en: Victorious are those virtuous ones who have, in every way, eternally acquired [merit] through the *pratyāhāra* sūtras.
It is a vast multitude of virtues and a complete cleansing of faults.
Just as this Kāśikā was composed by extracting the essence from other sources, so too is this Pañjikā made as a commentary upon it to the best of one's ability. ||2||
Regarding the passage beginning with "vṛttau" and so forth:
now, for what purpose is this verse presented at the commencement of the *Kāśikā*?
It is for the sake of avoiding disrespect toward that [work] and for the sake of establishing its authority.

For if this [work] had not existed previously, and this one were composed only after other treatises had been written, those who suspect the fault of redundancy would have no respect for it, but rather contempt.
But since this exists, that fault does not occur;

because by means of this, its specific excellence is declared—the cause of the complete and correct etymological derivation of all words—by the existence of which the ground for the suspicion of the fault of redundancy and for contempt is removed.
And reverence arises [for this work].
Furthermore, that distinction consists in its being endowed with a compendium of the essence of the system (tantra) which is scattered across various commentaries and such;
and since this is not possible in the earlier commentaries, how could there even be the suspicion of the fault of redundancy?
And in its absence, there would be no respect [for the grammar]; rather, due to the distinction previously mentioned, there is indeed respect.
And therein lies the *vṛtti*, which is an exposition of the sūtras composed by Pāṇini, as formulated by Cūlli, Bhaṭṭi, Nallūra, and others.
The *Bhāṣya* is the commentary on the statements composed by Kātyāyana, as formulated by Patañjali.
The word "likewise" (*tathā*) is used in the sense of inclusion;
the meaning is that it applies to the *Dhātupārāyaṇa*, the *Nāmapārāyaṇa*, and so forth.
Alternatively, it refers to similarity;
that is to say, just as a compendium of the essence of a scattered system is made in works such as the *Vṛtti*, so too [is one made] in the *Dhātupārāyaṇa*, the *Nāmapārāyaṇa*, and so forth.
The *dhātus* are the verbal roots beginning with *bhū*.
The *nāmas* are the nominal stems (*prātipadikas*). Those two treatises by which one reaches—that is, arrives at the limit or conclusion—of these are the *Dhātupārāyaṇa* and the *Nāmapārāyaṇa*.
The word *pārāyaṇa* is connected with each [term]:
namely, the *dhātupārāyaṇa* (the complete course of roots) and the *nāmapārāyaṇa* (the complete course of nouns).
The term is a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "those which have these as their beginning."
By the word "etcetera" (ādi), the training and so forth are included. "Scattered" (viprakīrṇasya) means that which is dispersed or expanded.
The meaning is "of the treatise on grammar" (*vyākaraṇa-śāstra*).
For that [treatise] is like a *tantra* (loom/warp);
threads stretched out in length are called a *tantra*.
Just as that which supports many transverse threads [is itself transverse], so too this [term] supports many objects to be characterized (*lakṣya*);
this is its similarity to the [example of the] thread (*tantra*).
Alternatively, *tantra* is grammar (*vyākaraṇa*), because words are stretched out (*tantryante*) or derived (*vyutpādyante*) by means of it.
Since roots have multiple meanings, the root *tan* here functions in the sense of "deriving" rather than its common meaning of "sustaining a family" (*trikuṭumbadhāraṇa*).
Or else, it means a system of tenets (*siddhānta*).
"Tantra means a primary system or a established doctrine," according to Amara.
Regarding the term *sārasaṃgraha*:
this word *sāra* is neuter and, by grammatical rule, refers to that which does not deviate from justice (*nyāya*).

And likewise, he will state under *ardharca-ādiṣu* (Pāṇini 2.4.31): "The word *sāra* is masculine when it means excellence (*utkarṣa*), and neuter when it means that which does not deviate from what is right (*nyāyād anapeta*). It is called a *saṃgraha* because by it both the characterized (*lakṣya*) and the characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) are grasped (*samantād gṛhyate*) or gathered together (*samantād gṛhyate*).
According to Pāṇini 3.3.58, the suffix *ghañ* is applied even in the sense of the instrument (*karaṇa*) after the roots *grah*, *vṛ*, *dṛ*, *niści*, and *gam*.
It is both "essence" (*sāra*) and "compendium" (*saṃgraha*), hence it is the *Sārasaṃgraha*. This, moreover, is precisely this particular commentary known as the *Kāśikā*.
Here, by the word "essence," freedom from defects is indicated.
For it is not possible for a treatise that possesses defects to be free from logical reasoning (*nyāya*),
because such a treatise is itself being brought to awareness by means of logical reasoning.
By the word "compendium" (*saṃgraha*), its possession of excellence (*guṇavattā*) is also indicated;
for otherwise, it would not be possible to correctly include all the definitions (*lakṣaṇa*) and the things to be defined (*lakṣya*) by means of this [work].

What, then, are the excellences here? They are: the quality of having desired supplementary additions (*iṣṭyupasaṃkhyānavattva*); the quality of having pure enumerations (*śuddhagaṇatva*); the quality of having explained the hidden meaning of the sūtras (*vivṛtagūḍhasūtrārthatva*); and the quality of having established the formation of words (*vyutpannarūpasiddhitva*).

And so he will say at the end of the treatise: "This commentary named Kāśikā contains desired supplementary rules, consists of pure groups [of words], has its meaning in the sūtras both explicit and hidden, and possesses established grammatical forms. Alternatively, this word *saṃgraha* is a noun derived from the action (*bhāvasādhana*).

"Compendium" (*saṃgraha*) means a collection, a summary; that is to say, the gathering together and establishing in one place of a treatise that has been scattered across various branches of scripture.
The word "essence" (*sāra*), however, denotes what is primary.
That portion of the textual composition by which the full mastery of the terminology is achieved is the essence.
"Sārasaṃgraha" means a compendium of the essence of the etymological derivation of words;
its composition is for the purpose of easy comprehension.
For it is easy to grasp that which is established in one place,
whereas that which is scattered is difficult to grasp. The mention of "extracting the essence" is for the purpose of excluding the preparatory elaborations (*parikara*).
For that [auxiliary] is a subordinate member (*aṅga*) because it assists the other;
the other, however, is the principal (*aṅgin*) because it is assisted by that very [auxiliary].
Now, as for the passage beginning with "atha" and so forth...
The word *atha* has the sense of "introduction" (*adhikāra*). An introduction is a commencement.
The word *atha* indicates this meaning: "the treatise on the instruction of words is now commenced."
If only "the instruction of words" (*śabdānuśāsanam*) were stated, there would be doubt as to whether the instruction of words is being commenced, recited, or merely heard.

However, by the employment of the word *atha*, this meaning is determined through the exclusion of other possible meanings: that it is being introduced. An *anuśāsana* is that by which words are instructed—that is, refined and explained.
"Instruction regarding words" is *śabdānuśāsanam*.

On this point, some raise an objection: since the rule "when both [the agent and the object] are possible, [the genitive is used] for the object" (Pāṇini 2.3.66) applies here, the sixth case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) would be employed;
and consequently, by the rule "and [the genitive] when there is an object" (2.2.14), there ought to be a prohibition of compounding.
And this is incorrect; for it is only where there is the possibility of both [the agent and the object] being expressed that this rule prescribes the sixth case (ṣaṣṭhī) for the object.

And where is there the possibility of both? Where there is the inclusion of both the agent and the object as established by the force of the context, as in: "Wondrous is the milking of cows by one untrained and not a cowherd."
Thus, the milking of cows that are difficult to milk by one who is untrained and lacks the skill of a cowherd is intended here to illustrate a marvelous feat;
and this marvelous expression can only be established as such if there is the mention of cows that are difficult to milk, along with an agent who is untrained and not a cowherd.
(Note: *edC, p. 4 begins with *durdohāṇāṃ*)
"Not otherwise" implies, by the force of the context, the inclusion of both [agent and object].

However, in the case of "instruction of words" (*śabdānuśāsanam*), since the intended meaning is merely that "this is the instruction of words and not of meanings," the mention of the teacher—the agent—is superfluous, as it can be understood even without being explicitly stated.
Therefore, in this case, there is no inclusion of either the agent or the object by the force of the context.
Consequently, there is no possibility of "attainment of both" at all.
And since that [attainment of both] is absent, the genitive case in the word *karmaṇi* is not applied by the rule *ubhayaprāptau karmaṇi* (2.3.66).
By which rule, then? It is by the rule *kartṛkarmaṇoḥ kṛti* (2.3.65).
Therefore, there will be a compound [of the word *vyākaraṇa*] like *edhmapravraścana*.
Alternatively, this genitive case is one characterized as "the remainder" (*śeṣa-lakṣaṇā*); thus, this is not to be questioned.
Furthermore, this name of grammar, "Instruction in Words" (*śabdānuśāsana*), is etymologically significant.
Therefore, since the purpose has already been indicated by that very [statement], it need not be stated explicitly.
For the activity of those by whom words are taught proceeds with that [purpose] as its objective;
and whatever is the objective for whose sake one acts, that becomes the purpose of that [activity].
This is what is meant: the instruction of words is its purpose.
And this is the immediate purpose;
however, the indirect purposes, such as the preservation of the Veda and so forth, are to be understood from the Bhāṣya.
The relationship, however, is characterized by the state of being the means and the goal.

That relationship which exists between grammar, the means (*sādhana*), and the linguistic instruction, which is the goal (*sādhya*), is already included within the [category of] purpose (*prayojana*).
[The question arises: "Of which words?"
But how can there be a reference by means of the word *kiṃ* to words that have become subordinate (*guṇībhūta*) within an instruction (*anuśāsana*)?
This is not a fault;
for it is observed that even a subordinate element, though included within the principal, may be mentally extracted and referred to by the word *kiṃ*.
For example: "This is the king's man; of which king?
What, then, is the intention of the questioner here?
He thinks as follows: in the expression "instruction of words" (*śabdānuśāsana*), the word "word" (*śabda*) denotes the universal.
And a word denoting a universal cannot, in the absence of context or other indicators, function with reference to a specific instance.
Furthermore, there are many types of sounds, such as the roar of the ocean and so forth.
Therefore, it follows that their exposition is also required;
however, it is grammar that is introduced here,
and that is an auxiliary of the Veda.
Furthermore, a limb (aṅga) is something that provides assistance;
and in this way, it assists the Veda,
provided that by means of it both Vedic words and worldly words— which are dependent upon it— are refined.
However, worldly words are beneficial to the Veda,

because their meanings are explained by means of them. Therefore, within the context of this treatise on the grammatical instruction of words, it is specifically these [Vedic] words that are intended to be analyzed.
But this does not apply even to the roar of the ocean and the like.

For, were such sounds to be derived [grammatically], one might think that grammar would no longer be an auxiliary limb (*aṅga*) of the Veda; thus, with this in mind, he says "of worldly [words]," and so forth.
"Worldly" (*laukika*) means those known in the world.

In this context, while the term *vidita* is understood from the preceding rule, the suffix *ṭhañ* is applied according to *lokasarvalokāṭ ṭhañ* (Pāṇini 5.1.44). Alternatively, *laukika* means "those who exist in the world" (*loke bhavā*).

By virtue of belonging to the class beginning with *adhyātma* (Pāṇini 4.3.60, Vārttika), the suffix *ṭhañ* is applied; thus we have *vaidikāḥ*. The separate mention of the Vedic [words] from the worldly ones is for the purpose of indicating their preeminence, just as when one says, "The Brāhmaṇas have arrived, and Vasiṣṭha has also arrived."

In this context, although Vasiṣṭha’s arrival is already established by his very status as a Brāhmaṇa, he is mentioned separately for the purpose of manifesting his preeminence. This manifestation of preeminence, however, serves to eliminate corruption among those who follow the Vedas with diligence; for it is observed that when they corrupt [the language] in sacrificial rites, there is a great transgression, as seen in the words "helayo helaya."
Alternatively, since those words which are used for the purposes of worldly affairs are already well-known as being "worldly" (*laukika*), Vedic words are mentioned separately.
Among these, worldly words have an indefinite sequence of phonemes, such as *gauraśvaḥ*, *puruṣaḥ*, *hastī*, and so forth;
whereas Vedic words have a fixed sequence, such as *śanno devīr abhiṣṭaye*, and so forth.
For in this grammatical exposition (anvākhyāna), the recitation of every individual word (pratipadapāṭha) must be accepted.
That too has three varieties,
distinguished by the instruction of correct words, corrupt words, or both.
Moreover, because words are infinite, that [complete enumeration] is impossible in every respect.

For it is thus reported that Bṛhaspati indeed taught Indra, for a thousand divine years, the complete recitation (*pārāyaṇa*) of words arranged word-for-word, yet he did not reach the end. Since there was no reaching the end even with such a teacher, such a student, and such a duration of study, how could it occur today among a generation of short-lived people?
Thinking that there is no other means [to achieve this], he says "How? and so forth.
How is there instruction? The meaning is that in no way whatsoever is the grammar of words an "instruction" (anuśāsana).
Alternatively, in this context, the word *anuśāsana* functions as a noun denoting the action (*bhāvasādhana*).

Instruction (*anuśāsana*) is refinement (*saṃskāra*). Since no refinement of words is possible in any other way, [the author] says "by means of the conceptualization of the division into base-forms (*prakṛti*) and so forth," etc., in order to show that alternative method by which one grasps a vast multitude of words with very little effort.
That which is produced first from a suffix (pratyaya) is called the base (prakṛti). Those for which the base comes first are "base-initial" (prakṛtyādayaḥ).
The word "initial" (ādi) is used to include suffixes and the rest.
Their "distinction" is their state of having unmixed forms.
The "conceptualization" of that [distinction] is the mental construction by means of a conceptualizing intellect.
Likewise, through such conceptualization, there is the instruction of words, which is grammar (*vyākaraṇa*), or rather, the teaching (*anuśāsana*).
This is the instrumental case used in the sense of cause;
for without it, there can be no grammar (*vyākaraṇa*) as instruction (*anuśāsana*),
nor without that [instruction], can the teaching of words be accomplished.
By the phrase "by means of conceptual construction," he demonstrates this:

that when the ultimate reality of entities such as *prakṛti* (primordial matter) and so forth has subsided, the division into *prakṛti* and so on is merely a conceptual construction; it is only the aggregate that denotes some object.
[He says] "by means of a definition possessing general and specific characteristics."
The instrumental case ending here is used in the sense of "instrument.

"Commonality" (*sāmānya*) and "particularity" (*viśeṣa*) together constitute "commonality-and-particularity"; that definition in which these two reside is a "definition possessing commonality and particularity.
(Ed. C, p. 6 begins with *yasmil*).

In that regard, the definition of a general rule (*utsarga*) is like that which possesses a commonality (*sāmānyavat*). For example, in the rule *karmaṇy aṇ* (Pāṇini 3.2.1), the elements *dhātoḥ* ("from a verbal root") and *karmaṇi* ("when there is an object") constitute the commonality.
The characteristic of an exception (*apavāda*) is that it possesses specific qualifications (*viśeṣavat*).
For example, in the rule *āto 'nupasarge kaḥ* (Pāṇini 3.2.3),
the terms *ataḥ* ("from a root ending in /ā/") and *anupasarge* ("when not preceded by a prefix") constitute the specific qualifications.

In that regard, by means of a definition possessing commonality (*sāmānyavat*), through the conceptualization of distinctions such as "nature" (*prakṛti*) and so forth, one arrives at a vast flood of words such as "potter," "reaper of stalks," or "reaper of arrows.
By means of a definition possessing particularity (*viśeṣavat*), however, one arrives at [words] such as "heel-protector," "cowherd," or "wool-giver.
This should be understood in the same way elsewhere as well.
"Now," and so forth.
He thinks as follows:
"The instruction of words has been undertaken."
In that case, instruction is appropriate only for one by whom words are taught;
yet, by the teaching of these [phonemes], no refinement (*saṃskāra*) of any word is effected.
Consequently, the intention of the question is that this constitutes a statement of something irrelevant (*aprastutābhidhāna*).
Regarding the phrase "of the phonemes" (*varṇānām*): the phonemes are *a* and so forth; their initial utterance is the instruction (*upadeśa*).

"Regarding the phrase 'for the purpose of pratyāhāra': *pratyāhāra* refers to the traditional collection of phonemes (*akṣarasamāmnāya*) characterized by a specific sequence and specific *anubandhas*, such as *aiuṇ* and so forth—so called because the phonemes (*varṇas*) are "drawn together" (*pratyāhriyante*) or condensed within it.
The instruction of the phonemes is for the sake of ensuring that such a [collection] exists."
It might be argued: "Since that too is irrelevant to the subject at hand, this very same fault remains. To this he says: "The [term] *pratyāhāra* [is used] for the sake of brevity," and so forth.
Brevity (*lāghava*) is the state of being brief (*laghu*).
Furthermore, that [attainment] requires little effort. For an object that can be accomplished with little effort is called "light" (*laghu*) due to its connection with minimal exertion.
By means of that lightness, there is the purpose of the application and accomplishment of grammatical rules such as *ḍhralope pūrvasya dīrgho ’ṇaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.3.111). This is the meaning.
For when there is a *pratyāhāra* (abbreviated term), the rule "that which begins with [a letter] together with the final one" (Pāṇini 1.1.71) applies.
When that rule applies, technical designations (*saṃjñā*) such as *aṇ* for the vowels beginning with *a* are established.

Consequently, wherever the inclusion of the vowels beginning with *a* is desired, they are all indicated by the designation *aṇ* and so forth; thus, the formulation of the treatise is accomplished with brevity.

And if that [the middle] were absent, the operation of the grammatical treatise beginning with "In its absence, [the name of the middle is determined] by the first through the last" (Pāṇini 1.1.71), "along with its cause," and so forth, would not occur;
for those two [the first and the last] are not possible in the absence of a specific arrangement [of sounds].
And if that [designation] were not in operation, the previously mentioned designations would not exist.

Consequently, in every rule (*sūtra*) where the inclusion of a certain number of sounds—beginning with *a* and so forth—is intended, those sounds would have to be specified by their own forms (*svarūpeṇa*) alone; thus, the operation of the treatise would lack brevity (*lāghava*).
Therefore, since this very [designation] is established with little effort for the sake of producing the subject matter at hand, there is no occasion for the aforementioned fault.

1 | AIUṆ | Now, why is it that vowel-based operations (*ackārya*) such as *ād guṇaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.1.87) do not occur here? Because of the preservation of the original form (*prakṛtibhāva*) by the rule *plutapragṛhyā ac* (Pāṇini 6.1.125).
[Note: The commentary on page 7 begins with *acīti*.]

Their status as *pragṛhya* is due to the prescription of the *pragṛhya* designation by the rule *nipāta ekājanāṅ* (Pāṇini 1.1.14). Their status as *nipāta* (particles), however, results from their inclusion among the words beginning with *ca*.

For this very reason, because they are *nipātas*, there is no audible manifestation of the case endings (*vibhakti*) that would arise whether they possess meaning (*arthavat*) or lack meaning (*anarthavat*).

In this context, regarding the state of being meaningless, it should be understood that the production of case endings occurs even for a meaningless particle because of the supplementary rule (*upasaṃkhyāna*) that extends the designation of "nominal stem" (*prātipadika*) to it. "By this sequence" means by this order.
But what is the reason that this very sequence is adopted,
and not another sequence?
To that it is said:
In this context, by the mention of *aṇ*, the inclusion of all three—*a*, *i*, and *u*—is intended. However, when there is a mention of *iṇ*, the inclusion of *a* is not intended;
whereas, when there is a mention of *uṇ*, the inclusion of both *a* and *i* is intended.

And since this [result] would not be achieved by resorting to a different sequence, this very sequence is adopted for these [sounds]. Someone might suspect that—because of the supplementary rule (*upasaṃkhyāna*) "after a phoneme, the suffix *kāra*" (Pāṇini 3.3.108, Vārttika)—the suffix *kāra* has not been applied here; therefore, these are not actually phonemes (*varṇa*), but rather something else entirely that merely imitates the shadow of those [phonemes], being partial components of the diphthongs (*sandhyakṣara*) and so forth.
To refute that, he says: "the phonemes" (*varṇān*).
The suffix *kāra*, however, is added as an extension (*upasaṃkhyāna*) to the rule *rogākhyāyāṃ ṇvul* (Pāṇini 3.3.108), which states that the suffix *ṇvul* is applied diversely (*bahulam*).
Therefore, the sense is that because of this statement of diversity (*bahulavacanāt*), even though [the letter *ka*] possesses the nature of a phoneme (*varṇatve*), the suffix does not apply.
Since the letter *ṇ* is included within both the preceding and following phonemes, it occupies a middle position.
It is not the final [element];
therefore, the designation *it* should not apply to it.

Even if, somehow, it were different, one might still have the misconception that—due to its lack of predominance according to the principle to be stated later—just as the operations pertaining to vowels (*ackārya*) do not apply to it there, so too the designation *it* would not apply; it is for the sake of such a person that it is said to be "final."

Although this [letter] occupies a middle position relative to the preceding and following phonemes, it nevertheless possesses the status of being final (*antya*) with respect to the preceding phoneme.
And since that status exists, it must be designated by the technical term *it*, even though it is not primary,
on account of the force of the instruction (*upadeśa*).
Otherwise, the instruction of those [indicatory letters] would be useless.
The purpose of teaching the indicatory letters, such as *ṇ* and others, is so that designations like *aṇ* (Pāṇini 1.1.69) may occur according to the rule *ādir antena sahet* (Pāṇini 1.1.71).
And that purpose would not be achieved if the designation *it* did not exist; this is the intended meaning.
Regarding the passage beginning with "tasya" (of him):
the word "eka" (one) takes the third case ending (*tṛtīyā*) because it is used in connection with the sense of accompaniment (*sahārtha*).
The word "tasya" takes the sixth case ending (*ṣaṣṭhī*) because it denotes the object (*karman*).

In the rule-statement (*pradeśavākya*), that letter *ṇ* is employed together with a single *a* for the purpose of indicating the named entity (*saṃjñin*). For that [letter *ṇ*] is the name (*saṃjñā*) of the phonemes beginning with *a* only when accompanied by the vowel *a*, neither as a solitary [phoneme] nor as accompanied by any other phoneme.
Therefore, for the sake of communication, it is employed together with that very [phoneme],
neither alone nor accompanied by other phonemes.
Others, however, say:

In "tasya," the genitive case is used in the sense of the agent; in "ekena," the instrumental case is used in the sense of accompaniment. Therefore, this is the meaning: [he who possesses it] together with one [other].
The letter *ṇ*, when accompanied by the initial letter, becomes the indicator (*grāhaka*) of the other letters falling between it, as well as of the initial letter itself.
Others say:

Since verbal roots have multiple meanings, the root *grah* (to take) here functions in the sense of "uttering," as in the expression "by a nominal stem that possesses [the capacity for] utterance. Therefore, the meaning is this: it occurs together with one [other word].

How is it determined that *iṇ* (Pāṇini 8.3.78) is not included by the vowel *i* in the rule for *sīdhvam*? It is because of the combined mention of the vowels *i* and *u* in the rule *aci śnudhātubhruvām yvoḥ* (6.4.77).

If this [the *i* of *sīdhvam*] were to be included by the *i* of *iṇ*, then for the sake of brevity, he would have simply mentioned *iṇ*. In the case of the combined mention *yvoḥ*, there are three and a half morae (*mātrā*); in the case of the mention *iṇ*, there are only three.

In that case, since the matter is established by a simpler formulation (*nyāsa*), the fact that one undertakes a more cumbersome effort indicates that this letter *ṇ* is not included within the letter *i*.
But then, why is there no inclusion by the letter *u* in the rule *kṛ-vā-pā-ji-mi-svi-sādhya-śūbhyo uṇ* (Uṇādi 1.1)?
Because there is nothing else to be included other than the letter *u*.
And because that [term] is designated by its own form alone—
as in "the short *a*-vowel," and so forth—
"usage" (*prayoga*) refers to the verbal root and the like, since it is employed (*prayujyate*).
In that context, the short vowel *a* is *saṃvṛta* (closed) in its utterance. It is called *saṃvṛta* because of its association with the quality of being closed (*saṃvṛtaguṇa*),
just as a cloth is called "white" due to its association with the quality of whiteness.

"But the long and protracted [vowels] possess openness (*vivṛtatva*). This means they possess the quality of openness (*vivṛtaguṇa*). Thus the authors of the *Śikṣā* say: "The vowels have open articulation (*vivṛtakaraṇa*); among them, *e* and *o* are more open (*vivṛtatara*)."
From those two as well, *ai* and *au*; from these two also, the vowel *ā* is subsumed within the vowel *a*. Regarding the phrase "of them," and so forth:

In this treatise, the short vowel *a* is accepted as having the quality of being "opened" (*vivṛta*) so that the technical designation *savarṇa* (homogeneous) may apply to those [vowels] such as the short and others according to the rule *teṣāṃ hrasvādīnāṃ tulyāsyaprayatnaṃ savarṇam* (1.1.9).

Otherwise, because the effort (*prayatna*) would be different, there would be no *savarṇya*; consequently, in forms such as *daṇḍāḍhakam*, the substitution of a long vowel by the rule *akaḥ savarṇe dīrghaḥ* (6.1.101) would not occur.

Now, one might object: even if the "opened" quality is merely asserted, the substitution of a long vowel for a short or protracted *a* before a homogeneous vowel would still result, since the protracted vowel is considered non-existent (*asiddha*) when that [substitution] is to be performed.
This is not a fault;
for the *pluta* vowel is established as valid within vowel-sandhis (*svarasandhi*), since the *pluta* is already established in those contexts.
Otherwise, the rule prescribing the preservation of the original form (*prakṛtibhāva*)—namely, *plutapragṛhyā aci* (Pāṇini 6.1.125)—would be rendered purposeless.

And here, although it was stated that "the open [vowels] are recognized as homogeneous," nevertheless, because of the statement "for the sake of establishing their homogeneity with those [semi-vowels]," it is understood that they are "more open.
For the homogeneity of an open sound with one that is more open is not possible,
due to the difference in their articulatory effort (*prayatna*).
Or [it may be understood] by the force of the declaration of openness (*vivṛtatva*).
Even for that which is less open, there will be homogeneity (*sāvarṇya*) with that which is more open.

If only "here" (*iha*) were said, then, due to proximity and because it is the subject under discussion, one would understand that only the vowel from the *akṣarasamāmnāya* (the traditional alphabet) is being declared as open.
It does not reside in a root, a nominal stem, an affix, or an indeclinable.

Consequently, because there is a difference in effort (*prayatna*), there would be no phonetic similarity (*sāvarṇya*); and since it would not be included by the traditional list of vowels (*akṣarasamāmnāyika*), it would lack the status of being a vowel (*actva*).

And because that [condition] is absent, the rule "it is pacified" (*śāmyati*) would not apply; for since the technical designation *ac* does not apply here, the substitute (*sthānin*) being a non-vowel lacks the property of being an *ac*, and thus, by the rule *śamām aṣṭānāṃ dīrghaḥ śyani* (Pāṇini 7.3.74), the lengthening of the vowel would not occur. Furthermore, in the word *dṛṣad*, the rule stating that the final syllable of a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) is acute would not apply, because that [designation of being a stem] possesses the properties of vowels (*aj-dharma*).
[The example] *nāyaka*.
In this case, because the *akāra* of the substitute (*pratyāya*) is not a vowel (*anact*), the rule for the substitution of *āy* and so forth would not apply there.

Furthermore, in the word *avanamati*, the rule stating that particles (*nipāta*) and prefixes (*upasarga*)—with the exception of *abhi*—are acute-accented on the first syllable (*ādyudātta*) would not apply.

Moreover, since there is no phonetic similarity (*sāvarṇya*) between the *akāra* found in the statement of the continued application (*anuvṛtti-nirdeśa*) and the long vowel, the long vowel would not be included [by that *akāra*].
What is the fault in that? [If the rule were applied as stated,] by the rule *asya cvau* (Pāṇini 7.4.32), the substitution of *ī* would apply only here: *śuklībhavati*;
but it would not apply in the case of *mālībhavati*. Furthermore, by the rule *yasyeti ca* (Pāṇini 6.4.148), the elision of the vowel *a* would apply only here: *dākṣiḥ*, *plākṣiḥ*.
However, this would not apply in the case of *vālāki*.

Therefore, the term "in this treatise" (*śāstre*) has been included for the purpose of demonstrating that whatever is merely a vowel (*avarṇa*) here in this science, all of that is declared to be *vivṛta* (open).

But even if there were homogeneity (*sāvarṇya*), would not the inclusion of homogeneous sounds by means of the letter *a* situated in a rule of general application (*anuvṛtti-nirdeśa*) already be established?

Because of the absence of the designation "anaṇ. For those vowels such as *a* and so forth that appear in the general enumeration (*anuvṛtti-nirdeśa*) are not *aṇ*; rather, they are those [vowels] found in the traditional list of phonemes (*akṣara-samāmnāya*).
If it is argued that there is no fault because [the word] relies on the side of the genus (*jāti*), we say: no.
This is not a fault, because the treatise on the apprehension [of words] rejects the position of the genus.
For in this case, two things exist within individual instances (*vyakti*).
There are both similarity and difference. In that regard, sometimes one or the other is intended to be predominant.
When similarity is intended, because that similar portion is common to all individual instances, there occurs an implication of all individuals without exception.
Because the difference [between the individuals] is not apprehended.

Thus, in this inclusive reference (*pratyāhāra*), since the similar portion is the primary element in the instruction, the status of being an *aṇ* (the short vowel 'a') is established for all individual instances of the sound-class *avarṇa* that serve as the basis for the recurring designation.
But what is the distinction between this similarity and the universal (*jāti*) of the *avarṇa* class? This is the distinction.
And this similarity exists only among the short instances of the phoneme *a*, not among the long or protracted ones; however,
the universal (*jāti*) of the phoneme *a* does exist even in the long and protracted instances—
this has already been established.
Now, how is it understood that the vowel *a* is declared to be "open" (*vivṛta*) in this treatise? To this, he says "of that," and so forth.

If the open *a* had not been previously declared, then one would not have performed the restoration (*pratyāpatti*) of it by means of the rule *a a* (Pāṇini 8.4.68) for the sake of its non-application [in the case of doubling]. For "restoration" is the re-attainment of a form after it has deviated from its own nature.

How could that [activity] be possible for one whose essential nature (*svarūpa*) is indeed unchanging? Alternatively, if it is asserted that [the treatise] is already fully disclosed, then even at the conclusion of that treatise, its application would have to be of that very same nature; anticipating this objection, he says "of that," and so forth.
The word *artha* here signifies cessation (*nivṛtti*).

As in the expression "smoke for the sake of mosquitoes. The meaning is that there should be a cessation of the application of that [term] when its purpose has been fulfilled. Alternatively, the word *artha* signifies "purpose" (*prayojana*).
By the word "tasya" (of that), the previously mentioned [subject] is referred back.
That whose purpose is the application (prayoga) is described as such.
Because it functions as an adverbial modifier (kriyāviśeṣaṇa), it takes the neuter gender.
This is what is meant:

for that [sound] which has been closed and fallen away from its own nature, a reversion to its state of application (prayoga) will be effected; since this occurs at the conclusion of the treatise, it follows that for such a sound, this is indeed the state of application.
2. ṛḷḳ.
Its apprehension occurs by means of three [factors].
How is apprehension obtained by means of three?
If it is a suffix attached to the whole, and not a suffix attached to a part.
And yet, if the adjunct belongs to the individual parts and not to the whole, there would be apprehension by only one [part].
This is not a fault;
for the usage regarding the adjuncts is established by convention (*pratijñā*).
The thesis, however, is human in origin;
and a person, while making a thesis in both cases, does not cease [the process],
because there is no contradiction.

For being connected to the whole is not contradicted by the claim that [the suffix] is connected to the parts; otherwise, neither would be connected to the other. Therefore, it is rightly said that the inclusion is effected by three [factors].
This should be applied everywhere in this manner.
In this treatise, the instruction regarding the phonemes (*varṇa*) is for a specific purpose.
With the intention that no purpose whatsoever can be served by the instruction of the phoneme *ḷ*, he says: "the phonemes beginning with *a*."
"Prayoga" (application) refers to that which is applied, such as a verbal root and so forth.

"Ananyatrabhāva" (occurrence nowhere else) is the meaning of the object (*viṣaya*). [The compound] "pracuraprayogaviṣaya" is a *bahuvrīhi* meaning those for whom the object of application is abundant and extensive.

Alternatively, *prayukti* means application (*prayoga*), which is utterance (*uccāraṇa*). [The term *prayuktiviṣaya*] is a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*) meaning "the object of that [utterance]. [The term *pracuraprayuktiviṣaya*] is a possessive compound (*bahuvrīhi*) with the word *pracura*.
"For them, the purpose [of the treatise] lies in its easy comprehension through instruction. "Easy comprehension" (*sujñāna*) means that it is understood with ease.
For what purpose is this purpose stated? It is stated for the sake of removing the opportunity for the objection: "Why is the purpose of teaching the sound *ḷ* alone being asked?"
For if this were not stated, and only the purpose of the letter *ḷ* were asked, then there would be occasion for this statement:
"The letter *ḷ*, however, is employed only in the context of the root *ḳḷp*. The word "however" (*tu*) is intended to distinguish it from [the letters] beginning with *a*.

It might be argued that since that [element] is related to *klp*, its instruction must be provided for the sake of those operations which apply to vowels (*ac*); therefore, he says "of *klp*" and so forth.
If it is indeed *asiddha*, what follows from that? To this he says: "In that case, only the vowel *ṛ*" and so forth.
"Because of the prescription of *lat*," and so forth. "The prescription of *lat*" (*latvavidhāna*) refers to that grammatical treatise by which the state of being *lat* (*latva*) is prescribed.
The suffix *lyuṭ* is used here in the sense of the instrument (*karaṇe*).
Alternatively, *bhāve* means "in the sense of an abstract state" (*vidhiḥ* = *vidhānam*). Thus,
it is a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*) meaning "the prescription of the substitution of *l*."
"Then, the subsequent [rules]," and so forth.
By this, he demonstrates that the substitution of *l* is established (*siddha*) in those cases.
For in the preceding case, the subsequent is not established; however, in the subsequent case, the preceding is not [unestablished].

Regarding the term *kḷptaśikha*: this is a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "one whose top-knot (*śikhā*) is arranged (*kḷptā*). Here, a protracted vowel (*pluta*) is prescribed by the rule *guroranṛtaḥ* (Pāṇini 8.2.86). And that [rule], by the rule *acaśca* (1.1.28), brings forth the original element (*sthānin*) as its referent.

Because the phoneme *ḷ* is not taught among the vowels (*ac*), it would not possess vowel-status (*actva*); consequently, [the rule] "in *prakḷpta*" would not apply. In this case, by the rule "particles (*nipāta*) are acute on the first syllable, and prefixes (*upasarga*) except for *abhi*," the vowel *a* of the word *pra* becomes acute.
The vowel *ḷ* is also originally acute (*udātta*) by virtue of its being a verbal root vowel.
Once the accent of the *niṣṭhā* suffix has been applied, it subsequently becomes grave (*anudātta*) according to Pāṇini 6.1.158: "A word is grave except for one [acute] syllable.

When the compound is formed according to Pāṇini 2.2.10 (*kugatiprādayaḥ*), the rule for the acute accent on the final syllable of a compound would apply; however, by Pāṇini 6.2.49 (*gatiranantaraḥ*), the preceding member retains its original accent (*prakṛtibhāva*), and thus the prefix *pra-* alone remains acute.

Therefore, by the rule *tasmāt parasya ḷkārasya udāttādanudāttasya svaritaḥ* (Pāṇini 8.4.66), the circumflex (*svarita*) accent is prescribed for the following *ḷ*-sound when it follows an acute (*udātta*) vowel. That [circumflex] would not occur if the *ḷ* were not a vowel (*ac*), because it possesses the properties of a vowel (*aj-dharma*). For example: *kḷptaḥ*, *kḷptavān*.
By the rule *anaci ca* (Pāṇini 8.4.47), doubling is prescribed for the consonants *ya* and *ra* following a vowel (*ac*). That [doubling] would also not occur if [the *ya* or *ra*] were not a vowel.
To refute the statement that "it is employed only when situated in the root *kḷp*", and to demonstrate another purpose, he says "yac ca" and so forth.
The capacity other than the power of uttering the word *sādhu* is "incapacity" (*aśakti*). That which is produced from that is "born of incapacity" (*aśaktijam*).
It is maintained that even the imitation of such [an utterance] possesses correctness (*sādhutva*).
Because there is a difference in meaning, they are distinct words;
and because they are employed by the learned,
they are like other correct words.
But surely, since the original (anukārya) is ungrammatical, the imitation (anukaraṇa) must also be ungrammatical,
according to the rule that "an imitation is like its original"?
This is not so.
For in that case, a grammatical *prakṛti* (base form) is resorted to;
and by the rule "as the base," it is precisely a grammatical operation that is extended [by analogy].
Furthermore, an ungrammatical word-form (*asādhuśabdarūpa*) is not a grammatical *prakṛti*.
Nor should one attempt to establish the status of being an "incorrect word" (apaśabda) based on the technical treatises;
for it is not possible even for grammar to declare something an incorrect word,
since its function is solely for the refinement of correct words (sādhuśabda).

Therefore, even the imitation of an incorrect word (*apaśabda*) is indeed correct. In that case, even for the *ḷ*-sound situated therein, vowel-operations (*ackārya*) would not occur if its instruction were not among the vowels— as in the example "kumāryy ḷtaka."
In this case, since *actva* (the status of being a vowel) applies, the *yaṇ* substitute occurs for the *ḷ*-sound when followed by [a vowel].

Now, one might object that even the purpose of teaching the *ḷ*-sound is established through the principle of "correspondence according to number" (*saṃkhyātānudeśa*) in the rule *iko yaṇ aci* (6.1.77).
For if the *ḷ*-sound were not taught, there would be three substituends and four substitutes; because of this discrepancy in number, the correspondence according to number would not apply.
% (edC, p.12 begins with *saṃkhyātānudeśo*) Therefore, the application according to numerical order (*saṃkhyātānudeśa*) is also a valid purpose for it;
yet this is not the case.
Let there be no enumeration of the numbered items.
Even in its absence, the determination will be made by the paribhāṣā "sthānentaratama" (1.1.50).
In that case, the designation *it* has another purpose.

For if there were no *upadeśa*, then in cases such as *gamḷ* and *sṛpḷ* in the sense of "going," the designation *it* (by Pāṇini 1.3.2, *upadeśe 'j anunāsikaḥ*) would not apply. And if that [designation] were absent, the suffix *aṅ* (by Pāṇini 3.1.55, *puṣādidyutādyuditah parasmaipadeṣu*) would not occur.
This is not so.

Even if there were no instruction [of the *ḷ*], since the designation of the *aṅga* would be prescribed from this very root beginning with *ḷ*, the technical name *it* would be established; thus, the instruction serves no purpose regarding the *akṣaras*.
Therefore, the purposes mentioned previously remain valid, and they were stated without relying on the rule that "the designation *savarṇa* must be declared for the *ṛ*-vowel and the *ḷ*-vowel."

For here, since this [principle] is relied upon, even if the instruction of the sound *ḷ* were absent, the inclusion of *ḷ* would be established simply by the fact that *ḷ* is grasped by *ṛ* according to the rule *aṇ udit savarṇasya ca*.
As for the rule 3.1.2 (*eoṅ*), the phrase "and the preceding part" (*pūrvāṃś ca*) was not stated therein.
Because it is impossible for this [term] to be grasped by the preceding rules.
Now, why is it not grasped here by the letter *a* in the rule *ṣidbhidādibhyo ’ṅ* (Pāṇini 3.3.104)? Regarding this, some say:

in the rule *ādirantyena sahet* (Pāṇini 1.1.71), the phrase "provided it is not a suffix" (*apratyaya*) from the rule *aṇuditsavarṇasya cāpratyayaḥ* (Pāṇini 1.1.69) is understood to carry over (*anuvartate*).
By this, the following meaning is established:
the initial [letter] becomes the grāhaka (the grasper) by means of the final [letter], provided that it is not itself a suffix (pratyaya).
And since this is a suffix, it does not become a grāhaka.
And in this way, even in rules such as "a word (pada) consists of that which ends in a nominal suffix (suP) or a verbal suffix (tiṅ)" [Pāṇini 1.4.14], the suffix would not be included as a referent.

Therefore, one should understand that here, due to the lack of conventional usage (anabhidhāna), there is no inclusion of the pratyāhāra. For derivatives formed by kṛt, taddhita, and compound suffixes are characterized by their conventional usage.
Furthermore, when suffixes beginning with 'a' arise by the rule *ṣidbhidādibhyo'ṅ* (Pāṇini 3.3.104), the intended meaning is not expressed.
In this case, however, there is the rule *śāsa idaṅhaloḥ* (Pāṇini 6.4.34).

Why does the term *aṅ* in the rule *ṛdṛśoraṅi guṇaḥ* (Pāṇini 7.4.16) not constitute a pratyāhāra (abbreviation) including the vowel *a*, as in [the pratyāhāra] *aṇ*? Because here *aṅ* refers specifically to that which resembles *ciṇ* and that which resembles *caṅ*.
For in the rule *śāsa idaṅhaloḥ* (Pāṇini 6.4.34), the phrase *bhañjeśca ciṇi* (Pāṇini 6.4.33) is understood to carry over (*anuvartate*).
In the rule *ṛdṛśoraṅi* (6.1.127), the phrase *ṇau caṅy upadhāyā hrasvaḥ* (7.4.1) is also [relevant].
Therefore, by the maxim of the frog-leap (*maṇḍūkapluti*), the mention of *caṅ* is carried over [from that rule].
By means of that mention of *caṅ*, which serves as a common locus of reference, *aṅ* is qualified.
And it is not the case that *caṅ* and *aṅ* are identical, because they are entirely distinct.
In that regard, the meaning is understood as if by implication (*sāmarthyāt*).
For words employed with reference to objects other than their primary meanings convey a sense as if the word "as it were" (*iva*) were used, even without its actual employment.
For example: "The boy is fire," or "The Vāhīka is a cow.
By this, the following meaning is established:

"Caṅ-iva aṅ" means an "aṅ" that is similar to "caṅ. And what is the "aṅ" that is similar to "caṅ"? It is that which is prescribed in place of "cli. Thus, the term "aṅ" is understood to refer specifically to that which occupies the position of "cli."
But this does not apply to the *pratyāhāra*.
Likewise, in the rule *śāsa idaṅhaloḥ* (6.4.34), when *aṅ* is qualified by the mention of *ciṇ*, it should be understood that only that *aṅ* which occurs in place of *cli* is intended.
If so, why is there no use of the *pratyāhāra* [formed] with the vowel *i* in these cases: *sani ca* (6.1.9), *iṅaśca* (2.4.48), *parimāṇākhyāyāṃ sarvebhyaḥ* (3.3.21), and *iṅaśca* (3.2.16)?
In the former case, [the rule] does not apply;
for by the prescription of *kittva* in *iko jhal* (Pāṇini 1.2.9),

since the substitution of *gam* is prescribed for the root *iṅ* when this *san*-pratyāhāra follows, the status of having an *ik* as its final element would be absent, and thus the prescription of *kittva* would be rendered purposeless due to the non-application of *guṇa*.
In the preceding case, it does not occur.
For if it were so, one would have formed the pratyāhāra with the letter *k* alone as in *ika*.
Indeed, there is no possibility of a suffix *san* following a verbal root ending in *ṅ*, such that the inclusion of the letter *ṅ* in the pratyāhāra would be purposeful.
It does not occur even in the subsequent [suffix],
because that would result in redundancy.
For instance, after stems ending in *i*, the suffix *ac* prescribed by the rule *erac* ought to apply.
Even from words ending in *u*, the suffix *ap* is applied by the rule *ṛdor ap*;

there are no words ending in *ḷ* at all. For words ending in *e* (and *ai*), the substitution of *ā* must occur by the rule *ādeca upadeśe’śiti* (Pāṇini 6.1.45), even prior to the production of the suffix.
Therefore, those [other vowels] also do not exist at the time of the application of the suffix;
only the vowel *ṛ* remains.
Consequently, if a *ghañ* suffix were intended, the inclusion of the *pratyāhāra* would be purposeless.
One should simply say *ur*.
Even in the rule *krīṅjīṇāṃ ṇau* (Pāṇini 6.1.48), because *krīṇāti* and *jayati* are mentioned separately, there is no inclusion by means of the vowel *i*.
If it is argued that the separate mention is for the purpose of restriction—so that [the substitution] may apply only to those two among the roots ending in *i*—that is not so.
Even so, one should perform the *pratyāhāra* (abbreviation) by means of the letter *ka* alone.
This is because the substitution of *āt* for roots ending in *e* is already established by the general rule itself.
Furthermore, in the rule *iṅ-dhāryoḥ śatrakṛcchriṇi* (Pāṇini 3.2.130), the term *iṅ* refers to the verbal root *iṅ*, due to its association (*sāhacarya*) with the verbal root *dhārayati*.
It should be understood that this does not apply to *pratyāhāra*.
4. *AIAUC*:
By this rule, "the first [element] together with the last," the technical designation *aj* is prescribed for the vowels beginning with *a*.
And just as that [vowel lengthening] occurs for the vowels beginning with *i*, it would likewise apply to the consonants beginning with *ṇ* when they are attached [as suffixes],
because they too are taught in that context.

Consequently, with the intention that—just as the substitution of *yaṇ* occurs in those nominal stems (prātipadika) such as *dadhyatra* and so forth under rules like *iko yaṇ aci*, it might likewise occur in cases such as *dadhiṇakārīyati*—he says "in the pratyāhāras," and so on.

[The question] "How [is it] not [to be applied] in the mentions of *ac*? implies the remainder: "it must be done. "Mentions of *ac*" (*aj-grahaṇāni*) refers to the utterances (*uccāraṇāni*) of this technical term (*saṃjñā*) "ac" within the rule-statement sentences (*pradeśavākya*).
When those [vowels] are present, how could the grammatical operations pertaining to vowels (*ackārya*) not occur for the sounds beginning with *ṇa*? The meaning is that they certainly would occur.
This is because of established usage (*ācārāt*).
*Ācāra* means conduct; it refers to the behavior of the teachers (*ācārya*).
Therefore, because of this indicative evidence, [the suffix *ghañ*] does not apply [in the sense of "doing"].
This is shown by the rule: "The *uṇādi* suffixes are applied diversely."
In the case of *tṛṣimṛṣikṛśeḥ kāśyapasya* and *ṅamo hrasvādaci ṅamuṇ nityam*,
[the author] does not apply the *yaṇ* substitution when *ṅasi* and *ṅas* follow, as indicated by the initial *ṇ* in the rule *ṅasiṅasoś ca*. From this, he provides an indication (*jñāpaka*).
Even though the designation *ac* exists, operations pertaining to *ac* do not take place;
or rather, by this activity of the Teacher, it is made known that these [sounds] do not even possess this designation *ac*.
For if they were indeed designated as *ac*, the Teacher would have performed the operations pertaining to *ac* upon them.

Having thus established the non-existence of technical names (*saṃjñā*) by means of an indicator (*jñāpaka*), he now says "because they are not primary" (*apradhānatvāt*) in order to establish it through reasoning (*nyāya*). Technical names such as *aṇ* and so forth are pronounced with *anubandhas* (indicatory letters) for the purpose of teaching their forms.
Consequently, because they are employed for the sake of another, they experience a state of non-primacy.
But the others are employed for their own sake; therefore, they possess predominance. Consequently, the designation *aj* applies only to them, and not to the indicatory letters (*anubandhas*).
For when both the primary and the non-primary are in proximity, it is the primary alone that enters into a relationship with the effect,
not the other;
and thus the author of the Bhāṣya has said.
"It is established because the understanding of the operation applies to the primary element.
If this were so, even the letter *a* would not have this designation;
for in the communication of a designation, it too certainly possesses the status of being a constituent part (*aṅga*).

Because of the force of the continued application of the phrase "of its own form" (*svasya ca rūpasya*), the fault does not arise, as it is understood that [the term] "becomes that" (*tasya bhavati*) applies.

By means of these two reasons just mentioned, it has been demonstrated that although the presence of the indicatory letters (*anubandhas*) is admitted at the time of the formulation of the technical name (*saṃjñā*), the name itself does not exist [at that time]. Now, in order to demonstrate that the name will not occur precisely because they are not present there, he says: "And there is elision" (*lopaś ca*), etc.
One who is strong is indeed stronger;
the suffix *tarap* is used here for the sake of the word's own meaning,
just as in the rule *alpāctaram*.
For those [sounds] designated as *it* are indeed *anubandhas*.
Therefore, since the designation *ac* applies to them, the rule "its elision" (*tasya lopaḥ*) must apply even prior to that [designation],
because it possesses greater force.

How, then, can there be a designation (*saṃjñā*) for those [elements] which do not exist? And if that designation does not exist, how can there be the occurrence of an operation (*kārya*) based on its apprehension? Furthermore, the elision (*lopa*) possesses greater force because it is subsequent and because it is obligatory;
for the rule concerning elision is subsequent to the rule concerning designations.
Thus, it also possesses the quality of being subsequent.
Because it would entail both the performed and the unperformed [states], there is permanence. Even when the designation has been made, the elision must occur; even when it has not been made.
However, the designation does not occur once the elision has been performed,

because the things designated (saṃjñin) no longer exist. If this were the case, then just as the elision of the indicatory letters (anubandha), such as the letter ṇ, occurs first for those falling within the suffixal endings (aṅga), so too would it occur for the letter c.
Consequently, the designation "aj" would not be established.
By the force of the statement itself, its [the final consonant's] elision will not occur prior [to the formation of the designation].
Or, even if that [consonant] has not been elided, the vowel *a* will be the designation in conjunction with that which previously existed.
However, for those beginning with *ṇa* that have lost their status as *ajanta* (ending in a vowel), they cannot receive this designation (*saṃjñā*),
because the [designation] *it* has its scope limited to those beginning with *i*.
Here, these phonemes beginning with *a* are intended to consist of multiple constituent parts.

The first half-mora of that [sound] is acute (udātta). This is because of the rule (Pāṇini 8.2.107): "In the case of an *ec* vowel that is not a *pragṛhya*, when it is not followed by a call from afar, the first half is acute and the second half becomes *i* or *u*.
Furthermore, certain constituent parts of some sounds resemble other phonemes;
for example, the *repha* (*r*) in the sound *ṛ*.
In the letter *ḷ*, there is the letter *l*.
In both *e* and *ai*, there are the letters *a* and *i*.
In both *o* and *au*, there are the letters *a* and *u*.
In the case of long vowels such as *ā* and so forth, there are short counterparts such as *a* and so forth.

In that regard, are these constituent parts (*avayava*) of phonemes such as *ṛ* and so forth included by the term "phoneme" (*varṇa*), or not? If the former alternative were held, then in examples such as *agne iha* or *vāyo udakam*, the rule for lengthening a vowel when followed by a homogeneous vowel (*akaḥ savarṇe dīrghatvam*) would apply. Furthermore, in cases such as *praṇīya* and *ālūya*, the short *ṛ*-sounds (*hrasvā ṛayaḥ*) would be subject to the insertion of the augment *tuk*.
These and other such faults also follow in this view;
they are to be understood from the Bhāṣya.

In the alternative view, however, the letter ṛ must be explicitly mentioned in the rules for the insertion of the augment *nuṭ*, for the substitution of *la* (the *l-ṛt* rule), and for the modification (*vināma*) [of the vowel].

Regarding the rule for the insertion of *nuṭ* before *tavāt*: in the case of the root *ṛdh* (meaning "to increase") in the *liṭ* [perfect] tense, as in *ānṛdhatuḥ* and *ānṛdhuḥ*, the *ṛ*-vowel does not include the *r*-sound within its scope when *hal* is mentioned [in grammatical rules]. Consequently, because the condition of being "two consonants" (*dvihaltva*) is absent, the *nuṭ* augment prescribed by Pāṇini 7.4.71 (*tasmānnuḍ dvihalaḥ*) would not apply.
In the rule prescribing the substitution of *l*, the substitution of *l* for the *r* of *kṛp-* by Pāṇini 8.2.18 (*kṛpo ro laḥ*) would not be established as it was already established;

likewise, in the rule prescribing nasalization, the substitution of *ṇ* in *mātṛṛṇām* and *pitṛṛṇām* would not occur. Therefore, he says "among the phonemes," etc., meaning among the phonemes beginning with *ṛ*.
"Parts of letters" refers to the *repha* (the sound *r*) and so forth. They are called "parts" (*ekadeśa*) for the purpose of making known that they possess the nature of being letters themselves.
This is what is meant:

The "parts of phonemes" (*varṇaikadeśa*) are those parts which constitute the very essence of the phonemes. For if only the term "parts" (*ekadeśa*) were used, someone might have the misconception that these parts are indeed distinct entities separate from the phonemes themselves.
Since musical instruments and the like also possess parts that are portions of phonemes, he says "those whose forms are similar to other phonemes" in order to exclude them; that is,
those parts whose form is similar to other phonemes are "parts whose forms are similar to other phonemes."
The meaning is that they have identical forms with other letters that are not constituent parts [of them].
Regarding the word "teṣu" (in them): it refers to the partial portions of the letters.
"An operation on that [element]" means an operation on another phoneme, such as the lengthening [of a vowel] when a homogeneous vowel follows (*akaḥ savarṇe dīrghaḥ*).
But what is the reason that it does not exist? He says:
"For it conforms to its shadow," and so forth.
"Its shadow" means its form.
It is the mere form (ākāra) of the other phonemes, beginning with 'a',
that they imitate;
for they possess a form identical to it.
But they are not those very [parts] themselves; for identity does not arise merely by conforming to their form. For instance, in a cow, there exist parts that conform to the parts of a gavaya.
Nor do they possess that nature as their own essence.
What, then, is the reason why they are not those very things? To this he says: "separately," and so forth.
"Effort" (*prayatna*) means exertion, which is the activity of the articulatory places (*sthāna*) and the organs of pronunciation (*karaṇa*).

The teachers maintain that there is a certain phoneme which is to be produced—that is, brought into existence—by a distinct effort different from the one used for the preceding phoneme, and by a different manner of articulation;
these phonemes are [therefore] composed of parts.
For if they were [mere] phonemes, they would have to be produced by a separate effort.
But this is not the case;
for it is by that very effort which constitutes the collective meaning that those [phonemes] are brought to completion.
Thus, by resorting to the position of non-perception (*agrahaṇaka*), the objection regarding the faults inherent in the position of perception (*grahaṇaka*) has been refuted.
But surely the position of "grahaṇaka" (the act of grasping) has also been established in the Bhāṣya,
since the faults associated with it have been refuted;
why then has that been abandoned?
Because there would be much that requires remediation [if they were included], whereas in the view that they are not grasped (*agrahaṇaka-pakṣa*), little requires remediation;
therefore, that very position was adopted by the author of the *Vṛtti*.

If, then, they are not grasped, the inclusion of the vowel *ṛ* in the rules for the augment *nuṭ* and so forth remains necessarily to be performed; to this he says: "In the rules for *nuṭ*, substitutes, and elision," and so on.
The meaning is that a rebuttal must be provided for the objection that arises regarding the application of the *nuṭ* augment and other rules in the case of the vowel *ṛ*.
In that regard, first, concerning the rule for *nuṭ*, the *repha* (the sound *r*) situated within the vowel *ṛ* is included by the term "consonant" (*hal*).
Therefore, even in this instance, the *nuṭ* augment occurs for a stem consisting of two consonants.
"Ānṛdhatuḥ" and "ānṛdhuḥ"—this has been explained by the author of the commentary himself. Now, is this *r* situated within the vowel *ṛ* a constituent of the phoneme (*varṇātmaka*)? He says: no.
For it was just now stated that those [phonemes] merely imitate that [original sound], and are not that very thing itself.
Well then, are those phonemes such as *ha* and so forth, which are taught in the traditional list of syllables (*akṣarasamāmnāya*), of the nature of phonemes? No, he says.
For he will state later regarding *hayavaraḍ* and so forth: "having taught these phonemes.

Now, how is it that by the inclusion of the consonants (*hal*), which consist of phonemes, there is also the inclusion of the *repha* (the sound *r*) situated within the *ṛ*-vowel, even though that *repha* does not itself consist of the *a*-phoneme? The intention is that this occurs by virtue of the force of the mention of "two consonants" (*dvihala*).
For in that context, one need only have said "after that [consonant], *nuṭ* [is inserted]."
And even when this is stated, there is no over-extension to cases such as *āṭatur* and *āṭuḥ*,
because the rule *aśnoteśca* (Pāṇini 7.4.72) serves a restrictive purpose:
if a reduplicated root (*advihala*) undergoes this change, it applies only to the root *aś*, and not to any other.
If it is argued that [the mention of] *dvihala* is for the purpose of excluding [the root] *aś*, this is incorrect.
For if this were the sole purpose, he would have formulated the prohibition simply as *na aś*.
Thus, even without the mention of *dvihala*, [the rule holds].
Since [the desired forms] are already established, the purpose for which he makes the mention of "dvihal" (a word consisting of two vowels) is this:
so that it may apply to those things that imitate the shadow of a dvihal.

Even for that [letter] which has one primary *hal* and another part that is a limb (*avayava*), it is worthy of being designated as a *hal* by way of metaphorical usage because of its similarity in form;
the purpose [of the rule] is so that this may also apply to it.
And how is this obtained? If the direct hearing (*śruti*) of the word "hal" applies there even to the manifestation of the letter *r* situated in the vowel *ṛ*, which imitates the shadow of a *hal*.
It is not otherwise.
Therefore, by the mention of "two consonants" (dvihal), the *repha* situated within the vowel *ṛ* is also included;
otherwise, the mention of "two consonants" would be purposeless.

The term *repha* is used there according to common convention; for among those who maintain that a [single] phoneme (*varṇa*) is grasped as a whole, even the portion consisting of the *ṛ*-vowel is commonly known as *repha*.
It is stated thus on account of their similarity.
For indeed, due to similarity, that designation is applied even to that [object],

just as one says "the boy is fire" (*agniḥ māṇavakaḥ*). Alternatively, in the rule *rādibhyaḥ* (Vārttika on Pāṇini 3.3.108), the word *varṇāt* does not carry over from the preceding rule *varṇāt kāraḥ*.

Therefore, the suffix *iph* occurs even after that which consists of a non-*a*-vowel, either by virtue of the rule of *bahulā* (diversity) or because it is understood that the suffix *kāra* occurs even after a non-*a*-vowel consisting of a constituent part similar to the letter *l*,
namely from the letter *ḷ*. Thus it should be known.
Even in the rule prescribing the substitute *l*, the general term *ra* is employed;
by this, both the pure *repha* (the letter *r*) and that which resides within the syllable *ṛ* are included.
Likewise, *la* is also a general term.
Therefore, a substitution of the letter *l* alone is prescribed in place of the letter *r* alone;

likewise, the letter *ḷ* arises from the *ṛ* vowel by means of a partial modification (*ekadeśavikāra*). Consequently, such grammatical references as Pāṇini’s rule *luṭi ca kḷpaḥ* (1.3.93) and others become logically justified.
This has been explained by the author of the Vṛtti himself under the rule *kṛpo ro laḥ* (Pāṇini 8.2.18):
"The term *ra* is employed as a general term (*sāmānya*).

That is to say, setting aside the distinction caused by being a phoneme (*varṇa*) or not being a phoneme, there exists a generality that resides in both the individual instances of the letter *r* (*repha-vyakti*)—both those consisting of a phoneme and those not consisting of a phoneme.
Since the word-cognition and the conceptual cognition "ra" are identical even for those two [sounds] which are distinguished by the difference between being a phoneme and not being a phoneme,
those two are what are apprehended;
however, the individual manifestation of the *repha* is not itself of the nature of a phoneme.
"By that" means that by the employment of a general term, both are included,
because that generality exists in both.
The word "also" (api) implies that this too is indeed a general term (sāmānya).
It is understood as "it is employed.
In this case as well, it would have to be stated that there is the inclusion of both: the letter *la* by itself and that which resides within the letter *ḷ*.
It is not stated because it is understood through the preceding rule.
Therefore, [the text says] "then this," and so forth.
Since both the *repha* (r) and the *lakāra* (l) are thus included, this substitution of *lakāra* is prescribed in place of the solitary *repha*.
Because of its closest proximity, the *ḷ*-vowel [is substituted] for the *ṛ*-vowel as well.
Now, even if both are included in the rule, how is it determined that the *ḷ*-vowel occurs in place of the *ṛ*-vowel? For the *repha* residing in the *ṛ*-vowel does not itself become the *ṛ*-vowel.
What then? It is a part of that [sound].
Nor does the *l* sound residing in the *ḷ* sound become the *ḷ* sound; what then? It is a part of that.

Since both are thus included, the meaning obtained is this: the *l* sound residing in the *ḷ* sound is the closest (the most similar) to the *r* sound residing in the *ṛ* sound, by virtue of being a single portion of the same phoneme (*varṇaikadeśatayā*).
However, in order to refute the objection that "the sound *ḷ* does not actually occur in place of the sound *ṛ*," it was stated: "by way of a modification of one part.

This means that the *repha* (the letter *r*) is a constituent part of the *ṛ*-sound, which is itself a single unit; and the letter *l* is a constituent part of the *ḷ*-sound, which is the modification of that [part].
Or rather, it is a partial [substitution];
or rather, it is the letter *la* situated in place of the letter *ḷ* as a partial [substitute];
that itself is the modification (*vikāra*).
The substitution of the letter *ḷ* for the letter *r* residing within the vowel *ṛ* is indeed a partial modification (*ekadeśavikāra*).
The word "door" (*dvāram*) means "entrance" or "means. By this, it is prescribed that the entire substitute *ḷ* takes the place of the entire original *ṛ*.

For if a separation of the sounds *ṛ* and *ḷ* from the *r* and *l* residing within them were possible, then it would be possible to prescribe the *l*, which is a single part of *ḷ*, as a substitute for the *r*, which is a single part of *ṛ*.
However, such a separation of those two [sounds] from that [diphthong] is not possible.
Therefore, the substitution of *ḷ* for *ṛ* is prescribed in the manner already stated.
The introduction of the phrase "and so" (*tathā ca*) and what follows is for the purpose of strengthening the point just stated;

because, in this way, the substitution of *ḷ* for *ṛ* is prescribed by means of a single instance. And this being the case, grammatical citations such as *luṭi ca kḷpaḥ* (Pāṇini 1.3.93) become logically consistent.
Not otherwise. By the word "ādi" (and so forth), there is the inclusion of the two rules: *ṛdupadhāc cākḷpicvṛtaḥ* (Pāṇini 3.1.110) and *tāsi ca kḷpaḥ* (7.2.90).

Regarding the rule for the substitution of *ṇ* (the *vināma-vidhi*), it has been stated that "it should be added that [the substitution occurs] even after an *ṛ*-vowel. Alternatively, this is established because the mention of the sound *ra* refers to the general class of sounds (*śruti-sāmānya*). Furthermore, since the substitution of *ṇ* occurs even when there is an intervention by a portion (*bhakti*) of an *a*-vowel, the inclusion of the words *nṛnamana* and *tṛpnoti* in the *kṣubhnādi* group should be understood as being for the purpose of prohibiting the substitution of *ṇ*.
Or rather, the author of the *Vṛtti* himself has provided a counter-argument, stating that it is precisely this [rule] which indicates that the substitution of *ṇ* occurs even after an *ṛ*-vowel.
"It is established by the indication of the commonality of sound (*śruti-sāmānya*).
"Sound" (*śruti*) refers to the perception of the form *ra*; that which possesses this is the sound *ra*, namely the letter *repha*.

Here, setting aside the distinction between being a phoneme (*varṇatva*) and not being a phoneme (*avarṇatva*)—which exists between the isolated [letter *ra*] and the *ra* situated within the syllable *ṛ*—that which is common to both, the mere *repha*, is what is indicated here.
But the individual manifestation of the *repha* is not identical with the phoneme itself.
By this, the substitution of *ṇ* is established even in cases such as *tisṛṇām*, *catasṛṇām*, *mātṛṛṇām*, and *pitṛṛṇām*,
because that commonality of the sound *ra* exists even in the vowel *ṛ*.
It might be argued as follows: in the phoneme *ṛ*, there are three constituent parts (*varṇāvayava*).
Among these, the *repha* consists of half a mora (*ardhamātrā*).
In that case, it is established simply by the mention of the commonality of the sound *ra*.

The subsequent explanatory passage (*jñāpakagrantha*) serves as a refutation of the objection that [the rule for *ṇatva*] is obstructed by that portion of the vowel (*avarṇabhakti*) which follows the letter *r*.

Since the author includes the words *nṛnamana* and *tṛpnoti* in the list of *kṣubhna*-type words in order to prohibit *ṇatva*, this indicates that *ṇatva* occurs even when there is an intervention by a portion of the vowel.
Otherwise, the mention of those two [repha and lakāra] there would be purposeless, because of the absence of their occurrence (*prāpti*);
for prohibitions are preceded by occurrence.
Even though the individual instance of the sound *repha*, consisting of a phoneme, is being indicated, he says "or rather" (*athavā*) and so forth in order to show that it is already established.

It has been indicated that, because of the general reference to the sound *ra* mentioned in the preceding sūtra, the substitution of *ṇ* occurs even when separated by a subsequent *avaṇa*-portion (*bhakti*).
However, the distinction here is that [the substitution occurs] immediately after the *ṛ*-sound itself, as it is not included in the preceding sūtra.
Others, however, declare that all these counter-arguments are formulated on the basis of the view that accepts the inclusion of parts of phonemes (*varṇaikadeśa*).
And this is incorrect;

for it is only appropriate to offer a rebuttal precisely where it was stated that one must provide a counter-argument regarding the short vowel *ṛ* in the rules concerning the insertion of *nuṭ*, substitution (*lādeśa*), and euphonic change (*vināma*).

Otherwise, by adopting the position of non-inclusion (*agrahaṇaka-pakṣa*) and yet attempting a rebuttal even under the position of inclusion (*grahaṇaka-pakṣa*), the author of the commentary (*vṛttikāra*) would merely reveal his own lack of skill.
5. *Hayavaraṭ*:
Its mention occurs by means of the single vowel *a* in the rule *śaś choṭi* (Pāṇini 8.4.63).
Here, the expression *śaś choṭi* should be understood as an illustration (*upalakṣaṇa*) for all the rules that provide specific applications (*pradeśavākya*).
In such explanations, there is inclusion by means of the letter *a*, but not by means of any other phoneme; this is the intended meaning here.
It does not mean, however, that inclusion occurs by means of the letter *a* only in this very sūtra.
In the rule *aṭkuṣvāṅnumvyavāye 'pi* (8.4.2),
it is accepted that the vowel *a* is included by the mention of *a* in the rule *dīrghād aṭi* (8.3.9).
Now, why is there not also inclusion by the vowel *a* in the rule *luṅlaṅlṛṅkṣvaḍudāttaḥ* (6.4.71)?
This is because of the rule *prāksitādaḍvyavāye ’pi* (Pāṇini 8.3.63).

For within this pratyāhāra, since any one of the vowels beginning with *a* is included, there must be an *aṅga* ending in a final vowel [to which the augment is added] according to the *alontyaparibhāṣā*. This is because each individual vowel possesses the designation *aṭ*.
Since each one of the letters beginning with *a* is individually a substitute (*ādeśa*),

and thus by virtue of being included by the mention of the "last" [letter], the intervention of the augment *aṭ* would not be possible. Now, even if they were not designated as such individually, the status of being a substitute might still be attributed to them collectively.
In this way, because it consists of more than one *al* (phoneme), it would be a substitute for the whole (*sarvādeśa*).

And if that were so, the original element (*sthānin*) would no longer be the letter *s*; therefore, in the case of *abhyaṣuṇot*, what would be separated by what, such that the retroflex (*mūrdhanya*) substitution could occur? Furthermore, why is this [the *s*] not included by the letter *i* in the rule *ardhadhātukasyeḍvalādeḥ* (Pāṇini 7.2.35)? If you say it is because of the mention in the rule *viditaḥ* (Pāṇini 5.1.43), [we reply: yes.
For in this *pratyāhāra* [of *ik*], by the rule *ādeḥ parasya* (Pāṇini 1.1.54), one of the vowels beginning with *i* would be the substitute for the *t* [in *vid-ta*];
and thus the form *viditam* would not be possible.

Now, why is there not also a grasping by means of the vowel *i* in the rule *dīdhīvevīṭām* (1.1.6)? [The answer is: because of the specific indications in rules such as *jayati*, *sambhavati*, and *avaharati* (Pāṇini 4.4.2, 5.1.52).
For if this were a *pratyāhāra* (abbreviation), then because it would exclude the quality (*guṇa*), such grammatical indications as these would not be possible.
Desiring to point out the fault that arises when the letter *r* is taught as following the letter *y*, he says "this," and so forth.
However, the teaching [of *r*] as subsequent [to *y*] is for the sake of its inclusion within the *val* group, as in the case of *jīradānuḥ* [from the root] *jīv* with the suffix *adānuk*.
The rule *godhāyā ḍhrak* (Pāṇini 4.1.129), which results in the form *gaudhera*, is intended so that the elision of *v* and *y* by the rule *lopo vyor vali* may apply;
furthermore, it serves the purpose of ensuring that the letter *v* is not included in the term *ral*.

For if the letter *r* were taught as preceding the letter *v*, then by the rule *ralo vyupadhād halādeḥ saṃś ca* (1.2.26), the suffix would optionally be *kittva* in forms such as *devitvā* and *dideviṣati*.
But surely, even if *ra* were taught after the letter *ya*, the letter *va* would still be included by the mention of *ra* (in the rule *ralo vyupadhāt...*);
for it is also taught among the *jaś* sounds.
This is not so.
Because they are produced by distinct qualities and because their difference is established;
as it has been said:
"They maintain that a phoneme is brought about by separate efforts."

This is because the former [the letter *va*] is produced with the articulatory organs slightly separated (*apṛṣṭa*) due to being a semi-vowel (*antaḥstha*), while the other [the letter *ba*] is produced with the organs in contact (*spṛṣṭa*) due to being a stop (*sparśa*).
Furthermore, this letter *va* is dental-labial (*dantoṣṭhya*). However, that which is intended in the sequence *ja-ba-ṅa-ḍa-da-śa* should be understood as purely labial (*oṣṭhya*).
But surely, because of the intervention of the letter *va*, this [letter *ra*] is not after the letter *ya*;

what then? It is after the letter *va*. Why, then, is it said to be "after the letter *ya*"? Even when there is an intervention, the word "after" (*para*) is still used; for example, as in "old age is after childhood. Thus, there is no fault.
In this case, even though the state of being old (*vṛddhabhāva*) is intervened by youth (*yauvana*), the application of the word *para* (subsequent) occurs.
If [the letter] is taught as subsequent to *ya*, then what follows? To this he says: "by the inclusion of *ya*" and so forth;
that is, by the inclusion—that is, the utterance—of this technical designation (*saṃjñā*) *yar*.

Thus, by the mention of this technical term *yay*, the meaning is "by means of utterance. Alternatively, by the mention—that is, the inclusion—of the *saṃjñins* (the things named) that begin with *ya*; the meaning is "by the inclusion of those *saṃjñins* beginning with *ya*."
"When there is grasping" means when there is appropriation (*upādāna*). However, by the grasping of that [appropriation], there is the grasping of that [name-and-form],
because that too is designated by that same name and because it is included within it.

In the case of *svarṇayati*, because the rule "ṛ, ṭu, and ṣ are retroflex" (*mūrdhanya*) establishes that they share the same place of articulation, when a *na* follows the *repha* (the sound *r*), the *repha* undergoes substitution by a *ṇa*—which is a homogeneous sound (*parasavarṇa*)—due to the absence of any specific exception.

But if this were so, would not the *paribhāṣā* regarding the "most similar substitute in the place of articulation" (*sthānentaratama*) be sublated? For the *ṇa* is not the most similar substitute for the *repha*, owing to the difference in their effort (*prayatna*).
This is not so;
for this objection is raised by relying upon the view that the individual is the word-meaning.
Therefore, one should not suspect sublation by the rule regarding the "nearest" (sthānentaratama-paribhāṣā).
For that rule operates only where both a nearest and a non-nearest [substitute] exist;
however, in this case, there is no nearest substitute, because the grammatical rule applies to each individual instance as a distinct entity.
However, because they are infinite, not all grammatical markers (lakṣaṇas) can be explicitly stated.

In that regard, if this marker pertaining to the [phoneme] *ṇ* were not to apply even to the immediately following *ṇakāra* due to a difference in effort (*prayatna*), then it would be entirely useless.
