Therefore, this paribhāṣā should be understood to apply when the word-meaning is a genus (*jāti*), and not when it is a substance (*dravya*).

In the case of *madrahrada-bhadrahrada*, this *repha* following the vowel and the letter *ha* becomes a *yar*. Consequently, the doubling [of the consonant] applies by the rule *aco rahābhyāṃ dve* (8.4.46), because from the preceding rule *yaro'nunāsike'nunāsiko vā* (8.4.45), the term *yar* is understood to carry over (*anuvartate*) here. When that doubling occurs, there would be the audible pronunciation of two *rephas*.

If it is argued that the elision of one [of the two *r* sounds] will occur by the rule *ro ri* (Pāṇini 8.3.14), we say no; for when an elision is to be performed, reduplication (*dvirvacana*) is considered non-existent (*asiddha*).
If that is so, then the elision of one [of them] will occur by the rule *halo yamāṃ yami lopaḥ* (Pāṇini 8.4.64).
For if this elision were established, there would be doubling [of the consonant].
Even so, in one alternative case, the hearing of two *repha*s (visarjanīya) would result;
for in that context, the option (*anyatarasyām*) from rule 8.4.62 (*jhayo ho’nyatarasyām*) continues to apply, as does the mention of the augment *aṭ*.
Even if that [substitution] were not to apply, nevertheless, by virtue of the power of the rule prescribing reduplication, the elision will not occur;
otherwise, the prescription of reduplication would be purposeless. As in the example: *kuṇḍaṃ rathena*.
According to the rule *anusvārasya yayi parasavarṇaḥ* (Pāṇini 8.4.58),
since no other *parasavarṇa* is possible for [the *anusvāra*] other than that, the *repha* itself would be the *parasavarṇa* of the *repha*.
One should not raise the objection that "since there are no homogeneous (*savarṇa*) sounds for the *repha* and the sibilants (*ūṣman*), the *repha* is also not homogeneous with another *repha*";
for that statement was made in reference to other phonemes,
because other phonemes, as the case may be, possess different points of articulation (*sthāna*) and efforts (*prayatna*).
However, among the various manifestations of the letter *r*, there is indeed mutual homogeneity (*sāvarṇya*), because they share the same place and effort of articulation.

Others, however, explain that when the letter *r* follows an *anusvāra*, the latter would become the nasal *ṇ* as its homogeneous substitute (*parasavarṇa*), on the grounds that they share the same place of articulation. But this is incorrect.
For one does not become a *savarṇa* (homogeneous) merely by similarity of place of articulation.
What then? By similarity of place of articulation and similarity of effort (*prayatna*).
And the letter *ṇa* is not of the same effort as the letter *ra*, because the *ra* is slightly unaspirated (*īṣat-pṛṣṭa*) while the *ṇa* is fully contacted (*spṛṣṭa*).

Thus, when the opponent has raised an objection based on the view that the individual (*vyakti*) is the meaning of a word, [the author], wishing to state a rebuttal based on the view that the universal (*jāti*) is the meaning of a word, says: "This is not a fault," and so forth.
"In the form" (*ākṛtau*) means "in the universal" (*jātau*). For some, the universal is the meaning of a word; for others, it is the substance (*dravya*).
For Pāṇini, however, both [the general rule and the exception] apply, according to the requirements of the linguistic usage (*lakṣya*). Thus,
in certain instances, one or the other is resorted to.
In that regard, when the universal (*jāti*) is accepted as the meaning of a word, it is the universal alone that is denoted by the word; however,
the individuals (*vyakti*) which serve as its substrata are understood by implication,
because it is impossible to cognize a universal without its substratum.

In this view, properties such as being the locus (*sthānitva*), being the substitute (*ādeśatva*), posteriority (*paratva*), and non-intervention (*avyavahitatva*)—which are useful for the grammatical refinement (*saṃskāra*) of words—are mediated through the individual instances (*vyakti*).
Therefore, a rule such as *yaro 'nunāsike 'nunāsiko vā* (Pāṇini 8.4.45), when it operates, operates only upon those individual instances that possess the universal (*jāti*).
Because it operates there [upon the individuals], it is said to have operated upon the universal.
Furthermore, among those individuals, there is no proximity or remoteness with respect to the universal (jāti) such that it would apply only in some cases and not in all.
This is because the relationship [between the universal and its instances] is undifferentiated.
Therefore, when it applies there, it applies everywhere, provided it is not sublated by either verbal testimony or logical reasoning.
And thus, when it has occurred in this manner, it has occurred with respect to the aggregate.
"Once" means one time; not again and again, because the purpose of the characteristic is fulfilled by its occurrence just once.

In this view, how does the rule *yaro 'nunāsike 'nunāsiko vā* operate? Does it apply without distinction to all entities that possess a universal (*jāti*), or does it apply specifically to only some? If it were without distinction, the aforementioned defect would remain exactly as it was.
If, however, it is to be stated that it applies specifically, then [the author] says *yaro 'nunāsika* and so forth.

By this, because the *sthānentaratama-paribhāṣā* (the rule regarding the closest substitute) is brought into play, it operates only with respect to those [substitutes] that are the closest (*antaratama*).
He shows that it does not apply to others with the words "tadanena" and so forth.

Since it operates only among those that are most similar (*antaratama*), therefore, by this definition, those sounds such as *ṅ* which are the most similar to the sounds such as *g*—by virtue of both place (*sthāna*) and quality (*guṇa*)—are prescribed as nasal (*anunāsika*). "Yathāsvam" means "according to its own."
The meaning is that those which are most similar to others are prescribed for them.
Regarding the phrase "of the *ga*-sounds and so forth," the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) includes the *ja*-sounds and others.
In the expression "the *ṅa*-sounds and so forth" as well, the word "and so forth" includes the nasalized consonants (*anunāsika*) such as *ña* and others.
In that regard, they are most similar by way of place of articulation and quality.
For example, among the letters *ga*, *ja*, *ḍa*, *da*, and *ba*, the letters *ṅa*, *ña*, *ṇa*, *na*, and *ma* correspond respectively.
Thus, since "the letters *a*, *kuh*, and the visarga are guttural," the throat is the common place of articulation for both the letter *ga* and the letter *ṅa*.
The *icuyaśa* sounds are palatals; thus, the places of articulation for the letters *ja* and *ña* are the palate (*tālu*).
The *ṛṭuraṣa* sounds are retroflexes; thus, the place of articulation for the letters *ḍa* and *ṇa* is the roof of the mouth (*mūrdhan*).
The *ḷtulasā* sounds are dentals; thus, the place of articulation for the letters *da* and *na* is the teeth (*danta*).

The *upū* and *upadhmānīya* are labials; thus, the lips are the place of articulation (*sthāna*) for the letters *ba* and *ma*. However, the quality (*guṇa*) of all these is identical, because of the statement that "the mode of articulation (*karaṇa*) for the stops (*sparśa*) is contact (*spṛṣṭa*)."
The consonants beginning with *ka* and ending with *ma* are the *sparśa*s (stops).
However, those which [arise] neither from the place of articulation nor from the quality (*guṇa*) are as follows.
The term "most proximate" (*antaratama*) is required here;
its connection is with the phrase "all those are excluded," which is to be stated later.
Their exclusion consists precisely in their non-employment.
"Either by position alone or by quality alone"—
in this case as well, "the most similar" is to be understood from the context,
and the connection is as before.
In that regard, the nasalized [consonants] are not the closest [substitutes] either by position or by quality;
they are like *ga*, *ja*, and *ḍa*.
Furthermore, *ya*, *va*, and *la* are both nasalized and non-nasalized.
These [substitutes] are indeed the closest (*anantaratama*) to those [original sounds] in terms of both place (*sthāna*) and effort (*guṇa*).
However, the inclusion of the term "nasalized" (*sānunāsika*) is because in rules such as *yaro 'nunāsike* (Pāṇini 8.4.45), the nasalized sound is prescribed as a substitute.

In that case, there is no closeness by way of place (*sthānata āntaratamyam*) between the letter *ga* and the letter *ya*, because their places of articulation are respectively the throat (*kaṇṭha*) and the palate (*tālu*).
Because the places of articulation for *ja* and *la* are the palate and the teeth respectively;
and because the places of articulation for *ḍa* and *va* are, respectively, the roof of the mouth, the teeth, and the lips.
Furthermore, there is no similarity between them even in terms of their phonetic qualities (*guṇa*).

Because the consonants beginning with *ga* have a complete contact (*spṛṣṭa*) as their mode of articulation; because the consonants beginning with *ya* have a slight contact (*īṣatspṛṣṭa*) as their mode of articulation;
and because of the statement that the semi-vowels (*antaḥstha*) have a slight contact as their mode of articulation.
The semivowels are *y*, *r*, *l*, and *v*.
By virtue of their place of articulation alone, the nasalized vowels (*anunāsika*) are the most similar;
for example, the nasalized counterparts of *j*, *d*, *b*, and *n* are *y̐*, *l̐*, *v̐*, and *ṅ̐* respectively.

In this context, the letter *ya* has the same place of articulation as the letter *ja*, because both have the palate (*tālu*) as their place of articulation. The letter *la* [has the same place] as the letter *da*, because both have the teeth (*danta*) as their place of articulation.
The letter *va* [has the same place] as the letter *ba*, because both have the lips (*oṣṭha*) as their place of articulation.

Although the teeth are the predominant place of articulation for the internal *v*, nevertheless, there is indeed a similarity based on proximity (*āntaratamya*) because both share the lips as a common place of articulation, just as in the case of *u* and *au*. The place of articulation for *u* is the lips; however, for *o*, it is also the throat, according to the rule: "The places of articulation for *o* and *au* are the throat and the lips."
Nevertheless, since they share the same place of articulation—the lips—there is indeed an internal similarity (*āntaratamya*) between them.
And just as there is internal similarity between those two despite the difference in one's place of articulation, so it is also between the letters *ba* and *va*.
There are also internal similarities based on quality (*guṇa*) alone, such as that between *ṅa*, *ṇa*, and *na* among the *ja*, *ba*, and *ḍa* series.
Because all [these sounds] possess the quality of being produced at the back [of the mouth].
In terms of their position, there is no internal proximity among them,
because the *jabagaḍada* sounds are produced respectively at the palate, the lips, the roof of the mouth, and the teeth.
But *ṅa*, *ṇa*, *na*, and *ṇa* [are excluded] because their places of articulation are the throat, the head, and the teeth.
Regarding the phrase "iti" and so forth: the particle "iti" is used here in the sense of a reason (*hetu*).

Since it is thus established that by virtue of both place (*sthāna*) and quality (*guṇa*), only those sounds which are the most similar (*antaratama*) are prescribed by this rule while all others are excluded, therefore, although *ṇakāra* is the most similar to *repha* by place alone— since both share the same place of articulation, namely the roof of the mouth (*mūrdhan*)—
there is no similarity in terms of quality.
And because of the distinction between qualities such as being touched (*spṛṣṭa*) and so forth;
since the letter *r* is included within the *ya*-class,
this is the reason for its undergoing the operations belonging to that class.
The meaning is that the doubling occurs because [the *y*] has reached the status of a *yaṇ*.
For that [doubling] applies to the *repha* (*r*) because it is included within the *yaṇ*, just as it does for other *yaṇ*s.
Regarding the passage beginning with *tad* and so forth:
the status of the letter *r* as the cause for doubling (*dvirvacana*) is directly taught (*sākṣācchiṣṭa*), that is, explicitly prescribed (*pratyakṣavihita*).
This is because, in the rule *aco rahābhyām* (Pāṇini 8.4.46), the doubling is enjoined by taking the letter *r* itself as the cause.
But the *yarkārya* (the grammatical operation concerning *y*) is inferred from its inclusion within *yar*;
and since direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) is stronger than inference (*anumiti*), the doubling of the letter *r*—which is directly enjoined by its status as a cause (*nimittabhāva*)—is set aside.
For example: "Let the Brāhmaṇas be fed."
"Let Māḍhara and Kauṇḍinya serve [the food]," it is said.

For here, the instrumental capacity of Māḍhara and Kauṇḍinya toward serving—which is directly enjoined—sublates their instrumental capacity toward eating, which was merely inferred from their being Brāhmaṇas.
If this is so, then there is a fault regarding curd, water, and the like.
For in the rule *iko yaṇ aci*, since the vowel (*ac*) is included within [the condition], the status of being a cause for the substitution of *yaṇ* for *ik* is inferred; however,
the substitution of *yaṇ* itself is directly taught,
because it is prescribed by taking *ik* as the direct recipient of the operation (*kāryin*).
Consequently, the status of being a cause (nimittabhāva) is sublated by that very [suffix] which is directly prescribed.

In that case, there is no fault because the individual (vyakti) is dependent upon the word-meaning (padārtha). It has been stated that when the individual is the word-meaning, the grammatical rule (lakṣaṇa) operates with respect to each specific instance (pratilakṣyam).

In that case, if the status of being a cause were sublated for the *ik* vowels by the substitution of *yaṇ*, then the grammatical rule (*lakṣaṇa*) concerning objects such as *dadhyudaka* would become useless.

Therefore, so that this fault does not occur, the status of being a cause is not sublated due to the force of the rule itself. However, in the present instance, the word-meaning (*padārtha*) is based upon a genus (*jāti*).

In that regard, because the genus (*jāti*) is one, the grammatical rule "acorahābhyām" is also singular; and that rule finds its application in cases such as *arkkaḥ* and *markkaḥ*. Therefore, although [the rule] does not prescribe reduplication for words like *madrahrada*, there is no risk of it being useless, and thus it is not stated twice.
Regarding the word *repha*:
by the use of the particle *iti*, the fact that the meaning just mentioned serves as the reason for the absence of doubling (*dvirvacana*) is indicated. [This applies to] the *anusvāra* and so forth.

The meaning of the word "api" (also) is that not only does [the rule] *na kevalaṃ yaro'nunāsike 'nunāsiko vā* (Pāṇini 8.4.45), which prescribes an optional nasal substitute, establish what is most similar (*antaratama*) by operating only once, but rather it also establishes the rule *anusvārasya yayi parasavarṇaḥ* (Pāṇini 8.4.58).
One might object: even if it establishes what is most similar, nevertheless, in this case, there must indeed be a *parasavarṇa* substitute consisting of the letter *r*.
Because that [anusvāra] is also the closest [substitute], he says "na ca" and so forth.
The connection is: "And there is no homogeneous (*savarṇa*) letter for the *repha*. Of what kind is it that does not exist?
"Most similar to the *anusvāra*": this means that which is most like the *anusvāra*. For this reason, there is no *parasavarṇa* (substitution by the following sound) in the case of *kuṇḍaṃ rathena*.
But how, then, is [the *anusvāra*] "most similar to the *anusvāra*"?
Is there no homogeneous (*savarṇa*) sound for the *repha*? It is said: for the *repha*, the *repha* alone is its homogeneous; no other phoneme is.
And that [homogeneous sound] is not the closest (*antaratama*) to the *anusvāra*.
This is due to the difference in place of articulation and the difference in quality.

For the *repha* (the sound *r*), the place of articulation is the palate (*mūrdhan*). As for the *anusvāra*, however, its place is the nose, according to the rule stating that "the *anusvāras* and *yamās* are nasal" (*nāsikya*).
Even though there is a *guṇa* [quality] for the letter *repha*, it consists of slight contact (*īṣatspṛṣṭatā*);
however, that does not exist for the *anusvāra*.

For this quality of being the closest (antaratama) is intended to belong only to the semivowels (*antaḥstha*), and not to others. Although—given that the third and fourth letters of the classes, the semivowels, *hakāra*, the *anusvāra*, and the *yamas* (the third and fourth letters following a *visarga*) are all nasalized (*nāsikya*), possess a constricted glottis (*saṃvṛtakaṇṭha*), and have voiced emission (*nādānupradāna*) and are voiced (*aghoṣavat*)—it is possible for the *repha* (the letter *r*) to be a homogeneous (*savarṇa*) substitute for the *anusvāra* by virtue of the external effort (*bāhyaprayatna*) known as "constricted glottis" and so forth; nevertheless, this rule for the *parasavarṇa* is not capable of prescribing a substitute based on similarity through mere external effort alone.
Where there are sounds most similar in terms of both place of articulation and quality, there the *anusvāra* takes the *parasavarṇa* (the following sound).
This is because [the rule] has already fulfilled its purpose in cases such as *śaṅkitaḥ* and *kuṇṭhitaḥ*.
Here, even in terms of place of articulation, the nasal cavities (*nāsikā*) of the *anusvāra* are most similar to those of *ṅa* and *ṇa*.

Because those two [the *anusvāra* and *visarga*] also have the nose as their place of articulation (*sthāna*), according to the statement: "The [nasal stops] *ñ*, *ma*, *ṅ*, *ṇ*, and *na* have both their own respective places of articulation and the nose as their place of articulation.
This is also true by way of their quality (*guṇa*).
This is because they are followed by the previously mentioned qualities of the *anusvāra*,
according to the statement, "As are the third [letters], so are the fifth. For,

by this passage beginning with "the third and fourth of the groups," those qualities common to the *anusvāra* which were stated for the third letters of the groups, such as *ga* and so forth, are here indicated for *ṅa* and the others.
One should apply the *repha* even by virtue of a mere quality if it occurs repeatedly;
for one should not assume that its repeated occurrence is purposeless,
since it has been stated that it does indeed occur repeatedly.
"uraḥ kena," etc. [The forms] *uraskaḥ* and *uraspāḥ* are derived as follows: *uraḥ kāyati* (he calls out "chest") and *uraḥ pāti* (he protects the chest).
The roots are *kai* and *gai* in the sense of sound (*śabda*), and *pā* in the sense of protection (*rakṣaṇa*).
Thus, by these two rules: *ātaḥ anupasarge kaḥ* (Pāṇini 3.2.3), [the suffix] *ka* is added;

and *āto lopa iṭi ca* (Pāṇini 6.4.64), there is the elision of the vowel *ā*. This forms an *upapada-samāsa* (compound with an adjunct). Then, the case-ending (*sub*) is elided. Finally, by *sasajuṣo ruḥ* (Pāṇini 8.2.66), the final *s* is replaced by *ru*.
By the rule *tasya kharavasānayor visarjanīyaḥ* (8.3.15), the *visarjanīya* [is substituted] for that [final *r*].
Then, by the rule *kupvoḥ ka-pau ca* (8.3.37), the *visarjanīya* is replaced by the *upadhmānīya* or *jihvāmūlīya*, as appropriate.
6. LAṆ:
This letter *ṇ* is doubled; it occurs both before and after [the vowel *a*]. Consequently, a doubt arises regarding the inclusion of *ṇ* in rules where *aṇ* is mentioned.
Is it [the case] by the rule for *pūrvā* or by the rule for *pra*?
Therefore, in order to exclude that, he says:
"The mentions of *iṇ*, etc. and so forth.

In this regard, just as all references to *aṇ* are understood to include the subsequent *ṇ* [by the rule *aṇuditsavarṇasya cāpratyayaḥ*], so it was explained in the section on *aiuṇ*. However, those references to *aṇ* which might also be thought to include the subsequent [letter] must be understood as referring to the preceding one. Which ones are they? For example: *ḍhralope pūrvasya dīrgho’ṇaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.3.11).
Regarding the mention of *aṇ* in these sūtras— namely, *ke’ṇaḥ* (7.4.13), *aṇo’pragṛhyasyānunāsikaḥ* (8.4.57), and *uraṇ raparaḥ* (1.1.51)—
in the first of these sūtras (*ke’ṇaḥ*), the inclusion of the word *vṛḍha* among the *dṛḍhādi* group serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*) that the subsequent mention of *aṇ* does not apply here.
For if [the form] were derived from another root, the form *vṛḍha* would not exist;
consequently, the inclusion of *vṛḍha* among the *dṛḍhādi* words would be untenable.

From the root *vṛh* in the sense of "exertion," when the past passive participle suffix (*niṣṭhā*) is applied, and after the substitution of *ḍha* for *ha*, the substitution of *dha* for *ḍha*, and the elision of *ḍha*, the form *vṛḍha* arises.
Furthermore, since the rule *acaś ca* (Pāṇini 6.1.101) is brought into proximity by the mention of "long" (*dīrgha*), it must be vowels (*ac*) alone that become long.

Thus, if the intention were for the lengthening to apply even to those vowels falling within the interior [of the compound] due to a subsequent vowel, he would have used the term "vowel" (*aj*) for the sake of clarity;
or else, he would not have used it at all.
Since the lengthening of all vowels is established by this very rule (1.2.28), *acaḥ*,
the mention of *aṇ* [in 1.2.29] is understood to refer back to the preceding [rule].
Furthermore, by the rule *ke’ṇaḥ* (7.4.13), since it is impossible for *hal* sounds to follow *ka-* when they are *aṇ*s, the shortening is prescribed only for vowels (*ac*).
In that case, if the shortness (*hrasvatva*) of all vowels (*ac*) were intended, he would have used the term *aj* alone for the sake of avoiding ambiguity;
or rather, he would not have used it at all,
since the desired meaning would have been established simply by the phrase "of the vowel (*acaḥ*)" which is brought to mind by the mention of "short" (*hrasva*).
By the third rule as well, a nasalized vowel (*anunāsika*) is prescribed for an *aṇ* at the end of a word.
Since there are no consonants (*hal*) that are *aṇ* at the end of a word, the nasalization must be prescribed for vowels (*ac*) alone.
In that case, if the intention were to prescribe nasalization for all vowels, one would simply have used the term "vowel" (*aj*) to avoid ambiguity.

Alternatively, one should not even perform that [substitution]. For it is only vowels (*ac*) that receive the designation *pragṛhya*, not consonants (*hal*). In that case, by the maxim of "connection with the negative particle" (*nañ-iva-yukta-nyāya*), since there is a prohibition of the *pragṛhya* status, the operation will be understood to apply only to that which is similar [to a vowel], namely, the vowels themselves.
Therefore, even there, by the force of the mention of *aṇ*, it is understood that the mention of *aṇ* refers only to the former [Pāṇini 1.1.69].

Furthermore, regarding Pāṇini 1.1.51 (*uraṇ rapara*), the rule 6.4.11 (*hotṛpraśāstṛṛṇām*) serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*) that here the mention of *aṇ* does not refer to the latter [Pāṇini 1.1.69].
For if the mention of *aṇ* referred to the latter, then by the rule *nāmī* (6.4.3), a long vowel would be followed by *rapara*.
Furthermore, the grammatical designation *praśāstṛṛṇām* would not be possible.
Moreover, no consonants (*hal*) other than the letter *r* are ever prescribed in any treatise as substitutes for the vowel *ṛ*.
For instance, according to the rule *iko yaṇ aci*, it would have to be the letter *r*.

Furthermore, there is no distinction made in the substitution of the vowel *ṛ* for the sake of the agent (*kartṛ*) in forms such as *itvā* and so on, whether the substitute *r* is followed by another *r* or not followed by an *r*.
For if the *r*-substitute were applied, one of the two *r*s would have to be elided by the rule *ro ri* (Pāṇini 8.3.14).
Therefore, this inclusion of the term *aṇ* [in the rule] would also serve only to prevent the application of the subsequent *ṇ*.

In that case, if the intention were for *raparatva* (the substitution of *r*) to apply to all vowels being prescribed in place [of *i* and *u*], one would have used the term *aj* alone for the sake of avoiding ambiguity. Therefore, it is certain that this mention [of *a*] occurs only with the preceding *ṇ*.
"An *aṇ* denotes its own homogeneous (*savarṇa*) sounds, except when it is a suffix" (Pāṇini 1.1.69)—this is one [reason].
Furthermore, in this context, the use of the *tapara* marker in the rule "ur ṛt" (7.4.7) is the indicative sign (*liṅga*).

For that [marker] is employed so that, even if the *ṛ* were to include its homogeneous sounds, in a form such as *acīkṛtat*, a long vowel would not replace the long original (*sthānin*) by virtue of being the closest in similarity (*āntaratamya*).

Furthermore, if in rules such as *aṇudid* the term *aṇ* were to be understood by means of the preceding *ṇakāra*, then the vowel *ṛ* would not be a grasper (*grāhaka*) of its homogeneous sounds (*savarṇa*) because it is not an *aṇ*.

Consequently, even for a long substitute, there would have to be a short vowel exactly as heard in the original rule; thus, he would not have made the addition of *tapara* (the *ṝ*), since there would be nothing to exclude.
And it has been done. Therefore, it is understood that by the subsequent letter *ṇ*, there is the inclusion of *aṇ*.
But even if there were inclusion of *aṇ* by the subsequent *ṇ*, how could the letter *ṛ* possibly be a grasper (*grāhaka*) of its homogeneous sounds (*savarṇa*) in the rule *ur ṛt* (Pāṇini 7.4.7)?
Because it is being taught [as a substitute].
[Objection: There is a prohibition stating that when a vowel is being taught as a substitute, it does not include the homogeneous vowels (*savarṇa*).
[Response: This is not so.
For he will say there: "And this [element] is not to be substituted; what then? Its own form is permitted for the purpose of precluding other substitutes.

In the case of *acīkṛtat*, [the root is] *kṛt* in the sense of "informing" (*saṃśabdana*). It belongs to the *curādi* class, so *ṇic* is added. Then *luṅ* (the aorist suffix). By the rule *ṇiśribrūsū...* (3.1.48), *caṅ* is substituted for *cli*. By *urṛt* (7.4.7), the *ṛ* of *ṛkārasya* becomes *ṛ*. There is the elision of *ṇi* by *ṇilopaḥ* (6.4.51). By *caṅi* (6.1.11), reduplication occurs. By *urat* (7.4.66), *a* is substituted. By *halādiḥ śeṣaḥ* (7.4.60), all but the first consonant are elided. By *sanvallaghuni* (7.4.93), the *ī* substitution occurs. By *dīrgho laghoḥ* (7.4.94), lengthening occurs.
Now, why is the mention of *aj* (vowels) not simply omitted here? The intention is that if it were so, doubt would certainly arise.
What is the reason? It is because one cannot proceed in this manner; therefore, he says: "For even among the semivowels (*antaḥstha*), etc.
The semivowels are of two types, excluding the letter *r*.

Because of the statement that [the letters] are both nasalized (*sānunāsika*) and non-nasalized (*niranunāsika*), the *ya*, *va*, and *la* sounds are of two types, distinguished by being nasalized or non-nasalized. Should these be taught as non-nasalized or as nasalized even within the *pratyāhāra* (phonetic summary)? If they were non-nasalized, then in cases such as *sa* + *yyanta*, when the *parasavarṇa* (substitution with a homogeneous sound) of the *anusvāra* occurs before a *yay* (a *ya*, *ra*, *la*, *va*, or *ha*) according to Pāṇini 8.4.58, the substitution would result in nasalized *ya* and so forth due to phonetic proximity (*āntaratamya*). Since those [nasalized sounds] are not taught within the *pratyāhāra*, the property of being a *yar* (a *ya*, *ra*, *la*, *va*, or *ha*) would not exist for them; consequently, the doubling (*dvirvacana*) of a *yar* prescribed by Pāṇini 8.4.47 (*anaci ca*) would not take place.

If, however, the term *aṇ* were not included [in the definition], then by the rule "an [vowel] includes its homogeneous counterparts" (*aṇ savarṇān gṛhṇāti*), the doubling of these [sounds] would also be established.

But one might object: even if doubling occurs, since the rule *halo yamāṃ yami lopaḥ* (P. 8.4.64) prescribes the elision of one [of them] when followed by a *yam*, the hearing of three *yakāra*s is simply impossible.
In that case, what is the purpose of the effort to provide for reduplication? This is not so;
for that elision is optional, because the term "anyatarasyām" (optionally) from rule 8.4.62, *jhayo ho'nyatarasyām*, continues to apply here.
In that case, in the alternative where there is no elision, the hearing of all three [anusvāra, anunāsika, and parasavarṇa] indeed occurs. However,
if they were taught with the nasalization (sānunāsika), then the substitution of the *parasavarṇa* for the *anusvāra* would not occur when a non-nasalized (*niranunāsika*) sound follows,
because those [nasalized sounds] are not included among them.

Regarding the phrase "in those beginning with *ha*," and so forth: the followers of Pāṇini maintain that the nasalization (*anunāsikya*) is prescribed [only] where they intend it; they acknowledge the nasal quality in those specific instances, and not elsewhere.
And by them, that [the *it* designation] is asserted for the vowel *a* when it occurs before the letter *l*,
but not in the case of *ha* and the others;
this is because [the rule] specifies "that which has the *it* designation."

Because the designation *it* is prescribed by the rule "In the Upadeśa, a non-vowel nasal is [called] *it*" (Pāṇini 1.3.2), he demonstrates the fruit of the promise regarding nasals by means of the words "by that" (*tena*) and so forth.
Since the inclusion of the *ṛ*-vowel and the *ḷ*-vowel under the designation *savarṇa* has been added as a supplement, the *ṛ*-vowel, when being grasped, also grasps the *ḷ*-vowel.
Consequently, there is the rule "Ṛ followed by *u* is replaced by *r*" (*ur ṛt paraḥ*).
Just as when the *aṇ* is prescribed as the substitute for the vowel *ṛ*, it is followed by *r*, so too it is intended that for the vowel *ḷ* it is followed by *l*.
Therefore, the nasalized [vowel] is formally declared.
By the rule *tena ādir antena sahet* (Pāṇini 1.1.71), there occurs the inclusion of the *pratyāhāra* "ra" in the rule *uraṇ rapara* (Pāṇini 1.1.51).
This [includes] from the letter *ra* up to the letter *a* in *laṇ*. And that being so, the substitute for the vowel *ṛ* becomes followed by *rapara* (i.e., having *r* as its subsequent element).
But for the letter *ḷ*, there is the rule "followed by *l*" (*lapara*). Consequently, forms such as *tavalkāraḥ* become grammatically justified. 7. *JñAMAṅAṇANAM*.
Its inclusion [in the pratyāhāra] occurs by means of three [vowels].
Now, why is this [the letter ṛ] not also included by the vowel *a* in the rule *sṛjidṛśorjhaly am akiti* (Pāṇini 6.1.58)? Because of the specific mention in *sākṣād draṣṭari* (Pāṇini 5.2.91).
For if this were a pratyāhāra, the word *draṣṭṛ* would not be established, due to the prescription of the substitution of the vowel *a* for the initial [of the suffix] within this pratyāhāra.

In that case, why does [the substitution] not occur by means of the *repha* (the letter *r*) in the rule *bhrasjo ropadhayo ram anyatarasyām* (Pāṇini 6.4.47)? Furthermore, how is this certain—that this *ram* is what is intended here, and not *am*? For the *saṃhitā* (the phonetic combination) is identical in both cases; therefore, there ought to be doubt as to whether this is *ram* or *am*.

If it is argued that certainty arises from the commentary (*vyākhyāna*), then if the commentary is accepted as the cause of certainty, certainty will arise from that alone in all such cases—both here and elsewhere—regarding matters of doubt; what, then, is the purpose of setting forth other reasons (*hetu*) by those who compose excessively voluminous treatises? Furthermore, as for one who thinks that in the rule *bhrasjo ropadhayo ram* (Pāṇini 6.4.47), there will be no inclusion of the pratyāhāra [of the vowels] due to the application of a restricted option (*vyavasthitavibhāṣā*), he should be addressed as follows:
(EdC, p. 29 begins with *niścaya*) Is the inclusion of *raṃ* being optionally chosen by this mention of "either one" (*anyatarasyām*)? That is, is it that "in the optional case, *raṃ* is taken"?

Or is it that a rule is being prescribed, such that "in the optional case, *raṃ* is prescribed"? If it is the inclusion of *raṃ*, then this is the inclusion of the letter *r* itself in its own form, accompanied by the phonetic marker *m*.

Is it not obtained that this does not apply to *pratyāhāra*? This is established by the rule of "optionally fixed" (*vyavasthitavibhāṣā*); for the augment *ram* would not occur optionally, because the inclusion of the term *anyatarasyām* has already served its purpose in providing an option for the inclusion of *ram*. Indeed, there is no second occurrence of the term *anyatarasyām*.
By that [interpretation], a restrictive rule (*vidhāna*) would have to be postulated.
However, in the other alternative, a conditional rule (*pākṣika-vidhāna*) is established.

But as for that which was intended—that by means of a fixed option (*vyavasthita-vibhāṣā*), this is the formal mention (*svarūpeṇa grahaṇam*) of the letter *ra* itself, accompanied by the indicatory mark *m*, and not of a technical abbreviation (*pratyāhāra*)—that is untenable.
Because there is oneness [of purpose] regarding the non-mention of either one;
for that has already been utilized by way of an optional rule (*vidhānavikalpa*).

Furthermore, from what source does this determination arise that "this is a fixed option" (*vyavasthitavibhāṣā*)? If you say "from the commentary" (*vyākhyāna*), then why resort to tradition now? To say "it will not be a reference to a *pratyāhāra* precisely because of the commentary"—this is trivial.
It is observed that the inclusion [of the suffixes] by means of the *pratyāhāra* (abbreviated term) also occurs through the letter *ñ*.
If this is so, for what purpose was it said "by three"? It is to show that in the rule *ñamantāḍḍaḥ*, the *pratyāhāra* is not necessarily intended to be included.

For here, even if the actual forms of the letters *ñ* and *m* were employed, the suffix *ḍa* would still be established after anything else ending in *m*, even without the inclusion of the *pratyāhāra*.
Because of the rule governing the predominance of the majority.
(2) But even so, it should have been stated as "by four" (*caturbhiḥ*). For in the rule *yamirñamanteṣu*, this [term] is not seen to be included by the letter *ñ* either.
This would be true if this were said with reference to mere apprehension;
however, this was not stated intending mere apprehension,
but rather a specific kind of apprehension.
It is based on the Sūtra.
Is this not a citation from the Sūtra? What then? It is the status of being an *āniṭ*-kārikā.
"Ke-cid" and so forth:

having reflected that these *pratyāhāra* groups mentioned immediately prior should be formed by the very same *ña* that occurs in the group "jha-bha-ñ," certain teachers perform the rejection (*pratyākhyāna*) of the letter *m*.
Their intention is that, in the event of such a rejection, the letter *ña* must be substituted for the letter *m* in rules such as *pumaḥ khayy am-paraḥ* (Pāṇini 8.3.6).
By stating "this being so" (*tathā ca sati*) and so forth, he demonstrates the fault in rejecting the suffix *makāra* as an *anubandha*.

For if the rule were read as *ṅñaḥ hrasvād aci ṅañuṇ nityam* (Pāṇini 8.3.32), then since *jha* and *bha* would also be included within the *pratyāhāra*, they too would become augmentals (*āgama*). This objection arises.
The rebuttal must be stated that these two will not occur because *jha* and *bha* do not exist at the end of a word (*padānta*).

When that has been stated, an objection is raised: "But surely, since both *labh* and *ubj* take the suffix *kvip*, both [the *b* and *j*] would indeed exist as word-final sounds; thus, the rule *jhalāṃ jaśo 'nte* (Pāṇini 8.2.39) would apply, and the question arises: how could those two [sounds] exist [as *g* and *d*]? This is the further objection. The further response is: "But surely there would be an inequality because of the absence of the incoming *jhabh* sounds."

For instance, there are three augments—ṅ, ṇ, and n—whereas the augments themselves are five: ṅ, ṇ, n, jh, and bh. Consequently, because of this numerical discrepancy, one might raise the objection that the rule of "correspondence according to order" (yathāsaṃkhyam, Pāṇini 1.3.10) would not apply to them. This is the further challenge.
This is not a fault.

In the Sūtra, as many augments (āgama) are taught, so many augments are also taught for those which receive them (āgamī). Therein, without regard for the specific linguistic forms to be characterized (lakṣya), it is established that the augments such as Ṅ and others occur according to their respective order; subsequently, the application of the grammatical operations will take place according to the requirements of each case.
First, for those who maintain that there are augments (āgama), they will apply [the rule] according to the respective order.

However, since the letters *jha* and *bha* do not exist as augments at the end of a word (*padānta*), one must state a further rebuttal: that because they do not exist as augments, the [original] augments themselves will also not occur.

Thus, through the rebuttal of many such objections, there would be excessive complexity in the process of establishing the absence of augments based on the reason that the augments *jha* and *bha* do not exist.
Therefore, the intention is that the rejection of the letter *m* is improper. 8. JHABHAÑ.
9. Gha ḍha dha ṣa | 10. Ja ba ga ḍa da śa | 11. Kha pha cha ṭha tha ca ṭa ta va |
But surely, this [sound] is already included by the letter *cha* alone, and *kha* and *pha* are not contained within it.
For what purpose, then, are they mentioned here? To this, he says: "The mention of *kha* and *pha*, etc."
The meaning is that these two are mentioned so that they may also be included within the subsequent *pratyāhāras*; this is the purpose [of their inclusion].
12. KAPAY.
13. ŚAṢASAR | 14.
HAL | Here, other phonemes are taught only once.
The letter *hakāra* is taught twice. Desiring to know the purpose of this double teaching, he asks, "Now, for what purpose," and so forth.

Regarding the word *snihitvā*: the root *ṣṇiha* means "affection. By the rule *ādeḥ ṣṇaḥ snaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.1.64), the initial *ṣṇa* is replaced by *sna*. The suffix *ktvā* is applied by the rule *samānakartṛkayoḥ pūrvakāle* (Pāṇini 3.4.21). The augment *iṭ* is added.

Regarding *alikṣat*: the root *liha* means "to taste. This is the *luṅ* (aorist) tense. By *ho ḍhaḥ* (Pāṇini 8.2.31), *h* becomes *ḍh*. By *ṣaḍhoḥ kaḥ si* (8.2.41), there is the substitution of *k* for *ḍh*. By *ādeśapratyayayoḥ* (8.3.59), there is the substitution of *ṣ* for *s*. Regarding *rudihi* and *svapihi*: these are formed from the roots *rud* and *svap* using the imperative (*loṭ*) for the sense of injunction and so forth. By *ser hy apic ca* (3.4.87), *hi* is substituted for *si*. Due to belonging to the *adādi* class, there is elision (*luk*) of the suffix *śap*. By *rudādibhyaḥ sārvadhātuke* (7.2.76), the augment *iṭ* is added.

*adāgdhām*: [The root] *dah*, meaning "to reduce to ashes," is used here in the *luṅ* (aorist) tense. For this, the suffix *cli* is applied. By the rule *tasthasthamipām* (Pāṇini 3.4.101), the ending *tas* is replaced by *tām*. Then, by *cleḥ sic* (3.1.44), the suffix *sic* is added. By *vadavrajeḥ* (7.2.3), a *vṛddhi* vowel substitution occurs. By *dāderdhātor ghaḥ* (8.2.32), the initial *d* is replaced by *dh*. By *jhalo jhali* (8.2.26), there is the elision (*lopa*) of the *sic*. By *jhaṣastathordho'dhaḥ* (8.2.40), the *t* is replaced by *dh*. Finally, by *jhalāñ jaś jhaśi* (8.4.53), the *gh* is replaced by *g*. Thus, *adāgdhām* is formed.
In that regard, if the letter *ha* were not included in the mention of *ra*, *śa*, and *va*, then the rules concerning *kit*, *tva*, and *iṭ* would not apply.

Furthermore, if *ha* were not included in the mention of *jhal*, then because the substitution of *gha* would also be considered asiddha, the *siC* suffix following a *gha*—which is not a *jhal*—would not undergo elision by the rule *jhalo jhali* (Pāṇini 8.2.26).
Therefore, so that this [letter *ha*] may be included in the mentions of *śal* and *jhal*, there is a re-enunciation of what has already been taught.
If these purposes are indeed [served] by instruction from another alone, then let it be so;
for by that alone these are accomplished.
With the intention that the previous instruction should not be performed, he says: "In that case, regarding *hayavaraḍ*, etc."
Regarding the phrase "in the case of the mention of *aṭ*, etc.":

if [the augment] had not been taught previously, then because of the mention of *aṭ* and the mention of *aś*—and since there would be no mention of *a*—the substitution of *ru*, the nasalization (*anunāsikatva*), the substitution of *ya*, and the elision of *ya* would not occur in the word *mahān*. [The derivation is as follows:
from the word *mahaḥ*, the suffix *su* is added; then by *ugidacām* (Pāṇini 7.1.70), the augment *num* is inserted.

By the rule *sāntamahataḥ saṃyogasya* (Pāṇini 6.4.10), the vowel is lengthened. Then, by the rules *halṅyābbhyo dīrghāt sutisyapṛktaṃ hal* (6.1.68) and *saṃyogāntasya lopaḥ* (8.2.23), [the suffix] is elided. When *mahān hi* is established, since the letter *ha* follows, the substitution of *ru* occurs for the final *n* by the rule *dīrghād aṭi samānapāde* (8.3.9). By the rule *āto 'ṭi nityam* (8.3.3), the preceding vowel becomes nasalized (*anunāsika*). Since the term *aś* is included in the scope of the following rule, the substitution of *ya* occurs for the *ra* by the rule *bho bhago agho* (8.3.17) et cetera. While the condition *aśi* is still in effect, the elision of *ya* occurs by the rule *hali sarveṣām* (8.3.22).
Regarding the rule *haśi ca* and so forth:
this is another purpose for the previous instruction.

For if that [instruction] were not present, in the example *brāhmaṇo hasati*, the letter *ha* would not be included by the mention of *haś*; consequently, when that [condition] is absent, the substitution of *ru* for *r* would not occur before the following [sound].

From the word *brāhmaṇa*, the suffix *su* is added. By the rule *sasajuṣo ruḥ* (8.2.66), *ru* is substituted [for *s*]. By *haśi ca* (6.1.114), *u* is substituted [for *r*]. By *ād guṇaḥ* (6.1.87), the *guṇa* [vowel *o*] is formed. Regarding "from one," etc., the ellipsis is that "the subsequent [sounds] are to be understood."
The word "syuḥ" (they should be) is to be connected with what is about to be said.
The ablative case in "ekasmāt" (from one) is characterized by its relation to direction.
The meaning is that the letters beginning with *ṅ* should be understood as following immediately after a single phoneme (*varṇa*).
Alternatively, the ablative case in "ekasmāt" (from one) is used with the elision of a verbal suffix ending in -lyap;

just as one says "he looks from the palace" (*prāsādāt prekṣate*) after having climbed the palace (*prāsādam āruhya prekṣate*), so too the meaning is that in the constituent sentences (*pradeśavākya*), the letters beginning with *ṅ* should be grasped after one letter has been uttered or taken up. That, moreover, is a single letter.

In the [Śivasūtra] "eoṅ | jhabhañ | aiuṇ | khaphachaṭhathacaṭatav | hayavaraḍ," that very [pratyāhāra] by which the inclusion of the letters beginning with *ṅ* was stated should be understood. In the rule "dvābhyāṃ ṣaḥ," the word "pare" (subsequent) which was supplied, as well as the verbal form "syuḥ" (they may be), is transformed into the singular number for the sake of the sense.
The meaning is that after pronouncing the two preceding [letters], the letter *ṣ* should be taken.
The same meaning is to be understood for what follows as well.
But where are the two [preceding letters]?
In the rule *jhabhañ* and *ghaḍhadhaṣ*, those very [pratyāhāras] by which the inclusion of the letter *ṣ* was stated are used;

thus, *kaṇam* would apply to exactly three [letters]. Those three, moreover, are: *ṛḷk*, *laṇ*, and *ña-m-a-ṅa-ṇa-na-m*. In the rule *ña-m-a-ṅa-ṇa-na-m*, those very [pratyāhāras] by which the inclusion of the letters beginning with *k* was explained are used.

Regarding the statement "the *jña* and *ca* [pratyāhāras] are to be understood from four [letters]," those four are again *a-i-au-c*, *k-p-y*, and so forth; in this context, it is intended that by the letters *c* and *y*, the inclusion of both the letter *ca* (the *c* in *ca*) and the letter *ya* (the *y* in *y*) is meant.
"Raḥ from five [consonants]" means that those five are [the consonants] ś, ṣ, s, r, and h; for in the rule "śa-ṣa-sar," there is the inclusion of the letter *ra*.
This has been established by the rule itself: "After the six [roots], *śal* [takes *iṇ*]. Furthermore, those six are as follows: [the six roots beginning with *tan*].
In the case of *jabagaḍadaś* and *hal*, those by whom the inclusion of the letters śa and la was stated should be understood [as authoritative].
Thus end the *pratyāhāra* sūtras.
[The first quarter of the first chapter.
Regarding the rule *vṛddhir ādaic*, some explain this as a three-word sūtra.

Others, however, considering it to be a collective (*samāhāra*) compound—namely *ācca aicca* = *ādaij*—interpret it as a two-word sūtra: *vṛddhir ādaic*. For if it were a copulative (*itaretarayoga*) compound, there would have to be a plural ending due to the multiplicity of its members.

But surely, even in a collective compound (*samāhāra*), the suffix *ṭac* would apply as a compound-final element (*samāsānta*) by the rule "after a *dvandva* ending in *cuda*, *ṣa*, or *ha*" (Pāṇini 5.4.106); [this does not occur] because the application of the rules for compound-final elements is non-mandatory (*anitya*). That non-mandatory nature will be made known in the sixth book (*Aṣṭādhyāyī* 6.1.133).

Now, why does the substitution of *k* (*kutva*) not occur according to the rule "after *atha*" (Pāṇini 8.2.30)? Because, by the rule "the words *ayas*, *maya*, etc., are treated as *bha* in the Vedic language" (Pāṇini 1.4.20), they possess the designation *bha*.
Since the word "ādi" (and so forth) denotes a class or type, this term "aiccha" is to be understood as belonging to the group beginning with "yasmaya" [as prescribed by Pāṇini 1.4.20].

[Objection: But is it not said that [the rules] apply "in Vedic" (*chandasi*)? And this is not Vedic; so how can there be the designation *bha*? [Response: There is no fault, because "the Sūtras are like the Veda. Now, is this Sūtra purposeless, like the various statements regarding the acute accent (*udātta*) and so forth? Or is it for the purpose of teaching correctness (*sādhutva*), such that the correctness of the word *vṛddhi* and of the vowels *ā*, *ai*, and *au* is declared by this [Sūtra]? Or is it for the purpose of restricting usage, such that the word *vṛddhi* must be used only for *ā*, *ai*, and *au*? Or is it for the purpose of providing substitutes (*ādeśa*), such that the word *vṛddhi* [is the substitute] for *ā*, *ai*, and *au*?

Is it a designation (*ādeśa*)—that "these" [the *ā*, *ai*, and *au*] are "of that" [the term *vṛddhi*]? Or is it for the purpose of establishing a relationship between the source and what comes from it (*āgamāgamisambandha*), such that the word *vṛddhi* is an augment (*āgama*) "of these" or "to that"? Or is it for the purpose of establishing a relationship of qualifier and qualified (*viśeṣaṇaviśeṣyabhāva*), such that the word *vṛddhi* is the qualifier "of these" or "to that"? For here we observe the use of a single case-ending (*ekavibhaktikatva*), and a relationship of qualifier and qualified is observed between two words with a single case-ending, as for example in "a blue lotus" (*nīlam utpalam*).

Or is it for the purpose of establishing a relationship between the name and the named? For that [relationship] is indeed seen even between two words in the same case-ending, as in the example, "This is a jackfruit tree" (*ayaṃ panasaḥ*). Among these, first of all, the initial position is not tenable.

For the Teacher, possessing superior knowledge regarding the world of beings, committed to the welfare of others, with a concentrated mind, having arranged protective measures for his disciples, composed the Sūtras with great effort, preceded by auspicious rites.

In this regard, it is impossible for even a single word to be meaningless, let alone such an extensive composition of a Sūtra! Nor can it be understood that the correctness (*sādhutva*) of the term *vṛddhi* and of the vowels *ā*, *ai*, and *au* is being enjoined by this [rule], because their correctness has already been established by other grammatical rules (*lakṣaṇa*). For instance, this word *vṛddhi* is taught without qualification:

from the root *vṛdhu* (meaning "to increase," Dhātupāṭha 759), the suffix *ktin* is added according to Pāṇini 3.3.94; then, by 8.2.40, the substitution of *dh* occurs; and finally, by 8.4.53, the letter *dh* is changed to *d*.

Even *ai* and *au* are included in the traditional list of phonemes (*akṣarasamāmnāya*) because they are taught [as such]. If it is argued that while *ai* and *au* are taught in the traditional list of phonemes, the vowel *a* is not, [we reply: there is no fault, because since the class (*jāti*) of the sound *a* is taught, that [individual instance] is also included. Or, even if the individual instance of the sound *a* were taught, there would still be no fault.
Because when the letter *a* is mentioned [in a rule], it includes the vowel *ā* as well.

Furthermore, this [mentioning of *a*] cannot even be for the purpose of restricting usage (*prayoganiyama*). For if it were for the purpose of restricting usage, then in rules such as "vṛddhi before *sic*" (P. 7.2.1) and "vṛddhi for *mṛj*" (P. 7.2.114), the use of the word *vṛddhi*—which follows vowels other than *a*, *ā*, *i*, *ī*, and *u*, *ū*, *e*, *ai*, and *o*, *au*—would be untenable.

For how indeed could one, having oneself established a rule, then employ that very [element] after something other than *ā* or *aic*? But another [author], in order to demonstrate that this [rule] does not serve to restrict usage, says: "And it is not commenced for the purpose of restricting usage. [Objection: But surely this [sūtra] is commenced precisely for the purpose of restricting usage, namely: *te prāg dhātoḥ* [Pāṇini 1.4.80]? [That is to say,] those elements designated as *upasargas* (preverbs) and *gatis* (indeclinables) must be employed only before the verbal root (*dhātu*). When this is urged by the opponent, he provides the rebuttal: "That rule is either rejected or not [accepted], because such undesirable results are observed [if it were accepted]."

For no one, when they ought to use the form *prapacati*, uses the form *pacati pra*. Even if [the rule] were not rejected [as unnecessary], there would still be no fault; because this is a restriction regarding technical designations (*saṃjñā-niyama*), not a restriction regarding usage (*prayoga-niyama*). That is to say, those particles beginning with *pra* receive the designations "motion" (*gati*) and "prefix" (*upasarga*) only when they are employed before a verbal root.

Furthermore, even if it were for the purpose of restricting usage (*prayoganiyama*), there would still be no fault; for a restriction on the usage of worldly words employed in their meanings is being undertaken, and the word *ādi* is a worldly word. Why, then, would there be a statement intended to restrict its usage? In that case, what was said—that "that rule (*yoga*) is rejected"—is incorrect. For it is not reasonable to reject something that possesses meaning. If it is argued that it is meaningless, then the very suspicion of meaninglessness would apply here as well.

If one were to hold the view that the author of the Sūtras composed even some sūtras that are meaningless, then anyone who accepts his authority must admit that everything he composed is meaningful in some way or another. Furthermore, the solution offered by resorting to the position that [the sūtras] are restricted by technical terminology is also contradicted by the Vṛtti.

It is clearly stated by this passage from the *Vṛtti*—namely, "those [terms] termed *gati*s and *upasarga*s must be employed before the verbal root"—that a restriction regarding usage (*prayoga-niyama*) alone is being adopted.

Furthermore, it is not appropriate for one who sets out to explain the *Vṛtti* to provide an interpretation that contradicts it. As for what was said regarding "of worldly words" (*laukikānāṃ śabdānām*) and so forth, that too is not sufficient to dispel the suspicion that [the rule] is intended as a restriction on usage.

For instance, rules such as *vibhāṣā supo bahuc purastātu* [Pāṇini 5.3.68], *avyayasarvanāmnām akac prāk ṭeḥ* [Pāṇini 5.3.71], and *kṛñcānuprayujyate liṭi* [Pāṇini 3.1.40] show that even unformed elements like *bahuc* and others are restricted by the grammatical treatise (*śāstra*) to specific applications; in such cases, one must indeed raise the doubt: "Is this for the purpose of restricting usage, or for some other purpose?"—but enough of this digression.
Therefore, the solution previously stated is the appropriate one. Furthermore, this cannot be understood as being for the purpose of substitution (*ādeśa*).

If the term *vṛddhi* were prescribed as a substitute for *ā*, *ai*, and *au*, then the following references would be untenable: the rule "yāti, vāti, drāti, psāti" (Pāṇini 8.4.17), the rule "āt" (7.2.85), and the rule "ātaḥ" (5.4.99). Alternatively, if *ā*, *ai*, and *au* were to be substituted by the term *vṛddhi*, even so, references such as "āto ṅitaḥ" (6.3.28) and "āta au ṇalaḥ" (6.3.39) would not be possible. For this very reason, it is also not tenable that this [term *vṛddhi*] is intended for the purpose of an augment (*āgama*).

Nor is the term *vṛddhi* [used] for the augment (*āgama*) when it has been prescribed, nor do the previously mentioned designations apply to it or to them. However, another says: "In the prescription of a substitute (*ādeśa*), there must be a genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) to express the relationship between the original element (*sthānin*) and the substitute; likewise, in the prescription of an augment, there must be one to express the relationship between the part and the whole. But here, no genitive is found; therefore, due to the absence of the genitive, this is neither for the purpose of a substitute nor for the purpose of an augment. This is incorrect, because we see the prescription of substitutes even without a genitive, as in the rules *vināpi* (P. 6.1.68), *aniteḥ* (P. 8.4.19), *antaḥ* (P. 8.4.19), and *naśca* (P. 8.4.21).

Furthermore, since the rule for the application of *āgama* (augment) is seen even without a genitive case—namely, in the rule "na yvābhyāṃ padāntābhyāṃ pūrvau tu tābhyāmaic" [Pāṇini 7.3.3]—this [genitive] might also be considered for the purpose of establishing the relationship between qualifier and qualified (*viśeṣaṇaviśe�ṣyabhāva*).
For indeed, the relationship of qualifier and qualified occurs only when there is both possibility (*sambhava*) and deviation (*vyabhicāra*), as in the case of "blue lotus.
However, in this context, there is neither the possibility of *ādaic* being in the word *vṛddhi*, nor the possibility of *vṛddhi* being in them (*ādaic*).

Now, one might object: just as the word *utpala* (lotus), while applying to all lotuses, is delimited from other objects by the word *nīla* (blue), such that the delimited [word] becomes the qualified (*viśeṣya*) and the delimiting word *nīla* becomes the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*), so too in this case, whichever of these two is delimited would be the qualified, and whichever is the delimiter would be the qualifier. This is not so;
for this is only possible when both words possess meaning, as in the case of the expression "blue lotus" (*nīlotpala*).
However, the *ā*, *ai*, and *au* vowels do not possess meaning.

Granted that there may indeed be a relationship of qualifier and qualified (*viśeṣaṇa-viśeṣya-bhāva*) between these two, nevertheless, this [distinction] is not appropriate for the purpose of establishing this [rule]; because it serves no purpose, and furthermore, because it is irrelevant to the subject at hand. For in this treatise on the instruction of words (*śabdānuśāsana*), whatever statement is made that does not contribute to the refinement (*saṃskāra*) of words is entirely useless.

And this [distinction] does not contribute to the refinement of words, because by means of the relationship of qualifier and qualified as explained here, no refinement—whether in the form of a specific accent (*svara*) or a specific phonetic form (*rūpa*)—is achieved for the term *vṛddhi* or for the vowels *a*, *ai*, and *au*.

If it is argued that their *saṃskāra* (grammatical refinement) consists precisely in the relationship of qualifier and qualified (*viśeṣaṇaviśeṣyabhāva*), then this is saying far too little [as stated in 1.1.1].
For one must also state "blue lotus" (*nīlotpalam*), in order to establish the relationship of qualifier and qualified between words such as "blue" and "lotus."

And it has not been stated [that this is so]; therefore, since this is not intended as a *saṃskāra* (grammatical refinement), its status as serving that purpose (*tādārthya*) is not possible. Now, one might object: "Is it not observed that even for words with identical case-endings, there is the superimposition of qualities (*tadguṇasamādhyāropa*), as in the example ‘The boy is a lion’? Therefore, this [word] will serve that purpose"—this is the alternative view some have devised. Even for the sake of that [objection], this is not the case; because even if such a superimposition of qualities were present here, it would be useless, as it serves no purpose for the subject at hand (*prakṛta*).

Therefore, concluding by way of elimination that this [rule] is intended solely for the purpose of establishing the relationship between the name (*saṃjñā*) and the named (*saṃjñin*), he says: "The word *vṛddhi* is [used] as a name," and so forth.
Granted that it serves that purpose by way of elimination, how is it obtained that "the word *vṛddhi* is the name and *ā*, *ai*, and *au* are the named"?
Why is the reverse not the case—that is, that *ā*, *ai*, and *au* are the technical terms (*saṃjñā*) and the word "vṛddhi" is the thing named (*saṃjñin*)? The reverse cannot be possible.
For the purpose of creating a technical term is for the sake of brevity; that which, when uttered, results in brevity in the application rules (*pradeśa*), must be intended as the technical term.

And when the word "vṛddhi" is uttered—even though it consists of multiple syllables—there is brevity, whereas with *ā*, *ai*, and *au* there is not; because when the word "vṛddhi" is uttered, it consists of four morae (*mātrā*), but with *ā*, *ai*, and *au*, it would consist of five.

Nor can it be imagined that there is brevity because the designation (*saṃjñā*) applies to each of *ā*, *ai*, and *au* individually, for without a specific purpose, the formulation of a single designation for multiple elements would be fruitless.
Furthermore, designations apply to recurring [elements].
The word "vṛddhi" recurs, whereas the word "ādaic" does not; therefore, there is no reversal such that "the word *vṛddhi*" [would be the name].
The mention of "word" (*śabda*) is for the purpose of excluding the object (*artha*).
For if that were not stated, since meaning is understood from the word, the object itself might be understood to possess the status of a name (*saṃjñātva*).

Although the name has already been prescribed [previously], it is nevertheless prescribed here because the lineage of teachers and students has come to an end; thus, it is indicated by means of a present-tense verbal form.

Where one intends to refer to a collective whole (*samudāya*), one employs the dual form of the word, as in "both [parts] are termed *abhyasta*" (Pāṇini 6.1.5); or else, one uses a significant technical term (*saṃjñā*) that is meaningful according to its derivation, such as "a cluster (*saṃyoga*) consists of consonants situated between [vowels]" (Pāṇini 1.1.7). For in that case, the technical term is established for this purpose so that it may apply to the collective whole.
We shall clarify this further below.

But here there is no such statement by which this designation would apply to the collection as a whole. Therefore, considering that this designation applies to each individual [element], he says "each one. Now, one might ask: even here, for the sake of brevity, when a single-syllable designation ought to have been made, why was a large designation like "vṛddhi" employed? It is so that the designation might apply to the collection as a whole. This is not the case; for this designation serves the purpose of auspiciousness (*maṅgala*).

For this very reason, she (the name *saṃjñā*) is mentioned first. Otherwise, since a name must exist before the thing named (*kāryin*), it would have been mentioned here just as it was previously in the rule "adeṅ guṇaḥ" [P. 1.1.2] and elsewhere; for instance, one might have specified the vowels *ai* and *au* as being included in the *pratyāhāra*. Consequently, some person of dull intellect might fall into the error of thinking that these letters do not belong to the set of vowels (*amī varṇāḥ*). Therefore, to dispel that misconception, he says: "of the letters" (*varṇānām*), and so forth.
Because of their proximity, someone might have the misconception that this designation applies only to those things produced by them; therefore, in order to dispel that, he says: "in general.
The intention is that this follows from the principle of pervasion (*vyāpti*).
To clarify the meaning of "in general," he says: "of those produced by them," and so forth.

Those produced by the word *vṛddhi* are "conditioned by that" (*tad-bhāvita*); others than those are "not conditioned by that" (*atad-bhāvita*). Regarding the use of *āT* (the long vowel *ā*) with the *T* marker: does it serve, as stated in [Pāṇini 1.1.70], to include even those sounds that differ in quality (*guṇa*) provided they are of equal duration, or to exclude those of different durations? First, the former position is not tenable; for in this treatise, accents such as the acute (*udātta*) and others are not considered to be differentiators of phonemes. Why is this so? Because of the mention of "acute" in [Pāṇini 6.4.71]: *luṅlaṅlṛṅkṣvaḍudāttaḥ*; otherwise, he would have simply pronounced the augment *aṬ* as being endowed with the acute accent itself.

The second [position] also is not tenable. For if the letter *a* were the grasper (*grāhaka*) of its own class-members (*savarṇa*), then, since it would grasp even the letter *a* belonging to a different time, the use of the *tapara* (the *t* following the vowel) would be justified for the purpose of excluding the grasping of those belonging to different times, so that the designation (*saṃjñā*) might not apply to them as well.
However, this [short *a*] is not a grasper of its own class-members, because it is not an *aṇ*, owing to its non-inclusion in the traditional list of phonemes (*akṣarasamāmnāya*).
Therefore, the use of the *tapara* is useless.
Therefore, [one might ask] why it should not be done at all; to this he says: "The inclusion of the letter *t*," and so forth. That which has *ec* as its meaning or purpose is described in that way.

But surely, even a *pluta* (protracted) vowel would be included when the word-meaning is the universal (*jāti*), because the universal of the sound *a* inheres in that as well; in that case, if the *tapara* (the *t*) were not employed, its designation would also occur. Therefore, the employment of *tapara* for the purpose of excluding that is indeed justifiable for the sake of the form *ā* as well. So why is it said, "for the sake of *e*"? It is thought thus: even when resorting to the position of the universal, it is understood by the force of the long pronunciation that only those individual instances of the sound *a* consisting of two morae (*mātrā*) are resorted to;
for otherwise, for the sake of brevity, one would simply have stated "ad".

Nor can it be assumed that the long vowel (*dīrgha*) is pronounced for the sake of excluding the short vowel (*hrasva*), because even when a long vowel is pronounced, the inclusion of the short vowel would still follow, since the class (*jāti*) of the *a*-vowel is present there as well. Nor was it stated as "āT" (with a long vowel) merely to avoid ambiguity, because this sound is unique to itself among other phonemes, or because there is no possibility of confusion when it is not in *saṃhitā* (continuous flow). Now, one might object: in the rule *taḥ paraḥ* (Pāṇini 1.1.70), a *bahuvrīhi* compound is adopted meaning "that after which *ta* follows"; however, in the present case (*aic*), the *tapara* (a sound followed by *t*) does not exist. Therefore, how can the use of *tapara* be for the sake of excluding the short vowel? To this, he says: "In those two cases as well, [the term] *tapara* means 'that after which *ta* follows'."
The word "also" (*api*) indicates that it is not only that which follows *t* which is called *tapara*, but also that which follows *tā* is likewise *tapara*.
What is meant is this: in this context, one should resort not only to the *bahuvrīhi* compound, but also to the *pañcamī-tatpuruṣa* compound.
We shall demonstrate how both of these are to be understood right there in that very place.

The particle *iti* here indicates cause; since this is so, that [vowel] is also "with a following *t*" (*tapara*). Therefore, the meaning is that the inclusion of *t* (the *tapara* marker) is for the sake of excluding the long vowel (*aijartha*). By the phrase "in cases such as *khaṭvailakā*," etc., he clarifies that very purpose of the *tapara* marker. In *vṛkṣa elakā* → *vṛkṣailakā*:

if the *tapara* marker were not applied here, then by the rule *vṛddhireci* [Pāṇini 6.1.85], a single substitute would take the place of the combination of the three-moraic *ā* and *e*; and due to proximity (*āntaratamya*), if that [three-moraic vowel] were also designated as a *vṛddhi*, the resulting *ekāra* would necessarily be three-moraic.

In cases such as *khaṭvā odanam* → *khaṭvaudanam* and *khaṭvā elakā* → *khaṭvailakā*, where both the preceding and following groups consist of four morae (*caturmātra*), the vowels *a* and *e* would also [be subject to the rule] becoming four-moraic. To prevent this fault, the addition of *t* (as in *tapara*) is made to exclude the designation of *vṛddhi* for *ai* and *au* when they consist of three or four morae. For example:
*āālāyanaḥ* and *aitikāyanaḥ*. Here, after the words *āla* and *aitika*, there is elision by Pāṇini 4.1.99 and 6.4.148, followed by *vṛddhi* substitution by 7.2.118 (*kiti ca*).

In the case of *aupagavaḥ*, the suffix *aṇ* is applied after the word *upagu* [Pāṇini 4.1.83]. In the case of *aupamanyavaḥ*, the suffix *añ* is applied after the word *upamanyu* [Pāṇini 4.1.104]. In both instances, the substitution of *av* for *an* occurs [Pāṇini 6.4.146], followed by the application of *vṛddhi* [Pāṇini 7.2.117].

These four are also examples of those [suffixes] being treated as such. Now, an objection is raised: since the objects of the first three [suffixes] among those three *sañjñins* have already been shown, for what purpose is the fourth introduced? Some say: "Because of the difference in the cause of *vṛddhi*; in the first two examples, the *k-it* suffix is the cause of *vṛddhi*, while in the third it is the *ṇ-it* suffix, and in the fourth it is the *ñ-it* suffix.
But this is incorrect.
For instance, in the rule [1.1.3], having cited *akārṣīt*, *ahārṣīt* is cited as well; yet there is no difference in the cause for the *vṛddhi* (vowel strengthening) in those cases.
Similarly, in the rule [1.1.4], having cited *loluvaḥ*, further examples such as *popuvaḥ* and *marīmṛjaḥ* are presented;

however, there is neither a difference in the cause for elision (*lopa*) nor a difference in the cause for the prohibition (*pratiṣedha*) that serves as the reason for presenting these additional examples.
Generally, even in other general grammatical rules (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*), an additional presentation of examples is observed even in the absence of a difference in the underlying cause (*nimitta*).

As for the one who says, "Even though the domain of the vowel *au* has already been shown by the example 'aupagavaḥ', the example 'aupamanyavaḥ' is presented additionally because of a difference in accent (*svarabheda*)," his position is also incorrect; this should be understood from the very reason just stated.
If there is a difference in the cause (*nimitta*) or a difference in the accent (*svara*), it should be understood that a further example is provided in every case; for instance,
*śālīyaḥ* and *mālīyaḥ* are examples of that which has not been conditioned by such [a cause].

For here, in the context of the technical designation *vṛddhi*, the introduction of the suffix *cha*—in the rule "That whose first vowel among the vowels is a *vṛddhi* is called *vṛddha*" (Pāṇini 1.1.72)—is intended to manifest that very [designation] which is its result. For when the designation *vṛddha* exists, the suffix *cha* is prescribed by the rule "After a *vṛddha* [stem], in the sense of 'born from' and so forth" (Pāṇini 4.2.114). However, no example is shown here for the long vowels *ai* and *au* when they have not undergone such a transformation (*atadbhāvita*), because they are understood through the very reasoning followed here.

When an operation is shown for the designation *vṛddhi* of a vowel-sound (*ākāra*) that has not been produced by that [specific rule], it is understood precisely through that [designation] that the same operation applies to those two as well.
What, then, are the examples for these two? They are *raimayam* and *naumayam*.
Here, since the designation *vṛddhi* applies to the vowels *ai* and *au*, the designation *vṛddha* follows as before.

And when that [condition] exists, the suffix *mayaṭ* occurs according to the rule: "In the sense of 'modification of that,' [the suffix *mayaṭ* is applied], as in *rāyamayaḥ* (made of wealth) and *nāvamayaḥ* (made of a boat)" [Pāṇini 4.3.144]. However, the inclusion of the vowel *taḥ* (the long *ā*) here serves all purposes;
that is, its purpose is for every case, and thus it is so described. The word *tu* (however) indicates a distinction from what preceded.
In that [previous rule], it was for the sake of *hrasva* (short) vowels only; here, however, it is for all purposes, including for the sake of *a* and for the sake of *eṅ*.

For if the *tapara* marker were not present, since *adeṅ* would not include its homogeneous (*savarṇa*) counterparts, this designation would apply even to those of different durations when the marker is present.

Consequently, in the word *taritā*, by virtue of being the closest [substitute], a long vowel would result as the *guṇa* substitute for the long vowel itself. [Objection: But surely the designation *vṛddhi* will supersede the designation *guṇa*; so how can this contingency arise? [Reply: This is not so.
For when there is the governing rule (*adhikāra*) of "one technical term" (*eka-saṃjñā*), one technical term is superseded by another; however, here there is no governing rule of "one technical term.

It might be argued: even in the absence of a governing rule of "one technical term," just as the technical term *gotra* is superseded by the technical term *yuvan* according to [Pāṇini 4.1.163], and just as the technical term *sārvadhātuka* is superseded by the technical term *ārdhadhātuka* according to [Pāṇini 3.4.115] and [3.4.116], so too will the technical term *guṇa* be superseded by the technical term *vṛddhi*. This is incorrect.
In the rule prescribing the technical term *yuvan*, the mention of the augment *t* is made for the purpose of restriction (*niyama*).
Therefore, it is logical that the designation *gotra* is sublated by the designation *yu* (*yuvat*).

It is likewise logical that the designation *ārdhadhātuka* is sublated by the designation *sārvadhātuka*, because of the statement [of Pāṇini]: "When two designations apply simultaneously, the later one sublates the earlier" (Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.4.2).

If there were a co-occurrence (*samāveśa*) of the designations *sārvadhātuka* and *ārdhadhātuka*, there would be no relationship of sublation and sublated; in that case, the aforementioned statement would be purposeless.
But here, there is no such basis by which the designation of *guṇa* would be sublated by the designation of *vṛddhi*.
Even if it were somehow sublated, the designation of *guṇa* would still apply even to that which has three morae (*trimātrika*),
for it cannot be sublated by that [designation of *vṛddhi*], because the latter does not have that as its scope.
If the designation "guṇa" were applied even to that which has three moras (*trimātra*), it would follow that a three-mora vowel is also a *guṇa*.

For just as a single-mora *a* is not the closest similar [substitute] for the vowel *ṛ* in terms of duration, so too a three-mora [vowel] is not; how then is this [distinction] obtained? It must be that its *guṇa* substitute is only a short [vowel], and certainly not a three-mora *ā*.

Furthermore, if the designation *guṇa* were to apply even to vowels occurring at different times, then in the case of *khaṭvā indraḥ* = *khaṭvendraḥ* and *khaṭvā urvī* = *khaṭvorvī*, because the substituend (*sthānin*)—which consists of the preceding and following elements taken together—is three morae (*trimātra*), the *guṇa* would likewise be three morae by [Pāṇini 6.1.87].
And in the case of *khaṭvā īṣā* = *khaṭveṣā* and *khaṭvā uḍhā* = *khaṭvoḍhā*, because it is four morae (*caturmātra*), the *guṇa* would be four morae.
Therefore, for the sake of all these cases, the addition of the *tapara* marker (the letter *ṛ*) must be made.
Regarding the passage beginning with "taritā":

from the roots *tṛ* (meaning "to cross over" or "to swim across," Dhātupāṭha 969), *ci* (meaning "to collect," Dhātupāṭha 1251), and *stu* (meaning "to praise," Dhātupāṭha 1043), the suffix *tṛc* is applied by Pāṇini 3.1.133 (*ṇlultṛcau*). Then, by Pāṇini 7.2.35, the augment *iṭ* is added; by Pāṇini 7.3.84, *guṇa* substitution occurs; the nominative singular ending *su* is added; and by Pāṇini 7.1.94 (*ṛduśanaspurudaṃso'nehasām ca*), *anaṅ* is substituted for the final vowel and following consonant; finally, by Pāṇini 6.4.8 (*sarvanāmasthāne ca*), the vowel is lengthened.
These three are, respectively, examples of *eṅ* and *at* when they have been modified by that [substitution].
"Paṭhanti" and "paṭhan" are examples of *at* having been modified by that [substitution];
here, because the final *a* receives the designation *guṇa*, the substitution of the subsequent form (*pararūpatva*) occurs according to Pāṇini 6.1.97.
The word "paṭhan" here ends in a present participle suffix (śatṛ).

An example of an operation for that which is not conditioned by such a suffix (*atadbhāvita*) is "ahaṃ pace" and so forth. An example of an *o*-vowel that is not conditioned by such a suffix is not shown here, as it is impossible. "This is a *paribhāṣā* (technical rule)."
It does not have jurisdiction because it is not marked with the svarita accent;
nor is it a rule prescribing guna or vṛddhi, since those two will be prescribed by other rules. [The phrase] "for the purpose of restricting the substituendum" means:

*Sthāniniyamaḥ* means "restriction regarding the substituendum" (*sthānin*); it is that which operates upon one specific [element] by excluding other possible substituenda. That which has this as its purpose or objective is described as such. The statement "a restriction is prescribed where there was the contingency of non-restriction" refers to cases where the substituendum is not explicitly mentioned, such as in rules like *[[Pāṇini 7.3.84]]* and *[[Pāṇini 7.2.1]]*. In those instances, when non-restriction would otherwise apply, he establishes a restriction for these [elements]: "only *ik* [is substituted], and not anything else."

Therefore, that alone should be understood as its scope, and not that place where the term itself is directly mentioned, such as [Pāṇini 6.4.146] and [7.2.116], and so forth; for in those cases, there is no possibility of the application of the rule at all. Furthermore, this is a *paribhāṣā* (interpretive maxim) characterized by a formal indicator (*liṅga*), and its indicator is the mention of "guṇa" and "vṛddhi," which serves as its point of application.

And thus two genitives appear: one is "ikaḥ" [Pāṇini 6.4.119], and the second is such as "iko yaṇaci" [Pāṇini 6.1.77]. In that case, since there is freedom of choice, the desired result is established according to one's wish.
A relationship of qualifier and qualified (*viśeṣaṇa-viśeṣya-bhāva*) is established between them.

In the case of "mideḥ," since an *ik* (a vowel) cannot possibly be at the end of the root, it is not possible for it to be a qualifier of the *aṅga* (stem). Therefore, here the *aṅga* itself is qualified by the *ik*: "the *ik* which belongs to the *aṅga* of the root *mid*."

Because that [element] is not present in its original position (*sthānaṣṭhabhāva*), when the final letter (*antyasya*) is not present, a single *guṇa* substitution is established for whatever [vowel] stands there.

In examples such as [Pāṇini 7.3.84], the status of having an *ik* vowel at the end of the *aṅga* is possible; and by qualifying the *aṅga* in this way, the desired result is achieved through the application of the rule *tadantavidhi* (the inclusion of what ends with that).
Therefore, the *aṅga* (stem) qualified by *ik* is specified, meaning "of a stem ending in *ik*.

This being the case, because this [genitive] is a genitive of location (*sthāna-ṣaṣṭhī*), Pāṇini's rule 1.1.52 (*yasmin vidhis tadādāv algrahaṇe*) applies; consequently, *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* substitutions occur only for a stem ending in *ik*, and not for any other.
[The phrase] "by its own technical name" (*svasañjñayā*) [is used].
The intention to be explained here is as follows:
"In place of *ik* alone. He demonstrates the nature of that restrictive rule (*niyama*) for the sake of which this *paribhāṣā* exists, using the example "akārṣīt.
[The root] *ḍukṛñ* (meaning "to do," Dhātupāṭha 1472); [in the] *luṅ* [tense]; [by P. 3.1.44] *sic*; [by P. 7.2.1] "vṛddhi" [occurs]; [by P. 7.3.96] *iṭ*.
Thus, regarding the form *ahārṣīt*:
here, the specific rule is *hmañ haraṇe* (Dhātupāṭha 899). [The question] "What is the purpose of [specifying] *ika*? [is answered by: *ita*.
It should be understood that the inquiry regarding the whole is made by way of one part;
for by the mere mention of "guṇa" and "vṛddhi," no meaning whatsoever is included without the inclusion of the term "i.
[As in the example] "yānam."
