If the suffix *lyuṭ* were applied to the root *yā*, the substitution of *a* would occur by virtue of being the closest internal equivalent (*āntaratamya*) when the *guṇa* is prescribed.
Consequently, when the two *a*s undergo the substitution of a single subsequent form (*pararūpa*) according to Pāṇini 6.1.104 (*ato guṇe*), the undesirable form *yanam* would result.
[This is illustrated by] the word *glāyati*.

Regarding the rule *glai mlai harṣakṣaye* (Dhātupāṭha 903–904), here the *guṇa* substitute for the diphthong *ai* would be *e*. Consequently, once the substitution of *ay* (*āyādeśa*) is applied, the undesirable form *glayati* would result.
[The correct form is] *umbhitā*.
The roots *ubha* and *umbha*, meaning "to fill" (*dhātupāṭhaḥ* 1319, 1320), take the suffix *tṛc* along with the augment *iṭ*.
In this case, the *guṇa* substitution of *o* for the labial consonant *k* would occur;

subsequently, when the *vṛddhi* substitute *āv* is applied, the undesirable form *ubhavitā* would result. Now, how is this distinction—that they are taught by their own technical names (*svasañjñā*)—obtained, given that the term "own name" (*svasañjñā*) does not appear in the rule itself? To this, he says: "The repetition of the mention of *guṇa* and *vṛddhi*" and so forth.

In this context, the mention of *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* from the two preceding sūtras is understood by anuvṛtti (carry-over). While that [anuvṛtti] is already present, the reason for repeating the mention of *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* here is this: "This restrictive rule (*niyama*) should apply where *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* are prescribed by their own technical names (*svasañjñā*), but it should not apply elsewhere. By the force of this repetition of *guṇa* and *vṛddhi*, the fact that one of the two mentions of *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* has the technical name as its primary referent is established. From this, the meaning is obtained that the restriction applies when there is a prescription by means of the technical name itself.

For otherwise, if such a preceding restriction were not intended here, then—since a fixed restriction would already be established by the continued application of the mention of *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* from the context—the repeated mention of *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* here would be purposeless; this is the underlying intention.
By the words "let it not be here" (*iha mā bhūt*) and so forth, he demonstrates that a restriction of this kind is what is to be excluded, as in the example "dyauḥ.
Here, the vowel *au* is substituted [by the rule] *diva aut* (Pāṇini 7.1.84).
When an *al* (a vowel or consonant) is prescribed by its own form (*svarūpeṇa*), it applies only to the final [element], not to the initial. For example, in the word *panthāḥ*,
the substitution of *ā* prescribed by the rule *pathimadhyṛbhukṣāmāt* [Pāṇini 7.1.85] applies only to the final [phoneme], not to the initial.
By the rule *ito 'tsarvanāmasthāne* [Pāṇini 7.1.86], the vowel *i* is replaced by *a*; by the rule *tho 'nthaḥ* [Pāṇini 7.1.87], the letter *th* is replaced by the substitute *nth*.
Thus, the form is *iyam*.
The substitution of *a* (atva) occurs precisely through the intervention of this [rule], not by the suffix *ekā*.
By the rule *daśca* [Pāṇini 7.2.109], the letter *d* is replaced by *m*.
However, if this paribhāṣā were to apply in the case of the word *saḥ*, the substitution of *yatva* for the *tyadādi* stems would certainly not occur.

[One might argue: "The substitution of *s* by the rule *tadoḥ saḥ sāvana-ntyayoḥ* [Pāṇini 7.2.106]—but is it not the case that the restriction on the substituend (*sthānin*) in the rule *anaśca* [Pāṇini 1.2.28] is intended to apply only to the prescription of its own technical name (*sañjñā*), and that this very restriction must exclude forms such as *dyauḥ*?"

For the author of the *Vṛtti* will state there: "When a rule is prescribed by its own technical name (*svasañjñā*), it is a restriction (*niyama*). The term *aj* (vowel) continues [to apply]. Let it not occur here: *dyauḥ*, *panthāḥ*, *saḥ*, *dyubhyām*, *dyubhiḥ*" (Kāśikā 38). Therefore, whatever must be accomplished by such a restriction is already established by that alone; there is no purpose in this further mention of *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* for the sake of such a restriction. This is true; however, in the comprehension of the meaning in this way, those listeners who are of dull intellect and beginners would experience a burden in their understanding.

Therefore, in order to favor them and to establish a restriction (*niyama*) for the formulation of technical names (*saṃjñāvidhāna*) here so that the meaning may be clear, the mention of *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* is repeated. One might ask: "In this case, since whatever is to be prescribed by something has already been prescribed by this very rule, should a restriction not be made regarding the formulation of technical names? This is not so; for if such a restriction were not applied to short vowels (*hrasva*), then in the forms *dyubhyām* and *dyubhiḥ*, the letter *u*—being prescribed in its own form by [Pāṇini 6.1.131]—would apply only in place of a vowel (*ac*), and not in place of the final phoneme (*alo 'ntyasya*).

Indeed, by this rule alone, the vowel (*ac*) cannot be excluded, because it is designated as *guṇa* or *vṛddhi*. The designation of "root" (*dhātu*) has been applied to a word of the stated dimension;

when the entire [word] is elided, since *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* would necessarily apply there in relation to the *ārdhadhātuka* suffix, what is the use of the prohibition? Therefore, considering that the word "root" applies to a portion of the root by virtue of the power of the formulation of the prohibition, he says: "A portion of the root is the root.
[This refers to the condition] "when there is elision of a root" (*dhātulope*).

If this [term] *dhātulopa* is a *tatpuruṣa* compound meaning "the elision of a verbal root," then the mention of *ārdhadhātuka* must be a qualifier for *guṇa* and *vṛddhi*: "When there is the elision of a verbal root conditioned by an *ārdhadhātuka* suffix, those *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* substitutions that would otherwise occur do not take place.

Alternatively, it might be a qualifier for the elision itself: "When there is an elision of a verbal root conditioned by an *ārdhadhātuka* suffix, *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* do not occur. In the former case, a prohibition would apply to the form *knopayati*; therefore, a remedy must be provided for that.

But in the second [view], this fault does not arise; for in the case of *knopayati*, the elision is not caused by the *ārddhadhātuka* suffix, but rather caused by the *katvala*. However, in the second alternative, [the rule] would apply in the case of *preddham*.

For here there is indeed an elision conditioned by an *ārdhadhātuka* suffix. But is this not a prohibition of *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* characterized by the vowel *i*? And yet, is there no *guṇa* here characterized by *i*? This is not so; for even here, the *guṇa* that occurs in place of both [the *i* and the following vowel] is indeed characterized by *i*, and it receives the designation of either of the two [substitutes]. To illustrate: in the forms *mātuḥ* and *pituḥ*, an *aṇ* followed by *r* occurs in place of both [the *u* and the following *s*].
Therefore, even under the view that the term [ārdhadhātuka] qualifies the elision (lopa), a counter-argument must indeed be made regarding the *tatpuruṣa* compound;
however, thinking that nothing needs to be countered in the case of the *bahuvrīhi*, and showing that this is indeed a *bahuvrīhi*, he says: "Of that," and so forth.
By this, it is shown that the term *ārdhadhātuka* qualifies the elision.

And thus, [the term] *ārdhadhātuka* is applicable only if it serves as the cause (*nimitta*) for that [substitution]; consequently, the over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) does not arise in the case of *knopayati*. Regarding the phrase "in that case" (*tatra*) and so forth:
it has also been explained that the *ārdhadhātuka* affix is not a qualifier of the *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* substitutions by way of being their cause.
Consequently, there is no over-extension (atiprasaṅga) even in the case of *preddha*, for the substitution of the *guṇa* vowel [for *r*] is not caused by an *ārdhadhātuka* suffix.
Regarding the phrase "those two" (*ye te*),
it is expressed in the feminine gender because it stands in grammatical apposition with the feminine term "guṇavṛddhī."

However, its feminine gender [is established] by the extended application (*atideśa*) of the rule *strīliṅgatā* (Pāṇini 1.4.3). And since that extended application applies to the meaning, those two—*yad* and *tad*—also become feminine when they refer to that same meaning.

Now, one might object: since a restrictive rule (*niyama*) is the subject under discussion, it would be more appropriate for this prohibition to apply specifically to that [restriction]; why then does he say, "In that case, those *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* substitutions which would otherwise occur do not take place"?
Because of the predominance of those two [guṇa and vṛddhi];
for they are invariably assisted [by the conditions], whereas the restriction (niyama) is subordinate because it exists for their sake.
Therefore, this prohibition is logically applicable only to guṇa and vṛddhi, as in the examples *loluvaḥ* and *popuvaḥ*.

From the roots *lūñ* in the sense of "cutting" (*dhātupāṭha* 1483) and *pūñ* in the sense of "purifying" (*dhātupāṭha* 1482), the suffix *yaṅ* is applied by the rule *dhātorekācaḥ* [Pāṇini 3.1.22]. There is reduplication by the rule *sanyaṅoḥ* [Pāṇini 6.1.9], and the strengthening of the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*) occurs by the rule *guṇoyaṅalukoḥ* [Pāṇini 7.4.82]. When the suffix *ac*—belonging to the *pacādi* class—is added to the *yaṅ*-stem and subsequently elided by *pacādyaci* [Pāṇini 3.1.134], there is a prohibition of the strengthening (*guṇa*) caused by that suffix. This being the case, the substitution of *uvaṅ* occurs by the rule *aci śnudhātukabhruvām* [Pāṇini 6.4.77]. Thus, the form *marīmṛjaḥ* is derived.

The root *mṛj* in the sense of "cleansing" (*mṛjū śuddhau*, Dhātupāṭha 1066) undergoes *yaṅ* as before; there is reduplication, *ura* substitution, and by [Pāṇini 7.4.66] through [7.4.60] to [7.4.90], the augment *īr* is added.
By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) in the rule *lolūyādibhyaḥ*, the forms *popūya* and *marīmṛjya* are included.
Regarding *lūñ*: "he will cut" (*lavitā*).

As long as the designation "root" (*dhātusañjñā*) has not yet occurred, the elision of the letter *ñ* takes place by the rule "the rule for elision is stronger than all rules for grammatical operations" (*vyā.pa.* 70). Subsequently, the [stem] *lū* receives the designation "root. Therefore, because the elision of *ñ* is not an elision of a root (*dhātulopa*), this serves as a counter-example. [The example is] *reḍ*.

The root *riṣ* (and *ruṣ*) is listed in the Dhātupāṭha as meaning "to injure" (1232, 1230). By the rule [Pāṇini 3.2.75], the suffix *vic* is applied; the letters *i* and *c* are for the purpose of ensuring that the general designation (*sāmānyagrahaṇa*) is not obstructed in the application of [Pāṇini 6.1.67], and the letter *v* is elided by this very same rule. Then, by the rule [Pāṇini 7.3.86], *guṇa* substitution occurs. Finally, by the rule [Pāṇini 8.2.39], the letter *ṣ* is replaced by *ḍ*.

But surely both of these counter-examples are deficient in two respects: for in those cases, there is no elision of the verbal root (*dhātulopa*), nor is there an occasion for [the application of] an *ārdhadhātuka* suffix. This is not so; for when the term *dhātu* (root) is present, a *bahuvrīhi* compound is obtained due to the proximity of the two words. And that being the case, the elision has an *ārdhadhātuka* suffix as its cause. For if the term *dhātu* were absent, and it were merely stated, "there is no elision before an *ārdhadhātuka*," then the prohibition would apply only to those *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* substitutions that are dependent upon an *ārdhadhātuka* suffix.

Regarding the word *roravīti*: from the root *ru* meaning "to sound" (*dhātupāṭha* 1034), there is the suffix *yaṅ*; by [Pāṇini 7.4.78], there is the elision (*luk*) of *yaṅ*; then the suffixes *laṭ*, *tip*, and *śap*.
Due to its inclusion in the *adādi* class, there is the elision of *śap* by [Pāṇini 2.4.72]; and by [Pāṇini 7.3.94], the augment *iṭ* is optionally applied.

The *guṇa* substitution caused by a sārvadhātuka suffix is not prohibited here. But is this not deficient in two respects? Just as the *guṇa* caused by an ārdhadhātuka suffix does not occur, so too should the elision (*lopa*) not occur. This is not so; for when the term "ārdhadhātuka" is present [in the rule], since it functions as the external referent (*anyapadārtha*) of the compound, its application is not resorted to [for the elision], and thus the elision caused by that [suffix] is obtained. And if that were the case, while the rule "na dhātulope" (P. 1.1.4) were stated merely as such, the meaning of the sentence would be: "Whichever *guṇa* or *vṛddhi* occurs, they both take place when there is elision."
And because [the term] is not further specified, the prohibition is understood to apply to every instance of *lopa* (elision). For example, in the form *abhāji*:

the root *bhañj* (Dhātupāṭha 1453) meaning "to break," followed by the suffix *luṅ*, then *cli* (by Pāṇini 3.1.43), which becomes *ciṇ* (by 3.1.66); then the elision of the *ta*-suffix by *iṇo luk* (6.4.104); and finally the elision of the nasal by *anunāsikalopaḥ* (6.4.33).
Regarding the word "rāga":
here too, there is the elision of the *n* [of the suffix] according to Pāṇini 6.4.27.
The root is "rañj" in the sense of "coloring" (Dhātupāṭha 1167); the suffix *ghañ* is applied in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāva*).

Although there is a *ru* vowel here, nevertheless, because the term *ika* is carried over [from the previous rule] and because an *ik* vowel is impossible in this context, the prohibition does not apply to the *vṛddhi* that would otherwise be required by [Pāṇini 7.2.116].
Thus we have *knopayati*.

[The root] *knūyī* [meaning] "to sound" (Dhātupāṭha 485) takes *ṇic* by [Pāṇini 3.1.26], and the *guṇa* substitution occurs by [Pāṇini 7.3.36, which applies to roots] beginning with *arti*, *hi*, and *ī*.
Regarding the word *preddham*:

from the root *ñīndhī* in the sense of "to shine" (Dhātupāṭha 1448), the suffix *kta* is applied; by the rule *aniditām* [Pāṇini 6.4.24], there is the elision of the nasal; and by the rule *jhaṣastathordho'dhaḥ* [Pāṇini 8.2.40], the letter *t* is changed to *dh*.

By [Pāṇini 8.4.53], the *dh* of the verbal root becomes *d*; and by [Pāṇini 2.2.18], the compound *pragatamiddham* is formed. If the rule *kṅiti* were a locative of reference (*parasaptamī*), then the prohibition would apply only to the immediately preceding *ik*, such that it would not apply to separated instances like *citaḥ* and *citavat*, nor to cases like *bhinnaḥ* and *bhinnavāt*, because in [Pāṇini 1.1.66] the mention of the term *nirdiṣṭa* (specified) serves the purpose of indicating immediate proximity.

Thinking that this [term] must apply everywhere when it is a locative of cause (*nimitta-saptamī*), because the relationship between cause and effect exists even when [the terms] are separated, he says: "This is a locative of cause.
A locative [case] due to a cause is a "locative of cause" (*nimitta-saptamī*).
This compound is formed by the division of the rule (*yogavibhāga*) "the fifth case" (*pañcamī*) [in Pāṇini 2.1.37].
Furthermore, that seventh case [locative] is to be understood by the rule *yasya ca bhāvena bhāvalakṣaṇam* (Pāṇini 2.3.37).
For, by the status of being a cause (*nimittabhāva*), the occurrence characterized by the application of *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* is indicated.

Now, even if this is a locative of cause (*nimittasaptamī*), why is a prohibition obtained for something separated [from the cause]? Because the technical rule (*paribhāṣā*) beginning with *tatra tasmin* (Pāṇini 1.1.65) does not apply there.

[[1.1.5]] Thus, because this *ik-paribhāṣā* would also apply due to its being [a rule] requiring attention (*ādara*), there would be no designation of *vṛddhi* in forms such as *śālīyaḥ* and *mālīyaḥ*.

Just as this *ik-paribhāṣā* applies only within the context of a specific injunction (*vidhi*) because it serves as a subordinate element (*aṅgaśeṣa*) to that injunction, so too does this *ānantarya-paribhāṣā*.
Furthermore, in this case, *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* are not being enjoined; rather, even though they have been enjoined elsewhere, they are here specifically qualified by the condition *kṅiti*.
Therefore, since that technical rule (paribhāṣā) does not apply here, the prohibition is established even for what is immediately preceding.
[The phrase] "those two which are *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* caused by *k* or *ṅ*" means: those two whose cause is *k* or *ṅ*.

Furthermore, those [operations] which occur when *k* or *ṅit* is present are to be understood as qualified by *kṅit*. By this, he shows that the mention of *kṅit* is a qualifier of *guṇa* and *vṛddhi*.

Now, one might object: since it is the primary element by virtue of being that which is prescribed (*vidhīyamāna*), it would be more logical for this to be a qualifier of the prohibition (*pratiṣedha*) itself? This is not so; for where a quality (*guṇa*), having undergone its own refinement (*saṃskāra*), is capable of providing great assistance to the primary element, it undergoes its own refinement in order to provide greater assistance to that primary element, and thereby enters into a relationship with the primary element.
As it has been said: "A quality, having undergone its own refinement, serves the principal; for in this way it exists for the benefit of the principal."

Thus [ends the previous discussion]. Here, however, by qualifying *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* through the mention of *kṅit*, a great benefit is rendered to the primary prohibition (*pratiṣedha*), since that [prohibition] is established even for [roots] separated [from the suffixes].

Regarding the form *bhinnaḥ*: from the root *bhidir vidāraṇe* (Dhātupāṭha 1439), the suffix *kta* is added; then, by the rule *radābhyāṃ niṣṭhātonaḥ* (Pāṇini 8.2.42), the substitution of *na* occurs for the final letter of the *niṣṭhā* suffix.
Regarding the word *mṛṣṭaḥ*:

by the rule *vraśca* [Pāṇini 8.2.36] and others, the letter *j* of the root *mṛj* becomes *ṣ*; then, by the rule *ādeśapratyayayoḥ* [8.3.59], the *ṣ* becomes *ṣṭ*. However, in forms such as *cinute*, by the rule *kṅiti ca* [1.1.5], the suffixes are designated as *kṅit*.
In the case of *cinvanti*, the substitution of *yaṇ* occurs by [Pāṇini 6.4.87] *huśnuvoḥ sārvadhātuke*.

Here, in these examples—*citaḥ*, *citavān*, *stutaḥ*, *stutavān*, *cinataḥ*, *cinvanti*—there is, as appropriate, a prohibition of the *guṇa* substitution conditioned by either a *sārvadhātuka* or an *ārdhadhātuka* suffix; in *bhinnaḥ*, *bhinnavān*, there is a prohibition of the *guṇa* conditioned by a light penultimate vowel (*laghūpadha*); and in the remaining cases, there is a prohibition of the *vṛddhi* substitution [conditioned by the suffix *kta*] according to [Pāṇini 7.2.114].

Regarding the rule *glājisthaśca ksnuḥ*: if this suffix *ksnu* were *kit*, then in the word *sthāsnus*, the substitution of *ī* for the final vowel of the root *sthā* (by means of the rule *ghumāsthāgāpājahātisām aṭi kṅiti* [Pāṇini 6.4.66]) would occur. Therefore, to avoid that result, it is asserted that *ksnu* possesses the property of being *git*.
For it will be stated there: "This suffix [sn] is *git*, not *kit*. Therefore, the substitution of *ī* for [the final vowel of] *sthā* does not occur" (Kāśikā 2.41).
And since it is *git*, the prohibition stated in [Pāṇini 1.1.5], "before *k* and *ṅ*," which would apply in forms such as *bhūṣṇuḥ* and *jiṣṇuḥ*, does not take effect.

Therefore, in order to avoid this fault, he says: "The letter *ga* also occurs here," and so forth (*kārikā* 241). The meaning is that it has undergone *cartva* (the substitution of *ca* for *ja*). This *cartva* is prescribed by the rule *khari ca* [Pāṇini 8.4.54].

For if the *gittva* (the status of having an indicatory *g*) of the suffix *ksnu* were intended, then in the word *bhūṣṇu*, the prohibition regarding a *kit* suffix stated in *śrayukaḥ kiti* [Pāṇini 7.2.11] would not apply. This is not a fault; for even in that case, the letter *ga* which has undergone *cartva* is what is indicated.

For instance, in Jayāditya’s commentary (*vṛtti*) on [Pāṇini 3.2.139], there is this passage: "In [the rule] 1.1.5, the letter *g* is indicated as having become a *catur* (a substitute for *ca*), and therefore the *guṇa* substitution does not occur.
Likewise, in [the rule] 7.2.11 (*śrayukaḥ kiti*), the letter *g* is also indicated; therefore, the augment *iṭ* does not occur after the root *bhū*.
(Kāśikā 241).

Regarding the rule *śrayukaḥ kiti* [Pāṇini 7.2.11], there is a passage in Jayāditya’s commentary (*vṛtti*) stating: "The letter *g* is also indicated here as being included within the *cat* (the *caturthī* case ending), so that [the form] *bhūṣṇuḥ* may be produced. However, Vāmana does not accept all of this. For instance, in the commentary composed by him on that very same sūtra, he writes: "Some explain the inclusion of the letter *g* through the indication of two *k*s here, so that [the form] *bhūṣṇuḥ* may indeed be produced."

Furthermore, because this is a scriptural instruction (*sautratvāt*), in the rule *śrayukaḥ kiti* (Pāṇini 7.2.11), the substitution of *u* for *ru* was not applied—presumably because the substitution of *c* for *t* was considered asiddha—and instead the *visarjanīya* was applied.

[In response, it is argued: "In the rule [3.2.139], by the elision of the vowel *ā* in *sthā-ā*, the form *sthāsnu-* is established; therefore, this [objection] is of no consequence" (Kāśikā 802). He thinks as follows: if the suffix *ksnu* were marked with *k* (*kit*), then the substitution of *ī* for the root *sthā* would apply; thus, to avoid that, it is appropriate to declare it as marked with *g* (*git*).

Furthermore, in the case of *jiṣṇuḥ* and *bhūṣṇuḥ*, the letter *ga*—which has undergone the change to *ca* (i.e., *c*)—is specified in the rules [Pāṇini 1.1.5] and [Pāṇini 7.2.11] (*śrayukaḥ kiti*) for the purpose of excluding the augment *iṭ* and the *guṇa* substitution as appropriate; thus, its mention would be meaningful. However, the suffix *ksnu* is not *git*; rather, it is simply *kit*.

Therefore, what is the point of specifying the letter *ga* (as *ca*) for the sake of prohibiting *iṭ* and *guṇa*? Moreover, even if *ksnu* were *kit*, the substitution of *ā* for the root *sthā* would still apply.

Therefore, in the rule *glājisthaśāca ksnuḥ* [Pāṇini 3.2.139], the vowel *ā* is elided [as a *praśleṣa*] so that, for the root *tiṣṭhati* ending in the suffix *ksnu*, only the vowel *ā* may occur, and whatever else might otherwise result shall not; this is the purpose. Consequently, since the word *sthāsnu* is already established by that very rule, the description here of the elision of the letter *g* (in *stheśabhāsa...* [Pāṇini 3.2.175]) is of no consequence. [The example] is "kāmayate."
Regarding the rule *kamerṇiṅ* [Pāṇini 3.1.30], the prohibition of *vṛddhi* [by Pāṇini 7.2.116] does not apply here;
thus we have *laigavāyanaḥ*.

When the suffix *phak* is applied to the word *liṅgu* by [Pāṇini 4.1.97] *naḍādibhyaḥ phak*, the prohibition of *guṇa* substitution [by Pāṇini 1.1.5] does not occur [before the *phak*]. Now, one might object: "Since this is already covered by the rule concerning *ukāra* vowels, this counter-example is inappropriate. This is not so; for here the letter *ca* is employed for the purpose of drawing back (*anukarṣaṇa*) the term *ikaḥ*. In that case, due to the force of being drawn back by the letter *ca*, the term *ikaḥ* abandons its status as a meaning-based referent (*arthapadārthatā*) and assumes the status of a formal referent (*svarūpapadārthatā*).

Otherwise, if the word *artha* were being drawn forward by the particle *ca*, it would refer only to its own meaning as a word-meaning (*padārtha*). In that case, the employment of *ca* for the purpose of drawing it forward would be redundant, since the recurrence of the word-meaning *artha* would already be established by its being marked with the *svarita* accent. However, when that [word *artha*] has its own form (*svarūpa*) as its meaning and is present here, the sense becomes this: "Those *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* operations which are prescribed by means of the term *ika*—that is, those *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* operations which are prescribed after uttering the word *ika*—do not take place when *k* or *ṅit* suffixes are the cause."

Furthermore, in the case of *laiṅgavāyanaḥ*, the guṇa substitution is not prescribed by explicitly uttering the word "ikaḥ" (as in Pāṇini 1.1.3); for the technical rule (*paribhāṣā*) regarding "ik" does not apply there. Its non-application is due to the fact that the substituendum (*sthānin*) is directly specified as the vowel *u*. Indeed, that rule applies only where the substituendum is not directly specified.

[Objection: But if the word *svarūpa* (the word-form itself) is present here by virtue of the word *ika*, then the locus (*sthānin*) would not be specified; consequently, it would not be known for what the prohibition of *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* applies. [Response: This is not a fault.

By the force of the context (*sāmarthya*), this prohibition of *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* is understood to apply to *ika* alone. For *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* are not prescribed after having uttered this word *ika*.

Alternatively, although the *ik-paribhāṣā* is a subsidiary element of the rule (*vidhyaṅga*), nevertheless, even though there is no actual prescription of *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* here, it is brought to mind by being referred to through the particle *ca*.
Indeed, this is precisely the purpose of employing the particle *ca*: namely, to bring the *ik-paribhāṣā* into proximity.
Consequently, since that [paribhāṣā] is present, this prohibition is understood to apply only in those cases where it (the paribhāṣā) is operative.
And where does this [paribhāṣā] operate? Where the original element (*sthānin*) is not explicitly mentioned.
But here the original element *is* mentioned; therefore, because the paribhāṣā regarding the letter *i* has no application, this serves as a counter-example.
"Of *mṛj*" and so forth.
But how is that [vṛddhi] obtained even when it is desired? Listen to how it is obtained:

in the rule *aco ñṇiti* (Pāṇini 7.2.115), the word *vṛddhiḥ* from [7.2.114] is understood to carry over; furthermore, the mention of *anyatarasyām* from [7.2.101] also carries over by way of the "frog-leap" maxim (*maṇḍūkapluti*), and that is a restricted option (*vyavasthitavibhāṣā*).
Then, a separation of the rule (*yogavibhāga*) is made for the word *acaḥ*.

In the case of the root *mṛj*, when followed by a suffix beginning with a vowel other than *a*, the substitution of *vṛddhi* is optional; otherwise, it does not occur at all. [The statement] "here there is also a prohibition of the *guṇa* substitution for a light penultimate vowel" indicates that this is a point of transition (*saṃkrama*). Others, however, explain that this passage should have occurred immediately after the subsequent sūtra containing the examples "kaṇitā āḥ" and "raṇitā āḥ," but it was written here by scribes who were confused by a misplaced *kāku* intonation.
Alternatively, it should be understood that this result is shown by means of the locative case in the sense of cause (*nimitta-saptamī*).
In the forms *acinavam* and *asanuvam*, because the suffix *laṅ* is marked with the *ṅ*-sign (*ṅit*), the substitute for it—namely *mip*—is also *ṅit*.

By the principle of *sthānivadbhāva*, since *mip* is *ṅit*, its substitute *am* is also *ṅit* as before; consequently, the prohibition of *guṇa* for the *vikaraṇa* (the augment *nu*) would follow based on that *ṅit* status.
He asks, "Why does it not occur? and replies with "I have done" (*acinavam*), etc.
By the word "etc. (*ādi*), forms such as "I have made" (*akaravam*) are included. [The phrase] "of the *lakāra*" refers to...
The substitute for *lakāra* is also called *lakāra* by way of metaphorical designation (*upacāra*), because it is preceded by *lakāra* through a traditional lineage.

Even though this [metaphorical] acceptance is granted, the fact that the augment *śit* was added to the substitute *śānac* in the rule *sati ca* (Pāṇini 3.1.83) indicates that the status of being "as if the original" (*sthānivadbhāva*) does not necessarily apply to operations concerning *anubandhas*.
This is the conclusion reached; hence the statement beginning with "the mention of *ṅit*-ness," and so forth.

If an operation prescribed for a *ṅit* [affix] were to apply to the *lakāra* when it is *ṅit*, then since the prohibition of *guṇa* would already be established by the *ṅit*-ness of the *liṅ* itself in forms such as *cinuyāt*, the author would not have made the *ṅit*-doubling (*ṅdvicana*) of that *yāsuṭ* [augment] in the rule *liṅaśiśyośca* (Pāṇini 3.4.103). Yet, he has done so; therefore, it is understood that "an operation prescribed for a *ṅit* does not apply to the *lakāra*. Regarding the rule *dīdhīvevyoḥ*:
this is the mention of these two roots—*dīdhīṅ* in the sense of "shining" and "playing" (Dhātupāṭha 1076), and *vevīṅ* in the sense of "equal to *veti*" (Dhātupāṭha 1077).

But why is it not understood that the inclusion here refers to these [other] roots: *dīṅ* in the sense of "decay" (DhP 1134), *dhīṅ* in the sense of "disregard" (DhP 1136), *veñ* in the sense of "weaving" (DhP 1006), and *vī* in the senses of "motion," "procreation," "beauty," "throwing," and "eating" (DhP 1048)? If the inclusion of these were intended, one would have made the formulation *vī-ve-dhī-dīṭām* for the sake of avoiding ambiguity.
However, it has been formulated otherwise.
Therefore, only the two previously mentioned roots are included here.

Regarding the term *iṭaḥ*: this refers to that which is prescribed by the rule *ārdhadhātukasya* [Pāṇini 7.2.35] and others. Now, why is there no inclusion of the root *iṭ* (as in *iṭ, kiṭ, kaṭī gatau*, Dhātupāṭha 318, 319, 320)? This would indeed be appropriate, given its association with other roots (*dhātusāhacarya*). This is not the case; for here, although the rule *alpāctaram* [Pāṇini 2.2.34] requires that *iṭ* be placed first, the author instead places it later, thereby indicating: "One should understand that there is some other reversal [of the expected order] here as well."

Therefore, since the mention of "element" (*dhātu*) would have applied by association with the term "element," it is understood that the mention refers specifically to its opposite, namely "tradition" (*āgama*).
[The word] "ādīdhyana" is formed with the suffix *lyuṭ*.

Regarding the word *ādīdhyakaḥ*: [it is formed] with the suffix *ṇvul*. Regarding the forms *kaṇitā āḥ* and *raṇitā āḥ*: in the section of verbal roots (*dhātupāṭha*) whose meaning is "sound," beginning with *aṇa raṇa kaṇa* (DhP 444, 445, 449), the roots *kaṇi* and *raṇi* are recited. From these two, when the suffix *luṭ* follows, the affix *tās* is applied by the rule *syatāsī lṛluṭoḥ* [3.1.33]. Then, by the rule *luṭaḥ prathamasya* [2.4.85], etc., the replacement of *ti* by *ḍā* occurs; there is the elision of the *ṭi* (the final vowel and following consonant); and the augment *iṭ* is added by the rule *ārdhadhātukasya* [7.2.35], and so forth.
He explains why an example of *vṛddhi* for *iṭ* has not been shown: "Vṛddhi is not possible for *iṭ*.

Vṛddhi is prescribed for a stem (*aṅga*) when a suffix beginning with *ñ* or *ṇ* follows, and this *iṭ* belongs to the *ārdhadhātuka* [suffixes]. Furthermore, the designation "stem" (*aṅga-sañjñā*) does not apply to an *ārdhadhātuka* [element] when it occurs before a suffix beginning with *ñ* or *ṇ*.

Therefore, *vṛddhi* does not occur after *i*. "Interval" (*antara*) means a gap, a fissure, an opening, or a period devoid of phonemes; that which has no such interval is described as such. Regarding the phrase "by those of different classes," and so forth: *antaraṃ* = *chidraṃ* = *vivaraṃ* = a period devoid of phonemes (*varṇaśūnyaḥ kālaḥ*). Those for whom no such interval exists are called "those [without interval]. "By those of different classes," etc.
The expression "by those of different classes" is used because in the world it is observed that only those of different classes act as separators.

For instance, when someone is asked by another, "Is there anyone in the next house over in the Brāhmaṇa family?", he replies, "There is none in the next house; a Vṛṣala family resides between these two."

If there were a designation (*sañjñā*) for each individual consonant (*hal*) when pronounced in conjunction—as in *nirvāyāt* and *niryāyāt*, where the substitution of *e* would occur by [Pāṇini 6.4.68] *vānyasya saṃyogādeḥ*; or in *saṃskṛṣīṣṭa*, where the augment *iṭ* would occur by [7.2.43]; or in *saṃskriyate*, where *guṇa* substitution would occur by [7.4.29]—many such other defects as these have been individually pointed out in the Bhāṣya regarding the status of each consonant as a designatum.

Even if those [objections] have been somehow removed with effort in that very context, nevertheless, the fault of excessive complexity (*pratipatti-gaurava*) incurred in the process of understanding the object to be established by means of such avoidance remains unavoidable.
However, there is not even a suspicion of such a fault when the name-bearer (*sañjñin*) is the aggregate (*samudāya*).
Therefore, having reflected that the aggregate alone is the appropriate name-bearer, he says: "The aggregate is the name-bearer."

But surely, effort is undertaken only where one desires an effect for those things that coexist with that effort; for example, [in the rule] *ubhe* is mentioned [at Pāṇini 6.1.5], yet no such effort has been made here. So how can the designation (*saṃjñā*) be obtained for the collective whole? There is no fault here, for effort has indeed been made even in this case: namely, the formulation of a long designation. For it is said, "The formulation of a designation is for the sake of brevity" (*Vyāḍīya-paribhāṣā* 135); thus, the formulation of a long designation cannot be conceived of unless there is a specific purpose.
Therefore, it should be understood that the designation "mahatī" was applied here in order to indicate that the one possessing the designation is great;
as it has been said: "The intention of the teachers is perceived through a gesture, a glance, or by means of an extensive composition of aphorisms.
And in this way, the one possessing the designation becomes "great" only if the entire aggregate is the possessor of the designation, not each individual *hal*.

Therefore, this is appropriate: that the "collection" (samudāya) is the named entity. To one who might object that the designation [of *saṃyoga*] for two [consonants] is not established because of the use of the plural form in the rule "halo" (*halaḥ*), he says: "And with respect to the genus," and so forth.
The word "and" (*ca*) has the sense of "because.
Because the plural is used with respect to the genus (*jāti*), the designation of *saṃyoga* is thereby established for both two and many [consonants].

The examples for the forms beginning with *agni* should be understood from the rule *tilān srāvapati* (Pāṇini 8.3.26), where the option (*vā*) is in force; and from the rule [8.3.29], where *dhuṭ* is in force, as well as from *naśca* (8.3.30), which optionally introduces *dhuṭ*, and *khari ca* (8.4.54), which changes it to *t*.
In that context, when *dhuṭ* is not present, the form is *nasatayoḥ*.

But when it exists, there are the forms *natasatarayaḥ* and *titaucchatram*. The form [of *titaucchatram*] is derived by applying the suffix *ḍau* according to Pāṇini 6.1.160 (*tanoterḍauḥ sanvacca*), which results in the elision of the *ṭi* (the penultimate vowel) and reduplication.

"There would be elision of the final consonant of a conjunct" (Pāṇini 8.2.23). This is the intention: that if there were a technical designation (*saṃjñā*) of the vowel *a* by the vowel *u* here [in the term *ukāra*], then [the *a*] would be dropped.
Furthermore, one should not suspect the teaching of the vowel *u* (*ukāra-upadeśa*) to be purposeless once the elision has occurred.

Where the designation *pada* does not exist—as in *titaunī* and so forth—it is because [the *saṃyoga*] is heard [there]. "Pacati" is the counter-example for the form (*rūpa*), while "panasam" is the counter-example for the grammatical operation (*kārya*), based on the thought that "the elision [prescribed by] *skoḥ saṃyogādyor* would apply. The sense is that if the designation *saṃyoga* were to apply even to the *s* and *n* when they are separated by an intervening vowel. By the statement "the nose together with the mouth is *mukhanāsikā*," he shows that this word *mukhanāsikā* is a *tatpuruṣa* compound, not a *dvandva*.
The *tatpuruṣa* compound, however, is to be understood as belonging to the class beginning with *mayūravyaṃsaka*.

For if it were a *dvandva* consisting of "mouth and nose," there would be singularization (*ekavadbhāva*) by the rule *prāṇitūryasenānām* [Pāṇini 2.4.2]. Consequently, there would be neuter gender by the rule *sa napuṃsakam* [Pāṇini 2.4.17].
And that being the case, the shortening of the final vowel of the nominal stem would result by the rule *hrasvo napuṃsake prātipadikasya* [Pāṇini 1.2.47]; such is the intended meaning.

Now, an objection is raised: since the suffix *lyuṭ* has been applied in the sense of an instrument (*karaṇa*) in the word *anayā*, the feminine suffix *ṅīp* ought to follow that ending by the rule *ṭiḍḍhāṇañ* [Pāṇini 4.1.15]. Consequently, when a *bahuvrīhi* compound is formed with that ending, the designation "that which is articulated through the mouth and nose" (*mukhanāsikāvacanaḥ*) would be untenable. This is not so; for this word *vacana*—by virtue of the frequentative statement (*bahulavacanāt*) in [Pāṇini 3.3.113]—is derived as an object (*karmasādhana*). Thus, *vacana* refers to a phoneme (*varṇa*) in the sense of "that which is articulated" (*ucyate*), and not to the nose. For this very reason, he says: "that which is articulated by means of it. In the word "articulated" (*uccāryate*), the verbal suffix (*lakāra*) denotes the passive (*karman*).
Having understood it thus, this compound *mukhanāsikāvacanaḥ* should be known as a genitive (*ṣaṣṭhī*) compound, not a possessive (*bahuvrīhi*) one.

Regarding the phrase *anusvāryaiva*: when the *anusvāra* is being uttered, the operation belongs to the nose and not to the mouth; therefore, [the designation] would apply only to that [anusvāra], but not to *ñ, ma, ṅ, ṇ, n*, nor even to the half-moon-shaped (*ardhacandrākṛti*) phoneme in [the mantra] *abhra ā~ apaḥ* (Ṛgveda 5.48.1), because the mouth also participates in its utterance.

The intention is that when this operation prescribed by [Pāṇini 8.4.45] is to be performed, there would be the inclusion of the *anusvāra* alone, and not of the *ṅ*-class sounds (*ṅ*, *ñ*, *ṇ*, *n*, *m*) and so forth.

But surely, according to the maxim of "the inhabitants of the palace" (*prāsādavāsinyāya*), they too will be included? Just as when it is said, "Let the inhabitants of the palace be brought," those who reside in the palace itself are included, as well as those who reside both in the palace and on the ground.

Just as [vowels] are brought in without fear [of over-extension], so here too, if only "uttered by the nose" (*nāsikāvacana*) were stated, there would be the inclusion of the *anusvāra*—which is uttered by the nose—as well as the *ṅ*-class sounds (*ṅ*, *ñ*, *ṇ*, *n*, *m*), which are uttered by both the mouth and the nose; consequently, the statement that [the rule] would apply to the *anusvāra* is incorrect.

If one were to say this, would it not follow that the same should apply to the *anusvāra* as well? This is not so; for in this case, three views are possible: (1) one view is that "the nasalized phoneme (*anunāsika*) is entirely produced by both the nose and the mouth"; (2) [another view is that] "its first part is produced by the mouth";

and (3) the third [view is that] "it colors both of the immediately preceding parts—those produced by the nose and those produced by the mouth—in such a way that even those parts appear as if they were produced by the nose.
Of these two immediately preceding views, one or the other is intended by Pāṇini.
And this "prāsādavāsinyāya" (the logic of the palace-dweller) does not apply here in any respect.

For if the sounds such as *ṅ* were to be pronounced entirely through the nose and also through the mouth, then by the logic of the palace-dweller, if it were merely stated that they are "pronounced by the nose," their inclusion [in the category of nasal consonants] would follow.
But this is not the case for the [nasal stops], because they are pronounced only partially through the nose and the mouth.

In that case, if the mention of the "mouth" (*mukha*) were not made, there would be no inclusion of those [sounds]; and in their absence, the designation (*saṃjñā*) would not apply. Thus it was rightly said: "For it would apply only to the *anusvāra*," and "lest it apply to *ka*, *ca*, *ṭa*, *ta*, and *pa*. For these sounds, beginning with *ka*, are articulated by the mouth alone and not by the nose; therefore, if the mention of the "nose" (*nāsikā*) were not made, it would apply to those [nasal sounds] alone.

And thus, in the cases of *śaktaḥ* and *suptam*, there would result the elision [of the nasal] by the rule beginning with *anudāttopadeśavanatitanotyādīnām* (Pāṇini 6.4.37), while in the case of *odanapak*, there would be lengthening by the rule *ato dīrgho yañi* (Pāṇini 7.3.101). Now, for what purpose is this extensive technical term (*sañjñā*) formulated? It refers to that in which the nose functions subsequently (*anu*), or alternatively, that which functions subsequently to the nose; or else, that which functions after the nose. Since the mouth is the subject under discussion, it is understood to refer to that very [mouth].
Regarding those two views, of which Pāṇini accepts one or the other: in the former, the nose functions after the mouth; in the latter, the mouth [functions] before the nose.
The assignment of these names according to their literal meaning (anvartha-sañjñā) is for the purpose of indicating the acceptance of one or the other of the two views previously mentioned.

The indication of that acceptance, however, is for the purpose of refuting those who might object to the inclusion of the word "mouth" (*mukha*) by resorting to the maxim of "the one living in the palace" (*prāsādavāsinyāya*). The word *tulya* is derived by forming the suffix *yat* according to the rule *nau-vayo-dharma-* [Pāṇini 4.4.91], based on the etymology "that which is measured by a balance is equal" (*tulayā sammitaṃ tulyam*).

Now, since it is impossible for effort (*prayatna*) to be measured by a balance, one might raise the objection that this is an impossible qualification (*asambhavadviśeṣaṇa*). To such an objector, he replies with the words "the word *tulya*" and so forth.

He thinks as follows: "The word *tulya* is used solely for the sake of etymological derivation (*vyutpatti*), but here there is no sense of 'weighing on a scale' (*tulā-artha*), nor is there the sense of 'measured by a scale' (*asammita-artha*).
This word *tulya* is a synonym for *sadṛśa* (similar). For instance, when 'tulya' is said, it becomes a synonym for 'sadṛśa', but not for 'measured by a scale'."

This word *āsya* also ends in the suffix *ṇyat*. It is derived from the root *as* (in the sense of "to throw" or "to cast") with the suffix *ṇyat* in the instrumental sense (*karaṇe*) according to [Pāṇini 3.3.113]: "that by which food is thrown or cast.
Thus, *āsya* means "the mouth."
Furthermore, that [region] extends from the lips up to the *kākalaka*.

The *kākalaka* is the elevated portion on the neck, which in common parlance is called the "throat-jewel" (*kaṇṭhamaṇi*). There is also a derivative form of the word *āsya*: when the suffix *yat* is applied according to Pāṇini 4.3.55 (*tatra bhavaḥ*), the vowel *a* is elided according to 6.4.148, and the *y* is elided according to 8.4.64, resulting in the form *āsyam*.
And this [term *āsya*] denotes the palate and other organs situated within the mouth.

In that regard, if this were the inclusion of the previous word *āsya*, then the designation *savarṇa* (homogeneous) would apply even to *ka, ca, ṭa, ta, pa*, because they are equal in their meaning as denoted by the word *āsya* ending in the suffix *ṇyat*, which refers to the locus of effort.

Having seen this fault in taking the word *āsya* as ending in a *taddhita* suffix, he says—showing that this is the inclusion of the word *āsya* ending in a *taddhita* suffix—"that which exists in the mouth (*āsye bhavam*) is *āsya*."

What, then, is that? He says: "the place of articulation such as the palate," etc. That in which the phonemes are produced is the "place" (*sthāna*). By the word "etc. (*ādi*), the nose and other organs are included.

But is it not the case that the nose, having its function outside the mouth, does not constitute the "mouth" (*āsya*)? This is not so; for it is not the nose situated outside the mouth that is intended here, since phonemes are not produced therein. What then? There is a membrane stretched within the mouth, like the skin of a drum (*paṇava*); the line connected to it, which, when struck by the breath, produces the phonemes—that is what is intended here as the "nose. How, then, is it known that this is the reference to the word *āsya* ending in a secondary derivative (*taddhita*) suffix? It is because of the similarity with the term *āsya*.
If there were a reference to that which does not end in a *taddhita* suffix, then the mention of "mouth" (*āsya*) would be purposeless;

for in all cases, the effort [of articulation] is equal when the meaning expressed by the suffix itself is intended. Indeed, there is no such thing [to be excluded] for the sake of which the mention of "mouth" would be necessary.

Now, one might argue that whether the *visarjanīya* possesses a homogeneous counterpart (*savarṇa*) or not, there is a purpose [for the rule], nor is there any fault. [This is addressed by the phrase: "contact and so forth" (*spṛṣṭatādi*).
By the word "etc. (*ādi*), [the qualities] such as slight contact (*īṣatspṛṣṭatā*) and so forth are included.

"'A quality of the phoneme' (*varṇaguṇaḥ*)" means a property (*dharma*) of the phonemes (*varṇa*), such as *a* and the others. "'That which has an equal effort in the oral cavity' (*tulya āsye prayatno yasya*)"—[this is the definition of a homogeneous phoneme].

By this, he shows that the word *tulyāsyaprayatna* is a three-membered *bahuvrīhi*. A *bahuvrīhi* certainly occurs even when its members have different grammatical referents (*vyadhikaraṇa*), provided they convey the intended meaning; for example: *kaṇṭhekālaḥ* ("the one who has Kāla [Śiva] on his neck") and *urasilomā* ("the one who has hair on his chest"). Now, why is it not accepted as a *bahuvrīhi* containing a *dvandva*—that is, "that whose *āsya* and *prayatna* are equal" (where *āsya* and *prayatna* form a *dvandva* compound)? He thinks thus: if a *bahuvrīhi* containing a *dvandva* were accepted, the effort (*prayatna*) would not be qualified by the place of articulation (*sthāna*), such as the palate (*tālu*).
Consequently, there would be no designation of mutual homogeneity (*savarṇasañjñā*) between the letters *ka* and *ṅa*, because their external effort (*bāhyaprayatna*) is different.
The external effort of *ka* consists of the throat being wide open (*vivṛtakaṇṭhatva*) and so forth; that of *ṅa* consists of the throat being closed (*saṃvṛtakaṇṭhatva*) and so forth.

And if the designation *savarṇa* (homogeneous) were non-existent, the letter *ṅ* would not occur in the word *śaṅkitā* [by Pāṇini 8.4.58]. Now, even if there is a difference in their external effort (*bāhya-prayatna*), their internal effort called "contact" (*spṛṣṭatā*) is the same for these two; by relying on that, will the designation *savarṇa* come to be? If this were so, then even though there is a difference between the internal efforts of *ś* and *c*—namely, being "open" (*vivṛta*) and "contacted" (*aspṛṣṭa*) respectively—the designation *savarṇa* would still apply based on the common external effort they share, such as being produced with the throat open (*vivṛtakaṇṭhatva*).

Consequently, the counter-example to be cited later, "aruścyotati," would not be appropriate. Now, in the case of a three-word *bahuvrīhi* compound, the effort (*prayatna*) is qualified by the place of articulation, such as the palate (*tālu*).
Therefore, setting aside external effort, only internal qualities such as contact (*spṛṣṭatā*) and so forth are grasped.
For that alone is possible within the mouth at the palate and other locations, and nothing else.

When internal effort (*ābhyantara-prayatna*) is taken into account, even though there is a difference in external effort (*bāhya-prayatna*), the *k* and *ṅ* sounds still receive the designation of being homogeneous (*savarṇa-sañjñā*), because their internal effort is identical and it is precisely that [internal effort] which is intended here. Nor does it follow that the *c* and *ś* sounds would incur the designation of being homogeneous simply because their external effort is identical; for that [external effort] is not what is intended here, and that which is intended here is not the same [in both cases]. Therefore, it is proper to rely on a three-word *bahuvrīhi* compound; it is not a *dvandva*-embedded compound.

If, then, a three-membered *bahuvrīhi* compound is resorted to, [one might object that] because of the difference in case endings and because of its lack of predominance, this [place] would not be specified as being equal; consequently, the designation of *savarṇa* (homogeneous) would apply even to those located in different places. This is not a fault.
For when a locus is presented in relation to something to be contained (*ādheya*), it is understood to be equal to that very thing which is contained.
To illustrate: when it is said, "The meal of Devadatta and Yajñadatta is equal in a bronze vessel," it is understood that the bronze vessel is also equal for them both.

Since this meaning—that "whatever [sound] has the same place of articulation and effort (tulyāsyaprayatna) in relation to another, it receives the designation *savarṇa* (homogeneous) with respect to that one alone"—is not obtained from the explicit statement here, there arises the following objection: "In that case, whatever sound has the same place of articulation and effort in relation to a certain sound, it would also receive the designation *savarṇa* in relation to something else. Anticipating this objection, he says: "in relation to one of the same class" (*samānajātīyaṃ prati*).

This means that whatever sound has the same place of articulation and effort in relation to a specific sound of the same class, it receives the designation *savarṇa* in relation to that one, and not in relation to anything else.

And this is obtained because the words *tulyāsyaprayatna* and *savarṇa* are relative terms. For a relative term, even without the explicit mention of its correlative, necessarily brings that correlative to mind through proximity to another word, just as in the expression "one must serve one's father," it is not explicitly stated "in oneself," yet this is understood from the relationship itself: "he who is the father of someone."
The same applies here as well.

Although it is not explicitly stated that "whatever has the same place of articulation (*tulyāsyaprayatna*) as another is designated as homogeneous (*savarṇa*) with respect to it," nevertheless, by virtue of the connection, it is understood that what has the same place of articulation and effort is designated as homogeneous only with respect to that which belongs to the same class.
Alternatively, *savarṇa* means "having the same color" (*samāno varṇaḥ*), and this is a designation based on its etymological meaning (*anvarthasañjñā*).
Therefore, the designation *savarṇa* (homogeneous) applies only with respect to that which is of the same class (*tulyajātīya*).

For in this way, its *varṇa* (phonetic quality) is the same, provided that the designation *savarṇa* applies only with respect to that very [same class], and not with respect to a different class (*vijātīya*). "Four," and so forth.
Efforts (*prayatna*) are of two kinds: internal (*ābhyantara*) and external (*bāhya*).
Among those, four internal articulations (*vṛtti*) have been shown;
the external ones, however, are eleven.

What, then, are they? They are: opening (*vivāra*), closure (*saṃvāra*), aspiration (*āśrāsa*), sonority (*nāda*), voiced (*ghoṣa*), voiceless (*aghoṣa*), weak breath (*alpaprāṇa*), strong breath (*mahāprāṇa*), acute (*udātta*), grave (*anudātta*), and circumflex (*svarita*).

In this regard, the wind called *prāṇa*, impelled by effort from the region of the navel, moves upward and is restrained with effort at one of the various locations beginning with the chest; being so restrained, it strikes that location, and from the striking of the location, sound (*dhvani*) arises.
In the ether (*ākāśa*), there is the perception of similarity (*sāvarṇya-śruti*), which is the acquisition of self by the similar phoneme (*savarṇa*).
In that process, when the location is struck while the phoneme-sound (*varṇa-dhvani*) is arising, then from the striking of the location, sound arises.
The manifestation of a phoneme (*savarṇa*) in space is its coming into being.

In that process, when the place of articulation (*sthāna*), the articulator (*karaṇa*), and the effort (*prayatna*) touch one another while the phoneme-sound is being produced, that is "contact" (*spṛṣṭatā*).

When they touch slightly, that is "slight contact" (*īṣatspṛṣṭatā*); when they touch in close proximity, that is "contractedness" (*saṃvṛtatā*); and when they touch from a distance, that is "openness" (*vivṛtatā*). These are the four internal efforts (*ābhyantara-prayatna*).

Furthermore, their internal nature arises precisely at the time of production through the operation of the places of articulation (*sthāna*), the points of contact (*karaṇa*), and the effort (*prayatna*).
Among these, the *sparśas* (contact consonants) have the quality of being produced by complete contact (*spṛṣṭa-karaṇa*).
The *sparśas* are those beginning with *ka* and ending with *ma*; "contact" (*spaṣṭatā*) is their phonetic quality (*guṇa*).
*Karaṇa* means *kṛti*, which is the manner of articulation.
Those whose *karaṇa* is accompanied by contact (*spṛṣṭatā*) are called *spṛṣṭakaraṇāḥ*.
The same should be understood for the other cases as well.
The semivowels (antastha) have a slight contact in their production; the semivowels are y, r, l, and v. The organs of articulation for the sibilants (ūṣman) and the vowels (svara) are wide open.
All vowels whatsoever are called *ac*.

The *uṣman* sounds are *ś*, *ṣ*, and *s*. Now, what are the characteristics of the *bāhya-prayatnas* (external efforts)? That same vital air (*prāṇa*), having ascended upwards and being obstructed at the head, when it strikes back against the abdominal cavity (*koṣṭha*), then, as the cavity is struck and the opening of the throat (*galabila*) is constricted, the phonetic property known as *saṃvāra* (constriction) arises.
From its being wide open, there is *vivāra* (opening).
When the throat-opening is constricted, the indistinct sound is *nāda* (resonance); when it is wide open, it is *śvāsa* (breath).
Some explain that the two [nasal sounds] occurring above [the consonants] are the *anupradāna*.
Others say that *anupradāna* is that which is given (*pradīyate*) after (*anu*), following the completion of the phoneme (*varṇaniṣpatti*).

Still others maintain that *anupradāna* is the *anusvāra*, according to the rule "like the resonance (*anusvana*) following the ringing of a bell (*ghaṇṭānirhrāda*)," meaning just as one experiences a resonance following the ringing of a bell, so it is here.

In that regard, when a sonant (*ghoṣavat*) sound is produced by the impact of the breath against the place of articulation, then, due to the conjunction with the sound of the resonance (*nāda*), it becomes voiced (*ghoṣa*). When a surd (*aśvasa*) is produced, then, due to the conjunction with the sound of the breath (*āśvasa*), it becomes voiceless (*aghoṣa*). When the air is great, it is "great-aspiration" (*mahāprāṇa*); when the air is slight, it is "small-aspiration" (*alpaprāṇa*). When the effort follows all the limbs and is intense, then there is constriction of the body and narrowness of the throat-opening; and because of the rapid movement of the air in the tone, there is roughness—this they call the acute accent (*udātta*).

When the effort is weak, there occurs relaxation of the limbs, enlargement of the cavity of the throat, and smoothness of the voice due to the slow movement of the air; this they call *anudātta* (unraised).

The *svarita* arises from the proximity of the *udātta* and *anudātta* tones; such are the external efforts (*bāhyaprayatna*). Furthermore, their externality consists in their arising after the time of the production of the phoneme, by virtue of the air.

Among those, the first and second letters of the classes, the sibilants (śa, ṣa, sa), the visarjanīya, the jihvāmūlīya, the upadhmānīya, and the first and second *yamas*, have an open throat (*vivṛtakaṇṭha*), are produced with breath (*āsānupradāna*), and are voiceless (*aghoṣa*). Among these, the first letters of the classes and the *yamas* are weakly aspirated (*alpaprāṇa*); all others are strongly aspirated (*mahāprāṇa*). Furthermore, the third and fourth letters of the classes, the semivowels (*antaḥstha*), the *hakāra*, the *anusvāra*, and the third and fourth *yamas*, have a closed throat (*saṃvṛtakaṇṭha*), are produced with resonance (*nādānupradāna*), and are voiced (*ghoṣavat*). Among these, the third letters of the classes and the semivowels are weakly aspirated.
All others are *mahāprāṇa* (aspirated).

As the third [consonants] are, so are the fifth; their additional quality is *ānunāsikya* (nasality). Regarding these two types of efforts—external and internal—that have been described, for the purpose of the technical designation *savarṇa* (homogeneous) here, the four internal efforts previously mentioned, such as *spṛṣṭatā* (contact), are relied upon, and not the external ones such as *vivāra* (opening), because they are excluded by the mention of the word "mouth" (*āsya*).
For it is only contact and the rest that occur within the mouth, not opening and the rest.

If this is so, for what purpose is the mention of "effort" (*prayatna*)? Let it simply be "having the same oral cavity" (*tulyāsyam*); for by the mention of "oral cavity" (*āsya*) alone, efforts such as contact (*spṛṣṭatā*) and the rest—which serve as causes for the designation of homogeneity (*savarṇasañjñā*)—are indeed obtained, just like the locations such as the palate, since they too reside in the mouth (*āsye*). This is true; nevertheless, both are employed in order to exclude [the application of] the operation [of the rule] to each [factor] individually.

Otherwise, just as a place of articulation (*sthāna*) functions in the designation of homogeneous sounds (*savarṇasañjñā*) independently of other places of articulation, so too would effort (*prayatna*) function independently of the place of articulation, and the place of articulation would function independently of effort. Consequently, there would be the designation of homogeneity for sounds that have different efforts but the same place of articulation, as well as for those that have different places of articulation but the same effort. With the words "a a a" and so forth, [the author] demonstrates which sounds, to what extent, and of what nature possess a mutual and permanent designation of homogeneity.
For all the *a*-sounds, the place of articulation is equally the throat, according to the rule: "The *a*, *ku*, *ha*, and *visarjanīya* are guttural (*kaṇṭhya*).

For the *i*-sounds as well, it is the palate, according to the rule: "The *i*, *cu*, *ya*, and *śa* are palatal (*tālavya*). And for the *u*-sounds as well, it is the lips, according to the rule: "The *u*, *pu*, and *upadhmānīya* are labial (*oṣṭhya*)."
For the *ṛ*-vowels as well, [the place of articulation] is the "head" (*mūrdhan*), according to the rule "ṛ, ṭu, ra, and ṣa are retroflexes" (*mūrdhanya*).

For the *ḷ*-vowels as well, it is the "teeth" (*danta*), according to the rule "ḷ, tu, la, and sa are dentals" (*dantya*). And for the *e*-vowels and *ai*-vowels, it is the "throat and palate" (*kaṇṭhatālu*), according to the rule "e and ai are produced in the throat and the palate."
Regarding the *o*-sounds and the *au*-sounds, [the rule] "o and au are produced at the throat and the lips" indicates that their place of articulation (*sthāna*) is the throat and the lips.

As for their effort (*prayatna*), however, for all of these—namely the sibilants (*ūṣman*) and the vowels (*svara*)—there is the opening of the articulators (*vivṛtaṃ karaṇam*); thus, they possess openness (*vivṛtatva*).
Therefore, because they share the same place and effort, the vowels beginning with *a* are designated as *savarṇa* (homogeneous) with one another.
The same applies up to the letter *au*.

The semivowels (*antaḥstha*) are divided into two types: nasalized (*sānunāsika*) and non-nasalized (*niranunāsika*), excluding the letter *r*. These also bear the technical designation "homogeneous" (*savarṇa*) with respect to other semivowels of their own kind.

Regarding the statement "there are no homogeneous (*savarṇa*) sounds for the *repha* [the sound *r*] and the sibilants (*ūṣman*)," the intended meaning is that other phonemes such as *a* and so on are of a different class (*vijātīya*) from them.
However, the *repha* and the sibilants, being of the same class (*tulyajātīya*) and having the same place and effort of articulation (*tulyasthānaprayatna*), are indeed homogeneous (*savarṇa*).

In this regard, first concerning the letter *ra*: other phonemes than *ṛ*, *ṭu*, *ra*, and *ṣa*—as well as those beginning with *ya* and *va*—are not homogeneous (*savarṇa*) with it, because they have different points of articulation (*sthāna*) and different efforts of articulation (*prayatna*).

For instance, according to the rule—"The letters *a*, *kuha*, and *visarjanīya* are gutturals; *i*, *cu*, *ya*, and *śa* are palatals; *ṛ*, *tu*, *la*, and *sa* are dentals; *u*, *pu*, and *upadhmānīya* are labials; *e* and *ai* are gutturo-palatal; *o* and *au* are gutturo-labial"—the respective points of articulation for *a* and the others are the throat and so forth.
However, for the letter *ra*, since *ṛ*, *ṭu*, *ra*, and *ṣa* are "cerebrals" (*mūrdhanya*), its point of articulation is the palate (*mūrdhan*).

Regarding the vowels such as *a* and others mentioned immediately above, their organ of articulation (*karaṇa*) is "open" (*vivṛta*); thus, for both the sibilants (*ūṣman*) and the vowels, there is openness.

However, those letters such as *ka* and others which fall within the consonant groups (*varga*), their organ of articulation is "contacted" (*spṛṣṭa*); thus, for the stops (*sparśa*), there is contact.
For the letter *ra*, the organ of articulation is "slightly contacted" (*īṣatspṛṣṭa*); thus, for the semivowels (*antaḥstha*), there is slight contact.
The letters *ś* and *s* are also not homogeneous (*savarṇa*) with the letter *r*, due to a difference in their places of articulation (*sthāna*) and efforts (*prayatna*).
For those two are, respectively, palatal and dental,
whereas *r* is retroflex (*mūrdhanya*).
The effort (*prayatna*) for those two [the *ṛ* and *ṝ* sounds] is also openness (*vivṛtatva*).
For the letter *r*, however, it is exactly as previously stated.

Due to the difference in effort, the letters *ṛ*, *ṝ*, *ṣ*, and *ūṣman* are not homogeneous (*savarṇa*) with the letter *r*; this is not, however, due to a difference in place of articulation (*sthāna*), because they too are produced at the root of the tongue (*mūrdhan*).

However, there is a difference in the effort (*prayatna*) between the sounds *ṛ* and *ṣ*: as before, they share the quality of being "opened" (*vivṛta*), whereas for the sound *r*, it is that same previously mentioned [effort].

For the *ṭ*-class (*ṭavarga*), the effort is "contact" (*spṛṣṭa*). Furthermore, the sounds *y*, *v*, and *l* do not belong to the same phonetic class (*savarṇa*) solely due to a difference in place of articulation (*sthānabheda*), and not because of a difference in effort; for these also possess the quality of being "slightly contacted" (*iṣatspṛṣṭa*).
Nevertheless, a difference in place of articulation does exist for *y*, *v*, and *l*, since they are respectively palatal, dental, and labial.
In this same way, the *visarjanīya*, the *jihvāmūlīya*, the *upadhmānīya*, and the *anusvāra*—

as well as these *yamās*, namely *kuṃ*, *khuṃ*, *guṃ*, and *ghuṃ*— do not constitute *savarṇa* (homogeneous) sounds with the letter *r* precisely because their places of articulation (*sthāna*) and efforts (*prayatna*) are dissimilar.

For the *visarjanīya* has its place in the throat (*kaṇṭha*), the *jihvāmūlīya* in the root of the tongue (*jihvya*), the *upadhmānīya* in the lips (*oṣṭhya*), the *anusvāra* and the *yamās* in the nose (*nāsikya*), while the *repha* (*r*) has its place on the palate (*mūrdhanya*).

As for the effort previously mentioned regarding that [repha], it does not exist at all for the *visarjanīya* and the others. Thus, there is no other similar (*savarna*) phoneme for the *repha* besides another *repha*. By this same method, it should be understood that for the sibilants (*ūṣman*) such as *śa* and the rest, there is likewise an absence of similarity (*sāvarṇya*). Regarding the phrase "belonging to a class" (*vargya*) and so forth: that which exists in a class (*varga*) is "class-member" (*vargya*).

By the rule *digāditvād yat* [Pāṇini 4.3.54], followed by the elision of the vowel *ā* according to *lopo vyor vali* [Pāṇini 6.1.66], the form *vargya* is derived. A phoneme belonging to a class (*vargya*) is homogeneous (*savarṇa*) with another phoneme of its class that falls within the same class, provided they share the same place of articulation (*sthāna*) and effort (*prayatna*), such as the letter *ka* being homogeneous with the letter *kha*. This should be understood to apply in other cases as well.
Regarding the phrase "of those with different places of articulation" (*bhinnasthānānām*), etc.:

for all these consonants beginning with *ka*, although they have the same effort (*prayatna*) because they possess the quality of being produced by contact (*spṛṣṭa*), they have different places of articulation (*bhinnasthāna*) according to their sequence, since their places are the throat, palate, head, teeth, and lips respectively.
[Examples are given: *tarptā*, *tarptum*.
The forms [of the words] are derived from the roots *tṛpa* and *tṛnpha*, meaning "to satisfy" (Dhātupāṭha 1307, 1308), in the suffixes *tṛc* and *tumun*.
Regarding the phrase "of those with different efforts" (*bhinnaprayatnānām*), etc.:

since the vowels beginning with *i* are all palatal (*tālavya*), they share the same place of articulation; however, they possess different efforts (*prayatna*) as appropriate, due to their respective qualities of being open (*vivṛta*), touched (*spṛṣṭa*), or slightly touched (*īṣatspṛṣṭa*).

Although the effort (*prayatna*) for the vowels *i* and *ś* is indeed identical, nevertheless, because the author will state an exception regarding them, they do not possess the status of being *savarṇa* (homogeneous).

The form *aruścyotati* is the present tense (*laṭ*) form of the root *ścyutir kṣaraṇe* (Dhātupāṭha 41). In that case, the *s* of the word *arus* situated later [in the compound] undergoes the substitution of *r* (*rutva*).
For that [visarga], there is a *sakāra* by the rule "vā śari" (Pāṇini 8.3.36); for that [sakāra] as well, there is the substitution of a *śakāra* by the rule for *ścutva*.
Thus we have "hotṛkāraḥ.

But how does the substitution of *ṛkāra* occur here, since there is no most similar (*antaratama*) substitute for the entire complex [of *ṛ* and *l*] which would serve as the original locus (*sthānin*)? To this he says: "Of both," and so forth.
The letter *ṛ* is a retroflex (*mūrdhanya*), whereas the letter *ḷ* is dental (*dantya*).

In that case, if a single long vowel that is both retroflex and dental could exist as the most similar (*antaratama*) substitute for those two, then that most similar one would be the substitute. However, since such a vowel does not exist, the substitute must be that which is most similar to each individual component.

Even in that case, if the long *ḷ* were to exist, it too would occur by way of alternation (*paryāyeṇa*), yet it does not exist. Therefore, by the principle of elimination (*pāriśeṣyāt*), that which is the most similar (*antaratama*) to the single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) of the entire complex is precisely the *ṛ*-vowel. He states the reason for the contingency expressed as "even though they have the same place of articulation and effort" (*tulyāsyaprayatnau*), because a prohibition presupposes a contingency.

In the case of *daṇḍahasta*, both the vowel *a* and the consonant *ha* have the same place of articulation (*tulyasthānatva*) because both are produced in the throat (*kaṇṭhasthāna*), and they have the same effort (*tulyaprayatnatva*) because both are produced with an open articulation (*vivṛtakaraṇa*). In the case of *dadhi śītam* as well, for the very same reason there is the same effort, and both have the same place of articulation because both are palatals (*tālavya*).
[The author] demonstrates the result of the prohibition: "the long vowel substitution (*savarṇadīrghatva*) does not occur."

But surely, in the rule *akaḥ savarṇe dīrghaḥ* [Pāṇini 6.1.101], the word *aci* is understood from 6.1.97; therefore, even if the prohibition were not present, lengthening would not occur, as in the example *kumārī śete*. Thus, these two examples are inappropriate. It might be argued: because the vowels *a* and *i* include their homogeneous counterparts (*sāvarṇya*) by 1.1.69, they possess the status of being vowels (*actva*); nevertheless, since they are taught among the consonants (*hal*), they also possess the status of being consonants (*haltva*). Therefore, they are not merely *akāra* and *ikāra*, but are also *hal*s. This is true.

Furthermore, this is the intention of the author of the *Vṛtti* here: first of all, the rule "for the sake of another" (*anyārtham*) must necessarily be applied [to Pāṇini 1.1.10] in order to prevent the elision (*lopa*) of the word *yasya*. That which was formulated for the sake of another would also serve this purpose.

Thus, the cumbersome process of comprehension that would otherwise result from having to understand the absence of lengthening (*dīrghatva*) by means of the continued application (*anuvṛtti*) of the previous rule is thereby dispensed with. [The example is] "vaipāśaḥ."

In the rule *vipāśi bhava ityaṇ* (Pāṇini 4.3.148), the vowel *i* being prescribed includes the letter *ś* as well by virtue of their homogeneous nature (*sāvarṇya*). Consequently, the elision (*lopa*) of that [ś] would result.

Regarding the term *ānahuha*: [it means] "the modification of *anaḍuh*. In this context, according to [Pāṇini 6.4.148], the vowel *ā* (in *ānaḍuha*) would include the consonant *h* as well; consequently, as before, there would be its elision (*lopa*). In this regard, is it understood that "whatever dual ending beginning with *ī* or *ū* is *pragṛhya*," or rather, "whatever dual ending having *ī* or *ū* at its end is *pragṛhya*"? In the first case, the designation *pragṛhya* would not apply to forms such as *pacete*, because here the dual ending is not merely the vowel *e*; rather, it is the entire word-element *āte*.

Having observed this fault in the first position, he states the second position, beginning with: "ending in *ī*, *ū*, or *e*," and so forth. Now, one might object: even in this position, forms such as *agnī* would not be established, for here the dual ending is *ī* and so on, but it does not end in *ī* and so on. [To this we reply: there is no fault, because by the rule [Pāṇini 1.1.21], the status of being "like the end" (*antavadbhāva*) occurs. Thus, *agnī*.
The lengthening [of the vowel] occurs by rule 6.1.102.

Here, since the designation *pragṛhya* applies, the lengthening prescribed by rule 6.1.97 (*akaḥ savarṇe*) does not take place when the word *iti* follows, due to the preservation of the original form (*prakṛtibhāva*) by rule 6.1.125. In the case of "vāyu" as well, the substitution of *yaṇ* occurs by rule 6.1.77.
In the remaining examples as well, there is the substitution of *ay*. In the case of *khaṭve*, the substitution of *śī* occurs by the rule *auṅa āpaḥ* [Pāṇini 7.1.18].

In the forms *pacete* and *yajete*, the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) suffixes *ātām* and *āthām* occur because the roots are marked with the *svarita* accent; the final vowel is replaced by *e* according to Pāṇini 7.1.34, and the *y* is elided according to Pāṇini 6.1.66.
In the examples *vṛkṣāv atra* and *plakṣāv atra*, [the same process applies].

This is a dual form; however, it does not end in *ī*, *ū*, *e*, or *at*. Therefore, because the rule for the preservation of the original stem (*prakṛtibhāva*) does not apply, the substitution certainly takes place:
"kumāryatra."

When the suffix *ṅīp* is applied according to [Pāṇini 4.1.20], the word *kumārī* ends in the vowel *ī*, and not in the dual case-ending; therefore, since there is no *prakṛtibhāva* (the preservation of the original form), the *yaṇ* substitution indeed occurs. Now, what is the purpose of the marker *t* (in *tapara*)? If it is argued that it is for the sake of excluding the protracted (*pluta*) vowel, we say no; for the protracted vowel is desired [to be included]. And how the designation *pragṛhya* is established for the protracted vowel even when the marker *t* is applied has been explained in the Bhāṣya by the passage beginning: "The protracted vowel is asiddha; because it is asiddha, its duration is exactly that [of the short vowel]" (MBh 1.66).

If it is argued that [the *t* after *ta*] is for the purpose of including those [sounds] distinguished by other qualities (*guṇa*) at that same time, we say no; because of the rule "In this science, qualities do not cause differentiation" (Pāṇini 1.1.69), he says: "The addition of *t* after *ta* is for the sake of removing ambiguity.
For if the addition of *t* after *ta* were absent, there would be a substitution of *yaṇ* for both the vowel *ī* and the vowel *ū*.
Consequently, there would indeed be ambiguity: "Is this a reference to the letters *y* and *v*, or rather to the vowels *ī* and *ū*? Thus, it must be stated [that the *t* is added].
The meaning is that it must be explained.

In this regard, it has been explained as follows: the term *śākalya* which is about to be mentioned applies here by way of the "lion's glance" (*siṃhāvalokita*) maxim, and that [rule] is a fixed option (*vyavasthita-vibhāṣā*). Consequently, there will be a prohibition for *maṇīva* and so forth, as in: *maṇīva*, *dampatīva*, and *rodasīva*. Words such as *maṇīva* and the others end in the dual number.

In that case, even though there is no *pragṛhya* status, the single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) "a long vowel before a homogeneous vowel" (*akaḥ savarṇe dīrghaḥ*, P. 6.1.101) indeed occurs [in the form] "the *m* which is related to *adas*. Here, the genitive case is used to denote a relationship characterized by the distinction between part and whole (*avayava-avayavibhāva*). In the example "amī atra," from the word *adas*, the substitution of *śī* for *jas* occurs by P. 7.1.17; then the substitution of *at* for the final vowel by P. 7.1.102; then the *guṇa* substitution by P. 6.1.97 resulting in the single form *e*; then the substitution of *ī* for *e* by P. 6.1.87; then the substitution of *i* for *ī* by P. 8.2.81; and finally the substitution of *m* for *d* by P. 8.2.80. This [sūtra] is commenced for the sake of the dual number of *adas*.
Regarding the form *amū āsāte*:
the dual ending of the pronoun *adas* is *au*.

By the rule *tyadādīnām aḥ* [Pāṇini 7.2.102], the final vowel is replaced by *a*, and by *vṛddhir eci* [Pāṇini 6.1.88], there is *vṛddhi* (resulting in *āda-au*). Then, by *adaso’serdādudo maḥ* [Pāṇini 8.2.80], in place of the long *au* of *adas*, an *u* is substituted because it is the closest similar sound (*antaratama*). Here too, since the operation concerning the *ū* (the substitution of *u*) is considered *asiddha* (non-existent) for the purposes of the preceding rule, the application of that preceding rule does not occur.

Therefore, this [sūtra] is commenced for the purpose of setting aside the rule "that which precedes is as if not established" (8.2.1). But how can this [rule 8.2.1] be set aside by the force of the statement [of the present sūtra]? This is not so; for if [the present rule] were merely for the sake of what is already established by the rule "the status of a *pragṛhya* applies when [the following vowel] is established" (6.1.127), then that statement would suffice. But it is not thus; for the commencement of a grammatical rule (*yoga*) is not prompted by a single purpose alone. If this were the only purpose, he would have stated it right there: "A nasalized [vowel] follows a non-*pragṛhya* *aṇ*, except in the case of *adas*."
In the example "śamytara, dāḍimyatra," the suffix *ṅīṣ* is applied by the rule "ṣidgaurādibhyaśca" [Pāṇini 4.1.41], and the vowel *a* is elided by the rule "yasyeti ca" [Pāṇini 6.4.148]. Thus,
this long *ī* occurs after the letter *m*, but it is not connected to the word *adas*.
Regarding the form *amuke'tra*:

the suffix *akac* is added by [Pāṇini 5.3.71] *avyayasarvanāmnām akac*, then *jas* is replaced by *śī* by [7.1.17], followed by *guṇa* by [6.1.87]. When the forms *amuke* and *atra* stand together, the substitution of the single preceding form (*pūrvarūpa*) occurs by [6.1.109] *paratra cātraśabde*. Regarding the word *śe*: since the phonetic feature of *śe* (the sound *śe*) is not specified, it would follow that the word *śe* occurring in *kāśe* and *kuśe* would also be included; therefore, with the intention of stating a specific distinction, he asks: "What is this *śe*?"
Regarding "supām" and so forth:

the intention is that the word *śe*—which results from applying the seventh case singular to the words *kāśa* and *kuśa* and then applying *ādguṇaḥ* [Pāṇini 6.1.87]—is not included here, because its occurrence is merely incidental (*lākṣaṇikatvāt*). In the forms *yuṣme* and *asme*, the substitution of *śe* for the genitive plural occurs by [the rule] *supāṃ suluk* [Pāṇini 7.1.39]; or alternatively, the change to *śe* belongs to the nominative plural itself, due to its Vedic character (*chāndasatvāt*), and thus [the rule regarding the genitive plural] does not apply.
In *tve* and *me*,
there is the substitution of *śe* for the locative singular and the ablative singular [of *yuṣmad* and *asmad*].
