In that context, because the *samprasāraṇa* of the root *āp* has been prescribed by the rule *vacisvapi-* [P. 6.1.15], it occurs before *pit* suffixes; however, it does not occur before *kit* suffixes, because it has not been prescribed by anything in that case.

Furthermore, because this single sentence finds its purpose solely in the accomplishment of the prohibition regarding *kit* suffixes, it cannot logically function again by way of an injunction (*vidhi*).

Now, if it were to function by way of an injunction—namely, that it applies as "let there be"—then the scope of the injunction would be precisely where there is no prior application (*prāpti*); thus, the meaning of the injunction would apply optionally only to *pit* suffixes, and not to *kit* suffixes, since [the rule] has already fulfilled its purpose there.

However, there is no fault in the formulation of the technical designation (*saṃjñā*); for when that designation exists, the prohibition (*pratiṣedha*) which operates brings about an equalization of that very domain which previously existed through the distinction between what is caused by *samprasāraṇa* and what is not. It effects an equality by making everything identical in being caused by *samprasāraṇa*. When that has been equalized, the optional rule (*vikalpa*)—applying both to a suffix marked with *kit* and one marked with *pit*—accomplishes the operation optionally in all cases by means of the positive injunction (*vidhi*), such that *samprasāraṇa* occurs in one alternative. Since non-application (*aprāpti*) remains established in the other alternative, everything desired is accomplished.

Therefore, since [the conditions for this designation] would apply both when [a rule] has been reached and when it has not been reached, this technical name (*saṃjñā*) is prescribed for the sake of providing an option (*vibhāṣā*). For example: *śuśāva*.

[The root is] *ṭuośvi* "to go, to grow" (Dhātupāṭha 1010); [the suffix] *liṭ*; [the substitute] *ṇal*; when the *saṃprasāraṇa* has been performed, the *vṛddhi* and the substitution of *āv* [take place].
In the forms *śuśuvatuḥ* and *śiśīyatuḥ*, the substitutions *iyaṅ* and *uvaṅ* are applied by the rule *aci śnudhātu* [Pāṇini 6.4.77]. Regarding the term *bhūta*:

where something prescribed by another grammatical rule is restated by means of a past tense case-ending for the sake of another grammatical operation—as in the rules [6.3.139] and [6.1.108]—therein it is called *bhūta*.

Regarding the term "future" (*bhāvī*): where something is indicated for the purpose of being prescribed by means of a suffix that is yet to be applied, it is called "future. For example, in the rule *ṣyaṅaḥ saṃprasāraṇam* [Pāṇini 6.1.13], it is "future. For in this case, there is no *iṅ* (the verbal root) in place of *ṣyaṅ* or in place of *vasu* (the suffix), such that the rule could be said to "weave the cloth" (*śāṭakaṃ vayati*) for it.
That *i* occurs in place of *yaṇ*, for which the technical designation "vocalization" (*samprasāraṇa*) applies;
as in the examples "iṣṭam" and "uptam," [the substitution] from here on is vocalization.
In the word *gṛhītam*, there is also vocalization (*samprasāraṇa*) by the rule beginning with *grahijyāvayi* [Pāṇini 6.1.16].
By the phrase "some" (*kecit*), he shows the opinion of those who do not rely on a future designation (*bhāvinī saṃjñā*).
But how can these two meanings of a single sūtra be obtained from a single sentence? Either by means of *tantra* (simultaneous application) or by repetition (*āvṛtti*).

But has it not been stated that in a rule prescribing a technical name (*saṃjñā-vidhi*), the word-form itself (*śabda*) is understood to be the referent? Therefore, it is logical that the phoneme (*varṇa*) alone should be the named entity (*saṃjñin*); how then could the meaning (*artha*) be so? If you argue that this is as in the rule *na veti vibhāṣā* (Pāṇini 1.1.44), that is not correct; for in that case, the particle *iti* is employed for the purpose of indicating the meaning, whereas here it is absent—thus [your objection] is invalid. Even here, it is indeed logical because either the principle of *tantra* (simultaneous application) or the principle of *āvṛtti* (repetition) is resorted to. And the evidence for these two possible interpretations of the sūtra’s meaning is the indication of a specific case-ending (*vibhakti-viśeṣa-nirdeśa*).

Since in prescriptive rules such as "the *samprasāraṇa* of *ṣyaṅ*" (P. 6.1.13), he employs a designation using the present tense (*bhāṣamāṇavibhakti*), it is understood from this that "the meaning of the sentence" (*vākyārtha*) is the technical name (*saṃjñin*).

And since in rules such as "[after an element] ending in *yat*, etc. (P. 6.3.139), he employs a designation using the past tense (*bhūtavibhakti*), it is determined from this that "the phoneme" (*varṇa*) is [the name].
Therefore, it is logical that even the meaning of the sentence may function as a technical name.
"What is the nature of this sentence-meaning? To this he says: "The locus of the substitute," and so forth.

With the words "In that case," etc., he demonstrates the division of the scope for the two immediately preceding meanings of the sūtras: [the first applies] where a phoneme is not possible in a rule of prescription (*vidhi*).
In a prescriptive statement such as "There is vocalization (*samprasāraṇa*) for *ṣyaṅ*" (P. 6.1.13), the first meaning of the sūtra presents itself.

In rules such as *anavāde tu* [P. 6.3.139], because the rule is prescribed for that which is to be enjoined (*vidheya*), the first [vowel] is ineffective; therefore, the second [vowel] is taken. Regarding the form *aduhitarām*: here, since the *ik* vowel is the substitute (*sthānin*) for the *yaṇ*, the *Bhāṣya* states that it would receive the designation of *samprasāraṇa*. And if that were the case, the lengthening rule *halaḥ* [P. 6.4.2] would undesirably apply. To refute this objection, he says: "Because of the correspondence of number (*saṃkhyātānudeśa*), etc."—here there are four *yaṇ* vowels as substituends (*sthānin*), and there are likewise exactly four *ik* vowels as substitutes (*ādeśa*). Therefore, by the principle of correspondence of number, as stated in *yathāsaṃkhyamanudeśaḥ* [P. 1.3.10], a correspondence of number must take place.
And consequently, the *samprasāraṇa* designation applies only to that *i*-vowel which stands in the place of *y*;

however, in this case, the *i*-vowel does not stand in the place of *y*, but rather in the place of *l*. Therefore, how could there be any occasion for that [designation] here? [In the root] *druh* "to injure" (*dhātu-pāṭha*).

In the *laṅ* [past tense], by the extension (*atideśa*) of Pāṇini 3.1.87, "that which has an action equal to that of the object behaves like the object," the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) applies to this reflexive object-agent (*karmakartṛ*).
Since the suffix *yak* is prohibited by 3.1.89, the suffix *śap* is applied.
Because it begins with *t*, there is *luk* (elision). With *aduhi* established, *tarap* is applied by [Pāṇini 5.3.56] *tiṅaśca*.
Then *ām* is applied by [Pāṇini 5.4.11] *kimettiṅavyayaghādāmvadravyaprakarṣe*.
The mention of *tarap* here is for the purpose of the technical designation (*saṃjñā*) "aṅga. This [sūtra] is an exception (*apavāda*) to that *paribhāṣā*.
Consequently, by virtue of its connection with that, this too is understood to be a *paribhāṣā*.

If, however, the rule were that what is initial becomes final and what is final becomes initial, then suffixes such as those beginning with *taddhita* (P. 4.1.76) and ending with *kṛt* (P. 3.4.67)—namely, those starting from P. 3.2.16 and P. 3.2.3—would also become both initial and final.
Nor should one suspect that the *ṅīp* suffix prescribed by the rule *ṭiḍḍhāṇañ* [Pāṇini 4.1.15] would have no scope of application because the *ṭi*-element belongs to the beginning of the suffix;
for its scope will be where the *ṭi*-nature is established for the base itself and not for the suffix, as in the case of *nadaṅ*, *bhaṣaṅ*, and so forth.
Furthermore, if the *ṭi*-element were at the beginning of the suffix, forms such as *kurucara* would be the only ones established.

But if the two [elements] were final, then in the case of *vidhyoḥ* (from *vidhi* + *oḥ*), since the *kip* suffix would fall within the base (*prakṛti*) according to Pāṇini 3.3.92, it would be included by the mention of "root" (*dhātu*);

consequently, the accent prescribed by Pāṇini 6.1.174 would not apply because of the prohibition in 6.1.175. To this he says: "Because the mention of the genitive (*ṣaṣṭhī*) applies [here] by way of the 'lion’s glance' maxim (*siṃhāvalokita-nyāya*)."

[Objection: Even so, [the suffixes] *ādy* and *anta* would still apply by [P. 3.2.8] and [P. 5.2.2]. [Response: This is not a fault. According to the principle "exceptions stated earlier sublate the rules immediately following them, but not those that follow later" (Vyāḍiparibhāṣā 9), this will be an exception specifically to the application of *sthāne-yoga* (substitution), and not to the condition of being followed by a suffix (*pratyaya-paratva*).

Another says: Since the two parts—the beginning and the end—and a part cannot exist without a whole, they subsist by implying the whole. Therefore, in the context of the relationship between part and whole, when a part is prescribed as either the beginning or the end, that part must be indicated by means of the genitive case; thus, by implication, it is understood that "that which is indicated by the genitive of a part" [is meant].
But this is not the case.

These two suffixes (pratyaya)—namely, those beginning with [the letter ñ] and ending with [the letter ṇ]—would result in being applied to the beginning and the end [of the root], because here the bases (*prakṛti*) are indicated by a genitive case expressing a part-whole relationship (*avayava-ṣaṣṭhī*). What then is the case? It is that genitive which stands in the sense of an ablative (*pañcamyarthe ṣaṣṭhī*), as in the rule "supāṃ supo bhavanti" (Pāṇini 7.1.39). Regarding the form *bhīṣayate*: from the verbal root *ñibhī* (meaning "fear," Dhātupāṭha 1084), the causative suffix *ṇic* is added; then, by [Pāṇini 1.3.68] and [7.3.40], the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) suffix is applied. In this context, if the word *acaḥ* (from Pāṇini 4.3.31) were an ablative, it would stand in grammatical apposition (*samānādhikaraṇatva*) with this [current] ablative [expressing the sense of "from the end"].

Then, by the rule *tataḥ* [Pāṇini 7.1.72], the augment *num* would have to follow the final vowel in this very case, as in *kuṇḍāni*; for here there is indeed a final vowel belonging to the neuter. However, in the case of *payāṃsi*, it would not occur [after the final vowel], because by the rule *alo 'ntyasya* [Pāṇini 1.1.52], it would instead apply in place of the *s* itself. For here, what is not final is not the vowel, but rather the *s*. Therefore, showing that this is a genitive used in the sense of specification (*nirdhāraṇa*), he says: "of vowels" (*acām*), etc. The plural number is used in the sense of a class (*jāti*).
In the *sūtra* as well, the singular number in "of this" (*asya*) refers to the class (*jāti*) alone.

If, then, this were a genitive of selection (*nirdhāraṇa-ṣaṣṭhī*), then since the final [letter] would not be specifically qualified, the augment *mit* might follow any final [letter] whatsoever without distinction; for there is no second mention of the vowel *a* by which the final [vowel] could be specified. This is not a fault; for in common usage, a selection is understood only among members of the same class. Thus, when it is said, "Among cows, the black one is the most beautiful," only a cow is understood—not a female goat, nor a mare.

Therefore, here too, among vowels, that which is determined as the final by virtue of being the last— relative to the limit of the preceding vowels— is understood to be of the same class as the vowels themselves.
Consequently, it will follow immediately after the very last vowel.

This [sūtra] has been commenced for the purpose of setting aside (apavāda) the notion that [an element] is in place of [another] (sthāneyogitva) when followed by an affix (pratyaya). Among these, for the purpose of setting aside the notion of being in place of another: by the rule *śemucādīnām* (Pāṇini 7.1.59), the augment *num* occurs [after the root *muc*], as in *muñcati*;
and by the rule *napuṃsakasya jhalacaḥ* (Pāṇini 7.1.72), it occurs [in the neuter], as in *payāṃsi*.

This is for the purpose of setting aside [the rule regarding] the posteriority of the suffix (*pratyayaparatva*). [The example is: *ruṇaddhi*. Now, one might object: "According to the principle that 'exceptions preceding [a general rule] set aside only the rules immediately following them, not those further ahead' (*vyā.pa.9*), it would be logical for this to be an exception only to the application of the *sthāni* (original element), and not to the posteriority of the suffix. This is not so; for if it were so, the designation of *mit* for the augment *śnam* would be useless because it would have no scope of application. If you argue that it is not useless because its purpose is to ensure the audible pronunciation [of the nasal], we say no; for there is the explicit grammatical indication (*nirdeśa*) in [Pāṇini 7.3.92].
If it were intended for the purpose of hearing [the suffix], the instruction would have been "tṛṇam ha im";
therefore, it is logical that this is an exception (apavāda) to the requirement of being followed by a suffix.

If this were so, then because of the rule "that which falls within [the domain of] something is included by the mention of that" (Vyāḍi-Pāṇini 21), the *śnam* augment—which falls within the domain of the verbal root—would not receive the designation of "affix" (*pratyaya*) due to its being mentioned along with the root and because it occurs before the affix; and consequently, the designation of *it* (indicating the elision of the following sound) would not apply to the letter *ś* at the beginning of the affix according to Pāṇini 1.3.8. This is not a fault; for since it is prescribed within the governing context (*adhikāra*) of "affixes," it will receive the designation of "affix" despite its occurring before the affix and despite its falling within the domain of the root, just as the final syllable of *bahuc* and *kac* receives the designation of "acute-accented" (*antodātta*).

In the case of *bahupaṭavaḥ* and *uccakaiḥ*, even though the [designation] *pratyaya* does not apply by virtue of [the rule's] posteriority, the final acute accent (*antodāttatva*) indeed occurs by the rule *citaḥ* [Pāṇini 6.1.157].
Regarding *masjeḥ* and so forth:
the designation *anuṣaṅga* was applied to the penultimate *nakāra* by the ancient teachers.
Regarding the root *ṭumasjo* in the sense of "purification" (Dhātupāṭha 1416), [the author] will state that the augment *num* is applied [by Pāṇini 7.1.60].

If that *num* were placed after the final vowel, then by the rule *skoḥ saṃyogādyoḥ* (8.2.29), there would be no elision of the *s* [of *masj*], and by the rule *aniditām* (6.4.24), there would be no elision of the *n* [of *nas*]; this is because they respectively do not follow a vowel (*anādittva*) and are not *upadha* sounds (*anudhattva*).
Therefore, the *num* must be inserted before the final *j*, between the *j* and the *s*.
And how it is obtained from the preceding [letter] after the final one will be explained in the seventh [chapter].

Regarding the word "magnaḥ": by [Pāṇini 8.2.45], there is the substitution of *ṇ* for the *ṣṭhā*-suffix; because that [substitution] is not yet established (*asiddha*), by [Pāṇini 8.2.30], the *k*-treatment (*kutva*) of the letter *j* results in the letter *g*.

In the word *maṅktā*, as before, when the letter *g* is applied, it undergoes *cartva* (the substitution of a voiceless unaspirated stop) by [Pāṇini 8.4.54], becoming *k*. Then, by [Pāṇini 8.3.24], an *anusvāra* is substituted;
and by [Pāṇini 8.4.58], the letter *ṅ* is substituted.

This [rule] should be understood as occurring before the suffix *bhakta*; otherwise, when *khaś* is applied after the root *lih* by [Pāṇini 3.2.32], and when *mum* is applied by [Pāṇini 6.3.67], in the form *vahaṃlih*, the *anusvāra* prescribed for a word-final position by [Pāṇini 8.3.23] would not occur, because it would no longer be at the end of a word (*apadāntatvāt*). "Intended for the restriction of application" (*yoganiyamārthā*):
"restriction of application" (*yoganiyama*) means a restriction of relationship (*sambandhaniyama*); that which has this as its purpose or motive is described as such.

If this [rule] is intended for the restriction of application—namely, that whatever genitive case occurs in the grammatical treatise is used only in the sense of "substitution" (*sthāne-yoga*), and not in any other sense—[then the rule is established].

This being the case, the genitive in *evaṃ sati* (Pāṇini 6.4.89) would also denote only a relation of "substitution" (*sthāneyoga*), and not a relation of "part-to-whole" (*avayava*) or "connection" (*avisamvāda*). Consequently, because the genitive of substitution (*sthāna-ṣaṣṭhī*) is applied even in the final rule [of this section], the vowel *ū* would replace the final *h* of *goha* (by Pāṇini 6.4.89). Furthermore, by the statement [of Pāṇini] *iti* (7.1.101), it would follow that the vowel *ū* replaces the penultimate (*upadhā*) alone as well. Therefore, he says: "In this treatise, whichever genitive has a fixed connection," and so forth.
By means of this [rule], a restriction is established to avoid the contingency of non-restriction (*aniyamaprasaṅga*).

Where does the contingency of non-restriction arise? Where there is doubt; for example, in the rule *[[2.4.52]]*. For here, there is a doubt: "Is it in place of *asti*, or rather in the immediately following [element]? In the previous case, however, because the substitute characterized by the *upadhā* (the penultimate vowel) was distinguished from the specific whole [as its locus], it was certain that this [substitution] applies only to the part; therefore, this [present rule] has no application there.

Regarding the phrase "sthāneyogaiva": the term *sthāne* is a locative of cause (*nimittasaptamī*), and *yogaḥ* means connection (*sambandhaḥ*). By this, it is stated that [the substitution] occurs only through a connection caused by position.
Clarifying this very point, he says: "In the case of *sthāna-yoga*, when the cause has become the cause," and so forth.
That [substitution] is to be understood as occurring when *sthāna-yoga*—that is, the state of being a cause—has been attained.
For here the word *bhūta* functions in the sense of the word *prāpta* (attained); just as in the expression "become a god" (*devabhūta*), the meaning is "one who has attained the state of a god."

By employing the term *nimittagrahaṇam* (the grasping of a cause), he shows that in the *sūtra*, this is a locative case of cause (*nimitta-saptamī*). Furthermore, "connection" (*yoga*) here is characterized by the relationship between the original element (*sthānin*) and its substitute (*ādeśa*). Why is this so? Because that [substitute] itself is the cause for the original element.
The word *sthāna* (place/position) is derived in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāvasādhana*); "standing" (*sthiti*) is the "place.
Furthermore, that [place] is threefold: "removal" (*apakarṣa*), "cessation" (*nivṛtti*), and "consequence" (*prasaṅga*).
In the case of the statement "Let the goat be tied in the place of the cow," "removal" is what must be understood by the word *sthāna*.

In the case of "a pungent medicine [should be used] in place of phlegm," there is cessation (*nivṛtti*). In the case of "the site of *darbha* grass should be strewn with *śara* grass," there is extension (*prasaṅga*).

Of these two meanings, neither is possible here: the first is not possible because the relationship between word and meaning is eternal; the second is not possible because the verb *as* (to be) is taught in a general sense.

Therefore, considering that the third meaning alone is intended, he says: "And the word *sthāna*. *Prasaṅga*, however, refers to the occasion (*avasara*) for time, which serves as the cause for purposeful action (*arthakriyā*). Thus: "In the sense of *prasaṅga* [used] in place of *asti*."
The meaning is that the occasion for time, which serves as the cause (nimitta) for that action characterized by the accomplishment of one's own purpose, has arrived.

By the phrase "in the context of [the word] *prasaṅga*, [it is] the cause of the connection," etc., he demonstrates the possibility [of this interpretation] within the illustration of the meaning of the Sūtra.
Furthermore, the term "Brāhmaṇa" is merely an illustrative example (*upalakṣaṇa*).

For even in the case of *asteri* and so forth, the genitive (*ṣaṣṭhī*) would indeed result, since the relation [of cause and effect] has arisen as the basis [for the suffix]. But what are the many meanings of the genitive, such that this [rule] regarding the genitive is stated for the purpose of excluding other objects of relation? To this he says: "For there are many," and so on.
For in the case of a word, there exist relations based on proximity, immediate succession, modification, part-whole, and so forth;
however, these are not like the relations of offspring and progenitor, etc. Therefore, he says: "as many as are possible in a word."

Now, regarding the term *sthāneyoga*: is this a non-compound (*asamāsa*) or a compound (*samāsa*)? If it were a non-compound, then because the word *yoga* is masculine, its designation in the feminine gender would be improper, and grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the word *ṣaṣṭhī* would not be achieved, since *yoga* would not be in the genitive case. Therefore, it must be a compound. Is it a *tatpuruṣa* or a *bahuvrīhi*? If it were a *tatpuruṣa*, then the two aforementioned defects would apply, as well as the undesirable consequence of the elision (*luk*) of the locative case-ending. If it were a *bahuvrīhi*, even so the elision of the case-ending would remain unavoidable here. To address this, he says: "*ṣaṣṭhī sthāneyogā*" and so forth.

The meaning has been explained. This is a *paribhāṣā* (technical rule) intended to restrict the application of substitutes, namely: "among those being obtained as substitutes. By this, he shows that this is not an injunctive statement (*vidhāyaka-vākya*), but rather a restrictive rule (*niyamārtha*) stating: "among those obtained through other rules—both those that are the closest (*anantaratama*) and others—it is only that which is the closest that occurs.
For if it were an injunctive statement, it would result in an over-extension even to cases such as *dadhi madhu*.

What, then, is the undesirable consequence here? To the extent that, due to proximity (*sāmnidhya*), those very words *dadhi* and *madhu* would become the substitutes for [the phonemes], and for those two substitutes there would be yet other words *dadhi* and *madhu* which would be their substitutes, and for those others yet others—thus, because of the prescription of an endless succession of substitutes, there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*).

Consequently, there would be no application of words toward the communication of meaning, because the activity of the explanatory treatise (*anvākhyāna-śāstra*) would never cease. For it is only upon the completion of the treatise that those [substituted] forms are employed, and not otherwise; this is the undesirable consequence.

But surely, once the characteristic has operated, its purpose having been fulfilled, it will not operate again? This is not so; for that which was stated applies where an operation is for the sake of a specific purpose. Here, however, the most similar [substitute] is prescribed spontaneously, and thus its operation does not cease. Even if this were a restrictive rule (*niyama*), if it were to restrict those things already prescribed, the statement would be entirely purposeless.

For if one were to say to someone who has already finished eating, "Do not eat," what would that person have achieved by those words? Therefore, the function [of the rule] is fulfilled only when the word is in the state of being acquired, because it functions in conjunction with other rules. Regarding the term "sadṛśatamaḥ" (most similar): this explains the meaning of the word *antaratama* (nearest). Regarding the phrase "arthataḥ" (in terms of meaning), etc.:

from the word *vataṇḍa*, the suffix *yañ* is applied in the sense of a female offspring according to Pāṇini 4.1.108; then, by 4.1.109, there is the elision of the vowel *a*. Then, the compound *vataṇḍī cāsau yuvatiśca* ("she who is both a Vataṇḍī and a young woman") is formed according to Pāṇini 2.1.65 and following.

In that context, when the substitution of the masculine form (*puṃvadbhāva*) is to be applied by the rule beginning with *tatrānena* [Pāṇini 6.3.42], every masculine word would be applicable. However, by this [rule], for the word *vataṇḍī*, which denotes the offspring of Vataṇḍa, the word *vātaṇḍa*—which is semantically the most similar (*antaratama*) to the meaning of "offspring of Vataṇḍa"—is what actually occurs. In forms such as *pākaḥ*, the suffix *ghañ* is used in the sense of an abstract action (*bhāve*).
As for the phrase beginning with *cakārasya*...
According to *Āpiśali-śikṣā* 4.3, "the first letters of the vargas are *alpaprāṇa*," thus the letters *ca* and *ka* are *alpaprāṇa*.

According to *Āpiśali-śikṣā* 4.2, "the first and second letters of the vargas, along with *śa*, *ṣa*, *sa*, *visarjanīya*, *jihvāmūlīya*, *upadhmānīya*, and the two *yamas*, are *vivṛtakaṇṭha*, *āsanupradāna*, and *aghoṣa*," thus they are *aghoṣa*.
Regarding the passage beginning with "of the letter *ja*," etc.:

"The third and fourth letters of the [five] classes (*varga*), the semivowels (*antaḥstha*), the letter *ha*, the anusvāra, and the *yamas*—namely the second and fourth [consonants]—as well as the nasals (*nāsikya*), have their place of articulation in the throat (*saṃvṛt-kaṇṭha*), possess nasal emission (*nādānupradāna*), and are voiced (*ghoṣavat*); they are 'great-breathed' (*mahāprāṇa*)," while [the others] are 'small-breathed' (*alpaprāṇa*).
Examples are "amuṣmai" and "amūbhyām."

In the singular dative case of *adas* and when followed by *bhyām*, the substitution of *yadādi* (the *yatva* rule) applies; then, by the rule "guṇe" [Pāṇini 6.1.97], there is the formation of a single substitute (*pararūpa*) [resulting in *ebhyaḥ*].

By the rule "smai" [Pāṇini 7.1.14], the form *smai* is substituted [for *bhyām* after *adas*]. In the case of *bhyām*, by the rule "supi ca" [Pāṇini 7.3.102], a long vowel is substituted; consequently, for a short vowel, a short *u* is produced, and for a long vowel, a long one. Regarding the phrase "while the word *sthāna* is understood to be present": the word *sthāna* under discussion here indeed signifies "occasion" (*prasaṅga*).
The meaning obtained is this: "When [substitutes] are to be applied in place of those [originals], that which is the most similar (antaratama) occurs.

Now, one might object: where there is multiple types of similarity, the similarity based on the place of articulation (tālu, etc. is stronger; therefore, so that this [specific case] may occur, the word *sthāna*—denoting the place of articulation—is mentioned once again.

If this is so, would it not follow that only proximity based on position (*sthāna*) is specifically adopted here as the criterion for substitution, while proximity based on means such as measure (*pramāṇa*) and the like would be abandoned? This is not a fault, for the connection is made there by splitting the sentence: "In place [of those being obtained], the most similar (*antaratama*) substitute occurs.
In the preceding sentence, the word *sthā* denotes "occasion" or "context" (*prasaṅga*), whereas in the subsequent one, it denotes the physical location such as the palate (*tālu*).
When the connection is thus established through the division of sentences, the inclusion of proximities based on position and other factors is understood in the former sentence.
In the second [alternative], however, there is the relative strength or weakness of those very [criteria].
The term "in the place" (*sthāne*) is a locative case used in the sense of a cause (*nimitta-saptamī*).
By this, the following is stated: where there is more than one proximity (*āntarya*), that which is the most proximate by way of the place as the cause is precisely what occurs.
The mention of the suffix *tamap* is an indicator (*liṅga*) for the distinction between sentences;
for by it, excellence (*prakarṣa*) in similarity is intended to be conveyed.
And that [excellence] occurs only when there is more than one similarity, in relation to another similarity.

And if there were syntactic unity (*ekavākyatā*), then since other types of similarity would have been excluded by the mention of "place" (*sthāna*), with respect to what would there be an excellence of similarity? Therefore, from the inclusion of the term *tama*, a syntactic split (*vākyabheda*) is inferred; otherwise, it would be purposeless. In the word *cetā*, there is proximity by place (*sthānata āntarya*) because the vowel *i* is palatal (*tālavya*) while the vowel *e* is both labio-palatal (*kaṣṭha-tālavya*). However, for the vowels *i* and *ā*, there is also proximity by measure (*pramāṇa*) because they both consist of one mora (*mātrika*). In the word *stotā*, [the same applies].
Here too, because the vowel *u* is labial and the vowel *o* is both guttural and labial, there is proximity (*āntarya*) by way of place of articulation (*sthāna*).
However, between the vowels *u* and *ā*, the proximity is as before, by way of measure (*pramāṇa*).

In that case, if the mention of "place" (*sthāna*) were not repeated, the *guṇa* substitute might sometimes be *a* due to proximity by measure, and sometimes it would be *e* or *ai* due to proximity by place.

Furthermore, because of the mention of "position" (*sthāna*), the *e*-vowels and *o*-vowels alone occur due to the greater strength of the internal proximity (*antarya*) created by position, and never the *a*-vowel.
Regarding the phrase "of the aspirated," "the aspirated," etc.:
the particle *iti* indicates a reason; the meaning is that since the second [consonants] are aspirated, the second [consonants] were expected for the aspirated *h*.

In this manner, in sentences such as "those possessing *nāda* [are] those possessing *nāda*," the sense of a reason (*hetu*) is to be applied. Regarding the statement in the *Śikṣā*, "The sibilants (*ūṣman*) beginning with *śa* are [homogeneous] by virtue of having the same place of articulation (*sthāna*); the second [consonants] are [homogeneous] with *ha*; the fourth [consonants] are [homogeneous] with *ha*": the phrase "the second" refers to the second letters of the classes (*varga*), such as *kha* and so on;
whereas the phrase "the fourth with *ha*" refers to the fourth letters of the classes, such as *dha* and so on.
That which has a common place (*sthāna*) is *sasthāna*.
In the term "*sasthānena*," the third case ending is used in the sense of a qualifier indicating a particular state (*itthambhūtalakṣaṇe*).
The second [consonants] of each group are characterized as *ūṣman* by virtue of their similarity (*sasthāna*).
This means: "Just as their *ūṣman* is similar in its place of articulation, so too these second consonants of the groups are *ūṣmans*.

Alternatively, this is an instrumental case used in the sense of equality; the word "equal" (*tulya*) is to be supplied, and the equality is to be understood as being through the quality of being *ūṣman*.
In this regard, the letter *ha* is a homorganic (*sasthāna*) to *kha*; *śa* is to *cha*; *ṣa* is to *ṭha*; and *sa* is to *tha*.
There is no sibilant (*ūṣman*) that is homorganic to *pha*. Therefore, its nature as a sibilant is specifically characterized because it resembles them.
The meaning is that, just as the letter *ha* is a spirant (*ūṣman*), so too are those [other letters].
Regarding the phrase "possessing resonance" (*nādavataḥ*) and so forth:
by the previously mentioned passage beginning with "the third and fourth of the classes," it was stated that the third letters and the letter *ha* possess resonance.
Regarding the statement "those which are *ūṣman* and possess *nāda*":

the quality of being *ūṣman* for the letter *ha* is declared by the rule "the sibilants (*śādayaḥ*) are *ūṣmans*" (Āpiśali Śikṣā 1.4.8); the possession of *nāda* for the fourth letters [of the guttural and labial classes] is declared by the rule "the fourth letters [are associated] with *ha*" (Āpiśali Śikṣā 1.4.1); and for the third and fourth letters of all the classes, it is by the previously mentioned rule [beginning with] "the third and fourth [letters] of all the classes" (Āpiśali Śikṣā 1.4.5). In this regard, three positions are possible: one position is that both [the substitution of *aṇ* and the *rapara* status] are prescribed for the place of *u* by this [rule].
The second position is that "the *aṇ* prescribed by another rule is subsequently made to have *r* as its final element (*raparatva*) alone by this [present rule].

The third [position] is that "the *aṇ* being prescribed in place of *u* by another rule is, at the very time of its prescription, produced by this [rule] in conjunction with that other rule as qualified by *raparatva*."

In that regard, if the first alternative (pakṣa) is adopted, the acute (*udātta*) and other accents would not apply to the position of *ṛ*, because they would be sublated by this [rule]; in *kṛti* [by P. 6.1.197], the initial acute would not occur; and in *prakṛtam*, once the natural accent (*prakṛtisvara*) has been applied to the initial acute of the first member [by P. 6.2.49], the subsequent rule [P. 6.1.158] would not result in an unaccented (*anudātta*) syllable, nor would [P. 8.4.66] result in a circumflex (*svarita*).

Even if the acute and other accents were prescribed in the place of the vowel (*ac*), nevertheless, since these have no other scope, only an *aṇ* specifically prescribed for the place of *ṛ* would be followed by *ra*.

Furthermore, regarding those other substitutions (*ādeśas*) prescribed word-for-word in place of *ṛ*—such as by other rules like "ṛta id dhātoḥ" [Pāṇini 7.1.100]—the substitution of *ra* for the final element (*raparatva*) would not apply to them. Consequently, forms such as *kirati* would not be established. Now, if the second alternative is adopted, then when a *guṇa* is prescribed for the root *tṛ* before suffixes beginning with *tṛc* and so on, by virtue of its measure (*pramāṇa*) and proximity (*āntaratamya*), a long vowel would result from a long vowel; thus, forms such as *taritā* would not be established.

Furthermore, since there is no specific degree of similarity (*antaratamya*) between the vowel *ṛ* and any particular vowel designated as "vṛddhi" when the vṛddhi substitute is prescribed for the suffixes beginning with *ṇvul*, all vowels designated as "vṛddhi" would apply in alternation.
Consequently, undesirable forms such as *nāyakaḥ* and *stāvakaḥ* might also occur as optional alternatives.
Having observed that these two initial positions are thus defective, he adopts the third position and says: "When an *aṇ* is about to be applied in place of *ṛ*," and so forth.

By this other definition, he shows that at the very time the *aṇ* is being prescribed, this paribhāṣā operates in conjunction with it to prescribe [the substitute] as qualified by the substitution of *r*.

And this is obtained through the recurrence (*anuvṛtti*) of the mention of "place" (*sthāna*) here from two previous instances; for if "place" were to recur here only from the preceding instance, the meaning "in place of *u*" would not be obtained.
But by the second [interpretation], the word *prasajyamāna* [is understood].

For instance: since the mention of *sthāna* (place) in the locative case is being carried over from the context, by its force it becomes nominative (*prathamānta*). Furthermore, this word *sthāna* signifies "occurrence" (*prasaṅga*).

Consequently, when *aṇ* is qualified by *sthāna*—as in "*aṇ sthānam*" (the *aṇ* is the place)—then the meaning that arises is: "*aṇ* only as it is occurring. Thus, [the term] "*prasajyamānaḥ*" [is used].
The phrase "being connected by way of a logical consequence" (prasaṅgena) means precisely that.

As for the word "only" (eva), it functions as a restriction; furthermore, because all sentences possess restriction as their implicit result through the process of exclusion (vyavaccheda), this [restriction] is obtained here as well.

How, then, does this [substitute] become a *sthāna* (place)? Indeed, it does not become a *sthāna* at all; rather, through its connection with that [original], there occurs the designation (*vyapadeśa*) of "place" for it. For example, in the command "Bring in the sticks" (*yaṣṭīḥ praveśaya*), there is a designation of the men by means of their connection with the sticks. But is it not the case that the rule "In place of [something], the most similar [element]" (*sthāne 'ntaratamaḥ*) applies? This is not a fault; for, due to the mark of the *svarita* accent, whichever [element] presents itself in a particular context, it presents itself there as the designator of only that meaning which is capable of undergoing that specific grammatical operation, by virtue of its functional capacity (*sāmarthya*).
Therefore, although in the previous sūtra the word *sthāna* denotes the locus such as *tavādi*, nevertheless here, as it occurs, it functions specifically to denote a contingency (*prasaṅga*).

Thus, because this [sūtra] is not an independent prescriber of an *aṇ* characterized by having *r* as its final element (*rapara*), the defect that existed in the first alternative does not apply here. Consequently, an *aṇ* prescribed by another rule is not subsequently made *rapara* by this [sūtra]; rather, the *aṇ* which is already in the process of arising (*prasajyamāna*) through another rule attains the status of being *rapara* with the assistance of this [sūtra].

Therefore, the fault that exists in the second alternative does not apply here at all. For in the rule prescribing *ra*-substitution for the *ṛ*-vowel, just as the *ṛ*-vowel itself possesses the sound *r*, the substitute likewise possesses the sound *r*.
Consequently, by the principle of closest similarity (*antaratama*), a substitute for the *ṛ*-vowel—which possesses the sound *r*—is one that likewise possesses the sound *r*.
Other [substitutes] designated as *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* are excluded.

If, then, it were to become followed by *r* (*rapara*) only when it was being applied (*prasajyamāna*), then because it would consist of more than one phoneme (*anekāl*), it would follow that it is a substitute for the whole word (*sarvādeśa*). This is not a fault; for the author provides the instruction "he crosses" (*tarati*), from which it is made known that it is not a substitute for the whole word. In the case of "the agent" (*kartā*) and "the remover" (*hartā*):

from the roots *ḍukuñ karaṇe* (Dhātupāṭha 1473) and *hṛñ haraṇe* (Dhātupāṭha 899), the suffix *tṛc* is applied by [Pāṇini 3.1.133]. Then, by [Pāṇini 7.3.84], there is *guṇa*, and by [Pāṇini 6.1.1], there is doubling (*dvitva*).
Regarding the forms *kirati* and *girati*:

from the roots *kṛ* in the sense of "scattering" (*dhātupāṭha* 1410) and *gṛ* in the sense of "swallowing" (*dhātupāṭha* 1411), the suffix *laṭ* is applied; by [Pāṇini 3.4.78], *tip* is substituted; because they belong to the *tudādi* class, *śa* is added; and by [Pāṇini 7.1.100], the vowel *ṛ* is changed to *i*.
Regarding the forms *dvaimāturaḥ* and *traimāturaḥ*: [these are derived from *dvi-mātṛ* and *tri-mātṛ* with the suffix *aṇ*].

The offspring of two mothers, or the offspring of three mothers: by the rule *māturut saṃkhyā-sambhadrapūrvāyāḥ* [Pāṇini 4.1.115], the suffix *aṇ* is applied, and by *ukāraś cāntādeśaḥ* [Pāṇini 7.3.117], the final vowel is replaced by *u*, resulting in *vṛddhi*.
Thus, "kheyam" (to be dug).
By the rule *kyap* (Pāṇini 3.1.111), the suffix *kyap* is applied, and the letter *i* is substituted for the final vowel;
thus, "Saudhātakiḥ. By the rule *sudhāturakaṅ ca* (Pāṇini 4.1.97), the suffix *iñ* is applied.
When the substitution of *ak* for *akaṅ* is made by virtue of that [substitution], it does not have *r* as its subsequent element (*rapara*), because it is not an *aṇ*.

Now, why is that which is an *aṇ* here not followed by *r*? Because it is not the substitute (*anādeśatvāt*). For in this case, the entire complex (*samudāya*) is the substitute, not its constituent part.

This is not a fault. For that which occurs in place of two things specified by the genitive case receives the designation of either one, just as one says, "the son of Devadatta" or "the son of Devadattā. The mention of *al* (the phoneme) is a qualifier of the final [element], not of the substitute (*ādeśa*); otherwise, he would have said simply "of the final" (*antyasya*).
Furthermore, in this context, the substitute is understood to consist of a single phoneme (*ekāl*);
he will state its status as a substitute for the whole (*sarvādeśatām*) in the rule *anyasya* (Pāṇini 1.1.55).
Regarding the phrase "of that which is indicated by the genitive" (*ṣaṣṭhīnirdiṣṭasya*):

even though this is a general statement, because of the governing rule "the genitive [indicates] a relation to a substitute" (*ṣaṣṭhī sthāneyogā*, 1.1.49), it should be understood as referring to that which is indicated by a genitive of position (*sthāna-ṣaṣṭhī*). Otherwise, suffixes such as *ṭit*, *kit*, and *mit*—being prescribed by means of a genitive indicating a relationship with a part (*avayava-ṣaṣṭhī*)—would apply to the final letter of the element. As in the rule: "The substitution of *id* for *goṇī*" (*id goṇyāḥ*, 1.2.50).
This sixth [rule] is interpreted as "the final *al* of the sixth case becomes short": that is, the final vowel of the sixth case ending is shortened.

In the example "pañcagoṇiḥ" (worth five bundles), there is a compound formed by [Pāṇini 2.1.51]: "purchased for five bundles. Then, by [Pāṇini 5.1.37], the suffix *ṭhak* is applied. Subsequently, by [Pāṇini 4.4.1], the suffix *ka* is added. Finally, by [Pāṇini 5.1.28], "there is elision (*luk*) of the suffixes following *adhyardha* and a *dvigu* compound, except when they form a technical name (*saṃjñā*)," there is elision of that [suffix].

If [the rule] "a substitute occurs for the final [element] of that which is designated by the genitive case" (Pāṇini 1.1.52) applies, then because of the continued application of the word "idaḥ" from [Pāṇini 7.2.111], the substitution would apply only to the final letter of that form which is being prescribed as *id*.

Consequently, the form *ābhyām* would not be established. This is not a fault; for by the metarule (*paribhāṣā*) "when there is more than one [substitute], the substitution of the final letter does not take place, except in the case of modifications of reduplication" (Vyāḍiparibhāṣā 62), this will not occur. Regarding the example *hotāpotārau*:
it is a *dvandva* compound of the words *hotṛ* and *potṛ*. When the suffix *au* follows, the substitution of *ānaṅ* occurs, followed by *guṇa* and the replacement of *ṛ* with *ra*.

The long vowel [in *mātāpitarau*] is formed by the rule *aptṛntṛc* (Pāṇini 6.4.11). This is an example for the alternative view in which there is no *ekaśeṣa* (retention of one member) according to the rule *mātāpitarau* (Pāṇini 1.2.70).

If a substitute beginning with *ṅ* (ṅit) applies even to the final letter [of the stem], then the *tātaṅ* substitute would also apply to the final letter; therefore, he says "in the case of *tātaṅ*" and so forth.
In that regard, it is for the purpose of prohibiting *guṇa* in forms such as *cinutāt*, for here there is the application of *guṇa* characterized by being a *sārvadhātuka* suffix.
The purpose [of the word] "from *mṛṣṭa*" is to prohibit *vṛddhi*.

For here, by the rule "there is *vṛddhi* for *mṛj*" (Pāṇini 7.2.114), *vṛddhi* would otherwise apply. Thus, since the *ṅit*-marking of *tātaṅ* has its scope in the prohibition of *guṇa* and *vṛddhi*, when that [marking] has an opportunity [to function], *tātaṅ* becomes a substitute for the whole [stem] by the rule "in place of [the final phoneme], [the substitute] is for the whole" (Pāṇini 1.1.55), because it is subsequent [to the other rules].
The scope for the rule *ṅicca* (Pāṇini 1.1.53) is exemplified by forms such as *hotāpotārau*.

The scope for the rule *anekāl* (Pāṇini 1.1.55) and others is exemplified by forms such as *bhavitā*, where the suffix is not marked with *ṅ*. When both rules would apply—as in *jīvatāt* and so on—the substitution of *tātaṅ* occurs as a replacement for the entire stem (*sarvādeśa*) because it possesses more than one phoneme (*anekāl*) and is further defined by its status as "higher" (*para*) in the sequence of rules. Thus we have *jīvatād bhavān* and *jīvatāt tvam*. Here, *jīvatāt* is derived from the imperative (*loṭ*) by the rule *āśiṣi liṅloṭau* (3.3.173); the *tip* ending is replaced by *uḥ* by the rule *eruḥ* (3.4.86), and then *tātaṅ* is substituted for *tu* by the rule *tu hrostātaṅ* (7.1.35). This [rule *ṅicca*] is an exception (*apavāda*) to the rule *alo'ntyasya* (1.1.52).
In the treatise, nowhere is an operation prescribed by first pronouncing the word *para*.
Therefore, with the intention that this [rule] would thus be without scope, he says: "And where," etc., and "where there is an indication of the ablative case."
By the rule *iti vacanāt* [Pāṇini 1.1.67], where there is an indication by the ablative case (*pañcamī*), an operation (*kārya*) is taught for what follows.
Regarding the form *āsīnaḥ*:

from the root *āsa* in the sense of "sitting" (Dhātupāṭha 1021), with the suffix *laṭ*, the ātmanepada is applied because it is marked with an anudātta vowel; then the suffix *śānac* is added, and *śap* is elided due to the root belonging to the *adādi* class.
In the case of *dvīpam*, *antarīpam*, and *samīpam*:
having analyzed [the compounds] as "that in which waters have gone twice," "waters have gone within," or "waters have come together," they are *bahuvrīhi*s.

The suffix *a* (which becomes *a* by rule Pāṇini 5.4.74, *ṛkpūḥ*) is added as a compound-final suffix (*samāsānta*). Although the suffix *śit* is multiliteral (*anekāl*) due to its indicatory letter *ś*, its separate mention as *śit* is for the purpose of making known the principle that "multiliterality is not caused by an indicatory letter" (*nānubandhakṛtamanekāltvam*).

Its purpose, however, is the non-substitution of the whole (sarvādeśa) in rules such as [Pāṇini 6.1.131] and others. "Position" (sthāna) means occasion (prasaṅga), and its nature has been explained previously. "Extended application" (atideśa) is of many kinds: extended application of the cause (nimitta), extended application of designation (vyapadeśa), extended application of the rule (śāstra), extended application of form (rūpa), and extended application of the operation (kārya).

In this regard, first of all, the transfer of a cause (*nimitta*) is impossible. For the properties such as being a verbal root (*dhātu*), which constitute the cause for the application of a word, cannot—by means of the individual instances (*vyakti*) such as roots—be made to extend to another entity as a substitute. Just as, when it is said, "One should behave toward this Kṣatriya as one would toward a Brāhmaṇa," the cause for the application of the word "Brāhmaṇa" cannot be extended to the Kṣatriya, so too here, because of this impossibility, the transfer of a cause is not resorted to.
Nor is there a transfer of designation (*vyapadeśātideśa*); for [the substitute] is non-different from the relationship between the name and the named (*saṃjñā-saṃjñi*).
For if there were a relationship between a name and its bearer, the use of the suffix *vat* would be purposeless, since that [relationship] would be established even without it.
Furthermore, because [the name] is not the primary factor here, it is not appropriate to rely on the extension of designation (*vyapadeśātideśa*).
For this very reason, the extension of the technical rule (*śāstrātideśa*) is also [inapplicable].
Furthermore, even those two [the substitute and the original] are subordinate with respect to the effect, because they have become constituent parts of it.
It is also improper to resort to the extension of the form [of the original], because it would be fruitless.
For if the form of the original were extended to the substitute, the substitute would be rendered purposeless.

In this case, even though there is an extension (*atideśa*) of the *rūpa* (form), the substitute (*ādeśa*) is not rendered useless, because its purpose is for the sake of being heard after the reduplication (*dvirvacana*).
Therefore, since resorting to another type of extension is improper, an extension of the operation (*kāryātideśa*) is adopted:
"it functions in the same manner as the original element (*sthānin*)."
Because it has the same effect as that [original], according to Pāṇini 5.1.114: *tena tulyam*.
Regarding the phrase "in those which have the substituend as their locus" (*sthānyāśrayeṣu*): this is a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "those for which the substituend is the locus.
Regarding the phrase "in those which do not have fire as their locus" (*analāśrayeṣu*).

Having formed the *bahuvrīhi* compound "ala-āśraya" (that which has *al* as its locus), the negative compound (*nañ-samāsa*) "na aḷāśrayāṇi" (not having *al* as their locus) is formed as "analāśrayāṇi.
To clarify the very meaning just stated, he says: "sthānyalāśrayāṇi," etc. Those for which the substitute (*sthānin*) *al* is the locus are described in that way.

By the term "dependence on *al*," he shows that the expression *alvidhi* found in the Sūtra is a compound formed by eliding the final member of the second word— namely, it is a compound where the first member is *al-āśraya* (depending on *al*) and the second member is *vidhi* (rule), resulting in *alvidhi*. Furthermore, having formed that initial compound, a negative (*nañ*) compound is then made according to the rule for the *mayūravyaṃsaka*-class and others,
resulting in *na alvidhiḥ*, i.e., *analvidhiḥ*.

Furthermore, what is a rule (*vidhi*) based on a suffix (*anla*)? That which depends solely on a phoneme (*varṇa*) is [suffix-based]; however, that which depends on a word-form aggregate (*samudāya*) is not suffix-based. By using the word "action" (*kārya*) as a synonym for the word "rule" (*vidhi*) through its function as an object (*karman*), he demonstrates its status as an object by stating: "it is ruled (*vidhīyate*)," thus it is a "rule" (*vidhi*). "What is the example? is the question.
"The purpose [of this work] is the substitution of the *dhātu* and so forth"—this is the reply.
"Purpose" (*prayojana*) means that by which one is employed; and since one is employed by means of an example, it follows that the answer is in accordance with the question.

But surely, since [the substitution] is to be applied when an *ārdhadhātuka* suffix follows, what is the purpose of this substitute here? To this he says: "In the domain of the *ārdhadhātuka*" and so forth. [The word] "having taken as base" (*prakṛtya*) and so on:
the compound is formed by [Pāṇini 2.2.18] *kugati-prādayaḥ*; then, by [Pāṇini 7.1.37] *samāse 'nañ-pūrve ktvo lyap*, the suffix *lyap* replaces *ktvā*. [The example is] *dadhikam*.
"Prepared with curd" (dadhnā saṃskṛtam) [Pāṇini 4.2.18].
"Of today" (adyatanam):
by the rule "sāyaṃ-ciram" [Pāṇini 4.3.23] and others, the suffix *ṭa* is applied, there is the augment *tuṭ*, and the substitution of *yan* for *ya*.
"akurutām kuru-tam":

this is the *laṅ* (imperfect) of the root *kṛ*. By the rule "tasthasthamipām" [Pāṇini 3.4.101], *tas* becomes *tām* and *thas* becomes *tam*. Because the root belongs to the *tan*-class [Pāṇini 3.1.79], there is *guṇa* strengthening of the root vowel.
Then, by the rule "ata ut sārvadhātuke" [Pāṇini 6.4.110], the short *a* is replaced by *u*.
"The village is our own, the countryside is our own"—here, by the rule "yuṣmadasmadoḥ ṣaṣṭhī" [Pāṇini 8.1.21], the substitutes *vas* and *nas* are applied. [Question:
"What is the purpose of using the term *vat*? [Answer: The intention is that even without it, that meaning is understood, as in cases such as "asaṃyogālliṭ kit" [Pāṇini 1.2.5].

Regarding the passage beginning with "sthāno" and so forth: generally, in this section, sūtras such as [Pāṇini 1.1.1] *sthāne* have been observed to serve solely the purpose of establishing the relationship between a technical name (*saṃjñā*) and that which is named (*saṃjñin*).
Therefore, in the absence of the suffix *-vat*, it is understood that the technical name is being prescribed for the substitute (*ādeśa*) in place of the original element (*sthānin*).
The particle *vat* is used for the purpose of ensuring that this [substitution] is not understood [as applying to the original element itself].
Why, then, is the designation (*saṃjñā*) of the substituend (*sthānin*) and the substitute (*ādeśa*) not desired? He says: "Even its own basis," and so forth.

For a designation exists for the purpose of making known the designated object (*saṃjñin*); it does not itself undergo the grammatical operation, but rather the designated object, being made known by it, [undergoes the operation].

In this context, if the designation (*saṃjñā*) were to belong to the substituendum (*sthānin*), then the grammatical operation (*kārya*) would apply only to the substitute (*ādeśa*) as the designated entity, and not to the substituendum which serves as the basis for the designation.

Consequently, by the rule *vadhādeśātmanepadam* (P. 1.3.28), the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) would apply to the substitute *vadhi*, and not to the root *han*. However, when the suffix *-vat* is employed, this becomes a case of extended application (*atideśa*). Through extended application, the operation associated with one thing is brought about in another; yet, the operation inherent to that [original] thing itself is not thereby negated. For instance, in the extended application "one should behave toward this Kṣatriya as toward a Brāhmaṇa," the operation connected with that Brāhmaṇa is produced in the Kṣatriya.
But it is not the case that the Brāhmaṇa’s own entitlements, such as being the first to eat and so forth, are excluded.

By the word "also" (*api*) in the phrase "even his own entitlements," it is indicated that even those things dependent on another—which are obtained through extension (*atideśa*)—are included in the injunction (*ādeśa*).
This is what is meant by "struck" (*āhata*).
By the rule *hanter luṅi* (Pāṇini 1.2.14), there is the *kittva* designation;
by the rule *anudāttopadeśa...* (Pāṇini 6.4.37) and others, there is the elision of the nasal (*anunāsikalopa*);
and by the rule *hasvādaṅgāt* (Pāṇini 8.2.27), there is the elision (*luk*) of the suffix *sic*.

Regarding the form *āvadhiṣṭa*: by [Pāṇini 2.4.42], there is the substitution of *vadh* for *han*, followed by the augment *iṭ*; then, by [Pāṇini 6.1.64], there is the substitution of *ṣ* and *ṭ*. [Question: "What is the purpose of mentioning the term 'substitute' (*ādeśa*)? [Answer:
This is a relative term, meaning "that which takes the place of" (*sthānin*).

In this regard, just as when it is said, "He is as stout as his father," even without the explicit mention of "son" here, it is understood that he is the son because of the nature of relative terms (*sambandhiśabda*), so too, when it is said "like the original element" (*sthānivat*), even without the mention of "substitute" (*ādeśa*), it is understood that the substitute itself becomes like the original because of the nature of relative terms; such is the intended meaning.
Regarding the phrase "of that which is inferential" (*ānumānikasya*) and so forth:
in rules such as Pāṇini 1.1.56, both the original element (*sthānin*) and the substitute (*ādeśa*) are directly expressed by the word.
In the expression *pacatu*, both the original element (*sthānin*) and the substitute (*ādeśa*) are inferable.
For instance, in the rule *eruḥ* [Pāṇini 3.4.86], it is not actually the phoneme *i* alone that is the original element, but rather the word *ti*;
nor is the substitute merely the phoneme *u*, but rather the word *tu*.
However, the pronunciation of the single parts *i* and *u* is for the sake of brevity.
By means of these parts, it is the whole that is prescribed as the substitute for the whole.
Just as a horned animal is inferred from the observation of its single part, the horn, so too is the word *ti* and the word *tu* [inferred] from their single parts, *i* and *u*.

In this treatise, between that whose connection with an action is perceived directly from the word itself and that whose [connection] is inferred from some meaning, context, or other factor, the former is held to be primary and the latter its opposite. For instance, regarding the rule *[[Pāṇini 2.3.19]]*, the author of the Vṛtti, having cited examples such as "he has come with his son," will state: "In this case, the father’s connection with the action and so forth is expressed by the word, whereas that of the son is merely implied; thus, the son lacks primacy."
And when both the primary and the secondary are present, it is logical that the understanding of the effect applies only to the primary.
Thus it has been said: "It is established because the understanding of the effect pertains to the primary.

For in this context, if the word *ādeśa* (substitute) were not mentioned, then the status of being a *sthānin* (original element) would apply only to that which experiences primacy by virtue of being prescribed as something to be taken up by the term *ādeśa*, and not to the secondary element which is merely inferential.
Therefore, the mention of "substitute" (*ādeśa*) is made so that the status of being "like the original" (*sthānivadbhāva*) may also apply to it;
by this means, even in cases such as *pacatu*, the designation "word" (*pada*)—according to the rule *suptiṅantaṃ padam* (Pāṇini 1.4.14)—is established.

But how is this determined? That by the rule *eruḥ* [Pāṇini 3.4.86], through the medium of its single constituent part, the entire word *tuḥ* is prescribed as a whole, and not merely the substitution of *u* for the mere vowel *i* as it is heard [in the original form]; because in the case of *pacatu*, the grammatical operation dependent on the designation of a *pada* (word) is observed; for that [designation] does not occur without the designation of a *pada*, nor does that occur without the treatment as a *tiṅ* (verbal suffix), nor does that occur without the prescription of the entire complex [as a substitute].

For when that [prescription of the whole] exists, the status of being a *tiṅ* is obtained through the principle of *sthānivadbhāva* (the substitute behaves like the original) which has been established with effort; it cannot be otherwise. This point is settled.

Now, when that which is inferential has been apprehended, how is the apprehension of the other obtained? It is thought thus: the single rule *sthānivat* should be formulated; by this rule, the substitute (*ādeśa*) is understood as the primary element because it is a relative term. Then follows a second rule concerning the substitute, for the sake of the status of being "like the original" (*sthānivadbhāva*) of that which is inferential.
And here, the word *sthānivat* continues to apply.
Thus, the inclusion of what is prescribed by both perception and inference is justified.
The phrase "in the case of a rule concerning a vowel" (*analvidhau*) is a supplement (*śeṣa*) to both rules.

"Regarding *dyupathityadādeśā*," and so forth: the substitutes *aut* (for *div*) and *āt* (for *pathin*, *mathin*, and *ṛbhukṣan*) do not behave as *sthānivadbhūta* when the elision of *su* (*sulopa*) is to be performed, because that [elision] proceeds by depending solely on a consonant (*hal*), and thus does not depend on a vowel (*al*). Why is this stated? The status of being *sthānivadbhūta* has been stated to apply in cases where a rule does not concern a vowel (*analvidhi*); this [sūtra] is for the sake of cases where a rule does concern a vowel (*alvidhi*). In forms such as *paṭayati*, the *vṛddhi* substitution [of *ai* for *a-i*] depends on a vowel, because the vowel *a* is the penultimate (*upadhā*) and is therefore a vowel (*altvāt*).

"Therefore, some say that [the substitute] does not obtain by virtue of what precedes; others say it is for the sake of a restrictive rule (*niyama*), meaning that only when a preceding operation is to be performed does the substitute behave like the original (*sthānivadbhavati*) if it is caused by what follows. Regarding the statement "the mention of *sthānin* is by means of *ac*," he shows by the word "of *ac*" (*acaḥ*) that it possesses the sense of the sixth case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) denoting the locus (*sthāna*).
Regarding the statement "the locative [in *parasmin*]," etc.

The intention is that it is not a genitive of the remote (*parasaptamī*), because the word "para" itself already expresses the sense of "another. Regarding the phrases "in the case of a preceding rule" (*pūrvavidhau*) and "in its domain" (*viṣaye*):

since the subject under discussion is the status of being like the original (*sthānivadbhāva*), it is understood that [the substitute] becomes like the original in the domain of a preceding rule, and not in any other context. This is the meaning.
The term *pūrvavidhi* means "a rule concerning what precedes. This word *vidhi* is derived as either an object (*karman*)— meaning that which is prescribed (*vidhīyate*)—
or as an action (*bhāva*)— meaning the act of prescribing (*vidhānam*).
In this [rule], which functions as a *karmasādhana* (denoting the object), the genitive case in "of the preceding" (*pūrvasya*) is characterized by a remainder (*śeṣalakṣaṇā*).
The meaning is: when an operation is to be performed upon that which is related to the preceding—that is, that which is fixed and has already acquired its existence.

However, in the case of a *bhāvasādhana* (denoting the action), the genitive in "of the preceding" is characterized by its connection to a verbal derivative (*kṛdyoga*), and thus denotes the object (*karmani*).
The meaning is that the operation must be performed upon the preceding [element] which has not yet been established.
That is to say, it is to be applied to the preceding element.

Furthermore, "preceding-ness" here is relative to the substitute (*ādeśa*), relative to the vowel (*ac*), or relative to the cause (*nimitta*), because these very factors—the substitute and so forth—are present in this context.

In that regard, the substitute (*ādeśa*) is proximate due to its being marked with the *svarita* accent, whereas the other two [the elision and the augment] are mentioned specifically in this very rule.

But surely there is a fault in all three cases; how then can "priority" (*pūrvatva*) be maintained in relation to the substitute and the others? For if priority were maintained in relation to the substitute—as in the case of *paṭayati* and similar forms—the status of the original element (*sthānivadbhāva*) would not be established; for in those instances, the elision (*lopa*) is the substitute, and priority or posteriority cannot exist with respect to it.

Because that [elision] is of the nature of non-existence (*abhāva*). It might be argued: "Since there is a sequence relative to the substituendum (*sthānin*) of the elision, that [sequence] will exist even with respect to the substitute (*ādeśa*) by way of that [substituendum], and thus it will be figurative (*aupacārika*). This is incorrect; for when a primary sequence exists—as in the case of *bahukhadvaka* and similar forms—it is improper to postulate a figurative one.

There is no fault, however, if one adopts the view that "the individual instance (*vyakti*) is the word-meaning. For when the individual instance is the word-meaning, the grammatical rule (*lakṣaṇa*) operates with respect to each specific object of description (*pratilakṣyam*).

In that case, if [the rule] were not applicable in instances such as *paṭayati* because the sequence [of operations] is metaphorical (*aupacārika*), then this rule—which has that very subject matter—would be rendered purposeless due to having no scope of application; therefore, this first position is indeed faulty. As for the second [position], however, this fault certainly does not arise.

For instance—the meaning of that rule is: "When an operation (*vidhi*) is to be performed regarding what precedes a vowel (*ac*), that [vowel] behaves as if it were the original substitute (*sthānivat*). And here, because of the statement *na yvābhyāṃ padāntābhyām* [Pāṇini 7.3.3], the substitution of *yaṇ* must occur even before the substitution of *aij*.

Consequently, since there is no "precedence" (*pūrvatva*) of *ai* and *au* relative to the vowel (*ac*), the status of being a *sthānivat* does not apply; and due to the absence of that, the substitutions of *āy* and *āv* for *ai* and *au* would also not be obtained. However, in this context, it is accepted that the term *acaḥ* is in the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhanta*) for the purpose of qualifying the substitute (*ādeśa*), and not in the ablative case (*pañcamyanta*).
In that case, [the substitute] becomes a word ending in the fifth case (*pañcamy-anta*).

However, this is the fault: here, in the form *tanvanti*, the augment *iṭ* would apply to the *upratyaya* due to the substitution of *yaṇ*; for no operation is prescribed here concerning a preceding fixed vowel (*acaḥ pūrvasya*), such that the augment *iṭ* would not occur by virtue of the *sthānivadbhāva* of the *yaṇ* substitution. But in the third alternative, the *yaṇ* substitution itself is what precedes the cause.

When *iṭ* is to be prescribed for that which is established [as a substitute], the status of being a substitute (*sthānivadbhāva*) is obtained, and thus there is no occurrence of the contingency of *iṭ* in the case of *tanvanti*; however, the defect that exists in the first position would also apply here.

In the cases of *vaiyākaraṇaḥ* and *sauvaśvam*, the semivowels (*y* and *v*) also occur before the cause. Now, it might be argued that the status of being a substitute is stated when an operation is to be prescribed for what precedes the cause, and yet here no operation whatsoever is prescribed for the *y* and *v* that precede the cause.

The substitution of *ā* and *y* is not the operation for *y* and *v*; what then? It is the operation for *ai* and *au*. This is not so; for whatever operation applies to *ai* and *au* necessarily applies to *y* and *v* as well, because those two are parts (*bhakta*) of them and constitute their constituent elements (*avayava*). To this it is replied: the fault mentioned regarding the first and last positions does not apply here; because *ai* and *au* are "external" (*bahiraṅga*), since they depend upon a secondary derivative suffix (*taddhita*) and depend upon an entire stem (*aṅga*); whereas *ā* and *y* are "internal" (*antaraṅga*), because they do not depend on the secondary derivative suffix and depend only on individual phonemes (*varṇa*).

Because of the rule "that which is *bahiraṅga* is asiddha with respect to that which is *antaraṅga*" (Vyāḍi 42), the substitutions *āy* and *āv* for *ai* and *au* will not occur [before the application of the augment *iṭ*]. Furthermore, the defect stated regarding the other alternative (*pakṣa*) does not arise at all; for in that case, since everything desired is not accomplished when the term is used in the sense of an object (*karmasādhana*), the term is also resorted to in the sense of an action (*bhāvasādhana*). Consequently, in the case of *tanvanti*, when the substitution of the preceding vowel *a* for the yet-to-be-finished *iṭ* must be performed, the status of being a *sthānivadbhāva* is established.

There is no fault even if [the suffix *iṭ*] is understood as an instrument (*karmasādhana*); for in this case, it is precisely the *yaṇ*-substitute that precedes the vowel (*ac*), and it is only when its application is to be prescribed that [the rule operates].

Indeed, an augment *iṭ* is not prescribed for some fixed element preceding the *yaṇ*-substitute; rather, it is prescribed for the *yaṇ*-substitute itself. However, if it is understood as a state (*bhāvasādhana*), there is no fault; because the *iṭ* is prescribed precisely for that which is not yet established prior to the *yaṇ*-substitution.
Therefore, even in that case, the word *vidhi* must be accepted as having the sense of an action (*bhāvasādhana*). [In the example] *paṭayati*:

the suffix *ṇic* is applied by the rule "one does that, one describes that" (*tat karoti tad ācaṣṭe*), and the elision of the suffix *ṭi* occurs by the rule "in the presence of *ṇi*, the nominal stem is treated like the suffix *iṣṭhan*" (*ṇāviṣṭhavad prātipadikasya*).

Now, an objection: since there is an intervention here, the state of being "prior" (*pūrvatva*) is not possible; this is not a fault, for the word "prior" (*pūrva*) applies even when there is an intervention, as in: "Pāṭaliputra is prior to Mathurā."

But surely, the suffix *ṇic* is introduced after a word governed by the second case (*dvitīyā-samartha*). In that case, since the designation "word" (*pada*) applies by relying on the internal case-ending, and once the rule for changing a final consonant to a voiced one (*jaśtva*) has applied, the form should be *paḍayati*.

If it is argued that the change to a voiced consonant does not occur because of the status of the elided *ṭi* as a *sthānivadbhāva* (as if it were still present), we say no; for there is a prohibition against *sthānivadbhāva* regarding the rule for *jaśtva*. This is not a fault; for in the rule *tad ācaṣṭe*, the word *tat* does not mean "after a word governed by the second case. From what, then? It means "after the object" (*karmaṇi*). How is this known? Because the intent is to specify the meaning.
This is what is meant: the causative suffix *ṇic* occurs in the sense of "he causes that which is designated as an object (*karman*) to be expressed.

Therefore, because the suffix *ṇic* arises from a form not ending in a verbal root (*asu-bandha*), the designation of a "word" (*pada*) does not apply, and consequently, the substitution of the voiced unaspirated stop (*jaśtva*) does not take effect.
Thus, we have *avadhīt*.

In *hanterluṅ*, the word *vadha*—which ends in a short vowel—is the substitute [for *han*] by the rule *hano vadha luṅi* (Pāṇini 2.4.42). Then, by *ārdhadhātukasyeṭ* (7.2.35), the augment *iṭ* is added. By *astisico'pṛkta* (7.3.96), the augment *iṭ* is added to the root *as* and the suffix *sic*; subsequently, by *iṭa īṭi* (8.2.28), there is the elision of *sic*. Regarding the phrase "characterized by having a consonant as the final element" (*halantalakṣaṇā*): because the mention of the term *hal* continues from the preceding rule *vadavraja* (7.2.3) onwards, the *vṛddhi* [vowel substitution] is characterized by having a consonant as the final element.
Regarding the example *bahukhaṭvakaḥ*:

one might object that since it will be stated later that "with respect to a rule concerning accent (*svara*), there is no substitution of the original form (*sthānivadbhāva*)," there is no possibility of *sthānivadbhāva* occurring here at all; therefore, this example is inappropriate. This is not so; for that prohibition is specific: "in the case of accent, lengthening (*dīrgha*), and the elision of *y*, a substitute for an elided element (*lopājādeśa*) does not behave like the original. Now, this is not a substitute for an elided element (*lopājādeśa*), and thus it is not an accent. Consequently, the acute accent (*udāttatva*) of the vowel *a* following the *kh* is not prevented.

By [Pāṇini 6.2.173], there is only the udātta accent on the final syllable of the compound. In the word *praśnaḥ*, the suffix *naṅ* is applied by [Pāṇini 3.3.90] and the following rules: "The roots *yaj*, *yāc*, *yat*, *vat*, *chapa*, and *praccha* [take *naṅ*]."

"Regarding the rule *tuki na sthānivadbhavati*: the meaning is that when *tuk* is to be applied, it does not behave as a substitute (*sthānivadbhavati*). For some maintain that if this were the case, then once the substitution of *śa* for the mere letter *ś* had been made, the *tuk* prescribed [by the rule] would still be heard due to the status of being a substitute; however, this is incorrect. For in this instance, because it is an *antaranga* operation, *tuk* must necessarily occur first by the rule *che ca* [Pāṇini 6.1.71]. Nor does the principle *vārṇād āṅgaṃ balīyaḥ* apply here, because the two operations have different bases (*nānāśrayatvāt*)."

Where a single cause (*nimitta*) results in both a phonemic operation (*vārṇa*) and a morphological operation (*āṅga*) occurring simultaneously, the following principle applies: as in *iyāya*. Here, depending on the vowel *ā*, the rule *abhyāsekārasya* [Pāṇini 6.1.77] would require the substitution of *yaṇ*, while the rule *abhyāsasyāsavarṇe* [Pāṇini 6.4.78] would require the substitution of *iyaṅ*. In that case, because the principle *vārṇādāṅgaṃ balīyaḥ* ("a morphological operation is stronger than a phonemic one") [Vyāḍiparibhāṣā 39] applies, only *iyaṅ* occurs.

However, in the word *praśna*, [the rule for] the nasalized substitute *śā* depends on the nasal [of the suffix], whereas the augment *tuk* depends on the letter *c*; therefore, because they have different bases (*anāśrayatva*), the aforementioned principle does not apply.

Therefore, the augment *tuk* must necessarily occur here. This must certainly be understood in this way; otherwise, it would contradict what the author of the *Vṛtti* will state regarding [Pāṇini 6.4.19]: "Because it is *antaraṅga*, when *tuk* has been applied by [the rule] *che ca* [6.1.71], this substitution applies to that which possesses the *tuk*. Others, however, explain: "In the rule *cchvoḥ śūḍanunāsike ca* [6.4.19], the letter *ch* was taught by one teacher to his pupils as being indicated along with the *tuk* augment (*satukka*), while by another it was taught as being without the *tuk* (*tugvirahita*)."
Regarding the term "of the pure" (*śuddhasya*), both of these are authoritative.

In the case of duality, the member (*aṅga*) is qualified either by the *cha* or the *chv*, or the member is qualified by the letters *cha* and *va*. Among these, in the first position, the meaning is that for whatever *cha* belongs to the member, there is the substitution of *śa*.

This is the meaning of the sentence; furthermore, because the form *satuk* (with the augment *tuk*) is taken as the substituendum (*sthānin*), once the internal operation (*antaraṅga*) of *tuk* has been applied, the rule *nānārthake alo’ntyavidhiḥ* (Vyāḍi-Pāṇini 62)—which restricts substitution to the final letter when the element is not used in its literal sense—does not apply. Consequently, the substitute occurs for the entire aggregate. When the letter *cch* is specified with the augment *tuk* in the rule for *ś*, as in the word *praśna*, then the mention of *aj* is indeed not a counter-example; for in that case, there is no occasion for the application of *tuk*.
But when the stem (*aṅga*) is qualified by the letters *cha* and *va*, then the status of being the substituendum (*sthānitva*) belongs to the stem ending in *cha*.
On this view, it should be understood that in the rule prescribing *ś* (P. 7.1.59), the letter *cha* alone is intended.

However, because the substitution of *tuk* occurs first due to its being an internal operation (*antaraṅga*), the rule regarding the final letter (*alo'ntyaparibhāṣā*) subsequently applies, resulting in the substitution of *ś* for the letter *cha* alone.

When that [condition] has been accomplished, the *tuk* augment ceases due to the absence of its cause; just as in *sthātā*, where once the substitution of *ṣ* has ceased, the substitution of *ṣṭu* also ceases.
In this view, *praśnaḥ* serves as a counter-example for the mention of the vowel (*aj*) in the rule.

If there were here the status of being a substitute (*sthānivadbhāva*), there would be a recurrence of the *tuk* augment because its cause is present, as in *pratyaṣṭhāt*, where the substitution of *ṣṭu* occurs.

The meaning of the rule *tuki nāsthānivadbhavati* is this: with respect to that very *tuk* which had previously been elided due to the absence of its cause, there is no "non-substitution" (*asthānivadbhāva*) when it subsequently reappears; thus, there is indeed a reappearance. Regarding the phrase *pūrvavidhiḥ*:
one might object that if there were such a reappearance of the *tuk* here, the designation of the suffix *naṅ* as having the marker *ṅ* (i.e., being *ṅit*) would be purposeless.

For that [designation] is made either for the sake of vowel-lengthening (*prasāraṇa*) in the case of the root *pracch*, or for the sake of prohibiting *guṇa* in the case of the root *vicch*. In that regard, there should be no vowel-lengthening in *naṅ* for the root *pracch*, because of the specific grammatical exception (*nipātana*) [Pāṇini 6.1.117].

If, when there is the status of being like the original (sthānivadbhāva), there were a recurrence of the augment *tuk*, then it might indeed be for the purpose of prohibiting the *guṇa* substitution; however, since the *guṇa* would not occur simply because the penultimate vowel is not heavy (*alaghūpadhatvāt*), this [prohibition] would be entirely purposeless. It is not purposeless, because it serves to indicate the rule: "The teaching regarding augments is not eternal" (*anityam āgamaśāstram*).

Regarding the knowledge of impermanence within the teaching of the *Āgama*, that which will be stated under [Pāṇini 7.2.36], *snukramoranātmanepadanimitte*—"In the case of *kram*, however, since it falls within the scope of the *ātmanepada* when used in the sense of the agent, a prohibition must be stated when the *ātmanepada* does not occur"—need not be stated. Furthermore, such grammatical indications as *uchi uñche* (Dhātupāṭha 215) and *vicha gatau* (Dhātupāṭha 1424), as well as others, become justified. [The form] *ākṛṣṭām* [is thus established].

From the root *kṛṣ* in the sense of "tearing" (*vilekhane*, Dhātupāṭha 990), with the prefix *āṅ*, the suffix *luṅ* is applied. The *cli* suffix is replaced by *sic*—this being an exception to *ksa* due to the supplementary rule *spṛśamṛśakṛṣatṛpadṛpāṃ sij vā* (Vārttika 207). Then, the augment *am* is added according to *tastām* (Pāṇini 6.1.59), followed by the *yaṇ* substitution and the *vṛddhi* replacement according to *vadavraja-* (Pāṇini 7.2.3). Regarding the form *vaiyāghrapadyaḥ*:
it is a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "one whose feet are like those of a tiger. The final syllable is elided according to [Pāṇini 5.4.138].
In the case of *vyāghrapādi*, since it belongs to the *gargādi* group, the suffix *yañ* is applied; by [Pāṇini 6.4.130], there is the substitution of *pad* for *pād*.
Regarding *ādīdhye*:
because it belongs to the *adādi* class, there is the elision (*luk*) of the *śap* suffix.

Now, why does the elision (*lopa*) not occur before the substitution of *e* for the final vowel (*ṭi*)?
