It would have occurred if, when the rule "in the presence of another" (*parasmin*) were stated, the elision were non-permanent (*anitya*) because it would not apply once the substitution of *e* for *ṭi* has taken place due to the absence of the status of being like the original (*sthānivadbhāva*). However, the substitution of *e* for *ṭi* is permanent (*nitya*) because it applies whether [the elision] has been performed or not.
Therefore, that [substitution] occurs first. Thus: "he gauḥ."

Because the [suffix] is marked with the indicator *ṇ* by the rule *goto ṇit* [Pāṇini 7.1.90], there is *vṛddhi* [vowel strengthening] of the *sarvanāmasthāna* [case ending] by the rule *vṛddhir eci* [Pāṇini 7.2.115].
The phrase "when the elision of the vocative suffix (*sambuddhi*) is to be performed" is [governed] by the rule *sambuddhau ca* [Pāṇini 6.1.69].
Regarding the term "bābhravyasya": [it is derived] from *babhru* as its offspring (*apatyam*).

By the rule *madhubabhvorbāhṛṇakauśikayoḥ* [Pāṇini 4.1.106], the suffix *yañ* is applied; then, by the rules [6.4.146] and [6.1.79], the substitution of *vānta* (the *au* of *yañ*) occurs, followed by the initial *vṛddhi* increment, resulting in the form *bābhravya*. Once established as *bābhravya*, the elision of the vowel *a* occurs by the rules [4.2.114] and [6.4.148].
[The statement] "the substitute *ava* is not treated as if it were the original element (*sthānivat*)" [is made].

Now, one might object: even if the status of being a *sthānivadbhāva* (substitution of the original element) did not apply, the rule "an operation conditioned by a specific phonetic combination (*saṃnipāta*) is not a cause for the destruction of that combination" (Vyāḍi’s Paribhāṣā 12) would mean that the elision of *y* (*yalopa*) should simply not occur here. For instance, since the [suffix] *yak* obtained its very existence through the substitution of *av* for *ā*, it is unable to subvert that [combination]. This is not so; for in this case, it is the entire aggregate (*saṅghāta*) that is characterized by the *saṃnipāta*, not the individual consonant (*hal*). Or, even if that [consonant] were characterized by the *saṃnipāta*, there would still be no fault, because the *paribhāṣā* regarding operations conditioned by a specific phonetic combination is not of universal application (*anitya*).
However, its impermanence (*anityatva*) will be made known by the rule *na lopaḥ supsvara* [Pāṇini 8.2.2] and others. Regarding the form *naidheyaḥ*:

from the root *ḍudhāñ* preceded by the prefix *ni-* (Dhātupāṭha 1092), by [Pāṇini 3.3.92], there is the elision of the long *ā*; with *nidhi* thus established, the suffix *ḍhak* is applied by [Pāṇini 4.1.122], which requires a base consisting of two syllables.

But surely, since a genitive compound (*pañcamī-samāsa*)—namely *pūrvasmād vidhiḥ* = "an operation [occurring] after what precedes"—is also intended, there ought to be the status of being a substitute (*sthānivadbhāva*) even when an operation is to be performed after what precedes; for he will state under [Pāṇini 7.3.50]: "In the case of *māthitikaḥ* (meaning 'one whose merchandise is *mathita*'), once the suffix *ya* has been elided by [Pāṇini 4.3.134], the substitution of *ka* for *ika* would be obtained by the status of being a substitute according to [Pāṇini 7.3.51: *isusuktāntāt kaḥ*]."

A rule characterized by a combination [of causes] is not a cause for its own subversion, because the elision of the letter *a* possesses the status of being "as if it were the original" (*sthānivat*); for it is stated that "even with respect to a preceding operation, [an element] is treated as if it were the original."

Thus, since by this rule the status of being a *sthānivadbhāva* (as if occupying the original position) occurs even for an operation based on what precedes [the *ādeśa*], one might argue that in cases such as "he gauḥ" (*he gauḥ*), the *sthānivadbhāva* must necessarily apply, and therefore these counter-examples (*pratyudāharaṇa*) are incorrect. This is not a fault; for in cases such as these, the *sthānivadbhāva* indeed applies, yet these are not improper counter-examples because the *sthānivadbhāva* applies only when an operation is to be performed based on what precedes [the *ādeśa*], and in these instances, that condition is absent.

For this very reason, because it is non-eternal (*anitya*), this [augment *iṭ*] is subordinate (*apradhāna*); thus, in the commentary on this sūtra, it was not presented as coming from the preceding rule in order to demonstrate that very subordination. But how is its non-eternality determined? It is determined by the inclusion of the term *seṭ* in [Pāṇini 6.4.52]. This is done for the following purpose: so that when *iṭ* has been applied, the elision of the *ṇi*-affix may take place.

For if the elision of the *ṇi*-affix were to occur while *iṭ* had not yet been applied, then in the case of *kāritam*, the augment *iṭ* would not occur, due to the prohibition [of *iṭ*] by the rule *ekācaḥ* (Pāṇini 7.2.10).

And so it will be stated there: "What is the purpose of [the word] *seṭ*? [Consider] *saṃjñāpitaḥ paśuḥ*. By the rule *sanīvantardha* [Pāṇini 7.2.49], the augment *iṭ* is optionally applied to the root *jñap*. Then, by the rule *yasya vibhāṣā*, there is a prohibition of *iṭ* in the case of the *niṣṭhā* suffixes.
Now, if the word *ekāc* (having one vowel) continues to apply there, then in the case of the *niṣṭhā* suffix, [one might think] 'here the augment *iṭ* must necessarily occur'."
The mention of *seṭ* would be redundant; it is included for the purpose of determining the time [of its application].

It is intended so that the elision of *ṇi* may occur once the augment *iṭ* has been applied. For if that elision of *ṣṭi* were not performed, then in the case of *kāritam*, the prohibition [of *iṭ*] by the rule "after a root that is monosyllabic in the original statement and has an anudātta vowel" (Pāṇini 7.2.10) would apply to the augment *iṭ*.

And if the status of being a substitute (*sthānivadbhāva*) were always to apply when an operation is to be performed based on what precedes [the elided element], then, since the elision of *ṇi* would be subject to that status, there would be no occasion at all for the prohibition of *iṭ* due to the word having more than one vowel; thus, he would not have included the mention of "seṭ" (having the augment *iṭ*), yet it is indeed included. Therefore, it is understood that "the status of being a substitute is not constant with respect to an operation based on what precedes."

Therefore, in cases such as *gaur-* (cow), when an operation (*vidhi*) is to be performed based on what precedes, the status of being a substitute (*sthānivadbhāva*) does not apply. Now, what is the purpose of including the term "operation" (*vidhi*), since the desired result would be established by the phrase "of what precedes" (*pūrvasya*) alone? For one might argue that the genitive case will be understood in relation to the operation—meaning "when an operation is to be performed on what precedes. This is not correct; for if the term "operation" were absent and it were simply said "of what precedes" (*pūrvasya*), then if it were indeed said "of what precedes," the status of being a substitute would not apply to an operation based on what precedes.
Conversely, if it were said "based on what precedes" (*pūrvasmāt*), the status of being a substitute would not apply to an operation performed on what precedes.

Since both a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*) and an ablative compound (*pañcamīsamāsa*) are obtained when the word *vidhi* is included, it is established in all cases. Therefore, the inclusion of the word *vidhi* must be made for the sake of these two compounds. Here too, the word *vidhi* functions as both an abstract noun (*bhāvasādhana*) and an object noun (*karmasādhana*), and it is connected with each [of the two terms] individually.

In this regard, as appropriate, in some cases it is understood as an abstract action (*bhāvasādhana*), and in others as an object (*karmasādhana*). Among these, in the rule concerning reduplication (*dvirvacana*), it is an abstract action; for in that case, only that [action] is to be prescribed, since there is no further operation to be performed upon that which is already established. But elsewhere, it is an object.

For in that case, since other operations are prescribed for the final element of a word (*padānta*) and so forth when it is situated there—as in "kau staḥ" (where do they two stand? and "yau staḥ" (which two stand?)—the substitute [of *as*] would have to be treated as the original (*sthānivat*) when the operations of *ā* substitution and *yaṇ* substitution are to be applied, following the rule of *tas* in the present tense (*laṭ*) of the root *as*, with the elision of *śap* due to its belonging to the *adādi* class. But how could it be treated as the original, given that grammar is employed solely for the refinement (*saṃskāra*) of words? A word such as "staḥ" is refined independently of any other word; therefore, with respect to an operation concerning what precedes a vowel that has not been previously modified, there must be the status of being the original (*sthānivadbhāva*).

Furthermore, this type of phenomenon is not possible within a word-formation (*pada-saṃskāra*) that is independent of other words; for when a word such as *staḥ* is being formed, another word such as *kāu* is not in proximity.

Now, is this a royal decree—that the grammatical instruction (*śabdānuśāsana*) must be performed solely for the sake of word-formation? Or is this the intention of the author of the treatise itself? If you ask this, the answer is no; for by the rule *yuṣmadyupapade madhyamaḥ* [Pāṇini 1.4.105], which prescribes the second person (*madhyama-puruṣa*) when *yuṣmad* and so forth are in apposition, the author has indicated that this treatise is also employed for the sake of sentence-formation (*vākya-saṃskāra*).

In this context, having first established the word *kau* and so forth, when the refinement (*saṃskāra*) of the word *staḥ* and the like is being performed, the rule of "substitution for the original" (*sthānivadbhāva*) would apply because the vowel *au* and so on would precede that which was not previously prescribed.

Therefore, a prohibition is stated. Now, one might object: even if the rule of substitution for the original is prohibited in cases such as *dadhyatra*, since the external replacement (*yaṇādeśa*) is considered unestablished (*asiddha*), the internal reduplication (*dvirvacana*) should not occur.
Why, then, does he say: "It occurs by virtue of this specific statement"?

Nor can it be argued that "because of the prohibition of *sthānivadbhāva*, the rule *asiddhaṃ bahiraṅgam* (Vyāḍi-Pāṇini 42) does not apply. This objection is invalid because the prohibition of *sthānivadbhāva* serves a purpose in cases where both [operations] depend on a single word, such as in *paṭvyau*, *paṭvyaḥ*, *śucyau*, *śucyaḥ*, and so forth. In these instances, since the prohibition of *sthānivadbhāva* is meaningful, there is no fault. Indeed, reduplication (*dvirvacana*) alone is *bahiraṅga*, because it depends upon many factors.
Likewise, the three rules—"hrasva," "uttarasya yaro 'naci," and "aco rahābhyām"—require that [the preceding vowel];
whereas the substitution of *yaṇ* (yaṇādeśa) requires only two: "iko 'ci. Regarding the word "vare":
surely, since this is a compound, there ought to be elision (*luk*) of the locative case ending?
How, then, is there the designation "in *vare*"? For this very reason, by virtue of a specific grammatical irregularity (*nipātana*), there is no fault in the absence of elision (*aluk*).
Others, however, explain that there is an elision of the vowel *ī* here (*īkāra-praśleṣa*).

And they establish the connection as follows: "In the case of a substitute for *aj* (a vowel) occurring in *vare*, it is not like the original (*na sthānivat*) with respect to a rule [concerning] *na*, nor is it like the original with respect to a rule [concerning] *ī*."

Therefore, in the case of *āmalakyāḥ phalam* ("the fruit of the *āmalaka* tree"), the suffix *mayaṭ* is applied by the rule *vṛddha-śarādibhyaḥ* [Pāṇini 4.3.142]. By the rule *tasya* [Pāṇini 4.3.163], there is elision (*luk*) of that suffix. Then, when the feminine suffix *ṅīṣ*—characterized by the *gaura-* group—is elided by the rule *ataḥ* [Pāṇini 1.2.49], the elision of the final vowel would follow by the rule *yasyeti ca* [Pāṇini 6.4.148] due to the status of that [elided suffix] as if it were still present (*sthānivadbhāva*).
However, because the prohibition of *sthānivadbhāva* applies with respect to an operation conditioned by a following long *ī*, this elision does not occur.

But surely it has been stated that "a substitute for a vowel (aj-ādeśa) caused by a subsequent element (para-nimittaka), as well as an elision (lopa), is treated as the original (sthānivat) in a rule concerning a preceding element"; and since there is no sequence (paurvāparya) involving an elision (luk), the status of being *sthānivat* will not occur here [in the case of *luki*]. Therefore, the insertion of the vowel *i* (*ikāra-praśleṣa*) is useless.
[Objection: Even in the case of an elision (*lopa*), there is no sequence; thus, in forms such as *paṭayati*, the status of being *sthānivat* would likewise not occur. [Response:
If, in that case [of *luk*], a sequence is possible by way of the original element (*sthāni-dvāraka*), then it should be the same here as well.

However, those who do not accept the elision (*praśleṣa*) of the vowel *ī* perform a split of the rule (*yogavibhāga*) for the sake of deriving the form *āmalakam*—meaning "the modification (*vikāra*) of the *āyalakya* fruit"—as follows: [The word] *yāyāvaraḥ*:

from the sense "he goes excessively," the suffix *yaṅ* is applied by the rule *dhātor ekācaḥ* [Pāṇini 3.1.22], followed by reduplication, shortening of the reduplicated syllable, lengthening by the rule *yaṅo 'ci ca* [7.4.30], and then the suffix *varac*. Once the *at* (the *a* of the reduplication) has been elided by the rule *ato lopaḥ* [6.4.48], the *yakāra* is dropped by the rule *ato lopaḥ* [6.4.48]. This elision of *at* is caused by a subsequent factor (*paranimittaka*), because it is prescribed when an *ārdhadhātuka* suffix follows.

If the elision (*lopa*) of *at* is caused by what follows (*paranimittaka*), then the objection arises: "In the rule *aco yat* [Pāṇini 3.1.97], why is there the mention of *ac*, since you will state that *ṇyat* follows bases ending in a consonant? Having raised this objection, [the author] will later state: "So that it may apply even to those which were previously vowel-ending—such as *ditsyaṃ* and *dhitsyam*. This would be contradictory; for when the elision of *at* is caused by what follows, a derivation with *yat* cannot possibly occur from what was previously a vowel-ending, because the elision of *at* did not exist prior to its production. And its non-existence is due to the absence of the subsequent cause. [Response: There is no contradiction, because there is a difference between the two positions.

In this context, the term *ārdhadhātuke* (in an *ārdhadhātuka* suffix) continues to apply. There are two positions regarding this: that it is a locative of domain (*viṣaya-saptamī*), and that it is a locative of sequence (*parasaptamī*). When there is an intention to express the *ārdhadhātuka* category in its generality, a temporal sequence between generalities is not possible; therefore, it is a locative of domain. However, when there is an intention to express specific instances of the *ārdhadhātuka*, a temporal sequence between those instances is possible; therefore, it is a locative of sequence.

When the priority or posteriority of the general category (*sāmānya*) is intended by means of its individual instances (*vyakti*), even then the locative of reference (*parasaptamī*) alone is used. In that regard, according to the first position, when an *ārdhadhātuka* suffix is the object [of application], the elision of *at* occurs prior to the arising [of the suffix]; in the other case, however, it occurs after that [suffix] has arisen.
In this context, the purpose of the mention of *ac* in the rule *aco yat* (Pāṇini 3.1.97) will be explained with reference to the first position;
whereas what was stated here—that the elision of *at* is conditioned by a subsequent factor—refers to the other position.

Therefore, there is no contradiction because the objects [of the two rules] are different. However, in the view that the locative case is *para-saptamī* (referring to what follows), the mention of *ac* there should be understood as being solely for the sake of clarity. How, then, is it known that the *para-saptamī* view is also intended there? It is known from the inclusion of the phrase beginning with "ity-ādi" (in Pāṇini 6.4.149).
For that [mention of *ac*] is made for this purpose: so that it should not be understood [as applying only] to that which ends in a consonant (*halanta*).
For if this were understood [in that way], the suffix *yuc* would not apply in the case of *jugupsanaḥ* and *mīmāṃsanaḥ*, because they would end in a vowel (*ajanta*).

Furthermore, if this [reference to] "ārdhadhātuke" were intended as a locative of scope (i.e., "when an ārdhadhātuka follows"), rather than a locative of sequence (i.e., "after an ārdhadhātuka"), then the mention of "ādi" (beginning) would be useless; for once the elision of the vowel *a* has occurred within the scope of an ārdhadhātuka, both *jugupsati* and *mīmāṃsati* would still be stem-final in consonants (*halanta*).
Therefore, by virtue of the mention of "ādi," it is understood that the view of the locative of sequence is also accepted there.

However, in the view that [the locative] is used in the sense of the object (*viṣayasaptamī*), the inclusion of "and so forth" (*tatrādi*) should be understood as being for the sake of clarity alone. As for the examples "itching" (*kaṇḍūtiḥ*), "one who wishes to act" (*cikīrṣakaḥ*), and "one who wishes to take" (*jihīrṣakaḥ*):
the suffix *ṇvul* is applied to the words *cikīrṣa* and *jihīrṣa*.
"Of *śiṣ* and *piṣ*"— that is,
of *śiṣ* (Dhātupāṭha 1452) meaning "to distinguish" and *piṣ* (Dhātupāṭha 1453) meaning "to crush.
[This applies] when the doubling (*hitva*), the substitution of *dhi* for *adhi* (*adhitva*), the change of *s* to *ṣ* (*ṣṭutva*), and the change of *s* to *j* (*jaśtva*) have occurred.
When the substitution of *hi* for *se* is made by [Pāṇini 3.4.87], the substitution of *dhi* occurs by [6.4.101];
then, by [8.4.41], there is the substitution of *ṣṭu*, and by [8.4.53], the substitution of *jaś*.

But surely, in this case, there is no possibility of the application of *sthānivadbhāva* (the status of being like the original) at all; for it is stated that "when there is an operation concerning what precedes an *ac* (vowel) that has not been [previously] enjoined (*anādiṣṭāt*), one becomes like the original (*sthānivadbhavati*)," and yet the nasal (*am*) does not precede such an *ac*. So why is there a prohibition? This is not a fault; because the original (*sthānin*), the letter *n*, possesses the quality of preceding [the vowel] even with respect to that which has not been enjoined, its substitute—the *anusvāra*—is also understood, by virtue of *sthānivadbhāva*, to precede the *ac* that has not been enjoined. [This is illustrated by the example] *śiṣanti*, etc.

But for what purpose is another example introduced, since it would have been more appropriate to cite the very example already mentioned, namely *śiṇḍhi* and so forth? He thinks as follows: if that same example were cited, then one might fall into the error of thinking that wherever there is a *parasavarṇa*, there must necessarily be an *anusvāra*, because it is precisely in those cases that the *parasavarṇa* is prescribed. Consequently, since the prohibition of *sthānivadbhāva* (the treatment of a substitute as the original) applies by necessity to the rule for *parasavarṇa*, it would follow that the prohibition of *sthānivadbhāva* has already been established for the rule for *anusvāra* as well; thus, someone might think that the separate mention of *anusvāra* need not be made. To prevent this misconception, another example is provided.

Therefore, that alone is a suitable example where the *parasavarṇa* substitution is not possible, namely: *pratidivnā*. This form is derived from the root *div* with the suffix *kanin* according to the rule *kaninyuvṛṣi* etc. (*Dhātupāṭha* 6.51). [The mention of] *hali ca* [is for this purpose].
The rule *upadhāyāñca* [Pāṇini 8.2.78] has been written here by modern scribes out of negligence;
for indeed, regarding *upadhāyāñca* [8.2.78], he will state later: "But in the case of *pratidīvna*, there is lengthening by [the rule] *hali ca* [8.2.77].

Now, even if the status of being a substitute (*sthānivadbhāva*) is prohibited, one would expect the prohibition of lengthening here by the rule *na bhakurchurām* [8.2.79]; so why does he say, "It occurs because of this specific statement"?

Nor can it be assumed that the prohibition [of *sthānivadbhāva*] does not apply here by virtue of the prohibition of *sthānivadbhāva* itself; for the prohibition of *sthānivadbhāva* serves a purpose in the case of *pipaṭhīḥ*.

For in this case, when *kvip* is applied to *pipaṭhiṣati*, after the elision of *a* (*ato lopaḥ*) and the substitution of *ru* (*rutvam*), since the substitution of *ru* is "as if not yet established" (*pūrvatrāsiddham*) according to Pāṇini 8.2.1, the substitution of *ṣ* (*ṣatva*) is likewise not established. If the *sthānivadbhāva* were not prohibited, then, because of the elision of the vowel *a* being as if it were still present (*sthānivadbhāvāt*), the rule governing the lengthening of a *bha*-stem ending in *r* or *v* (Pāṇini 6.4.157) would be prohibited by the governing context of Pāṇini 8.2.76.
And this [word] ending in *ra* and *va* is not designated as *bha*; rather, it ends in *na*.
Thus, "sagdhiḥ" is a descriptive compound (*viśeṣaṇasamāsa*) meaning "equal enjoyment" (*samānā gdhiḥ*). The substitution of *sa-* for *samāna-* is according to [Pāṇini 6.3.84].
Regarding *babdhām*:

from the root *bhas* in the sense of "devouring" or "shining" (*dhātupāṭha* 1100), by [Pāṇini 8.4.54], the *jaś*-substitution for the *bha*-sound of the reduplication becomes *ba*. Regarding *cakṣatuḥ* and *jakṣuḥ*:

by [Pāṇini 2.4.40], there is the substitution of *ghas* [for *ad*]; then, by [Pāṇini 7.4.62], the *cutva*-substitution for the *gha*-sound of the reduplication becomes *jha*; and as before, its *jaś*-substitution becomes *ja*.
Regarding the substitution of *ghasl* in the plural, it is by the rule "for *luṅ* and *san*, *ghasl*" [Pāṇini 2.4.37]. For example: *bahukhaṭvakaḥ*.

In this case, because of the status of being "as if the original" (*sthānivadbhāva*), the acute accent (*udāttatva*) does not apply to the letter *kh*. Rather, by [Pāṇini 6.2.173], it applies only to the vowel *a* of the word *tv-*. Thus we have *kiryoh*, *giryoh*.
Furthermore, by [Pāṇini 8.2.76] and [8.2.77], the lengthening (*dīrghatva*) does not occur.
And this has been stated by relying on the position that words are derived (*vyutpatti-pakṣa*), where the words *kiri-* and *giri-* are derived according to the rule *kṛgroricca* [Uṇādi 2.24].

However, under the position that words are not derived (*avyutpatti-pakṣa*), even though the status of being a substitute (*sthānivadbhāva*) does not apply, the lengthening of the vowel does not occur at all because they lack the status of being verbal roots (*dhātutva*).

Thus, relying on the position that words are not derived, he will state under the rule *upadhāyāñca* [Pāṇini 8.2.78]: "The *uṇādi*-derived items are un-derived nominal stems (*prātipadika*); therefore, there is no lengthening in cases such as *kiryoh* and *giryoh*."

Regarding the word "vāyvoḥ," the elision of *y* (by rule P. 6.1.66) does not occur. Previously, an extension (*atideśa*) of the grammatical operation was established; however, this [present rule] is now commenced for the purpose of extending the form itself.

Alternatively, according to the view that [the reduplication] occurs before the cause, a prohibition regarding the rule for reduplication would have applied by the immediately preceding sūtra; therefore, the commencement of this [present rule] should be understood as intended to counteract that.
In the rule [Pāṇini 1.1.59], both locative endings refer to terms in apposition (*samānādhikaraṇa*).
Therein, *aj* is the qualificand (*viśeṣya*), and reduplication (*dvirvacana*) is the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*).
The purpose of this relationship between qualifier and qualificand will be demonstrated in the counter-example *dudyūṣati*.
But how, then, is it expressed by the word *dvirvacana* (reduplication)? Because it is the cause (*nimitta*) of reduplication.
For this very reason, the author of the *Vṛtti* says: "when an *ac* vowel is the cause of reduplication.
Indeed, a thing receives the designation of its cause, just as, for example, [the term] *āyuṣya* is applied to *ghṛta* (clarified butter).

Since this [term *ajādau*] is also a locative of the subsequent (*parasaptamī*), it should be understood as "in that which begins with an *ac* vowel," according to the rule *yasmin vidhis tadādāv algrahaṇam* (Vyāḍi-Pāṇini 127).

Furthermore, because the word *parasmin* is the subject under discussion, it is understood as "in a subsequent [element] beginning with an *ac* vowel. Alternatively, since reduplication (*dvirvacana*) is a cause for qualifying a suffix, the mention of "reduplication" brings the suffix (*pratyaya*) to mind; thus, it is understood that the suffix must begin with an *ac* vowel.

If, then, a substitute for a vowel beginning with *ra* (i.e., *r*) behaves like its original (*sthānivat*) when it occurs before a vowel beginning with *ra*, then the form *papau* would not be established, because the substitute there does not occur before a vowel beginning with *ra*; rather, it occurs before a vowel (*ac*) itself. [Response: Even here, by virtue of "designation-like behavior" (*vyapadeśivadbhāva*), the status of beginning with *ra* exists, so there is no fault.

[Objection: In that case, this would not be established: *cakratuḥ*. For the substitution of *yaṇ* is prescribed only before a vowel (*ac*), and not before something beginning with *ra*. [Response: This is not a fault; for the substitution of *yaṇ* which is prescribed here before a vowel (*ac*) certainly occurs even before something beginning with *ra*.

If a substitute for a vowel (ac) were to behave like its original (sthānivat) whenever there is a cause for reduplication (dvirvacana), then it would remain so in every state, even after the reduplication has already occurred; therefore, he says: "only when the reduplication is to be performed.
By the word *eva* ("only"), he shows that the status of being a substitute does not exist at any time other than the time of the act of reduplication itself.

But how is this obtained, given that there is only one mention of *dvirvacana* (doubling), and by that [mention] the vowel (*ac*) is not specifically qualified? The thought is as follows: the second mention of *dvirvacana* also carries over here from the immediately preceding sūtra. Alternatively, having formed a *ekaśeṣa* compound as *dvirvacanañ ca*, the term *dvirvacane* is used [in the sūtra]. There, by the first mention of *dvirvacana*, the meaning "when a vowel is the cause of doubling" is obtained; but by the second, the meaning "only when doubling is to be performed" is obtained.

Since the status of being a substitute (*sthānivadbhāva*) is prescribed here when a doubling (*dvirvacana*) is to be performed, this [substitution] is understood solely for the sake of the operation of doubling.

When doubling is prescribed for that which possesses a vowel (*sāc*), it does not apply to that which lacks a vowel (*anack*); thus, its purpose as an operation of doubling is appropriate. Its purpose as an operation of doubling is appropriate.

Regarding this [rule] intended for the purpose of reduplication (*dvirvacana*), one might—out of delusion—think: "In cases such as *cakratuḥ* and *cakruḥ*, when reduplication is applied to this [root] which lacks a vowel (*anacka*), the desired form of the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*) is not established. To address such a person, he says: "And this is a transfer of form (*rūpātideśa*).

The word "and" (*ca*) is used for emphasis; the meaning is that it is indeed a transfer of form, not a transfer of grammatical operation (*kāryātideśa*). But how is this certainty reached—that "this is a transfer of form"? From the mention of the vowel (*aj-grahaṇa*).
This is its purpose: so that [the rules] "jeghrīyate" and "dedhmīyate" do not apply here.

Furthermore, if this were an extension of the operation of reduplication (dvirvacana-kāryātideśa) rather than an extension of the form itself (rūpātideśa), then the mention of the vowel *a* (*ajgrahaṇam*) would be useless.
Let there be the status of being a substitute (*sthānivadbhāva*) in this case; nevertheless, there would be no difference whatsoever.

For instance: even if there is the status of being like the original (sthānivadbhāva) here, there must still be the operation of reduplication; and even if there is no status of being like the original, there must still be that operation—since in both cases there is a consonant (sāckatvāt). Therefore, how can this serve as a counter-example? How then does the mention of the vowel *a* (aj-grahaṇa) become purposeful? If this were a substitution of form (rūpādeśa), such that when the form of *ra* is extended [to other vowels], the mention of *a* were not made, then even here, since the form would be extended, there would be reduplication of *dhrā* and *dhmā*, and thus an undesired form of the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsarūpa*) would result.
Therefore, it is determined that this is a transfer (atideśa) of form because of the mention of the letter *a*.

If this is so, the suffix *vat*—which is based on a distinction [between the original and the substitute]—would not apply; for since the original element (*sthānin*) itself has merely regained its own form, how could there be a distinction? There is no fault, because the intended distinction of form is based on the fact that these are transfers by virtue of being transfers. To clarify the meaning of what was stated—that "doubling (*dvirvacana*) must be performed"—he says: "restricted in time" (*niyatakāla*).
By the words "when doubling has been performed," etc., he demonstrates that very restriction of time. For example: *jaghnatuḥ*.

By [Pāṇini 7.3.55], there is the substitution of *k* for the letter *h*. Regarding the form *āṭiṭat*: the root *aṭ* takes the causative suffix *ṇic* in the sense of "causing to move"; then the *luṅ* (aorist) suffix is applied, followed by *caṅ* (the reduplication marker). By [Pāṇini 6.1.11] and [Pāṇini 6.1.2], there is reduplication of the second syllable beginning with a vowel. Then, by [Pāṇini 6.4.72], the augment *āṭ* is inserted.
Regarding the passage beginning with *ninaya*:
when, by [Pāṇini 7.1.91], there is no *ṇit*-designation, there is *guṇa*; when there is the *ṇit*-designation, there is *vṛddhi*. As for *jagle* and *magle*:
from the roots *glai* (meaning "loss of joy," Dhātupāṭha 904) and *mlai* (meaning "bending of the limbs," Dhātupāṭha 904), the substitution of *ā* occurs by [Pāṇini 6.1.45].

In the case of the *bhāva* (impersonal) voice, the *ātmanepada* affixes are used; by the rule *liṭastajhayo-reśirec* [Pāṇini 3.4.81], the substitute *eś* is applied. [The objection is: "There would be no hearing of the long vowel *ā*.

When the mention of *dvirvacana* (reduplication) is not made for the purpose of delimiting the time [of application], then even at a later stage the form of the original element (*sthānin*) would still persist, and consequently, there would indeed be the hearing of the long vowel *ā*.

However, the elision of the final *ā* (āto lopa) finds its scope in examples such as "goda" and the like; whereas when the vowel *ā* is actually heard, there would be a *vṛddhi* (vowel strengthening) with the following vowel,
as in "dudyuṣati."

When the augment *iṭ* is not applied in the alternative view by the rule *sanīvantardha* [Pāṇini 7.2.49], then there is *kittva* (the status of being *kit*) by the rules [1.2.9] and [1.2.10], and from that follows *ūṭh* by [6.4.19].
And that *ūṭh* is not the cause for reduplication.

In that case, if *añ* were not qualified as being the cause of reduplication, then even the *yaṇ*-substitution that occurs after *ūṭh* would undergo the treatment of a *sthānivadbhāva* (as if it were the original element).

In this way, the form of the reduplicated syllable would be heard as ending in the vowel *i*. However, when the cause for reduplication is understood to be the following *c* (the letter *c*), then reduplication occurs of the element *dyu*. In that case, through the application of the rules for "remainder of the consonant" (*halādiśeṣa*) and "shortening" (*hrasvatva*), the form of the reduplicated syllable in *dudyūṣati* is established as ending in the vowel *u*. [The sūtra] begins with "non-appearance" (*adarśanam*), etc.

But surely, the words *adarśana* (non-seeing) and *anupalabdhi* (non-apprehension) are general terms for non-apprehension, whereas the words *aśravaṇa* (non-hearing) and *anuccāraṇa* (non-articulation) are specific terms for non-apprehension. For instance, when the words "non-hearing" and so forth are uttered, it is the non-apprehension of sound itself that is understood, not non-apprehension in general; and yet, general and specific terms do not have the same meaning. So why does he say, "it is not a different thing"?
He thinks as follows: even general terms function with reference to a specific instance by virtue of the context.

And here, words are the subject under discussion because they are what are to be explained; therefore, although the terms "non-perception" (*adarśana*) and "non-apprehension" (*anupalabdhi*) are general in expression, nevertheless, by the force of the context, they refer here specifically to the non-apprehension of words.
Here, technical designations (*saṃjñā*) such as *vṛddhi* and so forth have been prescribed for words.

Similarly, here too, the term *adarśana* (non-appearance) itself should have the technical designation (*saṃjñā*) of "elision" (*lopa*). Consequently, since the word *adarśana* would be substituted for [the word *lopa*] in all instances where elision is prescribed, that very [word *adarśana*] would become the substitute. To this he says: "By these words," and so forth. How is this obtained previously? He thinks as follows: from rule 1.1.44, the particle *iti* continues to apply for the purpose of indicating the meaning [of the technical terms].
By this, a restrictive determination (*avadhāraṇa*) is understood, as in: "For action disciplines a substance, not a non-substance.
Even without the instrumental particle (*itikaraṇa*), the designation of the word's own form (*śabdasvarūpa*) is indeed established, as in [P.

1.1.22]. Therefore, by the force of the continued application of the instrumental particle, the meaning "non-appearance" (*adarśana*) which is perceived is what receives this designation, not the word itself. Furthermore, the designation "elision" (*lopa*) is made as a grand one so that it may be understood as a designation according to its literal meaning (*anvarthasaṃjñā*).

*Lopana* means *lopa*; the meaning is non-perception or non-utterance. Furthermore, this term "non-appearance" (*adarśana*) is not itself a form of sound whose nature is non-existence; rather, it refers to its object. Therefore, because the designation is understood according to its literal meaning, this is a designation for the object itself.
If, then, this designation [of "elision"] applies only to an object (artha), there would be an over-extension (atiprasaṅga).
For every word is not observed outside its own domain;
consequently, in the case of *trapu-jatu*, the non-observation of the suffix *kvip* would have to be designated as "elision" (*lopa*).

And this being the case, since the rule *piti kṛti tug* (Pāṇini 6.1.69) would result in the application of the augment *tuk* to a short vowel by the rule *evañca sati* (Pāṇini 1.1.62), he says: "of that which is applicable," and so forth.

Is this technical term (*saṃjñā*) for mere non-appearance? No; rather, it refers specifically to the non-appearance of that which is applicable through either the grammatical system (*śāstra*) or from some other source (*artha*).

Thus, here there is no possibility of the *kvip* suffix in any way; so how can there be the possibility [of its application]? How is this distinction obtained, since there is no mention here of "that which is applicable" (*prasakta*), nor has that been done? The thought is as follows: from the rule *sthānivat*, the term *sthānin* (the original element) is carried over here as well. *Sthānin*, *prasaṅgavat*, and *prasakta* are synonyms. By this, the following meaning is obtained: "this is the designation for that non-appearance (*adarśana*) of what was applicable. [Example: *gaudheraḥ*.
The substitution of *ey* occurs; by the rule [Pāṇini 6.1.66], there is the elision of the *yakāra* that is applicable according to the grammatical treatise.
In the case of *paceran*, the *sīyuṭ* is also [elided] by the treatise.
In other instances as well, the applicability should be understood accordingly.

In the words *jīradānuḥ* and *āstremāṇam*, there is the elision of the *v* in the first member. Regarding *āstremāṇam*: from the root *strivu* (meaning "to move" and "to dry," Dhātupāṭha 1109), which takes the suffix *manin* according to the rule *sarvadhātubhyo manin*, the second singular form is derived by applying the substitution of *e* for the penultimate vowel (*upadhā*) through lengthening, resulting in *āstremāṇam*.
Regarding the phrase "of another, such as an *anubandha*":
this refers to an *anubandha* such as the letter *k*.

By the word "etc. (*ādi*), the *s* of *sīyuṭ* is included. Just as the term "vṛddhi" is a designation for both those things transformed into that state and those not so transformed, so too the designations such as "elision" (*luṅ*) would apply even to that which is not so transformed; consequently, there would be a confusion of technical designations (*saṃjñā-saṃkara*).
For if there were a confusion of technical names (*saṃjñā*), they would become intermingled; therefore, he says: "And because multiple names are prescribed," and so forth.

If these names were to apply even to that which has not been conditioned (*bhāvita*) by them, then the prescription of multiple names would be purposeless, since the accomplishment of all grammatical operations would be achieved by just one name.

Therefore, because multiple names are prescribed, that name belongs only to that specific absence of a suffix (*pratyaya-adarśana*) which was conditioned—that is, brought about—by the utterance of that particular name, and not to any other; thus, no confusion occurs.

In that case, however, the fault of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśraya*) would follow; for instance, non-observation (*adarśana*) qualified by a technical name (*saṃjñā*) must be brought about, and once that non-observation of the suffix exists, it must be brought about by the technical name. To this he says: "And in the rules prescribing [operations]" (*vidhipradeśeṣu ca*), and so forth. That non-observation is prescribed, and for that which is thus prescribed, technical names such as *luk* and so on occur. Since the understanding occurs through the technical name that is yet to come into being (*bhāvinī saṃjñā*), the fault of mutual dependence does not arise. Regarding the word "atti": by [Pāṇini 2.4.72], there is *luk* elision of the *śap* suffix.
"He offers oblations" (*juhoti*). "The *varaṇa* trees. A village situated not far from *varaṇa* trees.

The suffix is elided by [Pāṇini 4.1.83] *tasya* and [4.2.82] *iti lup*, as in the examples *agastayaḥ* and *kuṇḍināḥ*. If the mention of the suffix (*pratyayagrahaṇam*) were not made, then for "many descendants of Āgastya," the suffix *ṛṣyaṇ* would apply according to [4.1.114] *ṛṣyandhakavṛṣṇikurubhyaḥ*.

The descendants of Kuṇḍinī are many; [the suffix] *yañ* is applied according to Pāṇini 4.1.105 because [the name] begins with *garga*. When the elision (*luk*) is effected by the rule "In place of *āgastya* and *kauṇḍinya*, there is *agasti* and *kuṇḍina*" (Pāṇini 2.4.70) before the case-ending *jas*, and *agasti* and *kuṇḍina* are the substitutes for those two words, *āgastya* and *kauṇḍinya*; then, due to this inequality, three substitutes would apply alternately to each of the original bases (*sthānin*) specified in the genitive case.
In that situation, when the elision (*luk*) occurs, it would follow that only the case-ending itself would be heard.

Furthermore, if [the substitution] were to apply to the final letter of the base, then *āgastyaḥ* and *kauṇḍinyaḥ* would result; however, *agastayaḥ* and *kuṇḍināḥ* are what is intended. Even if there were a substitution of *kuṇḍina-ja-* for the word *āgastya-* and a substitution of *āgastya-* for the word *kauṇḍinya-*, the undesired result would still follow.
For it is intended that the form of the word *āgastya-* in the nominative plural (*jas*) is *agastayaḥ*, whereas that of the word *kauṇḍinya-* is *kuṇḍināḥ*.

For this very reason, those two are introduced in the sequence "āgastyaḥ" and "kuṇḍinaḥ. Now, even if by virtue of internal similarity (*āntaratamya*) the word *āgastya* undergoes the substitution of the word *agasti*, and not *kuṇḍina*; and if the word *kauṇḍinya* undergoes the substitution of *kuṇḍina*, and not the word *agasti*—even so, there is no escape from the occurrence of the undesired result. To explain: although in this way "āgastyaḥ" and "kuṇḍinaḥ" are established, nevertheless, when a suffix beginning with *ac* (such as *-añ*) is intended after a word ending in *cha* or *chha* that belongs to the *prāgdīvyatīya* group, the rule [Pāṇini 4.2.114] would not apply because the base (*prakṛti*) has undergone *vṛddhi*.
However, since this designation is prescribed specifically for the non-observation of that [suffix] when a suffix (*pratyaya*) is present, the elision (*luk*) occurs only for that [suffix].

Even when there is an intention to express a suffix such as *parija* and so on, because the elision is prohibited by the rule "there is no elision before a vowel in the case of *gotra*" (Pāṇini 4.1.89), the suffix *cha* is applied after a word ending in a *vṛddhi* vowel.
Thus, "the students of the Agastis" is *āgastīyāḥ*.

However, from the word *kauṇḍinya*, even though there is elision (*luk*), only the suffix *aṇ* occurs by [Pāṇini 4.2.111], resulting in *kauṇḍinyāścātrāḥ*. Therefore, the fault of the absence of the suffix *cha* in that case should not be raised. Regarding the term *pratyayalakṣaṇam*:
it is a *bahuvrīhi* compound where the meaning of another word (*anyapadārtha*) is the effect, [meaning] "that for which the suffix (*pratyaya*) is the characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*)."

With the words "on account of the suffix" (*pratyayanimittam*) and so forth, he states the purpose for the commencement of the sūtra. Now, one might object: "But this is already established even by the rule of *sthānivadbhāva* (the substitute being treated like the original). This is not so; for even an operation based on the suffix (*alāśrayam*) is desired when a suffix is elided, provided it is conditioned by that suffix (*pratyayalakṣaṇam*).
Thus, in the case of *agnicit*, the augment *tuK* indeed occurs, even though it is based on the suffix [by Pāṇini 6.1.71].
[The form is] *agnicit*.

The suffix *kvip* is applied by [Pāṇini 3.2.91]. The elision of the *ti* is performed by the rule concerning *halṅyādi* [6.4.69]; the *śap* is elided because the root belongs to the *adādi* class [2.4.72]. By [8.2.32], *dh* is substituted for *t*. By the rule beginning with [8.2.37], *bhaṣ* (the letter *dh*) is substituted for the *baś* (the letter *d*). By [8.2.39], *jaś* (the letter *g*) is substituted for the *jhal* (the letter *dh*) at the end of a word, so that *gh* becomes *g*. Then, by [8.4.55], *c* is optionally substituted for *g* at the end of a word, resulting in *k*. Regarding the term "suffix" (*pratyaya*), it is understood from the preceding sūtra as "in the present tense."
The ātmanepada suffix is applied by the rule *āho yamahanaḥ* [Pāṇini 1.3.28]. The elision of the penultimate vowel (*upadhālopa*) occurs according to the rule *gamahana* [Pāṇini 6.4.98, etc.].
The substitution of *gh* for *h* is applied by the rule *ho hanteḥ* [Pāṇini 7.3.54].
Regarding the word *saṃgmīya*: from the root *gam* preceded by the prefix *sam*, the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) is applied according to [Pāṇini 1.3.29] *samo gami* etc.;
the substitution of *at* for *iṭ* occurs according to [Pāṇini 7.1.100] *iṭo't*.
By [Pāṇini 7.4.78], there is the elision (*luk*) of the *śap* suffix.

As before, there is the elision of the penultimate vowel (*upadhā-lopa*). It is stated that "the elision of the nasal does not occur" by means of [Pāṇini 6.4.37], *anudāttopadeśa*, etc. Thus, we have *raikulam*.
This is a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*). The form *gohitam* is derived by [Pāṇini 2.1.36], which begins with the rule *caturthī*.

In this case, there is the elision (*lopa*) of the sixth and fourth case endings in the singular number; however, because the substitutes *tvā* and *mā* are prescribed before a vowel (*aci*), that rule relies upon the phoneme (*varṇa*), not the suffix (*pratyaya*). Therefore, since those two [substitutes] are caused by the phoneme, they are not caused by the suffix, and thus [the rules for the suffixes] do not apply. But is it not the case that here the suffix is elided? What then? It is *luk*. This is not so; for the term *lopa* is a general designation for non-appearance (*adarśana*), whether it has been brought about by a specific rule (*tadbhāvita*) or not so brought about (*atadbhāvita*).
Therefore, even *lug* is indeed a type of *lopa*. Regarding the term "that which has *lu*": that in which the word *lu* exists is "that which has *lu*" (*lumān*).
What, then, is this? It is the technical term (*saṃjñā-śabda*) beginning with *lug*.
And this is the instrumental case (*tṛtīyā*): *he tau va*, or [it is used] in the sense of a characteristic mark (*itthambhūtalakṣaṇa*).

When a suffix is elided by that which bears the designation *lup*, the meaning is: "by that reason" (*tena hetunā*) or "characterized by that. Now, from where is this word *pratyaya* (suffix) obtained? Because the technical designations such as *luk* and so on are prescribed specifically for the non-appearance of a suffix, as in the rule: "when a suffix is elided by the word *lup*, that which is the stem (*aṅga*)."

Furthermore, that [suffix] which was the cause for obtaining the designation "base" (*aṅga*) must be understood as depending upon that very same suffix as its condition (*nimitta*). Although it is stated without qualification that "the operation characterized by that suffix does not take place," it is understood—by virtue of proximity—that the specific suffix which was elided by *lumat* and served as the condition for the designation "base" is what is meant by "characterized by that. For example, in the case of *gargāḥ*:
by [Pāṇini 4.1.105] and [2.4.64], there is elision (*luk*) when there is plurality.

In this case, the vṛddhi [vowel substitution] prescribed by *taddhiteṣvalacāmādeḥ* [Pāṇini 7.2.117] does not occur. Regarding the form *mṛṣṭaḥ*: from the root *mṛj*, the suffix *tas* is applied; due to its inclusion in the *adādi* class, there is elision (*luk*) of the *śap* affix; the substitution of *ṣ* occurs by the rule *vraścādi*; and the substitution of *ṣṭu* occurs. Thus, the vṛddhi [prescribed by 7.2.114] does not take place.
Regarding the form *juhutaḥ*:
when the suffix *tasi* follows, after the reduplication (*ślau*) has been applied to roots such as *hu*, the *guṇa* substitution characterized by a *sārvadhātuka* suffix does not take place.
In all cases, that very suffix depending upon which the designation of an *aṅga* (base) arose is itself the cause for operations such as *vṛddhi*.

And here, because no specific [condition] is relied upon, not only is the operation prescribed under the heading of *aṅga* (stem) prohibited, but also that which is prescribed under a heading other than *aṅga*.

Consequently, in the cases of *gargāḥ*, *bidāḥ*, and *uṣṭragrīvāḥ*, the acute accent on the first syllable—though prescribed by [Pāṇini 6.1.197] and its successors—is not applied, even though it is prescribed under a heading other than *aṅga*.
And here, in the case of *atrayaḥ*, there is the acute accent on the final syllable of the *taddhita* suffix, according to [Pāṇini 6.1.159] *kitaḥ*.

"Gargas" and "Bidas"—from these, respectively, the *yañ* suffix is applied according to the rule for the *garga*-class (*gargādibhyaḥ yañ*). Then, by the rule "after *vidada* and others, when not preceded by a seer, the *añ* suffix is applied" (*anṛṣyānantarye vidadibhyo 'ñ*), the *añ* suffix is added; subsequently, [the *yañ*] is elided by the rule "of *yañ*, *ña*, and *ṅīp*" (*yañañoś ca*). [The example] "camel-necked" (*uṣṭragrīvā*) is as follows:
In the case of *pratikṛti*, there is the elision (*lup*) of the suffix *kan* prescribed by [Pāṇini 5.3.96] according to [5.3.100].

In the case of *Atrayaḥ*, there is the elision (*luk*) of the suffix *ḍhak* prescribed by [4.1.122] in the sense of "descendant of Atri" when applied to a plural number, according to [2.4.65], *atribhṛgukutsavasiṣṭha...*.
[The examples] are "five" and "seven."
By the rule *ṣaḍbhyo luk* [Pāṇini 7.1.22], there is elision (*luk*) of the suffixes *jaś* and *śas*. Thus we have *payaḥ sāma*;
here too, by the rule *ato 'm* [Pāṇini 7.1.24].

In this case, although the suffix is elided by *lumat* and the designation of "stem" (*aṅga*) is based on that [suffix], nevertheless, by the rule of "suffixal indication" (*pratyayalakṣaṇa*), the designation of "word" (*pada*) certainly occurs according to Pāṇini 1.4.14: "That which ends in a *sup* or *tiṅ* is a word. For that [designation] is not an operation of the stem alone, but rather of the entire aggregate including the case-ending; indeed, the preceding portion is the stem.
And here, the designation of "word" does not arise by depending on that very same suffix by which the designation of "stem" occurred when it was elided by *lumat*.
Since the designation of "word" is present here, in the form *payaḥ*, the substitution of *r* occurs by Pāṇini 8.2.66.
The *visarjanīya* of [the words] *khaḥ* and *avaṣaṭ* undergo the grammatical operation (*padakārya*) pertaining to a word (*pada*). For example: *pañca*, *sapta*, *sāma*.
Here too, the elision of the *n* according to *nalopaḥ prātipadikāntasya* [Pāṇini 8.2.7] is an operation pertaining to a word (*padasaṃjñākārya*).

Regarding the word "kāryate": here, the *lakāra* (verbal suffix) is in the passive voice (*karmani*) from a causative (*ṇyanta*) root. [One might ask: "Is the suffix not elided by Pāṇini 1.1.63 (*na lumatāṅgasya*)? No; rather, it is because the mention of "elision" (*lopa*) from 6.4.48 continues into this rule [6.4.51]. Therefore, the vowel-lengthening (*vṛddhi*) indeed occurs by virtue of the suffix being present as a formal characteristic (*pratyayalakṣaṇa*). The term "antyādi" is a *bahuvrīhi* compound: that form of a word which has as its beginning the final vowel (*ac*) among the vowels is what is thus described.

Now, one might object that since the word *antya* (last) here requires *ācām* (of the vowels), it lacks the necessary semantic capacity (*asāmarthya*) to form a compound with the word *ādi* (first). This is not a fault; for the word *antya* is a relative term (*sambandhiśabda*). Since relative terms are inherently dependent and thus convey their meaning through such dependence, a compound is permitted even when there is dependence, as in the example "Devadatta’s teacher’s family" (*devadattasya gurukulam*).
[The rule] "the genitive case is used in the sense of selection" (*nirdhāraṇe ṣaṣṭhī*) applies here.

If this genitive case were [intended] for the purpose of selection (*nirdhāraṇa*) by the rule *yataśca nirdhāraṇam* [Pāṇini 2.3.41], then since selection occurs when there is a collection of many, the singular number in the word *acām* would be incorrect; rather, because of plurality, the plural number ought to have been used. Therefore, he says: "The singular is used in the sense of a genus (*jāti*).
The meaning is that it is because the genus is one. [He continues:
"Of the vowels (*acām*) situated together, whichever is the final."

But how is this distinction obtained, given that there is no second mention of the word *aja* here, nor is it the subject under discussion? The thought is as follows: in common usage, selection (*nirdhāraṇa*) is well-established only for things of the same class.
For instance, in the expression "the black cow is the one with the most milk among cows," even without a second occurrence of the word "cow," it is understood to be a cow alone.
Therefore, although there is no second mention of *aja* here, it is determined that only a member of the same class—an *aja*—is being selected.
The final existence is "antya," with the suffix *yat* applied according to the rule for the group beginning with *diś*.
Regarding the term "tadādi": the analysis of the compound is "that (*tat*) is the beginning (*ādi*) of which."
The forms beginning with *icchabdaḥ* are examples of word-forms (*rūpa*).

As for the grammatical operation (*kārya*) regarding the word *iccha*: when the technical designation *ṭi* applies, as in the case of explaining "one who has piled the fire-altar" (*agnicit*), the causative suffix *ṇic* is added; then, by the rule *ṇāviṣṭhavat prātipadikasya* (Vārttika 813), there is elision of the *ṭi* portion, resulting in *agnicayati*.
[Examples of dual endings] are *ātām* and *āthām*.

The grammatical operation resulting from the designation *ṭi* for these two is as follows: by [Pāṇini 1.1.55] *ṭeretvam*, we have the examples of the operations *pacete* and *pacethe*. Now, how can the vowel *i* in *vah* and *mah* receive the designation *ṭi*, given that there is no final element (*anta*) which could be designated as "the beginning of a set of vowels" (*aj-ādi*)? This is not a fault; by virtue of the designation of a thing as being what it is not (*vyapadeśivadbhāva*), it will be designated as both "the beginning" and "the final. In the rule [Pāṇini 1.1.65] *alo’ntyāt*, the two ablative cases are in apposition.

Regarding the phrase "in a collection of phonemes at the beginning of a root, etc.": [an objection is raised] "But surely there is no mention here of a 'collection of phonemes' (varṇasamudāya), nor is it the subject under discussion.
So how is this meaning obtained? [The answer is: Because of the mention of the "final" (antya); it is only the final [phoneme] of a collection that is the *al* [pratyāhāra], not a solitary one.
Therefore, by the mention of "the last" (*antya*), this meaning is obtained: "only an *al*. Precisely because of the use of the particle *eva*, the *al*-aggregate is excluded.
Now, since there is no second mention of the term "*al*" here, why does this technical name (*saṃjñā*) not apply to the *al*-aggregate as well? [The answer is: It is from common usage (*loka*).
In common usage, when it is said of these Brahmins, "Let the one before the last be brought," only the single one preceding the last is brought, not the aggregate.
Even so, why does this designation not apply to a [sound] that is separated by an interval? For the word "preceding" (*pūrva*) indeed applies even to what is separated.

This is precisely because of the worldly analogy: when it is said in common usage, "Bring what precedes the *hrantī*," no one brings something separated by an interval, but rather only that which is immediately adjacent.

If this designation [of *upadhā*] applies only to a single vowel (*al*) and not to a collection of consonants (*hal*), then that which will be stated in rule 7.4.10—namely, "In the prescription of qualities following a *saṃyoga*, the mention of 'having a *saṃyoga* as a preceding element' (*saṃyogopadha*) must be made"—would be contradicted. For if the designation *upadhā* applied only to a single vowel, it would be impossible for a *saṃyoga* (which consists of a collection of several non-contiguous consonants) to possess the status of being an *upadhā*.

There is no contradiction, however, because the *upadhā* status belongs to a member of the *saṃyoga*, and thus the collection as a whole is designated in that way by virtue of the property of its constituent part.

A collective whole is designated by means of its constituent parts; for example, "this city is wealthy. Alternatively, the mention of *upadhā* there should be understood as an indicator that the conjunction [of vowels] has a short vowel (*a*) preceding it.
Forms such as *akāra* are examples of the word-forms.

As for the grammatical operation, when the designation *upadhā* applies to the vowel *a*, there is *vṛddhi* (vowel strengthening) in cases such as *pācakaḥ* and *pāṭhakaḥ* according to Pāṇini 7.2.116.
Regarding the roots *ikāra*, *lkāra*, *bhedaka*, *chedaka*, *vartaka*, and *vardhaka*:
here, the *guṇa* substitution applies by the rule *pugantalaghūpadhasya* [Pāṇini 7.3.86]. Regarding the word *śiṣṭaḥ*:
the root *śāsu* (meaning "to instruct," Dhātupāṭha 1075) takes the *niṣṭhā* suffix; the change of the penultimate vowel to *i* occurs by the rule *śāsa idaṅhaloḥ* [Pāṇini 6.4.34].
For in that context, the term *upadhā* is understood to carry over from the sūtra beginning with *aniditām* [Pāṇini 6.4.24].
The substitution of *ṣ* occurs by the rule beginning with *śāsivasi* [Pāṇini 8.3.60].
[The phrase] "from the whole" (*samudāyāt*) and so forth follows.
[This is] from the combination of the letter *a* and the letter *s*.

The meaning is that the preceding *ś* should not receive the designation *upadhā* (penultimate). For if it were so, the substitution of *it* (the short vowel *i*) would apply to that very [letter]. Why is this [stated]? Because in rules such as [Pāṇini 6.1.77], the relationship between locus and located (*ādhāra-ādheya-bhāva*) in expressions like "before a vowel" (*aci*) is based on proximity (*pratyāsatti*), just as in the expression "a hamlet dwells in the Ganges" (*gaṅgāyāṃ ghoṣaḥ prativasati*).

In this regard, just as that proximity of the *gaṅgā* (the vowel *i*) occurs with respect to the preceding [element], so too does it occur with respect to the following one. Consequently, in cases such as *dadhi-udaka*, it is not known whether the *yaṇ*-substitution belongs to the preceding element or to the following one. Since such a doubt arises, this *paribhāṣā* is commenced for the purpose of providing a restrictive rule (*niyama*).

If it is argued that this [paribhāṣā] is commenced as being within the scope of doubt—meaning it applies wherever there is doubt—then by that logic, *dadhyudakam* would be established; however, this is not established: namely, *dadhya atra*.
But surely this is established even without the paribhāṣā, for there is no doubt here.
In that case, this would not be established: *samid atra* and *agnicit atra*.

For if this technical rule (*paribhāṣā*) were not applicable where there is no doubt—because it would not present itself here—the substitution of *yaṇ* would indeed occur even when there is an intervention. Therefore, an effort must be made so that this technical rule applies even in cases where there is no doubt. This [effort] is as follows: first, the rule *tasmin* (Pāṇini 1.1.66) should be formulated; for by this much alone, the desired objective is accomplished.

In this regard, the meaning is as follows: the particle *iti* need not have been employed to preclude the possibility of taking [the word] in its own form (*svarūpa*). For nowhere in the treatise is a word heard that is indicated by the locative case, such that one might suspect it refers to its own form.
That he composes a long sūtra when the matter could have been established with a short one indicates that this is a paribhāṣā of great scope.
This is for the sake of indication (*sūcanārtham*).

And thus, this [rule] becomes one of great scope (*mahāviṣayā*) if it operates everywhere—both in cases where there is doubt and elsewhere. It might be argued: "When it is stated 'that which is indicated by the locative case' (*saptamīnirdiṣṭe*), although the locus (*adhikaraṇa*) is indeed indicated by the locative, nevertheless, because that [locus] has the thing contained within it (*ādheya*) as its primary element, according to [Pāṇini 1.4.45], the *yaṇ* substitution is understood to apply to that vowel (*ac*) which is situated immediately before the *lyap* suffix; consequently, it would apply only here: *dadhi bhuṅkte*, but not here: *dadhy atra*."

"If there were no such fault in the alternative formulation (*yathānyāsa*), then this great sūtra would not have been composed"—this is not so. When [Pāṇini] provides the instruction *yadayaṃ* (P. 1.1.20), it indicates that the grammatical operations such as the substitution of *yaṇ* apply only to the locus (*adhikaraṇa*) and not to the thing contained therein (*ādheya*).

Furthermore, even in the alternative formulation, because the locus is primarily intended to convey the thing contained, the operation of *yaṇ*-substitution and the like applies precisely to the thing contained; thus, this paribhāṣā is present everywhere, and everything desired is established. In this case, by the rule *yadayaṃ* (P. 1.1.68), there must be the apprehension of the actual form itself.

Consequently, this *paribhāṣā* would apply only where that word *tasmin* is uttered, as in the rule: "In place of *yuṣmad* and *asmad*, [the substitutes] *yauṣmāka* and *āsmāka* [are used] before *aṇ* and *cha*" (Pāṇini 4.3.2).

For in this case, the purpose of that *paribhāṣā* is the exclusion of what follows (*paranivṛtti*), as in: *yauṣmākīṇam*—give to you; *āsmākīnam*—give to us. However, in cases such as *yuṣmabhyaṃ dehi yauṣmākīṇam* (give to you, [it is] yours) and *asmabhyaṃ dehyāsmākīnam* (give to us, [it is] ours), this *paribhāṣā* does not apply. Therefore, he says: "*tasmin*," meaning "when there is a reference to the sense of the locative case."

He thinks as follows: for the particle *iti* has been employed here, and it serves to set aside the view that [the word] denotes its own form (*svarūpa*) and establishes that the word *tasmin* denotes an object (*arthapadārthakatvam*). Consequently, there is the apprehension of the object alone.

Now, since that object must necessarily be indicated by some word or other, it is indicated by the word *tasmin*, which expresses a general sense because it possesses multiple meanings. But surely, since priority and posteriority are not possible between a word and its meaning, and thus such a relation is impossible with the object itself, it will be understood through the word that denotes it; therefore, there is no fault.

In this regard, the following objection is raised: the particle *iti* is employed so that there may be the apprehension of the meaning (*artha*) and not the apprehension of the word-form (*svarūpa*). And that apprehension of the word-form is suspected on the basis of the rule *tasminnaṇi cayuṣmākāsmākau* [Pāṇini 4.3.2]; for if there were to be an apprehension of the word-form, one would have used the term "preceding" (*pūrva*) in that very rule, yet it was not so done. Therefore, it is understood that even without the particle *iti*, there will be the apprehension of the meaning alone and not of the word-form; thus, is there not a lack of purpose for it?
This is established; however, for the sake of easy comprehension by those of dull intellect who are unable to grasp [the meaning] directly, the particle *iti* has been employed.
The term *nirdiṣṭa* (indicated) is an adjective qualifying the sense (*artha*).
And in this treatise, in sentences such as [Pāṇini 6.1.77], wherever there is the sense of the locative case, that [sense] is everywhere indeed "indicated" (*nirdiṣṭa*).
That qualification "specified" (*nirdiṣṭa*) is useless because there is no deviation [from what is intended]; therefore, he says: "The mention of 'specified' (*nirdiṣṭagrahaṇam*)," and so forth.
That whose meaning is immediate succession (*ānantarya*), i.e., non-interruption, is described as such.
But how does that have the sense of immediate succession? Because it is understood from that.
For this prefix *diś-* has the action of uttering as its meaning; even though it is here [in *nirdiṣṭa*] devoid of sound, it indicates immediate succession (*nairantarya*).

In that context, when the *prādi*-compound *nirdiṣṭa* (meaning "pointed out" or "indicated") is formed from *nir-antaraṃ diṣṭaḥ*, it is clearly understood to mean "uttered immediately after. To the question, "For what purpose, then, is immediate succession relied upon? he says: "Agnicid atra," etc.
This word *pūrva* also applies even when there is an intervention.

In this regard, the intention is that if immediate succession (*ānantarya*) were not relied upon, then [the rule] would apply even when there is an intervention. Now, one might object: "The term *aci* is understood as a locative of proximity (*upaśleṣika-adhikaraṇa*), and what is intervened by something else cannot be proximate; therefore, what is the purpose of specifying the mention of 'immediate succession'? This is incorrect; for if the mention of "specified" (*nirdiṣṭa*) were absent, it would be impossible to understand it as a locative of proximity.
This is because the word "preceding" (*pūrva*), even when referring to something that is intervened, effects the exclusion of only what follows, and not of what precedes even if it is intervened.
However, when the term *nirdiṣṭa* (specified) is employed, proximity (*pratyāsatti*)—which is denoted by the locative case expressing a point of contact (*aupaśleṣikādhikaraṇa*)—is understood.
And that [proximity] is not set aside by the mention of *pūrva* (preceding); rather, the meaning obtained is that only the exclusion of what follows (*para*) is effected.
Consequently, an operation does not apply to that which is separated [by an intervening element].

Furthermore, the mention of the word *nirdiṣṭa* (indicated) must indeed be made for the sake of what follows. For what purpose is this? [In response: That which occurs here under [Pāṇini 8.1.28] is not a case-ending (*kāraka-vibhakti*); rather, it is characterized by connection with direction (*dig-yoga*) according to [Pāṇini 2.3.29]: *dikśabdād añc-uttarapada*. Since the word *dik* (direction) must be supplied there, a doubt arises: when the elision (*nighāta*) of the preceding [verb] is to be performed, is it done after supplying the word *pūrva* (preceding), or after supplying the word *para* (following)? To resolve this doubt, this technical rule (*paribhāṣā*) is commenced for the purpose of restriction: "The mention of *nirdiṣṭa* is understood as a governing term (*anuvartate*)."
The sense is that because it has the meaning of "immediate succession" (*ānantarya*), an operation does not apply to what is separated [by another element].
Here too, the particle *iti* is employed for the purpose of indicating the meaning.
With the intention that, by this means, the meaning of the ablative case is grasped rather than the actual form of the word itself, he says: "from that" (*tasmāt*).

"An explanation of the meaning of the fifth case. Now, one might object: since the particle *iti* will carry over from the preceding rule (*pūrvasūtra*), what is the purpose of this *iti* being mentioned again? It is for the purpose of making it known that a portion [of the previous rule] carries over in this manner; by this, it is explained that the mention of "that which is indicated" (*nirdiṣṭagrahaṇa*) shall carry over just like the word *iti*. Another, however, says: "But here the particle *iti* removes the dependence on the limit (*avadhimattva*) of the limit (*avadhi*)."
Therefore, it is understood that [the rule] pertains to what follows the limit (*avadhi*), not to the possessor of the limit (*avadhimat*).
Furthermore, the particle *iti* is not intended to exclude the mention of the word's own form (*svarūpa*), because its own form is absent [in this context].

As for the rule *yad api* (Pāṇini 6.1.103), even there, since a *śas* suffix cannot occur before a long vowel resulting from the homogeneous substitution (*pūrvasavarṇadīrgha*), no doubt arises [regarding the application of the rule].

"Therefore, the word 'iti' is used solely for the purpose of excluding the dependence of the limit (*avadhi*) upon that which possesses the limit (*avadhimat*). To this, it is replied: if the particle *iti* is employed to ensure that the operation applies only to the subsequent [element] relative to the limit and not to that which possesses the limit—in order to remove the dependence of the limit upon the possessor of the limit—then there is no need for it; for that is established by common worldly usage alone. Indeed, in the world, when one says, "Let him who is after that teacher be fed," it is he who is after the limit (the teacher) who is fed, not the one who possesses the limit.

Therefore, here too, even without the employment of the word *it*, the operation will apply to the suffix itself (*uttara*), not to that which possesses the suffix (*avadhimat*). As for what was said—that even in the rule [Pāṇini 6.1.103], the suffix *śas* cannot occur before the long vowel of the same quality as the preceding (*pūrvasavarṇadīrgha*)—that too is incorrect. For instance, when the suffix *śas* follows words such as *hrasva* and *ādi*, and the long vowel of the same quality as the preceding has been established in the preceding words *vṛkṣa* and so on ending in *śas*, one observes in expressions such as *gacchata ān vṛkṣān upalabhate* and *gacchato vṛkṣān ān upalabhate*.

A *śas* [ending] certainly occurs after a long vowel resulting from the substitution of the homogeneous preceding vowel (*pūrvasavarṇadīrgha*). Now, where there is a mention of both [the base and the suffix], which one should undergo the grammatical operation? In that case, whichever [genitive] is without scope (*anavakāśā*) will cause the other genitive to be understood as a genitive of relation; therefore, the operation will apply to that which is indicated by the genitive. For example, in the rule *[[P. 7.2.82]]*, the locative is without scope, and thus it will cause the fifth case (*pañcamī*) in the preceding rule *[[P. 7.2.80]]*, which has scope, to be understood as a genitive. Thus, the operation will apply to that which is indicated by the genitive.

Likewise, in the rule *īdāsaḥ* [Pāṇini 7.2.83], the genitive case is prescribed by the previous rule *ānaḥ* [Pāṇini 7.2.82] which has its own scope (is *sāvakāśā*). Where both [rules] have their own scope, the fifth (ablative) case, by virtue of being subsequent (*paratvāt*), will displace the sixth (genitive) case of the preceding rule.
For example, in the rules *yaṅo 'ci ca* [Pāṇini 7.3.52] and *yaṅo vā* [Pāṇini 7.3.50], the fifth case has its own scope.
The term *ām* here is a locative used for the sake of what follows.
In that context, the ablative *ataḥ* functions as a substitute for the genitive of the locative *ām*; thus, *suṭ* is applied to the *ām* that follows a pronominal (*sarvanāman*).

However, regarding the rules [Pāṇini 6.1.75] and [6.1.76], although the locative *che ca* [6.1.71] has its scope in the preceding rule, nevertheless, because it is marked with the *svarita* accent, it is considered to have no further scope once it has been carried over from the previous application.
Therefore, that seventh case (saptamī) will be treated as a sixth case (ṣaṣṭhī) [by the principle of *vipariṇāma*].
The fifth case (pañcamī), however, having established the relationship of priority (paurvāparya), becomes applicable elsewhere and thus recedes.
Consequently, this is the meaning of the sūtra: when a *cha*-suffix follows a long vowel (*dīrgha*), the augment *tuK* occurs for that very long vowel which precedes it.

In this regard, although the locative case in [Pāṇini 3.1.67] is without scope, it does not cause the substitution of a genitive for the ablative *dhātoḥ*, even though that ablative does have scope. For otherwise, substitutes such as *yaK* and so on would belong to the verbal root (*dhātu*) itself.

Consequently, because the subsequent rule [Pāṇini 3.1.2], *paraśca*, would be sublated, the purposeful addition of indicatory letters (*anubandha*) for *yaK* and the others would result in futility. Indeed, if they were substitutes of the verbal root, their status as "subsequent" (*para*) would not be possible; rather, they must occur after the verbal root. [This is stated in the commentary beginning with: "In the science [of grammar], its own... and so forth.
In common usage, the mention of "the treatise" (*śāstra*) [is used] because it is the meaning alone that is to be grasped.

Regarding the rule *śabdasya* (Pāṇini 1.1.68), the genitive case is used in the sense of the agent; the meaning is that the word causes its own form to be grasped, that is, it makes it known or conveys it.
But what is the difference between the word and its own form, such that there is this genitive case based on their distinction, as in the expression *śabdasya*?
In the ultimate sense, there is no distinction whatsoever regarding the actual entity.
For instance, the "own-form" (svarūpa) of a word is its very nature (svabhāva).
If that [own-form] were something different from the word, the word would indeed be devoid of its own nature.
However, even though no real distinction exists, the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) occurs by relying on a distinction constructed by the intellect (*buddhi*).

For the intellect, arising through the maturation of its own seeds and assuming a particular form, brings about a distinction even when no distinction exists in the actual object—just as in the cases "Rāhu’s head" or "its own nature.

By the word "only" (*eva*) in the phrase "not the meaning of *bāhu*," he shows what is excluded. He states an exception to what would otherwise be over-extended: "except for technical grammatical terms (*aśabdasaṃjñā*)," and so forth.
To the question, "For what purpose, then, is this undertaken? he says: "By means of the word," and so forth.
When a word is uttered, the object is understood as being useful for a specific action, not the word's own form.

For instance, when it is said, "Let the cow be perceived," one strives to perceive the object itself, not the word's form; however, in the case of grammar (*vyākaraṇa*), an operation such as the application of suffixes is not possible for the object, because there is no temporal sequence between the word and that [object].
Nor is there any utility for the present context in an affix prescribed by virtue of its meaning;
for when it is stated [by Pāṇini 4.2.33] "of that," this understanding does not arise:
"whatever is the meaning of the word *agni*, that is the recipient of the operation here, and this operation is prescribed for it."

And therefore, regarding those words which denote that object as something to be enjoined—for example, for the proponents of the universal (*ākṛti*), when the word "the cow is to be milked" (*gaur duhyatām*) enjoins the universal, because the operation is impossible there [in the universal] and possible in the individual (*vyakti*) which is its substrate, and due to their constant association, the cognition occurs with respect to that very individual and not the universal; so too here, this [sūtra] is commenced so that there may be no such cognition of those [words] which denote that [universal].

The genitive case in *tadvācinām* is used in the sense of the object (*karmaṇi*). The meaning is that this [paribhāṣā] is commenced for the purpose that [the rule] should not be understood as referring to those words that express the [meaning]. In this regard, some say: "Since both the word-form itself and its synonyms would be subject to the operation, this paribhāṣā is for the sake of restriction (*niyamārthā*), so that it may apply only to the word that is actually heard [in the sūtra], and not to its synonyms. Others, however, hold that "a paribhāṣā possesses a formal indicator (*liṅginī*)," just as the terms *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* serve as indicators in [Pāṇini 1.1.3].
Or [it may be] a supplement to another rule; for example, in the rule "In case of conflict, the subsequent operation prevails" (Kātantra 67), it becomes a supplement to the subsequent rule.
However, others maintain that since no indicative mark (*liṅga*) nor status as a supplement to another rule exists for this, it is a definition-rule (*saṃjñā-sūtra*).

Even though the word "definition" (*saṃjñā*) is not explicitly uttered in the commentary (*vṛtti*), nevertheless, by stating "one's own form is what is to be understood from a word," the author of the commentary has effectively declared that this is indeed a definition.

In the case of the word "fire" (*agni*) and others, there exists a form common to other words, such as "wordness" (*śabdatva*), and also a unique form, such as "fire-wordness" (*agniśabdatva*). Among these, the term "its own" (*svam*) is employed for the purpose of excluding the common form and grasping the unique form of "fire-wordness" and so forth. For that [unique form] is indeed its own form, whereas the other belongs to others as well. Because it is not taught [by another] with respect to cognition, the word's own form is proximate, not its meaning; for the opposite is true of the latter, and because [the form] is never to be abandoned, and because it possesses an eternal connection [with the word].
For instance, imitative words (*anukaraṇa-śabda*) abandon their meaning but not their own form (*svarūpa*).

Moreover, the meaning is common (*sādhāraṇa*), whereas the form is unique (*asādhāraṇa*), because the meaning can be conveyed by other words as well. Thus, because it is proximate, eternally connected, and unique, the form alone is the "own" (*sva*) of the word, not the meaning.

Consequently, since the inclusion of the form is already established by the very mention of "its own" (*sva*), the mention of "form" (*rūpa*) is intended to indicate that in grammar, the meaning is accepted just as the form is.
By this, the rule "by the mention of that which has meaning, not that which is meaningless" (Vyāḍīya-paribhāṣā 1) becomes established.

Furthermore, although the word "of sound" (*śabdasya*) is already established from the very context of the instruction on words (*śabdānuśāsana*), the explicit mention of "sound" is for the purpose of making known this principle: where a term is mentioned with reference to the word itself, its own form (*svarūpa*) is understood, and not when it is mentioned with reference to its meaning.
Consequently, in the rule *tena* (Pāṇini 3.4.40), there is no apprehension of the word's own form.

However, that this instruction is intent upon the actual meaning is understood from the unbroken tradition of the teacher’s oral teaching. For instance, in the case of *āgneyam*, the suffix *ḍhak* is applied in the sense of "Agni is its deity.
