Similarly, in the case of *audaiātkam*, the suffix *ḍhak* is applied here in the sense of "prepared by Udaiāta."

Because of the recurrence of the word "ityasya" from [Pāṇini 4.2.18] *udaiāto-'nyatarasyām*, there is the substitution of *ka* for *ṭhak* by [Pāṇini 7.3.51] *isusu-ktāntātkaḥ*. Regarding the phrase "in the case of the mention of *ghu*" and so forth:

if even a technical term (*saṃjñāśabda*) such as *ghu* were to denote its own form, then although there is the governing rule (*adhikāra*) of "root" (*dhātu*) in [Pāṇini 3.3.92], the suffix *kvip* would still apply after the word *ghu* due to the specific mention of *ghu*;
the mention of "prefixes" (*upasarga*) would, however, serve as an indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*) for words beginning with *pra*.
For example: "The substitution of *aṅ* for *nāsikā* occurs when forming a name, provided that [the word] is not *nasa* or *asthūla*" (Pāṇini 5.4.118–119).

Furthermore, in the case of *kumārīgha*, since the word *gha* is a technical term (*saṃjñāśabda*) that conveys its own form, the rule Pāṇini 6.3.43 would entail the shortening of the vowel when the word *gha* follows. Now, one might argue that by the very force of the formulation of the technical term, the term itself is not taken in its own form, for a technical term is created for the purpose of conveying the thing it names (*saṃjñin*). If the technical term were also to convey its own form, the formulation of the technical term would be purposeless. This is not so.

For by the capacity of the instruction regarding technical names (*saṃjñā*), one would cause the bearer of the name (*saṃjñin*) to be understood, and by the capacity of the formulation of the technical rule (*paribhāṣā*), one's own form [would be understood].
Therefore, should a prohibition be made? It need not be made; because of the *jñāpaka* (indicatory mark), a word that is a technical name will not be a grasper of its own form.

When [Pāṇini] prescribes the technical name *ṣaṭ* for a numeral ending in the letter *ṣ* in the rule *yadayam* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.1.24), he makes known that a technical term (*saṃjñāśabda*) does not denote its own form (*svarūpa*). For otherwise, since the word *ṣaṭ* would have denoted its own form in the rule *ṣaṭ-catur-bhyaś ca* (7.1.22), the elision (*luk*) would occur even from there; thus, he would not have assigned the name *ṣaṭ* to a numeral ending in *ṣ*.

The word *ṣaṭ* indeed ends in the letter *ṣ*, and no other [number-word does]; this is true. Nevertheless, for those who might experience difficulty in understanding the meaning through the medium of a technical indicator (*jñāpaka*), the prohibition "it is not a grammatical term (*aśabda-saṃjñā*)" was formulated to avoid that.

The inclusion of the word *śabda* (word) is intended to demonstrate that the prohibition applies only to a technical term used in grammar (*vyākaraṇa*) and not to a common worldly term. Regarding the phrase "of those ending in *s* and *t*" (*sittadviśeṣāṇām*), etc.: where the inclusion of specific forms is desired, there the letter *s* should be made an *it*-marker, as in *vṛkṣasya* and *mṛgas*.

Regarding the passage beginning with "tato vaktavyaḥ" (then it should be stated): having made this mention of the *sit* suffix, this technical rule (*paribhāṣā*)—namely, "sittadviśeṣāṇām" and so forth—should be formulated either in the first chapter or elsewhere.

It should be stated that whatever has the letter *s* as its *it*-marker is the designator of those specific instances of it, such as *khadira* and others which are specific instances of [the general category] *vṛkṣa* and so forth.

In this same way, it should be understood in cases such as *pitparyāyavacanasya ca svādyartham* (Kātyāyana-vārttika 519) and so forth; moreover, this intended meaning is established through reasoning (*nyāya*). We shall demonstrate later, as the occasion arises, how it is established for the sake of easy comprehension. The introduction of the text beginning with *sittadviśeṣāṇām* is for the purpose of facilitating understanding. This is a technical rule (*saṃjñāsūtra*), not a governing rule (*paribhāṣā*);
for the latter serves the purpose of restriction (*niyamārthā*).

Furthermore, it was not previously established that [the letters] following an *aṇ* would include their homogeneous counterparts (*savarṇa*) as well as others, such that a restriction could be made stating that "only the homogeneous counterparts are included.
Therefore, the intention is that by means of the subsequent *ṇ*, the inclusion of homogeneous counterparts for *ṛ*-vowels and so forth is also established.
And the inclusion of a *pratyāhāra* by means of a subsequent *ṇ* has been demonstrated in the rule *a i u ṇ*.
From the preceding sūtra, the phrase "its own form" (*svarūpam*) is carried over here.
By virtue of the context, this undergoes a change of case-ending and becomes a genitive.
Thus, showing that when *aṇ* is mentioned as its own form, both *aṇ* and *udic* serve as the designators (*grāhaka*), he says: "and of its own form."
"ādguṇaḥ" and so forth:
just as *devendra* occurs here, so too *ādguṇa* (the single substitute for the preceding and following vowels) occurs in *khaṭvendra*.
Just as the substitution of *it* occurs in *paṭībhavati*, so too it occurs in *mālībhavati*.
Just as there is elision in the case of *dikṣi*, so too there is [elision] in the case of *cauḍi*.
The suffix *iñ* is applied to the word *cūḍā* because it belongs to the *bāhv-ādi* group.
[The rule] beginning with "vowel and nasality" (*svarānunāsikya*) [applies].
An acute (udātta) vowel mentioned in a rule includes even those that differ from it in other accents;
likewise for the grave (anudātta) and the circumflex (svarita).
Similarly, a nasalized (sānunāsika) vowel includes the non-nasalized (niranunāsika), and the latter includes the former. [This applies] except in the case of "long" (dīrgha).
If the prohibition "not a suffix" (*apratyayaḥ*) were not stated, then even a suffix would be a grasper (*grāhaka*) of its homogeneous sounds (*savarṇa*);

and consequently, even a long vowel would [be so grasped]. But is it not the case that this which is said—"not a suffix"—is far too limited? It should rather be stated: "that which is not a suffix, nor a substitute (*ādeśa*), nor having *ṭi*, *kit*, or *mit* [as an indicatory letter]."
This has been illustrated in the case of a substitute (*pratyaya*).
Regarding a replacement (*ādeśa*): from *asmāt* comes *itaḥ* (by [Pāṇini 5.3.7] *itastasil*), and from *asmin* comes *iha* (by [Pāṇini 5.3.11]).

For here, if there were the inclusion of homogeneous vowels (*savarṇagrahaṇa*), then if the substitution of *iś* for the *tyad*-class stems occurred before the *yatva* (change to *ya*) had taken place, an *ikāra* of three morae (*trimātra*) would result by the principle of closest proximity (*antaratamya*); whereas if it occurs after the *yatva* has taken place, it is a quarter-mora (*ardhacaturtha-mātra*).
If the *pararūpa* substitution [of Pāṇini 6.1.97] has not yet been applied, then it remains as such; but if it has been applied, then it would consist of less than three and a half morae (*mātrā*).
Alternatively, since there is neither a duration of three and a half nor four and a half morae, it would instead be two or three morae.
Regarding the suffix *-tṛc*: in *lavitr̥*, if the inclusion of homogeneous vowels (*savarṇagrahaṇa*) were to apply, the long vowel would also result.
Regarding the rule *kit-bhuvo ṅguṇ luṅ-liṭoḥ* [Pāṇini 6.4.88], as in *babhūva*, there might also be a nasalized (*sānunāsika*) vowel here;
for the *yaṇ* substitutes are indeed both nasalized and non-nasalized.
Regarding *mit*—as in *caturanuḍuhorām udāttaḥ* [Pāṇini 7.1.98–99], as in *anaḍvān*—there might also be a long vowel here.

Should it then be stated in this way? It need not be stated. The particle *ca* is employed here; it will serve the purpose of a collective conjunction (*samuccaya*) with the negation that has not been explicitly mentioned. By means of this, those [elements] such as substitutes (*ādeśa*) whose status as "graspers" (*grāhaka*) is not desired will not be graspers of their homogeneous counterparts (*savarṇa*). Others, however, say: "In the expression *apratyaḥ*, there is no mention of a technical term (*saṃjñā*) here; what then? It is a mention based on etymological meaning (*anvartha*).
A *pratyaya* is that which is recognized, prescribed, or produced."
Therefore, the meaning of the term *apratyaya* is this: "An *aṇ* being produced (*bhāvyamāna*) does not include its homogeneous counterparts" (Vyāḍi 35).
Since *haś* and the others are also produced—that is, they are brought into existence—they too are *pratyayas*; consequently, they do not become the graspers of their homogeneous counterparts.
Furthermore, the purpose for including the particle *ca* must be stated.

If it is argued that the purpose [of the particle *ca*] is to draw back (*anukarṣaṇa*) the rule "its own form" (*svarūpam*), we say no; for because it has already been drawn back, its recurrence in what follows would not occur.

Furthermore, this purpose is not tenable, since its recurrence is already established by its being marked with a circumflex accent (*svarita*). Now, if it is thought: "The word 'its own' (*svam*) ending in the nominative is the subject under discussion, whereas here the requirement is for something indicated by the genitive; therefore, the particle *ca* is employed so that through effort its status as ending in the genitive may be achieved"—this too is not the case.

For the transformation of the case-ending is established by the very force of the meaning. He demonstrates that *tapara* is a *bahuvrīhi* compound, [explaining it as] "that which has *t* followed by it," and also as a *pañcamī-tatpuruṣa* compound, "that which is further than even *t*.
It should be understood that this latter [compound] is formed through the division of the rule (*yogavibhāga*) "the fifth case" (*pañcamī*).
But how can these two compounds be obtained when there is only a single word *tapara*? There is no fault here, for even a single word, through repetition, will have a twofold division.
For here, the purpose of the inclusion of *ta* in the long vowel (*taparakaraṇa*) in the rule *bahuvrīher liṅgam* (Pāṇini 7.1.9) is indeed [to indicate this];
for a genitive tatpuruṣa compound is not applicable here.
For it is an *avarṇa* (a-vowel) that is intended as *tapara* here, not the case-ending *bhis*.

If, moreover, this were a *pañcamī-tatpuruṣa* compound, then the *t* would be followed by *para* (i.e., it would be *tapara*). Since it is stated here that a "letter followed by *t*" (*tapara*) is meant, and since that [the *t*] is not a letter, but rather the aggregate of them, the evidence for it being a *pañcamī-tatpuruṣa* is the employment of *tapara* in [Pāṇini 1.1.70]. For a *bahuvrīhi* construction is not appropriate here.

If it were a *bahuvrīhi* compound, then the vowel *ā* would have the *tapara* designation (the *t* following it). However, the *tapara* marker is not for the sake of the vowel *ā*, but rather for the sake of the *ai* diphthong. This has been explained in that very context. The term "of a homogeneous sound" (*savarṇasya*) is understood [from the previous rule], and a single phoneme (*varṇa*) cannot be homogeneous with itself, whereas a collection of phonemes can. Therefore, even though no specific distinction is stated, it is understood that only a phoneme is "followed by *t*" (*tapara*). Thus he says: "A phoneme followed by *t*" (*taparo varṇaḥ*).
The term *tatkālasya* is a bahuvrīhi compound, meaning "that which has this time.
This designation is incorrect;
for it is as follows: by the word *tat*, that which has *t* as its final element (*tapara*) is referred to, and *tapara* refers to a phoneme (*varṇa*).
Time, however, is held to be a specific kind of action.
Thus it has been said: "Others, who know time, understand time—which is distinct according to the different types of its recurrence—as the movement of the sun, the planets, and the lunar mansions."

[This refers to] *vā|pa|3.9.76*. How, then, can there be grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) between the two words *tapara* and *kāla*, which denote distinct qualities—namely, a specific phoneme and a specific action? [The answer is: "That which has a duration like that [of the phoneme] is *tatkāla*.
To demonstrate the meaning of this, he says: "*ātmanā*" and so forth.

Although, due to the proximity of the term *tapara*, it is appropriate for the word *ātman* to refer to that [phoneme] here; nevertheless, in this context, by virtue of association (*sāhacarya*), it refers to the action of pronunciation known as "duration" (*kāla*), which is associated with that [phoneme].

Why is this so? Because it is impossible for an action to be identical with a phoneme followed by *t* (tapara). The designation [of the duration] by that word is possible through association (*sāhacarya*).

What is meant by this is: "of that which has a duration equal to the action associated with the phoneme followed by *t*"; that is to say, it refers to that whose act of pronunciation is of the same kind as the act of pronunciation of the phoneme followed by *t*.

"Of that which is endowed with another quality" means: of that which has been articulated as distinguished by a quality called a *dharma*—such as the acute (*udātta*) accent—and which is then connected with other qualities such as the acute and so forth. "And of its own form" is included here as well, because that [phrase] recurs [from the previous rule].

In this case, is this sūtra for the purpose of restriction (*niyamārtha*) or for the purpose of an injunction (*vidhyartha*)? If *aṇ* is understood as carrying over [from the previous rule], then, since the matter would already be established by the preceding rule—"When something is already established, its restatement is for the purpose of restriction" (Kātyāyana-Pariśiṣṭa 62)—the rule means that an *aṇ* followed by *t* (*tapara*) is a grasper (*grāhaka*) only of its own duration (*tatkāla*), and not of anything else. If, however, *aṇ* has ceased to carry over, then it is for the purpose of an injunction. In the first of these two positions, the long vowel *ā*—which is followed by *t* and is non-nasal (*niranunāsika*)—is employed in the sūtra "The nasal of *viṭ* and *van* becomes *āt*" (Pāṇini 6.4.41), on the principle that "phonetic qualities (*guṇa*) are differentiators."
According to this view, there would be no grāhaka (perceiver) for the nasalized [vowel], because it is not an *aṇ* (short vowel).
Consequently, the substitute (*ādeśa*) would be only the non-nasalized one.

However, thinking that in the other alternative, even though the qualities (*guṇa*) are indeed differentiators, this fault does not arise, he adopts the second position and says: "This is for the purpose of an injunction (*vidhyartha*)."
He explains how [the rule] has an injunctive purpose, stating: "The term *aṇ* does not recur.

[This refers to the rule] "of *aṇ*s and others," and so forth. It is logical that the technical rule (*grahaṇaka-śāstra*) applies only to other [sounds] with a following *t* (tapara), because for those [sounds], their inclusion by the preceding [rule] is unestablished (*asiddha*).

Since the status of being a *grāhaka* (that which causes the substitution) for the *aṇ* vowels is already established by the preceding rule, [the author] asks, "How is this so? and replies with the rule beginning with "*ato bhisa ais*" and so forth. It might be argued that even here, that [preceding rule] would apply because it is of no other occasion (*anavakāśatvāt*); therefore, he says, "*ataḥ parāḥ*" and so forth. In rules such as [Pāṇini 6.1.87], the *aṇ* vowels ending in *a* have their scope; however, for this [present rule], there are long vowels ending in *t* that are not *aṇ*. For example, [as in Pāṇini 6.4.41]. The intention is that among those *aṇ* vowels ending in *t*, when both [rules] would apply, this very *grahaṇaka-śāstra* (the rule governing the application of substitutes) prevails due to its posteriority. Thus: *vṛkṣaiḥ*, *plakṣaiḥ*.

The third-person plural ending is *bhis*. By the rule *ato bhisa ais* [Pāṇini 7.1.9], there is the substitution of *ais*; by the rule *vṛddhir eci* [Pāṇini 6.1.85], there is *vṛddhi* [vowel strengthening].

Regarding the forms *abjāḥ* and *gojāḥ*: the root *janī* (Dhātupāṭha 1149) means "to be born" (*prādurbhāve*). Thus, [the analysis is] "born in the waters" (*apsu jāyate*) and "born among cows" (*goṣu jāyate*), according to [Pāṇini 3.2.67]. Regarding the form *khaṭvābhiḥ*: [it is derived from *khaṭvā* + *bhis*].

But how can this be a counter-example, since by the rule *pūrvatrāsiddham* (P. 8.2.1), when the status of being "like the preceding" (*pūrvavadbhāva*) applies according to *antādivacca* (P. 6.1.85), the substitution of *ais* must indeed occur here? Furthermore, since there is no single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) with *yat* [following] that would have the vowel *t* as its marker (*tapara*), what would be excluded by that marker? [The answer is: *kīlālapābhiḥ*, *somapābhiḥ*, and so forth. This is not a fault; for under the rule *antādivacca* (P. 6.1.82), he will state: "In a rule dependent on a specific phoneme (*varṇāśrayavidhi*), the status of being 'like the end' or 'like the beginning' is not desired."

For instance, [the rule] "na bhavati" (it does not occur) applies because of the absence of the state of being either "anta" (end) or "ādi" (beginning) in the case of things like *khaṭvābhiḥ*. Alternatively, in the word "ataḥ," there is an elision (*praśleṣa*) of two *a*-vowels, so that [the substitute] may apply to the *a* that is actually heard. This [rule] is formulated to avoid a prescription regarding the actual form (*svarūpa-vidhi*). This too is a technical definition (*saṃjñā-sūtra*).

With respect to a thing that has no beginning, a preceding thing cannot possess the status of being a "beginning"; and with respect to a thing that has no end, a subsequent thing cannot possess the status of being an "end.
Furthermore, in this context, the statuses of being a "beginning" and an "end" cannot logically be mutually dependent upon one another.

For if this were the case, since there would be an entity possessing a name that is distinct from [the first and last], the name would consist of the first element together with the final one, and would be subject to accentuation (*svarita*) itself.
Consequently, for the purpose of the subsequent application of this rule [Pāṇini 1.1.68], there would be the undesirable consequence (*asaṅga*) of its being treated as *svarita*.

Therefore, considering that by the force of the words "first" (*ādi*) and "last" (*anta*), an entity falling between them—distinct from the first and last—is implied as the named (*saṃjñin*), he says: "of those falling in between them."
This plural form *jātau* [is used] because it refers to the class; otherwise, the sound *hreṅ* would not have *o* as its technical name (*saṃjñā*).

Now, one might object: "Since the words 'beginning' (*ādi*) and 'end' (*anta*) denote parts located in fixed positions, and since parts belong to a whole that is a composite (*samudāya*), it is logical that by the words 'beginning' and 'end' the whole itself is implied as the named entity (*saṃjñin*), because these words are relative terms (*sambandhiśabda*).
This being the case, it should have been stated simply as: "of those falling in the middle of that composite."

He thinks as follows: since [the author] provides the instruction by applying the *yaṇ*-substitution for the letter *y* after a collection of phonemes in rules such as Pāṇini 1.1.67 (*iko yaṇ aci*), it is understood that the collection of phonemes is not the designated entity (*saṃjñin*); rather, it is the individual phonemes themselves. Otherwise, if the collection of phonemes were the designated entity, he would have provided the instruction by applying the *yaṇ*-substitution for the entire series of phonemes following it. If it is argued that this was not done because it is impossible, we say no; for the substitution of the entire series of phonemes is indeed possible.

If it is argued that, since the designation (*saṃjñin*) belongs to the aggregate (*samudāya*), the grammatical operation (*kārya*) cannot possibly apply [to it], then if the operation cannot apply when [the designation] refers to the aggregate, let the individual phonemes (*varṇa*) themselves be the designata; for the operation is possible there—what is the use of an aggregate? [This is said] so that there might not be a grasping by means of the term *ṭā*.
But is it not the case that even that [individual phoneme] lies at the very end of that same extent [of the aggregate]? No; because that extent is not intended to be expressed (*avivakṣitatvāt*).

The letter *ṭ* [in Pāṇini’s rule] is for the purpose of qualifying the third-case singular [in the rule], as in "dvitīyāṭaussvenaḥ" (P. 2.4.34), and not for the purpose of forming a *pratyāhāra* (abbreviated designation). Now, what is the purpose of including the word "beginning" (*ādi*)? It is so that the entire collection [of letters from the beginning to the end] should not be the technical name (*saṃjñā*). This is not necessary, because "technical names possess the property of recurrence. Only the initial element recurs in the rules (*pradeśavākya*), not the entire collection. Therefore, even without the inclusion of the word "beginning," it is understood by implication that the initial element alone, together with the final one, constitutes the technical name, and not the entire collection.

If that is so, then the inclusion of the word "ādi" (beginning) is for the purpose of clarifying a meaning already established by implication. Now, what is the purpose of including the word "saha" (together), since the sense of "together" is understood from the instrumental case itself, as in the rule *vṛddho yūnā* [Pāṇini 1.2.65]? This is not so; for the instrumental case also occurs in the sense of "characteristic of a state" (*itthambhūtalakṣaṇa*). If that were the case, then only the first letter would be designated by the name *saṃjñā*, being characterized by the last letter which has the designation *it*.

Consequently, in the application rules (*pradeśa*), the case-ending would not arise after the entire group in forms such as *akaḥ*, *ikaḥ*, and *aci*, because they would not be nominal stems (*aprātipadikatva*) due to their lack of meaning.

However, because of the inclusion of the word *saha* (together), the designation (*saṃjñā*) is understood as being co-existent; thus, since the entire group functions as a technical name (*saṃjñā*), it possesses the status of a nominal stem (*prātipadika*), and consequently, a case-ending is obtained. The inclusion of the letter *it* (the marker *ṭ*), however, is for the purpose of ensuring that this [group] does not become a technical name by means of the letter *c* in the rule *caṭatavaḥ*, which is designated as *nit* in the context of the rule *aci*. Its being "final" is as previously stated, and not with respect to the entire group. If that were the case, the designation *it* would apply to it by Pāṇini 1.3.3; to prevent this, a separation of the rules (*yogavibhāga*) must be made in the rule beginning with 1.3.4, stating "not so. This is an exception to the general rule "a word's own form [is its meaning]."
This too is a definitional rule (*saṃjñāsūtra*),
not a governing rule (*paribhāṣā*); for here the characteristic of a governing rule— namely, the nature of a restriction— is not present.
In the word *yena*, the third case ending (*tṛtīyā*) is used in the sense of the instrument (*karaṇe*).

*Vidhīyate* means "it is performed as something previously non-existent"; thus, *vidhi* is derived from the root with the suffix of the object (*karman-sādhana*). It ends in the suffix *ki*, according to the rule *upasarge ghoḥ kiḥ* [Pāṇini 3.3.92]. Regarding the phrase *tadantasya*:
it is a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "that which has this as its end."
By the word "tat" (that), that very sound which functions as the instrument (*karaṇa*) is referred back.
This word "anaṭ" denotes a part, and a part belongs to a whole.
Therefore, he says, "it becomes a designation for the whole," so that this designation is understood to belong to that [whole] itself—as in the example "avaśyalāvyam."
Regarding the term *avaśyapāvyam*:

from the roots *lūñ* "to cut" (Dhātupāṭha 1484) and *pūñ* "to purify" (Dhātupāṭha 1483), after the vowel strengthening (*vṛddhi*) has been applied, the substitution of *āv* occurs according to [Pāṇini 6.1.79]; then, a compound is formed because it belongs to the *mayūravyaṃsakādi* group.

The *m* is elided by the rule *lumpedavaśyamaḥ kṛtyeṣu* (Kāśikā 6.1.149). Now, why is it that a designation (*saṃjñā*) ending in a vowel (*ejanta*) is not possible here [by P. 1.1.69]? What would be the consequence? In forms such as *cayanaṃ*, *cāyakaḥ*, *lavanaṃ*, and *lāvakaḥ*, because the substitute consists of more than one phoneme (*anekāl*), the *ay-ādi* substitutes would apply as replacements for the whole (*sarvādeśa*). This is not a fault; for according to the principle *nirdiśyamānasyādeśā bhavanti* (Vyāḍiparibhāṣā 106), the substitutes will apply only to the [vowel] that is explicitly mentioned (*nirdiśyamāna*), and not to the entire word ending in that vowel. Alternatively, this particular grammatical rule (*yoga*) simply does not have such a scope of application; therefore, it does not operate here.

For it has been stated that the third case ending (*tṛtīyā*) is used in the sense of the instrument (*karaṇa*); and since there can be no instrument without an agent (*kartṛ*), the agent is also implied.
Furthermore, because it is a relative term, the word "end" (*anta*), which denotes a part, brings to mind the whole (*samudāya*) by its proximity.
And due to the context, both the intrinsic nature (*svarūpa*) and the agent are brought into proximity in three ways.
In some cases, [the agent] is indicated by explicit mention (*nirdeśa*); for instance, in the rule *īdūdeddvicanam* [Pāṇini 1.1.11], the dual number (*dvivacanam*) is mentioned as the agent.
Thus, by means of the instruments (*karaṇa*) consisting of *ī*, *ū*, and *e*, it prescribes the designation *pragṛhya*.

In other cases, [the agent] is established through context (*prakaraṇa*); for example, in the rule *erac* [Pāṇini 3.3.56], because the governing rule *dhātoḥ* [Pāṇini 3.1.91] is in force, the verbal root (*dhātu*) is present as the agent by virtue of the context.
He prescribes *it* (the suffix *san*) by means of the instrument *i*.

In some cases, this is due to semantic necessity (*sāmarthya*); for example, in the rule *[[P. 3.1.7]]*, here *san* is prescribed after the verbal root (*dhātu*) itself and not after anything else. Thus, by semantic necessity, the verbal root is present as the agent (*kartṛ*). That [root], being the agent, prescribes the *kit*-status of *san* by means of the instrument *i*. Therefore, in cases such as *īdūdeddvivacanam* [[P. 1.1.11]], since both the agent and the instrument are present, that [rule] falls within the scope of this sūtra, and consequently, the extension of the designation to what ends with those [elements] (*tadantavidhi*) occurs there.

But in this case [of rule 6.1.78], no agent (*kartṛ*) is present by way of any specific mode, nor is an instrument (*karaṇa*) possible without an agent; therefore, since neither the agent nor the instrument is present, this is not the domain of the present sūtra, and thus a *tadantavidhi* (the application of a grammatical operation to that which ends with a specified element) is not possible. The phrase "it must be stated" (*vaktavyaḥ*) means "it must be explained.

In that regard, the following explanation is given: in rules such as *dvitīyā śrita* (Pāṇini 2.1.24), the nominal suffixes (*sup*) are qualified by words like *śrita*, and not the words like *śrita* by the nominal suffixes.
The rule of "extension to that which ends with [the element]" (tadantavidhi) applies by means of the qualifier (viśeṣaṇa), not by means of the qualified (viśeṣya).

Since in the expression *ayena* the third case (*tṛtīyā*) denotes the instrument (*karaṇa*), and the instrument is dependent and exists for the sake of another, whereas the qualified is not, therefore the extension to that which ends with [the element] does not apply to the qualified elements such as *śrita* and so on.
[As in the example: *naḍādibhyaḥ phak*.

Here too, the *naḍa*-class and others are qualified by the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) under discussion, and not the nominal stem by the *naḍa*-class and others; therefore, here as well, there is no application of the rule for "that which ends with" (*tadantavidhi*). Regarding the phrase "with the exception of [rules concerning] *ugit* suffixes and the mention of phonemes": the nominal stem is qualified by an *ugit* suffix and by a phoneme. And when there is a qualification, the rule for "that which ends with" certainly applies. The phrase "in whatever [element] a rule is prescribed," etc., states that while the rule for "that which ends with" would otherwise apply, the rule for "that which begins with" (*tadādividhi*) is now being taught.
The phrase "yasmin" indicates that when a locative case is specified, it shows the rule applies to what begins with that [element].

Wherever there is a mention of an *al* (phoneme) in the locative case and a rule for what precedes is prescribed, it should be understood as applying to what begins with that; the meaning is "at the beginning of an *al*."

If, then, the rule for that which ends in *tad* (the whole) were to apply there as well, it would apply only here—namely in *śriyau*; but it would not apply here in *śriyaḥ*. However, when the rule for that which begins with *tad* (the whole) is in force, it applies even here; and because of the rule "and of its own form" (*svasya ca rūpasya*), it certainly applies even in the case of *śriyau*. When it is said, "of that which [ends in] *yasya*," a designation is prescribed for that very verbal form whose beginning among the vowels is termed *vṛddhi*. And since that [beginning] is necessarily of the nature of a whole, by implication, even by the general term *yasya*, the whole alone is denoted.
The word *yasya* ("of which") is stated for the purpose of indicating a technical designation (*saṃjñā*).

By the phrase "in the midst of vowels" (*acāṃ madhye*) and so forth, [the author] demonstrates that there is a selection (*nirdhāraṇa*) of a single part from a whole that possesses the designation *vṛddhi*; thus, he shows that the genitive case in *acām* is a genitive of selection (*nirdhāraṇa-ṣaṣṭhī*).
Here, the word *ādi* functions in the sense of "commencement" (*upakrama*); "commencement" means that which is commenced, i.e., that which is uttered first.

Because of the use of the plural number in the word *acām*, one might raise the objection that the designation *vṛddhi* should apply only to that which is the initial element among many vowels (*ac*), and not to that which is between two; in order to refute this, he says "*acām*" and so forth. If, then, this [genitive] in *acām* were a genitive of selection (*nirdhāraṇa-ṣaṣṭhī*), then since a selection can only occur from among members of the same class, the meaning would be that the *vṛddhi* [designation] should apply only to a vowel (*ac*) among vowels.

And this being the case, there would be no designation for that which begins with the vowel *ā*, such as *Ālāyana* and so forth, because the primary status (*mukhyatva*) of *ā* as a vowel does not exist, since it is situated within a consonant (*akṣa*).

It might, however, be considered figurative (*upacarita*), because by the rule [Pāṇini 1.1.69], even that which is not a vowel (*anac*) performs the function of a vowel (*ackārya*). But when the primary sense is available, it is not proper to resort to the figurative; for between the primary and the figurative, the operation is understood to apply to the primary. This is not a fault; by the principle of pervasion (*vyāpti*), the status of *ā* as a vowel will be accepted in its figurative sense. Otherwise, he would have prescribed the term *aij* alone, rather than *vṛddhi*.
*Śālīyaḥ*, *mālīyaḥ*, and so forth.

Here, since the designation *vṛddha* applies, the suffix *cha* occurs by [Pāṇini 4.2.113] *vṛddhācchaḥ*. Now, one might object: the words *śālā*, *mālā*, and *kāpaṭu* should not receive this designation (*saṃjñā*), for their initial sound is not designated as *vṛddha*; rather, it is a *hal* (consonant). This is not so; for although a *hal* is present here, it is not taken into account, because the status of being "initial" (*āditva*) is relied upon with respect to vowels (*ac*) alone. This is precisely the purpose of the mention of *aj* [in the definition of *vṛddha*].
How indeed could that state of being preceded by *aj* and so forth be understood [if the term *aj* were not used]? Otherwise, it would simply have to be applied there [to the whole].
When the mention of *aj* is made, the meaning becomes correct:
"among vowels (*ac*), whichever one has the designation *vṛddhi* and is situated before *aj* and the others."
This means that for any [vowel] other than the vowels [a, i, u], that which is designated as *vṛddhi* is pronounced first;

by this, the designation is established even for words such as *śālā*. In the case of "sābhāsannayanaḥ," because the designation *vṛddhi* does not apply here, only the suffix *aṇ* occurs, and not the suffix *cha*.

If, however, the mention of "ādi" (beginning with) were not made, then this designation would apply even to that [vowel] among the vowels of a word like *sabhāsan-nayana* where some vowel bearing the technical name *vṛddhi* occurs.

Although the word *vṛddhi* is heard here, nevertheless the *paribhāṣā* characterized by that [word] does not apply. This is because that [paribhāṣā] operates only where *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* are prescribed for a specific fixed substitute (*niyata-sthānin*).
And this has already been stated previously.
Furthermore, there is no prescription of *guṇa* or *vṛddhi* here; therefore, that [technical term] has no operation in this context.
Consequently, even for one for whom an initial element bearing the designation *vṛddhi* has an indefinite locus, its designation is nonetheless established.
"Or [it refers to] a name," and so forth.
This designation is to be understood as applying to those words—such as "Devadatta" and the like—which are uttered by persons for the sake of conventional usage.

The term *nāmadheya* (name) is conventionally established (*rūḍha*) with respect to these alone, and not with respect to those words such as "cow" and the like, which are based on causes such as genus (*jāti*) and so on, and which fall within beginningless linguistic usage.

[Objection: Since *kāśyādi* is listed [in the *gaṇapāṭha*], there ought to be the suffixes *ṭhañ* and *ñiṭha* by [Pāṇini 4.2.115] *kāśyādibhyaḥ*; therefore, the example *devadattīyaḥ*, which ends in the suffix *ch*, is incorrect. [Response: This is not a fault. For the word *devadatta* used there is that which is based on the action "giving to Devadatta" (*devadatta iti kriyā-nimittakaḥ*), and it is that very word which is listed there, not the word as a proper name (*saṃjñā-śabda*). Therefore, when the word *devadatta* has become a proper name (*saṃjñā-bhūta*) and is designated as *vṛddha*, then the suffix *cha* occurs; otherwise, the suffix *aṇ* applies. [The rule] *gotrāntāt* and so forth [is explained as follows].

Likewise, the suffix *cha* occurs after a word ending in the patronymic suffix *gotra*, whether it is uncompounded and derived from a base with a *vṛddhi* vowel, or likewise when compounded and not having a *vṛddhi* vowel. For example:

*ghṛtarauḍhiḥ*. This is a compound formed by the rule: "In the section concerning words in apposition, there is an addition [to the list] for *śākapārthiva* and similar compounds, and there is elision of the final member" (Vārttika 83).

Thus, for the offspring of one whose name ends in *uttara*—as in *pāṇinasyāpatyam*—"the suffix *iñ* is applied after [stems ending in] *at*" (*Pāṇini 4.1.95*), resulting in *pāṇinī*. Regarding the *bāhvādi* group, it is stated: "After *sambhūya* and *ambhas*, there is elision of *sal*" (*Gaṇasūtra* 66). The word *kāśyapa* ends in the suffix *añ* because it belongs to the *bidādi* group. Examples include *jaihvākātāḥ* and *hāritakātāḥ*.
The word *kātya* ends in the suffix *yañ* belonging to the *garga*-class. One who is fickle-tongued is a *kātya*, thus [the compound] *jihvākātya*.

One who eats greens is a *kātya*, thus [the compound] *haritakātya*. From these two, the general suffix *aṇ* applies; by [Pāṇini 6.4.148], there is the elision of the vowel *a*, and by [Pāṇini 6.4.151], there is the elision of the letter *y*. [The phrase] "for the sake of the subsequent rule" means...
Since this [rule] has a purpose in the subsequent sūtra, one might ask: "If it continues [into that rule], why does it not also apply for this purpose? To this he says: "It is not connected here.
The intention is that if it were also connected here, the meaning would be: "That [word] which has *tyad* and so on as its initial vowels is strengthened like them.
Consequently, it would apply only in cases such as *tvatputraḥ*, but it would not apply to *tyad* and so on when they stand alone.

But surely, in examples such as *tvatputraḥ* (“your son”) and *matputraḥ* (“my son”), pronouns like *tyad* and so on function as secondary members (*upasarjana*); and since their status as pronouns (*tyadāditva*) has been revoked when they are secondary members, how can this contingency arise? If the rule *yasyācāmādiḥ* is connected here, then even though they are secondary members, by virtue of that specific statement, the technical designation would apply only to those [pronouns] that remain [as primary], and not to them alone [when isolated]. How, then, can that which is being carried over (from a previous rule) be disconnected here? Because it continues to apply to its own inherent connection: by the rule *tyadādīni ca* [Pāṇini 1.1.73], pronouns are also designated as "vṛddhi."

"That which has a *vṛddhi* vowel as its initial among its vowels is called *vṛddha*. This is the rule for *vṛddha*. The mention of "among its vowels" (*ācām*) continues [from the previous sūtra], while the mention of "*vṛddhi*" has ceased.
Thus, the mention of "*vṛddhi*" has ceased.
In this way, a word connected with *vṛddhi* cannot be connected with the pronouns *tyad* and so on [in the form of *tvad* and *mad*]. For example,
in *tvādāyaniḥ* and *mādāyaniḥ*,

the suffix *phiñ* is applied by the rule *udīcāṃ vṛddhādagotrāt* [Pāṇini 4.1.157], and the substitutes *tvā-* and *mā-* are applied to *yuṣmad* and *asmad* by the rule *yūyavayau jasi* [Pāṇini 7.2.93].
The particle *ca* has the sense of including what has not been explicitly stated (*anuktasamuccayārtha*).

By means of it, there is no need to state [the rule] "optionally for a proper name" (*vā nāmadheyasya*, Vārttika 15), and so forth. Regarding the phrase "in the naming of a region of the Easterners" (*prācāṃ deśābhidhāne*), the meaning is: when there is the naming of that region which belongs to the Easterners (*prācām*).
By this, he shows that the qualification "of the Easterners" (*prācām*) is not intended as an optional alternative;
rather, it is explained that the phrase "according to the opinion of the Easterners" (*prācāṃ matena*) is not meant to be emphasized. [The examples are] *eṇīpacanīyaḥ*, and so forth.

The suffix *cha* is applied after [words] such as *eṇīpacana*. In the case of *āhicchatraḥ* and *kānyakubjaḥ*, the suffix *aṇ* alone is applied after the words *ahicchatra* and *kānyakubja*. In the case of *devadattaḥ*...

The suffixes *ṭhañ* and *ṇiṭh* prescribed by the rule *vṛddhādhikāre vihitaḥ* [Pāṇini 4.2.117] do not apply here; furthermore, they do not apply because of the inclusion of the word *kāśyapa* in the *kāśyapādi* list. For the word *devadatta* cited there is used as a name derived from an action (*kriyānimittaka*), whereas this is a counter-example concerning a technical name (*saṃjñāśabda*). And this should be understood to apply when the designation "vṛddha" does not exist, according to the rule *vā nāmadheyasya* (Vārttika 15).
Regarding the term "gomatāḥ":
everything exists here, but it is not a name for a location.
For instance, the river Gomatī is in the eastern region; it is not the region itself.

For a river is not grasped by the mention of a region, because in the rule *nadīdeśo 'grāmāḥ* (Pāṇini 2.4.7), the river is mentioned separately [from the region]. Furthermore, in rules such as *eṅ prācāṃ deśe* (Pāṇini 1.1.75) and *udīcāṃ vṛddhādagotrāt* (Pāṇini 4.1.157), the terms "eastern" (*prāc*) and "northern" (*udac*) are heard, yet their distinction is not understood. Therefore, in order to understand that, he says: "The eastern and northern," and so forth.

There is a river named Śarāvatī; the region situated to its east is the eastern region (prāgdeśa), and that to its north is the northern region (udagdeśa). It is she who divides these two—she establishes them through division; for when that boundary exists, their distinction is fully understood.
For what purpose does she divide them? "For the sake of establishing the words of the learned."
This is for the sake of the etymological derivation of words by wise grammarians.
How does he analyze the word *kṛtam*? He says: "Just as a swan [separates] milk and water.
Regarding the term *kṣīrodakam*, the singular form is used according to Pāṇini 2.4.6: "The singular is used for non-living things when they belong to the same genus (*jāti*)."
In some places, the reading is *kṣīrodake*.
This should be understood according to the rule: "Every *dvandva* compound may optionally be treated as a singular" (*Pāṇini* 2.4.6).
Just as a swan separates milk and water that have come together into a mixture and establishes them individually without confusion, so too does the Śarāvatī [separate] the east and north.
Because of the constant connection between *yat* and *tat*, by the statement "she" (*sā*), even though it is not explicitly stated, the word *yā* is understood.
That which divides [the directions], may she protect us, may she guard us.

However, regarding the well-known reading in that verse where it says *prāgudīcāv*, one must consider: how is the long *ī* possible when it is taught for a stem designated as *bha* by the rule *uda īt* [Pāṇini 6.4.139]? And how is it that the augment *num* does not occur by the rule *kathaṃ ca* [Pāṇini 7.1.70]? This requires further reflection.

Regarding this, they explain as follows: in the rule *ac-pratyanvavapūrvāt sāmalomnaḥ* (Pāṇini 5.4.75), the suffix *ac* is applied by means of a *yogavibhāga* (separation of the rule). Consequently, when an *ac*-ending follows, the designation *bha* applies and the substitution of *ī* occurs. The augment *num* does not occur because the *sarvanāmasthāna* ending is separated from the stem by the *ac* suffix. However, others form the compound *prāgudīcam* as a collective (*samāhāra*).
According to them, when the compound suffix *ṭac* is added by the rule *dvandvāccudaṣahāntāt samāhāre* (Pāṇini 5.4.106), the substitution of *ī* and the absence of *num* occur as before.

In some places, however, the reading is *prāgudīcā*. There, the plural number is used because of the intention to express plurality with respect to the constituent parts; the meaning is that [the suffixes] divide those belonging to the eastern region and those belonging to the northern region. In the *Kāśikā-vivaraṇapañjikā* composed by the venerable teacher Jinendrabuddhi, who is a disciple of the Bodhisattva, this concludes the first quarter (*pāda*) of the first chapter. Here, three alternative views are possible: either the letter *ṅ*, bearing the technical designation *itsaṃjñaka*, is prescribed by this [sūtra]; or, those suffixes following roots beginning with *gāṅ* and the *kuṭādi* group which are not marked by *ṇ* or *k* (i.e., *añṇit*) become *ṅit*; or, the letter *ṅ* bearing the technical designation *itsaṃjñaka* [is prescribed].

The meaning is that they become related to the marker *ṅ*; for it is only if the letter *ṅ* is prescribed as their *anubandha* (indicatory letter) that they become *ṅit*, and not otherwise. For Devadatta does not become "possessor of brindled cows" (*citragu*) without brindled cows. Alternatively, this [sūtra] establishes the technical name (*saṃjñā*) "ṅit": those affixes following *gāṅ* and the roots beginning with *kuṭ* that are not marked by *aṅ* or *ṇ* become *ṅit*, which is to say they acquire the designation *ṅit*.

Or, this may be an extension (*atideśa*): those affixes following *gāṅ* and the roots beginning with *kuṭ* that are not marked by *aṅ* or *ṇ* become *ṅit*, meaning they behave as if they possess the *ṅit* designation.
In the first alternative (*pakṣa*), when the ablative case in the rule *gāṅkuṭādibhyaḥ* is interpreted as a genitive in place of the nominative *añṇit*,

the letter *ṅ* would result in being a substitute (*ādeśa*) for the initial *al* (phoneme), according to the statement *alo 'ntyasya*. In the second alternative, however, there would be no comprehension of the named entity (*saṃjñin*) in the rule *aniditāṃ hala upadhāyāḥ kṅiti*, because of the difference between the words [the *saṃjñā* and the *saṃjñin*].

For the term *ṅit* is one thing, and the term *kṅit* is another. Furthermore, in the rule "in the case of the mention of *ṅit*, [the reference is] to *grah* and so on" (Pāṇini 6.1.16), it would follow that only these specific technical names (*saṃjñin*) are intended to be included, and not *yaṅ* and the others, according to the principle: "Between the artificial and the non-artificial, the application of the operation is understood to apply to the artificial" (Vyāḍiparibhāṣā 6).

Even if these defects could somehow be avoided, the fault of excessive complexity (*pratipattigaurava*) incurred in establishing the operation through the avoidance of those two initial positions remains unavoidable.

Thinking that there is no fault whatsoever in the third position, he relies on that very one and says: "This is an *atideśa* (extended application). If this were so, the instruction should have been made by means of the suffix *-vat*, otherwise its meaning would not be understood. This is not so; for words employed in the sense of another's referent convey the meaning of *-vat* even without the suffix *-vat*, as in "the boy is a lion" (*siṃho māṇavakaḥ*) or "the Vāhīka is an ox" (*gaur vāhīkaḥ*). [In the rule] *gāṅ*, the substitute for *iṅ* is taken, as in the rules "*iṅaśca*" [P. 2.4.48], "*gāṅ liṭi*" [P. 2.4.49], and "*vibhāṣā luṅlaṅoḥ*" [P. 2.4.50].
This refers to the substitution *gāṅ* that will be taught in place of *iṅ*, and not to the root *gāṅ* "to go" (Dhātupāṭha 950).

Why, then, is there no reference to the root *gāṅ* "to go" (DhP 950)? To this he says: "Of the *ṅ*-letter," and so forth. The purpose of the *ṅ*-letter belonging to the substitute for *iṅ* is this: so that in this rule (*sūtra*) only that [substitute] might be understood, and nothing else, for the sake of the middle voice (*ātmanepada*). Is this not the case? No; for the middle voice is already established by the status of being a substitute (*sthānivadbhāva*).

Therefore, only the substitute *iṅ* is understood [by the term *gāṅ*]; otherwise, the letter *ṅ* would be purposeless. But one might object: "The letter *ṅ* may serve to include both [the root *gā* 'to go' and the substitute *iṅ*] as a general reference; so how could it be purposeless? This is not the case. For if those two were identical, then the letter *ṅ* would have the function of a general reference; however, they are not identical. This is because the *ṅ* of the root *gāṅ* (meaning 'to go') serves the purpose of indicating the *ātmanepada* endings, whereas the *ṅ* of the other (*iṅ*) has no such application anywhere.
Therefore, because they do not have the same referent (*asamānārthatva*), the inclusion of the general term is incorrect; thus, the substitute *gāṅ* is taken [as the specific one].

But for what purpose is it pronounced here? Why not simply say *gā*? It cannot be done in this way; for if that were the case, according to the rule "when there is the mention of a base without an *anubandha*, there is no [mention] of one with an *anubandha*" (*Vyākaraṇa-paribhāṣā* 53), only the root *gai* ("to sing," Dhātupāṭha 916–917) would be included. For the *kuṭ*-class of roots begins from *kuṭa* ("to bend," Dhātupāṭha 1366) and extends up to *kuṅ* ("to sound," Dhātupāṭha 1401).
Immediately after that, because of the formation of *vṛt*, it is impossible for those [roots] exceeding it to belong to the *kuṭādi* group. Regarding the form *adhyagīṣṭa*:
since the *sic* affix is marked with the *ṅ* indicatory letter (*ṅittva*), the substitution of *ī* occurs by the rule *ghumāsthāgāpājahātisām hali* (Pāṇini 6.4.66).
For here, from the rule *kṅiti* (6.4.63), the word *kṅiti* is understood as a governing term (*anuvartate*), and from the rule *īd yati* (6.4.5), the word *īt* is also understood.
Regarding the form *adhyagīṣata*:
this is the substitution of *ad* [for *gā*] according to [Pāṇini 2.4.45].

Now, why is no example provided for the substitution of *gāṅ* that occurs in the *liṭ* [perfect tense]? He thinks as follows: this [substitution] belongs only to the *luṅ* [aorist]; here, the mention of *liṭ* serves no purpose, because it is already established by the rule to be stated later: "The *liṭ* following a root ending in a consonant is *kit*" [Pāṇini 1.2.5].
"Utkuṭitā": [derived from] the root *kuṭ* in the sense of "crookedness" (*kauṭilye*; Dhātupāṭha 1366). "Utpuṭitā."
The root *puṭ* is listed in the Dhātupāṭha (1367) with the meaning "to join together" (*saṃśleṣaṇe*).

Now, why does the ātmanepada not occur in the form *uccukuṭiṣati* (from the desiderative *san*), given that the *san* suffix is marked as having the *ṅit* designation? It is because of the governing rule concerning the "original instruction" (*upadeśa*).
For in that context, the term "in the original instruction" (*upadeśe*) from [Pāṇini 1.3.2] *upadeśe 'janunāsikaḥ* continues to apply.
And here, the status of being marked with *ṅ* (ṅittva) is not original (*aupadeśika*), but rather derivative (*ātideśika*).
[This applies to] the rule beginning with "of *vyac*" (*vyaceḥ*). The root *vyac*, meaning "to deceive" (*vyājīkaraṇe*), is listed in the *tudādi* class, prior to the *kuṭādi* group.
Regarding the word *vicītā*:
because it has the marker *ṅit*, there is *saṃprasāraṇa* here by the rule [Pāṇini 6.1.6] beginning with *grah-*.
Regarding *uruvyacāḥ*: [the same applies].
The suffix *asun* is added by the rule *sarvadhātubhyo'sun* (Dhātupāṭha 3.2.75). [In *bhrāśa*,] the vowel is lengthened by *[[6.4.14]]*. Regarding the phrase "a suffix beginning with *iṭ*":

that which has *iṭ* as its initial element—such as *tṛc* and so on—is what is meant. Now, why is there not a reference to the *iṭ* of the third person singular (*uttama-puruṣa*)? For its status as having the *k*-marker (*kit*) is already established by that very rule [1.2.4]. This is not the case; for where it is not established by that [rule], there would be a mention of *iṭ* for the purpose of prescribing the *ṅ*-marker (*ṅit*) for the third person singular.
And where would it not be established by that [rule]? In the case of the benedictive (*liṅ*) of the *ārdhadhātuka*—in the form *udvijiṣīya*.

Therefore, it is correct to take the singular number of the first person (*uttamapuruṣa*), and not the augment (*āgama*); this is because of two technical rules (*paribhāṣā*): "when there is the mention of something meaningful, that which is meaningless is not included" (Vyāḍiparibhāṣā 9), and "between a suffix and a non-suffix, only the suffix is to be taken" (Vyāḍiparibhāṣā 72).

Even if, by some means, the inclusion of *iṭ* were accepted, even so, only that [augment] itself would obtain the status of being marked with *ṅ* (ṅittva), and not the suffix beginning with it. Why, then, does he say: "A suffix beginning with *iṭ* becomes marked with *ṅ*"? He thinks as follows: the word *ādi* ("beginning with") is understood from [Pāṇini 1.1.73], and by that, *iṭ* is qualified.

Furthermore, the first-person singular [suffix] does not possess the status of being the "beginning" [of a suffix]; what then? It is the augment (*āgama*) alone; therefore, that [augment] alone is taken.

And since there is no purpose for that initial [element] alone to possess the *ṅit* property, it is understood by implication that the *ṅit* property belongs to the suffix beginning with *iṭ*. Thus, in "udvijitā," because of the *ṅit* property, the *guṇa* substitution prescribed by [Pāṇini 7.3.86], "for a root ending in *pu*, *g*, or *ṇ*, and having a light penultimate vowel," does not occur. Likewise in "prorṇuvitā."

Since the *guṇa* substitution is prohibited by the fact that [the suffix] has the marker *ṅ*, the substitute *uvaṅ* is applied by the rule "aci śnudhātu" (Pāṇini 6.4.77) and so forth. [The term used is] "apit."

Is this a *prasajya-pratiṣedha* (absolute negation) or a *paryudāsa* (relative negation/exclusion)? And what difference does it make here? In the former case, after the augment *āṭ* has been applied to the third person singular of the imperative (*loṭ*) by [Pāṇini 3.4.92], and subsequently by [Pāṇini 6.1.85]—which states that when a single substitute occurs for two vowels where the latter is a *pit*, it behaves like the latter—the single substitute for the vowel of the *āṭ* augment and the vowel of the *tud-* stem would be included under the term "pit" because it follows a *pit*. Since it is a *pit*, the prohibition of the *ṅit* designation by the rule *api* [Pāṇini 1.2.4] would apply, and consequently, the *guṇa* substitution of the verbal root would result.

But in the other alternative, in the case of *acyavante* and *plavante*, since the single substitute (*ekādeśa*) for the *śap* ending and the vowel *ā*—which belongs to both a *pit* and a *pit*—is distinct from the *pit*, the status of being *ṅit* would apply [to the suffix], and consequently, the *guṇa* substitution for the root would not occur? As for the distinctness of the single substitute from the *pit*, it is because everything is treated as if it were the beginning [of the following element] (*ādibadbhāva*), and thus it is included by the mention of the subsequent element (*paragrahaṇa*). It is said in reply: let it be exactly as you wish; there is no fault in either case. First, there is no fault in the former view; because in the case of *tudanti* and so on, the single substitute belongs to the *pit* itself, and not to both the *pit* and the non-*pit*.
For instance: [Pāṇini 3.4.92] prescribes the *pit* designation specifically for the imperative (loṭ) first person, but not for the augment *āṭ*.

There is no fault in the other case either, because by the rule "except when *apit*" (*apit*), the *sārvadhātuka* suffix is qualified—meaning that a *sārvadhātuka* other than one marked as *pit* is called *apit*.
Furthermore, the vowel *ā* at the end of the word *anta* is not the *sārvadhātuka* itself; rather, it is a part of it.

Furthermore, that which is *sārvadhātuka* here does not undergo a single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) with it, and that with which there is a single-substitute is not *sārvadhātuka*. Therefore, although this single-substitute is other than [the portion] ending in *pit*, nevertheless, since it is not *sārvadhātuka*, how could there be the possibility of its having the *ṅit* designation? Or, let there be the *ṅit* designation; even if it has that *ṅit* designation, there is no possibility of the absence of *guṇa* in that [situation]. Because of the rule "that which pertains to the letters is stronger than that which pertains to the stem" (*vārṇād āṅgaṃ balīyaḥ*), in forms such as *cyavante* and *plavante*, the *guṇa* must indeed occur prior to the substitution. As for *kurutaḥ*: [The text continues: "In *kurutaḥ*, the *u* is substituted for the *ṛ* of the root *kṛ* by the rule 'ru' (Pāṇini 7.1.100). Then, by the rule 'ato guṇe' (Pāṇini 6.1.97), *guṇa* is applied to the *u* of the suffix *tas*. However, because of the rule 'pugantalaghūpadhasya ca' (Pāṇini 7.3.86), *guṇa* is subsequently applied to the *u* of the root *kṛ*. Now, one might ask: why is there not *guṇa* for the *u* of the suffix *tas*? It is because the *u* of the suffix is not *laghūpadha* (having a light vowel as its penultimate). [The text continues: "In *kurvanti*, the *u* is substituted for the *ṛ* of the root *kṛ* by the rule 'ru'. Then, by the rule 'ato guṇe', *guṇa* is applied to the *i* of the suffix *jhi*. But why is there not *guṇa* for the *u* of the root? It is because the *u* of the root is not *laghūpadha*. [The text continues: "In *kurvaḥ*, the *u* is substituted for the *ṛ* of the root *kṛ* by the rule 'ru'. Then, by the rule 'ato guṇe', *guṇa* is applied to the *as* of the suffix *vas*. But why is there not *guṇa* for the *u* of the root? It is because the *u* of the root is not *laghūpadha*. [The text continues: "In *kurmaḥ*, the *u* is substituted for the *ṛ* of the root *kṛ* by the rule 'ru'. Then, by the rule 'ato guṇe', *guṇa* is applied to the *mas* of the suffix *mas*. But why is there not *guṇa* for the *u* of the root? It is because the *u* of the root is not *laghūpadha*. [The text continues: "In *kurute*, the *u* is substituted for the *ṛ* of the root *kṛ* by the rule 'ru'. Then, by the rule 'ato guṇe', *guṇa* is applied to the *ta* of the suffix *te*. But why is there not *guṇa* for the *u* of the root? It is because the *u* of the root is not *laghūpadha*. [The text continues: "In *kurvāte*, the *u* is substituted for the *ṛ* of the root *kṛ* by the rule 'ru'. Then, by the rule 'ato guṇe', *guṇa* is applied to the *āte* of the suffix *āte*. But why is there not *guṇa* for the *u* of the root? It is because the *u* of the root is not *laghūpadha*. [The text continues: "In *kurvate*, the *u* is substituted for the *ṛ* of the root *kṛ* by the rule 'ru'. Then, by the rule 'ato guṇe', *guṇa* is applied to the *ante* of the suffix *ante*. But why is there not *guṇa* for the *u* of the root? It is because the *u* of the root is not *laghūpadha*. [The text continues: "In *kurve*, the *u* is substituted for the *ṛ* of the root *kṛ* by the rule 'ru'. Then, by the rule 'ato guṇe', *guṇa* is applied to the *e* of the suffix *e*. But why is there not *guṇa* for the *u* of the root? It is because the *u* of the root is not *laghūpadha*. [The text continues: "In *kurvahe*, the *u* is substituted for the *ṛ* of the root *kṛ* by the rule 'ru'. Then, by the rule 'ato guṇe', *guṇa* is applied to the *vahe* of the suffix *vahe*. But why is there not *guṇa* for the *u* of the root? It is because the *u* of the root is not *laghūpadha*. [The text continues: "In *kurmahe*, the *u* is substituted for the *ṛ* of the root *kṛ* by the rule 'ru'. Then, by the rule 'ato guṇe', *guṇa* is applied to the *mahe* of the suffix *mahe*. But why is there not *guṇa* for the *u* of the root? It is because the *u* of the root is not *laghūpadha*. [The text continues: "In *cakre*, the *e* is substituted for the *ṛ* of the root *kṛ* by the rule 'ṛto ṅi' (Pāṇini 7.2.40). Then, by the rule 'ato guṇe', *guṇa* is applied to the *e* of the suffix *e*. But why is there not *guṇa* for the *e* of the root? It is because the *e* of the root is not *laghūpadha*. [The text continues: "In *cakrāte*, the *e* is substituted for the *ṛ* of the root *kṛ* by the rule 'ṛto ṅi'. Then, by the rule 'ato guṇe', *guṇa* is applied to the *āte* of the suffix *āte*. But why is there not *guṇa* for the *e* of the root? It is because the *e* of the root is not *laghūpadha*. [The text continues: "In *cakrire*, the *e* is substituted for the *ṛ* of the root *kṛ* by the rule 'ṛto ṅi'. Then, by the rule 'ato guṇe', *guṇa* is applied to the *ire* of the suffix *ire*. But why is there not *guṇa* for the *e* of the root? It is because the *e* of the root is not *laghūpadha*. [The text continues: "In *cakṛṣe*, the *e* is substituted for the *ṛ* of the root *kṛ* by the rule 'ṛto ṅi'. Then, by the rule 'ato guṇe', *guṇa* is applied to the *se* of the suffix *se*. But why is there not *guṇa* for the *e* of the root? It is because the *e* of the root is not *laghūpadha*. [The text continues: "In *cakrāthe*, the *e* is substituted for the *ṛ* of the root *kṛ* by the

Consequently, when there is the designation *ṅit*, no *guṇa* substitution occurs for the *vikaraṇa*. For this root *kṛ*, the substitution of *u* (as in *karoti*) takes place by [Pāṇini 6.4.110], because in that rule the term *kṅiti* is understood from the preceding sūtra [Pāṇini 6.4.98] beginning with *gamahana*. Since the *liṭ* suffix is prescribed after a verbal root (*dhātu*) alone and not after anything else, the root is brought into proximity by the force of the *liṭ* itself. Furthermore, that root is qualified by the mention of "not being a conjunct" (*asaṃyoga*), and by virtue of this qualification, the rule of "specifying the end of a compound" (*tadantavidhi*) applies. Thus he says: "from a root ending in a non-conjunct."

If, then, the *kittva* (the status of being *kit*) is prescribed for the *liṭ* suffix following a verbal root ending in a consonant cluster (*saṃyoga*), then forms such as *vavṛte* and *vavṛdhe* would not be established, because the *guṇa* substitution ought to occur due to its higher priority. The scope of *kittva* is exemplified by *ījatuḥ* and *ījuḥ*, while the scope of *guṇa* is exemplified by *vartitvā* and *vardhitvā*. In cases such as *vavṛte* and *vavṛdhe*, where both rules apply, the *guṇa* alone would prevail on account of its higher priority; however, this is not the case.

Since the word *para* signifies "desired," *kitva* alone is desired; *kitva* itself is the highest [desire], and therefore that alone will occur—thus there is no fault. Furthermore, in this context, if the exclusion (*paryudāsa*) "not from a conjunct" (*asaṃyogāt*) is resorted to, then when something other than a conjunct is grasped, by the maxim of the negative particle and the word *iva* (*nañ-ivayukta-nyāya*), only a similar [element] would be grasped. Since a single consonant (*hal*) other than a conjunct is similar to a conjunct, *kitva* would apply only to what ends in a consonant (*halanta*), and not to what ends in a vowel (*ajanta*). Consequently, forms such as *cakre* and *cakruḥ* would not be established.

Therefore, this is an absolute negation (*prasajya-pratiṣedha*), not an exclusion (*paryudāsa*). [The rule] "if it is not due to *saṃyoga*, [the substitution of *guṇa* does not occur] for roots beginning with *yaj-* when a *kit* suffix follows" (Pāṇini 6.1.15) prescribes [the absence of *guṇa*] when there is a *kit* suffix, not when there is a *ṅit* suffix—as in "bibhidatuḥ," "bibhiduḥ.
Due to the *kit* status [of the suffix], by [the rule] "after a root ending in *i* or *u*, when a *kit* suffix follows" (Pāṇini 7.3.86), there is an absence of *guṇa*.
In the forms *sastraṃse* and *dadhvaṃse*, because there is an absence of the *kittva* designation, the elision of the nasal (*anunāsikalopa*) does not occur by [Pāṇini 6.4.24] *aniditām*.

The roots *stransu* and *dhvansu* are listed in the Dhātupāṭha (754–755) as meaning "falling down"; since they are marked with an indicatory vowel *ṅ* (indicating *anudāttet*), the *ātmanepada* endings are used, and the substitution of *e* for the final vowel occurs according to [Pāṇini 3.4.81].
Regarding *bibheditha*: [the suffix] *sip* [is used]; [the augment] *iṭ* is applied by the rule of *krādiniyama*. Regarding *samīghe*:

[the root] *ñīndhī* in the sense of "shining" (*dīptau*; Dhātupāṭha 1448); as before, the *ātmanepada* [suffixes are used], followed by the replacement with *eś*; due to its being *kit*, there is the elision of the nasal according to [Pāṇini 6.4.24], *aniditām* etc.; then reduplication; and finally, the lengthening of a vowel in homogeneous combination according to [Pāṇini 6.1.97], *akaḥ savarṇe dīrghaḥ*.

Why does the augment *ām* not occur [after the root *indh*] by rule 3.1.36 (*atha*)? Because this [rule] has the domain of *mantra*s, and in that context there is the governing restriction (*adhikāra*) "not in a *mantra*" (*amantre*). If that is so, since a *mantra* is indeed *chandas*, then by rule 3.4.117 (*chandasyubhayathā*), the suffix would be treated as *sārvadhātuka*; and consequently, by rule 1.2.4 (*sārvadhātukam apit*), it would have the *ṅit*-designation. Precisely because of that *ṅit*-designation, the elision of the nasal (*anunāsikalopa*) will occur. So why is the *kit*-designation prescribed for the *liṭ* following *indh*? It is for the sake of providing an indication (*jñāpana*).
By this, it is indicated that this *ām* is not universally obligatory (*anitya*).

If [the augment] *ām* were permanent, then because it would necessarily intervene, the *liṅ* suffix could not follow immediately after the root *indh*, and thus the prescription of *kittva* (the status of having *k* as an it-marker) would be untenable; therefore, this *ām* is non-permanent.
Consequently, the usage *samīdhe* is also justified even in the spoken language (*bhāṣā*). As for *babhūva* and *babhūvitha*:
due to *kittva*, the *vṛddhi* and *guṇa* substitutions do not occur respectively. Then, by the rule *bhuvo vug luṅaliṭoḥ* [Pāṇini 6.4.88], the augment *vuk* is applied.

By the rule *bhavateraḥ* [Pāṇini 7.4.73], the substitution of *a* occurs for the reduplication (*abhyāsa*). Now, one might object: "Since *vuk* applies whether the guna and vṛddhi substitutions have already taken place or not, *vuk* is permanent (*nitya*), because it applies regardless of whether those operations have occurred. Once *vuk* has been applied by virtue of its permanence, there is no possibility at all for guna and vṛddhi to occur, because the root *bhū* would then lack a light penultimate vowel (*alaghūpadha*) and would not end in a vowel (*anajanta*). Therefore, the mention of *bhū* [in the rule] is useless. This is not so; for according to the principle that "a rule which applies to a different word-form is non-permanent" (Vyāḍipāda 100), *vuk* itself is also non-permanent.
Furthermore, because the operations of *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* would take precedence, once they have been applied, the substitution of *vaṅ* would not occur.
Therefore, the mention of the root *bhū* must be made.

Now, if it is argued that even when *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* have been applied, "that which is modified in one part is not different [from the original]" and thus there is no change of word-form (*śabdāntaratva*), then in that case, it would be possible to omit the mention of *bhū*.

That is done for the sake of clarity. Now, regarding the form *babhūva*, how is there a prohibition of the *vṛddhi* [substitution] by [Pāṇini 7.2.115], given that the word *ekācaḥ* continues to apply [from 7.2.10]? If it is argued: "By [Pāṇini 1.1.5] *kṅiti ca*, the *vṛddhi* characterized by an *it* (i.e., the *it-śāstrīya-vṛddhi*) is prohibited, but this *vṛddhi* is not characterized by an *it*, because its locus (*sthānin*) is explicitly specified [in the rule]," we reply: here, by the force of the prescription of *kit*-ness, there will be a prohibition even of *vṛddhi* not characterized by an *it*; otherwise, the prescription of *kit*-ness would be purposeless. This is not so; for that [prescription of *kit*-ness] is intended to prohibit *guṇa* in the case of the third person singular ending *thal* and the first person singular ending *ṇal*.

In that case, the mention of *ṅit* also continues [from the previous rule]. Since there is no other purpose for its continuation, it will therefore also result in a prohibition of *vṛddhi* even when it is not characterized by *ṅ*.

[The statement] "the mention of *indh* is for the sake of [avoiding] a conjunct" (*saṃyoga*)—this is because, due to its ending in a conjunct, the [prohibition] would not be established by the preceding rule.
Regarding the statement "for the sake of the root *bhū* with the affix *pi*":
it is not for the sake of *pi*; because that [root *bhū*] does not end in a conjunct consonant, it is already established by the preceding rule (*api* = *apit*).

Here, the mention of *bhavati* by means of the *śtip* affix is for the purpose of excluding the elision of *yaṅ* (*yaṅluk*); that is, so that the *liṭ* affix following a stem ending in the elided *yaṅ* does not acquire the *kit* designation.
Regarding the form *bobhāva*:

it has been stated thus—"That which is specified by means of *śtip*, *śap*, an indicatory letter (*anubandha*), or a class name (*gaṇa*), as well as any instance where a single-vowel (*ekāj*) term is mentioned—these five do not apply in the case of *yaṅ*-luṅ."

Regarding the example *(pu|pa|94)*, namely *anthigranthi* and so forth: the meaning is that this should be explained as having the purpose of ensuring that the *liṭ* [perfect tense] suffixes of these roots—*śranth* and *granth* in the sense of "binding" (*sandarbhe*; Dhātupāṭha 1512, 1513), *dambh* in the sense of "deceiving" (*dambhe*; Dhātupāṭha 1290), and *ṣvanj* in the sense of "embracing" (*pariṣvaṅge*; Dhātupāṭha 973)—are treated as *kit*.

In this regard, the following is the explanation: the particle *ca* is employed for the purpose of including what has not been explicitly mentioned; by means of it, there will be the *kittva* (the status of being *kit*) of the *liṭ* [perfect] even for roots such as *śranth*, ending in a conjunct consonant (*saṃyoga*).
Thus, *śrethatuḥ* and so forth:
due to the *kittva*, there is the elision of the nasal according to [Pāṇini 6.4.24], *aniditām*.

In the rule *tṛphalabhajatrapaśca* [Pāṇini 6.4.122], because the particle *ca* has the sense of including what is not explicitly mentioned (*anuktasamuccaya*), the substitution of *e* for *ai* and the elision of the reduplication (*abhyāsalopa*) apply even when the root is situated between multiple consonants,
as in *pariṣasvaje*.
The middle voice (*ātmanepada*) is used here because the root begins with an unaccented vowel (*anudāttettva*).

When the rule *sthādiṣv abhyāsena cābhyāsasya* [Pāṇini 8.3.64] is in effect, the substitution of *ṣ* for the initial *s* of the preceding [root] occurs by the rule *upasargāt sunoti* [Pāṇini 8.3.65], etc.

However, regarding the *sakāra* of another [root], there is a prohibition of *ṣatva* by the rule "there is no *ṣatva* for [the *s*] following *sad*, *si*, and *svañj* in the *liṭ*. [The roots are: *muḍ* "to cleanse" (DhP 1516), *mṛd* "to crush" (DhP 1515), *gudh* "to be angry" (DhP 1517), *kuṣ* "to extract" (DhP 1518), *kliś* "to afflict" (DhP 1522), *vad* "to speak clearly" (DhP 1009), and *vas* "to dwell" (DhP 1942). [The author] will state that there is a prohibition of *kittva* by the rule "not [after a root] having an indicatory *ṭ* when followed by *ktvā* with an augment *iṭ*" (*na ktvā seṭ*).

[Objection: But surely this very rule will serve as a restrictive one (*niyamārtha*), meaning that the *ktvā* suffix is *kit* only after roots such as *mṛḍ*, and not after others. Consequently, forms such as *devitvā* and *sevitvā* would be established. Why, then, will [the author] state the prohibition [in 1.2.18]? [Reply: It is for the sake of clarity; otherwise, some might suspect a contrary restriction, namely, that the *ktvā* suffix is *kit* only after roots such as *mṛḍ*, and not after any other.
Regarding the phrase "an anticipation" (*purastādapakarṣaḥ*) and so forth: "anticipation" (*apakarṣa*) means an exception (*apavāda*).
Regarding "having afflicted" (*kliśitvā*), the augment *iṭ* is applied by [Pāṇini 7.2.50]. Regarding "having spoken" (*uditvā*) and "having dwelt" (*uṣitvā*).

There is vocalization (*saṃprasāraṇa*) by the rule *vacyādi* [Pāṇini 6.1.15]. From the root *vas* (to dwell), there is the substitution of *ṣ* by the rule *śāsivasidhasīnāṃ ca* [Pāṇini 8.3.60], and the augment *iṭ* by the rule *vasatikṣudhoḥ* [Pāṇini 7.2.52]. The roots are: *rudir* (to shed tears), *vida* (to know), *muṣ* (to steal), *graha* (to seize), *ñiṣvap* (to sleep), and *praccha* (to inquire). Regarding the phrase "for the sake of the injunction for *grahi*": this means that the specific mention of *grahi* is intended to establish a particular grammatical operation.
This is so that there may be a re-enactment of the *kittva* (the status of being *kit*), which was prohibited by the rule *na ktvā seṭ* [Pāṇini 1.2.18].
The statement beginning with "The root *svapi* is for the sake of the rule itself" and so forth means "for the sake of the desiderative (*san*) suffix."

Now, he asks why there is no statement regarding the meaning of the suffix *ktvā*: "Indeed, *ktvā* is like a *kit*. For in the case of the roots *svap* and *pracch*, because the prohibition of *iṭ* applies by the rule *ekāca upadeśe'nudāttāt* [Pāṇini 7.2.10], *ktvā* does not become *seṭ*; therefore, the prohibition [of *guṇa*] by the rule *na ktvā seṭ* [Pāṇini 1.2.18] does not operate. Consequently, "indeed, *ktvā* is like a *kit*," as in the example *ruditvā*.
The suffix *ktvā* [is applied] as in [[3.4.21]];
thus, "having taken" (*gṛhītvā*).
By the rule beginning with *grah-* [[7.2.37]], there is *saṃprasāraṇa* according to [[6.1.16]].
In *jighṛkṣati*:

by [Pāṇini 8.2.31] *ho ḍhaḥ*, there is the substitution of *ḍha*; by [8.2.41], there is the substitution of *ka*; by [8.2.37] *ekāco baśo bhaṣ* and so forth, there is the substitution of *gha* for *ga*; and by [7.2.12], there is the prohibition of the augment *iṭ*. In *suṣupsati*: [the same process applies].
The semivowel substitution (*saṃprasāraṇa*) occurs by the rule *vacyādi* [Pāṇini 6.1.15].

In the form *pipṛcchiṣati*, there is also semivowel substitution by the rule *grahādi* [Pāṇini 6.1.16]; then, by the rule *che ca* [Pāṇini 6.1.71], the augment *tuk* is added, and by the rule *stoḥ ścunā ścuḥ* [Pāṇini 8.4.40], the change to the *ścutva* sound [the palatal *ch*] occurs. The word "having finished with *ktvā*" means that the discussion of *ktvā* has concluded.
Since the *kit* status of the *ktvā* suffix is indeed inherent (*aupadeśika*) when it begins with a *jhal* sound, its recurrence [in the rule] would be purposeless.
However, the term *sangrahaṇa* (the act of grasping) occurs here in the nominative case; its grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the word *jhal* is thus established.

Therefore, by implication, the rule of *tadādividhi* (specification of that which begins with something) is understood; hence he says: "A *san* beginning with a *jhal* letter becomes *kit*. Now, why does the rule of *tadantavidhi* (specification of that which ends with something)—namely, "a *san* ending in a *jhal*"—not apply? He thinks as follows: from the rule concerning the technical term *vṛddha* [Pāṇini 1.1.72], the mention of *ādi* (beginning with) is carried over here, and by that, the *jhal* is qualified; therefore, only *tadādividhi* is understood, not *tadantavidhi*.

If, however, this were an *anta-vidhi* (an operation affecting the end of a word), what would happen? It would apply only where, after the elision (*lopa*) of the final *a*, the root ends in a *jhal* consonant—such as in *cikīrṣitā* and so on; but it would not apply in cases like *cikīrṣati*, because the root would then end in an *at* vowel. This status of ending in an *at* vowel arises because the single substitute for both the *sañ* and the letter *k* is treated as the final element (*antavadbhāva*) with respect to the preceding portion. Now, why is the root *ika* from the Dhātupāṭha (*ik smaraṇe*, 1047) not understood here? Because it is more appropriate to take *jhal* as a *pratyāhāra* (a technical abbreviation for consonants); furthermore, it is because the word *jigīṣu* is listed among the *gargādi* group [of patronymic suffixes].

For if there were a mention of "dhātu" (root), the *kittva* (the property of being marked with *k*) of the suffix *san* following the root *ji* would not occur; and thus the word *jigīṣu* would not be established. Furthermore, if there were a mention of "dhātu," the rule [Pāṇini 1.2.10], which states that "a consonant (*hal*) standing near a root (*dhātu*) does not [cause the elision of the *i* of the suffix *ik*]," would also become inapplicable.
Therefore, it is logical that only the *pratyāhāra* (the technical abbreviation) is intended to be included, and not the word "dhātu."
In *cicīṣati*,
there is lengthening by [Pāṇini 6.4.16].
The prohibition of *iṭ* is applied by the previously mentioned rule [Pāṇini 7.2.10], *ekācaḥ*.

Even further on, wherever there is no hearing of the word *iṭ*, the prohibition should be understood to apply by this very [rule]. However, where there is a specific exception, that must indeed be stated— as in the case of *tuṣṭūṣati*.
By [Pāṇini 7.4.61], there is the elision of the remaining consonants (*khayaḥ śeṣaḥ*).
Thus, "śiśayiṣate" is formed;
by [Pāṇini 1.3.62], the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) is applied.

In the same way, in what follows as well, the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) should be understood to apply immediately after *icchā-sannanta* by this very rule. As for the phrase "For what purpose, then... and so forth, the intention will be explained hereafter:
"Lest there be *guṇa* substitution."
He states that for which this is said.
To reveal the intention with which he asked the question, he says: "ajjhanagamāṃ sani" and so forth.
If the *guṇa* substitution were to occur even after the lengthening has been applied, then the lengthening would be rendered purposeless (*vaiyarthyam*).
"Therefore, lest the [rule for] lengthening be rendered purposeless, the lengthening will be the sublater of that guna.
To point out the fault here, he says: "In that case, just as... and so forth.
Just as lengthening—which, in the absence of *kittva* (the *kit* designation), has no other scope—becomes the sublater of *guna*, so too [is it said]: "Therefore," and so forth.

Since this fault would thus attach itself to this [rule] if it were not commenced, therefore this *kittva* (the designation *kit*) is commenced in order to provide an occasion for lengthening (*dīrghatva*).
Now, even when this is commenced, why does this fault not occur? To this he says: "in *cicīṣati*" and so forth;
because when *kittva* is present, the *guṇa* is barred by that very [designation].

In forms such as *cicīṣati* and *tuṣṭūṣati*, the lengthening (of the vowel) occurs because it has its own scope; and by virtue of being subsequent, it does not preclude the elision of the *ṇi*-affix (*ṇilopa*).

For when there is the status of being *kit*, it cannot be said that just as the lengthening precludes the *guṇa* substitution, so too does it preclude the elision of the *ṇi*; because the *guṇa* is not precluded by the lengthening, but rather by the status of being *kit*.

Here, the scope for lengthening (*dīrghatva*) has been shown, whereas the scope for the elision of *ṇi* (*ṇilopa*) is as follows: *pāktiḥ* from *pācayati*, *yāṣṭiḥ* from *yājayati*, and so forth. In the case of *jñīpsati*, where both [rules] would apply, the elision of *ṇi* alone occurs by virtue of its being subsequent (*paratvāt*), thereby superseding the lengthening.
