[The roots are: *jñā* in the sense of "understanding" (DhP 1507); *māraṇatoṣaṇaniśāmaneṣu* (DhP 811); and *micca* (DhP 1624)—the suffix *ṇic* is added because these are read in the *curādi* group. The augment *puk* is applied by the rule *artihyī* etc. (Aṣṭādhyāyī 7.3.36).
The shortening [of the vowel] occurs by the rule *mitāṃ hrasvaḥ* [Pāṇini 6.4.92].

Others, however, read the root as *jñapa māraṇatoṣaṇaniśāmaneṣu* (Dhātupāṭha 1624); from that, the suffix *ṇic* is added, followed by the desiderative suffix *san*. By the rule *sanīvantardha-* [Pāṇini 7.2.49], there is optionally an absence of the augment *iṭ*. Then, by the rule *kāpjñapṛdhāmīt* [Pāṇini 7.4.55], the substitution of *īt* occurs, and by the rule *ata ekahalmadhye-* [Pāṇini 6.4.120], there is the elision of the reduplicated syllable. By the rule *taḥ* [Pāṇini 6.4.51], there is the elision of the suffix *ṇi*. [The statement] "the *kittva* of *ik*" and so forth [is explained as follows].

Now, for what purpose is the *kittva* (the property of being marked with *k*) prescribed for the subsequent *san* suffix, and for what purpose is the rule split (*yogavibhāga*) as "after an *ik*, [there is *kittva*] when followed by a *jhal*"? Should not this single sūtra simply be read as: "after an *ik*, [there is *kittva*] when followed by a *jhal* or after a word ending in a *hal*"? He states the purpose: "so that *guṇa* does not occur. In forms such as *cicīṣati*, *guṇa* would apply by [Pāṇini 7.3.84]; it is for the sake of preventing that that *kittva* is prescribed.

This purpose does not exist; because the rule for lengthening (dīrghatva) is commenced when the rule for *guṇa* has not yet applied—therefore, due to the commencement of the lengthening, the *guṇa* will not occur. Otherwise, the mention of "lengthening" (*dīrgha*) would be meaningless.

But surely the mention of lengthening is meaningful in the case of *cukūṣate*, for here, since the suffix is marked with *ṅ* by the rule *gāṅkuṭādibhyaḥ* [Pāṇini 1.2.1], the *guṇa* substitution does not take effect? This is not so; for the commencement of a grammatical rule is not prompted by a single example alone.
If this were the intended purpose, [the author] would simply have used the term *ṇi*.

Alternatively, with respect to the mere aggregate [of sounds], the technical rule (*paribhāṣā*) beginning with "before a word-initial" (*purastādapadādāḥ*) does not exist at all. The term *ikaḥ* is understood to carry over [from a previous rule].

In this context, if the word *anta* were to denote a constituent part (*avayava*), there could be no connection between *ik* and a consonant (*hal*), for an *ik* cannot possibly be a constituent part of a consonant.

For that which is commenced by something else, being non-different in location from it, becomes its part—as, for example, threads are parts of a cloth. And [the word] *hala* is not commenced by the [word] *anta*; therefore, this word *anta* does not denote a "part. Rather, considering it appropriate that it denotes "proximity," he says: "This word *anta* denotes proximity."

[Objection: But surely the term *dhātu* is implied here by the force of the context; therefore, with respect to that, the consonants (*hal*) will possess the status of being its constituents (*avayava*). [Reply: This is not so; for in that case, the word *anta* would be redundant, since the rule of "specification of what ends in that" (*tadantavidhi*) is already obtained by the rule *yena vidhis tadantasya* (Pāṇini 1.1.72).
Furthermore, he demonstrates that this is a *karmadhāraya* compound through the specific analysis: "that which is both a consonant (*hal*) and an end (*anta*).
[Question: Of what, then, is this the end? [Answer: Of the *ik* under discussion.

If this is so, then since "that which is dependent is incapable [of forming a compound]," the formation of a compound for the word *anta*—which is itself dependent on another—would not be possible. This is not a fault; for in this case, the word *anta* is the principal member (*pradhāna*). And it will be made known in the second chapter (at Pāṇini 2.1.56) by the inclusion of the term *sāmānyāprayoga* that a compound is indeed possible even for a principal member when it is dependent. The phrase *igantāt* is a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*).

But surely, "ika" ending in the ablative case is the subject under discussion; how then can there be a genitive compound? This is not a fault; for although the ablative form is the subject, nevertheless, here—given the relationship between the proximate and the proximal—it undergoes a change of case-ending to assume the state of being in the genitive:
namely, "from that which is proximate to an *ik*" or "belonging to an *ik* situated nearby. [As in the example: "he desires to know" (*bubhutsate*).
The root *budh* is listed as *avagamane* (Dhātupāṭha 1172). By the rule *ekāco baśo bhaṣ* (Pāṇini 8.2.37) and others, the substitution of *bhaṣ* occurs.
In subsequent cases as well, wherever the substitution of *bhaṣ* applies, it should be understood through this very rule.
By the rule *khari ca* (Pāṇini 8.4.54), there is the substitution of *cari*—that is, the letter *t* replaces the letter *dh*.
In the form *yiyakṣate*,
there is no vocalization (*saṃprasāraṇa*) by virtue of the rule beginning with *yajivraścādibhyaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.1.15).
If the word *amant* were to mean "that which is near," then the *kittva* (the status of having an *it*-augment) of the *san* following the root *dambh* would not be established.
For instance: since that *hal* which is adjacent to the *ik* is not posterior to it, and that which is posterior to it is not adjacent to the *ik*, he says "of *dambhi*" and so forth.

By the term *hal*, the class (*jāti*) of *hal* is denoted, not the individual (*vyakti*). Therefore, according to the view that "the class is those very individuals with their distinctions abandoned," there is no intervention for those individuals when they are relied upon as being *hal*.

Therefore, since the *san* suffix following immediately after that very class (*jāti*) of consonants (*hal*) which is proximate [to the root], the *kittva* (the status of being *kit*) prescribed for the *san* of the root *dambh* is already established.

Even when the class, which is a distinct entity, is entirely present in each individual instance (*vyakti*) and is partless and one, there is still no intervention; because it is an individual instance that acts as an intervener between another individual instance, but not the class, since that class is bodiless (*aśarīrin*).
Consequently, even in this view, since the *san* follows immediately after that very class of consonants which is situated nearby, the *kittva* of the *san* following *dambh* occurs.

Regarding that universal (*jāti*) which is distinct from the individual (*vyakti*), both its being proximate to the *ika* and the *sann* suffix’s being subsequent to it—which depends upon that universal—must be understood as mediated through the individual.

In this context, because the individual *n* is proximate to the *ika*, the *hal*-universal residing in it is also proximate to the *ika*; and because the *sann* suffix is subsequent to the individual *bh*, it is also subsequent to the universal residing in it. However, for a universal, proximity to the *ika* independent of the individual is not possible.
Nor is the posteriority of the suffix *san* relative to the universal (*jāti*); both of these [proximity and posteriority] should be understood as mediated by the individual (*vyakti*).

In this context, since the individual instance of the letter *n* is proximate, the universal of the consonant (*hal-jāti*) residing in that [individual] is also proximate; thus, because it is posterior to the individual instance of the letter *bh*, the suffix *san* is also posterior to the universal that serves as its substrate. However, proximity cannot exist for a universal independently of an individual, nor can the posteriority of *san* be relative to a universal; for a universal is incorporeal.

If, then, both of these [properties] are mediated by the individual (*vyakti*), then in that case, the opposite would also be mediated by the individual. [For example: because the individual *bh* is not proximate, the genus (*jāti*) would also not exist; because the individual *n* is not subsequent, the genus would also not exist. Consequently, even though the term *hal* denotes the genus, the *kittva* (the status of being marked with *k*) of the suffix *san* following the root *dambh* would not be established. This is not so.

Although for a genus (*jāti*), proximity and its opposite are mediated by the individual (*vyakti*), and although for a suffix (*san*) as well, posteriority and its opposite are mediated by the individual and depend upon the genus; nevertheless, since the *kit* status will apply here based on that which is the proximity of the general property of being a consonant (*hal-tva-sāmānya*) and that upon which the posteriority of the suffix depends, the opposite case, even though it exists, is simply not taken into account, in accordance with the requirements of the linguistic examples (*lakṣya*).

But is it not the case that what is called "the nature of being a *hal*" (*haltva*) is indeed a universal (*jāti*), for it does not exist? To explain: the technical term "*hal*" functions solely by virtue of convention, like words such as *ḍittha* and so on.

For it cannot be maintained that there exists an undifferentiated universal called "the nature of being a *hal*" among the phonemes *ha*, *k*, and so forth, in the same way that there exists an undifferentiated universal such as "cowness" (*gotva*) among cows and the like; this is because there is no basis for such a [universal] to exist.

Furthermore, it was stated that [the derivation] is established because the mention of *haL* in the rule for *dambh-* refers to the genus (*jāti*); however, this is not so. Even in the view of those who maintain that the referent of a word is a genus (*jātipadārthavādin*), in the case of proper names such as *Devadatta* which denote a single entity, a genus is nevertheless admitted on the basis of the multiplicity imagined through the differences in its states. How much more so, then, in the case of technical terms (*saṃjñāśabda*) like *haL*, which have multiple phonemes as their domain! Otherwise, the established principle of the relationship between word and meaning would be over-extensive (*ativyāpin*).

Furthermore, you must first be asked this: what is the basis for the existence of a universal (*jāti*) in cows and the like, by virtue of which it is accepted there? If you say it is "the application of a non-different designation and cognition toward things that are different," then these two [conditions] are equally present in the other case as well. For just as those two [designation and cognition] occur in cows and the like—even though they are different—following after [the perception] subsequent to the convention (*saṅketa*), so too do they occur in the case of the phonemes *ha* and so forth. And just as those two do not occur in them prior to the convention, so too they do not occur in cows and the like either.

Therefore, since those two—the designation and cognition as non-different among things that are different—which serve as the grounds for the conviction in the existence of a universal (*jāti*), also exist in the case of *hal*s (consonants), one must likewise admit a universal called *haltva* there. It is not the case that there is an absolute rule that universals such as *gotva* exist only in cows and the like. [The examples] "dhipsati" and "dhīpsati" are illustrations of this in cases where, according to the rule "sanīvantardha" (Pāṇini 7.2.49) and others, the augment *iṭ* does not occur.
By [Pāṇini 7.4.56], there is the substitution of *i* for the vowel; by [7.4.58], there is the elision of the reduplication (*abhyāsa*).

By [8.4.54], "and before a *khari* sound," there is the substitution of *c* (the *cartya* rule), whereby the *bh* becomes *p*. Since the suffix is marked with *k*, there is no elision of the nasal by [6.4.24], "of those not having *it* as an *it*" (*aniditām*).
By the *bhaṣ*-rule, the *d* becomes *dh*. [This applies] when the *liṅ* and *sic* follow in the *ātmanepada*.

But how can the *liṅ* [augment] occur when the ātmanepada suffixes follow, given that it is only the *sic* [augment] that can occur before ātmanepada suffixes, not the *liṅ*? He thinks as follows: here the word *liṅ* refers to the *sīyuṭ* [augment], which is a part of the *liṅ*, just as in [Pāṇini 1.1.4] the word *dhātu* refers to a part of a verbal root (*dhātu*).
Therefore, by this method, the *kit*-status is prescribed for the *sīyuṭ* itself.

Alternatively—just as in the rule *halṅyābbhyo dīrghāt* (Pāṇini 6.1.66), this qualification "after a long [vowel]" applies only to those two [suffixes] *ṅī* and *āp* for which lengthening is possible, so too here, this qualification applies only to that *sic* after which the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) can occur. The mention of the middle voice is for the purpose of excluding the active voice (*parasmaipada*). As in the example:
*abhistaṣṭa*.
The suffix *liṅ* is used here according to [Pāṇini 3.3.173] *āśiṣi liṅloṭau*; because it is marked with a *svarita* accent, the *ātmanepada* (middle voice) is employed.
In the same way, in subsequent cases as well, the *ātmanepada* should be understood by this very rule for roots marked with *svarita* or *ñ*.
The augment *suṭ* is applied according to [Pāṇini 3.4.107] *suṭ tithoḥ*.

In the active voice (*kartari*), the suffix *śnam* does not occur, nor does the elision of the final *s* of the *liṅ* (as prescribed by Pāṇini 7.2.79), because [the former] applies to *ārdhadhātuka* affixes and both [the latter and *śnam*] are prescribed for *sārvadhātuka* affixes. Regarding "bhutsīṣṭa," one should understand that the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) is applied to the root *budh* by virtue of Pāṇini 1.3.12 (*anudāttaṅita ātmanepadam*).

Even in subsequent cases, the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) for the agent after roots marked with an *anudātta* vowel or the suffix *ṅit* should be understood by this very rule. Regarding the form *abhitta*:
there is the elision of *sic* by [Pāṇini 8.2.26] *jhalo jhali*.
In the word *abuddha*,
the letter *t* is changed to *dh* by [Pāṇini 8.2.40], and the preceding *dh* is changed to *d* by [Pāṇini 8.4.53]. In the word *yakṣīṣṭa*:
Because of the *svarita* accent, the *ātmanepada* ending is used.
As before, there is the substitution of *ṣ* for *s* and *k* for *t*.
[The rule] "for there would be vocalization (*saṃprasāraṇa*)" applies.

By the rule *vacy-ādi-sūtra* [Pāṇini 6.1.15], we have *adrākṣīt*. [In this form,] the augment *iṭ* is applied by the rule *asti sico 'pṛkte* [Pāṇini 7.3.96], and then *vṛddhi* substitution occurs by [the rule] *sici vṛddhiḥ parasmaipadeṣu* [Pāṇini 7.2.3].

The changes to *ṣatva* and *katva* are as before. Furthermore, since *liṅ* and *sic* are being carried over [from previous rules], they bring the verbal root (*dhātu*) into proximity, because it is precisely from that [root] that those two [suffixes] are prescribed.

And since [the rule] "na ca ṛkāreṇa viśiṣyate" (Pāṇini 1.1.72) indicates that the designation of the end of a word (*tadantavidhi*) is understood by means of the phoneme *ṛ*, he says: "from a verbal root ending in the phoneme *ṛ*," and so forth.

Now, why is there not a reference to the root *ṛ* "to go" (Dhātupāṭha 1098)? This is the style of the Teacher: wherever he intends to refer to a specific root, he provides its indication by means of the *śtip* affix, as in "and in the case of *ṛ* and *piparty*" (Pāṇini 7.4.77) and "after *sṛ*, *śās*, and *ṛ*" (Pāṇini 3.1.56). Since no such indication by *śtip* has been made here, this is a reference to the vowel *ṛ* itself, and not to the root. In the form "akṛta," there is the elision of the suffix *sic* according to [Pāṇini 8.2.27], "after a short vowel, the suffix *sic* is elided."
The form *variṣīṣṭa* is derived from either the root *vṛṅ* or *vṛñ*;
the augment *iṭ* is applied by the rule *liṅsicorātmanepadeṣu* [Pāṇini 7.2.42]. The form *saṃgasīṣṭa* is likewise formed.

The *ātmanepada* ending is applied by the rule *samo gamṛcchi* [Pāṇini 1.3.29]. In the form *samagata*, the elision of the suffix *sic* occurs according to the rule *hrasvāṅgāt* [Pāṇini 8.2.27]. In the form *āhata*, [the same applies].
> [[1.3.28]] Thus, the *ātmanepada* [ending] is applied.
As before, there is the elision of *sic*.
[The form is] *āhasata*.

Regarding the rule *ātmanepadeṣvanataḥ* (Pāṇini 7.1.5), which prescribes the substitute *at*: Now, since the mention of *sic* was already under discussion, for what purpose is *sic* mentioned again? He says: "The mention of *sic* is for the purpose of excluding the *liṅ*. For the previously mentioned mention of *sic* is connected with the *liṅ*; therefore, if that [mention] were to carry over, one might suspect that the *liṅ* would also carry over. Consequently, the mention of *sic* is made in order to exclude that.

Now, one might object: "In the case of the optative (*liṅ*) of the root *han*, there ought to be the substitution of *vadh* for *han*; and even if the *kit* designation were present there, nothing undesirable would result. So why is the mention of *sic* made for the purpose of excluding the optative? To this, he says: "In the subsequent [rules]," and so forth.

The intention is this: if the marker *liṅ* were to carry over (*anuvartate*) here, then it would carry over into what follows, and consequently, by the subsequent rule, that [root] would also possess the *kit* designation. However, someone might have the misconception that because the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) does not qualify the *sij* affix in this commentary (*vṛtti*), the middle voice has been discontinued; therefore, in order to dispel that, he says: "The mention of the middle voice," and so forth. To the question, "Why does this not also apply here? he replies: "But here," and so forth. By the rule "And in the *luṅ* [after *han*]" (Pāṇini 1.2.14), the substitute *vadh* is applied to *han* in the parasmaipada *luṅ*; and that [substitution] is obligatory (*nitya*).

Its permanence, however, is due to the inclusion of the term *anyatarasyām* ("optionally") in the subsequent rule (Pāṇini 3.1.54). Since there is no purpose for the *kittva* (the designation as having a *k*-marker) when the substitute *vadh* is permanent, the recurrence (*anuvṛtti*) of the term *ātmanepada* here is not justified. Now, for what purpose is the *kittva* prescribed for the *sic* suffix following the root *han*, given that the *ṅittva* (the designation as having a *ṅ*-marker) already applies to the *sārvadhātuka* suffix following *sic* by [Pāṇini 1.2.4]? In that case, the elision of the nasal vowel is already established by [Pāṇini 6.4.24]: *aniditām...*.
If it is argued that [the rule] does not succeed because the suffix *sic* is marked with the *it*-indicator (*it*), we say no; for the vowel *i* in *sic* is intended merely for ease of pronunciation.
For it will be stated under [Pāṇini 3.1.44] that "the vowel *i* is for the sake of pronunciation.

Even so, if it is argued that because the suffix *cli* is marked with the *it*-indicator, *sic*—by virtue of its status as a substitute (*sthānivadbhāva*)—is also considered to have the *it*-indicator, and thus [the desired result] does not succeed, we say no; for the vowel *a* in *cli* is intended merely for ease of pronunciation.
For he will state under [Pāṇini 3.1.43] that "the vowel *i* is for the sake of pronunciation.

If this is so, then since the status of being *ṅit* is already established, the fact that he again prescribes the *kit* status of the suffix *sic* after the root *han* indicates the following: with respect to the external *sārvadhātuka* suffix, the elision of the nasal (by Pāṇini 6.4.24, *aniditām...*) does not occur for a stem ending in *sic*. By this, forms such as *āraṃsta*, *amaṃsta*, and *āyaṃsta pādam* are established.

Otherwise, if the nasal were elided, the undesirable form *āyatā* would result. Now, one might object: since the root *yam* is listed in the Dhātupāṭha as meaning "to cease" (*uparama*), how can it here function in the sense of "enticing" (*gandhana*)? To this he says: "Because it has multiple meanings.

In the rule [1.3.28], the term *akarmaka* ("intransitive") from [1.3.45] is understood to carry over. Therefore, one might ask: since this root is transitive here, how is the Ātmanepada used? To this he says: "Even though it is transitive," and so forth.
The transitivity (*sakarmakatva*) of the root *pad* and others exists here because of the presence of the act of stepping;
as in "he lifted his foot" (*udāyaṃsta pādam*), which means he drew it up. [Regarding] "the act of splitting" (*dārakarma*).
The word *karma* denotes action; the meaning is "the act of marriage. [Pāṇini 1.2.17] *sthā-dhvoḥ ic ca*.

[[1.2.17]] By the word "ca" (and), he shows that the *kit* status is conjoined with the *sic* suffix. But for what purpose is the *kit* status prescribed for *sic*, given that its fruit is the prohibition of *guṇa* [vowel strengthening]? For, by the very force of prescribing the vowel *i*, there will be no *guṇa*; otherwise, one would simply have prescribed the vowel *i* alone. This is not so; for the prescription of the vowel *i* would be for the sake of brevity (*lāghava*).
Pronouncing a short vowel is more concise than pronouncing a long one.
Regarding the term *upāsthita*:

since the mention of the root *sthā* continues from [Pāṇini 1.3.22] *samapravibhyaḥ sthaḥ* through [1.3.25], the rule *sannipātalakṣaṇo vidhiranimittaṃ tadvighātasya* (Vyāḍi-paribhāṣā 12)—which states that a grammatical operation conditioned by a specific phonetic configuration does not cause the destruction of that very configuration—prevents the substitution of *it* (the augment *i*) from obstructing the *sic* suffix. Therefore, how could there be elision [of the *sic*]? This is not so; for it is not said that the *it*-substitution applies to the *sic*, but rather that the letter *i* becomes the final substitute and the *sic* becomes marked with the *k*-sign (*kit*). Even if the *it*-substitution were caused by the *sic*, there would still be no fault, because that paribhāṣā is not universal (it is *anitya*).

The fact of its being *anitya* (non-eternal) will be made known in the seventh chapter (*Kāśikā* 7.1.13). Regarding the phrase "and *ic*" and so forth: the word *hetu* (cause/reason) is to be supplied here.
Consequently, when the word *hetu* is employed according to [Pāṇini 2.3.26], the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) occurs for the sense of "of whom" (*kasya*).
*Takāret* means "having *takāra* as its *it*" (*it*), or that which has *takāra* as its *it* is *takāret*; the state of being so is *takārettva*.

Regarding the instruction *iccēti*, for what reason is the state of having *takāra* as its *it* applied to the vowel *i*? The meaning is: for what purpose is the vowel *i* made *tapara* (followed by *t*)?
Alternatively, this genitive case is used in the sense of a "residual" (*śeṣa*) characteristic when there is a desire to express a relationship with the grammatical operation (*kārya*).
For what purpose is the *t* following the *i* (the *tapara*) employed?

It means: so that [the substitution] may not be long (*dīrgha*). For if the *tapara* were absent, when *aṇ* is mentioned, it includes its homogeneous counterparts (*savarṇa*); thus, since the *i* would include its homogeneous sounds, the rule of "the most similar [substitute] in place" (*sthānentaratama-paribhāṣā*) would apply, and in a case like *aditā*, a long vowel would take the place of a long vowel. To prevent this from occurring, the *tapara* is employed. In the phrase "even excluding *ṛ* and *ḷ*," the word "that" (*saḥ*) refers back to the long vowel.

Even without this very statement, the long vowel would be established by the rule *ghumāsthāgāpājahātisām aṭi* [Pāṇini 6.4.66]; therefore, the intention is that the long vowel will not occur due to the force of this specific statement.
[One might argue] that the long vowel will not occur because of the principle: "An *aṇ* being taught (*bhāvyamāna*) does not include its homogeneous counterparts" (Vyāḍipāda 30).
However, this rebuttal has not been stated, because even an *aṇ* being taught sometimes includes its homogeneous counterparts.

For instance: when the suffix *au* follows *adas*, the substitution of *tyadādi* [elements] occurs; once the *vṛddhi* has been applied, the letter *u* prescribed by [Pāṇini 8.2.80] is enjoined. Because this includes its homogeneous sounds (*savarṇa*), it replaces the long *au* with a long vowel itself—resulting in *amū*. [The phrase] "lest there be a protracted (*pluta*) vowel in the immediate [successor]" means that since the rule is commenced for the sake of something dissimilar—that is, for the sake of the immediate [vowel]—how is this so? Because the short vowel is substituted in place of the dissimilar *ā*, and not the protracted one.
Therefore, the *tapara* (the *t* following the vowel) must be employed for the purpose of precluding the protracted (*pluta*) vowel.
But even this is not a necessary purpose,
because it is traditionally taught that "the protracted vowel occurs in its proper domain."
The word *ca* (and) indicates a reason (*hetu*).
For it has already been stated that the protracted vowel (*pluta*) occurs specifically in cases such as calling from a distance (*dūrāddhūta*) and so forth [Pāṇini 8.2.84].

If the protracted vowel were prescribed here by this rule, then it would have to apply everywhere—in those specific cases like calling from a distance, as well as elsewhere. Consequently, even in the case of calling from a distance and so forth, since that [protraction] would already be established [by the previous rule], there would be the fault of restating what has already been said (*uktānuvāda-doṣa*), because one would be performing what has already been done.

Therefore, lest the fault of repeating what has already been stated (*uktānuvāda*) occur regarding the *pakṣa*, [the vowel] will remain short alone and not be protracted (*pluta*); thus, the inclusion of the phoneme *t* (in the rule *taparaḥ*) is rejected in the *Bhāṣya*. Others, however, explain that by the statement "and the protracted [vowel] is prescribed in its proper domain," the inclusion of *t* is not being rejected; rather, its purpose is being explained. In domains such as calling from a distance, the protracted vowel is desired and intended, yet it would not be obtained [otherwise]. By the paribhāṣā "in place of [something], that which is most similar" (1.1.50), only a long vowel would be prescribed in place of a long vowel.

But has it not already been stated that the long vowel is indeed established? However, the restatement of what is already established would be for the purpose of subverting the protracted (*pluta*) vowel.
And the protracted vowel is desired in cases such as calling from a distance.
Therefore, the marker *t* must be added [to the rule] so that the long vowel does not subvert that [protracted vowel].

When this is considered, the *pluta* vowel indeed occurs in the eighth case. Since the *kit*-status of the suffix *ktvā* is established by its very presence (*aupaveśika*), it would follow that even a *seṭ* (a suffix with an *iṭ* augment) would be included because it is grasped by the term *ktvā*; therefore, this prohibition is commenced:
"The suffix *ktvā*, when accompanied by an *iṭ* augment, is not *kit*."

Now, does the *kit* status [of the suffix] not occur here because the *it* designation for the letter *k* is prohibited, or because the operation of a *kit* suffix is prohibited? For if it were intended here that the absence of *kit* status (*akitva*) is to be established by prohibiting the *it* designation of the letter *k*, then the author would have composed the rule "laśakvaseṭktvātaddhitayoḥ" within the section on *it* designations.
In that case, indeed, a double prohibition would not have to be made.

Therefore, because of the prohibition of that grammatical operation which is dependent upon *kit*-ness, this rule effects the non-*kit* status of the *seṭ* suffix *ktvā*; it does not, however, effect the prohibition of the *it*-designation for the letter *k*. Now, what is the purpose of including the *anubandha* (indicatory letter) here, when one could simply say "na tvā," thereby making the sūtra more concise? This is not the case; for if the letter *k* were not pronounced, someone might understand [the rule] to apply even to the undesirable [suffix]. Indeed, the *seṭ* suffix *ktvā* has no *anubandha* *k* at all, since it is pronounced without such an *anubandha*.

Thus, in order that it may not be understood in that way, the term with the *anubandha* is pronounced. But which [root] among those marked with *iṭ* (*seṭ*) is pronounced without an *anubandha* in the rule? Even so, only those marked with *iṭ* would be included, and not those without *iṭ* (*aniṭ*), because they possess the *anubandha*. Regarding "nigṛhītiḥ":

by the rule "titutratatha" (Pāṇini 7.2.9), there is a prohibition of *iṭ* for roots beginning with *grah*, as stated in the Vārttika (Vārttika 831): "The prohibition of *iṭ* for *grah* and others must be stated. Therefore, the prohibition of *iṭ* by the rule "titutratatha" etc., does not apply here. Regarding "upasnihitiḥ":
[the root] "sniha" is in the sense of affection (Dhātupāṭha 1200). Regarding "nikucitiḥ".

In these three examples—*kuncu*, *kruncu*, and *kauṭilya-alpībhāva* (Dhātupāṭha 185, 186)—there occurs, respectively, *saṃprasāraṇa*, the prohibition of *guṇa*, and by virtue of the *kit* designation, the elision of the nasal according to [Pāṇini 6.4.24]. [The rule] begins with "not after a root having the augment *iṭ*" (*na seṭ*).

By this much—namely, by the application of the rule that there is no *kit* suffix when a *seṭ* [augment] follows—the forms such as *devitvā* are established. But what is the purpose of explicitly mentioning *ktvā*? If one asks: "Without that mention of *ktvā*, since there would be no *kit* suffix, would the rule not apply to the *niṣṭhā* [past participles] in cases such as *nigudhitaḥ*, *nigudhitaḥ*, *nigudhitavān* from the root *gudha* (Dhātupāṭha 1120, 'to envelop')? This is not so; because of the restriction regarding the *niṣṭhā*. Since there is a restriction in the rule *niṣṭhā śīṅasvidimidi* (Pāṇini 1.2.19), it will not apply to the *niṣṭhā*: namely, that the *niṣṭhā* after roots beginning with *śīṅ* is *seṭ* and *kinna* (not *kit*), but not after other verbal roots.

One should not suspect a reverse restriction (viparīta-niyama) such as "only the *niṣṭhā* [suffixes] follow roots beginning with *śīṅ*," for there is no construction in the grammatical treatise intended for an unintended purpose; thus, that [restriction] will not occur.

In that case, however, there would be a prohibition of the *kit*-status for the *liṭ* [affix], and consequently, in forms such as *jagmiva* and *jagmuḥ*, the elision of the penultimate vowel (*upadhā-lopa*) by the rule *gamahana-* [Pāṇini 6.4.98] would not take place. To this, he says: "On account of an indicator (*jñāpaka*), there is no [prohibition] in the case of the *parokṣā* [perfect tense].
Since the *liṭ* is prescribed for the remote past (*parokṣa*), its mention is termed "the remote past" (*parokṣā*); in that case, the prohibition of *kit*-status will not apply.
How so? From an indicator (*jñāpaka*).

What is that indicator? He says: "They know [the rule] 'the mention of *jhal* in the context of *san*'" (Pāṇini 1.2.8). Since he provides this qualification of *san* in the rule *sani ca* (1.2.9), it is understood from that that this prohibition—"there is no *seṭ*"—applies to an original (*aupadeśika*) *kit* status, and not to one that is transferred (*ātideśika*).
The inclusion of the term *jhal* is indeed for the purpose of ensuring that the *kit*-status does not apply in cases such as *hi-śiśayiṣate*.

For if the prohibition "not when there is an *iṭ*" (*na seṭ*) were to apply even to a *kit*-status that is extended by analogy (*ātideśika`), then the mention of *jhal* would be redundant. [One might argue: "Let there be *kit*-status here; the prohibition 'not when there is an *iṭ*' will apply to it. Therefore, this prohibition applies to the *kit*-status that is directly prescribed (*auddeśika*), and not to that which is extended by analogy.

The mention of *jhal* would be an indicator (*jñāpaka*) for this meaning: so that in the rule *sthādhvoricca* [Pāṇini 1.2.17], the substitution of *i* occurs before a *sic* beginning with a *jhal*-consonant, but not before one beginning with a vowel—as in *upāsthāyiṣātām*.

For here, by the rule *syasicsīyuṭtāsiṣu* [Pāṇini 6.4.62] and others, the treatment as *ciṇ* (*ciṇvadbhāvaḥ*) applies, as does the substitution of *i*; and in that case, because it is subsequent, the augment *iṭ* takes precedence over the *ciṇvadbhāva*.

When the *ciṇvadbhāva* (treatment as if ending in *ciṇ*) applies, the suffix *yuk* is added by [Pāṇini 7.3.33]. In that case, if the mention of *jhal* were not present, the substitution of *it* would apply even before affixes beginning with *iṭ*, resulting in *it* taking the place of the letter *y*. This, however, does not occur; for the substitution of *it* is prescribed in conjunction with the *kit* designation. Indeed, the *kit* status is the primary factor, while the *it* status is taught as a secondary (*anvācaya*) provision. Therefore, in the absence of the *kit* status, that *it* status will not occur.

Now, why does the *kittva* (the property of being marked with *k*) not also apply here in the rule *sthādhvoricca* [Pāṇini 1.2.17]? Because it is prohibited by the very rule *na seṭ* [Pāṇini 1.2.18]. [The commentary states: "It is equal to [the substitution of] *r* in *sudhīvan*. This *it*-substitution is equal to the substitution of *r*.
And in what example? In the form *sudhīvanī*.

In the word *sudhīvā*—meaning "one who possesses beautiful intellect" (*śobhanā dhīvā yasyāṃ sā*)—the suffix *ṅīp* is prohibited by [Pāṇini 4.1.12]. Just as the substitution of *r* for *v* (by [Pāṇini 4.1.7]) is prescribed in conjunction with the application of *ṅīp*, and thus does not occur in its absence, so too the substitution of *i* for *u* (the *it*-augment), which is prescribed in conjunction with the application of the suffix *ktvā*, will not occur in its absence. For what purpose, then, is the mention of *ktvā*? The mention of *ktvā* must be made so that the prohibition of *kittva* does not apply to the suffix *kvasu*. Thus ends the section on *ktvā*.
In the case of *kvasu*, there is an original (*aupadeśika*) *kit* status; its prohibition would apply by the rule "not after a root with the augment *iṭ*" (*na seṭ*).
Consequently, in the form *jagmivān*, the elision of the penultimate vowel (*upadhā-lopa*) would not occur. [Therefore, it is said:
"The *kit* status is for the sake of *vasu*, because of the extended application (*atideśa*)."

The words "it will not occur" are to be supplied [to the argument]. Let it be granted that there is a prohibition of the *kit* status prescribed by direct rule (*aupadeśika*); even if that exists, the elision of the penultimate vowel (*upadhā-lopa*) will still take place by virtue of the *kit* status that is extended by analogy (*ātideśika*).
For it has already been stated that, because of the mention of the term *jhal*, there will be no prohibition of the *kit* status that is extended by analogy.
Therefore, the mention of *ktvā* need not be for the sake of the suffix *vas*. If that is so, then the purpose is *nigṛhīti*;
the meaning is that the mention of *ktvā* is for the sake of ensuring that the prohibition does not apply to the suffix *ktin*.

In the form *jagmivān*, the augment *iṭ* is applied to the suffix *kvasu* by [Pāṇini 7.2.68]; the *num* augment is added by [Pāṇini 7.1.70]; the elision of the final consonant (*hal*) and the following vowel (*aṅyādi*) occurs by [Pāṇini 6.1.68] and [8.2.23]; and the lengthening of the vowel occurs by [Pāṇini 6.4.10] (*sāntamahataḥ*). The roots are: *śīṅ* "to sleep" (Dhātupāṭha 1032); *ñiṣvidā* "to perspire" (Dhātupāṭha 1188); *ñimidā* "to be unctuous" (Dhātupāṭha 1243); *ñikṣvidā* "to be unctuous or to release" (Dhātupāṭha 1244); and *ñidhṛṣā* "to be bold" (Dhātupāṭha 1269). Thus, the form *śayitavān* is derived.
The vowel is lengthened by [Pāṇini 6.4.14].
Regarding the form *śayitaḥ*:
the suffix *kta* is applied in the sense of the agent according to [Pāṇini 3.4.72], "The roots meaning motion and those that are intransitive," etc.
In examples such as *prasveditaḥ*, by the rule [Pāṇini 3.4.71], the prefix *pra-* indicates the beginning of an action (*ādikarma*), that is, its commencement. Regarding *pradharṣitaḥ*:
this is an example other than when there is impudence (*vaiyātya*);
for in that case, by the rule *dhṛṣiśasīvaiyātye* [Pāṇini 7.2.19], there ought to be a prohibition of the augment *iṭ*.
It is traditionally taught that when the base form (*prakṛti*) is mentioned, the form with the elision of *yaṅ* (*yaṅluk*) is also included.

Therefore, in *yaṅluk*, the substitution of *yaṇ* is applied by the rule "eranekācaḥ" [Pāṇini 6.4.82]. *Titikṣā* means forbearance or patience. If this were the case, one might ask: "Should not the word 'patience' (*kṣānti*) alone have been used, for in that way the sūtra would be more concise? This is true; however, it was not done so as to provide variety. Regarding the term "*apamṛṣitam*" (unwiped away).
The meaning is "unaffected," since verbal roots have multiple meanings.
This multiplicity of meaning is understood from the inclusion of the term *titikṣā* (endurance).

For if that were not the case, since the root *mṛṣ* is recited specifically in the sense of endurance, [the author] would not have included it, as there would be nothing to exclude. It has been stated: "it does not take the augment *iṭ*."

> [[1.2.18]] From this [it follows]: Now, one might object that *iṭ* should certainly not be applied after the suffixes *ktvā* and *niṣṭhā* following the root *pūṅ*, because of the prohibition in [Pāṇini 7.2.11], *śrayukaḥ kiti*.

To the one who would argue that the continued reference (*anuvṛtti*) to the term *seṭ* (having an indicatory *ṭ*) is therefore useless, he replies with the words, "And *iṭ* is prescribed after *pūṅ*," and so forth.
To the question, "Why has an example of the *ktvā* suffix not been shown here?", he says: "Of the *ktvā* suffix," and so forth.

If indeed the *kittva* (the property of being *kit*) of the *ktvā* suffix were prohibited by this rule (*yoga*), then an example of it would have been presented; however, it is not prohibited by this [rule]. Why then? Because it is already prohibited by [Pāṇini 1.2.18] itself. Therefore, the intention is that no example of it has been shown.
In order to reinforce the prohibition [of *iṭ*] by the rule *ktvā-pratyayasya* (Pāṇini 1.2.18), he says "And thus," etc.

Regarding the sūtra *pūṅśca* (Pāṇini 7.2.51), the followers of Bhāradvāja—considering that those rules which occur between two optional (*vibhāṣā*) rules are mandatory (*nitya*)—have stated: "The absence of *kit*-status is mandatory for the suffixes beginning with *iṭ*.
These two, moreover, are the suffixes *iṭ* and so forth, namely *ktvā* and the *niṣṭhā* suffixes.

If, then, the prohibition of *kit* were permanent (*nitya*) for both [suffixes] beginning with *iṭ*, then the mention of *ktvā* would be purposeless. For its mention is meaningful here only for the sake of establishing the non-*kit* status optionally (*vikalpena*), and not otherwise; since the permanence of the prohibition of *kit* is already established by the rule itself (Pāṇini 1.2.18). Anticipating this objection, it was stated: "The mention of *ktvā* is for the sake of what follows."

What is the purpose of pronouncing the root *pūṅ* with its *anubandha* (the marker *ṅ*)? It is so that there may not be a prohibition of *kittva* for forms such as *popuvitaḥ*, *popuvitavān*, and *popuvitvā* derived from the *yaṅ*-lopa (reduplication with elision of *yaṅ*). [Objection: The pronunciation with the *anubandha* is not appropriate for the purpose of excluding *pūñ*, because the prohibition of *iṭ* is already established by the rule *śrayukaḥ kiti* (Pāṇini 7.2.11), since there is no occurrence of the *seṭ* suffixes *ktvā* and *niṣṭhā* after *pūñ*. [Response: [The word] "niṣṭhā" has been removed [from the context].
And because it is attracted from the preceding sūtra.
Regarding "having tied" (*grathitvā*):
in the alternative where [the suffix] is *kitt*, there is the elision of the nasal according to [Pāṇini 6.4.24], *aniditām*.

Regarding "guphitvā": the root *guph* and *gunph* mean "to bind" (Dhātupāṭha 1317, 1318). Regarding "riphitvā": the root *riph* means "boasting, fighting, censuring, harming, and giving" (Dhātupāṭha 1306).

But surely, even in the absence of this [present] option, an option should occur here by [the rule] *ralo vyupadhāt* (Pāṇini 1.2.26) and so forth; and is there not any distinction between these two options? If that is the case, then by the force of the mention of the penultimate vowel (*nopadha*), the option produced by another rule is also sublated by this one.

But surely, a root with *ṛ* as its penultimate vowel will serve as a counter-example (*pratyudāharaṇa*) for the mention of "having a penultimate vowel" (*nopadhagrahaṇasya*), namely *ṛpha* and *ṛnpha* in the sense of "injuring" (Dhātupāṭha 1315, 1316), as in *arphitvā*. This is not so; for here we must derive three forms from these two roots: *arphitvā*, *ṛmphitvā*, and *ṛphitvā*.

This [result] is indeed established by this very rule, whether or not the mention of "having a penultimate vowel" (*nopadhagrahaṇa*) exists. First, when the mention of "having a penultimate vowel" does exist, because of the prohibition [by Pāṇini 6.4.19], "for *ṛpha* which has *an* as its penultimate," the form *arphitvā* is established.
However, in the case of the root *ṛmph*, since this option applies even when it does not have a penultimate *n*, the other two forms *ṛmphitvā* and *ṛphitvā* are established.
Even if the mention of "not having a penultimate [nasal]" (*nopadha*) were absent, these three forms would still be established provided this option exists.
Therefore, it is rightly stated that *repitvā* is the counter-example.

Since the rule of *tadantavidhi* (extension of a grammatical operation to that which ends with the specified element) is established by [Pāṇini 1.1.72], the inclusion of the word *anta* (end) is for the purpose of indicating: "In this section concerning the *ktvā* suffix, *tadantavidhi* does not apply without a specific effort.

Consequently, in the subsequent sūtra, the root *ṛ* is taken in its own form (*svarūpeṇa*), and not as ending in that [root]. The roots *vañcu* (in the sense of deceiving; DhP 1703) and *luñca* (in the sense of removing; DhP 187) are mentioned. The term *ṛta* refers to a verbal root found in the Sūtras, where the suffix *īyaṅ* is prescribed by [Pāṇini 3.1.29]:
*ṛterīyaṅ*. It is stated that "*īyaṅ* is optionally applied to *ṛti* in the *ārdhadhātuka* domain."
By means of the rule *ādāya ārdhadhātuke vā* [Pāṇini 6.4.62], the form *vavitvā* is derived; [and by the rule] *aniditām...* [Pāṇini 6.4.24].
Thus, there is the elision of *n*. Regarding "vaktavā," there is optionally the absence of the augment *iṭ* by [Pāṇini 7.2.56].
The letter *ca* is for the purpose of making it clear that the mention of *vā* (optionally) is *svarita*-accented.
By this, the mention of Kāśyapa in the subsequent sūtra is for the sake of honor (*pūjārtha*); otherwise, it would be understood as having the sense of an option (*vikalpārthatā*).

And thus, because it stands between two optional rules (*vibhāṣā*), this rule would become compulsory (*nitya*). [Examples of the roots are: *ñitṛṣā* in the sense of thirsting (DhP 1228), *mṛṣa* in the sense of endurance (DhP 1164), and *kṛśa* in the sense of making thin (DhP 1227). "The mention of Kāśyapa is for the sake of honor."
"The knowledge concerning this very subject belongs to Kāśyapa alone and not to others"—this manifestation of unique knowledge is itself an act of worship.
Through that act of worship, an act of worship characterized by the manifestation of the great significance of the treatise (*śāstra*) is also thereby performed.
Such indeed is the great significance of the treatise, that even those seeking liberation (*mumukṣu*) pay heed to it in such a manner.

Therefore, why does the mention of Kāśyapa not serve as an alternative? To this he says: "The particle *vā* indeed continues [from the previous rule]. Since the *kittva* (the status of being a *kit* suffix) is prohibited by the rule *ktvā-pratyayaś-ca* (Pāṇini 1.2.18), and since the *san* suffix is also established as non-*kit* (*akit*) by its very nature, this [prohibition] applies in both cases by way of a positive injunction (*vidhi-mukhena*) alone; thus, in one view, *kittva* occurs. Examples are *didyutiṣate* (as found in the *Kāśikā* and *Padamañjarī*) and *vididyutiṣate*. In these, the *samprasāraṇa* (vowel substitution) of the reduplicated syllable occurs according to the rule *dyutisvāpyoḥ saṃprasāraṇam* (Pāṇini 7.4.67). An example is *eṣiṣiṣati*.

From the root *iṣ* in the sense of "desire" (Dhātupāṭha 1351), after the augment *iṭ* has been applied, the doubling of the second monosyllabic vowel occurs according to [Pāṇini 6.1.2], resulting in *bubhūṣate*. According to [Pāṇini 1.2.10], the *kittva* (the property of being marked with *k*) applies invariably.

For the sake of brevity, although one could have simply said "from a root ending in *i* or having *u* as its penultimate letter" (*iṇ-upadhāt*), the expression "having *u* or *ū* as its penultimate letter" (*vy-upadhāt*) was used to indicate that all references to *iṇ* refer to the *iṇ* group ending with the subsequent *ṇ*.

By this, what was stated regarding the rule *laṇ*—"all references to *iṇ* refer to the *iṇ* group ending with the subsequent *ṇ*"—becomes justified. A vowel whose duration is that of *ū* is called *ūkāla*.

But surely this designation is improper; for instance, *ū* is a word, whereas time is an action—how, then, can there be grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) here? This is not a fault; because, by virtue of association (*sāhacarya*), the word *ū* here refers to the act of utterance associated with *ū*. Even so, it remains improper; because that utterance associated with *ū* belongs only to the vowel *ū*, and not to any other vowel.

How then could that vowel have the duration of *ū* by means of an action connected with something else? For Devadatta does not become "possessor of brindled cows" (*citragu*) because of brindled cows belonging to Yajñadatta. This is not a fault; for it has been stated here that the sense of the suffix *-vat* (indicating similarity) is intended. Thus, what is meant is this: a vowel whose duration is equal to the duration of the act of pronunciation associated with the syllable *ū*—which is pronounced as a long sound—is called "having the duration of *ū*" (*ū-kāla*).

Now, one might think: "But surely, *ūkāla* is a single technical term (*saṃjñin*), whereas the technical names (*saṃjñās*) are three; therefore, due to this discrepancy in number, the assignment of terms according to their numerical order (*saṃkhyātānudeśa*) does not apply. To address such a person, he says: "*ū* [stands for] the three," and so forth.

The meaning is that the designation *ū* was made by applying the rule of long substitution (*dīrghatva*) as a single substitute (*ekādeśa*) for the three *mātrika* vowels according to Pāṇini 6.1.101 (*akaḥ savarṇe dīrghaḥ*).
But how is it known that this is a designation of the three by means of a conjunctive compound (*praśleṣanirdeśa*)? It is because of the force of the prescription of the three technical names.
Indeed, the assignment of multiple names for a single entity is not purposeful unless there is a distinct purpose for each.
Furthermore, in this case, there is no distinct purpose in assigning multiple names to a single thing.

If this were a single word intended as a technical term (*saṃjñā*) such as "short, long, and protracted," then because the purpose of creating a technical term is brevity (*lāghava*), it would be inappropriate to employ such a large technical term.

Furthermore—terms that function as technical designations (*saṃjñāśabda*) possess the property of recurrence (*āvṛtti*) in various rules (*pradeśa*). However, this [compound] is not a term functioning as a designation for a collective whole, nor is this collective whole repeated in the various rules; rather, it is the individual terms "short" (*hrasva*), "long" (*dīrgha*), and "protracted" (*pluta*) that recur. Therefore, considering that the reference is made by forming a *dvandva* compound of those terms, he says: "short, long, and protracted," and so forth. As for the singular form of the *dvandva*, it is due to the rule stating: "Every *dvandva* optionally becomes a singular."

But surely, since this is a dvandva compound functioning as a singular (*ekavadbhāva*), it ought to be neuter by the rule *sa napuṃsakam* [Pāṇini 2.4.17]; so how is there a masculine designation? This is because the designation follows the style of the Sūtras. It has been stated that "in the Veda there is a transposition of genders" (*chandasi liṅgavyatyaya*). Since "the Sūtras are like the Veda," this masculine gender is not contradictory.

By the sequence "u, ū, ū3," he shows that the coalescence (*praśleṣa*) of these [vowels] occurs in this specific order. But from what source is this certainty derived—that this alone is their sequence? He thinks as follows: because the rule [Pāṇini 8.2.93] prescribes the protracted (*pluta*) vowel for the particle *hi* when it consists of a single mora (*ekamātrika*), it is understood that the final [mora] is not a single mora. For if it were the final [element], it would receive the designation of a protracted vowel (*plutasaṃjñā*).
And in that case, the prescription of the *pluta* (protracted vowel) would be purposeless.

Furthermore, even a final [vowel] consisting of two morae (*dvimātrika*) does not [become *pluta*], because the *pluta* is prescribed for a two-moraic [vowel] by the rule *[[Pāṇini 8.2.87]]*. For if it were indeed final, it would possess the designation *pluta*; and if that were so, the prescription of a *pluta* for a *pluta* would be redundant.
Therefore, they do not consist of one mora (*mātrā*) or two morae at the end.

Nor does one consist of one mora in the middle, because of the force of the rule prescribing lengthening (*dīrgha*) in both [Pāṇini 7.3.101] *madhye...* and [7.3.102] *supi ca*. If there were one mora in the middle, then that would receive the designation of "long" (*dīrgha*); however, the mention of a long vowel for what is already long would be redundant. Therefore, since there is one mora at the beginning, by the principle of elimination (*pāriśeṣya*), there are two morae in the middle and three morae at the end.
In the expression "u ū ū3," the letters *u* and so forth refer to the act of pronunciation associated with those very sounds. Thus,
by the rule "time is the *aj* [vowel]," there is the elision of the letter *ya*.

But has it not already been stated that this *u* being grasped as a vowel (*aṇ*) includes its homogeneous counterparts (*savarṇa*), and thus, since the long and protracted forms of *u* are included by virtue of this *u*, they too would receive the designation "short"? To this, he says: "The mention of time (*kāla-grahaṇa*)," and so forth.

For when there is a mention of time, those for whom these designations are prescribed obtain their respective qualifications—namely, having one measure (*ekamātrika*), two measures (*dvimātrika*), or three measures (*trimātrika*).

For instance, when the apprehension of duration (*kāla*) is involved and the completion of the sentence is applied to each [term] individually, three *bahuvrīhi* compounds arise: that whose duration is *u* is *ukāla*; that whose duration is *ū* is *ūkāla*; and that whose duration is *ū3* is *ū3kāla*.
In these cases, the referents of the other members of the compound (*anyapadārtha*) are vowels (*ac*) having respectively one, two, and three morae (*mātrā*).

Since a vowel (*ac*) having the measure of one *mātrā* is simultaneous with the act of pronunciation accompanied by the sound ‘*u*’; likewise, a vowel having the measure of two *mātrās* is simultaneous with the act of pronunciation accompanied by the sound ‘*ū*’; and likewise, a vowel having the measure of three *mātrās* is simultaneous with the act of pronunciation accompanied by the sound ‘*ū3*’.

This being the case, when the designation of "short" (*hrasva*) is prescribed for a vowel whose measure is one *mātrā*, even though the long and protracted vowels are included by means of the term ‘*u*’, that designation does not apply to them, for they do not have the measure of one *mātrā*.
Therefore, in *ālūya* and *pariṇīya*, the substitution of *tuṅ* (guṇa) does not occur based on a short vowel.
In the cases of *pratyakṣya* and *prarakṣya*:

from the roots *takṣū* and *tvakṣū* in the sense of "making thin" (Dhātupāṭha 655, 656), and *rakṣa* in the sense of "protecting" (Dhātupāṭha 658), when a compound is formed, the suffix *lyap* is applied by the rule *samāse'nañpūrve ktvo lyap* (Pāṇini 7.1.37).

In that case, since the two consonants *h* and *l* following another [consonant] possess the property of having the duration of *ū* (*ūkāltva*) when they form a *saṃyoga*, the designation "short" (*hrasva*) would apply even without the mention of *aj*. Consequently, the insertion of *t* (*tuk*) based on the short vowel would undesirably follow, as in the example *titaucchatram*.
Here, because the aggregate of the vowels *ā* and *u* has the duration of *ū* and thus possesses a measure of two morae (*dvimātrikatva*), the designation "long" (*dīrgha*) would apply.
Consequently, the optional insertion of *t* (*tuk*) prescribed by Pāṇini 6.1.76 would undesirably follow.

But if *aj* is not included [in the definition], the designation *dīrgha* (long) does not apply, because a collection of vowels (*ac-samudāya*) is not captured by the inclusion of *aj*. Now, one might argue: "Even if that *dīrgha* designation exists based on the whole, this *hrasva* (short) designation will still apply based on its constituent part; moreover, the *tuṅ* (the substitution of *ū*) based on that [short vowel] is simply non-obligatory. This is not so; because it is subsequent, the optional application of *tuṅ* based on the *dīrgha* would take precedence.

Furthermore, in such a case, there is no application of the principle of "repeated application" (*punar-prasaṅga-vijñāna*). That principle applies where a preceding rule, while operating, does not subvert the cognition of a subsequent rule; in that situation, it is said: "It is established by the principle of repeated application. But here, the obligatory rule (*nitya-vidhi*) subverts the cognition of the optional rule (*vikalpa-vidhi*), because of the mutual contradiction between an obligatory and an optional rule.

Consequently, by the very technical rule (*paribhāṣā*)—"In the event of a conflict when both apply simultaneously, that which is subverted remains subverted"—there would necessarily be an option (*vikalpa*).

Therefore, this mention of *ac* is a technical rule (*paribhāṣā*) characterized by a gender marker, intended to restrict the locus [of application]; it applies to the specific rules (*pradeśa*) such as "the neuter base takes the short vowel" (*hrasvo napuṃsake prātipadikasya*, P. 1.2.47). When that rule applies, two genitive relations arise, since there is freedom in choosing the relationship between qualifier and qualified. In the rule "the neuter base takes the short vowel," the base (*prātipadika*) is qualified by the vowel (*ac*), meaning "of a base ending in a vowel," and not the vowel being qualified by the base.

For if the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) were qualified by the vowel (*aj*), such that [the rule would mean] "the vowel belonging to the nominal stem," then even a vowel situated in the middle [of the stem] would undergo shortening, as in *suvāg brāhmaṇakulam*.

However, when the vowel qualifies the nominal stem, the genitive case [in the rule *prātipadikasya*] denotes the locus (*sthāna-ṣaṣṭhī*), not a partitive relation (*avayava-ṣaṣṭhī*); therefore, the shortening of the vowel occurs only for the final vowel (*alo 'ntyasya*).
In the rule [Pāṇini 8.2.82], the term *ṭi* which is being mentioned qualifies the vowel *ac*: "the *ac* that is part of the *ṭi*.
By this, the protracted (*pluta*) vowel occurs even for a vowel situated in the middle of the *ṭi*.
However, if the *ṭi* were qualified by the vowel *ac*—meaning "the *ṭi* which ends in a vowel"—then it would apply only here: *devadattā3*; but it would not apply here: *agnicit*.
By the letter *ca*, *aj* is drawn back [from the previous rule]; its purpose will be stated right here.

Examples such as *atiri-* and so forth have been explained under [Pāṇini 1.1.48]. In the word *cīyate*, the suffix *lakāra* is used in the sense of the object (*karman*). He states the reasoning for the rule "the restriction applies in the formulation of technical designations" (*saṃjñāvidhāne niyamaḥ*) with the words: "*aj* continues [to be understood]."

When the term *ac* (vowel) is not explicitly mentioned [in a rule], the terms beginning with "short" (*hrasva*) that are being carried over from previous rules function only to present the vowels themselves; for those [vowels] are already present by their own nature.
Consequently, while having their own forms as their sole referents, they serve as qualifiers for the vowel being prescribed.

In this context, the connection is made as follows: "In place of *a*, there occurs a vowel (*aj*), which is being prescribed by such technical designations (*saṃjñā*) as 'short,' 'long,' or 'protracted.'"

The words *dyauḥ*, *panthāḥ*, and *saḥ* have been explained in [Pāṇini 1.1.3]. In these cases, by the rules *diva aut* [7.1.84] and *pathimathyṛbhukṣāmāt* [7.1.85], the vowels *au* and others are prescribed in their own forms; since they are not prescribed by means of technical designations such as "long" (*dīrgha*), they occur in place of consonants (*hal*) alone, and not of vowels (*ac*).

In the cases of *dyubhyām* and *dyubhiḥ*, the vowel *u* prescribed by the rule *diva u* is not enjoined with the technical designation of "short" (*hrasva*); therefore, it occurs in place of the consonant alone, and not of the vowel.

But surely, the three examples beginning with *dyauḥ* are already established by the very restriction regarding the prescription of technical names (*saṃjñā*) in the rule *iko guṇavṛddhiḥ* [Pāṇini 1.1.3], for those examples were previously presented as counter-examples (*pratyudāharaṇa*) to that rule as well; therefore, there is no purpose in this restriction being prescribed by means of a technical name. True, this is so; however, he thinks thus: a restriction must be made in the prescription of the technical name for the sake of forms such as *dyubhyām* and *dyubhiḥ*.
The sound *hrū* has neither the designation of *guṇa* nor the designation of *vṛddhi*; for this is established by the very rule previously stated regarding the formulation of designations.

Therefore, this rule for formulating designations is made for another purpose, in order to favor even those who are forgetful and do not remember the purpose of the previous rule—namely, for the sake of forms such as *dyauḥ*, *panthāḥ*, and *saḥ*. As for the accents (*udātta* and so on), they are well-known in both common usage and the Veda.
To one who might object, "What is the use of formulating these designations?", he replies with the words beginning with "the words *udātta* and so on."

By the word "ādi" (and so forth), the anudātta and svarita accents are included. The particle "eva" (only/itself) is to be understood as displaced [in the compound], following the word "varṇadharme" (the property of the phoneme).

In both worldly and Vedic usage, terms such as "udātta" and the rest are well-known as referring specifically to that which is the property—namely, the quality—of the phonemes, and not to the vowel (ac) itself.

Therefore, in this grammar, properties such as the acute accent (*udātta*) and others are designated—that is, they are defined—as belonging to that vowel (*aci*) which possesses them; otherwise, because the words "acute" and so forth are heard in the specific rules (*pradeśa*), one might understand them as properties of the phoneme itself rather than as designating that which possesses them—this is the intended meaning. The word *uccais* has two senses: first, it denotes excellence of audibility (*śrutiprakarṣa*), as in "he speaks loudly" (*uccair bhāṣate*) or "he reads aloud" (*uccaiḥ paṭhati*). Second, it denotes a measure or locus (*pramāṇādhikaraṇavācī*), as in "Devadatta stands tall" (*uccaiḥ sthito devadattaḥ*); here, "tall" (*uccaiḥ*) refers to a measure, and its locus is what is expressed by the word *uccais* in this context.
Therefore, in this context, he says "loudly" (*uccaiḥ*) in order to show that the meaning of the second instance of the word "loudly" is being taken, and not that of the other.

However, the meaning of the word "loudly" as used in a sentence such as "he speaks loudly," which is the excellence of the hearing (*śrutiprakarṣa*), is not what is intended here by the word "loudly. If it were so intended, then in the case of whispered pronunciation (*upāṃśu*), the designations of *udātta* (high-pitched) and so forth would not apply; for there would be an absence of excellence, and since the *udātta* and others depend upon the presence of excellence, they would not be distinguished from one another.
For indeed, the very same [vowel] that is high (*uccaiḥ*) with respect to one thing becomes low (*nīcaiḥ*) with respect to another.

And thus, everything would be *udātta* (high-pitched); the intention is that even the most *anudātta* (low-pitched) is intended [to be relative]. Regarding the phrase "produced by the place" (*sthānakṛtam*) and so forth: let the specific measure (*pramāṇaviśeṣaḥ*) be called [the *udātta*]; the place (*sthāna*), which serves as its substratum, becomes high.
And in this way, not everything would be udātta.
The meaning is that what is called "anudātta" is [actually] high-pitched (*uccaiḥ*). Regarding the term "bhāgavatsu":
those which possess parts (*bhāgāḥ*) as their constituents (*avayavāḥ*) are "bhāgavanti."
Those portions are situated in the places of articulation, such as the palate and so forth, arranged in an upward and downward sequence.
"Place" (*sthāna*) is expressed by the word *uccais* [in the rule]; why then is the designation (*saṃjñin*) qualified by "highness" (*uccais*)? Because it is produced from a high place.
In that regard, when the place of articulation is the same, that which is produced in the upper portion—that is, the higher part—is designated as *udātta* (acute).

If it were merely stated that "the vowel produced in the upper portion of the place [of articulation] receives the designation *udātta*," then the same aforementioned fault of instability would persist. For instance, the very same point on the palate or other places of articulation that is high in small-bodied individuals becomes low in large-bodied individuals when compared to their respective palatal regions. Therefore, the term "equal" (*samāna*) is stated as a qualification of the place of articulation.

This is obtained because, since the purpose of creating a technical name (*saṃjñā*) is brevity, when a single-syllable name ought to be made, the creation of a multi-syllable name indicates that there is an increase in meaning due to the increase in the text. One might object: "From the increase in the text, we only perceive that some additional meaning intended by the Teacher is meant here; how is this specific meaning, namely 'equality' (*samānatva*), obtained? It is obtained from the uninterrupted tradition of oral instruction (*upadeśapāramparya*).

Furthermore, that similarity is to be understood as arising from the non-difference of the speaker, and not from the non-difference of the locations such as the palate; otherwise, the acute accent (*udātta*) would depend solely on the palate and not on the throat and other places.
Since the speaker is one, even though the palates and other locations are distinct, they are rendered similar by means of him; thus, when this is recognized, the aforementioned fault does not occur.
As for what the characteristic of this vowel (*aj*) produced in the upper part [of the vocal tract] is, he says: "In which," and so forth.
The explanation of "āyāma" is "nigraha.
Nigraha means stiffness.
Saṃvṛtakaṇṭhatā means the closure of the opening of the throat.
For this very reason, as the breath exits slowly, it dries out the parts of the throat;
there arises dryness and lack of oiliness. Regarding the phrase "ye te ke":

from the words *ka* and so forth, the substitution of *yat* for the pronominal base occurs [by Pāṇini 7.1.97], followed by the substitution of the single subsequent form [6.1.97]; then the substitution of *śī* for *jas* [7.1.17], followed by the substitution of the single subsequent form [6.1.87].
In this case, the base is acute by the accent of the nominal stem (*prātipadika-svara*);

then the accent of the case ending (*vibhakti-svara*) applies according to [Pāṇini 6.1.172]; and finally, the single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) receives the accent according to [Pāṇini 8.2.5]. The term *anvavasarga* is explained as *mārdava* (gentleness).
The meaning is "laxity. "Glossiness" is the explanation of "softness," and "greatness" is also [the explanation] of "extensiveness."
Precisely because the opening of the throat is large, the air exiting quickly does not dry out the parts of the throat;
therefore, the tone becomes smooth (*snigdha*). The words *tva*, *sama*, *sima*, and *nema*—meaning "not high-pitched"—are recited in all the lists of *sarvādi* (words beginning with *sarva*) alone.
"Low" (anuccāni) means "not high," that is, unaccented (anudāttāni).
In the passage beginning with "namaste rudra," the word *te* is unaccented by virtue of the governing rule "temayāvekavacane" [Pāṇini 8.1.22].
By the eighth [sūtra], *rudrādayo’pi* (8.1.19), all [the vowels] become anudātta. The words *udātta* and *anudātta* are technical designations (*saṃjñā*) for specific [vowel] qualities.

For a designation, when uttered in the rules (*pradeśa*), brings to mind the designated entity (*saṃjñin*). By means of those two [terms] being carried over (*anuvṛtta*) here, there is the understanding of the udātta and anudātta vowels which have been presented.
Therefore, the designation *svarita* is prescribed for a vowel (*ac*) consisting of a combination (*samāhāra*).

The word *samāhāra*—derived in the sense of an abstract noun as "the act of combining" (*samāharaṇam*)—is conventionally established in common usage (*loke*) to denote a collection (*samudāya*). Should someone object that since no collection of vowels (*acsamudāya*) consisting of both acute (*udātta*) and grave (*anudātta*) tones is possible, the designation itself cannot exist due to the impossibility of its referent (*saṃjñin*), he replies with the words "And by virtue of [its] capacity" (*sāmarthyācca*), and so forth.

This is said: "A combination of the acute (udātta) and the grave (anudātta) is designated as circumflex (svarita). However, there is no possibility of a vowel (ac) consisting of a technical (pāribhāṣika) combination of acute and grave. Therefore, by implication, only those two properties known in common worldly usage and in the Veda as acute and grave are understood here, not the vowels themselves. But even so, the same fault remains: this designation is prescribed for a vowel that consists of the acute and grave well-known in the world. To what, then, does it apply? It applies to that vowel in which the acute and grave, as established in both the world and the Veda, are combined.
Furthermore, since the combination of two things can occur even within a single entity, how could there be an impossibility of the possessor of the name (*saṃjñin*)?
By stating "that in which they are combined," it is shown that this word *samāhāra* functions as a locative instrument (*adhikaraṇasādhana*) and not as an abstract state (*bhāvasādhana*).
"Are combined" (*samāhriyete*) means they are brought together; the sense is that they are perceived in conjunction.

Regarding the word *śikyam*: when the suffix *yat* is present [from rule 4.1.83], the rule *śraṃseḥ śi kuṭ kicca* (Dhātupāṭha 817) applies; thus, from the root *śraṃs*, with the suffix *yat*, the substitution of the word *śi* for the root, and the addition of the augment *kuṭ*, the form is established.
Because it bears the marker *t*, it is svarita-accented.
Regarding the word *kanyā*:
according to the rule *tilyaśikyamatrikāśmaryadhānyakanyārājanyamanuṣyāṇāmantaḥ* (Phiṭ-sūtra 4.76), the final syllable is svarita.
Regarding the word *sāmānyaḥ*: [the same applies].
In *sāmani sādhuḥ*, the suffix *yat* is applied according to [Pāṇini 4.4.98].
In *kveti*, the suffix *at* is applied to the word *kim* ending in the locative case, according to [Pāṇini 5.3.12]: *kimo 't*.
The substitution of *kvā* [by Pāṇini 7.2.105] occurs [in the word] *kvāti*. The term *ādau* means *āditaḥ*; here the suffix *tasi* is used in the sense of the locative case.
This very mention is an indicator (*jñāpaka*) for the rule "the suffix *tasi* occurs after words beginning with *ādi*.
Consequently, in the section concerning *tasi*, the supplementary rule (*vārttika*) "an addition must be made for words beginning with *ādi*" need not be formulated.
Regarding the term *adṛḍhahrasvam*: it means "half of a short [vowel]. The compound is formed according to *ardhaṃ napuṃsakam* (Pāṇini 2.2.2).

Furthermore, one might argue that by the rule *paravalliṅgam* [Pāṇini 2.4.26], the word should take the masculine gender because the word *hrasva* is masculine; however, this is not the case. For the word *hrasva* is applied by taking up the quality (*guṇa*) of a specific measure; and according to the principle that "words expressing qualities (*guṇavacana*) take the gender and number of their substratum," the word *hrasva*, being a word expressing a quality, possesses all three genders just like the word *śukla*. Anticipating the objection that since the term *hrasva* has been established as the technical name for a single-mora (*mātrika*) vowel, its division would apply only to that and not to the long (*dīrgha*) and protracted (*pluta*) vowels, he says: *arddhahrasvam* and so forth.
The half-measure of a short vowel is not firm; therefore it is called an "unfirm measure" (*adṛḍhamātrā*). Consequently, by the term "unfirm short" (*adṛḍhahrasva*), the unfirm measure is indicated.
And for that very reason, it was stated [in the rule] as "of that" (*tasya*).
This is for the purpose of specifying the three types of circumflex vowels (*svarita*): the short, the long, and the protracted.

And if the mention of "short" (*hrasva*) without the qualification "solid" (*adṛḍha*) is an indication (*upalakṣaṇa*) of [any] non-solid *mātrā*, then the mention of the three [quantities] becomes meaningful; otherwise it would not.

Regarding the statement "the mention of 'short' is not the primary factor" (*atantra*): "not the primary factor" means it is for the sake of indication, just as in the expression "let the curd be protected from crows," where the crows [represent all potential thieves].
Therefore, this division of the *svarita* applies to all [vowels] beginning with the short ones.

Now, one might object: even so, the division of the eighth *svarita* is not established, because it is unestablished (*asiddha*). This is not so; for a subsequent rule is unestablished with respect to a preceding rule.
And this is not a rule; what then? It is for the purpose of explaining the division of that which has already been prescribed.
Alternatively, this is established by the *yogavibhāga* (separation of rules) of the rule "na" at [Pāṇini 8.2.3]. Regarding the phrase "or it is like *evaśri*" (*evaśrirvā*):
this preceding portion is acutely accented (*udātta*) and more distinct.

Being colored by that, the subsequent portion—as if having assumed its very form—is like a crystal gem colored by a substrate; because its phonetic character is differentiated from the pure acute accent, it does not deserve the designation of "grave" (*anudātta*).
It does not even deserve the designation "acute" (udātta), because it is merely a coloring [of the preceding part].
Therefore, some say that there is only one tone (ekaśruti).

Others, however, say: when the subsequent part is not colored by the preceding part—which has not yet produced an excellence of form—then, because it appears in its own nature, it is designated as "non-acute" (anudātta).

But when, like a crystal gem by means of a proximate object, it is overcome and colored by a preceding acute (*udātta*) accent that is more intense, it attains, as it were, the form of that [preceding accent] and is then designated as *ekaśruti*.
This is because its *śruti*—its hearing—is non-different, single, and of identical form with the hearing of the preceding part.

For at that time there is no distinction between the preceding and following [syllables] with respect to the *svarita* hearing; since both are perceived as possessing the quality of being acute (*udātta*). Thus it is said: "The sentence becomes *ekaśruti*."

By the mention of "sentence" (*vākya*), he excludes both the word (*pada*) and a portion of a word (*padaikadeśa*); for these two lack the capacity for addressing (*sambodhana*). Since a sentence possesses the capacity to function as the instrument when an address is to be made, it is that [sentence] for which the single accent (*ekaśruti*) is prescribed.

He asks, "From where, then, does that sentence [arise]? and says: "That by which one addresses from a distance. By this, the status of the sentence as an instrument (*karaṇa*) with respect to the vocative case is demonstrated.
The word "from a distance" (*dūrāt*) takes the ablative case ending according to Pāṇini 2.3.35.

By the statement “*sambodhanaṃ sambuddhiḥ*,” etc., he demonstrates that the term *sambuddhi* (vocative case) is taken here in its etymological sense (*anvartha*), and not as a technical (*pāribhāṣikī*) grammatical designation. If the technical *sambuddhi* were being taken here, then in the example “*devā brāhmaṇāḥ*,” there would be no single accent (*ekaśruti*); for the technical *sambuddhi* does not exist in that instance. However, when it is taken in its etymological sense, it occurs; the point is that the *sambuddhi*, which consists of the action characterized by addressing, is present here as well.
But from what is this adoption of the literal meaning determined? From the mention of "distance" (*dūra*).

When there is an adoption of the literal meaning, the vocative case arises by means of the word *dūrāt* [in the rule *dūrāt sambodhane*]. {This line does not appear in the Kāśikā}. It says: "When addressing someone from a distance."
Therefore, the term *dūra* (far) functions as an ablative (*apādāna*) in its literal sense;
however, if it were taken in its technical (*pāribhāṣikī*) sense, it would be entirely irrelevant,
for there is no "distance" associated with the case-ending of a vocative (*āmantrita*).
Although distance is not fixed, nevertheless, that place where speech established by ordinary effort is not heard should be understood here as "distant.

Regarding the phrase "of vowels" (*svarāṇām*), etc.: {this line does not exist in the Kāśikā} "non-distinction" (*avibhāgaḥ*) is the explanation of the nature of single-intonation (*ekaśruti*); the subsequent commentary explains it as the concealment of distinctions (*bhedatirodhānam*).

It is stated that *ekaśruti* (monotone) consists in the non-perception of specific accents such as the acute (*udātta*) and so forth, and the cognition of the mere phonemes (*varṇa*) such as *a* and so on. For example: "Come, O boy Devadatta! [with a protracted vowel]. In this very sense, there is a protracted vowel (*pluta*), and it is acute (*udātta*); for this is under the governing rule: "The final syllable (*ṭi*) of a sentence is protracted and acute" (Pāṇini 8.2.82).
The coalescence (*samāveśa*) of that single-syllable accentuation (*ekaśruti*) with the acute accent (*udātta*) is intended here, for the purpose of excluding the protracted (*pluta*) vowel.
He will explain how this is obtained later on.

In the counter-example, the threefold accentuation (*traisvarya*) alone occurs; therein, the vowel *ā* is acute by virtue of the rules "Particles are acute on the first syllable" (*phi-sū* 4.80) and "Preverbs are also [acute], except for *abhi*" (*phi-sū* 4.81).
In the word *gaccha*, there is the *nighāta* (elision of accent) by the rule *tiṅṅatiṅaḥ* [Pāṇini 8.1.28].
In the word *bhoḥ*, there is the acute accent (*udātta*) because of the rule *nipātā ādyudāttāḥ*.
In the words *māṇavaka* and *devadatta*, there is the *nighāta* by the rule *āmantritasya ca* [Pāṇini 8.1.19]. [The rest of the verse begins with] *agnirmūrdhā divaḥ*, etc.
The roots *agi* and *ragi* mean "to go" (*gatyarthāḥ*) [Dhātupāṭha 146, 144].
While the rule *vījyājvaribhyo niḥ* [Daiva 1.18] is in force, the suffix *nip* is applied by the rule *aṅgernirnalopaśca* [Daiva 1.20], and there is also the elision of the letter *n*.
The word *agni*, by virtue of the accent of the suffix, is udātta on its final syllable.

The root *mūrv* is listed as "binding" (*bandhane*) in the Dhātupāṭha (575). Following the rule *akanin yuvṛṣitakṣirājidhanvidyupratidivaḥ* (Uṇādisūtra 6.51), which prescribes the suffix *kanin*, the word *mūrdhan* is established with the suffix *kanin* by the subsequent rule *ānnukṣanpūṣanplīhankledansnehanmūrdhanmajjannaryamanviāpsanparijmanmātariānmaghavan* (Uṇādisūtra 6.55). Thus, due to this specific grammatical derivation (*nipātana*), the word is udātta-accented on its first syllable.
Furthermore, the substitution of the letter *dha* for the letter *va* occurs here solely by virtue of this same derivation.
The root *div* is listed as "playing and so forth" (*krīḍādau*) in the Dhātupāṭha (1107); the suffix *ḍivin* is applied [to form *divin*].
The vowel *i* is for the sake of pronunciation (*uccāraṇārtha*).
Even though [the base] is not a nominal stem (*abha*), the elision of the *ṭi* suffix occurs by the rule *ṭeḥ* [Pāṇini 6.4.143], due to the power of the inclusion of the *ḍit* marker.
When the form *div* is established, the final syllable of the case-ending becomes udātta by the rule *diva ut* [Pāṇini 6.1.171].
The word *kakud* is accented on the final syllable because of the rule: "A nominal stem (*prātipadika*) ending in a consonant has an acute accent on the final syllable" (Phiṭ-sūtra 1.1).

The word *pati*, being formed with the suffix *ḍati* according to the rule "from the root *pā* [comes] *ḍati*" (Dhātu-pāṭha 1.27), is acutely accented on its first syllable by the accent of the suffix (*pratyaya-svara*). Consequently, in the genitive compound *kakutaḥ patiḥ* = *kakutpatiḥ*, the final syllable is acutely accented by the rule "sa" (Pāṇini 6.1.223).
