From the root *prath* in the sense of "expansion" (*prakhyāne*) [Dhātupāṭha 1553], the suffix *ṣivan* is applied with vocalization (*saṃprasāraṇa*) according to Aṣṭādhyāyī 6.1.124: *pratheḥ ṣivan saṃprasāraṇañca*.
Thus, from the word *pṛthivī*, the feminine suffix *ṅīṣ* is added. By the accent of the suffix (*pratyayasvara*), the initial vowel of the suffix *ṅīṣ* following the verbal root becomes udātta.
The sixth case singular ending is *ṅasi*. By the rule *āṇ nadyāḥ*, it becomes anudātta.
There is a long vowel by way of *savarṇadīrgha*.
The substitution of *yaṇ* occurs by [Pāṇini 6.1.77].
The case ending is acute by [Pāṇini 6.1.174].
Thus: *ayam*.

From *idi paramaiārye* (Dhātupāṭha 63), by [Pāṇini 7.1.58], the augment *num* is applied; from *indeḥ kamirnalopaśca* (Pañcapādī 596), the suffix *kam* is added and there is elision of the *n*. The word *idam* is oxytone due to the suffix *kam*. When the nominative singular (*su*) follows, by *ido'y puṃsi*, the form *id* of *idam* undergoes substitution. Thus: *apām*.

From the verbal root *āplṛ* in the sense of "to pervade" (Dhātupāṭha 1260), the suffix *kvip* is applied according to Pāṇini 3.2.178 (*āpnotehr yasvaśca*), which also causes the shortening of the vowel; this form is then put in the genitive plural. By Pāṇini 6.1.165 (*ūḍidampadādyappumraidyubhyaḥ*), the case-ending receives the udātta accent.
Consequently, the word *apām* has its final syllable accented.
From the root *ri* in the sense of "going" (*dhātupāṭha* 1404), the suffix *asun* is applied according to *struribhyāṃ tuṭ ca* (*daśapādī* 9.62). There is the augment *tuṭ*.
The word *retāṃsi* is accented on the first syllable by virtue of the *nit*-accent rule.

Regarding the word *jinvati*: from the root *ji* in the sense of "to conquer" (*ji jaye*, Dhātupāṭha 561), the suffix *laṭ* is applied; the substitution of *śatṛ* occurs; then, by way of irregularity (*vyatyayena*), the suffix *śnu* is applied according to [Pāṇini 3.1.85]; and finally, the substitution of *yaṇ* occurs according to [Pāṇini 6.4.87].
The suffix *ṅīp* is applied by [Pāṇini 4.1.45];
the shortening occurs by [Pāṇini 7.3.107];
and the elision of the case-ending *su* occurs by [Pāṇini 6.1.69].
While the rule [Pāṇini 8.2.88] is in effect, [Pāṇini 8.2.89] prescribes the substitution of *praṇava*.
And that [substitute] is protracted (*pluta*) and acute (*udātta*), because of the governing context [of Pāṇini 8.2.82].
They call *praṇava* either the vowel *o* or the syllable *oṃ*.

Due to the force of the rule prescribing the acute (*udātta*) for the *praṇava* and because [the *praṇava*] is not yet established [as finished], the grave (*anudātta*) does not apply to what follows a word [according to Pāṇini 8.1.19]; however, it does apply to the remainder.
When these accents have been obtained, a single uniform accent (*ekaśruti*) is prescribed so that it "may not occur in recitation" (*saṃpāṭhe*).
Recitation (*saṃpāṭha*) refers to the time of private Vedic study (*svādhyāya*).

Regarding the passage beginning with *mamāgne*: [the root] *asu* in the sense of "to destroy" (*kṣapaṇe*; Dhātupāṭha 1209), followed by the suffix *madik* according to *yuṣyasimyāṃ madik* (Pāṇini Daivīvyākaraṇa 6.50).
The word *asmad* is accented on the final syllable due to the accentuation of the suffix.
In the case of the singular genitive ending, there is the substitution of *aś* by [Pāṇini 7.1.27], *yuṣmadasmadbhyāṃ ṅaso’ś*, and for *asmad*, the substitution of *mam* by [Pāṇini 7.2.96].
Due to the status of being like the original (sthānivadbhāva), it is udātta on the final syllable; then, by [Pāṇini 6.1.97], there is the substitution of the subsequent form (*pararūpa*).
The word *agni* undergoes *nighāta* (elision of the accent) according to [Pāṇini 8.1.19].
Regarding the word *varcas*: from the verbal root *varc* meaning "to shine" (Dhātupāṭha 162), the suffix *asun* is applied according to [Uṇādi-sūtra 9.49].
The word *varcas* is acutely accented on its first syllable due to the *nit*-accent rule.
The root *hveñ* is listed as 1008 in the *Dhātupāṭha*, meaning "in competition.
According to [Pāṇini 3.3.72], *ap* is the suffix when preceded by *ni*, *abhi*, or *upa*, and there is also vocalization (*saṃprasāraṇa*) of the vowel.
By [Pāṇini 2.2.19], *upapada* compounds with non-finite verbs (*atiṅ*) are formed.

When the rule [Pāṇini 6.2.139] would have caused the original accent (*prakṛtisvara*) of the final member to apply, the rule [6.2.144]—with *antaḥ* [6.2.142] still in force—prescribes that the final syllable is udātta. In the locative plural, the substitution of *e* by [7.3.103] *bahuvacane jhalyet* occurs; due to the status of the substitute being like the original (*sthānivadbhāva*), the vowel *e* remains udātta. From the root *as* "to be" (Dhātupāṭha 1065), in the imperative (*loṭ*), third person singular (*tip*), the substitution of *u* by [3.4.86] *eruḥ* takes place, and because it belongs to the *adādi* class, there is elision of the suffix *śap*. By the rule [8.1.28] *tiṅaṅatiṅaḥ*, the word *astu* becomes anudātta (unaccented).
"Japa is an imitative mantra.
By the statement "japa," the explanation of its meaning is that it is an imitative mantra (*anukaraṇamantra*).
*Anukṛti* means imitation (*anukaraṇa*).
In every mantra, clear articulation is required; this is what is meant by an "imitative mantra.
For this very reason, it says: "the practice of whispering" (*upāṃśuprayoga*).
This refers to recitation as if submerged in water. In some places, the reading is "non-performance mantra" (*akaraṇamantra*).

In this context, the meaning is as follows: that which has an easy (*īṣat*) performance or pronunciation is an *akaraṇa-mantra*; for the negative particle (*nañ*) here has the sense of "slight" (*īṣad*). The word *vi* is a particle (*nipāta*). According to the rule "Particles are acute-accented on the first syllable" (*phi-sūtra* 4.80), it is acute-accented. The root *viś* means "to enter" (*dhātupāṭha* 1424). Because the word *vi* ends in the suffix *kvan*—according to the rule "The suffix *kvan* is added after the roots *aś*, *pruṣ*, *laṭi*, *kaṇi*, *khaṭi*, and *viś*" (*daṇḍin-ukta-uṇādi-sūtra* 125)—the word *vi* is acute-accented on the first syllable by virtue of the *nit*-accent rule.
The term *sama-a-triṇam* is a descriptive compound (*viśeṣaṇasamāsa*).

It bears the udātta accent on the final syllable of the compound. Regarding the verb root *dah* (in the sense of "reducing to ashes," Dhātupāṭha 991): in the imperative (*loṭ*), second person singular (*sip*), the substitution of *hi* for *si* occurs; then, by [Pāṇini 6.4.105], there is elision (*luk*) of *hi*. Because the rule [Pāṇini 8.1.28] prescribing the suppression (*nighāta*) of an accented word before another accented word applies, the word *daha* is unaccented (*anudātta*).

Some read it with a protracted final syllable as *vahā3*; for them, since they do not wish to admit an arbitrary innovation (*sāhasa*), the protraction must be stated on the basis of the rule: "In all cases, the protracted vowel may optionally be stated" (*ma-bhā-3.420*). And that [protracted vowel] is acute (*udātta*). Others, however, read it ending in *-ā* (*vahā*); for them, the long vowel *ā* occurs because it belongs to Vedic usage (*chāndasa*).
For even a short vowel becomes long by way of metrical or phonetic substitution (*vyatyaya*), as in the words *puruṣaḥ* and *nārakaḥ*. [The phrase] "melodies situated in specific sentences" means...

As stated by Jaimini: "The designation *sāman* applies to songs. Here, *gīti* means a specific kind of sound (*dhvani-viśeṣa*). Why is the word *karman* (action) included? One might ask: why not simply say "in the sacrifice" (*yajñe*), since sacrificial mantras serve the purpose of sacrificial acts and would thus apply to sacrificial rites? This is true; however, the inclusion of the word *karman* is for the sake of clarity.

Or rather—this is for the purpose that it may apply even to those sacrifices not well-known [in common usage], such as the *pañcayajña* and others; otherwise, if only "in a sacrifice" (*yajñe*) were said, it would apply only to those sacrifices well-known [in common usage], such as the *āgneya* and so forth. The statement "here the word *vauṣaṭ* is indicated by the word *vaṣaṭ*" is intended to show that they share the same etymological root; both of them denote the act of giving to the gods.
Just as the gift to the gods is given by means of the word *vaṣaṭ*, so too it is given by means of the word *vauṣaṭ*.
Therefore, because they share the same purpose, the word *vaṣaṭ* indicates (*lakṣayati*) the word *vauṣaṭ*.

The inclusion of the word *kāra* is for the purpose that, setting aside its status as having meaning as its referent (*arthapadārthakatva*), it may be used in the act of giving with the word as its referent (*śabdapadārthakatva*), so that it may possess a higher pitch (*udāttatara*).

In the inclusion of the term *kāra*, [the word] is seen as having "sound" (*śabda*) as its referent, as in the case of the particle *evakāra*. Others explain the inclusion of *kāra* so that it might apply to other instances as well;

by this, in the expression *astu śrauṣaṭ*, this [word *śrauṣaṭ*] becomes more highly accented (*udāttatara*). The suffix of excellence in *uccais-tarām* is to be understood in relation to that protracted vowel (*pluta*) prescribed for the word *vauṣaṭ* by the rule *brāūhi-preṣya-śrauṣaḍ-āvahānām ādeḥ* [Pāṇini 8.2.91]; for that [protracted vowel] is acute (*udātta*), and since the excellence [of accent] exists in comparison to the acute protracted vowel prescribed for the end of a *yājyā* verse by the rule *yājyāntaḥ* [Pāṇini 8.2.90].

Alternatively, this word ending in the suffix *prakarṣa* (intensity) is simply another term for its own form (*svarūpa*). Others, however, say: by the rule [Pāṇini 6.1.158], the *pluta* vowel is acute (*udātta*), while the other is more gravely accented (*anudāttatara*). [Examples include] "iṣe tvā" and so forth.
[The root] "iṣu" [is used] in the sense of "desire" (Dhātupāṭha 1351); [the suffix] *kvip* is applied [by Pāṇini 3.2.178].

In the sense of "he possesses *iḍ*," the suffix *a* is applied by means of the supplementary rule (*upasaṃkhyāna*) "not a suffix" (*apratyayaḥ*) under the governing heading of elision (*lugadhikāra*). This suffix is acute on the first syllable (*ādyudātta*) by the accent of the suffix (*pratyayasvara*). From the word *iṣ*, the seventh case singular ending is applied. For the word *yuṣmad* ending in the second case, the substitute *tvām* is applied; this is unaccented (*anudātta*), because of the governing heading [of the rule] beginning with *8.1.18*.

In the word *agne*, the first syllable is acute (*ādyudātta*) by virtue of Pāṇini 6.1.199. [The form is derived as follows: from the root *yā* in the sense of "reaching" (Dhātupāṭha 1049), preceded by the prefix *āṅ*, there is the imperative (*loṭ*), the second person singular suffix (*sip*), and for *sip* there is the substitution of *hi*. The prefix *āṅ* is acute according to Phiṭ-sūtra 4.81: "And prefixes are acute, with the exception of *abhi*."

By the rule *tiṅṅatiṅaḥ* [Pāṇini 8.1.28], there is the *nighāta* (elision of accent) of the word *yāhi*. In the root *vī* (meaning "to go," etc., Dhātupāṭha 1019), the suffix *ktin* is udātta by the rule *mantrē vṛṣēṣapaca...* [Pāṇini 3.3.96]. In the singular dative case ending, there is *guṇa* substitution, followed by the *ay* replacement; both of these, by virtue of being *sthānivadbhāva*, are udātta, while the remainder is anudātta. The word *agni* is, as before, oxytone (*antōdātta*) due to the accent of the suffix *ni*.
In the second person singular [ending] *ami*, there is the substitution of the preceding vowel (*pūrvatva*).
The root *īḍ* (in the sense of "praising") is listed as number 1019 in the Dhātupāṭha;
because it is marked with an anudātta vowel, it takes the ātmanepada endings.
By the rule *tiṅṅatiṅaḥ* [Pāṇini 8.1.28], there is the *nighāta* (elision of the accent) of the word *iti*.

Having analyzed *puraḥ* as *pūrvasmin deśe* ("in the eastern region"), the suffix *asi* is applied by the rule *pūrvāparādharāvarāṇāmasi puradhavaścaiṣām* [Pāṇini 5.3.39], and the word *pūrva-* undergoes the substitution *pura-*. The word *puraḥ* is oxytone (accented on the final syllable) due to the accent of the suffix.
In the case of the past passive participle (*niṣṭhā*) of the root *dhā*, there is the substitution of *hi* [by Pāṇini 7.4.42].

When it has received the technical designation of a *gati* [by Pāṇini 1.4.67], a compound is formed [by Pāṇini 2.2.18]. Although the rule for the acute accent on the final syllable of a compound would have applied [by Pāṇini 6.1.223], the word *puraḥ* retains its original accent on the final syllable by virtue of the accentual rule for the first member of a compound [Pāṇini 6.2.49].
The word *śam* is a particle (*nipāta*) because it belongs to the *ādi* group;
by the accent rule for particles, it is udātta on its first syllable.
The genitive case of the pronoun *asmad* undergoes the substitution of *nas* by the rule *bahuvacanasya vasnasau* [Pāṇini 7.1.21], which is anudātta due to the governing context of anudātta vowels.
The suffix *ac* is applied after the root *div* in the sense of the present tense and so forth.
In the *pacādi* group, [the word] *devaḍ* is recited.

By the rule *ṭiḍḍhāṇañ* [Pāṇini 4.1.15], the suffix *ṅīp* is introduced; by the rule *anudāttau suppitau* [Pāṇini 6.4.148], there is elision of the vowel *a*; and by the rule *yasyeti ca* [Pāṇini 6.4.148], there is elision of the final vowel; thus, by the rule *citaḥ* [Pāṇini 6.1.163], the *ṅīp* is udātta.

In the second person plural, there is the substitution of the long vowel homogeneous with the preceding one according to [Pāṇini 6.1.102]. From the verbal root *stuñ* (meaning "to praise," Dhātupāṭha 1043), the suffix *ap* is applied by [Pāṇini 3.3.57] after the prefix *abhi*; this results in *guṇa* and the replacement of the vowel (*avādeśa*).
Through the transposition of phonemes (*varṇavyatyaya*), the letter *v* becomes *y*.

When the rule *gatikāraka* [Pāṇini 6.2.138] would have required the original accent (*prakṛtisvara*) of the final member of the compound, the rule *antaḥ* [Pāṇini 6.2.142], which is still in force, applies via [Pāṇini 6.2.144], resulting in the acute accent (*udātta*) on the final syllable of the second member. Thus, by [Pāṇini 6.1.87] and [8.2.5], the word *abhiṣṭaye* has its acute accent on the final syllable. This is called the *Subrahmaṇyā Nigada*.
The root *gad* occurs in the sense of "prose composition" (*apādabandha*), for prose is indeed called *gadya*. The prefix *ni-* denotes excellence.
That which is recited loudly, continuously, and without word-division (*apādabandha*) is designated as *nigada*.
Because it is characterized by the *Subrahmaṇyā* formula, it is referred to in the feminine gender as "the *Subrahmaṇyā*," namely:
*subrahmaṇyom*.

Some claim that [the word] *subrahmaṇyā* is derived from the rule *sādhuḥ* (Pāṇini 4.4.98), which takes the suffix *yat*, and that by the rule [regarding] *svaritatva* (Pāṇini 6.1.185) and the rule [regarding] the substitution of the syllable *oṃ* (Pāṇini 8.2.89), the vowel *oṃ* is substituted [for the final *ā*]. This is incorrect; for the *Kāśikā* (on 8.2.89) will state: "Having elided the final syllable of either a *pāda* or a half-verse (*ardharca*), they prescribe the insertion of a three-mora *o*-vowel or the syllable *oṃ* in place of the remainder beginning with that initial syllable; this they call the *praṇava*.
Furthermore, in the *nigada* recitation, there is no fixed division into *pādas*, nor is there a fixed division into half-verses.
Therefore, the word *o* exists as a particle (*nipāta*) that is meaningless [in itself].
Its single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) with the circumflex (*svarita*) accent is circumflex.
[This is governed by the rule: "An address (*āmantrita*) is acute on its first syllable."
By this [rule] from the sixth chapter, [it is stated]:
"The circumflex (udātta) is produced by the *tsayāna*.
Now, one might object that this circumflex is unestablished (*asiddha*); however, by virtue of this specific statement, its status as unestablished does not apply.

But is it not possible to state that the purpose of the utterance is "subrahmaṇyom"? For when the entire *nigada* is characterized by the word *subrahmaṇyā*, it is not appropriate to cite this single instance—
"the vowel *a* is acute"—
on the basis of the accent of the particle (*nipāta*).

"Then the following [syllable] is anudātta (unaccented) or svarita (circumflex)," according to the rule *tiṅṅatiṅaḥ* [Pāṇini 8.1.28], once the suppression of accent (*nighāta*) has been applied by the rule [8.4.66]. "The last one."
The letter *cha* has the form of *a*. "There are four acute [vowels]" means those other than the letters *va* and *cha*.
"The two unaccented [syllables]" refers to the letters *va* and *cha*. "The second syllable" refers to [the second syllable of the word].
The form of the word *medhā* [is such that] "the remainder is unaccented" (*śeṣamanudāttam*). In the word *medhā*, whatever is other than the two vowels [is unaccented].
"By the preceding [rule]" means by the rule "Medhātithi’s sheep. "In the same way, the first two syllables are acute" means that they are likewise accented.

If "gaurāvaskandin" is a compound vocative, it is accented on the first syllable. Even if they recite "gauḥ" as a separate word, nevertheless, when that too is included, because the entire vocative is accented on the first syllable, there are two acute accents according to the previously stated rule beginning with [Pāṇini 8.1.66]. As in: "ahalyāyai jāraḥ."

The fourth case ending is used in the sense of the sixth case, according to the supplementary rule (*vārttika*) "the fourth case may be used in the sense of the sixth" (*ṣaṣṭhyarthe caturthī vaktavyā*) at [Pāṇini 2.3.62], or alternatively, by way of transposition (*vyatyaya*) according to [Pāṇini 3.1.85]. The entire vocative form is accented on its first syllable because the word *kauśika* has entered into the subsequent vocative.
"Thus, Gautama said"—
the meaning is that this is equivalent to [the phrase] "O Kauśika Brāhmaṇa.
"'Two [vocatives] are acute'."
In each of the two preceding examples, the meaning is "the first [syllable].
Regarding the statement "the exclamation *āḥ* is udātta," it is by virtue of the accent of the nominal stem (*prātipadika-svara*).
"The term 'udātta' (acute accent) carries over" refers to the rule beginning with "mantre vṛṣa" [Pāṇini 3.2.96]. "Two [syllables] are acute" means...
Those two [cases] were previously shown in the rule "Come again" (*tau punarādī āgaccha*);
namely, by the rule *padāt paramāmantritaṃ nihanyate* (Pāṇini 8.1.19),
[which states that] "an vocative following a word is unaccented," once both words have been made udātta at their beginning because they are vocatives.

Because of the rule *vibhāṣitaṃ viśeṣitaṃ viśeṣavacane bahuvacanam* [Pāṇini 8.1.74], and because of the rule *pūrvasyāvidyamānavattvāt* [Pāṇini 8.1.19], the *nighāta* (anudātta accent) does not occur even for the word that follows. Consequently, both words retain their respective initial acute accents (*ādyudāttatva*) as prescribed by the sixth book [of Pāṇini]. This is what is meant by "the *nighāta* of the remainder" (*śeṣanighāta*).

By this [rule], *Pāṇini* 6.1.158, the plural number in the phrase "of those that are unaccented" (*anudāttānām*) is used in the sense of a genus; therefore, it applies even in the case of two [syllables]. Thus, the word *imam* has its final syllable accented (*antodātta*).

Because the word *idam* ends in the suffix *kam*, it is oxytone by the accent of the suffix (*pratyayasvara*). When its *tyadādi* substitution occurs and the subsequent monophthongization (*pararūpa*) takes place, that single substitute (*ekādeśa*) is also acute because it is [replaced] by an acute vowel. The phrase "only at the time of the rule" (*vidhikala eva*) is used because the application of the *nighāta* (elision of the accent) is prescribed only at the very moment the rule is being formulated (*vidhikāla*).
"All these [words] are unaccented by means of the suppression (nighāta) of the vocative," it is said.

Although there is the rule "a preceding vocative is as if non-existent" (Pāṇini 8.1.72), nevertheless, because all [the words] would result in being suppressed in relation to the word *me*, [the rule] states:
"A vocative in the nominative case is udātta on its first syllable."
By the rule [Pāṇini 6.1.19],
"The second syllable of that [word] is circumflex (svarita)," according to [Pāṇini 8.4.66].
Regarding the rule "tataḥ pareṣāmanudāttānām" [Pāṇini 8.1.73]:

since the negation of non-existence (avidyamānatva) applies here, the subsequent syllables are unaccented (anudātta) because of the prescription of the *nighāta* accent by the rule "māṇavakāt parayoḥ" [Pāṇini 8.1.19]. [The commentary adds:
"It should not occur in the case of an *avagraha*."

*Avagraha* is the unjoined recitation (*asaṃhitāpāṭha*). Now, since [the rule] *svaritāt* [P. 1.2.39] is in the ablative case, and because the mention of "that which is specified" (*nirdiṣṭagrahaṇa*) in [the rule] *tena* [P. 1.1.67] has the sense of immediate succession (*ānantarya*), there would be no possibility of *avagraha* occurring at all; for just as a phoneme (*varṇa*) is an intervening element, so too is time. Why, then, is the word *saṃhitā* mentioned? It is for the purpose of making known that time resulting from the ablative specification is not an intervening element. Consequently, in the rule *tiṅaṅatiṅaḥ* [P. 8.1.28], even in the case of *avagraha*, a finite verb (*tiṅanta*) following a non-finite verb (*atiṅanta*) is pronounced with a low pitch (*nihanyate*). Thus: "In the word *mātaraḥ*, [the first syllable] is unaccented (*anudātta*)."

The state of being unaccented (anudāttatva), however, is due to the accent of the case-ending (vibhaktisvara). In the word *mātaraḥ*, the suffix *jas* is added to the stem *mātṛ*; by [Pāṇini 7.3.110], the guṇa substitution occurs;
and the *s* of *jas* becomes *r*.
In that case as well, when followed by a non-śas ending, the substitution of *u* occurs according to Pāṇini 6.1.113.

When the acute accent (*udātta*) is applied to the case-ending by 6.1.165 (*uḍidampadam...*), the *o* in *eṅaḥ padāntādati* (6.1.109) is substituted; this *o* also becomes grave (*anudātta*) by virtue of its status as a *sthānivadbhāva*. Thus, it is said:
"when an acute [vowel] follows it."

Regarding the form *vibhaktyakāre*: "the vowel *i* is unaccented" (*ikāro'nudāttaḥ*) because it is connected with the word *sarasvatī*; for the rule "and [in the case] of the vocative" (*āmantritasya ca*, Pāṇini 8.1.19) prescribes the grave accent (*nighāta*) for the word *sarasvatī*.

"Therefore, it is not elided" (tasmān na nihanyate)— this is because of the prohibition of elision (*nighāta*) at the beginning of a verse-quarter (*apādādau*), as stated in [Aṣṭādhyāyī 8.1.18]. "The first syllable"— this refers to...

The *śakāra* and *okāra* are acute (*udātta*), according to the rule at Pāṇini 8.1.19. Regarding the form *ghṛtaspṛk*: by the rule at 8.2.62, there is *kutva*, whereby the *śakāra* becomes *khakāra*; then, by the rule for *jaśtva*, the *khakāra* becomes *gakāra*.
Regarding the form *adṛḍhabhāk*.
By [Pāṇini 8.2.30], the letter *ja* becomes *ga*.

In both cases, by [Pāṇini 8.4.56], there is *cartva*, whereby *ja* becomes *ka*. Once the designation *apṛkta* has been applied to the following [element] by [Pāṇini 1.2.41], the elision of the letter *v* occurs by [Pāṇini 6.1.67].
For in the counter-examples (*pratyudāharaṇa*), [the suffix] does not occur due to the absence of that [condition]. Regarding *darviḥ*:
from the root *dṛ* "to split" (Dhātupāṭha 1493), the suffix *vin* is applied by the rule *vṛ dṛbhyāṃ vin* (Daiva 1.23). Regarding *jāgṛviḥ*.
The root *jāgṛ* is listed as "to wake" (*nidrākṣaye*) in the Dhātupāṭha (1072). The suffix *kvin* is applied by the rule *jṛśṛstṛjāgṛbhyaḥ kvin* (Dhātupāṭha 1.24).

Regarding the word *surāḥ*: the root *ṣūñ* is listed as "to press" (*abhiṣave*) in the Dhātupāṭha (1247). From the derivation *surāṃ sunoti*, the suffix *kvip* is applied according to Pāṇini 3.2.130; thus we have *surāsut*, with the augment *tuk* added after the short vowel.
The suffix *ṇic* is applied by the rule "one says that" (*tam ācaṣṭe*, Vārttika 201).
The elision of the *ṭi* portion [of the stem] occurs by the rule "the operations pertaining to a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) as if it were ending in *iṣṭhan* apply when *ṇi* follows" (Vārttika 813).

Furthermore, from the verbal root *surā-sav-*, there is the suffix *kvip*; the *ṇi* is elided; this is the nominative singular; the *su* is elided by [Pāṇini 6.1.68] *halṅyābbhyo dīrghāt sutisy apṛktaṃ hal*; then the *ru*-tva and *visarjanīya* [substitutions] occur.
Here too, if the term "affix" (*pratyaya*) were not included [in the rule], then upon the elision of the *ṇi*, the vowel of the verbal root would receive the designation *apṛkta*.
If that designation were present, the elision of the *s* of the verbal root would occur by [Pāṇini 6.1.68] *ato lopaḥ*.

[Objection: But surely, even if the mention of "affix" (*pratyaya*) were not made, the technical designation (*saṃjñā*) would be understood according to the rule: "Between [a term consisting of] an affix and [a term consisting of] a non-affix, only that which is an affix is to be taken" (Vyāḍipāda 72). So for what purpose is the mention of "affix" made? [Answer: It is made for the sake of clarity. [Objection: Then for what purpose is the mention of "single" (*eka*) made? [To prevent the designation from applying] to a collection of *al*-sounds. [Reply: That is not necessary; it will not apply by virtue of the force of the mention of *al* itself. Otherwise, the mention of *al* would be useless—if the designation were to apply even to a collection of *hal*-sounds.
In this way, then, the mention of *hal* here serves to indicate that the mention of *hal* implies the mention of the genus (*jāti*).

By means of this, what was stated under [Pāṇini 1.2.10]—namely, "The form is established because the mention of *hal* in the root *dambh-* denotes the genus"—becomes justified. "Tatpuruṣa" is the name for a specific type of compound (*samāsa*), and it consists of the single word *eka*.
Co-referentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) is the occurrence of multiple words, which possess distinct grounds for application (*pravṛttinimitta*), with respect to a single referent.

Consequently, this designation [of *tatpuruṣa*] would apply only where there is co-referentiality of the *tatpuruṣa* compound with an external word—as in examples such as *rājapuruṣaḥ śobhanaḥ* ("the king’s man is handsome")—for here the *tatpuruṣa* indeed possesses co-referentiality with something, namely with the word *śobhana*.

To refute the objection that [the designation of *tatpuruṣa*] would not apply in cases such as *pācakavṛndārikā*, because here the *tatpuruṣa* lacks coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with anything—since there is no employment of another word—he says: "a *tatpuruṣa* whose words are coreferential" (*samānādhikaraṇapadaḥ*). "Coreferential" (*samāna*) means non-different (*abhinna*). Those words whose referent (*adhikaraṇa*), i.e., their expressed meaning, is one and the same are "coreferential words. A *tatpuruṣa* which has such words as its basis is a "coreferential-word *tatpuruṣa*."

By this, he demonstrates that because the words whose referents are identical [in meaning] constitute a *tatpuruṣa* compound, the term "co-referential" (*samānādhikaraṇa*) in this rule refers to the *tatpuruṣa* by way of metaphorical designation (*upacāra*).

But how is it justified to adopt a metaphorical sense when the primary co-referentiality of the *tatpuruṣa*—in relation to its second member—is possible? It is because of the employment of the lengthy technical name "karmadhāraya."

For here, since the purpose of creating a technical name (*saṃjñā*) is for the sake of brevity, by the author employing the long name "karmadhāraya" when a much shorter name could have been used, this meaning is indicated: "In this case, some other inversion has also been adopted regarding the technical name.

Consequently, according to the principle that "between the secondary (*gauṇa*) and the primary (*mukhya*), the operation is understood to apply to the primary" (Vyāḍipāda 4), it is not understood that the term refers only to a primary co-referential compound (*samānādhikaraṇa*). [This is clarified by the phrase] "having the same denotation" (*samānābhidheya*).
Because the words whose meanings constitute that [compound] have a common referent, the *tatpuruṣa* compound is also said to have a common referent by way of metaphorical designation (*upacāra*),
as in "supreme sovereignty" (*paramarājyam*) or "excellent sovereignty" (*uttamarājyam*). The compound is formed by [the rule] beginning with Pāṇini 2.1.61.

When it is a *karmadhāraya* compound, the rule *ity uttarapadādyudāttatvam* (Pāṇini 6.2.130) does not apply, resulting in the acute accent on the first syllable of the final member. For example, in *pācakavṛndārikā*,
there is the substitution of the masculine form (*puṃvadbhāva*) by the rule *vṛndārakanāgakuñjaraiḥ* (Pāṇini 2.1.61).
In the case of *pācikābhāryaḥ*,
this is a *bahuvrīhi* compound;
therefore, the prohibition [of the feminine suffix] by rule 6.3.37 certainly applies here.
Regarding the term *brāhmaṇarājyam*:
this is a genitive tatpuruṣa compound.

Consequently, the final syllable of the compound does not receive the udātta accent; rather, the first syllable of the second member (*uttarapada*) is udātta. The mention of "in a compound" (*samāse*) here is an indication of the locative case.

In compounds such as *kaṣṭaśrita*, there is no word-form (*śabdarūpa*) that is designated by the nominative case (*prathamānirdiṣṭa*). For instance, once the compound has been formed, the case-ending arises from that very compound itself, and not from the individual word [that was] situated therein.

Nor is it appropriate to assume that a constituent part of the compound possesses the status of being "designated by the nominative" based on the nominative that arose at the time of the sentence (*vākya*) from the word expressing the meaning of the compound; because the term "in a compound" (*samāse*) is an indication of the locus (*adhikaraṇanirdeśa*).

In that regard, when a compound (*samāsa*) has been formed, that from which the nominative case (*prathamā*) arises is alone what is designated as "stated in the nominative" (*prathamā-nirdiṣṭa*) within the compound; it is not that from which the case-ending arises at the time of the sentence (*vākya*). For that [word] is stated in the nominative only in the sentence, and not in the compound, because it was already stated in the nominative prior to the formation of the compound. Consequently, since the designatum (*saṃjñin*)—that which is stated in the nominative—is impossible once the compound is formed, the designation (*saṃjñā*) itself would be impossible. To refute this objection, he says: "That which is indicated by the nominative case-ending."
A treatise whose purpose is a compound is understood here as "the treatise on compounds" (*samāsaśāstra*).

In that context, this technical designation (*saṃjñā*) is prescribed for that which is indicated by the first case (*prathamānirdiṣṭa*), and not for [words] such as *kaṣṭaśrita*; for in a compound, there is nothing indicated by the first case, whereas in the treatise on compounds, there exists a designatum (*saṃjñin*) indicated by the first case—so how could there be a non-establishment of the designation? But how is it that when "in a compound" (*samāse*) is stated, that which is indicated by the first case in the treatise on compounds obtains the status of being the designatum? To this he says:
"In 'in a compound' (*samāse'), the treatise on compounds is understood."

But how, when it is stated "in a compound" (*samāse*), can the rule for compounds (*samāsa-śāstra*) be understood [to be meant]? Because the word "compound" (*samāsa*) is applied there by virtue of being for that purpose (*tādārthyāt*). For indeed, a thing is designated by the name of its purpose; as for example, a jasmine flower intended for a lamp is called "the lamp," and a pillar intended for Indra is called "Indra."

The function of the designation *upasarjana* (secondary member) in cases such as *kaṣṭaśrita* and others is the placement [of the word] at the beginning, according to the rule "the *upasarjana* comes first" (*upasarjanaṃ pūrvam*, Pāṇini 2.2.30). Regarding this, the following objection is raised: in the expression *rājñaḥ kumārīṃ paśya rājakumārīm paśya* ("look at the king's daughter"), the word *rājan* is prescribed as the first member in the rule for compounds by the sixth case (*ṣaṣṭhī*, Pāṇini 2.2.8), and the word *kumārī* is so prescribed in the rule for compounds by the second case (*dvitīyā*, Pāṇini 2.1.24). Since both would possess this designation (*upasarjana*) within the rules for compound formation, two defects would follow: a lack of restriction regarding which word should be placed first, and the shortening of the vowel of the *upasarjana*.

And here, in the case of *rājñaḥ kumāryāḥ svam* ("the property of the king's daughter"), since both [words] ending in the genitive case are designated as the first member (*prathamānirdiṣṭa*) in the rule for compound formation, both would receive the technical designation of "subordinate" (*upasarjana*). If that were so, those same two faults would arise. This is not a fault; for this very purpose was served by establishing the technical term "subordinate" (*upasarjana*) as a grand designation: so that it might be understood as a term based on its meaning (*anvarthasaṃjñā*). That which is non-principal is the subordinate, and that which is principal is not subordinate. Furthermore, the non-principal depends upon the principal, because it is a relative term.

In this regard, it should be understood from the rule of *saṃnaddha* that whatever is subordinate (*apradhāna*) with respect to something else is a subordinate member (*upasarjana*) with respect to that thing.
Furthermore, a word ending in the second case (*dvitīyānta*) becomes a subordinate member only in relation to words such as *śrita*, and not merely by virtue of ending in the second case.
And in this instance, words such as *śrita* do not exist.
In the case of *rājñaḥ kumāryāḥ svam* (the property of the king's daughter), the same solution applies here as well.

Here too, with respect to the word *kumārī*, the word *rājan* is subordinate (*aprādhānya*); however, it is not the case that the word *kumārī* is subordinate with respect to the word *rājan*. Therefore, the designation of "subordinate element" (*upasarjana*) applies to the word *rājan*, and not to the word *kumārī*.

If this were indeed a designation based on the meaning (*anvarthasaṃjñā*), then in cases such as *pācakavṛndārikā*, *puruṣavyāghraḥ*, *ardhapippalī*, and *pūrvakāyaḥ*, the meaning of the first member alone would be predominant; thus, the predominance here would belong to the [words] beginning with *pācikā*. Consequently, although these [words] are designated as the first members in the rules for compound formation—namely, Pāṇini 2.1.62, 2.1.56, 2.2.2 (*ardhaṃ napuṃsakam*), and 2.2.1 (*pūrvāparādharottaramekadeśinā sahaikādhikaraṇe*)—nevertheless, the technical designation of "subordinate" (*upasarjana*) would not apply to them. Why? Because they are predominant.

If this is so, then there is no fault, because in the subsequent sūtra the particle *ca* will serve the purpose of including what has not been mentioned [in the preceding]. However, another holds this view: "In the previously mentioned compounds such as *pācakavṛndārikā*, the first two cases are established by the rules *ādyantau* [2.1.57] and *ābhyām* [2.1.55]; the remaining two cases, however, are established by the rule *ṣaṣṭhī* [2.2.8] alone."

Therefore, the commencement [of the sūtra] beginning with *tasmāt* (Pāṇini 2.1.62) is not for the sake of that [specific meaning]; what then? It is for the sake of the technical designation (*saṃjñā*) "secondary member" (*upasarjana*). [The opponent argues: "By this, even though words such as *pācika* lack primacy, they will still receive this designation"—but this is incorrect. For indeed, the commencement would be for the purpose of stating these specific qualifications: "that which is being honored," "when there is no application of a general term," "the neuter gender," and "having a single substratum."

If this were the purpose of the undertaking [of the rule], then the designation *upasarjana* (secondary element) being prescribed here for that which is not primary would not apply to the primary element. This undertaking is intended for the sake of specifying that which is not primary.
The word *vibhakti* (case-ending) denotes either the *sup* suffixes or it signifies "division" (*vibhāga*).
"Division" refers to the power of the *kāraka* (grammatical relation), based on the etymology: "that by means of which the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) is divided."
Regarding the phrase "when [the compound] is being prescribed":
this refers to the time of the sentence that expresses the meaning of the compound;
for it is at that time that the prescription of that compound occurs.

By this, he demonstrates that the term *samāsa* (compound), which continues to apply [from the previous rule], refers to a sentence expressing the sense of a compound, and not to the technical rule (*śāstra*) concerning compounds.

For in a rule concerning compounds, every form of word would necessarily possess only a single case-ending; thus, the mention of "having a single case-ending" (*ekavibhakti*) would be redundant. This is the intended meaning. Indeed, every nominal stem (*prātipadika*) is used with one case-ending or another in turn.
Therefore, because of the force of the mention of "a single case-ending," a restriction is understood here; hence he says: "that which has a fixed case-ending.
Clarifying that very point, he says: "in the second [example], when there is a related word," and so forth, as well as:
"even when the preceding word lacks a case-ending."
The word *niṣkrānta* denotes a substance (*dravya*) which has become subordinate to the agent-power (*kartṛ-śakti*).
Since that [substance] is augmented by the powers of multiple instruments (*sādhana*), it comes to possess case-endings for multiple instruments due to its connection with other actions.
However, "the subsequent member (*uttarapada*) must end in the ablative case."
Because it possesses the functional capacity of an *apādāna* (ablative) manifested in relation to the action of departing (*niṣkramaṇa*).

In the expression *niṣkauśāmbiḥ*, there is the application of the technical term *upasarjana* (secondary member), which results in the shortening of the vowel according to the rule *gostriyor upasarjanasya* [Pāṇini 1.2.48]. Now, by what rule is the status of *niḥ* as an *upasarjana* prescribed here, such that its placement before the other member occurs? If you say it is by the preceding sūtra (*prathamānirdiṣṭaṃ samāsa upasarjanam*), this is not correct; for that sūtra prescribes the designation *upasarjana* for that which is non-principal (*apradhāna*), whereas in this case, *niḥ* is the principal element.
If that is the case, then [the desired result] will follow because the particle *ca* has the sense of including what has not been explicitly mentioned (*anuktasamuccaya*).

However, others say: "Let there be no designation of *nis* as a subordinate element (*upasarjana*); even in its absence, its prior placement (*pūrvanipāta*) will occur by virtue of the rule [Pāṇini 2.2.30], *prathamānirdiṣṭaṃ samāsa upasarjanam*. This is incorrect; for when prior placement is to be effected, the designation of a subordinate element does not exist at all for that which possesses a single case-ending.

In that context, if *nis* were not designated as a subordinate element, then in the given example, since that designation would be absent for both [members of the compound], an unrestricted prior placement of either one would undesirably follow.

Now, why is it that words such as *ardhapippalī* do not receive the designation of *upasarjana*? In this context, the term *vibhāṣā* (optionally) from the rule *vibhāṣā cchandasi* [Pāṇini 1.2.36] is carried over by the maxim of the frog’s leap (*maṇḍūkapluti*); moreover, this is a restricted option (*vyavasthitavibhāṣā*).
Consequently, in cases such as *ardhaṃ pippalyāḥ* = *ardhapippalī*, even though *pippalī* and the like are joined with the same case-ending, they do not receive the designation of *upasarjana*.
For if they did, then the shortening of the vowel would occur. [The author notes: "This word *artha* here signifies that which is denoted (*abhidheya*)."
By this [statement], he excludes [other meanings] by means of the mention of the "purpose" (*prayojana*) and so forth.

For the word *artha* has the sense of "purpose," as in: "He has come for this purpose" (*anena arthena āgataḥ*), which is understood to mean "for this motive. It also has the sense of "cessation," as in: "Smoke is for the sake of mosquitoes" (*maśakārtho dhūmaḥ*), which is understood to mean "for the sake of warding off mosquitoes."
The word *artha* also denotes wealth, as in "Devadatta is *arthavān*," which is understood to mean "he possesses wealth.
It also denotes the meaning [of a word], as in "this is the *artha* of this statement," which is understood to mean "this is its denotation (*abhidheya*).
However, in the present context, only the sense of "denotation" is intended.

Furthermore, that which is denoted is fourfold, distinguished by genus (*jāti*), quality (*guṇa*), action (*kriyā*), and substance (*dravya*). For this very reason, the application of words is fourfold. Among these, for words denoting a genus, the genus is the denotation—as in "cow" (*go*). If the designation of a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) were prescribed only for that which possesses a meaning, then the designation of nominal stems would not apply to words such as "hare's horn" (*śaśaviṣāṇa*), which express non-existence, because of the absence of a meaning. This is not so; for it has been stated [in the Vārttika]: "The word 'meaning' (*artha*) signifies that which is denotable" (Kāśikā 1.2.45). Thus, even non-existence is indeed denotable.

Otherwise, this statement "because of the absence of meaning" (*anarthābhāvāt*) would not be worth uttering, since it would be meaningless; for a meaningless statement does not deserve to be employed.
Therefore, even for words denoting non-existence (*abhāva*), the designation *prātipadika* certainly applies. [The objection] "lest it apply to that which ends in *na*" refers to the word *adhi*.

But surely there will be a prohibition by the rule *na dhātuḥ* ("not a verbal root"); for these two forms [dharā and dharām] belong to the roots *vana* (DhP 463, meaning "to assemble") and *dhana* (DhP 1104, meaning "wealth"), which are verbal roots. This is not so; the words *vana* and *dhana* also exist as underived (*avyutpanna*) nouns, and this is their usage here.

If, in this case, the designation of nominal stem (*prātipadika-saṃjñā*) were to apply to that which ends in *n*, then the addition of case-endings (*sub-utpatti*) would occur; and consequently, when the designation of "word" (*pada-saṃjñā*) is established, the elision of the *n* (*nalopa*) would take place.

But is it not the case that [the rule applies to] what is "not a root" (*adhātu*) and "not an affix" (*apratyaya*)? This is not so; for there exist even meaningless roots, such as *iṅ* in the sense of "studying" (DhP 1046) and *ik* in the sense of "remembering" (DhP 1047). These two possess meaning only when preceded by the prefix *adhi*, not when they are alone. As for the assignment of meanings to these two in the list of roots (*gaṇapāṭha*), it should be understood that this was done by superimposing the meaning of the whole onto its parts. Even though their meanings are thus superimposed, they still receive the technical designation "root" (*dhātusaṃjñā*) by virtue of their inclusion in the list of roots.
Thus, there are also suffixes that are meaningless,
such as in *yāva* and *yāvaka*.
For in these cases, it is not possible to ascertain the meaningfulness of the suffix through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*).

Even without that *kan* suffix, the meaning is understood from the word *yāvat* itself; therefore, it is rightly said that [the suffix] is meaningful. Regarding the form *ahan*: due to its belonging to the *ad*-class, there is elision (*luk*) of the *śap* suffix; the *tip* ending is elided by [Pāṇini 6.1.68], and the augment *aṭ* is applied.
And since that [root] is included by the mention of *han*, even when that [mention] is made, *han* belongs only to the giver.

Here, without the mention of the verbal root (*dhātu*), the designation of a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) would occur prior to the arising of the suffix; however, the elision of *n* occurs only later, once the suffix has arisen and the word-status (*padatva*) is established.
Alternatively, even the designation *prātipadika* would occur only after the production of the suffix; therefore, the mention of *dhātu* (verbal root) must be made.

But surely, in this case, the prohibition "not a suffix" (*apratyaya*)—by virtue of the rule for suffixal characteristics (*pratyayalakṣaṇa*)—should apply; so what is the purpose of mentioning *adhātu* (non-root)? This is not so; when the designation *prātipadika* is to be applied, the elision of *n* (*nalopa*) must take place, and regarding that elision of *n*, the prohibition "not before the *ṅi* case-ending or the vocative" (*na ṅisambuddhayoḥ*) serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*) that the prohibition "not a suffix" by virtue of suffixal characteristics does not operate.

If, by the definition of a suffix (*pratyaya*), there were a prohibition of the designation "nominal stem" (*prātipadika-saṃjñā*) in cases such as *he rājan* because it is not a suffix, then the prohibition in the rule *na ṅi-sambuddhayoḥ* [Pāṇini 8.2.8] would be purposeless, since there would be no possibility for the application [of the rule].

Now, how is the designation *prātipadika* (nominal stem) applied to words such as *bhid*, *chid*, *lū*, and *pū*, given that since those ending in *kvip* do not abandon their status as verbal roots (*dhātu*), these are indeed roots? In this case, shouldn't there be a prohibition by the rule "not a root" (*adhātu*)? This is not a fault; let it not be by this [present rule], but it will be by the subsequent rule because they end in a *kṛt* suffix. Nor does this [present rule] sublate the subsequent application, because it resides in a different sentence. Or, according to the principle: "Exceptions in the middle sublate preceding rules, not subsequent ones" (Vyāḍiparibhāṣā 10). Examples: *kāṇḍe*, *kuḍye*.
These two forms end in the dual number of the nominative case.
By the rule *śībhāvaḥ* (Pāṇini 7.1.19), the substitution of *śī* occurs.

And in this context, by the principle *pratyayagrahaṇe yasmāt sa vihitastadādestadantasya* (Mahābhāṣya, Paspaśāhnika, Sūtra 7), there will be a prohibition regarding that which ends in the suffix, and not regarding the suffix alone.

But is it not the case that, because of the mention of the word *anta* (end) in [Pāṇini 1.4.14], it has been indicated that "in other rules prescribing technical names (*saṃjñā*), when a suffix is mentioned, there is no inclusion of what ends with that suffix"? Consequently, the prohibition "not a suffix" (*apratyayaḥ*) would not apply to what ends in a suffix. This is not a fault; for that prohibition applies in the context of a rule prescribing a technical name, and this is not a rule prescribing a technical name. What then? It is a rule prescribing a prohibition.

Now, for what purpose is this prohibition of non-suffixes stated, given that in the subsequent sūtra the mention of *kṛt* and *taddhita* will serve as a restrictive rule (*niyama*)—namely, "only that which ends in a *kṛt* or *taddhita* suffix receives the designation *prātipadika*, not that which ends in any other suffix," such as *kāṇḍe* or *kuḍye*? This is not so; for if this prohibition were absent, then by the principle "in a rule prescribing a technical designation (*saṃjñā*), when a suffix is mentioned, there is no inclusion of what ends with it (*tadantavidhi*)," the designation *prātipadika* would apply only to the *kṛt* and *taddhita* suffixes themselves, and not to that which ends in them.
And the inclusion of "that which ends in this" (tadanta) is desired for the sake of assigning the technical designation of *prātipadika* to forms such as *bhicchillūḥpūḥ*.

Although the prohibition [of the *prātipadika* designation] would apply when a suffix (*pratyaya*) follows, we shall demonstrate in the subsequent sūtra how the designation of *prātipadika* is nevertheless obtained for that which ends in a *kṛt* or *taddhita* suffix.

Now, one might object: "In the cases of *kāṇḍe* and *kuḍye*, the designation of *prātipadika* applies to the base even before [the addition of] the case ending; and once the single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) with the case ending has been made, since the base retains its status as a *prātipadika* by virtue of the rule regarding what precedes and follows (*antādivadbhāva*), the shortening would indeed apply even if the condition 'not being followed by a suffix' (*apratyaya-grahaṇa*) were not stated. This is not so.

It will not [apply] by virtue of the force of the inclusion of the term *apratyaya* (not a suffix); otherwise, the inclusion of *apratyaya* would be purposeless. The double prohibition—stating "not a root (*adhātuḥ*) and not a suffix (*apratyayaḥ*)"—is for the sake of dispelling the suspicion that this might be a genitive *tatpuruṣa* compound. If it were stated simply as "not a root-suffix" (*adhātupratyayaḥ*), there would be a suspicion that it is a genitive *tatpuruṣa*: namely, "that which does not belong to a suffix of a root. In this case, the rule "in other instances where a suffix is mentioned in a technical definition (*saṃjñā-vidhi*), there is no extension to what ends with it (*tadanta-vidhiḥ*)" does not apply;
because this statement is made when a prohibition has already been reached by the term *apratyaya*.
The term "non-affix" (*apratyaya*) is stated as a prohibition against that which ends in an affix.

Bearing in mind that, therefore, wherever there is a prohibition of a technical name (*saṃjñā*), this [present rule] being commenced applies only to that which ends in such [an affix], he says: "Because of the exclusion (*paryudāsa*) of 'non-affix' in the preceding sūtra, [the name applies] to that which ends in a *kṛt*-affix," and so forth. Now, for what purpose is the mention of "compound" (*samāsa*)? Since a compound possesses meaning, its technical name would be established by the previous rule alone; to this he replies: "Of meaningful aggregates," and so forth.

This is a genitive of specification (*nirdhāraṇa-ṣaṣṭhī*). The mention of "compound" (*samāsa*) is for the purpose of restriction, so that the designation of *prātipadika* may apply specifically to a meaningful compound among those collections of sounds that possess meaning. If this were the case, would not a meaningful collection consisting of a base and an affix fail to receive the designation of *prātipadika*—as in *bahupaṭavaḥ* and *uccakaiḥ*? What is the fault here? [The answer is: In the rule *citaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.1.157), it is stated that "the *cit* [ending] applies to a base along with its [preceding] element for the sake of the suffixes *bahu* and *kac*."
This is established by the explicit statement (*vacana*): "The acute accent (*citsvara*) is prescribed with the inclusion of the *prakṛti*.

In the case of *bahupaṭavaḥ*, once the suffix *bahu-c* has been applied, if the designation *prātipadika* were not [granted], then—due to the absence of *prātipadika* status—the production of the case-ending (*sub*) would not occur; and even if the case-ending had been produced, it would not be subject to elision (*luk*) by [Pāṇini 2.4.71].
Consequently, in *bahupaṭavaḥ*, the accent would fall on the vowel of the *jas* ending, whereas it is desired that it fall on the vowel *u*.

However, when it is a nominal stem (*prātipadika*), after the elision (*luk*) of the previously produced case-ending has occurred, whatever other case-ending subsequently arises does not become part of the base (*prakṛti*), because it occurs at a time subsequent to the production of the suffix *bahuc*. Therefore, setting aside that [subsequent ending], the preceding portion alone becomes the bearer of the accent (*svarabhāk*).
Consequently, the accentuation of the vowel *u* is established.

In the case of *uccakaiḥ*, since it lacks the status of a nominal stem (*prātipadika*), the case ending would not arise from the entire complex [stem + suffix]. And if that [case ending] were absent, the status of being a word (*padatva*) would not exist.

Consequently, in the expression *uccakaiḥ paṭhati*, the low-pitched accent (*nighāta*) prescribed by the rule *tiṅṅatiṅaḥ* [Pāṇini 8.1.28] would not occur. Therefore, should it not be stated that the designation of "nominal stem" applies to the entire complex of base and suffix? It need not be stated, because the restriction applies to those of the same class; thus, only those of the same class are excluded by the restriction.

And that which is of the same class [as the compound] is a collection of sentences (*vākya-samudāya*) distinct from a collection of nominal stems ending in case-suffixes (*subanta*), not a collection of bases and suffixes (*prakṛti-pratyaya*).

Therefore, this suffix *tas* will not effect an exclusion by way of restriction; this is not so, for there are also compounds consisting of a collection of both items ending and not ending in case-suffixes, such as *prakartā* and *prakāraka*.

For here, according to the rule "there is a prescription for the compounding of prefixes (*gati*), agents (*kāraka*), and secondary words (*upapada*) with *kṛt*-derivatives prior to the arising of case-endings" (Vyāḍi, Pāṇini-vṛtti 138), a word ending in a case-ending that functions as a prefix or an agent is compounded with a *kṛt*-derivative that does not itself end in a case-ending; thus, this compound would be a collection of both a word ending in a case-ending and one not ending in a case-ending. Consequently, if the restriction were understood to apply even to items of the same class [namely, those ending in case-endings], then the designation of "nominal stem" (*prātipadika*) would not apply to *bahupaṭavaḥ* or *uccakaiḥ*.

Thus, the activity of the Teacher indicates that the designation *prātipadika* applies to the aggregate consisting of both base and suffix; for this reason, he teaches the prohibition of that which ends in a suffix by stating "not a suffix" (*apratyaya*). Regarding the term "in the neuter gender" (*napuṃsakaliṅge*):

it is a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "that whose gender is neuter. Furthermore, that neuter-gendered object should be understood as being of the nature of a substance (*dravya*); for the quality of being neuter belongs to a substance.
"Alo'ntyasya" (P.
1.1.52) is a *paribhāṣā* rule. In the word "grāmaṇīḥ," the suffix *kvip* is applied according to the rule "satsūdviṣa... (P. 3.2.61), etc.
The substitution of *ṇ* occurs by virtue of the supplementary rule (*upasaṃkhyāna*) "and after *agra* and *grāma*" (Kāśikā Vārttika 5064).

In the cases of *kāṇḍe* and *kuḍae*, because of the prohibition "that which is not a suffix" (*apratyayaḥ*), the designation of *prātipadika* does not apply; therefore, the shortening of the vowel does not take place. Now, one might object: since the single substitute for both a *prātipadika* and a non-*prātipadika* is treated as being like the final element of the former and the initial element of the latter, it is included under the term *prātipadika*; consequently, when the term *prātipadika* is employed [in the rule], the shortening would still apply. To this, he replies: "By the force of the employment of the term *prātipadika*," and so forth.

The point here is that if there were the state of having an end (i.e., if the term were finite), the mention of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) would be purposeless, because there would be nothing to exclude. Regarding the statement, "‘Strī’ refers to the inclusion of feminine suffixes," he states the reason for this as "because of its being marked with a svarita accent.
Since the svarita accent is applied to the mention of ‘strī’ here, comprehension arises through the principle of "governance by what is marked with a svarita" (*svaritenādhikāraḥ*).

With reference to the rule *tena* [Pāṇini 4.1.3], there is the inclusion of those suffixes such as *aṭ* and others that have been prescribed; it does not refer to a mere word denoting the feminine meaning, nor to the specific form of the word *strī* itself. To clarify that the term *upasarjana* (subordinate element) is a qualifier for both, he says: "of a subordinate *go*, of a subordinate feminine suffix," and so forth.

To further clarify the rule beginning with "of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) by means of those two," he says: "of that which ends in a subordinate word *go*," and so forth. The analysis of the compound is: "that of which a subordinate word *go* is the final member."

Thus, when there is *tadantavidhi* (the application of a grammatical rule to that which ends with a specified element) for a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) by means of a subordinate term (*upasarjana*) and a feminine suffix (*strīpratyaya*), as in *goḥ kulam* → *gokulam* and *rājñaḥ kumāryāḥ putraḥ* → *rājakumārīputraḥ*, the shortening of the vowel does not occur for the word *go-* and the word *kumārī-*. Otherwise, it would occur here as well. For in these cases, the word *go-* and the word *rājakumārī-* indeed possess the status of a subordinate term (*upasarjanatva*); this is the intended meaning. [The example] is *citraguḥ*.

The term *go* receives the designation of *upasarjana* by the rule *prathamānirdiṣṭam* [Pāṇini 1.2.43], whereas in cases such as *niṣkośāmbiḥ*, it does so by the rule *ekavibhakti cāpūrva* [Pāṇini 1.2.44]. Regarding *atitantrīḥ*: the root *tatri* is listed in the Dhātupāṭha (1678) with the meaning "to support a family"; by the rule *idito num* [Pāṇini 7.1.58], the augment *num* is added; and by the rule *avitṛstṛtantrībhyaḥ* [Daiva-nighaṇṭu 1.82], the suffix *i* is applied, resulting in *tantrīḥ*.
From the root *lakṣ* in the sense of "seeing" or "marking" (*dhātupāṭha* 1538), with the augment *muṭ* and the suffix *ī* according to *lakṣermuṭ ca* (*Aṣṭādhyāyī* 4.1.84), we have *lakṣmīḥ*.
From the root *śriñ* in the sense of "service" (*dhātupāṭha* 897), with the suffix *kvip* according to *kvibvacipracchi* etc. (*Vārttika* 288), and the lengthening of the vowel, we have *śrīḥ*.

The compound *atyādayaḥ krāntyādyarthe dvitīyayā* (Vārttika 91) is a *prādi-samāsa*. If the word *strī* is taken to mean "affixes prescribed under the heading of *strī*," then, because of the rule *pratyayagrahaṇe yasmāt sa vihitastadādestadantasya* (Bhāṣya Sūtra 7), which implies the inclusion of the ending [of the base], the shortening of the vowel would not be established in the case of *atirājakumārī*; for the affix *ṅīp* is not prescribed after the word *rājakumāra*, but rather after the word *kumāra*. This, however, is not a fault.

This technical rule (*paribhāṣā*) is established in the sūtra *yasmātpratyayavidhistadādi* [Pāṇini 1.4.13]. In that context, the term *vā* ("optionally") is understood to carry over from *vā'ṅgasya* [Pāṇini 1.4.5], and this is recognized as a restricted option (*vyavasthitavibhāṣā*).
Consequently, because it is a restricted option, this rule does not apply in certain instances at all.

Alternatively—the particle *ca* (and) is carried over from [Pāṇini 1.2.46], and it serves the purpose of including what has not been explicitly mentioned; therefore, there is no fault, as shortening will also occur in cases such as *atirājakumārī*. Regarding the statement "there is a prohibition in the case of a Bahuvrīhi compound ending in *īyas-"*: this means that there is a prohibition for a feminine suffix prescribed after a stem ending in *īyas-* when it occurs at the end of a Bahuvrīhi compound. How, then, is this obtained? It is obtained through the continued application of the term *vibhāṣā* (optionally) from [Pāṇini 1.2.36]: *vibhāṣā chandasi*.
And there is no over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) in this case, because the *vibhāṣā* (optional rule) is established as restricted. Regarding the form *bahuśreyasī*:

since it means "most praiseworthy," the suffix *īyasun* is applied by the rule *dvivacanavibhajyopapade tarabīyasunau* [Pāṇini 5.3.57]. By the rule *praśasyasya* [Pāṇini 5.3.60], the word *praśasya* undergoes the substitution of *śra-* when followed by the suffix *īyasun*; thus, there is the state of being treated like the original base (*prakṛtivadbhāva*). Then, the feminine suffix *ṅīp* is added by [the rules] *ṭiḍḍhāṇañ...*, *jāteśca*, etc. [Pāṇini 4.1.15, 6.3.45].

In the case of *bahuśreyasī* (meaning "one who has many excellent things"), the suffix *kap* does not apply by virtue of the rule *nadyutaśca* [Pāṇini 5.4.153]; this is because the suffix *kap* is prohibited by the rule *īyasaśca* [Pāṇini 5.4.156]. The term *adarśanam* [Pāṇini 1.1.59] refers to *luk* (elision), and that is an absence (*abhāva*). Since priority and posteriority (*paurvāparya*) are not possible in the case of an absence, the word *luki* here must be understood as a locative absolute (*sati-saptamī*), not as a locative of sequence (*parasaptamī*). Keeping this in mind, he says: "when there is the elision of the taddhita suffix."
Regarding the term *pañcendra*:

after the compound is formed by [Pāṇini 2.1.51] *taddhitārtha* etc., the suffix *aṇ* is applied by [4.2.24]; this *aṇ* is elided by [4.1.88], and the suffix *ṅīṣ* prescribed by [4.1.49] *indravaruṇa* etc. is elided by the present rule (*luk*).
When that [suffix] has ceased, the suffix *ānuk* also ceases, according to the principle that "when one of two things taught as being dependent on each other is removed, both are removed."

Regarding "pañcaśaṣkuliḥ": by the rule *adhyardhapūrvadvigor lug asaṃjñāyām* [Pāṇini 5.1.28], there is elision (*luk*) of the suffix *ṭhak*, which is prescribed in the sense of "bought with that" (*tena krītam*) for the secondary derivative (*ārhīya*). Regarding "āmalakam": [this is formed by the same process].
The suffix *mayaṭ* is applied according to [Pāṇini 4.3.144], "The fruit of *āmalakī* is a derivative (*vikāra*). As before, there is elision (*luk*).

*Śaṣkulī*, *badarī*, *āmalakī*, and *kuvalī*—these end in the feminine suffix *ṅīṣ* because they are included in the *gaurādi* group. Regarding "*gārgīkulam*" (the family of Gārgī): [it is formed by adding the patronymic suffix *yañ* to *garga*, followed by *ṅīp* to form *gārgī*, and then the neuter suffix *aṇ* to denote the family].

From the word *garga*, by the rule *yañaśca* [Pāṇini 4.1.16], the suffix *ṅīp* is applied; by [the rule] *yaṅścāp* [Pāṇini 6.4.148], there is the elision of the vowel *a*; and by [the rule] *halastaddhitasya* [Pāṇini 6.4.150], there is the elision of the letter *y*. Thus, *gārgyāḥ kulam* (“the family of Gārgī”) is a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*), with the elision of the genitive case-ending. Because the word *gārgī* is mentioned in the nominative case in the rules governing compounds, it possesses technical *upasarjana*-status (subordinate status). However, in the original examples [of the Mahābhāṣya], such as *indranī* and others, there is only the worldly sense of *upasarjana*-status.
Since both types of application are possible in this science, the worldly sense of being non-primary is here what constitutes *upasarjana*-status.
In common worldly usage, that which is subordinate is called *upasarjana*.
In the expression "O Gārgī," the word *gārgī* possesses precisely this worldly status of being subordinate. This is also seen in the cases of "Avantī," "Kuntī," and "Kurūḥ."
The feminine descendant of Avantī is a *gotra* name; the feminine descendant of Kunti is a *gotra* name—by [Pāṇini 4.1.171].
The feminine descendant of Kuru—by [Pāṇini 4.1.172], the suffix *ṇya* is applied.
By [Pāṇini 4.1.176], there is elision (*luk*). From the words *Avanti* and *Kunti*, by [Pāṇini 4.1.65], the suffix *ṅīṣ* is applied.

From the word *kuru*, the suffix *ūṅ* is applied by the rule *ūṅutaḥ* [Pāṇini 4.1.66]. Here, since both the suffix *ṅīṣ* and *ūṅ* denote the secondary meaning (*taddhitārtha*)—namely, a female descendant of the *gotra* lineage—the condition of being a subordinate member (*upasarjana*) does not exist in the worldly sense. Nor does it exist in the technical (*śāstrīya*) sense, because the rule for compound formation (*samāsa-śāstra*) applies only to elements not designated as the first member (*aprathamā-nirdiṣṭa*). Thus, we have the form *paṅgoṇiḥ*.

When the compound is formed by [Pāṇini 2.1.50] *taddhitārtha*, the suffix *ṭhak* is applied according to [4.3.128] *ārhīyaḥ*; its elision (*luk*) occurs as before. Regarding the statement "the rule *it* is a split of the yoga (*yogavibhāga*)," it means as follows: [the word *it* is separated from the preceding rule].
The inclusion of *it* here is indeed the indicator (*liṅga*).

For instance, if the rule were simply *goṇī*, with the term *hrasva* (short vowel) being understood by way of anuvṛtti from the previous rule, then once shortness is applied, the form *pañcagoṇiḥ* would be established perfectly well; what then would be the purpose of including *it*? This inclusion of *it*, being made, is understood as being for the sake of a *yogavibhāga* (splitting the rule). [Objection:

But surely there would be only the anuvṛtti of *luk* (elision) from the immediately preceding rule, not of *hrasva*. [Response: This is not so; for if *luk* were to be carried over, this present rule would be purposeless, since the elision is already established by the immediately preceding rule itself.
Therefore, only the mention of *hrasva* (short vowel) is carried over, not the mention of *luk* (elision). As in the example "pañcasūciḥ," it is similar to "pañcagoṇiḥ.
If a formal separation of the rules (*yogavibhāga*) were made, there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).
Since this [rule] would also apply excessively to other cases, he says "And that," etc.
If the substitution of *it* were to occur everywhere solely by virtue of the preceding rule, then the mention of "of *goṇī*" would be purposeless.
Therefore, because of the inclusion of the exclusion of *agoṇī*, this [rule] does not have universal application.
Therefore, this separation of the yoga (yogavibhāga) applies only to the case of the needle (sūcī) and not to other cases.
The inclusion of the marker *t* (taparakaraṇa) is for the purpose of excluding the long vowel;
for making a long vowel long would be purposeless.

If it is argued that, therefore, the long vowel will not occur even without the addition of *ta* (the *tapara* marker), we say no; for the purpose of making the vowel long is to prevent the short vowel from being substituted.

If it is further argued that since "an *aṇ* being taught (*bhāvyamāna*) does not include its homogeneous counterparts (*savarṇa*)," the state of having *ta* as a marker (*taparatva*) is unnecessary to exclude the short vowel, we say no; because that [short vowel] is not what is being taught.
For "being taught" (*bhāvyamānatva*) consists in the prescription of something previously unestablished.

Nor is there an injunction for something previously unestablished here; for, since elision (*luk*) and shortening (*hrasva*) would otherwise apply, that very long vowel *ī* is reintroduced by this rule. Therefore, the use of the phoneme *t* as a marker (*taparakaraṇa*) must be made. This [rule] is commenced because gender and number would otherwise apply to the denoted object (*abhidheya*).
The term *lupi* refers to the non-perception (*adarśana*) of an affix, and that [non-perception] is of the nature of non-existence (*abhāva*).
Furthermore, it is impossible to effect an extension (*atideśa*) of the functions of gender and number (*vyaktivacana*) in the case of non-existence.

Therefore, considering that the meaning of the affix which has been elided by the technical designation *lup* is intended to be expressed by the word *lup*, he says: "In the case of *lupi*, [it means] 'by the technical designation *lup*'," and so forth.
But how is this obtained, given that this designation refers to the non-appearance of the suffix (*pratyaya*) and not to the meaning of the suffix? It is due to association (*sāhacarya*).

For where there is elision (*lup*) of the suffix, the meaning of the suffix must necessarily be present. Thus it is said: "By the rule *yuktavat*, the meaning of the base (*prakṛti*) is expressed by the past passive participle suffix *ktavatu*."
Regarding this, he states the reason with the words "for that," and so forth.
"Connects" (*yunakti*) means he relates [them], that is to say, he makes them related to itself by means of a relationship characterized as the qualifier-qualified (*viśeṣaṇa-viśeṣya*) relation.

In that context, the meaning of the suffix (*pratyaya*), such as "the dwelling place of that" (*tasya nivāsaḥ*), is the qualified (*viśeṣya*), while the meaning of the base (*prakṛti*), such as the word "Pañcāla," is the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*).
Therefore, by means of what was previously understood—the exclusion of another owner—the meaning of the suffix is qualified. Regarding the phrase "Or else" (*atha vā*) and so forth:

previously, when the suffix *ktavat* was applied to the root *yuj* (Dhātupāṭha 1444), the form *yuktavat* was demonstrated; now, he demonstrates the form *yuktavat* again when the suffix *vati* is applied to that same root after the suffix *kta*.

Although, because a relationship is mutual, just as the meaning of the base (*prakṛti*) is connected with the meaning of the suffix (*pratyaya*), so too the meaning of the suffix is connected with the meaning of the base; nevertheless, since the extension (*atideśa*) of the gender and number associated with the meaning of the suffix would be purposeless [if applied to the base], it is understood that here the word *yukta* intends the meaning of the base itself. Thinking thus, he says: "The meaning of the base is connected. [He explains:
"The suffix *-vat* is used in the sense of the locative case (*saptamī*)."

Because of the indication by the locative case in the word *lupi*. The word *vyakti* (individual) also occurs in senses such as "manifestation," while the word *vacana* (number) occurs in senses such as "speaking"; therefore, so that there might not be a misunderstanding of those [other meanings], he says: "*vyaktivacane*" (in the individual and the number).
But what is the reason for relying on the terminology of the former teachers? To this he says: "*tadīyam*" (their own), etc. Why is this so? To this he says: "*tathā ca*" (and thus), etc.
The sense is that it is not logical to reject one's own [position]. Regarding "the Pañcālas are Kṣatriyas":

when there is the intention to express "many descendants of Pañcāla," the suffix [añ] is applied by Pāṇini 4.1.168; then, by 2.4.62, *tadrājasya bahuṣu tenaivāstriyām*, there is elision (*luk*) of that suffix. The phrase "the country inhabited by them" is connected with the upcoming term "of the Pañcālas."
"The country inhabited by the Pañcālas" — here, by [Pāṇini 4.2.81], there is elision (*luk*). From the word *kuru*, in the sense of "descendant," the suffix *ṇya* is applied by [Pāṇini 4.1.172].
From words such as *matsya* and others, the suffix *aṇ* is applied in the sense of offspring by [Pāṇini 4.1.168] *dvyañmagadha* etc.;

the rest is as before. Regarding "salted soup" (*lavaṇaḥ sūpaḥ*): [it means] "mixed with salt," and thus the suffix *iṣṭhak* is applied by [Pāṇini 4.4.1] *prāgvahatīṣṭhak*; then, by [Pāṇini 4.4.24] *tasya*, there is elision (*luk*) of that suffix.
In this case, the gender and number are the same as those of the referent (*abhidheya*).

For example, in the expression "the village not far from the *śirīṣa* trees" (*śirīṣāṇām adūrabhavo grāmaḥ*), the word *śirīṣāḥ* [is used]. Here, the suffix *aṇ* is applied by Pāṇini 4.2.70, and that suffix is elided by 4.2.82.
The inclusion of the term "expressive of an individual" (*vyaktivacana*) serves as the result [of this rule].
If "expressive of an individual" were not stated, then the status of being a tree (*vanaspatitva*) that exists in *śirīṣa* trees would also be extended by analogy (*atideśa*) to the village.

Consequently, in the expression *śirīṣavanam*, the substitution of *ṇ* for *n* (*ṇatva*) would undesirably apply according to Pāṇini 8.4.6: *vibhāṣauṣadhivanaspatibhyaśca*. [An example of the correct usage is: *harītakyaḥ phalāni* ("the fruits are *harītakī*").
The word *harītakī* ends in the feminine suffix *ṅīṣ*, as seen under the *gaurādi* group following the rule for *pippalī* and others.
From that, the suffix *añ* is applied by the rule *phale vikāre* (Pāṇini 4.3.136), which is then elided by the rule *tasya* (Pāṇini 4.3.167).

In this case, only the individual object (*vyakti*) undergoes the treatment of being like the base (*yuktavadbhāva*), while the number (*vacana*) remains according to what is expressed (*abhidheyavat*).
And this is obtained through the recurrence of the mention of *vibhāṣā* and by understanding it as an established option (*vryavasthitavibhāṣā*); for example:
"the thickets are forests" (*khalatikaṃ vanāni*). Here, the suffix *aṇ* [is applied] according to Pāṇini 4.2.70, and its elision (*lup*) occurs according to 4.2.82.

In this case, only the number (*vacana*) undergoes the treatment of being like that which possesses gender (*yuktavadbhāva*), whereas the individual (*vyakti*) remains exactly as it was in the denoted object (*abhidheyavat*).

This too is obtained just as before. Previously, because the gender and number residing in the meaning of the base (*prakṛti*) are extended (*atideśa*) to the meaning of the elided suffix (*lub-artha*), the extension of the individual and the number to qualifiers such as *ramaṇīya* and so forth is already established.

Although the grounds for the application (*pravṛttinimitta*) of the qualifiers are distinct, nevertheless, even though they differ, that very meaning of the *lu* suffix—which has been extended to denote the individual instances (*atideśavyaktivacana*)—is what is expressed by those [words] as they function therein. Therefore, since the expression of gender and number is already established through that [meaning] itself, this statement is intended to prohibit the [expression of] the genus (*jāti*). For example: *godauramaṇīyau*.
For there is a place named Godau; in the sense of "a village situated not far from those two," the suffix *aṇ* is applied.
By [Pāṇini 4.2.82], there is elision (*lup*) of that [suffix]. Thus: "Pañcāla is a country" (*janapada*) and "Godau is a village" (*grāma*).
Here, the words *janapada* and *grāma* denote a genus (*jāti*).

Since that very meaning of *lub* (elision) is expressed by those two [terms] through the form of a genus (*jāti*), those two [terms] would also be subject to the rule for "speaking of an individual" (*vyaktivacana*) as if they were like [the word itself]. Therefore, there is the prohibition: "of the genus" (*jāteḥ*). Regarding the phrase "of the meaning of the genus" (*jātyarthasya*) and so forth:

the meaning of a genus-word is the "meaning of the genus"; this prohibition of the treatment as if like [the word itself] (*yuktavadbhāva-pratiṣedha*) applies to that [meaning] by means of the term "not of a genus" (*ajāteḥ*), and not to the genus-word itself—this is the meaning.
What is established by this? To this he says: "By that," and so forth.

When the application of gender and number (yuktavadbhāva) to a meaning is prohibited, then just as a genus-word (*jātiśabda*) applying to that meaning does not take on its gender and number, so too the application of gender and number would not occur for its qualifiers either—such as in *bahvannam* ("much food") and the like—because words such as *ramaṇīya* ("pleasant") are not genus-words. The mention of the "door" (*dvāra*) is because a genus-word functions in the sense of the elided suffix (*lub-artha*), whereas qualifiers of the genus do not function directly in the sense of the elision.
For those [words] directly qualify the genus (*jāti*) itself.
When that [genus] is qualified, the meaning of the elision (*lup*) is also understood as being qualified; thus, by means of the genus, they become qualifiers of that [meaning of the *lup*].
This is expressed in the rule: "when there is *lup* of the suffix denoting 'human' (*manuṣya-lupi*)."

Regarding that which has the characteristic of a human (*manuṣyalakṣaṇa*), there is a prohibition of the treatment as if it were a compound (*yuktavadbhāva*) for its qualifiers. And this [prohibition] is obtained through the continued application of the term *vibhāṣā* (optionally), understood as a fixed option (*vyavasthitavibhāṣā*).
For example: "handsome like a scarecrow" (*cañcābhirūpaḥ*).
The suffix *kan* is applied according to Pāṇini 5.3.96 (*cañceva manuṣyaścañcā*), and its elision is effected by Pāṇini 5.3.98 (*lum manuṣye*). Thus,
the qualifiers such as "handsome" (*abhirūpaḥ*) take the gender and number of the thing they denote.
Regarding the word *vardhrikā*:
as before, the suffix *kan* and its elision (*lup*) apply. "That [usage] need not be taught" is the proposition; "because names are authoritative" is the reason.
Since words such as *pañcāla*, which have become conventional names, possess authority, therefore that [usage] need not be taught.
Furthermore, the status of being a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇatva*) is characterized by cognition.

All words indeed possess this status as a valid means of knowledge with respect to their own respective objects; and when it is said [of them], a distinction is understood therein: namely, that they convey their own meaning even when they differ in gender and number from the gender and number inherent in the denotatum (*abhidheya*).
For this very reason, he says: "For proper names (*saṃjñāśabda*) have various genders and numbers."
"Regarding the term *pramāṇa*:
the meaning is that *pramāṇa* refers to those words which convey [a meaning] or denote [it].

In this regard, one might think: "These words, such as *Pañcāla* and so forth, are not merely conventional names (*saṃjñāśabda*); rather, they are based on etymological derivation (*yoganimittaka*). To address this, he says: "*Pañcālā varaṇāḥ*," and so on.
Words whose basis is a connection (*yoga*) are *yoga-śabdas*.

For words such as "Pañcāla" do not apply to a country and so forth by virtue of a connection with the Kṣatriyas and others; rather, these are proper names (*saṃjñā*) for the countries and so forth. If these are proper names, then what follows? To this he says: "In that case, gender and number," and so on. This means they are not subject to grammatical prescription (*aśiṣya*).
