Why is this so? Because the gender and number of nouns of appellation are established by their very nature; therefore, he says "just as," and so forth.

Even for a single drop of water, the feminine noun *ap* is used in the plural; even for a single woman, the masculine noun *dāra* is used in the plural; and for a single house, the masculine noun *gṛha* is used in the plural; even for a single grain of sand, the feminine noun *sikatā* is used in the plural; and the word *varṣāḥ*, though referring to a specific period of time, occurs as a feminine plural.

Therefore, just as these words beginning with *ap* possess an inherent gender and number, so too do words such as *pañcāla*; thus, there is no purpose for the rule concerning the treatment of [names] like those that possess [their own] meaning (*yuktavat*).

If this is so, why was it stated previously? It was for the purpose of indicating the scope of the prohibition; for indeed, a prohibition cannot be made or understood if its scope has not been specified. Regarding the phrase "because the connection is not manifest" (*yogaprakhyānāt*): "connection" (*yoga*) refers to the relationship between a country and the Kṣatriyas and so forth; the meaning is "because that [connection] is not manifest," i.e., because it is not perceived.

For those words whose basis is a connection (*yoga*) denote the connection and then apply to the substance (*dravya*) possessing that connection; from such words, the connection is apprehended—just as, for example, from words like *daṇḍin* ("staff-bearer").

However, no such connection is apprehended from [words like] *Pañcāla* and so forth, in the same way that a connection is apprehended from words like *daṇḍa*. Therefore, these are not words based on connection; to this he says: "Not indeed," and so forth.
"Is made known" (*prakhyāyate*) means it is spoken of, it is manifested, or, in other words, it becomes an object of cognition.

Since the connection "the Pañcālas [are called] Varaṇā" is not perceived in this way, for that very reason we do not apprehend that the city is called "Varaṇā" due to its association with trees; what then? These are proper names whose grounds for application (*pravṛttinimitta*) are not required. If these are indeed proper names, he asks "What follows from that? and says: "Therefore, in this case," and so forth. The meaning has already been explained.

But surely, for the sake of deriving technical names (*saṃjñā*), a secondary suffix (*taddhita*) is indeed produced even for words, as in *hastī* [Pāṇini 5.2.133] and *kambalyam* [Pāṇini 5.1.3]. Why, then, is it said here that "the secondary suffix is not produced by [the rules] 4.2.69 and 4.2.70"? True, a secondary suffix is produced for the sake of deriving technical names. But where is it produced? It is produced where there exists a distinction created by the audible form (*śruti*). Since no such distinction exists here when the secondary suffix is elided (*lup*), the secondary suffix is not produced. [This refers to the rule] "when the application [of a term] is the authority" (*yogapramāṇe*).
The "measure of connection" (*yogapramāṇa*) is that by which the connection is made known;
furthermore, in this context, it refers to words such as *pañcāla* because they are the subject under discussion.

For, according to the view of others, such a word denotes a country or the like only after having denoted its own primary cause of application—the connection with the *pañcālas* and so forth—and not without having denoted it.
Therefore, the meaning is that the indicator (*pratyāyaka*) is the denoter (*vācaka*) of the connection (*yoga*).

"In its absence, there would be no perception" means that whatever is caused by a connection is not employed when that connection is absent, just like words such as *daṇḍin* ("staff-bearer") and so forth; this is the intended sense.
Regarding the passage beginning with "For [it is] by means of *yoga* as a means of valid cognition" (*yogapramāṇe hi*), etc.:
by employing the word "for" (*hi*) in the sense of a reason, he shows that the word "and" (*ca*) in the Sūtra functions as a reason.
It might be argued: "It is indeed the case that words such as 'Pañcāla' are not observed when there is an absence of *yoga*"; therefore, he says "And it is observed," etc.
The meaning has already been explained. Regarding the phrase "because it has another means of valid cognition" (*anyapramāṇatvāt*):

that whose cause for comprehension is another means of valid cognition—namely, that which is characterized by the expression of an object—is "that which has another means of valid cognition" (*anyapramāṇa*); the state of being such is "having another means of valid cognition" (*anyapramāṇatva*). As for the statement, "in a compound, some word is primary": [this refers to the fact that in a *tatpuruṣa* compound, the final member is predominant].
Just as in the word *rājapuruṣa*, [the term] "puruṣa" [is the subordinate member]. Regarding the phrase "the principal and the subordinate," and so forth:
in the compound *rājapuruṣa*, as before, the former is the subordinate (*upasarjana*) and the other is the principal (*pradhāna*).
And they state this together with the primary meaning:
"the base and the suffix," and so forth.
However, [the analysis] is impossible because there are infinite varieties.
For instance: when the *bahuvrīhi* compound "citraguḥ" (one who has brindled cows) is formed, an object other than the quality (*guṇa*) and the possessor of the quality (*guṇin*) is expressed.

Here, the word for the quality—the term "brindled" (*citra*)—is subordinate because it is a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*); the word for the possessor of the quality—the term "cow" (*go*)—is primary because it is the qualificand (*viśeṣya*).
In some cases, an object other than the two subordinates is denoted, as in "plakṣanyagrodhau" (the *plakṣa* and the *nyagrodha* trees).

For instance, not only do the base (*prakṛti*) and the suffix (*pratyaya*) together express the meaning of the suffix, but in some cases they also express the meaning of the base, as in the case of self-referential (*svārthika*) suffixes such as *śuklatara* and *śuklatama*.

Similarly, some maintain that by its very nature, the verbal root (*prakṛti*) expresses the primary meaning in verbs—according to the principle that "the verb has action as its primary meaning. Others, however, believe that in verbs it is the meaning of the suffix itself, being the predominant factor, that is expressed in the form of a potentiality (*śakti*), just as in certain instances by means of case-endings (*vibhakti*); but it is not the possessor of the potentiality—the referent (*padārtha*)—which has attained the status of a substance (*dravya*), that is expressed.
Therefore, when there is a connection with another action, another capacity manifests, as in "see the agent.

It is impossible to teach all such infinite varieties of the capacity for denoting meaning; thus, the comprehension of meaning arises solely from worldly usage. To explain how this is known, he says: "By those who... and so forth.

This is easy to understand. Regarding the rule *vibhāṣopayamane* (Pāṇini 1.2.16) in the *Bālamano ramā-vibhāṣopayamana*: from the rule *yamo gandhane* (1.3.28), the word *yamaḥ* is carried over; from *hanaḥ sic* (1.2.14), the word *sic* is carried over; and from *asaṃyogāt* (1.2.5), the word *kit* is carried over. Thus he says: "After the root *yama*, the *sic* affix is optionally *kit* when [the action] refers to marriage."
The meaning is that the word *upayama* is used in the sense of marriage;
"Rāma upāyata Sītām" means he accepted her as his wife.

In the alternative view where the *sic* suffix is marked with the *kit* designation, the *m* is elided by the rule "anudāttopadeśa... (*Pāṇini 6.4.37*), and then the *sic* itself is elided by the rule "hrasvādaṅgāt" (*Pāṇini 6.1.68*). Regarding *udavoḍhā*:
the meaning is that he accepted [her] as his wife.

In the alternative view where the suffix *sic* is treated as having the *kittva* designation, the *makāra* is elided by the rule "anudāttopadeśa... (Pāṇini 6.4.37), and then the *sic* is elided by the rule "hrasvādaṅgāt" (Pāṇini 6.4.103).
Thus we have *udavoḍhā*. As for *udvāha*, it means the formal taking [of a wife] as a spouse.
Regarding the phrase "in the gandharva form of marriage" (gandhanāṅge upayame tu): the meaning is "in a marriage preceded by violence," that is to say,
in the rākṣasa form of marriage.
"Having killed and having split open the heads, one should take [the bride] while she weeps from those who are weeping;
that is the Rākṣasa marriage," according to the Smṛti. [The rule] "there is always kit-ness" applies here.
The phrase "by the preceding sūtra" (*pūrvasūtreṇa*) is to be supplied [to complete the sentence] in the rule *yamo gandhane*.

If this optional rule (*vibhāṣā*) were to apply even to the *upayamana* (marriage) that is a subordinate part of *gandhana* (hinting), then it would be an *aprāptavibhāṣā* (an option regarding what has not otherwise been established).
Consequently, its inclusion among the *aprāptavibhāṣās* in the Bhāṣya on the rule *na veti vibhāṣā* would be contradicted.

Therefore, the sense is that one must resort to the *pūrvavipratiṣedha* (the rule of priority). *Bālamanoramā*: "The statement that the meaning of the primary suffix (*pradhānapratyayārtha*) [is the predominant factor] is [rejected], because the meaning [of a word] has other means of proof" (Pāṇini 1.2.56). Now, as an incidental digression, he refutes another statement formulated by previous teachers: "The meaning of the primary suffix. Regarding "the meaning of the suffix":

the meaning of the statement of the previous teachers—that "with respect to the meaning of the base (*prakṛtyartha*), the meaning of the suffix is the primary [element], i.e., the qualificand (*viśeṣya*), whereas the meaning of the base is its qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*)"—that too [is rejected]. It has already been stated: "because the meaning has other means of proof."
Regarding the question of how this reason is also applicable here, he says: "The word *tulya* (equal) is for the purpose of drawing forward the [previous] reason.

But how does the word *tulya* serve to draw forward the reason? It is thought that *tulyam* is an adverbial modifier of the act of refutation (*pratyākhyāna*); that is, this refutation is equal to the refutation mentioned immediately prior.
And thus it becomes equivalent if that which is its cause is also the cause of this.
Therefore, by the force of the inclusion of the word "equivalent" (tulya), the preceding term "cause" (hetu) is carried over.
Consequently, the word "equivalent" serves the purpose of drawing in the word "cause."
"From improper rising," and so forth.
Rising from bed during the last watch of the night is said to be proper. "Reclining" means sleeping; that too is proper during the first watch of the night.

Thus, the entire day, the last watch of the preceding night, and the first watch of the coming night—this is what is meant by "the present time. Regarding the phrase "a day with both halves of the night" and so forth:
the whole day and both halves of the night [constitute the period].

"Furthermore, according to others, the 'present time' refers to the period between the night that has passed and the night yet to come. By the words "This single entity called birth," etc., [the author] states the purpose for the commencement of the Sūtra.
Now, one might object: "Does number not exist in birth? For it is a property of substance (*dravyadharma*).

Even though that number which is included within the category of qualities (*guṇapadārtha*) as established in the Vaiśeṣika system does not exist there, nevertheless, in our own philosophical view, where "qualities are the differentiators," that number which consists of mere differentiation (*bhedamātra*) certainly exists; thus there is no fault.
Regarding the phrase "the designation of a genus" (*jāterākhyā*): *ākhyāna* is *ākhyā*, meaning communication.
Regarding the phrase "in a single object": [it refers to] one referent.

"A thing denoted by a genus (jātyākhyo 'rthaḥ) [is what is meant by] 'the meaning of a genus (jātyarthaḥ) takes the plural'"; by this he shows that it would not indeed fail to occur after qualifiers of the genus such as *sampanna* and so forth; the intention is that those [words] are not words denoting a genus (*ajātiśabda*).
But how is the plural treatment of the meaning of the genus obtained? Because of the inclusion of the etymological sense (*anvartha*).
Here, "plural" (*bahuvacana*) does not refer to the technical grammatical category of the plural; what then? It refers to the etymological sense.
*Ukti* means expression or speech.

The term *bahuvacana* means "the expression for many. Since the expression for many cannot possibly apply to a single object, by implication the meaning "one who possesses many kinds" (*bahuvid*) is understood with respect to a single object. Thus, in this manner, the sense of a genus (*jāti*) comes to be expressed as plural.
"By that," and so forth.

Since the plural number is prescribed for the meaning of a genus (*jāti*), by that [rule], the plural is justified for qualifiers of a genus when they do not refer to a genus, just like words denoting a genus. For example, "Devadatta":
the word *devadatta* is an arbitrary name (*yadṛcchāśabda*).
By this [term], a single entity that is followed by multiple individuals is not being denoted;
for a genus (jāti) has multiple individuals as its substratum.
Consequently, since there is no such thing as a genus called "Devadattatva," the plural form does not occur here.

[Objection: But surely here, due to the difference in states, the property of being Devadatta has multiple substrata. [Response: This is not so; for if this were the case, the mention of "genus" (*jāti*) would be purposeless, since a genus is possible everywhere.

Therefore, by the force of the mention of "genus," it is understood that only those words recognized in common usage as genus-words are intended here by the term "genus-word. And the word *devadatta* is not recognized in common usage as a genus-word. [As in the example: "A likeness of Kāśyapa is 'Kāśyapa.
Here, *kāśyapa* is derived from "the descendant of Kāśyapa" using the suffix *añ* according to Pāṇini 4.1.104: *anṛṣyānantarye vidādibhyo’ñ*. Thus, it is *kāśyapa*.

From that [word], by the rule *iva-arthe eva-pratikṛtau* [Pāṇini 5.3.96], the suffix *kan* is applied; then, by the rule *lum manuṣye* [Pāṇini 5.3.98], there is elision (*lup*). Thus, it is said: "This is a generic term (*jāti-śabda*)."

According to the rule "The word *gotra* [is used] together with *caraṇas*" (Pāṇini 4.1.63, Mahābhāṣya), this [term] ends in a *gotra* suffix; however, it is not expressed here in the form of a genus (*jāti*). What then? It is an image (*pratikṛti*).
If that is so, then when the intention is to convey a genus, there ought to be a plural form.

And here, it is not the communication of a single genus that is intended; what then? It is the communication of individual representatives. In the expression "rice and barley" (*vrīhi-yavau*), this rule prescribes a plural form when there is a single referent consisting of a genus.
But here, two referents consisting of genera are intended.
The word *vaktavya* means "to be explained. In this regard, the explanation is as follows: the rule *anyatarasyām* is a fixed option (*vyavasthitavibhāṣā*).
Consequently, it will not apply when a numeral is employed.

Alternatively, in the expression "one grain of rice has ripened" (*eko vrīhiḥ sampannaḥ*), the word "one" (*eka*) being employed manifests the oneness of the object denoted by the genus (*jāti*); and that [oneness] is contradicted by plurality.

Therefore, because of the contradiction between oneness and plurality, the treatment as plural (*bahuvadbhāva*) will not occur here. In this case as well, there is an extension of plurality to the meaning (*artha*), according to the rule:
"The meaning which belongs to *asmad* (the first person pronoun) becomes treated as plural."
Therefore, even when a finite verb (*tiṅanta*) occurs there, it takes a plural ending,
as in "we say" (*vayaṃ brūmaḥ*),
and so forth, [even] when [the referent] is singular or dual.

It is appropriate that [the use of the word "we"] occurs when there is oneness; but how can it occur when there is duality? For duality is not possible for the referent of the word "we," since the word "we" has the self (ātman) as its object, and the self is one. This is not a fault; for when "selfhood" is metaphorically attributed to another—as in "this is my second self"—then, because the word "we" applies there as well, it is possible for it to have duality as its object.

Alternatively, according to the rule that "among the pronouns beginning with *tyad*, whichever is subsequent remains," the word *asmad* alone, being what remains, expresses the meaning of *yuṣmad* as well; thus, the occurrence of two meanings is established, and the dual meaning is logical.

Now, if the word *asmad* is employed in the plural, then this [word] has a single referent and not a dual referent; yet if it has a dual referent and not a single referent, how is its application to either a single referent or a dual referent determined? It is determined by context (*prakaraṇa*), just as the word *ārāt* is understood to apply to both the meanings of "far" and "near."
In the word *aham*, the substitution of *ām* occurs by [Pāṇini 7.1.28], and the replacement of *ah* by *ha* occurs by [Pāṇini 7.2.94]. In the word *vayam*, [the same applies].

From *yasi* > [Pāṇini 7.2.91] > [Pāṇini 7.2.93] the substitution of *vay* for *ita*; then [Pāṇini 7.2.90] yields *āvām*. When the suffix *au* is applied, [Pāṇini 7.2.92] provides the substitution of *āv*;
and by [Pāṇini 7.2.88], "and of the first case," etc., the substitution of *āt* occurs.
"It should be stated" means "it should be explained.

As for the explanations: one must rely on the fact that the inclusion of the term *anyatarasyām* (optionally) which follows [from a previous rule] is a restricted option (*vyavasthitavibhāṣā*). This is as in the rule: *yuṣmadi gurāvekeṣām* ("when *yuṣmad* refers to a person of high status, according to some").

This [point] is also included by the sūtra itself because the particle *ca* has the sense of an unexpressed conjunction (*anukta-samuccaya*). As it is said: "The particle *ca* is for the purpose of drawing forward both [terms]. Now, one might object: "There are only two stars in the constellation Phalgunī, and likewise two in Proṣṭhapada; since these are duals, the plural number will apply to them precisely because they are duals. So what is the use of the particle *ca* for the purpose of drawing forward the word 'two'? To this we reply: In that case, this [use of *ca*] makes known that the mention of "constellation" (*nakṣatra*) is intended as an illustration (*upalakṣaṇa*) for luminaries (*jyotis*) in general.
Therefore, this also becomes established: "the Pūrvaphalgunīs have risen" and "the two Pūrvaphalgunīs have risen.

If it were not made known that the mention of "nakṣatra" (lunar mansion) is intended as an indication for "jyotis" (luminary/light), then this [usage] would not occur here; because the status of being a *nakṣatra* for luminaries exists only when there is conjunction with the moon, and not otherwise; at other times, they are merely *jyotis*. Furthermore, in the expression "the Pūrvaphalgunīs have risen," the word *phalgunī* is not used as denoting a *nakṣatra*, but rather as denoting a mere luminary (*jyotis*).

In this context, since the quality of being a *jyotis* (luminous body) exists even in a single [constellation], it is appropriate to include the word "ca" (and) in order to exclude that [single case] and to draw in the term "of two" (*dvayoḥ*).

If, however, the mention of *nakṣatra* were not for the purpose of indicating *jyotis*, then where would it apply? It would apply only here: "Today is Pūrvā Phalgunī," or "Today are the two Pūrvā Phalgunīs.
For indeed, the status of being a *nakṣatra* belongs to the two Phalgunīs here, because they are conjoined with the moon.

Thus it is said: [Pāṇini 4.2.3] the suffix *aṇ* occurs; [Pāṇini 4.2.4] its hearing does not occur because it has been elided. For example: *phalgunyau māṇavike* ("two young girls born under the asterism Phalgunī").
This means "born under the two Phalgunīs."

The suffix *ṭa* is applied by the supplementary rule (*upasaṃkhyāna*) "after *phalgunī* and *āṣāḍhā*, [the suffixes] *ṭā* and *an*" (Vārttika 4.2.35). Then, the feminine suffix *ṅīp* is applied by the rule "after [stems ending in] *ṭi*, *ḍha*, *āṇ*, *añ*, etc. (Pāṇini 4.1.15). Regarding the example "the boys Tiṣya and Punarvasu," the suffix *aṇ* is applied after the words *tiṣya* and *punarvasu* by the rule "after [names of lunar mansions], *aṇ*" (Pāṇini 4.2.3).
By the rule *tasya* [Pāṇini 4.2.4], there is elision (*lup*).

Consequently, for "a boy born under Tiṣya" and "two boys born under Punarvasu," the suffix *aṇ* is applied by the rule *saṃdhivelādi* [Pāṇini 4.3.16] et cetera; this suffix is then elided by the rule *śraviṣṭhāphalgunyanurādhā* [Pāṇini 4.3.34] et cetera.
[The phrase] "so that it may also apply to synonyms" [is stated].
When there is the mention of "nakṣatra" (asterism), this [rule] occurs because of the mention of the actual object (*artha*).
And when there is the mention of "śabda" (word), it has been stated that this *paribhāṣā* applies;
in its absence, it applies to synonyms as well.

Regarding the term *siddhyapunarvasū*: the word *siddhya* is a synonym for *tiṣya*. He demonstrates the analysis of the compound by its constituent parts as: "those for whom *tiṣya* and those two *punarvasū* [are the lords]."
The collective whole, however, should be understood as the meaning of the compound.
Now, regarding the expression *tiṣyapunarvasavaḥ*: it is men whose minds are perverted by a *bahuvrīhi* [interpretation] who speak thus;
consequently, this is not a compound of lunar mansions (*nakṣatra*) at all.

To one who might argue, "In that case, what is the purpose of including the term *dvandva* (copulative compound) for the sake of excluding this [possibility]?", he replies with the words "Tiṣya and so forth" and so on.

Due to the fault of their own description, when perceivers see Tiṣya and the others, they perceive those very Tiṣyas and so forth in a reversed manner; thus, they are expressed by means of a *bahuvrīhi* compound, but they are not [actually] persons.
Therefore, this is indeed a compound of lunar mansions (*nakṣatra-samāsa*).

Regarding the expression *tiṣyapunarvasvidam*: by what rule, then, does it take the singular form (*ekavadbhāva*) here? If one suggests it is by the rule *jātiraprāṇinām* [Pāṇini 2.4.6], that is not correct; for this is a proper name (*saṃjñāśabda*), like the word *devadatta*.
This is not a generic term (*jātiśabda*), for a genus consists of multiple individuals, whereas Tiṣya and so forth do not.

Furthermore, it will be stated: "And when the primary meaning is the genus (*jāti*), this singular treatment (*ekavadbhāva*) applies to substances denoting genera, not when there is an intention to express specific, fixed substances. And here, there is indeed an intention to express specific substances; therefore, the singular treatment is not justified by the rule *jātir aprāṇinām*. Nor is there any other rule for singular treatment [applicable here]. In that case, since Tiṣya and Punarvasu are stars, the dual compound (*dvandvasamāsa*) ought to take the plural ending because of their plurality.
And since the inclusion of the plural number (*bahuvacana*) would otherwise be purposeless, he says: "Every *dvandva* is optionally [singular]," and so forth.
Since this [sūtra] employs the plural number for the sake of precluding the singular, it is understood that there exists this paribhāṣā: "Every *dvandva* is optionally singular" (Vārttika 91).

Therefore, the intention is that the inclusion of the plural here is made for the purpose of precluding the singular. When the *bahuvrīhi* compound "of those having the same form" (*sarūpāṇām*) is formed, the substitution of *sa-* for *samāna-* occurs by the rule "light, country," etc. (Pāṇini 6.3.84).
In this context, the word *rūpa* refers to "intrinsic form" (*svabhāva*).
In the expression “of words that have the same form” (*sarūpāṇāṃ śabdānām*), the genitive case denotes selection (*nirdhāraṇa*).
Therefore, among those having the same intrinsic form, that which is similar in kind and possesses the same form remains as a single [representative], and not that which has a different form.
For selection (*nirdhāraṇa*) occurs only among things of the same class (*samānajātīya*), not among things of different classes (*vijātīya*).
Alternatively, this genitive case denotes a collective whole (*samudāyalakṣaṇā*); and that which falls within a collective whole consisting of similar items is itself similar, not dissimilar.
Therefore, only the similar item remains.
Regarding the term *ekavibhaktau*:
the word *eka* has the meaning of "identical" (*samāna*), as in the example *ekadhana*.
This is a compound formed according to [Pāṇini 2.1.48] *pūrvakālaika*, etc., consisting of the words "this" (*ekā*) and "case-ending" (*vibhakti*).
The same applies here in the rule *ekamekaśeṣaḥ*.

However, in this context, the word *eka* denotes a number (*saṃkhyā*), while the word *śeṣa* expresses a specific state through exclusion (*nivṛtti*), not merely a state of remaining. For this very reason, it is said: "One remains; the others are excluded."
"vṛkṣaśca vṛkṣaśca vṛkṣau" and so forth: this is a *ekaśeṣa* (retention of one) of uninflected forms, because the case ending is not conditioned [by the presence of another word];
for this [operation] is not prescribed by depending upon a subsequent case ending.
The phrase "in a single case-ending" (*ekavibhaktau*) is an indicator of similarity of form (*sārūpya*), not a specification of a cause.
When certain forms are observed following a single case-ending, the *ekaśeṣa* (retention of one) of the nominal stems occurs even while that case-ending has not yet been produced.
Once the *ekaśeṣa* has been performed, the case-ending is subsequently applied.

Alternatively, the *ekaśeṣa* (retention of one) applies only to those forms that include their case-endings. How so? For by the word "vibhakti" (case-ending), the grammatical relation (*kāraka*) is denoted, since it is that by which the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) is divided.

What is thus stated is this: when there are several forms of identical appearance (*sarūpa*) belonging to a single, common, and undivided grammatical relation, the *ekaśeṣa* occurs among those very forms that share a single grammatical relation.

If this is so, then the statement in the *Vṛtti*, "when [the case-ending] follows" (*parataḥ*), would be untenable; for a *kāraka* is a power inherent in the object, and it is not possible for words to have a sequence of priority and posteriority (*paurvāparya*) by means of that [power]. Furthermore, if the *kāraka* were denoted by the word "case-ending" (*vibhaktiśabda*), how could the formation of a single remainder (*ekaśeṣa*) of words accompanied by case-endings be obtained? It is replied: First of all, the statement in the *Vṛtti* is indeed tenable. This word "para" signifies "desired" (*iṣṭa*). Thus, "when [the case-ending] follows in a single case" (*ekavibhaktau parataḥ*) means "when one case-ending is desired. Moreover, this is either a locative of domain (*viṣayasaptamī*) or a locative of existence (*sati-saptamī*).
When one *kāraka* is intended as the locus (*viṣaya*), the seventh case ending (*saptamī*) is optionally used;
that is to say, when one *kāraka* is intended as the locus.
Furthermore, what constitutes an intended *kāraka*? That which is intended to be expressed (*vivakṣita*).

Therefore, because this is intended to be expressed, the *ekaśeṣa* (retention of one) of the case-endings (*vibhakti*) caused by their own respective factors (*kāraka*) is obtained. Furthermore, this *ekaśeṣa* occurs when there is an intention to express coexistence (*sahabhāva*).

This happens only if it is desired to denote the meaning of all [words] simultaneously by means of a single [word]; it does not happen otherwise. Now, an objection might be raised: "The word-meaning (*padārtha*) is the genus (*jāti*), and the genus is indeed one; since the genus is singular, there is no possibility at all for many words [to apply], so what is the purpose of undertaking the rule for *ekaśeṣa*? In response to this challenge, the author—relying on the view that "the substance (*dravya*) is the word-meaning"—states: "For each object" (*pratyartham*), and so forth.

"Pratyartham" means that since the application and occurrence of words is with respect to each individual object (*artha*), there is the denotation of many objects by a single word. In this view, since the denotation of the objects must be performed by each [word] individually, the consequence would be the use of multiple words; as many as those objects are, so many words would have to be employed, yet it is desired that there be only a single word. Therefore, the rule for "retention of one" (*ekaśeṣa*) is commenced. [Question: "What is the purpose of mentioning the term 'form' (*rūpa*)?"
He thinks as follows: if the term *rūpa* (form) were employed, the meaning would have to be understood by following two words, which results in a burden of comprehension (*pratipatti-gaurava*).

When *samānām* (of similar things) is stated, however, the meaning is understood by following a single word, resulting in ease of comprehension (*pratipatti-lāghava*); therefore, should one not simply employ the term *samāna*? [The answer is: the term *rūpa* is used so that [the designation] may apply even when the objects are different.

If the mention of "form" (*rūpa*) were not made, then, because no distinction would be specified, the rule would apply only where the word and its referent are identical—as in *vṛkṣāḥ* and so on—but it would not apply in cases such as *akṣāḥ*, due to the difference in meaning. For instance, the word *akṣa* occurs in the sense of a sense organ, a part of a chariot, and the *bibhītaka* fruit; likewise, the word *pāda* occurs in the sense of a *kārṣāpaṇa* coin, a quarter of a verse, a foot, and a toe; and the word *māṣa* also occurs in the sense of a type of grain and so forth. [The mention of form is made] so that [the rule] does not apply when there is a remainder consisting of two or many [referents].

Now, one might object: "If the singular number is intended in the word *śeṣa* (remainder), then there will be no remainder for two or many [elements]. This is not so; because it is that which is being prescribed here, the *śeṣa* itself is the primary element (*pradhāna*), and the singular number is not intended to be significant with respect to a primary element.

For instance, the technical designation *karman* (object) is established by the rule *kartur īpsitatamaṃ karma* [Pāṇini 1.4.49]; since that which is most desired by the agent is the primary element, the designation *karman* applies to two or many even when the singular number is not intended to be significant.

However, when it is a subordinate element (*guṇa*), number is intended to be expressed (*vivakṣyate*). For example, in the rule *ṅyāpprātipadikāt* [Pāṇini 4.1.1], since the case-endings beginning with *su* (the *svādayaḥ*) are what are being prescribed, they are the primary element (*pradhāna*); whereas the *ṅyāpprātipadika* is the subordinate element. Therefore, in that context, number is intended to be expressed. Consequently, the case-endings are applied only to each individual item. Yet, in accordance with the requirements of the grammatical definition (*lakṣaṇa*), number is sometimes not intended to be expressed even in the case of a subordinate element, as in this very same rule: *sarūpāṇām*.
Therefore, when two similar forms [occur], one remains. [The author says] "let there not be a substitute" (*ādeśo mā bhūt*).
If the term "remainder" (*śeṣa*) were not mentioned, the rule "of similar forms" (*sarūpāṇām*) would be a genitive of location (*sthāna-ṣaṣṭhī*); consequently, there would be a substitution.

And in that case, since the word *āś*—ending in the suffix *kvan* according to the rule *aśū-pruṣi-laṭi-kaṇi-khaṭi-viśibhyaḥ kvan* (Dhātupāṭha 8.125)—is acute on the first syllable due to the *nit*-accent, then in the place of two *āś* words both acute on the first syllable, the substitute would necessarily be one having two initial acute syllables, by virtue of being the closest analogue (*āntaratamya*). [Examples such as] *payaḥ* and so forth [follow].

In the case of *ekaḥ payaḥ śabdaḥ*, the first word ending in the nominative (*prathamānta*) is the agent (*kartṛpada*), while the second ends in the accusative (*dvitīyānta*) and is the object (*karmapada*); thus, because they possess different case endings (*bhinnavibhaktikatva*), they do not have a single subsequent case ending (*naikavibhaktiparatva*), and therefore the rule for a single remainder (*ekaśeṣa*) does not apply. In the example *brāhmaṇābhyām*, the first word *brāhmaṇa* ends in the instrumental (*tṛtīyānta*), whereas the second ends in the dative (*caturthyanta*).

Therefore, even here, there is no identity of case endings. This word *vṛddha* exists as a common (laukika) term, which refers to one who is in the final stage of life; it also exists as a technical (śāstrīya) term [defined by Pāṇini at 1.1.73]; and it exists as a designation of the ancient teachers (*pūrvācārya*), namely: "the descendant whose lineage has become obscured is called *vṛddha*. In that regard, if the common term were taken, then by association with it, the word *yuvan* would also have to be understood as referring exclusively to a common term denoting a specific stage of life; consequently, the rule would undesirably apply to cases such as *ajaśca varkaraśca* ("the goat and the kid"), for the goat (*aja*) is said to be a specific type of animal in its old age, while the young one is the *varkara*.
Now, if the technical (śāstrīya) sense were adopted, then [the term] would also apply in cases such as *aupagavaḥ* and *aupagaviḥ*; having considered this, he says: "The word *vṛddha*," and so forth.
By this, he shows that the mention of *vṛddha* refers to the technical designation established by the former teachers.
But how is this obtained? From the explicit instruction (*upadeśa*).

Alternatively, one might think as follows: although the word *yuva* is conventionally established in common usage (*loka*) as referring to the second stage of life, nevertheless, by the force of the technical rule (paribhāṣā) [Pāṇini 4.1.163], only that which refers to a descendant (*apatya*) is taken here. Therefore, due to its association with that, it is logical that the word *vṛddha* should also be understood as referring specifically to the sense of a descendant.
As for the mention of *gotra*, it was not included for the sake of variety.

Regarding the rule "in the case of speech with a youth" (*yūnā saha vacane*): by the inclusion of the word *saha* ("with"), it is shown that this third case ending (*tṛtīyā*) occurs in connection with the sense of "together" (*sahayoga*).

Therefore, because the third case is prescribed in connection with "being together," it is understood that the formation of a single remainder (*ekaśeṣa*) takes place when there is an intention to express coexistence.

With the words "In the case of identity" (*samānāyām*) and so forth, he shows the scope of that [rule] where the difference arises solely from the cause of the *vṛddha* and *yuvan* suffixes. "Form" (*ākṛti*) is the ground for the application of a word, such as being a *Gārgya* and so on; when that is identical—that is, undifferentiated—where [the forms] differ only through the *vṛddha* and *yuvan* suffixes themselves, and not through anything else such as the base (*prakṛti*), the meaning is that in such a case the difference exists solely due to the cause of the *vṛddha* and *yuvan* suffixes. "And Gārgya," etc. [is the example].

From the words *garga* and *vatsa*, the suffix *yañ* is applied because they belong to the *gargādi* group, resulting in *gārgyaḥ* and *vātsyaḥ*. From these two, the suffix *phak* is applied according to [Pāṇini 4.1.101] for the sake of a younger descendant (*yūnyapatye*), yielding *gāgryāyaṇaḥ* and *vātsyāyanaḥ*. Thus, *gārgyaś ca gāgryāyaṇaś ca* form "the two Gārgyas," and *vātsyaś ca vātsyāyanaś ca* form "the two Vātsyas.
Here, the sense of "younger descendant" is understood through context and other such factors.

Regarding the phrase "and Garga": this word *garga* is a designation for the root-prakṛti (the original progenitor); it does not refer to the elder [descendant], nor to the youth. Regarding the phrase "Gārgya and Vātsyāyana": [these are derived from the respective *gotra* names].
In this case, there is not only a distinction caused by the suffixes for the elder and the younger generation, but also one caused by the base (*prakṛti*).
The word *bhāgavitti* denotes a descendant in the lineage (*gotrāpatya*) and ends in the suffix *iñ* from the word *bhagavitta*. [The rule states: "and *bhāgavittika*."

The suffix *ṭhak* [is applied] by the rule 4.1.148, which follows from 4.1.147 (*bhāgavittī-śabdād-yūni-apatye*) with the word "in a sense of contempt" (*kutsane*) being carried over. This statement is made because the previous rule does not suffice due to the addition of the cause for morphological variation (*vairūpya*) in the feminine meaning.
By the statement "and like the masculine" (*puṃvac-ca*), this is an extension of that designation.
[The word] "feminine" (*strī*).

Is this the mention of a feminine suffix (*strīpratyaya*), or the mention of a word functioning with a feminine meaning (*stryarthavṛttiśabda*), or the mention of the meaning (*arthagrahaṇa*) itself? If it were the mention of a feminine suffix, then by this [rule], only that [suffix] would be set aside—namely, "the feminine suffix becomes as in the masculine"—but the feminine meaning itself would not be set aside. Consequently, in the case of *gārgyaś ca gāgryāyaṇaś ca* (Gārgya and Gāgryāyaṇa), where [the form] *gargāḥ* is derived while the condition *astriyām* ("provided it is not feminine") is still in force, the elision (*luṅ*) prescribed by Pāṇini 2.4.64 would not occur. Furthermore, in the case of *iha tu gargān paśyati* ("here he sees the Gargas"), the substitution of *n* for *t* (prescribed by 6.1.103) would not occur.

In the second view, however, by this [rule] the masculine-like form (*puṃvadbhāva*) is applied to the word functioning in the sense of a female, but there is no cessation of its feminine nature; nevertheless, that same fault would remain. But if "meaning" (*artha*) is taken [as the referent], there is no fault at all; therefore, considering that this is a mention of the meaning of the female, he says: "The meaning of the female becomes like the masculine. How, then, is this mention of the meaning obtained? It is said: because the feminine suffixes depend upon that which is to be expressed (*abhidheya*).

The meaning lacks primacy because it is not independent; it becomes subordinate through its dependence on the primary element. Its lack of primacy, however, results from its dependence on that which is to be expressed.
The meaning [of the suffix] is not primary because it does not depend on anything else;
however, when there is a conjunction of a primary and a subordinate element, it is logical to grasp the primary one. Therefore, only the feminine meaning is grasped, as in "Gārgī" and "Vātsī."
From the words *gārgya* and *vātsya*, by the rule *yañaśca* [Pāṇini 4.1.16], the suffix *ṅīp* is applied; as before, there is the elision of the vowel *a* and the consonant *y*.
Thus, *dākṣī*: here too, *ṅīp* is applied as before.
Regarding the phrase *dākṣāyaṇaśca*: [the suffix] *phak* is applied according to [Pāṇini 4.1.101], *dākṣerapatyam*. "If the distinction is only that which is characterized by gender" means:

if this were the case, it would not apply here in the example, "This is a bull (*gauḥ*) and this is a cow (*gauḥ*); these two cows (*gāvau*) stand," for in this instance there is no distinction whatsoever caused by gender. Let it not be by this rule; will it not be by the rule beginning with *sarūpāṇām* [Pāṇini 1.2.64]? This is not so; for if it were by that [rule], the single-remainder (*ekaśeṣa*) would undesirably apply even to the word *strī* (cow).
Consequently, the feminine gender might also occur, since gender is not prescribed by rule but depends on worldly usage.

However, when the *ekaśeṣa* (retention of one) is performed for feminine forms, the masculine sense is intended to be expressed; thus there is no fault. Alternatively, a split of the rule (*yogavibhāga*) is made: "pumān" [is a separate rule].
By this, even here where no distinction based on female or male exists, the *ekaśeṣa* of the masculine alone occurs.
And this being so, there is no over-extension (atiprasaṅga), because the desired result is established through the division of the rule (*yogavibhāga*);
for instance, in the cases of *brāhmaṇī*, *kukkuṭī*, and *mayūrī*.
Here, the suffix *ṅīṣ* is applied according to the rule *jāter astrīviṣayād ayopadhāt* [Pāṇini 4.1.63].
Regarding the example "the cock and the peahen" (*kukkuṭamayūryau*):
here, the distinction is not made solely on the basis of female and male; rather, it is also based on form and sound.
As in the case of "Indrāṇī."
By the rule *indravaruṇa* [Pāṇini 4.1.49], the suffix *ṅīṣ* is applied and the augment *ānuk* is added.
Regarding the term *prācī*:

from the root *añc-* preceded by the prefix *pra-*, the suffix *kvin* is applied according to the rule *ṛtvik* [Pāṇini 3.2.59], and *kutva* (the substitution of *ku*) occurs according to the rule *coḥ kuḥ* [Pāṇini 8.2.30]. Thus, we have *prāñc-*; with the addition of *ṅīṣ* and *ānuk*, it becomes *prācī*. "And before that" means *prācī*. Thus, *prācī* is derived from *pra-añc-* with *kvin*, followed by the application of *kutva*.
From a word ending in a feminine suffix, the *astāti* suffix is applied by the rule "from words denoting direction" (Pāṇini 5.3.27) et cetera;
its [elision] occurs by the rule "of that" (Pāṇini 5.3.30).
Thus, [the form] is *prācī*.

In the rule *prākchabdāt* (Pāṇini 6.3.45), the suffix *ṅīp* is added due to the supplementary inclusion (*upasaṃkhyāna*) of the root *añc*. [The form] *prāk* is an indeclinable (*avyaya*), according to the rule *prāgityavyayam* (Pāṇini 1.1.38). [The term] "not neuter" (*anapuṃsakena*) [is used].
Regarding the phrase "kima" and so forth:

[An objection is raised]—"But surely, even without the mention of the neuter gender, a single-remainder formation (*ekaśeṣa*) does indeed occur by means of rules such as *sarūpāṇām* (Pāṇini 1.2.64). Therefore, what is the distinction here, such that the single-remainder formation is prescribed by that [rule], and not by this one alone? To this he says: "'And it is not treated as a singular' (*ekavacca na bhavati*).
If the single-remainder formation were to occur by this [present rule], then there would be the state of being treated as a singular (*ekavadbhāva*) in some instances.
However, when *ekaśeṣa* (the retention of one) has taken place, this [rule] does not apply.
Now, for what purpose is it stated "of this" (*asya*)? If "of this" were not stated, the phrase "as a singular" (*ekavat ca*) would also carry over into the subsequent rule.
Consequently, in the subsequent case where *ekaśeṣa* is to be performed, the status of being a singular (*ekavadbhāva*) would undesirably follow for that [retained element].

Therefore, this mention of "of this" (*asya*) is for the purpose that the singular collective form (*ekavadbhāva*) may apply specifically to this neuter [compound], but not to that which will undergo *ekaśeṣa* in the subsequent rule. For if the word "of this" were present, it would be redundant; thus, to avoid such redundancy, the term *ekavat* does not carry over to the subsequent rule.
But surely it will not be carried over simply because it lacks the *svarita* accent?
If that is so, then that very lack of *svarita* is being explained in this manner for the sake of clarity.
Here, the vowel *e* is carried over.
Therefore, in the cases of *hima* and *himānī* (snow and heavy snow), and *araṇya* and *araṇyānī* (forest and great forest), [the feminine suffix] does not occur.

According to the rule *indravaruṇādibhyaḥ* (Pāṇini 4.1.49) and the statement *himāraṇyayormahatve* (Vārttika 352), "greatness" (*mahattva*) is another specific qualification [for the application of the suffix]. [The example] is *pitarau* (parents).
The *guṇa* substitution [of *o* for *ṛ*] occurs by the rule *ṛto ṅi* [Pāṇini 7.3.110].
Thus we have *mātāpitarau*.

The substitution *ānaṅ* occurs by the rule *ānaṅ ṛto dvandve* [Pāṇini 6.3.24], and the mother (*mātṛ*) is placed first because she is more venerable. Regarding the statement "the inclusion of the word *sarva* is for the sake of completeness": this means that the term *sarva* is used to indicate totality.

Otherwise, one might suspect that the phrase "except for the neuter" (*vinā tenānapuṃsakena*) from a previous rule continues here; consequently, [the rule] would not apply together with a neuter noun.

Or else, one might suspect that the phrase "if there is a distinction based on that" (*tallakṣamaścedeva viśeṣaḥ*) continues here; consequently, it would apply only where the distinction is created by *tyad* and so forth—as in *sa ca yaśca yau* and so on—but it would not apply here in cases such as *sa ca devadattaśca tau*.
Therefore, the word *sarva-* is included.
"And that [person] and Devadatta—those two.

When there is a desire to express a specific distinction, this is the example; but when there is a desire to express a general sense, then Devadatta is also connected with the word *tat* (that), and thus it is established by the rule itself, "Of those having the same form" (*sarūpāṇām*, Pāṇini 1.2.64).
"Whichever is subsequent."
Priority (paratva) should be understood as being relative to the order in the *gaṇapāṭha*. Regarding the term "village-born" (*grāmyāṇām*): those who exist in a village (*grāme*) are "village-born.
[The suffix] *ya* is applied according to [Pāṇini 4.2.93]: *grāmādyakhañau*.
But surely, "treeness" cannot belong to a *saṅgha* (an assembly), nor can "youthfulness" be excluded from it;
therefore, the qualification "among those who are not young" (*ataruṇeṣu*) is inappropriate. To this he says: "The mention of 'not young' (*ataruṇagrahaṇam*)," and so forth.
This qualification is indeed stated, yet it cannot apply to the *saṅgha*; therefore, by implication (*sāmarthyāt*), the *saṅgha* of others [i.e., trees] is understood.
Regarding "gāvaḥ imāḥ": the subsequent application of the word *imāḥ* is for the purpose of manifesting the feminine gender. Regarding "etau gāvau": [the same applies].

But how can this be a counter-example, since the *saṅgha* (group) exists even when there are only two? This is not a fault, because it might be thought that the mention of *saṅgha* would be redundant, as there would be nothing to exclude.
[The phrase] "among those with many hoofs" (*anekaśapheṣu*) and so forth:
the meaning is that this should be explained as having the sense that this *ekaśeṣa* (single-remainder compound) occurs among those things which have many hoofs—that is, many claws or hooves.

In this regard, the following is the explanation: the phrase "of one or the other" (*anyatarasyām*) is understood to carry over here, and it is recognized as a restricted option (*vyavasthita-vibhāṣā*). Consequently, [the rule] applies only to animals with uncloven hooves (*anekaśapha*), and not elsewhere. Thus ends the second quarter of the first chapter in the *Kāśikā-vivaraṇapañjikā*, composed by the venerable Master Jinendrabuddhi, who is a teacher of the Bodhisattvas. Those whose beginning is *bhū* are called *bhūvādayaḥ*.
The term *bhūvādayaḥ* refers to those verbs recited in the ten classes (*daśagaṇī*).
Regarding the passage beginning with "it becomes" (*bhavati*),

since the designation "root" (*dhātu*) applies here, the suffix *laṭ* is introduced by the rule "the *laṭ* [suffix occurs] in the sense of the present tense" (Aṣṭādhyāyī 3.2.123), while the governing rule "after a root" (3.1.91) continues to apply. By stating that "words such as *bhū* and so forth receive the designation 'root'," he demonstrates that this designation of "root" is established solely through the recitation of the list of roots (*gaṇapāṭha*).

By this, it is stated that for [roots] such as *aṇapayati* and *kaḍḍhayati*, the designation "root" (*dhātusaṃjñā*) does not apply. If this were so, someone might fall into the error of thinking that even words like *yā*, *vā*, and *div*—which denote pronouns, alternatives, and heaven respectively, which share the same phonetic form as roots, yet do not express an action—would also acquire the designation "root. Therefore, in order to refute that, he says: "The word 'root' (*dhātuśabdaḥ*)," and so forth.

For teachers desire that the formation of technical names (*saṃjñā*) be for the sake of brevity; thus, when a single-syllable name ought to be employed, the reason for resorting to the long name used by previous teachers is this: so that this name may apply to those very same things to which they assigned the designation "root" (*dhātu*).
And they established the designation "root" only for those words that express action (*kriyā*);
therefore, here too, by resorting to the terminology of the previous teachers, the designation "root" is prescribed only for those words that express action.

The point is that [the suffix *ghañ*] does not apply to words such as *yā*, *vā*, and *div*, which are identical in sound to verbal roots (*dhātu*) but do not denote an action. Now, if one forms the *bahuvrīhi* compound *bhūrādiryeṣām* ("those for whom *bhū* is the first"), and if the word *ādi* is cited in *saṃhitā* (continuous) form, then by the rule *vānto yi pratyaye* [Pāṇini 6.1.79], the *yaṇ* substitution would apply, resulting in the form *bhvādayaḥ*. Alternatively, if it is cited without *saṃhitā*, it would be *bhū ādayaḥ*. Therefore, from where does this letter *v* come, such that when it exists, the citation becomes *bhūvādayaḥ*? To this, he says: "of *bhav* and so forth," and so on.
In the enumeration of the *saṃjñins* (the items to be named), such as *bhū* and so forth, this letter *va* is employed for the purpose of auspiciousness (*maṅgala*).
That which has auspiciousness as its meaning or purpose is described as such. That word "auspicious" (*maṅgala*) is a synonym for *dharma*; that is to say, it means the goal of *dharma*.

Just as in the Veda, in the passage "We worship Tryambaka," the letter *ya* has no perceived purpose and thus its recitation is for the sake of merit (*dharma*) alone, having an unseen purpose (*adṛṣṭārtha*), so too is it here with the letter *va*.

Alternatively, in the world, the acquisition of something previously unobtained is considered auspicious (*maṅgala*), such as curds and other items at dawn; likewise here, the acquisition of the previously unobtained letter *va* is an auspicious and praiseworthy matter.
The word *maṅgala* signifies that which is praiseworthy.

And so it has been said: "Treatises that begin with an auspicious word, have an auspicious word in the middle, and end with an auspicious word, become renowned; they come to possess heroic men and long-lived men" (*Mahābhārata* 1.1.1).

Here, at the beginning, the word *vṛddhi* is auspicious; in the middle, there is this letter *va*; and at the end, the word *udaya* [is used] according to the rule *svari-dato-yam* [Pāṇini 8.4.66]. [The commentary begins: "*bhuvo vārtham*" and so forth.

Alternatively—in the rule *bhūvādayaḥ*—this usage of the word *ādi* is not for the sake of "beginning," nor does it refer to the syllable *va* used for the purpose of auspiciousness; rather, it refers to the word *vādi*, which is derived from the *uṇādi* suffix.

The term *vādayaḥ* means "those that speak" (*vadanti*), that is, "designators. This is derived from the verbal root *vad* by the rule: *vasivapiyajirājivrajisadihanivāśivādivāribhya iñ* (Uṇādisūtra 4.128).

In [the rule] 1|53), the suffix *kartari* (denoting the agent) is applied. Although the word *vadī* is mentioned there as having a *ṇi*-affix (*ṇyanta*), nevertheless, by virtue of the rule of "diversity" (*bahulavacana*), it occurs even after roots that do not take the *ṇi*-affix (*aṇyanta*). Regarding the term *bhvarthāḥ*:
this is an adjective qualifying those *vadīs*; *bhū* means "becoming," with the suffix *kvip* in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāva*) according to the group beginning with *sampad*.

The meaning of the root *bhū* is general action (*kriyāsāmānya*). Those whose meaning is *bhū* are "bhvarthāḥ. Why, then, are they called bhvarthāḥ? Because "they express the meaning of *bhū*. The particle *iti* indicates a reason; that is, because they express—that is, denote—the meaning of the root *bhū*, therefore they are called bhvarthāḥ.

It has been stated that verbal roots such as *bhū* and others, which are expressive words like *vā* and so forth, receive the designation "root" (*dhātu*). Thus, in this sūtra, the "designata" (*saṃjñin*) are what are remembered—that is, intended or accepted.

Therefore, it is effectively stated that those words expressing action, beginning with *bhū*, receive the designation "root. Consequently, words such as *yā*, *vā*, and *div*, which have the same phonetic form as roots but do not express action, do not receive the designation "root.
Furthermore, by the force of their inclusion in the list of roots (*gaṇapāṭha*), their status as roots is also accepted.
By this, it is stated that even verbal roots such as *aṇapayati* ("he causes to send") and others do not receive the designation of *dhātu* (verbal root).

In this interpretation, the expression *bhūvādayaḥ* should be understood as a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*), meaning "those whose beginning is *bhū*" (*bhuvovādayo bhūvādayaḥ*). Alternatively, the word *ādi* here is used immediately after the root *vā* (from the Dhātupāṭha 1050: *vā gatigandhanayoḥ*);
thus, those for which *vā* is the first (*ādi*) are called *vādayaḥ*.

The word *ādi* (and so forth) denotes a type (*prakāra*); the meaning is "of such types. A type, moreover, consists in similarity, which in turn exists by virtue of having action as its essence; as he says: "those whose meaning is existence" (*bhvarthāḥ*).
Their state of having existence as their meaning follows from the reason that they express the meaning of the root *bhū*.

Words of this or similar kind are considered to be *saṃjñins* (the things named) in this sūtra. Thus, it is stated that by this method, the designation *dhātu* applies only to those [roots] beginning with *bhū* that denote action (*kriyā*).
Consequently, words identical in sound to roots, such as *yā*, *vā*, *div*, and so forth, do not receive the designation *dhātu*;
for they do not denote action, since they express accomplished entities (*niṣpannavastu*).
For an action (*kriyā*), whose nature is being accomplished, is partless in some respects, yet possesses sequential parts in others, and its essence is that of an unaccomplished entity.
However, its inclusion in the list of verbal roots (*gaṇapāṭha*) is accepted as before.
Consequently, words such as *aṇapayati* do not receive the designation of "verbal root" (*dhātusaṃjñā*).

Regarding this explanation as well: *bhūvādayaḥ* is a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*). And the genitive should be understood as characterized by the relationship between the signified and the signifier (*vācyavācakasambandha*). [The word] *upadeśaḥ* [is derived from the root *diś* with the prefix *upa*] in the sense of an instrument (*karaṇe*), according to the rule *iti karaṇe ghañ* (Pāṇini 3.3.19). Now, it might be objected: "It is stated that [the suffix *ghañ* is applied] when there is a technical name (*saṃjñāyaṃ*), and yet this is not a technical name. This is not so; because of the statement "in various instances" (*bahulavacanāt*) in the rule *iti bhāve* (Pāṇini 3.3.18), it occurs even when it is not a technical name, so there is no fault.
Regarding the phrase "the words of the treatise," this is its explanation: "the recitation of the sūtras and the recitation of the *khilas*.
The *khilapāṭha* is the *dhātupāṭha*.
By the inclusion of the word "and" (ca), the list of nominal stems (prātipadika-pāṭha) is also included.

Now, how is there nasality (*ānunāsikya*) for [the letters] *ra*, *la*, *ga*, *ja*, and so forth? For their nasality is not recited in the list [of the Śivasūtras]. If it occurs even for those not explicitly recited, then why does it not occur for *bhū* and the like? To this he says: "The followers of Pāṇini are those who have nasality by convention" (*pratijñānanāsikyāḥ pāṇinīyāḥ*), and so on.
Those for whom nasality exists by way of a formal agreement (*pratijñā*) are "those who have nasality by convention."

Precisely where the followers of Pāṇini declare that there is nasalization (*ānunāsikya*), there it exists even if it is not explicitly recited, but not elsewhere. This declaration, moreover, does not apply without restriction; rather, it must occur only where the Teachers (*ācāryāḥ*) remember it. Just as the quality of being circumflex (*svaritatva*) and the quality of being unaccented (*anudāttatva*) are understood through such remembrance, so too is nasalization.

If, then, nasalization (*ānunāsikya*) exists merely by virtue of being a formal assertion (*pratijñāmātra*), for what purpose is it recited in certain instances, such as *ḍupaca~ṣ pāke* (Dhātupāṭha 996)? It is for the purpose of demonstrating that such a meaning is to be asserted as nasalized. For example, in the case of *abhra ā~ apaḥ*, because the nasalization is prescribed here by [Pāṇini 6.1.126] *ata upadhāyāḥ* following the subsequent rule, it does not receive the technical designation *it*.

But surely [the substitution] will not occur simply by the force of the prescription for the nasalized vowel (*anunāsika*); so what is the purpose of including the term "instruction" (*upadeśa*)? For if it were marked with the *it*-designation, there would be elision according to Pāṇini 1.3.9, and consequently, the prescription of the nasalized vowel would be rendered useless. This is true; however, he thinks as follows: the term "instruction" must certainly be included for the sake of subsequent rules. Being made for the sake of subsequent rules, it will also serve to clarify the meaning here. Alternatively, this direction regarding counter-examples has been shown by the author of the Vṛtti.
But here is a counter-example: *dadhi brāhmaṇakulam* ("the Brahmin family [is] curd").
If this were a technical name (*saṃjñā*) here, then by rule 7.1.58, the augment *num* would occur.

Now, it might be argued: "Since it is stated that 'of a verbal root' (*dhātoḥ*), the *num* is prescribed for a verbal root, and this is not a verbal root, but rather a nominal stem (*prātipadika*); so how could there be *num*? This is not the case; because of the principle that "words ending in *kvip* do not lose their status as verbal roots" (Vyāḍi-Pāṇini 132), it possesses the status of a verbal root due to its being a form ending in *kvip*.

From *ātmanaḥ* with the desiderative suffix *icchati*, [we derive] *dadhīyati*; from *dadhīyati* with the suffix *kvip*, we have *dadhi*. In the case of *brāhmaṇakulaṃ dadhi*, there is the elision of the vowel *a* by [Pāṇini 6.4.48]. Because of the mention of "elision" (*lopa*) at the beginning of [Pāṇini 6.1.66], the elision of the *yakāra* occurs first.
By [Pāṇini 6.1.67], there is the substitution of *v* for [the final consonant].

By the rule regarding the indication of the elision of an affix (*pratyayalopalakṣaṇa*), there is lengthening according to [Pāṇini 7.4.25]: "before non-weak endings and before *sārvadhātuka* affixes not marked with *k*.
Then, by [Pāṇini 1.2.47]: "there is shortening of the nominal stem in the neuter," there is shortening.

When the nasalization (*anunāsika*) is applied by [Pāṇini 8.4.57], the suffix *num* would occur because of the rule: "Verbal roots ending in *kvip* do not lose their status as verbal roots" (Vyāḍiparibhāṣā 132).

In the case of *aśmā* and *bhasma*, the letter *m* in the rule "āto manin" (Pāṇini 3.2.74) does not receive the designation *it*. For if it were so, then the suffix *manin*, which is prescribed after bases ending in consonants by [Pāṇini 3.2.75], would follow after the final vowel; [the intention is] that it should not apply to all vowels.

[This applies] even to those related to "poor" (daridra) and so forth. Regarding the term *antya*, it means "that which exists at the end. The suffix *yat* is applied according to the rule for the group beginning with *diś*.
This word *anta* refers to "conclusion."
For example: "this forest ends here.
That by which a collection is completed is the "end" (anta). "At the end" (ante) means at the conclusion; that which occurs at the end is "final" (antyam).
Regarding *haliti*: because the word *hal* has both genders, the term *antya* (final) is indicated here in the neuter gender.
As for the phrase "of the root-initial," etc.:
by the word "etc. (*ādi*), there is the inclusion of the rules for suffixes, nominal stems (*prātipadika*), affixes (*pratyaya*), augments (*āgama*), and substitutes (*ādeśa*).

In that regard, the letter *ṇ* occurs in a root—as in *ḍukṛñ* (Dhātupāṭha 1472); in a sūtra—as in *aiuṇ* (Māheśvara Sūtra 1); in a nominal stem (*prātipadika*)—as in *navaṭ*; [the suffix] *nadaṅ* is recited among the *pacādi* group; in an affix—as in [Pāṇini 3.1.5]; in an augment—as in [Pāṇini 4.3.138]; and in a substitute—as in *cakṣiṅaḥ khyāñ* (2.4.54). Examples include *agnicit* and *somasut*.

In the case of the roots *cinoti* and *sunoti*, [the forms] *agni-cit* and *soma-sut* are derived using the suffix *kvip*, with the application of *tuk*. Now, however, in the recitation of the *hal-pratyāhāra* (the list of consonants), the final letter *l* does not obtain the designation *it*; for there would be mutual dependence (*itaretarāśrayatva*).
To explain: the term *hal* is used as a *pratyāhāra* only when the designation *it* has been established by the rule *tasya lopaḥ* (Pāṇini 1.3.9).
And only when that *hal-pratyāhāra* exists can the letter *l* receive the *it* designation by the rule *hal-antyam* (Pāṇini 1.3.3).
This mutual dependence (*itaretarāśrayatva*) is indeed quite evident.
Since it is stated that "operations based on mutual dependence are not formulated in the treatise" (*Vyākaraṇa-paribhāṣā* 28), he says: "*haL-ya-sya l-haL*" and so forth.
That which, even without a difference in repetition (*āvṛtti*), effects the benefit of many things is called *tantra*.
For example, a well-kindled lamp benefits many students;
here, however, it is a specific effort that is intended by the word *tantra*.
By means of that *tantra*, it should be understood that the second mention of the term *hal* is included or adopted here.
Just as when one says "oto dhāvati" (the sheep runs), two sentences are uttered with a single effort, so too here the intention is that two *hal* words are uttered with a single effort.
In the expression "hasya laḥ" (*ha-l*), the genitive case denotes a relationship of proximity (*samīpisāmīpya*).
Regarding the phrase beginning with "tena":

Since a second mention of *ha* has been made according to the principle of *tantra*, the designation *it* is applied directly to the letter *la* in the *pratyāhāra* recitation—which is situated immediately after *ha*—as being the designated object (*saṃjñin*) itself, and not by virtue of its inclusion in the *pratyāhāra* as a whole.
This being the case, in the rule [Pāṇini 1.3.3] *halantyam*, there is no fault of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśraya*) regarding the *pratyāhāra* recitation.
*Bālamano ramā*: Pāṇini 1.3.3, *halantyam*, is a single-word sūtra.
The analysis of the compound is *hal-antyaṃ hal-antyam* (the final consonant among the consonants).

Since the group beginning with *śauṇḍa* is an *ākṛtigaṇa*, there is either a locative compound (*saptamī-samāsa*) according to the rule *saptamī śauṇḍaiḥ*, or a *sup-supā* compound. Here, the word *hal* refers to the technical term (*saṃjñā*) as used in the sūtra.
In the rule "upadeśe'janunāsika it," the term *it* is carried over from the preceding sūtra. Thus he says: "in the sūtra 'hal'... and so forth, [concluding with] "...it would be an *it*."
The meaning is that it should have the designation *it*, because the topic under discussion is designations (*saṃjñā*).

And thus, by this rule, the designation *it* for the letter *l* in the [previous] *hal* rule is established without depending on its *hal* designation; therefore, there is no circular dependency—this is the intended sense. From the *Bālamanoramā*: *halantyam* (Pāṇini 1.3.3). To the question "What follows from that?", he says: *halantyam*.
This is the second sūtra in the [repeated] section.
The analysis of the compound is *hal antyam*.
The word *hal* exists even as a neuter noun, because of its grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the neuter term *antya*.
In the rule *upadeśe 'janunāsika it*, the terms *upadeśe* and *it* are carried over from the preceding sūtra.
Thus he says: "the final [element] in the upadeśa," and so forth.

The Bhāṣya states that this refers to the final element among roots (*dhātu*), nominal stems (*prātipadika*), particles (*nipāta*), the technical abbreviations (*pratyāhāra*), sūtras, suffixes (*pratyaya*), substitutes (*ādeśa*), and augments (*āgama*).
Now, what is this so-called "instruction" (upadeśa)? To that he says: "Instruction is the first utterance.
The prefix *upa* signifies "first," and the root *diś* refers to the act of uttering.
The term *bhāva* [is used here] because of the rule "the suffix *ghañ* occurs in the sense of *bhāva*.

This is clear from the Bhāṣya on the sūtra "ādeca upadeśe" (Pāṇini 6.1.45). [The scope of the term *dhātu* includes] the Dhātupāṭha, the Sūtrapāṭha, the Gaṇapāṭha, the Uṇādisūtras, the Vārttikas, and the teaching of grammatical gender.
The instructions based on the authority of traditional scripture are proclaimed as "upadeśas."
Thus, the aforementioned ancient *kārikā* has been refuted in various ways in the *Prakriyā-prakāśa* (a commentary on the *Prakriyā-kaumudī*).

[The question is asked: "In the rule *upadeśe 'j anunāsikaḥ*, what is the purpose?"—[the answer is: it is so that in the rule *idamasthamuḥ*, when the suffix *thamu* is added, although the letter *m* is at the end of the suffix, its *itsaṃjñā* (the designation of an *it*) should not apply once the vowel *u*—which serves merely for pronunciation (*uccāraṇārtha*)—has been removed.

Therefore, it is established that by the repetition of the second rule (*halantyam*), the *itsaṃjñā* of the final letters such as *ṇ*, *k*, and others within the fourteen-sūtra section is accomplished.
To the question "What follows from that?", he says: "Then, upon the establishment of the technical designation *it* for [the letters] beginning with *ṇ*.

This means that after the designation *it* has been established by means of the letter *ṇ* and so forth, the designations *aṇ* and others are established by the rule *ādirantyena* (Pāṇini 1.1.71). In the word *vṛkṣāt*, if the letter *t* were to receive the designation *it*, then by the rule *titsvaritam* (Pāṇini 6.1.179), it would become *svarita*-accented. In the forms *apacāt* and *apacatam*: the suffix *laṅ* is applied to the root *pac*; then, by the rule *tasthasthamipāṃ tāntantāmaḥ* (Pāṇini 3.4.101), the substitutes *ta* and *tam* are applied in place of *tas* and *thas*.

In the rule *kimo't* [Pāṇini 5.3.12], it is understood that the letter *u* is an indicatory marker (*anubandha*) for the sake of protecting the *m* of the word *prāg diśo vibhaktiḥ* [Pāṇini 5.3.1] from being designated as an *it*.

For if [the letter *m*] were eternal (*nitya*), then by this very prohibition, the designation *it* would not apply to the letter *m*, and thus the inclusion of the indicatory letter *u* (*ukāra-anubandha*) would be purposeless. Here, why does the inclusion of the *ṭu*-group (the retroflex class) by the mention of *ṭu* not result in the inclusion of the *ṭa*-group according to the rule "aṇudit savarṇasya cāpratyayaḥ" [Pāṇini 1.1.69]? Because the nasality (*anunāsikatva*) of the letter *u* is not admitted, and because of the mention of *ṭu* in the rule "cuṭū" [Pāṇini 1.3.7].
If there were an inclusion of the *ṭa*-group here, then since the beginning of a suffix would already be established by this very [rule], the mention of *ṭu* would be purposeless.
[The example is] "minnaḥ."
By [Pāṇini 7.2.16] and [3.2.187], there is a prohibition of the augment *iṭ*.
Thus, "vepathuḥ" [is derived];
[it is formed] by [Pāṇini 3.3.89]: "The suffix *athuc* follows a verbal root ending in *ṭu*."
Regarding "paktrimam":
it is derived from *pāka* with the suffix *ma*, according to the rule *ktrermam nityam* [Pāṇini 4.4.20].
Regarding "uptrimam": [it is derived similarly].
By the rule *vacyādi* [Pāṇini 6.1.15], there is *samprasāraṇa*. In the case of *paṭūyati*, there is lengthening by the rule *akṛtsārvadhātukayoḥ* [Pāṇini 7.4.25].
In the case of *kaṇḍūyati*:

But how is this designation of *it* applied here, given that in the Sūtra the verbal roots *ṭu* and *ḍu* are presented with short vowels, whereas these two [forms] have long vowels? This is not so; for although they come to have long vowels once the lengthening has been applied, they nevertheless have short vowels in their original enunciation (*upadeśa*). And the term "in the enunciation" (*upadeśe*) is understood to carry over here from Pāṇini 1.3.2.
In that regard, because the word *paṭu* is listed among the *pṛthvādi* group, the fact that the root *ṭu* has a short vowel in its enunciation is established.
Likewise, because the word *kaṇḍū* is listed in the rule "from *kaṇḍvādi* etc., *yak*" (Pāṇini 3.1.27), the root *ḍu* also has a short vowel in its enunciation.
For the *kaṇḍvādi* group is of two kinds: verbal roots (*dhātu*) and nominal stems (*prātipadika*). Among these, the verbal root *kaṇḍū* ends in a short vowel;

however, the nominal stem *kaṇḍū* ends in a long vowel. Alternatively, even if the word "in the original instruction" (*upadeśe*) does not carry over [from the previous rule], nevertheless, since that which has undergone a partial modification remains essentially the same as the original, the application [of the rule] certainly occurs once the lengthening has been performed.
Regarding the term *ñikāryati*:
the suffix *kyac* is applied as before;
however, since the word *ñikāra* is not recited anywhere [in the lexicon], the designation *it* does not apply to it here.
If it were so, the form would not be established when the elision is performed—as in *rajakī*.
[The suffix] *ṅīṣ* is applied because of the marker *ṣ* according to Pāṇini 4.1.41.

Now, by what rule is there the elision of the nasal here? If you say it is by Pāṇini 6.4.24 (*aniditām*), no; for that rule specifies "before a *kṅit* suffix," and here there is no *kṅit* suffix. This is not a fault.

Regarding the rule *janījṛṣknasurañjau ñamantāśca* (Gaṇasūtra on the Dhātupāṭha, 817), the assignment of the technical designation *mit* serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*) that for the root *rañj*, the nasal is elided even when a suffix other than one marked with *k* or *ṅ* follows. Otherwise, since the vowel *a* of *rañj* would not be penultimate when followed by the causative suffix *ṇi*, the rule [Pāṇini 7.2.116] requiring Vṛddhi substitution would not apply; thus, some maintain that the assignment of the *mit* designation would be purposeless. Others hold that because the word "and" (*ca*) in [Pāṇini 6.4.27] has the sense of an inclusive conjunction (*anuktasamuccaya*), the nasal of *rañj* is occasionally elided even when a suffix other than one marked with *k* or *ṅ* follows. The term *ṣaḍdantaḥ* is a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "one who has six teeth. By the rule [Pāṇini 5.4.141], the word *datṛ* is substituted for *danta*; the vowel *ṛ* is for the purpose of triggering operations related to *ugit*-stems. According to the Vārttika [765]: *ṣaṣa utvaṃ datṛdaśadhāsūttarapadādeḥ ṣṭutvañca*, because the word is read in the *pṛṣodarādi* group, there is *utva* (the substitution of *u*) for the final letter of *ṣaṣ*, and by [Pāṇini 6.1.87], there is *ṣṭutva* (the substitution of *ṣṭu*) for the initial letter of the subsequent member; thus, the *d* of *datṛ* becomes *ḍ*.

When *ṣoḍat* is established, the suffix *ṇic* is applied according to the rule *tat karoti tad ācaṣṭe* (Vārttika 200, 201), meaning "he causes that to be done" or "he expresses that. Then, by the rule *ṇāviṣṭhavat kāryaṃ prātipadikasya* (Vārttika 813), which prescribes the treatment of the nominal stem as if it were in the superlative degree (*iṣṭhan*), the *ṭilopa* elision occurs—resulting in *ṣoḍayati*. From this, the suffix *ac* (of the *pacādi* class) is added, and the *ṇic* suffix is elided, yielding *ṣoḍa*. Regarding the word *ṣaṇḍaḥ*: the root is *ṣaṇu* (meaning "to give," Dhātupāṭha 1464). By the rule *ñamantāḍḍaḥ* (Dhātupāṭha 5.7), the suffix *ḍa* is added. Due to the frequentative usage (*bahulavacanāt*) [of the rule], the substitution of *s* for *ṣ* (*satvam*) does not take place.
Alternatively, *ṣaṇḍa* is an unanalyzed (*avyutpanna*) nominal stem (*prātipadika*). As for *ṣaḍika*:
from the word *ṣaḍ-aṅgulidatta*, the suffix *ṭhac* is applied in the sense of "affection" (*anukampā*) by [Pāṇini 5.3.78], *bahvaco 'manuṣyanāmnaṣ ṭhaj vā*.
By [Pāṇini 5.3.83], *ṭhājādāv ūrdhvaṃ dvitīyādayaḥ*, there is elision of *aṅgulidatta*; then, by [Pāṇini 7.3.50], there is the substitution of the vowel *i*.

By the rule *ṣaḍaśabdasya* [Pāṇini 6.4.148], there is the elision of the vowel *a*; because that elision is treated as if it were the original element (*sthānivadbhāva*), the word *ṣaṭ* is not subject to the designation *bha* by the rule *ṣaṭśabdasya* [Pāṇini 1.4.18] due to the intervention [of the elided vowel]. Because the word retains its status as a *pada* by relying on the internal case-ending, the substitution of *jaś* occurs by the rule *padasya* [Pāṇini 8.2.39], whereby the letter *ṣ* becomes *ḍ*. If this *ṣ* were to receive the designation *it*, then the suffix *ṅīṣ* would apply in the feminine by the rule *striyām* [Pāṇini 4.1.41].
Although this word *ṣaṇḍa* refers to a bull, its application to female cows is indeed possible due to their connection with the characteristics of a bull (*ṣaṇḍadharma*).

Even though these [words] such as *ṣoḍa* and others are based on secondary indication (*lākṣaṇika*), nevertheless, because the letter *ṣ* is specified by its mention in the enunciation (*uddeśagrahaṇa*), these become counter-examples for the rule regarding the mention of an affix (*pratyayagrahaṇa*).
For in these cases as well, the letter *ṣ* occurs in the enunciation—as in *aviṣaḥ* and *mahiṣaḥ*.

The root *ava* is used in the sense of "protection" (*rakṣaṇe*; Dhātupāṭha 600), and *maha* in the sense of "worship" (*pūjāyām*; Dhātupāṭha 1867). Regarding the rule *avimahyoṣṭiṣac* (Pāṇini 5.2.117), one might object: since the word *bahula* ("variously") is present in the rule *naṅ ca* (5.2.116), there is no designation as a suffix (*pratyayasaṃjñā*) here at all; even if such a designation were to exist, the designation *it* would not apply because of the word *bahula*. So why is the mention of "beginning" (*ādi*) carried over [from the previous rule]? The intention is this: the mention of "beginning," which must necessarily be carried over for the sake of subsequent rules, will also serve to clarify the meaning here. As in the example: *kauñjāyanyaḥ*.

From that which ends in *cphañ*, by [Pāṇini 5.3.113], the suffix *ñya* is applied in the sense of the base itself (*svārthe*). He will state that "there is the substitution of *ey* for *cha*"; this is an exception (*apavāda*) to the designation *it*.
Regarding "śāṇḍikyaḥ":

by [Pāṇini 4.3.92], the suffix *ñya* is applied in the sense of "one whose ancestral home (*abhijana*) is Śaṇḍika," for in that rule the phrase "this is his ancestral home" (*so'syābhijanaḥ*) is understood to carry over.
Regarding "mandurajaḥ": [it is formed with the suffix *aṇ*].

By [Pāṇini 6.3.63], the word *mandūra* undergoes shortening. Regarding the form *ānna*: by [Pāṇini 5.2.1] *annāṇṇaḥ*, the suffix *ṇa* is applied in the sense of "one who has obtained food," resulting in *anna + ṇa* = *ānnaḥ*.
For in that [rule], the word *labdha* is understood from the rule *tatra hi* (Pāṇini 4.4.84).

Now, for what purpose is a separate rule (*pṛthagyoga*) made? Why not simply make a single rule, namely *cuṭuṣāḥ pratyayasya*? To this he says: "The making of a separate rule," and so forth. He shows the purpose of making this rule optional by means of the rule *tena vittaḥ* (Pāṇini 5.2.26) and others. The example is *priyaṃvadaḥ*.
The suffix *mum* is applied according to [Pāṇini 3.2.38] and [6.3.67],
resulting in the form *jiṣṇuḥ*;
this is according to [3.2.139].
According to those who desire the *kṣnu* suffix to have the marker *ṅ*, this is an example of the letter *g*;

however, according to those who desire it to have the marker *k*, this also becomes an example of the letter *k*. [The word] "cūḍālaḥ" [is formed] with the suffix *lac* by rule Pāṇini 5.2.96 (*matvarthe*).

But surely this designation will not apply here due to the absence of a purpose? If it is argued that the purpose is to make the syllable preceding the *lit* suffix udātta, we say no; for since the accent of the *cit* suffix is an exception (*apavāda*) to all other [accents], once the final udātta of the suffix has been established by the general rule for suffixal accents, the purpose of employing the *cit* marker is this: that the accent of the *cit* itself alone should occur, so that whatever other accent would otherwise apply shall not take effect.

But this is a counter-example: [the word] *lomaśaḥ* [is formed] by the suffix *śa-* according to [Pāṇini 5.2.100], *lomādyasya santi*. This too is not [a valid objection], because here also, due to the absence of any purpose (*prayojana*), the designation *it* will simply not occur.

In that case, here is a counter-example: *karṇalalāṭāt kan alaṅkāre* [Pāṇini 4.3.65], where *kan* is used in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāva*). Thus we have *karṇikā*. If this were a technical name (*saṃjñā*), then by the rule *kiti ca* [Pāṇini 7.2.118] and others, there would be *vṛddhi* (vowel strengthening), and consequently, the desired form would not be established at all. If this is so, why is only this example presented and not the others? The intention is as follows: the term *ataddhite* (except when a *taddhita* suffix follows) is employed for this very purpose, and in order to avoid the burden of comprehension for those of dull intellect even in this instance, [examples such as] *cūḍālaḥ* and *lomaśaḥ* are given.

It may also be for this purpose. Now, for what reason is the word "tasya" (of that) stated?
