If this is so, what is the purpose of mentioning the *ṅit* [suffix]? For it follows that elsewhere there should be no ātmanepada. It is said in reply: it is taught for the sake of the accent (*svara*). In the *luṅ* form *mā hi mṛta*, once the anudātta has been applied by the rule "after a root taught with an anudātta *ṅit* suffix, the following *sārvadhātuka* is anudātta" (Pāṇini 6.1.180), the root retains its final udātta. Here, the suppression of accent (*nighāta*) prescribed by "a *tiṅ* [is unaccented] after a non-*tiṅ*" (Pāṇini 8.1.28) is prohibited by the rule "also after *hi*" (Pāṇini 8.1.34).
The augment *aṭ* is also [prohibited] by the rule *na māṅyoge* [Pāṇini 6.4.74].
In the word *amṛta*,
there is the elision of *sic* by the rule *hrasvād aṅgāt* [Pāṇini 8.2.27].

In *mṛṣīṣṭa*, the suffix *liṅ* is used in the sense of a benediction (*āśis*). Because of the rule *tasya* [Pāṇini 3.4.116], it is treated as an *ārdhadhātuka* suffix, and thus there is no insertion of the *vikaraṇa* suffix. By the rule *sārvadhātukārdhadhātukayoḥ* [Pāṇini 7.3.84], the augment *suṭ* is applied. Then, by the rule *vali* [Pāṇini 6.1.66], there is the elision of the semivowel *y*.
In *mriyate*: [the same process applies].

Because it belongs to the *tud-ādi* class, the suffix *śa* is applied; by the rule *riṅ śayagliṅkṣu* [Pāṇini 7.4.28], there is the substitution of *riṅ*; by the rule *aci śnudhātu* [Pāṇini 6.4.77] and others, there is *iyaṅ*.
Thus: *mariṣyati*. By the rule *iṭ ca* [Pāṇini 7.2.70], the augment *iṭ* is added. "As before" means...
The suffix *vati* is applied by [Pāṇini 5.1.115].

The word "pūrva" (prior), being a relative term, requires a point of reference (*avadhi*). And since that point of reference is explicitly stated [in the rule], it is understood as being present; thus he says: "the root which is prior to a *san*. If this were so, then since the mention of "*san*" would already be utilized for the purpose of establishing the status of the point of reference, the *ātmanepada* would occur after a root ending in *san*; however, this is not obtained there. From what, then, would it arise? From the mere root? This is not the case; for if it were so, the sequential enumeration of the *parasmaipada* roots would be rendered meaningless.
Now, could it be from a suffix ending in *pratyaya*? Even so, the inclusion [of the word *pratyaya*] would be purposeless; one would have to say "as before, from a suffix" (*pūrvavat pratyayāt*).

Therefore, having abandoned the *san* which is close at hand, it is not logical to assume another unmentioned [suffix] that is not connected; thus it is understood that [the suffix *kyac*] occurs only after a stem ending in *san*.
With the words beginning with "by which" (*yena*), he explains the meaning of the suffix *-vat*.
Regarding the phrase "that very [condition] is the cause":

the fact of having an *anudātta* vowel and the fact of being marked with *ṅ* remain causes even when the root is in another state, by virtue of the force of the statement concerning the *saN*-intensive. For example: *asisiṣate*.
When *iṭ* has been applied, by [Pāṇini 6.1.2], there is reduplication of the syllable *si*.
Thus we have *nivivikṣate*.
The root *viś* means "to enter" (Dhātupāṭha 1424); as before, the markers *kittva*, *ṣatva*, and *katva* apply.
In the case of *ācikraṃsate*, the augment *iṭ* does not occur because it is conditioned by the occurrence of the ātmanepada endings. [Similarly] in *śiśatsati* and *mumūrṣati*.
In this case, the preceding portion of the suffix *san* possesses the status of being a cause for the middle voice (*ātmanepada*), as seen in forms such as *śīyate* and *mriyate*.
Consequently, someone might have the misconception that the middle voice must necessarily occur here; therefore, in order to dispel that, he says: "It does not occur here," and so forth.
He asks, "What is the reason? and replies: "For not," and so forth.
What then? It is "even that which has a *śit* augment, etc.
Here, by the word *śit*, it is meant that [the element] is characterized by having a *śit* augment (*śidbhāvitva*) and is related to a *śit* augment (*śitsambandhitva*).

By the word "etc.," the inclusion of the *luṅ* and *liṅ* suffixes is intended; however, that is not present here. For in this case, the portion preceding the *san* suffix does not possess the state of being characterized by a *śit* augment nor is it related to a *śit* augment, because a *śit* suffix is absolutely impossible in this context. Nor are there *luṅ* or *liṅ* suffixes following the root *mriyate*.

Therefore, since *śad* and *mṛ* do not possess the conditions for the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) here, the middle voice does not occur. Why, then, does it not occur here in *anucikīrṣati* and *parācikīrṣati*? For the middle voice is prescribed for the root *kṛ* in the sense of "hinting" (*gandhana*) and so forth; thus, one might argue that even when these senses are not intended, the middle voice should still occur after the desiderative suffix (*san*). To this, he says: "And of that which... and so on. Because the active voice (*parasmaipada*) is prescribed by [Pāṇini 1.3.79] for the root *kṛ* in the sense of "hinting" and so forth in its prior state—namely, before the addition of the desiderative suffix—the absence of the middle voice is established for *kṛ*.

Therefore, because there is no cause for the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) even after these two roots when followed by *san*, [the suffix] does not occur. Now, as for [the forms] *jugupsate* and *mīmāṃsate*, how is there a middle voice, given that it is stated [in Pāṇini 1.3.62], "The [suffixes of the middle voice] are like those of the preceding [root]" (*pūrvavatsanaḥ*), and yet in the case of *gup* and the others, the middle voice does not occur prior to the addition of *san*; thus, due to the absence of this extension (*atideśa*) of the preceding state, the middle voice should not occur? To this, he says: "In this case," etc.
[The form] *jugupsate*:
here, *san* is added by [Pāṇini 3.1.5].
Regarding the form *mīmāṃsate*:

the suffix *san* is applied by [Pāṇini 3.1.6], *mānbadha*, etc.; then, by [Pāṇini 7.4.79], *sanyataḥ*, the vowel of the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*) undergoes *it*-vṛddhi (change to *i*), followed by lengthening.

But how is this so here? For while the fact that the root is unaccented (*anudātta*) is an indicator (*liṅga*) regarding the parts beginning with *gup*, it is not an indicator regarding the whole such as *jugupsā*; therefore, he says: "What is effected in a part," and so forth.

Just as a mark made on a part of a cow, such as its ear, serves to distinguish the whole animal, so too the property of having an anudātta vowel (anudāttettva) applied to a root such as *gup* serves to distinguish the whole verbal form, such as *jugupsate*.

If this were the case, then [the ātmanepada ending] would also apply in instances such as *gopayati*, *tejayati*, and *saṅketayati*. True; it might be argued as follows: "The characteristic mark (*liṅga*) produced by a suffix on a single member becomes a qualifier of that entire complex (*samudāya*)—that complex which that member does not deviate from. However, a complex ending in *san* (desiderative) is never deviated from, whereas one ending in *ṇic* (causative) is deviated from; therefore, the ātmanepada should not occur here.
This argument is incorrect, because even a complex ending in *san* can be deviated from, since forms such as *gopayati* are possible even without that [desiderative suffix].

Therefore, since there is no possibility of a whole (*samudāya*) that is not invariably associated with [the property of] having *gup* as its initial member, the fact that the designation "having an anudātta vowel" (*anudāttettva*) has been applied to the individual parts such as *gup* will serve as the distinguishing mark (*liṅga*) for the whole.
Consequently, the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) would indeed result even from forms such as *gopayati*.
If this is so, then in the rule [Pāṇini 1.3.87], the particle *ca* is employed in the sense of including what has not been explicitly mentioned (*anuktasamuccaya*).

Therefore, this will serve as an exception (apavāda) to the parasmaipada and ātmanepada suffixes that would otherwise apply after roots such as *gup* when they are followed by the causative marker (*ṇi*). Regarding the rule *āmpratyayavat* [Pāṇini 3.1.35]:
the suffix *vati* is applied here with a genitive case-ending (*ṣaṣṭhīsamarthāt*).
In the expression *kṛño'nuprayogasya* [Pāṇini 3.1.40], both genitives are in apposition (*samānādhikaraṇe*).

Regarding the passage beginning with *īkṣāñcakre*: the roots *īkṣ* (to see, DhP 610), *īh* (to strive, DhP 632), and *ūh* (to deliberate, DhP 648) take the *liṭ* suffix. By the rule *ijādeḥ* [Pāṇini 3.1.36] and others, the *ām* affix is applied; then by *āmaḥ* [2.4.81], there is the elision (*luk*) of the *liṭ*. Since it is now a nominal stem (*prātipadika*), the case endings (*sup*) would normally follow, but because it is an indeclinable (*avyaya*) due to being listed among the *svarādi* group, there is the elision of the case endings (*subluk*). Furthermore, by the rule *kṛñ ca* [3.1.40], the root *kṛ* is employed after the *liṭ*-ending verb. By stating that "this undertaking is for the sake of something not intended for the agent," it is implied that this is for the purpose of a mandatory injunction (*vidhi*).
In this regard, he says "If," etc., in order to point out the fault in this injunctive sense:
"He made [them] upright" (*udubjāñcakāra*).
The root *ubj* means "to straighten" (Dhātupāṭha 1303); with the prefix *ut*, the periphrastic perfect (*liṭ*) is formed, and the augment *ām* is applied as before.
By the rule *parasmaipadānām* [Pāṇini 3.4.82] and others, *tip* is replaced by *ṇal*,
resulting in *udumbhāñcakāra*. As for the objection regarding the form *ubhayam*, the resolution is provided by the rule *ubha umbha pūraṇe* [Dhātupāṭha 1319, 1320].
"How so? [The question arises because] it is impossible to accomplish both of these by a single effort; therefore, he says "as before" (*pūrvavat*), and so forth.
Here there is not indeed one effort; rather, there are two: "like the *ām*-affix" (*āmpratyayavat*) is one effort, and the continued application of the term "as before" (*pūrvavat*) is the second.
Therein, the rule (*vidhi*) is established by the former effort, and the restriction (*niyama*) by the other.

If the *ātmanepada* occurs after the verb *kṛ* when used with a secondary application (*anuprayoga*), it happens exactly as before, and not otherwise. Therefore, forms such as *udubjāñcakāra* do not occur [in this context], for the *ātmanepada* is not possible for roots like *ubj*, because they belong to the *parasmaipada* class. [An example of the correct formation is] *īkṣāmāsa*.
"Yes, there is the subsequent application (anuprayoga) of the root *as*.

Regarding the form *īkṣāmbabhūva*, the author says 'How then? and so forth, with the intention that in the rules *bhavetaraḥ* [Pāṇini 3.1.73] and *kṛñ ca* [Pāṇini 3.1.40], only the root *kṛ* is intended to be included."
Regarding the statement "the mention of the *pratyāhāra* [of the suffixes] beginning with *kṛñ*," etc.:
therein, the inclusion (*sanniveśa*) of both *ās* and *bhū* is also present within that *pratyāhāra*. Therefore, the intended meaning is that their subsequent application (*anuprayoga*) also occurs.
If this is so, then the subsequent application of *sampad* would also follow, since its inclusion therein is indeed established by the rule [Pāṇini 5.4.53].
Even though such an arrangement exists, there is no fault because that [arrangement] is not grasped by the term *pratyāhāra*;

we shall explain how it is not grasped later on in another context. Now, what is the purpose of the phrase "as if having the suffix *am*" (*am-pratyayavat*)? For if that were absent, the ātmanepada would apply only to the subsequent usage (*anuprayoga*)—as in "Devadatta does" (*devadattaḥ karoti*)? Here too, the word "as before" (*pūrvavat*) is understood to carry over.

Nevertheless, one might ask here: "Does he strive? Does he act? When it is stated that the suffix *ām* is used, it is understood—by virtue of proximity—that the subsequent application (*anuprayoga*) belongs specifically to *ām* itself, and not to the mere application [of any root]; thus, there is no over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). Regarding the root *yuj* in the sense of "concentration" (Dhātupāṭha 1177), since it is marked with an indicatory vowel *u* (anudāttet), the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) is already established; therefore, with the intention that its mention here is inappropriate, he says: "*yujir yoge*" ("the root *yuj* in the sense of connection"). As for "*prayuṅkte*" ("he employs"):
because it belongs to the *rudh*-class, the vowel *a* is elided by Pāṇini 6.4.111.

By [Pāṇini 8.2.30], *kutva* occurs—that is, the letter *ja* becomes *ga*; by [8.4.54] (*khari ca*), *catva* occurs—that is, the letter *ga* becomes *ka*; by [8.3.24] (*naśca*) and so forth, the *anusvāra* is applied; and by [8.4.58], the letter *ṅa* is substituted. Regarding the statement, "It should be stated that [the rule applies] when preceded or followed by a vowel" (*svarādyantopasṛṣṭād iti vaktavyam*): a vowel (*svara*) is the letter *a* (or any vowel); that which has a vowel as its initial or final element is called *svarādyanta*. The meaning to be explained is this: the *ātmanepada* ending occurs after the root *yuji* when it is accompanied by—that is, connected with—such a word. This is the sense in which it should be interpreted.

In this regard, the explanation is as follows: in this sūtra, the word *pra* is intended to indicate any prefix (*upasarga*) ending in a vowel; the word *upa* is intended to indicate any [prefix] beginning with a vowel. Therefore, the Ātmanepada occurs when the root *yuji* (to join) is joined with any such prefix, whether it ends in a vowel or begins with one. Why does it say "preceded by a prefix beginning or ending in a vowel"? Consider the example: *niryunakti*. It is understood that the rule "from an intransitive [verb]" (*akarmakāt*) carries over from that context; thus, it is maintained that the Ātmanepada is desired even for the transitive root *kṣṇu* (to sharpen).
For this very reason, an example of a transitive verb has been presented:
"he sharpens the weapon" (*saṃkṣṇute śastram*).
Due to its belonging to the *adādi* class, there is elision (*luk*) of the *śap* suffix.
Regarding "saṃkṣṇuvāte," the substitution of uvaṅ occurs by the rule "aci śnudhātu" (Pāṇini 6.4.77) and so forth. Regarding "saṃkṣṇuvate."
The instruction is as before: "by way of the prohibition of *avana*," and so forth. *Avana* means protection.

By that prohibition, it is understood that the root *bhuji* belonging to the *raudhādika* class is intended, and not the one belonging to the *taudādika* class—namely, the root *bhuji* in the sense of "to bend" (*kauṭilye*), as listed in the Dhātupāṭha (No. 1417).

For just as when it is said, "Let a cow with its calf be brought," only that cow which can possibly have a connection with a calf is brought, and not a buffalo or other such animal; so too here, by the prohibition of *ava-ni* (to protect), only that root belonging to the *raudhādika* group whose action (*vṛtti*) occurs in the sense of non-protection (*anavana*) is understood. Therefore, it is recognized that only that [root] is to be taken.

Consequently, in the forms *nirbhujati* and *vibhujati*, the ātmanepada does not occur for the root belonging to the *tudādika* group. [Regarding the example] "The elephant-keepers mount the elephant":
this was stated for the purpose of demonstrating the object (*karman*) in the case of the root *aṇ*.
An illustration of this is: *ārohayate hastī svayameva* ("The elephant causes itself to mount").

In the case of *ārohanti hastinaṃ hastipakāḥ* ("The elephant-keepers mount the elephant"), for the root *ruh* preceded by *ā-*—which, according to the Dhātupāṭha (859), means "to grow from a seed" or "to appear"—two actions are to be expressed: descending (*nyagbhavana*) and causing to descend (*nyagbhāvana*).
In that context, the elephant is the agent of the action of descending, while the elephant-keepers are the agents of the action of causing to descend.
The meaning is "making the elephant submissive" (*nyagbhāvayant-*).

When, however, because of being well-trained and easily managed, the elephant itself attains extreme compliance toward the act of subjugation, then that elephant is intended as the *prayojaka* (the instigator) with respect to the mahouts, while the mahouts are intended as the *prayojya* (the one to be instigated).
The elephant instigates the mahouts, saying, "Mount me," and thus, when the relationship of the instigator and the instigated is intended to be expressed, the causative suffix *ṇic* is applied.

Thus, in subsequent cases as well, since the agency of the object (*karman*) is intended to be expressed, the suffix *ṇic* is prescribed when there is an intention to express the state of being an instigator (*prayojaka*).

Once that [suffix] has arisen, when the objects (*prayojya*) are no longer intended to be expressed because their purpose has been fulfilled through the determination of their own nature, then—since the relationship between the instigator and the instigated has ceased—the root *ruh* functions merely in the sense of "becoming subordinate" (*nyagbhavana*).
An example of this is: *ārohayate hastī svayameva* ("the elephant causes itself to mount").

For instance, that which was the object (*karman*) in the causative (*ṇyanta*) becomes the agent (*kartṛ*) in the same causative form when [the causative suffix] *ṇic* is applied. Furthermore, even when the relationship between the instigator (*prayojaka*) and the instigated (*prayojya*) has ceased, the suffix *ṇic* does not cease; this is because there is no cause for its cessation.

Just as the root *pac* does not cease to denote "cooking" even when Devadatta’s activity has ceased—as in "the rice cooks by itself"—so too here, it should be understood that even when the activities of the instigator and the instigated have ceased, the suffix *ṇic* does not cease. [This applies to examples such as] "they sprinkle," and so forth.

In this case as well, when the elephant being bathed—due to its being well-trained and well-disciplined—exhibits an excellence of conformity toward the act of bathing, then, if one intends to express its status as the *prayojaka* (instigator) and that of the mahouts as the *prayojya* (the one being instigated), the suffix *ṇic* is applied.

When that has been done, as before, if the *prayojyas* are not intended to be expressed, that which was the object (*karman*) in the *aṇ*-ending form becomes the agent (*kartṛ*) in the *ṇi*-ending form.
[This is illustrated by] "they see," and so forth.

Here too, because the king who is being seen attains a state of extreme favorability toward the act of seeing, when his status as the *prayojaka* (instigator) is intended to be expressed, and the servants are intended as the *prayojya* (the one instigated), the suffix *ṇic* is applied. Once that has been prescribed, as before, when there is no intention to express the *prayojya*, that very king who was the object (*karman*) of the root *dṛś* in its non-causative (*aṇyantā*) state becomes the agent (*kartṛ*) in the causative (*ṇyantā*) state. Furthermore, in all these examples, the action itself remains exactly the same in the causative state as it was in the non-causative state.

Even though the causative suffix (*ṇic*) is present, because the relationship between the instigator and the instigated has been set aside and no other action arises, we have forms such as *gaṇayati*. The root *gaṇ* (in the sense of "counting," Dhātupāṭha 1853) is listed among the roots ending in *u* and *ṛ* (the *curādi* class).
From that, the causative suffix *ṇic* is added, and by [Pāṇini 6.4.48], there is the elision of the vowel *ā*.
When its prior rule is to be applied, because of the status of being *sthānivat*, the *vṛddhi* substitution [prescribed by] *ata upadhāyāḥ* [Pāṇini 7.2.116] does not occur:
"The cowherd counts the herd of cows;
the herd itself counts."

In this context, when *gaṇa* is intended to be expressed as the instigator (*prayojaka*)—since it conforms to the process of counting—and *gopālaka* is intended to be expressed as the one being instigated (*prayojya*), then the causative suffix *ṇic* is applied.
Once that has been applied, as before, when the status of the "instigated" is not intended to be expressed, that which was the object becomes the agent.

Nevertheless, because of the rule stating "in the case of the root *aṇ*" (*aṇau*), the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) does not occur; for previously, in the state of the root *aṇ*, *gaṇa* was not the object, but rather [the object] was only in the state of the causative (*ṇyanta*).

But as for what the author of the Vṛtti will say—after stating that some offer the counter-example *cetayamānaṃ prayojayati cetayate* (he causes one who is conscious to act, [and thus] he is conscious) regarding the rule *aṇau* in [Pāṇini 1.3.88]—that is incorrect. For it has been stated: "The rule applies to the causative *ṇic* formed by *hetu*;

by proximity, the prohibition should also logically apply to that alone. If that were true, then even the counter-example *gaṇayati gogaṇaṃ gopālakaḥ* (the cowherd counts the herd of cows) and *gaṇayati gogaṇaḥ svayameva* (the herd of cows counts itself) would be improper. But this is not so; because the distinction [between the agent and the object] is not intended to be expressed.

For if a distinction were intended, then by the rule for the causative suffix *ṇic* (*hetumaṇṇic*), the prohibition would apply only to that [causative] due to proximity, and not to the *cur*-class *ṇic* which is remote. However, no distinction is intended here, because the term "of *ṇi*" (*ṇeḥ*) refers to the genus (*jāti*). Therefore, the rule prescribes *ṇic* in general; consequently, the prohibition must also apply to *ṇic* in general. Thus, this counter-example is appropriate. In the sūtra beginning with "aṇāvakarmakāt" (Pāṇini 1.3.88), the term "aṇau" refers specifically to the causative *ṇic*.
For this very reason, since the rule [for the suffix] applies only to the causative (*hetumaṇic*), it is logical that the prohibition should apply to that alone due to its proximity.
We shall demonstrate exactly how the causative is understood there.

However, no such basis exists here by which one could determine that the term "of *ṇi*" (*ṇeḥ*) refers exclusively to the causative; for even among the roots of the *curādi* class, some are not invariably followed by the causative suffix, and because there exist certain roots where the causative is optional (*vibhāṣitaṇic*), it is possible for those very roots—which are *aṇyant* (without the causative) when they have an object—to possess the status of an agent when they are in the *curādi-ṇijanta* form.

Therefore, it is evident that the author of the Sūtras intended here by the term *ṇeḥ* the inclusion of the causal suffix (*ṇic*) in general. Now, in the case of *gogaṇaḥ svayameva gaṇayati* ("the herd of cows counts itself"), why does the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) not occur, given the extension [of the rule] by the principle *karmavat karmaṇā tulyakriyāḥ* [Pāṇini 3.1.87]? It is because the state (*bhāva*) resides in the agent (*kartṛsthabhāvakatvāt*).

For here, this verb *gaṇayati* denotes a specific kind of cognition consisting of a determination based on enumeration, which is precisely what is called "counting" (*saṃkhyāna*). And that specific cognition resides in the agent, because it inheres in him, and not in the object.

Therefore, because the action resides in the agent (*kartṛsthabhāvakatva*), the *ātmanepada* ending does not occur here. It is desired that the *ātmanepada* occurs through the extended application (*atideśa*) of the "object-like status" (*karmavadbhāva*) for those actions residing in the object (*karmasthakriyā*) and those whose state resides in the object (*karmasthabhāvaka*), but not for others. In examples such as *lunāti dātreṇa* ("he cuts with a sickle"), although the sickle is an instrument (*karaṇa*), it possesses a specific operation due to its sharpness; thus, when there is a desire to express its agency (*prayojakatva*) toward the person who is the reaper, the causative suffix *ṇic* is applied. This is according to the rule beginning with *ṇau cedgrahaṇam*.

In this context, if it were merely stated that "that which is the object in the *aṇ* [causal] state becomes the agent," then by implication it would be understood that the object of the *aṇ* becomes the agent specifically in the *ṇi* (causal) state. Thus, what is the purpose of the phrase "if in the *ṇi*"? It is so that this mention of "if in the *ṇi*" may be understood as requiring the same action (*samānakriyārtha*)—namely, that if the very same action which existed in the state of being an object occurs in the state of being an agent, then [the Ātmanepada suffix applies].
This is what is meant: if the very same meaning of the verbal root that had an object is intended to be expressed as having that same thing as its agent, then the Ātmanepada occurs; not otherwise.

Therefore, in the example "The elephant-keepers mount the elephant; being mounted, the elephant kills those who are afraid and sprinkles them with urine," the *ātmanepada* affix does not occur after the root *siñc* ("to sprinkle"), because the action is different. For indeed, the elephant was intended as the object (*karman*) prior to the action of mounting, but at a later time, in the action of sprinkling, it is the agent (*kartṛ*).
[This is stated: "The mention of the word *yat* is for the purpose of excluding other objects."

When that which is the object (*karman*) in the causative form (*ṇyanta*) becomes the agent (*kartṛ*) in the non-causative form (*an-ṇyanta*), provided it is not a different object, then the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) occurs; not otherwise. But is this not contradictory—for one and the same thing to possess both the state of being an object and the state of being an agent at the same time? This is not contradictory; for one is a property of the actual entity (*vastudharma*), while the other is a property of the speaker's intention (*vivakṣādharma*). When independence (*svātantrya*) is intended, there is the property of being an agent because it is a property of intention; and when it is being carried along (*āruhyamāṇatā*) that is intended, there is the state of being an object because it is a property of the actual entity—as in the example:
"He causes men to ascend the bank" (*sthalam ārohayati manuṣyān*).
In this case, there is also another object (*karmāntara*).
Because [the rule] says "human beings" (*manuṣyān*), it is not the case that the Ātmanepada suffix does not occur simply because the elephant alone is the object.

If this were so, then in the example "he sprinkles those who are afraid with urine" (*bhītān secayati mūtreṇa*), the Ātmanepada would not occur due to the presence of another object; for here too, there is indeed another object—namely, "those who are afraid. Therefore, should it not be stated that [the rule] "if there is a *ṇi*-causal" (*ṇau cet*) is for the sake of [indicating] a single action (*samānakriyārtham*)? This is not the case, for "those who are afraid" (*bhītān*) is not the object of the root *sic* ("to sprinkle"), but rather the object of the root *ā-ruh* ("to mount").

The meaning is that one who, being afraid, mounts [the horse] while wetting himself with urine; this is incorrect, for in such a case as "ārohramāṇa," the middle voice (ātmanepada) and the suffix *śānac* would not occur due to the existence of another object (*karmāntara*).
If that is so, then the suffix *śānac* is certainly not prescribed here; what then? It is the suffix *cānaś*, prescribed by the rule "tācchīlyavayovacanaśaktiṣu" (Pāṇini 3.2.129).

In this context, if the mention of "if [the causative] in *ṇi*" (*ṇau ced*) were not made for the purpose of ensuring the identity of the action, then since the very object of the non-causative form *ārohayati* becomes the agent of the causative form *ārohayate*, that same elephant would be both the object and the agent; thus, the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) would indeed occur.

Therefore, the mention of "if [the causative] in *ṇi*" must be made for the purpose of ensuring the identity of the action. Regarding the question, "What is the purpose of saying 'as the agent' (*kartā*)?", [the answer is:

by this rule, the middle voice is prescribed specifically when there is an agent; for in the case of the abstract state (*bhāva*) or the object (*karman*), it is already established by the rule *bhāvakarmaṇoḥ* (Pāṇini 1.3.13).
Therefore, the intention is that the agent is obtained through the force of the context (*sāmarthya*).

He says—“The elephant-keepers mount the elephant; the chief keeper makes them mount it”—in order to show that the mention of the agent is made for this purpose: the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) occurs only when that which was the object in the non-causative (*aṇyanta*) form is intended as the agent in the causative (*ṇyanta*) form, and not otherwise.

In this case, the elephant which was the object in the non-causative form is not intended as the agent in the causative form; rather, it is the chief keeper (*mahāmātra*). Therefore, the middle voice does not occur here.

And this [result] is obtained from the mention of the *kartṛ* (agent); for that [mention of the agent] serves no other purpose. Now, it might be argued: "It has been stated that the mention of *yat* is for the sake of excluding another object (*ananyakarmārtha*). And here, there exists another object called 'the elephant-driver' (*hastipaka*); therefore, [the rule] will not apply simply because of the mention of *yat*. So what is the use of this mention of *kartṛ* for the purpose of its exclusion? This is not so. For if the mention of *kartṛ* were not made, then the mention of *yat*—which is employed to demonstrate the meaning "that which is the object under the causative (*aṇau*) becomes the agent (*kartā*) itself under the non-causative (*ṇau*) if it was the agent"—would indeed be meaningful. Thus, by mentioning the *kartṛ*, the mention of *yat* becomes purposeful in establishing that very point.

If, however, the mention of the "agent" (*kartṛ*) were not made, that [rule] would simply not have to be applied; how then could the identity of the object (*samānakarmatā*) be understood? The example "he remembers the thicket of trees" (*smarati vanagulmasya*) is given for the purpose of demonstrating the object in the context of the *aṇ* (causative) suffix. It was stated in order to show the object (the domain) by means of its correlate, the status of being a "remainder" (*śeṣatva*) within the scope of the object.

But surely, in this case, there is no object (*karman*); for that [object] is intended to be expressed as a residual element (*śeṣa*). To explain: while the term "residual" (*śeṣe*) from [Pāṇini 2.3.50] is being carried over, this genitive is prescribed by [Pāṇini 2.3.52], *adhīgarthadayeśāṃ karmaṇi śeṣe*, when the object is intended to be expressed as a residual element. Therefore, this should be illustrated as: *smarati vanagulmam* ("he remembers the thicket").
Alternatively—even if it is intended as a subordinate element (*śeṣatva*) to that [action], nevertheless, because it is being remembered, its status as the object (*karmatva*) exists in reality.

Regarding the form *smārayati*: the root *smṛ* is listed in the Dhātupāṭha (807) with the meaning "to remember. When the causative suffix *ṇic* is applied because the thicket of trees (*vanagulma*) is intended as the prompter (*prayojaka*), the designation *mit* is assigned due to its inclusion in the *ghaṭādi* group; consequently, by the rule *mitāṃ hrasvaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.4.92), the shortening of the vowel occurs.
Regarding the word *enam*:

since the designation *karman* (object) applies by the rule "verbs meaning motion, cognition, or eating" [Pāṇini 1.4.52], the substitution of *enad* for *idam* occurs by the rule "the second case ending [is used] for *idam* and *adas*" [Pāṇini 2.4.34].

Now, one might object: the inclusion of the term *sa-* (with an object) is intended to exclude cases where there is no other object; and here, since there is another object, namely the *kokila* (cuckoo), the *ātmanepada* (middle voice) will not occur due to the existence of that other object. Therefore, what is the purpose of including the phrase *anādhyāne* (except in the sense of meditation/contemplation) to exclude such cases? This is not so; this counter-example is presented with the intention of expressing a case where there is merely meditation (*ādhyāna*).

The expression "enama" (it [the forest thicket] itself) should be understood as intended to demonstrate the meaning that the forest thicket is the agent and not the cuckoo. Thus, "the forest thicket reminds the forest thicket" means that it causes itself to be remembered by itself.

When the causative suffix (*ṇic*) has been elided, because the cuckoo—the object of the action—is intended [as the agent], the relationship between the instigator (*prayojaka*) and the one being instigated (*prayojya*) ceases; consequently, the verb *smarati* with its causative ending (*ṇyant*) reverts to its original meaning.

Now, one might object: "Recollection is a property of sentient beings, and a forest thicket is insentient; how then can it recollect? This is not so; for even in the case of insentient things, there is a metaphorical attribution (*upacāra*) of properties belonging to sentient beings—just as one says, "the riverbank wishes to fall.
Thus, it is said that "the root *ruh* has its action residing in the agent" (*kartṛstha-kriya*).
Because the object of that [action], which consists in the state of being subordinated, is inherent in the elephant-drivers;

and because "the root *dṛś* has its state of being located in the agent" (*kartṛsthabhāvaka*), since the object of that [action], namely the act of seeing, is established in the agents, the servants; and [because of the rule] "*hetubhaye*" (when fear arises from a cause).
"Fear of the cause" (*hetubhaya*) is a compound meaning "fear arising from a cause. Here, *bhīti* means fear— that is, terror or the apprehension that something undesirable might occur.
"From that, fear arises":
if fear arises from that instigator designated as the "cause" (hetu), then the middle voice (ātmanepada) occurs, and not otherwise.

If this were so, the meaning of the root *smi* would not be specified; because fear is the meaning of *bhī* alone and not of *smṛ*, it would follow that the middle voice would also occur in forms such as *vismāyayati*.
In cases such as *muṇḍo vismāpayate* ("the shaven-headed man causes amazement"), [the rule] would not apply; therefore, he says "the mention of *bhaya*" (*bhayagrahaṇam*), and so forth.
For the mention of *bhaya* is intended as an illustration of the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*).

If the meaning of the verbal root arises from an instigator (*prayojaka*), this is the sense intended. Consequently, even if amazement (*vismaya*) arises from that very same cause—if this meaning is obtained—then the sense of the root *smi* (to smile/be amazed) is likewise specifically qualified.
*Vismayaḥ* means wonder.
Regarding the term *muṇḍaḥ*:
he is called *muṇḍaḥ* because he is endowed with the quality (*guṇa*) of being shaven-headed (*muṇḍa*).
Regarding the form *bhīṣayate*:

from the root *ñibhī* in the sense of "fear" (Dhātupāṭha 1084), there is optionally (*vibhāṣā*) the substitution of *ā* for the root vowel according to [Pāṇini 6.1.51], and by the subsequent application of [Pāṇini 6.1.56], the *ā* is applied in one alternative;
then, by [Pāṇini 7.3.40], the augment *ṣuk* is added.
Regarding "vismāpayate":

the root *smiṅ* is listed in the Dhātupāṭha as *smiṅ īṣaddhasane* (Dhātupāṭha 948). By [Pāṇini 6.1.57], the vowel is lengthened (*āttva*); by [Pāṇini 7.3.36], *rtihyī* etc., the suffix *puk* is added. Regarding "he terrifies him with a key."
In this case, the fear arises from the *karaṇa* (instrument), not from the *hetu* (agent/causal agent) as the instigator (*prayojaka*).
Therefore, the *ātmanepada* (middle voice) ending does not occur.

Furthermore, the substitution of *ṣuk* also does not occur here, for that is desired only for roots ending in long *ī*; this is because, in the rule [Pāṇini 7.3.40], there is an elided mention (*praśleṣa*) of the vowel *ī* in the form "bhī ī."

Regarding the statement "he causes wonder by means of his form" (*rūpeṇa vismāyayati*), here the wonder arises precisely from the instrument (*karaṇa*) and not from the cause (*hetu*). As for the phrase "because there is no distinction" (*viśeṣābhāvāt*):

how can there be an absence of distinction when, in fact, there is indeed a distinction between these two, namely, being without an *anubandha* (*niranubandhaka*) and being with an *anubandha* (*sānubandhaka*)? Consequently, according to the metarule (*paribhāṣā*) "when a term without an *anubandha* is mentioned, that which has an *anubandha* is not included" (*niranubandhakagrahaṇe na sānubandhakasya*), there ought to be no inclusion of *līṅ* [in the rule].

Is it not then incorrect to say that both are grasped because there is no distinction between them? This is not a fault; for here, the suffix *lyap* occurs with its indicatory letter (*anubandha*) dropped. When the indicatory letter is dropped, only two things remain as differentiators: the meaning and the fact of being a different word.
In this case, first, the meaning of these two is one and the same, and furthermore, they are not different words.

A difference in words arises from a difference in the verbal root (*prakṛti*) or a difference in the suffix (*vikaraṇa*). However, there is neither a difference in the root nor a difference in the suffix between these two forms ending in *ṇi*; for both have the suffix *śap*. Furthermore, the substitution of *ā* [for the penultimate vowel] by [Pāṇini 6.1.51] applies to both as well.
And so he will say: "What is this [meaning] of the root *lī*? It is an indication [of the meaning] by means of the suffix *ya*, which is adventitious to both *līna* and *atilīyate*.
"[The meaning is] subordination" (*nyagbhāva*);
that is to say, the sense of being overcome.
Regarding the phrase "by means of matted locks" (*jaṭābhiḥ*):
the third case ending is used in the sense of cause (*hetu*).
For matted locks are indeed the cause for attaining honor and other such benefits.

For instance: "He who has matted hair is a great ascetic in this world"—thus he is honored by those who have conceived such a conviction. Regarding the term *mithyopapadāt*: an *upapada* is a word uttered in proximity; that which has the word *mithyā* as its *upapada* is described as such. An example is: *padaṃ mithyā kārayate*.
Since the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) endings have already indicated the repetition here, by [Pāṇini 8.1.4], reduplication does not occur.
"Sāpacāram" means "with fault" (i.e., defective).
By this, he explains the meaning of the word *mithyā* as "corrupted by defects of vowels and so forth," thereby clarifying the meaning of the preceding term itself.

By the word "ādi" (and so forth), "rūpa" is included. Regarding the term "asakṛt" (repeatedly), he demonstrates the meaning of the word "abhyāsa" (repetition) by means of an example. Regarding the phrase "when intended for the agent" (*kartṛbhiprāye*).
"‘It goes toward the agent’ (kartāram abhipraitīti) [3.2.1].

If the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) were to apply wherever the fruit of the action generally goes toward the agent, then it would also occur here in cases such as *pacanti pācakāḥ* (the cooks cook) and *yajanti yājakāḥ* (the sacrificers sacrifice).

For in these instances, the fruit of the action—the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*)—goes toward the sacrificers who are the agents, and the wages go toward the cooks; therefore, he says: ‘The fruit of the action,’ and so forth."
In this context, that result which is the primary factor of an action is what is understood;
and since the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) and so forth are not the primary results of an action, there is no over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).
To the question, "What, then, is that primary [result]? he says: "That for the sake of which," and so on.
By this it is meant that the sacrifice and other such rites are undertaken for the sake of that [result], and not for the sake of the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) and so forth.
"For the sake of what" means for the sake of heaven (*svarga*) and the like, and not for the sake of the sacrificial fee and the like.
For instance, rituals such as sacrifice are undertaken for the sake of heaven and the like, but not for the sake of the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) and so forth.
The phrase "for the sake of which" (*yadartham*) is an adverbial modifier of the action.
By the word *yat*, the fruit which constitutes the primary element of the action is indicated.

If the intention were merely to grasp the fruit alone—regardless of what that purpose or motive for the commencement of the action might be—then the inclusion of the term "fruit" (*phala*) would be redundant, because there is no such case where the fruit of an action does not intend toward the agent. Consequently, one should have simply stated: "when [the fruit] is intended by the agent" (*kartṛ-abhiprāye kriyāyāḥ*).

Even when this has been stated, once the sixth [case-ending] has conveyed that the intention belongs to the agent (*kartṛ*) in relation to the action, it is understood by implication that the fruit alone possesses the agent's intention regarding the action;
for no other thing related to the action intends toward the agent. Therefore, by the force of the mention of "fruit" (*phala*), the primary fruit is what is grasped.
Alternatively, because it is the primary factor, the primary result alone is understood;
as it has been said: "Because the understanding of the effect resides in the primary factor, [the rule] is established.
In this interpretation, the mention of the "result" (phala) is for the sake of clarity, since the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) is prescribed when the agent is the object.

If it is argued that the agent must be declared to be proximate [to the action] because it is understood that the fruit belongs to him alone, he says: "And that," etc. The meaning has already been explained. "Heaven and so forth," etc.
By the word "etc. (*ādi*), rice and other such items are also included.
With the words "nevertheless" (*tathāpi*) and so forth, [the author] demonstrates that the fruit consisting of the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) and the like is secondary.
That for the sake of which an action is undertaken is the primary fruit intended here.

Furthermore, rituals such as sacrifice are undertaken for the sake of heaven and the like, not for the sake of the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) and so forth. Therefore, because it is not the motive, that [the fee] is not primary. Consequently, even though it is directed toward the agent, the ātmanepada suffix does not occur.

Now, for what purpose is the inclusion of the term *abhipragrahaṇa* (the prefix *abhi-*)? It is so that [the definition] may apply even when the fruit is remote. For the fruit of an action is twofold: proximate and remote. Among these, the proximate is that whose accomplishment occurs immediately after the operation [of the cause]. The remote, however, is that which, once the operations have ceased, arises only after a long time due to the ripening of latent impressions (*saṃskāra*), depending on other intervening causes and being characterized by a lapse of time.
Among these, the first is primary with respect to origination because it is proximate, directly perceived, and free from deviation;
the other, however, is secondary with respect to origination because it is remote, inferable, and subject to deviation.
Although that [remote result] is also primary since the action is undertaken for its sake, nevertheless, in comparison to a result that is not remote, its lack of primacy certainly remains.

In this regard, if the inclusion of *abhi* were not made, then [the rule] would apply only to cases such as *lunīta* ("mow") and *punīta* ("purify"), where the fruit of the action is immediate (*aviprakṛṣṭa*).

However, it would not apply to cases such as *yajate* ("sacrifices"), where the fruit of the action, such as heaven (*svarga*), is remote (*viprakṛṣṭa*), because grammatical operations are understood to apply to the principal element.
But when *abhi* is included, there is no fault; for the word *abhi* denotes "facing toward" (*ābhimukhya*), while the word *pra* denotes the commencement of an entity (*sattvārambha*).
Therefore, when the intentionality toward the mere commencement is relied upon for the accomplishment of the result, it becomes established in all cases.

Now, one might object: "Even if the term *abhi-pra* were not included, the [suffix] would still apply to the roots such as *yaj* (to sacrifice) and others—even for a remote result—simply because of the attachment of specific suffixes (*anubandha*); otherwise, that [term] would be redundant. This is not so; for it is meaningful in cases such as malevolent magic (*abhicāra*), where a result is observed to be immediate.

Therefore, the inclusion of the word *iti* must indeed be made for the purpose that [the suffix] may occur even when the fruit is remote and not the primary factor. With the words "by way of censuring the right course" (*nyāyāpavādena*), he shows the intention by which one who desires wealth censures the right course. "He exerts himself" (*udyacchati*) means:
"The physician (*vaidya*) [exerts himself in] medical treatment" (*cikitsā*);
the meaning is that he makes an effort to master the science of medicine. It is a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "one for whom there are no [other] prefixes."

This [rule] is intended for the sense of the transitive (sakarmaka) verb, because it is already established by the rule *kṛta-sakarmakārtheñ* (Pāṇini 1.3.45). In that context, five sūtras beginning with *svaritañitaḥ* (Pāṇini 1.3.72) are understood to follow: "when the fruit of the action is intended for the agent, provided it is appropriate."

By what is it indicated? It should be understood that it is indicated by the ātmanepada [suffix] because of its being the subject under discussion. [The objection: "When it is already indicated by an upapada, [the suffix] would not apply," because words whose meaning has already been expressed are not employed.

By this, he shows that this is an *aprāpta-vibhāṣā* (an option where [the rule] was not otherwise established). But is it not the case that in the example *svaṃ yajñaṃ yajate*, [the application of the suffix] is not possible because the word *sva* is an *upapada*? For, under the heading of the second verbal root (*dhātu*), it is stated: "In that context, what is situated in the seventh case is called an *upapada*" (*Pāṇini 3.1.92*). Since the word *sva* is not of such a kind, he says: "That which is heard in proximity," and so forth. By this, he demonstrates that the term *upapada* is taken in its etymological sense—as a word uttered in proximity (*upa-uccārita*)—and not in its technical (*pāribhāṣika*) sense.
And this is understood because a literal sense is impossible;
he provides an example for the first sūtra among the five beginning with "one's own sacrifice" (*svaṃ yajñam*),
and for the second beginning with "one's own son" (*svaṃ putram*).
"In this way, one should cite [an example] from the *Pañcasūtrī*.
The phrase "elsewhere as well" is to be supplied.
The meaning is that one should cite examples not only from the sūtra contained within the *Pañcasūtrī*, but also from elsewhere.
He causes his own mat to be made, or he makes it himself. He gathers his own rice, or he gathers it himself. He lifts his own burden, or he lifts it himself.

"He stretches his own garment" (*svaṃ vastramāyacchate*, *āyacchati vā*) or "he recognizes his own cow" (*svaṃ gāṃ jānīte*, *jānāti vā*). These are examples as appropriate for the sūtras beginning with *ṇicaśca* [Pāṇini 1.3.74]. "By the preceding [rule]" (*pūrveṇa*).
By the rule beginning with *anudāttahitaḥ* [Pāṇini 1.3.12],
[the suffix] would apply "everywhere," that is,
even to all [stems] without exception.
"This is said for that purpose" means:
since the *parasmaipada* (active voice) would otherwise apply in all cases, this is stated to exclude it; for the word *artha* has the sense of "exclusion.
Likewise, as in the expression "smoke for the sake of the mosquito."
Thus, it is stated that this [sūtra] is for the purpose of restriction (niyamārtha).
By the words "from which roots" and so forth, he demonstrates the status of being a "remainder" (śeṣatva). By the phrase "by whichever qualification," etc.
By means of the suffixes (*anubandha*) and so forth:
"yāti" and "vāti" are examples of the remainder of a suffix;
"āviśati" and "praviśati" are examples of the remainder of a prefix and also of the remainder of meaning.

In this way, examples such as "he performs [an action] other than indicating" (gandhana) and so forth are to be understood. Now, one might object: by the rule *śeṣāt* (Pāṇini 1.3.78), which consists of a word ending in the fifth case (*pañcamyanta*) and is in grammatical apposition with the verbal root (*dhātu*), it is the root itself that is qualified, not its meaning. Consequently, the active voice (*parasmaipada*) would result even in cases where the meanings are not among those beginning with "indicating" (*gandhana*). This is not so; for the meanings beginning with "indicating" are indeed the meanings of the verbal base (*prakṛti*) itself. Therefore, when the term *śeṣa* ("remainder") is excluded from those meanings, it also excludes them. For example: *pacyate*, *gamyate*.

But surely, if there were a *parasmaipada* ending here, then the rule [Pāṇini 1.3.13] would be rendered purposeless because it would have no scope; this is not so, for it does indeed have its scope. What, then, is that scope? It is that which is not a *śeṣa*—namely, *āsyate*, *śayyate*, *kriyate*.
For the property of having an *anudātta* vowel and the property of being marked with *ṅ* constitute non-*śeṣa* status.

To one who might object that in the rule *śeṣāt kartari* [Pāṇini 1.3.78], the mention of the agent (*kartṛ*) is taken in a general sense, he replies with the words "in the case of the agent who is also the object" (*karmakartari*), and so forth.
He refutes this by means of the rule *kartari karmavyatīhāre* [Pāṇini 1.3.14] and others, stating:
"the agent who is indeed the agent himself."
"Pure" means one who is an agent devoid of the nature of an agent, as it were. Regarding "abhikṣipati":
the suffix *śa* is applied because it belongs to the *tudādigaṇa*. Regarding "parimṛṣyati":
the suffix *śyan* is applied because it belongs to the *divādigaṇa*. [This is also] by the rule "upācca."
The particle *ca* has the sense of conjunction (*samuccaya*) with respect to what precedes it. [An example is:
"He causes Devadatta to cease. Now, one might object: the root *ram*, preceded by the prefix *upa*, is indeed intransitive (*akarmaka*).
Likewise, when preceded by *upa*, this [root] has the sense of destruction—as in "they have ceased" (*uparatāni*) or "they have perished" (*naṣṭāni*), which is understood.
Or it has the sense of desisting—as in "he desists from his Vedic study" (*svādhyāyāduparamate*), which is understood as "he turns back.
And for a verb occurring in this sense, transitivity is not possible.

He states that the example provided for a transitive verb is appropriate: "uparamayati, meaning 'he causes to cease'. By this, he demonstrates that the root *upa-ram* functions in the sense of the causative suffix (*ṇic*) and thereby establishes its transitivity;
for a root that is intransitive becomes transitive when it occurs in the sense of the causative.
Now, how is it further possible for the root *anta* to function in the sense of the causative (*ṇyartha*)? It has been stated as such.

For one of this kind, its status as transitive (*sakarmakatva*) with respect to the object of the action (*prayojya*) is indeed established. Now, for what purpose is a separate rule (*pṛthagyoga*) made? [One might suggest: "Let there be only a single rule, 'na vyāṅparyupebhyo ramaḥ'. To this he says: "The making of a separate rule," and so forth. The meaning has already been explained. "As much as has been eaten" (*yāvadbhuktam*).
> [[2.1.8]] Thus ends the section on *avyayībhāva* compounds. Regarding the word *bhuktam*:
the suffix *kta* is applied according to [Pāṇini 3.3.114], *napuṃsake bhāve ktaḥ*.
The meaning is that one desists from as many meals as there are.
Alternatively, "yāvadbhuktam" is an avyayībhāva compound in its literal sense, expressing repetition.

The meaning is that one should desist from food after having eaten. [The following are listed from the Dhātupāṭha: *budha* in the sense of "understanding" (DhP 1172); *yudha* in the sense of "combat" (DhP 1173); *ṇaśa* in the sense of "disappearance" (DhP 1194); *janī* in the sense of "manifestation" (DhP 1149); *ih* in the sense of "studying" (DhP 1046); *cyuṅ*, *jyuṅ*, *jhayuṅ*, *pruṅ*, and *pluṅ* in the sense of "motion" (DhP 955–958); and *du*... [text truncated].
The roots *dru* and *su* are listed in the Dhātupāṭha as meaning "to go" (*gatau*) at numbers 944, 945, and 940 respectively.
Regarding the form *janayati*,
the designation *mit* is applied by the rule beginning with *janījṛṣ* (Gaṇasūtra/Dhātupāṭha 817).
The shortening of *mit* [vowels] occurs; thus,
in "adhyāpayati," there is the substitution of *āt* by [Pāṇini 6.1.48].

As before, [the term] *puk* [is applied]. Regarding the phrase "examples concerning this," the meaning is that these examples— such as *prāvayati* and so forth— are, respectively, examples concerning attainment (*prāpti*), dissolution (*vilayana*), and flowing (*syandana*).
In common usage, *syandana* is well known as "flowing" or "movement.
Beyond that, it should be understood as "causing to flow.
*Prāvayati* means "causes to reach" (*prāpayati*), and *drāvayati* means "causes to melt" (*vilāpayati*).
*ruāāvayati* means "he causes to flow" (*syandayati*). According to *Bālamano ramā*, rule 1.3.86, *vibhāṣā'karmakāt*:
the terms *upāt*, *rama*, and *parasmaipada* are understood from the preceding context. Therefore, it says: "from *upa* and *ram*."
From *budh*, *yudh*, *naś*, *jan*, *iṅ*, *pru*, *dru*, and *ru* [the suffix] *ṇiC* [is applied].
(Pāṇini 3.1.86). This is a *dvandva* compound of *budha*, *yudha*, *naś*, *jana*, *iṅ*, *pru*, *dru*, and *ru*.
[Examples include: "He causes the lotus to bloom" (*bodhayati padmam*).
The word "sūrya" (sun) is to be supplied [as the agent]. The root *budh* has the sense of "blooming. The lotus blooms.

The meaning is that the sun causes that [lotus] to bloom. However, the *parasmaipada* ending does not apply here by the rule "after a root that is intransitive in the *aṇ* [causal] sense and has a sentient agent," because in the *aṇ* sense, the lotus is the agent and thus lacks a sentient agent. [An example of the rule is: "he causes the pieces of wood to fight."
"The pieces of wood fight by themselves";
the meaning is that "he causes them to fight.
Because the agent is not endowed with consciousness (*acittavat*), the application of the rule *aṇāvakarmakāt* does not occur.

For this very reason, "he causes Devadatta to fight" (*yodhayati devadattam*) was not cited as an example, because [the desired form] is already established by the rule *aṇāvakarmakāccittavatkartṛkā* (Pāṇini 1.3.88). The same should be understood for subsequent cases as well.
For instance, in the case of "he destroys suffering" (*nāśayati duḥkham*).
"Suffering perishes" means that Hari destroys it;
"He produces happiness" means that happiness arises, and Hari generates it.
Regarding "he causes to study":
the meaning is that the injunction (vidhi) studies the Veda, and he causes that [Veda] to be studied.
He provides an example of the root *pru* in the sense of "motion" (*gatau*)—namely, *prāvayati*.
Considering that it has the sense of "going," he says: "the meaning is 'he causes to reach'.
Regarding "he causes to melt": clarified butter (*ājya*) flows; the meaning is "he causes that to flow."
Considering that the root *dhā* has the sense of "becoming liquid," he says: "the meaning is 'he causes to flow' (*syāndayati*).

As for the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) in the phrase "who generates joy in his devotees" (*prītiṃ bhaktajanasya yo janayate*), it is merely a scribal error. Alternatively, the devotee generates joy toward Hari as the object of their own self; [the text] then uses the form derived from the causative suffix (*ṇic*) with the further suffix *ṇau*, meaning "Hari generates that [joy]."

They say that the genitive case in "bhaktajanasya" is used because the agent who causes the action (*prayojyakartṛ*) is intended to be expressed as a subordinate factor (*śeṣatva*). Regarding "nigārayati," [the root] *gṛ* is listed in the Dhātupāṭha (1410) with the meaning "swallowing.
Regarding "āśayati": [it is derived from the root *śī*].
The root *aś* is used in the sense of eating (*bhojane*; Dhātupāṭha 1523);
thus, "he causes to eat" (*bhojayati*).
The root *bhuja* is used in the senses of protecting and eating (*pālanābhyavahārayoḥ*; Dhātupāṭha 1046); thus, "he moves" (*calati*).
The root *cal* means "to shake" (*dhātupāṭhaḥ* 832).
Due to its inclusion in the *ghaṭādi* group, it has the *mittva* designation; consequently, as before, there is shortening [of the penultimate vowel].
Thus: *copayati*.
The root *cup* is listed as "in the sense of slow movement" (Dhātupāṭha 403).
[The form] "kampayati" [is derived from] the root *kap*,
which means "to move" (Dhātupāṭha 375).
This rule (*yoga*) also has the sense of "having an object" (*sakarmaka*) and the sense of "having an agent that is not sentient" (*acittavat-kartṛka*).
This is because, for those [roots] contrary to those [conditions], the desired result is already established by the rule *aṇāvakarmakāccitavatkartṛkāt* (Pāṇini 1.3.88).
Among the examples presented therein, two—*cali* and *kamp*—are intransitive (*akarmaka*); for these two, this rule is intended to apply to cases where the agent is not sentient.

"But for the remaining [roots], the meaning of 'having an object' (sakarmaka) must be stated"—this means it must be explained. In this regard, the explanation is as follows: from [Pāṇini 1.3.85], the term *vibhāṣā* ("optionally") is carried over by "frog-leap" (*maṇḍūkapluti*), and that is understood to be a restricted option (*vyavasthitavibhāṣā*).

Therefore, the *parasmaipada* ending occurs invariably after roots other than *ad*, but it does not occur at all after *ad*. For example, in "ādayate devadattena" (he causes Devadatta to eat), the designation of *karman* (object) does not apply by virtue of the rule *gatibuddhipratyavasānārthaśabdakarmākarmakāṇām aṇikartā sa ṇau* [Pāṇini 1.4.52]; this is because of the statement: "There is a prohibition for the roots *ad*, *khād*, *nī*, and *vah*" (Vārttika 64). [The word] "cetayamānam" (being conscious).

The root *cit* in the sense of "perceiving" (*saṃjñāna*) belongs to the curādigaṇa; it is intransitive and has an agent possessing consciousness (*cittavat*). This refers to the rule for the causative suffix *ṇic*.

In this rule, the mention of *ṇic* from the sūtra beginning with *budha* (Pāṇini 1.3.86) is understood here, and that is specifically the *hetumaṇic* (the causative suffix); for no other *ṇic* is possible after roots such as *budh*.

Since the prescription concerns the *hetumaṇic*, it is logical that its prohibition alone should apply due to proximity (*pratyāsatti*). For exactly the same kind of thing that is the subject of the prescription must be the subject of the prohibition, owing to proximity.

For instance, when it is said, "Let the Brāhmaṇas enter, except for those who study other [Vedas]," the exclusion (paryudāsa) is understood to apply to those of the same class as those for whom entry was prescribed, due to their proximity.
{The printed reading is `ārohramāṇaḥ`; however, it is `ārohamāṇam`.} The middle voice (ātmanepada) is applied by the rule Pāṇini 1.3.67, *ṇer aṇau yaḥ*, etc.

Although here the causative suffix (*ṇic*) is prescribed with the intention of expressing that the elephant is the instigator (*prayojaka*) with respect to the elephant-keepers (*hastipaka*), nevertheless, in the state of being under the influence of the causative suffix (*ṇyantāvasthā*), the elephant-keepers are not intended to be the objects of instigation (*prayojyatvena*). Otherwise, the rule "that which is the object in the non-causative base (*haṇau*) becomes the agent in the causative (*ṇau*)" would not hold.
In that case, when the status of being an object of instigation is not intended, the form *ārohayamāṇa* means "he himself causes [himself] to mount.
When another person then employs that one who is causing [himself] to mount, then a second causative suffix (*hetumaṇṇic*) is applied.
After that [suffix], the *ātmanepada* ending occurs by the rule *ṇicaśca* [Pāṇini 1.3.74].

Therefore, *ārohayate* is indeed the appropriate counter-example. Regarding the term *pā*, according to the principle *lugvikaraṇālugvikaraṇayoralugvikaraṇasyaiva grahaṇam* (Vyākaraṇa-paribhāṣā 50), only the root *pā pāne* (Dhātupāṭha 925) is taken, and not *pā rakṣaṇe* (Dhātupāṭha 1056).
The roots *damu upaśame* (Dhātupāṭha 1203) and *yama uparame* (Dhātupāṭha 984)—these two are preceded by the prefix *āṅ*—and *yasu prayatne* (Dhātupāṭha 1210) [are also included].

The roots *muh* (in the sense of "bewilderment," Dhātupāṭha 1198) preceded by *pari*; *ruc* (in the sense of "shining," 745); *nṛt* (in the sense of "waving the limbs," Dhātupāṭha 1116); *vad* (in the sense of "distinct speech," Dhātupāṭha 1009); and *vas* (in the sense of "dwelling," Dhātupāṭha 1005)—the inclusion of *vas* in the sense of "covering" does not occur here for the very reason stated previously.
The phrase "by the two preceding rules" means "without them."
The root *nṛt* also has the meaning "to move";
by the word "also" (*api*), it also has the meaning "to cause the agent who possesses consciousness to act.
As for the form *pāyayate*: [it means "he causes himself to drink"].
When there is a desire to express that *pāti* is intransitive (*akarmaka*), the *parasmaipada* ending occurs,
as in *pālayati*. The augment *luk* is applied by the supplementary rule (*upasaṃkhyāna*) stating, "The elision [*luk*] of [the suffix] should be stated for *pāti*" (Vārttika 2 on Pāṇini 7.3.37).
In *damayate*,
as before, there is the shortening [of the penultimate vowel] according to Pāṇini 6.4.92 (*mitāṃ hrasvaḥ*). In *āyāmayate*, [the same applies].

Now, one might object that since this [root] is also included among the *pi*-roots, it ought to take the suffix *hrasva*; to this he says: "the root *yam* except in the sense of 'encircling' (*pariveṣaṇa*).
For in that context, the word "not" (*na*) is understood to carry over from the rule "not after *kam*, *yam*, and *cam*" (Gaṇasūtra on the Dhātupāṭha, root 817). [The word] "āṅ" [is used].

The mention of the vowel *ā* as qualified by the word *sva* (itself) is for the purpose of understanding it as a prefix (*upasarga*). Consequently, there is no inclusion of that vowel *ā* which is merely a formal imitation of a prefix. [Regarding the rule] "An addition of *dheṭ* to the *pā-* group," the term "in the *pā-* group" is a locative of domain (*viṣaya-saptamī*).
The purpose of the term *upasaṃkhyāna* is to provide an additional rule (*pratipādana*).
An additional rule must be formulated regarding the prohibition of the *parasmaipada* for the root *dheṭ* when it falls within the scope of the *pā-* [roots].
The meaning is that this very prohibition of the *parasmaipada* which applies to the scope of the *pā-* roots also applies to *dheṭ*.

In this regard, the following is the demonstration: the word "na" (not) is separated [from the previous rule] by means of *yogavibhāga* (splitting the rule); by that, the prohibition will apply to the root *dheṭ* as well.

If this is so, since the result is already established by "na" alone, is the mention of "pādīnām" (of the roots beginning with *pā*) purposeless? It is not purposeless; it is for the sake of making known that the preceding rule does not have universal application (*asarvaviṣayatva*).
Thus, we have the form "dhāpayete."
From the root *dheṭ* "to drink" (*dhātupāṭha* 902), the substitution of *ā* for the initial vowel occurs by [Pāṇini 6.1.44] *ādeca upadeśe'śiti*, and the augment *puk* is added as before.

Regarding the word *śiśum*: the accusative case is used because it receives the technical designation *karman* (object) by [Pāṇini 1.4.52] *gatibuddhipratyavasānārtha...*. Regarding the form *lohitāyati*: [the suffix *kāmyac* is applied].
Regarding the sense "that which was not red becomes red," the suffix *kyaṣ* is applied according to [Pāṇini 3.1.13].
The lengthening of the vowel occurs by [Pāṇini 7.4.25]: "before a non-ṛt affix and before a sārvadhātuka affix.
Thus, one says "paṭapaṭāyati" (it crackles).

When the suffix *ḍāc* is applicable to the word *paṭat*, there is reduplication by virtue of the supplementary rule (*upasaṃkhyāna*) "there is frequently reduplication before *ḍāc*" (Vārttika 888). Then, by the rule "after an imitation of an indistinct sound" (Pāṇini 5.4.57), the suffix *ḍāc* is added. Consequently, regarding the final *t* of the word *paṭat* and the *p* that follows it, [the question is] "how?"—meaning, "not in any way.
He asks for the reason why this is not obtained, and says: "Insofar as," etc.

For the *ātmanepada* [suffixes] are restricted by rules such as "anudāttaṅitaḥ" (Pāṇini 1.3.12); therefore, it cannot be understood that they apply to a form ending in *kyaṣ*. He provides the rebuttal with the words "In that case, then," etc. "Optionally" (*vikalpitam*) means "alternatively" (*vibhāṣitam*), that is to say, occurring only occasionally (*pākṣikam*).

But surely, since the *ātmanepada* is excluded by the *parasmaipada*, it cannot be understood because it is not present; to this he says: "And that," etc. When the fruit of the action is intended to belong to the agent (*kartṛ*), the *ātmanepada* would have applied; however, the *parasmaipada* was prescribed by two rules beginning with [Pāṇini 1.3.49] as an exception (*apavāda*) to that.
By the prohibition established in the immediately following rule against that exception, the *parasmaipada* is removed and the *ātmanepada* is brought into proximity.
When an exception (*apavāda*) has been set aside, there must necessarily be an application (*utsarga*) by rule.
Thus, the *ātmanepada* [suffix], which is brought to mind here by the prohibition, is connected [to the rule].

If, then, by this [rule] the *ātmanepada* alone is optionally prescribed for the agent (*kartṛ*), one might ask how the *parasmaipada* is obtained in the alternative case; to this he says: "by that," and so forth. Now, since the root *dyut* is singular, the use of the plural form is not appropriate; to this he says: "due to association with that," and so forth.

Just as, by association with a single person holding an umbrella, others who accompany him are also called "umbrella-bearers"—as in the expression "the umbrella-bearers are walking"—so too here, by association with *dyuti* (light), *jñāti* and the others are designated as "*dyuta*.
But how is this intended meaning established when there is a designation for only one? To this he says: "Because of the use of the plural number," and so forth.
For he demonstrates that this meaning is established even without the word "etc. (*ādi*), since its sense is thereby obtained.
Regarding the phrase "ending with *kṛp*":
by this, he indicates that those which are recited after *kṛp* do not belong to the *dyutādi* group.
This is understood from the fact that the *vṛt* marker is placed immediately after it, serving as an indicator for the completion of the list.
Regarding the form *vyadyutat*:
because it belongs to the *puṣādi* class, the suffix *aṅ* is applied.

If this is so, then since *aṅ* is prescribed for these very roots, the *parasmaipada* (active voice) endings will follow from them; what is the purpose of this rule? This is not the case; for by virtue of this indicator (*jñāpaka*), it is understood that the *parasmaipada* endings are obligatory in the *luṅ* (aorist) tense.
Furthermore, one might suspect that the *ātmanepada* does not occur elsewhere than after the root *lū*.

But surely it will not occur elsewhere by virtue of the power of the designation as having an *anudātta* vowel? This is not so; the designation as having an *anudātta* vowel would be for the sake of [the rule] *yujir yoge* (Pāṇini 3.2.149).
Therefore, this rule (*yoga*) must be formulated.
He rolled about.

[The root] *luṭh* [is used] in the sense of "striking against" (*pratīghāta*) [according to the Dhātupāṭha, roots 747 and 749]. Regarding the phrase "in the presence of *syat* and *san*" (*syasanoḥ*), this is a locative absolute construction (*satī saptamī*).

In forms such as *vatsyati*, since the word *asici* (in the absence of *sic*) is carried over from the rule *se'sici* [Pāṇini 7.2.57], and since the word *parasmaipade ca* (and in the case of the Parasmaipada) is carried over from the subsequent rule *na vṛdbhyaścatubhryaḥ* [Pāṇini 7.2.59], there is a prohibition of the augment *iṭ*.
However, in the Ātmanepada,
the *iṭ* augment indeed occurs, as in *vivṛtsati*.
> [[1.2.10]] Thus, due to the *kit* suffix, there is an absence of *guṇa*. As for the phrase "the letter *ca*, then," and so forth:
the intention is that since [the forms] *syasanoḥ* would already be established by virtue of belonging to the *vṛt-ādi* group, this is a rule for optional variation (*vikalpa*).
By the words "if that is so, then" and so forth, it is understood that a specific rule (*viśeṣavidhāna*) serves as an exception (*bādhaka*) to a general rule (*sāmānyavidhāna*).

But surely, if this *prāpti* (attainment) subverts the attainment of *kṛp*, would it not follow that its recitation in [the list of] *dyutādi* verbs is rendered useless? This is not so; for it is for the sake of the *aṅga* (stem). But surely, the *svarita* accent is intended for *syasanoḥ*; therefore, there will be no subversion of that [rule]. True, this is so; however, the author of the Sūtras placed the *ca* for the sake of variety, not for the sake of the *svarita* accent.
[Thus we have the form] *kalptā*.

When the two governing rules (adhikāra) from the previous section continue to apply, there is a prohibition of the augment *iṭ* by [Pāṇini 7.2.60] *tāsi ca kḷpaḥ*. Then, the substitution of *ḍa* [by 7.1.3] and the change of *ḍa* to *la* [by 8.2.18] result in the form *cikḷpsati*.

As before, due to the *kit* designation, there is an absence of *guṇa*. Thus ends the third quarter (*pāda*) of the first chapter in the *Kāśikā-vivaraṇapañjikā*, composed by the venerable Master Jinendrabuddhi, who is a teacher of the Bodhisattvas. Regarding the rule "that which is subsequent" (*yā parā*):

where there is a conflict (*vipratiṣedha*), that which is subsequent prevails, according to the statement "In a conflict, the subsequent [rule takes effect]" (*vipratiṣedhe param*, Pāṇini 1.4.2). And regarding "that which has no scope" (*anavakāśā ca yā*).
Even that technical term for which there is no scope anywhere else proceeds by way of being an exception (*apavāda*), thereby setting aside other technical terms.

If this is so, then for this very reason there will be no co-occurrence (*samāveśa*) of technical terms; what then is the purpose of the governing rule (*adhikāra*) regarding "one technical term"? This is not the case, for it is only when there is a conflict (*virodha*) that something functions as an exception.

But *vipratiṣedha* is indeed contradiction (*virodha*), and that contradiction occurs only when there is an authority (*adhikāra*) for a single designation (*ekasaṃjñā*), not when there is none. For instance, where there is no authority for a single designation, there is no *vipratiṣedha* at all, as in the case of the designations for suffixes (*pratyaya*) and so forth. Therefore, when this authority exists, contradiction arises.

And when that contradiction exists, by the rule "in case of contradiction, the latter [prevails]," the latter prevails, because it is an exception (*apavāda*) and is thus without occasion (*anavakāśa*).

Therefore, this designation (*adhikāra*) must be established. If that is so, it must be stated that there is a co-occurrence (*samāveśa*) of the designations *aṅga*, *bha*, and *pada*—as in *bābhravyaḥ* and *dhānuṣkaḥ*.
From the word *babhru*, the suffix *yañ* is applied by [Pāṇini 4.1.106]: *madhu-babhru-vrīhi-kauśikānām yañ*.

In that case, because it is a *bh* element and because it is a stem (*aṅga*), there is initial *vṛddhi*; then, by [P. 6.1.79], there is the substitution of *ava*. From the word *dhanus*, the suffix *ṭhak* is applied by [P. 4.4.57] "that which has this as its weapon" (*tadasya praharaṇam*); then, by [P. 7.3.51] "after [stems ending in] *is*, *us*, *uk*, or *t*, there is *ka*," there is the substitution of *ka*. Here, because it is a word (*pada*), by [P. 8.3.39] "for *iṇ*, there is *ṣa*," there is the substitution of *ṣ*. It need not be stated that there is initial *vṛddhi* because it is a stem. The option (*vā*) from [P. 1.3.90] "from here onwards" continues to apply, and that is a restricted option (*vyavasthitavibhāṣā*).
Therefore, in some cases, there will be the co-occurrence of technical designations (*saṃjñā-samāveśa*).
"Elsewhere" means both in common worldly usage and in the technical treatises.
First, regarding worldly usage: the co-occurrence of designations such as Indra, Śukra, and Purandara is observed.

In the grammatical treatise (*śāstra*) as well, there is the suffix (*pratyaya*), such as the *kṛt* and *kṛtya* suffixes. Likewise, because of the overlapping of designations (*saṃjñā-samāveśa*) elsewhere, it would also occur here; therefore, this [rule] is for the purpose of restriction so that only one designation may apply at a time. For example:
"the root *bhid* [is called *dhātu*], the root *chid* [is called *dhātu*]."
The scope for the designation *laghu* (light) is as follows;
its purpose, however, is seen in forms such as *bhettā* and *chettā*,
where the *guṇa* substitution applies by the rule *pugantalaghūpadhasya* [Pāṇini 7.3.86].
Regarding the forms *śikṣir* and *bhikṣir*:
this is the scope for the designation *guru*.
The purpose is [to form] *śikṣā* and *bhikṣā*.
The suffix *it* (the letter *i*) is applied here.
However, the designation "light" (*laghu*) does not apply in this case due to the absence of any purpose for it. Here, both [designations] would apply: as in *atatakṣat* and *ararakṣat*.
Because it is subsequent [to the preceding rule], it indeed receives the designation *guru*.

In the case of the roots *takṣū* and *tvakṣū* in the sense of "making thin" (*dhātupāṭha* 655, 656) and *rakṣa* in the sense of "protecting" (*dhātupāṭha* 658), after adding the causative suffix *ṇic*, the aorist marker *luṅ*, and the substitute *caṅ* for *cli*, there is the elision of *ṇi*. Then, by the rule *caṅi* [6.1.11], reduplication occurs. If the designation *laghu* were to apply here, then by the rule *sanvallaghuni* [7.4.93] and others, the state of being like the *san* suffix (*sanvadbhāva*) would result.

He says that because of the absence of that [condition], it does not occur: "as if *san* were present when there is a light vowel," and so forth. "This rule" refers to the rule for the treatment as *san*.
This example has been stated for [the case of] another [suffix].
Now, that which applies when there is no room [for another designation] is being stated: *ayam te yonir ṛtviyaḥ*.

Since the season (*ṛtu*) has arrived, the suffix *ghas* is applied by [Pāṇini 5.1.104–106], resulting in *ṛtviyaḥ*. When the substitution of *iy* for *ghas* is made, both the designation *pada*—by [Pāṇini 1.4.16] "and before a *sit* suffix"—and the designation *bha*—by [Pāṇini 1.4.18] "before a suffix marked with *ṅ*"—would apply. However, because there is no room [for the latter], the designation *pada* alone prevails.
If the designation *bha* were to apply [to the entire stem], then by rule P. 6.4.146, a *guṇa* substitution would occur.
However, the scope for the *bha* designation is found in forms such as *aupagava*.
The mention of the limit "up to *kaḍāra*" (P. 1.4.1) is for the sake of variety; otherwise, he would have simply said "up to *dvandva*" (P. 1.4.10).

Indeed, there would be no purpose for prescribing a single technical designation (*eka-saṃjñā*) from the word *akaḍāraḥ* onwards, prior to the mention of *dvandva*, such that the inclusion of this limit would be meaningful. [The term] "conflict" (*virodha*) means "contradiction" (*vipratiṣedha*).
This is because the word *vipratiṣedha* is well-known in common usage as denoting contradiction;
for when something contradictory is stated, speakers say, "This is spoken of as a contradiction," and it is understood to mean "contrary."
In order to show the scope of that prohibition, he says: "Where," and so forth.
*Prasaṅgau* means those two things which are entailed or enjoined; i.e., the two injunctions.
"*Anyārthau*" means [injunctions] for other purposes.
The two for whom the object (*artha*)—that is, the purpose—is elsewhere, in another domain, are described as such.
The meaning is that they have accomplished their purpose in another sphere, in a different location.
[This refers to] "in one."
"In the undivided" means simultaneously, i.e., at one and the same time.
The word "it" (sa) is connected with the phrase "this prohibition."

That contradiction is "contradicted" (vipratiṣiddha); the meaning is that it is the object of contradiction. Because it is the object of contradiction, here the word "contradiction" is used for the object by means of the subject, in order to indicate the object through the subject.
For neither does the contradiction logically apply to the contingency, nor does it have that as its locus.
Regarding the phrase "conflict between two of equal strength" (*tulyabalavirodha*):

it is a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "that in which there is a conflict between two things of equal strength. This explanation is provided by relying on the position that this refers to a *jāti* (a futile rejoinder).

In the view that the meaning of a word is a substance (*dravyapadārthapakṣa*), however, this is the distinction: "having different purposes" means those two whose purpose (*artha* = *prayojana*) is other, i.e., distinct.
The rest is the same.

Furthermore, in the expression "in case of conflict" (*vipratiṣedhe*), the locative case is used in the sense of existence (*sati-saptamī*). This refers to the rule concerning "general rules and exceptions" (*utsargāpavāda*) and so forth.

Where there is a conflict (vipratiṣedha), that is the scope for the application of this rule (yoga). And since conflict occurs only between two rules of equal strength, not between those of unequal strength,
this has been explained by the author through the passage beginning with "for where two [rules] apply to different purposes," which demonstrates its specific domain.
