Furthermore, there is no equality of strength between general rules (*utsarga*) and exceptions (*apavāda*), etc.; therefore, such cases do not fall within the scope of this [general] yoga. Consequently, the stronger rule alone prevails therein. In that regard, the general rule operates universally; for example: *ārdhadhātukasyeḍvalādeḥ* [Pāṇini 7.2.35], because the augment *iṭ* is prescribed for any *valādi* (consonant-initial) suffix in general. The exception is the specific rule; for example: *neḍvaśi kṛti* [Pāṇini 7.2.8], because the prohibition of *iṭ* is prescribed specifically for the *valādi* suffixes beginning with *vaś* when followed by a *kṛt* suffix.

Furthermore, that which is prescribed as a specific rule (*viśeṣavidhi*) is stronger; for instance, in the case of "Let curd be given to the Brāhmaṇas, but buttermilk to Kauṇḍinya," the offering of buttermilk, being specifically prescribed, will indeed set aside the offering of curd, which is prescribed as a general rule.

Therefore, when *kṛt* suffixes follow, the augment *īṭ* does not occur; rather, there is only a prohibition, as stated in the rule *stheśabhāsapisakaso varac* [Pāṇini 3.2.175], which says "the augment *īṭ*.
Between the obligatory (*nitya*) and the non-obligatory (*anitya*), the obligatory is stronger, just as in the case of *ais* for *bhisa* [Pāṇini 7.1.9].
For that [substitution] would indeed apply when the substitution of *e* by [Pāṇini 7.3.103], namely *bahuvacane jhalyet*, has been performed;

and it would also apply when it has not yet been performed—on the grounds that the substitution of *ais* for *bhisa* is prescribed after an *a*-ending stem by resorting to the consideration of what was previously so (the stem having formerly ended in *a*). And a rule that applies whether or not another operation has already taken place is considered obligatory (*nitya*).

And so he will say there [in Pāṇini 7.1.9]: "If it is argued that *ettva* (the substitution of *e*) applies to *bhis* because it is subsequent, then where would *ais* occur? Even when *ettva* has been applied, *ais* would still apply by virtue of its prior existence (*bhūtapūrvatva*); thus, in that case, *ais* is permanent (*nitya*). Since *ais* is permanent, *ettva* does not obtain; for its cause, the suffix beginning with *jhal*, has already been prescribed. The scope of *ettva* (as in *vṛkṣeṣu*) is when it is original (*ādya*), whereas in this case, since it exists, it is improper to rely on the notion of its prior existence.
Therefore,
that which is impermanent is weak, because it depends upon the existence or non-existence of another;
by contrast, that which is permanent is strong.

Therefore, in the case of *vṛkṣaiḥ*, the substitution of *et* (the short *e*) does not occur; rather, only the substitution of *ais* takes place. This is because it is observed in common worldly experience that between an internal (*antaraṅga*) and an external (*bahiraṅga*) operation, the internal one prevails.
For in the world, having risen in the morning, one first performs internal tasks such as washing the face, and only afterwards begins to perform external tasks such as going to the king’s palace.
It should be understood in this same way in the grammatical treatise (*śāstra*).
One whose desire is for heaven is *dyukāma*; his descendant is *dyaukāmi*, according to the rule *ata iñ* [Pāṇini 4.1.95].

Although the suffix *iñ* is prescribed after the word *dyukāma*, nevertheless, according to the principle that "the followers of Pāṇini do not undo what has been formed" (*akṛtavyūhāḥ pāṇinīyāḥ*), even an already established grammatical operation may be set aside. Thus, in the analytical derivation where *div-kāma-iñ* is established, once the substitution of *u* for *div* by [Pāṇ. 6.1.127] has occurred, the substitution of *yaṇ* would be required; however, because it is subsequent, the rule for *vṛddhi* (Pāṇ. 7.2.117) would apply. But the substitution of *yaṇ* is performed first because it is an internal (*antaraṅga*) operation, and subsequently the *vṛddhi* of the vowel *u*.
The *yaṇ*-substitution is internal because it depends upon individual phonemes (*varṇāśrayatvāt*).
However, *vṛddhi* is considered extraneous (*bahiraṅga*) because it depends on a *bahu* compound and a *taddhita* suffix.

The rule "an internal operation (*āṅga*) is stronger than one based on phonemes (*vārṇa*)" (Vyāḍiparibhāṣā 39) does not apply here, because the two operations depend on different bases (*vyāśrayatvāt*). Regarding the phrase "in the case of non-application," etc.:

when the view is held that "the universal form (*ākṛti*) is the meaning of the word," then, since the two rules have already fulfilled their purpose elsewhere, when a conflict (*vipratiṣedha*) arises, there results a total non-application due to mutual obstruction; just as if there were a single servant belonging to two people of equal power, and they both command him simultaneously with tasks in different directions.

Therefore, if that [word] seeks non-contradiction, it does not operate toward the effect of both [individuals]. However, in the case of a substance as the referent (*padārtha*), since the definition applies to each individual, and because its purpose would remain unfulfilled, the application of the two definitions would result in alternation (*paryāya*). For example, there would be an alternation in the act of eating from a single vessel for Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, and others who do not eat together. In that context, since the purpose is fulfilled when the operation occurs upon the genus (*jāti*) as the referent, this is commenced for the sake of a rule: "When there is a conflict (*vipratiṣedha*), the subsequent operation takes place."
In that case, if [an operation] were to apply even when [another] has already taken effect, then that too would indeed occur.
Regarding this, it is said: "It is established through the understanding of recurrence (*prasaṅga*).

However, since the two rules would both apply alternately because the individual word-meaning (*vyakti*) has not yet fulfilled its purpose, this [sūtra] serves as a restrictive rule (*niyamārtha*): "In the event of a conflict (*vipratiṣedha*), the subsequent [rule] alone takes effect, not the preceding one."

Regarding this, it is said: "When two rules apply simultaneously and there is a conflict, that which is sublated remains sublated" (Vyāḍipāda 40). [The rule] *ī ca ū ca yū* [is cited]. Now, one might object: since the substitution of the long vowel homogeneous with the preceding (*pūrvasavarṇadīrgha*) for the first two case endings is prohibited by [Pāṇini 6.1.102], and the *yaṇ* substitution [of *i* and *u* for *y* and *v*] takes effect, the form should be *yvau*.
Why, then, is the term *yū* used? To this he replies: "This is a citation without case endings (*avibhaktika*)."

Because the case-ending is elided by the rule *supāṃ suluk* [Pāṇini 7.1.39], no case-ending exists after this; thus it is called "without a case-ending" (*avibhaktika*). "Those which denote a female are termed 'feminine' (*stryākhyau*)."

But surely, when the suffix *aṇ* is applied by [Pāṇini 4.1.83] and the augment *yuk* is added by [Pāṇini 7.3.33], they ought to be designated as feminine (*stryākhyau*). So how can they be called "designated as feminine" (*stryākhyau*)? If you argue that this form arises when the suffix *kap* is applied by [Pāṇini 3.2.3], we say no; for in this case, the root *cakṣiṅ* is accompanied by a prefix. Therefore, he says: "Because of the observation of forms such as *mūlavibhuja*.

The suffix *kap* is also desired after words like *mūlavibhuja*. Accordingly, he will state in the third chapter, in the section on *kap*, the Vārttika: "An addition should be made for *mūlavibhuja* and the like" (Vārttika 232).

Because the word *stryākhyau* is seen in lists such as *mūlavibhuja-ādi*, the suffix *kap* is applied. Is this technical designation (*saṃjñā*) prescribed here for the vowels *ī* and *ū* themselves, or for those [stems] that end in them? If the first alternative were adopted, it would not apply to feminine forms derived through suffixation—such as *he lakṣmi* and *he yavāgvi*; for in these cases, it is the entire composite forms that are called "feminine," and not the vowels *ī* and *ū*. Having observed this flaw in the first alternative, he adopts the second alternative and says: "ending in the vowel *ī* or ending in the vowel *ū*," and so forth.

But is it not the case that, because of the inclusion of the word *anta* (end) in [Pāṇini 1.4.14], the rule of "specification by the end" (*tadantavidhi*) is not obtained when a suffix (*pratyaya*) is mentioned in a rule prescribing a technical name (*saṃjñāvidhi*) elsewhere? This is not a fault; for the fact that he teaches the prohibition in [Pāṇini 1.4.4], "those which are not the substitutes *iyaṅ* and *uvaṅ*," indicates that in this section, the rule of specification by the end does apply. Otherwise, the prohibition would be purposeless. For there is no feminine noun consisting of the mere vowels *i* or *u* that is a substitute for *iyaṅ*; rather, it is that which ends in them—as in the example *kumārī*.

The suffix *ṅīṣ* is applied by [Pāṇini 4.1.20], resulting in "gaurī. Alternatively, the suffix *ṅīṣ* is applied by [Pāṇini 4.1.41]: "The suffix *ṅīṣ* is added after [stems ending in] *ṣit* [roots] and after 'gaura' and so forth."
Regarding "śārṅgaravī": [the suffix] *ṅīn* is applied after *śārṅgarava* and others according to Pāṇini 4.1.73. Regarding "lakṣmīḥ": [it is derived with the suffix *kṛt*].

From the root *lakṣ* (meaning "to see" or "to mark," Dhātupāṭha 1538), the suffix *ī* is applied according to the rule *avitṛstṛtantribhya īḥ* (Daiva 1.82). While this rule is in force, the rule *lakṣermuṭ ca* (Daiva 1.84) applies; by the word *ca* ("and"), the augment *muṭ* is added, and the vowel *ī* is also included.
Thus, we have *brāhṛbandhūḥ*.
Here, the suffix *ūṅ* is applied according to the rule *ūṅutaḥ* (Pāṇini 4.1.66).
The letter *ṅ* is for the purpose of specification according to [Pāṇini 6.1.175].

Regarding the word *yavāgūḥ*: from the root *yū* in the sense of "mixing" (*miśraṇe*; Dhātupāṭha 1033), the suffix *āgūc* is applied by [Uṇādisūtra] 10.4, which states: "After the roots *su*, *yū*, and *vac*, the suffixes *anyuc*, *āgūc*, and *ajaknuC* [are added]. Thus, the form *yavāgūḥ* is derived.

These are examples of feminine forms (*rūpa*). However, the grammatical operation (*kārya*) applies to cases such as *ambārthanadyorhrasvaḥ* [Pāṇini 7.3.107]. In the instances *mātre* and *duhitre*, because the designation *nadī* (feminine noun) does not apply, the suffix *āṅ* prescribed by *āṇnadyāḥ* [Pāṇini 7.3.112] does not occur.
As for *grāmaṇīḥ* and *khalapūḥ*, these two function as masculine.
Because there is no perception of the feminine suffix *nī* in that [form], the shortening prescribed by the rule *ambārthanadyorhrasvaḥ* [Pāṇini 7.3.107] does not occur.
The form *grāmaṇīḥ* is derived from *grāmaṃ nayati* ("he leads the village") with the suffix *kvip* according to the rule *satsūdviṣa...* [Pāṇini 3.2.61].
The substitution of *ṇ* for *n* occurs according to the Vārttika *agragrāmābhyāṃ ca* [Kāśikā 5064].
In the expression *khalaṃ punāti*, the suffix *kvip* is applied according to [Pāṇini 3.2.178] *anyebhyo 'pi dṛśyate*.
In the expression *grāmaṇye striyai*,
the substitution of *yaṇ* is applied according to [Pāṇini 6.4.82].

In the case of *khalapve striyai*, here too [the rule] *oḥ supi* [P. 6.4.83] applies. Since in this instance the feminine gender (*strītva*) is expressed by the word *strī* as a separate word (*padāntara*), the designation *nadī* does not apply; consequently, the substitution of *āṅ* does not occur.

However, in the case of words such as *iṣu* and *aśani*, which possess both genders, femininity resides in the word-meaning itself; thus, the designation *nadī* (feminine noun) applies correctly—as in *iṣvai* and *aśanyā*.

If the designation *nadī* (feminine) does not apply when femininity is expressed by another word, then in the case of *paṭvai striyai*, since the word *paṭu* is observed to denote even a male, the femininity here would be expressed by another word; thus, the *nadī* designation should not apply. This is not so; for another word is of two kinds: in some cases, it excludes other denotable objects of a generality for a word whose application is suspected to be too broad—for example, in the case of the word *go* [cow], [the word] *vāk* [speech] excludes [other meanings] such as cattle;
in other cases, it actually brings about the application [of the term], as in the case of a Vāhīka [barbarian], where one says "the Vāhīka is a cow."

In this context, when a general term such as *paṭu* (clever) comes to reside in a specific instance through its connection with another word, that [specificity] is already included within the word itself; therefore, it is not excluded by the mention of "gender" (*ākhyā*).
However, in the case of the word *grāmaṇī* (leader), the application of femininity is brought about by another word and is not [inherently] delimited [by the word itself];
thus, it is set aside by the mention of "gender."

However, because these two are action-words (*kriyāśabda*), their primary application (*mukhyā vṛtti*) is established in the masculine. There is a distinction [from the word *paṭu*], for while the word *paṭu*—which denotes the quality of skill—is primary even when applied to another [the possessor of that quality], this is not the case here. Regarding the rule: "Those *yū* (vowels *i* and *u*) which are substitutes for *iyaṅ* and *uvaṅ* are not designated as *nadī*," this prohibition is understood to apply to words ending in *yū* by way of the *yū* themselves, and not to *iyaṅ* and *uvaṅ* alone; for there is no possibility of those alone being designated as *nadī*.

For there do not exist two feminine nouns (*stryākhyau*) consisting solely of the vowels *i* and *u*; for instance, in "he śrīḥ" and "he bhrūḥ," because the designation *nadī* (feminine stem) is absent, the shortening prescribed by the rule "a mbārthanadyor-hrasvaḥ" [Pāṇini 7.3.107] does not occur.

From the root *śriñ* in the sense of "service" (Dhātupāṭha 897), by applying the suffix *kvip* according to the rule "kvib-vaci-pracchi-śri-ru-ā-dru-pru-jv-ām dīrgho 'samprasāraṇaṃ ca" (Vārttika 288), and then performing the lengthening of the vowel, the form *śrīḥ* is obtained.

From the root *bhramu* in the sense of "unsteadiness" (Dhātupāṭha 1205), by applying the suffix *ḍū* according to the rule "bhramer ḍūḥ" (Daiva 1.177), and then dropping the final *ṭi* (the *u*), the form *bhrūḥ* is obtained.

Because the suffixes *iyaṅ* and *uvaṅ* are prescribed for both [feminine bases] by rules such as *aci śnudhātu* (Pāṇini 6.4.77), the vowels *i* and *u* become substitutes when they occupy the position of *iyaṅ* and *uvaṅ*. Regarding the form *he stri*:

from the verbal roots *ṣṭai* and *styai*, meaning "to sound" and "to congeal" respectively (Dhātupāṭha 911 and 910), there is the substitution of *ā* by rule *ādeca upadeśe'śiti* (Pāṇini 6.1.44). From the root *styai*, the suffix *ḍraṭ* is applied; the portion *ṭi* is elided by *ṭeḥ* (Pāṇini 6.4.155), and the *vṛddhi* vowel is elided by *ato lopaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.4.48). Then, the feminine suffix *ṅīp* is added by *ṭiṭḍhā* (Pāṇini 4.1.15) and subsequent rules.

In this case, because there is no prohibition of the designation *nadī*, the short vowel [of the stem] indeed remains. Since the rule [Pāṇini 6.4.79] prescribes *iyaṅ* for the word *strī*, the long vowel *ī* is the substitute in place of *iyaṅ*. Now, what is the purpose of including the term "place" (*sthāna*)? If it is argued that it is so that the prohibition may apply to those [stems] which are in the place of *iyaṅ* and *uvaṅ*, we say no; for if this were the intended purpose, one should have simply said "of *iyaṅ* and *uvaṅ*" (*iyaṅuvaṅoḥ*). Even so, the meaning remains the same: the designation *nadī* does not apply to those two vowels (*yū*) which are related to *iyaṅ* and *uvaṅ*.

And who are those two relatives of theirs? They are *iyaṅ* and *uvaṅ*, which serve as their original bases (*prakṛti*). Even without the mention of the word "sthāna" (place/position), the prohibition will be understood as applying to those that stand in the place of *iyaṅ* and *uvaṅ*.
What then is the purpose of including the word "sthāna"? It is so that the prohibition may apply where there is the presence or actual production of *iyaṅ* and *uvaṅ*;
but it should not apply where they are superseded by an exception (*apavāda*), as in the forms *ādhyai* and *varṣābhvai*.
From the root *dhyai* in the sense of "thinking" (*cintāyām*, Dhātupāṭha 908), the suffix *kvip* is applied by [Pāṇini 3.2.130], and there is vocalization (*samprasāraṇa*).
This vocalization is obtained because of the inclusion of the term *dṛśi*;
for indeed, in that very rule, the mention of *dṛśi* is for the purpose of including other specific injunctions.
Having stated that in some cases there is lengthening and in others reduplication, he will say [in a Vārttika]: "And there is vocalization (*samprasāraṇa*) for the root *dhyai*" (Vārttika 292).
For that which has undergone vocalization, the *yaṇ* substitution occurs in the singular dative case by the rule "for *eṅ* and for polysyllabic words" (Pāṇini 6.4.82).

This also applies to the word *varṣābhū*. Even though the phonetic similarity in *saṃhitā* is the same, the term *ām* refers to the genitive plural ending, and not to the accusative singular; for in the latter case, the grammatical operation pertaining to the designation *nadī* does not apply.

Nor is there a reference to the *ām* that is the substitute for the seventh case ending (*saptamī*); for that *ām* is prescribed by [Pāṇini 7.3.116] only after the designation *nadī* has been applied. In the form *śrīṇām atra*, if the *nadī* designation applies, the augment *nuṭ* is added by [Pāṇini 7.1.54]: *hrasvanadyāpo nuṭ*.

Here, the phrase "called feminine" (*stryākhyāt*) continues to apply. Since this designation of *nadī* is prescribed in connection with case endings (*vibhakti*), it is logical that the *nadī* designation applies only to a word-form (*śabdarūpa*) called feminine that is connected with a case ending. Consequently, where only a part [of a compound] is called feminine, the *nadī* designation does not apply—such as in *atiśriyāṃ brāhmaṇānām* ("among the Brahmins who surpass Śrī") and *atibhruvāṃ brāhmaṇānām* ("among the Brahmins who surpass the eyebrows"). If the term *yū* were not carried over here for the purpose of qualifying the short vowels, then it would also apply here in cases such as *mātre* and *duhitre*; therefore, it is carried over here.

Even if [the word *hrasva*] is understood as following [from a previous rule], if it follows as having the nominative case-ending (*prathamānta*), then a relationship of qualifier and qualified (*viśeṣaṇaviśeṣyabhāva*) between two nominative forms regarding shortness (*hrasvatva*) would not be possible. Therefore, by virtue of the sense of the context, it arises here with the genitive case-ending (*ṣaṣṭhanta*). Hence he says: "And the short vowel is related to *y* and *v*. But what is the short vowel related to those two? It is the short vowel that is homogeneous (*savarṇa*) with them; by implication, this refers to the vowels *i* and *u*, for no other short vowel can be homogeneous with the long *ī* and *ū*.
Regarding "kṛtyai" and "kṛtaye":

when the designation *nadī* applies, then—as before—the augment *āṬ* is added; otherwise, however, because it bears the designation *dhī* according to [Pāṇini 1.4.7] "the remainder is *dhī*, except for *sakhi*," the *guṇa* substitution occurs by [Pāṇini 7.3.111]. Here too, in cases where a portion of a word-form related to a case ending is feminine in gender, the designation *nadī* does not apply according to the previously stated rule—as in *atikṛtaye brāhmaṇāya* and *atiśriye*. Regarding "sakhyā": [the following applies].
By the rule *ghisaṃjñāyāḥ* [Pāṇini 7.3.120], the substitution of *nā* does not occur.
In the forms *sakhye* and *sakhyuḥ*, by the rule [Pāṇini 7.3.111], there is no *guṇa* substitution.
In the form *sakhyau*, by the rule [Pāṇini 7.3.119], the substitution of *at* does not occur.
The substitution of *au* occurs by [Pāṇini 7.3.118] *aut*.
This has also been stated regarding the form *sakhyuḥ* [by 6.1.112].

Here, in the case of *susakhiriti*—meaning "one whose friend is excellent"—and in the phrase *susakher āgacchati*, a prohibition would apply by means of the rule for extension to what ends in that (*tadantavidhi*). However, that does not occur because of the prohibition: "There is no extension to what ends in a nominal stem when that stem is used with a specific suffix" (Vyāḍiparibhāṣā 89).
In this context, there are two kinds of *ghisaṃjñā*: that which depends on a constituent part (*avayavāśrayā*) and that which depends on the whole (*samudāyāśrayā*).

Of these, that which depends on a constituent part is prohibited, whereas that which depends on the whole certainly does occur, because it is not prohibited. [The phrase] "when the *ghisaṃjñā* of the word *pati* has been established" implies, as a supplement, "by the immediately preceding rule itself."
The term *prajāpatinā* is a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*).

If this [rule] were commenced once the designation *ghisamjñā* was already established, then—according to the principle that "when something is already established, a new commencement serves as a restrictive rule" (*siddhe satyārambho niyamārthaḥ*)—the restriction would indeed be obtained even without the particle *eva*. Why, then, is the particle *eva* employed? To this he says: "The employment of the particle *eva*" and so forth.
For, without the particle *eva*, one might even suspect the opposite: namely, that "only the husband is the compound."

Consequently, [the rule] would not apply in cases such as *dṛḍhamuṣṭi*, whereas it does apply when the particle *eva* is present. Thus, since the use of the particle *eva* occurs immediately after a compound word (*samāsaśabda*), the restriction (*avadhāraṇa*) applies to something other than that [compound]; therefore, the word *pati* alone is restricted, not the compound. In this context, if the intended meaning were that the word *pati* ending in the sixth case (*ṣaṣṭhīvibhaktyanta*) becomes *ghi* or *jña*, then the mention of *yukta* would be purposeless; one should have simply said "the sixth case" (*ṣaṣṭhī*).

Therefore, since the term *yukta* (connected) is employed, the meaning understood is "connected with another word ending in the genitive case"; hence he says: "*ṣaṣṭhantena*" (with a genitive-ending [word]), and so forth.

Furthermore, if the word *pati* were to have the designation *ghit* when ending in the genitive, what would happen? It would apply only in a case such as *patyuḥ*, but here it would not apply: *kruñcānām apataye namaḥ*. In the example "*mayā patyā*," the word *pati* is connected with the instrumental case.
From *asmad-*: by [Pāṇini 7.2.91] and [7.2.97], there is the substitution of *mā*; by [7.2.89], there is the substitution of *y*. In the word *bhettā*, there is *guṇa* substitution by [7.3.86].

In the form *acīkarat*: from the root *kṛ*, there is the causative suffix *ṇic*, the *luṅ* (aorist) tense, the augment *aṭ*, the substitution of *caṅ* for *cli*, and the elision of *ṇi*. By the rule "ṇau caṅyupadhāyāḥ" [Pāṇini 7.4.1], the penultimate vowel is shortened.
The statement "oḥ puyaṇjyapare" [Pāṇini 7.4.80] is an indicator (*jñāpaka*) that what is performed after a *ṇi* suffix is treated as if it were in its original position (*sthānivat*).

By the rule *caṅi* [Pāṇini 6.1.11], the root *kṛś* is reduplicated. By *urat* [7.4.66], the substitution of *at* occurs, followed by the replacement of *r* with a vowel (*raparatvam*). When the designation *laghu* applies, the rule *sanvallaghuni* [7.4.93] causes the treatment as *saN*, which results in *it*-lengthening by *sanyataḥ* [7.4.94]. Thus we have *kuṇḍā* and *huṇḍā*.

The roots are *kuḍi* (meaning "to burn," Dhātupāṭha 270) and *huḍi* (meaning "to gather," Dhātupāṭha 269). Because of the instruction that the formative process is like that of the original teaching (*upadeśivadvacana*), the augment *num* is applied at the very stage of the original teaching.
Regarding "śikṣā" and "bhikṣā":
the suffix *akāra* (forming *śikṣā*) is applied by [Pāṇini 3.3.103] *śikṣa vidyopādāne*, and the suffix *ṭāp* is applied by [Pāṇini 4.1.4] *ajādyataṣṭāp*. Regarding "īhāñcakre" and "uhāñcakre":
these two are explained in the rule beginning with [Pāṇini 1.3.63] *āmpratyayavat*.

In this context, however, the designation *guru* (heavy) applies; thus, by the rule *ijādeśca gurumato 'nṛcchaḥ* [Pāṇini 3.1.36], the suffix *āna* (the ātmanepada marker) is applied. The form *kartā* is the periphrastic future (*luṭ*).
The forms *kariṣyati* and *akariṣyat* are the periphrastic future (*luṭ*) and the conditional (*lṛṅ*), respectively.
In this context, the *guṇa* substitution [is applied] by the rule "aṅgasaṃjñāyāḥ kāryam atra" (Pāṇini 1.1.56), and the augment *iṭ* is added as appropriate by the rule "ārdhadhātuka" (Pāṇini 7.2.35).

Regarding the statement "the word *yasmāt* is for the purpose of indicating the technical name (*saṃjñin*)," this means that the indication of the named entity (*saṃjñin*) is its purpose; that which has this as its aim is described in that way.

Now, one might raise the objection: "But isn't the *saṃjñin* (the thing named) already indicated here by the phrase 'beginning with that' (*tadādi*)? So how can it be said that [the word] is for the purpose of indicating the *saṃjñin*? Anticipating this inquiry, he says, "Because of its connection with 'beginning with that' (*tadādisambandhāt*)," in order to show the reason why the phrase "because" (*yasmāt*) serves to indicate the *saṃjñin*. This is because, when the word "because" is present, it establishes a connection between that which is under discussion and the phrase "beginning with that. That is to say: "That which is the beginning of that after which a suffix is prescribed is 'beginning with that' (*tadādi*)."

If this [word] *tasmāt* were not stated, what would be connected by the pronoun *tat*, which refers back to the subject under discussion? This [objection] is incorrect; for if that were the case, the designation *aṅga* (stem) would apply to the suffix and so forth when followed by a suffix, and consequently, in forms such as *kariṣyāvaḥ* and *kariṣyāmaḥ*, the *guṇa* substitution for the verbal root would not occur.
Therefore, in order to specify the particular item to be designated, the word *tasmāt* must be stated;
for only when there is a connection with this [word] can that specific item intended as the designatum (*saṃjñin*)—which is indicated by the rule *tadādi*—be properly pointed out, and not otherwise.

> [[1.3.17]] Thus, the restriction is that there is a rule [for the addition of a suffix] after a prefix (*upasarga*), but not for the suffix itself; for that [suffix] is prescribed by another rule. > [[1.3.17]] This is merely an illustration.
> [[1.3.18]] This too should be understood as included here.

The meaning is that the designation *aṅga* would apply starting from that [initial letter], and consequently, the augment *aṭ* would be inserted before the prefix (*upasarga*). Regarding the example "strī iyatī":
since this is its measure, the suffix *vatup* is applied by the rule *kimidambhyāṃ vo ghaḥ* (Pāṇini 5.2.40).

There is the substitution of *gha* for *va*, the replacement of *iy* [for *idaṃ*], the substitution of *ī* for *idaṃ* by *idaṃ kimor īśkī* (Pāṇini 6.3.90), and the elision of the vowel *i* by *ṭeḥ* (Pāṇini 6.4.148).
By [Pāṇini 4.1.45], the suffix *ṅīp* is applied, resulting in *iyatī*.

From the word *strī*, the nominative suffix *su* is added; its elision occurs by [Pāṇini 6.1.68], *halṅyābbhyo dīrghāt sutisyapṛktaṃ hal*, leaving the form *strī iyatī*. If the term "vidhi" (prescription) were not included [in the rule], then when the suffix *iyat* follows, the word *strī* would receive the designation of an *aṅga* (base); consequently, the elision of the vowel *i* would undesirably apply by [Pāṇini 6.4.148], *yasyeti ca*.

But surely, because of the rule "asiddhavad atrābhāt" (Pāṇini 6.4.22), the elision of the vowel *i* itself is unestablished (*asiddha*); so how can there be this occasion for its elision? The intention [of the objection] is that unestablishedness applies only within the scope of the section concerning prior operations (*prāgbhādhikāra*). This is not the intended meaning.

For the author of the *Vṛtti* will state there: "The phrase 'as if unestablished' (*asiddhavat*) is a governing heading (*adhikāra*); whatever we shall follow from here until the end of the chapter is treated as if unestablished. Likewise, since the particle *ā* is used in the sense of inclusion (*abhividhi*), unestablished status (*asiddhatva*) applies even within the governing heading of *bh*. If this is so, then by the mention of the word "rule" (*vidhi*), it is indicated that this unestablished status within the governing heading of *bh* is non-permanent (*anitya*);
consequently, it is unnecessary to state the rule: "The *vuk* and *yuṭ* augmentations are to be declared as established in relation to *avaṅ* and *ayaṇ*" (Vārttika 776).

*vuk* [is applied] as in *babhūva*, and *yuṭ* as in *upadidīye*. Now, one might object: "In this way, because of the status of the substitute (*sthānivattva*) for the elision of the vowel *i* according to [Pāṇini 1.1.57], there would be no occasion at all for the elision of the vowel *i* in the word *strī*. This is not so; for that which precedes a non-ṣat-pratyaya consisting of more than six syllables becomes a substitute (*sthānivat*) with respect to the operation concerning what precedes it. Thus, the vowel *i* in the word *strī*—which was previously part of the form *iyī* after its formation—is subsequently connected with the word *strī*.

Now, even if the term "vidhi" (prescription) were included [in the rule], why would the designation *aṅga* not apply? For there is indeed a prescription of a suffix after the word *strī*, and the suffix *iyac* certainly exists as something following it. This is not a fault; for when the term "vidhi" is present, the designation *aṅga* is prescribed for that element from which the suffix is prescribed, by virtue of proximity (*pratyāsatti*).

But here, the suffix prescribed after the word *strī* is not "subsequent" (*para*) because it has been elided; and the suffix *iyac*, which is prescribed as subsequent, is not prescribed from that [word *strī*]. Now, for what purpose is the mention of "that which begins with it" (*tadādi*)? For even without it, when it is stated merely that "the base (*aṅga*) is that from which a suffix is prescribed, provided a suffix follows," this meaning is obtained—namely, that by virtue of the constant connection between *yat* and *tat*, that from which the suffix is prescribed becomes designated as a base (*aṅga*) when a suffix follows. To this he says: "The mention of 'that which begins with it'... and so forth.

If the term *tadādi* (beginning with that) were not present, then only that element from which the suffix is prescribed would possess the status of an *aṅga* (base), and not the entire form beginning with *saha*, nor even the whole complex including the suffix *san* and the augment *num*; for in those cases, the suffix is prescribed as following [the base], not as beginning with it. When the inclusion of *tadādi* is made, a *bahuvrīhi* compound is adopted—meaning "that whose beginning is that from which the suffix is prescribed"—and by this means, the designation of *aṅga* is established for the entire complex, including *saha*, the suffix *san*, and the augment *num*. Thus, the mention of *tadādi* is for the sake of the suffixes beginning with *syat* and the augment *num*.

By the inclusion of the word "ādi" (and so forth), there is the inclusion of suffixes and augments situated between the base (*prakṛti*) and the suffix (*pratyaya*); this is because the augment *num* serves as an indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*).

In the case of *kariṣyāvaḥ*, since the suffix is prescribed after [the base] *kar-iṣya*, when the designation of "base" (*aṅga-saṃjñā*) applies to the entire aggregate beginning with that [base] up to the suffix, the lengthening [of the vowel] occurs by [Pāṇini 7.3.101]; otherwise, where would it apply? It would apply in cases such as *vāvāvaḥ* and *vāvāmaḥ*.

The roots *aya*, *vaya*, *maya*, *paya*, *taya*, *caya*, and *ṇaya* mean "to go" (*gatau*) [Dhātupāṭha 474–480]. In the form with the elision of *yaṅ* (*yaṅluk*), there is lengthening of the reduplicated syllable according to Pāṇini 7.4.83; and the elision of *y* occurs before the endings *-vas* and *-mas* according to 6.1.66. Here, the lengthening of the root occurs without a verbal suffix (*vikaraṇa*), because the suffix *śap* is elided by the rule "the *śap* of roots beginning with *ad*" (2.4.72).
Its status as belonging to the *ad*-class is due to its inclusion in the list beginning with "and *carkarīta*" (Dhātupāṭha 1081).
"*Carkarīta*" is a technical term used by ancient grammarians for the elision of *yaṅ*.
Regarding the word *kuṇḍāni*:
by [Pāṇini 7.1.20], there is the substitution of *śi* for the case-ending;
by [Pāṇini 7.1.72], there is the insertion of *num*.

In that case, according to the view that this *num* is an initial augment (*parādi*), the lengthening is established even without [the rule] *supi ca* [Pāṇini 7.3.102], because the base (*aṅga*) designation applies to the form including *num*. Even when it is a final augment (*pūrvānta*), the lengthening is established by [the rule] *ato dīrgho yañi* [Pāṇini 7.3.101], which follows from the governing rule *aṅgasya* [Pāṇini 6.4.1]. However, when it is not part of the base (*abhakta*), it is not established, because it is not a portion of the base.
Furthermore, this [word] is not a *bhakta* (subordinate element); such is the view of the author of the Sūtras.

For that reason, he formulated the rule regarding "that which begins with it" (*tadādivacana*) even for the sake of the augment *num*, as in the examples "for the sake of *śri*" and "for the sake of *bhū*."

In the example *śriya idaṃ* and *bhruva idam*, there is a compound by the rule *caturthī tadarthārtha* (Pāṇini 2.1.36), etc.; for here there is indeed a prescription for the singular number of the dative case.

If, however, the term *pratyaya* (suffix) were not repeated [in the rule], then the designation *aṅga* (stem) would apply to the words *śrī-* and *bhū-* when followed by the word *artha-*, and consequently the substitutions *iyaṅ* and *uvaṅ* would occur.

But since the term *pratyaya* is repeated when the locative case is specified, the designation *aṅga* does not apply to the words *śrī-* and *bhū-* when followed by the word *artha-*, and therefore *iyaṅ* and *uvaṅ* do not occur.

However, when the word *pratyaya* (suffix) is mentioned again in connection with the locative case (*saptamī*), there is no fault. For it is understood thus: "when a suffix is prescribed after that [base]," and the suffix which was prescribed after that [base] has been elided.

Even though the designation *aṅga* (base) is obtained for that [element] even when it is elided by virtue of the rule *pratyayalakṣaṇa*, the grammatical operation (*kārya*) is not obtained, because of the prohibition of the *pratyayalakṣaṇa* rule by [Pāṇini 1.1.63]. Regarding the statement "the mention of the *pratyāhāra* ‘sup-tiṅ’":

it is indeed appropriate to mention the *pratyāhāra* ‘tiṅ’, since there is no other word ‘tiṅ’. But how can it be the mention of the *pratyāhāra* ‘sup’, given that the locative plural [suffix] exists and why would its mention not occur? This is not a fault, because of the prohibition [by Pāṇini 8.2.8].

If there were a mention of the *sup* suffixes including the seventh case plural (*saptamībahuvacana*), then because the status of being a *pada* would not apply to the *ṅi* and vocative (*saṃbuddhi*) endings, the elision of *n* (the *nalopa*) would not even arise; thus, the prohibition [of the rule] would be purposeless. For example, in the case of "brāhmaṇāḥ," when the status of being a *pada* is present, [the rules] P. 8.2.66 and P. 8.3.15 apply.

Regarding the phrase "they recite" (*paṭhanti*): since this constitutes a *pada*, the *nighāta* (anudātta accent) applies by the rule *tiṅṅatiṅaḥ* [Pāṇini 8.1.28]. Now, one might object: "By the rule *pratyayagrahaṇe yasmāt sa vihitastadādestadantasya* [Paribhāṣā 24] or by [Pāṇini 1.1.72], even without the inclusion of the word 'end' (*anta*), the designation will apply only to that which ends with the suffix; so what is the purpose of including the word 'end'? To this, he says: "In the case of the *pada* designation," and so forth.

If, by the inclusion of the term "ending in" (*anta*) here, the point that "in other rules prescribing technical names (*saṃjñā-vidhi*), there is no extension [of the name] to what ends with that" were not made known, then in the rule *tarab-īyasun-au* (P. 1.1.22), the name *gha* would apply to the entire form ending in *tarap*, and not to the suffix alone.

Therefore, in this context, the inclusion of the term "ending in" is made known for this purpose: so that in other rules prescribing technical names, when a suffix is mentioned, there may be a prohibition of the extension to what ends with it.
Consequently, the name *gha* applies only to *tarap* and *tamap* themselves, and not to what ends in them.

In the expression *gaurībrāhmaṇitarā*, the short vowel [of the first member] does not occur before the word *brāhmaṇitarā* ending in the suffix *-tarap*, because the suffix *-tarap* is designated as *agha*. If only the suffix were designated as *agha*, then the shortening of the word *brāhmaṇī* would indeed occur when it follows that [suffix]. In the expression *bhavadīyaḥ* and so forth, a secondary derivative (*taddhita*) occurs in the sense of a possessive suffix (*śaiṣika*). Due to its status as a word (*pada*), the substitution of a voiced unaspirated stop (*jaś*) applies by the rule *jhalāñ jaśo 'nte* (Pāṇini 8.2.39).

In the case of *ūrṇāyuḥ*, when the suffix *yus* is applied according to [Pāṇini 5.2.123], the designation *pada* supersedes the designation *bha*; consequently, the elision of the final vowel *ā* does not occur by [Pāṇini 6.4.148].
Similarly in the case of *ṛtviyaḥ*.

Regarding the statement "the season has arrived," [the suffix] *ṛtviya* is derived by [Pāṇini 5.1.106] *ṛtoraṇ*. Because it is a *pada*, there is no *bha*-status, and thus the [substitution] dependent on that [status] does not occur [by Pāṇini 6.4.146]. Here, if the suffixes beginning from the seventh case plural up to *kap* were intended to be included, then one would not have formulated the prohibition "not before a non-sarvanāmasthāna [suffix]" (*asarvanāmasthāne*), because there would be no possibility [of its application]. Since that [prohibition] was indeed formulated, it is understood that the suffixes beginning from the first case singular up to *kap*—namely, *su* and the others—are what are intended. Therefore, he says: "In *svādiṣu*, starting from the singular suffix *su*.
[Examples: *rājatvam*, *rājatā*.
*rājataraḥ*: the suffix *tarap* is applied by [Pāṇini 5.3.57]. *rājatamaḥ*: the suffix *tamap* is applied by [Pāṇini 5.3.55] and the following rules. *rājānau*, *rājānaḥ*.
In this case, because the designation *pada* does not apply, the elision of the *n* does not occur.

If that were so, then in the word *rājā* as well, it would not occur, since by the rule for *pratyayalakṣaṇa*, the designation *pada* would be absent because [the suffix] is not an *asarvanāmasthāna*. This is not a fault; the activity of the Teacher indicates that the designation *pada* does indeed apply when *su* follows, since he teaches the prohibition in the rule "not before *naṅi* and the vocative" (*naṅisambuddhayoḥ*).
In this context, the word "vocative" (*sambuddhi*) would be redundant, because the elision of *n* would not apply simply due to the absence of the *pada* designation.

Alternatively—this [term] "asarvanāmasthāne" is an exclusion (*paryudāsa*), not a simple negation (*prasajyapratiṣedha*); therefore, the designation *pada* is prescribed for cases other than *sarvanāmasthāna*, but *sarvanāmasthāna* itself is not prohibited.

Consequently, by the preceding rule, the designation *pada* will apply there when *su* follows. Alternatively, even if it were a simple negation, there would be no fault, because of the principle "a rule or a prohibition applies to what is immediately contiguous" (Vyāḍipāda 12); thus, only that application which is immediate is prohibited, not that which is separated.

By that [rule], there is the elision of the vowel *a* according to [Pāṇini 6.4.148]. In the rule "after *ya* or *ca*" (*yaci*), the mention of the letters (*varṇagrahaṇa*) is in the locative case. Therefore, by the principle "when a grammatical operation is prescribed with reference to a specific element, it applies to that which begins with it" (*yasmin vidhis taddādāv grahaṇe*), one might think the rule should apply here; hence he says "beginning with *ya*" (*yakārādau*), and so forth.

In cases such as *gārgya*, when the designation *bha* is established, there is the elision of the vowel *a* according to [Pāṇini 6.4.148]. It has been stated: "An addition (*upasaṃkhyāna*) must be made for the words *nabhas*, *aṅgiras*, and *manus* before the suffix *vat*."
In this case, the result is that the technical designation *pada* (word) supersedes the designation *bhas* (nominal stem).

The phrase "like the sky" (*nabha iva*) is intended to demonstrate similarity of meaning; it does not, however, function as the suffix *vati* derived from a base in the nominative case. Rather, it is formed according to Pāṇini 5.1.114, *tena tulyam*, meaning "it behaves similarly to the sky," as in the example *āṅgirasvat*.
It is the same as before.
Regarding "manuṣvat":
because the term *bahula* ("variously") is understood to carry over to the rule *jane ruṣiḥ* (Dhātupāṭha 9.37), the suffix *usi* is applied to the root *man* (meaning "to know," Dhātupāṭha 1176).
By [Pāṇini 8.3.59], the substitution of *ṣ* occurs.
With *manuṣ* established, the suffix *-vat* is applied as before, resulting in *manuṣvad*.

If the designation *pada* were to apply here, then because the substitution of *ṣ* would be considered non-existent (*asiddha*), the substitution of *r* (ruṭ) would occur; consequently, the undesirable form *manurvat* would result.

The term *upasaṃkhyāna* (supplementary addition) is explained here as follows: from the rule *siti ca* [Pāṇini 1.4.16], the particle *ca* ("and") is understood to carry over (*anuvartate*), and it serves the purpose of including what has not been explicitly mentioned.
By means of this, the designation *bha* will apply to *nabhas*, *aṅgiras*, and *manus* when followed by the suffix *vat*. Regarding the form *vṛṣaṇvasva-āyoḥ*:

since the internal case-ending (*vibhakti*) would cause the designation *pada* to apply, the designation *bha* is prescribed; and the application of that [designation] is obtained precisely through the carry-over of the particle *ca*.

In *vṛṣṇo'āḥ*, although the substitution of *ṇ* (ṇatva) is technically non-existent (*asiddha*) because it occurs within a *bha*-stem, nevertheless, the elision of the nasal (*nalopa*) is not dependent on the word-form (*padanibandhana*), and thus the prohibition of *ṇatva* by [Pāṇini 8.4.37] applies. The expression "tasau" is a reference to the phonemes *t* and *s*.

Since a possessive suffix (*matvarthīya*) cannot be added to a mere phoneme, it is understood through the force of the context that this refers to words ending in those phonemes (*tadantavidhi*). Thus he says, "ending in the letter *t*" and so forth.
The phrase "in a possessive suffix" consists of two words in different grammatical cases (*vyadhikaraṇa*), forming a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*).
The term *matvartha* means "that which has the sense of the possessive suffix. In this context, it refers to that [word] in which the suffix occurs.

Alternatively, when the words are in apposition (*samānādhikaraṇa*), by association with the word *matu*, the meaning co-occurring with the possessive suffix *matup* is expressed—namely, "in that which has the sense of the suffix *ṇatup*," and not "in that which [the suffix occurs]. The inclusion of the word *artha* (sense) is so that [the suffix may occur] even elsewhere than where the possessive suffix *matup* itself occurs; for otherwise, if it were stated as *matau* ("in the possessive suffix"), it would apply only to the possessive suffix itself and not to others.

If the inclusion of the possessive sense (*matvartha*) were made, the suffix *matup* would not occur; for that [possessive sense] is a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*), and it is illogical for a qualifier to be connected with an operation. Indeed, when it is said, "Let the owner of brindled cows (*citragu*) be brought," the cows, who constitute the qualifier, are not brought as well. This is not a fault; for even a qualifier is sometimes distinguished by an operation, just as when it is said, "Let the Brāhmaṇas from Devadatta’s house be brought"—if Devadatta, who is the qualifier of the house, happens to be a Brāhmaṇa, then he too is indeed brought.
Regarding "udaiātvāna":
because it is treated as a *bha* stem, the designation of a *pada* is absent, and thus the substitution of the *jaś* sound (the dental *n*) is established.

Furthermore, the substitution of *v* [for *m*] occurs by the rule *jhayaḥ* [Pāṇini 8.2.10], the augment *num* is added by the rule *ugidacām* [Pāṇini 7.1.70], and the lengthening of the vowel occurs by the rule *sarvanāmasthāne cāsambuddhau* [Pāṇini 6.4.8].

In the case of *payasvī* and *yaśasvī*, because [the stem] has the designation *bha*, the substitution of *ru* does not occur. When the rule *indranpūṣāryamṇāṃ sau* (Pāṇini 6.4.12) is being carried over, the lengthening [of the vowel] occurs by the rule *sau ca* (Pāṇini 6.4.13). If the designation *bha* were to be prescribed here, then the designation *pada* would not apply; and if the designation *pada* were to be prescribed, then the designation *bha* would not apply here. In that case, there would be no co-occurrence (*samāveśa*) of the designations *bha* and *pada*, because of the governing principle that only one designation applies at a time.

However, this fault does not arise if one is prescribing correctness (*sādhutva*); for in that case, the designation *bha* is prescribed for some words that bear the designation *pada*, while for others it is prescribed for those bearing both designations. Therefore, it is more appropriate to prescribe correctness itself; with this in mind, he says: "The forms beginning with *ayasmaya*" and so forth.
But how is their correctness prescribed? To this he says: "In the section concerning the designations *bha* and *pada*" and so forth.

The door, the mouth, or the means—therein lies the grasping of speech. Nevertheless, because the suffix *mayaṭ* is prescribed for the sake of grammatical correctness (*sādhutva*) precisely in this case of the word *ayas*, the suffix *mayaṭ* occurs even after a Vedic verse (*chandas*). Consequently, due to its status as a *bha*-stem, the substitution of *ru* (for *s*) does not take place. Regarding the form *sarkvatā*:
the possessive suffix *matup* is applied in the sense that "this [person] possesses *ṛc*s."
Because it is a *pada*, there is the substitution of *k* by [Pāṇini 8.2.30] *coḥ kuḥ*.
Because it is a *bha*, the substitution of *j* by [Pāṇini 8.2.39] does not occur.
"This is an *ākṛtigaṇa* (an open class)."

Because the word "ādi" (and so forth) denotes a class or type. By stating, "the number 'many' is prescribed for that [base] by this [sūtra] as its expressed meaning," he demonstrates that the purpose of this grammatical rule is prescriptive (*vidhi*). In this regard, some hold the view that "the meaning of a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) consists of five factors: its own meaning, substance, gender, number, and object (*karman*), etc."
According to some, "the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) consists of a triad: its own referent (*svārtha*), substance (*dravya*), and gender (*liṅga*).
In that context, the "own referent" (*svārtha*) is the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*), comprising essential nature (*svarūpa*), genus (*jāti*), quality (*guṇa*), and substance (*dravya*).
Substance (*dravya*), however, is the qualified (*viśeṣya*), and it, moreover, consists of genus, quality, and substance.

In that regard, when a genus qualified by the form of a word is expressed—as in "cow"—then the form of the word, being the qualifier, constitutes its own meaning (svārtha), while the genus, being the qualificand, constitutes the substance (dravya).

But when a quality qualified by a genus is expressed—as in "the white quality of the cloth"—then the genus, being the qualifier, constitutes its own meaning, while the quality, being the qualificand, constitutes the substance.

However, when a substance such as a cloth is expressed as qualified by qualities—as in "a white cloth"—then the quality, being the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*), becomes its own primary referent (*svārtha*), while the substance, the cloth and so forth, which is the qualified (*viśeṣya*), remains the substance itself. Furthermore, when even one substance becomes a qualifier for another substance—as in "bring in the sticks" or "bring in the spears"—then the substance such as the stick, having attained the state of a qualifier, is the primary referent; whereas the other substance, having attained the state of the qualified, is the substance itself, such as the person and so forth.
In some cases, even a relation (*sambandha*) constitutes its own meaning—where a suffix arises caused by a relation—as in *daṇḍī* ("staff-bearer") and *viṣāṇī* ("horned").
Here, the relation between the staff and the person is the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*), while "staff-bearer" (*daṇḍī*) is the substance (*dravya*).
In some cases, even an action (*kriyā*) constitutes its own meaning—where a suffix arises caused by an action—as in *pācakaḥ* ("cook") and *pāṭhakaḥ* ("reader").
Others maintain that the relation between action and its factors (*kriyākārakasambandha*) is the primary meaning (*svārtha*) here.

Gender (*liṅga*), such as femininity and so on; number (*saṃkhyā*), such as singularity and so on; and the specific factors of action (*kāraka*) such as the object (*karman*) and others to be mentioned later [constitute this]. Among the two views previously stated, the second view is the one adopted here by the author of the *Vṛtti*. As for the fact that action alone is the denotation of the verbal root (*dhātu*), there is no dispute among the teachers (*ācārya*) on this point.

In this regard, while the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) possesses the aforementioned threefold meaning and the verbal root (*dhātu*) consists of action, if this rule were not stated, then—according to the principle that "suffixes whose meaning is not specified occur in their own sense" (*svārthe bhavanti*)—the plural suffixes *jas* and so forth prescribed after a nominal stem would apply only to those three meanings and not to the number "plurality.
Likewise, the plural suffixes *jhi* and so forth prescribed after a verbal root would apply only to the action itself and not to the number "plurality."
Therefore, since this very [sūtra] prescribes that plurality (*bahutva*) is the expressed meaning (*vācyatva*) of that [suffix], this serves as a rule of injunction (*vidhi*).

Just as by this rule (*yoga*) plurality is prescribed as the expressed meaning of the plural suffix (*bahuvacana*), so too by rules such as *[[2.3.2]]* and others, the object (*karman*) and so forth are prescribed for the second case endings (*dvitīyā*) and the rest;
and by *[[3.4.69]]*, the object and so forth are likewise prescribed for the verbal suffixes (*lakāra*).

Therefore, these rules as well must be understood as having injunctive force (*vidhyartha*). For those who hold the view that the meaning of a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) consists of five [factors], all five meanings are denoted by the nominal stem itself, and the case-endings (*vibhakti*) serve merely to manifest them. In that regard, according to the principle "suffixes whose meaning is not specifically prescribed apply in their own sense" (*anirdiṣṭārthāḥ pratyayāḥ svārthe bhavanti*), even without this specific statement, the plural suffix *jas* and others are already established after the nominal stem to express plurality.

In this regard, since [the application of number] would otherwise apply indifferently even to other categories such as singularity and so forth, this [rule] serves as a restriction (*niyama*) by means of which it is regulated. Why, then, did the author of the *Vṛtti* adopt the view that "the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) consists of the three" [number, gender, and substance]? Because it is logical.
For instance, in expressions such as "see the tree" (*vṛkṣaṃ paśya*), meanings such as number and the object (*karman*) are not perceived without the case-endings (*vibhakti*).

Although in cases such as *payaḥ payo jarayati* ("milk digests milk"), the meaning of number, object, and so forth is understood even without a case-ending, nevertheless, in instances such as *payasī*, *payāṃsi*, and *payasā*, a case-ending is invariably required for the sake of understanding number, object, and the like.

For it cannot be said that, just as in the word *gargāḥ* the meaning of "offspring" is understood through the plural ending without the *yañ* suffix, so too in *gāgryaḥ* the base alone expresses the meaning of "offspring."

Moreover, in cases such as *payaḥ payo jarayati* ("milk digests milk"), the meaning of number, object, and so forth is understood precisely through the power of the production of specific case-endings (*vibhakti*). For it is from that very specific case-ending which has been produced that this particular meaning is understood, and not from anything else; thus, it is logical that the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) consists of exactly three factors [number, gender, and substance]. If, then, plurality (*bahutva*) were prescribed as the expressed meaning of the plural number (*bahuvacana*), then in the Sūtra the mention of "plurality" would have to be made by means of an abstract suffix (*bhāvapratyaya*); otherwise, the number "plurality" would not be understood. It need not be so made.
Even without the abstract suffix (*bhāvapratyaya*), there can be an expression where the state (*bhāva*) is the primary referent, as in the example: "the whiteness of the cloth" (*paṭasya śuklaḥ*).

Now, even so, since the state is a single entity, the plural form "in many" (*bahuṣu*) would not be appropriate; this is not a fault. For, having superimposed the distinction belonging to the substance—which is the substratum of the number "many"—onto the quality of "manyness," the expression "in many" is made using the plural. Furthermore, this is intended to make it known that the word "many" (*bahu*) here expresses number (*saṃkhyā*) and does not express magnitude (*vaipulya*).

Therefore, "plurality" (*vaipulya*) is not what is expressed by the plural number; thus, in expressions such as *bahurodanaḥ* ("much rice") or *bahuḥ sūpaḥ* ("much soup"), the singular number alone occurs after the word *bahu* when it signifies abundance, and not the plural. If the number "many" (*bahutva-saṃkhyā*) were prescribed as the meaning of the plural, then in the example *vṛkṣaṃ paśya* ("look at the tree"), the plural would result, because two numbers are present here: the collective number (*samudāya-saṃkhyā*), which is oneness (*ekatva*), and the distributive number (*avayava-saṃkhyā*), which consists of the plurality inherent in the parts such as fruits, roots, and branches.

Even for this [number], there certainly exists a relation characterized by inherence in a single substratum with the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*). To explain: the number "plurality" (*bahutva*) inheres in those individual components [of the aggregate], and the meaning of the nominal stem—the aggregate itself—inheres in that very same [substratum]. Consequently, the plural suffix would follow from that [meaning of the stem]; therefore, he says: "the object [of the action] and so forth," etc.

Since *karman* and the others are expressed by words in the same case-ending, they are proximate to the number "plurality"; therefore, due to that proximity, the plural suffix occurs precisely when their own plurality is intended.

For in the example "see the tree" (*vṛkṣaṃ paśya*), it is the aggregate alone that is most desired as being pervaded by the action of seeing, and thus it alone attains the status of the object (*karman*), not the individual parts. So how could there be any occasion for the plural suffix? [The author addresses this with] "In *karman* and the others," etc.;
*karman* and the others are the denotata of the plural suffix.

That plurality belongs only to many [entities] such as objects (*karman*) and so forth; therefore, by implication (*sāmarthyāt*), the meaning results that [the plural suffix occurs] when there are many objects and so forth. If, then, the number "plurality" is prescribed as the denotation of the plural case-endings (*vibhakti*), then the case-endings beginning with *su* (the nominative) would not occur after indeclinables (*avyaya*), which lack number; consequently, they would not receive the designation of "word" (*pada*). To this he says: "And where," etc. Now, one might object: in the rule prescribing the case-endings (*svādi-vidhāna-sūtra*), number, object, and so forth are already established as the meanings of the case-endings by another treatise (*śāstrāntara*); therefore, he will state that this [present work] forms a single syntactic unit (*ekavākyatā*) with that [other treatise].

Why, then, would the *svādi* suffixes be considered "generally prescribed"? For it is not the case that the status of *svādi* as generally prescribed is established by the syntactic unity (*ekavākyatā*) of the rule for *su-au-ja-s*, etc., with another grammatical rule such as "the plural number is used for many" (*bahuṣu bahuvacanam*) or "the dual number is used for two" (*dvayor dvivacanam*).

In that case, there is no fault, because it has been stated that [the suffixes] are "generally prescribed" (*sāmānyavihitāḥ*), since by means of the *jñāpaka* (indicatory evidence), the production of *svādi* suffixes occurs generally even from indeclinables (*avyaya*). What, then, is that *jñāpaka*? It is the elision (*luk*) of the *sup* suffixes produced after an indeclinable, as in [Pāṇini 2.4.82]: "There is elision (*luk*) of the case-endings produced after an indeclinable. For elision is not possible for those [suffixes] that have not been produced. Regarding the rule "in the sense of two or one" (*dvyekayoḥ*): this too is an indication where the state (*bhāva*) is the primary factor; otherwise, because of the plurality [of the word *dvyeke*], the plural number would result. But when the indication is primarily concerned with the state, it is appropriate to use the dual number, as these two meanings—duality and singularity—are two.
With the words "this too," etc., he shows that this yoga also has the purpose of being an injunction (*vidhi*). Regarding the phrase "the denotation of meaning" (*arthābhidhānam*):

that by which a meaning (*artha*)—that is, the expressed object (*vācya*)—is denoted is "the denotation of meaning. Regarding the statement "the qualifier 'kāraka' refers to the domain of technical designations such as *apādāna* (ablative), etc.": [it means that the term *kāraka* applies specifically to those entities which fall under the technical grammatical categories of *apādāna* and so forth.]

That whose domain consists of technical designations (saṃjñā) such as "ablative" (apādāna) and so forth is described as such. By the word "and so forth" (ādi), the inclusion of "dative" (sampradāna) and the others is intended.

Now, why does this designation not apply to "the fixed" (dhruva) and the rest which are about to be mentioned? The thought is this: if these were being indicated by means of technical designation-words (saṃjñā-śabda), then this [word *viṣaya*] would have been indicated in the nominative case; however, since it is indicated here in the locative case, this is not a designation for "the fixed" and the rest.

The locative case in *kārake* is used in the sense of selection (*nirdhāraṇa*). Since selection occurs among many, how can there be a singular designation? It is singular with respect to the general category.

Alternatively, since "sūtras are like Vedic [usage]," the singular is used despite the fact that the plural would otherwise be required by the rule *vyatyayo bahulam* [Pāṇini 3.1.85]. Thus, among the various *kārakas*, that *kāraka* which is fixed (*dhruva*) receives the technical name *apādāna*.

In this way, it should be understood in other cases as well. This word "kāraka" exists indeed as a derivative term—ending in the suffix *ṇvul* and being a synonym for "agent" (*kartṛ*)—and it also exists as a technical term (*saṃjñāśabda*), being an underived synonym.

In this context, if the previously mentioned [definition] were to be accepted here, then the term *kāraka* would not apply to the [factors] beginning with the ablative (*apādāna*). For example, the word *kartṛ*—as in the rule *kartṛkaraṇayos tṛtīyā* (Pāṇini 2.3.18)—is derived in the sense of an agent (*kartṛ*), and the word *kāraka* is likewise derived. Furthermore, the agent (*kartṛ*) is independent (*svatantra*), whereas the ablative and the others are dependent (*asvatantra*). Therefore, how could they be designated by the term *kāraka*? Indeed, if the designation *kāraka* did not apply to them, they would not be included among those referred to by the term *kāraka*.

Now, if their independence were somehow admitted, then the designation "agent" (*kartṛ*) would necessarily follow in those cases as well; consequently, in instances such as *grāmād āgacchati* ("he comes from the village") and *upādhyāyāya gāṃ dadāti* ("he gives a cow to the teacher"), the third case ending (*tṛtīyā*) would necessarily follow after words like "village. Furthermore, there would be the fault of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśraya*). For instance, the derivation of the term "kāraka" (factor) occurs subsequent to the designation "agent," and once that [derivation] exists, the designation "agent" would occur by means of the term "kāraka. Much would have to be explained in this manner, and in providing such explanations, there would be excessive complexity in comprehension.

However, there would be no fault in taking the word *kāraka* as a synonym for *nimitta* (cause); thinking that it is precisely this [meaning] which is intended, he says: "This word *kāraka* is a synonym for *nimitta*.
As in the example "He comes from the village" (*grāmād āgacchati*).
In this case, the village possesses the status of a cause (*nimittabhāva*) with respect to the action of coming, which has the village as its fixed point (*dhruva*).

If the village were not established here as the limit (*avadhi*), then the act of coming would not be accomplished; therefore, the village is a *kāraka*. In the example "the leaf of the tree falls" (*vṛkṣasya parṇaṃ patati*), the tree is intended here as a relation (*sambandhitva*), but not as a cause (*nimittatva*).
Because of the mention of the term *kāraka* in the definition of *apādāna*, that which is not intended as a cause does not receive the designation of *apādāna*.

This is not a suitable counter-example for the mention of *kāraka*; for by the very mention of *dhruva* [in Pāṇini 1.4.24], the designation of *apādāna* is precluded here, since that which serves as a fixed point (*dhruvam*) when separation (*apāya*) is to be accomplished is indeed the *apādāna*. For the author of the Vṛtti will say: "That which serves as a fixed point when separation is to be accomplished" (Kāśikā 1.4.24). Nor is the tree intended here as a fixed point; what then? It is intended as a related entity (*sambandhin*). This is not so; for the tree, whose status as a fixed point is intended, is intended precisely as a related entity.

The meaning is that the leaf belonging to the tree, which has become the limit (avadhi), falls. For the intention to express [the tree] as a related entity (sambandhitva) does not contradict the intention to express it as a limit.

Therefore, it is only the state of being a limit that was intended for the tree, while its mere status as a related entity was intended; it was not intended that it serves as the cause (nimitta) for the separation (apāya), even though such causality exists. What, then, is improper here? [As in the example: "He asks the boy's father about the way."

Regarding the rule *akathitaṃ ca* [Pāṇini 1.4.51], which prescribes the designation of "object" (*karman*) for that which is "not mentioned" (*akathita*), if the governing condition *kārake* [Pāṇini 1.4.81] were absent, this would apply even to the boy (*māṇavaka*). How so? This word *akathita* is a synonym for "unmentioned. Since no specific category is under discussion and no particular distinction is introduced, when it is employed, it would apply everywhere without distinction to anything merely unmentioned.

Consequently, if it were simply stated as "that which is not mentioned," then everything—whether a factor of action (*kāraka*) or not a factor of action—would be "unmentioned," and thus it would follow that everything is "unmentioned."

Just as the father was not designated by specific terms such as "ablative" (*apādāna*) and so forth, so too the boy (*māṇavaka*) [was not]; therefore, he too would receive the designation of "object" (*karman*).
However, because the word "in a *kāraka*" (*kārake*) is present, the designation applies only to the father, who is the cause for the act of questioning, and not to the boy.
For the boy is not intended to be expressed as the causal factor (*nimitta*) with respect to the act of questioning; rather, he is intended as being related to the father.

If this were a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) of *dhruva* and so forth, rather than a technical name (*saṃjñā*), then in those instances where the word "kāraka" is employed—such as in [Pāṇini 6.2.148] and similar rules—the inclusion of the *apādāna* and other cases by the term "kāraka" would not occur. However, there is no such fault if it is taken as a technical name; for a name, when it recurs, conveys the named object. Therefore, he says: "In the designations of *kārakas*," and so forth.

Wherever there is the mention of the term "kāraka," this conventional usage—characterized by the communication of the intended meaning—is to be understood through this very qualification; for even in other contexts, the term "kāraka" is employed as a synonym for "nimitta" (cause).
And that cause is precisely the *apādāna* and so forth, for nothing other than those constitutes a cause of action.

Therefore, by the mention of "kāraka" (participant in an action), there is the inclusion of the *apādāna* (ablative) and the others. Others, however, say: because of association (*sāhacarya*), the *apādāna* and the rest—which are associated with that which qualifies a *kāraka*—are expressed by the word "kāraka"; thus, their inclusion occurs precisely through that [mention of] "kāraka.
Alternatively, the mention of "kāraka" should be emphasized;
by that, this rule [Pāṇini 1.4.23], namely *tataḥ*, becomes applicable.

Therefore, by the mention of the "participant" (kāraka), the *apādāna* and the others will be included. "Departure" (*apāya*) means separation; that is to say, disjunction. Since that [disjunction] resides in two things, just as he who departs by means of that disjunction is connected with the departure, so too that from whom he departs is also connected with the departure. Consequently, the ablative case (*pañcamī*) ought to occur in both instances; for this very reason, he says: "That which is stated to be fixed (*dhruva*) when there is departure. [And he adds: "When departure is to be accomplished."

This is a locative of object (*viṣaya-saptamī*). The meaning is: "that which has become the object of departure by virtue of being the thing to be accomplished. Although in common usage the word *dhruva* denotes a state of uniformity—as in "his character is constant" (*dhruvam asya śīlam*) or "his form is constant" (*dhruvam asya rūpam*)—nevertheless, since no purpose is served here by that [uniformity] when "departure" (*apāya*) is what is to be accomplished, constancy (*dhruvatā*) is not required with respect to the departure. Rather, that very [constancy] is what is employed, and it consists precisely in the state of being a limit (*avadhi-bhāva*).

In proximity to that *apāya* (separation), the word *dhruva*—through its connection characterized by contiguity (*saśleṣa*)—expresses the state of being a limit (*avadhi*) for that which is falling away; therefore, he says "that which has become a limit.
For this very reason, when *apāya* is the thing to be established (*sādhya*), that which serves as the limit is here denoted by the word *dhruva*.
Consequently, the designation of *apādāna* is established even in cases such as "he fell from a running horse" (*dhāvato'śvāt patitaḥ*).

For even in this case, although there is motion (*calatva*) and although [the agent] has not yet departed from [the object], the status of being an *avadhi* (limit) exists. Now, how is the designation of *apādāna* (ablative) applied here in such instances as "he feels aversion toward unrighteousness" (*adharmāj jugupsate*), "he desists from unrighteousness" (*adharmād viramati*), and "he neglects righteousness" (*dharmāt pramādyati*)? For indeed, no actual departure (*apāya*) occurs here. How so? Departure is preceded by the attainment of an effect (*kārya-samprāpti-pūrvaka*), and here there is no attainment of an effect. To this, he says: "In the case of roots meaning 'aversion' (*jugupsā*), etc.
The meaning is that an *upasaṃkhyāna*—that is, a supplementary rule (*pratipādana*)—must be made for the designation of *apādāna* when roots with the sense of aversion and so forth are employed.

In this regard, the following is the demonstration: "The technical term *apādāna* (ablative) is made large [in scope] for the purpose of indicating that this designation has a wide range of application. And thus it becomes wide-ranging if its scope includes not only those things designated by the terms mentioned in the sūtras, but others as well; otherwise it would not. Therefore, in the employment of roots such as *jugupsā* ('aversion'), even in the absence of physical separation (*apāya*), the designation *apādāna* will apply.

Alternatively: "There is indeed separation (*apāya*) here; for separation does not occur only when preceded by the attainment of a physical effect. What then? It also occurs when preceded by the attainment of a mental state."

In this context, first of all, one feels aversion toward unrighteousness (*adharma*) and desists from it. Only that person who acts with foresight perceives thus: "This so-called unrighteousness is a cause of suffering; therefore, a conscious being ought not to perform it. He perceives thus: "Nothing desirable is accomplished through this unrighteousness; there is only suffering resulting from its undertaking. Reflecting in this way, he grasps it with his intellect, and having grasped it, he turns away from it.
And thus, it is established that according to the rule "the fixed point of departure (*apādāna*) is that from which there is a certain falling away," [unrighteousness] is indeed the *apādāna*.
Regarding the word "pramādyati": [the root] *mad* is used in the sense of "intoxication" (*herṣe*) [Dhātupāṭha 1208]; the lengthening of the vowel occurs by [Pāṇini 7.3.74].

Now, how is there the designation of "ablative" (*apādāna*) here in the case of "he does not come from the village"? And why would it not be so? Because the village is not connected with the act of departing (*apāya*).

That in whose presence there is separation (*apāya*), that [separation] is prohibited by the action of coming which has the point of departure (*apādāna*) as its instrument; if that [action] is absent, how could there be separation? This is not a fault, for here, once the designation of "point of departure" has arisen, it is subsequently connected with the prohibition; otherwise, the scope of the prohibition would not have been shown. Thus, the action of coming which has the point of departure as its instrument is intended to be prohibited. In that case, if the prohibition were applied at the very outset, then because of the absence of separation, the designation of "point of departure" would not be established for the village, which would be unrelated to it.

Consequently, that action of coming which has the ablative as its instrument and serves as the object of the negation cannot be demonstrated [prior to the negation]; nor can a negation be stated here when its object has not been demonstrated. Therefore, the designation of "ablative" (apādāna) occurs first, and subsequently there is the connection with the negation; this is the sequence. *Bhīti* is fear (*bhī*); *trāṇa* is protection (*trā*). [The suffix] *kvip* is applied because [the root belongs to] the *sampad-ādi* group. *Bhī* and *trā* together form *bhītrau*.
Those whose meanings are "fear" (*bhī*) and "protection" (*trā*) are "those whose meanings are fear and protection" (*bhītrārthāḥ*).

Regarding the phrase "of those whose meaning is 'to fear' (*bibheti*)," and so forth: by virtue of association (*sāhacarya*), the words *bibheti* and *trāyati* here function as representatives of the meanings "to fear" and "to protect."
Those whose meaning is "to fear" are "those whose meaning is *bibheti*. Those whose meaning is "to protect" are "those whose meaning is *trāyati*. [The word] "fears" (*bibheti*)—thus it is said.
The root *ñibhī* in the sense of "fear" (Dhātupāṭha 1084) belongs to the *jauhotyādi* class.
Regarding the form *udvijate*:
the root *ovijī* in the sense of "fear" and "trembling" (Dhātupāṭha 1460) belongs to the *taudādi* class and is anudātta.
Regarding the word "trāyate": the root *trai* meaning "to protect" belongs to the Bhūvādigaṇa (Dhātupāṭha 965). Regarding the phrase "he fears in the forest":
here the fear is not from the forest itself; rather, it is from thieves and the like who reside there.

But surely, in this case, the technical designation *adhikaraṇa* (locus) will prevail as an exception due to its higher status. Moreover, the term *dhruvam* (the fixed point) is understood from the previous rule, and it has been stated that "that which is fixed is the limit (*avadhi*).

Now, the forest is not intended here as a limit; so what is the purpose of including the mention of "the cause of fear" (*bhayahetu*) to exclude that? If this is so, then this is an elaboration (*prapañca*) of the preceding rule.
For separation (*apāya*) does not necessarily occur only after physical contact (*kāyasamprāpti*); rather, it may also occur preceded by mental contact (*buddhisamprāpti*).

Furthermore, there is here also an attainment [of an object] preceded by cognition; for instance, in the case of the expression "he fears thieves," a person who is discerning perceives thus: "If the thieves were to see me, my death would be certain. Reflecting in this way, he attains them through his intellect, and having attained them, he turns away from them.
In that regard, the meaning is already established by the word "certainly" (*dhruvam*) and so forth.
Therefore, this is an elaboration of what was stated previously.
Furthermore, no consideration of relative importance (guru-lāghava) is made regarding the elaborations (prapañca).

In this way, the subsequent applications (yoga) are also to be understood as mere elaborations of the preceding one; for the examples of those [subsequent ones], such as "he is defeated because of his study" and so forth, are already established by the preceding rule itself.
And how they are thus established has been demonstrated in the Bhāṣya itself.
Therefore, even in that case, one need not consider the relative weight or lightness [of the consequences]. "It cannot be endured" means it cannot be experienced.
"He fails because of study" means he is unable to overcome the study; he does not master it.
> [[1.3.19]] Thus, the *ātmanepada* [is used].
In the example "he conquers his enemies" (*śatrūn parājayate*), the meaning is "he overcomes."

But surely, because it is subsequent [in the order of rules], the designation *apādāna* will not apply here since it is superseded by the designation *karman*; so what is the purpose of including the term *asoḍha* (not having endured) for the sake of its exclusion? This is true; however, in an elaborate exposition (*prapañca*), one does not consider the relative weight or brevity [of the formulation], and this is indeed an elaborate exposition.
For in this case, there is a departure (*apāya*) preceded by a mental connection (*buddhi-saṃsarga*) resulting from study.

For instance—a person who is lazy thinks thus: "This study leads only to suffering. Seeing this with his intellect, he undertakes it, and having undertaken it, he desists from it. Therefore, it is established by the preceding [rule] alone. Those whose meaning is "prevention" are called *vāraṇārthāḥ*, as in the example:
"He keeps the cows away from the barley."

In the word *gāḥ*, the designation *karman* (object) is applied because the cows (*go*) are intended as that which is most desired to be reached. From the word *go*, by [Pāṇini 7.1.93], the vowel substitution *āttva* occurs; when *rutva* has been applied, by [Pāṇini 8.3.17], *yatva* occurs, and then by [Pāṇini 8.3.22], there is the elision of *y*. Regarding *vārayati*:
the root *vṛñ* is used in the sense of "covering" (Dhātupāṭha 1813); the suffix *ṇic* is added according to the *curādi* class.

Regarding the term "nivartayati": the root *vṛt* means "to turn" (*vartane*; Dhātupāṭha 758); here it takes the causative suffix *ṇic*. An example is: "He turns the cows away from the barley in the field."

In this context, the designation *apādāna* does not apply to a field that is not desired (*anīpsita*); rather, the term *īpsita* (desired) is included [in the rule]. Now, one might object: "Since the designation *apādāna* would be sublated here by the designation *adhikaraṇa* due to its higher status, the field will not receive the designation *apādāna*; therefore, the inclusion of the word *īpsita* is unnecessary. This objection should not be raised, because it has already been answered. The phrase "in the case of concealment" (*antarddhau*) is a locative of occasion (*nimitta-saptamī*).

The locative is used according to the rule "the locative is used after a cause when there is a connection with an action" (*nimittāt karmayoge*), as in the example: "one kills the leopard for its skin" (*carmaṇi dvīpinaṃ hanti*).
This itself is the indicator: that the locative case occurs when there is a connection with an object (*karman*) following a cause (*nimitta*).
For here, there is indeed a connection with the object of non-perception (*adarśana*).
[The word] "by which" (*yena*) [indicates this].
