And here, the word *pra* is not connected with the action of leading (*nayana*), but rather with the action of going (*gamana*); thus, it does not receive the designation of *upasarga* in relation to the verb *nayati*. [The rule] "the addition of the word *marut*" refers to the context of the application of the suffix *tva*.

This is the remainder [of the argument]; for otherwise, by the rules "particles (*nipāta*) have the first syllable acute" (*phi-sū* 4.80) and "prepositions (*upasarga*), with the exception of *abhi*, [also have the first syllable acute]" (*phi-sū* 4.81), the word *marut* would also have its first syllable acute.
However, the word *marut* is intended to have the final syllable acute.

The meaning of the word *upasaṃkhyāna* is "explanation" or "demonstration"; thus, the meaning is that an explanation must be made regarding the designation of the word *marut* as a preposition (*upasarga*).

In this regard, the following is the demonstration: the rule "upasargāḥ" is treated as a separate *yogavibhāga* (splitting of a rule). And here, the term "prādayaḥ" (the particles beginning with *pra*) is not connected [to it].
Consequently, the designation *upasarga* applies to the word *marut* when the suffix *tva* is prescribed.

Precisely because of this *yogavibhāga* (separation of rules), it should be understood that the designation *upasarga* applies to the word *pra* when the rule for *aṅga* is being prescribed, as well as to the word *antaḥ* when the rules for *aṅgin*, *vidhi*, and *ṇatva* are being prescribed.
This *yogavibhāga* is indicated by the citations of [Pāṇini 5.2.101] and [1.4.71].
Following that, the second rule is "in connection with an action" (*kriyāyoge*).

And here, the term "prādayaḥ" (the particles beginning with *pra*) is connected [to the rule]. For what purpose is this? It is for the sake of making known that the preceding rule does not have universal application (*asarvaviṣayatva*), since it is already established by that [preceding] rule; thus, there is no over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). Furthermore, it is for the purpose that the designation "upasarga" (preverb) should not apply to the particles beginning with *pra* when they are not in connection with a verb.
Regarding the word *maruttaḥ*:

when the suffix *kta* is applied by [Pāṇini 7.4.47], because of the mention of two *t*s, there is a replacement of the entire root *dru*. Now, one might object that since the designation "prefix" (*upasarga*) does not apply here, the word *karot*—not ending in a vowel—is not subject to that [substitution]; to this he says: "By virtue of the power of the rule for the technical designation," and so forth.

Just as in the case of *hrusaraja*, where by the force of the application of the marker *ḍit* the elision of the *ṭi* occurs even for that which is not a nominal stem (*abha*), so too here the substitution of *t* will occur even from a base that does not end in a vowel (*anajanta*). Otherwise, this rule would be purposeless; the point is that for the word *marut*, there is no other grammatical operation once it has received the designation of an upasarga. Regarding the statement "the addition of the word *ac*," the meaning of the term *upasaṃkhyāna* here is the same as before.

The derivation [of *śraddhā*] is also exactly that. But surely, isn't it already established that *śraddhā* is formed precisely by its inclusion in the *bhidādi* group? Why then is the designation "preposition" (*upasarga*) applied to the word *śrac-* for the sake of establishing that? He thinks thus: the inclusion there [in the *bhidādi* group] is not of Vedic origin (*anārṣa*). *Bāla-manoramā*: "Prepositions, etc. (1.4.58). "Prepositions, etc. (*prādayaḥ*).
The terms "not denoting a substance" (*asattve*) and "particles" (*nipātāḥ*) are understood to carry over [from the previous rule].

Regarding this, he says: "adravya" (non-substantive) and "tathā" (thus). The meaning is that they are termed *nipātas* (indeclinables). [From the Bālamanoramā: "Upasargas [are so called] when in connection with a verb" (Pāṇini 1.4.59); "having prefixed" (*prakṛtya*).
When there is the notion of motion (*gati*), the compound is formed according to [Pāṇini 2.2.18].
In the case of a compound not preceded by *nañ*, the suffix *ktvā* becomes *lyap* according to [Pāṇini 7.1.37]. Thus, it is "the subject under discussion" (*prakṛta*).
While the rule *kte ca* [Pāṇini 6.2.45] is being carried over, by the rule *iti* [Pāṇini 6.2.49], the word *pra* is acute on its first syllable by virtue of its original accent (*prakṛtisvara*).

In the phrase *yat prakaroti*, although the rule *tiṅṅatiṅaḥ* [Pāṇini 8.1.28] would have required the elision of the accent (*nighāta*) for the *tiṅ* following the particle *pra*, this is prohibited by the rule *nipātairyadyadi* [Pāṇini 8.1.30] et seq.; consequently, because the suffix *tip* is marked with *p*, it is unaccented (*anudātta*).

According to the rule *satiśiṣṭasvarasya balīyastvam anyatra vikaraṇasvarebhyaḥ* (Vārttika 9 on Pāṇini 6.1.164), the accent of the suffix-initial (*pratyayādyudāttatva*) does not override the accent of the *vikaraṇa*. However, it is the accent of the root itself that applies— by the rule *dhātoḥ* (Pāṇini 6.1.156)—
and the remainder becomes unaccented (*anudātta*).

Since the prefix *pra-* would have been acute-accented (*ādyudātta*) by the rule *upasargāścābhivarjam* (Phiṭ-sūtra 4.81), [the present rule applies]. While the suspension of accent (*nighāta*) from [Pāṇini 8.1.28] is still in force, [Pāṇini 8.1.71] prescribes that when followed by a finite verb (*tiṅanta*) containing an acute accent, the preceding word becomes unaccented (*anudātta*).
For in that context, the term "unaccented" (*anudātta*) is understood to carry over from [Pāṇini 8.1.67]: "After words such as *kāṣṭha*, that which is praised [by them] is unaccented."

And these three purposes are to be understood as applying to the technical term *gati* (preverb) in what follows. Now, for what purpose is this division of rules (*yogavibhāga*) made; why not simply include the mention of *gati* in the preceding rule itself? To this he says: "The division of the rule is for the sake of what follows.
By the words "in what follows" and so on, he demonstrates that the division of the rule serves a subsequent purpose.

He asks: if the designation *upasarga* (preposition) were also to apply in what follows, what would happen? To this he says: "In the case of *ūrī syāt*, etc. [He further notes: "The particle *ca* is for the purpose of the co-inclusion of the designations."

If the word *ca* were not present, because of the governing rule for a single designation (*ekasaṃjñādhikāra*), there would be an option (*paryāya*) between two designations for a single object, rather than their co-occurrence (*samāveśa*).
By the words "it is *praṇīta*" and so forth, he demonstrates the result of the co-occurrence of designations:
"there is an accent [of the prefix] according to the rule *gatiranantaraḥ*."
In both examples, the rule "the substitution of *ṇ* and *ṣ* occurs after a prefix" applies; thus,
in *praṇītam*,
the substitution of *ṇ* [occurs] by [Pāṇini 8.4.14].
Regarding "abhiṣiktam":
the substitution of *ṣ* [for *s*] occurs by the rule "after a prefix, in the case of *sunoti*" (Pāṇini 8.3.65) and so forth. Regarding "kārikā" and so on:
this supplementary rule (*upasaṃkhyāna*) must be made for the purpose of indicating the meaning of verbal roots.
The word *kārikā* ending in the suffix *ṇvul*, which has a different meaning [from the one under discussion], takes the form *kārikāṃ kṛtvā*.
The meaning of the word *upākhyāna* is "explanation.

In this context, the explanation is as follows: because the particle *ca* in the subsequent sūtra serves to include what has not been explicitly mentioned, the word *kārikā* receives the designation *gati*. [This applies to] the rule beginning with *punaścanasau*, and so forth.

Furthermore, the meaning is that the two words *punaḥ* and *cana* are to be explained as having the form of being designated as *gati*s (prepositional particles) in the domain of Vedic usage (*chandasi*). This explanation, however, should be made by relying on the fact that the particle *ca* in the subsequent sūtra has the sense of including what has not been explicitly mentioned (*anuktasamuccayārthatā*). An example is: *punar-ūtyam*.

The root *ṣivu* is listed in the Dhātupāṭha as "to sew" (1108). With the suffix *niṣṭhā*, because it is marked with the *u*-diacritic (*udit*), there is an optionality regarding the augment *iṭ* by Pāṇini 7.2.56, and consequently, by 7.2.15, the prohibition of *iṭ* applies. By 6.4.19, the *va* is replaced by *ū* before a nasal, resulting in the *yaṇ* substitution. Thus, we have *sūta*.
Then, by 7.4.42, *nah* is substituted for *na*, and by 6.2.49, the original accent (*prakṛtisvara*) is maintained, resulting in an udātta on the first syllable. Hence, the form is *cano-hitam*.

The word *canaḥ* is indeed udātta on its first syllable by the rule "Particles (*nipātāḥ*) are udātta on their initial [syllable]" (Phiṭ-sūtra 4.80). Regarding the statement "those ending in *cvi* and those ending in *ḍāc*": one might object that, since the inclusion of the word *anta-* ("ending in") in the definition of a "word" (*pada*) indicates the principle—"In other rules prescribing technical names (*saṃjñā-vidhi*), when a suffix is mentioned, there is no 'mentioning of what ends in that' (*tadantavidhi*)" (Paribhāṣā 81)—it follows that only the suffixes *cvi* and *ḍāc* themselves should be designated as *gatis*. Why, then, is it said "those ending in *cvi* and those ending in *ḍāc*"? The intention is this: the rule [Pāṇini 1.4.59] "before a finite verb" (*tiṅi*) is still in force, and it is not possible for a mere suffix alone to have a connection with an action (*kriyā-yoga*). Therefore, the mention of the words "ending in *cvi*" and "ending in *ḍāc*" is made to indicate that the suffixes are to be understood as ending in those specific elements. Thus, the designation of *gati* applies to words ending in *cvi* and *ḍāc*.

Therefore, because of the application of the power of the rule for the recurrence of *kriyāyoga*, the designation is understood to apply only to that which ends in [the suffixes mentioned]; thus, the designation indeed applies to that which ends in them.

However, since no specific distinction is provided, it would follow that the designation applies whenever there is a connection with a verbal root (*dhātu*) in general; hence he says: "In the case of *cv-* and *āc-," and so forth.
The suffix *cv-* is prescribed in the sense of "becoming what one was not before" (*abhūtatadbhāva*) when used in conjunction with the roots *kṛ*, *bhū*, or *as* (Pāṇini 5.4.50).

In the rule *avyaktānukaraṇāt* (Pāṇini 5.4.57) and others as well, because the connection with the roots *kṛ*, *bhū*, and *as* is carried over (*anuvṛtti*), the suffix *ḍāc* is also prescribed in that very context. Therefore, since *cvī* and *ḍāc* cannot possibly be joined with anything other than verbal roots, the designation *gati* is prescribed for them when they are joined with *kṛ*, *bhū*, and *as*. Consequently, by association with those, the same applies to *ūry-ādi* words when they are joined with those very roots.
Since the meaning of *cvī* (the suffix used for nominalization) is not perceived in words such as *ūry-*, he states "to explain" them, beginning with "urī, urarī," and so forth.
Because words from *śrauṣaṭ* through *svadhā* are listed among the *cādi* group, they receive the designation of *nipāta* even when not joined with a verb.
The word *āviṣ* is recited among the *sākṣāt-prabhṛti* group.
By the rule *tena tasya* [Pāṇini 1.4.98], when used in conjunction with the verb *karoti*, the designation *gati* is optionally applied; thus,
in the form *śuklīkṛtya*, the substitution of *i* for *ya* occurs by the rule *yasyeti ca* [Pāṇini 6.4.148].
Regarding "paṭapaṭākṛtya," the word *paṭapaṭā* is derived [as an avyaya] in the rule Pāṇini 5.4.57 (*avyaktānukaraṇasyāta itau*); and regarding "not followed by *iti*."

Regarding the word *atipara*: would it be a *tatpuruṣa* compound by means of a *yogavibhāga* (splitting of the rule) such that "the word *para* [is used] after *iti*" (*ite para*), or would it be a *bahuvrīhi* such that "that after which *iti* follows" (*itiḥ paro yasmāt*)? If the first alternative were adopted, then there would be a prohibition in the case of *itikhāṭkṛtya*, but here it would not apply—namely in *ita* (meaning "having made the sound *khaḍ* he has come")—and this is undesirable. However, in the second alternative, this fault does not arise; therefore, adopting that very view, he says: "that after which *iti* follows. [The example is] *niraṣṭhīvat*.

Because of the prohibition stated in the rule *subdhātuṣṭhivuṣvaṣkatīnāṃ pratiṣedho vaktavyaḥ* (Vārttika 671), which applies to the root *ṣṭhivu* (meaning "to spit," Dhātupāṭha 560), the substitution of *s* [for *ṣ*] by Pāṇini 6.1.64 does not occur. Furthermore, by the rule *ṣṭhivuklamucamāṃ śiti* (Pāṇini 7.3.75), there is lengthening of the vowel. Regarding the phrase *prītyatiśayaḥ = ādaraḥ* (the Kāśikā states: "Excessive affection is respect"), it is explained as follows: *prītisambhrama* means "agitation caused by affection. The meaning is an action such as rising from one's seat or offering a seat, preceded by affection. Thus, *prītisambhrama* refers to agitation (or respectful zeal) arising from affection.
Regarding the phrase "indifference toward humiliation": *paribhava* means contempt;
*tiraskāra* means disregard; and *audāsīnya* means indifference.
*kartavyam* means that which ought to be done, namely, rising from one's seat, offering a seat, and so forth, as well as inspection (*pratyupekṣā*).

*Paribhavaudāsīnyam* (disregard for contempt) is a compound formed by the rule of *yogavibhāga* ("the third [case-ending]")—that is, *paribhavena udāsīnyam*. Alternatively, it is a copulative compound (*dvandva*): *paribhavaś ca audāsīnyaṃ ca paribhavaudāsīnyam*.

Now, for what purpose are "non-respect" (*anādara*) and "unreal" (*asat*) included [in the definition]? Why is it not simply stated that "respect" (*ādara*) is "real" (*sat*)? Furthermore, how then would the term *asat* receive the designation of an indeclinable (*avyaya*) in the case of non-respect? And how would operations such as compound formation (*samāsa*) apply? If, by the rule of extension to what ends in a specific element (*tadantavidhi*), the term *asat* also receives the designations of particle (*nipāta*) and prefix (*gati*), then—since the designation of indeclinable is prescribed for the particle *sat*—the designation of indeclinable will also apply to the term *asat*, because the extension of the rule to that which ends in a specific element has been formally added (*upasaṃkhyāna*) to the rules governing indeclinables.

And in this case, since a word ending in a *sup*-affix (*subanta*) is the subject under discussion, the compound being prescribed for a word ending in a *sup*-affix that has a *gati* as its prior member will apply to the word *asat* as well.
Furthermore, in the rule *gatiśca* [Pāṇini 2.2.18], the term *pūrvapada* (prior member) is understood from the preceding context;
and in the rule [8.1.70], the term *pada* (word) is likewise understood.

Since the original accent (*prakṛtisvara*) is prescribed for the first member of a compound ending in *gati*, the aforementioned grammatical operation would apply; however, how could there be an understanding of "disrespect" (*anādara*)? For if the term "disrespect" (*anādara*) were not included [in the rule], then by the negation of respect (*ādara*) through the particle *nañ*—as in "it is not existent" (*na sat*)—if respect is prohibited, what else could it be but disrespect? This argument is not correct; for a *tatpuruṣa* compound formed with *nañ* conveys a meaning that is similar to its positive counterpart, just as in the command, "Bring a non-Brāhmaṇa" (*abrāhmaṇam ānaya*).

In this context, if the inclusion of the term "disrespect" (*anādara*) were not made, then that which resembles something existent would be considered non-existent only in cases where the application of respect is expected—for example, "he went after having shown disrespect to his teacher. However, in a case where respect is not even expected, it would not apply—such as "he went after having shown disrespect to a servant. But when the term "disrespect" is included, it is understood as a *bahuvrīhi* compound: "that in which respect is absent" is "disrespect" (*anādara*). Thus, it applies to both cases.

Since a *bahuvrīhi* compound occurs both in the sense of absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*) and in the absence of application (*prasaktibādha*), the designation is established in all cases. Therefore, the mention of "disregard" (*anādara*) must be made; and when that is done, the mention of "dissimilarity" (*asadṛśa*) must also necessarily be made.

Otherwise, what would be distinguished by the inclusion of the term *anādara* (disrespect)? For the designation *gati* is prescribed for that which exists in the sense of disrespect; however, the occurrence of the word *sat* in the sense of disrespect is not possible. If it is argued that although it is not possible for that [word *sat*] itself, it is possible for the word *asat*, which ends in it—this is true; it is indeed possible, but the designation *gati* is not obtained for it, because there is no rule of extension (*tadantavidhi*) applicable here. In the present context, there is no such extension, nor is there anything previously mentioned (*prakṛta*) here; therefore, the inclusion of *anādara* is intended to convey the meaning of the word *asat*.

If, however, just as in the case of the rule "goṣpadaṃ sevitāsevitapramāṇeṣu," where the mention of *asevita* (unfrequented) is understood to serve the purpose of excluding the meaning of the word *goṣpada* because that word cannot apply to what is unfrequented, so too here the mention of *anādara* (disrespect) would be understood to serve the purpose of excluding the meaning of the word *asat* because the word *sat* cannot apply to disrespect; then it would have been possible not to include the word *asat*. Yet, since the mention of *asat* is actually made, it is for the sake of clarity:
[namely,] "having honored" and "having dishonored."

In this context, the words *sat* and *asat* signify "the beautiful" and "the ugly," or alternatively, "that which exists" and "that which does not exist. According to Pāṇini 1.4.63 (*sadasatī samarthye*), the indeclinables *sat* and *asat* are designated as *gati*s when they respectively denote respect and disrespect. The meaning is that these two indeclinables, *sat* and *asat*, bear the technical name *gati* when they are present [in the sense of] respect and disrespect, respectively.
"Having honored" means having shown respect.
"Without honoring" means [the opposite].
The meaning is "having shown disregard.
In the compound *gati-samāsa*, the suffix *ktvā* becomes *lyap*. [This is as in the expression] "having made a sound like 'khāḍ'."

It should not be argued that because the word *iti* intervenes here, the designation *gati* will not apply simply due to the absence of connection with a verb; for there is a connection with a verb in some way or another. The point is that the rule *te prāgdhātoḥ* (P. 1.4.80) is intended solely to regulate usage, meaning "those *gatis* and *upasargas* must be employed only before the verbal root, and not after it.
Regarding P. 1.4.63, *sadasatī ādarānādarayoḥ*: [The words] *sat* and *asat* [are designated as *gatis*] when expressing respect (*ādara*) and disrespect (*anādara*).
The meaning is that the two indeclinables *sat* and *asat*, when used respectively to express respect and disrespect, are designated as *gati*s. [The example] *satkṛtya* means "having shown respect."
"Having treated with disrespect" (*asatkṛtya*); the meaning is "having shown disregard.
In a *gati*-compound, the suffix *ktvā* becomes *lyap*. [As in the example: "having done enough" (*alaṃ kṛtvā*).

The word *alaṃ* occurs in the sense of sufficiency (*paryāpti*). This word *antaḥ* occurs in the sense of the middle (*madhya*) as a locus (*adhikaraṇa*), and also in the sense of inclusion (*parigraha*).

In this context, since inclusion is prohibited, the designation (*saṃjñā*) is prescribed here [as "indeclinable"]. As for its reading among the *svarādi* group, that is for the purpose of granting the designation of indeclinable even in the sense of inclusion. [Thus we have the example:
*antarhasya*.
The meaning is "having struck in the middle. The elision of the nasal [is indicated by] "iti," which means that it is to be explained as something that must be stated.
The explanation has already been provided previously.
Regarding the term "antardhā":
by the rule *ātaścopasarge* [Pāṇini 3.3.106], the suffix *aṅ* is applied.
Regarding "antarddhiḥ," the suffix *kip* is applied according to [Pāṇini 3.3.92]. Regarding "antarṇayati":

The substitution of *ṇ* [for *n*] occurs by the rule *upasargādasamāse’pi* [Pāṇini 8.4.14]. The word *kaṇe* is an indeclinable (*nipāta*) that functions as a form ending in the locative case. Furthermore, it is not understood here as signifying an excess of desire;
for in that case, the limiting condition (*upādhi*) "the obstruction of faith" (*śraddhāpratīghāta*) would be applicable.
The word *manas* is also understood to function as "desire" (*abhilāṣa*) due to its association with that [ear], as in the expressions "having struck the ear" and "having struck the mind.

Here, the word *karṇe* refers to a minute particle of rice (*taṇḍulāvayava*) acting as the locus (*adhikaraṇa*), while the word *manas* refers to the intellect (*cetas*). Regarding the term *puraskṛtya*:

in the sense of "come from a preceding place," the suffix *asi* is applied to the word *pūrva* by the rule *pūrvādharāvarāṇāmasi puradhavaścaiṣām* (Pāṇini 5.3.39), and the word *pūrva* undergoes the substitution *pura*.

> [[1.1.38]] This designation *avyaya* (indeclinable) is a technical term devised by the ancient masters (*pūrvācārya*) for the letter *s*, which occurs in place of the *visarjanīya*. > [[8.3.40]] Thus, [the rule applies to] the letter *s*: "having placed the city (*puraḥ*) before him, he went.
The phrase "having placed before him" (*puraḥ kṛtvā*) serves as a counter-example (*pratyudāharaṇa*).

The mention of *pūḥ* and *parāḥ* in this context is for the purpose of demonstrating that the word *puraḥ* is not an indeclinable (*avyaya*), by virtue of its association with them. [The root] *pṛ* (meaning "to protect" and "to fill," Dhātupāṭha 1489) takes the suffix *kvip* according to the rule *bhrājabhrāsa-* (Pāṇini 3.2.177).

It has been stated that [the rule] "udoṣṭhapūrvasya" [Pāṇini 7.1.102] applies, as does the substitution of *r* for *ra*. Because there is an absence of the designation *gati*, the operations such as compounding (*samāsa*) do not occur here; furthermore, by the rule "[8.3.40]," the substitution of *s* for the *visarjanīya* also does not take place.

[Objection: But surely, if the technical designation *gati* were to apply here, then once the *gati*-compound is formed, the case-ending (*sup*) would have to be elided; in that case, the form *puraḥ* would not occur. And if that [form] does not exist, the designation itself would also cease to apply. [Response: This is not so. Even though the case-ending has been elided and the form *puraḥ* might not exist [in isolation], the designation does not thereby cease to apply; for that which has undergone a modification in one part is not different from the original (Vyāḍi-Pāṇini 16). The word *astaṃ* ends in *m* and is an indeclinable (*avyaya*). Its status as an indeclinable is to be understood either from the very fact that it is qualified by the term "indeclinable" [in the rule], or because it belongs to the class of words beginning with *ca* (the *cādi* group).
"In *astaṃ* [the word] *kāṇḍaṃ* has gone" (*astaṃ kṛtvā kāṇḍaṃ gataḥ*).
[The root] *asu* [is used] in the sense of "throwing" (*kṣepaṇe*; Dhātupāṭha 1209); the suffix *niṣṭhā* [is applied], and as before, there is the prohibition of *iṭ*.
The particle *ca* is for the purpose of drawing forward [the rule] *avyayam* (Pāṇini 1.4.67).

If this is so, would there not be a lack of its recurrence in what follows because it has not been carried over? There is no such fault, for the particle *ca* will recur in the subsequent [sūtras] as well for the purpose of carrying that [term] forward. "The indeclinable word *accha* has the meaning of the word *abhi*";
*abhi* signifies direction toward (*ābhimukhye*).
"To be spoken clearly" (*acchodya*).
The semivowel substitution (*samprasāraṇa*) occurs by virtue of its inclusion in the *yajādi* group according to the rule Pāṇini 6.1.15.
The term *accham* means "unclouded" (*akaluṣam*). An "instruction" (*upadeśaḥ*) is the statement of a meaning for the sake of another;
since that serves to cause the other to understand, he says: "Instruction is for the sake of another."

"Having done that" (*adaḥ kṛtvā*) means "having performed this. "Remaining hidden" (*tiro bhūtvā sthitaḥ*) means "having become crooked" or "having become turned away. [This is stated] because the rule regarding the suffix *cvī* applies to words such as *sākṣāt*.
That by which the meaning of *cvī* is expressed or stated is "the statement of the meaning of *cvī*" (*cvyarthavacanam*), that is, the explanation of the meaning of *cvī*.

By this it is meant: in this rule for technical designation (*saṃjñāvidhi*), that statement of the meaning of *cvī* must be made by which the meaning of *cvī* for words such as *sākṣāt* and others is conveyed.
For what purpose? So that when something not directly manifest (*asākṣādbhūtam*) is made manifest (*sākṣāt kriyate*), it may receive the technical designation of a *gati*.

However, when no non-manifestation is produced, but rather some other specific quality is produced in that which has already become manifest—that is, in that which has attained the state of being perceptible—then let it not be [so].
This applies to cases such as "false" and so forth.
When [the designation] is applied to things that are not false or to things that are false, let it be as it should be; otherwise, let it not be.

The explanation is as follows: here, the mention of *cv-i* from [Pāṇini 5.4.50] and the mention of *artha* from [Pāṇini 1.4.69] are both carried over by the maxim of the frog-leap (*maṇḍūkapluti*). Consequently, the designation of "gati" is prescribed for *sākṣāt* and the others when they function in the sense of *cv-i*.
Alternatively, because this is understood as a fixed option (*vyavasthitavibhāṣā*), the designation will apply to them only when they function in the sense of *cv-i*.
The sense of *cvy-artha* (the state of becoming something else) is possible in both ways: for words ending in *cv-i* and for those not ending in *cv-i*.

In that regard, when there is the suffix *cv-i*, the designation (*saṃjñā*) is obligatory by rule [Pāṇini 1.4.61]; otherwise, however, the designation of *gati* is optional by this [present] rule. Furthermore, because of the restricted optionality (*vyavasthita-vibhāṣā*) of this sūtra, it applies only to cases involving the sense of *cvy-artha*.
There is also the grammatical justification (*nipātana*) for its having a final *m* sound.

In the word *agnau*, *vaśe*, and so forth, one should recognize particles that resemble case endings (*vibhaktipratirūpaka-nipāta*). The words *prāduḥ* and *āviḥ* belong to the *ūry-ādi* group; the words *urasi* and *manasi* are particles resembling case endings.
[The example is] "having placed upon the chest" (*urasikṛtya*).
The meaning is "having accepted. "Having brought to mind" means "having ascertained. "In the middle of the word" means...
The two [words] are similar in form to words ending in the seventh case.
Regarding "nivacane":
it is an indeclinable compound (avyayībhāva) in the sense of absence, as in the examples *nitṛṇam* and *nivusam*.

Regarding the expression "having made a statement" (*nivacanekṛtya*): by virtue of the power of its utterance, there is no elision (*aluk*) of the locative case even in a compound. The same applies in subsequent cases. For example: *hastekṛtya*, *pāṇaukṛtya*.
In the case of the locative (saptamī), there is no elision (aluk) as before.
Regarding "dārakarma" (the act of taking a wife), it means the making of a wife. Regarding "bandhane" (in binding), this is a locative of cause (nimitta-saptamī).

Since the word *prādhvam* functions in the sense of "conformity," it is not appropriate as a qualifier for the word "binding" (*bandhane*); therefore, by virtue of the contextual force (*sāmarthyāt*), it is understood as a qualifier of its meaning. Hence he says: "that conformity," and so forth.
That whose cause is binding is described in that way [i.e., *prādhvakaraṇa*].
[This refers to] the expression *prādhvaṃkṛtya*.
The meaning is: having made it favorable by means of a bond as the cause.
Regarding the phrase "having made it ready for the journey" (*prādhvaṃ kṛtvā*): it is understood as having made the cart capable of traveling on the road, that is, having directed it toward the road.
By [Pāṇini 5.4.85], the suffix *itac* is applied as a compound-final (*samāsānta*) affix.
By [Pāṇini 6.4.144], there is the elision (*lopa*) of the *ṭu*.
"Pragatamadhvānam" (gone along the path) is a *prādi*-compound.

Since the application [of the term *gati*] here is already established by the maxim "that which is explicitly stated takes precedence" (*lakṣamapratipadokta-paribhāṣā*) [Vyā|pā|3], the mention of the word *bandhana* (binding) is for the purpose of indicating that the word *prādhvam*, though derived from a rule (*lākṣaṇika*), also receives the designation *gati* when it is connected with *bandhana*.

Consequently, when the orientation of the cart toward the road is intended to be expressed through the binding itself—by implication—the form *prādhvaṃkṛtya śakaṭaṃ gatam* ("having made the cart face the road, he went") is also established. Regarding the phrase "in the domain of comparison" (*aupamye viṣaye*): [as stated in the Kāśikā]. "In the domain of comparison" means:
that by which something is compared is a *upamā* (comparison).

[The suffix] *it* [is applied] by [Pāṇini 5.2.117] *ity-aṅ*. Its state (*bhāva*) is "similarity" (*aupamya*); [the suffix] *dhyañ* [is applied] by [Pāṇini 5.1.119]. Furthermore, that [similarity] is a relationship between an action and its factors (*kriyā-kāraka-sambandha*).

This is because of the statement: "In compounds, primary derivatives (kṛt), and secondary derivatives (taddhita), there is the expression of a relation, except in cases of conventional usage, distinct forms, or invariable relations.
By the inclusion of the word "viṣaye" (in the locative case), he shows that this is a locative of domain (*viṣayasaptamī*).

Furthermore, it is possible for livelihood (*jīvikā*) and secret doctrine (*upaniṣad*) to function as the standards of comparison (*upamāna*), thereby serving as the objects of the respective comparisons; for without those [standards], the comparison itself would not exist.
"Making it a livelihood," and so forth; that is, having made it like a livelihood.
The meaning is "having made it like a secret doctrine (upaniṣad).
A livelihood (*jīvikā*) is a means of subsistence.

*Upaniṣad* means a secret or a cause. That which is similar to it is called *jīvikopaniṣad*; thus, by the terms *jīvikā* and *upaniṣad*, it is compared to a livelihood and a secret. This is for the purpose of restriction.

Furthermore, regarding the restriction (*niyama*), would it be a restriction on the designation (*saṃjñā-niyama*)—meaning that those prefixes (*prādayaḥ*) receive the designations "motion" (*gati*) and "preverb" (*upasarga*) only when they are employed before a verbal root (*dhātu*)? Or would it be a restriction on usage (*prayoga-niyama*)—meaning that those prefixes, being designated as "motion" and "preverb," must be employed before the verbal root? If the former restriction were adopted, then this would be understood as a partial statement regarding the rules for designations: "Those prefixes, when employed before a verbal root, receive the designations 'motion' and 'preverb'."
Furthermore, since the designations "motion" (*gati*) and "preverb" (*upasarga*) have not yet been established, the reference "those [are] the designations 'motion' and 'preverb'" would be untenable.

However, since the designation "particle" (*nipāta*) has already been established, by the word "those," only particles would be referred to; consequently, there would be a restriction regarding the designation "particle.
In the other case, however, by virtue of this restriction, this rule (*yoga*) becomes a part of the sentences that establish the designations "motion" and "preverb," and thus no such fault arises.

Furthermore, if the restriction of technical names (*saṃjñā-niyama*) were intended, its result would be the cessation of the names for those [prepositions] not used before a verb; but that is incorrect, because even if the names were applied, nothing undesirable would follow for those not used before a verb.

For the other type of restriction (*prayoga-niyama*), however, the result is the absence of usage before anything else, and that is correct, since the status of being a motion (*gati*) or preposition (*upasarga*) is not desired for those [words] when they are not used before a verb.
Therefore, a restriction of usage alone is logical; relying on that, he says: "Those are designated as *gati* and *upasarga*."
"And so forth" (*tathā ca*):

the meaning is that it is exactly like, or similar to, the rule (*niyama*) that has been established. Now, one might object: when "prapaṭhati" ought to be used in the sense of "he recites," one instead uses "paṭhati pra"; therefore, since no undesirable consequence is observed, this [rule] is useless. This is not so; for although those items termed *gati*s and *upasarga*s are not seen following a verbal root (*dhātu*) in the common language (*bhāṣā*), they are indeed seen in the Vedic language (*chandas*).

In this regard, a learner of dull intellect, having observed the usage of these [prepositions] after a verbal root in the Veda (*chandas*), might think: "Just as they are employed after a verbal root in the domain of the Veda, so too should they be employed in the spoken language (*bhāṣā*). To address such a person, the rule is intended for the purpose of providing a formal derivation; thus, there is no risk of it being redundant. Now, for what purpose is the mention of *te* (‘those’)? Since, by virtue of the context, the connection of those designated as *gati* and *upasarga* with the requirement of being placed before [the verb] would already be understood, he says:
“The mention of *te*, etc.”

If *te* were not mentioned, then because the elements designated as *gati*s would immediately precede [the verb], they alone would be connected with the rule through the application of "prior usage" (*prākprayoga*).
However, by mentioning *te*, the *upasarga*s are also indicated; thus, their connection [with the rule] is also established.
Therefore, the mention of *te* is for the purpose that the restriction regarding prior usage may also apply to the *upasarga*s.

[Objection: "But surely, since prefixes (prādayaḥ) are designated as 'gatis' or 'upasargas' in relation to that [action] toward which they are joined, it will be understood—even without the mention of the word *dhātu*—that their usage must precede the verbal root (*dhātu*) itself; for action does not exist elsewhere than in the verbal root. So why is it stated [in the rule], 'after a verbal root (*dhātoḥ*)'? [Response: This is not so; [the word *dhātoḥ* is used] so that in cases such as *prakartum icchati* → *pracikīrṣati*, the prefix may also be placed before the verbal root. In this instance, the prefix *pra* is joined with the action denoted by the suffix *san*; thus, the designation of *gati* or *upasarga* would apply to *san* [if the rule did not specify *dhātoḥ*]. Therefore, [the mention of *dhātoḥ* is necessary].

Furthermore, if the mention of "root" (*dhātu*) were not made, [the prefix] would be applied immediately before that very [element]. However, because of the mention of "root," it is applied before the root *cikīrṣati*, and not before the suffix *san*. It has been stated that because of the rule regarding the usage of separated elements in Vedic (*chandas*), there is no usage of separated elements in the common language (*bhāṣā*). If this is so, then even when there is an intervention by a motion-word (*gati*), the application before [the root] would not be obtained—as in *samāharati* and similar forms. This is not a fault; for an element of the same class does not constitute an intervention. Since the category of "motion-words" (*gati*) and "prepositions" (*upasarga*) is what is being relied upon, there is no intervention.
Regarding "ā mandraiḥ" and so forth:
here, although there is an intervention by words such as "ā" and "mandraiḥ," the verbal root *yā* is placed before them.
Thus: "āyāhi."
By this, he shows the connection with the word *aṅga yāhi*. The plural number is used in the expression "karmapravacanīyāḥ" because there will be many designata (*saṃjñin*) to be mentioned later.

The purpose of creating this long technical name (*saṃjñā*) is so that it may be understood as a descriptive term (*anvarthasaṃjñā*): those who have spoken of an action (*karman*) are "karmapravacanīyas.
[The suffix] *-anīyar* is used in the sense of the agent according to Pāṇini 3.3.113.
The word *karman* denotes action (*kriyā*).

And who have declared what to be action? Those who do not currently call it action. Thus, by means of establishing a name according to its etymological meaning, those who have indicated action, but have not [formally] declared it—those who do not currently call it action.

Thus, it is stated that those [words] which, by means of being given a name according to their literal meaning (*anvarthasaṃjñā*), have indicated an action (*kriyā*) in the past but do not indicate one at present, receive the designation *karmapravacanīya*.
If they do not indicate an action at present, what then? They indicate a specific relation (*sambandhaviśeṣa*).

For example, in the expression *śākalyasya saṃhitāmanuprāvarṣat* ("It rained after Śākalya’s recitation of the *saṃhitā*"), the word *anu* indicates the relation produced between the recitation and the rain, characterized as the state of cause and effect (*hetuhetumadbhāva*), by means of the act of listening (*niśamanakriyā*).

Since the designation *karmapravacanīya* applies, the second case (*dvitīyā*) occurs by [Pāṇini 2.3.8]. Thinking that "the word *lakṣaṇa* here refers to a mark (*cihna*)," someone objects with the words "For what purpose," and so forth. The other [author], however, [refers] to the sūtra beginning with [Pāṇini 1.4.90]. There, the word *lakṣaṇa* is understood as referring to a mark, that is, an indicator; but here, it refers to a causal factor (*hetu*). Therefore, with the intention that it is not established by that [previous rule], he says to him: "But the statement is for the sake of expressing the cause (*hetvartha*)," and so forth.
The word *tu* is used for emphasis, meaning "only the cause.
The word *hetu* here refers to an efficient cause (*kāraka-hetu*), not an indicative cause (*jñāpaka-hetu*); otherwise, this would not constitute a valid refutation.
That whose object is the cause is described as such.

The meaning of this statement is that it is intended so that the designation *karmapravacanīya* may apply to the prefix *anu* when it occurs in the sense of a cause (*hetu*). But for what purpose is this designation prescribed for it when it occurs in the sense of a cause? To this he says: "When [the sense of] a cause is expressed by the third case," and so forth.

For rain is the cause of the conjunction (*saṃhitā*); the sacrifice is the cause of the sprinkling (*seka*) following the *anūddhi*; for it is thus: having heard (i.e., perceiving) the conjunction, it rained.
And having heard [the word] *anu* used with the sense of "having sacrificed," he poured [the libation].

In that context, if this technical term (*saṃjñā*) were not applied to *anu* when it expresses a cause (*hetu*), then in examples such as *śākalyasya saṃhitāmanu raprāvarṣat*, the third case ending would occur by the rule *hetau* [Pāṇini 2.3.23]. Therefore, in order to prevent that [third case] and ensure that the second case ending alone occurs, this technical term is prescribed for *anu* when it denotes a cause. [The example is: *nadīmanvavasitā*.
The meaning of "saha" (together) is the meaning of the third case here,
because the third case is prescribed in connection with the sense of "saha" by [Pāṇini 2.3.19]. Regarding the word "anvavasitā":
This is the form of the root *ṣiñ* (meaning "to bind," Dhātupāṭha 1477) in its past passive participle (*niṣṭhā*) form. Regarding the expression "grammarians [follow] Śākaṭāyana":
this means that other grammarians are inferior in comparison to Śākaṭāyana.
Here, Śākaṭāyana is distinguished by the relationship produced through this comparison.

Then, when the sixth case-ending has been reached, the second is prescribed by way of its exception (*apavāda*), because the relationship residing in both [relata] is expressed by a single case-ending alone. Consequently, after the word *vaiyākaraṇa*, which denotes one of the relata, there is no further case-ending for the other relatum. That which is mounted upon the locus (*adhika*) is called the *adhi-karaṇa*.
And without that which is not greater, the greater cannot exist.

Therefore, this designation is understood to apply when there is a greater relationship produced by the action superimposed [upon it]. By the word "ca" (and), it is also [understood] in the case of the lesser.
"In the *upakhārī*, there is a *droṇa*.
This means that a *droṇa* is greater than a *khārī*.
The locative case is used according to the rule beginning with "yasmād adhikam" (Pāṇini 2.3.9).

Since the relationship has already been expressed by that very [word], the second case ending does not occur after the word *droṇa* according to [Pāṇini 2.3.8]. [The phrase] "by the related [word] under discussion" refers to [the word] *varṣa* and so on.
[The phrase] "of something" refers to...

Regarding "from Trigarta" and so forth: in the expression "apa trigartebhyaḥ," the ablative case is used according to Pāṇini 2.3.10, which states that the ablative is employed with the words *apa*, *āṅ*,
and *pari*.
Regarding "pari pari trigartebhyaḥ," there is reduplication according to [Aṣṭādhyāyī 8.1.5]. Regarding "odanaṃ pariṣiñcati," the meaning is that he sprinkles it on all sides.
By [Pāṇini 7.1.59], the *num* augment is applied.
Since the designation (*saṃjñā*) of "karmapravacanīya" does not apply here, only the designation of "upasarga" (preverb) occurs.

Consequently, by [Pāṇini 8.3.65], "upasargāt sunoti," the substitution of *ṣ* for *s* takes place. Where the author intends an operation to apply to both *maryādā* (limit exclusive) and *abhividhi* (limit inclusive), he explicitly mentions both, as in [Pāṇini 2.1.13] and so forth.

However, in this case, only the *maryādā* (limit) is taken, not the *abhividhi* (inclusive limit). Consequently, someone might have the misconception that this technical designation (*saṃjñā*) should not apply in the case of an inclusive limit; therefore, in order to dispel that [misconception], he says: "Because of the mention of the word" (*vacanagrahaṇāt*), and so forth.
For when the word is mentioned, a *bahuvrīhi* compound is obtained.
That rule in which the word "limit" (*maryādā*) occurs is the "mention of the word limit" (*maryādāvacana*).
In this regard, the meaning is as follows: where there is the apprehension of a limit (*maryādā*) in a sutra, the particle *āṅ* there is designated as a *karmapravacanīya*.

That sutra, namely [Pāṇini 2.1.13], contains the term *upātta* (employed) for the sense of *maryādā* (limit) and *abhividhi* (inclusiveness); thus, it applies in both cases. But what is the difference between exclusion (*varjana*) and limit (*maryādā*), such that, having mentioned exclusion in the preceding sutra, he employs the term "limit" here? This is the distinction: in the case of exclusion, there is understood a connection with something else through general association by excluding that [specific point], as in "it has rained up to the Trigartas"; for in this instance—

In whichever direction one situated [there] utters this sentence, it is understood that "it has rained" in that very region and likewise in all other directions, with the exception of Trigarta. However, when this sentence is used in the sense of a limit (*maryādā*)—as in "it has rained as far as Pāṭaliputra"—the connection is perceived with the raining of that specific region situated in the direction connected to that [limit]; this is the distinction. [The rule] "let it not apply in the sense of slightness (*īṣadartha*) or in connection with a verbal action (*kriyāyoge*)" refers to the word *ākaḍāra* in the sense of slightness.
In the case of *kriyāyoge samāharati*,
the ablative case does not occur because there was no technical designation (*saṃjñā*) in the preceding rule. In the other case, the *nighāta* (elision of the accent) occurs by [Pāṇini 8.1.70].

As for that form which exists in both speech and recollection, because it possesses the nature of being *aṅit*, there is no possibility of its being designated [by a technical name] here simply due to the pronunciation of the letter *ṅ*. Here, "characteristic" (*lakṣaṇa*) is intended to mean an indicator, a cause, or a mark.

That by which something is marked or characterized is a "characteristic. "Itthambhūta" refers to having attained a certain state; the description of such a state is "description of itthambhūta" (*itthambhūtākhyāna*).
The root *bhī* (meaning "to obtain") is marked as *ātmanepada* (Dhātupāṭha 1844).

From that point onward, according to the rule *ā dhṛṣādvā* (Dhātupāṭha 1805 onwards), it optionally takes the *ṇic* suffix; when the *curādi-ṇic* is not present, the form of the word ending in the *kta* suffix becomes *bhūta*.
A portion that is being accepted is called a *bhāga*.

As for the word *bhāga* (part) which is employed when a portion is not being accepted—as in "a part of the *priyaṅgu* plant" or "a part of the city"—that is due to its similarity to a portion that is actually being accepted.
*Vīpsā* (distributive repetition) is the desire to pervade objects.
Furthermore, these [meanings], such as indication (*lakṣaṇa*) and so forth, are not what is expressed (*dyotya*) by the prefixes (*pratyaya*) and the like.
What then? They are objects; for this very reason he says, "they are objects" (*viṣayabhūtā ayam*).

And this [statement] is connected with the definitions (*lakṣaṇa*) and so forth by changing the gender, according to the rule: "The gender and number are like those of the thing denoted" (*abhidheyavalliṅgavacanāni bhavanti*, Vyākaraṇa-paribhāṣā 73). And this is connected with the definitions and so forth by changing the gender, according to the rule: "The gender and number are like those of the thing denoted."

If words such as *lakṣa* (mark) and so forth are not what is indicated (*dyotya*) by [prepositions] like *prati*, then what do they indicate? They indicate a specific type of relation (*sambandhaviśeṣa*). For example, in the sentence "The lightning flashes toward the tree" (*vṛkṣaṃ prati vidyotate vidyut*), the tree is the mark (*lakṣaṇa*) and the flashing lightning is the marked (*lakṣya*); for the lightning flashes having reached the tree, the relation of being the marked and the mark produced by the action of reaching is here indicated by the word *prati*.
In the expression "Devadatta is kind toward his mother" (*sādhur devadatto mātaraṃ prati*),
the attainment of kindness by Devadatta with respect to his mother is expressed by the word *prati*.

Here too, the relationship between the mother and the attainment of kindness— characterized as the relation between object and subject— is expressed by *prati*, being produced precisely by the action of reaching (*prāpti*) such that [Devadatta] attains kindness upon reaching the mother.
Regarding the phrase "that which here [belongs] to me," and so forth:
the meaning is that whatever portion falls to my share, let that be given.
Here too, the relationship is one of owner and owned, produced either by the act of dividing or by the act of accepting.
In the word *mām*, the substitution of *mā* for the stem *asmad-* is applied by [Pāṇini 7.2.97]. Furthermore,
the substitution of *āt* (long *ā*) is applied by [Pāṇini 7.2.87].

In the expression "he waters tree after tree" (*vṛkṣaṃ vṛkṣaṃ prati siñcati*), the distributive repetition (*vīpsā*) is indicated solely by the reduplication. However, what is indicated by the word *prati* is precisely that relationship between the trees and the act of watering— characterized as the relation between the object to be accomplished and the means— which is produced by the action of pouring.
The trees and so forth are the *nimitta* (the cause or basis) of the action, while the sprinkling (*seka*) is the goal to be accomplished (*sādhya*).
Here, because the root *sic* is transitive, the accusative case is established for the trees—which are the most desired objects to be pervaded by the sprinkling—by the rule [Pāṇini 2.3.2] itself.

Since the technical designation *karmapravacanīya* supersedes the designation *upasarjana*, the substitution of *ṣ* for *s* (as prescribed by [Pāṇini 8.3.65], "after a prefix, *s* in *sunoti* etc. does not occur.
"He sprinkles around" (*pariṣiñcati*) means he sprinkles on all sides.
The passage beginning with "Now" (*atha*) and so forth constitutes an objection.
The term "avoidance" (*varjanā*) and so forth refers to the exclusion [of the word *apaśabda*].
The justification for this is precisely that it occurs in association with *apaśabda*.
For in that context, because of the governing rule (*adhikāra*) concerning *karmapravacanīya*, the inclusion of *apaśabda* in the sense of avoidance applies only to the act of avoiding.

The designation *karmapravacanīya* has been prescribed for that [word] by [Pāṇini 1.4.88]. Therefore, due to its association (*sāhacarya*) with that, the term *paraḥ* is understood here as having the sense of exclusion (*varjana*).

Consequently, even when used in conjunction with that [term], this fifth case is prescribed only in the domain of exclusion, and not in cases such as indication (*lakṣaṇa*) and so forth—as in the example: "May it not strike me here."
> [[6.4.111]] Thus, there is the elision of the vowel *a*.
Since the designation *karmapravacanīya* is absent, the status of being an *upasarga* remains intact.

Regarding the word "mām": although the root *as* (to be) is intransitive, even intransitive roots become transitive when accompanied by a prefix (*upasarga*). Therefore, the accusative case is used for the object according to [Pāṇini 2.3.2]. Now, one might object: since the word *abhi* indicates a connection with a portion (*bhāga*), it has no connection with the root *as*; so how can there be transitivity? This is not so; rather, the word *abhi* indicates the connection with a portion by way of its relationship with the root *as*. For otherwise, if there were no connection between it and *as*, it would not even be designated as a prefix (*upasarga*).
Consequently, the designation *upasarga* would not apply, and thus the substitution of *ṣ* in *abhiṣyāt* would also not occur. In the example "Abhimanyu is the match for Arjuna" (*arjunataḥ prati*),
Arjuna is the primary [standard of comparison],
and Abhimanyu is similar to him.

In the expression *so 'rjunam anukaroti* ("he imitates Arjuna"), the specific relationship produced by the act of imitation—the relation between the object of imitation (*anukārya*) and the imitation (*anukaraṇa*)—is indicated by the preposition *prati*.
The ablative case is used according to the rule *pratinidhipratidāne ca yasmāt* [Pāṇini 2.3.11]. For example:
*māṣān asmai tilebhyaḥ* ("He gives beans in exchange for these sesame seeds").

The meaning is that "the repayment" (*pratidānam*) here refers to the "returning" (*niryātanam*) of sesame seeds previously given, such as when one takes back sesame seeds and gives back *māṣa* beans. In this context, the relationship produced by the acts of giving and taking is characterized as the status of creditor and debtor. [This is based on] Pāṇini 1.4.92: *pratiḥ pratinidhipratidānayoḥ*, where *prati* signifies a representative (*pratinidhi*).
"Sadṛśaḥ" means a counterpart; "pratidānam" is the restitution of what has been given.
"Uktasaṃjñaḥ" means having the technical designation of *karmapravacanīya*.
The *Bālamano ramā* commentary states: "In the sense of a substitute (*pratinidhi*) and an exchange (*pratidāna*), [the suffix *cha* is applied]" (Pāṇini 5.3.92).
Regarding the word "here" (*atra*), it means "in the scope of the rule stated.
In the sūtra, the ablative case in the word *yasmāt* is used in the sense of the genitive; this is evident from this very indication.
As for the expression "the representative of Kṛṣṇa," it should be resolved by the principle that "what is established by an indicator [in a specific case] does not apply everywhere.
Thus, the resulting meaning is: "the fifth case ending occurs after a word joined with a *karmapravacanīya* when the relationship concerns representation or substitution. For example:
*pradyumnaḥ kṛṣṇāt prati*.
The meaning is that at the beginning of the battle and so forth, Pradyumna possesses a similarity as designated by Kṛṣṇa.
The meaning of the ablative case is similarity; *prati* is the indicator of that [similarity].
Regarding "from the sesame seeds" (*tilebhyaḥ*):
the meaning is that one returns the sesame seeds taken as a debt, either in their original form or by way of their value and so forth.
The fifth case ending (*pañcamī*) is used here in the sense of the object (*karman*). The phrase "denoting nothing other [than the substance itself]" means...
By this, he demonstrates that it is stated [in the rule] "because they do not denote a different meaning" (*anarthāntaravācitvāt*), and not because of a total absence of meaning (*arthābhāvāt*).
For if these two were "meaningless" (*anarthaka*) due to having no existing referent, this sūtra would be purposeless.
To explain: the technical designation *karmapravacanīya* is prescribed by this [sūtra] for the purpose of overriding the designations *gati* and *upasarga*.
Furthermore, the designations of "motion" (*gati*) and "preverb" (*upasarga*) do not apply to the meaningless *adhi* and *pari*,
because the rule for these designations prescribes them only with respect to that [object] toward which the prefixes (*prādayaḥ*) are connected with an action;
and since it is impossible for the two meaningless ones to be connected with an action.
Regarding the passage beginning with "kuto 'dhyāgacchati":

the word *kutaḥ* takes the ablative case (*pañcamī*) in the sense of an apādāna (point of departure). It does not take the accusative case by rule Pāṇini 2.3.8 (*karmapravacanīya*), because of the maxim: "The case ending denoting a kāraka is stronger than the case ending of an upapada."

The purpose for undertaking the sūtra has indeed already been stated. Why? Because [the word] *kim* takes the suffix *tasil* by Pāṇini 5.3.7, and undergoes the substitution of *ku* by 7.2.104. Since its designation as a *karmapravacanīya* overrides its designations as a *gati* or *upasarga*, the rule 8.1.70 does not apply, and thus there is no *nighāta* (anudātta accent).

Now, one might object: when it is said "he comes" (*āgacchati*), the act of coming is understood in its general sense; however, in the case of *adhyāgacchati* and *paryāgacchati*, because of their connection with the prefixes *adhi* and *pari*, an upward direction and a state of being on all sides are respectively perceived, which constitutes another distinction. Therefore, how can these two be said to express no different meaning? This is not so; for when those two prefixes are employed even while the specific meanings [of the roots] are already understood from context or some other source, then they should be known to express no different meaning.

But how [can there be usage] of two meanings already understood? This is not so; for when even those two meanings are employed, it would contradict the rule: "There is no usage of words whose meaning has already been expressed" (Vyākaraṇa-paribhāṣā 60)? True, the usage of a word whose meaning is already understood is indeed observed, as in the example: *dvau brāhmaṇau* ("two Brāhmaṇas").
This is because worldly usage pays no heed to considerations of prolixity (*guru*) or brevity (*laghu*). [Another example is]: *susiktaṃ bhavatā* ("it was well-watered by you");
here, the third case ending (*tṛtīyā*) occurs after the word *bhavat* in the sense of the agent.
But the second [alternative] does not occur, as before:
"the meaning of the verbal root is being praised.
Praise (*stuti*) is the manifestation of excellence; that itself is its honor (*pūjā*).
"The substitution of *ṣ* does not occur based on a prefix (*upasarga*).
The sense is that this is because the designation of "prefix" (*upasarga-saṃjñā*) is superseded by the designation of "karmapravacanīya.
[Example: "suṣiktam kiṃ tavātra" ("Was it well-poured for you here?").
"This is a mere dismissal, not an act of worship. [To this, it is replied: "It is simply 'you have been excessively praised.
Even when the fruit has already been accomplished, praise serves the purpose of inciting further activity;
the meaning is, "a beautiful deed has been done."

He clarifies the term "pūjā" (veneration): regarding the phrase "in the word-meaning" (*padārthe*), it is the meaning of another word that is indicated, not its own primary meaning (*svārtha*), nor even its own related meaning; the meaning of a word is "word-meaning" (*padārtha*).

The mention of "the meaning of a word" (*padārthagrahaṇa*)—whether understood as the meaning of the word itself or the meaning of a word related to it—would be redundant. For the meaning of the particle *api*, as well as the meaning of the phrase "there might also be [something] belonging to *api*," is simply the meaning of that very word; so what is the purpose of mentioning "the meaning of a word"? Therefore, he says "of another word," etc., implying that by the force of the mention of "the meaning of a word," the meaning of the specific word is understood:
"there might also be [something] of clarified butter" (*sarpiṣo 'pi syāt*).

Because the designation *upasarga* is superseded by the designation *karmapravacanīya*, the substitution of *ṣ* [for *s*] does not occur according to the rule *upasargaprādurbhyām astir yac paraḥ* (Pāṇini 8.3.87). Now, why does the accusative case not occur after the word *sarpiḥ*? Because it is impossible for that [word] to be connected with the word *api*; for it is the *mātrā* (measure/portion) of *sarpiḥ* that is connected with the word *api*, not *sarpiḥ* itself.
Why, then, does it not occur after the word *mātrā*? Because that [word] is never used [in such a context].

When it is indeed used, then it lacks the designation of *karmapravacanīya* altogether; for that designation is prescribed for a word that is not being employed to express the meaning of another word.
This is expressed by the phrase "by stating an additional meaning."

The "one who has authority" (*adhikārtho*) refers to one such as a root-digger (*mūlaka-saha-ruā-seka*), and the "possibility" (*sambhāvanā*) is the manifestation— i.e., the disclosure— of the non-obstruction of one's capacity for an action, such as watering, by means of his statement, as in:
"He might even water the roots of the radish," or "He might even praise the king."
The meaning is that his capacity for both sprinkling and praising is not obstructed.
The suffix *liṅ* is used here according to the rule *sambhāvane 'lamiti cet siddhāpyoge* [Pāṇini 3.3.154]. It signifies "permission for acting according to one's own will."

*Kāmacāraḥ* means acting according to one’s own will; *kāmacārābhyanujñānam* is the permission for such action. For example: "Pour, or praise. The meaning is: "You are permitted to pour or to praise as you wish."

"Shame on the wretch Devadatta!"—here the accusative case is used because of the supplementary rule (Vārttika 118): "The [accusative] should be employed after *dhik*, *upari*, and the other two [words], when these three are followed by a doubled word; it is also seen elsewhere. Regarding "He might even water an onion," the optative suffix (*liṅ*) is used according to [Pāṇini 3.3.169].
In "palāṇḍum" (onion), the accusative case is used in the sense of the object [Pāṇini 2.3.2].
In the examples "api siñca" (even sprinkle) and "api stuhi" (even praise), there is a simultaneous desirability (*cānīyamānatā*) of the two actions— praising and sprinkling— by a single agent.
Here, there is a conjunction (*samuccaya*).

By employing the word "and" (*ca*), which has the well-known sense of conjunction—such as in "sprinkle and praise"—it makes that very conjunction explicit in the example. Regarding the phrase "this [relation] exists between owner and owned": here, the relation is produced by actions such as protecting and being protected.
Regarding the passage beginning with "In that case" (*tatra*):
in every relation, something is restated (*anūdyate*) and something is described (*ākhyāyate*).
That which is well-known is restated; that which is unknown is described—that is, it is enjoined (*vidhīyate*), or made known. For example: "He who has earrings is Devadatta."
By way of restating *kuṇḍala* and by way of restating *Devadatta*, *devadattatva* (the state of being Devadatta) is predicated.

That which is predicated is the primary element (*pradhāna*), while the other is subordinate (*apradhāna*) as a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*). In that context, when the owner (*svāmī*)—being himself not previously established—is predicated, he becomes the primary element; consequently, because he is connected with the designation of a *karmapravacanīya*, the sixth case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) would apply based on the relation of distinction (*vyatireka*). To preclude that, the seventh case (*saptamī*) occurs according to the rule: "The seventh case is used for that which is superior (*adhika*) and for that which expresses the sphere of action (*ceṣṭāvacana*). [Pāṇini 2.3.9]

Since the relationship itself is already expressed by that very [genitive], the first case (prathamā) occurs after it, not the seventh (saptamī). However, when the relationship of ownership is enjoined because it is not otherwise established, then the opposite should be understood. The term "adhir īśvare" (the word *adhi* is used in the sense of lordship) continues to apply;
therefore, this is an optional rule (*vibhāṣā*) regarding what has already been established.
The verb *kṛ* preceded by the prefix *adhi* functions in the sense of "assignment.
Only that which has been assigned becomes noble (*ārya*), as in:
"That which will appoint me here."

In *mām*, the second case ending (*dvitīyā*) is used in the sense of the object (*karman*). Regarding the form *adhikariṣyati*: here, since the prohibition of the *nighāta* accent by the rule *nipātair yadyadi* (Pāṇini 8.1.30) applies, this word retains its original accent (*prakṛtisvara*), resulting in an udātta on the first syllable. Now, is *laḥ* to be understood as the nominative or the genitive? If it were the nominative, then the designation *parasmaipada* would apply only to the letter *l*, and not to its substitutes (*ādeśa*), such as *ti* and the others.
[Objection: Granted, they too might acquire that designation through the principle of *sthānivadbhāva* (the substitute being treated like the original).

However, in the rule [Pāṇini 3.4.77] *ityatra tu* "laḥ," the connection between *taṅ* and *āna* would not be tenable, for *taṅ* and *āna* themselves do not constitute the *l*-suffixes (*lau*). Here, the state of being *taṅ* and *āna* is expressed as the *l*-suffix itself being *taṅ* and *āna*. Alternatively, it should be explained that by virtue of association (*sāhacarya*), the substitutes (*ādeśau*) for *l*, namely *taṅ* and *āna*, are what is meant by the word "la."
Furthermore, if the desired meaning were established by means of an explanatory gloss (*vyākhyāna*), there would be an excessive burden in the process of comprehension (*pratipatti-gaurava*).
However, this fault does not exist in the case of the genitive interpretation; therefore, relying on that, he says: "The genitive [in the rule] 'laḥ' [is intended]," and so forth.

But surely even this position is indeed faulty: for if the designation *parasmaipada* were prescribed for the substitutes of *l*, it would not apply to the *tiṅ* suffixes, because they must instead receive the designations such as *prathamapuruṣa* (first person) and so on by the rule beginning with "teṣāṃ paratvāt" [Pāṇini 1.4.101].

But what would be the scope for the designation *parasmaipada* and for the [affixes] *śatṛ* and *kvasu*? This is not a fault; for when [Pāṇini] says, "There is *vṛddhi* in place of [the penultimate vowel] before *sic*, when *parasmaipada* affixes follow" (Aṣṭādhyāyī 7.2.1), this indicates that the verbal endings (*tiṅ*) indeed possess the designation *parasmaipada*. For that [vṛddhi] is prescribed when *sic* follows a *parasmaipada* affix, and the [affixes] *śatṛ* and *kvasu* cannot occur in the domain of *sic*. [The rule] "tip-tas-jhi," etc., is merely an illustration of their forms. [As for the example: "How many here are striking? (*katīha nighnānāḥ*).
The suffix *cānaś* is applied by [Pāṇini 3.2.129] *nipūrvoddhanteḥ*;
the elision of the penultimate vowel occurs by [Pāṇini 6.4.98] *gamahana* etc.;
and the substitution of *k* (kutva) occurs by [Pāṇini 7.3.54] *hohanterñṇinneṣu*.
If the *ānaś* affix were also designated as *ātmanepada*, then the verb *han* (to kill), which is *parasmaipada*, would not [take the *ātmanepada* endings]. The term *tiṅ* is the nominative plural.
What kind of things are the *tiṅ* affixes that are being named? The meaning is that they are such that there are three of each.
This is expressed in the neuter gender (*napuṃsakaliṅga*) in view of the number (*vacana*).
And this [word *tri*] is used twice for the sake of distributive repetition (*vīpsā*).

If there are three sets of three terminations belonging to the designations "first," "middle," and "last" persons, then—since there would be six things to be designated (*saṃjñin*) and only three designations (*saṃjñā*)—the rule of correspondence (*yathāsaṃkhyam*) would not apply due to the inequality of numbers.

In that case, if a single designation were to apply to multiple [terminations] because it would be redundant to prescribe multiple designations for a single [set], yet not three designations for each individual [termination], then even though each one would still be [designated], there would be a lack of fixed determination (*avyavasthā*). This is not a fault; for here, the mention of *parasmaipada* and *ātmanepada* continues by way of anuvṛtti.
And following that [rule], two groups are formed: one group consists of the nine *tiṅ* suffixes known as *parasmaipada*, and the second consists of the nine *tiṅ* suffixes known as *ātmanepada*.

In this regard, this sūtra is connected individually with the three triplets in the first group and the three triplets in the second group: "Among the *parasmaipada* *tiṅ*s, the three sets of three are called first, middle, and last (prathama, madhyama, uttama); likewise, among the *ātmanepada* *tiṅ*s, the three sets of three are called first, middle, and last."
For this being the case, there is no contingency of the absence of an enumeration according to number.
To demonstrate that very point, he says: "There are eighteen suffixes of *tiṅ*.
By the words "nine," etc., he shows two groups.

With the words "In that [context]" (*tatra*) and so forth, he establishes the connection of this sūtra with the three triplets (*trika*) in the first group; and also with the three triplets in the second group by means of the words "in the ātmanepada" (*ātmanepadeṣu*) and so forth. The plural number in the word "those" (*tāni*) is for the purpose of the co-occurrence of technical designations (*saṃjñā-samāveśa*); otherwise, since there is a governing rule for a single designation, the designations of person (*puruṣa*) and number (*vacana*) would apply alternatively due to the authority of the explicit statement. And in that case, the grammatical operations such as the addition of *āṭ* prescribed by the rule "thereafter" (*tatra*, Pāṇini 3.4.92) and so forth would become optional.
But this being the case, there occurs an overlapping of designations.

For by the word "tat" (that), those three [forms] each of which have acquired the designation "third person" are referred back as having the designations "singular" and so forth; thus, only those which have acquired the designations "first person" and so forth are also designated as "singular" and so forth.

But surely, the designations *prathama* and so forth apply to the triads, while the designations *singular* and so forth apply to each individual [element]; since their spheres of application are distinct, there is no contradiction even within the governing rule (*adhikāra*) for a single designation. This is not a fault. For the designations *puruṣa* (person) and so forth also apply to each individual [element], as there is no such thing as a "triad" other than the individual elements themselves. Therefore, it is only the *tib* suffixes and the like that are the bearers of these designations. The mention of the word *tri* (three), however, is for the sake of delimitation (*maryādārtha*). It establishes that the *tiṅ* suffixes, defined by the number three, are individually designated as *puruṣas*.

Therefore, since the designations such as *prathamā* (nominative) and so forth, and the designations such as *ekavacana* (singular) and so forth, have exactly the same scope, the word "those" (*tāni*) was stated for the purpose of ensuring the co-occurrence of these designations. The term *suv* is a *pratyāhāra* (abbreviated reference). It begins with the word *su*, the singular nominative case-ending, and ends with the letter *p* in *sup*, the plural locative case-ending.
Now, why is this *pratyāhāra* not understood as ending with the letter *p* in *kap* (the suffix *kap*)? Because that would result in the letter *p* in the plural locative *sup* becoming redundant.

Does this [the letter *k*] serve the purpose of indicating a low-pitched vowel (*anudātta*), or is it for the purpose of forming a pratyāhāra (a grammatical abbreviation)? In this regard, it does not serve the purpose of indicating a low-pitched vowel, because the status of being a *sup* suffix is already established by its very nature as having a low pitch.
Furthermore, if it were not even for the purpose of forming a pratyāhāra, it would be entirely meaningless.

Therefore, it is understood that this pratyāhāra is formed by that [letter *k*] alone, and not by the letter *p* of *kap*; for in the rules governing accentuation (*svaravidhi*), the letter *p* has already served its purpose. The letter *c*, however, is intended to ensure the co-occurrence (*samāveśa*) of technical names such as *puruṣa* and others.

Without that [rule], there would be an option (*paryāya*) due to the authority of the statement under the governing heading of "single designation" (*ekasaṃjñādhikāra*). As for the purpose of the *tiṅ* being a case-ending (*vibhakti*), it is the prohibition of the *it*-designation by the rule *na vibhaktau tusmāḥ* (Pāṇini 1.3.4). However, in the case of *sup*, there is this [designation] as well as others, such as the substitution of *tyadādi* forms. To show that this [designation] has a restricted scope, he says: "having introduced the heading *lasya*" and so forth.

And this is the reason for [the rule] being restrictive (*niyamārtha*). An undertaking is for the sake of restriction when it concerns something already established, not when it is unestablished. Furthermore, this restriction must be either a restriction on the meaning of the *upapada*—namely, that the second person is used only when *yuṣmad* is the *upapada*—or a restriction on the person (*puruṣaniyama*), namely, that the second person is used only when *yuṣmad* is the *upapada*. In that regard, if the first type of restriction is adopted, then in the cases "tvayā kurvatā" and "tvayā kurvāṇena," the substitutes *śatṛ* and *śānac* would not occur for the verbal suffix (*laḥ*) because *yuṣmad* is present as the *upapada*.
Therefore, for that purpose, another effort must be undertaken.
In the other case, however, nothing requires such effort; thus, relying on the second alternative, he says: "Of these, this...
and so forth, [referring to] both "the remote" and "the proximate."

But is it not the case that a word which is proximate to another is called an *upapada*—on the grounds that it is uttered in proximity (*upa-uccārita*)? And that which is separated [by other words] is remote (*viprakṛṣṭa*) in comparison to what is not separated; therefore, there ought to be a separation. This is not a fault, because the inclusion of both "proximate" and "remote" is not fixed, since they are relative, like "prior" and "posterior."

In this regard, although that which is separated is distant when compared to that which is not separated, nevertheless, when compared to something else that is even more distant, it becomes proximate; thus, in the other case, there must also be that which is separated.
If this is so, for what purpose is the mention of the term *upapada*? It is made for the sake of ensuring that [the designation] applies even when [the pronoun] has occurred previously.
Otherwise, if only "yuṣmadi" were stated, then by the rule [Pāṇini 1.4.105], the second person would apply only when *yuṣmad* occurs subsequently, and not when it occurs previously.

Because of the inclusion of the term *upapada*, this [designation] occurs here as well. An item used both before and after [a verb] is indeed an *upapada*. By explaining "in a coreferential [term]" (*samānādhikaraṇe*) as "having the same denotation" (*samānābhidheya*), he shows that the word *adhikaraṇa* in the sūtra is used in the sense of "denotation.

Furthermore, regarding that denotation, because of its proximity, it is understood to be precisely that [denotation] for which the *lakāra* (verbal suffix) is produced—whether in the agent (*kartṛ*) or the object (*karman*) among the *kārakas*; thus he says: "in the same *kāraka*" (*tulyakārake*), and so forth.
That whose agent (*kāraka*) is equal is described as such.
By the word *tulya*, the meaning of the word *samāna* (equal) is indicated.
[This applies] "whether it is actually employed or not employed."
By this, he explains the meaning of the term *sthānini* ("in the place of").

The word *sthāna* signifies "occasion" (*prasaṅga*). That which possesses such an occasion is called *sthānī*. And what has an occasion? Only that which has its meaning understood, yet whose word-form is not actually employed, has an occasion.

This is what is meant: even when *yuṣmad* is not employed—the word "even" (*api*) implying that it may also be employed. Why is the mention of "coreferential" (*samānādhikaraṇa*) made? So that [the rule] does not apply in the case of *tvayā pacyate*, where the coreferentiality is absent. For instance, *tvayā* here expresses the agent, since the third case ending is prescribed for the agent.
The word *pacyate* expresses the object (*karman*), because the suffix *la* is prescribed when the object is to be expressed. Regarding the phrase "when mockery (*prahāsa*) is understood":
where, due to the absence of actual fact, there is merely deception, mockery is understood by revealing the intention of the speaker.
Regarding the phrase "when *manya* is the subordinate word (*upapada*)": that which has the verb *manya* as its subordinate word—that is, a word uttered in proximity to it—is so described.
Because the middle element (*madhyama-dhātu*) is prescribed, it is understood that the *dhātu* is distinct from the other two; thus he says: "from the *dhātu*, [the suffix] *ṭa*.
And [it is stated]: "and that [compound] is treated as a singular" (*sa caikavat*).
Where there are two or many thinkers (*mantṛ*), there this treatment as a singular is prescribed.

In other cases, however, the singular number is established simply because the *mantr̥* (the agent) is one. Regarding the rule "in the case of the second and first persons": this refers respectively to the words *yuṣmad* and *asmad* when they are used as co-referential (*samānādhikaraṇa*) upapadas, even if they are not explicitly employed, because their meaning is nonetheless present.

Just as in the counter-example (*pratyudāharaṇa*), the previous mention of *upapada* was connected with the word *yuṣmad*; [one might think] that this would carry over here [to the present rule], but since it is impossible for that [previous *upapada*] to be connected with the root *man*, the term *upapada* is mentioned again.

The mention of *manyateḥ* by means of the *śyan* affix is for the purpose of ensuring that the root belonging to the *tanādigaṇa* (which takes *śnam*) is not included. Therefore, the following does not occur: *ehi manuṣe rathena yāsyāmi na hi yāsyasi yātastena te pitā*.

For such is the thought regarding *manoti*: when both these [pronouns], *yuṣmad* and *asmad*, are present as co-occurring words (*upapada*), how should it be? If the agentive capacities are expected to be restricted to their respective substrates, then the verb (*ākhyāta*) is used separately as well—namely, *pacasi* and *pacāmi*.

However, if, due to the absence of contradiction, the verbal suffix (*lakāra*) arises for both capacities, then by the rule of conflict (*vipratiṣedha*), only the first person (*uttama*) remains—namely, *tvaṃ cāhaṃ ca pacāvaḥ*.
Even though there is the rule that "among the *tyadādi* group, whichever is subsequent remains," this applies here.
In the expression "āvām pacāvaḥ" (the two of us cook), the word *asmat* must also have the sense of *yuṣmad* as its denotation; otherwise, the dual number would not be possible.

For the state of duality is not applicable to the word *asmat* alone. [Regarding the statement] "the word *para* functions in the sense of excellence," it is, for example, as in "param duḥkham" (extreme suffering).
Although the word *para* also occurs in the sense of "direction" (*dig*) and so forth, he shows here that it is understood as occurring in the sense of "excess" (*atiśaya*).
*Sannikarṣa* means proximity (*pratyāsatti*) and also contact (*saṃśleṣa*).
Showing that proximity is what is intended here, he says: "proximity (*sannikarṣaḥ*) is closeness (*pratyāsattiḥ*)."

But conjunction (*saṃśleṣa*) is not perceived, because it is impossible for it to exist among phonemes (*varṇa*). Conjunction occurs only between things that exist at the same time, yet phonemes cannot attain simultaneity; for they are uttered in succession and perish as soon as they have been uttered.
