Conjunction occurs only between things that exist at the same time, yet phonemes cannot attain simultaneity; for they are uttered in succession and perish as soon as they have been uttered.
Moreover, even if simultaneity were granted, a conjunction (*saṃśleṣa*) of phonemes is simply not possible.

To explain: conjunction would have to occur either through *saṃyoga* (physical contact) or through *samavāya* (inherence). In that regard, the former would apply only to substances and not to sound, because qualities (*guṇa*) are devoid of further qualities.
The latter is also impossible for sound, for one phoneme does not inhere in another phoneme; rather, sound inheres in space (*ākāśa*).
Furthermore, no distinction between conjunction (*saṃyoga*) and inherence (*samavāya*) is possible, because both are uniform in every respect.
Consequently, the qualification "further" (*paraḥ*) would be untenable.

However, since proximity (*pratyāsatti*) is differentiated by the distinctions created through dependence, it can be qualified by the term "further" when employed in terms of its degrees of excellence or deficiency; thus, its status as a qualification is logical.

What, then, is this "proximity" (*sannikarṣa*)? It is that which causes one to pronounce the phonemes (*varṇa*) following those that are already close. When the activity of the palate and other articulators that produce a preceding phoneme has ceased, and the activity of the palate and other articulators that produce the subsequent phoneme is initiated, they say that this takes half a *mātrā* of time. That [time] is the interval between phonemes; the proximity (*sannikarṣa*) is that in which there is an interval of half a *mātrā*.

If proximity (*sannikarṣa*) consists of a separation of phonemes (*varṇa*) by no more than half a *mātrā*, then how is it that in cases such as *dadhy atra*, the time of separation is not perceived, and the phonemes are experienced as being entirely joined together? This is not so. Why, moreover, is this [definition] undertaken, given that the teachers say that conjunction (*saṃhitā*) is simply the highest degree of proximity; for when it is said, "Study the *saṃhitā*," the student studies precisely that highest degree of proximity? This is not the case; in common worldly usage, the immediate succession of one word (*pada*) with another is called *saṃhitā*.
And so speakers say: "He studies the *saṃhitā*, not the individual words (*pada*); he studies the individual words, not the *saṃhitā*.
Furthermore, if this were not the case, the operation of *saṃhitā* would not occur within a single word, as in the examples *kumāryau* and *kurmāryaḥ*.
Since this rule prescribes the technical designation *saṃhitā* for a specific proximity (*sannikarṣaviśeṣa*) of phonemes, it applies everywhere. "Cessation" (*virati*) means "pause" (*virāma*).
The suffix *ghañ* is used in the sense of the action itself (*bhāve*).
A pause (*virāmaḥ*), which is the absence of the utterance of phonemes, receives the technical name *avasāna*.
He shows the second meaning of the word *virāma* by stating: "That by means of which one ceases [speaking] is a pause."

By virtue of the word *bahula* (in the rule Pāṇini 3.3.113), the suffix *ghañ* is applied even when not forming a technical name (*asaṃjñā*) according to Pāṇini 3.3.121. In this view, that final phoneme after which one ceases [speaking] is designated as *avasāna* (pause).

In that regard, in the former view, since there is an absence [of sound], there is no sequence of priority and posteriority; therefore, in the rule *kharavasānayoḥ* (Pāṇini 8.3.15), this locative case is understood as a locative of scope (*viṣayasaptamī*) with respect to the pause, and not as a locative of proximity (*parasaptamī*).

However, this locative case is used in relation to *khara*. Others, however, argue: if priority and posteriority (*paurvāparya*) are not possible in the absence of [a preceding sound], then the locative of the subsequent element (*parasaptamī*) in the rule *kharavasānayoḥ* [Pāṇini 8.3.15] would be untenable; and if that were so, the locative of the subsequent element would likewise be untenable in rules such as *ato guṇe* [Pāṇini 6.1.97].
Why? Because phonemes arise sequentially and perish as soon as they are uttered.
When *e* exists, *añ* does not exist; when *añ* exists, *e* does not exist.

Now, if it is maintained here that the genitive of the subsequent (*parasaptamī*) is intended by relying on a sequence of priority and posteriority (*paurvāparya*) imagined by the intellect, then those who consider that the same must be accepted even in the rule *kharavasānayoḥ* [Pāṇini 8.3.15] desire the genitive of the subsequent with respect to the pause (*avasāna*). Others, however, maintain that when the final phoneme has the designation "pause," the genitive in *kharavasānayoḥ* [8.3.15] is understood as follows: here, with respect to the pause, it is a genitive of the locus (*sthāna-ṣaṣṭhī*), meaning "the *visarjanīya* [substituted] for the *repha* [occurring] at the pause"; whereas with respect to the voiceless consonant (*khaR*), they say it is a genitive characterized by immediate succession (*anantarya-lakṣaṇā*).

In that view, in the sixth position [of the rule], the status as a substitute (*sthānitva*) for the *repha* which is carried over from "ro ri" (Pāṇini 8.3.14) is not contradicted; thus, even though there is only one case-ending (*vibhakti*), it is divided according to its application. Now, even in the alternative where [the *visarjanīya*] does not occur, there is indeed non-utterance (*anuccāraṇa*) in the preceding portion as well, and there too the *visarjanīya* would result—as in "ratha"—for here too there is utterance prior to the *repha*. This is not a fault, because in that context, the term "word" (*pada*) under discussion is qualified by the *repha*: "of a word ending in *repha*."
Nor does the word-form [“repha”] arise with the preceding *repha*.
But even so, this would be a designation (*saṃjñā*) for the meaning; thus, in the rule *kharavasānayor* (P. 8.3.15), the metarule *tasmādityuttarasya* (P. 1.1.66) does not apply.
For this metarule applies when a word is indicated by the locative case, but not when a meaning is indicated.

And if that [term *avasāna*] were not applied, then by the subsequent rule [Pāṇini 8.3.1], the *visarjanīya* would occur for the *repha* of the word *ratha*, which ends in *repha*, even though that preceding *repha* is separated [from the following *repha*]. This is not a fault; it will not occur because of an indicator (*jñāpaka*). Since the author provides the instruction [in Pāṇini 8.3.51] without applying the *visarjanīya* to the separated *repha*—namely, by stating *raḥ*—this indicates that the *visarjanīya* does not occur for a separated *repha*.
[Objection: But surely, in common usage in this world, the term *avasāna* will be understood as referring only to the final phoneme.
For it is well known in the world that the verb *ava-√so* (to end) is used with reference to the final phoneme (*antye varṇe*).

Thus, when someone asks, "With what does he end? speakers reply, "With the vowel *i* or with the vowel *u*. The meaning is that he brings about the conclusion [of speech] by means of a phoneme such as *i*.

Therefore, one should simply take the term *avasāna* (conclusion) to mean "a specific location," so that there is no need for the formulation of a technical name (*saṃjñā*) and its bearer (*saṃjñin*). This is not the case; for the root *syati* (from which *avasita* is derived) functions in the sense of completion—as in "the discussion has concluded" (*avasito vādaḥ*); it functions in the sense of comprehension—as in "the meaning has been understood" (*avasito 'rthaḥ*); and it functions in the sense of defeat—as in "Devadatta has been defeated in the dispute between the two."

In that case, if this [rule] were not undertaken, there would be doubt regarding the mention of "end" (*avasāna*): would it be the inclusion of the word *abhidhāna-avasāna*? However, one would have to formulate the rule as *hrantagrahaṇaṃ kartavyam*—"the mention of *hrantayoḥ*" (referring to *khar-antayoḥ*)? But even that is not [sufficient]; for in that case, there would be doubt: does it refer to the final phoneme (*varṇa*), or to the word (*pada*), or perhaps to the sentence (*vākya*)? In that regard, one would have to formulate the mention of "phoneme" (*varṇa-grahaṇa*) for the purpose of qualifying the final element.
Therefore, the relationship between the technical name (*saṃjñā*) and the named object (*saṃjñin*) must be established: "tree" (*vṛkṣaḥ*), "fig tree" (*plakṣaḥ*).
"The visarga is substituted for the final *r* before *kha* and *ra-vasana*" [Pāṇini 8.3.15];
as in "dadhiṃ madhu~" [Pāṇini 8.4.57].

For here, the term *avasāna* (pause) is understood to carry over from the rule *atra hi* [Pāṇini 8.4.56]. Thus ends the fourth quarter of the first chapter in the *Kāśikā-vivaraṇa-pañjikā* composed by the venerable Master Jinendrabuddhi, who was a disciple of the Bodhisattva. "This is a *paribhāṣā*" means:
a discourse (*bhāṣā*) that operates everywhere (*paritaḥ*) is a *paribhāṣā*.
And so it has been said: "A *paribhāṣā*, moreover, illuminates the entire treatise from a single location, just as a lamp placed upon a threshold."

How, moreover, is it known that this is a technical definition (*paribhāṣā*) and not a governing heading (*adhikāra*)? From the indicative mark (*liṅga*) consisting of the mention of "a rule concerning words" (*padavidhi*).
For in what follows, everything being repeated—such as the treatment as if it were a member of another word (*parāṅgavadbhāva*)—is indeed a rule concerning words (*padavidhi*).
In that case, if this were a governing heading, the mention of "a rule concerning words" would be purposeless, because there would be no absence [of such rules] to be delimited by it.

Regarding this technical rule (*paribhāṣā*), since a technical rule applies everywhere throughout the entire treatise even if it pertains to only one part [of it], if the term "prescription concerning words" (*padavidhi*) were not included, this rule would apply even to prescriptions concerning phonemes (*varṇavidhi*).
Therefore, the inclusion of the term "prescription concerning words," which is made for the purpose of excluding prescriptions concerning phonemes, becomes meaningful.
Consequently, by the indicative mark (*liṅga*) of the inclusion of the term "prescription concerning words," it is determined that this is a technical rule and not a governing heading (*adhikāra*).

If this is so, then for what purpose is the mention of *sāmarthya* (semantic connection) and *yukta* (joined) made in rules such as [Pāṇini 8.3.44] and [8.1.24], given that the term *pada* (word) is understood there from the previous context, and since these are rules concerning words (*padavidhi*), they would not apply in cases lacking semantic connection simply by virtue of being word-rules? This is true; however, we shall explain right there the specific purpose for which they are made. Furthermore, this word *vidhi* is indeed a noun derived from the action (*bhāvasādhana*)—meaning "the act of prescribing" (*vidhānam vidhiḥ*)—and it is also a noun derived from the object (*karmasādhana*)—meaning "that which is prescribed" (*vidhīyate iti vidhiḥ*).

In that regard, when a word expressing an action (*bhāva-sādhana*) is adopted for the term *pada-vidhi*, it refers to the "completion of words" (*padānām apariniṣpannānāṃ pariniṣpādanam*); thus, the genitive case in *padeṣu* is characterized by its connection with a verbal root (*kṛd-yoga-lakṣaṇā*), because those words are related to the act of completion. However, when a word expressing an object (*karman-sādhana*) is adopted, *pada-vidhi* refers to the grammatical operation—such as compounding—that is prescribed for words already established and fixed.
In that case, the genitive case in *padeṣu* is characterized as a residual relation (*śeṣa-lakṣaṇā*), because the operation being prescribed is presented as being connected to the words.

In this regard, if the word *vidhi* (rule) were understood here as having an active sense (*bhāvasādhana*), then only the prescription of case-endings (*vibhakti*) would be included, while compounding (*samāsa*), the treatment as if being a subordinate member (*parāṅgavadbhāva*), secondary derivative formation (*taddhitavṛtti*), and so forth, would not be included. For in those cases, there is no prescription of words that do not already exist; rather, the grammatical operations such as compounding are prescribed for words that are already established. However, thinking that if the word *vidhi* is understood in its other sense [the passive], those [operations] will also be included, he relies on the word *vidhi* as having a passive sense (*karmasādhana*) and says: "That which is prescribed is a *vidhi*."

But in this view as well, would not the prescription of case-endings (*vibhakti*) fail to be included? For by rules such as *na hi* [Pāṇini 2.3.2], no grammatical operation (*kārya*) is prescribed for words already established; rather, the words themselves are prescribed. If it were not included, so be it. Furthermore, we shall demonstrate later that nothing undesirable follows from its non-inclusion. [The term] "beginning with compounds" (*samāsādi*).

By the word "ādi" (and so forth), the inclusion of secondary derivative formations (*taddhita-vṛtti*) and others is intended. "Capable" (*samartha*) means "powerful" (*śakta*); that is to say, one who is competent in accomplishing its own function.
For in common worldly usage, such a person is called "capable."
The very communication of their own meaning is the function of words.
And all those words—whether worldly or Vedic—that are under consideration here are equally capable of performing that function of communicating their own meaning.
Therefore, by virtue of the inclusion of the qualification "capable," some specific distinction is intended.

And that distinction is as follows: when a sentence is employed for the sake of an operational function (*vṛtti*), its capacity to convey that meaning is understood through proximity; thus he says, "in the denotation of the meaning of the *vigrahavākya*," and so forth.

It is called *vigraha* because by means of it something is specifically grasped or understood (*viśeṣeṇa gṛhyate vijñāyate*). And that *vigraha* is the sentence itself. Alternatively, *vigraha* is the specific grasping; the sentence which serves for that grasping is the *vigrahavākya*.
This is a compound of the *madhyamapadalopa* (elision of the middle term) type, following the rule for *śākapārthiva* and similar formations.

"The meaning of the analytical sentence" (*vigrahavākyārtha*) refers to the sense conveyed by the analytical sentence. That which is capable of expressing—that is, making known—that meaning should be understood as "competent" (*samartha*). For example, this compound *rājapuruṣa*: the sentence whose meaning it expresses is *rājñaḥ puruṣaḥ* ("the king's man"); the word *rājapuruṣa* is capable of expressing that meaning, because that very meaning is understood from it as well.

Furthermore, that meaning consists of either conjunction (*saṃsarga*) and exclusion (*bheda*), or conjunction and exclusion together. Among these, the relation between a particular of its own [class] and a particular of its owner is called "conjunction. The differentiation of one's own [particular] from other owners, and the differentiation of another owner from one's own [particulars], is called "exclusion. In that regard, according to the view of those who maintain conjunction (*saṃsargavādin*), conjunction alone is the word-meaning; exclusion, however, is included within the object itself, for it is not grasped apart from what is excluded.
For two things being excluded from other related entities, their connection is not logically possible.

For the proponent of difference (*bhedavādin*), however, exclusion alone is the meaning of the word, while the connection is subsumed within the object; for there is no existence of ownership or the like for that which is being excluded if it is not already connected with other related entities.
For the proponent of both (*ubhayavādin*), however, both [exclusion and connection] constitute the meaning of the word.

If "competent" (*samartha*) were understood as that which is capable of expressing the meaning of the analytical sentence (*vigrahavākya*), then, in that case, competency would apply only to the domain of compounds (*samāsa*) and secondary derivatives (*taddhita*); consequently, this paribhāṣā would not apply to the rules concerning the treatment as an external member (*parāṅgavadbhāva*) and the prescription of case-endings (*vibhaktividhāna*), for in those instances there is no expression of the meaning of an analytical sentence. If it does not apply, so be it; nor does its non-application lead to any undesirable consequence. For instance, regarding the treatment as an external member, the author of the Bhāṣya will point out the fault of taking [the word] as a cause (*nimittagrahaṇa*).

And in that regard, there is indeed a functional capacity (*sāmarthya*) between the indicator (*nimitta*) and the indicated (*nimittin*), as in the example: "O King of the Madras, [you] are cutting with an axe.

Even regarding the prescription of case-endings (*vibhakti*), those which are case-endings of the factors of action (*kāraka*) are prescribed precisely for those factors of action such as the object (*karman*) and so forth; thus, they possess a connection with the action.

Furthermore, even among the case-endings used as adjuncts (*upapada-vibhakti*), such as those governed by the rule *yukte ca* (Pāṇini 2.3.19) and others, there is indeed a functional capacity, because of the inclusion of the term "connected" (*yukta*) and so on.

In that case, when such a connection exists, case-endings (*vibhakti*) are desired, but not on the basis of the capacity characterized by expressing the meaning of the analytical sentence (*vigrahavākya*).
Thus far, the word *samartha* has been shown to function in its primary sense. Now, in order to show its figurative function (*upacaritavṛtti*), he says: "Or rather" (*atha vā*), and so forth.

That which has capable words as its substratum is "that which rests upon capable words" (*samarthapadāśraya*); the state of being such is "the quality of resting upon capable words" (*samarthapadāśrayatva*).
For that reason, a compound is said to be "capable" (*samartha*).

Because the substratum (*āśraya*) is capable, the dependent (*āśrita*) is also designated as such by way of metaphorical transfer (*upacāra*), due to the transfer of the property of the cause to the effect—just as, for example, "the water of the reed-thicket" is called "the disease of the foot.
By the phrase "of those that are capable," he states that in a sentence, capability is characterized by the designation [of the words].
For instance, in the sentence "the king's man" (*rājñaḥ puruṣaḥ*), the king expects the man—thinking "this is his"—and the man also expects the king—thinking "I am his.

By the phrase "of those whose meanings are combined," he demonstrates that in a compound (*samāsa*), the words possess a capacity characterized by *ekārthībhāva* (the state of having a single unified meaning).
And *ekārthībhāva* is a specific state consisting in the commonality of meaning among words that were previously situated separately and possessed distinct meanings once they have been compounded.
For in a sentence (*vākya*), there is no commonality of meaning, because the meanings are distinct.
Precisely for this reason, a genitive case based on that distinction arises therein—as in "the king's man" (*rājñaḥ puruṣaḥ*).
In a compound (*vṛtti*), however, there is a commonality of meaning, because it denotes a meaning delimited by both words.

By this, the following is stated: for in a compound (*samāsa*), the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) enters into the qualified (*viśeṣya*) and becomes one with it (*ekārthībhāva*) along with the qualified; whereas in a sentence (*vākya*), the qualifier remains distinct from the qualified. That being absent—which is to say, that in the absence of which the word *ca* is employed in a sentence such as "the king's cow, horse, and man" (*rājño gauśca aśvaśca puruṣaśca*) to express a conjunction (*samuccaya*) based on distinction—in a compound, however, when that [distinction] is present, it ceases. This state of becoming one with a single meaning, as in "the king's cow, horse, and man" (*rājño gavāśvapuruṣāḥ*), is to be understood as *ekārthībhāva*.
"Look, Devadatta, what a pity! Viṣṇumitra has resorted to the teacher's house.

Here, the word *kaṣṭam* ("what a pity") is connected with *paśya* ("look"), but not with the word *śrita* ("resorted to"). Therefore, because there is a lack of semantic compatibility (*sāmarthya*), the compound does not take place.

Now, one might object: since words such as *śrita* are explicitly heard in the rule, we shall qualify the accusative case by those very words—namely, that it is the accusative related to *śrita* and the others. This designation is indeed possible.
But in the absence of that [restriction], it would be understood that the second case alone is compounded with words such as *śrita* (resorted to) and so forth.

In this way, a compound would indeed occur even for a word that is dependent on another—such as *mahat kaṣṭaṃ śritaḥ* ("one who has resorted to great hardship")—for here the second case ending occurs by virtue of being governed by words like *śrita*.
Therefore, the term *samartha* ("semantically connected") must be included [in the rule].
"What will you do with a crowd? Devadatta has been broken by a stone.
Here, the breaking is performed by "a stone" (upalena), which ends in the third case (instrumental).

Consequently, since there is the quality of being "done by that," it would follow that a compound (*samāsa*) should occur; however, it does not occur because of the inclusion of the term *samartha* ("having the same meaning").

But when the requirement of semantic competency (*samartha*) is observed, this is the meaning: if the refutation was indeed performed by that very same word ending in the third case which forms the compound, then the compound occurs.

However, in this case, the refutation was not performed by that [word]; therefore, the compound does not occur. In the same way, it should be understood that elsewhere too, due to a lack of semantic competency, no compound is formed. [This applies to the rule] "like a limb of another" (*parasyāṅgavat*).
Here, the word *aṅga* signifies a "part" (*avayava*). A compound becomes like a part of the subsequent [word], just as a limb is part of the body;
the meaning is that it is included by the mention of that [subsequent word].
Thus, he states that this is understood as an extension of identity (*tādātmyātideśa*) by saying: "This is an extension of identity.
Identity (*tādātmya*) means having the same nature (*tatsvabhāvatva*).
With the words "ending in a case-suffix" (*subanta*), etc., he clarifies that very extension of identity.
"A word ending in a case-suffix enters into the vocative.
This means that it is included therein.
For example: "aṭan kuṇḍena" (wandering with a bowl).

In this instance, the vowel *u* in the word *kuṇḍa* bears the accent of an address (*āmantrita-svara*). In other cases as well, the accentuation of an address accompanied by a case-ending should be understood in the same way. Regarding the example "pīḍae pīḍamāna":
O *pīḍamāna*, by your affliction I am *pīḍae*; that is to say, I am being tormented.

Regarding *pīḍa* in the sense of "immersing" (*avagāhane*; Dhātupāṭha 1544): with the causative suffix *ṇic* (curādi), the ātmanepada is used in both cases (the present participle and the periphrastic future). In one instance, there is the augment *iṭ* in the first person singular; in the other, there is the suffix *śānac*. The suffix *yak* is added because it is a sārvadhātuka, and the *ṇi* is elided. By [Pāṇini 6.1.186], the *iṭ* is unaccented (*anudātta*). The *yak* receives an acute accent (*udātta*) on its first syllable by the accent of the suffix (*pratyayasvara*). Thus, by [Pāṇini 8.2.5] "a single substitute for an accented and an unaccented vowel is accented," the vowel *e* is acute. However, for the word *pīḍamānā*, the rule [Pāṇini 8.1.19] applies: "there is a grave accent (*nighāta*) for a word beginning with *pīḍa* when it follows another word. Thus: "Gārgya is in the house" (*gehe gārgyaḥ*).

The word *geha* is oxytone due to its inclusion in the *uñchādi* group; the single-substitute vowel for the locative case ending is acute as before; and *gārgyaḥ* is ādyudātta (acute on the first syllable) by virtue of the *ñnī-t* suffix.
Thus, in this case, there is indeed a separate accentuation:
"O Devadatta, coming with a bowl."

If the mention of "another" (para) were not made, then a word ending in a case-suffix (subanta) would enter into the scope of the vocative even when it precedes [the first vocative]; consequently, there would be a grave accent (nighāta) for the word *āṭan* following the word *devadatta*, according to the rule *padāt paro 'ṭan* [Pāṇini 8.1.19].

But surely, when the mention of "another" (*para*) is made, since the word *kuṇḍa* would then behave as if it were a member of the subsequent word (*parāṅgavadbhāva*), and the sixth [rule] regarding initial accentuation (*ādyudāttatva*) having been applied, there ought indeed to be a suppression of tone (*nighāta*) for this *āṭan* following the word *devadatta*, which is a separate word (*padāt*)? This is not so; for that suppression occurs only when the word is not at the beginning of a verse-quarter (*apādādau*), whereas here the status of being at the beginning of a quarter (*pādāditva*) is intended. And in that case, the word *devadatta* is accented on its first syllable by the rule governing vocatives (*āmantritasvara*).
The same applies to *kuṇeḍanāṭan*.
Here, the suppression of tone for the vocative does not occur, because it stands at the beginning of a quarter.
"Just as a lump of clay might regain its own sound.

How, indeed, could a collection of *subanta* (inflected nominal) words, having become unified like a lump of clay and having attained a state of apparent oneness, "regain its own sound"? It is for this purpose that the term *aṅga* (stem) is included. But why is an effort made to ensure the attainment of its own sound once it has become unified? To this he says: "Of both," and so forth.

If the mention of "aṅga" (stem) were not made, then there would be one of the three types of extension: extension of effect (*kāryātideśa*), extension of rule (*śāstrātideśa*), or extension of designation (*vyapadeśātideśa*).

This being the case, just as the other [word] has the effect of being acute-accented on the first syllable (*ādyudāttatva*) and the rule for acute accentuation on the vocative (*āmantrita*), so too would it apply to the preceding word ending in a case-suffix (*subanta*); consequently, both words would have the acute accent on their first syllable.
However, when "aṅga" is mentioned, this becomes an extension of identity (*tādātmyātideśa*).

Therefore, the collection of *subanta* (inflected nominal) words, having become a single lump of clay (*mṛtpiṇḍībhūta*), receives the accent in the form of an initial acute (*ādyudātta*) belonging to the vocative; thus, there is no contingency of both [words] becoming initial acute.
[The rule] "so that the operation dependent on its own [form] may also take place" applies here:

in the example *āma kuṇḍenāṭan*, where the word *aṭan* follows a word ending in a case-suffix (*padāt parasya*), the elision of the accent (*nighāta*) prescribed by *āmantritasya* (Pāṇini 8.1.19) would otherwise apply; however, since the word *na* from *na luṭ* (8.1.29) is being carried over [as a governing particle], and because there is an absence of the condition of "separated by one intervening word" (*ekāntaratā*) in the case of *āma*, [the elision does not occur].

For if the suffix *vat* were not applied, the word ending in the case-suffix (*subanta*) would indeed be [the subject], and it would not be logical for such a form to have an interval of one syllable [from the preceding word].

However, when *vat* is applied, there are occasions when even its own substratum lacks the status of being a constituent part (*anaṅgatva*); thus, an interval of one syllable becomes possible, and by that means, the prohibition of the *nighāta* accent is established.
In this regard, the analysis of the accents is as follows: the word *ām* has its first syllable acute (*ādyudātta*) by virtue of being a particle (*nipāta*).

When the word *kuṇḍa* also undergoes the treatment of being like a subordinate member (*parāṅgavadbhāva*), it becomes udātta on its first syllable by virtue of the accent of the vocative (*āmantritānudātta*).
Likewise, when the prohibition of the *nighāta* (elision) applies, the element *aṭan* must also become udātta on its first syllable according to the rule of the sixth [chapter].
[The example is] "kūpe siñcan" ("sprinkling in the well").
In this case, since there is no status as a subordinate element (*parāṅgavadbhāva*), the *s* at the beginning of the word remains;
consequently, the prohibition of *ṣatva* (the change to *ṣ*) by [Pāṇini 8.3.111] would apply. For example: *carman-naman*.

Here too, because there is no status as a "member of another word" (*parāṅgavadbhāva*), the cause and the effect do not reside within the same word; thus, the substitution of *ṇ* (ṇatva) based on being in the same word does not occur. [This is stated in the rule: "When a word ending in a case-suffix (*subanta*) functions as a member of another word, [the rule applies] provided it is in grammatical coreferentiality (*samānādhikaraṇa*)," and so forth. But what is the reason that it would not apply when there is coreferentiality, such that this supplementary addition (*upasaṃkhyāna*) is made? He says: "Because of immediate proximity (*anantaratvāt*).

Since the mention of the term "specified" (*nirdiṣṭa*) in [Pāṇini 1.1.66] has the sense of immediate proximity, the rule would not apply when there is an intervention; therefore, this supplementary addition is formulated.

In the example "sīvyantīkṣṇayā sūcyā" ("sewing with a sharp needle"), because the word "tīkṣṇayā" is treated as if it were a subordinate member (*parāṅgavat*) of the word "sīvyant," it retains its initial acute accent even though it is separated [from the verb]. In the example "uccairadhīyāna" ("studying loudly"), however, because the word "uccaiḥ" does not undergo the treatment of being a subordinate member, it does not possess the initial acute accent that would otherwise be conditioned by its status as a vocative (*āmantrita*).
In its absence, there is only the final udātta accent in that case, because [the word] is recited among the *svarādi* group as not having a final udātta.

For it is stated in that very same [section] (*Pāṇini 1.1.37*), after teaching *sannatara*, *uccais*, *nīcais*, and so forth up to *pṛthak*: "These, beginning with *sannatara*, are recited as having the final udātta. When it is intended that *adhīyāna* constitutes the beginning of a *pāda*, then it has the initial udātta; otherwise, there is the *nighāta* (elision of accent) according to [Pāṇini 8.1.19]. [The phrase is] "according to seniority" (*yathāvṛddham*).
In this case, once the designation of "compound" (*samāsa*) is established, the grammatical operations beginning with [Pāṇini 1.2.46] take effect.

Now, for what purpose is the mention of *prāk* ("before")? For even without it, the word *prāk* will be supplied by virtue of the mention of the ablative case (*pañcamī*). Nor should one suspect that the word *parāk* might also be supplied, since *parāk* is also a term denoting direction; for if that were supplied, the designation of "compound" would apply to those [suffixes] which are subsequently enumerated after the mention of *kaḍāra*.

And thus, [the author] would have established the governing rule for compounds (*samāsādhikāra*) immediately after the mention of *kaḍāra*; however, it has been placed here. Therefore, by the force of its placement here, there will be an ellipsis (*adhyāhāra*) of the words "prior to this" (*prāk*). Consequently, he says, "The mention of 'prior' (*prāgvacana*)," etc., to show that the mention of "prior" is not for that purpose. Rather, the mention of "prior" is for the sake of ensuring that the technical term "compound" (*samāsa-saṃjñā*) co-occurs with the technical terms "avyayībhāva" and so forth in the subsequent rules.
For if that were not the case, this [term "compound"] would be sublated by those [other terms], which would otherwise have no scope [for application].

However, regarding this technical designation "compound" (*samāsa*), there would be scope for that compound which is formed by the *yogavibhāga* (splitting of a rule) of the word *saha* in [Pāṇini 2.1.4]: "That which has *saha* as its first member is a *tatpuruṣa*. This applies to examples such as *anuprāvarṣat* ("it rained after") and *anuvyacalat* ("he moved along"), where the compound is with a verbal suffix (*tiṅanta*). Even though there is thus scope [for both designations], because of the authority of the explicit statement within the governing heading on "single designation" (*ekasaṃjñādhikāra*), the operation would occur alternatively (*paryāyeṇa*), and not through co-occurrence (*samāveśa*).

However, when there is an explicit statement in the preceding rule (*prāgvacana*) directly incorporated into the Sūtra, there occurs a co-occurrence (*samāveśa*). How so? The connection is made as follows: "All those [compounds] situated before *kaḍāra* are designated as compounds (*samāsa*); being designated as compounds, they receive the designations of *avyayībhāva* and so forth. Therefore, the designation of a compound is merely the cause for the designations of *avyayībhāva* and the rest. And a cause is not obstructed by that which possesses the cause; otherwise, its status as a cause would not even exist. Thus, co-occurrence with the explicit statement in the preceding rule is logical.

If that [term *samāsa*] were merely supplied by implication (*adhyāhṛta*), then the meaning obtained would be: "As many as are established prior to being designated as *kaḍāra*, all those receive the technical designation (*saṃjñā*) of 'compound' (*samāsa*)," but not also: "Being designated as 'compounds,' they receive the designations of *avyayībhāva* and so forth.

However, when that term is explicitly mentioned (*sākṣāt upātta*) in the rule, this latter meaning is also obtained; otherwise, its explicit mention in the rule would be purposeless. In the case of *yathāvṛddham*, once it has attained the status of an *avyayībhāva*, the rule [Pāṇini 2.4.18] applies for neuter gender, and subsequently the rule [Pāṇini 2.4.83] applies.
"This is a designation based on its literal meaning (*anvarthasaṃjñā*).
[The term] *avyayībhāva* means that what was not an indeclinable (*avyaya*) becomes an indeclinable.
By the statement beginning with "the predominance of the meaning of the first member" (*pūrvapadārthaprādhānya*), he states the purpose of this designation based on its literal meaning.
Generally, in an *avyayībhāva* compound, the first member is an indeclinable (*avyaya*), while the second member is not; the whole compound is not an indeclinable.

If it acquires the property of that first member—namely, the status of being an indeclinable—by virtue of the first member, then, though its own nature is not inherently indeclinable, it becomes indeclinable in nature. And it acquires that property by virtue of the first member only if the first member is predominant, and not otherwise.
For it is logical that a thing, by virtue of its primary element, should abandon its own properties and undergo the acquisition of other properties.

Thus, this name being "significant" (anvartha-saṃjñā) demonstrates the predominance of the meaning of the first member in an *avyayībhāva* compound. By this, it is stated that when the meaning of the first member is predominant, then an *avyayībhāva* occurs, and not otherwise. By the phrase "those who are elders" (*ye ye vṛddhāḥ*), he explains that in the expression "according to seniority" (*yathāvṛddham*), the word *yathā* functions in the sense of distributive repetition (*vīpsā*).
"In the same way as Devadatta, so is Yajñadatta.
The meaning is that Yajñadatta is similar to Devadatta.
Now, one might object: this word "yathā" (as/in the manner of) requires an object of comparison (*upamāna*), namely "Yajñadatta," which is the object being compared (*upameya*).

In that case, since "that which is dependent is incapable [of forming a compound]" (*sāpekṣamasamarthaṃ bhavati*), the compound will not occur simply due to this incapacity; so what is the purpose of the prohibition "not when there is dissimilarity" (*asādṛśye*)? This is not so; for here the word *yathā* is not the standard of comparison (*upamāna*), but rather the entire expression "just as Devadatta" (*yathā devadattaḥ*).

Therefore, the incapacity belongs to that very [expression] because of its dependence on the object of comparison (*upameya*), and not to the word *yathā*. Regarding the term "determination of extent" (*iyattāparicchedaḥ*): the state of being this much is "extent" (*iyattā*), which is to say, measure (*parimāṇa*); the determination (*pariccheda*) of that is its ascertainment (*niścaya*).
With the words "as many vessels as there are," etc., he clarifies that very same limitation of quantity.

With the words "I do not ascertain," etc., he demonstrates the absence of any such limitation of quantity. In the expression "towards the tree" (*vṛkṣaṃ prati*), the word *prati* functions in the sense of a characteristic mark (*lakṣaṇa*), not in the sense of a measure (*mātra*).

Now, for what purpose is the explicit mention of *suP* [in the rule]? Since the mention of *suP* will carry over from the previous rule "A word ending in *suP* [is called *āmantrita*] when addressed" (Pāṇini 2.1.2), he says: "The mention of *suP," etc.
The mention of *sub* was previously connected with the indeclinable (*avyaya*); therefore, if that were to recur here, the indeclinable would also recur.

Consequently, this separate mention of *sub* is made for the purpose of excluding the indeclinable. Regarding the phrase "in the usage of gamblers" (*kitavavyavahāre*), etc.: how, then, is the usage of gamblers obtained even though it is not explicitly intended there? By its very nature, because the compound occurs there; for meanings are not extended [by grammatical rule], as they are worldly in nature.
"Of him," and so forth.
This connects with the phrase "the defeat of that striker. Here, *vipāta* means defeat (*parājaya*).
Regarding the word "of this" (*etasya*):
it is a reference to the sense-faculties and so forth themselves.
The singular number is used because of the intention to express non-difference.
This is connected with the phrase "falling otherwise than this.
Regarding the word "otherwise" (*anyathā*): what is intended by "otherwise-ness" is a state of being different from the manner of falling that was described in the case of victory.
"But when the five are of a single form, there is only victory.
The sense is that there is no compound [of the term] *pañcaparī* (five times).
For if, in the case of victory, the conduct of the dice and so forth were different from that [single form], then a compound would have to occur.
Furthermore, change is not possible when the five [fingers] are of a single form.
Therefore, victory occurs precisely when all five are of one form—whether they are turned upward or downward.
By this method, the justification for the statement "surpassing the four by one" is demonstrated.
"By another" (*pareṇa*) means "by way of excellence. "The words beginning with *akṣa* ending in the third case," and so forth;
otherwise, this compound is intended [to apply] in the *vṛtti*.

In that case, when the functions of the eyes and so forth are otherwise [than their primary roles], they possess either the status of an agent (*kartṛ*) or an instrument (*karaṇa*); therefore, since the instrumental case (*tṛtīyā*) must occur, only those words ending in it are compounded.
The phrase "of what was mentioned before" means "of the eyes and so forth."
Why is this so? Because it was previously stated that "akṣa" and the others are in the third case-ending (*tṛtīyā*).
The singular number is used because there is an intention to express non-difference (*abhedavivakṣā*).

Furthermore, this genitive (*ṣaṣṭhī*) is characterized by a relationship (*sambandhalakṣaṇā*) with respect to the word "vṛtta," intended as a residual relation (*śeṣavivakṣā*); thus, the word "vṛtta" must be supplied (*adhyāhartavya*).
Regarding the phrase "as it was not so":

if the manner in which the previously mentioned dice and other factors behaved during a prior victory does not occur in the same way at present, then this compound formation takes place, and not otherwise.

This compound serves to indicate that the previous behavior has changed; and since that change can be effected by even a single factor, it is useless to rely on the dual number and so forth. Therefore, he says: "when there is unity of the die and the counter."
The meaning is that [the rule applies] when *akṣa* and *śalākā* end in the singular number.

Thus, this very meaning, established by logic (*nyāya*), has been summarized in the verse. Alternatively, the subsequent mention of the term *vibhāṣā* (optionally) also connects here by way of the "lion's glance" (*siṃhāvalokita*) maxim; and that [optionality] is a restricted option (*vyavasthitavibhāṣā*).

Therefore, this meaning should be understood as established by the very statement [of the rule]. What is the purpose of the words "akṣādayaḥ" (dice, etc.)? [To exclude cases such as: "This did not happen with the die in the same way as it did previously in the victory. What is the purpose of the word "pariṇā"? [To ensure that] there is no compound with a mere nominal stem ending in *su*.

What is meant by "gambling transaction" (*kitavavyavahāra*)? It refers to a case where one does not play with dice or by means of dice in the same manner as when one previously won. Now, for what purpose is the mention of "limit" (*maryādā*) and "inclusion" (*abhividhi*)? Since the word *pañcamī* (the fifth case) is understood from the previous rule, and the fifth case is prescribed only in connection with the *karmapravacanīya* particle *āṅ*—as in the rule [Pāṇini 2.1.13], "The designation *karmapravacanīya* applies to *āṅ* in these two senses"—it follows that *āṅ* has this technical name only in these two meanings and not otherwise.

In that case, even without the inclusion of the terms *maryādā* (limit) and *abhividhi* (inclusiveness), the compound would occur for those two meanings alone and not otherwise? This is true; nevertheless, the inclusion of the terms *maryādā* and *abhividhi* is for the sake of easy understanding by those of dull intellect. [Examples: *abhyagni*, *pratyagni*.
The analysis (*vigraha*) is: *agnim abhi*, *agnaḥ prati*. The designation *karmapravacanīya*, however, is [assigned] by the rule *ekasya* [Pāṇini 1.4.91].
[This is derived] by [the rule] *aparasya* (Pāṇini 1.4.90) and so forth.

Here, fire (*agni*) is the indicator (*lakṣaṇa*); by means of it, the falling of locusts (*śalabhapāta*) is indicated. In this context, the words *abhi* and *prati* function in the sense of "facing toward" (*abhimukhya*); thus, the meaning understood is that the locusts fall only facing toward the fire, neither from afar (*pārāt*), nor from behind (*pṛṣṭhataḥ*). For example: *rūghnaṃ pratigataḥ* ("gone toward Rūghna").
One who sets out for Mathurā from Rūāughna but, due to confusion regarding the directions, returns to Rūāughna itself—in this case, Rūāughna is not the *lakṣaṇa* (indicator).
For that which one intends to reach when setting out is the *lakṣaṇa*.

But when, due to confusion regarding the directions, one returns to the very place from which one set out, how can that [place], being unperceived as a goal, be the *lakṣaṇa*? [In such a case, it is called] "Rūāughna. Thus, since the designation of "object" (*karman*) applies by the rule "and that which is not desired [by the agent] but is connected with the action" (Pāṇini 1.4.50), the second case ending (*dvitīyā*) is used for the object.
Regarding the example "yenāgnistena gataḥ" (He went in the direction where the fire is):

here, although the fire exists as a defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) and there is also a state of facing toward it (*ābhimukhya*), the words *abhi* and *prati* do not [function as such] here; therefore, there is no compound with the words *yena* and *tena*.
As for the examples "abhyaṅkā gāvaḥ" (cows marked on this side) and "pratyaṅkā gāvaḥ" (cows marked on that side).

The term *abhinavāṅkāḥ* is a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "those whose marks (*aṅka*) are new (*abhinava*) and fresh (*pratinava*). Here, the prefix *abhi-* signifies "new," while the prefix *prati-* signifies "fresh.
In this context, the "mark" (*aṅka*) refers to the characteristic brand on the cows; it does not mean "facing toward" (*ābhimukhya*).

But surely, since it occurs later in the sequence, the *bahuvrīhi* compound should take effect here; therefore, that will be the sublater [of the *avyayībhāva*], so what is the purpose of including the mention of "facing" (*ābhimukhya*)? It is not so; for if the mention of "facing" were absent, how could there be a *bahuvrīhi* because of the lack of remainder (*aśeṣatva*)? Alternatively, this indicates that the *bahuvrīhi* is superseded by the *avyayībhāva*.

By this, the expression *dvimuni vyākaraṇam* (Grammar [is two Munis long]) is established as an avyayībhāva compound. Otherwise, since the avyayībhāva would have fulfilled its purpose in its own sense, it would be superseded by the bahuvrīhi compound in the case of *dvimuni vyākaraṇam*—which refers to something other than its own members—due to the latter’s higher priority in the rules of application. Here too, because the word *anu* figuratively denotes length, it is spoken of as the word for length itself. In the example *anugaṅgaṃ vārāṇasī* (Vārāṇasī [is along the Ganges]), although both the Gaṅgā and Vārāṇasī possess length, nevertheless, because the Gaṅgā is more well-known for its length, the Gaṅgā alone is the defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) here, not Vārāṇasī.
For a characteristic must be well-known, not unknown.
Therefore, in this case, the compound is formed with the Gaṅgā alone, and not with Vārāṇasī;
as in the expression: "The extent of the Yamunā is indicated by the extent of the Gaṅgā."

It should be understood that [the word] *yamunayā* is used in the sense of "possessing that" (*tadvatī*) as a defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇabhūta*). For a nominal stem ending in a case-suffix (*subanta*) is compounded with another nominal stem ending in a case-suffix when it expresses a dimension (*āyāma*) characterized by the suffix *nu*, provided that this dimension-expressing suffix *nu* belongs to the first member; however, the suffix *nu* in *yamunāyāḥ* does not express the dimension of the Yamunā river.
There is no other extent than the extent of the Yamunā; therefore, this third case ending (*tṛtīyā*) is used in the sense of a cause (*hetu*).

The meaning to be understood is that the extent of Mathurā is indicated by the extent of the Yamunā as the cause—by means of the Yamunā, which possesses that [extent], and which serves either as a defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) or as an instrument (*karaṇa*). As for the inclusion of *tiṣṭhadgu* and the others in this section, since their grammatical correctness is already established by their recitation in the list of gaṇas, this mention is for the purpose of assigning them the technical designation of *avyayībhāva*; it is not for the purpose of forming a compound with a word ending in a case-suffix (*subanta*).
For this very reason, he says: "The compounds themselves are prescribed as such."
The very recitation of these words as they are is their "nipātana" (irregular formation).

By stating, "They bear the designation *avyayībhāva*," he indicates that only the technical name (*saṃjñā*) is being prescribed, and not that these form a compound with a word ending in a case-suffix (*subanta*). Examples are *tiṣṭhadgu* and *vahadgu*.
The substitution of *śatṛ* for the first member is prescribed by rule.

By the rule "the short vowel is substituted for the penultimate [vowel] of *go* when followed by *stari* or *tarī* in a compound" (Pāṇini 1.2.48), the vowel is shortened. That time during which cows stand is called *tiṣṭhadgu* (the time of standing cows).
The time when cows graze is the time *bahadgu*.

The particle *ca* has the sense of restriction (*avadhāraṇa*). If that [particle] were not present, there would be a compound with the word *parama* according to the rule *sanmahatparamottamotkṛṣṭāḥ pūjyamānaiḥ* (Pāṇini 2.1.60), resulting in *paramatiṣṭhadgu*.
However, because that particle has the sense of restriction, only those groups beginning with *tiṣṭhadgu*—that is, compounds of this specific kind—are established.
In the case of *āyatīgavam*,
there is an absence of the masculine form (*puṃvadbhāva*) and the presence of a compound-ending suffix (*samāsānta*). That time in which cows are coming is *āyatīgavam*.

In the expressions *khaleyavam* and *khalebusam*, the suffix *alac* is applied irregularly (*nipātana*) after a locative case-ending. [The corresponding forms with the present participle are] *lūyamānayavam*.
The suffix *śānac* is introduced as an irregular formation (*nipātana*). The same applies in the case of "pūyamānayava" (where barley is being purified).
These are words denoting time.
The group beginning with *tiṣṭhadgu* and ending with *saṃskriyamāṇabusa* [are avyayībhāva compounds]. Regarding the examples *samabhūmi* and *samapadāti*:

when the equality of the ground (*bhūmeḥ samatvam*) or the equality of the pedestrian (*padāteḥ samatvam*) is intended, the compound is an *avyayībhāva* because the meaning of the prior member (*pūrvapadārtha*) is predominant.

However, when there is a desire to express the predominance of the meaning of the subsequent member (*uttarapadārtha*), the compound *samapadātiḥ* or *samabhūmiḥ* becomes a *viśeṣaṇasamāsa*, which is a *tatpuruṣa*.
Others read the word *sama* ending in the letter *m*— as in *samambhūmi*, *samampadāti*,
*suṣamam*, *viṣamam*, *duḥṣamam*, and *parasamam*—
using the word *sama*.
And these, such as *suṣamā* and so forth:
these compounds, beginning with *suṣamā*, are those in which the meaning of the prior member (*pūrvapadārtha*) is predominant.
In this regard, one should understand the analytical sentences (*vigrahavākya*) to be "the excellence (*śobhanatva*) is *samā*" and so on.
When the meaning of the final member of the compound is predominant, however, it should be treated as either a *prādi-samāsa* or a *viśeṣaṇa-samāsa*, as appropriate. Regarding the term *āyatīsamam*:
the word *samā* denotes a year; thus, the compound is formed as *āyatī samam* (equal to a future year), which becomes *āyatīsamam*.

Thus, "equal to evil" (*pāpasama*) means equal to evil; "equal to merit" (*puṇyasama*) means equal to merit. Others, however, explain the third compound as *āyatyā sama* = "equal to the future" (*āyatīsama*); and so it is elsewhere as well.
*Prāhṇam* means the beginning of the day;
this [compound] is also one in which the meaning of the first member (*pūrvapada*) is predominant.
However, when the meaning of the second member (*uttarapada*) is predominant, it is simply a *tatpuruṣa*: "These two, Tiṣya and Punarvasu, have auspicious names in the forenoon."

Thus, in the case of *praratham*, *pradakṣiṇam*, *pramṛgam*, *apradakṣiṇam*, *samprati*, and *asamprati*, the purpose of the suffix *ic* [added] by the rule *ic karmavyatīhāre* (Pāṇini 5.4.127) is that the resulting form receives the designation of an indeclinable (*avyaya*) and the status of being neuter (*napuṃsakatva*). For example:
"This battle took place with clubs against clubs" (*daṇḍair daṇḍaiś ca prahṛtyedaṃ yuddhaṃ vṛttam iti*).

In this case, there is a compound according to [Pāṇini 2.2.27] *tatra tenedam iti sarūpe*; the suffix *ic* is added as a compound-final element (samāsānta) by [Pāṇini 5.4.127] *ic karmavyatīhāre*, and the vowel is lengthened by [Pāṇini 6.3.137], resulting in *daṇḍādaṇḍi*. Now, one might object: "Since the *mahāvibhāṣā* (the great option) is already in force, the alternative will be established by that alone; what then is the purpose of including the word *vā*? To this he says: "Because of the mention of *vā*" (*vāvacanāt*), and so forth. The meaning is already explained. If, then, because of the mention of *vā*, the genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*) occurs in one alternative, what is accomplished by the *mahāvibhāṣā*? To this he says: "By the *mahāvibhāṣā*" (*mahāvibhāṣayā*), and so forth. [The term] "*ekalakṣaṇa*" means...
It has a single nature. A continuum (*santāna*) is a series (*prabandha*);
because the members of the continuum possess a single characteristic, the continuum itself also possesses a single characteristic.
In that regard, there is the lineage by way of learning, characterized by a single feature: the lineage of grammarians (*vaiyākaraṇavaṃśa*) and the lineage of teachers (*upādhyāyavaṃśa*).
There is also the lineage by birth: the lineage of Brahmins (*brāhmaṇavaṃśa*) and the lineage of Kṣatriyas (*kṣatriyavaṃśa*). One who belongs to such a lineage is called "vaṃśya."
The suffix *yat* is applied because [the word] belongs to the *dig-ādi* group.
"Two sages" refers to Pāṇini and Kātyāyana.
Regarding the phrase "of grammar" (*vyākaraṇasya*), this is a genitive case used to denote a relationship. Thus, it means "of the grammar of the three sages" (*trimunivyākaraṇasya*).
The first two [refer to the author of the *Bhāṣya*], while the third is the author of the *Bhāṣya*.
"By knowledge" means by that which is called grammar (*vyākaraṇa*).
"Of those who possess it" refers to Pāṇini and others.
"The intention not to express distinction" means:

When those two sages are themselves designated as "Grammar" (*vyākaraṇa*)—that is, when a desire to express their non-difference is made in order to describe their connection with knowledge to an eminent degree—then grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) occurs, as in the expression "the Grammar of the Two Sages" (*dvimuni vyākaraṇam*). By the word *ca*, the term "number" (*saṃkhyā*) is drawn forward [from the previous rule].

By the use of the plural form, it is the meaning that is grasped here, not the phonetic form itself, nor the technical name; therefore, he says "with words denoting rivers," etc., so that the compound is understood to apply with all words expressing rivers.
And this [compound] is intended in the sense of a collective aggregate (*samāhāra*).
The particle *ca* is used for emphasis—meaning "only in the case of a collective compound (*samāhāra*), and not otherwise.

If this is so, should the term "collective" (*samāhāra*) be explicitly mentioned? It need not be mentioned; because for that very reason the compound of *akṣa* and the others occurs only in the context of gambling (*kitavavyavahāra*), for that same reason this [compound] will also be a collective: "seven Gaṅgās combined" is *saptagaṅgam*.
As before, there is shortening of the vowel.

But it does not occur when [the compound] has another word as its referent (*anyapadārtha*), such as *dvīrāvatīka* "a region having two Īrāvatīs," or *pañcanadam*, *saptagodāvaram*. Regarding *kṛṣṇaveṇṇā*: according to the rule, "The suffix *ac* is prescribed after a land preceded by *kṛṣṇa*, *udaka*, or *pāṇḍu*, provided that the river Godāvarī or a numeral precedes it," the suffix *ac* is applied as a compound-final element (*samāsānta*). Thus, *kṛṣṇaveṇṇā* is a descriptive determinative compound (*viśeṣaṇasamāsa*) meaning "that which is both Kṛṣṇā and Veṇṇā."
In the case of *śīghragaṅgaḥ*,
it is a *bahuvrīhi* compound. In the case of *kaṣṭaśritaḥ*,
since it has the designation of a *tatpuruṣa*, the original accent of the first member (*pūrvapada*) applies by the rule *tatpuruṣe tulyārtha* [Pāṇini 6.2.2] and so forth.

Now, he asks: "For what purpose is this great designation (*saṃjñā*) prescribed? and says: "And this is the designation of the former teachers. He asks: "What is the purpose of accepting that? and says: "The acceptance of that," and so forth. *Upādhi* means a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*).

What, then, is that specific condition (*upādhi*) belonging to it? He says: "A *tatpuruṣa* compound has the meaning of the final member as its predominant element. [This is stated] because, while the term *tatpuruṣa* continues to apply from the rule *samāsāntāḥ prayojanam* (Pāṇini 5.4.68), there is also the rule *rājāhaḥsakhibhyaṣṭac* (Pāṇini 5.4.91) which applies to *dvigu* compounds as well, such as *pañcarājī*.

The compound *pañcānāṃ rājñāṃ samāhāraḥ* ("the collection of five kings") is formed by [Pāṇini 2.1.51]. By [2.1.52], it receives the designation of *dvigu*; then, by [6.4.144], there is the elision of the final vowel (*ṭilopa*). Thereafter, by the Vārttika 156—"A *dvigu* whose final member ends in *a* is used in the feminine"—it takes the feminine gender, and by [4.1.21], the suffix *ṅīp* is added. Thus we have *dvirahaḥ* ("two days") and *tryahaḥ* ("three days").

[The suffix] *ṭi* is elided by [Pāṇini 6.4.145], and [the word] assumes the masculine gender by [Pāṇini 2.4.29]: "The words *rātra*, *ahna*, and *aha* are masculine. In the case of *pañcagavam*, [the word] assumes the neuter gender by [Pāṇini 2.4.17]:
"That [compound ending in *go*] is neuter."

Even though the word ends in the vowel *a*, femininity does not occur, because of the statement: "An exception must be stated for *pātra* and so forth" (Vārttika 1.4.3). Regarding the phrase "in the case of *śrita* and so forth":

the meaning is that when words such as *śrita* are employed as the cause for forming a compound, an extension (*upasaṃkhyāna*)—that is, a formal presentation—must be made for the compounding of verbs like *gam* and *gāmī*.
By means of these [words] as well, the formation of a compound must be established.

In this regard, the following is the demonstration: the rule "dvitīyā" is split by means of *yogavibhāga* (separation of rules), whereby a compound is also formed with words such as *gami* and *gāmi*.
Nor is the mention of *śrita* and so forth redundant; for its purpose is to indicate that the scope of the preceding rule is not universal.
The word *ādi* (and so forth) denotes a class or type.

Since the purpose would be accomplished by the inclusion of either one of the two words, "gami" or "gāmi," both are included so that the rule may apply to the *uṇādi* suffixes as well as others. Otherwise, if only "gami" were used, then because the word "ādi" (etcetera) denotes a class or type, it would result in the inclusion of only those *uṇādi* formations that are of the same type as "gami. If, on the other hand, only "gāmi" were used, it would result in the inclusion of only those *uṇādi* formations that are of the same type as "gāmi.
Therefore, the inclusion of both must be made.

In the expression *grāmaṃ gamī* ("one who will go to the village"), the suffix *ini* is applied by the rule *gameḥ ini* (Pāṇini 3.2.168). And that suffix [denotes] the future time, according to the statement: *sa ca bhaviṣyatkāle* (Pāṇini 3.3.3).
In the expression *grāmaṃ gamī* ("one who will go to the village"),
the suffix *ṇini* is applied by [Pāṇini 3.3.170] *āvaśyakādhamaṇryayoḥ* (to express necessity or debt).
By [Pāṇini 2.3.70] *akenorbhaviṣyadādhamarṇyayoḥ*, there is a prohibition of the genitive case.

In the expression "odanaṃ bubhukṣuḥ" (one desiring to eat rice), the suffix *u* is applied [by Pāṇini 3.2.168] to the root *bhuj* followed by the desiderative suffix *san*. The genitive case is prohibited [by Pāṇini 2.3.69] by the rule beginning with "kena loka...".

In examples such as *kaṣṭaṃ śritaḥ* ("he has resorted to hardship"), the prohibition of the genitive case is likewise established by this very [rule], because "its connection with the accusative is not tenable.
This is because the meaning of the accusative is impossible here;
the word *iti* is used in the sense of a reason (*hetau*).

Since its connection with the second case ending (*dvitīyā*) is untenable, the mention of the second case ending is carried forward for the sake of subsequent rules, but not for this specific purpose. For example: *svayaṃdhautau pādau* ("his feet washed by himself").
[The root] *dhāv* (in the Dhātupāṭha 601) means "to go" and "to clean"; because it is marked with the letter *u*, the augment *iṭ* is optional.
Thus, there is a prohibition of the augment *iṭ*.
By [Pāṇini 6.4.19], *ūṭh* is substituted for *ch* and *śav*.
By [Pāṇini 6.1.89], there is *vṛddhi*.

Regarding the term *svayaṃvilīnamākhyam*: the root *līṅ* is used in the sense of "adhering" (*śleṣaṇe*; Dhātupāṭha 1139). Because it is marked with the *o*-diacritic according to the rule *svādaya oditaḥ* (Kāśikā 8.2.45), the substitution of *n* for *t* applies [by Pāṇini 8.2.45].

Furthermore, according to the maxim *kṛdgrahaṇe gatikārakapūrvasyāpi grahaṇam* (Vyāḍi’s Paribhāṣā 126), a compound is formed even when a prefix (*gati*) precedes [the verbal root]. Thus, the compound *svayaṃvilīna* is established.

"What, then, is the specific advantage here when this compound is used, since this form is established even without it? To this he says: "The status of being a single word," and so forth. And with the words "And that," etc., he rejects the status of the sentence-meaning for the negation by means of the particle *eva*. It might be argued: "Even if the negation is the meaning of a sentence, the sentence itself will still exist. To this he says: "For not," and so forth.
For by a sentence, only the relationship between the action and its factors (*kriyākāraka*) is understood, not delay.
As in the phrase "and climbing onto a bed," and so forth.
A contrary path is a "wrong path" (*vimārga*); setting out upon that is "departure" (*prasthāna*).
Having completed his studies and performed the ceremonial bath (snāna), one who has been granted permission by his teacher may ascend a couch.
However, to ascend a couch otherwise constitutes setting out upon a wrong path;
it is not merely the act of ascending a couch itself that is the transgression.
And here, in examples such as *khaṭvārūḍhaḥ*, one should understand that "climbing onto a bed" is an indicative mark (*upalakṣaṇa*) for setting out upon a wrong path.
But what is the reason that this very [meaning] is understood? To this he says: "All indeed," and so forth.

The form [*ārūḍha*] is derived from the root *ruh-* preceded by the prefix *ā-* with the suffix *kta*, after which the changes of *ḍha*-ness, *dha*-ness, *ṣṭu*-ness, elision of *ḍha*, and lengthening have been applied.
"Jālma" means one who acts improperly. Regarding the phrase "because it does not denote a substance" (*asattvavācitvāt*):
for the power of action (*karma-śakti*) has a substance as its substratum;
therefore, only that which denotes a substance can be connected with the accusative case, not that which does not denote a substance. Regarding "moving and non-moving" (*carācarāḥ*).
This is for the purpose of demonstrating that the connection is not absolute.

"Moving" (*caranti*) means "wandering," thus they are called "moving and non-moving" (*carācara*), meaning they are unstable. According to the rule *caricalipativadīnamacyākcābhyāsasya* (Vārttika 658), the root *car-* takes the suffix *ac*, undergoes reduplication, and receives the augment *ak* in the reduplicated syllable.
"Sometimes they go for a day" refers to the northern solstice;
"sometimes for a night" refers to the southern solstice.
By this, making manifest that very instability, he declares that there is no absolute conjunction between the day and the night with those muhūrtas.
In the phrase "aharatisṛtāḥ," the *n* of *ahan* is replaced by *r* according to [Pāṇini 8.2.69]. In the phrase "ahaḥ saṃkrāntāḥ," [the same applies].
The root *kram* (meaning "to step" or "to stride," Dhātupāṭha 473) takes the suffix *iṭ* as prescribed by the preceding rule, which is here prohibited.
A long vowel is substituted according to Pāṇini 6.4.15 (*anunāsikasya kvijhaloḥ*).
Thus, the form *māsapramitaḥ* ("measured by a month") is derived.
From the root *māṅ* in the sense of "measuring" (*māne*, Dhātupāṭha 1088), the suffix *niṣṭhā* is applied in the sense of the agent according to Pāṇini 3.4.71, *ādikarmaṇi kartari ca*.
By the rule 7.4.40, *dyatisyati* etc., the substitution of *ī* for *ā* occurs.
Thus, [the form] is *pramitaḥ*, meaning "he has begun to measure for a month."

By showing the conjunction of the moon with the first day (*pratipad*)—which is a single part of the month—the [author] expresses the absolute connection (*atyantasaṃyoga*) of the month with that [day].
For absolute connection is the pervasion (*vyāpti*) of the entire duration of time by its own constituent element.

However, there is no pervasion—that is, no conjunction—of the moon with the first day throughout the entire month here; therefore, this is not an absolute connection. [This is what is meant by] "complete conjunction" (*kṛtsnasaṃyoga*).

"Universal conjunction" (*kṛtsnasaṃyoga*) means the conjunction of the whole; "conjunction of the whole time"—that is, of a period such as a *muhūrta*—with its own related [quality], such as pleasure, is "absolute conjunction" (*atyantasaṃyoga*).
To clarify this very point, he says: "of time," and so forth, [giving the example]:
"pleasure for a *muhūrta*."
[[2.3.5]] This is the second [example].

Here, there is the pervasion (*vyāpti*) of a *muhūrta*—a portion of time—by its own associated pleasure (*sukha*). Regarding the phrase "produced by that" (*tatkṛta*), it is not a compound with the word expressing this meaning, and it lacks a case-ending (*avibhakti*).

Because the third case ending has been elided by the rule *supāṃ suluk* [Pāṇini 7.1.39], this [term] is a qualifier in apposition with *guṇavacanena*. For this very reason, when asked "By what kind?", he replies: "By that which is produced by it" (*tatkṛtena*).

By the pronoun *tat*, there is a reference (*pratyavamarśa*) to the previously mentioned word ending in the third case; thus, he shows that [the action] is "performed by means of that which ends in the third case.

Since it is not possible for a word expressing a quality (*guṇavacana*) to function as an instrument (*karaṇa*) by virtue of its own form ending in the third case, it is understood through the force of the context (*sāmarthya*) that it means "performed by means of the object denoted by that [word]. Therefore, he says: "that is to say, performed by means of the meaning of that which ends in the third case.

Furthermore, this should be understood as a qualification of the word expressing a quality by way of its meaning: namely, that the meaning of the word expressing a quality is something produced by the meaning of that which ends in the third case.

That too is stated in that way. This is what is meant: [the compound is formed] by means of the sense expressed by the word ending in the third case, which is the sense of a quality-possessing term (*guṇavacana*).
For it is indeed the *artha* (meaning/object) that is produced by the meaning of the word ending in the third case, and not the word "quality-possessing term" itself.

*Guṇamuktavān* means *guṇavacanaḥ*. According to [Pāṇini 3.3.113], the suffix *lyuṭ* is used here in the sense of the agent (*kartari*). Alternatively, it is used in the sense of the instrument (*karaṇe*): that by which a quality (*guṇa*) is expressed is *guṇavacanaḥ*.
That which, having first denoted a quality (*guṇa*), subsequently denotes the substance (*dravya*) possessing that quality, is called *guṇavacana*.

If it were stated simply as "by means of a quality" (*guṇena*), there would be an over-extension (*prasaṅga*) to cases such as *ghṛtena pāṭavam* ("cleverness by means of ghee"); therefore, the inclusion of the term *vacana* ("denoting") is for the purpose of excluding such instances.
When this [term] is present, a compound occurs only with that which, having denoted a quality, then denotes the substance possessing it, and not with that which denotes the quality alone.
Furthermore, words such as *pāṭava* (skill) and others do not first denote a quality and subsequently denote the substance possessing that quality; rather, they denote the quality itself.
Because of the inclusion of the term "number" (*vacana*), there is no compound with them, as in the examples *śaṅkulākhaṇḍaḥ* (broken by a wooden mallet) and *girikāṇaḥ* (crippled by a mountain).

In this context, the words *khaṇḍa* and *kāṇa*, having first denoted the qualities consisting of the actions of being broken (*khaṇḍana*) and being closed (*nimīlana*), subsequently denote the substances possessing those qualities—either through the elision of the possessive suffix (*matup-lopa*) or through metaphorical identification (*abhedopacāra*). Thus, they are "words denoting qualities" (*guṇavacana*).

Regarding the phrase "having grain as its purpose" (*dhānyārtha*): here the word *artha* (purpose/object) is used in the sense of "produced by that"; for instance, it is said that "he was made hairy by the cows."

However, this word *vapāvān* (fatty) does not express a quality (*guṇa*), and thus it is not a "quality-expressing" (*guṇavacana*) term; consequently, no compound is formed with it. A compound occurs with the words *yukta* and *sadṛśa*, because when they are joined with those [words], the rule "the third case ending is prescribed after words having the sense of 'equal' (*tulyārtha*), except for *atula* and *upama*" (Pāṇini 2.3.72) ordains the third case. But how can a third-case compound be justified with the other words, such as *pūrva* and so on? For no third case is prescribed by any rule in connection with them. To this he says: "Precisely for this reason," etc., which is easy to understand. [The Vārttika] states: "An addition [should be made] regarding *avara* among *pūrva* and the others."
The meaning is that while words such as *pūrva* and others are established as causes for forming compounds, the word *avara* must be specifically added—that is, its inclusion must be explained.

The meaning is that a third-case compound (*tṛtīyā-samāsa*) is also established by means of the word *avara*. In this regard, the explanation is as follows: the term *bahulam* ("diversely" or "optionally") is employed in the subsequent rule.

Therefore, a compound is also formed with the word *avara*. In the example "he has stayed by means of alms" (*bhikṣābhir uṣitaḥ*), the third case ending is prescribed [by Pāṇini 2.3.23] because it denotes a cause (*hetu*). There is vocalization (*samprasāraṇa*) of the root *vas* according to the sūtra beginning with *vac* [6.1.15], the substitution of *ṣ* according to "of *śās*, *vas*, *si*, and *ghas*" [8.3.60], and the augment *iṭ* according to "after *vas* and *kṣudh*" [7.2.52].
"In 'he has reaped grain with a sickle,' the substitution of *ṇ* for *t* in the *niṣṭhā* [past participle] suffix occurs by the rule *lvādibhyaśca* [Pāṇini 8.2.44].
In 'one who steals on foot' (*pādahārakaḥ*)," [the same applies].
It is called "pādāhāraka" because it is carried by means of the two feet (*pādābhyām*).
In the expression "by means of the two feet," the word *pādābhyām* is either in the ablative (*pañcamī*) or the instrumental (*caturthī*) case.
The term *hāraka* is derived from the root *hr̥* with the suffix *ṇvul* in the sense of the object (*karman*), according to Pāṇini 3.3.113.

Regarding the term *galecopaka*: it means "one who causes [something] to move slowly in the throat. The suffix *ṇvul* is applied here as before, from the root *cupa* (meaning "to move slowly," according to the Dhātupāṭha, no. 403).
> [[6.3.14]] Thus ends the section on the owl. Regarding the phrase "employed for praise or blame" (*stutinindāprayuktam*):
that which is employed or set in motion by either praise or blame is "employed for praise or blame.
The meaning is that it is uttered for that purpose.
Regarding the phrase "the statement of a superimposed object" (*adhyāropitārthavacanam*):

it is a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*) meaning "the statement (*vacanam*) of that which is a superimposed object (*adhyāropito'rthaḥ*), i.e., that which, though non-existent, has been mentally projected. This is according to the rule *kartṛkaraṇayoḥ kṛti*.
Since an operation cannot apply to the meaning itself, it is understood to apply to the nominal ending that expresses that meaning. For example, in the word *kākapeyā*:
from the root *pā* "to drink" (Dhātupāṭha 925), the suffix *yat* is applied by [Pāṇini 3.1.97], and the substitution of *ī* for *a* occurs by [Pāṇini 6.4.65].

In this case, the manifestation of the river’s being full of water is a praise of the river; however, the meaning attributed here—namely, "drinkable by crows"—is a superimposed sense, such that the river is so full of water that it can even be drunk by crows standing on its bank.
Regarding the example "ālehraḥ kūpaḥ" (a shallow well), according to [Pāṇini 3.1.124] *ṛhaloṇryat*, the manifestation of the well’s proximity to water is a praise of the well.
Furthermore, the meaning superimposed here is "the state of being a watering place"—that is, a well so close to water that even dogs drink from it;
and "grass that can be cut by breath.
In this context, the praise of the grasses consists in manifesting an excellence surpassing that of Māra.
Furthermore, the meaning superimposed here is "cuttable by steam"— that is, the grasses are so soft that they can indeed be cut even by steam.
Regarding the phrase "rice to be gathered with thorns," this too is a praise of the rice, intended to highlight its extreme purity and its state of being perfectly cooked.

Furthermore, the "excessive meaning" (*adhikārtha*) superimposed here is the state of being "collectible even with a thorn"—that is to say, such is the excellence of the rice's clarity and its softness from cooking that it can be gathered even by means of a thorn.

Thus far are the examples regarding the statement of excessive meaning when employed for praise. Regarding the statement of excessive meaning when employed for censure, these same [examples] are to be understood.
For instance, in the phrase "the Kākekā river," the manifestation of having little water is a censure of the river.

Furthermore, the meaning superimposed here is precisely that previously mentioned state of being "drinkable by crows" (*kākapeyatva*). In the same way, in the case of *ālehra* and so forth, the superimposed meaning should be understood as being exactly that which was stated before—namely, that the river is so small in water that it can even be drunk by crows.

In the expression *ālehraḥ kūpaḥ* ("a well of *ālehra*"), there is also a censure consisting in the manifestation of its impure water—namely, that the rice (*odana*) is so small that it is even consumed by thorns. Now, one might object: since the previous rule already establishes a compound for the sake of expressing abundance, why is this [present rule] necessary? To this he says: "Of the previous," and so forth.
Those indeed are well-comprehended rules for which there is an elaboration (*prapañca*).
This elaboration is provided for the sake of ensuring that [the rule] is well-comprehended, as in the case of "curd-rice" (*dadhyodana*).
But surely, the relationship between grammatical factors (*kāraka*) is produced by action (*kriyā*), not inherently?
Furthermore, no action whatsoever is heard here in the formation of a compound; thus, there is an absence of semantic competency (*sāmarthya*).
And when semantic competency is absent, there can be no compound.

If it is argued that a compound occurs even in the absence of semantic competency by virtue of the power of the specific grammatical rule (*vacana*), then it would follow that in the case of "āsyatāṃ dadhnā" (let curd be sipped) and "odano bhujyatāṃ devadattena" (let rice be eaten by Devadatta), a compound would also occur. To this, he says: "In the formation [of a compound]," and so forth.
When the act of pouring an additive does not take place, the relationship between that which is to be refined (*saṃskārya*) and that which refines (*saṃskāraka*) is impossible.

Since both of these exist here, the action is understood as being included within the compound precisely because of their existence. Furthermore, since the connection between the food and the condiment is mediated by that [action], there is indeed semantic competency (*sāmarthya*). [This explains] the rule beginning with "for the sake of that" (*tadarthena*).
If the compound were to occur merely on the basis of being for that purpose (*tādarthya*), then the mention of *balirakṣita* would be redundant.
For instance, in cases such as *kuberabaliḥ* (an offering for Kubera) and *gorakṣitam* (protected by a cow), the state of being for that purpose is understood from those very examples.

Therefore, by the indicative mark (*liṅga*) provided by the mention of *balirakṣita*, it is understood that "a compound occurs when there is a relationship of material cause and effect (*prakṛti-vikāra-bhāva*) based on being for that purpose."

Now, one might object: "Should not the mention of *bali* and *rakṣita* be for the sake of the dative case (*caturthy-artha*)? This is not so; for the designation *sampradāna* (recipient) is intended for that which is aimed at by the action of the verb *dā* (to give), or by the [principal] action itself. But here, there is no being aimed at either by the action of *dā* or by the [principal] action; therefore, how could there be a dative in the sense of a recipient? To the question, "By what, then, does the dative occur in the sense of *tādarthya* (being for the sake of that)? he says: "Precisely from this," and so forth.
If the dative did not occur in the sense of *tādarthya*, then the mention of *tadartha* (for the sake of that) would be purposeless.

Therefore, this very fact—that a compound is prescribed with a word ending in the fourth case (caturthī) in the sense of "for the sake of that" (*tādarthya*)—is the indicator (*jñāpaka*) that the fourth case occurs in the sense of being for the sake of something. Regarding the phrase "with *arthena*" and so forth, the word "should be formed" (*kartavyam*) is to be supplied as the remainder.
A "nitya-compound" is said, i.e., described; by means of which [rule], that statement concerning nitya-compounds is to be explained.

This is what is meant: an explanation must be provided for that word *artha* by which a compulsory compound (*nityasamāsa*) is indicated. Here is that explanation: the term *vibhāṣā* (optionally) is understood to carry over [from the previous rule], and it is understood as a restricted option (*vyavasthitavibhāṣā*). Therefore, there will be a compulsory compound with the word *artha*, and it will possess all genders (*sarvaliṅgatā*).

When the rule *paravalliṅgaṃ dvandvatatpuruṣayoḥ* [Pāṇini 2.4.26] would have required the compound to take the gender of the final member, the present rule prescribes that it may take any gender.
