However, this is already established because gender is based on common usage (*lokāśrayatvāt*). Alternatively, all of this is established through the continued application of the term *bahulam* ("variously").

In the expressions *go-hitam* and *go-sukham*, the dative case is used according to the rule *caturthī cāśiṣy-āyuṣya-* [Pāṇini 2.3.73]. However, when used in conjunction with *hita*, the dative occurs even when it is not a benediction (*āśis*). For he will state: "The dative should be prescribed in connection with *hita*" (Vārttika).

123) Thus [it is said]: "It should be stated as 'bhayabhītabhītibhībhiḥ'. The meaning is that this should be explained as having the sense that a compound is formed with all three words beginning with *bhīta* as well.
To explain this himself, he says: "Of the preceding," and so forth.

For just as the rule *yathā-eva-hi* (Pāṇini 2.1.32) prescribes a compound for a word ending in the third case, yet—because the mention of the term *bahulam* (in various ways) implies that all restrictive conditions (*upādhi*) may be disregarded—a compound occurs even for words ending in other case-endings, such as *pādahārakaḥ* and *galecopakaḥ*, so too will a compound occur in cases such as *vṛkabhītaḥ*.

Therefore, this subsequent rule (*yoga*) should be understood as being for the purpose of illustrating examples of that very same previous *bahulam* rule, or rather, for the sake of detailed exposition (*prapañca*).
This is indicated by the phrase "And thus" (*tathā ca*), etc.

Since this is already established by the previous mention of *bahulam* (in various cases), this [present rule] is merely an elaboration (*prapañca*) of that very point; therefore, by that same *bahulam* mention, forms such as *grāmanirgataḥ* ("one who has gone out from the village") are also established.
By the word "etc. (*ādi*), examples such as *vṛkabhītaḥ* ("frightened by a wolf") are included. [The suffix] *śas* is applied [after *alpa*] according to Pāṇini 5.4.42: *alpaśaḥ*.
"The fifth [case-ending] is compounded when it is few."

The meaning is that the fifth case (*pañcamī*) which is produced from a few nominal stems (*prātipadika*) is compounded, but not from all nominal stems. For example: *stokānmuktaḥ* (released with little effort), *kṛcchrānmuktaḥ* (released with difficulty). Here, the fifth case is used according to the rule *karaṇe stokālpakṛcchra* [Pāṇini 2.3.33].
Also: *antikādāgataḥ* (come from nearby), *dūrādāgataḥ* (come from afar).

[The locative case is applied] by the rule *dūrāntikārthebhyo dvitīyā ca* [Pāṇini 2.3.35]. Because of the use of the plural number in the word *śauṇḍaiḥ*, the sense of "and so forth" (*ādi*) is understood; thus he says: *śauṇḍādibhiḥ*.

If it is asked: "By what rule is the compound of that which ends in a locative case prescribed with words such as *śauṇḍa*?"—if you say it is by the rule *saptamī śauṇḍaiḥ* [Pāṇini 2.1.40], that is incorrect. For instance, the locus (*adhikaraṇa*) is a kāraka, and that depends upon an action (*kriyā*).
Furthermore, in a compound such as *akṣaśauṇḍa*, no action whatsoever is heard;

so how could there be the possibility of a locus (*adhikaraṇa*) here? Nor can it be argued that the locative case will occur by virtue of this very rule when joined with words like *śauṇḍa*, for then the undesired consequence would arise even in the case of *devadattaḥ śauṇḍaḥ*. Therefore, he says "in the compound" (*vṛttau*), etc.;
for in this case, the action of "frequenting" (*prasakti*) certainly exists.

Since that [meaning] is included within the very sense of the compound (*samāsārtha*), a verbal form is not employed in the commentary because it is already understood. There is no fault in using the locative case for the locus (*adhikaraṇa*) which is its instrument (*sādhana*). For in this context, the word *antaḥ* is recited as having the locus itself as its primary meaning.
In its application, the reason for the locative case being in grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with that [word] is precisely this:

in the case of *vane'ntar*, *vanāntar*, or *vasatīti*, when the meaning of the prior member is predominant, there occurs only an *avyayībhāva* compound by the rule "an indeclinable [used] in the sense of a case-ending" (*vibhaktyarthe yadavyayam* 2.1.6); thus, *antarvaṇam*.
Here, the word *adhi* is recited; when the locus (*adhikaraṇa*) is predominant, there is an *avyayībhāva*: *adhistri*.
But when the substrate (*ādheya*) is predominant, it is a *tatpuruṣa* compound—as in "dependent on Brāhmaṇas" (*brāhmaṇādhīna*).

The word *brāhmaṇādhi* alone is not employed, because by the rule beginning with *aṣaḍakṣāśit* (Pāṇini 5.4.7), the suffix *kha*, which is used in its own sense (*svārthika*), is prescribed as obligatory after a word ending in *adhi*. [The statement] "by *dhvāṅkṣeṇa* there is the inclusion of the meaning" [is explained as follows].
This is because the instruction has the meaning as its primary focus.

For it has been established previously that where an instruction has the word-form as its primary focus, there is the apprehension of the formal essence; whereas elsewhere, there is only the apprehension of the meaning.
Furthermore, the fact that this instruction has the meaning as its primary focus is understood from the uninterrupted tradition of the teachers' oral transmission.

This is either a reference to the meaning (*artha*) due to the continued application of the term "frequently" (*bahula*), or rather, since it is stated that [the compound occurs] "in the sense of reproach" (*kṣepe*), and reproach is indeed brought about by the meaning, it is more appropriate to take this as a reference to the meaning itself.
And when there is a reference to the meaning, the compound also occurs with synonyms of *dhvāṅkṣa*; therefore, he says: "by a word expressing *dhvāṅkṣa*," and so forth.
Regarding the phrase "like a crow at a sacred bathing place" (*tīrthe dhvāṅkṣa iva*):
the word *iva* is employed to demonstrate that the censure of the crow is understood only when it stands in the relation of a standard of comparison (*upamāna*), and not otherwise.

However, in a compound (*samāsa*), because the meaning of the standard of comparison is already included within the compound itself, the word *iva* is not used as its meaning has already been conveyed.

For just as crows do not remain long at a sacred bathing place (*tīrtha*), so too anyone who is not steadfast regarding a task is called a "crow-at-the-tīrtha" (*tīrthadhvāṅkṣa*). As it has been said: "The meaning is 'unsteady'.
Unsteadiness regarding a task is precisely what constitutes "neglect" (*kṣepa*). [Regarding the rule] "A compound is desired only with that which ends in the suffix *yat*":
how, then, is this obtained by means of the suffix *yat* alone? Because of the recurrence of the word "in small measure" (*alpaśas*), as in the example "to be paid monthly" (*māsadeya*).
As before, there is also the substitution of *ī* for *ai*.
Here, the locative case (*saptamī*) should be understood as denoting the *upaśleṣika* (proximate) locus.

For the day that occurs when a month has elapsed is proximate to that month; or [the locative may be understood] by the rule "when one state indicates another state" (*yasya ca bhāvena bhāvalakṣaṇam*, Pāṇini 2.3.37).
For by the state of exceeding a month, the state of being a debt is indicated.

Now, if it is said "debt" (*ṛṇa*), then this [distinction] is not established—namely, that "this *sāman* is to be sung in the forenoon; this *anuvāka* is to be studied in the morning. Therefore, he says "debt," etc.
For a debt is necessarily to be discharged; thus, it is accompanied by an obligation (*niyoga*).
Therefore, by association, the necessity (*niyoga*) of that [debt] is indicated.
And this is understood from the indicative mark (*liṅga*) of the plural designation in the word "by means of *kṛtya*-suffixes" (*kṛtyaiḥ*).

How so? The plural number in "by means of *kṛtya*-suffixes" is intended here as significant; and that [plurality] is due to the diversity of bases when the mention of "debt" (*ṛṇa*) serves as an indicator for the necessity [of repayment].

The undesirable consequence arises when the *kṛtya* suffix is analyzed separately, but not otherwise, because the compound is intended to be formed with that very suffix due to its unity. Regarding the phrase "an attribute of the aggregate":

the term "in the sense of a name" (*saṃjñāyām*) is not an adjective qualifying either the prior member or the subsequent member; rather, it qualifies the aggregate—meaning, if the name is understood through the aggregate as a whole.

To show what is established when this is the case, he says "by that" (*tena*), and so forth. He states the justification for this very point with "for not" (*na hi*), and so forth. Regarding the passage beginning with "But you shall see this day's conduct and the night's conduct," there are no parts of the day or parts of the night here; rather, it is the entire day and the entire night. Therefore, there is no compound here. [The commentator notes: "In that case, *tatra* ends in the locative case."
Because of its similarity to the locative case (*saptamī*).
Here, the suffix *tral* itself is expressed by the word "locative" (*saptamī*),
for a thing may receive the name of another due to its similarity to it.

For example: "The Vāhīka is a cow. Furthermore, the suffix *tral* expresses similarity through the sense of the locative (*saptamī*), because it has the meaning of a locus (*adhikaraṇa*). Just as the locative case is employed to convey a locus, so too is the suffix *tral*.
Now, why is the seventh case-ending not understood here as being primary? Because it is impossible for it to exist within the word *tatra*;
its impossibility, however, is due to the fact that its meaning has already been expressed by the suffix *tral*.

But another says: when suffixes such as *tral* and others take the place of case-endings, then this [word] becomes ending in the seventh case precisely through the principle of "acting like the original" (*sthānivadbhāva*).
It is incorrect to say that the author of the *Vṛtti* did not adopt the view of substitution (*ādeśapakṣa*) in this case;

for here the word *anta* signifies a "part" (*avayava*). The locative suffix *traL* is used because it is that which has an "end"—that is, a part—as its final member. This is illustrated by the example: "the position of a mongoose on heated ground" (*avataptenakulasthitam*).
> [[6.3.14]] Thus, there is no elision (*aluk*) of the locative case ending.
What, then, is the censure here? It is instability regarding one's duties.
As he says: "And this fickleness," and so forth.

Just as mongooses do not remain for long in a heated place, so too, when someone undertakes certain matters but does not persist in them for long, this expression is used regarding him: "like a mongoose in a heated place" (*avataptenakulasthitam*).
In phrases such as "the water has dried up," the futility of an undertaking is the point of censure.
For this very reason, he says: "That which is done fruitlessly is described in this way."

Regarding "mūtritam in the sense of flowing": the root *mūtra* is listed as 1909 in the Dhātupāṭha, belonging to the curādi group. Regarding "the purpose of the recitation is the inclusion of *yuktāroha* and so forth":
that recitation is so described because its purpose or objective is the inclusion of *yuktāroha*, *ahrīka*, and others, or by means of *yuktāroha* and others.

But for what purpose is the inclusion of those [words] ending in *kta* within the *yuktārohi* and other groups desired? He says: "So that there may be the acute accent (*udātta*) on the first syllable of the preceding member. For in the case of the *yuktārohi* group, the acute accent on the first syllable of the preceding member is prescribed by the rule *yuktārohyādayaśca* (Pāṇini 6.2.81).
In that regard, if those words ending in *kta* were not recited [in this list], then they would not have the acute accent on their first syllable.

But how, then, are [the compounds] such as *pātresamita* included by the mention of *yuktārohin* and others, such that the initial acute accent (*ādyudāttatva*) prescribed for them also applies to *pātresamita* and the rest? To this he says: "For in the case of *yuktārohin* and others," and so forth.
Regarding the statement, "In cases such as *udumbaramaśaka*, there is a derisive comparison (*upamayā kṣepaḥ*)," he explains:

one who is confined to that very place and does not go anywhere else is considered to be of limited scope, thinking, "There is nothing beyond me"; such a person, whose range is unseen, is called an *udumbaramaśaka*.
In the same way, elsewhere too, there is an insult resulting from contempt. Regarding the phrase "by the practice of what is forbidden":
whoever performs a prohibited act is called a "man with his mother."
Regarding the phrase "by way of being effortless": one who is incapable of doing anything at all is designated by such terms as "a hero in a lump" (*piṇḍīśūra*) and so forth.
As for the word "and" (*ca*), it serves the purpose of emphasis (*avadhāraṇārtha*).
[The rule] is stated so that only those compounds such as *pātresamita* and the like should be *yat* (possessing the suffix *yat*), lest another compound form applicable to them should occur.

Therefore, in the case of *paramapātresamitāḥ*, no other compound is formed by [the rule] *sanmahat* (Pāṇini 2.1.60) and so forth. Regarding the phrase "employed with distinct grounds for application" (*bhinnapravṛttinimittaprayuktasya*) and so on:
the inclusion of the term "distinct grounds for application" is for the purpose of excluding synonyms (*paryāya*).
The inclusion of the word "eka" (one) is for the purpose of excluding [compounds] such as *gaura-ādi*.
The statement "the term 'prior in time' (*pūrvakāla*) is a specification of the meaning" is because the specification is governed by the primary significance of the meaning.
The meaning is that, for that reason, there is no apprehension of the word's own form (*svarūpa*).
[This is stated] because "the apprehension of the own form applies to the remaining [words]," since the indication has the word itself as its primary object.
"By 'the earlier time [is understood] through the later time.

But how is this specific meaning obtained even though it is not explicitly stated? Because "earlier time" is a relative term (*sambandhiśabda*). Indeed, an "earlier time" is not possible without depending on a "later time. Therefore, when the "earlier time" is grasped, the "later time" is also necessarily grasped.
For example: "bathed and anointed."

In the expression "first bathed, afterwards anointed," the word *snāta* (bathed) is applied by reason of the act of bathing (*snāna*), and the word *anulipta* (anointed) by reason of the act of anointing (*anulepana*); since both function with respect to a single object, there is grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*).

Regarding the term *ekaśāṭī*: the masculine form is applied according to [Pāṇini 6.3.42] and following, because it consists of "one" (*ekā*) and "a garment" (*śāṭī*). The forms beginning with *pūrveṣukāmaśamī* are names of villages.
"pūrvā" and "eṣukāmaśamī" [combine] as "pūrveṣukāmaśamī.
This sentence has been composed merely to demonstrate the division of the preceding and following members for those of dull intellect;
for in this case, there should not have been a sentence at all.

For a technical designation (*saṃjñā*) is not understood through a sentence alone. To demonstrate the distinction among even the single locative case based on the difference in its scope, he says: "In the domain of the meaning of a secondary derivative (*taddhita*)," and so forth.

If it were understood that "when the meaning of a *taddhita* is to be expressed" [is the condition], then in forms such as *pāñcanāpitih*, the *taddhita* suffix would be impossible, because its meaning would already have been expressed by the compound itself. Bearing this in mind, he stated "in the domain of the meaning of a *taddhita*" in order to show that this is a locative of scope (*viṣaya-saptamī*) with respect to the meaning of the *taddhita*.

*Taddhita* suffixes are those beginning with *aṇ*; their meaning consists of [designations such as] offspring (*apatya*) and so forth, and it is in that domain [that the rule applies]. The word "domain" (*viṣaya*) has the sense of "occurrence nowhere else," just as in the expression "water is the domain of fish. For example: *paurvaśālaḥ*.

In the case of "pūrvasyāṃ śalāyāṃ bhavaḥ" (born in the eastern region), when the sense of a secondary derivative (*taddhita*) is to be expressed as the domain [of the compound], first the compound is formed; then there is the elision of the case-ending (*subluk*);
and finally, the secondary derivative suffix is applied.
Regarding the term *pūrvaśālāpriyaḥ*: "that for whom the eastern hall (*pūrvā śālā*) is dear (*priyā*)"; this is first a *bahuvrīhi* compound of the three preceding words.
Subsequently, when the word *priya* stands as the final member (*uttarapada*), there is a *tatpuruṣa* compound of the two preceding words.
When that [compound] exists, as in the case of *śālā*, there occurs the acute accent on the final syllable of the compound;

for it is said: "In the case of a collective compound (*samāhāra*), a word denoting a direction (*diṅ-śabda*) is not possible. (Note: The original manuscript reads *dikśabdaḥ* and the *Padamañjarī* agrees.)
For a collection (*samāhāra*) is an aggregate (*samūha*),
and that occurs only among distinct objects existing at the same time.
Their simultaneity arises from the mind’s simultaneous apprehension of those objects, not because they are non-distinct entities.

And it expresses the division only by means of calculation (*saṃkhyā*), because that [calculation] denotes a divided object, whereas a word for direction (*dik-śabda*) does not, since its scope is restricted.
Therefore, a word for direction cannot occur in a collective aggregate (*samāhāra*); thus, it is not compounded therein, as in the example "five rivers" (*pañcanadī*).

Regarding the compound *pañcānāṃ nāpitānām apatyam* ("the offspring of five barbers"), when the sense of a secondary derivative (*taddhita*) is the domain, the compound is formed first; subsequently, by the rule *ata iñ* (Pāṇini 4.1.95), the form *pañcanāpiti* is derived, and finally, *pañcakapālaḥ* is formed.

In the case of *pañcasu kapāleṣu saṃskṛtaḥ* ("prepared in five potsherds"), when the meaning of a secondary derivative (*taddhita*) is the governing factor, the compound is formed first, and subsequently the suffix *aṇ* is applied.
By the rule *tasya* [Pāṇini 4.1.88], there is elision (*luk*) of that suffix. Thus, one arrives at *pañcagavadhanaḥ* (as the printed reading is *pañcagavadhanam*).

In the expression *pañca gāvo dhanam asya* ("five cows are his wealth"), first there is a *bahuvrīhi* compound of the first three words. Subsequently, with the word *dhana* as the final member (*uttarapada*), the preceding two words form a *tatpuruṣa*. When that [compound] exists, the suffix *ṭac* is applied as a compound-final suffix (*samāsānta*) according to Pāṇini 5.4.92.
For in that context, the term *tatpuruṣa* is understood to carry over from the rule *tatpuruṣasyāṅguleḥ* [Pāṇini 5.4.86].
Regarding the example *pañcapūlī*: the analytical explanation (*vigraha*) is "the collection of five bundles."

The singular number is applied by the rule *dvigurekavacanam* (Pāṇini 2.4.1). Femininity is established by the statement *akārāntottarapado dviguḥ striyāṃ bhāṣyate* (Vārttika 156), which results in the suffix *ṅīp* by the rule *ṭiḍḍhāṇañ...* (Pāṇini 4.1.15). Now, an objection is raised: "Since *samāhāra* means 'collection' (*samūha*), and a collection is already included within the category of 'the meaning of a secondary derivative' (*taddhitārtha*), the explicit mention of *samāhāra* is redundant; for it would be established simply by the phrase 'the meaning of a secondary derivative'. This is not so. For in the case of *pañcakumārī*, once the secondary suffix denoting a collection has been elided by the rule *luk taddhitaluki* (Pāṇini 1.2.49), the feminine suffix would also have to be elided by the rule *yasyeti ca* (Pāṇini 6.4.148). Therefore, the explicit mention of *samāhāra* is necessary to prevent that.

However, when a collective aggregate (*samāhāra*) is grasped as a distinct entity, it is precisely in this context that the non-occurrence of a secondary derivative (*taddhita*) suffix is designated as its technical name (*samākhyā*).
Consequently, this fault does not arise;
for example, the aggregate of five girls is *pañcamakumāri*.

When the technical designation *upasarjana* (secondary member) applies by the rule *ekavibhaktiś cāpūrvanipāte* [Pāṇini 1.2.44], then by the rule *gostriyor upasarjanasya* [Pāṇini 1.2.48], the shortening of the vowel occurs.

But how, in this case, is there the state of having a single case-ending (*ekavibhaktitva*)? It is because of its connection with only one [case], namely the genitive (*ṣaṣṭhī*). For a collective (*samāhāra*) is an aggregate (*samūha*), and when there is a relationship with that [aggregate], the genitive alone must occur.

Therefore, although the word *samāhāraḥ* (collection) is joined with the word *kumārī* (girl) through many case-endings—such as "the collection of girls" (*samāhāraḥ kumārīṇām*), "see the collection of girls" (*samāhāraṃ kumārīṇām*), and "by the collection of girls" (*samāhāreṇa kumārīṇām*)—the word *kumārī* is joined only with the sixth [genitive] case; thus, there is "uniformity of case-ending" (*ekavibhaktikatvam*). [The suffix] *ṭac* is applied according to the rule "there is a compound-final suffix" (*samāsānto bhavati*), because of the recurrence [of the rule] "after words meaning 'king,' 'day,' or 'friend,' [the suffix] *ṭac* [is added]" (*rājāhaḥsakhibhyaṣṭac*, Pāṇini 5.4.91). Here, the word *kutsita* (despised) expresses a conventional meaning (*rūḍhi*).
And thus, the *niṣṭhā* suffix does not denote the past tense.
Furthermore, by the word "contempt" (*kutsana*), the property that causes contempt is understood—on the grounds that "one is despised or censured by means of this.
The use of the plural number, however, is for the purpose of excluding the prescription of the [verbal] form itself.
By this, a compound is understood with words expressing contempt along with that which is contemptible, but not a compound of the word *kutsita* with the word *kutsana*.
Therefore, he says: "words expressing the contemptible," and so forth.
This compound is to be understood as occurring when there is contempt for the cause of the application of a word (*śabdapravṛttinimitta*).
But how is this obtained? From proximity (*pratyāsatti*).

For that which is the basis for the application (*pravṛttinimitta*) of a word is proximate; therefore, it is logical that the compound should occur only when that [basis] is used in a derogatory sense (*kutsā*), as in "a grammarian who is like a needle of chaff" (*vaiyākaraṇakhasūciḥ*).
The analysis of the compound is: "he is both a grammarian (*vaiyākaraṇa*) and a 'sky-pointer' (*khasūci*).
One who, when questioned regarding grammar, points to the sky—that is, looks toward the empty space—is called such because he is devoid of ready wit.

In this case, the quality of being a grammarian is the ground for the application of the word *vaiyākaraṇa*, and that [quality] is here disparaged. Furthermore, that [quality] consists in the relationship of being a student of grammar or the relationship of being a knower of grammar. It is by means of that ground that the word *vaiyākaraṇa* applies to the person.
In the same way, it should be understood that a compound is also used elsewhere when there is contempt for the basis of a word's application,
as in "yājñikakitavaḥ" (a fraudulent sacrificer). Here, he is a "kitava" (cheat) only in the sense of being like a cheat.

For just as a gambler engages in gambling while considering only the possession of wealth, asking "What do you have?", and not considering [the opponent's] caste or other qualities; so too, a ritualist who, when engaged in officiating at sacrifices, out of greed considers only the wealth of one unworthy of sacrifice and not his fitness for sacrifice—he is called a "gambler among ritualists.
Therefore, it is said: "One who is intent on the greed to officiate for those unworthy of sacrifice," and "one who is stubbornly perverse like a Mīmāṃsaka."
It is understood that the Mīmāṃsaka, having failed to obtain the fruit of studying Mīmāṃsā, has become an atheist (*nāstika*). And [in the case of] "the grammarian-thief" (*vaiyākaraṇaścauraḥ*):
surely a grammarian who is suspected of being a thief is indeed contemptible, and the word "grammarian" refers to him as such.
He asks, "How then is this counter-example appropriate? and replies with the words beginning, "For here...

For, by reason of proximity, the contempt must apply to that which is the ground for the application of the word (*śabda-pravṛtti-nimitta*). However, in this case, the ground for the application of the word *vaiyākaraṇa* is not being censured; because even a thief may correctly know or study grammar.

Therefore, it is not the basis for the application of the word that is being censured here; what then? That which possesses the quality of being a grammarian (*vaiyākaraṇatva*) is censured. However, that "grammarian-ness" is merely an incidental indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*). Just as one says, "He who trembles is an Āttha," where trembling is an incidental indicator of the Āttha, so too in the expression "a contemptible grammarian" (*kutsito vaiyākaraṇaḥ*). In this case, the grammarian is the thief; thus, "grammarian-ness" is simply a secondary characteristic. As in: "He who trembles is an Āttha"—here, trembling is an incidental indicator of the Āttha. [The example is: "a contemptible grammarian."
In this case, there exists a word that is contemptuous (*kutsita*) and denotes something contemptible;
however, the word *brāhmaṇa* itself is not a term of reproach. It has been stated that "the words *pāpa* and *aṇaka* denote reproach.

If this is so, one might ask: since the compound is already established by the preceding rule alone, for what purpose is this stated? Anticipating this doubt, he says "of those two" (*tayoḥ*), and so forth.

If there were a compound with the preceding [word], then, because the word *kutsita* (contemptible) would be indicated as the first member [of the compound], it would undergo prior placement (*pūrvanipāta*), whereas the words *pāpa* (evil) and *āpaṇaka* (shopkeeper) would undergo posterior placement (*paranipāta*). Therefore, this [sūtra] is commenced for the sake of ensuring prior placement.
The inclusion of the term *kutsita* is for the sake of clarity.

Otherwise, since the term "contemptible" (kutsita) would already follow from the preceding rule (*pūrvayoga*), that [present rule] would not need to be formulated at all. Regarding the statement, "That by which something is compared is the *upamāna* (standard of comparison)":
the meaning is that the *upamāna* is that by means of which an object is determined through similarity.
For example, in the expression "the *gavaya* is like a cow," the cow is the *upamāna*, for it is by means of its similarity to the cow that the *gavaya* is determined.
The meaning understood is: "As is a cow, so is a gavaya.

A universal (*sāmānya*) is that which is common to many; and since the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) is mentioned here, and because that [standard] depends upon the object of comparison (*upameya*), it is understood that the common property (*sāmānya*) belongs specifically to both the standard and the object of comparison. Thus he says: "Of the standard and the object of comparison," and so forth.
"This compound is formed with words denoting the object of comparison as qualified by that [property]."
This compound occurs with words that express the object of comparison (*upameya*) as qualified by that common property (*sāmānya-dharma*).
But when it is asked, "Why [is it said] 'with words expressing the common property'?", this specific qualification is obtained by logical necessity (*nyāya*).

For instance, those which have expressed a common property are called "words expressing the common property" (*sāmānyavacana*), just as those which have expressed a quality are called "quality-expressing words" (*guṇavacana*).

And when do they become words denoting a common property (*sāmānyavacana*)? When, having expressed the common property, they refer to the substance (*dravya*) that possesses it as qualified by that common property.

And since that [substance] possessing the common property is understood to be the object of comparison (*upameya*) precisely because the word for the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) is a relative term (*sambandhiśabda*), this very meaning established by logic was demonstrated by the author of the *Vṛtti* in the example:
"Devadattā is dark like a sword-blade" (*śastrīśyāmā devadattā*).

In this case, the *śastrī* (knife) is the standard of comparison (*upamāna*), and Devadattā is the object of comparison (*upameya*). A well-known thing serves as the standard of comparison, not an unknown one.
It is the *śastrī* alone that is well known for its dark quality, not Devadattā.
The commonality between these two is the shared property of "darkness" (*śyāmatva*).

Having expressed that darkness, the word *śyāmā* functions—either through metaphorical identification (*abhedopacāra*) with Devadattā or through the elision of the possessive suffix *matup*—and thus it becomes a term expressing a general property.

But surely, the rule "by a word in grammatical coreferentiality" (*samānādhikaraṇena*) continues to apply here; and since the word *śastrī* applies to a knife while the word *śyāmā* applies to Devadattā, there should be no compound because of their lack of coreferentiality (*vaiyadhikaraṇya*)? This is not so.

In all cases, because there is a distinction between the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) and the object of comparison (*upameya*), their designators necessarily stand in grammatical coordination (*vaiyadhikaraṇya*). And this very fact is stated [in the rule]; therefore, even though there is coordination, the compound will be formed by virtue of the specific force of the statement. Alternatively, the word *śastrī* (knife) here also refers to Devadattā;
thus, this is a compound based on grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) itself: "she who is both a knife and dark" is *śastrīśyāmā*.

But surely this word *śastrī* denotes a genus (*jāti*), and by taking "being a knife" (*śastrītva*) as its basis for application (*pravṛttinimitta*), it applies to that which possesses it; yet that quality of being a knife does not exist in Devadattā. So how can it apply there? This is not a fault; for there is also the view that "all these words apply to a substance (*dravya*) by taking up a quality (*guṇa*). In that case, the word *śastrī* will apply to Devadattā by taking up the quality of blackness (*śyāmatva*).
Or else, Devadattā will be denoted by the word *śastrī* on the basis of similarity (*tāddharmyāt*).

For it has been stated previously that a thing receives the name of another due to its possessing the same properties (*tāddharmya*). Furthermore, this possession of the same properties here consists in having the quality of being dark (*śyāma-guṇatva*).
An example is: "The rice grains are like hoes."
For husks indeed serve as a point of comparison;
for instance, by means of such similarities as length and so forth, rice grains are compared to them.
However, the word "rice grain" (taṇḍula) is not a term denoting a universal (sāmānya).

But surely the word *taṇḍula* (rice) also denotes a substance possessing that [quality] by taking up the universal *taṇḍulatva* (the state of being rice); thus it is indeed a word denoting a universal (*sāmānyavacana*). Is this counter-example, therefore, not incorrect? This is not so; for it has been stated that the common property (*sāmānya*) is that which is shared between the object of comparison (*upamāna*) and the object compared (*upameya*). And *taṇḍulatva* does not belong to husked grains (*phālānām*), but rather only to unhusked rice (*taṇḍulānām*). [This is established] by the force of the rule: "by words expressing the object of comparison."

Although the phrase "by words denoting the standard of comparison" (*upamānavacanaiḥ*) is not explicitly mentioned in the rule, nevertheless, because the word *upamitam* (that which is compared) depends upon both the object of comparison (*upameya*) and the standard of comparison (*māna*), it is a relative term; thus, it implies the status of being a standard of comparison for words such as *vyāghra* (tiger).
Consequently, even though no specific [quality] is expressed, it is understood by implication that the compound is formed with those words denoting the standard of comparison.
This applies provided that "a word expressing a common quality (*sāmānya*) is not employed."

The common property (*sādhāraṇo dharmaḥ*) of the object of comparison and the object compared—such as valor (*śaurya*) and so forth—is the "commonality" (*sāmānyam*). If the word expressing that [commonality] is not employed, then a compound occurs; it does not occur otherwise. Now, one might object: since the commonality is already included within the compound, there is no employment of words expressive of it; so what is the point of this prohibition? This is not so; for while the common property—the commonality—is indeed included within the compound, its specific instances are not.

In that case, since there would be no prohibition [against compounding], the use of a word expressing a specific common attribute (*viśiṣṭasādhāraṇadharma*) would indeed occur; thus, should a prohibition be made? No, it need not be made. Why? Because when a general term (*sāmānyaśabda*) is employed, that which depends upon it becomes dependent and therefore incapable of forming a compound (*asamartha*). Precisely because of this incapacity, the compound will not take place. This, however, indicates the following rule: "A compound does indeed occur even for a principal element (*pradhāna*) when it is dependent.

In this context, the men (*puruṣa*) are the principal element because they are the objects of comparison (*upameya*), whereas the tiger and so forth are subordinate because they serve as the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) for their sake.
What is the purpose of this indicator (*jñāpaka*)? It is so that forms such as *rājapuruṣaḥ śobhanaḥ* (the king’s man is handsome) are established. [The objection is:
"Since the rule *viśeṣaṇaṃ viśeṣyeṇa* (an adjective is compounded with the noun it qualifies) would already apply.

But surely, he will state that a compound occurs between an adjective and a noun in apposition (*samānādhikaraṇa*); however, because there is a difference between the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) and the object of comparison (*upameya*), there is a lack of apposition (*vaiyadhikaraṇya*). So how can the application of *viśeṣaṇaṃ viśeṣyeṇa* be reached here? The thought is this: this compound occurs when words denoting the standard of comparison, such as *vyāghra* (tiger), are used with words denoting the object of comparison, such as *puruṣa* (man).

And how there is grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) when words expressing a standard of comparison function with respect to the object of comparison has already been explained in the preceding rule itself. Regarding the statement "a differentiator is a qualifier" (*bhedakaṃ viśeṣaṇam*):

[the root *śiṣ* is listed as *śiṣlṛ viśaraṇe* in the printed editions; however, according to the *Padamañjarī*, it is *śiṣlṛ śeṣaṇe*, preceded by the prefix *vi-*]. From the root *śiṣlṛ* meaning "to distinguish" (Dhātupāṭha 1451), with the prefix *vi-* and the suffix *lyuṭ* in the sense of an instrument, we derive *viśeṣaṇam*. That by which something is distinguished is a "qualifier."
Its definition is as follows:

"The differentiator" (*bhedaka*) is that which, having operated upon an object possessing multiple modes by way of a general form, distinguishes it from other modes and establishes it within one specific mode; this is the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*).
[As for the view that] "the qualified (*bhedyam*) is the qualifier," [it is as follows:]...

The qualificand (*viśeṣya*) is that which is to be qualified (*viśeṣaṇīya*). From that verbal root preceded by the prefix *vi-* (√*viś*), the suffix *ṇyat* is applied in the sense of the object according to Pāṇini 3.1.124 (*ṛhaloṇryat*). Its definition is this: "that which is to be distinguished" (*bhedyam*).
That object which possesses multiple modes and, being distinguished from other modes, is established within a single mode, is the "divisible" (bhedya), that is, the qualificand (viśeṣya).

Now, for what purpose are both the qualifier (*viśe�ṣaṇa*) and the qualified (*viśeṣya*) employed? It might be argued that it would suffice to employ only one of them, since they are relative terms and the understanding of the other follows from the employment of either one. This is true; however, both are employed to indicate that a compound occurs only where both the preceding and the following words function individually as qualifier and qualified, as in the case of *nīlotpalam* ("blue lotus"). Here, the meaning of "blue" is distinguished from [other things] such as bees, and by means of the word "lotus," it is established as referring specifically to a lotus.

Even the meaning of "lotus" is established as "blue" by being excluded from red lotuses and so forth through its connection with the meaning of "blue"; thus, there exists a qualifier-qualified relationship for each term individually.
Where this [relationship] does not exist, however, there is no compound, as in the case of "a tree is a *śiṃśapā*.
For a tree deviates from being a *śiṃśapā*, whereas a *śiṃśapā* does not deviate from being a tree.
Therefore, because it excludes that [tree] from other types such as the *palāśa* and so forth, the term "śiṃśapā" serves as its qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*), and not the qualified (*viśeṣya*).

The "tree," however, is the qualified; since the meaning of "śiṃśapā" does not deviate from "treeness" (*vṛkṣatva*), it does not serve as its qualifier. Now, should one never say "the śiṃśapā tree" or "the mango tree"? One should indeed use a determinative compound (*viśeṣaṇasamāsa*) when the specific application of words such as "śiṃśapā" is not restricted to a particular instance.

For instance, words such as *śiṃśapā* are denoters of the fruit, the tree, and the root; thus, they are general terms (*sāmānyaśabda*). Because their referents deviate from "treeness" (*vṛkṣatva*), there is no relationship of qualifier and qualified (*viśeṣyabhāva*) [between them]. Furthermore, the word "tree" (*vṛkṣa*) becomes the qualifier.
However, when—due to some context or meaning—the meanings of "tree" and so forth have already been determined, then [the application of the general term] should not occur.

But surely, since the word "tree" has its function already determined by the meaning of "tree," its employment at that time would be untenable, because its meaning has already been expressed, according to the rule: "That which has its meaning already expressed is not employed" (*Vyāḍipāda 60*).
And consequently, there would be no possibility of a compound at all.

So why is the mention of "both" (*ubhaya*) made for the sake of excluding that? This is not so; for in common usage, the employment of words whose meaning has already been expressed is observed, as in the example: "Bring two cakes. If, then, a compound must occur wherever both [words] stand in a relationship of qualifier and qualified (*viśeṣya-viśeṣaṇa-bhāva*) toward each other, then in such a case there would be the status of being a subordinate member (*upasarjana*) for each individually, because both are qualifiers here, and because in this rule the qualifier is designated by the nominative case. Consequently, one might even have *utpalanīlarasam* (the blue-lotus-flavor).
But is it not the case that "blue lotus" is always intended [to be a compound]? This is not a fault, because one member is primary (pradhāna) and the other is secondary (apradhāna).
If both were primary, there would be no application of two unrelated terms in a single place, as they would not benefit one another.
Even if both were secondary, since both would depend upon the primary, they still could not benefit each other; thus, their application in a single place would likewise be impossible.

Therefore, in a single expression, one element is primary (*pradhāna*) while the other is secondary (*apradhāna*). That which is secondary receives the technical designation *upasarjana*, and not the other; for the designation *upasarjana* is based on its etymological meaning: *upa* (near) + *sṛjati* (it casts its own meaning near the qualificand). The word *nīla* is secondary because its referent, the quality (*guṇa*), is subordinate; however, the word *utpala* is primary because its referent, the substance (*dravya*), is predominant.

Therefore, it is only the word *nīla* (blue) that is subordinate (*upasarjana*), and not the word *utpala* (lotus); thus, there is no occasion for the previously mentioned fault to arise. In cases where both [words] are present, they may take the subordinate role alternately, as in *kubjakhañja* and *khañjakubja*. Now, from what is the predominance (*prādhānya*) of the substance (*dravya*) determined here? It is said: as in the instruction, "One should sacrifice a red goat" (*otaṃ chāgam ālabheta*), because even if the quality of being red (*otaguṇa*) is absent, a goat of another color may still be sacrificed; yet in the absence of a goat, a substance possessing the quality of redness that is something other than a goat cannot be sacrificed.
For a sacrificer does not achieve his purpose by sacrificing a ball of flour in the absence of a goat.

And if the substance were subordinate to the quality, then just as a ball of flour is not sacrificed in the absence of a goat, so too, in the absence of the specific quality [of being a goat], even another animal possessing some other quality would not be sacrificed. Yet it is not the case that such an animal is not sacrificed; therefore, the substance alone is primary, not the quality.
But surely, the word *utpala* is not established as being a word for a substance (*dravyaśabda*) either.
Likewise, there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) regarding the word *nīla*, since it does not abandon its own substrate, the substance, until its destruction.
Therefore, because the universal (*jāti*) is identical in nature with the substance, the word based upon that [universal] [applies] from the very production of the substance.
Furthermore, qualities (guṇas) either persist or do not persist in this substance; they come into being and pass away.

Therefore, these [qualities] are not identical with the substance itself, and thus the word for substance is not established as being caused by them. Enough of this digression. Regarding the example "Takṣaka is a serpent":
surely Takṣaka is indeed a qualifier of the serpent? For instance, when "serpent" is said, the universal (sāmānya) of serpents is understood, not a particular (viśeṣa) serpent.

When "Takṣaka the serpent" is said, it is understood that a specific kind of serpent is distinguished from non-Takṣakas; however, this counter-example is incorrect. This is not so, for it has been stated: "A compound occurs where one [word] exists in both [positions]. But Takṣaka never functions as the qualified object (*viśeṣya*) of the meaning of "serpent. Why does he not so function? Because Takṣaka's being a serpent is never subject to deviation (i.e., he is invariably a serpent).

But is it not the case that, since the word *takṣaka* has many meanings, the snake itself is indeed properly used as a qualifier for the sake of excluding other types [of *takṣakas*]? This is not so; a proper name does not possess the same capacity to denote meaning as an action-word (*kriyāśabda*).
For an action-word conveys its meaning by following its constituent parts (*avayavārtha*), whereas a proper name does so through its collective form (*samudāyarūpa*).

According to the principle that "the conventional usage of a whole is stronger than the etymological usage of its parts" (*Vyākaraṇa-paribhāṣā* 108), when that [collective usage] is present, there arises no expectation whatsoever regarding the meaning of the action-word.
Regarding the expression "the red Takṣaka":
here, "red" is the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*), while "Takṣaka" is not the qualified (*viśeṣya*),
because his being red is never subject to deviation (i.e., it is invariably present).

If, then, Takṣaka is not the substantive (viśeṣya), then "red" would also not be an attribute (viśeṣaṇa); for an attribute depends upon a substantive. Nor is it possible to imagine that something other than Takṣaka, such as a cloth, is the substantive with respect to which "red" could be considered an attribute. For in that case, since something other than "red" and so forth—such as "intense poison"—would be the attribute, it would follow that Takṣaka himself would have to be the substantive in relation to that.

"Therefore, others maintain that both [terms] are mentioned for the sake of clarity; this is an elaboration of the preceding [rule], since it is already established by that alone. For here too, there exists a mutual relationship of qualifier and qualified between each of the preceding and following words. [The statement] 'the mention of *śreṇī* and so forth is for the purpose of the sense of *cvy-anta*' [is made]."
The compound is intended to apply to those words that signify the transformation of something into what it was not previously.
For when the meanings of words such as *śreṇi* (guild) and others are brought into completion where they were previously unaccomplished, then a compound is desired.

However, when those meanings are already accomplished and are merely being treated in another form—such as when one intends to express the sense "the guilds have been made," "punished," or "honored"—then a compound is not desired.
Furthermore, it should not be suspected that the word *kṛta* cannot function in the sense of words such as *daṇḍita* ("punished") and so forth;
for the root *kṛ* denotes action in general,
or because verbal roots possess multiple meanings.

The meaning of the statement "the mention of the sense of *cvī* in [the context of] *śreṇi* and so forth" is as follows: that by which the sense of *cvī* is expressed—that is, made known—is "the expression of the sense of *cvī*" (*cvyarthavacana*). The meaning is that an explanation must be provided for that [expression] by which the sense of *cvī* is understood when *śreṇi* and other such words are employed as the cause of compounding (in the form of *karmadhāraya*). Thus, it means: "an explanation must be given."

In this regard, the following is the explanation: the term *bahulam* (optionally) is understood here; therefore, the compound occurs only for those meanings of *cvi* that involve the suffix *cvi*, and not for those that do not.

Regarding the phrase "of those ending in *cvi*" and so forth: since the suffix *cvi* is prescribed optionally, there are two kinds of meanings of *cvi*: those ending in *cvi* (*cvyantāḥ*) and those not ending in *cvi* (*acvyantāḥ*).
In this context, the compound is formed by this [rule] for those beginning with *śreṇi* and ending with *acvi*.

However, for those ending in *cv*, since they possess the designation of *gati* by the rule *gatiśca* [P. 1.4.61], the compound will occur by the subsequent rule *upasarjanaṃ pūrvam* [P. 2.2.30]. This word *viśiṣṭa* indeed exists as having a restrictive sense when it denotes excellence (*ādhikya*).
For example: "Devadatta and Yajñadatta are both learned, handsome, and discerning."

Devadatta, however, is distinguished from Yajñadatta by his Vedic study (*svādhyāya*); it is understood that he is superior *by means of his Vedic study alone*. Other qualities, meanwhile, remain exactly the same.
And there exists [the use of the comparative suffix] in the sense of superiority without restriction, as for example: "Devadatta and Yajñadatta are both eloquent, handsome, and discerning."
But Devadatta is distinguished from Yajñadatta by his Vedic study; it is understood that he is superior in terms of Vedic study.
Other qualities, whether equal or numerous, are not intended to be expressed here.

Although these two sentences are identical in form, nevertheless, a difference in meaning is understood from context and other factors, just as in the case of the word *ārāt*, which has a distinction between the meanings of "far" and "near."

In this regard, if the word *viśiṣṭa* were taken as denoting "excess" (*ādhikya*) without restriction, then [the rule] would also apply to the case of *siddhaṃ ca tad abhuktaṃ ca*, because here too there is a word ending in *-kta* that is in excess by virtue of the negative particle (*nañ*).
Therefore, he adopts the word *viśiṣṭa* as denoting "excess" with a restriction, stating: "that of which the distinction is by the negative particle itself," and so forth. [He adds:
"beginning with the root" (*prakṛtyādikam*).
By the word "ādi" (and so forth), the inclusion of suffixes (*pratyaya*) and prefixes (*upasarga*) is intended.
Regarding the term "anañ":
that which has no *nañ* (negative particle) in it—that is, a *ktānta* (ending in a *kta* suffix) in which no *nañ* exists—is called *anañ*.
"Both that which is done and that which is not done.
But how can a single entity be both done and not done? There is no fault here, because the designation is applied to the whole by means of the properties of its parts.
It is called "done" due to its connection with the portion that has been done, and that very same thing is called "not done" due to its connection with the portion that has not been done.

Alternatively, that for which something was intended is considered "not done" (akṛta) due to incapacity regarding that purpose; for example, because he lacks the capacity to perform the duties of a son, even a son is called "sonless" (aputra).

If a compound is formed with *nañ* alone as the qualifier, while everything else—the base (*prakṛti*) and so forth—is identical, then a compound would not occur with that [base] which has an additional *nuṭ* augment or the *iṭ* augment. To address this, he says: "*nuḍiṭau*" and so on.

Since the *nuṭ* and *iṭ* augments belong to that which is qualified by *nañ*—namely, the word ending in the *kta* suffix—they are included by the mention of that [suffix]; therefore, those two are not differentiators of this [compound].

The meaning is that they are non-differentiators. Therefore, even though it is additional, it remains qualified by the negative particle (*nañ*) alone; thus, a compound with it certainly occurs, as in *aśitānaśitena*.
The augment *nuṭ* is applied by [Pāṇini 6.3.74].
Thus, "by the afflicted and the unafflicted.
In one alternative, the augment *iṭ* is applied by [Pāṇini 7.2.50].
It is impossible to exclude the negative particle (*nañ*).
If that *nañ* were to be compounded, then the state of being qualified by the *nañ* would not be possible, because [the word] would be connected with two *nañ*s.

Therefore, since the meaning "only that which is qualified by the *nañ* is not compounded" is obtained simply from the mention of "qualified by the *nañ*," the inclusion of the term "not *nañ*" (*anañ*) is redundant.
That is done for the sake of clarity: "of *kṛtāpakṛta* and so forth," etc.
An enumeration (*upasaṃkhyāna*)—that is, a formal presentation—must be made for *kṛtāpakṛta* and the like.
In this regard, the following is the presentation: the term *bahulam* ("in various instances") is understood to carry over here; by that, a compound is formed even for *kṛtāpakṛta* and the rest.
Regarding the term “done and undone”:
it is "done" because of the performance of one part of that [action] which is desired; and it is "undone" because of the performance of one part of that [action] which is undesired.
Regarding the term "bhuktavibhuktam":
it is "eaten" (*bhukta*) because it has been consumed, and "vitiated" (*vibhukta*) because of its unpleasantness.
Here, the prefix *vi-* conveys the sense of being unpleasant, as in the word *virūpa* (deformed).
Alternatively: "that which has been eaten and that which has returned" is *gatapratyāgatam*;
"that which has gone and that which followed it after" is *yātānuyātam*;
and [the compound] *krayākrayikā*.

The word *kraya* refers to a large purchase, whereas a small purchase is called *krayikā*. Because it is connected with a part of a purchase (*kraya*), it is a "purchase" (*kraya*); because it is connected with a part of a small purchase (*krayikā*), it is "small-purchaseness" (*krayitā*). Thus, [the compound] *krayākrayikā* means "a large purchase and a small purchase," and the vowel lengthening occurs according to [Pāṇini 6.3.137].
Thus, "puṭa" and "puṭikā" form the compound "puṭāpuṭikā";
"phala" and "phalikā" form "phalaphalikā";
and "māna" and "unmānikā" form "mānonmānikā."
"In the section on co-referentiality," and so forth.
Here too, the meaning of the word *upasaṃkhyāna* is "presentation" (or "stating").
And the presentation is just as before. "Because of the statement 'with words denoting those worthy of honor and those being honored,'" and so forth.

The substitution of *hrasva* (short vowel) occurs for the final syllable of the subsequent member (*uttarapada*) only if the words are expressive of worship (*pūjāvacana*), and not otherwise; therefore, by the mention of "being worshipped" (*pūjyamāna*), it is understood that *sat* and the others are words expressive of worship.
For this very reason, the suffixes *śatṛ* and *śānac* are not included under the word *sat*, since those two do not denote worship—as in the example:
"An excellent cow [has emerged] from the mud. (*utkṛṣṭā gauḥ kardamāt*).
The meaning is "extracted.

Now, how is the compound *mahādrumaḥ* (great tree) or *mahodadhiḥ* (great ocean) formed, since no sense of "honor" (*pūjā*) is understood here? What then? It is the exceeding of the measure of the object denoted by the second member of the compound. Even if this is so, it will still be possible due to the continued application of the rule regarding the term *bahulam* (variously). Words such as *vandāraka* ("one who pays homage") are generic terms (*jātiśabda*). And when they function as a standard of comparison (*upamāna*), they become words expressing honor.

In this regard, since the formation is already established by the rule *vyāghrāder ākṛtigaṇatvāt* (Pāṇini 2.1.56), this new rule is commenced so that the suffix may apply even when used in a general sense. The statement "that which is being honored" (*pūjyamānam*) implies that words such as *vṛndāraka* are understood here as terms denoting honor;
for otherwise, the state of being honored would not be logically possible. An example is: "the elephant Suṣīma."
But surely, the rule "the qualifier [is compounded] with the qualified" (*viśeṣaṇaṃ viśeṣyeṇa*) still applies;

and since there is no Suṣīma other than Nāga, is this not simply a name for Nāga himself? If that is so, then this direction for a counter-example has been shown by the author of the Vṛtti. However, the actual counter-example here is: *devadatto nāgo yasmānmūrkhaḥ* ("Devadatta is a 'Nāga' because he is a fool"). [The rule] *jātiparipraśna eva vyutpādyete* ("only when there is an inquiry regarding a genus are they derived") is established by the rule *vā bahūnām* (Pāṇini 5.3.93), while the rule *kiṃyattadaurnirdhāraṇe* (5.3.92) is understood to be in force.

It might be argued: "For the purpose of qualifying which word is the mention of 'inquiry concerning a genus' (*jātiparipraśna*) intended? To this he says: "The word *katara* also," and so forth. "That very [mention] makes it known.

If, then, the word *katama* were taken as occurring only in the sense of an inquiry concerning a genus, the mention of "inquiry concerning a genus" would be redundant; for even without it, by the aforementioned principle, the words *katara* and *katama* would be understood as occurring only in the sense of an inquiry concerning a genus.
"And so," and so forth.

Precisely because the word *katama* functions elsewhere than in an inquiry regarding a genus (*jāti*), this counter-example of yours—"Devadatta, who is he?"—is appropriate. Otherwise, it would not be appropriate; for that [word] does not function anywhere other than in an inquiry regarding a genus. "Who is the friend? (*kiṃsakhā*).
The substitution of *anaṅ* occurs by [Pāṇini 7.1.93] *anaṅ sau*.

Now, one might ask: why does the compound-final suffix *ṭac*—prescribed by [Pāṇini 5.4.91–92] *rājāhaḥ sakhibhyaṣṭac*—not apply in cases such as *kiṃrāja*? To this he replies with the words *kimaḥ kṣepe* and so forth.

Here, the word *na* ("not") is understood from the preceding rule [Pāṇini 5.4.69] *na pūjanāt*. Since the formation of a compound is already established by the rule beginning with *viśeṣaṇam*, this present statement is for the purpose of prescribing the posterior position (*paranipāta*) of the word.
These are words denoting qualities (*guṇaśabda*).
In that case, if there were a compound with that [word], their prior placement (*pūrvanipāta*) would result.

Now, for what purpose is the mention of *dhūrta*? Since this is a word of censure (*kutsana*), is the compound not already established by the rule "with a word of censure" (Pāṇini 2.1.53)? To this he says: "The mention of *dhūrta* is for the sake of excluding cases where there is no censure."

The compound is understood to apply when there is contempt for the cause of the word's application (*śabdapravṛttinimitta*), and not when there is contempt [for the person] itself. "Established words (*rūḍhiśabda*) denoting praise are to be understood.
For words expressing praise are of three kinds: some are genus-words (*jātiśabda*) which, when employed in relation to another object, express praise, such as "Devadatta is a lion.
Some are quality-words (*guṇaśabda*) which become expressions of praise through the connection between a quality and its possessor (*guṇin*), such as "a beautiful village" or "an excellent cook."

Some are conventional words (*rūḍhiśabda*), such as *matallikā* and others; for these, excellence alone is the word-meaning. Therefore, here, because of the mention of "words" (*vacana*), those conventional words which function specifically in the sense of praise are understood. For example: *goprakāṇḍam*.
"Śobhanaḥ" means excellent or praised.
The separation of the *yoga* (rule) is for the sake of avoiding ambiguity.

If only the preceding rule were taken to include words expressing praise, then a doubt would arise: "Is the word 'praśasta' connected individually with each of the items beginning with *poṭā*, or is it connected with the word 'praśaṃsā'? If it were connected with *poṭā* and the others, there would be a compound even with their synonyms. [The rule continues: "With words such as *khalati* when they are in grammatical apposition," and so forth.

If this is so, for what purpose is there the specification in the feminine gender as "jaratībhiḥ"? One should have specified it simply as "jaradbhiḥ," for the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) of the masculine word *yuvan* with the feminine word *jaratī* is not logically possible. To this he says: "The specification in the feminine gender as 'jaratībhiḥ'," and so forth. But how can this specification enable one to understand this technical rule (*paribhāṣā*)? If this [rule] did not exist, then the specification "jaratībhiḥ" would be purposeless.

And thus, because this falls under the section concerning co-referential (samānādhikaraṇa) compounds, this compound is understood to be with the word *jaratī*, which is co-referential. Now, since that [word] is feminine, it cannot have co-reference with the word *yuvan*, which refers to a masculine; so how can this grammatical instruction (*nirdeśa*) be meaningful? It would be meaningful if this technical rule (*paribhāṣā*) were established: for if that rule exists, it follows that when the word *yuvan* is mentioned, the word *yuvati* is also included. Thus, there is co-reference between the words *yuvati* and *jaratī*, and only when that exists does their compounding occur.

The mention of *tedavaṃ jaratībhiḥ* indicates that this technical rule (*paribhāṣā*) exists. [Objection: Even so, when a compound with *jaratī* is being taught, it would not apply to *jarat* [in the masculine], as in *yuvajarann*? [Reply: This is not a fault; for in another recension (*vṛtti*), it is read as *jaradbhiḥ*. Since the Teacher has instructed his students in both ways, both forms are established. [And] "and synonyms of *tulya*."

Now, why is the apprehension of the word-form (*svarūpa*) not understood here? It is thought as follows: in the rule *kṛtya*, there is an apprehension of the meaning; therefore, by association with that, it is proper to understand only the meaning "equal" (*tulya*). Since no grammatical operation (*kārya*) is possible upon that meaning, it is understood that the compound applies to those words which express that meaning. Thus, the mention of the term *ākhyā* (name) is for the purpose of including those having the same designation (*nāmadheya*). Otherwise, even in the case of *gaur vāhīkaḥ* ("The Vāhīka is an ox"), the compound would occur; for here the word *go* has the sense of similarity.
For all words, when employed in reference to another object, convey similarity.
However, if the term "name" (ākhyā) were used [in the rule], then since the word *go* here does not have an identical name [with the other member], the compound would be prohibited.
In examples such as *bhojyoṣṇam*, words like *uṣṇa* are qualifiers (*guṇavacana*).
In that case, if this *yoga* (rule) did not exist, there would be the prior placement (*pūrvanipāta*) of those [words] when forming a descriptive compound (*viśeṣaṇasamāsa*).
Therefore, this rule is commenced for the sake of their subsequent placement (*paranipāta*),
as in the example "tulyamahān" (equal to great).
Although a compound by the rule "sanmahat" and so forth would apply here, nevertheless, this very [rule] takes effect because it is subsequent.
Its scope is when the term has the same designation—as in *tulya-ota*. And its scope is when the term does not have the same designation—as in *mahāpuruṣa*.
In the example "bhojya odanaḥ" (rice to be eaten), the word *odana* here denotes a genus (*jāti*). The rule [Pāṇini 2.1.57] continues to apply.

In that case, if both color-words were intended here as denoting their own specific forms (*svarūpa*), the relationship of qualifier and qualified (*viśeṣaṇa-viśeṣya-bhāva*) would not be possible, because they would have identical meanings.

For it is not possible for that very same thing to function as both the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) and the qualified (*viśeṣya*) of Devadatta. Furthermore, even if one were to grasp the intrinsic nature (*svarūpa*) of one [term] and the object-meaning (*artha*) of the other, then the word "color" (*varṇa*) would be the general term and the second word, such as "black" (*kṛṣṇa*), would be the particular term.
Consequently, each would lack the status of being both a qualifier and a qualified.
It has already been stated that the purpose of including the term "both" (*ubhaya*) [in the rule] is that a compound occurs only where both [conditions] are present.
Therefore, he says—beginning with "denoting a specific color," etc.—that the inclusion of the word "meaning" (*artha*) is understood to apply in both cases:
"a black-spotted deer" (*kṛṣṇasāraṅgaḥ*), "a red-spotted deer" (*lohitasāraṅgaḥ*).

But surely, the words *kṛṣṇa* and *lohita* refer to the parts, whereas the word *sāraṅga* refers to the whole—just like the word *śabala*. How then can there be grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) between a word such as *kṛṣṇa*, which functions with respect to a part, and a word such as *sāraṅga*, which functions with respect to the whole? To this he says: "By way of the parts," and so forth. It is called "black" because of its connection with black parts, and "red" because of its connection with red parts.

Precisely because the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) here is figurative, a compound does not apply by [Pāṇini 2.1.57] and so forth; therefore, this [definition] is commenced so that the designation "great" (*mahatī*) may be understood as a "significant designation" (*anvartha-saṃjñā*).
Consequently, the subordinate element (*upasarjana*) is that which is non-primary.
And in this context, it is not the whole aggregate that is non-primary; rather, it is the primary element itself.
Since the members [of a compound] exist for the sake of that [whole], they are subordinate;

therefore, words denoting the members, such as *kṛṣṇa*, possess the status of a subordinate term (*upasarjana*), but not a word denoting the whole, such as *sāraṅga*. "The word *kumārī* is compounded with those [words] only when it is in the feminine gender."
However, he indicates this by the restriction "but not in the masculine gender.
The sense is that grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) between a masculine form and a feminine form is not possible. [The phrase] "by them in both ways" [is used].
It is both feminine and masculine.

But how can a compound, when being stated with masculine bases (*puṃlliṅga*), be [formed] with feminine bases (*strīliṅga*)? To this he says: "When there is the mention of a nominal stem (*prātipadika*). This has already been explained. [The example is] "catuṣpādaḥ" (four-footed).
Those which have four feet are *catuṣpād*. By the rule [Pāṇini 5.4.138], there is elision of the final part [of the word].
It is stated: "It should be specified that [the suffix applies] to a genus consisting of four-footed animals."
The meaning is that this form of the rule must be explained as follows: only those words denoting four-footed animals (*catuṣpād*) that express a genus (*jāti*) are compounded with *garbhiṇī*.

This is the explanation here: the term "genus" (*jāti*) from the sūtra [Pāṇini 2.1.64] *poṭā-ādi* is understood here; therefore, only that which denotes a genus of four-footed animals is compounded with *garbhiṇī*, and nothing else. Thus, for example, *mayūravyaṃsakaḥ*.
He is both a peacock (*mayūra*) and a deceiver (*vyaṃsaka*), hence *mayūravyaṃsaka*.
Although the word *vyaṃsaka* ought to have been placed first according to the rules of compound formation, it is read here with the final position for the sake of its specific usage.
Thus, this applies to all compounds beginning with *mayūravyaṃsaka* and ending with *yavanamuṇḍa*.
In the Vedic language (*chandasi*), there is the rule "hastegṛhya" and so forth;

however, in a compound where *nañ* does not precede, *ktvā* becomes *lyap* according to [Pāṇini 7.1.37]. In the common language (*bhāṣāyām*), however, it becomes "hastegṛhītvā," "punardattvā," and so on.

Regarding the rule "ehīḍādayo 'nyapadārthe" (Pāṇini 2.2.74): when the action [expressed by the verb] "come" (*ehi*) and "praise" (*īḍa*) occurs within a particular ritual act, that act is called "ehīḍam. Similarly, there is "ehiyavam."
"Ehi-vāṇijā" refers to that action in which one says, "Come, merchant.
Similarly, there are "apehi-vāṇijā" (Go away, merchant) and "prehi-vāṇijā" (Depart, merchant).
"Ehisvāgatā" refers to that action in which one says, "Come, welcome."
Thus: *apehisvāgatā*;
that in which there is "bring the mat" is *prohakaṭā*;
likewise *prohakardamā* and so on, ending with *āharavasanā*.
The term *kṛndhivicakṣaṇā* refers to that action [expressed] by the words *kṛndhi vicakṣaṇa*.
The term *uddharotsṛja* is a compound of two finite verbs (*tiṅanta*).
Since the rule "a verb [is compounded] with a verb when there is continuity" (Gaṇasūtra 20) already establishes this, the present statement is for the sake of non-continuity.
That action in which one draws out and then discards is called *uddharotsṛjā*.
Furthermore, this compound has the action as its primary element.
"Jumping up and falling down," "shaking off the best," and likewise "lifting up and casting away"— such [expressions] refer exclusively to the domain of non-continuity.

The word *uccāvacam* is derived as an irregular formation (*nipātana*). It is analyzed as *udak ca avāk ca*. Furthermore, it is analyzed as *uccaiś ca nīcaiś ca*, and thus the form *uccanīcam* is derived as an irregular formation.
*Ācita* and *upacita*, when analyzed (*vigṛhya*), form *ācopacam*;
*ācita* and *parācita* form *ācaparācam*;
and *niścita* and *pracita* form *niścapracam*.
Having nothing is "akiñcana";
having bathed, he is "akālaka";
having drunk, he is "asthiraka."
The reading "bhuktvāsuhitaḥ" is for the sake of having the udātta accent on the final syllable; furthermore, the absence of the suffix *lyap* is treated as an irregularity (*nipātana*).
Likewise in the case of "proṣyapāpīyān."
Singleness of word and singleness of accent result from a compound;
for example— *utpatyapākalādi*,
*nityarohiṇī*.
Niṣaṇṇaśyāmā,
Apehiprasavā, and Iha-pañcamī.
Regarding the phrase "iha dvitīyā":

in a compound, there is both a single word-form (*aikapadya*) and a single accent (*eka-svarya*). According to the rule, "The root *jah* [is used] frequently with an object to express repetition, and it denotes the agent," the form *jahi* is the second person singular of the imperative (*loṭ*).
A verbal form ending in *ta* is frequently compounded with its object when frequency (*ābhīkṣṇya*) is implied, provided that the agent is expressed by means of the compound.
One who says "Go away, old man! repeatedly is called "one who goes away, old man" (*jahijoḍaḥ*).
In *jahistamba*, there is the imperative (*loṭ*), the second person singular suffix (*sip*), and the substitution of *ja* [for *hi*] according to Pāṇini 6.4.36.
In this context, the status of being the object belongs to "joined" (*joḍa*) and so forth.
Regarding the phrase "the verb" (*ākhyāta*) and so on: a word ending in a *tiṅ* suffix is compounded with another word ending in a *tiṅ* suffix when continuity of action (*kriyāsātatya*) is implied.
Where it is repeatedly said, "Eat! Drink!", there the compound *aśnītapibata* is employed.
This compound has action as its primary meaning.
In this same way, compounds such as *pacatabhṛjjata* and others are to be understood.
When it is said, "Salt, break [it]," that is *bhindhilakṣaṇā* (the indicative function of breaking).
Likewise, [it applies to] "Cook the salt."

Thus ends the first quarter of the second chapter in the *Kāśikā-vivaraṇapañjikā*, composed by the venerable Ācārya Jinendrabuddhipāda, who follows the tradition of Bodhasattva. Regarding the statement "by virtue of contextual capacity (*sāmarthya*), words denoting a part [are compounded]":

for if words such as *pūrva* (eastern, etc. did not denote a part, then the status of being a "possessor of parts" (*ekadeśin*) would not be understood for the subsequent member of the compound; this is because a possessor of parts is dependent upon its parts.
Therefore, it is understood that although words such as *pūrva* are stated in a general sense, they are compounded as denoting a part due to contextual capacity.

In order to clarify the meaning of the statement that "the mention of a single substratum (*ekādhikaraṇa*) is a qualification for the proponent of the 'one-part' view (*ekadeśin*"), he says: "And one," and so forth.
"One" means a substance (*dravya*) qualified by the number one.
By the term "single substance" (*ekadravya*), he shows that the word "substratum" (*adhikaraṇa*) here is employed in the sense of "substance."

Now, one might object: "The word *ekadeśinā* ends in the third case (*tṛtīyā*), whereas *ekādhikaraṇe* ends in the seventh case (*saptamī*); how, then, can a relationship of qualifier and qualified (*viśeṣaṇaviśeṣyabhāva*) be established between these two through grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), given that they have different case endings? And why would it not be so? Because their meanings are different. This is not the case; for it is said, "Sūtras are like Vedic [language]" (*chandovat sūtrāṇi bhavanti*), and because of the frequentative usage (*bahulavacanāt*) in the rule *pṛthagyogakaraṇasāmarthyād vā* (Pāṇini 3.1.85), the seventh case in *ekādhikaraṇe* has precisely the sense of the third case, according to the rule *na lokāvyayaniṣṭhākhalarthatṛṇām* (Pāṇini 2.3.69).

Therefore, there is no fault of having different meanings. Regarding the statement, "This rule is an exception to the genitive compound," because of the expression "by one who [possesses] a part," words such as *pūrva* (eastern/preceding) and so forth are understood to denote a part.
For words denoting a related entity necessarily bring to mind their counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*).

In that context, regarding the relationship between a part and a whole, when the genitive case is produced according to the rule for the "part" (*ekadeśin*), the compound would be required by the rule *ṣaṣṭhī* [Pāṇini 2.2.8]; therefore, this present rule is an exception (*apavāda*) to that.

In the example *pūrvakāyaḥ*, the body (*kāya*) is the whole (*ekadeśin*), and it is a single substance because it is possessed of a singular number. [The analysis is] "the front part of the body from the navel."
The ablative case in "nābheḥ" (from the navel) is used in the sense of spatial relation (*digyoga*).
The intended meaning is that which is above the navel and in front of it belongs to the body;
therefore, in this context, the navel is not a part-possessor (*ekadeśin*).
What then? The word *nābhi* (navel), which denotes the limit (*avadhi*), when ending in the fifth case, is not compounded.
However, for the word *kāya* (body), which denotes that which is a part (*ekadeśin*) [of the whole], compounding does indeed occur.

Even though the word *pūrva* (prior) is dependent (*sāpekṣa*), because the body (*kāya*) is the principal element, it has been established in the rule [Pāṇini 2.1.56] that a compound is formed even with a principal element that is dependent.

"First, address the students—this is the original reading and the one accepted by the *Padamañjarī*. Here, the compound [of *chātrāṇām* and *āmantraya*] does not occur because the students are the possessors (*ekadeśin*) qualified by the number plural.
Now, one might object: "In this case, since the subsequent rule applies, there will be a prohibition of the genitive compound by the rule *na nirdhāraṇe* [Pāṇini 2.2.10]."

[Note: The printed reading is *tat kimevādhikaraṇe*. What is the purpose of including the term "single substratum" (*ekādhikaraṇa*)? This is not [necessary]. If the word "address" (*āmantrayasva*) were not required, then the sentence would be completed with only the preceding "of the students" (*chātrāṇām*); in that case, since there would be no selection (*nirdhāraṇa*), this would not be the scope of that prohibition, and thus a compound would occur even with a part-whole (*ekadeśin*) possessing multiple numbers, provided there is no single substratum.

Now, since every sentence is completed by means of an action (*kriyā*), if one were to supply some action—such as "of the students"—to the phrase *pūrvaṃ chātrāṇām* and thereby conceive of a selection (*nirdhāraṇa*), then likewise there would be a selection in the case of *pūrvaṃ kāyasya*.

For here too, the action of pulling out (*ākarṣaṇa*) exists as the cause for selection. And thus, this rule being commenced within the very scope of that [preceding] rule would indeed be an exception (*apavāda*) to it.

Furthermore, a conflict between a general rule (*utsarga*) and an exception (*apavāda*) is not logically tenable; so how could the prohibition "not in the case of selection" (*na nirdhāraṇe*, Pāṇini 2.2.10) apply by virtue of its subsequent position, such that [the rule] "of that which is preceded by a numeral, *vi*, or *sāya*" (*saṃkhyā-visāya-pūrvasya*, etc. would be restricted? Since the author says [in 6.3.110], "after *sāyam*," one understands from this indicative mark (*jñāpaka*) that a compound of *ahan* occurs with every part-whole (*ekadeśin*).

Otherwise, the fact that the word *ahan* is preceded by *sāya* would be impossible, and thus that statement would be incorrect. [Regarding the term *ardha*: "But when it denotes an equal division, the word *ardha* is neuter and has a fixed gender; it is this [neuter] that is being referred to here."
If this is so, should one simply use the term *sama* (even)? This cannot be done, because the word *sama* has multiple meanings.

For instance, it also applies to a place devoid of elevations, depressions, and the like—as in the injunction "one should sacrifice on even ground," which means one should sacrifice on ground free from elevations, depressions, and so forth.

Furthermore, even if it is said that [the term] refers to an equal division (*samapravibhāga*), in that case too there would be heaviness [of the formulation]; therefore, should the mention of the neuter gender (*napuṃsakagrahaṇa*) be made? It need not be made. For by the very fact that the word *adr̥ḍha* is indicated in the neuter gender, the inclusion of the neuter will occur. This is not so; for if the mention of the neuter were not made, it would be understood that the neuter indication is based on the form of the word itself, as in the rules "in a neuter [word]" (*napuṃsake*, Pāṇini 1.2.47) and "in a *bahuvrīhi* compound ending in *bandhu*" (*bandhuni bahuvrīhau*, Pāṇini 6.1.14). Consequently, the status of the word *adr̥ḍha* as being inherently neuter would not be relied upon.

In this way, even that which possesses the neuter gender (*napuṃsakaliṅga*) would be subject to the same rule. Therefore, in order to establish the neuter gender for the word *ardha*, it must be stated that "it is neuter. For example:
*ardhapippalī*.
The feminine gender [of *paravalī*] is established by the rule *paravalliṅgam* [Pāṇini 2.4.26].
Now, why does shortening not occur here by the rule *athātra* [Pāṇini 1.2.48]? Because it is not a secondary member (*anupasarjana*).
Its status as a secondary member, however, is determined by the rule *ekavibhakti ca* [Pāṇini 1.2.44].
From this point [sūtra 7.4.44], the term *vibhāṣā* (optionally) is understood to carry over; and that has been explained as a restricted option (*vyavasthitavibhāṣā*). For example: *grāmārddhaḥ*.

The meaning is "one part of the village. In the expression "half of Devadatta’s animal," there is no compound with the word *Devadatta*, because Devadatta is not a "possessor of multiple parts" (*anekadeśin*).

The term *hrasva* (short) does not refer to a part [of a word], but rather to the master (*svāmī*). However, with the word *paśu* (animal), which is a part [of a compound], a compound is indeed formed. Even though the word *paśu* is dependent [on another element], a compound still occurs because of the predominance of *paśu*: for example, *adṛḍhapaśur devadattasya* ("Devadatta’s weak animal"). "Because of the inclusion of the option (*anyatarasyām*), that [compound] also becomes a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*)"—thus it is said.
But surely these words, beginning with *dvitīya*, end in a *pūraṇa* suffix.
