For example: *māṇavakam upanāthati*, which means "he entreats the boy. [This applies] to the root belonging to the *bhvādi* class; it does not apply to the one belonging to the *divādi* class, because that root is specified as being used in the sense of "injury" (*hiṃsā*).

And because this [suffix] does not apply there, it follows that only the causative (*ṇyanta*) form will be understood; so what is the purpose of specifying the causative form? Who, moreover, says that it is a specification of the causative form? For here, this vowel *i* has been used for the purpose of indicating the verbal root, according to the rule: "The suffixes *ik* and *śtip* are used for indicating a verbal root" (Vārttika 319).

If this is so, how is the long vowel *ā* heard in the form *jāsī*? It is said: the vowel *ā* was pronounced and then a modified form was indicated; this modified indication is made so that it should apply only where this specific form occurs, and not here—such as in the case of *dasyum ajījasat*.

In the *luṅ* [aorist] tense, by the rule "after the causative suffix *ṇi*, [the *cli* is replaced by] *caṅ*" (Pāṇini 3.1.48), the *caṅ* substitute is applied. Then, by "in the presence of *caṅ*, there is shortening of the penultimate vowel" (7.4.1) and "before *caṅ*, [the root is reduplicated]" (6.1.11), reduplication occurs. By the rule "as in the case of *saN* when the light syllable follows" (7.4.93), the status of *saN*-like behavior (*sanvadbhāva*) is applied; by "in *saN*, [the vowel] *a* becomes *i*" (7.4.79), the substitution of *i* occurs; and finally, by "the long vowel [is substituted] after a reduplicated syllable" (7.4.94), the lengthening takes place. This very purpose applies even to the roots *naṭ* and *krath*: namely, that the designation as *vakṛt* (having a *kṛt* suffix) should not apply here, so that forms such as *dasyumanīnaṭat* ("he caused the Dasyu to dance") and *dasyumacikrathat* ("he caused the Dasyu to strike") do not occur.

The purpose [of this rule] is also the lengthening of the vowel in *kratha*, as shown by the author of the Vṛtti when he states, "the lengthening occurs by way of an irregular derivation (*nipātana*).
The reading in the Vṛtti is *niprahan* (not *niprahanti*). Here, the mere indication of the verbal root and the prefix is what is intended.
However, there is no single composite (*saṃghāta*) consisting of the two prefixes, nor is there a fixed sequence (*ānupūrvī*); for those two are not intended to be significant.

Therefore, it is understood that the words *ni* and *pra* are included whether they are used separately or together, and even in reversed order. Thus he says: "There is the inclusion of the composite, the separate, and the reversed. For example: *caurasya praṇihanti*.

The substitution of *ṇ* [for *n*] occurs by the rule *nergadanada-* [Pāṇini 8.4.17]. Regarding the example "he causes the thief to dance" (*caurasyonnāṭayati*), since the vowel lengthening (*vṛddhi*) is already established by the root *naṭ* meaning "to tremble" [Dhātupāṭha 7.2.116], for what purpose is it stated that "the lengthening is by way of a formal irregularity (*nipātana*)"? To this he says: "For this... and so forth.
"It would apply to a short vowel" refers to the rule *mitāṃ hrasvaḥ* [Pāṇini 6.4.92]. An example is *caurasya pinaṣṭi*.

The root *piṣ* is used in the sense of "crushing" (*sañcūrṇana*; Dhātupāṭha 1452). Because it belongs to the *rudhādi* class, the suffix *śnam* is applied. In the expression "he crushes the grains" (*dhānāḥ pinaṣṭi*), there is no violence (*hiṃsā*), because that [violence] is a property belonging only to sentient beings.

And this [sūtra] has been commenced so that the rule may apply even to those actions whose agent is non-existent, as in: *caurasyojjāsayati devadattaḥ* ("Devadatta causes the thief to be terrified") and *śatasya vyavaharati* ("He deals with a hundred").
The meaning is that he employs a hundred in buying and selling, or rather, he gambles with it.
In *śatasya paṇate* as well, the meaning is the same.
The *ātmanepada* ending occurs because the root is marked with the *anudātta* accent. [The question] "Why does the *āya* suffix not occur?
implies that it would have applied by virtue of the rule *gaka-pū-dhūpa-* (Pāṇini 3.1.28).
Regarding the phrase "of that which has the sense of praise" (*stutyarthasya*), and so forth:

although the root *paṇ* is listed [in the Dhātupāṭha] as having both the senses of "transaction" (*vyavahāra*) and "praise" (*stuti*)—as in "paṇa vyavahāre stutau ca" (Dhātupāṭha 439)—nevertheless, the suffix *āya* is desired only after *paṇ* in the sense of praise, not in the sense of transaction.
On this point, the author of the Vṛtti himself will state the reasoning later.
Because of its association with *paṇi* in the sense of "praising," the *paṇi* here produces that very meaning [of praising], and not the sense of "transaction.
The expression "he transacts with a tally-stick" (*śalākāṃ vyavaharati*) means "he counts."
In this case, because it functions for the purpose of worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*), there is a difference in meaning [from the literal sense].
"He praises the Brahmins" (*brāhmaṇān paṇayati*) means "he extols them."

Since the root *vyavahṛ* does not function in the sense of "to bargain" (*paṇayati*), there is no identity of meaning [between them]. In the example "he praises the Brāhmaṇas" (*brāhmaṇān dīvyati*), the meaning is "he praises";
the lengthening of the vowel occurs by [Pāṇini 8.2.77] *hali ca*.
If this were to apply only to that specific meaning, then it would have been more appropriate to include the mention of *div* (to play/gamble) in the previous rule itself.

Why, then, is there this separation of rules (*yogavibhāga*)? To this, he says: "The separation of the rule is for the sake of what follows. For example: *śalākāṃ prati dīvyati* ("He plays with a stick"). In other senses such as "playing" and so forth, the root *div* is employed. *Bāla-manoramā*: *vibhāṣopasarge* (2.3.59). The rule "optionally [the suffix *kvip* is added] when a prefix is present. *Śalākāṃ prati dīvyati*. In a different sense, such as "playing" and so forth, the verb *dīvyati* is used. *Bāla-manoramā*: *vibhāṣopasarge* (612, 2.3.59). "Optionally [the suffix *kvip* is added] when a prefix is present."
The meaning is that when a prefix (*upasarga*) is present, the genitive case may optionally be used for the object of the root *div* in the sense of "gambling" (*vyavahāra*) or "betting" (*paṇa*).
[From the *Bālamanoramā*: Regarding the rule *preṣyabrāuvorhaviṣo devatāsaṃpradāne* (Pāṇini 2.3.61): [the words] *preṣya* and *brāu* [are mentioned], and [the phrase] *devatāsaṃpradānake*.
The meaning is: "that for which the deity is the recipient.
Regarding the term *preṣya-brāhmaṇayoḥ*:
the root *īṣ* (meaning "to go") belongs to the *divādi* class and takes the suffix *śyan*; by virtue of the prefix (*pra*), it functions in the sense of "impelling."
The analysis of the compound is *preṣyaś ca brāhmaṇaś ca* (a servant and a Brahmin).
Regarding the word *karmaṇaḥ*:
the meaning is that the term *karmaṇi*, which is understood from the rule *adhīgartha-*, is transformed into the genitive case.
Regarding the word *haviṣaḥ*:
the word *havis* does not refer to the generic form itself, but rather to words that denote specific types of sacrificial offerings (*havir-viśeṣa*), according to the commentary.

Thus, it refers to those words denoting specific sacrificial offerings which serve as the objects of the actions expressed by the *preṣya* and *brāhmaṇa* formulas, wherein the deities are the recipients (*saṃpradāna*), according to the commentary.

And thus, it is established that the genitive case is used after a word denoting a specific oblation (*haviḥ*) which has become the object of the *preṣya* and *brāhmaṇa* formulas expressing an action where the deity is the recipient (*devatā-saṃpradāna*). This follows from the [author's] own commentary. Here too, the term "remainder" (*śeṣa*) does not carry over, as indicated by the commentary.
And thus, this is an exception to the second [rule]:
"For Agni, of the goat.
This is an instruction (sampraiṣa) performed by the Adhvaryu priest directed toward the Maitrāvaruṇa.

O Maitrāvaruṇa, announce—that is, make known by means of the *praiṣa*—the oblation consisting of the fat (*medas*) called the omentum (*vapā*), which belongs to the goat and is to be offered with Agni as the deity: "Let the Hotṛ sacrifice;
let Agni enjoy the omentum and the fat of the goat; O Hotṛ, perform the sacrifice. This is the meaning.

In this regard, although in the Kalpasūtras only "agnaye chāgasya vapāyā medasaḥ preṣya" (Prompt [the Hotṛ] for the fat of the omentum of the goat for Agni) is seen, and not "haviṣaḥ" (of the oblation) as well, nevertheless, such a *praiṣa* (directive) should be understood as existing in some recensional branch (*śākhā*) on account of its citation in the Bhāṣya.
By the word *medas*, a specific kind of flesh resembling a piece of cloth is denoted.
Or [one may say]: "anubrūhi" (recite after).

In the *Kalpasūtras*, one sees [the formula]: "I shall direct [the Hotṛ] for the fat of the omentum of the goat-offering to Agni," but not even the word "of the offering" (*haviṣaḥ*). Nevertheless, such a *praiṣa* (direction) should be understood as existing in some recensional branch (*śākhā*), as evidenced by its citation in the *Bhāṣya*.
By the word "fat" (*medas*), a specific part of the flesh resembling a piece of cloth is denoted.
Or [the formula is]: "Recite after me" (*anubrūhi vā*).

In the Kalpasūtras, one sees only: "I shall give the command for the omentum and the fat of the goat-oblation for Agni," but not even the word "of the oblation" (*haviṣaḥ*). Nevertheless, such a *praiṣa* (ritual command) should be understood as existing in some recensional tradition (*śākhā*) based on examples cited in the Bhāṣya.
By the word *medas*, a specific kind of flesh resembling a piece of cloth is denoted.
Or [the command is]: "Recite the invitatory verse" (*anubrūhi vā*).
"Recite the invitatory prayer (*anuvākyā*) for the omentum and the fat of the goat-offering to Agni"—this is the example.

O Maitrāvaruṇa! The meaning is: "Make manifest by means of an invitatory prayer that which is the offering related to the goat, consisting of the omentum known as *vapā*, which is about to be presented to Agni.
What is the purpose of the two, the *preṣya* (direction) and the *anuvāka* (recitation)?
Offer the omentum and the fat of the goat as an oblation to Agni.
What is the oblation?
"Direct [the assistant] to offer cow-dung to Agni."
What is the purpose of the condition "when the deity is the recipient"?

[Consider: *māṇavakāya puroḍāśaṃ preṣya* ("Send the sacrificial cake to the boy"). It must be stated that there is a prohibition when the oblation (*havis*) is qualified by its being "already set forth" (*prasthita*).
"Command [the Hotṛ] regarding the oblation of the goat—the omentum and the fat—set forth for Indra and Agni.
Regarding the word "prasthitam," it means "unmanifested" (avyaktam). Thus ends the Brāhmaṇa section.
The word *brāhmaṇa* is a designation for the *Śatapatha*.
In the phrase "of the village," the genitive case is used in the sense of a remainder (*śeṣa-ṣaṣṭhī*).
With reference to the word "in the assembly," the phrase "on that day" serves as an illustration.

By the rule *svamornapuṃsakāt* [Pāṇini 7.1.23], there is elision (*luk*) of the suffix *am*. While the word *ahan* [from Pāṇini 8.2.68] is being carried over, by the rule [8.2.69], the *n* is replaced by *r*, which then becomes a *visarjanīya*. Thus, *dīvyeyuḥ*.

In the case of *liṅ*, *jher jus* [Pāṇini 3.4.108] results in the substitution of *jus*; then, by *liṅaḥ salopo 'nantyasya* [Pāṇini 7.2.79], there is the elision of *s*. Since the sixth case (genitive) would optionally apply to that which has a prefix (*sopasarga*), why does this rule not serve to mandate the second case (*dvitīyā*) invariably? He says: "of that which has a prefix" (*sopasargasya*).

By the rule *vyavasthitavibhāṣā* [Pāṇini 2.3.59], the second case will necessarily occur in the Vedic language (*chandas*) as well; therefore, this statement is not tenable for that purpose. [This refers to] "of the root *iṣ* belonging to the *divādi* class."
The mention of the root *iṣ* (meaning "to go," Dhātupāṭha 1127) by means of the suffix *śyan* is for the purpose of excluding other roots that share the same form.
The mention by means of the second person singular imperative (*loṭ*) is for the purpose of excluding other *lakāra*s, other persons, and other numbers.
The phrase "only in that context" [means that the rule applies only when the aforementioned conditions are met].
This applies only to the singular number of the middle person in the imperative mood,
as in "agnaye chāgasya" and so forth.
"Chāga" is a derivative (vikāra) of "chāga."

In that context, Agni is the deity as the recipient (*sampradāna*); the offering (*havis*) consisting of the fat (*vapā*) and other products of the goat is the object to be given (*sampradeya*). [Regarding the objection: "But [the text says] *preṣya*... [as stated in the *Kāśikā* and *Padamañjarī*].
By [Pāṇini 6.4.105], there is the elision (*lup*) of *hi*. In the case of "anubrūhi," there is the substitution of *hi* by *hir* according to [Pāṇini 3.4.87]: *sehir apicca*.
Because it belongs to the *ad-ādya* class, there is elision of the *śap* suffix.
This rule applies even in the domain of the spoken language (*bhāṣā*), as the word "Vedic" (*chandas*) is mentioned in the subsequent sūtra. Thus:
*juhudhi*.
By [Pāṇini 6.4.101], there is the substitution of *dhi* for *dhā*. Thus: "Command [the assistant] regarding the cow-dung for Agni.

Now, one might object: since cow-dung is indeed an oblation (*havis*), how can this serve as a counter-example? It is not so; because the mention of the deity as the recipient already establishes that the word is a relative term referring to an oblation, the explicit mention of "oblation" (*havis*) again indicates that what is intended is an oblation consisting of food fit for consumption.

And it is not appropriate to offer cow-dung as food; thus, the counter-example [is given] starting with "of the oblation that has been set forth" (*haviṣaḥ prasthitasya*). By the word *prasthita* ("set forth"), that oblation which is qualified is designated as "the set forth.
Regarding that, a prohibition of the genitive case must be stated.
The meaning is that it must be explained.
In this regard, the explanation is as follows: the term *vibhāṣā* (optionally) is carried over from rule 2.3.59, and that is a restricted option (*vyavasthitavibhāṣā*).
Consequently, [the suffix] does not apply to *prasthita* when it refers to an oblation (*havis*). [Question: "What is the purpose of including the term *bahula* (in various ways)?"

This is the question of one who considers that [the desired forms] are already established simply by the continued application of the term *vibhāṣā* (optionally). [The examples are: "kṛṣṇo rātryai" (Kṛṣṇa for the night) and "himavato hastī" (an elephant from the Himalayas).
In these cases, because of the inclusion of the term *bahulam* (in various ways), the fourth case ending (*caturthī*) occurs even in the sense of the seventh case (*saptamī*).
"Vaktavyā" means "it must be explained. In this regard, the following is the demonstration: the term "bahulam" (optionally/in various ways) is employed here.
Therefore, in some cases the dative case occurs even where the genitive would otherwise be expected;

in other cases it is something else entirely—this is indeed the intended meaning of the mention of the term *bahulam* (in various ways). In the example "he sacrifices with ghee" (*dhṛtasya yajate*), the root *yaj* here functions in the sense of worshipping a deity, and in that context, ghee functions as the instrument (*karaṇa*). In the example "five times" (*pañcakṛtvaḥ*), [the suffix *kṛtvasuc* is applied].
Regarding "dvirahnaḥ": [the rule] "dvitricaturbhyaḥ suc" [Pāṇini 5.4.18 applies]. For it is understood that [the action] occurs twice, thrice, or four times;
this is the sense, based on context and so forth.

But surely, since the meaning of the context and so forth is external (*bahir-aṅga*), and since the purpose of the rule "five times" (*pañcakṛtvaḥ*) has already been fulfilled there, this [rule] would not apply here? If that is so, then this teaches that even the meaning of the context and so forth is a cause for the case-endings (*vibhakti*). Therefore, in the rule *vṛddho yūnā* (Pāṇini 1.2.65), when the sense of accompaniment (*sahārtha*) is understood, the third case ending occurs. As for the word *āsikā*, it is formed by the suffix *ṇvuc* in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāva*), according to the rule *paryāyārhaṇotpattiṣu ṇvuc* (Pāṇini 3.3.111).
Regarding the form *ruāṣṭā*:
[it is derived from] the root *sṛj* with the suffix *tṛc*, according to [Pāṇini 6.1.58].
By [the rule] *vraścādinā* [8.2.36], there is the substitution of *ṣ*. [The commentary says: "Let this not apply when used in conjunction with a *taddhita* suffix."

Now, why is the term *kṛt* not included [in the rule] for the purpose of preventing [the application of the rule] when a finite verb (*tiṅ*) is used? Because in that case, the sixth case ending is prohibited by the rule *na lokāvyayaniṣṭhā* (Pāṇini 2.3.69).
In the example *kṛtapūrvī kaṭam*, the suffix *ini* is applied by the rule *pūrvādiniḥ* (Pāṇini 5.2.87), with the word *iniḥ* being carried over from the preceding rule *kṛtapūrvī* (Pāṇini 5.2.86).

In this case, since the agent (*kartṛ*) is already expressed by the secondary derivative suffix (*taddhita*), this very sentence [of the rule] does not apply, and thus there is no over-extension (*prasaṅga*). However, since the object (*karman*) has not been expressed by that [suffix], if the mention of the *kṛt* suffix were absent, the genitive would apply to the object such as "the mat" (*kaṭa*).

But surely this sentence itself is untenable; for indeed, because the object is already expressed by the past passive participle (*niṣṭhā*), the accusative case should not occur here, nor should the secondary derivative suffix, due to a lack of semantic capacity (*asāmarthya*).
That incapacity, moreover, arises from the requirement of dependence (*sāpekṣatva*).

For instance, in the expression "the mat was made by him previously" (*kṛtaḥ kaṭo 'nena pūrvam*), the word *kṛta* depends upon the mat (*kaṭa*). This is not the case here; how could the past passive participle (*niṣṭhā*) arising from a verbal root express the status of the mat as the object (*karman*)? For its capacity is only to denote the object in general, not a specific object. How then, in a sentence, is the status of the mat as the object expressed by that [participle]? In that case, such an expression would be logical, because of its grammatical coordination (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the word *kṛta*.

But when a *taddhita* suffix has been produced, grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) ceases due to the unification of meaning (*ekārthībhāva*). Consequently, by what means would the status of the mat and so forth as an object (*karman*) be expressed? However, since the action is the meaning of the base (*prakṛti*), just as it undergoes a connection with the instrument (*sādhana*) while being subordinate in a sentence, so too does it do so in a derivative formation (*vṛtti*). Thus, the status of the word "mat" as an object is justified in relation to the sense of "making. Therefore, the accusative case must certainly be employed. Furthermore, there must be a sentence that possesses the same meaning as the derivative formation; yet in the derivative formation, no external object such as a mat is perceived, by which an affix could be produced.
In the sentence, the dependence on an object such as "mat" (kaṭa) is understood to be purposeless;
therefore, the analysis (vigraha) must be made thus: "that by which [something] was previously made.
Consequently, there is no state of being dependent (sāpekṣatva), and the secondary derivative suffix (taddhita) is indeed valid. As for the phrase "otherwise, however" (itarathā hi):

The meaning is that if the reference to "the remainder" (*śeṣa*) continues [from the previous rule], then one would have simply said, "and when a *kṛt* suffix follows, in the sense of the agent" (*kartari ca kṛti*). Even if this were stated, since the word "remainder" (*śeṣa*) continues and the particle "ca" (and) is employed, the term "in the sense of the object" (*karmaṇi*) is indeed obtained; so what is the purpose of explicitly mentioning "the object" (*karman*) again? Therefore, the repetition of the mention of "the object" is for the purpose of terminating the jurisdiction of the section concerning "the remainder."
Furthermore, by the repetition of the term *karman*, the cessation of the previous mention of *karman* is indicated.

When that [previous mention] ceases, the mention of *śeṣa* (remainder), though it continued as connected to it, also ceases. The statement "‘ubhayaprāptau’ is a *bahuvrīhi* compound" serves to dispel the suspicion that it might be a *tatpuruṣa*.
He will state the purpose for resorting to the *bahuvrīhi* compound.
Because it is the subject under discussion, the term "both" (*ubhaya*) is connected with the agent and the object.
By the phrase "in which there is the possibility of both [agent and object] with respect to a *kṛt*-affix," the intention is that this occurs in relation to one and the same action.

He demonstrates the nature of the restrictive rule (*niyama*) "only when [the action] relates to an object" (*karmaṇyeva*). This is not, however, a reversed restriction (*viparītaniyama*) stating that the genitive occurs only when both [agent and object] are present;
for if it were so, the prescription of the genitive in the object case by the preceding sūtra would become redundant.

"In the phrase *āścaryo gavāṃ doho 'gopālakena* ('It is a wonder, the milking of cows by one who is not a cowherd'), the suffix *ghañ* is applied to the root *duh* in the sense of an abstract action (*bhāva*). In that case, since both [the agent and the object] would otherwise be expected to take the genitive, the genitive occurs only for the object, *goṣu* (of the cows), and not for the agent, *agopālakena* (by the non-cowherd)."

And here, the term *prayoga* ("employment") does not carry over from the rule *kṛtvo'rthaprayoge* [Pāṇini 2.3.64]. Consequently, the genitive case occurs even when the object (*karman*) is merely implied, as for example in the rule *antardhau yenādarśanamicchati* [Pāṇini 1.4.28], where the status of the object is understood for the unexpressed *ātman*.
Thus: "drinking" (*pānam*).
The suffix *lyuṭ* [is applied] in the sense of the abstract action (*bhāva*) according to [Pāṇini 3.3.115].
However, it does not apply here: "It is a marvel that there is both the cooking of the rice and the appearance of the Brāhmaṇas.
For in this case, the application of the suffix does not occur for both simultaneously.

Likewise, in the expression "the cooking of rice" (*odanasya pākaḥ*), the application [of the genitive] occurs only with respect to the object, the rice, and not with respect to the Brāhmaṇas as agents.

For the Brāhmaṇas are not intended here as the agents of the cooking; rather, they are intended as the agents of the manifestation [of the rice]. Furthermore, in the expression "the manifestation of the Brāhmaṇas" (*brāhmaṇānāṃ prādurbhāvaḥ*), the application of the genitive occurs only with respect to the Brāhmaṇas as agents—since the suffix *kṛt* [in *prādurbhāvaḥ*] denotes the agent—and not with respect to the rice as the object.
For *odana* (rice) is not the object (*karman*) of the act of appearing (*prādurbhāva*), because the root *bhū* is intransitive (*akarmaka*).
Rather, it is intended as the object of the act of cooking (*pāka*) itself. Regarding the phrase "of [roots] ending in *a* or *ā*" and so forth:
this is a prohibition of the aforementioned restrictive rule (*niyama*).
The meaning is that this form of the rule must be explained as signifying that there is no restriction when the suffixes *a* and *kā* are employed.

In this regard, the explanation is as follows: the term *bahulam* (optionally/in various ways) is understood to carry over from [Pāṇini 2.3.62], "In the Vedic language, [the dative] is used diversely in the sense of the fourth case"; therefore, there will be no restriction regarding the employment of the suffixes *a* and *kā*. As for the rule "In the remaining cases, optionally" (*śeṣe vibhāṣā*), its meaning also must be explained by resorting to the inclusion of the term *bahulam*.
Regarding the term *bhedikā*:
the suffix *ṇvuc* is applied as in the previous case to form the abstract noun.
Regarding the term *cikīrṣā*: [the suffix *aṅ* is applied to the desiderative stem].
The suffix *a* is applied by [Pāṇini 3.3.102] *a-pratyayāt*. In the example "approved by the kings" (*rājñāṃ mataḥ*), the suffix *kta* is applied by [Pāṇini 3.2.188] *mati-buddhi-* etc.;
here, the genitive case in *rājñām* denotes the agent.
But the *kṛt* suffix [denoting] action is expressed by the [suffixes] *niṣṭhā*.

Now, why does it not occur here in examples such as *śīlito devadattena* ("practiced by Devadatta") or *rakṣito devadattena* ("protected by Devadatta"), given that even for words like *śīlita*, the suffix *kta* is prescribed specifically for the present tense because the particle *ca* in [Pāṇini 3.2.188] has the sense of an inclusive "and" (*anuktasamuccaya*)? Even though this is so, there is no fault, because the suffix will not occur here due to the continued application of the term *bahulam* ("variously").
Alternatively, the fact that the action is in the present tense is understood from the very context.

The word-meaning (*padārtha*), however, establishes only the state of being an entity (*bhūtatva*), not its present existence (*vartamānatā*). But for one whose word-meaning is actually present, the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) certainly occurs upon the use of that [word], as in: "Hariścandra was dear to his subjects like [the god] Hari. [The author] explains the supplementary rule (*upasaṃkhyāna*) with the words "And thus," etc., stating: "It is established through the understanding of the 'remainder' (*śeṣa*)."

He who initiates the supplementary rule (*upasaṃkhyāna*) demonstrates that even when the agency (*kartṛtva*) is not intended to be expressed, the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) alone occurs and not the instrumental (*tṛtīyā*). This is shown by the statement: "When that [agent] is employed, the genitive case ending occurs.
According to the possibility of the situation, where the agent alone is possible, it occurs in the sense of the agent; for example: *idameṣām āsitam* ("this is what was sat by them").
Here, because the root *ās-* (to sit) is intransitive (*akarmaka*), only the agent is possible, not the object (*karman*).
But where an object (*karman*) is possible even for the agent (*kartṛ*), the rule applies to both cases, as in: *idam eṣām bhuktam odanasya* ("this rice has been eaten by them").
Since the root *bhuj* is transitive, the object—namely, the rice—indeed exists.

Why does the restriction (*niyama*) of [Pāṇini 2.3.66] not apply here? It is understood that this restriction applies precisely to prevent the application of the genitive case prescribed by [Pāṇini 2.3.65]: *kartṛ-karmaṇoḥ kṛti*.
"Either a rule or a prohibition applies to what immediately precedes" (Vyā.pa. 19), or "Exceptions in the middle sublate preceding rules, not subsequent ones" (Vyā.pa. 10).

Although it could have been stated simply as *adhikaraṇe ca* ("and in the sense of location"), the inclusion of the term *vāci* ("in speech") is for the purpose of ensuring that this is not understood as a mere illustration (*upalakṣaṇa*) of what is expressed by the locative case.

For if it were intended as a mere illustration, then even when a *kta*-suffix is used in the sense of "staying," "going," or "eating"—which are meanings other than [location]—the sixth case would still occur upon its employment.
However, when the suffix *kta* is used in the sense of an abstract action (*bhāva*) following the word *vācigrahaṇa*, the genitive case does not occur.
In that case, only the instrumental case is used for the agent (*kartṛ*), as in: *hahānenāsitam* ("sighing was done by him").

For here, the *kta* suffix does not denote the locus (*adhikaraṇa*); rather, according to the rule *kto’dhikaraṇe ca dhrauvyagatipratyavasānārthebhyaḥ* (Pāṇini 3.4.76), because of the particle *ca* ("and"), it is prescribed both in the sense of the action (*bhāva*) and the agent (*kartṛ*) as well as the locus (*adhikaraṇa*), just as it is otherwise obtained.
But when the suffix *kta* occurs in the sense of the agent (*kartari*), then because the meaning is already expressed by that very suffix, the genitive case does not occur there.

In the example *iha ime āsitāḥ*, the word *ca* has the sense of conjunction (*samuccaya*) with respect to what precedes it. Regarding the statement "the suffixes *kikin* are also included," although there is no inclusion of *ki* and *kin* by the mention of *l*—because they are substitutes for *l* and thus [normally] do not undergo the status of being like the original (*sthānivadbhāva*)—nevertheless, they must be included by means of the extended application (*atideśa*) from the rule *liṭ ca* (Pāṇini 3.2.115).
For when there is an extension of a specific rule, the extension of the general rule follows as an inseparable consequence, because the specific is invariably concomitant with the general.
Therefore, since the prohibition is based on the general rule, it is established for *kikin* suffixes as well; thus, their inclusion is also appropriate.
The form "pacamānaḥ" contains the suffix *śānac*.
The ātmanepada ending is used because of the svarita accent on the affix. In the form *pecānaḥ*,
the suffix *kānac* is applied according to the rule [Pāṇini 3.2.106].
There is reduplication.
By the rule *ata eka* [Pāṇini 6.4.120] and others, there is the substitution of *e* for the radical vowel and the elision of the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsalopa*).
Thus, *pecivān*.

The suffix *kvasu* is applied by [Pāṇini 3.2.107] *kvuśca*. Once the substitution of *e* for the root vowel and the elision of the reduplication have been performed, the augment *iṭ* is added by [Pāṇini 7.2.67] *vasvekājāddhasām*. Then, the nasal augment *num* is added by [Pāṇini 7.1.70] *ugidacām*.
The long vowel [is applied] by the rule *sāntamahasaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.4.10),
as in the examples *dadiḥ* and *papiḥ*.

By the rule *kikinoranyataraḥ* (Pāṇini 3.2.171), either the suffix *ki* or *kin* is applied. Due to the extended application (*atideśa*) of the rule *liṭ ca* (Pāṇini 3.4.115), reduplication occurs. Then, by the rule *ato lopaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.4.64), the vowel *ā* is elided.
Regarding "cikīrṣuḥ":
[the suffix] *u* is applied after roots ending in *san*, *ās*, *sañj*, and *bhikṣ* [by Pāṇini 3.2.168].
Regarding "alaṅkariṣṇuḥ": [the suffix] *iṣṇu* is applied [after the root *kṛ* with the prefix *alam*].

The suffix *iṣṇuc* is applied by the rule *alaṃkṛñ* [Pāṇini 3.2.136], as in *āgāmukaḥ* (found in both the *Kāśikā* and the *Padamañjarī*). The suffix *ukañ* is applied by the rule *laṣapatapada* [Pāṇini 3.2.154]. Regarding the phrase "in the prohibition of *uka*" (*ukapratiṣedhe*), and so forth:
The word "is being explained" (*pratipādyate*) is to be supplied as the ellipsis.
The explanation, however, should be carried out by relying on the continued application of the term *bahulam* ("in various ways"). Thus: "having done so. (*kṛtvā*)
The suffix *ktvā* [is applied] by the rule *samānakartṛkayoḥ* [Pāṇini 3.4.21]. Regarding the phrase "in the prohibition of indeclinables" (*avyayapratiṣedhe*) and so forth,
here too the ellipsis of the sentence should be understood as before,
and the explanation is likewise just as before.
Alternatively, the author of the Vṛtti has provided an explanation at [Pāṇini 2.4.18] with the words, "This entire section is recited among the *svarādi* [words]" (Kāśikā on 1.1.42),
or by the principle that "a rule conditioned by a technical name (*saṃjñā*) is not universally obligatory" (Vyāḍi’s Paribhāṣā 64).
Thus we have *udetoḥ*.
From the root *i* preceded by *ut*, the suffix *tosun* is applied according to Pāṇini 3.4.16 (*abhāvalakṣaṇe stheṇkṛñvadicari*),
resulting in *visṛpaḥ* ("gliding forth") and *īṣatkaraḥ* ("easy to do").
By the rule *īṣad* [Pāṇini 3.3.126] and others, the suffix *khal* is applied;
thus we have *īṣatpānaḥ*.
[The elision of the final vowel occurs] by the rule *ātṛno nakārāt*.
The meaning is: "from the *n* that belongs to the *tṛn* suffix used in the sense of habit (*tācchīlika*).
Regarding the word "pavamānaḥ":
it is derived from the root *pūṅ* (meaning "to purify," Dhātupāṭha 966) with the suffix *śānan* [according to Pāṇini 3.2.128].

Regarding "naḍamaghnānaḥ": the suffix *cānaś* is applied according to [Pāṇini 3.2.129], "The suffix *cānaś* is used in the sense of habitual action, age, or ability. The elision of the penultimate vowel occurs according to [Pāṇini 6.4.98], "In the case of *gam*, *han*, etc. and so forth.
The substitution of *k* for *h* in *han* occurs by [Pāṇini 7.3.54], *ho hanteḥ*, and so forth.
Regarding *adhīyan*:
the substitute *śatṛ* is applied by [Pāṇini 3.2.130], *iṅa dhāryoḥ śatrakṛcchriṇi*.
The substitution of *iyan* occurs;
there is a long vowel with the prefix;
thus, "kartā."
The suffix *tṛn* is applied by the rule *ā kvestacchīla* (Pāṇini 3.2.134). Regarding the statement "the optional application of the *śatṛ* suffix after the root *dviṣ*":

when the *śatṛ* suffix follows the root *dviṣ*, an optional designation must be made; this is because of the metaphorical treatment (*upacāra*) of the identity between the denotative word and the denoted object.
By the word *vā*, the meaning of "option" (*vārtha*) is expressed.
The meaning of "vā" is also "vikalpa. That by which something is expressed or made known is called a "vācaka-śabda" (denotative word).
The meaning is that its explanation must be provided.

In this regard, the explanation is as follows: the term *bahulam* (optionally) is understood here [from a previous rule]. Therefore, there will be an optional prohibition of the present participle suffix *śatṛ* after the root *dviṣ*.
In the form *dviṣan*, the suffix *śatṛ* is applied by [Pāṇini 3.2.131]. [The phrase] "it will apply to that which is not *aka* in the future tense" [is explained as follows].
[The suffix *luṭ* is not used] for the sense of debt (*ādhamaṇrya*), because that [future tense] is impossible there; however,
it is used for "what will be" (*bhaviṣyat*) and for debt,
because that [suffix] is possible in both cases.

But is it not the case that here there ought to be a correspondence of numbers (*saṃkhyātānudeśa*) because of the equality [of the number of items]? This is not so; for a correspondence of numbers occurs by means of a circumflex accent (*svarita*), and here the status of being circumflex is not formally asserted for that purpose.
[Example: *kaṭaṃ kārako vrajati* ("He goes, making a mat"). Here, the suffix *ṇvul* is applied by the rule *tumunṇvulau* [Pāṇini 3.3.10].
In the expression "grāmaṃ gamī" (one who will go to the village), the suffix *ini* is applied to the root *gam*. And because of the rule [Pāṇini 3.3.3], that suffix refers to a future time.
Regarding "śataṃ dāyī" (one who owes a hundred): [the suffix] *ṇini* is applied in the sense of necessity and debt [according to Pāṇini 3.3.170]. Regarding "yavānāṃ lāvakaḥ" (a reaper of barley).
The suffix *ṇvul* is applied by [Pāṇini 3.1.133] *ṇvultṛcau*. Thus, "one who necessarily acts" (*avaśyaṃkārī*) is formed with the suffix *ṇini* in the sense of necessity.

Regarding the phrase "the fulfiller of a hundred years": the root *pūrī* in the sense of "to fill" (*āpyāyane*) belongs to the curādigaṇa (Dhātupāṭha 1151). From it, the suffix *ṇvul* is applied according to Pāṇini 3.1.133 (*ṇvultṛcau*) to denote future time.
For that [suffix] occurs in all three times.
[The question arises: "Is this the inclusion of the *aka* prescribed under the heading of the future (*bhaviṣyat*)?
Here, indeed, "future" (*bhaviṣyat*) is emphasized by its accentuation.
The understanding of a governing rule (adhikāra) occurs through an accented vowel (*svarita*).
Therefore, this refers to the suffix *aka* prescribed by the future governing rule, and not to every instance of it— as in "the boy is to sing the Sāmans" (*geyo māṇavakaḥ sāmnām*),
where the word *geya* is derived in the sense of the agent by the rule *bhavyageya* [Pāṇini 3.4.68].
In the word *geyaḥ* (to be sung), derived from the sense "one who sings," the genitive case in *sāmnām* (of the Sāmans) is always used in the objective sense (*karmaṇi*).
Regarding the phrase "it should be stated" (*vaktavyaḥ*),
the meaning is that it should be explained.

In this regard, the following is the explanation: In the rule *na lokāvyayaniṣṭhā* [Pāṇini 2.3.69], the particle *na* should be treated as a separate *yogavibhāga* (separation of rules). By means of that, when both [agent and object] are applicable in the case of a *kṛtya* suffix, there will be a prohibition of the sixth case (*ṣaṣṭhī*).
Thus, one obtains the form *kraṣṭavyā śākhā grāmaṃ devadattena* ("the branch is to be pulled toward the village by Devadatta").
According to the rule *kṛṣeḥ* [Pāṇini 6.1.59], the augment *am* occurs.

[The rule] "the sixth case (genitive) should not occur when Devadatta is the agent" [is stated]. Thus, it has been said that when both [agent and object] are eligible [to take the genitive], a prohibition of the genitive must be stated for the *kṛtya* suffixes.
However, in the case of the object, such as the branch (*śākhā*), the genitive will not occur precisely because it is already expressed by the *kṛtya* suffix.

Precisely because the village (*grāma*) is not the primary object, just as *kṛtya* suffixes occur with respect to the primary action and not the non-primary one, so too does the sixth case ending [occur].
And here, the village is not the primary object; what then? It is the vegetable (*śāka*). The phrase "with words having the same meaning" means with words having a similar meaning.
The inclusion of the word "meaning" (*artha*) is for the purpose of including those [words] which express a state of having the same meaning independently of other words.
By that proximity to another word, particles such as *iva* are excluded—as in "the gavaya is like a cow" (*gaur iva gavayaḥ*) or "as is a cow, so is a gavaya.

The inclusion of the term *artha* (meaning) is not for the purpose of excluding the word's own form (*svarūpa*), because the prescription of the word's own form has already been set aside by the very mention of the plural number.

Here too, in the expression "equal to his father in wisdom" (*pitus tulyaḥ prajñayā*), the genitive case does not occur after the word *prajñā*, because wisdom is intended [as a factor] either as a cause (*hetu*) or as an instrument (*karaṇa*). Otherwise, the third case ending would have been attracted [by the rule].

Because it is heard [as such] in the immediately following sūtra; for this very purpose is the inclusion of the term *anyatarasyām*. Thus, that very [term] is drawn forward by means of the particle *ca*. Since the inclusion of the meaning (*artha*) would already be established simply by the mention of the third case (*tṛtīyā*), the explicit mention of the word "meaning" (*artha*) is understood to indicate that the word "meaning" itself is a distinct cause [for the application of the rule].
But how, then, is the inclusion of "meaning" (artha) established by the mention of the third [case-ending]? It is understood that this rule (yoga) is incomplete [and thus requires supplementation].

And since that [singular number] occurs only through the meanings (*arthaiḥ*) and not through the words (*śabdaiḥ*), the inclusion of the word "meaning" (*artha*) is established by implication (*sāmarthyāt*). Thus ends the third quarter of the second chapter in the *Kāśikā-vivaraṇapañjikā*, composed by the venerable teacher Jinenndrabuddhipāda, who was a disciple of the Bodhisattvas. Here, if the technical singular number (*pāribhāṣika-ekavacana*) were taken, then the subsequent application of the singular would not occur in the case of "this group-of-five-baskets (*pañcapūlī*) is beautiful," because the subsequent application (*anuprayoga*) would lack the status of a compound (*advigutvāt*).

If the technical (pāribhāṣika) term "singular" were intended here, then one would have said, "the singular [form] of a dvigu compound. Therefore, bearing in mind that this refers to the etymological (anvartha) singular and not the technical one, he says: "The expression of one is the singular. By this, showing that the word *ekavacana* is a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*), he demonstrates its etymological nature:
"The expression of one—that which denotes one—is the singular."

It is called *vacana* because it "speaks" (*vakti*), according to [Pāṇini 3.3.113], where the suffix *lyuṭ* is used in the sense of the agent. He says "of that which has a single meaning," etc., in order to clarify the meaning of "singular number" (*ekavacana*) by means of a synonym. Now, one might object that "singular number" should be in the masculine gender; why? Because a *dvigu* compound is masculine. This is not so; since the commonality of gender is intended, the reference is made using the neuter gender as a general term, and thus there is no fault.

"In this manner" means by means of the inclusion of the word "vacana" (singular number) which is significant according to its literal meaning (*anvartha*). It is not possible, even by hundreds of utterances, to make a word that expresses multiple meanings express only a single meaning, because the capacity of words to denote meanings is inherent (*svābhāvika*). Since this "utterance" (*vacana*) is stated, it is understood by implication (*sāmarthya*) that this is an extended application (*atideśa*); therefore, he says: "The singular form (*ekavadbhāva*) is prescribed for a *dvigu* compound whose referent consists of multiple things."
To clarify the meaning of this very point, he says: "A *dvigu* compound has a singular form.

If that were so, then even a *dvigu* whose meaning is a secondary derivative (*taddhita*) would incur singular status—for instance, in the case of *pañcakapālau* or *pañcakapālāḥ*, meaning "prepared in five dishes" or "those prepared in five dishes"—therefore he says: "And of the *samāhāra-dvigu*," and so forth.
The word "and" (*ca*) is used for emphasis.
The meaning is that [the rule applies] only to a *samāhāra-dvigu*.

But how is it understood that the reference is restricted to the *samāhāra-dvigu* alone? It is thought thus: by the word "and" (*ca*) in the rule *dvandvaśca* (Pāṇini 2.4.2), the term *dvigu* is drawn forward [as an anuvṛtti].
This is so that the singular treatment (*ekavadbhāva*) of the *dvigu* may occur in the very same sense in which the *dvandva* becomes a single unified meaning (*ekārthībhavati*).

A *dvandva* compound becomes a single unified meaning (*ekārthībhāva*) only in the case of a collective (*samāhāra*), and not otherwise. Therefore, the singular treatment (*ekavadbhāva*) applies to a *dvigu* compound only in that same context; thus, it is logical that this rule refers specifically to a collective *dvigu*. If, however, this rule refers only to a collective *dvigu*, then the extension (*atideśa*) would be purposeless; for the following reasons: the meaning of a *dvigu* is a collection (*samāhāra*); and a collection is derived from the sense of an action (*bhāvasādhana*). A collection (*samāhāra*) is the act of collecting (*samāharaṇa*), which is a group (*samudāya*), and that is indeed one.

In that case, since the singular number is already established by logical necessity (*nyāyaprāpta*), would the composition of this sūtra not be fruitless? This is not so; for, according to the view that "the aggregate (*samudāya*) is non-different from its constituent members (*samudāyin*)," the singular number for the aggregate is not established because the aggregate consists of multiple substances (*anekadravyātmaka*). It is for this reason that this [sūtra] has been commenced. Thus it is stated in the Bhāṣya: "Because a word is produced for each substratum (*adhikaraṇa*) and because of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with number, the singular number is prescribed for the *dvigu* compound.
Here, "for each substratum" means "for each substance" (*pratidravyam*).
In the production of speech, a number-denoting case-ending arises as the motivator, inherent in the substance that serves as the referent.
And the referent of a *dvigu* compound consists of multiple substances;
for instance, "five [fruits] taken together."

Since the bundles being tied together are delimited by the number five and because of their coreferentiality with that number, one might think, "These are five substances," and thus the singular number for the aggregate would not be established.
In that case, in the absence of this rule, the plural number would apply due to the multiplicity [of the constituents].

Therefore, the meaning of the sentence is that the singular state (*ekavacana*) is specifically prescribed. According to the view that "the aggregate is something other than its constituents," this sūtra must indeed be rejected.
And so it is stated in the Bhāṣya: "Or rather, [there is no need for this], because the aggregate is a single entity.
Or rather, there is no purpose in undertaking the yoga-rule itself, because this object called an "aggregate" (samāhāra) is indeed one.
The meaning of the sentence is that, because there is oneness (*ekatva*) in that case, the singular number will be used. Regarding the form *pañcapūlī*:
since it is feminine by the rule "A *dvigu* compound whose final member ends in short *a* is stated to be feminine" (Vārttika 156), the suffix *ṅīp* is applied to the *dvigu* by Pāṇini 4.1.21.

By the words "because the meaning is one" (*arthasyaikatvāt*) and so forth, he demonstrates the result of the extension of the meaning. Here, does the word *aṅga* (limb/part) terminate in the whole collection, or does it terminate in each individual member? In that regard, if it were to terminate in the collection, then this would constitute a single sentence; and in that case, a confusion (*vyatikara*) would follow. There would be a singular form for a *dvandva* compound of the limbs of living beings, musical instruments, and armies when they are joined together and their constituent parts are intermingled. However, if it terminates in each individual member, this fault does not arise.
For in that context, three sentences are established, beginning with "the *dvandva* compound of parts of living beings (*prāṇyaṅga*) becomes singular.

Regarding its own domain, where a sentence ending in the plural number is employed, by the first sentence the singularization (*ekavadbhāva*) is prescribed for a compound consisting of parts of living beings joined with other parts of living beings;
by the second sentence, however, it is for parts of musical instruments joined with other parts of musical instruments.

By means of the third [rule], there is no risk of confusion regarding the members of an army (*senāṅga*) with other members of an army; for there is no fourth rule by which a *dvandva* composed of intermingled parts would possess a single referent. Thinking thus, he adopts the position that the sentence is completed for each individual member and says: "Of the word *aṅga*" and so forth.
Likewise, he expects the rule that a *dvandva* of musical instruments (*tūryāṅga*) becomes singular.
The same applies here in the case of *senāṅgānām* (of the parts of an army) as well.
Regarding the term *pāṇipādam* (hands and feet):
if, in this context, even a limb of a living being is included by the mention of "living beings" (*prāṇi*), then the formation is established by the rule *jātir aprāṇinām* [Pāṇini 2.4.6].
For example: "paṇava-mṛdaṅgam" (the small drum and the kettle-drum);
and "rathikā-ārohān" (charioteers and riders).
In the latter case, the plurality of the referents of the compound term must be shown as "rathikāś ca ārohāś ca" (charioteers and riders).

Since multiplicity alone is the cause for being a component of an army, in the absence of multiplicity there can be no status as a component of an army; therefore, it should be "rathika-aśvārohau" (charioteers and horsemen). [The opponent argues: "In the case of elephants and so forth, because of their higher status, it must necessarily follow the option regarding animal-dvandvas."

By the rule *vibhāṣā vṛkṣamṛga* (Pāṇini 2.4.12) and so forth, and by the phrase *itaretarayoge* (Pāṇini 2.4.26) and so forth, he demonstrates the purpose of the section on *dvandva* compounds. By the phrase *prāṇyaṅgādīnāṃ samāhāra eva* (Pāṇini 2.4.2), he clarifies that this is for the sake of an optional rule (*viṣayavibhāṣā*) regarding specific domains. By the phrase *caraṇaśabda* (Pāṇini 2.4.3) and so forth, he shows the scope of the present sūtra.

For instance: when the word *caraṇa* refers to a specific branch of study (*adhyayana-viśeṣa*) taught by Kaṭha and others, then [the formation of the name] is established by the rule *jātir aprāṇinām* [Pāṇini 2.4.6]. But when [the word *caraṇa*] has as its cause the branch [of Vedic study], then [it is explained as follows]:
"that which has a branch as its cause" is a *bahuvrīhi* compound.

Regarding the phrase "of that which is apprehended by another means of valid cognition" (*pramāṇāntarāvagatasya*): a *pramāṇāntara* (another means of valid cognition) is a means of valid cognition other than the word (*śabda*); this, moreover, refers to perception (*pratyakṣa*) and so forth.

The mere mention (*saṅkīrtana-mātra*) of that which has been apprehended—that is, determined—by such a means through the word is what is meant; the word "mere" (*mātra*) is intended to exclude the actual comprehension of the object's meaning.
"Udagāt," "pratyaṣṭhāt":

from the root *iṇ* with the prefix *ud-* and from the root *sthā* with the prefix *prati*, in the *luṅ* (aorist) tense; the substitution of *gā* [for *iṇ*] occurs by the rule *iṣo gā luṅi* [Pāṇini 2.4.45], and the elision of *sic* occurs by the rule *gātisthā* [Pāṇini 2.4.77].
"Kaṭhakālāpam."

Those who study what was taught by Kaṭha are called *Kaṭhas*. From the word *kaṭha*, the suffix *ṇini* is applied in the sense of "taught by" (Pāṇini 4.3.104); then [the feminine suffix] *ṅīp* is applied (4.1.15); from that, the suffix *aṇ* is applied (4.2.59); then [the substitution of *y* for *v*] is applied (4.2.64); and [the elision of the final vowel and consonant] is applied (4.2.66), resulting in the formation of the term referring to that subject. Those who study what was taught by Kalāpin are called *Kalāpas*.

Regarding the meaning already stated, although the *prakṛtibhāva* (non-elision of the final vowel) would have applied by the rule *kalāpino’ṇ* [Pāṇini 4.3.108], the elision of the suffixal *ṭi* occurs by the Vārttika: *sabrahmacāripīṭhasarpikalāpikuthumitairatikijājalilāṅgaliśilāliśikhaṣṭiśūkarasadmasuparvaṇām upasaṃkhyānam* (Vārttika 798).
Thereafter, the suffix *aṇ* is applied by [Pāṇini] 4.2.59.
By [Pāṇini 4.2.64], there is elision (*luk*); and as before, there is the designation *tadviṣayatā*. Thus:
*kaṭhāś ca kālāpāś ca* becomes *kaṭhakālāpam*.
"But when the instruction occurs for the very first time" means:

when there is an initial communication of a meaning by means of a word through verbal testimony (*śabda*), which has not been previously understood by any other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)—whether in response to a question or as a reply—that is "instruction" (*upadeśa*). When that occurs, this is the counter-example:
"They went north" (*udaguḥ*).

By the rule *ātaḥ* [Pāṇini 3.4.110], the suffix *jhi* is replaced by *jus*; then, by the rule *jharo jhari savarṇe* [Pāṇini 6.4.68], there is the substitution of the subsequent form (*pararūpatva*). It should be stated: "The [substitution of *jus* for *jhi*] also applies after the roots *sthā* and *iṇ* when followed by the aorist (*adyatanī*)."
The meaning is that this must be explained.
Here is the explanation: from the sūtra "tulyārthairatulopamābhyām" (Pāṇini 2.3.72), the term "anyatarasyām" (optionally) is carried forward by anuvṛtti.
And that is understood to be a restricted option (*vyavasthitavibhāṣā*).

Therefore, by that [rule], there will be a singular collective form (*ekavadbhāva*) for the Vedic branches (*caraṇa*) in the past tense (*adyatanyām*) when used as a restatement (*anuvāde*), but not elsewhere. "Past tense" (*adyatanī*) is a technical term (*saṃjñā*) for the *luṅ* [suffix] coined by the ancient teachers (*pūrvācārya*).
For example: *anandiṣuḥ*.

The root *tud* is listed in the Dhātupāṭha as "ṭunadi samṛddhau" (67). According to Pāṇini 3.4.109, *sijabyastavidibhyaśca*, the suffix *jhi* is replaced by *jus*. Thus, from *udyanti*, the substitution of *yaṇ* for *ik* occurs according to Pāṇini 6.4.81 (*iko yaṇ*). [The term] "in the Adhvaryu Veda" refers to this.

By this word "adhvaryu," he shows that the Yajurveda is indicated here [by secondary implication]. Now, why is it not understood that the mention of "adhvaryu" is merely a qualifier for the specific sacrifice (*kratu*) belonging to that particular officiant (*ṛtvij*) named adhvaryu? Because it is impossible; for what sacrifice belongs to him alone? Rather, it belongs to one whose nature involves both expenditure and acquisition. Even if he possesses agency in that sacrifice, that agency is common to other officiants as well; therefore, it is improper to qualify that sacrifice by means of the single person, the adhvaryu.

But surely, for the sake of excluding that sacrifice which is prescribed by the *Atharvaveda*, why would the qualification "by a single Adhvaryu" not suffice? For there are no other Adhvaryus [besides him]. This is not so; if this were the intended purpose, then he would have simply made the prohibition "one who is not an Atharvan. For a direct prohibition conveys a more concise understanding. Alternatively, he could have used the term "Trayi" (the three Vedas).

If the sacrifice (*kratu*) were qualified by the *adhvaryu*, then that [qualification] would also apply to the phrase "the arrow and the thunderbolt" (*iṣuvajrau*), for even the arrow and the thunderbolt are sacrifices of the *adhvaryu*; since those two also have him as their performer.
Therefore, the Veda belonging to the *adhvaryus*—those who know the Yajurveda—is indicated by the word *adhvaryu*. That, moreover, is the Yajurveda.

In that regard, whatever sacrifice (*kratu*) is prescribed in the *Adhvaryu-veda* is called an "Adhvaryu-sacrifice. By the word "prescription" (*vidhāna*), both the instruction on the procedure (*itikartavyatopadeśa*) and the performance consisting of execution (*prayoga-anuṣṭhānātmaka*) are expressed.

If, however, the meaning of the rule were that "a copulative compound (*dvandva*) of words denoting Adhvaryu-sacrifices ending in non-neuter genders becomes singular," then the coreferential (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) reference in the rule to the term "Adhvaryu-sacrifice," the term "non-neuter" (*anapuṃsaka*), and the term "copulative compound" (*dvandva*) would be untenable.

Therefore, one might think that it should have been stated as "of those [words] denoting the *adhvaryu* and the *kratu* which are not neuter"; hence he says: "The *adhvaryu* and the *kratu* are not neuter. He adds: "This is a figurative designation (*gauṇa*. Figurative means non-primary or metaphorical; this is the meaning.
The term *adhvaryukratu* refers to a *dvandva* compound consisting of parts of the *adhvaryu* and the *kratu*; it is designated as *adhvaryukratu* by way of metaphorical usage (*upacāra*).
That same compound, when its constituent parts do not have the neuter gender, is called *anapuṃsaka*. It should be understood that this figurative designation is employed for the sake of brevity.

If, however, by the term *anapuṃsakam* (non-neuter) the copulative compound (*dvandva*) itself were intended in its primary sense, then this [rule] would be understood as an exception (*apavāda*) to the rule *sa napuṃsakam* [Pāṇini 2.4.17]. For example: *arkāmedham*;
that is, *arkaśca āmedhaśca* = *arkāmedham*.
"Sāyāhna" and "Atirātra" form the compound "sāyāhnātirātram. Regarding "iṣuvajrau" and so forth:
sacrifices such as the *iṣu* and *vajra* are not possible [for the Adhvaryu], for they are not prescribed in the Adhvaryu Veda;
rather, they are in the Sāma Veda.
Regarding the phrase "rājasūyavājapeye":
these two words, *rājasūya* and *vājapeya*, also exist in the masculine gender.
This is the counter-example for when they are employed in the neuter gender.

Regarding the phrase "in the Soma sacrifices": those sacrifices in which the drinking of Soma is prescribed are the Soma sacrifices; it is precisely in reference to them that the word *kratu* is conventionally established.

Nor do the Darśa-Pūrṇamāsa sacrifices refer to the Soma sacrifices; for, because of the inclusion of the rule "not a neuter" (Aṣṭādhyāyī 2.4.4), there is no grasping of the literal form here. Indeed, the general class of sacrifices (*kratusāmānya*) does not possess a neuter gender. The word *adhyayana* is derived as an abstract noun (*bhāvasādhana*)—meaning "the act of studying"—or as an object noun (*karmasādhana*)—meaning "that which is studied."
Regarding the term "adhyayanataḥ":

the suffix *tasi* is applied according to the Vārttika rule "ādyādibhyas-tasy-upasaṃkhyānam" (Vārttika 634), which prescribes *tasi* after words ending in the third case (*tṛtīyā*) when they express a cause (*hetu*).
Therefore he says: "by means of study as the cause.
Regarding the term "not remote" (*aviprakṛṣṭā*):
those whose names are not remote are called "those with non-remote names" (*aviprakṛṣṭākhyāḥ*).
The remoteness of the cause consists in its being common to others and so forth.
Furthermore, that cause is precisely the study designated by the name "recitation" (ākhyāna) as included in the Sūtra,
namely "the *padaka* and *kramaka*."
"One who studies the *pada* is a *pādaka*; one who studies the *krama* is a *kramaka*" [Pāṇini 4.2.61].
"The *kramaka-vārtika*";
one who studies the *vṛtti* is a *vārtika*.
[The suffix] *ṭhak* is applied after words ending in *kratu*, *uktha*, etc., and after *sūtra* [Pāṇini 4.2.60].
But how is it that for one who studies the *pada-pāṭha*, there is a lack of remoteness from the *krama-pāṭha* due to the cause of study? To this he says: "recitation" (*sampāṭha*), etc.
Because the recitation of the *padas* and the *krama* is not significantly different.
The book (*grantha*) is also of that same nature, and is therefore proximate [to the *padapāṭha*].
Furthermore, since the *krama-pāṭha* must be studied after having studied the *pada-pāṭha*, for that reason as well, the *saṃpāṭha* (the *krama-pāṭha*) is proximate to those two.

And thus, the designation "one who knows the *padapāṭha*" (*padaka*) or "one who knows the *kramapāṭha*" (*kramaka*) given to the student on account of that study—the *saṃpāṭha*—is also proximate; this is the intended meaning.
Regarding the term *pitāputrau*:
by [Pāṇini 6.3.25], there is the substitution of *ānaṅ*.
For in that rule, the word *putra* is understood as a carry-over from [Pāṇini 6.3.22].
In this case as well, the designations "father" and "son" are applied to those who are closely related because the cause [for these terms] is common to both.
For indeed, the relationship of producer and produced is the cause for both of them. As in the example: "the sacrificer-grammarian."
One who studies the *yajña* is a *yājñika*; [the suffix] *ik* is applied by [Pāṇini 4.2.59] after *kratu*, *uktha*, and so forth. One who studies grammar (*vyākaraṇa*) is a *vaiyākaraṇa*.
[4.2.59] *ity-aṇ*. There exists here the basis for these two designations in the fact of study (*adhyayana*), but not immediate proximity (*pratyāsatti*).

For there is no proximity of action between them—whether through the study of sacrifice (*yajña*) or the study of grammar (*vyākaraṇa*)—nor is there proximity of text. This [compound] is also designated as a coordinate compound (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) by way of a figurative application (*gauṇyā vṛttyā*), being a collective dvandva of generic classes (*jāti-dvandva*).

A *dvandva* compound whose constituent members denote a genus (*jāti*) is called a "genus" (*jāti*). Furthermore, there is no grasping of the actual form (*svarūpa*) of the genus, because of the prohibition [by Pāṇini 2.4.6] stating "not for non-living beings" (*aprāṇinām*). For example: *ārāśastri*.

The short vowel [is substituted] by the rule *hrasvo napuṃsake prātipadikasya* (Pāṇini 1.2.47). Thus, we have *nandakapāñcajanyau*. This is a *dvandva* compound consisting solely of two proper names (*saṃjñāśabda*), not of two generic terms (*jātiśabda*). By this, he demonstrates that the phrase *aprāṇinām* (Pāṇini 2.4.2) functions as a *paryudāsa* (an exclusion).
Therefore, he says "that which is joined with *nañ* or *iva*" and so forth to show what the meaning is:
"color, taste, smell, and touch" and so forth constitute the class of qualities (*guṇajāti*);
"going, contracting, and extending" constitute the class of actions (*kriyājāti*).

Regarding the phrase "and when the genus is predominant": when there is an intention to express the genus as primary, then, because the genus is predominant, genus-words undergo the state of being treated as a singular (ekavadbhāva).

Regarding the phrase "not when there is an intention to express specific substances restricted to a particular place, etc.": when there is an intention to express specific substances restricted to a certain location and so forth, then even upon the employment of a genus-word, the state of being treated as a singular does not occur.
Whence is this [conclusion]? Because of the designation "jāti" (genus), the primary genus is intended, not the secondary one.
And this is obtained from the fact that the operation is understood to apply to the principal element.
This is what is meant: when the genus itself is employed by depending upon a particular individual, then there is no singular number.

But when it is employed without relying on a specific individual, then there is indeed the singular form (*ekavadbhāva*), as in "badarāmalakāni" (jujube and myrobalan fruits). Here, there is a cognition of the jujubes and myrobalans as individuals; it is not a cognition of the words as generic classes (*jāti*).

For this very reason, the plural number is based on the individuals (*vyakti*); otherwise, since the genus (*jāti*) is singular, there would only be the singular number and not the plural. This [rule] "of non-living beings" (*aprāṇinām*) is an exclusion (*paryudāsa*).

By means of that, the following meaning is obtained—according to the maxim of "that which is joined with *nañ* or *iva*" (*vyā.pa. 65*)—there is no application of the singular collective form (*ekavadbhāva*) for color, taste, touch, and so forth.

In the prohibition "of those lacking breath" (*aprāṇinām*), the plurality that is heard implies plurality even in the positive injunction. Consequently, a *dvandva* compound consisting of multiple bases alone becomes a singular, not one consisting of two bases—such as *ārāśastriau*. This word *viśiṣṭa* expresses distinction (*bheda*). Although in the rule *ktena nañviśiṣṭenānañ* (Pāṇini 2.1.60), the word *viśiṣṭa* is explained as referring to an excess with a restrictive sense (*sāvadhāraṇādhikya*), that too is understood precisely through the medium of distinction.
Therefore, the author of the *Vṛtti* also says, "even those of different genders," and provides the example "agrāmāḥ.
Because of this prohibition, he states that there is no grasping of the actual forms of these two [words] by saying "of those denoting rivers," and so forth.

If the intended meaning of the rule here were that a *dvandva* compound consisting of words denoting rivers as well as words denoting regions becomes a singular (*ekavadbhāva*), then how could there be a reference in grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the present subject, namely the *dvandva* "nadīdeśa"? To this he says: "A *dvandva* whose constituent parts are rivers is called 'nadī'," and so forth. By this, he shows that the mention in the rule is figurative (*gauṇa*).
If "nadīdeśa" were a *dvandva* compound, then a *dvandva* whose parts are intermingled—where one part is a river and another is a region—would undergo the state of being a singular.

Furthermore, if this were a *dvandva* compound, would it be a collective (*samāhāra*) or a copulative (*itaretarayoga*)? In the former case, by the rule "that [compound] is neuter" (*sa napuṃsakam*), it would be neuter; in the latter case, however, there would be a dual ending. Seeing this fault, he says: "nadīdeśa. "This is not a compound at all, but a mere enumeration. "Madrakekayāḥ": both Madras and Kekayas are "Madrakekayāḥ."

Now, why is the mention of "river" (*nadī*) made? Is it not the case that the mention of "river" is already established by the very mention of "region" (*deśa*)? To this he says: "The mention of 'river' is because [a river] is not a region. Why, then, is a river not a region? He says: "For a region is a country (*janapada*)," because the word "region" is conventionally fixed (*rūḍha*) in that sense alone.
Furthermore, when a river is called a "region," that is due to its being located therein (*tātsthyāt*).
For there is indeed the application of a term based on location, as in the expression, "the platforms are shouting.
"And so forth" refers to this.
Therefore, "country" (*janapada*) alone is what is meant by "region" (*deśa*), and nothing else such as mountains and so forth.
And by establishing this, the mention of "region" does not include mountains and the like. Regarding the phrase "not villages" (*agrāmāḥ*) and so on:
in common worldly usage, the mention of "village" includes the mention of "city"; for instance, when it is said, "the village pig is not to be eaten," even the city pig is not eaten.

Consequently, if the prohibition "not villages" (*agrāmāḥ*) were applied here, it would also apply to cities (*nagara*). Therefore, in the prohibition "not villages," the exclusion of cities must be stated; that is to say, the prohibition of cities—which follows from the phrase "not villages"—must be explicitly stated as a counter-prohibition (*pratiṣedhasya pratiṣedhaḥ*), meaning it must be explained.
By that, the rule [of inclusion] for cities indeed remains in effect.

In this regard, the explanation is as follows: by making a distinction between "village" (*grāma*) and "town" (*nagara*) in the rule *yad ayam* (Pāṇini 7.3.14), he indicates that in this grammatical treatise, the term "village" does not include towns.
Consequently, the prohibition "not [in] a village" (*agrāmāt*) does not apply to towns. Regarding the phrase "on both sides" (*ubhayataśca*) and so forth: the meaning of "in both" is "on both sides."
Where some parts are villages and some are cities, only that prohibition which applies to villages should be stated—that is to say, it must be explained.
Here is the explanation: in the case of *agrāmāḥ*, this should be understood as a *prasajya-pratiṣedha* (absolute negation), meaning "if there are no villages in the *dvandva* compound.

Therefore, even where there is only a trace (*gandha*) of a village, the singular collective form (*ekavadbhāva*) does not occur. This word *kṣudra* certainly exists in the sense of a miserly person; for example, in *kṣudro devadattaḥ*, it is understood to mean "miserly."
And [the term] exists in the sense of being deficient in virtue or deficient in limbs, as in the expression "from low-born women" (*kṣudrābhyaḥ*);
here, women who are unfaithful to their husbands and those who are deformed are included by the mention of "low-born.
And it exists in the sense of diminution of size, as in "small grains" (*kṣudrās taṇḍulāḥ*).
But here, due to the proximity of the word *jantu* (living being), it expresses the smallness of the body of a living creature.
Therefore, it is understood that the word *kṣudra* is used in the sense of a decrease in size; thus he says: "Small (*kṣudra*) means having a diminished dimension.
The meaning is "having a small body."
Furthermore, the measure [of what constitutes a "small creature"] is not fixed due to differences in relative perspective;
thus, it is unstable—this is the meaning. He presents traditional authorities (*smṛti*) regarding the referent of the term *kṣudrajantu*: "A *kṣudrajantu* may be one that is boneless.
[The root] *kṣudir* means "to crush" (Dhātupāṭha 1443); it is called *kṣudra* because it is crushed (*kṣudyate*).
The suffix *rak* is applied according to the *uṇādi* rule "sphāyī-tañci" (Uṇādi Sūtra 8.31).
A "small creature" (*kṣudrajantu*) is one that is both small and a living being. Regarding the term "boneless" (*anasthi*).
One whose bones are not found—meaning one that has only a mouthful of skin, blood, and flesh—is a "small creature" (*kṣudrajantu*).
Alternatively, another Smṛti states: "or one who is merely small."
That which can be crushed is a "small creature" (*kṣudrajantu*).
By the force of the word's meaning, the term "small creature" is well-known in the world as referring to creatures such as mosquitoes and the like,
which do not possess their own blood when caught in a net.
Those for whom even a heap the size of a cow-hide (gocarma) does not cause a man to fall [from his caste] when killed are called well-known "small creatures" (kṣudrajantu).
Another Smṛti states: "Or those whose hundred fit into a handful.
Those living beings whose hundred fill a handful—that is, when the hands are joined in the añjali gesture—or by which a handful is filled with a hundred, they are small creatures.
"Some even from a mongoose," they say;
some describe it thus: "creatures as small as a mongoose are considered minor beings.
"This very Smṛti is the authority," they say.
Because this [Smṛti] is the upholder of all Smṛtis;
for thus, when small creatures are indicated by this, even those small creatures shown in other Smṛtis are included within them.
He asks, "Why are the other Smṛtis not also authoritative? and answers with the words beginning with "of the others" (*itarāsām*).
There is a contradiction with the Smṛti rule stating, "The memory [of the consumption] of bones and so forth extends even to the mongoose.
Therefore, these [Smṛtis] are not accepted as authoritative; by that, this is established in all cases:

because of the use of the plural number in the term "small creatures" (*kṣudrajantavaḥ*), the singular collective form should occur only when there is a plurality of constituent parts, just as in other instances of plural reference.
In this context, it does not apply to lice, nits, gadflies, and mosquitoes;
for this rule is commenced for the purpose of referring to species of living beings.

[Question: "What is the purpose of the term 'small creatures' (kṣudrajantavaḥ)? [Answer: But if this sūtra were absent, what would serve as a counter-example? It is thought thus: otherwise, the sūtra would have to be formulated simply as "jantavaḥ" (living beings), and from that, an over-extension (atiprasaṅga) would result. In common usage, the word "opposition" (virodha) denotes merely the state of being an adversary.

Thinking that if this [term *vaira*] were taken here, it would also apply to cases such as "shadow and light" or "fire and water," he says—“*virodho vairam*” (hostility is enmity)—in order to show that what is intended here is hostility.
He considers it thus: from [Pāṇini 2.4.8], the term *jantu* (living being) is understood to carry over;
therefore, it is understood that what is taken here is the hostility between living beings.
And that [nature] is indeed of the essence of enmity; thus it is said, "the Śāśvata is eternal. By the term "śaśvat," the three periods of time are expressed.
In that context, the word *śātika* means "being there. [The suffix] *ṭhañ* is applied according to Pāṇini 4.3.11 (*kālāṭ ṭhañ*).
By virtue of this very irregular derivation (*nipātana*), the suffix *ka* does not occur even after a word ending in *tān*.
And that which exists throughout the three periods of time is eternal.
"Gopāli-Śālaṅkāyanāḥ":
both the Gopālins and the Śālaṅkāyanas are [collectively called] Gopāli-Śālaṅkāyanāḥ.

Since there is no contradiction here regarding the cognition [of the object], the treatment as a single unit (*ekavadbhāva*) does not occur. As for the statement, "The particle *ca*, moreover, serves to conjoin this very [term]," because there is no other relevant element to be conjoined, the particle *ca* is understood to serve the purpose of conjoining this very treatment as a single unit.
He asks, "What results from that? and says: "By that, [the rule] 'paśu-śakuni'... and so forth.

The scope for the optional application (*vibhāṣā*) regarding animals and birds is: *mahājorabhram* / *mahājorabhrāḥ*, *haṃsacakravākam* / *haṃsacakravākāḥ*. The scope for the obligatory singular formation (*ekavadbhāva*) of those who are eternally opposed is: *brāhmaṇanāstikam*, *āśṛgālam*, *āmahiṣam*.

In the case of *kākolūkam*, since both [the general rule and the optional rule] would apply, the optional rule (*paśuśakunivibhāṣā*) would prevail due to its posteriority. However, because the particle *ca* here serves to include this very [rule], it becomes a singular compound invariably by this [present rule]. Although the root *siñ* (Dhātupāṭha 1248), meaning "to bind," functions in the sense of binding, nevertheless, preceded by *nirava*, it functions in the sense of "expulsion. Thus he says: "Exclusion (*niravasāna*) means expulsion (*bahiṣkaraṇa*).
Those by whom the vessel is not purified even through ritual consecration are therefore excluded from that—that is, set apart from it.

The meaning is that they do not obtain the opportunity to eat there. Words such as *go-aśva* (cow and horse) are listed in the group (*gaṇa*) with the formation of a singular collective (*ekavadbhāva*).
By this [sūtra], only their grammatical correctness (*sādhutva*) is prescribed, but not the formation of a singular collective; showing this, he says: "Words such as *go-aśva*."
This statement concerns the optional formation of copulative compounds (*dvandva*) for animals beginning with "ox" (*go*) and ending with "goat" (*aja*).
Regarding the three starting with "hunchback" (*kubja*) and "dwarf" (*vāmana*), [the rule] is not otherwise established.

Is there no contradiction up to the *caṇḍāla*? When a copulative compound does not express contradiction but functions merely in the sense of conjunction (*cārtha*), then it is said here that "there is one [person] up to the *caṇḍāla*."
The rule "strīkumāraṃ dāsīmāṇavakam" is stated because [the previous rule] does not apply.

Regarding "śāṭīpicchakam," although it is established by the rule "jātiraprāṇinām" (Pāṇini 2.4.6), this specific reading is for the purpose of excluding cases where there are many constituent members. As for "uṣṭrakharamuṣṭraśaśam."
This is for the purpose of making obligatory what would otherwise be optional by the rule *paśu-dvandva-vibhāṣā*.

The recitation of items beginning with *mūtra-śakṛt* and ending with *māṃsa-śoṇita*, which belong to non-living species, is for the purpose of including those that do not consist of many constituent parts.
The mention of *darbha-śara* and so forth is for the purpose of overriding the optionality regarding grasses (*tṛṇa*) that would otherwise apply.

Regarding the three [categories] beginning with *dāsī* and *dāsa*, the rule for *ekaśeṣa* (retention of one) under Pāṇini 1.2.64 does not apply due to this very irregularity (*nipātana*). It is said: "In the group beginning with *go-ādi*, the formation of the *dvandva* compound follows the order as pronounced.
How so? Because the form is accepted exactly as it appears.
For in the Gaṇapāṭha, this rule is based on the specific forms of these words by which,
when uttered in that manner, they undergo the application of the dvandva compound characterized by singular number.
However, "this rule does not apply to other forms."
When the *avaṅ* substitution [prescribed by Pāṇini 6.1.123] does not occur, then the rule provided by this present sūtra does not apply once another form has arisen;

rather, only the optional rule regarding the *dvandva* of animals (*paśudvandvavibhāṣā*) operates. Here, by the mention of "trees" (*vṛkṣa*) and so forth, there is the inclusion of words denoting specific types of trees and the like.
How so? Because here the *dvandva* is qualified individually by the words "tree" and so on, this optionality is therefore restricted to those of the same genus.
It applies to dissimilar things even when they belong to the same class, but not to those that are identical in their own form;
for there is no *dvandva* compound among them, due to the rule of *ekaśeṣa*. Furthermore, it does not apply to synonyms, even though they are dissimilar.

This is because there is no occurrence of *dvandva* (copulative compounds) among them. The absence of *dvandva* is due to the absence of simultaneous application and the absence of a combined meaning. Furthermore, the absence of the sense of "and" (*ca*) is due to the absence of a distinction between the meanings.

For distinctness of meaning requires distinct substrata, and it is not possible for synonyms to have distinct meanings. Therefore, this option (*vibhāṣā*) applies only to those words that denote specific types such as "tree" (*vṛkṣa*), which possess their own individual forms.
Consequently, in the case of "trees" and so forth, it is understood as a reference to the specific types themselves, not a reference to their individual forms, nor a reference to their synonyms.

Now, why is it not understood that the inclusion of words expressing both general and specific [meanings] is intended, since a *dvandva* compound of words expressing general and specific meanings is possible, as in the example "cows and bulls" (*govālīvardam*)? It is not so, because such usage is not established by linguistic convention (*anabhidhānāt*).

For there is no such expression in common usage as "tree and *dhava*" (*vṛkṣadhavam*); this is because the meaning of the word "tree" is already understood from the word "dhava" itself, which expresses that same meaning, and because when a word such as "dhava" is employed, a word such as "tree" is unfit for employment.

In the case of *govālīvardam*, however, since the word *go* (cow) refers specifically to female cattle when in proximity to the word *balīvarda* (bull), both terms are denotative of specific [sub-classes]; thus, a *dvandva* compound is appropriate.

Regarding those [compounds] here that do not denote living beings, since a singular form (*ekavadbhāva*) would necessarily apply by the rule *jātir aprāṇinām* [Pāṇini 2.4.6], this statement is for the purpose of making it optional (*vibhāṣā*). For the remaining [compounds], it applies where [the singular form] was not otherwise established.

Even though the term *mṛga* (wild animals) and others are already included by the mention of *paśu* (domestic animals), for what purpose are they mentioned separately? It has been stated that this *dvandva* compound of members belonging to the same class becomes a singular (*ekavadbhāva*).
