Since this is already established by the mention of *paśu*, the separate mention of *mṛga* and others is for the purpose that there may not be a mutual *dvandva* among them [within the category of wild animals]. When the rule could have been stated simply as "the *dvandva* of domestic animals" (*paśudvandva*), the specific mention of "horse and mule" (*aśvavaḍabau*) is for the sake of restriction (*niyamārtha*); it is so that the rule does not apply to other synonyms of these two, such as *hayavaḍave*. Regarding the phrase "having many constituent elements" (*bahuprakṛtiḥ*): [The commentary continues: The mention of *mṛga* and others is for the sake of excluding the mutual *dvandva* among them. If it were stated merely as "the *dvandva* of domestic animals," then the rule would apply even to synonyms like *hayavaḍave*. By mentioning *mṛga* and others, it is indicated that the rule applies only to those specifically named. Furthermore, the mention of *mṛga* and others serves to exclude the application of the rule to other similar classes, such as *śvacaṇḍālau* (dog and outcaste). Thus, the mention of *mṛga* and others is for the purpose of restricting the scope of the rule. As for the mention of "horse and mule," it is for the purpose of restriction (*niyamārtha*), so that the rule does not apply to other synonymous pairs, such as *hayavaḍave*. The mention of "having many constituent elements" (*bahuprakṛtiḥ*) is for the purpose of excluding the application of the rule to compounds consisting of only two members. For example, in the case of *kuśāśca kāśāśca palāśāśca* ("kuśa grass, kāśa grass, and palāśa trees"), since there are more than two members, the rule applies; however, in the case of *kuśakāśapalāśāḥ*, where there are exactly three, the rule does not apply because it is not a "compound with many constituent elements" in the sense intended here. That whose base (*prakṛti*) consists of many meanings or ends in the plural number is called *bahuprakṛti*.

The meaning is that a *dvandva* compound of these—namely, words with many meanings such as *phala* and so forth, or those ending in the plural—is treated as a singular (*ekavadbhavati*). Regarding the phrase "of those not denoting a substance" (*adravyavācinām*):
by this, he shows that the word *dravya* here refers to a substance (*adhikaraṇa*), and not to a substratum (*ādhāra*).

For words that express mutually contradictory things do not have their function [of denoting] in a single substratum (ādhāra), because the power of the substratum is the meaning of the case-ending (vibhakti).

Regarding the example "cold and hot": these two are contradictory by virtue of the very opposition characterized by non-coexistence; thus, they are termed "expressing mutually contradictory things" (vipratiṣiddhavācin).
The same applies to pleasure and pain as well. Regarding the phrase "desire and anger":
since even one who is angry may act out of desire, these two are not mutually exclusive. Regarding the phrase "according to their respective [natures]":
this means according to each one's own specific characteristic (lakṣaṇa).

In that regard, since the three terms beginning with *dadhipayasī* (curd and milk) denote side dishes (*vyañjana*), there is the possibility of optional singular formation (*vibhāṣaikavadbhāva*). Now, one might object: "In the case of *sarpirmadhunī* and *madhusarpiṣī*, the singular formation will not occur simply because these are included among the *rājadantādi* group [which mandates specific word order]. This is not so; for the singular formation of side dishes is only optional. Therefore, in the alternative where that singular formation does not occur, the inclusion [in the *rājadantādi* list] would serve only to ensure the deviation from the rule regarding initial placement (*pūrvanipāta*).
In the other view as well, this recitation here is for the purpose of prohibiting the treatment as a singular unit (*ekavadbhāva*).

If that is so, since [the desired forms] would be established by this very rule, the inclusion in the *rājadantādi* group would be useless? It is not useless, because it serves the purpose of the plural number, as in "clarified butter and honey" (*sarpirmadhunī*) or "honey and clarified butter" (*madhusarpiṣī*).

But is it not the case that even there, the two words are read only in the dual number? Even if this is so, nevertheless, because the *paranipāta* (the placement of the second member first) depends on the word-form (*śabda*), whereas duality is a property of the meaning (*artha-dharma*), duality is not taken into account. However, since the treatment as a singular (*ekavadbhāva*) depends on the meaning, when that [singular treatment] is prohibited, it is appropriate to intend to express the number. In the case of the five [names] beginning with "Brāhma-prajāpatī," there is the application [of the singular rule] because the aggregate (*samāhāra*) is one.
Regarding the phrase "white and black" (śuklakṛṣṇau) [in the rule] beginning with *Pāṇini 2.4.13*,

there is the application [of the dual number] because the collection (*samāhāra*) of items such as "fuel and sacrificial grass" (*idhmābarhiṣī*) constitutes a single entity. Furthermore, the substratum (*adhikaraṇa*) is the meaning of the base word (*vartipadārtha*).
*vartana* and *vartaḥ* form a compound (*samāsa*).
The suffix *ghañ* is used in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāve*). That which possesses *varta* is *vartin*; thus, it is a constituent member of the compound.

The term *varttipada* consists of the word *vartti* and that word (*pada*); the meaning of that word is called the "locus" (*adhikaraṇa*). But how does it possess the status of a locus? To this he says: "For that... and so forth. A locus is a substratum (*ādhāra*).
Furthermore, the meaning of the constituent words (*varttipadārtha*) serves as the substratum for the meaning of the compound (*samāsārtha*), because the latter inheres (*samavāya*) in the former.
The meaning of the compound, which is a whole (*avayavin*), is initiated by the constituent word-meanings as its parts (*avayava*); and the whole inheres in its parts.
[The word] "of that" (*tasya*) refers to this.
Regarding the meaning of the word *varttin*:

[in the example] "these ten—[note: this phrase is absent in the *Kāśikā* and *Padamañjarī*]—are these teeth-and-lips," there is the application [of the rule] by [Pāṇini 2.4.2], "And a dvandva compound... Since the "extent of the substratum" (*adhikaraṇaitāvattva*) is the subject under discussion, proximity is understood only in relation to that; therefore, he says: "in the vicinity of the extent of the substratum."

Regarding the expression "upadaśaṃ dantauṣṭham" (nine or eleven teeth and lips): here, the number ten constitutes the measure of the locus (*adhikaraṇaitāvattvam*). That which is near to it is either nine or eleven.
In this context, the word "ten" denotes that measure.

The prefix *upa* signifies proximity (*sāmīpya*). But how is it that the optional application of the singular form for a *dvandva* compound is obtained for the subsequent usage (*anuprayoga*)? To this he says: "of an indeclinable" (*avyayasya*), and so forth.
Although the optionality is obtained for the subsequent usage as well through the extension of the meaning (*arthātideśa*), this statement is introduced to show that there is also another solution.
In that regard, the *avyayībhāva* compound of an indeclinable with a numeral is prescribed by the rule "An indeclinable [compounded] with a case-ending... (*avyayaṃ vibhakti* 2.1.6) and so on.
The *bahuvrīhi* compound is also prescribed by the rule beginning with "A numeral, an indeclinable, *āsanna*, etc. [Pāṇini 2.2.25].

In this regard, regarding the option of singular formation (*ekavadbhāva*), when there is a *dvandva* of a single meaning, the *avyayībhāva* of a single meaning alone is employed as a subsequent application (*anuprayoga*).
Furthermore, its status as having a single meaning arises because proximity (*sāmīpya*) is its primary referent.

Although an *avyayībhāva* compound is an indeclinable (*avyaya*), nevertheless, it possesses non-dual unity—characterized by the absence of differentiation—and thus there is indeed grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*).
In other cases, however, a *bahuvrīhi* with a plural meaning is employed after a *dvandva* that has a plural meaning;
for the plural meaning of the *bahuvrīhi* is predominant due to its proximity [to the *dvandva*].
For a *bahuvrīhi* compound, being proximate [to its members], assumes the number and distinction of its primary element and thus possesses a plural sense,
as in "upadaśam" (near ten). While [the rule] Pāṇini 5.4.107 is in effect, the suffix *ṭac* is applied as a compound-final affix by Pāṇini 5.4.108, which states "also after *ana*."
By [Pāṇini 6.4.144], there is elision of the *ṭi* suffix.
Regarding "upadaśāḥ":

in a *bahuvrīhi* compound where the member denoting a number is the thing to be counted (*saṃkhyeya*), the suffix *ḍac* is applied by [Pāṇini 5.4.73]. Regarding "pañcagavam": [the suffix *aṇ* is applied].
The suffix *ṭac* is applied by [Pāṇini 5.4.92].
The inclusion of the word "with" (*sa-*) is for the purpose that this rule should apply even to a *dvigu* compound.

Otherwise, according to the principle that "a rule or a prohibition applies only to what is immediately preceding" (Vyāḍipāda 19), it would apply only to the *dvandva* that is immediately adjacent, and not to the *dvigu* which is separated; however, this is not the case. The term "singular number" (*ekavacanam*) is understood from the previous context, and since it is connected with the word "neuter" (*napuṃsakam*), how could there be any separation? For here, no specific *dvandva* is required by this rule through its connection with the singular number; rather, it requires the singular number alone.

In that case, the inclusion of the word "sa" (he) is for the purpose of encompassing what is well-known. This "sa" will be a restatement (*anuvāda*), and a restatement applies only to that which is already established.
Thus, this arrangement of genders is explained according to how they are observed in usage.
By this, in the case of a *dvandva* treated as a single unit (*ekavadbhāva*), its neuter gender is understood to be obligatory;
whereas for a *dvigu*, it is not fixed.
Consequently, the statement "a *dvigu* whose final member ends in *a* is used in the feminine" (Vārttika 156) becomes logically justified.
In the word *pañcapūlī*, the suffix *ṅīp* is applied by [Pāṇini 4.1.21].

This very rule prescribing *ṅīp* for a *dvigu* compound within the section on feminine formations is an indicator (*jñāpaka*) that "in some cases, a *dvigu* is spoken of as feminine. For example: *pañcakhaṭvam* and *pañcakhaṭvī*.

When the shortening of the penultimate vowel (*upasarjana-hrasvatva*) has been applied, the suffix *ṅīp* is optionally added, resulting in "pañcatakṣam" or "pañcatakṣī. When the elision of the nasal (*nalopa*) has been applied, the suffix *ṅīp* is optionally added, resulting in "adhistri.
This is an *avyayībhāva* compound according to the rule "avyayaṃ vibhakti... (Pāṇini 2.1.6) and others.
The shortening [of the final vowel] occurs by the rule *hrasvo napuṃsake prātipadikasya* [Pāṇini 1.2.47].
The compound *unmattagaṅgam*, *lohitagaṅgam* is formed by [the rule] *pūrvapadārthaprādhānye* [Pāṇini 2.1.21].

As before, there is shortening [of the vowel]. It was argued that "a compound whose primary meaning is that of the first member would necessarily lack gender," because in examples such as *adhistrī*, the first member lacks gender.
"The gender [of a compound] is that of the expressed meaning when the external referent (anyapadārtha) is predominant.

In examples such as *unmattagaṅgam* ("the Gaṅgā where people are mad"), a location (*deśa*) is the expressed meaning; since that [location] is masculine, the masculine gender would follow. In the case of *puṇyāham*, it is a *karmadhāraya* compound.
The suffix *ṭac* is applied as a compound-final element (*samāsānta*) by the rule *rājāhaḥsakhibhyaṣṭac* [Pāṇini 5.4.91].
The statement regarding its masculine gender is provided by the rule *pathaḥ saṃkhyāvyayādeḥ* [Vārttika on 2.4.30]. Thus, we have the form *vipatha*.
161) Thus, since the rule for taking the gender of the subsequent word would have applied, this specific statement is made:
[Pāṇini 2.4.18] "The compound ending in *itaC* is neuter.
For example: *catuṣpatham*.
This is a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*).
As for the collective dvigu compound, however, it is already established by the preceding rule.

The suffix *a* is added at the end of the compound according to [Pāṇini 5.4.74]: *ṛkpūrabdhūḥpathāmānakṣe*. Since there is no such thing as a *tatpuruṣa* consisting solely of the negative particle *nañ*, he states "the *nañ*-compound" (*nañsamāsam*) to indicate that a *nañ*-compound is intended here.
He will state: "Optionally [the feminine suffix ṭāp is applied] after *senā*, *surā*, and *chāyā*.

Since there is no purpose for this governing rule (*adhikāra*) in connection with the immediately following rules, he bypasses them and introduces the more distant rule beginning with "Optionally [the feminine suffix ṭāp is applied] after *senā*, *surā*," etc. [Pāṇini 2.4.25]. The fact that this rule serves no purpose in the subsequent immediately following rules has been established in the Bhāṣya by such statements as: "For in the case of a technical name (*saṃjñā*), there is neither a *tatpuruṣa* nor a negative compound (*nañsamāsa*) [ending in *kaṇṭha*] among the Uśīnaras, nor is there a *karmadhāraya*."
Regarding the term *dṛḍhasenaḥ*:
it is a *bahuvrīhi*.

Now, as for this designation "not a negative (*nañ*) or a *karmadhāraya*," what is its meaning? For if there were a *dvandva* compound here consisting of the negative and the *karmadhāraya*, would it then be a collective (*samāhāra*) or a copulative (*itaretarayoga*)? In the former case, the neuter gender would result; in the latter, however, a dual number would follow.
Since this explanation is based on the Sūtra itself, there is no fault in either case.
For it is said: "The Sūtras follow the rules of Vedic usage.

And he will explain in the third chapter that in Vedic usage there is a transposition of gender and number. Regarding the present context, since the rule for "ending in that" (*tadanta-vidhi*) does not apply [to the general term], he states—namely, "a *tatpuruṣa* compound ending in *kanthā*"—that the rule for "ending in that" is understood to apply to the specific *tatpuruṣa* under discussion by means of the word "kanyayā" (by the girl).
Regarding "sauśamikantham": it is a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*) meaning "the ragged garment (*kanthā*) of the Sauśamīs. Regarding "dākṣikanthā": [it is likewise a genitive compound].
"This is the name of this village; however, it does not exist among the Uśīnaras, but rather elsewhere. Regarding the term *upajñā*: "it is understood (*upajñāyate*) thus, therefore it is *upajñā*.
[The suffix] *aṅ* is applied in the sense of the object according to Pāṇini 3.3.106, *ātaścaupasarge*. "It is commenced (*upakramyate*) thus, therefore it is *upakrama*."
In this case, the suffix *ghañ* is applied in the sense of the object (*karman*) by [Pāṇini 3.3.19].
The prohibition of *vṛddhi* is established by [Pāṇini 7.3.34], "not for that which has a high-pitched vowel in its original form" (*nodāttopadeśasya*), and so forth.
As for the statement, "even though [the suffix applies] to that which is to be first known (*upajñeya*) and to that which is to be first undertaken (*upakramya*)," and so on.
*Upajñeya* means "to be fully understood.
*Upakrama* means "that which is to be undertaken.
*Ādi* means "primacy" or "the beginning."
"Pāṇinyupajñam" is a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*). By this, it is meant that it was first composed by him.
Regarding the term "akāla":
he did not establish a section on time (*kāla*) within his own grammar. [This is known from the statement: "The *Daśahuskarana* was composed by Vyāḍi."
Vyāḍi also, among the rules that apply simultaneously in time, has prescribed a technical definition (*paribhāṣā*) stating that "the earlier [rule] takes precedence in time.

The term *vālmīkiślokāḥ* is a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*) meaning "the verses of Vālmīki. Regarding the statement "abundance is a property of the meaning of the prior member," he provides the reason here: "of locusts, etc. and so forth.
In expressions such as *śalabhacchāyam* ("the shadow of locusts"), the plurality of the locusts and so forth is understood; for a shadow cannot exist without them.

Therefore, the plurality is an attribute (*dharma*) of the prior member of the compound, such as the locusts. [Question: "Why does this not apply here in the case of *rājasabhā* ('the king's assembly')?
The intention is that, according to the rule [Pāṇini 2.4.23], it ought to apply precisely in this instance.
"‘That is incorrect,’ and so forth.
By this, he confirms with the authoritative statement of the Master that ‘it is intended only for a synonym’ (Kāvyālaṅkāra-vṛtti 2.4.23).
Since it is intended only for a synonym, it is for this very reason that this was said."

Regarding the phrase "{jitparyāyavacanasyaiva-kāśikā| jaditparyāyavacanasyaiva}" and so forth: how is it that this meaning—"only [the word] expressing a synonym of *jita*"—is obtained, given that such a statement does not exist in this sūtra? The thought is as follows: Surely there is the mention of "pūrva" (preceding); therefore, this meaning is obtained from the mention of "pūrva. How so? If there were a mention of the actual form (*svarūpagrahaṇa*), one would have said simply "rājāmanuṣyāt" (after *rājan* when not preceded by a non-human). For the ablative case itself will supply the word for direction (*dikśabda*). Furthermore, for a *tatpuruṣa* compound ending in *sabhā*, there is no other [word] besides the word "pūrva" [that could serve as a qualifier].

Since the word *dik* (direction) can be supplied by ellipsis (*adhyāhāra*), what is the purpose of including the term *pūrva* (preceded by)? It is included so that the term *artha* (meaning) may be understood.

When *artha* is understood, the double prohibition—namely, "not preceded by a king" (*arāja-pūrvā*) and "not preceded by a non-human" (*amanuṣya-pūrvā*)—is explained as follows: [the compound] means "not preceded by a king" and "not preceded by a non-human.

By this, according to the maxim of "that which is connected with *nañ* or *iva*" (*nañ-iva-yukta-nyāya*), words synonymous with "king" (*rāja-paryāya*) are understood as similar to it, but specific individuals such as Candragupta and others are not, for they do not denote the general concept of "king" (*rāja-artha*).

Alternatively—the term *vibhāṣā* from the rule *arthagrahaṇe 'smin* (Pāṇini 2.4.16) continues here by way of the "frog-leap" maxim (*maṇḍūkapluti*), and that [optionality] is understood as a restricted option (*vyavasthitavibhāṣā*). Consequently, in this case, the word *īrā* will be understood only as a synonym for *prayāya*, and not anything else. For the word *amanuṣya*—which does not appear in the *vṛtti*—is used in its conventional sense (*rūḍhi*) to refer to *rakṣas*, *piśāca*, and so forth.

If this is so, does it not contradict what he will cite under the rule *anuṣyakartṛke ca* [Pāṇini 3.2.53]—namely, *jāyāghnas tilakālakaḥ*, *patighnī pāṇirekhā*, *śleṣmadhnaṃ madhu*, and *pittaghnaṃ ghṛtam*? This is not a fault; for in this case, the particle *ca* is employed, serving to conjoin that very same rule.

Thus, because of this re-enactment of the rule, or by virtue of the statement *kṛtyalyuṭo bahulam* [Pāṇini 3.3.113], the suffix will occur even in cases other than those involving *rakṣas*, *piśāca*, and so forth.

Alternatively—the word *amanuṣya* is of two kinds: there is this unanalyzed (*avyutpanna*) one which refers to *rakṣas*, *piśāca*, and so forth; and there is the analyzed (*vyutpanna*) one, which is a negative compound (*nañ-samāsa*). In this context [of the present rule], the conventional (*rūḍhi*) unanalyzed word is taken. In the rule *amanuṣyakartṛke ca* (Pāṇini 3.2.53), however, the non-conventional (*arūḍhi*) analyzed word is taken; thus there is no contradiction. As in the example: "Devadatta’s assembly" (*devadattasabhā*).

The word *devadatta* is not a synonym for "king," nor does it denote a non-human being. This word *sabhā* indeed exists as a term for a "hut"—as in "a long hut" (*kadīrghā sabhā*) or "a short hut" (*hrasvā sabhā*). It also exists as a term for a "gathering" (or assembly), as in "the assembly of Brāhmaṇas" (*brāhmaṇānāṃ sabhā*) or "the assembly of women" (*strīṇāṃ sabhā*). Since the word *āśālā* here excludes the sense of a "hut," the other meaning is understood; therefore, he says: "it denotes a gathering," and so forth. [Regarding the term] *āniśam*.

The night in which intoxicated *ānīs* roam is an *āniśā*; it is called *āniśā*. For what purpose is this [rule]? Here, this *dvandva* compound is like a snake, having its meaning as the primary factor (*arthapradhāna*). When it consists of members of different genders, there is no single gender that can favor both the preceding and following words—which are of different genders—by which the whole aggregate could be designated.
Furthermore, because it is impossible for both [genders] to apply simultaneously, it is impossible to provide such a designation.
Therefore, since there would otherwise be an option, this statement is made as a restrictive rule (*niyamārtha*) regarding the *dvandva*.

The *tatpuruṣa* compound is also of two kinds: that which has the meaning of the first member as its predominant factor (*pūrvapadārthapradhāna*) and that which has the meaning of the second member as its predominant factor (*uttarapadārthapradhāna*). Therefore, regarding that *tatpuruṣa* which has the meaning of the second member as its predominant factor, since it is predominant itself, the gender of the subsequent member will naturally belong to the entire aggregate; thus, a rule concerning it would be purposeless. However, regarding that [tatpuruṣa] which has the meaning of the first member as its predominant factor, since the gender of the first member would apply there, the gender of the second member is prescribed; therefore, in that case, this [rule] serves a prescriptive purpose.
Regarding the phrase "of the *dvandva* and the *tatpuruṣa*":
this indicates that the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) is used for "of the *dvandva* and the *tatpuruṣa*," not the locative (*saptamī*).
If this were the locative, then the gender of that which follows would apply to the preceding member in both the *dvandva* and the *tatpuruṣa*; for the word "following" (*para*) is a relative term.

Furthermore, in the case of *mayūrī-kukkuṭau* (a peahen and a cock), the feminine suffix of the first member would be removed; likewise, even in a *tatpuruṣa* compound such as *ardha-pippalī* (half a long pepper), the feminine suffix of the first member would [otherwise] occur. Therefore, this is a genitive [case ending].
This being so, it is understood that this is an extension (*atideśa*) of the meaning of the compound;
since the feminine suffix of the first member is neither prohibited nor enjoined, there is no occasion for the aforementioned defects to arise.

Because the gender of the compound’s meaning is extended [to the subsequent member], the subsequent usage (*anuprayoga*) is also a qualifier of the compound’s meaning alone; thus, it takes on that very same gender. For example: *kukkuṭamayūryāv ime* ("these two, a rooster and a peahen").
The shortening of the penultimate vowel (*upasarjana-hrasvatva*) does not occur here, because the technical designation of "subordinate element" (*upasarjana-saṃjñā*) is absent.

For this was stated previously: "The purpose of the technical term *upasarjana* (secondary member) is that the designation may be understood as descriptive of its meaning—that is, 'the non-primary is the *upasarjana*'.

And since in a *dvandva* compound all constituent members are primary, the designation *upasarjana* does not apply there. Furthermore, it has already been explained in the very rule prescribing the *upasarjana* designation that even in cases such as *ardhapippalī*, where there is a single case-ending (*ekavibhakti*), the designation *upasarjana* does not apply to the word *pippalī*.

"It should be stated" means it should be explained. In this regard, the purpose of mentioning *tatpuruṣa* again while the [rule] 2.1.22 is still in force is so that the subsequent gender (*paravalliṅgatā*) may apply specifically to that particular type of *tatpuruṣa*.

Therefore, in the case of *dvigu*, *prāpta*, *āpanna*, *alam-pūrva*, and *gati* compounds, the rule regarding taking the gender of the final member (*paravalliṅgatā*) does not apply. Otherwise, if this rule for taking the gender of the final member were to apply to every *tatpuruṣa* compound, then [the author] would have simply stated: "The gender of a *dvandva* and [a *tatpuruṣa*] is that of the final member" (*paravalliṅgaṃ dvandvasya ca*).
For by the word "and" (*ca*), it would already be understood that the previously mentioned *tatpuruṣa* is intended. Thus, we have the example: *pañcakapālaḥ*.
A *dvigu* compound is formed in the sense of a secondary derivative (*taddhita*).
There is elision (*luk*) of the suffix *aṇ*, which arises in the sense of "prepared" according to Pāṇini 4.4.88.
Thus, we have *prāptajīvikaḥ*.
The compound is formed by the rule *prāptāpanne ca dvitīyayā* [Pāṇini 2.2.4]. Regarding the example *alañjīvikaḥ*,
it is formed by the rule *paryādayo glānādyarthe caturthyā* (or rather, *vā*).
93) Thus ends the section on compounds (*samāsa*).
Regarding the example *niṣkauśāmbiḥ*, [it is formed] by the rule:

"Words beginning with *nis* [form a compound] with a word ending in the fifth case when meaning 'departed from' and so forth" (Vārttika 94). It is stated that "for *aśva* and *avaḍava*, the status of being a singular unit (*ekavadbhāva*) is optionally prescribed."

By the rule *vibhāṣā vṛkṣamṛga* [Pāṇini 2.4.12] and so forth, it is said: "This is an extension of meaning (*arthātideśa*), not a formal irregularity (*nipātana*). For if it were a formal irregularity, the mention of the word *pūrvavat* would be redundant; one should have simply stated *aśvavaḍavau*.

By the statement "the dual number is not the governing factor" (*dvivacanamatantram*), etc., he demonstrates the result of the extension of the meaning (*arthātideśa*). For if [the rule] were merely a formal substitution (*nipātana*), the gender would not follow the preceding [member] when there is a different number; rather, this rule is an exception (*apavāda*) to the subsequent gender. Thus, in the case of *hemanta-śiśirau*, it is an exception to the neuter gender, because the subsequent word *śiśira* is neuter. [The example] *ahorātre* [is also given].
This is an exception to the masculine gender.

Since the masculine gender would otherwise apply by the rule *chandasi liṅgavyatyaya uktaḥ* (Pāṇini 2.4.29), the reversal of gender is stated by the rule *paravalliṅgam* (Pāṇini 2.4.26). Thus, the feminine and neuter genders would have been obtained [for the compound] because the word *rātri* is feminine and the word *ahan* is neuter.
"dvirātraḥ" means the collection of two nights. A *dvigu* compound is formed for the sake of expressing a collective (*samāhāra*) by the rule "taddhitārtha... (Pāṇini 2.1.50) and so forth.
The compound-ending suffix *ac* is applied by the rule *ahaḥ sarvaikadeśasaṃkhyātapuṇyācca rātreḥ* [Pāṇini 5.4.87].

For here, the word *ac* is understood from the preceding rule *ac pratyanvavapūrvāt sāmalomnaḥ* [Pāṇini 5.4.75]. In the case of *pūrvāhṇaḥ*, the analysis is "the part of the day (*ahnaḥ*) that is prior (*pūrvam*). The compound is formed by the rule *pūrvāparaprathama...* [Pāṇini 2.2.1] et cetera. Then, the suffix *ṭac* is added by the rule *rājāhaḥsakhibhyaṣṭac* [Pāṇini 5.4.91], followed by the substitution of *ahan* for *ahar* by the rule *ahnaṣṭakhoreva* [Pāṇini 5.4.88]. Finally, the nasalization (*ṇatvam*) occurs by the rule *ahno'dantāt* [Pāṇini 8.4.7].
Regarding "dvayahaḥ": as before, it is a *dvigu* compound in the sense of a collective (*samāhāra*). As before, the suffix *ṭac* is applied.
By [Pāṇini 5.4.89], the designation *avahna* is prohibited;
by [Pāṇini 6.4.145], there is the elision (*lopa*) of the *ṭi*.
[The term] is "anuvākādayaḥ."
Some say: this is a *bahuvrīhi* compound; it is an *anuvāka* because the *vāk* (speech) is recited (*anu-krānta*) by means of this.
This statement is made because the feminine and neuter genders would otherwise have been applicable.
Others, however, believe that since this [suffix] is *ghañ*, it is masculine by virtue of its inherent capacity (*sāmarthya*).

For in that case, the suffix *kta* is an exception (*apavāda*) for the neuter gender in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāva*), and the suffix *ktin* applies in the feminine. Consequently, by implication, the former remains restricted to the masculine. However, that which is prescribed when not denoting the agent (*akartari kārake*) occurs in both the masculine and the neuter, because there is no subverting rule (*bādhaka*) to the contrary.

But it does not occur in the feminine; for since [the suffix] -ghañ is prescribed after roots other than those ending in *i* (Pāṇini 3.3.94) when the agent is not the factor [of the action], that [suffix], being prescribed by a specific rule, subverts the [general] -ghañ.
And here, the suffix -ghañ is prescribed after the root *vac* (Pāṇini 3.3.19). That which is recited as a passage is an *anuvāka*.
Thus ends the compound.
In this view, since the neuter gender would otherwise apply, this specific rule is stated. Regarding the term *apadha*:
when there is no prohibition of the compound-ending suffix by [Pāṇini 5.4.72], then the vowel *a* is added as the compound-ending suffix by [Pāṇini 5.4.74]: *ṛkpūrabdhūpathāmānakṣe*.

When there is no mention of a compound-ending suffix (*samāsānta*), then the masculine gender alone prevails—as in *apanthāḥ*. Because of the use of the plural number in the rule *ardharca-ādayaḥ*, the sense of "beginning with" is understood; thus he says, "*ardharca-ādayaḥ*," and so forth. Regarding the phrase "*śabdarūpāśrayā caiṣā*":
that which has the form of the word as its basis is so described.
The meaning is that this dual-gender application is prescribed by relying on the form of the word, without regard for the meaning.
The gender of a word denoting an action follows that of its expressed object: thus, *bhūtaṃ kuṇḍam* (a prepared pot), *bhūtā śāṭī* (a prepared garment), *bhūto ghaṭaḥ* (a prepared jar).
The gender of a derivative (*yaugika*) word follows that of its expressed meaning: thus, *lavaṇaṃ śākam* (salted vegetables), *lavaṇā yavāgūḥ* (salted gruel), *lavaṇaḥ sūpaḥ* (salted soup).
[In the case of] "mixed with salt," the suffix *ṭhak* is applied by the rule *saṃsṛṣṭe* (Pāṇini 4.4.22).
By [Pāṇini 4.4.24], there is elision (*luk*) of that suffix.

For this very reason, because it denotes a state already accomplished when joined with the meaning of a secondary derivative (*taddhita*), this word *apūrva* refers to merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*).
"[In the means of accomplishing that]"—thus [it is said].

The meaning is that whatever possesses the status of being an auxiliary (*aṅga*) with respect to the acquisition of the unseen (*adṛṣṭa*) is the means (*sādhana*) for it; this, moreover, is sacrifice (*yāga*) and so forth.
The word *karman* ends in the letter *n* and is of both genders, as in the expression "the sequence is the action" (*kramaḥ karma ca*). Regarding the phrase "instruction is the statement":
it is the initial presentation by means of words.
"Anavādeśa means 'stating subsequently. This refers to a subsequent explanation.
And he will explain later what kind of subsequent explanation is intended here.
"From these two students," and so forth—
this is an *ādeśa* (original enunciation).
"And so, from these two," and so forth— this is an *anvādeśa* (subsequent reference).

Furthermore, by the word "atho," an anvādeśa (subsequent reference) is expressed here. Now, one might object: once the substitution of *tyad* and so forth has been applied, and the elision [of the final vowel] occurs before a consonant (*hali lopa*), forms such as *atho ābhyām* are indeed established; therefore, only the anudātta accent should be prescribed, while the explicit statement of the substitute (*ādeśavacana*) is redundant. To this, he says: "The statement of the substitute," and so forth. Even when the suffix *akarac* is applied according to [Pāṇini 5.3.71], because of the governing rule [from 6.4.149, *idama iś*], there is no elision of the form *id-*; thus, without the statement of the substitute, the desired form would not be established.

But is it not the case that, by the rule *nanu ca* [Pāṇini 7.2.113], since there is elision (*lopa*) of the form *id* when followed by a consonant (*hal*), this [present rule] is for the purpose of ensuring that [the substitution] occurs when followed by a vowel (*aj-ādi*)? This is not so; for by virtue of the logical necessity (*sāmarthya*), the substitution must occur only when followed by a consonant, once the forms *smai*, *bhyām*, and so forth have been produced. Therefore, the statement of the substitute is for the sake of including the element with the augment *ka* (*sākacka*). And since this [rule] has been commenced for the sake of the form with *ka*, the addition of the marker *ś* is for the purpose of ensuring the replacement of the whole (*sarvādeśa*); otherwise, by the rule *alo’ntyasya* [Pāṇini 1.1.52], only the final letter would be replaced.

If it is argued that [the rule] will not apply because there is no purpose [for it], we say no; the statement of *a* for *a* is understood to be for the purpose of precluding the substitution of a long vowel (*dīrgha*). Now, what is the purpose of stating that it is *anudātta* (unaccented), given that once the case-ending has been made udātta by [Pāṇini 6.1.171], the base will become *anudātta* by [Pāṇini 6.1.158], which states that "in a word, all syllables except one are *anudātta*"? This is not so; the statement of *anudātta* is for the sake of including the case-ending, so that the entire form including the case-ending may be *anudātta*. Consequently, in the case of subsequent reference (*anvādeśa*), the word *abhyām* becomes entirely *anudātta*.

If *anvādeśa* (subsequent reference) were merely a subsequent utterance, why would it not occur here in the example: "Feed Devadatta, and this Yajñadatta"? For here too there is indeed an *anvādeśa*, and consequently, by rule [2.4.34], the substitution of *enad* would apply; therefore, he says: "In this case, it is not merely a subsequent utterance," and so forth.

"Therefore, it does not occur here" means that in this instance, there is no second presentation of the same referent (*abhidheya*) which was previously presented by a word; rather, it is a different referent altogether.
For instance, there is first the presentation of Devadatta, and subsequently that of Yajñadatta.

But how is this distinction obtained, given that the term *anvādeśa* is well-known merely as a subsequent utterance, and a general term does not settle upon a specific meaning without the proximity of another word? This is not a fault; because the mention of *vibhāṣā* from the rule *vibhāṣā senā* [Pāṇini 2.4.25] continues here, and that is understood as a restricted option (*vyavasthitavibhāṣā*).
Therefore, in this context, only such a specific type of *anvādeśa* (subsequent reference) is to be understood here, not *anvādeśa* in its general sense.
The intended meaning is that it is appropriate to accept the mention of a qualified *anvādeśa*.

Furthermore, whatever he will say there—beginning with "where, having prescribed something... (*yatra kiñcid vidhāya*)—that too should be understood as being based on this very same principle. [The commentary continues: "Now, in this case... (*atho atra*).
Regarding the phrase "atho ataḥ":
"The repetition is for the sake of making [the following vowel] anudātta.
According to the rule *etado'ś* (Pāṇini 5.3.5), the substitution *aś* for *etad* in the ablative case would be udātta; however, [this is not the case here].
The statement "it is intended [that the suffix] be anudātta" is for the purpose of specifying the anudātta accent.

Now, what is the purpose of the phrase "of *tra* and *tas*," given that by the rule "and *tra* and *tas* are anudātta," their status as causes [for the accent] will be understood? This is not so; for it might also be understood as a cumulative addition (*anvācaya*), as in the rule "after a word denoting the agent, *kyaṅ* [is added], with the elision of *sa*" (Pāṇini 3.1.11). In this case, *kyaṅ* would apply without distinction.
Thus, in this case, there is first an indistinct (aviśeṣeṇa) substitution of *tra* and *tas*.

However, where those two (*tra* and *tas*) are seen, they are both unaccented (*anudātta*). Therefore, it must be stated that "the forms *tra* and *tas*" [are used] for the purpose of establishing them as the cause [of the accent].

Now, what is the purpose of making *tra* and *tas* unaccented, since the accent of the *lit* suffix itself will render them unaccented? This is not so; for in this instance, the accent of the *lit* suffix does not apply, because an unaccented substitute is being prescribed.

But surely, once the accent of the *lit* suffix has been applied, the accent of the substitute (*ādeśa*) is then applied? If this is so, one might understand the accent of the substitute as an exception (*apavāda*) to the accent of the *lit* suffix; yet, a general rule (*utsarga*) does not apply where there is scope for an exception. Therefore, just as in the case of *goṣpadapram*, since there was no prior state of being unaccented (*anudātta*) due to the *lit* suffix, only the accent of the primary suffix (*pratyaya*) occurs; so it would be here as well. Thus, the statement [of the rule] is for the sake of making the *trata* and *sas* suffixes unaccented. Consequently, this entire word becomes unaccented. Although one could have simply said *tāu*, the use of *tratasoḥ* is for the sake of clarity.
The suffix *pramiti* is applied after *goṣpada*, as in *goṣapadapramiti*; the suffix *vindarajīvoḥ* [Pāṇini 3.4.30];
and the suffix *pūreḥ* after *carma* and *udaya* [Pāṇini 3.4.31].

The suffix *ṇamul* is applied [after a word ending in a vowel] by the rule *varṣapramāṇa ūlopaścādanyatarasyām* (Pāṇini 3.4.32), and there is also the elision (*ūlopa*) of the vowel *ū*. In the compound *dvitīyāṭaussvenaḥ*, *dvitīyāṭausaḥ* is a *dvandva* (copulative) compound consisting of *dvitīyā*, *ṭā*, and *auṣ*.
From the rule *idamo'nvādeśe* (Pāṇini 2.4.32), the terms *idamaḥ* and *anvādeśe* are understood to carry over (*anuvartate*).
From the rule "etadas-tratasoḥ," the word "etad" is also [understood].
He explains this with the words beginning "in the second case," etc.
He explains the term "anāvādeśa" as "something," etc.
"To enjoin" (vidhātum) means "to cause to understand something not previously known" (apūrvam bodhayitum).
Having cited an instance of a restatement (anvādeśa), he demonstrates it with the words "as for example" (yathā).
In the presentation of examples, the word *yathā* [is used].

However, in the rule "One should know that this *ām* is marked with *ṅ* when it signifies a slight degree (*īṣadartha*), connection with an action (*kriyāyoga*), limit (*maryādā*), or inclusion (*abhividhi*); but it is unmarked (*aṅit*) in the sense of a sentence (*vākya*) or recollection (*smaraṇa*)," there is no substitution of *enad*, because the first half of the verse is a restatement (*anuvāda*) due to its connection with the word *yat*.

In the phrase "of that which has been employed to accomplish some task," it is clear from the Bhāṣya that in the preceding sentence, the employment [of the word] was intended in whatever way possible, and there is no insistence that it must be this specific instance alone. Thus end those ending in *m*. Now, those ending in *ṇ*.
Regarding *vijiti* from the root *gaṇ*: the root *gaṇ*, meaning "to count," belongs to the *curādi* class and ends in the vowel *a*.
From this, with the prefix *su-* and the suffix *ṇic* added in the sense of the root itself (*svārthe*), [the form *saṃgaṇayati* is derived].
Because of the status of the substitute as the original (sthānivadbhāva), there is no vṛddhi of the penultimate vowel.

From that, the suffix *vic* is applied; by the rule "it is also seen after other [roots]," the *ṇi* is elided, followed by the elision of the single-consonant suffix (*apṛkta*). Then, the case endings (*sup*) are produced, and the *su* is elided by the rule beginning with *halṅyāb*. Thus, the form *sugaṇ* is obtained.
*Sugaṇau* and *sugaṇaḥ*, etc., remain unchanged.
In the locative plural (*sup*), by the rule *ṅṅoḥ kuk ṭuk śari*, there is an option for the insertion of *ṭuk*.
Intending that *ṭha* replaces *ṭ* according to the rule *cayo dvitīyāḥ*, he says: *sugaṇṭhsu*.
The second form in the absence of *ṭu* is stated as *sugaṇṣu*. The form in the absence of *ṭuk* is stated as *sugaṇsu*.
[And] *sugāṇ*.
From the verbal root *gaṇ*, there is the suffix *ṇic* because it ends in *a*; there is elision of the *a* (allopa).

Because that [elision] is treated as if it were still present (*sthānivadbhāva*), there is no vṛddhi strengthening of the penultimate vowel. From that [root with *ṇic*], there is the suffix *kvip*; there is elision of *ṇi* and elision of the single-consonant suffix (*apṛktalopa*).
The long vowel [ā] is applied by the rule *anunāsikasya kvijhaloḥ*;
thus the form is *sugāṇ*.
[The forms] *sugāṇau*, *sugāṇaḥ*, and so forth, follow accordingly.

Furthermore, one should not suspect that the *sthānivadbhāva* (the status of being like the original) applies to the elision of the *ṇi* suffix and the elision of the *āl* augment when a long vowel is to be produced; for such status is prohibited in the case of the prescription of a long vowel, and it is also prohibited with respect to a rule concerning *kvip*.
Thus end those [roots] ending in vowels. Now, those ending in consonants.

Regarding the word *rājan*, he states the specific rule: "Because it is subsequent" (*paratvāt*). This means that, in comparison with the elision of the *hal-ṅy-ādi* suffixes, the lengthening [of the vowel] occurs first by the rule "before a *sarvanāmasthāna* ending, except for the vocative singular," and only thereafter does the elision of the *hal-ṅy-ādi* suffixes take place.

Nor should it be argued that, according to the maxim "in the case of a conflict, that which is sublated remains sublated," the elision of *hal* and *ṅī* etc. cannot occur here; for the principle is established by the rule "it is accomplished through the recognition of recurrence" (*punaḥ prasaṅgavijñānāt siddham*), because the maxim "in the case of a conflict, that which is sublated" is not universally applicable. This is the intended meaning. [Regarding] "the elision of *na*" (*nalopa*).

The meaning is that there is elision (*lopa*) of the letter *n* by the rule "there is no elision of what stands at the end of a nominal stem" (*na lopaḥ prātipadikāntasya*). Regarding the form *dadhyāt*:
this is the optative (*liṅ*) in the sense of a benediction (*āśis*), and [by the rule] Pāṇini 3.4.116, it receives the designation of an ārdhadhātuka suffix.

Regarding the word "hanyāt" (he should kill), the suffix *liṅ* is used according to the rule "vidhinimantraṇa... (Pāṇini 3.3.161) and so forth. Furthermore, this [locative case] is a locative of domain (*viṣayasaptamī*).

If [the word *para*] were in the locative case (*parasaptamī*), then forms such as *bhavyam* would not be established. To explain: because the roots *as* and others end in a consonant (*halanta*), when the suffix *ṇyat* is applied by the rule *ṛhaloṇryat* (Pāṇini 3.1.124), the subsequent rules *asterbhūḥ* (2.4.52), *ajer vyaghañapoḥ* (2.4.56), and *cakṣiṅaḥ khyāñ* (2.4.54) would apply.
In that case, once *vṛddhi* has been applied to two of them and the *yuk* augment added to the third, undesirable forms such as *bhāvyaṃ*, *pravaiyam*, and *ākhyāyyam* would result.
However, if this were a locative of domain (*viṣayasaptamī*), then when the status of being an *ārdhadhātuka* is intended, the substitutions would occur even before the suffix has arisen.

Consequently, because the stem would end in *ac*, the suffix *yat* would be applied by [Pāṇini 3.1.97] *aco yat*; then, after *it* is applied by [Pāṇini 6.4.65] *īdyati*, the *guṇa* substitution would apply to all [the vowels], and finally, the *ava* substitution would apply to the root *as* by [Pāṇini 6.1.80] *asterbhūḥ*. Thus, forms such as *bhavyam*, *praveyam*, and *ākhyeyam* would be established.
Therefore, this is a locative of domain, not a locative of sequence (*parasaptamī*).

But how can this be understood as a locative of domain (*viṣayasaptamī*), given that the technical rule (*paribhāṣā*) "when there is a doubt regarding the sequence of words" (P. 1.4.2) applies, making a locative of posteriority (*parasaptamī*) alone logical, rather than a locative of domain? This is not so; because of the general indication in [P. 6.4.46], and in a general case there is no actual sequence of prior and posterior. If it is argued that sequence exists through the intellect (*buddhi*), we say no; for in that case, there would be unnecessary complexity (*gaurava*). Alternatively, the mention of *ac* in [P. 3.1.97] "aco yat" is the indicator (*jñāpaka*) that this is indeed a locative of domain.
"Subsequently, according to what is obtained," and so forth.

The meaning is that once the substitutes have been applied, whatever [suffix] is subsequently applicable from whichever [base], that occurs from that. In the word "prajagghya," the suffix *ktvā* is used according to [Pāṇini 3.4.21]:
"The suffix *ktvā* is used for two actions having the same agent when the first in time is expressed."
Thus ends the section on compound formation. Regarding the rule "In a compound not preceded by *nañ*, *lyap* replaces *ktvā*" [Pāṇini 7.1.37], we have the form *jagdhaḥ*.
By the rule *jhaṣas tathordho’dhaḥ* [Pāṇini 8.2.40], the letter *t* becomes *dh*;
by the rule *jhalāṃ jaś jhaśi* [Pāṇini 8.4.53], there is *jaś*-ness, whereby *dh* becomes *d*;
and by the rule *dalopaḥ* [Pāṇini 8.4.65], there is elision.
To the question, "Why does the augment *num* not apply here by [Pāṇini 7.1.58]? he says: "The vowel *i* is for the sake of pronunciation (*uccāraṇārtha*).

Just as in the case of "√*ad* (to eat)" (Dhātupāṭha 1011), where the vowel *a* is for the sake of pronunciation, so too should the vowel *i* here be understood. Now, what is the purpose of including the mention of *liṭ*? Is it not already established by [the rule] "*ti-kitī*" alone? It is not so established; because, due to the subsequent status of the suffix *ktvā*, the substitution of *lyap* would apply. This is not correct; since the substitution of *jagdhi* is *antaraṅga* (internal), it must take effect first.
Its status as *antaraṅga* (internal) is due to its being based on a single word (*ekapada*);
whereas the substitution of *lyap* is *bahiraṅga* (external), because it is based on a compound (*samāsa*), and a compound is based on multiple words (*anekapada*).

In that case—once the substitution of *jagdhi* is established, because it is *antaraṅga*, the rule *ti-kiti ca* [7.2.116] is understood to apply. This indicates that there is an annulment (*bādhanam*) of *antaraṅga* operations by *lyap*. Consequently, when the suffix *ktvā* is added to the roots *dhā* and *hā* preceded by *sam-* and *vi-*, then while the condition *ti-kiti* is still in force from the rule *dyati-syati-māti-sthāmi-ti-kiti* [7.4.40], the substitution of *hi* (by 7.4.42–43) would have been required, overriding the substitution of *lyap*.
However, due to this very indicator (*jñāpaka*), the substitution of *lyap* prevails and annuls [the application of *hi*]; thus we have *saṃdhāya* and *vihāya*.
Thus, in *nirdāya* and *durdāya*, the substitution of *dadā-* [for *dā-*] does not occur by virtue of [Pāṇini 7.4.46].
In *prasthāya*, the substitution of *it* [for the final vowel] does not occur by virtue of [Pāṇini 7.4.40].
In *prakhanya* and *prakhāya*, the obligatory substitution of *āt* [for the root vowel] does not occur by virtue of [Pāṇini 6.4.42]; rather, by virtue of [Pāṇini 6.4.43], it occurs only optionally.
For in that context, the mention of *āt* (the long vowel *ā*) continues from [Pāṇini 6.4.41] *vihvanoranunāsikasyāt*.
Consequently, the lengthening [of the penultimate vowel] does not occur by [Pāṇini 6.4.18] *prakramya*.
For in that case, the mention of "long" (*dīrgha*) continues from [Pāṇini 6.3.111], and the mention of *jhal* continues from [Pāṇini 6.4.15] along with the condition *kṅiti*.
In *āpṛcchya*, the substitution of *ś* [for *s*] does not occur by the rule *cchvoḥ śūḍanunāsike ca* [Pāṇini 6.4.19].
In *pradīvya*, the substitution of *ūṭh* does not occur by this very same rule;
rather, there is lengthening by the rule *hali ca* [Pāṇini 8.2.77].

In the example *prapaṭhāti*, the augment *iṭ* does not occur by virtue of the rule *ārdhadhātukasya* [Pāṇini 7.2.35]. In *aghasat*, because the root is marked with *ḷ*, the substitution of *aṅ* for *cli* occurs according to the rule on the *puṣādi* group [Pāṇini 3.1.55]. In *jighatsati*:

By the rule *saḥ syārdhadhātuke* [Pāṇini 7.4.49], the *s* is replaced by *t*. Regarding the statement "*ghaslṛbhāve 'cy upasaṃkhyānam*" (an addition should be made for the substitution of *ghaslṛ* when an *ac* follows): the meaning is that when the substitution of *ghaslṛ* is to be applied, an addition—that is, a formal explanation—must be provided for its occurrence even before an *ac* vowel. The explanation there is as follows: in the subsequent sūtra, the letter *ca* serves to include what has not been explicitly mentioned; by virtue of this, the substitution of *ghaslṛ* occurs even before an *ac* vowel.
In *praghasaḥ*, the suffix *ac* is applied according to Pāṇini 3.1.134 (*pacādyac*). In *ghāsaḥ*,
the suffix *ghañ* is applied in the sense of an abstract action (bhāve).

Regarding "praghasaḥ": by [Pāṇini 3.3.59], the suffix *ap* is applied. Although the rule could have been formulated as a single compound—"luṅsaṅghañapsu ghaslṛ"—the division of the rule (*yogavibhāga*) is for the sake of variety. Regarding "ghastām": [this is formed with the substitution of *ghaslṛ*].
*laṅ*, *tas*, *tām*; because it belongs to the *ad-ādi* class, there is elision (*luk*) of the *śap* suffix.
By the rule "In the Vedic language, [the augment] *aṭ* is frequently absent even when not preceded by *māṅ*" (Pāṇini 6.4.75), there is an absence of the augment *aṭ*.
Alternatively, this is an example from the *luṅ* tense.
In the word *mantra*, there is the elision (*luk*) of the suffix *cli* by the rule *ghasahvara* (Pāṇini 2.4.80) et al.
In the word *sagdhiḥ*, the suffix *ktin* is applied in the feminine by the rule *striyāṃ ktin* (Pāṇini 3.3.94).
By [Pāṇini 6.4.100], there is the elision of the penultimate vowel;
by [Pāṇini 8.2.26], there is the elision of the letter *s*.
However, if the elision of *s* of the suffix *sic* were prescribed by this very rule, then one should regard it as a Vedic (chāndasa) elision of a phoneme—as in the example *iṣkartāram adhvarasya*.
As before, the letter *t* becomes *dh*;
then the *gh* undergoes *jaś*-substitution. The compound is formed by [Pāṇini 2.1.58], and the substitution of *s* for *samāna-* occurs by [Pāṇini 6.3.84].
Regarding "attām":
by [Pāṇini 8.2.26], there is the elision of *sic*;
*tas* becomes *tām*.
By the rule *khari ca* [Pāṇini 8.4.54], the letter *d* is changed to *t*.
Alternatively, this is an illustration for the *laṅ* [aorist] tense.

Now, as to why the term *bahulam* ("diversely") is used—why not simply use the term *anyatarasyām* ("optionally")? Anticipating the objection, "In that case, what would become of the *guṇa* substitution?", he says: "That very term will also serve the purpose of the subsequent rule."
By this, he demonstrates the advantage that since *anyatarasyām* is included here, it need not be included again in the subsequent rule.
[Objection: In that case, the inclusion of *anyatarasyām* right here will carry over (*anuvartiṣyate*) into the subsequent rule.
[Reply: But what would happen if *bahulam* were to carry over into the subsequent rule? One might suspect that some other grammatical operation (*kārya*) would also take place.

The meaning "in some cases it is indeed otherwise" is certainly intended by the inclusion of the term *bahulam* (diversely); for instance, in the case of *ghastām*, the elision of the penultimate vowel (*upadhā-lopa*) does not occur,
even though it would have been applicable by [Pāṇini 6.4.100].

It does not occur because of the inclusion of the word *bahula* (diversely). [The rule] says "when *liṭ* follows. Now, one might object: since the word from [Pāṇini 6.4.46] (*guṇo yaṅ-liṭoḥ*) is understood here, and it has been stated that "in an *ārdhadhātuka*" is a locative of scope (*viṣaya-saptamī*), then the statement "when *liṭ* follows" is improper. This is not improper; for the meaning of the term *ārdhadhātuka* is the general property of being an *ārdhadhātuka*, which is common to many suffixes. And with such a general property, temporal sequence (*paurvāparya*) is impossible.

For that [priority or posteriority] occurs either spatially or temporally; however, since a universal (*sāmānya*) is not spatial, is temporal, and is eternal, spatial or temporal priority and posteriority with respect to it are impossible. Therefore, the locative case in *ārdhadhātuke* is correctly interpreted as a "locus-condition" (*viṣaya-saptamī*). Here, however, in the rule *liṭi*, the *ārdhadhātuka* suffix is mentioned, and with this, priority and posteriority are indeed possible.
Furthermore, when the substitute *ghaslṛ* is prescribed upon the occurrence of *liṭ*, nothing undesirable follows.

Therefore, this [ablative case] is properly a locative of the other (i.e., the *parasaptamī*). In the form *jakṣatuḥ*, there is elision of the penultimate vowel (*upadhālopa*) by the rule *gamahana* [Pāṇini 6.4.98], the substitution of *ṣ* by the rule *śāsivasighasīnāñca* [Pāṇini 8.3.60], and the substitution of *c* by the rule *khari ca* [Pāṇini 8.4.54].

*āda*, *ādatuḥ*, *āduḥ*. [In these forms] there is lengthening of the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*) by [Pāṇini 7.4.70]. Now, one might object: for the root *ghaslṛ* "to eat" (Dhātupāṭha 715), the forms will be *jāghāsa*, *jakṣatuḥ*, *jakṣuḥ*; and for the root *ada* "to eat" (Dhātupāṭha 1011), the forms will be *āda*, *ādatuḥ*, *āduḥ*. Furthermore, there exists another root *ghas*, because the suffix *kmarac* is prescribed [after it] by [Pāṇini 3.2.160]. So, why is this optional rule formulated here for the perfect tense (*liṭ*)? It is for the purpose of making known that the other root *ghas* does not have universal application.

Therefore, in that case, where there is neither gender nor number [in the grammatical rule], its application does not occur, whether in a *sārvadhātuka* or an *ārdhadhātuka* [suffix]. The letter *i* is for the sake of pronunciation;
it is not an *anubandha*.
The intention is that, because of this, the augment *num* does not occur.
Regarding the term *uvāya*:
there is vocalization (*samprasāraṇa*) by the rule "of the reduplicated syllable of both classes" [Pāṇini 6.1.17].
In the forms *ūyatuḥ* and *ūyuḥ*, there is likewise vocalization by the rule beginning with *grah-ādi* [Pāṇini 6.1.16].
Now, he asks why there is no *samprasāraṇa* (vocalization) of the letter *yakāra*, and says: "In the case of the *liṭ* [perfect], for the *ya* of *vayaḥ*" (*liṭi vayo yaḥ*), etc.
"[There is] no *samprasāraṇa* for *veñ*.
That which was applicable by the rule concerning *vaci* and others (*vacyādi-sūtra*) does not take place because of the prohibition: "for *veñ*" (*veñaḥ* 6.1.39).

For in that context, the word *na* (not) continues from [Pāṇini 6.1.37]. Since forms such as *uvāya* and so on would not be established because the root *vay-* is ātmanepada, this sūtra is commenced. "And this substitute ends in the vowel *a*"—from what [source] is this known? This is the style of the Teacher: wherever in this section there is a consonant-final substitute, he adds the vowel *i* for the sake of pronunciation, as in *jagdhi* and so forth.

Therefore, because it is not made to end in *ik*, it is understood that this substitute ends in *ak*. Regarding the phrase "characterized by having a consonant as its final" (*halantalakṣaṇā*): the *vṛddhi* that is prescribed by [Pāṇini 7.2.3] is what is meant by "characterized by having a consonant as its final. [The purpose is stated: "So that there may be an option regarding the *ātmanepada* forms in the *luṅ* [tense], but not in the *luṅ* [tense]."
By this, he shows that the division of the *yoga* (sūtra) serves a subsequent purpose.

For if it were a single *yoga*, since the term *liṅ* would also carry over to the subsequent rules, there would likewise be an option for the *ātmanepada* endings there as well. "Āvadhiṣṭa" [is an example] where the *ātmanepada* ending occurs by [Pāṇini 1.3.28].
In *āphadhiṣata*,
there is the substitution of *ava* [for *apa*] according to [Pāṇini 7.1.5].
In *āhata*, [the same applies].

In the case of *agāt*, there is the designation *kittva* (by rule 1.2.14), the elision of the nasal by the rule beginning with *anudāttopadeśa* (6.4.37), and the elision of the suffix *sic* by the rule *hrasvādaṅgāt* (8.2.27). In the case of *aguḥ*, the suffix *sic* is elided by the rule *gatisthā* (2.4.77) and so forth. As for *aguḥ*: [the same applies].

By the rule *ātaḥ* [Pāṇini 3.4.110], *jus* is substituted for *jhi*, and by the rule *ato guṇe* [Pāṇini 6.1.97], the subsequent form (*pararūpa*) is applied. Regarding the phrase "while *luṅi* is being carried over," etc.:

since the mention of *luṅ* is already being carried over from the rule *luṅi ca* [Pāṇini 2.4.43], the reason for making the mention of *luṅ* again is so that [the substitution] may also apply in the case of parasmaipada endings.
"And always in the ātmanepada.

By this, he shows the following: for the previous mention of *luṅ* was connected with both the mention of *ātmanepada* and the non-mention of *anyatarasyām*; therefore, if that were to recur here, those two would also recur. And in that case, the substitute would occur optionally only in the *ātmanepada*.
Therefore, the term *luṅ* is mentioned again for the purpose that it may apply universally and eternally; thus,
in the example *agāyi*,
the suffix *ciṇ* is applied by [Pāṇini 3.1.66].
The suffix *yuk* is applied by [Pāṇini 7.3.33].

Then, by [Pāṇini 6.4.104], there is the elision (*luk*) of the letter *t*. Regarding the statement "it should be stated that [the rule] applies like *iṇ*," the meaning is that this should be explained as having the following sense: just as the substitution of *gā* occurs for *iṇ* in the *luṅ* tense, so too does it occur for the root *ik* (meaning "to remember") listed as number 1047 in the Dhātupāṭha.

In this regard, the following is the explanation: from the rule [Pāṇini 7.4.78], the mention of *bahulam* (diversely) continues by way of the "frog-leap" maxim (*maṇḍūkapluti*). By that means, even for the root *i*, there will be the substitution of *gā* in the *luṅ* tense. Thus, *gamayati*.
Because of the designation *mit* in the rule "janījṛṣknasurañjo'mantāśca" (Dhātupāṭha Gaṇasūtra 817), there is shortening [of the penultimate vowel]. Thus, *jigamiṣati*.
> [[7.2.58]] Thus, there is the augment *iṭ*. In the form *pratīṣiṣati*,
by the rule [[6.1.2]] and by this rule [[6.1.9]], there is reduplication of the syllable *sa*.
The substitution of *i* [for the final vowel] occurs by the rule *sanyataḥ* [Pāṇini 7.4.79].
The *i* of the prefix [upa-] coalesces with the *i* of the verbal root [by Pāṇini 6.1.101].
He demonstrates that the analysis of the sūtra beginning with *iṅaśca* [Pāṇini 2.4.48] is intended for subsequent purposes through its division (*yogavibhāga*).

For if there were a single conjunction (*ekayoga*), the suffix *ṇi* would also carry over into the subsequent rules; consequently, this substitution would undesirably apply there as well. [In the example] "adhijigāṃsate," the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) is applied by [Pāṇini 1.3.62], and the lengthening of the vowel is applied by [Pāṇini 6.4.16]. [In the example] "adhijage":
By [Pāṇini 3.4.81], this *eś* [substitute] is applied; by [Pāṇini 6.4.64], there is elision of the vowel *ā*;
and there is reduplication of the word *gā*.

But surely, when the *liṭ* suffix follows, because the *ta*-portion is subsequent, the substitution of *aiś* must occur first; afterwards, the substitution of *gāṅ*; and since this substitution of *gāṅ* occurs when reduplication is the cause, by the rule "that which takes the place of an *ac* is like the original" (*sthānivadbhāva*), the reduplication of the vowel *i* would result. So how can there be reduplication of *gā*? This is not so.

Since the substitution of *gāṅ* is internal (*antaraṅga*) because it depends only on the *liṅ* suffix, whereas the substitution of *āṅ* is external (*bahiraṅga*) because it depends on a specific substitute for the *liṅ*, the substitution of *gāṅ* must therefore occur prior to the substitution of *āṅ* due to its internal status. Consequently, since this substitution of *ac* (i.e., *āṅ*) is caused by the reduplication (*dvirvacana*), the status of being a "substitute" (*sthānivadbhāva*) does not apply; how then could there be the possibility of reduplication of the vowel *i*?
[This is why] it is said: "The inclusion of the indicatory letter (*anubandha*) in *gāṅ* is for the sake of specification."

In the *gāṅ-kuṭādi-sūtra* [1.2.1], when it is stated "from *gāṅ* and the *kuṭādi* group," there would be the inclusion of even the root *kai* and *gai* meaning "to sound" (Dhātupāṭha 916, 917). Consequently, why would there not be an application of this rule in the case of *agāsīt naṭaḥ* ("the actor sang")? The reason why this does not occur has been shown right within the *gāṅ-kuṭādi-sūtra* itself. Now, one might object: "Surely the inclusion of *iṅ*, which is marked with the *ṅ*-sign (*ṅit*), will occur there by virtue of its being a *sthānivadbhāva* (substitute behaving like its original); so what is the purpose of the *ṅ*-sign? To this he says: "For not... and so forth.
For in that context, there is the inclusion of the actual form *gāṅ*.
And that [status] is not obtained through the treatment as being like the original (sthānivadbhāva);
what then? It is the operation (kārya).
For this is an extension of the operation (kāryātideśa) based on the rule "yasmāt" (Pāṇini 1.1.56), not an extension of the form (rūpātideśa). Thus, [the example] "adhyaiṣṭa."

By [Pāṇini 6.4.72], the augment *āṭ* is applied; by [Pāṇini 6.1.87], "and after *āṭ*," there is *vṛddhi*. According to the *Bālamanoramā*: "The option regarding the *luṅ* and *lṛṅ* [tenses] is optional" (2.4.50). Thus, the option regarding the *luṅ* and *lṛṅ* [tenses].

He completes the remainder [of the commentary]: "it may be *iṅ* or *gāṅ*. The intention is that this follows from the recurrence (*anuvṛtti*) of [the rules] *iṅaśca* and *gāṅ liṭi*. When the form *adhi a gā s ta* is established in the *sic* suffix, [the rule] *āgastyakauṇḍinyayor agastikuṇḍinac* (Pāṇini 2.4.70) applies for *āgastya*.
"Agastyas," "Kuṇḍinas":
[these forms arise] from the elision of the ṛṣyaṇ suffix after the word *agastya*.
The instruction regarding Agastya and others pertains to the *prakṛti* (base form). The word *kauṇḍinya* ends in the suffix *yañ* from the *garga*-class;
in the plural, there is elision (*luk*) of the suffix *yañ*.

The base forms *kuṇḍina* and so forth [are taught] in the section beginning with "from *yaska* and others, in the sense of a lineage" (*yaskādibhyo gotre*) and ending with "of *āgastya* and *kauṇḍinya*" (*āgastyakauṇḍinyayoḥ*).
Now follows the present topic from the fourth chapter: "the suffix *ṇa* is applied in view of the verbal root *iṅ*, etc."
The phrase "this [rule] which is a locative of posteriority" means that this locative of posteriority in the rule "saṃścaṅoḥ" is with respect to the affix *ṇi*.
[For example: "adhijigāpayiṣati."

With the causative suffix *ṇic*, the augment *puk* is applied by [Pāṇini 7.3.36] *artihyī* etc.; then the desiderative suffix *san*, the augment *iṭ*, and the substitution of *guṇa* and *ayādeśa* [occur].
Thus: *adhyāpipayiṣati*.
By [Pāṇini 6.1.48], there is the substitution of *ā* for the root vowel; by [Pāṇini 6.1.2], there is reduplication of the element *pā*.
Thus, one says *adhyajīgapat*.
Furthermore, by [Pāṇini 3.1.48], the suffix *caṅ* is applied.
By the rule *ṇau caṅyupadhāyā hrasvaḥ* [Pāṇini 7.4.1], there is shortening of the penultimate vowel;

by the rule *sanvallaghuni* [Pāṇini 7.4.93], the status of being like the *san* suffix applies, resulting in *ittva* (the substitution of *i*) by the rule *sanyataḥ* [Pāṇini 7.4.79]; and by the rule [7.4.94], there is lengthening of the *i*. Thus, one says *īhāmāsa*.
The suffix *ām* is applied by [Pāṇini 3.1.36] *īhateḥ*.
By [Pāṇini 2.4.81] *āmaḥ*, there is elision (*luk*) of the *liṭ* suffix. Then, by [Pāṇini 3.1.40] *kṛñcānuprayujyate liṭi*, the root *as* is employed after the *liṭ* suffix.
This is because the inclusion of the term "re-utterance" (*pratyāhāra*) implies that the root *as* is intended to be included.

In the rule *kṛñ cānuprayujyate liṭi* (Pāṇini 3.1.40), the term *kṛñ* is understood as a pratyāhāra (a grammatical abbreviation). It begins with the word *kṛ* from the rule *abhūtatadbhāve kṛbhvastiyoge sampadyakartari* (5.4.50) and extends up to the letter *ñ* in *ā-kṛño ñakārāt* (5.4.58).

By means of this inclusion of the pratyāhāra, the root *as* is also included; the sole purpose of this inclusion is so that the form *āsa* may occur when this [root] is used in conjunction with the aforementioned suffixes.

If the substitution of *bhū* were to occur even when *as* is used as an auxiliary (*anuprayoga*), then the form *āset* would not be possible when *as* is used as an auxiliary; thus, the inclusion of the *pratyāhāra* [the term *kṛ-bhv-as-*, which includes *as*] would be purposeless.

Consequently, one should simply have stated: "In the perfect tense (*liṭ*), *kṛ* is used as an auxiliary. Even in that case, there would remain the doubt whether this refers to the *pratyāhāra* or merely to the root *kṛ*; by including the *pratyāhāra*, such a doubt is removed. Furthermore, since the *pratyāhāra* has been included, it follows by the force of that inclusion that the substitution of *bhū* does not occur for *as* even when it is used as an auxiliary.
With the words "And so it is said," etc., he confirms the very point just mentioned by means of the statement of an authoritative teacher (*āptavacana*).

[The rule] *bhū* is stated with a long vowel so that a short vowel might not be heard in the formation of the past participle (*niṣṭhā*)—as in *bhūtaḥ* or *bhūtavān*. [Furthermore, the rule] *aster* is indicated by the suffix *śtip* so that it might not apply to the root *as* (to be). But this is unnecessary; for by the metarule (*paribhāṣā*) "that which lacks an indicatory letter (*anubandha*) [supersedes that which has one]," it will not apply to *as*. The letter *ṛ* is made its indicatory letter (*anubandha*) for the purpose of distinguishing it [from *as*] by the rule *idito vā* [Pāṇini 7.2.56].
The letter *a* in *asteḥ* is for the purpose of pronunciation (*uccāraṇārtha*), not an indicatory letter (*anubandha*).
In that case, some say that the mention [of the root] with the suffix *śtip* is for the sake of variety;
others say it is because the paribhāṣā concerning "that which lacks an indicatory letter" applies only to the domain of rules prescribing suffixes (*pratyayavidhi*). Thus: "the speaker" (*vaktā*).
The substitution of *k* [for *c*] occurs by the rule [8.2.30].
Regarding "ūce":

the *samprasāraṇa* (vocalization) occurs by the rule [6.1.15] concerning the root *vac* and others. "The *ātmanepada* [middle voice] ending does not necessarily occur" means that it is not obligatory.

For if it were [otherwise], the addition of the indicatory letter *a* would be purposeless. Therefore, the *ātmanepada* ending shall occur when the fruit of the action is intended for the agent (*kartṛ*), and not otherwise. Regarding the phrase "also beginning with *kśa*":
the vowel *a* in the letters *ka* and *śa* is for the sake of pronunciation.
The substitute *khyāñ* in this form must be stated [as the replacement for *cakṣ*].
But how is such a substitute obtained even though it is desired? Because of the continued application (*anuvṛtti*) of the previously mentioned term "diversely" (*bahulam*).

Therefore, because of the continued application of the term "diversely," one must provide the explanation that there is a prohibition of the substitute in the case of *varjana* (avoiding) and in the case of *asan* (non-existence). Thus: *saṃcakṣyā*.
By the rule *ṛhaloṇryat* [Pāṇini 3.1.124], we have *nṛcakṣas*.
By the rule *sarvadhātubhyo'sun* [Daiva-Uṇādi 9.49], there is lengthening [of the vowel] according to *6.4.14*.
Thus, *vicakṣaṇaḥ*.
The suffix *lyuṭ* is applied in the sense of the agent according to [Pāṇini 3.3.113]. Regarding the word "extensively" (*bahulam*) and so forth:

the meaning is that one should explain this as having the sense that, in technical names (*saṃjñā*) and in Vedic usage (*chandas*), operations such as the substitution of *jagdhi* do not occur extensively.
For what purpose? For the sake of food (*anna*).
The words *anna* and so forth are correct (sādhavaḥ) as they are;
however, their explanation must be carried out by relying on that very mention of the term *bahulam*.
Thus: "anna."

The substitution of *jagdhi* for *ad* does not occur here; this is because the term *bahulagrahaṇa* (the mention of "in various instances") continues to apply by way of the "lion's glance" (*siṃhāvalokita*) maxim.
Regarding the word *vadhaka*:

although the substitution of *vadha* for *han*, prescribed by the rule *hano vadha* [Pāṇini 2.4.42] and so forth, is stated to occur in the *liṅ* and *lyuṭ* suffixes, it also occurs when the *ṇvul* suffix is added to the root *han*.

Regarding the word "gātram": the suffix *ṣṭran* is derived according to the *uṇādi* rules; the substitution of *ga-* for *gam-*, which is prescribed by [Pāṇini 2.4.45] in the context of the *luṅ* (aorist), occurs here as well.
Regarding the word "vicakṣaṇaḥ":
the substitution of *khyāñ* for the root *cakṣiṅ* does not occur before the suffix *lyuṭ*.
However, the word *ajira* is an irregularly formed (*nipātita*) derivative from the *uṇādi* class, ending in the suffix *kirac*, according to the rule "ajira-śiśira-śithira" (*Dhātupāṭha* 8.27).
Precisely because of this irregular derivation (*nipātana*), the substitution of *vī* [for *vi*] prescribed by the rule *ajeghañapoḥ* (Pāṇini 2.4.56) does not occur.
By the word "etc. (*ādi*), forms such as *praghasa* are included. In the case of *pravāyakaḥ*, the suffix is *ṇvul*.
In the word *pravayaṇīyam*, the substitution of *ṇ* [for *n*] occurs by [Pāṇini 8.4.29], which prescribes the suffix *anīyar*.
"An addition (*upasaṃkhyāna*) must be made regarding *kyap* when there is a prohibition of *ghañ* and *ap*.
This means that an addition—that is, a formal statement—must be made concerning the prohibition of *kyap* which would otherwise apply when *ghañ* and *ap* are to be used.
The genitive case in "of *kyap*" (*kyapaḥ*) is employed because *kyap* is intended as being related to the prohibition, serving as the cause for that prohibition.

In this regard, the following is the demonstration: by the rule *saṃjñāyāṃ samajanipatamanavida* [Pāṇini 3.3.99] and so forth, the suffix *kyap* will be prescribed for the root *aj* when a name (*saṃjñā*) is to be understood. Furthermore, a name possesses a fixed sequence of phonemes; however, once a substitution (*ādeśa*) has been applied, the name is no longer perceived. Therefore, because the suffix *kyap* is prescribed specifically for the purpose of forming a name, the substitution of *vī* does not take place.
It is held that "in the case of an *ardhadhātuka* suffix beginning with a consonant (*val*), an option is desired."

But how is it that even when *iṭ* is desired, it is obtained? Because the root *aj* is udātta; for that root is listed among the verbal roots (*dhātu*) as being udātta in the sense of "to go. If there were a permanent substitution of *vī* for this root, then its listing as udātta would be purposeless; for *iṭ* does not apply when the substitution of *vī* has been prescribed, because [the resulting form] is anudātta. [The statement] "the term *yu* refers to the suffix *lyuṭ*" is [the explanation].
Because nothing else is possible [to denote].
In the expression "the staff is a means of driving" (*pravayaṇo daṇḍaḥ*), the suffix *lyuṭ* is used in the sense of an instrument (*karaṇe*), as it is by means of this that one drives.

The original form [is maintained]. This is because, according to the rule *ṇyādayo gotrapratyayāḥ* (Pāṇini 4.1.94), the suffixes for the younger generation (*yuvan*) are prescribed only after those that already end in a suffix denoting a lineage (*gotra*).
Thus, it says: *tasmād yūni ñ* (Pāṇini 4.1.95).
By the rule *ata iñ* [Pāṇini 4.1.95],
the word *kauravya* is listed among the *tikādi* group,
immediately after the word *aurasa*.

"There is the inclusion of the *kṣatriya* lineage therein" means that, due to association with the word *aurasa*, which ends in the suffix denoting a *kṣatriya* lineage, the word *aurasa* indeed ends in the suffix for a *kṣatriya* lineage according to [Pāṇini 4.1.166]: "The suffix *añ* after a *kṣatriya* [denoting] a country. Thus, "[the suffix] *aṇ* after *ṛṣi*."
By means of this [sūtra],
namely *kurvādibhyo ṇyaḥ*,
he derives the word *vāmarathya*.

Therefore, [the suffix] *aṇ* is applied as a secondary derivative (*śaiṣika*) by the rule "from Kaṇva and others, in the sense of lineage" (*kaṇvādibhyo gotre*). But surely the word *vāmarathya* is listed among the *kurv-ādi* group, not among the *kaṇv-ādi* group; so how can this have been stated? Even though it is not listed there, nevertheless, because of the reading "for Vāmarathya, as for Kaṇva and others, with the exception of the accent," its status as belonging to the *kaṇv-ādi* group exists; thus, since it was stated in this way, there is no fault. Regarding "Dākṣāyaṇa": the suffix *phak* is applied by [Pāṇini 4.1.101]. Regarding "not from a non-Brahmin or from a mere lineage": [this is the restriction].
In this regard, some have stated: "When there is elision (*luk*) of *aṇ* and *iñ*, there should be an addition to the rule for the *yuvan*-suffix after the mere lineage (*gotra*) of a Kṣatriya.
For them, [the suffix] would not apply after the lineage of a Vaiśya; therefore, the mention of "mere" (*mātra*) is for the purpose that it should also occur after the lineage of a Vaiśya.
For lineages of Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, and Vaiśyas are possible; among these, excluding the Brāhmaṇa lineage, [the suffix] occurs after every other [lineage].
However, in the preceding rule, the mention of *mātṛ* (mother) is for the purpose that [the suffix] might apply even after a *kṣatriya* gotra that does not end in a *tadrāja* affix.
For he demonstrates this by showing the addition (*upasaṃkhyāna*) of the *up* affix after a *tadrāja* affix when there is elision (*luk*) of *aṇ* and *iñ*,
as in the examples of *vaiśya* gotras such as *bhāṇḍījaṅghiḥ*.
Because the *brāhmaṇa* gotra is excluded here, it does not apply in this case— namely, *dākṣāyaṇa*.
Regarding the phrase "characterized by being a part of Śālva," this was stated with reference to the *kṣatriya* gotras.
Regarding the form *bhāṇḍījaṅghi*, it should be understood that in the Vaiśya gotra, only the suffix *iñ* is applied by the rule *ata iñ* [Pāṇini 4.1.95].

The statement "it is established by the observation of [names] such as Paila" indicates that because the group beginning with Paila is an *ākṛtigaṇa* (an open-ended class), these [names] are to be seen therein. [The rule] "or *aṇ* after *pīlā*" is stated.
For in that case, because the term *aṇ* is understood from the rule [Pāṇini 4.1.112], it is said:
"The others, beginning with Paila, end in *iñ*.
Here, the word *audañci* ends in *iñ* because it belongs to the *bāhv-ādi* group.
The word *hradañcu* is recited among [the roots] beginning with *bāhu*.
The pronunciation of the vowel *u* is not essential (*atantra*),
because it serves merely to indicate the verbal root (*dhātu*).
The suffix *kvin* is applied by the rule [Pāṇini 3.2.59] *ṛtvig-dakṣi...* etc., because of the word *udañc*.
The offspring of *udañc* is *audañciḥ*.

Due to a grammatical irregularity (*nipātana*), the elision of the nasal [prescribed by Pāṇini 6.4.24] *aniditām...* etc., does not occur; furthermore, the elision of the vowel *a* occurs by [Pāṇini 6.4.138] *acaḥ*.
The word *bhauliṅgi* is a derivative of a part of *śālva* ending in the suffix *iñ*.
As for the remaining [names], they should be understood as ending in *iñ* by virtue of the rule *ata iñ* [Pāṇini 4.1.95].

Regarding the reading *śālaṅki*: how is that possible, since according to the reading in the *naḍādi* group—*śalaṅku śalaṅkañ ca* [Gaṇasūtra 67]—the form should be *śālaṅkāyana*? Some say that there is another base word *śalaṅku*, and from that this *iñ* is prescribed.

From this very rule of irregular derivation (nipātana), it is understood that the suffix *iñ* is applied after the word *śalaṅku*; furthermore, others hold that in connection with that [suffix], there is the substitution of *śalaṅka* for the original base.
Regarding the rule "and after a *tadrāja* [term], the suffix *aṇ*": after a term designated as *tadrāja*, there is the elision (*luk*) of the *yuva* suffix that follows the suffix *aṇ*.

The term *apatyam* (offspring) [is used] here; by the rule *dvyañmagadha* (Pāṇini 4.1.168), the suffix *phiñ* is applied, which is elided (*luk*) by this [present rule]. Elsewhere, the mention of "eastern" (*prāk*) is seen to have the purpose of providing an option (*vikalpa*); therefore, he says "*gotraviśeṣaṇam*" and so forth, so that an option might not be understood here as well. In the list beginning with *taulvali*, the words *āntarahāti* and *pauṣkarasādi* end in the suffix *iñ*. For in the *bāhvādi* group, the word *antaraha* and the word *puṣkarasat* are recited; in this case, there is vocalization (*vṛddhi*) of both members because they belong to the *anuraśatikādi* class.

The remaining [names], however, end in the suffix *iñ* by virtue of [Pāṇini 4.1.95] *ata iñ*. Regarding the phrase "occurring in the plural" (*bahuṣu vartamānasya*), the meaning is "occurring in multiple referents" (*bahuṣvartheṣu vartamānasya*). Now, why is it not explained as "when the plural number follows" (*bahuvacane parataḥ*)? It is impossible to state it thus; for the word *bahu* denotes number (*saṃkhyā*), and does not denote the plural case-ending (*bahuvacana*).

If, however, the intended meaning here were "when a plural [number] follows," then one would not have formulated the prohibition "not in the feminine" (*na striyām*); for there is no possibility of its application.
