Indeed, there is no possibility of elision (*luk*) when a plural follows that is separated by a feminine suffix produced from a *tadrāja* stem. Furthermore, if elision were prescribed when a plural follows in the case of *attrayaḥ*, the *udāttanivṛtti-svara* (the accent of the disappearance of the acute) would result.

How so? From the rule *attrerapatyāni bahūni* [Pāṇini 4.1.122], the suffix *ḍhak* is applied; when its udātta accent on the final syllable is established by *taddhitasya* and *kitah* [Pāṇini 6.1.170, 165], and then the elision (*luk*) of the suffix occurs before the plural case-ending *jas* by *atribhṛgukutsavasiṣṭha* [Pāṇini 2.4.65], the rule *udāttayaṇo halpūrvāt* [Pāṇini 6.1.161] would result in the udātta accent for the case-ending. Therefore, the meaning is precisely this: "occurring in the sense of the plural."

The phrase "in the case of many" (*bahuṣu*) is a qualifier for that which ends in a *tadrāja* suffix, not for the *tadrāja* suffix itself; otherwise, a fault would arise in the case of a *dvandva* compound—for instance, in the example *āṅgaśca vāṅgaśca sauhṛdśca* (the Aṅgas, Vāṅgas, and Sauhṛdas), the suffix *huṅ* would not apply; for here the *tadrāja* suffix does not denote many [individuals], but rather that which ends in the *tadrāja* suffix does, since a *dvandva* denotes multiple substrates simultaneously.

Therefore, this qualification applies only to that which ends in a *tadrāja* suffix, not to the *tadrāja* suffix itself. However, the commentary (*vṛtti*) passage—"the *tadrāja*-named suffix, when occurring in the plural and not being feminine, undergoes elision (*luk*)"—is to be interpreted as follows: "of the *tadrāja*-named suffix which is related to that which ends in a *tadrāja* suffix and occurs in the plural and is not feminine, there is elision (*luk*) of that *tadrāja*-named suffix. How so? This capacity is obtained precisely for that which ends in a *tadrāja* suffix.
Indeed, the suffix designated as *tadrāja* does not belong to that which ends in it.
Furthermore, the mention of "ending" (*anta*) was not made in the rule [Pāṇini 2.4.62], because the ending in that suffix is obtained by the very paribhāṣā regarding the mention of a suffix.

Nevertheless, when elision (*luk*) is prescribed for that which ends in a suffix, it is understood to apply to the suffix alone; for, according to [Pāṇini 1.1.61], the technical term *luk* is prescribed only for the non-appearance of a suffix.
"By that very [suffix]" means by that which ends in the suffix denoting a kingdom (*tadrājapratyaya*). Examples are: *aṅgāḥ*, *vaṅgāḥ*, *suhmāḥ*.
There are many descendants of Aṅga;
by the rule *dvyañmagadha* [Pāṇini 4.1.168], the suffix *aṇ* is applied, which is then elided (*luk*).
Thus we have "the Lohadhvajās" and "the Vrīhimantas."
The suffix *ñya* is applied by the rule *pūgāññyo'grāmaṇīpūrvāt* [Pāṇini 5.3.112], and there is its elision (*luk*). Thus, "aupagavāḥ" (the descendants of Upagu).
By the rule *prāgdīvyato'ṇ* [Pāṇini 4.1.83], "priyavāṅgāḥ" (those for whom the Vāṅgas are dear) is a *bahuvrīhi* compound.

In this case, the elision does not occur by means of the *tadrāja* suffix, but rather by means of the compound (*samāsa*). Nor is that [compound] one ending in a *tadrāja* suffix; therefore, because the *tadrāja* suffix has not been prescribed for it, [the elision would not apply].

If that is so, then since a *dvandva* compound also does not end in a *tadrāja* suffix, would there not likewise be no elision in that case either? This is not so; even if the *dvandva* as a whole does not end in a *tadrāja* suffix, nevertheless each individual member of the *dvandva* ends in a *tadrāja* suffix and possesses the sense of a *gaha* (a settlement). Therefore, the elision certainly occurs in that instance.

Furthermore, "in the case of many" does not mean the inclusion of the meaning [of plurality]; for where there is the meaning of "many," there must necessarily be a plurality produced by that very [meaning]. Why then [use] the phrase "by that very [plurality]"? He thinks as follows: because it is internal (*antaraṅga*), if at the time of the production of the *tadrāja* suffix only that plurality which arises [at that moment] were taken—and not that which depends on another word—then there would be no elision (*luk*) in the case of *dvandva* compounds.

The inclusion of the word "tenaiva" (by that very [suffix]) indicates that this is a second effort: namely, that the plurality belonging to that which ends in a suffix is effected by that very suffix, and it occurs in all such cases even when depending on another word.

If this were so, would it not also apply here in the case of *priyavāṅgāḥ*? This is not a fault, for the particle "eva" is used here; it establishes a restriction with respect to only those of the same class, meaning only that plurality which is effected by [suffixes] characterized by elision (*lopin*).

Furthermore, in the case of *priyavāṅgaḥ*, the plural number was not formed by those [names] that undergo elision (*lopin*), because here some words undergo elision while others do not. And such being the restriction, even in a *dvandva* compound where there are both words that undergo elision and words that do not, [the plural] does not occur—according to [Pāṇini 2.4.62]. Here, in the case of *gārgyakāśyapayoḥ*, elision would apply according to [Pāṇini 4.1.101].
However, for *gālava*, since it ends in the *ṛṣyaṇ* suffix, there is no occurrence of elision (*luk*).
Thus: *āṅgyaḥ*.

The suffix *ṅīp* is applied by the rule *ṭiḍḍhāṇañ* [Pāṇini 4.1.15]. Someone might have the misconception that this term "gotra" refers only to the technical definition—namely, "the lineage beginning with the grandson" [Pāṇini 4.1.162]—and not to the common, worldly sense. Therefore, in order to dispel that notion, he says: "And elsewhere, that which is to be enjoined by a suffix," and so forth.
It is understood from this that both meanings are possible within this grammatical system (*śāstra*).

When the worldly *gotra* (lineage) is mentioned, the technical (*śāstrīya*) *gotra* is included therein; however, there is an indicator (*jñāpaka*) that the worldly *gotra* is not included when a suffix is prescribed. This is because, having used the term *gotra* in [Pāṇini 4.2.39], he employs the term *rājanya* [in 4.2.53]; this indicates that the worldly *gotra* is not taken when a suffix is prescribed. For example: "The students of Yāska" (*yāskāś chātrāḥ*), where the suffix *aṇ* is applied by [Pāṇini 4.3.120].

The word *puṣkarasat* is also recited here; for what purpose? Since [the formation] would be established by the rule "after a base with many vowels, *iñ* is added in the case of the Easterners and the Bharatas" (Pāṇini 4.1.161), one might ask why it is not already accounted for. It is not so established; for the prohibition [of *iñ*] in the rule "not after [bases ending in] *yañ*" (Pāṇini 4.1.162) would apply. For some read "taulvalyādayaḥ" (those beginning with Taulvali) in the list of Gopavana and others, and the word *puṣkarasat* is read among those beginning with Taulvali. And since there is a reading of the Taulvalis and others in the list of Gopavana and others, this very reading of the word *puṣkarasat* among the Yaska and others serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*) [that the prohibition does not apply]. Regarding "Gārgya": the feminine suffix *ṅīp* is applied by the rule "and after a base ending in *yañ*" (Pāṇini 4.1.16).
By [Pāṇini 6.4.148], there is the elision of the vowel *i*, and by [Pāṇini 6.4.150], there is the elision of the consonant *y*.
For in that context, the term "ya" is carried over from [Pāṇini 6.4.149], and the term "lopa" (elision) is carried over from [Pāṇini 6.4.134].
Thus, we have the form "vaidyaḥ."
"From *śārṅgarava* and so forth, the suffix *yañ* takes *ṅīn*" [Pāṇini 4.1.73]. Examples include *dvaipyāḥ* and *autsāḥ*.
Here, *yañ* and *añ* are applied in the sense of secondary (*śaiṣika*) suffixes such as "born from" (*jāta*) and so on. This refers to the rule beginning with "*yañādīnām*" and so forth.

Since it is stated that the elision (*luk*) of the suffixes *yañ* and others occurs when there are many [objects], this rule is formulated because [elision] would otherwise apply even in the case of singularity and duality.

Furthermore, the expression "in one or two" (*ekadvayoḥ*) is a reference where the number is the primary meaning, just as in the rule “the dual and singular endings are used for two and one” (*dvayekayordvivacanaikavacane*); that is to say, it refers to the states of singularity and duality. The word *upasaṃkhyāna* means "explanation" or "addition. The word "should be done" (*kartavyam*) is to be supplied [as the verb].
In this regard, the following is the demonstration: from the rule *vā yau* [Pāṇini 2.4.57], the word *vā* ("or") is carried over by means of the "frog-leap" (*maṇḍūkapluti*) maxim.
The particle *ca* ("and") is employed here for the purpose of including that which has not been explicitly stated.
Consequently, in a *tatpuruṣa* compound, there is the elision (*luk*) of the genitive case ending after one or two of the suffixes beginning with *yañ*.

If the word *vā* (or) is understood to carry over, then there would be an option even in the case of many [suffixes]. This fault does not arise, because the option is understood as being restricted (*vyavasthitavibhāṣā*). Regarding the example "āṅgakulam":

here, the suffix *aṇ*, which bears the technical name *tadrāja*, is applied after the word *aṅga*; however, this suffix is not one beginning with *yañ*, because in this section it is prescribed before the suffixes beginning with *yañ*.
Regarding "upagāgryam":
this is an *avyayībhāva* compound formed according to the rule "an indeclinable [preceded by] a case ending" (Pāṇini 2.1.6) and so forth.
Regarding "paramagārgyaḥ": [this is a *tatpuruṣa* compound].

By [Pāṇini 2.1.61] and so forth, a *tatpuruṣa* compound is formed of two words ending in the nominative case. Regarding "Ātreyyaḥ"—the printed reading is "Ātreyaḥ"—[the suffix] *ṅīp* is applied by [Pāṇini 4.1.15]:
*ṭiḍḍhāṇañ*.
Regarding "Bharatāḥ": [this is likewise derived].

Those for whom Bharata was the first name-giver are the Bharatas. In examples such as "Pannāgārāḥ" and others, the suffix *iñ* [Pāṇini 4.1.95] is applied, followed by its elision (*luk*). As for "Bālākayaḥ": [the same process applies].
The suffix *iñ* is applied because [the word] belongs to the *bāhv-ādi* group. Regarding the form *hāstidāsyaḥ*, the suffix *iñ* is applied by [Pāṇini 4.1.95]: *ata iñ*.
Regarding "ārjunāyanaḥ":

the suffix *phak* is applied by [Pāṇini 4.1.101] "yañiyośca. He shows that since this is included within the group beginning with *vida* (the *vidādi-gaṇa*), the elision [of the suffix] would otherwise have been required; thus he gives the example "śaigravāḥ."
Now, since others such as Harita and so forth are also recited here, why is it determined that there are only this many? To this he says: "Of the remaining," and so on.
"A reading due to negligence" means a reading that is not of Vedic (or authoritative) origin.

If their recitation is due to negligence, then in that case, because they are not included among the *bidādi* group, the suffix *añ* would not apply to them either; therefore, he says "for they," and so forth.
For they are indeed recited in the fourth chapter, among the *bidādi* group, prior to the *gopavanādi* group; thus, this undesirable consequence does not arise.

As for the reading of these [names] after the eight beginning with Gopavana and so forth, that is said to be a mistaken reading. Although the genitive case ending is uttered after a form ending in a suffix, nevertheless, the elision (luk) is understood to apply to the suffix itself, not to the whole word ending in that suffix; for this technical term "elision" (luk) is prescribed for the non-appearance of a suffix, not for the non-appearance of a word ending in one. Having considered this, he says: "In the case of the gotra-suffixes of Āgastya and Kauṇḍinya. These are two genitives in apposition. The meaning is: "of those two which are the constituent gotra-suffixes of Āgastya and Kauṇḍinya."
Showing those two conditions in their own form, he says: "After *aṇ* and *yañ*.
Although the elision (*luk*) of *yañ* is already established, it is nevertheless prescribed again so that its sublation by the substitute *kuṇḍina* might not be understood [as intended].
For the word *kuṇḍinī* has its acute accent on the middle syllable.
When the suffix *ini* is applied according to [Pāṇini 5.2.115] in the derivation "kuṇḍam asyāsti" (he who has a water-pot), by virtue of the accent of the suffix (*pratyayasvara*),
the rule "that which is a substitute should also be like that" would apply;
thus, by the principle of *sthānivadbhāva*, the word would become middle-accented (*madhyodātta*).
Because of the presence of the *cit* marker, the middle-udātta accent does not occur.
Why, then, is this substitution not made for the two other suffixes? To this he says: "of those two," and so forth.
If this substitution were made only for the two other suffixes, then the prohibition [in Pāṇini 6.1.217] beginning with "na" would not apply.

Since this prohibition applies to the elision (*luk*) and not to the substitute (*ādeśa*), the substitute would indeed occur here; consequently, by the rule *avṛddhādaṇ*, only the suffix *aṇ* would apply. Thus, the undesired form *āgastāḥ* would result. Even if the substitute were considered *vṛddha* due to its status as a *sthānivat* (acting like its original), and thus included under the term *vṛddha*, the form would still be *āgastīyāḥ* and not the desired *āgastīyāḥ*. Furthermore, the status of being *sthānivat* cannot be obtained here, because the designation *vṛddha* is not a rule concerning phonemes (*alvidhi*).

In this case, when there is elision (*luk*) of the suffix, once the substitute has been prescribed for what remains, and the elision itself is then prohibited by [Pāṇini 4.1.89], the form becomes established by [Pāṇini 4.2.114].

"There is no distinction therein" means that even if the designation *vṛddha* were present, by the exception [stated in] [Pāṇini 4.2.111], it must be formed with the suffix *aṇ* alone; thus, there is no difference in the case of Kauṇḍinya. [The rule applies to] "roots and nominal stems."

If this were the locative case (saptamī), then the meaning would be understood as follows: "The elision (luk) occurs of that case-ending which is proximate to both a verbal root (dhātu) and a nominal stem (prātipadika).

Since proximity is not possible without immediate contact (upaśleṣa), this rule would apply here as well in the case of *vṛkṣaḥ* and *plakṣaḥ*, for even here there is contact between the nominal stem and the case-ending.

Therefore, considering that the genitive case (ṣaṣṭhī) is more appropriate, he says: "Of the case-ending (*sup*), [the elision occurs] when [the nominal stem] has the designation 'verbal root' (*dhātusaṃjñā*)," and so forth.

But how can a case-ending (vibhakti) receive the designation of *dhātu* and the designation of *prātipadika*? To this he says: “contained within that,” and so forth. [Objection: Even so, the case-endings would merely be parts of the *dhātu* and *prātipadika*, and thus they would not themselves be designated as *dhātu* nor designated as *prātipadika*. [Response: There is no fault here, for words that apply to wholes also function with respect to their parts. As in the example: *putrīyati*.

In the expression *ātmanaḥ putram icchati* ("he desires a son for himself"), the substitution of *i* [for the final vowel] occurs by [Pāṇini 7.4.33]; then, by [Pāṇini 3.1.32], it receives the technical designation of a verbal root (*dhātu*). Since this [suffix] *kyac* is prescribed after a word ending in a case-suffix (*subanta*), it applies only to that which already possesses a case-suffix; therefore, in this instance, the case-ending becomes part of the verbal root.
Regarding the example *kaṣṭaśritaḥ* ("one who has resorted to hardship"):
the compound *kaṣṭaṃ śritaḥ* is formed by [Pāṇini 2.1.24], beginning with the rule "the second case [is compounded] with *śrita*," etc.

By the rule *[[1.2.46]]*, the designation *prātipadika* (nominal stem) is established; since a compound (*samāsa*) occurs only of those [elements] ending in case-suffixes (*subanta*), this [designation] applies only to that which already possesses a case-suffix.
Therefore, even here, the case-suffix is included within the *prātipadika*.

However, in the cases of *vṛkṣaḥ* and *plakṣaḥ*, because the prohibition of the *prātipadika* designation applies to what "ends in a suffix" (*apratyaya*), there is no *prātipadika* designation for that which includes the case-suffix; thus, there is no inclusion of the case-suffix within the *prātipadika*. [This is illustrated by the example] *trādhvam*.

The root *traiṅ* meaning "to protect" (*dhātupāṭhaḥ* 965) belongs to the *bhūvādigaṇa*. In the *loṭ* [imperative] mood, there is the substitution of *dham*; the final vowel is changed to *e*; and by the rule *savābhyām ām vāmau* [Pāṇini 7.1.91], there is the substitution of *ām*. Regarding the phrase "when a suffix beginning with a vowel follows": the mention of "suffix" (*pratyaya*) is intended to show that the term "vowel" (*ac*) here does not refer to the technical *pratyāhāra* (abbreviation). For if the intention were to employ the *pratyāhāra*, he would have used the letter *ṇ* in the form *aṇi* instead.
The intention is that no vowels other than *ac* can follow after a suffix ending in *yaṅ*. This very mention of *ac* is the indicator (*jñāpaka*) that all verbal roots fall within the *pacādi* group.
[Thus we have] "loluvaḥ."

The suffix *yaṅ* is applied by the rule "dhātor ekāco halādeḥ kriyāsamabhihāre" [Pāṇini 3.1.22]; reduplication occurs by the rule "dvi-va-canaṃ" [Pāṇini 6.1.9]; and the *guṇa* substitution occurs by the rule "guṇo yaṅ-lukoḥ" [Pāṇini 7.4.82]. When the form *lolūya* is established, the suffix *ac* (forming a nominal stem) is added by the rule "pacādyac"; the *yaṅ* suffix is elided; the prohibition of *guṇa* is applied by the rule "na dhātulopa" [Pāṇini 1.1.4] et cetera;
and the *uvaṅ* substitution is applied by the rule "aci śnu-dhātu" [Pāṇini 6.4.77] et cetera.
"Sanīruāṃsaḥ | Danīdhvaṃsaḥ.
[The roots] *ruāṃsu* and *dhvansu* [are used] in the sense of "falling down" (*avaruāṃsane*)—(Dhātupāṭha 754, 755). The operations of the *yaṅ* [intensive suffix] are applied as before.

Because of the prohibition [stated] in [Pāṇini 1.1.63], the elision of the nasal [of the root] by means of the technical designation of an affix (pratyayalakṣaṇa) according to [Pāṇini 6.4.24], *aniditām* etc., does not occur.
By [Pāṇini 7.4.84], *nīgvañcu* etc., the augment *nīg* is added to the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*). Thus:
*lālapīti*, *vāvadīti*.
By [Pāṇini 7.4.83] *lapervadeca*, there is lengthening of the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*).

By [Pāṇini 7.3.94] *yaṅo vā*, the augment *iṭ* is optionally applied. It is said that "the suffix *śap* is what is being carried forward (*anuvartate*), not *yaṅ*," because it is only *śap* that is formally declared to be *svarita*.
In the case of *juhoti*,
there is reduplication by [Pāṇini 6.1.10] *ślau*. In the case of *bibharti*...

The substitution of *at* by [Pāṇini 7.4.66] *urat* applies; the substitution of *apṛkta* by *ra* by [Pāṇini 1.1.51] *rapara* applies; and the substitution of *it* by [Pāṇini 7.4.76] *bhṛñām it* applies.
Regarding the form *nenekti*:

the root *ṇijir* is listed in the Dhātupāṭha (1093) as meaning "purification and nourishment. By the rule *nijāṃ trayāṇāṃ guṇaḥ* (Pāṇini 7.4.75), there is a substitution of *guṇa*, and by *ślau* (6.1.10), there is reduplication. Regarding *dāti* and *dhāti*:
although the previous rule would have required reduplication for the roots *dā* and *dhā* when followed by *ślu*, it is here prohibited extensively (*bahulam*).
The *śap* suffix is elided. Regarding the form *vivaṣṭi*:

the root *vaś* (meaning "to desire," Dhātupāṭha 1080) would normally undergo the elision of *śap* due to belonging to the *adādi* class; however, here *ślu* is applied instead. By the rule *ślau* [Pāṇini 6.1.10], reduplication occurs. While the rule *bhṛñām it* [7.4.76] is still in force, the substitution of *i* for the penultimate vowel is applied by [7.4.78]. Finally, the change to *ṣ* is effected by the rule on *vraśca*-type roots [8.2.36].
By [Pāṇini 8.4.41], there is the substitution of *ṣṭu* for *tu*.

Regarding the term "vibhakti": the root *bhaj* in the sense of "service" (*sevā*) belongs to the *bhvādi* class (Dhātupāṭha 998). There is *ślu* replacement for *śap*, the *it* designation is as before, and by [Pāṇini 8.2.30], there is the substitution of *ku* for *j*.
In some places, the reading is *vivakti*. This should be understood as belonging to the root *vaca* (Dhātupāṭha 1063), "to speak," which belongs to the first class (*adādi*). Regarding *agāt*:
the substitution of *gā* [for *i*] occurs by the rule *imo gā luṅi* (Pāṇini 2.4.45).
"Apāt" [is derived from] "pā pāne" (Dhātupāṭha 925); [it means] "he drank.
"Abhūt" [is derived from] "bhū sattāyām" (Dhātupāṭha 1); [it means] "it was."
By the rule *[[Pāṇini 1.1.5]]*, there is a prohibition of guṇa. Regarding the statement, "In the mention of *gā* and *pā*, there is the mention of *iṇ* and *pibati*":
first, the mention of the substitute *iṇ* is understood precisely from the form *gāti*, because of its indication by means of the *śtip* affix.

For an indication made with *śtip* is performed for the purpose of referring to that which is devoid of a verbal suffix (*vikaraṇa*), so that there may be the mention of only that which has the *luk*-elision of the suffix; otherwise, if the intention were to mention the root *gāyati*, he would have simply said *gā*.

If that is so, then by the rule "In the case of the mention of *gam*, *ā*, and *grah*, there is no distinction" (Vyāḍīya-paribhāṣā 124), there would be the inclusion of both [roots]; what, then, is the purpose of the mention by means of the *śtip* affix? Therefore, this very mention by means of the *śtip* affix indicates: "This is the inclusion of only the substitute [root] *im*, not of the root *gāyati*.

Furthermore, regarding the mention of *pā*, that it refers specifically to the root *pibati* is understood through the paribhāṣā: "Between a root with a *luk*-suffix and one with a non-*luk*-suffix, only the one with the non-*luk*-suffix is included" (Vyāḍīya-paribhāṣā 50).
[Thus we have the form] *aghāsīt*.
From the roots *kai* and *gai* meaning "to sound" (*dhātupāṭha* 916, 917), the augment *suk* is added by [Pāṇini 7.2.73]. Then there is *sic* and *iṭ*;
*iṭ* is applied by [Pāṇini 7.3.96], "after *asti* and *sic*, before an affix consisting of a single phoneme."

By the rule *iṭa īṭi* [Pāṇini 8.2.28], there is the elision of *sic*. Thus, *apāsīt*. [The root] *pā* "to protect" (Dhātupāṭha 1056) undergoes the same operations as before, such as the addition of *suk* and so forth. [Thus,] *āgāsātām*.
The *ātmanepada* endings are used for the *karmavat* (passive-like) construction. [The suffixes] *ātam*, etc.

Now, for what purpose is the elision (*luk*) of *sic* prescribed, rather than simply saying "of *li*" (*ler eva*)? Is it not the case that by doing so, the purpose is achieved here as well, and the mention of *li* need not be made in the subsequent rule? This is not so; for if the elision of *li* were understood here, the accent in forms such as *mā hi gātām* (derived from *gā* with *mā hi*) would not be established, since that [final syllable] is intended to be acute (*udātta*).
Even in the case of *aguḥ*, the substitution of *jus* for *jhi*—by means of [Pāṇini 3.4.110] *ātaḥ* and [3.4.109] *sijabhyastavidibhyaśca*—is not established.

Therefore, it must be stated that there is elision (*luk*) of *sic* itself. [Regarding the roots: *ghrā* in the sense of "taking up a smell" (DhP 926), *dheṭ* in the sense of "drinking" (DhP 902), *śo* in the sense of "making thin" (DhP 1145), *cho* in the sense of "cutting" (DhP 1146), and *ṣo* in the sense of "concluding action" (DhP 1147).
[The phrase] "since the [substitution of *jus*] would apply invariably to *dheṭ* by the preceding rule... [is used].

Because it is designated by the technical term *ghu*. In the alternative where there is no elision (*aluk*), the operations such as *sag* (the addition of *s*) and so forth are applied as before. The mention of *dheṭ* with its indicatory letter (*sānubandhaka*) is for the purpose of excluding *dhāñ*.
If the *kṛt* affix *ātva* were specified, then there would be the inclusion of the root *dhā* as well,
as in "adhrāsātām," where the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) occurs in the sense of the object. [And] "atata."
The *ātmanepada* ending is applied by the rule *svaritañitaḥ* [Pāṇini 1.3.72].
The elision of the nasal is effected by the rule *anudāttopadeśa* [Pāṇini 6.4.37], etc.,
as in the form *ataniṣṭa yayam*.

This [form] ends in the third person plural. While the term *sic* is understood from the previous rule, the mention of *liṭ* again is for the purpose of excluding the operations of *sic* such as those prescribed in [Pāṇini 6.1.187], and for the sake of subsequent rules.
Regarding the form *akṣan*:
it is derived from the root *ad* (meaning "to eat," Dhātupāṭha 1011) in the *luṅ* tense; by [Pāṇini 2.4.37], *ghaslṛ* is substituted for *ad*.

From that [root *hvar*], by [Pāṇini 3.1.43] *iḍitaścler*, the *cli* suffix is introduced; its elision (*luk*) occurs by this [present rule]; *jhi* is replaced by *anta*; the *ik* (the letter *i*) is elided by [Pāṇini 3.4.100] *itaśca*; the *t* is elided by [Pāṇini 8.2.23] *saṃyogāntasya*; the penultimate vowel is elided by [Pāṇini 6.4.98] *gamahanajana...* and so forth; the substitution of *ṣ* occurs by [Pāṇini 8.3.60] *śāsivasighasīnāṃ ca*; the substitution of *jaś* occurs by [Pāṇini 8.4.53]; and the substitution of *car* occurs by [Pāṇini 8.4.54] *khari ca*. The mention of *hvareti* is by means of the adventitious vowel *a*. Thus: *mā hvaḥ*.

In *luṅ*, there is the elision of *tiṅ* due to its being followed by a *guṇa*-augment and a following vowel; the elision of *hal* and *ṅi* etc. according to [Pāṇini 6.1.68]; and the absence of the augment *aṭ* by the rule *na māṅayoge* [6.4.74]. Thus we have *prāṇaḍ*. Regarding this: from the root *ṇaś* in the sense of "disappearance" (Dhātupāṭha 1194), the operations such as *luṅ* apply as before. By the rule *vraścādi-* [8.2.36], there is the substitution of *ṣ*; then by [8.2.39], there is the substitution of *j*—that is, the letter *ḍ* replaces the letter *ṣ*. For that [ḍ], by the rule *vāvasāne* [8.4.55], there is the substitution of *c* (the retroflex *ṭ*), resulting in the letter *ṭ*. Finally, by the rule *upasargādasamāse’pi* [8.4.14], there is the substitution of *ṇ*.
In some places, the reading is *prāṇak*. There, while *ku* is being carried over from [Pāṇini 8.2.62], *kutva* (the substitution of the guttural *k*) occurs by [Pāṇini 8.2.63].
[The form] is *āvaḥ*.

From the root *vṛñ*, there is the suffix *tip*; the *guṇa* substitution occurs, followed by the replacement of the vowel with *ra* (*raparatva*); then, by [Pāṇini 6.1.68], there is the elision (*lopa*) of the suffix *sip*.
Thus, "dhak. From the root *daha* in the sense of "reducing to ashes" (Dhātupāṭha 911), there is the suffix *sip*; by [Pāṇini 6.1.68], there is the elision of the suffix *sip*.

By the rule *iti hasya ghaḥ* [8.2.32], *ha* becomes *gh*. By the rule *ekāco baśo bhaṣ* [8.2.37] and so forth, *da* becomes *dha*; for *dha*, there is *jaś*-ness, resulting in *ga*; for that, there is *car*-ness, resulting in *ka*. Regarding the augment *āṭ*, there is a prohibition by the rule *bahulaṃ chandasyāmāṅyoge’pi* [6.4.75].
Thus: *āprāt*.
From the root *prā* in the sense of "filling" (Dhātupāṭha 1061), the suffix *tip* is applied.
Regarding the form *parāvarka*: from the root *vṛj*, *tip* is applied; there is the guṇa substitution for the light penultimate vowel, and then elision according to Pāṇini 6.1.68 (*halṅyādinā*).

Due to the restriction [niyama] "of that which ends in r or s" (Pāṇini 8.2.24), there is no elision of the final consonant of the conjunct (*saṃyogāntalopa*). The substitution of *g* for *j* occurs as before, and its substitution by *k* occurs through the rule of *cartva*. Thus: *akran*.
In the case of *kṛ*, there is the substitution of *anta* for *jhi*; then, by the rule *saṃyogāntalopaḥ*, the final consonant is elided. Regarding the form *ajñata*:

the substitution of *at* for the *jh* of the root *jan* occurs according to [Pāṇini 7.1.5], followed by the elision of the penultimate vowel as before, and finally the substitution of *c* for *j* according to [Pāṇini 8.4.40].
In some places, the reading is *ajñan*. In that case, the suffix *jhi* occurs, and consequently the *parasmaipada* ending should be applied.
[This] is the usage in the *Brāhmaṇa*.
This work on the explanation of the mantra, which follows immediately after the mention of *jan* in the mantra, is the Brāhmaṇa.
An example concerning that [case where *jan* appears with the elision of *luK*] has not been presented, because it is stated that "in the mantra, *jan* is seen with the elision of *luK*.
If, then, the elision occurs outside of the mantra, for what purpose is the mention of "mantra"? To this he says: "The mention of 'mantra'," and so forth. "He performed effort" (*īhāñcakre*).
The root *iṣ* is listed in the Dhātupāṭha as "īha ceṣṭāyām" (632). In the periphrastic perfect (*liṭ*), the suffix *ām* is applied by the rule "ijādeśca" (Pāṇini 3.1.36).

Because this *ām* ends in *m*, the entire form ending in *kṛt* receives the designation of a nominal stem (*prātipadika*). The nominative singular suffix *su* is added; however, because *ām* is included in the list beginning with *svarādi*, it is an indeclinable (*avyaya*), and thus the *su* is elided by the rule "avyayādāpsupaḥ" (Pāṇini 2.4.82). By the rule "kṛñ ca" (Pāṇini 3.1.40), the root *kṛ* is employed after the *liṭ* suffix. The middle voice (*ātmanepada*) is applied by the rule "āmpratyayavat" (Pāṇini 1.3.63), followed by the substitution of *eś* for the *liṭ* suffix, reduplication, and the application of the rules governing the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*). Finally, the *m* of *ām* is replaced by an anusvāra by the rule "mo 'nusvāraḥ" (Pāṇini 8.4.58).

Why then does [the rule] not apply here in *jagāma* and *śaśāma*? Because we state that the term *arthavat* ("meaningful") is understood [in the rule], and this [element *āma*] is meaningless (*anarthaka*). However, the suffix (*pratyaya*) is meaningful according to the principle: "suffixes whose meaning is not explicitly stated occur in their own sense" (Puṣpasūtra 90). Why then does it not apply here in *āmo rogaḥ*? Because of the maxim: "between that which is taught by a general definition and that which is taught by its specific form, only the latter is taken," and this [element *āma*] is taught by a general definition (*lākṣaṇika*). [The example] is *tatra śālāyām*.
From the word *tad*, by adding the suffix *tral* in the sense of the locative case, there is the designation "vibhakti" (case-ending) according to Pāṇini 5.3.1;
then the substitution of *ya* for *tad* etc. occurs, followed by the addition of *ṭāp*, and finally the application of the masculine form (*puṃvadbhāva*).

By the rule *iti tralo 'vyayatvam*, the *tral* suffix is an indeclinable (*avyaya*); consequently, there is elision (*luk*) of the feminine suffix *ṭāp* produced from it. But how can *ṭāp* be produced from an indeclinable? If you say it is by the rule *ajādyataṣṭāp* [Pāṇini 4.1.4], that is not so, because *ṭāp* is prescribed for the feminine gender, whereas an indeclinable lacks gender. Therefore, since the occurrence of *ṭāp* from an indeclinable is impossible, is not the statement regarding the elision of *ṭāp* after an indeclinable redundant? It is not redundant; for this is a designation where the possessor of the quality (*guṇin*) is primary—that is, *ṭāp* and the other suffixes apply when the referent possesses femininity.

And when that word *śālāyām* denotes the referent (*padārtha*) "femininity," the indeclinable *tatra* occurs [in place of it]. Although femininity here is the meaning of the sentence (*vākyārtha*), nevertheless, it is precisely by virtue of being the sentence-meaning that the feminine suffix is indicated; and once the feminine suffix is present, femininity becomes the very referent of the word (*padārtha*). Consequently, the elision (*luk*) of the suffix *ṭāp* must be stated, as in the examples *kṛtvā* and *hmatvā*.

Thus, by [Pāṇini 1.1.40], the suffix *ktvā* is an indeclinable (*avyaya*), and consequently, there is elision (*luk*) of the case endings (*sup*) produced from it. If it is asked, "By what rule is the production of case endings (*sub-utpatti*) from an indeclinable?"—and if one suggests it is by the rule [Pāṇini] 4.1.2 beginning with *svādi*, that is not so; for in that context, by another rule beginning with [Pāṇini] 1.4.21, the case endings beginning with *su* are restricted (*niyata*) to those [words] that possess number (*saṃkhyā*), whereas indeclinables lack number.

It might be argued: "Wherever number exists, the rules for *svādi* suffixes—such as 'the plural [suffix] is used for many' (*bahuṣu bahuvacanam*) [Pāṇini 1.4.21] and so forth—are applied. However, since indeclinables (*avyaya*) are devoid of number, the *svādi* suffixes, which are prescribed generally, must indeed apply to them. This is incorrect; for by the rule for *svādi* suffixes [Pāṇini 4.1.2], there is syntactic unity (*ekavākyatā*) with other rules of the science such as 'the plural [suffix] is used for many' [1.4.21], because the *svādi* suffixes are prescribed therein.

To explain: it has been stated there that number, object, and so forth are the meanings of the *svādi* suffixes as prescribed by other rules of the science; therefore, this [rule for *svādi* suffixes] forms a single syntactical unit with those.
And if there were syntactic unity [between the rule for case endings and the rule for indeclinables], how could there be a general prescription of *svādi* (case endings) etc.?

For there is no other defining characteristic by which *svādi* etc. could be prescribed in a general sense. Therefore, this very statement of the elision (*luk*) of the *sup* suffix produced after an indeclinable is the indicator (*jñāpaka*) that case endings do indeed occur after indeclinables.
Indeed, the elision (*luk*) of that which has not yet arisen is not possible.

This very point serves as the indicator (*jñāpaka*), for it was stated with this in mind: "But from indeclinables (*avyaya*), which are devoid of number, the case-endings (*svādi*) prescribed in general do indeed exist. [And] "When this [elision] is prohibited, there is simply the hearing (*śravaṇa*) of the ablative (*pañcamī*).
How so? Because two meanings are prescribed here, and in the prescriptive rule (*vidhāyaka-vākya*), there are exactly two.
In this context, the rule *nāvyayībhāvādataḥ* is one sentence that prescribes the aforementioned prohibition;
the rule *am tvapañcamyāḥ* is a second sentence that prescribes the substitution of *am*, and in that case, it requires the reference to *ataḥ*.

For this very reason, two sentences are presented in the *Vṛtti*: "The elision (*luk*) of the case-ending (*sup*) following an avyayībhāva compound ending in *a* does not occur"—this is the first sentence; and "but there is the substitution of *am* for it, except in the case of the fifth [case-ending]"—this is the second.

In this context, by the expression "except for the fifth case" (*apañcamyāḥ*), only the substitution of *am* for the fifth case is prohibited, in accordance with the principle that "a rule or a prohibition applies only to what immediately precedes" (*anantarasya vidhir vā bhavati pratiṣedho vā*). The elision (*aluk*) prescribed by the preceding sūtra, however, is not prohibited.
For this very reason, when elision does not occur, the fifth case ending is indeed heard.

If there were a single syntactical unit (*ekavākyatā*), then because two operations would be enjoined through a single application of the text, the prohibition "except for the fifth case" would apply to both operations.
Excluding the fifth case, these two operations are to be understood [as applying].

However, in the case of a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*), the phrase "except for the fifth case" (*apāñcamyāḥ*) depends on the immediate substitute *am*, and not on the non-elision (*aluk*) prescribed by another sentence.

Therefore, being connected with the phrase "except for the fifth case," the non-elision (*aluk*), though prescribed as a general rule, also extends to the fifth case; consequently, the actual hearing of the fifth case-ending is indeed appropriate.

This meaning is also obtained by the word *tu*. Now, it may be argued: "Verbal actions require their factors (*kāraka*s), and it has been stated that an *avyayībhāva* compound is one in which the meaning of the first member is predominant. Since the meaning of the first member is an abstract state (*asattvabhūta*), there can be no connection with an action in its absence; therefore, since the status of being an *apādāna* (ablative) and so forth does not exist, how could case-endings such as the fifth (*pañcamī*) arise from an *avyayībhāva*? This is not so; even when the meaning of the first member is predominant, a connection with an action is possible in relation to the subordinate meaning of the second member, as in the example: "Bring five bundles (*pañcapūlīm ānaya*)."

In that case, even though the abstract state (*bhāva*) is predominant, the connection with the action depends upon the substance (*dravya*) which has become subordinate. For example, in *sumadram*, there is an *avyayībhāva* compound according to [Pāṇini 2.1.6], *avyayaṃ vibhakti* etc., in the sense of abundance.
Similarly, in *unmattagaṅgam*.
By this [rule 2.1.21],
namely "ekaviṃśatibhāradvājam" [by rule 2.1.19], the substitutes *ḍā*, *rau*, and *ras* respectively take the place of the parasmaipada and ātmanepada suffixes.

If this is so, then since *tip*, *tas*, and *jhi* are each designated as the first person (*prathamapuruṣa*) among the *parasmaipada* endings, and likewise *ta*, *ātām*, and *jha* among the *ātmanepada* endings, there would be a discrepancy in number—six original bases (*sthānin*) and three substitutes (*ādeśa*)—and thus, due to the absence of a one-to-one correspondence (*anudeśa*), all the substitutes might apply to each base in turn. This is not a fault; for the assignment will be determined by immediate proximity (*ānantarya*). And that proximity is established by meaning: "that which has a single meaning [replaces] that which has a single meaning, that which has two meanings [replaces] that which has two meanings, and that which has many meanings [replaces] that which has many meanings.
Thus, [the term] "agent" (*kartā*) [is used].

> [[3.3.15]] *tip*, *tasyānekāltvāt*—because it has more than one *al* (phoneme), this [suffix] *ḍā* is a substitute for the whole [stem]. Now, an objection might be raised: "But surely, the status of having more than one *al* is not caused by an *anubandha* (indicatory letter) [according to *Vyāḍi-paribhāṣā* 14], and since the letter *ḍ* is an *anubandha*, how can there be the status of having more than one *al* such that it would be a substitute for the whole? This is not a fault; for as long as the substitution for the whole has not yet occurred, the designation *it* does not apply by the rule *cuṭū* [[1.3.7]]. And in the absence of the *it*-designation, it is not an *anubandha*; thus, because it possesses more than one *al*, it becomes a substitute for the whole.
Even for *ḍittha*, there is the elision of the final syllable (*ṭilopa*) by [Pāṇini 6.4.143] *ṭeḥ*. Thus we have *kartārau* and *kārtāraḥ*;
here, the elision of the *s* occurs by [Pāṇini 7.4.51] *rica*.
Forms such as *adhyeta* and so forth belong to the root *iṅ* "to study" (Dhātupāṭha 1046).
In this case, even though the substitution of *e* for *ī* (by Pāṇini 7.1.91) would apply later, the substitutions beginning with *ḍā* (ḍā, ḍu, ṇa) take effect first because they are *antaraṅga*.
Their status as *antaraṅga* is due to their depending solely upon the original element (*sthānin*) itself.

The substitution of *et* for *ṭi* is extrinsic (*bahiraṅga*), for it depends not only on the substituend but also on the verbal root (*dhātu*); this is because the term "of the verbal root" (*dhātoḥ*) is governed [by Pāṇini] up until the end of the third chapter.

The rule *thāsaḥ se* (Pāṇ. 3.4.80) serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*) that the substitution of *et* for *ṭi* does not apply to substitutes of *tiṅ*. Consequently, even when the substitutes *ḍā*, *rau*, and *ras* have been applied, the substitution of *et* does not take place.

In the word *kartāsi*, there is the elision of the letter *s* by [Pāṇini 7.4.50]. Thus ends the fourth quarter of the second chapter in the *Kāśikā-vivaraṇa-pañjikā* composed by the venerable Ācārya Jinendrabuddhi, who is a follower of the Bodhisattva. The word *pratyaya* is introduced as a technical term (*saṃjñā*) for the purpose of brevity in the treatise.

If the designation *pratyaya* were to be prescribed for many individual bases—namely, the *san*-suffix, the *kyac*-suffix, and the *kyaṅa*-suffix—each by means of separate rules, then there would be prolixity (*gaurava*) in the treatise because of the multiplicity of those bases.
For they do not possess such a commonality that, by taking that as a basis, the designation could be prescribed for many at once by a single rule, as is the case in [Pāṇini 1.1.73].

But surely this exists as a *sa*-group (*sav*), and thus the sūtra could be formulated as "that which has *sa* as its affix" (*sapratyayaḥ*), with the *sa*-group being understood by taking the letter *s* of the suffix *san* up to the letter *p* of the suffix *kap*. This is not so;

for there are many other *p*s, such as those in [Pāṇini 3.1.34] and [Pāṇini 3.1.106]. In that case, if one were to rely on proximity and take the immediately preceding *p* for the purpose of the *sa*-group, then the *sa*-group would be understood as ending with the *p* of *sip* alone.
Now, if pervasion (*vyāpti*) is apprehended, then by the rule *taptanaptanāthanāśca* [Pāṇini 7.1.45], the suffix *tanap* would have to end in the letter *p* itself.
This might be argued: "The principle of pervasion alone must be resorted to."

Nor will there be a rejection of the *pratyāhāra* [term] *tap* by means of the letter *pa*; rather, it is only *ka*, because of the indicative power (*jñāpaka*) of the rule "kapa eva" (Pāṇini 6.3.68). Otherwise, since the technical designation of "suffix" (*pratyaya-saṃjñā*) would apply even in the sixth [chapter], this [rule] would be purposeless. This is not so; for a rule serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*) only when there is no other purpose. But here there is indeed a purpose. What is it? It is so that [the suffix] may be specifically dependent on the suffix *am*, and not merely dependent on the general category of "suffix. Thus, this [rule] would serve as a restrictive injunction (*niyama*), so how could it be redundant?
Furthermore, even if the abbreviation (*pratyāhāra*) were somehow obtained through the letter *ka* alone, there would still be an excessive burden of comprehension (*pratipatti-gaurava*).

Therefore, considering that it is more appropriate to establish this technical term (*saṃjñā*) by means of a governing rule (*adhikāra*) for the sake of brevity, he says: "The word *pratyaya* is governed as a technical term.

If this is so, it must present itself with each individual [element] it governs; and once it has presented itself there, it would connect only with the initial elements and not with the bases (*prakṛti*) and so forth—thus, there is no reason for such a restriction.
Therefore, this designation would also apply to *prakṛti* (base), *upapada* (co-occurring word), *upādhi* (condition), *vikāra* (modification), and *āgama* (augment).
Among these: *prakṛti*—as in [Pāṇini 3.1.5]; *upapada*—as in *stambakarṇayo ramijapoḥ* [3.2.13]; *upādhi*—as in *haraterdatināthayoḥ paśau* [3.2.25].

Although there is no purpose for the designation of the object (*artha*) itself, nevertheless, since it exists for that which expresses it, the designation would indeed apply to that [the expressive word].

A *vikāra* (modification) [is defined by P. 3.1.108], and an *āgama* (augment) [by P. 4.3.138]. Furthermore, when these possess the technical designation of *pratyaya* (suffix), they would have the status of being subsequent (*para*) and the quality of having the acute accent on their first syllable (*ādyudātta*). Although it is impossible for *gup* and the others to be simultaneously subsequent (*para*) with respect to one another, or for *san* and the others to be so, nevertheless, they might occur alternatively—sometimes *gup* and the others would be subsequent, sometimes *san* and the others, or otherwise, *gup* and the others might be subsequent to something else entirely. To address this, he says: "the base and the subordinate word" (*prakṛtyupapada*), and so forth.
And this has been stated precisely as it follows from logical necessity.

How so? Since *prakṛti*, *upapada*, and *upādhi* are indicated by means of the ablative (*pañcamī*) and other case endings in order to establish another grammatical operation, their verbal form ending in the fifth or other case endings is unfit to convey the relationship between a name (*saṃjñā*) and the named (*saṃjñin*).

For instance: either there is a relationship between a name (*saṃjñā*) and the named (*saṃjñin*) through grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with a word ending in the nominative case, where the named—having the form of the name impressed upon it by the intellect—is presented together with the name as having entered into a relation of non-difference, such as in [Pāṇini 1.1.1];

or, when there is an intention to express the difference between the name and the named, the named is presented with the genitive case, being separated from the name-word which is employed as its own-form (*svarūpa*), such as in [Pāṇini 1.1.68].
However, since *prakṛti* and the others exist by taking up specific case-endings suitable for assisting another, it is impossible to establish a relationship of technical name (*saṃjñā*) with them.
Nor is it reasonable to assume that a technical name will apply to them through the ellipsis of a case-ending suitable for the relationship between a name and its bearer;
for ellipsis is appropriate only when there is no scope for the explicit statement, but not when such scope exists.
Furthermore, there is room for [the designation] *sannādi* (beginning with *san*).
Moreover, because the *prakṛti* (verbal root) and the other elements are subordinate, the designation is inappropriate for them;
for in common worldly usage, it is observed that an operation applies to the principal element, as when many people are walking and someone asks, "Who is this going? and he replies, "The king."
In that case, both the one who asks and the one who answers place their trust in the principal element, the king.
Therefore, here too, because the grammatical operation is understood to apply to the principal element—the *saN* suffix and so forth—it will be designated by that very term.
Its primacy, moreover, arises from its being prescribed as something not previously established.

Since *prakṛti* (bases) and the like have their essential natures already determined in the recitation of the *dhātu* and other lists, they are subordinate because they serve as the basis for the introduction of suffixes such as *san*. Therefore, how could they possess a technical name (*saṃjñā*)? Although *āgama* (augment) and *vikāra* (modification) are presented in the nominative case—being fit for the relationship between a name and the named—and possess primacy due to being the objects of prescription (*vidheya*), nevertheless, they do not receive a technical name; for the term "suffix" (*pratyaya*) is made a grand technical name. The purpose of this is so that the name may be etymological (*anvarthasaṃjñā*): it is called a "suffix" (*pratyaya*) because one perceives meanings (*artha*) by means of it. And one does not perceive any meaning through modifications or augments.

If, then, this were a designation based on its literal meaning (*anvarthasaṃjñā*), the designation "suffix" (*pratyaya*) would not apply to [elements] such as those mentioned in rules 5.4.28 and 5.4.29, because of the absence of that meaning.

The meaning [of a word] is twofold: worldly (*laukika*) and technical (*śāstrīya*). Among these, the former is understood through the word-base (*prakṛti*) alone, while the latter is understood through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*). But that [technical meaning] does not exist for them [the suffixes], because their meaning is understood from the base itself even without the suffixes? This is not a fault; for although their meaning is not apprehended through positive and negative concomitance, it is nevertheless apprehended from this very authoritative statement: "Suffixes whose meanings are not explicitly stated [convey] their own meaning" (Puruṣottamadeva’s *Paribhāṣāvṛtti* 90).

Therefore, since those [suffixes] also convey their own meaning, they too would be termed *pratyaya* (suffixes); thus, this over-extension is avoided, and it is established that the designation *pratyaya* does not apply to *prakṛti* (bases) and the like. Regarding the forms "kartavyam" and "karaṇīyam," when the suffixes beginning with *tavyat* receive the designation *pratyaya*, the designation *aṅga* (base) applies to what precedes them by the rule "yasmāt pratyayavidhiḥ" (Pāṇini 1.4.13).

Now, why is *tavyat* and so forth cited as an example immediately after that [the section on *kṛt* suffixes], skipping over *san* and the others which are separated from it? Because in the case of *tavyat* and so forth, there is the possibility of the grammatical operation (*kārya*) associated with the technical name "suffix" (*pratyaya-saṃjñā*) applying even to those beginning with an acute accent (*ādyudātta*);

however, in the case of *san* and the others, that is not possible, because [their accentuation] is already barred by the accent of the verbal root (*dhātu-svara*). The phrase "this too is a governing rule (*adhikāra*)" means that it is not only [the term] "suffix" (*pratyaya*) [that is a governing rule].
This is the meaning of the word "also" (*api*).
"In every [application], it stands present"—this indicates the distinction between a *paribhāṣā* (a metarule) and an *adhikāra* (a governing heading).
A *paribhāṣā*, being situated in only one place, operates throughout the entire treatise; it does not, however, stand present at every individual rule (*pratiyoga*).
"Or it is a *paribhāṣā*":
this indicates an alternative view.

The nature of a *paribhāṣā*—namely, that it operates throughout the entire treatise even though it belongs to only one part—is not explicitly shown in the commentary (*vṛtti*), because it is understood by way of demonstrating the nature of a governing rule (*adhikāra*).

For if this *paribhāṣā* were to operate upon the actual application [of a rule] and be active in the accomplishment of the grammatical effect (*kāryasiddhi*), then there would be no distinction between an *adhikāra* and a *paribhāṣā*; consequently, their separate presentation here would be fruitless.
Furthermore, this *paribhāṣā* possesses an indicator (*liṅginī*), and its indicator is precisely the technical designation *pratyaya*.
The expression "of a verbal root" (*dhātoḥ*) is an elliptical indication (*upalakṣaṇa*) for a stem (*prakṛti*) that denotes an action; by this, even that which ends in a *tiṅ* suffix is included.
Even that [word] can be designated as denoting action because action is its primary meaning;
for designations are made according to what is primary, as in the case of "the royal capital" (*rājadhānī*).
[This is stated in the rule: "Or [it is derived] from the nominal stem" (*prātipadikād vā*).
This is an elliptical reference to a verbal root (*prakṛti*) that does not denote an action; by this, feminine suffixes ending in *ṅī* and *āp* are also included.
Regarding the form "taittirīyam": the suffix *chaṇ* is applied in the sense of "proclaimed by" according to [Pāṇini 4.3.102], *tittirivaratantukhaṇḍikokhācchaṇ*.

From that [suffix] ending in *tad*, the suffix *aṇ* is applied by [Pāṇini 4.2.59]. Its [elision] occurs by [Pāṇini 4.2.64]. Now, for what purpose is the letter *ca* (the "and") used; for there is nothing previously mentioned here that could be conjoined by means of *ca*? To this he says: "The letter *ca*, moreover," and so forth.

Since there is no other element to be compounded, the particle *ca* is understood here as having the sense of compounding; therefore, even under the heading of "frequently" (*bahulam*), when suffixes are prescribed for [words] such as *ṛṇa* and so on, their posteriority is not made optional. But for what purpose is this stated? So that it may be subsequent and not prior. This is not a valid purpose, for he states that which he intends to be prior: "The suffix *akac* comes before the final vowel of indeclinables and pronouns" (Pāṇini 5.3.71).

"Will that other suffix which follows this [rule] be considered 'para' (subsequent) even without being explicitly stated? This is not so; for only those suffixes whose position is specifically restricted by a rule would be considered "restricted in position. That which is different from these and is not restricted in position might sometimes be subsequent, sometimes prior, and sometimes intermediate. Therefore, must it be stated that it is "para"? It need not be stated; because the ablative case in the expressions *dhātoḥ* and *pratipadikāt* is characterized by its connection to spatial direction (*digyoga-lakṣaṇā*), as there is no other cause for the ablative case, such as the *apādāna* kāraka.

Therefore, will this very [rule] supply the word "subsequent" (*paradik*)? This is not so; rather, there would be a supply of the word "prior" (*pūrvadik*), and thus even the prior [elements], such as *sann* and others, might sometimes [be affected].

[Objection: In that case, will the determination be made by this metarule (paribhāṣā): *[[1.1.67]]*? [Reply: This is not so; for the scope of this [metarule] is where an operation (*kārya*) is prescribed for what follows an element specified in the ablative (*pañcamī*), whereas *sann* and others are not specified in the genitive (*ṣaṣṭhī*). Furthermore, even in those cases where an operation related to them is prescribed, it is precisely they who are the things to be brought about (*bhāvyamāna*).

But is it not the case that the technical designation (*saṃjñā*) and the grammatical operation (*kārya*) of being an "affix" (*pratyaya*) are prescribed? It is not so. Furthermore, how can the designation and operation of being an affix be prescribed for those [elements] which do not yet exist? Moreover, what would be the recourse in the case of those for whom even the designation of "affix" is not prescribed—such as *kaṇeṣṭhaḥ* (Pāṇini 5.2.64) and *śamerḍhaḥ* (5.2.29)? For the designation of "affix" is not desired for these; thus, in words such as *kaṇṭhaḥ* and *śaṇḍhaḥ*, the operations prescribed for an affix, such as the substitution of the vowel *i*, do not take place.

If this is so, would not the "subsequent-ness" (*paratva*) being predicated of the suffix also fail to occur? It will occur by virtue of the governing force (*adhikāra*) of the rule *paraśca*. For if this statement were absent, even though that Paribhāṣā were present, the subsequent-ness would be optional in the case of the *uṇādi* suffixes, because they are prescribed under the governing rule *bahulam*. Therefore, this must be stated. By the words "when there is the contingency of a suffix with an indefinite accent," etc., he demonstrates the purpose for the commencement of the Sūtra.

That whose accent (*svara*) is indefinite (*aniyata*) and unsettled (*avyavasthita*) is "that which has an indefinite accent"; this forms a *karmadhāraya* compound with *pratyaya*. Then, a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*) is formed with the word *prasaṅga* [resulting in *aniyatasvarapratyayaprasaṅga*]. When there is the occasion (*prasaṅga*) of such an indefinite-accented suffix (*pratyaya*), this statement is made for the sake of making the initial syllable (*ādi*) acute (*udātta*).
In some places, the reading is *aniyatasvaraprasaṅge*.
In this context, having formed an *aviśeṣa-samāsa* (non-qualificative compound) of the word *aniyata* with the word *svara*, a *ṣaṣṭhī-samāsa* is formed with the word *prasaṅga*.
Since there is an occurrence (*prasaṅga*) of indeterminate accents such as the acute (*udātta*) and so forth, the statement is made for the purpose of making the initial syllable acute.
[This applies] to the rule beginning with "and in polysyllabic words" (*anekākṣu ca*), etc.
Those which have many vowels are called *anekācaḥ*.

Since there is no fixed rule regarding the position [of the accent] among those suffixes that have many vowels, this statement is made for the purpose of making the initial syllable acute: so that the acute accent may belong only to the beginning, and not to the middle or the end.

In the case of suffixes (*pratyaya*) consisting of more than one vowel (*anekāc*), since there is no fixed position [for the accent] within the suffix itself, even if the mention of "the beginning" (*ādi*) were absent, an indeterminate placement of the accent would not be possible. Therefore, it is stated: "and in the case of those with more than one vowel. For if the mention of "the beginning" were omitted for suffixes with more than one vowel, an accentuation on the beginning, middle, or end would result without restriction. This [mention of the beginning] is not intended to serve as a rule that the first syllable of a suffix with more than one vowel must be acute; because, in the case of suffixes where the beginning is unaccented (*anudātta*), there is simply no possibility of an acute accent occurring on the middle or the end.

For instance: when he intends [a vowel] to be unaccented (*anudātta*), he attaches the phonetic marker *p* to it, as he says in [Pāṇini 3.1.4]; when he intends it to be circumflex (*svarita*), he attaches the marker *t* to it, as he says in [Pāṇini 6.1.185]; and when he intends it to have monotone (*ekaśruti*), he employs the term "monotone" [in the rule], as he says: "Monotone is used in addressing from a distance" [Pāṇini 1.2.33].

When he desires a suffix to have the acute accent (*udātta*) on the final syllable, he attaches the marker *c* to it; as it is said: "The final syllable of that which has *c* as its marker is acute" (Pāṇini 6.1.169). When he desires it to have the acute accent on the middle syllable, he attaches the marker *r* to it; as it is said: [Pāṇini 6.1.217]. Now, will not any other suffix than these two be acute on the first syllable even without an explicit statement? This is not so.

For only those whose accent is specifically prescribed would have a fixed accent; however, for a suffix whose accent is not prescribed, its accent would result in being unrestricted—sometimes acute (udātta), sometimes another accent.
Even when it is acute, it might occur sometimes at the beginning, sometimes in the middle, and sometimes at the end.
Therefore, this must be done [by the present rule]. [The commentary states: "This is an exception to the preceding [rule]."
Because its commencement does not take place until that [suffix] has been reached.

The term *su* refers to the pratyāhāra (the entire set of nominal suffixes), not to the locative plural ending; for the latter would already be established as unaccented by virtue of its being marked with the *p*-diacritic (*pit*).
For this very reason, the commentary (*vṛtti*) employs the plural form *supaḥ* in its reference.

And this mention of *pratyāhāra* refers to the *sup*-suffixes alone by means of the letter *p*, and not to anything else, because that [mention] has no other purpose. For example, in "pacati" and "paṭhati," it is the *śap* suffix that is the illustration, not the *tip*; for the latter is already established by rules such as "tāsyanudātta" (Pāṇini 6.1.180). Furthermore, the technical designation (*saṃjñā*) of "affix" (*pratyaya*) is indeed already under discussion.
This is for the sake of clarity.

The term *pratyaya* is introduced as a technical designation (*saṃjñā*), because its referent is already understood from the statement: "until the end of the fifth chapter" (Pāṇini 3.1.1). Now, even if the designation *pratyaya* were present here, the suffix *san* would certainly not be [called] a *pratyaya*; for this is an etymological designation (*anvarthasaṃjñā*): "that by which meanings are conveyed (*pratiyante*) is a *pratyaya*. Yet, no meaning whatsoever is conveyed by *san*, because it is devoid of meaning (*anarthaka*); indeed, no specific meaning of *san* is specified here.

Nor is it reasonable to assume that the suffix will occur in its own sense according to the principle that "suffixes whose meaning is not specified occur in their own sense" (*PuPā 90*), for the intended meaning of "concealment" and so forth is not perceived from a form ending in *saN*. If it is argued that even though it is meaningless, it will function as a technical name (*saṃjñā*) by virtue of being prescribed under the heading of suffixes, [we reply: no; for if that were the case, it would also apply to modifications (*vikāra*) and augments (*āgama*) by rules such as *3.1.108* and *4.3.138*. This is not a fault; the suffix *saN* certainly has a meaning. What, then, is this meaning? It is censure (*nindā*) and so forth.
As it has been said: "The suffix *san* is employed in the sense of censure (*nindā*), forbearance (*kṣamā*), and the counteracting of disease (*vyādhipratīkāra*)" (Vārttika 178).
But how is it determined that the meanings of *san* are censure and so forth? By means of positive and negative concomitance (*anvayavyatireka*).

For when the suffix *san* is present, those meanings are understood in examples such as *jugupsate*; however, when *san* is absent—even though roots like *gup* are present—they are not understood in forms such as *gopayati*.
Therefore, since *san* indeed possesses meaning, it correctly receives the designation of an affix (*pratyaya*).
Because [the root] in *jugupsate* lacks the status of being an *ārdhadhātuka*, the augment *iṭ* does not occur.
However, there is an absence of *ārdhadhātuka* status because the suffix *san* is not prescribed by the rule *dhātoḥ* [3.1.91].
By the rule *kuhoścu* [7.4.62], the substitution of *c* occurs—resulting in the letter *j*.
Thus: *titikṣate*.

The substitution of *ga* for *ja* [by Pāṇini 8.2.30] results in the letter *ga*; its substitution by *ka* [by Pāṇini 8.4.54, "and before a *khari*"] results in the letter *ka*. [Thus we have] *nindākṣamā* and so forth. But how is the desired form obtained in the case of *nindā* and the others? The term *vā* (or) which will be mentioned later is understood as a supplement (*śeṣa*) to everything, and that is a restricted option (*vyavasthitavibhāṣā*).
Therefore, one is always virtuous regarding censure and the like, but not otherwise.
And this is a general rule; he will explain it differently for the sake of countering disease.
Or else, "weeds" refers to those grown in a field for the sake of grain that must be treated—that is, destroyed.
Alternatively—*kṣetriyaḥ* means an adulterer.
"Another's wife" (*paradārāḥ*) is "another's field" (*parakṣetram*); the meaning is that he is to be treated or restrained there.
It is also seen in the sense of doubt: "My mind wavers" (*vicikitsati me manaḥ*).

Although doubt may arise here due to the connection with a prefix (*upasarga*), nevertheless, it is held that the meaning is expressed by the verbal root (*dhātu*) alone, while the prefix merely serves as an indicator (*dyotya*).
Therefore, the mention of "remedying disease" is intended as a general rule;
for in common usage, the term *cikitsati* is generally employed in the sense of remedying a disease.
"Elsewhere" means in concealment and so forth. "He conceals" means:

The causative suffix *ṇic* is applied in the sense of "causing to do" (*hetumaṇṇic*), as in *tejayati* and *saṅketayati*. These two belong to both the *curādi* and *bhvādi* groups because they are listed in both the *curādi* and *bhvādi* classes. Now, one might ask: how is the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) prescribed for forms such as *jugupsate*, which are derived from a desiderative (*sannanta*)? For we do not observe the middle voice being used for roots like *gup* prior to the addition of the desiderative suffix *san*. To this, he says: "The addition of the indicatory letters (*anubandha*) in the case of *gup* and the others," and so forth.

The intention is that the *ātmanepada* endings should occur. In the case of the roots beginning with *gup*, the *anubandha* has been added for the purpose of being *anudātta*; therefore, the *ātmanepada* occurs by virtue of the rule *anudāttaṅita ātmanepadam* [Pāṇini 1.3.12].

Now, one might object: "Even if the *anubandha* were applied, the *ātmanepada* should still not occur after those roots, because they are separated from the suffixes by the *san* suffix. This is not so; it will occur by the force of the application of the *anubandha*.

Alternatively, according to the principle that "a grammatical marker applied to a constituent member serves as a qualifier for the whole" (*avayave kṛtaṃ liṅgaṃ samudāyasya viśeṣakaṃ bhavati*), the groups beginning with *jugupsā* themselves are those marked with the anudātta accent; therefore, the ātmanepada ending will occur after them precisely through that constituent member. This being the case, whatever objection might arise here has already been raised and refuted under the rule *pūrvavatsanaḥ* [Pāṇini 1.3.62].

Now, for what purpose is the letter *a* taught in the suffix *san*, given that it ought to be elided by the rule *tasyārdhadhātuke* [Pāṇini 6.4.48], and even in the case of a *sārvadhātuka* suffix, it would be subject to a single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) with the *śap* augment; thus, whether the teaching of the letter *a* exists or not, there appears to be no difference? This is not so; for here, in the form *pratīṣiṣati*—where the suffix *san* is prescribed after the root *iṇ* preceded by *pra*—if the teaching of the letter *a* did not exist, then the doubling (*dvirvacana*) of the second vowel as prescribed by the rule *ajāderdvitīyasya* [Pāṇini 6.1.2] would not apply to the syllable *si*, because the suffix *san* would be devoid of a vowel (*anackatvāt*).
When there is the instruction of the letter *a*, the [doubling] occurs for that second monosyllable which begins with *sa*.

The purpose of the instruction of the letter *ap* is for that very reason. The two roots *mān* and *bandh* are anudātta-its, while the remaining ones are svarita-its. Here, because of the mention of "long" (*dīrgha*), the technical rule (*paribhāṣā*) "of a vowel" (*acaḥ*) from [Pāṇini 1.2.28] is brought to bear; thus, the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*) is qualified by the vowel. Consequently, when a long vowel is prescribed for a reduplicated syllable ending in a vowel, it necessarily depends upon the *halādiśeṣa* (the retention of the initial consonant) operation; for without that, the reduplicated syllable would not end in a vowel.

Since that [the substitution of *i*] exists, nothing remains to be awaited; therefore, immediately after that, the long vowel (*dīrgha*) must occur. Consequently, occurring in place of the short vowel (*hrasva*) of the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*), it would subvert the *it*-designation of the root *bhū*, whereas for the remaining [roots], it would subvert the short vowel. Thus, for one who might think that an undesirable form would result, he says: "The long vowel occurs in place of the *i* of the reduplicated syllable. But how is the long vowel of the *i* obtained, given that a specific rule (*viśeṣavidhi*) subverts a general rule (*sāmānyavidhi*)?

[The rule *guṇo yaṅlukor* 7.4.82] applies, and since the long vowel (*dīrgha*) is specifically prescribed [by *aco ñṇiti* 7.2.115], would this not then override the short vowel (*it*) prescribed by the general rule and apply instead to the letter *a* itself? Therefore, it is considered thus: this must have been indicated in the rule *dīrgho'kitaḥ* [7.4.83]—namely, that "in the case of modifications of the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*), exceptions (*apavāda*) override the general rules (*utsarga*).
The purpose of including the term *akitaḥ* [in 7.4.83] is so that [the long vowel] does not occur here: as in *yaṃyamyate* and *raṃramyate*.

If general rules (*utsarga*) were indeed sublated by exceptions (*apavāda*) even in the case of modifications of the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa-vikāra*), then—since the exception *nuk* would have been applied—the long vowel would not occur simply because the stem would no longer end in a vowel other than *a*; what then would be the purpose of the rule *akitaḥ*?

Furthermore, it has already been applied. Therefore, this [rule] indicates that there is no relationship of sublation and sublated (*bādhyabādhaka-bhāva*) among the modifications of the reduplicated syllable.
Thus, we have *bībhatsate*.

By the rule *ekāco baśo bhaṣ* [Pāṇini 8.2.37], the letter *b* becomes *bh*; and by the rule *khari ca* [Pāṇini 8.4.54], the letter *dh* becomes *t*. Regarding the phrase "in the subsequent sūtra" and so forth:
here, only a general injunction for *san* is required by the mention of the option (*vā*), and not specifically an injunction that follows immediately.
Therefore, this is understood to be a supplement (*śeṣa*) to all three rules.

The inclusion of the word "all" (sarva) is for the purpose of making it known that the rule [Pāṇini 3.1.5] beginning with *gup* is also understood as a supplement (*śeṣa*); otherwise, it would be understood as a supplement only to the immediately preceding rule.
Regarding the form *mānayati*:
it is either derived from the causative suffix *ṇic* added because of the sense of "causing" (*hetu*), or from the *cur*-class suffix *ṇic*, since this root is also listed in the *cur*-class.

Regarding the statement "{niśānayati - kāśikā} niśānam," [the suffix] *ac* is applied according to the rule for roots beginning with *pac*. Since the status of being an object (*karman*) is logically established for that which is most desired by the agent to be reached through the action,
and not otherwise, some action must necessarily be expected.

And since no other [action] is heard here, and desire (*icchā*) is brought to mind as the meaning of the suffix, it is logical that it alone should be expected; this is due to the principle of proximity (*pratyāsatti*). Therefore, he says "the object of *iṣ*" (*iṣikarma*), etc., because the status of being an object (*karmabhāva*) is understood for that which is pervaded by that very [desire]. "The object of *iṣ*" (*iṣeḥ karma*) is a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*).

Since similarity necessarily depends on a counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*), a counter-correlate must be sought; and since no counter-correlate is explicitly mentioned in the rule (*sūtra*), he says "by *iṣ* itself," etc., because by the previously stated reasoning, the counter-correlativity is understood to belong to *iṣ* alone.

The term *samāna-eka-kartṛka* is a bahuvrīhi compound meaning "having a single common agent. Now, one might object that the status of being an object (*karmatva*) is not applicable to the verbal root (*dhātu*), because that [objecthood] is a property of the meaning (*artha-dharma*), whereas the verbal root consists of sound (*śabda-ātmaka*).

If it is argued that in usages such as *karoti dhātum icchati* (“he desires the verbal root”), the verbal root itself is observed to possess the status of an object (*karman*), we reply: no, we do not say that the verbal root can never have the status of an object. Rather, what we say is that it is impossible for that [root] which is taken up here as the *bhāvanā* (efficient force) that causes the arising of the desiderative suffix (*san*) and which possesses a common agent (*samānakartṛka*). This is because the state of having a common agent belongs to an object that is yet to be accomplished (*sādhyamāna*), whereas the status of being an object belongs to something whose nature is already established (*siddhasvabhāva*). Furthermore, the fault regarding the verbal root’s status as an object was stated while provisionally accepting its having a common agent; now, even that [common agency] is simply not possible.

For instance: a verbal root (*dhātu*) is both the word and the agent of the action; it does not [itself] express "the state of being an object" (*karmatva*), and so forth. Regarding the phrase "by way of the meaning" (*arthadvāraka*):
that for which the meaning is the door or the means is "by way of the meaning."

Because the object (*karman*) is the meaning [of the root], and because there is identity of agent (*samānakartṛkatva*), even a verbal root denoting that [object] is said to have an object and a common agent by metaphorical attribution (*upacāra*) of the property of the meaning. This is the intention: just as in the rule "A *dvandva* compound consisting of parts of living beings or musical instruments... (Pāṇini 2.4.2), because the meaning [the parts] belongs to a living being, even that which denotes it is called a "part of a living being. In the case of *cikīrṣati*, the meaning of the root *kṛ* is pervaded by desire (*icchā*); therefore, due to this identity, it has an object and a common agent with the desiderative root *iṣ*. For the very one who is the agent of *iṣ* is also the agent of that [root *kṛ*].
Therefore, by that means, the sense is that the root *kṛ* (to do) also has the same agent as its object (*sakarmaka*).

From that, [the suffix] *san* is applied; because of the rule *san-ṅit* (Pāṇini 1.2.9), there is the absence of *guṇa* due to the *kit* status of *san*. Then, by the rule *aj-jhan-gamāṃ sani* (6.4.16), there is lengthening; by *ṛta iddhātoḥ* (7.1.100), there is the substitution of *it*; then *rapara* (substitution of *r*); by *hali ca* (8.2.77), there is lengthening; while *iṇkoḥ* (8.3.57) is being carried over, by *iṇkoḥ* (8.3.59), there is the substitution of *ṣ*; then reduplication and the operations pertaining to the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*). [The question is: "What is the purpose of mentioning the word *dhātu* (root)?"
The mention of "dhātu" (root) is made here for this purpose: so that [the suffix] might not occur after a word ending in a case-suffix, such as *gamanam icchati*.

But surely, even in the absence of the mention of "dhātu," the suffix *san* cannot possibly arise from that [case-ending], because it is barred by the exception [stated in Pāṇini 3.1.8]; therefore, by the principle of elimination (*pāriśeṣya*), it will necessarily occur only after a root even without the mention of "dhātu. With this intention, he says: "Let there be no derivation [of *san*] from [a root] preceded by a prefix (*sopasarga*)."

When the meaning of the verbal root, as qualified by a prefix, is pervaded by the agent’s desire (the sense of the desiderative suffix *iṣ*), then that very root, qualified by the prefix, undergoes the status of being an object (*karman*). Consequently, by means of that [object], the verbal root itself, together with its prefix, would be designated as the "object" (*karman*); and thus, the suffix [denoting the object] would arise after the form including the prefix. Furthermore, in the case of *prācikīrṣat*, when reduplication is applied according to the rule *sanyoḥ* [Pāṇini 6.1.9]—"reduplication occurs of the first monosyllabic element ending in a suffix marked with ṣ or ṇ"—it would result in the reduplication of the entire complex beginning with the prefix *pra*. Moreover, in the case of the imperfect (*laṅ*), if the designation "stem" (*aṅga*) were applied to the root together with its prefix, the augment *aṭ* would have to be inserted before that [complex].

If, then, it is accompanied by a prefix (*sopasarga*), would there not be an absence of derivation from the *karmadhātu* because that [verbal root] is intransitive? This is not so; for when the composite whole (*samudāya*) possesses the status of an object (*karman*), its constituent parts (*avayava*) also experience that status of being an object, since the composite is of the nature of its parts. Indeed, the status of the parts as objects is the very means (*abhyupāya*) for the status of the composite as an object; otherwise, if the parts did not attain the state of being objects when the composite is the object, then in the expression "he desires a great son" (*mahāntaṃ putram icchati*), the second case ending (*dvitīyā*)—which is characterized by being an object—would not apply to the parts.
As in the example: "he desires [to go] by means of going."
The mention of the suffix -lyuṭ is for the purpose of demonstrating its status as an instrument (karaṇa).
For indeed, the non-occurrence of the suffix saN after a verbal root is the counter-example;
in this case, there is the condition of having a common agent (samānakartṛkatva).

For instance: he who is the agent of desiring (*iṣ*) is the very same as the agent of going (*gam*); for he desires some object by means of his own act of going, which has attained the status of an instrument (*karaṇa*). However, since the state of being an object (*karman*) for the act of going is not established through the mediation of a [separate] meaning, it does not occur; hence [the example]: "He desires Devadatta’s eating" (*devadattasya bhojanam icchati*).
In the expression "of Devadatta" (*devadattasya*), the genitive case is used for the agent according to Pāṇini 2.3.65, *kartṛkarmaṇoḥ kṛti*.
For here, Devadatta is the agent of the eating (*bhojana*), whereas Yajñadatta is the agent of the desiring (*iṣ*); thus, there is no identity of agent (*samānakartṛkatva*).
[The phrase] "he knows how to do" (*kartuṃ jānāti*) [is an example].

Because of the inclusion of the word "desire" (*icchā*), the sense of "desiring" does not exist here in the meaning of the verbal root. But surely it has been stated that the suffix *san* occurs after a verbal root whose object is [also] the object of the verb *iṣ* (to desire), provided it has the same agent as that [verb *iṣ*];

and since in this case there is no suffix expressing "desire," neither is there for the root the state of being the object of *iṣ*, nor the state of having the same agent as *iṣ*. Therefore, this counter-example is incorrect due to the deficiency of three constituent factors? This is not so; for when the word "desire" is present, those two qualifiers are obtained through proximity (*pratyāsatti*).

But in the absence of that [restriction], since the verbal root is understood to have an object with respect to any action whatsoever, and since the identity of agent is understood merely in relation to the counter-correlative (the object), what is improper here? [The statement] "By the mention of the option (*vā*), the sentence also occurs"—this refers to the subsequent sūtra as the ellipsis.
