However, in this case, because the rule is prescribed precisely from *samānakartṛkeṣu tumun* [Pāṇini 3.3.158], the sentence *kartāram icchati* will indeed occur.
For if that word were eternal, its utterance would be purposeless.
Furthermore, another purpose for the utterance has already been stated; the word "also" (*api*) serves to include that as well.
[This is explained by the passage beginning with] "Because of the rule 'from a verbal root' (*dhātoḥ*)," and so forth.

Because the designation *ārdhadhātuka* is prescribed for a suffix by the rule *ārdhadhātuke śeṣaḥ* [Pāṇini 3.4.114] after the word *dhātoḥ* has been uttered—meaning that a suffix is designated as *ārdhadhātuka* when it is prescribed after a verbal root (*dhātu*)—in this case, since the suffix *san* is prescribed after the word *dhātoḥ*, it does not receive the *ārdhadhātuka* designation; for its prescription is not performed in that manner. Regarding the statement "an addition [should be made] in the sense of possibility" (*āśaṅkāyām upasaṃkhyānam*):
*āśaṅkā* means probability (*sambhāvanā*), and that is a property of the speaker.

In the expression "the riverbank wishes to fall," since the bank is insentient, desire is not possible; therefore, [the suffix] does not apply. This usage occurs only in the context of "I fear the bank will fall," as in "he wishes to die."
As before, there is the substitution of *k* and lengthening [of the vowel].
It has been stated that [the rule] "udoṣṭhapūrvasya" [Pāṇini 7.1.102] applies, as well as the substitution of *r* for *u*.
Here, although the living being (*jīva*) possesses consciousness, because it is dear [to the speaker], the desire of the dog to die does not arise; thus [the desired form] would not be obtained.
And this application is to be understood in the sense of the statement: "I fear that he will die.
The word *upasaṃkhyāna* means "explanation" or "demonstration.
The phrase "it should be formulated" (*kartavya*) is to be supplied as an ellipsis.

As for the demonstration: a split of the rule (*yogavibhāga*) should be made as "dhātoḥ" (from a root); by this, *san* will occur even in the sense of apprehension (*āśaṅkā*). [The phrase] "from that which ends in *san* prescribed for the sense of desire" (*icchā-sanantāt*) and so forth means that the prohibition of *san* must be explained as applying to a *san* that follows a *san* prescribed in the sense of desire.
We shall provide that explanation later.

The suffix *san* which occurs in its own sense (*svārtha*)—from that which ends in such a *san*, the suffix *san* is added again; thus, "desire" (*icchā*) is made a qualifier [of the action], as in *jugupsiṣate*.
By [Pāṇini 6.4.48], there is the elision of the vowel *a*.

Regarding the phrase "from a *śaiṣika*," etc.: that meaning which is other than those beginning with *āptaya* and ending with *adūrabhava* is the *śeṣa* (remainder); that which occurs therein is *śaiṣika*. [The suffix] *ṭhañ* is applied by the rule *adhyātmādibhyaṣṭhañ* (Vārttika 456).
From such a *śaiṣika* [base], a subsequent suffix of the same form (*sarūpa*) is prohibited.

From *śālāyāṃ bhavaḥ* (that which exists in a hall), [by Pāṇini 4.2.114] we get *śālīyaḥ*. From *śālīye bhavaḥ* (that which exists in what exists in a hall), however, the suffix *cha* does not occur again. But a different form certainly occurs: from *ahicchatre bhavaḥ* (that which exists in Ahicchatra), [by Pāṇini 4.1.83] we get *āhicchatraḥ*; then from *āhicchatre bhavaḥ*, [by Pāṇini 4.2.113] we get *āhicchatrīyaḥ*, because *cha* follows a base ending in *aṇ* that has the *vṛddhi* vowel. The suffix whose meaning is "existing" in the sense of the possessive (*matup*) is called *matubarthīyaḥ*; thus, by [Pāṇini 4.2.138], there is the suffix *cha*. A suffix whose meaning is "possessing the sense of the possessive" is called *matubarthikaḥ*; thus, by [Pāṇini 5.2.115], there is the suffix *ṭhan*.
A suffix expressing the sense of *matup* (possessive) is not desired after another suffix that expresses the sense of *matup*, provided it is of the same form (*sarūpa*).

For example, from *daṇḍa asyāsti* ("he has a staff"), one forms *daṇḍikaḥ* by adding *ṭhan* as before; however, from this *matup*-type suffix (*daṇḍika*), the suffix *ṭhan* does not apply again to form *daṇḍikikaḥ*.

But if the suffixes are of different forms (*virūpa*), it certainly occurs: from *daṇḍa asyāsti* one forms *daṇḍī* (using *in*), and from *daṇḍinaḥ asyāṃ śālāyāṃ santi* ("there are staff-bearers in this hall"), one forms *daṇḍimatī śālā* (using *matup*) after the word ending in *in*.
Regarding the statement "from *sannata* [the suffix] *san* will not arise," the term "homogeneous" (*sarūpaḥ*) is to be connected [to it].

Although in that case there is no deviation regarding the formal homogeneity (*rūpasārūpya*) of the suffix *san*, nevertheless, by virtue of the capacity of the qualification, formal homogeneity of meaning (*arthasārūpya*) is resorted to.

Therefore, it is understood that [the suffix *san*] follows a desiderative (*icchā-sananta*) [root], because it was previously stated: "A prohibition must be stated for [the suffix *san*] following a desiderative" (Vārttika 181). However, when *san* occurs after roots such as *gup* in the sense of censure (*nindā*) and so forth, that indeed becomes a desiderative (*icchā-san*). And thus, an example has been cited from such a formation. All of this has been cited precisely because it is established by logical necessity (*nyāya-prāpta*).
How so? For a base (*prakṛti*) that is already established serves as the cause for the application of an affix.

However, at the time when an affix denoting a derivative meaning (*śaiṣika*) with the same form (*sarūpa*) is prescribed, there exists no established base ending in such an affix; nor does there exist an established base ending in such an affix at the time when an affix expressing the sense of *matup* (*matvarthīya*) with the same form is prescribed; nor does there exist a base that has attained its own existence from a base ending in the desiderative suffix (*icchāsan*) while that suffix itself is being prescribed. This is because, by rules such as [Pāṇini 4.3.53], derivatives such as *śaiṣika* with the same form are themselves yet to be produced (*bhāvyamānatvāt*).

Therefore, because they lack an existent material cause (*prakṛti*), they do not arise from the kind of material cause previously described. The word *ātman* is understood here as that which, by excluding what is other, expresses its own counter-correlative (*pratiyogin*) object; it is not, however, that which refers to the person (*puruṣa*) who possesses internal activity and is the enjoyer (*bhoktṛ*). If that were taken here, it would be ineffective. Consequently, it could not qualify either "desire" (*icchā*) or the nominal ending; for in that case, desire simply does not belong to anything other than the self, so its being a qualifier of that [other] would be illogical.

Even a word ending in a case-suffix (*subanta*), when connected with another [word], becomes connected to the self [of that other word] as well; for both of them are related to the same self. Therefore, it is also improper for that [suffix] to function as a qualifier of a *subanta*; thus, only that which expresses a counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) to something else is accepted.
For only in this way can the exclusion of the suffix *kap* be effected, and not otherwise.

Here too, because of the proximity of desire (*icchā*), the status of being the object (*karmatva*) is understood as belonging to that which is pervaded by that very [desire]; thus he says: "of the object of desire" (*iṣikarmaṇaḥ*). If desire were qualified by the mention of the self (*ātman*), then this would also apply here—as in "he desires the king's son"—for when the king's son is also desired, the desire belongs to the desirer himself.
Therefore, considering it appropriate to qualify the word ending in a case-suffix (subanta) by means of self-reproach, he says: "belonging to the seeker who is related to the self.
That the word ending in a case-suffix is related to the self should be understood as being mediated through its meaning.
Now, how is it obtained that this [reproach] belongs specifically to the seeker? Because the seeker is brought into proximity by the desire itself, which brings him near.
Why is this so? Because without that [suffix], it would not exist.

Regarding the form *putrīyati*: the substitution of *i* (ittva) occurs by [Pāṇini 7.4.33]. Now, does the inclusion of the term *su* (sub) here serve to exclude nominal stems (*prātipadika*), or to exclude verbal roots (*dhātu*)? In that regard, its purpose cannot be to exclude nominal stems, for there is no distinction whatsoever between a suffix being produced from a word ending in *su* and one produced from a nominal stem.

It is also not tenable [to say that the mention of *su*] is for the purpose of excluding the verbal roots (*dhātu*), because it would then sublate the *san* suffix prescribed after them; with this intention, he asks: "What is the purpose of mentioning *su*? [The answer is: "So that it does not occur from a sentence. He states the purpose of mentioning *su*: if the mention of *subanta* (inflected words) were absent, [the suffix] might occur even from a sentence; therefore, the mention of *su* is made to exclude that.

Now, is it then the case that [the suffix] *mahāputrīya* must absolutely not occur? It must occur when this sentence is formed as a compound: *mahāputram icchati* ("he desires a great son"). But when this sentence is *mahāntaṃ putram icchati* ("he desires a great son"), then it must not occur.
Furthermore, the mention of "sentence" (*vākya*) should be understood as an indication for a collection of words (*padasamudāya*).
Therefore, the occurrence [of the suffix] is suspected from the collection *mahāntaṃ putram*, yet this is not a sentence, because its meaning is not complete.

Furthermore, what would happen if [the compound] were not formed? If there were no semantic integration (*ekārthībhāva*)—characterized by the absence of *asāmarthya* (lack of capacity)—between the words *mahat* and *putra*, which have become subordinate (*guṇībhūta*) to the meaning of the suffix, then the compound would not occur.
Consequently, the substitution of *ā* prescribed for the subsequent member by Pāṇini 6.3.46 would not take place.

Alternatively, since the word *putra*, being subordinate to the meaning of the suffix, would lack the qualification of being "honored" (*pūjyamānatā*), the compound would not occur by virtue of Pāṇini 2.1.61 and following; and in the absence of that compound, the substitution of *ā* would likewise not occur.

Now, when *sub-grahaṇa* (the mention of *sub*) is being applied, why does it not apply here, since this [word] ends in *sub*? It is not so; because of the paribhāṣā regarding the mention of an affix (*pratyayagrahaṇaparibhāṣā*), when there is a mention of *sub*, only that which begins with the element from which *sub* was produced is understood. And in this case, *sub* is not produced from the sentence (*vākya*), but rather from a constituent part (*avayava*).
Therefore, production [of *sub*] does not occur from the sentence.

In that case, why does it not occur from the word *putra*, which is merely a constituent part [of the compound]? Because it does not convey the meaning. For there must be a suffix following a phrase whose meaning is identical to that of the derivative formation (*vṛtti*); and the meaning understood here from the phrase "one who desires a great son" is not conveyed by a form ending in a suffix.

For instance, the meaning of the sentence "he desires a great son" (*mahāntaṃ putram icchati*)—namely, [the desire for] someone who is a great [person] such as the King of Vārāṇasī—is understood. Similarly, when it is said "he acts like one desiring a great son" (*mahāntaṃ putrīyati*), this meaning—that he behaves toward someone as if toward a great son—is understood as being of a different category from the sentence-meaning [of the previous example]. [An example of this is: "he desires the king's son" (*rājñaḥ putraṃ micchati*). [Objection: But surely, because there is a lack of semantic competency (*asāmarthya*) due to the presence of mutual expectancy (*sāpekṣatva*), the suffix will not occur; what is the purpose of including the term *ātman* [in the rule]? How is there a lack of competency? Is it not because of the statement: "That which is expectant is incompetent" (*Cāndra-vyākaraṇa 2.1.27*)? [Response: This is not so.
In that case, when [the meaning] is determined independently through the sense or the context, then [the suffix] applies.
And it applies here: *pāpamicchati* ("he desires evil"), *aghamicchati* ("he desires misfortune").
For in this instance, even without the employment of a third subsequent word, the sense of "another's" (*parasya*) is understood; indeed, no one desires evil for themselves.
Regarding the passage beginning with "the letter *ka*," etc.:

if the letter *ka* were not present, there would be no apprehension of this [term], because in the rule at [Pāṇini 1.4.15] there is the apprehension of that which possesses the *anubandha* (indicatory letter) *ka*.
The letter *ca* is for the purpose of preventing its obstruction.

If the letter *ca* were not present, however, since *kyac*, *kyaṅ*, and *kyaṣ* would all have two indicatory letters (*dvyanubandhaka*), there would be no obstruction to their general inclusion [in the rule].
But the letter *ca* is not for the sake of making the word *antodātta* (oxytone); for that is already established by the rule *ghātoḥ* [Pāṇini 6.1.156].
Thus it is said: "it must be stated."
The meaning is that [the suffix] must be explained.
As for the explanation: it should be done by resorting to the fact that the term *vā* (or) which follows [in the previous rule] is a *vyavasthitavibhāṣā* (an option restricted to specific cases).
Consequently, the *kyac* suffix does not occur after words ending in *m* or after indeclinables (*avyaya*). [This applies to the rule] beginning with "in the Vedic language" (*chandasi*), etc.
The meaning is that this form of the rule must be explained as signifying that the suffix *kyac* occurs even for the desire of another in Vedic usage (*chandasi*).

As for the explanation: when *kyac* has been applied, the rule teaches the substitution of *i* for the vowel of the word *agha* in order to block the application of *it* [by Pāṇini 7.4.37]; this indicates that in Vedic usage, *kyac* occurs even for the desire of another. For no one indeed desires evil (*agha*) for themselves.

Regarding the word *aghāyavaḥ*: by the rule [Pāṇini 3.2.170], there is the substitution of *ā* for the vowel; the suffix *u* is added; by the rule [Pāṇini 7.3.109], there is *guṇa* substitution; and finally, the replacement with *ava*. Now, one might ask: since both these suffixes, *kyac* and *kāmyac*, are prescribed after a word ending in a case-suffix (*subanta*) when there is a desire for an object for oneself, why were they not formulated as a single rule? To this he says: "The separation of the rules" (*yogavibhāgaḥ*), and so forth. If the rule were formulated as a single unit, namely *supa ātmanaḥ kyackāmyacau*, then both suffixes would continue to apply in the subsequent rules as well.

But surely, even if there were a *yogavibhāga* (separation of rules), only *kāmyac* would follow by virtue of immediate proximity, not *kyac*. This is not a fault; for here the letter *ca* is employed for the purpose of carrying over (*anukarṣaṇa*) *kyac*. The purpose of carrying over *kyac* is so that it may continue into the subsequent rule, as there is no application [of *kāmyac*] here. If it is asked why *kāmyac* also does not carry over, the answer is: no, because of the force of the *yogavibhāga*. Now, why does the letter *ka* not receive the designation *it* according to [Pāṇini 1.3.8]? To this he says: "The letter *ka* [does not receive the designation *it*]," and so forth.

But is it not the case that the only operation [to be performed] is elision (*lopa*)? It is not an operation; for here, the instruction of a phoneme is intended either for the sake of an operation or for the sake of its being heard. In this instance, there is no operation to be performed. Therefore, if it were not for the sake of its being heard, the instruction would be purposeless.

In that case, this would be the purpose: so that there might be the prohibition of *guṇa* in *agnikāmyati*. This is not a valid purpose, because *guṇa* is prescribed for the *aṅga* [stem] before both *sārvadhātuka* and *ārdhadhātuka* suffixes. Furthermore, a suffix prescribed after a verbal root (*dhātu*) is designated as *ārdhadhātuka*; however, this suffix is not prescribed after a root, but rather after a word ending in a nominal suffix (*subanta*). In that case, this would be the purpose: so that there might be the *saṃprasāraṇa* substitution by rule 6.1.15 (*vac-svapi-yaja-...*) in *upayaṭkāmyati*. This too is not valid, because in that rule, the verbal roots beginning with *yaj* are specified as being characterized by the marker *k*—that is, "the *k*-marked suffixes following *yaj* and the others."
And what is the *kit* [augment] for the roots beginning with *yaj*? It is that which is prescribed after the roots beginning with *yaj*, but this [augment] is not prescribed in that manner.

Even assuming there is a purpose [for it], he states another solution: "because of being preceded by the letter *c*. He thinks as follows: let the arrangement be made in this way, namely, that the instruction is given with two *c*s—as in *supa ātmanaḥ kyac* and *kāmyac*; thus, that *c* will bear the technical designation *it*, and it will serve to protect the *k* from receiving the *it* designation.

Now, what is the purpose of the second *ca* (and)? For, by the rule "of a verbal root" (*dhātoḥ* 6.1.162), the final acute accent is already established. Here, in the form *putrakāmyiṣyati*, even though the accent of the suffix *satiśiṣṭa* [the suffix *san*] would apply, the power of the marker *c* ensures that the accent of *kāmyac* itself occurs. As in: *upayaṭkāmyati*. [Analysis: By [Pāṇini 3.2.73], there is the suffix *vic*; from "he desires the *upayaj*" there is *kāmyac*. By the rule beginning with *vraśca-* (8.2.36), there is the substitution of *ṣ* for *j*; its *jaś*-substitution is *ḍ*; and for that too, by the rule *vāvasāne* (8.4.55), there is the *car*-substitution of *ṭ*. [Objection: "The suffix *kyac* recurs, not *kāmyac*."
And the reason for this has been stated previously:

since the verbal suffix (*pratyaya*) expresses the sense of "acting" (*ācārakriyā*), the objecthood (*karmatā*) of the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) is established in relation to that, due to proximity (*pratyāsatti*), as in the previous case. Regarding the phrase "and from a locus" (*adhikaraṇācca*) and so forth, the meaning is that the rule should be explained as having the sense: "the suffix *kyac* occurs after a word denoting a locus when the sense is 'acting'."

The explanation, however, should be carried out as before, by carrying forward the word *ca* (and) and relying on its function of including what has not been explicitly stated (*anuktasamuccaya*). This suffix *kyaṅ* is prescribed in conjunction with the elision of *sa*. Therefore, it would apply only where there is the elision of *sa*—as in *payāyate* and so forth—but here it would not apply—as in *kākaḥ śyenāyate* and so forth.
For this is a single sentence, and the *ca* serves as a conjunction; thus, what is meant is that both *kyaṅ* and the elision of *sa* occur.
And thus, because these two are prescribed simultaneously, there should be no occurrence of *kyaṅ* in the absence of the elision of *s*.

For when these two are prescribed simultaneously, the grammatical operation does not apply in the absence of either one, as in the rule "the substitution of *i* for [the final of] *sthā* and *dhvṛ*" (Pāṇini 1.2.17). Therefore, he says: "prescribed as an addition" (*anvācaśiṣṭaḥ*), and so forth.
This is what is meant by this.
This *ca* is not for conjunction (*samuccaya*), but rather for inclusion (*anvācaya*).

In that case, there are two sentences: [the rule] "it occurs everywhere after the agent" (*kartuḥ bhavati sarvatra*) and "where there is the letter *sa*, there its elision also occurs" (*yatra tvasti sakārastatra tasyāpi lopaḥ*).
Therein, by the first sentence, the *kyaṅ* suffix—being prescribed as primary without regard to the rule for the elision of *sa*—also operates even when the elision of *sa* is being prescribed.

Regarding the form *śyenāyate*: the lengthening [of the vowel] is by the rule *akṛtsārvadhātukayoḥ* [Pāṇini 7.4.25]. It is said that "the mention of the option (*vā*) is also connected to the rule for the elision of the *s*"; otherwise, the form *payasyate* would not be established.
"And that is a restricted option (*vyavasthitavibhāṣā*).
Otherwise, there would be an optional elision of *s* even for *ojas* and *apsaras*.

By this [statement], he clarifies what was said [in the Vārttika]: "For *ojas* and *apsaras*, the elision is obligatory, but for *payas*, it is optional" (Vārttika 185 on Pāṇini 2.1.92); namely, that this is indeed a restricted option.
Now, regarding the question of why the elision of *s* does not occur in the forms *haṃsāyate* and *sārasāyate*, he says: “In the rule for the elision of *s*,” and so forth.

If, even in the rule for the elision of *s*, this [word] *kartuḥ* were in the ablative case (pañcamī), then—because of the non-application of [Pāṇini 1.1.52, which states that a substitute takes the place of that which follows the ablative]—the elision of *s* occurring wherever it might be situated would also apply here. However, in the rule for the elision of *s*, this *kartuḥ* is not in the ablative case; what then? It is in the genitive case (ṣaṣṭhī).

Because a change of case occurs for the sake of the meaning, the genitive of locus (*sthāna-ṣaṣṭhī*) is established. And when the genitive of locus is present, by the rule *alo'ntyasya* [Pāṇini 1.1.52], the elision must apply only to the final letter. Therefore, in forms such as *haṃsāyate*, there is no elision. [The sūtra begins with] *ācāre* and so forth.
The particle *kyaṅ* is also for the purpose of indicating the object [of the action]; by that, *kyaṅ* is prescribed as an exception (*apavāda*) to *kvip*.

Here, because *avagalbha* and others are taught with the low-pitched (*anudātta*) letter *m* as an indicatory mark (*anubandha*), the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) occurs in forms such as *avagalbhate*; furthermore, *kvip* is optionally prescribed after *avagalbha* and others. To this extent, since {the root *galbha* in the sense of "boldness" (DhP 3.92)}, *avagalbha* in the sense of "being bold" (DhP 3.92), *klībṛ* in the sense of "lack of boldness" (DhP 3.81), and *huḍṛ*, *hoḍṛ* in the sense of "motion" (DhP 3.52, 3.54) are all marked as *ātmanepadin* verbs, [the rule applies].

In this regard, when the *lakāra* (verbal suffix) is applied to these [roots], forms such as *avagalbhate* will result; however, when the *kṛt* suffixes have been produced first to form nominal stems (*prātipadika*), and then the *kyaṅ* suffix is produced, the form *avagalbhāyate* will result. This is the purpose of the optional rule for the application of *kvip*: so that in the form *avagalbhāñcakre*, the *ām* augment may occur by the rule *kāspratyayādāmamantre* [Pāṇini 3.1.35].
Otherwise, if *ām* were prescribed only after a root ending in a suffix, it would not apply here, because [the base] would end in a suffix rather than a suffixless root.
[This is stated in the rule: "From all nominal stems (*prātipadika*)."

The inclusion of *avagalbha* and others must also be made for the purpose of attaching the indicatory letters (*anubandhas*). Here, it is expected that "optionally *kvip*" applies to the sense of conduct (*ācāra*).
Consequently, the resulting syntactical formulation is: "*kvip* occurs after all nominal stems (*prātipadika*) specifically in the sense of conduct."

Now, for what purpose are the *k* and *p* markers attached as *anubandhas* to the suffix *kvip*, given that the purpose of the *k* marker is to prohibit *guṇa* substitution, and no *guṇa* is applicable here? This is because *kvip* is not prescribed after a verbal root (*dhātu*), and thus it lacks the status of being a *sārvadhātuka* affix;
for *guṇa* is taught [only] for *sārvadhātuka* and *ārdhadhātuka* affixes.

Furthermore, the purpose of the *p* marker is to mark the vowel as unaccented (*anudātta*), but that is not possible for *kvip*; because it is devoid of vowels (*anacka*) and because it is entirely elided (*sarvalopitva*) according to Pāṇini 6.1.67.

If it is argued that these two [suffixes] are for the purpose of not obstructing the apprehension of the general meaning (*sāmānyagrahaṇa*), we say no; for the non-obstruction of the apprehension of the general meaning is established by either one alone.
Otherwise, even for *vij* and *viṭ*, an *anubandha* would have to be added for that purpose—this is what must be considered. Regarding the word "in becoming" (*bhuvi*):
"becoming" is *bhū*; the suffix *kvip* is applied in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāva*) because it belongs to the *sampadādi* group.

Here, by the mention of *hal*, the *bhṛśādi* group is qualified as far as possible; because this is a specific qualification (*viśeṣaṇa*), there is no *tadantavidhi* (extension of a rule to that which ends with such an element). Thus he says: "and of those ending in a consonant" (*halantānām ca*), etc.
Here too, as before, the elision of the consonant (*hal-lopa*) is taught as a secondary addition (*anvācaya-śiṣṭa*); therefore, even in its absence, the suffix *kyaṅ* certainly occurs.

In the rule for the elision of the consonant, the genitive case "from *bhṛśādi*" (*bhṛśādibhyaḥ*) becomes a locative of reference (*sthāna-ṣaṣṭhī*), due to the necessary transformation of the case-ending according to the sense.
In that regard, since the restriction [of Pāṇini 1.1.52] applies, in examples such as *bhṛśāyate*, there is no elision of a non-final consonant (*ahalantyasya halaḥ*).

Now, one might object: "Since the words beginning with *bhṛśa* are many, the term *acvebhyaḥ* should be in the plural to correspond to them; why then is there a reference in the singular as *acveḥ*? To this he says: "*acveḥ*" and so forth.
The phrase "after *bhṛśa* that is not *acvi*" and "after *śīghra* that is not *acvi*" is connected to each [word] individually.

Therefore, the singular number is logical. As for the passage beginning with "For what purpose, then," etc., this is a question made under the governing rule *ac-ah* (Pāṇini 6.4.129). He asks why it should not be applied, saying: "Insofar as," etc.

By the rule beginning with *abhūtatadbhāve* and so forth, the suffix *cv-* is prescribed in connection with the verb *bhū*. In that case, because the meaning has already been expressed by that [suffix] itself, the suffix *kyaṅ* will not occur after words ending in *cv-*, on the principle that "what has already had its meaning expressed is not employed" (*uktārthānām aprayogaḥ*).

But might it not be argued that *kyaṅ* would indeed occur, overriding the subsequent employment [of the verb]? This is not so; for rules that have no other scope are subverting, whereas *kyaṅ* does have its own scope.

Where [does this apply]? It applies to those words beginning with *abhṛśa* that end in *ac*; for the suffix *cv-* is prescribed optionally after a word ending in *ac*. Since the term *ac-* is understood to carry over [from the previous rule], when both [the original form and the *cv*-derived form] would apply to words ending in *ac*, the latter must necessarily occur due to its higher status [in the order of rules] because of the subsequent application (*anuprayoga*). Therefore, he says: "similar to that," and so forth. The prohibition of *ac-*—namely, the rule *nañivayuktamanayasadṛśādhikaraṇe tathā hyarthagatiḥ* (Vyāḍipañjikā 65)—is intended so that words like *abhṛśa* might be understood as being similar to those ending in *cv-*. Otherwise, how could they be recognized as such? Thus is the purpose of the prohibition regarding *ac-*.

Since the suffix *cv-* has as its domain the transformation of something that did not previously exist into something else (*abhūtatadbhāva*), its similarity is based solely on the object itself, not on the word-form and so forth; thus he says: "from those whose domain is the transformation of what was not into that [which it becomes]," and so on.
Here, in the list of *bhṛśādi* words, some read *manas* and other such terms with prefixes; from those very forms with prefixes, the suffix would have to be applied.
Consequently, in the case of *udamanāyata*, because the form with the prefix would be designated as a *aṅga* (base), the augment *aṭ* would have to appear before the prefix.

In the case of *sumanāyya gataḥ*, since the verbal root with its prefix (*sopasarga*) has entered into the formation ending in *-kvā*, there would be no prefix distinct from that [root], and thus a compound would not occur; consequently, the suffix *-lyap* would not be obtained? This is not so; for just as in the case of *prakartum aicchat*, where even though the object is the root together with its prefix, the suffix is applied to the root alone—having extracted it from the prefix by virtue of the mention of "the root" (*dhātu*)—so too will it be here. If it is argued that in that case there is an explicit mention of "the root," [we reply] that here too the reason is that the mention of "a word ending in a case-suffix" (*subanta*) is understood to carry over. Words such as *sumanas* are collections of words ending in case-suffixes.
Why does *kyaṅ* not occur after a collection of words ending in a nominal suffix (*subanta*)? It is said: even in the rule for *laṅ*, the term "root" (*dhātu*) is understood to carry over.

Now, while the word "elision" (*lopa*) is already being carried over from [Pāṇini 3.1.11], what is the purpose of mentioning "elision" (*lopa*) again? It is for the purpose of excluding the letter *s*.

For the previous mention of *lopa* (elision) was connected with the letter *s*; therefore, if that were to recur [in the present rule], its recurrence would also follow, and consequently, elision would undesirably apply even to that which is not followed by a suffix (*ananta*). Otherwise, its recurrence would be purposeless. [The example] "lohitāyate" [is formed] by [the rule] Pāṇini 1.3.90, which prescribes the Ātmanepada voice. [The example] "paṭapaṭāyate" [is formed similarly].
From the word *paṭat*, the suffix *ḍāc* is applied by [Pāṇini 5.4.57] *avyaktānukaraṇāt*.

By [the Vārttika] *ḍāci bahulaṃ dve* (Vārttika 888), reduplication occurs before the suffix *ḍāc* itself, because the term *ḍāci* in the rule is a locative of scope (*viṣayasaptamī*). Once *ḍāc* has been applied, the *ṭi*-elision takes place.

In the case of reduplication, the *pararūpa* (substitution of the subsequent form) applies to the *takāra* which is a constituent of the word *ac*, according to [Pāṇini 6.1.97]: "In reduplication, the single substitute for both is the form of the subsequent [element]"—thus, the letter *pakāra*.
Regarding the statement "the prescription of *kyaṣ* after *lohita* and words ending in *ḍāc*" and so forth:
the meaning is that this prescription of *kyaṣ* by the rule concerning *lohita* and others applies specifically after the word *lohita* and after words ending in *ḍāc*.

But surely, other word-forms such as *nīla* and so on are also listed among *lohita* and the others; therefore, the suffix *kyaṣ* ought to apply to them as well. To this he says: "In the *bhṛśādi* group," and so forth.
Those words other than *lohita* should be understood as belonging to the *bhṛśādi* group.
As for their inclusion here [in the *lohita* group], that is due to negligence.
The intention is that [the word] is not an *ārṣa* (Vedic) term because it arose in a recent time.

If, then, other words are recited among the *bhṛśādi* group, the inclusion of the word "etc. (*ādi*) would be purposeless, for there is nothing else that could be included by it? To this he says: "Those which," and so forth.
It should be understood that those which are recited among the *lohita* group due to negligence should instead be recited among the *bhṛśādi* group.
But this is not the case for *varman* and the others when they are not explicitly listed [in the *gaṇa*].
Therefore, since they are included by the mention of "etc. (*ādi*), only *kyaṣ* occurs;
thus, one says *varmāyate*.
> [[8.2.7]] Thus, there is the elision of *n*. By the rule `akṛtsārvadhātukayoḥ` [[7.4.25]], there is lengthening.

Words such as *nidrā* are listed here; although they denote a mere quality (*dharma*), they nevertheless refer to a substance (*dravya*) when occurring in the scope of the *kyap* suffix, due to the inherent nature of the expressive power of words. For example: *nidrāyate*.
The meaning is that one who was sleepless becomes possessed of sleep. But how can those words not explicitly listed in the gaṇa be considered *lohitādi*? To this he says: "And this is an *ākṛtigaṇa*.
How is this known? To this he says: "And thus," and so forth.
He says "keyati" (it is for the purpose of grasping the general) and states "naḥ kye.

In this regard, one might think that the letter *k* is appended to the end of that which ends in *n* among those enumerated, for the sake of the technical designation "pada"; thus he says "na hi," and so forth.

But how is it that *ḍāc* occurs in connection with *kyaṣ*, given that the rule *kṛbhvastiyoge* (Pāṇini 3.1.40) continues [from the previous sūtra], so that *ḍāc* is prescribed only in connection with roots such as *kṛ*, *bhū*, and *as*, and not with *kyaṣ*? To this he says: "{The printed reading is `kṛbhvastibhireva`} ‘as if in connection with *kṛ*, *bhū*, and *as*’, etc.
This very prescription of *kyaṣ* after words ending in *ḍāc* indicates that just as *ḍāc* occurs in connection with *kṛ*, *bhū*, and *as*, so too does it occur with *kyaṣ*.
Otherwise, the mention of *ḍāc* would be purposeless if *ḍāc* were not to occur in connection with *kyaṣ*.

But surely, when the suffix *ḍāc* occurs in connection with the root *bhū*, then *kyaṣ* will occur after that which ends in it; so how can there be pointlessness? This is not so; for *kyaṣ* cannot occur here now, because the meaning [of becoming] has already been expressed by the verb *bhū* itself.

The intention is that, according to the maxim regarding the connection with *mañi*, *kyaṣ* is understood to occur in the sense of "the transformation of something into what it was not," due to the continued application of the rule *acveriti*.

For just as in the previous sūtra, due to the prohibition by *acveḥ*, the suffix *kyaṅ* is prescribed for the domain of "becoming that which one was not" (*abhūtatadbhāva*) according to this principle, so too here [is it prescribed] by *kyaṣ*. [The objection is: "Only *kyaṅ* is carried over, not *kyaṣ*," because only *kyaṅ* is marked with the *svarita* accent.

[The reply is: From the very mention of *kaṣṭāya* in the rule "from a word in the fourth case-ending" (*caturthī-samarthāt*), the fourth case-ending is obtained as the governing case; therefore, by its force, the suffix is understood [to apply].

This word *kramaṇa* exists in the sense of "stepping" (*pādaviharaṇa*) and also in the sense of "crookedness" (*anārjava*). Since the term "stepping" (*kramaṇa*) would otherwise denote that [action] without distinction, the qualification is employed so that the suffix might not be understood as referring merely to stepping. *Jihṛm*, *pāpa*, and *anārjava* are synonymous.

Therefore, when the term is qualified by "crookedness" (*anārjava*), the suffix is understood to apply specifically to that stepping which is characterized by crookedness, and not to stepping in general.

And this is obtained because the term *vā* (or) from the rule *dhātoḥ karmaṇaḥ* [Pāṇini 3.1.7] and others, which continues to apply here, is understood as having a restricted optionality (*vyavasthitavibhāṣā*).
In the expression *kaṣṭāya kramaṇe*, the dative case is used in the sense of purpose (*tādarthye*).
Thus, one says *kaṣṭāyate*.
The meaning is that it performs a difficult progression, which is non-straightforward.
"This is said to be too little" because it does not encompass all the illustrative examples (*lakṣya*).
He asks, "How then should it be stated? and replies with the printed reading: *satrakaṣṭa*, etc.

Although in this alternative analysis (*nyāsa*) there is no mention of a case-ending that expresses the required semantic relation (*samarthavibhakti*), nevertheless, because the governing rule for nominal suffixes (*sub-adhikāra*) is in force, the appropriate case-ending compatible with that sense must be supplied.

Thus, *sattrāyate* means "he intends to perform a sacrificial session" (*satraṃ cikīrṣati*), which signifies "he desires to commit sin. Similarly, one says "the goat steps into difficulty" (*ajaḥ kaṣṭaṃ krāmati*).
In this context, the root *krami* means "to step" or "to move the feet. The word *kaṣṭam* is an accusative object; the meaning is that he steps into a difficult or impenetrable place.
Alternatively—"kaṣṭam" is an adverbial modifier (kriyāviśeṣaṇa).
The meaning is that the unborn one moves in such a way as to be "difficult" or "painful. Even when it is not an adverbial modifier, "kaṣṭam" ends in the accusative case.
For it has been established in such rules as *karaṇe ca stokālpa* [Pāṇini 2.3.33] that "the qualifiers of an action are the object" (*kriyāviśeṣāṇāṃ karmatā*).
Therefore, in the counter-example (*pratyudāharaṇa*) of this rule, there is the mention of the word *kaṣṭa* ending in the second case (*dvitīyānta*).

It is understood that in the primary examples (*mūlodāharaṇa*) as well, the second case—the governing case-ending (*samarthavibhakti*)—is to be supplied. The word *karmaṇaḥ* is in the ablative case (*pañcamī*), because of its grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the two words *romantha* and *tapas*, which also end in the ablative.
Even though there is grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with those two [words], the dual number does not occur, because the sentence is completed with each [word] individually.
Regarding the term *vartticarau*: "turning" (*vartana*) is *vartti*; it is derived from the causative root (*ṇyantāt*) with the feminine suffix *ktin*.

But surely the suffix *ktin* should not occur here, because it is superseded by *yuc* according to [Pāṇini 3.3.107]. There is no fault, for *ktin* will occur precisely due to this very irregular derivation (*nipātana*).
In "caraṇaṃ cariti," the suffix *kvip* is applied because the root belongs to the *sampadādi* group. "In the movement of the jaw," and so forth.
Regarding the chewing of what has been swallowed after having vomited it up again— which involves the movement of the jaw—
the form [of the verb] with the suffix *kyaṅ* derived from the word *romantha* should be explained as having this meaning.
This explanation, however, must be carried out by continuing the mention of the particle *vā* and relying on its status as an option (*vibhāṣā*) restricted to specific cases (*vyavasthita-vibhāṣā*).
The mention of *vā* (or) must necessarily be carried over [from the previous rule], so that the sentence "the worm *vartayati* the *romantha*" may be formed.

[In the expression] "the worm *vartayati* the *romantha*," it means that it makes into a ball (*guṭikā*) the substance called *romantha*—which is either what has been vomited out (*udgīrṇa*), cast outside, or what has been swallowed (*avagīrṇa*) and emerged through the back. This is the meaning.
Therefore, in this case, the movement of the jaw does not exist;
however, it certainly exists in the primary example, as in *romanthāyate*.
The meaning is: having drawn back again what was swallowed, one chews it.
That chewing consists precisely of the movement of the jaw. Others, however, explain the cognition of the movement of the jaw differently.

There exists this word *romantha*, which has the action as its meaning; by deriving a *ṇic* suffix from the nominal stem *romantha* according to the rule "the meaning of the verbal root [is added] after a nominal stem" (*dhātvartha*), and then forming a noun with the suffix *ghañ*, it refers to the chewing of that which was swallowed, having drawn it back up again.
And there exists this word as a denoter of a substance, which denotes a substance characterized by the act of rumination, whether it has been regurgitated or swallowed.
In this context, the term refers to that which expresses action (*kriyā*), because even when it applies to a substance (*dravya*), it does so only by means of an action.

Therefore, it is secondary (*gauṇa*) with respect to the substance and primary (*mukhya*) with respect to the action; and according to the principle that "between the secondary and the primary, the grammatical operation is understood to apply to the primary" (Vyākaraṇa-paribhāṣā 4), [the suffix] occurs only from that which expresses action, not from that which expresses a substance. Thus: "After *tapas*, the *parasmaipada* [suffixes] also [are used]."

The word "vaktavyam" (it must be stated) is required [as a supplement]. Since the *ātmanepada* would otherwise result due to the *ṅit* designation, the *parasmaipada* must be stated—that is, explained.

This explanation, however, must be made by relying on the fact that the option (*anyatarasyām*)—which is carried over from the rule "napuṃsakamanapuṃsakena" [Pāṇini 1.2.69] etc. to the rule "anudāttaṅitaḥ" [Pāṇini 1.3.12] by the maxim of the "frog-leap"—is a restricted option (*vyavasthitavibhāṣā*).
Therefore, the ātmanepada suffix does not occur after *tapas* when it takes the *ky-aṅ* suffix.
Due to its absence, by [Pāṇini 1.3.78], the parasmaipada suffix alone occurs. Regarding the statement, "It should be stated that [the suffix applies] also after *phena*":
this is to be explained as meaning that the *ky-aṅ* suffix occurs after the word *phena* when it denotes the sense of vomiting (*vamana*).

The explanation, however, is as follows: one should proceed by carrying forward the letter *ca* from the sūtra *bhṛśādibhyaḥ* [3.1.12] in the sense of an unexpressed collective inclusion (*anuktasamuccayārtha*). Here, by the word *karaṇa*, action (*kriyā*) is meant, not the most effective instrument (*sādhakatama*).
This is because, due to the governing rule (*adhikāra*) of *karmaṇaḥ* [3.1.15], the suffix must occur only after words that denote objects such as sound (*śabda*) and so forth.

In that case, if the suffix were applied to the most effective instrument, the base and the suffix would be unrelated; furthermore, since the status of being an object depends upon an action, in the absence of an action, the status of being an object could not exist.

Therefore, having determined that the word *karaṇa* (instrument) refers precisely to the act of doing (*karoti*), he says: "In the sense of the instrument, in the meaning of 'doing'. Regarding the example *sudina* and so forth, this should be explained as follows: the suffix *ky-aṅ* occurs after words such as *sudina* when they function as objects (*karman*) in the sense of "making" (*karoti*).
As for the explanation itself: here too, one must proceed by carrying over (*anuvartya*) that very particle *ca*, which serves to include what has not been explicitly mentioned.

For this very reason, by means of the particle *ca* (and), which has the sense of including what was not explicitly mentioned, there is also the inclusion of *aṭ* and the others. Consequently, forms such as *aṭāyate* are also established. [The expression] "*aṭāṭṭa*" and so forth:
the meaning is that "the inclusion" (*grahaṇam*) of *aṭ* and the others means their "adoption" (*upādānam*).
And this [sūtra] is commenced because the suffix *ṇic* would otherwise apply by the rule "tat karoti" (Pāṇini 3.1.26); that too is desired, as in *śabdayati* and *vairayati*.

Therefore, it should be understood that the recurrence of the particle *ca* is for the sake of this meaning as well. Regarding the phrase "in the sense of feeling (*vedanā*) and experience (*anubhava*)," experience is the apprehension of an object through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).

But surely, in common usage, the word "feeling" (vedanā) is seen to denote mere perception; how then is this specific distinction obtained? We shall explain in the subsequent sutra how it is so obtained.
An agent is an instrument of action, and an instrument of action exists only in relation to an action.
And here, "feeling" is heard as the action, and no other.
Therefore, he alone is understood to be the agent of that [feeling];
and he alone is understood to be the experiencer of that [feeling].

Consequently, even though the term is used without distinction, the word "agent" (kartṛ) is taken here as referring to the experiencer who is the agent—this is what is meant by the phrase "if [the feeling belongs] to the agent who is the experiencer," and so forth.
By this mention of the "agent" (*kartṛ*), he shows that pleasure and the like are qualified [by it], but not feeling (*vedanā*).
If feeling were qualified by the mention of the agent—such that feeling would belong to the agent—then here too [the following] would occur: "The preparer feels Devadatta’s pleasure.
For the feeling indeed belongs to the preparer as well, since he too is its agent.
For just as the one being served experiences pleasure, so too does the server.

However, this much is the distinction: one experiences it through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), while the other does so through inference (*anumāna*). For if [the self] were in no way the agent of that [action], the statement "it experiences" would not be possible; indeed, one who is not an agent is not said to experience.
Therefore, the point is that the inclusion of the agent as a qualification for pleasure and the like is logical.

But surely, even if [pleasure and so forth] are qualifiers of happiness and the like, that same fault remains; for pleasure and the rest are related to the prover as well, by way of a relationship characterized as the state of being produced and producer? This is not so; for in every case, pleasure and the rest are related to an agent (*kartṛ*), and this mention of "agent" is indeed made.

Therefore, by the force of the mention of "agent," it is specifically that agent who is the substratum (*āśraya*) and the inherent cause (*samavāyi-kāraṇa*) of pleasure and the rest that is understood.
By means of that relationship consisting of the relation between substratum and superstratum (āśrayāśrayibhāva), the suffix is understood to denote pleasure and so forth as related to the agent.
Furthermore, the agent is not the inherent cause (samavāyikāraṇa) of pleasure and so forth; what then? It is the instrumental cause (nimittakāraṇa).

Those pleasures and so forth which belong to the agent—the inherent cause of pleasure and so forth—and which are related to it by way of the relation between substratum and superstratum, are perceived through direct perception (pratyakṣa).
Therefore, it is rightly stated that the apprehension of that [object] has the nature of experience (*anubhava*), such that "in feeling (*vedanā*) there is experience of the object.

If, however, by the mention of the agent (*kartṛ*), pleasure (*sukha*) and so forth are qualified and not feeling itself, then the genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*) "in the feeling of the agent" would not be possible due to a lack of semantic connection (*asāmarthya*). There is no fault here because this is a scriptural formulation (*sautra*); even if there is a lack of semantic connection, the compound will occur because of the specific rule. Alternatively, it is simply not a compound at all; the absence of the genitive ending is due to its elision according to the rule *supāṃ suluk* (Pāṇini 7.1.39). [The phrase] "in a particular instrument (*karaṇaviśeṣe*) when there is honor (*pūjā*)" [is also explained in this way].

By the word "ādi" (and so forth), attendance (*paricaryā*) and wonder (*āścarya*) are included. By the phrase "of *namas*" (*namasaḥ*) and so on, he demonstrates the division of the scope for the meaning just stated immediately preceding.

Although this meaning follows from the general rule regarding the instrument (*karaṇa*), it is nevertheless obtained through the inherent nature of the expressive power (*abhidhāna-śakti-svābhāvya*) even without an explicit statement; just as the roots *pac* and others function in the sense of "softening" (*vikleda*) and so forth, and the *bahuvrīhi* compound functions in the sense of possession (*matvartha*).
"One pays homage to the gods" (*namasyati devān*).

Now, one might object: since the word *namaḥ* exists within the word *namasyati*, shouldn't the dative case be required by the rule "In connection with *namaḥ*, *svasti*, etc. [Pāṇini 2.3.16]? This is not so; for, according to the principle "When a meaningful item is being mentioned, an item that is meaningless is not included" (Vyāḍiparibhāṣā 1), it is impossible to treat the meaningful word *namaḥ* as being present here.

Alternatively, by the principle "The case ending denoting the grammatical relation (*kāraka*) is stronger than the case ending of a subordinate word (*upapada*)" (Cāndraparibhāṣā 69), the accusative case alone is applied.

The case-ending expressing a *kāraka* (grammatical participant) is stronger because it is independent of a connection with a secondary word (*upapada*), whereas the case-ending of a secondary word is weaker because it depends upon another word. For example: *namasyati*.
The meaning is that he pays homage;
"he serves" (varivasyati) means that he attends upon.
"Citrīyate" means "to cause wonder. Regarding "from the tail," and so forth:
*udasana* is throwing upwards; *paryasana* is throwing all around.

When the sense is that of raising up (*udasanana*), the word *ut-* is employed for the sake of indicating that meaning—as in *utpucchayate*. When the sense is that of shaking about (*paryasanana*), the word *pari-* is used—as in *paripucchayate*.

By the rule "the operation of the suffix *iṣṭhan* applies to the nominal stem" (*ṇāviṣṭhavat kāryaṃ prātipadikasya*; Vārttika 813), the elision of the final vowel (*ṭilopa*) occurs due to the application of the *iṣṭhavadbhāva* treatment.
*Samācayanaṃ* means piling up;
*arjanaṃ* means the acquisition of what has not been obtained;

*paridhānaṃ* means clothing. By the rule "After a nominal stem (*prātipadika*), [the suffix] *ṇic* is applied frequently in the sense of verbal action (*dhātvartha*), and it is treated like *iṣṭhan*" (Dhātupāṭha, Gaṇasūtra 186), the suffix *ṇic* is established after words such as *muṇḍa*.
And this is merely an elaboration of that very point.
Although the elaboration beginning with "it performs that" and so forth has already been stated, it is nevertheless repeated here for the benefit of those of dull intellect.
[This refers to the phrase] "or upon its cessation."
Upon the cessation of eating,
[the text says] "he takes milk as his vow" (*payo vratayati*); the meaning is that he consumes milk.

The expression "he vows [himself to] the food of a *vṛṣala*" (*vṛṣalānnaṃ vratayati*) means that he does not eat the food of a *vṛṣala*. Likewise, "he takes up the plough" (*haliṃ gṛhṇāti*) becomes *halayati*, and "he takes up strife" (*kaliṃ gṛhṇāti*) becomes *kalayati*. Now, one might ask: by this, he shows that even in the rule (*sūtra*), only *hali* and *kali* are intended to be included; however, the substitution of *at* for *a* has been applied to them so that the *sanvadbhāva* (the treatment as if preceded by the suffix *san*)—as prescribed by rules such as *sanvallaghuni* (Pāṇini 7.4.93)—might not occur.
Therefore, the inclusion of *halikalyoḥ* is appropriate.
For instance, the causative suffix *ṇic* is not difficult to obtain here, as it is established by the very *gaṇa*-sūtra itself;
this [mention] is stated merely for the sake of elaboration (*prapañca*).

And that *prapañca* (elaboration) is indeed applicable even to the inclusion of *hal* and *kal*. However, this is the distinction: when there is the inclusion of those ending in *akāra*, then by the very *gaṇasūtra*, *ṇic* would also apply to those ending in *īkāra*. Once that [suffix] has been applied, by virtue of the treatment as *iṣṭhavadbhāva*, *ṭilopa* would apply, as well as *vṛddhi* according to [Pāṇini 7.2.115]. Both of these are *anitya* (non-obligatory).

For instance, although *ṭilopa* applies whether [the suffix] has been applied or not (*kṛtākṛtaprasaṅgitva*), it is *anitya* because it results in the acquisition of a different form (*śabdāntaraprāpti*).

For instance, when the *vṛddhi* [substitution] has been applied, the substitution of *ai* for *aikāra* would apply; when it has not been applied, the substitution of *i* for *antikā* would apply. However, since the *vṛddhi* becomes non-applicable once the *ṭilopa* (elision of the suffix) has occurred, it is considered non-eternal (*anitya*).
This non-application occurs because the stem no longer ends in *ac*.

Between these two non-eternal rules, the *vṛddhi* prevails due to its higher priority; once that has been effected, the *ṭilopa* follows. Even then, the stem does not become one whose *aglopya* (the initial vowel is elided).

And this being the case, if the treatment as *san* (i.e., *sanvadbhāva*) were to apply by [Pāṇini 7.4.93] *sanvallaghuni*, and consequently the lengthening of the vowel of the reduplicated syllable were to apply by [Pāṇini 7.4.94] *sanyataḥ*, then the undesired forms *acīkalat* and *ajīhalat* would result.

However, when the inclusion of the words *halika* and *kalika*—which have undergone *attva* (the substitution of *a* for *ā*)—is accepted, although the *vṛddhi* (vowel strengthening) occurs because it is a subsequent rule, nevertheless, even when that *vṛddhi* has taken place, the suffix *am* is elided; thus, the base (*aṅga*) becomes one whose final vowel is elided (*aglopī*).
Consequently, due to the treatment as *san*, the desired forms *acakalat* and *ajahalat* are established.
In this context, only those two [roots] are to be understood for whose inclusion the desired result is achieved, but not those for whose inclusion an undesired result would follow;
for it is not appropriate to establish a rule in a grammatical treatise for the sake of an undesired outcome. Regarding the term *ekāc*:
this is a *bahuvrīhi* compound and not a *tatpuruṣa*, because of the qualifying term *halādeḥ*.
"It occurs in the sense of the intensification of an action. By this, he shows that the intensification of an action is a qualifier of the verbal root.
"Therefore, the suffix yaṅ occurs."

Where [is this used]? According to the rule, "suffixes whose meaning is not specified apply in their own sense" (Pāṇini 3.4.90), it occurs in that very context of *kriyāsamabhihāra* (intensive repetition of an action). The primary sense of *samabhihāra* is the gathering together in one place of things scattered in various locations, resulting in the formation of a single mass. However, since actions—which perish as soon as they arise—cannot coexist simultaneously, and since multiple actions cannot be denoted at once by a single verbal root (*dhātu*), such a primary *samabhihāra* is impossible. Therefore, to show the secondary sense of *samabhihāra*, he says: "frequency," and so forth.
Both of these [types of action] receive the designation "conjunction" (*samabhihāra*) figuratively due to their similarity to actual conjunction.

Just as there is a conjunction of substances that have been brought together and are not separated from other substances, so too this same [conjunction] occurs for actions that are not separated from other actions; such is the similarity.
Furthermore, action is of two kinds: primary (*pradhāna*) and secondary (*apradhāna*).
In this context, the primary action (*pradhānakriyā*) is such as softening (*vikledana*), while the subordinate action (*guṇakriyā*) is such as placing [the pot] on the fire (*adhiśrayaṇa*).

Therein, he who brings the cooking to its final result and, without undertaking another action, begins the cooking again, performs the repetition of the primary action; the repetition (*samabhihāra*) of these is their recurrence. On the other hand, he who performs the subordinate actions, such as placing on the fire and so forth, in their entirety without interruption by other actions, performs the repetition of the subordinate actions; the repetition of these is their intensification (*bhṛśārthatā*).

Or, it denotes an excess of the result, that is, an intensification of the meaning. For instance, one who, having attained the state of burning, continues to burn or shines intensely, is said to "blaze forth" (*jājvalyate*) or "shine brilliantly" (*dedīpyate*).
As for the form *pāpacyate*: [it is derived from *pac* with the intensive suffix].
The doubling [of the verb] occurs by the rule *dvirvacanam* [Vt. 885], and the lengthening occurs by the rule *dīrgho 'kitaḥ* [Pāṇini 7.4.83].

In this case, doubling does not occur according to the rule *kriyāsamabhihāre dve bhavataḥ* (Vārttika 886); for the suffix *yaṅ*, which is prescribed when there is intensity of action (*kriyāsamabhihāra*), possesses the inherent capacity to manifest that very intensity on its own. However, the imperative (*loṭ*) which will be taught in the rule *kriyāsamabhihāre loṭ loṭo hisvau vā ca tadhvamoḥ* [Pāṇini 3.4.2] is itself incapable of manifesting the intensity of action and therefore requires doubling.

This [suffix] *sa* is not prescribed for the repetition of an action (*kriyāsamabhihāra*), but rather for the object and other grammatical roles (*karmādiṣu*), according to the rule: "In the sense of the object and so forth" (Pāṇini 3.4.69).
Therefore, when it is employed, reduplication certainly occurs—as in: "He cuts, indeed, cutting again and again" (*lunīhi lunīhītyevāyaṃ lunāti*) and "he shines intensely" (*dedīpyate*).
The *guṇa* substitution [is applied] by the rule *guṇo yaṅ-lukoḥ* [Pāṇini 7.4.82]. Thus, we have the form *bhṛśaṃ prāṭati*.

If the mention of the word "dhātu" (root) were not present [in the rule], the meaning of the sūtra would be: "The suffix *yaṅ* occurs after a monosyllabic word beginning with a consonant that denotes the intensification of an action (*kriyā-samabhihāra*).
However, this is not the intended sense.

Furthermore, the suffix *yaṅ* would undesirably apply to the root *aṭ* preceded by *pra*; for the composite whole consisting of *pra* and *aṭ* possesses the aforementioned qualifications. This undesirable consequence does not arise, however, when there is the mention of "root" (*dhātu*), because this [composite] is not a root, but rather a combination of a root and a prefix (*upasarga*).
Regarding the form *jāgarti*:
the *śap* suffix is elided because the root belongs to the *adādi* (second) class.
Now, for what purpose is the mention of "action" (*kriyā*) [in the definition], instead of simply saying "repetition" (*samabhihāra*)? It is not so.

It might also apply when there is a repetition of the means (*sādhana*). This is not so; for this [term] is a qualifier of the base (*prakṛti*), and the occurrence of the base in the sense of a repetition of the means is not possible.

Moreover, the term "in the sense of an instrument" (*karaṇe*) [from Pāṇini 3.1.17] is understood here; by that, "repetition" (*samabhihāra*) is qualified. If repetition is connected with an instrument, then how could there be the possibility of its application to repetition of a means of accomplishment (*sādhana*)? This, then, is the purpose: so that it may apply to the repetition of mere action (*kriyā*). Otherwise, because the understanding of the grammatical operation would pertain to the principal element, it would apply only to the repetition of the principal action, not to the repetition of a subordinate action (*guṇakriyā*). [The examples begin with] *sūci* and so forth.

The roots *sūca* in the sense of "backbiting" (Dhātupāṭha 1873), *sūtra* in the sense of "untying" (Dhātupāṭha 1908), *mūtra* in the sense of "urinating" (Dhātupāṭha 1909), *aṭa* in the sense of "going" (Dhātupāṭha 295), *ṛ* in the sense of "going" (Dhātupāṭha 1098), *aśa* in the sense of "eating" (Dhātupāṭha 1523), and *ūrṇūñ* in the sense of "covering" (Dhātupāṭha 1039)—among these verbal roots (*prakṛti*), they must be included in the rule prescribing the *yaṅ* affix; and that [inclusion] belongs only to the former [set].

Because the particle *ca* has the sense of including what is not explicitly mentioned (*anuktasamuccaya*), it is understood [that these roots are included]. To the question, "For what purpose, then, is there this mention of these verbal roots (*prakṛti*)?", he says: "For the sake of those having multiple vowels (*anekāc*), those beginning with *ha*, and so forth. That which has "having multiple vowels," "beginning with *ha*," and so forth as its purpose (*artha*)—i.e., its motive—is described as such. The mention of the three roots *sūci* and the others, which belong to the *curādi* class and take the causative suffix (*ṇic*), is for the sake of [the rule concerning] those with multiple vowels; that of *ūrṇoti* is for the sake of both those with multiple vowels and those beginning with *ha*; but for the remaining ones, it is solely for the sake of those beginning with *ha*.
In *sosūyate*,
there is the elision of the *ṇi* suffix by [Pāṇini 6.4.51], and as before, there is the *guṇa* strengthening of the reduplicated syllable. In *aṭāṭayate*:
> [[6.1.2]] Thus, there is doubling of the letter *ṭ*, the application of the rule *halādiḥ śeṣaḥ* [6.4.65], and lengthening. In the form *arāryate*,
there is *guṇa* substitution by the rule *yaṅi ca* [7.4.30].
The doubling of the single-consonant *ry* in the second [syllable] does not apply by the rule "of a single consonant" (Pāṇini 6.1.3),
because of the statement: "there is a prohibition of the *r* that follows a *y*" (Vārttika 651).
Regarding "aśāśyate":
there is reduplication of the second monosyllabic element, namely "śya".
Regarding "prorṇunūyate": [the same applies].

Here too, the word *nu* is doubled; however, the letter *r* is not doubled, because there is a specific prohibition to that effect: "It is not desired in cases such as *bhṛśaṃ rocate* (it shines intensely) and *bhṛśaṃ śobhate* (it looks beautiful intensely)."

The status of the rule "tadarthaṃ vā" as having a restricted option (*vyavasthitavibhāṣā*) should be explained as following from the context. [The word] "dhātoḥ" (of a root) alone [is understood]; "in the sense of motion" (*gatau*) is an attribute of the base form (*prakṛti*).
The meaning is "from a verbal root denoting motion. He expresses this very same point by means of another synonym: "from a verbal root expressing motion," as in *caṅkramyate* and *daṃdramyate*.
The roots *kramu* (meaning "to step") [DhP 4.73], *drama*, *hamma*, and *mīmṛ* (meaning "to go") [DhP 4.66, 4.67, 4.68] take the augment *num* by [Aṣṭādhyāyī 7.4.85].
One who performs coming and going over a very short distance, thereby accomplishing a winding motion, is said to be *caṅkramyate* or *dedramyate*.

Now, what is the purpose of including the word *nitya* ("always"), given that the sentence will not even arise here due to the lack of conventional usage? For the sentence "he moves in a winding way" (*kuṭilaṃ krāmati*) cannot convey the meaning of the verbal derivative *caṅkramyate*.

For instance, from the sentence *kuṭilaṃ krāmati* ("he moves crookedly"), a doubt arises: "Is it the crookedness of the motion, or the crookedness of the mind? However, in the case of the verbal derivative *caṅkramyate*, there is no doubt, as only the crookedness of the motion is understood; thus he says, "The mention of 'nitya' (constant)," and so forth.
The scope is the crookedness of motion.
That which has the restriction of the *yaṅ* suffix as its purpose (*artha*)—that is what is meant by that expression.
By the phrase "because it expresses motion" (*gativacanāt*), etc., he shows the purpose of the rule;
by the phrase "but not," etc., he indicates that which is excluded by it.

"Always" (*nityam*) means at all times: because it expresses motion, the suffix occurs only in the sense of crookedness (*kauṭilya*), and never in the sense of the intensification of an action (*kriyāsamabhihāra*).

Therefore, in the sense of "he moves excessively" (*bhṛśaṃ krāmati*), the *yaṅ* suffix—which would otherwise be required by the preceding rule—is not applied. The roots are as follows: *luplṛ* in the sense of cutting (*chedane*) [DhP 1431]; *ṣadlṛ* in the senses of falling apart, moving, and sinking (*viśaraṇa-gaty-avasādaneṣu*) [DhP 1427]; *abhra*, *vabhra*, and *cara* in the sense of moving (*gatyarthāḥ*) [DhP 556, 557, 559]; *japa* and *jalpa* in the sense of distinct speech (*vyaktāyāṃ vāci*) [DhP 397, 398]; and *jabhī* (or *jabha*, or *jṛbhi*) in the sense of bending the limbs (*gātravināme*).

(*Dhātupāṭha* 388, 389): *daha* in the sense of "reducing to ashes" (*bhasmīkaraṇe*); (*Dhātupāṭha* 991): *daṃśa* in the sense of "biting" (*daṃśane*); (*Dhātupāṇini* 1410): *gṛ* in the sense of "swallowing" (*nigaraṇe*).

By the phrase "when there is censure regarding the meaning of the verbal root" (*dhātvarthagarhāyām*), he explains the meaning of [the rule] "when there is censure regarding the action" (*bhāvagarhāyām*). [Thus, the sense is: "he censures that which is being destroyed."
"Blameworthy" (*garhita*) is an adverbial modifier (*kriyāviśeṣaṇa*).
By this, a censure of the state of being (*bhāvagarhā*) is understood here.
The blameworthiness [of cutting] is due to its lack of purpose and because it is corrupted by faults.
In the same way, the state of being censurable (*garhitatva*) should be understood in what follows as well.
Regarding the word *cañcūryate*,
the suffix *nuk* is applied by [Pāṇini 7.4.87].
The substitution of *u* [for *a*] occurs by [Pāṇini 7.4.88] *utparasyātaḥ*, and the lengthening occurs by [Pāṇini 8.2.77] *hali ca*.
Regarding *jañjapyate*:
the augment *nuk* is applied by [Pāṇini 7.4.86] *japajabha-* and so forth.

By the rule *ṛta iddhātoḥ* [Pāṇini 7.1.100], there is the substitution of *i*, followed by the substitution of *ra* for *ṛ*, reduplication, the elision of the *repha* (*r*) and *yakāra* (*y*) of the word *giryā* by the rule *halādiśeṣaḥ*, the *guṇa* substitution as before, and finally the substitution of *la* by the rule *pūrvatrāsiddham* [Pāṇini 8.2.1] applied to *latvam*. In the expression "he recites well" (*sādhu japati*), there is no censure of the meaning of the verbal root; rather, it is praise.

"In the expression *mantraṃ japati vṛṣalaḥ* (the outcaste mutters a mantra), the censure of the agent (*sādhana*), namely the *vṛṣala*, is understood; for a *vṛṣala*—that is, a *śūdra*—lacks the qualification to mutter Vedic mantras. The inclusion here of words other than those beginning with *cura* is for the sake of elaboration (*prapañca*), since [the formation] is already established by the rule: "After a nominal stem (*prātipadika*), the suffix *ṇic* is applied diversely (*bahulam*) in the sense of verbal activity (*dhātvartha*), and it is treated like the suffix *iṣṭhan*. [The examples] begin with *arthaveda*.
The word *vaktavya* means "to be explained.

As for the explanation: because of the rule *prātipadikāddhātvarthe bahulam* (Pāṇini 3.1.13), which serves to prescribe other grammatical operations, the augment *apuk* occurs for these [roots] in conjunction with the suffix *ṇic*.
However, in the case of the word *satya*, it should be understood that the augment *āpuk* occurs due to the specific irregularity (*nipātana*) in the rule *satyāpa* (Pāṇini 3.1.25).
"Vipāśayati" means "he releases the bond. "Nirūpayati" means...
The meaning is "he sees form. In the case of *abhiṣeṇayati*,
the substitution of *ṣ* [for *s*] occurs by the rule beginning with *upasargāt* [Pāṇini 8.3.65].

Regarding the form *tvacayati*: one might object that the word *tvac* ends in a consonant (*halanta*). Therefore, when the causative suffix *ṇic* is added, since the rule *ṇāviṣṭhavat* (Vārttika 813) applies, the status of being like the superlative suffix *iṣṭhan* would cause the elision of the final vowel (*ṭilopa*). Once that elision is applied, the rule *prakṛtivadbhāvaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.4.163) would apply, and subsequently the rule *vṛddhir eci* (Pāṇini 7.2.116) would require a *vṛddhi* strengthening. Thus, how can it be that the form is *tvacayati*? To this he replies: "This word *tvaca* ends in the vowel *a*. This is indeed a different word ending in *a*, which has the same meaning as the word *tvac*.

For this very reason, there is the mention of *tvaca-* ending in *-a* in the sūtra; when that *-a* is elided, no vṛddhi occurs due to the status of the substitute (*sthānivadbhāva*). [The rule] "after *cur* and so forth, in the sense of the root itself" applies to stealing and the like.

But surely, since topics such as narratives (*ākhyāna*) and the like are not included here in this Sūtra, how can they be obtained? And if they are not obtained, how can they be indicated? To this he says: "Because it is inherent" (*svābhāvikatvāt*), and so forth.
The denotation of meaning by words is inherent, not something resulting from explicit instruction (*vācanika*); for it has already been stated that the latter is impossible.
Therefore, whatever word is inherently the designator of a particular meaning, it is entirely appropriate to indicate that meaning even if it is not explicitly included in the Sūtra.

"Yathāyatham" means that which belongs to each respective [word]. But are these words beginning with *kaṇḍū* verbal roots (*dhātu*) or nominal stems (*prātipadika*)? In that regard, if they were verbal roots, then when the suffix *yak* is applied, the form *kaṇḍūḥ* would not be established;
rather, *kaṇḍūyā* would result.

But surely, the word "or" (vā) will carry over [from the previous rule]; therefore, when the yaṅ suffix is absent, the form *kaṇḍūḥ* will result? This is not so; for it is impossible for a case-ending (*sub*-vibhakti) to arise directly from a verbal root, since such endings are prescribed only after nominal stems (*prātipadika*).

It might be argued: "When *kvip* is applied after a root ending in *yaṅ* by [Pāṇini 3.2.178], and when the *a* is elided by [6.4.48] and the *y* is elided by [6.1.66] before a *val* suffix, the form *kaṇḍūḥ* will be established. This is incorrect; for *kvip* is prescribed in the sense of the agent (*kartṛ*), whereas *kaṇḍūḥ* denotes merely a sensation (*vedanāmātra*) and not an agent. Nevertheless, because the class beginning with *sampad* is an open-ended group (*ākṛtigaṇa*), one may derive *kaṇḍūḥ* by applying *kvip* in the sense of the abstract state (*bhāva*). Even so, forms such as *mantuḥ* and *valgūḥ* would still not be established.

If, by the recurrence of the word *vet* (or *vā*), the suffix *yak* does not occur after the words *manu* and *valgu*, then a case-ending (*vibhakti*) would not be applicable to them; consequently, the forms would be *manu* and *valgu* without a case-ending.

Alternatively, if the suffix *kvip* is applied after having prescribed *yak* for those two, even so, the undesired forms *mantūḥ* and *valgūḥ* would result. For once *yak* has been applied, lengthening must necessarily occur by the rule *akṛtsārvadhātukayoḥ* [Pāṇini 7.4.25].

Now, if *kaṇḍv-ādayaḥ* were nominal stems (*prātipadika*), then the addition of the suffix *yak* would be purposeless; for that [suffix] is added so that the prohibition by *na dhātu-lopa-aardhadhātuka-ya-ṅ-āḥ* [Pāṇini 1.1.4] may apply to the guna substitution that would otherwise be required by *sārvadhātuka-ārdhadhātuka-yoḥ* [Pāṇini 7.3.84]. If they were nominal stems, this purpose would not be achieved, because one might object that a suffix prescribed after a nominal stem does not receive the designation *ārdhadhātuka*. To address such an objection, he says: "They are of two kinds," and so forth.
In this context, the locative case is used in the sense of selection (*nirdhāraṇa*).

Among those roots and nominal stems (*dhātu-prātipadika*), the suffix *yak* is applied after those roots which belong to the *kaṇḍv-ādi* class; the justification for this is found in the rule "under the heading of 'roots'. To strengthen this very point, he says: "And thus," and so forth.

Since the suffix is prescribed from roots (*dhātu*) in this manner—because the context is that of roots and not nominal stems (*prātipadika*)—the letter *k* is attached as an indicatory marker (*anubandha*) to the suffix *yak* for the purpose of prohibiting *guṇa*. For if *yak* were to be applied to nominal stems, it would not be an *ārdhadhātuka* suffix; consequently, since there would be no possibility of *guṇa* occurring at all, the addition of the indicatory *k* to prohibit it would be purposeless. Thus, [the rule] "it is a root because of the context of roots" applies.
The phrase "it produces an affix" is to be supplied as the remainder [of the sentence].

From the rule *dhātor ekācaḥ* (Pāṇini 3.1.22), the term *dhātu* ("verbal root") is understood to carry over. Therefore, only a verbal root such as *kaṇḍū* and others produces the affix, not a nominal stem (*prātipadika*).
Regarding the phrase "of what," and so forth:
for this reason as well—the attachment of the *kakāra* (the letter *k*) as an *anubandha*—the verbal root (*dhātu*) produces a suffix (*pratyaya*).
Otherwise, the employment of the *kakāra* as an *anubandha* would be entirely purposeless according to the manner previously stated.

Therefore, because the suffix *ya* is prescribed for *kaṇḍū* and others which have become verbal roots (*dhātu*), and because the indicatory letter *k* is attached to them, their status as verbal roots is understood.

For it would not be logical to prescribe the suffix *ya* for those that have not become verbal roots, nor would it be appropriate to attach the indicatory letter *k*, as there would be no purpose for doing so.
Now, how is it determined that *kaṇḍū* and the others are nominal stems (*prātipadika*)? To this he says: "And he says," and so forth.
The particle *ca* indicates the reason (*hetau*).

If these were merely verbal roots (*dhātu*), then once the suffix *yak* was applied, the lengthening [of the vowel] would already be established by the rule *akṛt-sārvadhātuka-ardhadhātukayoḥ* (Pāṇini 7.4.25); consequently, he would not have pronounced the long vowels in *kaṇḍūñ*, *hmaṇīṅ*, and *mahīṅ*. Yet he does pronounce the long vowels. Therefore, it is concluded that "the root is optionally designated" (*dhātur vibhāṣitaḥ*). The meaning is that their status as verbal roots is optional.

But surely, in the alternative view (*pakṣe*), where the suffix *yaṅ* does not occur, the long vowel must be pronounced for the purpose of ensuring that when a suffix such as *kvip* follows roots ending in *ay*, forms like *kaṇḍūḥ*, *kaṇḍūtiḥ*, and *kaṇḍūtavān* are heard with the long vowel. So how can it be said that [the long vowel] is useless? Furthermore, how can suffixes such as *kvip* follow roots ending in *ay*, given that *yak* is optional? And why is it optional? Because of the continued application of the word "or" (*vā*). This is not so; for this rule is compulsory (*nitya*). Its compulsion, however, follows from the fact that the mention of "or" (*vā*) has been withdrawn.

But from what source is that cessation understood? From the formulation of the rule beginning with *āyādayaḥ* [Pāṇini 3.1.31]. If the term *vā* ("or") were to carry over here, it would also carry over into the subsequent rules, and thus one would not need to formulate this rule at all, thinking, "The *āya*-suffixes and others will optionally occur. Furthermore, if that rule were not formulated, the *āya*-suffixes and others would not apply even before *sārvadhātuka* affixes optionally; for the mention of *vā* is a *vyavasthitavibhāṣā* (a restricted option).

Therefore, because the rule beginning with "tasmād āyādayaḥ" (Pāṇini 6.1.80) is formulated, it is understood that the mention of the term *vā* ("optionally") has ceased; thus, the suffix *yaK* must necessarily occur.
Consequently, if these [words] were not *prātipadika*s according to this view, the vocalization of the long vowel [in the sūtra] would be purposeless.
Therefore, by the force of the vocalization of the long vowel, they possess *prātipadika* status; this is the definitive position.

In that regard, under the view that [the items] belong to the *dhātu* (verbal root) class, forms such as *kaṇḍūyate* are established; however, under the view that they are *prātipadika* (nominal stems), if the *yaK* suffix were not present, forms such as *kaṇḍūḥ*, *mantuḥ*, and *valgūḥ* would result.

As for those ending in the vowel *a* that are listed among the *kaṇḍvādi* group—such as *magadha* and others—the elision of the *a* occurs by [Pāṇini 6.4.48]: *aniditāṃ hala upadhāyāḥ kṅiti*, resulting in *magadhyati*, *sukhyati*, and *duḥkhyati*. The two words *leṭ* and *loṭ* are listed [in the *gaṇapāṭha*]; they are understood here by their own form (*svarūpa*) and not as grammatical suffixes (*pratyaya*), because of their association with the *kaṇḍvādi* group which consists of words representing their own forms. [The commentary continues with] "for the purpose of praise," and so forth.
The roots are listed in the Dhātupāṭha in this sequence: "paṇa [is used] in the sense of trading and praise" (Dhātupāṭha 439), and "pana, and [also in the sense of praise]" (Dhātupāṭha 440).

In that context, under "pana ca" (Dhātupāṭha 440), the term "praise" (stuti) is understood to carry over [from the previous rule], but not the meaning of "trading" (vyavahāra). Therefore, while *paṇi* has both the meanings of trading and praise, *pani* has only the meaning of praise.
Consequently, here, by virtue of its association with *paṇi* which has the meaning of praise, *pani* is also taken as having only the meaning of praise.
Therefore, being engaged solely in praise, he produces conviction, but not in regard to worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*).

In the expression "of a hundred" (*śatasya*), the genitive case is used for the object according to [Pāṇini 2.3.57]: "The genitive is used for the object when [the verbs] *vyavahṛ* (to deal) and *paṇ* (to bet) are employed with a capable [agent]."

In this regard, why does the *ātmanepada* not occur in the form *paṇāyati*, given that this root *paṇ* is listed as having an *anudātta* vowel? In that case, just as the *ātmanepada* occurs after the simple root by the rule "from roots with an *anudātta* vowel or marked with Ṅ" (*anudāttaṅitaḥ* 1.3.12), it ought to occur likewise after a form ending in the *āya*-affix. To this he says: "The indicatory letter," and so forth. For that which is its indicatory letter has already served its purpose—having effected the *ātmanepada* operation—in the case of *paṇati* when devoid of the *āya*-affix; therefore, the *ātmanepada* does not occur after a form ending in the *āya*-affix, because that [form] constitutes a different verbal root. [The term used is] "sautraḥ" (found in the sūtra).
Because it is recited in the Sūtra;
that which exists in the Sūtra is "sautra.
It is said: "It functions in the sense of compassion (ghṛṇā)."
*Ghṛṇā* means *jugupsā* (disgust).
This [suffix] occurs there by its very nature.
