Now, why is it called *īya*, rather than being called simply *cha*; for if *cha* were used, with the substitution of *īya* for it, the form *ṛtīyate* would be established? It is not established; because the augment *iṭ* would apply first due to its higher priority, the substitution of *īya* would not occur, as the suffix would no longer begin with a vowel.

But surely, because it is *antaraṅga*, the substitution of *ī* alone will take place; its *antaraṅga* status follows from the statement: "The rule that [the stem] behaves as if it were taught (*upadeśivat*) is for the sake of obtaining the desired accent" (Vārttika on Pāṇini 7.1.2). If this is so, then this teaches: "The suffixes *āya*, *anna*, and so forth, do not apply to verbal roots. By this, forms such as *śaṇḍhaḥ*—derived by adding the suffix *ḍha* to the root *śam*—are established.
Alternatively, it is because of the statement: "In the rules governing accent, the behavior as if taught is for the sake of obtaining the accent."

Therefore, since there would be no status of being "internal" (*antaraṅga*), the augment *iṭ* would apply by virtue of its priority; hence, *īyaṅ* is prescribed. [The inclusion of] the letter *ṇ* is for the sake of *vṛddhi*, so that *vṛddhi* may occur according to [Pāṇini 7.2.116]: *aca upadhāyāḥ*.

If this is so, for what purpose is the designation *mit* prohibited for the root *kam* in the rule *na kampamicamām* (Dhātupāṭha 817), lest the shortening prescribed by *mitāṃ hrasvaḥ* (6.4.92) should take place? This is not the case; it will not occur precisely because of the force of the application of the marker *ṇ*; otherwise, the application of the marker *ṇ* would be purposeless.

Is it not purposeless? No, because it serves the purpose of including the general term [in the rule]. Furthermore, when the suffix *ṇiṅ* is absent by virtue of the rule *āyādaya ārdhadhātuke vā* [Pāṇini 3.1.31], the designation *mit* is prohibited so that shortening (*hrasvatva*) does not occur in the case of the causative *ṇic*. By the phrase "in the domain of the *ārdhadhātuka*," he shows that the term *ārdhadhātuka* functions as a locative of domain (*viṣayasaptamī*).

He states, "when there is the intention to express an *ārdhadhātuka*," because the status of being in the domain of the *ārdhadhātuka* is possible only when that [suffix] is present in the mind through the desire to express it, and not otherwise.

But with what intention is the locative case of the object (*viṣayasaptamī*) resorted to? He thinks as follows: In the case of the locative of another [element], is the arising (*utpatti*) of the suffix considered, or its non-arising (*nivṛtti*)? If it is arising, then when the suffix *ktin* is prescribed for the root *gup* in the feminine, if the suffix *āya* does not arise there, then the desired form *guptiḥ* is established as intended.

But when it does arise, then by the rules "of *at*" [Pāṇ. 6.4.48] and "when *val* is elided" [Pāṇ. 6.1.64], once the vowel *a* has been made, if there is no subsequent non-arising, then the desired form *gopāyati* is established as intended.

But when [the suffix] *gopa* occurs, one encounters the undesirable consequence that "protection" (*gupti*)—whether it exists or does not exist—is not established as a desired result upon its cessation. However, if the locative case is taken as denoting the object (*viṣaya-saptamī*), then since the arising is optional, it will arise.
In the case of the term *ārdhadhātuka*, if there is an intention to express the *ārdhadhātuka* state, the option applies from the very beginning.

In that regard, according to the view that [the suffix] does not arise, when the suffix *ktin* is prescribed after a feminine base, the form *guptiḥ* is established; whereas according to the view that it does arise, *gopāyā* results.
Nor is *gopātiḥ* an undesirable consequence, because the suffix *ktin* does not occur after a base ending in the suffix *āya*.
Nor does the undesirable form *gopā* result, because the suffix *āya* itself does not arise.
Regarding the phrase "in the event of the undesirable consequence of [the suffix] nitya":
the meaning is that, by means of the three preceding sūtras, [the suffixes] āya and so forth would have applied to [words such as] māyā and others.
Regarding the phrase "at its production" and so forth: [it refers to the application of the suffix].
The arising of those [suffixes], such as *āya* and others, is postulated when the *ardhadhātuka* suffix is the domain, but not the cessation of those that have already arisen.

For if their cessation were postulated, then when the *āya* suffix has ceased while the *ardhadhātuka* remains as the domain, the suffix *a* would be prescribed by the rule *a pratyayāt* [Pāṇini 3.3.102] according to the characteristic of the suffix (*pratyayalakṣaṇa*). Consequently, even though the locative case indicates the domain (*viṣayasaptamī*), the undesirable form *gopeti* would result; this is the intended meaning.
Regarding the phrase "as appropriate" (*yathāyatham*):

The meaning is that whatever is obtained from something arises from it subsequently, following the conceptualization of its production. By the specific phrase "those which have *san* and so forth at their end," he demonstrates a *bahuvrīhi* compound.

For a *bahuvrīhi* certainly occurs even with words in different grammatical cases (*vyadhikaraṇa*) when the meaning is clear, as in *kaṇṭhekālaḥ* ("the one who has a dark throat") and *urasiloma* ("the one who has hair on his chest").
By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), there is the inclusion of all suffixes beginning with *kyac* and ending with *ṇiṅ*.
Regarding the term "collections" (*samudāya*):
it refers to collections consisting of both base (*prakṛti*) and suffix (*pratyaya*).

By this, he indicates that this is a *tadguṇasaṃvijñāna* bahuvrīhi compound; otherwise, the designation "verbal root" (*dhātu*) would be prescribed only for those bases characterized by *san* and so forth.
Regarding the phrase "{dhātusaṃjñāḥ - *Kāśikā* and *Padamañjarī*}: `dhātusaṃjñakāḥ`":
those for whom "dhātu" is the designation are called *dhātusaṃjñakāḥ*.

Here, the word *dhātu* refers to its own form (*svarūpa*) as the referent, not to the referent consisting of the roots *bhū*, *vā*, and so forth. Otherwise, the roots *bhū* and so on would become the designations for those ending in *san* and so forth; and that is incorrect, for there is no purpose whatsoever in establishing such a vast number of designations.
Furthermore, designations (*saṃjñā*) are subject to recurrence;
for there is no rule in any treatise stating that all [roots] beginning with *bhū* and so forth must recur. Therefore, the word *dhātu* does not denote those [roots].
For here, in this rule prescribing technical designations, there is the inclusion of suffixes (*pratyaya*) such as *san* and others.

And in this regard, by the inclusion of the term *ca* (and) in [Pāṇini 1.4.14], it has been indicated that: "When a suffix is mentioned, it denotes that which begins with the element from which that suffix is prescribed and ends with the suffix itself" (Paribhāṣā 44).
This paribhāṣā is prohibited when a suffix is mentioned in a rule prescribing a technical name (*saṃjñā*).

In that context, if the mention of "ending in" (*anta*) were not made, the rule for "ending in that" (*tadanta-vidhi*) would not apply; yet it is desired. Therefore, the mention of "ending in" is made for that purpose. Regarding this, one might object, thinking that by this mention of "ending in," a previously non-existent *tadanta-vidhi* is being established, and thus [the objection] would be: "If this technical designation (*saṃjñā*) is prescribed for those ending in *san* and so forth, then in the case of *devadattaḥ prācikīrṣat*, the designation would undesirably apply to Devadatta as well as to the prefix. To this he replies: "By the very paribhāṣā regarding the mention of an affix (*pratyayagrahaṇa-paribhāṣā*)," and so on.

Indeed, by the mention of "end" (*anta*), a previously non-existent rule regarding the end of that [element] is not being established; what then? Since the designation of a "word" (*pada*) was prohibited by the mention of "end" in the rules prescribing such designations, it is here restored by the very paribhāṣā concerning the mention of an affix (*pratyayagrahaṇa*). The meaning is that, having been obstructed while its operation had already commenced, it proceeds once more.

Consequently, the technical name applies only to the entire aggregate beginning with that from which the *san* and other affixes were prescribed, and not to something beginning with a different word; this is the intended sense.

Now, immediately after [the sūtra] *atha* (1.3.1), why was it not stated that "those ending in *san* and so forth [are also verbal roots]" (*sanādyantāśca*)? For if this were the case, the term *dhātu-* would not need to be mentioned twice. This cannot be done; for if it were done in that way, there would be no definite limit to the number of suffixes beginning with *san*.
However, by doing it here [as it is], the inclusion of all suffixes up to and including *ṇiṅ* is understood.

If that is so, why was it not stated immediately after [Pāṇini 1.3.1] *tarhi* (in 1.3.2) that "and *bhūvādayaḥ*"? This too is not [the case]; for if it were done in this way, since [the suffixes] beginning with *san* depend on what has been previously enumerated (*anukrānta*), the *bhūvādayaḥ* would also have to depend on what has been previously enumerated. Consequently, only those beginning with *gup* that have been previously enumerated would receive the designation *dhātu*, and not others such as *bhū* and the rest. Alternatively, if *bhūvādayaḥ* did not depend on what has been previously enumerated, then *san* and the others would likewise not depend on it; and thus there would be doubt as to whether *san* and the others should be understood as extending up to *kap*.
Therefore, it is logical to follow the original arrangement. Here there are two forms of *lṛ*: one belonging to *lṛṭ* and the second to *lṛṅ*.
Since the inclusion of both is desired and no distinction is made between them, these two, together with the third, *luṅ*, constitute three causes [for the application of the rule].
However, there would be an inequality in that there would be two *nimittas* (causes/conditions), whereas [the rule] speaks of "two.
Therefore, for one who might object that a numerical correspondence (*saṃkhyātānudeśa*) would thus be impossible, he replies with the words "the form *lṛ*" and so forth.

By discarding the *anubandhas* (indicatory letters) *ṭ* and *ṅ*, there is no difference in the resulting forms; thus, the form *lṛ* is common and identical to both *lṛṅ* and *lṛṭ*. Consequently, the duality of the *nimittas* also holds.

The intention is that, because of this, the correspondence according to number (*saṃkhyātānudeśa*) is not contradicted. For this very reason, he says: "according to the order" (*yathāsaṃkhyam*), and "he will do" (*kariṣyati*).
The suffix *luṭ* [is applied] as in *iti*; the augment *iṭ* is added by the rule *ṛddhanoḥ sye* [Pāṇini 7.2.70]. Regarding *akariṣyat*:
the suffix *lṛṅ* is applied, the augment *aṭ* is added, and the vowel *i* is elided by the rule *itaśca* [Pāṇini 3.4.100].

Regarding the term *kartā*: by the rule *anadyatane luṭ* [Pāṇini 3.3.15], the suffix *luṭ* is applied; then, by the rule *luṭaḥ prathamasya* [Pāṇini 2.4.85] and others, the substitution of *ḍā* for *tip* occurs, followed by the elision of the *ṭi* (the final vowel and following consonant). Regarding the phrase "the inclusion of the *it*-marker," and so forth: *iditkaraṇam* etc. means that the addition of the marker *it* [to the root *kṛ*] serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*) for the application of the augment *num*. This is because the marker *it* is prescribed for roots ending in vowels (*ajādīnām*) to indicate that the augment *num* should be inserted after the penultimate vowel (*upadhā*) when the suffixes beginning with *śap* follow. Since the root *kṛ* ends in a consonant (*halanta*), the marker *it* would otherwise have no purpose; therefore, its presence indicates that the augment *num* applies even to roots ending in consonants. Thus, *num* is added, resulting in the form *kar-t-ā*. Furthermore, since *num* is a marker (*itsaṃjñaka*), it is elided by the rule *tasya lopaḥ* [Pāṇini 1.3.9]. Consequently, the form becomes *kartā*. As for the statement "the *it*-marker is not for the sake of accent (*svarārtham*)," this is because the accent is already established by the rule *citaḥ* [Pāṇini 6.1.163], which prescribes an acute accent (*udātta*) on the final syllable of a word that has a *cit* marker. Therefore, the marker *it* is not intended to serve the purpose of determining the accent. Finally, regarding the statement "the *it*-marker is for the sake of the feminine suffix (*strīpratyayārtham*)," this is because the marker *it* is prescribed for roots ending in vowels to indicate that the feminine suffix *ṭāp* should be added. Since the root *kṛ* ends in a consonant, the marker *it* would otherwise be redundant; thus, its presence indicates that the feminine suffix *ṭāp* applies even to roots ending in consonants. Consequently, *ṭāp* is added, resulting in the feminine form *kartṛ*. As for the statement "the *it*-marker is not for the sake of the feminine suffix," this is because the feminine suffix is already established by the rule *ṭiḍḍhāṇañdvayasajdaghnañmātractayapṭhakṭhañkañkvarapaḥ* [Pāṇini 4.1.15], which prescribes the suffix *ṅīp* for words ending in *ṭi*, *ḍha*, *ṇa*, *añ*, *dvayasaC*, *daghnaC*, *mātraC*, *tayap*, *ṭhak*, *ṭhaÑ*, *kaÑ*, or *kvarap*. Therefore, the marker *it* is not intended for the purpose of adding the feminine suffix. As for the statement "the *it*-marker is not for the sake of the elision of the *ṭi* portion (*ṭilopārtham*)," this is because the elision of the *ṭi* portion is already established by the rule *ṭeḥ* [Pāṇini 6.4.143], which prescribes the elision of the *ṭi* portion of a verbal root (*dhātu*) before the suffixes *śas* and those beginning with *s*. Since the root *kṛ* ends in a consonant, the marker *it* would otherwise be redundant; thus, its presence indicates that the elision of the *ṭi* portion applies even to roots ending in consonants. Consequently, the *ṭi* portion is elided, resulting in the form *kartā*. As for the statement "the *it*-marker is not for the sake of the elision of the *ṭi* portion," this is because the elision is already established by the rule *ato lopaḥ* [Pāṇini 6.4.48], which prescribes the elision of the final vowel (*akāra*) of a verbal root (*dhātu*) before the suffixes *śas* and those beginning with *s*. Therefore, the marker *it* is not intended for the purpose of the elision of the *ṭi* portion. "Thus, *iccāsāv it* means 'that which is both *it* and has *it* as its designation'; the formation of that is *iditkaraṇam*. The meaning is: the formation of the letter *i* which has the designation *it*.

Alternatively: that *tāsi* (the suffix *tās*) which has *idit* [as its marker] is *idit-tāsi*; the formation of that is *iditkaraṇam*, meaning the formation of the letter *i* belonging to the *tāsi* which has the designation *it*."

"‘For the purpose of preventing the elision of the nasal’ (anunāsikalopapratibandhārtham). For if that [marking as *it*] were not present, there would be the elision of the nasal according to [Aṣṭādhyāyī 6.4.24], *aniditām*. Therefore, the marking as *it* is for this purpose: so that there may be its prevention—that is, an obstruction to its operation."
Regarding the word *mantā*:
it is derived from the root *man* in the sense of "knowing" (*jñāne*, Dhātupāṭha 1176), or from *manu* in the sense of "understanding" (*avabodhane*, Dhātupāṭha 1471).
The middle voice (*ātmanepada*) is applied according to Pāṇini 1.3.12: *anudāttaṅita ātmanepadam*.

Regarding the term *saṃgantā*: here too, from the root *gam* preceded by the prefix *sam*, the rule *samo gami* [Pāṇini 1.3.29] applies. Since the *ṭi*-lopa (elision of the suffix) is applied in both cases, one might expect the elision of the nasal (*anunāsika-lopa*) by resorting to the *ātmanepada* because of the *ṅit* designation. This [elision] is prevented by the inclusion of the marker *it*. If, then, the inclusion of the marker *it* in *tās* is for the purpose of obstructing the elision of the nasal, this being so, does it not contradict what will be stated under [Pāṇini 7.1.58]: "In the case of *tās* and *sic*, there is no operation of the marker *it*; therefore, the vowel *i* is recited without the nasal (*niranunāsika*) for the sake of pronunciation"? There is no contradiction, because they were composed by different authors.

This is indeed the statement of Jayāditya, while that [other view] belongs to Vāmana. In the *Vāmanavṛtti*, however, the vowel *i* in the roots *tāsi* and *sici* is taught as being for the purpose of pronunciation (*uccāraṇārtha*) and not as an indicatory letter (*anubandha*); therefore, no contradiction should be suspected. With what intention, then, did Jayāditya treat the *i*-vowel of *tāsi* as having the function of preventing the elision of a nasal (*anunāsikalopa*), whereas Vāmana treated it as being merely for the purpose of pronunciation? Let that intention be heard: the non-application of the rule of "asiddha" (as if not having taken effect) within its own domain is non-eternal (*anitya*), and Jayāditya will demonstrate that non-eternality in that very context.

The intention here is that the elision of *ṭi* prescribed by the *ābhīya* rule is not considered *asiddha* in this context because that rule is not universally obligatory (*anitya*); thus, it was stated that the *ikāra* of *tāsi-* serves the purpose of preventing the elision of the nasal.
Vāmana, however, considering that the *asiddha* status does indeed apply here, stated that it serves the purpose of mere pronunciation (*uccāraṇārtha*).
For if the elision of *ṭi* were considered asiddha (non-existent for the purposes of the preceding rule), the elision of the nasal (*anunāsikalopa*) would not apply;
therefore, it is incorrect to claim that the long vowel *ī* is intended to prevent that [nasal elision].

Indeed, just as the teacher Gonardīya—relying on the application of the *sannipātalakṣaṇaparibhāṣā*—stated that in the case of *atijaraṃ brāhmaṇakulam tiṣṭhati*, one ought to have *atijarair brāhmaṇakulaiḥ*.

Others, however, relying on the non-application of this technical rule (*paribhāṣā*) due to its lack of permanence, say that *atijarasam brāhmaṇakulam* should become *atijarasar*. Likewise, it should be understood that the two authors of the *Vṛtti* have stated these two purposes by relying both on its existence as a scriptural rule and on its lack of permanence. Others explain that, relying on the view that "the section concerning what is unestablished (*asiddha-adhikāra*)" precedes [this rule], it was stated that the purpose of the letter *i* is to prevent the elision of the nasal (*anunāsika-lopa*); whereas, relying on the view that "the section concerning what is unestablished" occurs together with it, it was stated that its purpose is for the sake of pronunciation (*uccāraṇārtha*).
And this [point] is impossible to understand, because Jayāditya and Vāmana did not adopt the position that "the scope [of the suffixes] is established prior to the existence [of the verbal base].
That they did not adopt it is made manifest in the commentary (*vṛtti*) on that very point, and thus it should be understood from there alone.

Furthermore, these [suffixes] *sva* and so forth are exceptions (*apavāda*) to all [suffixes] such as *yaṅ*, by the maxim of "that which was not previously applicable" (*yenāprāpte*) and because of their being internal (*antaraṅga*). Their internality, however, arises because they are prescribed precisely at the stage of the *l* [augment]. Regarding "joṣiṣat": the root *juṣ* (Dhātupāṭha 1288), meaning "to delight in" or "to serve," is used in the sense of the optative (*liṅ*) with the suffix *leṭ*.
The letter *i* in *sip* is for the purpose of pronunciation; the letter *p* is for the sake of the accent. By [Pāṇini 3.4.94], the augment *aṭ* is added.

By [Pāṇini 3.4.97], there is the elision of the letter *i*. By [Pāṇini 7.2.35], the augment *iṭ* is applied because the *ārdhadhātuka* suffix begins with a consonant other than a semivowel. There is the *guṇa* substitution for the light penultimate vowel. By [Pāṇini 8.3.59], the change to *ṣ* occurs. Thus, we have *tāriṣat*.

From the root *tṛ* in the sense of "floating" or "crossing over" (*dhātupāṭha* 969), by [Pāṇini 7.3.84] and [3.1.85], there is a transposition of phonemes (*varṇavyatyaya*) whereby the vowel *a* of the root becomes *ā*.
The remainder is as before. Thus: *mandiṣat*.

Regarding *madī*: according to the *Dhātupāṭha* (*stutimodamadasvapnakāntigatiṣu*), and specifically the entry *stutimodanasvapnagitiṣu* (DhP 1.13), the augment *num* is applied by [Aṣṭādhyāyī 7.1.58]. Regarding *padāti*:

the root *pada* in the sense of "going" (DhP 10.1169) belongs to the *divādi* class and is *anudātta*; the *parasmaipada* ending is used by way of transposition (*vyatyaya*), along with the *śap* suffix, and there is the lengthening of the homogeneous vowel (*savarṇadīrgha*) together with the augment *aṭ*.
The elision of the letter *i* does not occur here in the case of *tip*; this is because the word "optionally" (*vā*) is understood from the rule [Pāṇini 3.1.96]. Regarding the form *cyāvayāti*:
the roots *cyaṅ*, *chyuṅ*, *jyuṅ*, *jhayuṅ*, *pruṅ*, and *pluṅ* are listed in the Dhātupāṭha (nos. 955–958) with the meaning "to move."
The suffix *ṇic* is added because of the causal sense (*hetu*).

Regarding the addition of the marker *p* to *sip*: in the form *bobhūyiṣātām*, where the acute accent (*udātta*) would otherwise apply by the rule for the "cessation of the acute" (*udāttanivṛtti-svara*), the marker *p* is intended to ensure that the syllable remains unaccented (*anudātta*).
From the word *bobhūya*, which ends in *yaṅ*, the *ātmanepada* middle voice affix *leṭ* is applied; the third person dual ending *tas* is used, and the *ṭi*-portion of this affix is replaced by *e*.

By the rule *eta ai* [Pāṇini 3.4.93–94], the augment *āṭ* is applied; then, by the rule *sārvadhātukam apit* [Pāṇini 6.1.186], the *sārvadhātuka* suffix is unaccented. Due to the force of the *pit* designation, this unaccented status awaits the accent of the *sip* suffix, even though it is an internal (*antaraṅga*) operation. Once that has been effected, the augment *iṭ* is added to the *sip*.
And that [augment] is unaccented because of the rule *āgamā anudāttāḥ* (augments are unaccented).
By [Pāṇini 6.4.48], there is the elision of the udātta vowel *a* of the *yaṅ* suffix.
Its status as udātta, however, is due to the accent of the verbal root (dhātusvara).

When [Pāṇini 6.1.161] would have applied to make it udātta, the fact that the suffix is marked with the letter *p* causes the *iṭ* augment to become anudātta. By the term "affix" (*pratyaya*) in this context, the affixes beginning with *sañ* (desiderative) and so forth are included.

By the paribhāṣā "in the case of the mention of a suffix, [the rule applies] to that which ends with it" (PuPāVṛ 44), or by [Pāṇini 1.1.72], the designation of that which ends in [the suffix] is understood. Furthermore, because of the governing context of "roots" (dhātu), roots are specified here by the mention of "suffixes"; thus he says, "from roots ending in suffixes.
It was stated [earlier] with reference to the alternative view that the root ends in a consonant (*halanta*), namely, "the suffix *ām* occurs.

However, in the alternative view where the root ends in a vowel (*adanta*), it should have been said, "the suffix *ām* occurs," but that was not stated; for it is understood from the very fact that *ām* will be taught later as having the marker *m* (i.e., being *amit*) precisely because the root ends in a vowel.

The term *amantra* here is a locative of domain (*viṣaya-saptamī*), not a locative of proximity (*para-saptamī*). Therefore, because of the exclusion of mantras, this rule is understood to apply specifically to the spoken language (*bhāṣā*) and the *brāhmaṇa* texts.

A *brāhmaṇa* is a treatise consisting of the very explanation of mantras. Now, one might object: "By the maxim of the particle *na* joined with a negative (*nañ-iva-yukta-nyāya*), [the prohibition] should apply only to the *brāhmaṇa*, not to the spoken language. This is not so; for if it were not intended to apply even to the spoken language, he would have simply said "*brāhmaṇe*" [without mentioning *bhāṣāyām*].
Regarding the form *kāsāñcakre*:
by [Pāṇini 2.4.81] *āmaḥ*, there is the elision (*luk*) of the suffix *liṭ*.

Since that [suffix] has been elided because it was a substitute for *liṭ*, the designation of a nominal stem (*prātipadika-saṃjñā*) applies by [Pāṇini 1.2.46], which states that when a suffix is elided, the operations conditioned by that suffix still take place. Then the case-ending *su* is added. Alternatively, because the word *svar-ādi* is recited [in the list of indeclinables], the designation of an indeclinable (*avyaya-saṃjñā*) applies—either by the inclusion of the particle *ca* in the rule [1.1.38] as having the sense of an unmentioned collection, or otherwise—and thus there is the elision of *su*.

Now, by the rule *atha* [Pāṇini 6.1.68], the elision (*lopa*) of the nominative suffix *su* will occur here; what is the use of the designation "indeclinable" (*avyaya-saṃjñā*) in this case? [Examples: *lolūyāñcakre*—this is formed with the suffix *ām* after the root *lolūya* ending in *yaṅ*. *nonāva*—this is formed similarly.

The root *ṇu* is used in the sense of "praising" (*stuti*; Dhātupāṭha 1035). By the rule *ṇo naḥ* [Pāṇini 6.1.63], the *ṇ* is changed to *n*. With the suffix *yaṅ*, we have the form *nonūyate*. At this stage, by the rule *yaṅo 'ci ca* [Pāṇini 2.4.74], there is elision (*luk*) of the *yaṅ*. Then follows the suffix *liṭ*, the suffix *tip*, and by the rule *parasmaipadānām* [Pāṇini 3.4.82], *ṇal* is substituted for *tip*. Vṛddhi then occurs.

In this case, by the principle of "characterized by the suffix" (*pratyayalakṣaṇa*), the suffix *ām* would apply after a stem ending in a suffix; however, because of the specific statement "not in the case of a mantra" (*amantra*), it does not occur. Regarding the rule *kāsyanekācaḥ* and so forth:
the meaning is that one should remove the mention of the suffix (*pratyaya*) and instead employ the mention of "having more than one vowel" (*anekāc*).
He asks "For what purpose? and replies: "For the sake of *culumpa* and so forth.

For according to the original formulation (*yathānyāsam*), after the word *ka*, which denotes Prajāpati as well as Viṣṇu, when the suffix *kvip* is applied to form a word for habitual action (*ācārakvip*), the suffix *ām* would undesirably follow even from that derivative; furthermore, it would not apply to roots such as *cakāsṛ* and others that do not end in a suffix. Therefore, this alternative formulation (*nyāsāntaram*) is to be understood.

Others, however, believe that because the mention of "affix" (*pratyaya*) implies "having more than one vowel" (*anekāc*), this [rule] need not be formulated; but this is incorrect. For it is not tenable that the mention of "affix" is intended as an implication for "having more than one vowel," since there exist both monosyllabic affixes and monosyllabic roots.
We shall demonstrate later how this alternative formulation (*nyāsāntara*) is to be rejected, as in the examples:
*cakāsāñcakāra* and *daridrāñcakāra*.
The roots *cakāsṛ* in the sense of "shining" (Dhātupāṭha 1074) and *daridrā* in the sense of "poverty" (Dhātupāṭha 1073) [are cited].
Regarding the form *culumpāñcakāra*:

although the root *culumpati* is not listed among the standard verbal roots (*dhātu*), its status as a root should be understood on the authority of Kātyāyana’s statement that "the inclusion of the term 'more than one syllable' (*anekāj*) in the rule for *kāspratyayādāmamantre liṭi* is for the sake of including *culumpa* and others. Now, why does the designation *it* not apply to the letter *m* of *ām*? To this he says: "Because *ām* has the designation *am*," and so forth.

That which has the letter *m* as its final element is "this" (*idam*); "not this" (*na idam*) is *amidam*. The state of being that is *amittvam*. He asks, "How is there the state of being *amit*? and replies with the words "because it ends in *a*" (*adantatvāt*), and so forth.
For if it were to end in the letter *m*, the technical designation *itsaṃjñā* would apply to that *m*.
Nor does this [suffix] end in the letter *m*; rather, it ends in the vowel *a*.

Therefore, the vowel *a* itself—by undergoing the designation *it* according to the rule "In the original instruction, an *anunāsika* [nasal] is designated as *it*" (Pāṇini 1.3.2)—prevents the letter *m* from receiving the designation *it*.
This is just as, for example, in the case of the root *vid*, its lack of *guṇa* substitution follows from its being *am-ita* (having *m* as an *it*) due to its ending in the vowel *a*.
For even in the absence of the [guṇa] quality, in the case of the root *vid*, as in *vidāñcakāra*, the substitution occurs only at the beginning because of its ending in the vowel *a*.

Now, since it ends in *a*, when the *a* is elided by Pāṇini 6.4.48 (*ato lopaḥ*), the vowel *i* does not become a *upadhā* (penultimate) due to the status of being a *sthānivadbhāva* according to 1.1.57 (*tasyāḥ*). Consequently, the *guṇa* substitution for a light *upadhā* does not take place.
However, its ending in *a* is established by the rule 3.1.38 (*videḥ*), which prescribes the ending in *a* by way of a *nipātana* (irregular formation) in conjunction with the suffix *ām*.
Having accepted that the suffix *ām* ends in the letter *m*, he says "because of the prescription of *āścakāsaḥ*" in order to establish its status as an *am-it*.
The connection is with the previously mentioned [rule] that *ām* is an *am-it*; for the suffix *ām* is prescribed after the root *ās-* by the rule "after *day*, *ā*, and *ās*" (Pāṇini 3.1.37).

And because of the supplementary rule (*upasaṃkhyāna*) stating that "the mention of 'having more than one vowel' in the case of roots ending in *kāsi* is for the sake of [roots like] *culump*" and so forth, [the suffix *ām* is applied] after the root *cakās-*.

By the inclusion of the word "ādi" (and so forth), *cakās* is also included. The purpose of assigning the technical designation *it* to the letter *m* is that it should follow after the final vowel (*aco 'ntyāt paraḥ*). For if *ām* were not designated as *it*, then the prescription of *ām* for *āś* and *cakās* would be rendered meaningless.

For there is no distinction whatsoever between those two [roots] as to whether a *pa* (the augment *ām*) occurs after the final vowel or does not occur; for in both cases, by the rule *ato lopaḥ* [6.4.48], that very same form would result. Thus, how can this prescription of *ām* for the roots *āś* and *cakās* be meaningful? It would be meaningful only if *ām* were an *am* (i.e., if it ended in *m*), and not otherwise. Since there is no other purpose, the *it* designation will not apply due to the absence of such a purpose.

One should not entertain the doubt that "the long vowel substitution for homogeneous vowels (*savarṇadīrghatva*) will not occur here because of the power of the rule [prescribing] *āṬ*," nor that "the *paribhāṣā* [stating that a rule applies only when its cause is not separated by anything other than vowels or semivowels] will not apply"— this is unacceptable for one who does not wish to contradict the observed linguistic data (*lakṣya*).
For in that case, an undesirable form would result.
Furthermore, it is not logical for an undesirable meaning to be established in a treatise.

If, then, [the root] *am* were indeed [treated as] ending in *t*, the grammatical instruction *āmamantra* would be untenable; for by the rule of homogeneous lengthening (*savarṇadīrgha*), it ought to have been *āmāmantre*. To this he says: "The subsequent form (*pararūpa*) applies, as in the case of *katanta*. Just as there is a subsequent form in the rule *sarvatra lohitādikatantebhyaḥ* (Pāṇini 4.1.18), so it is here as well; thus, there is no inconsistency in the instruction. [Note: The printed reading is *ijādeḥ*. "Of that which begins with *ij*" (*ijādeḥ*).
The term *ādi* [in the compound] is a *bahuvrīhi*;
*ic* is the inclusion of the *pratyāhāra*;
and *gurumān* means "that which has a *guru* [heavy syllable]."
"Devoid of *ṛcchati*" means abandoned by *ṛcchati*;
the meaning is that he is devoid of its form. "In the act of striving (*īhācañkre*)"—thus [it is said].
Regarding the root *īh* in the sense of "exertion" (Dhātupāṭha 632), we have the form *ūhāñcakre*.
Regarding the root *ūh* in the sense of "reflection" (Dhātupāṭha 648),
we have *tatakṣa* and *rarakṣa*.
The roots *takṣū* and *tvakṣū* mean "to make thin" (Dhātupāṭha 655, 656); *rakṣa* means "to protect" (Dhātupāṭha 658). Regarding the forms *iyaja* and *uvapa*:

in the case of the root *yaj* and *vap*, when the first person singular (*uttama*) ending *ṇal* follows, there is an absence of the designation *ṇit* according to Pāṇini 7.1.91; consequently, due to the absence of *vṛddhi* [vowel strengthening], there is an absence of the condition of having a heavy syllable (*gurumattā*).

Some maintain that *iyeṣa* and *uvoṣa* are counter-examples. Regarding the roots *iṣu* in the sense of "desiring" (DhP 1351) and *uṣa* in the sense of "burning" (DhP 696): in the *ṇal* suffix, there is the *guṇa* substitution for the light penultimate vowel, followed by reduplication. Then, by [Aṣṭādhyāyī 6.4.78], the substitutions *iyaṅ* and *uvaṅ* apply. Now, one might object: "Once *guṇa* has been applied, these two [roots] also become 'heavy' (*guru*), so shouldn't the augment *ām* necessarily occur? The answer is: it should not occur. According to the principle "a rule conditioned by a specific configuration [of sounds] is not a cause for the destruction of that configuration" (Vyāḍiparibhāṣā 12), the presence of the *liṭ* suffix constitutes the configuration that causes the root to be heavy. Thus, the very condition that triggers *guṇa* prevents the application of *ām*.
Furthermore, the term *gurumattā* (the state of having a heavy syllable) in the rule *āmaḥ* [Pāṇini 2.4.81] precludes only the *liṭ* (perfect tense).

Alternatively, the suffix *matup* in *gurumataḥ* denotes constant connection (*nityayoga*); therefore, it should apply only to that which is constantly connected with a heavy syllable. Now, this is not the case for the roots *iṣ* and *uṣ*, as they do not have a constant connection with a heavy syllable. If this were so, then in the form *ucchāñcakāra* from the root *ucchi* (meaning "to dwell," Dhātupāṭha 216), the rule would not apply once the *tuk* augment has been added? This is not a fault; for the prohibition regarding the root *ṛcch* indicates that the rule applies even to that which acquires a heavy syllable due to an adventitious cause (*āgamanimittā*).
Regarding the word *ānarchcha*:

from the root *ṛccha* in the sense of "motion, loss of the senses, or becoming embodied" (Dhātupāṭha 1296), there is the insertion of *tuk* by [Pāṇini 6.1.71], the substitution of *guṇa* by [Pāṇini 7.4.11], reduplication, the replacement of all but the first consonant by the first one (*halādiśeṣa*), lengthening by [Pāṇini 7.4.70], and the addition of the augment *nuṭ* by [Pāṇini 7.4.71].

But is it not the case that the mention of *guṇa* for the root *ṛcch* immediately before the *liṭ* suffix in [Pāṇini 7.4.11] serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*) that the augment *ām* does not apply to *ṛcch*?
For if that [condition] were present, it would not have been indicated that "heaviness" (gurumattā) belonging to that [root] arises even from the cause of its arrival (āgamanimitta).
Therefore, the prohibition "anṛccha" must be stated. Regarding "of the root ūrṇoti," etc.:
because it begins with *ij* and because it possesses heaviness, the suffix *ām* would apply.
Therefore, a prohibition must be stated; that is to say, it must be explained.

The explanation, however, is as follows: because the term *anyatarasyām* (optionally), which is to be mentioned later, is understood by way of the "lion's glance" (*siṃhāvalokita*) principle to apply here as a *vyavasthitavibhāṣā* (restricted option), [the prohibition] must be formulated.
Thus: *prorṇunāva*.
> [[6.1.2]] Thus, there is reduplication of the syllable *nu*, but the letter *r* is not reduplicated; > [[6.1.3]] because of this prohibition. "Or rather," and so forth.
[The root] *ṇu* is used in the sense of "praise" (*stuti*; Dhātupāṭha 1.35).
"It occurs in the same manner as *nu*" means that its state is the "state of being like *nu*.
The meaning is that it functions similarly to the suffix *nu*.
But what is the purpose for which it must be expressed in such a way? To this he says: "The non-occurrence of *yaṅ* is the purpose."

When there is the substitution of *nu* for *nū*, just as the suffix *yaṅ* occurs after the root *nū*—as in *nonūyate* according to [Pāṇini 3.1.22] *dhātor ekācaḥ*—so too does it occur after the root *ūrṇu*: *prorṇonūyate*.
Regarding the statement "and for the purpose of prohibiting *ām*," it is required that the substitution of *nu* be stated.
When that is present, just as *ām* does not occur after the root *nū* because it belongs to the *ani* class and lacks the augment *guṇa*, so too it does not occur after the root *ūrṇu*: *prorṇunāva*.
Regarding the rule *ekācaśceḍdupagrahāt*, it is connected with the statement "the treatment as having a penultimate *u* (*nuvadbhāva*) should be stated.
Here, the ablative case is used according to *karmaṇi lyablope* (Pāṇini 2.3.28), as in the examples: "he looks from the palace" (*prāsādāt prekṣate*) or "he looks from the seat" (*āsanāt prekṣate*).
The phrase "the inclusion of *iṭ*" refers to the prohibition of *iṭ*.

This is what is meant: while the rule *ekācaḥ* [Pāṇini 7.2.10] is being carried over, the inclusion of *iṭ* prescribed by the rule *śrayukaḥ kiti* [Pāṇini 7.2.11] is made with reference to this very point; namely, that the status of *nu* should be stated for the root *ūrṇu*.

Consequently, just as there is a prohibition of *iṭ* for the root *nū* by the rule *śrayukaḥ kiti*—as in *nutaḥ*, *nutavān*—so too is there a prohibition for the root *ūrṇu*—as in *proṛṇutaḥ*, *proṛṇutavān*.

Alternatively, in the expression *iḍupagrahāt*, this ablative case (*pañcamī*) is used in the sense of a cause (*hetu*), as in [Pāṇini 1.2.53]. The meaning is that because the augment *iṭ* is prescribed for roots with a single vowel (*ekāc*) when there is an *upagraha* (i.e., the Ātmanepada), for that reason—that is, for that purpose—the status of being "like *ūrṇu*" (*nuvadbhāva*) must be stated for the root *ūrṇu*.
Now, what is the purpose of the particle *ca* in the rule *ijādeśca*? It serves to include what has not been mentioned; by means of it, [the rule] *kāsyanekācaḥ* (Vārttika) [is applied].
Thus, it need not be stated [in the rule].

For even according to the alternative formulation (*anyāsa*), forms such as *cakāsāñcakāra* are established by means of the letter *ca*. Now, one might object: "If this were not stated, would it not follow that the suffix *ām* could also be applied after a root ending in a suffix that consists of a single vowel (*ekāc*)? If this is not desired, then one must accept that the upcoming mention of the word *antarasyām* (‘optionally’) is a governing reference (*anuvṛtti*), and that it functions as a fixed option (*vyavasthitavibhāṣā*). As in the example: *palāyāñcakre*.

In *parāyāta*, there is the substitution of *l* for *y* by the rule *upasargasyāyatau* [Pāṇini 8.2.19]. Due to association (*sāhacarya*) with *uṣ* and *jāgṛ*, the root *vid* is understood here as the one meaning "knowledge" that takes the *parasmaipada* (active voice), and not the two *ātmanepada* roots meaning "existence" and "investigation," nor the *ubhayapada* root meaning "acquisition. Because of its association with *jāgarti* from the *adādi* class, only the *adādi* root *vid* is taken; thus he says, "*vida jñāne*" ("*vid* in the sense of knowing").
In *viveda*, because it lacks a final long vowel (*adantatva*), the *guṇa* substitution indeed occurs.
The fact that the root *vid* ends in a short vowel (*a*) is understood through its connection with [the rule regarding] *ām*; therefore, the absence of *guṇa* occurs only there and not elsewhere.

Hence he says: "Because it is asserted that *vid* ends in a short vowel, there is no *guṇa* before *ām*. Regarding the phrase "of *bhī*, *hī*, *bhṛ*, and *hu*," the genitive case is used in the sense of the ablative.
"Supām supo bhavanti" means "the case endings (sup) become [other] case endings (sup). Regarding "śluvat": it is like ślu; thus, "śluvat."
By the rule *Pāṇini 5.1.116*, the suffix *vati* is applied after a word ending in the seventh case (*saptamī*).
This is an extension of grammatical operations (*kāryātideśa*). For this very reason, it is said: "In this [context], the operation is as in the *ślu* [elision]."
Regarding the phrase "doubling and the substitution of *i*":
doubling occurs by the rule *ślau* [Pāṇini 6.1.10], and the substitution of *i* occurs by the rule *bhṛñāmit* [Pāṇini 7.4.76].
If this extension (*atideśa*) did not exist, the doubling dependent on the *liṭ* suffix would not take place when there is an intervention by the augment *ām*.

Otherwise, this [result] would not occur at all; for in the rule prescribing that [guṇa], from the rule "There is guṇa for the three [roots] ending in ṇ, j, or ñ before ślu" (Pāṇini 7.4.75), the term "before ślu" (ślau) is understood by anuvṛtti.
Therefore, the extended application (atideśa) "as if it were ślu" (śluvat ca) is established for the sake of accomplishing both of these. Regarding the phrase "is employed after" (anuprayujyate):
the two words *anu* and *pra* are each in the nominative case.

The word *yujyate* is a form ending in the third person singular of the middle voice (*ātmanepada*). Regarding the phrase *ām-pratyayasya*: it is a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "that from which the suffix *ām* arises."

By the word *paścāt* (afterwards), the author explains the meaning of the prefix *anu*, thereby refuting its prior application (*prākprayoga*). Furthermore, because all sentences have the nature of being restrictive (*sāvadhāraṇaphala*), the rule that the root *kṛ* is employed immediately after the *ām*-affix is established here as a restriction; thus, its application with an intervening element is refuted. For if *kṛ* were applied with an intervening element, it would not be "applied after the *ām*-affix" alone, but rather after another word as well. By the phrase "when *liṭ* follows," he states that there is no application when any other suffix follows.

But surely, by the rule *āmaḥ* [Pāṇini 2.4.81], there ought to be a *luk*-elision of the *liṭ* [perfect] suffix; so how can *kṛñ* be employed as an auxiliary (*anuprayujyate*) when *liṭ* follows? This is not a fault; for the meaning here is not that *kṛñ* is employed as an auxiliary whenever a *liṭ* is prescribed by another rule and follows it.

Now, an objection is raised: "Since it is stated that *kṛñ* [is used], the subsequent employment (*anuprayoga*) of the roots *bhū* and *as*, as in *pācayāmbabhūva* and *pācayāmāsa*, would not be established. To this he says: "By means of the pratyāhāra ‘*kṛñ*’," and so forth. Having taken the word *kṛ* from the rule *iti* (Pāṇini 5.4.50), this is a reference to a *pratyāhāra* by means of the letter *ñ* in the rule *kṛño dvitīyatṛtīyaśambabījāt kṛṣau* (Pāṇini 5.4.58).
By that *pratyāhāra* reference, the three roots *kṛ*, *bhū*, and *as* are included;
and since all three are contained therein, there is no fault.

Even so, the subsequent application (*anuprayoga*) of the root *as* is not established; for by the rule *[[P. 2.4.52]]*, there ought to be the substitution of *bhū* for *as*. To this he says: "by virtue of that" (*tatsāmarthyāt*).
By virtue of the inclusion of *kṛ*, *bhū*, and *as* within the pratyāhāra, the substitution of *bhū* for *as* does not take place.
The purpose of including these [three] in the pratyāhāra is so that the subsequent application of *as* may occur.

If the substitution of *bhū* were to apply to every instance of the auxiliary verb (*anuprayoga*), the mention of the *pratyāhāra* [of roots] would be useless; one would simply have said, "the root *kṛ* is used as an auxiliary in the periphrastic perfect (*liṭ*).
Even in that case, the doubt—"Does this mention of *karoti* refer to the root *kṛ*, or to the *pratyāhāra*?"—would be avoided.

If, then, there is the inclusion of the *pratyāhāra* "kṛñ" [in the rule], then in that case, by [Pāṇini 5.4.53], the employment of *sampad* as an auxiliary verb would follow, because *sampad* is included within that *pratyāhāra*. This is not a fault; for the term "dhātu" (root) is understood to carry over from [Pāṇini 3.1.32], and by that, *kṛñ* is qualified—meaning "that *kṛñ* which is a root. Now, *sampad* is not a root; what is it then? It is a combination of a root and a prefix (*upasarga*). Therefore, it is not employed as an auxiliary. [As in] "pācayāmbabhūva":
from the causative form of *pac*, the suffix *ām* is added by [Pāṇini 3.1.35], and by [Pāṇini 6.4.55], the substitution of *ay* for the *ṇi* occurs.
By the rule *bhavateraḥ* [Pāṇini 7.4.73], the vowel *a* is substituted for the reduplication.

By the rule *bhuvo vug luṅaliṭoḥ* [Pāṇini 6.4.88], the augment *vuk* is added. But for what purpose is this stated, since this [word] ends in *am* and its verbal meaning is unmanifest? For from this, there is only the manifestation of the time of the action, not of the means (*sādhana*), person (*puruṣa*), or number (*saṃkhyāna*).

For indeed, their manifestation does not occur without a word ending in a verbal suffix (*tiṅanta*). Therefore, since the meaning is not yet complete, the subsequent employment (*anuprayoga*) of the root *as* (in the form *āma*) will take place so that there may be the subsequent employment of *kṛ*, *bhū*, and *as*; [the printed reading is: "so that it may be for *kṛ*, *bhū*, and *as*, and not for *pac* etc.
If it is argued that it should not be for *pac* etc., we say no; because *pac* etc. express specific meanings, the subsequent employment of them is untenable.

When a word expressing a specific meaning is employed as a subsequent application (*anuprayoga*), is it applied after a form ending in *ām* that expresses a general meaning, or one that expresses a specific meaning? In this regard, first of all, a word expressing a specific meaning cannot be applied as a subsequent application to a form ending in *ām* that expresses a general meaning, because such a thing is impossible. For the roots *kṛ*, *bhū*, and *as* express general meanings, and no suffix *ām* has been prescribed after them by anyone. Furthermore, regarding a form ending in *ām* that expresses a specific meaning, would a subsequent application be made with a word expressing a specific meaning that is synonymous with it, or one that has a different meaning? In that case, a synonymous word is certainly not applied as a subsequent application, because its meaning has already been expressed.

And because it is desired to employ [the root] after that [periphrastic formation], there occurs the manifestation of all meanings such as the action (*kriyā*), time (*kāla*), and so forth, through the suffix *ām*.

By virtue of this capacity, only that [root] should be employed as the subsequent verb (*anuprayoga*) where the manifestation of all [meanings] occurs. In that case, even if it has a different meaning, a preceding root that has the same meaning as the one ending in *ām* does not deserve to be employed as the subsequent verb; for its own meaning would not be manifested.

An auxiliary (*anuprayoga*) is employed for the purpose of manifesting the meaning of the root ending in *āma*; however, the means (*sādhana*) and other factors related to the meaning expressed by that *āma*-ending cannot be manifested by a verb whose meaning is entirely different.
They can, however, be manifested by a verb that expresses a general sense.

For when a specific term is in proximity, a general term is restricted to that specific meaning; thus, when general terms such as *kṛ*, *bhū*, and *as* are employed following an ām-ending [verb], they function with respect to that very specific meaning expressed by it. Therefore, since the employment of these very terms—*kṛ*, *bhū*, and *as*—will occur, should this [sūtra] not be commenced? This is not so; for just as *kṛ*, *bhū*, and *as* denote general action (*kriyāsāmānya*), so too does the root *vid*. Consequently, *vid* might also be employed [following the ām-ending]. Therefore, this [sūtra] is commenced in order to exclude that.
And it is for the purpose of excluding constructions with an intervening word, so that there may not be [the usage] "pācayāṃ cakāra devadattaḥ.
However, the non-exclusion of such constructions with an intervening word is obtained through a specific restriction (*avadhāraṇa*).

This restriction is obtained because all sentences have the result of exclusion (*vyavaccheda*), because the particle *ca* has the result of restriction, or because *ca* has the sense of an unexpressed conjunction (*anukta-samuccaya*).

And it must be undertaken for the purpose of removing misconceptions; furthermore, the removal of misconceptions is obtained because [the term] *anu* has the sense of "subsequently. Regarding the statement "the suffix *ām* is prescribed after the root *vid* in the *loṭ* [mood]," since the *ām* prescribed after the *liṭ* [perfect tense] would not apply to the *loṭ*, it is therefore treated as an irregular formation (*nipātana*). Moreover, based on the presence of *ām*, the *guṇa* substitution [of the vowel] of the light penultimate syllable would apply; thus, its absence is also [established].

Since the elision (*luk*) prescribed by [Pāṇini 2.4.81] *āmaḥ* does not apply to the imperative (*loṭ*), there is elision of the imperative. It has been stated that the auxiliary verb *kṛ* is used after the perfect (*liṭ*); however, it would not be applicable after the imperative. Therefore, it must also be understood as being applied by nipātana (irregular prescription) in all cases.
Thus: *kurvantu*.

The plural ending; the substitution of *ant* for *jhi*; the substitution of *u* for *e* by [Pāṇini 3.4.86]; the *guṇa* strengthening of the root based on the *vikaraṇa* suffix; the substitution of *ut* for the final *a* before a *sārvadhātuka* suffix by [Pāṇini 6.4.110]; and the *yaṇ* substitution for the *vikaraṇa*. Regarding the phrase "the particle *iti*" and so forth:
since the mention of the forms of the imperative (*loṭ*) serves as an illustration, he says "not only" and so forth in order to demonstrate what is intended by the particle *iti*.
"Let them do" (*kurutām*): here, *tām* is substituted for the suffix *tas* by the rule beginning with *tasthas* [Pāṇini 3.4.101]. "Do" (*kuru*).
In *sehrapicca* [Pāṇini 3.4.87], there is the suffix *hi*; by the rule *utaśca pratyayāt* [Pāṇini 6.4.106] and others, there is elision (*luk*) of *hi*.
In *kurutam*, this is the suffix *tam* [of the second person dual]. In *abhyutsādayām*, [the suffix is *mip*].
Thus, once the compound has been formed, this [word] ending in the nominative case is indeed singular;
likewise, *prajanayām* is also so.
The remaining forms ending in *ām* are likewise exclusively nominative.
"Akaḥ": this is the first person singular ending of the *luṅ* (aorist) tense of the root *kṛ*.
"akrana" is the third person plural ending;
"sadijaniramīṇām" is [the genitive plural].

The root *ṣadlṛ* is used in the senses of "falling apart," "going," and "depressing" (Dhātupāṭha 1427); *janī* is used in the sense of "manifestation" (Dhātupāṭha 1449); and *ramu* is used in the sense of "playing" (Dhātupāṭha 853).
Regarding the term "of those ending in *ṇi*":
this refers to those [roots] that have been converted by the causative suffix *ṇic*.

Regarding the term "pacateḥ": because it is prescribed for the *liṭ* [perfect tense], it would not apply to the *liṅ* [optative]; therefore, it is treated as an irregularity (*nipātana*). Regarding the term "asya": [it refers to the root].

[The form] is derived from the causative of either *punāti* or *pavati*; it is stated that "it is an irregularity (*nipātana*) in the conditional (*lṛṅ*) and the optative (*liṅ*)," because [otherwise], as in the previous case, it would not be obtained.
Regarding the statement "there is also the absence of *guṇa* even for those that are seen":

the *guṇa* substitution prescribed by [Pāṇini 7.3.86] *pugantalaghūpadhasya* would apply; therefore, the absence of that *guṇa* is established as a *nipātana* (irregularity). For example: *abhyutsādayām*.
The substitution of *ray* for the preceding vowel;
the elision (*luk*) of the *luṅ* suffix;
[the rule] "of *ak*" (*akaḥ*).

From the root *kṛ* in the *luṅ* tense: the augment *aṭ*, the suffix *tip*, the *cli* substitute; its elision by the rule "in mantras, [the *cli*] of *ghas*" (Pāṇini 2.4.80); *guṇa* substitution; replacement of the vowel by *ra* (*raparatvam*); elision of *ti* by "when followed by *ra*" (Pāṇini 6.1.68); and the *visarjanīya* for the *repha*. Regarding "abhyudasīṣadat":

the suffix *caṅ* is applied by the rule "after *ṇi*, *śri*, etc. (Pāṇini 3.1.48); shortening of the penultimate vowel by "when *caṅ* follows a causative suffix" (Pāṇini 7.4.1); reduplication by "when *caṅ* follows" (Pāṇini 6.1.11); the *halādiśeṣa* (retention of the first consonant); and since the condition for "behaving like *san*" (*sanvadbhāva*) applies when there is a light syllable (Pāṇini 7.4.93), the substitution of *it* occurs, followed by lengthening by "when *sa* follows" (Pāṇini 7.4.94).
This process should be understood to apply accordingly in subsequent cases as well. Regarding "prajanāyām":
because [the root] belongs to the class beginning with *janī*, *jṛṣ*, *knasu*, and *rañj* (Dhātupāṭha 817), it is marked with the *mit* designation, and thus there is shortening of the vowel.
Regarding "cikayām": [this is derived from the root *ci*].
The letter *ka* is also elided here;
the *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* substitutions take place,
resulting in *acaṣīt*.
By [Pāṇini 7.3.96], the augment *iṭ* is applied; there is vowel lengthening (*vṛddhi*) before the suffix *sic*. Thus, "ramayām";
by [Pāṇini 6.4.92], the short vowel is substituted for the roots marked with *mit*.
In "pāvayām," there is the elision (*luk*) of the optative suffix (*liṅ*) by [Pāṇini 2.4.81] *āmaḥ*.
In "kriyāt," [the same applies].

In the case of *kṛ* with the optative (*liṅ*) in the sense of a benediction (*āśis*), there is the suffix *tip*; by [Pāṇini 3.4.100], *itaśca*, there is the elision of the *ikāra*; then *yāsuṭ* is added; by [Pāṇini 7.4.28], *riṅ śayagliṅkṣu*, there is the substitution of *riṅ*; and by [Pāṇini 8.2.29], *skoḥ saṃyogādyor ante ca*, there is the elision of *s*. Thus, "pāvyāt. Similarly, for the optative, because it is an *ārdhadhātuka* suffix, there is the absence of *śap* by [Pāṇini 3.4.116]; and by [Pāṇini 6.4.51], there is the elision of *ṇi*.
Regarding "vidām": this is from the root *vid* in the *luṅ* tense; the suffix *ām* is applied, there is an absence of *guṇa*, and the *luṅ* marker is elided (*luk*).
Regarding "akran": [this is from the root *kṛ*].

From the root *kṛ* (to do), the suffix *luṅ* is applied; *cli* replaces it; the final *jhi* is replaced by *an*; the vowel *i* is elided by *itaśca* [Pāṇini 3.4.100]; there is the elision of the final consonant due to being at the end of a conjunct (*saṃyogāntalopa*); the *cli* is elided by *mantre ghasahvara* [Pāṇini 2.4.80]; the augment *aṭ* is added; and the *yaṇ* substitution occurs. Thus, "avediṣuḥ" is formed:
the augment *iṭ* is added to *sic*, and *jus* replaces *jhi* by *sijabhyastavidibhyaśca* [Pāṇini 3.4.109].
"The particle *iti* is for the purpose of showing usage"—
this means that other similar instances should also be understood as occurring in the Vedic language (*chandas*). "The vowel *i* is for the purpose of pronunciation"—
this means that its sole purpose is pronunciation, and there is no other objective.

By this, he shows that the grammatical operation [dependent on] the designation *it* does not take place. "The letter *c* is for the sake of the accent" means that there should be the acute accent (*udātta*) on the final syllable according to [Pāṇini 6.1.157]: *citaḥ*.

Now, why is it not understood that in the rule *mantre ghasahvaraṇaśavavṛdahādvṛckṛgamijanibhyo leḥ* [Pāṇini 2.4.80], the letter *e* is for the purpose of a general inclusion (*sāmānyagrahaṇa*), and the letter *c* is for the purpose of preventing its obstruction? One thinks thus: there is no suffix *liṭ* after the roots *ghas* and so forth in the Veda for which this letter *i* (in *liṭ*) would serve as a general inclusion; and since that purpose of general inclusion does not exist, the purpose of the letter *c*—namely, to prevent its obstruction—is also untenable.

In that case, why do the vowel *i* and the consonant *c* in the rule *āmaḥ* [Pāṇini 2.4.81] not serve to prevent the general inclusion [of all forms]? For there, from the rule *mantre ghasa...* [2.4.80], the term *liṭaḥ* is carried over; and in the absence of *i* and *c*, by the principle "when a form without an *anubandha* is mentioned, it does not include one with an *anubandha*" (Vyāḍi-Pāṇinian Paribhāṣā 53), only that [specific *liṭ*] would be included, not *liṅ* and *liṭ*. This is not so; let there be no recurrence of the mention of *liṅ* here—by way of generality, the elision (*luk*) will apply to the suffix as a whole; and nothing undesirable follows from this being the case.

For there is no grammatical operation (*pratyaya*) for which the elision (*luk*) would result in anything undesirable. Even if the reference to *liṅ* were to continue [from a previous rule], there would be no fault; for when there are multiple things to be grasped, a general term is used to grasp them, and for that which follows *ām*, there is nothing else to be grasped. Indeed, nowhere does another usage of *liṭ* occur after *ām*; therefore, due to the absence of any other possibility, it is *liṭ* alone that is understood.

In this regard, there is no purpose for the vowel *i* (in *pū*) for the sake of grasping the general sense (*sāmānya*), nor for the sake of not obstructing that [general sense] by means of the letter *ca*. Now, one might object: "But in forms such as *pāvayāṅkriyāt*, isn't there another *liṅ* suffix? This is not so; it is established precisely through grammatical irregularity (*nipātana*). And that irregularity must necessarily be resorted to; otherwise, even if the vowel *i* were applied and the letter *ca* were used to prevent its obstruction, the form *abyutsādayami* would not be established.
Therefore, the previously stated purpose alone is logical.

We shall demonstrate later how the particle *ca* has the sense of "and so forth" (*yathottara*). Now, for what purpose is the suffix *cli* attached, and then *sij* and others prescribed for it, rather than simply prescribing *sic* as the general rule (*utsarga*) and then prescribing *ksa* and others as its substitutes? It cannot be done in this way; for if it were so, in the rule [Pāṇini 1.2.12] *cleḥ siC*, since *cli* would be absent, the mention of *aniṭ* (non-iṭ-vowel) would be understood as a qualifier of the root—meaning "of a root that does not take iṭ. Consequently, the form *aghukṣat* from the root *guh* would not be established. This is because, since *guh* is marked with *ū* (*ūdittva*), the *iṭ* augment is optionally prescribed by [Pāṇini 7.2.44] *svarati-sūti-sūyati-dhūjūdito vā*, and thus it lacks the status of being *aniṭ*.
By the mention of *satyanigrahaṇa*, that very [rule] is qualified: "of *cli* which is without *iṭ*" (*cleraniṭaḥ*).

And because *cli* following *guh* optionally takes *iṭ*, when *iṭ* is absent, the suffix *ksa* is established by virtue of *cli* being without *iṭ*. "The letter *i* is for the sake of pronunciation" (*ikāra uccāraṇārthaḥ*).
By this, showing that there is no purpose other than pronunciation here, he indicates the absence [of the letter *i*] in the technical designation (*it-saṃjñā*).

But surely, even if the *ik* were not an *anubandha*, the elision of the nasal in *amaṃsta* would apply by the rule *aniditām* [Pāṇini 6.4.24]; therefore, why is this *ik* not considered an *itsaṃjñaka* (marked with *it*) for the purpose of prohibiting that elision? The thought is as follows: Even if the *ik* were not an *anubandha*, the elision of the nasal must still occur for a stem ending in *sic* simply because of the *anubandha* itself; this is known from the *jñāpaka* (indicative evidence) of the *kit* designation in the rule *hana sic* [Pāṇini 1.2.14]. For indeed, the purpose of applying the *kit* designation to the root *han* is so that the elision of the nasal may occur in forms such as *āhatā*.

If the elision of the nasal (*anunāsika-lopa*) were to occur for a verbal root ending in *sic*, then the making of *sic* a *kit* suffix after the root *han* would be purposeless. [The statement] "the letter *ca* is for the sake of accent" means it is for the sake of making the word end-acute (*antodātta*).

But surely, since the suffix *sic* is devoid of consonants (*anacka*), it is not possible for the letter *c* to serve the purpose of indicating an accent (*svarārthatā*)? There is no fault here, because once the augment *iṭ* is applied, it becomes possessed of a consonant (*sācka*). Even so, in the case of the *luṅ* tense, when the augment *āṭ* is applied, the word ought to be *ādyudātta* (accented on the first syllable) by the "remaining" accent (*atiśiṣṭasvara*); what then is the purpose of the letter *c*? In that case, its purpose as an indicator of accent will apply where the augment *āṭ* is prohibited by the rule *na māṅayoge* [Pāṇini 6.4.74].

But surely, even there, the *nighāta* (enclitic accent) should apply by the rule *tiṅṅatiṅaḥ* [Pāṇini 8.1.28]? In that case, where the *nighāta* is prohibited by the rule *hi ca* [Pāṇini 8.1.34]—as in examples such as *mā hi lāvīt*—there it will serve the purpose of providing the correct accent. But surely, since the *cit* designation would apply to the substitute *cli* by virtue of its being a *sthānivadbhāva* (treatment like the original), why is the letter *c* appended to the substitute? To this he says: "For the fact that augments are unaccented," and so forth. By the explicit statement that *yāsuṭ* is acutely accented, it will be made known that augments are otherwise unaccented.
And that [property] is not prescribed when another accent has already been reached.

For instance: those augments (*āgama*) such as *aṭ* and *ānuk* which are parts of the base (*prakṛti*), the accent of the base would apply to them; whereas those such as *iṭ* which are parts of the suffix (*pratyaya*), the accent of the suffix would apply. Therefore, the unaccented nature of the augment (*āgamānudāttatva*) sublates every other accent.
Consequently, just as it sublates the accent of the suffix, it would likewise sublate even the *cit*-accent produced by the status of being a substitute (*sthānivadbhāva*).
Therefore, the letter *ca* is also attached to the substitute (*ādeśa*).
The word *hi* means "because," and the word *iti* means "therefore.
Because it would otherwise subvert even the accent of the *cit* [marker], therefore the letter *ca* is attached twice, both to the original form (*sthānin*) and to the substitute (*ādeśa*).

But surely, in cases such as *mā hi lāvīt*, if the suffixal augment (*āgama*) were to be unaccented (*anudātta*), then the marking of the *cli* suffix with the *cit* marker would be purposeless due to the absence of any utility. Therefore, by the force of the *cit* marking of *cli*, the accent of the *cit* (i.e., the acute accent on the suffix) will not be sublated by the unaccented nature of the augment—thus, is the *cit* marking of *sic* redundant? It is not redundant, because it serves a purpose in certain instances. How so? For here, just as the rule *sarūpāṇām ekaśeṣaḥ* [Pāṇini 1.2.64] was initiated by resorting to the view that the word denotes the individual (*vyakti*), so too, in order to resort to the view that the word denotes the class (*jāti*), the letter *c* is appended [to the *cli*].

For when a word-meaning is an individual entity (*vyakti*), just as the *cit-svara* (acute accent on the *cit* suffix) applies to every individual instance, so too does the statement that the *yāsuṭ* augment is acute serve as an indicator (*jñāpaka*) of the anudātta (grave) nature of the verbal root.

Consequently, in the form *mā hi lāvīt*, the anudātta nature of the augment is indeed indicated by that rule. And thus, just as the *cit-svara* occurs here, so too must it occur by virtue of the anudātta nature of the augment; otherwise, the indicator regarding this subject would be rendered useless.

Furthermore, since the simultaneous occurrence of two *anudātta* (unaccented) vowels is impossible, there would have to be an alternation (*paryāya*). In that case, the *anudātta* nature of the substitute *c* would supersede the original *c* in one instance by virtue of being an *āgama-anudātta* (an unaccented augment). However, when the *c* is repeated [as an *it*], even though an *anudātta* is produced in one instance, once that has been produced, the *cit-svara* (acute accent) is produced again by the force of the fact that the *c* is marked with two *it*s; therefore, there is no fault. [The examples] beginning with "spṛśa-mṛśa" [follow].

When *kṣa* is about to be applied by the rule *spṛśimṛśikṛṣibhyaḥ* [Pāṇini 3.1.45], and when *aṅ* is about to be applied to *tṛp* and *dṛp* because they belong to the *puṣādi* group, it must be stated—or explained—that *sic* optionally applies. The explanation for this is as follows: in the rule prescribing *kṣa*, the term *anyatarasyām* ("optionally") is carried over from the rule *vidāṃkurvantvityanyatarasyām* [Pāṇini 3.1.41] by the maxim of the frog-leap (*maṇḍūkapluti*); likewise, in the rule for the *puṣādi* group, it is carried over from the rule *ātmanepadeṣu* [Pāṇini 3.1.54]. And that optionality is understood to be restricted (*vyavasthitavibhāṣā*) in both cases.
Therefore, the suffix *k* will optionally occur after the roots *spṛś*, *mṛś*, and *kṛṣ*, whereas it occurs invariably after others.
After the roots *tṛp* and *dṛp*, the augment *aṅ* will optionally occur, whereas after other roots beginning with *puṣ*, it occurs invariably.
Consequently, in that alternative where *k* and *aṅ* are absent, only the suffix *sic*, which is prescribed generally, occurs.

Regarding "aspṛkṣat": the root is *spṛś* (Dhātupāṭha 1422) meaning "to touch. The suffix *ksa* is applied; by [Pāṇini 8.2.36], *vraścādi*, there is the substitution of *ṣ*; by [8.2.41], there is the substitution of *k*; and by [8.3.59], *ādeśapratyayoḥ*, there is the substitution of *ṣ*. Regarding "asprākṣīt": [the same process applies].
Thus, there is the augment *it*; by the rule *vadavraja* (Pāṇini 7.2.3) and others, there is *vṛddhi*, and the substitution of *yaṇ* for the vowel *ṛ*. Regarding the form *aspākṣīt*:
it is formed with the suffix *sic*.

When there is no augment (āgama), then there is simply the vṛddhi of the vowel *ṛ*. In this same way, two forms each should be understood for the roots *mṛśa* (in the sense of touching, DhP 1425) and *kṛṣa* (in the sense of scratching, DhP 1286).
[The form] *atṛpat* [is derived from] *tṛpa* (in the sense of satisfying, DhP 1195).
"atrāpsīt, atāpsīt"—this is as before.
In the same way, the three forms of the root *du* (dhātupāṭha 1196), meaning "to gladden" and "to release," should also be understood. [The form] "aghukṣat" [is derived similarly].

Regarding *duha* "to fill" (Dhātupāṭha 1014): by the rule *ekāco baśo bhaṣ* [Pāṇini 8.2.37], the letter *d* undergoes *bhaṣ*-bhāva and becomes *dh*; then, by the rule *khari ca* [Pāṇini 8.4.54], the *dh* undergoes *cartva* and becomes *k*. Thus, we have *alikṣat*.
Regarding *liha* "to taste" (Dhātupāṭha 1016): by the rule *ho ḍhaḥ* [Pāṇini 8.2.31], the *h* becomes *ḍh*, and as before, there is *ṣatva* and *katva*.
Regarding *adhākṣīt*: the root *daha* means "to reduce to ashes" (Dhātupāṭha 991); as before, there is the substitution of *ḍha*, *ka*, *ṣa*, *bhaṣ*-bhāva, and *ca*.
Regarding *akoṣīt*: the root *kuṣa* means "to extract" (Dhātupāṭha 1518); there is the *guṇa* strengthening of the light penultimate vowel. Regarding *adarśat*: [the root is *dṛś*].
By the rule "aṅgasya ṛdhaśo 'ṅi guṇaḥ" [Pāṇini 7.4.16], there is a guṇa substitution;
thus, "adrākṣīt."
> [[6.1.58]] This is the augment *it*.

By the rule `vadavraja` [[7.2.3]] and others, there is *vṛddhi* (vowel strengthening); as before, there is the substitution of *ṣ* and *k*. The letter *c* [in the sūtra] is for the sake of specification (*viśeṣaṇārtha*).
If, in the rule `caṅi` [[6.1.11]], the term *aṅ* were not mentioned, then doubling (*dvirvacana*) would also occur when *aṅ* is prescribed by the rule `asyativaktikhyātibhyo'ṅ` [[3.1.52]].

In the forms *acīkarat* and *ajīharat*, there is reduplication by [Pāṇini 6.1.11] *caṅi*. Then, by [Pāṇini 7.4.62], the *ur-atta* (substitution of *u*) occurs for the roots *kṛ* and *hṛ*; subsequently, by [Pāṇini 7.4.62], the *cutva* (substitution of *c*) occurs—the *k* becomes *c*, and the *h* also becomes *jh*. Then, by [Pāṇini 8.4.54], the *jh* becomes *j*.
The remainder is to be understood according to the example *abhyudasīṣadat*.
Regarding "aśiśriyat" and so forth:

from the root *śriñ* in the sense of "service" (Dhātupāṭha 897), and from *du*, *dru*, and *ru* in the sense of "motion" (Dhātupāṭha 944, 945, 940), the substitutions *iyaṅ* and *uvaṅ* are applied as appropriate by the rule *aci śnudhātu* (Pāṇini 6.4.77) and others.
Regarding "akārayiṣatām": [this is derived from the causative of the root *kṛ*].

In the case of the object (karman), there is a dual ending, namely *ātām*, followed by the augment *iṭ*, the substitution of *guṇa*, the replacement [of *ya* for *yat*], and the substitution of *ṣ*. Regarding the statement "there is an addition [to the rule] for the root *kam*":

one might ask, "Since the suffix *ṇiṅ* is applied by [Pāṇini 3.1.30], the *caṅ* [reduplication] after *kam* is already established simply because it ends in *ṇi*; why then is this addition made? To this he says: "The suffixes beginning with *āya*," and so forth. Thus, [the form] *acakamata* is derived.

The *ātmanepada* ending occurs because the root is marked with an *anudātta* vowel. As before, there is *kutva* (the substitution of *k*) for the reduplicated syllable. The phrase "in the alternative where *ṇiṅ* is absent, there is the treatment as *san*" indicates that this does not apply in the alternative where *ṇiṅ* is present. This is because the meaning of [Pāṇini 7.4.93], *sanvallaghuni caṅpare*, is that when a *ṇi* is followed by *caṅ*, and when an *aṅga* follows that *ṇi* which is followed by *caṅ*, the reduplicated syllable of that *aṅga* undergoes the operations of *san*. This meaning is not possible in the alternative where *ṇiṅ* is absent. Thus, [we have] *adadhat*.
By [Pāṇini 6.4.64], there is the elision of the vowel *ā*. As before, the substitution of the *jaś* sound (*jhal*) for the reduplicated syllable results in the letter *d*.
Thus: *adhāsīt*.

In the case of *luṅ*, [the suffix] *sic* is applied; by the rule *yama-ramana-mātāṃ sak ca ṭ* [Pāṇini 7.2.73], there is the augment *iṭ*, and by the rule *prakṛteśca sagāgamaḥ* [Pāṇini 7.3.96], there is the augment *sak* added to the root. Then, by the rule *iṭa īṭi* [Pāṇini 8.2.28], there is the elision of *sic*. Thus we have *aśīśayat*;
as before, the substitution of *iyaṅ* occurs.
"Even here, *aṅ* is optionally substituted," according to the rule *jṛstambhu* (Pāṇini 3.1.58) and others. "*Āt*" [refers to the augment].
In *āyateraḥ* [Pāṇini 7.4.18], there is the substitution of *atva* (short *a*), and by [Pāṇini 6.1.97], the subsequent form (*pararūpa*) is applied.
Thus, we have *āyīt*.
When the prohibition of *vṛddhi* is applied by [Pāṇini 7.2.5] and so forth, the *guṇa* substitution followed by the *ayādeśa* occurs.

Regarding "adhiṣātām": this is the dual ending for the object (karmaṇi), namely *ātām*. By the rule *sthāghvoricca* [Pāṇini 1.2.17], there is both the *kit* designation and the substitution of *it* (the short *i*). "This rule applies where the suffix *āya* is absent," because the term used [in the sūtra] is that which does not end in the suffix *āya*.
Because a verbal root ending in the suffix *āya* constitutes a different root altogether. Regarding the form *ajūgupatam*:

the root is *gup* in the sense of "protection" (*gupū rakṣaṇe*, Dhātupāṭha 395); it is in the *luṅ* (aorist) tense; there is reduplication; the suffix *thas* is replaced by *tam* according to [Pāṇini 3.4.101] *tasthasthamipāṃ tāmtamtāmaḥ*; and the vowel lengthening of the reduplicated syllable occurs according to [Pāṇini 6.1.7] *dīrgho'kitaḥ*.
Regarding *agauptam*:

by [Pāṇini 8.2.26], there is the elision of the suffix *sic*; because that [elision] is considered non-existent (*asiddha*), the *vṛddhi* substitution occurs according to [Pāṇini 7.2.3] and following, resulting in *agauptam*.
Regarding *agopiṣṭam*: [the same applies].

Because the root has an indicatory letter *ū*, the augment *iṭ* optionally applies by [Pāṇini 7.2.44] *svarati* etc.; since the prohibition of *vṛddhi* by [Pāṇini 7.2.4] *neṭi* applies, there is the *guṇa* substitution for the light penultimate vowel.
Thus, *agopāyiṣṭam*.
From the form ending in the *āya*-suffix, *sic* and *iṭ* are added [by Pāṇini 6.4.48]. This constitutes "the three forms."
The latter [rule] is: "after these [roots] ending in *ṇi*.
This refers to *ūnayati* and *elayati*, which end in the *cur*-class *ṇi*.
"By the former" refers to the preceding rule.
Regarding the form *auṇayīt* derived from the root *śriṇi* and so forth: there is the suffix *tip*, followed by *sic*;

the *sic* is elided by [Pāṇini 8.2.28] *iṭa īṭi*. Since that elision is considered "asiddha" (non-existent for the purposes of subsequent rules), when the rule for *vṛddhi* would otherwise apply, there is a prohibition by [Pāṇini 7.2.5] *hrmmyantalakṣaṇa*. Then, *guṇa* and *āy-ādeśa* are applied, followed by *āṭ* by [Pāṇini 6.4.72], and finally *vṛddhi* by [Pāṇini 6.1.87] *āṭaśca*.
Regarding the form *auṇināt*:
there is reduplication according to [Pāṇini 6.1.2],
and the elision of the *ṇi* suffix.
Regarding the form *dhvanayīt*:

by this very rule of irregular derivation (*nipātana*), there is the shortening of the final vowel [to *i*] as in *dhvanayīt*. Because of its status as a *sthānivadbhāva* (substitutional equivalence), the *vṛddhi* increment prescribed by [Pāṇini 7.2.116], *ata upadhāyāḥ*, does not occur. Furthermore, the prohibition of the augment *aṭ* applies because of [Pāṇini 6.4.75], *bahulaṃ chandasyamāṅyoge’pi*.
In *adidhvanat*,
the substitution of *it* occurs due to the application of the *sanvadbhāva* rule. In *aililat*, [the same applies].
> [[6.1.2]] Thus there is reduplication of the root *li*, and as before,
the augment *āṭ* is applied. Regarding "ārdidat," here too there is reduplication of the second monosyllabic (*ekāc*) portion, as before.
The letter *r* (repha), however, is not doubled, because of the prohibition: "There is no doubling [of a consonant] after *r*" (*na dvirucyate*).
[In the case of *āṭ*,] there is *vṛddhi*. Or, it is the substitution of *brāūñ* [for *vac*], according to the rule:
"*brāūñ* is the substitute for *vac*" (*brāūño vaciḥ*).
"Or it is a substitute for *cakṣiṅ*," meaning "the root *cakṣiṅ* is replaced by *khyāñ*" [Pāṇini 2.4.54]. Thus,
[the form] is *paryāsthata*.

The ātmanepada ending is applied due to the supplementary rule (*upasaṃkhyāna*) "there is [the substitution of *um*] after the prefix *upa-* when followed by the roots *as-* and *ūh-*" (Vārttika 49). Thus, from *avoc-at*,
[by Pāṇini 7.4.20] *vaca* is replaced by *um*, resulting in *ākhyat*.
As before, there is the elision of the vowel *ā*. Regarding the form *ahvat*:
as before, there is the elision of the vowel *ā*.
Now, for what purpose is this division of the rule (*yogavibhāga*) made? Why not simply have one single rule, namely *asyativaktikhyātilipisicihvaśca*? To this he says: "separately," and so forth.

The separation of the rule (*yogavibhāga*) in the subsequent sūtra is for the purpose that the option regarding the *aṅ* substitute should apply specifically after roots such as *lipi*, etc., when the *ātmanepada* endings follow. If there were a single rule, the suffixes beginning with *hras* would also carry over to the subsequent [sūtras], and consequently, the *aṅ* substitute would undesirably apply optionally even after those [roots]. The *ātmanepada* ending occurs by the rule "after a root marked with a svarita accent or a ñit marker. This is because the roots *lip* and *sic* have a svarita accent, while the root *hve* has a ñit marker.

In the case of *alipta* and *asikta*, by [Pāṇini 8.2.26] there is the elision of the suffix *sic*; because that [elision] is considered established (*siddha*) by [Pāṇini 8.2.26], the *guṇa* substitution for a light penultimate vowel would have applied. However, by [Pāṇini 1.2.11], due to the *kit* designation, it does not occur; and by [Pāṇini 8.2.30], there is the change to a guttural (*kutva*). Those roots which have *ḷ* as their indicatory letter (*it*) are called *lṛdita*.

The *puṣādi* group indeed exists as a sub-group within the *bhvādi* class—beginning with *puṣa puṣṭau* (DhP 700), *śriṣu śliṣu pruṣu pluṣu dāhe* (DhP 701–704), and so forth; there is also a sub-group within the *divādi* class—beginning with *puṣa puṣṭau* (DhP 1182), *śuṣa śoṣaṇe* (DhP 1183), and so forth; and there is also a sub-group within the *kryādi* class—beginning with *puṣa puṣṭau* (DhP 1529), *muṣa steye* (DhP 1530), and so forth. Therefore, in this context...
To the question "Of which [group] is there the inclusion?", he says: "The *puṣādi* group is a sub-group within the *divādi* group," and so forth.

If the *bhvādi* group were being included, he would not have made a separate mention of the *dyutādi* group immediately after the *puṣādi* group, because they would already have been included by the mention of the *puṣādi* group itself; therefore, that [the *bhvādi* group] is certainly not what is being included.

Nor indeed is the *kryādi* sub-group included; for in that [sub-group], only four roots are recited: the two previously mentioned, namely *khac* (DhP 1531) "to become manifest" and *grah* (DhP 1533) "to take," provided these were intended to be included, one would have made them *ṛdit* (marked with ṛ). Thus, the mention of the *puṣādi* group would not be necessary. Therefore, by the principle of elimination (*pāriśeṣya*), the inclusion of the *puṣādi* roots belonging to the *divādi* sub-group is understood.
Now, why were *puṣ* and the others not made to have the marker *ḷ* (*lṛdit*)? It is because they cannot be made *lṛdit*.
For if they were *lṛdit*, then since they are recited with the markers *u* (*udit*) and *ā* (*ādita*), there would be an absence of the two operations prescribed by [Pāṇini 7.2.56] and [7.2.16].
