And for what reason were *dyut* and the others not made *lṛdit*? For the very same reason that *puṣ* and the others were not made *lṛdit*, so too were *dyut* and the others.
For among those [roots] as well, some recite them starting from the beginning.
Among them, the *puṣādi* group extends up to the end of the *ādivādi* group.

As for the marker *vṛt* placed after the root *ṣṇiha* (meaning "affection") in the Dhātupāṭha, that is intended to mark the end of the *ravādi* group, not the *puṣādi* group; such is the tradition of the Teachers (*ācāryas*).

The roots beginning with *dyut* and ending with *kṛpū* (Dhātupāṭha 762) are included [in the *vṛt* group]; the root *vṛt* follows immediately after, because of the marker *vṛt* placed after *ghaṭa* (Dhātupāṭha 763). Regarding the form *adyutat*, the *parasmaipada* ending is used optionally by rule 1.3.91.
Regarding "aātat": [the root] *i* in the sense of "going" (*gatau*, Dhātupāṭha 742). [Examples:
*agamat*, *aśakat*.
The roots *gam-lṛ* in the sense of "going" (Dhātupāṭha 982) and *śak-lṛ* in the sense of "ability" (Dhātupāṭha 1261).
Regarding the form *vyadyotiṣṭa*:
because it belongs to the class of roots with an anudātta indicatory vowel (*anudāttettva*), the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) is employed.
Regarding "aloṭiṣṭa": [the root] *ruṭ* and *luṭ* mean "to strike back" (*pratīghāta*) [Dhātupāṭha 747, 748]. Regarding "asarat" and "aśiṣat": [these are derived from the roots *sṛ* and *śās*].
Thus, there is the substitution of *i* (by Pāṇini 6.4.34), and the substitution of *ṣ* (by Pāṇini 8.3.60).
Regarding the form *ārat*:

as before, there is *guṇa*, then *āṭ* because the root begins with a vowel (Pāṇini 6.4.72), and finally the long vowel by the rule for homogeneous sounds (*savarṇadīrghaḥ*). Regarding *pṛthak* and so forth: [the same applies].

If the rule were formulated as a single compound yoga, namely *puṣādidyutādlṛditsarttiśāstyasartibhyaśca*, then the parasmaipada (active voice) suffixes alone would apply after the roots beginning with *sarti*, and not the ātmanepada (middle voice) suffixes.
Therefore, the separate formulation of the yoga is for the purpose that the ātmanepada suffixes may also apply after these very roots.
[The example given is] *samaranta*.

The ātmanepada ending is applied by the rule *samo gami* [Pāṇini 1.3.29] because the root *ṛ* is preceded by *sam*. The absence of the augment *aṭ* is due to the rule *bahulaṃ chandasyamāṅayoge’pi* [Pāṇini 6.4.75]; this usage is Vedic (*chāndasa*).

Now, one might ask: if the augment *aṅ* indeed occurs in the ātmanepada endings, then what is the purpose of the particle *ca* (and) used for the purpose of carrying over [the rule] to the parasmaipada endings? To this he says: "And that," etc.

The word *tat* refers back to the rule *parasmaipadeṣu*. It will find its application later on, for it does not find its application right here; otherwise, the formulation of a separate rule would be purposeless. *I* and *r* together are *ir*; that which has these as its indicatory letters (*it*) is called *irit*.

In that context, the letter *i* [in *ik*] receives the designation *it* by the rule "The *u*, *ṛ*, and *e* vowels, when nasalized, are called *it*" (P. 1.3.2), and the letter *r* [in *ir*] receives it by the rule "The *r* is called *it*" (P. 1.3.3). Alternatively, the designation *it* applies to the entire group [of letters] *ir* itself, and not to each individual constituent part. That which has this group *ir* as its *it*-designation is called *irit*.
It should be understood from this very statement that the *it*-designation belongs to the group;
for no other rule has prescribed the *it*-designation for that [group].
Regarding "abhaitsīt":
there is *vṛddhi* by the rule "vadavraja" [Pāṇini 7.2.3] and so forth, and the augment *iṭ* by [Pāṇini 7.3.96].
[The forms] "aruddha" and "abhitta" [are formed similarly].

The *ātmanepada* ending occurs because the root has a *svarita* accent. As before, there is the elision of *sic*. The addition of the marker *u* to the root *stambh* is for the purpose of specification by the rule [Pāṇini 7.2.56]. Thus, "astabhat" (he obstructed); here, the nasal is elided according to the rule [Pāṇini 6.4.24] "aniditām."
"*Āt*," and so forth.
This was explained under [Pāṇini 3.1.49]:
"By employing either *glucu* or *gluñc*, the three forms are established."

How so? If *gluc* were to be adopted, then with the prefix *aṅ* and the suffix *sic*, the two forms *aglucat* and *aglocīt* are established; however, with *gluñc* and the suffix *sic*, a third form, *agluñcīt*, would result. On the other hand, if *gluñc* were to be adopted, then with the prefix *aṅ* and the suffix *sic*, the two forms *aglucat* and *agluñcīt* are established;
but with *gluc* and the suffix *sic*, a third form, *aglocīt*, would result.

If this is so, for what purpose is both [reasons] taken up? For the three-fold nature is what is to be proven, and that is indeed established even by the taking up of either one; to this he says: "Because of the difference in meaning," and so forth.
The word *tu* (but/however) is used for emphasis.
For the meaning of these two is indeed distinct.
In that case, if only one [of the two] were taken, then for that very meaning which is not taken, the form *aglucat* would not be established.
Therefore, because they have distinct meanings, both are taken.
"Some," and so forth.
Because verbal roots have multiple meanings (*anekārthatva*), it is not contradictory for them to have non-differentiated meanings.

Therefore, the forms *upādāna* and *gluñcat* are established from both [roots]. The roots are: *ḍukṛñ* "to do" (DhP 1472), *mṛṅ* "to die" (DhP 1403), *dṛ* "to split" (DhP 1493), and *ruha* "to be born" (DhP 859).
Among these, for the first three, the suffix *sic* would apply; and for *ruha*, the suffix *kṣa* would apply by the rule *śala igupadhādaniṭaḥ* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 3.1.45).
In *akarot*,
the guṇa substitution is as before. In *amarat*, [the same applies].
The *parasmaipada* ending occurs by way of transposition (*vyatyaya*).

However, in the common language (*bhāṣā*), the forms are *akārṣīt*, *amṛta*, *adārīt*, and *arukṣat*. Regarding the phrase "by virtue of the capacity" (*sāmarthyāt*) and so forth, the word "ta" refers to the suffix *ta*.

There exists indeed the third person singular middle voice (*ātmanepada*), and there also exists the second person plural active voice (*parasmaipada*) for which this [suffix] is prescribed as a substitute. Since this root is *ātmanepadi*, the active plural cannot occur here; therefore, by the principle of elimination (*pāriśeṣya*), the third person singular middle is understood. This very establishment through elimination is what constitutes "semantic force" (*sāmarthya*).
Thus: "it arose" (*udapādi*).
By [Pāṇini 6.4.104], there is elision (*luk*) of the suffix *ta*. Thus, "udapatsātām":
[the suffix] *ātām* undergoes the substitution of *ca* for *t* by [Pāṇini 8.4.54].
Regarding the form *udapatsata*:
the substitution of *jhi* by *at* [as prescribed by Pāṇini 7.1.5] applies here;
furthermore, the option (*vā*) has ceased to apply in this context.
Because of the mention of *anyatarasyām* ("optionally") in a subsequent rule. [The roots] "janī prādurbhāve" (DhP 1149) and "budha avagamane" (DhP 1172) [are intended].
By this, [it is implied that] one reads "jana janane" (DhP 1105) and "budhir bodhane" (DhP 875, occurring in the *bhvādi* class as 858 and in the *divādi* class as 1172) simply as "budha avabodhane.
[The form] "adugdha" [is derived from the latter].

By [Pāṇini 3.1.45], the suffix *kṣa* is applied; for that suffix, while the term *kṣasya* is being carried over from [Pāṇini 7.3.72], [Pāṇini 7.3.73] prescribes its elision (*luk*) after the roots *duh*, *diha*, etc. By [Pāṇini 8.2.32], the substitution of the voiced unaspirated stop (*jaśtva*) occurs as before, resulting in *adohi*.

The suffix *ta* occurs when the action is intransitive (*śuddhe karmaṇi*); therefore, the *ciṇ* affix applies here as a rule. This is a prohibition of the *ciṇ* that would otherwise have been obtained through the extended application (*atideśa*) of the rule "like the object" (*karmavat*).

Regarding the form *aruḍha*: there is elision of the *sic* by [Pāṇini 8.2.26]; since that elision is considered non-existent (*asiddha*), the *guṇa* substitution for the light penultimate vowel (*laghūpadhaguṇaḥ*) would have applied, but it does not occur because the *sic* is treated as having the *kit* designation by [Pāṇini 1.2.11]: "In the ātmanepada, the *liṅ* and *sic* are *kit*."

As before, there is the substitution of *ja* for *ś*. This is a prohibition of *ciṇ*, which would otherwise have been applicable by the extended rule (atideśa) "tapastapaḥ karmakasyaiva" [Pāṇini 3.1.88]. For example: *atapta tapas tāpasaḥ*.
The meaning is that the ascetic (*tāpasa*) performs penance (*tapas*) characterized by fasting and so forth, thereby causing himself suffering.
In this context, *tapas* (asceticism) is the agent (*kartṛ*) and the ascetic (*tāpasa*) is the object (*karman*).
However, when that ascetic, reduced to skin and bone, performs austerity for the sake of heaven, then the usage is: "The ascetic performed austerity" (*atapta tapas tāpasaḥ*).
Now, in this case, *tapas* is the object and the ascetic is the agent.

And here, the word *tapas* refers to a specific kind of knowledge that is the cause for attaining heaven and other such goals. The root *tap* also means "to acquire"; thus, the meaning is that an ascetic (*tāpasa*) is one who has acquired this specific knowledge.
Regarding the phrase "anvavātapta pāpena karmaṇā" (he was tormented by a sinful deed):
the meaning is that he was subsequently tormented or struck down by that sinful deed which was previously committed.
Here, the *lakāra* (verbal suffix) is used in the sense of the object (*karman*). This is according to the rule: "In the two meanings of state (*bhāva*) and object (*karman*)."
This is a qualifier of the word *ta*:
"the *ta* that occurs in the sense of the abstract action (*bhāva*) or the object (*karman*).

Now, what is the purpose of including the mention of *ciṇ*? For is it not the case that the mention of *ciṇ* continues from [Pāṇini 3.1.60]? It might be argued: "Since that [mention of *ciṇ*] is connected with the optional rule [Pāṇini 3.1.61] *dīpajanabudhipūritāyipyāyibhyo 'nyatarasyām* and with the prohibition [Pāṇini 3.1.64] *na rudhaḥ*, if it were to continue here, it would necessarily continue as something still connected to those [rules]; however, this is not the case."
Because the mention of "either one" (*anyatarasyām*) has already been withdrawn in the two preceding rules, and because a prohibition must be preceded by a prior application;
if there were an application of *ciṇ* in the sense of the abstract action (*bhāva*) or the object (*karman*), then the recurrence of "not" (*na*) would be for the purpose of prohibiting it.
However, there is no application of that [rule] for those two [senses] by anyone, since in the rule prescribing *ciṇ*, the term "agent" (*kartṛ*) recurs in all instances.
He states that the mention of *ciṇ* again is redundant: "The mention of *ciṇ* is for the sake of clarity.

In the absence of the mention of *ciṇ*, those of dull intellect would experience difficulty in comprehension; therefore, to favor them, the mention of *ciṇ* is repeated in order to clarify the very meaning already established by logic. The term "in the sense of the impersonal (*bhāva*) or the passive (*karman*)" is understood from a previous rule, and showing that this qualifies the *sārvadhātuka* [affix], he says: "that which expresses the impersonal or the passive," and so forth.
That *sārvadhātuka* affix which occurs in the meanings of the impersonal or the passive is what "expresses the impersonal or the passive."
The suffix *ṇini* is used here in the sense of habit (*tācchīlya*) or necessity (*āvaśyaka*).

Now, why is it not stated thus: "when the abstract state (*bhāva*) or the object (*karman*) are to be expressed, *yaK* occurs before an *sārvadhātuka* suffix"? It is impossible to state it in this way; for in the grammatical treatise, the abstract state and the object are declared to be denoted by the *sārvadhātuka* suffix itself.
If one asks why this is so, it is because of the rule [Pāṇini 3.4.69].

[Objection: But surely, in cases such as *akāri kaṭo bhavatā* ("a mat was made by you"), *aśāyi bhavatā* ("it was slept by you"), and *abibharbhavān* ("you carried"), since the object and other factors are understood even in the absence of a *sārvadhātuka* suffix, it is not tenable that they constitute the meaning of the *sārvadhātuka*. For it is not logical that something which is understood in the absence of another thing should be the meaning of that [other thing], since the meaning is to be established through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*). [Reply: This is not a fault. For there is no such rule that something must possess meaning only because it is established through positive and negative concomitance. What then? It is a formal proposition (*pratijñā*). And that [meaning] is indeed established, as in the case of *kvip* and other suffixes.
And as for the statement "there is [the suffix] for the *sārvadhātuka*," this is trivial.

Regarding the form *śayyate*: the substitution of *ayaṅ* occurs by the rule *ayaṅ yi kṅiti* [Pāṇini 7.4.22]. As for the phrase "in the prescription of *yaṅ*" and so forth: one might object that since *yaṅ* will occur simply through the extended application (*atideśa*) of the rule "like the passive" (*karmavat*), what is the purpose of this supplementary rule (*upasaṃkhyāna*)? To this he replies: "Because of the conflict" (*vipratiṣedhāt hi*), and so forth.
The scope of [Pāṇini 3.1.68] *kartari śap* is: "the agent is pure" (*śuddhaḥ kartā bhavati*). The scope of [Pāṇini 3.1.67] *karmavat karmaṇā...* is: "the object is pure," as in *odanaḥ pacyate*.

In the case of *odanaḥ svayameva pacyate*, the status of being like the object (*karmavadbhāva*) would trigger the suffix *yak*. However, because of the inclusion of the word *vat* (in the rule *karmavat karmaṇā...*), so that [the properties of the object] may also apply to its own substratum (the agent), the suffix *śap* is also possible since agency is indeed present there. Since the rule for *śap* is subsequent to the rule for *yak*, *śap* alone would apply. Therefore, an addition (*upasaṃkhyāna*)—that is, an explicit statement—must be made regarding *yak* in the case of the agent-as-object (*karmakartṛ*).
The demonstration, however, is this: by virtue of the *jñāpaka* (indicative evidence), the suffix *yaK* will occur even in the case of the reflexive agent (*karmakartṛ*).
What is that *jñāpaka*? It is the prohibition [stated] at [Pāṇini 3.1.89].
For if *yaK* did not occur in the case of the reflexive agent, that prohibition would be purposeless.

It was stated—having accepted that the *śāstra*-based extension (*śāstrātideśa*) is stronger—that the *śap* [suffix] is more powerful due to the conflict (*vipratiṣedha*). However, this is not a *śāstra*-based extension; rather, it is an extension of the operation (*kāryātideśa*).

The sūtra for the extension of the operation itself is the independent prescriber of the operation of *yaK* and so forth, and that is the subsequent one. Therefore, due to the conflict, the *yaK* alone is more powerful. [Regarding the statement] "The letter *p* is for the sake of the accent":
this is so that there may be the non-acute (*anudātta*) quality by [Pāṇini 3.1.4].

"The letter *ś* [in *śyan*, etc. is for the purpose of establishing the designation *sārvadhātuka*," meaning that the status of being *sārvadhātuka*—by the rule "that which has *tiṅ* or *śit* is *sārvadhātuka*" (Pāṇini 3.4.113)—should occur. It should be understood that this same purpose applies to the *ś* of *śyan* and the others as well. "It is an exception (*apavāda*) to *śap*."

Because its commencement occurs only upon the attainment of that [suffix]; [the statement] "the letter *n* is for the sake of the accent" is so that, by [Pāṇini 6.1.197], the word may have the udātta accent on its first syllable.
In the word *dīvyati*, the long vowel is applied by [Pāṇini 8.2.77] *hali ca*. In the words *sanoti* and *kṣaṇoti*,
[the roots are] *ṣaṇu* in the sense of "giving" (Dhātupāṭha 1464) and *kṣaṇu* in the sense of "injuring" (Dhātupāṭha 1465).

"Niymārtham" (for the sake of restriction): this means that this very operation of the *tan*-class (*tanādi-kārya*) should occur; such is the restriction so that another operation of the *tan*-class does not occur in its absence. For if there were no purpose for the restriction, then just as the elision (*luk*) of *sic* is optional after other roots of the *tan*-class—such as *atat*, *atathāḥ*, *ataniṣṭa*, *ataniṣṭhāḥ*—it would likewise apply to the root *kṛ* as well.

But when that [suffix *luṅ*] is present, [the elision] does not occur; and in its absence, the elision governed by the eighth book [of Pāṇini], specifically *hrasvādaṅgāt* [8.2.27], takes effect—as in *akṛta* and *akṛthāḥ*. [Objection:

Even if that [suffix *luṅ*] were present, no undesirable consequence would arise regarding the operations such as *tan* and so forth, because even under the alternative view (*aluk-pakṣa*) where there is no elision, the elision prescribed by *hrasvāt* [8.2.27] would still apply. [Reply: This is not so; for since the elision of *sic* is about to be introduced [by *tanādibhyaḥ* 6.4.37] at a point where the elision [of *luṅ*] has not yet necessarily applied, the latter, being subsequently initiated, would sublate the former.

> [[8.2.1]] Thus, because it is not established (*asiddhatva*), one should not suspect that the prohibition of elision (*lopabādha*) is improper; for he will state this: "There is no *asiddhatva* regarding exceptions (*apavāda*), due to the authoritative force of the statement of the exception. If, then, another operation belonging to the *tan*-class is not desired for the root *kṛ*, why is it read only in the *bhū*-class? What, moreover, is the advantage of brevity (*lāghava*) in this case? Even if it were read in the *bhū*-class, its inclusion would necessarily have to be made in the rule prescribing the verbal suffix (*vikaraṇa-vidhi*); therefore, this objection is not valid. [The answer is: Since the suffix *śap* would apply by virtue of its being in the *bhū*-class, this specific statement is made.
"The substitution of *a* occurs"—this is according to the paribhāṣā rule "of the final [al]" (Pāṇini 1.1.52). As in the example: *dhinoti*.

Now, one might ask why the *guṇa* substitution for the light penultimate vowel (*laghūpadhaguṇa*) does not occur here; to this he says: "of the elision of *a*" (*allopasya*), etc. Because of the status of the elision of *a* as being "as if it were the original" (*sthānivadbhāva*) by [Pāṇini 1.1.57], the vowel *i* is no longer preceded by a light vowel (*anupadhatvāt*), and thus the *guṇa* does not take place. Furthermore, although it would have been sufficient to say "of *dhī* and *kṛvi*" (*dhivikṛvyoḥ*) for the sake of brevity, the inclusion of the suffix *num* (in the form *dhinvikṛṇvyoḥ*) is made in order to indicate that *num* occurs precisely at the stage of the original instruction (*upadeśāvasthā*).

Therefore, in the rule for the insertion of *num*, it need not be stated that "the mention of 'as if having an upadeśa' is for the sake of obtaining the desired accent. The letter *ca* is for the purpose of carrying over [the suffix] *śnā*. In the form *stabhnāti*, first there is the elision of the nasal by the rule *aniditām* [Pāṇini 6.4.24].
Because these roots are mentioned together with *śnu* and *śnā*, someone might have the misconception that they belong exclusively to those [secondary conjugation] domains.
Therefore, to dispel that, he says: "because their status as having the marker *u* is established," and so forth.
In these cases, the letter *h* is declared to bear the technical designation *it*; the result of this is the optional application of the augment *iṭ* before the suffix *ktvā*.
If these [suffixes] were restricted to the domain of vikaraṇas, the application of the marker *u* would be purposeless.
Therefore, by the very fact that the marker *u* is prescribed, it is determined that they apply to all [suffixes].
Here, the word "artha" (meaning/purpose) signifies "domain" (*viṣaya*).

The meaning is "having all things as its object. In the examples *puṣāṇa* and *muṣāṇa*, the suffix *loṭ* occurs in the sense of an injunction (*vidhi*) and so forth; by [Pāṇini 3.4.87] *sehrapicca*, the suffix *śnā* is applied because the roots belong to the *kryādi* class, and by this [rule], *śānac* is substituted for it.
The letter *ca* is for the purpose of making the final syllable udātta.
By [Pāṇini 6.4.105], there is elision (*luk*) of the suffix *hi*;
thus, "krīṇīhi. By [Pāṇini 6.4.113], there is the substitution of *i* for the vowel.

But surely, since the *śnā* affix is the subject under discussion, it alone will be understood here as the substitute; so what is the purpose of the mention "of *śna*" (*śnaḥ*)? To this he says: "The mention of 'śna' is a specification of the original element (*sthānin*)," and so forth. The purpose of the mention "of *śna*" is so that there may be the understanding that this word *śānac* is the substitute. But what is the reason that, in its absence, such an understanding would not arise? To this he says: "For [if it were not specified,] it would be another suffix," and so forth.

"All roots," even those recited in other groups, are its scope; thus it is so described. If the term "śnaḥ" were used as a short designation for the *sthānin* (the element being replaced), the recurrence of the suffix *śnā* would not be known.

Consequently, this suffix—which is an exception (*apavāda*) to *śānac*—would apply to all roots ending in consonants, and *śānac* would be its substitute; in that case, let there be no *guṇa* for *mid*. Otherwise, since this *guṇa* is commenced within the scope of the prohibition, just as it occurs here in *medyati*, it would likewise occur here in *midāna*.

Furthermore, because of the addition of the marker *śit* in the rule *śitkaraṇe tu* (P. 1.2.4), the status of being marked with *ṅ* (*ṅittvam*) applies once again. Consequently, although *guṇa* substitution is prescribed for the root *mid* even in cases where it is otherwise prohibited, it does not occur here. In this case as well, the purpose of both the marker *cit* and the marker *śit* is exactly as previously stated. [Note: This is not found in the Kāśikā. Example: *gṛhāṇa*.

The root *graha* (in the sense of "seizing" or "taking up," Dhātupāṭha 1533) takes the imperative suffix *loṭ*, the second person singular ending *sip*; this becomes *hi*, which is then replaced by *śnā*. This *śnā* becomes *śānac*, and the *hi* is elided [by Pāṇini 6.4.105]. Then, by [Pāṇini] 6.1.16, there is vocalization (*samprasāraṇa*) of the roots beginning with *grah*. Thus, the form *gṛbhāya* appears; this is the reading found in some places.
In that regard, [the Vārttika] states: *hmagrahor bhaś chandasi* (Vārttika on Pāṇini 8.2.32).
By [Pāṇini 8.2.32], it acquires the designation *bha*.
Regarding "badhāna": from the root *bandh* (meaning "to bind," Dhātupāṭha 1508), there is the elision of the nasal [of the root] by [Pāṇini 6.4.24]: *aniditām*.
The rest is as before. Regarding the term "yathāyatham":
that which is one's own respective object is "yathāyatham";
the meaning is "in whichever respective object."
Furthermore, as to what this so-called "exchange" (*vyatyaya*) is, he says: "Exchange is the act of going beyond" (*vyatigamanaṃ vyatyayaḥ*).
To clarify that very exchange, he says: "It is an interchange (*vyatihāra*), a commingling (*vyatikara*)," and so forth.
With the words "in some cases" (*kvacit*), etc., he demonstrates another mode of exchange.

Regarding "bhedati": this is the prescription of *śap* in place of *śnam*. In "marati" as well, there is *śap* in place of *śa*, and the *parasmaipada* ending occurs by way of substitution (*vyatyaya*).

Regarding "mriyate": it is from the root *mṛ*, which takes *riṅ* as before, and for that [root] there is *iyaṅ*. Regarding "neṣatu": this is the *loṭ* (imperative) of the root *nī*, with *tip*; by [Pāṇini 3.4.86], *tip* becomes *eruḥ*; after that, *śap* is added; there is *guṇa* substitution for the root vowel; and the *s* of *sip* becomes *ṣ*. An example of the state of having three *vikaraṇas* is: "{taruṣema vṛtram" — Kāśikā}, [and] "taruṣema dṛṣadam".

The suffix *liṅ* is used in the sense of a benediction (*āśis*). By the rule *nityaṃ ṅit* (Pāṇini 3.4.99), the *s* of *mas* and *vas* is elided. The augment *yāsuṭ* is added; because of this, the *liṅ* is treated as a *sārvadhātuka*, and thus the suffix *u* is applied. Following that comes *sip*, and after that, *aṅ*. Guṇa is substituted for the root vowel. The *ṣ* of *sip* undergoes the substitution of *iy* by the rule *ṣatva* (Pāṇini 7.2.80).
[The *iy*] combines with *aṅ* by the rule *aṅgasya* (Pāṇini 6.1.87), and the *s* is elided by the rule *saḥ syārddhadhātuke* (Pāṇini 7.2.79).

By [Pāṇini 6.1.66], there is the elision (*lopa*) of *y*. Now, why was it not stated simply as "transposition" (*vyatyaya*), rather than using the term "variously" (*bahulagrahaṇa*); for if the word "also" (*api*) were carried over from the preceding rule, one could connect it thus: "In the Veda, transposition occurs, and by the word 'also,' that which is otherwise established [also occurs]," whereby everything desired would be accomplished even without the mention of "variously"? To this he says: "The mention of 'variously' (*bahulagrahaṇam*)," and so forth.

The term *bahulam* (variously) is used for this purpose so that there may be a deviation—that is, a reversal—of every prescribed rule, whether it pertains to the original (*prakṛta*) or the non-original (*aprakṛta*). Otherwise, if the inclusion of *bahulam* were not made, [the rule] would apply only to the original elements beginning with *si* and ending with *śānac*, but not to others such as *śnam* and so forth; yet it is desired that it apply to those as well.
This is obtained only when *bahulam* is included.
To demonstrate this very point, he says: "sup-tiṅ-upagraha," and so on.

In that [verse], there is a transposition of case endings (*supām vyatyaya*): where "in the yoke" (*dhuri*)—referring to the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*)—would have been expected, the genitive is used in place of the locative.
Regarding verbal suffixes (*tiṅām*): in the phrase "those who fashion for the sacrificial post" (*ye yūpāya takṣati*), the plural form "they fashion" (*takṣanti*) would have been expected.
The primary *upagraha* (voice) is a specific action manifested by the substitution of suffixes (*lādeśa*).
However, in this context, the term *upagraha* is applied to the *parasmaipada* and *ātmanepada* endings because they serve as the cause for manifesting that [action].
What is meant is this: there is an "exchange" (*vyatyaya*) between the *ātmanepada* and *parasmaipada* endings.
He desires one who practices the *brāhmaṇa*; he fights with another, O Agni, being well-known.
"He desires" is what is obtained [from the context].
Regarding the indicative mark (*liṅga*): "They sit as if satiated with honey."
When *madhunā* was expected, it is [corrected to] *narasya*, meaning "of the first person" (*prathamapuruṣa*) and so forth—thus, "one should separate by means of the ten metaphors.

Regarding the word *viyūyāt*: in the context of the first person, the second person is used; from the root *yu* ("to mix," Dhātupāṭha 1033) with the prefix *vi*, the optative (*liṅ*) is formed in the sense of a benediction (*āśis*), followed by the suffix *sip*, then *yāsuṭ*, which causes lengthening according to Pāṇini 7.4.25, and the elision of the *s* according to 8.2.29.
Regarding *kāla* (time): [the rule applies] by one who is about to establish the sacred fires (*agnīn ādhāsyamānena*).
In the domain of the *luṭ* suffix, it is *luṭ*; here, the word *kāla* refers to the *luṅ* and other temporal suffixes because they have time as their object.
Indeed, a transposition of primary time itself cannot be effected.
*Halām*—the seed-syllable of the face has blossomed (*śubhitam*).
Although *śubhitam* would have been expected, [it is derived as follows]:

from the roots *śubha* and *śumbha* in the sense of "beauty" (Dhātupāṭha 1321, 1322), the past passive participle suffix (*niṣṭhā*) is applied, followed by the augment *iṭ*, and the substitution of the letter *pha* for the letter *bha*.
In the case of *acām*— [the rule states] "let pregnant wives sing near me" (*upagāyantu māṃ patnayo garbhiṇyaḥ*).
Although one would expect *patnyo garbhiṇyaḥ*,
the vowel *ī* is replaced by *i*.

Regarding the vowels—by rule [Pāṇini 6.1.220], the final syllable is udātta, as it occurs here: *āvatīṃ somavatīṃ prajāvatīṃ sūryavatīṃ dṛṣadam ita*; likewise, it would also occur here: *āvatī somavatī prajāvatī*.
However, when there is a reversal (of the accent), the word *satyā* retains its original accent (*prakṛtisvara*).
What, then, is the original accent? It is the acute accent on the first syllable (*ādyudāttatvam*).
For instance, the *ṅīp* suffix is unaccented because it is marked with *p*.

The *matup* suffix is likewise [unaccented] for that very reason. As for the word *āśa*, it is derived from the *Dhātu-pāṭha* rule "{*aśū-pruṣi-pluṣi-laṭi-kaṭi-kaṇi-khaṭi-viśibhyaḥ kvan*}" (*DhP* 8.125); since it ends in the *kvan* suffix, the word *āśa* is accented on its first syllable by the *nit-svara* rule.
The mention of the "agent" (kartṛ) is for the purpose of indicating the "factors of action" (kāraka) in general;
the meaning is that there is an interchange of the factors of action.
[This is seen] in the case of those who approach both Vedas.
Although *āsādayadbhyaḥ* would have been expected, the recipient (*sampradāna*) is treated as the instrument (*karaṇa*).

The term *yaṅ* is used to include the entire pratyāhāra (abbreviated designation), starting from *yak* in [Pāṇini 3.1.67] up to the *ṅ* in *liṅyāśiṣyaṅ* [3.1.86]. The meaning is that there is a transposition (*vyatyaya*) of the suffixes beginning with *yak* and ending with those marked by *aṅ*.
Regarding the form *muṇḍā śuṣmasya bhedatī*,
although the suffix *śnam* would have been expected,
the author of the treatise— Pāṇini— intends a substitution (*vyatyaya*) for these suffixes beginning with *śap*.
"And that [suffix] is also established by way of preponderance (*bāhulaka*). From the word "also" (*api*), there is an interchange of the *si* and other case endings.
The state of being preponderant is "preponderance" (*bāhulakam*); the suffix *vuñ* is applied here because it belongs to the *dvandva*, *manojña*, and so forth group (Pāṇini 5.1.132).
The word "and" (*ca*) indicates the reason.

Since, in this way, the transposition of both regular and irregular forms is established by means of the frequentative usage (*bāhulaka*), the term "frequentative" (*bahulagrahaṇa*) has been employed. Regarding the statement "it is an exception (*apavāda*) to *śap*":

one might object that the *liṅ* prescribed for the benedictive (*āśīḥ*) receives the designation *ārdhadhātuka* by [Pāṇini 3.4.116], whereas *śap* is prescribed for the *sārvadhātuka*; how then can it be called an exception to *śap*? To this he says: "In the Veda, both ways," and so forth. With the intention that this is seen only after roots such as *sthā* and not after others, he says: "*sthā-gā-gami*," and so forth.

Regarding the form *upastheyam*: from the root *sthā* preceded by the prefix *upa*, the optative (*liṅ*) is used in the sense of a benediction (*āśis*). The suffix *mip* is added; its replacement by *am* is effected by [Pāṇini 3.4.101], *tasthas*. Then *yāsuṭ* is added. Because it possesses both designations (as both ārdhadhātuka and sārvadhātuka), it is treated as a *sārvadhātuka*, and thus the elision of *s* occurs by [Pāṇini 7.2.79], *liṅaḥ salopo’nantyasya*.
In some places, the reading is *upastheṣam*;
there, because it is an *ārdhadhātuka*, there is no elision of *s*, and the *y* is elided before the *v* (by Pāṇini 6.1.66).
Regarding the word *upageyam*:
[the root] *gai* (meaning "to sing," Dhātupāṭha 917) undergoes the substitution of *ā* [for the vowel *i*] by [Pāṇini 6.1.45];
the remainder is as before.
Regarding "gamema": the *mas* of the *liṅ* following the root *gam* undergoes elision of *s* by [Pāṇini 3.4.99]. All [suffixes] such as *yāsuṭ* are as before.
Regarding "voceyam":
the root *vac* is used in the sense of "speaking" (*vaca bhāṣaṇe*, Dhātupāṭha 1842).

[Adding] the suffix *sip*, in that [suffix], [the augment] *aṅ*; when *aṅ* follows, [the substitution] *um* occurs for *vac* by Pāṇini 7.4.20; and for the [portion] *yā*, [the substitution] *iy* occurs by Pāṇini 6.1.87 in both cases.
"I might know" (*videyam*); [the root] *vid* means "to know" (*dhātupāṭha* 1064).
"I might be able" (*śakeyam*).

The root *śaklṛ* means "to be able" (Dhātupāṭha 1261). Regarding the form *āruheyam*: the root *ruh* [meaning] "birth" or "appearance" (from seed) (Dhātupāṭha 859); the substitution of *iy* and all other operations are as before. It is stated that "the suffix *ac* should be mentioned after the root *dṛś*."
For if there were *aṅ*, the *guṇa* substitution [prescribed by Pāṇini 7.4.16] would apply;
and in that case, the form *dṛśeyam* would not be established.
But when there is *ak*, due to its *kit* status, the absence of *guṇa* occurs.
Therefore, it must be stated—that is, explained.

The explanation, however, must be provided by virtue of the continued application of the term *bahulam* (in various cases). [The rule] "like the object" (*karmavat*) refers to Pāṇini 3.1.87, and not to 3.1.88, because of the nominative case ending in the word *tulyakriyaḥ*.
Otherwise, if it were "tulyakriye" or "tulyakriyasya," he would have made the indication using either the locative or the genitive case.
[The compound] "tulyakriyaḥ" means "one whose action is equal. Equal to what? To the object (*karman*).
The compound is justified because it conveys meaning despite being dependent [on other words].
This word "tulya" (equal) signifies "similar.
Furthermore, a similarity between the action and the object—the means of accomplishment—is not possible, because they are absolutely distinct.

For instance—action (*karman*) is a fully established substance, whereas activity (*kriyā*) has an essential nature that is not distinct from it. Therefore, in the expression "by means of action" (*karmaṇā*), this word "action" is used figuratively; by way of metaphorical transfer (*upacāra*) based on location (*tātsthya*), it refers to the activity residing within the action, just as in the phrase "the beds cry out," where the word "beds" refers to the people [on them].

The metaphorical designation (*upacāra*), however, is for the purpose that the status of being treated like an object (*karmavadbhāva*) should apply to those whose state (*bhāva*) resides in the object and whose action (*kriyā*) resides in the object, but should not apply to those whose state resides in the agent (*kartṛsthabhāvaka*) or whose action resides in the agent.
Having kept all this in mind, he says: "the action in the object is the 'object'.
By this, he explains that this word "object" (*karman*) denotes the action residing in the object.

And in order to demonstrate the meaning of the rule that results when the word *karman* (object) is used in the sense of an action residing in the object (*karmasthakriyā*), he says: "By an action residing in the object," and so forth.

This being the established meaning of the rule, one who—considering this word *tulya* (equal) to mean "common" (*sādhāraṇa*)—might object: "If an agent whose action is equal [to the object's], meaning one whose action is common, becomes like the object by virtue of an action residing in the object, then it would follow even in the case of 'Devadatta cooks rice' (*pacaty odanaṃ devadattaḥ*)."

Because even here, all the substances acting as *kārakas* proceed toward that which is the principal action; they proceed by means of that action residing in the object (*karman*), and thus the agent becomes one whose action is common [to others] by virtue of that action residing in the object—just as this [action] is related to the other *kārakas*, so too it is related to the agent—[the author] replies to that with the words "in which object" (*yasmin karmaṇi*), and so forth.
By employing the two words "tad-vat" and "yathā" in the sense of similarity, he explains: "this word *tulya* expresses similarity, not commonality."
In a case where an agent, even while assuming the state of an agent, exhibits such an action as was exhibited when in the state of an object, that agent becomes like an object (*karmavadbhavati*).

And since similarity must be based on some distinction, only the unique activity of the agent characterized by placing [the pot] on the fire and so forth is grasped, and not the common activity characterized by softening and so forth.

Furthermore, in the sentence *devadattaḥ odanaṃ pacati* ("Devadatta cooks the rice"), because Devadatta’s unique activity as an agent is dissimilar to the activities of the other factors (*kāraka*s), the status of being "like an object" does not apply.

Alternatively—when it is stated that "an agent whose action is similar [to the action] residing in the object (karman) becomes like the object (karmavadbhavati)," one might, thinking that the word *tulya* signifies "similarity," raise the following objection: "If this were so, then in the case of 'the granary being split splits the vessels,' the rule would also apply here; for the very same kind of action consisting of the separation of parts which is observed in the vessels is likewise observed in the agent, the granary. To this prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*), he says: "In whatever object" (*yasmin karmaṇi*), and so forth. By the word *saḥ* ("that"), the very same referent indicated by the word *yasmin* ("in which") is referred back.

By this, he refutes the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa) by demonstrating that an agent who possesses an action equal to an action residing in an object becomes "like an object" (karmavat) precisely through an action that has a single substance as its substratum.
And this is obtained through the principle of proximity (pratyāsatti).

For an action that inheres in the same substance is proximate, whereas one that inheres in a different substance is remote. Now, it might be argued: "The view is that power (*śakti*) is the factor of action (*kāraka*); however, the power of the object (*karman-śakti*) never attains the status of the agent (*kartṛ*). Therefore, it was incorrectly stated: 'in which action, even when it has become the agent'? This is not a fault, because when the distinction between power and the possessor of power is not intended to be expressed, what is being referred to is simply the substance (*dravya*) which is the substratum of that power. However, this other statement is indeed incorrect: "In the same way, the action is characterized as in the case of the object."

If it is argued that similarity is not tenable because the very same operation that exists in the state of being an object (*karman*) also exists in the state of being an agent (*kartṛ*), since such [similarity] must reside upon a difference—this is not a fault. Although the substance (*dravya*) possessing the states is non-different despite the difference in action caused by the difference in states, nevertheless, there is a difference in the states themselves: for the state of being an agent is indeed one thing, and the state of being an object is another. Since there is a difference in action due to the difference in states, the similarity resides in that [substance] which is their substratum. In this context, extension (*atideśa*) is of many kinds, based on differences in cause (*nimitta*), designation (*vyapadeśa*), scripture (*śāstra*), and grammatical operation (*kārya*).

In this case, there can be no transfer of the cause (*nimittātideśa*); for that which is the cause of the object—the state of being most desired by the agent—cannot be transferred to the agent, because there is no connection between the attributes of one thing and another thing possessing contradictory attributes.

Furthermore, the transfer of designation (*vyapadeśātideśa*) does not differ from the position of [mere] naming (*saṃjñāpakṣa*). In the position of naming, however, the fault that will be stated later would apply, and the inclusion of the suffix *vat* would be purposeless.

In the view that there is an extension of the *śāstra* (rule), however, it is the rule itself that is extended; once that has been extended, the *yak* and other affixes are obtained by those very rules. Consequently, if this were an extension of the rule (*śāstrātideśa*), then because they are subsequent, the *śap* and other affixes would be the sublaters (*bādhaka*) in the case of a reflexive agent (*karmakartṛ*), and a remedy would have to be provided for that.
But in the case of an extension of the operation (*kāryātideśa*), the *yak* and other affixes are prescribed by this very [sūtra] itself.

Therefore, since those *śap* and other affixes which depend on the agent would apply to the reflexive agent, they are sublated by the *yak* and others due to their being subsequent; thus, nothing needs to be remedied.

However, the primary [purpose] is the extension (*atideśa*) of the grammatical operation (*kārya*), because the rules of extension exist for that purpose. Therefore, demonstrating that this [sūtra] effects an extension of the operation, he says: "based on the action" (*karmāśrayāṇi*), and so forth.

Now, one might object: since there is a mention of the nominative case in the phrase "having the same action" (*tulyakriyaḥ*), it would be understood that the extension applies to the agent (*kartṛ*) ending in that [suffix], yet there is no explicit mention of the term "agent" (*kartṛ*) in the sūtra.

Although that which is under discussion (*prakṛta*) is also in the locative case (*saptamyanta*), the requirement here is for what is indicated by the nominative (*prathamānirdiṣṭa*). Therefore, he says "in the sense of the agent" (*kartari*) and so forth, [asking]: how can an extension (*atideśa*) be made without the mention of the agent in the nominative? Furthermore, he states "the *yak* affix and the middle voice" (*yagātmanepada*) and so forth to explain the purpose of this extension:
"it is split" (*bhidyate*) is an example of the *yak* affix;
"it was split" (*abhedi*) is an example of the *ciṇ* affix.

Regarding the term "kāriṣyate," the *ciṇvadbhāva* (the treatment as if it were the *ciṇ* [passive] affix) applies; for the *ciṇvadbhāva* is prescribed in the passive voice by rules such as *syasicsīyuṭ* [Pāṇini 6.4.62]. However, all of these examples pertain to the middle voice (*ātmanepada*). As for the phrase "even that which resides in its own [base]," and so forth:
That which does not occur even in the absence of an extended application (atideśa) is its own inherent basis; for example, the suffix *vat* is employed for this very purpose.

For if that were absent, this would be a rule for technical designation (*saṃjñā-sūtra*), and consequently, an agent whose action is similar to that of the object would receive the designation "object" (*karma-saṃjñaka*).
This being the case, because the verb would be transitive (*sakarmaka*), the *L*-suffix would not occur in the sense of the abstract state (*bhāva*) according to [Pāṇini 3.4.69].

But when the suffix -vat is employed, there is an extension (atideśa) [of the properties]. By that, the action belonging to the agent—which was previously unestablished—becomes the object, rather than the agency residing in its own substratum.
The nature of being intransitive is thereby removed, because that [agency] operates upon it.

By this, the application of the suffix *la* in the sense of the abstract state (*bhāve*) for intransitive verbs is established—as in "the granary is being split" (*bhidyate kusūlaḥ*). Now, one might ask: why does the accusative case not occur after the word *kusūla* in the sentence "the granary splits by itself" (*bhidyate kusūlaḥ svayam eva*), since this too is an object (*karman*)? To this he says: "In the case of the optative used as a benediction (*āśiṣi*), there is *aṅ*" (*liṅyāśiṣyaṅ*), and so forth. A grammatical reference (*nirdeśa*) containing two *l*-sounds is called "containing two *l*s."
If the instruction consists of two case-endings (*lakāra*), then what [is the result]? He says: "In that case," and so forth. The word *kāryam* (the grammatical operation) is to be supplied.

When there is an instruction with two case-endings, because of the recurrence of the term *la* from the rule *liṅyāśiṣyaṅ* [Pāṇini 3.1.86], it is only the agent (*kartṛ*) of the *lanti* [present tense] that becomes like the object (*karmavat*) with respect to the grammatical operation, and not the nominal stem (*prātipadika*).

The particle *iti* is used here in the sense of a reason (*hetau*). Since this is so, the accusative case does not apply to the word *kusūla*. [This is because of the rule] "by means of the instrument (*karaṇa*) and the locus (*adhikaraṇa*).

If the word *karmanā* were absent, an agent whose action is identical to that of an action residing in an instrument or a locus would also be treated like the object (*karmavat*). However, since this word is present, such a result does not occur.
Regarding the statement "the sword cuts well" (*sādhu asiś chinatti*):

when the agency (*kartṛtva*) of the blade is intended to be expressed, the sword is the agent here because it possesses an action equal [to that of the agent], namely the action characterized by the entry of the material to be cut, even though that action resides in the instrument.
Regarding the statement "the pot cooks well" (*sādhu sthālī pacati*).

In this context, when the locus (*adhikaraṇa*) is intended to be expressed as the agent (*kartṛ*), there is an agent who possesses an action equal [to that of the object] by virtue of an action consisting of supporting (*dhāraṇa*) which resides in the locus. Now, why does this not occur here: "Devadatta cooks rice" (*pacaty odanaṃ devadattaḥ*) and "the rice cooks itself" (*rādhyaty odanaḥ svayam eva*)? For even here, there is indeed an agent who possesses an action equal [to that of the object] by virtue of an action residing in the object (*karman*); for the very same kind of action characterized by softening (*vikledana*) which is observed in the rice when it is the object is observed when it is the agent as well, since the roots *pacati* and *rādhyati* have the same meaning. To address this, he says: "Because of the governing rule concerning verbal roots" (*dhātvadhikārāt*), and so forth.
This word *samāna* is a synonym for "one," as in the expression "the mother of Devadatta and Yajñadatta is the same" (*samānā mātā*),
which is understood to mean "the mother is one. From the rule *dhātor ekācaḥ* [Pāṇini 3.1.22], the term *dhātu* (root) is carried over by anuvṛtti.
Words such as "object" (*karman*) and others are relative terms (*sambandhi-śabda*). And those which are relative terms, by their very nature, bring to mind a specific correlate whose form is fixed.
For instance, when it is said, "One should act with devotion toward one's mother," even without the explicit mention of "one's own," it is understood to mean "toward one's own mother.
Therefore, [the term *karman*] brings to mind only that verbal root (*dhātu*) in relation to which the status of being an object (*karman*) belongs to something, and not any other.
And thus, since the mention of "root" (dhātu) continues [from the previous rule], this meaning is obtained:
when a certain root has a particular object presented, if that same root has that very object as its agent, then this extended application (atideśa) applies, and not otherwise.

Therefore, in the cases "Devadatta cooks the rice" (*pacaty odanaṃ devadattaḥ*) and "the rice cooks by itself" (*rādhyaty odanaḥ svayameva*), it does not apply; for it is impossible for the rice to be both the object and the agent in two different roots.

Alternatively—the singular number [expressed by] "of the root" (*dhātoḥ*) is intended here; therefore, the status of being like the object (*karmavadbhāva*) occurs only with respect to a single root. By the rule beginning with "of those whose action resides in the object" (*karmasthabhāvakānām*), he demonstrates the very meaning established by logic. For instance, the status of being like the object applies to an agent whose action is equivalent to an action residing in the object.
However, for roots whose action resides in the agent (*kartṛsthabhāvakānām*) or whose action resides in the agent (*kartṛsthakriyāṇām*), there is no such agent.

Although action (*kriyā*) is also included [by the rule] *kṛtyalyuṭo bahulam* (Pāṇini 3.3.113), and in that context even state (*bhāva*) is encompassed; nevertheless, here, due to the force of taking both terms, a distinction in meaning should be observed. That which is accomplished by means of an instrument involving physical motion is called "action" (*kriyā*), whereas that which is accomplished without physical motion is called "state" (*bhāva*). To show examples for those [grammarians] for whom the state resides in the object and the action resides in the object, as well as for those for whom the state resides in the agent and the action resides in the agent, he says: "The state of the root *pac* resides in the object."

In the case of the expression "the pot cooks by itself" (*pacyate ghaṭaḥ svayameva*), when the cooking of the pot situated in that very place is accomplished, then the cooking—whose nature is to be accomplished by means of an instrument characterized by a lack of motion—is located in the agent (*kartṛstha*). However, when the production of cooking occurs for a substance undergoing cooking as it moves to another location, then the action of the root *pac* is indeed located in the object (*karmastha*), as in the example "the rice is being cooked" (*pacyata odanaḥ*). This is expressed by the rule: "The action of the root *bhid* is located in the object" (*karmasthā ca bhideḥ kriyā*). For instance: "the granary splits by itself" (*bhidyate kusūlaḥ svayameva*).

For the action denoted by the root *bhid* (to split) is characterized by the separation of parts, and that occurs when another state is attained; thus, there is movement (*parispanda*), and therefore the action resides in the object (*karmasthā kriyā*).

As for the statement, "the state of being a sword-bearer (*asibhāva*) resides in the agent (*kartṛstha*)," the term *asibhāva* refers to the state of being [denoted] by the verbal root *ās* (to sit/be).

For "sitting" (āsana) is indeed a state of being (bhāva), because it is accomplished by means of the instrument of movement. Thus, when activity has ceased, one employs the expression "he sits"; the state of sitting is that which coexists with the duration of a month.
The compound is formed according to the *śākapārthiva* class (and others), resulting in *māsāsibhāvaḥ*.
When does this state of being seated (*āsibhāva*) coexist with the month (*māsa*)? It occurs when the expression *māsam āste* ("he sits for a month") is employed.
In *māsam*, the second case ending (*dvitīyā*) is used in the sense of the object (*karman*).

However, the designation "object" (*karmasaṃjñā*) applies because of the rule: "Time, state, and the distance to be traversed are designated as objects [of intransitive verbs]" (*kālabhāvādhvagantavyāḥ karmasaṃjñā hy akarmaṇām*, Vārttika 1.4.51).
The state of sitting (*āsibhāva*) resides in the agent, because it inheres in the sitter;
therefore, the construction *māsa āsyate svayam eva* ("the month sits by itself") does not occur.
"The action of the root *gam* (to go) resides in the agent.

Walking consists of the movement of the feet; and because it is accomplished through vibration (*parispandana*), it is an action. Furthermore, that action inheres in the mover, such as Devadatta, and not in the object, such as the village.

Therefore, because the action of staying [at home] is present, the expression "the village goes by itself" does not occur. Regarding the rule "only that which has *tapas* as its object," the word *eva* (only) is for the sake of clarity; for all sentences have exclusion as their result, and thus that meaning is already obtained.
If this were to apply even to that which does not have *tapas* as its object, then the mention of "having *tapas* as its object" would be purposeless.
By the restrictive phrase "not of one who performs another action," he shows what is excluded:
namely, "because of the difference in action.
This means because of the dissimilarity of the actions.

Since the *karmavadbhāva* (the treatment of an agent like an object) was previously prescribed for similarity of action, this [present rule] applies by way of dissimilarity; therefore, it is for the purpose of a new injunction (*vidhi*). For this very reason, because equality with an action residing in the object is not possible, the phrase *karmaṇā tulyakriyaḥ* (Pāṇini 3.1.87) does not carry over [into this rule].
By the words "fasting and so forth" (*upavāsādīni*), he demonstrates that very difference in action.
By the word "upavāsa" (fasting) and others, he explains the meaning of the word "tapas" (asceticism).

By the phrase "it means 'to cause suffering,'" he shows that in the state of action (*karmāvasthā*) of the ascetic, the root *tap* has the meaning of causing suffering. As in the expression: "one performs asceticism for the sake of heaven."
In this context, the word *tapas* refers to knowledge (*jñāna*), which is the cause for attaining heaven and other such goals.

By the phrase "it means 'to acquire' (*arjayati*)," he shows that in the state of being the agent (*kartṛ*), the root *tap* signifies acquisition. "It means 'to cause to turn back'"—that is, it does not mean "to cause pain"; for since austerity (*tapas*) is insentient, pain is impossible for it. In examples such as "it heats the gold" (*uttapati suvarṇam*), because gold is the object (*karman*), the treatment of the root *tap* as if it were the object (*karmavadbhāva*) does not apply. This is because "the *yak* and *ciṇ* affixes are not prescribed for the reflexive object (*karmakartṛ*)."

The term *karmakartṛ* (the object-agent) is a qualification. This is a prohibition of the *yak* and *ciṇ* suffixes which would otherwise apply by the rule *karmavat karmaṇā tulyakriyaḥ* [Pāṇini 3.1.87], and not of the *ciṇvad-bhāva* (the treatment as if having the *ciṇ* augment) in the passive and middle voices [by the rule *ciṇvadiṭ ca* 3.1.67].
This is for the purpose of showing that [the rule] applies even to those two [cases] which have been reached when the action is pure (*śuddha*).
And this is obtained through the technical rule (*paribhāṣā*): "A prescription or a prohibition applies to what is immediately preceding" (Vyāḍiparibhāṣā 19).
[The example is] *dugdhe*.
When *duh* is replaced by *śap*, there is elision (*luk*) because it belongs to the *ad*-class.
As before, the substitutions for *gh*, *jha*, and *jaś* take place.
Thus: *adugdha*.
When the *ciṇ* affix is prohibited, the *ksa* affix is applied; its elision (*luk*) occurs by the rule "the elision of *ksa* is optional" (*lug vā*, Pāṇini 7.3.73).
Thus we have "prasnute."
The root *snu* in the sense of "flowing forth" (*praruāvaṇe*) is listed in the Dhātupāṭha as number 1038. As in the previous case, there is elision (*luk*) of the *śap* suffix.
The form *prāsnoṣṭa* is derived from the *luṅ* tense.
Regarding the word "namate": the root *ṇam* (Dhātupāṭha 981) means "to bow" and "sound.
It should be understood that here the root *nam*, having the causative sense (*ṇyartha*) internalized, functions in the sense of the object (*karman*).

For in this way, the action resides in the object (*karmasthakriya*); otherwise, because the action would reside in the agent (*kartṛsthakriya*), there would be no possibility [of the action being attributed to the object], and thus the prohibition would be meaningless. However, when the sense of "self" (*svārtha*) is included within the root, the action resides in the object—as in: "Devadatta bows the staff," or "The staff bows by itself."
As in the state of the causative suffix (*ṇic*). Regarding the rule "in the prohibition of *yak* and *ciṇ*" and so forth:

the meaning is that when the prohibition of *yak* and *ciṇ* is to be applied, an extension (*upasaṃkhyāna*)—that is, a formal statement—must also be made for the prohibition of those [suffixes] in the case of *śranthi* and the others.
However, the inclusion of "not" (*na*) in the rule must be performed for the sake of establishing the desired result through a split in the yoga (*yogavibhāga*).
The mention of *ṇi* includes both the causative suffix *ṇic* (denoted as *hetumaṇṇic*) and the other [suffixes].
[The first part is] *hetumaṇṇic*.
"Devadatta causes the mat to be made" (*kārayati kaṭaṃ devadattaḥ*);
"the mat causes itself to be made" (*kārayate kaṭaḥ svayam eva*).
When the *yak* affix is prohibited, the *śap* affix [is applied].

In the example *acīkarata kaṭaḥ svayam eva*, since the *ciṇ* suffix is prohibited, the *caṅ* suffix is applied by the rule *ṇiśri* [Pāṇini 3.1.48]. Then, by the rule *ṇau caṅy upadhāyā hrasvaḥ* [7.4.1], the penultimate vowel is shortened.
By the rule *caṅi* [6.1.11], reduplication occurs, followed by the phonological operations pertaining to the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsakārya*).

The other is *ṇiṅ*: "After the words *puccha*, *bhāṇḍa*, and *cīvara*, [the suffix] *ṇiṅ* [is applied]" [Pāṇini 3.1.20]. For example: *utpucchayate gāṃ gopaḥ* ("The cowherd lifts up the tail of the cow") and *utpucchayate gauḥ svayameva* ("The cow lifts up its own tail").
When the root *yāc* (to beg) is prohibited [from taking the *śap* suffix], the *śap* is applied;
this should be understood to apply to subsequent cases as well. For example: *udapupucchata gauḥ svayameva* ("the cow wagged its tail by itself").
When *ciṇ* is prohibited, the substitution of *caṅ* occurs as before;
this should be understood to apply in subsequent cases as well.
[The roots] *śrantha* and *grantha*, meaning "to string together" (Dhātupāṭha 1512, 1513).
The roots *granth* and *śranth* are read at the beginning of the *cur*-class (Dhātupāṭha 1837 and 1838).

According to the rule "optionally up to *dhṛṣ*" (Dhātupāṭha immediately after 1805), there is an option regarding the causative suffix (*ṇic*). When that *ṇic* is absent, these are the examples; otherwise, the formation is established by the presence of *ṇic*.
Devadatta ties a knot.
The knot ties itself.
The knot tied itself.
Devadatta ties his girdle;
the girdle ties itself.

Since the roots *śranth* and *granth*—meaning "to tie"—are also listed in the Kryādi class (Dhātupāṭha 1512, 1513), this prohibition applies to them as well: Devadatta ties his girdle; the girdle ties itself.
> [[6.4.113]] Thus, there is the substitution of *i* for the vowel.
The girdle untied itself (*aśranthiṣṭa*).
Devadatta ties a knot (*grathnīte*).
The knot tied itself;
the knot untied itself. Devadatta tells the story.
He himself tells the story;
as before, there is elision of the suffix *śap*.
Devadatta told the story.
The word *avocata* is derived from the root itself:

by [Pāṇini 2.4.53] *brūño vaciḥ*, there is the substitution of *vac*; by [Pāṇini 3.1.52] *asyativaktikhyātibhyaḥ ṅaḥ*, there is the substitution of *aṅ*; and by [Pāṇini 7.4.20] *vaca um*, the augment *um* is applied.
Because the causative sense (*ṇyartha*) is inherent, it should be understood as having an action residing in the object (*karmasthakriyatva*).

Regarding the rule "of those that are intransitive when taking the middle voice" (*ātmanepadākarmakāṇām*): those verbal roots which are understood to be intransitive at the time of the prescription of the middle voice are called "those that are intransitive when taking the middle voice. For example: *vikurvate saindhavāḥ svayam eva* ("the Saindhava horses exert themselves by themselves").
This is the substitution of *it*.

In the example "the Saindhavas drew themselves apart" (*vyakṛṣata saindhavāḥ svayameva*), because the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) is prescribed by [Pāṇini 1.3.45] following the root *kṛ* preceded by *vi*, there is the absence of an object (*akarmakatva*) for the middle voice.

Here too, the root *kṛ*, existing in the sense of "leaping," has its causative meaning (*ṇyartha*) internalized and thus becomes a root whose action resides in the object (*karmasthakriya*). The mention of *rañj* with the elision of the nasal (*anunāsika*) is for the sake of brevity.
"These two are exceptions to the [affixes] *śyan* and *yak*, and to the *parasmaipada* and *ātmanepada* [respectively].
Thus, *śyan* is an exception to *yak*; however, the *parasmaipada* is an exception to the *ātmanepada*.
For example: "he colors" (*rajyati*).
By the rule *aniditām* [Pāṇini 6.4.24], there is the elision of the nasal. The mention of "the Easterners" (*prācām*) is for the purpose of providing an option;
by this, he removes the sense that it is for the sake of honor.
In that context, for the sake of honorific reference (*pūjārtha*), no alternative form (*vikalpa*) would be obtained.
By the words "it is censured" (*kuṣyate*) and so forth, he demonstrates what is intended when the prior mention is made for the sake of an alternative;
namely, the passage beginning with "and in the domain of *syāt*," etc.
By the word "etc. (*ādi*), forms such as *tāsi* and others are included. In the examples *cukuṣe* and *rarañje*:
the suffix is *liṭ*, the voice is *ātmanepada*, the affix is *tapratyaya*, and for that, *aiś* is the substitute.

Regarding *koṣiṣīṣṭa*: this is the optative (*liṅ*) in the sense of a benediction (*āśis*). [The suffix] *sīyuṭ* is added; then *suṭ* is added by Pāṇini 3.4.107; there is the *guṇa* substitution for the light penultimate vowel, the change to *ṣ*, and the change to *ṣṭu*. Regarding *raṅkṣīṣṭa*: [the same process applies].

There is a prohibition of the augment *iṭ* by the rule *ekācaḥ* [Pāṇini 7.2.10], and there is the substitution of *k* (kutva) by the rule *coḥ kuḥ* [Pāṇini 8.2.30], resulting in the letter *g*. Then, by the rule *khari ca* [Pāṇini 8.4.54], there is the substitution of *c* (cartva), resulting in the letter *k*. Thus we have *akoṣi* and *arañji*.
"Because of the governing rule (adhikāra) 'of the root' (dhātoḥ) in the prescription of the *yaṅ* [affix]" means that the mention of "root" (dhātu) which occurs in the prescription of the *yaṅ*—
namely, in the rule *dhātor ekācaḥ* [Pāṇini 3.1.22]— is the governing rule here. And this is the reasoning for the fact that the mention of "root" would otherwise be purposeless.
"But for the sake of the technical designations (*saṃjñā*) of *kṛt* suffixes and *upapada*s," he says;
this refutes the charge of pointlessness (*ānarthakya*).

Now, one might object: even by the previous mention of "root" (*dhātu*), the technical designations of *kṛt* suffixes and *upapada*s would be established, as in the example *kariṣyati*, where the suffix *syat* would receive the designation of *kṛt* by the rule *kṛdatiṅ* [Pāṇini 3.1.93].
Consequently, by the rule *tataśca* (Pāṇini 1.2.46), the designation of "nominal stem" (*prātipadika*) would apply; and that being present, the generation of case-endings (*sub*) would follow.

Furthermore, in the context of [the rule] *tatropapadam* (Pāṇini 3.1.92), which is part of the section beginning with *supo dhātuprātipadikayoḥ* (Pāṇini 2.4.71), the designation "governing word" (*upapada*) would also apply to the suffix *luṅ*. As a result, the meaning "after the suffix *luṅ* as a governing word, the suffix *cli*" would be possible.

Therefore, within this section on verbal roots (*dhātu*), so that the designations "kṛt" and "governing word" may apply here but not in the preceding sections, the term "verbal root" (*dhātu*) is mentioned once again.

If it is argued that these two technical terms (*saṃjñā*) will be prescribed by way of a governing heading (*adhikāra*), just like the term *pratyaya*, and therefore they will not apply to what precedes [the rule], we say: no; for the logic of the "lion's glance" (*siṃhāvalokita-nyāya*) also applies.
If they were prescribed by way of a governing heading, they might be suspected of applying even to what precedes;
in that case, an explanatory interpretation (*vyākhyāna*) would have to be provided.
Furthermore, the mention of "dhātu" (verbal root) is made light by this explanation.

Moreover, the mention of "dhātu" must necessarily be made for another purpose; being made for that other purpose, it will also serve to clarify the rule for the technical designation (*saṃjñā*) of *kṛt* suffixes and *upapada*s.
To demonstrate that very necessity for another purpose, he says: "for the sake of the designation *ārdhadhātuka*," and so forth.
The meaning to be understood here is that the word "ca" (and) is for the purpose of prescribing the *asarūpa* (non-homogeneous) rule;

that is, within this governing context of verbal roots (*dhātvadhikāra*) [beginning with P. 3.1.91], an *asarūpa* exception (*apavāda*) should be a sublater (*bādhaka*), but not in the preceding [context].
Consequently, there is no co-occurrence (*samāveśa*) of the suffixes *ksa* and others with *sic*.

But surely, the designation *ardhadhātuka* would be established even by the first mention of "dhātu"; what is the purpose of the second mention of "dhātu"? To this he says: "By [the rule] 'of a root' (*dhātoḥ*) and so forth. The meaning is that the second mention of "dhātu" is for the sake of ensuring that the designation *ardhadhātuka* applies only to that which is prescribed after the word "dhātu" has been uttered. Why, then, is the designation *ardhadhātuka* stated for that which is prescribed after "dhātu" has been uttered? He says: "So that it may not occur here. If the second mention of "dhātu" were absent, the designation *ardhadhātuka* would apply in cases such as *lūbhyām* and *lūbhiḥ*.

For in this case, there is indeed an affix following a verbal root (*dhātu*), on the basis of the principle that "those ending in *kvip* do not lose their status as verbal roots. Consequently, since it would possess the character of an *ārdhadhātuka*, the augment *iṭ*—which is conditioned by being an *ārdhadhātuka*—would undesirably apply.
However, when the second mention of the term "verbal root" (*dhātu*) is made, it functions by implication to denote a word-form consisting of a sequence of sounds (*śabdabandhapadātmaka*).
From this, the following meaning is obtained: that which is prescribed by the mention of "dhātu" (root) as such—by the designation "dhātu"—receives the technical name *ārdhadhātuka*.
Consequently, in forms such as *lūbhyām*, there is no status of being *ārdhadhātuka*;

for here the suffix is not prescribed by the rule "after a root" (*dhātoḥ*), but rather by the rule "after a nominal stem" (*prātipadikāt*). By the phrase "that which is indicated by the locative case," he explains the meaning of the expression "that which stands in the locative."

For this designation (*saṃjñā*) is prescribed for a word, and which [word] is "situated in the locative" (*saptamīstha*)? It is that of which there is a mention in the locative case, as in *kumbhakāraḥ*.

When the designation *upapada* is applied, the compound is formed by *upapadam atiṅ* (Pāṇini 2.2.19), and by *gatikārakopapadāt kṛt* (Pāṇini 6.2.139), the final member of the compound retains its original accent (*prakṛtisvara*). [The phrase] "the mention of *stha*" and so forth [is explained as follows].
That by which something is pointed out is a "nirdeśa" (designation).
That which has a locative case as its designation is a "saptamīnirdeśa. The inclusion of the term *stha* is for the purpose of understanding that [designation].
This is what is meant: the mention of *sthā* is for the purpose that there may be an understanding of that which is indicated by the locative case (*saptamī*) as being the name-bearer (*saṃjñin*).
If, however, the mention of *sthā* were not made, what would happen? To this he says: "For otherwise," and so forth.

For otherwise, if the mention of *sthā* were not made, then by the rule "In a prescription of a name (*saṃjñā-vidhi*), when a suffix (*pratyaya*) is mentioned, there is no inclusion of that which ends with it" (Paribhāṣā 81), that very locative case would be understood as the technical term *upapada*.

Furthermore, the notion that "the designation [saṃjñā] is not applicable to a non-existent designatum" would apply only in cases where the locative case (saptamī) is heard, such as in *stamberama* ("elephant") and the like.

One might argue: "This is not a mention of the suffix (*pratyaya*), but rather a mention of the actual form of the word *saptamī*. To this he says: "In cases where," and so forth; the meaning is already explained.
Regarding the passage beginning with "But because of the inclusion of *stha*," etc.:

when the inclusion of *stha* is made, due to the expansion of the text, that which is indicated by the locative case in the sūtra is designated as the technical term (*saṃjñin*); thus, everything becomes established, because all those for whom this designation is intended are indicated by the locative case in the sūtra.
For example, in the rule *stambakarṇayoḥ* [Pāṇini 3.2.13], the words *stamba* and *karṇa* are indicated in the sūtra by the locative case.
In the rule [Pāṇini 3.2.97], *upasaraja* and so forth are included;

and in the rule [Pāṇini 3.2.1], *kumbha* and so forth denote the object (*karman*). Now, since the purpose of creating a technical term (*saṃjñā*) is for the sake of brevity (*lāghava*), why is such a cumbersome term employed? To this he says: "The creation of a cumbersome term," and so on.
The word *upa* signifies proximity.

The designation *upoccārita* (pronounced near) for a word [occurring] as an *upapada* is established so that, when there is an understanding of the technical name (*saṃjñā*) according to its literal meaning (*anvartha*), the operation of the rule concerning semantic competency (*samarthaparibhāṣā*) may take effect; this is the purpose of creating this cumbersome designation.
To demonstrate what is accomplished when the rule concerning semantic competency is brought into play, he says: "Look at the jar," and so forth.
For when the designation is based on its literal meaning, a suffix (*pratyaya*) dependent upon an *upapada* becomes a rule regarding words (*padavidhi*).
And wherever there is even a trace of semantic connection (*padagandha*), the rule regarding semantic capacity (*samartha-paribhāṣā*) applies.
Therefore, in the case of "look at the jar" (*paśya kumbham*) and "he makes a mat" (*kaṭam karoti*), [the *samāsa*] does not occur.
For here, the jar has no semantic connection with the verb "to make"; what then? It has a connection with the word "look."

The word *pada* here is also etymological (*anvartha*), not technical (*pāribhāṣika*). For instance, a word ending in a case-suffix (*subanta*) receives the designation *pada*; and at the time when the designation *upapada* is prescribed for the suffix *ṭac*, it remains a word ending in a case-suffix. This is because, once the designation *upapada* has been applied, the suffix is prescribed based on that *upapada*, and the *upapada-compound* (*upapadasamāsa*) must also occur before the production of the case-suffix, according to the rule: "There is a statement regarding the compounding of prefixes (*gati*), non-agentive (*akāraka*), and *upapada* words with *kṛt*-suffixes prior to the production of the case-suffix" (Vyāḍīya-paribhāṣāvṛtti 138). Therefore, this word *pada* is etymological: that by which a meaning is reached (*padyate*) or understood is a *pada*.

The inclusion of the word *tatra* (in that case) is for the purpose that the designation *upapada* should apply when there is the status of being a cause (*nimittabhāva*) with respect to the suffix (*pratyaya*) situated in the locative case.
For if the word *tatra* were not included, the suffix would arise when *karman* is the *upapada*, but it would also arise when it is not an *upapada*.

As for the indication by the locative case in the expression *karmaṇi*, its purpose would be to assign the designation *upapada* to that [word] when it is possible for it to end in the locative; however, the meaning that the suffix must necessarily occur only when that [locative-ending word] exists is not obtained.

Therefore, the mention of "therein" (*tatra*) is for the sake of the purpose already stated. Now, one might ask: why is the mention of "therein" not intended to indicate that the governing rule (*adhikāra*) concerning verbal roots (*dhātu*) applies immediately [to what follows]? That is, so that the designation *upapada* might apply immediately within this governing rule concerning verbal roots? This is not the case; for this is established even by virtue of the governing rule itself. The designation *upapada* will be introduced as a governing rule, and by that, the designation will apply to the technical names (*saṃjñin*) to be mentioned hereafter. Thus, there is no need for the mention of "therein" for this specific purpose.

Regarding the passage beginning with "In this [context]" (*tatrāitasmin*), the commentary (*vṛtti*) is to be inferred as follows: "In this governing rule of verbal roots (*dhātvadhikāra*), that which is indicated by the locative case receives the technical designation *upapada*. And in that context, because the commentary requires supplementation (*sopaskāratva*), the meaning 'when there is a cause for a suffix' is obtained. As for the word "to be done" (*kartavyam*):
once the designation *kṛt* has been applied, the designation *prātipadika* applies by [Pāṇini 1.2.46].
In the word *cīyāt*, the term *liṅ* [is used] in the sense of a benediction (*āśiṣi*), and by this [rule], it receives the designation of *ārdhadhātuka*.

If the condition *atiṅ* were not stated, then even a *tiṅ* [ending] would receive the designation of *kṛt*; consequently, the lengthening [of the vowel] prescribed by the rule *akṛtsārvadhātukayoḥ* [Pāṇini 7.4.25] would not occur.

However, *atiṅ* becomes *satya* because it contains the sound *y*. It is a general rule (*utsarga-dharma*) that a general rule does not apply to the domain of an exception (*apavāda*). Yet, it is desired that some general rules do apply even to the domain of exceptions; since this cannot be established without an explicit statement, this [sūtra] is for that purpose.

But even if this [sūtra] were commenced, this intended meaning would still not be achieved. To explain: its connection would have to be either with the general rule (*utsarga*), or with the exception (*apavāda*), or with both. In that regard, if the first alternative were adopted, then by means of the word *vā* (or), which introduces an option, the meaning of this [sūtra] regarding existence and non-existence would be: "The general rule, being dissimilar, optionally applies in the case of non-feminine genders," and "optionally it does not apply. And in that case, there would be a permanent non-application of the exception within its own domain;
for nothing at all would have been done for the exception by this [sūtra], since it has no connection with it.

Furthermore, when an exception (*apavāda*) that possesses a subverting force (*bādhaka*) is present and is experienced as being non-optional (*avikalpā*), the general rule (*utsarga*) is not able to operate there; thus, the option (*vikalpa*) would apply only within its own proper domain.
Now, if the second alternative [is accepted], then the meaning would be this: "A dissimilar exception (*asarūpo 'pavādaḥ*) applies optionally (*vikalpena*) except in the feminine.
Even so, the operation of the general rule in the domain of the exception is still not obtained.

It is said that a general rule (*utsarga*) and an exception (*apavāda*) may optionally apply to a non-feminine [noun]. Even so, it is not possible for the general rule to operate within the domain of the exception;
for the general rule avoids the domain of the exception, since the exception is by nature subverting.

Moreover, that sublation remains in this position exactly as it was before, for it has not been removed by this [statement]. What then? Its presence and absence in its own domain have been established: it exists in one case, and it does not exist in another.
And there is no other statement whereby the general rule (*utsarga*) might stand aside from the scope of the exception (*apavāda*).
In the case where there is no exception, the general rule will apply even in the absence of a statement providing the [specific] occasion.

If it is argued that this is because there is no obstruction [to the operation of the general rule], we reply: True, this applies in the case of an obstruction to the *kārya* (the result); however, in the case of an obstruction to the *śāstra* (the rule), that which enjoins the *kārya*—being obstructed by an exception (*apavāda*)—must operate only by avoiding the domain of that exception. Once that [general rule] has operated, even if it subsequently undergoes operation optionally due to the exception, the operation of the general rule (*utsarga*) is not possible within the domain of that [exception], because the general rule has that very domain as its scope. If it is argued: "Let it be the case of an obstruction to the *kārya*," we say: No, for that is improper. For when the enjoining rule (*vidhāyaka-śāstra*) is not obstructed, an obstruction to its *kārya* is not logical.
For it is only by cutting off the cause that the effect can be cut off, and not otherwise;
indeed, as long as the lamp is not extinguished, its light is not extinguished.

Therefore, the exception (*apavāda*) itself subverts the general rule (*śāstra*); and when that [exception] has been subverted, even in the case where there is no exception, the general rule would never apply to the domain of the exception.
Now, if the third alternative were taken, the meaning would be this: "A non-homogeneous general rule (*utsarga*) optionally applies, as does an exception (*apavāda*).
Even so, there would be an optional application of both within their own respective domains, but not of the general rule in the domain of the exception; for the very reason stated previously.

Therefore, one might object that even if this [rule] were formulated, the intended meaning would still not be achieved. To that, he replies: "A non-homogeneous exceptional suffix (*apavāda-pratyaya*) is indeed subverting."

By this, he shows that the connection is with the exception (*apavāda*), and not that existence and non-existence are being conceptualized; rather, it is shown that [the exception] constitutes a sublation (*bādhakatva*) in a particular case. And thus, in that case where the exception does not act as a sublation, the general rule (*utsarga*) proceeds due to the absence of an obstruction; in this way, their coexistence (*samāveśa*) is established.

"Excluding the suffix prescribed under the heading of 'feminine' (*stryadhikāra*). But how is this meaning obtained from the expression "not in the feminine" (*astriyām*)?
