It is thought thus: "The mention of 'feminine' (*strī*) here is marked with a svarita accent, and through a svarita accent, the understanding of a governing heading (*adhikāra*) occurs; therefore, taking as a basis that which is prescribed under the heading of 'feminine,' a prohibition is understood to apply to those [suffixes] for which both a general rule (*utsarga*) and an exception (*apavāda*) have been prescribed."

Now, why is it not understood in this way: that when "feminine" (*strī*) is the meaning to be expressed, a dissimilar (*asarūpa*) exception or sublater does not apply? It is impossible to understand it thus; for if it were understood in this way, then in cases such as *lavyā* and *lavitavyā*, the suffix *tavya* would not occur.

If that is so, why is it not understood thus: "The suffix prescribed by the mention of the word *strī* in the rule *striyām* (Pāṇini 3.3.94) is what is expressed here by the word *strī*; and when [a suffix] is prescribed for the feminine (*striyām*), a dissimilar (*asarūpa*) exception or sublater does not apply"? This cannot be understood in this way; for if it were understood thus, then in the case of *vyāvakrośī* and *vyāvakruṣṭiḥ*, the suffix *ktin* would not occur in place of *ṇac*, because *ṇac* is prescribed by the rule *karmavyatīhāre ṇac striyām* (Pāṇini 3.3.43), while *ktin* is also prescribed for the feminine. Therefore, the meaning is exactly as stated previously.

If this is so, does the paribhāṣā "ktalyuṭtumunkhalartheṣu" (Pāṇini 3.3.114) not apply, since those suffixes are prescribed under the heading of "strī" (feminine)? Furthermore, in the case of *hasitam* and *hasanam*, the suffix *ghañ* would also apply by virtue of [Pāṇini 3.3.18] "bhāve" (in the sense of the abstract action).

Regarding the rule *samānakarttṛkeṣu tumun* [Pāṇini 3.3.158]: "In cases where there is a common agent, the suffix *tumun* is used"—does this not also apply in the domain of *icchati bhoktum* (he wishes to eat), where the rule *icchārtheṣu liṅloṭau* [3.3.157] would also be applicable? Regarding the example *īṣatpānam* (drinking slightly): does this not also fall within the domain of the rule *īṣadduḥsuṣu kṛcchrākṛcchrārtheṣu khal* [3.3.126], whereby the suffix *khal* would also be applicable? There is no fault here because the mention of the word *vā* (optionally) implies that the rule is a *vyavasthitavibhāṣā* (a restricted option), and thus it does not apply. The statement "*ṇvultṛcau* is a general rule" (*utsarga*) is made because it is prescribed as a general provision.
"The rule *igupadhāpīkiraḥ kaḥ* is an exception (*apavāda*)"—
this is because it is prescribed as a specific rule (*viśeṣavidhi*). The general rule (*utsarga*) is *Pāṇini 3.2.1*, while the suffix *kap* [prescribed by *Pāṇini 3.3.106*] is the exception.
But surely, since there is dissimilarity (asārūpya) caused by the *anubandhas*, that [suffix] would also be "dissimilar"; to this he replies with "not caused by the *anubandhas*" and so forth.
In this regard, the mention of the option (*vibhāṣā*) in [Pāṇini 3.1.139] is the indicator (*jñāpaka*).
For if dissimilarity were indeed caused by the *anubandhas*, the mention of the option would be purposeless.

Indeed, because of the dissimilarity (*asārūpya*) caused by the suffixes, the affix *ṇa* will optionally apply by the rule *śyādvyadha-* [Pāṇini 3.1.141]. The use of the plural number in the term *kṛtyāḥ* is due to the plurality of the technical names (*saṃjñin*).
Alternatively, the plural is used for the purpose of including *kṛt* suffixes not explicitly mentioned;
consequently, the need for the supplementary rule (*vārttika*) "the addition of *kelimara*" does not arise.
"He will state [later] that 'the suffixes *ṇvul* and *tṛc* [are applied]'.

Now, why is it not understood that the *ṇvul* in the rule "ṇvul is applied diversely when expressing a disease" (Pāṇini 3.3.108) serves as the limit for this section? It is because of an indicator (*jñāpaka*).

Since the author, having made the mention of *kṛtya* suffixes in the rule "after a word ending in *ghañ*" (Pāṇini 3.3.16), makes a separate mention of *tṛc*, it is known from this that it does not serve as a limit; otherwise, since *tṛc* would also be a *kṛtya* suffix, its separate mention would be purposeless.

If this were so, the preceding rule would be purposeless; therefore, by virtue of this very indicator (jñāpaka), this technical designation (*saṃjñā*) would not apply to a *tṛc* [stem]. This is not the case; for if this [present rule] did not exist, it would not apply to a *tṛc* stem by virtue of the indicator, yet it would certainly apply to a stem ending in the suffix *ṇvul*.

It might be argued: "The indicator (*jñāpaka*) depends on a specific rule (*yoga*); in this rule, the designation *kṛtya* applies—this meaning is indicated by the mention of the suffix *-tṛc*, and therefore the suffix *-ṇvul* will not occur either. [We reply: This would apply to other suffixes beginning with vowels as well, and there would be an excessive burden of comprehension (*pratipatti-gaurava*), because an indicator that depends on a specific rule is difficult to discern. Regarding the statement "the letters *t* and *r* are for the sake of accentuation" (*svarārthau*):
the letter *t* serves the purpose of the *svarita* accent according to Pāṇini 6.1.185.

The *repha* [in *vāstavya*] is for the purpose of making the middle syllable udātta. Regarding the rule "the suffix *tavyat* is added after the root *vas*, and it is also *ṇit* when denoting the agent": from the root *vas* (meaning "to dwell," Dhātupāṭha 1005), the suffix *tavyat* occurs in the sense of the agent, and that suffix is *ṇit*.
This need not be stated [as a separate rule], because it is already established by [Pāṇini 3.3.113].
One who dwells is a *vāstavya*.

There is *vṛddhi* [substitution] due to the presence of the *ṇit* suffix. Regarding the statement "the addition of *kelimara* should be included," the word *upasaṃkhyāna* means "explanation" or "demonstration. This demonstration has already been provided previously.
It is further stated: by virtue of the rule *bahulam* (in various ways) [Pāṇini 3.3.113], the suffix *kelim* will also be considered a *kṛtya*.
The letter *ka* is for the purpose of the operations of a *kit* suffix, and the letter *ra* is for the purpose of vowel accentuation.
Thus: "The beans cook themselves" (*pacelimā māṣāḥ*).

Due to the inherent nature of the word's power (*śabdaśakti*) and because of this plural number (*bahuvacana*), it occurs only in the case of the reflexive agent (*karmakartṛ*) and not elsewhere. Regarding the letter *t* [in *gātā*], [the *Kāśikā* states] that it is for the sake of the accent—specifically for the purpose of the rule "that which ends in *t* is acute, except for *nau*" (*yato 'nāvaḥ*)—and for the sake of specification; that is, it is for the purpose of making the initial syllable acute (*ādyudātta*).
[The example is] "it should be sung" (*geyam*).

From the roots *kai* and *gai* (meaning "to sound") [Dhātupāṭha 916, 917], there is the substitution of *ā* by [Pāṇini 6.1.45], the substitution of *i* by [Pāṇini 6.4.65], and then *guṇa*. Regarding the phrase "as far as" (*yāvatā*) and so forth:

here, verbal roots are of two kinds—those ending in a consonant (*halanta*) and those ending in a vowel (*ajanta*). Among these, [the suffix] *ṇyat* is desired after a root ending in a consonant by [Pāṇini 3.1.124]: *ṛhaloṇryat*. Therefore, by the principle of elimination (*pariśeṣya*), since the suffix *yat* will occur only after a root ending in a vowel even without the mention of *aj*, the mention of *aj* is redundant; this is the intended meaning. [The expression] "from that which was previously a vowel-ending" (*ajantabhūtapūrvāt*)...

This is a *karmadhāraya* compound meaning "that which is both vowel-ending (*ajanta*) and has previously been so. The mention of the vowel (*aj*) is for the sake of ensuring that the rule applies even to a word that was previously vowel-ending but is now consonant-ending (*halanta*), such as in the example *ditsyam*.
The form *dhitsyam* is derived from the roots *dāñ* and *dhāñ* with the suffix *san*, followed by reduplication;
the substitution of *ī* for *a* is applied by the rule *sani mīmā* [Pāṇini 7.4.54].
By [Pāṇini 7.4.58], there is the elision of the reduplication (*abhyāsa*).

By [Pāṇini 7.4.49], *tattva* (the substitution of *ta*) occurs. Even before the *ardhadhātuka* suffix has been produced, when its status as the domain [of the rule] is intended, by [Pāṇini 6.4.48], there is the elision of the vowel *a*.

In this state, if there were no censure (*garhaṇa*) of the unreal, [the rule] would not apply; because [the word] would not end in *ac*. But since that censure exists, it applies by resorting to its having previously ended in *ac*.
And it should be understood that this purpose is only optional (*pākṣika*).
In which case [is this] so? When the *ārdhadhātuka* suffix is intended as the object of application, it is prescribed by [Pāṇini 6.4.48].
When it is an *ārdhadhātuka*, then this [present rule] serves no purpose.
However, the mention of *aj* (the vowel) should be understood as being for the sake of clarity, as in the examples beginning with *taki-śas-* and so forth.

Regarding the roots *taka* (printed as *sahane*, Dhātupāṭha 117), *hasane* (Dhātupāṭha 117), *śasu hiṃsāyām* (Dhātupāṭha 727), *cate cade yācane* (Dhātupāṭha 865, 866), *yatī prayatne* (Dhātupāṭha 30), and *janī prādurbhāve* (Dhātupāṭha 1149)—an addition (*upasaṃkhyāna*) concerning the suffix *yat* must be made for these; that is, its prescription must be provided.
This prescription, however, should be made by relying on the mention of the term *bahulam* ("in various ways"). [Furthermore,] regarding the rule *hano vā vadha ca*:
the suffix *yat* occurs after the root *han*, as an exception (*apavāda*) to the suffix *ṇyat*.
Because of the mention of the word "vā" (or), the suffix *ṇyat* certainly occurs in the alternative case;
however, the suffix *yat* is obtained from that very same rule through the expression "bahulam" (diversely). When *yat* occurs, then there is the substitution of *badh* for the root *han*.
That [suffix] is also obtained through the recurrence of the term *bahulam* (variously) from rule 7.4.78 in the context of rule 2.4.42. Regarding the form *ghātya*:
there is the substitution of *t* by [rule] 7.3.32 (*hanastaḥ*), and the substitution of *k* by [rule] 7.3.54 (*ho hanteḥ*). It is *prākyam*.
Regarding the word *vākya*:
by the rule *cajoḥ* [Pāṇini 7.3.52], there is the substitution *kutva*. Thus, *kopyam*.
Regarding "gopyam":
from the root *kup* in the sense of "anger" (Dhātupāṭha 1233); from *gup* in the sense of "concealment and reproach" (Dhātupāṭha 970); and from *gup* in the sense of "confounding" (Dhātupāṭha 1234).
Regarding "āpyam": [it is derived from the root *āp*].
The root *āplṛ* means "to pervade" (*vyāptau*; Dhātupāṭha 1260). Regarding the term *anupasarge*:
by a transposition of case endings (*suj-vyatyaya*), the locative case is used in the sense of the ablative.
For this very reason, he says: "from those that are without a prefix" (*anupasargebhyaḥ*).
The meaning is "from those where no prefix (*upasarga*) exists.

Now, why is it not understood in this way: "other than a prefix is *anupasarga*"? It is impossible to understand it thus; for if it were understood in that manner, [the rule] would not apply to simple words. Since, by the maxim of "that which is joined with *nañ* or *iva*" (*nañivayukta*), there would be a reference to a nominal stem (*subanta*) similar to a prefix, the repeated mention of *sub* in the rule *supo dhātuprātipadikayoḥ* (Pāṇini 2.4.71) would be redundant, because this very term *anupasarga* would already be carried over (*anuvṛtti*) into that rule.
Therefore, the previously stated meaning alone is correct:

"for the sake of restriction" (*niyamārtham*) means that [the suffix] should apply only after a verb root that lacks a prefix (*anupasarga*), and not after those with prefixes (*sopasarga*). "After *car*" (*careḥ*), and so forth.
This [rule] is for the purpose of including the prefix (*upasarga*): namely, that which occurs when the root *car* has *āṅ* as its upapada, provided that "heavy" (*aguru*) is not denoted.

However, since this is established by the very fact of the *jñāpaka* (indicative evidence), it need not be stated as a separate supplement (*upasaṃkhyeya*). For this reason, he formulates [the rule] beginning with *sammānanotsañjanācāryakaraṇa* (Pāṇini 1.3.36); from this it is known that [the suffix] occurs after *car* with *āṅ* when "heavy" is not denoted.
In the expression "the teacher (*ācārya*) is the country," the meaning is that it is a place to be traveled to.

"Guru" means the initiator (*upanetā*). Regarding the word "avadyam": when the prefix *nañ* is used as an upapada with the root *vad*, the suffix *yat* is prescribed by rule 3.1.106, which supersedes the application of both *yat* and *kyap*; thus, *yat* alone is substituted here. Regarding "anudyam": [the same applies].
There is *saṃprasāraṇa* because [the root] belongs to the *yajādi* group; then, by the rules [Pāṇini 6.1.73 and 6.1.74], the augment *nuṭ* is applied. Regarding the form *paṇyam*:
although the suffix *ṇyat* would have been expected after the root *paṇ* in the sense of "commercial transaction," the form is here established as an irregular derivation (*nipātana*).
"Pāṇyam" means that which is to be praised. Regarding "varyā," although the suffix *ṇyat* would have been expected from the root *vṛ*, it is here prescribed as *yan*.
By the word "in the feminine" (*striyām*), he shows that the indication of gender (*liṅganirdeśa*) in the sūtra is intended as a pervasive rule (*tantrata*).
By the phrase "non-obstruction" (*apratibandhaḥ*),
he explains the meaning of the term "non-suppression" (*anirodha*).
"Absence of obstruction" means the absence of a blow against its expansion.
Regarding the word "by means of activity" (*vṛttyā*),
it refers to that which is to be suppressed.
The meaning is that its outward flow must be obstructed.
And this form is derived from the root *vṛñ* by applying the suffix *kyap* according to Pāṇini 3.1.109 (*eti-stu-śāsa-kyap*) and then adding the augment *tuk* according to 6.1.71;
thus we have "the officiating priests are to be warded off" (*vāryā ṛtvijaḥ*).

This is the form of the root *vṛñ*. Since there is no prohibition against the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) being shared with wealth, the feminine gender does not apply; therefore, only the suffix *ṇyat* occurs.

Is it not the case that [the suffix] *kyap* should apply here by the rule *eti-stu-śāsvṛ-* [Pāṇini 3.1.109]? This is not so; for in that rule, *vṛñ* (the root meaning "to choose") is what is intended to be included, whereas here the example is from *vṛṅ* (the root meaning "to choose" as a verb). Regarding the phrase "it must be stated" (*vaktavyam*), the meaning is "it must be explained.

In this regard, the explanation is as follows: two words meaning "desirable" (*artha*) are pronounced here by means of *tantra* (simultaneous application); one is ādyudātta (accented on the first syllable), and the other is antodātta (accented on the final syllable).

That which has the udātta accent on the first syllable is applied [as a substitute] for *vaiśyā*; the other, however, is for *svāminī*. Regarding the term *kālyā*, meaning "one whose time has arrived": while the rule [Pāṇini 5.1.104] is being supplied, [the suffix] *yat* is applied by [Pāṇini 5.1.107].
*Prajana* means "procreation"; the suffix *ghañ* is used in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāva*), and there is a prohibition of *vṛddhi* by [Pāṇini 7.3.35].
"Upasāryā" means "to be approached. Regarding "jīryate," [it is derived from] the roots *jṛṣ* and *jhṛṣ*, meaning "the loss of vitality" (*vayohānau*). (Dhātupāṭha 1130, 1131).
Regarding the term *saṅgamana*: *saṅgamana* means *saṅgati* (conjunction).
[The suffix] *lyuṭ* is applied according to [Pāṇini 3.3.115].
By this, he indicates that in the word *saṃtam*, the suffix *yat* is applied by [Pāṇini 3.3.114].
It is stated that "the suffix *yat* is introduced as an irregular formation (*nipātana*) when the agent is the meaning.
This is an exception (*apavāda*) to the suffixes *tṛc* and others.

Regarding the term *ajaritā*: this is a triplet (*tṛc*). [The commentary states: "The phrase 'not preceded by a prefix' (*anupasarga*) is understood [to carry over]. Now, one might object: in the rule *satsūdviṣa* (Pāṇini 3.2.61) and others, he will state that this mention of "prefix" (*upasarga*) is for the purpose of providing a technical indication (*jñāpaka*), namely, that elsewhere when there is a mention of "sup" (case endings), the mention of "prefix" does not apply. And so, by that very indication, it will not apply in the case of a prefix; why then is there the need here for the continued application of the mention of "not preceded by a prefix"? Some say it is for the sake of clarity.

In that regard, others maintain that the mention of the prefix (*upasarga*) is for the purpose of restriction (*niyama*), or that it should be understood here as not including a prefix (*anupasarga*) in order to show an option (*vikalpa*).
"Brāhmaṇodyam" means the speaking of a Brāhmaṇa.

The suffix *kyap* is applied in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāva*); as before, there is vocalization (*saṃprasāraṇa*) according to [Pāṇini 6.1.87], followed by a compound with an upapada. As for the statement "but that which does not carry over," it is because it was not drawn forward from the preceding rule. An example is: *brāhmaṇyam gataḥ* ("he has attained the state of a Brahmin").

The meaning is that he has attained the state of a Brahmin (*brāhmaṇatva*). Now, one might object: since [the suffix] *kta* is prescribed for the abstract state (*bhāva*) and the object (*karman*) by [Pāṇini 3.4.70], and the term "without a prefix" (*anupasarga*) is understood to carry over [from the previous rule], and since the verb *bhū* is intransitive when without a prefix, it follows by implication that [the suffix] will apply only to the abstract state and not to the object; so what is the purpose of explicitly mentioning "the abstract state" (*bhāva*)? To this he replies: "The mention of 'the abstract state' is for the sake of subsequent rules. By this, he indicates its utility in [the rule] *Pāṇini 3.1.108*: so that [the suffix] may apply only to the abstract state in that context.

Regarding the word *bhavyam*: by the rule *aco yat* [Pāṇini 3.1.97], the suffix *yat* is applied; then, by the rule *dhātorguṇaḥ* [Pāṇini 6.1.80], guṇa is substituted for the vowel, and *av* is the resulting substitute. Regarding *brāhṛhatyā*:
the meaning is "the killing of a Brāhmaṇa."
Regarding the word "dhātaḥ":
as before, this refers to the state of being a primary element (*tatvakatva*).
Why, then, is the *ghañ* suffix cited as a counter-example rather than the *ṇyat* suffix? To this he says: "But the *ṇyat*," and so forth.

He states the reasoning for that very point: "Because it cannot be denoted. For *kṛt*, *taddhita*, and *samāsa* suffixes are characterized by denotation (*abhidhāna*), yet the state (*bhāva*) cannot be denoted by the *ṇyat* suffix prescribed after the root *han*.

To explain: when *dhātya* is uttered, only the object (*karman*) is understood, not the state. Regarding the word *śiṣya*: [the root] *śās* is used in the sense of "instruction" (Dhātupāṭha 1075). By the rule *śāsa idaṅahaloḥ* [Pāṇini 6.4.34], there is the substitution of *i* for the final vowel; and by the rule *śāsivasi* [Pāṇini 8.3.60], there is the substitution of *ṣ* for *s*.
Regarding "ādṛtyaḥ":
the root *dṛṅ* meaning "to respect" (Dhātupāṭha 1141) is preceded by the prefix *āṅ*.
Regarding "juṣyaḥ": [it is derived from the root *juṣ*].
The root *juṣ* (in the Dhātupāṭha, no. 1288) means "to take pleasure in" and "to serve.
Now, for what purpose is the mention of *kyap*, given that the mention of *kyap* continues from [Pāṇini 3.1.106]? To this he says: "While *kyap* is being carried over," and so forth.
It is "for the purpose of subverting a sublater."
To clarify this, he says: "orāvaśyake" (after a root ending in *u* or *ṛ*, the suffix *kyap* is used when necessity is intended).

The scope for the application of [the suffix] *stun* (*stutya*) is where necessity is not intended to be expressed—as in *stutya*. The scope for [the suffix] *ṇyat* (as in Pāṇini 3.1.125) is another verbal root—as in *avaśyalāvyam*. Here, both would apply—as in *avaśyastutya*; however, because it is subsequent in the order of rules, *ṇyat* would be the sublater. But because of the repeated mention of *kyap*, even that is set aside and *kyap* occurs.
"By the mention of *vṛ*, the inclusion of the root *vṛñ* (to choose) is intended, not that of *vṛṅ* (to choose as a bride).

How so? From the rule *kṛṣirajoḥ* [Pāṇini 3.1.90] onwards, the mention of the *parasmaipada* (active voice) continues here; by this, the word *vṛ* is qualified—namely, "the word *vṛ* which belongs to the *parasmaipada*. And which is the word *vṛ* of the *parasmaipada*? That for which the status of being a cause (*nimittabhāva*) toward the *parasmaipada* is observed.
That [suffix] is observed after the root *vṛñ* (to choose) when it is used in both voices (*ubhayapadin*), but not after *vṛṅ* (to choose); for the latter is invariably middle-voiced (*ātmanepada*).

Therefore, the reference is only to *vṛñ* and not to *vṛṅ*. Regarding the rule beginning with "śaṃsi-duhi" and so forth, the meaning is that this must be explained as having the sense that the suffix *kyap* optionally occurs after these roots, beginning with *śaṃs*.
The explanation, however, should be made by relying on that very mention of the word *bahula* (in Pāṇini 3.3.113).
Regarding the form *śasyam*: it is derived from the root *śaṃsu* (meaning "to praise," Dhātupāṭha 728); the elision of the nasal [of the root] occurs according to [Pāṇini 6.4.24], *aniditām*.
Regarding the word *guhra*: [it is derived from] *guhū* "to conceal" (Dhātupāṭha 896). [The rule] beginning with *añjeḥ saṃpūrvād guhaśca* (Pāṇini 3.1.48) applies.
The meaning of the term *upasaṃkhyāna* is "an additional statement" (*pratipādana*).
And that [derivation] is as before.
[The root] *añj* is used in the senses of manifestation, wandering, beauty, and motion (Dhātupāṭha 1458).
As before, there is the elision of the nasal (*n*).

And this is a designation for clarified butter (*sarpiṣ*). The question—"How is it to be approached?"—is asked by one who considers that this form belongs to the root *iṇ*. [The answer is: "This form belongs to the root *īṅ*."

The form [of *upeyam*] arises from the root *iṅ* in the sense of "motion" (Dhātupāṭha 1143) when the suffix *yat* is applied according to Pāṇini 3.1.97 (*aco yat*), and not from the root *iṇ*. For if the suffix *kyap* were applied to *iṇ*, the form would have to be *upetavyam*. Regarding the phrase "excluding *kḷp* and *cṛt*":
this means excluding the roots *kṛpū* in the sense of "capability" (Dhātupāṭha 762) and *cṛtī* in the sense of "injury and binding" (Dhātupāṭha 1324).
Because the substitution of *l* for *r* is not established (*asiddha*), the root has *ṛ* as its penultimate vowel.
Regarding the form "kalpyam":
because the substitution of *l* for *r* is not established, the *guṇa* substitute *ā* applies to the *ṛ*-vowel itself.

It becomes *ṇyat*—that is, *kīrttyam*. When there is the intention to express an *ārdhadhātuka* suffix, after the elision of the *ṇic* affix by [Pāṇini 6.4.51], the status of ending in a consonant (*halanta*) arises; therefore, by [Pāṇini 3.1.124], it becomes *ṇyat* alone.
The lengthening occurs by [Pāṇini 8.2.77].

But has it not been stated that the purpose of including the mention of *ac* in [Pāṇini 3.1.97] *aco yat* is so that the suffix *yat* may apply even after a root that was previously vowel-ending, as in *ditsyam* and *dhitsyam*; and if that is so, should not *yat* likewise apply here after the causative (*ṇic*)? If this is the case, then since the *cur*-class roots are not invariably accompanied by *ṇic*, the suffix *ṇyat* occurs here after the non-causative form itself, and thus there is no fault. "It should be stated" (*vaktavyaḥ*) means it should be explained.

The explanation is as before. It should be rubbed with both hands; [the compound] *pāṇisargyā rajjuḥ* is a compound formed by *upapadam atiṅ* (Pāṇini 2.2.19). [The suffix *yat* is applied] by the rule *samavapūrvācca*.
The word *sṛji* is connected with the suffix *ṇyat*.

The particle *ca* is used for conjunction (*samuccaye*). It is not only when *pāṇi* is the upapada that *ṇyat* is to be stated; rather, it is also [to be applied] after [the root] preceded by *samava*. Regarding the form *kheyam*: the root *khanu* (Dhātupāṭha 878) means "digging" (*avadāraṇe*); the letter *n* is replaced by *ī*, according to Pāṇini 6.1.87.

Now, for what purpose is the long vowel (*dīrgha*) prescribed, since even if a short vowel (*hrasva*) were prescribed, the *guṇa* substitution would still occur by the rule *ādguṇaḥ*? And when the *guṇa* is applied to the short vowel, is there not some distinction [in the result]? It might be argued as follows: "The single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) must be declared to be non-existent (*asiddha*) with respect to the application of the augment *tuk*. In that case, if a short vowel were prescribed, then once the *guṇa* has been applied to the short vowel, the *tuk* would be based on the short vowel because it is non-existent with respect to the application of *tuk*; but if the long vowel is prescribed, it does not occur. Therefore, the prescription of the long vowel must be stated. But this is not so.

Since this substitution [of *i* for *ī*] occurring at the end of one word and the beginning of another must be stated as being "unestablished" (*asiddha*) for the application of the rule regarding the *tu*-augment, but not in all cases, he says: "The mention of the long vowel.
Why, then, is there a mention of the long vowel so that there may be a contraction (*praśleṣa*) of two *i*-vowels by means of the "long vowel of homogeneous phonemes" (Pāṇini 6.1.101)?
Why, moreover, is a second *i*-vowel mentioned, when the form *kheya-* would be established even with only one? To this he says: "In that case," and so forth.

The two *i*-sounds are taught here by means of a conjunctive reading (*praśleṣa*). In that context, the purpose of the second *i*-sound is so that the substitution of *āt* (long *ā*)—as prescribed by [Pāṇini 6.4.109] *ye ca*—may take effect as an exception to [the rule at 6.4.62]. The scope of [6.4.62] is, for example, *khāyate*, *khanyate*, *isi*; whereas the scope of this substitute (*asya* = *āt*) is that case where the substitution of *āt* does not occur. However, in the alternative where the substitution of *āt* does occur, both rules would apply simultaneously.

When both [rules] would apply simultaneously, the substitution of *ā* (āttva) would occur because it is internal (*antaraṅga*) and because it is taught [in a rule] that precedes [the other]. And when this [substitution of *ā*] exists, the substitution of *i* (ittva) occurs only after having set aside the substitution of *ā*.
Furthermore, the substitution of *ā* is internal because it is prescribed by relying on the generality of the suffix *kyap*;
the substitution of *i* is external because it is prescribed by relying on the specific [form of the] suffix *kyap*. [The meaning is: "they are to be supported."
By this, demonstrating that the word *bhṛtya* is a verbal noun (*kriyāśabda*), he refutes its status as a technical term (*saṃjñāśabda*).

Regarding the rule "after [the prefix] *sam*, optionally" (*saṃpūrvād vibhāṣā*): this option applies only when it is not a technical term; for otherwise, the suffix *kyap* would have been invariably applicable, and thus this would merely be an option for that which was already invariably prescribed.

This is obtained because the term *vibhāṣā* (optionally) which is to be stated hereafter serves as a supplement (*śeṣa*) to both rules, and because of the understanding that the option is not restricted (*avyavasthita-vibhāṣā*). [The rule] begins with "in the masculine, when it is a name" (*saṃjñāyāṃ puṃsi*).
The remainder of the sense is that this is a prohibition of the [previous] non-name (*asaṃjñā*) case.
By this, he states that the prohibition has its purpose fulfilled in the masculine: since the prohibition is thus fulfilled in the masculine, therefore the form *te-bhāryā* is not established.
The meaning is that, according to your opinion as the author of the Sūtra, the word *bhāryā* would not be established;
for if the prohibition [of the suffix *kyap*] were effective only with respect to the masculine, then *kyap* ought to occur in the feminine.

But surely it is said, "in the sense of a name (*saṃjñā*)," and the word *bhāryā* is a word denoting a name; for even when Devadatta is not supporting her, his wife is still called *bhāryā*. So how can there be the application of the suffix *kyap* here? We do not say that *kyap* must occur by this rule; rather, [it occurs] by the rule *saṃjñāyāṃ samajaniṣada-* (Pāṇini 3.3.99). To this, he gives the answer: "In the feminine, there is the scope for the abstract state (*bhāva*).

By the term "scope for the abstract state" (*bhāvādhikāra*), what is intended here is the operation characterized by the attainment of the status of being the expressed meaning (*abhidheya*) of the abstract state (*bhāva*); it does not, however, refer to a formal "heading" (*adhikāra*) within the technical system of the grammar.

In the section on feminine nouns (*striyām*), when the suffix *kyap* is prescribed by rules such as *saṃjñāyāṃ samajaniṣada* [Pāṇini 3.3.99], there is an extension of the jurisdiction of the *bhāva* (action/state); this is due to the inherent nature of the expressive power of words.
In that context, the *kyap* being prescribed applies only to the *bhāva*, not to the *karman* (object).
Thus, the form *bhāryā* is established.
The intention is that [the suffix] applies to the object (*karman*), because the feminine gender has jurisdiction over the abstract state (*bhāva*).
It is the abstract state alone that functions as the expressed meaning, not the object; therefore, the word *bhāryā* is established in the sense of the object.
For in the section on abstract nouns (*bhāva*), the suffix *kyap* must indeed apply to express the abstract state;

however, to express the object (*karman*), only the suffix *ṇyat* applies. This is an optional rule (*prāptavibhāṣā*) because *kyap* is prescribed by the rule "after a root ending in short *ṛ*, except for *kḷp* and *cṛt*" (Pāṇini 3.1.110).
Regarding "parimārgyaḥ": as before, there is the substitution of *k* for *g*, and by [Pāṇini 7.2.114], there is the *vṛddhi* strengthening of the root *gṛ*. Regarding "rājñā sotavyaḥ":

this shows that, due to a specific syntactic rule, there is an irregular formation (*nipātana*) when the word ending in the third case, "rājñā" (by the king), is the attendant word (*upapada*) and the object (*karman*) is expressed.

By the rule "rājā veha sūyate," even when the word *rājan* ending in the nominative case functions as the locus (*adhikaraṇa*), this is a formal irregularity (*nipātana*). From the root *ṣuñ* meaning "to press" (Dhātupāṭha 1247), the suffix *kyap* is applied;
therein, the absence of the *tuk*-augment and the lengthening of the vowel are both treated as irregularities.
Regarding the term *sūsartibhyām*:

from the roots *ṣū* (meaning "to impel," Dhātupāṭha 1408) and *sṛ* (meaning "to go," Dhātupāṭha 935), when the suffix *yat* would [otherwise] apply by [Pāṇini 3.1.97] *aco yat*, and the suffix *ṇyat* would apply by [Pāṇini 3.1.124] *ṛhaloṇryat*, the suffix *kyap* is prescribed as an irregular formation (*nipātana*).
Thus, [the form] *sūḥ* is derived from the sense of "he impels" (*suvati*).
Regarding action:
because he impels the worlds toward what is to be done,
when he has been praised, the activity of the world proceeds.
Regarding the phrase "when a pause (yati) occurs within a pāda," this refers to the rule [Pāṇini 8.1.106].
*Mṛṣāvādanam* means false speech (*mṛṣodyam*).
*kyap*, with *samprasāraṇa*; [this forms] a *upapada* compound.
By showing the meaning as "he pleases" (*rocate'sau*) through a suffix denoting the agent (*kartṛ*), he demonstrates that this is an irregular formation (*nipātana*) in the sense of the agent.
When suffixes beginning with *tṛc* would otherwise apply, the suffix *kyap* is prescribed as an irregularity (*nipātana*).

Regarding the rule "of *gup*" (*gupeḥ*): this refers either to the root *gup* in the sense of "concealing" (*gupa gopane*, Dhātupāṭha 970) or to the root *gup* in the sense of "protecting" (*gupū rakṣaṇe*, Dhātupāṭha 395).

Regarding the term *avyaya*: from the root *vyai* (listed as 764 in the Dhātupāṭha, meaning "fear" and "movement"), the suffix *kyap*—which is an exception to [the suffix] *tṛc* when used in the sense of the agent—is applied by way of irregular derivation (*nipātana*). Regarding *ujjheśca*: from the root *ujjh* (listed as 1304 in the Dhātupāṭha, meaning "to abandon").

"The suffix *kyap* is irregularly applied in the sense of the agent (*kartari*). This is an exception (*apavāda*) to [the application of] the suffixes *tṛc* and others. Regarding the statement "from the roots *puṣ* and *siddh*":
*puṣa* is [listed in the Dhātupāṭha as] "to nourish" (1182); *ṣidhu* is [listed as] "to be accomplished" (1192).
"The suffix *kyap* is prescribed [after the root] in the sense of location (*adhikaraṇe*). This is an exception (*apavāda*) to the suffix *lyuṭ*. "From the root *pav-* preceded by the prefix *vi-*.
[The root is] *paṅ* "to purify" (Dhātupāṭha 966).
Regarding the phrase "and of the root *nī*":
this refers back to [the condition] "preceded by *vi*.
Regarding the phrase "when *yat* would otherwise have been obtained": this refers to the same.
Because all three [words] end in a suffix that lacks a *vikaraṇa*:
*vipūya* is that which is putrefied;
*vinīya* is that which is led away, i.e., that which has attained completion.

A specific medicinal preparation prepared with oil or ghee combined with substances such as the three myrobalans (*triphalā*) and others is called a *kalka*. That which is to be conquered is "conquerable" (*jitya*). *Bṛhadbala* means *hali* (the plough). Regarding the word "pratigṛhya":

The semivowel substitution (*saṃprasāraṇa*) is applied by the rule *grahijyā* [Pāṇini 6.1.16], and the compound is formed according to *iti* [Pāṇini 2.2.18]. Regarding the term *asvairī*: the root *īr* (meaning "to go" and "to move," according to the Dhātupāṭha, no.
1018) is used here; the suffix *ṇini* is added in the sense of habitual action (*tācchīlika*) to form the word for one whose nature (*śīla*) is to be moved or to go by oneself (*svayam*).
By way of irregular derivation (*nipātana*), there is a vṛddhi [strengthening] of the vowel: *svairī* means "independent. One who is not independent is called *asvairī*.
[The term applies] "to the arms," etc.
The meaning is "in that which has become external.

The suffix *yañ* is applied according to the supplementary rule (*upasaṃkhyāna*) "and there is the elision of the sixth case-ending after *bahiṣ*," and in that case, there is the elision of the *ṭi* portion.
[This refers to the phrase] "and in the sense of 'to be included' (*pakṣye cārthe*)."
The word *pakṣya* denotes a group (*varga*).
It means "that which exists in a side" (*pakṣe bhavaḥ*), derived with the suffix *yat* according to the rule for the *dig-ādi* group.

"Pragṛhya" means a word that is not joined [with the following one]. Here, the meaning of the root *grah* (to seize) is "non-proximity. For vowels are not brought into proximity—that is, they are not placed in close contact—therefore it is called "non-proximity" (*asannikarṣa*).
"Avagṛhṇanti" means "they pause. Regarding the statement "for which an avagraha is made," therein,
within a compound word (*samudāyapada*), the constituent words (*avayavapada*) are variously paused— that is, they are explained by being separated.
Because the constituent parts (*avayava*) are grasped therein, it is called *avagraha*. [The form] *gṛhakāḥ* is derived by adding the suffix *kan* according to Pāṇini 5.3.76.
"Those who have been seized" means those who are restrained or brought under another's control.
"Elsewhere" means...
In both the masculine and neuter genders:
"vāsudevagṛhrāḥ" is a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*). [The rule] "and after *vṛṣan*" [is also applied].

The roots *vṛṣu*, *pluṣu* (listed as 703 in the Dhātupāṭha, meaning "to burn"), and *mṛṣu* (listed as 706 and 707, meaning "to sprinkle") [are mentioned]. Regarding the word *pattram*: it is that by which things fall (*patanti anena*).
[The suffix] *ṣṭran* is applied according to the rule beginning with *dāmnīśasa* (Pāṇini 3.2.182).
Regarding the word *yugyam*: [it is derived from *yuj* with the suffix *kyap*].
The root *yuj* is listed as *yujiryoge* (Dhātupāṭha 1444).

Regarding the word *yugyam*: it means that which is to be joined (*yojanīya*) by a vehicle, such as a cow or similar animal; thus, it is called *yugyam*. As for the term *amāvasyat*, the utterance of the indicatory letter *t* (*takārānubandha*) is intended to indicate that this is a *nipātana* (irregular formation) ending in the suffix *ṇyat*, and not one ending in the suffix *kyap*; otherwise, since *kyap* is the suffix currently under discussion, one might suspect that this word ends in the suffix *kyap*.
Moreover, the suffix intended here is *ṇyat*, not *yat*; otherwise, the irregular formation (*nipātana*) would be purposeless.
For in the context of *yat*, one would simply have said "after *amāvasyā*, optionally" (*amāvaser anyatarasyām*).
Furthermore, there is a fault in the irregular formation ending in the suffix *yat*.
The fault will be revealed later.

Furthermore, whatever fault exists regarding the irregular derivation (*nipātana*) of a form ending in the suffix *yat*, that same fault would apply to the form ending in *kyap*, and the absence of *samprasāraṇa* would likewise result in it being treated as an irregular derivation. Therefore, considering this irregular derivation to end in the suffix *ṇyat*, he says: "The suffix *ṇyat* occurs when [the word] *kāla* functions as a locus (*adhikaraṇa*). By means of the principle of partial modification (*ekadeśavikṛta*), he demonstrates the merit of this irregular derivation ending in *ṇyat*.
Indeed, the word *amāvasyā* itself has been prescribed as an irregularity (*nipātita*) to prevent the occurrence of *vṛddhi*.
In this case, the word *amāvasyā* does not apply under the alternative where *vṛddhi* is absent.

Consequently, by the principle that "that which is modified in one part is not different [from the original]" (*ekadeśavikṛtamananyavat*), when the word *amāvasyā* is included, the word *amāvāsyā* is also included.

Therefore, while the rule *pūrvāhṇāparāhṇādrāmūlapradoṣāvaskārād vun* [Pāṇini 4.3.28] is being carried over, the suffixes *vun* and *aṇ* are prescribed for the word *amāvāsyā* by the rule [4.3.30], and thus they are established for the word *āmāvasyā* as well.
Regarding the phrase "from *amāvāsi*" and so forth:

although there is only one base (*prakṛti*), the dual number is used in the reference because a distinction is intended on the basis of the difference between its properties of undergoing vowel strengthening (*vṛddhi*) and not undergoing vowel strengthening.
By stating "designating the self as 'I'," he indicates that others act otherwise. The term "of the two with the suffix *ṇyat*" means "of those ending in the suffix *ṇyat*."
"I cause them to fall into non-increase";
the word "optionally" (*anyatarasyām*) is to be understood as the remainder [of the rule].
He asks what is established by this and says: "In that way, the two possess a single occurrence."
The phrase "is established" (*prasiddhyati*) is to be connected with what is about to be said.
In some places, the reading is *tathaikavṛttitām*;
in that case, it is to be connected with the contextually relevant term "I shall establish" (*nipātayāmi*).
And the meaning of "I cause to fall" is "I accomplish.
Regarding the word "of those two," it is a reference to the new moon days (amāvāsyā) and the days of the waning moon (amāvasyā).

Furthermore, "function" (vṛtti) refers to the production of the two suffixes vun and naṇ. Those two which possess an identical function are "single-functioned" (ekavṛttī); their state is "single-functionality" (ekavṛttitā).

That [state] is established by producing the suffix ṇyat and then, by means of a formal exception (nipātana), preventing the occurrence of vṛddhi therein; for that which is modified in one part remains non-different from the original.
"And my accent is perfected," as stated in [Pāṇini 6.1.185];
thus, the state of having the final syllable as *svarita* (circumflex) is intended.

Regarding the word "sidhyati" (it is established): for those who, however, apply the suffix *yat* to the root *vas* with the prefix *am-*, and—by virtue of the mention of the option (*anyatarasyām*)—desire the suffix *ṇyat* as an alternative, their form *amāvāsya-* is indeed established; nevertheless, the accent is not established under the *yat*-suffix alternative. For, by the rule [6.1.213], the substitution of *svarita* is set aside, and the initial acute (*ādyudāttatvam*) would result for the word *vasyā-*. Furthermore, even when a compound is formed with the word *amā*, and the natural accent (*prakṛtisvara*) of the final member ending in a *kṛt*-suffix is applied by [6.2.139], the word *vasyā-* itself would remain acutely accented on its first syllable.
An *anta-svarita* accent is desired [for this word].

Furthermore, the previously mentioned state of having a single function (*ekavṛttitā*) is not established, because they are distinct words. For one [form] ends in the suffix *-yat*, while the other ends in the suffix *-ṇyat*; thus, in the case of *-ṇyat*, the absence of *vṛddhi* is prescribed as a grammatical anomaly (*nipātana*). This refers to the phrase "when *kyap* would otherwise have applied."

Because it has a soft consonant (*ṛdupadha*) as its penultimate, the reversal of the initial and final [elements] applies; thus, by means of a *nipātana* (irregular prescription), the letter *k*, which was at the beginning, is treated as being at the end, and the letter *t*, which was at the end, is treated as being at the beginning.
Regarding the passage beginning with *hvayateḥ*:

when the suffix *kyap* is applied to the root *hveñ* (meaning "to contend," Dhātupāṭha 1008), there is vocalization (*samprasāraṇa*) because it belongs to the *yajādi* class [Pāṇini 6.1.15], and lengthening occurs by [Pāṇini] 6.4.2.
However, when it is derived from the root *hu* (meaning "to give" or "to take," Dhātupāṭha 1083), then the absence of the *tuk*-augment and the lengthening are treated as irregularities (*nipātana*).
*Devahūvaḥ* means that in this [place] the gods are invoked (*hūyante*).
Regarding *acchivyaḥ*, the *Kāśikā* states:
"from the root *śiṣlṛ*, meaning 'to distinguish' or 'to leave as a remnant' (*viśeṣaṇe-viśaraṇe*). (Dhātupāṭha 1451).
The letter *ch* [is substituted] by [Pāṇini 8.4.63], and the substitution of *ścutva* [for *c*] occurs by [Pāṇini 8.4.40]. [The rule states:
"the suffix *yat* follows these two. Since the word ends in the vowel *ṛ*, the suffix *ṇyat* would otherwise have been expected [by Pāṇini 3.1.124].
"The substitution [of *stṛ*] occurs only when the feminine gender is intended;
otherwise, the mention of the feminine form *staryā* would be purposeless.
Regarding the word "āpṛcchyaḥ":
There is vocalization (*samprasāraṇa*) by [Pāṇini 6.1.16].
In the case of *pratiṣīvyaḥ*, there is lengthening by [Pāṇini 8.2.77] *hali ca*. In the case of *vadeṇryat*, [the suffix is applied] by [Pāṇini 3.1.97] *vadeṇryat*.
Regarding the rule *kyap* [Pāṇini 3.1.106], when both [the suffixes] *kyap* and *yat* would apply, [we have] the forms *bhāvyaḥ* and *stāvyaḥ*.
These are formed with the suffix *ṇyat*, which is an exception (*apavāda*) to the suffix *yat* applied to the roots *bhū* and *stu*. [The examples] beginning with *niṣṭarkya* follow.
The two summary verses are for the purpose of facilitating easy comprehension.
Regarding the word "vyatyayam" (reversal):
it means the inversion of the beginning and the end.

Regarding the phrase "ṇyad ekasmāt": this ablative case ending (*pañcamī*) occurs due to the elision of a word ending in *lyap* (the gerund suffix). The suffix *ṇyat* is applied with reference to the single word *niṣṭarkya*.
The suffix *ṇyat* is applied in order to establish a single word; thus,
"from four, *kyap*"—
this fourth case ending is used in the sense of purpose (*tādarthya*).
Regarding the four suffixes beginning with *devahūya* mentioned immediately before, the suffix *kyap* occurs for their sake—that is, for the purpose of accomplishing them.

This is according to the rule: "The suffix *yat* is prescribed after [stems ending in] *catur* and *turi*. This dative case (*caturthī*) also expresses that very same sense of being for the sake of something (*tādarthya*).

Immediately following that, there are four boundary markers ending with *khānyaparyanta*; for their sake—that is, for the purpose of establishing them—the rule occurs: "after one [marker], the suffix *ṇac*.
In these cases as well, the ablative case is used in the sense of the object (*karman*) when there is an ellipsis of a *lyap*-ending verb.
The suffix *ṇyat* is applied with reference to the single word *khānya*;
that is to say, for the purpose of deriving the word *khānya*.
And [the rule states] "and the word *ya*."
The word "ekasmāt" (from one) is used for the purpose of attraction (*anukarṣaṇa*). The suffix *ya* occurs with reference to the word *devayajyā*. Thus, there are two instances of the suffix *kyap*.
Two *kyap* suffixes occur for the derivation of the words *āpṛcchya* and *pratīṣīvya*.
Regarding the rule "the prescription of *ṇyat* follows *cut*," the meaning is that the suffix *ṇyat* occurs four times.

Furthermore, that [suffix] occurs in the remaining cases, such as *brāhma* and so forth; or alternatively, by the rule "after one [other than those specified]," the meaning is "after a single verbal root.
Regarding the rule "the suffix *kyap* after four [roots]," it means that the suffix *kyap* occurs after four verbal roots.

But surely, the verbal root (*dhātu*) is nothing other than *nī*; so how can it be said "from four roots"? There is no fault here, for the intention is to express a distinction even within a single [root] due to the difference in prefixes (*upasarga*).
Regarding the rule "and after the four, there is the prescription of *yat*":
the meaning is that the prescription of *yat* occurs after those four immediately preceding roots.
"ṇyadekasmāt": the suffix ṇyat is prescribed after the single root *khana*. "And the word *ya*": [this refers to the fact that the suffix *ya* is also applied].
In the word *devayajyā*, the suffix *ya* occurs from a single verbal root.

Regarding the statement "there are two *kyap* suffixes," there are two instances of the *kyap* suffix derived from the roots *ā-prach* and *piṣ* for the sake of forming the words *āpṛcchya* and *pratiṣīvya*. The phrase "the genitive case is used in the sense of the ablative" [is applied here].
By this [sūtra], [Pāṇini 2.3.39] *it-tha-thas-iṣ-tha-ma-ktram*, [the suffix *ktram* is applied].

But for which ablative case (*pañcamī*) is the genitive (*ṣaṣṭhī*) used here? It is for the ablative characterized by connection with a direction (*digyoga*). For in the rule for the formation of suffixes (*pratyayavidhi*), there must be an ablative due to the connection [with the word] *paraśca* [Pāṇini 3.1.2]. "That which has necessity is 'necessary' (*āvaśyakam*)."
The suffix *vuñ* is applied because [the word] belongs to the *manojñādi* group.

This very fact is the indicator (*jñāpaka*) that the elision of the *ṭi* (the final vowel and following consonant) occurs for indeclinables (*avyaya*) when a nominal suffix (*bha*) follows in general.

In this context, two possibilities are considered: first, that it functions as an *upapada*, since the term *upapada* is used in its mandatory sense; and second, that it functions as an *upādhi* (a qualifying condition), since the term is used in its sense of indicating what is to be expressed (*dyotya*).

In that regard, if it were understood thus—that [the suffix] applies when the word *āvaśyaka* (necessity) is an *upapada*—then it would not apply when *āvaśyaka* is to be expressed without being an *upapada*, as in the examples *lāvyaṃ* and *pāvyam*. He says, "when *āvaśyaka* is to be expressed," so that it may be understood in this way;
and this is obtained through proximity (*pratyāsatti*).

For an *upādhi* (limiting condition) is internal (*antaraṅga*) because it is manifested by another suffix, whereas its connection with an *upapada* (governing word) is external (*bahiraṅga*), since the meaning of that [connection] is expressed by a different word.
Regarding the phrase "the impossibility of accent and compound":
when the *upapada* is necessarily understood, the compound occurs by the rule *upapadam atiṅ* [Pāṇini 2.2.19].

And since that [suffix] exists, by the rule *tasmai ca sati* (Pāṇini 6.2.139), there is the accent of the original form of the final member (*uttarapada-prakṛti-svara*) based on the subordinate word (*upapada*), and the accent of the *tit* suffix does not occur. However, in the view that [the suffix] merely indicates [the meaning], there would be no compound at all, because the defining condition (*lakṣaṇa*) for it is absent. Even if, somehow, there were a compound other than an *upapada-compound*, even so, the accent based on the *upapada-compound* would not occur; consequently, the accent of the *tit* suffix would not be obtained, as there would instead be the oxytone accent of the compound (*samāsāntodāttatva*).
Regarding "avaśyalāvyam":

there is the elision of the *m* in *avaśyam* according to the rule "lumpedavaśyamaḥ kṛtye" (Pāṇini 6.1.142). [The compound is formed] by virtue of its inclusion in the *mayūravyaṃsaka*-group, and so forth.
He shows that because the *mayūravyaṃsaka* group is an *ākṛtigaṇa*, forms such as *avaśyalāvyaprabhṛti* and *lāvyaprabhṛti* are to be understood therein.
He asks, "How is the accent? and says: "And when there is the original accent (*prakṛtisvara*) of the second member," and so forth.

In this regard, the effort is as follows: in the rule [Pāṇini 6.2.139], the word *ca* from [Pāṇini 6.2.135] will be carried over (*anuvarttiṣyate*), and it serves the purpose of inclusive conjunction (*samuccaya*) for what is not already mentioned (*anṛkta*).

Therefore, even in cases such as *avaśyalāvyam*, the accent of the verbal root (*prakṛtisvara*) occurs. Regarding the phrase "an exception to [the rule] beginning with *yata-*": this is because the roots *ṣṛñ* (in the sense of "pressing," DhP 1247) and *yu* (in the sense of "mixing," DhP 1033) end in *r*. Furthermore, the roots *ḍuvap* (in the sense of "sowing seeds or weaving threads," DhP 1003), *rapa* and *lapa* (in the sense of "distinct speech," DhP 401, 402), *trapūṣ* (in the sense of "shame," DhP 374), and *camu* (in the sense of "eating," DhP 469) possess a vowel in the penultimate position (*adupadhatva*) and end in the labial class (*pavargāntatva*).

Regarding the word *dābhya*: the root *dabh* exists as a distinct verbal base (*prakṛti*) not listed among the standard roots, similar to *culump*. Regarding the statement "the suffix *ṇyat* is introduced by nipātana":
this is said because the suffix *yat* would otherwise have been expected.

If [the suffix] *ghañ* were applied to the sense of "non-eternal," there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) to jars and other such things as well, because they too are non-eternal; thus he says, "conventional" (*rūḍhaḥ*), and so forth.

Even though a basis for application (*pravṛttinimitta*) exists, words that are conventional function only with respect to a specific object due to their restricted scope, not with respect to an unspecified one, like the word "peacock" (*mayūra*) and others.
For not every creature that cries out loudly is called a peacock, nor is every creature that moves called a cow (*go*); rather, it is only a specific kind of living being [to whom these names apply].
Therefore, this conventional term applies only to the *dakṣiṇāgni* fire and not to jars and the like.
Regarding the phrase "because it is never awake," the meaning is that it does not burn continuously.
For its very flaming is its state of being awake.
He says "And that which... and so forth, in order to show that even in the *dakṣiṇāgni* (southern fire), it remains specifically [in that form] and not everywhere.
But does it have a different source (*yoni*) by virtue of which it is thus distinguished? To this he says: "For of that... and so forth.

*Yoniḥ* means "the cause. By the words "because of its being of a different nature" (*vaiākṛtyāt*) and so forth, he demonstrates the various types of *yoni*. Regarding the phrase "if it is argued that what is not brought [into existence] is non-eternal," the remainder of the sense is: "this would then apply even to jars and the like."
"It would be performed in the *dakṣiṇāgni* fire.
Regarding this [term] *ānāyya*, the grammatical derivation (*nipātana*) is made specifically for the *dakṣiṇāgni* fire and not elsewhere.
The optative suffix (*liṅ*) is used here in the sense of possibility (*sambhāvanā*).
The meaning is that this is possible, and not otherwise.
Regarding the phrase "and one should know him as having a single source":
having brought that [fire] denoted by the term *āhārya*, one should know—that is, recognize—it as being in the *dakṣiṇāgni* (southern fire), which shares a single source with the *āhavanīya*.

The word *ca* is used for emphasis—meaning "only in the case of a single origin. [This is illustrated by the rule] "otherwise, it would be *āneya*. In the case of impermanent things such as a jar, or in the case of the *dakṣiṇāgni* fire which has a different origin than the *āhavanīya* fire, when the suffix *yat* is applied according to Pāṇini 3.1.97 (*aco yat*), the form becomes simply *āneya*. By the specific compound *avidyamānā sammatiḥ*, he demonstrates that this is a *bahuvrīhi* and thereby dispels the suspicion that it might be a *tatpuruṣa*. He explains: "*sammatiḥ* means the state of being agreed upon (*sammatatā*)."
"Consensually approved" (*sammata*) means "honored" (*pūjita*).
The state of being consensually approved is "consensual approval" (*sammatatā*).
By this term *sammati*, he shows that what is denoted here is that which is honored. "If this is so," and so forth.
Furthermore, since honor is absent in a thief and the like, the application of the word *praṇāyya* to a pupil (*antevāsī*) would not be appropriate;
for the intention is certainly not that honor is non-existent in a pupil. In the phrase "he should recite the *Brāhma*," the word *brāhma* here refers to the Veda.
"Consent is also called longing"—
by the word "also," he shows that it is not merely worship.
"By the absence of that."

"By the absence of longing" means "by being free from desire"; the meaning is: by being devoid of the longing for the enjoyment of worldly objects. Regarding the term "pāyya": [the rule] *āto yuK* (Pāṇini 3.1.97) applies; it is used in the sense of specific sacrificial offerings (*havirviśeṣa*).
Wherever this [term] is established, it remains right there;
it does not apply to every mere oblation.
Thus [it is said]: "the *dhāyyā*."
As before, it is joined [with the word *yuk*]:
"the designator of a specific *ṛc*.
Not all *ṛcs* are denoted by the word *sāmidhenī*; rather, what is meant is the mantra for placing the fuel sticks (*samid-ādhāna*).
For instance, the word *sāmidhenī* is derived within the mantra for placing the fuel-sticks (*samid-ādhāna*).

Furthermore, not every *ṛc* verse is designated as a *sāmidhenī*; rather, he says "In that [context]" and so forth, showing that only a specific one is so called. But how can a general grammatical rule of derivation (*nipātana*) be restricted to a particular case? To this he replies: "The word *dhāyyā* is a conventional term (*rūḍhiśabda*). The word *dhāyyā* is a conventional term denoting a specific type of *ṛc*.
That very [meaning] is expressed by this [term], and no other.
How, then, is it known that this is a conventional (rūḍhi) word? To this he says: "And thus," and so forth.

If this were not a conventional word, then because it is prescribed as a nipātana-form in the *sāmidhenī* verses, it would not be seen in the specific sense of a *ṛc* verse in the passage "one should recite the *dhāyyās*"; yet it is indeed seen there.
Therefore, it is determined that this is a conventional term (*rūḍhiśabda*).

If, however, it is also seen in the context of the *sāmidhenī* verses, would the mention of *sāmidhenī* not be redundant? It is not redundant; for its purpose is to indicate a specific conventional usage. Regarding the word "from the root *pibati*":
[it refers to] *pā pāne* (Dhātupāṭha 925).
Regarding the rule "the suffix *yat* is used in the sense of an action (*adhikaraṇe*)":

since the suffix *lyuṭ* would otherwise be expected, what is the reason for deriving the word *kuṇḍapāyya* with the suffix *yat*, rather than using *ṇyat*? To this he replies: "Because [if it were formed with *ṇyat*], the accent would be governed by the rule 'yato ’nāvaḥ'."
If it ended in the suffix *pratyaya*, there would be acute accent (*udātta*) on the first syllable of the second member of the compound;
if it ended in the suffix *ṇyat*, there would be circumflex accent (*svarita*) on the final syllable—
as in *kuṇḍapānam*.

In cases other than when *kratu* is the object, only the suffix *lyuṭ* occurs. Regarding the rule "after *vah* preceded by *sam*" and so forth: since the root ends in a consonant, the suffix *ṇyat* would indeed be established [by P. 3.1.124]; however, if that were applied, vocalization (*samprasāraṇa*) would not occur because the suffix is not marked with *k*.

Even if vocalization were applied after *ṇyat*, lengthening by P. 6.4.2 (*halaḥ*) would not apply; for that rule prescribes lengthening of a stem whose final vowel is preceded by a consonant belonging to a part of the stem (*aṅga*) from which the vocalization follows. This case does not conform to that pattern; therefore, both [the suffix and the vocalization] are prescribed as a formal anomaly (*nipātana*).
The suffix *ṇyat*, prescribed as a general rule, does not suffice for the root *ūh* preceded by the prefix *sam*.

It is so that *ṇyat* applies only to the root *vah* preceded by *sam* when the object is fire (*agni*), but it should not apply here in the case of "a Brāhmaṇa who is to be carried together" (*saṃvoḍhavyo brāhmaṇaḥ*). [Therefore, the rule is stated: "By this, the word becomes oxytone.
For when a word ending in the suffix *yat* is thus prescribed, the word as a whole becomes oxytone by the accent of the suffix itself.
If the suffix *ṇyat* were present, however, the accent would be *svarita* due to the rule regarding *tit*.

Therefore, the intention is that the suffix *ya* is prescribed as an irregularity (*nipātana*), setting aside the original [suffix]. As for the statement, "The letter *ca* is for the sake of including the general term," etc., it means that there should be an inclusion of both *tṛc* and *tṛn* as a general category.

If that [term *niranubandhakaraṇa*] were not present, then according to the rule "when there is no mention of a suffix with an *anubandha*, there is no inclusion of one with an *anubandha*" (Vyāḍiparibhāṣā 53), there would be no inclusion of the suffix *tṛn*.

Now, why is it not for the sake of making the final syllable udātta? Because that is already established by the accent of the suffix itself (*pratyayasvara*). He says "each individually" and so forth, so that through proximity (*pratyāsatti*) the word "beginning with" might not be understood as connected only with the root *pac*; hence he says "nandi-vāśi" and so forth.

From these verbal roots— *naṃdi* in the sense of "prosperity" (Dhātupāṭha 67), *vāśṛ* in the sense of "sound" (Dhātupāṭha 1163), *madī* in the sense of "joy" (Dhātupāṭha 1208), *duṣa* in the sense of "corruption" (Dhātupāṭha 1185), *rādha* and *sādha* in the sense of "accomplishment" (Dhātupāṭha 1262, 1263), *śubha* and *śumbha* in the sense of "beauty" (Dhātupāṭha 1321, 1322), and *ruca* in the sense of "splendor" (Dhātupāṭha 745)— the suffix *lyu* occurs when they are causative (*ṇic*-formed) and a name (*saṃjñā*) is to be expressed.
Examples include *nandana* from *nandayati*, and so forth.

Regarding the term *dūṣaṇam*: by [Pāṇini 6.4.90], the substitution of *ū* occurs. However, for these roots when they do not end in the causative suffix *ṇic*, only suffixes such as *tṛc* and others are used, whether in non-technical (*asaṃjñā*) or technical (*saṃjñā*) senses.

The very purpose of including *graha* and so forth, as well as *nandi* and so forth, in the list (gaṇa) is this: that their grammatical correctness (*sādhutva*) should be established specifically within the domain of technical names (*saṃjñā*).
Otherwise, one would have merely listed the roots themselves in the list, and then, having indicated them here by means of the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), one would have prescribed the suffix.
[This is shown in the rule] "sahitapi" and so on.

From the roots *ṣaha* in the sense of "endurance" (Dhātupāṭha 1809), *tap* in the sense of "tormenting" (Dhātupāṭha 985), and *damu* in the sense of "pacification" (Dhātupāṭha 1203)—from these, when used in the non-causative (*aṇ*) form and employed as proper names (*saṃjñā*), the suffix *lyu* is applied. Examples include *jalpanaḥ*, and so forth.

The roots *jap* and *jalp* mean "articulate speech" (Dhātupāṭha 397, 398); *ram* means "play" (Dhātupāṭha 853); *dṛp* [according to the Dhātupāṭha, it means] "exultation and delusion" (Dhātupāṭha 1196), specifically "gladdening and releasing"; *kad* and *krad* mean "calling out and weeping" (Dhātupāṭha 70, 71); *kṛṣ* means "scratching" (Dhātupāṭha 990); *hṛṣ* means "to rejoice" (Dhātupāṭha 709); and *ard* means "to injure" (Dhātupāṭha 1828). One who injures (*ardayati*) people (*jana*) is Janārdana;
although the suffix *aṇ* would have been expected by rule, the suffix *lyu* (forming *-ana*) is used here.

The root *yu* (in the sense of "mixing" and "not mixing"—*dhātupāṭha* 1033) and *ṣūda* (in the sense of "flowing"—*dhātupāṭha* 1717). [The term] *madhusūdanaḥ* means "one who causes the honey to flow.
Here too, although the suffix *aṇ* would have been expected after an object (*karman*), the suffix *lyu* is used. The root *ñibhī* (in the sense of "fear"—*dhātupāṭha* 1084).

The suffix *ṇic* is applied by [Pāṇini 3.1.26]; [the form] "lavaṇaḥ" is derived from the root *lūñ* "to cut" (Dhātupāṭha 1483) by means of irregular derivation (*nipātana*). The substitution of *ṇ* for *n* occurs through irregular derivation.

The inclusion of *kṛtaṇatva* in the list [of *gaṇas*] is a grammatical irregularity (*nipātana*). The root *ṇaś* (meaning "to disappear," DhP 1194) preceded by the prefix *vi-* and the root *dam* (meaning "to subdue," DhP 1203)—both of these being followed by the causative suffix *ṇic*—form the compound *vittavināśana*. [Thus, it means] one who destroys wealth (*vitta*).

*Kuladamana* means "one who subdues a family. The short vowel [in *damana*] is applied by the rule *mitāṃ hrasvaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.4.92). Although the suffix *aṇ* would have been expected after the object [of the action], the suffix *lyu* (which becomes *-ana*) is used instead. Regarding *graha* and so forth:
*graha* is "to seize" (Dhātupāṭha 1533); *ṣaha* is "to endure" (Dhātupāṭha 1809), preceded by the prefix *ut*.
The root *tasu* (in the sense of "throwing," Dhātupāṭha 1212) and *dasu* (Dhātupāṭha 1213); like *das*, the former [root] takes the augment *puk*.
The root *bhas* (in the sense of "scolding" and "shining," Dhātupāṭha 1100) is preceded by the prefix *ut*.
The root *sthā* (in the sense of "cessation of motion," Dhātupāṭha 928) takes the suffix *yuk* according to Pāṇini 7.3.33.
The root *sthā* is [the base for] *sthāyī*.
The root *matri*—according to the Dhātupāṭha (*guptaparibhāṣaṇe*, Dhātupāṭha 1679)—means "to speak secretly," and it takes the suffix *ṇic* belonging to the *cur*-class.
The root *mṛd*—according to the Dhātupāṭha (*kṣode*, Dhātupāṭha 1515)—is preceded by the prefix *sam*.
The rule "saṃmṛdnāti" is intended to apply only when preceded by the prefix *sam*.

Regarding the rule "rakṣa-śru-vasa-va-pa-śāṃ nau": for the roots *rakṣ* (to protect, DhP 658), *śru* (to hear, DhP 942), *ḍu-vap* (to sow seeds or weave, DhP 1003), and *śo* (to thin, DhP 1145)—the suffix *ṇini* is applied when the word *ni* is used as an *upapada*.
"Niśāyī"— this is correct according to the previous rule. "Yāci," and so forth.

The roots *ṭuyācṛ* in the sense of "begging" (Dhātupāṭha 863), *hmañ* in the sense of "taking away" (Dhātupāṭha 899) preceded by the prefixes *vi-* and *ā-*, the same root (*hmañ*) again preceded by *sam-*, *vaja* and *vraja* in the sense of "going" (Dhātupāṭha 252, 253), *vada* in the sense of "distinct speech" (Dhātupāṭha 1009), and *vasa* in the sense of "dwelling" (Dhātupāṭha 1005)—for these [roots] whose meanings are prohibited [by other rules], the suffix *ṇini* occurs.
Regarding the phrase "of those that are prohibited":
the meaning is "of those whose meanings have been prohibited."
Since the negative particle (*nañ*) occurs only with words that have a prohibited meaning, it is understood that the suffix *ṇini* follows those words preceded by *nañ*.
But how can there be the employment of things that are prohibited? There is no fault here because there is no prohibition regarding their existence through metaphorical application (*upacāra*).

For the existence of word-meanings is not exclusively primary; rather, as has been stated, there is another, metaphorical existence of word-meanings through their objects, which is called "metaphorical existence."

In this regard, the negation applies only to that existence which is primary (*mukhyā*), and not to that which resides in the intellect (*buddhisthā*) and is figurative (*aupacāriki*); thus, its application based on that [primary existence] is not contradicted. Regarding the rule beginning with *acām*:
the suffix *ṇini* occurs after verbal roots ending in vowels (*ajanta*) that have inanimate agents (*acittakartṛka*) and for which [the suffix] has been prohibited.

"Acitta" means one for whom the mind (citta) does not exist; those actions whose agent is such [a being] are so described. Furthermore, this qualification functions by way of its referent (artha). Since the referent has an unconscious agent, the verbal roots denoting that referent are metaphorically (upacāreṇa) called by that same term.
"Viśayī and viṣayī in the sense of 'region'":
when the word *deśa* (region) is the meaning to be expressed, the words *viśayin* and *viṣayin*, ending in the suffix *ṇini*, are grammatically correct.
The suffix *ṇini* is applied to the roots *śīṅ* ("to sleep," Dhātupāṭha 1032) and *ṣiñ* ("to bind," Dhātupāṭha 1477), both preceded by the prefix *vi*.
And the absence of *vṛddhi* [substitution] occurs due to the rule of irregular derivation (*nipātana*).
Regarding the statement "the word *abhibhāvin* is used in the sense of the past tense," the word *abhibhāvin*, ending in the suffix *ṇini*, is grammatically correct when it refers to the past time.
The suffix *ṇini* is applied to the root *bhū* preceded by the prefix *abhi*. Thus, one who has overcome [others] is called *abhibhāvī*.
Similarly, there are the forms *aparādhī* and *uparodhī*.
From the roots *rādha* and *sādha*, meaning "to accomplish" (Dhātupāṭha 1262, 1263), and *rudhir*, meaning "to cover" (Dhātupāṭha 1438)— with the prefix *apa*— the suffix *ṇini* is applied,
resulting in the forms *paribhāvī* and *paribhavī*. These are derived from the root *bhū* preceded by the prefix *pari*.

In this alternative view (*pakṣe*), there is an absence of *vṛddhi*. [The examples are] "paca" and so forth: *ḍupacaṣ* "in cooking" (DhP 996); *vaca* "in speaking" (DhP 1842); *ḍuvap* "in the spreading of seeds or threads" (also "in cutting," DhP 1003); *vada* "in distinct speech" (DhP 1009); *cala* "in shaking" (DhP 832); *śala* "in going" (DhP 843); *patlu* "in going" (DhP 845).
[The form] "nadaṭ" [is derived from] *nada* "in sounding."
{nada—*Dhātupāṭha*: nada in the sense of indistinct sound (54).
The *ṭ*-suffix is for the purpose of [forming] the feminine suffix *ṅīp*.
{bhaṣaṭ—*Kāśikā*: bhasaṭ}.}
In the *Dhātupāṭha* (1100), {bhaṣa bhatrsane} means "to revile," and *bhasa* means "to revile" and "to shine"; the letter *ṭ* is for the purpose of [forming] the suffix *ṅīp*.

*gṛ* (to swallow) [DhP 1410], *miṣa* (to strive) [DhP 1352], *kupa* (to be angry) [DhP 1233], *miha* (to sprinkle) [DhP 992], *tṛ* (to swim or cross over) [DhP 969], *cura* (to steal) [DhP 1534], *gāhū* (to plunge or stir) [DhP 649], *jṛṣ* and *jhṛṣ* (to grow old) [DhP 1130, 1131], *mṛṅ* (to die) [DhP 1403], *kṣamūṣ* (to endure).

(dhātupāṭhaḥ-442), *tuda* "to pain" (dhātupāṭhaḥ-1281), *mṛd* "to crush" (dhātupāṭhaḥ-1515), *divu* "to play, etc. (DhP 1.107), *nṛtī* "to dance, to move the limbs" (dhātupāṭhaḥ-1116), *vraṇa* "to wound the body" (dhātupāṭhaḥ-1937) belonging to the *curādi* class; *dṛśir* "to see" (dhātupāṭhaḥ-988);

*ḍubhṛñ* "to support and nourish" (dhātupāṭhaḥ-1087)—from this [root], with the word *jāra* as an upapada, the suffix *ac* is applied. One who supports (*bibharti*) a paramour (*jāram*) is called a *jārabharaḥ*.

With the root *pac* (to cook), when preceded by the prefix *ā*, the suffix *aṇ* is applied in the sense of the object (*karman*), provided the following word begins with a vowel— thus, "one who cooks rice" is *āpacaḥ*.
It is said to be an *ākṛtigaṇa* (an open class) because the word *ādi* ("beginning with") in the compound *pacādi* has the sense of "of the same type."
And because this is an *ākṛtigaṇa* (an open class), words such as *cakradhara* and others are established. Regarding the term *vikṣipaḥ*:
due to the *kit* designation, there is an absence of *guṇa*.
Regarding the term *jñaḥ*: [the same applies].
By [Pāṇini 6.4.64], there is the elision of the vowel *ā*. Thus, "priyaḥ" [is derived from] the root *prīñ* (meaning "to satisfy") [Dhātupāṭha 1836], with the substitution of *iyaṅ*.

Regarding the word *kiraḥ*: from the root *kṛ* meaning "to scatter" (Dhātupāṭha 1409), there is the substitution of *i* for the root vowel according to Pāṇini 7.1.100 (*ṛta iddhātoḥ*), followed by the substitution of *ra* for the following vowel (*raparatvam*). Now, how are words such as *deva* and others formed, given that since the roots beginning with *div* have a penultimate *i*, when the suffix *ka* is added, the forms should be *divakaḥ*, *sivakaḥ*, and so on? To this, he says: "*devaseva*" and so forth.

The word *ādi* (and so forth) indicates a class or type. Regarding the rule *orāvaśyake* (Pāṇini 3.1.135): [the suffix *ṇyat* is applied after a root ending in *u*] when necessity (*avaśyaka*) is expressed. Thus we have *lāvyaṃ* and *pāvyam*.
In these cases, by the rule *aco ñṇiti*, there is *vṛddhi* (vowel strengthening), and then by the rule *vānto yi pratyaye*, the substitution of *av* for the final *o* occurs.

*Bālamanoramā*: "The suffix *ka* [is applied] after roots ending in a vowel (*ig-upadha*), after *jñā*, *prī*, and *kir*. (Pāṇini 3.1.135). Regarding the root *kṛ* in the sense of "scattering" (*vikṣepa*): when the vowel substitution (*ittva*) and the replacement by *ra* (*raparatva*) have occurred, the form becomes *kir*, ending in the letter *r*.
The ablative case here follows from the compound (*dvandva*) of these terms: *ig-upadha*, *jñā*, *prī*, and *kir*.
The suffix *kittvam* is for the purpose of prohibiting the *guṇa* substitution.
Regarding *jña*:
there is elision (*lopa*) of the final *ā*.
"Priya" [is derived from] the root *prīñ*; [the suffix] *ke* [is applied], and [the vowel] *i* becomes *iyaṅ*.
"Kira" [is derived from] the root *kṝ*.

From the root *kṛ*, with the suffix *kap* and the substitution of *it*, there is the replacement by *ra*. This is an exception to [the addition of] the suffix *ṇa*. It applies to what would otherwise be obtained by the rule *śyādvyadha* (Pāṇini 3.1.141) and so forth.
Thus, *suglaḥ*.

The roots *glai* and *mlai* [are used] in the sense of "loss of joy" (*dhātupāṭha* 903, 904); *pā* in the sense of "drinking" (*dhātupāṭha* 925); *ghrā* in the sense of "perceiving odor" (*dhātupāṭha* 926); *ṣmā* in the sense of "sound and contact with fire" (*dhātupāṭha* 927); and *dṛṭ* in the sense of "drinking" (*dhātupāṭha* 902). For these roots, when the suffix *ka*—characterized by their vowel *ā*—or *ṇa* would otherwise apply, the suffix *śa* is prescribed.

If the term *upasarge* (when preceded by a prefix) is understood to carry over, then *ka* applies; if it has ceased to apply, then when *ka* would otherwise apply, *ṇa* applies after roots that do not have prefixes.
For the root *dṛś*, the suffix *ka* applies as characterized by the rule for roots ending in *i* or *u*.
In forms such as *utpiba*, because the affix (*pratyaya*) is marked with *śit*, it receives the designation *sārvadhātuka*; consequently, by [Pāṇini 3.1.68], the affix *śap* is applied for the agent.

Then, by [Pāṇini 7.3.78] beginning with *prāghrā*, the substitutions *piba* and so forth are applied as appropriate. Regarding the statement "there is a prohibition when it is a technical name (*saṃjñā*)," it refers to the affix *śap* because that is the subject under discussion.
The statement "by tigers and so forth" (Pāṇini 2.1.55) is the indicative mark (*liṅga*) for that prohibition. Regarding the rule "not after a prefix" (*anupasargāt*):
by means of a transposition of case endings (*subvyatyaya*), the singular number stands in place of the plural. Examples include *limpaḥ*, *vindaḥ*, and so on.
*lipa* in the sense of "smearing" (Dhātupāṭha 1433); *vidlṛ* in the sense of "finding/obtaining" (Dhātupāṭha 1432).
The inclusion of the nasal (*num*) [in the root] is for the purpose of indicating that the *num* occurs only in the state of the original instruction (*upadeśāvasthā*).
*dhṛñ* in the sense of "holding/sustaining" (Dhātupāṭha 900); [this is used here] with the causative suffix *ṇic*.
Regarding the word "pārayaḥ": it is derived from the root *pāra* (meaning "to complete an action"), which belongs to the *curādi* group (Dhātupāṭha 1911, 1912);
or alternatively, it is derived from the root *pṛ* (meaning "to protect" or "to fill"), with the causative suffix *ṇic* added (Dhātupāṭha 1489).

The root *vid*—meaning "to know" (*vedanākhyāna*) and "to dwell" (*nivāsa*)—is listed as number 1708 in the *Dhātupāṭha* (from the *Padamañjarī*), belonging to the *curādi* group with the suffix *ṇic*. Alternatively, it may be any one of the roots beginning with *bid*, which have the sense of "knowing" and so forth, with the causative suffix *ṇic* added.
The root *ejṛ*, meaning "to tremble" (*kampane*), is listed as number 234 in the *Dhātupāṭha*, with the causative suffix *ṇic* added.
The root *cit* in the sense of "perception" (*saṃjñāna*) [is listed as] number 39 in the Dhātupāṭha; it takes the causative suffix *ṇic*.
The root *sah* in the sense of "endurance" (*marṣaṇa*) [is listed as] number 1809 in the Dhātupāṭha; it takes either the causal suffix *ṇic* or the *curādi* suffix *ṇic*.
[Examples include] *limpaḥ* and *vindaḥ*.

By [Pāṇini 3.1.77] and [7.1.59], the augment *num* is applied, resulting in *pralipaḥ* and *pravidaḥ* (the latter being absent in the *Kāśikā*). The suffix *ka* is applied by virtue of the rule for roots ending in *i* or *u* (*igupadhala-kṣaṇaḥ kaḥ*). Regarding the statement "after *limp-* with the prefix *ni-*" and so forth, the meaning is that this should be explained as having the sense: "the suffix *śa* occurs after the root *limp-* when the word *ni* is used as an *upapada*."
However, an explanation must be provided here regarding the particle *ca*, because it has the sense of including what has not been explicitly stated (*anuktasamuccaya*).
[The example] begins with "in the case of *go* and so forth" (*gavādiṣu*).
When words such as *go* and others function as the governing word (*upapada*), the suffix *śa* occurs when the context is that of a proper name (*saṃjñā*).

This is an exception (*apavāda*) to the suffix *aṇ* [prescribed by Pāṇini 3.2.1] when the object is *karmaṇi*. And that [exception] is obtained because the letter *ca* has the sense of an inclusive conjunction (*anuktasamuccaya*). It is an exception to the suffix *ṇa*, which would otherwise be obtained by [the rule] *śyādvyadha* (Pāṇini 3.1.141) and so forth.
For whom, however, does the exception not apply? Because of the continued application of the rule "not after a prefix" (*anupasargāt*). [The forms] *dadaḥ* and *dadhaḥ* [are derived as follows]:
once the suffix *śe* has been applied, the suffix *śap* is added.

Because this root belongs to the *juhoty-ādi* class, there is *ślau* (elision of the suffix); by the rule *ślau* [Pāṇini 6.1.10], there is reduplication; and by the rule *śnābhyastayor ātaḥ* [Pāṇini 6.4.112], there is the elision of the long *ā*.
Thus, "dāyaḥ" [is formed]; here, by the rule *āto yuk* [Pāṇini 7.3.33], the augment *yuk* is added.

Regarding the word *pradaḥ*: by rule [Pāṇini 3.3.106], the suffix *ka* is applied. Now, one might object: since the roots *dada* (in the sense of "giving," Dhātupāṭha 17) and *dadha* (in the sense of "holding," Dhātupāṭha 8) would become *dado* and *dadhaḥ* when the suffix *ac* is added, and since from the roots *dā* and *dhā* the forms *dāyaḥ* and *dhāyaḥ* would likewise result when the suffix *ṇa* is added, what is the purpose of this sūtra? This is not so; for if *ac* were used, the final syllable would be udātta by rule [Pāṇini 6.2.157].
But in the case of *śe*, there is only the accent of the negative particle (*nañ*): as in *adadaḥ* and *adadhaḥ*. Regarding the term *jvaliti*:
it is a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "those for which *jval* is the first.
The non-hearing of the case-ending is due to its elision by the rule *supāṃ suluk* [Pāṇini 7.1.39].
Regarding the term "kasantebhyaḥ":
it is a *tatpuruṣa* compound meaning "those that have *kas* as their end," where the word *anta* signifies proximity.
Alternatively, it is a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "those for which *kas* is at the end."
The word *anta* signifies either proximity or a limit.
The root *jval*, meaning "to blaze," is listed twice in the Dhātupāṭha—once among the *ghaṭādi* roots and once thereafter.
[The reference] "from them" (*tebhyaḥ*) refers to those.

In that case, if this qualification were absent, there would be doubt as to which "jvalādi" (jvala and so forth) roots are intended; therefore, to exclude those [others], the "jvalādi" group is specified as "those beginning with *kas*.
Thus, the sub-group (*gaṇa*) beginning with *ghaṭa* is not excluded.
The mention of *kas* is not for the purpose of excluding those that are recited after *kas*, because the reading is "after *kas*, *vṛt*" (*kasaṃ adhītya vṛt*).
