But surely, the inclusion of roots such as *jval* among *ghaṭ* and the others is for the sake of the designation *mit*; in that case, even without the mention of *kan* and *san*, only those ending in *kan* and *san* would be understood. Therefore, is this qualification (*viśeṣaṇa*) useless? This is not so; for if that [mention of *kan* and *san*] were absent, the listing of the preceding *jval*-type roots would serve a dual purpose—both for the sake of the *mit* designation and for the sake of the suffixes—whereas for the others, it would serve only the purpose of the suffixes. Therefore, the mention of *kan* must be made.
"An exception to *aca*":
because [the roots] beginning with *jval* are included within the group ending in *pac*. "An addition regarding the *ṇa* of *tan* must be made":
when the suffix *ṇa* is to be prescribed, the fact that *tan* also possesses a *ṇa* must be set forth.

The demonstration [of the application] should be provided later on, because the particle *ca* has the sense of including what has not been explicitly mentioned (*anuktasamuccaya*). [The root] *śyaiṅ* (in the sense of "going," Dhātupāṭha 963);
there is the inclusion of roots ending in long *ā*, such as *dā* and *dhā* etc.
[The root] *vyadha* (in the sense of "striking," Dhātupāṭha 1181); [the root] *ruāu* (in the sense of "going," Dhātupāṭha 940) preceded by *āṅ*, and again that same [root] preceded by *sam*.
The root *iṇ* "to go" (Dhātupāṭha 1045) preceded by *ati*; the root *ṣo* "in the sense of ending" (Dhātupāṭha 1147) preceded by *ava*;
the root *hrīñ* "in the sense of taking away" (Dhātupāṭha 899) preceded by *ava*;
the root *lih* "in the sense of tasting" (Dhātupāṭha 1016); the root *śliṣ* "in the sense of embracing" (Dhātupāṭha 1186); and the root *ās* "in the sense of breathing" (Dhātupāṭha 1069).

In this context, [the suffix] occurs only after those roots that are listed with prefixes (*sopasarga*); however, it occurs after the remaining roots both when they have prefixes and when they are without prefixes (*anupasarga*).

This is because the phrase "provided they are without a prefix" (*anupasargāt*) has ceased to apply here, as indicated by the subsequent mention of the term "without a prefix" (*anupasarga*) later on.
Regarding the phrase "and 'vibhāṣā'": it is connected with the word "ceased" (nivṛttam).
For the mention of *vibhāṣā* is indeed connected with [the condition] "when not preceded by a prefix" (*anupasargeṇa*).
Therefore, when that [suffix] is excluded, its [the other suffix's] exclusion also occurs.
Regarding the phrase "for the purpose of subverting the sublater":

since [the suffix *ka*] is prescribed as a specific rule by [Pāṇini 3.3.106], what could be the sublater of the suffix *ṇa*, which is prescribed as a general rule? It is for the purpose of subverting that [general rule].
This purpose of the inclusion of the root *avaśyati* should also be understood [in this way]. Alternatively, its mention is for the sake of restricting the prefix:
so that [the suffix] may apply only after the prefix *ava-*, as in the word *avaśyāyaḥ*.

Regarding the rule *āto yuk* [Pāṇini 7.3.33]: the word *dunyoḥ* is a genitive used in the sense of an ablative due to a metrical substitution (*subvyatyaya*); likewise, *anupasarge* is a locative used in the sense of an ablative. For this very reason, he says: "from the roots *du* and *nī*, provided they are not preceded by a prefix (*anupasarga*)."
Regarding "dāvaḥ":
[it is derived from] the root *du* (meaning "to afflict," Dhātupāṭha 1256).
Regarding "nāyaḥ": [it is derived from the root *nī*].

The root *ṇīñ* is used in the sense of "leading" (*prāpaṇe*) [Dhātupāṭha 901]. From this, the forms *praṇayaḥ* and *praṇayaḥ* are derived using the suffix *ac* according to the rule beginning with *pacādyac*, and the substitution of *ṇ* for *n* occurs by the rule *upasargādasamāse’pi* [Pāṇini 8.4.14]. The statement "this is an optional rule applied according to specific circumstances" (*vyavasthitavibhāṣā*) is clarified by the example beginning with "in the case of aquatic creatures" (*jalacare*).
"It should be stated that [the suffix] also applies after the root *bhū*.
This means it should be explained that after the root *bhū*, the suffix *ṇa* optionally occurs.
This explanation, however, must be made by means of a *yogavibhāga* (splitting of the rule) based on the word "optionally" (*vibhāṣā*). [The rule] "when the house is the agent" is as follows.
By this, he shows that "in the house" (*gehe*) is an adjunct (*upādhi*) of the agent, which is the meaning of the suffix, and not a governing word (*upapada*).
And this is understood from the inclusion of the word *gṛhapati* ("householder") in the list beginning with *apatya* ("offspring").
[As it is said: "And wives [are included] because they reside therein."
The word "house" (geham) is connected with what has been previously mentioned. By this, he indicates that the suffix occurs even when the "house" is used in a figurative sense.
And this is obtained through the simultaneous utterance of the word "house" twice, according to the principle of *tantra*.
Regarding "gṛham":
there is vocalization (*samprasāraṇa*) by [Pāṇini 6.1.16] *grahādinā*. Regarding "in the sense of an artisan as the agent":
by showing that [the term] functions as a qualifier (*upādhi*) as before, he excludes its status as a subordinate word (*upapada*).

And this [usage] is obtained from the application of the commentator (*bhāṣyakāra*) in the phrase "he gives the cloth to the washerman" (*rajakasya vastraṃ dadāti*), based on the enumeration [of roots] beginning with *nṛt*, *khan*, and *rañj*.
Furthermore, this is obtained because the term "optionally" (*vibhāṣā*) is understood to follow [from a previous rule], resulting in a restricted option (*vyavasthitavibhāṣā*);
specifically, by the rule "and there is the elision of the nasal in *rañj*" (*rañjeranunāsikalopaśca*).
This [fact] is also obtained from that very usage by the author of the Bhāṣya.

Furthermore, the fact that he teaches the designation *mit* for the root *rañj* in the rule "janījṛṣknasurañjo'mantāśca" (Dhātupāṭha 819 onwards) indicates that the elision of the nasal of *rañj* occurs even when a suffix other than one marked with *k* or *ṅ* follows.

The sole purpose of this *mit* designation is so that the shortening prescribed by "mitāṃ hrasvaḥ" (Pāṇini 6.4.92) may take effect; and if this elision of the nasal did not exist, there would be no occasion for such shortening.
Furthermore, when there is no lengthening (*vṛddhi*), the penultimate vowel (*upadhā*) does not become short.

Therefore, just as the elision of the nasal (*anunāsikalopa*) occurs for the root *rañj* after the causative suffix *ṇi*, so too does it occur after the suffix *ṣvan*. Because of this specific enumeration, the elision does not occur in forms such as *hvātā* and *hvāyaka*.

The addition of the marker *ṇit* to the suffix *ṣvan* is for the purpose of making the first syllable udātta; the letter *ṣ* is for the purpose of [triggering] the suffix *ṅīṣ*. Regarding the word "gāḥ":
this is a reference to the root *gai* (meaning "to sing," Dhātupāṭha 917), after the elision of the vowel *ā* has been applied by [Pāṇini 6.4.140].
For this very reason, he says: "of *gāyati*."

But surely, by the rule "In the case of the mention of *gā*, *mā*, and others, there is no distinction" (*Vyākaraṇa-paribhāṣā* 124), there ought to be a mention of even the root *gāṅ* 'to go' (Dhātupāṭha 950)? This is not so; because in the word *gāthaka*, the agency of an artisan is understood specifically in relation to the meaning of the root *gai* (to sing) due to the suffix *thakan*, and not in relation to the meaning of *gāṅ*. The letter *n* in *thakan* is for the purpose of making the initial syllable udātta. [The form] *gāyanaḥ* is derived by adding the suffix *yuk* according to [Pāṇini 3.1.147].
*gāyanī*: the suffix *ṅīp* is applied because of the presence of the marker *ṭi*; "the separation of the rule (*yogavibhāga*) is for the sake of what follows."
In the subsequent rule, the suffix *ṇyuṭ* alone is intended to be carried forward by the word "ca" (*and*), so that *thakan* shall not be included.
If the two were combined into a single rule as "goṇyuṭthakanau," then *thakan* would also be drawn in. Regarding the term "jahāteḥ":
it refers to the root *ohāk* in the sense of "abandoning" (Dhātupāṭha 1090).
Regarding the rule "jihāteśca":
the root *ohāṅ* in the sense of "going" (Dhātupāṭha 1089) is intended to be understood here.
The letter *k* is specified after the root *jahāti* precisely for the purpose of including both [roots] under a common designation.
For if that [letter *k*] were not present, then if this reference were by means of a single *anubandha*, it would not include the root *jahāti* which has two *anubandhas*;
and if it were by means of two *anubandhas*, it would not include the other [root].
Since both [terms] possess an *anubandha* when the letter *ka* is present, their general inclusion is justified by the rule:
"In the case of *vrīhi*, *kāla*, and the agent (*kartṛ*).
By this, he shows that *vrīhi* and *kāla* serve as qualifiers of the meaning of the suffix.
But it rejects [the status of] being an *upapada*;
this is understood from the rule at [Pāṇini 4.1.27].
As for the example "hāyanāḥ":

By the rule *[[Pāṇini 7.3.33]]*, the suffix *yuk* is applied. [The phrase] "because they abandon the water" indicates the ground for the application (*pravṛttinimitta*) of the word *hāyana* with respect to rice.
"He abandons the states of being"—
by this [expression] also, within a year; "having flowed forth"— this is a designation made by means of repetition.
However, the augment *num* has not been applied despite the word being neuter, because the rules governing augments (*āgama-śāsana*) are non-eternal (*anitya*).
Regarding the rule "the suffix *vun* is used in the sense of *samabhihāra*":

someone might have the misconception that since the word *samabhihāra* elsewhere means repetition (*paunaḥpunya*) and so forth, it must have that same meaning here as well; therefore, to dispel that [misconception], he says: "by the mention of *samabhihāra*" and so on.
"It is indicated" means "it is shown.
This is understood because verbal roots have multiple meanings.
Others say it is due to the continued application of the term *śilpinī* (the female artisan).

*Śilpī* means "one who performs well. Regarding the rule "the suffix *vun* is prescribed for one who performs well," he demonstrates the result of taking "performing well" as a mere indicative mark by saying "even once," and so forth.

This is a clarification of what was immediately preceding: "when a blessing (*āśis*) is implied," not when it is explicitly expressed. This is because, according to the rule *kartari kṛt* [Pāṇini 3.4.67], the agent alone is the meaning expressed by the suffix.

Regarding the phrase "from the mere root" (*dhātumātrāt*): it is because the intention is to express the generality of the verbal root (*dhātu*), because [the specific roots] *pru*, *sṛ*, and *vāñc* have been excluded,
and because no other specific root is relied upon here.
It is based solely on the elements (*dhātu*), and not on any specific [grammatical] distinction.

By employing the imperative (*loṭ*) in the sense of a benediction (*āśis*) in the words "may he live" (*jīvatāt*) and "may he rejoice" (*nandatāt*), he shows that *jīvaka* and *nandaka* have the same meaning as those [verbal roots].
He asks, "What, then, is this thing called *āśis* (blessing)? and says: "*Āśis* is a particular kind of prayer (*prārthanā-viśeṣaḥ*).
Prayer is the longing for an object that is not yet attained and is desired;
"and in this context, it has action as its object."
The term *kriyāviṣaya* is a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "that which has action as its object.
This meaning is understood from the mention of the verbal root (*dhātu*), because a verbal root denotes action;
thus, it refers to "the action of such-and-such [a root]."

It is thus wished that one may be the agent of the action of living and the action of rejoicing—that is, "may you have life and joy. Thus ends the first quarter of the third chapter in the *Kāśikā-vivaraṇapañjikā*, composed by the venerable Ācārya Jinendrabuddhi, who is a disciple of the Bodhisattvas. [Note: The term *karmani* here is not a reference to its own form (*svarūpa*), because of the prohibition [stated] in *aśabda-saṃjñā* (Pāṇini 1.1.67).

If, moreover, only the essential nature (*svarūpa*) were grasped in the context of "objects of action" (*karmapradeśa*), then the formulation of technical designations (*saṃjñāvidhāna*) would be purposeless; nor could there be a grasping of "action" (*kriyā*), for if that were grasped, the rule *kartrabhiprāye* [Pāṇini 1.3.72] would be untenable. For if "action" and "object" were grasped, the suffix would have to occur when a word expressing "action" is the attendant noun (*upapada*), yet here no such word expressing "action" exists as an attendant noun. Therefore, "object" is grasped according to the rule *kartur īpsitatamaṃ karma* [Pāṇini 1.4.49]. To demonstrate its subdivisions, he says: "threefold," and so forth.

Among these, the *nirvartya* (that which is produced) is that which arises while being non-existent, such as in the expressions "he makes a pot" (*kumbhaṃ karoti*) or "he builds a city" (*nagaraṃ karoti*).
For a pot and the like arise while indeed being non-existent; thus it is the *nirvartya* object.

The *vikārya* (that which is modified) is that of which some modification is prescribed while it already exists, such as "he cuts the stalk" (*kāṇḍaṃ lunāti*) or "he razes the city" (*nagaraṃ lunāti*).
The "object as modification" (*vikārya-karman*) is that in which a transformation of something already existing, such as a stalk of grass, is enjoined by means of cutting.

The "object as attainment" (*prāpya*) is that where neither the production of something non-existent nor the imposition of a modification upon something already existent is performed; rather, only a mere connection with the action is perceived, as for example: "He studies the Veda" (*vedam adhīte*) or "He practices the *carccā*.
Here, through the act of studying and so forth, only a connection with the Veda and the like is perceived, and not the production of something previously non-existent.
Nor is it the case that modification is simply the alteration of an existing thing; this is what is to be understood by the term "action" (*karma*).
Regarding the phrase "in all cases" (*sarvatra*), and so forth: because no specific distinction is mentioned among the three types [of action].

Regarding the rule "when *karman* is the upapada," why should it not apply when there is an *abhidhāna* (denotation)? [The answer is: because it would subvert the rule "a *kṛt* suffix [is used] when the agent is to be expressed" (Pāṇini 3.4.67). Thus, we have the examples beginning with *śīli*, *kāmi*, and so on. {In the *dhātupāṭha*, the root *śīl* is listed in the *curādi* group as meaning "to hold fast"; furthermore, the root *śīl* is also listed in the *bhvādi* group as meaning "concentration."} The root *śīl* in the sense of "concentration" (Dhātupāṭha 1878) belongs to the *curādi* class and ends in the causative marker (*ṇic*).
*kamu kāntau* (Dhātupāṭha 443): the root *kam*, with the causative suffix *ṇic*. *bhakṣa adane* (Dhātupāṭha 1557): the root *bhakṣ*, with the causative suffix *ṇic* belonging to the *curādi* class.
*cara gatyarthaḥ* (Dhātupāṭha 559): the root *car*, meaning "to move," preceded by the prefix *āṅ*.
The letter *ik* is for the purpose of indicating the verbal root (*dhātu*).
Since the suffix *aṇ* would otherwise apply to these [words], it must be stated—meaning explained—that *ṇa* [is to be applied].

Here is the explanation: by the maxim of the frog’s leap (*maṇḍūkapluti*), *ṇa* is carried over from rule 3.1.140, and the mention of *vibhāṣā* is carried over from rule 3.1.143; thus, both *ṇa* and *aṇ* are prescribed here when a direct object (*karman*) serves as the attendant word (*upapada*).

Here, because the term *vibhāṣā* (optionally) is understood from the previous rule and is recognized as a *vyavasthitavibhāṣā* (restricted option), the suffix *ṇa* alone will apply after words such as *śīlin*, while the suffix *aṇ* alone will apply after the remaining words.
Regarding these two, however, there is a distinction in the feminine gender: for the suffix *aṇ*, the feminine suffix *ṅīp* occurs, whereas for the suffix *ṇa*, the suffix *ṭāp* occurs.
The letter *ṇ* [in *ṇa*] is for the purpose of causing *vṛddhi*.

Regarding the statement “and the original accent of the first member (*pūrvapada-prakṛtisvaratva*)”: when the rule *gatikārakopapadānāṃ kṛt* [Pāṇini 6.2.139] would otherwise result in the original accent of the final member (*uttarapada-prakṛtisvaratva*), it must be stated—that is, explained—that there is also the original accent of the first member.

The explanation here is as follows: in the rule *tulyārtha* [Pāṇini 6.2.2], which begins with *tulyādau*, a formal split of the yoga (*yogavibhāga*) should be made by adding the word *tatpuruṣe*. By this means, the original accent of the first member will also apply to words such as *māṃsaśīla* and others.

The word *māṃsa* has its accent on the final syllable (*antodātta*), because it ends in the suffix *sa*, following the rule *vṛtṛvadihanikami-kaṣibhyaḥ saḥ* (DhP 9.21), with the addition of *man* and lengthening of the vowel according to *manerdīrghaśca* (DhP 9.23); thus, by the accent of the suffix (*pratyayasvara*). The word *kalyāṇa* has its accent on the middle syllable (*madhyodātta*), according to the rule *laghāvante dvayośca bahvaṣo guruḥ* (Phiṭ-sūtra 2.42).
This is its meaning: when there is a light syllable at the end, or when there are two light syllables at the ends, the heavy syllable that follows the word *bahvac* becomes acute (*udātta*).

The term *bahvaṣ* means "having many vowels" (*bahvaj*). Now, one might object: since forms such as *māṃsaśīla* ("one whose habit is meat") can be established by forming a *ghañ*-derived noun in the sense of an action from roots like *śī*, and then forming a *bahuvrīhi* compound with that, what is the purpose of this specific rule for *ghan*? This is not so; for if it were a *bahuvrīhi*, then in the case of *bahubhakṣa* ("one who eats much"), the final syllable of the second member would become acute according to Pāṇini 6.2.175.

Furthermore, the suffix *ṇa* must necessarily be stated for the purpose of non-obstruction; otherwise, when the sentence "he desires meat" (*māṃsaṃ kāmayate*) occurs, the suffix *aṇ* would also apply. Regarding the rule "and from *īkṣi* and *kṣami*":

the meaning is that the suffix *ṇa* occurs after these two—namely, *īkṣa* (meaning "to see," Dhātupāṭha 610) and *kṣamū* (meaning "to endure," Dhātupāṭha 1206)—and this [rule] must be explained accordingly.
The explanation, however, should be performed exactly as before. [The root] *hveñ* is used in the sense of rivalry (*spardhā*).
Regarding the rule "veñ tantusantāne" (DhP 2.40),
why is there not an inclusion of the root "vā gatigandhanayoḥ" (DhP 10.50)? Because [the latter] is intransitive,
whereas here the transitive [root] is being carried forward.
Regarding the statement "māṅ māne":
this is intended as an indicator for the root *mā* that has the marker *ṅ*.
By the rule "In the case of the mention of *gā*, *mā*, and others, there is no distinction" (*Vyāḍīya-paribhāṣā* 124), the inclusion of *meṅ praṇidāne* (Dhātupāṭha 961) is also desired.

Now, if there is no distinction in the case of the roots *gam*, *mā*, and *ā* [with respect to the application of the suffix *aṇ*], then would not the form *meti* also result from those two roots—namely *mīñ* in the sense of "injury" (DhP 1476) and *ḍumiñ* in the sense of "throwing" (DhP 1250)—once *āttva* has been applied within the domain of *ej*? Indeed, it does occur from these two with the suffix *aṇ* by virtue of the preceding rule.
[The example] *svargahvāyaḥ* [is formed] with the suffix *yuk* according to [Aṣṭādhyāyī 7.3.33]. [The word] *anupasarge* [means] "when there is no prefix."
Although there is the contingency of the ablative case (pañcamī) due to the transposition [of the rule], the locative case (saptamī) is used;
furthermore, this qualifies the verbal root (dhātu).
For this very reason, it says: "from those ending in long ā, provided they are not preceded by a prefix (anupasarga)."
In "godaḥ," as before, there is the elision of the letter *l*. In "pāṣṇam," [the same applies].

The root *tri* is listed as *traiṅ pālane* (Dhātupāṭha 965). Because of the inclusion of the term *supi*, [the rule] does not connect with *karmaṇi* (the accusative case), and furthermore, because the root *sthā* (*tiṣṭhati*) is intransitive.
In examples such as *samasthaḥ*, when a word ending in the locative case (*saptamyanta*) is the *upapada*, there is the phrase *atratyādi*.
The rule *supi* constitutes one *yoga*, and in that context, the word *ataḥ* is understood to carry over (*anuvartate*).
By the words "supi" and so forth, he explains the meaning of this rule;
"tataḥ stha" is the second rule.

The commentary states: "And [the suffix] *sth* occurs after a verbal root ending in *su*. This refers to the question beginning with "What... and so forth; it is the question of one who considers [the rule] already established by the preceding [sūtra]. [The purpose is:
"So that [the suffix] may also occur in the sense of the abstract state (*bhāva*)."
Because of the capacity for the initial undertaking (*ārambha*), [the suffix] will not apply to the agent (*kartṛ*).

Nor is another meaning specified; in that case, according to the principle that "suffixes whose meaning is not specified occur in their own sense" (*anirdiṣṭārthāḥ pratyayāḥ svārthe bhavanti*), it would refer to the state of being (*bhāva*) alone.
For that indeed is the inherent meaning (*svārtha*) of verbal roots.
In the example *{ākhūtthaḥ-kāśikā} ākhūttham*,
there is the substitution of the preceding vowel with its homogeneous counterpart (*pūrvasavarṇa*) by [Pāṇini 6.1.102]. Regarding the rule *parimṛjāpanudoḥ*,
the genitive case is used in the sense of the ablative through a transposition of cases (*subvyatyaya*).
The root *mṛj* (Dhātupāṭha 1066), meaning "to cleanse," is preceded by *pūri-*;
the root *nud* (Dhātupāṭha 1426), meaning "to impel," is preceded by *apa-*;
[and] "laziness" (*ālasya*), etc.
This [suffix] is a qualifier for the meaning of the suffix (pratyaya).
"Alasya" is simply "alasa" (lazy);
the suffix *ṣyañ* is applied in the sense of the base word itself according to the rule beginning with *cāturvarṇya*.
"Āharaṇa" means "one who brings";
[this is formed] with the suffix *lyuṭ* in the sense of the agent according to Pāṇini 3.3.113.
Thus, "one who brings happiness" is *sukhāharaṇa*.
The meaning is that this form of the word *ka* should be explained as having the sense: "Who becomes the agent of laziness or the acquisition of pleasure by this [means], and not otherwise?
In this regard, the explanation is as follows: here too, as before, the term *vibhāṣā* (optionally) is understood to follow, and that is a *vyavasthita-vibhāṣā* (a restricted option).
Therefore, *ka* occurs only when the agents are laziness and the acquisition of pleasure, and not otherwise.
"Another is *tundaparimārja*"; here, the suffix *aṇ* occurs in the sense of "absence of laziness. [Another example is] "*śokāpanodaḥ*."

That which merely dispels sorrow through the teaching of its antidote, but does not produce happiness, is indeed a non-protector (*atrāṇa*). Regarding the phrase "in this context" (*atra prakaraṇe*) and so forth:
the dative case is used in the sense of "for the sake of that" (*tadarthe*) according to the rule beginning with *mūlavibhuja-ādi*.
The word *ādi* (and so forth) expresses a category.

The meaning is that the employment and demonstration of the suffix *ka* must be carried out for the sake of forms such as *mūlavibhuja* and others, so that words like *mūlavibhuja* may be grammatically correct.

In this regard, the demonstration is as follows: from rule 3.2.2 up to rule 3.2.3, the particle *ca* (and) is understood by anuvṛtti; and since it serves the purpose of including what has not been explicitly mentioned, the suffix *ka* will thus apply after bases such as *mūlavibhuja*.
He splits the root.
{From the Dhātupāṭha:} *bhuja* in the sense of "crookedness" (Dhātupāṭha 1417).
They release the claws, thus they are "claw-releasers" (*nakhamucāni*).
The root *muc* is used in the sense of "liberation" (*mokṣaṇe*) [Dhātupāṭha 1430].
Regarding the expression "sesame seeds hidden by crows" (*kākagṛhāstilāḥ*),
the root *guh* is used in the sense of "concealment" (*saṃvaraṇe*) [Dhātupāṭha 896].
[The roots] are to be hidden from crows; this is an exception (*apavāda*) to the suffixes *tavya* and others.
The suffix *ka* is used in the sense of the object (*karman*). [An example is: "In what does the lily rejoice? (*kva modate kumudam*).

This is an exception (*apavāda*) to [the suffixes] *tṛc* and so forth. "The formulation is for the sake of [roots] with prefixes," because [the formation] is already established by [Pāṇini 3.2.3], *anupasargāt*. "[Of the root] *dadāti*."
This is an illustration of roots beginning with *dā*;
it is intended to include other roots beginning with *dā* as well, according to the statement: "In the case of mentions of *ga*, *mā*, and *ā*, there is no distinction" (Vyāḍiparibhāṣā 124).
[The rule applies] "when preceded by *pra*."
The meaning is "connected with the prefix *pra*.
In the sūtra, the word *pre* should be understood as being in the locative case (*saptamī*) in the sense of the instrumental (*tṛtīyā*), due to a transposition of cases (*subvyatyaya*).
[The example is] "one who knows the path" (*pathiprajñaḥ*).

The meaning is that "he knows the path. In the phrase "he tells about the cow" (*gāṃ sañcaṣṭe*), this indicates that the substitute *khyāñ*—as prescribed by the rule *cakṣiṅaḥ khyāñ* [Pāṇini 2.4.54]—is intended, and not the root *khyā* in the sense of "speaking" (*prakathane*, Dhātupāṭha 1060).

This is understood because the root *khyāti* preceded by the prefix *sam-* cannot possibly occur in such usage. Furthermore, according to the maxim "between a root with a *luk*-suffix and one without a *luk*-suffix, only the one with the *luk*-suffix is taken," the term *pā* refers to the root meaning "to drink" (*pānārtha*), and not the one meaning "to protect" (*rakṣaṇārtha*).

Although it is stated that "there is no distinction in the mention of *gā* and others" (*Vyākaraṇa-paribhāṣā* 124), nevertheless, due to its association with *pibati*, the term *gā* refers to the root with the *alug*-vikaraṇa suffix, and not to the root meaning "to go. Thus he says: "of *gāyati* and *pibati*.
The inclusion of the marker *ṭ* in *ṭak* is for the purpose of eliding the final vowel (*ā*).
The inclusion of the marker *ṭi* is for the purpose of deriving the feminine suffix *ṅīp*; it is not for the purpose of [the rule] *Pāṇini 1.1.46*.
Whence is this [conclusion]? Because the beginning and the end are [already] constituent parts (*avayava*).
Furthermore, it is not logical for a suffix (*pratyaya*) to be a constituent part, because of the rule stating "and what follows" (*paraśca* [Pāṇini 3.1.2]).

But might it not be the case that the genitive in *gāpoḥ* will indicate both the status of being a constituent part and the suffix *ṭak*? This is not so; this genitive is used in the sense of the ablative, or rather, it serves to qualify the agent—meaning "when *gā-* and *pā-* are the agents."
And this is appropriate, for in this way the dependence on a subsequent suffix (*pratyayaparatva*) is not sublated.

Furthermore, if [the suffix] were initial, the *kit* designation of *ṭak* would be purposeless. He states "of *surā* and *śīdhu*" etc., in order to exclude the final vowel of the upapada of the root *pibati*.
It has already been established that *pibati* is what is intended here, and not the root *pāti*.

Here, the term *vibhāṣā* from [Pāṇini 3.1.143] is understood to carry over; however, that is a restricted option (*vyavasthitavibhāṣā*). Consequently, [the suffix *kvip*] will apply when *surā* and *śīdhu* are the accompanying words (*upapada*), but not otherwise. The example *kṣīrapā* ("milk-drinker") is given as a feminine illustration in order to demonstrate that there is a specific rule regarding the feminine gender. The word "extensively" (*bahulam*) and so forth [is used].
The meaning is that this form [of the rule] should be explained as: "In the Vedic language, the suffix *ṭak* frequently occurs after the root *pā* (to drink).
The explanation, however, must be made by relying on the fact that the previously mentioned term *vibhāṣā* (optionally) continues to apply here as a *vyavasthita-vibhāṣā* (restricted option).
The result of this is that in the alternative case, the suffix *kap* occurs in the word *surāpā*. Regarding the phrase "lifting up is raising."
The meaning is "leading upward" (*ūrdhvanayanam*) that which is situated below (*adhaḥsthitasya*).
Regarding the term *aṃśaharaḥ*:
the meaning is "one who takes a share" (*svīkaroti*), not "one who throws upward. The phrase "in the section on vowels" (*ac-prakaraṇe*), and so forth.

The printed reading is *prātipadikagrahaṇe liṅgiviśiṣṭasya* ("when a nominal stem is mentioned, that which is qualified by gender is also included"). According to the rule *liṅgaviśiṣṭasyāpi grahaṇam* (Vyāḍīya-paribhāṣā 29), since the mention of *ghaṭa* would already include the mention of *ghaṭī*, the explicit mention of *ghaṭī* is for the purpose of indicating that this paribhāṣā is not universally valid (*anitya*). Its purpose, however, will be explained under the rule *dityadityādityapattyuttarapadāṇṇyaḥ* (Pāṇini 4.1.85). The word *upasaṃkhyāna* means "formulation" or "explanation."

In this regard, the demonstration is as follows: in the subsequent sūtra, the word *ca* (and) has the sense of including what is not explicitly mentioned; by means of that, the suffix *ac* will apply after the root *grah* when words such as *śakti* are present as *upapadas*. Regarding the phrase "in the sūtra" and so forth:

the meaning of *dhāri* is the meaning of the object to be supported (*dhārya*). In that context, when the root *grah* occurs with that meaning and a word is present as an *upapada*, an addition (*upasaṃkhyāna*)—that is, a formal demonstration—must be made regarding the suffix *ac*.
The demonstration is as follows:
"Another is merely a grasper of the thread.
This refers to one who takes up the thread alone but does not maintain it; in that case, there is no protection [from falling]. "This undertaking is for the purpose of lifting up."
Because [the desired meaning] is already established by the preceding rule alone when there is no lifting (*anudyamana*). Regarding "bone-lifter" (*asthiharaḥ*):
the meaning is that it refers to a stage of life capable of lifting a bone. The term "non-lifting" (*anudyamana*) is excluded.
Therefore, because there is no distinction [between the two cases], it follows that this rule applies even when the action is not being undertaken.

But surely, when the action is not being undertaken, it is already established by the preceding rule; for since the *tṛn* suffix would apply by virtue of its higher status, wouldn't the *ac* suffix also occur due to the provision for alternative forms (*vāsarūpa-vidhāna*)? This is not so; for he will state this: "In the case of suffixes expressing habitual disposition (*tācchīlika*), suffixes such as *tṛn* do not occur as alternatives.
"Habitual disposition" means "being of that very nature."
Furthermore, that is a mental state (*mānasa-dharma*).
Its occurrence is inferred by its independence from [any expectation of] a fruit.

By the words "one who brings flowers" (*puṣpāharaḥ*) and so forth, he illustrates the sense of habitual practice (*tācchīlya*). [The commentary states: "There is a distinction regarding the feminine gender. This is the reading of the root text (*mūla-pāṭha*).

For when there is a vowel (*aṇ*), the suffix *ṅīp* occurs, but when there is a vowel other than *a* (*ac*), the suffix *ṭāp* occurs. Regarding the statement "because *jap-* has sound as its object," one says "he mutters the *gāyatrī*" or "he mutters an *anuvāka*," since usage is observed only for cases where sound is the object. The phrase "the object is not possible" means that the ear is not of the nature of sound. The particle *iti* is used here in the sense of a reason.

Precisely because the word *karṇa* cannot function as an object (*karman*), the term *supi* (in the locative case) is connected here, and not *karmaṇi* (in the locative case denoting the object). Regarding the phrase "of *hasti* and *sūcaka*" and so forth:
the mention of *hasti* and *sūcaka* is a qualifier of the agent (*kartṛ*) who is the meaning of the suffix.
The meaning is that this rule prescribing the suffix *ac*—namely, *stambakarṇayo ramijapoḥ*—must be explained as having the sense that it applies when *hasti* and *sūcaka* are the agents.

The explanation, however, should be made by relying on the fact that this very [rule], following the mention of *vibhāṣā*, is of restricted optionality (*vyavasthitavibhāṣātva*). For example: *stamberamaḥ* (an elephant) and *karṇejapaḥ* (a slanderer);
here there is no elision (*aluk*) of the locative case ending according to [Pāṇini 6.3.14].

"Sūcakaḥ" means a slanderer. By the inclusion of the phrase "from the root alone," he indicates that the application [of the suffix] occurs even in cases where an exception (apavāda) would otherwise apply.
For in this way, [the suffix] occurs from the verbal root alone, even though it occurs in its domain after setting aside an exception;
and this meaning is obtained from the mention of the "verbal root" (dhātu).
Demonstrating the purpose of the mention of the "verbal root" through the rule "śami saṃjñāyām" and so forth, he clarifies the meaning expressed by the verbal root: "śami saṃjñāyām."
This is an elliptical reference to the sūtra;
the meaning is "in this sūtra, namely, *śami dhātoḥ saṃjñāyām*.
[The phrase] "*hetvādiṣu*" [is used].
By the word "ādi" (and so forth), the inclusion of *tācchīlya* (habitual nature), *anulomya* (conformity), and *yoga* (connection) is intended.
Since the suffix *ṭa* would apply by the rule *śamy-upapade karoteḥ saṃjñāyāṃ hetv-ādiṣu vivakṣiteṣu* [Pāṇini 3.2.20], the mention of the verbal root (*dhātu*) is made in order to preclude that.

The rule *śami dhātoḥ* [Pāṇini 3.2.14] has its scope in cases where there is a verbal root other than *kṛ* with *śam* as an upapada—for instance, *śaṃvada*. The rule *kṛño hetutācchīlyānulomye* [Pāṇini 3.2.20] has its scope in cases where *kṛ* is used with a different word as an upapada—for instance, *śrāddhaṃ karoti* resulting in *śrāddhakara*. However, when *śam* is the upapada of *kṛ*, both rules would apply to form a name, as in *śaṅkarā* (a bird so named).

For she (the base *śī*) possesses that suffix (*t*), and that notion (*saṃjñā*); thus, because it is subsequent, the suffix *ṭa* would apply. However, by the repeated mention of "root" (*dhātu*), the suffix *ṭa*—which is prescribed for the root alone—is set aside, and only *ap* occurs. The phrase "connected with *sup*" is supplied [to the rule] because *śī* is intransitive.

Since an intransitive verb can have a locus (*adhikaraṇa*) as its object, the term *sup* is connected here [in the rule], and not the term *karman* (object). Regarding the statement "an addition must be made for *pārā* and so on":
this introduction is for the purpose of excluding the locus (*adhikaraṇa*).
The phrase "pārābhyām" indicates that the word ending in the third case is the *upapada*.
In the cases of *uraḥśayaḥ* and *pṛṣṭhaśayaḥ*, it should likewise be understood that the *upapada* ends in the third case. Regarding "digdhasahaśayaḥ":
since he lies with (*saha*) one who is smeared (*digdha*), the compound is formed by the rule of *yogavibhāga* (separation of rules) under [Pāṇini 2.1.29], "the third case."

The compound with the upapada occurs after the suffix has been applied and prior to the arising of the case-ending; for example, *girau* and so forth. When *giri* is the upapada, the suffix *ḍa* is applied to the root *śī* in the Vedic domain, resulting in *giriśaḥ*.

The elision of the *ṭi* portion occurs because it is marked with the *ṭi*-indicator. All this is established by the word "variously" (*bahulam*) in [Pāṇini 3.1.85]. *Bālamanoramā*: Regarding the rule 744, 3.2.15, *adhikaraṇe śeteḥ*.
The meaning is that when a word ending in a case-suffix (*subanta*) expressive of the locus (*adhikaraṇa*) is used as an upapada, the suffix *ac* is added to the root *śīṅ*.
Regarding the phrase "pārādiṣu":
here, the term "expressing the locus" (adhikaraṇavācinī) is not connected [to the rule]. Indicating this, he provides the example: "pārābhyām."
"Regarding 'when *uttāna* and others are the agents':
this is a Vārttika.
Its meaning is that when words such as *uttāna* and others, denoting the agent, are used as upapadas, the suffix *ac* is applied after the root *śīṅ*."
"Upon the mountain":
this is a *vārttika*.
When "upon the mountain" (*girau*) is the upapada, there is the elision of the *ṭi* (the first vowel and following consonant) even of the root *śīṅ*.

Although this [suffix] ought to be explained within the Vedic system itself, nevertheless, it is explained here with the intention of demonstrating that in common usage (*loka*), the suffix *ḍa* does not occur, but rather the suffix *ac*. With this in mind, he provides an example of the suffix *ac* in common usage: *giriśayaḥ*. Why? Because the suffix *ḍa* is impossible in common usage; such is the intended meaning.
He explains: "It has a mountain," and so forth.

From the *Bālamano ramā*: "After the root *hṛ* [meaning 'to take'], when combined with *dṛti* and *nātha*, [the suffix *ka* is applied] in the sense of 'a beast' (Pāṇini 3.2.15). *Dṛti* means a leather bag.
The commentary states: *dṛtihariḥ* means *āā*.
It is an explanation of the word *nātha*: "the nose-rope. This means the rope passed through the nose.
Regarding "nāthahari":

this term is conventionally used for a specific type of animal with a rope passed through its nose. [The rule] "the formation of another suffix is for the sake of the feminine suffix ṅīp" means that because it has the marker *ṭi*, the suffix *ṅīp* is applied. [The statement] "this undertaking is for the purpose of excluding the sense of location" means...
This is already established by the preceding rule regarding the locative case.
For example: *bhikṣāñ carati* becomes *bhikṣācaraḥ*; *senāñ carati* becomes *senācaraḥ*.
The word *ādāya* is a form ending in the suffix *lyap*.

In the term *ādāyacaraḥ* (one who moves after taking), the suffix is applied because the object to be taken (*ādātavya-karman*) is not intended to be expressed, and only the prior time (*pūrvākāla*) is intended.
That is to say, it means "one who moves having performed the act of taking.
Therefore, the objection that the suffix cannot be established due to a lack of semantic competency (*asāmarthya*) arising from mutual dependence (*sāpekṣatva*) is not to be raised.

Even if it depends on the action (*karman*), there is no fault even so; by the force of the statement, the suffix occurs even when there is no [actual] capacity. The word *puras* is derived with the suffix *asi* according to the rule *pūrvādharāvarāṇāmasi puradhavaścaiṣām* (Pāṇini 5.3.39).
The word *agrataḥ* also ends in the suffix *tasi*, according to the supplementary rule (*vārttika*) *tasiprakaraṇe ādyādibhya upasaṃkhyānam*. [The form] *agre* [is likewise].
The substitution of the vowel *e* for the final syllable of the word *agra* is prescribed as an irregularity (*nipātana*) so that the form *agresaraḥ* may be obtained.

Now, one might object: "Is this not already established by the non-elision (*aluk*) of the locative case? True; when it is established, the suffix occurs with a locative case-ending as its governing word (*upapada*).

However, when [the analysis is] *agraḥ sarati* ("one who goes in front") or *agreṇa sarati* ("one who goes by means of the front"), where there is no locative ending, it would not be established; for that purpose, the substitution of the vowel *e* is prescribed as an irregularity. [The rule continues: "The suffix occurs when the word *pūrva*, denoting the agent, is the governing word."

By this [sūtra], the word *kartari* (in the sense of the agent) qualifies the *upapada* (the subordinate term), not the agent itself; thus he shows that the meaning of the suffix is being indicated. This is because the indication of that [meaning] is already established by the rule *kartari kṛt* [Pāṇini 3.4.67]. The intention is that an explicit mention here would be improper.

But surely there is a lack of semantic capacity (*asāmarthya*) in the case of *pūrvaḥ sarati* ("the one in front goes"); for this word *pūrva* denotes either a relative position (*vyavasthā*) or a part (*avayava*).

In the former case, a limit (*avadhi*) must be expected—such that "this is prior to that"—while in the latter, the referent is a whole (*avayavin*), as in "the front of the body. Since both cases require a correlative, and since there is a lack of semantic capacity when such a requirement exists, would there not be a failure of the suffix to arise? This is not a fault; for the word *pūrva* is a relative term (*sambandhiśabda*).

Surely, a grammatical operation (*vṛtti*) does indeed occur even when there is a requirement for expectancy (*sāpekṣa*), as in the example "Devadatta’s teacher’s family" (*devadattasya gurukulam*). These [words], however, are not *upapadas*. For if they were *upapadas*, the mention of the verbal root (*dhātu*) in rule 3.2.14 would be purposeless;
that mention was made specifically to prohibit the suffix *ṭa* after the root *kṛñ* when followed by *hetu* and the others.

If these were *upapadas*, there would be no possibility at all for the application of the suffix *ṭa*; consequently, the mention of "root" (*dhātu*) [in the rule] would be purposeless. Therefore, these are neither *upapadas* nor meanings of the suffix, because the agent (*kartṛ*) is the meaning of the suffix according to the rule *kartari kṛt* (Pāṇini 3.4.67).
Furthermore, it is not logical that they should cause a sublation [of that rule], as there is no contradiction.
Thus, it is appropriate that these function as qualifiers of the meaning of the suffix.
In that context, the suffix occurs in the sense of the agent (kartṛ), such that when it is expressed, its specific qualifications—such as being a cause (hetu) and so forth—are understood.
For this very reason, he says: "when the sense of cause, habitual disposition (tācchīlya), or compliance (ānulomya) is to be understood.
And: "a cause (hetu) is an unambiguous factor (aikāntikaṃ kāraṇam)."

By this, he shows that the word *hetu* (cause) refers to a worldly cause and not to a technical one. A technical cause is an instigator (*prayojaka*) of an independent agent (*svatantra-kartṛ*). If its inclusion here were intended, the form *kṛñaḥ* would be untenable; for the suffix *ṇic* does not arise in the sense of an instigator from a root ending in *ṇi*, but rather the suffix arises from a root already containing the sense of *ṇi* within itself. If it is argued that this is not so because the meaning of *ṇi* is not perceived in a form ending in the suffix *ap* [as in *kāra*], [we reply: this is not the case. (Note: The argument concerns the grammatical derivation of the term *hetu* in the context of Pāṇini’s rule *hetumati ca* [3.1.26]. The opponent suggests that the technical *hetu*—an agent who prompts another—is excluded because the suffix *ṇic* cannot be added to a root ending in *ṇi*. The author refutes this by pointing out that the meaning of *ṇi* is indeed present in forms like *kāra* via the suffix *ap*, which carries the force of *ṇi*.)

But surely, when a worldly cause (*laukika-hetu*) is apprehended, the agent (*kartṛ*) is distinguished by way of being its instrumental cause (*nimitta*); and that is incorrect, for there is no such thing as an "instrumental cause" of an agent that would need to be excluded by this qualification? This is not a fault. For once the status of the agent as an instrumental cause is established, the term *hetu* (cause) being employed again makes known its absolute necessity (*aikāntikatva*): namely, that the agent who is the absolute cause of [the action]. It is for this very reason it has been said: "The cause is the absolute instrument (*kāraṇa*).
*Ānulomyam* means "I act in conformity," which is the following of the mind of the one to be propitiated.

Regarding the term *yaśaskarī*: by the rule *ataḥ kṛkamikaṃsa* [Pāṇini 8.3.46] and others, the *visarjanīya* is replaced by *s*. From the *Bālamanoramā*: "In the sense of cause, habitual action, or favorability, after the root *kṛ*. (3.2.20) "The word *hetu* means a cause (*kāraṇa*)."
*Ānulomya* is the conforming to the mind of the one to be propitiated.
Regarding the phrase "among those things to be illuminated," the intended meaning is that the agent alone is what is expressed by the suffix.
However, the meaning is not "when *hetu* and so forth are upapadas," because of the [author's] own explanation.
It should also be understood as "when a *karman* is the upapada. Anticipating the objection that the rule *kupvoḥ* [would apply] to produce the jihvāmūlīya [visarga], he says: *ataḥ kṛ-kami*.
He provides an example regarding the reason (*hetu*): "Knowledge brings fame.
Here, knowledge is the cause of fame.
"One who performs ancestral rites" [is another example].
The meaning is that one whose nature is to perform the *śrāddha* rites.
"One who acts like a forest-dweller" (*vanakara*) means one who follows the instructions of his teacher and others.
Regarding the rule *bāla-manoramā-nāḍī-muṣṭyoś-ca* (7.3.20), it is stated that "the correspondence [of the respective terms] is not intended.
This, however, is clear from the Bhāṣya.
The terms *ghaṭī*, *khārī*, and so forth are clear. Regarding the phrase "according to what is appropriate":

the word *divā* (by day) is connected with [the rule] *supi*; because that [word] is primarily a locus (*adhikaraṇa*), it cannot logically function as an object (*karman*). However, since the remaining [words] are primarily entities (*sattva*), they can logically function as objects when connected with the verb *karoti* (to do); thus, they are connected with the term "object" (*karmaṇi*).

"The undertaking [of this treatise] is for the sake of [explaining] the meaning of 'no cause' and so forth," because [the refutation of] causes and the like has already been established by the preceding [work].
"The Sun" (Bhāskara).

But how is there a *s* here, since for the *s*, by the rules for *ru* and *visarjanīya*—namely, *kupvoḥ ka pau ca* [Pāṇini 8.3.37]—there ought to be either a *visarjanīya* or a *jihvāmūlīya*? To this he says: "Because of the irregular formation (*nipātana*) of the *s*," and so forth.
The very pronunciation of the *s* in the word *bhāskarānta* is itself the irregular formation. As in the example: *bahukaraḥ*.
The word *bahu* signifies abundance. Regarding the term *ahaskaraḥ*:
by the rule "of *ahan*" [Pāṇini 8.2.69], the *n* is replaced by *r*, which then becomes a *visarjanīya*.
In the case of *dhanuṣkaraḥ* and *aruṣkaraḥ*, the substitution of *s* [for *ṣ*] occurs by the rule *ataḥ kṛkami* (Pāṇini 8.3.46),
while the substitution of *ṣ* [for *s*] occurs by the rules [8.3.44 and 8.3.45].

Now, for what purpose is the inclusion of the word *ananta*? Since the word *ananta* also ends in *anta*, would it not suffice by the rule of "extension to that which ends in [the specified element]" (*tadantavidhi*) simply by mentioning *anta*? This is not the case; for in every rule involving an *upapada* (a subordinate word), an extension to that which ends in [the specified element] is not desired. Thus, the author of the *Vārttika*, the *Padakāra*, recites: "In a rule concerning an *upapada*, the mention of *bhaya*, *ḍāc*, and so forth, necessitates an extension to that which ends in [those elements]" (Pāṇini 1.1.73, Vārttika 9). If that is so, one might then object: "In the case of *nānatakaraḥ* and *anantakaraḥ*, a negative compound (*nañsamāsa*) could also occur with the word *anta*? Such a doubt should not be raised; for there would be a fault regarding the accent (*svara*).

For if [the word *ananta*] were present, the accent of the negative particle (*nañ*) would apply by the rule "In a *tatpuruṣa* compound, [the accent is that of] the first member when it has the same meaning [as the second]" (Pāṇini 6.2.2), and so on.

Consequently, the word *anantakara* would be acute-accented on its first syllable, because the negative particle is prescribed to be acute-accented by the rule "Indeclinables are acute-accented on the first syllable" (Phiṭ-sūtra 4.80). However, according to the rule "A *kṛt*-suffix [is acute-accented on the first syllable] after a prefix, a kāraka, or an upapada" (Pāṇini 6.2.138), the latter member of the compound would have the accent of its own base-form, resulting in an oxytone (acute-accented on the final syllable).
Therefore, the mention of *ananta* must be made. [This is stated in the verse: "The prescription of *aj* applies to *kim*, *yat*, *tat*, and *bahu*," and so forth.

The rule for the suffix *ac* must be prescribed when *kim* and so forth are used as governing words (*upapada*). But how is it that the suffix *ṭa* also follows here? [The answer is: by the maxim of the *māṇḍūkakalpa* (the frog-leap principle), *ac* also follows; furthermore, the mention of *vibhāṣā* (optionally) is also understood.

Because of the understanding that this is a fixed option (*vyavasthitavibhāṣā*), *ac* alone occurs after *kṛñ* when followed by *kim*, *yat*, *tat*, or *bahu*; whereas in the remaining cases, such as those beginning with *dvi*, only *ṭa* occurs.

Moreover, since the purpose of this rule's commencement is to exclude meanings such as "cause" (*hetu*) and so on, when specific meanings like "cause" are not intended to be expressed, then *ac* is prescribed after *kṛñ* following *kim*, *yat*, *tat*, or *bahu*; but when those specific meanings are intended, only *ṭa* occurs by virtue of the preceding sūtra.
Thus this application is established: "This birth is a 'servant' (kiṃkarī).

A servant is one whose nature is to serve; [here] it does nothing at all—that is to say, it is purposeless. Regarding the phrase "in the sense of the object," this is a mention of the word's own form.
Whence is this [known]? From the force of the inclusion of the word "action" (*karman*).

If the inclusion here were of the technical (Pāṇinian) "object," then the inclusion of the word "action" would be purposeless; for [the category of] "object" is already under discussion, and since the root *kṛ* is transitive, it will be connected with that very [technical object].

And thus it was stated previously: both [terms], "in the object" (*karmaṇi*) and "in a *sup*-ending word" (*supi*), recur [from the preceding rules]. Among these, in the case of transitive verbs, the term "in the object" applies; elsewhere, the term "in a *sup*-ending word" applies.
Therefore, this is indeed a mention of the actual form (*svarūpagrahaṇa*).
This is what is meant by "the mention of the object."

*Karma* means activity; its *nirdeśa* (designation) is its price. [The suffix] *ṭa* is obtained in the sense of cause (*hetu*) and so forth, by the rule *kṛño hetu* [Pāṇini 3.2.20]. Regarding the statement "it should be stated that [the suffix applies] in the case of rice (*vrīhi*) and a calf (*vatṣa*)," the mention of *vrīhi* and *vatṣa* serves to specify the agent (*kartṛ*).
The meaning is that this rule must be explained in such a way that what is prescribed by this *sūtra* occurs only when *vrīhi* and *vatsa* are the agents (*kartṛ*).

In this regard, the explanation is as follows: here too the term *vibhāṣā* (optionally) is understood to carry over, and it is a restricted option (*vyavasthitavibhāṣā*). Therefore, it will apply only when *vrīhi* and *vatsa* are the agents, and not elsewhere.

Because it is a permanent [term], the first syllable of the subsequent word is udātta. Regarding the phrase "when *paśu* is the agent," this indicates that the mention of *paśu* is a qualifier of the agent, which is the meaning of the suffix. Its status as the meaning of the suffix, however, follows from the rule "kṛt suffixes [denote] the agent" (Pāṇini 3.4.67).

But how is it determined that [the suffix] is merely a qualifier of the meaning of the suffix, and not rather its sublater? To this it is said: because a suffix is prescribed after a verbal root, the suffix must occur when there is a relation between the meaning of that [root] and something else which is to be expressed.
The meaning of the root is action (*kriyā*), and its relation is with a means (*sādhana*), not with the essential nature of the thing itself.
And the means is power (*śakti*), not the essential nature of the thing itself.

By the word "animal" (*paśu*), one expresses its own referent by way of its actual substance (*vastusvarūpa*), not by way of its capacity (*śaktisvarūpa*). Therefore, when the animal is made known as being devoid of capacity, it is not fit to be the meaning of the suffix.
Since that [meaning of the base] is not the meaning of the suffix, how could it, being powerless, sublate this meaning of the suffix?

Therefore, the meaning of the suffix prevails; thus it is rightly said that "the agent is qualified by it" in the case of the statement "in the sense of the agent when [the action is performed] upon an animal.
This principle should be observed elsewhere as well regarding the qualification of the meaning of a suffix. For example: "I invoke thee, accompanied by the Brāhmaṇas, accompanied by the Kṣatriyas."
In the intended sense of "he desires the *brāhmaṇ*-hood" or "he desires the *kṣatra*-hood," the suffix *-in* is applied.
From that [form ending in *-in*], the second case (*dvitīyā*) is used; its elision occurs by the rule *supāṃ suluk* [Pāṇini 7.1.39].
From the word *yuṣmad*, the substitute *tvā* is applied by the rule *yuṣmacchabdāddvitīyādibhakteḥ* [Pāṇini 8.1.23].
Regarding "gosanim": the meaning is "one who acquires a cow" (*gāṃ sanati*), with the suffix *in*.
When *am* follows that which ends in this suffix, there is the substitution of the preceding form (*pūrvarūpatva*).
"Pathirakṣī" means "those who protect the path"; this is a dual form, with the long vowel resulting from the substitution of the homogeneous vowel (pūrvasavarṇadīrghatva).
Regarding the term "havirmathīnām": having analyzed the compound as *haviḥ mathanti*, the suffix [ṇini] is applied;
from that [stem ending in the suffix], the genitive plural is formed. [The phrase] "from the causative" (*ṇyantāt*) refers to this.
By this, he dispels the doubt that this is an indication (*nirdeśa*) of the root *ayami* belonging to a different verbal base (*prakṛtyantara*).
Why, then, is it determined to be a causative form (*ṇyanta*)? Because of the presence of the marker *ś* in the suffix *khaś*.
If it were intended to include a different verbal base, the addition of the marker *ś* would be purposeless.
Indeed, that [the designation *śit*] is made for the purpose that, when a *sārvadhātuka* suffix follows, the rule for *śap*—which is dependent upon it—may take effect.

Now, whether the root *ej-* exists as a separate verbal base or not, there is no difference whatsoever regarding the presence or absence of *śap*. However, when the term *ṇi* is included [in the rule], the application of the *śit* marker becomes meaningful.
If that were absent, there would be the elision of *ṇi*; but when it is present, since *śap* is conditioned by the *sārvadhātuka* suffix, the elision of *ṇi* does not occur.

Some maintain that the status of being an *ārdhadhātuka* suffix causes the elision of the *ṇi* affix, but this is incorrect; for the addition of the marker *śit* would be for the sake of what follows.
If that were not present, then in the subsequent rule, there would be the substitution of *ā* for *dhā*, and the replacement of *dhmā* by *dham* would not occur.
Consequently, forms such as *stanandhayaḥ* and *nāsikandhamaḥ* would not be established.

Therefore, the causative nature (*ṇyantatva*) should be understood from that very commentary itself: "This letter *kh* is for the purpose of elision (*mum-artha*)," so that the augment *mum* may occur by the rule [Pāṇini 6.3.67], which operates under the governing heading [of 6.3.66].

"Śakāra has the purpose of providing the designation *sārvadhātuka*," meaning that the designation *sārvadhātuka*— as prescribed by [Pāṇini 3.4.113] "That which is marked with *ti* or *ś* is *sārvadhātuka*"— should apply. For example,
in the form *aṅgamejayaḥ*.
The *śap* suffix [is applied], followed by the substitution of *guṇa* and *āyādeśa*. Regarding the phrase "in the section on *khaś*" and so forth:

when words such as *vāta* and others are used as *upapadas*, an addition (*upasaṃkhyāna*) must be made to the roots *aja* ("to move, to throw," DhP 230), *dheṭ* ("to drink," DhP 902), *tuda* ("to afflict," DhP 1281), and *ohāk* ("to abandon," DhP 1090) within the section on *khaś*.
The word *upasaṃkhyāna* means "explanation" or "formulation."
In this regard, the following is the demonstration: in the rule [Pāṇini 3.2.30], there is the letter *ca*; and that has the sense of including what has not been mentioned.
By means of that, the suffix *khaś* will occur after verbal roots beginning with vowels when words such as *vāta* and others are used as upapadas. For example:
*śunindhayaḥ*.
The shortening [of the vowel] occurs by [Pāṇini 6.3.66].
Regarding the rule *śadrdhañjahāḥ*:

there is *ślu* substitution for the *śap* suffix after roots of the *juhotyādi* class; there is reduplication by [Pāṇini 6.1.10] because of the *ślau* condition; and there is the elision of the long *ā* by [Pāṇini 6.4.112] *śnābyasatyorātaḥ*. By the rule *stane dheṭaḥ* and others, he shows the examples while demonstrating the connection with the respective *upapadas* as appropriate.
Regarding the phrase "nāsikandhamaḥ":
the substitution of *dham* is applied by the rule [Pāṇini 7.3.78] beginning with *pāghrā*.
As for the passage beginning with "And this," etc.:
He states the reason for the absence of the rule regarding "as many as there are" (yathāsaṃkhya):

For the word *stana* has fewer syllables than *nāsikā*; since its prior placement ought to have been made according to the rule, the fact that it is not so placed indicates a deviation from the general characteristic.
Just as here the rule concerning prior placement deviates and does not apply to its own domain, so too does the characteristic of "as many as there are."
Therefore, from this sign of the deviation of the definition, the absence of a correspondence in order is obtained. Regarding the word "udi":
this is a locative case—meaning "when *ud* is present.
In that context, the distribution of the domains for the words *ut* and *kūla* is to be observed.
Because of the rule *[[1.4.80]]*, the word *ut* follows immediately after the verbal root, and the word *kūla* precedes it.

Alternatively—{the reading *uditi* is printed in the manuscript}—the term *udi* is a locative of reference (*parasaptamī*), meaning that the word *kūla* has the status of an *upapada* when *ut* follows it. [Objection:

Why does the word *ut* itself not also receive the designation of *upapada*, since there is a separate mention of the locative case for each? [Response: This is the style of the Teacher: wherever the status of *upapada* applies to each member individually, he expresses the locative case for the entire aggregate, as in the rule *nāḍīmuṣṭyoḥ* [[3.2.30]].
But here, since the reverse has been done, it does not constitute an *upapada*.
Furthermore, because the roots *ruj* and *vah* are transitive, the rule "after [a root] with an object" (*karmaṇi*) applies here;
however, the status of being an object is impossible for the word *ucchabda*, because it denotes a non-substantiality (*asattvavācitvāt*).
How can that [word] be an upapada?
In the case of *kūlamudrujaḥ*, [the suffix] *śa* is applied because it belongs to the *tud*-class; in the case of *kūlamudvahaḥ*, likewise.

Regarding *vahaṃlihaḥ*: since the root *liha* means "to taste" (*liha āsvādane*, Dhātupāṭha 1016), the *śap* suffix is elided due to its belonging to the *adādi* class; furthermore, because it is marked with the *ṅ* indicatory letter, there is an absence of *guṇa* substitution by [Pāṇini 1.1.5]. Regarding *prasthampacā* and *droṇampacā*:

the words *prastha* and *droṇa* are used figuratively (*upacāreṇa*) to refer to rice and other grains measured by those amounts; they do not refer solely to the specific measures themselves, such as the wooden vessels made of wood and so forth.

For here, the root *pac* signifies "moistening. And since moistening is not possible for a primary object such as a *prastha* (a measure of capacity), its connection [with the measure] is not tenable.

For this very reason, there can be no apprehension of the word's own form [as the primary meaning]; for a connection with the root *pac*, which denotes moistening, is not possible with a measure (*parimāṇa*) that has its own form as the predominant factor.

For although the word *prastha* and others denote that which is measured (*parimeya*), nevertheless, their designation as a measure (*parimāṇa*) is not contradicted, because they first function as measures. [The rule] "the beginning is for the sake of what is not a measure" is stated because [the formation] would already be established by the preceding rule in the case of a measure;
however, this is necessary because the words *mita* and *nakha* do not denote a measure.

For *mita-śabda* always denotes a measurable substance, whereas *nakha-śabda* denotes a limb of a living being. Regarding the term *aruntuda*: after the vowel *u* of the word *arus*, the augment *mum* is added by [Pāṇini 6.3.67]; then there is the elision of the final consonant of the conjunct (*saṃyogāntalopa*) by [8.2.23], followed by the substitution of a homogeneous sound (*parasavarṇa*) by [8.4.58]. Regarding *asūryampaśyāḥ*:
the substitute *paśya* is applied by the rule beginning with *prāghrā-* [7.3.78].
"Because of the connection of the negative particle with the term 'seeing' (*dṛśin*). This is the reason for the lack of semantic competency (*asāmarthya*).
For in this case, it is the act of seeing that is negated, not the sun itself.
Therefore, the negative particle (*nañ*) is connected only with the verb *paśyati* (to see), and not with *sūrya*; thus, there is a lack of semantic competency (*asāmarthya*).
By stating "they do not see the sun" (*sūryaṃ na paśyanti*), he demonstrates the connection of the negative particle with the verb *paśyati*.
When the sun is negated, the suffix must certainly not be applied, because it would not express the intended meaning.
This compound occurs even in the absence of syntactic expectancy (*asāmarthya*), because it is expressive (*gamakatvāt*) or because of this very statement.

Now, one might object: "Just as in the case of 'the king's wives do not see the sun,' so too [they do not see] other things such as other men; therefore, it is improper to specify [the sun] with a single qualifier. To this he says: "And this is intended for concealment (*guptiparam*)."

The statement "the wives of the king are not to be seen by the sun" (*asūryampaśyā rājadārāḥ*) is primarily intended for concealment (*gupti*), because it is employed for the purpose of establishing such concealment.

By the words "in this very way," etc., he demonstrates that its purpose is concealment. Regarding the form *ugrampaśya*, although [the rule] *dṛśeḥ khaś* [Pāṇini 3.2.64] would have applied, the suffix *khaś* is here treated as an irregularity (*nipātyate*).
As before, there is the substitution of *paśya*.
Regarding the term *irammadaḥ*:
it means "one who intoxicates with *ira*."
The root *mad* is used in the sense of "joy" (*harṣe*; Dhātupāṭha 1208).
Although suffixes such as *tṛc* would have been applicable, the suffix *khaś* is here prescribed by irregular derivation (*nipātyate*).
In that context, since the root belongs to the *divādi* class, the suffix *śyan* would have been applicable; its absence is also prescribed by irregular derivation.
Regarding the term *pāṇindhamāḥ*:
although the suffix *lyuṭ* would normally be expected in the sense of a locus (*adhikaraṇa*), the suffix *khaś* is prescribed as an irregularity (*nipātana*).

As before, the substitution of *dham* [for *dhmā*] takes place. The inclusion of the letter *ca* [in the sūtra] is for the purpose of qualifying [the rule] "there is shortening when *khaś* follows" (*khaci hrasvaḥ*).

If it were stated simply as *khe hrasvaḥ*, the shortening would apply even to the suffix *khaś*. One might object: "But surely, by the rule that when a suffix with one indicatory letter (*anubandha*) is mentioned, a suffix with two indicatory letters is not included (Vyāḍīya-paribhāṣā 52), this will not occur. To this he replies: "In that case, since one must rely on that technical rule (*paribhāṣā*), it is considered simpler to actually include the letter *c* [in the suffix]. One might further object: "But then forms such as *priyaṃvadaḥ* and *vaśaṃvadaḥ* are already established even with *khaś*; for what purpose is a separate suffix being created? He says: "The creation of a separate suffix is for the sake of subsequent rules."

In this context [of rule 3.2.39], another suffix is introduced for the purpose of ensuring that the short vowel occurs when *khac* follows *tāp*, as well as for the elision of the *ṇi*-affix, and so forth. Why, then, is *khac* not applied directly in the subsequent rule itself? It is for the sake of making it understood that *khac* also occurs here.

By this, the suffix *khac* is established for the root *gam* as well when a word ending in a *su*-affix (*sup*) is the upapada. If it is argued that "there is an addition (*upasaṃkhyāna*) of *gam* in the section on *khac*" (Vārttika 247), then in that context, another suffix is introduced for the purpose of providing the explanation (*pratipādana*) by means of the term "addition. This very [rule] should be understood as that explanation: "And *viha* [is substituted] for *vihāyas*.
When the word *vihāyas* is the upapada of the root *gam*, the suffix *khac* is applied, and by its co-occurrence (*sanniyoga*), the word *vihāyas* undergoes the substitution of *vihā*.
"It should be stated that [the suffix] *kha* is marked with the indicatory letter *ḍ*.

Because of this *ḍ*-indicatory letter (*ḍittva*), there would be elision of the final vowel (*ṭilopa*), since this word is recited separately from the rule "for *vihāyas*, [substitute] *viha*" (Vārttika 248). This is for the purpose of indicating that the property of having the *ḍ*-indicatory letter (*ḍittva*) is not universally obligatory (*anitya*); otherwise, the form *vihaṅgama* would not be established. [The rule] "and before the suffix *ḍe*" (*ḍe ca*), etc., [is cited].
And when the suffix *ḍa* follows the root *gam*, there is the substitution of *vihā* for *vihāyas*.
Thus, "vihaga" (bird).
But does the suffix *ḍa* not [otherwise] apply here? It occurs precisely by virtue of this specific rule.

Alternatively, he will state later on: "In the section on *ḍa*, it is seen in other cases as well" (Vārttika 256). [The phrase] "the inclusion of both" is used because there is no distinction between the two states when the suffix *ṇic* is applied. [The term] "the instruction contains two *t* sounds" is used.

In the rule "dviṣatparayoḥ," there are two *t* sounds; one of these is a constituent part (*avayava*) of the word *dviṣat*. By means of that [part], the word *dviṣat* is qualified—namely, that the word *dviṣat* is the governing condition (*upapada*) when it ends in *t*. Consequently, [the suffix] does not occur in the feminine, because [the word] ending in a feminine suffix does not end in *t*.

However, if the second *takāra* were not present, then by the rule "when a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) is mentioned, that which is qualified by gender is also included" (Vyāḍiparibhāṣā 29), it would apply even to the feminine form.
Thus, one would have *dviṣatīkāśikā*, [and] *dviṣatī*,
with the suffix *ṅīp* applied according to Pāṇini 4.1.45.
Because the word *dviṣat* ends in the present participle suffix *śatṛ* according to [Pāṇini 3.2.131], which prescribes the *ugit* designation. Regarding the term *śāstrita*:

having analyzed it as "done in the *śāstra*," one adds the causative suffix *ṇic* to the nominal stem *śāstra* in the sense of the verbal root's meaning; then, when the suffix *kta* is applied after that form, one obtains *śāstrita*.
The meaning is "prescribed by the *śāstra*."
Alternatively, "śāstrita" means one who has proceeded from this [path] taught by the *śāstra*, that is, one born from or engaged in the knowledge of the *śāstra*.
Or else, the word *śāstra* should be viewed as belonging to the *tārakādi* group;
thus, "śāstrita" means one for whom the *śāstra* has arisen.

Regarding the term *vācaṃyama*: it is derived by analyzing it as *vācaṃ yacchati* ("one who restrains speech"). By the rule *khaci* (Pāṇini 6.3.69), the absence of the augment *mum* in the first member is prescribed as a nipātana (irregularity). Now, one might object: "The suffix itself will be established by that very same nipātana; so what is the purpose of this [separate statement]? This is not the case. When the suffix *ac* is applied according to the rule *pacādyac*, and then a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*) is formed as *vāco yamaḥ*, the form *vācaṃyama* is successfully derived.
It indeed results [in the desired form], but in that case, the irregular derivation (*nipātana*) would be purposeless.
And this being so, the compound with an *upapada* would not be obligatory.
Therefore, the suffix *khac* must be prescribed, and the irregular derivation must also be performed—as in the word "dāri."

The root *dṛ* in the sense of "tearing apart" (*vidāraṇe*) is indicated here with the suffix *ṇic*. In the word *purandaraḥ*, the substitution of *mu* for the initial [of the prefix] is prescribed as an irregularity (*nipātana*). Regarding this, it is stated: "And [the substitution of *mu* occurs] after *bhaga* when [the root] *dṛ* follows."
The meaning is that this form of the rule—"the suffix *khac* occurs when *bhaga* is the upapada after the root *dṛ*"—must be explained.

The explanation here is as follows: the particle *ca* ("and") is carried over from [Pāṇini 3.2.37], and it does not serve to include what has not been mentioned; therefore, the suffix *khac* occurs when *bhaga* is the upapada after the root *dṛ*. Regarding the word "sarvaṅkaṣaḥ":

the roots *kaṣ*, *khaṣ*, *śiṣ*, *jaṣ*, *jaṣ*, *śaṣ*, *vaṣ*, *maṣ*, *ruṣ*, and *riṣ* have the sense of "to injure" (Dhātupāṭha 685–694). Regarding the phrase "in the case of a rule for an upapada," and so forth:

But surely the word *abhaya* is already established as a *nañ*-compound? It cannot be so; for since the [suffix-accent] is *satiśiṣṭa*, the rule *tatpuruṣe tulyārtha* [Pāṇini 6.2.2] would cause the initial syllable of the first member to be udātta by its original accent. However, by the rule *gatikārakopapadāt kṛt* [Pāṇini 6.2.139], beginning with *gatikārakopapadānām*, a final udātta is desired.
Therefore, it must be formed [as a *tatpuruṣa*].

Because it is an exception (*apavāda*), [the suffix] *khac* subverts *aṇ*; and when there is a desire to express [the meanings of] "cause" (*hetu*) and so forth, it also subverts the suffix *ṭa* because it is subsequent [in the order of rules]. Now, why was it not stated simply as "optionally after *kṣema*, *priya*, and *madra*" (*kṣemapriyamadre vā*)? What is the purpose of including the mention of *aṇ*? One might argue that since *aṇ* will occur by the rule "after [roots ending in] *khac*, optionally" (*khaci vikalpyate*), this is unnecessary. To this he says: "When it should have been said 'optionally' (*veti vaktavye*)," and so on.

If it were stated as "optionally after *kṣema*, *priya*, and *madra*," then because of the inclusion of the word "optionally" (*vā*), even that which is obtained by default (*yathāprāpta*) would be desired [as an alternative].

Consequently, when "cause" and so forth are intended to be expressed, the suffix *ṭa* would apply by the rule "after *kṛ*, [the suffixes *ṭa* and *aṇ* are used] in the sense of cause and habitual action" (*kṛño hetutācchīlya*). Therefore, [the mention of *aṇ*] is for the sake of subverting that [suffix *ṭa*].

Therefore, when there is a desire to express the sense of "cause" (*hetu*) and so forth, the suffix *aṇ* occurs, overriding the suffix *ṭa*. Here, the condition *supi* (after a word ending in a case-suffix) applies, not the condition *karmaṇi* (after an object); for the root *bhū* is intransitive (*akarmaka*).
[The phrase] "in the word *āśita* ending in a case-suffix," etc., follows.
Now, why is the reverse not the case—that is, why is it not that the meaning of the suffix is *āśita*, with *karaṇa* and *bhāva* as attendant words (*upapada*)? Because such a thing is impossible.

The word *āśita* denotes the agent (*kartṛ*) of the root *aś* (to eat); its connection with the verb *bhavati* is not tenable. For that which is the agent of *aś* cannot possibly be the meaning of the suffix of *bhavati*.
Therefore, the word *āśita* functions as an upapada (governing word), while the other two [words, *pīna* and *kṣāma*,] function as the meaning of the suffix.
And thus, this [suffix] becomes an exception (*apavāda*) to both *ghañ* and *lyuṭ*.

By the rule of "optionality when forms are dissimilar" (*vā'sarūpa-vidhi*), *lyuṭ* also indeed occurs—as in *āśitabhavana odanaḥ* ("rice for those who have eaten"). However, because it is the very form of *ghañ*, it is precisely that which sublates [the other]. This is due to the force of the technical designation (*saṃjñā*).

For names are of two kinds: some follow the meaning of their constituent parts (*avayavārtha*), such as *saptavarṇa* ("seven-colored"); others, however, are the opposite, such as *tailapāyikā* ("oil-drinker").

Here, in cases where there is a following of the meaning of the constituent parts—as in *viāmbhara*, *śatruntapa*, and so forth—the term "in the object" (*karmaṇi*) is connected [to the suffix]: he bears the burden (*viām bibharti*) is *viāmbhara*.

But where there is no following of the meaning of the constituent parts—as in *rathantaraṃ sāma* ("the Rathantara Sāman")—there, for the sake of etymological derivation (*vyutpatti*), the term "after a nominal stem ending in a case-suffix" (*supi*) is connected: it crosses by means of a chariot (*rathena tarati*), or it crosses on a chariot (*rathe tarati*).
Regarding the term *patiṃvarā*:
it is derived from the roots *vṛñ* in the sense of "choosing" (*varaṇe*, Dhātupāṭha 1254) and *vṛṅ* in the sense of "selecting for oneself" (*sambhaktau*, Dhātupāṭha 1509).
The analytical derivation (*vigraha*) is: she chooses a husband (*patiṃ vṛṇīte*), or they choose a husband for her (*patiṃ vṛṇute*).
"Śatruñjaya" means "one who conquers enemies. Regarding the term "dhāri," it is the inclusion of the root *dhṛ* when it is in its causative (*ṇyanta*) form.
"Yugandhara" means "one who bears the yoke";
there is shortening of the first member of the compound.
"Śatruṃsaha" means "one who endures the enemy."
"He scorches the enemy" is *śatruṃtapaḥ*;
"he subdues the foe" is *ariṃdamaḥ*. Although the root *dam* is intransitive, it will nevertheless become transitive by virtue of having the causative sense (*ṇyartha*) inherent within it.
The meaning is "he who tames his enemies. Regarding the statement, "whose son is Sautangami," he shows that by the designation of the son as Sautangami, the father's name is inferred to be Sutaṅgama;
for it is only when the father's name Sutaṅgama exists that the son can be designated by the word Sautangami, not otherwise.

Now, for what purpose is this separation of rules (*yogavibhāga*)? He says that the mention of *gam* was made in the preceding rule itself: "The separation of rules is for the sake of subsequent [rules]. This is so that the application of *gam* alone may continue into the following rules, while that of *bhṛñ* and the others does not; for if they were in a single rule, those others would also carry over. "The letter *ḍ* is for the purpose of eliding the *ṭi*."

[The suffix] *ḍit* [is used] so that the elision of the final phoneme (*ṭilopa*) by the rule *ṭeḥ* [Pāṇini 6.4.155] may occur. But how can the elision of the final phoneme be obtained even when the suffix is marked with *ḍ*, given that the elision of the final phoneme is prescribed for that which bears the technical designation *bha*, and here there is no *bha*-designation? To this he says: "*ḍity abhasyāpi*" and so forth.
The sense is that if the elision of the final phoneme were not to occur even when the suffix is marked with *ḍ*, then that [marking] would be purposeless.

But surely it will be for the sake of not being heard; so how could there be pointlessness? He thinks as follows: by making this reference to the form ending in the suffix *ḍa*—derived from the root *jan* after the elision of *ṭi* according to [Pāṇini 6.4.48] (*janerḍaḥ*)—it is understood that the letter *ḍ* is for the sake of not being heard.
Regarding the phrase "in all cases" (*sarvatra*), etc., the meaning of the word *upasaṃkhyāna* is "explanation" or "formulation."
In this regard, the following is the demonstration: the particle *ca* (and) is carried over from the rule *gamaśca* [Pāṇini 3.2.47].
Because its purpose is to include what has not been explicitly mentioned, the suffix *ḍa* will apply even when there is no governing word (*upapada*), as in the case of *sarvatra* and so forth.

Furthermore, the word *sarvatra* here is connected with the term *supi*, and not with *karmaṇi*; for since that [term *karmaṇi*] primarily denotes the power of the locus (*adhikaraṇa-śakti*), it is impossible for it to function as the object (*karman*).
The word *panna* is connected with the term "object" (*karman*) because it functions as an adverbial modifier (*kriyāviśeṣaṇa*).

For it has been established in the rule *karaṇe ca stokālpa-* [Pāṇini 2.3.33] and others that an adverbial modifier possesses the status of an object. Regarding the rule *uraso lopaśca* [Pāṇini 1.1.52], there is the elision of the *sakāra*. Regarding the rule *sudūroradhikaraṇa*.
The suffix *ḍa* is prescribed as an exception (*apavāda*) to *lyuṭ*.
By the rule of "optionality of dissimilar forms" (*vā'sarūpa-vidhi*), that [suffix] also occurs: *sugamanam*, *durgamanam*.
Why is it specified as "locus" (*adhikaraṇe*)? So that it does not apply when there is an "object" (*karman*).

By the rule *īṣadduḥsuṣu* [Pāṇini 3.3.126] and others, the suffix *kha* is applied, as in *sugamaḥ* (easy to go) and *durgamaḥ* (difficult to go). Regarding *nirgo deśe*: when the word *nir* is used as a prefix (*upapada*), the suffix *ḍa* is applied to the root *gam* when the locus (*adhikaraṇa*) is a place (*deśa*). A place where one goes out from is called a *nirga* place.
