In cases other than "leaving a place," only the suffix *lyuṭ* is used—as in *nirgamanam* ("departure"). Regarding the rule "*āśiṣi*" (in the sense of a benediction): this specifies the meaning of the suffix.
That suffix occurs when the agent is such that, when it is prescribed, a benediction is understood.
"One should kill a *timi*":

this is the optative (*āśīr-liṅ*) mood. The citation of the sentence containing the usage [of the word] is for the purpose of illustrating the word *timi*, since it has the same meaning. "The bringing of wood" (*dārāvāhana*), and so forth.
Only the substitution of *ṭ* is added as a supplementary rule (*upasaṃkhyāna*). As for the suffix *aṇ*, however, it is already established by the rule "aṇ pratyayaḥ" (Pāṇini 4.1.83).

Now, what is the purpose of including the mention of "the end" (*anta*)? For would it not suffice that [the substitution] applies to the "end" according to the rule "tasmād ity uttarasya" (Pāṇini 1.1.67)? It is not the case that rules prescribed by a genitive case apply only to the final letter of a word.
And here, the root *han* is not indicated by the genitive case; rather, it is indicated by the ablative. [Objection:
But surely, by virtue of the sense, there will be a change of case—so that the genitive of *hanaḥ* will be obtained? [Response: Even so, the mention of *anta-* (end) is for the sake of clarity.
In the example "dārvāhanti" (he strikes wood), the word *dāru* ends in the accusative case.

Because [the suffix] is elided by the rule *svamornapuṃsakāt* [Pāṇini 7.1.23], the accusative case ending is not heard. Regarding the phrase *cārau vā*: here too, the substitution is prescribed optionally;
however, the suffix *aṇ* is established as obligatory by the rule *aṇ ca* [Pāṇini 3.2.1].
Thus we have *cārvāghāṭaḥ*.

The substitution of *k* [for *h*] occurs by the rule *ho hanterṇinneṣu*; the substitution of *t* occurs by the rule *[[Pāṇini 7.3.32]]*. The statement *karmaṇi sami ci* is a qualification of the very rule *karmaṇy upapade* [[Pāṇini 3.2.1]]. The logical principle that was stated regarding the word *ud* serving as an *upapada* in that context should be understood here as well regarding the word *apa*.

"The undertaking is for the sake of one who has no master," because [the formation] is already established by the preceding rule in the sense of a blessing (*āśis*). "Kumāraghātī" (one who kills a boy):
as before, there is the substitution of *t* for *t* and *k*.
"By means of *nipātana* (irregular derivation), the word *śiras* becomes *śīrṣan*.

This means that the substitution of *śiras* by *śīrṣan* occurs precisely through the *nipātana* [prescribed] in the rule *kumāraśīrṣayoḥ* [Pāṇini 5.1.69], and not by the rule *śīrṣaṃ chandasi* [Pāṇini 6.1.60]. For in that latter rule, a different word *śīrṣan*, which has the same meaning as the word *śiras*, is irregularly derived (*nipātyate*); otherwise, forms such as *śīrṣaghātī* would occur only in the Vedic language (*chandas*), and not in the common spoken language (*bhāṣā*).
Furthermore, the grammatical reference "kumāraśīrṣayoḥ" would not be appropriate, for that [word] ends in *n*; yet this reference is made with a word ending in *a*, not one ending in *n*.

The second *i* in the suffix *ṇin* is for the purpose of protecting the *n* from being designated as *it*, while the *ṇ* is for the purpose of *vṛddhi* strengthening. That by which something is characterized or marked is a "characteristic" (*lakṣaṇa*). That which possesses such a characteristic is "possessing a characteristic" (*lakṣaṇavat*); [the locative case is used] in that sense.

By this, he shows that the word *lakṣaṇa* in the Sūtra is taken with the possessive suffix *-aka* (matvarthīya). And showing that it is an adjective qualifying the agent (*kartṛ*) of the suffix, he says: "when the agent possesses the characteristic" (*lakṣaṇavati kartari*).

Now, why does the word *lakṣaṇa* not function as a subordinate word (*upapada*)? Some say: "Because the root *han* is transitive, the rule 'in the sense of the object' (*karmaṇi*) applies here; therefore, if *lakṣaṇa* were to function as an *upapada* here, it would be qualified by the object."
Furthermore, it is not tenable for the object of the root *han* (to kill) to be "characteristic" (*lakṣaṇa*), for that [root] occurs in the sense of violence, and violence concerns living beings.

As for the argument that "because husband and wife possess the qualities of living beings, their status as the object is tenable," this too is untenable; for the word *lakṣaṇa*, which ends in the possessive suffix *-aka*, can also apply to a living being.
It is understood from the very commentary itself that "characteristic" cannot function as a subordinate member of a compound.
Or because it is not so expressed;
for the designation of both the wife and the husband as the agent is observed,
as in the expression "jāyāghnaḥ" (one who kills his wife).

Due to the presence of the *kittva* (the marker *k*), there is the elision of the penultimate vowel (*upadhālopa*) by the rule *gamahana* [Pāṇini 6.4.98], and as before, there is the substitution of *gh* for *h*.
Thus, we have *patighnī*.
Because of the marker *ṭi*, the suffix *ṅīp* is applied. The phrase "when the agent is not a human" (*amanuṣyakarttṛke*) [is used].

That whose agent (*kartṛ*) is a non-human (*amanuṣya*) is described as such; and this is a qualifier of the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*), because the meaning of the root belongs to the verb *han*. Therefore, he says: "{This type of sequence does not exist in the original text} ‘when the meaning of the root has a non-human agent’,” and so forth.

Now, why is the mention of “having a non-human agent” not a qualifier of the *upapada* (the accompanying word)? Because the term *karmani* (in the sense of the object) is understood by anuvṛtti (carrying over from the previous rule), and a connection between the object and a non-human agent is logically impossible.
For a means (*sādhana*) is connected with the action (*kriyā*), not with another *kāraka* (participant in the action).
Why is this not understood as a qualifier of the agent (*kartṛ*) of the meaning of the suffix? Because that [suffix] cannot have a non-human as its agent.
For it is impossible for there to be an "agent of an agent," but rather [an agent] of an action (*kriyā*).

But surely the mention of "agent" (*kartṛ*) need not be made, since even without it, the suffix is indeed obtained when the agent is non-human? This cannot be so; for if the mention of "non-human" were employed alone without the mention of "agent," it could also be understood as a qualifier of the governing word (*upapada*).

Therefore, the mention of the "agent" (kartṛ) must be made. That being so, since it is impossible for the mention of a non-human agent to be a qualifier of that [agent], it is proper that the meaning of the verbal root (dhātvartha) alone should be qualified by it.
[Question: "Why does it not occur here?"
Because the agent is an elephant, the meaning of the verbal root has a non-human agent;

it is thought that the suffix *ṭak* must necessarily follow from this. Regarding the phrase "when capability (*śakti*) is understood," by this he refutes the status of capability as a subordinate word (*upapada*).
By the rule "when *hastika* and *kapāṭa* are the objects as co-occurring words (*upapada*)," *hastika* and *kapāṭa* are qualifiers of the meaning of the suffix.

Now, why is it not understood thus: "when *śakti* is the co-occurring word, [the suffix applies] after the roots *hasti* and *kapāṭa* when the agent is a human"? For, since this is already understood through the very force of the rule's formulation, the root *han* (to kill) must function here with respect to the meaning of the verbal root when the object is *hastika* or *kapāṭa* and the agent is a human.
And in that case, since the result would be established by the previous rule alone, the formulation of this [present] rule would be redundant.

But when these two function as *upapadas* (governed words) and their capacity (*śakti*) is understood [as being directed toward another], it is recognized that the agent is a human; thus this fault does not arise. In the example "he kills an elephant with a special [weapon]," the phrase "with poison" (*viṣeṇa*) demonstrates the lack of inherent capacity [to kill].
For one who is himself unable to kill, he kills by means of other methods such as poison. [The examples] "pāṇigha" and "tāḍagha" [are provided].

The suffix *ṭa* is applied, the substitution of *gh* occurs, and the elision of the *ṭi* is prescribed by nipātana. Regarding the term "accau": it is a bahuvrīhi compound meaning "that in which *cv-* does not exist" (*na vidyate cviryasmin tatra accau*);
or it is a tatpuruṣa compound meaning "other than *cv-*" (*cver anyaḥ acviḥ*).
The meaning is "ending in *ac*.
This qualifies *adity-ādi* and so forth.
As for the singular number, it is connected with each of those [terms] individually.
By the phrase "in the case of *āḍhaka* and so forth," [the author] refutes that *āḍhaka* and the others are qualifiers of the agent (*kartṛviśeṣaṇatva*).
By the phrase "when the instrument (*karaṇa*) is the *kāraka*," he likewise rejects that the instrument functions as a subordinate word (*upapada*).

Now, why is it not understood thus: "when the instrument is the subordinate word, and *āḍhaka* and so forth are the agents"? Regarding this, some say: "In this context, *āḍhaka* and the others are primarily words (denoting objects), and it is not possible for such things to function as agents."
Furthermore, their primacy regarding the word (*śabdapradhānatva*) is understood from the prohibition [contained in the rule] *cvyanteṣvacvau*;
for it is the word alone that becomes possessed of the suffix *-cv-*, not the meaning.
The state of having the suffix *-cv-* belongs only to the word, not to the meaning.

In that case, if these [words] were primarily expressive of meaning (arthapradhāna), the qualification "in the sense of cvi" would be inappropriate, and the prohibition "not when [the word ends in] -vat" would be redundant.

Furthermore, even the exclusion (paryudāsa) would be purposeless; this is not so, because in usages such as *tsaryāpyāḍhaḥ* ("he makes *tsarya* complete"), *subhagaśabdaḥ sukhayati* ("the word 'subhaga' makes one happy"), and so forth, the status of the agent (*kartṛtva*) is observed.
Indeed, the determination of meaning from the commentary itself is beyond reproach.

Because the instrument (*karaṇa*) is indicated as the meaning of the suffix, the rule *kartari kṛt* [Pāṇini 3.4.67] does not apply. Now, one might object: "These are not meanings of the suffix *cv-*; those [meanings] necessarily end in *cv-*, whereas here, forms such as *āḍha* and so on, which do not end in *cv-*, are simply impossible. So why are they excluded? To this he says: "Because the suffix *cv-* is prescribed optionally," and so forth. The prescription is indeed optional because of the continued application (*anuvṛtti*) of the word "optionally" (*vā*) from [Pāṇini 5.4.50]: *cvau ca*. Examples include: *āḍhaṃ tailena kurvanti* ("they make it thick with oil"), and so on.
This [oil] was not previously non-existent and then made full by oil; rather, what happens is that the *āḍha* measure is anointed with oil.
Since verbal roots have multiple meanings, the root *kṛ* here functions in the sense of "anointing.
Therefore, because there is no manifestation of something previously non-existent, this serves as a counter-example.

Alternatively—let it be granted that there is indeed the manifestation of what was previously non-existent (*abhūtaprādurbhāva*), even so, he says "when the *prakṛti* is not intended to be expressed," and so forth, in order to demonstrate that this counter-example is indeed appropriate. For it is not every manifestation of what was previously non-existent that constitutes the meaning of the suffix *cvi*; rather, it is only a specific kind. This is because the mention of *prakṛti* will be shown in that context. *Prakṛti* is the prior state of the effect.

Therefore, where the effect (*kārya*) is dependent [on a cause] and the prior commencement of that effect is intended to be expressed as being brought into existence (*bhāvyamānatayā*), there it is "the manifestation of what was not previously existent" (*abhūtaprādurbhāva*); that alone is the meaning of the suffix *cvī*.

This is what is meant: when the prior state of the effect is intended to be expressed, then the meaning of *cvī* applies; it does not apply when the intention is merely the manifestation of what was not previously existent.

However, in the present case, without referring to the prior state and without dependence on a prior commencement, only the mere transformation of something into what it was not (*abhūtatadbhāva*) is intended to be expressed.
Therefore, even though there is the state of becoming what was previously not that, the suffix *cvī* does not apply.
Consequently, this serves as a counter-example: "āḍhyīkurvanti" (they are making rich).
Here, the suffix *cvī* is applied by the rule "abhūtatadbhāve kṛbhvastiyoge" [Pāṇini 5.4.50], and the substitution of *i* for the vowel occurs by the rule "cver dīrghāt" [Pāṇini 7.4.32].

"It must be [formed] with the suffix *lyuṭ*," because the suffix *lyuṭ* is prescribed by the rule *Pāṇini 3.3.117*. If it must be formed with *lyuṭ*, he asks "What follows from that? and says: "And not," etc.
In both cases, the form is identical and the accent is the same.

First, the form is indeed not different because the compound is mandatory in both instances; for it must be a *khyun*-upapada compound, and even with *lyuṭ*, it must be a *gati*-compound according to [Pāṇini 2.2.18]. Furthermore, because of the prohibition [by Pāṇini 6.3.66], the *mum* augment cannot occur, so there is no difference in form.

Nor does the accent become a distinguishing factor: where the *nit-svara* (accent on the first syllable) would apply when *khyun* is present, the *lit-svara* (accent on the first syllable) applies in exactly the same place when *lyuṭ* is used.
"By the force of the prohibition":
the prohibition "not after *ac* or *v*" (Pāṇini 3.2.56) is formulated in order to exclude the form *āḍhyīkaraṇa*.
In this way, its exclusion is achieved if, when *khyun* is absent, *lyuṭ* also occurs; otherwise, it would certainly [apply].
The meaning is that the negation would be "that very form," which would result in pointlessness. "In terms of meaning" means not in terms of words.
The purpose, however, is simply the force of the prohibition.
The phrase "and for the sake of the subsequent [rule]" shows the utility of the following sūtra.

In this regard, there is a distinction: when *khiṣṇuc* and *khukañ* are excluded, [the suffixes] beginning with *tṛc* must occur. In the case of *khyun*, the letter *kh* is for the purpose of the elision of the *mum* augment, and the letter *n* is for the sake of the accent (*svara*). Regarding the phrase "in the sense of the agent (*kartṛ*) among the kārakas": the mention of "agent" is for the purpose of excluding the instrument (*karaṇa*). One might object: "But surely, because it has not been explicitly stated, its recurrence [from a previous rule] would not occur? This is true; however, someone might mistakenly think that just as *āṭ* and the others recur, so too does their connection [to the agent]. Therefore, [the term "agent"] is mentioned to prevent such an error.
The mention of the agent (*kartṛ*) is for the sake of what follows: "because of being acute" (*udāttatvāt*), and so forth.

That which is other than acute is grave (*anudātta*); therefore, the prohibition of *iṭ* by [Pāṇini 7.2.10], "after a monosyllabic root that is grave in its original enunciation (*upadeśe*)," does not apply to the *ardhadhātuka* suffix prescribed after the root *bhū*. Consequently, the *iṭ* characterized by [the rule] beginning with *balādi* [7.2.35] must occur; and since the status of having an initial *i* is thereby established by that very [suffix], the intention is that the status of having an initial *i* need not be explicitly stated for the suffix *khiṣṇuc*.

He states the purpose of making the suffix begin with the vowel *i* in the words beginning with "nañastu": "If *khiṣṇu* were not made to begin with *i*, then even though it would become *ikārādi* (beginning with *i*) once the augment *iṭ* is applied, nevertheless, because it would be *lākṣaṇika* (derived through a grammatical rule), it would not be included by the mention of *iṣṇuc* in [Pāṇini 6.2.160]."

Furthermore, in the case of *anāḍhambhiṣṇuḥ*, if the rule for the final acute accent (*antodāttatva*) of the subsequent member following a negative particle (*nañ*) were not applied, it would not occur; yet it is desired that it should. Therefore, the rule for the final acute accent of the subsequent member following *nañ* is established, by which the suffix *iṣṇuc* is made to begin with the vowel *i*. Now, one might object: "Even though it begins with *i*, the suffix *iṣṇuc* prescribed in the rule *alaṃkṛñādi-* (Pāṇini 3.2.136) should be the one intended for inclusion, and not the other, because that [other] has only one indicatory letter (*ekānubandhaka*), whereas this [suffix under discussion] has two indicatory letters (*dvyanubandhaka*)? [Response: There is no fault here, because the very utterance of the vowel *i* [in the technical name of the suffix] serves as the authority (*sāmarthya*) for the inclusion of this suffix as well.

The letter *kha* is for the sake of the meaning "death" (*mumūrṣā*); the letter *ca* is for the sake of the vowel; the letter *ña* is for the sake of the *vṛddhi* [vowel] increment. Regarding this, it was stated: "The two terms *karmaṇi* and *supi* are carried over [from the previous rule]. Among them, in the case of transitive verbs, *karmaṇi* applies; elsewhere, *supi* applies.

Since this root *spṛś* is transitive, when it is said that "after the root *spṛś*, provided there is a *subanta* word as an *upapada* other than 'water' (*udaka*)," one who perceives a contradiction between the preceding and following statements says: "But surely... and so forth. The resolution is given by the words beginning with "This is not... and so forth.

But how is it that when the term *kartṛ* (agent) is included and its sense of accumulation (*pracaya*) is understood, a suffix is obtained when a word ending in a case-suffix (*subanta*) is the attendant noun (*upapada*)? To this he says: "in the mere presence of a word ending in a case-suffix," and so forth.

When there is merely a word ending in a case-suffix as the attendant noun, one sense of accumulation refers to the agent when the object (*karman*) is the attendant noun, while another refers to the instrument (*karaṇa*) and so on when they are the attendant nouns. Since there is a distinction [between these cases], an accumulation of the agent—which is differentiated by the distinction of those respective relations—is thereby obtained. For example: *ghṛtaspṛk* ("one who touches ghee").
Regarding the rule *kvinpratyayasya kuḥ* and so forth:
if it were stated simply as *kvipratyayasya kuḥ*, the suffix *kvip* would also be included; therefore, the letter *n* is appended [as an it-marker].

The letter *n* is not for the purpose of making the base (*prakṛti*) udātta-accented on its first syllable, because the root *spṛś-* consists of only one vowel (*ekāc*), and thus the desired accent is already established by the accent of that [root] itself.

The letter *ka* is for the purpose of prohibiting the *guṇa* [vowel substitution]; the letter *va* is for the purpose of specification according to [Pāṇini 6.1.67]. Regarding the phrase "he sacrifices at the proper season" (*ṛtau yajati*): he sacrifices during the seasons beginning with spring; that sacrifice in which the season itself is the deity is the "season-sacrifice," and thus it means "he performs that sacrifice.
Alternatively, it means "he sacrifices as impelled by the season."
In that sacrifice where the season (*ṛtu*) is the motivator, one performs the sacrifice prompted by the season;
in this view, the suffix *ṇic* is prescribed to be elided immediately after its introduction.
[The word] "ṛtvij" [is derived in this manner].
There is vocalization (*samprasāraṇa*) because [the root] belongs to the *yajādi* class (Pāṇini 6.1.15).

The phrase "it should be understood in some way or another" indicates that it must be etymologically derived by some means or other; it shows that the meaning of the individual components is not the governing factor.
"The state of having the udātta accent on the final syllable is prescribed as a nipātana.
This is for the purpose of overriding the fixed accent.
As in "dadhṛk."
In *abhyāsa*, there is the substitution of *at* by [Pāṇini 7.4.66], the retention of the initial consonant by [Pāṇini 7.4.60], and the change to the voiced unaspirated stop (*jaśtva*).
It is stated that "the substitution of *ṣatva* is also prescribed as an irregularity" (nipātana),
because [the rule] would otherwise not apply due to the prohibition in [Pāṇini 8.3.111].
The root *ṣṇih* is listed in the Dhātupāṭha as "to love" (1200); from the form *utsnihrati*, the word *uṣṇik* is derived.

By the rule beginning with "because of being taught together with irregular forms (*nipātana*)," the purpose of teaching these [roots] together with the irregular forms is so that they may undergo certain non-grammatical (*alākṣaṇika*) operations.
Consequently, a certain non-grammatical operation occurs in these cases.

This, however, is non-characteristic (alākṣaṇika)—namely, that which occurs even when the verb is transitive (*sakarmaka*), provided only a *subanta* (inflected nominal) follows as an attendant word (*upapada*).

In the case of *prāṅ*, there is the application of *num* by [Pāṇini 7.1.70], the elision of the *hal* and *ṅī* suffixes by [6.1.66], and the elision of the initial consonant cluster by [8.2.23]; then, as before, the *k*-substitution (*kutva*) of the letter *n*.
Regarding the term "from the simple [root] alone" (*kevalāt*):
even though the rule *supi* (Pāṇini 3.2.4) is in force, the suffix occurs only from a root that lacks an upapada, because of the indication by the rule for the irregular form (*nipātana*) *saha*;
or else, it is due to the force of the prescription of the *kvin* suffix.
For when there is an *upapada*, the suffix *kvip* ought to occur by the rule [Pāṇini 3.2.61], as in the case of *sad-* and others.
Regarding the phrase "from that which has an *upapada*" and so forth:

there is no difference between the suffix *kvip* and the suffix *kvin* after the root *yuj-* with an *upapada*, because the substitution of *k* for *g* (the *kutva*) is established by the rule [Pāṇini 8.2.30].

When the suffix *kvip* is applied by the rule *anupapadāt* [Pāṇini 3.2.71], the prescription of *kvip* becomes meaningful for the purpose of changing the *n* of *num* into a *k*-sound (*kutva*). Here, "not looking" (*anālocana*) is intended to mean mere visual cognition (*cakṣurjñāna*). If the root *dṛś-* does not actually apply there, then this suffix occurs, and not otherwise—as in the forms *tyādṛk* and *tyādṛśaḥ*.

While the rule [Pāṇini 6.3.89] is being carried over, the substitution of āt (ātvam) occurs by [Pāṇini 6.3.91]. It is said that "the letter *ñ* in *kañ* is for the purpose of specification in the rule *ṭiḍḍhāṇañ*.
If the letter *ñ* were not to be applied in *kañ*, then the letter *n* would have to be applied for the sake of the udātta accent.

And thus, [the rule] *kañ kanyāyām* (Pāṇini 4.1.15) must be formulated in this way. Consequently, if it were stated in that manner, the suffix *ṅīp* would also undesirably apply in cases such as *yādṛśī*; therefore, the letter *ñ* must be included for the purpose of qualifying that [rule]. Now, one might object: since the act of seeing (*darśana*) is inherent in the root *dṛś*, the act of seeing is indeed present in forms such as *tādṛk* and *tādṛśa*. For, in their etymological derivation, the teachers form these suffixes by instructing the sentence: "one sees him" (*taṃ paśyati*) or "in such a manner" (*evaṃprakāram*).

A *vṛtti* (compound) has the same meaning as the sentence (*vākya*), and that [action of] seeing (*darśana*) has the sense of "knowing" (*jñāna*). To the question, "How then does the root *dṛś* function here in the sense of non-observation? he says: "For words such as *tādṛś* are types of conventional (*rūḍhi*) words," and so forth. In conventional words, one must not rely on the meaning of the individual parts; rather, they exist by means of the collective meaning of the whole.
For this very reason, the etymological meaning of the components is not adopted here.
Even though an etymological meaning exists, the component meaning is not taken up, as in cases such as "a tiger (vyāghra) is so called because it smells from afar" (*vyājighrati*).
Therefore, although the action of seeing is employed for the sake of etymology in the sentence, it does not exist at all in the compound (*vṛtti*).

For instance, from words such as *tādṛk* and *tādṛśa*, a cognition arises regarding an object that is similar, but not regarding the act of seeing; thus, it is logical that the root *dṛś* functions in the sense of "not looking" (*anālocana*). Regarding the statement, "it should be stated that [the suffixes] *kvip* and *kan* occur after *dṛś* when *samāna* and *anya* are the accompanying words," the meaning is that this specific rule must be explained. The explanation for this is as follows: the particle *ca* ("and") is carried over (*anuvartate*) from the preceding sūtra, and its function here is to include (*samuccaya*) the aforementioned rule.
Therefore, the two suffixes will occur after the root *dṛś* when the words *samāna* and *anya* are used as upapadas.

Regarding the form *sadṛśaḥ*, while [the rule] Pāṇini 6.3.84 is still in effect, the substitution of *sa-* for *sam-* occurs by [the rule] 6.3.89. As for the mention of "object" (*karman*), it does not apply from the rule "spṛśo'nudake kvin" (Pāṇini 3.2.58) onwards.

But surely there are also verbal roots that take objects; so why is it not applied [to them]? The thought is as follows: in rules such as *spṛśo 'nudake kvin* (Pāṇini 3.2.58), the term *kartari* (Pāṇini 3.2.57) which is carried over (*anuvartate*) is understood for the purpose of accumulating agents (*kartṛpracaya*). Therefore, the word *supi* is applied, and not *karmaṇi*.
For in this way, the accumulation of agents is obtained, and not otherwise.

Now, for what purpose is the mention of "prepositions" (*upasarga*)? Since prepositions are indeed only [words] ending in case-suffixes (*subanta*), the inclusion of prepositions would already be established by the inclusion of *sub*[-anta] words; to this he says: "The mention of 'prepositions' is for the sake of an indication (*jñāpanārtha*).

It indicates that elsewhere, when there is a mention of *sub*[-anta] words, the mention of prepositions does not apply. Where else, upon the mention of *sub*[-anta] words, does the mention of prepositions not apply? To this he says: "In the rule *vadaḥ supi kyap ca* (Pāṇini 3.1.106)."
But is it not the case that in the rule *nanu ca* (Pāṇini 3.1.106), the term *anupasarga* ("not a preverb") is understood by anuvṛtti from the preceding rule 3.1.100?

Thus, the inclusion of the term *upasarga* ("preverb") here need not be understood as carrying over; rather, the inclusion of *upasarga* is for the purpose of providing an indication (*jñāpaka*). Others say it must be included to demonstrate an alternative (*vikalpa*). Regarding this, they say: "The author of the Vṛtti shows that this is merely the direction toward the purpose of the indication."

However, the purpose of this indicator (jñāpaka) is clearly as follows: in the rule [Pāṇini 3.2.58], because of the governing authority (*adhikāra*) of the term *supi* [from 3.2.4], if there were no indicator, then even when a preposition (*upasarga*) ends in a nominal suffix (*subanta*), the rule would apply—as in *upaspṛśati* and *saṃspṛśati*. By virtue of this indicator, it does not occur. [The phrase] "by way of association" (*sāhacaryāt*) and so forth [is used].

If the root *sū* deviates from its status as belonging to the Ādyādika class, whereas the root *dviṣa* in the sense of "enmity" (DhP 1013) does not so deviate, then by virtue of this association (*sāhacarya*), the form *sū* refers to the Ādyādika root *ṣūṅ* in the sense of "the release of the embryo from living beings" (DhP 3031), and not to the Taudādika root *ṣū* in the sense of "impelling" (DhP 1408).

But is it not the case that, by association with the *tud*-class root *sā*, this [root] is also understood here? This is not so; for just as the root *sū* deviates from its status as belonging to the *tud*-class, so too does *sad*, because it is recited among the *bhū*-class roots. Therefore, how could there be a reference here to the *tud*-class root by virtue of such association? The phrase "not of *sū*" is an indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*) for the verbal root whose form is *sū* belonging to the *ad*-class.

It is also not appropriate to include this [root] *ṣañ* "to give birth" (*prāṇiprasave*) from the *Dhātupāṭha* (1132), which belongs to the *divādi* class; for the same reasoning applies. [The opponent suggests:
"There should be the inclusion of both," because no distinction is specified.
"Not for the sake of gain" refers to the root *vidlṛ* in the sense of "to obtain" (Dhātupāṭha 1432). [The genitive ending] is used because the vowel *a* is intended to be expressed.

Here, the reason for not adopting the root meaning "to gain" (*lābha*) is that the enunciation of the form ending in *a*—namely, *vidaḥ*—in the sūtra is intended to be significant; therefore, because the root *vid* ending in *a* is listed in the *gaṇa*, it alone is understood, and not the one ending in *ḷ*. [Regarding] *śṛciṣat*:
{the root *sadlṛ* in the *dhātupāṭha*—} *sadlṛ* has the sense of "perishing" (*viśaraṇa*).
[Regarding] *mitradhruk*.

In the case of *druha* in the sense of "desire to harm" (*jighāṃsāyām*) [Dhātupāṭha 1197], the letter *k* is substituted by [Pāṇini 8.2.33] *vā druhamuha*. Then, by [Pāṇini 8.2.37] *ekāco baśo bhaṣ*, the substitution of *bhaṣ* occurs. Thus we have *godhuk*.
In the case of *duha* in the sense of "milking" (*prapūraṇe*) [Dhātupāṭha 1014], the substitution of *gh* occurs by [Pāṇini 8.2.32].
In the word *āyuk*, by [Pāṇini 8.2.30], there is the substitution of *k* for *g* (*kutva*), resulting in the letter *g*; as before, that *g* is replaced by *k*. In the word *śatrujit*:
"How is there the substitution of *ṇ* here?"—

the sense is that since the substitution of *ṇ* is prescribed by the rule "after a preceding word, when it is a name, except for *go*" (Pāṇini 8.4.3) specifically for names (*saṃjñā*), it should not occur here because it is not a name.
[The example is] "samrāṭaḥ."

The root *rājṛ* is listed in the Dhātupāṭha as "to shine" (822). By the rule *vraścabhrasja* [Pāṇini 8.2.36], the substitution of *c* for *j* results in the letter *ṭ*. By the rule *mo rājisamaḥ kvau* [Pāṇini 8.3.25], the letter *m* is substituted.
The letter *k* in *kvip* is for the purpose of prohibiting *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* strengthening;
the letter *p* is for the purpose of the *tuk* augment.
By [Pāṇini 6.1.67], there is the elision of the letter *v*.

The letter *i* is for the purpose of including the general term "that which is not a *pṛkta*" (verapṛktasya). Regarding the form "ardhabhāk," by [Pāṇini 6.1.67], there is the elision of the letter *v*.
The *vṛddhi* [substitution] occurs by the rule *pratyayalopalakṣaṇena* (P. 1.1.62), and the *kutva* [change of *ṣ* to *ṣṭ*] occurs by the rule *ṣṭunā ṣṭuḥ* (P.

8.4.41). The letter *ṇ* is for the purpose of effecting the *vṛddhi*, and the letter *i* is for the purpose of including the general category [of suffixes ending in *i*] by the rule *ikaḥ kāśe* (P. 6.3.64). Thus, the form is *jalāṣāṭ*.
By the rule *ho ḍhaḥ* [Pāṇini 8.2.31], there is the substitution of *ḍha*; for that, by *jaśtva*, there is *ḍa*; and for that, by *ṣṭunā ṣṭuḥ* [8.4.41], there is *ṭa*. Thus we have *pṛṣṭhavāṭ*.

As before, there is vṛddhi, followed by the substitutions of *ḍha*, *jaśtva*, and *cartva*. The separation of the *yoga* (sūtra-splitting) is for the sake of what follows, so that the term *bahu* may carry over into the subsequent rule, but not the term *sahi*.

For when there is a single application (ekayoga), there would be the recurrence of both [rules]. Since the suffix *cv-* was already obtained by the preceding rule, the suffixes *ñ* and *ṛḍ* are now prescribed.

The letter *ṭ* is for the purpose of [triggering] the feminine suffix *ṅīp*; the letter *ñ* is for the purpose of accentuation and for the purpose of *vṛddhi*. Only the suffix *yu* remains; its replacement is by *ya* according to [Pāṇini 7.1.1]: "In place of *yu*, [there is *ya*]. "Not within a *pāda*" (*anantaḥpādam*).
The word *antaḥ* has the same meaning as the word *madhya* (middle).

In the expression *antaḥpādam*, the meaning is "in the middle of a foot. An avyayībhāva compound is formed with the sense of a case ending according to [Pāṇini 2.1.6], *avyayaṃ vibhakti* etc.; thus, *na antaḥpādam* becomes *anantaḥpādam*.

And since *vah-* is the subject under discussion, this [rule] is understood as a specific qualification of that very [word]; therefore, he says: "if it occurs outside, provided it is not within a *pāda*.

Because the term *chandaḥ* (Vedic meter) continues to apply, the word *pāda* here indicates a *ṛk*-verse quarter. The meaning is: it does not occur outside [the sandhi] when it is in the middle of a *ṛk*-verse quarter.

In the counter-example (*pratyudāharaṇa*), because the suffix *vahi* occurs outside the middle of the word (*pādamadhya*), by that [rule], only the suffix *ṇvi* applies according to Pāṇini 3.2.64: *vahaśca*. "The mention of both" is because no distinction is made.
"In the same way," and so forth.

The meaning is that just as there is the inclusion of both [suffixes] in the two immediately preceding rules, so too there is [the inclusion of both] here, even though their meanings are possible [to be distinguished]. Regarding the statement,

"The letter *ṭ* is for the purpose of preventing the general inclusion," if the letter *ṭ* were absent, then by the paribhāṣā concerning suffixes with a single *anubandha* (Vyāḍiparibhāṣā 52), this [suffix] alone would be included in the rule *ṅy-āp-prātipadikāt* [Pāṇini 4.1.1], and not the suffixes beginning with *vij*.
However, because the letter *ṭ* has two markers (*anubandha*), the inclusion of all [suffixes] is justified. Regarding the phrase "for the sake of specification":

in the rule *viḍvanoranunāsikasyāt* (Pāṇini 6.4.41), the letter *ṭ* serves to specify; for if it were stated simply as *vi-vanoḥ*, there would be an inclusion of *kvip* and other suffixes as well, and consequently, elision would occur in forms such as *akarot*.
Regarding the term "abjāḥ":
it is "born in the waters," thus "abjāḥ. Likewise is "gojāḥ."
"One who wins cattle" is *goṣāḥ*; by [Pāṇini 8.3.108], there is the substitution of *ṣ*. "One who wins men" is *nṛṣāḥ*.
"One who digs a hole" is *vilakhāḥ*;
"one who strides toward curds" is *dadhikrāḥ*;
"one who goes at the front" is *agregāḥ*.

In the case of *kāmadudhā* and *gharmadughā*, there is no elision (*aluk*) of the locative case ending according to [Pāṇini 6.3.14]. Thereafter, the elision [of the final vowel] occurs according to [Pāṇini 6.1.67], and the substitution of *ā* for the penultimate vowel occurs according to [Pāṇini 6.4.41]. Thus: *kāmadudhā* (the cow that milks desires) and *gharmadughā* (the cow that milks the hot offering).
"Kāmadughā" means "one who milks desires";
"gharmadughā" means "one who milks the sacrificial oblation. Regarding the phrase "from these":
it refers to the combinations of roots and upapadas (governing words) such as *otu* and so forth.
"Roots and compounds with prefixes are treated as *nipātas* (irregular formations)," such as *otavā* and so forth.

But what is the reason that roots and compounds with prefixes are treated as *nipātas*, rather than having the prefixes and roots specified separately? To this he says: "For the sake of establishing operations that are not [governed by] general grammatical rules (*alākṣaṇika*)."
In forms such as *otavā*, the substitution of *r* (rutva) is prescribed by the rule *avayāḥ otavāḥ puroḍāśca*; likewise,
in *ukthaśāḥ*,
the substitution of *r* indeed exists by [Pāṇini 8.2.66].
Regarding the word "śaṃsateḥ":
this refers to the verbal root *śans* meaning "to praise" (Dhātupāṭha 728). The addition of the marker *ṇ* in the suffix *ṇvin* is for the purpose of making the first syllable udātta.
The inclusion of the marker *ṇ* is for the purpose of [triggering] *vṛddhi*.
The letter *i* is for the sake of specification [in the rule] "after *ik*" (Pāṇini 6.1.67). Regarding the phrase "of *ota*, *vāha*, etc. and so forth:

if this is stated, then there is no need for the rule "the forms *avayāḥ*, *otavāḥ*, and *puroḍāśaḥ*," because its lengthening is already established by the purpose of the substitution of *ru*. But is not that lengthening already established by [the rule] "after *a*, *i*, *u*, and *ṛ*" (Pāṇini 6.4.14)? It is indeed established; however, it is for the sake of those cases where it is not established by that [rule], so that it may apply there as well.
But where, then, is it not established by that [rule]? In the vocative singular (*sambuddhau*).

If, then, that is stated, then *ḍas* need not be mentioned; for by that very exception (*nipātana*), the absence of the suffix *t* will be established for *otavaḥ* and so forth? This is not so; it has already been stated that there would be no lengthening in the vocative. Now, if it must be said that the absence of *t* will be established by exception, then in the case of *otavobhyām*, the substitution of *u* for *o* would occur.

Therefore, the suffix *ḍas* must be stated, and a *nipātana* (irregular formation) must also be applied. [The statement] "the separation of the rule (*yogavibhāga*) is for the sake of what follows" means that in the subsequent sūtra, only *yaj* should continue to apply. [Regarding the form] *upayadbhiḥ*: there is the substitution of *ṣ* by the rule beginning with *vraśca-* (Pāṇini 8.2.36), and as before, the substitution of the *jaś*-class letter results in the letter *ḍ*.

Regarding the term "ubhayatvam": when the suffix *tva* follows, the letter *ṭ* is substituted for the *t* by the rule *khari ca* [Pāṇini 8.4.54]. Now, one might ask: since the word "mantra" will be understood as a carry-over from [Pāṇini 3.2.71], and a mantra is indeed nothing other than Vedic verse (*chandas*), for what purpose is the term "Vedic verse" (*chandas*) explicitly mentioned? To this he replies: "The mention of 'Vedic verse' is for the sake of including the Brāhmaṇas."

If the term *chandas* were not included, then even though the mention of *mantra* would continue to apply, it would not extend to the *brāhmaṇa*; for the *brāhmaṇa* is not grasped by the mention of *mantra*, since it is a different type of text.

The word *brāhmaṇa* refers to a specific type of text that consists of an explanation of *mantras*, but it does not refer to the *mantra* itself. Therefore, the term *chandas* is stated so that [the rule] may also apply to the *brāhmaṇa*.
Regarding the phrase "the inclusion of *vic" and so forth..."
If the *cit* marker were not applied, this [suffix] would have only one *anubandha*;

consequently, in the rule [Pāṇini 6.1.67], by the *paribhāṣā* regarding that which has only one *anubandha* (Vyāḍi-paribhāṣā 52), only this [suffix] would be grasped, and not *kvip* and the others. However, when the *cit* marker is present, there is no suffix with only one *anubandha*, and thus all are grasped. The letter *n* in *manin* is for the purpose of making the initial syllable udātta.
In the suffixes *kvan* and *kvanip*, the letter *p* is for the purpose of making the vowel *anudātta* (unaccented), and the letter *i* is for the purpose of pronunciation.
In *kvanip*, the letter *p* is for the purpose of triggering the operations of a *pit* suffix, and the letter *c* is for the purpose of attracting (*anukarṣaṇa*) the suffix *vic*.
[Thus], one who gives beautifully is called *sudāmā*.
The long vowel [ā] is substituted by the rule *sarvanāmasthāne ca* (Pāṇini 6.4.8) and so forth.
He stands like *ā* (the letter *ā*), thus he is *ātthāmā*;
the substitution of *t* for *s* occurs because the word belongs to the *pṛṣodarādi* group.
"One who possesses beautiful wisdom" is *sudhīvā*;
"one who drinks beautifully" is *supīvā*. By [Pāṇini 6.4.66], there is the substitution of *ī* for the vowel following the suffix *kvanip*.
"He gives abundantly" is *bhūridāvā*;
"he drinks clarified butter" is *ghṛtapāvā*;
"he drinks sweet drink" is *kīlālapāḥ*; and [the word] is *suśarmā*.
The root *śṛ* is used in the sense of "injuring" (*hiṃsāyām*; Dhātupāṭha 1488). The analysis of the compound is: "one who injures beautifully" (*śobhanaṃ śṛṇāti*). Regarding the form *prātaritvā*:
when the word *prātaḥ* is the governing term (*upapada*) for the root *iṇ*, the suffix *kvanip* is applied according to Pāṇini 3.2.171, followed by the insertion of the augment *tuk*.

Regarding "vijāvā": the root *jan* means "to appear" (Dhātupāṭha 1149). From the form *vijāyate*, the suffix *vanip* is applied; by the rule *viḍvoranunāsikasya* [Pāṇini 6.4.41], the vowel is lengthened. Regarding "agregāvā": [the same analysis applies].
The roots *gmlṛ* and *sṛplṛ*, meaning "to go" (*gatau*), undergo the substitution of *ā* as before.
Regarding *reḍasi*: the root *riṣa* means "to injure" (*hiṃsāyām*); as before, there is the substitution of the voiced stop (*jaśtva*) resulting in the letter *ḍ*.

"The mention of *dṛśi* (‘are seen’) is for the purpose of following actual usage. By this, it is meant that when [the suffixes] are understood through usage, these [suffixes] such as *manin* and others are grammatically correct (*sādhavaḥ*) only in those instances where they are actually observed; therefore, nothing new is being prescribed. By this, it is stated that "they are not to be applied universally. If they were seen after other roots as well, then the previous rule would be redundant; would it not have been enough to say simply that *manin* and the others are seen after all verbal roots? This is not so; for they occur invariably after verbal roots ending in long *ā*, whereas after roots not ending in *ā*, they occur only occasionally.

"However, [the rule] *pūrvayogaśchandasi* applies to Vedic, whereas we [apply it] even to the common language (*bhāṣā*). This is obtained through the recurrence (*anuvṛtti*) of the word *api* in the rule *nirupapadetrabhyaśca*, which serves to exclude all restrictive conditions (*sarvopādhivyabhicārārtha*). [Examples:
*ukhāsrāt*."
Regarding *praṇadhvat*: [the roots] *ruāṃsu* and *dhvaṃsu* mean "to fall" (*avaruāṃsane*). By the rule *aniditām* [Pāṇini 6.4.24], there is the elision of the nasal (*anunāsika-lopa*).

By the rule *vasuruāṃsudhvaṃsvanaḍuhāṃ daḥ* [Pāṇini 8.2.72], there is the substitution of *da*. By the rule *vā'ḍavasāne* [Pāṇini 8.4.55], there is optionally the substitution of *ca* (cerebralization).

Regarding "vāhābhraṭ": the root *bhranśu* means "to fall down" (Dhātupāṭha 1225). By the rule [Pāṇini 8.2.36] concerning *vraścādi*, there is the substitution of *ṣ*; as before, there is the substitution of *jaś* and then *car*. Then, by [Pāṇini 6.3.137], there is the lengthening of the vowel. Regarding the phrase "for the purpose of subverting the sublater," and so forth:
the suffix *ac* subverts *kak* and *kvip*, and this is for the purpose of subverting even that (*ac*).

The mention of the term *dhātu* (root) in the rule *acaḥ sthāstambhoḥ pūrvasya dīrgho’ṇaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.4.19)—which states that a long vowel is substituted for the penultimate short vowel of the roots *sthā* and *stambh* when followed by a suffix beginning with a consonant—is made for this purpose:
so that even when an exception (*apavāda*) has been prescribed [by a subsequent rule], the suffix *aj* may still occur when *śam* is the upapada and a technical name (*saṃjñā*) is intended.

Furthermore, if the rule *sthaḥ ka ca* (Pāṇini 3.2.77) were not stated, then—just as the mention of *dhātu* in the rule *kṛño hetutācchīlyānulomyeṣu* (Pāṇini 3.2.20) is understood to serve the purpose of prohibiting the suffix *ṭa* in those specific senses—it would likewise be understood here to prohibit the suffixes *kap* and *kvip* after the root *tiṣṭhati*.

And this being the case, when *śam* is the upapada and a name (*saṃjñā*) is intended, only the suffix *ac* would apply after the root *sthā*, and not the suffixes *kak* or *kvip*. However, when this specific rule (*yoga*) applies, it subverts *ac* so that both suffixes indeed occur.
Thus: *śaṃsthaḥ*.
The elision of the vowel *ā* occurs by [Pāṇini 6.4.64]. Regarding the form “*brāhmaṇānām antrayitā*” (one who addresses the Brahmins):

the root *mantr* (meaning "to speak secretly," Dhātupāṭha 1679) takes the augment *num* by [Pāṇini 7.1.58], followed by the causative suffix *ṇic* (from the *cur*-class). From that, the suffix *tṛn* is added in the sense of habitual action by [Pāṇini 3.2.135].
The phrase beginning with “*supi*” [refers to the rule for the locative case].

But is not the re-mention of *sub* redundant when *supi* [Pāṇini 3.2.4] is already being carried over? It is not redundant; for the previous mention of *sub* was connected with the prefix (*upasarga*), and thus, if that were to recur, that [connection] would also recur. Therefore, the mention of *sub* is made again in order to exclude the prefix. "From *ud* and *prati*, etc. [refers to Pāṇini 1.4.90].

Since the inclusion of the word *su* is for the purpose of excluding prefixes (*upasarga*), the rule would not apply when a prefix is present; therefore, this statement is made. An addition (*upasaṃkhyāna*)—that is, a formal explanation—must be provided for the case where the root *sṛ* has *āṅ* preceded by *ut* or *prati* as its attendant word (*upapada*). The explanation for this is as follows: from [Pāṇini 3.2.75], the word *api* (meaning "also") continues to apply here as well, in the sense of overriding all restrictive conditions (*sarvopādhivyabhicārārtha*). Consequently, in the form *udāsāriṇyaḥ*, the suffix *ṇini* occurs even though a prefix is present. [This is further supported by the rule] *sādhukāriṇi ca*.
The undertaking [of this rule] is for the purpose of excluding those who do not possess that habit.
By means of the particle *ca*, the phrase "the addition (*upasaṃkhyāna*)" is drawn over; its purpose is precisely to provide an exposition.
This exposition, however, should be carried out by relying on the word *api* as before, in order to indicate the deviation from all qualifications (*sarvopādhi*).

Alternatively—since [Pāṇini], after stating "tacchīla" (having that as one's habit) in the rule *tacchīlataddharmatsādhukāriṣu* [3.2.134], further includes the term "sādhukārin" (one who performs it well), he indicates that the suffix *ṇini* occurs even when denoting one who performs something well, even in the absence of habitual action (*atācchīlya*).
Thus, [we have] *brāhmaṇi vadaḥ* ("one who speaks like a Brāhmaṇa").
This rule (*brāhmaṇi vadaḥ*) is also commenced for the purpose of expressing non-habitual action, or for the purpose of denoting a genus (*jāti*).

Since [the formation] would already be established by the previous rule when denoting habit (*tācchīlya*) and not denoting a genus (*ajāti*), the present rule is not for the purpose of excluding the *asarūpa* principle;
for example, from *brāhmaṇa-vādin*, one forms *brāhmaṇavādī*.
The letter *ṇ* in the suffix *ṇini* is for the purpose of causing *vṛddhi*.

The second *i* is for the purpose of protecting the *n* from being designated as an *it*. Since suffixes are prescribed after a verbal root (*dhātu*) when there is an agent (*kartṛ*), it is understood that the agent expressed by the subordinate word (*upapada*) is the point of comparison for that [agent]; thus he says: "the agent expressed by the subordinate word" (*upapadakartā*), and so forth.

The agent expressed by the subordinate word is the "agent-subordinate-word" (*upapadakartā*); this is a compound with the middle term elided (*madhyamapadalopin*), according to the *śākapārthiva*-type group.
As in the example: "*uṣṭrakrośī*" (one who cries like a camel).

The roots *kruś* (DhP 856) meaning "to call out" and "to weep," and *ru* (DhP 1034) meaning "sound"— in the case of the term *dhvāṅkṣarāvī*, [the suffix] is introduced for the purpose of denoting non-habitual action (*atācchīlya*) or a class (*jāti*), because it would already be established by the preceding rule in the case of habituality (*tācchīlya*) and when not denoting a class. [The example] is "he eats."

The root *bhakṣ* in the sense of "eating" belongs to the curādigaṇa (Dhātupāṭha 1557). By stating, "And this is a qualifier of the aggregate [of the action and its object]," he refutes the suspicion that it might be a qualifier of the meaning of the suffix (*pratyayārtha*).
For if it were a qualifier of the meaning of the suffix, the suffix would apply only when the agent is the vow itself, and not to Devadatta who possesses that vow.
By the phrase "the root and the prefix" (*dhātūpapada*), etc., he shows that the vow (*vrata*) is a qualifier of the whole.
"A restriction (*niyama*) when there is the possibility of acting according to one's desire (*kāmacāra*).
*Kāmacāra* means activity prompted by desire; it is a restriction that applies when such [possibility] exists.

Since there is no fixed rule, when one has reached the state of engaging in sleeping and eating according to one's desire in a general sense, this [injunction] excludes that from other objects and applies specifically to places such as a bare ground (sthaṇḍila) and so forth; therefore, it is established as a restriction (niyama). Furthermore, two types of restriction are possible here: either of the form "one must sleep only on bare ground" and "one must eat only what is not *śrāddha* food," or of the form "one sleeps only on bare ground" and "one eats only what is not *śrāddha* food. In the case of the former type of restriction, the violation of the vow (*vratalopa*) would occur precisely at the time when one does not sleep on bare ground or does not eat non-*śrāddha* food.

Thinking that, therefore, the second restriction is appropriate, he says: "When there is lying down," and so forth. Regarding the phrase "repetition (*ābhīkṣṇya*) means frequency (*paunaḥpunya*)," [the analysis is as follows]: the state of occurring again and again is "frequency"; since it is a suffix added after an indeclinable, the *ṭi* portion is elided before any *bha*-suffix.
Regarding the phrase "the intended meaning is 'practice' (*āsevitā*)": [this refers to the sense of repeated performance].

That very [term] *abhīkṣṇya* (frequency). He clarifies it through two alternative formulations: "{Other than that which denotes habit (*tācchīlya*) — so state the Kāśikā and the Padamañjarī.}" By saying "other than that which denotes habit," he demonstrates the purpose of this rule by pointing out its lack of applicability to frequency under rules such as *supsyajātau* [Pāṇini 3.2.78], as shown in the example "those who drink astringent decoctions" (*kaṣāyapāyiṇaḥ*).
In whatever region drinking decoctions repeatedly results in good health, they drink decoctions for that reason, and not out of habit. Regarding the term "milk-drinkers" (*kṣīrapāyiṇaḥ*):

they too drink milk for that same aforementioned reason, or because of the absence of any other drink, even though there is no habitual inclination to do so; it is simply because there is no other alternative.
Regarding the term "sauvīrapāyinaḥ," here too,
this very reason for drinking *sauvīra* mentioned immediately above applies again and again.
[The suffix] *-in-* is applied according to [Pāṇini 4.2.92], which states that it occurs "everywhere."
The substitution of *ṇ* [for *n*] occurs by the rule beginning with *prātipadikāntanum* [Pāṇini 8.4.11]. Thus, we have *kulmāṣakhādaḥ*.
Regarding the phrase "the mention of the root *man*" [in Pāṇini 6.1.55]:
Regarding the rule "not [the root] *man*," this refers to the root *man* belonging to the *divādi* class (Dhātupāṭha 1176), namely *mana jñāne*;
it does not include the inclusion of the root *man* belonging to the *tanādi* class (Dhātupāṭha 1471), namely *manu avabodhane*.

Furthermore, when the suffix *ṇini* is applied to the root *man*, the form *darśanīyamānī* arises; that same form arises from the root *manu* as well. Therefore, what is the distinction here such that the inclusion of *manya* is desired and not *manu*? To this he says: "For in the subsequent rule," and so forth. Although there is no distinction here, in the subsequent rule there is a distinction caused by the verbal suffix (*vikaraṇa*). For when *khaś* is applied to *manya*, because it belongs to the *divādi* class, the suffix *śyan* occurs; but for *manu*, because it belongs to the *tanādi* class, the suffix *u* occurs. [The term] "self-pride" (*ātmamāna*) means "thinking about oneself" (*mananam*); the suffix *ghañ* is used in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāve*).
*Ātmamānaḥ* means "conceit regarding the self" (*ātmanaḥ mānaḥ*).
The genitive case is applied by the rule *kartṛkarmaṇoḥ kṛti* [Pāṇini 2.3.65], and the compound is formed by the rule *kṛdyogā ca ṣaṣṭhī samasyate* (Vārttika 83).
Now, why does the genitive case not occur in the sense of the agent (*kartari*)? Because of the force of the inclusion of the word "self" (*ātman*).
For a cognition of anything other than the self is impossible, since cognition is a quality of that [self].
Furthermore, this word "self" does not denote qualities such as pleasure and so forth; what then? It denotes the absence of another.
Even if one were to hold that "the Self is that which is not another," the apprehension of a self (ātma-grahaṇa) would still be purposeless.

For in this way, the meaning would be: "that cognition which exists in the cognizer regarding whatever cognition [he has]"; and that is incorrect, because every cognition belongs to the cognizer himself, even when he is conceiving of something else. Therefore, the genitive case here refers only to the object (karman). This is what is meant by the statement beginning with, "when the agent is the meaning of the suffix," and so forth.

But how, again, is this very same meaning—that the action and the agent are one and the same—logically justified? It is due to a distinction in capacity (*śaktibheda*), just as in the expression "the honey being drunk intoxicates.

[In the suffix] *khaś*, the letter *kh* is for the purpose of [triggering] the *mum* augment (Pāṇini 6.3.67), and the letter *ś* is for the purpose of designating it as a *sārvadhātuka* affix. This word *bhūta* has both the sense of "that which has passed" (*atikrānta*) and the sense of "own form" (*svarūpa*). In that case, it is not known in what sense of "past" (*bhūta*) the suffix is applied; therefore, he says "and because of the governing context of 'verbal root' (*dhātu')" and so forth, in order to clarify that.
The word *ca* (and) indicates a reason (*hetu*).

Since the term "from a verbal root" (*dhātoḥ*) is understood to carry over [from the previous rule], it is therefore understood that [the suffix] occurs after that which has become the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvarthabhūta*).

Now, one might object: since the context concerns verbal roots (*dhātu-adhikāra*), is it not more appropriate for this qualification (*viśeṣaṇa*) to apply specifically to the verbal root itself? No; because such a thing is impossible (*asambhavāt*).
When the verbal root (*dhātu*) is the subordinate element in this sense of "having become" (*bhūta*), the qualifier *bhūta* is inappropriate.

Therefore, because it is impossible for that [qualifier] to apply there, it is understood as a qualifier of its very meaning (*tadartha*). The suffix *ṇini* is what is carried over [from the previous rule], not *khaś*, because only *ṇini* is marked with the *svarita* accent.
To the question, "Where, then, is sacrifice the instrument? he says: "The Agniṣṭoma [sacrifice] is [the instrument] in the production of the fruit," and so forth.
The fruit is heaven; its *bhāvanā*—that is, its production—is the activity belonging to the sacrificer. In that regard, the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice serves as the instrument.

But surely, apart from the Agniṣṭoma, there is no activity of the sacrificer called *bhāvanā* in which the sacrifice could be intended as the instrument; for in that case, he produces the fruit known as heaven by means of this very sacrifice called the Agniṣṭoma. This is not so; for the general activity exists within the specific activity, since the specific does not deviate from the general. Indeed, it is the general activity itself that first enters into the mind of one desiring a result.

For instance—the practitioner, desiring the fruit and being himself motivated by the desire for that fruit, first imposes upon his intellect the general operation, thinking, "Heaven must be kept in mind. Then, the scripture—"One desiring heaven should sacrifice with the Agniṣṭoma"—establishes this meaning: "One should bring heaven into being by means of the Agniṣṭoma. Consequently, he adopts the Agniṣṭoma as the instrument (*karaṇa*) for the production of heaven.
Therefore, while the arising of heaven constitutes the general operation, the specific operation known as the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice becomes the instrument in the production of heaven.

Now, one might object: while that which is being performed experiences the state of being an object (*karman*), nevertheless, due to its distinct capacities (*śakti-bheda*), its status as an instrument (*karaṇatva*) is not contradictory. For example, in the expression "intoxicated by the honey being drunk," although the honey experiences the state of being an object, it simultaneously possesses the status of an instrument.

Thus, the meaning of the term *agniṣṭomayājī* is: "one who has brought about heaven by means of the Agniṣṭoma as an instrument. However, the word "heaven" (*svarga*) is not employed [in the compound] because it is separated from the formation of the derivative (*vṛtti*). As for the term *pitṛvyaghātī*: [it is explained as follows].
By [Pāṇini 7.3.32], there is the substitution of *t* for *d*;

by [7.3.54], the substitution of *gh* for *j*; and by [6.4.13], the lengthening of the vowel when followed by the suffix *su*. The mention of "contemptible" (*kutsita*) is an adjective qualifying the meaning of the suffix.
"Grasping" (*grahaṇa*) means that by which something is grasped;
that, moreover, is an explanation (*vyākhyāna*).
This is what is meant: that by which the agent, who is contemptible, is grasped as the meaning of the suffix—that must be provided as an explanation.

In this regard, the following is the explanation: the term *bahula* (diversely), which is to be mentioned later, is drawn back and connected here; therefore, the agent who performs a prohibited act such as the killing of a paternal uncle (*pitṛvya*) is censured only in that case, and not otherwise. Regarding the form *brāhṛhaḥ*:
the lengthening of the vowel is as before. It is stated that "the suffix *kvip* is prescribed after all verbal roots" by the rule [Pāṇini 3.2.76].
"And here, the restriction is fourfold," it is said.

These are: restriction of the verbal root (*dhātuniyama*), restriction of the accompanying word (*upapadaniyama*), restriction of the suffix (*pratyayaniyama*), and restriction of time (*kālaniyama*).
The particle *ca* (and) is used for emphasis—meaning "only fourfold."

This indicates a restriction on the verbal root (*dhātu-niyama*), stating that the root *han* occurs only with "brāhmaṇa" and other such words as its attendant noun (*upapada*), and not with any other.
Precisely for this reason, it is said: "The restriction applies to that which is other than the place where the particle *eva* is employed.
When the particle *eva* is used immediately after the attendant nouns, it restricts the root *han*.
This rule is generally applicable (*prāyika*); however, it is seen in some cases even when another word serves as the *upapada*, as in *madhuhetu*.
Its general applicability is understood from the fact that the term *bahula* (diverse/optional), which will be mentioned later, is drawn forward [to this point].
The restriction regarding the *upapada* is expressed as: "In the case of *brāhmaṇa* and others, the root *han* alone [is used], and not any other."

For here, the audible *e* of the root *han* restricts the governing word (*upapada*): when *brāhmaṇa* and so forth are the governing words, there is only the suffix *kvip* after *han* in the sense of the past (*bhūta*). "No other suffix" constitutes the restriction of time;
because when *kvip* is prescribed after *han* with *brāhmaṇa* and so forth as the governing words, the past tense is thereby restricted.

If it is argued that in words such as *brāhṛ* there is only the suffix *kvip* and no other suffix, then the *niṣṭhā* (past participle) suffix would also not apply—[as in] "he killed a Brāhmaṇa" (*brāhṛāṇaṃ hatavān*)? This is not a fault; according to the rule "exceptions [intervening] in the middle sublate preceding rules, not subsequent ones" (Pāṇini 1.4.2), only the suffixes *aṇ* and so forth are sublated, not the *niṣṭhā*. Even so, why would the suffix *tṛc* not apply here in the phrase "of the slayer of Vṛtra" (*vṛtrasyāhantuḥ*)? There is no fault, because the restriction is merely general. The restriction on the suffix is expressed as "only in the past tense, not in another," meaning that the suffix is restricted to the past tense.

But how is it that all four restrictions (*niyama*) are obtained at once? He says: "Regarding this very point," etc. The term *bahulam* (variously), which is to be mentioned later in the rule *brāhma-bhrūṇa-vṛtreṣu kvip bahulam* (Pāṇini 3.2.87), is drawn forward and connected with this present rule; thus, this fourfold restriction is obtained. [The phrase] "excluding the word *su*" is used because, since that [word *su*] denotes a non-substance (*asattva*), its status as an object (*karman*) is untenable.
Regarding the phrase "in auspicious rites" (*svādiṣu karmasu*):
this is stated by relying on the majority of cases, as in "a village of Brahmins" (*brāhmaṇagrāmaḥ*) or "a village of Bhaṭṭas" (*bhaṭṭagrāmaḥ*).
Why is this so? Because, with the exception of the word *su*, it is taught that [the suffix applies] only to those immediately preceding [the word].
"And here the restriction is threefold.

This is also obtained through the recurrence of the term *bahula* ("in many cases"). "The scope [of this rule] concerns the restriction regarding time, the secondary suffix (*upapada*), and the primary suffix (*pratyaya*)," as stated in the *Kāśikā*.
One for whom the objects [of the action] are restricted by time (*kāla*), accompanying words (*upapada*), and suffixes (*pratyaya*) is so described.

Furthermore, these are: restriction of time, restriction of the accompanying word, and restriction of the suffix. Among these, the restriction of time is as follows: after the root *kṛ*, when preceded by words beginning with *sva* (i.e., *sva*, *svin*, *snu*, *su*), the suffix *kvip* alone occurs only in the past tense (*bhūta*), and no other suffix occurs. It does not occur [in other tenses], as in: "one who has performed work" (*karmakāra*).

Restriction of the base (*upapadaniyama*): After words beginning with *su*, the suffix *kvip* occurs only after the root *kṛ*, and not after any other verbal root. For instance, one does not say *mantramadhītavān* (he has studied the mantra) using *kvip*; rather, only the suffix *aṇ* is used, as in *mantrādhyāya* (one who has studied the mantra). Restriction of the suffix (*pratyayaniyama*): After words beginning with *su*, the suffix *kvip* occurs after the root *kṛ* only when referring to the past (*bhūta*), not the present (*vartamāna*) or the future (*bhaviṣyat*). Therefore, when there is a desire to express the meaning "he performs a mantra" or "he will perform a mantra," the form *mantrakṛt* does not occur. [In contrast,] one says *śāstrakṛt* (author of a treatise).

The suffix *kvip* is applied by [Pāṇini 3.2.76]. The phrase "the domain of verbal roots (*dhātu*), time (*kāla*), upapadas, and suffixes (*pratyaya*)" is a bahuvrīhi compound as before; the external referent (*anyapadārtha*) is the restriction regarding time and so forth.

In this regard, there is a restriction of time (*kāla-niyama*): after the root *su* (to press), the suffix *kvip* occurs only when the action is completed in the past, and no other suffix; for one does not say "he pressed Soma" as *somasāvaḥ*. There is a restriction of verbal root (*dhātu-niyama*): *kvip* occurs after *su* only when *soma* is the object, and not with any other word as a subordinate element (*upapada*); here it does not occur: "he pressed liquor" as *surāsut*. There is a restriction of the subordinate element (*upapada-niyama*): *kvip* occurs after *su* only when *soma* is the object, and not from any other root; here *kvip* does not occur in the sense of "he bought Soma," but rather the suffix *aṇ* occurs, resulting in *somakrayaḥ*.

The restriction of the condition (*pratyayaniyama*): the suffix *kvip* occurs after the root *su* (to press) only when the action is completed in the past, and not otherwise. Consequently, when there is a desire to express the meaning "he presses Soma" or "he will press Soma," the form *somasut* does not occur. Here too, as previously stated, there is a restriction of time (*kālaniyama*): the suffix *kvip* occurs after the root *ci* (to pile) only when the action is completed in relation to the fire-altar (*agni*), and not otherwise. Therefore, when there is a desire to express the meaning "he has piled the fire-altar," the form *agnicāya* does not occur. There is also a restriction of the verbal root (*dhātuniyama*): the root *ci* occurs only when *agni* is the governing word (*upapada*), and not with any other. Consequently, the form *iṣṭakācit* (one who has piled bricks) does not occur.

The restriction regarding the *upapada* (governing word) is that [the suffix *kvip*] occurs only after the root *ci* when *agni* is the object, and not after any other verbal root; therefore, forms such as *agnikṛt* do not occur.

The restriction regarding the suffix is that after the root *ci* with *agni* as the object, the suffix *kvip* occurs only in the sense of the past (*bhūta*), and not at any other time; therefore, forms such as *agnicit* in the present or future do not occur. Regarding this, since the mention of "object" (*karman*) continues from the previous rule [Pāṇini 3.2.86], the fact that the object is mentioned again here indicates that it is intended to serve as the meaning of the suffix itself. Thus he says: "only when the *kāraka* is the object."

By the phrase "dhātūpapada" and so forth, he demonstrates that this mention of the term *agni* (fire) is intended as a qualifier for the entire compound. Regarding the statement "the mention of the term [is] for the purpose of conveying conventional usage (*rūḍhi*)," etc.:

this word *agni* denotes fire in general; if the mention of the term were not made here, the specific distinction would not be understood—namely, which [fire] is to be understood here. Therefore, the mention of the term is made for the purpose of conveying conventional usage. He asks: "What, then, is the reason that the mention of the term is made for that purpose? and replies with "for the meaning of 'fire' is," etc.
That specific arrangement of bricks for the purpose of the fire-altar is called *śyenacit* (the falcon-shaped altar); it is precisely in that context that this suffix is desired.

How is it obtained in that very context? When there is a mention of that which is well-known (*prasiddha*), the specific arrangement of bricks for the purpose of the fire-altar—which is being mentioned—is understood as the meaning of the suffix to be expressed, and nothing else. [This is stated] in the passage beginning with "while the word *karman* is present," etc., following from [Pāṇini 3.2.86]: *karmaṇi hanaḥ*.
"Again, the mention of *karman*," and so forth.

This is for the purpose that an action which, when experienced as being connected with an activity, brings about censure (*kutsā*) for the agent—that [action] should be the "action" (*karman*) serving as the cause of censure.

Even though the term *karman* was already carried over from the previous rule, the mention of *karman* again is for the sake of excluding that mention of *karman* which was intended to signify the object (*karman*) in the immediately preceding sūtra but was undesirable here.

Why is there no inclusion of the word *karman* (action)? Because it continues [from the previous rule] precisely by virtue of its being marked with the *svarita* accent. Regarding the example "seller of soma" (*somavikrayī*):
since the selling of soma is prohibited in the scriptures, the action called "soma," when connected with the act of selling, brings about censure for the seller.
Regarding "the sale of grain": [this is stated] "for the purpose of excluding other suffixes. Other suffixes refer to those such as *aṇ* and so forth; it is for the purpose of excluding them.
Even when [the verbal root] has ceased, the suffix remains as another suffix, as in the expression "he saw the other world.

And the reason for this is stated in the very sūtra *brāhma-bhrūṇa* (Pāṇini 3.2.87). There is the mention of the word "suffix" (*pratyaya*) in the rule regarding the locative case; there, by the paribhāṣā concerning the mention of a suffix, the inclusion of that which ends in it occurs. Thus he says: "when a word ending in the locative case is an upapada."
For this very reason, there is no apprehension of the word's own form (*svarūpa*).
In the case of *upasarajaḥ*,
by virtue of the application of the marker *ḍit*, there is elision of the *ṭi* even for that which does not bear the designation *bha*.

In the case of *maṇḍurajaḥ*, the vowel is shortened by [Pāṇini 6.3.63]. In the case of *buddhijaḥ*, since the intellect (*buddhi*) functions as the source (*apādāna*) according to [Pāṇini 1.4.30] "the material cause of that which is produced," the fifth case (*pañcamī*) is used for the source; thus, it serves as its *upapada*.

Words such as *buddhi* (intellect) and so forth are not genus-words (*jātiśabda*), because intellect and the rest are qualities of the self (*ātman*). Regarding the phrase "conditioned by a collection" (*samudāyopādhi*): he demonstrates that if a technical name (*saṃjñā*) is understood through a collection of verbal root, prefix, and suffix, then it constitutes the meaning of the suffix, and not otherwise—as in the example "{*prajāḥ*-Kāśikā} *prajāḥ*" (offspring).
This is the name for a collection of living beings.

If "prajā" is the sole example for this sūtra, then since one could simply state "pra-janaḥ saṃjñāyām" (the root *jan* with the prefix *pra-* forms [the word] when it is a name), the form "prajā" would be established even without the mention of the prefix (*upasarga*). Why, then, include the mention of the prefix? The mention of the prefix is for the sake of subsequent rules; it is so that [the suffix] may apply when there is a prefix, as in [Pāṇini 3.2.100], but not when there is a *karmapravacanīya*.

Furthermore, if a suffix is sometimes observed after a non-initial [root] in actual usage when another word is present as a governing term (*upapada*), then [the mention of the prefix] is also for that purpose: namely, [to ensure the application of the rule] "after *jan* preceded by *anu*," and so forth.

Now, why does the word *anu* not function as an *upapada* [in this context]? The reason why it does not is explained under the rule *udi kūlerujivahoḥ* (Pāṇini 3.2.31), and thus it is not explained here again. "All conditions" (*sarva upādhayaḥ*) refers to *upapada*s and so forth; the word "also" (*api*) is used for the purpose that there might be deviation (*vyabhicāra*) from these.
Regarding the phrase "even from another root," this refers to the root *khanu* (Dhātupāṭha 878), meaning "to dig."

"In another *kāraka* as well" means in a *kāraka* other than the agent (*kartṛ*), namely, in the object (*karman*). Regarding "done" (*kṛtam*), here there is an absence of *guṇa* substitution due to the presence of the *kit* suffix.
Regarding the form *kṛtavān*:

the augment *num* is applied by [Pāṇini 7.1.70] *ugidacām*; the lengthening is by [6.4.14]; and the elision of the final consonant (*hal*) and the following vowel (*i*), etc., as well as the elision of the final member of the conjunct (*saṃyogānta-lopa*), are by [6.1.66] and [8.2.23]. As for the phrase beginning with *niṣṭhāyām*, etc.: [the rule applies] when there is a *niṣṭhā* suffix.

When a suffix designated as *niṣṭhā* is to be prescribed, there is no established basis for that suffix designated as *niṣṭhā*, nor for this designation "niṣṭhā" itself. Why? Because of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśrayatva*). How is there mutual dependence? He says: "In the case of the designation," and so forth. Having uttered the designation "niṣṭhā," the prescription of the suffixes *kta* and *ktavatu* occurs here with reference to the past tense; and since those two [suffixes] must exist before the designation can apply, there is mutual dependence. As it is said: "Operations based on mutual dependence are not admitted in the grammatical treatise" (Vyāḍipañjikā 28).

Since the suffixes *kta* and *ktavatu* are recognized by their own form according to [Pāṇini 1.1.26], another technical designation (*saṃjñā*) can be prescribed for them, but not otherwise. Therefore, there is no establishment of the designation; and since that is not established, those two suffixes themselves are not established. [The term] "future" (*bhāvinī*) refers to this.
The meaning is "will come to be.
For example: "Weave a cloth for this thread.
This word *bhāvinī* is derived from the suffix *ini*, being formed by the rules *gameriniḥ* (Dhātupāṭha 6.57), *āṅi ṇit* (6.58), and *bhuvaśca* (6.59).
And that [suffix]—as in *bhaviṣyat* (Pāṇini 3.3.3)—is prescribed for the future tense.
Therefore, the word *bhāvinī* obtains the meaning "that which will come to be" (*bhaviṣyantī*).
The phrase beginning with "by virtue of the capacity" (*sāmarthyāt*) and so forth [follows].
That which, once arisen, has this designation "completion" (niṣṭhā) occurs in the past;
no other thing that has arisen has this designation "completion.
Rather, by implication, it applies only to the suffixes *kta* and *ktavatu*.
Regarding the phrase "in the beginning action" (*ādikarmaṇi*) and so forth:
here the word *karman* denotes "action. The meaning is: in that which is initial—that is, in the first stage characterized by action at the commencement of an activity.

As long as a mat reaches completion through its constituent actions, the time of the past (*bhūtakāla*) applies once those actions have been brought to an end (*apavarga*). However, since the whole is not yet fully accomplished at the first action, it remains strictly within the present (*vartamānakāla*).
In that case, the suffix *niṣṭhā* (the past participle marker) would not apply; therefore, it must be specifically stated and explained.
In this regard, the explanation is as follows: by the rule beginning with *yad ayam* [Pāṇini 3.4.71], he optionally applies the *niṣṭhā* suffix after a transitive verb;

or else, by the rule beginning with *yad vā* [Pāṇini 3.4.21], he indicates that the *niṣṭhā* suffix occurs after a verb denoting the commencement of an action (*ādikarman*). For example: *prakṛtaḥ kaṭam* ("He has begun the mat").
The prefix *pra-* here indicates the beginning of an action (*ādikarma*).

The very same meaning that is expressed by "Devadatta makes a mat" (*prakaroti kaṭaṃ devadattaḥ*) is expressed by "Devadatta has begun a mat" (*prakṛtaḥ kaṭaṃ devadattaḥ*). Regarding the form *suptvā*: [the suffix] *-tuK* is applied by [Pāṇini 6.1.71], the lengthening of the vowel occurs by [Pāṇini 6.4.8] and the following rules, and the elision of the *n* occurs by [Pāṇini 8.2.7]. Regarding the form *jaraṃ*.
Because *atṛn* is marked with the *ṅit* indicator, it receives the acute accent on its first syllable (*ādyudāttatva*).

The augment *num* is applied by the rule *ugidacām* [Pāṇini 7.1.70]. Regarding the form *dadarśa*: this is the root *dṛś* in the perfect tense (*liṭ*), with the suffix *ṇal*. There is reduplication, followed by the substitution of *at* for the reduplicated vowel according to *urat* [7.4.66], the replacement of *a* by *ra* (*raparatva*), the application of *halādiśeṣaḥ* [7.4.60], and finally the *guṇa* strengthening of the light penultimate vowel (*laghūpadhaguṇaḥ*) [7.3.86].
Regarding the form *ātatāna*:
the root *tanu* meaning "to expand" (Dhātupāṭha 1463), preceded by the prefix *āṅ*, undergoes *vṛddhi* substitution according to Pāṇini 7.2.116.
This grammatical operation applies when there is a connection between verbal roots.
> [[3.4.1]] Because of the continued application of the mention of "connection between verbal roots" (*dhātusambandha*),
[the rule] applies "even when there is no qualification" (*aviśeṣaṇena*);
that is, in the case of mere past time (*bhūtamātra*).
The *i* and *ṭ* of *liṭ* serve as qualifiers for the subsequent rule;
for if it were stated simply as "the *la*s, or *kānac*," there would be a grasping of all *la*-markers.
The *ṭ* is for the sake of the substitution of *et* for *ṭi*. The addition of *c* in *kānac* is for the sake of making it *udātta* on the final syllable.
The purpose of the *kit* designation is for the sake of the operations that apply to *kit* suffixes.

Furthermore, these operations—such as those beginning with the root *bandh* (Dhātupāṭha 1508), which ends in a consonant cluster (*saṃyoga*)—are prompted by roots ending in a cluster, and not by others.

While the rule *asaṃyogāllit* [Pāṇini 1.2.5] establishes this for non-cluster-final roots, even roots ending in clusters prompt the *kit* status in the spoken language (*bhāṣā*), but not in the Vedic language (*chandas*).
To this he replies: Since the *liṭ* [perfect] affixes possess the status of *sārvadhātuka* by rule [Pāṇini 3.4.113], they indeed have the *ṅit* property by rule [Pāṇini 1.2.4].
Whether it be *kit* or *ṅit*, there is no difference whatsoever in the Vedic language (*chandas*).

However, in the spoken language (*bhāṣā*), if the *kit* property did not apply to roots ending in a non-conjunct consonant, then the guna substitution prescribed by rule [Pāṇini 7.4.11]—which is introduced for the purpose of prohibition—would fail to apply here as it does in the cases of *nipaparatuḥ* and *nipaparur*; likewise, it would also fail to apply here in the case of *nipapurāṇaḥ*. But since the *kit* property does apply, that [guna substitution] does not occur.
In common usage (*bhāṣā*), however, the *kittva* [of the suffix] is meaningful.
From the root *pṛ* in the sense of "protecting" and "filling" (Dhātupāṭha 1086), preceded by the prefix *ni*, the suffix *kānac* is applied.
Due to its position after the reduplication, the substitution of *u* [for the radical vowel] occurs by Pāṇini 7.1.102, *udoṣṭhapūrvasya*, followed by the substitution of *ra* for the semivowel.
