By virtue of the rule *sthānivad ādeśo* (1.1.56), the word *pṛṣ* is reduplicated. Then follow the operations of *urat*, *atva*, *raparatva*, and *halādiśeṣa*. The substitution of *ṇ* for *n* occurs by the rule *aṭkupvāṅnumvyavāye’pi* (8.4.2).
That the suffix *kānac* is used in the colloquial (*bhāṣā*) [and not only in the Veda] is understood from this very [application as a] *jñāpaka*.

In *cikyānaḥ*, there is the substitution of *k* (kutva) for the letter *c* of the root *ci* following the reduplication, according to Pāṇini 7.3.58; then the *yaṇ* substitution occurs according to 6.4.82 and so forth.
In *suṣuvāṇaḥ*, [the same applies].

Regarding the reading *sunoteḥ* (it is printed as such): the substitution of *uvaṅ* [by Pāṇini 6.4.77] applies to the root *su*, and the change to *ṣ* [by 8.3.59] applies here. As for the statement "there will be a change of case":
although *liṭ* is introduced in the nominative case (*liṭ*), nevertheless, by virtue of the sense, there will be a change of case.

Because of its connection with the substitute (*ādeśa*), the subsequent *liṭ* will be understood in the genitive case. Therefore, even without the explicit mention of *liṭ*, since it is the subject under discussion, the substitute *kānac* will apply to *liṭ* itself; thus, the intention is that the mention of *liṭ* need not be made.
The phrase "even that which" (*yo'pi*) and so forth: even for that [verb] for which *liṭ* is prescribed by [Pāṇini 3.2.115], when there is the mention of *liṭ*, the substitution of *kānac* occurs.

However, if that [mention of *liṭ*] were absent, then by the principle "a rule or a prohibition applies only to what is immediately preceding" (Vyāḍiparibhāṣā 19), it would apply only to that [immediately preceding case], and not to *liṭ* in the sense of "remote past" (*parokṣe*).

Now, if the mention of *liṅ* (the optative suffix) were absent, why would *kānac* not be understood as another suffix? It is impossible to understand it thus; for if it were another suffix, the prohibition of the genitive case by the rule *na lokāvyayaniṣṭhākhalarthatṛnām* [Pāṇini 2.3.69] would not apply.

Consequently, in the form *agni-cikyānaḥ*, the genitive case would arise after the word *agni*. The addition of the marker *uk* to *kvasu* is for the purpose of [triggering] *num*. The addition of the marker *k* should be viewed as being similar to that in *kānac*.

For if that [augment] were not present, then just as the *guṇa* substitution does not occur here in *teratuḥ* and *teruḥ* according to the rule *ṛcchatyṛnām* [Pāṇini 7.4.11], so too would it not occur here in *tatīvān*.

[The root] *tṛ* [meaning] "floating" and "crossing" (Dhātupāṭha 969) undergoes the substitution of *i* by [the rule] *ṛta iddhātoḥ* [7.1.100], followed by lengthening by *hali ca* [8.2.77]; the reduplication is the operation pertaining to the abhyāsa. [The form] *jakṣivān* is explained as follows.
By the rule *liṭanyatarasyām* [Pāṇini 2.4.40], the root *ghas* is substituted for *ad*.

By *vasvekājāddhasām* [7.2.67], the augment *iṭ* is added. By *ato lopaḥ* [6.4.48], the penultimate vowel is elided. By *khari ca* [8.4.54], the letter *gh* is changed to *k*. By *śāsivasighasīnāñca* [8.3.60], the substitution of *ṣ* occurs. By *abhyāsasyāsavarṇe* [6.4.78], the substitution of *c* occurs for the reduplicated syllable, resulting in *jh*. By *jhalāṃ jaś jhaśi* [8.4.53], the letter *jh* is changed to *j*. Thus, we have *papivān*.
The root *pā* in the sense of "drinking" (Dhātupāṭha 925). The augment *iṭ* is applied as before; then, by [Pāṇini 6.4.64], there is the elision of the vowel *a*.

"The separation of the rule (*yogavibhāga*) is for the sake of what follows" means that in the subsequent sūtra, only *kvasu* should be carried over, and not *kānac*. Now, one might object: "In this section, the *liṭ* [perfect tense] is prescribed for the general past; therefore, it does not exist at all in the common language (*bhāṣā*). Consequently, how can it be understood that there is a substitution of *kvasu* for it? To this he says: "Precisely because of the prescription of the substitute," and so forth. From this very fact—that there is a prescription of *kvasu* as a substitute for *liṭ* in the common language—it is inferred that *liṭ* exists in the common language for the general past; otherwise, the prescription of the substitute would be purposeless.

For a substitute (ādeśa) is not possible for that which does not exist as a locus (sthānin). If, then, the *liṭ* [perfect tense] is inferred in the spoken language (*bhāṣā*) because of the prescription of its substitute, it would follow that *liṭ* occurs invariably after roots such as *sad-* in the spoken language. Consequently, by the rule "the *kvasu* suffix is optional," there would result the undesirable consequence of hearing finite verbal endings (*tiṅ*) in certain instances, and the substitution of *luṅ* [aorist] in its own domain would not be optional, since *liṭ* would be constant. This is not a fault; for *liṭ* is inferred by means of the sign (*liṅga*) that is the substitute. Therefore, when the substitute is absent, that inference of it is likewise non-existent.

If that [the *liṭ*] were non-existent, from where would there be substitutes for which its hearing might otherwise follow? In the view where the *liṭ* does not exist, who could prevent the occurrence of the *luṅ* and other suffixes in their own respective domains? Regarding the form *upasedivān*: from the root *ṣadlṛ* in the sense of "sitting" (Dhātupāṭha 854), there is the substitution of *e* and the elision of the reduplication by [Pāṇini 6.4.120], *ata ekahalmadhye*. Then, by [Pāṇini 7.2.67], *vasvekājāddhasām*, the augment *iṭ* is added; followed by the lengthening by [Pāṇini 6.4.10], *num*; and finally, the elision of the final consonant of the cluster (*saṃyogāntalopa*) by [Pāṇini 6.1.66], *halṅyādi*.

Regarding the form *upāsadat*: because of the inclusion of the word "or" (*vā*), in that alternative where the *liṭ* suffix does not occur, the *luṅ* suffix is used for the general past tense; then *tip* is applied, the *ikāra* is elided by [Pāṇini 3.4.100] *itaśca*, and *aṅ* replaces *cl* by [Pāṇini 3.1.56] *puṣādidyutādyuditaḥ parasmaipadeṣu*. Thus we have *upāsīdat*.
By the rule *prāghrādi* (Pāṇini 7.3.78), there is the substitution of *sīd* [for *sad*]. Thus, "upasasāda.
By the rule *tip-ṇal* (Pāṇini 7.1.116), there is *vṛddhi*.

Regarding the form *anūviṣān*: the root is *vas* in the sense of "dwelling" (*dhātupāṭha* 1005). The suffix *kvasu* follows the *liṭ* [perfect] tense, resulting in reduplication; then, by the rule *vacyādisūtra* [Pāṇini 6.1.15], there is vocalization (*samprasāraṇa*).

By the rule *liṭabhyāsasyobhayeṣām* [Pāṇini 6.1.17], there is vocalization of the reduplicated syllable; by the rule *śāsivasighasīnāñca* [Pāṇini 8.3.60], there is the substitution of *ṣ*; and finally, by the rule [Pāṇini 6.1.101], a long vowel is substituted for the vowel of the prefix *anu* together with the following vowel.
Regarding *anvavātsīt*:

[the suffix] *luṅ* [is applied]; by [Pāṇini 7.3.96], the augment *iṭ* [would apply], but there is a prohibition of *iṭ* by [Pāṇini 7.2.10] *ekācaḥ*; by [Pāṇini 7.4.49] *saḥ syārdhadhātuke*, *s* is substituted for *t*; and by [Pāṇini 7.2.3] *vadavraja* etc., *vṛddhi* [occurs]. Thus, *anvavasat*.
*laṅ*: *anūvāsa*.
[This is] the *liṭ* [affix]; the operations such as *samprasāraṇa* are as before.
Regarding the word "upaśuśruvān": the root is *śru* in the sense of "hearing" (Dhātupāṭha 942); the suffix *kvasu* follows the perfect tense (*liṭ*); there is reduplication; thus it means "he heard.
It is equivalent to "upāśrauṣīt."

By [Pāṇini 7.2.1], there is vṛddhi; as before, there is the prohibition of iṭ; by [Pāṇini 7.3.96], there is iṭ; and with the prefix, by [Pāṇini 6.1.101], we have *upāśṛṇot*. Here, *laṅ* is applied, by which [Pāṇini 3.1.74] the suffix *śnu* is added and the root changes to *śṛ*; then, by [Pāṇini 7.3.84], there is guṇa substitution for the *sārvadhātuka* and *ārdhadhātuka* affixes.
Regarding the form *upaśuśrāva*:
[the suffix] *liṭ*, [then] *tip*, [and then] *ṇal* [are applied]; by [Pāṇini 7.2.115], there is *vṛddhi*, followed by the substitution of *āv*.
In this case, the operation prescribed by this rule applies to the general state of having occurred (*bhūtasāmānye*).
By the rule *luṅ* [Pāṇini 3.2.110], the suffix *luṅ* is applied;

by the rule *anadyatane luṅ* [3.2.111], the suffix *laṅ*; and by the rule [3.2.115], the suffix *liṭ*. Thus, *laṅ* and *liṭ* occur when the action refers to the past, not of today, and is beyond the range of perception (*parokṣa*). Furthermore, because they are prescribed as specific exceptions (*viśeṣavidhi*), *laṅ* and *liṭ* would necessarily supersede this operation concerning the root *sad* and others.

The general past tense (*bhūtasāmānya*) is the scope for that grammatical operation; [the *laṅ* and *liṭ* suffixes apply] after roots other than *sad* and so forth, and after *sad* and so forth when there is a specific past tense (*bhūtaviśeṣa*), namely the non-recent and non-witnessed past (*bhūtānadyatanaparokṣa*). And in the case of the non-recent past where both [suffixes] would otherwise apply, the *laṅ* and *liṭ* should occur due to the two aforementioned causes. To one who might object that this grammatical operation is not prescribed by the rule itself, he says: "even in the domain of *luṅ* and *laṅ*," and so on.
The mention of *liṭ* and the mention of *vā* in this sūtra are carried forward (*anuvṛtti*) from the preceding rules [Pāṇini 3.2.111] *anadyatane laṅ* and [3.2.115] *parokṣe liṭ*.
Because of the force of that carry-forward, this [substitution] applies to *laṅ* as well.

In this context, the connection should be made as follows: *laṅ* occurs in the non-recent past; or, after roots such as *sad*, *liṭ* optionally occurs; and for *liṭ*, the substitute *kvasu* occurs invariably.

The *liṭ* [perfect] occurs in the sense of the remote past (*parokṣa*); alternatively, it occurs after roots such as *sad*. It is desired that the suffix *kvasu* replace *liṭ*, and this is prescribed by another rule: "The suffix *kvasu* follows the root *iṇ* preceded by the prefix *upa*. It should be understood that this is a substitute for *liṭ*. Regarding the phrase "lengthening of the reduplicated syllable" (*abhyāsadīrghatvam*), [the following applies].
By this [sūtra], namely 7.4.69, the phrase "by its power" (*tatsāmarthyāt*) and so forth is used.
By the power of the prescription of lengthening, the single-substitute lengthening (*ekādeśa*) of *akaḥ savarṇe dīrghaḥ* (P. 6.1.101) is prohibited; the meaning is that its operation is obstructed.
If there were only a single substitution (*ekādeśa*), the mention of "longness" (*dīrghatva*) would be purposeless, since longness would be established by the single substitution itself. [Objection:

But surely this would be the scope for the long vowel of the reduplication (*abhyāsa*) in the forms *iyatuḥ* and *iyuḥ*, where the substitution of *yaṇ* is applied according to [Pāṇini 6.4.81]: "In place of the form of a root..."? [Response: This is not its scope, because here [the rule] "as if it were the original" (*sthānivadbhāva*) must apply according to [Pāṇini 1.1.57]. How so? Because when a long vowel is produced by the rule for homogeneous vowels (*savarṇadīrghatva*), it can be designated as a "prior operation" (*pūrvavidhi*), since it is an operation dependent on what precedes.
That which is produced as belonging to both positions receives the designation of either one.

Furthermore, there is no prohibition of the status of being a *sthānivadbhāva* with respect to the rule for lengthening (*dīrghavidhi*) by the sūtra *na padānta* [Pāṇini 1.1.57]; because there is a prohibition of the status of being a *sthānivadbhāva* with respect to the rule for lengthening by the sūtra beginning with *svaradīrghayalopeṣu lopājādeśau na sthānivadeva* (Kāśikā on 1.1.59).

Since it is stated [in the Kāśikā on Pāṇini 1.1.59] that "in the case of vowel-lengthening (*svaradīrgha*) and the elision of *y* (*yalopa*), the substitutes for elision (*lopājādeśa*) do not behave as if they were the original (*sthānivat*)," there ought to be lengthening by way of the rule *akaḥ savarṇe dīrghaḥ* due to this status of being *sthānivat*.

This lengthening of the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*)—being without scope (*anavakāśatva*)—subverts the lengthening of homogeneous vowels (*savarṇadīrghatva*); thus it is established that, by virtue of its functional necessity (*sāmarthya*), the single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) is prohibited.
Regarding the phrase "In that case" (*tatra*) and so forth:

For when there is an obstruction to a single substitution (*ekādeśa*), there is the state of having multiple vowels (*anekāctva*); consequently, by the rule *iṭ ca* [Pāṇini 7.2.67], the augment *iṭ* would not apply, and thus it is introduced as a nipātana (irregularity).
As for the statement "there is a *yaṇ*-substitution for that which has the form of a verbal root" [by the rule *aci śnu-dhātu-...* 6.4.77], this too is indeed a nipātana.
In the case of *satyañjāda* and others as well, there is *samprasāraṇa* after the root *vas*.

Once the *samprasāraṇa* has been performed, the augment *iṭ* would apply; however, it is prohibited by [Pāṇini 7.2.67]. That very [prohibition] is here reintroduced by this rule of *nipātana*. What was prohibited is set into operation again, but it is not prescribed as something new.
"Therefore, it does not occur when [the suffix] begins with a vowel.

For since the rule is prescribed for the verb preceded by *api* without specifying a particular distinction, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of its application even when [the suffix] begins with a vowel; however, this is not the case for the production of the augment *iṭ*, because that [suffix] is characterized by beginning with a consonant (*valādi*). As in the example "upeyuṣā."

Once the *samprasāraṇa* has been performed, the substitution of *yaṇ* for the root vowel occurs, and by [Pāṇini 8.3.59], the status of being a *ṣatva* (the substitution of *ṣ* for *s*) is established. "And here the prefix (*upasarga*) is not the governing factor" means that the prefix is not the primary element in this context.

The status of being a *tan* [as a substitute] for that [root *gam*] is obtained through the continued application of the term "diversely" (*bahulam*) from the rule *tan-tasya* (Pāṇini 7.4.78). Regarding the form *upāgāt*:
the substitution of *gā* occurs by the rule *luṅi* (Pāṇini 2.4.45).
By the rule *gātisthā* (Pāṇini 2.4.77), there is elision (*luk*) of the suffix *sic*. Regarding the form *upait*:

this is the *laṅ* (imperfect) tense, with the suffix *tip*; due to its belonging to the *adādi* class, there is elision of *śap*; then *āṭ* is added by [Pāṇini 6.4.72], and by [Pāṇini 6.1.87] there is *vṛddhi* (vowel strengthening) after *āṭ*.

Regarding *upeyāya*: this is the root *i*, with the suffix *liṭ*, the *tip* ending replaced by *ṇal*. By [Pāṇini 7.2.115], there is *vṛddhi* substitution, followed by the *āy* replacement. Due to the status of being a *sthānivadbhāva*, the *ikāra* is not reduplicated. Then, by [Pāṇini 6.4.78], the *iyaṅ* substitution occurs, which merges with the *ikāra* to form *eyāya* by [Pāṇini 6.1.87]. Regarding *anāśān*: this is from the root *aś* in the sense of "eating" (*bhojane*; Dhātupāṭha 1523), with the suffix *liṭ* and the *kvasu* affix. There is reduplication. For the root *aś*, by [Pāṇini 7.4.70], there is lengthening of the reduplicated syllable and the absence of *iṭ*. The absence of *iṭ*, which would otherwise have been required by [Pāṇini 7.2.67] (*vasvekājāddhasām*), is established here as an irregularity (*nipātana*).
*nānā* and *anānā*: [this is] a negative compound (*nañ-samāsa*). By [Pāṇini 6.3.73], there is the elision of the *n*; by [Pāṇini 6.3.74], the augment *nuṭ* is added.

Regarding *nāśīt*: this is the *luṅ* [tense]. By [Pāṇini 8.2.28], there is the elision of the *sic* suffix after [the root] *aś* when followed by *īṭ*. As before, the augment *āṭ* is applied, followed by *vṛddhi*, and with the negative particle *nañ*, there is the long vowel by rule of homogeneous sounds (*savarṇadīrghatva*).
Regarding "nāśnāt": this is the *laṅ* [aorist] tense; *śnā* is applied because it belongs to the *kryādi* class, and there is the augment *āṭ*.
Regarding "nāśa": [this is the root].

The suffix *liṭ*, *tip*, *ṇal*, reduplication, lengthening of the abhyāsa (reduplicated syllable) as before, and the substitution of a long vowel for homogeneous vowels with the negative particle *nañ* [resulting in *ān*] from the root *vac*. Regarding "of *vac*" and so forth:

from the root *vac* in the sense of "speaking" (Dhātupāṭha 1063)—either by the substitution of *vac* [for *brū*] according to Pāṇini 2.4.53, or from *vac* preceded by the prefix *anu*—the *kānac* suffix, which is designated as *ātmanepada* in the sense of the agent, would not be applicable because [the root *vac*] is *parasmaipada*; nor would it apply to the other [root *anuvac*] because the fruit of the action is intended to accrue to the agent (*kartṛbhiprāyaphala*). Therefore, it is prescribed as an irregular formation (*nipātita*).

By the rule *vacy-ādi-sūtra* [Pāṇini 6.1.15], there is vocalization (*samprasāraṇa*) of the root; then, by the rule *liṭ-abhyāsasya ubhayeṣām* [Pāṇini 6.1.17], there is vocalization of the reduplication; subsequently, by the rule *akaḥ savarṇe dīrghaḥ* [Pāṇini 6.1.101], there is lengthening of the vowel *a* when followed by the prefix *anu*. Thus we have *anvavocat* and *anvabravīt*.
The *śap* [augment] is elided by *bruvo laṅliṭoḥ śapaḥ luk* [Pāṇini 2.4.53], and *īṭ* is added by *bruva īṭ* [7.3.93].
Thus, "anūvāca" [is formed]:

the *liṭ* [affix] takes *ṇal*, whereby there is *vṛddhi* [by 7.2.116]; as before, there is the single-substitute *samprasāraṇa* of the reduplicated syllable. The letter *ṅ* [in *bruviṅ*] is for the purpose of specification [by 3.4.99].

The letter *u* is for the purpose of specification [in the rule] "In *luṅ*, *laṅ*, and *lṛṅ*, the augment *aṭ* is udātta" (Pāṇini 6.4.71). This *luṅ* should be understood as referring to past time in general; for the *laṅ* and *liṭ* are prescribed for specific divisions of the past, namely the recent past (*anadyatana*) and the remote past. For example: *akārṣīt*.
> [[7.2.1]] Thus there is *vṛddhi*; as before, there is the augment *īṭ*.
Regarding "of *vasati*" and so forth:
since the suffix *laṅ* would otherwise apply for non-recent past time (*anadyatana*) from the root *vasa nivāse* (Dhātupāṭha 1005), it must be stated that *luṅ* applies instead.

The entire day, the fourth watch of the night that has passed, and the first watch of the coming night—this is "non-today" time (*anadyatana*). In that regard, when someone asks another who has risen during the fourth watch of the specific night that has passed, "Where did you stay?", he, while giving his reply during that specific night or by day, employs the *luṅ* (aorist) tense: "I stayed here."

And that [rule] does not apply here; because he has slept for three *praharas*—that is, for three *lakṣas*—of the first part of the remainder of that night, this constitutes his "non-today" (*anadyatana*) time, and therefore the *laṅ* suffix would be required. Consequently, the *luṅ* suffix must be stated—that is, explained.
However, the explanation here too must be made by resorting to the mention of the term "variously" (*bahulagrahaṇa*).
Thus: "in a continuous state of wakefulness."
If he remained awake throughout the entire remainder of that night without interruption, then the *laṅ* (imperfect) tense is used; however,
if he slept for even a single *muhūrta* during that specific part of the night, then only the *laṅ* is used— as in "I stayed here" (*avātsam*).

By the rule *luṅ, miṅ, tasthasthamipāṃ tāntantāmaḥ* [Pāṇini 3.4.101], the substitution of *am* occurs; by *vadavrajahalantasyācaḥ* [Pāṇini 7.2.3], vṛddhi is applied; and by *saḥ syārdhadhātuke* [Pāṇini 7.4.49], the *s* is changed to *t*. Regarding the term *anadyatane*:
if this were a *tatpuruṣa* compound, it would have to be either an exclusion (*paryudāsa*) or a simple negation (*prasajyapratiṣedha*).
In that case, according to the former view, the suffix would have to apply to something other than the current day (*adyatana*).

And thus, even in the case of "adya vā hyo vā abhokṣmahi" (I have not eaten today or yesterday), [the rule] would apply when there is a mixture of the current day and the non-current day. Since there exists a collection of the current and non-current days which is distinct from the non-current day alone, the sense arises that [the rule] does not apply to the other [purely current-day] case; consequently, it would apply to the general past. Therefore, the prohibition "anadyatane" (in the non-current) is a prohibition with respect to a specific type of past—the current day—and not with respect to the general past.

For the generality of the past (*bhūtasāmānya*) is not the same as a specific instance of the past (*bhūtaviśeṣa*); therefore, considering that the *tatpuruṣa* interpretation of the term is flawed, he says: "The term 'anadyatana' is a *bahuvrīhi* designation.

That in which the present day (*adyatana*) is non-existent is the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) characterized as the "past other than the present" (*anadyatanabhūta*). Here, the *laṅ* suffix occurs after a root referring to such a time, but it does not occur when there is a combination of both the present and the non-present, because in that case, a portion of the present day still exists.

Furthermore, it does not occur even in the mere generality of the past, for a specific instance is indeed contained within the generality, since the generality includes that specific instance within itself.
The meaning that "the *laṅ* [imperfect tense] should not occur where even a trace of the present day (*adyatana*) exists" is obtained when this is a *bahuvrīhi* compound.

If, then, this is a *bahuvrīhi*, it would follow that the *laṅ* occurs even for the present day itself; is there not a second present day within the present day? This is not so; because within the general category of the present day, there exists a specific portion of the present day such as a *muhūrta*. Therefore, it cannot be said that the present day is one in which the present day is non-existent—as in the expression, "Let us eat today or tomorrow."

The suffix *luṅ* takes the *ātmanepada* ending by [Pāṇini 1.3.66]. The suffix *mahiṅ* (the first person plural) undergoes the absence of *guṇa* because of the *kittva* of *sic*, according to [Pāṇini 7.2.42]: "In the case of *ātmanepada* endings, there is no *guṇa* for the root vowel after *liṅ* and *sic*. By [Pāṇini 8.2.30], there is *kutva*—the substitution of *ga* for *ja*; then, by [Pāṇini 8.4.54], there is *cartva*—the substitution of *ka* for *ga*. As before, there is the substitution of *ṣa*. Regarding the phrase "in the sense of the remote past" (*parokṣe ca*) and so forth:
the word *parokṣa* is a conventional term (*rūḍhiśabda*) that applies to an object beyond the reach of the senses.

"In the absence [of the speaker] and when known by the world" means when it is well-known in the world (*lokaprasiddhe*), within the range of the speaker's vision; "the *laṅ* ending" refers to that which is to be used, and it must be explained as being within the range of the speaker's vision. This explanation, however, must be made by resorting to the frequentative usage (*bahulagrahaṇa*) of that very rule. Now, is this not a contradiction to say, "in the absence [of the speaker] and within the range of the speaker's vision"? For an object that is "in the absence" (*parokṣa*) is said to be beyond the senses (*atīndriya*), whereas an object that has come within the range of the senses is "within the range of vision" (*darśanaviṣaya*). Therefore, if it is "in the absence," how can it be "within the range of vision"?

If it is an object of perception (*darśana-viṣaya*), how can it be "out of sight" (*parokṣa*)? This is not so; for it has been stated that it is an object capable of being perceived. There is no contradiction, as it is "out of sight" because it has not been [actually] experienced.

Regarding *aruṇati*: the root is *rudhir* in the sense of "obstructing" (Dhātupāṭha 1438); due to its belonging to the *rudhādi* class, there is the suffix *śnam*; then the suffix *tip*; and by the rule *halṅyābhyo dīrghāt sutisyapṛktaṃ hal* (Pāṇini 6.1.68), there is the elision of the *ti*.

The siege of Sāketa was within the range of vision for the speaker at that time and was well-known to the world; yet, because it was interrupted by other business and not directly experienced [by the speaker], it is also "out of sight" (*parokṣa*).
What is meant by "out of sight"? For example: *udagād ādityaḥ* ("the sun rose"). Here, the suffix *sic* is elided by the rule *gāti-sthā-* (Pāṇini 2.4.77).
The operations such as the substitution of *ādeśa* (and so forth) are to be applied as before.

Why specify "known by the world"? [Consider: *cakāra kaṭaṃ devadattaḥ* ("Devadatta made a mat"). Why specify "within the range of the speaker's vision"? [Consider: *jaghāna kaṃsaṃ kila vāsudevaḥ* ("Vāsudeva indeed slew Kaṃsa").

In the case of the root *han*, the *liṭ* suffix is used for the remote past (*parokṣa*); there is reduplication, and by [Pāṇini 7.3.55], the substitution of *gh* for *h* occurs—namely, the letter *h* becomes *gh*. Because the killing of Kaṃsa occurred in a distant past, it is not within the range of perception of a speaker in the present day;
therefore, a speaker contemporary with the killing of Kaṃsa would have used only the *laṅ* suffix: "Vāsudeva killed Kaṃsa" (*ahan kaṃsaṃ vāsudevaḥ*).
In the primary example as well, the speaker should be understood as being contemporary with the inhabitants of Sāketa.
For him alone is this [the city] within the range of vision, not for anyone else. Regarding "vatsyāmaḥ":

[this is] the *lṛṭ* (future tense), *mas* (first person plural ending); by [Pāṇini 3.1.33], *sya* is substituted; as before, the *s* becomes *t* by [Pāṇini 7.3.101]; [then] the vowel lengthening [occurs].
Regarding the phrase "the inclusion of the word *vacana*," etc.:

for if the inclusion of the word *vacana* were not present, the suffix would apply only when the word *abhijñā* itself is the upapada; however, because it is included, the suffix applies to all those words that express the meaning of *abhijñā*. As for the word "if" (*yadi*).
This is a locative absolute (*satī saptamī*).
And the term "word expressing recognition" (*abhijñāvacana*) is understood to carry over [from the previous rule].
Therefore, he states—beginning with "in the presence of the word *yat*"—that where the word *yat* occurs, the word expressing recognition is not necessarily required to accompany it.
In *avasāma*, there is the *laṅ* [suffix] after the root *vas*; by [Pāṇini 6.4.107], there is the elision of *s*, and as before, there is the lengthening of the vowel.
By the words "merely a dwelling" (*vāsamātra*) and so forth, he shows that this is not the scope of the subsequent rule.

For if another defining condition were required there, then the rule in the subsequent sūtra would be optional; that is not desired, therefore it does not require one. "This is an option in both cases" means: in a case where [the suffix] is already applicable, and in a case where it is not yet applicable. For when the word *yat* is absent, it is applicable by the rule *abhijñāvacane luṭ* (Pāṇini 3.2.112); when the word *yat* is present, it is not applicable due to the prohibition *na yadi* (Pāṇini 3.2.113).

*Ākāṅkṣaṇam* is *ākāṅkṣā* (expectancy); that which exists together with expectancy is *sākāṅkṣaḥ*. Expectancy is said to be the cognition of a relationship, and that is a property of a conscious being; therefore, it is understood that the term *sākāṅkṣaḥ* is an attribute of the speaker. Thus he says: "If the speaker is expectant. To clarify the meaning of this very point, he says: "If the speaker is expectant."
To clarify the meaning of this very point, he says: "Of the characterized and the characteristic," and so forth.

In that context, if this is required, then what is being stated is this: if the knowledge whose object is the relationship between the characterized (*lakṣya*) and the characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) is established for the speaker;
that is to say, if the speaker requires the relationship between the characterized and the characteristic.

"bhokṣyāmahe" (we shall eat). The *ātmanepada* ending for the root *bhuja-* is as before, along with the suffix *syapratyaya*; the substitution of *e* for *ṭi* occurs, and by [Pāṇini 8.2.30], there is *kutva*—the change of the letter *j* to *g*; then by [Pāṇini 8.4.54], there is *cartva*—the change of *g* to *k*; and the *s* becomes *ṣ*.
What, then, are the "characterized" (*lakṣya*) and the "characteristic" (*lakṣaṇa*), between whose relationship the speaker has an expectation? To this he says: "The garment is the characteristic."

The characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) is so called because it is fully known, for by means of it a person is characterized. "But food is the characterized (*lakṣya*)"—this is because it is not fully known; it is not a characteristic.
"It is said that 'the characteristic has been fully known,' as for example, 'smoke [is the characteristic] of fire. But [an objection is raised: 'Now then' and so forth.
For the meaning of a verbal root (*dhātvartha*) is an action (*kriyā*) consisting of successive parts that is being accomplished (*sādhyamānā*);
and that which is being accomplished is non-existent (*asat*)."
Furthermore, that [non-existent] is not an object of the sense-faculties, because those [faculties] have only existent things as their objects.

And whatever is not an object of the sense-faculties is "parokṣa" (imperceptible); for this alone is the meaning of the verbal root [in the term *parokṣa*]. Therefore, the inclusion of the term "parokṣa" is redundant, because there is nothing to be excluded—this is the intended meaning. [The opponent replies: "This is true," referring to what was stated immediately following.
If this is true, then for the purpose of excluding what was the term "imperceptible" (*parokṣa*) employed? He says: "But there exists," and so forth.

In cases where the things to be accomplished are perceptible, people have the misconception of perception regarding the meaning of the verbal root—the nature of the action—while that action has not yet been completed.

But surely, even when they are attended to, the means of accomplishment (*sādhana*) are not directly perceived (*pratyakṣa*), because they are of the nature of a power (*śakti*), and because power is to be inferred from its effect (*kārya*); for an effect is not produced by that which lacks power, and thus power is inferred in the production of an effect. So why is it said that the means of accomplishment are directly perceived? This is not a fault. For since "powers reside in substances," and because the substance is directly perceived, these [powers]—which consist of the nature of power—are figuratively said to be directly perceived as well, by attributing the property of the substratum to those things residing within it.

Alternatively—that [action] too, being dependent on the means of accomplishment (*sādhana*), is expressed by the word "means" because the distinction between the substance (*dravya*) and its power (*śakti*) is not intended to be emphasized. By this mention of "imperceptibility" (*parokṣa*), there is an assumption of perceptibility (*pratyakṣābhimāna*); that very thing is called "imperceptible. Thus he says: "where it does not exist.

Furthermore, imperceptibility is not possible for the highest person (*uttama*) with respect to the self (*ātman*) or the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*), because their means of accomplishment are perceptible.

Anticipating the objection that "in that case, since they are perceptible to the world, the highest person would be established [as an agent]," he says: "with respect to the object of the highest," and so forth.

For an action is to be accomplished by oneself; when it cannot be achieved due to distraction of the mind, then it becomes indirect (*parokṣa*). Therefore, even in the case of a superior object, there is the state of being indirect. That indeed occurs, as in the expression "he lamented" (*vilalāpa*).

The form [is derived] from the root *lap* preceded by *vi*, in the perfect tense (*uttama-puruṣa*) with the suffix *ṇal*. Regarding the phrase "in the case of absolute concealment" (*atyantāpahnave*), this is evident. Concealment (*apahnava*) means denial (*apalāpa*).
It is sometimes absolute, which is the negation of everything; and sometimes non-absolute, which is the negation of only one part.
Among these, that which is absolute is the negation of everything; in that case, the suffix *liṅ* should be prescribed, meaning it should be explained.
However, even here, the explanation must be carried out by resorting to the principle of "variety" (*bahulagrahaṇa*).
Someone was asked by another, "Are you set out for Kaliṅga? and so forth;
he replied, "I did not go to Kaliṅga.
In this case, there is an absolute negation (*atyantāpahnava*), because it is not merely the object, Kaliṅga, that is denied, but the act of going as well.
However, when there is a denial of the location alone but not of the act of going, then the *laṅ* suffix occurs even though the denial is not absolute—as in: "I did not stay in Kaliṅga.
Likewise, someone might be asked by another after entering the Deccan: "Was this task performed by you?
and he would reply: "I did not enter the Deccan."
Here too, there is an absolute denial.

For instance, not only is activity pertaining to the southern region prohibited, but even entry is forbidden. By the expression "the question to be asked," he shows that the word *praśna* is used in the sense of the object (*karmasādhana*).
For if it were used in the sense of the instrument (*karaṇasādhana*), the word *praśna* would denote that by which one is questioned.

And that being the case, since its acquisition of self-nature (*ātmalābha*) occurs at all times because it is being uttered, the mention of "immediate time" (*āsannakāla*) would be redundant. Furthermore, even if [the suffix] were used in the sense of an action (*bhāva*), it would not apply after verbal roots that denote a different meaning,
such as in the case of *agacchati*.

The roots *gamlṛ* and *sṛplṛ* mean "to go" (Dhātupāṭha 982, 983). In the form *iyāja*, there is the substitution of *cha* according to [Pāṇini 7.3.77]: *iṣugamiyāṃ chaḥ*. In the form *iyāja*, there is vocalization (*samprasāraṇa*) according to [Pāṇini 6.1.17]: *liṭabhyāsasyobhayeṣām*.
Regarding the word "jaghāna" (he slew): the slaying of Kaṃsa is what is being questioned here. That [event] is temporally remote in relation to the present speaker.

The Naiyāyikas describe a period within five years as "proximate" (*āsannakāla*), whereas that which has passed five years is "remote" (*viprakṛṣṭa*). Here, the killing of Kaṃsa is a remote time. [An example is: "Naḍa used to study in the past."

From the root *iṅ* preceded by the prefix *adhi*, the suffix *laṭ* is applied; the *ātmanepada* ending occurs according to [Pāṇini 1.3.13], the substitution of *e* for *ṭi* occurs according to [Pāṇini 3.4.79], and the lengthening occurs according to [Pāṇini 7.4.25]: "The long vowel is substituted for the *ik* of a non-*kṛt* or non-*sārvadhātuka* suffix. By [Pāṇini 6.1.97]: "A long vowel is substituted for *aka* when followed by a homogeneous vowel," the lengthening occurs together with the prefix. Alternatively, the *ātmanepada* ending occurs in the sense of the agent (*kartṛ*); due to its belonging to the *adādi* class, there is elision of the suffix *śap* according to [Pāṇini 2.4.72], and the substitution of *at* occurs according to [Pāṇini 7.1.5]; then, as before, the *iyaṅ* substitution for the root vowel occurs as appropriate. Thus: "*bravīti*."

Regarding *brāuva īṭ* [Pāṇini 7.3.93]: in the case of *kathayati*, the root *katha* (meaning "to compose a speech") is listed as number 1851 in the Dhātupāṭha; it belongs to the curādigaṇa and ends in a short vowel (*a*). From this, the suffix *ṇic* is added. Because of the status of being a *sthānivadbhāva* (as if it were the original element) by [Pāṇini 1.1.57], the *vṛddhi* substitution does not occur by [Pāṇini 7.2.116].

Now, for what purpose has this been commenced again? Since the previous rule provides for the case of the remote (*parokṣa*), it does not apply to the non-remote (*aparokṣa*); therefore, this is begun so that [the rule] may also apply there. But surely, in the preceding *yoga*, the mention of "remote" (*parokṣa*) will be withdrawn; once that is withdrawn, by the preceding rule alone it will apply both to the remote and the non-remote? This is true.

Someone might also raise this objection: "If the mention of *parokṣa* (the remote past) has ceased [in this rule], then the mention of *anadyatana* (not of today), which is connected to it, must also have ceased. So that this is not understood otherwise, the mention of *parokṣa* from the preceding sūtra is carried over (*anuvartate*). And while that is being carried over, this [present rule] must be formulated; otherwise, it would not apply to cases that are not *aparokṣa* (i.e., not remote). Regarding the phrase "*pṛṣṭaprativacane*" (in response to a question): *praśnaḥ* means *pṛṣṭam* (that which is asked); the suffix *niṣṭhā* is used here in the sense of the abstract action (*bhāve*). A reply preceded by a question is *pṛṣṭaprativacanam*. This is a *madhyamapadalopa* (middle-term elided) compound belonging to the class beginning with *śākapārthiva*.
"The phrase 'in the non-contemporary past' and 'out of sight' have ceased to apply," because they lack the svarita accent.
"Did you make a mat, Devadatta?"— this is the question.
"Indeed, I am doing it, sir"—this is a reply preceded by a question.
"Have you said anything there, Devadatta?"—this is the question.
"Indeed, I am doing it, sir"—this is the reply preceded by a question. "Has he not done it?"—this is the question.
Since a response does not occur preceded by a question, the *luṅ* [aorist] suffix alone is used.

But surely every response is indeed preceded by a question; therefore, the mention of "asked" (*pṛṣṭa*) is useless, as there is nothing to be excluded. This is not accepted; for this word "response" (*prativacana*) certainly exists in the sense of a statement following a question—that which does not occur without a question.

In the case of an *avyayībhāva* compound, there is the word *vacana*, as in *vacanaṃ vacanaṃ prativacanam* ("word after word, a response"), where the *avyayībhāva* occurs in the sense of repetition (*vīpsā*) according to [Pāṇini 2.1.6], "An indeclinable [is compounded] in the sense of 'according to'. There is also a word for "composure" (*samādhi*), because we see that the root *vac* preceded by *prati* is used in the sense of composure; for thus speakers say, "That which was not previously stated has been uttered by me," meaning it has been refined. Thus, since the word *prativacana* has multiple meanings, if the mention of "what is asked" (*pṛṣṭa*) were not made, it would apply to all these meanings.

But when this [rule] is being formulated, only that word which is a response preceded by a question is understood, and no other; thus there is no pointlessness in your objection. Regarding "nākarṣam": the substitution of *am* is as before. Regarding "in the word *purā*":
by this he shows that the word *purā* is taken here as a subordinate element (*upapada*), and not the form *puri*.

If this is indeed the case, then since this [word] ends in the vowel *ā*, would it not be incorrect to provide the locative form *purī* (ending in *ī*) as a reference? This fault does not arise because of the elision of the vowel *ā* due to a split in the rule (*yogavibhāga*) based on Pāṇini 6.4.140. Alternatively, why is it not understood that the word *pūḥ*—which is derived from the root *pṛ* (meaning "to protect" and "to fill," Dhātupāṭha 1086) by the addition of the suffix *kvip* according to the rule for the *bhrājādi* group (Pāṇini 3.2.177), followed by the substitution of *u* for the root vowel and the subsequent replacement of *r* as the substitute for *ṛ* (Pāṇini 7.1.102)—is also taken here as a subordinate term (*upapada*)? Because such a word cannot function in the sense of "not belonging to the current day" (*anadyatana*).

Since the word *purā* occurs in that very context, it is appropriate to take that [word] alone; he shows this by indicating that the present tense (*laṭ*) is drawn in by the particle *ca* in the rule "and after *purā*" (*luṅ ca*). He says, "according to their respective domains" (*yathāviṣayam*).

In the rule *yathā’sādṛśye* [Pāṇini 2.1.7], there is an *avyayībhāva* compound with *vīpsā* (repetition). Regarding the phrase "others as well," these refer to the *laṅ* (imperfect) and other such verbal suffixes.
"Vasanti" is [an example of] the present tense (*laṭ*);
"avātsuḥ" is [an example of the aorist].

In the case of *luṅ*, by the rule *sijabhyastavidibhyaśca* [Pāṇini 3.4.109], there is the substitution of *jus* for *jhi*; by the rule *vadavraja* [Pāṇini 7.2.3] and so forth, there is *vṛddhi*; and as before, there is the substitution of *t* for the *s*.
Thus, *avasan* is formed from *laṅ*.
Regarding the form *ūṣuḥ*: it is the *liṭ* [perfect] tense.

By the rule *parasmaipadānām* [Pāṇini 3.4.82], *jhi* is replaced by *jus*; there is reduplication; there is vocalization (*samprasāraṇa*) by the rule *vacyādisūtreṇa* [Pāṇini 6.1.15]; and by the rule *liṭabhyāsasyobhayeṣām* [Pāṇini 6.1.17], the same applies to the reduplicated syllable; finally, by the rule *śāsivasighasīnāñca* [Pāṇini 8.3.60], the substitution of *ṣ* occurs. Regarding the phrase "begun but not completed":
that which has been commenced—that is, set forth for accomplishment—and has not yet reached completion, is called "present" (*vartamāna*).

Since the term "present" (*vartamāna*) is mentioned within the governing rule for verbal roots (*dhātu-adhikāra*), it is understood as a qualifier of that very meaning [of the root]. Thus he says: "in the present," and so forth.
For it is not possible for the occurrence (*vṛtti*) of a verbal root to apply to something other than the meaning of the root itself.
The letter *ṭ* in *laṭ* (the technical designation for the present tense suffix) is for the purpose of specification.

The letter *a* [in the term *apṛkta*] is for the purpose of specification; otherwise, if *i* were uttered as *hr*, there would be the inclusion of the *liṭ* and other affixes. The *ś* in *śatṛ* and *śānac* is for the purpose of [designating them as] *sārvadhātuka*.
The *ṛ* is for the purpose of the operations associated with *ugit* stems. This [term *aprathamāsamānādhikaraṇa*] is an exclusion (*paryudāsa*).
In this grammatical treatise, the word *prathamā* is a technical term (*rūḍha*) restricted to the specific case-ending *su*.

Any case-ending other than the *prathamā*, such as the second (*dvitīyā*) and so forth, is called *aprathamā*. The word *samāna* here signifies "common" or "shared," as in the example: "Devadatta and Yajñadatta possess equal wealth."
This word *adhikaraṇa* denotes that which is expressed [by the term]; "that which is common (*samāna*) and that which is its locus (*adhikaraṇa*)" forms a *karmadhāraya* compound.
*Aprathamayā samānādhikaraṇam* = *aprathamāsamānādhikaraṇam*. The compound is formed by the split (*yogavibhāga*) of the rule *tṛtīyā* [Pāṇini 2.1.30].
Consequently, the locative case is applied by the rule *yasya ca bhāvena bhāvalakṣaṇam* [Pāṇini 2.3.37].
By means of an action (*bhāva*) that is not in grammatical coreferentiality (*asamānādhikaraṇa*) with the first case, the action denoted by the suffixes *śatṛ* and *śānac* is characterized.

The term "not the first" (*apramathā*) functions as an exclusion (*paryudāsa*), thereby including the second and subsequent cases; thus, by the maxim regarding the inclusion of what ends in a suffix (*pratyayagrahaṇaparibhāṣā*), there will be an application of the rule to that which ends in those suffixes. This is why he says: "provided it is not ending in the first case," and so forth.
"Of that" refers to the present tense suffix (laṭ).
"Coreferentiality" refers to [the relationship between the action and the agent].

Regarding the phrase *sāmānābhidheyam*: the meaning of the sentence is that the suffixes *śatṛ* and *śānac* occur only if coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇyam*)—that is, having the same denotatum (*sāmānābhidheyatvam*)—is possible with a word ending in the second case (*dvitīyāntena*), and not otherwise. By explaining it in this way, it is shown that in this context an exclusion (*paryudāsa*) of what is not coreferential with the nominative is intended, rather than a simple negation (*prasajyapratiṣedha*). For if a simple negation were intended, he would have said: "if there is no coreferentiality with a word ending in the first case (*prathamāntena*)."

Furthermore, what would happen if a non-presuppositional negation (*prasajya-pratiṣedha*) were resorted to? The suffixes *śatṛ* and *śānac* would not occur when the subsequent word is not in grammatical coreferentiality (*asamānādhikaraṇa*)—for instance, *bhajyata iti bhaktiḥ*, *kurvan bhaktir asya kurvadbhaktiḥ*, or *kurvāṇo bhaktir asya kurvāṇabhaktiḥ*.

Moreover, those secondary derivatives (*taddhita*) that function when not in coreferentiality with the first member would also fail to occur—for example, under the rule *praśaṃsāyāṃ rūpap* [Pāṇini 5.3.66], one could not have *kurvadrūpam* or *kurvāṇarūpam*; and under the rule *īṣadasamāptau kalpaśabdeśyadeśīyaraḥ* [Pāṇini 5.3.67], one could not have *kurvatkalpaḥ*.

But surely the fault remains even in the case of *paryudāsa* (exclusion), for it is not the case that [the rule] "two [verbs] occur when [one] is not ending in the first case" applies here, even though there is coreferentiality with a word in the nominative.
However, in the case of *prasajyapratiṣedha* (absolute negation), having first established the negation, it is improper to subsequently enjoin what has been negated, as in:
"See Devadatta cooking."
He shows coreferentiality with a word ending in the second case:
"pacatā" (by the one cooking). [He shows it] with a word ending in the third case.

By changing the case-ending [of *devadattena*] and connecting it as "by Devadatta" (*devadattena*), [the relationship is established]. Now, one might object: here there is grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) between the substitute for *laṭ* (*tiṅ*) and that which does not end in the nominative case, but not with *laṭ* itself, because *laṭ* is never actually used in application. There is no fault, however, because the property of the substitute is metaphorically attributed to the original base (*sthānin*); thus, coreferentiality is metaphorically attributed to *laṭ* as well. Now, what is the purpose of mentioning *laṭ*, since *laṭ* indeed continues from the immediately preceding rule? This might be the case: [but] this [word *laṭ*] ends in the nominative case.

The meaning here is conveyed by the use of the genitive case; therefore, one might argue that the mention of *laṭ* must be repeated for the sake of the genitive construction. However, this is incorrect. Even though the word ending in *laṭ* is in the nominative, its meaning will undergo a change of case (vibhaktivipariṇāma) so that it is understood as being in the genitive. To address this, he says: "While *laṭ* is still in force," and so forth.
The repetition of *laṭ* is for the purpose of excluding cases where there is coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the nominative.
By this, in some instances, it occurs even when there is coreferentiality with the nominative—as in *kurvan brāhmaṇaḥ* ("the Brāhmaṇa who is doing").
Regarding the form *san brāhmaṇaḥ*:
[the root] *as* meaning "to exist" (*dhātupāṭha* 1065) belongs to the *adādi* class, and thus there is elision of the *śap* suffix.
Then, by the rule *śnasoralopaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.4.111), there is the elision of the letter *a*.

In all instances such as "vidyamānaḥ" and so forth, the word "brāhmaṇaḥ" is to be understood as required. The root *vid* in the sense of "existence" (Dhātupāṭha 1171) belongs to the Divādi class and takes the Ātmanepada endings; here, the suffix *śyan* is applied.
[The form] "juhvat" is derived according to Pāṇini 3.2.78.

The root *hu*—meaning "to give" (*dāne*; according to the *Dhātupāṭha*, 1083; the *Bhāṣya* states it means "to take" or even "to please")—undergoes the *yaṇ* substitution by [Pāṇini 6.4.87]. By [Pāṇini 7.1.78], there is an absence of the *num* augment after a reduplicated stem followed by the suffix *śatṛ*. Thus, we have the form *adhīyānaḥ*.
The root *iṅ*—meaning "to study" (*adhyayane*; *Dhātupāṭha*, 11046)—is preceded by the prefix *adhi*.
As before, by the rule *aciśnu* [Pāṇini 6.4.77] and others, *iyaṅ* is substituted. Regarding the rule *māṅyākrośe*:

when the root *māṅ* is used as a subordinate word (*upapada*) and reproach (*ākrośa*) is implied, the suffixes *śatṛ* and *śānac* are applied to the present tense (*laṭ*). For example: *mā pacan*, *mā pacamānaḥ*.

But surely, in this very case, the *luṅ* (aorist) suffix ought to occur after *māṅ*, precisely because of this additional rule? There is no fault, because by the repeated mention of *laṭ* (present), the [aorist] does not occur in cases of abuse (*ākrośa*). The scope (*avakāśa*) for the rule *māṅi luṅ* [Pāṇini 3.3.175] is where there is no abuse. "Some maintain that the term *vibhāṣā* (optionally) is carried over" means that this is for the purpose of ensuring that the *śatṛ* and *śānac* suffixes occur optionally in examples such as *san brāhmaṇo 'sti* or *brāhmaṇo 'sti*.
By the use of the word "some" (*kecit*), it is implied that some do not follow [the rule].

Their intention is as follows: if those two [suffixes] were invariably applied when not in grammatical agreement with a nominative (*aprathamā-samānādhikaraṇe*), then the author would not have included the phrase "not in agreement with a nominative"; he would have simply said, "the *śatṛ* and *śānac* [are used].

In that case, the meaning would be this: since the *śatṛ* and *śānac* are prescribed generally for both cases—namely, in agreement with a nominative and elsewhere—the mention [of the condition "not in agreement with a nominative"] would not need to be made again.

Therefore, by the force of the inclusion of the term "not having the same referent as a word ending in the first case" (*aprathamāsamānādhikaraṇa*), those two [suffixes] necessarily occur only when they do not have the same referent as a word ending in the first case, whereas they occur otherwise when they have the same referent as a word ending in the first case.

If, then, they were to carry forward the mention of the option (*vibhāṣāgrahaṇa*), then just as in cases such as *san brāhmaṇaḥ*, *asti brāhmaṇaḥ*, *vidyamāno brāhmaṇaḥ*, and *vidyate brāhmaṇaḥ*, where they occur optionally; so too would they occur in cases such as *kurvadbhaktiḥ* and *kurvāṇabhaktiḥ*. To this he says: "And that," etc. "In that regard," etc.
Since there is an established option (*vyavasthitavibhāṣā*),
[the rule] says "according to observation" (*yathādarśanam*); that is, usages consistent with the observed linguistic data (*lakṣya*) should be inferred accordingly.
This is what is meant: [the suffixes] should be understood as being like the perception of an object.

In some cases, those two suffixes, *śatṛ* and *śānac*, are obligatory (*nitya*); in some cases, they are optional (*pākṣika*); and in some cases, they are non-existent (*avidyamāna*). Among these, they are obligatory in instances such as *kurvadbhaktiḥ*, *kurvāṇabhaktiḥ*, *kurvattaraḥ*, and *kurvattamaḥ*; they are optional in instances such as *san brāhmaṇaḥ* and *asti brāhmaṇaḥ*; and they are simply non-existent when followed by suffixes such as *tarap* and *tamap*.

Regarding the example *pacatitarām*: from the word *pacati*, the suffix *tarap* is applied by [Pāṇini 5.3.56] *tiṅaśca*; then, when the feminine suffix *ām* is applied by [Pāṇini 5.4.11] *kimaettiṅavyayaghādāmvadravyaprakarṣe*, the two [suffixes *ām* and *su*] do not occur. "The commencement [of this rule] is for the sake of [the case ending] coreferential with the nominative (*prathamā-samānādhikaraṇa*)"—here, a restriction (*avadhāraṇa*) is to be understood.

The previous rule (*pūrvayoga*) has the meaning of being non-co-referential with the nominative (*prathamā-asamānādhikaraṇa*), as well as, in some cases, the meaning of being co-referential with the nominative (*prathamā-samānādhikaraṇa*); this [present] rule, however, has exclusively the meaning of being co-referential with the nominative.

If, then, the previous rule also has the meaning of being co-referential with the nominative, then—this being the case—it might be argued that since those two [suffixes, *śatṛ* and *śānac*,] occur elsewhere even when co-referential with the nominative, they will likewise occur in the vocative (*sambodhana*), making this [present rule] redundant? It is not redundant; for it serves to provide a detailed exposition (*prapañca*) of that very same point. For example: "O cooking one" (*he pacan*).
> [[8.2.8]] Thus, due to the prohibition of *nalopa*, there is no elision of the *n*.
[In the form] `he pacamāna`, [the rule] `[[6.1.69]]` effects the elision of the case-ending (*su*). [The statement] "`And this is a qualifier of the meaning of the verbal root`" means:
Because the context concerns *dhātu* (roots).
Why then do these two [suffixes] not occur when there is an *upapada* (a governing word)? Because of the statement "of action" (*kriyāyāḥ*).
If they were to occur when there is an *upapada*, then the mention of "action" would be purposeless.

For an *upapada* is [an affix] that follows a verbal root (*dhātu*), and since that [root] expresses action (*kriyā*), even without the explicit mention of "action," both [the *hetu* and the *lakṣaṇa*] will be understood as having action as their domain.

Therefore, by the inclusion of the term "action" (*kriyāgrahaṇa*), when those two serve as qualifiers of the meaning of the verbal root, it is understood that in some cases the meaning of the root is the cause (*hetu*) of a substance (*dravya*) or its characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*); in some cases, it is the cause of a quality (*guṇa*); and in some cases, it is the cause of an action (*kriyā*).
Thus, the inclusion of the term "action" is appropriate for the purpose of excluding substances and the like; hence the statement "of an action" (*kriyāyāḥ*).
Regarding the phrase "having action as their object":
this is an explanation of the word *kriyāyāḥ*.
Those two for whom action (*kriyā*) is the object (*viṣaya*) are described in that way.

By this, it is indicated that the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) in the phrase "of the action" (*kriyāyāḥ*) is prescribed in place of the locative (*saptamī*) through a transposition of case endings (*sub-vyatyaya*). As in the example "those lying down eat" (*śayānā bhuñjate*):

because [the root] *śīṅ* is an exception [to the rule for *śap*], there is elision of *śap*, and by the rule "for *śīṅ* before a *sārvadhātuka* suffix" (*śīṅaḥ sārvadhātuke* 7.4.21), there is *guṇa* substitution.

In this context, "lying down" (*śayana*) is the defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*), and the act of eating (*bhujikriyā*) is the object (*viṣaya*). For it is by means of that [eating] that the act of eating is characterized; therein the root *śīṅ* (to lie down) occurs.
As for the expression "standing, they instruct," the substitution of *tiṣṭha* for the root *sthā* is according to the rule *pāghrādhmādheṭdṛśaḥ śaḥ* (Pāṇini 7.3.78).

In this case, "staying" (*avasthāna*) is the indicator (*lakṣaṇa*), by which the act of "instructing" (*anuśāsana*) is indicated. In the examples "he lives while earning" (*arjayan vasati*) and "he cooks while reciting" (*pacati paṭhati*), the relationship of indicator and indicated (*lakṣya-lakṣaṇa-bhāva*) between the two actions is not intended to be expressed.
"That which trembles is air (*vāyu*).

For here, trembling is the defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*), and by means of it, air is defined; however, this does not concern an action, but rather concerns a substance (*dravya*), because air is a substance.
"That which floats is light."
In this case, the quality (*guṇa*) known as "lightness" (*laghu*) is indicated by the act of jumping (*utplavana*); thus, that [quality] has the *guṇa* as its object, not the action.

Although in examples such as *varṣatīti dhāvati* ("he runs because it rains") and *hantīti palāyate* ("he flees because he is being struck"), the actions of running and fleeing are indicated by the acts of raining and striking, nevertheless the suffixes *śatṛ* and *śānac* do not occur. This is because the rule *Pāṇini 3.2.121* follows from the phrase *vyavasthitavibhāṣā* ("restricted option"); for by the use of the particle *iti*, the state of being a cause (*hetubhāva*) is made manifest.
Furthermore, the fact that the prior placement [of the word] is a characteristic mark (*liṅga*) of non-deviation is the indicator.
By this [sūtra 2.2.32], the rule regarding the prior placement (*pūrvanipāta*) of a word ending in *dhi* is shown to have exceptions;
that is, even though its own scope (*svaviṣaya*) exists, there are cases where it does not apply.

This specific mention [of *hetulakṣaṇayoḥ*] is the indicator (*liṅga*) of those exceptions. For if the prior placement of a word ending in *dhi* were subject to exceptions, [the author] would have formulated the rule as *hetulakṣaṇayoḥ*.

But when there is deviation [from the rule], expressions such as "smoke and fire" become justified. Now, one might ask: since this designation would apply to the *śatṛ* and *śānac* suffixes simply by virtue of being the subject under discussion, what is the purpose of mentioning the suffix *tu*? To this he says: "The mention of *tu*" and so forth. The meaning is that the mention of *tu* is for the sake of preventing confusion with other specific qualifiers (*upādhi*). The qualifier here is the present tense, because the *śatṛ* and *śānac* suffixes are prescribed for that time.

When the mention of *tau* (the suffixes *śatṛ* and *śānac*) is made for the purpose of including the grammatical property (*upādhi*), he asks: "What happens? and replies with the words "*śatṛśānajmātrasya*" and so forth.
The inclusion of the word *mātra* (only) is for the purpose of excluding the inclusion of the grammatical property.
For if the mention of *tau* were not made, the designation would apply only to those two [suffixes] exactly as they appear in their original form (*prakṛti*).

And what are those two like? They are prescribed for the present tense (*vartamānakāla*). Consequently, *sad* would not be the technical designation (*saṃjñā*) for the substitutes of *lṛṭ*, which are prescribed for the future tense (*bhaviṣyatkāla*).

[Objection: But surely those two are prescribed by the word *sat* in the rule *luṭaḥ sadvā* [Pāṇini 3.3.14]; therefore, by the force of that statement, they will indeed belong to the future? [Response: We do not say that their prescription is not established; rather, we say that once they have been prescribed, the subsequent designation (*saṃjñā*) does not become established.

Furthermore, in cases such as *brāhmaṇasya kurvāṇaḥ* ("of the Brahmin, doing") or *brāhmaṇasya kariṣyamāṇaḥ* ("of the Brahmin, about to do"), the prohibition of the sixth-case compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*) by the rule *pūraṇaguṇa-* (Pāṇini 2.2.11) would not apply [if the term *sat* were not used].

However, the inclusion of the word *sat* (meaning "being") serves the purpose of prohibiting the sixth-case compound specifically for those forms ending in the present participles *śatṛ* and *śānac* when they are themselves expressed by the word *sat*.

In the inclusion of *sat*, the designation (*saṃjñā*) is declared based on the mere form without regard for the specific qualifiers *śatṛ* and *śānac*; thus, the designation is established even for those [forms] that are not restricted to the present tense. Therefore, the suffixes *śatṛ*, *śānac*, and so forth, are prescribed for the present time.

Are these substitutes (*ādeśa*) for *la*, or are they suffixes (*pratyaya*)? In this regard, if the term *laṭ* is understood to carry over [from the previous rule], then they are substitutes for *la*; however, if it does not carry over, then they are suffixes.

If they were to be made substitutes for that [root], then the mention of the word *vibhāṣā* (optionally) would have to be carried over from [Pāṇini 3.2.121]; otherwise, in cases such as "Devadatta purifies" (*pavate devadattaḥ*) or "Devadatta sacrifices" (*yajate devadattaḥ*), one would hear the *tiṅ* endings.

But under the principle of suffix-characterization (*pratyayalakṣaṇa*), when by the rule of dissimilar forms (*vāsarūpavidhi*) the *laṭ* occurs, then the hearing of the suffix—that is, the hearing of the *tiṅ*—is established.

Furthermore, under the view that [the suffixes] are substitutes (*ādeśapakṣa*), by the rule *[[P. 3.4.69]]*, the suffixes *śānan* and so forth would apply even in the sense of the action (*bhāva*) or the object (*karman*), yet they are intended to apply only in the sense of the agent (*kartṛ*).

Under the view that they are independent suffixes (*pratyayapakṣa*), however, by the rule *[[P. 3.4.67]]*, they occur only in the sense of the agent, not in the sense of the action or the object. In this case, in the example *iha katīha maṇḍayamānaḥ*, if the suffix *cānaś* were applied [under the *ādeśapakṣa*], there would be an accentual depression (*nighāta*) by the rule *[[P. 8.1.28]]*; but under the *pratyayapakṣa*, this does not occur, because [the suffix] is not an *ārdhadhātuka*.

[If *cānaś* were treated as a suffix,] by [Pāṇini 3.1.67] and [3.1.68], the technical designation *ātmanepada* would apply; consequently, it would occur only after roots that are *ātmanepadins*—as in the example: "How many here are striking? (*katīha nighnānāḥ*). In the view that it is a suffix (*pratyaya*), however, there is no possibility of the designation *ātmanepada* because it is not a substitute (*ādeśa*). Thus, since there are many faults to be remedied in the view that it is a substitute, and even if they were remedied, there would be excessive complexity in understanding them, he adopts the view that it is a suffix and says: "The suffix *śānan* occurs."
The *śakāra* is for the purpose of designating the *sārvadhātuka* category.

In the example "pavamānaḥ," [the root] is *pūṅ* in the sense of "purifying" (*dhātupāṭha* 966); *śap* is applied [by Pāṇini 3.1.68], followed by [the substitution of *mā* for *śap*] according to [Pāṇini 7.2.82]. "If," etc. [refers to the following].
The question arises from one who considers that in rules such as *na lokāvyaya* [Pāṇini 2.3.69], the term *tṛn* refers specifically to the suffix *tṛn* alone.
[The answer is: "Because *tṛn* is used here as a designation for a *pratyāhāra* (a collective term).
For example: *somaṃ pavamānaḥ* ("purifying the Soma") and *naḍamāghnānaḥ* ("striking the reed").
This should be connected with the phrase "prohibition of the genitive" (*ṣaṣṭhī-pratiṣedha*).

If *tṛn* were taken as a reference to the suffix itself, then in cases such as *somaṃ pavamānaḥ*, where the suffixes beginning with *śānan* express the meaning of the suffix, there would be no prohibition of the genitive.
However, *tṛn* is not a reference to the suffix; rather, it is a reference to a *pratyāhāra* (a grammatical abbreviation).

And since words such as *caśānan* are included therein, the prohibition of the genitive (*ṣaṣṭhī*) indeed applies. Regarding the statement "the mention of *śatṛ* after the root *dviṣ* is optional" [Pāṇini 3.2.131]:

because the *śatṛ* suffix prescribed by that rule is included within this pratyāhāra, there would be a prohibition of the genitive when used in conjunction with it; consequently, in the case of *caurasya dviṣan*, the genitive would not optionally occur.

Therefore, when the form ending in *śatṛ* from the root *dviṣ* (meaning 'to hate,' Dhātupāṭha 1013) is employed, the genitive should be stated as an alternative to the accusative that would otherwise be required. As in the example *maṇḍamānāḥ*.
The root *maḍ* is listed in the Dhātupāṭha as *maḍi bhūṣāyām* (321); due to its *it*-marker, the augment *num* is added. With the causative suffix *ṇic*, it becomes *bhūṣayamāṇāḥ*.
The root *bhūṣ* in the sense of "adornment" (Dhātupāṭha 682) takes the causative suffix *ṇic*.
Regarding the phrase "casting off their armor," the suffix *śyan* is applied because the root belongs to the *divādi* class.
That very age is reached; staying there, they cast off their armor—*kavaca* meaning *sannāha*, "armour.
[The phrase] "bearing their crests" (*śikhaṇḍaṃ vahamānāḥ*).
Here too, such an age is understood wherein those currently existing wear a crest (*śikhaṇḍa*).

*Śikhaṇḍa* means a tuft of hair (*cūḍā*). The mention of the word "speech" (*vacana*) is for the sake of variety; for even without it, when age is understood, the suffix is indeed obtained, as in the rule *vayasi ca* [Pāṇini 4.1.20].

Regarding the word "nighnānāḥ," it is understood to mean "the power of killing. Regarding the phrase "when the agent is not subject to difficulty" (*akṛcchriṇi kartari*), this indicates that the term *akṛcchriṇī* is an attribute of the agent, which is the meaning of the suffix.
"One whose verbal root-meaning (*dhātvartha*) is not difficult and is easily accomplished is *akṛcchrī*"; thus, by [Pāṇini 5.2.115], the suffix *ini* is applied. "Adhīyan" (studying).
As before, [the suffix] *iyaṅ* [is applied].
Regarding "dhārayan": from the verbal root *dhṛṅ* in the sense of "remaining" (*dhātupāṭha* 1412), the causative suffix *ṇic* is added. Regarding "amitraḥ śatruḥ": [it means] "an enemy is a foe."
Because the word *amitra* is a conventional term (*rūḍha*) meaning "enemy" from the very beginning. Regarding the phrase "he hates":
due to its belonging to the *adādi* class, there is elision of the *śap* suffix. Regarding the phrase "connection with sacrifice":
the word *saṃyoga* functions as a *karmasādhana* (an object-oriented derivation).
For this very reason, the commentary states: "in the pressing connected with the sacrifice.
"Connected" means related; that which is connected with the sacrifice is "connected with the sacrifice" (*yajñasaṃyukta*).
And when is the pressing connected with the sacrifice? When it becomes an auxiliary part (*aṅga*) of the sacrifice.
Regarding the passage beginning with "sunvantaḥ" and continuing with "sarve yajamānāḥ":

by the term "sunvantaḥ" (those who press the Soma), he shows that the *yajamānas*— namely the performers of a *sattra* sacrifice who are the masters of the rite— are intended, and not merely those officiating as priests (*yājñikas*).

But how is this meaning obtained, given that just as the sacrificers (*yajamāna*) are the agents of the pressing (*abhiṣava*), so too are the officiating priests (*yājaka*)? To this he says: "The mention of connection" (*saṃyogagrahaṇa*), and so forth. Here, it should be understood that [the rule] *suño yajñe* applies; for even when stated thus, the connection of the pressing with the sacrifice is indeed obtained, because the sense of the root *sunoti* (to press) is understood here as having the sacrifice as its domain. Therefore, is it not unnecessary to include the mention of "connection"? It is included for the purpose of indicating the primary agent (*pradhānakartṛ*).

"Those who, having become the performers of the sacrifice, obtain the fruit while pressing the soma—these are the primary agents; they are the sacrificers (*yajamāna*), not the officiating priests (*yājaka*). By the phrase "in the sense of those whose habit it is, etc., among the agents," he shows that "those whose habit it is" (*tacchīla*) and so forth serve as qualifiers of the meaning of the suffix. "And this *āṅ* is used in the sense of 'inclusiveness' (*abhividhi*)," where inclusiveness means pervasion (*abhivyāpti*).
Here, *aṅ* does not signify a limit; therefore, this is an indication of the meaning even for the *kvip* suffix that will be mentioned later.
That [suffix] also occurs only in the sense of "having that as one's habit" (*tacchīla*) and so forth.
"That," etc.

The term "of a root" (*dhātoḥ*) [from Pāṇini 3.1.91] is understood here; however, a qualification such as "habitual disposition" (*śīla*) and so forth is not applicable to a root itself. Therefore, that which is the meaning of the root is indicated by the word "having that as its habit" (*tacchīla*) and so forth, functioning as a qualifier for the three [categories] beginning with "habitual disposition. That meaning of the root is the "habit" (*śīla*) of someone—he is "one whose habit is that" (*tacchīla*).
That very same thing is the "duty" (*dharma*) of someone—he is "one whose duty is that" (*taddharmā*).
"One who acts rightly" (*sādhukārī*) means one who performs that activity which is the meaning of the verbal root; this is the sense of "acting rightly.
Regarding the term "by nature":
the intention is that from this [nature] proceeds a mode of conduct that is independent of results.

The intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) is a mental phenomenon (*caitasika-dharma*), and that, moreover, is simply ethical discipline (*śīla*). "Independent of fruit" means being devoid of desire for a result.
"Therein" refers to [the aforementioned].
Regarding the meaning of the verbal root:
"conducting oneself in that manner" (*tadācāraḥ*).
This shows that conducting oneself in that manner is distinct from having that as one's habitual disposition (*tacchīla*).
"He who properly performs the meaning of the element"— here too, "without virtue" is to be connected [to this]. Regarding the word "properly":
The meaning is "praiseworthy.
It is neuter because it functions as an adverbial modifier (*kriyāviśeṣaṇa*). Regarding the term *muṇḍayitāraḥ*:

the suffix *ṇic* is applied according to Pāṇini 3.1.21 (*muṇḍamiśra*), meaning "those who make [them] bald"; then, by the application of the *iṣṭhavadbhāva* rule, there is the elision of the *ṭi* (the *a* of *muṇḍa*).
"The Śrāviṣṭhāyanas are those who shave the bride after she has been married"—so says the *Kāśikā*. "The Śrāviṣṭhāyanas shave the bride once she is married";
this is their family custom (*kuladharma*).
"The Āhvarakas carry away the food when the *śrāddha* ceremony is completed."
This is their usage:
"He who makes a mat well is the maker of the mat";
"he who walks with ease through the village walks well. [The rule] beginning with "in the prescription of *tṛn*" and so forth [applies].
The present undertaking is for the purpose of excluding that which has such a habit.
Regarding the rule for the suffix *tṛn*, it should be stated that *tṛn* is applied after a verbal root that is not preceded by a prefix when the sense of "priest" (*ṛtvij*) is to be expressed;
for example, "hotṛ."

The root *hu* [is used] in the sense of "giving" (*dāna*), according to the Dhātupāṭha (1083), which states: "In giving" (*dāne*); some say it means "taking" (*ādāna*), and the Bhāṣya says it also means "pleasing" (*prīṇana*).
[The word] "potā" [is derived from this].
The root *pūṅ* means "purification" (*dhātupāṭha* 966).
Regarding the term *udgātā*:
the roots *kai* and *gai* mean "sound" (*dhātupāṭha* 916, 917). There is a variation in the vowel.

If the suffix *tṛc* is present, the word becomes oxytone by its original accent (*prakṛtisvara*) according to Pāṇini 6.2.139. However, if the suffix *tṛn* were present, then while 6.2.49 is still in force, 6.2.50 would apply, and its original accent would result as before. Regarding the rule "of *nī*, there is also *ṣuk*": the augment *ṣuk* is to be understood as occurring after the *guṇa* substitution has taken place; otherwise, because the penultimate vowel would not be light (*laghu*), the *guṇa* substitution would not occur.
Alternatively, the *guṇa* substitution itself must be explicitly stated.

The term *ṛtvij* is understood here as well. This [sūtra] is also commenced for the sake of meanings other than habitual action (*atācchīlyārtha*). Regarding the rule "from *tviṣ*, *ṭa*" and so forth:

from the root *tviṣ* (Dhātupāṭha 1001), meaning "to shine," the suffix *tṛn* should be stated when a deity is to be expressed, and the vowel *a* is the substitute for the penultimate vowel (*upadhā*).
"And the state of being *aniṭ*":
since this [rule] is a supplement to all [the preceding rules], its status as *aniṭ* is established in the case of *pota*. "Of *kṣad*" and so forth:
*kṣad* is a verbal root belonging to the Vedic (Sūtra) tradition.

This is established because words such as *hotṛ* and others are derived from the Uṇādi list according to the rule "from the roots *guh*, *ṛ*, *pac*, *ci*, *vayi*, *ami*, *sad*, and *kṣad*, the suffix *tra* is applied" (Uṇādisūtra 4.166), since they are among those forms specifically prescribed (*nipātita*) in the Uṇādi section.

For in that [sūtra], these are prescribed as *nipātana* (irregularly formed) stems: *naptṛ*, *neṣṭṛ*, *tvaṣṭṛ*, *kṣatṛ*, *potṛ*, *hotṛ*, *bhrātṛ*, *jāmātṛ*, *pitṛ*, and *duhitṛ* (Pāṇini 6.4.11). The root *kṛ* preceded by *alam*; again, that same root preceded by *ni* and *ā*; the root *jan* meaning "to appear" (*prādurbhāve*) preceded by *pra*; the root *pac* meaning "to make manifest" (*vyaktīkaraṇe*); the root *pad* meaning "to go"; some read *pati* instead [of *pad*]; and the roots *śala*, *hula*, and *patlṛ* meaning "to go."

The root *mad* is listed in the Dhātupāṭha as meaning "joy and pride" (*harṣaglepanayoḥ*), while *mad* is also listed as meaning "the means of satisfaction" (*tṛptisādhane*)—these words and others are preceded by the prefix *ud*.

From the roots *ruc* (meaning "to shine" and "to please," Dhātupāṭha 745), *trapūṣ* (meaning "shame," Dhātupāṭha 374) preceded by *apa*, *vṛtu* (meaning "to turn," Dhātupāṭha 758), *vṛdhu* (meaning "to grow," Dhātupāṭha 759), *ṣaha* (meaning "to endure," Dhātupāṭha 1809), and *car* (meaning "to move," Dhātupāṭha 559), the suffix *iṣṇuc* occurs; this is an exception (*apavāda*) to [the suffix] *tṛn*. (Note: The reading in the manuscript is *tṛṇo'pavādaḥ*.)

But when the root *kṛ* preceded by *alam* is used in the sense of "adornment" (*maṇḍana*), then [by rule 3.2.151] the suffix *yuc* would apply; therefore, a prior counter-exception (*pūrvavipratiṣedha*) must be stated. Otherwise, the suffix *iṣṇuc*—which has its scope elsewhere than in "adornment"—would supersede [the suffix *yuc*] due to its higher status.

As for those roots listed here with prefixes, the suffix occurs only when preceded by those specific prefixes; however, in other cases, it applies without restriction, as in *dhārayiṣṇavaḥ* and *pārayiṣṇavaḥ*.

The root *dhṛ* is listed as *dhṛṅ avasthāne* (Dhātupāṭha 1412), and *pṛ* as *pṛ pālanapūraṇayoḥ* (Dhātupāṭha 1086). The causative suffix *ṇic* is added, and by the rule *ayāmanta* (Pāṇini 6.4.55), the substitution of *ay* for the penultimate vowel occurs. Regarding the statement "the separation of the sūtra is for the sake of what follows": this is so that only the word *bhavati* may be carried over (*anuvartana*) into the subsequent sūtra. Otherwise, if the single sūtra *ṇibhūbhyāñca* were formed, then the mention of *ṇi* would also be drawn along [into the next rule]. Examples include *bhājiṣṇu* and so forth.
This is common usage.

Its introduction even in this commentary is for the purpose of demonstrating the suffix *iṣṇuc* after the root *bhrājṛ* in the sense of "shining" (*dīptau*; Dhātupāṭha 181). Now, as to why the vowel substitution *ī* occurs in the word *sthāsnur* by means of the rule *ghumāsthāgāpā* [Pāṇini 6.4.66], he says: "And this [suffix] is marked with *p*," and so forth.
The substitution of *ī* occurs before suffixes marked with *k* or *ṅ*.
In this context, because the phrase "tatra" [from Pāṇini 6.4.63] is understood as a governing rule (*anuvṛtti*), this [suffix] is neither *kit* nor *ṅit*; what then? It is *git*.
As for the non-hearing of the letter *g*, it is due to its being indicated in its changed form (*cartva*) as *c*.

If that is so, then in the case of *jiṣṇu*, the substitution of *guṇa* would apply; for while *guṇa* is prohibited before an affix marked with *k* or *ṅ* by the rule "na kṅiti" [Pāṇini 1.1.5], it is not prohibited before one marked with *g*. To this he says: "And before *kṅit*" (*kṅiti ca*), etc. Indeed, in the rule "na kṅiti" [1.1.5], only the letters *k* and *ṅ* are indicated; what then? The letter *g* is also included, having been changed to *c* (by internal sandhi); therefore, even before an affix marked with *g*, there is no *guṇa*.

In that case, regarding the word *bhūṣṇu*, since the prohibition of *iṭ* prescribed by [Pāṇini 7.2.11] "after a root ending in *śr*, *y*, or *k*, before a *kit* suffix" would not apply to a *git* suffix, he says: "The letter *g* is indicated as having become a *c* (i.e., *k*) in the rule 'after a root ending in *śr*, *y*, or *k*, before a *kit* suffix,'" which connects with the subject at hand.
"'By that' means by the indication of the letter *g* as having become a *c*. 'Because *kasnu* is a *git* suffix,' etc."
That which has *ga* as its technical designation (*itsaṃjñaka*) is called *git*; the state of being that is *gittva*.
Because of this *gittva*, the vowel *i* does not occur in the word *na syāt*; thus, the vowel *ī* does not occur after the root *tiṣṭhati*.

But why does the *git* designation not apply here? He says: "Because of the teaching that *ītva* [the substitution of *ī*] occurs before *kṅit*," and so forth. The vowel *a* in the syllable *kakāra* is for the purpose of pronunciation (*uccāraṇārtha*).
Since it is taught that *ītva* occurs before *kṅit*, and this [suffix] is *git*, therefore the *ītva* prescribed before *kṅit* does not apply here because of its *git* status.
If this is so, then in the word *jiṣṇu*, the *guṇa* substitution would apply; therefore, he says: "the absence of *guṇa*" and so forth.
That prohibition of *guṇa* which occurs when the three sounds *ka*, *ga*, and *ṅa* bear the designation *it* must be remembered—that is, known.
In the rule [Pāṇini 1.1.5], the sound *ga* is specified as having undergone the change to *ca*.

If, then, [the letter *g*] is elided, one might object that in the word *bhūṣṇu*, the prohibition of *iṭ* by the rule *śrayukaḥ kiti* [Pāṇini 7.2.11] would not apply; therefore, he says: "It should be understood that the prohibition of *iṭ* occurs because [the root] *śri* followed by *yuk* is *aniṭ*.
If the letter *g* were subject to elision (*cartva*), the prohibition of *iṭ* by the rule *śrayukaḥ kiti* [7.2.11] would not apply. To this he says: "*śrayuko 'niṭtvam*" and so forth.
Thus, even the letter *g* is indicated as being subject to elision (*cartva*).

In this regard, it should be understood that even for the two letters *ka* and *ga*, which bear the designation *it*, there is the prohibition of the augment *iṭ* based on their being "non-*iṭ*-taking" (*aniṭ*) when followed by a consonant cluster (*śrayuk*).
