If the letter *ga* were treated as having become *ca* (as in *cakāra*), then in the rule *śrayukaḥ kiti* [Pāṇini 7.2.11], it would be specified as such, and consequently, the substitution of *u* [for the vowel] by the rule *haśi ca* [Pāṇini 6.1.110] would apply; however, since that [substitution] is considered "unestablished" (*asiddha*), there is no fault. Alternatively, because this is a Vedic-style (*sautra*) formulation, the reading is not in *saṃhitā* (continuous) form, and thus the rule does not apply—this is the solution. However, all of this is unacceptable to Vāmana.
This has been established in the passage beginning with "yathā nābhimataṃ tathā" (as it is not desired, so [it is]). Regarding the words "daṃśeḥ" and so forth,
the term *upasaṃkhyāna* functions in the sense of "explanation" or "addition."

The addition of the *ksnu* suffix must also be prescribed for the root *daṃśa* (meaning "to bite," Dhātupāṭha 898). The following is the justification for this: the particle *ca* ("and") is carried over from the preceding rule, and it serves the purpose of including what has not been explicitly mentioned; therefore, [the suffix] will apply to the root *daṃś* as well.
Thus, we have the form *daṃkṣṇavaḥ*.
The substitution of *ṣ* occurs by [Pāṇini 8.2.36] *vraścādinā*, and the substitution of *k* occurs by [Pāṇini 8.2.41].

The elision of the nasal vowel (*anunāsikalopa*) does not take place by [Pāṇini 6.4.24] *aniditām*, because the suffix *ksnu* is marked with the *g* indicator. However, for those who maintain that [the suffix] has the *k* indicator, they must apply a split of the rule (*yogavibhāga*) here—adding "not" (*na*)—to the rule [Pāṇini 6.4.30] *neti*, in order to prohibit the elision of the letter *n*.

Or else, another effort must be made by them: that the *nakāra* becomes an *anusvāra*, and that [the *anusvāra*] undergoes *parasavarṇa* substitution. [The roots involved are: *tras* in the sense of "trembling" or "agitation" (DhP 1741), *gṛdh* in the sense of "desire" (DhP 1246), *ñighṛṣ* in the sense of "boldness" (DhP 1269), and *kṣip* in the sense of "impelling" (DhP 1285). Regarding the form *trasnuḥ*:
there is a prohibition of the augment *iṭ* by the rule *neḍvaśikṛti* (Pāṇini 7.2.8).

Regarding the term *gṛghnuḥ*: by [Pāṇini 6.4.24], there is the absence of the *guṇa* substitution. [The roots are: *śamu* in the sense of pacification (DhP 1201); *tamu* in the sense of longing (DhP 1202); *damu* in the sense of cessation (DhP 1203); *śramu* in the sense of asceticism and exhaustion (DhP 1204); *bhramu* in the sense of instability (DhP 1205); *kṣamu* in the sense of endurance (DhP 1206); *klamu* in the sense of fatigue (DhP 1207); and *madī* in the sense of exhilaration (DhP 1208). [The mention of these roots] is for the sake of the *kutva* change in subsequent rules.
In examples such as *samparki*, it is so that the rule *cajoḥ ku ghiṇyatoḥ* [Pāṇini 7.3.52] may apply.
The statement "the letter *u* is for the sake of pronunciation" serves to exclude its status as an *anubandha*.
If [the vowel *u*] were a marker (*anubandha*), then for the word *śamin*, the form *śaminau* would result, and by the rule *ugidacām* [Pāṇini 7.1.70], the augment *num* would be applied.

Furthermore, in the case of *śaminitarām* and *śaminitamām*, while the rule [6.3.44] is in effect, rule [6.3.45] would optionally cause shortening; otherwise, the making of the short *u* as a marker would be purposeless.
Therefore, the vowel *u* serves solely for the purpose of pronunciation.
By the rule *hrasvatvaṃ ca* [Pāṇini 6.3.43], shortening occurs invariably. Regarding the form *śamī*:

the vowel-vṛddhi substitution prescribed by *ata upadhāyāḥ* [Pāṇini 7.2.116] does not take place, because it is prohibited by the rule *nodāttopadeśasya mṛjy-edhitām* [Pāṇini 7.3.34]. The lengthening occurs by the rule *sau ca* [Pāṇini 6.4.13]. Regarding the form *asitā*.
The root *asu* in the sense of "throwing" (Dhātupāṭha 1209) takes the suffix *tṛn*. The root *pṛcī* in the sense of "contact" (Dhātupāṭha 1462) is preceded by the prefix *sam*.

*rudhir* in the sense of covering (Dhātupāṭha 1438) preceded by *anu*; *yama* in the sense of cessation (Dhātupāṭha 984) and *yasu* in the sense of effort (Dhātupāṭha 1210) preceded by *āṅ*; *sṛja* in the sense of emission (Dhātupāṭha 1178); *jvara* in the sense of fever/disease (Dhātupāṭha 776) preceded by *sam*; *kṣipa* in the sense of impelling (Dhātupāṭha 1285); *raṭa* in the sense of speaking/reviling (Dhātupāṭha 297); *vada* in the sense of speaking or declaring (Dhātupāṭha 1009); and *daha* in the sense of reducing to ashes.

(dhātupāṭhaḥ-991), *muha* in the sense of "bewilderment" (dhātupāṭhaḥ-1198) preceded by *pari*; *duṣa* in the sense of "corruption" (dhātupāṭhaḥ-1185); *dviṣa* in the sense of "dislike" (dhātupāṭhaḥ-1013); *druha* in the sense of "desire to harm" (dhātupāṭhaḥ-1197); *duha* in the sense of "milking" (dhātupāṭhaḥ-1014); *krīḍṛ* in the sense of "sporting" (dhātupāṭhaḥ-350) preceded by *ā*; *vijir* in the sense of "separation" (dhātupāṭhaḥ-1094) preceded by *vi*; *tyaja* in the sense of "abandoning," specifically "the loss of vitality" (as per the Dhātupāṭha).

(Dhātupāṭha 986): *rañj* in the sense of coloring; (Dhātupāṭha 999): *bhaj* in the sense of service; (Dhātupāṭha 998): *car* in the sense of motion, preceded by *ati*; that same [root] preceded by *anu*; (Dhātupāṭha 1530): *muṣ* in the sense of stealing, preceded by *āṅ*; (Dhātupāṭha 1012): *han* in the senses of injury and motion, preceded by *abhi* and *āṅ*.
These are specified only in the context of their usage (*vṛtti*). "But not beginning with *tvat*" [is the rule].
It is connected with the word "is taken" (*gṛhyate*).
To the question "Why is the root belonging to the *ad-ādi* class not taken? he says: "But the *ad-ādi* [root] has a *lu*-class suffix (*lug-vikaraṇa*); therefore, it is not taken.
"The *paridevi* [root] belongs to the *bhū-ādi* class."
The connection is with the word "is grasped" (*gṛhyate*).
Now, why is there not an inclusion of the causative form of *pari-div*, which means "to play" and so forth? Because of its association with other [roots] that lack the causative suffix (*aṇ*).
[The rule] "is grasped in a general sense" applies.
Because there is no distinction; that is,
"there is the apprehension of both" for that very reason.
"By means of an irregular derivation (*nipātana*), there is the elision of the nasal.
In the rule *tyajaraja*, the very pronunciation of the form without the nasal is itself the irregular derivation.
[The example is] "samparkī."
The *guṇa* substitution for a light penultimate vowel [applies]. In the case of "āyāmī," there is *vṛddhi* [substitution] by [Pāṇini 7.2.116].
Regarding "parisārī":
here too, the vṛddhi [vowel substitution] occurs by [Pāṇini 7.2.115]. Regarding "abhyāghātī": [the same applies].
As before, in the case of *ghaṭ* and *tat*, [we have] *pralāpī* and *prasārī*. [The roots are] *lapa* in the sense of "distinct speech" (*dhātupāṭha* 402) and *sṛ* in the sense of "motion" (935).
[Then we have] *pradrāvī* and *pramāthī*.
*du dru gatau* (Dhātupāṭha 944–945); *madha viloḍane* (Dhātupāṭha 848);

"not for the meaning of covering"—this excludes the root *vasa ācchādane* (Dhātupāṭha 1023). *ṇidi kutsāyām* (Dhātupāṭha 66); *arda hisi hiṃsāyām* (Dhātupāṭha 1828, 1829); *khādṛ bhakṣaṇe* (Dhātupāṭha 49); *ṇaśa adarśane* (Dhātupāṭha 1194) preceded by the prefix *vi*, with the causative suffix (*ṇic*).

*Kṣipi* is exactly as mentioned before; likewise, *raṭi* and *vadi* preceded by *pari* are causative (*hetumaṇṇyanta*); and *vyāṅ-pūrva-bhāṣ* [from the root] *bhāṣ* meaning "clear speech" (Dhātupāṭha 612).

The term *asūya* refers to the form ending in *ya* from the *kaṇḍvādī* group. Here, since the suffix *yuc* would have applied to *kliś* in the sense of "afflicting" and to *bhāṣ* by virtue of [Pāṇini 3.2.149], *vuñ* is prescribed [instead].
But for the remaining [roots], the suffix *tṛn* is applied.

Now, one might object: since the rule *paraśca* [Pāṇini 3.1.2] applies, there ought to be a fifth case (*pañcamī*) indicating spatial relation, as in the commentary—“from roots such as *nind* and others. Why, then, is the first case used in the sūtra? To this he replies: “The first case is used in the sense of the fifth case.
The intention is that this is due to a transposition of case endings (*sub-vyatyaya*).
And from this collective dvandva compound, the nominative singular is used; however, the masculine gender is employed by way of grammatical anomaly (vyatyaya).
Regarding the word "asūyakaḥ," there is the elision of the vowel *a* according to [Pāṇini 6.4.48].

Now, for what purpose is the suffix *vuñ* prescribed after the roots *nind* and so forth, given that by the rule of "non-identity of form" (*vāsarūpa-vidhi*) alone, words such as *nindaka* would already be established? For indeed, the form is the same and the accent is the same; however, in this very case there is a distinction in accent: in the word *asūyaka*, when *vuñ* is applied, because of the marker *ñ*, the first syllable becomes acute (*udātta*), whereas if *ṇvul* were applied, the acute accent would fall on the syllable preceding the *lit* suffix. Therefore, *vuñ* should be prescribed only after the single root *asūy*, and not after the others such as *nind* and so forth. To this, he says: "Since it is already established by *ṇvul* alone," and so on.

If, in the case of those [suffixes] denoting habit and so forth (*tacchīlādi*), suffixes such as *tṛc* were also permitted by the rule of non-identity of form (*vā'sarūpavidhi*), then the suffix *vuñ* would not have been prescribed after words meaning "blame" (*nindā*) and the like; yet it has indeed been prescribed. Therefore, the prescription of *vuñ* indicates that the rule of non-identity of form does not apply to those denoting habit and so forth. Consequently, forms such as *alaṅkārakaḥ* and *nirākartā* do not possess grammatical correctness (*sādhutva*) when they denote habit and the like. *Movement* (*calana*) is a specific kind of action that causes the attainment of another location.
*Sound* (*śabda*) is an object of the sense of hearing.
"Calanaḥ, copanaḥ"—
[from] *cala* "to shake" (Dhātupāṭha 832) and *cupa* "in slow motion" (Dhātupāṭha 403).
"Śabdanaḥ"— [from *śabda* "sound"].
The root *śabda*—from the Dhātupāṭha (*śabda upasargād āviṣkāre bhāṣaṇe ca*, No. 1714)—is used in the sense of making a sound when preceded by an *upasarga*; it belongs to the *curādi* group.

Alternatively, the suffix *ṇic* is applied according to the rule *prātipadikād dhātvarthe bahulam* (Gaṇasūtra 1860, *curādi* 1915), and from this form ending in *ṇic*, the suffix *yu* is added according to the rule *śabdavairakalaha* (Pāṇini 3.1.17). Thus we have *ravaṇaḥ*.
In the case of *ru* (root 1034 in the Dhātupāṭha), we have *edhitā*.
In the case of *edh* meaning "to grow" (root 2 in the Dhātupāṭha),

[the forms] *jugupsanaḥ* and *mīmāṃsanaḥ* arise when the suffix *san* is applied according to [Pāṇini 3.1.5], and the lengthening [of the vowel] is performed according to [Pāṇini 3.1.6] starting with *mān-badha*.
In this context, the grammatical indicator (liṅga) applied to the members [of a compound] serves to qualify the whole, which ends in those [members].

Thus, if the mention of "beginning" (ādi) were not made, the rule would not apply to those two [words]; for, in the absence of the mention of "beginning," the rule of "ending-in-that" (tadantavidhi) would be understood as applying to a consonant (hal), namely: "from that which ends in a consonant and has an anudātta vowel.
However, the words *jugupsa* and *mīmāṃsā* do not end in a consonant; rather, they end in a vowel (ajanta).
Since the inclusion of the word "ādi" (and so forth) implies that [the elision] occurs even after consonant-final bases, the inclusion of "ādi" must be made.

And that [inclusion] must be made when the position is that "there is elision of 'at' before an *ārdhadhātuka* suffix," and not when the position is that "it occurs when an *ārdhadhātuka* suffix is the governing context.

For in that case, if the intention were understood as referring specifically to an *ārdhadhātuka* suffix, the mention of "consonant-final bases" would be purposeless, as there would be no basis for exclusion.
Therefore, by the force of the inclusion of *hl*, it will be understood as a qualifier of the initial [element]; thus, the inclusion of the word "initial" (*ādi*) need not be made at all.
In this context, the inclusion of the word "initial" should be explained merely for the sake of clarity. As in the example:
*vasitā*.

The root *vas* means "to cover" (Dhātupāṭha 1023). Regarding the word *javana*: the root *ju* is a Vedic (sautra) root; some say it functions in the sense of "going," while others say it refers to "speed" as a specific cause.

Regarding the forms *caṃkramaṇaḥ* and *dandramaṇaḥ*: from the roots *kramu* "to step" (Dhātupāṭha 473) and *drama* and *hamma* "to go" (Dhātupāṭha 466, 467), the suffix *yaṅ* is applied by [Pāṇini 3.1.23], followed by reduplication; then *nuk* is inserted by [Pāṇini 7.4.85], the vowel *a* is elided by [Pāṇini 6.4.48], and the semivowel *y* is elided by [Pāṇini 6.4.49].

Regarding the examples *jvalanaḥ* and *śocanaḥ*: the roots *jvala* and *hvala* mean "to move" (*dhātupāṭha* 804, 805), and *śuca* means "to grieve" (*dhātupāṭha* 183). Now, one might object: "In this context, roots such as *ju*, *caṅkram*, and *daṃdram* have the meaning 'to move,' while the root *pad* is anudātta and begins with a consonant; therefore, the suffix *yuc* is already established for these by the two preceding rules. What, then, is the purpose of including them here? To this he replies: "Of those having the meaning of moving," and so forth. If they were not included here, then in cases such as *caṅkramaṇo grāmasya* ("wandering about the village"), the suffix would not apply; for in such instances, the village and so on are intended to be the object (*karman*).
Therefore, these [roots] are mentioned for the purpose that [the suffix *tṛc*] may apply to transitive verbs (*sakarmaka*).
By the words "for the sake of an indicator" (*jñāpakārtham*), etc., he shows another opinion: "The suffix *tṛn* does not occur after the root *alaṃkṛ*."

This also serves as the purpose for the indicator (*jñāpaka*). One must supply the ellipsis: "it does not become correct [to say] 'alaṃkartā'. He asks, "How, then, is the mention of the word *pad* an indicator? and replies with the words beginning "for instance" (*tathā hi*).
The inclusion of the word *pada* here is made so that there may be coexistence (*samāveśa*) rather than sublation (*bādhā*) by the suffix *ukañ*, which is prescribed as a specific rule.

If the rule regarding dissimilarity (*asarūpavidhi*) were to apply even to suffixes expressing habitual action (*tācchīlika*), then coexistence with *ukañ* would already occur simply because of their dissimilarity; consequently, the prescription of *yuC* for *pada* would be redundant.

Therefore, this specific prescription [of *yuC*] is intended solely as an indicator (*jñāpanārtha*) that [the rule of dissimilarity] does not apply here, since it is prescribed by the general definition [in Pāṇini 3.2.149].

If, then, the absence of the *vāsarūpa* rule (Pāṇini 3.1.94) were being indicated here, the suffix *yuc* would not be established in forms such as *gantā* (by Pāṇini 3.2.149), because *dhinuṇ* is prescribed by the rule *vau kaṣa* (3.2.143). To this he says: “And it is for the most part (*prāyika*),” etc. That it is for the most part will be demonstrated in the subsequent sūtra. The suffix *yuc* is prescribed when the suffix *tṛn* (Pāṇini 3.2.135) would otherwise apply. Here, even in the subsequent rules, wherever no specific distinction is intended, it should be understood that [the new suffix] is an exception (*apavāda*) to *tṛn* alone.
Regarding "roṣaṇaḥ": [it is derived from] the root *ruṣ* in the sense of "anger" (Dhātupāṭha 1670). Regarding "by the preceding [rule]":
because [the form] is already established by [Pāṇini 3.2.149] and subsequent rules.

Now, why is this not understood as being for the purpose of prescribing the suffix *yuc* after the roots *aya*, *vaya*, *raya*, and *ṇaya* (as per Dhātupāṭha 474, 475, 482, 480)? It is impossible to understand it thus; because [the forms] from *nayati* are already established by the rule "anudāttetaśca" (Pāṇini 3.2.149) and so forth.
Therefore, this [sūtra] is for the purpose of prohibition, as in the examples *knayitā* and *kṣmāyitā*.

The roots *knūyī* in the sense of "moistening" (*unde*) and "making a sound" (*śabda*) [DhP 485], *kṣmāyī* in the sense of "shaking" (*vidhūnane*) [DhP 486]; *ṣūda* in the sense of "flowing" (*kṣaraṇe*) [DhP 25], *dīpau* in the sense of "shining" (*dīptau*) [DhP 1150], and *dīkṣa* in the sense of "shaving the head" (*mauṇḍye*) [DhP 609]—these are the examples. The objection begins with "But surely" (*nanu ca*), and the resolution begins with "By the rule *vā'sarūpeṇa*" (*vā'sarūpeṇa*).

It might be argued that this has already been indicated by the fact that there is no rule for dissimilar forms (*vāsarūpavidhi*); therefore, there would be no occasion for the suffix *yuc*. To this he replies with "pertaining to habitual action" (*tācchīlika*), etc.
And this very [point] is the indicative mark (*liṅga*) of its being a general rule (*prāyika*).

For if there were an absence of the *asarūpa* rule (the rule allowing non-identical suffixes) everywhere, then, because [the action] would already be precluded by the suffix specifically prescribed for that case, the prohibition [of the present rule] would be redundant.
By the words "And thus," etc., he demonstrates the coexistence with the suffix denoting habit (*tācchīlika*), thereby strengthening the fact that the indicator is merely general (*prāyika*).
The example is "kamrā" (one who desires).
The suffix *ra* is applied by the rule *namikampi* [Pāṇini 3.2.167].
Regarding the form *kamanā*,
the suffix *yuc* is applied by the rule *anudāttetaśca halādeḥ* [Pāṇini 3.2.149].
Regarding the word *kamprā*: [it is derived from] the verbal root *kapi* in the sense of "trembling" (Dhātupāṭha 275). The objection begins with "from the root *sūd*" and so forth;
the resolution begins with "it is not permanent" and so forth.
"It is understood through the division of the rule (*yogavibhāga*).

Regarding the proof for its non-eternality: although a single rule "nayasūdadīpadīkṣa" ought to have been formulated, the fact that he performs a division of the rule indicates that there is some specific distinction between this [rule] and the preceding prohibition.
That specific distinction is indeed its non-eternality.
Although the suffix *yuc* would also apply after the roots *dīp* and *dīkṣ*, it does not occur because of non-usage (*anabhidhāna*). [Examples: *upasthāyukāḥ* (Kāśikā); *upasthāyukaḥ*.
[The suffix] *yuk* is applied by the rule *āto yuk ciṇkṛtoḥ* [Pāṇini 7.3.33].
[Example: *pravarṣukāḥ* (Kāśikā); *pravarṣukaḥ*.
Regarding "vṛṣu mṛṣu secane" (Dhātupāṭha 706, 707),
[the word] "kāmukāḥ" [is derived from] "kamu kāntau" (Dhātupāṭha 443).

When the prohibition of *vṛddhi* would otherwise apply by the rule *nodāttopadeśa* [Pāṇini 7.3.34], in the case of the word *anācameri*, *vṛddhi* indeed occurs because of the statement: "In the case of *cam*, *kam*, and *vam*, it should be stated that [the rule applies]" (Vārttika 844). Thus we have *kiṃśārukam* and *kāśikā*; and *śārukaḥ*.
The root is *śṛ* in the sense of "injuring" (Dhātupāṭha 1488).
From the root *laṣ* preceded by *apa*, the suffix *dhinuṇ* occurs according to the rule *ape ca laṣaḥ* [Pāṇini 3.2.144].

For it was stated previously that in the case of suffixes expressing habitual disposition (*tācchīlika*), there is sometimes a co-occurrence [of multiple suffixes]. From the roots *pat* and *pad*, the suffix *yuc* also indeed occurs, according to the rule *jucaṅkramya* etc. [Pāṇini 3.2.150].
Regarding the root *sthā*, [the suffix *ki* occurs] by virtue of the rule "glājisthaśca ksanuḥ" [Pāṇini 3.2.139].
Regarding the root *gam*, both *ki* and *kin* occur in the Vedic language by the rule "ādṛgama... [Pāṇini 3.2.171] and so forth;

they also occur in the common language (*bhāṣā*) because of the supplementary rule: "In the common language, [the suffixes *ki* and *kin* are added] after the roots *dhā*, *kṛ*, *sṛ*, *jan*, *gam*, and *nam*" (Vārttika 284).

The suffix *ra* is applied to the root *kam* by the rule *namikampi-* [Pāṇini 3.2.167]. Since the suffix *yuC* would otherwise be applicable by the rule *jucaṃkramya-* [Pāṇini 3.2.150], the suffix *ini* is prescribed here.

The letter *i* is for the purpose of protecting the letter *n* from receiving the technical designation *it*. [The following roots are cited: *ji* in the sense of "victory" (DhP 561); *dṛṅ* in the sense of "respect" (DhP 1411); *śriñ* in the sense of "service," preceded by the prefix *vi-* (DhP 897); *iṇ* in the sense of "motion" (DhP 1045); *ṭuvam* in the sense of "vomiting" (DhP 849); *vyatha* in the sense of "fear and trembling" (DhP 764), preceded by the negative particle *nañ*; and *ama* in the sense of "disease," preceded by the prefix *abhi-* (DhP 1720).

The root *ṣū* preceded by *pra* is intended here (from Dhātupāṭha 1408, meaning "to impel"), and not the roots *ṣūṅ* (Dhātupāṭha 1031, meaning "the delivery of the fetus of a living being") or *ṣūṅ* (Dhātupāṭha 1132, meaning "the birth of a living being").
This is according to the maxim regarding roots without an indicatory letter (*niranubandhakaparibhāṣā*).

In the case of the suffix *kvarap* in the rule *iṇ-jibhyām*, the suffix *kvarap* occurs because of the statement: *iṇ-naś-jis-artibhyaḥ kvarap* (Pāṇini 3.2.163). It is said that [roots] ending in short *a* are listed in the *curādi* group.

Therefore, when elision (*lopa*) has been applied here, the intention is that, by virtue of the status of being a *sthānivat* (as if occupying the original position), neither *vṛddhi* nor *guṇa* occurs. After these [roots], since *iṣṇuc* would apply as before in the Vedic language (*chandas*), and since *kikin* would apply to the roots *drāti* and *dadhāti*,
*āluc* is prescribed instead— as in the example *spṛhayāluḥ*.
The substitution of *ay* is applied by the rule *ayāmantra* [Pāṇini 6.4.55] and so forth.
Regarding the phrase *āluci* and so on,
the root *śīṅ* is understood.
This means that the inclusion of the root *śīṅ* [in the rule] is for the purpose of further explanation;
that explanation must be provided so that the inclusion of *śīṅ* also takes effect when *aluc* is to be prescribed.

In this regard, the following is the explanation: the particle *ca* from the preceding sūtra is carried over here, and it serves the purpose of including what has not been explicitly mentioned. By means of it, the root *śīṅ* is also included as a verbal base (*prakṛti*). Here, there is the inclusion of three roots: *ḍudāñ* in the sense of "giving" (DhP 1091), *do* in the sense of "cutting" (DhP 1148), and *deṅ* in the sense of "protecting" (DhP 962); for there is the rule stating, "In the mention of *gā*, *mā*, and *dā*, there is no distinction [between their various forms]. (Vyāḍiparibhāṣā 124).
The roots are *dheṭ* "to drink" (Dhātupāṭha 902), *ṣiñ* "to bind" (Dhātupāṭha 1477), *śadlṛ* "to fall away" (Dhātupāṭha 1428), and *ṣadlṛ* "to dissolve, go, or perish" (Dhātupāṭha 1427).

Now, regarding the phrase "the calf sucks its mother" (*dhāruvatsaḥ mātaram*), why is the accusative case used here, when by the rule *kartṛkarmaṇoḥ kṛti* (Pāṇini 2.3.65) the genitive case ought to occur? To this he replies: "not with [words ending in] *la*, indeclinables, or past participles" (*na lokāvyayaniṣṭhā*).

The letter *u* is present, and together with it, the letter *a* is joined by means of the rule for lengthening homogeneous vowels (*savarṇadīrghatva*). Consequently, when the rule of "specification by the final letter" (*tadantavidhi*) is understood to apply, the genitive case does not occur upon the employment of a suffix ending in *u*; therefore, only the accusative occurs, and not the genitive.
But in that case, would there not be a lack of prohibition in the example "desirous of making a mat" (*kaṭaṃ cikīrṣuḥ*), because the suffix *u* does not end in *u*? [It is replied:
the suffix *ghinuṇ* also exists [in this context].

Because the verbal root *chand* ends in the vowel *u*, the suffixes *kikin* also occur [after it] by the rule *ādṛgamahan...* (Pāṇini 3.2.171). [The roots are: *bhañj* (to crush) [Dhātupāṭha 1453], *bhāsṛ* (to shine) [Dhātupāṭha 624], and *ñimidā* (to moisten/to release) [Dhātupāṭha 1243].
Regarding the form *bhaṅgura*, the substitution of *ku* [for the nasal] occurs by the rule *bhañjabhāsamido ghurac* (Pāṇini 3.2.161).
"The suffix [is used] in the sense of the agent who is also the object" means that it is being broken by itself.
But from what source is the suffix obtained in the sense of the agent who is also the object? To this he says: "By its own nature."

By its very nature, the suffix *pratyaya* denotes the reflexive object-agent (*karmakartṛ*), not the agent alone; therefore, it applies only to the reflexive object-agent. [The rule] "the mention of *vid* in the sense of knowing" refers to this root *vid* "to know" (Dhātupāṭha 1064).
Regarding the phrase "not for the sake of obtaining" (*na lābhārthasya*):

this refers to the root *vidlṛ* in the sense of "obtaining" (Dhātupāṭha 1432). This is an elliptical indication (*upalakṣaṇa*) for the root *vid* in the sense of "knowing"; therefore, the two roots *vid* meaning "existence" and "investigation" are certainly not included here.
In some places, however, for the sake of including these two by means of the word "ādi," the reading is *lābhārthasya*.
Why, then, is the meaning of "knowledge" (*jñāna*) included? He says: "by its very nature" (*svabhāvāt*).
By the suffix produced after the root *vid*, it is only the agent of the act of knowing who is understood as the inherent nature, and no other.
Therefore, there is the apprehension of the object of cognition, and not of anything else.
This refers to the suffix [denoting] the "object-as-agent" (*karmakartṛ*),
in the sense that "it is cut by itself."

In this context, "by its very nature" (*svabhāvāt*) refers to the very same reason mentioned previously. Regarding the forms *itvaraḥ* and *itvarī*, the suffix *ṅīp* is applied by the rule *ṭiḍḍhāṇañ* [Pāṇini 4.1.15] and others. Regarding the form *jāgarūkaḥ*:
The root *jāgṛ* is listed as "to wake" (*nidrākṣaye*) in the Dhātupāṭha (1072).

By the rule of irregular suffixation (*vāsarūpavidhi*), the suffix *tṛn* is also applied, resulting in the form *jāgarita*. Regarding the root *daṃś*, although the elision of the nasal (*anunāsikalopa*) by the rule beginning with *aniditām* [Pāṇini 6.4.24] would be established even when the *yaṅ* suffix is elided due to the principle of treating the suffix as present (*pratyayalakṣaṇa*), nevertheless, for the sake of brevity, it should be understood that the elision of the nasal is explicitly stated [in the rule].
As for the example *yāyajūkaḥ*:
By the rule *yajeryaṅi* [Pāṇini 7.4.83], there is lengthening; by *ato lopaḥ* [Pāṇini 6.4.48], there is elision of the vowel *a*. Thus, we have *jañjapūkaḥ* and *dandaśūkaḥ*.

By the rule *lupasada* [Pāṇini 3.1.24], the suffix *yaṅ* is applied; by the rule *japajabha* [Pāṇini 7.4.86], the augment *nuk* is added to the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*). Regarding the roots: *ṇam* (meaning "bending" and "sound," Dhātupāṭha 981); *kapi* (meaning "movement," Dhātupāṭha 375); *ṣmiṅ* (meaning "slight laughter," Dhātupāṭha 948); *kamu* (meaning "desire," Dhātupāṭha 443); *tṛha* and *tṛhi* (meaning "injury," Dhātupāṭha 1455, 1456); and *dīpī* (meaning "illumination," Dhātupāṭha 1150).

Since *kapi* has the meaning of movement and since *kami*, *dīpi*, and the others are *anudātta-it* (having an unaccented vowel as their indicatory marker), the suffix *yuC* would have been applicable; therefore, the suffix *ru* is specifically prescribed here.

Regarding the phrase "continuity of action" (*kriyāsātatyam*): the uninterrupted engagement in actions being performed is "continuity of action. In that context, the suffix itself functions as having another suffix. Regarding the statement "the *san* suffix is understood": [it refers to the desiderative suffix].

That which is prescribed by the rule *guptijkidbhyaḥ* [Pāṇini 3.1.5] and so forth is excluded by the statement *na sani dhātuḥ*. Therefore, the roots *ṣaṇu* "to give" (Dhātupāṭha 1464) and *vana* / *ṣaṇa* "to share" (Dhātupāṭha 463, 464) are not included.

And this is understood from the inclusion of the word *jigīṣu* in the *gargādi* group; for that [inclusion] is appropriate when there is a reference to a suffix (*pratyaya*), but not when there is a reference to a verbal root (*dhātu*). [The rule] "with *āṅ* before *śās* in the sense of desire," and so forth, is also understood from its mention together with *āṅ*.

The root *hrāṅ* is recited with the sense of "desire," not for the purpose of praise, as in the example "the mendicant hopes" (*āśaṃsu bhikṣuḥ*). Here, since the suffix *yuc* would have applied by [Pāṇini 3.2.149] *anudātteśca halādeḥ*, the suffix *up* is prescribed. Regarding the rule for the root *vid*: [the following applies].
The root *vid* is used in the sense of "knowledge" (*jñāna*) [according to Dhātupāṭha 1064].
However, for the others, there is no inclusion [of the meaning] either because they are not explicitly mentioned or due to the power of the grammatical rule of irregular formation (*nipātana*).
[This applies to the form] *iṣeḥ*.

Regarding the root *iṣ* in the sense of "desire" (*iṣu icchāyām*, Dhātupāṭha 1351), as well as the group of roots beginning with *iṣ* in the sense of "motion" (*iṣa gatau*, Dhātupāṭha 1127), there is no application of the aforementioned [suffixes]. Thus, the form is *icchuḥ*.

The substitution of *cha* is prescribed as a nipātana (irregular formation). By the rule *che ca* [Pāṇini 6.1.71], the augment *tuk* is added, and by the rule *stoḥ ścunā ścuḥ* [Pāṇini 8.4.40], the change to *ścu* occurs. Regarding the form *mitrayuḥ*:
from *mitram icchati*, the suffix *kyac* is applied according to [Pāṇini 3.1.8].

The lengthening [of the vowel] prescribed by *akṛtsārvadhātukayoḥ* [Pāṇini 7.4.25] would apply, as would the substitution of *i* (ittva) prescribed by [7.4.33]; however, neither of these two occurs because of the prohibition [by 7.4.35].
Thus we have *saṃsvedayuḥ*.
Here, the suffix *kyaṣ* is applied because the word belongs to the *lohitādi* group [Pāṇini 3.1.13].
Regarding the word *sumnayuḥ*:
there is a prohibition [of the suffix *kyac*] by the rule *devasumnayoḥ* (Pāṇini 7.4.38).

In the sense of "acting like *sumna*," the suffix *kyac* is applied according to the rule *kartuḥ kyaṅ salopaśca* (Pāṇini 3.1.11). Words employed in the sense of another referent convey the meaning of the suffix *vat* even without the suffix *vat* being present, as in: "The Vāhīka is a cow" (*gaur vāhīkaḥ*) and "The young boy is a lion" (*siṃho māṇavakaḥ*).

When it is said, "The Vāhīka is a cow" (*gaur vāhīkaḥ*), even without the suffix *vat*, the word "cow" is applied to another object; thus, through the similarity of the word-form, the Vāhīka is understood as being "like a cow.
Here, in the rule regarding *liṭ*, the term is employed for *kikina* in a sense other than its own primary meaning.
Therefore, he says, "And those two are like *liṭ*," indicating that an extended application (*atideśa*) is understood even in the absence of a connection with the suffix *vat*.
The meaning is that they become equal to the *liṭ* [perfect tense], i.e., they possess the same properties (*tulyadharmāṇau*).
The intention is that whatever grammatical operation (*kārya*) belongs to the *liṭ*, such as reduplication (*dvirvacana*) and so forth, that occurs for the *kik* and *kin* suffixes.
This is an extension of the operation (*kāryātideśa*), not an extension of the rule (*śāstrātideśa*); for, compared to the extension of the operation, the extension of the rule is secondary.
However, the extension (*atideśa*) from the rule is secondary because it is something to be performed (*kārya*).

If this were an extension of the operation (*kāryātideśa*), then by the rule *[[Pāṇini 3.4.99]]*, the designation *parasmaipada* would also apply to the suffixes *kik* and *kin*; consequently, those two suffixes would not occur after roots that are marked for the *ātmanepada*. This is not a fault; for the designation *parasmaipada* applies to the substitutes (*ādeśa*) of *l*, not to the letter *l* itself.
In that context, the genitive case in the word "of *la*" (*lasya*) is used in relation to the substitutes; the meaning is that the substitute of *l* receives the designation *parasmaipada*.
Furthermore, *kikin* are not substitutes for the *l*-suffixes; therefore, how could there be any occasion for the designation *parasmaipada*?
Why, then, do *tiP* and the other suffixes not occur? Because of the specific force (*sāmarthya*) of the rule prescribing those two [kikin].

If *tiP* and the others were to occur, the prescription of *kikin* would be purposeless—one should simply have prescribed the *liṭ* [perfect] suffixes—and yet, by means of *tiP* and the others, those such as "one who has that habit" (*tacchīla*) are not prescribed. They will not occur because of non-expression (*anabhidhāna*).

Why do the suffixes *kvasu* and *kānac* not occur here, and why is it that their presence does not result in meaninglessness (*ānarthakya*) for the suffixes *ki* and *kin*, given that *kvasu* and *kānac* are prescribed optionally by the rule "3.2.106–107"? They will simply not occur because of non-expression (*anabhidhāna*); for those two [suffixes] do not prescribe the sense of "one who has that habit" (*tacchīla*) and so forth, precisely because of such non-expression.
Furthermore, by the rule "3.4.69," the suffixes *ki* and *kin* do not occur even in the sense of the abstract state (*bhāva*) or the object (*karman*).

For just as by the suffix *ghurac* derived from the root *bhañj* according to [Pāṇini 3.2.161], the agent who is also the object (*karmakartṛ*) alone is expressed by its very nature and not merely the agent, so too by the suffixes *ki* and *kin* derived from a verbal root, the agent alone is expressed by their very nature, and not the state (*bhāva*) or the object (*karman*).
Regarding the statement "the letter *d* in *ād* is for the sake of ease of pronunciation," this is intended to exclude the possibility that it is a *tapara* (indicating that the vowel is short).
For this very reason, he says: "But this [letter] is not followed by *t*.
What, then, is the reason that it is not desired to be followed by *t*? He says: "Lest it be so," and so forth.
Thus, even the compound with the ablative case (*pañcamī-samāsa*)—namely, "that which is further than *t*" (*tasmāt api paraḥ*)—is resorted to.
> [[1.1.1]] In this context, the purpose is so that the designation *vṛddhi* should not apply to *ai* and *au* when they consist of three or four morae (*mātra*).

Consequently, if [the term] were *tapara* in this way, then even in the case of the phoneme *ṛ*, it would be *tapara*; and as a result, by means of *ṛ*, there would be the inclusion of its own duration—namely, those consisting of one mora—but not of the long ones.
What would be the fault in that? [The forms] *dadhiścakriḥ* and the like would indeed occur, but *taturiḥ*, *jaguriḥ*, and the like would not occur.
Therefore, lest this fault should occur, the use of the *t* in *tapara* (indicating a long vowel) is not desired here.
In the example "papiḥ somam," there is elision of the vowel *ā* by [Pāṇini 6.4.64], reduplication, and the shortening of the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*).

By the rule *na lokāvyayaniṣṭhā* [Pāṇini 2.3.69] and others, the prohibition of the genitive case applies; thus, from the word *soma*, the second case singular is used in the sense of the object (*karman*).
Regarding *dadhiḥ*:
[it is derived from] the root *ḍudāñ* "to give" (Dhātupāṭha 1091).
Regarding the word "tatuh": it has been stated that [the substitution of *u* for *ṛ* applies] by rule 7.4.78, and that the substitute is followed by *r* (raparatva) by rule 1.1.59;
therefore, due to the status of being a *sthānivadbhāva*, the word *tṛ* is reduplicated.
By [Pāṇini 7.4.66], there is the substitution of *at*, followed by the substitution of *ra* for the vowel, and the application of *halādiśeṣaḥ* [7.4.60].
Thus, from the root *gṛ* "to swallow" (Dhātupāṭha 1410), we have *jaguriḥ*.
Similarly, from the roots *jan* and *han*, we have *janmiḥ* and *jaghniḥ*.
The elision of the penultimate vowel occurs by the rule *gamahana* [Pāṇini 6.4.98].

The change of the letter *n* in the root *jan* to *ñ* occurs by the rule *janernakārasya* [Pāṇini 8.4.40], which prescribes the substitution of a sibilant (*ścutva*). The objection begins with the word *atha*. The resolution begins with *ṛcchatyṛtām* [Pāṇini 7.4.11]. The statement beginning with *utsargaśchandasi* [Pāṇini 3.4.117] provides the final answer.

A general rule (*sāmānyena vidhānam*) is an *utsarga* (a general injunction). This is what is meant: the production of the suffixes *kik* and *kin* should be understood as occurring from the verbal root alone, without taking into account any specific base (*prakṛti-viśeṣa*).
That is to say, they are to be prescribed from the mere verbal root.
He asks, "From what reason? and replies: "Because they are seen even after *sad* and others.

This means that since the suffixes *kikinau* must be applied as a general rule (*utsarga*) even after words such as *sad*, which are not included in the [specific] sūtras—for instance, in the forms *sediḥ* and *nemiḥ*.

The substitution of *e* for the root vowel and the elision of the reduplicative syllable (*ettvābhyāsalopau*) apply after the roots *ṣadlṛ* ("to dissolve, to go, to sink") [DhP 854] and *ṇam* ("to bow, to sound") [DhP 981], according to Pāṇini 6.4.120. Thus, we have *dadhiḥ* and *cakriḥ*. As before, there is the elision of the vowel *ā* following the suffix *ghañ*.
"Cakriḥ, sasriḥ"— here there is the substitution of *yaṇ* for the roots *kṛ* (to do) and *sṛ* (to go). "Jajñiḥ"— [likewise].
In the case of the root *jan*, there is elision of the penultimate vowel and the preceding *cu* (the *j*) as before;
thus, *nemiḥ*.
As before, there is the substitution of *at* and the elision of the reduplication; thus, *sahivahi*, etc.

It also occurs in the vernacular (bhāṣā), as in "sāsahiḥ" and so forth. From roots such as *sah*, the suffix *yaṅ* is applied; there is reduplication, and as before, the elision of the vowel *a* and the semivowel *y*. [Examples include] "svapnaka" and "tṛṣṇak".

From the roots *niṣvapa* (meaning "to sleep," Dhātupāṭha 1068) and *tṛṣ* (meaning "thirst," Dhātupāṭha 1228), the substitution of *k* for *p* occurs by rule 8.2.30; thus, the letter *g* [is replaced] by *k*.
Then, by rule 8.4.56, the substitution of *c* for *k* occurs; thus, the letter *k* [is replaced] by *c*.

The *ṅ* in *nañiṅ* is for the purpose of prohibiting *guṇa* in the case of *tṛṣ*, and the *i* is for the sake of pronunciation. For the root *śru*, the suffix *ukañ* also applies by rule 3.2.154 (*laṣapat-* etc.).

Since the suffix *yuc* would otherwise apply to the root *vand* by the rule *anudāttetaśca* [Pāṇini 3.2.149], this statement is made. "The suffix *krukac* should also be mentioned" means that another suffix, *krukac*, must be stated—that is, explained. Regarding this, the explanation is as follows: the particle *ca* ("and") is carried over from the preceding rule *ādṛgamahan* [Pāṇini 3.2.171]; and that particle serves the purpose of including what has not been explicitly mentioned. It serves the purpose of including what has not been explicitly mentioned.
Therefore, *kruk* will also occur. Regarding the term *sthāvara*:
the prohibition of *iṭ* is applied by [Pāṇini 7.2.10], *ekāca upadeśe 'nudāttāt*. Also in cases such as *īṣāra*, the prohibition is by [Pāṇini 7.2.8], *neḍ vaśi kṛti*.
Furthermore, although *ksnu* and *ukañ* are prescribed for the root *sthā* by the preceding rule, they also occur here by virtue of this specific statement.
Since the suffix *yu* would have applied to *īśabhās* as before, this rule is stated [to form] "yāyāvara."

As before, there is the elision of the letter *a* and the semi-vowel (*y*). [The following roots are cited: *bhrājṛ* (DhP 181) in the sense of "shining," *bhāsṛ* (624) in the sense of "shining," *urvī*, *turvī*, *thurvī*, *dhurvī* (DhP 569, 570, 571, 573) in the sense of "injury," *dyuta* (DhP 741) in the sense of "shining," *urja* (DhP 1549) in the senses of "strength" and "vitalizing," *pṛ* (DhP 1086) in the senses of "protecting" and "filling," *ju* (a root found in the *sūtra*-tradition), and *ṣṭuñ* (DhP 1043) in the sense of "praising," preceded by *grāvan*. Regarding the form *vibhrāṭ*: the substitution of *ṣ* occurs according to the rule *vraśca-* etc. (Aṣṭādhyāyī 8.2.36).
As before, there is the substitution of *jaś* and *cart*. In the word *dhūḥ*, there is the elision of the letter *v* by [Pāṇini 6.4.21], and the lengthening of the vowel by [Pāṇini 8.2.76].
Regarding the word *pūḥ*:
by [Pāṇini 7.1.102] *udoṣṭhapūrvasya*, there is the substitution of *u* (utvam) and the replacement of *r* (raparatva); as before, there is lengthening (*dīrghatva*).
Regarding [the rule] *javaterdīrghaśca*: [there is the substitution of *u* and lengthening].
How so? Some say that in the *sūtra* the word "jū" should be read with a long vowel.

Others, however, say that because it is seen in the subsequent *sūtra*, it is a remainder (*śeṣa*) for both rules; and that [remainder] is for the purpose of including another injunction, whereby a long vowel is prescribed for the root *javati*.
Thus, one who praises the pressing-stones is a *grāvastut*. The objection beginning with "For what purpose is this? and so forth is raised.
The resolution is that [the formation] is barred by those suffixes used in the sense of habit (*tācchīlika*).

This might be argued: "It will occur somewhere by means of the *vāsarūpa* rule"; to this he says: "And the *vāsarūpa* rule... This, however, has been stated in the rule beginning with *nindahiṃsa* (Pāṇini 3.2.146).

But has it not been established in the rule *nanu ca* (Pāṇini 3.2.153) that the indicator (*jñāpaka*) is merely occasional (*prāyikatva*), and that the rule for optional forms of dissimilar suffixes (*vā'sarūpavidhi*) does not apply here? To this he says: "of that very [root]" (*tasyaiva*). [The desired form] is produced by rules such as *bhū* (Pāṇini 3.3.130) and *bhaviṣya* (Pāṇini 3.2.76). Now, since the goal would be accomplished by the mere words "also from others" (*anyebhyo 'pi*), for what purpose is the inclusion of the term *dṛśi* ("seeing")? He shows other rules for the sake of including those cases for which the inclusion of *dṛśi* is intended, by means of the phrase "in some instances" (*kvacid*) and so forth.

Because the inclusion of the term *dṛśi* (‘as seen’) is for the purpose of encompassing other rules, and having done so, the author of the Vṛtti recites the rule beginning with *kvibvacipṛcchi* (Vārttika 288).
The intention is to show that those very other rules are included by means of the inclusion of *dṛśi*.

But how, again, does the inclusion of *dṛśi* encompass the other rules? For when *dṛśi* is present, this meaning is obtained: “Just as the roots ending in *kvip* are seen, in that very same way they are to be understood.”
And when that purpose is achieved, the rules for reduplication (*dvirvacana*) and so forth become subsumed.
Thus, in the case of *hita*, they are followed exactly as they are observed.

If reduplication and the rest are prescribed according to their proper application, then in the case of roots ending in *kvip*, reduplication is seen in some instances, while in others there is vocalization (*saṃprasāraṇa*); therefore it was rightly said: "The mention of the root *dṛś* (‘to see’) is for the purpose of including other rules. [The example] is *vāk*.
By means of the rule *vaceḥ* [Pāṇini 6.1.15], the absence of the *samprasāraṇa* (vowel substitution) that would otherwise have occurred is established,
resulting in the form *śabdaprāṭ*.
Similarly, by means of the rule *grahādīnām* [Pāṇini 6.1.16], the *samprasāraṇa* of the root *pṛcch* is also prevented.
By the rule *vraścādi* [Pāṇini 8.2.36], there is the substitution of *ṣ*; as before, there is the substitution of *jaś* and then *car*.
One who praises what is extended (*āyata*) is called *āyatastūḥ*. The root is *ṣṭuñ* in the sense of "praising" (Dhātupāṭha 1043).
"Kaṭaprūḥ" means "one who moves toward a mat"; [the root] *pruṅ* means "to go" (Dhātupāṭha 957). "Śrīḥ" [is another example].
The root *śri* is used in the sense of "service" (Dhātupāṭha 897).
[The words] *didyut* and *jagat*.
Thus, there is the elision of the nasal (*anunāsikalopa*).
Regarding *dadṛt*:
by [Pāṇini 7.4.66] *urat*, there is the substitution of *at*, followed by *raparatva* (substitution of *ra*), and then *halādiśeṣa* [7.4.60]. Regarding *dhīḥ*.

The root *dhyai* in the sense of "thinking" (*cintāyām*) [Dhātupāṭha 908] takes a long vowel by [Pāṇini 6.4.2], *halaḥ*. Regarding the phrase "of the creditor and the debtor" (*dhanikādhamarṇayoḥ*) and so forth:
a creditor (*dhanika*) is one to whom a debt is owed;
a debtor (*adhamarṇa*) is one who owes.

That which stands in the interval between those two, falling on the side of one's own party and serving as a cause for conviction, is called a *pratibhū* (surety), but not everyone [who stands there].
Therefore, when someone stands in the interval between two villages, there is no conviction [of ownership] in that case.
This is obtained from the inherent nature of the word's power (*śabdaśaktisvābhāvyāt*), or because of the recurrence of the term "is seen" (*dṛśyate*) from [Pāṇini 3.2.178].

In the continuation of this [sūtra], the term *pratibhūḥ* is intended as a technical name (*saṃjñā*). Why, then, is the mention of *antara-* necessary? Should it not simply be stated as "in the case of a technical name" (*saṃjñāyām*)? This is not so; for words that function as technical names (*saṃjñā-śabda*) involve the sublation of their status as denoting substances (*dravyatā*), and the word *pratibhū-* is not like that.

Nevertheless, even when Devadatta exists, that [word] does not necessarily apply [to him]. Regarding the word *vibhuḥ*: it is formed by the suffix *kvip* as before. Regarding the statement "there is an addition [of the rule] for *mitadrava-* and others": [this refers to the formation of such terms].
"Without distinction"—that is, both in the case of *saṃjñā* (proper names) and *asaṃjñā* (non-proper names).
The dative case in the rule "from *mitadrava* and so forth" (*mitadravādibhyaḥ*) is used in the sense of purpose (*tādarthye*).
The purpose is that words such as *mitadrava*, which end in the suffix *ḍu*, should be grammatically correct (*sādhavaḥ*).

The purpose of the word *upasaṃkhyāna* (supplementary addition) is to provide an explanation. And that explanation concerns the word *ḍu*, because it is the subject under discussion. In this regard, the explanation is as follows: the word *ḍu* also carries over from rule [Pāṇini 3.3.130]; therefore, the suffix *ḍu* occurs after *mitadrava* and others, even after other verbal roots (*dhātu*), provided there is another word [in composition]. Thus: "of the root *dhay*" (*dhayateḥ*).
The root *dheṭ* means "to drink" (Dhātupāṭha 902).
Regarding the term *dadhāteḥ*:
the root *ḍudhāñ* means "to hold" and "to nourish" (Dhātupāṭha 1092).
Regarding the phrase "in the case of an object as the kāraka":
by this, [the author] demonstrates that the object is the meaning of the suffix and thereby refutes its status as an *upapada*.
For if the object were indeed an *upapada*, he would have prescribed [the suffix] within this very section, namely under Pāṇini 3.2.1 (*karmaṇy aṇ*).

In this way, indeed, the mention of the object (*karman*) need not be repeated twice. [Objection: Even if the mention of the object need not be repeated, does it not follow that the mention of *ṣṭran* must be made in the subsequent sūtra? [Response: Let it be so; for the mention of *ṣṭran* is indeed lighter than the mention of the object. [Objection: Here, because of the continued application (*anuvṛtti*) of the word "present" (*vartamāne*), the suffix occurs in the sense of the present; but when [the rule] is applied there [in the subsequent sūtra], this is not obtained. [Response: This is not so; even here, when [the rule] is applied, the suffix does not occur in the sense of the present.

For when "dhātrī" is uttered, no specific [gender] is understood; rather, what is understood is a woman qualified merely by the relationship between action and its factors—namely, that she bears *āmalaka* fruits for the purpose of medicine.

Therefore, in the rule "in the sense of the object" (*karmaṇi*), this is indeed the meaning of the suffix (*pratyaya*), not an *upapada*. Regarding the entry "dāp lavane," just as in the sūtra "[1.1.20]," there is also the inclusion of "daip śodhane" (DhP 924).
If that is so, why does it not occur here as well? Because it is not so expressed.
For by its very nature, the suffix *ṣṭran* in the word *dātram* denotes an instrument for cutting (*lavana*), not an instrument for cleaning (*śodhana*).
This is because [the rule] states "when [denoting] the instrumental *kāraka*."
By this, demonstrating that it has the sense of an instrumental suffix (*karaṇapratyaya*), he refutes its status as a governing word (*upapada*).
If this were an *upapada*, then the inclusion of the word *daṃṣṭrā* in the list beginning with *ajā* would be untenable.
[The example is] "yoktram" (a yoke).

In the word *meḍhram*, there is the substitution of *ku* [for *ha*] by [Pāṇini 8.2.30]. Then, by [8.2.31], there is the substitution of *ḍha* for *ha*; by [8.2.40], the substitution of *gha*; by [8.4.41], the substitution of *ṣṭu*; and finally, it becomes *daṃṣṭrā* by [8.3.13].
[The suffix] *ṭāp* [is applied] because it begins with a vowel (*ajādi*). Regarding the rule "from *daṃś*" and so forth:

one might object, "Just as in the case of *tyajaraja* (Pāṇini 3.2.142), where the nasalized form of the root *rañj* is used to indicate that the nasal is dropped when the suffix *dhinuṇ* is added—resulting in *rāgī*—so too, when the suffix *ṣṭran* is added to *daṃś*, the nasal should be dropped. How then can this [nasalized form in the sūtra] function as an indicator (*jñāpaka*)? This is not a fault. If this nasalized indication were intended solely for the purpose of dropping the nasal when *ṣṭran* is added to *daṃś*, then the inclusion of the word *daṃṣṭrā* in the list of words beginning with vowels (*ajādipāṭha*) would be contradicted.
Therefore, its purpose is to serve as an indicator.

Regarding the word *naddhrī*: by the rule *naho dhaḥ* [Pāṇini 8.2.34], there is the substitution of *dh* for *nah*; by the rule *jhaṣastathordho'dhaḥ* [Pāṇini 8.2.40], there is the substitution of *dh* for the *t* of *tathoḥ*; by the rule *jhalāṃ jaś jhaśi* [Pāṇini 8.4.53], there is the substitution of the *jaś*-class sound (*d*) for the *dh*; and by the rule *ṛnnebhyo ṅīp* [Pāṇini 4.1.41], the suffix *ṅīp* is applied. As for those verbal roots beginning with *śas* that are *seṭ* (having an *iṭ* augment), there is a prohibition of the *iṭ* augment by the rule *titutratathasisusarakaseṣu ca* [Pāṇini 7.2.9]. "If that instrument (*karaṇa*) is a part of *hala* or *śūkara*."

By this, he demonstrates that in the rule *halaśūkarayoḥ*, the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) expresses a part-whole relationship (*avayava-ṣaṣṭhī*), and not a locative case denoting the thing to be expressed (*abhidheya-saptamī*).
[As stated in the *Kāśikā* and *Padamañjarī*: "The word 'mouth' (*mukha*) itself is what is meant; no other part such as the ear is intended. Thus, it is the mouth alone that is referred to.

And this is due to the inherent nature of the expressive power [of words]. There is the inclusion of the two roots *dhū* in the sense of "shaking" (*dhātupāṭha* 1398) and *ṣū* in the sense of "impelling" (1408). However, there is no inclusion of *dhūñ* in the sense of "trembling" (1487), nor of *ṣūṅ* in the sense of "the release of the embryo from living beings" (1031), nor of *ṣūṅ* in the sense of "the birth of living beings" (1132), according to the technical rule (*paribhāṣā*) stating: "When a root without an indicatory letter (*anubandha*) is mentioned, that which possesses an indicatory letter is not included. [The term] *barhiṣpavitram* is derived either from the root *pav* or *pun*.
"By this sacred grass (barhis) it has been purified.
*Barhiṣpavitra* refers to a product made of *kuśa* grass.
The term "encircling" (*veṣṭana*) refers to the wrapping around the forefinger (*pradeśinī*). [The word] is "minna."
> [[7.2.16]] Thus, there is a prohibition of the augment *iṭ*. By the rule `radābhyām` [[8.2.42]], there is the substitution of *n* [for *t*]. The same applies here in the case of `kṣviṇṇaḥ`.
The substitution of *ṇ* [for *n*] occurs by the rule *aṭkupvāṅnumvyavāye ’pi* [Pāṇini 8.4.2].
Regarding the word *dhṛṣṭaḥ*:

the prohibition of the augment *iṭ* is applied by the rule *dhṛṣiśasī vaiyātye* [Pāṇini 7.2.19], and the substitution of *ṣṭu* [for *ṣṭu*] is applied by the rule *ṣṭunā ṣṭuḥ* [Pāṇini 8.4.41]. Regarding the word *mataḥ*: [the formation follows the same principles].
In the root *man* (Dhātupāṭha 1176),
there is a prohibition of the augment *iṭ* by [Pāṇini 7.2.10] *ekācaḥ*, etc., and the elision of the nasal by [Pāṇini 6.4.37] *anudāttopadeśa*, etc. Thus,
the form is *iṣṭaḥ*.

From the *Dhātupāṭha*: *iṣ* in the sense of "desire" (*iṣu icchāyām*, *Dhātupāṭha* 1351). Because [the rule] ending with *iti* (Pāṇini 7.2.56) is optional, there is a prohibition of the augment *iṭ* by the rule ending with *iti* (Pāṇini 7.2.15), resulting in the form *buddhaḥ*.

In the root *budh* meaning "to understand" (Dhātupāṭha 858), there is the substitution of *dha* as before, the *jaś*-treatment of the letter *t*, and the change of *dh* to *d*. Thus: *pūjitaḥ*, *arcitaḥ* ("honored," "worshiped").

`{It is not found in the Bhvādi class; it is well known only as belonging to the Curādi class.} pūja, in the sense of worshiping` (Dhātupāṭha 1642); `arca, in the sense of worshiping` (Dhātupāṭha 204), [belonging to] the Bhvādi class.

And these two belong to the *curādi* class; therefore, when a suffix follows roots from the *curādi* group, there is the elision of the *ṇi* affix by [Pāṇini 6.4.52]. In examples such as *śīlitaḥ*, the roots are: *śīla* in the sense of "concentration" (Dhātupāṭha 658); *kṣamuṣ* in the sense of "endurance" (Dhātupāṭha 442); *kruśa* in the sense of "calling out" (Dhātupāṭha 856); *juṣī* in the sense of "pleasure and service" (Dhātupāṭha 1288); *ruṣa* in the sense of "anger" (Dhātupāṭha 1670); *hrmñ* in the sense of "taking away" (Dhātupāṭha 899); and *hrmaṣ* in the sense of "satisfaction."

(dhātupāṭhaḥ-1229) *hm̐ṣu* "in falsehood" (dhātupāṭhaḥ-709); *tuṣa* "in satisfaction" (dhātupāṭhaḥ-1184); *kamu* "in desire" (dhātupāṭhaḥ-443); *yama* "in cessation" (dhātupāṭhaḥ-984); *kaṣa* "in injury" (dhātupāṭhaḥ-685); *mṛṅ* "in giving up life" (dhātupāṭhaḥ-1403)—these are the forms of these roots in their respective order.

Among them, the first two (*hm̐ṣu* and *tuṣa*) are *seṭ* (taking the augment *iṭ*). Furthermore, for any root here that ends in *u*, *ū*, *i*, or *ī*, there is a prohibition of *iṭ* by the rule [Pāṇini 7.2.15] *niṣṭhāyām seṭi*.
However, for that which has been augmented with *iṭ*, there is a prohibition of *iṭ* by the rule "after a root ending in *śū* or *īḍ*, there is no *iṭ* before the *niṣṭhā* suffix" [Pāṇini 7.2.14].
For roots ending in *hm* or *ṣ*, the *iṭ* is optional by the rule "after *hm* or *ṣ*, [there is no *iṭ*] before *loman*" [Pāṇini 7.2.29], etc.
Thus, [the forms] *kāntaḥ* and *kṣāntaḥ* are established. (The *Kāśikā* does not contain this.)
The vowel lengthening [occurs] by rule 6.4.15.
In the word *ākruṣṭaḥ*, the substitution of *ṣ* [for *s*] occurs by rule 8.2.36, beginning with *vraśca*.
Regarding "saṃyataḥ":
as before, there is the elision of the nasal vowel (*anunāsika*).
Regarding "amṛtaḥ": [the same applies].
The suffix *kta* is used after roots meaning "to go" (*gati*) and others when they denote the agent (*kartṛ*).

Regarding the phrase "as before" (*pūrvavat*): the meaning is that just as the past participle (*niṣṭhā*) is used in the sense of the present for words such as *śīla*, so it is also for the word *amṛta*. As in the example "he has slept" (*suptaḥ*).
In the case of the root *svap*, there is vocalization (*samprasāraṇa*).
In the form *śayitaḥ*,
because the prohibition of *kittva* applies by the rule "the *niṣṭhā* affixes [are not *kit*] after *śīṅ*" (Pāṇini 1.2.19), *guṇa* substitution occurs.

Regarding the word *āśitaḥ*: the root *aś* meaning "to eat" (Dhātupāṭha 1523) is preceded by the prefix *āṅ*; then there are *lip* meaning "to smear" (Dhātupāṭha 1433) and *tṛp* meaning "to satisfy" (Dhātupāṭha 1195).
Among these, *aś* and *śīṅ* are *seṭ* (having an *iṭ* augment); the remaining ones are *aniṭ* (without an *iṭ* augment).
The prohibition of the augment *iṭ* is applied by the rule "ekācaḥ" [Pāṇini 7.2.10] and others.

Although verbal roots such as *śīl* (to practice) and so on are derived for the present tense, nevertheless, in examples such as *śīlito devadattena*, *rakṣito devadattena*, and *ākruṣṭo devadattena*, the genitive case prescribed by "ktasya ca vartamāne" [Pāṇini 2.3.67] does not occur.

How it does not occur has been explained in that very same place. Thus ends the second quarter of the third chapter in the *Kāśikā-vivaraṇapañjikā* composed by the venerable Ācārya Jinendrabuddhi, who was a disciple of the Bodhisattva. Regarding the phrase "from what exists in the preceding [rule]": Now, why was the mention of "existing in the preceding" not omitted there? Indeed, it would have been appropriate to omit it there. For if that were omitted, this [present rule] would not need to be formulated. This is not so; it must necessarily be formulated, because some [grammarians] maintain that [the suffixes] apply only to what has already occurred (*bhūta*).
Furthermore, if the mention of "present time" (*vartamāna*) were not carried over from the preceding rule, then *uṇādi* suffixes would not apply even to the future tense.
Consequently, the rule [Pāṇini 3.3.3] would have to be understood as a restrictive rule (*niyamārtha*) meaning: "The roots *gam* and others take these suffixes only when referring to the future.
Therefore, the mention of "present time" must be carried over to the preceding rule.
Regarding the word *vatra*:

while the rule *āto manin* (Pāṇini 3.2.74) is being carried over, the suffix *manin* is applied by [3.2.75], and the prohibition of the augment *iṭ* is applied by [7.2.8]. Regarding the word *bhasma*: [it is formed similarly].
The root *bhās* [is listed] in the Dhātupāṭha as "to shine" (*bhrāsa-bhartsana-dīptyoḥ*, 1100).
Regarding the phrase "the mention of *dṛś*" and so forth:

he demonstrates that by the mention of *dṛś*, this meaning is conveyed—that a suffix should be applied in the past tense (*bhūta*) only where the learned (*śiṣṭas*) employ it in accordance with specific usage, and not everywhere. Regarding the phrase "of the suffix itself" and so forth...

For this will be the case: forms such as *gamyā* and others will be grammatically correct (*sādhavaḥ*) only if the future tense is prescribed for the suffix itself; however, if the suffix were to have another tense, they would not be correct in the future. Therefore, by this method, the future tense is prescribed specifically for the suffix.

In the example *grāmaṃ gamī* ("one who will go to the village"), the suffix *ini* is applied according to *gameriniḥ* (Dhātupāṭha 6.57), and the vowel lengthening occurs according to *sau* (Pāṇini 6.4.13).
Since the genitive case is prohibited by the rule *akenorbhaviṣyadādhamaṇryayoḥ* (Pāṇini 2.3.70), the accusative case is applied after the word *grāma* according to *karmaṇi dvitīyā* (2.3.2).
Regarding the form *āgāmī*:

while the suffix *ini* is in force by the rule *gameriniḥ* (Dhātupāṭha 6.57), the suffix *ini* is added by the rule *āṅi ṇit* (Dhātupāṭha 6.58); because it is marked with *ṇ*, there is vocalic strengthening (*vṛddhi*) of the penultimate vowel.

Regarding the word *prasthāyī* and so forth: from the roots *ṣṭhā* (meaning "to stop," DhP 928), *budh* (meaning "to awaken," DhP 1172), *yuj* (meaning "to concentrate," DhP 1177), and *yā* (meaning "to go," DhP 1949), the suffix *ṇini* is applied according to Pāṇini 3.2.78. By Pāṇini 7.3.33, the augment *yuk* is added after the roots *yā* and *sthā*. For the root *yuj*, the substitution of *k* occurs according to Pāṇini 7.3.52 (*cajoḥ ku ghiṇṇyatoḥ*).
Regarding the word *bhāvī*:

while the rule *āṅi ṇit* (Pāṇini 5.2.47) is in effect, the suffix *ini* is applied by the rule *bhuvaśca* (Pāṇini 5.2.48); because the suffix is marked with *ṇ*, there is *vṛddhi* [vowel strengthening]. [The Vārttika] states: "An addition [should be made] for the non-today (*anadyatana*)."

But what is the reason that it is not established? This instruction is formulated using the *lṛṭ* suffix with the sense of "it will be" (*bhaviṣyati*). Consequently, it would apply only to the general future within the domain of *lṛṭ*, and not to the non-contemporary future; thus, the *luṭ* suffix would have no scope, as its domain is sublated by *lṛṭ*. Therefore, an addition (*upasaṃkhyāna*) must be made for the non-contemporary future.
Here, the word "addition" (*upasaṃkhyāna*) means "formulation" (*pratipādana*).

In this regard, the following is the demonstration: the term *bahulam* ("optionally") is understood here by way of anuvṛtti (carrying over from a previous rule); therefore, [the suffixes] will occur even in the non-immediate future (*anadyatana*). And these roots beginning with *gam* are sublaters (*bādhaka*) of both the *luṅ* (aorist) and *lṛṭ* (periphrastic future), because they are exceptions (*apavāda*). As for their being exceptions, it is according to the principle of *yenanāprāpti* (Pāṇini 1.4.2). [Objection: But surely, by the rule of *vāsarūpa* (Pāṇini 3.1.94), the *luṅ* and *lṛṭ* would also be applicable, since the phrase "in the future" (*bhaviṣyati*) is carried over (*anuvṛtti*) into that rule [for *gamyādayaḥ*]? [Reply: True; even with this *anuvṛtti*, [the suffixes] would still occur only optionally (*pakṣe eva*). [Objection: Is this not so? [Reply: This is not the case; for if it were so, the *anuvṛtti* would be purposeless. As in the example: *yāvadbhuṅkte*.
> [[1.3.66]] This is the *ātmanepada* [suffix].

> [[6.4.111]] There is the elision of the phoneme /t/ [in the suffix -syate]. Regarding the example "as much as he will give, so much will he eat" (*yāvaddāsyati tāvadbhokṣyate*): since its measure is that [of the gift], it has that same measure; thus, by the rule *yattadetebhyaḥ parimāṇe vatup* [[5.2.39]], and while the [context] of *[[6.3.89]]* is being carried over, the substitution of /ā/ occurs by *[[6.3.91]]*.
"He will go forth" (*purā vrajiṣyati*).
[The root] *pṛ* is used in the senses of "protecting" and "filling" (*pālanapūraṇayoḥ*, Dhātupāṭha 1489).

By the rule *bhrājabhāsa-* etc. (Pāṇini 3.2.177), the suffix *kvip* is applied; by the rule *udoṣṭhapūrvasya* (Pāṇini 7.1.102), the substitution of *u* occurs; and the third case singular is used in the sense of the instrument (*karaṇe*).

But surely, the particles *yāvat* and *purā* are unanalyzed (*avyutpanna*) even now; and since they have been analyzed [in this rule], their inclusion will occur by the very paribhāṣā "that which is taught by a rule and that which is taught as a word-form" (Vyā.pa. 3). Therefore, for what purpose is the mention of the term "particle" (*nipāta*)? Some say it is to avoid the difficulty of comprehension for those of dull intellect. Others say it is to indicate that this paribhāṣā is not universally valid (*anitya*). The purpose of indicating its non-universality will be explained later. [The example is: "When shall he eat? (*kadā bhoktā*).

[Objection: But surely, because of the continued application (*anuvṛtti*) of the word "in the future" (*bhaviṣyati*), this must apply only to the scope of *lṛṭ*, not to *luṭ*. Therefore, only *lṛṭ* should have been cited as an example in its alternative form; why then has *luṭ* also been cited? [Response: It is thought thus: because of the continued application (*anuvṛtti*) of the rule "optionally when *kadā* and *karhi*" from [Aṣṭādhyāyī 3.3.5] to [Aṣṭādhyāyī 3.3.15], there must be an option for *luṭ* even within the scope of *lṛṭ*.

"Karhi bhokṣyate? (When will he eat?). This is the *lṛṭ* [future tense]. Now, one might object: since the word *karhi* is derived [by Pāṇini] as referring to a time other than the immediate future (*anadyatana*) in [Aṣṭādhyāyī 5.3.21], wherever it is employed, a time other than the immediate future must occur there; therefore, how can there be the application of *lṛṭ*? Should it not rather optionally be *luṭ* by [Pāṇini 3.3.15]? This is not so; because the word *bhokṣyate* exists solely in reference to a future time.
The understanding of the non-recent past tense occurs from the sentence when the word *karhi* is in proximity;
however, the *lṛṭ* affix does not apply to a meaning that is understood from a sentence.
For it is the individual word (*pada*) that is refined here, and the meaning understood from the sentence is not utilized in the refinement of the word.

Therefore, when a general future tense is intended to be expressed, the *lṛṭ* suffix occurs; likewise, when a specific future tense not belonging to the current day is intended, the *luṅ* suffix occurs. Regarding the phrase "the usage of *kim*" and so forth:
what, then, is the usage of *kim*? He says: "By the mention of 'usage' (*vṛtta*)... and so on.
By the word "that" (*tat*), the word *kim* is connected: one should understand that this form of the word *kim*, ending in a case-suffix, is [to be understood] by the mention of "usage."

The suffixes *ḍatara* and *ḍatama*—as in the rules *kiṃyattadaunirdhāraṇe dvayorekasya ḍatarac* [Pāṇini 5.3.92] and [5.3.93]—should be understood through the mention of *vṛtta* as being connected specifically with the word *kim*.

Furthermore, by the technical rule (*paribhāṣā*) regarding the mention of a suffix, it should be understood here that the meaning refers to that which ends in *ḍatara* and *ḍatama*; this is how the sense is to be known.
Thus, it is called "exclusive specification" (*parisaṃkhyāna*).
The meaning is "a restriction.
By this, [the suffix] does not occur in words such as *kiṃtarām*, *kiṃgauḥ*, and *kiṃpuruṣaḥ*; for those have been excluded by the enumeration of what constitutes a *kiṃvṛtta*.
[As in the example: *bhojayanti*.
The suffix *laṭ* follows the causative suffix *ṇic*.
In the form "bhojayitāraḥ," the substitution of *ras* for *jhi* occurs by [Pāṇini 7.1.3], and the elision of the *s* occurs by [Pāṇini 7.4.51].

"One who desires to obtain asks" (*labdhukāmaḥ pṛcchati*). This is because, in the examples provided, the desire to obtain (*lipsā*) is understood. Since this [usage] is possible only when there is a desire to obtain and not when it is absent, one might ask: "In a case where the accomplishment of what is desired to be obtained is understood, there must necessarily be a desire to obtain; thus, since it is already established by the preceding rule, for what purpose is this new rule begun? To this, he says: "This rule is begun for the sake of [words] not ending in *kiṃ*."

If this is so, why was the term *kiṃvṛtta* not included in the previous sūtra itself, and instead the suffix prescribed directly? In that case, this [present] rule would not need to be commenced. This is not correct; for just as when the accomplishment of what is desired (*lipsyamānasiddhi*) is understood, there occurs both the *kiṃvṛtta* (the interrogative form) and the *akiṃvṛtta* (the non-interrogative form), so too it might occur even where the desired object is understood without the accomplishment of what is desired. However, in that case, it is intended that it should occur only when there is a *kiṃvṛtta*. Therefore, the inclusion of *kiṃvṛtta* must be made in the preceding rule. And since that is present, this [present] rule must also be commenced for the sake of the *akiṃvṛtta*.

"He encourages the giver" means that he generates enthusiasm in him regarding the giving of food. By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) in the phrase "commands and so forth," injunctions (*vidhi*), invitations (*nimantraṇa*), requests (*āmantraṇa*), entreaties (*adhīṣṭa*), and others are understood.
"He comes" (*āgacchati*).
By [Pāṇini 7.3.77], the substitution of *ch* occurs.

Regarding the term "adhyayanapraiṣasya": an instruction (*praiṣa*) concerning study (*adhyayana*) is an "instruction for study" (*adhyayanapraiṣa*); this is a compound with elision of the second member (*uttarapadalopa*), following the class beginning with *śākapārthiva*.
"Now, you should study the Vedic meters (*chandas*).
Here, the suffix *loṭ* [is used] according to Pāṇini 3.3.163;
and that is an injunction (*praiṣa*) concerning the subject of study.

With regard to the arrival of his teacher, there is the status of being a cause for the command to study; thus, the arrival of the teacher is the occasion for the command (*praiṣa*). "The compound [is formed] by means of irregular derivation (*nipātana*)," and so forth.

The irregular derivation (*nipātana*) occurs in the very utterance of the word *ūrdhvamauhūrtika*. Having analyzed it as *ūrdhvam muhūrtāt*, the compound is formed from this very irregular derivation.

Then, by the rule *bahvaco 'ntodāttāt* [Pāṇini 4.3.67], the suffix *ṭhañ* is applied; subsequently, there is vṛddhi of the first syllable of the second member (*uttarapada-vṛddhi*), which occurs precisely because of this specific grammatical exception (*nipātana*). Since "that which is to be" (*bhaviṣyat*) is the subject under discussion, it is understood that the term *audhrvamauhūrttika* serves as its qualifier; thus he says, "And this [term] refers to that which is to be," and so forth.
Furthermore, this word *audhrvamauhūrttika* applies to what is imminent for the present moment.
"Subsequent to a muhūrta" (ūrdhvamauhūrttike) means "in the vicinity of the present.

Regarding the form "āgacchet": the suffix *yāsuṭ* is applied; by [Pāṇini 7.2.80], there is the substitution of *iy* for the vowel; by [Pāṇini 6.1.87] and [6.1.66], there is the elision of the letter *y*; and by [Pāṇini 7.2.79], there is the elision of the final *s*. As for the phrase "the matted locks of one who intends to beg" (*bhikṣiṣya ityasya jaṭāḥ*).

The suffix *lṛṭ* [is applied]; because it has an *anudātta* indicatory vowel (*it*), the *ātmanepada* endings are used; the first person singular ending; the augment *iṭ*; the substitution of *e* for the final *ṭi* [of the suffix]; and by [Pāṇini 6.1.97], the subsequent form (*pararūpa*) is substituted.

Here, the word *jaṭā* is a subordinate term (*upapada*) for the sake of the action of begging, but the word *jaṭā* does not denote an action itself; for matted locks (*jaṭā*) are substances (*dravya*). [As in the example: "A staff will fall upon you as you run."

The root *dhāv* is used in the senses of "going" and "purifying" (*dhātupāṭha* 601). From this, the present tense suffix *laṭ* is applied, which undergoes the substitution of *śatṛ*; this is the genitive singular.
Alternatively, from the root *sṛ* meaning "to go" (*dhātupāṭha* 935), the substitution of *dhāv* occurs by the rule *prāghrādisūtra* [Pāṇini 7.3.78].
In this case, the action of "running" (*dhāvati*) is a subordinate element (*upapada*), but it does not serve as the purpose for the main action.

The word *artha* here signifies purpose (*prayojana*). Whatever one undertakes with a specific aim is the purpose of that action; however, this person does not run toward the falling of the staff for its own sake, but rather for the sake of some other task. The objection beginning with "Now" (*atha*) and so forth is as follows:

[the suffix is] "prescribed by a general rule" (*sāmānyena vihita eva*), because the suffix is prescribed without distinction both when another action is to occur at a future time and when it serves as a subordinate element (*upapada*) to an action intended for the sake of another action.
The refutation begins with "lṛṭā" and so forth.

[Pāṇini] will prescribe *lṛṭ* by the rule "lṛṭ śeṣe ca" [3.3.13]; since that *lṛṭ* is prescribed as a specific exception, it would sublate [the present rule]. To prevent its sublation, this [rule] is prescribed again here. Now, why was it not stated that *tumun* is sublated by [the rule concerning] a word expressing the purpose of an action (*kriyārthopapada*)? Because their meanings are different.
For there can be no relationship of sublated and sublator between two things that have different meanings, and the suffixes *ṇvul* and *tumun* have different meanings.
To explain: *ṇvul* occurs in the sense of the agent (*kartṛ*), whereas *tumun* occurs in the sense of the action (*bhāva*).
How is this known? From the inclusion of the term "in the sense of *tumun*" (*tumartha*) in the rule *tumarthe seseṇa* [Pāṇini 3.4.9].

If the suffix *tumun* were to apply in the sense of the agent (*kartari*) based on the rule "kṛt [suffixes] are used in the sense of the agent" (Pāṇini 3.4.67), then suffixes such as *śeṣan* and others would also apply in that same sense; consequently, he would not have included the mention of "the sense of *tumun*" (*tumarthagrahaṇa*). Yet he has included it. Therefore, from the inclusion of the mention of the sense of *tumun*, it is understood that *tumun* does not apply in the sense of the agent. Furthermore, no other meaning is specifically prescribed for it; thus, according to the principle that "suffixes whose meaning is not specifically prescribed apply in their own inherent sense" (Puṣpabhūti-pāda 90), it is understood that *tumun* occurs only in the sense of "becoming" (*bhāva*).

Regarding what was stated—that [the future tense suffix] *lṛṭ* is superseded by a word expressing purpose through the use of a verbal root (*kriyārthopapada*)—he says "by the rule of alternative forms" (*vāsarūpavidhinā*), etc., in order to refute that.
Then he says "if this is so," etc.
By this, he explains that the prescription of the suffix *ṇvul* serves as an *jñāpaka* (indicative evidence).

For if, when a verbal root meaning an action is used as an upapada (governing word) for another action, suffixes such as *tṛc* were to apply by the rule of "non-identity of form" (*vāsarūpa*), then the suffix *ṇvul* would also occur—since it expresses the same meaning as *tṛc*—by virtue of that *vāsarūpa* rule; consequently, the author would not have prescribed it here again. Yet he has prescribed it. Therefore, by this prescription of *ṇvul*, it is made known that in this specific case, suffixes such as *tṛc* do not apply by the rule of "non-identity of form. By the words beginning with "therefore," he demonstrates the purpose of this technical indication (*jñāpana*).
The example is "the agent" (*kartā*).
In the triplet beginning with "vikṣipaḥ," the letter *n* in the suffix *tumun* is for the purpose of making the initial syllable udātta, while the letter *u* is for the purpose of pronunciation.

The letter *l* in the suffix *ṇvul* serves to make the vowel preceding the suffix acute when the suffix is marked with *l* (by Pāṇini 6.1.193); the letter *ṇ* serves for the purpose of *vṛddhi* strengthening. Regarding the term "expressive of the action" (*bhāvavacanāḥ*): they are called *vacanāḥ* because they express (*bruvanti*) [the action]; the suffix *lyuṭ* is used in the sense of the agent due to the rule of diversity (*bahulagrahaṇāt*). Thus, "expressive of the action" (*bhāvavacanāḥ*) means those which are the expressions (*vacanāḥ*) of the action (*bhāvasya*).

Furthermore, he says "having introduced [the topic] with 'in the sense of an action' (*bhāve*)," etc., in order to show that their status as denoters of action (*bhāvavacanatva*) results from their being prescribed in the section on action (*bhāvādhikāra*). "Having introduced" means having made it the subject matter (*adhikṛtya*).
"The *ghañ*-suffixes and so forth" refers to [the rules beginning with Pāṇini 3.3.18].
By the word "etcetera" (ādi), goats and so forth are included.
"For what purpose? and so on constitutes the objection; "by that which is prescribed when there is a word signifying an action as a subordinate element" and so on constitutes the resolution.
It might be argued: "They will be formed by the rule *vāsarūpa*.
To this he says: "And it has been stated that the *vāsarūpa* rule does not apply.
This was stated in the preceding sūtra. [Then follows: "Now," and so forth.

One should simply say "in the sense of being" (*bhāve*). If this were stated, it would serve as the rule for the introduction of *ghañ* and other suffixes; consequently, those suffixes would apply without distinction to every verbal root (*dhātu*), because no specific restriction has been provided. By the inclusion of the term "utterance" (*vacana*), this meaning is obtained: those suffixes prescribed in the sense of being function in such a way that they become expressers of being. To demonstrate how they become expressers of being, he says, beginning with "And how," using a series of questions.
Regarding the phrase "by the consistency of the name":

this means not by way of exclusion (*vyatireka*), nor by way of lack of restriction (*aniyama*). On this point, some say: because of the mention of the word "utterance" (*vacana*), those very prescriptive sentences (*vidhi-vākya*) by which their existence is established are the ones that apply when there is a verbal root as a subordinate element (*upapada*) for the sake of another action; in this way they become denoters (*vācaka*), and not otherwise. Others, however, say: this very *sūtra* is the prescriptive rule, by virtue of the force of the mention of the word "utterance."
By this rule as well, their formation occurs in the same manner as by their own specific prescriptive rules (*vidhivākya*).
For if that rule were to apply only when [the suffix] *bhāva* is present, it would not apply in any other context either.
Therefore, it is prescribed once again. This refers to the rule beginning with "karmaṇyaṇ" (Pāṇini 3.2.1).
This has been made known by the rule *tumunṇvulau* [Pāṇini 3.3.10] and others: that the rule regarding optional forms (*vāsarūpavidhi*) does not apply here.

Therefore, although the suffix *aṇ* is prescribed after a word functioning as a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*), nevertheless, due to the absence of the *vāsarūpa* rule, the suffix *ṇvul*—which would otherwise be superseded when the subordinate word denotes the purpose of an action (*kriyārthopapada*)—is not barred; thus, it is prescribed once again.
"Because it possesses an exception (*sopapavāda*), it supersedes *ṇvul*."
This is because [the suffix] *ṇvul* has not yet been reached when [the subsequent rules] begin, and because it is prescribed as a specific rule.
Regarding the phrase "kādīn," the connection is that they "sublate" [the preceding rules].

By the word "ādi" (and so forth), the inclusion of *ṭak* and others is intended.
