Regarding the statement, "Therefore, it occurs even in the domain of exceptions (*apavāda*)," the exceptions are the suffixes beginning with *ka*, which are prescribed in place of the general *aṇ*; it occurs even in their domain.

> [[3.3.12]] This provides scope for a non-vowel-final (*anākārānta*) verbal root as an upapada—for example, *kāṇṭalāvo vrajati* ("he goes after cutting throats"); whereas [[3.2.3]] provides scope for a vowel-final (*ākārānta*) verbal root as an upapada—for example, *godaḥ* ("cow-giver"). Here, however, both would apply in the case of *godāyo vrajati*; yet, because it is subsequent (*paratva*), the suffix *aṇ* occurs. Similarly, [[3.2.8]] *gāpoṣṭak* provides scope for *surāpaḥ* ("liquor-drinker") and *śīdhupaḥ* ("mead-drinker"), while *aṇ* has the same scope. Here, both would apply in the cases of *surāpāyo vrajati* and *śīdhupāyo vrajati*. [The rule begins with] "by the word *ca*" and so forth.
By this, he shows that the word *ca* is for the purpose of drawing back (*anukarṣaṇa*) the rule *kriyāyāṃ kriyārthāyām*.
[The example is] "I shall do" (*kariṣyāmi*), where the augment *iṭ* applies by [Pāṇini 7.2.70]. [The term] "those designated as *sat*" (*satsaṃjñau*).
Because they are prescribed by the rule *tau sat* [Pāṇini 3.2.127], the suffixes *śatṛ* and *śānac* bear the technical designation *sat*.
But how can *śatṛ* and *śānac* occur after the suffix *lṛṭ*? To this he says: "In cases not coreferential with the nominative," and so forth.

Just as *śatṛ* and *śānac* optionally occur after *laṭ* when it is not coreferential with the nominative, so too do these two, bearing the designation *sat*, occur after *lṛṭ* by means of a fixed option (*vyavasthitavibhāṣā*).

The suffixes *śatṛ* and *syaN* always occur [with the future stem] when not in coreferential relation with a word ending in the nominative case (*apathamāsamānādhikaraṇa*), etc.: *kariṣyantaṃ paśya* ("see him who will do"), *kariṣyamāṇaṃ paśya* ("see him who will be done"); *he kariṣyan*, *he kariṣyamāṇa* ("O you who will do," "O you who will be done"); *arjayiṣyan vasati* ("he dwells intending to acquire"); *kariṣyadbhaktiḥ* ("one whose devotion will be performed"), *kariṣyamāṇabhaktiḥ* ("one whose devotion will be performed"); *kariṣyadrūpaḥ*, *kariṣyamāṇarūpaḥ* ("one whose form will be made"). Thus it is when not in coreferential relation with the nominative. However, when in coreferential relation with the nominative, there is an option: *kariṣyati devadattaḥ* ("Devadatta will do") or *kariṣyan devadattaḥ*; *kariṣyate devadattaḥ* or *kariṣyamāṇo devadattaḥ*.

While the term *lṛṭ* was already in effect, the repetition of *lṛṭ* is for the purpose of indicating the original element (*sthānin*). Otherwise, it might be understood that the two [suffixes] designated as *sat* are distinct suffixes altogether. Alternatively, it is for the sake of ensuring that the rule applies to the mere *lṛṭ* itself. Consequently, this also applies to the *lṛṭ* used in the sense of "not today" (*anadyatana*), as in: *āho agnīnādhāsyamānena*.
These two [suffixes] do not apply to this [root]; for there is the governing rule *bhaviṣyati* (P. 3.3.3), and this [root] is prescribed for the future tense.

However, it should be understood that the suffix *lṛṭ* applies to the non-todays-past (*anadyatana*) because of the split of the rule (*yogavibhāga*) in the subsequent sūtra containing the term *anadyatana*. The letter *ṭ* in *lṛṭ* is for the sake of the substitution of *et* (by P. 3.4.79); the vowel *ṛ* is for the sake of specification in the rule *ṛta id dhātoḥ* (P. 3.1.33). "The term *anadyatana* is a Bahuvrīhi compound" is the explanation.
"Non-present" (*anadyatana*) means that its existence does not occur on this [day].
By the words "by that" (*tena*) and so forth, he demonstrates the purpose of resorting to the *bahuvrīhi* compound;
and since this has already been largely explained under [Pāṇini 3.2.111], it should be understood from that very source.

"Today he will come or go"—the meaning is "he will come today or go [tomorrow]. Regarding the rule beginning with "in lamentation" (*paridevane*), the *luṅ* suffix is prescribed for the future not belonging to the current day (*anadyatana*); however, it does not apply to the general future (*bhaviṣyatsāmānya*), yet it is desired there. For this purpose, the present rule is stated.
*Paridevana* means lamenting.
Regarding the term "*āstanī*," this is another technical designation for the *luṭ* [future tense] used by certain teachers.

"Should be stated" means it should be explained. In this regard, the following is the explanation: from [Pāṇini 3.3.13] onwards, the particle *ca* (and) is understood by anuvṛtti; and that particle serves the purpose of including what has not been explicitly mentioned.
Therefore, in the case of lamentation (*paridevana*), the *luṅ* suffix will occur for the future sense, as in "it will be.

But this other [usage], such as "when indeed will he go? and so forth, shows that the *luṅ* occurs in the non-past (*anadyatana*) time alone; thus he says: "In the grammatical analysis (*padānvākhyāna*) and in grammar (*vyākaraṇa*), that word—such as 'he goes' (*gantu*) and so forth—occurs in the non-past time alone.
When its application is to the non-past or to the general future, it occurs either from the meaning or from the context; thus the sentence-meaning is established."
Furthermore, the meaning of a sentence is not the cause for the grammatical refinement (*saṃskāra*) of a word; rather, it is the meaning of the word itself.
Therefore, the rule "the *luṅ* [suffix] is used for what is not of today" is established.
By this principle, the statement that the *laṅ* [suffix] is used in expressions of lamentation (*paridevana*) and so forth is correct.

In the case of *luṭ* as well, the letter *ṭ* is for the purpose of [triggering] the substitution of *ṭi*; the letter *u* is for the purpose of specification according to [Pāṇini 2.4.85]. The suffix *ghañ* is prescribed as an exception (*apavāda*) to [the suffixes] *ṇvul*, *tṛc*, and *ka* (which is conditioned by the rule regarding roots with *ik* as an upadhā), and also to the *ac* suffix of the *pacādi* class [prescribed after] the root *spṛś*. In the form "pādaḥ," there is the *vṛddhi* substitution according to [Pāṇini 7.2.116].

If this is so, is it not the case that the term *pada* is not established? Indeed, it is not unestablished, because of the specific rule (*nipātana*): “A word (*pada*) is unaccented, with the exception of one [syllable]” (Pāṇini 6.1.152). Regarding the statement “it should be stated that *spṛś* [takes *ghan*] in the sense of affliction (*upatāpa*),” the meaning is that it should be explained as having the sense that the suffix *ghan* occurs after the root *spṛś* when it means “affliction,” which is to say, disease.

In this regard, the explanation is as follows: the word “optionally” (*vā*) from the rule “the suffix *sa* is optionally used for the future marker *lṛṭ*” (Pāṇini 3.3.14) is carried over [to this rule], and that is a restricted option (*vyavasthitavibhāṣā*).
Therefore, the suffix *ghañ* occurs only when the agent (*kartṛ*) is implied, and not otherwise.
"There is a difference in accent" means that if the suffix *ac* were present, there would be udātta on the final syllable; however, with *ghañ*, the word would have udātta on its initial syllable.
The letter *ñ* in *ghañ* is for the purpose of [triggering] *vṛddhi* and for the purpose of making the first syllable udātta.

The letter *gh* is for the purpose of applying the substitution of *k* in accordance with the rule *cajoḥ kughiṇṇyatoḥ* [Pāṇini 7.3.52]. Regarding the phrase "of the root *sṛ*": it refers to the root *sṛ* meaning "to go" (Dhātupāṭha 935).

Regarding the phrase "when the agent is stable" (*sthire kartari*): by this, it is shown that the mention of "stable" (*sthira*) is an adjective qualifying the agent who is the meaning of the suffix, and not an adjunct (*upapada*). "The *ghañ* suffix occurs":
this is an exception (*apavāda*) to [suffixes] such as *tṛc*.
He asks: "What, then, is this so-called 'stable'? and replies: "'Stable' means persisting through another time," and so forth.
He states the justification for that very point: "'That [which lasts] for a long time,'" and so forth.
The root *sṛ* has the meaning of "going."
And that [agency] is possible only for an agent who persists through an interval of time, not for one who perishes immediately after attaining self-existence.

Therefore, it is only an agent who persists through an interval of time who is logically fit to be the agent (*kartṛ*) of the action (*gati*), which is the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātu*); this is precisely what is expressed here by the word "stable" (*sthira*). If the action of going is possible only for one who persists through an interval of time, then the inclusion of the term "stable" would be redundant; for an unstable entity cannot logically be the agent of the act of going. It is not redundant, however, because its purpose is so that the suffix may apply to an agent who goes with excellence—that is, one who moves continuously.
For this very reason, the inclusion of the word *ciraṃ* ("for a long time") was made in the commentary (*vṛtti*) in the statement, "staying for a long time, it flows through another period of time.
[The example] *candasāraḥ* is a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsaḥ*). [It is said: "It should be stated that [the rule applies] in the case of *vyādhi*, *matsya*, and *bala*."
This undertaking has an unstable meaning;
the sense is that this form of meaning—namely, that the suffix *ghañ* occurs after all three of these, beginning with *vyādhi*—must be explained.
The explanation here, however, should be made by relying on the recurrence (*anuvṛtti*) of the word "and" (*ca*).
In the word *atīsāraḥ*, there is lengthening [of the vowel] according to [Pāṇini 6.3.122]. In the word *rāgaḥ*,
there is the elision of the nasal [vowel] according to [Pāṇini 6.4.26] and [6.4.27].

But surely, since this indication by means of the word *bhāva* ending in the suffix *ghañ* is made with the verb *bhavati*, the specification of the meaning of the suffix is restricted solely to the domain of *bhavati*; consequently, the suffix would apply only when that which is to be expressed is the "being" (*bhāva*) of *bhavati*, and that could be denoted by a suffix produced from *bhavati* itself. Therefore, the suffix ought to occur only from that [verb]. How then does it occur after *paci* and other roots in forms such as *pākaḥ*, *tyāgaḥ*, and *rāgaḥ*? To this he says: "expressing the general action," and so forth.

For the general notion of action (*kriyāsāmānya*), which underlies the meanings of all verbal roots, is the meaning of the root *bhū*. Therefore, when an indication of meaning is made by means of that which expresses the general notion of action, it becomes applicable to the domain of all verbal roots; thus, the intention is that a suffix occurs even after roots such as *pac* and others. Now, an objection: the meaning of a verbal root consists of a sequence of prior and posterior stages and is not yet fully accomplished. Consequently, if a suffix were to occur with that [meaning] as its expressed object (*vācya*), then because that meaning has not attained the status of a substantial entity (*asattvabhūtatva*), the connection of the meaning of the suffix with gender and number would not be established. To this, he says: "And the meaning of the verbal root," and so forth.
The particle *eva* serves to exclude the suffix.

The meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) is expressed by the root alone, and not by the suffix. If so, how is it that suffixes such as *ghañ* and others are prescribed? To this he says: "That which belongs to it," and so forth.

The "perfectedness" (*siddhatā*) or "accomplishment" (*niṣpannatā*) of that meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*)—which is the property (*dharma*) in which suffixes such as *ghañ* and others are prescribed—is what is meant here. Therefore, it is logical that the meaning of the suffix (*pratyayārtha*) is connected with gender and number; the sense is that the property belonging to that [meaning] is of the nature of a substance (*sattvabhūtatvāt*). As for the word "bhāva" (being)—this is indicated in the masculine gender and in the singular number.

Consequently, the suffixes would apply only to the masculine gender, only in the singular number, and not when joined with another gender nor in another number. This being the case, in the rule [Pāṇini 3.3.94], the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) between these two terms—*bhāve* ("in the sense of an action") and *striyām* ("in the feminine")—would be untenable; rather, there would be a lack of coreferentiality (*vaiyadhikaraṇya*).

Consequently, the suffix *ktin* would not occur in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāva*) when applied to a feminine noun; rather, it would occur only in other senses such as the object (*karman*) and so forth. Furthermore, regarding the abstract state, in masculine gender forms like *pākaḥ* and *pākāḥ*, there would have to be only the singular number. Since the word *bhāva* is capable of denoting a meaning of a certain grammatical nature, it ought to be joined with a suffix that expresses a meaning of that same nature and not otherwise. Therefore, he says: "In this context, neither the masculine gender nor the singular number is restrictive."

That which is suitable for connection with all genders and numbers, which serves as the cause for the general meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*), and which is adopted as the cause for the suffixes—that alone is the primary factor; neither gender nor number is so.

In that regard, since it is impossible to specify [the object] through gender and number without the general meaning of the nominal stem, these two are mentioned because they are inseparable from it. Once that general meaning of the nominal stem has been understood, however, since gender and number have already fulfilled their purpose, suffixes indeed occur even when another gender is present.
The word "pakti" [is derived] by applying the rule for the abstract state (bhāve) [Pāṇini 3.3.94].
The word "pakva" [is derived] similarly.
The suffix *kta* is used in the sense of an impersonal action (*bhāva*);
thus, "pacanam" (the act of cooking).
The suffix *lyuṭ* is applied according to [Pāṇini 3.3.115].

In this case as well, if the masculine gender were the governing factor for the abstract action (*bhāva*), then because grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) between the word for the action and the neuter noun would be impossible, there would be a lack of coreferentiality (*vaiyadhikaraṇya*). Consequently, the suffix *lyu* would not occur in the neuter abstract sense, but rather only in a different meaning altogether. Furthermore, the presentation of the objection and its resolution is based on the equality of the form *pacana-* when the abstract action is masculine; otherwise, since the suffix *lyuṭ* is prescribed with reference to a different kind of abstract action, this point would simply not need to be raised here.
The words beginning with "pāka" are examples of the abstract suffix (*bhāvapratyaya*) according to another statement. Regarding "prāsa":

the root *asu* means "to throw" (Dhātupāṭha 1209). Regarding "praseva": the root *ṣivu* means "to sew" (Dhātupāṭha 1108). In both cases here, the suffix *ghañ* is applied in the sense of the object (*karman*).
Regarding the term "āhāra":
[it is derived from] the root *hr̥* in the sense of "taking" (*haraṇe*, Dhātupāṭha 899).
Thus, "madhurāhāraḥ" means "sweet food."
It is either a *karmadhāraya* or a *ṣaṣṭhī-tatpuruṣa* compound. Regarding the word "meṣaḥ" (*ram*):
from the root *miṣ* in the sense of "to compete" (*spardhāyām*) [Dhātupāṭha 1352], the suffix *pacādyac* is applied.
Regarding the word "kartavyaḥ": [it is derived from the root *kṛ* with the suffix *tavya*].

"The suffix *tavya* [is used] in the sense of the object (*karman*). [Regarding the statement] "The letter *ca* is for the purpose of preventing ambiguity regarding the technical name (*saṃjñā*)," this *ca* is out of its proper sequence and should be understood immediately after the word *saṃjñāyām*; by that, the meaning of "and" (*ca*) is indicated.

By indicating the meaning of the word "and" (*ca*) in the phrase "and in the case of a name" (*saṃjñāyāṃ ca*), this [word *ca*] serves to show that there is deviation from the scope of "name"; therefore, it also applies in the case of what is not a name. If this were so, one might ask: "Why not formulate the suffix in a general way without mentioning 'name,' so that the particle *ca* would not have to be used for the purpose of showing deviation from 'name'? This is true; nevertheless, the mention of "name" is made to indicate that while it generally occurs in the case of a name, it occurs only occasionally in the case of what is not a name. In the word *dāyaḥ*, the suffix *ghañ* is applied to the root *dā* in the sense of the object (*karman*), and the *yuk* augment is added as before.
The term *lābhaḥ* is formed with the suffix *ghañ* precisely in the sense of the object (*karman*). Regarding the phrase "the mention of *kāraka*" and so forth:

for if the rule were formulated as *akartari* (excluding the agent) by way of exclusion (*paryudāsa*), then even without the explicit mention of *kāraka*, through the maxim of the connection with *nañ* and *iva* (Pāṇini 2.2.6), the understanding would arise that [the suffix applies] to such a *kāraka* other than the agent—namely, to the object and so forth—just as in the case of *abrāhmaṇaḥ*, which refers to someone like a Brāhmaṇa, such as a Kṣatriya.
Therefore, in the case of *paryudāsa* (exclusion), even without the mention of *kāraka*, the suffix is understood to apply only to a *kāraka*; thus, the mention of *kāraka* need not be made.
However, in the case of *prasajyapratiṣedha* (absolute negation), it must be mentioned; for there, only the negation of the action is perceived, and not another similar entity.

In that context, if only "in the sense of non-agent (*akartari*) and when it is a technical name (*saṃjñāyām*)" were stated, the meaning would be understood as "it does not occur in the sense of agent."
And thus, because there is no other prescriptive rule (*vidhāyaka-vākya*), the suffix would not occur in relation to the action (*karman*) and so forth.
Where, then, would it occur? It occurs in its own meaning (*svārtha*), according to the principle: "Suffixes whose meaning is not specifically prescribed occur in their own meaning" (*Puṃ-pāṭha* 90).

But has it not already been prescribed in its own meaning by the preceding rule? This is not so; for it has been stated: "The *ghañ* and other suffixes are prescribed in reference to that property called 'accomplishment' (*siddhatā*) which belongs to the meaning of the verbal root."

Therefore, why is the mention of "kāraka" (participant in an action) made in the case of a *prasajya-pratiṣedha* (absolute negation)? To this he says: [the rule] is established even without the mention of "kāraka" in the case of a *paryudāsa* (relative negation); that very [negation] will be accepted. Why then is the mention of "kāraka" made here? To this he says: "It is made," and so forth.

If, then, this *nañ*-compound were merely an exclusion (*paryudāsa*), the mention of "kāraka" (participant) would be purposeless; for even without it, a suffix is obtained only when there is a kāraka. However, when it is a simple negation (*prasajyapratiṣedha*), the mention of "kāraka" becomes meaningful, because in that case a suffix is not obtained as referring to a kāraka even without that mention. And this has been demonstrated immediately prior. Therefore, by the mention of "kāraka," it is indicated that the compound exists even in the case of a simple negation.

In the rule *tena* [Pāṇini 2.1.32], a compound is obtained when there is a *prasajya-pratiṣedha* (absolute negation). Consequently, what was stated—that "the substitution of *ā* is unconditional, and the prohibition applies to *śit* affixes"—becomes logically consistent.

But what is the reason for resorting to *prasajya-pratiṣedha* in that case? It is so that even before the production of the suffix, once the unconditional substitution of *ā* has been applied, forms such as *suglaḥ* and *sumlaḥ* may occur according to [Pāṇini 3.3.106].

But if an exclusion (*paryudāsa*) were adopted there, then [the rule] would have to apply as *āttva* (the substitution of /ā/) when a suffix beginning with *tṛc* or another such suffix follows; consequently, a suffix characterized by ending in /ā/ would not occur after roots such as *glāyati*.

But does not the activity of the Teacher indicate that suffixes characterized by having "ā" as their final vowel occur after roots ending in vowels—since he teaches the suffix *aṇ* [in Pāṇini 3.2.2] for the purpose of setting aside *kap*—therefore, even if a relative exclusion (*paryudāsa*) is adopted for the term "not ending in *i*" (*aśiti*), the suffix characterized by having "ā" as its final vowel is established for roots ending in vowels on the basis of this indicator (*jñāpaka*)? This is not so; this indicator is understood to apply only to cases where there is an object (*karman*) as a co-occurring word (*upapada*). Therefore, in the rule "not ending in *i*" (*aśiti*), it is proper to adopt a simple negation (*prasajyapratiṣedha*).
And its existence here is indicated by the mention of the "participant" (*kāraka*).

But what is the reason that a simple negation (*prasajyapratiṣedha*) is not established, such that it must be understood as conveying the existence [of something else]? The reason is its lack of semantic capacity (*asāmarthya*). For when there is semantic capacity, a compound (*samāsa*) ought to occur, and that does not happen in the case of a simple negation.

This is because, in that case, the negative particle (*nañ*) is connected with the verb, not with the subsequent word—as in the example "one handful of rice" (*eka-staṇḍula-niścāyaḥ*), where the suffix *dhañ* is applied even though [the rule] *Pāṇini 3.3.58* would have required it.
In the case of *dvau śūrpaniṣpāvau*,
although *ṛdorap* [Pāṇini 3.3.57] would also apply,
the substitution of *ṣ* for the *visarga* occurs by [Pāṇini 8.3.41].

"Two *kāra*s. [The root] *kṛ* means "to scatter" (*vikṣepa*; Dhātupāṭha 1409). Now, one might ask: since the suffix *ghañ* is already established by rule Pāṇini 3.3.28 in cases such as *dvau śūrpaniṣpāvau*, for what purpose is this stated here? The intention is as follows: when the term *sarva* ("all") is employed for other purposes, the suffix is established elsewhere even in the expression of measure (*parimāṇākhyā*). Furthermore, the suffix *hap* would also be appropriate after the prefix *ni-*; however, the scope of rule 3.3.28 is where the expression of measure is not understood.

But what is the distinction when *ghañ* is applied by that [rule] or by this [present rule]? What logic is being explained? None at all. [Objection: Is it not the case that "from a root" (*dhātoḥ*) is a general governing rule (*adhikāra*), and not a specification of a particular root? Even without the mention of "all" (*sarva*), *ghañ* will occur from any root whatsoever; so for what purpose is the mention of "all"? To this he says: "The mention of 'all'... and so forth.

Furthermore, what is the reason that an exception (*bādhā*) is not established when there is no mention of "all" (*sarva*)? To this he says: "In the preceding," and so forth. According to the principle: "Exceptions [stated] earlier subvert the immediately following rules, but not those that follow later" (Vyāḍiparibhāṣā 9), if there were the mention of "all," the *ghañ* suffix would subvert only the immediately following *ac* suffix, but not the *ap*.
If, however, the term "all" (*sarva*) were not included, it would exclude even water;

therefore, the inclusion of "all" is so that there may be exclusion [of the suffix] even in the case of water. Furthermore, this word *parimāṇa* is conventionally established (*rūḍha*) in reference to measures such as the *prastha* and the like, but not in reference to number (*saṃkhyā*). Consequently, how could this suffix, being prescribed for the expression of a measure (*parimāṇa*), occur in cases such as *ekaḥ taṇḍulaniścāyaḥ* ("one handful of rice"), where number is what is understood? To this he says: "The mention of *ākhyā* (name/designation)" and so forth. The mention of *ākhyā* here is made for the purpose of excluding—that is, abandoning—the conventional sense (*rūḍhi*).
Therefore, when conventional usage (*rūḍhi*) is abandoned, number (*saṃkhyā*) is also included.
For, by the force of the inclusion of the term "name" (*ākhyā*), the measure (*parimāṇa*) is [intended]; hence, its inclusion is also appropriate.

The intention is this: if, due to the inclusion of the word "all," this *ghañ* suffix were to subvert even what follows it, it would likewise subvert the *sthī* suffixes as well. Thus, [the rule] is stated.
For this very reason, he says: "But the feminine suffixes are not superseded.
How, then, is this meaning obtained? From the indication by the word *sarvebhyaḥ* in the ablative case.
For when there is an indication in the ablative, the word *sarva* is understood to be in grammatical apposition with the verbal root (*dhātu*).
Therefore, by the inclusion of the word "all" (*sarva*), there is an annulment of the exception based on the *prakṛti* (the original form), but not of that based on the meaning (*artha*).
If, however, the exception based on the meaning were also intended to be annulled, then one would have uttered the word "all" (*sarva*) in the locative case as "in all" (*sarvasmin*).
[As it stands, we have] "one *tila*-height" (*ekā tilocchritiḥ*).

From the root *śri* with the prefix *ud-*: by [Pāṇini 3.3.94], [Pāṇini 8.4.40] there is the substitution of *c*, and by [Pāṇini 8.4.63] there is the substitution of *ch*. Regarding the phrase "dārajārau" and so forth:
the words *dāra* and *jāra* are treated as irregularly formed (*nipātita*).

What is elided here? From the roots *dṛ* "to tear" (DhP 1493) and *jṛṣ* "loss of vitality" (DhP 1130), when followed by the causative suffix *ṇic*, the suffix *ṇic* is elided before the agentive suffixes *tṛc* and others, as well as the suffix *ghañ*. But surely, since the elision of *ṇic* is governed by [Pāṇini 6.4.51], once that elision has occurred, the designation *mit* would apply to these roots according to [Pāṇini 6.4.92] (*janījṛṣknasurañjo'mantāśca*). Consequently, even though the *ṇic* has been elided, the rule for the shortening of roots designated as *mit* would undesirably apply to the root *jṝ* by virtue of the "characteristic of the affix" (*pratyayalakṣaṇa*).

If it is argued, "Let there then be shortening of the measured [vowel], and subsequently, the *vṛddhi* substitution will occur by virtue of the *ghañ* suffix," this is incorrect. For the *vṛddhi* substitution based on the *ghañ* suffix does not apply, because when there is the status of being a substitute (*sthānivadbhāva*) according to Pāṇini 1.1.57, the operation is intervened upon by the *ṇic* suffix. However, when elision (*luk*) occurs, since that [elision] is not a cause for the subsequent rule, the status of being a substitute does not exist; thus, the *vṛddhi* substitution takes place by relying on the *ghañ* suffix. Furthermore, the shortening of the vowel does not result by means of the "characteristic of the suffix" (*pratyayalakṣaṇa*), because of the prohibition of the characteristic of the suffix by Pāṇini 1.1.62: "When a suffix is marked with *lu*, there is no [application of a rule] to the stem (*aṅga*)."
Therefore, elision (*luk*) must be stated [as the solution]. Regarding the statement "it is an exception to *ac*":

although the suffix *ac* prescribed by [Pāṇini 3.3.56] *erac* would apply here, the *ghañ* that is being prescribed after a word ending in the vowel *i* should be understood as an exception specifically to *ac*.
Thus, we have the form *adhyāyaḥ*.
The suffix *ghañ* is applied in the sense of the object (*karman*). Regarding the rule "and after that which ends in it, there is optionally *ṅīṣ*":
this means that *ṅīṣ* is to be introduced after a word ending in *ghañ* when it occurs in the sense of the ablative (*apādāna*).

In this regard, the following is the demonstration: in the rule *voto guṇavacanāt* [Pāṇini 4.1.44], the word *vā* should be treated as a *yogavibhāga* (separation of the rule). By means of that, the suffix *ṅīṣ* will apply after a word ending in *ghañ* which is prescribed for the feminine in the sense of the *apādāna* (ablative). And when the connection with a male (*puṃyoga*) is not intended to be expressed, then *ṅīṣ* is established. However, when the connection with a male is intended to be expressed—as in "the wife of a teacher" (*upādhyāyasya strī*)—then *ṅīṣ* is established by the rule *tasyāpatyam* [Pāṇini 4.1.92] itself.
The term *upādhyāyī* refers to one who approaches and studies under a teacher (*upetyādhīyate*). Regarding the rule *śṛ vāyu-varṇa-nivṛtteṣu*:

since the root *śṛ* is listed as *śṛ hiṃsāyām* (Dhātupāṭha 1488), the suffix *ghañ* is prescribed when *vāyu*, *varṇa*, and *nivṛtti* are to be expressed. This prescription should be carried out either by relying on the particle *ca* itself for the purpose of including unstated items, or by resorting to the inclusion of the term *bahulam* (in various ways) from Pāṇini 3.3.113.

*Nivṛtta* means warding off (*nivāraṇa*). Warding off is said to be the cause for the cessation of suffering from cold and so forth. Regarding the phrase *akṛtanīśāraḥ*, the meaning is "one who has not performed the warding off of cold."

As before, there is lengthening of the prefix. "An exception to *ap*" means it is an exception to what was obtained by [Pāṇini 3.3.57] *ṛdorap*. It should be understood that even the suffix *ghan* prescribed by the subsequent rule for stems ending in *u* is an exception specifically to *ap*. "From those without a prefix" (*anupasargebhyaḥ*).

The term *anupasargebhyaḥ* is a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "those for which no prefix (*upasarga*) exists. By providing this analysis with a word ending in the ablative case, he demonstrates that in the rule, the word *anupasarga*—which appears in the nominative—is used as a locative through a transposition of cases (*subvyatyaya*). Regarding the question, "How is there 'the power of the king' (*prabhāvo rājñaḥ*)?", the intention is that because of the explicit mention of "no prefix," the prefix *pra-* here should not function as a governing word (*upapada*).
And how is it that "the policy of the king" (*nayo rājñaḥ*) [is formed]? [As stated in the *Kāśikā*: "How is it..."]
It is considered that the suffix *ghañ* should be applied here when there is no prefix (*anupasarga*). Thus: *vikṣāvaḥ* [from the root] *kṣu* "to sound" (Dhātupāṭha 1036). And: *unnāyaḥ*;
here, by [Pāṇini 8.4.45], the nasalization (*anunāsika*) optionally occurs.

"How is there an 'unnaya' (bringing up) of the meanings of words?"— the intention here is that the suffix *ghañ* must occur because it is preceded by the prefix *ud*. "A general apprehension"— because no specific [instance] is mentioned.

"The connection with the prefixes is according to their respective order. The prefix *ni-* is connected with the root *pū*, and *abhi-* with *lū*. But surely there are three roots—*pūñ*, *pūṅ*, and *lūñ*—and only two prefixes; therefore, due to this discrepancy, the correspondence according to order (*yathāsaṃkhyam*) should not occur? There is no fault here, because the form *pū* is one and the same when the specific indicatory letters (*anubandha*) have been discarded as common factors; thus, there is no discrepancy. This [rule] is an exception to what would otherwise be obtained by the rule *ṝdorap* (Pāṇini 3.3.57).

Even later on, when the suffix *ghañ* is prescribed after a root ending in *ṛ*, it should be understood as an exception (*apavāda*) specifically to *ap*. [The statement] "there is the inclusion of both" is because no distinction is made. Now, would *dhānya* here be the meaning of the base (*prakṛti*), or would it be the meaning of the suffix (*pratyaya*)? First of all, it cannot be the meaning of the base; for *dhānya* (grain) is a substance (*dravya*), whereas a verbal root (*dhātu*) denotes action (*kriyā*).

The meaning of the suffix is indeed applicable to the word *dhānya* (grain); however, because it has already been expressed by the suffix, the use of the word *dhānya* in the expression *dhānyasyotkāraḥ* (a winnowing of grain) would not be justified.
Even if such usage were to occur, since the meaning is already included within the sense of the suffix, the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) is not appropriate—namely, in *dhānyasyotkāraḥ*.

There would instead have to be grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the word ending in the suffix; for the meaning of the suffix is realized only when there is coreferentiality with the word ending in that suffix, as in *dṛtihariḥ paśuḥ* (a beast that tears apart).

Therefore, this [suffix] does not express the meaning of the suffix (*pratyaya*), nor does it express the meaning of the base (*prakṛti*); rather, it is a qualifier of the meaning of the base. Thus, there is no inclusion of the root *kṛ* in the sense of "injury" (*hiṃsā*) [as listed in Dhātupāṭha 1496].
He asks: "What is the reason? and replies: "Because it is not so expressed (*anabhidhānāt*)."
Due to the inherent nature of the power of words, the two terms *ud* and *kara* denote only the scattering of grain, not violence.
It is logical that only that whose meaning is expressed by the suffix should be understood [as the object of the rule], and not anything else. As in the example: "a heap (*utkāra*) of grain."

The meaning is that "scattering" (*vikṣepa*) belongs to the giver. By the passage beginning with "in which place they praise together," he shows that the word *saṃstāva* has the sense of a locus (*adhikaraṇasādhana*). Regarding "the *barhiṣprastara*": the substitution of *ṣ* for the *visarga* occurs according to Pāṇini 8.3.41, *idudupadhasya cāpratyayasya*. Regarding "the *tṛṇavistara*": the meaning is a covering of grass. This word *chandas* exists indeed in the context of the Mantras and Brāhmaṇas; there is another [meaning] referring to a specific arrangement of syllables, of which *gāyatrī* and others are the particular varieties.

In this context, which of those meanings is intended? To this he says: "The *vṛtta*," and so forth. He provides the justification for this very point: "Because of the mention of the name. For if the intention here were the mantra and Brāhmaṇa, he would not have mentioned the name; he would simply have said "in the *chandas*."
Even when it is stated in this way, the inclusion of both *mantra* and *brāhmaṇa* is indeed obtained, as in the rule at [Pāṇini 7.4.78] and others.
Therefore, because of the mention of the name, "meter" (*chandas*) is understood here by recurrence (*anuvṛtti*).
[The term is] "viṣṭārapaṅkti."
The substitution of *ṣ* [for *s*] occurs by [Pāṇini 8.3.94].

Someone might have the misconception that the word *viṣṭāra* alone here is a name for a meter ending in the suffix *ghañ*; in order to dispel that, he says: "the word *viṣṭārapaṅkti* here," and so forth.
Therein = in the word *viṣṭārapaṅkti*.
"It exists as a constituent part (*avayavatvena vartate*).

This should be connected with the statement that "it is a word-form ending in the suffix *ghañ*. If the word-form ending in *ghañ* is not the name of a meter (*chandonāma*), but rather the word *viṣṭārapaṅkti*, then in that case the form ending in *ghañ* exists as a constituent part. If this is so, then how is it understood that this [term] is the name of a meter? For when the name of a meter is intended, this is the meaning: namely, that the word ending in the suffix becomes the name of a meter.

And since this would be the case, he says that the intended meaning is not tenable: "The locative case here is locative absolute (*adhikaraṇa-saptamī*), [expressing] 'in the name of a *chandas*. By this, he demonstrates that the meaning to be understood here is: "the suffix occurs when the name of a *chandas* is the locus (*adhikaraṇa*) of the word ending in the suffix," and not that "it occurs when the name of a *chandas* is merely implied. Regarding the phrase "an exception to *apa*" (Pāṇini 4.2.70), this refers to what was obtained by [the rule] Pāṇini 3.3.58. As for the statement "In the *Chandas*, however," etc., the printed reading of the Vārttika is seen as: "{In the *Chandas*, the suffix *uṇ* is desired after the root *vi-pūrvād api-ṣyati* in the senses of lifting up and throwing down}. "In the *Chandas*, however," and so forth [is explained].

The specific sacrificial vessel by which the oblation is offered is called *sruc*. The raising (*udyamana*) of it is its being lifted upward; the lowering (*nipātana*) of it is its being brought downward. It should be understood that the suffix *ghañ* is prescribed for these two meanings in the Vedic domain (by Pāṇini 3.3.18).
And that [suffix] is obtained by [the rule] *sa ca* (Pāṇini 3.3.113). Thus, [the form] "nigrābham" is explained.

The substitution of *bh* for *h* occurs due to the inclusion of *grah* in the Vedic language (*chandasi*) as an exception (*upasaṃkhyāna*). Since the root *grah* denotes an action (*kriyāvācitva*) and a fist (*muṣṭi*) is not of the nature of an action, [the substitution] is not possible there for the root *grah*. Therefore, he says—"if the meaning of the verbal root has the fist as its object"—in order to indicate that the scope of the meaning of *grah* is understood here as referring to the grasping of a fist.

This word *muṣṭi* exists in the sense of a measure—as in *śākasya muṣṭiḥ* ("a handful of vegetables")—and it exists in the sense of a particular arrangement of the fingers, as in *muṣṭinā hanti* ("he strikes with his fist"). Now, if the word were taken here in the sense of a measure, this rule would be rendered purposeless, because [the desired form] is already established by [Pāṇini 3.3.20]. Therefore, it is understood that the word is taken in the sense of a particular arrangement of the fingers; thus he says: "A *muṣṭi* is a configuration (*saṃniveśa*) of the fingers. *Saṃniveśa* means a particular arrangement. As in:
"What a grasp (*saṃgraha*) the wrestler has!"
The meaning is "the firmness of the fist. For this very reason, he says: "It is called 'firmness of the fist'. Regarding the phrase "of the objects" (*padārthānām*) and so forth:
the word *pada* denotes a real entity (*vastu*).
*Apacāra* means contemptible conduct; that is to say, the non-performance of what ought to be performed.

Just as in the world the failure to do what is required is censured as improper, its opposite—peaceful conduct—is *anapacāra*. To clarify this very meaning through a synonym, he says: "the performance of what ought to be performed."
The term *yadyatprāptim* is an *avyayībhāva* compound used in the sense of distribution (*vīpsā*), according to the rule *yathāsādṛśye* [Pāṇini 2.1.7].

*Karaṇam* means "accomplishment" (*sampādanam*). What is meant is this: the accomplishment of those things that are reached through reasoning, scripture, or worldly renown—that is *abhreṣa*. [Regarding the word *bhreṣa*: in the root list, *bhreṣṛ* means "to go"; *bhreṣaṇam* is *bhreṣaḥ*; it is a deviation from one's own nature (*svarūpāt taccalanam*).
Non-deviation (*abhreṣa*) is the non-departure from the essential nature of deviation (*bhreṣasvarūpa*).
For things remain unmoved from their essential nature only if they do not overstep what has been attained.
"By means of measurement" (*parimāṇena*).
Thus, by [the rule] 8.4.14, there is the substitution of *ṇ* for *n*.
"He strikes" means he obstructs.
"By leading all around."
This is an explanation of the meaning of the term "by way of transformation" (*pariṇāmena*): namely, "non-transgression" (*anatipātaḥ*),
which means "not overstepping," and "transgression" (*atipātaḥ*) is its opposite.

The meaning is "transgression" (*atikrama*). *Paryāya* is indeed the same as *anupātyaya*; since the desired result would have been established by the continued application of the term *anupātyaya* alone, the inclusion of the word *paryāya* is for the purpose of overriding a potential sublation. This is so that, when the sense of inclusive limit (*abhividhi*) is intended, the suffix *ghañ* itself may apply even after [the rule regarding] *parimāṇa* has been overridden. And thus, because there is an increase in the word, an increase in the meaning is obtained; however, the word *paryāya* is not the primary designator of this specific meaning. [Regarding the phrase] "by the mention of *hastādāna-grahaṇa*" and so forth...

Appropriation (*upādāna*) that does not depend on other means for its swift execution is *pratyāsatti* (proximity); it arises from that very [appropriation] itself. Therefore, by the mention of "taking with the hand" (*hastādāna*), the proximity of the object to be grasped is indicated, because of the constant association (*sāhacarya*) between the meaning denoted by the word "taking with the hand" and proximity. [In the example] "on the top of the tree" (*vṛkṣaśikhare*) and so forth, the mention of "the top of the tree" indicates that the object to be taken is not proximate. "Piling up" (*rāśīkaraṇa*) means the bringing together in one place of what was scattered.
Regarding the term *cikhallinikāya*: *cikhalli* is a country (*janapada*), and its *nikāya* is its inhabited region.
Now, what is the purpose of including the word "beginning with" (*ādi*)? It is so that it may not apply to the meaning (*artha*).

If this is so, should it not be stated as "caḥ kaḥ"? In that case, the inclusion of the word "ādi" (beginning) is for the purpose that when [the suffix] is produced from a form ending in *yaṅ* (intensive), the second *ca* should not be substituted by *ka*, according to the rule "{in the absence of an end, [the substitute takes the place of] what stands in the vicinity of the end" (Śākalya 56). Regarding the phrase "by the entry into a single property," the meaning is "by following a single property. Because of the governing context of "of a verbal root" (Pāṇini 3.1.91), that which is the object expressed by the verbal root is understood here, and not the object as a grammatical factor (*sādhana*).
Thinking that the verbal root (*dhātu*) does not have its application there [in the sense of "action"], he says: "Action (*karma*) is *kriyā*.
Regarding the statement "the particle *ca* is for the sake of specification":

why does the particle *ca* not serve the purpose of making [the word] oxytone (*antodātta*)? It cannot serve the purpose of making it oxytone, because the suffix *añ* is prescribed after a stem ending in the negative particle *nañ*.

By the rule of *satiśiṣṭa* accent, the word should be *ādyudātta* (accented on the first syllable); in that case, how could there be the possibility of it being *antodātta* (accented on the final syllable)?
Therefore, the particle *ca* is indeed for the purpose of specification (*viśeṣaṇa*).
If only "in the feminine" (*striyām*) were stated, then [the suffix] would also apply in the case of *prājñā*.

Regarding the forms beginning with *vyāvakrośī*: from the roots *kruś* (to call out or to weep; Dhātupāṭha 1365), *likh* (to arrange letters; Dhātupāṭha 1365), and *has* (to laugh; Dhātupāṭha 721), the suffix *ṇac* is applied. Then, by the rule *ṇacaḥ striyām* [Pāṇini 5.4.14], the suffix *añ* is added in the sense of the base itself (*svārthe*). By the rule *ṭiḍḍhāṇañ* [Pāṇini 4.1.15], the feminine suffix *ṅīp* is added. By the rule *aijāgama-pratiṣedhaḥ* [Pāṇini 7.3.6], the substitution of *ai* is prohibited. Thus, only the initial *vṛddhi* (vowel strengthening) takes place. As for the form *vyatipākaḥ*: [it is derived similarly].
In that case, because the state (*bhāva*) is masculine, the suffix *ghañ* occurs.

Now, why was *ṇac* not mentioned in this very same section [beginning with Pāṇini 3.3.94]? What advantage would there be in doing so? [One might say: "The mention of the feminine (*striyām*) need not be repeated twice. There is indeed an advantage: however, the rule of optional forms (*vāsarūpavidhi*) would not apply; for there is a prohibition by the rule *astriyām*.
Consequently, since there would be no co-occurrence (*asamāveśa*) of *ktin* and *ṇac*, the form *vyāvakruṣṭiḥ* would not be established.

But if this [interpretation] were adopted, the suffix *ṇac* would not be established; because, in the rule Pāṇini 3.1.94 (*ato 'nekācaḥ*), due to the fact that the mention of "feminine" (*strī*) is marked with a svarita accent, the prohibition in 3.1.94 (*na striyām*) is understood to apply only to the domain of suffixes prescribed under the heading of "feminine," and not to the domain of feminine suffixes in general.
Therefore, the other [interpretation] alone is logical, as in the examples "vyāvacorī" and "vyāvacarcī."

From the roots *cur* (Dhātupāṭha 1534) and *carc* (Dhātupāṭha 1712)—both belonging to the *curādigaṇa* and taking the causative suffix *ṇic*—the suffix *yuc* would apply by [Pāṇini 3.3.107]. Since that suffix is prescribed for specific cases and is subsequent [in the order of rules], it would normally be the sublater; nevertheless, in these instances, only the suffix *ṇaṅ* is desired. Thus we have *vyatīkṣā* and *vyatīhā*.
From the roots *īkṣ* (Dhātupāṭha 610) meaning "to see" and *īh* (Dhātupāṭha 632) meaning "exertion"—by [Pāṇini 3.3.103]—only the suffix *ac* occurs.
It is not possible to perform [the action] because it is desired [only] in certain cases where there is a sublater (*bādhaka*), and not everywhere.
Furthermore, the status of being a sublater for the suffix *akāra* should be understood as previously explained.
Regarding the term "vyātyukṣī":
The root *ukṣ* means "to sprinkle" (Dhātupāṭha 657).
In this case, even in the domain of the prohibitive negative particle *a-* [which would normally cause the substitution of *guṇa*], only the augment *ṇat* occurs.
[Question: "How is this diversity obtained?"
"Not in any way";
the meaning is that there is an absence of any cause for its attainment,
as indicated by [the rule] 3.3.113.

Therefore, he shows that this variety is obtained by saying "sāṃkūṭinam. [The suffix] *aṇ* is added in the sense of the base itself (*svārthika*) to the word ending in the *inu* suffix derived from the root *kūṭ* (meaning "to torment," according to others) [Dhātupāṭha 1890]. Because of the rule [Pāṇini 6.4.15], there is no elision of the *ṭi* [of the suffix] by the rule [Pāṇini 6.4.144], due to the preservation of the original form (*prakṛtibhāva*) by the rule [Pāṇini 6.4.164]. [Then] "saṃrāvaḥ" [is formed].

The suffix *ghañ* is applied by the rule *upasarge ruvaḥ* [Pāṇini 3.3.22], as in the word *saṃdrāvaḥ*. Regarding this, it is also governed by the rule *ataḥ* [Pāṇini 3.3.23]. Now, one might ask: since the term *bhāve* (in the sense of an action or state) continues to apply from the previous rule, for what purpose is it mentioned again? To this he says: "In the sense of an action (*bhāve*)."

Regarding the phrase "in the present" (*vartamāne*) and so forth: the inclusion of the term *bhāva* here is redundant; being redundant, it is understood as intended to exclude the application of the *vā-sarūpa* rule.
Consequently, there is no co-occurrence (*samāveśa*) of the suffix *tṛn* with the suffix *kta*.

But surely, the term *kāraka* (agent) also recurs [from the previous rule]; therefore, why is the mention of *bhāva* (action/state) not made for the purpose of excluding that? The thought is as follows: although both *bhāve* and *kārake* are present in the context, a restriction is established by virtue of observing actual usage, as in the case of the suffix *ṇac*. For even though both are present there, because it conforms to the observation of the target forms (*lakṣya*), it is understood to apply to *bhāva* alone and not to *kāraka*, even without an explicit re-mention. In the same way, here too, *inuṇ* will be understood to apply only to *bhāva*. Therefore, it is appropriate that the mention of *bhāva* is repeated solely for the purpose of negating the application of the rule regarding alternative forms (*vāsarūpavidhi*).
If this is so, then just as there is no co-occurrence (*samāveśa*) of *ghañ* and *inuṇ*, there would likewise be none with *lyuṭ*; therefore, he says: "But with *lyuṭ*," and so forth.
This has already been explained.
The letter *ṇ* in *inuṇ* is for the purpose of causing *vṛddhi*.

The letter *u* is for the sake of pronunciation. This is a statement made because [the suffix] would otherwise have been obtained by the rule *grahavṛdṛ...* (Pāṇini 3.3.58). Regarding the phrase "because of the capacity for the continued application seen": the capacity for the continued application (*anuvṛtti*) of the suffix *ghañ* is seen through its presence in actual usage, whereas for *inuṇ*, it would have to be inferred.
Furthermore, when two [suffixes] whose capacities have been observed are in proximity, it is logical that the one whose capacity has been observed first should be applied.
Therefore, some maintain that only *ghañ* continues [from the previous rule], and not *ap*.
However, in this way, even in rules such as *grahavṛdṛ* (Pāṇini 3.3.58), only *ghañ* continues, and not *ap*.
Therefore, it is explained otherwise: where the capacity for the continued application (*anuvṛtti*) of that which is under discussion is observed, there is *svaritatva* (the acute accent).
For it is in that case that the capacity for the continued application of the word under discussion is seen within the treatise (*śāstra*).
What is meant by this is: *svaritatva* is asserted only for the suffix *ghañ*, and not for *inuṇ*.

Therefore, because of its acute accent (*svarita*), the suffix *ghañ* alone is carried forward [by *anuvṛtti*], and not *inuṇ*. It is an exception (*apavāda*) to what was obtained by the rule "after the roots *grah*, *vṛ*, *dṛ*, etc. (Pāṇini 3.3.58). "There are grains called *nīvāra*."

By this [explanation], although this word is derived by means of the term *dhānya*, which expresses a general category, he shows that—due to the inherent nature of the expressive power (*śakti*) of words—the form ending in the suffix actually refers only to a specific kind of grain.
The lengthening of the vowel occurs by the rule *upasargasya ghañi* [Pāṇini 6.3.121]. Regarding the form *nivarā*:
it is called *nivarā* because it is "shut off" (*nivriyate*).
Even though it ends in the suffix *ghañ*, it occurs in the feminine gender.

And thus, the statement in the section on genders that forms ending in *ghañ* and those ending in *ghu* are masculine should be understood as being merely general (prāyika). Regarding the phrase "an exception to [the suffixes] *ac* and *ap*":
because the root *śri* ends in the vowel *i*, it is an exception to *ac*; whereas for roots such as *yu*, because they end in the vowel *u*, it is an exception to *ap*.
Regarding the phrase "How is it that all elevations end in falling?",
the intention is that the suffix *ghañ* should be applied here because of the presence of the prefix *ud*.
The response beginning with "That which will be stated," etc., provides the resolution.

If, then, the mention of *vibhāṣā* (optionality) is connected here, would it not follow that affixes would optionally apply even to roots such as *yu* and others? There is no fault, because it does not follow due to *vyavasthita-vibhāṣā* (restricted optionality). Regarding the rule *rauteḥ* [3.3.22], since the suffix *ghañ* would necessarily apply by [the previous rule], this sūtra is commenced also for the sake of *plavati*, which ends in the vowel *u*. Although [the suffix] would also be obtained by the rule *grahavṛdṛ-* [3.3.58] etc., this [sūtra] is an exception (*apavāda*) to that; thus, *ghañ* is prescribed in the alternative (*pakṣe*). "From some cause" means:
because of the context concerning the transgression of the action of being (*sattva-karma*). "And through connection with a merchant," and so forth.
For the "scale-string" (*tulāsūtra*) is generally associated with, that is, concomitant with, merchants; therefore, by virtue of that association, it is indicated by connection with merchants.
Here, the merchants do not possess primacy.
Consequently, that very scale-string and so forth is the denotation of the word *tadanya* ("other than that"). [This applies to] the phrase "those yoked to chariots," and so on.

But how is this further established, given that the word *raśmi* (ray) is a general term, just as it applies to a rope used for tethering a horse, so too does it apply to the rays associated with the moon, the sun, and so forth? The thought is as follows: just as in the case of the rule *dhānyānāṃ bhavane kṣetre khañ* [Pāṇini 5.2.1], even though the word *dhānya* is general, only a specific type of grain is understood because the suffix [denoting a field] expresses a specific grain due to the inherent nature of the word's power (*śabdaśakti*);
likewise, although the word *raśmi* denotes a generality, nevertheless, by its inherent nature, when followed by a suffix, it refers specifically to a particular kind of rope.
Therefore, the inclusion [of the root] is appropriate. Regarding the term "vṛṇoteḥ":
the mention with the *śnu*-suffix (*vṛṇoti*) is for the purpose of excluding the root *vṛṅ*.
Here too, as before, since it expresses a general sense, it applies to cases other than that denoted by the word "covering" (*ācchādana*).

In this alternative view, the suffix *ap* occurs by the rule "grahavṛdṛ... [Pāṇini 3.3.58]. The statement "the letter *ca* is for the sake of specification" means that even without it, the term *apratyaya* would still include what is not a suffix (*apratyaya*) in the rule "thāthādi... [Pāṇini 6.2.143]. The phrase "in the prescription of *ac*" and so forth [is explained as follows].
The purpose of the term *upasaṃkhyāna* (supplementation) is to provide a formal derivation (*pratipādana*).
This derivation, however, must be carried out by relying on the rule *pūraṇaguṇasuhitārthasadavyayatavyasamānādhikaraṇena* [Pāṇini 2.2.11].

Others, however, desire the establishment of forms such as *bhaya* through the irregular formation (*nipātana*) in the rule *varṣapramāṇa ūlopaścāsyāntarasyām* [Pāṇini 3.4.32]; yet that is not correct, because of the doubt: "Is this the utterance of the words *bhaya* and *varṣa* in the neuter gender, or in the masculine gender?"
"Vaktavyau" means "they are to be explained. The explanation, however, must be carried out by relying on that very mention of the term *bahula* (in the rule Pāṇini 3.1.85).
Regarding the forms *javaḥ* and *savaḥ*:

from the root *ju* mentioned in the Sūtra [Pāṇini 3.2.150], and also from the root *ṣuñ* meaning "to press" (Dhātupāṭha 1247), the suffix *ac* is applied by the subsequent rule even though it would have been obtained by the previous one. There is a distinction in accent: for if the suffix were *āna*, the word would be udātta on the first syllable; however, when the suffix is *ac*, the word becomes udātta on the final syllable. Thus, "the inclusion of the marker *p* is for the sake of the accent."
> [[3.1.4]] This is so that the lack of udātta (anudāttatva) may occur.
In the rule *ṛdorap*, the vowel *ṛ* should be followed by a *t* (i.e., *ṛt*).
This being the case, according to the principle "that which follows even *tād* is *tapara*," the vowel *u* would also be subsequent to it.

And because of the application of the *paribhāṣā* rule "tataśca" [Pāṇini 1.1.70], this [substitution] would occur only here—in *yavaḥ* and *stavaḥ*; however, it would not occur in *lavaḥ* and *pavaḥ*. But in the case of the letter *d*, by the rule "aṇ includes its homogeneous phonemes" (*aṇ savarṇān gṛhṇāti*)—as in the example "he takes from the earth" (*bhuvaḥ gṛhṇāti*)—it occurs even after a long vowel.
Therefore, this *u* includes its homogeneous phonemes.

And here the indicative mark (*liṅga*) is the rule at [Pāṇini 1.4.31]. If the letter *t* followed by *pa* were present, however, the suffix *ap* would not occur after the root *bhū*; consequently, the form "prabhavaḥ" as used in the rule would be untenable.

Since no other purpose for that letter *d* is possible—given that its purpose is merely for ease of pronunciation—he says, "the letter *d* is for the sake of ease of pronunciation. The term "vṛ" is a general inclusion of both the roots *vṛṅ* and *vṛñ*.
[The term] "dṛ" is likewise.

The root *dṛś* is used in the sense of "respect" (*ādare*) [Dhātupāṭha 1411]. Regarding the statement "it is an exception (*apavāda*) to the rule for *niścinvati*," this refers to what would otherwise have been obtained by the rule *er ac* [Pāṇini 3.3.56].

Now, for what purpose is the inclusion of *ni* [in the rule]? For even if *aci* were prescribed here, there would be no difference [from the previous rule], since that very same form results in both cases. To this he says: "The inclusion of *ni* is for the sake of the accent (*svarārtham*). This means it is for the sake of making it *anudātta*. But one might object: the suffix *ghan* being prescribed by [Pāṇini 3.3.40] after the root *ci* would not apply [if *ni* were not included], because it would also apply after *ni-cinoti*. Therefore, is it not appropriate to include *ni* in order to block that [application]? This is not so; for even after *ni-pūrva* *cinoti*, this *ghan* is desired by way of a prior counter-exception (*pūrvavipratiṣedha*).

But surely, even for the sake of accent, the mention of *niś* is not at all appropriate; for when the rule *tathāpi* (Pāṇini 6.2.139) applies, which prescribes the original accent (*prakṛtisvara*) of the second member, it is instead governed by the rules *antaḥ* (6.2.142) and *ādyudāttaḥ* (6.2.144), which result in the word being oxytone (*antodātta*). Likewise, even when the suffix is present, it ought to be unaccented (*anudātta*)? This is not a fault; by the force of the mention of *niś*, the accent prescribed by the rule *tathāthādi* (6.2.144) does not apply in that context.

In the absence of that subsequent word (*uttarapada*), when [the suffix] remains in its original form (*prakṛtibhāva*) due to the low-pitched (*anudātta*) nature of *ap* and the final acute (*antodātta*) nature of the verbal root, the word *niścaya* becomes middle-acute (*madhyodātta*) by the accent of the whole word (*kṛtsvara*); however, if *ac* were present, it would be final-acute (*antodātta*). Regarding the rule "of *vaś* and *raṇ*" and so forth: *vaś* (DhP 1080) means "desire" (*kānti*), and *raṇ* (DhP 445) means "sound" (*śabda*). Verbs such as *aṇ*, *raṇ*, etc. (DhP 444–453) have sound as their meaning.
For those two roots, *vaś* and *raṇ*, an addition (*upasaṃkhyāna*)—that is, a formal statement (*pratipādana*)—must be made.

In this regard, the following is the demonstration: the letter *ca* (and) is used here for the purpose of including what has not been explicitly mentioned; by that, it will also apply to the roots *vaśi* and *raṇi*. Regarding the rule "the suffix *ka* [is applied] in the sense of *ghañ*" and so forth:

the meaning of *ghañ* is "state" (*bhāva*) and also the "object" (*karman*) excluding the "agent" (*kartṛ*); in those cases, the application of the suffix *ka* must be prescribed for the sake of words like *sthā*.
However, this is already established by the rule itself [Pāṇini 3.3.113].

The term *pā* refers to the root meaning "to drink," not the root meaning "to protect," according to the paribhāṣā rule regarding the elision of suffixes (*vyā|pa|50*). In the word *prasthaḥ*, the vowel *ā* is elided by [Pāṇini 6.4.64].
Regarding "praśnaḥ":
[it is derived from] the root *ṣṇā* in the sense of "cleansing" (*dhātupāṭha* 1052).
Regarding "āvidhaḥ": [it is derived from the root *vyadh*].
The root *vyadh* means "to strike" (*tāḍane*; Dhātupāṭha 1181).
By the rule *grahijyā-* (Pāṇini 6.1.16) and others, there is vocalization (*samprasāraṇa*).
Thus, [the word] *vighnaḥ*.
The elision of the penultimate vowel (*upadhālopa*) occurs by [Pāṇini 6.4.98] *gamahana* etc., and the substitution of *k* for *h* (*kutva*) occurs by [Pāṇini 7.3.54] *ho hanteḥ* etc.
Regarding the word "weapon" (*āyudham*): the root *yudh* means "to fight" (Dhātupāṭha 1173). [The rule states: "The suffix *ap* is added after the root *ad*."
This is an exception to *ghan*.
From this point onward, even in subsequent cases, it should be understood that the suffix *ac* prescribed after bases ending in consonants is an exception to *ghan*,
as in the examples "vighasaḥ" and "praghasaḥ."

By [Pāṇini 2.4.38], there is the substitution of *ghasl*. Now, for what purpose is *ad* prescribed here, rather than prescribing it from the root *ghas* itself as a separate base? What advantage would there be in doing so? Would it not mean that the transformation of *ad* into *ghas* need not be performed? True, this is so; nevertheless, *ad* is prescribed here for the sake of subsequent rules—so that in the rule "after *na*, there is *ṇa*" [3.3.60], it may apply to *ad*, but not to *ghas*. Regarding the statement, "The mention of *vīṇā* is for the sake of [the verb] with a prefix": if, even in the domain of the lute (*vīṇā*), the [suffix] were to occur only after a prefix, then the mention of *vīṇā* would be redundant.
Because the suffix is prescribed generally for words that do not have a prefix, it is established even in the case of *vīṇā*. Regarding "parimitaḥ":

it means measured, limited, or delimited. A handful (*muṣṭi*) consisting of two, three, or four substances such as radishes, which is tied together for the sake of common usage, is designated by such terms as *mūlakapaṇaḥ* (a handful of radishes). Regarding "vidyāmadaḥ" (the intoxication of learning):
"Intoxication by knowledge" (*vidyayā madaḥ*). The compound is formed by [Pāṇini 2.1.31] *kartṛkaraṇe* and so forth. "Madness" (*unmādaḥ*).

Even here, although the inclusion of *mad* should have been made precisely at [Pāṇini 3.3.61]—following [Pāṇini 2.2.18]—the formulation of the rule as *mado 'nupasarge* (Pāṇini 3.3.67) is for the purpose of indicating that this grammatical operation is not universally obligatory (*anitya*). By means of this, the form *māda* is established. Now, one might object: since *madaḥ* [from Pāṇini 3.3.67] is understood as a governing word (*anuvartate*), it should be stated there that [the suffix applies] after *pra* and *sam*; even so, the desired form would certainly be established. Why, then, is it treated as an irregular formation (*nipātana*)? To this he says: *prasaṃbhyām*, etc.

In this context, since no other [meaning] than *pramada* (excessive joy) and *saṃmada* (intense delight) is heard through the word *rūḍhi* (conventional usage), and since these two are indeed conventional words, it is understood that they alone are intended.
Furthermore, a restrictive sense (*avadhāraṇa*) is to be seen here, because all sentences possess an inherent restrictive nature.
Therefore, the irregular formation (*nipātana*) is for the sake of the conventional meaning.
This meaning results precisely in the sense of the words *pramada* and *sammada*.

By means of this sūtra, the technical derivation (*vyutpatti*) of these two specific conventional terms (*rūḍhi-śabda*)—namely *pramadau* and *sammadau*—is established so that it does not apply to other words; such is the purpose of the irregular formation (*nipātana*).
For if, following the inclusion of the root *mad*, one were to state merely "after *pra* and *sam*," then even when the root *mad* follows both *pra* and *sam* combined, the suffix would still occur.
Likewise, when *pra* and *sam* occur after another prefix, or when *mad* occurs after *pra* and *sam*, [the rule] would still apply.
Consequently, the sūtra would have to account for conventional words (*rūḍhiśabda*) such as *prasaṃmadaḥ*, *abhiprasaṃmadaḥ*, and *pratisaṃmadaḥ*, and not merely for *pramadaḥ* and *sammadaḥ*.
However, since the term is specifically prescribed (*nipātana*), a restriction is understood: these two [prefixes] must occur individually—neither joined together nor accompanied by any other prefix.

By this, the sūtra becomes established in its conventional meaning: "The suffix *ap* is indeed established after the root *grah*"—by the rule beginning with *grahavṛdṛ* [Pāṇini 3.3.58]. If this is so, for what purpose is there a formal nipātana (irregular derivation)? He says: "For the sake of the substitution of *l*," and so forth. "Nihavaḥ" (calling).
The root *hveñ* (meaning "in competition" and "in sound"—*dhātupāṭha* 1008) is used here in the sense of "competition.
When the semivowel-vocalization (*samprasāraṇa*) has been performed, the rules for *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* substitutions apply.

Since the four forms beginning with *nihavaḥ* are already established for the root *hu* when preceded by prefixes such as *ni*, this specific rule is intended to exclude the suffix *ghañ* from the root *hvayati* when preceded by *ni* and other such prefixes. Thus, the form is *āhvāyaḥ*.

The suffix *yuk* is applied by [Pāṇini 7.3.33]. The word *nipāna* is derived from the sense "they drink therein," using the suffix *lyuṭ* in the locative sense according to [Pāṇini 3.3.117]. To the question of why the word *āhāva* refers to a reservoir for water, he says: "For in that case," and so forth.
By this, he demonstrates the basis for the application (*pravṛttinimitta*) of the word *āhāva* to a reservoir for water. Regarding the phrase "the mention of the state (*bhāva*)," and so forth:

But surely, just as in the rule *yathā* (Pāṇini 3.3.43), although two [categories] are under discussion, the suffix will be understood to denote only the action (*bhāva*) by virtue of observing the linguistic usage (*lakṣyadarśana*), so too here [in our case]. Why, then, is there the mention of "action" (*bhāva*) for the purpose of excluding the rule *akartari ca kārake* (Pāṇini 3.3.19)? This is true; however, even though this meaning is already established solely through the power of observing the linguistic usage, it is explicitly stated by the mention of "action" for the benefit of those of dull intellect.

Now, just as in the rule *atha yathā* (P. 3.3.44), where the term *bhāve* is already in force, the repeated mention of *bhāva* is understood to be for the purpose of excluding the *vāsarūpa* principle, why is it not understood in the same way here as well? Because of the observation of actual usage (*lakṣyadarśana*).
For we actually see forms such as *hūtam*, *hvānam*, and *hūtiḥ* [ending in *kta* and others].
In the case of *ghañ* and so on, the action (*bhāva*) occurs by the *vāsarūpa* principle. And "that [suffix] is udātta at the end."
Because the word *vadha* is pronounced with an acute accent on the final syllable in the Sūtra;
by the rule beginning with "there" (*tatra*), he demonstrates how that which is desired is established when the substitute *vadha* has the acute accent on its final syllable:
even when the elision of *a* occurs by Pāṇini 6.4.48, the acute accent of the *ap* [suffix] remains by Pāṇini 6.1.161.

Regarding the word *dhātaḥ*: the suffix *ghañ* is applied to the root *han* in the sense of the object (*karman*) and other *kārakas*; the substitution of *t* for *h* occurs by the rule *hanasta’ṭiṇṇaloḥ* [Pāṇini 7.3.32]; and the substitution of *k* (or *g*) for *h* occurs by the rule *ho hanteḥ* [Pāṇini 7.3.54] and others. As for the phrase "the letter *c* is out of its proper sequence," and so forth: *dhātaḥ* | *karmādau kārake ghañ*, *hanasto’ṭiṇṇaloḥ* [7.3.32] iti tatvam; *ho hanteḥ* [7.3.54] ityādinā kutvam | *cakāro bhinnakramatvāt* ityādi |
The connection is that the particle *ca* is not connected with the substitute (*ādeśa*). Why is it not connected? Because its position is different.

If the sequence of this *ca* were "of *han*, *vadha* and [the suffix]," then it would not be uttered immediately after the substitute; therefore, because its position is different—that is, due to the difference in sequence—it is not connected with the substitute, but rather with the affix under discussion (*prakṛta*). And so, in order to show the connection with what is under discussion, he says: "And *ap*," and so forth.

The suffix *ap* occurs, and due to the recurrence of the word "ca" (and), that which is otherwise applicable also occurs; by this, the suffix *ghañ* also occurs. In the example "abhravānaḥ," this is a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhī-samāsa*).

The meaning is "the hardness of the cloud. If the word *ghana* were derived [only] when the referent is a physical form—as in "thick curd" (*ghanaṃ dadhi*)—then it would fail to denote curd that possesses physical form; for how could a word derived in reference to one thing apply to something else? To this he says: "By means of a word denoting a property (*dharma*), the substratum (*dharmī*) is expressed.
This is a metaphorical identification (*abhedopacāra*) based on the elision of the possessive suffix *matup*, as in the expression "a white cloth" (*śuklaḥ paṭaḥ*).

By the word "white" (śukla), the meaning is "a cloth possessing the quality of whiteness. Regarding the term "antarghana": it is derived from the root *han* with the suffix *ap* in the locative sense (*adhikaraṇe*), meaning "that in which living beings are killed.
Regarding the phrase "even for you, it must certainly be grasped": [this refers to the necessity of accepting the aforementioned point].
And because the teacher has instructed the students in both ways. Regarding the term "atyādhāna": the word *ati* denotes the sense of "above," while the root *ā-dhā* means "to place."
That upon which something is placed or set is its *ādhāna* (receptacle); the suffix *lyuṭ* is used here in the sense of the locus (*adhikaraṇa*). Thus, [the word] is *udghanaḥ*.

In the word *apaghana*, the suffix *ap* is used in the sense of the locus (*adhikaraṇa*) because it is "shaken off" (*uddhanyate*) therein; in the word *apaghana*, the suffix *ap* is used in the sense of the instrument (*karaṇa*) because one is struck by it (*apahanyate*). Regarding the phrase "and there," it refers even to what was mentioned immediately prior.

Regarding "ghanādeśaḥ": this is due to the recurrence (anuvṛtti) of the term "ghana" from the rule "mūrttau ghanaḥ" [Pāṇini 3.3.77]. Regarding "stambaghnaḥ": [this is formed by the addition of the suffix -ka].

As before, there is the substitution of *ku* for *kva* and the elision of the penultimate vowel (*upadhā-lopa*). Regarding "vali-ghaḥ," there is optionally (*vibhāṣā*) the substitution of *la* [for *va*] according to Pāṇini 8.2.22. Regarding "āśraya-śabdaḥ" and so forth:
*āśrayaṇam* (the act of taking refuge) is *āśrayaḥ*; it means service (*sevā*).

And since that [action] occurs where there is proximity (*pratyāsatti*), the substratum (*āśraya*) is accompanied by proximity. Therefore, the word *āśraya* indicates proximity (*sāmīpya*), because its meaning is associated with proximity. For example, in the expression "the mountain-slope" (*parvatopaghnaḥ*), an object situated near a mountain is expressed. Likewise, in the rule "the suffixes *saṅgha* and *udgha*" (*saṅghodghau*).
*Saṃhananam* means the *saṅgha*.
*Udghaḥ* is that which is struck (*hanyate*) or known (*jñāyate*) as preeminent (*utkaṭam*); the suffix *ap* is applied in the sense of the object (*karman*).
How, then, does the root *han* function in the sense of "knowing"? Because it has the meaning of "going" (*gati*).
This is because all roots whose meaning is "going" have the meaning of "knowing. The word *ni-mita* means "measured on all sides" (*samantānmita*).
The meaning is that it is equal in height and in circumference from every side.
In order to demonstrate this single meaning by means of a more well-known expression, he says: "That which possesses height and circumference is so described.
Height (*āroha*) means elevation;
circumference (*pariṇāha*) means breadth.
Regarding the phrase "nighā vṛkṣāḥ":
they are called *nighāḥ* because they are struck down (*hanyante*) or known (*jñāyante*) without distinction.
Even in the sense of the object (*karman*), the meaning is that they are entirely equal.

In this way, they are known to be without distinction if they are equal on all sides both in height and in circumference. Regarding the word *uptrimam*: there is vocalization (*samprasāraṇa*) by the rule "vacisvapi... [Pāṇini 6.1.15] and so forth;
the letter *k* in the suffix *ktri* is for the purpose of prohibiting *guṇa*. Regarding the word *vepathuḥ*: [it is derived from the root *vyp* with the suffix *athuc*].
*Vepanam* is *vepathuḥ*.
Since both of these occur in the sense of an action (*bhāva*) by their very nature, this [suffix] is understood as an exception (*apavāda*) to the suffix *ghañ*.
Furthermore, the suffix *ghañ* does not apply even by the rule of optional forms (*vāsarūpavidhi*), because such a form is not attested (*anabhidhānāt*).

Furthermore, the letter *ca* in *athuc* has the sense of "and" (*svarātha*). [The following roots are included]: *yaja* (to worship the gods, etc., DhP 1002), *ṭuyāc* (to beg, DhP 863), *yata* (to strive, DhP 30), *viccha* (to go, DhP 1423), *praccha* (to desire to know, DhP 1413), and *rakṣa* (to protect, DhP 658). Here, because it is inherent [in the rule], *yāc* and the others [are understood].

Since those [roots] ending in *naṅ* function in the masculine, *naṅ* does not serve as an exception (*apavāda*) to *ghañ*. Furthermore, according to observed usage, by the rule of optional forms (*vāsarūpa-vidhāna*), *ghañ* also occurs—as in *yāga*. However, because a root ending in *naṅ* such as *yāc* functions in the feminine by its very nature, *naṅ* serves as an exception to the suffix *a* (the long *ā*) that would otherwise be obtained by Pāṇini 3.3.103.
Because of the statement [Pāṇini 3.3.113], the rule regarding dissimilar forms (*vāsarūpavidhi*) does not apply.

The letter *ṅ* is for the purpose of prohibiting *guṇa*; that is, it is so that the *guṇa* substitution of the light penultimate vowel (*laghūpadhaguṇa*) does not occur in the case of the root *vicch*.

But surely, because it is antaranga (internal), the *tuk* augment must first apply by the rule *che ca* [Pāṇini 6.1.71]; in that case, since the root does not have a light penultimate vowel (*alaghūpadha*), the *guṇa* substitution will not occur anyway. Therefore, why should the letter *ṅ* be added to the suffix *naṅ* for the purpose of prohibiting that *guṇa*?
The very fact that *ṅ* is attached to *naṅ* is the indicator (*jñāpaka*) of the principle: "The teaching regarding augments is not eternal" (*anityam āgamaśāsanam*).

If, then, because it is non-eternal (*anityatva*), [the rule] *tutunapupluñcaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.4.19) prescribes the substitution of *ś* for the letter *ch* when accompanied by *t*, how could that substitution not apply to the solitary [letter *ch*]? This is not a fault; for the expression *cchvoḥ* contains two instances of the letter *ch*.
Therein, one is accompanied by *t* (*satukka*), while the second is solitary (*kevala*). Therefore, the substitution of *ś* will indeed apply even to the solitary [letter *ch*].

If, however, the instruction were written with two *cch*s—as in "cchvoḥ"—then the dual number would not apply because there are many substituends. This is not a fault, for since this is a Vedic (sūtra-style) formulation, the dual number will occur by way of a substitution for the plural. Furthermore, the instruction must necessarily be written with two *cch*s; otherwise, in the rule [Pāṇini 6.4.21], there would be no elision of the single [element], because a single *cch* is not the original form (*aprakṛtatvāt*). The explicit mention [of the dual] would then serve only for the purpose of eliding the *v*.
In "yajñaḥ" and "yācñā," the letter *n* becomes *ñ* by [Pāṇini 8.4.40], which prescribes the substitution of *ścutva*.
In "yatnaḥ," [the same applies].
> [[7.2.8]] Thus is the prohibition of *iṭ*. In the examples "viśnaḥ" and "praśnaḥ," the substitution of *ś* for *ch* occurs by the rule beginning with "cchvoḥ" [[6.4.19]].

In the word *rakṣṇaḥ*, the substitution of *ṇ* for *n* occurs by [Pāṇini 8.4.41]. Now, one might ask: why does the vocalization (*samprasāraṇa*) of the vowel in *praśnaḥ*—by means of the rule concerning *grahijyā* and so forth ([Pāṇini 6.1.16])—not occur here? To this, he says: "of *pracch*" and so on.
"What is the indicator? To this he says: "And in the case of a question," and so forth. "The *kip* suffix occurs"—this is an exception (*apavāda*) to the *ghan* suffix.
"The purpose of making it *kit* is for the sake of elision."

> [The rule] "6.4.64" is intended so that there may be the elision of the vowel *ā*. Because the locative case is specified separately for the object (*karman*) and the locus (*adhikaraṇa*), neither of them functions as an *upapada* (governing word), nor do they constitute the meaning of the suffix. Therefore, one of them is the *upapada* and the other is the meaning of the suffix:
the object is the *upapada*, and the locus is the meaning of the suffix.
He states—beginning with "when the object is the *upapada*"—that this distinction is understood from the commentary and from observation of the linguistic examples (*lakṣya*).

Now, what is the purpose of including the mention of *adhikaraṇa* (locus), since the suffix would be obtained in the sense of locus simply by the continued application (*anuvṛtti*) of the rule "and when [the action] is not the agent, but another *kāraka*" [Pāṇini 3.3.19]? To this he says: "The mention of *adhikaraṇa*," and so forth. If the mention of *adhikaraṇa* were absent, the suffix under discussion would apply even in other senses—such as the abstract state (*bhāva*), or toward other *kārakas* such as the instrument (*karaṇa*)—therefore, the mention of *adhikaraṇa* is for the purpose of excluding those. Regarding the phrase "in the sense of *bhāva* etc.": by the word "etc. (*ādi*), the inclusion of the non-agent *kāraka* is intended.

"Ghañ, ac, and ap are exceptions" means that for those [roots] ending in *i*, *ac* is the exception; for those ending in *ṛ* and those ending in *u*, *ap* is the exception; and for the remaining ones, *ghañ* is the exception. "It should be stated" means it should be explained.
The explanation, however, should be made by relying on [Pāṇini 3.3.113]:
*vyākhyānaṃ tu*. [The examples are] "attainment" (*āptiḥ*), and so forth.

[The roots are: *āplṛ* in the sense of pervading (Dhātupāṭha 1260); *rādha* and *sādha* in the sense of accomplishment (Dhātupāṭha 1262); *dīpī* in the sense of shining (Dhātupāṭha 1150); *ruānsu* and *dhvansu* in the sense of falling (Dhātupāṭha 754, 755); and *ḍulabhaṣ* in the sense of obtaining (Dhātupāṭha 975).

Because the root *labh* has the marker *ṣ*, when the suffix *aṅ* would otherwise apply by the rule *ṣidbhidādibhyo 'ṅ* [Pāṇini 3.3.104], the suffix *ktin* is prescribed instead by the rule *śeṣebhyas tu gurutvāt* [Pāṇini 3.3.103] to form the word *iṣṭiḥ*. In this case, there is vocalization (*samprasāraṇa*) according to the rule for the *vac*-group [Pāṇini 6.1.15]. Similarly, one forms *kīrṇiḥ*, *gīrṇiḥ*, and *śīrṇiḥ*.
The substitution of *i* for the vowel [of the root] occurs by the rule *ṛt-id-dhātoḥ* [Pāṇini 7.1.100], and the substitution of *ṇ* [for *n*] occurs by the rule beginning with *raṣābhyām* [8.4.1].
