Just as the substitution of *ṇ* for the *t* of the suffix *niṣṭhā* (past passive participle) occurs in forms such as *kīrṇaḥ* by the rule *radābhyām* [8.2.42] and others, so too does it occur here for the suffix *ktin*.

Just as the substitution of *ṇ* for the *t* of the suffix *niṣṭhā* occurs in *lūnaḥ* by the rule *radābhyām* [8.2.42], so too does it occur for the suffix *ktin* in forms such as *lūniḥ* and *yūniḥ*. [The phrase] "it subverts that which is an exception to the *aṅ* [augment]" means:
The meaning is that this [suffix] is an exception (*apavāda*) that subverts the suffix *aṅ* which would otherwise be obtained by the rule *sthādibhyaḥ* [Pāṇini 3.3.106].
As for the example "paktiḥ," it is an exception to the rule *ṣidbhidādibhyo'ṅ* [Pāṇini 3.3.104].
Regarding "prasthitiḥ":
the substitution of *i* for the root vowel occurs by [Pāṇini 7.4.40] *dyatisyati* etc.
Regarding "saṅgītiḥ": [the same rule applies].

The substitution of *ī* occurs by the rule *dhumāsthāgāpājahātisām hali* (Pāṇini 6.4.66). And here, according to the principle *gāmādāgrahaṇeṣv aviśeṣaḥ* (Vyāḍiparibhāṣā 124), there is the inclusion of both *gai* (to sing, Dhātupāṭha 917) and *gāṅ* (to go, Dhātupāṭha 950).
[The root] *pā* [is also included].
As before, the term "bhāva" (action/state) is understood in the sense of the verbal root's meaning (*pāna*), not in the sense of preservation (*rakṣaṇa*).
Regarding the phrase "the mention of *bhāva*," and so forth:
"another meaning" refers to a kāraka other than the agent (*kartṛ*); the mention of *bhāva* is for the purpose of excluding that. Regarding the question "How [is this]? and so forth...

If this *ktin* suffix is an exception (*apavāda*) to an exception (*apavāda*) of the *aṅ* [suffix], then how is the form *avasthā saṃsthā* established? The intention is that it cannot be established in any way. [The author replies: "In the sense of *vyavasthā*" and so forth.

This very mention of the word *vyavasthā* ending in *aṅ* in the Sūtra is itself the indicator (*jñāpaka*); therefore, there is no absolute supersession (*atyantabādha*) by *ktin*, and thus forms such as *avasthā* are also established.

Regarding the term *atyantāya*: this is an indeclinable (*nipāta*) that resembles the four case-endings, just like *cirāya*. [The following are the verbal roots: *vṛṣu* and *mṛṣu* in the sense of sprinkling (*secane*; DhP 706, 707); *iṣu* in the sense of desiring (*icchāyām*; DhP 1351); *ḍupacaṣ* in the sense of cooking (*pāke*; DhP 996); *mana* in the sense of knowing (*jñāne*; DhP 1176); *vida* in the sense of knowing (*jñāne*; DhP 1064); *bhū* in the sense of existence (*sattāyām*; DhP 1); *vī* in the sense of motion, pervasion, procreation, etc. (*gativyāptiprajanādiṣu*; DhP 1048); and *rā* in the sense of taking (*ādāne*; DhP 1057).
Regarding the phrase "of the base and the suffix":
the dual number is used because there is an intention to express the general category of bases; otherwise, since bases are many, the plural would have been required.
"The connection is through the transformation of the case ending."
The first case ending [nominative] applied to words such as *vṛṣan* is, by implication, transformed into the fifth case (ablative);
through this, the relationship between the base and the suffix is established, for otherwise the relationship would be untenable.
Thus: "the notion" (*matiḥ*).

The elision of the nasal [of the root *pac*] occurs by the rule beginning with *anudāttopadeśa* (Pāṇini 6.4.37). Regarding the phrase "in all cases" (*sarvatra*) and so forth: the suffix *kin* is prescribed after roots such as *vṛṣ* both in mantras and in non-mantric contexts;
the same applies to the root *pac* by virtue of the rule *sthāgādisūtra* (Pāṇini 3.3.95).
If this is so, for what purpose is this stated? He says: "for the sake of the udātta accent.
Regarding the rule *iṣeḥ stutau* and so forth:

he will state that there is a nipātana (irregular formation) of the root *iṣ* as *icchā*; therefore, the suffix *ktin* is prescribed here, otherwise [the form] would have occurred only by way of that nipātana.

The suffix *ktin* alone should be prescribed after [roots] beginning with *vṛṣ*. The mention of the acute accent (*udātta*) is for the sake of subsequent rules, so that the *kyap* [suffix] prescribed by "the suffix *kyap* occurs after *vraj* and *yaj* in the sense of abstract action" (Pāṇini 3.3.98) may be acute. Thus, it is said: "The statement is for the sake of the accent."
But it is not for the sake of the meaning of the suffix,
because [the desired form] is already established by [Pāṇini 3.3.94]. Nor is it for the sake of the augment *ūṭ*, because that too is already established by [Pāṇini 6.4.20], namely *jvaratvara* etc.
Regarding "yauteḥ":
this refers to the root *yu* (meaning "to mix" or "to separate," according to the Dhātupāṭha 1033).
And regarding "javateśca": [this refers to the root *ju*].
From the verbal root *ju* mentioned in the sūtra [Pāṇini 3.2.150],
there is "lengthening" (*dīrghatvam*); by the word "and" (*ca*), there is also "acute accent" (*udāttatvam*).
The suffix *ktin* is established by the general rule alone;
[the word] "is dissolved" (*lyate*) refers to the root *ṣo* in the sense of "ending" (*antakarmaṇi*), as found in the Dhātupāṭha (1147).
"The absence of *it* is also prescribed as a *nipātana*.

This means that by the rule "for *dyati*, *syati*, etc. (Pāṇini 7.4.40), the augment *it* would apply; therefore, its absence is prescribed as a *nipātana*. Or else, [the form is derived] from the root *san*.

Regarding the root *ṣaṇu* in the sense of "giving" (Dhātupāṭha 1464), the suffix *sāti* is established by applying the rule *janasanakhanām* [Pāṇini 6.4.42], which effects the substitution of *ā*. This is the remainder of the explanation. If this is so, for what purpose is there a formal derivation (*nipātana*)? He says: "for the sake of the accent," and so forth.

For if there were no nipātana (irregular derivation), the word *sāti* would have its initial syllable accented acute (*ādyudātta*). The nipātana is for the purpose that it should instead have its final syllable accented acute (*antodātta*). [This is stated] by the rule: "From the root *han*, or from *hi* or *nī*."

Regarding the term *heti*: when it is derived from the root *han* (to strike), then the substitution of *e* for the letter *h* is prescribed as a *nipātana* (irregular formation); the elision of the nasal (*anunāsika*), however, is already established by the rule *anudāttopadeśa...* [Pāṇini 6.4.37] and so forth.
But when it is derived from the root *hi* (meaning "to go" and "to understand," Dhātupāṭha 157), then *guṇa* (vocalization) is prescribed as the *nipātana*.
Thus: *kīrttiḥ*.

From the root *kṛt* (Dhātupāṭha 1653), which belongs to the curādigaṇa and takes the causative suffix *ṇic*, the suffix *yuc* would normally apply according to [Pāṇini 3.3.107]. However, *ktin* is prescribed here as an irregular formation (*nipātana*).

By [Pāṇini 7.1.101], the substitution of *i* for the radical vowel occurs, and by [Pāṇini 8.2.77], the lengthening of the vowel takes place before a consonant (*hal*), resulting in *ijyā*. In this term, the semivowel is replaced by its corresponding vowel (*samprasāraṇa*) according to the rule on the *vacyādi* group [Pāṇini 6.1.15].

If an acute accent (*udātta*) is prescribed, he asks: "What is the purpose of the marker *pit*? and replies: "The marker *pit* is for the sake of what follows," and so on. Regarding the statement "the term *bhāve* is not marked with a svarita accent," etc.:
the svarita quality is not applied to that very mention of *bhāva* which was made in the sūtra [Pāṇini 3.3.95] beginning with *sthā-gā-*.
The governing rule (*adhikāra*) is precisely this: *bhāve* [3.3.18–19].
Regarding the word *samajyā*:
the substitution of *vī* [for *sam*] does not occur by the rule *ajeḥ vy-ghañ-apoḥ* (Pāṇini 2.4.56), because of the statement that this applies "when it is a technical term" (*saṃjñāyām*).
For once the substitution of *vī* has been applied, the word is no longer understood as a technical term; indeed, a technical term must have a fixed sequence of phonemes.
Regarding the word *nipatyā*: it is that in which things fall (*nipatanti*). [The root] *ṣadlṛ* is used in the senses of "falling apart," "going," and "sinking" (Dhātupāṭha 854).
"Niṣīdantī tasyām" means "sitting upon it. "Nipatyā" means "falling upon it," for they fall upon it.
Regarding the word *matyā*:
it is called *matyā* because they think (*man*) by means of it.
As in the previous case, there is the elision of the nasal (*anunāsika-lopa*), and the augment *tuk* is added after the short vowel.
By means of it they know;
in it they press the soma;
in it they lie down.
The substitution of *ayaṅ* [is applied] by the rule *ayaṅ yi kṅiti* [Pāṇini 7.4.22].

*Bharaṇam* is *bhṛtyā*. *Āyana* is derived from *eti tayā* [Pāṇini 3.1.112]. Regarding this, it was stated: "Because it is observed in the masculine as a technical name (*saṃjñā*), the form *bhāryā* is not established for you; since there is the suffix *ghañ* in the sense of abstract state (*bhāva*) when feminine, *bhāryā* is thus established. However, here it is stated that "the term *bhāva* is not intended to be emphasized" (Kāśikā on Pāṇini 3.3.98). Thinking that the previous and subsequent statements are contradictory, he asks: "How? and so forth.

If the term *bhāve* [from Pāṇini 3.3.18] were not here intended as a governing heading (*svarita*), how could it be said that "there is a governing heading for *bhāva* in the feminine"? For if *bhāve* were not intended as a governing heading, the existence of a governing heading for *bhāva* here would not be logical. The resolution is provided by the statement: "The governing heading for *bhāva* is the operation of the agent to be produced" (*bhāvādhikāro bhāvyavyāpāraḥ*), and so forth. By the term "governing heading for *bhāva*" (*bhāvādhikāra*), the operation is intended there as the thing to be expressed. That operation, moreover, is characterized by the attainment of the state of being denoted by the word *bhṛtya*.

Therefore, this is what is meant: for the word *bhṛtyā*, derived by the rule "samaja-niṣada... and so forth, only its abstract state (*bhāva*) becomes the denoted meaning, and not a grammatical relation (*kāraka*) excluding the agent.

Consequently, the form *bhāryā* is established as referring to the object (*karman*) kāraka. However, this is not a scriptural restriction [imposed by the technical term *bhāva*], because that [restriction] would not apply here due to the absence of the *svarita* accent; thus, let there be no intention to denote the abstract state (*bhāva*) in that context.

Regarding [the forms] *samajyā* ("assembly") from the sense "they assemble therein," *niṣadyā* ("sitting") from "they sit therein," and *vidyā* ("knowledge") from "one knows by means of this"—it is not the case that these are incorrect due to the [restriction of the suffix] *kyap* to the instrumental and other [kārakas]. How, then, while the rule "after roots meaning 'to go' and those ending in long *ī*, when used in the sense of the abstract action (*bhāva*) or a non-agent (*akartṛ*) kāraka" (Pāṇini 3.3.18–19) is being followed in all instances, is this restriction obtained—that in some cases the abstract action (*bhāva*) becomes the expressed meaning of the *kyap*-derived form, while in others it is specifically a non-agent kāraka? It is obtained through the force of technical designation (*saṃjñā*).

Where a designation (*saṃjñā*) is understood through an affix (*pratyaya*) that arises [denoting] an action (*bhāva*), there the action alone attains the status of being the expressed meaning (*abhidheyatva*), while the other [the agent] remains indifferent (*audāsīnya*). But where a designation is understood through an affix that has arisen [denoting] a factor other than the agent (*akartṛ-kāraka*), there that [factor] attains the status of being the expressed meaning, while the action assumes indifference.

Thus, while the term "designation" (*saṃjñā*) is already being carried over [from a previous rule], its mention again here is for the sake of the action; for the previous mention of "designation" was connected with a factor other than the agent.
Consequently, [if the term were not repeated], the designation would apply only to a *kāraka* (participant in an action) excluding the agent (*kartṛ*), and not to the abstract state (*bhāva*).
Therefore, the term "designation" (*saṃjñā*) is mentioned again for the purpose that the designation may indeed apply even to the abstract state (*bhāva*).
Now, how is it that *bhṛtiḥ*, *matiḥ*, and *āsutīḥ* are formed? It is by virtue of irregular derivation (*nipātana*).

What, then, is the purpose of the rule for optional application (*nipātana*)? It is as follows: [Pāṇini 3.2.22, 3.2.188, and 5.2.112]. "A split in the yoga (*yogavibhāga*) must be made here," it is said. Thus, from the rule *kṛñaḥ kyap*, the form *kārya* is established; then, by the rule *śa ca*, the forms *kriyā* and *kṛti* are produced according to what is obtained. Consequently, three forms are established. Among these, by the rule *kṛñaḥ*, the form *kṛtya* is established, and by the rule *śa ca*, the two forms *kriyā* and *kṛti* are formed.
When the word [√iṣ] denotes an abstract state (*bhāva*), then by Pāṇini 7.4.28, the substitute *riṅ* is applied.

However, when it denotes a factor other than the agent (*akartari kārake*), then because there is no *ya*-affix, the suffix *śa* alone follows the verbal root; once the substitute *riṅ* has been applied, *iyaṅ* is substituted for it by Pāṇini 6.4.77 (*aci śnudhātu...*).

The letter *ś* serves the purpose of indicating that the following is a *sārvadhātuka* affix. By the very nature of its expressive power, the suffix *śap* occurs in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāva*), not in the sense of a factor (*kāraka*).

Regarding the phrase "and the absence of *ya*": by rule Pāṇini 3.1.67, the suffix *yak* would [otherwise] apply; therefore, its absence is prescribed as a nipātana (irregularity). [The word] "desire" (*icchā*).

The substitution of *ch* [for *ś*] occurs by the rule *iṣugami* [Pāṇini 7.3.77]. Regarding the examples beginning with *paricaryā*: the roots *cara* (meaning "to move," Dhātupāṭha 559), *sṛ* (meaning "to move," Dhātupāṭha 965), and *mṛga* (meaning "to seek," Dhātupāṭha 1900)—the latter being vowel-ending in the *curādi* class—as well as *aṭa* and *paṭa* (both meaning "to move," Dhātupāṭha 295, 296), take the suffix *śa* in the sense of an abstract action (*bhāva*). As before, there is the replacement of *ya* [for the root-final consonant], and for *sṛ*, there is *guṇa*. For *mṛgayati*, there is no elision of the vowel *a*; rather, there is the elision of the *ṇi* suffix by the rule *ṇeraniṭi* [Pāṇini 6.4.51].
Regarding "aṭāṭā": [this is derived] from the root *aṭ* with reduplication and the substitution of *tva* for the reduplicated syllable. Regarding "or the vowel *a* of *jāgarti*":
when the suffix *śa* is applied, there is *guṇa* substitution according to Pāṇini 3.1.67 and 7.3.85.

Regarding the term *jāgarā*: since there is the governing rule "after a verbal root" (*dhātoḥ* [Pāṇini 3.1.91]), it is understood that the mention of a "suffix" (*pratyaya*) serves as a qualifier for the verbal root; thus he says, "after verbal roots ending in suffixes. As for *cikīrṣā*:
the feminine suffix *ap* is added to the word *cikīrṣa*, which itself ends in the desiderative suffix *san*.
In the word *putrīyā*, there is the substitution of *i* [for the final vowel] by [Pāṇini 3.1.8] and [7.4.33]. In the word *putrakāmyā*, [the same applies].
The suffix *kāmyac* [is applied] as in *iti kāmyac*. Regarding *lolūyā*:

the suffix *yaṅ* is applied by [Pāṇini 3.1.22], "After a root that has a single vowel and begins with a consonant. Since the governing rule [Pāṇini 3.1.91], "after a root," is in force, it is understood that the mention of "heavy" (*guru*) and the mention of "consonant" (*hal*) serve as qualifiers for that very [root]. Thus he says: "A root which is heavy and ends in a consonant," and so forth.

But how, when it is said "of the guru," is a root (*dhātu*) possessing a *guru* [vowel] understood? By implication (*sāmarthyāt*). For no *guru* designation has been prescribed for any root ending in a consonant (*hal*), yet this term "of the guru" is stated; therefore, it is understood that by implication, the root possessing the *guru* [vowel] is expressed by the word "guru" through the metaphorical identification (*abhedopacāra*) of the designation with the designated.

Indeed, even without the possessive suffix *-mat*, the expression of both the quality and the possessor of the quality is accepted through metaphorical identification—as in the case of "the white cloth."

Now, why is the reversal not understood for the purpose that [the suffix] should apply only to roots beginning with *rudh* and not to roots such as *kuḍ*, namely: "a root which ends in a heavy vowel (*guru*) and consists of a single consonant (*hal*)"? Because of an indicator (*jñāpaka*): since this [author] provides the mention of the word *ceṣṭā* without a suffix in the rule "the second and fourth cases are used after a verb meaning 'to go' when there is movement, provided it is not a path" (Pāṇini 2.3.12), and also the mention of the word *śaṅkā* from the root *śaki* (meaning 'doubt') in the Dhātupāṭha (86), it is known from this that there is no reversal here.
For in the opposite case, there is neither "effort" (*ceṣṭā*) according to the teacher, nor even "doubt" (*śaṅkā*).

[The forms] beginning with *kuṇḍā* are the forms of these roots: *kuḍi* in the sense of "burning" (Dhātupāṭha 270), *huḍi* in the sense of "aggregation" (Dhātupāṭha 269), *īha* in the sense of "effort" (Dhātupāṭha 632), and *ūha* in the sense of "reflection" (Dhātupāṭha 648). [The phrase] beginning with "among those recited in the *gaṇas*" and so forth.

The roots *bhī* and others are listed in the [dhātu-]gaṇa as ending in the suffix *aṅ*. If, moreover, *aṅ* were prescribed here for those [roots] while it were prescribed for nominal stems (*prātipadika*), that would be improper, because the context is that of verbal roots (*dhātu*). Therefore, having extracted and separated those bases which constitute their constituent parts, they are indicated by the mention of "the *bhī*-class and others" in the rule *ṣid-bhidādibhyo 'ṅ*.

Furthermore, these [roots] are: *bhid* in the sense of "splitting" (Dhātupāṭha 1439); *chid* in the sense of "dividing into two" (Dhātupāṭha 1440); *vid* in the sense of "knowing" (Dhātupāṭha 1064); *kṣip* in the sense of "impelling" (Dhātupāṭha 1285); *guh* in the sense of "concealing" (Dhātupāṭha 896); *ḍudhāñ* in the sense of "sustaining and nourishing" (Dhātupāṭha 1092); and *medhṛ* in the sense of "intelligence and injury" (Dhātupāṭha 1070) [or, according to another reading, "union"].

The verbal roots *hiṃs* and *saṃkliś* (Dhātupāṭha 868, 869); *ṛ* in the sense of "going" (Dhātupāṭha 1098); *hman* in the sense of "taking away" (Dhātupāṭha 899); *hukṛñ* in the sense of "making" (Dhātupāṭha 1472); *kṣi* in the sense of "destruction" (Dhātupāṭha 236), or alternatively *kṣi* in the sense of "dwelling and going" (Dhātupāṭha 1407); *tṛ* in the sense of "floating and crossing over" (Dhātupāṭha 969); *ghṛñ* in the sense of "holding" (900); *likha* in the sense of "arranging letters" (Dhātupāṭha 1365); *cuda*...

The following [roots] are to be understood: *samucchraya* (Dhātupāṭha 1592), meaning "to rise up"; *pīḍa* (Dhātupāṭha 1544), meaning "to press down" or "to enter deeply"; *ḍuvapa* (Dhātupāṭha 1003), meaning "to sow seeds" or "to continue a lineage," and also "to cut"; *vasa* (Dhātupāṭha 1942), meaning "to dwell"; *mṛjūṣ* (Dhātupāṭha 1066), meaning "to purify"; and *krapa* (Dhātupāṭha 771), meaning "compassion" and "going. These are to be known.

If, then, the primary forms (*prakṛti*) are being specified, the recitation of *bhid* and the others in the list (*gaṇa*) is purposeless. On the other hand, if they are recited, the rule for the suffix (*pratyaya-vidhāna*) is purposeless. The recitation in the list is not, however, purposeless, because it serves to include well-known forms. Its purpose is to ensure that their grammatical correctness (*sādhutva*) applies only where these groups such as *bhid* and the rest are already established in usage, and not elsewhere. Thus, what was stated in the Bhāṣya—“*bhidā* in the sense of splitting” (Gaṇasūtra 29)—and so forth, becomes logically justified.

Nor is the prescription of the suffix [with the augment *ṭi*] purposeless, for it serves to eliminate ambiguity. For if that were not present, there would be doubt: "Are the suffixes beginning with *ka*, and so forth, prescribed by another rule such as Pāṇini 3.1.135 (*kṛdādibhyaḥ kaḥ*)? Or is it only the suffix *aṅ*? In the former case, when the feminine gender is intended to be expressed, the suffix *ktin* would result. Why? Because the purpose [of the rule] is to eliminate ambiguity.

Therefore, the prescription of the suffix is not meaningless. Regarding the word *ārā*: [as in] *guhā giryyoṣadhyoḥ*. The word *guhā* is correct only when referring to a mountain (*giri*) or a medicinal herb (*oṣadhī*), and not elsewhere.

And here, the word *giri* refers to a single part [of the mountain], according to the principle: "Words that function for a whole also function for its parts" (*Vyākaraṇa-mahābhāṣya*, Pāda 1, Sūtra 85).
By "cave" (*guhā*), a certain specific part of the mountain is meant; "cave" (*guhā*) is also the name of a medicinal herb.
In other cases, the suffix *ktin* occurs after the root *guh*, as in *gūḍhiḥ*. [The rules applied are:
*ho ḍhaḥ* [Pāṇini 8.2.31], *jhaṣastathordho'dhaḥ* [8.2.40], *ṣṭunā ṣṭuḥ* [8.4.41], and *ḍhralope pūrvasya dīrgho'ṇaḥ* [6.3.111]. Examples include *hārā*, *kārā*, and *dhārā*.
When the *guṇa* substitution has been applied, lengthening is prescribed [by way of *nipātana*], as in "lekhā" and "rekhā. Here,
the *guṇa* of the root *likh-* is prescribed by way of *nipātana*.
In this alternative view, there is a substitution of the letter *ra* for the suffix *lakāra*.
Regarding the form *cūḍā*:
the root *cud* undergoes the substitution of *ḍa*, and the penultimate vowel is lengthened; these are established as irregularities (*nipātana*).

Regarding "ārā śastryām": the word *ārā* is correct when it refers to a knife; here too, after the application of the *guṇa* vowel, lengthening is prescribed by way of irregular derivation (*nipātana*). Regarding "ārttir anyā": [it means] "suffering is something else."

By the rule *arterāṅpūrvasya ktin* (Pāṇini 6.1.91), there is a single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) [of *ar* for *āṅ-ar*], and the substitution of *r* follows (*raparatvam*). Thus: "a stream on a precipice" (*dhārā prapāte*).
"Where there is a pouring forth, there one holds [it]," as in *jaladhārā* ("stream of water") and *kṣīradhārā* ("stream of milk"). Regarding the phrase "belonging to the *cur*-class":

this is connected individually with each [root] beginning with *citi smṛtyām* (Dhātupāṭha 1535). Regarding the phrase "when *yuc* would have been applicable": [this refers to the application of the suffix *yuc*].

This is by the rule *ṇyāsasaśrantho yuc* [Pāṇini 3.3.107]. As for the root *kumbi* which is recited in the *Bhvādi* class, there ought to be an *a*-suffix by the rule *ṇvultṛcau* [Pāṇini 3.3.103]. However, whether there is an *a*-suffix or the *aṅ* suffix, there is no distinction whatsoever in the case of *kumbi*; therefore, that root does not necessitate its inclusion here. [The sūtra continues with] *śradantaroḥ*, etc.
"Like a prefix, as it were":
whatever operation occurs with respect to a prefix—characterized by the production of suffixes—that very same operation occurs for those two [prefixes] as well.
Thus, just as *pradhā* and *upadhā* occur when the prefix *pra-* and *upa-* are present, so too do *śraddhā* and *antardhā* occur when *śrad-* and *antara-* are present.
Nor is this grammatical derivation to be accomplished by means of an *upasaṃkhyāna* (supplementary rule); for the word *śraddhā* attains its correctness through its inclusion in the *tārakādi* group.

The word *antardhā* is also [established] by way of an indicator (*jñāpaka*). Since [Pāṇini] provides the citation of the word *antardhi* ending in the suffix *ki* in the rule "one desires non-perception by means of that which is in concealment" (*antardhau yenādarśanam icchati*, Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.4.28), it is known from this that the word *antar-* serves as the cause for the operation of a prefix (*upasarga*). For otherwise, the suffix *ki* would not apply by the rule "after that [word], when it is an attendant word" (*tasmann upapade*, Aṣṭādhyāyī 3.3.92); consequently, the citation "in the case of concealment" (*antardhau*) would be untenable. [The phrase] "it is an exception to [the substitution of] the vowel *a*" [is explained as follows].
Regarding the forms obtained as appropriate by the two rules *a pratyayāt* [Pāṇini 3.3.102] and *kṛnmejantaḥ* [Pāṇini 3.3.103]:
as for the question "How is *āsyā* [formed]?",
it is not formed in any way [by those rules].
The meaning is that *āsi* shall be [the suffix] by this rule, and it will be *yuc*, not anything else.
This is the rebuttal to [the objection] beginning with "ṛhalorṇyat" [Pāṇini 3.1.124].

[Objection: But surely the suffix *ṇyat* would occur by the rule of optional forms (*vāsarūpavidhi*), and that rule of optional forms does not apply in the feminine because of the prohibition "not in the feminine" (*astriyām*) [Pāṇini 3.1.94]. So why is it said that "*ṛhalorṇyat*" will result in *ṇyat*? To this he says: "vāsarūpa," etc.
And this very point has been established there [in the Mahābhāṣya] with the words "an addition" (*upasaṃkhyānam*). The meaning is "establishment.

The establishment here is as follows: the term *bahulagrahaṇa* (the mention of "diversely") which is about to be stated is a supplement (*śeṣa*) to both rules; by means of that, [the suffix] will apply to *ghaṭṭi* and other such words.
"It should be stated" means it should be explained. That explanation itself must be carried out by relying on the inclusion of the term "frequently" (*bahula*).

Regarding "anveṣaṇā": [the root] *iṣ* means "to go" (Dhātupāṭha 1127), or [it means] "repetition" (?). "An exception to *ktin* and so forth"—by the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), [the suffixes] *aṅ* and others are meant. "The mention of 'ākhyā' (name/designation)," etc.

If the name of a disease consists of a suffix, then this suffix occurs; it does not occur otherwise. The mention of "naming" (ākhyā) is for the purpose of confirming this rule. It does not apply to a disease expressed by another word, such as *bubhukṣā* (hunger) or *bhasmaka* (consumption).
Regarding the phrase "the inclusion of the word *bahula*," and so forth:
the prescription of the suffix *ṇvul* even outside the domain of designating a disease constitutes a deviation (*vyabhicāra*); for that purpose, the word *bahula* is included.

By means of this, the suffix is established even when there is a specification of the root-meaning (*dhātvartha*). Another meaning is as follows: the deviation (*vyabhicāra*) is the occurrence of this rule in other domains than the specific scope of the prescription of *ṇvul* for designating a disease; for that purpose, the word *bahula* is included.
By this, everything beginning with the rule "The suffixes *ik* and *tip* are used when a verbal root is cited" (Vārttika 3.19) is subsumed.
Regarding the word *pracchardikā*:
the root *charda*, meaning "to vomit," belongs to the *curādi* class.
Regarding "pravāhikā": [it is derived from] the root *vaha* in the sense of "carrying" (Dhātupāṭha 1004). Regarding "pracarcikā": [it is derived from the root *carc*].
The root *carc* (meaning "to study") is listed as number 1712 in the Dhātupāṭha; it belongs to the *curādi* group.
Here, although the suffix *ktin* would normally apply after the root *vah*, the suffixes *ṇvul* and *itar* take the suffix *yuc* instead. Thus, we have the form *śiro'sti*.

The root *ard* is used in the sense of "injury" (*hiṃsā*) [Dhātupāṭha 1828], or in the sense of "going" (*gati*) and "begging" (*yācana*) [Dhātupāṭha 55]. By the rule *khari ca* [Pāṇini 8.4.54], the change to the *car* sound (*t* for *d*) occurs.

A genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*) is formed with *śiras*. Then, the following grammatical operations must be applied: the substitution of *u* by the rule *eṅi pararūpam* [6.1.109], the substitution of *vṛddhi* by *vṛddhireci* [6.1.87], and the substitution of *o* by *oto gārgyasya* [6.1.113].

Regarding the rule *ikśtipau*: the letter *k* is for the sake of the operations pertaining to a *kit* suffix; by means of it, in the case of *pacati*, the *śap* [augment] occurs based on the *sārvadhātuka* [suffix]. Now, one might object: "The *śap* is prescribed when a *sārvadhātuka* suffix denotes the agent (*kartṛ*), but here the agent is not the meaning of the suffix; so how can there be the possibility of *śap*? [Response: The addition of the marker *ś* is for the purpose of establishing the technical designation (*saṃjñā*) of *sārvadhātuka*; by virtue of this, *śap* will occur even when the *sārvadhātuka* suffix does not denote the agent. Otherwise, the inclusion of the marker *ś* would be purposeless.
If this is so, would it not also apply [to *eva*]? It will not apply because it is not so designated; for it is stated that "the suffix *kāra* follows a phoneme" (*varṇāt kāraḥ*).

Since it is said "from a phoneme," does it not follow that the suffix *kāra* cannot be established after *eva*? There is no fault here, because by virtue of the mention of the term "diversely" (*bahulagrahaṇa*), the suffix will occur in some instances even after what is not a phoneme.
Alternatively, *kāra* means "making" (*karaṇa*); thus, this is a genitive compound meaning "the making (*kāra*) of *eva*."
Regarding the rule *matvarthāc chaḥ*:
here, the elision of the vowel *a* must also be stated,
for otherwise [the suffix] would not apply because [the base] lacks the designation *abha*.
Due to the inclusion of the word "bahula" (in the rule), the elision of the suffix *vā* will occur,
as in the cases of "iṇajādibhyaḥ" and "ik kṛṣyādibhyaḥ."
This is for the purpose of explaining the non-derivational (adhātu) [nouns].

Words such as *ājya* and others should be understood as technical names (*saṃjñāśabda*). Regarding the term *uddālakapuṣpabhañjikā*, it is a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*) according to [Pāṇini 2.2.8] "uddālakapuṣpabhañjikā."

Furthermore, the genitive case here is characterized by its connection with a *kṛt* suffix, according to the rule *kartṛkarmaṇoḥ kṛti* [Pāṇini 2.3.65]. In this sūtra, the mention of "narration" (*ākhyāna*) comes first, followed by "inquiry" (*paripraśna*); however, in the commentary (*vṛtti*), the presentation of "inquiry" is placed first, followed by "narration," as in the phrase "when inquiry and narration are understood. To one who might ask, "For what reason has this reversal been made in the commentary?", he replies: "Inquiry comes first," and so on.
The explanation proceeds by way of prior inquiry; therefore, in the commentary (*vṛtti*), the presentation of the inquiry and its illustration is made first, followed by the explanation.
The intention is that there is no purpose for deviating from this sequence.
To the question, "Why then is the inquiry not specified first in the *sūtra* and the explanation afterwards? he says: "In the *sūtra*," and so forth.

By the rule *alpāctaram* [Pāṇini 2.2.34], since the order of words in a *dvandva* compound is fixed, it is shown that the word *ākhyāna*, having fewer syllables, is placed first in the sūtra. [The example] "kāṃ kārimiti" [is derived from] the suffix *iñ*.
"What *kārikā*? means "what [action] characterized by the suffix *ṇvul*?"—
that is, "what action (*kriyā*)?"
By [Pāṇini 3.3.100], the suffix *śa* is applied. Regarding the phrase "which action" (*kāṃ kṛtyām*),
the suffix *kyap* is used there because of the letter *ca* [in that rule].
Regarding "kāṃ kṛtim":
the suffix *ktin* is applied by means of a grammatical split (*yogavibhāga*). Regarding "kāṃ gaṇim": [the same applies].
The root *iñ*, meaning "to count" (*gaṇa-saṃkhyāne*), is listed in the *cur*-class (the tenth class) as ending in a long vowel (*adanta*). [The example is:
"Which courtesan? (*kāṃ gaṇikām*).
The suffix *ṇvul* [is applied]; [in the case of] "gaṇanām," the suffix *yuc* [is applied].
Likewise: "kāṃ pācim" and so forth;
"kāṃ pācim akārṣīḥ", "kāṃ pācikām", "kāṃ pacām";
"kāṃ yājim", "kāṃ yājikām" and so forth, as well as "kāmiṣṭim".

"Which *pāṭhi*, *pāṭhikā*, or *paṭhiti*?"—this is an exception (*apavāda*) to [the suffixes] *kta*, *ktin*, and so forth. By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), [suffixes such as] *ā* and others are meant. For example: *agragāmikā*.
It leads to the foremost.
This is a compound formed with the genitive case characterized by its connection with a verbal derivative (*kṛt*).
[The phrase] "for the sake of the accent" (*svarārtham*) is used.
This is for the purpose that the accentuation of the final syllable (antodāttatva) should occur;

for if the suffix *ṇvul* were present, the acute accent would fall on the syllable preceding the suffix. [The rule] "they occur elsewhere than where they are prescribed" applies here. If this is so, does it follow that the statement of the meaning in rules such as [Pāṇini 3.4.70] becomes useless? This is not the case; for by virtue of the grammatical connection (*yoga*), the *kṛtya* suffixes and others are intended for meanings such as the abstract action (*bhāva*) and so forth, whereas they occur only rarely in other grammatical relations (*kāraka*).
And since that mode of conduct of theirs is established when the designation of "what is not beneficial" (anartha) is present, how could it be purposeless? [The example] "snānīyam" [is used];
here the *kṛtya* suffix is applied in the sense of the instrument (*karaṇa*).
[The example] "dānīyaḥ" [is used].
In the sense of the recipient (*sampradāna*), it is said "it is given to him" (*dīyate tasmai*);
regarding the word "apasecana," it is derived with the suffix *lyuṭ* in the sense of the object (*karman*), meaning "that into which something is poured" (*apasicyate tad*).

Regarding the term *avarodhāvaṇam*: it is that which is "obstructed" (*avarudhyate*). From the root *sṛ* meaning "to go" (Dhātupāṭha 935), with the causative suffix (*ṇic*) and the suffix *lyuṭ* in the passive sense, [the form *avarodhana* is derived].
As for *bhojanāḥ*, it means "that which is eaten" (*bhujyate*).

"Ācchādanāni" means "those which are covered. The suffix *lyuṭ* is used here in the sense of the object (*karman*). Thus, "the king's meals" (*rājño bhojanāḥ*) and "the king's coverings" (*rājña ācchādanāni*) are genitive compounds (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*).

"Praskandana" and "prapatana": [the suffix] *lyuṭ* is applied in the sense of the ablative (*apādāna*), as in "that from which one leaps forth (*praskandati*) or falls down (*prapatati*). Now, for what purpose is the mention of the term "variously" (*bahula*)? Since this meaning is already understood—namely, that by the very force of the commencement of the rule, the *kṛtya* and *lyuṭ* suffixes occur not only where they are specifically prescribed but generally elsewhere as well—he says: "Because of the mention of 'variously,'" and so forth.

By this, other *kṛt* suffixes as well, even when prescribed in one context, are desired in other contexts according to the intended meaning; and that is established through the mention of "variously."
Thus, he indicates that the inclusion of the term *bahulam* (in various ways) has been made. Regarding the example "pādahārakaḥ":

although the suffix *ṇvul* is prescribed [by Pāṇini 3.1.133] in the sense of the agent (*kartari*), it occurs here in the sense of the object (*karmaṇi*) due to the inclusion of *bahulam*. Furthermore, by [Pāṇini 3.4.70], the suffix *kta* is established in the sense of the abstract state (*bhāve*).

"Since this *kta* suffix [prescribed] for the neuter gender and the abstract state (*bhāva*) is superseded by the specifically prescribed *lyuṭ*, the formulation of the rule (*yoga-ārambha*) is necessary. Regarding the statement "the division of the rule (*yogavibhāga*) is for the sake of what follows":

it is so that only *lyuṭ* may be carried over (*anuvṛtti*) in the subsequent [rule], and not *kta*. Regarding the statement "the statement is for the sake of obligatory compounding (*nityasamāsa-artha*)": that which has obligatory compounding as its purpose (*artha*) or motive is described in that way.

But how does this statement mean that it is a compulsory compound (*nityasamāsa*)? He says: "For a compound with an *upapada* is a compulsory compound. For by this rule, a suffix is prescribed when an *upapada* (an accompanying word) in the objective case is present; thus, there will be an *upapada* compound, and that is compulsory because the mention of "compulsory" (*nitya*) from [Pāṇini 3.4.68] continues to apply to its formulation. An example is: "drinking milk is happiness" (*payaḥpānaṃ sukham*).

But how is this an illustration of it? For in this case, pleasure does not arise from contact (*saṃsparśa*); rather, it arises from eating (*abhyavahāra*). This is not a fault; for all those acts such as eating do not occur without contact, and thus, because contact is an inseparable concomitant (*nāntarīyakatva*), it is not [explicitly] required [to be mentioned]. [The example is: "The rising from the couch is pleasant. Here, by the rule *pūrvasavarṇaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.1.102), there is the substitution of the preceding vowel.

In this case, there is bodily pleasure for the agent, but not for one being contacted by the object of the action (*karman*); rather, it is for one [contacted] by the point of departure (*apādāna*) called the couch.
Regarding the phrase "the worship of the fire-pit" (*agnikuṇḍasyopāsanam*):
the root *ās* (Dhātupāṭha 1021) is preceded by the prefix *upa*.
Here, pleasure arises from non-contact; for that [pleasure] occurs precisely for one who is being touched while the fire-pit is being worshipped.

Regarding the expression "bathing of the guru" (*guroḥ snāpanam*): the root *ṣṇā* is used in the sense of "cleansing" (*śauce*; Dhātupāṭha 1053). The causative suffix *ṇic* is added, and by the rule *arti-hrī-* [Pāṇini 7.3.36], the augment *puk* is inserted.
But surely, even here the teacher is the agent of pleasure, so there is pleasure for the agent;

how then can this serve as a counter-example? To this he says: "The teacher [is not the agent] of the act of bathing (*snāpayati*). By this he shows that agency is not intended here with reference to pleasure, but rather with reference to the action itself.

And here, the teacher is not the agent (*kartṛ*) of the act of bathing; rather, it is the disciple. For the teacher, [the bathing] becomes merely the object (*karman*). The designation of "object" for the teacher is established by the rule *gati-buddhi-* (Pāṇini 1.4.52) and others; for when that [verb] is intransitive (*akarmaka*), even though he is the one who bathes, he is designated as the agent (*kartṛ*).
[The word] "embracing" (*pariṣvañjana*) [is used].

The root *ṣvanj* is used in the sense of "embracing" (*pariṣvaṅge*; Dhātupāṭha 976). By the rule *upasargāt sunoti* [Pāṇini 8.3.65] and others, the cerebral nasal (*mūrdhanya*) is substituted. Regarding the phrase "mental joy" (*mānasī prītiḥ*):
by this, he demonstrates that the particular joy arising from embracing one's son is a physical pleasure (*śarīrasukhatva*).
Regarding "mardanam":
[the root] *mṛd* means "to crush" (*kṣode*; Dhātupāṭha 1515).
"In all cases, the uncompounded form is cited as a counter-example."

But there is no absence of the *lyuṭ* suffix, because *lyuṭ* occurs everywhere by virtue of the preceding rule. By the statement "in the sense of the instrument (*karaṇa*) and the locus (*adhikaraṇa*) as kārakas," he shows that the instrument and the locus are the meanings of the suffix.
Why do the instrument and the locus not occur here as *upapadas*? Precisely because of the mention [of them] in the rule "in the sense of the instrument and the locus."

For the two words *karaṇa* and *adhikaraṇa*, ending in the suffix *lyuṭ*, denote respectively the instrument (*karaṇa*) and the locus (*adhikaraṇa*). In that case, if these two were to have *dadhi* as their subordinate word (*upapada*), this grammatical instruction would not be possible.

If this were so, then there would be a rule for the suffix contingent upon the instruction, and the instruction contingent upon that suffix; thus, a circular dependency (*itaretarāśrayatva*) would result. This is not the case, because words are eternal (*nityatva*).
Nothing new whatsoever is produced, because words are eternal; rather, their mere existence is described [by grammar]. Thus, there arises the fallacy of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśrayatā*).
For example, the term "wood-cutter" (*idhmapravraścanaḥ*).
The root *pra-vraśc* means "to cut" (Dhātupāṭha 1292); thus, *idhmānāṃ pravraścanaḥ* is a genitive compound meaning "the cutter of fuel-sticks.
Regarding *palāśa-śātanaḥ*: the root *śadlṛ* means "to destroy" (Dhātupāṭha 1428); the substitution of *t* for *d* occurs by the rule *hetumaṇṇic* (Pāṇini 7.3.42).
Regarding the word *godohanī*:
the suffix *ṅīp* is applied by the rule *ṭiḍḍhāṇañ* [Pāṇini 4.1.15]. As for the phrase "if [the name] is understood by the aggregate," etc.:
if the technical name (*saṃjñā*) is understood through the aggregate of the base (*prakṛti*) and the suffix (*pratyaya*), then the suffix occurs; otherwise, it does not.
Regarding the phrase "for the sake of non-completeness" (*akārtsnyārtham*): *akārtsnya* means incompleteness or lack of totality; that which has this as its purpose or object is so described.
By this, he demonstrates that the cognition has a non-totalizing scope.

Regarding the term *dantacchadaḥ*: the root *chad* means "to cover" (*apavāraṇe*; Dhātupāṭha 1935) and takes the causative suffix *ṇic*. According to Pāṇini 6.4.96, *chāder ghe 'dvayupasargasya*, there is shortening [of the penultimate vowel], and the compound is formed as previously described.

Regarding the term *prasādhana*: from the roots *rādha* and *sādha* in the sense of "accomplishment" (*saṃsiddhi*) [Dhātupāṭha 1262, 1263], with the causative suffix *ṇic*, the suffix *lyuṭ* is applied in the sense of the instrument (*karaṇa*) by the preceding rule; then, the compound is formed according to *kugatiprādayaḥ* [Pāṇini 2.2.18]. The phrase "in the very same sense as before" means in the sense of both the instrument (*karaṇa*) and the locus (*adhikaraṇa*).

[Objection: But surely the suffix *ghañ* is already established for words such as *gocara* by the previous rule itself; why then is this new rule (*yoga*) commenced? [Response: To this he says: "and after a consonant" (*halaśca*), etc. [Objection: But the term "affix" (*pratyaya*) will be carried over (*anuvartate*) from there, so by that means *ghañ* will occur in *gocara* and other such cases. [Response: However, there would be an excessive burden of comprehension (*pratipatti-gaurava*), because the continued application (*anuvṛtti*) of the term "mostly" (*prāya*) would not be indicative [of its necessity]. Regarding "of the root *stṛ*" (*stṛṇāteḥ*): it is from the root *stṛñ* "to cover" (Dhātupāṭha 1484).
Regarding the phrase "prāyānuvṛtteḥ" and so forth:

when the word *prāya* is understood as being carried over [from a previous rule], the suffix *ghañ* is applied after the verbal roots *tṛ* and *sṛ* when a word ending in *upadhi* follows, provided that it is a name (*saṃjñā*) and functions as a qualifier (*upadhibhūta*). This is the meaning obtained.
[The commentary adds: "Not when it is a name."
Because this condition (*upādhi*) is generally applicable, it sometimes occurs even when there is no [specific] designation. For example: *veṣṭaḥ*.
[The root is] *veṣṭa* in the sense of "encircling" (*veṣṭane*; Dhātupāṭha 255). Also: *mārgaḥ*, *apāmārgaḥ*.
{The root-list for √mṛj—} (Dhātupāṭha 1066).

By the rule *cajoḥ* [Pāṇini 7.3.52], there is the substitution of *k* (kutva); by *mṛjervṛddhiḥ* [7.2.114], there is vṛddhi; and by *upasargasya ghañi* [6.3.121], there is lengthening. "The present rule is begun for the sake of those ending in non-consonants (*ahalanta*)," because for those ending in consonants (*halanta*), the result is already established by the preceding rule. The objection beginning with "But surely... is as follows.
The resolution is that the statement is intended to exclude water.
The meaning is that if this were not commenced, then [the designation] would apply to water as well by virtue of the preceding rule. Thus, "an oil-puddle" (*tailodaṅkaḥ*).
This is a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*). Furthermore, the genitive case here is characterized by its connection with a *kṛt* suffix [denoting the object], as in "water-drawing" (*udakoñcanaḥ*),
where the suffix *lyuṭ* is used in the sense of the object (*karman*).
"From what [reason] is 'gha' [used]? and so forth.

He thinks as follows: since *gha* was prescribed by the rule "In the masculine, when it is a technical name" (*puṃsi saṃjñāyām*, Pāṇini 3.3.118), etc., and since the suffix *ghañ* has been ordained [by subsequent rules], it would therefore be more appropriate for *ghan* alone to occur in that domain once *gha* has been superseded.
[The phrase] "because there is no distinction" means this.

For there is no difference here whether the suffix *ghañ* or *gha* is applied to the root *añc*. The intention is that if *gha* were applied even in the case of *udaka*, the prohibition of *anuk* would serve no purpose. Now, one might object: "If *gha* is applied, the word *udaṅka* becomes oxytone by the accent of the suffix (*pratyayasvara*); but if *ghañ* with the augment *ḍhi* is applied, it would be acute on the first syllable by the accent of the *ñit* suffix (*ñitsvara*). Why, then, is it said that there is no difference? To this he replies: "Even when *ghañ* [is applied]," and so forth.

"By means of the suffix prescribed by [Pāṇini 6.2.144] *thāthādisvareṇa*, the suffix *ḍa* should be stated," and so forth. Everywhere, the word "should be stated" (*vaktavya*) has the meaning "should be explained. In this regard, the explanation is as follows: the letter *ca* is used here, and it serves to include what has not been mentioned; therefore, suffixes such as *ḍā* and others will also occur.

But is it not the case that the particle *ca* is for the purpose of carrying over (*anukarṣaṇa*) the suffix *ghañ*? This is not so; for *ghañ* is established by its very being marked with the *svarita* accent. Now, for what purpose is the suffix *gh* prescribed after the root *khan*, given that its prescription is for the sake of the *kutva* change (of *kh* to *k*), and yet no part of *khan* consists of a *ku*-sound? If this is so, then it indicates this: that this suffix occurs after other roots as well. By this, forms such as *khalaḥ*, *bhagaḥ*, and *padaḥ* are established. [This applies] to the words *su* and *iccha*.
But how can a specific [meaning] be obtained even when [the rule] is stated in general terms? To this he says: "Because of possibility" (*sambhavāt*).
Wherever something is possible, there that [thing] serves as a qualifier.

The word *kṛcchra* occurs only in the sense of difficulty (*duḥśabda*), not in the sense of non-difficulty (*akṛcchra*). However, for the other two [prefixes], it occurs only in the sense of non-difficulty, not in the sense of difficulty. Therefore, *kṛcchra* is indeed a qualifier of *dus* alone, while *akṛcchra* belongs only to the other two.
"‘The mat is easy for you to make’ (īṣatkaraḥ kaṭo bhavatā) means that the mat is made by you without difficulty or effort. ‘It is easily done’ (īṣatkāryaḥ)."
The suffix *ṇyat* is applied by the rule *ṛhaloṇryat* [Pāṇini 3.1.124].

Here, the word *īṣat* functions in the sense of *manāk* (slightly). It is stated that "the letter *l* is for the sake of accentuation," so that by the rule *liti* [Pāṇini 6.1.193], the vowel preceding the suffix marked with *l* becomes udātta (acute-accented).

Now, one might object: the grammatical operation of *khit* (the suffix *kha*), such as the shortening of vowels and so forth, is prescribed by rules like Pāṇini 6.3.66 for non-indicative (*anavyaya*) words; yet *īṣat* and the others bear the designation of "indicators" (*avyaya*). For what purpose, then, is the *khit* suffix applied to *khal*? To this he says: "The application of *khit* is for the sake of the *mum* augment in the subsequent rule. In the subsequent rule, *khal* will be prescribed even when a non-indicator is the upapada; the *khit* suffix is applied so that the *mum* augment may occur there according to Pāṇini 6.3.67. Furthermore, the agent and the object function as *upapadas*, but they do not constitute the meaning of the suffix itself.

Furthermore, if these two were the meaning of the suffix, the suffix would occur only when words such as *īṣat* are used as governing words (*upapada*); consequently, the inclusion of the marker *k* would be purposeless, because the grammatical operation conditioned by *k* is prescribed for non-indeclinables (*anavyaya*), whereas words like *īṣat* are indeed indeclinables. Therefore, for this reason as well, it is determined that the governing words are the agent and the object, and not these two [the agent and object] themselves which constitute the meaning of the suffix.

In this context, neither the agent (*kartṛ*) and the object (*karman*) nor *īṣat* and the others are individually the cause for the suffix; what then? It is their collection. By the particle *ca*, a co-occurrence (*sanniyoga*) is established, whereby the agent and object, as well as *īṣat* and the others, function simultaneously as *upapadas*; it cannot be otherwise. If this is so, how can there be a simultaneous compound of two *upapadas*? Who, indeed, says that there is a simultaneous compound? For first, having formed a compound with the subsequent *upapada*, the compound with the preceding one occurs afterwards.
What, then, is the further governing term (*upapada*) here? It is the agent (*kartṛ*) and the object (*karman*).
How is this known? From the force of the application of the suffix *khi*.
For the application of *khi* is for the purpose of [triggering] the augment *mum*, and the addition of the augment *mum* is prescribed for that which is not an indeclinable (*anavyaya*).

In that case, the designation *khit* for the words beginning with *īṣat* and for the verbal root [in the context of immediate succession] would be purposeless. For example: *īṣadāḍham bhavaṃ bhavatā*.
The meaning is: "You are becoming firm without difficulty."
"Devadatta is being made somewhat wealthy by you.
The meaning is: "Devadatta is being made rich without difficulty by you. Regarding the rule *kartṛkarmaṇoḥ* and so forth:
the sense of *cvī* is the state of becoming that which one was not previously (*abhūtatadbhāva*).
The meaning is that this form of the rule—namely, "when *kartṛ* and *karman* are the *upapada*s signifying those [meanings], the suffix *khal* occurs"—must be explained.

In this regard, the explanation is as follows: the term "mostly" (*prāya*) is carried over by the maxim of the frog-leap (*maṇḍūkapluti*); therefore, the suffix occurs only when the agent (*kartṛ*) and the object (*karman*) signify the sense of *cvy-artha* (becoming something else), and not otherwise. For example:
*svādukena bhūyate*.

In this case, because the sense of the *cv*-suffix (*cvi*) is not intended to be expressed, the suffix does not occur. Regarding "sūpasadanam": [it is derived from] the root *ṣadlṛ* ("to perish, to go, to sink") preceded by the prefix *upa*. Regarding "sudohanam": [it is derived from] the root *duh* ("to milk").

"It should be stated" means it should be explained. Here is the explanation: the word *api* ("even") is used here, and it serves the purpose of indicating that there are exceptions to all [the rules]. By this, it is shown that the suffix *yuc* occurs even after these [roots] in the vernacular (*bhāṣā*): *śāsu* "to instruct" (DhP 1075), *yudh* "to fight" (DhP 1173), *dṛśir* "to see" (DhP 988), *ñidhṛṣā* "to be bold" (DhP 1269), and *mṛṣa* "to endure" (DhP 1164).

But how is it determined that the word *api* signifies "even" (*sarvavyabhicāra*) in this context? It is because of the commencement of the sūtra. For if only the deviation regarding the sense of motion (*gatyartha*) were intended here, this sūtra would not have been begun, and the term "motion" (*gatyartha*) would not have been included in the preceding sūtra. If it were to express the state of being near (*samīpasya bhāvaḥ*), then that might be the case; however, if that were so, there would be no compound between a present [action] and its proximity, because of the absence of a relationship.

For proximity (*sāmīpya*) does not have a connection with the present tense itself, but rather with what is near to it, because that [proximity] is a quality of the latter. Therefore, thinking that this suffix will occur here in its own primary sense (*svārtha*), he says: "Proximity is simply being near" (*samīpam eva sāmīpyam*).

But for what purpose is this formulation made by prescribing the *ṣyañ* suffix in its own primary sense, instead of simply saying "near to the present," which would be more concise? To this he replies: "The fact that *ṣyañ* has its own primary sense is made known. This indicates that the *ṣyañ* suffix may also occur in its own primary sense.

The suffix *ṣyañ* has been applied here as a *svārthika* (denoting its own meaning) in order to indicate this specific sense: that *ṣyañ* occurs in its own primary meaning (*svārthe*). The phrase "for the sake of establishing [terms such as] *cāturvarṇya* and others" states the purpose of this very indication.
By the word "etc. (ādi), the inclusion of the four stages of life (cāturāśramya) and so forth is intended.
"I am coming" (*ayam āgacchāmi*) has this meaning: it refers to the sense of "I have come" (*ayam āgamam*).

Regarding the word *āgamam*: it is the third person singular (uttamaikavacana) of the aorist (*luṅ*). By the rule *tasthasthamipām* [Pāṇini 3.4.101], the substitution of *am* occurs for *mi*. By the rule concerning the *puṣādi* class [Pāṇini 3.1.55], *aṅ* replaces *cl*. Thus, the form is *āgamam*, as in "I have come. Regarding *eṣa gacchāmi*: this means "I am going here."
The meaning of "eṣa gamiṣyāmi" (I shall go) is as follows: [Pāṇini 7.2.58] provides the augment *iṭ*, resulting in "gantāsmi" (I am about to go).

*luṭ*, *tāsi*, *mip*. Now, for what purpose is the mention of "vat" (the suffix -vat)? Since the meaning that "when it is stated 'in proximity to the present, [the suffixes] are used in the present,'" these suffixes prescribed for the present time are understood to apply in proximity to the present, one might ask why the word "vat" is used. To this he says: "The mention of vat," and so forth. If the word "vat" were not there, only the formal shape (*rūpa*) of these suffixes would be indicated by the term "present time," but their base (*prakṛti*) and other factors would not be taken into account; consequently, they would arise from the verbal root alone.

But when the suffix *vat* is employed, total similarity (*sarvasādṛśya*) is understood; since the suffix *vat* is prescribed only in that specific context, no confusion arises. To demonstrate this very absence of confusion, he says: "by which," and so forth.

For total similarity occurs only if those [suffixes] which are prescribed for the present tense by a particular qualifier are used for the proximity of the present (*vartamānasāmīpya*) by that same qualifier, and not otherwise.
"By means of the root, the prefix, and the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*). By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), there is the inclusion of the limiting adjunct and that which is not denoted by the suffix.
Examples are "the purifying one" (*pavamānaḥ*) and "the sacrificer" (*yajamānaḥ*).

> [[3.2.128]] That which is prescribed [by the suffix] occurs after those two very [roots] even when there is proximity to the present time, and not after another root. In the example *alaṅkariṣṇuḥ*, the suffix *iṣṇuc* is prescribed after the root *kṛñ* preceded by *alam* when the agent is characterized by habituality and so forth; it occurs after that very same [root] even when there is proximity to the present time.
And regarding that very same meaning, in the expression *aparud agacchat* ("he went [there] last year"), the *laṅ* suffix occurs precisely when remoteness (*viprakarṣa*) is intended.

In the case of *varṣeṇa gamiṣyati* ("he will go within a year"), the *lṛṭ* suffix likewise occurs. Furthermore, by the words "he who thinks" (*yo manyate*) and so forth, he rejects the sūtra with respect to a particular cognizer.
"‘The movement through another time,’ and so forth.
‘Another time’ refers to a past or future time proximate to the present; its ‘movement’ is its cognition.

This [cognition] arises from the word ‘I am coming’ even when it pertains to a specific present time, provided it is employed immediately after the sentence ‘When, Devadatta, will you go? rather than from the sentence ‘I am going.’"

Even if time were accessible through a sentence (*vākya*), the commencement of the Sūtra would be appropriate only if it were useful at the time of the grammatical formation (*saṃskāra*) of the word (*pada*); however, it is not useful there. This is because the grammatical treatise effects the formation of the word, not of the sentence. When the word is being formed, only that time which is accessible through the word is useful; therefore, the intention is that [time] is accessible through the sentence.
The particle *iti* serves as a reference back to what has been under discussion.
Thus, for one who thinks—that is, understands—this [treatise], it need not have been commenced at all.

This is because those very conditions (*pratyaya*) for which it was commenced are already established by the rule "the present tense is used for the present" (*vartamāne laṭ*, Pāṇini 3.2.123) and others within the grammatical system itself.

By the inclusion of the word "section" (*prakaraṇa*), he shows that not only should this single sūtra not have been commenced, but even rules such as "in the sense of praise, as if past" (*aśaṃsāyāṃ bhūtavacca*, Pāṇini 3.3.132) should likewise not have been commenced.
"‘Such a one,’ and so forth.
And thus, it is stated that this [work] must indeed be commenced for the sake of that person who is not such a comprehender, namely, one of dull intellect;
for he is not capable of understanding through such a method."
"And so," and so forth.

Since, in that case, time understood through the sentence is not utilized at the time of the grammatical formation (*saṃskāra*) of the individual words, this being so, expressions such as "Ah! He will do" (*āḥ kariṣyati*) are justified.
For even there, the word "he will do" (*kariṣyati*) occurs precisely in the future tense; thus, by the rule *lṛṭ* (Pāṇini 3.3.13), the suffix *lṛṭ* is established.
This time, however, is the future non-remote (bhaviṣyadanadyatana).

Even if a subsequent time were perceived, it would still not be taken into account during the formation of word-meanings (*pada-saṃskāra*), as it constitutes the meaning of the sentence (*vākyārtha*).

If the time conveyed by the sentence were nevertheless relied upon during the formation of word-meanings, then forms such as *kariṣyati* would be untenable—since, in that case, the suffix *luṭ* alone would have to be used for the future non-remote. [As an example of this time, one says] *āgamat*.
The suffix *niṣṭhā* [denotes the past tense] in the word *āgata*.
The elision of the nasal [of the root] occurs by the rule beginning with "anudāttopadeśa" (Pāṇini 6.4.37).
"Adhīmahe": from the root *iṅ* (to study), the suffix *luṭ*, the ending *mahiṅ*; due to its belonging to the *adādi* class, there is elision (*luk*) of the *śap* augment [Pāṇini 2.4.72].
"Adhyagīṣmahi": likewise.

In the *luṅ* [aorist], by the rule "optionally in the *luṅ* and *lṛṅ*" (Pāṇini 2.4.50), there is the substitution of *gāṅ* for *iṅ*; and because *sic* is marked with the *ṅ*-sign by the rule "the *gāṅ*, *kuṭ*, etc. (Pāṇini 1.2.1), there is the elision of the *i* by the rule "of *ghu*, *mā*, *sthā*, etc. (Pāṇini 6.4.66). One might ask: since there is an extension (*atideśa*) of the past tense (*bhūta*), why do the *laṅ* (imperfect) and *liṭ* (perfect) endings not also apply? To this he says: "In the case of an extension of a general property," and so forth. This is an extension of the general property of being past, whereas the *laṅ* and *liṭ* are suffixes that denote specific types of the past.

"In the extension of general rules, there is no extension of specific ones; therefore, those two [rules] do not apply here. [This is stated because] "the rule *bhūtavat ca* is an exception (*apavāda*) to this [present rule].
This is because the present rule is commenced even when *bhūtavat ca* would otherwise have applied.

Now, what is the purpose of including the term *vacana* (utterance)? Since everything is already established by the rule *kṣipre lṛṭ*, he says: "The inclusion of the term *vacana* is for the sake of expressing synonyms (*paryāya*)."

For if the mention of the word *vacana* (denoting) were not present, the suffix *lṛṭ* would apply only when the word *kṣipra* itself is the upapada; however, since it is present, it applies to all those words that denote "quickly. Now, what is the purpose of mentioning *lṛṭ*? One might ask: why not simply say "in the sense of *kṣipra*," since the extension (*atideśa*) of the rule "as if past" (*bhūtavat*) pertains to the future tense, and once that [past-tense application] is prohibited, the desired result is already established by the rule "the present tense (*laṭ*) in the remaining cases" (*laṭ śeṣe ca*)? To this he replies: "When one ought to say 'not' (*na*)," and so forth.

When it should have been stated simply as "na" (not), the inclusion of the term "luṭ" serves this purpose: so that *lṛṭ* may also occur in the sense of the future not belonging to the current day (*bhaviṣyadanadyatana*). Otherwise, *luṭ* alone would be the exception (*apavāda*) to *lṛṭ*. [Example: "I hope that I might study" (*āśaṃse yukto'dhīyīya*). Here, from the root *iṅ*, there is the suffix *liṅ*, the augment *sīyuṭ*, the first person singular ending, and the augment *iṭ*. By the rule *iṭo't* [Pāṇini 3.4.106], there is the substitution of *at*; because the suffix is marked with *ṅ* (*ṅittvāt*), there is no *guṇa* strengthening; by the rule *liṅaḥ salopo'nantasya* [Pāṇini 7.2.79], the *sakāra* is elided; the *iyaṅ* substitution occurs for the root vowel, and it is combined with the prefix [by Pāṇini 6.1.101].

"I hope that I shall study quickly. In this instance, although the word *kṣipram* (quickly) is an upapada and the word *āśaṃse* (I hope) is also an expression of hope (*āśaṃsā*), nevertheless, because it is subsequent [in the order of rules], only the suffix *liṅ* occurs, not *lṛṭ*. However, the scope for *lṛṭ* is where there is no upapada expressing hope—as in: "We shall study quickly. By the phrase "proximity of times" (*kālānāṃ sāmīpyam*), he shows that here proximity related to time is intended.

But how, moreover, is it established that by the general statement [of proximity], only proximity related to time is understood? From the rule *vartamānasāmīpye* onwards, this section is for the most part concerned with time.
Why is that? Because words such as *vartamāna* (present) and so forth are terms denoting time.
Furthermore, there is a prohibition regarding the *laṅ* and *luṭ* suffixes, and those two are prescribed specifically for [particular] times.
Therefore, it is understood that proximity of time is resorted to here precisely through the connection with those two wherever they may be.
To the question of what kind that [proximity] is, he says: "by a similar class," and so forth.
The mention of "similar class" is for the purpose of excluding those of a different class.

If [the time] were understood as being separated by mere duration of time, then in examples such as "On that full moon day which has passed, the teacher kindled the fires," there would be no sense of proximity, because it is separated from the new moon day and other lunar days.
Therefore, non-separation by a member of the same class [of days] is what is intended.
[This is shown by the example] "He gave."
The elision (*luk*) of *sic* occurs by the rule *gātisthā* [Pāṇini 2.4.77].
In the form *adhyāpipat*,
the causative suffix (*ṇic*) is applied by the rule *ṇicaśca* [Pāṇini 1.3.74].

The substitution of *ā* [for the root vowel] occurs by [Pāṇini 6.1.48]; the augment *puk* is added by [Pāṇini 7.3.36], etc.; then the *luṅ* tense; the *caṅ* suffix is applied to the *cli* by [Pāṇini 3.1.48], etc.; then the reduplication of the syllable beginning with *pī* occurs by [Pāṇini 6.1.2]; the augment *āṭ* is added by [Pāṇini 6.4.72]; the vowel increase (*vṛddhi*) occurs by [Pāṇini 6.1.87]; and there is the elision of the *ṇic* suffix. Regarding the phrase "this full moon day which has passed":
this is said with reference to that full moon day which is not separated by any other full moon day.

For although that [Full Moon] is separated from the New Moon and other lunar days, nevertheless, because it is not separated by a time of a different kind—namely, the time called the Full Moon—it does not transcend proximity.

Regarding the form *agnīnādhita*: from the root *dhā* preceded by the prefix *ā*, there is the substitution of *i* by [Pāṇini 1.2.17], the *sic* affix is treated as *kit*, and the *sic* is elided by [Pāṇini 8.2.27].
"Adita" is a form of the root *dā* (to give),
as before.

Regarding *yakṣyate*: this is the *lṛṭ* suffix after the root *yaj*, with the augment *sya*; when that is present, the substitution of *k* for *ṣ* occurs by [Pāṇini 8.2.41]. In forms such as *ādhita*, the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) is applied everywhere by [Pāṇini 1.3.72], etc.

For what purpose are two prohibitions stated? Could it not simply be said: "Not in the case of continuous action (*kriyāprabandha*) or proximity (*sāmīpya*), as in the case of the immediate past (*adyatana*)"? For in the cases of continuous action and proximity, the *luṅ* and *lṛṭ* suffixes—denoting the immediate past—are intended, and not the *laṅ* and *lṛṭ* suffixes denoting the non-immediate past.
Since those two [tenses], the *laṅ* and the *luṭ*, would indeed be established even when stated in this way, he says: "Two negations," and so forth.

He thinks as follows: if it were merely stated that "the *lṛṭ* is used for the continuity and proximity of action as in the case of *nādya*," then this very sūtra would be prescriptive; consequently, a confusion would arise—the *lṛṭ* in the domain of the *luṅ*, and the *luṅ* in the domain of the *lṛṭ*.
For no such distinction is specified here.

When the scope of the prohibition is stated as "the *luṅ* [aorist] is used for the past (*bhūte*) and the *lṛṭ* [future] for the future (*bhaviṣyati*"), this fault does not arise; therefore, nothing at all is prescribed by this rule. Rather, only a prohibition of the non-recent (*anadyatana*) tenses is effected. When those [non-recent tenses] are prohibited, the general rules (*utsarga*), such as *luṅ* and others, come into effect in their respective times through their own prescriptive statements, being freed from the exceptions (*apavāda*). Thus, the two prohibitions are stated in order to permit what is otherwise obtained [by the general rules]. *Bālamanoramā*: "In the sense of continuity of action (*kriyāprabandha*) and proximity (*sāmīpya*), it is not like the non-recent. (Pāṇini 3.3.135). It is not like the non-recent.
The continuity of an action (*kriyā-prabandha*) means its constancy (*sātatyam*). Thus it is said: "in the constancy of an action.
By the phrase "as in the case of the non-recent past" (*anadyatana-vat*), the *laṅ* and *luṭ* suffixes prescribed for the non-recent past and the future are intended.
Regarding this, he says: "Not *laṅ* or *luṭ*" (*na laṅluṭau*).
This means that *laṅ* does not occur for the remote past (*anadyatana-bhūta*), whereas *luṅ* does not occur for the remote future (*anadyatana-bhaviṣyat*).
He provides an example of the prohibition of *laṅ* when there is continuity of action (*kriyāsātatya*): "He ate food as long as he lived" (*yāvajjīvam annam adāt*).
In the *Laghu-śabdendu-śekhara*, by the rule *gātisthāghupābhūbhyaḥ sicaḥ* (Pāṇini 2.4.77), there is the elision (*luk*) of *sic*.
Regarding the example for proximity (*sāmīpya*), he says: "proximity" (*sāmīpyam iti*).
"This which... (*yeyam iti*).

Even when there is an interval of several days and nights in the dark fortnight following the full moon, proximity indeed exists, because there is no intervention by another full moon of the same kind.

Regarding the form *ādhitā*: from the root *dhā*, in the *luṅ* tense, the vowel *i* is substituted for the root by the rule *sthādhvoricca*; the *sic* suffix is treated as *kit*, and its elision occurs by the rule *hrasvādaṅgāt*.
Regarding the phrase "he did not sacrifice with Soma," the words "of this very full moon that has passed" are to be supplied as an ellipsis.
Now, he provides an example of the prohibition of the *luṭ* (future) suffix when there is continuity of action: "this very new moon."

"One will sacrifice with the Soma"—the phrase "in that upcoming new moon [day]" is supplied [from the context]. According to Pāṇini 3.3.135 (*bhaviṣyati maryādāvacane 'varasmin*), when there is a statement of a limit in the future, [the suffix *lṛṭ* is used]. In the *Bālamano ramā*, it is stated: "In the future, when there is a limit..."
The word *avarasmin* is to be analyzed as a locative;
*anadyatanavat na* means that the *luṅ* [aorist] suffix does not apply.
The *bhāṣya* states, "for the purpose of prohibiting a continuous sequence of action," and Kaiyaṭa says, "and for the purpose of excluding proximity.
As for this [which is referred to]:

The construction is as follows: for one residing in a certain particular region, regarding this path that must be traveled starting from Pāṭaliputra and so forth, "we shall drink barley-meal (saktu) and the like" in that which is *avara*—the eastern portion—of Kauśāmbī, which lies in the middle of that path.
Here, by the word *kauśāmbyāḥ*, the sense of a limit (*maryādā*) is understood;
by the word *avaram*, the sense of being posterior or lower (*avaratva*) is understood.
The intention here is that the *luṅ* [aorist] will not occur for the future time, but rather only the *lṛṭ* [periphrastic future];
this is because of the rule concerning the division of time (*kālavibhāga*). "The previous sūtra" refers to [Pāṇini 3.3.13].

The meaning is that the rule is the sūtra: *bhaviṣyati maryādāvacane 'varasmin*. Now, one might object: "But isn't this already established by the previous sūtra even in the case of a temporal limit (*kālamaryādā*)? To this he says: *ahorātra*.
Thus, the aforementioned rule—*bhaviṣyati maryādāvacane*—does not apply to a division related to a day-and-night (*ahorātra*). This is the meaning.

Now, one might ask: "Why is there not just a single sūtra, 'In the sense of defining a limit, and in the division of time other than days and nights, [the suffix *luṭ* is used] for the future'? To this he says: 'The separation of the yoga (yogavibhāga) is for the sake of what follows.
This will become clear in the subsequent sūtra:
'This year which is to come.'"
An example of a temporal limit is "from Āgrahāyaṇī";
this means from the full moon day of Mārgaśīrṣa.
"Engaged" means "endowed with the observances.
"We shall study" means... [the rest of the sentence].
The point here is that the suffix *luṭ* (the periphrastic future) is not used, but rather *lṛṭ* (the simple future).
Regarding the phrase "possessing fifteen nights":
it is a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "that fortnight which has fifteen nights."
In the rule *ac-pratyanvavapūrvāt*, the suffix *ac* is applied as a compound-ending (*samāsānta*) due to a *yogavibhāga* (separation of the rule) regarding the term *ac*.
Alternatively, *pañcadaśarātraḥ* is the collective aggregate (*samāhāra*) of fifteen nights;
here, the suffix *ac* is applied as a compound-ending according to the rule *ahnaḥ sarvaikadeśasaṅkhyātapuṇyāt*.

However, the rule "a neuter [compound] preceded by a numeral" does not apply here because of the statement: "Gender is not to be taught, for gender depends on common usage. Regarding the phrase "when there is a statement of a limit (*maryādāvacane*)," the inclusion of the word "statement" (*vacana*) is so that it may also apply in the sense of inclusive limit (*abhividhi*).
Furthermore, an inclusive limit is indeed a specific type of limit.
That very same *maryādā* (limit) is called *abhividhi* (inclusive limit) when it is connected with an operation (*kārya*), but it is called *maryādā* when it is not so connected.
In this context, because of the mention of the word "vacana" (statement), no specific distinction is intended; therefore, the rule applies merely upon the utterance of the term *maryādā*.

Even without the mention of the word "vacana," there would be no prohibition regarding *abhividhi*; for wherever one desires an operation within an *abhividhi*, one either uses the term *abhividhi*, as in [Pāṇini 2.1.13], or uses the word "vacana," as in [Pāṇini 1.4.89].
The term "vacana" (word) is employed so that [the rule] may apply even in the sense of inclusion (*abhividhi*).
"In the latter" (*avarasmin*) means "subsequent to" (*arvāk*).
"One should go"—
this indicates the future state of the path.
"That which is lower than that"— this refers to the present state.
By this, the division of the path is indicated by "twice";
by this also, the absence of obstruction to action is indicated;
and [the intention] "we shall enjoy" is indicated.

By [Pāṇini 1.3.66], the ātmanepada ending is applied; by [8.2.30], the letter *g* is substituted; and by [8.4.54] (*khari ca*), the *g* is changed to *k*, resulting in *adhyaimahi*. Regarding *apibāma*: the ending *mahiṅ* is used, followed by the augment *āṭ* by [6.4.72]; then, by [6.1.87] (*āṭaśca*), vṛddhi is applied, and by [6.1.74], the semivowel substitution (*yaṇ*) occurs for the prefix. Thus, *apibāma*.

By the rule *pāghrādisūtra* [Pāṇini 7.3.78], there is the substitution of *piba*; by the rule *sārvadhātuka-ārdhadhātukayoḥ* [Pāṇini 7.3.84], there is the elision of the *sakāra*. "We shall eat" (*bhoktāsmahe*) is in the *luṭ* (periphrastic future) tense.

Regarding the statement, "And he will explain the specific detail therein," [it refers to] the rule *anahorātrāṇām* (Pāṇini 2.4.29). The compound *kālamaryādāvibhāge sati* is a *dvandva* formed by the conjunction of the words *maryādā* and *vibhāga*.
Through this, there is a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*) with the word *kāla*.
Regarding the phrase "and of them":
it is appropriate that there is a prohibition of division with respect to them by means of those [actions], because the division is related to them.
However, when there is a division of another [object] by means of them, then it is not appropriate, for in that case the division is not related to them.
What then? It is that which possesses a relationship [to the action] as it is being divided (*vibhajyamāna*).

Even so, because the division is performed by day and night, the relationship [of the place] to the action does indeed exist; since the cause is related to its effect (*naimittika*), there is no fault.

If the statement were for the purpose of prohibiting [division] by day and night, then by implication (*sāmarthyāt*) a prohibition of the division of time alone would be understood, and not the division of space, for there is no connection between the division of space and day and night. Therefore, he says: "The separation of the *yoga* (rule) is for the sake of what follows."
The purpose of the subsequent sūtra is so that the division [of the rule] may apply only to time (*kāla*), and not to place (*deśa*).
[In the example] *abhuñjmahi*, there is the elision of the vowel *a* according to Pāṇini 6.4.111. [The phrase] "an illustration of the threefold rule" refers to this.

In that regard, in the first [case], there is a division of time expressed by another word into days and nights; in the second, there is a division of time expressed as "day and night" by means of time expressed by another word; in the third, there is a division of time expressed as "day and night" by means of time expressed as "night.
"In every way" (*sarvathā*) means by every manner.

The meaning of the word *sarvathā* (in every respect) is as follows: whether the division of another [period] is by means of days and nights (*ahorātra*), or whether those [days and nights] themselves are divided by something else, or even if they are divided by days and nights themselves—in all these cases, there is a prohibition.

Regarding the phrase "contact with days and nights" (*ahorātrasaṃsparśa*): the connection of days and nights with a division is "contact with days and nights. It is stated that "in all instances, suffixes [indicating] non-recent time (*anadyatana*) should be cited as examples."

Regarding the "past not of today" (*bhūtānadyatana*): in all such cases, the *luṅ* [aorist] should be cited, as in "we were engaged in study there" (*tatra yuktā adhyaimahi*) or "we ate rice there" (*tatraudanam abhuñjmahi*).

Regarding the "future not of today" (*bhaviṣyadanadyatana*), however, the *luṭ* [periphrastic future] should be cited in all such cases, as in "we shall be engaged in study there" (*tatra yuktā adhyetāsmahe*) or "we shall eat rice there" (*tatraudanaṃ bhoktāsmaha*).
The phrase "and so forth" (*ityevamādikam*) includes, by means of the word "etc. (*ādi*), rules such as "the *liṅ* [optative] is used after 'how' (*katham*)" (Pāṇini 3.3.143), and others.
"Due to some deficiency" means due to the occurrence of adverse conditions or the lack of other necessary causes.
"It would have come about" [is the meaning].
The suffix *syap* is applied by [Pāṇini 3.1.33].
The elision of the vowel *i* occurs by [Pāṇini 6.4.100],
resulting in "āhvāsyat."
The root *hveñ* (listed as 1008 in the Dhātupāṭha) is used in the sense of "rivalry" (*spardhā*) and "sound" (*śabda*).
Regarding the example *paryāsiṣyata* found in the Kāśikā,
it refers to the root *ās* (listed as 1021 in the Dhātupāṭha) in the sense of "sitting" (*upaveśana*), which is marked as *anudātta*.
In that context, "that which has become the cause" (kāśikā) means "that which has become the cause of that.
It is the cause of the cart's overturning.
By this, he demonstrates the relationship between cause and effect (*hetu-hetumadbhāva*) as the basis for the inferential mark (*liṅga*).
Regarding the phrase "having understood the sign and the signified":

having repeatedly observed previously that when Kamala was called, the cart did not turn over, one understands—by means of a logical mark (*liṅga*)—that even a future calling of Kamala will be the cause of the cart not turning over.
Furthermore, the logical mark (*liṅga*) is the common property (*dharma*) of "the calling of Kamala."
"And there is the 'transgression' (*atipatita*) of that. This refers to the transgression of Kamalaka’s summons and the overturning of the cart.
