Therein, the transgression of Kamalaka’s summons is understood through signs such as Kamalaka’s departure to another region; the transgression of the overturning of the cart is understood here through the loading of heavy cargo onto the cart and so forth.

"From this statement" means from such statements as "if he had invited Kamalaka," and so forth. Now, for what purpose is the mention of *kriyā* (action)? It need not be stated that "the conditional suffix *lṛṅ* occurs when there is non-occurrence (*atipatti*) of the condition for the optative (*liṅ*)," because even without the mention of *kriyā*, the specific meaning "when there is non-occurrence of the meaning of the verbal root" would be obtained due to the governing context of the verbal root (*dhātu-adhikāra*). Therefore, one might think the mention of *kriyā* is redundant. This is not so;

for while it is heard that "it occurs when there is the condition for *liṅ*," since the connection with what is currently under discussion is stronger than the connection with what has already passed, it is understood that the non-occurrence must be of that very thing which constitutes the condition for *liṅ*.

Consequently, by the rule "after *uta* and *api* when they are semantically connected" (Pāṇini 3.3.152), the suffix *liṅ* would undesirably apply both when there is the expression of semantic capacity (*sāmarthya*) and when there is the expression of possibility (*atipatti*).
Therefore, the mention of "action" (*kriyā*) must be made. Starting from "after *uta* and *api*" and so forth:
this prescription of the suffix *lṛṅ* applies to those conditions for *liṅ* beginning with the rule "after *uta* and *api* when they are semantically connected" (3.3.152).
He asks, "Whence is this? and says: "Previously," and so forth.

Since it will be stated later that "[the suffix *liṅ* is used] when [an action] is prior" (Pāṇini 3.3.141), then by the principle of elimination (*pāriśeṣya*), the prescription of *liṅ* for the past tense remains restricted only to those rules beginning with "[the suffix *liṅ* is used] when [an action] has been completed" (Pāṇini 3.3.141). However, it does not apply to cases such as "he has eaten," and so forth.
He demonstrates the conditional (kriyātipatti) [usage] with the rule "vā ā utāpyoḥ. By this, he shows the elision (praśleṣa) of the particle *aṅ*.

If there were an elision of *aṅ* here, then the rule "vā utāpyoḥ" would not apply; for once the guṇa substitution has occurred by virtue of the subsequent rule, the preceding [vowel] ought to undergo vṛddhi [with the following vowel]. There is no fault here, however, because this is a Vedic-style (sautra) formulation.

By virtue of its being an irregular formation (*nipātana*), a single substitution (*ekādeśa*) will first be made with the preceding element, and then *aguṇa* [substitution] will be applied with the following element according to Pāṇini 6.1.87.

Now, one might object: when used in conjunction with *āṅ*, the ablative case is prescribed by the rule "the ablative is used with *apa*, *āṅ*, and *pari*" (Pāṇini 2.3.10); however, the ablative does not occur after *āṅ* when it follows a word, because *āṅ* is not a nominal stem (*aprātipadika*).
[This applies to the examples beginning with] "in the sense of a limit" (*maryādāyām*), and so forth.

If this *āṅ* were used in the sense of "inclusivity" (*abhividhi*), then by the rule *utāpyoḥ samarthayoḥ* [Pāṇini 3.3.152], the potential mood (*liṅ*) would optionally apply; however, it is intended to be mandatory.
Therefore, this *āṅ* denotes a limit (*maryādā*), not inclusivity.
And thus, "it remains as it was obtained."
"The optative suffix (*liṅ*) and so forth; because of the inclusion of the word 'or' (*vā*). [Objection: "It would not apply to the general time (*kālasāmānya*).

By this, he indicates that this is a rule for the general time by showing the recurrence (*anuvṛtti*) of terms such as *bhaviṣyati*, which denote specific times—namely, "those prescribed for specific times.
For the *laṅ* and *liṭ* are prescribed for the past as a specific time, while the *luṅ* and *lṛṭ* are prescribed for the future.

The present tense suffix *laṭ*, being prescribed for all [tenses] in common with time (*kālasāmānye*), sublates those [other tenses] due to its higher priority, as in the example "he causes to sacrifice" (*yājayati*). This is formed by adding the causative marker *ṇic* to the root *yaj*, followed by *laṭ*.

"Because of the absence of a condition for the conditional (liṅ)" means that although the non-occurrence of an action (kriyātipatti) is intended here because the conditions for the conditional—such as cause and effect—are absent, nevertheless the conditional suffix does not occur. "The mention of 'optionally' (vibhāṣā)" and so forth:
the mention of "optionally" is for the purpose of preventing the sublation of those [suffixes] such as the conditional which are prescribed for other times.

If this is so, the particle *ca* (and) is redundant; for by the very mention of the option (*vibhāṣā*), the present tense (*laṭ*) would indeed be established as not being set aside. True, it is established in the sense of the present time; however, it is not established for other times. For in that case, when the word *katham* is used as an attendant term (*upapada*), there is no application of the present tense; how then could it be established by the mention of the option? Therefore, the particle *ca* must be employed for the sake of the present tense. "He should cause to sacrifice" (*yājayet*)—this is the optative (*liṅ*).
"yājayiṣyati" (he will cause to sacrifice)— this is the *lṛṭ* [future tense].
"ayīyajat" (he caused to sacrifice repeatedly)— this is the [periphrastic] perfect.

In *ayājayat* (he caused to sacrifice), there is the substitution of *luṅ*, the *cleḥ caṅ* [3.1.44], shortening before *ṇi* when followed by *caṅ* [7.4.1], elision of the *ṇi* suffix, reduplication according to *caṅi* [6.1.11], and the change of *a* to *i* according to *sanyataḥ* [7.4.79]. Similarly, in *yājayāñcakāra* (he performed the act of sacrificing repeatedly).

The *liṭ* [perfect] suffix: by the rule *kāspratyayādām* [Pāṇini 3.1.35], the suffix *ām* is added; by *āmaḥ* [2.4.81], there is elision (*luk*) of the *liṭ*; because that [suffix] is an indeclinable (*avyaya*), there is elision of the case endings (*sub-luk*); by the rule *kṛñ ca* [3.1.40] and others, the root *kṛ* is employed after the *liṭ* followed by *ām*; for this, the suffix *ṇal* is applied, followed by reduplication, the operations pertaining to the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa-kārya*), and the substitution of *ā* by the rule *ayāmanta* [6.4.55].

In this context, how is it that there is a cause for the *liṅ* [optative], and what is this "censure" (*garhā*)? Since the *liṅ* is prescribed for censure, when there is a desire to express the past tense, the *lṛṅ* (conditional) occurs in the case of the non-occurrence of the action (*kriyātipatti*), because of the rule *bhūte ca* (Pāṇini 3.3.141), which operates while the term "past" is in effect. When there is a desire to express the future tense, the *lṛṅ* must necessarily occur everywhere, because of the rule *liṅnimitte lṛṅ kriyātipattau* (Pāṇini 3.3.139), which operates while the term "future" is in effect. Regarding the phrase "in the case of a word ending in *kim*" (*kiṃvṛtte*):
by the inclusion of the word *vṛtta*, that which ends in its specific case-ending is understood.

Regarding the rule *ḍataratamau ca*: why was it not stated simply as "in the case of an interrogative particle (*kiṃvṛtta*), [the affix] *lṛṭ* [is used]"? For *liṅ* is the subject under discussion, and by the word *ca* ("and"), its inclusion alone would have been understood; so what is the purpose of mentioning *liṅ*? To this he says: "The mention of *liṅ*, etc.

For if the mention of *liṅ* were absent, just as *liṅ* would be included by *ca* due to being the subject under discussion, *laṭ* would also be included, since that too is indeed the subject under discussion.

Therefore, the mention of *liṅ* was made in order to exclude *laṭ*. Here, there are two meanings and likewise two suffixes; consequently, someone might have the misconception that they must correspond according to their respective order (*yathāsaṃkhyena*). To dispel that, he says "the one with more syllables" (*bahvacaḥ*), and so forth. For the word *amarṣa* has fewer syllables than the word *anavaklṛpti*; thus, although its placement first would have been required by the rule *alpāctaram* [Pāṇini 2.2.34], the fact that the word *anavaklṛpti*, which has more syllables, is placed first here demonstrates that this is intended to show an intentional deviation from the general grammatical rule (*lakṣaṇavyabhicārārthatā*).

Just as here the rule for prior placement (*pūrvanipāta*) does not apply to its own domain due to deviation, so too is the rule for correspondence in order (*yathāsaṃkhya*). Therefore, there is no correspondence in order. The inclusion of the word "also" (*api*) is so that [the rule] may apply even in the case of an interrogative particle (*kiṃvṛtta*); otherwise, if only "non-interrogative" (*akiṃvṛtta*) were mentioned, it would not apply in the case of an interrogative particle.

If, as in the case of the rule *upakādibhyo 'nyatarasyām* [Pāṇini 2.4.69], the mention of *advandva* (non-dvandva) there is for the purpose of terminating the governing scope (*adhikāra*) of *dvandva*, so too here the mention of *akiṃvṛtta* (not a *kiṃvṛtta*) would be for the purpose of terminating the governing scope of *kiṃvṛtta*. If it is explained that once that [scope] has ceased, both suffixes will apply to both *kiṃvṛtta* and *akiṃvṛtta*, then the inclusion of the word *api* could indeed be omitted. Nevertheless, it is included for the sake of clarity. As for the statement, "the word *kiṃkila* is a compound": [it refers to the fact that it is treated as a single unit].

By this, he refutes the idea that the words *kiṃ* and *kila* are each individually an *upapada*. Why, then, are they not each individually an *upapada*? Because the word *kiṃ* alone cannot function in the senses of "impossibility" (*anavaklṛpti*) and "intolerance" (*amarṣa*), whereas it can do so when combined [with *kila*]. Regarding the statement "it is an exception to the gender," it refers to what was previously applicable. [The phrase] "there is no cause here for the gender" [indicates that the rule does not apply].

Because [the suffix] *lṛṭ* alone is prescribed. "An exception to *lṛṭ*" refers to that which is obtained by the rule beginning with *anavakḷpti* (Pāṇini 3.3.145). "[There should be] an addition for *yadā* and *yadi*" means...
The purpose of the term *upasaṃkhyāna* (supplementary addition) is to ensure that the conditional suffix *liṅ* occurs and the conditional suffix *lṛṅ* does not.

Regarding this, the following is the explanation: from the rule [Pāṇini 3.3.145] beginning with *anavaklṛpty-*, the word *api* is carried over here as well; it serves the purpose of including what has not been explicitly mentioned, and by means of it, the suffix will also apply after *yat* and *yadi*. Thus, it is said: "it is an exception (*apavāda*) to the future suffix *lṛṭ*."

[This refers to] that which was obtained by the rule *anavakḷpty-ādi-sūtra* [Pāṇini 3.3.145]. Now, one might ask: "Why was the inclusion of *yat* and *yatra* not made in the preceding rule itself; what is the purpose of this separation of rules (*yogavibhāga*)? To this he says: "The separation of rules is for the sake of the subsequent [rules]. This is so that only *yat* and *yatra* may carry over into the following rules, and not *jātu* and *yad*.
"The rule of correspondence by number (*yathāsaṃkhya*) is not intended here," because of the very same sign of deviation from the [usual] definition mentioned previously.
And that— namely, the prior placement of the polysyllabic term— is the sign of deviation from the definition throughout this entire section, and not merely in that specific sūtra.
Alternatively—since there is no svarita accent here to indicate the sense of "correspondence in order," the correspondence does not occur.

For it was stated previously: "Correspondence in order occurs by means of the mark of the svarita. By the rule beginning with *yaccayatrābhyām*, he shows the remainder as being dependent on *yat* and *yatra*;
the remainder cannot be understood as being dependent on "wonder" (*citrīkaraṇa*), because "wonder" is what is being marked by the svarita accent in this context.
Regarding the form *ārokṣyati*:
the root *ruh* (Dhātupāṭha 859) means "to sprout from a seed" and "to appear. [The substitution of] *ḍha* for *ha* is prescribed by Pāṇini 8.2.31, and [the subsequent change] by 8.2.41.

Regarding the phrase "it would be a marvel if he were to eat": here, a marvel is understood in the sense of impossibility (*anavaklṛpti*). Since the *lṛṭ* (future) suffix is prohibited when a marvel serves as the cause, the rule "In the prescription of the *liṅ* after *jātu* and *yad*, there is an addition [of the *liṅ*] for *yadā* and *yadi*" (Vārttika 331) applies; thus, the *liṅ* occurs in the sense of impossibility. The term "of two capable [things]" (*samarthayoḥ*) is used.
In this context, semantic competency (*sāmarthya*) based on grammatical roots (*dhātu*) is not relied upon;
for that [competency] is already obtained simply by virtue of those two being *upapadas*.
Therefore, what is understood here as "competent" (*samartha*) refers to mutual semantic competency as expressed by words.

Furthermore, neither of those two definitions—namely, that characterized by mutual expectancy (*vyapekṣā*) nor that characterized by unification of meaning (*ekārthībhāva*)—is possible here; for both of them would apply [to the same case] alternatively. Therefore, the capacity (*sāmarthya*) defined as having a common meaning (*samānārtha*) is what is expressed here by the word "capable" (*samartha*). To this end, he says: "The two of these have a common meaning. Regarding the form *kuryāt*: when the suffix *u* is added, there is *guṇa* substitution and the replacement of *r* (*raparatva*); then, by the rule *ata ut sārvadhātuke* [Pāṇini 6.4.110], there is the substitution of *u*, and by *ye ca* [Pāṇini 6.4.109], there is the elision of the vowel *u*. [The example is: "May you eat at my pleasure. (*kāmo me bhuñjīta bhavān*).
By this [statement], he reveals his own intention to another: "The determination of fitness.
Fitness (*yogyatā*) means capacity (*sāmarthya*); the determination (*adhyavasāna*) of that [fitness] is what is meant.
That by which it is determined or ascertained is the "determination of fitness," which is knowledge; it is called "possibility" (*sambhāvanā*).
To clarify that same point by means of another formulation, he says: "the conviction regarding capacity" (*śakti-śraddhāna*).
Capacity is efficacy; that knowledge by which it is believed is "the conviction regarding capacity.
"That" refers to this [conviction].

Regarding "sambhāvanam paryāptyā": this means by way of capacity. By this, he shows that the word *alam* used here is understood in the sense of sufficiency (*paryāpti*), and not in the sense of adornment (*bhūṣaṇa*) and so forth.
"Capable" (*paryāptam*) means empowered, that is, competent to accomplish its own function.
Its own function, moreover, is the discernment of an object contrary [to what was previously perceived].
"Unfailing" (*avitatha*) means that its object exists;
by this, it is accepted that its meaning is precisely that of "sufficiency" (*paryāpti*).
For it is thus that its object becomes the opposite [of what is commonly held]: if it is non-erroneous because its object is existent, and not otherwise. "Alamaḥ" means "of the word *alam*."

Why is this so? Because by means of the particle *iti*, the word *alaṃ* is established as having the meaning of "word" (*śabda-pada-artha*) rather than being displaced from its status of having the meaning of "object" (*artha-pada-artha*).

The meaning of *alam* as "sufficiency" (*sambhāvana*) does not admit of a qualifier; consequently, would not the statement—"Now, this *alam* is qualified"—be contradicted? This is not a fault. A repetition of the word *alam* will be made; therein, one instance of it, being included in the sūtra, will have the sense of the word *artha*; while the other instance, having fallen away from the status of the word *artha* due to its connection with the particle *iti*, is understood here to have the sense of the word *śabda*.
[This is indicated by the phrase] "the sense of *ca*" (*cārtha*). This follows either from the sense or from the context.

"And it is not employed [in the *Kāśikā*]—it is not employed," because the meaning has already been understood. "In such a case where there is the condition of possibility (*saṃbhāvanopādhika*)—[as stated in the *Kāśikā*] 'where there is the condition of the possibility of action' (*kriyāsambhāvanopādhike*).
That whose object is characterized by the possibility of action as its specific condition is described in that way.
"Even one might split a mountain with one's head"—as before [Pāṇini 6.4.111].
Here, the capacity for splitting a mountain which is attributed to a man is possible only through his knowledge; because it is not false, this attribution is sufficient.

"He will probably go"—here, there is a possibility (*sambhāvanā*) understood from the word *prāyas*, but there is no sense of "sufficiency" (*alam-artha*). Therefore, when the intention is to express future time, only the suffix *lṛṭ* occurs, not *liṅ*. [The *Kāśikā* states: "In the future tense. This is to be understood as "it is desired."

But how can the future tense be obtained through the term *vibhāṣā*, given that there is no mention of the future tense here in the sūtra even without the mention of *vibhāṣā*? To this he says: "Because the mention of *vibhāṣā* follows [from the previous rule].
By that, the *liṅ* suffix is obtained as *vibhāṣā*.

Since the word *liṅ* continues from the sūtra beginning with "after *uta* and *api*" (Pāṇini 3.3.152), the fact that *liṅ* is mentioned again [in this rule] serves to indicate that the future tense is obtained.

Furthermore, the purpose of including the term *liṅ* [in the rule] is so that [the suffix] may occur in a specific time, namely the future. Consequently, in examples such as "he kills, therefore he flees" (*hanti iti palāyate*), when the present tense is intended, only the *laṭ* suffix occurs.
In this case, the killing is the cause (*hetu*), and the fleeing is the effect of the cause (*hetumat*).

In *palāyate*, the substitution of *l* for *t* is applied by [Pāṇini 8.2.19]. In *bhuṅktām*, once the substitution of *e* for *et* has been made, *ām* is added. It should be stated that this applies when there is the expression of one's own desire (*kāmapravedana*).

The meaning is that this form of the rule—namely, "these two, the optative (*liṅ*) and the imperative (*loṭ*), occur in the expression (*pravedane*) or manifestation (*prakāśane*) of desire (*kāmasya*)"—is to be explained in this way.

The explanation here is as follows: the term "expression of desire" (*kāmapravedana*) is carried over from [Pāṇini 3.3.153]; therefore, these two suffixes occur only when there is an expression of desire.

In this context, what is the purpose of mentioning *liṅ*? Why not simply say "after verbs meaning 'desire,' there is also *loṭ*"? Even if *liṅ* were brought forward by the particle *ca*, it would still be the previously mentioned *liṅ*. This is not the case; for it has been stated that [the use of *loṭ*] is optional (*vibhāṣā*) regarding future time. Therefore, if that [previous rule] were to follow, there would be an optionality. To prevent that, the mention of *liṅ* is made once again. Since *tumun* is prescribed after those [verbs] for which *liṅ* and *loṭ* were previously obtained, it is said: "It depends solely upon the verbal root (*prakṛti*) of *tumun*."

Since the suffix *tumun* is prescribed after a verbal root (*dhātu*), by virtue of proximity (*pratyāsatti*), it is understood that the identity of the agent (*samānakartṛkatva*) must depend upon that very root—namely, that the agent of the base form (*prakṛti*) of *tumun* must also be the agent of the verbs expressing desire. For example, in "he desires to eat" (*icchati bhoktum*), the agent of the verb *iṣ* (desire) is the same as the agent of *bhuj* (to eat); thus, there exists here a case of identical agents. In such instances, the suffixes *liṅ* and *loṭ* would otherwise apply by virtue of being subsequent rules (*paratvāt*). To prevent this from occurring, [the rule for *tumun*] is stated. Furthermore, the suffix *ṇvul* should not apply; this is the purpose [of the rule]. For example: "He desires Devadatta while he is eating" (*devadattaṃ bhuñjānam icchati*).

In this case, Devadatta is the agent of the action of "being" (*bhūj*), whereas he is other than the agent of "desiring" (*icchati*); thus, there is no common agency (*samānakartṛkatva*). Therefore, when the present tense is intended, only the suffix *laṭ* occurs.
Regarding the phrase "due to non-expression" (*anabhidhānāt*):
for here, the intended meaning cannot be expressed by the suffix *tumun* as it arises [in its place].
And [the suffixes] characterized by verbal expression consist of primary derivatives (kṛt), secondary derivatives (taddhita), and compounds (samāsa).
Alternatively, it means "due to non-expression";
that is, because there is an absence of the expression "desiring to act" (icchan kartum).

For it is the well-known usages of the world that are subsequently explained in the treatise, and not things such as "one might wish to do," which are not so established in common usage. Regarding the example "bhuñjīyādhīya" (he should eat while studying), [the suffix] *iṭ* is replaced by *at* according to Pāṇini 3.4.106. But why is this stated, since the optative (*liṅ*) will occur here by the rule of non-identity of form (*vāsarūpa-vidhi*) alone? This is not the case; because the optative and imperative (*loṭ*), being exceptions, would otherwise apply and thus obstruct [the formation], the suffix *tumun* is prescribed for the purpose of setting aside those two.
Since it is sublated by that [rule], just as the *loṭ* [suffix] does not occur, so too the *liṅ* [suffix] would not occur either.
Therefore, this is stated for the purpose of prescribing the *liṅ*. "The separation of the rule (*yogavibhāga*) is for the sake of what follows."

In the subsequent sūtra, it is intended that only *liṅ* (the optative suffix) should carry over, and not *tumun* (the infinitive suffix). Regarding "instigation" (*preraṇa*), it means an injunction (*niyoga*). "Invitation" (*nimantraṇa*) is the performance of an injunction.

Even in the absence of desire, when there is the certain necessity (*avaśyambhāvena*) of performing an action because its non-performance would result in the loss of merit (*adharma*), that performance is called an invitation.
"Acting according to one's will" (*kāmacārakaraṇam*): "acting according to one's will" (*kāmacāra*) means the movement of desire (*icchāpracāra*).
That which is performed by means of that is the invitation (*āmantraṇam*).

This is what is meant: [the term] "invitation" (*āmantraṇam*) refers to that which is performed solely by desire and not by lack of desire, because there would be no fault even in its non-performance.

In this context, would this meaning—namely, the injunction (*vidhi*) and so forth—be a qualifier of the meaning of the verbal root (*prakṛti*), or the meaning of the suffix (*pratyaya*), or a qualifier of the meaning of the suffix? If the first alternative were adopted, then it would not be established in cases where the verbal root itself expresses meanings such as injunction; for example, in *vidadhyāt* ("one should perform"), *nimantrayet* ("one should invite"), *āmantrayet* ("one should address"), or *adhīcchet* ("one should desire to study"). For in these instances, there are no other qualifiers such as injunction existing apart from the meaning of the root. This defect would have to be remedied. Even if it were remedied, there would be excessive complexity in comprehension (*pratipatti-gaurava*).

Now, as for the second [alternative]: having seen the defect in these two [positions]—namely, that the optative (*vidhi*) and other suffixes would be the denoters of the meanings of the suffixes, which are the state (*bhāva*), the object (*karman*), and the agent (*kartṛ*)—he resorts to the third position and says: "And the optative and others," etc.
Those very meanings of the suffixes are the state, the object, and the agent;

since the suffix is prescribed for them by the rule *laḥ karmaṇi ca* [Pāṇini 3.4.69], he considers that this meaning consisting of the optative and so forth is their qualifier, and thus says: "In those qualified by the optative and others," etc.
By this word "etcetera" (ādi), the inclusion of invitations and so forth is intended;
by the second [word], the inclusion of the states of being and the object;
and [the example] is "he sat."
Due to the property of beginning with a vowel (*adāditvāt*), there is the elision (*luk*) of *śap* [by Pāṇini 2.4.72].
Thus, "adhyāpayet" [is formed];

here, as before, there is the substitution of *ātv* and the elision of *śap*. If the *loṭ* suffix occurs only in the sense of injunctions (*vidhi*) and so forth, for what purpose is this split of the rule (*yogavibhāga*) made? To this he says: "The split of the rule is for the sake of the subsequent [rules]."
In the subsequent sūtra, so that only the *loṭ* [suffix] may be carried over and not the *liṅ*,
[the example] "karotu" is given;
for it has been stated [in Pāṇini 3.4.86] that "eruḥ" [replaces the *loṭ* ending].
Regarding "adhyāyai":

by [Pāṇini 3.4.92], the augment āṬ is applied; when the substitution of *e* for *ṭi* is made, [by 3.4.93] *e* becomes *ai*, and [by 6.1.87] there is vṛddhi due to the preceding āṬ, resulting in the guṇa and ay-ādeśa substitutions for the base. Regarding "kāryaḥ":
by [Pāṇini 3.1.124], the suffix *ṇyat* is applied after roots ending in *ṛ* or a consonant.

Regarding the word "kṛtyaḥ," the suffix *kyap* is applied by [Pāṇini 3.1.120]. The question "For what purpose is this? and so forth expresses an objection (*dveṣya*). The response beginning with "Because it is prescribed as a specific rule" (*viśeṣavihita*) and so forth provides the resolution (*parīhāra*).

For the *kṛtya* suffixes are prescribed generally, whereas the *loṭ* suffix is prescribed for specific meanings such as command (*praiṣa*) and so forth. Therefore, since they are specifically prescribed for those [specific] domains like command, the *kṛtya* suffixes would be sublated in those contexts; hence, it is restated [here].

He refutes the resolution [offered] by the rule *vāsarūpa* and others. With the words "If this is so," etc., he demonstrates that the prescription of the *kṛtya* suffixes for commands (*preṣa*) and the like serves as an *jñāpaka* (indicative evidence). Now, an *jñāpaka* occurs only when there is no other purpose; but here there is indeed a purpose. What is it? That by means of which the *kṛtya* suffixes would apply to commands and the like according to a restriction, and not elsewhere? This is not so; because such a restriction is undesired.
For *kṛtya* suffixes are seen elsewhere as well—as in "it is to be dried by grass" (*tṛṇena śoṣyam*) and "it is to be awakened by a wise man" (*budhena bodhyam*).
That [usage] would not be established if there were a restriction [to the sense of command], for in these cases, commands and the like are not understood.
Therefore, a restriction is not intended here; nor is it proper in the grammatical treatise to assume a formation whose meaning has not been specified (Bhāṣya on Pāṇini 3.4.69).
Therefore, it is logical that this is merely an indicator (*jñāpaka*), because the prescription of the *kṛtya* suffixes necessarily occurs.
By the inclusion of the word "necessarily" (*avaśyam*), he shows that [the rule] does not apply in any case whatsoever.

And this is obtained even from what follows the heading of *strī* (feminine), since the rule of non-identity of form (*vāsarūpavidhi*) is sometimes understood through the formal promise (*pratijñāna*) of the *svarita* accent.

Therefore, when words such as *kāla* (time) and others are used as upapadas, the suffix *lyuṭ* also occurs by virtue of the rule regarding dissimilar forms (*vāsarūpavidhi*), as in *kālo bhojanasya* ("it is time for eating").
However, if the rule regarding dissimilar forms did not apply in every respect, then only the suffix *tumun* would invariably occur by [Pāṇini 3.3.167].
By the statement "some say," it is implied that others do not accept a distinction between these two cases. And [the phrase] "and according to what is obtained" [is used].

"Loṭ and the kṛtya suffixes"— this is an exception (*apavāda*) to the *liṅ* [optative] and the kṛtyas. "An exception to the *liṅ*"— this refers to that which is obtained by the rule concerning injunctions (*vidhi*) and so forth, which is prescribed immediately following [the present rule].
In *adhyāpaya*,
the substitution of *hi* for the imperative suffix *si* applies by Pāṇini 3.4.87, and its elision follows from 6.4.105. In *juhudhi*, the same applies.

The substitution of *dhi* [for *hi*] occurs by the rule *6.4.101*. The phrase "the mention of *praiṣa* (command) and so forth is connected here" means that if a command (*praiṣa*) and such are not understood here, then the substitution does not take place there; this is the intended meaning.

When it is said, "It is time for eating," a command is understood from that, namely, "May you eat. Therefore, with the intention that the mention of *praiṣa* and so forth continues to apply here [and thus the substitution *dhi* should occur], he asks: "Why does it not occur here? and so on.

It might be argued: "Because of the evidence (*jñāpaka*) provided by the prescription of the *kṛtya* suffixes for commands (*praiṣa*) and so forth—which indicate that feminine gender is intended—the rule of non-identity of form (*vāsarūpa*) does not apply even after [the present sūtra]. What then? It is *anitya* (not universally obligatory). Therefore, it occurs in some instances. And this was already stated previously in the passage beginning with "In that case, this indicates... (Kāśikāvṛtti on 3.3.163). "An exception to *tumun*" means an exception to what was obtained by the preceding sūtra. "Voḍhavyaḥ" (to be carried).
The rules *ho ḍhaḥ* [Pāṇini 8.2.31], *haśi ca* [8.2.40], *vā śari* [8.4.41], *ḍho dhe lopaḥ* [8.3.13], and *lopaḥ śākalyasya* [6.1.127] must be applied.
The objection beginning with "Now" (*atha*) and so forth is to be rejected;
the rebuttal beginning with "This which... (*yo'yam*) and so forth is the resolution.

It has already been stated that the rule regarding optional forms (*vāsarūpavidhi*) does not necessarily apply after the section on *strī* (feminine suffixes). Regarding the word "necessary" (*āvaśyakam*), the suffix *vuñ* is added because it belongs to the *manojñādi* group.
As for the phrase "this is a limiting condition" (*upādhirayam*), [it refers to the fact that the application of the suffix is contingent upon a specific state].
The meaning is that it is a qualifier of the sense of the suffix (*pratyaya*).

Regarding the statement "not an *upapada*": the intention is that if it were an *upapada*, the forms would not be *kārī* and *hārī*. This has already been established under [Pāṇini 3.1.125] that an *upādhi* is necessarily required, whereas an *upapada* is not; therefore, here too, one must state that the status of being an *upādhi* is necessary in that same manner.

Because it is taught together with that [word *saha*], the state of being a debtor (*ādhamaṇrya*) is also merely an attribute (*upādhi*), not a subordinate term (*upapada*). If one were to think: "If an attribute that is necessary is not a subordinate term, then by the rule [Pāṇini 2.2.19] there would be no compound; nor is there any other rule by which a compound could occur here," he says in response to such a person: "The compound is formed because it belongs to the class beginning with *mayūravyaṃsaka*," as in the example *saharūpaṃ dāyī*. Since the genitive case is prohibited by the rule [Pāṇini 2.3.70]—"The sixth case [is not used] after a word ending in *akan* when expressing a future action or a debt"—the second case alone is employed. The objection beginning with "For what purpose... and so forth is raised.
The rebuttal is: "by that which is specifically prescribed. The dismantling of that rebuttal is: "in the case of the agent," and so forth.
The support of the rebuttal according to the opinion of others is: "some say," and so forth. [The example is:
"bhavyageyam" (that which is to be performed or sung).

"For words that function with reference to wholes also function with reference to their parts" (Śābarabhāṣya on Pāṇini 2.1.56). Thus, words such as *bhavya* and *geya* here refer to the verbal action (*kṛtya*) which constitutes a part [of the whole process].
Regarding the phrase "denoting the agent":
by the rule for *bhavya*, *geya*, and so forth, these are optionally prescribed as irregular forms (*nipātana*) denoting the agent.
The division of the *yoga* (rule-segmentation) is for the sake of what follows. This [term] is also a qualifier of the meaning of the base (*prakṛti*).

This is stated with the intention of the preceding [rule] in order to exclude the status of being a *upapada*. Regarding "he may live" (*jīvyāt*): there is the elision of the *s* by the rule *skoḥ* [Pāṇini 8.2.29].

Now, for what purpose is the mention of *liṅ*? [One might argue: "It is already established by the rule *loṭ ca* [Pāṇini 3.3.162]; for by the force of the particle *ca*, *liṅ* will also be drawn along [into the scope of the rule]. This cannot be so; for just as *liṅ* is drawn along by the particle *ca*, the *kṛtya* suffixes would likewise be drawn along.

[Objection: But the *kṛtyas* will be excluded; once they are excluded, the particle *ca* will serve only to draw along *liṅ*. [Reply: This is true; however, if their exclusion were understood in this way, there would be an exclusion of *liṅ* as well.
If it is argued that [the *liṅ*] will continue to apply by virtue of the commentary (*vyākhyāna*), even so, there would be an excessive burden on the understanding (*pratipatti-gaurava*).
Therefore, for the sake of avoiding the burden of [repeated] practice, it is proper that it remain exactly as it was originally arranged.

Why was the term *āśis* (benediction) not included right here in the rule concerning injunctions and so forth (*vidhyādi-sūtra*) [Pāṇini 3.3.161]? For in that way, the mention of the optative (*liṅ*) and imperative (*loṭ*) would not have been necessary. This is not possible; if it were read in the rule concerning injunctions and so forth, then by rules such as [Pāṇini 3.3.165], there would be an annulment (*bādhā*) due to their higher status (*paratva*). However, since it is placed here, this present rule will be the annulor of those [subsequent rules] due to its higher status; thus, this undesirable consequence does not arise.

Furthermore, the mention of "benediction" (*āśis*) must necessarily be made for the sake of the subsequent rule—so that [the suffixes] may apply in the sense of a benediction according to Pāṇini 3.3.174. The phrase "by the aggregate" (*samudāyena*) means by the aggregate of the base (*prakṛti*) and the suffix (*pratyaya*).
By this, he shows that the technical designation (*saṃjñā*) has the aggregate as its condition.

Regarding the word *tanti*: since the root *tan* (meaning "to extend") is listed as [Dhātupāṭha 1463], the rule [Pāṇini 6.4.15] would require lengthening of the vowel, and the rule [Pāṇini 6.4.37] beginning with "anudāttopadeśa" would require the elision of the *anusvāra*; both of these are prohibited by the rule [Pāṇini 6.4.39]. Regarding the word *sāti*: [the same applies].

In *ṣaṇu* (meaning "to give," Dhātupāṭha 1464), there is the substitution of *ā* [for the vowel] by [Pāṇini 6.4.42]. Regarding *devadattaḥ*: after the root *ḍudāñ*, the substitute *dad* occurs in the case of the *niṣṭhā* suffix [by Pāṇini 7.4.46], and then the substitution of *t* for *d* occurs [by Pāṇini 8.4.54]. Regarding *mā karṣit*: [this is explained as follows].

> [[6.4.74]] Thus, there is an absence of the augment *aṭ*. That which has the word *sma* following it as its additional element after the root *māṅ* is described as such. Thus ends the third quarter of the third chapter in the *Kāśikā-vivaraṇapañjikā*, composed by the venerable Ācārya Jinendrabuddhi, who is a disciple of the Bodhisattvas. Regarding the statement "the word *dhātu* [is used] in the sense of the meaning of a root":
he demonstrates that, having applied a metaphorical designation (*upacāra*) of the expression to the expressed object, the "meaning of the root" (*dhātvartha*) is here indicated by the word *dhātu*.

This word *dhātu* (root) applies only to [the list of roots] beginning with *bhū*; for there can be no connection between another word and a word like *dhātu* that has already become subordinate within its own primary sense. Therefore, this word *dhātu* applies to the meaning of the root (*dhātvartha*) itself, not to the roots *bhū* and so on. Consequently, the phrase "connection with a root" (*dhātusambandha*) is understood to mean "connection with the meaning of a root. Thus he says: "The connection of the meanings of roots is 'dhātusambandha'.
But how is this connection? He says: "The relationship of qualifier and qualified (*viśeṣaṇaviśeṣyabhāva*)."
"Even those spoken at the wrong time," and so forth.

"Yathākāla" means one’s own proper time. The compound *yathākāla* is an *avyayībhāva* used in the sense of distribution (*vīpsā*), according to Pāṇini 2.1.7 (*yathā'sādṛśye*). Thus, "spoken at the proper time" is *yathākāloktāḥ*. The compound is formed by the rule of *yogavibhāga* (separation of rules) under Pāṇini 2.1.39 (*saptamī*). Those which are not spoken at the proper time are *ayathākāloktāḥ*.

This is what is meant: by their respective prescriptive rules, whatever suffixes have been prescribed for specific times, those suffixes remain grammatically correct even when applied at times other than those.

He shows examples such as *agniṣṭomayājī* and so forth. In all these cases, the meaning expressed by the verbal suffix (*tiṅanta*) is the qualificand (*viśeṣya*), while the meaning expressed by the nominal suffix (*subanta*) is the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*).

Regarding the statement, "One who has performed the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice" (*agniṣṭomayājī*), this is a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "one for whom the time [of the sacrifice] has passed. Its status as having a past time is due to the prescription of the suffix *ṇini* under the rule *bhūtādhikāre* (Pāṇini 3.2.85).
Regarding the phrase "janitā" (will be born), it refers to the future tense. It is a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "that which has a future time.
Its status as having a future time follows from the rule prescribing the suffix *lṛṭ* for the future not of today (*bhaviṣyadanadyatana*).
Regarding the word "tatra":
it is the locative case used in the sense of selection (*nirdhāraṇa*).
Between those two—past time and future time—that which is past time becomes grammatically correct when connected with future time.

In the case of "one who has performed the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice" (*agniṣṭomayājī*), although the past tense is connected with the future tense in the word "will be born" (*janitā*), it results in being understood as the future tense itself. In the second example as well, "done" (*kṛtaḥ*) is the past tense, because the suffix *niṣṭhā* is prescribed for the past;
"will be" (*bhavitā*) is the future tense, just as before.
In that regard, the past tense (*bhūtakāla*), even when connected with another [word], is grammatically correct.
In the third case as well, "future" (*bhāvī*) refers to the future tense; this is because of the rule: "[The suffix *luṭ* is used] for the future" (Pāṇini 3.3.3).
"Was" (*āsīt*) refers to the past tense; this is because the *laṅ* suffix is prescribed for the past not belonging to the current day (*bhūtānadyatana*).

In this regard, even a future time, when connected with a past time, becomes valid. Here, in the expression "the son of one who has performed the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice will be born," the past time, being connected with the future time, results in a future time.
Thus, the meaning understood here is: "He is his son who will sacrifice with the Agniṣṭoma.
Furthermore, a future time, when connected with a past time, does not attain the status of a past time; for the meaning understood here is not: "He is his son who has sacrificed with the Agniṣṭoma."

In the other two examples as well, the qualifier attains the time of the qualified; for in those cases, this meaning is understood: "That mat which will be made was that [which] he was about to make," and "That duty which had not yet come to be was that which existed.
How does this occur? Why does the reverse not happen? To this he says: "The qualifier, etc.
For a qualifier is a subordinate element (*guṇa*) because it exists for the sake of another; that is to say, it is not the primary element (*apradhāna*).
And that [auxiliary] must perform its service for the primary act, which is the qualificand.

Now, without abandoning its own time and without adopting the time of the primary, it is not capable of performing the act of assisting the primary; therefore, the time of the primary is maintained as the limit. Furthermore, the primary is the object to be assisted. It is not logical for the primary to adopt the time of the auxiliary; otherwise, if the time of the primary were to adopt the time of the auxiliary, then its status as the primary would be lost.

Therefore, no reversal occurs. Now, for what purpose is the mention of "affix" (*pratyaya*) [in this rule], since the term "affix" continues from the previous context? To this he says: "In the section concerning affixes," and so forth.

The previous mention of "affix" was connected with the verbal root (*dhātu*); therefore, when that is relied upon here, it results in the correctness of those affixes prescribed within the governing heading of the verbal root.
However, in this present mention of "affix," only the affix in general is intended; for that reason, the mention of "affix" is repeated.
Regarding the phrase "at a different time":
this means at a specific time, that is, at a time other than the present one.
The example given is "He was possessed of cows."

The term *gomān* (possessing cows) refers to the present time, because the suffix *matup* is prescribed by the rule *tad asya* [Pāṇini 5.2.94] and its successors, which takes the word *asti* (is) as expressing the present time. That [suffix], when connected with the past and future times, becomes grammatically correct. By stating "and this [serves to specify] the meaning of the base (*prakṛti*)," he thereby rejects [the view that it functions as] a subordinate word (*upapada*).
The intention is that if [the suffixes] were merely *upapadas*, they would not arise from the root alone—as in the example "āditya.

In this regard, there are two positions: either *hi* and *sva* would be substitutes for the *tiṅ* endings, or they would be substitutes for the *loṭ* ending. Now, one might object: "There is no occasion at all for the first position to be suspected, because of the explicit statement 'of the *loṭ*'; so how can it be suspected? It is indeed reasonable to suspect it, on the grounds that even though it is a substitute, it receives the designation "*loṭ*" because it occupies the place of the *loṭ*.

For in that case, if the former position were adopted, then in the example "bhuṅkṣva bhuṅkṣvetyevāhaṃ bhuñje" (I eat [thinking], "Eat, eat!"), because the suffix is marked with *p* (pittvāt), it would not possess the status of being marked with *ṅ* (ṅittva); consequently, the elision of the vowel *ā* by the rule "śnaṣorallopaḥ" (Pāṇini 6.4.111) would not occur. Furthermore, both [the *parasmaipada* and *ātmanepada* substitutes] would apply indiscriminately to both *parasmaipada* and *ātmanepada* endings, due to the absence of a restrictive cause. This result is obtained only when the substitution is prescribed generally for the place of all *tiṅ* affixes; otherwise, the *hrādeśa* (substitution of *hi*) would apply to *parasmaipada* endings, while the *svādeśa* (substitution of *se*) would apply to the others.
Therefore, considering this position to be faulty, he resorts to the second position and says: "And of that *loṭ*," and so forth.
He will provide a rebuttal to that position in which the fault occurs, stating:
"Or rather, let there be those ending in *tad-dhvam*."
The word *loṭ* is required [as the subject].
*Ta* and *dhvaṃ* are *taṣvama*; that *loṭ* for which these two are yet to come into being (*bhāvin*) is "that which has *taṣvama* as its future state" (*taṣvambhāvī*).

By this, he shows that the very *loṭ* suffix itself is the substitute (*sthānin*) for such meanings; because of its purpose (*tādathryāt*), the word *ta* is designated by the term *ta* in the sūtra, and the word *dhvaṃ* is designated by the term *dhvaṃ* for the sake of the substitution (*ādeśa*).

Now, why are *ta* and *dhvam* not understood as the substituends (*sthānin*)? For it is impossible to understand them as substituends; if they were also substituends, then *hi* and *sva* would likewise apply to the substitutes of *loṭ*. If it is argued that we shall qualify *ta* and *dhvam* by saying "those which are *ta* and *dhvam* of *loṭ*," and thus this fault does not arise—even so, there would be an excessive burden of comprehension (*pratipatti-gaurava*).

It is more logical that only the *loṭ* [mood] is the substituendum (*sthānin*) for *ta* and *dhvam*, and not for *ta* and *dhvam* themselves. If, then, *hi* and *sva* are substitutes for *loṭ*, they would not be substitutes for *tiṅ*s; and in that case, by the rule *tiptasjhi... [P. 1.4.99]*, those two would receive the designation *parasmaipada*. Consequently, by the rule *śeṣātkartari parasmaipadam* [P. 1.3.78], both would occur only after roots that are inherently *parasmaipada*.

Furthermore, because they would be situated within *tiṅ*s, the complex ending in them would not be considered a *tiṅ* ending, and thus the rule *tiṅṅatiṅaḥ* [P. 8.1.28] would not apply, resulting in the absence of the *nighāta* (anudātta accent). To address this, he says: "And there is a splitting of the yoga (*yogavibhāga*)," etc., namely: "*loḍityeva*" (the word *loṭ* alone [is the subject]).
By this, he shows the continuation of the term *loṭ* in the second yoga.
Regarding the phrase "possessing the properties of *loṭ*" (*loḍdharmāṇau*), etc.:
those two possess the properties of *loṭ* because they share properties such as being verbal suffixes (*tiṅ*) and so forth, just like *loṭ*.

But surely, properties such as being *tiṅ* belong to the substitutes (*ādeśa*) of *loṭ*, not to *loṭ* itself? There is no fault here, because by means of the substitute, the properties such as being *tiṅ* also belong to the original element (*sthānin*), namely *loṭ*.

How, then, do those two [substitutes] come to possess the properties of *loṭ* when there is a split of the rule (*yogavibhāga*)? When there is a split of the rule, in the second rule the word *loṭ* which recurs [from the first rule] undergoes a change of case by implication; thus, having attained the state of being in the genitive case, it qualifies *hi* and *su*: "those *hi* and *su* which are substitutes of *loṭ*."

Furthermore, those *hi* and *sva* which will be prescribed by the rule "sehir apicca" [Pāṇini 3.4.87] in place of the substitutes *sip* and *thās* of the imperative (*loṭ*), are themselves prescribed here in place of the imperative with their respective specific features already included; they are not something entirely new.
By this, the meaning that "those two possess the properties of the imperative" is indeed obtained.
Regarding the phrase "by that," and so forth:
Therefore—in the manner described above—the *hi* and *sva* substitutes take the place of the imperative (*loṭ*);
by this, the status of being active-voice (*parasmaipada*) and middle-voice (*ātmanepada*) is established through their distinct distribution according to their respective domains.
In that regard, the status of being active-voice is established for the word *hi*, because the *hi* belonging to the imperative is designated as active-voice.

The status of being an *ātmanepada* is restricted to the word "self" (*sva*), because the word "self," when connected with the imperative (*loṭ*), bears the technical designation of *ātmanepada*. Furthermore,
"the status of being a *tiṅ* suffix applies to both as well," because both of those [words] connected with the imperative possess the nature of a *tiṅ* suffix.

But surely, *sip* and *thas* are related to the substitutes for *loṭ*, because they are their substitutes, and not to *loṭ* itself; so how can they be designated as being related to *loṭ*? There is no fault here, for *loṭ* is related to them by way of those substitutes.

If, then, these two possess the properties of the *loṭ* [imperative], then they would likewise have the designation of the singular number (*ekavacana*) and the designation of the middle person (*madhyamapuruṣa*), because those two also possess the properties of the *loṭ*. Consequently, there would be no forms of the *loṭ* occurring in other numbers or other persons? This is not a fault; for if the designations of singular number and middle person were already established [by general rules], this rule would be purposeless, since the substitution of *hi* and *sva* for the singular middle person would be accomplished even without this rule—as in the example: *lunīhi lunīhi*.
The reduplication [of the verb] occurs by the rule *kriyāsamabhihāre dvau bhavataḥ* (Vārttika 886). The substitution of *i* for the vowel [of the root] occurs by the rule *lunanti* (Pāṇini 6.4.113).
The elision of the long *ā* occurs by the rule *śnābhyastayor ātaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.4.112).

With the words "Or rather" (*atha vā*) and so forth, he demonstrates the purpose of including the word "or" (*vā*) in the rule *vā ca tadhvamoḥ*. Regarding the form *alāvīt*: there is *vṛddhi* by [Pāṇini 7.2.1], *iṭ* by [Pāṇini 7.2.35], *iṭ* by [Pāṇini 7.3.96], and the elision of the *sic* suffix by [Pāṇini 8.2.28]. Regarding the form *alāviṣṭām*: [the same process applies].
By the rule *tasthasthamipām tāntantāmaḥ* [Pāṇini 3.4.101], the suffix *tas* is replaced by *tām*.
Regarding the form *alāviṣuḥ*:
by the rule *sijabhyastavidibhyaśca* [Pāṇini 3.4.109], the suffix *jhi* is replaced by *jus*.
"In this same way, examples should also be cited for the middle and highest persons.
For instance: "Cut! Cut!"—[in response to this] you have cut, both of you have cut, or all of you have cut;
or alternatively: "Cut! Cut!"—[in response to this] all of you have cut.

"‘Lunīhi lunīhi’ (‘Reap, reap!’)—thus indeed did I reap; ‘āvāṃ alāviṣva’ (‘We two have reaped’); ‘vayam alāviṣma’ (‘We have reaped’). In this same way, examples should also be cited for the middle and highest persons.
[‘Lunīhi lunīhi’]—thus indeed will you reap, ‘yuvāṃ laviṣyathaḥ’ (‘you two will reap’), ‘yūyaṃ laviṣyatha’ (‘you all will reap’).
Or else: ‘lunīta lunīta’ (‘Reap, reap!’)—thus indeed will you all reap."
"Cut! Cut!"—thus [he says], "I shall cut," "we two shall cut," or "we shall cut. Regarding the form *adhīyāt*:
this is the substitution *iyan*.
Regarding the form *adhīyate*: [this is the substitution *iyat*].
> [[7.1.5]] This is the substitution of *it*.
"In this manner, [the rule] should be illustrated for all *lakāra*s" (as stated in the *Kāśikā* and the *Padamañjarī*).
Regarding the *laṅ*: *lunīhi lunīhi*—in this very way, he cut (*alunāt*), these two cut (*alunītām*), and these [many] cut (*alunan*).
"Reap, reap!"—thus you reaped; "you two reaped"; "you all reaped.
Or else—"Let him reap, let him reap!"—thus you all reaped.
"Reap, reap!"—thus I reaped; "we two reaped"; "we all reaped."

"Study! Study!"—saying this very thing, he studied; these two studied; these [many] studied. "Study! Study!"—saying this very thing, you studied; you two studied; you all studied. Or else—"Study! Study!"—saying this very thing, you all studied.
"Study! Study!"—thus I studied (*adhyaiṣi*), we two studied (*adhyaiṣvahi*), and we all studied (*adhyaimahi*).

In other tenses (*lakāra*s), examples are not provided here for fear of excessive prolixity; one should supply them for oneself by following this same method. Now, regarding "Cut! Cut! (*lunīhi lunīhi*), how is there reduplication (*dvirvacana*) here, given that the repetition of the action (*kriyāsamabhihāra*) is already understood through the verbal root (*dhātu*) itself?

Is it because the *loṭ* suffix is prescribed after a verbal root that expresses an action qualified by that [intensity]? Or rather—if it is argued that reduplication occurs once that [meaning] has been understood—then reduplication would also apply to a form ending in *yaṅ*. Therefore, he says: "In the manifestation of the repetition of action," and so forth.

Although the *loṭ* suffix occurs after a verbal root that denotes an action qualified by the repetition of action (*kriyāsamabhihāra*), nevertheless, that manifestation of the repetition of action is not effected by the verbal root; what then? It is effected by the *loṭ* suffix itself.
That [suffix] is capable of effecting that [intensive meaning] only when accompanied by reduplication, not alone; for it is not prescribed there [in the sense of intensification].
Indeed, it (the *loṭ* suffix) is prescribed for the objects and so forth by the rule *loṭ ca* [Pāṇini 3.4.69], but not for the repetition of an action (*kriyāsamabhihāra*).

Therefore, since the *loṭ* suffix is itself incapable of manifesting that [meaning] when it must be manifested, it requires reduplication; the point is that reduplication occurs of that which ends in it.
But by what [rule] is it stated that the reduplication requires [the sense of] "intensive repetition of an action"? To this he says: "In the case of intensive repetition of an action," and so forth;
"the *yaṅ* affix, moreover," and so forth. For the *yaṅ* affix is indeed prescribed specifically for the intensive repetition of an action.
Therefore, since that [element] being prescribed there is itself capable of manifesting it, it does not require reduplication (*dvirvacana*).
The sense is that reduplication does not occur for that which ends in it. Regarding the phrase "the superimposition of multiple actions" (*anekakriyādhyāhāra*):
the meaning is the accumulation of several actions.
By this, he shows the distinction between *samuccaya* (conjunction) and *samabhihāra* (repetition).
*Samabhihāra* is either frequency or intensity, and it is possible only for a single action;
whereas *samuccaya*, on the other hand, pertains to multiple actions—as in "wander through the village."
[The suffix] *luk* [is applied] by [Pāṇini 6.4.105].

Here, there is a conjunction (*samuccaya*) of various acts of wandering (*aṭana*), which have attained distinction due to the difference in their means (*sādhana*). Regarding the phrase "Or else" (*atha vā*) and so forth: by the first occurrence of the word "or" (*atha vā*), he demonstrates the option (*vikalpa*) established by the mention of "or" (*vā*) in [Pāṇini 3.4.2], *vā ca tadhvamoḥ*; by the second, that established by the mention of "optionally" (*anyatarasyām*) in [Pāṇini 3.4.3]. He clarifies the meaning of the sentence beginning with "In the previous rule prescribing the imperative" (*pūrvasmin loḍvidhāne*) and so forth, by means of the passage beginning with "from whichever root" (*yasmāddhātoḥ*) and so forth.
Regarding the phrase "in connection with a verbal root" (*dhātusambandhe*) and so forth:

because the phrase "in connection with a verbal root" (*dhātusambandhe*) is carried over [from the previous rule], the injunction for the *loṭ* suffix applies only when there is a connection with a verbal root. Therefore, the subsequent employment [of the suffix] is already established, for without that [subsequent employment], there can be no connection with a verbal root, since such a connection resides in two things. If this is so, for what purpose is this statement? To this he says: "But for the sake of [prescribing] the specific manner [of application]. (*yathāvidhyarthaṃ tu*).

Now, why is it not for the purpose of excluding either a separated usage or a preceding usage, as in the rule "The root *kṛ* is used after [another verb] when the *liṭ* suffix follows" (Pāṇini 3.1.40)? No; because both of those are also desired.
For a separated usage is indeed desired: "Devadatta cuts [the grass], saying, 'Cut!
Cut! A preceding usage is also desired: "Devadatta cuts, saying, 'Cut! Cut!'"
Therefore, it is logical that this [rule] is intended solely for the purpose of a prescription (*vidhi*).

But one might object: since the rule *nanu ca* (Pāṇini 3.4.5) permits the employment of another verbal root having the same meaning, there will be "employment according to the original form" (*yathāvidhyanuprayoga*) in the case of the intensive repetition of an action (*kriyāsamabhihāra*); so what is the point of this present statement? This is not so; for in that case, the restriction (*niyama*) would apply only to the case of conjunction (*samuccaya*), whereas in the case of the intensive repetition of an action, there would be "employment according to the original form" both for the primary root and for another root having the same meaning. Therefore, this must be commenced. [The purpose is] "to exclude the employment of every specific [root]."

If this were not commenced, then the subsequent employment (*anuprayoga*) would necessarily apply only to as many roots as those for which the *loṭ* suffix is prescribed; therefore, this [sūtra] is intended to prevent that.
Now, one might object: even without this statement, the subsequent employment of the general verb alone will occur by virtue of parsimony (*lāghava*).

If there were application of all specific terms [simultaneously], one would say, "Eat rice, drink barley-meal, eat fried grains," and then [the general term] "he eats, he drinks, he eats" would apply to all of them; consequently, only the word *taru* (tree) would be used, while words such as *vanaspati* (forest-plant) and others would be eliminated. But this is not the case; therefore, in the usage of worldly language, there is no concern for brevity or prolixity.

But surely, in examples such as *bhrāṣṭramaṭa* ("wander from frying pan to fire"), there is a conjunction (*samuccaya*) of the *kārakas* (factors) themselves, such as the frying pan and so on, and not of the action, because that [action] is singular; and since "residing in multiple substrates" is a universal (*sāmānya*), and that is impossible for an action which is unitary, how then is the subsequent application (*anuprayoga*) of a word expressing a universal justified? To this he says: *bhrāṣṭramaṭa*, etc. The meaning has already been explained. Regarding the term *yathāyatham*:
it means "according to each respective [case]."
The meaning is: that which is one's own domain, in that [domain] it [occurs].
Regarding "akarat," the substitution of *aṅ* for *cl* occurs by [Pāṇini 3.1.59]. Regarding "akaram," [the same applies].
*mipo'm* | *avṛṇīta*— this is the aorist (*laṅ*) of the root *vṛñ*; because it belongs to the *kryādi* class, the suffix *śnā* is applied, and the substitution of *ī* for *u* occurs as before.
Regarding "mamāra": this is the *liṭ* [perfect] suffix.

By the rule "mriyater luṅ-liṅoś ca" (Pāṇini 1.3.61), which restricts the usage, the *parasmaipada* [active voice] ending is applied. The *ṇal* suffix is added; there is *vṛddhi* [vowel strengthening], followed by the substitution of *ra* for *ṛ* (*raparatva*). Then, because of the status of the original position (*sthānivadbhāva*), the root *mṛ* is reduplicated. Next, the substitution of *u* for *ṛ* (*urat*) occurs, followed by the substitution of *ra* for *ṛ*, and finally the *halādiśeṣa* [retention of the first consonant]. Regarding "neṣat" and "takṣiṣat": these are examples of the *leṭ* [subjunctive] mood.

In *nayati* and *takṣate*, the suffix is *leṭ*; the *tip* ending undergoes the elision of its *i* by *itaśca lopaḥ parasmaipadeṣu* (Pāṇini 3.4.97); the suffix *sip* is added by *sib bahulaṃ leṭi* (3.1.34); and *āṭ* is prefixed by [3.4.94]. In *takṣiṣat*, the augment *iṭ* is applied by *ārdhadhātukasya* (7.2.35).

Examples such as *joṣiṣat* and others have been explained under the rule *sib bahulaṃ leṭi* (3.1.34). "Negotiation" (*upasaṃvāda*) means "discussion"; it refers to making a formal agreement regarding what ought to be done.
These two are synonyms for the word *upasaṃvāda*.
By the words "If you [should] for me," etc., he shows the nature of the agreement (*saṃvāda*);
and by the words "On account of the cause," etc., he shows the nature of the doubt (*āśaṅkā*).
"Following" means pursuing; that is to say, inference.
"Reasoning is conjecture."
There are two ways of explaining this apprehension:
"I myself," and so forth. The gods said to Paśupati, "Destroy Tripura," and he replied, "I alone am the lord of the bound souls (paśu)."
When it was said, "Take the portion belonging to Bṛhatī," the Sun spoke this: "Your cups shall indeed be taken with me at their head;
your vessels shall indeed be declared to have me as their deity.

Regarding the word "īśai": the root *īś* (meaning "to rule") [Dhātupāṭha 1020], in the third person singular, with the augment *iṭ*, the substitution of *e* for the final *ṭi*, and by [Pāṇini 3.4.93] the substitution of *ai* for *e*.

Regarding *gṛhrāntai*: the root *grah* is used in the sense of "taking" (*upādāna*) [Dhātupāṭha 1533]. By applying the rule for the object [karmaṇi] [Pāṇini 3.1.67], there is vocalization (*samprasāraṇa*) according to the rule for *grah* and so forth [Pāṇini 6.1.16].

The remaining derivation is as before. Regarding *ucyāntai*: the root *vac* is used in the sense of "speaking" (*paribhāṣaṇa*) [Dhātupāṭha 1063]; there is vocalization (*samprasāraṇa*) according to the rule for *vac* and so forth [Pāṇini 6.1.15].
The remainder is as before. Regarding "patāma" (*patlṛ* "to go," Dhātupāṭha 845), the suffix *mas* takes the augment *āṭ* according to Pāṇini 3.4.94.
By the phrase "by the movement of the tongue" and so forth, he demonstrates the previously mentioned definition of doubt (*āśaṅkā*) through an example.
"This is precisely the meaning of the optative suffix (*liṅ*).
It refers to the relationship between cause and effect.
How so? First, in the case of a mutual agreement (*upasaṃvāda*), it consists of a formal stipulation characterized by such an expression as: "If you do this for me, I too will give this to you."
In that context, the "instrument" (karaṇa) is the cause (hetu), and "giving" (dāna) is that which possesses the cause (hetumat); thus, a logical agreement is the meaning of the optative suffix (liṅ).
Furthermore, "suspicion" (āśaṅkā) is the pursuit of an effect based on a cause;
there too, the cause is the "cause" (hetu) and the pursuit of the effect is "that which possesses the cause" (hetumat)—thus, suspicion as well is indeed the meaning of the optative suffix.

If this is so, since [the desired result] is already established by the preceding rule, for what purpose is this stated? To this he says: "The statement is for the sake of making it obligatory (*nityārtha*). It might be argued that it would be obligatory by the preceding rule alone; to this he says: "In the previous sūtra," and so forth. How is this known?
Because of the statement "kṛt-affixes [denote] the agent" (*kartari kṛt*), he considers that the sense of *tumun* is properly restricted to the agent alone.
"By the force of the statement," and so forth.

If the *kartṛ* (agent) alone were the meaning of the suffix *tum*, the mention of "the meaning of *tum*" would be purposeless; for by virtue of being a *kṛt* suffix, the *say*-class suffixes (*sayap*) and others would already apply to the agent.
Therefore, from the indicative mark (*liṅga*) of the inclusion of "the meaning of *tum*," it follows that *tumun* does not apply to the agent.
"It is drawn away" means it is removed;
that is to say, it does not occur when [the agent] is the grammatical subject (*kartṛ*).
It might be argued that its meaning will be "action" (*karman*) and so forth; to this he says, "And not," etc.
"In another" means in action and so forth.
If, then, [the suffix] does not occur in the case of *karman* and so on because they are not specified, it would likewise not occur in the case of *bhāva*.
He says—starting with "anirdiṣṭārthāḥ"—that even in the case of *bhāva*, the suffix *tumun* is indeed not specified.

Because another meaning is specified, whatever base (*prakṛti*) is employed as the cause for the suffixes, the suffixes whose meanings are not specified occur in their own sense (*svārtha*) due to the proximity of that very meaning; furthermore, in this context, that "own sense" is *bhāva*.
Whence is this [conclusion]? From the governing context of "verbal root" (*dhātu*), and because a verbal root denotes an action (*bhāva*).

If that were so, one might simply use the term "action" (*bhāva*) for brevity. But this is not possible; for if "action" were used, then by the rule *kartari kṛt* (Pāṇini 3.4.67), the suffix *tumun* would apply only when the agent (*kartṛ*) is intended.
However, when the term "the meaning of *tumun*" (*tum-artha*) is used, it is indicated that even for *tumun*, the meaning is indeed "action," and thus there is no fault whatsoever.
Regarding "vakṣe":
from the root *vac* in the sense of "speaking" (Dhātupāṭha 1063), with the suffix *se*, there is the substitution of *k* according to [Pāṇini 8.2.30].
Regarding "eṣe": [the same applies].
The suffix *sen* follows the root *iṇ*. Regarding the word "jīvase": it is derived from the root *jīv*, meaning "to sustain life" (Dhātupāṭha 562).
This very same example applies to both conditions (*pratyaya*), though the accent differs.
Regarding the term *preṣe*: it is derived from the root *iṇ* with the prefix *pra*, followed by the suffix *kse* [according to Pāṇini 6.1.87].
Regarding "śriyase":
from the root *śriñ* in the sense of "service" (*sevāyām*) [Dhātupāṭha 897], the suffix *ksen* is applied, resulting in the vowel change to *iyaṅ*.
Regarding "upācaradhyai": [it is derived from the root *car* with the prefix *upa* and the suffix *adhyai*].

The root *car* means "to go" (Dhātupāṭha 559), preceded by the prefix *upa-aṅ*. This is an illustration of both suffixes; however, there is a distinction between them due to the difference in accentuation, as in the form *āhuvadhyai*.
Regarding *pā pāne* (Dhātupāṭha 925): for the suffix *śadhyai*, the substitution of *piba* occurs by the rule *prāghrādisūtra* [Pāṇini 7.3.78]. Regarding *mādayadhyai*:
the root *madī* (Dhātupāṭha 815) in the sense of "joy" takes the causative *ṇic* affix, followed by the suffix *śadhyai*, resulting in the application of *guṇa* and the substitution of *ā*.
"pātavai" means "for drinking";
"sūtave" means "for giving birth."
Regarding *ṣūṅ* "to release the fetus of living beings" (Dhātupāṭha 1031): [the suffix] *tavya* is added, and because it is marked with *ṅ*, there is no *guṇa* substitution.
Examples such as *gantave* ("to go") follow in order from the roots *gam*, *kṛ*, and *hṛ*. Regarding *prayai*:
by the rule *ato lopa iṭi ca* (Pāṇini 6.4.64), the vowel *ā* is elided. Regarding *dṛśe*: [the same applies].
The suffix *ka* is applied to the root *dṛś*.

Regarding the form *vikhyai*: the suffix *ka* is irregularly applied (*nipātyate*) to either the root *cakṣiṅ* or the root *khyāti*, preceded by the prefix *vi*. Regarding the form *vibhājamam*: [the suffix *kamu* is applied].
From the root *bhaj* preceded by the prefix *vi*, the suffix *ṇamul* is applied;
thus, "apalupam.
[The root] *lup* is listed as "luplṛ cchedane" (Dhātupāṭha 1431). [The suffix] *kamul* is applied after the roots *abhicara* and *iṣ*. Thus, "abhicaritam."
The suffix *tosun* is applied after the root preceded by the prefix *abhi*. Thus, we have "vilikhaḥ" and "vitṛdaḥ.

The suffix *kasun* is applied to the root *likh* and to *tṛd*—as found in the Dhātupāṭha (*tṛdir hiṃsādānayoḥ*, DhP 1446). Regarding the statement "the meaning of kṛtya suffixes is the abstract state (*bhāva*) and the object (*karman*)," [it refers to this].
Because the *kṛtya* suffixes are prescribed [by Pāṇini 3.4.70] for the states of being (*bhāva*) and the object (*karman*). Regarding the form *antetavai*:
it is derived from the root *iṇ* preceded by the prefix *anu*, with the suffix *tavai*.
"Paridhātavai"—
this is derived from the root *dhā* preceded by the prefix *pari*.
"Paristaritavai"— this likewise [is derived from the root *stṛ* preceded by *pari*].
[The word *paristaraṇa*] is derived from the root *stṛñ* "to cover" (Dhātupāṭha 1252) preceded by the prefix *pari*.
[The word *avagāha*] means "plunging";
it is derived from the root *gāhū* "to stir" (Dhātupāṭha 649) preceded by the prefix *ava*.

Regarding the term *didṛkṣeṇya*: from the root *dṛś* (to see), the suffix *san* is added; there is reduplication; the substitution of *ur*; the substitution of *ra* for the final consonant; the substitution of *i* for the radical vowel by the rule *sanyataḥ* [Pāṇini 7.4.79]; the absence of *guṇa* strengthening by the rule *na abhyāsasyāsavarṇe* [Pāṇini 7.3.85]; the substitution of *ṣ* for the initial consonant by the rule *vraścādi-* [Pāṇini 8.2.36]; and the substitution of *ka* for *sa* by the rule *saḥ kāt* [Pāṇini 8.2.41]. Once the form *didṛkṣa* is established, the suffix *kenya* is added. Similarly, regarding the term *śuśrūṣeṇya*.

From the root *śru*, the desiderative suffix *san* is applied; by [Pāṇini 6.4.16], there is lengthening of the vowel, and the reduplication undergoes the operations pertaining to the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*). When the form *śuśrūṣa* is established, the suffix *kenya* is added. Regarding the term *katrtvam*: it is the abstract noun (*bhāva*) derived from the root *kṛ*.
"Even in the *sayādi-sūtra*, the suffix *tava* is prescribed.
The *sayādi-sūtra* is the rule concerning *sa* and so forth; even there, in that [rule] by which *sa* and the others are prescribed, the suffix *tava* is also prescribed.
"From that which has the sense of *tum*," and so forth.

If, however, the rule for that [suffix] were a prescription for the abstract action (*bhāva*) alone in the sense of *tumun*, it would be redundant, since [the meaning] is already established by this very [rule]. Therefore, although it is stated there that it has the sense of *tumun*, nevertheless, one should understand that the suffix *taven* is prescribed elsewhere than that—namely, in the case of the object (*karman*) and other factors such as the agent (*kartṛ*). "The suffix *eś* is introduced as an irregular form (*nipātana*). The addition of the marker *ś* is for the purpose of assigning it the technical designation of *sārvadhātuka*.

Therefore, when [the suffix] is prescribed for an *ardhadhātuka* [context], the substitution of *khyāñ* by the rule *cakṣiṅaḥ khyāñ* [Pāṇini 2.4.54] does not occur in a *sārvadhātuka* context. Regarding the phrase "until the completion" (*āsaṃsthātoḥ*) and so forth: by the word "completion" (*saṃsthā*), the conclusion is expressed, which indicates the act of seating on the sacrificial altar (*vedyām sadanam*).
[As in the injunction: "It should be established before the rising of the sun."
In this case as well, the act of kindling the fire is [indicated] by the rising of the sun;
in expressions such as "before the calves [are driven out]," the sitting down is indicated by the driving out of the calves;
and in expressions such as "before the [morning] chanting," the offering is indicated by the chanting.

In the example beginning with "purā pracaritoh," the act of *pracarana* (moving forward) itself constitutes the offering (*āhavana*). In the two subsequent examples, there is an impossibility of the offering. Regarding the phrase "of the two expressing negation" (*pratiṣedhavācinoḥ*), this is an explanation of the term "of the two negations" (*pratiṣedhayoḥ*). By this, he demonstrates that because they express negation, the words *alam* and *khalu* are referred to by the word "negation" (*pratiṣedha*) in the sūtra.

For there is indeed a designation by the name of that which it denotes; as in [Pāṇini 2.4.8], where words such as *yūka* (louse) and *likṣā* (nit), because they denote small creatures, are expressed by the term "small creature" (*kṣudrajantu*).
Regarding the word "ornament" (*alaṅkāra*), the suffix *ghañ* is used in the sense of the action itself (*bhāve*).

In this context, the word *alaṃ* signifies "ornamentation" (*bhūṣaṇa*). As in the example: *alaṃ vāle rodanena* ("Enough, child, with weeping"). [The suffix] *lyuṭ* is used here in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāva*). [An objection is raised: "If it is argued that the rule of optional forms (*vāsarūpavidhi*) applies..."

Even without the mention of "prāk" (before), the option (*vikalpa*) is indeed obtained; for if you think that a dissimilar exception (*asarūpa-apavāda*) is necessarily sublated [by the general rule], then in that case, the mention of "prāk"—meaning "prior to the heading on feminine nouns (*stryadhikāra*)"—is stated for the sake of providing an option, having kept in mind that there is no rule of non-identity of form (*asarūpa-vidhi*) after that point. [The example is] *apamitya*.

The substitution of *ā* [for *i*] occurs by [Pāṇini 6.1.45]; the compound is formed by [Pāṇini 2.2.18]; the replacement of *ktvā* with *lyap* occurs by [Pāṇini 7.1.37], which states that in a compound not preceded by the negative particle *nañ*, *ktvā* becomes *lyap*; the substitution of *i* for *y* occurs by [Pāṇini 6.4.70]; and [the lengthening of the vowel] occurs by [Pāṇini 6.1.71]. Now, one might object: "The suffix *ktvā* is already established here by [Pāṇini 3.4.21], 'When two actions have the same agent, [the suffix is used] for the earlier in time,' since there is indeed a common agent here as well. For the very same person who performs the act of driving away (*apamayate*) is the one who begs (*yācate*). Why, then, is it prescribed [again]? To this he replies: "Because there is no prior time," and so forth.
Since one first asks for something and afterwards removes it, there is no state of prior time; therefore, the suffix *ktvā* is prescribed even when [the action] has not yet been reached.

Let it be prescribed that [the suffix] *nam* occurs [after the root *yāc*]. However, there is this objection: when the suffix *ktvā* occurs after the root *mā* (*mi*) by virtue of the rule [Pāṇini 3.4.21], would it not then also occur after the root *yāc* by virtue of that same rule? This is not a fault, because in the rule "of two [verbs] having the same agent" (3.4.21), the phrase "of the northerners" (3.4.19) is understood, and that is a restricted option (*vyavasthitavibhāṣā*). Therefore, when *ktvā* occurs after *mā*, it will not occur after *yāc*.
[The commentary states] "because of the mention of 'of the northerners'" and so forth.
The mention of "of the northerners" here is for the purpose of providing an option.
Therefore, even that which has been previously obtained occurs as an alternative.
[The suffix] *ktvā* follows the root *yāc*;

the *laṭ* and other [suffixes] follow *mā*. Someone might suspect that this mention of *māṅ* refers to the root *māṅ* in the sense of "measuring" (*māṅ māne*, Dhātupāṭha 1142); in order to refute that, he says: "This is the mention of the root *meṅ* after its vowel has been changed to *ā*."

But from what is this understood? From the inclusion of the term *vyatīhāra* (exchange). The root *miṅ* alone occurs in the sense of exchange, not the root *māṅ*; therefore, it is recognized that this is indeed a reference to *miṅ*.

For what purpose, then, was such a reference made? [One might ask: "If there were doubt when it is used, should it not have been stated unambiguously as simply *miṅ*? To this he says: "It is for the sake of providing an indication (*jñāpanārthaḥ*)."

When the designation *me* ought to have been used, the fact that the designation *kṛtātvasya* (of that which has undergone the change to *ā*) was made with its *anubandha* is for the purpose of providing a technical indication (*jñāpana*).
By this, it is indicated: "The status of not ending in a vowel (*anejantatva*) is not caused by an *anubandha*.
With the words "By this," etc., he demonstrates the purpose of this indication.
If this meaning were not made known, then because [the root] would end in a consonant (*hal*), it would not possess the quality of ending in *ej* (a vowel).

What would be the fault in that? The inclusion of *daip* would not be included by the mention of *dāp*; for their forms are different. Consequently, there would be no prohibition of *daip* in the rule *dādhā ghvadāp* (Pāṇini 1.1.20).
When this meaning has been made known, it becomes so. Here, these two words, *para* (subsequent) and *avara* (prior), are relative terms (*sambandhi-śabda*).

One becomes "subsequent" in relation to what precedes it, and one becomes "prior" in relation to what follows it. Furthermore, relative terms necessarily bring to mind their respective counter-correlates (*pratiyogin*). Therefore, although no specific usage is explicitly indicated in the sūtra, it is understood that the connection with *para* and *avara* pertains specifically to "the subsequent" and "the prior"; thus he says: "of the prior by the subsequent," and so forth. "The mountain is qualified by its connection with the subsequent river."
For instance, when it is said "the mountain not having reached the river," a mountain characterized by its connection with a subsequent river is understood;
that is, "the river is qualified by its connection with a preceding mountain.

This is because, when it is said "the river having crossed the mountain," the river is understood as being characterized by its connection with both a preceding mountain and [itself]. Since the governing topic is the verbal root (*dhātu*), it is understood that the state of having a common agent (*samānakartṛkatva*) belongs specifically to the meanings of the roots; thus he says: "those two meanings of the roots which have a common agent," and so forth.
And this genitive case is used in the sense of specification (*nirdhāraṇa*).

Furthermore, this word *samāna* signifies "one and the same. Now, one might object: "The capacity (*śakti*) is the grammatical factor (*kāraka*), whereas [the action] prior in time is something else; so how can 'having the same agent' (*samānakartṛkatva*) be understood? To this he says: "Of the capacity and the possessor of the capacity," and so forth.
There is the power (*śakti*) and the possessor of power (*śaktimān*); there is the possessor of power and power (*śakti-śaktimantau*).
Here, no distinction is intended between that which is the substratum of power and that which is the power itself.
Therefore, Devadatta alone, as the substratum of power, is the agent; and since he is one and the same for both actions, it is logical that they share a common agent (*samānakartṛkatva*).
Regarding the word "pītvā":
as before, there is the substitution of *ī* for *ai*.
