Here, the dual number is employed in the expression "samānakartṛkayoḥ" (of two [actions] having the same agent); therefore, only two actions will be presented, not many. Consequently, would this rule apply only when two actions are presented and not when many are? To this he says: "The dual number," and so forth.

Because this instruction has action as its primary focus, the dual number is not the primary element here; rather, it is used because of its necessary concomitance. Therefore, the instruction was formulated using the dual number.

An indication must necessarily be made by some word or other; therefore, since the dual number is not a restrictive factor, [the rule] applies even when there are many actions, as in: *brāhmaṇe bhuktavati vrajati* ("When the Brāhmaṇa has eaten, he goes").

Here, the Brāhmaṇa is the agent of the action of eating (*bhujikriyā*), whereas Devadatta is the agent of the action of going (*vrajatikriyā*); thus, there is an absence of a common agent (*samānakartṛkatva*).
[Another example is: *vrajati jalpati ca* ("He goes and he speaks").

Because the action occurs simultaneously here, there is no temporal priority [of one action over another]. The form *vyādāya* is derived from the root *dā* preceded by the prefix *vi-*. The form *saṃmīlya* is likewise derived from *mīl*.

This refers to the root *mīla*, *smīla*, and *kṣmīla* in the sense of "winking" (*nimeṣaṇe*) from the Dhātupāṭha (517, 519, 520), with the prefix *sam-* and ending in the causal suffix *ṇic*. But what is the reason that [the rule] is not established? He says: "Because there is no prior time (*apūrvakālatvāt*), the purpose of the word 'addition' (*upasaṃkhyāna*) is to provide an explanation. In this regard, the explanation is as follows: the word *ca* from the preceding rule (*pūrvayoga*) is carried over (*anuvartate*), and it has the sense of including what has not been mentioned (*anuktasamuccayārtha*). Therefore, in cases such as *mukhaṃ vyādāya svapiti* ('having opened his mouth, he sleeps'), the rule will apply even in the absence of a prior sequence of actions. The phrase "accompanied by reduplication" (*dvirvacanasahitau*) and so forth [is explained as follows].

For the capacity of the suffixes *ktvā* and *ṇamul* belongs only to those accompanied by reduplication (*dvirvacana*) when used to indicate frequency (*ābhīkṣṇya*), not to them alone; this is due to the inherent nature of the power of words (*śabdaśaktisvābhāvya*).
Therefore, the intention is that reduplication must be prescribed here.
To the question, "By what [means] is there reduplication here?", he says: "In the case of frequency," and so forth.
Regarding "pāyampāyam":
[the suffix -ya is applied] by [Pāṇini 7.3.33] "āto yuk". Regarding "anākāṅkṣe":
that for which there exists no *ākāṅkṣā*—that is, no expectation (*apekṣā*)—is so described.
Regarding the phrase "but *ktvā*, even though prescribed by the preceding rule":

because of the word *api* ("even"), it is appropriate that what is prescribed by the immediately preceding rule is prohibited—on the grounds of the maxim: "A prescription or a prohibition applies to what is immediately antecedent" (Vyākaraṇa-paribhāṣā 99).
But how can there be a prohibition of what was prescribed by the preceding rule? [The answer is: because the prohibition is formulated with reference to the specific context (*prakaraṇa*).
This prohibition is made with reference to the section on the prior time (*pūrvakāla-prakaraṇa*), such that what would otherwise apply under that section does not take place.

Therefore, it is logical that there is a prohibition even of that which was prescribed by the preceding sūtra. The statement "the term *ābhīkṣṇye* (repetition) does not recur" is the reasoning for the claim that "this is an optional rule (*vibhāṣā*) where [the application] was not previously established."

But is it not the case that this is a *prāptavibhāṣā* (an option for what is already established), since it is commenced when the suffix *ktvā* is already applicable by the rule "when two actions have the same agent" (*samānakartṛkayoḥ*, Pāṇini 3.4.21)? This is not so; for this is called a *aprāptavibhāṣā* (an option for what is not yet established) with reference to the suffixes *ktvā* and *ṇamul* prescribed by the immediately preceding rule.

As for the suffix *ktvā* alone which is prescribed by the rule "when two actions have the same agent," the mention of the term *vibhāṣā* need not apply to it at all; because the meaning conveyed by it is already established by the rule regarding alternative forms (*vāsarūpavidhi*).
With the words "But surely" (*nanu ca*) and so forth, [the author] refutes the purpose of the optional rule (*vibhāṣā*) mentioned immediately prior. [He does so by stating:
"In cases where *ktvā* and *ṇamul* [are prescribed]," and so on;
for by the very rule of "non-identity of form" (*vāsarūpa*), [the suffixes] *laṭ* and the others would optionally [apply].

Since that purpose for which the mention of *vibhāṣā* (optionality) is made regarding the *siddha* [rules], it is indicated that where both *ktvā* and *ṇamul* are prescribed simultaneously, the rule of "non-identity of form" (*vāsarūpavidhi*) does not apply.
What is the purpose of this indication? He says: "By that," and so forth; "the compound with an *upapada*," and so forth. [The question arises:
the compound with an *upapada* (as prescribed by Pāṇini 2.2.19) would apply; why does it not occur? He says: "It has been stated," and so forth.
It was stated previously [at Kāśikāvṛtti 2.2.20]: "An upapada that has the same rule of application as *am* itself is compounded.

In the case of *agne-bhṛtīni*, the upapadas have the same rule of application as *am* and another *ktvā* suffix; therefore, they are not compounded. In the expression *caurāṅkāram*, the augment *mum* is applied by [Pāṇini 6.3.67].
Regarding the phrase "the making of a thief" (*caurakaraṇam*) and so forth: here, the verb *kṛ* (to do/make) signifies the act of uttering.
In the abusive statement "You are a thief," the utterance of the word "thief" is for the purpose of accomplishing that very abuse.
For without that [prior state], the accusation cannot be established—
namely, "but he is not made a thief"—
because it would be impossible.

Nor can the state of being a thief be produced in a person even by a Brahmin’s saying "you are a thief" a hundred times. [Regarding the statement] "the mention of 'artha' (meaning) is for the sake of [including] the meaning 'sweet'":

but surely, because of the rule [Pāṇini 1.1.68], there ought to be a reference to the word-form itself? This is not so; for since it is already established that "of the word" (*śabdasya*) follows from the context of the instruction on words (*śabdānuśāsana*), the explicit mention of "word" (*śabda*) is made for the purpose of indicating that where a term is used as referring to the word itself, its own form (*svarūpa*) is understood, whereas where it is used as referring to the meaning, the meaning is understood. And here, the reference is to the meaning. Therefore, the inclusion of "meaning" (*artha*) alone is appropriate.
However, that the instruction is intent upon the actual meaning is understood from the uninterrupted lineage of oral instruction handed down by the teachers.
And since the suffix is obtained even when the word is used in its synonyms provided the sense of "meaning" is grasped, he says: "in the sense of 'delicious' (*svādu*)," and so forth.

Now, for what purpose is the form ending in *m* (*svādumi*) prescribed as an irregularity (*nipātana*), if it is argued that it is so that the upapada ending in *m* may be heard? No; if this were the sole purpose, it need not have been prescribed as an irregularity, because *khamuñ* is the subject of the immediately preceding rule, and thus that very suffix would have been prescribed here.

To refute the objection that "once this [suffix] is prescribed, the upapada will naturally possess the final *m* by virtue of the suffix itself," he says: "In the case of *svādumi*," and so forth. By this, he demonstrates the following: although the state of having a final *m* is established when the suffix *khamuñ* is applied, the prohibition of the long vowel *ī* (in the feminine) is not established. Consequently, from the word *svadu* as an upapada, the suffix *ṅīṣ* would be triggered by the rule *voto guṇavacanāt* [Pāṇini 4.1.44], and thus an undesirable form would result. However, when the final *m* is specifically prescribed by nipātana, the occasion for the application of *ṅīṣ* does not arise, because its cause has been precluded.
Therefore, even one who employs *khamuñ* must necessarily introduce a form ending in *m* as a nipāta (irregular form) for the purpose of prohibiting the application of *ī*.

Although the opponent's intention is that "once *khamuñ* is applied, the status of ending in *m* will be achieved by the *mum* augment itself," he says "of that which ends in *cvī*" (*cvyantasya*) and so forth to indicate that this is not the case everywhere.

By this, he shows the following: if the status of ending in *m* were not introduced as a nipāta, then even when *khamuñ* is applied, the upapada ending in *cvī* would not possess the status of ending in *m*; because such a word is an indeclinable (*avyaya*).
This is because of the governing rule (*adhikāra*) "and in the case of *mum* and *vidhi*" [Pāṇini 6.3.66].

Therefore, even by one who prescribes the suffix *khamuñ*, the nipātana (irregular designation) of its having a final *m* must be performed. If this were so, why not simply perform the nipātana of having a final *m* and prescribe the suffix *khamuñ* as the one currently under discussion? It is impossible to prescribe *khamuñ*; for if *khamuñ* were the suffix, the nipātana of its having a final *m* would be understood for the sake of making it an indeclinable (*avyaya*), and consequently, lengthening (*dīrghatva*) would necessarily occur by the rule "and in the case of *cvau*" [Pāṇini 6.3.63].
If the suffix *ṇamul* were present, it would be understood as an exception (*apavāda*) to all other rules; consequently, even the rule for lengthening (*dīrghatva*) would not apply.

Furthermore, the suffix *ṇamul* must necessarily be prescribed for the sake of subsequent rules; and when it is prescribed for those subsequent instances, there is neither economy (*lāghava*) nor, conversely, complexity (*gaurava*) here. He asks, "In what sense do these suffixes occur? and answers with the words, "And because of the governing context of *tumun*," and so forth.
"These" refers to those [suffixes] prescribed in the section concerning the sense of "tum.
"If this is so," [he says].
The meaning is that [the suffix] occurs when there is a sense of "for the sake of" (tum-arthe).
Regarding the phrase "by the suffix of the root *bhuj*," etc.:
although the agent is not expressed by the suffix *ṇamul*, nevertheless, because it is expressed by the suffix *laṭ* of the root *bhuj*, the third case ending should not occur.

But surely, the agent is characterized by capacity (*śakti*); moreover, the capacity regarding the act of making something tasty is one thing, while the capacity regarding the act of eating is another. In that case, even though the capacity regarding the act of eating is expressed by the present suffix (*laṭ*), since the designation "agent" does not apply to the other capacity [because it is unexpressed], would it not follow that the third case ending (*tṛtīyā*) must indeed occur? To this he says: “And not in this,” etc.
For here, in the section concerning a common agent, the distinction between capacities is not intended to be expressed;
therefore, Devadatta, who possesses the capacity, is the agent.
And since that [agent] is mentioned as being one and the same, how could there be the contingency of a third [case-ending]?

For what reason is the separate mention [of the agent] not intended? To this he says: "For when there is a common agent," and so forth. Even while conceding the intention to express a distinction, he states another resolution: "When the primary power is expressed," and so forth.

But what determines the primary and subordinate status of the agent and the capacity [of action] in this case? It is determined by the action (*kriyā*); for that which effects sweetness (*svāduṅkāram*) is subordinate because it exists for the sake of the act of eating.
The act of eating, however, is primary because it is that which is to be assisted by the former.
And since the primary and subordinate status belongs to the action, the primary and subordinate status of the agent and the capacity—which have that action as their object—also follows accordingly.

In that case, when the primary power (*pradhāna-śakti*) has been expressed, the non-primary power (*apradhāna-śakti*) manifests—that is, it appears—because it has also been expressed, since subordinate factors (*guṇas*) follow the principal factor.

Therefore, the meaning is that the third case-ending (*tṛtīyā*) does not occur. Regarding the phrase "established non-usage" (*siddhāprayoga*): that for which non-usage is established is so described.
"Because it is meaningless," and so forth.
It is "meaningless" either because of the absence of a referent (*abhidheya*) or because of the absence of a purpose (*prayojana*).
"In this very way," [it is said].
The meaning is that it is indeed purposeless.

By the phrase "he eats otherwise" (*anyathā bhuṅkte*) and so forth, having kept that very purposelessness in mind, he demonstrates the established fact of its non-usage. For whatever meaning is understood when the verb *karoti* is not employed in the expression "he eats otherwise," that same meaning is understood even when *karoti* is employed in the expression "he eats in another manner" (*anyathākāraṃ bhuṅkte*).
Therefore, the root *kṛ* (to do) is redundant.

But how can it be redundant when it is actually being employed? These affixes beginning with *anya* express "manner" (*prakāra*). When they denote the manner of the meaning of the verb used in conjunction with them (*anuprayoga*), then the root *kṛ*, being qualified by them, expresses that very manner; and since that manner is already understood from elsewhere [the suffix itself], *kṛ* becomes redundant.

If this is so, since its meaning is already understood, would its employment not be precluded? It is not so; for the employment of even an understood meaning is observed—as in "Bring two cakes" or "I am cooking. In the expression "He eats with his head otherwise," the word *anyathā* (otherwise) expresses the manner of another word, namely *śiras* (head). That manner is not understood without the verb *karoti* (does/makes). For if *karoti* were not employed, the manner characterized as "otherwise" would be perceived only as pertaining to the act of eating (*bhujikriyā*), and not as pertaining to the head.
Rather, it would be understood that the head itself is being eaten;
therefore, the verb *karoti* (to do) here is not used in its primary sense (*śuddha-prayoga*). Regarding the phrase "in response to an expression of malice" (*asūyā-prativacane*):
a reply born from malice is a "response to malice."
Regarding the passage beginning with "yadyasūyan": the form *asūyan* is the present participle (*śatṛ*) of the root *asūy*,
which belongs to the *kaṇḍv-ādi* class and takes the suffix *ya*.
This is connected with the phrase "he answers.
"He answers" (*prativakti*) means he speaks back; the sense is that he utters a reply.
[The word] "he asks" (*pṛcchati*).
This [term] ends in the locative case.
When someone asks a question, if one replies while showing *asūyā* (disrespect or malice), then that reply given in response to what was asked is called an "insulting reply" (*asūyā-prativacana*).
[The commentary continues with] "in whatever manner," and so forth.
When one asks the question, "How will you eat?", this statement beginning with "In whatever manner" (*yathākāram*) is a response characterized by true indignation (*asūyā*).
When one asks the question, "How will you eat?", this is the response [given] out of true indignation.
"‘As I shall eat after having done [this], so you shall see’—this is not a reply in the spirit of malice;
rather, it is an explanation [of the rule]: ‘when the word *karman* is used as an upapada, [the suffix *ṇamul* is applied] when it is qualified by totality (*sākalya*)’."

By this, he shows that "the grasping of the whole" (*sākalyagrahaṇa*) is a qualifier of the object (*karman*). [The *Kāśikā* states: "Whichever Brāhmaṇa he knows—[he knows, obtains, or reflects upon him].
By this, he shows that the roots *vid*, *labh*, and *vicār* (in the sense of reflecting) are included.

Why, then, is there no apprehension of the meaning of existence (*sattā*)? Because that [root] is intransitive (*akarmaka*), and because [the rule] specifies "in the case of an object" (*karmaṇi*). Regarding "of *vindate*": this refers to the root *vidlṛ* in the sense of "acquisition" (Dhātupāṭha 1432). Regarding "of *pūrayate*":
by this indication, he explains that this is the inclusion of the causative form (*ṇyanta*).

The term "in this [sūtra], the object (karman) is understood to be present. However, an object is not possible for the root *pṛ* when it is in its causative form (*ṇyanta*); for verbal roots that are intransitive become transitive when they take the causative suffix.
Therefore, it is understood that this mention refers to the causative form. [This is indicated by the phrase] "by the whole [complex]."
By means of the combination of the root, the suffix, and the upapada;

by this, he shows that the measure of the year is a qualifying attribute (*upādhi*) of the aggregate. As for the question, "What is the purpose of the mention of *asya* (of this)?", the intention is that since *pūrayati* (fills) is the subject under discussion, its elision will be understood even without the explicit statement "of this."
"It should not apply to the *upapada*.

If "of this" (*asya*) were not stated, then just as the measure of the year (*varṣapramāṇa*) is understood as a qualifier of the entire complex (*samudāya*), so too the elision of *ū* would be understood as a qualifier of the entire complex.

That is, it would mean that the elision of the final *ū* occurs for a complex consisting of a base (*prakṛti*), an affix (*pratyaya*), and an *upapada*; consequently, the elision would apply to the *upapada* as well.
Therefore, so that this fault may not occur, the word "asya" (of this) is stated. Regarding the term "from a causative" (*ṇyantāt*), this is a reference to the form including the *puk* augment.
And the *puk* occurs only when a causative suffix (*ṇic*) follows, by virtue of the rule "after the roots *ṛt*, *hi*, etc. (*arttihyī* 7.3.36).
Therefore, from this very explanation, it is understood that the root [√mṛd] is in its causative form (*ṇyanta*).
Regarding the phrase "in the sense of clothes" (*celārtheṣu*):
it is a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "those for which cloth is the price."

By this, he shows that *cela* is used in the sense of its referent (*arthagrahaṇa*). And the reasoning regarding the inclusion of the referent (*arthagrahaṇa*) which was stated in [Pāṇini 3.4.26] is to be understood here as well for the inclusion of the referent.
"Celaknopam" (the wetting of a cloth).

There is elision of the *y* of *vali*; there is *guṇa* substitution by [Pāṇini 7.3.86], "of that which ends in *pu*, *g*, or *ṇ*, and whose penultimate vowel is light"; and there is elision of the *ṇi*. Regarding "of *kaṣa*":

it is recited in the section of roots meaning injury as "√*kaṣa* √*śiṣa*" (Dhātupāṭha 685, 687). Regarding "of *piṣa*": it is "√*piṣlṛ* in the sense of pulverizing" (Dhātupāṭha 1452). Regarding "with total destruction (*samūlaghātam*)"—

Having applied [the rule] *iti kṛtvam* (Pāṇini 7.3.54) and *iti tatvam* (Pāṇini 7.3.32), [it is said]: "This undertaking is for the purpose of non-violence (*ahiṃsā*)," because [the formation of the word would already be] established by the rule to be stated later, *hiṃsārthānām* (Pāṇini 3.4.48), in the case of violence.
"[It is] for the purpose of making it an obligatory compound (*nityasamāsa*)."
The word "even" (*api*) implies "even for [a root] whose meaning is violence.

This rule is commenced so that there may be an obligatory compound (*nityasamāsa*) according to [Pāṇini 2.2.19]. However, when a suffix is subsequently added, it would instead be optional by virtue of [Pāṇini 2.2.21]: "The compounds beginning with the third case are optionally [compounded]."

Regarding the rule *yathāvidhyanuprayogārthaśca* (Pāṇini 3.4.46): this is so that there may be the subsequent employment (*anuprayoga*) of that very root after which the suffix *ṇamul* was prescribed; otherwise, when that suffix is applied, there would be the subsequent employment of a different root. Now, one might object: since the root *han* signifies "injury" (*hiṃsā*), then by virtue of its higher status [in the order of rules], the subsequent employment should be by that [root] alone; how then is this introduction of the rule justified for the sake of making the compound obligatory and for the sake of subsequent employment according to the specific rule, in the case of *han* meaning injury? To this he says: "By means of a prior counter-exception" (*pūrvavipratiṣedhena*), etc. By the phrase "denoting anointing" (*snehanavācini*), [the word] "in anointing" (*snehane*)...
He explains the meaning of this [sūtra] with the words "ending in vṛtti. The fact that it ends in *vṛt* is understood from the very statement itself. Regarding "svapoṣam":
when the word *sva*, denoting the self (*ātman*), is used as an upapada, the suffix is applied.
"Like the nourishment of a cowherd" refers to that which expresses one's own [possession]; "like the nourishment of wealth" refers to that which expresses wealth.

In the word *pitṛpoṣam*, the suffix denotes the sense of "knowing. In the word *naṣṭaḥ*, the substitution of *ṣ* for *s* is applied by the rule *naśervraścādi-* (Pāṇini 8.2.36), and the augment *num* is elided by the rule *aniditām-* (Pāṇini 6.4.24). In the phrase *puruṣeṇoḍhaḥ*, [the suffix *-kta* is applied].

By the rule *vaher vacy-ādi-sūtreṇa* [Pāṇini 6.1.15], there is vocalization (*samprasāraṇa*); by *pūrva-rūpa* [6.1.108], the preceding form is substituted; by *ho ḍhaḥ* [8.2.31], *ḍha* replaces *ha*; by [8.2.40], [8.4.41], and [8.3.13], and finally by [6.3.111], the long vowel is applied. Thus, it means "it is filled from above" (*ūrdhvaṃ pūryate*). The sense is that it becomes filled from above. Because the root is marked with an indicatory *anudātta*, the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) is used, and because it belongs to the *divādi* class, the suffix *śyan* is applied. Regarding the term *ghṛtanidhāyam*: [it is explained as follows].

The reasoning is as before. Here, in examples such as *mūlakenopadaṃśaṃ bhuṅkte* ("he eats with a radish as a side-dish"), the third case ending (*tṛtīyā*) denotes the instrument (*karaṇa*), and that which ends in the third case—such as *mūlaka*—is the subordinate term (*upapada*). Now, is that instrument [the means] of the root *upa-daṃś* or of the root *bhuj*? In this regard, it cannot belong to *upa-daṃś*; for when one thing is being indicated (*upadiśyamāna*) or chewed (*upadaṃśyamāna*), something else becomes the instrument. But here, that very radish and so forth is what is being chewed, and nothing else.

However, the status of being an *upapada* certainly applies to *bhuji*, but the technical designation (*saṃjñā*) of "upapada" would not occur, and consequently, the *upapada-samāsa* (compound with an upapada) would also not occur. This is because the application of the grand designation "upapada" is for the purpose of activating the paribhāṣā rule concerning semantic competency (*samartha*). Therefore, when that [paribhāṣā] is present here, the designation of "upapada" must apply to that which has semantic competency toward a specific element. In this case, the designation of "upapada" must apply to *bhuji* in relation to *karaṇa*.

Anticipating the objection that "the capacity of radishes and the like is directed toward the act of eating (*bhuji*), not toward the act of nibbling (*upadaṃśi*"), he says: "And radishes and the like [are used] in relation to nibbling," and so forth.

Although radishes and the like function as instruments (*karaṇa*) with respect to eating, their capacity is nonetheless compatible with being connected to the act of nibbling; for they are its object (*karman*).
Furthermore, the connection with the act of nibbling does not cease simply because there is a connection with the act of eating, since there is no contradiction between them.

Therefore, its status as an *upapada* (secondary word) is indeed established, and that being so, there is an *upapada-samāsa* (compound with a secondary word). Regarding the phrase "when there is a difference in action":
by the mention of the "difference in action," he indicates the domain of the suffix *ktvā*.
Where there is a sequence of actions (*paurvāparya*) and a single agent (*samānakartṛkatva*), that is the domain of the suffix *ktvā*.
Since both of these occur when there is a difference in action, the scope of the suffix *ktvā* is thus indicated:
"having eaten with radish, he eats" (*mūlakenopadaśya bhuṅkte*).

By the rule *aniditām* [Pāṇini 6.4.24], there is the elision of the nasal. Because of the governing heading *dhātusaṃbandhe* (in connection with verbal roots), there must be an auxiliary verb (*anuprayoga*), since [the action] resides in two [verbs].

In this regard, because of proximity, the identity of the object (*samānakarmatva*) is understood only with reference to the root used in the subsequent application (*anuprayoga*); thus he says: "by the root used in the subsequent application," and so forth.
Regarding the word *kālayati*:
{the root *vela* is for the instruction of time (some say *kāla* is a separate root)—Dhātupāṭha; the root *kala* is for casting aside—Dhātupāṭha; the root *kāla* is for wasting—Dhātupāṭha (1880)}.
Regarding the term *dantatāḍam*: the root *taḍ* meaning "to strike" (Dhātupāṭha 1579) belongs exclusively to the *curādigaṇa*. [The compound thus means] "having struck with a staff," and so forth.

In this case, the thief is the object (*karman*) of the root *han* ("to strike"), whereas the cow is the object of the subsequently employed root (*anuprayoga-dhātu*); thus, because there is an absence of a common object (*samānakarmakatva*), only the suffix *ktvā* occurs. [The form] is "āhatya" (having struck).

By the rule *anudāttopadeśa* [Pāṇini 6.4.37] and others, there is the elision of the nasal (*anunāsikalopa*). [The word] "the word *upa*" is connected with each [of the following roots]. This is so that [the suffix *kha*] may apply only after the roots *rudh* and *kaṣ* when preceded by *upa*. [An example is: *pārāupapīḍam*.
The root *pīḍ* in the sense of "immersing" (*avagāhane*) belongs to the *curādi* class (Dhātupāṭha 1544).
Regarding the phrase "of *karṣati*" and so forth:

the root *kṛṣ* is listed in both the *bhvādi* group (in the sense of "plowing," *vilekhane*, Dhātupāṭha 990) and the *tudādi* group (Dhātupāṭha 1286); here, however, the *bhvādika* one is intended, not the *taudādika* one, because of the indication by the suffix *śap*.

The designation [of the word *śapa*] as having the *nirdeśa* (indicatory) form is obtained from its pronunciation with the quality of *kṛta*. Regarding the phrase "from the fury of battle" (*yuddhasaṃrabhāt*):

*saṃrambha* is a specific modification of speech and body preceded by mental agitation; *yuddhasaṃrambha* is the fury directed toward battle; because of that, they draw very close, meaning they approach. Regarding the phrase "the measure is the length" (*pramāṇamāyāmaḥ*):
this is according to the statement, "But *āyāma* shall be the measure (*pramāṇa*)."
By means of another word whose meaning is more commonly known—namely, *daighryam* (length)—he clarifies the very meaning of the word *pramāṇa* (measure). He says: "an increase of two fingers.
The combination of two fingers (*aṅguli*) is *dvyaṅgulam*; the suffix *ac* is applied here according to the rule *tatpuruṣasyāṅguleḥ* [Pāṇini 5.4.86].

By that two-finger [measure], the length of the *khaṇḍikā* is determined. Regarding the term "rising from bed" (*śayyotthāyam*), the *pūrvasavarṇa* [substitution] applies according to Pāṇini 6.1.107, and the *yuk* suffix is added according to 7.3.33; by such means, he demonstrates the sense of urgency (*parīpsā*). Regarding the term "drawing out the gaps" (*randhrāpakarṣam*).
The meaning is that he is so eager that he does not even wait for a vessel; drawing the milk directly from the opening of the breast, he drinks it with his mouth.
Regarding the phrase "drawing from the frying pan" (*bhrāṣṭrāpakarṣam*):

he is so eager that he does not even wait for a container to be provided; drawing [the food] directly from the frying pan, he eats it with his hand. He will explain in the fourth [chapter] that the term *svāṅga* (one's own limb) refers to something that is not liquid and so forth.

Regarding "akṣinikāṇam": the root *kaṇ* means "to close" (Dhātupāṭha 1715); it belongs to the *curādi* class and is preceded by the prefix *ni*. "That limb which, when severed, does not cause the living being to die—that is 'taken' (*hr̥tam*)."
The hands, feet, and so forth are non-permanent, because they are sometimes absent even while a living being is alive. However,
that limb by whose severance a living being dies is permanent, such as the head and so on.

Furthermore, its permanence [is established] because it is always present within living beings. Regarding the phrase "affliction (*parikleśa*) is vexation (*vibādhana*) from all sides," the word "from all sides" (*sarvataḥ*) explains the meaning of the prefix *pari-*, and the word "vexation" (*vibādhana*) likewise explains the root *kliś-* [as expressed by the prefix *vi-*]. Regarding the phrase "by means of [the objects] beginning with the visible, and [the activities] beginning with action":
By the word "etc. (ādi), the triad beginning with the husband is included. "Without remainder" means in its entirety.
"Of things" (*padārthānām*) means of houses and so forth. "Intent" (*tātparyam*) means the repetition of actions; that is the meaning of "frequency" (*ābhīkṣṇyam*).

With the words "pervasion in a substance" (*dravye vyāptiḥ*) and so forth, he demonstrates the distinction between the objects of that which is being pervaded (*vyāpyamāna*) and that which is being practiced (*āsevyamāna*). If the suffix occurs when the meaning is either that which is being pervaded or that which is being practiced, then since those two meanings possess both permanence (*nityatā*) and distributive repetition (*vīpsā*), there ought to be a dual number according to [Pāṇini 8.1.4]. Why, then, does this not occur? He says: "by the same [word]" (*samānena*), etc. Although a compound (*samāsa*) is not prescribed for those two meanings, as has already been explained previously.
And so the author of the Bhāṣya will say:
"Because of the statement 'repetition [vīpsā] occurs in the case of sup-suffixes,' it is meant that reduplication of a word denoting a substance occurs when there is the sense of pervasion (vyāpti).

Because of the statement 'constancy [nityatā] occurs in the case of tiṅ-suffixes,' it is meant that reduplication of a word denoting an action occurs when there is the sense of necessity (āseṣyamānatā)."
"House after house": this is the reduplication of a word that is not inherently repetitive. "Entering house after house."

Regarding the statement "of a word denoting an action," the author first raises an objection beginning with "But surely... and then refutes the opponent's view starting with "for the purpose of excluding *ktvā*.

It might be argued as follows: since both *ktvā* and *ṇamul* are prescribed by the rule [Pāṇini 3.4.22], if *ṇamul* were again prescribed after roots such as *viś* for the sake of repetition (*āsevā*), then the suffix *ktvā* would also apply there. Therefore, is it not the case that *ṇamul* is stated once more for the purpose of excluding that [application of *ktvā*]? This is not so; for [the application of *ktvā*] is indeed desired.
It is accepted that the suffix *ktvā* is prescribed after roots such as *viś* in the sense of repetition (*hrāsa*), as in: "having entered [the house] repeatedly, he sits.
Therefore, the re-mention of *ṇamul* for the purpose of excluding that [suffix] is incorrect. Regarding the phrase "for the sake of the object denoted by a word ending in the second case," etc.:

if it were not employed for the purpose of excluding *ktvā*, then the re-statement would be for the purpose of assigning the technical designation of *upapada* (governing word) to that which ends in the second case.

By this [rule], because of the governing heading "and when a second-case [word] follows" (Pāṇini 3.4.53), the suffix is prescribed when a word ending in the second case is the *upapada*. Therefore, the status of being an *upapada* is obtained for that which ends in the second case. But for what purpose is the status of being an *upapada* desired for a word ending in the second case? To this he says: "the *upapada* compound," and so forth.
The mention of *pakṣa* (option) is because the formation of a compound is prescribed optionally by the rule *tṛtīyāprabhṛtīny anyatarasyām* [Pāṇini 2.2.21].
One might argue: "In that case, when *ṇamul* is prescribed, the designation of *upapada* will still occur. To this he says: "For by that," and so forth.
For *ṇamul* is not prescribed in connection with an *upapada* by that [rule], because there is no word present in the locative case (*saptamī*) [to which it could apply].

Therefore, when the suffix *ṇamul* is prescribed by that [rule], there would necessarily be an absence of the status of being an *upapada*. Regarding the rule "after the roots *as* and *tṛṣ*" (*asyatitṛṣoḥ*):
*asu* is listed as "in the sense of throwing" (Dhātupāṭha 1209), and *tṛṣ* is listed as "in the sense of thirsting" (Dhātupāṭha 1228).
[The phrase] "he intervenes in the action," etc., [is explained as follows].

The suffix *ṇic* is applied by the rule "tat karoti" (Pāṇini 3.1.26), etc., [in the sense of] "he causes an interval. [In the analysis] "he causes an interval (*antaram*) in an action; [thus] he is one who has another action," the suffix *aṇ* is applied according to the rule for the object (*karmaṇyaṇ*), and there is the elision of the *ṇic*. Showing that the word *antara* here refers to an intervention (*vyavadhāna*), he says: "one who intervenes in an action.
[The example is] "he causes to drink" (*pāyayati*).
The root *pā* in the sense of "drinking" (Dhātupāṭha 925) takes the suffix *ṇic*.
By the rule *śācchā* [Pāṇini 7.3.37], the augment *yuk* is added. Thus, it is said:
"The act of drinking by the cows is interrupted by excessive eating and by thirst."

And because this drinking and the drinking that will take place after two days have passed lie between those two [acts of] satiating and quenching thirst, [the phrase] "having made them drink today," etc., explains the meaning of "he makes the cows drink [after] a lapse of two days. Following this, the meaning of other [expressions] is also understood; therefore, they are not explained [here]. [The expression is] "having fasted for two days."

The root *vas* in the sense of "dwelling" (Dhātupāṭha 1942) undergoes vocalization (*samprasāraṇa*) by [Pāṇini 6.1.15], and the suffix *ktvā* is replaced by *lyap*. The substitution of *ṣ* occurs by [Pāṇini 8.3.60]: *śāsivasighasīnāñca*.

Here, the root *vas* refers to "dwelling" (*upavasana*), which is characterized by the intervention of the act of eating (*bhujikriyā*). If the rule *asyatitṛṣoḥ* were not stated here, then this [substitution] would also apply in this case.
"Movement is not interrupted.
Just as in the example of impurity (*mala*), where the act of drinking is interrupted by the intervening actions of spitting and thirsting, it is not so here with movement.
And in that case, the accusative case is used according to the rule *āhagamahanaḥ* (Pāṇini 2.3.5).
Because the entire day is occupied by the act of shooting arrows, the word *iṣu* (arrow) is used in the sense of the object (*karman*) itself—
as in "he causes the cows to drink [them] after having shot them for a yojana. In this case, the word denoting distance (*adhvan*) is the subordinate term (*upapada*).
In some cases, such as with *ruāudhna*, the meaning is that after having made [the child] drink [milk], one makes him drink again after traveling a distance of one *yojana*.
Both [terms], *adhvakarmakam* and *na kālakarmakam*, are *bahuvrīhi* compounds. Regarding the root *ā-diś-*:

it is the root *diś* (Dhātupāṭha 1283), "to bestow," preceded by the prefix *ā*. Regarding the phrase "in the case of reporting something contrary to what was intended": [this refers to the usage of the verb].

"Whatever is intended and desired" means "according to what is intended. The compound *yathābhipretam* is an *avyayībhāva* formed with the particle *yathā* used in the sense of distribution (*vīpsā*), according to Pāṇini 2.1.7: *yathāsādṛśye*. "Not according to what is intended" (*ayathābhipretam*) means that which is not desired; it means "unpleasant. [The word] "I declare" (*ācakṣe*).

From the root *cakṣiṅ* preceded by the prefix *āṅ*, the suffix *laṭ* is applied. By the rule *thāsaḥ se* [Pāṇini 3.4.80], *thās* is replaced by *se*. Then, by the rule *skoḥ saṃyogādyor anteca* [Pāṇini 8.2.29], there is the elision of the letter *k*. Next, by the rule *ādeśapratyayayoḥ* [Pāṇini 8.3.59], there is the substitution of *ṣ* for *s*. Finally, by the rule *iṇkoḥ* [Pāṇini 8.3.57], there is the substitution of *ṣ* for *t*. Thus, we have "uktam" (it was said). Where was this stated? It was stated in the rule *kvoktam* [Pāṇini 3.4.47].
Furthermore, this statement is intended to establish the formation of a compound with an *upapada* (an accompanying word).
> By this [sūtra], the *upapada* compound may optionally occur.

But why does the compound occur with that *ktvā* which is prescribed by this [sūtra], and not with that which is prescribed by [the rule] "of two [actions] having the same agent" (*samānakartṛkayoḥ*) [Pāṇini 3.4.21]? To this he says: "For thus," and so forth.
> At this point [in the commentary on 2.2.22], the phrase "beginning with the third case" (*tṛtīyāprabhṛtīni*) [from 2.2.21] is understood as a governing rule (*anuvartate*).

Therefore, by this [rule], a compound occurs only with that [suffix] for which *ktvā* is prescribed as an option, but not with the other, because *ktvā* is prescribed when words beginning with the third case (*tṛtīyā*) are used as *upapadas*. Now, what is the purpose of mentioning *ṇamul*, since *ṇamul* is already understood from the previous context? To this he says: "In the section on *ṇamul*" and so forth. "Equal status" (*tulyakakṣatva*) means having equal force (*tulyabalatva*).
"By that," and so forth; he shows the purpose of the indicator (*jñāpaka*). [The purpose is:
if it were stated as "and *ktvā*."

If the particle *ca* were not used to deliberately draw forward (*anukṛṣṭa*) the suffix *ṇamul*, it would not carry over (*anuvarteta*) into the subsequent rule, because there would be no deliberate effort [to do so].

Just as, by that same [particle], the suffix *ktvā* is understood to be mentioned as a secondary element (*anvācīyamānatā*), and consequently, due to its non-primary status, it would not carry over into what follows.

When *ṇamul* is mentioned again, however, because they are mentioned together (*sahanirdeśāt*), there is no relationship of subordinate and principal between *ktvā* and *ṇamul*; thus, both carry over. This is illustrated by the example "having made [it] horizontal" (*tiryakkṛtvā*).

The word *tiro’ñcati* is formed with the suffix *kvip* by [Pāṇini 3.2.59], *ṛtvig-ādinā*. When the letter *c* is changed to *j* by [8.2.39], the substitution of *k* (known as *kutva*) occurs by [8.2.62], resulting in the letter *g*. Then, the substitution of *c* for *g* (known as *cartva*) results in the letter *k*. Finally, the replacement of *tirya-* occurs by [6.3.94]. Thus, the root text reads: "having placed the wood (*kāṣṭhaṃ*) crosswise (*tiryakkṛtvā*), he went to the section (*kāṇḍam*). That is, having made it non-straight (*anṛju*).

The meaning is "having placed [the word] at the end. Now, as for this mention of *tiryaci*: since the designation *bha* applies, when the elision of the vowel *a* occurs by [Pāṇini 6.4.138] *acaḥ*, the form ought to be *tiraścī*; therefore he says: "*tiryaci*" and so forth.
For in all cases, a word that serves as an imitation (*anukaraṇa*) is an imitation of the very form of the word itself.
However, there is this much distinction: in some cases there is an imitation of the word as its referent (*śabdapadārtha*), and in other cases an imitation of the meaning (*artha*).

In this context, although it would have been sufficient to say merely "imitation" (*anukaraṇa*), the inclusion of the term "form of the word" (*śabdarūpa*) is for the purpose of making known that this imitation refers specifically to the form of the word alone, devoid of meaning.
This is what is meant: this is an imitation of that animal sound which has "word" as its referent, but it is not that very [animal] sound itself.
Therefore, because it is a different word, the elision of the vowel *a* does not occur; such is the intended sense.

One might object: "Even so, according to the rule *anukaraṇaṃ prakṛtivad bhavati* (Vārttika on Pāṇini 1.1.16), should there not be the elision of the vowel *a*—the operation belonging to the original form (*prakṛti*)—in this case as well? To this, he says: "And not," and so forth. He provides the justification for this very point: "Because it would entail the destruction of the form being imitated. If the operation of the original form were to apply here, then the very form of the imitation—the sound *tiryak*—would be destroyed, that is, it would no longer be perceived.
The meaning is that one should not perceive the imitation (*anukaraṇa*) as being exactly like that which is intended to be imitated, without the loss of its original form.
Since this defect arises when there is an imitation "as if it were the original" (*prakṛtivat*), therefore, in this case, the imitation must not be treated as if it were the original.

However, the rule "the imitation is as if it were the original" (*prakṛtivadanukaraṇaṃ bhavati*, Vyāḍipāda 113) should be understood to have its scope where there is an imitation of a word whose referent is a meaning (*arthapadārtha*).
He explains where and how an imitation (*anukaraṇa*) occurs as if it were the original form (*prakṛti*), stating: "The [substitution] of *aś* for *etad*, etc.
Both "the substitution of *aś* for *etad*" and "the substitution of *aś* for *adas*" are imitations of words whose referents (*padārtha*) are the words themselves.

If an imitation that has a word as its referent were also to undergo the status of being the original form (*prakṛtibhāva*), then, once the operations based on the original form—such as the substitution of *yat* and so forth for the *tyad*-class pronouns—had been applied, the forms would have been *etasya* and *amuṣya*.

Just as the state of being a base (*prakṛtibhāva*) does not occur here [in the case of *kṛ*], so it is also in the case of *tiryac*. "In this instance, correspondence according to order (*yathāsaṃkhya*) is not intended.

But how is it that it is not intended even though it is applicable, given that there are two bases and likewise two suffixes—there being thus a basis for the application of correspondence according to order? [The answer is: because of the mention of *kṛ* and *bhū*, which serves as a sign of non-deviation from the rule.

When this suffix is being prescribed, it ought to be introduced by a fifth case ending characterized by disjunction (*digyoga-lakṣaṇā*), based on the connection with the rule *paraś ca* [Pāṇini 3.1.2]. Therefore, since the fifth case should have been used in the formulation as *kṛbhūbhyām*, the fact that it is instead formulated as *kṛbhvoḥ* serves as a sign of deviation from the general rule.

When a suffix (*pratyaya*) is prescribed here, it ought to be introduced by means of a fifth case (*pañcamī*) characterized by a relation of direction (*digyoga-lakṣaṇā*), according to the connection with [Pāṇini 3.1.2] *paraśca*. In that context, while a fifth-case designation such as *kṛbhūbhyām* should have been employed, the fact that there is this sixth-case designation *kṛbhvoḥ* is a sign of a deviation from the rule; therefore, it should be understood that there is no correspondence according to numerical order (*yathāsaṃkhya*). [The form] *mukhataḥ* is derived by the suffix *tasi* [according to Pāṇini 5.4.45]. [The form] *mukhīkṛtya*...
Here, the word *mukha* ends in *cvi*.
The suffix *cvi* is applied according to [Pāṇini 5.4.50] *abhūtatadbhāve*, etc., and the substitution of *i* for *a* occurs according to [Pāṇini 7.4.32].
[The compound means] "it rests upon the face."

In *tasu upakṣaye* (Dhātupāṭha 1212), the suffix *kvip* is applied by [Pāṇini 3.2.130]. By [Pāṇini 6.1.66], there is the elision of the *su* (the nominative case ending), followed by the application of *rutva* and *visarjanīya*. Here, the word *tas* is a verbal root (*dhātu*), not a suffix (*pratyaya*).

Consequently, the suffixes *ktvā* and *ṇamul* do not apply after a form ending in *tas* when it is designated as such; rather, only *ktvā* applies by [Pāṇini 3.4.21], which states "when two actions have the same agent. Thus, [the commentary says]: "there is no meaning [of the suffix] nor the meaning of the root."
The meaning not accompanied by the suffix *na* is called *nā*, and that accompanied by the suffix *dhā* is called *dhā*.
That suffix whose meaning is *nā* is "having *nā* as its meaning" (*nārtha*), and that suffix whose meaning is *dhā* is "having *dhā* as its meaning" (*dhārtha*).
[The phrase] "having divided into two" (*dvidhākṛtya*) [is used].
Regarding "having divided into two":
the suffix *dhamuñ* is applied by the rule *dvitryośca dhamuñ* [Pāṇini 5.3.45].
Regarding "having made into two parts" (*dvedhākṛtya*).
The term *edhāc* [in Pāṇini 5.3.46] means "having increased," that is, "having set aside" or "having separated.

If the mention of the suffix (*pratyaya-grahaṇa*) were not present here, then because the words *hiruk* and *pṛthak* have the sense of "separation" (*asahārthatva*), they would lack the status of being meanings [of the suffix]; consequently, the suffixes *ktvā* and *ṇamul* would apply even when these two are used as *upapadas*.
Since the requirement is already established by the continuation of the mention of the suffix from the preceding rule, the repeated mention of the suffix here is for the sake of easy understanding.

For the previous mention of *pratyaya* would have been carried over with effort because it was part of a compound (*samāsaikadeśa*). In the example "having separated the pieces of wood, he went" (*nānā kṛtvā kāṣṭhāni gataḥ*),
the sense of the suffix *cvi* is not present here, because the state different from the original form (*prakṛti*) is not intended to be expressed.
Regarding the phrase "the mention of *artha* is for the sake of [excluding] *dhā*": that whose purpose (*artha*) or motive is the suffix *dhā* is described as such.

For there are many suffixes that have *dhā* as their meaning; if the word *artha* were not mentioned, only the suffix *dhā* itself would be included, and not the other suffixes that share its meaning.
But when there is the mention of "suffix" (*atha*), their inclusion also occurs.
Now, why does the mention of "meaning" (*artha*) not also apply here? To this he says: "But not when there is only one.

For the mention of "meaning" is made in cases where many things to be grasped are possible; however, in the case of a suffix that is only one and not a *pratyaya*, its [inclusion] is established even without the mention of "meaning," and thus the mention of "meaning" is not for that purpose.

But surely, even *ghamuñ* and the others will be included by the mention of *dhā* through the principle of *sthānivadbhāva*; therefore, the inclusion of the term *artha* for the sake of *dhā* is also improper? This is not a fault; for there is also a suffix with the meaning of *dhā* that is not a substitute (*agha-ādeśa*), according to the rule: "The suffix *ḍa* is seen after words ending in *ghamuñ* in the sense of self (*svārthe*)" (Vyāḷī-Pañjikā 610). Therefore, the inclusion of the term *artha* must be made for the sake of *dhā*. However, we say this: the inclusion of the term *artha* need not be made even for the sake of *artha*. For there are two suffixes with the name *na*: one is without an indicatory letter (*niranubandhaka*), and the second is with an indicatory letter (*sānubandhaka*).

In that case, if the mention of "meaning" (*artha*) were not present, then according to the rule *niranubandhagrahaṇe na sānubandhakasya* (Vyāḍipañjikā 53), there would be a reference only to the suffixless form, and not to the one with an *anubandha*, nor to *nañ*.

However, when the mention of "meaning" is present, there is a reference to that [suffix] as well. Now, one might object: since the mention of *bhū* continues from the rule *[[P. 3.4.61]]*, for what purpose is *bhuvaḥ* stated here? To this he says: "The mention of *bhū*" and so forth.

For previously, the mention of *bhū* was connected with the root *kṛ*; therefore, when that [root] is carried over [into the subsequent rule], its [mention of *bhū*] would also be carried over. Hence, the mention of *bhū* is repeated here in order to exclude it. The indication *anvac* is explained by the term *tiryac*.
Regarding *anvagbhūya*:
after the suffix *kvip* has been applied as before, and after the substitution of the *jaś*-sounds (*j-ś*) has been applied to the end of that [form], this is the resulting form.

"Having become an attendant (anvagbhūtvā) [he stays]," means "having become a follower (anucara), he remains. Now, one might ask: since the suffix *tumun* is already established by the rule *tumunṇvulau kriyāyāṃ kriyārthāyām* [Pāṇini 3.3.10] when words such as *śak* (to be able) are used as governing words (*upapada*), for what purpose is this new rule commenced? He says: "This commencement is for the sake of cases where there is no [other] action.
This commencement is made so that *tumun* may occur even with words like *śak* when they do not signify another action.
In expressions such as "he is not able to eat" (*na hi śaknoti bhoktum*), it is understood that the following word denotes an action (*kriyārthopapada*).
What then [is the case]? It is something else entirely, a different meaning.
In this context—at least in cases such as "he is able to eat," "he is capable of eating," or "he knows how to eat"—proficiency (*prāvīṇya*) is understood.

In the expression "he is weary of eating" (*glāyati bhoktum*), an incapacity for that [action] is understood; in "he prepares to eat" (*ghaṭayati bhoktum*) and "he deserves to eat" (*arhati bhoktum*), there is merely the fitness for it.
In "he begins to eat" (*ārabhate bhoktum*) and "he sets out to eat" (*prakramate bhoktum*), there is simply another action of the commencement of eating itself.
In "he obtains to eat" (*labhate bhoktum*), there is a refusal [of the request].
In expressions such as "there is [something] to eat" (*asti bhoktum*), there is merely the sense of possibility. "Sufficiency" (*paryāpti*) means "non-deficiency," that is to say, completeness.
Regarding the phrase "in those qualified by the sense of 'enough'": [this refers to the usage of the infinitive].

Although words such as *bhūṣaṇa* (ornament) and others have the sense of "sufficiency" (*alam*), nevertheless, since it is only capacity (*sāmarthya*) that is possible in the context of expressing sufficiency, that alone is understood—either through the observation of usage, through the comprehension of the meaning, or through grammatical explanation (*vyākhyāna*). Therefore, the meaning becomes: "in those [words] qualified by the sense of sufficiency."

If this is so, why was it not stated simply as "in the case of capacities" (*sāmarthyeṣu*)? It cannot be stated in that way; for if it were stated thus, [the rule] would also apply in cases such as "he eats by means of capacity" (*sāmarthyena bhuṅkte*) or "he eats by means of strength" (*balena bhuṅkte*).
However, there is no fault in the formulation as it stands; for in these instances, what is seen is not sufficiency (*paryāpti*), but rather ease (*saukarya*).
The meaning is that this is easy to accomplish.

What is intended here is merely the possibility of its occurrence; the sense is that the formation of such a word is indeed possible. For what purpose is this [sūtra]? So that suffixes such as *tṛc* may apply when the agent (*kartṛ*) is the referent.
Where, then, would they otherwise apply? Suffixes whose meaning is not specifically prescribed apply in their own sense (*svārthe*). (Pāṇini 3.4.75)

But is it not the case that where one desires an affix in its own sense (svārtha), one employs the term "bhāva" [as a qualifier], as in the rule for *ghañ* and other suffixes which specifies "in the sense of an action" (*bhāve*)? And yet these *ghañ*-suffixes do not occur in their own sense; what then? They occur in reference to its property known as "establishedness" (*siddhatā*).

Likewise, in the rule regarding the prescription of *lakāra*s and so forth (Pāṇini 3.4.69), the *lakāra*s themselves are not prescribed in their own primary sense; what then? They are prescribed in the sense of its property called "sādhyatā" (the state of being an object to be accomplished). Although there is a prescription of *ghañ* and other suffixes as well as *lakāra*s in the sense of "bhāva" (action/state), nevertheless, this distinction of scope is obtained due to the inherent nature of the expressive power of words. For *ghañ* and the others have the capacity to express only the established state (*siddhatā*) of the root-meaning, whereas the *lakāra*s [express] only the state of being to be accomplished (*sādhyatā*).

Thus, since suffixes (*pratyaya*) that have no specified meaning apply in their own sense (*svārthe*), it would follow that suffixes such as *tṛc* and others would also occur in that same sense. Therefore, this [sūtra] is commenced so that they may occur only in the sense of the agent (*kartṛ*). In this regard, there are two views: is this a supplement (*śeṣa*) to the rules for the origin of *kṛt* suffixes—such as "the suffixes *ṇvul* and *tṛc* occur in the sense of the agent" or "the suffixes *lyu*, *ṇini*, and *ac* occur in the sense of the agent after roots like *nandi*, *grahi*, and *pac*"? Or is it a specification of meaning (*arthādeśa*) for those *kṛt* suffixes already prescribed by their respective independent prescriptive rules?
Subsequently, the meaning would be indicated by this [sūtra]: "Those [suffixes] which have not been made or prescribed by other rules [occur] when the agent (kartṛ) is to be expressed.

In that case, if the second alternative were adopted, then just as the meaning is declared by this [sūtra] for suffixes such as *tṛc* and others, so too it would be for *khyun* and others; because no distinction is mentioned, they too would apply to the agent.
Furthermore, since instruments (*karaṇa*) and other factors are mentioned in their own individual prescriptive rules, they would also apply to suffixes such as *kaṇ*.

Although it is not possible for a single suffix (*pratyaya*) to apply simultaneously to both the agent (*kartṛ*) and the instrument (*karaṇa*), nevertheless, by the force of the explicit statement (*vacana-sāmarthya*), they would apply alternately to the agent and the instrument. Therefore, this position is faulty; thus, relying on the first position, he says: "Of the rules for the production of *kṛt* suffixes," and so forth.
By this, he states that these [rules] and the present one constitute a single syntactic unit (*ekavākyatā*).

If this were so, then this [remainder] would have to be supplied even in sentences such as "khyun" and others, on the grounds that these too possess this remainder; consequently, in this view, the fault that occurs in the second position would also apply here. To this, he says: "In those cases where," and so forth. He provides the reason for this very point: "Because of the expectancy for meaning. For a remainder belongs only to those [sentences] which, being incomplete, expect a meaning, and not to others.
Therefore, since those very sentences in which no meaning is specified possess a requirement for completion (*sākāṅkṣatva*), it is logical that this [section] constitutes their supplement (*śeṣa*).
The prescriptive sentences regarding the *tṛc*-suffixes and others do not specify meanings and thus stand in need of meaning.
For instance, when it is stated, "The suffixes *ṇvul* and *tṛc* occur," there arises a requirement for a specific meaning: "In what sense do these two occur?"
Therefore, since this is a supplement to those very [rules], it applies only to them.
Regarding the statement "not in the rules concerning *khyun*, *nā*," and so forth,
the word "applies" (*upatiṣṭhate*) is understood.
The connection is with what has been previously stated:
"directly," and so forth.
This is the reason for its non-occurrence.
Sentences such as *khyu* and others do not possess a requirement for further meaning (*arthākāṅkṣā*), because in them the meanings of the instrument (*karaṇa*) and so forth are directly specified.

Therefore, since these [sentences] do not have that [requirement], this [suffix] is not their subordinate element (*śeṣa*), and thus it does not apply to them; consequently, this undesirable consequence (*doṣaprasaṅga*) does not arise. In the case of words such as *bhavya*, the [suffixes] *geya*, *pravacanīya*, and *upasthānīya* are transitive (*sakarmaka*).
Therefore, since the [suffix] would otherwise apply to the object (*karman*) of those [verbs], there is an exceptional rule (*nipātana*) for its application to the agent (*kartṛ*).
For the remaining intransitive [roots], [the suffix *kṛtya*] is used in the sense of the abstract state (*bhāva*) and the agent (*kartṛ*).

Regarding the word "bhavya": [it is derived by adding] *yat* [after a vowel ending root] according to Pāṇini 3.1.97; [then] *guṇa* [substitution occurs]; and [finally] the substitution of *ava* [for the vowel *o*] occurs according to Pāṇini 6.1.80.
Regarding the word *geya*:
by [Pāṇini 6.4.65] *īdyati*, there is the substitution of *ī* for the vowel, and then *guṇa*.
Regarding the word *sāmnām*: [the same rule applies].
In the case of the object, the sixth case (genitive) is applied by the rule governing connection with a *kṛt* suffix. Regarding the word "upasthānīyaḥ," the suffix is *anīyar*.

Regarding the word "janya": in the rule *aco yat* [Pāṇini 3.1.97], the suffix *yat* is applied by the supplementary rule (*vārttika* 213): "There is an addition of *taki*, *śas*, *yati*, *cati*, and *janī*.
Regarding the word "āplāvya": [it is derived from the root *plu* with the suffix *yat*].
From the root *plu*, by [Pāṇini 3.1.125] the suffix *ṇyat* is applied; there is vṛddhi, and as before, the substitution of *ā* for *au*.
Thus, "āpātyaḥ.

By the preceding rule [3.1.124], *ṛhaloṇryat*, because it is designated as a *kṛt* suffix, the letter *l* would apply only in the sense of the agent (*kartṛ*), not in the senses of the action (*bhāva*) or the object (*karman*). Therefore, this [sūtra] is commenced so that it may also apply in those two senses.

Regarding the phrase "having abandoned the indicatory letters (*anubandha*) such as *la*," etc.: having set aside the specific indicatory letters that distinguish the ten *lakāra*s beginning with *laṭ*, the general term "laḥ" is taken;
and this [term] ends in the nominative plural.
He dispels the doubt regarding the fifth and sixth case endings.

If [the word *anantara*] were in the ablative (*pañcamī*), the meaning would be specified as belonging only to that which follows the letter *l*; consequently, the *lakāra* would apply only to the agent (*kartṛ*). Furthermore, in this sixth case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) alone, it would be understood as having the sense of immediate succession (*ānantarya*);
thus, the specification of the meaning would belong only to that which is immediately following the *lakāra*, and the same fault that arose in the case of the ablative would follow.

In this case as well, is the genitive understood in reference to the substitutes (*ādeśa*)? Even so, by this [rule], the meaning of the substitutes of the *lakāra* would be indicated; thus, this very object (the meaning of the domain) would remain unindicated. But surely, the *lakāra* itself is never used [in actual speech]; how then can its meanings, such as the object (*karman*) and so forth, belong to it? There is no fault, because these meanings will be understood as belonging to its substitutes by virtue of their functional capacity (*sāmarthya*).
Thus: "They do not occur in the sense of the abstract state (*bhāva*) after roots that have an object."

Because of the statement "after intransitive verbs" (*akarmakebhyaḥ*); otherwise, that [statement] would be purposeless. By the phrase "of those two, namely *bhāva* and *karman*," he shows by means of the word "of those two" (*tayoḥ*) that there is a reference back to the expression "*bhāvakarmaṇoḥ*. Now, one might object: In the immediately preceding sūtra there are two sentences—the first being "the *l*-suffixes occur in the sense of the object and the agent," and the second being "and they also occur in the sense of the impersonal action (*bhāva*) after intransitive verbs, as well as in the sense of the agent. In that case, is it not more appropriate that the word "of those two" (*tayoḥ*) refers specifically to the agent and the impersonal action mentioned in the immediately preceding sentence? This is not a fault.

When the author employs the term *kartari* ("in the sense of the agent") in the subsequent rule [Pāṇini 3.4.71], it is understood that there is a reference (*pratyavamarśa*) only to the "state" (*bhāva*) and the "object" (*karman*). If there were a reference only to the state and the agent, the mention of the agent would be redundant; for its application to the agent is already established by this very rule. In that case, it would have been more appropriate to say simply "and in the object" (*karmaṇi ca*), since the suffix would not otherwise apply to the object by any other rule. However, since there is here a reference to both the state and the object, the mention of the agent is appropriate so that the suffix may apply to the agent where it would otherwise not be obtained.
As it is obtained in the case of both the action (bhāva) and the object (karman).
Therefore, a reflection upon only the action and the object is appropriate.

By the words "the particle *eva*," etc., the purpose of the particle *eva*—namely, exclusion (*vyavacchedya*)—is for the sake of removal (*apakarṣaṇa*), that is, for the sake of cessation (*nivṛtti*). [The example is] "it was slept" (*śayitam*).

Because the prohibition of *kittva* (the status of being a *kit* suffix) by the rule *niṣṭhā śīṅaḥ* [Pāṇini 1.2.19] and others applies here, *guṇa* substitution occurs. Thus we have *īṣatkaraḥ* and *sukaraḥ*, with the suffix *khal* applied by the rule *īṣadduḥsuṣu* [Pāṇini 3.3.126].
Similarly, we have *īṣadāḍhaṃbhavam*.

Here too, [the rule] "of the agent and the object [there is the sixth case-ending] after the roots *bhū* and *kṛ* [when used with the prefix *pra-*, 3.3.127]" applies. "In the sense of the beginning of an action" (*ādikarmaṇi*) is a descriptive compound (*viśeṣaṇasamāsa*), meaning "that which is both the beginning (*ādi*) and the action (*karman*).
[The term] "moment of action" (*kriyākṣaṇaḥ*) refers to this.

By this, [the author] shows that the word *karman* denotes the action (*kriyā*), and not the means (*sādhana*) as the object. But how is it determined that "it denotes the action"? It is because of the qualification by the word "beginning" (*ādi*). Since there is a beginning, middle, and end among the many moments of an action, it is appropriate to establish that the first moment of action—which distinguishes it from the preceding non-existent state—is the "initial object" (*ādikarman*).

By the inclusion of the word "ādi" (beginning), it cannot be specified by that term that the action of accomplishment (*sādhana-karman*) is indeed one and the same; for since the word "ādi" is dependent upon a beginning that is not itself beginningless, it does not apply there, as there is nothing to be excluded (*vyavacchedya*). Furthermore, showing that [the suffix] is prescribed by the rule *niṣṭhā* [Pāṇini 3.2.102] while *bhūte* [3.2.84] is still in force for the case of an initial action (*ādi-karman*), he says: "In that," and so forth.
Since the first moment of action, being already accomplished, is "past" (*bhūta*), its intended expression as past is logical.

In the example "Devadatta has made a mat" (*prakṛtaḥ kaṭaṃ devadattaḥ*), the suffix *kta* denotes the agent. Since the agent is already expressed by that very suffix, the third case ending does not occur after the word *devadatta*.
However, because the object (*karman*) has not been expressed [by a verbal suffix], the accusative case (*dvitīyā*) indeed occurs after the word *kaṭa*, as in:
*prakṛtaḥ kaṭo devadattena* ("The mat was made by Devadatta"). Here, the suffix *kta* is used in the sense of the object.
Because *karṇa* has already been expressed by that [instrumental suffix] itself, the accusative case does not occur.
Since the agent (*kartṛ*) has not been expressed, the third case (instrumental) indeed occurs after the word *devadatta*, as in:
"It was done by Devadatta" (*prakṛtaṃ devadattena*).

The suffix *kta* is used here in the sense of a state (*bhāve*). Everywhere, the prefix *pra-* indicates the commencement of an action (*ādikarma*). Now, one might object: at the time when the action capable of producing the mat is first initiated, the mat has not yet been accomplished; at that moment, only the grass and other materials which serve as the causes of the mat exist, and the mat does not yet exist in its finished state. Therefore, how can there be grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) between the word "mat" and the word "commenced" (*prakṛta*), which denotes a past time? In response: the word "mat" is applied by way of figurative indication (*tādārthya*) to that specific transformation produced in the grass and other materials by the very first moment of the action. And that [transformation] is indeed past.
Thus, there is no fault. Regarding the word "upasthitaḥ":
the substitution of *i* occurs by the rule "dyatisyatimāsthāmiti kiti" [Pāṇini 7.4.40].
Regarding the word "anūṣitaḥ": [it is derived from the root vas with the prefix anu].
By *vacyādi* (Pāṇini 6.1.15), there is *samprasāraṇa*; by *vasatikṣudhoh* (7.2.52), the augment *iṭ* is added; and by *śāsivasighasīnāñca* (8.3.60), there is the substitution of *ṣ*.
In the word *anujātaḥ*, [the rule] *jātaḥ* (6.4.42) applies, resulting in the substitution of *āt*.
Regarding the word *ārūḍhaḥ*:

by [Pāṇini 8.2.31] *ho ḍhaḥ*, [8.2.40] *jhaṣastathorddho'dhaḥ*, [8.4.41], [8.3.13], and [6.3.111], there is the substitution of *ḍh* and the lengthening of the vowel. Regarding the word *anujīrṇaḥ*: [the same rules apply].

The root *jṛ* is listed in the Dhātupāṭha as "jṛ vayohānau" (1494). By the rule *ṛta iddhātoḥ* [Pāṇini 7.1.100], the substitution of *i* for *ṛ* occurs; by *hali ca* [8.2.77], lengthening takes place; and by *radābhyām* [8.2.42] et cetera, the substitution of *n* for *r* is applied. Now, one might object: since roots such as *śliṣ* are inherently intransitive (*akarmaka*), the desired form is already established; so what is the purpose of including them here? To this he says: "śliṣādayaḥ" etc.
"For that purpose" means for the sake of their transitive (*sakarmaka*) usage. The example given is "goghnaḥ" (a cow-killer).
This very form is derived from the root *han* with the suffix *ac* (the *pacādyac* class);
it is prescribed as a substitute for the dative case (*sampradāna*), and there is also elision of the penultimate vowel (*upadhā-lopa*).

Alternatively, the suffix *ṭak* is prescribed, and the elision of the penultimate vowel is established by the rule *gamahana* [Pāṇini 6.4.98] and so forth, while the substitution of *k* for *h* (*kutva*) is established by the rule *ho hanteḥ* [Pāṇini 7.3.54] and so forth.

If the form *goghnaḥ* is prescribed as an irregular formation (*nipātana*) when [the cow] is the recipient of the action, then it would follow that even a *caṇḍāla* or similar person could be designated by that term; for even those who kill a cow in order to give it to such a person would be considered "well-doers" (*sukṛtin*). Therefore, he says: "By the force of the irregular prescription," and so forth.
Just as in this case, by the force of the irregular prescription, a certain non-technical grammatical operation (*alākṣaṇikaṃ kāryam*) is obtained, so too is a specific meaning (*arthaviśeṣaḥ*).
Consequently, although *goghnaḥ* is prescribed as an irregular formation without qualification, it nevertheless applies only to a specific [person].
Therefore, the designation applies to the officiating priest and others, but not to anyone else such as a *caṇḍāla*.

If that is so, then when a cow is killed for the purpose of giving [its meat], it would follow that the person does not acquire the designation "cow-killer" (*goghna*); to this he replies with the words "even though not," and so forth.

Just as one who is not actually cooking is called a "cook" (*pācaka*) by virtue of his fitness [for the task], so too, even though there is no actual killing of a cow, one is called a "cow-killer. {These are formed with *uṇādi* suffixes—Kāśikā}. These are indeed suffixes belonging to the *uṇādi* class.
Thus [it is said]:
those suffixes which begin with *uṇ* are called "the *uṇādi* suffixes.
But what, then, are those *uṇādi* suffixes? To this he says: "The suffix *mak* after the roots *śyai*, *dhū*, and *sū*," and so forth.
By the word "etcetera" (ādi), words such as *maṅkvant* and others are included.

If these are indeed *uṇādi* suffixes, then since *uṇādi* suffixes are conventional (*rūḍhi*) words and thus lack a relationship between action and its factors (*kriyākāraka*), their occurrence in the sense of the ablative case (*apādāna*) would be impossible. This is not a fault; for even among conventional words, some do possess a relationship between action and its factors, as in the case of *tailapāyikā* and others.
Therefore, this objection is not to be raised.

Regarding the phrase "by those two" (*tābhyām*) and so forth: one might object that if this sūtra did not exist, this reference (*nirdeśa*) as "by those two" would be untenable, because the *apādāna* (ablative case) has not been previously introduced; therefore, how could there even be occasion for an exclusion (*paryudāsa*)? This is not a fault, for this [sūtra] serves a single purpose. If this were omitted, the sūtra would have to be formulated in this way: "After that [suffix], and after an *apādāna*, the *uṇādi* suffixes occur elsewhere."

And likewise, if this were not stated, then there would indeed be an exclusion (*paryudāsa*). Now, for what purpose is the reference to the recipient (*sampradāna*) and the source (*apādāna*) made by means of the word *tābhyām* (from those two)? It might be argued that only this much should have been said: "elsewhere than these [two], the *uṇādi* suffixes [apply]," for since they are the subject under discussion, the *uṇādi* suffixes will be understood as applying elsewhere than to those two. To this he says: "For the purpose of referring back to the recipient," and so forth; and "Otherwise, indeed," and so forth. The meaning is: if the reference to those two were not made by means of the word *tābhyām*.

Regarding the phrase "because of being immediate" (*anantaratvāt*) and so forth: according to the maxim "a rule or a prohibition applies to what is immediate" (*vyā.pa.* 19), there would be an exclusion (*paryudāsa*) of the ablative case alone, were it not for the specific mention "by those two.
[The example given is] "agriculture" (*kṛṣiḥ*).
The suffix *ik* is applied by the rule *ik kṛṣyādibhyaḥ* (Vārttika 324),
as in *tantuḥ*. The suffix *tun* is applied by the rule *sitanigamimasisacyāvidhāñkruśibhyastun* (Dhātupāṭha 1.122).

Regarding the word "carman": [it is] *manin*. Now, one might object: this is not a well-known convention in the world—that roots meaning persistence (*dhrauvya*) are intransitive (*akarmaka*), and those meaning consumption (*pratyavasāna*) are transitive (*sakarmaka*). How, then, is this meaning obtained? To this he says: "It is a convention established within its own school" (*svanikāyaprasiddhiḥ*).
"Its own school" (*svanikāya*) refers to the community of grammarians (*vaiyākaraṇasaṅgha*); therein lies this convention.
Regarding the phrase "in the [senses of] agent, action, and locus":
[the suffix *kta* is applied] to the action (*bhāva*) and the object (*karman*) by the rule beginning with "only to those two" (Pāṇini 3.4.70).
As for the phrase "this belongs to them": [it refers to the following].
The genitive case is used by the rule *adhikaraṇavācinām* [Pāṇini 2.3.68]. As for the question "How so? and so forth, consider the examples:

*bhuktā brāhmaṇāḥ* ("the Brāhmaṇas have eaten") and *pītā gāvaḥ* ("the cows have drunk"). Here, the past passive participle (*niṣṭhā*) denotes the agent; otherwise, because the agent would not be expressed [by the suffix], the third case would have to appear after the words *brāhmaṇa* and *go*, which denote the agent.

Since no one has prescribed the suffix *kta* in the sense of the agent after roots meaning "consumption" (*pratyavasāna*), why does he not read this [sūtra] immediately after that one? For if that were the case, there would be this advantage: the mention of *kta* need not be repeated twice.

In that case, it should be stated as follows: "The suffix *kta* occurs after roots beginning with *maṇ*, and also after [roots] *śliṣ*, *śīṅ*, *sthā*, *ās*, *vraj*, *jan*, *ruh*, and *jṛ*; and after those whose meanings are 'staying' (*dhrauvya*), 'motion' (*gati*), or 'eating' (*pratyavasāna*), when used in the sense of the locus (*adhikaraṇa*)"; and in this way, the twofold mention of *kta* and the mention of "those meaning motion and those being intransitive" would not need to be made. However, it is impossible to state it thus;

for if it were stated in this manner, just as the suffix *kta* would occur in the sense of the agent (*kartṛ*) after roots meaning 'staying', it would also occur after those meaning 'eating', and that is not desired.
Therefore, let it remain exactly as it was stated: "The letter *a* is for the sake of pronunciation.

By this, he dispels the suspicion that it is an *anubandha* (indicatory letter). For if this were an *anubandha*, there would be a grasping (*grahaṇa*) only of *laṅ* and *laṭ* as qualified by the *anubandha* *a*, and not of others such as *liṅ* and so forth.
"In a specific object" means in the agent, the object, and so forth;
"in a specific time" means [at a particular time].

Regarding "in the present [tense] and so forth," the phrase "like the traditional list of phonemes" (akṣarasamāmnāya) means that just as in the traditional list of phonemes, the letters beginning with 'a' are stated in their sequential order within a pratyāhāra, so it is here. [The question is: "Why then is there not a grasping of the letter *l* alone?"
The sense is that no specific [suffix] is prescribed.
Regarding the word "cūḍālaḥ," [the suffix] *lac* is applied by [Pāṇini 5.2.96].

Regarding the phrase "the section on verbal roots" (*dhātvadhikāra*): the term *dhātoḥ* (from [Pāṇini 3.1.91]) follows as a word ending in the fifth case (*pañcamī*), and by this, the *lakāra* is qualified—meaning, "of that *lakāra* which is prescribed after a verbal root.

In the context beginning with [Pāṇini 3.4.69], the meanings designated as agent (*kartṛ*), object (*karman*), and abstract action (*bhāva*) are carried over (*anuvartante*) here; and by these, the *lakāra* is further qualified—meaning, "of that *lakāra* which is prescribed when there is an agent and so forth."

The meaning is that by this [rule], only the specific *lakāra* is grasped, not every [instance of it]. "The letter *p* is for the sake of the accent" means that it should be *anudātta* (unaccented), according to the rule "The *sup* and *tiṅ* suffixes are *anudātta*" (Pāṇini 3.1.4). "The letter *ṭ* in *iṭ*, etc. and so forth.

But even if this qualifying meaning were absent, nothing undesirable would follow, because in the rule *iṭo't* [Pāṇini 3.4.106], the augment *iṭ* is prescribed as being *ad*, and therefore no other *ikāra* (the vowel *i*) could possibly be a substitute for *liṅ*.
If one argues that there exists an *ikāra* that is a constituent part of *tiṅ* and so on, we say no; for those are substitutes for *l* (*lādeśa*), not for *a*.
Indeed, *tiṅ* and the others are *lādeśas* as composite wholes, and the *ikāras* and so forth are not their constituents.

Regarding the rule *arthavadgrahaṇe* (Vyāḍi-paribhāṣā 1), when there is the inclusion of a meaningful *ik* vowel, there arises the contingency that the suffixes beginning with *kṛt* and *taddhita* would also be included. For these [suffixes] are not themselves meaningful, since only the complete groups such as *tiP* and so on possess meaning.
Therefore, the marker *ṭ* need not be applied at all? True, it need not be applied for one who is capable of understanding in this way; however, for one who is incapable, it must indeed be applied.

Why is it not understood that the letter *ṣ* [in *laṣ*] is for the purpose of ensuring that this [augment *ṭi*], which has become an *āgama*, is prescribed in its specific location according to the rule *atha* (Pāṇini 1.1.46)? To this he says: "By *ti* etc. and so forth.
"Equality" (*tulyatva*) means similarity; that [similarity] exists because they are taught in a single grammatical connection (*ekayoganirdiṣṭatvena*).
When that is the case, by virtue of the genitive case in the rule *lasya* (Pāṇini 3.4.77), a relationship with all of *ti* etc. is established.
In the second [interpretation], however, it is indeed *iṭ* itself.

In that regard, whichever position is adopted such that all [elements] receive favor, that alone is fit to be accepted; thus, this genitive case must be understood as a "genitive of location" (*sthāna-ṣaṣṭhī*).
Furthermore, since *iṭ* also becomes a substitute by that [rule], the letter *ṭ* is not for the purpose of indicating a specific location, as is the case with [the *ṭ* in] *deśa*.

Alternatively—the similarity with *tiP* and so forth, which results from their being taught in a single grammatical rule (*ekayoganirdiṣṭatva*), is an indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*) of association (*sāhacarya*).
The meaning is: "because of similarity with *tiP* and so forth" [is equivalent to] "due to association with them.
Through association, there is the determination of a doubtful meaning, as in the example: "the cow with its calf."

Likewise, here too a doubt arises: "Is this a substitute (*ādeśa*) or an augment (*āgama*)?
