Nevertheless, because of its association with *tiP* and others whose status as substitutes is beyond doubt, it is determined that this is indeed a substitute. Consequently, the letter *ṭ* does not serve the purpose of indicating a substitute.

If this is so, then in the rule *phalipāṭinamimanijanāṃ guk paṭinākidhataśca* (Dhātupāṭha 1.103), since the *guK* augment would be similar to the substitutes *paṭi* and others, would the *guK* augment also become a substitute? This is not a fault; for the word "augment" (*āgama*) from [Aṣṭādhyāyī 6.1.137] is understood there, and the designation (*saṃjñā*) is not conveyed by a substitute, but rather by an augment.
Therefore, it should be understood that an *āgama* (augment) possesses the status of being a substitute (*ādeśa*).

In this regard, when even a single genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) is connected with a substitute, it is a genitive of locus (*sthāna-ṣaṣṭhī*); however, when it is connected with an augment, it is a genitive of part (*avayava-ṣaṣṭhī*), as in the rule "the letter *ṅ* [is the augment] of *mahiṅ*" and so forth.
Now, why is the letter *ṅ* not for the sake of [marking] the property of being *ṅit*? Because that is already established by the rule itself: *tasya* (Pāṇini 1.2.4).
Regarding the rule *ṭita ātmanepadānāṃ ṭere* (Pāṇini 3.4.79), [the question begins]: "Why does this not apply here? and so forth.
The intention is that since the *śānac* suffix is also related to a *lakāra* that bears the designation *ātmanepada*, it too ought to undergo the substitution of *etva* for its *ṭi*.
[Regarding the phrase] "by those under discussion" (*prakṛtaiḥ*) and so forth:
among the *tib* and other suffixes under discussion, those which are *ātmanepada*—in this way, the *ātmanepada* suffixes are specified here; therefore, this fault does not arise.
Indeed, [the suffix] *śānac* is not included among the *tiṅ*-affixes.
For the sake of brevity, although one could have said "of those ending in *ṭ*, there is *taṅ*," the expression "of the *ātmanepada*s" is used for the sake of stylistic variety.

Now, if it were stated simply as "of the *taṅ*s," would there not be an inclusion of the *tas* affix by means of the letter *t* through the formation of a *pratyāhāra*? No, this will not happen, because of the paribhāṣā rule regarding the inclusion of meaningful elements (*arthavadgrahaṇaparibhāṣā*).

If that is so, would [the substitution] apply to that which is prescribed in the place of *tha*? No; the term *tiṅ* will be understood as referring to those [suffixes] included among *tiṅ*-suffixes such as *tib* and the rest.

Or rather, by proximity, the inclusion of the *ta*-group (*ta-pratyāhāra*) will be understood through the word *ta* belonging to the *ātmanepada*. However, there is no basis for a universal application, because one must follow the established usage of the linguistic examples (*lakṣya*). For instance, in *peciṣe*: this is *liṭ*; by the rule "in *liṭ*, after a root ending in *a* with one consonant between [the root-final and the suffix], provided the suffix does not begin with a substitute," there is the substitution of *e* and the doubling of the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*).
Regarding "paktāse":
[the suffix] luṭ, [followed by] tāsi; then, by [Pāṇini 7.4.50], there is the elision of the letter *s*. Regarding "pakṣyase": [this is formed with] lṛṭ.

By [Pāṇini 8.2.30], there is *kutva*—the substitution of the letter *k*. Now, why does the substitution of *s* not occur for the letter *th* alone—that is, by the rule *thaḥ saḥ*? For once *th* has been changed to *s*, and the subsequent portion [of the suffix] has been changed to *e* by [Pāṇini 7.1.91], the desired form would indeed be established. This is not possible; for if it were so, the same would apply even to the *th* that occurs in the word *hrārthāś*. If you argue that this does not happen because of the qualification "prescribed after a verbal root" (*dhātoḥ*) due to the governing context of "verbal roots" (*dhātvadhikāra*), we say no; for such a case is impossible.
For such a *takāra* (the letter *t*) is not possible as being prescribed after a verbal root (*dhātu*).

Now, might it be specified that [the rule applies] to what follows immediately after a verbal root? Even so, the substitution would apply only to the subsequent [suffix], and not to the other *vikaraṇas*, because of the intervention; therefore, let it remain exactly as in the original formulation (*yathānyāsam*).

Since the ending in *e* is already established by the substitution of *et* for the final vowel (*ṭi*), the fact that the substitute is made to end in *e* is for the purpose of indicating that "the substitution of *et* for the final vowel of *tiṅ* substitutes does not occur."

Therefore, in forms such as *ḍātā*, *urastā*, and so forth, the substitution of *et* for *t* does not occur—resulting in *paktā*, *paktārau*, and *paktāraḥ*. [Regarding the rule: "The letter *ś* is for the sake of making the replacement apply to the whole.
If that [letter *ś*] were absent, then by the rule "after [an element mentioned in] the governing heading of 'dhātu' [1.1.67]," the substitution would apply only to the following *t*.
But when *ś* is present, by the statement "after [an element ending in] *ś* [1.1.55]," the substitution applies to the entire [element].

Now, why is it not stated as *śe*? It cannot be done in this way; for if it were *śe*, it would receive the technical designation *pragṛhya*. And in this case, in the word *vyatipapa*, there would be the substitution of *pi* [for *pā*].

But when *eś* is present, it does not occur; for he will state this: "Whatever [substitution] occurs in relation to a phoneme, one should know that it applies to that which begins with it. As in *papaktha*.

Thus, there is the absence of *iṭ*. In some readings, the form *pecitha* appears; in that case, *iṭ* is applied by the rule [7.2.63], and then *e* is substituted for *ay* and the reduplication is elided by [6.4.121].
Regarding the word *peca*:

because of the governing rule *dhātoḥ* [Pāṇini 3.1.91], and by [Pāṇini 1.1.67] and [1.1.54], the letter *th* is replaced by the vowel *a*. Then, by [Pāṇini 6.1.97], there is the substitution of a single subsequent form (*pararūpa*) for the two *a*s.

Alternatively—since the substitute must correspond to the original in terms of its semantic scope (*āntaratamya*), it is logical that the multi-syllabic *akāra* should be replaced by a multi-syllabic substitute; thus, it applies to the entire aggregate [of the stem and suffix], as in *peciva* and *pecima*.
The augment *iṭ* is applied here according to the rule for roots beginning with *kṛ* (Pāṇini 7.2.13). [The root] *vid* means "to know."

By this, it is understood that the term *vid* refers to the root √vid meaning "to know," and not to other roots. He thinks as follows: the word *vidaḥ* is in the ablative case; therefore, by the rule Pāṇini 3.4.79 (*vido laṭo vā*), there ought to be a substitution for the immediately following suffixes beginning with *ti*. Furthermore, no *parasmaipada* suffixes can follow any other root than this *vid*, because they would be separated by the *vikaraṇa* suffixes.
Because the roots *vicārayati* and *sattāyati* are marked with the *ātmanepada* (middle voice) suffix, the occurrence of the *parasmaipada* (active voice) suffixes is untenable;
therefore, only the root meaning "to know" (*jñāna*) is understood here. Regarding the phrase "only five," etc.:

[an objection is raised]—"But surely there is no second mention of 'five' here, nor is there a mention of 'etcetera' (*ādi*) intended as a qualifier for the substitutes (*ādeśa*). In that case, all the substitutes beginning with *ṇal* should apply alternately in place of all five [roots]. So how is the meaning obtained that 'only five substitutes, beginning with *ṇal*, occur'? To this he says: "Because of the connection with the substituends (*sthānin*)," etc.

For here, only the first five *sthānin*s (substitutes) have been specified; and by the technical rule (*paribhāṣā*) "of those [five]," a connection with only the first five is possible, not with the others.
To explain: only among the first five is there *āntaratamya* (phonetic proximity), because they share the same meaning;
it does not exist for the others, because the opposite is the case.

Therefore, because of the connection with the substituends (*sthānin*), it is logical that even in the case of the substitutes (*ādeśa*), the number five and the status of being "first" are understood; thus, there are exactly five substitutes, beginning with *ṇal*.
Regarding the form *āttha*:

by the rule *āhasthaḥ* [Pāṇini 8.2.35], the *h* of *āha* becomes *th*; then, by the rule *khari ca* [Pāṇini 8.3.55], there is *cartva* (substitution of a voiceless unaspirated stop) for that *th*, resulting in *t*.
Regarding the word "bravīti": [the rule] *brūva īṭ* [Pāṇini 7.3.93] applies. Regarding the word "pareṣām" (of others):
it refers to the suffixes beginning with *tha*.

Now, for what purpose is this word *brāuvaḥ* stated again? Since the word *brāuva*, which ends in the fifth case (ablative), will simply undergo a change of case-ending to become sixth-case (genitive) ending, one might think it will be understood as such. To this he says: "The repetition of the word *brāuvaḥ*" and so forth.
For a change of case-ending is appropriate only when the related term (*sambandhin*) is not explicitly heard.

Here, however, since *parasmaipadānām* [of the active endings] refers to the very *ti*-suffixes and others under discussion, they are already present as the related terms in the sixth case; therefore, a change of case-ending is not appropriate.
If "brāuvaḥ" were not stated again, then just as the *ṇal* and other affixes belong to the *parasmaipada* [verbs], so too would this substitution (*āhauddeśa*) apply to them.
Therefore, "brāuvaḥ" is stated again so that *brāuvaḥ* may serve as the substitute for those [affixes].
[Otherwise] it would belong only to the *parasmaipada* [affixes].
The ellipsis is "if 'bhuvaḥ' were not stated again. And this is the reason for the repetition of "'bhūvaḥ'.
The word *hi* has the sense of "because" (*yasmāt*).

Since, in the absence of this repetition, the substitution of *ah* would apply only to the *parasmaipada* endings, therefore the repetition of the word "brūvaḥ" must be made. [The rule] "tām-ādayaḥ" refers to those whose prescription is made by [the rule] "tasthasthamipāṃ tāmtamtāmaḥ" (Pāṇini 3.4.101) and so forth.
[The phrase] "and the elision of *s*" (salopaśca).

There is the rule "yasya nityaṃ ṅitaḥ" (Pāṇini 3.4.99). Regarding "aḍāṭau" and so forth: by the rule "luṅlaṅlṛṅkṣvaḍudāttaḥ" (6.4.71), *aṭ* is prescribed; by the rule "āṭaśca" (6.4.72), *āṭ* will be prescribed as an operation for the *laṅ* [tense]. Furthermore, by the rule "laṅaḥ śākaṭāyanasyaiva" (3.4.111), there is the substitution of *jus* for *jhi*.

And no specific distinction is introduced here; therefore, the intention is that just as the operation of *tām* and so forth occurs due to the extension (*atideśa*), so too must the operation of *laṅ* occur. [The suffix] *mip* undergoes elision by [Pāṇini 3.4.100] *itaśca*, and its substitution by *am* also takes place.
This is a point of contention (*deśyam*).

Because the substitution of *u* by rule 3.4.86 (*eruḥ*) and the replacement of *m* by *niḥ* (rule *merniḥ*) will both be prescribed as exceptions (*apavāda*) to those two [rules], it is said that "that [substitution] is a restricted option" (*vyavasthitavibhāṣā*). By this, he considers that only the substitution beginning with *tām* occurs, and not that beginning with *aṭ*. [This applies to] the forms *hinyoḥ*, etc.
*Hi* and *ni* form *hinī*; it must be stated that there is a prohibition of the substitution of *u* for these two, otherwise forms such as *lunīhi* and *pacāni* would not be established.
[The objection is raised: "Or rather, it is due to the power of the pronunciation.
For if, once the vowel *ī* had been applied, the substitution of *u* were required, then [the author] would have pronounced the vowel *ū* instead.

For this is indeed the lighter method for deriving the word. Nor does the brevity of the sūtra depend on the pronunciation of the vowel *i*; rather, when *u* alone ought to have been pronounced, he pronounces *i* for this purpose: namely, so that the substitution of *utva* (the replacement of *u* by *ū*) shall not occur. In the case of "lunīhi," since the status of being a *pit* (causing *guṇa*) is prohibited by [Pāṇini 1.2.4], the status of being a *ṅit* applies; consequently, by [Pāṇini 6.4.113], the substitution of *itva* (the replacement of *i* by *ī*) takes place.

Regarding *rāghnuhi*: the root *rādh* (and *sādh*) is listed [in the Dhātupāṭha] as "to accomplish" (1262, 1263). Because it belongs to the *svādi* group, the suffix *śnu* is applied. Here too, as in the previous case, because the suffix is marked with *ṅ*, there is no *guṇa* substitution.

Now, for what purpose is the rule formulated as *guru-sūtra* (a heavy rule), rather than simply stating *se rhi ṅicca*? It cannot be done in this way; for if the status of being *ṅit* were prescribed [there], then by virtue of *sthānivadbhāva*, the status of being *pit* would certainly still apply.

Consequently, due to the status of being *ṅit*, the operations of a *ṅit*—such as the prohibition of *guṇa*—would occur, and due to the status of being *pit*, the property of being *anudātta* (unaccented) would also occur. Therefore, let it remain exactly as it was originally stated: "The status of being *pit* is optionally negated."
Regarding the phrase "the substitute" (*lādeśaḥ*): because that [original] is immediate, whereas the substitute, being separated by it, is not immediate; thus, it is treated as an option.
Regarding the word *yuyodhi*:

the root *yu* (Dhātupāṭha 1033) means "to mix" (*miśraṇe*) and also "not to mix" (*amiśraṇe*). By the rule *bahulaṃ chandasi* (Pāṇini 2.4.76), there is *ślu*-elision of the *śap* suffix; by the rule *ślau* (6.1.10), there is reduplication.
Here too, because the suffix is *pit*, it does not possess the property of being *ṅit*; therefore, *guṇa* substitution does not occur.
By [Pāṇini 6.4.103], there is the substitution of *gh* for the root vowel.
Regarding "prīṇīhi":
the root *prīñ* (meaning "to satisfy" and "to desire," according to the Dhātupāṭha, entry 1474) belongs to the *kryādi* class; therefore, the suffix *śnā* is applied.

Here too, since there is no *apit* [affix], the substitution of *ī* occurs as before. This is an exception (*apavāda*) to the rules "for *ut* and for elision" (*utthalopayoḥ*). Specifically, it applies to the cases where the substitution of *u* for *e* is obtained by the extended application (*atideśa*) of *eruḥ* [Pāṇini 3.4.86], and where the elision of the vowel *i* is obtained by the extended application of the rule *itaśca* [Pāṇini 3.4.100] which prescribes such elision in the *laṅ* tense.

In the word *pacāni*, [the augment] *āṭ* is applied by [Pāṇini 3.4.92]. Here, there are two positions: either the *loṭ* (imperative) is qualified by the vowel *e*, or the vowel *e* is qualified by the *loṭ*. If the first position were adopted, then because the *e* would be a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*), and because the rule of "extension to that which ends with [the qualifier]" (*tadantavidhi*) applies to a qualifier, the suffix *ām* would be prescribed for a *loṭ* ending in *e*. Consequently, since [the substitute *ām*] consists of more than one phoneme (*anekāl*), it would result in the undesirable consequence (*doṣa*) that it becomes a replacement for the whole (*sarvādeśa*). This fault must be addressed. However, in the second position, the vowel *e* itself is the primary element (*pradhāna*) because it is the thing being qualified.

Furthermore, since the rule of *tadantavidhi* (extension of a grammatical operation to that which ends with the specified element) does not apply to the principal element itself, this will apply to the vowel *e* alone; thus, there is nothing further to be addressed.
Therefore, relying on the second alternative, he says: "of the vowel *e* belonging to the *loṭ* [imperative]," and so forth. For example: *pacatām*.

In *ṭeretve kṛta ām*, as in *iha pacāvedam* and *yajāvedam*, although the *guṇa* substitution is included by the mention of the imperative (*loṭ*) due to the treatment of the end as the beginning (*antādivadbhāva*), nevertheless, because of the principle that "the external (*bahiraṅga*) is [regarded as] non-existent when the internal (*antaraṅga*) is to be applied" (Vyāḍi-Pāṇini 42), the *ām* replacement does not occur;
for while the *guṇa* is external— since it depends on two words— the *ām* replacement is internal.

The status of being internal (*antaraṅga*) is due to having a single word as its locus. For example, in *pacasva*, the substitution of *se* for *thās* (according to Pāṇini 3.4.80) results in the form [ending] with *vakāra*.
In *pacadhvam*, [the same applies].

"When *ṭeret* has been applied, the substitution of *am* occurs; and that [suffix] is the first person (*uttama-puruṣa*) and is marked with *p*. Now, why is the property of being *pit* not assigned to *āṭ* itself? Because it would be purposeless. For the property of being *pit* would serve either to mark [the suffix] as unaccented (*anudātta*) or for the sake of *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* substitutions. In that regard, the unaccented nature of *āṭ* is already established simply by virtue of its being an augment (*āgama*). Furthermore, *āṭ* cannot be the cause for *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* substitutions because it is not a suffix (*apratyayatvāt*).

Therefore, since the status of being a *pit* (having *p* as an *it*) with respect to the first person (*āṭ*) is purposeless, it is prescribed for the last person (*uttama*) alone—as in "karavāṇi. Because of its *pit* status, the last person does not possess the status of being a *ṅit*; consequently, *guṇa* substitution occurs.
Regarding "karavai":

there is *vṛddhi* [substitution] by the rules *eta ai* [Pāṇini 3.4.93] and *āṭaśca* [Pāṇini 6.1.87]. Regarding "an exception to *ām*": it is an exception to what would otherwise be obtained by the rule *āmetaḥ* [Pāṇini 3.4.90].
"Let him cook this; let him sacrifice this.

When the *loṭ* suffix is replaced by the *laṅ* substitute according to Pāṇini 3.4.85 (*loṭo laṅvat*), the substitution of *śap* occurs, and then by Pāṇini 6.1.87 (*ato dīrgho yañi*), there is lengthening (vṛddhi). Regarding the phrase "alternately": why do these two not occur simultaneously? He thinks thus: these two are prescribed as having the marker *ṭi*, and the status of being *ṭi* is for the purpose of prescribing [the accent] on the initial syllable.
Furthermore, two things cannot simultaneously possess the status of being "first" (*ādi*), because a single point of origin (*ādideśa*) is already occupied by one; thus, simultaneity is not tenable.
Examples such as *joṣiṣat* have been explained under [Pāṇini 3.1.34], and they are also explained here.

Regarding *joṣiṣat*: the root *juṣ* (Dhātupāṭha 1288) means "to take pleasure in" or "to serve. The *i* in *sip* is for the sake of pronunciation; by [Pāṇini 3.4.97], *aṭ* is added, followed by the elision of the *i* [by 6.4.64]. Then, by [7.2.35], the augment *iṭ* is applied, the *guṇa* of the light penultimate vowel occurs, and by [8.3.59], the *ṣ*-substitution takes place. Regarding *tāriṣat*: the root *tṛ* (Dhātupāṭha 969) means "to swim" or "to cross over. By [7.3.84], there is a lengthening of the vowel of the root through irregular substitution (*vyatyaya*). The remainder is as before.
Regarding "mandivat": the root *mad* is listed as "madi stutimodamadasvapnakāntigatiṣu" (Dhātupāṭha 13); by the rule "idito num" (Pāṇini 7.1.58), the augment *num* is added. Regarding "padāti":

the root *pad* is listed as "pada gatau" (Dhātupāṭha 1169) in the Divādi class and is anudātta; there is a substitution for the Ātmanepada with the Parasmaipada; the suffix *śap* is added, and by the rule "akaḥ savarṇe dīrghaḥ" (Pāṇini 6.1.97), the long vowel results from the combination with the augment *aṭ*; finally, the suffix *tip* is applied.
The elision of the vowel *i* does not occur here; this is because the option (*vā*) is carried over from the rule *tadvidhau* [Pāṇini 3.4.96]. Regarding the form *cyāvayati*:

the roots *cyuṅ*, *jyuṅ*, *pruṅ*, and *pluṅ* mean "to move" (Dhātupāṭha 955–958), and the causative suffix *ṇic* is applied due to the presence of a motive. Regarding the form *mantrayete*: [the root *mantra* takes the suffix *ṇic* when used in the sense of "to consult," etc., according to Pāṇini 3.1.21].

Regarding the root *matri* (from the Dhātupāṭha 1679, meaning "to reproach in secret"), with the causative suffix *ṇic*, the *śap* affix, and the substitution of *guṇa* and *ayādeśa*—this is the reading in the manuscript.
[The question is: "Why does [the augment] *āṭ* not occur [in forms such as] *padāti* or *vidyut*? etc.

Regarding the phrase "by virtue of the capacity of the rule": if the substitution of *ai* were to apply to the augment *āṭ*, he would have prescribed the augment *aiḍ* itself; it is thought that in this way there is economy of procedure (*prakriyālāghava*). Regarding "śāsai":
this is the first person singular ending *iṭ*, with the substitution of *e* for the final *ṭ*.

The examples beginning with *īśai* have been explained under the rule *upasaṃvādāśaṅkayoḥ* [Pāṇini 3.4.8]. Regarding *dadhasa*: from the root *ḍudhāñ* in the sense of "holding and nourishing" (Dhātupāṭha 1092), there is the substitution of *se* for *thās* [3.4.80], the elision (*ślau*) of *śap*, reduplication by the rule *ślau* [6.1.10], the augment *aṭ*, and the elision of the vowel *a* by the rule *ata ekahalmadhye* [6.4.120]. As for the phrase "the mention of the parasmaipada," etc.:

But surely, the substitution of *e* for *ṭi* will serve as a superseding rule (*bādhaka*) in cases such as the augment *iṭ*; so what is the purpose of mentioning *parasmaipada*? This is not so; for the scope of the *ṭi*-to-*e* substitution is other *lakāra*-initial forms, whereas the elision of *it* applies to *parasmaipada* forms. When both rules would apply simultaneously, the elision of *it* would occur by virtue of its being the subsequent rule. [Thus we have] *karavāva*, where *āṭ* is added by [Pāṇini 3.4.94].
[The commentary begins with] "The mention of the 'first person' (*uttama*)," and so forth.

If, then, the mention of the "highest" (uttama) person is made for the purpose that [the suffix] should not occur in other persons, is that so? No; rather, only the mention of *vas* and *mas* should be made. Here too, this is the meaning: it is unnecessary to mention the letter *s*. Would the elision of *s* not occur by the very rule concerning the final letter (*alo’ntyaparibhāṣā*)? It is impossible to make the mention of *vas* and *mas*; for if that were done, when *tau* (the suffixes *tas* and *tha*) occur in place of another person by means of *vyati*, the elision would still occur; and when *thas* is substituted in place of the highest person, the elision would not occur.

Only when the term *uttama* (first person) is explicitly mentioned does the fault not arise; for, by the principle of *sthānivadbhāva*, the designations *madhyama* (second person) and *uttama* apply to the forms *bhavantī*. Since there is no rule for the coexistence of two designations, the designation *madhyama* is superseded by the designation *uttama*. Furthermore, if the mention of the letter *s* were not made, then when other numbers are substituted for the *uttama* [person] through transposition (*vyatyaya*), there would be the elision of even other phonemes. Therefore, let it remain exactly as in the original formulation: *apacāvāpacāma*.
In *laṅ*, [the substitution of] a long vowel occurs by [Pāṇini 7.3.101]. Thus, *apacāt*.
In *luṅ*, *apākṣīt*.

In *apākta*, there is *vṛddhi* by [Pāṇini 7.2.3] *luṅ-vadavraja-* etc., and *iṭ* by [Pāṇini 7.3.96]. In *apāktām*, there is *vṛddhi* as before, and the elision of *sic* by [Pāṇini 8.2.26]. In *pacet* and similar forms, the *liṅ* suffix is applied by [Pāṇini 3.3.161] *vidhi-nimantraṇa-* etc.; the *sakāra* is elided by [Pāṇini 7.2.79] *liṅ-salopo’nantasya*, and its elision occurs along with the *śap* by [Pāṇini 6.1.87] *vali lopaḥ*. In *pakṣīṣṭa* and similar forms, the *liṅ* is used in the sense of benediction (*āśis*); the *kutva* of the letter *c* occurs by [Pāṇini 8.2.30], and the *ṣatva* of the letter *k* occurs by [Pāṇini 8.3.57] *iṇkoḥ*. [The phrase] "belonging to the domain of the *parasmaipada*" [is used].

By this, he shows that the locative case in the rule "in the *parasmaipada*s" (*parasmaipadeṣu*) is a locative of scope (*viṣayasaptamī*), not a locative of sequence (*parasaptamī*). A locative of sequence is not possible here, because the *liṅ* [optative] lacks *parasmaipada* endings.
[The phrase] "when the unaccented status of the augment has been obtained" [is used].
How, then, is it determined that an augment (*āgama*) is unaccented? Precisely because of the explicit statement that *yāsuṭ* is accented.

For if augments were not unaccented, the rule prescribing their accentuation would be purposeless; since *yāsuṭ* is a part of the suffix, its initial vowel would already be established as accented by the accent of the suffix itself.

Objection: Should not the mention of the acute accent (*udātta*) be for the sake of those [suffixes] ending in *pi*, since they are indeed unaccented (*anudātta*), and thus the *yāsuṭ* augment belonging to them would also be unaccented if the word "acute" were not stated? Response: This is not so; if this were the intended purpose, he would have simply said "api. Therefore, this mention of the acute accent is merely an indicator (*jñāpaka*) that the augments are unaccented. As it is said: "Because there is no possibility of operations conditioned by the marker *ṅ* in that case."

The intended meaning is that this does not apply to all [suffixes]. Why is this so? Because in the case of *uṣyāt*, the *samprasāraṇa* (vocalization) prescribed by the rule *grahijyā-ādi* (Pāṇini 6.1.16) is possible only when the suffix *yāsuṭ* follows, which is marked with the indicator *ṅ*.
For the *samprasāraṇa* is dependent solely upon the presence of the indicator *ṅ*; since no specific [suffix] is mentioned [in the rule], it applies only where *ṅ* is present.

In that regard, if the *ṅittva* (the property of being marked with *ṅ*) were prescribed for *yāsuṭ*, then there would be favor shown only to the single case of the *samprasāraṇa* (vocalization) of the root *grah*.

However, since the prescription of *ṅittva* for the *liṅ* (optative) suffix results in favor toward the entire operation of *ṅit*—namely, the prohibition of *guṇa* and *vṛddhi*—*ṅittva* is prescribed specifically for the *liṅ*.
[This refers to the phrase] "of the operations of *ṅit*."
The meaning is "in the presence of suffixes marked with Ṅ or Ṇ. Regarding the form *kuryāt*:
there is guṇa of the root based on the vikaraṇa suffix, *ut* substitution by [Pāṇini 6.4.110] *ata ut sārvadhātuke*, and the elision of the vowel *u* by [Pāṇini 6.4.109] *ye ca*.
They would form [the word] as *kuryuḥ*;
by [Pāṇini 6.1.96], there is the substitution of the single subsequent form (*pararūpatva*).
[The example is] *acinavam*.
In *mipo'm*, there is guna [substitution] because of the absence of the *ṅit* designation;
and this is the purpose of the indicator (*jñāpaka*). [Namely,] that "this *kit* status belongs only to the affix."

If this is so, does it not contradict the rule that the *yāsuṭ* augment added to the *liṅ* in the sense of benediction (*āśis*) becomes *kit*? There is no contradiction; the mention of *yāsuṭ* is merely an indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*) for the *liṅ* itself. Thus, by means of its constituent part (*liṅavayava*), the *kit* status is prescribed for the *liṅ* itself by this rule, because the *liṅ* has *yāsuṭ* as its constituent part. [This applies] "not to the augment" (*nāgamasya*).
Regarding the phrase "of the augment" (*nāgamasya*), here too it should be understood to mean "of the augment alone. Regarding the phrase "due to the absence of purpose" (*prayojanābhāvāt*).
The meaning is that it is not because every *kit* suffix lacks a purpose.

Why? Because by the rule [Pāṇini 6.1.15] *vacy-ādi-sūtra*, the *samprasāraṇa* (vowel substitution) that occurs for the roots *vac* and *svap* is possible even before the *yāsuṭ* augment when it is a *kit*.
For the *samprasāraṇa* is prescribed for any *kit* suffix in general, since no specific [suffix] is mentioned.

If the prohibition of *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* is exactly the same [in both cases], then what is the distinction between being marked with *ṅ* (*ṅit*) and being marked with *k* (*kit*), such that *kit*-ness would be prescribed when that [*ṅit*-ness] has already been obtained? To this he says: "The *samprasāraṇa*," and so forth.
If it were marked with *ṅ*, the *samprasāraṇa*—which is to be enjoined by the rule beginning with *vac-ādi* (Pāṇini 6.1.15)—would not occur when there is a *kit* suffix.
Furthermore, the *guṇa* enjoined by [the rule] *sārvadhātukārdhadhātukayoḥ* (Pāṇini 7.3.84) would also not occur.
In the case of *iṣyāt*,

there is the elision of the *s* sound according to [Pāṇini 8.2.29]. In the case of *vacyāt*, because of the absence of the *kit* designation, the vocalization (*samprasāraṇa*) of the root *vac* does not occur.
Regarding "jāgṛyāt":

by the preceding sūtra, the suffix is marked with Ṅ (ṅit), and therefore there is no guṇa substitution. In both cases, because they belong to the adādigaṇa class, there is elision of the suffix śap. Regarding "kṛṣīran": [the same applies].

"The *liṅ* [mood] is used in the sense of benediction (*āśis*). Regarding "may I do" (*kṛṣīya*), it is the *liṅ* in the sense of benediction. "This is not a part of the substitute" (*naivāyam ādeśāvayavaḥ*).

Because only the letter *a* is the substitute. If this is so, since this *a* is prescribed as a substitute, would it not—by the rule "A vowel (*aṇ*) and an *u-dit* [element] denote their homogeneous counterparts (*savarṇa*), provided they are not suffixes" (Pāṇini 1.1.69)—be a grasper of its homogeneous sounds? It will not be so, because of the principle: "An *aṇ* being in the process of being taught (*bhāvyamāna*) does not include its homogeneous counterparts" (Vyāḍi-pāda 35). Or, even if there were inclusion of homogeneous sounds, by the principle of closest proximity (*antaratamya*), only a one-mora (*mātrika*) sound would result. Now, why is the letter *a* not substituted for the augment *iṭ* in forms such as *lāviṣīṣṭa*? He says: "There is no inclusion of the augment *iṭ*."
Regarding this, he states the reason: "In the case of the mention of that which has meaning," and so forth.

Now, one might object: even suffixes (*āgama*) certainly possess meaning; for instance, the meaning of the optative (*liṅ*) is expressed only when accompanied by *yāsuṭ*, not by the suffix alone. This is not so; for while other verbal suffixes (*lakāra*) are seen to have meaning even without it, suffixes (*āgama*) are never seen to have meaning in that way.

Therefore, they do not become meaningful [in that context]. Now, is the *liṅ* (optative) qualified by the letters *t* and *th*—meaning "that *liṅ* which stands in the place of *t* and *th"*? Or is it [qualified] such that "those two [suffixes] belong to the *liṅ* which has *t* and *th*" as its substituends? In this regard, if the first alternative were adopted, then because it is the qualified element (*viśeṣya*), the *liṅ* would possess primacy.
Consequently, since grammatical operations apply to the principal element, the augment *suṭ* would be added to the *liṅ* itself.
And in that case, because it is both subsequent in order and specifically prescribed (*viśeṣavihita*), the *suṭ* would supersede the *sīyuṭ*.
Therefore, considering that this [first] position is faulty, he states the second position with the words "of the two related to the *liṅ*.
To clarify the meaning of what was stated—that the augment *suṭ* occurs after the letters *t* and *th*—he says, "the letters *t* and *th* are the augments.
The intention is that they are the primary elements by virtue of being the qualificands (*viśeṣya*).

Regarding what was stated— "of the *liṅ* and its related element"— he says "the *liṅ* is its qualifier" in order to clarify its meaning. As for "the *sīyuṭ*, however, is an augment belonging to the *liṅ* itself," the *t* and *th* are excluded by the word "itself" (*eva*).
"By that," and so forth.

Since, for this reason, the *takāra* and *thakāra* are the substitutes for *suṭ*, whereas for *sīyuṭ* it is only the *liṅ* [augment], therefore, because they occupy different positions (*bhinnadeśatva*), *sīyuṭ* is not superseded by *suṭ*.
Nor is a relationship of sublation (*bādhyabādhakabhāva*) appropriate between two things occupying different positions, due to the absence of contradiction (*virodhābhāva*).
"May he plough," "may you plough"— these are the forms in the third person singular and second person singular. Likewise,
"may they two plough," "may you two plough"— these are the forms in the dual.
[The suffixes] *āt*, *ām*, *ātha*, and *ām* [are applied].

In all cases, the *liṅ* [is used] in the sense of benediction (*āśis*). Because of the rule "and *u*" (Pāṇini 1.2.32), there is an absence of *guṇa* due to its being marked with *k*. [In the form] *paceyuḥ*: the substitution of *iy* [occurs] by [the rule] "after *pac*" (Pāṇini 7.2.80), and the subsequent form (*pararūpa*) [is applied] by [the rule] "of the preceding and following" (Pāṇini 6.1.87). By the mention "and of *vid*" (*vetteśca*), he shows that only the root belonging to the *lug-vikaraṇa* class is intended here.

For the suffix *jhi* occurs only after that very [root], not after other roots ending in *vid*, because they are separated by the *vikaraṇa*. Since the roots meaning "existence" (*sat*) and "investigation" (*vicāraṇā*) are *ātmanepada*, the suffix *jhi* is impossible there; therefore, it is logical to understand the inclusion of only those roots that have the *luk*-vikaraṇa.
Regarding the statement, "The mention of 'abhyasta' is for the sake of [excluding] 'as'":

if the mention of 'abhyasta' were for the sake of [excluding] 'as', then in that case, *jus* would also apply to *jhi* when it is related to *laṭ* and so forth; therefore, he says, "'ṅit' is also understood.
By this, *jus* will occur only for *jhi* that is related to the marker *ṅ*, and not for others—this is the intended meaning.
Regarding the forms *abibhayuḥ* and *ajihyayuḥ*:

the root *ñi bhī* (meaning "fear," Dhātupāṭha 1084) and *hrī* (meaning "shame," Dhātupāṭha 1085) undergo *guṇa* substitution by [Pāṇini 7.3.83] *juji ca*. Then, by [Pāṇini 2.4.75] *juhotyādibhyaḥ śapaḥ śluḥ*, there is elision (*ślu*) of the suffix *śap*; and by [Pāṇini 6.1.10] *ślau*, there is reduplication. Regarding the form *ajāgaruḥ*: [the same process applies].

Because the root *ad* belongs to the class beginning with *adādi*, there is elision (*luk*) of the *śap* suffix. For the root *jāgarti*, the designation *abhyasta* (repeated) applies by the rule "the six beginning with *jakṣ* [are called *abhyasta*]" (Pāṇini 6.1.6). Regarding the rule "after *sic*, for the *jhi* following an *ā*-ending [root]," it is stated that the *jhi* is immediately subsequent to both [the root and *sic*]. Considering that such immediate succession after both is impossible because of the intervention of *sic* after the *ā*, he asks: "How? and so forth. [The answer is: "When there is elision of *sic*."

When the elision (*luk*) of *sic* is applied by the rule *gātisthā* [Pāṇini 2.4.77], then, by virtue of the characteristic of the affix (*pratyayalakṣaṇa*), *sic* becomes possible immediately after [the root].
This is because of the statement "after that which ends in the vowel *a*," since [the root] is heard immediately preceding it.
"By means of hearing" (*śrutyā*) means by means of the perception accomplished through the sense organ of hearing (*śrotrendriya*).
Thus, since proximity (*ānantarya*) is established by both [the *sic* suffix and the audible *s*], it follows by implication that *jus* replaces *jhi* after a form ending in *sic* with *luka*.
For proximity to two [elements] is not possible when the *sic* is actually being heard.
"The letter *t* is for the sake of ease of pronunciation," because there is no [other] form to be excluded;
for a suffix beginning with *s* cannot occur after either a short or a protracted vowel. "Since it is already established by the preceding rule," [it is said].

Even though the *sic* affix has been elided, he demonstrates the purpose of the restriction "abhūvinn" by means of the rule for the presence of an affix (*pratyayalakṣaṇa*), because the *jhi* affix is not immediately followed by *sic*. The augment *vuk* is applied by the rule "bhuvo vug luṅaliṭoḥ" [Pāṇini 6.4.88]. Now, one might object: "But this cannot be obtained here by the preceding rule, for in this case there is no immediate succession of *jhi* with respect to *sic*; so why is it being prohibited? To this he replies: "by the rule for the presence of an affix," and so forth.
For when [the suffix] has been elided by the rule regarding the characteristic of an affix (*pratyayalopa*), there is immediate succession; therefore, the rule would apply by the preceding one.
Thus, the *jus* substitution is prohibited by this restrictive rule (*niyama*).

If, then, this is for the sake of restriction, it would not apply even in the case of *akārṣuḥ*, because here the *jhi* does not follow immediately after a root ending in *at* with the elision of *sic*. To this he says: "of the same class," and so forth.
Therefore, this *jus* is prescribed after a form ending in the elision of *sic* for the purpose of restriction (*niyamārtha*).
And that restriction depends upon a similar class; thus, it excludes only that which belongs to the same class.
What is of the same class? Another form ending in the elision of *sic*.

And in the case of *na cākārṣuḥ*, this is not the scope of the rule stating that "the *sij* suffix is elided before the *jhi* ending," and therefore the *jus* substitution indeed occurs, as in *āyuḥ* and *avuḥ*. As before, there is the elision of *śap*, and as before, there is the substitution of the subsequent form (*pararūpa*). "Only the *laṅ*" and so forth:
the *jus* substitution must be prescribed for the *jhi* belonging to that [tense].
This was stated with reference to the *tiṅ* suffixes. Why is this so? Because the suffixes *laṅ* and *liṅ* can also follow immediately after a stem ending in *ā*;

furthermore, since the substitution of *jus* for those two is prescribed by the very rule beginning with *tatsambandhinostu* (Pāṇini 3.4.108), this [present statement] is not made with reference to them.

The particle *eva*, however, serves to exclude the conditional (*lṛṅ*), because the root is separated from the suffix *syap*. That [suffix] should be understood as that for which there is no occurrence of the conditional (*laṅ*) by way of extension (*atideśa*).
On the other hand, that for which the occurrence of the conditional (*laṅ*) is prescribed by way of extension is called "the conditional" (*laṅ*) figuratively.

In ultimate reality, however, this is indeed the *loṭ* [imperative] and not the *laṅ* [imperfect]. Regarding the phrase "that which [occurs] by virtue of being like the *laṅ*," the term *laṅ* is connected [to the compound]. The mention of *laṅ* is made for the purpose that the primary *laṅ* itself may be understood, so that it does not become equivalent to the *laṅ*.

But by what means does the treatment as *laṅ* (*laṅvad-bhāva*) occur? He says: "The *loṭ* [is] like the *laṅ*" (*loṭo laṅvat*). For by this rule (Pāṇini 3.4.85), when the operations of the *laṅ* are extended to the *loṭ*, it acquires the status of being like the *laṅ* due to its connection with the operations of the *laṅ*. Thus, through a metaphorical application (*upacāra*), it is designated as *laṅ* because it resembles the *laṅ*.

The meaning here is as follows: if the mention of *laṅ* were not made for the purpose of including the primary *laṅ*, then—due to the extension (*atideśa*) provided by the rule "the *loṭ* is like the *laṅ*" (Pāṇini 3.4.85)—just as the operations such as *tām* and so forth apply to the *loṭ*, this [operation of *jus*] would likewise apply.
Therefore, the mention of *laṅ* is made in order to avoid this fault; let there be no *jus* here, owing to the specific effort of mentioning *laṅ* in the context of the *loṭ*.

As for that [substitution] which is prescribed by the rule *sijabhyastavidibhyaśca* [Pāṇini 3.4.109], why does it not occur in cases such as *vibhyatu*, *jāgratu*, and *vidantu*, since there is no other effort involved therein? To this he says: *sijabhyasta* etc.

But how is it that, without further effort, the preceding *jus* does not occur in the imperative (*loṭ*)? To this he says: *jusbhāvamātraṃ hi* etc. For this *jus* is not qualified here by the primary *laṅ*; rather, it is merely the state of being *jus*.
The *jus* that is prescribed in this section applies only to the primary *laṅ*, not to any other;
therefore, even the preceding [form] does not take *jus*.
The mention of the single letter *e* is for the sake of what follows.
Now, why is the particle *eva* not used for that very purpose? Because its function is to express an injunction (*vidhi*).
Indeed, the meaningfulness of the particle *eva* is not tenable in a sentence whose purpose is an injunction;
for it is employed for the sake of restriction (*niyama*), not for the sake of injunctions.

And this is not for the purpose of restriction (*niyamārtha*); for a rule (*vidhi*) that is commenced when [the matter] is already established serves as a restriction (Kāśikā on Pāṇini 1.4.1). However, this is not commenced when [the matter] is already established.
Therefore, the particle *eva* is solely for the sake of what follows. [Objection:

Might the particle *eva* here be for the purpose of ensuring it applies according to the opinion of Śākaṭāyana alone, so that it does not apply according to the opinions of others? [Reply: No; because even without that [particle], this restriction is already established.

If it were not for the opinion of others, the mention of Śākaṭāyana would be purposeless. Regarding the term *adviṣu*: due to its belonging to the *ad*-class (the second class of roots), there is the elision (*luk*) of the suffix *śap*. In the examples "bhavati" and "nayati," once the verbal suffix (*tiṅ*) has received the designation *sārvadhātuka*, the suffix *śap* is applied by virtue of that designation in the sense of the agent (*kartṛ*). Since this *śap* also belongs to the *śit* category and is thus *sārvadhātuka*, the *guṇa* substitution occurs by Pāṇini 7.3.84: *sārvadhātukārdhadhātukayoḥ*.
In *roditi*,
as before, there is the elision of *śap* [by Pāṇini 3.1.68], and then the augment *iṭ* [is applied by Pāṇini 7.2.76].
In *pavamānaḥ* and *yajamānaḥ*, [the same applies].
Because that [suffix] is *sārvadhātuka*, there is the *śap* augment; because that too is *sārvadhātuka*, there is *guṇa* substitution for the root. Regarding "lavitā":
the suffix *tṛc* is applied, and by the rule *ārdhadhātukasyeḍvalādeḥ* [Pāṇini 7.2.35], the augment *iṭ* is added.
Regarding "vṛkṣatvam": [the suffix *tva* is applied].
Regarding "lūbhyām": it is derived from the root *lū* with the suffix *kvip*, followed by the dual ending *bhyām*. Regarding "jugupsate": [it is derived from the root *gup* with the suffix *san*].
The suffix *san* is applied by the rule *gupādibhyaḥ san* [Pāṇini 3.1.5].
Since suffixes such as *tva* and others are not considered *ārdhadhātuka*, there is no application of the augment *iṭ*.

It has been stated that *vṛkṣatvam* is a counter-example, because the suffix *tva* is not prescribed after a verbal root (*dhātu*). However, [the objection] that forms such as *lūbhyām* are incorrect is unfounded, according to the maxim "those ending in *kvip* do not lose their status as verbal roots" (Vyāḍiparibhāṣā 132); for the suffix *myām* is prescribed only after a verbal root, and the suffix *san* is also prescribed after a verbal root, since *gup* and others are verbal roots. This is not so; for precisely to avoid this very fault, it was stated that [the suffix is prescribed] "after that which is designated by the word *dhātu*."
And this is its meaning: "that which is prescribed after the word 'dhātu'"; that is to say, that which is prescribed by uttering the word *dhātu*.

For in the defining rule (*lakṣaṇa*) for that [suffix], there is the mention of *dhātu*, and the suffixes *bhyas* and *āmsan* are not prescribed in such a manner; because in the rule prescribing them, neither the governing heading (*adhikāra*) of *dhātu* nor the explicit mention of *dhātu* is possible.

But how is the meaning "that which is prescribed by means of the designation *dhātu*" obtained? For the term *dhātu* occurs only once [in the rule], and since that [single mention] has already served its purpose in excluding suffixes that are not *dhātus*, it is not capable of expressing any further specific distinction? The thought is this: either the second occurrence of the word *dhātu* is understood as being carried over from the rule prescribing *yaṅ* (Pāṇini 3.1.22), or from the rule *śamidhātoḥ saṃjñāyām* (Pāṇini 3.2.14). In that case, by one *dhātu*, the exclusion of non-*dhātu* suffixes is effected; [by the other, the specific application is established].
[The word *apara*] is excluded; by another [word], the suffix (*pratyaya*) is specified as "that which is prescribed after a verbal root (*dhātu*).

Why is the term *śeṣa* ("remainder") mentioned? It is so that [the designation *pratyaya*] does not apply to *tiṅ* and *śit*; otherwise, since there would be no governing rule for a single designation, there would be a co-occurrence (*samāveśa*) [of designations] just as with the designations *ādi-pratyaya* and so on. [For example, in the form] *śekitha*:
because the *liṭ* [affix] is an *ārdhadhātuka*, [the augment] *iṭ* is applied by [Pāṇini 7.2.63].
In this regard, the intended meaning is that [the substitution] occurs only for the root *ṛ*, and not for other verbal roots (*dhātu*s).
Thus, by [Pāṇini 6.4.121], there is the substitution of *i* and the elision of the reduplication,
as in *jagle* and *mamle*.

Because it is an *ārdhadhātuka* [affix], there is the elision of the vowel *ā* by [Pāṇini 6.4.64]. Now, he refutes what was stated in the passage beginning with "But surely... (*nanu ca*), namely that [the *ārdhadhātuka* designation] is an exception (*apavāda*) to the designation *sārvadhātuka* (Kāśikā 3.4.115). His intention is this: elsewhere, because of the governing rule on the non-simultaneity of designations (*ekasaṃjñādhikāra*), there is a co-occurrence [of designations], as in the case of the designations *pratyaya* and so forth. But here, there is no governing rule on the non-simultaneity of designations; therefore, it is incorrect to say that this *ārdhadhātuka* designation is an exception to the *sārvadhātuka* designation. [The author replies: "This is true," and so forth, thereby supporting the fact that it is indeed an exception. [The example is given: "laviṣīṣṭa" (as found in the manuscript reading). "laviṣīṣṭhāḥ. (Note: *laviṣīṣṭhāḥ* is the manuscript reading for *laviṣīṣṭa*).
By [Pāṇini 3.4.107], *suṭ* is added; there is the change to *ṣ* and the change to *ṣṭ*. {The printed reading is "astaye," but it is "svastaye."} Regarding "svastaye":
the root is *as* in the sense of "existence" (Dhātupāṭha 1065); the suffix *ktin* is applied in the feminine.
Because it is treated as a *sārvadhātuka* suffix, the substitution of *bhū* for *as* does not occur. Regarding "viśṛṇvire": [the root is *śru*].
Here, because the *liṭ* [perfect] suffix is treated as a *sārvadhātuka*, the *śnu* affix is applied according to Pāṇini 3.1.74, as well as the substitution of *śṛ*.
Thus we have *sunvire* and *upastheyāma*.

In the case of the root *sthā*, there is the suffix *liṅ*, followed by *yāsuṭ* and *mas*. [The substitution of] *i* occurs by [Pāṇini 7.4.24]. Now, since all of this is already established by [Pāṇini 3.1.85], for what purpose is this new rule begun? He says: "It is precisely for the sake of [the application of] the rule *vyatyayo bahulam* (‘there is a great variety of irregularities’). The meaning has been explained. Thus ends the fourth quarter of the third chapter in the *Kāśikā-vivaraṇapañjikā* composed by the venerable Ācārya Jinendrabuddhi, who is a disciple of the Bodhisattva. And the third chapter is completed. “This is a governing heading (*adhikāra*)” because it has not been marked with a circumflex accent (*svarita*).
"Up to the completion of the fifth chapter"—
by this he shows the limit of the governing rule (*adhikāra*).
Beyond that, it does not continue, because it lacks the *svarita* accent.

"In [the section] beginning with *svādi* and ending with *kapparyanta*": this indicates the scope of the governing rule (*adhikāra*). "The term *ṅī* is a general designation for *ṅīp*, *ṅīṣ*, and *ṅīn*" and so forth.
The term *ṅī* here refers to the general category of *ṅī* alone, excluding its specific indicatory letters (*anubandhas*).
The phrase "of *ṭāp*, *ḍāp*, and *cāp*:
*āp*" is connected with the preceding statement that there is a general inclusion.

Now, since the suffixes beginning with *ṅī* are many, one might ask: "Should there not be a plural ending? How then is there a singular designation in the rule *ṅyāpprātipadikāt* [Pāṇini 4.1.1]? To this he says: "Of these," and so forth.
The meaning is that this designation of the *ṅī*-suffixes and others is made here by means of a collective (*samāhāra*) *dvandva* compound;
for if it were a *dvandva* of mutual conjunction (*itaretarayoga*), there would necessarily be a plural ending.
And this *dvandva* compound is not one of mutual conjunction (*itaretarayoga*), but rather one of collective aggregation (*samāhāra*).

Since that [aggregation] constitutes a single meaning, the singular number alone is appropriate. The explicit statement "it is a designation of an aggregate" is for the purpose of excluding mutual conjunction and for the purpose of excluding other types of compounds; otherwise, a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*) such as "the nominal stem of *ṅī* and *āp*" (*ṅyāpoḥ prātipadikaṃ ṅyāpprātipadikam*) might also be suspected.

Therefore, that which is a nominal stem (prātipadika) consisting of a compound ending in a *ṅī* or *āp* suffix— such as *rājakumārī* and the like— is the source [for the suffix], but not from *kumārī* and the like when they are used alone.
Since the nominal stem is the base (*prakṛti*) precisely by virtue of the rule for the application of *ṅī* and *āp*,
this reference is made by means of a collective copulative compound (*samāhāra-dvandva*).

In that context, however, three [elements]—the feminine suffix *ṅī*, the suffix *āp*, and the nominal stem (*prātipadika*)—are taken as the bases; therefore, it occurs from all [of them]. Now, how is the analysis (*vigraha*) here? Some say: "The feminine suffix *ṅī*, the suffix *āp*, and the nominal stem.

But surely, because the technical designation "nominal stem" is prohibited by the rule "that which is not a suffix" (Pāṇini 1.2.45), the derivation of case endings would not occur for the word *ṅī*? It is replied: this is not a suffix, but rather an imitation (*anukaraṇa*) of a suffix.

Even so, would there not still be a prohibition on the grounds that "an imitation follows the nature of the original" (*prakṛtivadanukaraṇaṃ bhavati*) [Pāṇini 8.4.46]? This is not a fault. For imitation is twofold: of the meaning and of the mere sound.
The Teacher has indicated this by his dual instruction—through both the application and non-application of the *iyaṅ* substitute in rules such as [Pāṇini 7.1.18] and [Pāṇini 7.1.19].
Therefore, in this case, only the sound is imitated, and not the sound accompanied by its meaning.

Therefore, in this case, there is no prohibition at all by the rule *apratyayaḥ* [Pāṇini 1.2.45]. However, the extension (*atideśa*) "as if it were the original form" (*prakṛtivat*) applies when the imitation (*anukaraṇa*) possesses meaning. Now, one might object: even so, shouldn't there be elision of the final consonant and the following vowel (*halṅyādilopa*) according to [Pāṇini 6.1.68]? It is said in reply: the elision of *su* occurs after a stem ending in a feminine suffix marked with *ṅ*, not after the mere suffix *ṅī*.

If it is argued that [the suffix] *ṅīp* would apply by virtue of the principle of "behaving like that which possesses a designation" (*vyapadeśivadbhāva*), we say no; for it is stated that "the principle of behaving like that which possesses a designation does not apply to what is not a nominal stem" (*Pāṇini 1.1.65*), and this [word *pūrvā*] is indeed a nominal stem.

Therefore, [the suffix applied] is *ṅīṣ*. Now, if it is argued that this is a *paribhāṣā* (metarule) concerning the domain of suffix-vidhis, because it is made known in the rule *pūrvādiniḥ* (Pāṇini 5.2.85–87), [we reply: this is not a suffix-vidhi; what then? It is a vidhi for elision (*lopa*). Consequently, the *paribhāṣā* does not apply, and thus the principle of "behaving like that which possesses a designation" certainly exists; therefore, the rule for elision proceeds.
Therefore, there must be elision (*sulopa*) [of the case-ending], as in the rule *ṅī ca*.

This analysis, *ṅīśca*, is based on assuming the general application of the technical rule (*paribhāṣā*). However, another says: "In actual usage, in words such as *kumārī* and *gaurī*, the vowel *ī* that occurs is itself reproduced here with its case-ending elided; thus, it remains simply *ṅī*."

If this is so, why is the letter *ṅ* attached for the purpose of denoting the general category (*sāmānyagrahaṇa*)? Would it not follow that, because it possesses meaning through the meaning of the item being imitated (*anukriyamāṇa*), the production of case-endings would occur once again, and consequently, the form *ṅīḥ* would have to result [by P. 4.1.41]? This is not the case; for there is a prohibition by the rule *apratyayaḥ* (P. 1.2.45), which relies on the designation of "that which has the characteristics of an affix" (*pratyayalakṣaṇa*) with respect to the case-ending that existed at the prior time. Alternatively, one might argue: "On the basis of the *jñāpaka* [in P. 8.2.8], the designation 'nominal stem' (*prātipadika-saṃjñā*) is not prohibited by the rule *apratyayaḥ* (P. 1.2.45) through the characteristics of an affix."
This is incorrect; this *jñāpaka* (indicative evidence) pertains specifically to the domain of the rule for the elision of *n*.

Therefore, it is established that here there is no prohibition of the designation *prātipadika* by means of the rule *pratyayalakṣaṇa*. Now, it might be argued: if they are suffixes (*pratyaya*), then by the statement "and [they] follow" (*paraśca*, Pāṇini 3.1.2), the case-endings (*svādayaḥ*) occurring after [the base] imply a preceding base (*prakṛti*), for otherwise their status as "following" would not be possible, since that status of being subsequent depends upon a prior element; and no base other than those ending in *ṅī* and so forth is possible [in this context].

In this context, even without the explicit mention of "ṅy-āp-prātipadika," this very base (*prakṛti*) is obtained by the principle of elimination (*pāriśeṣya*). To explain: other bases are the verbal root (*dhātu*)—which includes that which ends in a *tiṅ* affix—and the sentence (*vākya*).
As for suffixes (*pratyaya*), they include the *svādi* group, the *ṭābādi* group, and the *aṇādi* group.

Among these, a verbal root cannot be followed by *svādi* suffixes; for those [suffixes], being prescribed in relation to meanings such as singularity and so forth, imply a word (*śabda*) possessing those [meanings].
Nor does the verbal root possess oneness and so forth.

Furthermore, if it is argued that [suffixes] arise without distinction, but a restriction is applied to those that have already arisen—even so, their arising from the verbal root is not tenable; for the *svādi* suffixes, which are prescribed generally, are superseded by the *tavyadādi* suffixes, which are prescribed specifically.
If it is then suggested that the *ṭābādi* suffixes might instead arise from the verbal root—this might be so.

If the mention of *ṅyāpprātipadika* were not present, then from verbal roots ending in *a*, such as *jugups* and others, the suffix *ṭāp* would apply by [Pāṇini 4.1.4] *ataḥ*; from verbal roots ending in *ap*, such as *vañc* and others, the suffix *ṅīp* would apply by [Pāṇini 6.3.45]; and from verbal roots ending in *n*, such as *man* and others, the suffix *ṅīp* would apply by [Pāṇini 4.1.5] *ṛnnebhyo ṅīp*. But this is not the case; for the suffixes *ṭāp* and so on are prescribed in the sense of feminine (*striyām*), whereas a verbal root denotes an action (*kriyā*). And since an action is non-substantial (*asattvabhūta*), it has no connection with gender (*liṅga*), because gender is a property of substance (*dravya*).
By this, the derivation of feminine suffixes such as *ṭāp* from verbal forms (*tiṅanta*) and from sentences (*vākya*) is refuted, because both of those are primarily concerned with action (*kriyā*).
Furthermore, the derivation of primary suffixes (*aṇ* etc. from a verbal root (*dhātu*) is likewise untenable;
for they are prescribed only when there exists a relationship with meanings such as "offspring" (*apatya*).

Since the meaning expressed by a nominal stem (*dhātu*) is not a sentient being (*asattvabhūta*), just as its connection with femininity is impossible, so too is its connection with meanings such as "offspring" (*apatya*).

By this, the derivation of suffixes such as *aṇ* from verbal forms (*tiṅanta*) or from sentences is refuted; for even the meaning of those [verbal forms], which is primarily action (*kriyāpradhāna*), lacks a connection with "offspring" and the like.
Even though a connection exists in a case such as "the offspring of him who cooks for Devadatta," it does not occur because of the *jñāpaka* rule *tiṅaśca* (Pāṇini 4.1.78).

If it is argued: "Let those *taddhita* suffixes which are prescribed in connection with meanings such as 'offspring' (*apatya*) and so forth not arise according to the principle just stated; however, those which are prescribed in their own sense (*svārtha*) ought indeed to occur"—this is a mere pretense. For just as the occurrence of [suffixes] like *su* (the nominative case-ending), though prescribed generally, is not possible because they are superseded by [suffixes] like *tavyat*, which are prescribed for specific cases, so too the occurrence of even *svārthika* suffixes, though prescribed generally, is likewise impossible because they are superseded by *svārthika* suffixes like *tumun*, which are prescribed for specific cases.
If it is asked, "In that case, would there be *ke* suffixes after verbal roots ending in *tiṅ*?"—they will not occur, because of an indicator (*jñāpaka*).

Since [Pāṇini] in certain rules for the formation of *taddhita* suffixes mentions the term *tiṅ*—as in "and after *tiṅ*" (*tiṅaśca*)—and since he mentions *tiṅ* in certain rules for the formation of *taddhita* suffixes—as in "and after *tiṅ*" (*tiṅaśca*)—this indicates that *taddhita* suffixes do not occur after verbal forms ending in *tiṅ*.
If it is then asked, "Would they occur after a sentence?"—they will not occur, due to the absence of conventional usage (*anabhidhāna*).

For when it is said, "Devadatta’s ākaḥ" (*devadattasyākaḥ*), meanings such as the unknown (*ajñāta*) that belong to the sentence-meaning are not indicated by the suffix *kap*; rather, they are indicated solely by the word *āśa*. Likewise, there should be no occurrence of [suffixes] such as *su* after a verbal ending (*tiṅanta*). This is because their meanings—such as singularity (*ekatva*) and so on—are already expressed by the verbal endings themselves, and it is not proper to employ words whose meaning has already been expressed, according to the rule: "There is no employment of what has already had its meaning expressed" (*uktārthānām aprayogaḥ*, Vyāḍi-Pāṇini 60). If it is objected: "But is not the employment of even those whose meaning has been expressed observed, as in the case of *ekaḥ*, *dvau*, and *bahavaḥ*?"—[the reply is: The employment here is justified because of the inclusion of the term "number" (*vacana*) [in the sūtra].

For in the rule beginning with *prātipadika*, the inclusion of the term "number" (*vacana*) serves this very purpose, because that technical rule (*paribhāṣā*) applies there. Consequently, the operation of a pronoun (*sarvanāma*) is established even for [words] such as *sarva* when they are qualified by gender (e.g., *sarvā*).

If this is so, could one not—relying on this very principle—omit the mention of the suffixes *ṅī* and *āp* [in the rule *ṅyāpprātipadikāt*]? This is not possible; for the designation of a nominal stem (*prātipadika-saṃjñā*) cannot apply to a meaningful verbal form (*śabda-rūpa*) qualified by gender, because of the prohibition [stated in Pāṇini 1.2.45]: *apratyaya*.

Furthermore, in a rule prescribing the designation of a nominal stem (*prātipadika-saṃjñā*), it is not possible to indicate all meaningful elements as the designata by means of their own form, because they are infinite in number.

If this is so, then this paribhāṣā would likewise not apply to the rule "as in the case of *iṣṭhan* for a nominal stem" (*ṇāviṣṭhavat prātipadikasya*, Vārttika 813); since its own form is not being grasped there, the status of being treated like *iṣṭhan* would consequently not occur for those [nominal stems] qualified by gender.

What fault is there in that? [One might argue: in the case of *kumārīmācaṣṭe* and *kumārīyati*, the elision of the *ṭi* suffix would not occur. This is not a fault; for the treatment as if it were an *iṣṭhan* suffix (*iṣṭhavadbhāva*) is desired extensively (*bahulam*). Thus, it is recited in the *Cura*-class [of roots]: "After a nominal stem (*prātipadika*), in the sense of a verbal root, [the suffix *ṇic* is added] extensively, and it is treated like the *iṣṭhan* suffix" (Cura-ga-sūtra 186). Therefore, by virtue of this extensive application (*bahulavacana*), the treatment as if it were an *iṣṭhan* suffix will apply even to a form qualified by gender. Furthermore, with the words "Moreover," etc., he adds another purpose. The word *tat* refers back to the mention of the feminine suffixes *ṅī* and *āp*.
The mention of *ṅī* and *āp* is for the purpose that the formation of *taddhita* suffixes may occur from bases ending in *ṅī* and *āp*. For example, in the form *kālitarā*:

from the word *kāla*, the suffix *ṅīp* is applied by the rule [Pāṇini 4.1.42] (*janapada-ādi-sūtra*), and from that base ending in *ṅī*, the suffix *tarap* is applied by the rule [Pāṇini 5.3.57] (*dvivacana-vibhajya-upapade*), after which the short vowel is substituted by the rule [Pāṇini 6.3.43].
Regarding the form *hariṇitarā*:

from the word *harita*, the feminine suffix *ṅīp* is applied by the rule *varṇādanudāttāt topadhāto naḥ* [Pāṇini 4.1.39], whereby the *t* is replaced by *n*. If the mention of *ṅī* and *āp* were absent in the rule *aṭkupvāṅ* [Pāṇini 8.4.2], then because of its higher status, the comparative suffix (*ātiśayika*) would apply first. However, since this mention exists, and because the bases ending in *ṅī* and *āp* are relied upon as the stems when a secondary suffix (*taddhita*) is prescribed, the *ṅī* and *āp* must occur first; thus, the prescription of the secondary suffix is established from that which ends in them.

But surely the feminine suffix (*strīpratyaya*) is *antaraṅga* (internal), whereas the *taddhita* suffixes are *bahiraṅga* (external). For instance, because of the governing rule [Pāṇini 4.1.82], they arise after that which ends in a case-ending (*vibhaktyanta*); and case-endings depend upon [grammatical relations] such as the object (*karman*), while the object and so forth are *bahiraṅga* because they are caused by external actions. Consequently, since their cause is *bahiraṅga*, the *taddhita* suffixes themselves also depend solely on what is *bahiraṅga*.

Since a gender marker (*liṅga*) does not depend on any other related element, it is "internal" (*antaraṅga*); therefore, suffixes such as *ṭāp* and others, which are caused by that [gender], are also internal. Consequently, because they are internal, the suffixes *ṭāp* and so forth must necessarily apply first, and only afterwards would secondary nominal suffixes (*taddhita*) apply to the stem ending in those [feminine markers]. Thus, is the mention of *ṅī* and *āp* (i.e., feminine endings) redundant? This is not so; for in the statement "the mention of *ṅī* and *āp* is for the purpose of introducing secondary nominal suffixes after what ends in them," by the term "secondary nominal suffixes" (*taddhita*), only those secondary suffixes used in their own sense (*svārthika*) are intended.

To indicate this very point, the suffix *tarap* is cited in its own sense (*svārthika*) after feminine suffixes such as *kālitara* and *hariṇitara*. Among the *svārthika* suffixes, the rule *samarthānām* [Pāṇini 4.1.82] does not apply.

For the author of the Vṛtti will say: "This governing rule extends up to the limit of the *svārthika* suffixes" [Vārttika on Pāṇini 5.3.1], because there is no utility for [the application of that rule] among the *svārthika* suffixes.

And this being the case, since the suffixes expressing the same meaning (*svārthika*) ought to arise from the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) itself without depending on the production of case-endings (*vibhakti*), how can they be considered "external" (*bahiraṅga*)? But even so, forms such as *kālitara* would not serve as examples; for the suffix *tarap* is external.

For although that [suffix] does not depend on the production of a case-ending, it certainly depends on an external object as its counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*); however, since a feminine suffix does not depend on any such counter-correlate, it possesses the status of being "internal" (*antaraṅga*). This is not a fault; this direction of examples was merely shown by the author of the *Vṛtti*. These, however, are the examples that should be presented here: *enikā*, *śyenikā*, and *rohiṇikā*.

For in this case, if the secondary derivative (*taddhita*) were to occur first, then when the suffix *kap* is applied to the words *etaśya*, *taroha*, and *roha* with the intention of expressing meanings such as "unknown" (*ajñāta*), the feminine suffix *ṅīp* and the nasal *n* would not occur by virtue of the rule: "After a vowel that is anudātta and followed by *t* as an upadhā, [the suffix *kap*] is replaced by *na*" (Pāṇini 4.1.39).

If, then, the mention of *ṅī* and *āp* is for the purpose of prescribing secondary suffixes (*taddhita*) after words ending in those vowels, then the compound-final suffixes (*samāsānta*) would also have to be added only after such words. Consequently, in the case of "there are many *gomat* [possessors of cows] in this city," the following would occur: first, the feminine suffix *ṅīp* would be applied according to Pāṇini 4.1.45; then, the suffix *kap* would be applied according to 5.4.153, resulting in the form *bahugomatīkā*, whereas the desired form is *bahugomatkā*. This is not a fault. For the compound-final suffixes do not arise from the completed compound itself; rather, they arise from the final member of the compound even before the compound has been formed, based on its meaning.

For thus the author of the Vṛtti will say regarding [Pāṇini 7.4.14] *na kapi*: "This short vowel [prescribed by 6.3.43] also does not occur before the suffix *kap*; since the compound must be formed after *kap* has been added when the final member of the compound is short, the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) of the compound does not end in a feminine suffix."

Furthermore, in the sentence "there are not many cattle-owners in this city," since the final member of the compound refers to a feminine entity as part of the compound's meaning, the feminine suffix must be applied first, followed by the compound, and then the feminine suffix; thus, through this sequence of suffixes, *bahugomatī* is established. If, however, the compound-endings (*samāsānta*) were added from the final member after the compound had already been formed, then in the rule *nañastatpuruṣāt* [Pāṇini 5.4.71], the phrase "those which will be mentioned following *nañ*" would apply.

The statement in the Vṛtti—"samāsāntas do not occur after a *tatpuruṣa* compound ending in *ṛk* and so forth"—would be contradicted; for one would have to say that "samāsāntas do not occur after those [compounds] which have the meaning of a *tatpuruṣa*. However, because *nañ* is the subject under discussion, it is understood as that very [negation].
Furthermore, in the rule *tatpuruṣāt* [Pāṇini 5.4.71], the word *tatpuruṣa* refers by extension (*tādārthya*) to the meaning of a *tatpuruṣa* when it occurs as a final member of a compound.

In that context, since *ṛk* and so forth are explicitly mentioned, it is understood as referring specifically to *ṛk* and the rest; and the two ablative cases in "after a *tatpuruṣa* ending in *ṛk* etc. are in different grammatical relations (*vyadhikaraṇa*).

Therefore, this is the meaning: when *ṛc* and so forth follow the negative particle (*nañ*), that negative particle has those [words] as its proximate elements; consequently, the *tatpuruṣa* compound-final suffix does not occur after such a word denoting *ṛc* and so forth.
Alternatively, the word *anta* denotes a constituent part; thus, both ablative cases are in grammatical apposition because they share the same referent.
That very subsequent member of the *tatpuruṣa* which ends in *ṛc* and so forth is precisely what is meant.
It has been stated that [the rule applies] "from the end of that" and "from the meaning of a *tatpuruṣa*.

Consequently, this is the meaning: compound-endings (*samāsānta*) do not occur after a final member (*uttarapada*) which is a *tatpuruṣa* having the sense of that [compound], provided it is preceded by the negative particle *nañ*. That, moreover, refers to the sense of a *tatpuruṣa* ending in that [negative particle].

By virtue of the contextual force (*sāmarthya*), only that which begins with *ṛc* and so forth is understood as the final member (*uttarapada*). In that case, does this not contradict the following commentary (*vṛtti*) on the rule *bahuvrīhau saṃkhyeye ḍajabahugaṇāt* [Pāṇini 5.4.73]: "The suffix *ḍac* occurs after a *bahuvrīhi* compound ending in anything other than *bahu* or *gaṇa*, provided that the *bahuvrīhi* occurs in reference to a numeral (*saṃkhyeya*)"? There is no contradiction; for here, it is stated that the final member itself is called "the *bahuvrīhi*" because it serves the purpose of the *bahuvrīhi*.

This is the meaning: the suffix *ḍac* occurs after that which serves as the final member (*uttarapada*) of a *bahuvrīhi* compound when it denotes a number. In this manner, other contradictions of this kind should also be resolved.

Thus, this remains established: the mention of *hrāp* is for the purpose of prescribing a secondary derivative (*taddhita*) after that [which ends in *hrāp*]; the mention of *ṅyāp* is for the purpose of prescribing a secondary derivative after that [which ends in *ṅī* or *āp*] due to a conflict of rules (*vipratiṣedha*); and because of this conflict, the secondary derivative is more powerful. If this is so, why is the mention of *ti* and *ūṅ* not understood in the same way for the rules *yunastiḥ* (Pāṇini 4.1.77) and *ūṅutaḥ* (Pāṇini 4.1.66), such that a secondary derivative would arise after that which ends in *ti* or *ūṅ*—as in *yuvatitarā* and *brāhmaṇabandhūtara*? [This is because of the rule *ūṅutaḥ* (6.3.44).]

Shortening (*hrasvatva*) should not be applied optionally; for the mention of *ṅī* and *āp* is intended as an illustration (*upalakṣaṇa*). Having introduced [the rule] with "those whose formation [is prescribed]" (P. 6.3.43), the mention of *ṅī* and *āp* here is for the purpose of illustrating those cases. Therefore, it should be understood that the mention of *tyūṅ* is also effectively included here. If the mention of *ṅī* and *āp* were merely illustrative, one might argue that the mention of only one would suffice, since even by one the feminine suffixes (*strīpratyaya*) are indeed illustrated. This is true; however, both are mentioned for the sake of variety (*vaicitrya*).

By this optional suffix added in its own sense (*svārthika*), the feminine suffix is intended to be superseded. In that regard, when there is supersession, then after the word *lohita*, when the suffix *kan* is applied and the feminine suffix *ṭāp* is added, and the substitution of *i* for *t* has occurred, the form should be *lohitikā*. However, when there is no supersession, then by the rule "from a low-pitched vowel [denoting] a color, having *t* as its penultimate, *na* replaces *t*" (Pāṇini 4.1.39), the suffixes *ṅīp* and *nakāra* are applied; and when *kan* is added and the shortening occurs by the rule "after *ka*, the vowel of the suffix *aṇ* is shortened" (Pāṇini 7.4.13), the form should be *lohinikā*.

Therefore, this must indeed be stated: "Or there is the sublation of the gender by the suffix *lohitā*. Regarding the statement "the secondary markers (*anubandha*) beginning with *u*," therein the *u* of the nominative singular is for the sake of pronunciation. Why is it not understood as being for the purpose of the qualification "not [ending] in *ah*" (Pāṇini 7.1.93)? Because there is no [form] to be excluded.

The letter *ja* in *jasaḥ* is for the purpose of ensuring unambiguous pronunciation; for if it were absent, once the substitution of *au* for *as* had been applied, there would be doubt as to which suffix was being pronounced, and thus an explanatory gloss would have to be provided.
Now, why is it not understood as a qualifier in the rule *jasaḥ śī* [Pāṇini 7.1.17]? Because even if it were stated as *asaḥ śī*, there would be no over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).
Furthermore, the letter *ṭ* in *auṭ* is for the purpose of including the entire group *suṭ* by means of a technical abbreviation (*pratyāhāra*).
This passage does not exist in the Vṛtti, yet it must have been there;
it has now disappeared due to the error of a scribe or similar causes.

The substitution of *ś* for *ṣ* in the case of *auṭ* [the nominative-accusative dual ending] by means of the *c*-substitution (*cartva*) according to Pāṇini 8.4.54, *khari ca*, is intended to ensure an unambiguous pronunciation.

The letter *ś* is for the purpose of removing ambiguity; otherwise, if only *hrauḍas* were stated, there would be doubt: "Is this the pronunciation of the letter *ṭ*, or of the letter *ḍ*? In that case, because of the pronunciation of *ḍ*, there would be the elision of *ṭi*.

[Objection: Even with the presence of *ś*, doubt must certainly arise: "Is this the pronunciation of the letter *ḍ* which has undergone the change to *c* (i.e., *ṭ*), or of the letter *ṭ* itself? [Response: This is not so; for if it were the letter *ḍ*, the pronunciation of *ś* would be useless. Therefore, [the letter *ś*] serves as a qualifier in the rule *atha* [Pāṇini 6.1.103] for the sake of distinction in the rule *ata upadhāyāḥ* [Pāṇini 7.1.12].

In rules such as *supāṃ suluk* [Pāṇini 7.1.39], there is an elision (*praśleṣa*) of the vowel *ā* in the form *suluk pūrvasavarṇa ā āt śe*. In that context, if the marker *ṭ* were not present, this [elided *ā*] would also be included in the reference. The phrase "number, object, and so forth" refers to another grammatical rule, namely *saṃkhyākarmādayaśca* [Pāṇini 1.4.21], which states that numbers are prescribed in the sense of the nominative case (*svādi*) and so on.
And by [the rule] beginning with *karmādayaśca* (Pāṇini 2.3.2), there is "a single syntactical unity (*ekavākyatā*) between this [rule] and that. Thus,
when there is plurality of the object (*karman*), the suffix *śas* occurs.
In the case of the object (*karman*), for the numbers two and one, there are the dual endings *au* and *auṭ*.

In this way, a single syntactical unit (*ekavākyatā*) should be understood in other instances as well. If, however, this [rule] forms a single syntactical unit with that [preceding rule], then the following statement would be contradicted: regarding [Pāṇini 2.3.2], "This instruction applies where number is possible; however, from indeclinables (*avyaya*), which are devoid of number, the case-endings (*svādi*) prescribed in general certainly exist. For, if there were a single syntactical unit, the case-endings would be prescribed specifically for meanings such as singularity and so forth associated with the object and other relations, and thus they could not be described as being "prescribed in general."

This is not tenable. Furthermore, as for what was stated there—namely, that "the plural number prescribed by the rule *ṅyāpprātipadikāt svādayaḥ* and *lasya tibādayaḥ* is here enjoined as having the quality of plurality (*bahutva*) as its expressed meaning"—that too is certainly contradictory. For it is not logical to enjoin the expressed meaning of plurality for a plural suffix that has already been prescribed within a single syntactical unit (*ekavākyatā*).

By combining this with the conclusion of that treatise, since the plural number is prescribed only for the count of plurality, there is first of all no contradiction. For even in the case of a single syntactical unity (*ekavākyatā*), how the general prescription of the suffixes *svādi* is justified has been demonstrated right here [in 1.4.21].

As for the second contradiction that was raised, that too does not exist at all. It should be understood that the intended meaning there is that [the rule] has attained syntactic unity (*ekavākyatā*) with the rule *prātipadikāt svādayo lasya tibādaya iti bahuvacanam vihitam* (Pāṇini 1.4.21). Furthermore, regarding the point that by this sūtra the number "plurality" is prescribed as the denotable meaning (*vācyatvena*), the intended meaning should be seen as follows: that it has attained syntactic unity with the rules of the *svādi*-group (Pāṇini 4.1.2) and with the rule *lasya* (Pāṇini 3.4.77), etc.

And thus, the plural number is prescribed only for a collection (*saṃhati*); and since its plurality as a numerical value is enjoined as being expressed only through that collection, how can there be any contradiction? Now, one might object: "The rule *bahuvacanam* [Pāṇini 1.4.21] is a single teaching, and its syntactic unity (*ekavākyatā*) is with the rule *svādi-* [Pāṇini 4.1.2]; therefore, that [unity] is not possible with another teaching such as *lasya* [Pāṇini 3.4.77]. Or, if there is syntactic unity with that [rule *lasya*], it is not possible with the rule *svādi-*? There is no fault at all.

These two statements are uttered within the *tantra* (the grammatical system). In that regard, one statement forms a single syntactic unit (*ekavākyatā*) with the rule beginning "svādi" [Pāṇini 2.4.71], while the other does so with another rule of the science beginning "lasya" [Pāṇini 3.4.77]. Alternatively, the absence of contradiction is demonstrated in another way:

here, would the suffixes beginning with *su* (the case endings) be prescribed by this rule [2.3.2] independently, without regard for such rules as those mentioned above?
