Or would they be prescribed having regard for them, thereby entering into a single syntactic unit with them? These are the two positions.

In that regard, according to the first position, the case-endings (*svādayaḥ*) are prescribed without distinction; however, for those thus prescribed, a restriction is made by another rule of the science, such as "where number is possible, there [the plural] is used for the plural" (*bahuṣu bahuvacanam*, Pāṇini 1.4.21), which prescribes them as expressing numbers such as singularity associated with the object (*karman*) and so forth. As for the indeclinables (*avyaya*) which are devoid of number, the case-endings prescribed in a general sense simply exist for them. According to the second position, however, the case-endings are prescribed specifically for meanings associated with the object and so forth, such as plurality and the like.

In that context, the first alternative was adopted [in Pāṇini 1.4.21], but here the second is adopted; thus there is no contradiction, because the statement is made by resorting to a different alternative. Now, in the case of the second alternative, how can there be the production of *su*-suffixes (*sub*) from indeclinables (*avyaya*), since the production of *svādi* suffixes is not possible from those [indeclinables] which lack number, object, and so forth within a single syntactical unit? This is not a fault; it will occur by virtue of an indicator (*jñāpaka*).

Since this [sūtra] teaches the elision (*luk*) of the *sup* produced after an indeclinable [by Pāṇini 2.4.82], it indicates that the production of case-endings (*vibhakti*) occurs even from indeclinables.
In the case of *kumārī*, the suffix *ṅīp* is applied by [Pāṇini 4.1.20]. In the case of *gaurī*: [the same applies].
The suffix *ṅīṣ* is applied by [Pāṇini 4.1.41].
In the case of *śāṅrgaravī*, the suffix *ṅīn* is applied by [Pāṇini 4.1.73], which states that after the *yañ* suffix following *śāṅrgarava* and others, *ṅīn* is added.
As for *khaṭvā*: [it is formed with the suffix *aṅ*].
The suffix *ṭāp* is applied by the rule *ajādyataṣṭāp* [Pāṇini 4.1.4],
resulting in *bahūrājā*.
The suffix *ḍāp* is applied by the rule *ḍābubhābhyāmanyatarasyām* [Pāṇini 4.1.13].
Regarding the term *kārīvagandhyāḥ*:

it means "one whose scent is like the scent of dried cow dung" (*karīṣasya gandha iva gandho yasya*). [The suffix *ya* is applied according to] Pāṇini 5.4.135 and 5.4.137, resulting in the shortening of the vowel [to *i*].

In the case of *karīṣagandher apatyam* ("the offspring of Karīṣagandhi"), there is the elision of the vowel *a* by [Pāṇini 6.4.148], followed by the *vṛddhi* substitution by [Pāṇini 7.2.117] and so forth. Then, the replacement with the suffix *ṣyaṅ* occurs by [Pāṇini 4.1.78], "for *aṇ* and *iñ* that are not Vedic (*anārṣa*), when the penultimate syllable is heavy," and the feminine suffix *cāp* is added by [Pāṇini 4.1.74], "after *yaṅ*, *cāp*. Regarding the statement, "Because of the prescription of *ṅī* and *āp* by this very rule," this indicates that when a suffix is prescribed under the governing heading (*adhikāra*) of "in the feminine" (*striyām*), there is no such thing as a base (*prakṛti*) ending in *hrasva-i* or *ā*.
Furthermore, this serves as the reason for the principle that "in this section, only the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) is connected [to the operation]."

For if, in this section, a base (*prakṛti*) ending in *ṅī* or *āp* were possible, then *ṅī* and *āp* would also be connected [to the rule]; however, such a form ending in *ṅī* or *āp* is not possible here, and therefore those two are not connected in this context. Furthermore, regarding femininity (*strītva*), there is a difference of opinion among the teachers, and in some views, a flaw is observed. In that regard, the view of some is as follows: "A woman is one who possesses breasts and a narrow waist; a man is said to be one who is hairy; and that which is the interval between the two, in the absence of these, is the neuter."
Thus:
in "stanakeśavatī," the suffix *matup* is used in the sense of abundance or excellence;
and in "lomaśaḥ" as well, the suffix *śa* is applied according to the rule *lomādipāmādibhyaḥ śaḥ* (Pāṇini 5.2.100).

Regarding the phrase "the interval between both," the meaning is that it is similar to both the female and the male. Furthermore, that similarity consists in possessing gender. If this is so, then that which possesses both [characteristics] combined would result in being neuter.
For the form of the aggregate (samudāya) is indeed similar to the form of the constituent members (samudāyin) by virtue of being its indicative mark; therefore, he says: "in the absence of that.
That in which both of these are absent is "neuter" (napuṃsaka).
Consequently, this fault does not arise.
If it were stated only that "in the absence of those two, it is neuter," then indeclinables and verbal forms (tiṅanta) alone would possess neuter gender.

Even if it were stated only that "it is that which lies between the two," then compounds such as *kukkuṭamayūryau* (the cock and the peahen), which are considered to be an aggregate of genders, would undesirably result in being neuter.
Therefore, both [conditions] have been stated: "that which lies between the two" and "in the absence of those two."

Thus, that which is neither female nor male, and which possesses the characteristics of a gendered entity, is called neuter (*napuṃsaka*); consequently, it is stated that indeclinables (*avyaya*) and verbal forms (*tiṅanta*) do not possess the status of being neuter. In this view, the suffix *ṭāp* would undesirably apply to the word *bhrūkuṃsa*, for in its case, a connection with breasts and hair is perceived. A *bhrūkuṃsa* is a dancer who wears women's attire; he is said to be a man.

Furthermore, because beds (*khaṭvā*) and the like lack breasts and hair, they would not possess femininity; and because trees and the like lack body hair, they would necessarily lack masculinity. Conversely, because donkeys (*khara*), huts (*kuṭa*), and so forth do have body hair, they would possess masculinity; consequently, in the phrase *kharakuṭīḥ paśya*, the rule [Pāṇini 8.2.46] requiring the substitution of *ṇ* for *n* would apply. However, the view of others is as follows: there are three states—contraction (*saṃstyāna*), procreation (*prasava*), and stability (*sthiti*). Contraction, which has the nature of diminution, is femininity; that object in which it exists is feminine. Procreation, which consists of increase, is masculinity; that in which it exists is masculine. Stability is neuter. Thus, the female gender is defined by the presence of contraction. The state consisting of that condition which is devoid of both increase (*upacaya*) and decrease (*apacaya*) is "neutrality" (*napuṃsakatva*); that in which this exists is a "neuter" (*napuṃsaka*). Even in this view, since all three—concretion (*saṃstyāna*), and so forth—are present everywhere, it would follow that every single entity is simultaneously female, male, and neuter. If you argue: "There is no such fault, because femininity occurs only when concretion is intended to be expressed, masculinity only when production (*prasava*) is intended to be expressed, and neutrality only when stability (*sthiti*) is intended to be expressed," this is incorrect. For instance, even when it is said, "the girl is growing" (*upacīyate kumārī*), the girl remains female and does not become male.

In the expression "the tree diminishes" (*apacīyate vṛkṣaḥ*), even when there is an intention to express diminution (*saṃstyāna*), the word "tree" remains masculine alone and does not become feminine. In the expressions "the pot increases" (*upacīyate kuṇḍam*) or "the pot diminishes" (*apacīyate vā*), even when there is an intention to express either increase or diminution, the word "pot" remains neuter alone and becomes neither masculine nor feminine. Thus, because of these differing views regarding femininity among the teachers and because of the observation of such faults, he asks: "'Feminine' (*striyām*) is said; what is this 'feminine'? and so forth.
The author of the commentary (*vṛttikāra*), however, having understood the intended meaning, speaks while relying on another view: "'Particular universals' (*sāmānyaviśeṣāḥ*)" and so forth.
"Universals and particulars.

Thus, they are universals because they are common to things of the same class, and they are particulars because they are distinguished—meaning they are excluded—from one another and from those of different classes; hence they are "universals-and-particulars" (*sāmānyaviśeṣa*).
This is as in the case of "femininity" and so forth, which are like "cowness" and so forth.

For just as the general-peculiarities such as "cowness" (gotva) and so forth are the causes of non-differentiated cognitions and designations even with respect to their own distinct substrata, so too are "femininity" (strītva) and the rest.
Just as "cowness" and the like subsist in all members of the same class and are excluded from those of different classes, so too do "femininity" and the like.
Therefore, they too are general-peculiarities, exactly like those.

But surely, since universals and particulars (sāmānyaviśeṣas) pervade all individuals, even in this view the same consequence of having all genders everywhere would follow; why then was this view adopted after abandoning the other view? To this he says: "Individuals are of many kinds. They are called *vyaktis* because they are manifested (*vyajante*) by these [universals]; that is, they are the substrata of the universals and particulars.
Those universals and particulars for which there are individuals of many kinds are described as such.

By this, he indicates the following: because the manifestors that serve as the substrata for general and particular properties are diverse, only a certain general or particular property is manifested by a certain substratum, and not every [property] by every [substratum].
This is because the potencies of things have restricted domains.

In that regard, when a certain object manifests only femininity and neither masculinity nor neuter-ness, it is indeed a woman, not a man, nor a neuter; when it manifests only masculinity, it is indeed a man; and when it manifests neuter-ness, it is indeed a neuter.
However, that which manifests two or three [genders] is considered to possess two or three genders—such as *ardharcaḥ*, *ardharcam*; *padmaḥ*, *padmam*; *taṭaḥ*, *kaṭī*, *taṭam*.
Therefore, in this view, there is no occasion for the aforementioned defect.

But then, how can that which is the substratum of a general-particular [entity] and is not a manifester [of gender] become feminine, masculine, or neuter through association with them? To this, he says: "In some cases," and so forth.

For in cases such as space (ākāśa) and the self (ātman), gender-specific universals (*sāmānyaviśeṣa*) such as femininity and so forth are manifested solely by instruction in certain instances, and not manifested by their substratum, because those substrata are beyond the reach of the senses.
In that regard, that in which femininity is manifested by instruction is a woman, as in: "This is space.
That in which masculinity is [manifested] is a man, as in: "This is the self."

Where there is neuter-ness, that is indeed neuter, as for example: "this is space" (*idam ākāśam*). He asks: how is it that femininity and so forth are sometimes manifested by mere instruction? He says: "as for example," and so on.

For qualities such as Brahminhood and Kṣatriyahood have no such substrate that could manifest them; this is because their substrates—such as the universal-particulars (sāmānya-viśeṣa) and space—are beyond the reach of the senses.
The manifestation of [qualities] such as Brahminhood occurs only through instruction, based on similarity elsewhere and by relying upon that [instruction].
Just as it is with those, so too is it in some cases with femininity and the like.
But what is this "femininity"? Is it the meaning of the suffix (*pratyaya*), or is it a qualifier of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*)? To this he says: "And femininity," and so forth.

When the word *strī* (woman) denotes "femininity" (*strītva*) even without a suffix expressing an abstract state (*bhāvapratyaya*), then, when femininity is the meaning to be expressed, the suffixes *ṭāp* and so forth occur; thus, femininity becomes the meaning of the suffix.

For just as the word *go* (cow), in the view that the word's referent is a genus (*jāti*), denotes "cowness" (*gotva*) even when devoid of a suffix expressing an abstract state, so too does the word *strī* denote femininity.

But when the word *strī* (feminine) also applies to the substance (*dravya*) possessing that [quality] by taking "femaleness" (*strītva*) as its qualifier, then this position also holds: "The suffixes *ṭāp* and so forth occur after that nominal stem (*prātipadika*) which occurs in the feminine"; thus, femaleness becomes a qualifier of the base (*prakṛti*).
Therefore, it is appropriate in both ways.

But how, then, is it appropriate in both ways? For if "femininity" (*strītva*) is the meaning of the suffix, then femininity would become the primary element; in that case, a genitive case expressing a relation of distinction (*vyatireka-lakṣaṇā*) would result, as in "the femininity of Devadattā. Consequently, there would be no grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) in the expression "Devadattā is a girl" (*kumārī devadattā*). Furthermore, in the dual and plural, the forms *kumāryau* and *kumāryaḥ* would not occur, because femininity is a single entity. Moreover, a plural suffix would not be applicable, as in *gārgyāyaṇī*.

Regarding the forms *kārīṣagandhyā* and *kālitara*, since the feminine gender (*strītva*) is one, and that [gender] has already been expressed by the suffix *ṣpha* and so forth produced at the very first stage, the vowel *ī*—as in the word "strī"—would not occur. For in the printed reading of the *Daśapādī Uṇādi-sūtra*, it is seen as "strī," being denoted by the suffix *ḍraṭ* according to the rule "styāyater ḍraṭ" (Pāṇini 4.1.3); therefore, there would be a genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) characterized by distinction [between the base and the suffix]. Why is this not the case? Because the distinction between the general and the particular is not expressed by a word ending in a feminine suffix, such that there would be a genitive case characterized by distinction.

But why is it not expressed [in the plural]? Because of the inherent nature of the word’s power (*śabdaśaktisvābhāvyāt*). Furthermore, the dual and the plural are also applicable; for even when there is oneness of the general and the particular, the words denoting them adopt the number of their substrata (*āśrayasaṃkhyā*), precisely because of the inherent nature of the word’s power.
Therefore, because the substratum is manifold, the dual and plural numbers will occur.

In cases such as *gārgyāyaṇī*, femininity is expressed by two feminine suffixes; it is not expressed by a single suffix such as *ṣyaṅ*. Thus, even though there are multiple suffixes, this is entirely appropriate.
Alternatively—in the case of *gāgryāyaṇī*, the suffix *ṅīṣ* will occur by virtue of the presence of the marker *ṣ* in the suffix *ṣpha* prescribed by [Pāṇini 4.1.17]: *prācāṃ ṣpha taddhitaḥ*.
In the case of *kārīṣagandhyā*, the suffix *āp* will occur after a stem ending in *ṣyaṅ* by virtue of the rule [Pāṇini 4.1.74]: *yaṅaścāp*.
Regarding the term *kālitarā*:

the feminine suffix *ṅīṣ* prescribed by the rule *jānapadādi* [Pāṇini 4.1.42] expresses femininity as not qualified by excellence (*aprakarṣa-viśiṣṭa*), and not as qualified by excellence (*prakarṣa-viśiṣṭa*). Therefore, since that [excellence] has not been expressed, the suffix *ṭāp* will occur after the word ending in the superlative suffix *tara*. Alternatively, the suffix *ṅīp* will occur either due to the indicative mark (*liṅga*) in the rule *strī* [Pāṇini 4.1.3], or by the force of the inclusion of the marker *ṭ* [in *ṅīp*].

In the view where the meaning of the base (*prakṛti*) is qualified [by gender], however, the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) expresses the substance itself as qualified by femininity, while the suffixes such as *ṭāp* and others are merely indicators (*dyotaka*).
In that case, because there is no distinction [between the stem and the suffix], the genitive case does not arise; likewise, the dual and plural numbers do not apply either.
Since the substance is manifold, it is entirely appropriate for multiple suffixes to occur.

For just as the feminine suffixes *ṭāp* and so forth occur in words such as *khaṭvā*, even though the feminine gender is already expressed by the nominal stem (*prātipadika*), so too do numerous suffixes such as *ṣpha* occur in words like *gārgyāyaṇī*.

Since the feminine gender is indicated by this very [suffix], it is rightly said: "It is appropriate in both ways. Regarding the rule "from *aja* and so forth, and from that which ends in *a*" (*ajādyatadantāt*):
the meaning is "from that which ends in the vowel *a*."

Now, why is it that the word-form itself is not understood [to be included] in cases such as *śarad* and *darad*, following the rule "after a word ending in something other than *śabda*"? It is because of an indicative mark (*liṅga*).

What is the indicative mark? It is the mention [in the sūtras] such as "when there is a desire to express that and so forth" (Pāṇini 2.4.21) and "of that which is preceded by *ya* or *ka*" (Pāṇini 7.3.46).
For if the word-form itself were being grasped, those [rules] would not be applicable.
"The letter *p* is for the purpose of including [the suffix] in general.
For if the letter *p* were not present in the rule *ṅyāpprātipadikāt* [Pāṇini 4.1.1], there would be no inclusion of this [suffix].
"The letter *ṭ* is for the purpose of preventing interference with the inclusion in general."

For if the letter *ṭ* were not present, then according to the rule "when a suffix with one indicatory letter (*anubandha*) is mentioned, it does not include one with two indicatory letters" (Vyāḍi-Pāṇini 52), there would be the inclusion of only the suffix *ṭāp*, and not of *ḍāp* or *cāp*; this is because they possess two indicatory letters.
[Examples are] *śubhaṃyāḥ* and *kīlālapāḥ*, where the suffix *vic* is applied by the rule "it is seen after other roots as well" (Pāṇini 3.2.75).

"What would happen, moreover, if *ṭāp* were applied here as well? To this he says: "By *halṅyābhyo dīrghāt sutisyapṛktaṃ hal*" and so forth. "In the case of a word characterized by a genus (*jāti*)" means:

"A feminine suffix is added after a genus-word that does not denote a female, provided its penultimate vowel is not *y*, according to Pāṇini 4.1.63. "In the case of a word characterized by connection with a male (*puṃyoga*)" means: [according to Pāṇini 4.1.48].
Regarding the rule [Pāṇini 4.1.48]: "When *puṣpa* or *phala* is the final member of the compound"; and regarding [Pāṇini 4.1.64]:
"Also when the final members are *pāka*, *karṇa*, *parṇa*, *puṣpa*, *phala*, *mūla*, or *bāla*."
"In the sense of age" (vayolakṣaṇe); [this refers to] Pāṇini 4.1.20;
"in the sense of the suffix *ṭi*" (ṭillakṣaṇe).

Regarding the rule *ṭiḍḍhāṇañ* [Pāṇini 4.1.15], there is the statement: "And *śūdrā*, provided it is not preceded by *amahat*" (referring to Pāṇini 4.1.49), and so forth. Now, one might object: since the rule *āmanmahataḥ* [Pāṇini 6.3.46] and others require that the vowel be lengthened (*ātva*) here, one should instead say "not preceded by *amahat*" (*amahatpūrvā*). This is not the case; for that lengthening (*ātva*) is prescribed when the word is used in its primary sense (*arthapradhāna*), whereas this instance concerns the form of the word itself (*śabdapradhāna*). Thus, "preceded by *mahat*" (*mahatpūrvā*) refers to that feminine base which has the word *mahat* preceding it.

"Prohibition of that which is preceded by *mahat*. This explains the meaning of the term *amahatpūrva*. Here too, the word "jāti" (genus/class) is connected [to the rule], so that the prohibition may apply to words denoting a genus. Let it not be the case here: *mahatī śūdrā* = *mahāśūdrā*.

In this case, the word *śūdra* in the latter member of the compound refers to the [social] class (*jāti*), not to the collective entity consisting of the form "great-śūdra" (*mahatīśūdrā*). But how can there be an application of the rule for that which is preceded by *mahat* when it is stated that [the term refers to] a class, such that a prohibition must be articulated? To this he says: "The word *mahāśūdra* denotes the Ābhīra class.
For it is precisely the collective entity of the word *mahāśūdra* that occurs in reference to a class.

For this very reason, the form *mahāśūdrī* is derived with the suffix *ṅīp* by the rule *jāter astrī* [Pāṇini 4.1.63] and others. Now, one might object: "Even so, there is no possibility for the suffix *ṭāp* at all; for how could a suffix arising after the word *śūdra* apply to *mahāśūdra*? To this he says: "In that case, the rule of *tadantavidhi* (application of a grammatical operation to a complex form ending in a specified element) does not apply," and so forth. [The opponent asks: "How can there be a *tadantavidhi*?"
In no way [is it formed].
He considers that this is because the rule of extension to what ends in such an element (*tadantavidhi*) is prohibited when the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) itself contains the suffix;
thus, [the form] is *atidhīvarī*.
Regarding the word *atipīvarī*:

from the roots *dadhāti* and *pibati*, the suffix *kvanip* is applied by the rule *āto maninkvanivvanipaśca* [Pāṇini 3.2.74]. The substitution of *ī* for *a* occurs by the rule *ghumāsthāgāpājahātisām hali* [Pāṇini 6.4.66].

Thus, the compound is formed as *atikrāntā dhīvānam* (one who has surpassed the wise) and *atikrāntā pīvānam* (one who has surpassed the fat), according to the rule *atyādayaḥ krāntādyarthe dvitīyayā* [Pāṇini 2.2.18].

In this case, once the rule regarding *tadanta-vidhi* (the application of an operation to that which ends with a specified element) has been made known, the suffixes *ṅīp* and *ṅīṣ* do not apply by the rule *vanorac* [Pāṇini 4.1.7].

However, if *tadanta-vidhi* were not made known, then the term *vanaḥ* would be understood as a reference to the suffix itself; and according to the principle that "when a suffix is mentioned, there is a reference to that which begins with the element from which it is prescribed and to that which ends with it" (Puṣpasūtra, Paribhāṣāvṛtti 44), these two suffixes would apply only here—namely, in *dhīvarī* and *pīvarī*—but not in *atidhīvarī* and *atipīvarī*. [Furthermore, they would not apply] in *atibhavatī*.

Regarding the term *atimahatī*: the word *bhavat* alone is listed among the *sarvādi* (the group beginning with *sarva*) as having the marker *ugit*, while *mahat* is listed in the *gaurādi* group. In the absence of this indicator (*jñāpaka*), the suffixes *ṅīp* and *ṅīṣ*—which are prescribed for words ending in *ugit* and for the *gaurādi* group respectively—would apply only to the words *bhavat* and *mahat* themselves. Consequently, they would not apply in forms such as *atibhavatī* and *atimahatī*; however, when this indicator exists, they do apply.

If this is so, then by the rule for *tadanta* (application to that which ends with [a specific stem]), would not the suffix *ṭāp* also apply to the *dvigu* compound *pañcājī*, which is a collection (*samāhāra*) of five goats? This is not a fault; we shall qualify [the rule] by [specifying] "in the feminine gender" (*striyām*) in relation to *aja* and the others. For in the rule *ajādyataḥ* [Pāṇini 4.1.4], there is a genitive case; therefore, the connection should be made as follows: "The suffix *ṭāp* applies to that which is feminine belonging to *aja* and the others," meaning to the state of femininity (*strītva*) residing in the denoted object (*vācyārtha*) of the words *aja* and so forth, by way of the relation of inherence (*samavāya*).

Furthermore, in the word *pañcājī*, femininity (*strītva*) is not inherent in the meaning denoted by the word *ajā*; rather, it is inherent in the meaning denoted as a collective (*samāhāra*). This is indicated by the rule: "The feminine suffix *ṭāp* is applied after [a compound] ending in *ajā*, when the sense of 'taking away the former' (*pūrvāpahāṇā*) or 'taking away the latter' (*aparāpahāṇā*) is intended."
Because it ends in a *lyuṭ* suffix. Regarding "prākpuṣpā":
those which face forward are *prāñci*; [the suffix] *kvin* is applied by the rule *ṛtvigdadhṛk* [Pāṇini 3.2.59].
That which has flowers facing forward (*prāñci*) is *prākpuṣpā*. "The letter *ṅ* is for the purpose of including the general category" means...
For if that [term *sarvanāmasthāna*] were not present, then in the rule *ṅyāpprātipadikāt* [Pāṇini 4.1.1], the mention of *ṅī* would refer only to *ṅīp* and *ṅīṣ*,
and not to *ṅīp*. "In whatever way" (*yathākathañcit*) means by whatever manner whatsoever.

If it is possible for a vowel (*varṇa*) to be *uṅit*, or if it is a suffix (*pratyaya*), or even a nominal stem (*prātipadika*), then in any case where one of these is possible, that is what is meant by the "form of a word ending in *uṅ*.
By this, he shows that the qualification belongs to the form of the word ending in *uṅ*, and not to the nominal stem itself.

If this were a qualification of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) itself, it would apply only here—in cases such as *bhavatī* and *mahatī*; however, it would not apply in *arvatī*, because the substitution of *tr* for the letter *n* has already been made [by rule 6.4.127], so that the phoneme *t* alone is the *ugit* (possessing the marker *k*), not the nominal stem. Furthermore, it would not apply in *gomatī*, for here too the suffix *matup* alone is the *ugit*, not the nominal stem. Therefore, the intention is that it is proper for this to be a qualification of the word *ugit* itself.

That form consisting of the word *ugit* is an adjective (*viśeṣaṇa*) of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*), and since a rule involving a suffix applies to that which ends in what is denoted by the adjective, he says "from that which ends in this" (*tadantāt*), and so forth.

If, then, the feminine suffix *ṅīp* occurs after a nominal stem ending in a form consisting of the word *ugit*, then the form *bhavatī* would not be established; for in this case, there is no nominal stem ending in the word *ugit*, because there is no other nominal stem ending in that [which would contain] the word *ugit* following the stem *bhavat*. This is not a fault; because of the principle of "behaving like that which possesses a designation" (*vyapadeśivadbhāvāt*), it will apply from that which ends in such [a stem].

But surely, by the rule "the treatment as having a designation applies [only] when not with a nominal stem" (*Śākalya-pariśiṣṭa* 65), there should not be such a designation here? This is not so; for in the rule *rugit*, it is not a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) that is being referred to. What then? It is a reference to both nominal stems and non-nominal stems, because the term *ugit* includes both vowels and suffixes—as in *pacantī* and *yajantī*, where the feminine suffix *ṅīp* follows a present participle in *-śat*. Thus, there is a prohibition regarding verbal roots that end in *ugit*.

The word "is being explained" (*pratipādyate*) is to be supplied as the remainder [of the sentence]. Regarding the statement "there must be an addition for the root *añc*," the meaning is that the application of the suffix *ṅīp* to the root *añc* must be established. In this regard, the following is the explanation for both cases: in the rule [Pāṇini 4.1.8], the phrase "optionally" (*anyatarasyām*) will be treated as a separate rule (*yogavibhāga*), and that [optionality] applies as a supplement to all three rules: [Pāṇini 6.3.45], [4.1.7], and [4.1.8].

And that [rule] is a *vyavasthitavibhāṣā* (an option restricted by specific conditions). Therefore, the suffix *ṅīp* occurs invariably after a nominal stem ending in a word containing the phoneme *u* or *ṛ* (*ugit*), and after the root *añc* ending in *u* or *ṛ*; but it does not occur at all after others. Others, however, provide a different explanation: in the case of *ukhāsrat* and *parṇadhvat*, only the relationship between the action and the agent is intended to be expressed, not femininity; hence, *ṅīp* does not occur.
However, because of its grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the word *strī*, the cognition of femininity (*strītva*) results.
And in the rule *strīyam* [Pāṇini 4.1.3], the position that there is coreferentiality with the word *strī* is not maintained.
But in cases such as *prācī* and so on, femininity is intended to be expressed; therefore, the suffix *īkāra* occurs here.
Regarding "ukhāruāt" and "parṇadhvat":

[the forms] *ukhāruāt* and *parṇadhvat* are derived from the roots √ru (to cry out) and √dhvans (to fall) with the suffix *kvip* by [Pāṇini 3.2.75], and the lengthening of the vowel in *ukha-* is applied by [Pāṇini 6.3.137].

In the word *prācī*, the suffix *kvin* is added to the root √añc preceded by the prefix *pra-*, the vowel *a* is elided by [Pāṇini 6.4.138], and the lengthening of the vowel in the prefix is applied by [Pāṇini 6.3.137]. The term "*vanaḥ*" refers to the inclusion of both the suffixes *kvanip* and *vanip*.

Now, as for the form *vann* which is produced when the suffix *vic* is applied by [Pāṇini 3.2.75] to the roots *baṇa* and *ṣaṇa* (Dhātupāṭha 463, 464) meaning "to produce," and *vanu* (Dhātupāṭha 1470) meaning "to beg"—why is that form not accepted here? If the suffix *vic* were seen after those two roots, it would be so; however, it is not seen, because it is not prescribed (*anabhidhānāt*).
Regarding the word *śarvarī*:
from the root *śṛ* (Dhātupāṭha 1488) meaning "to injure," the suffix *vanip* is applied by [Pāṇini 3.2.75], followed by *guṇa* substitution and the replacement of the vowel with *ra*.
Regarding the term *paralokadarśī*: the suffix *kvanip* is applied by that very rule [Pāṇini 3.2.75]. Regarding the phrase *vano na haśaḥ*:
the word "in some cases" (*kvacit*) is to be understood as the ellipsis.

When the suffix *vanip* follows a root ending in *haś*, and is prescribed after such a root, then the feminine suffix *ṅīp* and the substitution of *ūph* do not occur for the final vowel of the resulting nominal stem (*prātipadika*) in certain instances. For example, in the word *sahayudhvā*:

from the root *yudh* (meaning "to fight," Dhātupāṭha 1173), the suffix *kvanip* is applied by [Pāṇini 3.2.94], [3.2.95], and [3.2.96] (*sahe ca*). Then, by [6.4.7] and [6.4.8] (*sarvanāmasthāne*), the vowel is lengthened, and finally by [8.2.7], the *t* is replaced by *d*. Thus, *sahayudhvan* becomes *sahayudhvā*.

In some cases, however, the prohibition does not apply at all—as in *śarvarī*. Here, the suffix *vanip* follows a root ending in *r*, which is a consonant (*haś*). In *avāvarī*, although the suffix *vanip* is prescribed after a root ending in a consonant (*haś*), the prohibition still does not take effect. [The root] *oṇṛ* (in the sense of "removing," Dhātupāṭha 454) takes *vanip* by [Pāṇini 3.2.75], and the substitution of *ā* occurs by [Pāṇini 6.4.41: *viḍvanoranunāsikasyāt*], followed by the substitution of *ava*.
And it should not be said that one must simply state "not after *van*, nor after a consonant" (*vano na haśaḥ*). [This is the reading found in the printed edition.]
It must be stated that the mention of *antara* in [Pāṇini 4.1.8] is a supplement (*śeṣa*) to this rule as well. And that is understood to be a restricted option (*vyavasthitavibhāṣā*).
Therefore, where the suffixes *ṅīp*, *ṅīṣ*, and *pha* are not desired, they will not occur. Thus, the word *pāda* is cited here as having the compound-final suffix (*samāsānta*) applied.

Now, why is it that the form *pād*—which is produced from the root *pad* "to go" (Dhātupāṭha 1169) by adding the causative suffix *ṇic* and then applying the *kvip* suffix according to [Pāṇini 3.3.130]—is not understood to be what is being referred to here? It would be so understood if the *kvip* were seen after the verb *pādayati*, but it is not seen; for there is no such linguistic usage (*anabhidhāna*).
[The examples are] *dvipāt* ("two-footed") and *dvipadī* ("two-footed female");
these are *bahuvrīhi* compounds meaning "one who has two feet."

"While ‘elision of the syllable *pād-*’ (Pāṇini 5.4.138) is being carried over, there is the elision of the vowel *a* by [5.4.140], and then the substitution of *pad-* by [6.4.130]. Regarding the statement "‘In an *ṛc*’ is a specification of the object denoted," this refutes the suspicion that it might be a specification of the domain. For if it were a specification of the domain, the meaning would be: "When the domain is an *ṛc*—that is, within the *Ṛgveda* collection—the feminine suffix *ṭāp* shall apply to a nominal stem ending in the word *pād-*"; and in that case, it would apply only to the *Ṛgveda* and nowhere else.

The intention is that, in the explanation of what is to be designated, [the suffix] occurs everywhere. This was stated in order to dispel the doubt that "whatever is obtained from whatever source is entirely prohibited," and that this prohibition applies specifically to *ṅīp* because of its immediate proximity.

But surely, in this context, *ṭāp* (by the rule *ṭābṛci* [Pāṇini 4.1.9]) is the immediately preceding [suffix], so how can there be immediate proximity to *ṅīp*? [The answer is: because [the former] is not marked with the svarita accent.

In this case, it is logical that the suffix *ṭāp* follows immediately after the suffix *ṅīp*. Now, an objection is raised: the technical names "ṣaṭ" (six) are indeed number-words (*saṃkhyāśabda*), and number-words convey only the numerical distinction of a substance (*dravya*), not its feminine gender (*strītva*). Any perception of its feminine gender arises through grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with another word. Furthermore, the position that [the suffixes] are coreferential with a feminine [substantive] was not established in the rule [Pāṇini 4.1.3]. Thus, since there is no possibility at all for a feminine suffix to apply after those [number-words], the prohibition is meaningless? This is not so.

Number is indeed a quality (*guṇa*), because it is recited as such in the Vaiśeṣika *Guṇasūtra* (1.1.6): "Number, dimensions, distinctness, conjunction, and disjunction. And for words expressing qualities, the gender and number [of the word] follow those of the substratum (*āśraya*), as in: "a white cloth" (*śuklā śāṭī*), "a white blanket" (*śuklaḥ kambalaḥ*), "a white garment" (*śuklaṃ vastram*); and likewise "white," "two whites," "whites. This being the case, when there is a prohibition [of the feminine suffix], just as a feminine suffix occurs after words like "white," so too would it occur after those designated as "six" (*ṣat-saṃjñaka*), as in: "five Brāhmaṇīs" (*pañca brāhmaṇyaḥ*).
By [Pāṇini 7.1.22], there is elision (*luk*) of the *jas* suffix.
Regarding the form *svasā*:
by [Pāṇini 7.1.93], *anaṅ* is substituted [for the final vowel of the stem]; then, as before, by [Pāṇini 6.4.7], there is lengthening of the vowel.

The words *tisṛ* and *catasṛ* are also listed among the *svarādi* group; for what purpose is their inclusion there? For, when a case ending (*vibhakti*) follows, the forms *tisṛ* and *catasṛ* ought to occur [by Pāṇini 7.2.99]. In that case, if these two were to serve as the cause (*nimitta*) for the application of the feminine suffix *ṅīp*, which is characterized by being added after a stem ending in long *ī*, the immediate sequence (*ānantarya*) with the case ending would be disrupted by them. And this has been stated: "A rule characterized by a specific grammatical configuration (*sannipātalakṣaṇa*) is not the cause of the destruction of that very configuration" (Vyāḍīya-paribhāṣā 12).

Therefore, since the feminine suffix *ṅīp* will not apply by the very rule of the technical definition (*paribhāṣā*) regarding the "conjunction" (*sannipāta*) [of phonemes], what is the need for this prohibition? If so, then this [prohibition] indicates that this *paribhāṣā* is not universal (*anityā*).
By this, forms such as *yā* and *sā* are established.

For even here, in the case of the rule "the substitution of *ya-* for the pronouns beginning with *tyad-* before a case-ending," the vowel *a-* would not be the cause for the application of the suffix *ṭāp*; for if *ṭāp* were present, the immediate sequence (*ānantarya*) of the case-ending [with the stem] would be destroyed.

However, because the technical designation (*paribhāṣā*) is indeed non-permanent (*anityatva*), the suffix *ṭāp* occurs [instead]. Regarding the passage beginning with "of those having the designation *ṣaṭ*," etc.: in cases such as *pañca brāhmaṇyaḥ*, since the rule "an operation applies to what is immediately preceding, or there is a prohibition thereof" (Vyāḍiparibhāṣā 19) effects a prohibition of the immediately preceding *ṅīp*, and once the *ṅīp* has been prohibited, the *ṅ* is elided by [Pāṇini 8.2.7], whereby the state of ending in the vowel *ā* arises; why then would the suffix *ṭāp* not be produced? It certainly would be produced, because the cause [for its application] is present.

If it is argued that [the substitution] would not occur because the elision of *n* (nalopa) is considered non-existent (*asiddha*), this is not so; for the non-existence of the elision of *n* is stated only with respect to those rules specifically enumerated in [Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.1.58], beginning with "ṅṇoḥ kukṭuk śari" [8.2.2].

Since the rule for the suffix *ṭāp* is not enumerated therein, how could the elision of *n* be considered non-existent in that case? Demonstrating that the rule for *ṭāp* is indeed enumerated there, he says: "Because of the pratyāhāra," and so forth.
In the term *cāp*, the letter *p* related to *cāp* serves as an indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*).
This is what is meant by "sub":

here, the *pratyāhāra* is not formed by the letter *p* belonging to the *sup* (the seventh case plural ending), but rather by the *p* belonging to *cāp* in the rule *yaṅaścāp* [Pāṇini 4.1.74]. Therefore, even the prescription regarding the feminine suffix *ṭāp* is indeed a *sub*-prescription, because *ṭāp* is also included within that *pratyāhāra*.

And therefore, even in the case of the prescription of the *ṭāp* suffix, since the elision of *n* (*nalopa*) is treated as non-existent (*asiddha*), everything desired is established; it is indeed established. [However,] there is a fault regarding the *it*-status [of the vowel].
The compound *bahucarmā* is a *bahuvrīhi* meaning "one who has many hides in this city.

By [Pāṇini 5.4.154], the suffix *kap* is applied, followed by *ṭāp* and the elision of the nasal (*nalopa*). Now, one might expect that by [Pāṇini 7.3.44], *it*-strengthening (*ittva*) would be desired here so that the form would be *bahucarmikā*; however, that does not occur, because in this case the vowel *a* is not preceded by the letter *k*. To ensure the correct result, the entire compound is treated as ending in all case-terminations (*sarvavibhaktyanta*).
*Subvidhi* means a rule concerning *sup*, or a rule [applied] when *sup* follows.

If *ṭāp* were also considered *sup*, then since the substitution of *it* (shortening) is stated to occur even when that [ṭāp] follows, that too would be a *subvidhi*—on the grounds that it is a rule [applied] when *sup* follows.
Consequently, when that [ṭāp] is to be applied, the elision of *n* (*nalopa*) would be treated as non-existent (*asiddha*). This, however, is incorrect for the formation of the *cāp* pratyāhāra.
"Therefore, not both.
Since there is thus a fault in including [the word] *cāpā* in the pratyāhāra, therefore both *ṭāp* and *ṅīp* are prohibited.

For how is the meaning "in the feminine" required here? With respect to this meaning, it is said that "that which occurs"—since both *ṅīp* and *ṭāp* are prescribed for the sense of the feminine, both occur [as applicable]. Examples: *vāmā*, *pāmā*.
The suffix *manin* is applied after the roots *dadāti* and *pibati* by [Pāṇini 3.2.74], and the lengthening of the vowel occurs as before by [Pāṇini 6.4.7].

Now, regarding the forms *samīma*, *sīmānau*, *sīmānaḥ*; and *atimahimā*, *atimahimānau*, *atimahimānaḥ*—how is the prohibition [of the elision of *m*] established here? For the mention of *man* in the rule refers to the meaningful suffix *man*.

Furthermore, unlike words such as *dāma* or *pāma*, which possess meaningfulness through the sense of their suffixal element (*pratyaya*), words such as *sīma* do not possess meaningfulness through any such [suffixal] meaning. For the word *sīma* is an unanalyzed nominal stem (*avyutpanna-prātipadika*), and its meaningfulness belongs to that [stem] itself, not to the *manas* which constitutes its [supposed] component.

Even here in the case of *atimahimā*, the suffix *man* does not possess meaningfulness (*arthavattva*). To explain: when the intended meaning is "the state of being great" (*mahato bhāvaḥ*), the suffix *iman* is prescribed after the word *maha-* by [Pāṇini 5.1.122]. In that instance, meaningfulness belongs to *iman* alone, and not to *man*, which is merely a portion of it; therefore, he says: "*an-in-as-man-grahaṇāni...*" and so forth. By reciting this statement, the author of the Vārttika indicates that when *an*, *in*, or *man* are mentioned, the paribhāṣā regarding the mention of meaningful elements (*arthavadgrahaṇaparibhāṣā*) does not apply.

By this, there is the inclusion of these [words] even though they are meaningless (*anarthaka*); and it is thereby stated that the rule of "having that as its final element" (*tadantavidhi*) applies to both these meaningless and meaningful [elements]. Consequently, the prohibition is established even in cases such as *sīmā* and *atimahimā*. Regarding the statement, "A *bahuvrīhi* compound in which the penultimate vowel is elided (*anupadhālopa*) is the example here":
how is this obtained, since no specific distinction has been mentioned? To this he says: "For [in the case] of those whose penultimate vowel is elided," and so forth.

Since [Pāṇini] will state an optional rule for that which has a penultimate vowel elision in the sūtra *ana upadhālopino 'nyatarasyām* (4.1.28), therefore, by the principle of elimination (*pāriśeṣya*), the scope of this [present rule] is the Bahuvrīhi compound that does not have a penultimate vowel elision. An example of that is *suparvā*, and so forth;
these are Bahuvrīhi compounds meaning "she whose joint is beautiful" and "he whose skin is beautiful."

And in this case, the elision of *a* by [Pāṇini 6.4.137], "not after a word ending in a double consonant," does not occur. Thus we have *atirājī*. This is a *tatpuruṣa* compound according to [Vārttika 91 on Pāṇini 2.2.18]: "Words beginning with *ati* [form a compound] with a word in the accusative when meaning 'surpassing' (*krānta*) and so forth. Now, is the purpose of including the option (*anyatarasyām*) here that, in the alternative case where the suffix *ḍāp* is excluded, there should also be a prohibition [of the suffix *ṅīp*]? Or is the purpose that, in the alternative case where both *ḍāp* and the prohibition are excluded, the suffix *ṅīp* should also occur? Of these, the first [interpretation] is incorrect; for since both *ḍāp* and the prohibition are explicitly stated, both will occur by the very force of the statement (*vacanasāmarthyāt*).

The second [alternative] is also untenable. For, by the mention of "anyatarasyām" (optionally), is it intended that *ṅīp* is prescribed for a *bahuvrīhi* compound that does not elide its penultimate vowel (*anupadhālopin*) in one case, or for one that does elide its penultimate vowel (*upadhālopin*)? Regarding these, the first alternative is not tenable; for if *ṅīp* were prescribed here for the case of a non-eliding penultimate vowel, the statement of the prohibition would be purposeless. The second alternative is also not tenable, because *ṅīp* will be prescribed as an optional alternative by the specific rule "ana upadhālopino 'nyatarasyām" [Pāṇini 4.1.28].

Nor is it appropriate here to include the mention of "one or the other" (*anyatarasyām*) with the thought, "We shall not apply [the rule] to one or the other"; for that must certainly be included so that, when the suffix *ṅīp* is excluded, both the suffix *ḍāp* and the prohibition [of *ṅīp*] may apply—namely, in the forms *bahurājñyau*, *bahurājānau*, and *bahurāje*.

Otherwise, since the suffix *ḍāp* and the prohibition would find their scope in cases like *suparvā* where there is no elision of the penultimate vowel (*anupadhālopin*), they would be superseded by *ṅīp* due to its higher status in the order of rules (*paratvāt*).

Therefore, thinking that the mention of *anyatarasyām* (the option) must indeed be made even for what is about to be stated, he says—having taken all of that into account—"What is the purpose of the mention of *anyatarasyām*?
The sense is that it is useless.
[He then states the rule] beginning with "In a *bahuvrīhi*," etc.

By this [rule], the mention of *anyatarasyām* would be purposeless, as it would result in an option (*vikalpa*) even for that operation which is prescribed by this very rule within a *bahuvrīhi* compound—
since whatever is otherwise established must be presented as an option,
and [in this case] the feminine suffixes *ṅīp* and *ṅīṣ* would not be applicable due to the prohibition [stated in] "ṅībrophāvaprāptau" (Pāṇini 4.1.12).

Therefore, for the sake of prescribing that [suffix], the term *anyatarasyām* ("optionally") must be employed. How so? A split of the rule (*yogavibhāga*) is made here; in that context, the mention of *bahuvrīhi* is carried over, and this [mention of *anyatarasyām*] follows by the maxim of the frog-leap (*maṇḍūkapluti*). Consequently, after a *bahuvrīhi* compound ending in a suffix marked with *v*, the suffixes *ṅīp* and *ṅīṣ* are obtained optionally, as well as the substitution of *ū* for the final vowel. Thus, forms such as *bahupīvā*, *bahudhīvā*, *bahupīvarī*, and *bahudhīvarī* are established.

Others, however, say: because of the mention of "either one" (*anyatarasyām*) following the mention of "both" (*ubhābhyām*), the suffixes *ṅīp* and *ṅīṣ* are obtained after a *bahuvrīhi* compound ending in *van*.

The term "from both" (*ubhābhyām*) [in Pāṇini 4.1.13] is not an ablative; what then? It is an instrumental. The meaning is that when there is a feminine gender in a *bahuvrīhi* ending in *van*, the speaker must convey it by means of both suffixes, *ṅīp* and *ṅīṣ*.

But is not the purpose of including the mention of "both" (ubhābhyām) in the rule *ḍābubhābhyām* [4.1.13]—namely, that the suffix *ḍāp* occurs after both types of bases, those ending in the suffix *man* and those ending in *an* when they are *bahuvrīhi* compounds? It is thought thus: because of the *svarita* accent, the suffix is obtained from both even without the explicit statement "from both" (*ubhābhyām*). Regarding the word "everywhere" (*sarvatra*), it refers to the section on feminine gender.

But does it not fail to carry over in rules such as *na* [4.1.33] and *ṭāṅasiṅasām* [4.1.65], since the qualification "of that which ends in *at*" (*tasyātaḥ*) is untenable there due to its impossibility? To this he says: "When that exists," and so forth.
Where [an application] is possible, there it functions as a qualifier; however, where it is not possible, it continues [to apply] solely for the sake of what follows.

Why does it not occur here in the case of *pacamānā*? The intention is that since the suffix *śānac* possesses the property of being *ṭit* by virtue of its status as a substitute (*sthānivadbhāva*), the suffix *ṅīp* ought to occur even after a word ending in that.
"Because *laṭ* has two indicatory letters (*anubandha*).

By this, he shows that there is no application of *laṭ* here due to the technical rule (*paribhāṣā*): "When a term with one indicatory letter is mentioned, [it does not include] a term with two indicatory letters" (Vyāḍiparibhāṣā 52); for *laṭ* has the letter *ṭ* as its second indicatory letter. "How is it in the case of *lyuḍ* and so on?"—the ellipsis is to be supplied as "the vowel *ī* occurs."
By the word "ādi" (and so forth), [rules] such as Pāṇini 3.2.8 and others are included.

Since suffixes such as *lyuṭ* also possess two indicatory letters (*anubandha*), they ought to be included by the mention of *ṭit*; consequently, the feminine suffix *ṅīp* would not apply to words ending in them, and thus forms such as *cākrikā* and *sāmagī* would not be established.
[The author says: "By the force of the inclusion of the *ṭit* [indicatory letter]."
If even those [suffixes] were not included by the mention of *ṭi*, then the application of the marker *ṭ* would be purposeless, as no other purpose is possible.
Therefore, despite having two markers (*anu-bandha*s), suffixes such as *lyuṭ* are understood through the force of the application of *ṭ*; thus there is no fault.
If one then argues that the present tense (*laṭ*) should likewise be understood solely by the force of the application of *ṭ*, he says: "In the other case."
For in the case of *laṭ*, the result [of the rule] is the substitution of *e* for *ṭi* by Pāṇini 3.4.79 (*laṭaḥ śatṛśānacāv aprathamāsamānādhikaraṇe*).
Therefore, even if there is no actual inclusion [of *laṭ*], the inclusion of the *ṭi*-marker would not be rendered useless.
Consequently, by the force of the inclusion of the *ṭi*-marker, forms such as *lyuṭ* are understood; thus, there is no fault.
In that case, one might argue that even *laṭ* should be included by virtue of the very fact that it is marked with the *ṭi*-sign; to this he says: "In the other case.
For in the case of *laṭ*, the purpose of marking it with the *ṭi*-sign is the substitution of *e* for *ṭi* according to [Pāṇini 3.4.79].
Therefore, although this [present rule] does not include *laṭ*, nevertheless, the marking of it with the *ṭi*-sign would not result in being useless.

Therefore, since the purpose of the marker *ṭ* has already been fulfilled, it is incorrect to include this [root] under that rule. Regarding the example "paṭhitā vidyā" (the science has been studied), how is it connected here? Since the augment *iṭ* is a part of the suffix, the suffix possesses the marker *ṭ*; consequently, the feminine suffix *ṅīp* ought to occur. How then does the form "paṭhitā" come to be? [The answer is: "The *ṭ*-marker of an augment is not a cause [for grammatical operations]."
It is understood that [the suffix] *ṅīp* applies because it is the subject under discussion.
How is it known that this [suffix] is not caused by [the presence of] a marker? He says: "In the rule *ṭauṭaulau*, etc.

Since the addition of the augment *tuṭ* would already be established by its being marked with *ṭi*, the fact that the suffix *ṭi* is prescribed again in the rule *sāyaṃciraṃprāhṇeprage'vyayebhyaṣṭyuṭyalau tuṭ ca* (Pāṇini 4.3.23) is an indicator (*jñāpaka*) that the *ṭi*-marker on an augment does not serve as a cause for the application of *ṅīp*. Examples: *soparṇeyī*, *vainateyī*.

From the word *suparṇī*, which ends in the feminine suffix *ṅīṣ* indicating a genus (*jāti*), and from the word *vinatā*, which ends in the feminine suffix *ṭāp*, the suffix *ḍhak* is applied by [Pāṇini 4.1.120]. The substitution of *ey* for *aya* is effected by the rule [Pāṇini 7.1.2], *āyaneyīnīyiyaḥ*.

Now, one might object that according to the maxim "when a term without an *anubandha* is mentioned, it does not include a term with an *anubandha*" (Vyāḍiparibhāṣā 53), the mention of *ḍhak* should not include *ḍha*; to this he replies: "The word *ḍha* is without an *anubandha*," and so forth.

But is there not this suffix *ḍha* without an indicatory letter (*niranubandhaka*), as in [Pāṇini 5.3.102]: *śilāyāḥ ḍhaḥ*? This is not so; for by its very nature, this suffix occurs only in the neuter. Then is there this one by virtue of its inherent nature—the reading printed as *sabhāyā ḍhaśchandasi*—namely [Pāṇini 4.4.104–106]: *sabhāyā yaḥ*? Even this does not occur in the feminine, because the word *sabheyī* is never observed to be used in the Vedic language (*chandas*).

Therefore, since the suffix *ḍha* with its indicatory letter (*anubandha*) does not exist in the feminine, the paribhāṣā concerning suffixes without indicatory letters (*niranubandhaka-paribhāṣā*) does not apply here; otherwise, the mention of *ḍha* would be purposeless. Regarding the phrase "even in *ṇe*":
this means that whatever grammatical operation is performed for *aṇ*, it may also sometimes occur for *ṇa*, and sometimes it does not.
But where, then, does an operation prescribed for *aṇ* also apply to *ṇa*? It applies in the case of suffixes expressing habitual character (*tācchīlika*).

For this has been indicated in the rule *tathā hi* (Pāṇini 6.4.172): that even when the suffix *ṇa* is applied, the operation conditioned by the suffix *aṇ* takes place. How so? For the word *kārma* is an irregular formation (*nipātana*) for the purpose of eliding the *ṭi* (the penultimate vowel) in the sense of habitual action (*tācchīlya*). If the operation conditioned by *aṇ* did not also apply when *ṇa* is used, the irregular formation would be purposeless;

because once *ṇa* is applied to the word *karman* in the sense of "one whose habit is work" (*karma śīlam asya*) by the rule *chattrādibhyo ṇaḥ* (Pāṇini 4.4.62), the elision of the *ṭi* would already be established by the rule *ata upadhāyāḥ* (Pāṇini 6.4.144).

If it is argued that [the form] is not established because of the preservation of the original stem (*prakṛtibhāva*) by the rule *an* (Pāṇini 6.4.167), this is not so; for the preservation of the original stem is prescribed specifically with respect to the suffix *aṇ*. In that context, the word *aṇi* is carried over from the preceding rule [6.4.164].

Thus, since it has been indicated that "even in the case of the *ṇa*-suffix expressing habitual action (*tācchīlika*), the operation performed for *aṇ* takes place," the operation performed for *aṇ* occurs only there and not elsewhere—as in the examples *caurī* and *tāpasī*.

In the case of *curāśīlā* and *tapaḥśīlā*, the suffix *ṇa* is applied according to the rule *chattrādibhyo ṇaḥ* [Pāṇini 4.4.62]; since it is stated that "even when *ṇa* is applied, the effect of *aṇ* occurs," the feminine suffix *ṅīp* is added.
Regarding *dāṇḍā* and *mauṣṭā*: [the suffix] *ṇa* is applied in the sense of a game, according to the rule *daṇḍaḥ praharaṇam asyāṃ krīḍāyām, muṣṭiḥ praharaṇam asyāṃ krīḍāyām* [Pāṇini 4.2.57].

Now, why is there not a reference to the *pratyāhāra* starting from the letter *a* in *aṇ* up to the letter *ṇ* in *laṇ*? Because of the separate mention of *ṭi* and the others. For if there were a reference to the *pratyāhāra*, the mention of those [suffixes] would be purposeless, since [the desired forms] would already be established by [the suffix] *aṇ* itself. [Examples: *autsī*, *audapānī*. [These are formed] with the suffix *añ* according to Pāṇini 4.1.86: "The suffix *añ* is applied after [words meaning] 'spring' (*utsa*) and 'well' (*udapāna*) [to denote 'belonging to']."*

Now, for what purpose is the word *añ* mentioned again in the rule *śāṅgaravādyaño ṅīn* [Pāṇini 4.1.73], since the desired form is already established by that very [previous mention of *añ*]? For that same form and that same accent are indeed achieved; for instance, when *ṅīn* is applied, the word becomes ādyudātta (accented on the first syllable) by [Pāṇini 6.1.197]. Even in the case of *autsī*, which is derived from the word *utsa* ending in *añ*, once *ñit*-accentuation has made it ādyudātta and *ṅīp* has been added, that same ādyudātta quality remains. To this, he replies with the words *śāṅgaravādyañaḥ*, etc.

The feminine descendant in the lineage (*gotra*) of *Bida*—having applied the suffix *añ* by the rule *anṛṣyānantarye bidādibhyo 'ñ* [Pāṇini 4.1.104], which yields *baida*—would, because it is a genus (*jāti*) according to the rule *gotraṃ ca caraṇaiḥ saha* [Kāśikāvṛtti 4.1.63], be subject to the suffix *ṅīṣ* by the rule *jāter astrīviṣayādayopadhāt* [Pāṇini 4.1.63].
To prevent that, the mention of *añ* is made again in the rule *śāṅgaravādyaño ṅīn* [Pāṇini 4.1.73].

If this is so, then the mention of *añ* here should not be made, since by that [rule] alone the forms beginning with *autsī* are established. This is not correct; for the mention of *jāti* (genus) from [Pāṇini 4.1.63] *jāterastrīviṣayādayopadhāt* carries over into [4.1.48] *tasyāpatyam* and so forth. Thus, in the case of *baidaḥ* derived by *añ*, his wife is *baidī*; in the sense of connection with a male (*puṃyoga*), the suffix *ṅīṣ* is desired there. Therefore, the mention of *jāti* must be carried over into that rule.

Furthermore, in the case of *autsī*—derived from *utsa* with the suffix *añ* intended to convey the meaning "this is from the *utsa*"—the long vowel *ī* would not apply there because it is not a genus (*ajāti*). Therefore, the mention of *añ* must indeed be made here as well. The pronunciation of the indicatory letters (*anubandha*) in *dvayasaC*, etc., is for the purpose of including the suffixes;
for there are also nominal stems (*prātipadika*) such as *dvayasa* and others, and if the indicatory letters were not pronounced, those [stems] might also be understood as being included.

The word *taya* also could potentially be a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) ending in the vowel *a*, derived from the verbal root *taya*—from the list of roots (*dhātupāṭha*) meaning "to go" (roots 474, 485, 479, 480). Therefore, the letter *p* is pronounced in order to exclude that possibility. [Examples follow: *ūrudvayasī* and so on;

since her thighs are the measure [of her height], or her knees are the measure, the suffixes *dvayasaC* and others are applied according to Pāṇini 5.2.37. *Pañcatayī*: since she has five parts, the suffix *tayap* is applied according to Pāṇini 5.2.42. *Ākṣikī*, *śālākikī*.

In the expressions "he plays with dice" (*akṣair dīvyati*) and "he plays with sticks" (*śalākābhir dīvyati*), the suffix *ṭhak* is applied by the rule *tena dīvyati khanati* [Pāṇini 4.4.2], and the *ikādeśa* (substitution of *i*) takes the place of *ṭha*. Regarding the form *lāvaṇikī*:
it means "one whose merchandise is salt" (*lavaṇaṃ paṇyam asyāḥ*), according to [Pāṇini] 4.4.52.

Now, for what purpose are *ṭhak* and *ṭhañ* mentioned separately? Why not simply use the general term *ṭha*, omitting the specific indicatory letters (*anubandha*) that distinguish them? To this he replies: "separately," and so forth.

If there were a general inclusion by the term *ṭha*, then *ṭhan* and the others would also be included; therefore, they are mentioned separately to exclude them. The word *ādi* (etcetera) is for the purpose of including *ñiṭha* and the rest. Consequently, when the suffix *ṭhan* is applied [by Pāṇini 5.2.115] in the sense of "one who has a staff," the form *daṇḍikī* does not occur; and when the suffix *ñiṭha* is applied [by Pāṇini 4.2.116] in the sense of "born among the Kāśis," the form *kāśikī* does not occur. The mention of the indicatory letter *k* [in the rule *kaño'nubandhagrahaṇam*] is for the purpose of excluding those very forms and others. Thus: *yādṛśī*, *tādṛśī*.

In the rule *tyadādiṣu dṛśeranālocane kañ ca* [Pāṇini 3.2.60], the suffix *kañ* is applied; by *yattador āttvam* [Pāṇini 6.3.91], there is the substitution of *ā* for the final vowel of *yat* and *tat*. The pronunciation of two indicatory letters (*anubandha*) in *kvarap* is for the purpose of excluding *varac*, which is prescribed by the rule *stheśabhāsa-* [Pāṇini 3.2.175] and others. If this is so, then only one indicatory letter should have been pronounced, since even with one, the exclusion of *varac* is indeed accomplished? This is true; nevertheless, two indicatory letters are pronounced for the sake of easy comprehension by those of dull intellect. Thus: *itvarī* (a woman who wanders), meaning "not a wife" (*na-ārī*).

By the rule *iṇnaśjasartibhyaḥ kvarap* [Pāṇini 3.2.163], there is the augment *tuk* after a short vowel. The mention of the indicatory letter (*anubandha*) in *khyan* is for the sake of brevity; otherwise, if the genitive plural were used, there would be a cumbersome pronunciation due to the addition of the augment *nuṭ* and the lengthening of the vowel before *nām*. Thus, we have *āḍhaṅkaraṇī*.

The suffix *khyun* is applied by the rule *āḍhasubhaga* (Pāṇini 3.2.56) in the sense "that by which one who is not wealthy (*anāḍha*) is made wealthy (*āḍhya*). This is further governed by the rule *nañ-snañ-īkak-* (Pāṇini 6.3.75), etc.
The word *upasaṃkhyāna* means "formulation" or "supplementary statement.

The formulation here is as follows: in the subsequent sūtra, the particle *ca* ("and") serves to include what has not been explicitly mentioned; therefore, the suffix will also apply after words such as *nañ*.

Regarding "straiṇī" and "pauṃsnī": these are formed by the suffixes *nañ* and *sañ* respectively according to the rule "strīpuṃsābhyāṃ naṅ-snañau bhavanāt" [Pāṇini 4.1.87], meaning "this belongs to a woman" (*striyā iyam*) and "this belongs to a man" (*puṃsa iyam*).
Regarding "śāktīkī" and "yāṣṭīkī": [these denote those who live by the profession of using a spear or a staff].
His weapon is an inexhaustible spear (*śakti*).

Regarding the forms *taruṇī* and *talunī* in the sense of "wine" (*surā*)—that is, in the context of words such as *surā*—the feminine suffix *ṅīp* should be understood after the words *taruṇa* and *taluna*. For wine and the like possess no age, since age is a property belonging only to living beings. In the case of wine and the like, only the state of being fresh is conveyed by the words *taruṇa* and *taluna*.

But when age (*vayaḥ*) is intended to be expressed, then by virtue of their inclusion in the *gaura-* group, the suffix *ṅīṣ* must occur. In that case, there is a difference in accent: for the words *taruṇa* and *taluna* are derived with the suffix *unan* according to the rules *kṛvṛdāribhya unan* (DhP 5.52) and *tro raśca lo vā* (DhP 5.56); thus, by the accent of the *nit* suffix, they are udātta on the first syllable. When *ṅīp* is applied there, the word remains udātta on the first syllable; but when *ṅīṣ* is applied, the word becomes udātta on the final syllable due to the accent of the suffix. [Thus we have] *gārgī*.
Regarding "vātsī":

from the words *garga* and *vatsa*, the suffix *yañ* is applied [by Pāṇini 4.1.105] for the feminine offspring; then the suffix *ṅīp* is applied [by 4.1.15], resulting in the elision of the vowel *a* [by 6.4.148] and the elision of the letter *y* [by 6.4.150]. As for the statement "the mention of 'offspring' (*apatya*) must be made": that by which offspring is grasped is the "mention of offspring" (*apatyagrahaṇa*).

This is the explanation being stated: the commentary should be formulated in such a way that the suffix *yañ* is understood as qualifying "offspring" (*apatya*). Here is that explanation: the mention of "of the Easterners" (*prācām*) in the subsequent rule, which serves the purpose of providing an option, is also connected with this present rule; furthermore, that [option] is understood as a restricted option (*vyavasthitavibhāṣā*). Consequently, the suffix occurs invariably after a word ending in *yañ* when prescribed in the sense of offspring; however, it does not occur after a word ending in *yañ* when prescribed in senses such as "born in" (*jāta*) following the word *dvīpa*.

Now, for what purpose is this separation of rules (*yogavibhāga*)? One might ask: "Why not simply include the mention of *añ* in the preceding rule itself? To this he says: "The separation of rules is for the sake of the subsequent [rules]. This is so that in the following rule, the suffix *ṣpha* may apply only after a stem ending in *yañ*, and not after those beginning with *ṭi* and the rest. "The letter *ṣ* is for the sake of the feminine suffix *ṅīṣ*" means that it is so that the suffix *ṅīp* (as prescribed by Pāṇini 4.1.41) may apply.

Now, one might object: "Even if the suffix *ṣpha* is applied, the suffix *ṅīṣ* should not occur at all, because femininity is already manifested by the suffix *ṣpha* alone. To this, he says: "by two suffixes," and so forth.
For the suffix *ṣpha* alone is not capable of manifesting femininity; thus, it requires *ṅīṣ*. Since femininity is manifested only by those two together, *ṅīṣ* must indeed occur.
Regarding the phrase "the mention of *taddhita*," etc.:

the mention of *taddhita* is for the purpose that the designation *prātipadika* (nominal stem) should apply by virtue of the rule "A *kṛt*, a *taddhita*, and a compound [are *prātipadika*s]" (Pāṇini 1.2.46).
However, the *prātipadika* designation is [further] for the purpose that the suffix *ṅīṣ* should apply.

But surely, even without that [suffix], the suffix *ṅīṣ* will occur by the very power of the *ṣit* designation; otherwise, the *ṣit* designation would be purposeless, as there would be no other motive. Nor should one fear the over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) that it might also apply to the root *trapūṣ* ("to be ashamed," Dhātupāṭha 374), because the *ṣit* designation on a root has its utility in the rule for the suffix *aṅ*—"from roots marked with *ṣit* and from *bhidādi* etc., the suffix *aṅ*" (Pāṇini 3.3.104)—and because of the governing context "after this" (*ataḥ*). True, this is so; however, there would be a burden of comprehension (*pratipattigaurava*).
Therefore, for the sake of easy comprehension, the inclusion of the term *taddhita* [is made], as in the phrase "the inclusion of the word *sarvatra*" and so forth.
The inclusion of the word *sarvatra* in the subsequent sūtra is purposeless;

for that [inclusion] is made so that [the rule] might apply according to the opinion of all teachers, but this serves no purpose, because by virtue of the fact that [the preceding rule] is not marked with the *svarita* accent, the inclusion of the previous [term] must necessarily apply according to the opinion of all.

Therefore, the inclusion of the word "sarva" (all) in the subsequent sūtra is purposeless; hence, it is drawn back [to the present context]. He asks, "For what purpose? and replies, "To override the overriding rule.

By stating, "He will teach *cāp* after *āvaṭa*," he clarifies the meaning of "to override the overriding rule. The scope (*avakāśa*) of *cāp* after *āvaṭa*—according to the opinion of the Northerners—is *āvaṭā*; the scope of the rule "after a word ending in *gha* or *añ* from the *garga*-class, *cāp*" is *gārgyāyaṇī*. In the case of both rules applying after *āvaṭa* according to the Easterners, *cāp* would occur by virtue of its being the subsequent rule.
Because of the inclusion of the term "sarvatra" (everywhere), it will indeed be *ṣpha*—as in *āvaṭyāyanī*. Regarding Pāṇini 4.1.17: *vṛddhetkosalājādāññyaṅ*.

The meaning is that the suffix *ñyaṅ* is applied after [words denoting] a country (*janapada*) or a Kṣatriya who are designated as *vṛddha*, provided they end in the vowel *i* or *u*, as well as after the word *kosala* and the word *aja*, when deriving the sense of "descendant.
The term "from a *vṛddha*" [is used].
The meaning is "is explained.
Regarding the terms *āmbaṣṭhyaḥ* and *sauvīryaḥ*:
the words *āmbaṣṭha* and *sauvīra* denote both a country and the kṣatriyas thereof.
"Iditi": this indicates an example ending in "id".
"Āvantya" refers to [the example].
The word *Avanti* refers both to a country and to its king; likewise,
the word *Kosala* refers both to a country and to its king.
"Ajādasyāpatyam" (the offspring of Ajāda). This analysis [of the compound] applies when it denotes a king;
however, when it denotes a country, the analysis is "the king of the Ajādas."

*Bālamano ramā*: *ṣpha* [is added] after [stems ending in] *yañ* in the sense of feminine gender, according to the Easterners; this is a *taddhita* suffix. The term *yañ* is understood from the previous rule, and *striyām* (in the feminine) is supplied from the context. The word *ṣphe* has its nominative case-ending elided.
Thus he says: "from that which ends in *yañ*," and "independent" (*svatantra*).
For that word *kata* which does not constitute a part of another [compound] but stands alone is an independent nominal stem (*prātipadika*).
However, the word *kata* which is a constituent part of the compound *kurukata* lacks independence, because it is bound to the whole.
But what is this word *kata*, which is an independent nominal stem (*prātipadika*)? To this he says: "from the word *kapi*" and so forth.
[Examples: *lauhitāyanī*, *śāṃsityāyanī*.
From the words *lohita* and *śaṃsita*, the suffix *yañ* is applied because they belong to the *garga*-class.
Regarding "vābhravyāyaṇī":

here too, from the word *babhru*, the suffix *yañ* is applied by [Pāṇini 4.1.106] *madhubabhruvor brāhmaṇakauśikayoḥ*; then, by [6.4.146], there is the substitution of *vānt* (i.e., *au*), and from the stems ending in *yañ*, the suffix *ṣpha* is added. Regarding "but from *kaṇva*" and so forth...
The word *śakala* is desired before the word *kaṇva*, but [the word *śakala*] is after the word *kata*.
What happens when this is so? He says: "The preceding and following," and so forth.
This being the case, the two groups—the preceding and the following—consist of those that end with and begin with them [respectively].
By the word *tat*, the word *śakala* is referred back.
Those two groups, the preceding and the following, of which *śakala* is respectively the end and the beginning, are the "groups ending in and beginning with that.
For example, the preceding group begins with *lohita* and ends with the word *śakala*.
The subsequent group (gaṇa), beginning with Kaṇva and including Śakala and others, follows.
But what is the purpose of making the preceding and subsequent groups end with and begin with those respective terms? He says: "In that regard, the suffix *ṣpha* is the purpose.
When the preceding group ends with *śakala*, the suffix *ṣpha* serves as its purpose.

The purpose of [placing] *uttara* after *śakala* and the others is that they are listed among the nominal stems (*prātipadika*) in a different order. They are listed among the nominal stems in this sequence: *kapikata*, *kurukata*, *anaḍuh*, *kaṇva*, *śakala*.
"That [order] must be established in this way."
It should be established according to the lineage shown by the passage beginning with "From Kaṇva, Śakala was the first.
Therefore, this is what is meant: the two names *kurukata* and *anaḍuh* should be read in another place, while the word *śakala* should be read between the words *kataka* and *kaṇva*.
[The author] "thinks" (*manyate*)—thus says the author of the Ślokavārttika.
But how, given such a reading, are the suffixes *ṣ* and *phaṇ* established from the word *śakala*? He says: "From those ending in *kata*" (*katantebhyaḥ*), and so forth.

The term *katanta* is a *tatpuruṣa* compound meaning "that which has *kata* as its end. The substitution of the single form [for the final vowel and consonant] occurs by virtue of the irregularity (*nipātana*) "from those ending in *kata*.
The term *katanta* is a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "those [words], such as *lohita* and others, which have the word *kata* at their end."
The word *śakala* ends in *kat*, and the words *lohita* and so forth also end in *kat*; thus, by the rule of "single remainder" (*ekaśeṣa*) for similar forms, we have *katantaśca katantāśca*.

By the phrase "in the same way" (*tathā*), he shows that just as there is a single remainder of both the *bahuvrīhi* and *tatpuruṣa* compounds in the case of *katantebhyaḥ*, so too is it here in the case of *kaṇvādibhyaḥ*.

*Kaṇvādiḥ* means the beginning of *kaṇva*, namely the word *śakala*; those beginning with *kaṇva*—such as *gokakṣa* and others—are called *kaṇvādayaḥ*. Then, *kaṇvādiśca kaṇvādayaśca* results in *kaṇvādayaḥ*, with a single remainder as before.
"Not included by the operation of a *tatpuruṣa* [compound]" means:
in the rule "after words ending in *kata*" (Pāṇini 4.2.111), it is not included by the operation of a *tatpuruṣa*, that is, by a *tatpuruṣa* compound.
For example, the word *madhyāpīta*.
Regarding the two groups [of suffixes] beginning with *kataka* and *aṇva*, or the "two suffixes":
these are the *ṣpha* suffix and the *aṇ* suffix.

"Pratipadyate" means "it obtains. For when it is included within the operation of that *tatpuruṣa* compound, this is the meaning that arises for the present rule: after the word *śakala* ending in *kat*, as well as after words ending in *yañ*, and after the words beginning with *lohita* which end in *yañ*, the suffix *ṣpha* occurs in the feminine.
By that [rule], the word *śakala* acquires the suffix *ṣpha*,
resulting in *śākalyāyanī*. Even in this case, since the word *śakala* is included through its occurrence as a *tatpuruṣa* compound, the meaning is as follows:

The meaning is that the suffix *aṇ* occurs in the sense of secondary derivatives (*śaiṣika*) after words such as *kaṇva*, which end in the word *śakala* and possess a patronymic suffix (*gotrapratyaya*), and after words beginning with *kaṇva* and ending with *gokakṣa* that possess a patronymic suffix. By this rule, the word *śakala* also acquires the suffix *aṇ*; thus: "these are the pupils of Śākalya" = *śākalāḥ*. As for the question, "How is *kauravī* [formed]?", it is the inquiry of one who believes that the suffix *hīp* is prescribed here directly from the word *kauravya*.
Demonstrating that the feminine suffix *ṅīp* is prescribed here after the word *kuru* ending in the suffix *aṇ*, he says: “*tasyedam*,” etc., and “*kauravyamāṇḍūkayoḥ*,” etc.
Whatever grammatical operation is prescribed for *kauravya* and *māṇḍūka* by this rule must also be extended (*upasaṃkhyāna*) to *āsuri*;
that is to say, the suffix *ṣpha* must also be applied to *āsuri*.

In this regard, the following is the demonstration: the letter *ca* is added here, and it serves the purpose of including what has not been explicitly mentioned; therefore, the suffix *ṣpha* will also apply after the word *āsuri*.
Thus, we have *āsurāyaṇī*. [The derivation is as follows:
from *asura*, the suffix *iñ* is applied by [Pāṇini 4.1.95], *ata iñ*; then, the suffix *ṣpha* is applied to that which ends in *iñ*.

Regarding the statement, "since *iña* would [otherwise] apply by [Pāṇini 4.2.110]," one must perform a *yogavibhāga* (splitting of the rule) there by adding "not" (*na*). By that, even from the word *āsuri*, [the suffix *cha*] will occur—prohibited by [Pāṇini 4.2.114]—as in: "The *kalpa* taught by Āsuri is the *Āsurīya*. Regarding the term "*yauvanādi*," the word "etcetera" (*ādi*) is for the purpose of including "old age" (*vṛddhatva*) and so forth.
"By direct statement" (*śrutyā*) means:

that nominal stem which, by mere hearing alone and without depending on context or other factors, first conveys the stage of youth, functions here "by direct statement," as in the word "maiden" (*kumārī*).

But is it not the case that this word *kumārī* does not refer to the first stage of life; where, then, does it apply? [If you say] "in the absence of connection with a male," for it is indeed used even for an old woman—as in "an old maiden" (*vṛddhā kumārī*)—this is not so. For the word *kumārī* is conventionally established (*rūḍha*) only in the first stage of life. As for its application even to an old woman, that is due to her similarity (*sādhamryāt*) to a maiden, and not due to the absence of connection with a male. For a thing may receive the name of another due to similarity, as in "the Vāhīka is an ox" (*gaur vāhīkaḥ*). [The rule says: "in the final stage of life."

The meaning of this rule is that the suffix *ṅīp* occurs when [the word] is not in the "last" (*acarama*) stage; such is the interpretation of this sūtra. Herein lies the explanation: the mention of "the first stage of life" (*prathamavayas*) here is an indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*) for the "not-last" stage of life; therefore, the suffix *ṅīp* occurs even in other cases where one is not in the last stage of life. But what is the reason that it would not be established if only the first stage of life were being grasped, such that the meaning of the sūtra must be explained in this way? To this he says: "These two [words] express the second stage of life," and so forth.
In this regard, some maintain that there are four stages of life—childhood, youth, middle age, and old age.
Accordingly, they say: "What will one do in the fourth stage, having failed to study in the first, failed to acquire wealth in the second, and failed to practice austerity in the third?"

Thus it is said. Others maintain that there are three stages: childhood (*kaumāra*), youth (*yauvana*), and old age (*sthāvira*). Accordingly, they say: "The father protects her in childhood, the husband protects her in youth, and the son protects her in old age; a woman does not deserve independence. Some others maintain that there are three stages: infancy (*bālya*), middle age (*madhyatva*), and old age (*vṛddhatva*). Accordingly, they say: "One is called a child until sixteen, as long as one subsists on milk and rice; one is middle-aged until seventy, and beyond that, one is called old."
Thus, among all these [ages], youth is the second stage of life (*vaya*).

Now, one might object that since the words *vadhūṭī* and *ciraṇṭī* denote the first stage of life, [the suffix] would not apply here; therefore, some explain that "the first stage of life" is used here as an indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*) for the final stage of life. However, he who thinks: "Some, indeed, maintain that there are only two stages of life: having grouped together all those states that possess growth, they establish them as the first stage of life; and having grouped together all those states characterized by decline, they establish them as the second stage of life."
And so it has been said: "As long as one prospers through food, one must prosper; thereafter, one will be joined with misfortune. It is relying on this very insight that this *sūtra* was composed.
Therefore, the suffix *ṅīp* also occurs in the words *vadhūṭī* and *ciraṇṭī*; thus, these two denote the second stage of life (youth).

One must strive to ensure that this text is not contradicted by the statement, "A woman who has attained youth is so designated. For in this philosophical system, youth is not included within the second stage of life, because the state of youth is characterized by growth. Now, as for the description "lying on her back with red-soled feet"—since childhood is understood here, and it is only a child who lies on her back with red-soled feet—therefore the suffix *ṅīp* ought indeed to be applied. To this he says: "These are not words denoting age.
The meaning is that these words do not express age.

In this context, by the mere hearing of the nominal stem *uttānaśayā*, there is first understood a general relationship between an action and its factors: "she who lies on her back" (*uttānā śete* = *uttānaśayā*).

Following the rule [Pāṇini 4.1.1] which continues the mention of the suffix *ac*, and specifically by the supplementary rule [Vārttika 3.2.15] stating "after *uttāna* and others when they denote the agent," the suffix *ac* is applied; then, by the rule [Pāṇini 6.3.33], "the feminine form is like the masculine," the masculine form is substituted.
