It is also called the "place" because it is the basis for the arising of the *dharmatā-niṣyanda* itself. Or else, it is called the "place" because it is the basis for the arising of the *dharmatā-pratisaṃvid*, which is the cause of the *dharmatā-niṣyanda*. It is also called the "place" because it is the basis for the arising of the *dharmatā-niṣyanda* itself. Or else, it is called the "place" because it is the basis for the arising of the *dharmatā-pratisaṃvid*, which is the cause of the *dharmatā-niṣyanda*. It is also called the "place" because it is the basis for the arising of the *dharmatā-niṣyanda* itself. Or else, it is called the "place" because it is the basis for the arising of the *dharmatā-pratisaṃvid*, which is the cause of the *dharmatā-niṣyanda*. It is also called the "place" because it is the basis for the arising of the *dharmatā-niṣyanda* itself. Or else, it is called the "place" because it is the basis for the arising of the *dharmatā-pratisaṃvid*, which is the cause of the *dharmatā-niṣyanda*. It is also called the "place" because it is the basis for the arising of the *dharmatā-niṣyanda* itself. Or else, it is called the "place" because it is the basis for the
That which is produced by a person.
Regarding the word "bhājī":
from the root *bhaj* in the sense of "bestowing" (*viśrāṇana*), belonging to the *curādi* class, with the suffix *ṇic*.

By [Pāṇini 3.3.107], the suffix *yuc* would apply; however, by this very irregular derivation (*nipātana*), the suffix *aṅ* is applied, and from that which ends in *aṅ*, the suffix *ṅīṣ* is added. Thus, "śrāṇā."
The suffix *kta* is applied to the root *śrā* (meaning "to cook," Dhātupāṭha 810).

According to the rule *saṃyogāderāto dhātoryaṇvataḥ* [Aṣṭādhyāyī 8.2.43], the substitution of *na* for *ta* occurs; furthermore, by the rule *aṭkupvāṅanumvyavāye'pi* [Aṣṭādhyāyī 8.4.2], the substitution of *ṇa* for *na* occurs. Thus, the word "nāga" [is derived]. And so forth.

The word *nāga* is of two kinds: denoting a genus (*jāti*) and denoting a quality (*guṇa*). Therefore, because it here denotes "thickness" (*sthaulya*), it does not produce the suffix *ṅīṣ* as one denoting a genus; for it is not possible for "thickness" to be the denotation of a genus. Nor does it denote another quality; for from a word denoting "elephant" (*nāga*) that ends in *ṅīṣ* and expresses another quality, no other quality is understood, but rather thickness itself. Consequently, when this word, having expressed the quality of thickness, applies to a substance, then it produces the suffix *ṅīṣ*, and not otherwise.
"Elsewhere," and so forth:

when the word *nāga*, which primarily denotes a quality such as length (*daidhya*) and the like, exists elsewhere [than in its primary sense] and qualifies a substance (*dravya*), it then produces the feminine suffix *ṭāp*.
"But from that which expresses a genus (*jāti*)," and so forth.
Because [the word] expresses a genus such as "elephant-ness" (*hastitva*), the suffix *ṅīṣ* occurs by the rule "after a genus-word denoting a female" (*jāterastrīviṣayāt*) and so forth.
Regarding the phrase "if it is a color" (*varṇaśced*): the meaning is that if the word denotes a substance (*dravya*) and color is its basis for application (*pravṛttinimitta*).
"Another is 'black'"— this is its arbitrary name. "Another is 'blue'"— thus [it is called].
"Covering" refers to garments and the like.
It does not apply everywhere in the absence of covering;
rather, it applies "to blue and so forth, to medicinal herbs, to water, and to living beings."
This is due to the inherent nature of the word's expressive power (*śabdaśakti*), since the word *nīla* functions only in that specific sense.

Alternatively, the term *vā* (or) from [Pāṇini 4.1.38] is carried over here; and since that is a restricted option (*vyavasthitavibhāṣā*), it will apply only to these two meanings and not to others. Thus, it is said:
"only when it is a technical name (*saṃjñā*)."
This alternative [interpretation] is indeed without a covering;
it too is obtained from that very same source through the persistence of the verbal root *grah* (to seize),
as in the expression "an iron product" (*ayovikāra*).
The term *phāla* is indeed a specific name for that which is called *kuśānyā*;
it is simply an object made of wood or other materials, having that particular shape.
Regarding the phrase "one who desires another": she is one whose nature it is to desire an object other than sexual intercourse. She is called "one who possesses a desire for sexual intercourse."
Because the word *maithunecchā* (desire for sexual intercourse), ending in the suffix *-ā* denoting possession (*matvarthīya*), is employed [as a bahuvrīhi].
"Keśaveśaḥ"—
this refers specifically to one who has that name.
Regarding the phrase "kavarānyā":

since she possesses color (*varṇa*), the suffix *matup* applies; however, due to its elision or through metaphorical identification (*abhedopacāra*), that which refers to the substance (*dravya*) should be understood [as the word]. This word *śoṇa* denotes color. According to the rule "of colors ending in *taṇ*, *ni*, or *ti*" (*Phiṭ-sūtra* 2.33), it is acute-accented on the first syllable (*ādyudātta*).

Since [the form] is already established by [Pāṇini 4.1.40], this statement is for the purpose of restriction (niyama): it is so that [the term] may apply to "one who rinses his mouth" (pracāman), and not to others. "A quality-word (guṇavacana) is one that has expressed a quality"—this is because the suffix *lyuṭ* is prescribed in the sense of the past tense (*bhūta*). Furthermore, it should be understood as that which, having first denoted a quality, subsequently denotes the substance possessing that quality either through the elision of the *matup* suffix or through metaphorical identification (*abhedopacāra*).
Regarding the terms "sharp" (*paṭvī*) and "soft" (*mṛdvī*):

here, having denoted the qualities of sharpness and softness respectively, the words *paṭu* and *mṛdu* refer to the substance possessing those qualities; thus, they are "expressive of qualities" (*guṇavacana*). Regarding "pure" (*śuci*):
the word *śuci*, having operated upon the quality of purity, operates upon the substance; therefore it is "expressive of a quality," but it is not [the same as] that which ends in the vowel *ū*.

Regarding the word *ākhu*: this denotes a genus (*jāti*), not a collection (*gaṇa*). As for the statement "the suffix *ṅīp* is prescribed after words denoting qualities (*guṇavacana*) for the sake of making the initial syllable udātta":
it is the suffix *ṅīp* that is to be applied after words denoting qualities, not *ṅīṣ*.
There is a distinction regarding the accent.
For what purpose? For the sake of making it acutely accented on the first syllable (*ādyudātta*).

Since the acute accent of the vowel *ī* is prescribed by [Pāṇini 6.1.174] for words that are acutely accented on the final syllable (*antodātta*), there would otherwise be no distinction between the suffixes *ṅīp* and *ṅīṣ*.

However, among those words that have the acute accent on the first syllable (*ādyudātta*), the *ṅīp* suffix remains unaccented (*anudātta*); therefore, for that purpose, *ṅīp* must be prescribed. Now, it may be objected: "But *ṅīṣ* is the subject under discussion (*prakṛta*); how then can *ṅīp* be prescribed? This is not a fault; for here it is *ṅīp* alone that is carried over by the maxim of the frog-leap (*maṇḍūkapluti-nyāya*), and not *ṅīṣ*, because the latter is not marked with the svarita accent. [The example is] *vasvī*.

Regarding the root *vas* in the sense of "dwelling" (Dhātupāṭha 1942), when the rule *bhṛ-mṛ-śī-tṛ-carit-sarit-dhani-nāsti-da-u-ḍu-dhanim-i-masjibhya uḥ* (Daiva 1.92) is in force, and also the rule *dhānye nit* (Daiva 1.94), the suffix *u* is applied by the rule *śṛ-vṛ-snihitrapy-asivasihaniklidivandhimanibhyaśca* (Daiva 1.95). This suffix is marked with *ṇ* (ṇit), and because it is *ṇit*, the word becomes udātta on its first syllable.

Furthermore, this word *vasu* is a quality-denoting term (*guṇavacana*), for it denotes a substance (*dravya*) that possesses the quality after having first denoted the quality itself, namely "wealthiness" (*vasutva*).
The word *paṭu* likewise causes the suffix *ṅīp* to be elided because it is udātta on its first syllable.

The roots *aṭa* and *paṭa* mean "to go" (*gatau*; Dhātupāṭha 296, 297). With the causative suffix *ṇic*, the suffix *up* is applied according to *phalipāṭinamimanijanāṃ guk paṭinākidhataśca* (Daiva-Uṇādi-sūtra 1.103); for *pāṭi*, there is the substitution of *paṭi*. Due to the continued application of *dhānye nit* (Daiva-Uṇādi-sūtra 1.94), the word is accented on the first syllable because of the *nit* designation. Furthermore, since the word *mṛdu* is accented on the final syllable by the accent of the suffix, there is no difference between the feminine suffixes *ṅīp* and *ṅīṣ* in this case.

Regarding the root *mrada* in the sense of "softening" (*mardane*; Dhātupāṭha 767), when the suffix *ku* is being carried over from the rule *kubhraśca* (Daiva 1.107), the suffix *ku* and the process of *samprasāraṇa* (vowel substitution) occur by virtue of the rule *prathimradibhrasjāṃ samprasāraṇaṃ ca* (Daiva 1.113). As for the statement "there is a prohibition regarding the word *kharu* and those having a conjunct consonant as a penultimate letter" (*kharusaṃyogopadhapratiṣedhaḥ*), this means that there is a prohibition [of the application of the suffix] after the word *kharu* and after words having a conjunct consonant as their penultimate element.
It must be stated, however, that this [prohibition] is obtained precisely through the understanding that the option (*vā*) in the rule is a restricted option (*vyavasthitavibhāṣā*).
The inclusion of *ta* in *utaḥ* (with a long vowel) is for the purpose of excluding the long vowel; therefore, it does not apply in the case of *paṭuḥ*.
From the desire for *paṭu*, the suffix *kyac* is applied by *supa ātmanaḥ kyac* [Pāṇini 3.1.8], and a long vowel is substituted by *akṛtsārvadhātukayoḥ* [Pāṇini 7.4.25].
When *paṭūya* remains, the suffix *kvip* is added; then the *a* is elided by *verapṛktasya* [Pāṇini 6.1.67], and the *y* is elided by *lopo vyor vali* [Pāṇini 6.1.66].

In this context, by the very inclusion of the qualifier "utaḥ," the non-inclusion of a technical (śāstrīya) *guṇa* is established, for there is no word ending in the vowel *u* among the *hrasva* vowels or the *eṅ* diphthongs.
In common usage, however, a subordinate element is sometimes called a *guṇa*, as in the expression "we are *guṇa-bhūta*," which is understood to mean "we are not the primary [element]."

For in the rule "The suffixes *tva* and *tal* are used to denote that [quality] when a word for a substance (*dravyaśabda*) is applied because of the existence of a certain quality (*guṇa*)," the word "quality" (*guṇa*) refers merely to a qualifier. This is because the abstract suffix (*bhāvapratyaya*) occurs even in the case of a genus (*jāti*). However, in this context, he states the definition—"It resides in a substance (*sattva*) and departs from it"—in order to specify what kind of quality is intended here. Since all sentences have the function of exclusion (*vyavaccheda*), the restriction "only in a substance" (*sattva eva*) should be understood.
"Substance" (*sattva*) means a material entity (*dravya*); the meaning is that it resides only there, that is, it takes that very thing as its substratum.
"It departs" (*apaiti*) means it goes away from that state of being, just as blackness in a mango fruit first appears and then departs once redness has arisen.
Regarding the phrase "it is seen among different classes" (*pṛthagjātiṣu dṛśyate*):
those whose classes (*jāti*) are separate (*pṛthak*) or manifold are "those of different classes" (*pṛthagjātayaḥ*); therefore, it is seen among them, the "different classes."
For [the universal] "cowness" is not seen in individual cows such as Māṇavaka;
yet, the quality "white" seen in a white cow is also seen in conch shells and other objects.
By all of this, it is stated that *jāti* (universal) is not a quality (*guṇa*).
For a universal does not reside in substance alone.

Just as *sattā* (existence) subsists in all three—substance, quality, and action; *dravyatva* (substanceness) in substance alone; *karmatva* (actionness) in action alone; and *guṇatva* (qualityness) in quality alone; likewise, a universal residing in a substance does not depart from it. From its birth until its destruction, because it does not abandon its supporting substance, a universal is not observed in different classes of substances.

For the universal "cowness" (gotva) is not seen in individual cows and the like, nor is the universal "horseness" (aśvatva) seen in cows and the like; thus, there is no contingency of a universal being a quality (guṇa). However, this might apply to action (karman); for that too resides only in a substance when it is active, and departs from it when it becomes inactive. [This is addressed by the rule: "It is seen in separate classes."
It is observed in jars, cloths, and so forth;
therefore, redness is a quality (*guṇa*), and it is produced through contact with fire.
[The sūtra states: "And that which is not born of action."

Action (*kriyā*) is activity (*vyāpāra*). That which is produced from that is "produced by action" (*kriyāja*). That which is not produced by action is "not produced by action" (*akriyāja*), meaning eternal (*nitya*), such as the quality of magnitude (*mahattva*) and so forth in space (*ākāśa*) and other substances.
Thus, by demonstrating these two modes—the producibility and non-producebility of a quality (*guṇa*)—the exclusion of the status of being a quality from action (*karman*) is accomplished.
For action is only producible; it is never non-producible.

Even so, it follows that substance (dravya) would possess the nature of a quality (guṇatva), for these properties are found in it as well. To explain: if that [substance] also resides in its constituent parts which are themselves substances, and departs from them—just as the body is a whole (avayavin)—then it indeed inheres in its parts such as the hands and feet; and because it perishes upon their destruction, it departs from them. Furthermore, it is observed among distinct classes of things, being seen in elephants and other such beings.
Substance (*dravya*) also possesses the two aforementioned modes:

because a composite substance (*avayavidravya*) is produced, whereas space (*ākāśa*) and so forth are not produced in that way. To this he says: "That quality has non-existence as its nature" (*asattvaprakṛtir guṇaḥ*).
"Nature" (*prakṛti*) means intrinsic character (*svabhāva*).

That which has *sattva* as its substance (*dravya*) is "of the nature of *sattva*" (*sattvaprakṛti*). That which is not of the nature of *sattva* is "not of the nature of *sattva*" (*asattvaprakṛti*). A quality (*guṇa*) is that which, though endowed with the aforementioned properties, does not possess the nature of a substance (*dravyasvabhāva*).

"Substance" (*dravya*) means having the nature of a substance; therefore, a quality is not [a substance]. In the list beginning with *bahu*, it is read: "*śaktiḥ śastre*" (the word *śakti* [takes the suffix *ṅīṣ*] when referring to a weapon). This is its meaning: when a weapon is to be expressed, the suffix *ṅīṣ* occurs after the word *śakti*—thus, *śaktiḥ* or *śaktī*.
What is meant by "weapon" (*śastra*)? It means *śakti* (a spear) or *sāmarthya* (capability).
Others, however, read two words: *śakti-śastrī*—namely, *śakti*, *śaktī*, *śastri*, and *śastrī*.
[The rule applies] from this point onward for words denoting parts of living beings (*prāṇyaṅga*).

The suffix *ṅīṣ* optionally occurs after a word ending in *ikāra* (the vowel *i*) that denotes a limb of a living being: *dhamaniḥ* or *dhamanī*. Why "ending in *i*"? [Consider: *samarthā grīvā* ("a capable neck").
Why "a limb of a living being"? [Consider: *śreṇiḥ* ("a row").

"From a word ending in a kṛt-affix that has an indicatory letter *ik*, except for those ending in *ktin*. "Some say: 'from any [word] except those ending in *ktin* and those having a feminine meaning.
The meaning of this has been explained precisely in the commentary on [Pāṇini 4.1.31].

If the suffix *ṅīṣ* occurs after every word ending in *aktin*, for what purpose is there the recitation of words such as *śakaṭa* and others with a final *i*-vowel in the list (*gaṇa*)? It is for the sake of elaboration (*prapañca*). Furthermore, the recitation is for the purpose of providing an exception to the prohibition [of *ṅīṣ*] that would otherwise apply by the rule "after a word ending in *aktin*. In the case of *paddhati*, the substitution of *pad* [for *pāda*] occurs according to [Pāṇini 6.3.54]: *pādasya padājyāti-gau-pada-paṅktiṣu*. Thus, *pāda-hati* becomes *paddhati*.

Regarding the rule "after *candrabhāga*, [the suffix] *ṅīṣ* [is applied] when 'river' (*nadī*) is to be expressed": after the word *candrabhāga*, the suffix *ṅīṣ* occurs when a river is the meaning to be expressed—thus, *candrabhāgī* as a river.
Why specify "when a river"? [Because otherwise it would apply to] a deity named *Candrabhāgā*.
Regarding the word *ahan*: this term does not occur in the feminine when used alone;
therefore, it must be cited as ending in that [feminine suffix] within a compound.
The autumn (*śarat*) in which the days are long is called *dīrghāhnī*.
From this [word], both the prohibition of the feminine suffix *ṅīp* and its application occur.

Furthermore, the suffix *ḍāp* also occurs by the rules "in a *bahuvrīhi* compound ending in *an*, [the feminine suffix is added]" (Pāṇini 4.1.12) and "optionally *ḍāp* after both [suffixes *an* and *ap*]" (Pāṇini 4.1.13); or else, the suffix *ṅīp* occurs by the rule "optionally [after a word] ending in *an* when the penultimate vowel is elided" (Pāṇini 4.1.28).
By that, the feminine suffix *dhātu-rūpya* (the form of the root) occurs.

If the word *bahu* is a quality-word (*guṇavacana*), for what purpose is its inclusion here, since the suffix *ṅīṣ* is already established by the preceding rule? To this he says: "of that," and so forth. Now, for what purpose is the mention of "always" (*nitya*), since even when the alternative [suffix] is established by the preceding rule, it will necessarily occur by the very force of its formulation? To this he says: "The mention of 'always' is for the sake of what follows. "Prabhvī," and so forth.

With "bhuvaḥ" being carried over from the rule *bhuvaḥ saṃjñāntarayoḥ* [Pāṇini 3.2.179], the suffix *ḍu* is applied by the rule *vipraśabhyo ḍvasaṃjñāyām* [Pāṇini 3.2.180]; the feminine suffix *ṅīṣ* is added to that which ends in this suffix. Thus, *svayambhūḥ* is a form derived from the root *bhū* with the *kvip* suffix.

But surely, since "bhuvaḥ" is a fifth-case [ablative] form derived from the word *bhū* with a long vowel, the suffix must then follow only after a long vowel and not after a short one; to this he says: "This fifth case is indeed from the short vowel. If that is so, the mention "bhuvaḥ" would be untenable, for once the guṇa substitution has been applied by [Pāṇini 7.3.111], the mention should have been "bhoḥ"? To this he says: "It is a Vedic (sautra) mention. It is stated that there is a transposition of phonemes (*varṇavyatyaya*) in the Veda (*chandas*).

This shows that the substitution of *uvaṅ* was applied to its quality (*guṇa*). Regarding the term "due to connection with a male" (*puṃyogāt*), the ablative case is used in the sense of cause according to [Pāṇini 2.3.25]:
*vibhāṣā guṇe'striyām*.
"Connection" (*yoga*) means relationship (*sambandha*).
Regarding the term *ākhyāyām*:
this is a locative case used in the sense of the ablative, according to [Pāṇini 2.3.42].
It is called *ākhyā* (name) because it is by means of this that the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadika-artha*) is expressed; thus, it is a name by virtue of its function.
Regarding the phrase "in the designation of a male":
the meaning is that it serves as the designator of a male.
For that [word], due to its connection with a male, currently refers to a female; it does not refer to a male.

In past time, [the word] was a denoter of the male; therefore, the mention of "having occurred" (*bhūta*) is made. This is what is meant: if a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) was previously a denoter of the male, but subsequently functions in the feminine due to connection (*puyoga*), then the suffix *ṅīṣ* occurs after it. But how is the mention of the "male"—which has become subordinate through connection—properly a qualifier, given that the word "in the feminine" (*striyām*) continues [from the previous rule] and thus [the qualification] would apply only to the female? This is not so; for that which functions in the feminine due to connection with a male necessarily denotes the female. Therefore, this qualifier would otherwise be entirely purposeless.
Is this then a qualification of "connection with a male" (*puṃyoga*)? No, because it is impossible.
For there is no such nominal stem (*prātipadika*) which, prior to the connection with a male, refers to a female and serves as the designation for that connection with a male.

Indeed, all words such as *gaṇaka* and others which refer to a female due to connection with a male were already expressive [of that female] before [the connection]; they did not [originally] belong to the connection with a male.

However, those words such as *puṃyoga* which denote the connection with a male do not at all apply to a female by virtue of that connection with a male. Nor is there any such other word mentioned in this context, nor is any heard, to which the mention of the name (*ākhyā*) could be connected.
Therefore, it is understood that the connection here is specifically with the male, even though he is a subordinate factor (*guṇabhūta*).
"Gaṇakī," and so forth.
One who calculates is a *gaṇaka*; [the suffix] *ṇvul* is applied.
"Pratiṣṭhita" means *praṣṭha*; [the suffix] *ka* is applied according to Pāṇini 3.2.136.
The retroflex *ṇ* [in *mūrdhanya*] is due to the irregular derivation (*nipātana*) prescribed by [Pāṇini 8.3.92]. All these [words] are denotative of a male.
However, when they subsequently refer to a female due to connection with a male (*puṃyoga*), the suffix *ṅīṣ* is applied after them.
"Because the ground for the application of the word exists in the masculine.

That which constitutes the ground for the application of words such as *gaṇaka* (calculator) and the like—the essential nature of actions such as counting—exists in the masculine, but not in the feminine, nor in the neuter.
Therefore, these [words] apply to the masculine gender.
The meaning is that these words are denoters of the male.
How, then, do they apply to the female? To this he says: "Through connection with that," and so forth.
"Connection with that" (tadyoga) is the relationship [expressed as] "this belongs to that," characterized by the relation of owner and owned.
Therefore, even these masculine words function by their very nature to denote a female.

Just as a woman receives bathing, anointing, sprinkling, and so forth through association with those [male] things, so too does she receive the application of those same terms. In the case of "Devadattā," the word *devadatta* does not denote the female through association with the person named Devadatta.
What then? It is from herself alone; for this designation was applied to her:
"she who has been touched," meaning "she who has given birth."
The term "nirluṭhitagarbhā" means the same.
The words *parisṛṣṭa* and *prajāta*, when applied to a woman, function by taking the occasion of childbirth as their basis.
These words—*parisarga*, *prajana*, and *prasava*—are synonymous.
And for that procreation, union with a male is the cause, because it does not exist without him.
Therefore, it exists in the female due to the cause of union with a male. "It exists" [is the phrase].
"But it is not the case that the vowel *ī* does not occur because [the word] is called a masculine term.

Regarding "these words," the plural number is to be understood with reference to other words of this same class; otherwise, since there are only two words—namely *parisṛṣṭa* and *prajāta*—one would have had to say "these two words. [The commentary states: "An exception must be stated for *gopālikā* and others."
The phrase "for the sake of derivation" (*siddhyai*) is the ellipsis of the sentence.
For the sake of deriving words such as *gopālikā* and others, there is a prohibition of the suffix *ṅīp*.

However, that [prohibition] is to be established by relying on the fact that the option (*vā*) following from [Pāṇini 4.1.44] *voto guṇavacanāt* is a restricted option (*vyavasthitavibhāṣā*). Furthermore, it must be stated: "After *sūrya*, when denoting a deity, the suffix *āp* should be prescribed."

But surely, one need only state the prohibition regarding *ṅīṣ*; once *ṅīṣ* is prohibited, *ṭāp* will occur, and with *ṭāp*, the form *sūryā* is indeed established? This is not so; for although the form is established, the accent is not, because this word *sūrya* is ādyudātta (accented on the first syllable).
To explain: in the rule *rājasūyasūrya-* [Pāṇini 3.1.114], it is introduced as ending in *kyap*; therefore, by virtue of *kyap* being marked with *p*, it is anudātta (unaccented).
However, the verbal root—whether *sū* (to bring forth) or *sṛ* (to flow)—is antodātta (accented on the final syllable) by the general accent rule for roots.

In that case, if the suffix *ṭāp* were applied, there would be anudātta (unaccented) status; however, when [the suffix] *sat* is present, the final syllable becomes udātta (accented). The inclusion of the marker *p* is for the purpose of general reference in the rule *ṅyāpprātipadikāt* [Pāṇini 4.1.1].
Thus: *sūrī*.

The feminine form of *sūrya* when it denotes a human woman is *sūrī*, and it takes the suffix *ṅīṣ*; there is the elision of *ya* by the rule "sūryatiṣyāgastyamastyānām" [Pāṇini 6.4.149]. Regarding the phrase "of those":
it refers to the *indrāṇīs*.
Regarding the phrase "but of others": it refers to...

[This concerns] *himā* and so forth. Now, for what purpose is *ānuk* prescribed? Why not simply say *anuk*, since by that [the form] would be established through the rule for long vowels of homogeneous sounds (*savarṇadīrghatva*)? It is not established; for by [Pāṇini 6.1.97], the substitution of the subsequent form (*pararūpa*) would apply.
[Objection: This will not happen due to the force of the explicit utterance of the vowel *a*; for if it were a case of the subsequent form, one would have to state simply *nuk*.
In that case, it will come about through the capacity of the pronunciation of the letter *r*;
thus it is also understood that the *l*-sandhi simply does not occur.
Therefore, lest this be so understood, the suffix *ānu* must indeed be stated.

Alternatively: [the word] *indra* is derived from the sense "he praises Indra" (*indram ācaṣṭe*). By the rule *tat karoti tad ācaṣṭe* (Vārttika 200, 201), there is the causative suffix *ṇic*. Then, by the rule *ṇāviṣṭavat prātipadikasya* (Vārttika 813), there is the elision of the *ṭi* (the final vowel and following consonant). From the root *indrayati*, the suffix *kvip* is applied, and the *ṇic* is elided, resulting in *indraḥ*. The prescription of the suffix *ānuk* is for the purpose that the long vowel *gha*—that is, the letter *ā*—should be heard in the form *indrāṇī*. For if *ānuk* were present, the long vowel would not be heard. Now, one might object: "In this case, the suffix *ṅīṣ* should not occur, because of the governing rule *ataḥ* (from a stem ending in short *a*)? [The answer is: It will occur by virtue of the force of the explicit utterance of the long vowel. [The rule] "in the sense of greatness, [the suffix *kan* is added] after *himā* and *araṇya*" [is also cited].

When *himā* and the others, though joined with the quality of greatness (*mahattva*), are connected with the feminine gender, then this is declared by the present rule to be the prescription of these two—the suffix and the augment—when there is a desire to express femininity; however, it is not said that this is an exception (*apavāda*) to the feminine suffix.
For the suffix occurs only when femininity itself is intended. Regarding "after *yava*, when defect is implied":
when a defect is understood, the suffix *ṅīṣ* occurs in the feminine—*yavānī*, meaning "defective barley. Regarding "after *yavana*, when [a script] is meant": [the suffix *ṅīṣ* occurs].
Regarding the phrase "the script of the Yavanas" (*yavanānāṃ lipiḥ*):

although the suffix *ṅīṣ* would have applied under rule 4.3.120, it does not occur here because the meaning of that [suffix] has already been expressed by *ṅīṣ* itself. As for the statement "and the substitution of *ṇa* for the *da* of *ācārya*": [this applies when the word *ācārya* is used].

This is not something that needs to be stated as new, because it is already included among the *kṣubhnādi* group [of words]. As for the statement, "This rule applies only in the sense of self-same status (*svārtha*)," the word "only" (*eva*) excludes connection with a male (*puṃyoga*).
For if this rule were to apply in the case of connection with a male, then even a Śūdra woman who is the wife of a Kṣatriya would have to be called *kṣatriyāṇī*.

Therefore, this rule is for the sake of the word's own meaning alone— namely, that a *kṣatriyā* is [the wife] of a *kṣatriya*. However, in the case of a connection with a male (*puṃyoga*), the suffix *ṅīṣ* must necessarily occur by means of the preceding sūtra, "liṅ ca."
To what does that *lit*-ness belong? To the suffix *ānuk*.
For instance, the word *mudgalānī* is recited in the *Āmnāya* with the second syllable as acute (*udātta*);

however, if the suffix *ṅīṣ* were *lit*, the third syllable would be acute. By the phrase "that which has a preceding instrument" (*karaṇaṃ pūrvaṃ yasmin*), he demonstrates that both the mention of "having a preceding instrument" (*karaṇapūrva*) and the mention of "purchased" (*krīta*) are qualifiers of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*).
This word *pūrva* denotes a constituent part (*avayava*).
The meaning is: "that in which the instrument (*karaṇa*) is a constituent part.
Now, why is it not understood that the term *karaṇapūrva* is a qualifier of the word *krīta* itself? Because it is impossible.

Does the word *krīta* qualify by taking the word *pūrva* as denoting a constituent part—meaning "the instrument in the preceding [word]"? Or does it take *pūrva* as a word denoting a relative position—meaning "the instrument which precedes this"? In that regard, the first alternative is not possible, for in this case no other word denoting an instrument can logically be a constituent part of the word *krīta*. However, the second alternative is possible; yet, it would apply even to a sentence—as in "bought with a goat" (*ajā-krīta*), since here the word denoting the instrument (*aja*) indeed precedes the word *krīta*. But when [the rule] is qualified by reference to a nominal stem (*prātipadika*), this fault does not occur.
The word *krīta* in the expression *na hrīṇa krīta* is not a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) ending in the suffix *krīta* that functions as a constituent part;
rather, it is a sentence (*vākya*).
Therefore, the nominal stem under discussion, which is a general term, is qualified by the word *pūrva*, which denotes a specific constituent part.

Even by the word *krīta*, that very same nominal stem (*prātipadika*) preceded by an instrumental [word] is intended. Therefore, if that [stem] were being qualified, it would follow by implication that the rule applies to what ends in it (*tadantavidhi*). Thus he says: "from the nominal stem *krīta*. Examples are: *vastrakrītī* ("bought for a garment") and *vasanakrītī* ("bought for clothing").

In this context, according to the rule *gatikārakopapadānāṃ kṛdbhiḥ saha samāsavacanaṃ prāk subutpatteḥ* (Vyāḍi-Pāṇini-Vṛtti 138), which states that words denoting motion (*gati*), grammatical relations (*kāraka*), and secondary words (*upapada*) are compounded with *kṛt*-derived nouns before the addition of case-endings (*sup*), there is a compounding of the instruments *vas-tra* and *vas-ana* with the word *krīta* even prior to the addition of case-endings, resulting in *sukrītā* and *duṣkrītā*. Because they are secondary words (*upapada*) following a word denoting motion (*gati*), there is a compounding with the word *duṣ-* even prior to the addition of case-endings, according to the rule *kugatiprādayaḥ* (Pāṇini 2.2.18). In the form *duṣkrītā*, the substitution of *ṣ* occurs by the rule *idudupadhasya cāpratyayasya* (Pāṇini 8.3.41). [The phrase] "compounded with a word ending in *ṭā*" refers to this process.
It should be understood that this applies only to those two [suffixes] which end in a case-ending (*subanta*).

Since the status of being a *kṛdanta* is established once the feminine suffix *ṭāp* has been applied, one must consider here whether *ṭāp* should be applied first or the case-ending. Because it is more internal (*antaraṅga*), *ṭāp* is applied first.
Since the case ending (*vibhakti*) is external (*bahiraṅga*), the compound is formed between two words that end in case endings.
Internality (*antaraṅgatva*) and externality (*bahiraṅgatva*) regarding the feminine suffixes *ṭāp* and *vibhakti* have been explained in the rule *ṅyāpprātipadikāt* [Pāṇini 4.1.1].
To the question, "Once *ṭāp* has been applied, why does *ṅīṣ* not occur?", he says: "And because of the word 'from this' (*ataḥ*)," and so forth.

But how is a compound with a word ending in *ṭāp* established, given that it is stated: "The compounding of *gati*s, *kāraka*s, and *upapada*s with *kṛt*-derived words occurs prior to the arising of case-endings" (*Vyāḍiparibhāṣāvṛtti* 138)? Since [the rule] requires the compound to occur while the word is still in its *kṛt*-derived state, he says: "Of *gati*s, *kāraka*s, and *upapada*s," and so forth. But why is it said to be "frequently" (*bahulam*)? He says: "The agent and the instrument," and so forth.
For by this [rule], namely *Pāṇini* 2.1.32, the compounding of *gati*s, *kāraka*s, and *upapada*s with *kṛt*-derived words is prescribed.

And because of the inclusion of the term "bahulam" (variously), in some cases [the compound] occurs while still in the state of a *kṛt*-derivative, even before the production of case-endings (*sup*), and in other cases otherwise. Therefore, the teachers state that "the rule regarding the compounding of prefixes, verbal roots, and secondary words with *kṛt*-derivatives occurs before the production of case-endings" (Vyāḍiparibhāṣāvṛtti 138) is applied "variously. Consequently, the intention is that a compound is sometimes obtained even with a feminine suffix ending in *ṭāp*, as in the example "abhraviliptī."
From the root *lipa* (in the *Dhātupāṭha*, no. 1433), the suffix *kta* is applied.

When the intended meaning is "smeared with few clouds," a compound is formed as previously described before the addition of case endings (*sup*). However, the word *alpa* ("few") is not employed [separately] because its meaning is already conveyed [by the compound].

"Anointed with sandalwood" (*candanānuliptā*) means "anointed with much sandalwood. Regarding "pierced by a conch shell" (*śaṅkhabhinnī*), the substitution of *n* [for *m*] occurs according to Pāṇini 8.2.42: *radābhyām*.

Although the rule *niṣṭhā* [Pāṇini 2.2.36] would require that the past participle ending in *niṣṭhā* be placed first in a compound, it does not apply here because of the Vārttika: *jātikālasukhādibhyaḥ paravacanam* (Vārttika 116).
For words such as *śaṅkha* denote a genus (*jāti*);
it is precisely for this reason that the final syllable receives the udātta accent according to [Pāṇini 6.2.170].
Regarding the term *galakotkṛtī*:
the suffix *kta* is applied to the root *kṛtī* in the sense of "cutting" (*chedane*; Dhātupāṭha 1435). Regarding the term *keśalūnī*: [it is derived from the root *lū* with the suffix *ini*].

He raises the objection regarding the substitution of *n* [for *t*] based on the rule *keśān lunāti* (Pāṇini 8.2.44). Regarding the form *pādapatitā*, the final syllable is udātta due to the *tatpuruṣa* compound according to the rule *pādapatitā* (Pāṇini 2.1.32). [The objection is: "There is a prohibition of the suffix *jāta* after a word that has an udātta on the final syllable."

Regarding the prescription of the suffix *ṅīṣ* after a *bahuvrīhi* compound that is oxytone (*antodātta*), there is a prohibition when the word ends in *jāta*; and since this [prohibition] is obtained precisely from the inclusion of the term "end" (*anta*) [in the rule], it need not be stated.

Should one not simply omit the mention of "end" here? Even without it, just as in the case of *varṇād anudāttāt* [Pāṇini 4.1.39], where it is understood as "ending in an anudātta vowel," so too here it would be understood as "ending in an oxytone vowel. It is done for this purpose: so that the rule applies to a *bahuvrīhi* that is invariably oxytone, but not to one that is optionally oxytone.
Furthermore, in the case of *dantājātā* and *stanajātā*, because of the optional addition of the feminine suffix *ṅīṣ* by [Pāṇini 4.1.71], this rule will not apply.

Alternatively, the mention of *vā* ("optionally") in the subsequent sūtra is a carry-over (*śeṣa*) for both rules, and it is a restricted option (*vyavasthitavibhāṣā*); therefore, it will not apply to words ending in *jāta*.
It should be understood that in this interpretation, the inclusion of the word *anta* ("ending in") is solely for the sake of clarity. [This applies] "to *pāṇigṛhītī* and others, in specific senses."
The word "for the sake of accomplishment" (*siddhaye*) is to be supplied as the remainder.
For the sake of accomplishing [the forms] *pāṇigṛhītī* and so forth, the suffix *ṅīp* occurs only in specific instances, not everywhere.
This is also obtained through the rule of restricted option (*vyavasthitavibhāṣā*).
However, the specific distinction regarding the taking of the hand (pāṇigrahaṇa) should be understood:
she whose hand is taken for the purpose of becoming a wife, preceded by the presence of fire as witness, is called "one whose hand has been taken" (pāṇigṛhītī).
[The phrase] "in whatever manner" [is used].

The meaning is: "by some manner other than the one already stated. Regarding the phrase "not after *bahu* and so forth" (*abahunañ*), the sense is that this should be explained as having the effect that the suffix *ṅīṣ* does not occur after words preceded by *bahu* and others.
This explanation, however, must be made by relying on the fact that the very mention of the word *vā* (in Pāṇini 4.1.45) is a *vyavasthitavibhāṣā* (an option restricted to specific cases).
In the phrase “*jātikālasukhādi*,” etc.,
in the word “*bahukṛte*,” there is the udātta accent on the final syllable according to Pāṇini 6.2.175.
In the words “*akṛtā*” and “*sakṛtā*,” [the accentuation] is according to Pāṇini 6.2.172 (*nañsubhyām*).

In examples such as *māsajātaḥ* and so forth, [the rule] applies according to Pāṇini 6.2.170. Regarding the phrase "from that which does not have a non-body-part as its prior member" (*asvāṅgapūrvapadāt*):
"non-body-part" (*asvāṅga*) means that which is not a body part; a *bahuvrīhi* compound whose prior member is such is described in that way.
For example: *sāraṅgajagdhī*.

The root *ad* is listed as "ada bhakṣaṇe" (Dhātupāṭha 1011). By the rule "ado jagdhiḥ" (Pāṇini 2.4.36), the substitute *jagdhi* is applied; by [the rule] "ekāco baśo bhaṣ jhaṣantasya sdhvoḥ" (Pāṇini 8.2.40), the *t* is changed to *gh*; and by [the rule] "jhalāṃ jaś jhaśi" (Pāṇini 8.4.53), there is the elision of the *gh*. Thus we have "palāṇḍubhakṣitī. The root *bhakṣ* is listed as "bhakṣa adane" (Dhātupāṭha 1557); the causative suffix *ṇic* is added according to the *curādi* class.

Regarding "surāpīti": the substitution of *i* occurs by the rule *ghumāsthāgāpājahātisām aṅi* (Pāṇini 6.4.66). In all such cases, the final syllable of the second member (*uttarapada*) is udātta-accented according to the rule *jātikālasukhādibhyo ’nācchādanāt* (Pāṇini 6.2.169) et cetera. Regarding "vastracchannā" and "vasanacchannā": [the same rule applies].

The word *cchanna* is derived from the root *chad* (meaning "to cover" or "to conceal," Dhātupāṭha 1833), which belongs to the *cur*-class and takes the suffix *ṇi*; with the suffix *kta*, the form *cchanna* is established by the rule *vā vāntaśāntapūrṇa-* [Pāṇini 7.2.27].

Since the rule *anācchādanāt* [Pāṇini 6.2.169] prohibits the acute accent on the final syllable of the second member, the original accent (*prakṛtisvara*) is applied; consequently, because the remaining syllables are unaccented (*anudātta*), there is no acute accent on the final syllable here. In this compound, the first member (*pūrvapada*) is acute on its initial syllable: one instance by the accent of the *nit* suffix, and the other by the accent of the *lit* suffix.
From the root *thasa* in the sense of "covering" (*ācchādane*; Dhātupāṭha 1023), with the suffix *ṣṭran*, we get *vastram*.
From the root *vas* in the sense of "clothing" (*vasanam*), with the suffix *lyuṭ*, we get *vāsaḥ*.

By the rule beginning with "bahulam," it should be explained that in the Vedic language (*chandasi*), the feminine suffix *ṅīṣ* occurs frequently in the sense of a technical name (*saṃjñāyām*). This is the intended meaning.

In that regard, because the non-mention of the word "or" (*vā*) implies a fixed option (*vyavasthitavibhāṣā*), the feminine suffix *ṅīṣ* will occur frequently in both technical names (*saṃjñā*) and Vedic verse (*chandas*).

[Objection: But since this very rule establishes its status as a *bahuvrīhi*, the suffix *ṅīṣ* will occur by that rule alone; for what purpose, then, is this [separate rule] stated? To this he says: "And *pravṛddha*," etc.
He shows that it is a *tatpuruṣa* through a specific analysis [of the compound], as in the example "moon-faced" (*candramukhī*).

The compound *candra iva mukham asyāḥ* ("her face is like the moon") is a *bahuvrīhi*. In this case, by the rule *prathamānirdiṣṭam* [Pāṇini 1.2.43] and others, the word *mukha* receives the designation of *upasarjana*.
[An example is] *atikeśī* ("having beautiful hair").
Thus ends the compound.
By the rule *ekavibhakti ca* [Pāṇini 1.2.44], the word *keśa* attains the status of an *upasarjana*. Regarding the term *aṅga*:
the meaning is that it must be explained as having the form of the statement, "the suffix *ṅīṣ* occurs after *aṅga* and other words when they are *upasarjanas*."

For what purpose? Because the suffix *ṅīṣ* does not apply due to the presence of a conjunct consonant (*saṃyoga*) as the penultimate element, this form of the rule must be explained for that purpose. This is the explanation: in the subsequent sūtra, the particle *ca* serves to include what has not been explicitly mentioned; by it, the suffix *ṅīp* applies to words such as *aṅga* and others that have a conjunct consonant as their penultimate element. [The word] "not liquid" (*adrava*).

The wind that issues forth from the mouth and nose is *prāṇa*; one who possesses this *prāṇa* is *prāṇin*. That which exists therein is "situated in a living being" (*prāṇistha*). The mouth and so forth are called "one's own limbs" (*svāṅga*). If this were the case, then phlegm (*kapha*) would also be a "limb," and consequently, the suffix *ṅīṣ* would undesirably apply in the term *bahukaphā* (one with much phlegm). To this, he says: "not liquid" (*adrava*). Because of the inclusion of this qualification, this undesirable consequence does not arise, since phlegm is by nature liquid.

Even so, knowledge might be considered its own *aṅga* (limb/member), because it resides in a living being and is not liquid; consequently, would the suffix *ṅīṣ* not apply in the case of the term *bahujñānā* as well? To this he says: "possessing form" (*mūrtimat*).
That which has dimension—such as shortness and so forth—belonging to those substances that are not all-pervading is "form" (*mūrti*); that which possesses this is "possessing form.
And that [form] does not exist in knowledge, because knowledge is devoid of qualities (*nirguṇatvāt*).
Furthermore, because qualities and knowledge are attributes of the self (*ātmaguṇatva*), there is no possibility of their being considered one's own limbs (*svāṅgatva*).
Even according to those for whom form (*mūrti*) is a specific kind of touch such as hardness and so forth, knowledge does not possess form; for there is no touch in knowledge.
Nevertheless, even in this case, a swelling known as *āyu* would indeed attain the status of being one's own limb, since it possesses the aforementioned qualifying characteristics.
Furthermore, since the suffix *ṅīṣ* would otherwise apply in the case of *bahuśophā*, he says "not born of a morbid change" (*avikārajam*).
A "morbid change" (*vikāra*) means an imbalance of the bodily constituents (*dhātu*), that is to say, a disturbance of the elements (*bhūta*); what is produced from that is "born of a morbid change.
That which is not born of a morbid change is "not born of a morbid change" (*avikāraja*).

Thus, by the force of this specific qualification regarding the material cause (*upādāna*), even a swelling (*śopha*) would not attain the status of being one's own limb (*svāṅga*). If a limb were defined as that which resides in a living being, then hair fallen on a road or elsewhere would not be one's own limb; consequently, the expression "a woman with long hair on the road" (*dīrghakeśī rathyā*) would not be established. To address this, he says: "not residing in that" (*atatstham*), and so forth.
"Located in that" means situated in that living being (*tatstham*); "not located in that" (*atatstham*) means not situated in that living being—i.e., not situated in a sentient being (*aṇistham*).

Even so, hair and the like are considered one's own limbs (*svāṅgam*) provided they were previously seen on a living being. In that case, would not facial features such as the mouth of a statue lack the status of being one's own limbs because they do not reside in a living being? Consequently, in the expression *dīrghamukhī pratimā* ("a long-faced statue"), the suffix *ṅīṣ* would not occur? To this he says: "If it belongs to that [living being] in that way. (Note: This refers to the rule *svāṅgāccopasarjanādasaṃyogopadhāt*, Pāṇini 4.1.54, which prescribes the feminine suffix *ṅīṣ* for words denoting parts of the body that are not preceded by a conjunct consonant, provided they are *upasarjana* and denote a limb of a living being.)

If that limb of a living being is connected to it in such a way—that is, joined with it in a particular configuration—and if it is likewise connected in that same manner even when belonging to a non-living thing, then it possesses the status of being its own limb (*svāṅgatva*).
Alternatively: if this [limb] of that living being is joined in the same way as it is in a living being, then it is also a limb of its own. There is another reading: *tena ced etat tathā yutam*.
If that which is connected to a living being by a certain mode—such as a particular configuration or the like—is likewise connected to a non-living thing, it is still its own limb (*svāṅga*).

Alternatively, if the mouth and so forth of that non-living thing are joined together in the same manner as they are in a living being, it is still its own limb. Or again, if that substance situated in a non-living thing is joined with the mouth and other limbs in the same way as a substance belonging to a living being, it is still its own limb.

The meaning in every respect is this: if a limb such as the mouth and so forth belonging to a living being is exactly like that same limb belonging to a non-living being, then it is likewise [treated as] its own limb (*svāṅga*). Regarding the rule beginning with "when characterized by the suffix *bahuC*" and so on: since a prohibition would have applied by the rule "of the nose and the belly" (Pāṇini 4.1.56) when characterized by the suffix *bahuC*, this statement is made [as an exception].

For the remaining cases, the rule *asaṃyogopadhāt* [Pāṇini 4.1.54] serves as an indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*) for a conjunct consonant (*saṃyoga*). Regarding this, it is said: "The prohibition characterized by the presence of the prefixes *saha*, *nañ*, or *vidyamāna* certainly remains in effect.

Now, as for the case of *nāsikā* and *udara*, this rule—according to the principle that "exceptions stated earlier subvert the immediately following rules, but not those that follow later" (Vyāḍipāda 9)—subverts only the prohibition characterized by the suffix *bahuc*, which is immediately adjacent, and not the prohibition characterized by the prefix *saha* and so forth.

Regarding the words beginning with *oṣṭha*, according to the rule "Exceptions [apavāda] set aside preceding rules" (*vyākaraṇa-paribhāṣā* 10), the suffix characterized by having a *saṃyoga* as its penultimate letter (*upadhā*) applies first; thus, we have *sahanāsikā*, *anāsikā*, and *vidyamānanāsikā*.
As for *bimboṣṭhī*:

she whose lips are like the *bimba* fruit is *bimboṣṭhī*; here, the substitution of a single subsequent form (*pararūpa*) is applied by the supplementary rule (*vārttika* 687): "In a compound, the substitution of a single subsequent form may optionally be stated for *o* and *u* followed by *aṣṭha*."

Those, however, who read the vowel *au* as in "bimbauṣṭī" apply the *vṛddhi* [vowel substitute] according to Pāṇini 6.1.88. Regarding the statement "it should be stated that [the suffix applies] after 'puccha'," the meaning is that one should provide an explanation to the effect that the feminine suffix *ṅīṣ* occurs after nominal stems ending in "puccha.
For what purpose? So that it may also apply after a stem ending in "puccha" even when it has a conjunct consonant (*saṃyoga*) as its penultimate element (*upadhā*).
The explanation, however, should be made by relying on the fact that the particle *ca* has the sense of including what has not been explicitly mentioned:
"having a beautiful tail" (*kalyāṇapucchī*) means "she whose tail is beautiful. "Variegated" (*kabara*), and so forth.
The suffix *ṅīṣ* occurs after words ending in *puccha* when preceded by *kabara* and others.

This [application] is also obtained from that very [sūtra], either through the inclusion of the particle *vā* (or) or because the option (*vibhāṣā*) is restricted (*vyavasthita*). That which has a variegated tail is *kabarapucchī*.

Thus, in the cases of *maṇipuccha*, *viṣapuccha*, and *śarapuccha*, the word *puccha* does not undergo prior placement [as a compound member]; this is because of the rule: "In the case of prior placement of the locative case, there is a statement that [the word] follows words such as *gaḍu*" (Vārttika 115).
"From the comparison, from the subject, and from the tail"—
the word "always" is connected [to this].
This also is obtained from the two reasons previously stated.

Since this is already established by the rule *pucchācceti vaktavyam* (Vārttika 364), the repeated mention of *puccha* here is for the sake of elaboration (*prapañca*) or to ensure its obligatory application (*nityārtha*).
That which has a tail like that of an owl is called *ulūkapucchī*. In the phrase *kalyāṇakrīḍā*, the word *krīḍā* is feminine in gender.
This is because of the reading in the *Liṅgakārikā*: "The breast, the armpit, the tongue, the neck, attachment, family, desire, and illusion.
The analysis of the compound is: "She whose breast (*kroḍā*) is auspicious (*kalyāṇī*).
The masculine form is applied according to Pāṇini 6.3.34, *striyāḥ puṃvat*.
The shortening of the final vowel of the *uttarapada* occurs by the rule *gostriyoḥ* [Pāṇini 1.2.48] and so forth.
Consequently, there is a prohibition of the suffix *ṅīp*, which would otherwise have applied by the rule *svāṅgāccopasarjanāt* [Pāṇini 4.1.54] and so forth; thereafter, the suffix *ṭāp* is added.
Thus, we have *mahālalāṭā*.
The substitution of *āt* [for *tva*] occurs by the rule beginning with *āmanmahat* (Pāṇini 6.3.46). Regarding the term *sakeśā*: it means "that which exists together with hair.
The compound is formed by the rule *tena saheti tulyoge* (Pāṇini 2.2.28).
By [Pāṇini 6.3.82], there is the substitution of *sa-* for *saha-*.
Regarding "akeśa":

it means "one for whom hair (*keśa*) does not exist. According to the Vārttika (102), "A negative particle forms a *bahuvrīhi* compound with words having the sense of 'existent,' and there is elision of the final member," there is the elision of the word "vidyamāna" (existent).

Now, what is the purpose of including the word "pūrva" (preceded by)? One might argue that it should simply be stated as "saha-nañ-vidyamānāt" (preceded by *saha*, *nañ*, or *vidyamāna*); for by this ablative case (*pañcamī*), when the limb of one's own body (*svāṅga*) is qualified, the status of being preceded by *saha* and so forth is indeed obtained. This is not so; for the ablative case would qualify the limb of one's own body by way of posteriority—meaning "that limb of one's own body which follows after *saha* and so forth. Consequently, there would be the possibility of forming compounds with something other than a limb of one's own body following after *saha* and so forth, such as in the analysis: "one whose face is beautiful and present" (*kalyāṇa-vidyamāna-mukhā*). Alternatively, the analysis could be: "one whose face is present" (*vidyamāna-mukhaḥ*), and then "one whose [face] is beautiful and present" (*kalyāṇa-vidyamāna-mukhaḥ*).

When the term *pūrva* (preceding) is included, because the word *pūrva* denotes a constituent part (*avayava*), the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) is qualified by having *saha* and so forth as its preceding element. Thus, when it is understood that "from a nominal stem ending in a limb of the body (*svāṅga*) which has *saha* and so forth as its constituent part," the prohibition does not apply here. For this [stem] does not have *saha* and so forth as its constituent part; rather, it has the word *kalyāṇa* as its constituent part. Therefore, there is no occurrence of the undesired consequence. Regarding the form *sūrpaṇakhā*:
the substitution of *ṇ* occurs by the rule *pūrvapadāt saṃjñāyām agaḥ* [Pāṇini 8.4.3].

Now, why is she called the Rākṣasī Śūrpaṇakhī? Because it is not a conventional name (*saṃjñā*). It is said [in Pāṇini’s grammar] that [the substitution of *ṇ* for *n*] occurs when there is a conventional name (*saṃjñāyām*), and this is not a conventional name.
For instance, the substitution of *ṇ* (ṇatva) does not occur by the rule beginning with "pūrvapadāt" (Pāṇ. 8.4.3).

This designation for her is etymological (yaugika), based on her connection with nails shaped like winnowing baskets (*śūrpa*); that is, she is called *Śūrpanakhī* because her nails (*nakha*) are like a winnowing basket (*śūrpa*). Now, why is this form introduced as ending in long *ī* (*īkāra*), instead of simply saying "in the Veda [the word] *dīrghajihvā* [is formed]"? If it is argued that by saying it thus, a prohibition would be understood from the context of prohibitions, we say no; for since the suffix would not apply due to the word ending in a conjunct consonant (*saṃyogopadha*), and because prohibitions must presuppose a prior application of a rule, it follows by implication that this is indeed a positive injunction (*vidhi*). Thus he says: "The introduction [of the form] is for the sake of making it obligatory (*nityārtha*)."

Because the suffix *ṅīṣ* under discussion is optional by virtue of being prescribed as such, it would be understood as optional here as well; however, due to this specific grammatical anomaly (*nipātana*), it becomes compulsory. Regarding the phrase "the scope of prescription and prohibition" and so forth:

the scope of prescription consists of a word denoting a bodily limb (*svāṅga*) that is a subordinate member (*upasarjana*), as well as a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) ending in a conjunct consonant (*saṃyoga*) or beginning with *nāsikā*.
The scope of prohibition consists of a nominal stem ending in a conjunct consonant, as per [Pāṇini 4.1.56] and [4.1.57].

By this, he indicates the following: the prescriptive rules (vidhi-śāstra) such as *svāṅgāccopasarjanād asaṃyogopadhāt* [Pāṇini 4.1.54] and so forth, as well as the prohibitive rules (pratiṣedha-śāstra) such as *na kroḍādibahvacaḥ* [Pāṇini 4.1.56] and so forth, are both applicable here. Therefore, the suffix *ṅīp* is to be prescribed only in those cases where *ṅīṣ* has been enjoined; however, in those cases where *ṅīṣ* is prohibited, *ṅīp* is likewise prohibited.
By the phrase "where *ṅīṣ* is enjoined" and so forth, he demonstrates the result with respect to the scope of the prescription.

But what, then, is the distinction between the suffix *ṅīp* and [the others], since in both cases the resulting form is identical? To this he says: "There is a distinction in accent. For because *ṅīp* is marked with *p*, it is unaccented (*anudātta*); however, for *ṅīṣ*, there is acute accent on the first syllable (*ādyudātta*) by virtue of the accent of the suffix itself.
An example is *prāṅmukhī*.

By the rule *ṛtvigādi* (Pāṇini 3.2.59), the suffix *kvin* is added to the root *añc*; by the rule *aniditām* (6.4.24), there is the elision of the nasal; and by the rule *ṛnnebhyo ṅīp* (4.1.5), the suffix *ṅīp* is applied, resulting in *prācī*. The word "in the eastern direction" (*prācyāṃ diśi*) is expressed as "having the face [turned] toward the east" (*prāṅmukha*). By the rule *dikśabdebhyaḥ saptamīpañcamī* (5.3.27) et cetera, the suffix *astāti* is introduced; by the rule *astāti ca* (5.3.40), this suffix is elided; by the rule *luk taddhitaluki* (1.2.49), the feminine suffix is also elided; by the rule *avyayād āpsupaḥ* (2.4.82), the case ending (*sup*) is elided, resulting in *avyaya* status by the rule *avyayād āp-supaḥ* (2.4.82); and finally, by the rule *halṅyābbhyo dīrghāt sutisyapṛktaṃ hal* (6.1.68), the case ending is elided. Thus, she whose face is turned toward the east is *prāṅmukhī*. The *ṅ* is added by the rule *ṅiti ca* (1.1.5). Hence, the form *prāṅmukhā*.
The suffix *ṭāp* [is applied].

But surely, when *ṅīp* is excluded, there ought to be *ṅīṣ* by the rule "also after a word denoting a limb of one's own body that is an upasarjana" (Pāṇini 4.1.54)? This is not so; the activity of the Teacher indicates that where there is an option (*vibhāṣā*) between a general rule (*utsarga*) and an exception (*apavāda*), the general rule does not apply once the exception has been set aside—this being why he employs the mention of the word "optionally" (*vā*) in the rule "after a word ending in *ū*, optionally" (Pāṇini 4.1.118).

If [the suffix] *ḍhak* were to apply here by virtue of the rule "after *mukta*, [there is] *ḍhak*" (*muktād ḍhak*), what would be the purpose of including the mention of *vā* ("or")? Therefore, from this mention of *vā*, it is made known that where even the general rule (*utsarga*) is optional (*vibhāṣā*), the general rule does not apply once one has been released by an exception (*apavāda*).

But how is the general rule optional? By the Great Option (*mahāvibhāṣā*). The suffix *aṇ* is the general rule [by Pāṇini 4.1.83], while *ḍhak* is the exception [by 4.1.120]; if *aṇ* were to apply even after being released by that [exception], what would be the purpose of the mention of *vā*? One would not say so; rather, it is for the sake of excluding the default *aṇ*.
By the words "it is not so here" (*iha na bhavati*), etc., he demonstrates the result of the requirement for negation (*pratiṣedhāpekṣā*).
Regarding the examples "prākkroḍā" and "prāgjaghanā," because the rule [Pāṇini 4.1.56] also applies here by way of *anuvṛtti*, the suffix *ṅīṣ* does not occur.
Regarding the term *prāggulphā*:

here too, by [Pāṇini 4.1.63] *asaṃyogopadhāt*, and by [3.2.64] *vahaśca*, the suffix *ṇvi* is applied. There is elision of the entire suffix *ṇvi*. By [7.2.116] *pratyayalakṣaṇena*, there is *vṛddhi* (vowel strengthening). Then, by [6.4.132], the *uṭh* substitute for the *v* occurs, being designated as *saṃprasāraṇa*; this is because the term *saṃprasāraṇa* is understood from [6.4.131]. The letter *ṭh* is for the purpose of specification, according to [6.1.89].

By [Pāṇini 6.1.108], there is the substitution of the subsequent form (*pararūpa*); by [Pāṇini 6.1.89], there is the *vṛddhi* single-substitute for the vowel of the first member (*pūrvapada*) together with the [subsequent vowel]. Thus, "sakhī" [is formed]:
the suffix *ṅīp* is added to the word *sakhi*.

By means of the elliptical supplement "she has no child," he shows that it is a *bahuvrīhi* compound; and in the case of a *bahuvrīhi* compound beginning with the word *aśiśu*, the form *aśī* is prescribed as a *nipātana* (irregular formation).
But he shows that it is not a *tatpuruṣa* compound meaning "that which belongs to him.
For in a *tatpuruṣa*, it does not occur that "a child" becomes "a non-child.
[The example is] "friend" (*sakha*).
By [Pāṇini 7.1.93], the substitute anaṅ is applied; by [Pāṇini 6.4.7] and [6.4.8], "and in the case of a sarvanāmasthāna," the vowel is lengthened.

Although one could have simply said "sakhyaśiśubhyām," the fact that this specific formation (nipātana) is employed has this purpose: so that it may apply to other words of identical phonetic form as well; thus, "sakhī" is that which exists together with a friend (*sakhi*). Regarding the term *jāteḥ* [in the rule], since grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with "from the nominal stem" (*prātipadikāt*) would otherwise be impossible, that nominal stem which denotes a genus (*jāti*) is here expressed by the word "genus" (*jāti*) through the metaphorical application of the denoted to the denoter. For this very reason, the author of the commentary (*vṛtti*) says: "that nominal stem which denotes a genus.
[The phrase] "not having a feminine scope" (*astrīviṣayāt*) [is used].

The word *viṣaya* (domain/subject) is used even when there is no occurrence elsewhere; for this very reason, the author says in the commentary: "If it is not restricted to the feminine alone. That whose existence is not limited to the feminine alone, but occurs both in the feminine and elsewhere—that is *astrīviṣaya*. It is called a *jāti* (genus). To answer the question "What is this so-called *jāti*?", he says: "*Ākṛtigrahaṇā*" and so forth. That by which something is formed (*ākriyate*) or manifested is *ākṛti*; it refers to configuration (*saṃsthāna*).
For instance: "bad form" (*durākṛti*) refers to a poor configuration (*duḥsaṃsthāna*), while "good form" (*svākṛti*) refers to a fine configuration (*susaṃsthāna*).
That by which something is grasped is called "grasping" (*grahaṇa*); the suffix *lyuṭ* is used here in the sense of an instrument (*karaṇe*).
That which has the grasping of form is "form-grasping" (*ākṛtigrahaṇā*), meaning that which is manifested by configuration (*saṃsthānavyaṅgyā*).

But surely, because the word *grahaṇa* is in grammatical apposition with the word *ākṛti*, it must function as feminine, and thus, by the rule *ṭiḍḍhāṇañ* [Pāṇini 4.1.15], the suffix *ṅīp* should be applied; when a compound is formed with that [feminine] ending, the suffix *kap* is added by the rule *tadantena samāse kṛte* [Pāṇini 5.4.153], and consequently, the form *ākṛtigrahaṇīkā* would result. This is not a fault; for the word *grahaṇa* was first derived in the sense of a general instrument (*karaṇasāmānya*), and only afterwards is it connected with a specific [object].

In that context, when another word is in proximity, whatever specific gender-connection it has is considered *bahiraṅga* (extrinsic). Therefore, the compound is formed after first constructing the sentence with the *antaraṅga* (intrinsic) common gender alone, as in the case of [Pāṇini 2.1.68].
By this definition, it is stated that the universal (*jāti*) is of a general nature, characterized by "cowness" (*gotva*) and so forth.
For "cowness" and the like are grasped through their form (*ākṛti*), because they are manifested by the configuration (*saṃsthāna*) possessing horns and other such features.

By this definition, specific castes such as Brāhmaṇahood and the like are not subsumed. For these are not manifested by configuration (*saṃsthāna*); since the configuration of their substratum is not distinct—because the configuration of a Brāhmaṇa is exactly the same as that of a Kṣatriya and others—the author states a second definition, beginning with "And of the marks" (*liṅgānāṃ ca*), and so forth.
Even that universal which does not possess all genders, and which is manifested by non-configuration (asaṃsthāna), is a genus (*jāti*), such as "Brahmin-hood" (*brāhmaṇatva*) and so forth.
For it possesses both the feminine and masculine genders—as in *brāhmaṇaḥ* and *brāhmaṇī*—but it does not possess the neuter gender; thus, it does not partake of all genders.

Even in the case of Brahmin-hood and the like, manifestation through demonstrative indication (*uddeśa*) must be accepted; otherwise, since [the name] Devadatta possesses two genders—as in *Devadattaḥ* and *Devadattā*—it would follow that this too is a genus.

And this [term] is not intended to be a genus-word (*jāti-śabda*); what then? It is a technical name-word (*saṃjñā-śabda*). This is for the purpose of providing a rule (*vidhi*). Therefore, even though they possess all genders, they possess the status of a genus (*jātitva*) by virtue of the previous definition, as in the case of *taṭaḥ*, *taṭī*, and *taṭam*.

"One who resorts to all marks" (*sarvaliṅgabhāk*) is derived with the suffix *ṇvi* according to the rule *karmaṇy upapade* (Pāṇini 3.2.1). Now, one might object: since the word *sarva* depends upon *liṅga*, the suffix *ṇvi* after the root *bhaj* would not be applicable when *sarva* is the subordinate term (*upapada*), because [the rule] relies on the subordinate term; furthermore, the compound of the subordinate term (*upapadasamāsa*) would not occur due to a lack of semantic connection (*asāmarthya*). This is not a fault. For just as in the case of "Devadatta’s teacher’s family" (*devadattasya gurukulam*), a compound occurs despite the lack of semantic connection because it conveys the meaning (*gamakatvāt*), so too both [the suffix and the compound] will occur here. And that genus (*jāti*) is defined as "grasped by a single enunciation" (*sakṛdākhyātanigrahyā*).
*Sakṛt* means once; *ākhyātā* means taught; *nigrrāhrā* means to be grasped with certainty.
By this, he demonstrates the characteristics of a universal (*jāti*), namely: its manifoldness, its eternity, and its complete presence in each individual instance.

Since it is taught once with respect to a black or white cow-individual, yet is to be grasped with certainty even in a cow-individual different from that, for that very reason it is eternal and completely present in each [individual].
If it were not one, then when a cow is designated once, it would not be apprehended in another individual body.

And if it were not eternal, then upon the destruction of that body, because it too would be destroyed, it would not be apprehended in another body. Furthermore, if it were not fully present in its entirety within each individual, then it would not even be apprehended in its entirety within that very body in which it was designated, let alone in another body! For if it were present only partially, then only the part would be apprehended, not the universal (jāti).
A genus does not become a part of a genus, because that would entail the consequence of its being manifold. He states the third definition of a genus with the words "and lineage" (*gotraṃ ca*), etc.

According to the technical rule *apatyaṃ pautraprabhṛti gotram* (Pāṇini 4.1.162), "lineage" (*gotra*) has a specific technical meaning; however, in this context, both the worldly sense of lineage and offspring in general are intended.
The *caraṇa* is manifold according to the divisions of Vedic recension (*adhyayana*).
Together with the *caraṇas*, the *jāti* (birth) becomes the *gotra*.
*Gotra* refers to [lineages] such as Nāḍāyana and so forth.
Although the commonality such as being a Nāḍāyana is conceived in the same way as a *gotra*, it is nevertheless not manifested by shape (*saṃsthāna*).
Furthermore, because it exists in all genders— as "Nāḍāyana is a man," "Nāḍāyanī is a woman," and "Nāḍāyana is a neuter"—
the phrase "and *gotra*" was stated in order to establish that *gotra* is a genus (*jāti*).

The word *caraṇa* (branch of Vedic study) is a term for an action, because it is applied in connection with the act of studying; since it is thus a term for an action rather than a term for a genus (*jāti*), the phrase "together with the *caraṇas*" was stated in order to establish that its referent is indeed a genus. The examples "a hen," "a sow," and "a peahen" are illustrations of a genus as apprehended through its form (*ākṛti*).
"Brāhmaṇī, vṛṣalī"—
these do not possess all genders.
"Nāḍāyanī, cārāyaṇī"— [these likewise].
Regarding the characteristic of the lineage (*gotra*):
by the rule *naḍādibhyaḥ phak* [Pāṇini 4.1.99], the suffix *phak* is applied in the sense of a descendant,
resulting in the forms *kaṭhī* and *bahvṛcī*.

Regarding the characteristics of the feet: "muṇḍā" [is used] because of its connection with the quality of being shaven. It refers to a non-feminine object when one says, "This person is shaven (muṇḍaḥ)," as in "Devadatta is shaven," since the word *muṇḍa* applies to a male as well.

But it is not a genus-word (*jāti-śabda*); rather, it is a quality-word (*guṇa-śabda*). As for "fly" (*makṣikā*), because it is always restricted to the feminine gender, the word *makṣikā* has the feminine as its scope. As for "Kṣatriya woman" (*kṣattriyā*).
In this context, *gotra* means "birth" (*jāti*).

Because the suffix *gha* is prescribed for the offspring of a *gotra* by the rule *kṣattrāddhaḥ* [Pāṇini 4.1.138], and because it possesses the gender of its source, it constitutes a *jāti*. Furthermore, since the word *kṣattriya* is used even for males, the term *kṣattriya* does not refer exclusively to females. As for a word with *y* as its penultimate vowel (*yopadha*), however, there is the rule: "In the prohibition regarding words with *y* as their penultimate vowel, there is no prohibition for *hayá*, *gavaya*, *mṛga*, *uṣṭra*, *khasa*, and *manuṣya*."

How, then, is this [prohibition] obtained? Because the particle *ca* in the subsequent sūtra has the sense of including what has not been explicitly stated. For by that [subsequent rule], since the suffix *ṅīṣ* is prescribed after words such as *hayagavaya*, this prohibition does not apply;
thus we have "matsī."
In the case of *sūryatiṣyāgastyamatsyānām* [Pāṇini 6.4.149], there is the elision of the *ya*-affix. Regarding *manuṣī*, the *ya*-suffix is applied by [Pāṇini 4.1.161], along with the augment *ṣuk*.
And the generic nature (*jātitva*) of these, such as horses, gavayas, and so forth, is to be understood from the apprehension of their form (*ākṛti*). Regarding the term "rice-cooker" (*odanapākī*):

it is a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*) meaning "the cooking of rice. However, this is formed merely for the sake of etymological derivation; the literal meaning of its constituent parts does not exist [in the word as a whole].
The feminine suffix *hras* occurs only in certain classes [of words].

This should be understood to apply to words such as *śaṅkukarṇī* and others as well. Regarding *avantī* and *kuntī*: by the rule [Pāṇini 4.1.171] and [4.1.176], the suffix [denoting lineage] is elided after the words *avanti* and *kunti*, and then the suffix *ṅīṣ* is applied.

Regarding "dākṣī" and "plākṣī": [the suffix] *iñ* is applied by [Pāṇini 4.1.95]. For in all cases, a lineage (*gotra*) is indeed a genus (*jāti*). Regarding "viṭ" and "darat": [these are formed with the suffix *aṇ*].
The suffix *viś* is applied in the sense of offspring (Pāṇini 4.1.168).

From *darada*, the suffix *aṇ* is applied by the rule for the *dvyañ-magadha* group (4.1.168); then, by the rule "and after *at*" (4.1.175), there is elision (*luk*) of those two suffixes in the feminine.
Here too, "lineage" (*gotra*) means "caste" (*jāti*).
In the case of "tittiri," the genus (jāti) is apprehended through its form (ākṛti).
In the case of "udameyī," [the same applies].

"From this [root], *iñ* [is added]" (Pāṇini 4.1.95). Here, "lineage" (*gotra*) means "birth" (*jāti*). Regarding the statement "there is an addition of *iñ*," the meaning is that an addition of the suffix *ṅīṣ* must be made after a word ending in *iñ*.
For what purpose? For the sake of expressing non-birth (*ajāti*).
This is so that [the suffix] might also apply to words ending in *iṅ* even when they do not denote a genus (*ajāti*).

In this regard, the following explanation is given: here, a split of the rule (*yogavibhāga*) is made with the word "from this" (*itaḥ*); by means of that, [the suffix] will also apply to words ending in *iṅ* even when they do not denote a genus.

Then follows the second rule, "of the genus of humans" (*manuṣyajāteḥ*), which serves to indicate the non-obligatory nature (*anityatva*) of the preceding rule. Consequently, [the suffix] applies invariably in the case of the genus of humans, but elsewhere according to usage.
This applies only in certain cases, not everywhere;
for example, in the case of *sautaṅgamī* and others.

One might object: since the suffix *iñ* is prescribed by the rule *ata iñ* [Pāṇini 4.1.95] specifically for the offspring of a *gotra*, and a *gotra* is indeed a genus (*jāti*), why is it said that "the addition of *iñ* is for the sake of non-genus meanings"? To this, he says: "From *sutahgama* and so forth," etc.

By the rule *sutaṅgamena nirvṛtā nagarī* (Pāṇini 4.2.80) and so forth, the suffix *iñ* is applied because [Avantī] belongs to the *sutaṅgama*-class. The inclusion of the letter *t* in the word *itaḥ* is for the purpose of excluding long vowels;
therefore, this suffix does not apply to the word *avantī*.

One desires *avantī*. By the rule *akṛtsārvadhātukayoḥ* [Pāṇini 7.4.25], there is lengthening; thus, when *avantī ya* remains, the vowel *a* is elided by *kvip* [Pāṇini 6.4.48]. First, because of the mention of "elision" (*lopa*), the *y* is elided by *apṛktalopāt prāk* [Pāṇini 6.1.66], and subsequently, the *v* is elided by *paścāt* [Pāṇini 6.1.67]. Then, when *avantī* remains, if the specification *tapara* (indicating a short vowel) were not made, then from this form as well [the suffix] would occur, and consequently, the elision of *su* by *tataḥ* [Pāṇini 6.1.68] would result; thus, *avantīḥ* would not be established. As for *kurūḥ*: [The derivation is: one desires the Kurus. By the rule *kuruśubhayoḥ kyac* [Vārttika on Pāṇini 3.1.10], the suffix *kyac* is added. Then, by *kyaci ca* [Pāṇini 7.4.33], the *u* is replaced by *ī*. Then, by *eranekāco 'saṃyogapūrvasya* [Pāṇini 6.4.82], the *u* is replaced by *ya*. Thus, *kurīya* remains. Then, by *kyasya vibhāṣā* [Pāṇini 6.4.50], the *kyac* is optionally elided. When it is elided, *kurīya* remains. Then, by *kyaci ca* [Pāṇini 7.4.33], the *u* is replaced by *ī*. Then, by *eranekāco 'saṃyogapūrvasya* [Pāṇini 6.4.82], the *ī* is replaced by *ya*. Thus, *kurya* remains. Then, by *kyaci ca* [Pāṇini 7.4.33], the *u* is replaced by *ī*. Then, by *eranekāco 'saṃyogapūrvasya* [Pāṇini 6.4.82], the *ī* is replaced by *ya*. Thus, *kurya* remains. Then, by *kyaci ca* [Pāṇini 7.4.33
The feminine descendant of Kuru is formed by the suffix *ṇya* according to Pāṇini 4.1.170 (*kurunādibhyo ṇyaḥ*), which is elided by 4.1.174 (*striyām avanti-*) and so forth.
Here, "lineage" (*gotra*) refers to caste (*jāti*). Thus, [the word] is *brāhma-bandhūḥ*.
*Brāhṛbandharāyāḥ* [is derived from] *vīro bandhur asyāḥ*; thus it is a *bahuvrīhi* compound.
The words *brāhṛbandhū* and *vīrabandhū* refer to a specific genus (*jāti*). Its status as a genus, moreover, is due to its not possessing all genders (*asarvaliṅgabhāktvāt*).

For those two [suffixes] are indeed feminine and masculine, not neuter. The use of *ta* in *utaḥ* (the long vowel *ū*) is for the sake of ease of pronunciation, not for the purpose of excluding the long vowel; this is because there is no word denoting a human genus that ends in the long vowel *ū*. As for the mention of "the letter *ṅ*" and so forth...

If the marker *ṅ* were not applied to *ūṅ*, then [the marker] in rule 6.1.175 would also not need to be applied; for there exists no other *ū*-vowel possessing the *ṅ*-marker. Consequently, if it were stated as "not after a root or a feminine suffix ending in *ū*" (*nodhātvoḥ*), then even in cases such as *yavāgvā* and *yavāgvai*, there would be a prohibition of the acute accent that would otherwise apply to the third case and subsequent case endings by rule 6.1.174.

But surely, because the vowel *ū* is specified as being meaningful (*arthavat*), the rule "when that which is meaningful is mentioned, that which is meaningless is not [included]" (*arthavadgrahaṇe nānarthakasya*) will prevent this from applying to the meaningless [portion]. For the word *yavāgū-* is derived from the suffix *āgūc* according to the rule *sṛyuvacibhyo 'nyujāgūjaknuc-aḥ*; in that case, the element *āgūc* alone is meaningful by virtue of its suffixal meaning, while the vowel *ū* is indeed meaningless. This is not so; for this paribhāṣā is not established as applicable to the mention of individual phonemes (*varṇagrahaṇa*), and since this is a mention of a phoneme, the paribhāṣā does not apply.

Now, what if one were to apply [the rule] in this way? Even so, there would be the inclusion of the suffix *ū* by the rule "from the roots *kṛṣ*, *cam*, *tan*, *nidhā*, *nisṛj*, and *kharj*, the suffix *ū*" (Pāṇini 3.2.164).
Consequently, a prohibition would undesirably apply in cases such as *kharjvā* and *kharjve*.
Therefore, the marker *ṅ* must be employed for the sake of specification.

Now, for what purpose is the long vowel pronounced? Should not simply *ūṅ* be stated, since by the rule *dīrghāj-jaś-śasoḥ* [Pāṇini 6.1.101], a long vowel includes its own long counterpart? To this he says: "The pronunciation of the long vowel," and so forth.
If the long vowel were not pronounced, then by the subsequent rule [Pāṇini 5.4.154], the suffix *kap* would optionally apply; therefore, the long vowel is pronounced in order to preclude that.

But how is it that by the long pronunciation [of the vowel], the *kap* suffix is excluded? Should *ūṅ* be applied immediately after the compound *brāhma-bandhū-as*, or should *kap* be applied? In that case, because it is subsequent [in the order of rules], *kap* would apply; however, due to the elision (*praśleṣa*) of the vowel *u* by means of the long pronunciation, there is a re-statement (*punarvidhāna*). This re-statement, being of the same class as the rule for *kap* and applicable at the same time, excludes only the application of *kap*—which is its own specific category—and not the application of the case-endings (*svādi*) and so forth. The case-endings, however, certainly do occur after a word ending in *ūṅ*, because both *tyūṅ* and *ūṅ* are included in the technical term *tyadādi*; or else, it is due to an indicative mark (*jñāpaka*), namely the grammatical reference in [Pāṇini 1.1.71]: *āśuraḥ āśravā*.
Therefore, *brāhmaṇbandhu* always ends in the vowel *u* alone, and never ends in the suffix *kap*.
