Regarding *adhvaryu*: from the sense "one who desires the sacrifice" (*adhvara*), the suffix *kyac* is applied, followed by the suffix *up*; then, by the rule *kavyaghvarapṛtanasyarci lopaḥ*, the vowel *a* is elided. [The rule] beginning with *aprāṇijāteśca* and so forth [is now applied].

The meaning is that this form of the rule—"the suffix *ūṅ* occurs after a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) that does not denote a genus of living beings"—must be explained. The explanation for this is as follows: in the rule [Pāṇini 4.1.68], the particle *ca* (and) serves to include what has not been explicitly mentioned; by means of it, the suffix will occur after those denoting non-living genera that are excluded from the group beginning with *rajjū-* (e.g., rope), such as *alābūḥ* (a bottle-gourd) and *karkandhūḥ* (a jujube fruit).

But what difference is there whether this [suffix] *ūṅ* is present or absent, since in both cases the form is the same and the accent is likewise? For instance, the word *alābu* is derived in the *Uṇādi-sūtras* precisely by means of the suffix *ū*: in the rule "from *kṛṣ*, *cam*, *tan*, *dhani*, *sarji*, and *kharji*, [the suffix] *ū*" (*Daiva 1.164*), while the rule "after a *ṇit* [suffix]" (*Daiva 1.168*) is still in force, and by the reading "after the prefix *nañ*, from *labi* with the elision of *na*" (*Daiva 1.170*), the suffix *ū* must be applied to the root *labi* (meaning 'to hang down') preceded by the negative particle *nañ*.

Thus, by the rules *vartamāne ṇit* and *nañi lambernalopaśca* (Pāṇini 3.2.168 and 3.2.167), the suffix *ū* is applied to the root *labi* (meaning "to descend," listed as number 379 in the Dhātupāṭha) preceded by the negative particle *nañ*; furthermore, by the rule *idito num* (Pāṇini 7.1.58), the augment *num* is added, and the elision (*lopa*) of the letter *n* is prescribed for the form that has thus acquired the *num* augment.

The word *karkandhū* is also derived with a final long *ū* by the rule *andūdṛnbhūjambūkaphelūkarkandhūdidhiṣūḥ* (Dhātupāṭha 1.176), which occurs within the context of the rule *nṛtiśṛdhyoḥ kūḥ* (Dhātupāṭha 1.174). Why, then, is the suffix *ūṅ* prescribed here? It is so that in forms such as *alābvā* and *alābvai*, the prohibition of the acute accent on the first syllable of the case-ending—as prescribed by [Pāṇini 6.1.175]—may take effect. For if that [suffix *ūṅ*] were not present, then just as it does not occur in *khalapvau* and *khalapvaḥ*, it would likewise not occur here. [The rule continues: "In *āśurasya*, there is also elision of the *u* and the *a*."
However, this [form] is established by the very rule of irregular derivation (*nipātana*) "āśuraḥ āśravā" (Pāṇini 6.4.19), so it need not be explicitly stated. Regarding "vṛttoruḥ":
she whose thighs (*ūru*) are rounded (*vṛtta*)—that is, whose thighs are circular—is "vṛttoruḥ. (Note: The printed reading is *parimaṇḍalā ūrū*.)

For the sake of brevity, it should have been stated "after *arvant-*," yet it is stated as "after a compound whose final member is *ūru-*. This is for the purpose that the rule should apply where the word *ūru-* alone is the final member (*uttarapada*). Otherwise, if it were stated as "after *arvant-*," then in a case such as *hastisvāmyūrūḥ*—meaning "she whose husband's thighs are like those of an elephant" (where *svāmyūrū-* is the prior member)—the suffix would also apply there, because this too is a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) ending in *ūru*. However, when "final member" (*uttarapada*) is specified, there is no fault; for in this case, *ūru-* is not the final member of the nominal stem, but rather *svāmyūrū-* is the final member [of the entire compound]. Thus we have the form *saṃhitorūḥ*.
The word *saṃhita* signifies "joined together" (*saṃśliṣṭa*), meaning "the thighs are joined together. Regarding the statement, "it should be stated that [the suffix] follows *sahita* and *saha*":
the meaning is that this rule must be explained as having the sense that the suffix *ūṅ* occurs after a nominal stem ending in the word *uru* when it follows either *sahita* or *saha*.

In this regard, the explanation is as follows: the letter *gh* is inserted here, and it serves the purpose of an inclusive conjunction (*ayuktasamuccaya*); by means of that, the suffix will also apply after *sahita* and *saha*.
The inclusion of the word "ādi" (etcetera) in the sūtra is an indicator (*liṅga*) for the continued application (*anuvṛtti*) of the rule "the word *ūru* is the subsequent member.

Otherwise, the meaning would be understood as: "the suffix occurs only after nominal stems such as *saṃhitā* and so forth. For if there were continued application by virtue of the *svarita* accent alone, even with this [word *ādi*], the suffix would undesirably apply only where *ūru* is the subsequent member, even when a middle member exists—namely, from the words *saṃhita-svāmī-ūru*, and not from the word *saṃhita-ūru*.

Because the word *ūru* functions as a subordinate member (*guṇabhāva*), it cannot serve as a qualifier here. The word *kadru* denotes a specific color; therefore, although the suffix *ṅīṣ* would have been required by the rule *voto guṇavacanāt* [Pāṇini 4.1.44], that requirement is blocked by the prohibition *kharusaṃyogopadhayoḥ* (Vārttika 349). Since the feminine form would then not be expressed by the nominal stem itself, this statement [of the Vārttika] is provided.

Furthermore, because the word *kamaṇḍalu* does not denote a living being, the suffix *ūṅ* would have applied by the rule *aprāṇijāteścārajjvādīnām* (Vārttika 369); this [statement] is for the purpose of restriction regarding the Vedic language (*chandas*).

Alternatively—this [word] refers to a rope (*rajjvādi*); therefore, since there is a prohibition [of the feminine suffix *ṅīp*], this statement is for the purpose of establishing its application. Regarding the words "baidī" and "aurvī": from the bases *bidu* and *aurva*, the suffix *añ* is applied by the rule *anṛṣyānantarye* (Pāṇini 4.1.104). Since these end in *añ*, they denote a lineage (*gotra*). Because they denote a genus (*jāti*), the suffix *ṅīṣ* would have been required by the rule governing genus-words; however, the suffix *ṅīn* is here prescribed instead. There is a difference in accent (*svara*) [between the two].
Regarding the phrase "these are infinite":

from the word *gotama*, the suffix *aṇ* is applied in the sense of offspring according to [Pāṇini 4.1.114], *ṛṣyandhakavṛṣṇi* etc.; however, for the remaining [names], the suffix is applied by [Pāṇini 4.1.92], *tasyāpatyam*.
From the word *gautama*, because it is listed in the *gaura-ādi* group, the feminine suffix *ṅīṣ* also occurs.
"These [names] end in ḍhak" because they belong to the *śubhrādi* group. "Kāmaṇḍaleyaḥ" [is derived in this way].

There is the elision of the letter *u* by the rule *ḍhe lopo 'kadr̥vāḥ* [Pāṇini 6.4.147]. Since the suffix *ṅīp* would otherwise apply to these words by the rule *ṭiḍḍhāṇañ* [Pāṇini 4.1.15], this statement is made as an exception. Thus, the form is *vātsyāyana*.
From the word *vatsa*, which ends in the *yañ* suffix [according to Pāṇini 4.1.105], the suffix *phak* is applied [by Pāṇini 4.1.101],
resulting in *mauñjāyana*.
From the word *muñja*, the suffix *phak* is applied [by Pāṇini 4.1.99].
"Birth" (jāti) means the characteristic of the lineage (gotra). For even the worldly sense of lineage is included therein.
In the world, even a youth is called by his *gotra*; for instance, speakers say, "He is a Gārgyāyaṇa by *gotra*. Regarding the phrase "ending in *ḍhak*":
since the word *kekasa* belongs to the *śubhra* group, the suffix *ñyaṅ* is applied; thus, it is also [an example] of one ending in *ñyaṅ* that does not end in *ḍhak*.
The suffix *ñyaṅ* is applied after the words *kapi* and *śibi* in the sense of "offspring" according to Pāṇini 4.1.171.
Since the suffix *cāp* would also have been applicable by Pāṇini 4.1.74, this statement [is made] as a restrictive rule.
Thus: *ehi*, *paryehi*.

From the root *īh* meaning "exertion" (Dhātupāṭha 632), preceded by the prefix *ā*, and also from roots preceded by *pari* and others, the suffix *in* is applied according to the rule *sarvadhātubhyaḥ* (Uṇādisūtra 1.46; though in the Vṛtti it is seen that the suffix *in* occurs after all roots).
Since the word belongs to the *bahv-ādi* group, the suffix *ṅīṣ* would have been required by the rule *kṛdikārādaktinaḥ* (Gaṇasūtra 50); hence this specific statement [is made].
Thus, it ends in *yañ*.

Because [the word *udapāna*] belongs to the *gargādi* group, both the suffixes *ṅīp* (by *yañaśca* 4.1.16) and *ṣpha* (by *ṣphāntācca* 4.1.17) would otherwise apply; this statement [is made] to prevent that.
The printed reading is *udapānaḥ*, [but the intended form is] *audapānaḥ*.

The suffix *aṇ* is applied by [Pāṇini 4.3.76] *udapānād āgataḥ*. Since this word is recited among the *utsādi* group, there is no difference when the suffix *añ* is applied—whether it be *ṅīp* or *ṅīn*, for in both cases it must be accented on the first syllable according to [Pāṇini 6.1.197]. Bearing this in mind, he says: "The form ending in *aṇ* from *śuṇḍika-* serves as the purpose. Regarding the term "genus" (*jāti*).

Because *arāla* and *caṇḍāla* do not possess all genders, they are [treated as] jāti [names]. Regarding *vataṇḍa*, since the suffix *ṅīṣ* would otherwise apply by virtue of its being characterized as belonging to the *gaura*-class, this rule is stated as an exception.
By the principle of "that which is caused by a suffix" (*pratyayalakṣaṇa*), the application of both *ṅīṣ* and *pha* is barred by Pāṇini 4.1.16 and 4.1.17.

The feminine descendant of Vataṇḍa [is formed] by the suffix *yañ* according to Pāṇini 4.1.108; that [suffix] is elided according to 4.1.109. Regarding the rule "In the case of a name (*saṃjñā*), [the suffix] *ṅīn* is applied after the words *bhogavat* and *gaurimat*":
when a name is understood, the suffix *ṅīn* is applied after the words *bhogavat* and *gaurimat*.
This statement is made because the suffix *ṅīp* would otherwise have been required by Pāṇini 6.3.45 due to their ending in the suffix *mat*.

But surely, the word *bhoga* ends in the suffix *ghañ*, and the word *gauri* ends in the suffix *iñ* according to Pāṇini 4.1.95 (*ata iñ*); therefore, both of these are udātta on the first syllable due to the accent of the *ñit* suffixes.
The suffix *matup* added to them is anudātta because it is marked with *p*.

Thus, when either *ṅīp* or *ṅīn* is prescribed after *bhogavat* and *gaurimat*, there would be no difference; for what purpose, then, is *ṅīn* prescribed after them? To this, he says: "In order to ensure the constant short vowel in the *ghādi* group."
In rules such as [Pāṇini 6.3.43], the suffix *ṅīn* is prescribed after those two [stems] so that the short vowel may always occur—as in *bhogavatitarā* and *gaurimatitarā*.
If, however, the suffix *ṅīp* characterized by the presence of the marker *uk* were applied, then while [6.3.44] continues to apply, [6.3.45] would cause the shortening of the vowel optionally.

Now, even when *ṅīn* is applied by this [rule], why does the shortening not optionally occur by [6.3.45], given that this [shortening] occurs optionally for *bhogavat* and *gaurimat* precisely because they are *ugit* stems?
And that which is prescribed by this sūtra is not considered prescribed by the term *nadī* (feminine noun) because the status of being *ugit* is not relied upon [in that context].
Why is it said "when it is a name" (*saṃjñāyām*)? [Consider] *bhogavatī*, *gaurimatī*;
here the suffix *ṅīp* applies [by 4.1.45].

And here, in the case of *ghā* and so forth, there is only optional shortening: *bhogavatitarā* or *bhogavatītarā*, *gaurimatitarā* or *gaurīmatītarā*. Regarding the rule "and [the substitution of] *vṛddhi* for *nṛ* and *nara*":
for the word *nṛ*, this is stated because the suffix *ṅīp* would otherwise apply by the rule *ṛnnebhyo ṅīp* [Pāṇini 4.1.5].
For the word *nara*, the suffix *ṭāp* would otherwise apply by the rule *ajādyataḥ* [Pāṇini 4.1.4], or else the suffix *ṅīṣ* applies because it denotes a genus (*jāti*).

The status of being a *jāti* (genus), however, arises from the apprehension of the form (*ākṛti*). Furthermore, *vṛddhi* occurs for both of these; and that [vṛddhi] takes the place of the *ṛ*-vowel in the word *nṛ* by virtue of the rule "the final letter" (*alo'ntyaparibhāṣā*, Pāṇini 1.1.52).
Once the elision of the *i* in the word *nara* has been performed by the rule "of that which [ends in i or u]" (*yasyeti*, Pāṇini 6.4.148), it takes the place of the vowel *a*.

But surely, by the rule *anantyavikāre 'ntyasadeśasya* (Vyāḍi-Pāṇini 63), the substitution should apply to the *repha* alone? This is not a fault; because the genitive case is used for that which is the immediate constituent (*prakṛti*) of the *vṛddhi*, and since the substitute applies where there is a genitive, the vowel *a* is understood as the locus (*sthānin*). Some read the word *putra* here, but since it does not denote a female in its simple form, this is taken as ending in a compound suffix (*samāsānta*). Being present with a compound suffix, it becomes feminine when it acquires the same meaning as the word *duhitṛ*—as in *pradyotaputrī* and *śailaputrī*. [The phrase] "according to what is appropriate" (*yathāyogam*).

According to the possibility [of application]: here, the letter *k* in the rule *ṅyāpprātipadikāt* [Pāṇini 4.1.1] is for the purpose of including the general category, and the letter *c* is for the purpose of not obstructing that. Thus, since both [the *k* and *c*] have their purpose elsewhere [in other rules], they override the rule *evamubhayoranyatra caritārthayoḥ* [Vārttika 3.1.4] by virtue of being subsequent, and the acute accent on the final syllable (*antodāttatva*) of the feminine suffix *cāp* occurs by the rule *citaḥ* [Pāṇini 6.1.157].
Regarding the statement "this is a general inclusion of *ñyaṅ* and *ṣyaṅ*":
setting aside the distinctive indicatory letters (*anubandha*), this is an inclusion of the general category of *yaṅ* alone.

But how is the inclusion of both [suffixes] justified? For it might be argued that only the inclusion of *ñyaṅ* is appropriate there; since *ñyaṅ*, being prescribed for the sense of "offspring," is incapable of expressing femininity and thus requires a feminine suffix, whereas *ṣyaṅ* does not, because it is prescribed specifically for the feminine. This is not so; for if there were no inclusion of both, the marking of *ṣyaṅ* with the indicatory letter *ṅ* would be purposeless.
Indeed, the sole purpose of that *ṅ* in this rule is the inclusion of both; nothing else follows from it.
Therefore, by the force of the *ṅ*-marking, the inclusion of *ṣyaṅ* also occurs.
"Āmbaṣṭhā," and so forth.

From the words *āmbaṣṭha*, *sauvīra*, and *kosala*, the suffix *ñyaṅ* is applied in the sense of "offspring" according to [Pāṇini 4.1.171]; and from that which ends in *ñyaṅ*, the feminine suffix *cāp* is added.
Thus: "Kārīṣagandhyā."
This has been explained in the *svādi* section [Pāṇini 4.1.2].
Regarding the form *vārāhyā*: from the word *varāha*, the suffix *iñ* is applied according to [Pāṇini 4.1.95].
Regarding "Bālākī": from the word *balākā*, the suffix *iñ* is applied according to the rule for the *bāhv-ādi* group.

In both cases, the substitution of *ṣyaṅ* is applied by the rule beginning with "aṇiñoḥ anārṣayoḥ" (Pāṇini 4.1.78), and the feminine suffix *cāp* is added after that form. Regarding "Śārkarākṣī," and so forth.
Regarding the statement "from *śarkarākṣa*, *pūtimāṣa*, *gorakṣa*, and words ending in *yañ* such as *garga*, the feminine suffix *āp* [is applied]":

this refers to the rule *yañaśca* [Pāṇini 4.1.16]. Regarding the word *yuvati*: once the designation of a secondary derivative (*taddhita*) has been established, the designation of a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) occurs by the rule *kṛttaddhita* [Pāṇini 1.2.46] and so forth.

Now, one might ask: "Is the use of the plural in the term *taddhitāḥ* not possible? For just as in the case of [P. 3.1.1] *dhātoḥ*, where even though the singular is used, that designation applies to all the many suffixes such as *san* and others that are to be mentioned, so too here the designation should have been made using the singular alone? To this he says: "The plural," and so forth.

The purpose of employing the plural when the singular should have been used is this: so that there may be the inclusion of those *taddhita* suffixes which have not been explicitly stated by the rule-formulations (*lakṣaṇavākya*) and have not been directly expressed.

Consequently, rules such as "pṛthivyā ñāñau" (Vārttika 3.1.115) need not be formulated. Since those suffixes are already established by the very use of the plural number [in Pāṇini’s sūtra] for the purpose of including unmentioned secondary suffixes (*taddhita*), the purpose of creating this extensive technical term (*saṃjñā*) is so that it may be understood as a descriptive (*anvartha*) designation: "those which are beneficial (*hita*) to them are *taddhita*. By the word "them" (*tad*), both worldly and Vedic words are referred to; since these are the subject under discussion because they are what are to be explained, the suffixes beginning with *aṇ* occur only in those cases where they are applicable, and wherever they do occur, they are beneficial to them, and not elsewhere.

Therefore, the fact that secondary suffixes (*taddhita*) have the characteristic of denotation is established. Now, why is the section on secondary suffixes not placed at the very beginning of the section on feminine suffixes? What would be gained by doing so? [The answer is: It would be established that secondary suffixes are "nominal stems" (*prātipadika*) because they are infinite; consequently, in the rule *ṅyāpprātipadikāt* [Pāṇini 4.1.1], the mention of *ṅī* and *āp* would not need to be made, nor would the mention of "secondary suffix" be required in [the rule] *taddhitāḥ* [4.1.76], nor the mention of the vowel *i* in [the rule] *taddhiteṣvacāmādeḥ* [6.4.148], since this would already be accomplished by the term "secondary suffix" alone. [Objection: It is impossible to do so.

If it were done in this way, then the purpose previously stated for the inclusion of *ṅī* and *āp* would not apply; for the *ṅ* in *ṅīp*, *ṅīṣ*, and *ṅīn* would be subject to the designation *it* by the rule "not when a *taddhita* suffix follows" (Pāṇini 1.3.8).
Furthermore, in this case, the substitution of *guṇa* [of *i* with *e*] would occur in the word *paṭvī* by the rule "after *paṭu*" (Pāṇini 6.4.146).
Therefore, let it remain exactly as it was originally formulated: "[*ṅīp*] is an exception to *ṅīp*."
Because it ends in the letter *n*, the suffix *ṅīp* would apply by the rule *ṛnnebhyo ṅīp* [Pāṇini 4.1.5].
Now, why does the suffix *ṅīṣ* not apply by the rule *athedantāt* [Pāṇini 4.1.65]? Because it does not denote a human species (*amanuṣyajāti*).
For the word *yuvati* does not express a human species; rather, what does it express? It expresses an age (*vayaḥ*).
For he exists only in the state of youth, not in the states of childhood or old age.

Furthermore, such words are not *jāti* (generic) terms; for those [generic terms] apply across all conditions and instances based on their genus (*jāti*), like the word "cow" (*go*) and others. Here, in the rule "of *aṇ* and *iñ*" (*aṇiñoḥ*), is only the suffix (*pratyaya*) being taken, or the entire complex ending in it? If the first alternative were adopted, the qualification "when the penultimate syllables are heavy" (*gurūpottamayoḥ*) would be untenable. For heaviness of the penultimate syllable is not possible for *aṇ* and *iñ*; rather, it belongs to the complex ending in them.

Therefore, considering that it is appropriate to adopt the second alternative, he says: "In the case of those nominal stems (*prātipadika*) ending in *aṇ* or *iñ* which are prescribed after a *gotra* [name], provided they are not Vedic (*anārṣa*). If this were a reference to the entire aggregate consisting of the suffix *aṇ* or *iñ*, then the qualification "not Vedic" (*anārṣayoḥ*) would not be applicable; for the aggregate as a whole is prescribed only after a Vedic seer (*ṛṣi*). However, this qualification is indeed applicable to *aṇ* and *iñ*; for those two are prescribed after either a Vedic seer or someone else.

The qualification "in the *gotra*" is also appropriate only for the suffixes *aṇ* and *iñ*, not for the entire complex [of suffixes]; for in this context, the technical term *gotra* is understood according to the rule *apatyaṃ pautraprabhṛti gautram* (Pāṇini 4.1.162), and therein only *aṇ* and *iñ* are prescribed, not the entire complex. This is not a fault; since these two qualifications cannot apply to the entire complex, they are understood by implication to refer to the individual parts, *aṇ* and *iñ*. For this very reason, the author of the *Vṛtti* says: "In the *gotra*, those *aṇ* and *iñ* which are prescribed as non-Vedic (*anārṣa*)."

In this case, would this *ṣyaṅ* substitution be [the substitute] itself, or would it be an affix (*pratyaya*)? Now, since there is a mention in the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī-nirdeśa*), it must undoubtedly be a substitute by this very rule; therefore, is not the suspicion regarding the second alternative (that it is an affix) improper? This is not so; for even in the prescription of an affix, a mention in the genitive case is observed, as in "after *gā* and *pā*, the affix *ṭhak*" (*gāpoṣṭhak*). Therefore, the suspicion regarding the alternative that it is an affix is indeed appropriate. In that regard, if it were an affix, the form *audamedheya* would not be established.

The feminine descendant of Udamegha is formed by adding *iñ* (Pāṇini 4.1.95) to the base *udamegha*, resulting in *audameghi*. From that form, the suffix *ṣyaṅ* is applied by this rule [Pāṇini 4.1.73], with the elision of the vowel *i* according to Pāṇini 6.4.148 (*yasyeti ca*), and then the feminine suffix *cāp* is added by Pāṇini 4.1.74, yielding *audamedhyā*. Regarding her descendant, the suffix *ey* is substituted [by Pāṇini 4.1.120].
In that context, the elision of *y* is desired by the rule "tasmin" (Pāṇini 6.4.151), but it does not apply here because the *y* is not part of a patronymic suffix (*apatyayaka*).

If one objects, "But surely [the elision applies] by the rule 'nanu ca' (Pāṇini 6.4.150)?"—no; for in that rule, the word "īti" is understood as a governing term (*anuvartate*) from the preceding sūtra.

In the view that [the suffix] is a substitute (ādeśapakṣa), since the suffixes *aṇ* and *iñ* denote offspring (*apatya*), the substitute *ṣyaṅ* also denotes offspring by virtue of its status as a substitute (*sthānivadbhāva*); thus, the elision of *y* is established. With the intention that the view of substitution alone is correct, he says: "The substitute *ṣyaṅ* occurs.
Now, even in the view of substitution, [the form] *auḍulomyā* would not be established, because the word *loman* is listed among the *bāhv-ādi* group.

Since there is no connection with the offspring of that [stem] alone, the entire complex ending in it is taken; thus, from *uḍuloman-* "the offspring of Uḍuloman," when the suffix *iñ* is applied by virtue of its belonging to the *bāhv-ādi* group, and *ṣyaṅ* is substituted for it, the elision of the final syllable (*ṭilopa*) is desired by rule 6.4.144, yet it does not occur because of the preservation of the original form (*prakṛtibhāva*) by rule 6.4.168.
However, in the view where the suffix is the subject, because *iñ* intervenes, there is no preservation of the original form for *ṣyaṅ*, and thus the elision of the final syllable takes place.
When the elision [of the *n*] by [Pāṇini 6.4.148] has been performed,
there is no intervention. Even when the elision [of the *y*] by [Pāṇini 1.1.57] has been performed,
because of the status of that elision as *sthānivadbhāva* (as if it were the original element), there is indeed an intervention.
There is no fault even in the view that [the suffix] is a substitute (ādeśa), because it is established by its sequence (ānupūrvī).
For here, the status of having a heavy penultimate syllable (gurūpottamatva) is not possible if the elision (lopa) has not yet occurred.
In that case, the elision of the *ṭi* occurs first for that very [suffix] *ṣyaṅ* when it follows *iñ*, and only thereafter does the status of having a heavy penultimate syllable arise.

Consequently, by the sequence beginning with *ṣyaṅ*, [the substitution] is established as being valid. Now, this is the fault in the view that it is a substitute (*ādeśa*): because it consists of more than one phoneme (*anekāl*), it would result in a total replacement (*sarvādeśa*). If it is argued that by the rule *ṅicca* [P. 1.1.53], it should result in a final-element replacement (*antādeśa*)? This is not so; for because of the prohibition of the exception (*apavāda-pratiṣedha*), it results in a total replacement. [The question arises: "Should *ṅicca* [P. 1.1.52] be treated as a final-element replacement, or, due to having more than one phoneme, as a total replacement? In that case, because of its higher status (*paratva*), the total replacement would apply, just as in the rule *tuhrostātaṅṅāśiṣyanyatarasyām* [P. 7.1.35]. To this, he says: "Of that which is being pointed out" (*nirdiśyamānasya*), and so forth.

Just as it is understood that the substitute *pad* applies to the word *pād* itself and not to a composite ending in the word *pād*, so too this [substitution] is understood to apply only to the specific *aṇ* and *iñ* being indicated.
Where, then, should there be a universal substitution (*sarvādeśa*)? It is where the genitive case is uttered for the composite, as in the rule *tuhror* (P. 7.2.31).
As for the statement, "The letter *ṅ* is for the purpose of including the general class," [it means that it serves to indicate the entire suffix].
For if that were not the case, in the rule *yaṅaścāp* [Pāṇini 4.1.74], there would be the inclusion of only that which follows from [the previous rule] 4.1.171, and not of *ṣyaṅ*.
[The commentator states: "The letter *ṣ* is for the purpose of preventing the non-application of that [rule].

In that context, when a term with a single *anubandha* is mentioned, there is no inclusion of a term with two *anubandhas*; thus, there would be the inclusion of only *tyaṅ*, and not of *ñyaṅ*. This word *uttama* exists both as a derived nominal stem (*prātipadika*) ending in the suffix *tamap*, and as an underived (primitive) one.

In that case, if this were the apprehension of one who has already mastered [the language], the form *vārāhri* would not be established; for one who possesses mastery abides in words of four syllables or more.

Just as, from the word *hrasva*, the suffix *tamaP* is prescribed in the sense of excellence (*atiśāyana*) to denote that which has "risen" (surpassed) [others], and that which has "risen" exists only in relation to that which has not yet risen.

In the case of three [items], two are "risen" (*udgata*) and one is "not risen"; since this [one] is not "risen" in comparison to those two, when there is a desire to express the meaning that "this is more eminently risen than these two," the suffix *tamap* does not arise, because it is superseded by *tarap*, which is specifically prescribed for two items. However, in the case of four [items], three are "risen" and one is "not risen"; therefore, this [one] is "risen" in relation to those three that are "risen.

When there is a desire to express the meaning that "this is more eminently risen than these [three]," the suffix *tamap* arises. Consequently, it applies only when there are four [items]; and since the word *uttama* ("highest") is established only in that context, the form *vārāhṛtama* would not be established.

For, having considered that "there are not four here," [the author] shows that this word *uttama* is taken in its non-conventional (avyutpanna) sense; thus he says: "The word *uttama*, by its very nature" (*svabhāvāt*), and so forth. Indeed, the word *uttama* is non-conventional (*avyutpanna*) by its very nature when it denotes the last among three or more, but it is not conventional (*vyutpanna*) in that sense. For in its conventional sense, it denotes the last among four or more. Therefore, by the passage beginning with "The word *uttama*, by its very nature," it is shown that the non-conventional (*avyutpanna*) sense of the word *uttama* is what is intended here.

Thus, for one who is unlearned, even the form *vārāhī* would be established [by the rule] "ṭiḍḍhāṇañ...". However, this is a mistaken reading; for just as in the case of *baidī*, where the suffix *ṅīn* occurs after the word ending in *añ* due to its being a genus (*jāti*) according to Pāṇini 4.1.73 (*śāṅgaravādyaño ṅīn*), so too here it ought to be formed with *ṅīn* alone.
But its status as a *jāti* (generic class) follows from its being a *gotra* (lineage).

Therefore, one should read the text here as: "In the case of [patronymics] such as Śāṅgarava ending in *añ*, the suffix *ṅīn* occurs," resulting in forms such as *vāsiṣṭhī* and *vaiyāghrapadī*. [The suffix] *iñ* is applied by the rule "ṛṣy-andhaka-" (Pāṇini 4.1.114), etc.
"Aupagavī, kāpaṭavī"— here, the suffix *aṇ* is applied by the general rule [Pāṇini 4.1.83] to the words *upagu* and *kapata*. "Āhicchatrī,
vaiyāghrapadī"— here [the suffix *cha* is applied].
> [[4.3.25]] *ity-aṇ* || "Gotra" (clan) and that which is a part of it is "gotrāvayavaḥ.
Here, however, by applying a metaphorical designation (*upacāra*) to the object denoted, the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) that expresses that [object] is referred to by the term "gotrāvayava.

Now, one might object: in such an analysis (*vigraha*), because the word "avayava" (part) functions as a qualifier, it should be placed first—just as the word "nīla" (blue) is placed first in the compound "nīlotpala" (blue lotus).
Because the group beginning with *rājadanta* is an *ākṛtigaṇa*, the qualifier will have the position of the subsequent member (*paranipāta*).
Furthermore, "lineage" (*gotra*) here is taken in its worldly sense, not in its technical (*pāribhāṣika*) sense.
In common usage, the primordial progenitor who provides the name for the line of descendants originating from himself is called "lineage."

For instance, there was a certain primordial and preeminent person named Bharata; because of him, all his descendants—sons, grandsons, and so forth—are designated as "Bharatas. This word *avayava* exists in the sense of a "part" (*ekadeśa*), and by virtue of its connection with that part, the whole (*avayavin*) is called a "collection" (*samudāya*).
Furthermore, it exists in the sense of separation—*avayuti* meaning *avayava*, in the sense of being distinct (*pṛthagbhūta*).
Although the root *yu* is listed in the sense of "mixing," nevertheless, because verbal roots have multiple meanings, the prefix *ava-* conveys the sense of separation (*pṛthaktva*).
It is used in the sense of being subordinate (*apradhāna*), as in the examples: "this is a member of the family" (*kulāvayava*) or "this is a member of the community" (*saṅghāvayava*).
From these, it is understood that this person is subordinate to the family and the community.

In that regard, if a word denoting a part (*ekadeśavācin*) were taken [as the referent], then the mention of *upādāna* would be purposeless; one should simply say "from a *gotra*. For even a part of a *gotra* is indeed a *gotra*, just as a part of milk is called "milk. Furthermore, if it were taken as referring to something distinct—that is, existing elsewhere than the *gotra* itself—then the suffixes *aṇ* and *iñ* prescribed after [names] such as *puṇika* would be applied; and this is undesired. Thus, since there is a fault in taking either a word denoting a part or a word denoting a distinct entity, only that which expresses the subordinate element (*apradhānavācin*) is taken here.
Regarding the phrase "parts of the lineage" (*gotrāvayavāḥ*):
this is a qualifier for the *śrutis* such as "Puṇika" and so forth;
the meaning is that they denote secondary lineages.
Regarding the phrase "considered to be *gotra*":
this means they are intended as *gotra*, that is, they are well-known in common usage as denoting *gotra*;
however, the meaning is not that they are recited in the chapter on *gotra*.
For this very reason, they are secondary, because they are not listed in the *Gotrādhyāya* (the chapter on lineages).

Regarding the term "designations of families" (*kulākhyāḥ*): *kula* means lineage (*gotra*); they are called "designations" (*ākhyā*) because they designate [it]—that is, by means of the lineage, and so forth.
Regarding the word "tataḥ":
[it means] from the *śruti* words such as *puṇika*, which are characterized by the aforementioned qualifiers.

If that is so, then since *ṣyaṅ* would indeed occur after those [words] where *aṇ* and *iñ* are prescribed for the *gotra* [lineage], this rule (*yoga*) would be purposeless, as it is already established by the preceding one. To this he says: "The commencement [of this rule] is for the sake of cases where the penultimate syllable is not heavy (*agurūpottama*)."
"From *pauṇikī* and so forth":

from the words *puṇika*, *bhuṇika*, and *mukhara*, there is the feminine suffix *cāp* applied to that which ends in *iñ*—by [Pāṇini 4.1.95] *ata iñ*—as well as to [stems ending in] *ṣyaṅ*. Thus: "The suffix *ṣyaṅ* occurs in the feminine after *krauñci* and others.

Now, an objection may be raised: previously the position of the base (*prakṛti*) was adopted; why then is the position of the suffix (*pratyaya*) adopted here? The purpose is to demonstrate that even when that [suffix-based] position is adopted, there is no fault here.
"The beginning [of this rule] is for the sake of those whose penultimate syllable is not heavy," and so forth.
This beginning is intended for those who are listed here ending in *iñ* and *aṇ*;
however, for others, it is intended for the suffixes *maṇin* and *iñ*.

Among these, the first group begins with *krauḍi* and others ending in the suffix *iñ*, prior to the word *caupayata*. The words beginning with *caupayata*, however, end in the suffix *aṇ* up to the word *saudhātaki*.
The word *saudhātaki* itself ends in *iñ*, according to the rule *sudhātor akaṅ ca* [Pāṇini 4.1.97].
[The example is] "the daughter of a *sūta*."
The suffix *ṣyaṅ* occurs after the word *sūta* when it denotes a young woman who has reached puberty: *sūtyā*. In other cases, only the suffix *ṭāp* is used:
*sūtā*. Regarding the rule "after *bhoja* when denoting a Kṣatriya": the suffix *ṣyaṅ* occurs after the word *bhoja* when the Kṣatriya caste is to be expressed.
This is an exception (*apavāda*) to the feminine suffix *ṅīṣ* which denotes a genus (*jāti*). In other cases, only the suffix *ṭāp* occurs—as in *bhojā*.

Those following that [suffix] up to the word *gaukakṣya* end in the suffix *iñ*; furthermore, that [word *gaukakṣya*] ends in *yañ* from the *garga*-class. Regarding the rule "In the sense of a lineage (*gotra*), [the suffix *cha*] is obligatory by the preceding [sūtra]," and so forth.

When the suffix *iñ* is prescribed for a descendant beginning with a grandson (*pautra*), then, since [the application of] the previous rule "for *aṇ* and *iñ*" (Pāṇini 4.1.78) would otherwise be obligatory, this [suffix] is prescribed as an option. However, when it applies to an immediate descendant (a son), it is prescribed in a case where it was not previously applicable at all. "This governing rule (*adhikāra*) extends up to the limit of secondary suffixes (*svārthika-pratyaya*).

Secondary suffixes (*svārthika*) are those that occur in the sense of the base itself (*prakṛty-artha*); the suffix *ṭhañ* is added here because the word belongs to the *adhyātma* group (Pāṇini 4.3.60).

The term *svārthika* refers to those suffixes whose limit (*avadhi*) or boundary (*maryādā*) is such; that is to say, "as far as the rule *prāgdiśo vibhaktiḥ* [Pāṇini 5.3.1]. By this, showing the sūtra from which the secondary suffixes (*svārthika-pratyaya*) subsequently proceed as their limit, he explains that this governing heading (*adhikāra*) extends prior to that very sūtra [5.3.1].
But what is the reason that this governing rule (*adhikāra*) does not apply even to secondary suffixes (*svārthika*)? To this he says: "In the case of secondary suffixes," and so forth.
Regarding the phrase "of those that are capable" (*samarthānām*), the meaning is "of those whose meanings are connected."

Furthermore, the state of being related (*sambaddhārthatā*) exists because it resides in two things; it occurs only when there is a counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*). However, in the case of suffixes used in their own sense (*svārthika*), no distinct meaning other than that of the base word (*prakṛti*) is possible, for which another word would have to be employed to convey the sense, and in relation to which there could be "capacity" (*samarthatā*). Therefore, since capacity is absent in the case of *svārthika* suffixes, the rule "of those that are capable" (*samarthānām*) is not applicable here.
For this very reason, because of the absence of a counter-correlate, the rule "from the first [word]" (*prathamāt*) is likewise not applicable.

For if there were another word as a counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*), then a doubt might arise: "Does the cognition proceed from the first [word] or from the second? Consequently, the statement "from the first," which persists [in the rule], would be meaningful for the purpose of excluding that doubt. But when a second counter-correlate does not exist, its persistence is of no use.
Thus, it is said: "In that case, even the alternative (*vikalpa*) is not established."
The meaning is that it is "indeterminate" (aniyata).
For some [suffixes] added for their own sake (*svārthika*) are always [present].

Thus, in the rule *aṣaḍakṣāśitaṅgvalaṃkarmālam* [Pāṇini 5.4.7] and others, the author of the Bhāṣya will provide an enumeration: "Which suffixes, then, are constant? Those beginning with *tamap* up to *kā*, those beginning with *ñya* up to *vun*, those beginning with *ām* up to *mayaṭ*, and the compound-final suffixes [added] after *bṛhatī* and words denoting a genus."

In this regard, those suffixes beginning with *tamap* (as per Pāṇini 5.3.55) and ending before the suffix *ka* (as per 5.3.70) are obligatory (*nitya*). Likewise, those beginning with the suffix *ñya* (as per 5.3.112) and ending before the suffix *vun*—in the rule "After *pāda* and *śata*, when preceded by a numeral, *vun* is added in the sense of repetition (*vīpsā*), and there is elision of the final phoneme" (5.4.1)—are obligatory. Similarly, those suffixes beginning with *ām* (as per 5.4.11) and ending before the suffix *mayaṭ* (used in the sense of "made of that," *tatprakṛtavacana*) are obligatory.

Thus, the suffix *ka* prescribed by [Pāṇini 5.4.6], the suffix *ca* prescribed by [Pāṇini 5.4.9] as "after a word ending in *jāti*, when expressing a kinsman (*bandhu*)," and all those compound-final suffixes such as *ḍa* and others—all of these are compulsory (*nitya*).
Therefore, the optionality regarding secondary suffixes (*svārthika*) is not established.

Consequently, it has been stated that even the mention of "vāk" (speech) is not fixed therein; it sometimes follows and sometimes does not. Here, is the qualification "from the first" (*prathamāt*) intended for the sentence of usage (*prayoga-vākya*) or for the defining rule (*lakṣaṇa-vākya*)? If it is the former, then there is no restriction regarding the order of words in a worldly sentence, as we see the usage "pātram āhara" and "āhara pātram.
And thus, when the expression "apatyam upagoḥ" is used, the suffix would arise from the word *apatya* by virtue of its being in the nominative case.

But surely, by this first word in the genitive case included in the sūtra—which is an imitation (anukaraṇa) word—the word that constitutes the non-worldly sentence (*alaukikavākya*), though mentioned later, is imitated; because it is the first [word], it receives the designation "first.

Therefore, even when the worldly sentence "the offspring of Upagu" (*apatyam upagoḥ*) is employed, the suffix will arise from the word *upagu* alone—since it has received the designation "first" in the manner already described—and not from the word *apatya*.

If it is argued that there is no fault even when the first alternative is adopted, this is a triviality; for when the primary [meaning] is possible as the first, it is not proper to accept the secondary.

Therefore, even though the word *upagu* has primacy in a secondary sense, the suffix would arise only from the word "offspring" (*apatya*) in its primary sense as the first, and not from the word *upagu*.
Furthermore, this would result in excessive complexity in comprehension (*pratipatti-gaurava*).
In the second case, however, no fault arises at all; for the employment of words in defining statements (*lakṣaṇavākya*) is fixed.
Therefore, relying on that, he says: "defining statements," and so forth.

Among those [words] that are semantically capable, the first is determined as the base of the suffix (*pratyayaprakṛti*), just as in the example: "Among cows, the black one is the most abundant in milk," where the black cow is distinguished among cows by its state of being the most abundant in milk.

If, then, the suffix occurs after that which is capable [of being designated] first, this being the case, in the rule *tasya* (Pāṇini 4.1.92), the pronoun *tasya* is a general term (*sāmānyavācin*). Since it is mentioned first as a general term, the suffix would apply only to a general term and not to a specific term; for instance, it would not apply to a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) such as *upagu*. Is it not the case that in the defining statement (*lakṣaṇavākya*), that [specific term] is not mentioned first? To this he says: “*tasya*,” etc., and “for the purpose of indicating a specific characteristic” (*viśeṣalakṣaṇārtham*).
The meaning is that it is for the purpose of indicating a specific distinction.
For if "of that" (*tasya*) were not intended to indicate a specific distinction, then its capacity [to function as a genitive] would not exist;
for this term "of that" does not, independent of context and the like, settle upon specific instances.

Furthermore, no benefit is conferred upon the offspring by this [suffix] when it is not restricted to specific [descendants], because the word for "offspring" (*apatya*) already conveys the general relationship, as it is a term denoting a relative in general.
Consequently, in the absence of such a benefit, there would be no functional capacity [for the suffix].
To this, it is replied: "of that" (*tasya*).
Therefore, by implication, this [word] has the purpose of indicating particulars (*viśeṣa*).

Thus, those particulars which are indicated—that is, expressed—become auxiliaries by conveying a related entity as qualified through the exclusion of other related entities; it is in this way that its capacity with respect to them is established.
Consequently, this generality (*sāmānya*) of that [word] should be understood as having the purpose of indicating particulars.

Therefore, its primacy is understood as belonging to the specific terms such as *upagu*, and consequently, the suffix arises from that [specific term] alone, not from the word expressing the general [genitive relation]. For example: "The blanket is the offspring of Upagu for Devadatta.
Here, the word *upagu* is connected with the blanket, not with the offspring.
The word *apatya* (offspring) is also connected with the word *Devadatta*, not with the word *Upagu*.

Therefore, since there is no connection between the word *upagu* and the word *apatya*, no suffix arises from it. [The rule] "so that there may also be a sentence" means that if the word *vāk* were not included, then when the offspring is expressed by a sentence, the suffix prescribed for that meaning would preclude the formation of a sentence.

But surely, when the meaning is the same, that which is governed by a grammatical rule (*śāstrānvita*) excludes that which is not so governed (*aśāstrānvita*). For example, by the rule *gameḍoḥ* (Pāṇini 3.1.26), the word *go*, being governed by the rule, excludes the word *gāvī*, which has the same meaning but is not governed by the rule; however, it does not exclude words like *ḍittha*, which have a different meaning.

Furthermore, the meaning of a *vṛtti* (derivative formation) and a *vākya* (sentence) is not identical; for in a *vṛtti*, the semantic capacity (*sāmarthya*) consists in the unification of meaning (*ekārthībhāva*), whereas in a sentence it consists in mutual expectancy (*vyapekṣā*). This is not so; for even though there is this difference in the mode of expression, the primary meaning does not differ. To illustrate: when it is said, "Bring Upagu’s offspring," the very same object that is qualified by the relationship of being an offspring is brought; and when it is said, "Bring the offspring of Upagu" (*aupagavam*), that very same object is brought. It is precisely with respect to the primary meaning that a word conforming to the grammatical rules (*śāstrānvita*) sets aside one that does not conform to them (*aśāstrānvita*). Otherwise, even the word *go* would not set aside the word *gāvī*.

For there is indeed a difference in meaning between those two as well; for instance, the word *go* denotes "cowness" (*gotva*), whereas the word *gāvī* denotes that same thing as well as its ungrammaticality (*aśāstrīyatva*). Therefore, in the absence of the mention of the suffix *vā*, just as the word *go* excludes the word *gāvī*—despite the difference in their secondary meanings—on account of the identity of their primary meaning, so too would a *taddhita* suffix that is governed by grammatical rules exclude a sentence that is not so governed.
Consequently, the mention of *vā* is made so that the sentence form may also be possible.
"If this is so," and so forth.

If, by the inclusion of the word "or" (*vā*), the presence or absence of the secondary derivative (*taddhita*) brings about the presence of the sentence, then when the sentence is absent, the secondary derivative must necessarily occur.
Consequently, the compound formation (*samāsavṛtti*) such as *upagvapatyam* ("the offspring of Upagu") would be sublated by the secondary derivative formation (*taddhitavṛtti*).

"There is no such fault," and so forth; the meaning has already been explained. [An objection: This reference "prāgdīvyataḥ" (before *dīvyat*) is incorrect, since he will state "dīvyati" (Pāṇini 4.4.2) and not "dīvyat. In that case, if the word *dīvyati* were taken as the limit (*avadhi*), the reference ought to have been "dīvyateḥ. To this he replies: "It is a part of that," and so forth. If the entire word *dīvyati* were taken as the limit, this reference would indeed be improper; however, it is not the entire word that is taken, but rather a part of it, namely the word *dīvyat*. Thus, there is no fault.

Now, for what purpose are the terms *divyad* and *prāk* included? Why not simply make the governing rule (*adhikāra*) *naṇ* alone? It cannot be done in this way; for if it were so made, since the *aṇ* would be interrupted by other governing rules such as [Pāṇini 4.1.120], one would have to repeat the mention of *aṇ* again in rules such as [Pāṇini 4.2.1]: *tena raktaṃ rāgāt*.

However, when the extent of the governing rule is declared by means of a limit (*avadhi*), then this [suffix] is permitted for all meanings falling within that limit; thus, there is no need to repeat the mention of *aṇ*.
Therefore, the mention of *dīvyat* must first be made in order to indicate the extent of the scope (*adhikāra*).
The mention of *prāk* must also certainly be made for the purpose of indicating that very [word] as the limit.
For if that were absent, when it were stated "the suffix *aṇ* after *dīvyat*," the word *dīvyat* would be understood as the base (*prakṛti*) of the suffix *aṇ*.
"In all three views," and so forth.

But how is it that this application of *aṇ* is obtained by avoiding the domain of exceptions (*apavāda*), given that while that governing rule (*adhikāra*) exists, *aṇ* would apply even in the domain of exceptions because it presents itself with every individual rule—for instance, in "after *ataḥ*, there is *iñ* and *aṇ*"? Otherwise, its mention there would be purposeless. Even in the view that it is a metarule (*paribhāṣā*), since "in the meanings of 'descended from' (*prāgdīvyataḥ'), *aṇ*" is stated without distinction, how would the general metarule, as it operates, avoid the domain of exceptions? This is true even in the case of a positive injunction (*vidhi*).

If all those bases (*prakṛti*) that occur prior to the rule *prāgdīvyataḥ* were brought together here and the suffix *aṇ* were prescribed for them universally, then the universal prescription would otherwise be rendered meaningless. This is how [the author] thinks: by means of an indicator (*jñāpaka*), it will not apply in the domain of exceptions (*apavāda*). For instance, when he employs the term "optionally" (*vā*) or "either way" (*anyatarasyām*) in certain places—such as in *udaiāto'nyatarasyām* (Pāṇini 4.2.18)—that indicates that the suffix *aṇ* does not occur in the domain of exceptions. However, regarding the positive prescription (*vidhi*), there is a more extensive resolution.

For the suffix *aṇ* is not prescribed after those bases that occur before the word *prāgdīvya*; rather, it is prescribed for those meanings that occur before *prāgdīvya*. In that case, since the suffix *iñ* is produced from a specific base (*prakṛti*) within that same range of meaning, it will supersede *aṇ*.

Now, for what purpose is this limit (*avadhi*) adopted? Why not simply say "before *ṭhak*"—meaning "before the suffix *ṭhak*" as prescribed by [Pāṇini 4.4.1]? It cannot be done in this way; for then [the rule] beginning with [Pāṇini 4.2.18] would also be understood as having *ṭhak* as its limit.

"In that case, one should have stated: *prāk kaṃsīyāt*—that is, [Pāṇini 4.3.168] *kaṃsīyaparaśabdayoryañañau luk ca*. The meaning would have been: 'before that word which is *kaṃsīya*. Even so, it would be impossible to state [it thus]; for by that very rule [4.1.88], the suffix would also be produced after *kaṃsīya*, and consequently, in the case of *dvikaṃsaḥ* (the modification of two *kaṃsas*), the elision (*luk*) would not occur. Therefore, let it remain exactly as it was originally formulated. Regarding the rule *pattyuttarapadācca*:
by this, he shows that the word *uttarapada* is connected only with the word *pati*, and not with others such as *diti* and so forth."
And this [meaning] is obtained either through proximity (*pratyāsatti*) or from the explanation; for it must be stated that "also after *yama*.
This means that the suffix *ṇya* occurs after the word *yama*, and this form of meaning must be explained.

In this regard, the explanation is as follows: although it could have been stated here as "after a word ending in *pati*" (*patyantāt*) for the sake of brevity, the statement "after a word having *pati* as its final member" (*patyuttarapadāt*) is for the purpose of providing an additional rule.
Because of the abundance of the text, there may be a lack of clarity regarding the meaning;
therefore, the suffix *ṇya* will apply even after the word *yama*.

Alternatively, the particle *ca* is carried over from the preceding sūtra; thus, because it serves to include what has not been explicitly mentioned, [the suffix] will apply. "Of those whose speech, mind, and ancestors... and so forth.
The purpose of the term *upasaṃkhyāna* (supplementary addition) is to provide an exposition.

This exposition must be carried out either by relying on an increase in meaning due to an increase in the text, or by the continued application (*anuvṛtti*) of the particle *ca* (and), which serves to include what has not been explicitly stated.

In the case of *yāmyam* and so forth, the suffix *ṇya* is applied according to the requirements in senses such as "descendant" (*apatya*) and others belonging to the *prāgdīvyatīya* group. [This is governed by the rule] "After *pṛthivī*, the suffixes *ña* and *añ*."

These suffixes beginning with *ñ*—such as *ña* and *añ*—are established by the use of the plural number in [Pāṇini 4.1.76], which serves the purpose of including *taddhita* suffixes not explicitly mentioned; thus, they need not be stated separately.

In that regard, when the suffix *ña* is applied to the word *pṛthivī*, the feminine suffix *ṭāp* is added, resulting in *pārthivā*; however, when the suffix *añ* is applied, the suffix *ṅīp* is added according to [Pāṇini 4.1.15] (*ṭiḍḍhāṇañ*), resulting in *pārthivī*.
As for the rule "for *bahiṣ*, there is elision of the sixth case ending," and so forth...

But surely, since the elision of the *ṭi* suffix is already established by the rule "for indeclinables, there is elision of the *ṭi* whenever a *bha*-affix follows, for the sake of forms such as *sāyaṃprātika*," why is it stated again? To this he says: "The mention of the elision of the *ṭi*," and so forth. [The example] "ārātīyaḥ" serves to indicate that [the rule regarding the elision of the *ṭi*] is not universally obligatory (*anityatva*).

Regarding the rule *ārād bhavati* [Pāṇini 4.2.114]: the term *sthāmnaḥ akāraḥ* means that since the word *sthāman* alone is never used in the sense of "offspring" (*apatya*), it should be understood that the suffix *akāra* applies to a form ending in that word.
Thus, one who has such strength (*sthāman*) as his own is called *āsthāmā*; by virtue of belonging to the *pṛṣodarādi* group, the letter *s* is changed to *t*.

*Ātthāmaḥ* is the offspring of *ātthāman*; by [Pāṇini 6.4.144], there is elision of the *ṭi* (the final vowel and following consonant). Regarding the rule "after *loman*, in the sense of offspring": the word *loman* is listed among the *bāhv-ādi* group; since the word *loman* alone has no connection with offspring, it is understood that the rule applies to words ending in *loman*.
Here, when the intention is to express offspring and the suffix *iñ* would otherwise apply in the plural, the suffix *a* is prescribed as an exception to that.
The descendants of Uḍuloma are many, [hence they are called] *uḍulomāḥ*. Regarding the word "everywhere" (*sarvatra*):

it means in the sense of offspring (*apatya*) and elsewhere as well. Alternatively, it means that there would be the contingency of suffixes beginning with *aj* (such as *añ*) applying both in the sense of *prāgdīvyatīya* (relating to what precedes the suffix *dīvya*) and in other senses.
"The contingency of a suffix beginning with *aj*" (*ajādeḥ pratyayasya prasaṅgaḥ*) means its occurrence or application (*prāpti*).

In that regard, whatever occurs everywhere from the word *go*, if this is so, then for what purpose is the mention of *go* in the rule *[[5.1.2]]*? It is for the sake of elaborating upon this very point:
namely, the form *gavyam*.
It means "the offspring of a cow" or "one who moves with a cow.

Alternatively, the suffix *aṇ* applies where there is a relevant application for words beginning with *aja* and others; it does not apply elsewhere. For example: *gorūpyam* (cow-silver) and *gomayam* (cow-dung).
[The suffixes] *rūpya*, optionally [after words ending in] *hetu* and *manu* (Pāṇini 4.3.81), and *mayaṭ* (4.3.82). [The phrase] "beginning with *ṇya*" and so forth:
the word *lakṣaṇa* denotes a cause (*nimitta*) or a mark (*cihna*).
That which has a specific meaning as its mark is "that which has a specific meaning as its mark" (*arthaviśeṣalakṣaṇa*), and this is an exception (*apavāda*) to the suffix *aṇ*.
Therefore, by the rule of prior prohibition (*pūrvavipratiṣedha*), the suffixes beginning with *ṇya* (i.e., *ṇyat*, *ṇic*, etc. occur.
Nor need this be stated, because the word "para" signifies "desired," and thus [the desired result] is already established by that very term.
By the word "ādi" ("etcetera"), suffixes such as those mentioned in [Pāṇini 4.1.86] and so forth are included.

In this regard, there is scope for the suffix *ṇya*: as in *daityaḥ* and *vānaspatyam*. Since this *ṇya* is prescribed in all meanings such as "offspring" (*apatya*) and so forth, it is a general suffix; therefore, it is not characterized by a specific meaning. There is scope for the exception (*apavāda*) *aṇ*, which is characterized by a specific meaning: as in "the offspring of *Duli*" (*duler apatyam*), where by [Pāṇini 4.1.122], *ḍhak* is applied—resulting in *ḍauleyaḥ*. This *ḍhak* is prescribed specifically in the particular meaning of "offspring," and thus it is characterized by a specific meaning.

In this case, both [suffixes] would apply: *daityaḥ* as "the offspring of Diti," or *vānaspatyam* as "a collection of trees. The suffix *ṇya* occurs by means of a prior counter-exception (*pūrvavipratiṣedha*). Why is it said "on account of a specific meaning" (*arthaviśeṣalakṣaṇāt*)? Any exception to the suffix *aṇ* that is prescribed for a specific meaning rather than a general meaning necessarily applies, overriding *ṇya* and the others due to its subsequent position. For example: *uṣṭrapatiḥ* ("camel-leader") is the name of a leaf.

Regarding the form *auṣṭrapatyam* derived from *tasyoṣṭrapateridam iti* (Pāṇini 4.3.123) with the intention of expressing "this belongs to that camel-owner," the suffix *añ* is applied. This *añ*, which serves as the indicator for "this belongs to that" (*tasyedam*), is an exception (*apavāda*) to the suffixes *hyañ* and *aṇ*; it is not an exception to those suffixes whose application is conditioned by a specific meaning.
For meanings such as "offspring" (*apatya*) and so forth are specific meanings;
however, the meaning of "this belongs to that" (*tasyedam*) is a general one, not a specific meaning. [Question: "How then is *vāiteyaḥ* formed?"

If the suffixes beginning with *ṇya* (i.e., *ṇya*, *ṇvul*, etc. were to occur by means of an anterior counter-exception (*pūrvavipratiṣedha*) to the exception (*apavāda*) of *aṇ* based on specific meanings, then the form *daiteya* would not be established.
The intention is that even in this case, the suffix *ṇya* alone ought to occur [after the word *diti*]. This is expressed in the passage beginning with "from the word *diti*," and so forth.

When this word *diti* is derived from the root *do* in the sense of "cutting" (*avakhaṇḍane*, Dhātupāṭha 1148) with the suffix *ktic* according to Pāṇini 3.3.174 (*kticktau*), and the vowel substitution *itva* applied according to 7.4.40 (*dyatisyati-* etc.), then the feminine suffix *ṅīṣ* is added by the rule *kṛdikārādaktinaḥ* (Gaṇasūtra 50). Alternatively, if it is considered an unanalyzed nominal stem (*prātipadika*), then the suffix is added according to *sarvato'ktinnarthādityeke* (Gaṇasūtra 51).

Now, one might object: since it is a rule that "when a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) is mentioned, the form qualified by gender is also included" (Vyāḍīya-paribhāṣā 29), the mention of the word *diti* should also include the word *ditī*; consequently, just as the suffix *ṇya* occurs after the word *diti* by virtue of a prior counter-exception (*pūrvavipratiṣedha*), it ought to occur after the word *ditī* as well. To this, he replies: "The paribhāṣā regarding forms qualified by gender is not universal (*anityā*)."

Furthermore, its lack of permanence (*anityatva*) is to be understood from the elision of the word *ghaṭa* [in the rule], according to the Vārttika: "In the section on vowels (*ac-prakaraṇa*), there is an addition [to the rule] regarding the words *śakti*, *lāṅgala*, *aṅkuśa*, *yaṣṭi*, *tomara*, *ghaṭa*, *ghaṭī*, and *dhanus* after the root *grah*. [The phrase] "and of their exceptions" refers to [the suffixes] *iñ* and so forth. The word *vaṣkaya* is recited in the [Uṇādi] list as being used with the word *as*.
This is its meaning: the suffix *añ* occurs after the word *vaṣkaya*, provided that it is not in a compound (*ase* = *asamāse*).
The designation "compound" (*samāsa*) was established by the former teachers as "sa.
[Thus,] the descendant of *vaṣkaya* is *vāṣkaya*.
What is the purpose of [the condition] *asa*? In the case of *gauvaṣkayiḥ*, only the suffix *iñ* applies by [Pāṇini 4.1.95] *ata iñ*.
[This is stated] because of the rule *udasthānāddeśe*.
When the word *udasthāna* is used to denote a place (*deśa*), the suffix *añ* is applied. Thus, a place situated in *udasthāna* is called *audasthāna*.
Why specify "a place"? [Because otherwise: there is a certain person named *udasthāna*; his descendant is *audasthāniḥ*.
Regarding "pṛṣadaṃśe":
when the word *pṛṣat* is used in the sense of a "part" (*aṃśa*), the suffix *añ* is applied. Thus, a part of a spotted deer (*pṛṣat*) is called *pārṣada*.
What is the purpose of [the word] *aṃśa*? [It is to exclude] another who is a member of the assembly (*pārṣada*).

Only the suffix *aṇ* occurs. Here, the word *kuru* is recited; when there is a desire to express its descendant, the form *kaurava* would not be established, because by [Pāṇini 4.1.151] and [4.1.172], the suffix *ṇya* would be required.
For the suffix *añ* is prescribed generally, whereas the suffix *ṇya* is prescribed for a specific case.

And does that which is prescribed generally get superseded by that which is prescribed specifically? This is not a fault; this rule (*yoga*) will follow after those two rules. Even there, since the word *kuru* has no other scope when the meaning is "offspring" (*apatya*), the suffix *añ* will also apply from it.

Alternatively, when the intention is to express the meaning "offspring" according to [Pāṇini 4.3.120], the form *kaurava* will result. It should be stated: "After *grīṣma*, [the suffix *añ* applies] except in Vedic literature."
The meaning is that this form of the rule must be explained as follows: "the suffix *añ* occurs after the word *grīṣma* when the non-Vedic sense is to be expressed.
He asks, "For what purpose? and replies with "lest it occur here," and so forth.

This is for the sake of ensuring that when words such as *triṣṭubh* are to be expressed in the Veda (*chandas*), the suffix *ṛtvaṇ* alone—as prescribed by the rule *sandhivelādi* [Pāṇini 4.3.16]—should apply, and that *añ* should not occur.
Therefore, the suffix *añ* does not occur [after *grīṣma*] to form *graiṣmī triṣṭubh*.
The explanation for this is as follows: the word *vā* ("or") is understood [from a previous rule], and that is a restricted option (*vyavasthitavibhāṣā*).
Consequently, the suffix *añ* does not occur after the word *grīṣma* when a Vedic meter (*chandas*) is to be expressed.

"‘Vṛtta’ is taken [as the referent]" means that here *vṛtta* refers to those specific types such as *triṣṭubh*, *jagatī*, and so forth; therefore, it is the *chandas* (meter) that is taken, not the *veda*. In this context, the word "strī" (*woman*) is taken in its own form, not a word ending in feminine suffixes such as *ṭāp* and so on.

For [the author] will later state the suffix *ḍhak* [after a word] "ending in *strī*" (Pāṇini 4.1.120); by association with that, the word "puṃs" (*man*) is also understood to have that same property.
Its own form is also grasped [by the rule], as in "pausnam.

There is elision according to *saṃyogāntasya lopaḥ* [Pāṇini 8.2.23]. If the suffixes *nañ* and *san* were to occur after the words *strī* and *puṃs* prior to the application of the term *bhavana*, they would also occur in the sense of *vat*; consequently, forms such as *strīvat* and *puṃvat* would not be established. Therefore, he says: "*striyāḥ puṃvat*" and so forth.
Since he provides this instruction, *striyāṃ puṃvat* [Pāṇini 6.3.34], it is understood that the suffixes *nañ* and *snañ* do not occur in the sense of the suffix *vati*.

[Objection: But from this instruction, one can understand that the suffix *snañ* does not occur in the sense of *vati*, yet one cannot understand that the suffix *nañ* does not occur; consequently, the form *strīvat* would not be established. To this, he says: "And it depends on the rule," and so forth. Because of the instruction *puṃvat*, this rule [of *snañ*] does not apply in the sense of *vati*; for this reason, this indicator (*jñāpaka*) depends on the rule [itself], and not on the suffix *snañ*.
By this, even the example "like a woman" (strīvat) is established. [This is so] because of the svarita accent on the word "prāgdīvyataḥ.
[And it is so] because of the prohibition "not after bhavanāt."
By way of reversal:

would this [word] *dvigoḥ* be in the ablative case or the genitive case? If it were the ablative, then the meaning would be: "There is elision (*luk*) of the suffixes *ana*, *ap*, *pratyaya*, *prāg-dīvyat*, and *yatīya* when they follow a *dvigu* compound. Consequently, just as there is elision of that which is caused by the designation (*saṃjñā*) of a *dvigu*—as in *pañcakapālaḥ* (a sacrificial cake prepared in five dishes)—so too would it apply to that which is not the cause of the *dvigu* designation, such as in: "this fragment of the *pañcakapāla-puroḍāśa*."
> [[4.3.120]] Regarding *it-aṇ*—as in *pāñcakapālam*:

having observed this fault in the case of the genitive (*pañcamī*), he states, relying on the genitive (*ṣaṣṭhī*) alternative: "The word *dvigoḥ* [in the sūtra] refers to the genitive. That is, "[the suffix is applied] to that which is related to a *dvigu* compound."

The *samāhāra-dvigu* is prescribed by the rule *yasya taddhitārthe* (Pāṇini 2.1.51); it is "related to the *dvigu*" because its object (*tadartha*) is related to the *dvigu* through the medium of its meaning.
That [meaning] also, through that medium, is related to the *dvigu*.
[This is stated] "by way of being the cause."

This demonstrates that the elision (*lug*) occurs for that relationship which exists by way of the condition and the conditioned (*nimitta-naimittika-bhāva*), and not for that which exists by way of priority and posteriority (*paurvāparya-bhāva*).
And this is obtained because the relationship of condition and conditioned is more internal (*antaraṅga*);
for that is the primary connection of the *dvigu* with the secondary derivative suffix (*taddhita*), and therefore it is what is grasped.
However, because the state of being prior and posterior (paurvāparya) occurs even at a later time, it is considered external (bahiraṅga); therefore, it is not included [in the definition].

Regarding the example "pañcakapālaḥ": it is a compound formed by *taddhitārtha* [Pāṇini 2.1.50] in the sense of "prepared in five potsherds" (*pañcasu kapāleṣu saṃskṛtaḥ*). By [Pāṇini 2.1.52], it receives the designation of *dvigu*; by [Pāṇini 4.4.3], the suffix *aṇ* is applied, which is then elided (*luk*).
Regarding "dvivedaḥ":
the compound is formed as before, meaning "one who has studied two Vedas," with the suffix *aṇ* according to [Pāṇini 4.2.59]. Regarding "dvaidevavattiḥ":
this means "the offspring of two Devadattas," with the suffix *iñ* according to [Pāṇini 4.1.95].

Regarding the statement, "This belongs to the *pañcakapāla*, thus it is *pāñcakapālam*": here, the first suffix that arose in the sense of being prepared (*saṃskṛta*) is itself the cause for the *dvigu* compound, and not that which arises at a later time when there is a desire to express the meaning "this belongs to it. For the *dvigu* is not prescribed with reference to that [second] meaning as its object; rather, it is prescribed with reference to that suffix which was prescribed in the sense of being prepared.
Because it has that [the *dvigu*] as its cause, the elision (*luk*) does not occur here for that suffix which is prescribed by the rule "this belongs to that" (*tasyedam*).
Regarding the phrase "or rather" (*atha vā*) and so forth:
previously, the elision was prescribed for that *taddhita* suffix which is the cause of the *dvigu*; now, however, it is prescribed for the *dvigu* itself—thus there is a distinction.

But how is it that the elision (*luk*) occurs only for a *dvigu* compound? To this he says: "The term 'of the *dvigu*' (*dvigoḥ*) is a genitive of location (*sthāna-ṣaṣṭhī*). With the words "Now then" (*nanu ca*), etc., he refutes the explanation just stated.

The intention is as follows: since these technical terms (*saṃjñā*) such as *luk* and so forth have been prescribed for the non-appearance of an affix (*pratyaya-adarśana*), when *luk* is mentioned here, it is not capable of prescribing the elision of only a *dvigu*.
[To this he replies: "This is true."
Immediately after this was stated:

"If that is so, how is the elision (*luk*) of the *dvigu* compound obtained through the technical designation (*saṃjñā*)? To this he says: "But by way of metaphorical usage (*upacāra*)," and so forth. Metaphorical usage (*upacāra*) is that specific cognition which superimposes a state of being upon a thing that does not actually possess that state.

It is called *lakṣaṇā* because "one is characterized by means of it"; furthermore, in this context, it is indeed metaphorical transfer (*upacāra*). By this [term], that which is not a *dvigu* compound is characterized as having the form of a *dvigu*. Just as in the expression "the platforms cry," persons who do not possess the nature of platforms are characterized as having the nature of platforms, so too here, that which is not a *dvigu* compound is characterized as having the form of a *dvigu*. The basis for this metaphorical transfer is its being the cause of a *dvigu*; as it has been said: "The suffix itself, when it serves as the cause of a *dvigu*, is a *dvigu*."

For there is indeed a metaphorical designation of the effect in place of the cause, as in the expression "clarified butter is life. Regarding the phrase "then [the term] based on a *dvigu* compound" and so forth:
that for which a *dvigu* compound is the cause is described in that way.
That property which is the basis for metaphorical designation (*upacāra*) is what is intended here by the word "quality" (*guṇa*).
A conceptual construction based on a quality is "conceptual construction based on a quality"; this, moreover, should be understood as being essentially of the nature of metaphorical designation.

If, by means of metaphorical designation, the suffix is called a *dvigu* because it is the cause of the *dvigu*, why is that [compound] whose cause is the *dvigu* not also called a *dvigu* through figurative conceptualization? For even the term for a cause is indeed employed metaphorically for its effect, as in: "all this past good and bad karma is being experienced."

Regarding the term *pāñcakapālam*: this is the view that the suffix *aṇ* is applied in the sense of "this is a fragment of a five-pot-sherd cake" (*pañcakapālasya puroḍāśasyedaṃ khaṇḍam*). Since this suffix is produced after a *dvigu* compound, its cause is the *dvigu*; however, the *dvigu* status itself is not the cause. This is because the *dvigu* status is already established when the secondary derivative (*taddhita*) is being produced; thus, the *dvigu* status is not the cause, but rather the nominal stem (*prātipadika*).

For instance—it is not prescribed that "this is a *dvigu*"; rather, it is prescribed that [the suffix] occurs "after a nominal stem" (*prātipadikāt*). Therefore, even though the status of being a *dvigu* is present, it is not the cause for the suffix; nor can the suffix itself be designated as a *dvigu* by way of metaphorical attribution.
This is what is meant by "but the other [view]."
This is a *taddhita* suffix, the elision (*luk*) of which was shown in the primary example.

The phrase "only the cause of *dvigu*-ness" uses the particle *eva* to exclude the status of being a nominal stem (*prātipadika*). That is to say, it is only the cause of *dvigu*-ness and not the cause of being a nominal stem; for the *dvigu* compound is prescribed for that specific meaning, whereas it is not prescribed for the status of being a nominal stem—this is the distinction.

Consequently, the designation "dvigu" is applied figuratively (upacāra) precisely to that which is the cause of the dvigu; it does not apply even to that [suffix] which arises from an already formed dvigu. Regarding the phrase "If this is so," and so forth:
if the taddhita suffix which is the cause of the dvigu is here called a "dvigu" by way of figurative usage because it is the cause, then its elision occurs by the rule *bha-tha-vi*.

If this is so, how can there be elision here in the case of *pañcakapāla*—meaning "prepared in five potsherds"? For in this instance, once the *dvigu* compound has been formed as a collective (*samāhāra*) meaning "the collection of five potsherds," the secondary suffix (*taddhita*) prescribed subsequently does not serve as the cause for that *dvigu*. The refutation begins with "Not indeed here," and so forth.
He asks: "Why is it not produced? and answers with "For there would be three forms," and so forth.
The three words themselves constitute *traiśabdyam* (the state of having three words).
The suffix *ṣyañ* is applied in the sense of the base itself according to the rule for *cāturvarṇya* and similar formations.
Here, it is this *traiśabdyam* that we must establish.
The word *pañcakapālī* is established even without the production of a secondary derivative (*taddhita*); therefore, a secondary derivative is not produced from it.
By the phrase "prepared in five potsherds" (*pañcasu kapāleṣu saṃskṛtaḥ*), he demonstrates the threefold linguistic usage.
The phrase "of two words," and so forth, [follows].

The word *pañcakapālī*, which occurs in the sense of a collective compound (*samāhāra*), and the word *pañcakapāla*, which occurs in a compound within the scope of a secondary derivative (*taddhita*) meaning, both have the same referent. Since the analysis (*vigraha*) is performed by one of these two—the former—no production of a secondary derivative (*taddhita*) is to be understood from it. [The phrase] "production from the other" refers to the word *pañcakapāla*.
According to the logic of "goat and sheep" (*avyavika-nyāya*).

Just as in the case of *āvikam* ("goat's meat"), the analysis (*vigraha*) is made with the word *avi* (goat), yet the word *avi* itself triggers the application of the suffix; so it is here as well. The phrase "Now, why does this not occur here?
and so forth means that since the suffixes *rūpya* and *mayaṭ* are also causes for the formation of a *dvigu* compound, they too ought to undergo elision (*luk*). This is the intended sense.

The word "veti" (or "vā") is understood as it follows from [Pāṇini 4.1.82]. Now, one might object: even so, elision (*luk*) would apply optionally in all cases; therefore, he says "sā ca" and so forth.
The word "ca" (and) is used in the sense of a reason (*hetau*).
Since that *vyavasthitavibhāṣā* (restricted option) is understood, therefore, in cases such as *pañcakapāla*, the elision (*luk*) occurs invariably;
however, in cases such as *pañcagargarūpya*, it does not occur at all. Regarding the rule "before a vowel" (*aci*):
if this were a locative case (*parasaptamī*), a mutual dependency (*itaretarāśrayatā*) would result in the prescription of the suffix *cha*.

How so? [The derivation is as follows: "the many descendants of Garga" (*gargasyāpatyāni bahūni*). If there were *luk* elision of the suffix, the *cha* suffix would not occur. If it is argued that even when that [suffix] is elided, [the base retains its designation by the rule] "when that which causes the designation is elided" (*lupte'pi tasmin*), then—due to the prohibition against the elision of a suffix [which prevents the application of the rule "that which has a single vowel is called *pragṛhya*"]—there would be an absence of *vṛddhi*, and consequently, the technical designation *vṛddha* would not apply. And because of that, the *cha* suffix characterized by the *vṛddha* designation would not occur.
Therefore, for one who desires the *vṛddha* status of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*), there must first be non-elision (*aluk*) of the suffix.

If that *cha* suffix were to occur after an *aluk*, then the *cha* would have the *aluk* as its cause, and the *aluk* would have that *cha* as its cause; thus, there is clearly a circular dependency (*itaretarāśrayatva*).

Seeing this fault in the locative of "subsequent" (*parasaptamī*), he says—showing that this is a locative of "domain" (*viṣayasaptamī*)—"when a [suffix] beginning with *a-j* belonging to the *prāgdīvyatīya* group is the domain.
"Being the domain" means existing in the intellect even though it has not yet been produced.
Regarding "gārgīyāḥ":
these are the many descendants of Garga.
The suffix *yañ* is applied according to Pāṇini 4.1.105 because [the word] belongs to the *gargādi* group.

When there is the intention to express the meaning "students of Garga," and [the suffix] *ya*—which has not yet been produced after *aja* and so on—is brought to mind as the object [of the operation], the elision (*luk*) prescribed by Pāṇini 4.1.101 would apply; this [present rule] prohibits that. Then, once the initial *vṛddhi* has been applied and the designation *vṛddha* (based upon that) has been established, the suffix *cha* applies by 4.2.114. This is replaced by *īya*, and by 6.4.148 the *a* is elided, and by 6.4.151 the *y*.
Thus we have *vāstīyāḥ*. This is similar to the previous case.

Regarding the term *ātreyīyāḥ*: [the word] *ātreyī* is formed by adding the suffix *ḍhak* according to Pāṇini 4.1.122, as it denotes the many descendants of Atri. Although this suffix would normally be subject to elision (*luk*) by rule 2.4.65 (*atribhṛgukutsavasiṣṭhagotamāṅgirobhyaśca*), there is a prohibition of that elision when the suffix *cha* is to be applied in the sense of "pupils of the Ātreyas. Thus, *ātreyīyāḥ* means "the pupils of the Ātreyas."

Regarding "khārapāyaṇīyāḥ": it refers to the many descendants of Kharapa. By the rules [Pāṇini 4.1.99] and [2.4.63], the elision (*luk*) of that [suffix] would otherwise apply; however, there is a prohibition of this elision when the suffix *cha* is to be applied, as in "the students of the Kharapas" (*kharapāṇāṃ chātrāḥ*). Regarding "kaubalam" and "vādaram": [these are derived from *kubala* and *badara* with the suffix *aṇ*].

The words *kubalī* and *badarī* end in the feminine suffix *ṅīṣ* (by the rule *gaurādibhyaś ca*), and by the accent of the suffix (*pratyayasvara*), they are oxytone (acute on the final syllable); the remainder of the word is unaccented (*anudātta*). Consequently, when there is the intention to express the meaning "the fruit is a modification (*vikāra*) of the *kubalī*" or "the fruit is a modification of the *badarī*," the elision (*luk*) that would otherwise apply to those two [suffixes] by the rules *tasya* [Pāṇini 4.2.44] and *phale luk* [Pāṇini 4.3.163] does not take place when a suffix beginning with a vowel—specifically the suffix *cha*—is the context, provided the sense is "this belongs to the *kubala*" or "this belongs to the *badara*"; this is because of the inclusion of the term *gotra* [in the rule].
Regarding the suffix that occurs as a signifier (*vācaka*) in the sense of a *gotra* (lineage), there ought to be a prohibition of its elision (*luk*).
However, this suffix *añ* does not occur as a signifier in the sense of a *gotra*, but rather in the sense of a modification (*vikāra*); therefore, its elision indeed takes place.
When that [elision] has occurred, by the rule "when a *taddhita* suffix is elided" (*luktaddhitaluki*), there is also the elision of the feminine suffix.
When [the suffix] *añ* is elided, because there is no *vṛddhi* [strengthening], the status of being "old" (*vṛddha*) does not exist; therefore, only *aṇ* occurs, and not *cha*.
Thus, we have *gargarūpyam* and *gargamayam*;
