the forms [and the suffixes] *rūpya* and *mayaṭ* are as before.
If there were no elision (*aluk*) here, it would result in *gāgryarūpyam* or *gāgryamayam*.
[Instead,] it is *gārgīyam*.
By the rule *prākkrītācchaḥ* (Pāṇini 5.1.1), the suffix *cha* is applied; however, this is not a *prāgdīvyatīya* suffix, because it is prescribed after the word *dīvya* (in Pāṇini 4.1.83).
"Of the *gotra*" means "of the *gotra*-suffix. "Among many [suffixes], that which causes elision" [is applied].
That [suffix] for which elision is prescribed when it has arisen in the sense of "many" is called *bahuṣu lopī*.
Regarding the phrase "when there is the occurrence (*pravṛtti*) of that which ends in the plural," *pravṛtti* means the transition to another meaning.

This is what is meant: [the rule applies] when there is a transition to another meaning for that which ends in a plural suffix. And as for that "transition to another meaning," it should be understood that it occurs when a secondary suffix (*pratyaya*) is produced in reference to a youth (*yuvan*) from the end of that [plural form]; for at that time, the lineage-suffix (*gotra-anta*) is applied to the youth.

Regarding the phrase "dvayekayoḥ" (in the case of two or one): when a suffix denoting lineage (*gotra-pratyaya*) is produced after a word ending in that suffix to denote a single descendant in the younger generation (*yuvan*), or two descendants, then, upon the transition to another meaning, the *aluk* (non-elision) occurs. For example: *bidasyāpatyāni bahūni* (the many descendants of Bida).

The suffix *añ* is applied by the rule *anuṣyānantarye bidādibhyo’ñ* [Pāṇini 4.1.104]. Since that suffix undergoes elision (*luk*) when multiple [descendants] are intended, according to the rule *yaññośca* [Pāṇini 2.4.64], it becomes elided in the plural. When there is a desire to express a single or two young descendants (*yuvan*) derived from that [base ending in *añ*], the suffix *iñ* is applied by the rule *ata iñ* [Pāṇini 4.1.95]. Once the elision of that [suffix] has been effected by the rule *ṇyakṣattriyādisūtreṇa* [Pāṇini 2.4.58], and when the meaning of that which ends in a *gotra* suffix has shifted to another sense, the *gotra* suffix *añ* produced here in the plural also undergoes elision.

But how is it that [the substitution] does not occur, given that—because of the absence of an object [in the case of *aluk*]—the suffix *iñ*, belonging to the *prāgdīvyatīya* group and not denoting a genus (*ajāti*), has been introduced? For there is the metarule *pratyayalakṣaṇam* (Pāṇini 1.1.62).

Just as in the case of *go-hitam* ("beneficial for a cow"), which is a genitive-tatpuruṣa compound where the case-ending (*sup*) has been elided (*luk*); although one might rely on the fourth case-ending by means of the metarule *pratyayalakṣaṇam*, the replacement of the *ec* vowel in the word *go-* with *ava* (by Pāṇini 6.1.78: *eco 'yavāyāvaḥ*) does not take place, because [that rule] depends upon a phoneme (*varṇāśrayatvāt*).
Its dependence upon a phoneme, however, is due to the fact that [the replacement] is prescribed when a vowel (*ac*) follows.

Just as there is the paribhāṣā, "When [an operation] depends on a phoneme (*varṇa*), the rule concerning suffixes (*pratyayalakṣaṇa*) does not apply" (Vyāḍi-paribhāṣā 96), so too in cases such as *baidaḥ* and *baidau*, should there not likewise be no application [of the suffix-rule] because it depends on a phoneme due to the absence of elision (*aluk*)? This is not so; for here the absence of elision (*aluk*) does not depend on a phoneme, but rather on a secondary derivative (*taddhita*). However, the word *aci* is mentioned in this sūtra as a qualifier.
For this very reason, it is stated in the commentary (*vṛtti*): "A suffix beginning with a vowel (*aj-ādi*) that belongs to the *prāgdīvyatīya* class."

Therefore, since that technical rule (*paribhāṣā*) does not apply here, the rule "there is no elision (*aluk*) of the *gotra* [suffix] before a vowel-initial [affix]" (*gotre 'lug aci*) applies; by this very rule, the non-elision (*aluk*) is established here.
Furthermore, so that this [non-elision] does not occur when there are many *yuvan* [descendants], the supplementary rule (*upasaṃkhyāna*) "only in the case of two or one" is stated.
In that case, the form remains simply *bidāḥ*. [This refers to the phrase] "of that which ends in the singular or dual," and so forth.

When a patronymic suffix (*gotrapratyaya*) ending in the singular number and one ending in the dual number both undergo a transition to denote a plurality of persons designated as *yuvan* (descendants), elision (*luk*) must be stated.

In this regard, *baidaḥ* is the singular form denoting the lineage (*gotra*), and *baidau* is the dual form. Here, as before, the suffix *añ* is applied; then, when there is a desire to express the plurality of *yuvan* descendants of those two, the suffix *iñ* is added according to [Pāṇini 4.1.95]: *ata iñ*.

When the elision (*luk*) of that [suffix] has been effected by the rule *ṇyakṣattriyādibhyaḥ* (Pāṇini 2.4.58), the elision of the *añ* suffix, which is a *gotra* suffix, is also desired; however, that [elision] does not apply, and therefore an addition (*upasaṃkhyāna*) is made. But what is the reason that it does not apply? To this he says: "For in this case," and so forth.

By this rule [Pāṇini 2.4.64], *luk* (elision) is prescribed when [the suffix] has arisen in the sense of the plural; however, *añ* has not arisen in the sense of the plural, but rather in the sense of the singular or the dual. Therefore, [the elision] does not apply.

Thus, it is established that in all cases, when there is a plurality, it must be *bidāḥ*. Regarding the word "in the sense of the young" (*yūni*), [this is] the locative case used in the sense of the genitive [according to Pāṇini 3.1.85].
For this very reason, the author says in the commentary: "of the suffix *yuvan*.
By stating "when a suffix beginning with a vowel (*aj-ādi*) is intended," he shows that the locative case in *aci* is a locative of scope (*viṣaya-saptamī*).
If this were a locative of sequence (*parasaptamī*), then [the substitution] would occur even in cases where the suffix *cha* is not desired.
The intention is that [the suffix] ends in a *yuvan*-suffix because it denotes Buddhahood. Regarding the forms "phāṇṭāhmatarūpyam" and "phāṇṭāhmatamayam":
if there were elision (*luk*) here, these forms "phāṇṭāhmatarūpyam" and "phāṇṭāhmatamayam" would not occur.
[Also regarding] "bhāgavittikīyam."
The suffix *cha* [prescribed] after words ending in *prāg-dīvyatya* is like the preceding [rule]. For example: *gārgīyāḥ*, *vātsīyāḥ*.
There is elision of the *ka* and *ya* of the preceding member.

While the word *vā* (optionally) is still in force, the mention of *anyatarasyām* (alternatively) is for the purpose of indicating that the rule in the previous sūtra is compulsory (*nitya*). [Thus it is said: "It is connected with both the preceding and the subsequent suffixes."
In this regard, it is first connected with the preceding [rules], beginning with *aṇ* and so forth, because it is prescribed independently (*asaṃyukta-vidhānāt*).
If it were not to be connected with the preceding rules, one would have formulated a single rule simply as "the descendant of that [is formed by] *iñ* after *at*" (*tasyāpatyam ata iñ*).

However, since one makes *ata iñ* (Pāṇini 4.1.95) independent of *ataḥ* (Pāṇini 4.1.92), it is understood from this independent prescription that it pertains to the meaning of the preceding [rules]; thus, for now, it is connected with the preceding ones.
It is also connected with the subsequent [rules], because it is marked as *svarita* (circumflex) among them.
Regarding the word "tasya" (of that),
the reference is made in the masculine gender and in the singular number.
Consequently, the suffix would arise only from a masculine base and only when ending in the singular number;

it would not arise from feminine or neuter bases—such as in *devadattāyā apatyam* ("the offspring of Devadattā") or *kulasyāpatyam* ("the offspring of the family"). Nor would it arise from dual or plural endings—such as in *dvayormātrorapatyam* ("the offspring of two mothers") or *tisṛṇāṃ mātṛṇāmapatyam* ("the offspring of three mothers").
Now, is this designation made in the neuter gender? [If so,] it would not apply to the feminine or the masculine.

Here, the designation "offspring" (*apatyam*) is made in the singular number; therefore, it would apply to only one offspring, and not to two or many—such as *aupagavau* (the two descendants of Upagu) or *aupagavāḥ* (the many descendants of Upagu). To this prima facie objection, he says: "qualified by the meaning of the base," and so forth.
The word "is grasped" (*gṛhyate*) is to be connected with what is to be stated hereafter.
The meaning of the base (*prakṛti*) is the meaning of words such as *upagava*; by that [base-meaning], the genitive sense—the relationship between offspring and progenitor—is qualified.

Now, one might object: "In this context, the pronoun *tasya* (‘of that’) refers to a general term; yet for it, specific meanings such as *upagava* have been formed, by which the genitive sense is qualified. This is not a fault, because the word *tasya* serves as an indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*) of the specific instance.
Furthermore, its status as a specifier of a particular [substance] has already been established previously.
Therefore, a specific [patronymic] such as Upagu and the like is indeed the meaning of the base (prakṛti).
And [it was said]: "and merely offspring."

The word *mātra* is for the purpose of excluding anything additional, such as gender (*liṅga*) and so forth. In the phrase "gender, number, and so forth" (*liṅgavacanādika*), the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) includes time (*kāla*). For this indication is made by means of the present tense.
As it has been said: "Even where another verb of action is not explicitly heard, there too the verb *as* (to be), in the present tense, first person, though unexpressed, is understood to exist.
In that case, if the intention is to express the present time, it would not apply to other times.
Furthermore, what is the reason that gender, number, and so forth are not intended to be expressed? Because they are subordinate.
For a designation must necessarily be made by some characteristic mark (*liṅga*) or the like, because such a mark is inseparable [from the object];

therefore, it is included here, just as straw and so forth are taken up by one who seeks grain, even though they are not the primary object. The rule beginning with *tasyedam* (Pāṇini 4.3.120) also applies in the sense of "offspring" (*apatya*).

One who is the offspring of Upagu can be designated as "this is his [offspring]," because these—namely offspring (*apatya*), collection (*samūha*), residence (*nivāsa*), and modification (*vikāra*)—are the specific instances of the general rule *tasyedam* ("this belongs to him").

Consequently, since the suffix *aṇ* is already established for the sense of offspring by the rule *tataśca* (Pāṇini 4.3.120), for what purpose was this sūtra *tasyāpatyam* composed? [The answer is: "It was composed for the purpose of superseding [other rules]."

By this [sūtra 4.3.120], the *aṇ* suffix being prescribed becomes an obstacle to the *ch* suffix which would otherwise apply by [sūtra 4.2.114]. This [present sūtra] is composed for the purpose of subverting that; it ensures that the *ch* suffix is subverted by the *aṇ* suffix ordained by this very rule. But how can a non-śaiṣika suffix subvert a śaiṣika suffix? The domain of the śaiṣika suffixes consists of six meanings other than those beginning with "offspring" (*apatya*) and ending with the four meanings [of the fourth case].

And this [suffix] does not exist at all in the domain of *apatya* (offspring). Therefore, how could its non-existence subvert the suffix *cha*? To this he says: "This is merely the general rule (*utsarga*) for the remainder.
The intended meaning is that this grammatical rule (*yoga*) would not exist [if the specific rule were applied].
By the word "asau" (this one), because it is the subject under discussion, the meaning "his offspring" is referred back.
Even though the suffix *aṇ* has already been produced by the general rule (*utsarga*), that same meaning is expressed through association with that general rule.
This association with the general rule exists because that general rule prescribes *aṇ* and other such suffixes in that context.

Even here, when this rule (*kriyamāṇe*) is applied, because it enters into the scope of that [rule] (*ityetasminnanupraveśāt*), just as any other "remainder" (*śeṣa*) becomes a specific instance of it, so too does the sense of "offspring" (*apatyārtha*). For that [sense of offspring] also possesses a distinctness relative to what has been used, since it is not included within the limits of the "four senses" (*caturarthī*).
Consequently, because it is a remainder, the suffix *cha* would result in the sense of offspring.
In this yoga, however, [the term] *śeṣe* does not enter into [the rule at] Pāṇini 4.3.120, because it has already been employed [elsewhere].

Consequently, since there is no remainder (*aśeṣatvāt*), there is simply no possibility for the suffix *cha* to apply to the offspring (*apatya*). That very non-application is what is expressed by the word "sublation" (*bādhana*).
Now, he asks what the purpose of this [rule] for the sake of exclusion (bādhanārtha) is, and says: "The purpose of this is the formation of *vṛddha* bases.

The *vṛddha* nominal stems (*prātipadika*) are the purpose of this rule. Thus, in the cases of *bhānor apatyam* ("the descendant of Bhānu") resulting in *bhānavaḥ*, and *śyāmagor apatyam* ("the descendant of Śyāmaga") resulting in *śyāmagavaḥ*, the suffix *aṇ* becomes established.
If this technical term *yoga* were not present, then the meaning of "offspring" (*apatya*) would be understood as a residual category (*śeṣa*) according to the method previously stated;

consequently, the rule *vṛddhēbhyaś caḥ* [Pāṇini 4.2.114] would apply there. However, by the metarule *kṛtrimākṛtrimayoḥ kṛtrime kāryasaṃpratyayaḥ* (Vyāḍi-Patañjali 6), only the technical (*paribhāṣika*) sense of *gotra* is to be understood, because the word *gotra* is employed within the governing context of "offspring" (*apatyādhikāra*).

For the worldly *gotra* is merely offspring; if its inclusion here were intended, he would have said simply "one," since the worldly *gotra* is already understood from the context of the discussion on offspring. Therefore, by the specific mention of *gotra*, he states that the technical (*pāribhāṣika*) sense is meant—namely, "the *gotra* is the offspring beginning with the grandson"—and so on, [including] the phrase "by distinction."

"Bhedena" means by division (*vibhāgena*). "Prati apatyam apatyam" means for each offspring. The meaning is: when there is the contingency—that is, the possibility—of suffixes arising from all those offspring that are possible; since every offspring is connected to all [ancestors], the offspring of any one among Garga, Gārgi, Gāgrya, or Gāgryāyaṇa would be the offspring of all of them. Consequently, the suffixes characterized as belonging to the immediate lineage (*gotra*) following the original base (*paramaprakṛti*) would result [by over-extension].
Whatever is the offspring of Garga belongs to all those who are Gārgis, Gāgryas, and Gāgryāyaṇas.

For although here the analysis is performed with the word "Garga" as in "the offspring of Garga," nevertheless, this restriction—that the suffix must arise from the word "Garga" alone—is not obtained; rather, there is freedom of choice.

And so, when the suffix arises from the word *garga*, then by virtue of belonging to the *gargādi* group, the suffix *yañ* [Pāṇini 4.1.105] is applied; when it arises from the word *gārgi*, then the suffix *phak* [Pāṇini 4.1.101] is applied; and even when it arises from the word *gāgrya*, that same *phak* is applied; and when it arises from the word *gāgryāyaṇa*, then the suffix *iñ* [Pāṇini 4.1.95] is applied. Thus, when there was the possibility of various suffixes arising for each successive descendant according to these divisions, this restriction is established: "only one suffix occurs. By this, he demonstrates that it is a restriction regarding the suffix (*pratyayaniyama*).
The restriction regarding the suffix (*pratyayaniyama*), however, is obtained from the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) of the word *eka* with the word *pratyaya*.
Furthermore, in this rule, the word *eka* should be understood as denoting number (*saṃkhyāvacana*), as in the cases of "one," "two," or "many.
By means of the particle *eva*, the exclusion of two or more is effected: there is only one suffix, not two, nor many.
And since that single suffix occurs only from the ultimate base (paramaprakṛti) because of the mention of "one," it is stated by implication (*sāmarthyāt*).

For if it were produced from the word *gārgi*, there would be two [suffixes]—*iñ* and *phak*—and not one. Or if it were from the word *gāgrya*, even then there would be exactly two—*yañ* and *phak*. Or if it were from the word *gāgryāyaṇa*, there would be three—*yañ*, *phak*, and *iñ*. Therefore, by employing the mention of "one," it is stated by implication that the production of the gotra-suffix occurs only from the original base (*mūlaprakṛti*), so that a single suffix is established upon production from the original base itself.

But surely it is only the progenitor who is connected with the offspring; for this is seen in the world: seeing a child sitting on his grandfather’s lap, someone asks, "Whose is this? and he replies, "Devadatta’s. Thus, he designates the progenitor and not himself. Therefore, since there is no connection of all [ancestors] with the offspring, there would be no contingency of a distinct cognition arising for each individual offspring; and since there is nothing to be excluded, this rule was not commenced for the sake of restriction. To this, he says:

"All are joined with offspring. He states the justification for this very point: "Offspring (apatyam) is so called because of not falling away (a-patana). For that by means of which one does not fall into sins is the cause of one's offspring; it becomes one's offspring precisely because of that non-falling away. Therefore, even one who is produced through an intermediary is the offspring of the primary referent denoted by the root, because he too [is characterized] by not falling away from that.
Furthermore, the mention of the "primary prakṛti" (original base) should be understood as an illustration;
for even when the meaning expressed by another prakṛti is involved, that which is produced immediately [from it] is indeed an offspring (*apatya*).
As for what was stated—that when one asks "Whose is this?", it designates the progenitor and not oneself—it cannot be established thereby that the offspring is connected with the progenitor alone.

Because, in that case, it would not be the one for whom [the action] did not fall who is intended to be known; rather, it is the one who designates the agent, and not himself. For if it were the one for whom [the action] did not fall who was intended to be known, then he would certainly have designated himself as well.

Furthermore, if not everyone were connected with offspring (*apatya*), then this grammatical coreferential designation (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) of the words "offspring" (*apatya*) and "starting from the grandson" (*pautraprabhṛti*)—as in the rule *apatyaṃ pautraprabhṛti gotram* (Pāṇini 4.1.162)—would be untenable; for those males in relation to whom others receive the designation "grandson" and so forth would, in relation to him, be non-offspring (*anapatya*). Therefore, from this very designation as well, it is understood that all are connected with offspring—as in the example: "His son is also a Gārgya."
By the word "also" (*api*), his grandson and others are included as well. What, then, is the reason that even his son is called Gārgya? He says: "In all [cases]," and so forth.

Even in the case of *Gārgyāyaṇa*, since the lineage-descendant (*gotrāpatya*) is produced by one [generation] intervening [between the original ancestor and the descendant], the suffix *yañ* occurs there as well from the word *Garga*; therefore, his son also is a Gārgya.

By the phrase "from the word *garga*," he shows that [the suffix] occurs after the ultimate base (*paramaprakṛti*). And it has been stated that this is understood from the inclusion of the word "one" (*eka*). Alternatively, by the words "or rather" (*atha vā*) and so forth, he demonstrates the restriction regarding the base (*prakṛti-niyama*). This restriction of the base, however, is understood through the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) of the word "one" with the base.

It should be understood that the word "one" here functions as a restriction regarding primacy (*prāthamya*), just as in the rule: "The first and second letters of the classes have the throat closed (*saṃvṛtakaṇṭha*), have *ā* as their internal effort (*anupradāna*), and are voiceless; some are weak-breathed (*alpaprāṇa*), while all the others are strong-breathed (*mahāprāṇa*)."
For here, in the first case, it is understood that they have few vowels (*alpaprāṇa*).
This is an explanation of the word *eka*: "the first base" (*prathamā prakṛtiḥ*).
And what is the first? That which is the ultimate base (*paramaprakṛti*) not ending in an affix, such as *garga*, *naḍa*, and so forth.
"Prakṛti is restricted.
Only the first [vowel] of the base (*prakṛti*) produces the suffix (*pratyaya*), not any other; for example, words such as *gārgya*, *gāgrya*, and *gāgryāyaṇa* end in suffixes.
The offspring of Garga is *gārgya*; his son also is *gārgya*.
The descendant of Naḍa is Nāḍāyana; his son also is Nāḍāyana.

In all cases, even when the lineage (gotra) is produced through an intervening generation, the first base form produces the suffix. The word "also" (*api*) indicates that this is a restrictive rule (*niyama*), showing that it is not only the former [rule] that applies.

Since the suffix would apply to all [stems] when there is a connection with a descendant—even from those that are *paramaprakṛti*, *anantara*, or *yuvan*—if one intends to express a *yuvan*-descendant, a restriction is therefore made to exclude that:
"only from a *gotra* [stem].
This means: "only from that which ends in a *gotra* suffix."
By this, he shows the essential nature of the restrictive rule (*niyama*).
With the words "not merely," etc., he indicates what is excluded by the rule. [Examples:
*gārgyāyaṇaḥ*, *dākṣāyaṇaḥ*.

From a base ending in those suffixes *yañ* and *iñ* which are prescribed in the sense of lineage (*gotra*), [the suffix] *phak* is applied according to Pāṇini 4.1.101; for example, *aupagaviḥ* and *nāḍāyaniḥ*.
From a base ending in those suffixes *aṇ* and *phak* which are prescribed in the sense of lineage, the suffix *iñ* is applied according to Pāṇini 4.1.95; for example, *dākṣī*.
The offspring of Vakṣas is a female in the fourth [generation].
[The suffix] *iñ* is applied by [Pāṇini 4.1.95], and [the feminine suffix] *ṅīṣ* is applied by [Pāṇini 4.1.65]. [The questioner asks: "What, then, is being prohibited here?
He considers there to be a fault if everything were to be prohibited.

In order to expose that very defect, he says "yadi" and so forth. The meaning is: "there would result a lack of restriction regarding the feminine gender," which implies that the feminine suffix *yuv* would apply even after words such as *parama*, *prakṛti*, *anantara*, and *yuvan*.

"Because the designation *gotra* is sublated by the designation *yuvan*," [it is said]. However, in the rule "But when an ancestor is living, one is called *yuvan*," the word *tu* (but) is used for the purpose of restriction (*avadhāraṇa*).
By that [restriction], the [intended] expression is not obtained.
"From that," and so forth.
Since there is a fault in prohibiting both [the suffixes] for the *niyama* and the *yuvan* [suffixes], therefore, in order to eliminate that, a split of the rule (*yogavibhāga*) must be made.

In that regard, "from the *gotra*, in the sense of the *yuvan*" is one rule; by this, a restriction (*niyama*) is established, as he says: "A suffix occurs after a *gotra* [stem] in the sense of the *yuvan*."

Then follows the second rule: *astriyām*. By this, the operation that was prescribed for the term *yūni* is prohibited; as it is said: "That which was prescribed for the *yuvan* [stage] does not apply when it is feminine. It is stated: "Only the designation *yuvan* is prohibited."

How so? For in this rule, "not in the feminine" (*astriyām*), the term "in the young" (*yūni*) is understood to carry over from the preceding context; thus, it is understood that the grammatical operation prescribed for the "young" (*yuvan*) does not occur when [the referent] is feminine.
Furthermore, since the designation "young" (*yuvasaṃjñā*) is applied only to the "young," it is precisely that which is prohibited here. This is what is meant by "the designation 'young' itself."
By the particle *eva*, the exclusion of the *yuvan* suffix is established;
thus it is said: "She will be denoted by a *gotra* suffix.

Since the designation *yuvan* has been prohibited for her, the designation *gotra* remains unshaken. By the word "from this" (*ataḥ*), the stem under discussion is qualified; and because a rule involving a suffix applies to that which ends with the qualifier, he says: "from a nominal stem ending in the vowel *a*."

Now, why is it that *athātaḥ* is not understood as the form of the root *ata* (meaning "to go continuously," Dhātupāṭha 34) with the suffix *kvip*? [The answer is: because of the rule [Pāṇini 4.1.112].
That [suffix] is introduced for the purpose of superseding the suffix *iñ*.

If, however, there were a reference here to the actual form (*svarūpagrahaṇa*), then since there would be no possibility at all for the application of *iñ* after words beginning with *śiva*, the prescription of *aṇ* to supersede it would be purposeless; for words such as *krauḍi* and others ending in *iñ* are already listed [in the *gargādi* group].
Therefore, this [term] refers only to that which ends in the vowel *a*.

If this is so, then in the case of *asyāpatyam ir* ("the descendant of this"), the rule would not apply because it does not end in *a*; however, there is no fault here, as it becomes something ending in *a* by virtue of the principle of "behaving like that which possesses a designation" (*vyapadeśivadbhāva*). Examples are *śubhaṃyāḥ* and *kīlālapāḥ*.

In the rule *yāteḥ, pibateśca* (Pāṇini 3.2.74), the suffix *vij* is indeed attracted by the particle *ca* from the preceding rule *vijupeśchandasi* (Pāṇini 3.2.73). As for the question "How? and so forth:

from the word *daśaratha*, there ought to be the suffix *diñ* because it ends in the vowel *a*. Consequently, the use of the form *dāśarathāya*, which ends in the suffix *aṇ*, would not be justified; such is the intended meaning.

"Regarding the phrase *śeṣavivakṣāyām* and so forth: by this, he shows that the suffix *aṇ* is prescribed here when there is the intention to express the meaning "this belongs to Daśaratha," but not when there is the intention to express the meaning [of a descendant] according to Pāṇini 4.1.92. However, when one intends to express "the offspring of Daśaratha," then the suffix *iñ* indeed occurs—namely, *dāśarathiḥ*. As for *bāhaviḥ*:"
Regarding the word "kvacit":
it refers to those ending with Ajīgarta and so forth.
Since the names beginning with Bāhu and ending with Vaṭāku do not end in the letter *a*, this recitation is for the purpose of providing their inclusion [in the list].

Regarding the word *cūḍā*, since the suffix *ḍhak* would have applied by [Pāṇini 4.1.121] *dvya-caḥ*, and regarding the words beginning with *vṛkala* up to *puṣkarasat*, since the suffix *aṇ* would have applied by [Pāṇini 4.1.113] *avṛddhābhyo nadīmānuṣībhyaḥ*, this [Vārttika] is intended to ensure the application of the suffixes for the words beginning with *puṣkarasat* and ending with *loman*, as they do not end in the vowel *a*. [The Vārttika continues: "In the case of *amitaujas*, there is also the elision of *s*."
The suffix *iñ* occurs after *amitaujas*, and there is elision of the *s*. Thus, *āmitaujiḥ*.
It is recited as *udañc*; in that case, it should be understood that the letter *c* belongs to the root *añc*.

This [suffix] is not, however, ending in the vowel *a*; rather, it ends in the suffix *kvip*. Due to its being a *nipātana* (irregular formation) at the time of the application of the suffix, the elision of the nasal (*anunāsika-lopa*) does not occur.
"Audañciḥ" means the offspring of one who faces north (*udīc*).
The word "śiras" necessitates an interpretation where it stands at the end of a compound (*tadantavidhi*), because a neuter [word] alone cannot have a connection with the term "offspring" (*apatya*).
The offspring of Hastiśiras is Hāstiśīrṣi; in this case, by the rule *ity atra cakārasyānuktasamuccaya* (the inclusion of what was not explicitly mentioned), the offspring of Loman is Audhrvalomi.

Regarding the group beginning with Ajīgarta and ending before the word udaṅka, since the suffix *aṇ* prescribed by the rule *ṛṣyandhakavṛṣṇi* [4.1.114] would otherwise apply as a superseding factor, the specific rule *udaṅkaḥ saṃjñāyām* (udaṅka takes the suffix *iñ* when it is a proper name) is stated.
There is a certain person named Udaṅka; his descendant is Audañkiḥ.
According to the rule "sambhūyo'mbhasoḥ salopaśca," the suffix *iñ* is applied to the words *sambhūya* and *ambhas*, and there is the elision of the letter *s*—thus [we derive] Sāmbhūyiḥ and Āmbhiḥ.
Regarding the phrase "beginning with the arms and so forth":
by the word "and so forth" (prabhṛti), those which will be mentioned hereafter are included. "Those whose vision exists in the mundane state of the lineage" (gotrabhū).
*Darśana* means common usage (*prasiddhi*). *Bhāva* in the context of a worldly lineage (*laukika-gotra*) means the act of being designated by a name.
It should be understood that those who possess established usage regarding a worldly lineage are included among the *bāhu*-class [of stems].
"Exclusion of them elsewhere than that":
this exclusion is to be understood as applying to those for whom there is no perception of the worldly *gotra* (clan-lineage) itself, but rather perception of something other than that.

Thus, there was a certain primordial person named Bāhu, who is well-known as the founder of a designation; the males born within the lineage of his descendants receive the appellation "Bāhu," and it is from him that the suffix *iñ* is derived.
However, that which is internal to "idam" (this), namely the word *bāhu* (arm), becomes plural as *bāhavaḥ*.
This is understood both from the recurrence of the word "or" (*vā*) and from the recognition of an option (*vyavasthitavibhāṣā*) established by context.

Furthermore, regarding the grammatical operation prescribed for relative terms such as *āśu* (quick) and others, there is a prohibition [of that operation] based on their similarity [to the terms in question].
In this case as well, the very same reason stated previously should be understood.

According to the rule *rājāśur-ād-yat* [Pāṇini 4.1.137], the suffix *yat* after the word *āśura* occurs only when it is a relative term (*sambandhiśabda*), not when it is a proper name (*saṃjñāśabda*). Therefore, if there is someone named Āśura, his descendant is formed with the suffix *iñ* alone, resulting in *Āśuri*.
Regarding the phrase "saṃjñāśurasya":
that which is swift by virtue of its name (*saṃjñā*), and not because of its connection [to the act of going], is *saṃjñāśura*. Regarding the example "vyāsavaruḍa" and so forth:
the meaning is that this should be explained as having the sense that the suffix *iñ* is applied after names such as Vyāsa, and simultaneously with that, the substitution of *akaṅ* occurs.

In this regard, the following is the explanation: the word "ca" (and) from the preceding sūtra is carried over here, and it serves to include what has not been explicitly mentioned; by that, [the suffix] will also apply to Vyāsa and others. Regarding the form *vaiyāsakiḥ*:
by the rule beginning with *na yvābhyām* [Pāṇini 7.3.3], there is a prohibition of the *vṛddhi* substitution for the vowel *i*.

Now, one might ask: why was the word *sudhātṛ* not taught directly for the [suffixes] beginning with *bāhu*, and why was the substitution of *akaṅ* not applied there—as is done when *amitaujas* is recited in the *gaṇa* list with the rule "and the elision of *s*"—or even in the *sūtra* itself? For in that case, no specific advantage in terms of brevity (*lāghava*) would be obtained; thus, this objection is trivial. [The statement] "it is an exception (*apavāda*) to *iñ*" refers to the fact that words such as *kuñja* end in the vowel *a*. "The letter *c* is for the sake of specification" means:
If the letter *ca* were not included here, then it would likewise not be included in the rule *tataḥ* [Pāṇini 5.3.113], because the suffix *cphañ* does not exist there.
Consequently, if it were stated as *vātaphañor astriyām*, there would also be the inclusion of the rule *ādyādibhyaḥ phañ* [Pāṇini 4.1.110],
resulting in forms such as *kauñjāyanyaḥ* and *kauñjāyanyau*.

Since the suffix *ñya* is being carried over from the rule "after [words ending in] *pūga*, *añja*, *agra*, and *maṇin*, [the suffix] *ñya* is applied" (Pāṇini 5.3.112), the suffix *ñya* is added here in its own sense (*svārtha*) according to the subsequent rule (5.3.113).
Thus, we have *kauñjāyanāḥ*.

Because these are designated as *tadrāja* by the rule "those beginning with *ñya* are *tadrāja*" (5.3.119), the elision (*luk*) occurs according to the rule "of a *tadrāja* [suffix], when many [descendants are denoted]" (2.4.62), and so forth.

Furthermore, in this case, should there be the accentuation of the *ñit* [suffix], or rather the accentuation of the *cit* [suffix]? To address this, he says: "In the singular and dual," and so forth.

First, regarding the singular and dual, since the *cit* accent would apply while that suffix is present, and the *ñit* accent arises only after the *ñya* suffix has been prescribed, the *ñit* accent becomes "later-prescribed" (*satiśiṣṭa*); therefore, it must prevail by that alone.
However, in the plural, once the *ñya* suffix has ceased to apply, it is desired that the *cit* accent itself take effect, having set aside the former.

But how is that [the accent] obtained even though it is desired? If you say "by the power of the marker *ñ*," no; for by the power of the marker *ñ*, the *ñit-svara* (the acute accent on the *ñit* suffix) would also be obtained. If that is so, then a split of the rule (*yogavibhāga*) will be made in the section on accentuation: first there is this—"of a *cit*" [Pāṇini 6.1.157]; then "of a *taddhita*" [Pāṇini 6.1.158], where "of a *cit*" continues to apply. For what purpose is this? Because of its subsequent position, the rule "of the *para*" [Pāṇini 6.1.197] would result in the initial syllable being acute, and this [split] is for the purpose of subverting that.

Then, by the rule *kitaḥ* [Pāṇini 6.1.159], the final syllable of a word ending in *kit* becomes udātta when followed by a taddhita suffix. In the list of *naḍādi* words, the form *śalaṅku śalaṅkañ ca* is recited. Its meaning is this: the word *śalaṅku* produces a secondary suffix (*pratyaya*) and undergoes the change to *śalaṅka*; thus, the form *śālaṅkāyana* is derived. Regarding the phrase "in the *pailādi* group": [it refers to the fact that *śālaṅkāyana* is listed there].

In the list beginning with *paila*, the word *śālaṅki* is recited as ending in the suffix *iñ*; this is so that there may be elision (*luk*) of the secondary suffix (*yuvan-pratyaya*) derived from it, as in the example: "Śālaṅki is the father, Śālaṅki is the son. For in that context, the rule "after a word ending in *ṇya*, after a non-Kṣatriya name, and after an *ārṣa* [name] ending in *añ* or *it*" (Pāṇini 2.4.58) applies, and the phrase "elision in the case of a younger generation" (*yūni luk*) is carried over. Since that word *śālaṅki* is not appropriately included there—because it ought to take the suffix *phak* due to its inclusion in the *naḍādi* group—the objection arises: "How is it recited there as ending in *iñ*? He states the resolution for this: "In a specific lineage," and so forth.

Regarding the *kauśika* clan-name, grammarians prescribe the suffix *phak* (forming *kauśikāyani*) specifically after the word *śalaṅku*; elsewhere, however, only the suffix *iñ* occurs, which is not a fault.
That *iñ* is obtained because [the *bāhu* group] is an open-ended class (*ākṛtigaṇa*). Even granting that the rule for *phak* applies to the mere clan-name, [the point remains].
He states another solution with the words "Or rather" (*atha vā*), etc.
The mention of the state of being an *iñ*-descendant is an illustration;
for even the state of being a *śalaṅka* is indicated by the very fact that [the name] is recited in the list beginning with *paila*.
In the previous explanation as well, this very [rule] should be understood as the indicator (*jñāpaka*):
"In the *vṛṣagaṇa*, [the suffix *phak* is applied after *agniśarman*].
From the word *agniśarman*, when the *gotra* is *vṛṣagaṇa*, the suffix *phak* occurs: *āgniśarmāyaṇaḥ*.
In another [text], it is simply "Agniśarman.
One reads "amuṣya" (of him);
from that, by means of a nipātana (irregular formation), there is no elision of the case-ending, resulting in "āmuṣyāyaṇa" (the descendant of such-and-such).
Regarding the rule "kṛṣṇaraṇau brāhmaṇavāsiṣṭhayoḥ":
the words *kṛṣṇa* and *raṇa* produce the suffix *phak* when *brāhmaṇa* and *vāsiṣṭha* are respectively the meanings to be expressed. Thus, *kāṣrṇāyanaḥ* means "a Brāhmaṇa."
*Rāṇāyaṇa* is *Vasiṣṭha*;
the meaning is "one belonging to the Vasiṣṭha lineage.
In other cases, only the suffix *iñ* occurs—as in *Kāṣṇa* and *Rāṇi*.
He reads [the sūtra] as "kroṣṭu-kroṣṭañ-ca.
The word *kroṣṭu* produces the suffix *phak*, and it also undergoes the change to *kroṣṭan*—thus [the form] *krauṣṭāyanaḥ*. The objection begins with "And not," etc.;
the resolution is stated beginning with "This is true," etc.
The suffix *phak* is prescribed after those [words] beginning with *harita* that end in a *gotra* suffix.
Since no further *gotra* suffix can follow another *gotra* suffix,
it is understood by implication that even though the governing rule concerns *gotra*, the suffix applies to the *yuvan* (descendant) degree.

If this is so, for what purpose is the section on *gotra* (lineage)? He says: "The section on *gotra* is for the sake of what follows. Now, why does [the suffix] not occur after that which is prescribed by the rule *yañ* (Pāṇini 4.1.105) and that which is prescribed by the rule *vṛddhācchaṇ* (Pāṇini 4.2.114)—namely, the suffix *iñ* after *sutaṅgama* and others—since no specific distinction has been mentioned here? To this he says: "*yañ* after *dvīpa* when referring to the ocean," and so forth.
For by the mention of *gotra*, the two suffixes *yañ* and *iñ* are specified here as "those *yañ* and *iñ* suffixes which occur in the sense of *gotra*."

Furthermore, the suffix *yañ* is not prescribed by the rule "from *dvīpa*, etc. [Pāṇini 4.3.10] for the sense of a lineage (*gotra*); rather, it is prescribed for specific meanings such as "born there" (*jāta*). Nor is the suffix *iñ* prescribed after *sutaṅgama* and others for the sense of a lineage; rather, it is prescribed in four senses, beginning with "that which exists in this place" [Pāṇini 4.2.68, 70]. Therefore, [the suffixes] do not occur after words ending in those [suffixes]. If, then, *yañ* and *iñ* are qualified here by the mention of "lineage," and not by the meaning of the suffix itself, then it would not be understood where these suffixes occur. To address this, he says: "after that which ends in... and so forth.
To the question "Why is that?", he says: "Because of the statement 'the feminine [is formed] from *gotra* and so forth. Regarding this, [he explains]: "'*Gotra*' refers to this [term]."

If, then, the term *gotra* (lineage) is understood to carry over [from the previous rule], it would not be appropriate for the base forms *bhṛgu* and *vatsa* to qualify the meaning of the suffix, because by those two [bases] themselves, which already possess the *gotra*-suffixes, the meaning of the suffix—the descendant of a lineage—is capable of being qualified. Therefore, one might rightly say: "among the Bhārgavas, Vātsyāyanas, and Āgrāyaṇas"? This is not a fault; for by the force of the governing topic (*adhikāra*) of *gotra*, the two bases here are understood as referring specifically to the descendant of a lineage, having applied a metaphorical designation (*upacāra*) of the cause to the effect.

In order to demonstrate that very same application of the suffixes to the offspring of a lineage (*gotrāpatya*) for those two [suffixes], it is stated in the commentary: "If he is a Bhārgava, he becomes a Śāradvatāyana; if he is a Vātsya, he becomes a Śaunakāyana. "How so? and so forth.

If the suffix *phak* occurs after Droṇa and others in the sense of the offspring of a lineage, then how is it that in usages such as "Drauṇāyana" (the son of Droṇa), Āsthāman is called the "immediate descendant"? "It is not so here," [is the reply]. It is not the case that the present-day Droṇa is meant, nor that one is called "Droṇāyana" by means of the suffix *phak* in the sense of his immediate offspring. What then? "It is beginningless" (*anādi*).
This was stated for the purpose of demonstrating the possibility of [the name] being derived from *śruti*.
By means of the phrase "by which reason," he now demonstrates why he is called Ātthāman, the son of Droṇa, starting with "but from the contemporary," and so forth.
"But from the contemporary," etc.
This should be understood as referring to the exclusion of the ancient Droṇa. For the Droṇa of the *Mahābhārata* is certainly not contemporary; he is long past.
Yet, even an object that is long past attains a state of presentness when it is being contemplated by the mind, as in the expression: "Let Kaṃsa be killed today."

The designation of Ātthāman as "Drauṇāyana"—by means of a secondary suffix (*gotra-pratyaya*)—even though he is the son of the contemporary Droṇa, occurs through superimposition (*adhyāropa*). Superimposition is the attribution to something of that which does not actually exist there.
Of what is there the superimposition? Of the *gotra*.

Regarding the phrase "due to the similarity of sound" (*śrutisāmānyāt*): this is the reason for the superimposition (*adhyāropa*). There is a commonality of sound (*samānā śrutiḥ*) between Droṇa, who is the father of the eternally existing Aśvatthāman, and [the word] *droṇa*.

Therefore, because of the similarity of sound, perceivers whose minds are unsettled by this phonetic resemblance superimpose upon Ātthāman—the son of Droṇa who is a descendant of Bharata—the quality of being a *gotra*, which belongs to the lineage of the ancient Droṇa; through that superimposition, the designation "Droṇāyana" is applied to him. As for the passage beginning with "But those words here [which are] not names of sages," and so forth: [The text continues: "In the case of words such as ‘Vaiyāsaki,’ ‘Jātukarṇya,’ and ‘Maudgalya,’ the suffix *iñ* is applied according to the rule ‘From *vyāsa* and others, *iñ*’ (*vyāsavaruḍaniṣāda...*) to denote a descendant. However, since these individuals are not actually sages, the application of the suffix is based on a figurative usage (*upacāra*). Just as one might say, ‘This man is a lion’ when he possesses the qualities of a lion, so too the word ‘sage’ is applied metaphorically to these persons because they possess certain sage-like qualities. Furthermore, the word ‘sage’ is used here in its primary sense (*mukhya*) with respect to the lineage of Vyāsa and others, while it is used in a secondary sense (*gauṇa*) with respect to the individuals themselves. Thus, there is no contradiction. [The text concludes: "As for the statement ‘And because of the similarity of sound,’ etc.: even though the word ‘sage’ is used here in its primary sense with respect to the lineage, yet due to the similarity of sound, perceivers whose minds are unsettled superimpose the status of being a *gotra*—which is the property belonging to the lineage of the ancient Droṇa—upon Ātthāman, the son of Droṇa who is a descendant of Bharata. Through that superimposition, the designation ‘Droṇāyana’ comes to be applied to him. [The text ends with: "As for the passage beginning with ‘But those words here [which are] not names of sages,’ etc. (as previously cited).

But surely, in the Sūtra the word *ānantarya* is employed with an abstract suffix (*bhāvapratyaya*); in that case, it should be explained as follows: "Furthermore, regarding those words such as *putra* ('son') and others which do not denote a seer (*ṛṣi*), does the suffix occur only when there is immediate succession of offspring (*apatyānantarya*)? This is not so; for this suffix *ṣyañ* is not prescribed in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāve*), but rather in its own primary sense (*svārthe*), just as in the case of *cāturvarṇya*. Otherwise, the suffix would denote the property of being immediately successive in relation to the offspring (*apatyasya dharma ānantarye pratyayaḥ*), and not the offspring itself, yet that is what is intended here.

But how is it that, while the topic is *gotra* (lineage), the suffix is obtained only for the immediate offspring (*anantarāpatya*) after words denoting *ṛṣis* (sages)? Here, the mention of *gotra* is set aside;

[the rule] applies as "after words denoting *ṛṣis*, the suffix *svaṅ* occurs only for the immediate offspring. To this he says: "This is the application of the rule 'anṛṣyānantarya' (Pāṇini 4.1.104)," and so forth. "If this is the meaning," and so forth.

In this context, the phrase "immediate [descent] from a non-seer" (anṛṣyānantarya) serves to specify the intended meaning; for the rule prescribes an affix for the offspring immediately following a non-seer.

Consequently, one might think that no prohibition has been made regarding immediate descent from a seer; therefore, he says: "The word 'seer' (ṛṣi) here refers to the genus of seers (ṛṣijāti) or to the state of being a seer (ṛṣitva).
[The term 'immediacy'] applies to the offspring."
The compound is formed through a *yogavibhāga* (splitting of the rule) based on [Pāṇini 2.1.39] *saptamī*.
Subsequently, there is a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*) meaning "the uninterrupted succession of the offspring of a seer.

Thus, the meaning becomes this: the prohibition of the suffix *añ* would not have been established regarding the uninterrupted succession of offspring belonging to the state of being a seer (*ṛṣitva*).

Alternatively—*ṛṣyapatyāni* means "the ṛṣis and their offspring"; the meaning is that there should be no prohibition regarding the suffix *añ* in relation to the continuity (*nairantarya*) among them.
What is the fault in that? He says: "In this regard, this... and so forth.

There are seven Kāśyapa ṛṣis who are connected to one another through the relationship of parent and child, of whom the seventh is the Kāśyapa named Mitrāhu; there is continuity among the offspring of those who possess the status of being *uṣitva*.
In this regard, a prohibition of the suffix *añ* is desired for the descendants of sages (*ṛṣyapatya*) when there is continuity [of lineage], so that the form "kāśyapānām" may be obtained.
If the suffix *añ* were present, because it is not elided when applied to a plural, the form "kāśyapānām" would result;
however, since that prohibition does not apply in this particular sense, the form "kāśyapānām" is not established.

Therefore, the intention is that the meaning of the rule *anṛṣyānantarye* is understood as "it does not occur when there is an uninterrupted lineage of seers' offspring. Regarding the phrase "only in the form of an immediate offspring," what is intended here is not the offspring of a *gotra*.
What then? What then? It is the immediate offspring.

Therefore, by means of the suffix *ṛṣyaṇ*—which is prescribed for [lineages such as] Ṛṣi, Andhaka, and so forth, in the sense of immediate offspring [according to Pāṇini 4.1.114]—the designation "Kāśyapāḥ" will come to be.
To strengthen this very point, he says: "And necessarily," and so forth.

That prohibition whose scope (*viṣaya*) is the uninterrupted succession (*nairantarya*) of the offspring of sages (*ṛṣyapatya*) is described as such. The meaning is that when the prohibition is understood as applying to the uninterrupted succession of the offspring of sages, or to those who are themselves the offspring of sages— for example,
[the statement] "one is censured for saying 'Kauśika is a Vāsiṣṭha'."

What is the reason? Viśvāmitra performed austerity, thinking, "May I not be one who is not a seer (*ṛṣi*). Thereupon, he became a venerable seer. He again performed austerity, thinking, "May I not have a son who is not a seer. Thereupon, the venerable Gādhi also became a seer. He again performed austerity, thinking, "May I not have a grandson who is not a seer. Thereupon, the venerable Kuśika also became a seer.
Thus, there occurs either an uninterrupted succession of the state of being a seer among the descendants, or an uninterrupted succession of those who are the offspring of seers.

Furthermore, if it were understood that there is no continuity [of lineage] in the case of the offspring of sages (*ṛṣi*), then the form *kauśika* as a *viśvāmitra* would not be established. Regarding the rule "the wife of another and the axe" (*parastrī paraśuśca*): the word *parastrī* causes a suffix to arise and undergoes the substitution of *parasya*.

The offspring of another's wife is a *pāraśava*. As for the question "How is *mānavī* a progeny?"—since it must be included among the *gargādi* group, the suffix *yañ* should apply; consequently, the form *mānavī* would not be established.
The intention is that since the suffix *ṣpha* is prescribed after a word ending in *yañ* when it has the characteristic of [denoting] *lohita* and so forth, the form should be *mānavyāyanī*.
However, it is called "lineage" (*gotra*), for the suffix *yañ* is prescribed in the sense of lineage, not in the general sense of offspring.
Therefore, in that case, by the general rule, the suffix *aṇ* will apply, resulting in the form *mānavī*.
"How so? and so forth.

If it is said that [the suffix] is used for a *gotra*, then just as the suffix *yañ* does not occur after the word *garga* when referring to a direct descendant (*anantarāpatya*), so too it should not occur after the words *jamadagni* and *parāśara*. How then is it that the suffix *yañ* occurs in such cases as "Rāma, son of Jamadagni" (*jāmadagnya*) and "Vyāsa, son of Parāśara" (*pārāśarya*)? [Response: "It will occur through the superimposition of the form of a *gotra*.

When Rāma and Vyāsa, though they are direct descendants, are intended to be expressed as having the form of a *gotra*, then the superimposition of the form of a *gotra* is performed; thus, the occurrence of *yañ* is without fault.

It is not to be assumed that the desire to speak (*vivakṣā*) regarding what is non-existent is illogical; for the desire to speak is observed even with respect to what does not exist, such as "the Vindhya is a *vardhitaka*" (a small mound) or "the ocean is a *kuṇḍikā*" (a small water-pot).
When, then, there is a desire to speak of an intermediate descendant, he says: "But when there is a desire to speak of an intermediate descendant," and so forth.
[The example is] "vājāse."
The word *vāja* causes the suffix *yañ* to arise;

that is to say, when not in a compound (*asamāse*). Why [is it said] "when not in a compound"? [Consider] *sauvājiḥ*. If, then, since the word *babhru* is already established by its inclusion in the *gargādi* list, its mention here for the sake of *kauśika* is for the purpose of restriction (*niyamārtham*), then there is no need for its inclusion in the *gargādi* list; let its mention be solely for the purpose of an injunction (*vidhyartham*) regarding *kauśika*, and not for this [restriction]. To this he says: "Even its inclusion in the *gargādi* list," and so forth.

The reading [of *garga*] and others must also be included in the list so that the internal-group operation (*antargaṇakārya*) of *ṣpha* may apply by the rule "In all cases, after *lohita*, etc. (Pāṇini 4.1.18).

Now, why was *kauśika* not included in the list? What advantage would there be in doing so? In that case, the mention of *babhru* in the sūtra would no longer be necessary. This is true; however, the list is not the work of Pāṇini.
Pāṇini does not deserve criticism for not doing it this way;
for what has not also been done by the author of the Gaṇapāṭha? It was done for the sake of variety, for the composition of the Gaṇapāṭha by its author is indeed diverse—as in the case of *kāpeyaḥ*.

From this [rule] *itaścāmiñaḥ* [Pāṇini 4.1.122], the suffix *ḍhañ* is applied. If the word *kapi* were recited among the *gargādi* group, its inclusion here would be for the sake of restriction; since that is the case, let its inclusion here simply be for the purpose of a mandatory rule (*vidhi*) regarding the descendant of Aṅgiras—what need is there for its recitation among the *gargādi*? To this he says: "And for the sake of the grammatical operations pertaining to the *lohita* group," and so forth. For what purpose is this? The meaning is: this is purposeless. He asks: "What is the reason? and answers with "Insofar as... and so forth.
By the words "even in the case of Śiva and others," etc., he demonstrates the purpose [of the rule].

If this were not stated, then just as the suffix *yañ* occurs for [a descendant of] Āṅgirasa due to the inclusion [of the name] in the *Gargādi* group, so too would the suffix *aṇ* occur for [a descendant of] Śiva and others due to their inclusion in the *Śivādi* group.
Therefore, the repetition is for the sake of ensuring that the suffix *yañ* for Āṅgirasa supersedes the suffix *aṇ* for Śiva and others.

Now, since [the desired form] is already established by its inclusion in the *Gargādi* list, why has it not been stated that this [rule] is for the sake of restriction (*niyamārtha*) regarding the *Āṅgirasa* lineage? It is impossible to say so; for a rule serves as a restriction only when there is no other purpose.

But here there is a purpose, and that has indeed been demonstrated. Regarding "vātaṇḍāyanī": [this is formed] with the suffix *ṣpha*, which is characterized by the *lohita* group. Regarding "ye tv atra" and so forth...

Because of the statement [in Pāṇini 4.1.93], "no further gotra-suffix is applicable after that which already ends in a gotra-suffix," it follows by implication that even though the governing rule concerns non-gotra suffixes, when those items ending in a gotra-suffix are listed [in the Gaṇapāṭha], the suffix for the *yuvan* (descendant) is understood to apply to them according to [Pāṇini 4.1.94]. Thus: "after Śap, [the suffix is applied] when [referring to] Ātreya."
From the word *śapa*, if it refers to an Ātreya, the suffix *phañ* is applied; thus, *śāpāyana* is an Ātreya, whereas otherwise it is *śāpi*.

The word *vailya* ends in a *gotra* suffix; from that, the suffix for the younger generation (*yuvan*) is applied. *Vili* was a royal sage (*rājarṣi*); his descendant in the *gotra* line is *vailya*, and his young descendant is *vailiyāyana*.

The word *ānaḍuhra* also ends in a *gotra* suffix because it belongs to the *garga*-class and ends in *yañ*; from that [base] as well, the suffix *phañ* occurs only for the junior descendant (*yuvan*)—thus, *ānaḍuhrāyana* is the junior descendant.

In the feminine, only the suffix *ḍhak* occurs—as in *jāteyaḥ*, the offspring of *jātā*. [As stated in the rule: "In the case of *ātreyī*, [the form is used] when [referring to] a descendant of Bhāradvāja."
From the word *Ātreya*, the suffix *phañ* is applied if it refers to a descendant of Bhāradvāja: *Ātreyāyaṇa* when he is a Bhāradvāja; otherwise, *Ātreyi*.

[The rule] "Bhāradvāja [is used] for Ātreya" means that from the word *Bhāradvāja*, the suffix *phañ* is applied when the specific descendant is Ātreya: *Bhāradvājāyana* when he is an Ātreya; otherwise, the suffix *ṛṣyaṇ* is applied. [The term] "accordingly" (*yathāyatham*) means...
"According to their respective [rules].
For whichever suffix, such as *iñ* and so on, belongs to a particular [base], the suffix *aṇ* is prescribed in place of that [suffix] at the beginning of the word.

Now, what is the purpose of mentioning *aṇ*? Why not simply say "from *śiva* and so on"? If it is argued that if only "from *śiva* and so on" were stated, the suffixes *iñ* and so on—which are prescribed according to their respective rules—might occur instead of *aṇ*, and this is for the sake of ensuring that *aṇ* alone occurs; this is not so. This statement would be useless regarding the suffixes *iñ* and so on as prescribed by their respective rules, because even without this [mention of *aṇ*], they would be established.
Therefore, even without the mention of the suffix *aṇ*, it will indeed be *aṇ* alone [that applies].

But surely, if the mention of *aṇ* were absent, because *phañ* is the subject under discussion, the rule would be understood as applying to that (*phañ*) alone? This is not so; for if it were intended to prescribe *phañ* after words such as *śiva* and others, then one would have listed them right there among the *āyādi* group.
What, then, is the purpose? This word *auṣṭriṣeṇa* is listed among the *śivādi* group; consequently, the suffix *ṇya* would apply to it by [Pāṇini 4.1.152].

In this context, if the mention of *aṇ* were not made, this rule [P. 4.1.152] would have its purpose fulfilled merely by setting aside that [rule for *iñ*]; consequently, only *iñ* as prescribed [by P. 4.1.95] would apply, and not *aṇ*. Therefore, the mention of *aṇ* is made so that *aṇ* itself may apply. Regarding the phrase "in order to set aside the *iñ* of the Northern Grammarians":
by the rule "of the Northern Grammarians" (P. 4.1.153), *iñ* would otherwise be applicable; therefore, the word *takṣan* is read here in order to set aside that [*iñ*].

If that were the case, since the word *takṣan* is read here, the *iñ* of the Northern Grammarians is set aside; however, it follows that there would also be a setting aside of the *ṇya* suffix [prescribed by P. 4.1.152].
And so, would not the form *tākṣṇyaḥ* fail to be established? To this he says: "But the sublation of the suffix *ṇya* is not intended.
How is it that it does not occur even though it is not intended? Because of its association with words such as *supiṣṭa*.

Here, the word *takṣan* which is recited together with *supiṣṭa*, *mayūra*, *khara*, *dūra*, and *takṣan*—just as their recitation here is for the purpose of setting aside the suffix *iñ*—by virtue of that association, the recitation of this [word *takṣan*] will also be understood as being solely for the purpose of setting aside *iñ*.
In this context, the statement regarding *śiva* and others is for the purpose of setting aside the suffix *iñ* that would otherwise apply after words beginning with *bhūri*.
For *bhūri*, *saṃdhi*, and *muni*, the suffix *ḍhak* would have been applicable by rule 4.1.122.

Regarding *kuṭhāra* and *anabhimlāna*, as well as those beginning with *kakutstha*, the statement is for the purpose of subverting the suffix *iñ* that would otherwise apply after words beginning with *jaratkāru*.
Regarding the words beginning with *jāratakāru* and ending before *supiṣṭa*, the suffix *ḍhak* would otherwise apply by [Pāṇini 4.1.120].

Regarding the words beginning with *supiṣṭa* and ending before *takṣan*, the suffix *iñ* applies. For the word *takṣan*, the suffix *iñ* is applied according to the rule for agents (kārila-kṣaṇa) by the Eastern grammarians.
This is for the purpose of excluding *ṛṣṭiṣeṇa*, *senānta*, *lakṣama*, *ṇya*, and others.
Regarding the inclusion of the words *gaṅgā* and *ādi* where [the suffix] was not otherwise applicable, this has been explained by the author of the Vṛtti himself:
since the suffix *iñ* would have applied to words beginning with *bhūmi* prior to the rule for *yaska* and others, their inclusion here serves to exclude that.
The suffix *ḍhak* is applied to the word *bhūmi* by [Pāṇini 4.1.122];
likewise, the suffix *ḍhak* is applied to the word *ilā* by the rule *dvyacaśca* [4.1.121];
and in the same way, the suffix *ḍhak* is applied to the word *sapatnī* by [Pāṇini 4.1.120].

Regarding the rule *dvyaco nadyāḥ*: the suffix *aṇ* occurs after two-syllable words that denote rivers. For example, from *sandhyā*, we have *sāndhyam*; from *kulyā*, we have *kaulyam*. But surely the *aṇ* belonging to the class of proper names (*tannāmika*) already applies here? True, it does apply; however, it is superseded by the suffix *ḍhak* [according to Pāṇini 4.1.121].
Therefore, there is this statement for the purpose of overriding that [previous rule]:
"The forms *triveṇī* and *trivaṇaṃ*. Thus, the word *triveṇī* causes a suffix to arise and becomes *trivaṇaṃ*.

The offspring of Triveṇī is Traivaṇa. Although there is a technical definition (*paribhāṣā*) in another treatise stating that "the term *vṛddha* refers to an elided descendant," there is also a technical definition of *vṛddha* in this very treatise [at 1.1.73]. Consequently, regarding the prohibition of *vṛddha*, someone might have a doubt: "Of which *vṛddha* is there a prohibition—is it the prohibition of that which is defined here in this treatise, or of that which is defined by another treatise? Therefore, in order to dispel that doubt:

He shows that this is a prohibition of that which has been defined as "vṛddhi" in this grammar by the rule *vṛddhir yasya* (Pāṇini 1.1.73) and so forth. But how is it determined that this prohibition applies specifically to that which is defined here as "vṛddha"? Because a name of a river or a human being cannot possibly end with a *gotra*-suffix.
In this context, however, by the mention of "river" (*nadī*), only the worldly river is understood, and not the technical one.
Why is this so? Because of the association with the word *mānuṣī*, which functions in its worldly sense.
Now, why is there not a reference to the actual phonetic form of the words *nadī* and *mānuṣī*? Because of the prohibition regarding the *vṛddha* [technical] term.

For if the word-form itself were being referred to, the prohibition regarding "vṛddha" would be meaningless, as there would be no occasion for its application. Furthermore, because of the use of the plural number, it cannot be a reference to the word-form itself. For if the word-form were being referred to, since the words *nadī* and *mānuṣī* are duals, one would have used the dual number in the reference instead.
[Otherwise] it would be a property of the word-form (*śabdadharmah*), as in [the rule] *avṛddhābhyaḥ*.

If, then, this is a property of the meaning (*arthadharmaḥ*), how is it that by the rule *nadīmānuṣībhyaḥ* the base forms (*prakṛtayaḥ*) are indicated? For in this way, only a property of the meaning is indicated, not the base forms. To this he says: "By that," and so forth.
By that, through the metaphorical application (*upacāraḥ*) of the distinction of meaning.
The base forms (prakṛtis) denoting river-nouns are being pointed out.
Regarding the term "pratyayaprakṛtiḥ":
it is a genitive compound (ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa), meaning "the base form of an affix."
"An exception to the suffix *ḍhak*":
because the names of rivers that do not begin with a *vṛddhi* vowel and the names of human females end in feminine suffixes. Examples are "vaitastaḥ" and "nārmadaḥ."
The suffix *aṇ* is applied after the words *vitastā* and *narmadā*, as in *vaitastaḥ* and *nārmadaḥ*.
After the word *śikṣita*, [the suffix *ṭhak* is applied], as in *śaikṣitaḥ*. After [the word *suparṇī*], the forms *sauparṇeyaḥ* and *vainateyaḥ* [are derived].
The words *suparṇā* and *avinatā* are names of birds, not [names of] a river or a human female.

Regarding the term *śaubhaneya*: the word *śobhanā* occurs here as the name of a river or a human female, but not as a proper name (*saṃjñā*); rather, it functions as an adjective (*viśeṣaṇa*). "An exception to *iñ*" means: [End of excerpt]

Now, one might object: "Since the suffixes *ḍhak* and others apply after words ending in vowels other than *a*, excluding those beginning with *atri*, it would be more logical for [the rule under discussion] to be an exception (*apavāda*) to them. To this, he says: "But from *atri* and so forth," and so on. By the first word "and so forth" (*ādi*), the sages such as Jātaseṇa and others, as well as those belonging to the Andhaka clan such as Ugrasena and others, are included; by the second, the suffixes *ṇya* and others are included. In that regard, the scope (*avakāśa*) of the *ṛṣya-ṇ* suffix is [in the case of] Vāsiṣṭha; the scope of the *ḍhak* suffix [by rule 4.1.122] is Dauleya. When both are applicable after the word *atri*, the *ḍhak* suffix occurs because it is subsequent [in the order of rules], resulting in Āttreya.

The scope for the suffix *aṇ* is the same [as before]; the scope for the suffix *ṇya*, which follows *senānta*, is as follows: *kāriṣeṇyaḥ*, *hāriṣeṇyaḥ*. There is a sage named Jātasena; when both [suffixes] would apply, *ṇya* occurs by virtue of being subsequent:

*jātasenyaḥ*. The scope for the suffix *aṇ* after *andhaka* is *vāsudevaḥ*; the scope for *ṇya* is the same. There is a Vṛṣṇi named Śūrasena or Viṣvaksena; when both would apply, *ṇya* occurs by virtue of being subsequent: *śaurasenyaḥ*, *vaiṣvaksenyaḥ*.
The scope of *kuru-ṇya* is *nākula*; the scope of *ṇya* is the same. An Andhaka named Ugrasena: when both [suffixes] would apply, *ṇya* occurs by virtue of its posteriority—*augrasenyaḥ*.

The scope of *vṛṣṇi-aṇ* is *vāsudeva*; the scope of *ṇya* is the same. A Vṛṣṇi named Śūrasena or Viṣvaksena: when both would apply, *ṇya* occurs by virtue of its posteriority—*śaurasenyaḥ*, *vaiṣvaksenyaḥ*.

The scope for the application of *kurvan* is when the suffix *nākula* is not present; for *ṇya*, that same scope applies. *Bhīmasena* is a *kuru*; since both [suffixes] would otherwise apply, *ṇya* occurs by virtue of its higher status: *bhaimasenyaḥ*. The objection beginning with "How then... is the challenge.
The resolution of the challenge begins with "Some say...".
[The example is] "the accidental occurrence" (*kākatālīyam*).
The meaning is "not preceded by conscious intention. "Collected" means "accumulated."
"Always [plural]" refers to the fact that the lineages of Andhaka and the others are beginningless. Regarding "born of two mothers":
first, the *dvi* is applied in the sense of a secondary derivative (*taddhita*), and subsequently, the secondary derivative suffix is applied.

Regarding "sāmmāturaḥ": first there is a *prādisamāsa* (prepositional compound), and afterwards the *taddhita* suffix. Regarding "bhādramāturaḥ": first there is a *viśeṣaṇasamāsa* (attributive compound); then the *taddhita* suffix. Now, why is the statement not made regarding the meaning of the suffix? To this he says: "But the suffix," and so forth.

[This is] by the very rule characterized as *utsarga*, namely [Pāṇini 4.1.92]. Now, one might object: "The status of being preceded by a numeral and so forth is a qualifier of the word *mātṛ*; therefore, since the reference is made with respect to the word *mātṛ*, it is seen to be in the masculine gender (*puṃlliṅga*) alone. So how can there be a reference in the feminine gender (*strīliṅga*) as in the expression ‘*saṃkhyā-sambhadra-pūrvāyāḥ*’? To this he says: "The reference in the feminine gender is with respect to the meaning. This reference is dependent upon the meaning of the word *mātuḥ*, and that meaning is feminine.
The designation was made using the feminine gender.
By the words "by that" (*tena*) and so forth, he demonstrates the result of [the rule] being dependent on the meaning.

For when the designation in the feminine gender is dependent on the meaning, only that word whose meaning is feminine—namely the word *mātṛ*—should be understood; therefore, there is no inclusion of a female slave (*dāsīmātṛ*).
For its referent is not feminine; rather, it is masculine. A laborer who measures grain is called a *dhānyamāta*. Regarding the term *saumātra*:
first, it is a *prādi*-compound (*pra-ādi-samāsa*).

"Therefore, the general rule [Pāṇini 4.1.83] applies the suffix *aṇ*. Here, the words *Vatsa*, *Bharadvāja*, and *Atri* are employed as having their application restricted to the specific lineages (*gotra*) of Vātsya, Bhāradvāja, and Ātreya.

For this very reason, he says: 'If he is a Vaikarṇa, he is a Vātsya; if he is a Śauṅga, he is a Bhāradvāja; if he is a Cāgala, he is an Ātreya. Furthermore, that application of these [words] to the offspring of the lineage should be understood through the metaphorical transfer of the cause to the effect. And both of these [interpretations] are authoritative."

But how can that which is mutually contradictory also be a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*)? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "For this sūtra was composed by the Teacher in both ways; therefore, what contradiction is there? Here, by the mention of "feminine" (*strī*), words ending in feminine suffixes such as *ṭāp* and so forth are understood. Now, why is it not a reference to the word-form itself (*svarūpa*)? Because of the use of the plural number. For if it were a reference to the word-form itself, since that is singular, he would have used the singular number in the designation.

Why is there not a grasping of the word *strī* (woman) alone for the meaning "female"? Because the word *vimātṛ* (stepmother), which has the meaning "female," is included among the *śubhra* group [of words].

If, in this context, the word *strī* alone were intended to mean "female," then its inclusion in the *śubhra* group would be purposeless, since the suffix *ḍhak* would already be established by this very rule. [Examples:
*aiḍaviḍaḥ*, *dāradaḥ*.

In the case of *iḍaviḍa* and *varada*, only the suffix *aṇ* occurs, as in *iḍaviḍasyāpatyam* and *varadasyāpatyam*. While the suffix *ḍhak* was already in force, the explicit mention of *ḍhak* again is for the sake of making it obligatory. [This applies] when the offspring of *vaḍavā* is to be expressed as a male (*vṛṣa*).
"He who casts the seed into her womb is called a bull (vṛṣa) or a Vāḍaveya. As for the statement, "It is recorded as being from the krauñca and the kokila," the term *vṛṣa* is not required;
this is simply a rule regarding the offspring.
This is an exception (*apavāda*) to the suffix *ḍhak*. It is an exception to the suffix *aṇ* prescribed by the rule *tannāmikāṇ*.

For those two-syllable feminine stems that denote the names of rivers or human females, the suffix *aṇ* applies because it is specifically ordained for them; therefore, the suffix *ḍhak* is prescribed in order to set aside that [suffix *aṇ*]. The phrase "according to the requirements" (*yathāyogam*), and so forth, [is used].
First, for those [words] ending in /a/, this [suffix *iñ*] is an exception (*apavāda*).
From the words *śalākā*, *kurekā*, *ambikā*, *aśokā*, *khaṭvā*, *piṅgalā*, and *khaṇḍonmattā*, the suffix *tannāmikā-ṇ* applies.
From the word *vidhavā*, the suffix *ḍhrak* applies as a characteristic of a low-caste woman (*kṣudrā*).
From *kiṃkaṣā*, *rohiṇī*, *ajavasti*, *śakandhi*, *kṛkalāsa*, *sudatta*, and *paridhi*, the suffix *ḍhañ* is applied to denote the characteristic of four-footed animals.
From the word *godhā*, the suffix *ḍhrak* is applied; by the force of the explicit statement, that [suffix] also indeed occurs.
For the remaining words, the general suffix *aṇ* is applied; such is the meaning according to their respective application.
Regarding the rule "after *lakṣaṇa* and *śyāma*, [the suffix] *ḍhak* occurs in the *Vāsiṣṭha* lineage":
after these two words, *lakṣaṇa* and *śyāma*, the suffix *ḍhak* occurs when referring to a specific descendant of the *Vāsiṣṭha* lineage.
Thus, *lākṣaṇeyaḥ* refers to a *Vāsiṣṭha*, whereas *lākṣaṇiḥ* refers to another.
Śyāmeyyaḥ belongs to the Vasiṣṭha lineage, while Śyāmāyana belongs to another;
[the suffix] *phañ* is applied because [Vasiṣṭha] begins with a vowel (*a*). She who wanders through families is a *kulaṭā*.

Now, one might object that since the long vowel substitution (*dīrghatva*) applies when [the suffix] *aka* follows a word ending in a vowel of the same class (*savarṇa*), the form should be *kulāṭā*; to this he replies with "the subsequent form" (*pararūpa*), and so forth.
"By the very same [rule]" means by this very rule, *pūrveṇaiva* (Pāṇini 4.1.120).
The designation "prior" (*pūrva*) applies even when there is an intervening element, as in: "Pāṭaliputra is prior to Mathurā. Regarding "kaulaṭeraḥ":

once the substitution of *ey* has been made, there is the elision of *y* after a semivowel (*vali yalopaḥ*). Regarding "the female offspring of a *caṭakā* is a *caṭakā*": [this is derived from the feminine base].

When the elision (*luk*) has been applied by [Pāṇini 4.1.89] *iti luki kṛte*, the feminine suffix *ṭāp* must be applied again. Even from a masculine base, elision is indeed desired when the feminine is intended. Thus, this rule was originally *caṭakād airak*; at present, however, due to a scribal error, the reading is *caṭakāyāḥ*. [The example is] *godheraḥ*.
As before, there is the elision of *yal*. Regarding the statement, "The mention of the Teacher (*ācārya*) is for the sake of honor":

one might object that if the mention of the Teacher were absent, this rule would be mandatory (*nitya*); and in that case, there would be no co-occurrence (*samāveśa*) of the suffix *ḍhrak* with the preceding [suffix *kan*] in the word *āraka*.
Why, then, does the mention of the Teacher not serve the purpose of making it optional? To this he replies: "By the force of the explicit statement (*vacana-sāmarthyāt*)."
It is stated both as *ḍhra* and as *āra*; in that case, their co-occurrence will take place by virtue of the expressive power of the statement.
Therefore, the mention of the teacher (*ācārya*) is solely for the sake of honor.
As for the phrase "but it is an indicator" (*jñāpakam tu*), and so forth:
Since the suffix *rak* is already established [by Pāṇini 4.2.80], the mention of *āra* is for the purpose of providing a specific designation (*sañjñā*).

By this very fact, it is understood that this suffix also occurs after other bases; otherwise, the mention of *āra* would be redundant, as the form is already established by *rak*. Consequently, forms such as *jāḍāraḥ* (the offspring of a dull-witted person) and *pāṇḍāraḥ* are established, for these would not be established by *rak* alone. Thus, it is said: "by means of the property of the meaning."

Because the object [denoted] is insignificant, the constituent elements (*prakṛti*) that express it are also designated as "insignificant" (*kṣudra*) by way of metaphorical usage. As for the passage beginning with "How then," etc.:

since the rule for the suffix *ḍhak* requires the inclusion of feminine suffixes such as *ṭāp* and others, and because the word *pitṛṣvasṛ* does not end in a feminine suffix, the question arises from one who considers the application of *ḍhak* to be impossible.
Regarding the phrase "this very [fact]" and so forth:
this very reliance upon the word *pitṛṣvasṛ* as the cause for the suffix *ḍhak* makes known its status as such from the word *pitṛṣvasṛ*.
For a short vowel cannot logically function as a cause [for a grammatical operation]. [The commentary] states: "It refers to this [word] *pitṛṣvasṛ*."

Here too, according to the principle that "for what is immediate, there is either an injunction or a prohibition," only elision (*lopa*) would apply immediately [to the suffix], not *chaṇ*, because it is separated [by other elements]. Since both of these results are desired, he demonstrates the reason by which both are obtained with the words "of the father’s sister" (*pitṛṣvasuḥ*).

When this [term] is required here, it is understood as being in the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhanta*), just as in the rule for elision, *pitṛṣvasuḥ* [Pāṇini 4.1.132], where there is a genitive; thus the following meaning is established: whatever was stated regarding the father’s sister (*pitṛṣvasṛ*) applies to the mother’s sister (*mātṛṣvasṛ*) as well, so that by that [rule], the suffix *chaṇ* and the elision (*lopa*) of the *ḍhak* are obtained.
For both of these were indeed stated in reference to the father’s sister. Regarding the term *catuṣpādbhyaḥ*:
those things which have four feet are so designated.

There is elision [of the suffix] according to the rule *pādasya lopo hastyādibhyaḥ* [Pāṇini 5.4.138]. Here too, the bases (*prakṛti*) that denote those [meanings] are indicated by means of the property of their referents (*artha-dharma*). For this very reason, he says: "from the bases denoting four-footed [animals]."
The use of the plural number is for the purpose of excluding a rule that would prescribe their own specific forms.
In the phrase "of *aṇ* and the rest," the word "and the rest" (*ādi*) includes *ḍhak* and the other suffixes.
Regarding the passage beginning with *kāmaṇḍaleyaḥ*:

the words *kamaṇḍalu*, *śunti*, *bāhu*, and *jambu* denote species of four-footed animals. In these cases, there is the elision of the vowel *u* by the rule *ḍhe lopo’kadravāḥ* [Pāṇini 6.4.147]. This is an exception (*apavāda*) to the suffixes *aṇ* and others;
by the word "and others" (*ādi*), the suffix *ḍhak* is included.
The use of the plural number in the rule is intended to express the distinction between those two suffixes based on the difference in their respective bases.

Among them, for the words *aja*, *vastimant*, and *yū*, this [suffix] is an exception (*apavāda*) to the suffix *aṇ*; for the remaining words, it is an exception to the suffix *ḍhak* [prescribed by Pāṇini 4.1.122]. Regarding the phrase "if it refers to the Kṣatriya caste":
if the Kṣatriya caste is understood from the word ending in the suffix, then this [suffix] occurs.
One who is indeed childless of the king, even if not of the Kṣatriya caste, becomes [his] general protector (*trāṇa*).
And this is obtained through the understanding that the rule *vā* (Pāṇini 4.1.131), which recurs here, is a restricted option (*vyavasthitavibhāṣā*).
Thus: "a Rājanya."
By [Pāṇini 6.4.168], there is the preservation of the original form (*prakṛtibhāva*).
Regarding "rājñaḥ," here too, by [Pāṇini 6.4.167] *an*, there is the preservation of the original form. [The rule states: "the suffix *gha* occurs."

It should be understood that [the term] *gha* refers only to the suffix *gha*, and not to the suffixes *tarap* and *tamap*. But how is this obtained, given that *gha* is a technical name (*saṃjñā*) for *tarap* and *tamap*, and since a technical name, once uttered, causes the understanding of the named object (*saṃjñin*), it would be more appropriate to take those two [suffixes] alone? This is not a fault; for in a rule prescribing an affix (*pratyaya-vidhi*), wherever the word *gha* is heard, there the form itself (*svarūpa*) is taken. This is due to an indicator (*jñāpaka*).
