Since the author teaches the substitution of *iy* for the *gh* at the beginning of an affix (in Pāṇini 7.1.2), that indicates that wherever *gha* is heard in a rule prescribing an affix, it is the form itself that is taken.

For a substitution of *gh* for the initial sound of a suffix cannot occur when there is the mention of a nominal stem (*saṃjñin*) [by the term *prātipadika*]. Regarding the phrase "In the subsequent rule" and so forth:

since the prohibition of the preceding member (*pūrvapada*) occurs in the subsequent rule, it is understood that this technical rule (*paribhāṣā*), in which the mention of a nominal stem (*prātipadika-śruti*) exists, does not apply here.

For if it were to apply, then—because of the prohibition of the extension of a rule to what ends with a nominal stem (*tadantavidhi*) by one who mentions a nominal stem (P. 1.1.72)—that substitution would not occur after a preceding member anyway; thus, the prohibition "not after a preceding member" (*apūrvapadāt*) would be redundant.

Furthermore, an indicator (*jñāpaka*) depends upon a general rule; therefore, these two technical rules (*paribhāṣā*)—namely, "the treatment as if possessing a designation applies except for a nominal stem" (Śākalya-Pariśiṣṭa 65) and "an operation involving a nominal stem that includes a suffix is not desired to apply to what ends with that [stem]" (Vyāḍi-Pariśiṣṭa 89)—do not apply here either.

Consequently, the nominal stem ending in the word *kula* is understood as the word *kula* itself. Now, one might object: the word *pūrva* denotes a constituent part (*avayava*), yet no other word can logically be a constituent part of the word *kula*, because it is distinct from it and does not contribute to its formation. Therefore, since there is nothing to be excluded, how can this be a qualification of the word *kula* in the phrase "not preceded by another word" (*apūrvapadāt*)? To this he replies: "belonging to a compound," and so forth.
This [distinction] of "prior member" (*pūrvapada*) and "subsequent member" (*uttarapada*) occurs only when a compound exists.
Therefore, because there is an absence of a preceding member (*pūrvapada*) related to a compound, the word *kula* is qualified as "that which has no preceding member related to a compound.

And for what is it non-existent? For that which is not included within a compound—the solitary word *kula*. Thus, it is stated that this rule applies from the solitary word *kula*. Now, why is the word *pūrva* not accepted in its sense of "established order" (*vyavasthā*)? Because it is impossible.
In that context, when [the word] *hrasvīyamāṇa* is not present, a word such as *kula* from which a preceding member (*pūrvapada*) does not exist is called "without a preceding member" (*apūrvapada*).

Consequently, in the sentences *devadattaḥ kulyaḥ* and *devadattaḥ kauleyakaḥ*, the suffixes *yaṅ* and *ḍhakañ* would not occur; for here, the word *devadatta* exists as a preceding member (*pūrvapada*). [The question is: "What is the purpose of mentioning the word *pada*?"
Why was it not stated simply as *apūrvāt*? For even so, the desired result is achieved, and the sūtra becomes more concise—this is what [the author] thinks.
[The purpose is] so that the suffix may occur even after a compound whose prior member (*pūrvapada*) is *bahuc*.
If it were stated as *apūrvāt*, then when *bahuc* is the prior member of a nominal stem—that is, when it is prior to the element *bahuc* itself—the suffix would not be applied from that [stem].
But when there is the inclusion of the word *pada*, it occurs even from that [subsequent element], because that is not a preceding word (*apūrvapada*). For example:

*bahukulyaḥ*. Here, the suffix *bahuc* is applied according to [Pāṇini 5.3.68]: "The suffix *bahuc* is added after a nominal stem ending in a vowel to express 'not quite complete' (*īṣadasamāpta*). Thus, "a family that is not quite complete" is expressed as *bahukulam*.

The offspring of *bahukula* is *bahukulyaḥ*. [Regarding the statement] "the letter *t* is for the sake of the accent": this is so that the circumflex (*svarita*) accent may apply according to Pāṇini 6.1.185. Now, one might object: since the word *sapatnī* alone has been derived as feminine by [Pāṇini 4.1.35], how is the masculine usage *sapatnaḥ* justified? To this he says: "the word *sapatna* is a synonym for 'enemy' (*śatru*)," and so forth.
[The phrase] "in the sense of 'as if'" (*ivārthe*).
The meaning of *iva* is similarity (*sādṛśya*).

For just as a co-wife is a cause of suffering, so too is an enemy; thus, one who is like a co-wife is called a "co-wife" (*sapatnī*) [in a figurative sense]. [This applies] "according to the circumstances," and so forth.

Among those, because the first four end in feminine suffixes (*strī-pratyaya*), they are exceptions (*apavāda*) to the suffix *ḍhak*; for *vṛkañcin*, there is the suffix *aṇ*; and for the remaining ones, because they end in the letter *a*, there is the suffix *iñ*. "The term 'gotra' refers to offspring beginning from the grandson onwards.
This does not mean mere worldly offspring; for if that were the case, the mention of "gotra" would be redundant.
The point is that the inclusion of that [specific type of] offspring is already obtained simply by virtue of the governing context (*adhikāra*) of "offspring" (*apatya*).
Regarding the phrase "in the absence of recognition of the father": this refers to when [the father] is unknown.
By means of that designation made by the mother for the purpose of indicating the lack of recognition of that father, there would be contempt.
Regarding the example "gārgo jālmo gārgikaḥ":

from the word *garga*, which belongs to the *gargādi* group and ends in the suffix *yañ* (denoting a lineage), the feminine suffix *ṅīp* is applied by the rule *yañaśca* [Pāṇini 4.1.16]. When the *it* portion (*i*) is elided by the rule *halastaddhitasya* [Pāṇini 6.4.150], the form *gārgī* remains; subsequently, the suffixes *ṇa* and *ṭhak* are applied. The same applies to *glaucukāyanaḥ* and other such examples.

The feminine descendant (apatyam) in the lineage (gotram) of Glucuka is formed with the suffix *phin* by the rule *prācām avṛddhāt phin bahulam* [Pāṇini 4.1.160]; from that, the suffix *ṅīṣ* is applied by [Pāṇini 4.1.65], and subsequently the suffixes *ṇa* and *ṭhak*. Regarding "Kārikeya": from the word *kāraka* ending in the suffix *ṇvu*, the suffix *ṭāp* is applied; this word *kārikā* does not denote a lineage (*gotra*), therefore only the suffix *ḍhak* occurs.
Regarding "Aupagavi": [this is derived from Upagu].

The offspring of Upagu is a *gotra*; when it is a male, the suffix *ṇ* is applied. After a word ending in that [suffix], only the suffix *iñ* occurs. In this case, contempt should be understood as arising from some practice such as the performance of forbidden acts—for example, "the young brahmin Gārgeya.

Here, because the father is already known, the designation by his [the father's] maternal lineage is made for the purpose of identifying the mother; thus, there is no contempt, and consequently, the suffix *ḍhak* does not occur. The phrase "among the Sauvīras" is a qualification of the base noun (*prakṛti*).
"In Sauvīra," meaning that which is a *vṛddha* [stem] denoting a lineage (*gotra*) from Sauvīra; "from Bhāgavitti, the suffix *ṭa*, etc.
means the descendant of Bhagavitta is a lineage member (*gotra*).
From that which ends in *iñ* [by 4.1.95], the suffix *ṭhak* is applied— yielding *bhāgavittikaḥ*; and by [4.1.101],
the suffix *phak* is applied— yielding *bhāgavittāyanaḥ*.

*Tārṇabindavaḥ* [is derived from] *tṛṇabindu*, where the suffix *aṇ* is applied by the general rule (*autsargika*) to denote offspring; then, by the suffix *ṭhak*, we have *tārṇabindavikaḥ*. Since the suffix *ṭhak* was attracted (*anukṛṣṭa*) in the preceding sūtra, it does not carry over here; therefore, the mention of *ṭhak* is repeated again for the purpose of excluding the suffix *ṇya*. For the mention of *ṭhak* preceded by the word *vā* is connected with the suffix *ṇya*; thus, if that were to carry over, *ṇya* would also carry over. [The phrase] "the compound has *bhāga* as its prior member," and so forth.
Those suffixes (*ṭhak*) which are to be applied by this rule are enumerated in this verse.

A technical term (*vṛtti-śabda*) whose prior member (*pūrvapada*) is "bhāga" is described as such. First, there is *bhāgavitti*; second, *tārṇabindava*; and third, *ākaśāpeya*—these three words [are examples] where the suffix *ṭhak* is applied diversely (*bahulam*) after a *gotra* name.

The meaning is that although the suffix *yaṣṭhak* is stated to be applied diversely (*bahulam*) to a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) ending in a word denoting a Sauvīra lineage (*gotra*), it occurs only after those three, namely *bhāgavitti* and the others, and not after any others. Now, for what purpose is the mention of "vṛddha" (the technical term for stems containing the vowels ai, au, or vṛddhi), since the term "gotra" is carried over from the previous rule? We shall qualify it by the mention of "Sauvīra" itself; and since a nominal stem such as *bhāgavitti* which exists within a Sauvīra lineage is necessarily *vṛddha*, the mention of "vṛddha" is redundant because there is no possibility of its exclusion. To this, he says: "The mention of *vṛddha*," and so forth.
For that mention of *gotra* is a qualifier of the feminine; therefore, while it continues to apply, there would be a recurrence of the feminine, which is the qualified (*viśeṣya*).
Consequently, the mention of *vṛddha* is for the purpose of excluding that [feminine application].
It should be explained thus: only the mention of *gotra* will continue to apply because it alone is marked with the *svarita* accent, and not the word "feminine" (*strī*).
Furthermore, because of the [authoritative] commentary, the mention of *vṛddha* alone is sufficient. For example: *aupagaviḥ*. This is derived by adding *iñ* after a stem ending in *aṇ*.
But surely an enumeration was made; how then could there be the possibility of the suffix *ṭhak* from the word *aupagava*? That enumeration applies only when the mention of *sauvīra* is present.

For instance, Bhāgavitti and others are enumerated specifically as belonging to the Sauvīra lineage. In that context, if the mention of "Sauvīra" were omitted, the form *Bhāgavittāyanaḥ* would undesirably follow even from the word *Aupagava*, by means of the suffix *phak* as before. Now, one might ask: what is the purpose of the mention of *bahula* (diversity/optionality), for could not the same result—such as *Bhāgavittikaḥ* and *Bhāgavittikāyanaḥ*—be achieved simply by using the phrase *na vā* (or not)? To this, he says: "The mention of *bahula*," and so forth.
By the inclusion of the word "or" (*vā*), only optionality (*vikalpa*) is obtained, but not the diversity of limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*).
However, by the inclusion of the word "often" (*bahula*), that too is obtained.
Therefore, the inclusion of the word "often" is for the purpose that there may be the diversity—that is, the manifoldness—of the various specific limiting adjuncts.

To demonstrate that very diversity of conditions (*upādhi*), he says: "beginning with 'of a woman of the *go* caste'," and so forth. This is easy to understand. Regarding "and *yamunda*," and so forth:

those [words] for which the suffixes *cha* and *ṭhak* are prescribed by this rule are enumerated here by this verse; however, it should be understood that this is obtained precisely through the continued application of the mention of the term *bahula*.
An example for *yaman* has been shown by the author of the Vṛtti itself.
We shall now show examples for the other two: the descendant of *suyāman*, with the suffix *phiñ*, is *sauyāmāyaniḥ*; his descendant is *sauyāmāyanikaḥ*.
The descendant of *vṛṣan*, with the suffix *phiñ*, is *vārṣyāyaṇiḥ*; his descendant is *vārṣyāyaṇīyaḥ* or *vārṣyāyaṇikaḥ*.
These words, *yamunda* and so forth, are known as having the suffix *phiñ*; that is, they are understood to end in *phiñ*. These are the four rules beginning with [Pāṇini 4.1.147].
Among them, the first applies only in cases of censure, and the last applies only among the Sauviras.
One who knows grammar should remember that the two middle [names] belong to the Sauvīras and Kutsā; one should know this. Regarding the rule "alpāctarasya" (Pāṇini 2.2.34) and so forth:

the word *mimata* has fewer syllables (*alpāctara*). Although its prior placement (*pūrvanipāta*) would have been required by the rule "alpāctaram," the fact that it appears as the subsequent member (*paranipāta*) indicates a sign of deviation from the general rule. Just as this characteristic of prior placement deviates—that is, does not apply within its own scope—so too does the characteristic of "correspondence in order" (*yathāsaṃkhya*) deviate; thus, there is no correspondence in order.

Therefore, from each [condition] individually, two [rules] are established: *kauravyaḥ* is an exception (*apavāda*) to [Pāṇini 6.4.146 and 6.1.79], while [the suffix] *ṇya-* applies by [Pāṇini 4.1.172]:
*kurunādibhyo ṇyaḥ*, and so forth.

But for what purpose is another *ṇya*-suffix introduced after the word *kuru*, when this [suffix] alone would suffice—since the resulting form is indeed the same and the accent is also the same? To this he says: "But that [is] from a *kṣatriya*.
By this, he shows a difference in meaning;
for, by virtue of the governing rule [Pāṇini 4.1.168], that [suffix] occurs after a *kṣatriya*, whereas this one occurs after something other than that.
Consequently, one [term] has a *kṣatriya* as its progeny (*apatya*), while the other has a non-*kṣatriya* as its progeny; thus, the difference in meaning is indeed clear.
Demonstrating that there are also differences in grammatical form (*rūpa*) among many [such terms], he says: "designated as *tadrāja*" and so forth.
For because it is designated as *tadrāja*, there must be elision (*luk*) in the plural according to the rule *tadrājasya bahuṣu* (Pāṇini 2.4.62), as in the case of *kuravaḥ*.

"But this is indeed heard as 'kauravyāḥ'; the word *rathakāra* is recited [in the rule]. In that regard, the word *rathakāra* exists as a term denoting a caste (*jāti*), and it also exists as a term denoting an agent (*kārin*). Therefore, which of these two is recited here? To this he says: "The word *rathakāra* is recited here," and so forth. Now, why is it not also recited as a term denoting an agent? To this he says: "But [if it were] an agent," and so forth. For if the word *rathakāra* were a term denoting an agent, then by the very subsequent rule (*sūtra*) the suffix *ṇya* would already be established; what then would be the purpose of its recitation here? [It is for the sake of ensuring that] "the masculine form does not occur."

Regarding the rule *bhasyāḍhe taddhite* (Vārttika 731), which would otherwise require the application of the masculine form (*puṃvadbhāva*), this does not apply to the word *keśinī*. If it were to apply, then after the elision of the suffix *ṭi* by rule [6.4.144], the undesired form *kaiśyaḥ* would result. Why does it not apply? To this he says: "Because of the force of the mention of the feminine suffix. For if the masculine form were to apply, the mention of the feminine suffix here would be purposeless; he would have simply recited it in the masculine gender.

Even if it were read in the masculine gender, the suffix is established from the word *keśinī* as well by means of the paribhāṣā "that which is qualified by gender [is included]. Now, one might object: "Is the reading of the feminine form not intended for the purpose of excluding the masculine? This is not so; for the suffix will simply not apply to the masculine because it is not so designated. Regarding the phrase "like Kaṇva and others": this extension (*atideśa*) occurring in the section on "descendants" (*apatya*) is understood to apply to those ending in descendant-suffixes, such as those beginning with *kaṇva*.

Kaṇva and others are included within the group beginning with Garga; therefore, whatever grammatical operation applies to Kaṇva and others ending in *yañ* also applies to Vāmarathya, with the exception of accentuation. Regarding the phrase "elision and so forth" (*lugādikam*), the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) includes [suffixes] such as *ṅīp*.
According to the rule *kaṇvādibhyo gotre* [Pāṇini 2.4.64], the elision (*luk*) of the patronymic suffix occurs when there is plurality.
In the feminine, the suffix *ṅīp* is applied by the rule *yañaśca* [Pāṇini 4.1.16].
Furthermore, the suffix *ṣpha* is applied in the feminine alone by the rule *prācāṃ ṣpha taddhite* [Pāṇini 4.1.17].

The suffix *phak* is applied by [Pāṇini 4.1.101]. Then, for the secondary (*śaiṣika*) meanings, the suffix *aṇ* is applied by [Pāṇini 4.2.111] when that meaning is intended to be expressed. Finally, the suffix *aṇ* is applied by [Pāṇini 4.3.127]: "After stems ending in *añ*, *yañ*, or *iñ*, the suffix *aṇ* is applied when the meaning is a 'corporation' (*saṅgha*), a 'limb' (*aṅga*), or a 'characteristic mark' (*lakṣaṇa*)."
Just as these grammatical operations apply to Kaṇva and others, so too do they apply to Vāmarathya.
The examples for these are, respectively, *vāmarathāḥ* and so forth. [The rule states:
"The initial acute accent (*ādyudāttatva*) is not one derived by extension (*atideśika*)."

Just as words such as *kaṇva* and others ending in *yañ* have the acute accent on the first syllable (*ādyudātta*) by virtue of the accent of the *ñit* suffix, it is not so with *vāmarathya*; rather, it has the acute accent on the final syllable (*antodātta*) by virtue of the accent of the suffix itself.
[The rule] "after *samrāj*, when denoting a Kṣatriya" means that the suffix *ṇya* occurs after *samrāj* to denote a Kṣatriya; thus, the offspring of *samrāj* is *sāmrājya*.

Except for *sāmrājaḥ*. Here, because of the prohibition against the rule of "extension to what ends with [a specific element]" (*vyā|pa|89*) when a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) is accompanied by a suffix that causes grammatical operations (*grahaṇavat*), there is a literal apprehension (*svarūpagrahaṇa*) of the word *lakṣaṇa*.
For this very reason, he says: "from the word *lakṣaṇa*.
The term *kāri* is an apprehension of the meaning.

Since the action (*kārya*) does not exist in that sense, he says "and from words denoting an agent" (*kārivacanebhyaśca*) so that the suffix may be understood as expressing that [agent]. Why is there not likewise a literal apprehension (*svarūpagrahaṇa*) of the word *kārin*, just as there is of the word *lakṣaṇa*? Because of its inclusion among the *śiva*-group [of words], where it is read as *takṣan*. For its inclusion there is intended to block the *iñ* suffix which would otherwise be prescribed by the rule for agents (*kārilakṣaṇa*). If, however, there were a literal apprehension of the word *kārin* here, then since it would be impossible for the suffix to apply to words such as *takṣan*, the general suffix *aṇ* alone would have to apply; consequently, its inclusion in the *śiva*-group would be purposeless.

However, since the suffix *iñ* would otherwise apply by default when there is the apprehension of meaning (*arthagrahaṇa*), its inclusion in that rule is appropriate for the purpose of overriding it. Regarding the phrase "by the force of the statement" (*vacanasāmarthyāt*) and so forth:

both the suffix *ṇya* and the suffix *iñ* are mentioned; since their co-occurrence is established by the force of the statement itself even without the mention of the Teacher (*ācārya*), the mention of the Teacher is made for the sake of variety.
Because the mention of the Teacher is redundant, this meaning is obtained: namely, that an increase in the text results in an increase in the meaning.

But might the mention of "Ācārya" not be for the sake of honor? This is not so; for if that were the case, one would have to include the "Prācya" (Easterners) as well, since they too record the suffix *iñ* after words such as *senānta* and *lakṣaṇa*.
By the phrase beginning with "the word *takṣan*," he demonstrates the diversity [of usage].
Regarding "tākṣṇaḥ":
when the suffix *aṇ* is applied after *śiva* and others, there is elision of *a* according to [Pāṇini 6.4.135].
Regarding "tākṣaṇyaḥ": [the suffix *ñyaṅ* is applied].
The original form (*prakṛtibhāva*) is maintained by [Pāṇini 6.4.168]. Regarding the statement "the word *kauravya* is recited," and so forth:

this word *kauravya* indeed exists as a term denoting a *kṣatriya* lineage (*gotra*), ending in the suffix *ṇya* by [Pāṇini 4.1.172]; of those two [possibilities], the former is taken here. Why is this so? Because of its association with the word *aurasa*.

The word *aurasa* ends in the suffix *añ* [Pāṇini 4.1.168]; therefore, it denotes a Kṣatriya. By association with that, only the word *kauravya* which denotes a Kṣatriya—because it ends in a Kṣatriya suffix—is understood here. As for the phrase "But he who... and so on:

the word ending in the suffix *ṇya* [Pāṇini 4.1.151] denotes a gotra such as Brāhmaṇa and others. From that, by [the rule] *ata iñ* [Pāṇini 4.1.95], there ought to be only the suffix *iñ*. To this, one might object: "This is merely your own whim. To address this, he says: "And thus," and so forth.
Since this is so, there must necessarily be the suffix *iñ* for words such as those belonging to the *Brāhmaṇa* lineage (*gotra*).

For instance, in the rule *ṇyakṣattriyārṣañito yūni* (Pāṇini 2.4.58), earlier commentators also cited "the father is a Kauravya" and "the son is a Kauravya" as examples. If the suffix *phiñ* were applied here instead, that example would be untenable; for the elision (*luk*) of *phiñ* in the sense of a descendant (*yuvan*) is not prescribed after a word ending in the suffix *ṇya*, but rather after those ending in *aṇ* and *iñ*. Thus, it is maintained that "this suffix is desired [to be applied] from the very original base (*paramaprakṛti*)."

[This is] from the words *kośala* and *karmāra*. [The term *kauśalya*] ends in the suffix *ñyaṅ* according to Pāṇini 4.1.171, while the word *karmārya* ends in the suffix *ṇya* characterized by the agent (*kārin*) according to 4.1.152; [the phrase "from these two"] is for the purpose of excluding those two. If [the application of the suffix] is desired only for the original base (*mūlaprakṛti*), how can this modified form (*vikṛta*) be accepted as having the form of the base (*prakṛtirūpa*)? To this he says: "In connection with the suffix," and so forth. And this is not merely his own invention; rather, showing that this is the opinion of the teachers themselves, beginning with the author of the Bhāṣya, he says: "And thus," and so forth.

Furthermore, what is the distinction regarding the production [of a suffix] from the ultimate base (*paramaprakṛti*) versus from that which already ends in a suffix? When produced from the ultimate base, the suffix is obtained for the mere sense of "offspring" (*apatya*). However, when produced from that which already ends in a suffix, there is this specific distinction: by the rule *gotrādyūni* [Pāṇini 4.1.94], it applies specifically to "younger offspring" (*yūnyapatye*). Regarding the statement *yuḍ vādiṣṭasya*:

the inclusion of the word *ādiṣṭasya* (of that which is prescribed) is for the purpose that [the augment] should apply even when the substitution of *āyan* has been made; otherwise, because it would not be original (*anāditvāt*), the substitution of *āyan* would not occur.

In the case of *dāgavyāvaniḥ*, once the *guṇa* substitution [of *au* for *o*] has been applied by Pāṇini 6.4.146, the *av-ādeśa* [of *ai* for *e*] is applied by Pāṇini 6.1.79. In the case of *kāttrāyaṇiḥ*:
the suffix *aṇ* is added in the sense of "the descendant of Kartṛ," resulting in *kārtra-*; from that, the suffix *phiñ* is added.

Regarding "dākṣāyaṇaḥ": from the word *dākṣi*, which ends in the suffix *iñ*, the suffix *phak* is applied by the rule *pañiñośca* [Pāṇini 4.1.101] to denote a descendant in the fifth generation. The explanation and so forth is easy to understand. Regarding "from a *vṛddha* [stem]": [the suffix *phak* is applied].

In this context, only that which is technically defined as *vṛddha* (possessing a vowel in the first syllable) is understood, not what is well-known in other treatises, because of the prohibition [stated] as "from what is not a *gotra*. Regarding the phrase "from the word *kārin*" and so forth: the scope for the suffix *iñ*, which is characterized by the term *kārin*, is exemplified by *tāntuvāyiḥ*; the scope for *phiñ* is exemplified by *āmraguptāyaniḥ*. In the case of *nāpitāyaniḥ*, both would apply; however, because of its higher status (*paratva*), only *phiñ* occurs. Thus, "that which is *vṛddha* here is not a *gotra*."
"From the word *vākin* up to *kāka*":
by the word "etc. (*ādi*), the suffix *aṇ* is included; [this] rule is an exception (*apavāda*) to *iñ* and the others.

In this context, [the suffixes] *aṇ* and *iñ* are superseded by [the following rules]: for the words *carman* and *varman*, there is an exception to *aṇ*; for the remaining [words], there is an exception to *iñ*. Regarding the rule "there is elision of the *n* in *carman* and *varman*": for these two words, *carmin* and *varmin*, the suffixes *kuk* and *phiñ* are applied, and there is elision of the *n*. Since the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) would not end in *n* once *kuk* is added, the elision of *n* would not otherwise apply; therefore, it is specifically prescribed—resulting in *cārmikāyaṇiḥ* and *vārmikāyaṇiḥ*. As for the phrase beginning with "by that" (*tena*), etc.: *tena* (by that), etc. refers to the instrumental case. The suffix *cha* is applied after a word ending in the instrumental case to denote "one who studies or knows that. For example, from *sāman* ("Sāmaveda"), we derive *sāmikaḥ* ("one who studies the Sāmaveda"). The suffix *cha* is replaced by *ikaḥ*. Similarly, from *chandaḥ* ("Veda"), we derive *chandasaḥ* ("one who studies the Veda"). The suffix *aṇ* is applied after a word ending in the instrumental case to denote "one who goes by that way. For example, from *dakṣiṇāpathena* ("by way of the southern path"), we derive *dākṣiṇāpathakaḥ* ("one who travels by way of the south"). The suffix *ka* is applied. From *uttarapathena* ("by way of the northern path"), we derive *auttarapathikaḥ* ("one who travels by way of the north"). The suffix *ika* is applied. From *madhyamena* ("by the middle way"), we derive *mādhyamikaḥ* ("one who travels by the middle way"). The suffix *ika* is applied. From *pūrvapathena* ("by the eastern path"), we derive *paurvapathikaḥ* ("one who travels by the eastern path"). The suffix *ika* is applied. From *aparapathena* ("by the western path"), we derive *āparapathikaḥ* ("one who travels by the western path"). The suffix *ika* is applied. From *adhvānam* ("a road"), we derive *ādhvikaḥ* ("one who travels the road"). The suffix *ka* is applied. From *kāntāram* ("a wilderness"), we derive *kāntārakaḥ* ("one who travels the wilderness"). The suffix *ka* is applied. From *samvatsaram* ("a year"), we derive *sāṃvatsarikaḥ* ("one who travels for a year"). The suffix *ika* is applied. From *māsam* ("a month"), we derive *māsikaḥ* ("one who travels for a month"). The suffix *ika* is applied. From *ardhamāsam* ("half a month"), we derive *ārdhamāsikaḥ* ("one who travels for half a month"). The suffix *ika* is applied. From *ahar* ("a day"), we derive *āhnikaḥ* ("daily"). The suffix *ika* is applied. From *rātrim* ("a night"), we derive *rātrikaḥ* ("nocturnal"). The suffix *ika* is applied. From *puṇyāham* ("an auspicious day"), we derive *pauṇyāhnikaḥ* ("relating to an auspicious day"). The suffix *ika* is applied. From *puṇyarātrim* ("an auspicious night"), we derive *pauṇyarātrikaḥ* ("relating to an auspicious night"). The suffix *ika* is applied. From *puṇyāhorātram* ("an auspicious day and night"), we derive *pauṇyāhorātrikaḥ* ("relating to an auspicious day and night"). The suffix *ika* is applied. From *puṇyāhaḥ* ("an auspicious day"), we derive *pauṇyāhikaḥ* ("relating to an auspicious day"). The suffix *ika* is applied. From *puṇyarātriḥ* ("an auspicious night"), we derive *pauṇyarātrikaḥ* ("relating to an auspicious night"). The suffix *ika* is applied. From *puṇyāhorātraḥ* ("an auspicious day and night"), we derive *pauṇyāhorātrikaḥ* ("relating to an auspicious day and night"). The suffix *ika* is applied. From *puṇyāha-puṇyarātri-puṇyāhorātrāṇām* ("of the auspicious day, the auspicious night, and the auspicious day-and-night"), we derive *pauṇyāhika-pauṇyarātrika-pauṇyāhorātrikāḥ* ("relating to the auspicious day, the auspicious night, and the auspicious day-and-night"). The suffix *ika* is applied. From *puṇyāha-puṇyarātri-puṇyāhorātrebhyaḥ* ("from the auspicious day, the auspicious night, and the auspicious day-and-night"), we derive *pauṇyāhika-pauṇyarātrika-pauṇyāhorātrikāḥ* ("relating to the auspicious day, the auspicious night, and the auspicious day-and-night"). The suffix *ika* is applied. From *puṇyāha-puṇyarātri-puṇyāhorātrāṇām* ("of the auspicious day, the auspicious night, and the auspicious day-and-night"), we derive *pauṇyāhika-pauṇyarātrika-pauṇyāhorātrikāḥ* ("relating to the auspicious day, the auspicious night, and the auspicious day-and-night"). The suffix *ika* is applied. From *puṇyāha-puṇyarātri-puṇyāhorātrebhyaḥ* ("from the auspicious day, the auspicious night, and the auspicious day-and-night"), we derive *pauṇyāhika-pauṇyarātrika-pauṇyāhorātrikāḥ* ("relating to the auspicious day, the auspicious night, and the auspicious day-and-night"). The suffix *ika* is applied. From *puṇyāha-puṇyarātri-puṇyāhorātrāṇām* ("of the auspicious day, the auspicious night, and the auspicious day-and-night"), we derive *pauṇyāhika-pauṇyarātrika-pauṇyāhorātrikāḥ* ("relating to the auspicious day, the auspicious night, and the auspicious day-and-night"). The suffix *ika* is applied. From *puṇyāha-puṇyarātri-puṇyāhorātrebhyaḥ* ("from the auspicious day, the auspicious night, and the auspicious day-and-night"), we derive *pauṇyāhika-pauṇyarātrika-pauṇyāhorātrikāḥ* ("relating to the auspicious day, the auspicious night, and the auspicious day-and-night"). The suffix *ika* is applied. From *puṇyāha-puṇyarātri-puṇyāhorātrāṇām* ("of the auspicious day, the auspicious night, and the auspicious day-and-night"), we derive *pauṇyāhika-pauṇyarātrika-pauṇyāhorātrikāḥ* ("relating to the auspicious day, the auspicious night, and the auspicious day-and-night"). The suffix *ika* is applied. From *puṇyāha-puṇyarātri-pu

By virtue of the statement, according to the opinion of the northerners (*udīcām*), the suffix *phiñ* was prescribed optionally by the preceding sūtra; by this [present rule], the augment *kuk* is also optionally prescribed for that [suffix]. Consequently, there are three forms. "For the purpose of option" (*vikalpārthaḥ*) means for the sake of providing an alternative.
"It is accomplished by one alone" means...
"Because it has the sense of an option (*vikalpa*). Since "option" is the subject under discussion, it is understood [from the context].
Here, one must supply the question: "For what purpose is there the mention of 'all'?
To this, the answer begins with "In that case," and so forth.
Both the mention of "northerners" (*udīcām*) and the mention of "easterners" (*prācām*) are for the sake of honor.
As it is said, "The mention of *bahula* is for the sake of variety.
By process of elimination, it follows that the mention of *anyatarasyām* is intended to express an option (*vikalpa*).

With the words "in some cases" (*kvacit*) and so forth, he demonstrates that the inclusion of the term *bahula* (diversely) serves the purpose of variety. With the words "and thus" (*tathā ca*) and so forth:

since there is no sense of "offspring" (*apatya*) here, and having established this, the elision (*luk*) does not occur in the plural form *mānuṣāḥ*. For if the sense of "offspring" were present, the elision in the plural would necessarily follow by [Pāṇini 4.1.92]: *apatye kutsite mūḍhe 'lpe jātīye 'pi ca kaṇ*. "In offspring that is contemptible," and so forth.
This verse is intended as a supplementary rule (*upasaṃkhyāna*) for the word *mūrdhanya*.
[The formation of] the suffix *aṇ* is already established by the rule "the suffix *aṇ* is applied when there is a desire to express offspring" (Pāṇini 4.1.92).

Now, one might object: "But isn't *mūrdhanya* also already established by the continued application of the term 'diversely' (*bahulagrahaṇa*)? If that is so, then the meaning obtainable through the continued application of the term 'diversely' is precisely what is stated by this verse.
And that [term] applies specifically to a distinguished person in a particular context, such as a fool or a child, but not everywhere.
A "fool" (*mūḍha*) is one who is ignorant because he has not studied the Vedas.

One who is contemptible due to his very foolishness or because of practicing what is forbidden is called a *māṇava* belonging to the Brāhmaṇa caste. The word "etcetera" (*prabhṛti*) has the sense of the word "beginning with" (*ādi*).
The term *pautraprabhṛti* is a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "that of which the grandson (*pautra*) is the starting point.

If it were the case that any offspring beginning with the grandson is designated as a *gotra*, then even Garga would incur the designation of *gotra*, for he too is indeed a grandson in relation to someone. Furthermore, if the designation *gotra* were applied [to him], the suffix for a direct descendant (*anantarāpatya*) could not follow the word *gotra*. Anticipating this objection, the author says: "Because it is a relative term," and so forth.

The designation "gotra" is prescribed for those beginning with the grandson (pautra) and subsequent descendants. Since these terms, as well as the word "apatya" (offspring), are relative terms, they necessarily depend upon one who possesses offspring.
Therefore, the designation "gotra" is prescribed in relation to that which is the offspring of such a person.

Nor can it be designated that for one whose *potṛ* (great-grandson) is Garga, that Garga is his *aptaya* (lineal descendant), because the state of being a descendant (*apatyatva*) does not manifest there. Its non-manifestation is due to the fact that the descendant is not intended to be expressed there in its specific form. For even that state of being a descendant which exists there is not denoted by its actual nature; rather, it is prescribed as a descendant starting from the *potṛ*.

Therefore, since [the term *garga*] does not appear in its own form [as a descendant], there is no possibility of the technical designation (*saṃjñā*) "gotra" applying to Garga himself. Regarding the rule "*gargasya pautraprabhṛti*" (P. 4.1.105): when the descendant beginning with the grandson of Garga—namely, the offspring related to Garga—is designated as *gārgya*, the technical designation "gotra" applies; and while the word "gotra" is carried over from P. 4.1.98, the suffix *yañ* occurs for a descendant who is a *gotra*.
Thus, it is said: "This is merely a designation (*vyapadeśa*) for 'descendant'."
The word "one who possesses a name" (*saṃjñin*) is the ellipsis [to be supplied]. The intention is that this will be stated in the subsequent sūtra.

However, in the present case, since the status of being a descendant (*apatyatva*) is never absent in the grandson, he is understood as a descendant by means of the suffixes themselves; therefore, there is no purpose in including the term "descendant" (*apatya*) for the sake of designating the one who possesses the name.

In the subsequent sūtra, however, this [term] beginning with "pautra" (grandson) is modified to end in the genitive case (*pautraprabhṛteḥ*); thus, the designation *yuvan* (younger descendant) is intended for the offspring related to one starting from the grandson. And that [designation] cannot be obtained without the mention of "offspring" (*apatya*). For there exists something other than offspring related to one starting from the grandson; in that case, it would not be known whose designation this is. Therefore, some maintain that the mention of "offspring" is appropriate there for the purpose of specifying the bearer of the designation. But here, we see that the mention of "offspring" is appropriate for the purpose of specifying the bearer of the designation.

If the mention of *apatya* (descendant) were not made, then the argument previously stated for the sake of refuting an objection—that the word *apatya* is a relative term (*sambandhi-śabda*)—would be untenable.
Consequently, even the name *Garga* would indeed receive the technical designation of *gotra*.

Therefore, even here, the mention of *apatya* must certainly be made with reference to the named object (*saṃjñin*), so that the designation may apply to that which appears in the form of a descendant, and not to anything else.

But surely, since that very mention of *apatya* (offspring) which was introduced there [in P. 4.1.92] will serve as the designation for the thing to be named (*saṃjñin*), what is the purpose of another mention of *apatya* here? This is not so; for how could that which was established there as the meaning of the suffix (*pratyaya-artha*) serve as the designation for the thing to be named? One might argue: "Even though it was established there as the meaning of the suffix, nevertheless, since its purpose no longer exists here because it has been carried over (*anuvṛtta*), it will be understood as serving to designate the thing to be named. But this too is not the case.

The continuation of the governing rules (*adhikāra*) for the sake of what follows is observed, and the explanation would have to be made in this way; however, since a direct statement (*vacana*) is more concise than an explanation, the term "offspring" (*apatya*) must be explicitly stated.
[Examples: *kauñji-*, *gārgiḥ*.

Because there is an absence of the designation "lineage" (*gotra-saṃjñā*) for what immediately precedes it, that which is prescribed for the lineage by [Pāṇini 4.1.98] and [4.1.105] does not apply here. [The definition: "a continuous succession of ancestors."

*Abhajanāḥ* refers to the grandfathers and so forth; *prabandhaḥ* means lineage (*santānaḥ*). That which exists therein is called *vaṃśyaḥ*, where the suffix *yat* is applied according to the rule for words beginning with *diś*.
The term *pautraprabhṛtyapatyam* is a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsaḥ*).

Regarding the phrase "starting from the grandson" (*pautraprabhṛti*) and so forth: if this term "starting from the grandson" were to qualify *apatya* (descendant) through grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), such that "the descendant who is starting from the grandson"—then the designation *yuvan* (younger generation) would apply from that point onward, which is undesirable. Therefore, this is not a qualifier of *apatya* through coreferentiality. What then? By virtue of the sense, once the case-ending has been changed, it attains the status of a genitive ending and functions as a non-coreferential qualifier: "the descendant who is starting from the grandson. To demonstrate what is thereby accomplished, he says "by that" (*tena*) and so forth.

Since, when the case-ending has been thus changed, the word *apatyam* (offspring) is qualified by the genitive form *pautraprabhṛteḥ*, the designation *yuvan* (younger descendant) is prescribed starting from the fourth generation; and the cause for this change of case-ending is the word *apatyam*.
For the word *apatya*, being a relative term (*sambandhiśabda*), requires a correlate such as a cause, and in this context, the genitive serves as that correlate because it is proximate.

The phrase "of him, beginning with the grandson" (*pautraprabhṛti tasya*) requires this very [genitive]; therefore, it establishes the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) in that very place. If, then, because of the inability [of the term] *apatya* (offspring) [to govern itself], there is a transformation of the genitive for "beginning with the grandson," why does it not occur in the previous rule as well? Because in that [previous] case, the nominative (*prathamā*) has no other scope. For in the previous rule, the nominative has its purpose already fulfilled; therefore, it is not possible to transform it into a genitive. But here, since its purpose is not yet fulfilled, it can be transformed into the state of a genitive.

Regarding the term "gāgryāyaṇaḥ": here, since the designation *yuvan* (descendant) applies, a suffix denoting a *yuvan* descendant occurs after a base ending in a *gotra* suffix, according to [Pāṇini 4.1.94]. The word "tu" (but/however) is for the purpose of restriction (*avadhāraṇārtha*).

What, then, is the fault said to arise from the co-occurrence (*samāveśa*) of these two designations? [Consider the following: from the rule *śālaṅker apatyaṃ yuvā* (P. 4.1.101), the suffix *phak* is applied; and from *pailasyāpatyaṃ yuvā* (P. 4.1.156), the suffix *phiñ* is applied. Regarding these two, elision (*luk*) is prescribed by the rule *tayoḥ* (P. 2.4.59)—resulting in the forms *śālaṅkir yuvā* and *pailo yuvā*.

If there were a co-occurrence of the designations "lineage" (*gotra*) and "youth" (*yuvan*), then in the intended meaning "the students of the youth Śālaṅki," when a secondary suffix (*prāgdīvyatīya*) beginning with a vowel (*ajādau*) is to be applied, the suffix would not be elided according to the rule *gotrād yūni* (P. 4.1.89). Thus, the form would incorrectly remain as *śālaṅki-yuva*.

Therefore, the word "tu" (but) is employed for the purpose of restriction, so that the designation "gotra" should not apply to that youth. Because the word "brother" (*bhrātṛ*) is a relative term, it implies as its own referent (*saṃjñin*) that very person in relation to whom brotherhood exists.
The word "elder" (*jyāyān*) denotes one who is more praiseworthy or older;
and his status as elder is due either to qualities or to age.

Since [the term] "younger" exists in relation to a rival who is older, that very person is presented as the rival by the word *jyāyas* ("older"). Thinking that, therefore, the designation "younger" will be understood specifically in reference to a younger brother, he says: "A younger brother is designated as *yava*. With the words "those born before," etc., he justifies the commencement [of the rule] by showing that its purpose extends beyond the immediate family (*avaṃśya*).
By the phrase "because of not being a cause," the brother's lack of lineage-status is also indicated.
For he who is a cause, either directly or through a succession, is one belonging to the lineage; and since a brother is not a cause, he does not belong to the lineage.
"While Gārgya is living" means while his brother is living.

In the same way, "while Vātsya is living," one should understand that Vātsyāyana is his younger brother; or "while Dākṣi is living," one should understand that Dākṣāyaṇa is his younger brother. Regarding the term "country-dweller" (*janapadavṛtti*): a country such as Pañcāla has been mentioned as a "country" (*janapada*); however, when the word "kṣatriya" denotes a "kṣatriya-dweller," this is due to the metaphorical application of the name to the object denoted, or through association (*sāhacarya*).

Now, words such as *pañcāla* and others denote a country (*janapada*) when a secondary suffix (*taddhita*) is applied according to [Pāṇini 4.2.69] and that suffix is elided according to [4.2.81]. Therefore, how can eternal *kṣatriya* words be qualified by the status of being country-names, which belongs to a later time? Furthermore, how can a learned person explain how these words come to denote a country through their connection with the *kṣatriyas*?

For the author of the Sūtras, by rejecting the treatment as a *yukta* and the elision (*lup*) in the rules "That [name] is to be eaten" (Pāṇini 1.2.53) and "Because the name is the authority, there is elision due to the non-appearance of the connection" (1.2.54), has stated that the application of words such as *Pañcāla* occurs inherently, just as it does for Kṣatriyas in a region.
Just as words are eternal, so too is a region like Pañcāla; therefore, how could the status of being a word denoting a region be of later origin? [Examples such as] *Pāñcāla*:
the words *Pañcāla* and others, while existing in a country, denote Kṣatriyas by their very nature; from these, the suffix *añ* is applied in the sense of offspring.

Regarding "Aikṣvāka": in the rule beginning with *dāṇḍināyanahastināyana* (Pāṇini 2.4.174), the elision of the vowel *u* in the word *ikṣvāku* is prescribed as a nipātana (irregular formation). Regarding "Drauhya":
the word *drahru* denotes a kṣatriya specifically and is not a name for a country (*janapada*); therefore, only the suffix *aṇ* is applied.
Regarding the term *pāñcālir vaidehiḥ*:
here, the words *pañcāla* and *videha* are names of countries (*janapada-śabda*), not designations for Kṣatriyas. Rather, they denote Brāhmaṇas; therefore, the suffix *iñ* alone is applied.
Regarding the phrase "from a word identical in sound to 'Kṣatriya'," etc.:

a word that actually denotes a Kṣatriya is here called "Kṣatriya" by way of metaphorical usage (*upacāra*), just as the word for a country (*janapada*) is called "country. That which has a word identical in sound to "Kṣatriya" is thus described.

Therefore, it must be stated that from the word *kṣattriya*, when it ends in the sixth case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) and signifies a *rājanya* (a member of the royal class), a secondary suffix (*pratyaya*) is produced just as in the case of a descendant (*apatya*). This is an exception (*apavāda*) to the suffix *vuñ* which would otherwise apply by [Pāṇini 4.2.125].

Just as in the case of "the descendant of Pañcāla" (*pañcālasyāpatyam*) resulting in *pāñcālaḥ*, so too in the case of "the king of the Pañcālas" (*pañcālānāṃ rājā*), it results in *pāñcālaḥ*. Likewise, one says *māgadhaḥ*.

From the word *magadha*, the suffix *aṇ* is applied according to [Pāṇini 4.1.170], *apatye* and so forth; likewise, it is applied in the rule *tasya rājanyatra*. Here, by the mention of *vṛddha*, the term [defined] at [Pāṇini 1.1.73] is understood, for only that [term] can possibly be both a name of a country (*janapada*) and a designation of a Kṣatriya, whereas that which is defined in other grammatical systems cannot. Examples are *āmbaṣṭhyaḥ* and *sauvīryaḥ*;
from the words *āmbaṣṭha* and *sauvīra*, the suffix *ñyaṅ* is applied.
In the case of *āvantyaḥ* and *kauntyaḥ*, the suffix *ñyaṅ* is applied after the words *avanti* and *kunti*. In the case of *kaumāraḥ*, the suffix *añ* occurs.

"It should be stated that the suffix *ḍaṇ* [is applied]. This is an exception (*apavāda*) to the suffix *ñyaṅ* for the word *kṣattriya*. The letter *ḍ* is for the purpose of causing the elision of the *ṭi* (the final vowel and following consonant).
And this [suffix] is obtained through the "frog-leap" (*maṇḍūkapluti*) maxim by the recurrence of the word "optionally" (*vā*) from the rule "or, when another sapinda [is meant]" (Pāṇini 4.1.165).
In that case, would there not be an over-extension [of the rule]? No, it will not occur because the *vibhāṣā* (optionality) is fixed.

In the example "pāṇḍavaḥ from another [Pāṇḍu]," the word *pāṇḍu* refers to a Kṣatriya; when the general suffix *aṇ* is applied to it, the form *pāṇḍavaḥ* is obtained. This is an exception (*apavāda*) to both the suffixes *añ* and *aṇ*.
However, regarding the suffix *aṇ* characterized by having two syllables (*dvyaj*) [in the word *kuru*]:

since it was previously stated that [the suffix *aṇ*] follows the word *kuru* for the sense of "descendant" (Pāṇini 4.1.151), there is scope for that [suffix] when the word denoting a country (*janapada-śabda*) is not a *kṣatriya*. But when the word denoting a country is a *kṣatriya*, then because of its higher status, the suffix *añ* would apply; therefore, the suffix *aṇ* characterized by having two syllables would be an exception (*apavāda*) to that [suffix *añ*].
Therefore, another [suffix] is prescribed again in order to supersede that [previous one]. It is said: "It is desired [that the suffix] *añ* be applied.
This is characterized by the name [of the place].
How is this known? From the fact that *sālva* is an irregularly formed (*nipātana*) word.

"The constituent parts of those [names] denote the constituent parts of the territories and are common to the Kṣatriyas; therefore, they too receive the designation *sālva* figuratively. Regarding the phrase "because of being separated by the section on the technical designations of *gotra* and *yuvan*": for the reason that the section concerning the designations of *gotra* and *yuvan* was placed as an intervening separation is precisely this: so that there may not be a reference by means of the pronoun *te* ("those") in the rule *te tadrājāḥ* to those *aṇ*-suffixes and others that were previously mentioned but now separated [by the intervening section].
"And so it has been illustrated.
In the rule *tadrājasya bahuṣu tenaivāstriyām* [Pāṇini 2.4.62], an illustration based on grammatical operation (*kāryāśraya*) was given;
however, in this present section, the illustrations are based on form (*rūpāśraya*), such as *colaḥ* and *śakaḥ*.

There is elision (*luk*) of the suffix *aṇ* [prescribed] after the names of the two regions, Aṅga and Magadha; and there is elision of the suffix *añ* [prescribed] after Kerala. Thus: *Avantī* and *Kuntī*.
When the *taddhita* suffix has been elided, the feminine suffix *ṅīṣ* is applied by [Pāṇini 4.1.65].
Thus, "Kurūḥ" [is formed];
here the suffix *ūṅ* is applied by [Pāṇini 4.1.66]. The letter *t* [in the technical name *ūṅ*] is for the sake of clarity.

If there were a *takāra* [the marker *t*], the indication should have been "asya" (of this); and because the indication would be identical [to the word "idam"], there would be doubt: "Is this an indication of the vowel *a*, or rather of the pronoun *idam*?
However, when the *takāra* is present, this fault does not arise; for the designation "followed by *t*" (*tapara*) is well-established only with respect to vowels.
Furthermore, the *takāra* is not for the purpose of excluding the long vowel (*dīrgha*), since a long vowel is impossible in this context.
Regarding "Sūrasenī" and "Madrī":

when the suffix *añ* derived from the word *sūrasena* and the suffix *aṇ* characterized by having two vowels (*dvyañ*) derived from the word *mada* are elided, the feminine suffix *ṅīṣ* is applied according to [Pāṇini 4.1.63]: "The suffix *ṅīṣ* is added after a genus name (*jāti*) that does not denote a female, provided it has a vowel other than *y* as its penultimate letter."

Regarding the word *darat*: from the word *darat*, there is the elision (*luk*) of the suffix *aṇ* prescribed for the regions of Dvy-añ and Magadha [Pāṇini 4.1.168]. If the term *ataḥ* here refers to the phoneme *a*, then since the mention of a phoneme triggers the rule of "application to what ends with that" (*tadantavidhi*), this would also apply here in the cases of *āmbaṣṭhyāḥ* and *sauvīryāḥ*. Therefore, he says: "There is elision after *Avanti* and so forth," etc.

If the rule of application to what ends with that were to apply here, the explicit statement of elision after *Avanti* and so forth would be purposeless, as the result would already be established by this very rule.

Since this would not be established by the mere mention of the suffix *a* under the rule of "specification of what follows that" (*tadantavidhi*), the explicit statement of the elision (*luk*) for [the suffixes] from *Avanti* and so forth would be purposeless. [Examples: *pāñcālī*, *vaidehī*—[these are formed] by the addition of *añ* according to [Pāṇini 4.1.168], and then [the feminine suffix] *ṅīn* is applied according to [Pāṇini 4.1.73].
The suffix *aṇ* [is applied] by the rule beginning with "āṅgī-māgadhī" (Pāṇini 4.1.170).
The suffix *ṅīṣ* is applied by the rule *jāterastrīviṣayādayopadhāt* [Pāṇini 4.1.63].
From the words *bharga* and *śālva*, the suffix *aṇ* is applied according to the rule *dvyañmagadha-* [Pāṇini 4.1.168].
From the remaining words, however, the suffix *añ* is applied.
In the case of *bhārgī* and so forth, the suffix *ṅīṣ* is applied as before.
Regarding *yaudheyī*, *śaukreyī*, and *śaubhreyī*:

from the words *yaudheya*, *śaukreya*, and *śaubhreya*, the suffix *aṇ* is applied in the sense of the base itself (*svārthe*) by the rule "after *para*, *ādi*, *yaudheya*, etc., [the suffixes] *aṇ* and *añ* [are applied]" (Pāṇini 4.1.117).

In *bhārgī* and so forth, the suffix *ṅīṣ* is applied as before. Regarding the phrase "Of what, then," etc.: he reveals the intention with which he asked by means of the passage beginning with "How," etc., and the passage beginning with "The *para-* [group]," etc.

*Parśu-* refers to a *kṣatriya*; it shares the same base as the name of a region (*janapada*). Its feminine descendant is formed by the suffix *aṇ* according to [Pāṇini 4.1.170] and so forth; this *aṇ* is elided by [Pāṇini 4.1.77: *ataśca*]. Furthermore, the *aṇ* added in the sense of the base itself (svārthika) by [Pāṇini 5.3.117: *parādi-yaudheyādibhyo 'ṇañau*] is also elided.

Thus, regarding the word *rakṣāḥ*: from the word *asūra*, which is a name of a region (*janapada*), the suffix *añ* is applied according to the rule beginning with "from a word denoting a region" (*janapada-śabdāt*). From that form ending in *añ*, the suffix *aṇ* is added in the same manner as before to express the same meaning (*svārthika*), and there is elision of the feminine suffix (*ṭāp*) and the *yaṅ*.

With the words "And so," etc., the author strengthens this point by citing the evidence provided by the author of the *Bhāṣya*. Thus ends the first quarter of the fourth chapter in the *Kāśikā-vivaraṇapañjikā*, composed by the venerable Master Jinendrabuddhi, a disciple of the Bodhisattvas. This root *rañj* indeed exists in the sense of passion or attachment—as in "attached to the king" (*deve raktaḥ*) or "attached to a woman" (*striyāṃ raktaḥ*); and it also exists in the sense of a specific color—as in "red cow" (*rakto gauḥ*), meaning "reddish" (*lohita*).

There is the case of bringing about a different color in something white—such as "a red cloth," which means that having removed the white, another color such as red has been brought about. Here, the word is taken in its third sense, as stated in the passage beginning with "of the white.

This word *rāga* is indeed used both as an abstract noun (*bhāvasādhana*) and as an instrumental noun (*karaṇasādhana*); here, the second is intended, as stated in the passage: "that by which one is colored is *rāga*."
By the mention of "passion" (rāga), the meaning is intended to be grasped, not the word-form itself.

Therefore, it is understood that the suffix is applied to a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) that expresses a specific kind of passion, and not to the word *rāga* alone; hence he says, "from a nominal stem expressing a specific kind of passion.
Now, why does this not result in the grasping of the word-form itself? Because the reference is directed toward the meaning.

It has already been established previously that where a designation is intent upon the word-form (*śabdapara*), there the intrinsic nature (*svarūpa*) is grasped, but not where the designation is intent upon the meaning (*arthapara*).
Furthermore, the fact that a designation is intent upon the meaning is understood from the uninterrupted tradition of instruction passed down through the lineage of teachers.
If, then, [the author] says "How? with the intention of referring to the production of another color in what was white:
The refutation begins with "from analogy" (*upamānāt*) and so forth.

The sense is that just as in the expression "the Vāhīka is an ox" (*gaurvāhīkaḥ*), the word "ox" (*go*) functions to denote another object, namely the Vāhīka, through analogy; likewise here, the word "kāṣāya" and others function to denote the "donkey-ear" (*gardabhakarṇa*) and so on. Regarding the statement "the suffix *aṇ* is not desired after the words *śakala* and *kardama*," this is obtained through the continuation of the option (*vā*) by the "frog-leap" principle (*maṇḍūkapluti*) from the rule "after another [word] denoting a sapinda" (*vānyasmin sapiṇḍe*, Pāṇini 4.1.165).

And this being so, there is no over-extension of the principle, because the *vibhāṣā* (doctrinal alternatives) are established according to specific contexts. Here, some maintain that time is of the nature of action (*kriyā*), while others consider it to be of the nature of a substance (*dravya*), like space and so forth.

Both of these views are untenable in this context. If the former view were adopted, would the conjunction with a lunar mansion belong to an action inherent in a substance such as the sun, or to an action residing in the self [of time]? The first case is impossible, because [action] cannot be inherent in something else [other than its own substratum].
Otherwise, even space and other such entities would possess action.
For there could be no connection of a substance with an action that inheres in a different entity.

However, while an action residing in the self does have a connection with a constellation, the qualification "connected" (yukta) is not tenable [as applied to the asterism]; this is because there is nothing to be excluded [by such a qualification].

For it is never possible for time, which abides in the asterism Puṣya and so forth, to be conjoined with those very asterisms such as Puṣya; it is precisely to exclude this possibility that the term "conjoined" (yukta) is employed.
Thus, first of all, it is improper to rely here upon the view that "time is action.
The second [view] is also indeed improper; because what is intended here by "conjunction" is the cause for determining a specific point of time.
For indeed, it is precisely for the purpose of determining a specific time that terms such as *pauṣī* are employed in common usage.
And such a conjunction occurs only between those two things which possess proximity and remoteness, such as the asterism Puṣya and the moon;
for at one time there is proximity between them, and at another time there is remoteness.
Considering that there can never be any proximity or remoteness between the lunar mansion (*nakṣatra*) and time, because both are eternal, he says "How then," and so forth;
the intention is that [proximity] cannot be established in any way.
Indicating that the word "lunar mansion" (*nakṣatra*) used in the aphorism refers to the moon when it is situated near a lunar mansion, he says "situated near Puṣya and so forth," and so on.

For just as the word "Ganges" is applied to the region near the Ganges in the expression "a hamlet on the Ganges" due to proximity, so too here, words denoting specific constellations such as Puṣya are applied to the moon when it is in proximity to Puṣya and the others.
Thus, being applied to that [proximity], they produce a cognition.
Consequently, conjunction with the moon situated near Puṣya and the others is established as the cause for determining the specific divisions of time.
Because that particular state of the moon occurs only occasionally, the meaning is "conjoined with the moon situated near Puṣya"; for the word *puṣya* is applied to the moon when it is in that state.
Thus, [the term] is *pauṣī*.

In the rule *sūryatiṣyāgastyamastyānāṃ ya upadhāyāḥ* [Pāṇini 6.4.149], there is the elision of *y* by the statement *tiṣyapuṣyayornakṣatrāṇi yalopaḥ* (Vārttika 808), which says that for the words *tiṣya* and *puṣya*, when they denote asterisms (*nakṣatra*), there is elision of *y*. If this elision (*luk*) occurs without qualification, then it would also apply here in the cases *pauṣī rātriḥ* ("the night of Puṣya") and *pauṣamahar* ("the day of Puṣya"), because here too the status of being an asterism is understood without distinction. For instance, when one says *pauṣī rātriḥ*, no specific distinction such as "today" or "tomorrow" is understood. Therefore, he says: *na cet nakṣatrayuktasya* ("provided it does not refer to that which is joined with an asterism"), and so forth.
He thinks as follows: the phrase "thus" (evam) is understood from the previous context; therefore, it does not become a specific [sub-division] of that.
Regarding the expression "a specific [sub-division] such as night," he says "such as" (ādi), by which words specific units like *muhūrta* and *lava* are included.
Regarding the expression "as much as" (*yāvān*), and so forth.
He clarifies the very point just mentioned:
for how long a period of time is one conjoined with a lunar mansion (*nakṣatra*)? It is a day and night (*ahorātra*).

Thus, when the duration of time conjoined with the lunar mansion is not understood as a whole, but rather as a specific part of it—namely, the night or the day—this is not a case for the elision (*lup*) [of the suffix].

If this is so, how can even a portion of an affix be its object? [The answer is: by way of the whole, those things contained within it are grasped. Since the portions are also connected, the production of the affix is established by the preceding rule. Furthermore, here a portion of a member [of the compound] is the object of elision (*lup*).

In that case, [the elision] would apply here: *pauṣo 'horātraḥ* ("a day-and-night of the month of Pauṣa"). For when it is said that a certain duration of time is conjoined with a lunar mansion (*nakṣatra*), no distinction regarding that [time] is understood. Likewise, when "day-and-night" (*ahorātra*) is mentioned, it is not known whether it is past, future, or present. This is not a fault; for "no distinction" (*aviśeṣa*) here is a simple negation (*prasajya-pratiṣedha*). By this, it is understood that the elision does not occur where there is a distinction—such as night and so forth—of the time conjoined with the lunar mansion; it is not, however, the case that the elision occurs where there is no distinction. [Question: "Why does the treatment of the conjoined [element] (*yuktavad-bhāva*) not take place when there is elision (*lup*)?"

If [the suffix were applied directly], the word *śravaṇa* would have the masculine gender. The resolution is provided by the words "by means of irregular derivation" (*nipātanāt*) and so forth; its meaning has already been explained. The mention of *nakṣatra* (asterism) which was introduced in the context is here transformed into the genitive case by implication. Therefore, he says "from a dual compound of asterisms" (*nakṣatradvandvāt*), meaning that the suffix is understood to be applied after a dual compound consisting of asterisms.
"In both the specific and the non-specific," because the mention of "non-specific" has been excluded. "Today is the day of Rādhā and Anurādhā."

But surely, since there is no distinction [between the two cases], the *lup* elision ought to apply; so how can there be the hearing (i.e., the actual pronunciation) of the suffix? To this he says: "The *lup* is superseded by [the addition of] the suffix because it is subsequent. [Regarding the word] "from a *tīya*": the suffix *tīya* is applied by the rule "after *dvi*, *tīya*" [Pāṇini 5.2.53]. He will state [later] that after *tri*, the suffix *tīya* is applied with vocalization of the vowel [by the rule "after *tri*, vocalization and *tīya*"] [Pāṇini 5.2.55]; after a word ending in that [suffix], the suffix *īkak* should be stated in the sense of the same meaning (*svārtha*). [Regarding the phrase] "not from *vidyā*."

When expressing a branch of knowledge (*vidyā*), the suffix *tīya* and others do not occur [after the word for its founder]. Regarding the rule "from a lineage name (*gotra*), as in the case of *aṅka*":

just as when the meaning "its mark" (*tasyāṅkaḥ*) is intended to be expressed, a suffix is applied after a lineage name, so too is it desired when the meaning "a *sāman* seen by him" (*tena dṛṣṭaṃ sāma*) is intended to be expressed. For example:
"a *sāman* seen by Aupaveyi" (*aupavena dṛṣṭaṃ sāma*).
The word *aupagava* ends in a *gotra* suffix according to [Pāṇini 4.1.92].

Regarding the rule "the suffix *vuñ* occurs after a *gotra* or a *caraṇa*," just as the word *aupagavaka*— meaning "this mark belongs to Aupagava"— is formed by adding *vuñ* to the word *aupagava* which ends in a *gotra* suffix to denote a mark (*aṅka*), so too is it applied in the case of the rule "a *sāman* seen by him."

But is it not the case that in the rule *nāṅkārtha* (Pāṇini 4.3.126), the sense of "like a numeral" (*aṅkavat*) was not included? How then can the suffix *vuñ* be applied when it is said "like a numeral" (*aṅkavat*) by this [present rule]? This is not a fault; for in that [previous] rule, the meaning of the suffix prescribed by the expression "like a numeral" (*aṅkavat*) is intended here. Just as a suffix is desired in the sense [of the previous rule], namely *tena gotrapratyayāntāt* (Pāṇini 4.3.120), so too is it desired here in the sense of *tena dṛṣṭaṃ sāma* ("a Sāman seen by him"). The summary statement *dṛṣṭe sāmani* has its meaning already explained. *Bāla-manoramā*: "A Sāman seen [by him]" (1190, 4.2.7). A Sāman seen.
"By that very [word]" means that it indeed continues to apply.
The meaning is that, in the sense of "a sāman seen by him," the suffixes *aṇ* and others should occur after a word ending in the third case.
"In this sense" means: the suffix *aṇ* which occurs in the sense of "a *sāman* seen [in this]" is optionally treated as having an indicatory letter *ṭ* (*ḍit*). Thus, *auśanam*.
This is the form according to the view that there is elision of the *ṭi* (the final vowel and following consonant).
From the *Bālamanoramā*: "After *kali*, the suffix *ḍhak* [is applied]" (Pāṇini 4.2.7).
This is a *vārttika*. [Note: The two examples do not appear in the root text; it is seen as simply *vāmadevyam*. The forms are *vāmadevyam* and *vāgamadevyam*.

The first [form] has a circumflex accent (*svarita*) on the final syllable by virtue of the accent of the particle *ati*; the second has an acute accent (*udātta*) on the final syllable by virtue of the accent of the suffix. As for the question, "What is the purpose of making it marked with the *ṅit* designation?", one might consider the *ṅit* designation redundant because the elision is already established by rule 6.4.148—this refers to forms such as *ḍaḍḍau*. However, in the case of *na vāmadevyam* (not the Vāmadevya chant), while the word *nañ* is being carried over from 6.2.155, rule 6.2.156 prescribes that the final syllable of the subsequent member (*uttarapada*) is acute. To ensure that this rule does not apply here, the *ṅit* designation is made.

And when there is no mention of *ana* there, the accent belongs to the negative particle (*nañ*) itself, which is further acute (*udātta*), because of the rule: "Particles (*nipātāḥ*) have the acute accent on their first syllable" (Phiṭ-sūtra 4.80). Now, if the marker *ḍit* were applied, why would there not be a mention of *ana*? To this he says: by the metarule (*paribhāṣā*) "when there is a mention of a form without an indicatory letter (*niranubandhaka*), that which has an indicatory letter (*sānubandhaka*) is not included," the exclusion of both *ḍa* and *ḍaḍ* is also effected.

Even when [the word] *yat* is included, by the technical rule (*paribhāṣā*) "when a single marker (*anubandha*) is employed, [a substitute] with two markers is not [to be understood]," the form *yataḥ* is obtained.

Furthermore, the very fact that the marker *ḍit* is applied here is the evidence for the existence of these two technical rules. By the phrase "not having that meaning" (*atadarthe*) in the summary verse (*saṅgrahaśloka*), the rule [Pāṇini 6.2.156] is obtained;
the meaning is "in this rule."
Regarding "nañ-svare": *nañ-svara* means the accent (*svara*) of the negative particle (*nañ*). The remainder has already been explained. Regarding "*cārmaṇaḥ*": [it is derived from *carman*].
Because of the rule *an* [Pāṇini 6.4.167], the original stem form (*prakṛtibhāva*) applies, so the elision of the suffix *ṭi* does not occur.

Because of the rule *na saṃyogādvamantāt* [Pāṇini 6.4.137], the elision of the suffix *ap* (*allopa*) does not occur. Now, why does this [elision] not apply here in the case of *chāttraiḥ parivṛto rathaḥ* ("a chariot surrounded by students")? To this he replies: "completely encircled," and so forth. This root *vṛ* functions in the sense of "encircling" (*veṣṭana*), and its prefix *pari-* indicates the state of being on all sides (*sarvato bhāva*).

Therefore, that which is surrounded on all sides must be the object of the suffix; however, the chariot is not surrounded on all sides by the students, and thus there is no occasion for the application of the suffix there.

As for the usage "the chariot surrounded by students" (*chāttraiḥ parivṛto rathaḥ*), it is figurative (*gauṇa*) through the superimposition (*adhyāropa*) of being surrounded upon [the chariot]. And when the primary sense of being surrounded exists, it is not proper to resort to a figurative, superimposed meaning. [In the example] *pāṇḍukambalī*, the long vowel is applied by [Pāṇini 6.4.13] *sau ca*. [The objection] "since it is already established by the suffix expressing possession (*matvarthīya*")...
For whatever is completely enveloped by something, that [thing] belongs to it.

Thus, since the form is established by the suffix *ineni* in the sense of possession according to Pāṇini 5.2.115, the explicit mention of "that" (*yat*) and "this" (*tat*) is for the purpose of excluding the suffix *aṇ*.
If [the desired form] could be obtained [otherwise], this rule would not have been commenced.

If this statement were not present, then the suffix *aṇ* would apply by rule 4.2.10, and consequently the form would be *pāṇḍukambala*, whereas *pāṇḍukambalī* is what is intended. Therefore, [the word *pāṇḍukambala*] is stated for the purpose of excluding *aṇ*. Regarding the phrase "the modification of a leopard (*dvīpin*) or a tiger (*vyāghra*)" and so forth:

when there is the intention to express the meaning "the hide is the modification of a leopard" or "the hide is the modification of a tiger," the words *dvaipa* and *vaiyāghra* end in the suffix *añ* by rule 4.3.154. Through these two words, the hide is denoted here because it is the modification of a leopard or a tiger.

Since it is possible for a chariot to be covered by leather specifically in its modification as the hide of a leopard or a tiger, and not by mere modification in general, it is understood that here the words *dvaipa* and *vaiyāghra* intend to refer to the leather itself. Regarding the phrase "in the expression of something unprecedented" (*apūrvavacane*), this means "the expression of what has not occurred before," that is, the designation of something new.
To the question "Of what is there the expression of something unprecedented? he says: "Of the taking of the hand," and so forth.

And although this was stated as a general rule, it is obtained here by the force of the specific grammatical injunction (*nipātana*). For just as some other non-technical (*alākṣaṇika*) operation is obtained by the force of a specific injunction, so too is this one.
[This applies to cases such as] "in both ways when feminine," and so forth.

If the word *kaumāra* denotes a male, even so its status as being "not preceded" (*apūrva*) occurs when it serves as a qualifier for the female alone and not for the male; thus, it is derived in this specific way and not otherwise—this is the meaning. Regarding the term *apūrvapati*: it is a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "one who has no husband previously."
She whose marriage ceremony with a husband has been completed is one who has a husband not previously [married to her].
The meaning is that the husband "attained" (upapanna) her, i.e., reached her. [The compound] is "one who has a husband not previously [married to her]."

This is also a *bahuvrīhi* compound: "in the sense of 'not having had [sexual intercourse] before' (*apūrvavacana*), [the form] *kaumāra* is irregularly derived (*nipātita*)," and so forth. What exactly is irregularly derived here? He says: "The suffix *aṇ* is prescribed after the word *kumārī*."
The meaning is that the suffix *aṇ* is applied by irregular derivation (*nipātana*) to the word *kumārī*.
When does this occur? He says: "when she is previously unknown" (*apūrvatvaṃ yadā tasyāḥ*).
For here, by means of this irregular derivation, either a male or a female is denoted; and in both cases, the condition of being "previously unknown" applies.
The meaning is that this nipātana (irregular formation) applies when it is a qualification of that woman and not of a man, and not otherwise;
[this is shown by the phrase] "or it is used with *kumāryā bhavati*.
By this, the formal rule (*yoga*) is rejected.

For he who has obtained a young girl (kumārī) is [referred to] as "kaumāra" there; thus, by the rule *tatra bhavaḥ* [Pāṇini 4.3.53], the word *kaumāra*, ending in the suffix *aṇ* in the sense of "belonging to that," is derived. Then, when the feminine suffix *ṅīṣ* is applied according to the rule for words denoting males (*puṃyogalakṣaṇe*), the form *kumārī* is established.
There is indeed no difference in accentuation.

For instance, even when the suffix *ṅīṣ* is applied [to *kaumāra*], and after the elision [of the final syllable] by Pāṇini 6.4.148, it ought to be accompanied by an udātta *ṅīp* according to 6.1.161.
Indeed, the suffix *ṅīṣ* is itself udātta on its first syllable due to the accentuation rule for suffixes (*pratyayasvara*).

But if this were the case, would it not follow that any other woman who is the cause for the designation "maiden" (*kaumāra*) would also be called *kaumārī*? This is not a fault; for by virtue of proximity (*pratyāsatti*), only she who is proximate to that [state of maidenhood] will be the *kaumārī* of that [man].
What, then, is its proximate cause? It is that which is the cause for the designation "childhood";
it is precisely that [state] because of which one is called "in childhood" (kaumāra), and nothing else.
Even though Vyāsa and others were also born of a maiden (kumārī), nevertheless, the suffix *aṇ* will not apply to them, because of the absence of such usage (*anabhidhānāt*).

And this non-mention must necessarily be resorted to; for otherwise, even if the technical name *nipātana* were applied, the suffix *aṇ* would indeed occur by the rule [Pāṇini 4.3.53]. By the phrase "and by the whole," etc., he shows that the vow (*vrata*) serves as a qualifier for both the base (*prakṛti*) and the suffix (*pratyaya*). The word *śāstritaḥ* is derived in the rule [Pāṇini 3.2.40]. Regarding *audaiātkam*:
the suffix *ka* is applied by [Pāṇini 7.3.51] because the word ends in *i*, *su*, *u*, or *t*. Regarding *kṣaireyī*: [the suffix *ṅīṣ* is added according to Pāṇini 4.1.45].
The suffix *ṅīp* is applied by [Pāṇini 4.1.15] *ṭiḍḍhāṇañ*. Regarding the phrase "if there is the desire to express it from that":
the word "from that" (*tataḥ*) refers to that which ends in a suffix.
This is what is meant: if in common usage there is a desire to express this [meaning] from that which ends in a suffix, then the suffix occurs in this way; not otherwise—this is the sense.
By the statement beginning with "and by that which ends in a suffix," he clarifies that a technical name (*saṃjñā*) is a qualifier of a whole.
"This is the name" refers to that which is understood through what ends in a suffix.

Regarding the word *pauṣī*: [the suffix] *aṇ* is applied by [Pāṇini 4.2.3], and the feminine suffix *ṅīp* is added to that which ends in it. [The commentary states: "It does not occur here" because the status of being a technical name (*saṃjñā*) is not understood.
For the names [of the days] do not end with the suffix *pratyaya* in the case of the ten-night period (*daśarātra*), nor do they in the case of a hired month (*bhṛtakamāsa*).
What, then, is the equivalent result? He says: "following the usage" (*prayogānusaraṇam*).
The meaning is that "following the usage" refers to the indication by usage (*prayogopalakṣaṇa*).

This is done for the purpose of specifying the scope of the application: the suffix should be produced where the usage is observed—namely, in the case of months, fortnights, and years—but not in the case of hired laborers' wages and the like.
This very point is also made by the use of the particle *iti*.
For it is thus: if there is a desire to express the meaning for common usage after a word ending in a suffix, then the suffix should be produced in that way, and not otherwise.

The particle *iti* is employed for this purpose; consequently, the worldly intention (*loka-vivakṣā*) pertains to the month, the fortnight, and the year, and not to the wages for a month and so forth.
Therefore, there is conformity with usage (*prayoga-anusaraṇa*), and the result is indeed the same for both.
[Regarding the passage] beginning with "the technical term" (*saṃjñā*).

But surely, just as the term *saṃjñā-śabda* is well-known in the world as having the result of following conventional usage, so too is the *itikaraṇa*; why then is its similarity to that [term] made known here? To this he says: "For this is not," and so forth.
For instance, in the world, this term *saṃjñā-śabda* is well-known as having the result of following conventional usage, whereas the *itikaraṇa* is not.
Therefore, the sense is that its similarity to that [term] is thus made known.

With the words "In the case of being the referent of a technical name" (*saṃjñārthatve*), he demonstrates the purpose of the indication [by the rule]. That whose meaning is equivalent to a technical name is "one whose meaning is the same as a technical name" (*saṃjñārtha*).

The word "equivalent" (*tulya*) is not employed because its meaning is already understood through the compound; the sense is that just as in the rule *rucyarthānām* [Pāṇini 1.4.33], the word "same" (*samāna*) is not used alongside the word "desire" (*ruci*).
The state of being the object of a name is "name-object-ness" (*saṃjñārthatvam*).
And this word *artha* signifies purpose (*prayojana*). [Thus it is said: "That becomes appropriate."

Since it has been indicated that the particle *iti* has the same meaning as a technical name (*saṃjñā*), it is stated that wherever the particle *iti* is used for the sake of following conventional usage, from each such instance an intended meaning (*vivakṣā*) arises; thus, [the rule] becomes logically consistent, because the purpose of the particle *iti* is to function as a technical name. Regarding the example "pūrṇamāsādaṇ":

a *bahuvrīhi* compound is formed in the sense of "that lunar day on which the month is full. From this very [technical name], the suffix *aṇ* is applied by virtue of this specific nipātana (irregular formation).
This [term] *paurṇamāsī* is derived from *pūrṇamāsa* with the suffix *aṇ* according to [Pāṇini 4.3.120];
it is the name for a specific lunar day (*tithi*).

The derivation, however, should be performed in some way or another. [According to] *Bāla-manoramā*: "From *kṣīra*, the suffix *ḍhañ* [is applied]" (Pāṇini 4.2.21); "In this [month], there is the full moon day (*paurṇamāsī*)," [and] from the word *iti*.
And this is established in the *Bhāṣya*.
[Thus we have] *pauṣī*.
The full moon day conjoined with the Puṣya asterism is *pauṣī*; the month in which that occurs is the *pauṣa* month.
From the word *pauṣī*, by the addition of the suffix *aṇ* and the elision of the vowel *ī* according to the rule *yasyeti ca*, [the form *pauṣa* is derived].
