It becomes equal to that which is certain [of its application], namely: "this existence is appropriate there. For example, Devadatta who exists in Rūghna is called "Rūghna," even though he does not always exist in Rūghna; for he inevitably departs at times for the northern regions and so forth, yet the suffix denoting existence (*bhavapratyaya*) still applies to him.

Furthermore, if "existence there" (*tatra bhavaḥ*) were [the sole meaning], then in the case of *jihvāmūlīya*—meaning "a phoneme existing at the root of the tongue"—the suffix *cha* prescribed by the rule *jihvāmūlāṅguleśchaḥ* (Pāṇini 4.3.62), which falls under the governing heading *tatra bhavaḥ* (4.3.53), would not apply; for a phoneme does not exist permanently at the root of the tongue. Therefore, since "mostly existing" (*prāyabhava*) is included within "existing there," it does not exceed the scope of that [heading]; thus, the mention of "mostly existing" is redundant. Regarding the phrase "fitness" (*avakḷpti*) and so forth:
fitness means possibility (*sambhāvanā*).

"Non-excess of measure" (*pramāṇānatireka*) means that the measure of the contained (*ādheya*) does not exceed the measure of the container (*ādhāra*), such that the contained enters into the container—as in "it fits in a *ruāudhna*. That which is possible within a *ruāudhna* does not exceed the measure of the *ruāudhna*; because it enters into it, an object such as an army is described in this way. For example: "silk cloth."

But surely, *vāru* cannot denote silk; rather, it denotes the silkworm, and therefore the term would apply only to the worm, not to the cloth. Furthermore, since no specific distinction is stated, it would follow that the suffix could also apply to the sheath belonging to a sword. To this he says: "This is a conventional usage" (*rūḍhireṣā*), and so forth. For a word based on conventional usage (*rūḍhi*) is derived in whatever manner possible; its etymological meaning need not necessarily be considered there, because in some cases the etymological meaning is impossible.

For instance, the word *tailapāyikā* is derived in the sense of "one who drinks oil," yet the literal meaning of its constituent parts need not necessarily be relied upon there, because in some cases the meaning of the parts is impossible.

That is to say, although the word *tailapāyikā* is etymologically derived as "one who drinks oil" (*tailam pibati*), it nevertheless applies to a certain specific creature even when that creature is devoid of the act of drinking oil.
Therefore, even if [the term] does not apply to a worm...

Now, what fault is there in [the word] arising from the sheath of a sword, such that a cognition [of the sword] is not accepted from it? [If you say: "It follows that it would denote the sword," [we reply:
if you argue that it is because the sword is possible therein, then it follows that when a cognition arises from another sheath, it would denote a worm, for the worm is also possible therein.
Or, if you say that even in that case it denotes the cloth by virtue of conventional usage (*rūḍhi*) and not the worm; [then we reply:]...

In that case, why is the term *varuā* used for [silk] produced from a cocoon (*kośa*), and not for a sword? He thinks as follows: although the suffix *ḍhañ* is prescribed after the word *kośa* in the sense of "produced therefrom" (*sambhūta*), nevertheless, from the word *kauśeya*, the meaning "produced therefrom" is not understood; rather, the meaning is "modification" (*vikāra*), due to conventional usage (*rūḍhi*).

Thus, *kauśeya-varuā* means "the modification of the cocoon is silk. And so it has been stated by the author of the Vārttika: "The suffix *ḍhañ* is applied to *kośa* in the sense of a modification, because the sense of 'produced therefrom' is not applicable" (*vikāre kośāḍḍhañ, sambhūtārthānupapatteḥ*).

Regarding [Pāṇini 4.3.42]: from the word *kauśeya*, the derivative (*vikāra*) is understood to refer to the cocoon of a silkworm, and not to the sheath of a sword, due to conventional usage (*rūḍhi*). Therefore, the suffix is correctly applied only after that word which denotes the source whose derivative is understood, and not after any other. The term "time" (*kāla*) is reiterated in order to qualify the subsequent base-words (*prakṛti*).
Furthermore, when the essential form (*svarūpa*) [of a word] is apprehended, subsequent bases (*prakṛti*) cannot be qualified, because an essential form is by nature unique.
Therefore, this refers specifically to the apprehension of meaning.
Thus, he says "from those expressing specific times" and so forth, in order to show that the suffix is understood to be applied from words denoting particular durations of time.
Regarding "haimanaḥ" and "śaiśiraḥ," the suffix *ṛtvaṇ* is applied by the rule *sandhivelādi-sūtra* (Pāṇini 4.3.16). From the *Bālamano ramā*: "kālāt sādhupuṣpyatpacyamāneṣu" (4.3.45).

The meaning is that when the senses of "sādhuh" (skilled/proper), "puṣpyat" (flowering), and "pacyamānam" (being cooked/ripening) are intended, suffixes prescribed for the locative case (*saptamyanta*) shall be applied after a word denoting time. Thus, [the suffix *ṭhañ*] is added in the sense of "proper [in that season]," "flowering [in that season]," and "ripening [in that season]."

From the root *puṣp* meaning "to blossom," which belongs to the *divādi* class, the form *puṣpyat* is derived by adding the suffix *śatṛ* (forming the present participle). In the expression *haimanaḥ prāvāraḥ* ("a winter cloak"),
the suffix *aṇ* is applied according to the rule "sarvatrāṇ ca talopaśca," and there is an elision of the suffix *it*.
Regarding "vāsantī," the suffix *ṅīp* is applied by the rule "ṭiḍḍhāṇañ..."; regarding "śāradā," the suffix *aṇ* is applied by the rule for [names derived from] seasons (*ṛtvaṇ*).
In the rule *tatra bhavaḥ*, the phrase *yāvat-kālāt* is understood to follow. In the *Bālamano ramā*, under sūtra 4.3.53 (*upte ca*), it is stated:
"The word *tatra* [is understood] as before."
When the sense of "sown" follows a word denoting time ending in the locative case, the prescribed suffixes shall apply. [The word] "sown" is derived from the root *ḍu vap* (to sow seeds).

The intention is that the past tense (*bhūtakāla*) is not intended to be expressed here. "The division of the rule (*yogavibhāga*) is for the sake of what follows" means that the suffix *vuñ* should apply only in subsequent cases; it should not apply to words such as *sādhu*, etc. "It is an exception (*apavāda*) to *ṭhañ*" refers to the suffix *ṭhañ* which would otherwise be obtained by the rule *kālāṭ ṭhañ* [Pāṇini 4.3.11].

Now, one might object: "The suffix *ṭhañ* is prescribed after words denoting time (*kāla*), yet the word *āyujī* does not denote time; therefore, how can *ṭhañ* apply here? Anticipating this doubt, he states—"joined with *aiṇī* and *āyujī*"—in order to demonstrate that the word *āyujī* does indeed denote time. But how can words such as *kalāpa* and others denote time, given that their usage is well-established in reference to peacocks and other such things? To this he replies: "words such as *kalāpa*, etc. He clarifies this point in the same way: "at which time," and so forth.
The word *āṭṭha* is conventionally established here as a specific type of tree;
therefore, since it is connected with time in its entirety, no specific point of time is indicated by means of it.

Consequently, he says—beginning with "because the fruits of what you have sown do not ripen"—in order to demonstrate that the word *āṭṭha* refers to the time associated with the ripening of those fruits.

Although the word *āṬṭha* occurs in the sense of a tree, it nevertheless occurs in the sense of its fruit. "It is an exception (*apavāda*) to *aṇ* and *ṭhañ*" means that it is an exception to *ṛtvaṇ* after the word *grīṣma*,
and an exception to *kālaṭ-ṭhañ* after the word *anaraśama*.

The term *avarasamā* means "inferior and equal. This statement is made because the suffix *ṭhañ* would otherwise apply by virtue of the rule *kālāt ṭhañ*. Therefore, it is intended that *ṭhañ* need not be explicitly mentioned; since the suffix *vuñ* is optionally prescribed, even without the mention of *ṭhañ*, *ṭhañ* itself occurs in its alternative case (*pakṣe*) as required by the general rule.
Regarding the phrase "the mention of *ṭhañ*," etc.:

if the mention of *ṭhañ* were not made here, then in cases such as *sandhivelā* [Pāṇini 4.3.16], because of the reading *saṃvatsarāt phalaparvaṇoḥ* (Gaṇasūtra 104), the suffix *aṇ* would apply by virtue of being an exception (*apavāda*) to the *aṇ* prescribed for *sandhivelā* and so on; thus, when time is intended to be expressed, *vuñ* would be set aside and only *aṇ* would occur. By the mention of *ṭhañ*, however, even *aṇ* is superseded and *ṭhañ* alone occurs. Examples: *naiśikaḥ*, *naiśaḥ*.

[The forms] *prādoṣikaḥ* and *prādoṣaḥ* [are derived as follows]: by rule Pāṇini 4.3.14, the suffix *ṭhañ* is applied after the words *niśā* and *pradoṣa*. When [the time] has been released by that [suffix], the suffix *ṛtvaṇ* applies to the word *pakṣa*. Since the term "time" (*kāla*) is understood to be recurring [from a previous rule], and since time itself does not pass away, it is understood that here the study [associated with time] is designated by the words *niśā* and so forth through a figurative application (*gauṇyā vṛttyā*), because it is concomitant with night.

For this very reason, he says: "The study associated with the night is 'night'"; and "This is an exception (apavāda) to the suffix *aṇ* and to *cha*. That which among the *digādi* group is a term like *vāpyādi* (meaning a large pond), for that the suffix *cha* is the exception; but for the remaining [terms], the suffix *aṇ* applies as a *prāgdīvyatīya* derivative. Now, what is the purpose of including *mukha* and *jaghana* in the *digādi* list, since they denote parts of the body and the subsequent rule (Pāṇini 4.3.55) will already apply to them? To this he replies: "In the case of *mukha* and *jaghana*.
For those words *mukha* and *jaghana* which denote parts of an army (*senāvayava*) are not words denoting parts of the body (*śarīrāvayava*).
For a body has as its intrinsic nature parts such as hands and feet, whereas an army does not have such a nature; what then is it? It consists of a collection of chariots and so forth.
Regarding the rule "udakāt saṃjñāyām":
when the word *udaka* occurs and a name (*saṃjñā*) is understood, the suffix *yaṅ* is applied—thus *udakyā*, which refers to a woman in her menses.
And here, neither the meaning of the base nor the meaning of the suffix exists;

and that non-existence of those two is understood by the mention of the term "saṃjñā" (name). In the case of a name, as in *audako matsyaḥ* ("a fish from the water"), the suffix *aṇ* alone occurs. [This rule] is an exception (*apavāda*) to *aṇ*.
Because its commencement does not apply until that [suffix] has been reached.

However, as for that which begins with *pāda* and so on, because it follows after that, it subverts the *yat* suffix and the *cha* suffix. Since the suffix *yat* would apply by virtue of [the words] *dṛti* and *kukṣi* being parts of the body, and since the word *kukṣi* is also listed among the *dhūmādi* group—whereby the suffix *vuñ* would apply by [Pāṇini 4.2.127]—the suffix *aṇ* is prescribed for the remaining [words], and the suffix *ḍhañ* is then ordained. He says "the word *asti*" etc., so that the word *asti* might not be understood as ending in a verbal suffix (*tiṅanta*).

According to the rule "those which resemble case-endings and accents are also called particles (*nipāta*)," this is a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) resembling a verbal form that bears the technical designation of a particle; it is not actually a verbal suffix.
And this has the same meaning as a verbal suffix (*tiṅanta*), as in "the Brāhmaṇī possesses milk" (*astikṣīrā brāhmaṇī*).
It also has a different meaning, as in "he exists in wealth," as in "he is possessed of [existence]" (*astimān*);
here it is understood as "wealthy."

In this case, since no specific distinction is stated, both [the singular and plural] are understood. Someone might have the misconception that because of the use of the plural number, the suffix must be applied only after a word ending in the plural; otherwise, he would have used the singular for the instruction. To dispel that [misconception], he says: "The word *grīvā*," and so forth.

He shows why the plural is used due to the specific meaning, and not merely to ensure that [the suffix] occurs only after a plural-ending word. "From *bahu*, *deva*, etc."—the meaning is that this form of the rule should be explained as: "The suffix *ñya* occurs after *bahu*, *deva*, and *pañcajana*."

In this regard, the explanation is as follows: the particle *ca* (and) occurs here; by virtue of it, the suffix *ñya* will also apply after *bahis* and the others. [The question] "What then? and so forth:

how is it that the suffix, which is stated generally as being applied after an *avyayībhāva* compound, applies specifically after *parimukha* and the rest? To this he says: "And of *parimukha* etc.," and so forth.
The word *ca* (and) is used in the sense of a reason (*hetu*).
There is no purpose for the inclusion of *parimukha* and so forth in the list of gaṇas;

for even if this [rule] were not there, its status would still be that of an injunction (*vidhi*). Therefore, it occurs only after *parimukha* and the others, and not after every avyayībhāva compound.
If this is so, one might say that it should simply have been stated as "after *parimukha* and the others"; to this he says: "Of those," and so forth.

For if it were stated simply as "from *parimukha* and so forth," then—even in the absence of the mention of *avyayībhāva*—the suffix would apply even from *tatpuruṣa* compounds such as *parimukha*. However, when that [mention of *avyayībhāva*] is present, it does not occur: *parimukha* is a *prādisamāsa* meaning "the face is encompassed" (*parigataṃ mukham*), and that which exists there is *parimukha*; here only the suffix *aṇ* occurs. Furthermore, the mention of *avyayībhāva* must necessarily be made in the latter half [of the rule]:
[Pāṇini 4.3.60] "after *pari* and *anu* preceded by [a word denoting a village]," so that it may apply to *avyayībhāva* compounds.
Regarding "pārihaṇavyam": [the substitution of] guṇa for o [is applied], and by [Pāṇini 6.1.79], there is the replacement of av. Regarding "aupakūlam": [the suffix cha is applied].
The term *avyayībhāva* is formed by [Pāṇini 2.1.6], *avyayaṃ vibhakti*, etc. However, since this [word] is not listed among the *parimukha* group, only the suffix *aṇ* occurs.

Here, how is *piramukham* an *avyayībhāva* compound? For it is only [compounds] with *apa*, *pari*, *bahiḥ*, *añcu*, and [words ending in] the fifth case that are compounded according to Pāṇini 2.1.11; and the fifth case occurs only when *pari* is used as a *karmapravacanīya*. Furthermore, the designation *karmapravacanīya* is applied by rule 1.4.88, yet in *parimukhe* no sense of exclusion (*varjana*) is understood; rather, what is understood is the sense of "on all sides" (*sarvatobhāva*). If this is so, then it will be an *avyayībhāva* by means of the rule-splitting (*yogavibhāga*) of the sūtra *avyayam* (Pāṇini 2.1.6). Others, however, [hold that] those which occur here...
The *avyayībhāva* compounds beginning with *parihāṇi* and so forth are formed by that very rule, [Pāṇini 2.1.12].
In this regard, even for those cases where exclusion (*varjana*) is not understood, they are formed by the split-off rule (*yogavibhāga*) [Pāṇini 2.1.6], "An indeclinable.
However, those beginning with *upasīra* and so forth, which have *upa-* as their prefix, are formed by [the rule] "An indeclinable," etc., [Pāṇini 2.1.6] when proximity (*sāmīpya*) is intended.
Regarding "anugaṅgam":
by [Pāṇini 2.1.16], it attains the status of an indeclinable (*avyayabhāva*).

Others, however, hold that compounds beginning with *anu*—such as *anusīram* and so on—attain the status of an indeclinable by means of [the rule] "that which begins with *anu* is an indeclinable in the sense of 'behind' (*paścāt*)" and so forth. As for the statement: "The word *antar* is compounded in the sense of a case ending (*vibhaktyartha*)."
By the rule beginning with *avyayaṃ vibhakti* [Pāṇini 2.1.6],

the meaning of the case ending (*vibhaktyartha*) is the locus (*adhikaraṇa*), because the word *antaḥ* has the locus as its primary sense. Regarding the statement "the suffix *ṭhañ* should be stated after the word *samāna*," the word "should be stated" (*vaktavya*) refers to what is to be explained.

In this regard, the explanation is as follows: although the rule would have been established simply by [the compound] *antaḥ-pūrva*, the additional inclusion of the word *pada* is made for the purpose of indicating that here the operation applies even when there is an additional element; therefore, the suffix *iñ* occurs even after words such as *samāna*. By this, it should be understood that the suffix *ṭhañ* occurs after *adhyātma* and so forth, after *ūrdhvanda*, *ūrdhvadeha*, and after words where *loka* is the final member. For example: *ādhyātmikam*.
Regarding the term "ādhyātmika":
*adhyātmam* means "with respect to the self" (*ātmani adhi*). This is an *avyayībhāva* compound in the sense of a case ending.
The vowel lengthening of both members of the compound is according to [Pāṇini 7.3.20]: *anuśatikādīnāṃ ca*.
"This *adhyātma* and so forth is a class of words based on their form (*ākṛtigaṇa*).

If this is so, then the rule "the suffix *ṭhañ* should be stated after words beginning with *samāna*" (Vārttika 454) and so on would be purposeless, since [the desired forms] would already be established by the rule "after [words] beginning with *adhyātma*. It is not purposeless; for it serves as an elaboration (*prapañca*) of this very point.
That is to say, the class beginning with *adhyātma* itself is being elaborated upon here.

Now, is it not the case that the word *ūrdhva* ends in the vowel *a*, so how has it come here to end in the consonant *m*? To this he says: "by the word *ūrdhva*" and so forth. [The examples] *aihaukikaḥ* (belonging to this world) and *pāralaukikaḥ* (belonging to the next world) show the vṛddhi strengthening of both members of the compound as before. [The forms] *mukhatīyam* and *pārātīyam* are derived by adding the suffix *tasi* according to [Pāṇini 5.4.45].
The suffix *matup* is added optionally by the supplementary rule (*vārttika*) "there is an addition [of the suffix] after *ādi* and others" (Vārttika 634).

The elision of the *ṭi* portion occurs by the rule "for indeclinables, there is elision of the *ṭi* when any *bha*-suffix follows" (Vārttika 842). Furthermore, it should be stated that the two suffixes *man* and *īyasun* are also applicable.
It depends on the word *madhya*. [As stated in the rule: "From *madhya*, the suffix *dinaṇ* is applied in the sense of 'midday'.
Thus, the word *madhya* undergoes the change to *madhyaṃ*, and the suffix *dinaṇ* occurs after it.
[The word] "of *sthāman*."

[The suffix] *aṇ* is applied after a nominal stem ending in the word *sthāman*. [In the example] *āsthāma*, it is a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "one whose strength (*sthāma* = *bala*) is present" (*āsyeva*). Due to its inclusion in the *pṛṣodarādi* group, the letter *s* is replaced by *t*.
From the sense "existing in *sthāman*" (*sthāmni bhavaḥ*), the suffix *aṇ* is applied, which is then elided. [This applies] also to stems ending in *ajina*.
The term *luk* (elision) is connected [to the following]. In the example "vṛkājinaḥ," there is elision of the *aṇ* suffix.
Regarding the term *samānasya*:
this is a genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) characterized by immediate succession.
The meaning is that the suffix *ṭhañ* is desired immediately after the word *samāna*.
Regarding the term "samānasya":
this is a genitive case characterized by immediate succession.
The meaning is that the suffix *ṭhañ* is desired immediately after the word *samāna*.
Regarding the phrase "in *adhyātma* and so forth":
the locative case is used here in the sense of a domain (*vaiṣayika-adhikaraṇa*).
The meaning is that the suffix *ṭhañ* is desired when *adhyātma* and the like constitute the subject matter (*viṣaya*).
Regarding the phrase "of one's own person and another," the word "and" (ca) implies that the suffix *īya* is also applied. This is according to the rule: "after *ūrdhva*, *dama*, and *deha*."

The meaning is that the suffix *ṭhak* is applied after the word *ūrdhva*, as well as after the words *dama*, *ūrdhva*, and *deśa*. Regarding the phrase "the suffix *īya* should be applied to the middle one," the word *atha* is used in the sense of conjunction (*samuccaya*).
The meaning is that the suffix *īya* should be applied immediately after the word *madhya*. [This is stated as:
"the two suffixes *maṇ* and *īya* are likewise," where the phrase "after the word *madhya*" is understood.
The suffixes *maṇ* and *mīya* are to be applied after the word *madhya*.

Regarding the rule "likewise from *ajina*": the meaning is that elision (*luk*) should be stated [as an exception] when the word ends in *ajina*. Regarding the example "pārigrāmikam": [this is derived from *parigraha* with the suffix *ṭhañ*].
From the *pari-* [rule] following an avyayībhāva compound ending in the word *grāma*: *pari-grāmāt* (Pāṇini 2.1.12) forms an avyayībhāva compound;
[the derivative form is] *ānugrāmikam*.

Regarding this as well: "because it is an exception" (*yato'pavādaḥ*) refers to what is obtained by the rule *śarīrāvayavācca* [Pāṇini 4.3.55]. "When *cha* is applicable" refers to the preceding rule. Furthermore, the word *karṇikā* is conventionally established (*ruḍha*) in the sense of a particular type of ornament;
and in the case of conventional words, there is no necessity that they must involve a connection with the ear. "{The portion of the sūtra is: 'in its explanation'}" means "its explanation."

*Vyākhyānam* means "that by which something is explained"; the suffix *lyuṭ* is used here in the sense of an instrument (*karaṇe*). Because of the word *ca* ("and"), it is understood that the rule applies to what occurs in that [context] as well.

Now, since *vyākhyāna* is the meaning of the suffix and the word *ca* is heard immediately after it, it would be logical for *ca* to carry forward (*anukarṣaṇa*) only those items of the same class as the meaning of the suffix, and not even the case-ending (*vibhakti*) expressing grammatical competency; for *ca* brings about a conjunction (*samuccaya*) of items belonging to the same class, as in [Pāṇini 4.2.40].

By the particle *ca* (and), which stands in proximity to the suffix (*pratyaya*), it is the suffix itself that is conjoined. For example, in the rule [Pāṇini 4.2.41], once the case endings of the governing word (*samarthavibhakti*) preceding the word "pādānāt" have been withdrawn, it would be more appropriate for the suffix to be applied even in the sense of "belonging to" (*bhava*) by the very force of the genitive case; thus, it was incorrectly stated there. Instead of saying "and in the sense of belonging to that" (*tatra bhave ca*), it would have been proper to say "and in the sense of belonging to that" (*tasya bhave ca*). To this, he replies: "In proximity to the meaning of the sentence," and so forth.
Here, by the use of the term *iti*, the meaning "explanation" (*vyākhyāna*) is what is being referred back, and not the meaning of the suffix used for explanation.

Therefore, the particle *ca* (and), being uttered immediately after the word ending in the suffix *iti*, is heard in proximity to the very meaning of the sentence as apprehended by that suffix; thus, it conjoins only a sentence-meaning of the same class.

For this reason, the locative case in the sense of "occurring therein" (*tatra bhave*) is employed precisely by the force of the rule itself; otherwise, he would have said simply, "and in its commentary" (*tasya vyākhyāne ca*).
He asks, "What then is this sentence-meaning? and replies: "In that which occurs therein," [meaning] "but the word *Pāṭalīputra* is not the name of the thing to be explained."
But surely, Pāṭaliputra is explained by means of Sukosalā; it must necessarily be that which is to be explained, for otherwise Sukosalā would not be its explainer.

Is the point that the word "Pāṭaliputra" becomes the name of that which is to be explained by that explanation? This is not so; the point is that if what is intended here is that which is to be explained, this [Sukosalā] is not its name.
Furthermore, what is intended here as that which is to be explained? That which is most well-known in the world as being that which is to be explained.
Whence is this [known]? From the mention of the name of that which is to be explained.

For in this context, the mention of the name of that which is to be explained must not be made for the sake of the meaning to be explained; because even without it, the cognition of the very name of that which is to be explained is established.
To illustrate: in the word "tasya" (of it), the correlative (*pratiyogi*) of "it" is already included in the explanation.
And that [suffix] is possible only for what is to be explained (*vyākhyātavya*), not for anything else.
Therefore, it is understood that by the rule "of that" (*tasya*) with the genitive case-ending, whatever is to be explained by force of context is precisely what is taken as its referent.

Consequently, even without the explicit mention of the name of the thing to be explained, the suffix will occur only after a word denoting the name of the thing to be explained; so what is the purpose of explicitly mentioning the name of the thing to be explained? It is done for this purpose: so that the suffix may occur only after a word denoting that which is well-known in the world as being "to be explained."
Grammatical treatises and the like are well-known specific types of texts in the world; they are not [places such as] Pāṭaliputra and so forth.

Even so, the mention of the word *vyākhyātavya* (to be explained) should not have been made; for, by the very force of mentioning that which is to be explained, the suffix would indeed be obtained from those words already well-known as being "to be explained. This is not the case. For, when the meaning of the suffix is "explanation," once the suffix is established from the word itself denoting "that which is to be explained," the mention of *vyākhyātavya* again serves to show that the suffix is obtained from those words which are well-known as being "to be explained," but it does not apply to things existing therein (*tatra bhava*), because there is no such force [of the rule] in that regard.

Furthermore, since in the sense of "existence" (*bhava*), those [suffixes] explained therein are more commonly established, it is desired that the suffixes be applied only to those specific bases that express that meaning, and not to just any base whatsoever. Therefore, within the governing rule for *bhava*, the term "name" (*nāman*) must be included in order to encompass the conventional meanings (*rūḍhi*). Now, for what purpose are the governing rules for *bhava* and "explanation" (*vyākhyāna*) established simultaneously? To this he says: "Of *bhava* and explanation," and so forth.
The simultaneous governing rule of these two is for the purpose of stating here the exceptions (*apavāda*) beginning with *ṭhañ*.

Now, why is it said that [the rule] is for the purpose of prescribing an exception (*apavāda*), so that there may be a specification of the meaning of the suffixes such as *aṇ* and others which are under discussion? To this he says: "For those two meanings have already been specified.
For those two meanings have indeed already been specified:
one is by the rule "born therein" (*tatra bhavaḥ*), and the other is by the rule "belonging to that" (*tasyedaṃ*).
This is because this explanation possesses a specific distinction: "The commencement [of the rule] is for the sake of [words] having an infinite acute accent.
If that is so, then these two examples alone—*rājasūyikam* and *vājapeyikam*—are appropriate.

This is because, in the words *rājasūya* and *vājapeya*, since the final member is a *kṛt*-derived stem, it has an acute accent on the middle syllable by its original accent (*prakṛtisvara*), and thus the final member here is acutely accented on its first syllable.

One [form] is [acute on the first syllable] by the accent of the whole (*kṛtsvara*) because it ends in a suffix, while the other is [acute on the first syllable] by the rule *yato ’nācaḥ* [Pāṇini 6.1.207].

Furthermore, when the compound is formed, the word remains acute on the first syllable due to the preservation of the original form (*prakṛtibhāva*) by the rule *samāse ca kṛte* [Pāṇini 6.2.139]; thus we have {āgniṣṭomikaḥ, nāvayajñikaḥ—Kāśikā} and "āgniṣṭomikaṃ nāvayajñikam.

These two examples are incorrect, because this [rule] does not apply since the words *agniṣṭoma* and *navayajña* are already acute on the final syllable by the accent of the suffix (*pratyayasvara*). Indeed, there is no difference whether the suffix *ṭhañ* is applied by the preceding rule or by this one.
This has been cited here because of its association with *kratu* (sacrifice).
It is understood that the word functions [as a derivative] due to association. The form *puroḍāśasyedaṃ* is oxytone (*antodātta*).
Therefore, when the suffix *ṭhañ* would otherwise apply by virtue of the rule *bahvaca-antodāttāt ṭhañ* [Pāṇini 4.3.67], [the following applies].

The word *puroḍāśa*, however, has its middle syllable udātta according to the rule "In a light [syllable] at the end, or when two [light syllables] precede, the heavy [syllable] is [udātta]" (Phiṭ-sūtra 2.42). While the suffix *aṇ* would have been applicable here, *ṣṭhan* is prescribed instead.
The letter *v* is for the sake of [forming] the feminine suffix *ṅīṣ*; the letter *n* is for the sake of making the first syllable udātta.
Their preparation is the *mantra* called *pauroḍāśa*.
[The term] means "that which is associated with the *puroḍāśa*.
By virtue of its capacity or through association, the word *puroḍāśa* refers to the *mantra* by which the *puroḍāśas* are prepared; it does not refer to the *puroḍāśas* themselves.
Why is this so? Because the mention of the name of that which is to be explained continues [from the previous rule].
For sacrificial cakes (*puroḍāśa*) are not more well-known as things to be explained. "An exception to *aṇ*"—by the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), the suffix *ṭhañ* is included.
In that regard, for those words ending in *ṛ* such as *udgātṛ* and others which consist of many syllables (*bahvac*) and are oxytone (*antodātta*), [the suffix] *ṭhak* is an exception to *ṭhañ*.
Furthermore, even from *brāhmaṇa*, *prathama*, and *adhvara*, only *ṭhañ* is applied;
these too consist of many syllables and are oxytone by the accent of the nominal stem (*prātipadika-svara*).
Even from a compound word consisting of both a noun and a verb, it is that very [suffix] which occurs;
moreover, it is polysyllabic and has its final syllable accented acute by the accent of the compound.
From the remaining [bases], there is the suffix *aṇ*.
Regarding the forms *pāṃśukam* and *pāñcahotṛkam*:
[the suffix] *ka* is applied by [Pāṇini 7.3.51], *isu-suk-tāntāt kaḥ*.

Since the words *pañcahotṛ* and *caturhotṛ* end in a *dvigu* compound, they are *ādyudātta* (acute-accented on the first syllable) by the rule [Pāṇini 6.2.29], *dvigau*, which prescribes the original accent (*prakṛtisvara*) of the preceding member.
For the first member [of the compound] is acute-accented by the rule *nraḥ saṃkhyāyāḥ* (Phiṭ-sūtra 2.28).
The word *puraścaraṇa*, ending in the suffix *lyuṭ*, is middle-accented by the rule *kṛduttarapadaprakṛtisvara* (Pāṇini 6.2.138).
The verbal noun (*ākhyāta*) is acute-accented on its first syllable by the rule *ākhyātaśabdaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.2.49). [The phrase] "for the sake of grasping the meaning through association" [is used].

And it should be understood that this is obtained by resorting to an *ekaśeṣa* (single-remainder) compound. Regarding the phrase "an exception to [the suffixes] *ṭhañ* and *añ*," the word "etc. (*ādi*) includes *ṭhak* and *cha*.
Among those [words ending in *cha*], for those consisting of many syllables (*bahvac*) and having the udātta accent on the final syllable, [the suffix] *ṭhañ* applies.
[The suffix] *ṭhak* is prescribed after words ending in *vidyā*, *nyāya*, *śikṣā*, and *śabda* when they denote a period of two years (*dvyaj-lakṣama*).
[The suffix] *cha* is prescribed after the word *vyākaraṇa* when it is *vṛddha*.

Why is the mention of *aṇ* necessary? It might be argued that it is unnecessary because [the suffix] *tā* is already prescribed after words such as *krayaṇa* and others, and if this were so, one might suspect that the exceptions beginning with *ṣṭhan* would not apply; for if those exceptions were not applied, their prescription would be rendered purposeless.

Therefore, that which is prescribed by the authority of the statement and would not otherwise be obtained because it is sublated by another will indeed take place; and is that [suffix] *aṇ*? To this he says: "The mention of *aṇ*" and so forth.

In that context, if the mention of *aṇ* were not made, then whatever here is a *vṛddha* [word] with an udātta accent on the final syllable—which would otherwise be sublated by *ṭhañ*—would, by virtue of the prior statement, result in *cha* alone. Therefore, the mention of *aṇ* is for the purpose of subverting *cha*, which is itself a sublater.
By this, the form *vāstuvidya* is established.
The word *vāstuvidyā* is a *vṛddha* [term], and as a compound, it is accented on the final syllable by the rule *samāsasya*. [The examples] beginning with *ṛgayana*: thus, *ṛgayana*.

The word *ṛgayana* is a noun derived from the action (*bhāvasādhana*), meaning "the path of the Ṛg-verses" (*ṛcām ayana*). Although the suffix *lyuṭ* (ana) is prescribed for expressing the action, nevertheless, by way of metaphorical transfer (*abhedopacāra*), it refers to the treatise that possesses that action; and as such, it is accented on the final syllable according to [Pāṇini 6.2.150].

As for those who derive the word *ṛgayana* using *lyuṭ* in the sense of the instrument (*karaṇe*), their word would be accented on the middle syllable by the rule of the original accent of the subsequent member of a compound (*kṛduttarapadaprakṛtisvara*); thus, its inclusion in the list would not be necessary, as it is already established by [Pāṇini 4.1.83]. The word *padavyākhyāna* is accented on the final syllable according to [Pāṇini 6.2.151].
Regarding the word *māna*:
when derived from the root *man* with the suffix *ghañ*, it is oxytone by [Pāṇini 6.2.144];
if, however, it is derived from the root *mināti* with the suffix *lyuṭ*, it is oxytone by [Pāṇini 6.2.150]. {This is not found in the Kāśikā or the Padamañjarī.}
Regarding the term *chandobhāva*:
by the rule *gatikārakopapadāt kṛt* [Pāṇini 6.2.138], it is accented on the final syllable due to the accent of a *kṛt*-suffix;
furthermore, it is derived from the verbal root *bhāṣ* with the suffix *a* [Pāṇini 3.3.103].
The word *chandoviciti* has its final syllable accented acute by [Pāṇini 6.2.151] and so forth;
the word *punarukta* has its final syllable accented acute by [Pāṇini 6.2.144].
The word *nirukta* is oxytone (accented on the final syllable) according to [Pāṇini 6.2.146]. The word *vyākaraṇa*, ending in the suffix *lyuṭ*, is middle-accented (accented on the middle syllable).

The word *nigama* is derived with the suffix *gha* by the rule beginning with [Pāṇini 3.3.119], *gocarasañcara*; it is oxytone due to the accent of the suffix (*pratyayasvara*). The words *vāstuvidyā*, *aṅgavidyā*, *kṣattravidyā*, and *kṣattriyavidyā* are all oxytone by virtue of the accent of the compound (*samāsasvara*).
The words *utpāta* and *udapāda*—the latter being explained as *ud-apa-āda*—are both oxytone by virtue of the rule [Pāṇini 6.2.143] concerning *thāthādi* compounds.
Regarding *saṃvatsara*:

since it is derived according to the rule *aśeḥ saraḥ* (Dhātupāṭha 8.50), with the continuation of that context, and then by the rule *vaseḥ saṃpūrvāccit* (Dhātupāṭha 8.51, 52), the word *saṃvatsara* is oxytone.
From the root *mṛh* (to destroy), the suffix *kta* is applied; with the augment *ūṭh* added before the *kta*, the word *muhūrta* is thus oxytone (accented on the final syllable).
The word *nimitta* also [is oxytone] by virtue of the accent of its nominal stem (*prātipadika-svara*).
As for the word *upaniṣat*: [it is derived from the root *sad* with the prefix *upa-ni*, followed by the suffix *kvip*].

The suffix *kvip* is applied to the root *sad* preceded by the prefix *upa-ni*. It is oxytone (accented on the final syllable) by the rule regarding the accent of *kṛt*-suffixes. Now, regarding the phrase "having come from the foot of a tree" (*vṛkṣamūlād āgataḥ*), why does the suffix not occur after the word *vṛkṣamūla*? To this he says: "The primary," and so forth.

The word *mukhya* (primary) means that which is intended as the principal [meaning]; it is this that is accepted here, and not the secondary principal [meaning] that is invariably concomitant (*nāntarīyaka*), for when the primary meaning exists, it is not proper to accept the other, non-primary meaning, because the understanding of the function pertains to the primary. Regarding the statement "the suffix *ṭhak* [is an exception] to the suffix *ṭhan* in the sense of 'place of origin'": this is stated thus because of its frequency, since the word *kṛkaṇa* is read in this context.
For there, it is an exception to the suffix *cha* which would otherwise apply by rule 4.2.145.

The word *tīrtha* is listed here among [the items] beginning with *dhūma*; therefore, this is an exception (*apavāda*) to the suffix *vuñ* prescribed by [Pāṇini 4.2.127]. Now, what is the purpose of including the mention of *aṇ*? One might ask: "Why not simply say that [the suffixes] after *śuṇḍika* and so on are exactly as prescribed [by the general rule], and why worry that if it were stated thus, it would only be an exception? For if an exception were being formulated, the explicit statement [of the general rule] would be redundant; therefore, even without the mention of *aṇ*, *aṇ* alone will certainly occur. To this, he says: "The mention of *aṇ*" and so forth.

The word *udapāna* is listed here as a term denoting a place of labor (*āyasthāna*), whereas it is also listed among [the words] beginning with *utsa*. In that case, if the mention of *aṇ* were not present, the suffix *ṭhak* [prescribed by Pāṇini 4.1.86] would be barred, and only the suffix *añ* would apply. Therefore, the mention of *aṇ* is for the purpose of subverting that sublater [of *ṭhak*].

By means of this, the form *udapāna* is established through the suffix *aṇ*. As for the phrase "the inclusion of the short vowel *a* (taparakaraṇa) is for the sake of ease of pronunciation," [it means that it is merely for phonetic convenience].

Now, why does [the suffix *takāra*] not serve to exclude [the application of] *dīrgha* (long vowel)? Because it is impossible. For among those [words] related by *vidyā* (learning) or *yoni* (lineage), there is no nominal stem (*prātipadika*) ending in the vowel *ṛ* for which the *takāra* could serve as an exclusion. Regarding the form *pitryam*:

[the substitution] *rīṅ* [takes the place of] *ṛt* [by Pāṇini 7.4.27], and [the final *ya*] is elided [by Pāṇini 6.4.148]. If it is said that the rule for the suffix applies like that of a *gotra* (clan name)—just as in the case of *aṅka*—then only the extension (*atideśa*) of the suffix *aṇ* would follow, not that of *vuñ*.

Since the mention of *aṅka* occurs only in the rule for *aṇ*—namely, in the rule *vuñ* [Pāṇini 4.3.126] which begins with *saṅghāṅkalakṣaṇa* [4.3.127]—one might ask: why is it mentioned here? To this he says: "By the mention of *aṅka*," and so forth.

Just as in the expression "Let the curd be protected from crows," the mention of "crows" is an indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*) of any harm in general, so too here the mention of *aṅka* is an indicator of the rule *vuñ* [4.3.120].

Therefore, this is the meaning of the sūtra: just as a suffix occurs in the rule *yathā* [Pāṇini 4.3.120], so too does it occur in the rule *tathā* [Pāṇini 4.3.74]. By this, the extension (*atideśa*) of the suffix *-vuñ* is also justified. [Objection: Even so, the extension of the suffix *-aṇ* would not be obtained, for there is no mention of "clan" (*gotra*) in the rule prescribing that suffix. [Response: There is no fault, because the term "clan" (*gotra*) is carried over (*anuvartate*) from the preceding sūtra.

He shows by which sūtra the suffix *aṇ* is prescribed, namely by the rule beginning with *saṅghāṅkalakṣaṇa* [Pāṇini 4.3.127]. Regarding the phrase "derived from a compound" (*samāsādgatam*), its meaning is "that which has come from a compound. But why is the ablative case used here? It is precisely because of the indicator (*jñāpaka*) that it must be derived from a non-compound.

Since he states the suffix after a word ending in the fifth case (the ablative), it is understood that the fifth case occurs when expressing a cause (*hetu*). [The statement] "the division of the rule (*yogavibhāga*) is for the purpose of avoiding a correspondence in order (*yathāsaṃkhya*)" means this: one might object, "But since the optional particle *anyatarasyām* permits the general rule (*autsargika*), there is no possibility of a correspondence in order arising due to the disparity [in number]? This is true; however, the division of the rule is made for the sake of someone who might think that a correspondence in order applies to *rūpya* and *mayaṭ* because they are being prescribed as something not previously established. [Regarding the commentary: "First" (*prathamataḥ*)—the meaning is "it is perceived first" (*prathama upalabhyate*).
By the word "first" (*prathama*), he explains the meaning of the prefix *pra*;
and by the word "is perceived" (*upalabhyate*), he explains the meaning of the root *bhū*.
Since roots have multiple meanings, the root *bhū* here functions in the sense of "perception. Thus, "is perceived" means "is understood."

"‘It originates from the Himavat’—by this [Pāṇini 1.4.31], the Himavat receives the designation of *apādāna* (ablative). [Regarding] Pāṇini 4.3.85: *hetumanuṣyebhyo 'nyatarasyāṃ rūpyaḥ* (the suffix *rūpya* is optionally used after words denoting a cause or a person):
[this applies] precisely to the sense ‘come from that’."
He provides examples from the *hetu* [category]—beginning with *samādāgatam* and so forth.
He provides examples of words denoting humans—such as *devadattarūpyam*. [The rule] *prabhavati* (Pāṇini 4.3.85) is derived from the *Bālamanoramā*.
The phrase "tata ity eva" (only from that) [applies];
however, the word "āgata" (arrived) is excluded.
The meaning is that, in the sense of "to have power over," suffixes should be applied as prescribed after a word ending in the fifth case (ablative).
*Prabhavaḥ* means "first manifestation.
It signifies that [the Ganges] originates from the Himavat;
the meaning is that she first becomes manifest on the Himavat.
In the expression "the source of *bhuvaḥ*," there is the status of an *apādāna* (ablative point).
[As stated in] *Bālamano ramā*: "The door emerges from" (1445, 4.3.85), "the door emerges from.
[The question is: "From what? (kānyeti).
The meaning is that it is the gateway to the district known as Kānyakubja. Regarding the phrase "but it is refined there," the word *tu* (but) is used for emphasis;
it is indeed refined in that city of Vidūra, but it does not originate from there. As it is said: "Vālavāya and Vidūra."
Only the word "Vālavāya" produces the cognition, not the word "vidūra.
The meaning is that [the mountain] is first perceived by means of the word "prabhavati" (originates/is found).
And it originates on the Vālavāya mountain.

Therefore, the word *vālavāya*, which denotes that from which [the lineage] originates, is implied as the base (*prakṛti*). Just as *viśravaṇa* and *ravaṇa* are themselves recited in the list beginning with *śiva*, [so too here].

However, because this occurs under the governing rule concerning offspring (*apatya*), the word *viśravas* alone is implied as the base, since it is that by which the relationship between those two [names] and their offspring or the progenitor is established.

*Viśravas*’ offspring is *Vaiśravaṇa*, namely Rāvaṇa. Alternatively, the word *vidūra* itself is a distinct base (*prakṛtyantara*) that denotes Bālavāya; the meaning is "it comes from afar," or "it originates from the mountain Bālavāya.
This being the case, to one who might say, "The word *vidūra* is not well-known there in Bālavāya," he replies: "One should apply it as in the case of *jitvarī*."

Just as merchants alone pronounce the city of Vāsāṇasī as "Jitvarī" for the sake of auspiciousness, but not ordinary people, so too do grammarians alone pronounce Bālavāya as "Vidūra. By the phrase "like Jitvarī," he indicates that conventional designations (rūḍhi) may have as their domain specific places and persons. He states "in those situated therein" and so forth because, since a path is devoid of action, its status as the agent of the act of going is not logically possible;
thus he shows that the movement residing in the person is metaphorically attributed (upacaryate) to the path.

Regarding the passage beginning with "Or else" (*atha vā*): here the root *gam* (to go) signifies "attainment. And for those [paths] such as Rūghna and so forth, there is indeed an attainment of this very path, characterized by immediate succession, which is accessible through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). But how can the "door," which is well-known as an instrument (*karaṇa*), be intended here as being independent? To this he says: "Just as," and so forth.

Just as a sword, although well known as an instrument (*karaṇa*) in the act of cutting, is intended to be expressed as independent [as the agent], so too [the door is intended as the agent]. Now, it might be argued: "Departure occurs for one who possesses consciousness, or for that which is impelled by one possessing consciousness—as in 'Devadatta departs'—but the door is not impelled by one possessing consciousness; therefore, its departure is not logical. This is not a fault;
for even in the case of insentient things, the conventional usage "it departs" is observed, such as in the statement: "The wind departs through this mouth of the cave."

If it is argued that [the accusative] is therefore not justified because of the act of "departing" (*niṣkrīyatva*), there is no fault; for when those situated within [the body] depart, one figuratively says, "it departs through the door. Now, one might object: since the suffix *-ta* in *kṛte* is a *niṣṭhā* (past passive participle) used in the sense of the object (*karman*), and since the object is already expressed by that suffix, the accusative case would not apply. To this he replies: "The accusative is used in relation to the expectation of the word *adhikṛtya*. The accusative is used in relation to the action denoted by the gerund (*lyabantena*), and the object of that action has not been expressed by anything else.

For according to the *niṣṭhā* [sūtra], only that which constitutes the work itself (*granthātmaka*) is designated as the object (*karman*), and not even that object of the action ending in a *lyap* suffix, such as Subhadra and others. [Examples:
"Gairimittra" is formed with reference to Girimitra;
"Yāyāta" is formed with reference to Yayāti. [The rule] begins with "lup," etc.
The dative case in *ākhyāyikāyai* is used in the sense of purpose (*tādarthye*).

The meaning is that there is elision (*luk*) of the suffix when [the word] *ākhyāyikā* is intended for the sake of an *ākhyāyikā*, that is, for the purpose of expressing an *ākhyāyikā*. Regarding the form *yamasabham*, its neuter gender is established by the rule *sabhārājā* (Pāṇini 2.4.23) and so forth.

If [the hymns] such as *Śiśukranda* are to be understood as being included within the *Indrajanana* and so forth, then for what purpose is there a separate mention of them? To this he says: "For the sake of elaboration," and so on;
and "This being the case," and so on.
The word *ca* (and) is used in the sense of a reason (*hetu*).

Since the inclusion of *śiśukranda* and so forth—being members of the *ākṛtigaṇa* beginning with *indrajana*—is for the purpose of illustrating that very class, this being the case, it need not be stated that there is a prohibition regarding gods (*deva*), asuras, and so on, because there is no possibility of their occurrence [in this context]. Furthermore, those very items such as *indrajana* from which this suffix *cha* is observed are [the ones intended], and it is not observed after words such as "god" or "asura. [And it is said: "A place is also called 'native land' (*abhijana*) by virtue of its connection with that [person]."
Just as the word "staff" (*yaṣṭi*) is applied to a person because of his connection with a staff—as in the command "bring the staffs"—so too the word "lineage" (*abhijana*) is applied to a region.
But who is this that is called "of noble lineage" (*abhijana*) due to a connection with lineage? To this he says: "In which," and so forth;
and "here, [the word] denoting a region," and so forth.

But how can there be a derivative suffix (*pratyaya*) from a secondary sense (*gauṇa*) when the primary sense (*mukhya*) is [the intended] "lineage" (*abhijana*)? To this he says: "Because of the proximity to the place of residence" (*nivāsa-pratyāsatter*). The word "residence" (*nivāsa*) is drawn over [from the previous rule]; by that, the lineage is qualified as "that which is the lineage and is a place of residence. Therefore, the suffix occurs only after words denoting a location, and not after [names of] kinsmen; for those [kinsmen] do not constitute a place of residence. What is the difference between residence and lineage? He considers that there is indeed no difference at all, because lineage is essentially the site of residence.
"Where," and so forth;

he shows the specific purpose. "The division of the rule (*yogavibhāga*) is for the sake of what follows" means that in the subsequent rules, there may be cognitions based on birth (*abhijana*), but these should not apply in the sense of a place of residence (*nivāsa*). [This applies to] "those who live by weapons."
The phrase "tadabhyam caturthī" (the fourth case ending [denotes the source] for that) excludes the fifth case ending.

For if this were a fifth case ending, the meaning of the rule would be: "when Parvata is the object to be expressed, the suffix cha occurs after 'āyudhajīvibhya' (those who live by weapons)"; however, this is not desired. Therefore, this is indeed the fourth case ending, not the fifth.
[The example is] "sāṅkāśyakāḥ."
> [[4.2.121]] || "An exception to [the suffixes] beginning with *aṇ*"— by the word "beginning" (*ādi*), [the suffixes] *cha* and so forth are meant.
According to the opinion of those who call Śaṇḍika and others "Parvātanas," this is an exception to the *cha* suffix obtained by the preceding rule.
Regarding those words that denote inhabited regions (*janapada*), [the suffix] *vuñ* is obtained by rule 4.2.125;

regarding the word *śaṇḍika*, the suffix *aṇ* is obtained by rule 4.2.132. As for the phrase "and so forth" (*prabhṛtayaḥ*), by the word "and so forth," these are included: *madhu*, *vasanta*, *kamboja*, *sālva*, and *kaśmīra*.

Regarding *Gandhāra* (the reading *mu* is *gandhāra*, while the ancient printed edition reads *gandhāri*), *Kiṣkindhā*, *Sāradī* (not found in the *Gaṇapāṭha*), *Urasa* (according to the *Kāśikā*), *Uras*, and *Darad*—for these, the suffix *vuñ* would otherwise apply by rule 4.2.125 and following; this statement [is made to override that].
Also, for *Takṣaśilā* and others, for *Kaumedura*, *Kāṇḍavāraṇa*, and *Grāmaṇī*, the suffix *cha* would otherwise apply by rule 4.2.114; [this statement is made to override that].
For the remaining [words], the suffix *aṇ* applies by rule 4.1.83. "Devotion" (*bhakti*) is so called because it is "shared in" (*bhajyate*) or "served" (*sevyate*).

The suffix *ktin* is used here as a *karmasādhana* (denoting the object) derived from the verbal root *bhaja* in the sense of "service" (*sevāyām*) [Dhātupāṭha 998]. Now, one might object: since non-sentient things such as place (*deśa*) and time (*kāla*) are excluded by the rule concerning the application of *nañ* and *iva* (Pāṇini 2.1.65), the term "sentient" (*cetanā*) will be understood as referring to the *prakṛti* (the source/origin) alone; so what is the purpose of explicitly including the term "non-sentient" (*acitta*)? This is not correct.

For without that term, it would not be known whether "not place and time" (*adeśakālāt*) is a specification of the *prakṛti* or a prohibition regarding place and time. In that case, an unintended meaning might also be understood—namely, from the word *adeśa* and from the word *akāla*.

However, if the term *acitta* were not included, there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*), and thus the prohibition [of the suffix] by the rule *adeśakālāt* would be understood [as applying to all cases].
And precisely because of this prohibition, the inclusion of the specific form [of the word] as *acitta-* does not occur;

for if the specific form were included, the over-extension regarding place and time would not require a prohibition. [Objection: But surely the suffix *ṭhak* will carry over from the previous sūtra, and by that alone, forms such as *māhārājika* are indeed established; so why is another suffix, *ṭhañ*, employed? To this he says: "The employment of another suffix," and so forth.
The separate formation of this suffix is so that the word may have the udātta accent on its first syllable by means of the *ñit* marker;

for if the suffix were *ṭhak*, the word would instead have the udātta accent on the final syllable according to the rule *kitaḥ* [Pāṇini 6.1.159]. From the *Bālamanoramāsudhā*: *sudhātur akaṅ ca* (4.3.99), "and *akaṅ* after *sudhātu*";
and "the suffix *iñ* follows" (*cādiñ*).
The meaning is that from the word *sudhātṛ* ending in the genitive case, the suffix *iñ* is added in the sense of "offspring," and the base undergoes the substitution of *akaṅ*.

In *akaṅ*, the letter *ṅ* is an *it* (indicatory), while the letter *a* is for the sake of pronunciation. By the rule "*ṅicca*," this [substitute] becomes an antādeśa (a replacement for the entire final portion).

Regarding this, he says: "Saudhātaki. [He explains] "Vyāsa": the meaning is that after *vyāsa*, *varuḍa*, *niṣāda*, *caṇḍāla*, and *bimba*, when the suffix *iñ* is applied, there is the substitution of *akaṅ* for the base. [From the *Bālamanoramā*: "After *mahārāja*, the suffix *ṭhañ* [is applied]," 1456, 4.3.99: *mahārājāṭṭhañ*.]
The phrase "so'sya bhaktiḥ" (this is his devotion) is the ellipsis [to be supplied].

Regarding "māhārājika": the analysis of the compound is "one whose devotion is to the Mahārāja. This is an exception to the suffix *cha* prescribed after a word ending in a vṛddhi vowel, such as "Vāsudeva."

[The suffix] *aṇ* [is applied] after the word *arjuna* by virtue of the general rule. Now, an objection is raised: "But the word *arjuna* denotes a Kṣatriya; therefore, it would be more appropriate to apply an exception (*apavāda*) to the suffix *vuñ*, which is obtained by the subsequent sūtra. The author considers this: "The term *bahulam* (‘in various cases’) is employed there [in that subsequent sūtra]; consequently, the suffix *nuñ* cannot even be applicable after the word *arjuna*. Therefore, only *aṇ* should apply here, and thus it is logical that [the subsequent sūtra] serves as its exception. The phrase beginning with "Now, an objection" (*nanu ca*) introduces the challenge. It might be argued: "There is a distinction between *vuñ* and *vun*; therefore, *vun* is prescribed after the word *vāsudeva*? To this he says: "And not here," etc.

Furthermore, whether the suffix *vuñ* or *vun* is applied to the word *vāsudeva*, there is no difference whatsoever; for in both cases, the form is identical and the accent is the same. As for the prohibition of the *puṃvadbhāva* (masculine treatment) that occurs when *vuñ* is applied—based on [Pāṇini 6.3.39]—that very same prohibition is indeed obtained when *vun* is applied, based on [Pāṇini 6.3.37].

By the phrase "saṃjñeṣaḥ" and so forth, he refutes what was stated: "But surely, by the rule 'nanu ca vāsudevaśabdādgotrakṣatriyākhyebhyaḥ' [Pāṇini 4.3.99], the suffix *vuñ* must indeed occur. He refutes that: the suffix *vuñ* is prescribed after words denoting a lineage (*gotra*) or a Kṣatriya name.

However, the word *vāsudeva* is neither a nominal stem denoting a lineage nor one denoting a Kṣatriya; therefore, how [could *vuñ* apply]? By this [discussion]—specifically by not applying the rule "alpāctaram" [Pāṇini 2.2.34] to place the word *arjuna* first—it is made known that that which is more venerable (*abhyarhita*) is placed first.

Therefore, in the case of *mātāpitarau*, *śraddhamedhe*, and *dīkṣātapasī*, the prior placement of the more venerable term is established by the very authority of the *śāstra*. The venerability of the word *vāsudeva* is due to its being a specific deity. [Examples: *glaucukāyanakaḥ*, *mlaucukāyanakaḥ*.
From the words *glucu* and *kamlucuka*, by the rule *prācām vṛddhāt phiñ* [Pāṇini 4.1.160], the suffix *vuñ* is applied to that which ends in *phiñ*.
For what purpose is the mention of the word *ākhyā* (name/designation)? Why not simply say "from *gotra* and *kṣatriya* [names]"? To this he says: "The mention of *ākhyā*," and so forth.

If the mention of *ākhyā* were not made, then the suffix would apply even to those who are somehow associated with the *kṣatriya* class, which is not desired. Therefore, the mention of *ākhyā* is made in order to include only well-known *kṣatriyas*.
Therefore it is said: "The learned one is not a Kṣatriya; his is devotion.
It is not well-known that the word "learned" (vidvat) is synonymous with the word "Kṣatriya.
Rather, its application to the Kṣatriya is understood through its grammatical coreferentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya) with the word "Kṣatriya."

Regarding the term *pāṇinīya*: [the suffix] *aṇ* is applied in the sense of "the descendant of Pāṇini"; by the rule beginning with *gāthividatha* (Pāṇ. 6.4.165), there is the preservation of the original stem-form (*prakṛtibhāva*). Then, [the suffix] *cha* is applied in the sense of "one whose devotion is to Pāṇini" (Pāṇ. 4.2.114), resulting in *pāṇinīya*. Similarly, "one whose devotion is to the Paurava" results in *pauravīya*. {This is not in the Kāśikā} regarding the phrase "words consisting of a single sound."
By this, he shows that the word *samāna* here signifies "one and the same. He explains the meaning conveyed by the word *sarva* in the phrase "the suffix and the base."
"Similarly, *aṅga* [is used] for a Kṣatriya, as in *asya bhaktiḥ* (his devotion).

By the rule *aṅgādibhyaḥ kṣattriyebhyo bahuṣvapatyeṣu* (Pāṇini 4.1.170), the suffix *aṇ* is prescribed; however, by the rule *tadrājasya* (Pāṇini 2.4.62), its elision (*luk*) is performed. In the plural, the names of the Kṣatriyas such as *aṅga* and others, who are lords of territories, become identical in form to the names of those territories themselves.

In this context, just as the suffix *vuñ* occurs after names of inhabited regions (*janapada*) such as *aṅga* and others in the domain defined by [Pāṇini 4.3.95], namely "this is his devotion" (*so'sya bhaktiḥ*), according to [Pāṇini 4.2.124], so too does it occur after words denoting inhabitants of a region—as in "the Brāhmaṇas of Pañcāla" (*pañcālā brāhmaṇāḥ*).

When the word *pañcāla* and others refer to those residing in Pañcāla through association (*sāhacaryāt*), then the Brāhmaṇas are identical in form to the name of the region when used in the plural; however, they themselves are not inhabitants of that region (*janapadinaḥ*).

Therefore, because there is no extended application (*atideśa*) [of the rule for inhabitants], only the suffix *aṇ* occurs—resulting in *pāñcālaḥ*. [The sūtra contains] the mention of "all" (*sarva*), and so forth.

If the term *sarva* (all) were not employed, then because the suffix (*pratyaya*) is that which is being prescribed, it would possess primacy; and since grammatical operations are understood to apply to what is primary, the extension (*atideśa*) would apply to that [the suffix] alone, and not to the base (*prakṛti*). Therefore, the term *sarva* is used so that the extension may also apply to the base.
"And that," etc.
And that transfer of the base (*prakṛtyatideśa*) causes the entire suffixation to apply only to the dual and singular, not to the plural.

The word *janapada* is not "vṛddha" (containing a *vṛddhi*-strengthened vowel) here; therefore, the word *janapada* is seen as non-*vṛddha*. However, in the plural, when the elision (*luk*) occurs according to Pāṇini 2.4.62—*tadrājasya bahuṣu tenaivāstriyām*—it becomes non-*vṛddha* even without the transfer of the base. For this very reason, the transfer of the base is useless in that case.
Therefore, for this purpose, the inclusion of the word "all" (*sarva*) need not be made [in the rule],
as in the phrase "when there are causes of *vṛddhi*" and so forth;
because when the base (*prakṛti*) is prescribed as non-*vṛddha* in the case of suffixes such as *vuñ* that cause *vṛddhi*, *vṛddhi* occurs once again.

Regarding the phrase "when the reduction is not performed according to the original form" (*prakṛtinirhrāsākṛte*), because of the inclusion of the term "all" (*sarva*), the reduction is by way of the original base (*prakṛti*). "Reduction" (*nirhrāsa*) means diminution through scarcity or decrease.
[The example is] "mādraḥ."
And with reference to this base (*prakṛti*), this base *madra* becomes "small" (*alpa*).

[The forms] *vārjyaḥ* and *vārjyau* are derived from the base *vṛji*. Now, one might object: since the suffix *vat* has the meaning of "complete similarity," the base will be extended by the very mention of *vat*; so what is the purpose of including the word "all" (*sarva*)? This is not the case; for just as in that instance the suffix *vat* does not extend the meaning of the deity—which is the specific meaning of the suffix—to the meaning of "complete similarity," so too here the form of the country (*janapada*) is not extended to the inhabitant of the country (*janapadin*).
Why, then, is the meaning of the suffix (*pratyaya*) not extended there [to the *vat* suffix]? Because the difference between those two is established by the *vat* suffix itself.

For the *vat* suffix is prescribed in the sense of similarity (*sādṛśya*), and similarity depends upon difference. If the meaning of the primary suffix (*bhāvārtha*) were also transformed into the meaning of a deity (*devatārtha*), then the *vat* suffix would not be applicable at all. Therefore, the *vat* suffix expresses the similarity of another operation, while it indicates the difference between the two meanings of the suffixes; and here too, it expresses the difference between the country (*janapada*) and its inhabitant (*janapadin*).
If "all" (*sarva*) were not included, the form *janapadin* would not be obtained for the word *janapada*.

Therefore, the inclusion of "all" is made. Regarding the phrase "the inclusion of 'frequently' (*bahula*)," etc., this is a definition that demonstrates the scope of the rule concerning identical words (*samāna-śabdatā*).
The plural marker is included for that purpose.
The phrase "otherwise, indeed," and so forth,
means that the plural marker would not be employed.

"In that very case" means in the plural number. It is only when the plural number is present and the *tadrāja* suffix has been elided (*luk*) that there is identity of form (*samānaśabdatā*), and it is precisely in that situation that the extended application (*atideśa*) would occur.
"It would not occur in the singular and dual numbers," because [the suffix] is absent there due to the identity of the word-form.
"But in the plural," and so forth.

However, when the plural number is employed, since the extended application (*atideśa*) is understood to apply to those names that share the same word-form with a country name in the plural, this [designation] is established even for the dual and singular. Regarding the phrase "spoken with excellence" (*prakarṣeṇoktam*):
"excellence" (*prakarṣa*) means intensity; thus, that which is explained or taught by such [an excellence] is called "spoken" (*prokta*).
It does not mean "composed" (*kṛta*).
But it is not said that "done" (kṛta) means "produced" (utpādita) or "proclaimed" (prokṣata). Why? He says: because the meaning has already been explained by [Pāṇini 4.3.116].

How can there be the suffix *aṇ* in *māthurī*, when there ought to be the suffix *cha* after a word ending in *vṛddhi*? This is not a fault; for he will state that the mention of *aṇ* in [Pāṇini 4.3.108] serves the purpose of allowing it to occur after other words as well, and thus the suffix *aṇ* occurs even from the word *māthura*.
Regarding "pāṇinīyam": the suffix *cha* is applied according to [Pāṇini 4.2.114] after the word *pāṇi*. Regarding "āpiśalam" and "kālakṛtsnam": [the suffix *aṇ* is applied].

From the words *āpiśali* and *kāśakṛtsna*, the suffix *aṇ* is applied by [Pāṇini 4.2.111] *iñaśca*. Thus, we have *taittirīyāḥ*. Here, the suffix *chaṇ* is applied; from those [words ending in *chaṇ*], the suffix *aṇ* is applied by [Pāṇini 4.2.59] *tad adhīte*, which is then elided by [Pāṇini 4.2.64]. The status of being "pertaining to that" (*tadviṣayatā*) is established by [Pāṇini 4.2.67] *chandobrāhmaṇāni ca tadviṣayāṇi*. But how is [the suffix] obtained in the Vedic language (*chandas*)? For there is no mention of "in the Vedic language" [in the rule]; thus he says: "from Śaunaka and others," and so forth. "The letter *ṇ* is for the sake of *vṛddhi* in what follows" means that in the subsequent rules, *vṛddhi* (vowel strengthening) should occur.
For here [in this specific rule], the letter *ṇ* has no purpose; its purpose is indeed for the sake of *vṛddhi*.

The words *kāśyapa* and *kauśika* possess the suffix *vṛddhi*. Regarding the phrase "and of that also," etc.: one might ask, "Is it not the case that the status of being the subject of that [suffix] is appropriate for the *chandas*, the *brāhmaṇas*, and so forth; how then can it apply to the *kalpas* as well? To this he says: "from Śaunaka and others," etc.

It might be argued: "Even if this [the suffix *cha*] were not established, for although [the word] 'in the Veda' (*chandasi*) from [Pāṇini 4.3.106], *śaunakādibhyaśchandasi*, does not carry over [to this rule], nevertheless, while the status of being a Vedic text (*chandas*) is being predicated for the *Brāhmaṇas* and so forth, the status of being a *Kalpa* would certainly not be established. For even if the rule from [Pāṇini 4.3.106], *śaunakādibhyaḥ*, were to carry over, this present rule would not cause the *Kalpa* to attain the state of being a Vedic text or the state of being a *Brāhmaṇa*. To this he says: "And [it applies] to those prescribed under the heading of *Chandas*," and so forth.
But how is it that even when desired, the designation *chandas* (Vedic) is applied to those [suffixes] prescribed under the heading of *chandasi*?

By that [rule], Pāṇini 4.3.106, these suffixes are prescribed as being applicable to the *prakṛtis* (bases) mentioned; thus, for all of them, there is the status of being within that domain (*viṣayatā*) even at the beginning of the Kalpa.
Alternatively, by means of a figurative assumption (*guṇakalpanā*), the status of being *chandas* is intended to be expressed for the beginnings of the Kalpas as well.

Now, one might object: since the particle *ca* in [Pāṇini 4.2.66] has the sense of including what has not been explicitly mentioned (*anuktasamuccaya*), the application of that rule to words beginning with *kalpa* was already established by that very [particle]; so for what purpose is it being established again in this manner? [The answer is: the particle *ca* could have been used there to establish the application of that rule to words beginning with *kalpa*, or else this present method could have been adopted—it is for the sake of showing this alternative. [This is explained in the commentary] starting with "by the contemporary person," and so forth.

The Kāśyapa of the present day is called "Kāśyapa" because he originates from the Kāśyapa lineage (*gotra*); likewise, the Kauśika of the present day is called "Kauśika" because he originates from the Kauśika lineage. In that regard, if the term "seer" (*ṛṣi*) is derived solely from the word *ṛṣi*—that is, if those who are recited in the *Pravarādhyāya* are considered seers—then are not these two [Kāśyapa and Kauśika] also recited therein? This is not a fault; by the force of employing a qualifier, this word *ṛṣi* is understood as a verbal noun (denoting an action): "a seer is so called because of seeing."

Therefore, by means of that prescriptive vision which is not shared with other persons, the two words *kāśyapa* and *kauśika* were established for those [two individuals]; hence this rule for the suffix *cha* is formulated. However, the contemporary words *kāśyapa* and *kauśika* are not of such a nature; with respect to them, only the suffix *cha* occurs. Because of the metaphorical application (*upacāra*) based on the intent to denote [the lineage], the words here designated by the term *kalāpivaiśampāyanāntevāsin* (pupils of Kalāpin and Vaiśampāyana) actually denote those who are pupils of Kalāpin and Vaiśampāyana.

For this very reason, he says: "of the pupils of Kalāpin. Now, one might object: those who are disciples of disciples (the *śiṣyaśiṣyas*) are indeed already included among the pupils of Kalāpin and Vaiśampāyana; therefore, it is incorrect to say that there were four pupils of Kalāpin and nine pupils of Vaiśampāyana. To this he replies: "those who performed [the study] directly," and so forth. Here, the root *kṛ* refers to the act of studying. Those by whom [the text] was studied directly are the "direct performers" (*pratyakṣakāriṇaḥ*).
Here, only these many disciples are intended.
What is incorrect in this? He asks for the reason why those who possess direct realization (*sākṣātkārin*) are included here, and not those who are separated [from that state]:
"Because of the mention of Kalāpin and Khāṇḍāyana."
The explanation of the reason:
"{tathā hi – kāśikā} tathā ca" and so forth;
this is the commentary on that very point.
Vaiśampāyana has Kalāpin as his pupil; those who are his pupils are indeed the pupils of Vaiśampāyana.

If those who are separated [by an intermediate generation] were also to be included as pupils there, then the mention of Kalāpin would be purposeless; one would simply have said, "from the pupils of Vaiśampāyana."

Likewise, there is Khāṇḍāyana, a pupil of Vaiśampāyana. In that case, if those who are even separated [by lineage] were to be included, then since [Khāṇḍāyana] would already be established by this very rule on account of being a pupil of Vaiśampāyana, the mention of the word "Khāṇḍāyana" among Śaunaka and the others would be entirely fruitless. Therefore, both the inclusion of the *kalāpin* here and the mention of the word "Khāṇḍāyana" among Śaunaka and the others are indicative marks (*liṅga*)—that is, indicators—that direct perception is to be included.
[The examples continue with] "Hāridraviṇaḥ," and so forth.

The suffix *ṇini* is applied after words such as *haridu* in the sense of "proclaimed" (*prokta*); from that form ending in *ṇini*, the suffix *aṇ* is added according to [Pāṇini 4.2.59]. Thereafter, by the rule *proktālluk*, there is elision of the *aṇ*. In the phrase *ulapena caturthena*, the third case (*tṛtīyā*) is used in the sense of accompaniment (*sahārtha*).
Thus we have *kālāpakam*.

This [group] of *kalāpin*s is called *kālāpaka*, by the rule *gotracaraṇād vuñ* [Pāṇini 4.3.126]. But surely, there is the rule *dharmāmnāyayor vuñ* (Vārttika 476); and since these pupils are neither *dharma*s nor *āmnāya*s, how can the suffix *vuñ* apply here? In that case, it will occur by way of a comparison (*upamāna*). The pupils are spoken of as being like *dharma*s, as in "the *kālāpaka* [group]."
Just as the Dharma is related to Kalāpi, so too are the disciples; this is stated for the purpose of comparison.
Ālambi is the name of a region in the East, and one born there is a "Caraka.
Likewise, both Palaṅka and Kamala.
There are three [schools] of the Prācya: these disciples of Vaiśampāyana, namely the Ṛca, Bhāruṇi, and Tāṇḍa, are the Prācyas. "The other three are the Madhyamīyas" refers to the Carakas;
those who belong to the Middle Country (madhyadeśa) are the Madhyamīyas.
In the *Gahādi* group, it is recited: *madhyamadhyamañcāṇ caraṇe* (Gaṇasūtra 99).

This is its meaning: the word *madhya* undergoes the state of becoming *madhyama*, and the suffix *cha* is applied after it; however, when *caraṇa* (Vedic school) is the sense of the suffix, the suffix *aṇ* is also applied.
In that regard, when the status of being a Vedic school (*caraṇatva*) is not intended for the *Ṛgveda* and so forth, then, once the suffix *cha* has been applied, the form *madhyamīyāḥ* results.
When there is the intention to express "foot" (*caraṇa*), the suffix *aṇ* is applied, resulting in the form *mādhyama*.
[The word] *udīcyaḥ* ("northerners") is derived by [the rule] *udakṣu bhavāḥ* (Pāṇini 4.2.101), etc.
Among the northerners (*udīcyeṣu*) is Śyāmāyani-caraka. Kaṭha and Kalāpin are also Carakas among the northerners; this has been stated for others as well by [the rule] *aparasyāpi* (Pāṇini 4.3.108).

But surely, among the disciples of Vaiśampāyana, the name *Caraka* belongs specifically to Kaṭha; so how can he be called *Caraka*? To this he says: "‘Caraka’ [is the name] of Vaiśampāyana," and so forth.

Even though they themselves do not have the name *Caraka*, it does belong to their teacher Vaiśampāyana; through that connection, his disciples are also spoken of in that way. Regarding "the Bhāllavins":
from *Bhāllava*, *Śāṭyāyana*, and *Aitareya*, the suffix *ṇini* is applied in the sense of "taught by."

From that suffix, [the suffix] produced by the rule *tad adhīte* [Pāṇini 4.2.59], according to [the rules] *chandaso nivr̥ttam* [4.2.64] and *tad viṣayaḥ* [4.2.66], etc., has that as its scope. Examples are *paiṅgī* and *āruṇaparājī*.
The suffix *ṇini* is applied after the words *piṅga*, *aruṇa*, and *parāśara*,
as in *yājñavalkāni* and *āśmarathaḥ*.

The elision of *y* occurs by the rule "āpatyasya" [Pāṇini 6.4.151] following the forms *yājñavalkya* and *ārṣeya*, which are derived from the *garga*-class stems *yājñavalkya* and *ārṣeya* with the suffix *yañ*.

Now, one might object: "Are not the *Yājñavalkya* and other such Brāhmaṇas also indeed proclaimed by ancient sages (*purāṇaproktāni*), since they are equal to other Brāhmaṇas in being proclaimed by ancient sages? To this he says: "Yājñavalkya," etc.
For this is the report regarding these narrative accounts (*ākhyāneṣu*): Yājñavalkya and others were later exponents than the other exponents.
And thus, there is no fault, because the author of the Sūtras employs conventional usage without regard for the actual ontological status [of objects].
The intended meaning is that this is established by the passage beginning with "Why does it not have that as its object? (4.2.66).
Regarding the phrase "pratipadam" and so forth:
by the technical rule *lakṣaṇapratipadoktaparibhāṣā* (Vyāḍiparibhāṣā 3), a term that is mentioned word-for-word (*pratipada*) serves as a qualifier.
Thus, having uttered the word "brāhmaṇa," the rule establishes that the suffix prescribed for Brāhmaṇas has that specific [Brāhmaṇa] as its domain.
Therefore, this [word *kalpa*] does not have that [the treatise] as its object.
Why, then, does it not [denote] the treatises (*kalpa*)? As in the case of: "The Kāśyapins study the *Kalpa* proclaimed by Kāśyapa"? [To this, the author replies: "And this... and so forth.

In the section on Vedic prosody (*chando'dhikāra*), whatever rule (*yoga*) is prescribed, its application is restricted to that specific context; however, this particular rule does not continue to apply within the section on prosody. Consequently, the suffix (*pratyaya*) prescribed by this rule does not have as its domain the students and knowers [of the texts] in the ritual manuals (*kalpas*), such as "the *paiṅgī-kalpa*" or "the *āruṇaparājī-kalpa*. Regarding the word "purāṇa": since the suffixes *ṭa* and *ṭil* are applied with the simultaneous occurrence (*sanniyoga*) of the augment *tuṭ* by the rule "sāṃyaciram" (Pāṇini 4.3.23), one would expect the form to be "purātanam.
To this, he says: "The absence of *tuṭ* occurs due to the irregularity (*nipātana*) of the word 'purāṇa'."
If this is so, does the ancient [form] not exist? To this he says: "Not indeed, nor... and so forth.

But surely, since it is said that "even exceptions (*nipātana*) are sublaters" (Vī.pā.vṛ. 109), there ought to be a denotative form? [The answer is: they are even non-denotative (Nī.pā.vṛ. 110); they are also not sublaters, and this has been established under [Pāṇini 7.3.42]. "[It is] an exception to *cha* and *aṇ*" means:
The suffix *cha* is an exception (*apavāda*) for those who are elders (*vṛddha*), whereas the suffix *aṇ* applies to the remaining [non-elders]. For example:
*śaunakinaḥ* and *vājasaneyinaḥ*.

The suffix *ṇini* is applied in the sense of "proclaimed by Śaunaka" or "proclaimed by Vājasaneya. From that form ending in *ṇini*, the suffix *aṇ* is added according to Pāṇini 4.2.58; then, by 4.2.64, the final vowel and consonant are elided. As before, its scope is restricted to that specific subject. The phrase beginning with "from the simple [word]" (*kevalād dhi*) and so forth serves as the reason for the statement that "it has a collective meaning" (*tat saṃhatārtham*).

Since he will state that *luka* (elision) occurs after *kaṭha* alone, therefore the reading *kaṭha-śāṭha* found here is for the sake of a collective meaning: "the Kaṭhas and the Carakas. When the suffix *prokta* has been elided, the *aṇ* that occurs [in place] of the student also undergoes elision by the rule *proktālluk* [Pāṇini 4.2.63]. As before, its scope is the same. [The example is] "the Kālāpas."
As before, there is the elision (*luk*) of the suffix *aṇ* produced after a word ending in the aforementioned suffixes when denoting an agent, and its scope is likewise established.

Regarding the passage beginning with "Now" (*atha*), one might object: "If the mention of *aṇ* were not made, then this rule, being prescribed for what was already applicable, would merely be an exception (*apavāda*) to the suffix *ṇini*. This is not so; for if that were the case, the statement [of the rule] would be purposeless.
Therefore, that which is prescribed but does not apply because it is set aside by this [rule], that alone will occur; and that is indeed the suffix *aṇ*.
Regarding the phrase "and so forth" (*evamādi*): by the word "etcetera," the inclusion of the Maudas, Paippalādas, Śākalas, and Jājālas is intended.
