If [you argue] that "if *asat* were not [stated], then in the case of *tvac-grahaṇa*, everything would fail to be established" (Pāṇini 4.2.114), [we reply: no, because the general rule (*autsargika*) for *aṇ* has been superseded by that [specific rule]. Regarding "the Chāgaleyins":
here too, just as before, there is the elision (*luk*) of the *aṇ* suffix produced after the name of the student (*adhyetṛ*), and its scope is the same.
This should be understood to apply to the two subsequent rules as well. Regarding "according to the respective order" (*yathāsaṃkhyam*), etc.
"In the *Bhikṣusūtra* [the suffix] *pratyaya* follows *pārāśarya*, and in the *Naṭasūtra* [it follows] *śilālin*.
And here, its having that as its object is intended. But how is that obtained even though it is merely intended? To this he says: "For that purpose," and so forth.

[Objection: But surely, by the very inclusion of "metre" (*chandas*) as a recurring term, its scope would already be established? [Reply: No; because the *bhikṣu-sūtra* and the *vanaṭa-sūtra* are not metres. Thus he says: "And by the attribution of a quality" (*guṇakalpanayā ca*), and so forth.

Here, "quality" (*guṇa*) is intended to mean that property which serves as the basis for the metaphorical designation (*upacāra*) of "metre"; the "attribution" (*kalpanā*) is that which has this as its cause.
Just as a metre is studied for a specific purpose, so too the *sūtra* accomplishes that same purpose.
The status of being *chandas* (Vedic) for the *bhikṣusūtra* and the *naṭasūtra* is figurative (*aupacārika*), based on such an attribution of qualities as "of a monk" and "of an actor.
Regarding the term *pārāśariṇaḥ*: the word *pārāśarya*, belonging to the *gargādi* group, takes the suffix *vañ*; by [Pāṇini 6.4.151], there is the elision of the *ya*.
In the case of *śailālinaḥ*,
there is the elision of the *ṭi* suffix by [Pāṇini 6.4.144]. In the case of *pārāśaram*,
the suffix *aṇ* is applied by [Pāṇini 4.2.111].
Regarding "śailālam":

the suffix *aṇ* is applied by the general rule (*autsargika*), and the elision of the *ṭi* portion occurs according to the Vārttika rule "nāntasya ṭilope sabrahmacāripīṭha" (Vārttika 798). Regarding "tena":
the third case ending is used according to Pāṇini 2.3.72, "tulyārthairatulopamābhyām."
Regarding the word *saudāmanī*:

because of the rule *an* [Pāṇini 6.4.167], there is no elision of the *ṭi* (the final vowel and following consonant) due to the preservation of the original stem-form (*prakṛtibhāva*). Now, since "by that" (*tena*) was indeed the subject under discussion, for what purpose is the third-case suffix (*tṛtīyā*) as a governing case-relation (*samarthavibhakti*) introduced here again? To this he says: "Since 'by that' is the subject under discussion," and so forth.
For in the preceding rule, "by that" was connected to the governing topic of Vedic meters (*chandaḥ*); therefore, if that were to carry over, that [topic] would also carry over.
Therefore, the third case ending is employed here once again as a governing case (*samarthavibhakti*) in order to terminate the jurisdiction of the Vedic language (*chandaḥ*).
But for what purpose is the jurisdiction of the Vedic language established in the preceding [rules]? To this he says: "In the preceding," and so forth.
Because the jurisdiction of the Vedic language applies to the preceding rules, their scope is thereby established.
Therefore, in that context, the governing authority of *chandasi* (in Vedic usage) must be applied.

However, since that [Vedic authority] would apply there, an effort must be made here to exclude it, so that the suffix might occur only in *chandasi*. Regarding the term *akālakam*, the meaning is "that which is devoid of the technical definitions (*paribhāṣā*) concerning time. But what is the difference between *kṛta* (made/composed) and *upajñāta* (discovered/invented), such that when the word *upajñāta* is already under discussion, the mention of *kṛta* is made? To this he says: "produced," and so forth. [This refers to the rule] *bāla-manoramā-saṃjñāyām* (Bālamanoramā on Pāṇini 4.3.119): *saṃjñāyām* (when it is a name).

The phrase "tenetyeva" means that when the sense is "done by him," suffixes should be applied as prescribed after a word ending in the third case, provided it is a technical name (*saṃjñā*). The term "in a literary work" (*granthe*) does not carry over [from the previous rule].
Thus he says: "The meaning of the non-literal (agraṃtha) [is as follows]. Regarding the rule *bāla-manoramā* 4.3.119, *saṅghāṅkalakṣaṇeṣvañyañiñāmaṇ*:

the meaning is that after a word ending in *yañ*, *añ*, or *iñ*, the suffix *aṇ* is applied when it refers to a *saṅgha* (a collection), an *aṅka* (a mark), or a *lakṣaṇa* (a characteristic), provided these are intended to be expressed with a feminine ending in *ī*.
This is a refutation of [the previous position]. Regarding "ghoṣa":
the meaning is that the rule "in the case of saṅgha, aṅka, lakṣaṇa, and ghoṣa" must be formulated.
And thus, there are three bases (*prakṛtis*) and four meanings of the suffixes (*pratyayārthas*); therefore, there is no correspondence according to their respective order (*yathāsaṅkhyam*).
Regarding "Gārgya":
the remainder [of the rule] is "a corporation (*saṅgha*), a mark (*aṅka*), or a hamlet (*ghoṣa*)."

Regarding "gārgam," the word "lakṣaṇa" (characteristic) is to be understood as the ellipsis. Similarly, in the case of "dākṣam, dākṣam," one might object that since the words *aṅga* and *lakṣaṇa* are synonyms, their separate mention is redundant; to this, he says: "by way of succession."
Just as a specific heated seal-imprint residing on a cow or similar animal is a "mark" (aṅka);
for its connection to the owner is mediated through the cow.
The word "directly" (sākṣāt) [is used] because...
The meaning is that the specific knowledge (*vidyāviśeṣa*) existing directly in Devadatta is his defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*).
Vedic knowledge is *vaidī vidyā*.
According to Amara, "a *ghoṣa* is a cowherd settlement" (*ābhīrapallī*), and [the phrase refers to] "a distinction in accent" (*svara*).
For if the suffix were *aṇ*, the word would be oxytone due to the accent of the affix (*pratyayasvara*);
however, when it is *añ*, it becomes ādyudātta (accented on the first syllable) due to the *ñit*-accent. Regarding the word "tasya":

this is a masculine designation; it would apply only to the masculine, not after dual or plural endings; and it would apply only to words denoting what is perceptible, not to words denoting specific qualities, because the word *tad* denotes only an object that is not present to the senses (*parokṣa*).

One might raise this objection: "Since the meaning of the suffix is also indicated by the singular number and the neuter gender in the word *idam*, it would apply only to a single object—specifically to that which is neuter—and not to anything else; furthermore, it would not apply to something remote (*parokṣe*), because the word *idam* denotes what is directly perceived (*pratyakṣa*)? Anticipating all of this, he says: "*prakṛtipratyayārthayoḥ*" and so forth.
In the base (*prakṛti*), only the general sense of the genitive case is intended.
In the meaning of the suffix as well, only that which is related to the genitive sense is intended—that without which the genitive sense would not be established.
With the words "yadaparam" (furthermore), he shows what is excluded by the word *mātra* (only/merely).
By the word *ādi* (and so forth), the quality of denoting a universal (*sāmānyābhidhāyitva*) is included.
The reason for intending this [meaning] in every instance has been stated precisely in the rule *[[Pāṇini 4.1.92]]*.

Now, why does this not occur here: *devadattasyānantaram* (after Devadatta), *devadattasya samīpam* (near Devadatta), and so forth? [The answer is: "In the case of *anantara* and so on," etc.; "because of non-expression" (*anabhidhānāt*) means that there is no communication of *anantara* and the others by means of an element ending in a suffix. [And as for the rule] "the suffix *tuḥ* after *saṃvah*"...
The meaning is "from the end of the root *vah*.
Regarding the form *sāṃvāhitram*:
from the root *vah* preceded by the prefix *sam*, there is the suffix *tu*, along with the augment *iṭ*, and the substitution of *yaṇ*.
"It is already established here by the rule [Pāṇini 6.1.83].
If this is so, for what purpose is the supplementary rule (upasaṃkhyāna) stated? He says: "For the sake of the augment iṭ," and so forth.

In this supplementary rule (*upasaṃkhyāna*), the augment *iṭ* would not occur because of the prohibition of *iṭ* by the rule "after a monosyllabic root that is unaccented in its original enunciation" (*ekāca upadeśe'nudāttāt* 7.2.10). Examples include *agnīghaḥ* and so forth. Regarding *agnīgha*: when the sense of a shelter or a house is to be expressed, the suffix *raṇ* should be stated [after the word *agnīgh*], and the designation *bha* should also be stated. Since the designation *bha* applies, there is no designation of a "word" (*pada*); consequently, due to the absence of the *pada* designation, the substitution of *jaś* (voiced unaspirated stops) does not take place. Regarding *samidhām* and so forth:

the suffix *vaṇyaṇ* should be stated—that is, explained—as being applied after the word *samidh* in the specific sense of a particular kind of fuel-wood (*samidh*) with which the fire is kindled by means of a specific mantra.
The explanation, however, should be stated by relying on the rule *havirnivāsasāmidhenīṣu* (Pāṇini 3.1.129).
Regarding the word *sāmidhenī*: the suffix *ṅīṣ* is applied [by Pāṇini 4.1.41], and the elision of *y* occurs [by Pāṇini 6.4.150]. "Not elsewhere" means: [the suffix does not apply] in other cases.

Regarding the rule for *sannāha* and so forth: in the rule *patrādvāhre* (Vārttika 4.3.120), the restriction (*avadhāraṇa*) must be understood here as "only after *pattra* [the suffix *añ* is applied] to denote a horse.
Why does it not occur elsewhere? Because of non-expression (*anabhidhāna*).

Now, why is this not formulated as a single rule together with the preceding one, namely: *pattrapūrvapatrādhvaryupariṣado'ñ*? It cannot be done in this way; for if it were, the suffix would undesirably apply even to bases other than those preceded by *pattrapūrva*.

In the case of the division of rules (*yogavibhāga*), since the word "chariot" (*ratha*) is carried over from the preceding rule, it is the chariot alone that is qualified by the mention of "preceded by *pattra*"; thus, there is no over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).

However, if it were a single rule (*ekayoga*), while "chariot" and so forth would be carried over, just as the chariot is qualified by being preceded by *pattra*, the chariot itself would likewise be qualified by *pattra* and the others; this would lead to an undesirable result.
Therefore, the division of rules alone is logical. [The example is] "Bābhraṇyaśālaṅkāyanikā."

Since the suffix *vuñ* occurs by its very nature (*svabhāva*) in the feminine, the suffix *ṭāp* is applied; the substitution of *ī* for *a* is then effected by the rule *pratyayasthāt* [Pāṇini 7.3.44]. When *vun* was already applicable, the prescription of *vuñ* is for the sake of the vowel lengthening (*vṛddhi*). And it is only non-*vṛddha* (non-penultimate-heavy) words denoting a lineage (*gotra*) or a school (*caraṇa*) that necessitate this, not those that are *vṛddha*.
For in their case, there is no difference whether *vuñ* or *vun* is employed.
Regarding "glau cukāyanaka":

[the suffix] *phin* is applied by the rule *prācām avṛddhāt phin bahulam* [Pāṇini 4.1.160], and from that which ends in *phin*, the suffix *vuñ* is added. Regarding "from a *caraṇa*" and so forth: [the suffix *vuñ*] is desired only after a *caraṇa* when referring to *dharma* or *āmnāya*, and not elsewhere, because of the lack of conventional usage (*anabhidhāna*). Therefore, due to this disparity, there is no correspondence according to the order of enumeration (*yathāsaṃkhyam*).

But if the mention of "sound" (ghoṣa) were not there, then since the three beginning with *añ* would also apply to the group beginning with *saṅgha*, there would be a confusion of application according to their respective order (*yathāsaṃkhyam*). Furthermore, the suffix would not be applied when there is sound [as in the case of the word *veda*].
In the example "Baidaḥ," the suffix *añ* is applied by the rule *anṛṣa-* [Pāṇini 4.1.104], and from that form ending in *añ*, the suffix *aṇ* is applied.

What is the difference between *aṅka* and *lakṣa*? There is indeed no difference at all; for it is considered that *aṅka* and *lakṣa* are synonyms. By the words "the characteristic" (*lakṣaṇam*) and so forth, he demonstrates the distinction.
A characteristic (lakṣaṇa) or mark is the property of that which is characterized (lakṣya) alone, and not of anything else; for example, knowledge belongs to the Vidas alone.
Indeed, characteristics belong only to those who possess them, such as the Vidas, and not to anyone else.
However, a mark situated on a cow or similar object does not belong to the cow or the like [as their defining essence].
What then? [It applies] to others than those, namely, the owners of cows and so forth.

Now, for what purpose is the *ṅit* marker applied to the suffix, since the bases ending in *añ* and *yañ* are already "vṛddha" (possessing the *vṛddhi* vowel)? To this he says: "The application of the *ṅit* marker," and so on;
[its purpose is] so that the suffix *ṅīp* may occur in the case of *baidī vidyā* ("the science of Baida").

And here, in the case of *baidīvidya*, the rule [Pāṇini 6.3.39] "in this [context]" serves to prevent the substitution of the masculine form (*puṃvadbhāva*); for this purpose the suffix is marked with the indicator *ṇit*, not for the sake of *vṛddhi*. It is said, "it is an exception to *vuñ*," because the word *śākala*, which denotes a Vedic school (*caraṇa*), possesses the characteristic of being a school name.
Regarding "śākalāḥ":

from the word *śākalya*, which ends in the suffix *yañ* (belonging to the *garga*-class), the suffix *aṇ* is applied in the sense of "proclaimed by" according to Pāṇini 4.2.111. Then, by Pāṇini 6.4.151, there is the elision of the *y* of the patronymic suffix when followed by a *taddhita* suffix beginning with a vowel.

When *śākala* is established, the suffix *aṇ* is applied by [Pāṇini 4.2.59], and by [4.2.63] there is elision (*luk*) of that suffix because it is taught as such—thus, *śākalāḥ*. A collection of them is *śākalaḥ*, or alternatively *śākalakaḥ*. This is an exception to the suffixes *vuñ* and *aṇ*. It is an exception to *vuñ* derived from the *caraṇa-lakṣaṇa* group beginning with *chandoga*, and to the general *aṇ* derived from the group beginning with *naṭa*. "Students for whom the staff is primary are *daṇḍamāṇavāḥ*."

He shows that this is a compound formed by the elision of the middle term (*madyamapadalopisamāsa*). Furthermore, it should be understood as belonging to the *mayūravyaṃsaka* group; for the *mayūravyaṃsaka* group is an open-ended class (*ākṛtigaṇa*).
"The suffix *vuñ* does not occur"—by this, he shows that this is a prohibition of *vuñ*. But how is it known that this is a prohibition of *vuñ*? To this he says: "The mention of *gotra*, etc."

For here, the mention of *gotra* (lineage) from [Pāṇini 4.3.126] continues; therefore, the meaning is this: in the sense prescribed by [Pāṇini 4.3.120], the suffix that would otherwise apply after a *gotra* word does not apply when referring to a *daṇḍamāṇava* or a *antevāsin*. Since the suffix *vuñ* alone would apply after a *gotra* word, this very prohibition is now enjoined for it. From the word *gaukakṣya*, which ends in *yañ* because it belongs to the *garga*-class [Pāṇini 4.2.111], the suffix *aṇ* is applied; as before, there is the elision (*yalopa*) of *ya*. Thus: "the Dākṣas."

From *dākṣi*, *plākṣi*, and *māhakīya*, the suffix *aṇ* is applied by [Pāṇini 4.2.111] *iñaśca*. "A different state of the material cause" (*prakṛter avasthāntaram*) means that a different state of the material cause (*prakṛti*), which is the cause (*kāraṇa*), is its being otherwise (*anyathātva*).
"Not a living being" (*aprāṇī*).
Regarding *prāṇinaḥ*, he will state the suffix *añ* [by P.
4.3.154]. Regarding *ādyudāttam*, he will state the suffix *añ* [by P. 4.3.140].

Regarding the term "not ending in *vṛddhi*": he will state that the suffix *mayaṭ* applies after a word with a *vṛddhi* vowel by rule 4.3.144; furthermore, for those words for which there is no specific, word-for-word (*pratipadam*) rule of application—such as "the suffix *yat* after *go* and *payas*" (4.3.158) and so forth—it would follow that the form should remain in its original state (*prakṛtibhāva*) by rule 6.4.167, which prescribes *an*. How then is the form *āśma* derived? To this he says: "In the sense of 'a modification of stone' (*aśmanaḥ vikāraḥ*), there is the elision of the *ṭi* [suffix]."

This supplementary rule (*upasaṃkhyāna*) has been formulated for the purpose of eliding the *ṭi* (the final vowel and following consonant) [of the base], namely: "The *vikāra* (modification) of the self [is expressed by these suffixes]. [This indicates that] words such as *aśman* and others are *ādyudātta* (accented on the first syllable) precisely because they have the *nit* suffix.
In that context, the words *aśman* and *bhasman*, because they end in the suffix *manin*, have their first syllable udātta by the accent rule [of the suffix] (*natsvara*).
The word *mṛttikā* also has its first syllable udātta because it ends in the suffix *tikan*—[according to Pāṇini 5.4.39].

Now, for what purpose is the mention of "of that" (*tasya*)? Since the mention of "of that" is already under discussion? To this he says: "{The section concerning 'of that'—as printed in earlier editions}" and so forth. "The section concerning 'of that'" etc. means that the topic of "of that" (the genitive) continues.
For that previous mention of "of it" (tasya) was connected with the secondary suffixes beginning with *gha* (*śaiṣika*), such as *gha*.
Therefore, if that [suffix] were to recur, those [suffixes] would also recur.
However, when this mention of "of it" is made, the preceding mention of "of it" is set aside.
Therefore, even in the present context, when the word "tasya" (of it) is used, the term "tasya" is stated again for the purpose of excluding the *śaiṣika* suffixes.

Now, an objection may be raised: the *gha*-suffixes and others are the primary elements because they are what are being prescribed; however, the mention of "tasya" is subordinate because its purpose is to serve that [prescription]. In that case, it would be improper for the primary element to be excluded while the subordinate element is being excluded. For just as the mention of "tasya" in the present context is connected with the *gha*-suffixes, so too is it connected with the *aṇ*-suffixes and others. This is not a fault, for if both were to be excluded, the commencement of the sūtra would be rendered fruitless.
Because there is no specific element to be prescribed, therefore the cessation of both does not occur.
But surely, by the force of the initial undertaking, it is understood that there is a cessation of one or the other of the two;
so, which are they—the *kādi* sounds or the *aṇ* sounds? There is indeed doubt.

This is merely a doubt; for in all cases of doubt, this principle applies: "The specific understanding is obtained from the explanation, for a rule is not rendered non-definitive by mere doubt" (Vyākhyānaparibhāṣā 75).
We shall explain [the sūtra] as meaning that "gha and the others cease," while the suffixes *aṇ* and so on will continue by virtue of their being marked with the *svarita* accent.

But surely, since gha and the others are not marked with the *svarita* accent, they would not continue; rather, it is by the statement "that very [suffix] belongs to it" (*tasyaiva tu saḥ*) that their continuation is indicated for the purpose of excluding the secondary (*śaiṣika*) suffixes.

By the rule beginning with "vikārāvayavayoḥ," he demonstrates a specific distinction. But by what means do the *gha* and other suffixes apply to *vikāra* (modification) and *avayava* (part)? It is by the rule [Pāṇini 4.3.120], because that [suffix] is a specific sub-class of *tasyedam* (belonging to this). Examples are: *hālaḥ* (made from barley) and *sairaḥ* (made from sesame).
If the secondary suffixes (*śaiṣika*) were to follow here, then by [Pāṇini 4.4.81], the suffix *ṭhak* would apply after the words *hala* and *sīra*.
When that is excluded, however, only *aṇ* occurs. Thus, in the example "a reed made of *mūrvā* fiber" (*maurvaṃ kāṇḍam*), the suffix is applied to the word *mūrvā* to denote a part.
Regarding the term "maurva-bhasma" (ash of the maurva plant):
by the phrase "from here onwards," etc., he demonstrates the distribution of the scopes of the suffixes that are about to be explained.
[The question] "How? [is asked].
In what manner is this distinction obtained?
He asks about the perceptible object with the words "both," and so forth;
he demonstrates the reason why this distinction of objects is obtained.

There, medicinal herbs (oṣadhī) end with the ripening of their fruit; trees (vṛkṣa) possess both flowers and fruits, while their specific varieties, the forest-creepers (vanaspati), possess only fruits.

In that context, by the mention of "forest-creepers," the specific types of trees [possessing only fruit] are understood, whereas by the mention of "trees," the inclusion of forest-creepers is also to be recognized.
Regarding the phrase "of the modification and the part," and so forth:
the simultaneous governing (yugapadadhikāra) is for the purpose of stating that "I shall explain the suffixes beginning with *aṇ* [and others] under a single governing rule.
Why does it not also serve the purpose of indicating the meanings of the suffixes beginning with *aṇ*? To this he says: "For those two have already been indicated."

For those two meanings have already been explained by the rule itself [Pāṇini 4.3.120]; since this [present rule] is a specific qualification of those two, it is an exception (*apavāda*) to *añ* and *mayaṭ*.

That is to say, it is an exception to *añ* which would otherwise apply by [Pāṇini 4.3.140], "from that which begins with an anudātta vowel," and an exception to *mayaṭ* which would otherwise apply by [Pāṇini 4.3.144], "from that which is vṛddha."

In that regard, although the word *bilva* would normally have its final syllable accented (*antodātta*) by the accentuation rule for nominal stems (*prātipadika-svara*), it instead receives either a circumflex (*svarita*) or an acute (*udātta*) accent according to the rule: *bilvatiṣyayor vāntasvaritatvam* (Phiṭ-sūtra 1.23).
The words *vrīhi* and *mudga* have their final syllables accented because they belong to the *ghṛtādi* group.
The words *masūra* and *godhūma* have their middle syllables accented according to the rule: *laghāv ante dvayoś ca bahvaṣo guruḥ* (Phiṭ-sūtra 2.42).
Similarly, the word *gavedhukā* is also derived from the root *iṣ* with the suffix *ksu*, as in *ikṣu*;
it is oxytone due to the accent of the suffix.
The word *veṇu* is also necessarily oxytone according to [Pāṇini 6.1.215].

The words *karpāsī* and *pāṭalī* end in the suffix *ṅīṣ* by virtue of [Pāṇini 4.1.63], "The suffix *ṅīṣ* is applied after a word denoting a genus that is not feminine and has a non-*y*-vowel as its penultimate. Because they end in the suffix *ṅīṣ*, they are oxytone due to the accent of the suffix *ṅīṣ*.
The word *karkandhū* is oxytone due to its being an irregularly formed (*nipātana*) term according to [Pāṇini 6.2.176]: *andūdṛgbhūjambūkaphelūkarkandhūdidhiṣūḥ*.
The word *kuṭīra* is oxytone by virtue of the rule beginning with [Pāṇini 6.2.179]: *laghāvante*.
All these [words] are anudātta in their initial syllables according to [Pāṇini 6.1.158].
Therefore, the suffix *añ* is prescribed for the purpose of excluding [other suffixes].

Now, what is the purpose of mentioning *aṇ*? Why not simply say that after words such as *bilva*, the suffix is applied exactly as ordained? This cannot be done; for here the word *pāṭalī* is listed as having a *vṛddhi* vowel, and thus when the suffix *mayaṭ*—which supersedes *añ*—would otherwise apply, the explicit mention [of *añ*] would result in *añ* alone.
However, because of the mention of *aṇ*, it is *aṇ* itself that occurs.
Therefore, the mention of *aṇ* is made. Regarding the phrase "according to what is appropriate" (*yathāyogam*):

the meaning of "according to what is appropriate" is that [the suffix *aṇ* is applied] after words denoting living beings, herbs, and trees for both modifications (*vikāra*) and parts (*avayava*), whereas after other words it is applied only for modifications.
The phrase "an exception to *añ*" means...
This refers to what would otherwise be obtained by the two rules *orañ* [Pāṇini 4.3.137] and *anudāttādeḥ* [Pāṇini 4.3.138].

The words *tittiḍīka*, *māṇḍūka*, *dardurūka*, and *madhūka* have the acute accent on the middle syllable according to the rule *laghāvante* (Phiṭ-sūtra 2.42), and therefore they have the grave accent on the first syllable (*anudāttādi*). Thus, this [suffix] is an exception (*apavāda*) to *orañ*, because [the base] begins with a grave accent.
Regarding the phrase "not containing living beings, etc.":

by the word "etc. (*ādi*), the states of being an herb (*oṣadhi*) and not being a tree (*avṛkṣa*) are included. Regarding the statement "anything other than that which begins with an anudātta vowel is the example here":
this is because [the case of] that which begins with an anudātta vowel is already established by the subsequent rule.

Regarding "daivadāravam" and "bhādradāravam": the words *devadāru* and *bhadradāru* have their initial syllable accented acute according to the rule *pītadravarthānām* (Phiṭ-sūtra 2.37). This is its meaning: those whose referent (*artha*) is *pītadru* are called *pītadravarthāḥ*; for those words denoting *pītadru*, the first syllable becomes acutely accented. Regarding "dādhittham," and so forth.

In the examples *dadhni tiṣṭhati* ("he stands in curd") and *kapau tiṣṭhati* ("he stands in a monkey"), the suffix *ka* is applied by the rule *supi sthaḥ* [Pāṇini 3.2.4], followed by the elision of the vowel *a* by *ato lopaḥ* [Pāṇini 6.4.48]. Due to its inclusion in the *pṛṣodarādi* group, the letter *s* is replaced by *t*. This forms an *upapada-samāsa* (compound with a subordinate word), which, by the accent of the compound (*samāsasvara*), results in the two words being oxytone (having the acute accent on the final syllable). Consequently, the words *dadhittha* and *kapittha* have anudātta vowels at their beginning. Regarding the statement "this is an option in both cases" (*ubhayatravibhāṣā*), it applies both where the rule would otherwise apply and where it would not.
In order to clarify that very option (*vibhāṣā*) regarding both cases, he says: "palāśakhadira," and so forth.
The word *palāśa* is oxytone (*antodātta*) because it belongs to the *dhṛtādi* group; the word *khadira* is also [oxytone] by virtue of the accent of the *ti* suffix.

While the rule *iṣimadimudikhidicchidibhidimandicanditisimihimuhimucirucirudhibandhiśuṣibhyaḥ kirac* (Dhātupāṭha 8.26) is in force, the form *khadira* is established as an irregular derivation (*nipātita*) ending in the suffix *kirac* by the rule *ajiraśiśiraśithilasthirasphirasthavirakhadirāḥ* (Dhātupāṭha 8.27).
The word *śiṃśapā* has its middle syllable accented acute (*madhyodātta*) according to the rule *pāntānāṃ gurvādīnām* (Phiṭ-sūtra 3.55).
Its meaning is this: for words ending in the sound *pā* that belong to the *guru* class and so forth, the second syllable becomes acute.

Alternatively, since [the word] follows from the rule *dvitīyaṃ prāgīṣāt* (Phiṭ-sūtra 3.50), and given the root *spadi* (meaning "to tremble slightly," Dhātupāṭha 14), the suffix *yuc* is applied by the rule *anudāttādeśca halādeḥ* (Pāṇini 3.2.149), resulting in *spandana*; thus, by the accent of the *cit* suffix, it is acute on the final syllable (*antodātta*).
According to the rule *kṛśṛgṛṭipaṭiśauṭibhya īran* (Uṇādi-sūtra 8.72),
the word *karīra* is udātta on its first syllable by virtue of the *ni*-accent.

Furthermore, according to the rules *kṛhmabhyāmīṣan* (Uṇādi-sūtra 9.9) and *śṛpṛbhyāṃ kit ca* (Uṇādi-sūtra 9.10), the word *śirīṣa* is likewise udātta on its first syllable by virtue of the *ni*-accent.

*vikaṅkata*, *pūla*, *asana*, and *vāsa* have their initial syllable accented acute by the rule *grāmādīnāṃ ca* (Phiṭ-sūtra 2.38). [The mention of these] is "an exception to the suffix -añ" (*año 'pavādaḥ*), because the word *śamī*— ending in the feminine suffix *-īṣ* due to its inclusion in the *gaurādi* group— is acutely accented on the final syllable by the accent of the suffix (*pratyayasvara*), and thus does not begin with an unaccented vowel.
The letter *ṭ* serves the purpose of [introducing] the suffix *ṅīp*. Regarding the phrase "of these two," the objection begins with "What is the use of this? and so forth;
the resolution begins with "Those specific cognitions," and so forth.
By the word "ādi" (and so forth), [rules] such as Pāṇini 4.3.157 and others are included.

If the phrase "of these two" (*etayoḥ*) were not stated, then when the subsequent specific suffixes beginning with *añ*—such as those following the rule for *yaḥ*—were to undergo vocalization (*samprasāraṇa*), they alone would apply because they are subsequent [in the order of the rules].
However, when "of these two" is stated, they optionally occur even in the case of specific suffixes; thus, forms such as *kapotamayam* are established.

Now, while this [sūtra] "of these two" (*etayoḥ*) is being formulated, how can the suffix *mayaṭ* apply to the scope of the *avada* rule? It does so because the phrase "of these two" serves the purpose of providing a second injunction; thus, the suffix *mayaṭ* occurs in the sense of both modification (*vikāra*) and constituent part (*avayava*). There are two [injunctions]: first, "of these two," and second, "the suffix *mayaṭ* occurs.
In that regard, if this were not a second injunction, it would merely serve the purpose of extension (*prāpaṇa*).
Therefore, even where [a form] is known to be sublated by specific cognitions, the mention of "vā" (optionally) must be made. Regarding the word *gavyam*:

when there is the intention to express the meaning "this belongs to a cow," the suffix *yat* is applied by the rule *sarvatra gorajādiprasaṅge yat* (Vārttika 383), and the substitution of *ava* for *go* occurs according to Pāṇini 6.1.79.

"Excrement is neither a modification nor a part"—this is understood from the context of the "cow. First of all, it is not a modification; for excrement is merely another state of the original substance (*prakṛti*), because it does not possess the characteristics of the cow (as opposed to the case of boiled rice, which does).
A part of a composite whole that assists the substance becomes its constituent cause (*ārambhaka-avayava*), such as the hand and so forth for the body; however, cow-dung is not like this.
To the question, "In what case, then, does this rule apply?", he says: "In the domain of 'this belongs to that' (*tasyedam viṣaye*).
Because the dung is produced from the cow, it is her effect; thus, the meaning of *tasyedam* (its belonging to that) applies here.
Therefore, this rule for *mayaṭ* applies only in that specific case. [Question:

"In that case, by what [suffix] should the derivatives for modification (*vikāra*) and part (*avayava*) be formed? [Answer: He says: "But in the case of modification and part," and so forth. "[It is] an exception to *aṇ*" means:

this word *piṣṭa* is udātta on its first syllable according to Pāṇini 6.1.205; therefore, the general suffix *aṇ* would apply to it, and this [rule for *mayaṭ*] is an exception to that. "[It is] an exception to *mayaṭ*" means: [it is an exception] to *mayaṭ*.
[This applies to] what was already obtained by the preceding sūtra. [Objection:

But since he will indeed teach *kan* in the sense of a name (*saṃjñā*), that rule [of *kan*] would be purposeless. [Response: This is not so; for that [suffix *kan*] applies to meanings such as "small" (*alpa*) and so on, whereas this [suffix *aṇ*] applies to the sense of a modification (*vikāra*).
Thus, this is meaningful, because of the difference in meaning. "The words *tila* and *yava* are udātta on the first syllable."
Therefore, the suffix *aṇ* would apply; hence, this [rule] is an exception (*apavāda*) to that.
As for the acute accent on the first syllable (*ādyudāttatva*) of those two, it must occur by the rule itself: *tṛṇadhānyānāṃ dvyaṣām* (Phiṭ-sūtra 2.27).

This is its meaning: for words consisting of two syllables denoting grasses or grains, the first vowel is udātta. Regarding "yāvakaḥ": [the suffix] *aṇ* is applied in the sense of a derivative product; from that which ends in *aṇ*, the suffix *kan* is added according to [Pāṇini 5.4.29]. Regarding "mauñjam": [the suffix *aṇ* is applied in the sense of "made of"].
Since the word *muñja* has an udātta accent on its first syllable, the suffix *aṇ* applies to it by the general rule (*autsargika*). Thus, [the form] is *gārmuta*.
[This is derived from] *mugror utiḥ* (Pāṇini 5.2.96); { *garmut* — Daivam}.
By the rule *garmut-ca* (Pāṇini 5.2.107), the word *garmut* is oxytone due to the accent of the suffix;
from that [word], the suffix *añ* is applied by [the rule] *tasmād-ṛt-vik-...* (4.3.140), resulting in the form *brāhmadhrya*.

By the rule *vṛdhivapibhyāṃ ran* (Pāṇini 4.1.117), the word *brādhna* is acutely accented on the first syllable due to the *nit*-accent; from that [word], by [Pāṇini 4.1.83] and *ṭiḍḍhāṇañ* (Pāṇini 4.1.15), the suffix *ṅīp* is applied.

Regarding the form *bailva*: why is there a mention of the possessive suffix *matup*? Why not simply say "not after *nod*, *vadhū*, or *bilva*"? To this he says: "The mention of *matup*. If it were stated as "after *ud*" (in the rule *nodvadhūbilvāt*), it would be a reference to the phoneme *u*.

In this context, since the mention of the term *varṇa* (color) applies the rule of "extension to that which ends with it" (*tadantavidhi*) everywhere, the mention of the suffix *matup* is made in order to prohibit that extension.
To the question, "But what would be the fault if there were such an extension to that which ends with it? he says: "In this very case," and so forth.
By the use of the particle *eva*, he shows that [the suffix] would not apply after words such as *muñja*.

Regarding the term *vaiṣṇavī*: the suffix *aṇ* is applied according to the rule for the *bilva*-class. The phrase "an exception to *mayaṭ* and so forth" includes *añ* by the word "and so forth" (*ādi*). Because there is a difference in their respective bases (*prakṛti*) and because plurality is intended for both, the dual number is used for both.
In this context, by the words *tāla* and *śyāmāka*, there is an exception to the suffix *mayaṭ* (prescribed for products of increase).

Furthermore, the word *bārhiṇa*—derived from *barhin* by the rule [Pāṇini 4.3.154] "The modification or part of a peacock" (*barhiṇo vikāro'vayavo vā*)—ends in a suffix denoting a modification or a part; therefore, this is an exception to the suffix *añ* which would otherwise apply to it by the rule [Pāṇini 4.3.155]. As for the remaining words, such as *indrāliśa* and others, there is the suffix *añ* characterized by having an initial low-pitched vowel (*anudātta*).

When *indra* is the upapada after the roots *liś* and *dṛś*, the suffix *ka* is applied according to the rule "there is an addition for *mūlavibhujādi* etc. in the section on *ka*" (Vārttika 232). By [Pāṇini 6.3.137], there is lengthening;
by [Pāṇini 6.2.139], due to the accent of the *kṛt*-suffix, the words *indrāliśa* and *indrādṛśa* have the udātta accent on the final syllable.
The word *indrāghu* is oxytone due to the accent of the compound (*samāsasvara*).
The word *capa*—derived from the root *cap* meaning "to soothe" (*dhātupāṭha* 399) with the suffix *ac*—is oxytone.
The word *pīyūkṣā* is middle-accented according to the rule beginning with "when there is a light syllable at the end" (*phi-sūtra* 2.42).

Even though, once the feminine suffix *ṭāp* has been applied, the condition "when a light syllable stands at the end" (*laghāvante*) no longer applies, it does indeed exist prior to the application of *ṭāp*; it is precisely in that state that the middle-acute accent (*madhyodāttatva*) occurs. [The author] reads: "after *tāla*, when a bow is denoted.
This means that the suffix *aṇ* is applied after the word *tāla* when a bow is to be expressed.
Thus, *tālaṃ dhanuḥ* ("a bow made of palmyra wood"), whereas anything else is *tālamayaṃ* ("made of palmyra").

Now, what is the purpose of including the mention of *aṇ*? Could it not simply be stated as "according to the rule as prescribed" (*yathāvihitam*)? It cannot be so; for after the word *bārhi*, the suffix *mayaṭ*—which is characterized by *vṛddhi* and *hrasva* [by Pāṇini 4.3.155]—is superseded by *aṇ*. In that case, by the force of its initial formulation, only *mayaṭ* would apply.
Furthermore, the word *śyāmāka* has its middle syllable accented acute (*madhyodātta*) according to the rule beginning with "when a light syllable is at the end" (*laghāvante*, Phiṭ-sūtra 2.42).

Therefore, [by the rule] *tasmāt* [Pāṇini 4.2.44], since [the suffix] *mayaṭ*—which is characterized by the term *vṛddha*—would supersede [the suffix *añ*] due to its higher status, the very commencement [of this new rule] ensures that only *añ* shall apply. By the explicit mention of *aṇ*, only *aṇ* occurs. [The phrase] "because of the mention in the plural," and so forth, [is used].
The sense is that if the apprehension of the essential nature (*svarūpa*) were intended, one would have made the designation using the singular number alone because of its oneness.
Regarding the phrase "of *mayaṭ* and so forth," the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) includes the suffix *nañ*.
The plural number is as before.
In that context, the suffix *mayaṭ* is set aside (apavāda) in favor of [the suffix *aṇ*] for those words such as *vṛddha*, *hāṭaka*, *jātarūpa*, and so forth;
however, for those such as *tapanīya* which begin with an anudātta vowel, the suffix *añ* is applied.

Regarding the term *tāpanīyam*: the word *tapanīya* is mid-toned (*madhyodātta*) according to the rule "when [the suffix] *yañ* follows, the penultimate syllable is acute" (*phi-sū-2.42*). Regarding the phrase "an exception to [the suffixes] *aṇ* and others":
by the word "others" (*ādi*), the suffix *mayaṭ* is included.
The plural number is as before.
In that context, for those animal-denoting words which have the acute accent on the first syllable, this [suffix] is an exception to *aṇ*;
however, for those which are *vṛddha*, *mayaṭ* is prescribed.

In the case of *rajata* and other such words as well, [the suffix] *añ* is an exception (*apavāda*) to *aṇ* when the word begins with an udātta vowel; however, it is an exception to *mayaṭ* when the word begins with an anudātta vowel and so forth. Since the suffix *añ* would already be established by the rule *tato hi* (Pāṇini 4.3.140), its restatement is for the purpose of ensuring that only *añ* is applied and not *mayaṭ*, which would otherwise apply by the rule *mayaḍ vaitayorbhāṣāyām...* (Pāṇini 4.3.143) and so on.
In that context, *rajatam* is oxytone due to its inclusion in the list beginning with *ghṛta*;
whereas *sīsam* and *loham* are proparoxytone according to the rule *nabviṣayasyānisantasya* (Phiṭ-sūtra 2.26).
This is its meaning: for a word denoting a neuter object that does not end in *i* or *u*, the first syllable is udātta.
*Nab* is the technical name (*saṃjñā*) for the neuter gender.

While the phrase "before the final [syllable]" (*antyāt pūrvam*) is understood [from the previous rule], by the rule *śiśṛmānodumbarabalīvardoṣṭrārapurūravasāṃ ca* (Phiṭ-sūtra 3.64), in the case of *udumbara*, the syllable preceding the final one is udātta.
In the case of *nīladāru*, *rohitadāru*, and *bibhītakadāru*, the acute accent falls on the middle syllable according to the rule *laghāvante* (Phiṭ-sūtra 2.42).
Some also recite the word *pītadāru*;
that is acutely accented on the first syllable according to the rule *nabviṣayasyānisantasya* (Phiṭ-sūtra 2.26).

Because the word *tri* ends in the suffix *ḍri* according to the rule *taraterḍriḥ* (Pāṇini 5.2.66), it is acute-accented on the first syllable (*ādyudātta*) by the accent of the suffix. The compound *trikaṇṭaka* is a *bahuvrīhi* meaning "one who has three thorns";
thus, by the rule *[[6.2.1]]*, the word *trikaṇṭaka* is acute-accented on the first syllable.
"Kaṇṭakaṃ karoti" (he makes a thorn) [is explained as] the suffix *aṇ* applied in the sense of an object (*karmaṇi*).

The word *kaṇṭakāra* has its final syllable accented (*antodātta*) by virtue of the accentuation rule for *kṛt*-suffixes. [The commentary says: "This is an exception to the suffix *mayaṭ*," because everything characterized by *vṛddhi* that ends in a *ñit* suffix is considered *vṛddha*. "[These suffixes are understood]" means...

But surely, by the paribhāṣā "the single-consonant suffix," the inclusion of *ṣṭlañ* would not be obtained? This is not a fault; for in the rule *ñitaśca*, the particle *ca* (and) serves to include that [suffix] as well.
Therefore, its inclusion will also take place.
By the mention of *orañ* in the sūtras from 4.3.137 through 4.3.141, the inclusion of these sūtras is to be understood; for they are non-different [in their application].
That very suffix *añ* which is prescribed by the rule *orañ* [Pāṇini 4.3.137] is carried over into these two rules.

By means of the example "the modification or part of *daivadāru*" (*daivadāravasya vikāro 'vayavo vā*), he demonstrates the illustrations and so forth for these suffixes as appropriate. [The examples are: *kāṃsya* ("made of bell-metal") and *pāraśava* ("made of iron").
"Beneficial for Kaṃsa" results in *kaṃsīya* by [Pāṇini 5.1.1] *prāk krītāc cha*.
"Beneficial for an axe" results in *paraśavya* by [Pāṇini 5.1.2] *u-gav-ādibhyo yat*.

According to [Pāṇini 4.3.168], when it is a modification (*vikāra*) or a part (*avayava*) of *paraśavya*, the suffixes *yañ* and *añ* occur respectively, with the elision (*luk*) of *cha* and *yat*: thus, *kāṃsya* and *pāraśava*; and for their modification or part, the suffix *añ* is applied by this same rule.
Regarding the term "bailvamayam": the word *bilva* [is formed] with the suffix *aṇ* by [Pāṇini 4.3.136]. From that, by the rule for *vṛddha* [words], only the suffix *mayaṭ* occurs.
Regarding the term *vaidamaya*:
by the rule *anṛṣya-ādinā-añ* (Pāṇini 4.3.104), the suffix *añ* is applied, resulting in *vaida*.

This suffix *añ* is marked with the indicator *ñ*, but it does not signify a modification (*vikāra*) or a constituent part (*avayava*). Consequently, the suffix *mayaṭ* alone is applied [to form *vaidamaya*]. Thus, it is stated that this is "an exception (*apavāda*) to [the application of] *aṇ* and the other [suffixes]."
By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), the inclusion of *añ* and the others is intended.
It is said: "Number (*saṃkhyā*) is also included by the mention of 'measure' (*parimāṇa*).

But how is this obtained, given that the word "measure" is conventionally established (*rūḍha*) for [units of capacity] such as the *prastha*, and not for number? This is not a fault; for just as [the *prastha* and so on] are the means of delimiting [a substance], so too is number.
Therefore, by means of this analogy, the word *parimāṇa* will also apply to number (*saṃkhyā*), in the sense that "number is like a measure" (*parimāṇam iva parimāṇam*).

But if this is so, is it not improper to employ a figurative sense (*gauṇa*) when a primary sense (*mukhya*) exists? This is the fault here: in this system (*tantra*), two instances of the word *parimāṇa* are uttered simultaneously; therein, the second word is accented, and by that, number is also included—as in the example *naiṣkikam*.
The suffix *iṣṭhan* is applied as before [Pāṇini 5.1.18]. Examples are: *śatyaḥ*, *śatikaḥ*;
and *saharūm*.

By the rule *śatamānaviṃśatikasahasravasanādaṇ* [Pāṇini 5.1.27] and by the rule *adhyardhapūrva* [Pāṇini 5.1.28], when the suffix *vat* is applied in the sense of similarity (*sādṛśya*), he demonstrates what is achieved as desired.
By the word "etc. (*ādi*), there is the inclusion of the base form (*prakṛti*) and so forth.
Thus: *dvisaharuām*.
The term *dvigu* is used here in the sense of a secondary derivative (*taddhita*), meaning "a modification consisting of two thousand.

Because the rule "there is extension [of the designation] to that which ends in such a word when preceded by a numeral, provided there is no elision (*aluk*)" (Vārttika on Pāṇini 5.1.20) permits this extension to the final member of the compound, just as in the case of the sense of "bought" (Pāṇini 5.1.37)—whereby elision may optionally occur—so it is here as well. Thus, we have the form *dvisāhasram*.

The vowel lengthening (*vṛddhi*) of the final member of the compound occurs by the rule *saṃkhyāyāḥ saṃvatsarapūrvasya* [Pāṇini 7.3.15]. Regarding the form *dvinīṣkaḥ*: just as the suffix *ṭhañ* is applied after the word *niṣka* in the sense of "purchased" according to *prāgvateṣṭhañ* [Pāṇini 5.1.18], and that suffix is optionally elided (*luk*) by the rule *dvitripūrvānniṣkāt* [Pāṇini 5.1.30], so too is it here.

Regarding the term *dvinaiṣkikam*: by the rule *parimāṇāntasyāsaṃjñānnāṇayoḥ* [Pāṇini 7.3.17], there is vṛddhi of the final vowel of the second member of the compound. The word *umā*, according to the *Phiṭ-sūtra* 2.27 which states "the word *umā* refers to grass or grain," is not udātta on its first syllable; the word *ūrṇā* is also udātta on its final syllable by the accent of the nominal stem (*prātipadika-svara*). Since the suffixes *aṇ* and *ña* would apply to these two respectively, the optional suffix *vuñ* is introduced. Regarding the statement "but for *pums*, *añ* occurs": if the suffix *ḍhañ* were to apply here to *pums*, he would have made the reference using the masculine gender alone.

In the case of a masculine gender designation, when a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) is mentioned, there is indeed the inclusion of that which is qualified by gender; thus, the suffix is obtained even from the word *eṇī*.

Therefore, because of the feminine gender designation itself, the suffix *añ* applies to the masculine, and not *ḍhañ*. However, regarding the scope of *mayaṭ*, it is prescribed [by the rule] "because of the mention of the contingency of [suffixes] beginning with *aj*."
Since the suffix *mayaṭ* does not begin with a vowel (*an*), it would not apply in that context; therefore, [the suffix] is prescribed there from the word *go*.

However, the word *payaḥ* ends in the suffix *asun* derived from the root *pā*, and by virtue of the *nit*-accent, it is udātta on its first syllable. Consequently, the suffix *aṇ* prescribed by the rule *prāgdīvyato’ṇ* [Pāṇini 4.1.83] would apply.
Thus, what is being prescribed here serves as an exception (*apavāda*) to that. As for the suffix *añ*, however, it indeed applies.
When there is elision (*luk*) of that [suffix], the prescription becomes purposeless because it is not heard [in the resulting form]. For example, in the case of *jambūni*:
once the elision has been applied, the gender of the expressed meaning becomes neuter.

Regarding the rule *hrasvo nupaṃsake prātipadikasya* [Pāṇini 1.2.47], and the sequence *jaśśasoḥ śiḥ* [7.1.20] and *num* [6.4.7] resulting in a long vowel: what then is the specific distinction that exists when *lup* occurs, such that this [long vowel] is prescribed even though *luk* is the general rule? To this he says: "The distinction is the state of being like the original compound (*yuktavadbhāva*). When *lup* occurs, there is the state of being like the original compound [according to 1.2.51]; thus, the distinction exists precisely when *lup* occurs. For example: *jambūḥ phalam* ("the fruit is a rose-apple").

In this case, by virtue of the treatment as if possessing the gender of the base (*yuktavadbhāva*), the gender inherent in the base itself prevails; therefore, the neuter gender does not apply. Regarding the phrase "in the section on *lup*" and so forth:
they wither through the ripening of their fruit, thus they are called *phalapākaśuṣaḥ*. The suffix *kvip* is applied according to the rule *anyebhyo 'pi dṛśyate* (Pāṇini 3.2.178).
"Vrīhayaḥ, mudgāḥ"— here there is elision (*lup*) of the suffix *aṇ* after words such as *bilva* [according to Pāṇini 4.3.134]. "Yavāḥ, māṣāḥ"— [likewise].

Therefore, [the suffix] *aṇ* is the general rule (*autsargika*). These [words] are ādyudātta (accented on the first syllable) by the rule "of grasses and grains" (*tṛṇadhānyānām*, Phiṭ-sūtra 2.27), etc. Regarding the statement "in the case of flowers and roots, [the suffix] is frequently elided" (*puṣpamūleṣu bahulam*):
when flowers and roots are to be expressed, the suffix *lup* is frequently applied.
In the case of *mallikā*, *vanamallikā*, *jāti*, *vidārī*, *aṃśumatī*, and *bṛhatī*, there is elision (*lup*) of the suffix *aṅ* characterized by anudātta vowels and so forth.

The words *mallikā* and *navamallikā* have the acute accent on the middle syllable according to the rule "when there is a light vowel at the end, or when there are two [light vowels], or when there are many heavy vowels" (Phiṭ-sūtra 2.42).

Furthermore, the word *jāti* has the acute accent on the final syllable because it ends in the suffix *ktic*, according to the rule "the suffixes *kvip* and *ktic* are used in the sense of a name" (Pāṇini 3.3.174).
The words *badarī* and *bṛhatī* are also oxytone because they end in the feminine suffix *ṅīṣ* according to the *gaurādi* group.
The word *aṃśumatī* ends in *ṅīp* by [Pāṇini 4.1.45];
since the stem *aṃśu* is oxytone by its own nominal stem accent (*prātipadika-svara*), [the resulting form] is middle-accented.
Regarding "pāṭalāni":
[the suffix] *aṇ* is applied according to the rule for the *bilva*-group.
Regarding "śālvāni mūlāni": [the same suffix is applied].
By the rule *anudāttādir lakṣaṇo ’ṇ*, the suffix *aṇ* is applied;
thus, the word *śālva* is udātta on its final syllable by the accent of the nominal stem (*prātipadika-svara*).
*Śālva* is that which is commonly known as *śāka*.
"In some cases, even something else [occurs]" means that in certain instances other than those [already mentioned], the elision (*lup*) occurs; furthermore,
there is the absence of both *tatpuruṣa* and *lup*.
In the case of *kadambaka* and so forth, there is the elision (*luk*) of the suffix *añ* as characterized by an anudātta vowel.
Words such as *kadamba* have the udātta accent on the middle syllable according to the rule *laghāvante* (Phiṭ-sūtra 2.42).
Regarding *balvāni*:
In this case, there is the absence of both [the suffixes].

However, since all of this is already established by the very recitation of the *harītaky-ādi* group, nothing new need be stated. For among the *harītaky-ādi* words, they read: "and those whose withering is caused by the ripening of the fruit" (Pāṇini 4.3.165), and "frequently in the case of flowers and roots" (4.3.166). Among the *harītaky-ādi* words, *kaṇṭakārikā*, *gargārikā*, and *śephālikā*—these, because they end in the suffix *kan* [by rule 5.3.87], are acute-accented on the first syllable due to the *nit-svara*.

By that very [rule], there is the elision (*lup*) of the general suffix *aṇ* after those [words]; however, after the remaining [words], there is the elision of the suffix *añ*, which is characterized by having an initial low-pitched vowel (*anudātta*). All of them have the high-pitched vowel (*udātta*) at the end, and thus they are "those beginning with an *anudātta*" (*anudāttādi*).

Among them, *kālā*, *drākṣā*, and *dhrākṣā*—those which are listed before these—are *antodātta* (having the high-pitched vowel at the end) because they end in the feminine suffix *ṅīṣ*. In that regard, *otapākī* and *arjunapākī* end in *ṅīṣ* according to the rule *pākakarṇaparṇa* [Pāṇini 4.1.64].

But for the remaining [words], because they belong to the *gaura*-class, [the suffix *ṅīṣ* is applied] by the rule *gaurādibhyaśca* [Pāṇini 4.1.41]. From the words *kālī*, *drākṣā*, and *dhṛkṣā*, which are oxytone (*antodātta*) by virtue of the accent of the nominal stem (*prātipadika-svara*), the feminine suffix *ṭāp* is added; then, by the rule *savarṇadīrgha* [Pāṇini 6.1.101], there is the substitution of a long vowel, and by the rule *udāttayaṇo halpūrvāt* [Pāṇini 6.1.174], this [long vowel] becomes udātta. Therefore, *kālī* and the others are also oxytone. As for the form *kaṃsīyaḥ*: [it is derived from *kāṃsya* with the suffix *cha*].
In the *Uṇādi* [section], the word *kaṃsa* is derived as ending in the suffix *-a*.

The word *paśu* is also derived with the suffix *ku*, following the rule *pṛthivīvyādhṛṣibhyaḥ kuḥ* (*DhP* 1.108), while the rule *āṅparayoḥ khaniśṛbhyāṃ ṇicca* (*DhP* 1.118)—which includes the statement that the suffix is also *ḍit*—is in force. Why, then, does elision (*luk*) not occur for these two [roots] and their suffixes? To this he says: "Because of the governing heading (*adhikāra*) of 'nominal stem' (*prātipadika*)," and so forth.

The term "from a nominal stem" (*prātipadikāt*) is understood [from the previous rule]; therefore, elision (*luk*) occurs for that which is prescribed after a nominal stem. However, these two [suffixes] are not prescribed after a nominal stem; rather, they are prescribed after a verbal root (*dhātu*). Consequently, elision does not apply to them. This is because [the suffixes] are themselves unaccented (*anudātta*).
For the word *paraśavya* has a svarita accent on its final syllable by virtue of [Pāṇini 6.1.185].
[The rule] "by that, [the compound] begins with an anudātta" applies;
and the word "iti" is understood to carry over there.

[This rule] follows from [Pāṇini 4.2.91]: *yasya ca*... Thus ends the third quarter of the fourth chapter in the *Kāśikā-vivaraṇapañjikā*, composed by the venerable Master Jinendrabuddhi, who is a teacher of the Bodhisattvas. In the *Harītaky-ādi* group, the words *kaṇṭakārikā*, *gargārikā*, and *śephālikā* end in the suffix *kan* (by Pāṇini 5.3.87). Because they are formed with this suffix, they are acute on the first syllable (*ādyudātta*) due to the accent of the *niṭ* suffix.

Consequently, the general suffix *aṇ* is elided after these. After the remaining words, however, the suffix *añ* is applied according to the rule for words beginning with an anudātta vowel (Pāṇini 4.2.44), as all of them are anudātta on the first syllable because they are acute on the final syllable (*antodātta*).

In this regard, those [words] such as *kālā*, *drākṣā*, and *dhrākṣā* which are recited before these [others] are oxytone because they end in the suffix *ṅīṣ*. Among them, *otapākī* and *arjunapākī* end in *ṅīṣ* by virtue of the rule "pākakarṇaparṇa" (Pāṇini 4.1.64).
As for the remaining [words], they take the suffix *ṅīṣ* by virtue of belonging to the *gaura*-class, according to the rule "gaurādibhyaśca" (Pāṇini 4.1.41).

From the words *kālā*, *drākṣā*, and *dhrākṣā*, which are oxytone by the accent of the nominal stem (*prātipadika-svara*), the suffix *ṭāp* is added; then, through the substitution of a long vowel with a homogeneous vowel (*savarṇadīrghatva*), the resulting vowel retains its acute accent according to the rule "udāttayaṇo halpūrvāt" (Pāṇini 6.1.174).

Therefore, *kāla* and the others are also finally accented (*antodātta*). Regarding *kaṃsīya*: in the *Uṇādi-sūtras*, the word *kaṃsa* is derived as ending in the suffix *sa*. The word *paśu* is also derived with the suffix *ku*; while the rule *pṛthivī-vyā-dhṛṣi-bhyaḥ kuḥ* (Uṇādi 1.108) is in force, it is formed by the suffix *ku* according to the rule *āṅ-parayoḥ khani-śṛbhyāṃ ṇicca* (Uṇādi 1.118).

"Why does elision (*luk*) not also occur for these two, namely the root (*dhātu*) and the suffix (*pratyaya*)? To this he says: "Because of the governing rule (*adhikāra*) concerning nominal stems (*prātipadika*)," and so forth.
The term "from a nominal stem" (*prātipadikāt*) is understood [from the previous rule]; therefore, elision occurs only for that which is prescribed after a nominal stem.
These two, however, are not prescribed after a nominal stem; rather, they are prescribed after a root. Consequently, elision does not apply to them.
"Simply because it is unaccented (anudātta)":
for the word *paraśavya* has a svarita accent on its final syllable by [Pāṇini 6.1.185].
"Therefore, it begins with an unaccented vowel."

The word *iti* is understood there [in the rule], following from [the rule] *yasya ca* (Pāṇini 6.4.148). Thus ends the third quarter of the fourth chapter in the *Kāśikā-vivaraṇapañjikā*, composed by the venerable Ācārya Jinendrabuddhi, who is a follower of the Bodhisattva. Now, for what purpose is the mention of *prāk* ("before")? It is for this purpose: so that the suffix *ṭhak*, which has been set aside by another suffix as an exception (*apavāda*) in a specific sense, may be reinstated in a subsequent section of the text.

For example: in this specific meaning [of "one who eats"], the suffix *aṇ* (prescribed by Pāṇini 4.4.4, *kulatthakopadhāt*), having been set aside, is reintroduced later for another meaning, namely in the sense of "one who crosses" (Pāṇini 4.4.5), so that it may apply again. [The commentary says] "In the section on *ṭhak*, etc.
This means that the suffix *ṭhak* is to be added after words such as *māśabda* in the sense of "he says" (*āha*) when they denote an action. [It is further noted:
"This rule for the application of the suffix is based on a syntactical sentence (*vākya*)."

For that alone is the meaning of the sentence; thus, it is not disregarded as having become a mere object of action. This is indicated by the statement: "The cognition arises from the very sentence that expresses that [meaning]," for a sentence is indeed a collection of words.
The collection of words consisting of the word *mā* and the word *śabda* is a sentence (*vākya*).

This should be understood in other cases as well. But how can there be an injunction for an affix (*pratyaya-vidhi*) from a sentence when the governing topic (*adhikāra*) concerns nominal stems (*prātipadika*)? To this he says: "from *prabhūta* and so forth," because of the repetition [of the rule].

If, indeed, the rule for the suffix were applied directly from the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) itself, then the subsequent supplementary rule—"*āhau prabhūtādibhyaḥ*" (Vārttika 483)—would be rendered purposeless, as its purpose would already be accomplished by this very [general] rule.

For even words such as *prabhūta* and the like would fall under the category of words beginning with *mā* (i.e., *mā*, *na*, etc.), and these, being expressive of the object (*karman*), would themselves produce the suffix; since they denote adverbs (*kriyāviśeṣaṇa*).
For the status of adverbs as objects (*karmatva*) will be established in the rule *tatpratyanupūrvamīpalomakūlam* [Pāṇini 4.4.28]. Furthermore, the meaning of the suffix is also "he says" (*āha*).
Therefore, because of the repetition in the rule *prabhūtādibhyaḥ* [Pāṇini 5.1.118], it is understood that the prescription of the suffix occurs only from a sentence.
[The rule] states: "from an adverbial modifier of action" (*kriyāviśeṣaṇāt*).

The word *prabhūta* and others, because they denote adverbs (*kriyāviśeṣaṇa*), express the specific quality of the action; thus, by applying a metaphorical designation (*abhidheyopacāra*) to the denoted object, they are said to be words for a specific quality of the action. The word *tena* (by that) is connected with each [item] individually.

Regarding the rule "the third case is used everywhere for the instrument," in forms such as *dīvyati* ("he plays"), the verbal suffix (*lakāra*) denotes the agent; since the agent is already expressed by that very suffix, the use of the third case for the agent is not appropriate.

Therefore, the third case (instrumental) occurs only in the sense of the instrument (*karaṇa*). Now, why does the third case not occur in the sense of the cause (*hetu*)? Because it is not so expressed (*anabhidhānāt*).

Although the instrumental could theoretically occur for the agent (*kartṛ*) as well—since the past passive participle (*niṣṭhā*) is prescribed here in the sense of the object (*karman*) in the word *jitam*—nevertheless, due to its association with words such as *dīvyati*, the instrumental is understood to occur only in the sense of the instrument.

In the expression *devadattena jitam* ("victory was won by Devadatta"), the third case ending (*tṛtīyā*) occurs in the sense of the agent (*kartṛ*); therefore, this is simply a sentence (*vākya*), not a suffix (*pratyaya*). In this sūtra, by using words such as *dīvyati* ("he plays") which end in the singular number and denote the present tense, there is an indication of a single number for the meaning of the suffix and of the present time. Consequently, one might object that a suffix would apply only when the meaning of the suffix is singular, and not in the dual or plural; likewise, it would apply only in the present tense, and not in the past or future. To one who would raise such an objection, he says: "There is no intention to express (*avivakṣā*) either number or time regarding the meaning of the suffix."
But there is no intention to express those two [number and time], because they are invariably concomitant.
For it must necessarily be expressed by some number and at some time;
yet those two are not the primary factors, nor is there an intention to express them.

If, then, number and time are not intended to be expressed, does it follow that the means [the instrumental case] is also not intended to be expressed, since they belong to the same context? This is not a fault; for when the utterance of a second word would be meaningless without the intention to express something, that thing must necessarily be intended to be expressed.

If, in cases such as *dīvyati* ("he plays"), one intends to express only the literal meaning [of the root], then the utterance of the second word [the suffix] would result in being purposeless; therefore, it is not logical to claim that even the means (*sādhana*) is not intended to be expressed. Here, in examples such as *dīvyati*, according to the principle that "a verb (*ākhyāta*) has action as its primary meaning," it is the action itself that is primarily denoted by the word, while the agent is subordinate. However, in the case of a secondary derivative (*taddhita*), such as *ākṣikaḥ* ("a gambler"), it is the agent alone that is expressed here as the primary element, while the action is subordinate. And this [position of yours] is incorrect.

Should someone object that just as this [agent] is expressed by means of a verbal suffix (*tiṅanta*) through the suffixes produced after verbs, so too should it be possible to express it when joined with a suffix ending in a *taddhita* [secondary suffix], [the author] says: "And even though the action is primary," and so forth.
This is the very nature of linguistic expression: that even while conforming to the primacy of the action, the *taddhita* becomes primarily focused on the agent.
Therefore, the state of being the agent must be taken into account here.

For neither *svabhāva* nor *svābhāva* deserves to be questioned. The division of the rule (*yogavibhāga*) is for the sake of what follows—namely, this exception (*apavāda*) [Pāṇini 4.4.4] should apply only to *saṃskṛta*, so that it does not apply in cases such as *dīvyati*; for this purpose, there is a division of the rule. "There is a difference in accent":
for if the suffix *ṭhak* were present, the affix *taddhita* would have its final syllable accented acute by the rule *kitaḥ ra* (Pāṇini 6.1.159).

When the suffix *ṭhañ* is present, the initial vowel becomes udātta by virtue of the *ñit-sarvanighāta* rule. In this section, the letter *ṣ* is seen in some cases as part of a *saṃhitā* (sandhi) and in others as an *anubandha* (indicatory letter) of the suffix itself; therefore, within the governing rule (*adhikāra*) for *ṭhak*, it is not known which is *saṃhitika* and which is the suffix’s *anubandha*.
Consequently, a systematic enumeration has been made to eliminate doubt, and this he does with the verse beginning "from *ākarṣa*, *parpa*, etc. (*ākarṣātparpādibhyaḥ*).

> [[4.4.9]], `pargādibhyaṣṭhan` [[4.4.10]], `bhastrādibhyaṣṭhan` [[4.4.16]], `kasusīdadaśaikadaśāt ṣṭhanṣṭhacau` [[4.4.31]], > [[4.4.74]], and > [[4.4.53]]; these six [suffixes] end in *vit*. Now, one might object: since suffixes ending in *vit* exist even after other bases, such as those beginning with > [[4.1.40]], why is it said that "these six" [end in *vit*]? To this he replies: "`In the governing context (*adhikāra*) of *ṭhak*," and so forth.

Because *ṭhak* is the subject under discussion, he shows that only those [suffixes] marked with the *ṣ* indicatory letter (*ṣit*) within its governing scope are included. But even so, there would still be seven [suffixes], since two *ṣit* suffixes are prescribed by the rule *kusīdādibhyaḥ ṣṭhan* (Pāṇini 4.4.31)? To this he says: "The number six, however, is relative to the prescriptive rules.
This is because there are seven *ṣit* suffixes;
by this very [principle], the *ṣit* suffixes are employed in these grammatical operations (*yoga*).

The meaning is that these six applications have the suffix *ṣit* as their purpose. "The letter *l* is for the sake of the accent" means that the vowel preceding the suffix marked with *l* (lit) shall be acute (*udātta*). "The letter *ṣ* is for the sake of [the feminine suffix] *ṅīṣ*" means...
So that the suffix *ṅīṣ* may apply according to [Pāṇini 4.1.41], we have the form *ākarṣikī*. It is said:
"A touchstone for the purpose of testing gold is called *nikaṣopala*."

It is drawn [to itself] because it is gold. Regarding *parpa* and other words, he recites "pādaḥ pacca" [Pāṇini 5.2.129]; its meaning is this: from the word *pāda*, the suffix *ṣṭhan* occurs, and by connection with that, the substitution *pad* takes place for *pāda*. Thus, *padikaḥ* and *padikī*. If this is so, why is the supplementary rule (*vārttika*) "the substitution of *pad* for *pād* in the sense of 'going' when the suffix *ika* follows" (Vārttika 740) stated? This is not a fault, because [the rule] "in *ika*" (Pāṇini 6.3.53) is not of ancient origin (*apaurāṇika*). Regarding "ṣvāgaṇikaḥ": a group of dogs is an *āgaṇa*.

But surely, since the word *āñ* is listed among the *dvārādi* group, by the rule *dvārādīnāṃ ca* [Pāṇini 7.3.4], which prohibits *vṛddhi*, there ought to be an augment instead; for in that case, the rule of "taking the beginning of the word" (*tadādividhi*) is desired. So how is it that the form *āāgaṇika* arises? To this he says: "*āāder iñi ṭaḥ*, etc.

Since the operation pertaining to the *dvārādi* group is prohibited, only the initial *vṛddhi* takes place. [The mention of] "buying and selling" (*krayavikraya*) is for the sake of including both the compound and its separated members.

In this treatise, the words *kraya* and *vikraya* are uttered by way of ellipsis (*tantra*). It should be understood that in one case they are taken in their collective sense, while in the other they are taken in their distributive sense. In the list beginning with *bhastrā*, the form *śīrṣebhāra* is recited. Therein, the substitution of *śīrṣan* for *śiras* occurs precisely because of this irregular derivation (*nipātana*); the compound is formed by the rule *saptamī* [Pāṇini 2.1.40], through a split in the application (*yogavibhāga*), and in the alternative view, there is no elision (*aluk*) of the locative case ending by [Pāṇini 6.3.14]. Regarding the term *paryāhāre*: it is called *paryāhāra* because it is carried around (*paritaḥ sa hyiyate*); it refers to a circular arrangement and the like. As for the statement "the word *tri* is understood here as that which ends in the suffix *ktri*": [this refers to the fact that the suffix *ktri* is applied after verbal roots ending in *ḍu*.]
Why is the word for number (*saṃkhyāśabda*) not included? Because it is not expressed. For when one says "three times" (*tris*), there is no comprehension of the intended meaning [of the suffix -ma].
[The example is] *uptrimam*.

Thus there is *samprasāraṇa*. Regarding the statement, "The inclusion of the word *nitya* (always) is for the purpose of precluding independence (*svātantrya*)," independence refers to the usage of the suffix *tri* alone, without the suffix *map*. The inclusion of *nitya* is intended to preclude that independence. Once the inclusion of *nitya* has served to preclude independence, the author demonstrates the resulting meaning by means of the phrase "{tryantaḥ - mu|pāṭhaḥ} tryantam" and so forth.
With the words "in another object" (*viṣayāntare*) and so forth, he explains that which is excluded by the particle *eva*.
An "other object" (*viṣayāntara*) is that object other than the referent of the suffix *mat*, in which no cognition occurs.
It should be understood that the mention of "eternal" (*nitya*) is for the purpose of excluding that [non-eternal case]. Regarding the term "having borrowed" (*apamitya*):

Thus, by [the rule] *ktvā* (Pāṇini 7.1.37), when its substitution by *lyap* is made, the form *apamitya* arises. And by [the rule] *tasya ca* (Pāṇini 1.1.40), it receives the designation of an indeclinable (*avyaya*). Therefore, even though the governing context requires a case-inflected word in the third case, the suffix is prescribed from this very word which lacks an inflection. Now, one might object: "By [the rule] *yena saṃsṛṣṭe* (Pāṇini 4.4.3) alone, the suffix will occur when there is contact; for that with which something is in contact becomes 'prepared' (*saṃskṛta*) by it. This is not so; for *saṃskāra* (preparation/refinement) is the imparting of excellence to what already exists, whereas *saṃsarga* (contact/commixture) is a state of oneness.

And in that case, there should not be [the suffix] *utkarṣa*; rather, upon contact with one's own pure substance, there is only *svaprakarṣa* (one's own excellence), not *utkarṣa*. The suffix is desired only when there is mere contact (*saṃsarga*); therefore, it must simply be said "it is mixed" (*saṃsṛṣṭa*). Let this alone be done; what is the use of this [rule] beginning with *kiṃ* [Pāṇini 4.4.3]? Even in the absence of contact, where something is refined (*saṃskṛta*), the suffix is desired—as in *vaidyika* ("learned"). Contact with knowledge (*vidyā*) is not possible; contact occurs only between two substances, such as between a staff and a person.

Because that property belongs to something corporeal, whereas knowledge (*vidyā*) is not corporeal. For the sake of prescribing [the suffix] after *kulattha*, *kola*, and *dhānya* (Pāṇini 4.4.4), the mention of "prepared" (*saṃskṛta*) must be made.

For the suffix is not desired merely after what is mixed, but rather after that which has acquired a quality produced by it. [Objection: But surely for those things mixed with flour (*cūrṇa*), the flour exists; thus, since it is established by the possessive suffix *-in* itself, this [mention of "prepared"] is useless? [Response: This is not so. It would be established by the possessive suffix when there is a desire to express existence (*astivivakṣā*), but it is not established when there is a desire to express being mixed (*saṃsṛṣṭavivakṣā*); for in that case, the suffix *-ṭhak* would apply.
If the suffix *ṭhak* has the purpose of denoting "for the sake of," how could this [word] be meaningless? Regarding the phrase "denoting a substance" (*dravyavācī*), and so forth:
this word *lavaṇa* is indeed a quality-word (*guṇavacana*) that refers to a specific taste, because taste is a quality (*guṇa*).
It is also a substance-word (*dravyavacana*), as in the expression "five salts."

In this regard, that which expresses a quality (*guṇavacana*) does not necessitate the elision (*luk*). For although a substance (*dravya*) is not actually conjoined with its qualities, nevertheless, words expressing qualities refer to the substance through the relation of identity (*abheda*), as in "this is that," such as: "the cloth is white" (*śuklaḥ paṭaḥ*), "the oil is pungent" (*kṣāraṃ tailam*), or "the curd is sour" (*amlaṃ dadhi*); likewise, the word "salt" (*lavaṇa*) will also function in the same way. Therefore, what is the use of elision? This must necessarily be understood in this manner; otherwise, elision would have to be prescribed even for words such as "sweet" (*madhura*) and so forth.
Substantive words (*dravyaśabda*), however, do not apply elsewhere because they establish non-difference through the identification "this is that.

Therefore, the word *lavaṇa*, being expressive of a substance, triggers elision (*luk*). Regarding the phrase "with seasonings" (*vyañjanaiḥ*), the use of the plural number is intended to exclude a rule that applies to the specific form [of the word].

By the word "tena" (by that), because it is the governing topic (*adhikāra*), when the third case (*tṛtīyā*)—the case expressing capacity—is present, there is a restatement of the third case for the sake of easy comprehension. While the rule *upasikta* [Pāṇini 2.1.39] is in effect, this is its purpose: so that it may apply to cases such as "rice mixed with broth," but not here: "a pot mixed with soup."
Regarding the expression "rice-gruel sprinkled with water":
water does not constitute a *vyañjana* (condiment/sauce), because the word *vyañjana* is conventionally restricted to things such as soup (*sūpa*) and the like.

[Objection: Is it not the case that whatever is sprinkled with *vyañjanas* becomes refined (*saṃskṛta*) by them; thus, in that context, "refined" would indeed be established? [Reply: It is not so established. For refinement (*saṃskāra*) consists in the addition of excellence to something already existing, and such [addition] is not possible in every instance where there is merely being sprinkled.

For instance, when rice and other foods, which have lost their natural flavors, are sprinkled with substances possessing distinct flavors, there is only a subtraction [of the original taste], not an addition.
And this is desired even at the very moment of being sprinkled.
Therefore, its separate commencement occurs prior to that. Thus it is said: "it proceeds."
The meaning is "he exerts himself.
The phrase "that is a qualifier of the process" (*tatprakriyāviśeṣaṇam*) and so forth indicates that the performance of the action expressed by the verbal root is what must be accomplished.
The word "vartate" (it exists) signifies the present; its meaning is "to act. For that [act], being connected as something to be performed, becomes the object (*karman*).
And because it is in grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with that [object], its qualifier is also joined with the status of being something to be performed.
That too is necessarily an object (*karma*).
It has been stated that even for an intransitive root (*akarmaka-dhātu*), the adverbial modifier itself functions as the object.

Although the word *tat* (that) already implies the second case (*dvitīyā*) as its governing inflection, the bases are here specified with the second case ending for the sake of clarity; otherwise, since the fifth case (*pañcamī*) is the logical rule in the formulation of suffixes (*pratyaya-vidhi*), they would have been specified in their stem form alone. [The example is] "prātīpikaḥ" (hostile).
The term *pratīpa* is a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "that in which water has gone back" (*pratigatā āpo 'smin*).

By the rule *ṛkpūrabdhūḥpathāmānakṣe* [Pāṇini 5.4.74], the suffix *a* is added as a compound-final element (*samāsānta*). Furthermore, by the rule *evañca* [Pāṇini 6.3.97], the substitution of *i* for the final vowel occurs.
But in other cases, by [Pāṇini 6.3.98], there is *utva* (the substitution of *u*) for the vowel other than that of the place of articulation; from that, the suffix *ṭhak* is applied. Thus:
*prātilomikaḥ*, *ānulomikaḥ*—as stated in the *Kāśikā* and the *Padamañjarī*. [The forms] *prātilomikam*, *ānulomikam* [are also derived]. [The analysis is:
"one whose body hairs (*loman*) go against [the grain]" and "one whose body hairs follow [the grain]," which are *bahuvrīhi* compounds.

The compound suffix *ac* is applied by the rule *ac praty-anu* [Pāṇini 5.4.75]. The word *prati* takes the ablative case by the rule *pañcamy-ayāṅ-paribhiḥ* [Pāṇini 2.3.10], and the compound is formed as an *avyayībhāva* by the rule *avyayaṃ vibhakti-* [Pāṇini 2.1.6]. From this, the suffix *ṭhak* is added. One who serves while facing away from one's own front—that is, excluding the direction toward oneself—is called *pārimukhika*.
The prefix *pari-* is used in the sense of "on all sides" (*sarvatobhāve*); thus, by the rule *tasya* (Pāṇini 2.2.18), it forms a *prādi*-compound.

One who serves wherever the master’s face is directed is called *pārimukhika*. Regarding the term "twofold" (*dviguṇam*), he shows that the word is applied metaphorically (*tācchabdyam*) because of its being for that purpose (*tādārthyāt*).

What is the intention of one who applies the word "twofold" (*dviguṇa*) to a thing that is not twofold and then forms a derivative suffix from it? He thinks as follows: the term "lender on double" (*dvaiguṇika*) refers to a creditor (*uttamarṇa*), yet he does not actually give away a twofold amount; what then? Having let [the principal] accumulate, he takes back a twofold amount. For otherwise, if the opposite were the case, it would indeed be a matter for praise, and not for censure. When the word "twofold" (*dviguṇa*) is used in the sense of "having that purpose" (*tādathrya*) with respect to a single object, then for one who gives that single object which has a twofold purpose, it results in being exactly twofold; thus, it is a matter for censure.

Furthermore, in this context, "censure" (garhā) is to be understood as the fact that what is given by the scripture when it is prohibited [elsewhere] becomes a cause of sin (pratyavāya). By the phrase "another base form" (prakṛtyantara), he rejects the proposed addition (upasaṃkhyāna).
Even there, because it serves that purpose, that which is given for the sake of vṛddhi is expressed by the word *vṛdhudhi*.

But surely, if that [derivation] were rejected, then when a suffix is added to the word *vṛddhi*, the form *vārdhika* would also result? This is not a fault; for by the analogy of *avyavi*, the word *vṛddhi* forms a sentence [only], whereas with the word *vṛddhuṣi*, there is both a sentence and a compound (*vṛtti*). Even there, regarding the matter of usury, having applied the word *daśaikādaśa* to ten things that have the sense of "ten plus one," the suffix is then added from that. In all cases, the intended meaning should be understood as previously explained.

"Ten and eleven" (*daśa ca ekādaśa ca*) is a coordinate compound (*samānādhikaraṇa-samāsa*). Now, one might object that grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) is not possible between two things that have different referents. However, there is no fault here, because the word "ten-and-eleven" (*daśaikādaśa*) also applies by metaphorical extension (*upacāra*) to the ten [objects] themselves within the context of the eleven objects. One who gives ten [objects] with the intention that they shall be exactly eleven is called "one who gives ten-and-eleven."
