Then, because of its superiority, [the suffix] *yat* is applied after words such as *śarīrāvayava* (body-part), as in "oil for the body" (*nābhyaṃ tailam*). Now, one might ask: when *yat* is applied according to the definition of a body-part, why does the state of *nabha* not occur? To this he says: "In the case of *go* and so forth, there is *yat*" and so on. For that [suffix] is prescribed together with the *yat* applied to *go* and other such words.

Therefore, according to the principle that "when those [elements] taught in conjunction with one another are absent in one, they are both absent" (Vārttika on Pāṇini 1.1.56), the negative particle *naÑ* does not apply.

In the case of *śunaḥ* and so forth, once the semivowel substitution (*samprasāraṇa*) has been applied to the element *an*, the form ends in *an*; consequently, by rule [Pāṇini 6.4.144], the suffix *ṭi* must necessarily be elided.

If that is so, does it not follow that [the substitution] does not occur due to the power (*sāmarthya*) of the *samprasāraṇa*? This is not the case; for according to the principle: "That rule is sublated for which the instruction is rendered purposeless, but that which is merely the cause of a rule is not sublated" (Vyāḍipāda 56), the fault remains as it was.

If it is argued that this is due to the power of the prescription of the long vowel (*dīrghavidhāna*), even so, it would still occur in one alternative (*pakṣe*). Therefore, it is explained otherwise.
Here, two *ca*s (and-s) are recited: "the *samprasāraṇa* and *ca*, and optionally (*vā*) lengthening (*dīrghatva*) and *ca*.

The second *ca* is out of its regular order and should be understood as being near the word *samprasāraṇa*. Since there is nothing else to be conjoined, it serves the purpose of conjunction (*samuccaya*), and thus it conjoins that very same [lengthening].
In that case, the *samprasāraṇa* is performed by one [element], while by the second there is the maintenance of that very same form.
Regarding the phrase "in connection with that" (*tatsanniyogena*), etc.: by the word "that" (*tat*), the state of length (*dīrghatva*) is referred back.
Because of that lengthening, the final udātta accent occurs; otherwise, by [Pāṇini 6.1.213], there would be the initial udātta accent. Regarding the rule "ūdhaso’naṅ ca":
the substitute *anaṅ* is applied to the word *ūdhas*, and by the force of the particle *ca*, [the substitution of *ya* for the final vowel] also occurs.

*Ūdhanyaḥ*: as before, there is the preservation of the original form (*prakṛtibhāva*). Now, one might object: "Is not *kambalya* already established by the very rule of irregular derivation (nipātana) in [Pāṇini 5.1.30], ‘*aparimāṇa-vistācita-kambalyebhyaḥ*’? For *kambalya* is indeed a specific measure; otherwise, the inclusion of the word *kambalya* there would be purposeless, since the word *kambalya* is the name for that specific measure. Furthermore, this suffix, being prescribed in the sense of a technical term (*saṃjñā*), occurs only in that context and nowhere else."

Is it not the case that the word *kambalya* here is a proper name (*saṃjñā*), and therefore there is no purpose for this [rule]? This is not so; for by means of a formal derivation (*nipātana*), it is understood merely that the word *kambalya* is correct when denoting a measure (*parimāṇa*), but it is not understood that this word ends in the suffix *-ya*. Consequently, the circumflex accent (*svaritatva*) on the final syllable would not occur. Therefore, this must be formulated for the sake of correctly understanding the circumflex accent.

Since the particle *ca* serves the purpose of drawing in (*anukarṣaṇa*) what was heard immediately preceding, one might object: "But will this not happen simply because [the word] has the *svarita* accent? In that case, the suffix *cha* would also [be drawn in]. One might further object: "But since it has been stated that *cha* occurs after the base alone when *cha* is in proximity, this [use of *ca*] must be for the sake of a restrictive rule (*niyama*); and that is undesirable. Since its scope is restricted, its connection [to the previous rule] would have the force of an injunction (*vidhi*); and between an injunction and a restriction, the injunction is superior. This is not so; even when *cha* is connected, its force as an injunction is possible.

How is it said, "with respect to *saṃjñā*"? For *saṃjñā* occurs even when the meaning of its constituent parts (*avayavārtha*) is not applicable; since those [words] whose constituent meanings are not applicable do not belong to the *aprākkrītīya* class, and thus there is an absence of suffixes such as *-hit*, is this [the word *saṃjñā*] for the sake of the suffix *-cha*? It might be so; therefore, should the letter *ca* be made to draw along (*anukarṣaṇa*) the suffix *-yat*? No, it need not be made; for the commencement and cessation of governing rules (*adhikāra*) occur according to what is desired, and thus the continuation will occur from that very [source], but not from *-cha*.
If that is the case, then the letter *ca* is for the purpose of drawing along [the rule] "from *u*, *go*, and so forth" (*ugavādibhyaḥ*).

For what purpose is this [rule]? Since the suffixes *añ* and others would apply by virtue of their higher position [in the order of rules] over [the suffixes] *sanaṅgu* and so on, it is for the purpose of subverting those.

Now, why does one not simply read [the rule] as "also after *kambala*, when it is a name" (*kambalācca saṃjñāyām*) within the *gava*-class itself? In that case, there would be no difference regarding the relative weight or brevity [of the formulation]; thus, this [separate rule] is somewhat superfluous. The word *havis* is recited in the *gava*-class; therefore, the suffix *yat* must necessarily follow it. Here, however, there is a reference to specific types of oblations (*havis*), and not to the word-form itself; for the technical rule concerning the word-form (*svarūpa-paribhāṣā*) applies in the *ugavādi*-sūtra.

For in that case, nothing prevents the technical rule (*paribhāṣā*) "of its own form" (*svarūpa*) from applying; therefore, it is the word-form itself that is grasped. Since the rule "of its own form" applies there, it does not apply here [in the present context]. Otherwise, if the rule "of its own form" were to apply here as well, then from a single independent word, two things would result—one eternal and one non-eternal—which is untenable in a single instance; thus, the reversal of the rule does not occur.
Alternatively, because the word *havis* is mentioned separately here, it is determined that the meaning is primary; otherwise, it would have been listed only among the *apūpa* and other such items.
Regarding the phrase "and from food-modifications" (*annavikārebhyaśca*):
"food-modifications" (*annavikāra*) refers to types of food. These produce the suffix *pratyaya* optionally (*vibhāṣā*), as in *udanyāḥ* or *udanīyāḥ*.

If this is so, since items beginning with *apūpa* (cakes) and ending with *kiṇva* (ferment) are already established here simply by virtue of being modifications of food, their inclusion in the list would be purposeless. However, when *apūpa* and the others are used metaphorically (*upacāra*) for other things due to some similarity of form, it is for that purpose that they are listed here.

Furthermore, if one intends to include cakes and the like by means of the inclusion of "food-preparations" (*annavikāra*), then it would also apply here: *yavāpūpāḥ* (barley-cakes) and *vrīhitaṇḍulāḥ* (rice-grains).
However, because they are explicitly mentioned in the *pratipadapāṭha*, the rule for *taddhita* suffixes is excluded.

But is it not the case that, because of the mention of "non-compound" (*asamāsa*) in [Pāṇini 5.1.20], there must necessarily be an application of the rule of extension (*tadantavidhi*) here? By this mention of "non-compound," the point being established is that there is an application of the rule of extension in the preceding rule. True, this is so; however, in the case of words such as *apūpa* ("cake"), it will not apply due to the force of their being listed as specific items (*pratipadapāṭha*). This very fact is the indicator (*jñāpaka*) that the dative case occurs in connection with the word *hita*.
Therefore, as for what was stated—"the dative should be prescribed in connection with *hita*"—[it is justified].

123) This [definition] is thus justified: it is called a *śarīra* (body) because it perishes (*śīryate*). If one were to argue that by this term even things such as jars would be included, he says: "The body is the aggregate of living beings.
By this, he shows that this is a conventional usage (*rūḍhi*).
In the case of [the word] "cow" and so forth, it denotes the parts of the body.
In this regard, however, there is no difference whatsoever between those bases (*prakṛti*) [ending in *an*] and these [bases ending in *in*], whether by this [rule] or by the preceding one.

Where there is a distinction—namely, "the substitution of *nābhi* and *nabha*" (Gaṇasūtra 106)—that distinction is to be understood as applying only in that specific case. For bases beginning with *khala* and ending with *vṛṣan*, there is elision [of the suffix] according to the rule *yasyeti ca* (Pāṇini 6.4.148).
Thus, [we derive] *brāhmaṇyam*.

Is it because of the prohibition [by Pāṇini 6.4.137], "not after a word ending in a conjunct consonant," that the elision of the vowel *a* [by 6.4.134] does not occur? And is it because of the rule [6.4.144], "the elision of the suffix *ṭi*," also does not occur due to the preservation of the original form (*prakṛtibhāva*) [by 6.4.168]? In this context, the word *vṛṣan* is understood as ending in the vowel *a*, but the word *brāhmaṇa* is not understood as ending in the vowel *a*.

Indeed, a doubt regarding the word *vṛṣan* is appropriate: once the *n* has been elided, is this [word] one ending in *a*, or rather one ending in *n*? This is because there arises the contingency of the suffix *yac* being excluded from the word *brāhmaṇ*. The intention is that the suffix *yac* is also excluded from the word *brāhmaṇ*. For this very reason, he says: "The suffix *ch* as well," and so forth. The particle *api* is used in relation to the suffix *yac*: not only does the suffix *yac* not occur, but the suffix *ch* does not occur either.
The absence of the suffix *cha* after the word *brāhmaṇa* should be applied here.

[Objection: But since these two [suffixes] are not mentioned here, why does the suffix *yat* not occur—given that [the rule] "after [words ending in] *a*, the suffix *yat* [is used]" (Pāṇini 5.1.5) applies—and why does the suffix *cha* not occur? [Response: He says: "Because of non-expression" (*anabhidhānāt*).

For when one says *vārṣīyam* or *brāhmaṇīyam*, the intended meaning is not understood; because the expressive power of words is restricted toward the communication of meaning, in some cases the meaning is expressed by means of a suffix, while in other cases it is expressed by means of a sentence.
Therefore, only the sentence remains: "beneficial for the bull" (*vṛṣṇe hitam*), "beneficial for the Brahmins" (*brāhmaṇebhyo hitam*).

This is because the meaning understood from the sentence is not denoted by the secondary derivative suffix (*taddhita*); such is the sense. Here, the word *aja* is employed in the masculine gender, because the word ending in *avi* (which ends in a consonant) would otherwise have been placed first [by the rule governing the order of members in a compound].
Had there been a reference to a word ending in the feminine suffix *āP*, the word *hṛdī* would have been placed first.

If the masculine form were not included in the selection, the rule *dvandve ghi* [Pāṇini 2.2.32] would be superseded, and consequently, the rule *ajādyadantam* [Pāṇini 2.2.33] would require that the feminine word *ajā* be placed first in the compound. Therefore, the masculine form is indeed intended.

Accordingly, following the principle that "when a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) is mentioned, the inclusion of its gender-distinct forms also occurs" (Vyāḍīya-paribhāṣā 29), the suffix is applied even from the feminine form: *ajābhyaḥ hitam* results in *ajathyam*.
By the rule *puṃvadbhāvaḥ* (6.3.35), there is the substitution of the masculine form.

For in that [section], the suffixes beginning with *tasil* are enumerated (*parisaṃkhyāyante*). Among them, since *ātman* is also enumerated, why is the elision of *n* (*nalopa*) not applied in the form *ātman*? Since this is a dual compound (*dvandva*), the elision of *n* would apply by the rule *na lopaḥ prātipadikāntasya* (8.2.7). To this he replies: "In *ātman*, etc. The elision of *n* is not performed for the purpose of indicating that *ātman* alone is its original form (*prākṛti*).
But what is the distinction [established] when this is the case? He says: "By that," and so forth. The meaning has already been explained.

If this is so, does it not follow that the word *vijana* (solitude) would be connected with the subsequent member of the compound? He thinks as follows: because the absence of the elision of the *n* in *ātman* shows that the syntactical completion applies to each [word] individually, and thus a deviation [of connection] has been demonstrated; therefore, due to proximity (*pratyāsatti*), it is connected only with the word *bhoga* (enjoyment), and not with the word *vijana*. Thus, there is no fault.
"It is desired [only] after a *karmadhāraya* compound," because of the traditional instruction of the lineage of teachers (*vāryapāramparyopadeśāt*).
This should be understood as established by the knowledge that this is a restricted option (*vyavasthitavibhāṣā*), following from the non-occurrence of the mention of the *vibhāva*.
One might expect that *viāsyajanaḥ* would become *viājanaḥ*, since by a compound such as *viāto jano 'syeti viājanaḥ* ("one whose people are wise"), it ought to be so;

yet, just as [the *cha* suffix] does not occur, the *cha* suffix likewise does not occur. Anticipating this objection, he says: "But the *bahuvrīhi*," and so forth. "Supplementary statement" (*upasaṃkhyānam*) means the act of providing an explanation.

In this regard, the following is the explanation: here, although one could have simply said "from *bhoga* preceded by a word denoting wealth" (*bhogāt samāsād iti*), the inclusion of the term "subsequent member" (*uttarapada*) is for the purpose of providing an additional rule.

And it should not be suspected that, this being the case, the suffix *kha* would apply after *bahubhoga*—meaning "one whose wealth is abundant"—in the sense of "slightly incomplete," as in *bahupūrvād īṣadasamāptau*; for the *pratyaya* *bahu* does not occur at the end of a compound.
Therefore, in this instance, there must necessarily be the suffix *cha*, resulting in *bahubhogīya*.
Therefore, it will also occur after *pañcajana*;
this is a technical term (*saṃjñāśabda*), and thus [the rule] *[[Pāṇini 2.1.50]]* applies as a compound. Likewise, it should be understood that it occurs after *sarvajana* as well.
Regarding the phrase "only from a *tatpuruṣa* compound":

even though no specific [compound] is mentioned, because of the instruction "from *mahājana*," this word *bhoga* must be derived from a *samānādhikaraṇa* (co-referential) compound. It is either a noun formed by means of the abstract action (*bhāvasādhana*)—meaning "the act of enjoying" (*bhukti* is *bhoga*)—or a noun formed by means of the object (*karmasādhana*)—meaning "that which is enjoyed" (*bhujyate* is *bhoga*). He states "the word *bhoga*" and so forth to show that this is an irregularly formed word denoting the body, and that it is this [body] which is being taken here.

The meaning is that the word *bhoga* denotes the body itself. Wherever this [word] occurs, it expresses a direct relationship and thereby acquires the reflexive suffix (*kha*). It occurs both in relation to action and to substance.

For instance: although there is a connection with both the act of eating and the substance [the food], nevertheless, because the connection with the body is primary, the cognition arises from that [the body].

If someone were to object, "Just as in the case of *rājācārya* (king-teacher), only the compound form occurs, so it must be here as well," he says in response: "The suffix *aṇ* [is applied] after *ācārya*. This is due to its inclusion in the *kṣubhna*-class of words.

"Or rather, from the two [roots] alone, there is only the formation of a sentence"—thus, the *cha*-suffix does not occur precisely because it is not so designated. Regarding the statement "or the mention of *ṇya* for all," he states an alternative:
that it is either due to the designation [of the suffix] or through the metaphorical application of the name of the designatum (*abhidheya*) to the designation (*abhidhāna*).

Here too, it should be understood that this is due to the continued application of the term *vibhāṣā* (optionality). Nor should there be any apprehension of an option between the two words *sarva* and *puruṣa*, because the optionality is restricted (*vyavasthita-vibhāṣā*).
[The rule is: "After *puruṣa*, [the suffix] *vadha* [is applied]."

In that regard, regarding the sense of "killing" (*vadha*), this is an exception (*apavāda*) to the suffix *aṇ* [Pāṇini 4.3.120]; regarding the sense of "modification" (*vikāra*), it is an exception to the suffix *añ* [Pāṇini 4.3.154]; and regarding the sense of "collection" (*samūha*), it is also an exception to the suffix *aṇ* [Pāṇini 4.2.37].

Regarding the sense of "a book composed by him" (*tena kṛte granthe*), it is specifically the suffix *aṇ* [Pāṇini 4.3.116]. In both cases, the inclusion of the marker *ñ* is for the sake of accentuation (*svarārtha*) and, in the case of *Caraka*, for the sake of vowel lengthening (*vṛddhi*).

The rule *māṇave tu* (Pāṇini 6.3.39) is for the purpose of prohibiting the *puṃvadbhāva* (masculine-like treatment). Thus, one whose wife (*bhāryā*) is a *māṇavī* is called *māṇavīnābhārya*. The compound *tadartham* ("for that purpose") is formed by the rule *caturthī tadarthā* (Pāṇini 2.1.36), etc.

This very statement is the indicator (*jñāpaka*) that in a compound where the final member is a word denoting "purpose" (*arthottarapada*), the gender belongs to the meaning of the whole compound, and not to the gender of the final member.
By this, that which was stated— "it should be stated that there is a compulsory compound with 'artha' and that it takes all genders" (Vārttika 78)— is established.
"Prakṛti is the material cause" means that a cause which belongs to the same class and functions within an undifferentiated continuum is called a material cause.

It is called *upādāna* (appropriation) because it is appropriated (*upādīyate*); [the suffix] *lyuṭ* is used in the sense of the object (*karman*) due to the rule of frequent usage (*bahulavacana*). [The term *upādānahetu*] is a genitive compound meaning "the cause of that [appropriation]. Regarding the phrase "of that very [cause]" and so forth:
the specific state (*avasthāviśeṣa*) that follows immediately after that very cause of appropriation is the transformation (*vikṛti*).

Regarding the phrase “expressing a modification” (*vikṛtivācinaḥ*) and so forth: one might object that, because of the rule [Pāṇini 4.1.82], since that meaning is indicated first and since the base (*prakṛti*) has that as its purpose, the suffix would logically apply only to that which expresses the base. This is not a fault; the mention of the “first” (the base) is made for the sake of restriction, so that when an operation applies both to the first and the non-first, it occurs only from the first. However, in this case, there is no possibility of application from the first at all.
"In the original form" (*prakṛtau*): because the original form has been established as the meaning of the suffix by means of the locative case. "Of the modification" (*vikṛteḥ*).

Since the fifth *vikṛti* (modification) serves as the *prakṛti* (original material), this [rule] does not apply to it; therefore, the suffix occurs only after a word denoting a *vikṛti*. By the phrase "in the sense of a *vikṛti*," he demonstrates that in the rule *tadartham*, the nominative has been substituted for the locative through a transposition of cases (*sub-vyatyaya*), and the neuter gender has been substituted for the feminine gender through a transposition of genders (*liṅga-vyatyaya*).

But surely it has been stated that grammatical irregularity (*vyatyaya*) occurs in Vedic (*chandas*), and this is not Vedic; so how can there be irregularity here? There is no fault, because "the Sūtras are like the Vedas" (*chandovatsūtrāṇi bhavanti*). [The phrase] "by the inclusion of its meaning," etc., refers here to the exclusion of other bases (*prakṛti*): for example, *yavānāṃ dhānāḥ* ("parched grains of barley") and *dhānānāṃ saktavaḥ* ("flour of parched grains").

In some cases, there is a connection between the modification (*vikāra*) and its material cause (*prakṛti*), as in "barley is the material cause of the grains" or "grains are the material cause of the flour. In other cases, the material cause has no other purpose [than that which the modification serves], as in "embers are the material cause of the wood.
To demonstrate what is intended by the phrase "for the sake of explaining that the material cause has no other purpose," he says: "And for the sake of the meaning of the suffix," and so forth.

In this context, the suffix is prescribed with reference to a modified form (*vikṛti*) within the archetypal form (*prakṛti*). For that [archetype], by virtue of being for the sake of that [modified form], it is possible to indicate the dative case alone to express that purpose (*tādarthya*).
Therefore, because the meaning of the suffix is for the sake of that [modified form], the dative case is obtained as the governing case (*samartha-vibhakti*) by virtue of its semantic competency.

Regarding the phrase "But some," etc.: for them, the fourth case (dative) is obtained from the statement itself as the governing case (samartha-vibhakti). As for the expression "for that purpose" (*tadartham*):

why is the genitive cited as a counter-example? The genitive expresses the sense of being for the sake of something (*tādarthyam*), as in "this belongs to the teacher" (*guroridaṃ*) or "for the teacher's sake" (*gurvartham*).
That being the case, even the sixth [case-ending] becomes a capable (samartha) case-inflection.
As for the counter-example "aṅgārāṇāṃ kāṣṭhāni" (wood of coals), it serves to exclude other bases; by that [exclusion], barley and so forth are rendered capable [of the relation]. For example:
"kāṣṭhāni aṅgārebhyaḥ" (wood from coals) and "iṣṭakāḥ prākārebhyaḥ" (bricks from walls).
Without this mention of "for that purpose" (tadarthagrahaṇa), it would not be known for what purpose [the suffix] is intended to be expressed.
Therefore, the intention is that the base (prakṛti) is intended to be expressed as having no other purpose.
The sense is that the mention of "for that purpose" was made in order to demonstrate this specific purpose.

And thus, since it is the very *prakṛti* itself that is distinguished by the exclusion of other *prakṛtis* when it is connected [to the suffix], the case ending of separation (*vyatireka-vibhakti*) occurs only for *yava* and so forth.

As for those who maintain that the fourth case (*caturthī*) is carried over [from the previous rule], for them the mention of *tadartha* is understood as a qualifier of the fourth case—meaning "the fourth case [is used] in the sense of being for that purpose" (*tādarthye caturthī*).
In that regard, "barley-gruel serves for urine" (*mūtrāya kalpate yavāgūḥ*) is the counter-example.

The recurrence of the word "of them" (teṣām) for a fourth time is purposeless, because its meaning is already conveyed by the inclusion of the word "for that purpose" (tad-artha). Thus, the genitive case which has the same meaning as "for that purpose" is further specified [by the word] "any" (yā kācit) in the suffix -itac.
The meaning is that [the well] is not even the material cause (*upādānakāraṇa*).

This might be argued: "A well is certainly not the material cause of water; therefore, the term 'modification' (*vikṛti*) need not be included in order to exclude that [well]. To this he says: "And it is," and so forth.
The word "and" (*ca*) is used for emphasis.
But surely water is produced from its own causes which are distinct [from the well]; how then can the well be its *prakṛti* (material cause)? To this he says: "Because it is produced therein.

For just as the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices constitute the *prakṛti*—serving as the basis for the origination of ritual properties such as the *prayāja* offerings—so too, because the well serves as the basis for the origination of water, it is the *prakṛti*. If this is so, then is water also its *vikṛti* (modification)? To this he says: "But surely," and so forth.
He states the proof for this very point: "Because of absolute difference.
For a modification (*vikāra*) is indeed a subsequent state of the primal matter (*prakṛti*), and thus it is not absolutely different from it, just as embers are [not absolutely different] from wood.
For those [embers], by virtue of existing within a continuous series that is non-different from the earthen substance, do not differ at all from the pieces of wood.
Water, however, because it possesses a distinct nature and exists within a distinct continuum, is absolutely different from the well;
therefore, there is no subsequent state [of the water] that is identical to the prior one, and thus no modification occurs. "But the sheath is not its material cause (prakṛti)."
Because it is not the cause of that [effect], and because it is the substratum of non-origination.
But surely, "prakṛti" (material cause) and "vikṛti" (modification) are relative terms.

And a relative term necessarily produces a cognition with respect to its counter-correlate; for instance, when it is said, "one must behave like a mother," it is not explicitly stated "in one's own mother," but it is understood as "in whichever woman is someone's mother."

This being the case, when the base (*prakṛti*) characterized as "well" (*kūpa*)—which serves as the material cause for a derivative form (*vikṛti*)—is intended to be expressed as the meaning of the suffix, then even in the absence of an explicit mention of the derivative form, the suffix is understood to apply precisely to whatever derivative form that well may take. Likewise, when a suffix is intended to be applied to the word *asi* ("sword"), which expresses a derivative form, the suffix is understood to apply to its very base (*prakṛti*) which serves as the material cause for that form, even in the absence of an explicit mention of the base. Therefore, by the mention of either one, everything desired is accomplished.

He says, "In that case, nothing undesirable follows," beginning with the words "for that purpose, for both as well. By this he intends the following: this might indeed be so if the words *prakṛti* (material cause) and *vikṛti* (modification) were necessarily relative terms; however, these two are not necessarily relative terms. For instance, this verb *kṛ* preceded by the prefix *vi-* certainly occurs in the sense of doing harm—as in "Devadatta acts perversely (*vikaroti*) toward his non-existence" [i.e., seeks to destroy him]; it occurs in the sense of a variety of movements—as in "the students move about restlessly (*vikurvate*)"; and it occurs in the sense of impropriety—as in "this independence of women is a perversion (*vikṛti*)."
The root *pra* exists in the sense of an effect—as in "the cloth is a modification (*vikāra*) of the threads";
it also exists in the sense of a cause—as in "the threads are the material cause (*prakṛti*) of the cloth"; and it exists in the sense of indifference—as in "the material cause of sentient beings.
These [latter two] refer to those things which are non-productive; it also exists in the sense of the removal of defects—as in "this person is restored to his natural state (*prakṛti*)."

There is [the case where] "it is naturally beautiful" refers to the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of things; there is [the case where] it refers to the basis for the arising of things, as when one says, "this is the archetype (*prakṛti*) of the New- and Full-Moon sacrifices. There is [the case where] "it is naturally beautiful" does not refer to the intrinsic nature of things; there is [the case where] it refers to the basis for the arising of things, as when one says, "the New- and Full-Moon sacrifices are the archetype of ritual acts. Thus, because these two terms have multiple meanings, their concomitance is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*); therefore, by grasping either one of them, the point is not established.
Nor can the intended relationship between material cause (*prakṛti*) and modification (*vikāra*) be expressed by either [of these two terms] alone.
Here, that which is a modification—consisting of the material cause and its subsequent state—is what should be understood.

But if the root *kṛ* preceded by the prefix *vi-* has multiple meanings, then should one not also strive to resolve the doubt regarding this [sūtra], namely Pāṇini 4.3.134? This is true; however, such is the style of the Teacher (Patañjali): in some places he relies on explicit statement, in some places on logic, and in some places on traditional authority. All of this is now being explained.

By that [suffix], everything is made understood. When *chadiḥ* is intended to mean a modification of leather (*carma-vikāra*), even then the suffix *ḍhañ* alone is desired—as in *chādiṣeyam carma* ("a leather shield"). [Objection: But would not the suffix *añ* apply by virtue of its higher status (being taught later) according to [Pāṇini 4.3.15]? [Reply: This is not a fault; for in the rule *carmaṇo’ñ*, the suffix *ḍhañ* from the rule for *chadiḥ* will be carried over (*anuvartiṣyate*). Just as a suffix arises after the word *chadiḥ* and the word *vali* when they are in the fourth case (*caturthī-samartha*) to express the relationship between material and modification (*prakṛti-vikāra-bhāva*), so too it ought to occur after the word *upadhi*. Anticipating this doubt, he says: "From the word *upadhi*" and so forth.
Here he states the reasoning: "It is placed upon" (*upadhīyate*), and so forth. By this, he shows [the application of] the rule *karmaṇy upasarge ghoḥ kiḥ*.
And by that, there is the denotation of a substance that has not yet attained its subsequent state.
If [the suffix] were to occur after the word *upadhi* when it denotes a modification (*vikṛti*), then it would likewise occur in other meanings;
however, it does not occur in the case of a specific base (*prakṛti*).
But there is no relationship of base and modification between the word *upadhi* and another word denoted by it, because they are not identical.

For instance: that very same part of a chariot which is denoted by the word *upadhi* (substratum) is also denoted by the word *aupadheya* (the thing based on the substratum) when it has not yet attained its subsequent state.

It might be argued: "When the word *upadhi* is derived in the sense of an action (*bhāvasādhana*), such that 'placing upon' (*upadhāna*) is the *upadhi*, then there is no difference, because it denotes an action. Furthermore, when the word *upadhi* denotes the modification (*vikāra*) of the substance of the action, and the word *aupadheya* denotes the causal substance (*prakṛtidravya*), then these two suffixes will apply to their respective specific bases. This is incorrect; for a modification of the substance of an action is not tenable, due to their absolute difference.

Therefore, from the word *upadhi*, the suffix is understood to have the sense of "located upon" (*stha-artha*) alone. Regarding the phrase "also on leather" (*carmaṇy api*) and so forth: *ñya* provides the scope for [the example] *aupānahraḥ muñjaḥ* ("munja grass used for sandals"), while *añ* provides the scope for *vādhrram* and *vāratram*. When leather is intended to be expressed as the material cause (*prakṛti*), both [suffixes] would apply; however, by the rule of priority (*pūrvavipratiṣedha*), only *ñya* occurs—namely, *aupānahraṃ carma* ("leather for sandals"). Is the word *carmaṇaḥ* in the ablative case (*pañcamī*) or the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*)? If it were the ablative, the suffix would apply only to the word "leather" itself, and not to words denoting modifications of leather. How is this obtained? From non-usage (*anabhidhāna*).
For indeed, a suffix is held to be a specific modification of the base (*prakṛti*).
And when a suffix is produced from the word *carman*, there is no expression of the intended meaning [of the base].

Therefore, this is not the ablative case (*pañcamī*), but rather the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*). Wishing to dispel the suspicion that it might be the accusative case (*dvitīyā*), he says "tat" and so forth.
The intention is that [the term] has no object (*akarmaka*).
He says "of this," and so forth, because the meaning of the whole (*avayavin*) is preceded by the meaning of its parts (*avayava*).
That which acts is an agent (*karaṇa*).

The suffix *lyuṭ* is used in the sense of the agent (*kartari*) due to the frequentative nature of the rule. The term *it-karaṇa* is a *karmadhāraya* compound meaning "that which is both an *it* [indicatory letter] and an instrument (*karaṇa*). This refers to the rule: "When there is a possibility [of usage], if the word *alam* is employed with the sense of 'sufficient,' provided that a completed action is not expressed" (Pāṇini 3.3.154).

But is it not the case that *prākārīyā iṣṭakāḥ* ("bricks for the wall") and *prāsādīyaṃ dāru* ("wood for the palace") are already established by the preceding rule? For indeed, when a wall or a palace is conceived through the plurality of certain bricks or a certain wood, those bricks and that wood become the "products" (*vikāra*) of the wall and the palace respectively, according to their sequence; and since the purpose (*tādathrya*) of the bricks and the wood exists [in relation to them], [the rule] applies. To this, he says: "*prakṛtivikāra*" and so forth. The meaning has been explained. "*Dvistadgrahaṇam*" and so forth.
Thus, this principle is demonstrated by this [sūtra]:
in examples such as *ityādi*, there is not a single meaning of the suffix;
rather, in that case, the connection with the case-ending expressing semantic competency (*samarthavibhakti*) is understood through the whole [compound].

Consequently, that [suffix] would occur only where the connection with the case-ending denoting capacity is possible through both meanings of the suffix—as in "a tree possessing branches" (*śākhāvān vṛkṣaḥ*) and so forth;
but it would not occur where the connection is with only one of the two—as in "Devadatta possesses cows" (*gomān devadattaḥ*) or "the mountain possesses trees" (*vṛkṣavān parvataḥ*) and so forth.

When this rule (*nyāya*) is demonstrated, it applies everywhere. Here, by the word *parikhā*, a moat (*kheya*) is meant. The mention [of the word *parikhā*] at the beginning is for the purpose that, when the suffix *ṭhañ* has been excluded by rules such as Pāṇini 5.1.65 and 5.1.66 which possess governing force (*adhikāra*), the suffix *ṭhañ* alone should apply in the subsequent mention of meanings such as in 5.1.72. There are two rules: one is "that which it deserves" (*tadarhati*, 5.1.62), and the second is "that which it is fit for" (*tadyogyaḥ*, 5.1.117). To which of these is it taken here as the limit? He says: "that which it deserves," and so forth.

Why is there no inclusion of the other [term]? He thinks as follows: if the inclusion of that were intended, he would have made the connection with *prāgvateḥ* (Pāṇini 5.1.18) alone, and not with *ārhāt*. But is it not the case that this [restriction] does not apply even in the sense of *vat*? Even though *ṭhak* is introduced in the sense of *vat*, nevertheless it should not occur there, because it is superseded by the *vati* suffix which is prescribed by a specific rule (*pratipadavihita*), or because of non-expression (*anabhidhāna*).
Therefore, it is logical that only the word *arha*, which is a part of the word *arhati*, should serve as the limit.
"Excluding the cow's tail and so forth.
How, then, is it known that this is a prohibition [of the suffix] after words other than "cow's tail"? Because no other meaning is possible here.
But might this not be the meaning: [the suffix applies] after a word other than "cow's tail," and after a numeral and a measure? This meaning cannot possibly be intended here.

If this were the intended meaning, then since [the desired form] would already be established by the very fact that *niṣka* and so forth are measures (*parimāṇa*), the restatement would be purposeless. But might it not be for the sake of restriction (*niyama*)—so that it should apply only when there is no compound? This is not so; for when a positive injunction (*vidhi*) exists, it is not logical for it to serve as a restriction. For if there were a restriction, one would have to abandon what was not to be expressed, which results in the subversion of the word.

Furthermore, since a statement that has already been established is being taken up again, there is the fault of restating what has already been said. However, in the case of an injunction (*vidhi*), there is neither sublation by the word nor the fault of restatement;
therefore, in the investigation of the possibility of an injunction versus a restrictive rule (*niyama*), it is proper that it be an injunction.

Since no other meaning is possible here, it is understood that this is a restrictive rule (*pratiṣedha*) [expressed by] "not after *go-puccha*. By means of this indicator (*jñāpaka*), the base form (*prakṛti*) is not intended to be expressed; for otherwise, why would he employ the suffix *ṭhañ* (in Pāṇini 5.1.44) for the purpose of excluding *ṭhak*? [Furthermore, it is stated:
"This vowel *ā* [in *ārhāt*] has the sense of inclusive limit (*abhividhi*)."

For if the letter *ā* were taken here as denoting a limit (*maryādā*), its inclusion would be purposeless, since the desired result is already established by the continued application of the rule for "prior" (*prāk*) [of the fifth case]. However, when the letter *ā* is taken as denoting inclusion (*abhividhi*), that which is intended is accomplished; to demonstrate this, he says: "The suffix *ṭhak* also occurs in the sense of 'deserving' (*arhati*).
"Number is the counting of distinctions."

"Differences" (*bhedāḥ*) are those things that are divided; they are distinct objects. That by which these are counted, enumerated, and delimited is "the enumeration of differences," namely oneness (*ekatva*) and so forth.
For when there is a distinction in number, the conceptualization of objects is performed by means of oneness and the rest.
Even the number one, when applied to many things arranged together, expresses a single, non-associated difference.
"Weight-measurement is *unmāna*.
This refers to that by which the weight of an object such as gold is lifted up; thus, it is the balance scale (*tulā*) and so forth. "Length-measurement is *pramāṇa*."
That by which the measurement of the extent of a horizontal object is determined is *pramāṇa* (measure), such as a span (*vitasti*) and so forth.
"Dimension (*parimāṇa*) is the measurement of height and circumference.
That by which an object such as grain is measured both in height and in circumference is *parimāṇa*.
Height (*āroha*) is elevation; circumference (*pariṇāha*) is breadth.

When the difference between number and measure has been asked, the specific demonstration of *unmāna* and the others is for the purpose of removing ignorance regarding that subject by way of that context.
The word "indeed" (*kila*) in the summary indicates that this is the opinion of the teachers, beginning with these examples.
"From all sides" means in terms of both height and circumference;
as it is said: "The number [of cubits] for the arms is from all sides."

"Is it because of unmāna, parimāṇa, or pramāṇa that number (*saṃkhyā*) is excluded [from being a measure]? Because it is not included therein. [The phrase] "an exception to *ṭhañ*" refers to the principle of "that which applies when another would otherwise apply" (Vyāḍipāda 49). Since words from *niṣka* up to *droṇa* are terms for *parimāṇa*, and since the word *ṣaṣṭhi* is a term for number (*saṃkhyā*), when *ṭhak* is excluded, *ṭhañ* alone would otherwise apply; therefore, this [present rule] is an exception to that very [suffix].

The phrase "of the non-prohibition of [rules] ending in that" means "of the non-prohibition of the rule regarding what ends in that. If, then, the suffix is understood to follow that which ends in such a word, one might object: "In that case, by the principle *vyapadeśivadbhāvo 'prātipadikena* (Pāṇini 1.1.65), a suffix would not be applicable to simple words [ending in such a suffix]. This is not a fault; for by the mention of "not in a compound" (*asamāse*), the cessation of the paribhāṣā *grahaṇavat* (Pāṇini 1.1.72) is indicated. And once that [paribhāṣā] has ceased to apply, the suffix occurs after that which ends in such a word.

And in that context, because "of its own form" (*svasya ca rūpasya*) is the subject under discussion [from *Kāśikā* 1.1.73], [the suffix] occurs even after a single [word]. As for the opinion that—"On account of the force of introducing something not previously mentioned, the reading of the single words would be for the sake of brevity"—this is trivial.
[The phrase] "and from here onwards," etc.

But how can the rule of "specification by the final letter" (*tadantavidhi*) be obtained even when it is desired, given that it is prohibited by the metarule: "There is no specification by the final letter when a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) is accompanied by a suffix"? This is because that metarule is not universal (*anitya*). Its non-universality is understood from the prohibition of the suffix in the *gargādi* group within the compound *vājāse*; for if the rule were universal, there would be no possibility at all for a suffix to arise from the word *vāja* in a compound, and thus it would not have been necessary to state the prohibition.
Regarding the term *dviśūrpa*:

having formed a *dvigu* compound in the sense of a secondary derivative (*taddhita*) meaning "purchased with two winnowing baskets" (*dvābhyāṃ śūrpābhyāṃ krītam*), this base is not one that ends in a *luk* elision; rather, the suffix *añ* is applied by the rule *saṃkhyāpūrvapadād añ* (Pāṇini 5.1.26), and its elision is effected by the rule *avyayārdhapūrvadvigor luk asaṃjñāyām* (Pāṇini 5.1.28).

Regarding the term *dviśaurpika*: by [Pāṇini 7.3.17], there is vṛddhi of the final vowel of the second member of the compound. As for what was stated—"it is accepted that for words preceded by a numeral, the rule applies to the whole ending in that [suffix]"—and what was also stated—"but it is not accepted for a base ending in a luk-elision"—he says "And so it has been said," etc., in order to confirm both of those points through authoritative tradition (*āptāgama*). "It is an exception (*apavāda*) to *kan*" means: [The suffix *ka* is applied] in the sense of "worth" (*mūlye*) after a word denoting a measure (*māna*), provided it does not end in *śūrpa*, *droṇa*, or *khārī*. (Pāṇini 5.1.26) In this context, the suffix *ka* is prescribed after a word denoting a measure, such as *śata*, *sahasra*, *niṣka*, *paṇa*, *pāda*, *māṣa*, *dharaṇa*, *kārṣāpaṇa*, *śatamāna*, *pala*, *rūpya*, *suvarṇa*, *hiraṇya*, *vāha*, *droṇa*, *ādhaka*, *kudava*, *pātra*, *śūrpa*, *droṇa*, and *khārī*. However, this is superseded by the suffix *ka* when the word ends in *śūrpa*, *droṇa*, or *khārī*. Thus, the suffix *ka* is applied in the sense of "worth" after the word *dvau śūrpau* (two *śūrpa-measures*). By [Pāṇini 7.3.17], the vṛddhi of the final vowel of the second member occurs. Now, regarding the statement "it is an exception to *kan*": since the suffix *ka* is prescribed here, it sets aside the suffix *kan* which would otherwise have been applicable by [Pāṇini 5.1.24]. Furthermore, although the suffix *ka* is generally prescribed after a word ending in *śūrpa*, *droṇa*, or *khārī*, it is specifically mentioned here to indicate that it applies even when these words are preceded by a numeral. This is because the rule [5.1.26] is understood to apply to all words denoting measures, including those ending in *śūrpa*, *droṇa*, and *khārī*, except for those ending in *śūrpa*, *droṇa*, and *khārī* themselves. Therefore, the suffix *ka* is indeed applied here, and it is an exception to *kan*. As for the phrase "it is an exception to *kan*": since the suffix *ka* is prescribed after a word ending in *śūrpa*, *droṇa*, or *khārī*, it sets aside the suffix *kan* which would have been applicable by [Pāṇini 5.1.24]. Moreover, although the suffix *ka* is generally prescribed after a word ending in *śūrpa*, *droṇa*, or *khārī*, it is specifically mentioned here to show that it applies even when these words are preceded by a numeral. Regarding that which is obtained by the subsequent sūtra:

"śatikam. While the rule [Pāṇini 5.1.57] is in effect, when the sense of a suffix denoting a "group" (saṅgha) is intended to be expressed [by Pāṇini 5.1.58], only the suffix *kan* occurs by virtue of the subsequent sūtra.
"The meaning of the suffix here is 'collection' (saṅgha).
That treatise named *Nidāna*, whose extent is one hundred chapters, is what is meant here by the meaning of the suffix.
And since that [treatise] consists of a collection of chapters delimited by the number one hundred, it is precisely the "collection" that constitutes the meaning of the suffix.

"Exactly one hundred in reality"—because the hundred chapters have no other purpose, they do not differ from the meaning of the base (*prakṛti*). That very same hundred of chapters is expressed by the base, and it is that same thing which is expressed by the suffix as well; thus, there is no difference here between the meaning of the base and the meaning of the suffix.
Therefore, by this [rule], a prohibition will apply wherever the meaning of the suffix is not distinct from the meaning of the base;
and it has been explained that [in such cases] the meaning is not distinct.

But surely, in the rules "saṅghe cānauttarādharye" (Pāṇini 2.4.2) and "saṅghāṅkalakṣaṇeṣv añ" (Pāṇini 5.1.58), the word *saṅgha* is understood to refer to a collection of living beings; how then can it be understood here as referring to a literary work? There is no fault, for it is used through metaphorical extension (*upacāra*).
Alternatively, in the rule concerning numbers (*saṃkhyā-sūtra*), a specific assembly is understood due to its association with technical terms (*saṃjñā-śabda*).

Even in the rule "in an assembly where there is no vertical stacking" (*saṅghe cānauttarādharye*, Pāṇini 2.4.2), because the term *nāman* is understood to carry over from the previous rule (Pāṇini 2.4.1), it is an assembly of living beings that is understood.
However, in the present case, since there is no occurrence of *yat*, there is no distinction, as even a collection of books (*gantha*) may be included.
Regarding the passage beginning with "But here," etc.:

One might object, "A negation ought to apply when 'hundred' is the expressed meaning; yet here, when one says 'a hundred cloth' (*śatyaṃ śāṭakaśatam*) or 'a hundredfold cloth' (*śatikaṃ śāṭakaśatam*), a hundred is indeed understood. So why does the negation not occur? To this he replies with "By means of a sentence," etc.
For the words *śatya* and *śatika* are general terms (*sāmānyaśabda*); and general terms do not function to denote a specific instance without [the aid of] context and so forth.

Therefore, as long as this other word "up to a hundred garments" (*yāvacchāṭakaśatam*) is not employed, the number-hundredhood of the meaning of the suffix is not apprehended. Consequently, because it is understood only upon the proximity of another word, it becomes the meaning of that other word, not the meaning of the suffix.
[This is expressed by the phrase] "not by direct audition" (*na śrutyā*).
The connection is that it is "understood.

Where the number-hundred of the meaning of the suffix is expressed by a word ending in a suffix independently of any other word, there it is understood through direct statement (*śruti*) by the mere hearing of that word ending in a suffix; for example, when it is said in the counter-example, "that which has a hundred as its measure is a *śataka*," it is indeed understood that the meaning of the suffix is also exactly a hundred.
But here, however, the state of being a hundred is cognized from the sentence (*vākya*).
Furthermore, at the time of the formation of individual words (*pada-saṃskāra*), the sentence-meaning does not possess the status of being a subordinate factor (*aṅga*) for those words;

for at that time, it remains a subordinate element (*upasarjana*). A prohibition applies to a suffixal meaning that is distinct from the meaning of the verbal root (*prakṛti*), but not to that which is understood through the distinct sentence as a whole.
To confirm this by means of the statement of an authoritative person (*āpta-vacana*), he says: "And so it has been said," and so forth.

When a prohibition of "hundred" (śata) is to be applied, what is meant by this is that there is no prohibition of the meaning of the suffix when it is "hundred," provided it is different from the meaning of the base (prakṛti).

In that case, what is other? The meaning of the base is "hundred"; what is other? The meaning of the suffix is "hundred. In that instance, there is only a positive injunction (vidhi), not a prohibition.

But by what [rule] would a compound be obtained here, such that the particle *ca* is employed for the purpose of prohibiting it and for the purpose of carrying forward the term *asamāsa* (non-compound)? To this he says: "Before *vati*, etc. [The example] "a fivefold cloth" (*pañcakaḥ paṭaḥ*) is an illustration of a worldly number (*laukikī saṃkhyā*).
[The examples] "manyfold" (*bahukaḥ*), etc., follow.
Regarding the one who has been reviled:
"one who is forty" (*catvāriṃśatkaḥ*). [This is formed] by [Pāṇini 7.3.51]:
*isusuktāntāt kaḥ*.
"Because of the inclusion of the word 'meaningful' (*arthavat*)," according to the paribhāṣā "the inclusion of that which is meaningful" (Vyāḍiparibhāṣā 1),
it follows that "there is no exclusion (*paryudāsa*) of the suffix *ḍati*."

The genitive case here denotes a part of a word (*avayava-ṣaṣṭhī*) with respect to the word *śabda*. There is no exclusion of the *ti* sound which is a single constituent part of the suffix; for that [part] has no independent meaning.
As in the example: *katikaḥ*.

"What is the measure of these?"—from this [question] the suffix *ḍati* is applied by [Pāṇini 5.2.41], and the elision of the final *ṭi* occurs by [Pāṇini 6.4.143]. Having analyzed the compound as "bought for how many" (*katibhiḥ krītam*), the suffix *kan* is added.

If there is a mention of the word *ti* when it is meaningful (*arthavat*), then an exclusion would not apply even to the *ti* belonging to the word *navati* (ninety); for it is the whole word *navati* that is meaningful through its specific numerical sense, not the word *ti* which is merely a part of it. This is not a fault; for within the word *navati*, the word *nava* (nine) has multiple meanings.

And so, since it is understood as a specific number from the word *nava* (nine), what follows after it is the word *ti*; from that, these [numbers] are recognized, because they exist when that [word *ti*] exists. [Objection:

In that case, the exclusion (*paryudāsa*) of the word *ti* would not apply to the word *aśīti*, for it would not have a meaning. Nor does the word *aśī* which precedes it have any meaning; rather, only the entire compound has meaning as a specific number. [Response: This is not so. Even though no meaning of the word *aśīti* is manifested, nevertheless it is asserted.
The word *aśīti* is derived in this way: the form *aśī-* arises from the eight *daśan*s (eight tens), and the suffix *ti* is added.

Whatever is the meaning of "eight tens" is the meaning of the word *aśī*, while the specific numerical distinction belongs to the suffix *ti* alone; therefore, it is not meaningless. Even so, does the prohibition regarding *viṃśati* not remain unestablished? It is indeed derived in this way: the form *viṃ-* arises from two *daśat*s (two tens), and the suffix *śati* is added.

In that regard, what is the purpose of the suffix *śati*? The very meaning that belongs to the two decades of the preceding portion is what is asserted by the suffix *śati*; it is a specific number (*saṃkhyāviśeṣa*), while the syllable *ti* has no [independent] meaning.
That is indeed desired.
What is included? From "twenty"—as in "that which consists of twenty" (*viṃśatika*).

Now, what is the purpose of including the mention of *anta* ("ending in") in the rule *atiśadantāyāḥ*, given that the word *atiśa* does not belong to the *prāgvatīya* class [and thus the suffix *-kan* would not apply to it by default]? One might argue that the extension to "that which ends in" (*tadantavidhi*) will occur simply by means of the technical rule concerning the mention of a suffix (*pratyayagrahaṇaparibhāṣā*). If that were so, then this very mention of *anta* serves the purpose of ensuring that the extension to "that which ends in" does not occur through this particular technical rule. What would be the consequence otherwise? In the case of *ekasaptatyā krītaḥ* ("bought for seventy-one"), the prohibition [of the suffix *-kan*] would not apply; for the suffix *ti* is not prescribed after the words *eka* and *saptadaśan*.

But when the inclusion of the suffix *ti* is made, since the word *ti* is heard at the end of the aggregate, the prohibition is established here as well. This is because [the words] ending in *vat* possess the designation of "number" (*saṃkhyā*), due to the prescription of that designation by the rule *bahugaṇavatuḍati saṃkhyā* (Pāṇini 1.1.22). As for the phrase "of that," and so forth...

But how can its derivation (*āgama*) by means of this suffix be understood, since there is no mention of *kan* here? Furthermore, that which is under discussion (*prakṛta*) is also indicated in the nominative; yet here the sense [required] is one indicated by the genitive. This is not a fault, because the rule *vatoḥ* (Pāṇini 5.2.39) is in the ablative case, and it will effect a genitive for the nominative *kan* according to the rule *pratyayasthāt kāt pūrvasya...* (Pāṇini 7.3.44). Thus, *tāvatkaḥ*: "that much is its measure" (*tat-parimāṇam asya*). By the rule *yattadetebhyaḥ parimāṇe vatuḥ* (Pāṇini 5.2.39), the suffix *vatu* is applied, and by *ātas tṛtīyād acām anyatarasyām* (Pāṇini 7.2.91), the vowel substitution (*ātva*) occurs. *Viṃśakaḥ*: "twenty."

By [Pāṇini 6.4.142], there is the elision (*lopa*) of the word *ti*; by [Pāṇini 6.1.97], there is the substitution of the single subsequent form (*pararūpatva*) due to the rule *ato guṇe*. The elision by [Pāṇini 6.4.148] does not occur because the elision is considered non-existent (*asiddha*) in this context according to [Pāṇini 6.4.22]: "In this [section], that which is taught is as if it were non-existent. Objection: But here, the designation of a word (*pada-saṃjñā*) is based on the internal case-ending (*vibhakti*); so how can there be the substitution of the single subsequent form? Response: In that case, since the non-existence (*asiddhatva*) of the rule is not absolute, the elision by [Pāṇini 6.4.148] will indeed take place; thus, there is no fault.
"But how is it that [the question] 'how then here [is there] *kan*? arises?

This question is raised with reference to the term *viṃśatika*, given that in the case of *tiṃraśatka*, the word *tri-* is understood as having its own meaning; therefore, since the exclusion (*paryudāsa*) does not apply there, the presentation of this question with reference to that [term] would be inappropriate. [The answer is:
"A division of the rule (*yogavibhāga*) will be made."
The intention is that it refers to the meaning of "thirty.

"An exception to *ṭhañ*" means it is not *ṭhak*, because the word *kaṃsa* denotes a measure. "An exception to *ṭhañ*" means it is not *ṭhak*, because the word *śūrpa* denotes a measure. "An exception to both *ṭhak* and *ṭhañ*" [the printed reading says "an exception to *ṭhañ*"].

*Śatamāna* is a measure (*parimāṇa*), while *sahasra* is a number (*saṃkhyā*); therefore, the suffix *ṭhak* would apply to these two [by Pāṇini 5.1.18], and this [rule] is an exception (*apavāda*) to that *ṭhak*. "Bought for twenty" is *viṃśatikaḥ*;
and that [suffix] can also occur when [the word] signifies a measure.

In that context, [the suffix] *ṭhañ* is an exception (*apavāda*) to [the rule for] *parimāṇa*; [the suffix] *ṭhak* is an exception to [the rule for] *aparimāṇa*; and [the suffix] *ṭhak* is an exception to [the rule for] the word *vasana*. Regarding the expression "adhyardhakaṃsa": a compound is formed in the sense of a secondary derivative (*taddhita*), meaning "bought with one and a half *kaṃsas*. According to the Mahābhāṣya: "Prior to the suffix *vat*, there is the application of the rule regarding the final element (*tadantavidhi*) to words preceded by a numeral, provided there is no elision (*aluk*)."
Thus, by the rule *kaṃsāt ṭiṭhan* [Pāṇini 5.1.25], the suffix *ṭiṭhan* is applied; its elision (*luk*) occurs,
resulting in *dvikaṃsam* ("worth two *kaṃsas*") and *adhyardhaśūrpam* ("one and a half *śūrpa*s").

The suffix *añ* is applied [to *śūrpa*] by the rule *śūrpādañ anyatarasyām* (Pāṇini 5.1.26); [the suffix] *ṭhañ* is optionally applied, and there is elision (*luk*) of that. If the elision of the *arhīya* suffix following a *dvigu* compound were prescribed [without qualification], would it not apply even to that which follows a *dvigu* ending in a *taddhita* whose *luk* has occurred—such as *dviśūrpaḥ paṭaḥ* ("a cloth bought for two winnowing-baskets") or *dviśaurpikam* ("bought with a cloth worth two winnowing-baskets")? This is not a fault; the term *vibhāṣā* (optionally) which is to be stated later also connects with the preceding rule. That is a restricted option (*vyavasthitavibhāṣā*).
Therefore, there will be no [vṛddhi] for what follows a dvigu compound that ends in a *taddhita* suffix with elision—such as *dviśaurpika*.

When the *ṭhañ* suffix belonging to the *prāgvatīya* group is applied, the vṛddhi of the final syllable of the second member occurs by [Pāṇini 7.3.17]. Examples are *pāñcalohitikam* and *pāñcakalāpikam*.
Of what? These are names for specific measures. [The analysis is as follows:

"That which has five *lohinyaḥ* as its measure" (*pañca lohinyaḥ parimāṇam asya*), and "that which has five *kapālāḥ* as its measure" (*pañca kapālāḥ parimāṇam asya*). Having analyzed these, a compound is formed in the sense of a secondary derivative (*taddhita*). By the rule *Pāṇini 5.1.57*, the suffix *ṭhañ* is applied. Then, by the rule *Vārttika 731* (*bhasyā’ḍhe taddhite*), due to the masculine substitution (*puṃvadbhāva*), the vowel *i* and the nasal *n* of the word *lohinī* are removed. [Regarding the term *adhyardha*: "The word *adhyardha* is indeed a number."
Having applied a metaphorical designation (*upacāra*) of the denoted object to the denoting word, it was stated that "the word *adhyardha* is itself a number.
Just as numbers such as one (*eka*) and so forth are worldly numbers, so too is the word *adhyardha*. [The question is:
"For what purpose is it employed separately? [The word *saḥ* does not appear in the Kāśikā.]
The word "of number" (*saṃkhyāyāḥ*) is to be supplied as the remainder [of the compound].
For here, because "preceded by *adhyardha*" (*adhyardhapūrvasya*) is mentioned separately from "two" (*dvi*), the mention of "number" occurs separately from that which is preceded by *adhyardha*.
Therefore, he asks in order to show the purpose for mentioning that word *adhyardha* separately.

With the words "for the sake of indication" (*jñāpakārtham*), etc., he states the purpose. He asks: "Why, then, does this [suffix] not undergo the grammatical operations pertaining to number? To which he replies with "of the number" (*saṃkhyāyāḥ*), etc. Regarding the form *adhyardhasahasram*:
there is elision (*luk*) of the suffix *aṇ* prescribed by the rule "after *śata*, *māna*, and *viṃśatika*" (Pāṇini 5.1.27).

Regarding the term *adhyardhasāhasrām*: by [Pāṇini 7.3.15], there is vṛddhi of the final syllable of the second member. Regarding the statement "there is an addition for *suvarṇa* and *śatamāna*": [this refers to the rule].
"Upasaṃkhyānam" means "addition" or "supplementation.

In this regard, the following is the supplementation: from the rule "vistācca" [Pāṇini 5.1.31], the particle *ca* ("and") applies here by way of the "lion's glance" (*siṃhāvalokita*) maxim; and since it serves the purpose of including what has not been explicitly mentioned, the rule thus applies even to the words *suvarṇa* and *śatamāna*. An example is: *adhyardhasuvarṇam*.
There is elision (*luk*) of the suffix *ṭhañ*, as in the example "adhyardhaśatamānam. This refers to the suffix *aṇ* prescribed by [Pāṇini 5.1.27] and subsequent rules;
thus, we have "adhyardhaśatamānam."

The vowel lengthening (*vṛddhi*) of the final member of the compound is applied by the rule *parimāṇāntasya* [Pāṇini 7.3.17]. Now, one might object: gold (*suvarṇa*) is a measure of weight (*unmāna*), not a measure of capacity (*parimāṇa*); therefore, how can there be vowel lengthening for it? This is not a fault; for when vowel lengthening applies to the final member, even a measure of weight is understood as a "measure" (*parimāṇa*). How is this known? From the fact that the word *śāṇa* is specifically excluded by the rule *asaṃjñāśāṇayoḥ* [Pāṇini 7.3.17].

If, then, measurement (*unmāna*) were not included therein, then since there would be no possibility at all for the application of the term *śāṇa* in the sense of measurement, [the author] would not have formulated a prohibition.

Why does the rule "after *adhyardha-* and *dvi-* [compounds], [the suffix *ṭhak* is applied] to *kārṣāpaṇa* and *sahasra* respectively" not apply here? Because the absence of such an application has been indicated by the deviation from the defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇavyabhicāra*).

In this regard, first of all: in the rule *adhyardhapūrvadvigoḥ* [Pāṇini 5.1.28], because the word *dvigu* has fewer vowels and ends in a vowel, its prior placement (*pūrvanipāta*) would follow. Furthermore, in the rule *kārṣāpaṇasaharuābhyām*, because the word *saharuā* has fewer vowels, its prior placement would likewise follow. These two rules, by indicating independence from other grammatical characteristics (*lakṣaṇāntara*), indicate the absence even of the maxim of "respective order" (*yatāsaṃkhyaparibhāṣā*); thus, the maxim of respective order does not apply here. The mention of *adhyardhapūrva* does not extend [to subsequent rules] because it is not marked with a svarita accent. For example: *dviniṣkam*.
In the expression "purchased for two *niṣkas*," because the suffix *ṭhak* is prescribed for non-similar [cases], the suffix here is *ṭhañ*, which undergoes elision (*luk*).
Thus we have "dvinaiṣkikam.
The vowel lengthening of the final member of the compound occurs by the rule beginning with "parimāṇāntasya" (Pāṇini 7.3.17).

Regarding the rule *bahupūrvācca*: the meaning is that this form of the rule—stating that there is optionally (*vibhāṣā*) elision (*luk*) of an *ārhīya* suffix after a *dvigu* compound whose first member is *bahu* and which ends in the word *niṣka*—must be explained. In this regard, the explanation is as follows: since the result is already established by the rule *dvitribhyāṃ niṣkāt*, the fact that the author adds the superfluous term *pūrva* indicates that "there is something else additional [to be understood]."
Therefore, it occurs even after words preceded by many [prefixes]. Regarding the statement, "The phrase 'preceded by two or three' is drawn forward by the letter *ca*," one might object:

"Since the term *dvitri* will continue to apply simply because it is marked with the *svarita* accent, why is this necessary? For if it were merely *svarita*, the extent of its governing scope (*adhikāra*) would not be known. This objection is trivial; for the extent of the governing scope will be understood from the commentary (*vyākhyāna*). If that is so, since the continuation of the phrase "preceded by two or three" is already established by the *svarita* accent alone, the fact that he adds the letter *ca* specifically for the purpose of drawing that forward indicates this: that something else additional is also present here.

By this, the elision (*luk*) is optionally applied even when the prefix *bahu-* precedes. Thus, "one *bista*" becomes *bahubistam*, and "two *bistas*" becomes *dvibistam*. In the latter case, the suffix *ṭhañ* is added in the sense of "that whose measure is two *vīstas*," and its elision (*luk*) occurs.
Regarding "dvibaistikam":

there is vṛddhi of the final syllable of the second member. The mention of "preceded by dvi, tri, etc. has ceased [to apply here], because it was not carried over from the previous rule, or because it lacks the svarita accent.
Since the suffix *aṇ* would have been applicable by the rule for *śatamāna* and so forth (Pāṇini 5.1.27), this rule ordains the suffix *kha* after its elision (*luk*).
"By virtue of the power of its specific prescription, there is no elision (*luk*) for this.
If there were elision, the prescription of *kha* would be purposeless;

for when both *ṇa* and *kha* are elided, there is no distinction whatsoever. Since *ṭhak* is prescribed by the rule "after *paṇa*, *pāda*, and *māṣa*" (Pāṇini 5.1.20) in the case of a non-compound, and since *ṭhañ* would otherwise apply, its elision is intended. Furthermore, since *ṭhan* and *ṭyan* are prescribed after the word *śata* in the case of a non-compound (Pāṇini 5.1.21), and since *kan* is prescribed in the case of a compound characterized by a numeral, [the specific prescription of *kha* serves a purpose].

Regarding the phrase "dvipādyam" and so forth: one might ask, why does the substitution of *pad* not occur here according to Pāṇini 6.3.53, *padyatyatadarthe*? True; however, in the rule 6.3.52 (*prāṇyaṅgāt*), the substitution of *pad* is prescribed only for words denoting a limb of a living being. Why is this so? Because its connection is established only with that which expresses motion, as indicated by the rule beginning with 6.1.140, *ājyātigopahvareṣu kṣepe*; it does not apply to a word denoting a measure.
Since that very term denoting a limb of a living being (*prāṇyaṅga*) is carried over into the subsequent sūtra as well, the substitution of *pad-* is intended for that [term] alone.

One might object: "This word *pāda* here also denotes a limb of a living being; therefore, the substitution of *pad-* ought indeed to occur here? To this he says: "The substitution of *pad-* does not take place.
Thus, although the substitution of *pad-* would apply by rule 6.3.53, it does not occur.
He asks, "What is the reason? and says: "In the rule beginning with *prāṇyaṅgasya* [Pāṇini 5.4.113], there is the mention of a foot that is a limb of a living being (*prāṇyaṅga*).
However, this [present rule] is a mention of measure (*parimāṇa*). [The *Kāśikā* states: "Measure" (*parimāṇa*)].

Because of its association with *paṇa* and other measures of quantity, "measure" (*parimāṇa*) is understood here as a *pāda* [of gold], not a limb of a living being; thus, there is no occasion for the substitution of *pad* [for *pāda*]. Examples include *sāptatikam*, *āśītikam*, *naiṣkikam*, and *pāṇikam*.
Here, the suffix *ṭhak* is applied.
The suffix *ṭhak* [is applied] by [the rule] "śatyam, śatikam" (Pāṇini 5.1.20),
resulting in "śatyam" and "śatikam."

Regarding the statement "dvikam, trikam" [under rule 5.1.21]: why does [the suffix *ka*] not apply here in cases where there is the expression of a general sense, such as in "devadattena krītam" (bought by Devadatta) or "pāṇinā krītam" (bought with the hand), given that the instrumental case (*tena*) is prescribed [by Pāṇini 2.3.18]? To this, he says: "tena," etc.
The third case ending is used in the sense of the instrument (*karaṇa*). Why [is it] "from the price" (*parimūlyāt*)? Therefore, there ought to be an affix [added].
[The word] "elsewhere" (*anyatra*) [is used].
"From anything other than a price"? The third case ending occurs in the sense of an instrument (*karaṇa*).

Regarding the phrase "because of non-expression": for the third case ending that arises in the sense of an agent (*kartṛ*), as well as the third case ending that arises in the sense of an instrument when it is not a price—no suffix produced after such endings is capable of conveying the intended object, provided that [the suffix] is intended to be expressed.

For instance, when it is said "daivadattikaṃ pāṇikam" (purchased from Devadatta, purchased for a hand), the meaning "purchased by Devadatta as the agent" or "purchased with the hand as the instrument" is not determined [by the suffixes alone]. In "devadattena," the third case ending denotes the agent (*kartṛ*), and in "pāṇinā," it denotes the instrument (*karaṇa*). Thus, this is what is being stated: because the relationship between the object of exchange and the substance that is proximate to the transaction is not expressed [by the suffixes].
"Simply because it is not so expressed.
For when "prāsthikam" (worth one prastha) is said, it is not understood that it was purchased with two prasthas or purchased with many prasthas.

Furthermore, what is the reason for that expression [of accumulation]? Such is the power of words; what need is there for another reason here! Moreover, since words such as *prastha* and others denote objects that are measures (*parimāṇa*) in their actual meaning, what is the reason for their application when there is an accumulation of those things to be expressed? [Objection: But in that case, accumulation would not be possible even in a sentence. [Reply: This is not a fault; for in a sentence, there exists a case-ending (*vibhakti*) that expresses accumulation, so the expression of accumulation is not contradictory. But in a compound (*vṛtti*), there is nothing that denotes accumulation; therefore, it is not appropriate to apply that [expression] in the domain of a compound.

If, then, [the suffix] should not occur after forms ending in the dual or plural, this being the case, expressions such as *dvikam* (bought for two) or *trikam* (bought for three) would not be established; therefore, he says: "But where... and so forth. Non-expression is the cause for the non-arising of the suffix after a dual-ending form. And where does that expression not occur? Where there is no comprehension of a distinction in number regarding the meaning of the base (*prakṛti*), because of a lack of evidence.
But here there is indeed a means of valid cognition:
the words "two" and so forth are themselves presented as bases (prakṛti).
For they convey an object delimited by a number that serves as their own ground for application (pravṛttinimitta).
Therefore, this is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for understanding the specific number of the object itself.
Consequently, the realization arises that "this reason—namely, 'because it is not denoted'—is present here.
[The phrase] "in the same way," and so forth, follows.

Just as in cases such as *trika*, because there is evidence for the non-existence of number in the meaning of the base (*prakṛti*), a suffix occurs even after a word ending in the plural, so too in cases such as *maudgika*, the base-word *mudga* and others serve as the evidence for understanding the number of their own referent. To demonstrate this, he says: "For not by one," and so forth.
Since a purchase is not made with a single individual instance of *mudga* and the like, plurality is understood through the recurrence of the word *mudga* and the rest even without a case-ending;
that serves as the evidence in that regard.

The mention of "one" (ekagrahaṇa) should be understood as an elliptical indication (*upalakṣaṇa*) of both [the singular and the plural], as they are not applicable to all three. Regarding the phrase "of the great elements" (*mahābhūtānām*), this refers to earth, water, fire, air, and space. Regarding the word "conjunction" (*sāṃhatyam*). [According to the *Kāśikā*: "The transformation of the great elements" (*mahābhūtapariṇāmaḥ*) means their production.
"Of the great elements" refers to earth, water, fire, air, and space. "Conjunction" means...

By the rule *śatamānādi-sūtra* [Pāṇini 5.1.27], the suffix *aṇ* is prescribed; it is "an exception (*apavāda*) to *ṭhañ* and the others. By the word "others" (*ādi*), the inclusion of *ṭhak* and so forth is intended. Now, one might object: since numbers and measures are excluded [from the scope of this rule], it could be said that *kan* and *ṭhak* are the exceptions; why then is it stated that it is an exception "to *ṭhañ* and the others"? This term "*ṭhañādīnām*" (of *ṭhañ* and the others) should be understood as a *bahuvrīhi* compound where the qualities of the members do not apply to the whole (*atadguṇasaṃvijñāna*).
It was stated with this very intention: "The suffix *ṭhak* is for the sake of [excluding] *āḍhakī*.
*Ṭhak* has been cited as a counter-example (*pratyudāhṛta*). Since all suffixes are potentially applicable, this was stated in order to supersede them.
"What is the suffix *kan* characterized by number (*saṃkhyālakṣaṇa*)? [Examples are: *pañcakaṃ*, *aṣṭakam*.
What is [the suffix] in *prāsthikaḥ*?"

The term *tasya* (of that) is understood from the rule *prāgvateṣṭhañ* [Pāṇini 5.1.18] up to this point [5.1.38]. For what purpose, then, is *tasya* mentioned again? To this he says: "In the section dealing with the genitive (*ṣaṣṭhī-prakaraṇa*), there is a further mention of the genitive case-ending as the governing case" (*ṣaṣṭhī-samartha-vibhakti-nirdeśa*), and so forth.
"Of the meaning of the suffix" (*pratyayārthasya*) means "of the cause."
Regarding the word "otherwise" (*anyathā*):

if the mention of the genitive case were not made for the purpose of excluding [the application of] suffixes, then just as *saṃyoga* (conjunction) and *utpāta* (calamity) would be qualifiers of the meaning of the suffix, so too *īrā* might be suspected of being a qualifier of that very same [meaning].
And in that case, the suffix would apply only when the cause is qualified by *īrā*. The letter *c* is for the purpose of including *īrā*.

The particle *iti* is used for the purpose of indicating the intended meaning (*vivakṣārtha*). In all cases, the mention of *ṭhañ* is for the purpose of excluding *ṭhak*; otherwise, if only the base were specified, *ṭhak* would apply by force of [Pāṇini 5.1.19] *ārhāt*. "In this, sowing occurs" (*vāpaḥ*)—this is derived from the locus (*adhikaraṇa*), with the suffix *ghañ* by [Pāṇini 3.3.121] *halaśca*. "The word *pātra* denotes a measure"—this is an exception (*apavāda*) to *ṭhañ*.
The reasoning here is as follows: if [the word *ārhīya*] were to denote "immeasurable" (*aparimāṇa*), then it would be an exception (*apavāda*) to the suffix *ṭhak*, not to *ṭhañ*.

Thus, in the form *pātrikī*, the feminine suffix *ṅīṣ* is applied by [Pāṇini 4.1.41]. Now, one might object: "Since there is a plurality of items such as 'increased' (*vṛddhi*) and so forth, the plural number ought to be used; therefore, how is it that this is indicated by the singular form 'is given' (*dīyate*)? To this, he says: "'Is given' is in the singular," and so on.

If the connection were made with *vṛddhi* and the others taken collectively, then the plural number would be required. However, that connection is not made with them collectively; rather, it is made individually. Therefore, only the singular number is used.

Here, the word *vṛddhi* is understood in its worldly sense as denoting a specific kind of wealth, and it is not a technical grammatical term (*saṃjñā*), because it is mentioned alongside *āya* and other terms that denote specific kinds of wealth.

For this very reason, he says "therein," and so forth. Interest (*vṛddhi*) is that wealth which is to be given by the debtor in excess of the creditor's own capital. Regarding the phrase "in villages and so forth":
By the word "etcetera," fields and so forth are meant.
Regarding the phrase "of cloth etcetera":
the material cause (*upādāna*) of things such as cloth that are being used is thread and so forth.
Whatever wealth is obtained through the sale of cloth and other goods in excess of its [original] value is "profit. This is called "the fee for protection" (*rakṣānirveśa*).
The king's share, which consists of the protection provided by the king to merchants, is termed the "fee for protection."

But is this not already included within the *apayāya* (expenditure)? Therefore, is the separate mention of *śulka* (customs duty) purposeless? This is not so; for in the expression "there is an income (*āya*) of five in this village," the village stands as the locus (*adhikaraṇa*) with respect to the income, because the income that arises is contained within it. However, this is not possible in the case of *śulka*. In the expression "there is a *śulka* of five in this hundred," the hundred is not the locus of the *śulka*; rather, the hundred serves to define the quantity of the *śulka*.
Therefore, because this [recipient] is distinct, the *śulka* (bride-price) is mentioned separately. Regarding the passage beginning with "But it is established" (*siddhaṃ tu*),

since grammatical roles (*kāraka*) arise from the speaker's intention (*vivakṣā*), he states "equally" (*samam*) and so forth, meaning that what is designated as the recipient (*sampradāna*) is intended here as the locus (*adhikaraṇa*).
The meaning has already been explained. [It is said: "This is an exception to *ṭhañ*.
It is not an exception to *ṭhak*; for the word *bhāga* denotes a measure (*parimāṇa*).
But is it not the case that the word *bhāga* also exists as denoting a mere part? True, it exists; however, it is not what is intended here.
For if that [word *rūpaka*] were taken [in its primary sense], a connection with "interest" (*vṛddhi*) and so forth would not be possible.

However, since it is well-known as a term denoting measure, it functions in the sense of a "fraction of a *rūpaka*," and thus a connection with "interest" and so forth is possible. Regarding the phrase "modifier of the base" (*prakṛtiviśeṣaṇam*) and so on:
"base" (*prakṛti*) refers to the nominal stem (*prātipadika*).

"The meaning is 'from *vaṃśa* and so forth when they constitute a burden. In this sense, only the words *vaṃśa* and the others produce the suffix directly. Now, one might object: "The words *vaṃśa* and so forth are indeed words, and the word *bhāra* (burden) is also a word; and it is not possible for a word to function as a coreferential qualifier (*samānādhikaraṇa-viśeṣaṇa*) for another word. Therefore, how can the meaning 'from those *vaṃśa* and so forth that have become a burden' be established? To this he says: "'The word *bhāra* [functions] by way of its referent (*artha-dvāreṇa*),' and so forth."
