Even from the mention of "vayas" (age), since suffixes such as *tva* and *tal* would apply according to their respective rules, the specific prescription of *añ* is made.
The inclusion of the word "vacana" (mention) is for the purpose of excluding a rule based on the literal form [of the word]; otherwise, it would apply to the word *vayas* itself.

In that regard, for words such as *udgātṛ*, *unnatṛ*, and *adhvaryu*, since they denote officiating priests (*ṛtvij*), the suffix *cha* would have applied by Pāṇini 5.1.135; therefore, the reading [of these words] is for the sake of the suffix *añ*.
Although the condition of having a light vowel as the preceding member would have applied to these words—*suṣṭhu*, *duṣṭhu*, and *vadhū*—[the rule] states:
"In the case of *subhaga* when used in a mantra. Thus, the word *subhaga* produces the suffix *añ* in the context of a mantra: *mahate saubhāgyāya*.
"All rules are optional in the Vedic language" (Pāṇini-purva-vṛtti 56);
thus, by the rule "after *ah*, *mad*, *bhaga*, and *sindhu*" (Pāṇini 7.3.19), the vṛddhi of the final syllable of the second member does not occur.
What is the purpose of the word *mantra*? [It is to indicate] *saubhāgyam*, because it belongs to the *brāhmaṇādi* group.

As for the reading of the remaining items here, it serves to provide the suffixes *-tva* and *-tal*. Regarding words ending in *hāyana*: when *-tva* and *-tal* would otherwise apply, the suffix *-aṇ* is prescribed.

But is it not already established that *-aṇ* applies to words ending in *hāyana* by rule 4.3.120? It is not so established; because of its higher status, it is superseded by *-tva* and *-tal*. Consequently, for the state or action of *āṣāḍhahāyaṇa*, the form *āṣāḍhahāyaṇa* (with *-aṇ*) would result from rule 4.2.114.
Therefore, the prescription of the suffix *aṇ* after words ending in *hāyana* is appropriate;
thus we have "yauvanam.
By the rule "an" [Pāṇini 6.4.167], there is the preservation of the original stem form (*prakṛtibhāva*).

In the case of *yuvā* and others, since the suffix *vuñ* would otherwise apply to the word *yuvan* by virtue of its inclusion in the *manojñādi* group—thereby setting aside the *añ* suffix which is prescribed for words denoting age—the word is included [in the *yuvādi* list] to ensure that *añ* applies instead.
For the word *sthavira*, the suffix *añ* applies by virtue of its denoting age; likewise, for the word *hotṛ*, the suffix *añ* alone applies because it belongs to the *udgātrādi* group.
Thus: "puruṣāse."
The suffix *aṇ* occurs after the word *puruṣa* when it does not form a compound; for example, *pauruṣam*. Why is it said "when not [in a compound]"? [Consider] *rājapuruṣatvam*.
This is a recitation [of the rule] because [the suffix *aṇ*] would otherwise not apply by [Pāṇini 5.1.129].
Since the word *āḍulu* ends in the vowel *ī*, the suffix *aṇ* is already established; however, this recitation is for the purpose of overriding the suffixes *tva* and *tal*.
[The example is] *hṛdayāsa*.
Does the suffix *aṇ* occur after the word *hṛdaya* when it is not in a compound? It occurs; thus, *hṛdya*. [This is because] the substitution of *hṛd* for *hṛdaya* applies by rule 6.3.50.
Why is it said "when not in a compound"? [To show that] the suffix *aṇ* occurs after the word *hṛdaya* when it is not in a compound.
In the rule *hṛd-am* [Pāṇini 6.3.50], there is the substitution of *hrad* for *hṛdaya*.

Why is it said "of *as*" (*asaḥ*)? [To exclude cases like] *paramahṛdayatvam*. Since the words beginning with *kuśala* and ending with *kṣetrajña* belong to the *brāhmaṇādi* group, the suffix *ṣyañ* would otherwise apply; this entry [in the list] is therefore made to prevent that. For the remaining words, however, the suffixes *tva* and *tal* apply.

But surely, since there is no rule of extension (*tadantavidhi*) for a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) that possesses a suffix, there would be no possibility of the suffix *aṇ* arising after a compound; thus, the prohibition regarding *puruṣāse* and *brahmadayāse* would be purposeless? It is not purposeless, for this is a locative of scope (*viṣayasaptamī*): when a compound is intended to be formed, the words *puruṣa* and *brahmada* are themselves the scope [of the operation]. If the prohibition were not stated, then when both the *nañ*-compound and the suffix *aṇ* (expressing an abstract state) were simultaneously applicable, the *aṇ* alone would occur by virtue of its being the subsequent rule.
However, because of the prohibition, the compound itself takes place first.
Then, that abstract suffix (*bhāvapratyaya*) for which there is a cause arises.

And what is this [cause]? It is the suffixes *tva* and *tal*: *apuruṣatvam*, *apuruṣatā*; *ahmadayatvam*, *ahmadayatā*. Here, the word ending in *hāyana* is first, while the group beginning with *yuvan* is second; the meanings are also only two—abstract state (*bhāva*) and object (*karman*). Therefore, by virtue of this capacity, one might expect a correspondence according to their respective order; however, because the rule regarding the subsequent placement of the shorter vowel [in *yuvan*] serves as an indicator of deviation from such a fixed sequence, it does not occur.
Or [it is so] because it is not marked with the *svarita* accent. Regarding the term "ending in an *ik*" (*igantāt*):
it is a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "that whose end (*anta*) is an *ik*.
The base noun (*prātipadika*) is the referent of the other member of the compound (*anyapadārtha*).

Regarding the phrase "in the case of grasping what precedes" (*laghupūrvagrahaṇe*), etc.: why is this [word *pūrva*] not qualified by itself? Because, within the meaning of a *bahuvrīhi* compound, it is subordinate (*guṇabhūta*) and thus cannot be connected with a qualifier.
Furthermore, this word *pūrva*, being a term denoting relative position (*vyavasthāśabda*), requires something else [to which it is prior].

And here, because another [element] has not been specified, it is not known from what [source] the preceding light [vowel] is derived. To ascertain that, he asks: "But from what is this preceding light [vowel]?
Relying on the principle of proximity (*pratyāsatti*), he says: "Because of its vicinity," and so forth.
For in this sūtra, the *ik* [vowels] are what are in close proximity, since they are explicitly mentioned (*śruta*).
Regarding the word "tena" (by that):
it is argued that the inclusion of the term *anta* (end) is redundant because it is already contained within [the compound] *laghupūrva*. This is because it would be fruitless;

for when it is stated "from that which has a light vowel as its prior member" (*laghupūrvāt*), since the rule of "that which ends in this" (*tadantavidhi*) applies to the nominal stem (*prātipadika*), its being the "end" is obtained by the very force of the context. Therefore, in this interpretation, the inclusion of the term *anta* is purposeless.

However, in the previous formulation, if the mention of "the end" (*anta*) were absent, the rule would be understood simply as *laghupūrvād vataḥ*; consequently, even an *ik* that is not at the end would be subject to the operation. In that case, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of suffixes being added even after words such as *laśuna* and *lakuṭa*. It is for this purpose that the mention of "the end" is made. [The question is: "How then is *kāvyam* derived?"

It must be otherwise; the intention is that because the word *kavi* has a light penultimate vowel (*laghupūrvagantatva*), [the suffix *vuñ* would apply]. Since [suffixes] such as *tva* and *tal* would otherwise be applicable, *vuñ* is specifically prescribed. Here, the word *uttama* is taken as an underived (*avyutpanna*) nominal stem (*prātipadika*). Considering its inherent nature—that it denotes the "last" among three or more—it says, "the last among three or more," and so forth.

However, if the form ending in the suffix *tamap* were taken, then the defect mentioned regarding *sutāra* in the rule *aṇioranārṣayoḥ* (Pāṇini 4.1.78) and elsewhere should be understood to apply here as well, following that same logic.

The term *upottama* means "near the last" (*uttamasya samīpam*). This is an *avyayībhāva* compound according to [Pāṇini 2.1.6]: *avyayaṃ vibhaktisamīpa*. When suffixes such as *tva* and *tal* would otherwise apply after a *dvandva*, the suffix *vuñ* is prescribed. From those among the *manojñādi* group that denote qualities, the suffix *ṣyañ* applies. After the words *caura* and *dhūrta*, *ṣyañ* applies alone because they belong to the *brāhmaṇādi* group. After the word *yuva*, *aṇ* applies because it belongs to the *yavādi* group. For the remaining words, however, *tva* and *tal* apply. Thus: *amuṣyaputraḥ*.
The non-elision (*aluk*) of the case-ending occurs by way of an irregular derivation (*nipātana*).

Here, in the *dvandva* and *manojñādi* groups, there are two sets [of bases], and the meanings of the suffixes are also only two—namely, the abstract state (*bhāva*) and the object (*karman*)—so that a one-to-one correspondence (*yathāsaṃkhya*) would follow; however, as before, this does not occur because the rule is not marked with the *svarita* accent.
Alternatively, the particle *ca* here is used in the sense of conjunction (*samuccaya*).

Since there is nothing else to be added to that [rule], the prescription of the suffix *vuñ* itself adds together the two meanings of abstract state (*bhāva*) and object (*karman*) individually. Therefore, from a single group [of bases], the suffix *vuñ* occurs both in the sense of an abstract state and in the sense of an object, but not according to their respective order (*yathāsaṃkhyam*); for otherwise, the addition (*samuccaya*) would be untenable. A designation based on offspring is called a "lineage" (*gotra*), and it is recited in the *Pravarādhyāya*. Furthermore, that which denotes persons engaged in the study of the Veda is the designation of the word "branch" (*caraṇa*).

Regarding the statement "the lineage (*gotra*) together with the [Vedic] schools (*caraṇa*)," since the technical terms *gotra* and *caraṇa* denote a genus (*jāti*), the suffix *añ* would have applied by rule Pāṇini 4.1.129; however, the suffix *vuñ* is prescribed instead. Here, there are two nominal stems (*prātipadika*) denoting lineage and school, and there are likewise two meanings; thus, one might expect them to apply respectively (*yathāsaṃkhyam*). This does not occur because the first member of the compound is marked as *svarita*. For this very reason, he says: "respectively, for the two meanings of abstract state (*bhāva*) and action (*karman*)."
Regarding the phrase "when praise and so forth have become the objects":
for indeed, a *bhāva* (verbal root meaning) cannot be any one of the things such as praise;
a *bhāva* is the ground for the application of a word (*śabdapravṛttinimitta*).
Furthermore, praise and the like do not constitute the basis for the application (*pravṛttinimitta*) of the words "lineage" (*gotra*) and "conduct" (*caraṇa*).
Nor does action itself possess the nature of praise and so forth.

For praise and the like are not conventionally established as the actions of lineages and conducts, in the way that heat and so forth are the actions of fire; this is because they [praise and the like] are of the nature of verbal activity (*kriyā*).

The suffix *vuñ* occurs when the object consists of the meanings of the *bhāva* (action/state) and *karman* (object), which function as the referents of the suffix by virtue of being that which is to be accomplished (*sādhyatayā*). This is expressed in the rule:
"one who knows that, one who has attained that" (*tadaveta-statprāptaḥ*), because the root *iṇ* here has the sense of motion (*gatyarthatvāt*).
Regarding the phrase "or known by him":

since the root *i* preceded by the prefix *ava* can also function in the sense of "knowing," the word *tat* here refers back to the abstract state (*bhāva*) or the action (*karman*) related to the lineage (*gotra*) and the school (*caraṇa*).
Regarding the form *gārgikayā*:
by [Pāṇini 4.3.151], there is the elision of *ya*. When the suffixes *tva* and *tal* would otherwise apply, the suffix *cha* is prescribed. Regarding the statement "it should be said 'not so'":
even though the suffix *cha* is prohibited as an exception, the suffix *tva* applies.
The formation [of the word *bhāva*] is established by the rule *tasya bhāvastvatalau* (Pāṇini 5.1.118).

Therefore, although one could simply say "not" (*na*), this specific statement is made so that there may be an exclusion of *tal* by means of *tva*. If only "not" were said, then when *cha* is prohibited, just as *tva* occurs, so too would *tal* occur.
But if your statement were not made, the sublation of *tala* would be established.
Thus ends the first quarter of the fifth chapter in the *Kāśikā-vivaraṇapañjikā*, composed by the venerable master Jinendrabuddhi, who was like a Bodhisattva.

— — — Now begins the fifth chapter, second quarter: "Bhavana" means that in which things come into being or are born; the suffix *lyuṭ* is used here in the sense of a locus (*adhikaraṇe*). "Are born" means they arise or originate.

By this, the root *bhū* in the sense of "arising" (*utpatti*) is understood here, not the one in the sense of "existence" (*sattā*). For if that [latter] were understood, then in the case of things already arisen elsewhere, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasajyeta*) that they would have to be located even in whatever place they are subsequently placed. If, however, the root *bhū* is understood in the sense of arising, then the mention of the "field" (*kṣetra*) would be purposeless. It is included for the sake of ensuring that the expression "the arising of mung beans in a granary" (*mudgānāṃ bhavanaṃ kusūle*) does not occur.

Nor does the inclusion of the word "bhavati" (comes into being) entail the undesirable consequence [of applying it] to a granary, for that is not the locus of the arising of mung beans and the like; what then? It is the locus of their existence (*sattā*). This is not so; for when the word "field" (*kṣetra*) is included, the verb "bhavati" here signifies arising.
How so? This word "field" denotes the substratum of the arising of grains.
Therefore, when that [word] is included, the ground does not receive the designation "field" with respect to mere existence; thus, it is logical that the verb "bhavati" applies to its arising.
But if the term "field" (*kṣetra*) were not employed, the word *bhavati* would be understood as denoting mere existence;
in that case, it would follow [absurdly] that even a granary (*kusūla*) is a field.
Furthermore, there is also a conventional usage of the word *bhavana* meaning "house," which too would be excluded by the word "field."

Now, how is the genitive case as the governing inflection (*samarthavibhakti*) introduced? For since [the rule] *tataḥ* (Pāṇini 5.1.119) follows, the genitive as the governing inflection is already established by that very rule. If this is so, then this [usage] indicates that preceding suffixes do not necessarily arise from a word governed by the genitive case.
Therefore, [we have the rule] *tataḥ* (Pāṇini 5.1.135).

The suffix *ccha* is established in its own sense (*svārtha*) after the word *hotrā* when it is in the nominative case (*prathamā-samartha*); thus, *hotrā* itself becomes *hotrīyam*. And in this way, the suffix *iyaN* is established in its own sense after words such as *catur-varṇa* when they are in the nominative case. [The statement] "This is stated because *khañ* would otherwise apply; in one alternative (*pakṣe*), that [suffix *khañ*] also occurs" is appropriate insofar as *khañ* occurs in the alternative after *tila*, *māṣa*, and *aṇu*; for these are grains (*dhānya*).
But since *umā* and *bhaṅgā* are not grains (*dhānya*), the [interpretation] that they are optional is not tenable;
for whatever is recited in Vedic sentences such as "sesame for me and barley for me," that alone is grain. Only barley and the like are recited in the mantra, not *umā* and *bhaṅgā*.

If even those two were considered grains (*dhānya*), they too should have been listed [among the seventeen]; therefore, it is understood that they do not possess the nature of grain. Consequently, the suffix *khañ* does not apply to them, for if it did, it would also occur optionally. Thus he says: "In the case of *umā* and *bhaṅgā*" and so forth. According to the traditional law (*smṛti*), there are seventeen types of grains;
among these, since *umā* and *bhaṅgā* are also enumerated as grains, their status as grain is indeed accepted.
Furthermore, as for their non-recitation in the Veda, that is because they are not applicable to Vedic rituals;
therefore, the intention is that they do not possess a lower status (adhānyatva) merely due to their non-recitation there. Here, the meaning of the suffix is established.
In that case, the hide would have either the status of an instrument (*karaṇatva*) or the status of an agent (*kartṛtva*).
In this regard, if [the word] possesses the status of an instrument (*karaṇatva*), then there must necessarily be an instrumental case ending (*tṛtīyā*) characterized as an instrument.

Alternatively, if it possesses the status of an agent (*kartṛtva*) itself, then since the genitive is prohibited by the rule *na lokāvyayaniṣṭhākhalarthatṛnām* [Pāṇini 2.3.69], the instrumental ending characterized as an agent remains.

Therefore, considering that the instrumental case—the "case of capacity" (*samarthavibhakti*)—is obtained through the force of the meaning of the suffix, he says: "from that which has the instrumental as its base of competency" (*tṛtīyāsamarthāt*).
And that designation "of all leather" (*sarvacarmaṇaḥ*) is formed by making a compound of the word *sarva* with the word *carman*.
To one who thinks, "Therefore, its connection is only with the word *carman*, for no other [word] can logically form a compound with it," he says: "And here the word *sarva*... and so forth.
If this is so, would a compound not fail to occur due to a lack of semantic capacity (*asāmarthya*)? To this he says: "In that case, this... and so forth.
The intention is that [the form *carmī*] arises precisely from this irregular derivation (*nipātana*).

Now, why is it not understood as being connected with "leather" (*carman*) itself? To this he says: "made entirely of leather. For in this case, the formation of a secondary derivative (*taddhita-vṛtti*) is desired to express the meaning of the entire sentence.
In this way, indeed, this very sentence-meaning is understood as being accompanied by the secondary derivative (*taddhita*):
in this sense, the function of the secondary derivative is obtained in the sentence-meaning only if the word "all" (*sarva*) is connected with "made" (*kṛta*) and not with "skin" (*carman*).

If the word "all" were connected with "skin," there would be either a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*) or a descriptive compound (*karmadhāraya*) in the form *sarvacarmaṇā*. In that case, if it were a genitive compound, the meaning understood from the secondary derivative would be "made by skin belonging to everything."

In a *karmadhāraya* compound, however, the meaning is "made with all leather. This [meaning] is not of two kinds—that which is understood from a word ending in a *taddhita* suffix—but rather only this: "made with all leather.

Therefore, since it is impossible to understand the connection of the word *sarva* ("all") with "leather," its connection with "made" (*kṛta*) alone is logical. [As for the term *darśana*: it is called *darśana*] "because it is seen in this."
The suffix *lyuṭ* is used here in the sense of the locus (*adhikaraṇa*).
In the word "yathāmukham," there is an *avyayībhāva* compound according to [Pāṇini 2.1.7], *yathā’sādṛśye*.
"Yathāmukha" means that which is similar to the face (*mukhasya sadṛśam*).
What, then, is that? It is a reflection (*pratibimba*) based upon a mirror (*ādarśa*).

Now, one might object: "Since there is a prohibition [of compound formation] by the rule 'asādṛśye' (Pāṇini 2.1.72), a compound should not occur here. To this he replies with "By way of irregular derivation" (*nipātanāt*), and so forth.
Furthermore, this compound is one in which the meaning of the first member is predominant (*pūrvapadārthapradhāna*).

Since the first member expresses a non-substantive (*asattvavacana*), the suffix is appropriately applied only when it is in the nominative case (*prathamā*). Alternatively, because of the *jñāpaka* (indicatory evidence) in [Pāṇini 2.4.83], case endings beginning with the accusative (*dvitīyā*) occur after an indeclinable compound (*avyayībhāva*); therefore, the suffix is appropriately applied due to its compatibility with the accusative case.
Regarding the expression "yathāmukhaṃ yatāmukhīnaḥ," it means "one who sees what is similar to the face. Here, the genitive case is used in the sense of the object (*karman*).

That in which the entire face is seen, such as a mirror and so forth, is described in this way. Now, for what purpose is the base (prakṛti) uttered in the accusative case in the sūtra? Is it for the sake of [triggering] the suffix by virtue of the power of that accusative? Or rather—this is not an accusative in [the rule] *pathyaṅgakarmapattrapātram*; for words like *pathin* are not connected with the action of "pervading" (*vyāpnoti*), but rather with the word *sarva*. Therefore, the status of being the object (*karmatva*) belongs to that [word *sarva*] alone, and not to its components such as *pathin* and the rest.

Why is that? Because that [word] is not in the dual; rather, by means of a transposition of case endings (*sub-vyatyaya*), this is the nominative in place of the ablative. Why? Because the compound *samāhāra-dvandva* is neuter, the substitution of *am* for the case-ending was made according to Pāṇini 2.4.83: *ato'm*.
Thus, [the word] is "pariśiṣṭam" (the remainder).

And regarding the rule "sarvādeḥ pathyaṅgakarmapattrapātram": words such as *pathin* do not occur at the beginning of a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) that begins with *sarva* and so forth. Therefore, by virtue of the logical necessity (*sāmarthya*), it is understood that the rule applies to those [stems] ending in these [words]; thus he says: "ending in *pathin*, *aṅga*, *karman*, *pattra*, or *pātra*."

Regarding the term *sarvapathīna*: "this is both *sarva* and *panthāḥ*"; thus, by the rule *pūrvakāla-* [Pāṇini 2.1.48] and others, a compound is formed. Then, by the rule *ṛkpūrabdhūḥpathāmānakṣe* [Pāṇini 5.4.74], the suffix *a* is added as the final member of the compound; hence [the form *sarvapatha*]. Now, one might object: once the compound-final suffix has been applied, the word no longer ends in *pathin*. To this we reply: there is no fault, because the rule [for the suffix *-īna*] applies on the basis of whatever in this case ends in *pathin*.

"But surely, because of the intervention [of other elements], the rule does not apply?"—[this is answered] by the inclusion of the term "compound" (*samāsa*). Since suffixes added at the end of compounds (*samāsānta*) are included by the mention of "compound," there is no intervention. This is established by the rule *tayor avyayībhāvaḥ* (Pāṇini 2.4.18).
Thus, it is said:
"The measurement of a cloth is expressed even though it is not connected with the body."
For, by virtue of his fitness for attainment, he is capable of reaching the body down to the tips of the toes.

Now, what is the distinction between pervasion (*vyāpti*) and attainment (*prāpti*), such that when it is said "he pervades," it is stated that "he attains"? Attainment is merely a connection; pervasion is that very same connection in its entirety—this is the distinction. [Regarding the rule] *anurāyāme* and so forth: when there is extension (*āyāma*), then [the compound is formed] according to Pāṇini 2.1.16.

When it denotes similarity (*sādṛśya*), then by the rule "the indeclinable *yathā* [is compounded] with what ends in *tara*" (Pāṇini 2.1.7), and subsequently by "an indeclinable [is compounded] with a word ending in a case-suffix" (Pāṇini 2.1.6) and so forth, the form *yathāpadam āyatam* is established; and likewise, *baddhopānad anupadīnā*. When denoting similarity, it is *yathā anupadam*, and thus it is called *anupadīnā* because the sandal is bound according to the size of the foot.
The meaning is "measured by the foot.
Even when the prefix *anu* signifies similarity (*sādṛśya*), this meaning should be understood [here], for similarity consists precisely in having an equal measure.
"To the right" (*pradakṣiṇam*).
*Ayana* means "going";
it may be said to consist of going clockwise (*pradakṣiṇa*). *Anaya* means "counter-clockwise" (*prasavya*).
That which is contrary to this is called *ayānaya* (wrong direction).

Having thus shown the meaning of the individual components (*avayavārtha*), he says "of those moving clockwise and counter-clockwise" (*pradakṣiṇaprasavyagāminām*) and so forth, in order to show the meaning of the whole (*samudāyārtha*). The plural number is used for the purpose of indicating the various causes of *ayānaya*.
If the pieces move both clockwise (*pradakṣiṇa*) and counter-clockwise (*prasavya*), then there is *ayānaya*; not otherwise.

In this context, one's own pieces move clockwise, while those belonging to the opponent move counter-clockwise. When these pieces, moving in such a manner, reach their respective positions and—due to that specific mode of movement consisting of clockwise and counter-clockwise motion—are not occupied (*asamāveśa*), meaning they are neither sat upon nor attacked by the opposing pieces belonging to the adversary, that is called *ayānaya*. It is not merely the act of moving clockwise and counter-clockwise itself that constitutes it.
This is the method: it should be understood that when the squares are occupied by pieces accompanied by allies, then [the capture is prevented];
for indeed, the squares of pieces that have allies cannot be occupied by others, whereas those that are without allies certainly can be.

Regarding the phrase "situated at the head of the board" (*phalakaśirasi sthitaḥ*): on that board where they play with dice, there is a well-known position at its head for the *kiṭavān* (gamblers); a *śāra* (man) situated there is called "the *ayānayīna*," because the word *ayānayīna* is conventionally established (*rūḍha*) in that very sense.
Others, however, explain it as: "to be led" (*neya*), meaning "to be moved" (*netavya*), but not having been moved from there.
Regarding this, they say that since the meaning "situated on the head" is untenable, the text must be understood as meaning "it is placed on the head of the board" (*phalaka-śirasi sthāpyate*).
Alternatively, [the term] *nītaḥ* (brought) may be used for *neyaḥ* (to be brought), because it serves as an indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*) of that state;
it is expressed by means of its future condition.
Even though all [the words] are related to both *ayā* and *anaya*, it has already been stated that the suffix arises from the qualificand (*viśeṣya*) alone.

Although the governing rule for the second case (*dvitīyā-adhikāra*) is already in effect, the repetition of the term "second case" is for the purpose of ensuring that the suffix occurs only after a word ending in the second case that is actually observed [in usage].
Consequently, the suffix arises from the word *ayānaya* when it ends in the second case and denotes a specific object to be led (*neyavacana*), and not from the mere word *neyavacana* itself.

That very method (*naya*) which proceeds clockwise and counter-clockwise is what has been shown by the passage beginning with "sa eva viśiṣṭaḥ. Now, regarding the word *ayānaya*: if this were a collective *dvandva* compound, it would have to be neuter, and thus [the form] would have to be *ayānayaṃ*. If, on the other hand, it were a *itaretarayoga* [compound], it would have to be dual because it consists of two members, and thus [the form] would have to be *ayānayau*. This is not a *dvandva*; rather, it is a *tatpuruṣa* compound belonging to the *mayūravyaṃsakādi* group: *anaya* accompanied by *aya* is *ayānaya*.

Now, regarding the expression *baddhābhakṣayatineyeṣu*, how can there be a *dvandva* compound of verbal forms (*tiṅanta*)? Who, moreover, says that this is a *dvandva*? If it is not a *dvandva*, how is the plural form *neyeṣu* justified? [The answer is: because the formulation is *sautra* (belonging to the Sūtras). Or rather, by means of a transposition of case endings (*sub-vyatyaya*), the plural is appropriate in place of the singular in Vedic usage. But surely it has been stated that the transposition of case endings occurs in Vedic; is this not Vedic? [To this we reply: "The Sūtras are like Vedic. (Mahābhāṣya)
Thus, there is no fault.
Alternatively, this is simply a *dvandva* compound and not a form ending in a verbal suffix (*tiṅanta*);
for this word "bhakṣayati" does not end in a verbal suffix.

What then? It is a particle (*nipāta*) resembling a verbal suffix (*tiṅanta*), having the same meaning as a verbal suffix, just like the word *asti* in the expression *astikṣīrā brāhmaṇī* ("a Brāhmaṇī woman who has milk"). But how is it possible to see the occurrence of this particle without a suffix, given that its formation is prescribed in conjunction with a suffix? To this he says: "It should be regarded as simply another word (*śabdāntara*). Regarding the form *gāmī*:
the suffix *ṇini* is applied in the sense of necessity (*āvaśyaka*) according to Pāṇini 3.3.170, *āvaśyakādhamaṇryayorṇiniḥ*.
Furthermore, this word *gāmī* functions in the future tense, as it is said: "One who will go is called *gāmī*."
And that [future] status is obtained from the rule "sā ca bhaviṣyati vṛttiḥ" (Pāṇini 3.3.3); thus he says "in the future," and so forth.
"By the rule 'akenorbhaviṣyadādhamaṇryayoḥ,' there is a prohibition of the genitive case. The intention is that by this, its capacity to govern the accusative case is established.
For the genitive case [ending] connected with a *kṛt* suffix is an exception to the accusative; therefore, when the genitive is prohibited, it must indeed be the accusative.
Regarding the example "avārapāram": this is a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*) meaning "the further shore of the near shore" (*avārasya pāram*).
And it should be stated that the prior placement of the genitive case [member] is optional;
by this, in one alternative, *pārāvāram* also occurs.
[The phrase] "even from a separated compound" means:
[The reading is marked as "bhavati-mudritaḥ"] "And from the opposite.

But how is it that, since the second case-ending is already obtained through the governing rule (*adhikāra*) alone, an additional mention of the second case is made here? By this, it is indicated that the suffix occurs after something additional to that [governing rule]. Consequently, the suffix is justified even after a compound that has been analyzed (*vigṛhīta*) and after the opposite.

Regarding the term "atyantam": it is either the absence of an end (*anta*) or the passing beyond (*atyaya*) an end. It is an *avyayībhāva* compound formed according to the rule *avyayaṃ vibhakti* [Pāṇini 2.1.6] and so forth.
Alternatively, *antamatikrāntam* is a *tatpuruṣa* compound according to the rule *kugatiprādayaḥ* [Pāṇini 2.2.18]. It is an adverbial modifier (*kriyāviśeṣaṇa*),
meaning "one who goes excessively."
Because in common usage the word *atyanta* is well known in the sense of "excessive" (*bhṛśa*).
Regarding the term *anukāmam*:
that which resembles desire (*kāma*) is *anukāma*.
The meaning is "in accordance with desire.
This is an *avyayībhāva* compound used in its literal sense (*yathārthe*).
This, too, is indeed an adverbial modifier (*kriyāviśeṣaṇa*) [of the verb]. [Regarding the phrase] "year by year" (*samāṃ samām*).

The doubling [of the word] occurs for the sake of distributive repetition (*vīpsā*), as indicated by the rule: "[8.1.4]". Therefore, it is said: "‘Samāṃsamām’ is a distributive repetition"; "a collection of *subanta* words is the base form (*prakṛti*)."
Because of the force of the statement within the governing context of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*),
[the meaning is] "it bears a fetus," since verbal roots have multiple meanings.

"Regarding the rule *pūrvapade supo’lugvaktavyaḥ*: when a taddhita suffix is produced, since the designation *prātipadika* applies by [Pāṇini 1.2.46], the elision of the case-ending (*subluk*) would follow by [Pāṇini 2.4.71]; therefore, its prohibition must be stated. They say that 'the verb *vijani* also occurs in the sense of the delivery of a fetus.'"

Thus he thinks: when [the action] occurs in the context of conceiving a fetus (*garbhadhāraṇa*), the locative case here is indeed the second case (*dvitīyā*) due to absolute conjunction (*atyantasamyoga*), not the seventh case (*saptamī*). The seventh case is appropriate in the context of releasing the fetus (*garbhavimocana*), as in the word *vijanau*. [The phrase] "merely the elision of *yat*" means: *pratyayalope pratyayalakṣaṇam* (P. 1.1.62) "When a suffix is elided, the operation conditioned by that suffix still takes effect. In this rule, the word *pratyaya* ("suffix") is mentioned twice. One instance refers to the suffix itself, while the other refers to the grammatical operations conditioned by it. Therefore, the meaning is: even when a suffix is elided, the operation conditioned by that suffix is still applied. For example: *paṭayatīti paṭuḥ* ("he makes cloth, thus clever"). Here, the suffix *śatṛ* (present participle marker) is elided after the root *paṭ* by P. 3.2.174 (*āto maninkvanibvanipaśca*). Although the suffix is elided, the operation conditioned by it—namely, the substitution of *ku* for the final letter of the stem—is still applied by P. 7.3.52 (*aṭkupvāṅnumvyavāye 'pi*), resulting in the form *paṭuḥ*. However, there is an exception: the operation conditioned by a suffix does not apply when the suffix is elided by P. 1.1.63 (*na lumatāṅgasya*). This rule states that when a suffix is marked with the elision indicator *luk*, *lup*, or *ślu`, the operation conditioned by that suffix is not applied. For example: *gomān* ("possessing cows"). Here, the suffix *matup* is elided by P. 5.2.94 (*matau bahvaco 'najirādīnām*), and because it is marked with *luk*, the operation of lengthening the vowel (*pūrvapadāt saṃjñāyām aṇiṇoḥ* / P. 8.4.3) is not applied. Thus, the form remains *gomān* rather than *gomān*. Furthermore, the operation conditioned by a suffix does not apply when the suffix is elided by P. 1.1.64 (*na padāntadvirvacanavareyalopasvarasavarṇānusvāradīrghajaścarvidhiṣu*). This rule specifies that certain operations are not blocked by the elision of a suffix when they concern: (1) the end of a word (*padānta*), (2) reduplication (*dvirvacana*), (3) the *vara* suffix, (4) the elision of *ya*, (5) accentuation (*svara*), (6) homogeneous vowels (*savarṇa*), (7) the nasalization (*anusvāra*), (8) lengthening (*dīrgha*), or (9) the substitution of *jaś* and *car* sounds. For example: *dadhi atra* ("curd here"). Here, the case ending *su* is elided by P. 6.1.68 (*svamornapuṃsakāt*), but the operation of sandhi (*iko yaṇ aci* / P. 6.1.77) is still applied to the final *i* of *dadhi* because the elision is not one of those specified in P. 1.1.64. Thus, the form becomes *dadhy atra*. Regarding the term *yalopamātram*: the word *mātra* here signifies "mere" or "only," indicating that the elision of *yat* alone is intended, without implying any other grammatical operations. This refers to the elision of the *yat* portion of the suffix *kyac* (or similar formations), which results in the base form being used directly. For instance, in the derivation of *putrakāmyati* ("desires a son"), the suffix *kāmyac* is added to *putra* by P. 3.1.9 (*supa ātmanaḥ kyac*), and then *kāmyac* is elided by P. 6.1.9 (*kyaci ca*) to form *putrakāmyati*. In such cases, the elision of *yat* is merely the removal of the suffixal element, leaving the base intact for further application of rules. Thus, the distinction between these rules lies in whether the elided suffix is marked with *luk*, *lup*, or *ślu* (which block operations), or whether it is simply elided without such markers (where operations conditioned by the suffix may still apply). This ensures the precise application of grammatical transformations across various morphological derivations.

For it is not the case that the entire *samā* (compound) is pervaded by the release from the womb (*garbhavimocana*); thus, by means of the word *mātra*, he shows that there is no elision of every case-ending.
[He says] "of the remainder," meaning of the suffix *ām*. [He says] "in the case of non-origination."
Regarding the *taddhita* suffix:

[the rule] "and of the final member" (*uttarapadasya ca*). Because of the word "and" (*ca*), it must be stated that there is elision of the preceding member (*pūrvapada*). Since the elision of the letter *y* is prescribed in connection with the suffix, it would not apply in its absence; therefore, this supplementary rule (*upasaṃkhyāna*) is provided for that case. [The phrase] "in a secluded place where birth is imminent" (*avaṣṭabdhe vijane āsanne prasave*).

In this instance, the meaning of the first two words is explained by the latter two respectively: "abhyamitrāt" (from the enemy). "Abhyamitram" means facing toward the enemy; it is an avyayībhāva compound according to [Pāṇini 2.1.14].
This is an adverbial modifier (*kriyāviśeṣaṇa*);

therefore, the second case (*dvitīyā*) alone is the governing case-ending (*samarthavibhakti*). Since the suffix *caraṭ* would have applied by the rule "In the sense of 'formerly existing,' [the suffix] *caraṭ*" (Pāṇini 5.3.53), the suffix *khañ* is prescribed here. Thus, "that in which cows stand is a *goṣṭha*" (cow-pen).
In *supiṣṭhaḥ* [Pāṇini 3.2.4], the suffix *ka* is applied; by the rule *ambāmbagobhūmi-* [Pāṇini 8.3.97] and others, the cerebral (*mūrdhanya*) substitute is applied.
Regarding *bhūtapūrve*:
that which existed previously is *bhūtapūrva*.

The compound is formed by [Pāṇini 2.1.4] *sup supā*. Regarding the statement, "the mention of 'having previously been' (*bhūtapūrva*) is a qualification of that very [word]," it should be understood as being mediated by the meaning, just as in sūtras such as [Pāṇini 3.1.7] *dhātoḥ karmaṇaḥ samānakartr̥kāt*, where there is both the state of being an object (*karmatva*) and the state of having a common agent (*samānakarttṛkatva*). For example: "that which is traveled in one day is *ekāhagama*."

The suffix *ghañ* is applied by the rule *akartari ca* [Pāṇini 3.3.19], and due to irregular derivation (*nipātana*), there is no *vṛddhi* strengthening. Then, the compound is formed by the rule *āto 'nupasarge kaḥ* [Pāṇini 3.2.3] and *āto dhātoḥ* [Pāṇini 6.4.140]. Thus: "having flown a hundred *yojanas*."
The meaning is: "having gone a hundred of those *yojanas* which are traversed in a single day.

The word "hundred" (*śata*), while denoting a number, functions by its very nature to take up its own corresponding numeral. Therefore, even when there is grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the word *āhvāna* (invocation) in the sense of many things—as in "a hundred invocations"—the word is used in the singular ending alone. [This is illustrated by the phrase] "in whatever way."
"In whatever manner" means by any means whatsoever.
He shows that one should not be overly attached to the literal meaning of the individual components by stating: "and there is the elision of the final member of the compound" (*uttarapadalopaśca*).
The final member (*uttarapada*) consists of the words *praveśana* (entry) and *avataraṇa* (descent); their elision (*lopa*) occurs.

"Shālīna means 'dull-witted'. For such a person, even though he is capable of giving a reply due to his dullness, when being respected by noble persons, he is unable to remain there—thinking, "The public is watching"—and therefore he deserves entry into a *śālā*.
This word *śālā* here denotes a small hut.

"Kaupīna means sin. For in the world, because it is censurable and unfit to be done, it is called *akārya* (unfit to be done); thus it is said that it deserves (*arhati*) descending into or entering a well (*kūpa*).
By implication, a certain part of the body is denoted by the word *kaupīna*.

Even the garment intended for covering that part of the body is called "loincloth" (*kaupīna*) because of its association with them, such as those who have gone forth (*pravrajita*). "Of various classes" means of many different castes. "Of unsettled livelihoods" means...
Those whose actions are indefinite:
"their activity is called a *vrāta*.
Because of its association with a *vrāta*, that too is called a *vrāta*.

Alternatively—when there is the intention to express the meaning "this belongs to the *vrātas*," although *cha* would [otherwise] apply, by virtue of this very irregular derivation (*nipātana*), *aṇ* occurs.
That, moreover, is the activity such as carrying loads and so forth.
[The phrase] "it is not desired in that case" refers to this.

But how is it that even though [the meaning] is desired, it does not occur? Because in the present *Mahāvibhāṣā*, the *vibhāṣā* (optionality) is fixed. [The rule states: "The form *sāptapadīna* is an irregular formation (*nipātana*).
What, then, is irregularly formed here? The suffix and the meaning of the suffix are under discussion;
and the meaning of the suffix *khañ* is "attainment" (*avāpti*).
The compound is formed in the sense of a secondary derivative (taddhita), meaning "attained by means of seven steps.
From the word *saptapada*, the suffix *khañ* is then applied. Regarding the phrase beginning with "How," etc.:
[it refers to] the action of a friend or the state of being a friend (*sakhyam*).

In that regard, if *sāptapadīna* were derived as a primary derivative (*nipātana*), its grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the word *sakhi* (friend) would not be possible; for the questioner’s intention is that "friendship itself does not become a friend.
Regarding the phrase "that which has a subordinate [element] as its principal" (*guṇapradhāna*), etc.:
that whose subordinate element (*guṇa*)—whether it be an abstract state (*bhāva*) or an action (*karman*)—is the principal is described as such.
When it functions with reference to the quality alone by way of primary denotation, then it should be understood as having the quality as its predominant factor;
"in that case, there is grammatical coreferentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya) with the word 'friend' (sakhi)," because both [words] function with respect to the same referent.
"But when," and so forth.

"Indication" (*lakṣaṇā*) means metaphorical usage (*upacāra*). When, through the metaphorical usage of non-difference between the property (*dharma*) and the possessor of the property (*dharmin*), the suffix *taddhita* functions by a figurative application (*gauṇyā vṛttyā*) toward a person (*puruṣa*) possessing number, then it becomes coreferential (*samānādhikaraṇa*) with that very [word].

Just as when the word *śukla* (white) refers solely to the quality (*guṇa*), it does not stand in grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with a word for a substance (*dravya*), as in "the white of the cloth" (*paṭasya śuklaḥ*); but when, through connection with the word "you" (*tvam*), it refers to the cloth, then coreferentiality occurs, as in "the white cloth" (*śuklaḥ paṭaḥ*); so too should it be understood here. Regarding the statement "In place of *hrogodoha*, there is the substitute *hiyaṅgu*": the meaning is that the word *hiyaṅgu* is the substitute for *hrogodoha*. *Hrau godohanaṃ* is *hrogodohaḥ*; this is a compound formed according to [Pāṇini 2.1.4], *sup supā*.

"The suffix *khañ* is applied in the sense of a modification" (Pāṇini 4.3.134); this is an exception (*apavāda*) to the suffix *ṣyañ* that would otherwise apply. Regarding the suffix *aṇ*, [the rule] "an exception to *aṇ*" (Pāṇini 4.3.120) applies; when *aṇ* is about to be applied, the suffixes *kuṇap* and others are prescribed.

Because there is no purpose for the letter *ja*, the designation *it* (as per Pāṇini 1.3.7) does not apply. Regarding the rule "those prescribed in a single yoga [are understood to recur]," the recurrence of words such as *ādi* occurs by virtue of their being marked with the *svarita* accent;
this is because their recurrence is contingent upon the formal declaration (*pratijñā*) of the *svarita* accent.

Even for those elements taught in a single *yoga*, the *svarita* accent occurs only where it is specifically prescribed, and not elsewhere. Therefore, it is logical that even among elements taught in a single *yoga*, there may be the recurrence (*anuvṛtti*) of only one part. For example: *vidyācuñcuḥ*, *vidyācaṇaḥ*. Now, why does the letter *c* in the rule *cuṭū* [Pāṇini 1.3.7] not receive the designation *it*? The reason for this has already been stated in that very place: the formulation of a separate rule is for the purpose of making known that this grammatical operation is not universally obligatory (*anitya*). [The rule states: "The suffixes *nān* and *añ* occur in the sense of the base itself (*svārthe*)."
This is because of the rule: "Suffixes whose meaning is not specified [express] their own base-meaning" (Pāṇini Sūtra 3.1.125).
The letter *ñ*, however, is for the purpose of making the initial syllable udātta.

*Bālamanaoramā*: "From *vi* and *nañ*, [the suffixes] *nān* and *añ* [are applied], provided that [the resulting sense] does not mean 'together' (*saha*). (Pāṇini 5.2.27). The compound *nasahe* functions as a distinct unit;
this is an adjective qualifying the base form (*prakṛti*).
Thus he says: "in the sense of non-accompaniment" (*asahārthe*).
Its explanation is: "in the sense of separation" (*pṛthagbhāve*).
After the words "from those ending in the present participial suffixes" (*vartamānābhyām*), the remainder of the rule, "from *vi* and *nañ*" (*vinañbhyām*), is to be supplied.
Regarding "its own meaning":
the sense is that the meaning of the suffix has not been specified. Regarding "the two suffixes": [this refers to the fact that they have been mentioned].
The phrase "various knowledges" (*nānājñā*) is to be supplied [in the verse] according to their respective order. Regarding the word *vinā*:
it is a form derived from the verbal root *vi* with the suffix *na*.
The meaning is "separately" (*pṛthak*). Regarding "various" (*nānā*): it is a form derived from the negative particle *nañ* with the suffix *nāñ*, resulting in initial vṛddhi.
The meaning is "separately" (*pṛthak*). However, if *na-saha* were the meaning of the suffix, then by the word *na*, it would be understood as "not with" (*na saha*).

This being the case, the sense would be: "not not with," but rather "together indeed. This is clear from the *Bhāṣya*: "Two negatives convey the original meaning. [The relevant rules are: *vinañbhyāṃ nānāñau nasaha* (Pāṇini 5.2.27) and *vaiḥ śālacchaṅkaṭacau*. (See also the *Bālamano-rāmā* and other commentaries.)
Regarding the phrase *kriyāviśiṣṭā*:

this means that the suffixes *śālac* and *śaṅkaṭac* are applied in their own sense (*svārthe*) after a word denoting a *kāraka* (participant in an action) qualified by an action (*kriyā*). This has been clarified in the Bhāṣya with the statement beginning *sasādhanakriyāvacanāt*.

This has been stated: prefixes (*upasarga*) are of such a nature that where some word expressive of an action (*kriyāvacī śabda*) is employed, they are said to qualify that action; where no such word is employed, they express the action along with its factors (*sādhanakriyā*). In this case, no word expressive of an action is employed; therefore, the suffix occurs after the prefix which expresses the action together with its factors.

And as for that word *bhavan*? Because of the rule "suffixes whose meaning is not specifically stated apply in their own sense" (*Pāṇini 5.3.125*), it applies in its own sense due to its unspecified meaning,
[yielding] "one whose horns have fallen off."

By this, he shows that the word *vi-* occurs in the sense of the action of going away (*vigamana*) when that action has the horns as its instrument (*sādhanā*). If the suffix were applied to an action accompanied by its instrument, then forms such as *viśālo gauḥ* ("the bull with wide [horns]") and *viśaṅkaṭo gauḥ* ("the bull with formidable [horns]") would not be established; for in these cases, the bull is not the instrument of the going away, but rather what is it? It is the horns. To this, he says: "Because of connection with that" (*tadyogāt*), and so forth.

Just as a cow is called "a dewlap" (*sāsnā*)—using the property of a part—due to its connection with parts such as the dewlap, so too a cow is called "wide" or "formidable" due to its connection with wide or formidable horns.
Regarding the phrase "In ultimate reality," and so forth:
the compound is for the sake of etymological derivation.
Therefore, here there is not only an absence of action accompanied by its means, but also an absence of the means itself.

Therefore, words expressing qualities such as *viśāla* and others are conventionally established in the world from the perspective of ultimate reality, just like words such as *śukla* (white) and so forth.
Consequently, one should not insist upon a distinction between the meanings of the base (*prakṛti*) and the suffix (*pratyaya*) in these cases, such as *viśāla*.
Thus, they are ultimately devoid of [independent] meaning.

It is stated that the suffixes *śālac* and *śaṅkaṭac*, even when applied to the root *vi*, are indeed devoid of meaning (*anarthaka*). Regarding the word "these": the plural number is used by taking in mind the words *saṅkaṭa* and others which are about to be derived, for they too are simply quality-words (*guṇaśabda*). It should be understood that everything is exactly as before: a suffix is added in its own sense (*svārthe*) to a prefix (*upasarga*) that expresses an action together with its means (*sasādhanakriyā*).

"Alābūtilomā," and so forth. An addition (*upasaṃkhyāna*) must be made for the suffix *kaṭac* when "dust" (*rajas*) is the meaning denoted [by the compound] from words such as *alābū*. This is an exception (*apavāda*) to the suffixes used for derivatives (*vikāra*); for the dust of things such as *alābū* is a modification (*vikāra*) of them.
Regarding the phrase "goṣṭhādayaḥ" and so forth:
the word "ādi" (and so on) indicates a class or type.

The names of animals are those beginning with the word "go" (cow); from these, when their locations and so forth are to be expressed as the referents, the suffixes *goṣṭha-ja* and others are to be prescribed.
In the desire to express this meaning, [the suffixes] *goṣṭha-ja* and so forth are prescribed for the sense of "place" (*sthāna*) and the others.
Now, one might object: is not everything, such as *kaṭa-ja* and so on, already included by the plural number in rule 4.1.76? True; this is merely an elaboration of the very sentence just mentioned.
[The example is] *avikaṭam*.
In this case, by [Pāṇini 4.2.37], the suffix *kaṭaṭ* is applied in the sense of a collection; thus,
"avipaṭam" refers to the expanse of scattered sheep.
Two camels are "a pair of camels" (*uṣṭragoyugam*); six elephants are "a herd of six elephants" (*hastiṣaṅgavam*); the oil of *iṅguda* is "*iṅguda-tailam*";
the essence of sesame is "*tila-tailam*."
"In the case of *bhavane kṣetre*," and so forth: a field for sugarcane is "an *ikṣu* field" (*ikṣuśākaṭam*) or "an *ikṣu* plantation" (*ikṣuśākinam*).
The field where roots grow is "mūlaśākaṭam" or "mūlaśākinam. Regarding "namanam natam," he shows that the past passive participle (*niṣṭhā*) is used here in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāve*).

"Belonging to the nose"—by this [expression] as well, the genitive case in "of the nose" (*nāsikāyāḥ*) indicates a relationship (*sambandha*). If these suffixes are to be applied when something bent is related to the nose, how then are both the nose and the person denoted by this [term]? To this he says: "Because of connection with that" (*tadyogāt*). [Question: "How are they 'thick' (*nibiḍāḥ*)?"
There is no connection with that here;
therefore, because of the absence of such a connection, the designation [of "simile"] is not tenable—this is the intended meaning. [The opponent suggests:
"It will arise from comparison (*upamāna*)."

"Because of density, the hair and the garments are equal to the nose in terms of density. Therefore, by virtue of that comparison, both of those will be denotable by the word *nibiḍa* (dense). Regarding the phrase "and because of the governing context of technical names (*saṃjñā-adhikāra*)," this refers to the continued application of the governing context of technical names from the sūtra beginning with *nate nāsikāyāḥ* [Pāṇini 5.2.31].

Regarding the phrase "having a restricted object": it is understood as referring specifically to that which is near and mounted upon a mountain. The intended meaning is that, because of this, [the compounds] *vṛkṣasyāsannam* ("near the tree") and *plakṣasyārūḍham* ("mounted on the *plakṣa* tree") do not occur.

Now, regarding the forms *upatyakā* and *adhityakā*, why does the substitution of *it* (the long vowel *ī*) not occur here by the rule *pratyayasthāt kāt pūrvasya* [Pāṇini 7.3.44]? To this he says: "By the rule *pratyayasthāt kāt*. If this substitution of *it* were to take place, the technical name (*saṃjñā*) would not be established; for the technical names are not of the form *nopatyikā* or *adhityikā*. Therefore, because of the governing context of technical names (*saṃjñā-adhikāra*), the substitution of *it* does not occur. By the word "in the sense of the object" (*karmaṇi*), he shows that there is a reference to the actual form of the word "object" (*karmaṇi*).
Now, why is the technical (pāribhāṣika) sense of the word *karman* not accepted here? Because it is impossible. It is impossible because the root *ghaṭ* is intransitive (*akarmaka*). [Note:

In the formation of the suffix *aṭhac*, the pronunciation of the vowel *a* is for the purpose of preventing the substitution of *i* for *ṭha*. The words *bubhukṣā* and *pipāsā* are recited among the *tārakā*-group [of words that take the suffix *aṇ*]. For what purpose is their inclusion there, since when the suffix *niṣṭhā* is applied to the two roots ending in *san* (desiderative), and the augment *iṭ* is added, one obtains the forms *bubhukṣitaḥ* and *pipāsitaḥ* (as in "Devadatta is hungry" or "Devadatta is thirsty")? True; however, because they are prescribed with reference to the past tense (*bhūta*), they would not be established in the present tense (*vartamāna*).
But by this [rule], it is established even in the case of the present tense.
Therefore, the reading of those two [sūtras] is justified:
"after *garbha*, when not denoting a living being."
The suffix *itac* occurs after the word *garbha* when the referent is not a living being (*aprāṇin*). Example: *garbhitāḥ śālayaḥ* ("rice grains that have been impregnated").

Why "not a living being"? [Consider: *garbhaḥ sañjāto 'syāḥ*, *garbhiṇī gauḥ* ("a cow in which a fetus has arisen; a pregnant cow"). Since the word *pramāṇa* is a relative term, its meaning as the object of the suffix is understood accordingly.
"First and second," and so forth.

The suffixes *dvayasaC* and *dadhnac* are prescribed for vertical measurement (*ūrdhvamāna*). That by which something is measured after being placed above—neither horizontally nor all around—is vertical measurement.
"Without distinction" means that the suffix *mātra* occurs everywhere— whether in the sense of weight (*parimāṇa*), measure (*unmāna*), or without distinction—
in such forms as "a mere *prastha*" (*prasthamātram*).
Because of the word *api*, it also occurs as "measuring a span" (*vitastimātra*). [The rule] "the elision of *mātraC* when expressing measure" (*pramāṇe loḥ*) applies here.

Furthermore, this term *luk* is a technical designation (*saṃjñā*) established by the ancient teachers. This elision (*luk*) is prescribed for the suffix *mātraC* that has been produced; it does not apply to the suffixes *dvayasaC* and *dadhnaC*.
Because the rule is prescribed for those [compounds] that have more than two members;
in this case, even the originative injunction (*utpatti*) does not apply,
according to the rule "for a *dvigu* compound, always."
Because a *dvigu* compound is not a measure-word (*pramāṇa*), and even if it were to end in a measure-word, there is no rule for eliding [the case-ending] after such a compound; therefore,
the elision (*luk*) is stated here as being already applicable by the preceding rule.

"What is the purpose of including the word 'nitya' (always)? For an option (*vikalpa*) has not been introduced [in the preceding rule] such that the inclusion of 'nitya' would be made for the sake of excluding it. Nor is it appropriate to include 'nitya' here in order to indicate that the preceding rule operates optionally.
The intention is that this [suffix] is not intended to be optional (*vibhāṣā*). By the words "in case of doubt" (*saṃśaye*), etc., he states the purpose of including the term *nitya* ("constant").

*Śravaṇa* is derived from the prefix *pra-*; the suffix *ghañ* is used in the sense of an abstract action (*bhāva*) according to Pāṇini 3.3.113 (*kṛtyalyuṭo bahulam*). Thus, *śrāvī* means "one who has hearing. Furthermore, this refers to the suffix *mātrac* which is about to be mentioned, as it is spoken of here in connection with measurement (*pramāṇa*).
Regarding the rule "stome ḍaṭ" and so forth:
that sacrifice whose measure is fifteen days is called "pañcadaśaḥ" (fifteen-day) or "pañcadaśī" (the fifteenth).
Because it ends in *ṭi*, the suffix *ṅīp* is applied. Regarding the rule "after *śan* and *śati*,
the suffix *ḍini* [is added]," this prescription applies without distinction both to the sense of a *stoma* and elsewhere.
Regarding "viṃśinaḥ":
[the suffix] ḍiniḥ is applied by [Pāṇini 5.2.137], followed by the elision of *ti* according to [Pāṇini 6.4.142], and the elision of the vowel *ya* (yasyeti lopaḥ).
[The examples are] "śamamātram" and "diṣṭimātram."
There are two examples of measure (*pramāṇa*):
"only a *prastha*" and "only a *kuḍava*" are examples of measurement (*parimāṇa*);
"fivefold" and "tenfold" are examples of number (*saṃkhyā*).
Where it is not determined whether there will be peace or not, the term *śamamātra* is employed.

This should be understood accordingly in other instances as well. Regarding the word *hāstinaṃ*: the preservation of the original stem form (*prakṛtibhāva*) occurs by the rule *hanaṇyanapatye* [Pāṇini 6.4.164].

Regarding "dvipuruṣī": the suffix *ṅīp* is applied by [Pāṇini 4.1.24], "After *puruṣa*, when it denotes a measure, one of the two [suffixes *ṅīṣ* or *ṅīp* is used]. Regarding "dvihastinī": [the same applies].

In this case, the suffix *ṅīp* is applied by the rule *ṛnnebhyo ṅīp* [Pāṇini 4.1.5]. Regarding the form *yāvān*: the vowel *a* is substituted [by *yasyeti ca* 6.4.148]; the augment *num* is added by *ugidacām* [7.1.70]; the lengthening occurs by *sarvanāmasthāne cāsambuddhau* [6.4.8]; and the elision of the final consonant (*hal*) and the following vowel (*ṅy-ādi*) occurs due to the rule for the elision of a conjunct at the end of a word (*saṃyogāntalopa*).

Thinking that the words *pramāṇa* and *parimāṇa* are synonyms, one might raise this objection: "Why is the term *parimāṇa* mentioned here, since the term *pramāṇa* is already understood by implication? To him, he replies: "While [the word] *pramāṇe* is being carried over," and so forth.

Furthermore, the distinction between these two, *pramāṇa* and *parimāṇa*, has already been explained previously: "But *parimāṇa* is on all sides, whereas *pramāṇa* would be length (*āyāma*). [This is stated in the rule: "The suffixes *ḍāc* and *tāp* [are applied] because of a difference in meaning."
This reference is made with respect to the technical designation *ḍāvatu* established by the ancient teachers (*pūrvācārya*), for they indeed applied the suffix *ḍāvatu* to these [words].
That which is distinguished is a "distinction" (*viśeṣa*); the state of being a distinction is "distinctiveness" (*vaiśeṣyam*).
The distinctiveness of the meaning is the specific quality of the meaning; such is the sense.

The word *pramāṇa* has one meaning, while the word *parimāṇa* has another; thus, these two have distinct meanings. Therefore, since there is a difference in their meanings, when the suffixes *ḍāp* and *vatup* are to be prescribed, the mention of the word *parimāṇa* is stated separately. The word "is stated" (*ucyate*) means "is performed. For what purpose is this separate mention made? He says: "In order to prevent [the application of] *mātra* and so forth."

He says that the separate mention is made for the purpose of ensuring that the suffixes beginning with *mātra* are not superseded, since the distinction in meaning is already established by the separate enumeration.

Now, if there is identity—that is, if the general base (*prakṛti*) is the same—then suffixes such as *mātraJ* and others, being prescribed, constitute general rules (*utsarga*). However, the suffix *vatU*, being prescribed from a specific base (*prakṛtiviśeṣa*), constitutes an exception (*apavāda*). According to the principle that "the general rule is set aside by the exception," if [the bases] were identical, suffixes such as *mātraJ* would not apply after the words *yad*, *tad*, and so on; consequently, forms such as *tanmātram asya pramāṇam* ("that is its measure") would not be established. Since there is no relationship of general rule and exception when the meaning is different, this undesirable consequence does not arise.
Furthermore, regarding the statement "The state [of being a suffix] is established for those ending in *ḍāp* and *ṭāP*," the term "*ḍāvatoḥ*" is in the ablative case.
When there is a difference in meaning, the derivation of suffixes such as *mātraj* and others from words ending in the suffix *vatup* is established.

The suffix *vatup* occurs in the sense of measure (*parimāṇa*): "that which is its measure" becomes *yāvān*. From that [form] ending in *vatup*, suffixes such as *mātraj* occur in the sense of measure: "that which has such a measure" becomes *yāvanmātram*.

Now, if there were identity [between the base and the suffix], then by the rule *uktārthānāmaprayogaḥ* (Vyāḍīya-paribhāṣā 60), since this meaning would not have been expressed by the possessive suffix *matup*, the suffixes *mātraj* and others could not follow that which ends in it; thus [forms such as] *tvāvataḥ* and *māvataḥ* would not be possible. Furthermore, for *yuṣmad* and *asmad* ending in *map*, the substitutes *tva-* and *ma-* [are applied] according to *yuṣmadasmador maparyantasya* (Pāṇini 7.2.98), and their accentuation is as before. [The form] *kiyān* [is derived similarly].
Regarding the word *iyān*:
by the rule *kimaḥ kī* [Pāṇini 5.2.40], *kim* becomes *kī*;
and by the rule *idama īś* [Pāṇini 5.3.3].

The elision [of the *vat* suffix] occurs by [Pāṇini 5.2.39], *yasyeti ca*. But by what rule is the substitution of *gh* for the *v* of the *vatup* suffix prescribed after *kim* and *idam*? To this he says: "Or else," and so forth; namely, "or by means of a division of the *yoga*."
By means of the rule *kim-idam-bhyām* alone, the suffix *vatup* is prescribed; thereafter, by the rule *vo ghaḥ*, the substitution of *gh* for the *v* of *vatup* is ordained.

Now, what is the purpose of including the mention of *v* (*vagrahaṇa*), since by the rule *ādeḥ parasya* [Pāṇini 1.1.54], the *gh* substitution is ordained for the *v* itself? Is it not the case that because [the substitute *gh*] consists of more than one phoneme (*anekāl*), it would result in a total replacement (*sarvādeśa*)? This is not a fault, for here the vowel *a* is merely for the sake of pronunciation (*uccāraṇārtha*) and is a mere phoneme (*varṇamātra*), not an actual substitute (*ādeśa*). How, then, is this to be understood? From the explanation (*vyākhyāna*).

In that case, since the substitute *va* is indeed lighter, it is proper to take it as the substituendum (*sthānin*). Even if the substitute for the entire complex (*samudāya-adeśa*) is adopted when *va* is not the substituendum, there is no fault; for the single-substitute form (*pararūpa*) will apply to the two *a*-vowels. [The compound] "the measure of a number" (*saṃkhyāyāḥ parimāṇam*) contains a genitive case ending in the sense of the object (*karman*), characterized by its connection with a *kṛt*-suffix.
*Parimitiḥ* means measure (*parimāṇam*). The sense is the delimitation by number. *Paricchedaḥ* is formed with the suffix *ghañ* in the sense of an abstract action (*bhāve*).
Regarding the phrase "from that which exists in the delimitation of number":
the intended meaning is "from that which exists in a number characterized by delimitation.
This very meaning of the statement will be made explicit later on.
"The substitution of *gh* for that *v*" is because of the continued application (*anuvṛtti*) of the rule "vo ghaḥ" (Pāṇini 8.2.32).
Regarding the phrase "because it is being questioned":
this refers to when the word *kim* functions to delimit a number.

And when does it occur? When number (*saṃkhyā*) is being inquired about. For a determination is not possible for that which is not being inquired about. And when it is being inquired about, then—because it is being inquired about—is it understood that the suffix occurs after the word *kim* when it denotes a number that brings about a determination, since the word *kim* functions with respect to a determination characterized by that inquiry?

That which has "delimitation" (*pariccheda*) as its limiting adjunct (*upādhi*)— that is to say, as its qualifier— is "that which has delimitation as its adjunct. By this, the intended meaning of the word *kim* when it functions in the sense of numerical delimitation has been clarified.
Regarding the word "kati":
there is elision (*luk*) by [Pāṇini 7.1.22] *jasaḥ*.
Regarding the phrase "or rather" (*atha vā*), and so forth.

And in this explanation, *saṃkhyāparimāṇe* is a *karmadhāraya* compound; by virtue of irregular derivation (*nipātana*), there is this reversal of the subordinate member (*upasarjana*). Furthermore, the word *parimāṇa* is derived as an instrument (*karaṇasādhana*), meaning "that by which something is measured. [The phrase] "of such a nature" means:
He clarifies the meaning of this by means of the phrase "having the nature of delimitation" (*paricchedasvabhāvā*).

That by which something is delimited is "delimitation" (*pariccheda*); that which has this as its nature is described as such. With the words beginning with "wherein" (*yatra*), he demonstrates for what purpose number is qualified by the mention of measure.

It might be argued: "There is no such distinction at all where number does not have the nature of delimitation; therefore, that qualification is useless. To this he says: "For in the case of 'kṣepa' (negation/exception)," and so forth. "What is this number of these ten?"—in this context, number is not intended as a delimiting factor.
For there is no restriction here, because the sentence is intended for the purpose of censure (*kṣepa*).

In this context, the word *kim* functions as censure and not as a question. Regarding the form *catuṣṭayī*: [the substitution of] *sa* occurs by Pāṇini 8.2.34 (*catur-ṛt-aḥ*), and the retroflex (*mūrdhanya*) replacement occurs by 8.3.101 (*tasya api*); then the feminine suffix *ṅīp* is applied by 4.1.15 (*ṭiḍḍhāṇañ...*). [The author asks: For what purpose is the mention of the suffix *tayap* [in the rule], since it will already follow from the current context? He replies with the words "The mention of *tayap*" and so forth.

If the mention of *tayap* were not made, then this suffix *ayac* would be understood as something entirely different from the suffix *tayap*, rather than being a substitute for *tayap*. What, then, would happen if it were a different suffix? The operations (*kārya*) pertaining to *tayap* would not apply to *ayac*. What are those? [The rule] beginning with Pāṇini 1.1.33 provides the optional designation (*saṃjñā*) of "pronominal" (*sarvanāman*) when the suffix *jas* follows—thus: *dvaye*, *dvayāḥ*; and by Pāṇini 4.1.15, the feminine suffix *ṅīp* is applied—thus: *dvayī*.

But surely, since that [suffix] was already prescribed by the preceding sūtra, its recurrence here is understood for the purpose of providing a substitute (*ādeśa*), as there is no other purpose—namely, in the rule *dvitribhyām* [P. 5.2.43]. The ablative case ending (*pañcamī*) will be converted into a genitive ending (*ṣaṣṭhī*) by [the rule] *pañcamīnirdeśaḥ* [Vārttika 1 on P. 1.1.67]; therefore, even without the explicit mention of *tayap*, the status of *tayap* as the original element (*sthānitva*) is indeed obtained. This is not so; for if the recurrence of *tayap* were not for another purpose, then its status as the original element would be understood through the force of that recurrence. However, it is for another purpose. Thus, the point is established.
However, its continued application (anuvṛtti) serves a purpose for what follows;
thus, by means of a separation of the rules (yogavibhāga), the suffix *tayaP* must be prescribed.
And that which is being continued cannot itself be prescribed.

Therefore, since the subsequent rule would otherwise apply, it is improper for *tayap* to be the substitute; thus, the mention of *tayap* is made. Regarding the phrase "by the force of the statement" (*vacanasāmarthyāt*), etc.:
if [the word] were to have its final syllable acute (*antodātta*), the prescription of an acute accent would be purposeless.
Furthermore, once *ayac* is applied, by the accent of the *cit* suffix itself, the principle that "the subsequently prescribed accent is stronger" (*satiśiṣṭasvaro balīyān*) would prevail.

Since the final acute accent (*antodāttatva*) is established by [Pāṇini 6.1.164], the initial acute accent (*ādyudāttatva*) would otherwise not be established; therefore, that which is being performed for its sake becomes a meaningful statement. "If it is a worldly number," etc.

Like *dvitrādi*. By the preceding rule (*yoga*), the suffixes *tayaP* and *tayap* are prescribed; by the subsequent rule, the substitution of *ayac* is prescribed as obligatory for that [suffix]. As in: "both gods and humans" (*ubhaye devamanuṣyāḥ*).
Those which have both as their two parts are called "both" (*ubhaye*).

How can there be two parts for gods and humans when there is a plurality [of them]? Even though there is plurality here, duality also certainly exists in the two bases (*prātipadika*); for in this case, the two groups are the two parts of the aggregate—one group being that of the gods and the other that of humans—and thus there is no fault.

*Bālamanauramā*: Regarding the rule *tadasminnadhikaṃ iti daśāntāḍḍaḥ* (Pāṇini 5.2.44): now, concerning suffixes denoting possession (*matvarthīya*). The meaning is that in the analytical statement (*vigraha*) "that is more in this" (*tadasminnadhikaṃ tadadhikamasmin*), the suffix *ḍa* shall occur after a compound ending in the word *daśan* which stands in the nominative case, in the sense of "in this. The mention of the word "end" (*anta*) is for the purpose of excluding the application of the rule regarding the inclusion of what ends with [a specific stem] (*tadantavidhi*) when a suffix is prescribed.
Precisely because of this indication, they say that the locative case (*saptamī*) here functions in the sense of the ablative (*pañcamyarthe*).
The *Bhāṣya* states: "The locative case is used for the locus of contact (*aupaśleṣika-adhikaraṇa*).
Kaiyaṭa explains: "The locus of proximity (*sāmīpika-adhikaraṇa*).
[The example is: "In this [quantity], there are eleven additional māṣas."
The meaning is "from this" (asmāt),
or "those which are attached to this" (asmin).

Nor should it be suspected that [the suffix] would also occur from the word *daśan* alone by virtue of the principle of "treatment like the principal designator" (*vyapadeśivadbhāva*), for it has been stated that "the treatment like the principal designator does not apply to what is not a nominal stem" (*aprātipadikena*).
*Bālamano ramā*: "After *ubha*, [the suffix] is always udātta" (Pāṇini 5.2.44). "And that is udātta" means it is udātta on the first syllable (*ādyudātta*).
It is clear in the Bhāṣya that the fact of being acutely accented on the final syllable (*antodāttatva*) is established by its very nature as a *cit* suffix.
Regarding this, it is clear in the Bhāṣya on the *sthānivadbhāva* rule that "only the suffix *ayac* is prescribed here, and not a substitute for *tayap*";
however, the statement in the root text (the Kāśikā) that it is "a substitute for *tayap*" follows the Vārttika. Thus ends the section on the fifth case-affixes in the Bālamanoramā.

Now begins the section on the *parasmaipada* (active voice) formation. He proceeds to determine the rules for the *parasmaipada* with the rule: "After the remainder, in the sense of the agent" (*śeṣātkartari*). Regarding the phrase "and by the meaning of the suffix," etc.: if the meaning of the suffix is of such a nature, and the meaning of the base is of that very same nature, then the suffix is applied, and not otherwise. To demonstrate that the meaning of the base is of the same class as the meaning of the suffix, he presents an example: "eleven *kārṣāpaṇas*."
The meaning of the base (*prakṛti*) is also exactly eleven *kārṣāpaṇas*; thus, the meaning of the base belongs to the same category as the meaning of the suffix (*pratyaya*).
Regarding the phrase "But here, however, not... and so forth:
for in this case, the hundred *kārṣāpaṇas* is the meaning of the suffix.
The meaning of the base word, however, is eleven *māṣas*;
and since these are of a different kind from the *kārṣāpaṇas*, the suffix does not apply.
[This is because] it is desired that [the suffix] occurs only after the words "hundred" (*śata*) and "thousand" (*sahasra*).

Why [is this so]? Because a suffix is desired after "ten" (*daśan*) and after "hundred" (*śata*) or "thousand" (*sahasra*) when they are preceded by that [word], but not after any other [number] such as "twenty" (*viṃśati*) and so on.

But how is it obtained from the sūtra when it is not explicitly mentioned? To this he says: "The particle *iti* is for the purpose of indicating the intended meaning," and so forth. "How," and so forth.
If a suffix were to be applied when there is an addition to a hundred or a thousand, then in this case—namely, "eleven hundred"—the suffix would not be obtained.
For here, the intention is that there is another number added, neither a hundred nor a thousand.
[The commentary] says: "Of hundreds," and so forth.
By this, he excludes other numerical values.

When the word *śata* (hundred), ending in the genitive case, is compounded with the word *sahasra* (thousand), then the compound *śatasahasra* denotes a thousand of hundreds. However, when the word *sahasra*, ending in the genitive case, is compounded with [the word] *śata*, then the compound *śatasahasra* denotes a hundred of thousands.

But surely, when the word *sahasra* ending in the genitive case is compounded, it should become *sahasraśatam*, as seen in the *rājadantādi* group? There is no fault, for its placement at the end [of the compound] will occur.

Thus it is established by the rule "in that case, of *śata* and *sahasra*" (*tatra śatasahasrayoḥ*), because the meaning expressed by *śatasahasra* is already included within the two words *śata* and *sahasra*.
Regarding the phrase "in the case of an excess" (*adhike*) and so forth:

in common usage, when there is an excess of the same kind as the meaning of the suffix, the grammatical operation known as a suffix is desired only for the numbers hundred (*śata*) and thousand (*sahasra*).
However, when the excess is of a different kind, and neither a hundred nor a thousand is intended to be expressed by the meaning of the suffix, then it is not desired.

Now, regarding the [number] "one hundred and eleven" (*śatasahasram*), in what case should the suffix *ḍa* be applied? To this he says: "of which," and so forth. "Number" (*saṃkhyā*) means counting or enumeration.
When there is an excess of that which possesses the number, the suffix *ḍa* should be applied.

And of what does the number consist? That which is exceeded is counted as the number. When hundreds are being counted, it is "a thousand of hundreds," which is *śatasahasram*; in that case, the suffix *ḍa* must be applied when there is an excess of hundreds. For example: "in this thousand, eleven is in excess" becomes *ekādaśaṃ śatasahasram*.
But when thousands are being counted—as in "a hundred thousands" (*sahasraśatam*)—then the suffix *ḍa* must be applied to indicate the excess of thousands:
for example, "one hundred thousand in which eleven thousands are in excess" (*ekādaśaṃ śatasahasram*).

Now, for what reason is the nominative case-ending (*prathamā-samartha-vibhakti*) employed [in the rule *tasmin*]? For surely the phrase "that has arisen for him" (*tad-asya sañjātam*, Pāṇini 5.2.36) continues to apply; in that case, should not the meaning of the suffix (*pratyayārtha*) itself be specified as "in this"? It cannot be so; for if that [phrase] were to continue, there would follow the continuation of its related referent "for him" (*asya*), which is the meaning of the genitive. And there is no contradiction between the meanings of the genitive and locative cases, given the specification "in this" (*asmin*). The previous meaning of the suffix does not cease; however, if that were to continue, the suffix would also occur in the sense of the genitive.
Therefore, in order to exclude that [previous] "of this" (*asya*), the word "that" (*tat*) is again introduced with the first case-ending (*prathamāvibhakti*) as its governing factor (*samartha*).

If this is so, since the meaning of the suffix in "of this" (*asya*) has been excluded, would it not follow that a suffix in the sense of the genitive (*ṣaṣṭhyarthe*) is not obtained in the rule *[[Pāṇini 5.2.47]]*? There is no fault here, because even though it has been excluded, it will recur by way of the "frog-leap" maxim (*maṇḍūkapluti-nyāya*).

Others, however, explain that "that" (*tat*) is an indicator (*jñāpaka*). They say: "That"—referring to what is under discussion—is an indicator; namely, that which is specified in rules such as *tadasya sañjātam* (Pāṇini 5.2.36) does not enter into the status of a subordinate member (*aṅga*) even when it is carried over (*anuvartamāna*) here, and thus a suffix is not applied in the sense of the genitive case. Now, one might object: in rules such as *tiṃraśadāder ḍaṭ* (Pāṇini 5.1.59), words like *triṃśat* end in the suffix *śat*; therefore, by the technical rule regarding the mention of a suffix (*pratyayagrahaṇaparibhāṣā*), a suffix would be obtained from that which ends in it. So, what is the purpose of explicitly mentioning the ending (*antagrahaṇa*)? To this, he says:
Regarding the statement "the mention of 'end' [is made] when there is a mention of 'six,'" etc.:

if the mention of "end" were not made, then by the *paribhāṣā* concerning the mention of a suffix (*pratyayagrahaṇa-paribhāṣā*), [the operation] would apply only to that which begins with the element from which the suffix is prescribed, and not to what follows it. Therefore, the mention of "end" is for the purpose that [the operation] may also apply to what follows that element.
