If, then, [the suffix] is prescribed after that [which begins with a number], the mention of "the end" (*anta*) is for the sake of including more than that; it would not apply to a solitary [number]. This is not a fault; the particle *ca* ("and") is used here, and it serves to include what has not been mentioned. Therefore, it will also occur after a solitary [number]. Regarding the statement, "The mention of 'number' (*saṃkhyā*) must also be made":
that by which a number is grasped is the "mention of number"; that must be made.
What, then, should be done? An explanation [is required].

The explanation there is as follows: from the rule *saṃkhyāyā avayave tayap* [Pāṇini 5.2.42], the term *saṃkhyāyāḥ* (of a numeral) is carried over; therefore, [the suffix] will occur only after a numeral, not after anything else. This applies to the rule *viṃśateśca* and so forth.
The meaning is that this must be explained as having the following sense: the suffix *ḍa* occurs after the nominal stem *viṃśati* and also after a nominal stem ending in *viṃśati*.

In this regard, the explanation is as follows: first, the suffix occurs directly after the word *viṃśati* as explicitly mentioned in the sūtra; furthermore, it occurs after a word ending in *viṃśati* because the particle *ca* has the function of including what is not explicitly stated.
In the passage beginning with "And the mention of 'number' (*saṃkhyāgrahaṇam*)," the same meaning applies as before.
The explanation is also the same as before: "that by which a quality is measured" means it is exchanged or sold.
"That too," and so forth.
For it is not possible to determine that the quality designated as "the thing to be measured" (nimeya) possesses the status of a part without [the measuring instrument] having the status of a part;

for when the root [instrument] lacks the status of a part, the designation "part" does not apply at all. Therefore, even though the status of being a part has not been explicitly stated for the measurer (nimāna), it is nevertheless understood through implication.
"Two parts of barley are its *nimāna*.

Now, although there is an exchange in both cases, nevertheless, the word *nimāna* is conventionally established (*rūḍha*) in the sense of "price" alone; therefore, only that which is intended as the price becomes the *nimāna*, and not anything else.
[The word] "of barley" (*yavānām*).
The genitive case is used in the sense of a "portion" (*bhāga*).
If this is so, then since the word *udaiāt* depends on something else, the occurrence of the secondary derivative (*taddhita*) would be contradicted.

[Objection: But the suffix is applied to the portion that begins with *ud*, not to *ud* itself; so how can there be grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) between the word ending in the suffix and the word *udaiāt*, as in the expression "the *udaiāt* consisting of two [parts]"? To this, he says: "But even in the case of a portion," and so forth.

In this case, moreover, the reason is the inherent nature of the expressive power [of the suffix]. Just as [suffixes] such as *aṇ* and others, although prescribed in relation to the connection between offspring and progenitor, denote the related party primarily due to the inherent nature of their expressive power—as in "Aupagavaḥ" (the son of Upagu) or "Dākṣiḥ" (the son of Dakṣa)—so too this [suffix], being prescribed in relation to a part (*bhāga*), denotes the possessor of the part (*bhāgin*) such as Udañc and the like. Furthermore, in the rule "guṇasya," singularity (*ekatva*) is intended to be expressed.

The singular number in the word *guṇasya* is intended to be significant. Now, it might be argued: "Even in the rule *taddhitāḥ* [Pāṇini 4.1.76], the plural number is not authoritative because it is not intended to be significant"; how then is it appropriate here to intend the singular number? This is not a fault; for in this case, one should form a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*) and apply the suffix only to express the measure of the quality (*guṇanimāna*), for in this way the sūtra becomes concise.

Since this is what ought to be stated, the fact that he utters the singular form *guṇasya* indicates this: namely, that singularity is intended here. By the words "by that" (*tena*) and so forth, he demonstrates the purpose of intending singularity. For when singularity is intended, this is the purpose: that [the rule] should apply when there is a comparison of a single quality, as in:
"two parts of barley, three of rice."
In this case, since the word "two" (*dvi*) functions as a measure for three parts, the suffix is not applied.

But surely, even when there is a desire to express oneness, the suffix should not be applied here, because of the rule stating: "The suffix is desired after a number that expresses a greater quantity"?
Indeed, the word "two" does not express a greater quantity here. If that is so, then the two parts of barley that exist are intended here as the things to be measured (*nimeya*).
The three parts that have arisen are [the basis] for the suffix *nimāna*.

In that case, if there were no intention to express oneness (*ekatva-vivakṣā*), then the suffix would apply to the three qualities (*guṇa*) that have arisen. Furthermore, regarding the rule "and from that which is more numerous" (*bhūyasaś ca*), it is desired that the suffix be applied to that which expresses a greater number of the meanings of the base (*prakṛtyartha*), and not otherwise.
"It does not occur here" because of the absence of expression,
or because of the recurrence of the particle *iti* from the sūtra beginning with "that is in excess in this" (Pāṇini 5.2.45).

If it is intended that [the term *nimāna*] applies only when there is a greater number of verbal units, then it would not apply in the case of the expression "two parts of barley are its measure" (*yavānāṃ dvau bhāgau nimānam asya*)? To this he says: "And [in the case of] 'greater'," and so forth. For even in such a case, it would follow: "two and a half parts of barley rise up," since here there is indeed an excess of the meaning of the base word (*prakṛti*) over the meaning of the suffix (*pratyaya*). To this he says: "It is a word denoting a quality" (*guṇaśabda*), and so forth. This word denoting a quality, although expressing a part, also expresses the equality of that part; however, the word "and a half" (*ardha*) does not denote an equal part.
"And it is seen even in the case of *nimeya*.

By what, then, is it prescribed that it is seen? By this very [rule]. How so? There are two sentences here; in one of them, the word *nimāna* has the sense of an instrument (*karaṇa-sādhana*)—that by which something is measured is a *nimāna*; but in the second, it has the sense of an object (*karman-sādhana*)—that which is measured is a *nimāna*. [This is established] by Pāṇini 3.3.113, where the suffix *lyuṭ* is applied in the sense of the object.

When [the word *guṇa*] is derived as an instrument (*karaṇa*), then the genitive case in "of the quality" (*guṇasya*) expresses the object; but when it is derived as an object (*karman*), then it expresses the agent.
For a quality is intended to be expressed as the agent because it is the instrument of the act of bartering.
Indeed, there is an intention to express the instrument as the agent, as in the example: "The axe cuts."

In that regard, by one sentence, a suffix is prescribed when the number (*saṃkhyā*) currently residing in the standard of measurement (*nimāna*) has the object of measurement (*nimeya*) as its expressed meaning (*abhidheya*). By another [sentence], a suffix is also stated when the number currently residing in the object of measurement has the standard of measurement as its expressed meaning.
And the basis for this syntactical split (*vākyabheda*) is the mention of "number" (*saṃkhyā*), following from the rule *saṃkhyāyā avayave tayap* [Pāṇini 5.2.42].
And thus, the mention of "number" (saṃkhyā) continues [from the previous rule]. This is the second [instance here].

In that regard, if there were only one sentence here, the second mention of "number" would be purposeless; however, when two sentences are constructed based on the inference from the Sūtra, it becomes meaningful.
Therefore, there are two sentences here:
"The two, rice and barley," and so forth. In this context, the two—rice and barley—are not intended as the measure for the portion of the *udaidha*; rather, it is the *udaidha* itself.

Thus, in the case of "two qualities" (*dvauguṇau*) and so forth, the word ending in the nominative case functions as the measure of the quality. For a portion of oil is not measured by two portions of milk.

The addition of the suffix *mayaṭ* with the augment *ṭi* is for the sake of [the feminine suffix] *ṅīp*: "two of molasses, one of grapes" (*dvimayī drākṣā*). Here, two mentions of the word "number" (*saṃkhyā*) are carried over; among them, by the first, the base (*prakṛti*) is qualified by the rule "from a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) expressing a number. But by the second, he says "by which," etc., in order to qualify the meaning of the suffix (*pratyayārtha*). By pronouncing the word "enumeration" (*saṃkhyāna*), he shows that the meaning of the suffix is qualified by the word "enumeration," which expresses a number.
For the word "number" (saṃkhyā) is of two kinds: that which expresses the act of counting and that which expresses the object counted.

In this context, if the meaning of the suffix were qualified by the word expressing the object counted, then the meaning would be as follows: "that by which a countable object, such as a handful and so forth, is completed—that is, made to exceed [the previous total] by another substance—is a 'pūraṇa' (completer). Consequently, the term would apply even in a case such as "a jar for five handfuls.
Therefore, it is proper to qualify the meaning of the suffix only with the word expressing the number itself.
Regarding the word "sampadyate," he explains its meaning as "it is filled. By this, he demonstrates that the meaning of the suffix is qualified by the expression of number.

The completion of a number is not the addition of an extra substance to substances, as in the case of [counting] fistfuls; rather, it is simply their attainment (*sampatti*). This is shown by the passage beginning with "it does not occur here," and so forth. For when a jar is produced, the number five does not become attained by means of fistfuls.

What then? In that case, there is merely the addition of another substance (*dravyāntara*) to those very five [categories] numbered by the suffix *ḍaṭ*. [The rule states: "The augment *maṭ* occurs after *ḍaṭ*. Now, why does the suffix *maṭ* not occur directly after the stem ending in *n*? It is not fit to be a suffix. For if it were a suffix, the recurrence (*anuvṛtti*) of *ḍaṭ* would be purposeless; since *ḍaṭ* has already been prescribed previously, the recurrence of what has already been prescribed cannot logically serve the purpose of its prescription.
And that [suffix] is understood to have the sense of *āgama* (augment).

But is there not any distinction in cases such as *pañcama* and so on—whether *maṭ* is an *āgama* or a suffix? For its form is the same, its accent is the same; what is the use of the subsequent rule? Let *maṭ* itself be the suffix. True, there is no distinction here; but in cases such as *viṃśatitama*, there is a distinction.
For in those cases, by [Pāṇini 5.2.56], the suffix *maṭ* would otherwise apply.
Words beginning with the twentieth [ordinal] would have the acute accent on the middle syllable by virtue of the accent of the suffix (*mayaṭ* being the printed reading).
However, when the suffix *ḍaṭ* is present, since it is assigned an acute accent on its initial syllable, and subsequently the augment is unaccented, they become oxytone (acute on the final syllable).
Therefore, for the sake of the subsequent rule, it is understood here as well that *ḍaṭ* alone is the suffix that is being carried over.

But how can the augment *maṭ* be prescribed for the suffix *ḍat*, given that the mention of *ḍat*—which was introduced in the nominative case as the subject under discussion—is now required [here] in the genitive case? To this, [the author says]: "from that which ends in *n*" (*nāntāt*), and so forth.

Although the mention of *ḍat* was introduced in the nominative case, nevertheless, because of its connection with the augment *maṭ* [by the rule] *pratyayasya lopaḥ* (Pāṇini 1.1.62), this fifth-case form (*pañcamī*) "from that which ends in *n*" (*nāntāt*) causes the first-case form *ḍat* to be interpreted as a sixth-case form (*ṣaṣṭhī*); thus there is no fault.
"The fifth" (*pañcamaḥ*).

In this case, the elision of *ṭi* does not occur; for once the suffix *maṭ* has been applied, the [stem] receives the designation *bha*. Now, one might object: "But surely, because it is subsequent, the elision of *ṭi* ought to take place first? This is not so; the augment *hr̥* is *antaraṅga* (internal), as it is prescribed in connection with the suffix itself. The elision of *ṭi*, however, occurs only after the suffix has been produced and the designation *bha* has been established, depending upon both the base and the suffix; thus, it is *bahiraṅga* (external).

"Eleventh" means "that which completes the eleven. But how is this obtained from this [rule], given that the mention of "number" (*saṃkhyā*) continues [from the previous rule]? For even a collection of numbers is included by the mention of "number," since it is formed with the sense "by means of which something is numbered. This must necessarily be understood in this way; otherwise, there would be no formation for words like *adaśata*. Thus, [the commentary begins] with "In this case, by the locative case," and so forth.
In the section concerning the suffix *pūraṇa*, the suffix *hray* is prescribed as being enjoined in conjunction with *ḍat*.
Although the locative case (*saptamī*) is not explicitly present there, it is nevertheless understood to follow after *ḍat*.
Therefore, by implication, there occurs a transformation of the case-ending; thus, that which is expressed as "after *ḍat*" (*ḍaḍiti*) is here transformed into the locative.
"The word *katipaya* is not a number.

Why? Because it lacks worldly status; it is not a number because it is not recognized as such in common usage. Nor is it technical (śāstrīya); for its designation as a "number" is not prescribed in the grammatical treatise (*śāstra*).
If it is not a number, how can the suffix *ḍaṭ* apply to it, since the augment *thuk* is prescribed [only] when that suffix follows? To this he says: "of that," and so forth.
From the very fact that the augment *thuk* is prescribed for the word *katipaya* when *ḍaṭ* follows, it is determined that the suffix *ḍaṭ* occurs after this word;
hence [the form] "sixth" (*ṣaṣṭhaḥ*).
The substitution of *ṣṭ* occurs;
here, the elision of the *ṭi* does not take place,
due to the force of the rule prescribing *thuk*.
The designation of the preceding part of the *āgama* is for the sake of applying the technical term *bha*.
If [the *āgama*] were made to begin with the subsequent element (*parādi*), then the designation *bha* would not apply; and if that were absent, the designation *pada* would apply by [Pāṇini 1.4.17].
Consequently, in the case of *ṣaṣṭhaḥ*, the substitution of the voiced unaspirated stop (*jaś*) would undesirably follow.

Regarding the term "fourth" (*caturthaḥ*): here, the substitution of *s* for the *r* occurs according to [Pāṇini 8.3.34]. However, if it belongs to the prior boundary (*pūrvānta*) and forms part of a technical name (*saṃjñā*), the substitution does not take place. Regarding the statement: "the suffix *tīya* is applied after the word 'two' (*dviśabda*)."

Now, why does the substitution of *tīya* for the suffix *ḍaṭ* not occur after the word *dvi*? Because it serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*). Since the author makes the reference using the feminine suffix *ṭāp* in the rule "dvitīyāṭṭā... [Pāṇini 2.3.2], that indicates that this is not a substitute. If this were so, then since the form would be established by this very rule, the prescription of the suffix would be purposeless. No; it is for the sake of the accent (*svara*).
For by virtue of being a *nipātana*, it would be oxytone according to the accent of the nominal stem (*prātipadika-svara*);
however, with the suffix *tīya*, it becomes circumflex-accented on the middle syllable (*madhyodātta*) by the accent of the suffix (*pratyaya-svara*).
Furthermore, if the suffix were not prescribed, one would have to rely on the principle that "even *nipātanas* can be restrictive exceptions" (*bādhakāny api nipātanāni bhavanti*).

109) Thus, *ḍaḍ* may also occur. If, however, this were a substitute (*ādeśa*) for *ḍaḍ*, what would happen? By the accentuation rule for *ḍaṭ*, the word *tīya* would be oxytone (having the acute accent on the final syllable), and in the feminine, because of the *ṭi*-marker, there would be the suffix *ṅīp*; consequently, the form *dvitīyā* as it is taught [in the grammatical tradition] would not be possible. [The answer is: "The term *aṇ* is understood there," from the rule [Pāṇini 6.3.111].

But surely, since the letter *ṇ* in the subsequent [sūtra] includes *aṇ*, would not the letter *ṛ* also be included as *aṇ*? To this he says: "And by the preceding [rule]," and so forth. Why is it not stated here simply as "*trestrica*" (and for *tri*, *ca*)? It is impossible to state it thus; for if it were stated in that way, there would be doubt: "Is this a substitute (*ādeśa*), or is it an affix (*pratyaya*)? Regarding the phrase "of what follows after *viṃśati* etc.," and so forth: But surely the affix *ḍaḍ* is separated from the word by the affix *tīya*; how then can the augment *tamaṭ* be understood [to apply]? To this he says: "Because of the governing context (*adhikāra*) of 'filling' (*pūraṇa*)."

Since the suffix *tamap* is prescribed after words such as *viṃśati* and others when the sense of completion (*pūraṇa*) is intended, and since no other suffix than *ḍaṭ* is possible in this context, it is understood that *ḍaṭ* itself is meant.
This is because the common worldly number-words beginning with *viṃśati* are included [in the rule],
according to the principle of pervasion (*vyāpti*).
Furthermore, those [numbers] beginning with twenty and twenty-one are included.

Why, then, would there be a need for them if they were not already situated within the rule *paṅktiviṃśati* etc. (Pāṇini 5.1.59)? [The answer is: "The mention of 'hundred' (*śata*) and so forth" means that the mention of 'hundred' and so forth is for the purpose of ensuring that the suffix applies after numerals such as 'hundred' and the like.

Now, what is the purpose of including the term *nitya* (invariably), since by the very force of the rule's commencement (*ārambha-sāmarthya*), the injunction will be understood as invariably applying? It might be argued that [the rule] would apply invariably from words such as *śata* onwards due to the force of its commencement; however, for words beginning with *māsa*, there would be an option (*vibhāṣā*) because of the recurrence (*anuvṛtti*) of the phrase "optionally" (*anyatarasyām*). [Objection: But surely the phrase "optionally" (*anyatarasyām*) will be excluded simply because it is not marked with a svarita accent? [Response: Then the inclusion of the term *nitya* is for the sake of clarity. [Question: Up to the word *śata*? [Response: From the word *ṣaṣṭi* onwards, they should be understood as starting with the suffix *-tama*.

Because the suffix *tamaṭ* is prescribed by its own specific rule for words such as *śata* and others. By the term "*matau*" (in the sense of the suffix *mat*), the possessive meaning (*matvartha*) is expressed, due to their constant association.

Regarding the phrase "*matvarthena*" and so forth: the case ending expressing grammatical competency is the nominative; "existence" (*astitva*) is the qualifier of the base (*prakṛti*); and "this belongs to this" is the meaning of the affix (*pratyaya*). All of this is "implied" by the mention of the possessive sense (*matvartha*).
It is brought near; that is to say, it is presented.
It is logical that when the suffix *matup* is mentioned, the meaning of the suffix is implied, because that [suffix] has that [meaning] as its domain.

How are the case endings for semantic competency (*samarthavibhakti*) and so forth implied? Through association with the meaning. Alternatively, because subordinate elements follow the principal, once the meaning of the suffix is presented by way of its predominance, that which is subordinate is also necessarily presented through the power of the suffix itself.
In this context, a word such as *asyavāmīya* is a sentence because it consists of multiple words.

And since the rule for including compounds (*samāsa-grahaṇa*)—which states that the designation of "nominal stem" (*prātipadika*) applies to meaningful collections—is for the purpose of restriction, these words do not possess the designation of "nominal stem. Therefore, one might object that the [suffix] does not apply to them because they are not nominal stems. To such an objection, he replies with the words "and words that are imitations," etc.
By the mention of "imitation" (*anukaraṇa*), he eliminates the status of being a sentence in the case of *asyavāmīya* and similar forms.

Indeed, imitation words (*anukaraṇa-śabda*) do not possess constituent parts that are *pada*s; therefore, how could they have the status of a sentence (*vākya*)? For if they did, they would lack the designation of a nominal stem (*prātipadika*).

By the phrase "having their own form as the primary element" (*svarūpamātrapradhāna*), he demonstrates that they possess meaning (*arthavattva*); for if they were meaningless, they would not receive the designation of a nominal stem, since the rule for the designation of a nominal stem applies only to those things that possess meaning. If they lacked the status of a nominal stem, [the application of suffixes] would not occur.
And in that case, the very absence of a condition would result.
The word "mere" (mātra) is for the purpose of excluding other meanings.
Those [words] whose primary denotable object is the mere essential nature (svarūpa-mātra) are described as such.

The word *ca* (and) has the sense of "because. Because imitation-words (*anukaraṇaśabda*) produce a suffix while having their own form as the primary element, therefore the grammatical operation known as a suffix is established even from multiple [sounds], since that [imitation-word] possesses the status of a nominal stem (*prātipadika*).
Its lack of nominal-stem status would otherwise arise either because it is a sentence (*vākya*) or because it is meaningless (*anarthaka*).
Nor is there the status of being a sentence in cases such as *asyavāma-prabhṛti*, because these are words of imitation (*anukaraṇa*).
Nor are they meaningless, because they possess meaning by virtue of their own form alone.

If, in examples such as *asyavāma*, there exist multiple constituent words within that word of imitation, then how is it said that [the suffix] is established even from a multi-word form? [The answer is: this is stated according to the conventional usage of others regarding what constitutes a "word."
The same applies to *asyavāmā* and others.
Since many of their constituent parts are well-known, it was stated thus on account of that well-known status, and not because they actually consist of multiple words.

Now, how can words of imitation (*anukaraṇa-śabda*) provide merely their own form, given that the object being imitated is their very denotation, and therefore that alone constitutes their primary form? This is not so; for here, a suffix is prescribed after a word ending in the nominative case that is coreferential with the verb *asti*.

Even though onomatopoeic words (*anukaraṇaśabda*) possess meaning through the object they imitate, when they are subsequently reflected upon by means of the particle *iti* or by the word "word" (*śabda*), they become nominally governed (*prathamāsamartha*) and coreferential with [the following] word. For it is not possible for those [words] which have become subordinate to a meaning to be nominally governed or to function as qualifiers (*upādhi*).

Thus, when it is said, "In this there is the short vowel 'a'," it is understood that the very word being imitated—which is made known by the onomatopoeic word—is what is nominally governed and functions as the qualifier, but not the onomatopoeic word itself.
Therefore, by means of the particle *iti* or by the word "word" (*śabda*), there must necessarily be a reflective reference (*pratyavamarśa*).

In the case of the expression "asyavāmīya," because one says "the word *asyavāma* exists in this [text]" or "it exists in this," the status of the word as a referent for a differentiated object is set aside, and its status as a referent for its own form (*svarūpa*) alone arises.

But if this is so, the possessive suffix (*matvartha*) is not justified; for the words of the sacred tradition (*āmnāya-śabda*) exist as the objects to be imitated (*anukārya*) in the case of *sūkta* and *sāman*, whereas the worldly words that are imitations (*anukaraṇa-śabda*) do not. This is not a fault; because of the presence of particles such as *iti*, which are causes for syntactic independence (*vākya-svātantrya-hetu*), the imitative words, being referred back by them, become meaningful in their own form; however, in a compound (*vṛtti*), they are meaningful only through the object to be imitated, because there is an absence of particles like *iti* which cause syntactic independence.

Since it is precisely in the *vṛtti* (the commentary) that the possessive suffixes expressing the sense of "having" (*matvartha*) are intended to be stated for the *sūkta* and the *sāman*, and not for the *vākya* (the sentence), what here is not appropriate? [The names] *āsyavāmīyam* [is so called] because the word *asyavāma* exists in this;

*kayāṣubhīyam* [is so called] because the word *kayāṣubhā* exists in this. And this grammatical construction is an exception (*apavāda*) to the general rules for possessive suffixes. [This is so] because in the immediately preceding sūtra, the suffix *cha* is prescribed only for the *sūkta* and the *sāman*; and because in another context, the suffix *cha* is not prescribed for the *adhyāya* or the *anuvāka*. He asks: "By what, then," and so forth.
Elision (*luk*) is not applicable when [the suffix] is shortened; indeed, this very elision is what he states.
Therefore, this very mention of elision indicates that there is a rule for the application of *cha* after the names of chapters (*adhyāya*) and sections (*anuvāka*). "And optionally," and so forth.
The word *ca* is used for emphasis, meaning "only by way of an option.
But how is it obtained as an option? Because of the continued application (*anuvṛtti*) of the term *anyatarasyām* from [Pāṇini 5.2.56].

If this is so, would it not follow that there is also an option for the suffix *cha* in the previous case? There is no fault, for the suffix will carry over by the maxim of the "frog's leap. When the suffix *cha* is to be elided (*luk*) by the rule *pūrveṇa cche tasya ca pakṣe luki prāpte vimuktādibhyo 'ṇ vidhīyate* (Pāṇini 5.2.60), the suffix *aṇ* is prescribed after words such as *vimukta*. When the suffix *cha* is to be elided (*luk*) by the rule *cchasya ca luki prāpte goṣadādibhyo vun ārabhyate* (Pāṇini 4.3.38), the suffix *vun* is prescribed. When the suffix *aṇ* is to be applied by the rule *aṇi prāpte vun vidhīyate*, [the suffix *kan* is prescribed]. In the case of words such as *ākarṣa*, when the suffix *cha* is to be applied to those that are *vṛddha* (having a long vowel in the first syllable), the suffix *kan* is prescribed for the remaining words when the suffix *aṇ* is to be applied.

The purpose of introducing another suffix (*pratyayāntarakaraṇam*) is so that, in this case, there may not be *guṇa* substitution for that which ends in *-u*, and there may not be the elision (*lopa*) by the rule *yasyeti ca* [Pāṇini 6.4.148] for that which ends in *-ī*.
If the suffix *vun* were applied, both of those [undesirable results] would follow;
consequently, unrefined speech (*aśiṣṭa*) would result here once again.

Furthermore, whether that [desire] exists in the forest or elsewhere, there is no distinction; thus, it does not require a separate condition (*pratyayāntara*). "Desire for wealth" (*dhane kāmaḥ*) means a longing directed toward wealth. Regarding "being occupied" (*prasita*):
although this root *si* belongs to the class "ṣiñ bandhane" (Dhātupāṭha),...
Although the root *pā* (in the form *bandh*) is listed in the sense of "binding," it nevertheless occurs here in the sense of "attachment" because roots have multiple meanings;
as in the expression "attached to [long] hair" (*keśeṣu prasitaḥ*).
The locative case [is used] by [Pāṇini’s rule] 2.3.44.
Furthermore, attachment (*āsakti*) is a property (*dharma*) whose object is action; thus, the action residing in the locus of the hair and so forth is expressed by the word "hair" and so forth.
For this very reason, he says: "When one is engaged in the arrangement of the hair and so forth, it is said thus."
"The plural number [is used] so that it may also apply to a collection of one's own body parts (*svāṅga*).

For if that [plural marker] were not present, just as a collection of provinces is not grasped by the term "province," so too a collection of body parts would not be grasped by the term "body part," and thus [the rule] would not apply to a collection of body parts; but when it is present, it does apply, otherwise there would be no purpose for it.

If it is argued that the purpose [of this rule] is to exclude the *svarūpavidhi* (the application of a suffix to its own form), we say no; for since the term *svāṅga* (one’s own limb) has been defined by the rule *adravaṃ mūrtam...* (Pāṇini 4.1.54), a *svarūpavidhi* is impossible here. Since the suffix *kan* would have applied by the preceding rule, the suffix *ṭhak* is prescribed [instead].
Thus, one says *ādyūnaḥ*, meaning "one who does not desire to win" (*avijigīṣuḥ*).

This is because, according to the rule *vivaḥ avijigīṣāyām* (Pāṇini 8.2.49), the substitution of *n* for the *t* of the past participle suffix (*niṣṭhā*) is prescribed only when the root *vi-vas* is used in the sense of "not desiring to win."

The word *udāraka* is formed by means of the suffix *kan* [added] after the prefix *uda*. The third case ending in *sasyena* is used either to denote association (*sahayoga-lakṣaṇa*) or to denote a characteristic mark of such a state (*itthambhūta-lakṣaṇa*).

As for the statement "this word *sasya* denotes a quality," although the word *sasya* also signifies grain—as in "rice is *sasya*" or "barley is *sasya*"—this was stated, namely "this is a designation," so that its [literal] sense as grain might not be understood here.

Is this [the word] *sasyaka*? It ends in the suffix *kan*. [The rule] "In the sense of the object (*karman*), only the second case (*dvitīyā*) occurs" means that when the second case would otherwise apply in the sense of the object, the sixth case (*ṣaṣṭhī*), characterized by its connection with a *kṛt*-suffix, is introduced as an exception to it.

And for that [sixth case], there is a prohibition by the rule "In the case of *akan* and *ṇin*, [the sixth case is not used] when referring to the future or a debt" (Pāṇini 2.3.70), because the suffix *ṇin* is necessarily present here.
Therefore, it remains without exception as the second [case] itself. Regarding the term *acirāpahṛtam*:

the word *acira* signifies a short period of time; its compound with the word *apahṛta*—meaning "the time which has been taken away from it"—is formed according to [Pāṇini 2.1.37]: *tena gata-rūḍhy-asamāptāḥ*. Regarding the phrase *pañcamīsamarthāt*: [it means] "from that which is in the fifth case (ablative) in its governing sense."

Precisely because of the specific mention [in the rule]. For no case-ending (*vibhakti*) relevant to the present context is being carried over here; rather, the ablative (*pañcamī*) is explicitly heard in the mention. Therefore, it is understood that the suffix occurs after a word-base governed by the ablative. Furthermore, that ablative case is used with the root *apa-hṛ* because it signifies "departure" (*apāya*). Since the base is connected with that [action], it becomes the point of departure (*apādāna*) itself; thus, it should be understood as characterized by the ablative. But for what purpose is this done, since it is derived for the sake of a technical name (*saṃjñā*), and the names *brāhmaṇaka* and *uṣṇika* apply only to a technical name? No; it applies even in other domains.
In order to demonstrate that very object, he says: "where," and so forth. The meaning has already been explained. Regarding the phrase "from an adverbial modifier" (*kriyāviśeṣaṇāt*):
for it has been established that an adverbial modifier functions as the object (*karman*).
Regarding the word *kāriṇi*: the suffix *ṇini* is used here in the sense of habitual action (*tācchīlye*).
Since the use of the genitive case is prohibited when this suffix is employed, the accusative case must necessarily be used for the object.

It is understood that the suffix is applied after words such as *śīta* (cold) when they function as adverbs and are in the second case (*dvitīyā*). Therefore, in this context, the words *śīta* and *uṣṇa*, when referring to the object of touch (*sparśa*), do not produce the suffix.
Where, then, do they produce it? In the sense of slowness (*māndya*) and rapidity (*śaighrya*), because the suffix *ṇini* occurs when necessity (*āvaśyaka*) is implied.
There is no entity that invariably produces both cold and hot sensations;
for even frost and sunlight do not necessarily produce them, as there is the possibility of obstruction.

However, the causal power (*kartṛśakti*) of entities is fixed; thus, it is entirely logical that in the exercise of that power, one may invariably produce [an effect] slowly while another produces it quickly. [This is explained by the rule: "There is the elision of the final member of a compound when a word is superposed [upon it]."
The word [droṇa] situated in the latter member of the compound is elided by way of a grammatical irregularity (nipātana).

But how can there be the use of the word *droṇa* ending in the nominative case—as in "an additional *droṇa* in a *khārī*"—and also its use ending in the instrumental case—as in "an additional *khārī* by means of a *droṇa*"? To this he says: "In the sense of the agent and the object," and so forth.

By the rule beginning with *gatyarthakarmakaśliṣa* (Pāṇini 3.4.72), the suffix *kta* is prescribed after the root *ruh* in both the active (*kartṛ*) and passive (*karman*) voices; consequently, the word *adhyarūḍha* occurs in the sense of both the agent and the object. Therefore, when the word *adhika* is derived in that same sense, it becomes a synonym for those two meanings. In that regard, when it functions as the agent (*kartṛ*), the nominative case (*prathamā*) occurs after the word *droṇa*, not the instrumental (*tṛtīyā*). When it functions as the object (*karman*), because the agent has not been expressed, the instrumental case occurs after the word *droṇa* due to the word *adhika*.
Because the object (*karman*) is already expressed [by another word], the nominative case alone occurs after the word *khārī*, and not the accusative—as in:

*adhikā khārī droṇena* ("A khārī is more than a droṇa"). But surely, in the case of *adhiko droṇaḥ khāryām asyām* ("A droṇa is more in this khārī"), since the object is not expressed [by another word], the accusative would result after the word *khārī*? This is not a fault; for when the author provides the rules *yasmād adhikam* (Pāṇini 2.3.9) and *tadasminn adhikam* (Pāṇini 5.2.45), he indicates that when used in conjunction with the word *adhika*, only the fifth (*pañcamī*) and seventh (*saptamī*) case endings occur. Regarding the term *anuka*: [it means "inferior" or "less than"].

From the word *anu*? What [is the example]? *abhika-abhīkaḥ*. Here too, it is from the word *abhi*. He says—“from the word *pārā*, being in the third case-construct”—because the third case-construct as the governing case-ending is obtained from the very statement [of the rule] itself. “From *ayaḥśūla* and *daṇḍājina*.”

Is it not already understood from the very mention of the third case ending that the third case is obtained as the governing case-ending (*samarthavibhakti*)? To this he says: "From the third case ending in construction with *abhyām*. This is a general reference to words ending in ordinal suffixes.
Now, why does this not become a reference to the specific word-form itself? Because the reference is primarily concerned with the meaning.
For it has been stated that a reference to the specific word-form occurs only when the reference is primarily concerned with the word itself.
How does a suffix (*pratyaya*) occur in its own sense (*svārthe*)? Suffixes whose meaning is not specifically indicated occur in their own sense (Pāṇini 3.4.75).
90) Having formed [the words] "dvika" and "trika," there is elision (luk) of the suffix -tīya.

Regarding the term *catuṣkam*: there is elision (*luk*) of the ordinal suffix *ḍaṭ* and of the augment *sathuk*; for the *visarjanīya* of the word *catur*, [the rule] *visarjanīyasya saḥ* [Pāṇini 8.3.34] applies; and for that [s], [the rule] *idupadhasya cāpratyayasya* [Pāṇini 8.3.41] applies, resulting in the substitution of *ṣ*.
Regarding the phrase *tāvatithena* and so forth: [it is formed by adding the ordinal suffix *thuk*].

It should be stated that the suffix *kan* occurs after a nominal stem ending in a *pūraṇa* (ordinal) suffix, provided it is in the third case (*tṛtīyā*) and has the sense of "he takes" (*gṛhṇāti*). Furthermore, there is always elision (*luk*) of the *pūraṇa* suffix. For example:
*ṣaṭkaḥ*.
The *jaśtva* substitution for the letter *ṣ* is *ḍ*; its *cartva* substitution is *ṭ*. And here, there is the elision (*luk*) of the *sathuk* augment after *ḍaṭ*. Thus, "pañcakaḥ."

In this case as well, [the suffix] *ḍaṭ* applies. Now, why does it not occur here: "he grasps a staff with his second hand"? To this he says: "The particle *iti* is for the purpose of indicating the intended meaning," and so forth; this is easy to understand. But surely a young camel is not bound by a chain alone; rather, it is by means of a rope and the like as well. So how can a chain be called a "bond"? To this he says: "Even though," and so forth.

Even though there exists something else there, such as a rope and so forth, nevertheless the chain (*śṛṅkhala*) indeed serves as the instrument for its being made into a string; it does not become that [string] by means of that [chain]. Therefore, the chain is called "binding.

Even if the rope and so forth are also binding, let them be! For it is not restricted here [to the definition] that it must be the chain alone. [This is stated] because [the sūtra] expresses an action along with its instrument.
The means (*sādhana*) is the mind (*manas*); the action (*kriyā*) is going (*gamana*). Together with that [means], there is the action of going.
By the statement "in that" (*tadvati*), the meaning is: "occurring in going which is accompanied by its means.
Thus, "[in] that which possesses it" (*tadvati*).
By that word, the action is referred back; the meaning is "possessing an action along with its means. Thus, "eager" (utsukaḥ).
The meaning is "extracted. Regarding the phrase "obtainable by implication" (*arthalabhyā*) and so forth:

"meaning" (*artha*) refers to the locus (*adhikaraṇa*) and other such factors; by that, the case-ending beginning with the seventh (the locative), though not explicitly stated here, is obtained as the governing case (*samarthavibhakti*).

The term "purpose" (*prayojana*) is expressed by the word "cause" (*kāraṇa*). It should not be stated separately that time (*kāla*) is also a cause of disease. This is not so; for time is not necessarily a cause of disease.
In that case, even when it is not a cause of disease, the mention of time is made for the purpose of indicating how [the fever] occurs from it.
Thus: "that which occurs on the second day is *dvitīyaka*."
In that case, regarding a fever arising from some other cause such as wind (vāta) and so forth, "time" is intended merely as a locus (adhikaraṇa), and not as a cause (hetu).

But how can a suffix [denoting time] arise from words such as *dvitīya* and so on, which are other than words for time (*kāla*), since these are not commonly known as words for time? These are general terms; it is only through the proximity of another word that their application to time is understood. This is not a fault. In a sentence, when there is the proximity of another word, these terms have their application to time; and the meaning of the base (*prakṛti*) residing in that application serves as the qualifier for the suffixes because of its immediate proximity, not the meaning residing in the sentence, because of its remoteness—as in the expression "produced by *viṣapuṣpa* flowers."
The third [type] is:
"He should eat hot food.
Here, the intended meaning is the relationship between cause and effect.
If [the suffix] is expressed by the sixth case-ending (*ṣaṣṭhī*) produced from the word *idam* itself, then from the word *uṣṇa*, only the first case-ending (*prathamā*) occurs.

Here, the suffix is prescribed after words expressing a specific time or purpose, not after the words *kāla* (time) or *prayojana* (purpose) themselves. Is it [the suffix] applied after words expressing a specific time, as in "occurring at a specific time"? Or after words expressing a specific purpose, as in "the fever is the agent of the action" or "the purpose"? And when there is a desire to express cause and effect, it applies to that which is related to the effect.

Furthermore, this restriction regarding the types [of suffixes] has not been stated in the Sūtra; how, then, is it obtained? To this he says: "In this [context], the mention of 'technical term' (*saṃjñā*) from the subsequent Sūtra is drawn back [into the present one]. By that, when that [subsequent rule] is present, the meaning becomes as follows: if it ends in a suffix and is a technical term, then [the suffix is applied]; and when that meaning exists, if it ends in a suffix and is indeed a technical term, then the suffix arises in this manner and not otherwise. Because of the proximity of the mention of "technical term," this restriction of every kind is obtained here.
For indeed, without that specific manner [of derivation], a name (*saṃjñā*) does not come to have another suffix.

But surely, the mention of "name" (*saṃjñā*) in the subsequent sūtra is a supplement (*śeṣa*) to that very [preceding rule]; how then can it be extracted from there? This is not a fault; for it is a supplement to both rules. How so? A division of the rules (*yogavibhāga*) will be made: first, "when food is the predominant element in this," and then "in the sense of a name. Thus, the mention of "name" will be understood as a supplement to both. [The meaning is: "provided that the food is the predominant object."

That whose object (*viṣaya*) is "mostly" (*prāyaḥ*) is described as such. By using the locative case in "in the grasping of the object" (*viṣayagrahaṇe*), it is shown that this is a locative of domain (*viṣayasaptamī*).
[The phrase] "the suffix (*pratyaya*) occurs" [is used].

Otherwise, in the case of the intention "guḍāpūpāḥ prāyeṇānnam" (jaggery-cakes are generally food), the case-roles become [determined by that intention]; because the object of the "generally" (*prāya*) is intended as the instrument (*karaṇa*), the third case ending occurs.

In *guḍāpūpikā*, there is the substitution of *it* for the vowel preceding the *ka* of a suffix, according to Pāṇini 7.3.44 (*pratyayasthāt kāt pūrvasyāta idvā syāt*). Regarding the statement "the suffix *ini* should be stated after *vaṭaka*," the meaning is that it must be explained [as a Vārttika].

In this regard, the explanation is as follows: since the inclusion of the term "name" (*saṃjñā*) here is conditioned by the presence of a suffix, wherever a word ending in a suffix constitutes a name, there a suffix must occur.

Now, the word *vaṭaka* does not end in the suffix *-kan* as the name of anything; therefore, *-kan* will not arise from it. And that suffix being absent, the possessive suffix *-in* will occur [to form] *vaṭakinaḥ*.

Regarding the rule *ṛnnebhyo ṅīp* [Pāṇini 4.1.5]: since the previous rule [4.1.4] would have applied the suffix *kan* by virtue of it being a technical name (*saṃjñā*), and since the formation of the word would otherwise have required a full sentence to express the possessive sense (*matvarthīya*), this rule is stated to supersede the suffix *matup*. Thus, for the form *kaulmāṣī*, the suffix *ṅīp* is applied by [Pāṇini 4.1.15] *ṭiḍḍhāṇañ*. It is said that "the letter *n* is for the sake of the accent."

But surely, it is taught that a vowel [is acute] when followed by that which has *nakāra* as its *it*, and since *nakāra* is an *anubandha* of the entire complex, there is no state of being followed by a *nit*? This is not a fault; *na-eva-it* is a *tatpuruṣa* compound.
Thus, when *nakāra* is designated as *it*, the acute accent will apply to the preceding element.
What, then, is prescribed here? He says: "one who studies the *Chandas*."
The word *śrotriya* is an irregular formation (nipātana) in the sense of "one who listens to the meaning of this [Veda].
Regarding the phrase "or by Vedic license" (*chandaso vā*) and so forth:

in the preceding case, a word was irregularly formed for the sake of the sentence-meaning, without the distinction between stem and suffix being present; however, here, both the stem and the suffix are irregularly formed in the sense of "one who has studied that."

In this case, although the *bahuvrīhi* compound is marked as *nita*, the accent is nevertheless established, because the suffix *ghan* follows a *nita* element. Regarding the phrase beginning with "How so?":

if the word *cchandaḥ* is prescribed by way of a grammatical anomaly (*nipātana*)—with the substitution of the word *śrotra* for the word *śabda* and the addition of the suffix *ghan*—in the sense of "one who studies that," then the form *cchāndasa* would not be established in this sense, since it is overridden by the rule of anomaly; such is the intended meaning. Regarding the phrase beginning with "The word *śrāddha*": the term *śrāddha* is the designation for a particular ritual action that is to be accomplished according to the procedure prescribed in the scriptures.
This word *karman* denotes action. That action in which there is faith (*śraddhā*) is called *śrāddha*; here, the suffix *ṇa* is applied according to [Pāṇini 5.2.101].
The phrase "in the means of accomplishing that" and so forth [is explained as follows].

Since the state of having been eaten (*bhuktatva*) cannot function as a qualifier of the action (*karman*), it is understood that [the word *bhukta*] gives rise to the suffix [denoting the past participle] after occurring in the sense of "that which accomplishes it" (*tatsādhana*), such as in the case of the root *bhū*.
Its occurrence in that sense is due to its being for the sake of that (*tādārthyāt*); just as, for example, the word *pradīpa* occurs in reference to a jasmine flower intended for a lamp.
[This refers to the rule regarding] "the mention of simultaneous time."
"That by which a simultaneous time is grasped" means "simultaneous apprehension of time";
this is the sense in which the explanation should be made.
For what purpose? He says: "Eaten today," and so forth.

The purpose [of this rule] is so that one who has eaten at a *śrāddha* on a particular day should be designated as "śrāddhika" on that very day, and not on any other day such as today. Regarding this, the explanation is as follows: the particle *vā* (or) also carries over here, and it is a restricted option (*vyavasthitavibhāṣā*); therefore, it is intended that the suffix applies only on the day the *śrāddha* was eaten, and not elsewhere. As for the phrase "pūrvaṃ gataṃ pītaṃ bhuktam," since the word *pūrva* functions here as an adverbial modifier (*kriyāviśeṣaṇa*), it becomes the object (*karman*); thus, the suffix is understood to follow a word in the second case (*dvitīyāsamartha*).
Regarding the word "pūrvaḥ":
the long vowel [ā] is applied by the rule "sau ca" (Pāṇini 6.4.13). The word "saha" signifies that which exists;
for this very reason, he says: "the existing preceding [element]."
By [Pāṇini 6.3.82], there is the substitution of *sa-* for *saha-*.

Regarding the example "he made a mat before" (*kṛtapūrvaḥ kaṭam*), one might object: "Since the object (*karman*) has already been expressed by the past passive participle (*niṣṭhā*), the second case ending (*dvitīyā*) should not apply here. This is not a fault. This *niṣṭhā* does not denote the object; rather, it denotes the action (*bhāva*). Even if it were to denote the object, there would still be no fault; for by the *niṣṭhā*, the object in its general sense is expressed, but not the specific object.

Therefore, since the specific object (*viśeṣakarman*) has not been expressed [by another suffix], the second case ending (*dvitīyā*) will occur. But is this not a sentence, because it consists of multiple word-parts such as "previously made" (*pūrvaṃ kṛtam*)? And since the mention of "compound" (*samāsa*) in the rule for nominal stems (*prātipadika*) is intended as a restriction—that only meaningful aggregates are designated as nominal stems—this [sentence] lacks the designation of a nominal stem.
How, then, is this a valid reason? To this he says: "sup-supā" and so forth;
"by two rules" and so forth.
If [the principle of] "behaving like that which has a designation does not apply to what is not a nominal stem" (Śākalya-smṛti)...

If this *paribhāṣā* were not to exist, then one would have formulated the rule as a single compound: *sapūrvātpūrvādiniḥ*. Why, then, use a split rule (*yogavibhāga*)? For if there were a single rule, the suffix would apply even after a simple [word] by virtue of the principle of "behaving like that which possesses a designation" (*vyapadeśivadbhāva*).

Since the author makes a separate rule—namely, *tadevamekayogena siddhe yat...* [Pāṇini 5.2.86]—this indicates that there exists the following *paribhāṣā*: "The behavior of that which possesses a designation does not apply with respect to what is not a nominal stem" (*vyapadeśivadbhāvo'prātipadikena*). (Śākaṭāyana)
65) Or rather, [it means] "by that which possesses grasping" (*grahaṇavatā*). (Vyā.)
Otherwise, how could such a technical rule (*paribhāṣā*) as "pa" (Pāṇini 1.1.72) not exist? One would not have formulated the rule "sapūrvācca" (Pāṇini 5.2.87).
For by the very rule "tadantavidhinā" [the principle of extension to what ends with a specified element], forms such as *kṛtapūrvī* would be established even by [the preceding rule] 5.2.86.

Since this suffix is already established by the previous rule (*pūrvayoga*) even from the word *pūrva*, the fact that he formulates this rule, "and also when preceded [by another word]" (*sapūrvācca*), indicates the existence of this metarule: "A nominal stem (*prātipadika*) that possesses a specific marker does not undergo the extension of a grammatical operation to what ends with it" (*grahaṇavatā prātipadikena tadantavidhir na bhavati*).
[Example: *iṣṭo yajñe*.

But how is there an accusative case here, since when [the word] *yajña* functions as the object (*karman*), there ought to be an accusative ending? To this he says: "of that which has the suffix *kta*, when it has *in* as its scope," and so forth. But why is it elided (*nipātyate*) in this way here? Having established the word *paryavasthātṛ*, the substitution of *path* for the constituent part *avasthātṛ* is made in one instance, while in the other, the word *pari* is substituted for that very same [part], and subsequently the suffix *in* is added. Regarding "anupadī": [it means] after the foot (*padasya paścāt*); it is an *avyayībhāva* compound in the sense of "after" (*paścāt*).
From that, the suffix *in* is elided. Regarding "the mention of *saṃjñā*" and so forth.
"The occurrence of a secondary derivative (*pratyayānta*) applies only when a specific meaning is to be expressed; this is the restriction of the meaning.
(Vārttika 802). Thus, there is the elision of the *ṭi* suffix.
[The commentary begins with] "The mention of 'technical term' (*saṃjñāgrahaṇam*)," and so forth.

For if the term "perceiver" (*saṃjñā*) were not included, then just as the one who observes is called a witness (*sākṣin*), so too would the giver and the receiver be called witnesses, since they also certainly observe. Because of the inclusion of the term "perceiver," however, only the observer is meant.
One who is a witness other than the giver and the receiver, being nearby, is the "observer" (*upadraṣṭṛ*).

But surely, the word *sākṣin* will be established as correct simply by the rule of irregular derivation (*nipātana*) in [Pāṇini 2.3.39]: "The [words] *svāmī*, *īśvara*, *adhipati*, *dāyāda*, and *sākṣin* [are formed with the suffix *ṇini*]. Furthermore, since this word is worldly in nature, its restriction of meaning will be understood exactly as it is used in common speech; therefore, is this [present rule] not useless? This is not so; for in that rule of irregular derivation, one cannot determine that the word *sākṣin* ends in the letter *n*, because there is no proof for it. Otherwise, there would be an unnecessary burden on the understanding of the listener when the intended meaning is already perceived in common usage.

Therefore, this is stated in order to avoid the burden of understanding that [the word] ends in the letter *n*. The suffix *kṛtya* [is applied] in the sense of possibility (*śakyārthe*) to form *cikitsya*.
Regarding the phrase "in the sense of the sentence-meaning" (*vākyārthe*), etc.:

is the word *kṣetriya* formed in the sense of the sentence "to be treated in another's field"? This word is introduced as a *nipātana* (irregular formation), without the division into base and suffix.
The letter *ca* is for the purpose of [indicating] that the final syllable is udātta.
Regarding the phrase "or from another's field" (*parakṣetrādvā*) and so forth,
the word *vā* indicates an alternative mode.

Alternatively—from the word *parakṣetra* (another's field)?—in that case, a suffix is applied in the sense of "one who should be treated" (*cikitsya*) after a word ending in the seventh case (*saptamī*), and there is the elision (*lopa*) of the word *para*.
[Thus] *parakṣetra* means "the body of another birth. By stating "because it is other than this present body, it is incurable," he demonstrates the meaning of the word *para*.

For that field which is cultivated for the sake of grain becomes a "foreign field" (*parakṣetra*) for weeds because they do not grow there [intentionally]. "And all this is authoritative," because everything has been established by the Teacher. By the phrase "this is a conventional usage" (*rūḍhireṣā*), he causes one to abandon the etymological meaning of the parts of the word.
But how is this conventional usage (*rūḍhi*) produced? To this he says: "And thus," and so forth.

If this conventional usage did not exist, there would be no lack of restriction regarding etymological derivation (*vyutpatti*); for in the case of non-conventional words, the meaning is necessarily restricted.
However, in the case of this conventional word, the lack of restriction regarding etymological derivation is appropriate.
For conventional (rūḍhi) words are derived etymologically in some way or another by means of an imagined meaning of their constituent parts.
But how can the self be inferred by means of instruments such as the eye? To this he says: "It is not without an agent," and so forth.
By this, he demonstrates the invariable concomitance (avinābhāva).
The particle *iti* is used here in the sense of a reason (*hetau*).
Why? Because the activity or cessation of the instruments (*karaṇa*) and so forth depends upon an agent (*kartṛ*); therefore, wherever those [instruments] exist, there must necessarily be an agent.
Thus, the self (*ātman*) is inferred by means of the inseparable mark (*avinābhāva-liṅga*) that is the instrument, such as the eye and so forth.
But how is it served by that [the self] as its own nature? To this he says: "By means of that," and so forth. For it is through the door [of the senses] that knowledge of objects arises for the self.
Therefore, in order to know objects, the self serves the sense organs, such as the eye and the rest.
"According to each"? That is, according to its own [nature].
Whatever is the object of a particular sense faculty, that is given to it.
"The particle *iti* has the sense of ‘manner’ (*prakāra*)":

this means that the particle *iti* indicates that the etymological derivation (*vyutpatti*) should also be performed in other such manners; for this very reason, he says "provided it is possible" (*sati sambhave*), and so forth.

When possible, the derivation should be made in such ways as: "it is called a *indriya* because objects (*viṣaya*) are led toward (*nīyante*) or connected with (*sambadhyante*) by it. Regarding the phrase "the word *vā*," and so forth: [this refers to its use as an alternative].
For if the word *vā* were absent, the dependence of the various modes of interpretation, such as "the mark of Indra" (*indraliṅga*) and so forth, would be understood;
for [without it], the derivation would be caused by their mutual expectation combined into a single conjunction.
But the word *vā*, being connected thus—"the mark of Indra" and "seen by Indra"—demonstrates their independence.

Thus, each individual category functions as a constituent part of the derivation independently of the other categories. Regarding the phrase "the meaning of the suffix": now, it is true that when something belongs to another, it exists in that thing, and when something exists in a thing, it belongs to that thing—just as, for example, branches are in a tree, or the branches belong to the tree. In such cases, the relationship would be established by the mention of either one alone; so for what purpose are both mentioned? This is not so; for there is no necessary co-occurrence between the meanings of the genitive (*ṣaṣṭhī*) and the locative (*saptamī*). For instance, cows may be on the Ganges, yet they do not belong to it.
Likewise, even when gone to another country, Devadatta’s son still exists, yet he is not [perceived] there;
therefore, both must be specified.
Thus, "it exists" is a qualifier of the substrate (*prakṛti*).

But surely, the relationship between a qualifier and a qualified (*viśeṣya-viśeṣaṇa-bhāva*) occurs only when there is both possibility and deviation, as in the case of "blue lotus. Now, there is no deviation from existence (*astitva*), as it has been said: "A category does not deviate from existence. Since there is nothing to be excluded by it, is this qualifier not purposeless? This is not so; by the very power of employing the qualifier, it is understood that it is a specific kind of existence (*sattā*) that is taken as the qualifier, and not mere existence (*sattāmātra*). Furthermore, that specific existence is precisely the existence of being (*sat-sattā*).

And since there is deviation (vyabhicāra) regarding that [existence], the relationship between the qualified and the qualifier (viśeṣyaviśeṣaṇabhāva) necessarily follows. But why is present existence (sampratisattā) taken as the qualifier? So that the cognition may occur with respect to that very [existence] and not with respect to past or future existence; for this purpose, [the rule] does not apply in cases such as "he had cows" or "he will have cows."

But surely, having prescribed the suffix *matup* for past and future existence—as in "one who possessed cows was" (*gomān āsīt*) or "one who will possess cows will be" (*gomān bhavitā*)—how can it be so employed? This is not a fault, because even when the time [of the action] does not correspond [to the tense of the suffix], their grammatical correctness is established by the rule regarding the connection with a verbal root (*dhātusaṃbandha*). Thus it is employed; it is not because the suffix is prescribed for past or future existence.

As for the statement, "If it has the sense of 'being' as its limiting adjunct (*astyarthopādhika*), then it means 'it becomes' (*bhavati*)," this means that if it is qualified there by a present existence, then it has the sense of "it becomes."
In the word *gomān*,

the augment *num* is applied by [Pāṇini 7.1.70] *ugidacām*; then the elision of the final consonant (*hal*) and the following vowel (*i*), as well as the elision of the final member of the conjunct (*saṃyogāntalopa*), take place.
The vowel is lengthened by [Pāṇini 6.4.14].

In the form *vṛkṣavān*, the substitution of *v* for *m* is applied by [Pāṇini 8.2.9], which states that *m* is replaced by *v* when it follows a short vowel or a long vowel preceded by a short vowel. Regarding "restriction of the scope" (*viṣayaniyama*): the existence of the suffix within its specific domain is what is meant by "restriction of the scope."
Showing further that this refers to a distinguished object such as "abundance" (*bhūman*) and so forth, he says: "*bhūmanindā*" and so on.
The state of being much is "abundance" (*bhūman*). [The suffix] *iman* is applied according to the rule *pṛthvādibhya imanij vā*.

By the rule *bahorlopo bhū ca bahoḥ* [Pāṇini 6.4.158], there is the substitution of *bhū* for *bahu* and the elision of the vowel *i*. Thus, one who possesses many cows is called *gomān*. Even if only one or two cows are present, one is not designated as *gomān*.
In the sense of censure: "kakudāvartī" (one with a hump-turn);
he is censured because of his fruitlessness.
In the sense of praise: one who possesses a praiseworthy form is called "surūpavān" (possessing a beautiful form).

In the sense of constant connection (*nityayoga*): "trees that have milk" (*kṣīriṇo vṛkṣāḥ*) refers to those trees with which there is a constant relation to milk. [An example of the suffix *ini* in the sense of excellence is: "a girl with a protruding belly" (*udariṇī kanyā*).
That which possesses an abdomen in an excessive degree is expressed in this way:
"one with a staff" (*daṇḍī*) in the context of association; here, the association with a staff is what is expressed.
Therefore, even though the staff exists here while he remains at home, he is not designated as "the one with a staff" (*daṇḍin*). Regarding the phrase "for the purpose of excluding others":
that whose purpose or function is the exclusion of other possessive suffixes (*matvarthīya*), such as *ini* and so forth, is described as such.
As for "how," etc.:
The repetition [of the rule] after *rasa* and so forth is for the purpose of excluding others;
the intention is that, consequently, forms such as *rūpiṇī kanyā* would not be established.
Regarding the phrase "generally" (*prāyika*), and so on:

The meaning [of the suffix] is primarily the exclusion of others (*anyanivṛtti*); thus, it is appropriate that it is generally the case that "this belongs to him" (*so 'syāsti*). Since it is generally characterized as the exclusion of others—as in the examples *rūpī* and so forth—it sometimes occurs otherwise as well. How, then, is its general nature (*prāyikatva*) understood? To this he says: "The particle *iti*," and so forth.
And here, the particle *iti* functions to indicate the intended meaning (*vivakṣārtha*).
Therefore, in cases where the world’s intention to speak arises from a word ending in the suffix *matup* itself, exclusion (*anyanivṛtti*) is effected by that [suffix]; not in all cases.
The phrase "Or rather" (*atha vā*) and so forth introduces another solution.
By the word "etcetera" (ādi), the inclusion of the sense organs such as the eye is intended.
[The term] "from quality" (guṇāt) is recited in the list;
furthermore, the mention of "quality" is a qualifier for all [the categories] beginning with taste.
"Therefore, this reading applies only to those [words] which denote qualities perceived by the sense organs such as the tongue. By this,
the exclusion of others is effected from those words ending in quality-denoting suffixes that are perceived by the sense organs such as the tongue, but not from others.

It might be argued: "In cases such as *rūpin* (possessing form) and so forth, is the possessive suffix (*matvarthīya*) produced from those qualities which are perceived by the sense organs? To this he says: "*rūpī*, *rūpika*" and so on.
In the words *rūpiṇī* and *rūpika*, what is understood is the quality of beauty, not the form perceivable by the visual organ.
Likewise, in the phrase "*rasiko naṭaḥ*" (the actor is a connoisseur), what is understood is the quality of aesthetic sentiment (*bhāva*), not the quality perceivable by the gustatory organ.
The *bhāvas*—such as the erotic (*śṛṅgāra*), the heroic (*vīra*), and the loathsome (*bībhatsa*)—are properties of composition. Regarding the term "ekācaḥ":

it means "from that which consists of a single vowel. From that which has one *ac* (vowel), only the suffix *matup* occurs—for example, *dhīmān* ("intelligent") and *svavān* ("possessing wealth"). Regarding the term "kaṇikālaḥ": [it refers to a specific type of rhythmic measure].
This word *kaṇikā* and others denote a limb of a living being (*prāṇyaṅga*), not a particular type of ornament.
Since it is desired [to apply the suffix] only to limbs of living beings, he says: "It should be stated that [the suffix applies] after a limb of a living being.
The meaning is that this form of the rule must be explained as having the sense that the suffix *lañ* occurs after a word ending in *ā* precisely because it denotes a limb of a living being.
In this regard, the following is the explanation: the particle *iti* follows as having the sense of "intended meaning" (*vivakṣārtha*).
By virtue of that, [the suffix] will apply only to the limbs of living beings and not to anything else.
Alternatively, because there is no conventional usage (*anabhidhānāt*), it will not apply to things that are not limbs of living beings.

But surely, since a monosyllabic word ending in *lac* would already have its final syllable accented by the accent of the suffix (*pratyayasvara*), for what purpose is the letter *c* [in *lacaḥ*]? To this he says: "By the accent of the suffix alone," and so forth. When the word *cūḍāla-* follows the nominative singular case-ending and the word *asi* is placed after it, there occurs the *nighāta* (elision of accent) according to Pāṇini 8.1.28; then the substitution of *r* by 8.2.66; then the substitution of *u* by 6.1.113; then the *guṇa* substitution *ā* by 6.1.87; and that [substituted vowel] becomes acute according to 8.2.5; finally, the single substitute (*ekādeśa*) is the subsequent form (*pararūpa*) by 6.1.109.

If the letter *ca* were not present, however, there would be a circumflex (*svarita*) accent according to the rule *svarito vānudātte 'padādau* [Pāṇini 8.2.6]. Therefore, the letter *ca* is employed to prevent that. If *la* were optionally applied by means of the mention of *anyatarasyām*, then in one alternative case, the suffixes would occur exactly as they are otherwise prescribed; thus, after a word ending in *a*, the suffixes *ini* and *iṭhan* would apply to words such as *sidhma*. To avoid this fault, he says: "by the mention of *anyatarasyām*" and so forth.
Because particles have multiple meanings, the term *anyatarasyām* here functions in the sense of "optionally" (*samuccaya*).
Thus it has been stated by the author of the Vārttika: "The term *anyatarasyām* signifies an option.

Some hold that because the possessive suffix *matup* is marked with the *svarita* accent, it is that very suffix which is optionally included in this context, and not any other suffix as might otherwise be required.

Others, however, say: "The mention of *anyatarasyām* is solely for the purpose of providing an option (*vikalpa*). It is not the case that both the suffixes *ini* and *ṭhan* are applied, because those two are already established by the *mahāvibhāṣā* itself.

If it were so, would another suffix be prescribed as an alternative? That too is not the case; because of the immediate proximity (*sannihita-pratyāsatti*), it is only the suffix *matup* that is intended to bring about what is already obtained."

Thus, when there is the mention of "either one" (*anyatarasyām*), the intention is that only the suffix *matup* is made optional; with this in mind, it was stated that [the suffix] is conjoined by the mention of "either one.
However, it is not the case that the suffix itself is made optional.
But surely, the meaning is that the presence or absence of the *lac* suffix is being effected?
Regarding the passage beginning with "tasmāt" (therefore):

since, in this manner, by the inclusion of the word "anyatarasyām," the suffix *matup* is conjoined [with the others] rather than the suffixes themselves being treated as optional alternatives, therefore the suffixes *ini* and *ṭhan* do not occur after those words which are listed here as ending in *ā*.
[This is stated in the rule: "In the case of *pāṣṇi* and *śramani*, there is also lengthening [of the vowel]."
The suffix *lac* occurs after the words *pārṣṇi* and *dhamani*, and there is lengthening of the vowel in those two: *pārṣṇīlaḥ* and *dhamanīlaḥ*.
Regarding the rule "after *vāta*, *danta*, *bala*, and *lalāṭa*, there is also *ūṅ*": for these words beginning with *vāta*, the suffix *lac* follows, and *ūṅ* is added after them.
vātūlaḥ,
dantūlaḥ,
balūlaḥ.
*Lalāṭūlaḥ*.
When contempt is implied, [the suffix *ūla* is added] after *jaṭā*, *ghaṭā*, and *kalā*:
*jaṭālaḥ*, *ghaṭālaḥ*, *kalālaḥ*.
What is the purpose of the term "kṣepa" (inclusion)? [As in] *jaṭāvān*.
[This is governed by the rule] "*kṣudrajantūpatāpācca*" ("and also after [words denoting] small creatures and affliction"). ["And also after [words denoting] small creatures and affliction"].
"Small creature" (*kṣudrajantu*) refers to the mongoose and similar animals.

"Affliction" (*upatāpa*) means disease. Regarding the phrase "when the object [of desire] is powerful and possessed of longing," by the mention of the two forms ending in the suffix *mat*, he indicates that the words *kāma* and *bala* are understood here as ending in the vowel *a* with the suffix *arśa-ādi*.

But surely the words *vatsa* and *aṃsa* do not denote desire and strength; what then? They denote a particular stage of life and a particular limb of a living being. Therefore, how can one be said to possess desire or strength by means of those two? To this he says: "In the domain of derivative function (*vṛtti*)," and so forth.

How is this known? To this he says: "For here," and so forth. The meaning is that the well-known meaning of the word *vatsa* in a sentence—which is characterized as a particular stage of life—and the object of the word *aṃsa*—which is characterized as a limb of a living being—do not exist [as such] here in the derivative compound (*vṛtti*), nor are they perceived.
Alternatively—"does not exist" (na vidyate) means "is not" (nāsti).
By this, the absence of those two meanings which are well-known in common usage—namely, [the meanings] consisting of age and a specific part of a living being—is shown.
Now, in order to show the existence of those two meanings which are intended here, he says: "vatsalaḥ," and so forth.

"Affectionate" (*snehavān*) means "possessing desire" (*kāmavān*). Thus, since in the sentence the meanings of "calf" (*vatsa*) and "shoulder" (*aṃsa*)—namely, age and a limb of a living being—do not exist [as primary referents], it follows that by the words *vatsala* and *aṃsala*, one who is "affectionate" and "strong" as previously stated is expressed. Therefore, it is known that in the context of grammatical function (*vṛtti*), the words *vatsa* and *aṃsa*, while denoting desire and strength, produce a cognition directed toward that which possesses them [the person].

The inclusion of the term *anyatarasyām* (optionally) throughout this entire section serves the purpose of adding the suffix *matup*. Therefore, for one who thinks that [the suffix] *matup* must necessarily occur, he says: "And this is not," and so forth.
By this very reason, it should be understood that even a full sentence does not occur.
For this meaning is not possible in the case of words such as *pāmā* and others, where [the base] *aṅga* is recited; in that context, the inclusion of *kalyāṇa* serves as a qualifier for *aṅga*.
A woman (*aṅganā*) is one who possesses beautiful (*kalyāṇa*), that is, excellent, limbs (*aṅga*). Why [include] *kalyā*? [To exclude] *aṅgavatī*.

"From *śākī*, *palālī*, and *dadru*, there is the suffix [ini] and shortening of the vowel. Thus, the suffix occurs after *śākī* and the others, along with the shortening of the vowel: *śākinaḥ*, *palālinaḥ*, *dadruṇaḥ*.
Some maintain that *śākī* means "great vegetables" (*mahacchākam*) and *palālī* means "great straw" (*mahāpalālam*).
A collection of various kinds of vegetables is called *śākī*; a collection of straw is called *palālī*.
Regarding the word "viṣvak" and so forth: the suffix is applied after the word *viṣvak*, and there is an elision of the final member of the compound.
And that [word *viṣuṇa*] is formed before the suffix has been applied and before the substitution of *yaṇ* has taken place.

When the word *viṣu* is present as an upapada to the root *añc*, the suffix *kvin* is applied by the rule "ṛtvig... (Pāṇini 3.2.59), resulting in the elision of the nasal (*anunāsika*). Thus, when the form *viṣvac* is established, the suffix *na* is not added in the sense of "one who possesses *viṣvañc*"; rather, there is an elision of the second member (*uttarapadalopa*) before the substitution of *yaṇ* has occurred, resulting in *viṣuṇa*.
This word *viṣuṇa* is thus treated as an irregular formation (*nipātana*).
It occurs in various senses.
Regarding the rule "lakṣmyā acca": the suffix *na* is applied after the word *lakṣmī*, and the letter *a* is substituted for the final [vowel]. Thus, one who possesses *lakṣmī* is called *lakṣmaṇa*.
"Jaṭā-ghaṭa," and so forth. When contempt is implied, the suffix *ilac* is added after words such as *jaṭā*. Examples: *jaṭilaḥ*, *ghaṭilaḥ*, *kalilaḥ*.

What is the purpose of the restriction "kṣepa" (in contempt)? [Examples: *jaṭāvān*, *ghaṭāvān*, *kalāvān*. Since the suffix *matup* would apply after words meaning "wisdom" (*prajñā*), and *ilac* would also apply because they are read in the *picchādi* group, while *matup* would apply to others, the suffix *ṇa* is specifically prescribed [after these]. In this sūtra, two bases (*prakṛti*) are introduced, and two meanings of the suffixes (*pratyayārtha*) likewise follow from the two bases. Thus, for one who thinks that there must be a correspondence in number (*yathāsaṃkhya*) even in certain applications such as [Pāṇini 5.2.98] and [5.2.104], he says: "But in the case of the two meanings of the suffixes..."

Why is it that even when desired, [the compound] does not occur? [The answer is: because in the rule *ityatrāṃśaśabdasya paranipātāt* (Pāṇini 2.2.37), the word *aṃśa* is placed last; this serves as an indicator (*liṅga*) for the deviation from the general rule.

For, although the word *aṃśa* would normally be placed first according to the rule *ajādyadantam* (Pāṇini 2.2.33), and although the word *bala* would also have been placed first according to the maxim *laghvakṣaraṃ pūrvaṃ nipatati* (Vārttika 108), this specific placement of *aṃśa* at the end demonstrates independence from other rules and thus shows a deviation from the rule of "correspondence in order" (*yathāsaṃkhya*) within this section concerning the suffix *matup*.
Therefore, in the entire section concerning the suffix *matup*, there is no correspondence between the [words] and their meanings in their respective order.
Why is this so? Because the indicator of deviation from the rule depends upon the context.
And why is that? From the [traditional] commentary (*vyākhyāna*).

Or, because two signs indicating deviation from the definition have been employed, if there were dependence on grammatical connection (*yoga*), one would have employed only one of them. Since the suffix *vin* is established by the rule "from the word *tapas*, because it ends in *as*, etc. [Pāṇini 5.2.121], and since the suffix *ini* is established from the word *saharu* because it ends in *ā* [Pāṇini 5.2.115], this further formulation is for the purpose that there may be no sublation by the *aṇ* suffix which is about to be prescribed.

Regarding the phrase "saharuāāttu" and so forth: by the rule [Pāṇini 5.2.115], the suffix *ṭhan* would also apply, but that too is set aside. By this, he shows that the repetition [of the word] indicates that there is an exclusion of *ṭhan* after the word *saharuā*. The phrase "in the section on *aṇ*" and so forth refers to the *jyotsnā*-group, which is an *ākṛtigaṇa* (an open class).
From which [bases] is the suffix *aṇ* seen in the sense of the possessive suffix *matup*? Those such as *jyotsnā* (moonlight) and others should be observed.
This word *upasaṃkhyāna* functions in the sense of "supplementation" (*pratipādana*).

In this regard, the supplementation is as follows: the particle *ca* ("and") in the subsequent sūtra has the purpose of including what has not been mentioned; by that, the suffix will apply even to *jyotsnā* and the like.
Regarding the term "kauṇḍala": one who is worthy of two earrings (kuṇḍala) is called thus;
another, however, is simply called "kuṇḍalī. "An example here is [the case of] ādeśa" means:

Because the suffix *luP* will be prescribed by the subsequent sūtra (*deśe lubilacau*), and because [the word *danta*] ends in *a*, the suffixes *ini* and *thaN* would otherwise apply according to Pāṇini 5.2.117. However, by the reading "from a word denoting a limb of one's own body" (*svāṅgāt*), the suffix *uraC* is prescribed after the word *danta*. Since the suffixes *matup* and *ini-thaN* would also apply as far as possible, the suffix *ra* is prescribed after words such as *ūṣa*.
Thus, we have *madhuraḥ*.
Here, the word *madhu* refers to a specific kind of taste.
"In the section on *rap*," and so forth.
The word *upasaṃkhyāna* (supplementary addition) functions in the sense of "explanation" or "establishment.
Here, this is the explanation: the particle *ca* ("and") is operative here from [Pāṇini 5.2.105], and it serves the purpose of including what has not been explicitly mentioned.
By this [rule], the suffix *ra* occurs after words such as *mukha* as well—
as in *nagapāṇḍupāṃśu* (or, according to the *Kāśikā*, *nagapāṃśupāṇḍubhyaḥ kāśikā*)— and so forth.
The meaning is that the rule must be explained in such a way that the suffix *ra* occurs after words beginning with *nagapāṃśu*.

The explanation, however, should be made by relying on that same recurrence of the particle *ca*. Since *dyu* (heaven) and *dru* (tree) form *dyudru*, the suffix *matup* would apply to them; [therefore] *ma* is prescribed [instead]. Thus, *dyumāḥ* means "one who has heaven," and by [Pāṇini 6.1.131], the substitution of *u* occurs.
Some say: "The word *dyu* is another base, a name for *ahan* (day); from that, this prescription of the suffix is made."
