"Is *matup* [used] in conventional (*rūḍhi*) words? No, it is not further optional.
This is because the meaning of a conventional word is not expressed by *matup*. Since *ini* and *thañ* would otherwise be applicable, this rule for *matup* is commenced.
Now, one might ask: "But isn't the term 'optionally' (*anyatarasyām*) already present in the context; why then is this repeated? To this he says: "But isn't it already present," and so forth.

"In the section on *vapa*, etc."—the particle *iti* is used here in the sense of a reason. Just as the suffix *vapa* is seen after the word *keśa*, so too is the suffix *vapa* observed after other words; therefore, this must be stated—that is, explained.
The meaning is that the explanation should be formulated in such a way that this [suffix] occurs after other [stems] as well.

In this regard, the explanation is as follows: here too, that very particle *ca* (and), which has the sense of collecting what was not explicitly mentioned (*anuktasamuccaya*), is understood to carry over; therefore, the meaning is that it occurs after others as well. [The phrase] "it also occurs after a short vowel" [is explained as follows]:
how, when there is a mention of a long vowel, can it be said that it occurs after a short vowel too? [The answer is: "In that case, they are indeed equal," and so forth.
The same kind of *saṃhitā* that is seen here for the long vowel is seen even when the short vowel is included.
Therefore, the intention is that the inclusion of the short vowel here is not contradictory.

In this regard, one might object: "Even though the *saṃhitā* is the same, nevertheless this is a single word in which the *yaṇ*-substitution has been applied; thus, there ought to be the selection of one or the other [of the two vowels] as its own form (*svarūpa*)."

In that regard, if there is the inclusion of the long vowel, it would not apply to the short; and if there is the inclusion of the short vowel, it would not apply to the long. To this he says: "in both ways. The rule was formulated by the Teacher in two ways.
Therefore, since there is the inclusion of both, there is no fault.

Now, what is the purpose of including the term *saṃjñā* (name), given that because the particle *iti* continues to apply, [the suffix] will not occur when it is not a name, as in the case of the suffix *map* after *dyu* and *drabhi*? If this is so, then the inclusion of the term *saṃjñā* should be regarded as an elaboration (*prapañca*) of that very same particle *iti*. This [suffix] is an exception (*apavāda*) to *ini* and *thañ*. When *vin* is about to be applied after the word *rajas* (Pāṇini 5.2.121), and *matup* is prescribed for others, [the suffix] *valac* is then ordained. Regarding the passage beginning with "In the section on *valac*," etc., this too is essentially explained by the explanation of the suffix *vap*.

Why does the lengthening [of the vowel] not occur here by [Pāṇini 6.3.118] *vale*? Because of the continued application (*anuvṛtti*) of the term "proper name" (*saṃjñā*) from [Pāṇini 6.3.116] *vanagiryoḥ saṃjñāyām*. When the suffixes *ini* and *iṭhana* would otherwise apply after the word *danta*, the suffix *vala* is prescribed. Regarding the word *śikhā*, the suffix *ini* will be stated [in Pāṇini 5.2.116]; in that context, it is said: "The suffix *ini* should be mentioned after *śikhā* and others" (Mahābhāṣya).
Thus [it is stated]. The mention of *śikhā* (peak) is for the sake of non-locality (*adeśārtha*), so that [the suffix] may apply in a case such as *śikhāvalā sthūṇā* ("a pillar with a peak").
However, in the case of locality (*deśe*), the suffix is already established as being specifically *cāturarthika* by the rule *deśe* [Pāṇini 4.2.69].

If this is so, then only this [definition] should be stated; what is the use of that [previous one]? This is not the case; for even that must indeed be stated so that [the rule applies] to meanings such as "accomplished" (*nirvṛtta*) and the like.
Here too, the mention of the term *saṃjñā* (name) is for the purpose of restating that very meaning.
For the restriction of the denotable object is established through the recurrence of the particle *iti*. Thus: "The feminine gender is not the essential factor."

Is it not subordinate because it is not intended to be expressed? The use of the feminine gender, however, is for the sake of variety. Therefore, the letter *a* followed by *t* (i.e., *at*) is understood by the word "ataḥ. For this very reason, he says: "from that which ends in the vowel *a*," and so forth. Now, why is it not understood as the mention of the actual form of the word *ac*, [meaning] "from the nominal stem *ac*"? It is improper for there to be a mention of the actual form here; for if it were a mention of the actual form, the prescription of the suffix *matup* after words such as *rasa* would be purposeless.
That [suffix *matup*] is prescribed for the purpose of excluding *ini* and *than*.

Since those two suffixes would not apply here if the [word-forms] were taken in their own form (*svarūpa*), what is the point of prescribing *matup* for that purpose? Why is the marker *t* added [to the end of the base]? [As in the example: "śraddhāvān. But surely, since words such as *māla* ending in long *ā* are listed among the *vrīhy-ādi* group, they will serve as restrictive rules (*niyama*)—meaning that [the suffixes *ini* and *than*] apply only after these specific words ending in long *ā*? This is not so; such a restriction would apply only to those of the same class [as the listed examples], whereas *ini* and *than* would still apply after bases ending in *ḍāp* and *cāp*.
Therefore, the letter *a* followed by *t* (i.e., *at*) must be employed [in the sūtra]. Thus: "kāryī" [is derived as] "one who has performed" (*kṛta*), with the suffix *ini*.
Regarding "taṇḍulikaḥ": the suffixes *ini* and *iṭhan* are applied after a genus name (*jāti*). Regarding "from *śikha* and so forth," and so on:
in both instances, the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) denotes a class or type (*prakāra*).

Those words such as *śikhā* and others, for which only the suffix *-ini-* is observed in the usage of the learned (*śiṣṭaprayoga*), are to be understood [as falling under this rule], for they have prescribed the suffix *-ṭhan-* after those [words].
However, this distinction of scope is understood precisely through the continued application of the particle *iti*.
[This is indicated by the word] "to be stated" (*vācya*).
The meaning is that this [term] must be explained.
In the phrase "in cases such as *yavakhada*," the locative case indicates the domain (*viṣaya-saptamī*).
The passage beginning with "If that is so, then... and so forth [follows].

Since the word *vrīhi* would have its own form (*svarūpa*) included [in the list] starting with *tuṇḍa*, its inclusion here would be understood as purposeless; therefore, by implication (*sāmarthyāt*), it is understood that by the mention of *vrīhi*, the meaning (*artha*) is intended.
To demonstrate what is established when the meaning is intended, he says: "one who has *śāli* rice is a *śālika*" and so forth. [Then follows:
"after *śiras*, except after the negative particle (*nañ*)."

The suffix *cha* (i.e., *ika*) occurs after the word *śīrṣan* following the negative particle *nañ*. By means of a formal irregularity (*nipātana*), the substitution of *śiras* for *śīrṣan* takes place—thus: *aśīrṣī*, *aśīrṣikaḥ*.
Others, however, read *śīrṣan* as a distinct word-form [independent of *śiras*].
However, its mention here is for the purpose of ensuring that it applies even in the *bhāṣā* (colloquial speech).

Otherwise, because of the rule [Pāṇini 5.2.60], forms such as *aśīrṣikaḥ* and *aśīrṣavān* would not occur in the *bhāṣā*. This sūtra is commenced because the suffixes *matup* and others are applicable according to the circumstances;
thus, it states: "By the word *ca*, the suffixes *ini*, *iṭhan*, and *matup* [are also included]."

By this [rule], the four suffixes are [added] after words such as *tuṇḍa*; furthermore, the suffixes *ini* and *ṭhan* are also [added]. Regarding the rule "after a word denoting a limb of one's own body (*svāṅga*), when enlargement (*vivṛddhi*) is expressed": a suffix occurs after a word denoting a limb of one's own body when enlargement is expressed. He has large ears: *karṇilaḥ*, *karṇikaḥ*, *karṇī*, *karṇavān*. Since the suffixes beginning with *matup* would otherwise apply, the suffix *ṭhañ* is prescribed.

And that [suffix] occurs after a *tatpuruṣa* compound with a common locus (*samānādhikaraṇa*) that has "one" (*eka*) as its first member, but not after every [compound] having "one" as its first member.
This is understood from the recurrence of the particle *iti*. For example:
*ekaṃ ca tacchataṃ ca* = *ekaśatam*; that which possesses this is *aikaśatikaḥ*.
In the case of a *ṣaṣṭhī-tatpuruṣa* compound: *ekaśatavān*. Regarding the question "How so? and so forth:

if the word *ataḥ* [from Pāṇini 5.2.114] is understood to carry over [to this rule], then the form *gośakaṭī-vān* would not be established, because that word (*gośakaṭī*) does not end in the vowel *a*; such is the intended meaning. [The objection continues:
"It will be [established] from that [other rule]."

The intention is that [the suffix] will follow after that which ends in this [suffix]. This is the meaning: by implication, it is understood that *ṭhañ* is prescribed after a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) ending in *a*, provided that it is preceded by "one" (*eka*) or "cow" (*go*).
Alternatively, there is no fault because [the suffix] will arise from that cause.

Regarding the passage beginning with "and necessarily" (*avaśyaṃ ca*), if the word *hrati* were not understood to carry over [from the previous rule], then the suffix would also apply after words such as *citra*, *kala*, and *lāṭikā* when used in connection with the rules for *dvandva*, *upatāpa*, and *gahra* (Pāṇini 5.2.129; 5.2.116). Regarding the passage beginning with "the mention of *nitya*," etc.

For if the term *nitya* (always) were not mentioned, the mention of *anyatarasyām* (optionally) would follow everywhere for the purpose of adding the suffix *matup*, and thus [the suffix] *ati* would occur alongside *matup*.
Therefore, the mention of *nitya* is for the sake of precluding that.
[The question is: "How [can it be said] 'because of possessing a single substance'?"

If the inclusion of the word *nitya* (always) is for the purpose of overriding the *matup* suffix, then one might think that in the case of *na hy ekadravyavattvāt*, the *matup* suffix after the word *dravya* preceded by *eka* would not be established.
To this, [the author] says: "By *ekena*" and so forth.

The meaning is that its grammatical correctness (*sādhutva*) must be demonstrated by forming a compound with the word *dravyavattvāt* according to Pāṇini 2.1.4 (*sup supā*), resulting in the form *ekena*. Regarding the phrase "the two, both, and *ubhaya*," and so forth:
In this context, a restrictive interpretation (*avadhāraṇa*) is to be understood:
only pairs and so forth cause lengthening, and not others, because they are long by their very nature.
"All of this is accomplished by the inclusion of the term *bahulam* (‘diversely’)."
The intention is that the word *vaktavya* (to be stated) is used here in the sense of "explanation. Regarding the form *ūrṇāyuḥ*:

because it is treated as a *pada*, it lacks the designation of *bha*, and thus the elision of the *y* in *yasya* does not occur. Now, why is *gmini* not simply stated instead? [One might argue: once the substitution of *jaś* has been applied, the form *vāggmī* is established; however, would not the nasalization (*anunāsika*) prescribed by Pāṇini 8.4.45 apply here? This is not a fault, for we shall understand this as a fixed option (*vyavasthitavibhāṣā*). If that is so, then what is the purpose of adding the letter *g*? He indicates this by stating: "This [suffix] is *gmini*."
When *bahubhāvate* (he treats as much) is used in its correct sense, even there, setting aside the suffixes *āl* and *jāṭac* which will be mentioned later, only *gmini* occurs.

Thus it becomes *hraṣika*. This is so provided that [the suffix] occurs even in the domain of an exception (*apavāda*), and not otherwise. And in this way, it should be understood that *āl* and *jāṭac* occur only when one treats something contemptuously as much, by the principle of remainder (*pāriśeṣya*). [This refers to the rule] "when contemptuous."
The intention is that the word *vaktavya* occurs in the sense of "to be explained. Regarding the term *vaktavyam*, the meaning to be explained is this:
the suffixes *alac* and *āṭac* occur after a word denoting one who speaks excessively in a contemptible manner. This is the form of the meaning to be explained.

The explanation has already been provided in the preceding sūtra. Since the word *sva* is listed among *rasa* and others in [Pāṇini 5.2.94] as having one vowel (*ekāc*), it would follow that the suffix *matup* applies; therefore, this [sūtra] is commenced. Regarding the phrase "denoting an Ārya":
the word *sva*, which denotes wealth, here denotes an Ārya.
And likewise: "That which is noble due to the possession of wealth is called 'wealthy' (*svavān*).

The word *sva* occurs in reference to other things such as the self (*ātman*). Depending on what is possible, suffixes such as *matup* and others are prescribed [after it]. And this is an *ākṛtigaṇa*.
Because it is not enclosed [by a case ending].
And this word "ādi" (etcetera) denotes a type; as in the rule "after a word denoting one's own limb that is deficient."
The suffix *ac* occurs after a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) that denotes a defective limb or a defective activity—for example, "one whose foot is lame" (*khañja-pāda*).

Now, one might object: the word *śukla* ("white") is a term for a quality (*guṇavacana*); therefore, does this not already succeed even by means of metaphorical identification (*abhedopacāra*) [between the quality and the possessor]? If that were so, then the mention of the word "color" (*varṇa*) was made for the purpose of ensuring that the suffix applies even to nominal stems denoting color when they function as substances (*dravyavṛtti*). For instance, buildings endowed with the quality of whiteness are called "white" (*śuklāḥ*); when these exist in a city, it is called a "white city" (*śuklaṃ nagaram*).

Since the final udātta accent would already be established by the accent of the suffix (*pratyayasvara*), the inclusion of the letter *c* is for the purpose of overriding the svarita accent prescribed by the rule *svarito vānudātte 'padādau* [Pāṇini 8.2.6], which applies to words meaning "one who has this" (e.g., *arśas-asyāsti*). Regarding the phrase *tadviṣayebhyaḥ*:
the word *tat* refers specifically to affliction (*upatāpa*) and censure (*garhā*). This is a bahuvrīhi compound meaning "those for whom affliction and censure are the objects (*viṣaya*)."

This qualification applies to all words denoting living beings, just as it does to *dvandva* compounds and the like. Why, however, is it not desired even when [the rule] would otherwise apply? Because of the continued application (*anuvṛtti*) of the word "ca" (and).
"Since the suffix is already established by [Pāṇini 4.3.115] *siddhe pratyaye*,
[the present rule] is for the purpose of setting aside [suffixes] such as *ṭhan*."
The repetition is for the purpose that [the suffix] might indeed be *ini* and not *ṭhan* or others;

by the word "ādi" (and so forth), the suffix *matup* is understood. It should be known that from this point onward, the subsequent rules (*yoga*) are for the purpose of restriction (*niyamārtha*). [The rule begins: "After the words *vāta* and *atisāra*..."
Although it is the fifth case (pañcamī), nevertheless, by virtue of the sense, there is a transformation of the case-ending (*vibhaktivipariṇāma*).
In connection with the augment (*āgama*), it is transformed into the sixth case (*ṣaṣṭhī*).
For this very reason, he says: "And by the application of that [suffix], the augment *k* occurs for those two."

Now, why is it that the augment does not belong to the suffix itself? Because the meaning is not expressed by the suffix when it possesses the augment *kuk*, and because its own form would not be established. [The rule] "it should be stated 'also after *piśāca*" means that this form of the meaning—that the suffix *ini* occurs after the word *piśāca*—must be explained.

In this regard, the following is the explanation: the term *bahulam* (‘diversely’) is understood to carry over from [Pāṇini 7.4.78]. Therefore, the suffix will also occur after the word *piśāca*. Regarding the phrase “when age (*vayas*) is to be expressed”:
how, then, is age expressed if words such as *pañcama* and so on produce the suffix while denoting time?
For this very reason, he says—“she has a fifth month”—in order to demonstrate that their function pertains to time.

Regarding the phrase "when [the suffix] *siddha* exists," and so forth: since the suffixes used for filling out the number end in the vowel *a*, the suffix *ini* is already established; however, when that is established, this further statement is understood to be for the purpose of restriction (*niyamārtha*), namely:
"only *ini* occurs."
It shows the essential nature of the restriction (*niyama*): "the suffix *ini* is restricted.
The restriction is to be understood as before.
"In this case," and so forth.

Since the word *mālā* is recited among the *vrīhy-ādi* group, its repetition here in the sense of "contempt" (*kṣepa*) is for the purpose of setting aside the suffix *matup*, and not the suffix *ṭhan*.
It is not stated as "from *sukha* and so forth," because it has already been excluded by this very [rule].
For the word *mālā* is included among the *śikhā-ādi* group; since it belongs there, it does not occur elsewhere except in the sense of contempt.

Because it belongs to the class beginning with *śikhā*, the suffix *matup* is also applied; since *matup* is optionally combined [with other suffixes] by the rule "anyatarasyām," we have both *mālī* and *mālāvān*. By means of the hand (*hasta*), only the hand itself is perceived, not the genus (*jāti*).

However, through the employment of the word "man" (*puruṣa*), the genus of man is understood. By the statement, "If the Brāhmaṇa-practitioner is indicated by the aggregate," he shows that the Brāhmaṇa-practitioner possesses the aggregate as a limiting adjunct (*upādhi*).

When one is initiated for the purpose of acquiring sacred knowledge (*vidyā*), there is a specific set of observances (*niyamaviśeṣa*) that must be practiced; one who performs these is a *brahmacārī*. The suffix *-in* is used here in the sense of necessity (*āvaśyaka*). Regarding this practice of specific observances, only the three [higher] castes have the entitlement, not the Śūdra; thus he says: "By the term *brahmacārī*, the member of the three castes (*traivarṇika*) is intended. One who exists within the three castes, being included therein, is a *traivarṇika*.

What, then, is the reason that only this [meaning] is intended? He says: "For he," and so forth. Why does [the suffix] not occur here: *puṣkarāṇi padmānyasmin deśe santi* ("lotuses, i.e., lotus-flowers, exist in this place")? Because of the continued application of the particle *iti*. Regarding the rule "and from a meaning that is not present" (*arthāccāsannihite*): if the term "not present" (*asannihita*) were used, there would be a contradiction with its existence. For if the object is not present, it does not indeed exist; if it exists, how can it be not present? Therefore, because of the employment of the qualifier, setting aside the qualifier "exists," the suffix is prescribed from the object by way of the condition of non-presence (*asannidhānopādhikāt*).
And because of the inherent nature of the power of denotation,
the term "one who desires" (arthī) refers specifically to one who possesses longing.

Not every non-proximate object becomes "possessing non-proximity" simply because of its reflection in a suffix; therefore, must a suffix be stated? It need not be stated. How, then, is it obtained without being explicitly stated? From the rule *pūraṇaguṇasuhitārthasadavyayatavyasamānādhikaraṇena* (Pāṇini 2.2.11), by means of the mention of the word *bahulam* ("diversely"), just as operations such as "the lengthening of the vowel in *aṣṭrā*, *mekhalā*, *dvaya*, *ubhaya*, *rajas*, *madya*, and so forth" (Bāla-manoramā 586) are accomplished, so too is this [case]. This is expressed by the words "and from that which ends in that," and so on.

The term "asannihitam" (not present) is understood to carry over; the meaning is that this form [of the suffix] is to be explained as having the sense that a cognition of "this" and so forth arises with respect to an object conditioned by its being not present.

The explanation has already been largely provided. [Objection: If, by the inclusion of the term *anyatarasyām* ("optionally"), the suffix is made optional—meaning that after words such as *bala*, there is an option for the *matup* suffix—then, when *matup* is excluded, both *ini* and *iṭhan* would occur according to what is otherwise prescribed. However, only *ini* is desired. How, then, is only *ini* obtained if, by the inclusion of *anyatarasyām*, *ini* is added cumulatively (*samuccīyate*) rather than *matup* being optionally excluded? Having this in mind, he says: "By the inclusion of *anyatarasyām*," and so forth.

But surely, if both *ini* and *iṭhan* were to occur, the formulation of the rule would be purposeless, since the suffix would be established even without it; therefore, does this fault not also apply to the optional occurrence of *matup*? This is not so; by the force of the rule's formulation, the meaning obtained is that either one of the two—*ini* or *iṭhan*—occurs, but not *ini* alone. Therefore, the mention of *anyatarasyām* must indeed be made for the purpose of including *ini*. [Examples: *prathiminī*, *dāminī*.

From the two roots *prathimin* and *dāmin*, by [Pāṇini 3.2.144] "after these, the suffix *ini*," there is the elision of the *ṭi* portion; then, by [Pāṇini 4.1.5] "the suffix *ṅīp* after bases ending in *ṛ* or *n*," the suffix *ṅīp* is applied.

Here too, the mention of "technical term" (*saṃjñā*) is merely an elaboration of the particle *iti*. Regarding the phrase "denoting water and happiness": according to their respective order, *kam* denotes water (*udaka*), and *śam* denotes happiness (*sukha*).

Regarding the word *śaṃyuḥ*: by [Pāṇini 8.3.23], *tasya* [by 8.4.59], there is a following homogeneous sound (*parasavarṇa*); the semivowel *y* is the nasalized substitute for *m*. Thus, both the *anusvāra* and the *parasavarṇa* are established.
Because these two [rules] are prescribed under the heading (*adhikāra*) of "word" (*pada*).

If, however, the designation "word" did not exist, then in its absence, due to the non-existence of *anusvāra* and *parasavarṇa*—which are dependent upon being a word—the undesirable forms *kamyuḥ* and *śamyuḥ* would result. Regarding the word *tuṇḍi*: since it is listed among the *tuṇḍa*-group in the rule *svāṅgādvivṛddhau* (Pāṇini 5.2.116), when the suffixes *ilac*, *ini*, *ṭhan*, or *matup* would otherwise apply, the suffix *vaṭ* is specifically prescribed after *tuṇḍa* instead of *matup*. Regarding the word *bali*: because it is listed in the *pāman*-group, *matup* does not apply; for the word *vaṭa*, however, *matup* alone is applied. "The word 'I' (*aham*) is a different word altogether. Thus it is said.

After the substitution [of *a*] for *asmad-* by [Pāṇini 7.2.94], and after the substitution of *at* for the words beginning with *tyad-* has been made, the form of the word *yat* is produced; however, the word *aham* is something entirely different from that—an unanalyzed (avyutpanna) word. Having thus shown the difference between the words, he says "it occurs in the sense of *ahaṅkāra*" (*ahaṅkāre vartate*) in order to show a different meaning. Examples are *ahaṃyuḥ* ("possessing ego") and *śubhaṃyuḥ* ("possessing auspiciousness").
As before, the anusvāra and the subsequent *parasavarṇa* [are applied].

Thus ends the second quarter of the fifth chapter in the *Kāśikā-vivaraṇapañcikā*, composed by the venerable master Jinendrabuddhi, who was a teacher of the Bodhisattvas. Now begins the third quarter of the fifth chapter. *Bālamanoramā*: *ahaṃśubhamoryus* (Pāṇini 5.2.140). [The suffix] *yus* is applied after the words *aham* and *śubham*. *Ahaṃyuḥ* ("one who thinks 'I am'")—the masculine gender is due to the usage of the Sage (*ārṣa*). *Vaṭibhaḥ*—[is derived from *vaṭi* with the suffix *bha*].
The root *vaṭ* means "to surround.
*Vaṭiḥ* is the act of surrounding (*vaṭanam*).
The analysis of the compound is: "one who possesses that [surrounding]."

*Bālamanoramā*: Regarding the rule *ahaṃśubhamoryus* (Pāṇini 5.2.140), which prescribes the suffix *yus* after the words *aham* and *śubham*, the author anticipates the objection that the case-ending (*sup*) should be elided in the forms *ahaṃyuḥ* and *śubhaṃyuḥ*, and thus says: "In *aham* etc. The status of being a *sit* [marker] is for the purpose of establishing *padatva* (the status of being a word).
By that [rule], because it is a word (*padatva*), the *anusvāra* is established as the *parasavarṇa*. Thus ends the section on possessive suffixes (*matvarthīya*) in the *Bālamanoramā*.
Now begins the section on the formation of denominative verbs (*nāmadhātu*). "Those [suffixes] should be understood as having the technical name 'case-ending' (*vibhakti*)."

Those for whom this word "vibhakti" is a technical designation (saṃjñā) are so described. Now, an objection might be raised: since the word *vibhakti* is the designation for *sup* and *tiṅ* suffixes, and a designation conveys its designated object (*saṃjñin*) when it is uttered in the rule-texts (*pradeśavākya*), the prescription that *sup* and *tiṅ* have the designation "vibhakti" would be redundant. Just as the word *vṛddhi*, although subordinate to its own denoted worldly meaning, functions as a designation for *ā*, *ai*, and *au*, so too the word *vibhakti* should be understood as functioning as a designation for *tasil* and other such suffixes.

Now, why is it not stated right there [in Pāṇini 1.1.73]: "The *sup* suffixes and those beginning with *prāg-diś-* are case-endings (*vibhakti*)"? If this were so, the term *vibhakti* would not need to be mentioned again [in Pāṇini 1.4.104]. This cannot be done; for if such a formulation were adopted, it would not be known from where the *prāg-diśīya* suffixes begin. Furthermore, since the word *diś* occurs multiple times in the treatise—as in "the suffix *yat* after *diś* and so on" (Pāṇini 4.3.54) and elsewhere—the limit [of the *prāg-diśīya* group] would also remain doubtful.

Furthermore, in order to indicate the limit for the shortening of the vowel *kā* as prescribed by rules such as *kiṃsarvanāmabahubhyaḥ* [Pāṇini 5.3.2], the phrase *prāgdiśaḥ* would have to be stated here once again.
Therefore, let it remain exactly as it was originally formulated:
*tataḥ*, *yataḥ*.

While [the rule] 7.2.84 is being carried over, [the rule] 7.2.102 causes the substitution of *at* for *kim*; by 1.3.4, there is a prohibition of the designation *it* for the letter *s*; and by 1.1.38, because it is an indeclinable (*avyaya*), there is elision (*luk*) of the case-ending.
Thus, "kutaḥ.
By [the rule] 7.2.104, "ki tihoḥ," there is the substitution of *ku* for *kim*.

Regarding the phrase "the rules for *tyad* and so forth": here, the forms beginning with *tyad* are dependent upon case endings (*vibhakti*). Regarding the word "thence" (*tataḥ*): [it is derived from *tad*].
The example for the substitution of *atva* (the replacement of *idam* by *adas*) according to the rule for *tyadādi* is "iha";
it is the case where the accent of the case-ending of *idam* [is affected].
From the word *idam* ending in the locative case, the suffix *hap* is applied [by Pāṇini 5.3.11], and the substitution of *iś* occurs [by 5.3.3].
Thus, when the case-ending (*vibhakti*) is present, the acute accent (*udāttatva*) of the element following *idam* is established by [Pāṇini] 6.1.171.
However, in this instance, the initial acute accent is already established by the accent of the suffix itself.
Therefore, this direction for providing examples has been shown.
However, the following example is appropriate here: "itaḥ. Here, the suffix *tasil* is applied to the word *idam*, and the direction is as previously stated.

If this were not the case, then when [the suffix] *tasi* is a case-ending (*vibhakti*), by the rule *liti* [Pāṇini 6.1.187], the accent would have to come from the affix; consequently, the first syllable of the preceding word (*pūrvapada*) would be acute (*ādyudātta*).
However, if that is so, the acute accent on the first syllable of *tasi* following *idam* is established by the rule *ūḍidamparaḥ* [Pāṇini 6.1.165].

But surely, even if it is a case-ending, the accent of the *lit* [affix] should prevail because it is subsequent [in the order of rules]? This is not a fault; for in the rule *liti* [6.1.187], the rule *ūḍidam* [6.1.165] and others will be carried over (*anuvarttiṣyate*) in order to override the accent of the *lit* affix.

But even so, does the acute accent of the case-ending (*vibhakti*) not still fail to be established? For in that rule [Pāṇini 6.1.168], the mention of "the third case and the following" (*tṛtīyā-ādi*) is understood as a governing term (*anuvartate*), and the suffixes beginning with *tasil* are not included by that mention of "the third case and the following.

From the singular of the third case up to the end of the fifth chapter, every suffix designated as a case-ending (*vibhakti-saṃjñaka*) is considered "the third case and the following. This is what is meant by the phrase "from this point onwards," and so on.

For "capacity" (*sāmarthya*) indeed means the state of having a relation; and that necessarily depends upon a counter-correlative (*pratiyogin*), since the coalescence into a single meaning occurs only when that counter-correlative exists, and not otherwise. "Primacy" (*prāthamya*) likewise depends entirely upon a counter-correlative; for it is only in relation to a second thing that something is called "first."

From this point forward, since the suffixes (pratyaya) apply only to the meaning of the base (prakṛtyartha), there is no possibility of a second counter-correlative (pratiyogin) within that scope; and due to the absence of such a correlative, there is likewise no possibility for "capacity" (sāmarthya) or "primacy" (prāthamya), because those two depend upon a counter-correlative.
Since this is so, both [the requirements]—"the section on capacity" (sāmarthyādhikāra) and "the mention of 'first'" (prathamagrahaṇa)—are rendered useless, and thus both are withdrawn.

If this is the case, does it not follow that the mention of the word "optionally" (vā) must also be withdrawn, since it is prescribed in the same grammatical rule (ekayoganirdiṣṭatvāt)? To this he says: "But the mention of 'optionally' (vāvacana) indeed continues."
The intention is that this is because it is *svarita* (accented).

Regarding the phrase "by that option" (*tena vikalpena*), he demonstrates the result of the continued application (*anuvṛtti*) of the word "optionally" (*vā*) in the subsequent sūtra. As for the question "Where?"—
> [[5.3.10]], as before? It is "bad state" (kubhāva). [The phrase] "enumeration of the *prakṛti*" means a complete listing of the *prakṛtis*.

Regarding the term *vaiyākaraṇapāśaḥ*: the suffix *pāśap* is applied in the sense of "deserving contempt" (Pāṇini 5.3.47). Furthermore, since this suffix occurs after the letter *vya* following the limit [of the word *vyākaraṇa*], it also occurs after other bases.

"Since [the rule] is already established by its being a pronoun (*sarvanāman*)," refers to the fact that *kim* possesses the status of a pronoun due to its inclusion among the words beginning with *sarva*.
"The mention of *kim*" and so forth...

Since this word *kim* is recited among the "dvyādi" (the group beginning with *dvi*), the exclusion "from *dvyādi*" (*dvyādibhyaḥ*) is applied to it. Therefore, even though it is a pronoun (*sarvanāman*), it is mentioned by its own specific term. If that is so, then the word *kim* should have been recited before the word *dvi*; for in that case, its separate mention would not be necessary at all. This is true; however, since there is no formal list of the *gaṇa*s here [in the sūtra], the author of the sūtra does not deserve censure.

Furthermore, according to the rule that "among the pronouns beginning with *tyad*, whichever comes later remains," when *kim* is intended to be expressed in conjunction with all the pronouns beginning with *tyad*, it would be expected to remain as *śeṣa*: *tvaṃ ca kaśca* → *kau*; *bhavāṃśca kaśca* → *kau*. Since this does not succeed in such a reading, let it remain exactly as in the original formulation. [This is because] "when there is a mention of 'many' (*bahu*), it is a mention of number (*saṃkhyā*)."

How, in this case, are "sarva" and the others indicated as the *saṃjñins* (the things named) by means of the technical name *sarvanāman*? Because they are mentioned together with it [the name], it is understood that the mention of the *saṃjñin* refers specifically to that which has been assigned the technical name *saṃkhyā* (number) by the rule *bahugaṇavatuḍati saṃkhyā* (Pāṇini 1.1.23), even though the word *bahu* is also used in that rule. For example, in the expression *bahoḥ sūpāt* ("from much broth"), the word *bahu* denotes abundance (*vaipulya*). As for the statement, "The letter *ś* is for the purpose of indicating a replacement for the whole (*sarvādeśa*)," [it serves to ensure that the entire original element is replaced].
For would it not be possible [to apply the rule] there?

If so, then when the *lopa* (elision) of the *rūpa* (the suffix *su*) is applied by Pāṇini 7.2.113 (*halṅyābbhyo dīrghāt...*), and the *guṇa* substitution is applied by 6.1.84 (*ādguṇaḥ*), the undesirable form *eha* would result from *etaḥ* + *iha*.

[Objection: But surely, once the substitution of *at* for the pronoun stem by 7.2.102 (*tyadādīnām at*) has been made, then by 6.1.94 (*ato guṇe*), the subsequent form (*pararūpa*) is applied, and after the elision of the *rūpa*, the substitute *it* takes the place of the final letter, whereby *itaḥ* becomes *iha*—is this not established? [Response: It would be established if the substitution of *at* for the pronoun stem were obtained first; however, that is not obtained, because the substitution of *it* (*itvam*) itself is indeed more *antaraṅga* (internal).

For this reason, [the substitution] involving suffixes such as *tasil* is *antaraṅga* because it depends solely on the suffix; whereas [the substitution] of *tyādi* is *bahiraṅga* because it depends upon the designation of the stem (*aṅga-saṃjñā*) and the fact that the following suffix is inflected (*vibhaktitva*). Therefore, the form *śākaraḥ* must be applied. In the rule "of *ra* and *tha*" (*rathoḥ*), there is a reference to the two phonemes.

In that context, by the principle "when a rule is prescribed with reference to a specific element, it applies to that which begins with it" (*yasmin vidhis tadādāv algrahaṇe*), it is understood that the operation applies to that which begins with *repha* and that which begins with *thakāra*, and so forth—this is what is meant by "beginning with *repha*" and so on.

How is it known that the letter *r* in [the suffix] *repha* is for the purpose of pronunciation? Because there is no *repha* containing the vowel *a* following the pronoun *idam*. [The statement] "the letter *ś* is for the purpose of a universal substitute" [is made].

But does it not apply to the final [sound]? If it were to apply before the substitution of *tyad*-class elements (*tyadādyatva*) has taken place, then its application to the letter *d* would result in being purposeless, for its vowel *a* is already obtained through the *tyad*-class substitution itself. On the other hand, if it were to apply in place of the vowel *a* after the *tyad*-class substitution has been made, it would likewise result in being purposeless, for there is no need to state the vowel *a* for the vowel *a*, and it has already been established. In that case, by virtue of the explicit statement, it will be a replacement for the whole even in the absence of the letter *ś*. This is not so; for there is indeed a purpose in stating the vowel *a* for the vowel *a*.
What [is the purpose]? Therefore, in this case, so that another [accent] which might otherwise apply does not occur.
But what is this [other accent]? It is the acute (udātta) on the syllable preceding the suffix marked with *l*. For that reason, the letter *ś* must be inserted.
"The suffix *thamu*—[the *Kāśikā* states that this *thamu* suffix must be added as a supplement]—must again be added as a supplement.
This is because it is not found [in the original sūtra].
"Must be added as a supplement" (*upasaṃkhyeya*) means it must be explained [as being required].
In this regard, the following is the demonstration: this very statement regarding the substitution [of *thakārādi*] serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*) that the form *idam-sthamuḥ* occurs.
But how indeed is this so? From the indicator. [If one were to argue:

"The suffix *thamu* will occur, and not *tham*; therefore, since *thakārādi* is prescribed without distinction by [Pāṇini 5.3.23], would the substitution apply to that very [suffix]?"—this is not a fault; for here, a specific [form] beginning with *thakārādi* is intended.

In the case of *etadaḥ* as well, the term *idamaḥ* is understood to carry over [from the previous rule], and that is not for the purpose of prescribing a substitute (*ādeśa*), because the substitute has already been prescribed previously. Therefore, it is understood as a qualifier of the suffix (*pratyaya*). Consequently, we shall qualify the suffix beginning with *tha* by means of this: "that which is prescribed by the word *idam* itself"—meaning that the suffix beginning with *tha* is prescribed by the word *idam* alone—and since only *thamu* is prescribed in this manner and not *thāl*, it is rightly said that the mention of the substitute (*ādeśavacana*) indicates that this [suffix] indeed exists even when it is not *thamu*. The term *dīti* refers to the seventh case ending (*saptamī*) beginning with the letter *da*.

In that case, since there is no suffix beginning with *da* that belongs to the *prāgdiśīya* class, one might ask how it is known that the rule applies when the suffix begins with *da*. To this he says: "in a *prāgdiśīya* suffix beginning with *da*," and so forth.
[The example is] "sarvadā brāhmaṇī."
> [[3.2.3]] , and from that, the suffix *ṭāp*.
From the *Bālamano ramā*: regarding the portion "and of the self" (*ātmanaśca*) in [Pāṇini 5.3.6], he takes it up separately in order to explain it, saying "and of the self.

He states that by the word "and" (*ca*), the phrase "non-elision of the third case" (*tṛtīyāyā alug*) is also drawn in, saying "there is non-elision of the third case of 'self'. The remainder of the rule is "when a subsequent member (*uttarapada*) follows."

Regarding the statement "it should be said that [the word] *pūraṇa* [is used]," the word *pūraṇa* itself is not taken here; rather, by the force of its being marked with the *svarita* accent, there is a reference to the suffixes prescribed under the governing rule (*adhikāra*) for ordinal numbers. Intending that, according to the principle "when a suffix is mentioned, it includes that which ends in it," he says: "at the end of an ordinal suffix. In the expression *ātmanāpañcamaḥ*, the meaning is "the self is the fifth."
The third case ending (instrumental) is used here in the sense of the first case (nominative), because [the word] belongs to the group beginning with *prakṛti*.
Alternatively, the meaning is "one who possesses the state of being the fifth created by himself";
in this case, the third case ending is used in the sense of the instrument (*karaṇa*).
By including the action of "making" (*karoti-kriyā*) within it, there is a compound [formed] with that [word] according to the rule *tṛtīyā tatkṛte*.
Both of these two positions are established in the Bhāṣya.
Now, one might object: Saṅkarṣaṇa, Pradyumna, and Aniruddha are the three manifestations (*vyūha*) of Viṣṇu.
It is established in the Viṣṇupurāṇa and other texts that Janārdana is the controller of these [three].
Regarding this, the Paurāṇikas say: "Janārdana, however, is himself the fourth.
In that case, since there would have to be *ātmanā caturthaḥ* (with the non-elision of the instrumental case ending), he says "janārdanastu" [to show the elision].
"Bahuvrīhi" means that when there is an analysis (vigraha) such as "that whose self is the fourth," it is a bahuvrīhi compound; this is the sense.

The intention is that even for a single entity, one may conceptually construct a distinction based on limiting adjuncts (upādhi), and thus intend to express both its status as the meaning of the constituent members (vṛttipadārthatva) and its status as the meaning of the whole compound (anyapadārthatva).
This is clearly stated in the Bhāṣya:

*bāla-manoramā*, *sarvasya so'nyatarasyāṃ di* (Pāṇini 5.3.6). Regarding *sarvasya saḥ*: the term *di* is the singular locative case (*saptamyekavacana*) and serves as an adjective qualifying the prāgdiśīya suffixes.
"In which [word] there is an affix" (*yasminvidhiḥ*) refers to the rule of "that-initiality" (*tadādividhiḥ*).
Thus he says: "the two *da*s in the suffixes belonging to the *prāgdiśīya* group.
An example is *sadā*. [The rule states: "the suffix *tasil* occurs."

Why are these suffixes beginning with *tasil* not treated as substitutes (*ādeśa*) in place of the fifth case endings (*pañcamī*) and so forth? For if this were so, the technical designation (*saṃjñā*) of "case ending" (*vibhakti*) would not need to be applied to them. It is impossible to treat these as substitutes; for if they were substitutes, the elision (*luk*) prescribed by [Pāṇini 2.4.71]—namely, that *tyap* [by 4.2.103] becomes *tya*, as in *tatastyaḥ* and *yatastyaḥ*—would not apply. Indeed, substitutes for case endings (*sub-ādeśa*) acquire, through the principle of "behaving like the original" (*sthānivadbhāva*), the grammatical operations dependent upon being case endings.
Consequently, in the word *tataḥ*, the suffix *tasi* would be unaccented (anudātta) according to [Pāṇini 3.1.4].
Why is this so? In *dheniti*, there is *guṇa* by [Pāṇini 7.3.111].
In *etarhi*, there is *dīrgha* by [Pāṇini 7.3.102].
In *tatra*, there is *etva* by [Pāṇini 7.3.103]: "In the case of a plural ending beginning with a *jhal*, [the final vowel of the base] becomes *e*."

In *kutra*, the substitution of *au* occurs by [Pāṇini 7.3.119]. Then, in *tatra*, the substitutions of *smāt* and *smin* occur by [Pāṇini 7.1.15]. Therefore, these are not treated as substitutes for *na*.

If this is so, then in the case of *tasyan* derived from the root *tasu upakṣaye* (DhP 1212), would the substitution *tasil* not apply by rule [Pāṇini 5.3.8], *taseśca*, because the form of the verbal root (*dhātu*) is followed by a word ending in the fifth case (*pañcamī*)? This is not a fault; it will not occur because the suffix is understood to be *svārthika* (having its own meaning).

These suffixes beginning with *tasil* are *svārthika* (having their own meaning). Among them, when the substitute *tasil* is prescribed, it is understood in such a way that, being applied in its own sense (*svārthe*), it does not transcend the status of being *svārthika*.

By the rule "after [a word ending in] the ablative case, provided it is not *ahīya* or *ūha*" (*apādāne cāhīyarūhoḥ*, Pāṇini 5.4.45), the *tasil* which occurs as a substitute for that *svārthika* suffix is itself indeed *svārthika*.

However, since the verbal root (*dhātu*) functions in a sense different from the nominal stem (*prātipadika*), the *tasil* occurring as a substitute for it is not *svārthika*. For example: "From where have you come? (*kuta āgataḥ*).
Is it because of the rule *[[5.4.45]]* due to its subsequent position? Once *tas* has been applied, *tasil* is substituted for it by this [rule].

But surely, even when *tasil* is applied, the form remains the same; so for what purpose is it prescribed? To this he says: “The prescription of *tasil* for *tas*,” and so forth. It is desired [only] when [the words] *sarva* and *ubhaya* function as adverbs (*avyaya*). Therefore, it does not occur here in the cases of *parisiñcati* and *abhiyāti*.

And here, the reason for the non-occurrence [of the suffix] is that the term *anyatarasyām* (optionally) is understood to carry over from the rule beginning with *sarvasya* [Pāṇini 5.3.6], and this is a *vyavasthitavibhāṣā* (a restricted option).
Therefore, [the suffix] occurs only when [the word] expresses the sense of "all" (*sarva*) or "both" (*ubhaya*), and not elsewhere. Regarding the word *kva*:

by the rule *kvāti* [Pāṇini 7.2.105], there is the substitution of *kva* for *kim*. As for the elision of the *t* in *kva*, although there is a prohibition by the rule *na vibhaktau tusmāḥ* [Pāṇini 1.3.4], the fact that this prohibition is not absolute is indicated by the presence of the vowel *u* in the rule *idamasthamuḥ* [Pāṇini 5.3.24]; thus, the *t* receives the designation *it* (and is subsequently elided).

Now, because of this negation, there is the notion that "it does not exist"; and also because of the absence of purpose [for the suffix]. [The rule states: "The state of being 'other' (itaratva) is relative to the fifth and seventh cases.
This is because the word *itara* is understood immediately following those cases.

Now, for what purpose is the inclusion of the term *dṛśi* ("is seen"), since the desired result is already established by the mere statement "*itarābhyo'pi*" ("also from others")? To this he says: "The inclusion of the term *dṛśi*," and so forth.
The mention of the word *dṛś* (seen) is for the purpose that the rule (*vidhi*) should be understood as being general (*prāyika*).
When that [word] is present, the meaning obtained is: "It occurs where it is seen when following the usage of the learned (*śiṣṭa*), but not elsewhere.
By this, the general nature of the rule is established.

Regarding the phrase "by that" (*tena*) and so forth: if the term *dṛśi* ("is seen") were included [in the rule], then only from those other [words] where the usage of learned authorities (*śiṣṭa*) is observed would the suffixes *tasil* and the others be applicable. Since such usages are observed from other words only in connection with *bhavat* and so on, the prescription of those suffixes applies only in that specific case.

If suffixes such as *tasil* and others also occur after words ending in *hrasva*, is the previous rule prescribing [suffixes] after the fifth (*pañcamī*) and seventh (*saptamī*) cases redundant? This is not so; for those two [cases] are intended by necessity, while the others occur in connection with words such as *bhavat*. And since both are obtained when this preceding rule and this present one exist together, how can there be redundancy? [The phrase] "the word *saptamyāḥ* (after the seventh case) is understood" follows because that word is marked with the *svarita* accent.
"But not from the others," because it is the opposite of that; "it is an exception to [the suffixes] traL and so forth."
Regarding the impossibility [of its occurrence]:

therein, from the word *kim*, it is an exception (*apavāda*) to the suffix *āt* which would otherwise be obtained by the rule *kimo't* [Pāṇini 5.3.12]. According to the opinion of some, *tarala* is also [included].

From that word [tad] as well, [the suffix *trā* is applied] by the rule "In the Vedic language, *trā*, *dā*, *hi*, and *lū* [are added after *tad*]" (Pāṇini 5.3.20). From the remaining [pronouns], however, [the suffix] *tral* is applied, as in "kadā" (when?).
"The substitution of *kā* for *kimaḥ* is an exception (*apavāda*) to [the rule] that would have applied by 5.3.11. "The letter *l* is for the sake of the accent (*svarārtha*)."
[The purpose is] so that the preceding [syllable] may have the acute accent (*udātta*) when there is a *lit* suffix [according to Pāṇini 6.1.193].

But one might object: just as in the case of *itaḥ*, the accent of the case-ending (*vibhaktisvara*) occurs by the rule "ūḍidam" (Pāṇini 6.1.165) and so forth, so too should it be here by that very same rule? This is not so; for while it is appropriate that the case-ending accent occurs in the case of *itaḥ* because the *lit*-status of *tasil* has already served its purpose elsewhere—in *paritaḥ* and *abhitaḥ*—here, however, the application of the *lit*-marker to *hil* has not yet achieved its purpose. Therefore, if it were sublated by the case-ending accent, its [the *lit*-marker's] purposelessness would result.

Therefore, only the *litsvara* accent occurs. The rule *dānīñ ca* is a *yogavibhāga* (splitting of a rule) for the sake of what follows—namely, so that in [Pāṇini 5.3.19] the suffix *dānīm* alone may apply, and not the suffix prescribed by the preceding rule. Regarding the term "meaningless" (*anarthakam*):
it is for the sake of variety.
Since there is no other [suffix], being meaningless [in itself], it becomes meaningful precisely through its variety.
"Because it is prescribed":
by [the rule] *sarvaikānya* (Pāṇini 5.3.15) and so forth. *Idā*:
likewise, through the transposition of phonemes (*varṇavyatyaya*), the letter *da* becomes *dha*.
"Idānīm" and "tadānīm": these are examples of the suffix *dānīm*. When the suffixes beginning with *tasil* would otherwise apply, the suffix *hil* is prescribed;
as in "kahi."

"Kadā, yadā, tadā"—this is according to [Pāṇini 5.3.15]: "After *sarva*, *eka*, *anya*, *kiya*, *tada*, and *yada*, the suffix *dā* is applied in the sense of time. "Sadyaḥ" (on the same day)—this is a conventional formation (*nipātana*) meaning that the cause and the effect occur on the same common day.
For example: "striking a vital point (marman) that causes instantaneous death. The meaning is that on the very day one is struck in a vital point, on that same day there is the taking of life.
And [the phrase] "and it is extensive" means:

*Uccair-āriśca* means "noble. Regarding *parasmād edyavi*: the suffix *edyavi* occurs after the word *para* when a day (*ahar*) is to be expressed. [The *Kāśikā* states: "A general term is differentiated by its specific instance (*viśeṣa*), which is its mode (*prakāra*). [The *Vārttika* states: "The separation of the rule (*yogavibhāga*) is for the sake of what follows."

He will state [later] that "after *thā*, when *hetu* follows" (Pāṇini 5.3.26); this is so that the suffix may apply only after *kima* and not after *idam*. [The rule is: "after those words which denote direction, place, and time.
But how can words for directions denote place or time? By their very nature (*svabhāvāt*).
For just as they denote directions by their own nature and not from any other cause, so too do they denote place and time.

If this is so, how is it that those existing in the three [dimensions] are designated by "directions" (*dik*)—as in the expression *dik-śabdebhyaḥ*? How, then, should it be designated? Should it not be *dig-deśa-kāla-śabdebhyaḥ*? This is not the case; for such a designation would have this result: [it would apply] even to the phrase *aindryāṃ diśi nivasati* ("he dwells in the eastern direction"), which we do not want. Since this [result] could be obtained by any one of these [terms], the designation by *dik* alone is appropriate, because by this designation the rule becomes concise. Furthermore, designation by *dik* is more concise, as the word *dik* has fewer syllables than the others; therefore, the designation is made by *dik*.

Even so, since the word *dik* (direction) primarily denotes direction, the qualification [“of place and time”] is inappropriate; for the word *dik* necessarily refers to direction. In that case, it should have been stated as “of place and time. This is not correct; for if it were stated thus, the word *dik* would merely serve as an indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*), and the suffix would apply only to those words denoting place and time, not to those denoting direction.
By including the mention of “direction,” however, it applies to those as well.

In this context, there are three case-endings (*vibhaktayaḥ*) and three meanings (*arthāḥ*), namely the directions and so forth; therein, someone might have the misconception that, due to their correspondence (*sāmya*), they must be applied according to their respective order (*yathāsaṃkhyena*). Therefore, to dispel that [misconception], he says: "In this [rule], application according to order is not intended.

Why, then, is a plural designation used here when a singular designation should have been employed? It is for the purpose of indicating that the suffix is to be applied individually to each of the directions and so forth, which possess multiple case-endings.

And thus, this suffix is formed from [a word] ending in many case-endings—provided that it occurs after a word denoting direction (*digvṛtti*) and ends in the seventh, fifth, or first case-ending, as well as after a word denoting place (*deśavṛtti*) and time (*kālavṛtti*).

Alternatively, the particle *ca* ("and") is carried over from the rule "thā hetau ca" (Pāṇini 5.3.26), and it conjoins only what is explicitly heard [in the text]. Therefore, the suffix occurs after each of those ending in the seventh, fifth, or first case-ending when they denote direction and so forth; it is not according to their respective order (*yathāsaṃkhyam*), for a conjunction would be contradicted by a correspondence based on order.

Alternatively, it has been stated that "correspondence according to order (*yathāsaṃkhya*) occurs when there is the *svarita* accent. However, in this case, the *svarita* accent would not be prescribed for the purpose of correspondence according to order; therefore, there will be no correspondence according to order. [This is indicated by] "before" (*puraḥ*) and "below" (*adhastāt*). By the rule to be stated later, Pāṇini 5.3.40, the suffix *-astāti* is added to the words *pūrva* and *adhara*. Consequently, by correspondence according to order, these two—*puraḥ* and *adhaḥ*—are the substitutes for the words *pūrva* and *adhara*, respectively.

"In the eastern direction (aindrī) he dwells. The word *aindrī* generally denotes any object related to Indra; however, in proximity to the word "direction" (*dik*), it refers specifically to a direction. Therefore, because it is not commonly known in the world as a synonym for "direction," the suffix [denoting direction] does not apply here.
[As in: "He went to the eastern village" (*pūrvaṃ grāmaṃ gataḥ*).

In this context, the word *pūrva* refers to a location because the village is of the nature of a place; however, it does not here end in the seventh case (*saptamī*) or other such case endings, but rather ends in the second case (*dvitīyā*). In the example "he dwells with a teacher who is to the east" (*pūrvasmin gurau vasati*), the word *pūrva* refers to the teacher as characterized by direction and so forth, but it does not refer to the directions themselves. Regarding the statement "the letter *a* is for the sake of specification": if the letter *a* were not included here, then the rule would have to be formulated as *ṣaṣṭhī tasarthapratyayena* (Pāṇini 2.3.30). This being the case, the suffix *tasil* would also be included [in the scope of the rule].
Furthermore, in the case of the expression *tataśca tato hetunā*, the genitive case would prevail by overriding the instrumental case.

Therefore, the letter *a* must be included for the sake of specification. Now, why is it that the letter *a* is not there for the purpose of preventing the hearing of the feminine suffix *ṭāp* when the words *dakṣiṇā* and *uttarā* refer to the directions? [The answer is: "In all compound formations (*vṛtti*), a pronoun takes the masculine form. (Vārttika).

104) Thus, because the feminine suffix *ṭāp* is already excluded by the very statement "as in the masculine" (*puṃvat*), one might object: "If the letter *k* were not present, the accent would be established by the accent of the affix itself; therefore, the letter *k* should not even be inserted. To this, [the answer is: "When there is a mention of an element with a single *anubandha*, an element with two *anubandhas* is not included" (Vyāḍīya-paribhāṣā).

"In that case, will there not be the inclusion of *tasil*? Even so, there would be an inclusion of either one [of the suffixes] in the rules for *tasil* (Pāṇini 5.4.44), *tra* (4.3.112), and *tasi* (4.3.113).
Therefore, the particle *ca* must be employed for the sake of specification: 'And the suffix *āti*.
This also is an exception (*apavāda*) to *astāti*."
Regarding the terms *dakṣiṇapaścāt* and *uttarapaścāt*:
[the suffix *ṭac* is applied] because he dwells in the southwestern direction (*dakṣiṇāparasyāṃ diśi*), thus it is *dakṣiṇapaścāt*; likewise for *uttarapaścāt*.
According to the rule "and when the second member ends in *ardha*," the word *aparasya* is connected [to this rule].
"Even without the preceding word, the state of being posterior (paścādbhāva) must be expressed"—
this is to be connected with what is under discussion, namely "of the other half-uttara-pada.
In all these instances, the word *vaktavya* ("must be expressed") occurs in the sense of "should be explained" (*vyākhyāna*).

In this regard, the following is the explanation: by means of the "lion’s glance" (*siṃhāvalokita*) from the subsequent rule, the particle *ca* ("and") is understood to apply here, and it serves the purpose of including what has not been explicitly stated.

By that, operations such as the substitution of *pañca* for the word *apara* when it follows a directional term as a prior member (*dik-pūrvapada*) are established. By the rules [Pāṇini 5.3.28], [5.3.35], [5.3.36], [5.3.37], and [5.3.38], which begin with *uttaradakṣiṇābhyām*, the suffixes *atasuc* and others would otherwise be applicable; however, the rule prescribing *astāti* even after *adhara* is formulated, and thus *astāti* indeed supersedes those [suffixes].
However, *atasuc* and the others certainly do occur optionally by virtue of an explicit statement (*vacana*).

And here, although there is a triad of both the suffixes beginning with *uttara*, the case endings beginning with the seventh (*saptamī*), and the qualifiers (*upādhi*) beginning with *diś*, nevertheless, there is no application according to numerical correspondence (*yathāsaṃkhya*).
Why? Because the fact that those meanings possess the *svarita* accent has not been formally asserted.

By placing the word *adhara*, which consists of fewer syllables, first—either as a sign of deviation from the general rule (*lakṣaṇavyabhicāra*) or to demonstrate that this [specific] rule is independent of other rules—he indicates that the rule for "correspondence according to order" (*yathāsaṃkhya*) is not required here. Consequently, there is no correspondence according to order with respect to the case-endings (*vibhakti*). Furthermore, with respect to the qualifying attributes (*upādhi*), since the word *dakṣiṇa* cannot function in the sense of time, it is said: "If it denotes proximity, it occurs between the limit (*avadhi*) and the object limited (*avadhimān*)."

But how is such a distinction obtained, given that the word for a limit (*avadhi*) is not heard in the sūtra, nor is the possessor of a limit (*avadhimān*)? Words such as "directional" (*dik-śabda*) function by depending on a limit; and the possessor of a limit also exists in dependence upon a limit. Thus, even though it is not explicitly stated, this distinction is obtained by implication, as in:
"He dwells below."

By the rule to be stated as [5.3.40], the word *adhara* undergoes substitution when followed by the suffix *astāti*. The phrase "prior to *asi*" refers to what will be stated in [5.3.39]: "When *asi* follows, *pur* and *dhava* are substituted for these."

Some believe that the suffix occurs solely from words denoting direction (*dik-śabda*); according to their view, forms such as *pūrveṇa vasati* ("he dwells to the east") are also valid. If the suffix were to occur solely from words denoting direction, then it would also occur after *atyanta*. Let it be so—[the suffix] will be elided by rule 5.3.30. This is not the case; for "intermediate exceptions (*apavāda*) supersede preceding rules" (Vyāḍipāda).

10) Thus, by this [rule], there is elision (*luk*) here only for *astāti*, and not for anything else. In that case, the term *anyatarasyām* constitutes a restricted option (*vyavasthitavibhāṣā*). Consequently, it will not apply to words ending in *añc*.

The letter *pakāra* (the *p* in *kārmaṇa*) is for the purpose of specification [by Pāṇini 2.3.31] and for the sake of the accent. [The rule applies to] that which is joined with it: the meaning is that the suffix *aṇ* is added in its own sense (*svārthe*) to a word denoting an action (*karman*) that is employed by the speech of a messenger conveying a specific message;
thus, "action itself" is *kārmaṇa*.
Because of the *prakṛtibhāva* (non-application of grammatical modification) by the rule "a-an," there is no elision of the suffix *ṭi*.
That action which is performed exactly as it was heard from the words of a messenger is called *kārmaṇa*.
This is what he says: "having heard the verbal [instruction]. [The suffixes] *-añ* and *-ī* are applied after the word *bhakta*.

[Objection: But would not the suffix *ādi* alone apply because it is the nearest [to the word]? [Reply: No; the particle *ca* ("and") is used here, for it includes even a preceding element that is separated [by others].

Therefore, *āc* will also occur. Since *tāt* is obtained after a word ending in a vowel (*pūrva-āc*), this rule beginning with *itas* is commenced so that there may be an option (*vibhāṣā*) regarding *tāt* even after a word ending in a vowel.

Now, for what purpose is this [word] *eṣām* stated, since that very genitive which occurs in [the rule regarding] *pūrva* and so on is understood as a genitive of the substituendum (*sthāna-ṣaṣṭhī*) once the suffix has been prescribed, and because the difference in relationship results in a difference in the meaning of the genitive? This is true; nevertheless, it is stated as *eṣām* for the sake of easy comprehension. But surely, because it is superseded by *asin* [in Pāṇini 5.2.127], the suffix *astāti* should not occur after *pūrva* and the others? To this he says: *idameva* and so forth. The meaning has already been explained. And [regarding] *prakāravacane ca jātīyar* [Pāṇini 5.3.69], this [suffix *thamu*] is its exception (*apavāda*).

It has been stated that *vidhā* means "manner" (*prakāra*) [in Pāṇini 5.3.23], and that [manner] also exists as a specific substance (*dravya*) or quality (*guṇa*). If that were also included here, then because of its connection with gender and number—either through the substance or the quality—the suffix ending would not be without gender and without number. And in that case, its status as an indeclinable (*avyaya*) would not be established, yet that is desired; for the suffix *dhā* is recited among the indeclinables, from *tasil* onwards up to *edhāc*.
However, there is no fault in accepting that [action] as its object; for, bearing in mind that action is never connected with gender and number, he says "And that," and so forth.

Action is the meaning expressed by the verbal root, such as "moistening" (vikledana) and the like; and since that is its object, it is described as such. But how is the apprehension of a particular [meaning] obtained when there is a general statement? This is precisely the purpose of including the word "object" (artha): so that there may be a specification of the mode; otherwise, he would have simply said "in the case of an injunction" (*vidhāyām*).

If, then, the manner (*prakāra*) is understood as the object of the action, would [the rule] not fail to apply in cases such as *navadhā dravyam* (substance in nine ways) and *navadhā guṇaḥ* (quality in nine ways)? This is not a fault; for here too, an action must be supplied:

"Substance is to be established in nine ways," and "Quality is to be established in nine ways," when they are analyzed (*vigṛhyate*). As for the example "Make into one" (*aikadhyam kuru*), this is an illustration of the shifting of the locus (*adhikaraṇavicāla*).

Regarding the expression *aikadhyam bhuṅkte*: [this is used] in the sense of restriction (*vidhi*). Here, the mention of *dhā* is understood by anuvṛtti from the previous rule, yet its application in that context was not intended to express restriction (*vidhi*), because it had already been prescribed there.

Therefore, because of the force of the subsequent application (*anuvṛtti*), the status of being a substitute (*sthānitva*) for the suffix *dhā* is understood; thus he says, "since it is obtained from the context itself. The ellipsis to be supplied is "the status of being a substitute for the suffix *dhā*. But what is the reason that [the rule] does not apply to that which is prescribed in the sense of 'prevention' (*vidhā*) when the mention of *dhā* is absent? To this he says, "for [the rule applies] only to that which is immediately preceding," and so forth.
For if the word *punaḥ* were not used, then according to the principle "a rule or a prohibition applies to what is immediately preceding" (Vyākaraṇa-paribhāṣā 19),
it would apply only to that which was prescribed for the purpose of determining the locus (*adhikaraṇavicāla*), and not to that which was prescribed for the purpose of supporting (*vidhāra*).
But when the word *dhāma* is included [in the rule], the substitution is established for the base *dhāma* alone—as in the example *matidvaidhāni*.

But surely, since secondary suffixes (*svārthika*) do not follow the gender and number of their base forms (*prakṛti-dharma*), there ought to be no [application of] gender and number here? This is not a fault; for sometimes secondary suffixes do indeed deviate from the properties of their base forms. For example: *cāturvarṇyam* (the state of being the four castes) from *catvāro varṇāḥ* (the four castes). Furthermore, this word *yāpya* occurs in the sense of "to be conveyed"—as in *grāmāntarād yāpyaḥ* ("to be carried from another village"); it occurs in the sense of "incurable"—as in *yāpyo rogaḥ* ("an incurable disease"); and it occurs in the sense of "contemptible"—as in *yāpyo 'yam* ("this one is contemptible"), where it is understood as "contemptible."

Regarding the suffix *pāśap* [which forms words like *yāpyapāśa*]: since it is understood to denote only that which is contemptible (*kutsita*), it is most appropriate to include the word *yāpya* itself as expressing that very meaning. For this reason, he says: "The contemptible is called *yāpya*. [In this sense], *yāpya* means "that from which qualities are removed (*apanīyante*)," and thus the *kṛtya* suffix is applied in the sense of the ablative (*apādāne*) according to [Pāṇini 3.3.113].
[The questioner asks: "Why does it not occur in that case?"
The intention is this: although he is proficient in grammar (*vyākaraṇa*), nevertheless, because of his bad character (*duḥśīlatva*), the suffix must indeed occur there.
Regarding the phrase "of whom" (*yasya*) and so forth:

a quality (*guṇa*) is the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) and a substance (*dravya*) is the qualified (*viśeṣya*). Although many qualities exist in that substance, nevertheless, when a word applies to—that is, functions with respect to—a substance due to the presence of a particular quality, by reason of proximity (*pratyāsatti*), the word must express the disparagement (*kutsā*) of that very quality; however, the bad character of the grammarian is not the basis for the application of the term (*pravṛttinimitta*).
What then? It is the thorough knowledge of grammar or its study.

And here, one must not assume that the suffix is used in the sense of "immoral" (*duḥśīla*). This is because [the suffix] *tīya* is prescribed under the heading of ordinal numbers (*pūraṇa*) by the rule *pūraṇapratyayo yastīyaḥ* (Pāṇini 5.2.48), either because it is enjoined within that section on ordinals or because it denotes an ordinal number.
Even by way of metaphorical usage (*upacāra*), a third [part] is called "completer" (*pūraṇa*).
Regarding the word "in a portion" (*bhāge*): the meaning is "in a part" (*aṃśe*).

But for what purpose is this [rule], since even when [the suffix] *ani* is applied, the form remains the same? To this he says: "The statement is for the sake of the accent (*svarārtham*). This is so that, in the analysis [of the compound], it may be acutely accented on the first syllable by virtue of the *nit*-accent.
"The mention of *pūraṇa* (ordinal numbers) is for the sake of subsequent rules."

[The suffix] is intended so that a suffix may occur after a word ending in a ordinal suffix (*pūraṇapratyaya*) in subsequent cases. And would not the term "ordinal" (*pūraṇa*), being applied for the purpose of exclusion, also be meaningful here? However, since that [suffix] is absent, its meaningfulness here is not tenable.
But is it not the case that [the form] *mukhapārātaserīyaḥ* [is derived from *mukhapāra*]?
460) Is there also such a thing as *pārātīyaḥ* even when [the suffix] is not used for filling out a word (*apūraṇa*)? To this he says: "The *mukhatīya* and others are meaningless.
By the paribhāṣā regarding the inclusion of meaningful elements (Vyāḍi-paribhāṣā 1), a *tīya* suffix that possesses meaning is understood here; however, *mukhatīya* and the like are meaningless.

Therefore, the intention is that even though the mention of *pūraṇa* (ordinal numbers) occurs [in the rule], its application will not take place [here]. For in the case of "according to the order" (*yathāsaṃkhya*), it is understood from the sixth [rule] that there is an application otherwise than [the immediate predecessor];
and since it would already be established by the preceding [rule] alone, the mention of the sixth [rule] would be purposeless.

Therefore, both [results] arise from both [rules]. By the word "and" (*ca*), it is meant "and as it was obtained [by the preceding rule]. It is understood that there is either the elision (*luk*) of *ākinic* or of *kan*.
Because of proximity,
and not because of that which is prescribed in another context, due to remoteness.
If "and that" and so forth were eternal, then its injunction would be purposeless.
Therefore, by the force of the rule, it occurs in the alternative case.

But what is the reason that the mention of "without a companion" (*asahāya*) is made for the purpose of excluding words denoting number? To this he says: "For if that were included," and so forth. If the mention of "without a companion" were absent, the word *eka*, even when it expresses a number, would also be included.
If that [non-accompaniment] were present, however, there would be no [term for] two or many;
for the number one does not exist in two or in many.
Non-accompaniment, however, applies even to a hundred, because of the absence of anything else of the same kind—as in the expression "a hundred without companions."
Therefore, by including the meaning of "companionship" (*sahāya*), the suffix is established even for two or many [persons].

Now, why is *ākinic* taught [instead], rather than simply saying *akanic*, since here too the desired form would be established through the rule of homogeneous long vowels (*savarṇadīrghatva*)? It is not established; for the rule of substitution with the subsequent form (*pararūpatva*) and the elision of the final vowel (*yasyeti lopa*) would apply.

Would it not be the case that these do not occur due to the functional power (*sāmarthya*) of the pronunciation of the letter *a*? This is not so; for there is indeed a purpose for the pronunciation of the letter *a*.

Why? So that there may not be another *avagraha* (word-division) based on the designation of a "word" (*pada*) within the designation of a "nominal stem" (*bhasaṃjñā*). Therefore, only *ākinic* should be prescribed. But for what purpose are these two words, which have the same meaning, taught, rather than just one of them? It cannot be done in this way; for here, a suffix is desired after a word denoting an object qualified by a past time (*atikrāntakāla*), and that past time would not be grasped if only one of the two were mentioned.
To illustrate: the word *bhūta* also occurs in the sense of the present, as in *bhūtavān*; however, the word *pūrva* also refers to direction and place.
Therefore, when only one of the two [words] is mentioned, that which has passed away [the past time] is not understood.
For this very reason, he says: "The word *bhūtapūrva* expresses a past time.
Now, why does the designation *it* (as in *cuṭ*) not apply to the letter *ca* [in *bhūtapūrva*]? Because that rule is not universal (*anitya*).

However, impermanence (*anityatva*) has been established in that very context. Here, that which is the qualifier ending in the sixth case (*ṣaṣṭhyanta*) is subordinate because it exists for the sake of another; the other, moreover, being assisted by that very [qualifier], is the qualificand (*viśeṣya*) and is primary (*pradhāna*). Since the comprehension of the action (*kārya*) occurs through the primary element, when a suffix is prescribed after a word ending in the sixth case, the suffix is understood to apply to the primary correlate ending in the sixth case, not to the meaning of the base (*prakṛtyartha*); likewise, the mention of "having existed previously" (*bhūtapūrva*) is understood to refer to that very [primary correlate] and not to the meaning of the base. Having considered this, he says: "after that which ends in the sixth case," and so forth.

However, the meaning of the suffix [in *atiśāyana*] should be understood as that which is the counter-correlative (*pratiyogin*) of the genitive case-ending. Regarding the word "excess" (*atiśāyana*):
it is formed with the suffix *lyuṭ*.
Although the root *śī* by itself occurs in the sense of sleeping, here the prefix *ati* causes it to function in the sense of excellence; for this very reason, he says: "excellence" (*prakarṣa*).

"Should it not rather be *atiśāyanam*? To this he replies: "The lengthening [of the vowel] occurs by way of irregular derivation (*nipātana*). But how is the word *atiśāyana* understood as being correct through such an irregular derivation? It is for the purpose of establishing its grammatical correctness (*sādhutva*). And this [term *atiśāyana*] is a qualifier of the base form (*prakṛti*).
He refutes the doubt regarding the suffix:

it need not be stated that for primary suffixes (*svārthika*), the meaning of the base (*prakṛtyartha*) serves as a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) of what is expressed (*dyotya*); for that [meaning] is already expressed by the base itself—as in the examples *paṭiṣṭhaḥ* and *laghiṣṭhaḥ*.
The elision of the *ṭi* suffix occurs by [Pāṇini 6.4.154].

Regarding the form *gariṣṭhaḥ*: by the rule beginning with [Pāṇini 6.4.157], "the substitutes *gura-* etc. [are applied] for *priya*, *sthira*, *sphira*, *urū*, *bahula*, and *guru*," the word *guru* undergoes the substitution of *gara-*.

To one who thinks that "there should be no further suffix after a word already ending in a suffix denoting excellence, because the excellence has already been expressed by that single suffix," he says: "And when...

This means: where the *ātiśāyanika* suffix (denoting excellence) is prescribed for the first degree of excellence, since that [excellence] has already been expressed by it, let there be no second suffix of excellence.

However, in the case of a different degree of excellence, it is indeed proper for another *ātiśāyanika* suffix to follow a word already ending in an *ātiśāyanika* suffix, because that [further excellence] has not yet been expressed; such is the sense.

After the suffix *iṣṭhan* [Pāṇini 5.3.60], together with the preceding [suffix] [Pāṇini 6.1.87]: the suffix *tamap* is a suffix expressing excellence (*prakarṣa*) following a word ending in the suffix *iṣṭhan*. Here, that excellence which is relative to a counterpart—that is, excellence relative to a previous excellence—is expressed by the suffix *iṣṭhan*.

But surely there is no rule prescribing this superlative suffix (*atiśāyika*) by which, once it is prescribed, another degree of excellence beyond it could be prescribed as a further superlative; for this is the only single rule. In that case, if the suffix denoting excellence were prescribed by this very rule, it would be impossible for such a suffix to follow a base that already ends in a superlative suffix; thus, the existence of a further superlative after a superlative is improper? This is not a fault.

In this context, because there is a distinction between the two suffixes being prescribed, these constitute two separate sentences: by one, the suffix *iṣṭhan* is prescribed, and by the other, the suffix *tamap* is prescribed after that [base] ending in *iṣṭhan*. Regarding the statement "the expression of two meanings is the dual (*dvivacanam*)," this shows that the term *dvivacana* is taken here in its etymological sense (*anvartha*), and not in its technical (*pāribhāṣika*) sense. For if the technical dual were intended, the suffix would not apply in the case of "Between us and Devadatta, Devadatta is more handsome," because the technical dual does not exist there.
However, when the term is understood according to its etymological meaning (*anvartha*), the upapada possesses a dual sense.
For instance, by the word *asmākam*, one meaning is expressed, since the plural number is prescribed [by Pāṇini 1.4.22] for the sake of a single referent;
and by the word *devadattasya*, a second meaning is also expressed. Thus, that upapada indeed becomes a dual expression in accordance with its etymological meaning.

Thus, since this [term] succeeds everywhere when understood according to its etymological meaning (*anvartha*), he considers that its inclusion here is appropriate. "To be divided" (*vibhaktavya*) means it should be made separate.

Furthermore, that which is being surpassed (*atiśayyamāna*) possesses the status of an *upapada*, not the agent who surpasses (*atiśayitṛ*); for otherwise, the suffix would not be prescribed [after such a word]. Now, one might object: "When the suffix *ṇyat* is applied by the rule *ṛhaloṇryat* [Pāṇini 3.1.124], the form should be *vibhājya*; how then is the form *vibhajya* justified in the grammatical instruction? To this he says: "It occurs as *yat* by way of an irregular derivation (*nipātana*). In this context, there are two *upapadas*, and likewise two bases (*prakṛti*) and two suffixes (*pratyaya*). Consequently, someone might have the misconception that the correspondence must follow the numerical order (*yathāsaṃkhya*). Therefore, in order to dispel that, he says: "And [the application of] numerical order is indicated by the mark of the *cara*."

For by demonstrating independence from other defining characteristics (*lakṣaṇāntara*), he indicates that even the characteristic of "correspondence in number" (*yathāsaṃkhya*) need not be relied upon here. Regarding the word *paṭīyān*:
