as before, there is the elision of *ṭi* [by Pāṇini 6.4.143], the lengthening of the vowel [by Pāṇini 6.4.14], and the elision of the final consonant of the cluster following a vowel or semivowel [by Pāṇini 6.1.68 and 8.2.23].
In the expression "The people of Mathurā are wealthier than the people of Pāṭaliputra," the fifth case ending (pañcamī) is applied by rule [Pāṇini 2.3.42].

Here, "pāṭaliputrakebhyaḥ" is the subordinate term (*upapada*) used in the sense of "distinguishing" (*vibhajya*); for the people of Pāṭaliputra are distinguished from—that is, set apart from—the people of Mathurā.

But is this not already established by the rule *dvivacanopapade* ("when a dual form is the upapada")? For here there is indeed a dual form as the upapada; to wit: "one heap of the Mathurans, another of the Pāṭaliputrakas"—and these two are expressed by a dual. Therefore, is the mention of *vibhajya* ("dividing") redundant? This is not so; for although there is a duality here in relation to the heaps, that duality is not what is conveyed by the word. What, then, is it? It is the distinction between the parts (*avayava-bheda*).
For this very reason, the plural form is used in the expression *māthurāḥ pāṭaliputrakebhyaḥ* ("the Mathurans [are superior] to the Pāṭaliputrakas").

In this case, there is no "two-meaning-ness" (dvyarthatā) even with respect to a class (rāśi), as in the example: "The people of Mathurā are more delicate than the people of Sāṅkāśya and the people of Pāṭaliputra.
Therefore, the mention of the term *vibhajya* ("having distinguished") must also be made. Regarding the form *pācakataraḥ*:
since this refers to a substance (dravya) possessing the capacity of an agent, the word *pācaka* denotes a substance.

Now, for what purpose is the particle *eva* used, since a rule being commenced when [the desired result] is already established serves as a restrictive rule (*niyamārtha*) even without it? To this he says: "The particle *eva*" and so forth. For if the particle *eva* were absent, a contrary restriction would be understood—namely, that [the suffixes] *ta* and *tama* apply only after words denoting qualities (*guṇavacana*) that begin with vowels (*ajādī*). Consequently, because the restriction applies to what follows the particle *eva*, there would be a restriction on the base (*prakṛti-niyama*). And thus, because the word denoting a quality would be restricted to those beginning with vowels, the suffixes *tarap* and so forth would not occur after them.

However, when the particle *eva* is uttered immediately after the base (*prakṛti*), this becomes a restriction regarding the meaning of the suffix (*pratyaya*) rather than a restriction regarding the base; thus, forms such as *paṭutaraḥ* and *paṭutamaḥ* are established. To ensure the establishment of these two as well, the rule "the suffixes *iṣṭhan* and *īyasun* [are added] after words expressing qualities" was not formulated. In that case, because these two [suffixes, *iṣṭhan* and *īyasun*] would serve as injunctions (*vidhi*) and would consequently sublate (*bādhaka*) the suffixes *tarap* and *tamap*, the absence of those two would mean that forms like *paṭutaraḥ* and *paṭutamaḥ* could not be established. [This is illustrated by the example: *karipṭhaḥ*.
From the word *kartṛ* [ending in] *tṛn*, [the suffix] *iṣṭhan* is added according to [Pāṇini 5.3.55], resulting in the elision of the syllable *tṛ*.

Regarding the form *dohīyasī*: from the word *dogdhrī* [ending in] *tṛn*, the suffix *īyasun* is added; once the elision of the syllable *tṛ* has occurred, the substitution of *gh* and so forth ceases due to the absence of its cause, and the feminine suffix *ṅīp* is applied according to [Pāṇini 4.1.5]. Now, one might object: since *ajādī* ends in the nominative case, how can a substitute be obtained when *aja* and others follow? To this he says: "in *ajādī* [of] *ati*."
Regarding the phrase "having that as its object" (*tadviṣaya*):
that which has that praiseworthy word as its object is *tadviṣaya*.
This shows that the restriction [imposed] by the rule *itaś ca* (Pāṇini 5.3.58) does not apply in that case.
"Likewise in the subsequent [rules] as well," refers to rules such as Pāṇini 5.3.62 and others.

In the case of "this one is better than these two," the suffix *īyasun* occurs when a dual-numbered word is the *upapada*. In the case of "this one is better than this one," the suffix occurs when a word used distributively (*vibhajya*) is the *upapada*.

In the former case, the genitive is used for selection (nirdhāraṇa) [Pāṇini 2.3.41], while in the latter case, the ablative is used [Pāṇini 2.3.42]. The separation of the rules (yogavibhāga) is intended to prevent the application of the rule of "correspondence in order" (yathāsaṃkhyam), and for the sake of what follows.
In the subsequent rule, it is so that only the substitution of *jya* occurs for the word *vṛddha*, and not the substitution of *śra*. Regarding the phrase "of the word *vṛddha*":
the meaning is "of this word, namely *vṛddha*."

By this, he shows that there is a literal apprehension (*svarūpagrahaṇa*) of the word "vṛddha. Now, one might object: since the word *vṛddha* has been established as a technical term (*saṃjñā*) by the rule [Pāṇini 1.1.73], therefore only the designated object (*saṃjñin*) signified by it is to be understood, and not its own form, according to the statement [Pāṇini 1.1.68]? This is not a fault; for the word "praśasyasya" (of that which is praiseworthy) is carried over here from the previous rule, and by that, the word *vṛddha* is qualified: "of that which is praiseworthy and old. In the case of a literal apprehension, the state of being praiseworthy is appropriate when the meaning of the word is an age-advanced person, but not in the case of a technical apprehension.

Alternatively—by the *sthāne'ntaratama* paribhāṣā (P. 1.1.49), that which is the most similar (*antaratama*) to the word *jya* is understood as its substitute; and since the word *vṛddha* alone is the most similar to it, it is logical that only that [word] should be taken.
Regarding the phrase "and of those two" (*tayośca*), etc.:
just as in the rule *yathā>...* (P. 5.3.60), the existence of affixes beginning with vowels (*ajādī*) was indicated by the absence of a restrictive rule (*niyamābhāva*), so too is it indicated here.

The absence of restriction regarding *aja* and so forth, however, should be understood as being due to the prescription of substitutes after [the suffixes] *para* and so on, just as before. Regarding the phrase "of the two causes" (*nimittayoḥ*) and so on:
the two causes are the two suffixes; because the prescription of substitutes occurs after them.
Why, then, is it not desired [to apply the rule] here? Because that which has fewer syllables (*alpāctara*) is placed last.
For that [term] expresses independence from other defining characteristics;
therefore, even the rule of "correspondence by order" (*yathāsaṃkhya*) is not required here.

If this is so, would it not follow that correspondence by order would also fail to apply between the original element (*sthānin*) and its substitute (*ādeśa*)? Let there be no correspondence by order; the determination will instead be made on the basis of "proximity" (*āntaratamya*).

But surely, if another defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇāntara*) is not required to establish the rule, then the maxim *sthāne 'ntaratamaḥ* [P. 1.1.50] would also not apply? This is not so; for the statement that there is no fixed rule (*vyavasthā*) established by the wording of the sūtra itself only makes known that there is no restriction imposed by the formulation of the rule, but it does not subvert a restriction established by the meaning (*arthakṛtā*). Moreover, this maxim *ādeśapratipattaye* [P. 1.1.49] must necessarily be taken into account.

How can the *paribhāṣā* "in its place, the most similar" (*sthāne 'ntaratamaḥ*)—which is a subsidiary element of that [rule]—be disregarded? Here too, a correspondence between the causes [the two words] is not intended; for its absence is understood from the fact that, despite the rule "that which begins with a vowel and ends in /a/ comes first" (*ajādyadantam*), the word *alpa-* is placed last rather than first, thereby indicating a disregard for the formal characteristic [of being alphabetically prior]. Furthermore, by the term *yuvan*, the actual form itself is intended to be referred to, not the state of the lineage being living. Why? Because here too the word "of that which is praiseworthy" (*praśasyasya*) from [Pāṇini 5.3.60] continues to apply; therefore, the word *yuvan* must be qualified as "the praiseworthy youth."

Praise is appropriate when the word-meaning is understood in its own form (*svarūpa*), as connected with the stage of life known as youth, which is esteemed by all the world; it is not so when it is understood in a technical (*pāribhāṣika*) sense.

Alternatively, according to the rule *sthāne 'ntaratamaḥ* [Pāṇini 1.1.50], it is understood that among those [sounds] in place of [an original], that which is most similar (*antaratama*) is the one that takes its place; and the word *yuva* itself is indeed the most similar.
Therefore, it is proper to take the word in its own form alone.

The inclusion of the term *anyatarasyām* (optionally) here applies only to the word *alpa*, not to the word *yuva*; for even without it, the optional alternative is already established by the rule: "In the case of *sthūla*, *ṭūra*, *yuvan*, *hrasva*, *kṣipra*, and *kṣudra*, [the final vowel] followed by *yaṇ* etc. is replaced, and there is *guṇa* substitution for the preceding [vowel]" (*Pāṇini* 6.4.156). Indeed, if the substitution were obligatory, the elision of what follows the *yaṇ* etc. would be impossible, nor would the preceding portion be subject to *guṇa*. Thus we have *yaviṣṭhaḥ* and *yavīyān*.

By the rule *sthūladūrādi-sūtra* (Pāṇini 6.4.156), that which follows the *yaṇ*-substitution and so forth is elided, and a *guṇa* substitution occurs for the preceding vowel. Because of its association (*sāhacarya*) with the suffix *matup*, only the possessive suffix *vin* is understood here—referring to [Pāṇini] 5.2.102 and 5.2.121. And by these two rules, this very statement regarding elision (*lug-vacana*) makes known that [the suffixes] beginning with *aj* are applied after [stems ending in] *u*. Thus: *rūpavān*.
In the sūtra *asmāyāmedhāsrajo viniḥ* (Pāṇini 5.2.120), the suffix *vini* is applied.

In the form *ruājiṣṭhaḥ*, there is no elision of the *ṭi* portion because of the preservation of the original stem (*prakṛtibhāva*) by rule *na kapi* (Pāṇini 7.4.14). Regarding the phrase "and those which have their own meaning" (*svārthikāś ca*), and so forth.

Qualifications such as praise and so forth pertain to the meaning of the base (*prakṛti*); the *svārthika* suffixes are indicators (*dyotaka*) of that [meaning], but they are not denoters (*vācaka*) of a different meaning.

If the suffix *rūp* is prescribed after a word existing in the sense of praise, it would not apply to a word existing in the sense of censure—such as "this man is *vṛṣalarūpaḥ*" (of the form of a low-born person) or "this man is *caurarūpaḥ*" (of the form of a thief).
For words like *vṛṣala* always express censure and never occur in the sense of praise, unlike words such as *kāka* and others? To this, he says: "Of the meaning of the base," and so forth.
The excellence (*vaiśiṣṭya*) of the meaning of the base (*prakṛti*) is its completeness (*paripūrṇatva*); when that exists, praise (*praśaṃsā*) occurs.

And thus, when even words such as *vṛṣala* possess the completeness of their referent, they then function in the sense of praise, and the suffix is therefore applied after them as well. When the completeness of the meaning of the base is achieved through the eating of onions or the drinking of liquor, they then function in the sense of praise, and the suffix is therefore applied after those too.
By means of eating onions and drinking liquor, he demonstrates the fulfillment of the essential meaning [of the term].
For the word *vṛṣala* has "Śūdra" as its denotation;
when he consumes even such things as onions—which are censured by virtuous people—then his Śūdra-ness reaches full completion.
"A Śūdra is one who eats everything and sells everything.
Furthermore, the meaning of the word *caura* (thief) is also fully realized through the act of stealing well-guarded property.

Now, as for the point: "Derivatives formed with suffixes having their own meaning (*svārthika*) follow the gender and number of the base" (Vyākaraṇa-paribhāṣā 74); the sense is that whatever gender and number belong to the meaning of the base, those same gender and number also apply to the form ending in the *svārthika* suffix.

Furthermore, in cases such as *pacatorūpam* (the form of two cooking [agents]) and *pacantirūpam* (the form of many cooking [agents]), should there not be dual and plural endings? To this he says: "The action is primary," and so forth.
Although both the action and the agent are denoted by the verb (*ākhyāta*), nevertheless, the action alone is its primary meaning.

And since gender and number ought to follow the base-meaning (*prakṛtyartha*) which is the primary element, it is appropriate for them to conform to the suffixes that express their own meanings (*svārthika*).
Action is the primary element, and there is only one action.
Therefore, dual and plural endings do not occur after a verbal form ending in the suffix *rūp*.
[Objection: In that case, would the neuter gender also not apply, since action lacks gender? To this, he says: "But the neuter gender," and so forth.
He states the reason for that very point: "Because the gender (liṅga) is based on the world.

If, then, the action is one, how are the dual and plural numbers not established in forms such as *pacataḥ* and *pacanti*? This is not a fault; for although the action is one, the means (sādhana) are many, and therefore the dual and plural will occur based upon those [means]. Would they then occur from a word ending in the suffix *rūpap*? No, they would not, because they have already been expressed by the verbal suffix (*tiṅ*).

But the singular number will indeed apply, because it is the general rule (*utsargika*), according to the statement: "The singular number shall be employed as the general rule. Here, the mention of *vibhāṣā* (optionality) is connected with the suffix *bahuc*, not with what precedes; therefore, the position of *bahuc* is not subject to optionality, and thus it remains obligatory. For this very reason, he says: "But that [suffix] is only before [the word].
By the word *eva* (only), he shows that the particle *tu* has the sense of restriction (*avadhāraṇa*).

If, however, the word *tu* were not used for the sake of restriction (*avadhāraṇa*), it would not be known whether the mention of *vibhāṣā* is connected with *bahuc*, or whether this [restriction] applies to what precedes. But by the word *tu*, having its sense of restriction, when that which precedes is restricted, it is understood—by the principle of elimination (*pāriśeṣya*)—that it is connected specifically with the mention of *vibhāṣā* in the case of *bahuj*.
As for the statement, "The addition of the marker *c* is for the purpose of making the final syllable accented (*antodātta*)."

Furthermore, for what does the acute accent on the final syllable (*antodāttatva*) arise due to the presence of the *cit* suffix? It arises for the entire complex (*samudāya*) together with its base (*saprakṛti*), because of the rule: "The *cit* suffix [is marked acute] along with its base, for the sake of [distinguishing] words having many vowels or the suffix *kac*" (Vārttika 6.1.169).

If this is so, when *paṭavaḥ* is derived from the nominal stem *paṭu*, would not the acute accent (*udāttatva*) apply to the suffix *jas*? This is not a fault; for when the suffix *bahuc* has been produced, the designation of nominal stem (*prātipadika-saṃjñā*) is applied by the rule "That which is meaningful, not a verbal root, and not a suffix, is a nominal stem" [Pāṇini 1.2.45]. Once that is done, the elision of the case-ending (*subluk*) is performed by the rule "The case-endings are elided after a verbal root and a nominal stem" [Pāṇini 2.4.71]. When that has been performed, the acute accent subsequently applied belongs to the vowel *u* in the word *paṭu*.

Furthermore, once the designation of a nominal stem (*prātipadika-saṃjñā*) has been applied and the elision of the case-ending (*sup-luk*) has occurred, another *jas* suffix arises; its acute accent (*udāttatva*) cannot be denied, for it is not a part of the original base (*prakṛti*).

But surely, since the mention of "compound" (*samāsa*) is a restrictive rule (*niyama*) regarding meaningful aggregates, a form preceded by the suffix *bahuc* should not receive the designation of a nominal stem? This is not a fault; the restriction applies to those of the same class (*tulyajātīya*).
And what is of the same class? That which is of the same nature as compounds.
Of what kind of elements is there a compound? Of those possessing distinct meanings and being connected.
Distinctness of meaning and connection occur only for those that possess separate referents;
however, it is not possible for indicators (dyotaka) to possess separate referents.

Now, why is the *sub*-elision performed first, and only afterwards the final acute accent (*antodāttatvam*), given that—because it is subsequent—the final acute accent ought logically to occur first? This is not so; for the elision (*luk*) is permanent (*nitya*), because it applies whether [the accent] has been applied or not. For that elision occurs even when the final acute accent has been applied, and it also occurs when it has not been applied; whereas the final acute accent occurs only when the elision of another element has taken place. Since a rule that applies to one thing when another has not occurred would be non-permanent (*anitya*), therefore the elision is indeed performed first.
"Raisins with much molasses.
But how can there be "incompleteness" (apūrṇatva) here, since the word *guḍa* denotes either the universal (*jāti*) of molasses or the substance (*dravya*) that is its substratum?

In that regard, the universal is indeed one and partless; thus, it is complete within every locus. And as for the substance, whatever is connected with it is likewise complete, because it is fully present throughout.

Therefore, is it not incorrect to use "incomplete" (*īṣadasamāpti*) here as a qualifier, because [the quality] is impossible [in the word itself]? And how could there be grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*)—as in "grape with much sugar" (*bahuguḍā drākṣā*)—since it would not be obtained by the word "grape" (*drākṣā*), given that its meaning is something else? Furthermore, why would the feminine gender not be justified by the rule: "Derivatives formed with suffixes having their own meaning (*svārthika*) follow the gender and number of the base" (*Vyākaraṇa-paribhāṣā* 74)? This is not a fault. Here, when a word is uttered, two things are perceived: the word and the object, as well as the universal (*jāti*) and the substance (*dravya*). Even qualities (*guṇa*) which are not the direct meaning of the word are included through their connection with the denoted object. Where both of these [word and object, or universal and substance] are present, there is completion (*samāpti*).

But where one of these two is absent, there the word *guḍa* (molasses) is applied here to a substance that lacks the genus (*jāti*) of molasses or is deficient in qualities such as sweetness; thus, a slight incompleteness [of meaning] is established, and grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) is likewise established. How so? When, first of all, the word *guḍa*, having been applied by some common property to something denoted by a word such as *drākṣā* (grape) which lacks the genus [of molasses], produces a cognition, then coreferentiality with the word *drākṣā* occurs, because both words function with respect to the same object.

But when it refers to one devoid of qualities, as in the case of the "molasses-like" person (*guḍajītīya*), even then there will be grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), just as in the expression "the Vāhīka is an ox" (*gaur vāhīkaḥ*). In that same way, the word "molasses" (*guḍa*) may also apply to one who lacks its qualities.

The word "molasses" (*guḍa*) is used here to mean "abounding in molasses," and since the grape is similar to that, it too will be designated by the term "abounding in molasses. Furthermore, the feminine gender is also appropriate, because gender is dependent upon worldly usage.
Furthermore, the rule that "secondary suffixes (*svārthika*) follow the gender and number of their base" (*vyākaraṇa-paribhāṣā* 74) is merely a general tendency.
Therefore, sometimes they even deviate from this rule, as in *kuṭīraḥ* and *śamīraḥ*.
The suffix is also applied in its own sense (*svārthika*).
By the words "because of the mention of *vibhāṣā*" and so forth, he explains the purpose of including the term *vibhāṣā*.

For if the mention of *vibhāṣā* were not present, then *kalpa*, *bā* (*vat*), and so on—which find their scope in verbal forms ending in *tiṅ*—would be superseded by *bahuc*, which is specifically prescribed after nominal stems (*subanta*). But since that [mention of *vibhāṣā*] exists, they also occur in that alternative case. Now, one might object: "Since *bahuc* occurs in a different location, there is no conflict with them; so how could there be supersession? Or, in the absence of supersession, even when *bahuc* has been applied, those suffixes must necessarily still occur, because the subsequent position remains unoccupied. This is not so. For a conflict between a general rule and a specific rule does not necessarily arise solely from a difference in location; rather, it arises from a difference in meaning as well.
Is the meaning [of the suffix] *bahu-c* the same as that of *kalpa-bādi* because it is indicated by *bahu-c*? In that case, *kalpa-bādi* would not apply to that meaning;
for there is no further indication (*dyotana*) of what has already been indicated (*dyotita*), just as there is no further denotation (*abhidhāna*) of what has already been denoted (*abhihita*).

Now, what is the purpose of including the mention of *suP* (*sub-grahaṇam*), since the mention of *prātipadika* continues, and there is no difference whether the suffix *bahu-c* arises from a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) or from a word ending in a case-suffix (*subanta*)? To this, he says: "The mention of *suP," etc.
For if the mention of *sub* were not present, because [the word] *tiṅaśca* [Pāṇini 5.3.56] is the subject under discussion, the suffix would consequently arise from that.

Therefore, the mention of *sub* is for the purpose of excluding that. Regarding the phrase "in the expression of that" (*tasya vacane*), the meaning is "in the utterance," that is, "in the indication."

With the words "And this [suffix] occurs after that which possesses a mode" (*prakāravati cāyam*), etc., he demonstrates the difference in scope between the suffixes *thāl* and *jātīyar*. When there is a difference in scope, even though *thāl* is prescribed for a specific case, it does not sublate *jātīyar*. The suffix *jātīyar* is established after a word ending in *thāl*, as in *kathañjātīyaḥ* ("of what kind?"). This suffix is not desired after a verbal form (*tiṅanta*).
Regarding the phrase "it will be accomplished" (*akariṣyate*):
how, then, are the existence and non-existence of these two obtained? To this he says: "The word *tiṅaśca* is understood [from the previous rule]," and so forth.
By the restriction "only in what follows," he shows that although [the word *tiṅaśca*] is understood here as well, it should nevertheless be connected with the suffix *kapratyaya*.

And although the term *vacana* (utterance) continues to apply from the preceding sūtra, that [suffix] must occur only where there is an utterance of a meaning such as "unknown" (*ajñāta*) by means of a suffix being produced;
however, that meaning cannot be expressed by the suffix *ka* when it is produced after a verbal form ending in a *tiṅ*, whereas it can be expressed by *akac*.
Therefore, the term *tiṅ* from [Pāṇini 5.3.56] *tiṅśca* should be connected with *akac* in the subsequent sūtra, not with the suffix *ka* here.

The inclusion of the word *prāk* (before) is for the purpose of indicating [the limit], and the inclusion of *iva* is for the purpose of defining the boundary; otherwise, the extent of the governing rule (*adhikāra*) would not be known. [Question: "Of what is this an exception (*apavāda*)? [Objection:

But surely, because they occupy different positions, there is no conflict between *kak* and *ac*; and in the absence of conflict, there can be no relationship of sublated and sublator. Therefore, how can it be said that "of what is this an exception"? [Response: This is not a fault. It has been stated that conflict does not necessarily arise solely from spatial position, but also from the meaning: "The meaning is the same as that of the *akac* suffix. Since that meaning has already been expressed by *akac*, the suffix *kap* will not apply to that meaning.

If, because of the recurrence of the term *prātipadikāt* (from the nominal stem), the suffix *akac* were prescribed before the final vowel (*ṭi*) of the nominal stem, forms such as *tvayakā* and *mayakā* would not be established. Alternatively, if it were prescribed before the case-ending (*sup*), even so, the form *yuṣmakābhiḥ* would not be established. Therefore, he says: "From the nominal stem, [before] the case-ending" (*prātipadikāt supaḥ*).

Regarding the phrase "both," etc.: but even if both are recurrent, why is this restriction not obtained—that in some cases it occurs before the final vowel of the inflected word (*subanta*), and in other cases before the nominal stem? To this he says: "In that regard," etc.
The mention of "vacana" (word) continues here for the purpose of restriction.

Therefore, where the expression of meaning can be accomplished by an affix produced before the nominal stem (*prātipadika*), it occurs before the nominal stem; where the expression of meaning can be accomplished by an affix produced after a word ending in a case-suffix (*subanta*), it occurs only after that *subanta*.
The addition of the marker *c* in *akac* is for the purpose of making it have an acute accent on the final syllable.
For that [suffix] belongs to the entire complex together with its base (*saprakṛti*).

And so he will state: "The suffix *cit* is added to a base ending in *kṛt* for the sake of expressing multiplicity" (Vārttika), and "the suffix *kā* should be prescribed after the root *tūṣṇīm*" (Vārttika).
[The suffix *kan* is applied] after [the root *śī*] in the sense of contempt (*kutsā*) and so forth, as far as possible.
The particle *ca* (and) serves to indicate the addition of a rule; thus: "In the sense of character (*śīla*), [the suffix *kan* is applied], and there is the elision of the *m*."

"Virtue" (*śīla*) is not said to refer solely to intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*); what then? It refers to restraint (*niyama*) as well. For instance, one who maintains perfect restraint is called a "virtuous monk" (*śīlavān bhikṣuḥ*). Therefore, even one who restrains his speech by being intent on restraint is called "silent. This is expressed in the rule beginning with "by the conjunction with *akac*" (*akacsanniyogena*), and so forth.

But how is this specific distinction—that [the substitution occurs] by way of the simultaneous application (sanniyoga) with *akac*—obtained, given that it is not stated in the Sūtra? To this he says: "The letter *ca*" and so forth. The purpose of the letter *ca* is precisely this: that the letter *da* should take the place of the letter *ka* by way of its simultaneous application with *akac*. This is the intended meaning. Regarding the phrase "unknown in its specific quality" (*ajñātaviśeṣa*), it means "unknown."

If that which is absolutely unknown were to be considered "unknown," then in the absence of any cognition of the object whatsoever, the very nature (*prakṛti*) of the object would not exist; for an object that is entirely unperceived cannot serve as a subject of linguistic usage (*prayoga*). Therefore, it is understood that what is intended here by "unknown" is that whose specific attributes (*dharmāntara*) are unknown while it is known in its own form (*svarūpa*); that is, "unknown" means having its particularities (*viśeṣa*) unperceived.

To clarify this very point, he says: "By its own [form]," and so forth. "Own form" refers to the nature of being a self (*ātmatva*) and the like; "particular form" refers to the relationship between property and owner (*svasvāmisaṃbandha*) and the like. "Out of compassion," and so forth.
*Abhyupapatti* is indeed assistance (*anugraha*).
[Examples include] *svapitaki*, *āsitaki*.

[In these cases,] the suffix *iṭ* is applied, and due to the root belonging to the *adādi* class, there is the elision (*luk*) of *śap*. [The term] *nītiḥ* refers to a policy consisting of means such as conciliation (*sāma*) and bribery (*dāna*).

By the word "ādi" (and so forth), the inclusion of *bheda* (sowing dissension) and *daṇḍa* (punishment) is intended; however, since these two are not possible in the case of compassion (*anukampā*), only the single policy of *sāma* (conciliation) and *dāna* (gift-giving) is understood by the term "ehaki.

[The derivation is as follows: from the root *iṇ* preceded by the prefix *āṅ*, the second person singular imperative ending takes the substitute *hi* according to Pāṇini 3.4.87 (*sehir apicca*). Now, one might ask: "Is the suffix not already established here by the preceding rule (*pūrveṇaiva*)? Since compassion is indeed understood here, for what purpose is this? To this he says: "By the preceding rule alone," and so forth.

"One whose connection with compassion is proximate" refers to one who is showing compassion toward someone for whom that connection is immediate. This proximity of the connection pertains to every object of compassion; since compassion is enjoined based upon that [proximity], it is logical that it should be enjoined only from that person toward whom one is proximate through compassion—namely, from the very person previously being shown compassion—and not from a remote person such as a son-in-law (*ghātr*) and so forth.
Therefore, this [rule] is intended so that [the suffix] may also apply in the present case from that [remote person].
"From that which is remote" means from that which is distant. It is distant because compassion does not have that [remote object] as its basis.

For in that [derivation], the word *dhāna* and so forth are not the base; rather, it is the person being shown compassion, such as Devadatta. In the forms *devikaḥ* and *yajñikaḥ*, once the word *datta* has been elided according to Pāṇini 5.3.83 (*ājādyudhvaṃ dvitīyādacaḥ*), the vowel *a* is elided according to 6.4.148.
In every counter-example, *ka* alone is to be understood;
for instance, "madrabāhukaḥ.
One whose arms are Madra-like is *madrabāhuḥ*.

This is not a name; rather, it is an adjective. For what purpose is the mention of "human" (*manuṣya*)? So that [the suffix] does not apply in a case such as *devahastako hastī* ("an elephant with the hand of a god").
For what purpose is the mention of "name" (*nāma*)? So that [the suffix] does not apply in cases such as *mṛgakaḥ* ("little deer") or *matsyakaḥ* ("little fish"). [The example is: *deviyaḥ*.
In *ghan*, there is elision as before;
in *devilaḥ*, the suffix *ilac* [is applied];
and in *devikaḥ*.

Regarding the question "Who is Devadattaka?", [the suffix] *ka* is applied after words such as *upendra* (as in *upendradatta*). Why is the mention of *prāk* (before) not for the purpose of indicating an option (*vikalpa*)? To this he says: "For it is by the word 'or' (*vā*) alone," and so forth.

In this context, the word *vā* ("or") is understood from the preceding rule; therefore, since the option has already been established by that alone, the inclusion of the word *tad* ("that") would not be justified. Regarding the phrase "the mention of the name":

for if the mention of the name were absent, there would be a grasping of the universal (*jāti*) and its own form (*svarūpa*). Therefore, the mention of the universal is for the purpose of ensuring that there is no grasping of the own form. As for the example, "a certain person named Vyāghrājina": [it serves to illustrate the point].
The skin of a tiger is *vyāghrasyājinam*; one whose skin is like the skin of a tiger is *vyāghrājinaḥ*.

According to the rule "A *bahuvrīhi* compound may be formed with a word preceded by a locative case or a standard of comparison, and there is elision of the final member" (Vārttika 99), when the *bahuvrīhi* is formed and the final member is elided, the form *vyāghrājinaḥ* is produced.

Now, why was it not stated simply as "atha ajinalopaśca" (and then there is the elision of *ajina*), rather than using the term "uttarapada" (subsequent member)? It cannot be done in this way; for if someone named Vyāghra-mahājina were to be treated with compassion [and called] "Vyāghraka," when the elision of the word *ajina* is prescribed, the word *mahat* would not be dropped. However, when the elision is prescribed for the subsequent member (*uttarapada*), it occurs. Therefore, let it remain exactly as it is in the original formulation.

*mahadajinam* means "having a great skin" (*mahājinam*). Just as there is a "great skin" of a tiger (*vyāghrasya mahājinam*), so too this [elephant] has a great skin; thus, as before, it is a *bahuvrīhi* compound with the elision of the final member (*uttarapadalopī bahuvrīhiḥ*), followed by the suffix *kan*. Regarding the phrase "in this section," etc.:

by this, he shows that the elision occurs for those [suffixes] beginning with vowels (*ājādi*) which are prescribed in this specific section, but it does not occur for those prescribed in other sections.
And this is understood from the fact that the two [suffixes] beginning with vowels prescribed in this section are carried over (*anuvṛtti*) here.

Now, for what purpose is the mention of "after" (*ūrdhva*)? Since the rule *dvitīyādacaḥ* uses the ablative case, even without the mention of "after," by the principle that "an operation [affects] that which follows [the element denoted by the ablative]," the elision would apply only to that specific word-form which stands after the second vowel. To this, he says: "The mention of 'after' (*ūrdhvagrahaṇam*)," and so forth. If the mention of "after" were absent, by the rule *tasmādityutarasyādeḥ* (P. 1.1.54), there would be an elision of the initial portion of that which follows the second vowel; when that [mention of "after"] exists, however, everything [following the second vowel] is set aside.
Therefore, the mention of "after" is for the purpose that the elision of the whole [portion following the second vowel] may occur.

Now, what is the purpose of including the mention of *ṭha*, since the desired result would already be established by the rule "after [a suffix] beginning with a vowel" (*ajādau*) once the single-substitute replacement (*ekādeśa*) of *ṭha* has been performed? To this he says: "The mention of *ṭha," etc. The mention of *ṭha* is for the sake of ensuring that the rule prescribing the suffix *ka*—namely, *isusuktāntāt kaḥ* [Pāṇini 7.3.51]—applies even when the second letter of the suffix *uka* remains, before the single-substitute replacement has taken place, provided that the elision of everything following the second letter occurs while the suffix is still in its *ṭha*-state.

In this regard, the following objection might be raised: "Once the single-substitute (ikādeśa) has been applied, and since the [resulting form] begins with a vowel (ajādi), when the portion after the second vowel is elided, the substitute will be included by the mention of 'ṭh' due to its status as a *sthānivadbhāva* (acting like the original); thus, the substitution for 'ka' will take place. To this, he says: "For, in the case of a characteristic based on being the first of a vowel," and so forth.

In this rule prescribing the substitute, the mention of 'ṭh' there would have to be either a mention of a single phoneme (*varṇagrahaṇa*) or a mention of a cluster (*saṅghātagrahaṇa*). Among these, if it were a mention of a single phoneme, then because it is not a rule concerning a phoneme (*alvidhi*), the status of acting like the original (*sthānivadbhāva*) is not possible.

Although [the condition] is applicable when a cluster (*saṅghāta*) is grasped, nevertheless, according to the principle that "an operation characterized by a combination [of sounds] is not the cause of the destruction of that combination" (Pāṇini-vyākaraṇa-paribhāṣā 12), the *u* sound produced by the cluster consisting of the *aj*-beginning nature [of the suffix] would not effect the immediate succession with the suffix *ṭha*.

Consequently, just as in the case of *māthitikaḥ*—derived from *mathitaṃ paṇyam asya*—where even though the *ya* is elided by the rule *yasya* (Pāṇini 6.4.148), the single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) does not occur because the *t* maintains immediate succession with the *ṭha*, so too [in the case of *vāyudatta*], the form *vāyukaḥ* would not result.
Therefore, since *u* has already been mentioned as being in the second position, the mention of *ṭh* is for the purpose of prescribing *ka*;
and the meaning of that [mention] is that there is elision (*lopa*) of it.
And that [substitution] occurs only for the initial [portion], not for the whole;

or rather, this *la* is a substitute for *l* (the entire suffix), and because it consists of more than one phoneme (*anekāl*), it replaces the whole. [This applies] by the rule "after the second vowel."

When the second [vowel] is to be elided, it should be stated that the elision of the word-form beginning with that [second vowel] occurs when the *sandhyakṣara* (diphthong) constitutes the second [vowel].

Although the elision of what follows the *sandhyakṣara* would also have been applicable, the rule "of those preceded by a monosyllabic prior member" (*ekākṣarapūrvapadānām*) and so forth prescribes the elision of what follows the second vowel; this [present rule] is an exception (*apavāda*) to that.
[The term] "monosyllabic" (*ekākṣara*) [is used].
Furthermore, this word *akṣara* also refers to a syllable (*ac*).
For those compounds whose prior member consists of a single syllable (*ekākṣara*), the elision of the subsequent member (*uttarapadalopa*) should be stated. For example: *vāgāśīḥ*.

Considering that *vāc* is the object of the blessing (*āśis*), a *bahuvrīhi* compound is formed despite the lack of grammatical coreferentiality (*vaiyadhikaraṇya*). Having analyzed the compound as *anukampita-vāg-āśīḥ*, when the suffix *ṭac* is applied, there would be elision of everything after the second vowel. That being the case, with the form *vāc-ika-* established, once the elision of *y* is performed by [Pāṇini 6.4.148], the designation *pada* would not apply due to the status of the substitute (*sthānivadbhāva*) according to [Pāṇini 1.1.57].

Therefore? Based on the case-ending (*vibhakti*) contained within that [compound], the designation *pada* applies according to [Pāṇini 1.4.17] *sup-antam padam*, whereby the substitution of *ku* (i.e., *g*) would result in *vāgika*. However, when the word *āśis* has its final element elided, because that [substitute] is not an *aj-ādeśa* (a substitute for a vowel), there is no *sthānivadbhāva* (the status of being like the original); thus, the designation *bha* indeed occurs. Consequently, since the designation *pada* is thereby negated, the *kutva* (substitution of *g*) and other operations dependent upon the *pada* designation do not take place, and thus *vācika* is established. "How? and so forth.

If it is stated that there is elision of the second member (*uttarapada*) when the first member (*pūrvapada*) consists of a single syllable, then the form *ṣaḍika* is not established. Even here, if the elision of the second member were applied before the designation *bha* had arisen and the designation *pada* had been set aside, then—by rule 8.2.39, which prescribes the substitution of the voiced unaspirated stop (*jaś*) for the *ṣakāra* of the word *ṣaṣ*—the form *ṣaḍika* would not be established. [The solution is: "And that [elision] occurs for those whose euphonic combination (*sandhi*) has not yet taken place. If the elision occurs precisely when there is no euphonic combination of vowels, then it is established; otherwise, it is not.

Therefore, it must be stated that the elision occurs only for *śevala* and the others when no vowel sandhi has been applied. Regarding the statement "the short vowel is the counterpart of the long," that [short vowel] should be understood as being relative to that [long vowel] in comparison with which it becomes long.

But surely, when there is a decrease in length, it becomes short; and since there is smallness wherever there is a decrease in length, is this not already established by the preceding rule? It is not so established; for there is no such necessary restriction that wherever there is a decrease in length, it must necessarily be characterized by smallness. For instance, even when there is a decrease, an object that possesses the quality of largeness remains large and does not become small—as in the words *kuṭīraḥ* and *śamīraḥ*.

Since suffixes added in the sense of the base itself (*svārthika*) follow the gender and number of the base, should it not be feminine by virtue of the feminine gender inherent in the base, rather than masculine? To this he says: “Even though they are *svārthika*,” and so forth. If the suffix were prescribed after words such as *vatsa* (calf) in the sense of "slenderness," then the suffix would apply without distinction even to those calves and others that are slender in their bodies, because no specific qualification has been provided? To this he says: “Of whichever quality,” and so forth. A "quality" (*guṇa*) is a qualifier; the "substantive" (*dravya*) is the thing qualified.
The cause for the application (*pravṛttinimitta*) of words such as *vatsa* is a specific stage of life (*vayoviśeṣa*) and the like.

When words such as *vatsa* (calf) and so forth apply—that is, function—with respect to a substance (*dravya*) as the qualified object (*viśeṣya*), it is precisely that cause of application (*pravṛttinimitta*) belonging to the word *vatsa* and so on which undergoes attenuation (*tanutva*), and not attenuation in general. Why is that? Because of proximity (*pratyāsatti*). When a suffix is prescribed after base words (*prakṛti*) such as *vatsa* and so forth, no other cause of application is proximate; therefore, it is logical that the suffix should occur when that very [cause] is attenuated. "Its attenuation" means the attainment of the second stage of life.
At the time of reaching the third stage of life, the attenuation of the ground for the application of the term "bull" (*ukṣan*)— which belongs to the second stage of life—
is certain to remain;
"its attenuation consists in having another father."
The meaning is "born from a donkey as a father. In that case, one born from a donkey as a father is called an *ātara*. Its "slowness" (*tanutva*) refers to its feeble capacity for carrying burdens.
One who is not capable of carrying a load is called *ṛṣabhatara*.

However, when his capacity for carrying a load becomes weak—that is, diminishes—then there is "thinness" (*tanutva*). [The rule] states: "The suffix is applied to those being singled out. How is it understood that this means "to those expressing what is being singled out"? Because, once the suffix has been produced from that very [base], the act of singling out is understood.
Regarding "Mahāvibhāṣā" and so forth:
[the rule] "after a capable [word], from the first [member]" (Pāṇini 4.1.82) is intended so that the suffix may occur when there is the sense of "derivation" (niṣariṇa).
"In 'of the two' (*dvayoḥ*), the case ending is one of selection (*nirdhāraṇa-vibhakti*) from a collective.

This refers to either the genitive (*ṣaṣṭhī*) or the locative (*saptamī*). Furthermore, that [selection] is governed by the rule: "And [the sixth case ending is used] when there is a selection from among [a group]" (*yataśca nirdhāraṇam*, Pāṇini 2.3.41).

"‘Of one’ (*ekasya*) is a specification; it is a specification of that which is being singled out (*nirdhāryamāṇa*). This is so that [the rule] may apply when one thing is being singled out from among many. Now, an objection is raised: "Is not singling out (*nirdhāraṇa*) the separation of a single part from a whole? Since the word ‘of two’ (*dvayoḥ*) indicates a collection of parts from which a single part is to be singled out, and since such a collection can only consist of one part when a single part is to be singled out, the singling out will necessarily apply to only one even without the mention of the word ‘one’ (*eka*). Therefore, the mention of ‘one’ is useless. This is not so.

For if that [word *eka*] were not present, the genitive case in *dvayoḥ* would be understood as a genitive of object (*karma-ṣaṣṭhī*), meaning "if two are pointed out from somewhere"; consequently, the suffix would also apply here: "In this village, who are Devadatta and Yajñadatta?
Therefore, the mention of *eka* must be made. Regarding the phrase "from those whose scope is a question concerning a genus" (*jāti-paripraśna-viṣayebhyaḥ*):
those for whom there is a question concerning a genus as far as possible are described in that way.
"What is your clan, together with your conduct? (Mahābhārata)
Thus, its status as a genus (*jāti*) is established.
And is that *kaṭha*-genus being inquired about by means of the word "what" (*kiṃ*)? In this context, the word "what" serves as the object of the inquiry regarding the genus.

"Whichever among you is a Kaṭha, let him come"— in this instance, the words *yattama* and *tatama* refer exclusively to the genus (*jāti*), and do not function as interrogative pronouns. "Whichever among you is a Kaṭha, let him come."

In this context, the words *yat* and *tat* refer exclusively to genus (*jāti*), not to the scope of an inquiry (*paripraśna*), because such is impossible; for an inquiry is not made by means of those two, but rather by the word *kim*.
For this very reason, he will state: "The mention of 'inquiry' is a qualification of *kim* alone, and not of *yat* and *tat*, because it is impossible.
[And] "the mention of 'optionally' (*vā*) is for the sake of the suffix *akac*."
[The rule] is stated so that *akac* may also occur as an alternative.
If this were the case, the sentence would not be established; for when the suffix *ḍatamac* does not occur, there must necessarily be *akac*. To this, he says: "By the *mahāvibhāṣā*" and so forth.
And here, the *mahāvibhāṣā* follows for the purpose of optionalizing the suffix; since the suffix is made optional by it, the sentence will also occur as an alternative.

"But the mention of *jāti* (genus) is connected with all [the cases]. Since *jāti* occurs everywhere, when a word is qualified by *jāti* and so forth, would its status as the object of inquiry be obtained simply by implication (*sāmarthyāt*)? This is not so; for it (*jāti*) also functions in the sense of censure (*kṣepa*). In that case, if the term "inquiry" (*paripraśna*) were not mentioned, then when *jāti* functions in the sense of censure, the suffix would still apply. [The phrase] "in its own domain" [is used].
In one's own domain;
therein, the exclusion of one out of two is the scope of the suffix *ḍatarac*, while the exclusion of one out of many is the scope of the suffix *ḍatamac*.
The particle *ca* (and) serves the purpose of attraction (*anukarṣaṇa*).
For if that [condition] were absent, then by the rule "a suffix either applies to what immediately precedes or it prohibits it" (Vyāḍi-paribhāṣā 19),

only the suffix *ḍatama* would apply; because the rule "the suffix *ḍatara* applies when selecting one out of two" continues [to govern], and the rule "the suffix *ḍatama* applies when selecting one out of many" continues [to govern].

"Why is the mention of 'prāk' (before) not for the sake of providing an option? To this he says: "The option (*vikalpa*) indeed continues. It was stated that the word "option" (*vikalpa*) continues from the immediately preceding rule; by that very [continuation], the option regarding the suffix (*pratyaya-vikalpa*) is established. Therefore, the mention of *prāk* is solely for the sake of honor (*pūjārtha*), not for the sake of providing an option. [This applies to] "by one who has studied grammar," and so forth.

But how is it that *vyākaraṇa* (grammar) is a form of disparagement (*avakṣepaṇa*), given that its study is prescribed by the scriptures because it is an auxiliary (*vedāṅga*) to the Vedas? Even so, in cases where one brings forth such disparagement toward a specific person, the status of that [study] as disparagement is established with respect to him, because it serves as a cause for fault.

By the rule beginning with "parasya" [Pāṇini 5.3.74], he shows the division of the suffix *kan* used in the sense of disparagement. Regarding the statement, "the mention of *pratikṛti* (image/representation) is a qualifier of that," it means that the usage should occur where there is similarity pertaining to a representation.

In the expression "the cow is like the gavaya," there is similarity, but not one pertaining to a representation; for a cow is not a representation of a gavaya. That which is made of wood and so forth is indeed called a "representation" (*pratikṛti*). Furthermore, the term *cañcā* refers to a straw man; and because of its similarity [to a human], a person is called a *cañcā*.

According to the rule *lupi yuktavadvyaktiyacane* [Pāṇini 1.2.51], the gender remains that of the base form itself. Now, one might object: "Does not the status of being 'like the base' (*yuktavadbhāva*) fail to apply here because of the statement *manuṣyalūpi pratiṣedhaḥ* (Vārttika 21)? This is not so; the prohibition applies to qualifiers (*viśeṣaṇa*), not to that which ends in *lup*. Thus, in the case of *devapadyaḥ*, it is a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*) meaning "the path of the gods" (*devānāṃ panthāḥ*).

By the rule *ṛkpūrabdhūḥpathām ānakṣe* [Pāṇini 5.4.74], the suffix *a* is added as a compound-final (*samāsānta*), followed by *kan*, and then the case-ending (*sup*) for that. Regarding the phrase "from this point onward" and so forth:
since the suffix *kan* would otherwise apply there according to the rule *pratikṛtau* [Pāṇini 5.3.96], from this point forward these specific suffixes are employed;
for in the case of something not being a representation (*apratikṛti*), or when it is not designated as such, the expression would otherwise have to be conveyed through a full sentence alone.

But in the case of *saṃjñā* (a name), whether it is a derivative form (*pratikṛti*) or not a derivative form (*aprakṛti*), only the suffix *ḍhañ* is applied; for example, *vastiḥ* = a modification of a fence (*vṛti-vikāraḥ*).

In the word *vāsteyī*, the feminine suffix *ṅīp* is applied by the rule *ṭiḍḍhāṇañ* [Pāṇini 4.1.15]. Regarding the phrase "from a compound whose object is the meaning of 'like' (*iva*)," the term *ivārtha* means "the meaning of *iva*," namely similarity (*sādṛśya*), and that which has this as its scope (*viṣaya*) is so described.

If [the suffix] *śas* is prescribed after a compound whose object is the sense of "like" (*iva*), would it not then also apply in cases such as *śastrośyāmā* ("dark like a knife") and *puruṣavyāghra* ("tiger-like man")? This is not a fault, for in these instances the compound does not function in the sense of "like"; rather, it is the first member or the second member [that functions thus]: "dark as a knife" (*śastrīva śyāmā*) and "this man is like a tiger" (*puruṣo 'yaṃ vyāghra iva*).

Furthermore, even if [the word] functions in the sense of a part (*ekadeśa*) as if it were the whole (*iva*), and thus the compound is said to express the meaning of *iva*, nevertheless, because that meaning has already been expressed by the compound itself, the suffix will not occur. As for the compound, in what sense does it function like *iva*? This suffix is prescribed where there is another meaning similar to the meaning of the compound; as in the statement, "this very thing is like something else," due to the governing influence of the term *iva*.
"Atarkitopanataṃ" means arrived unexpectedly, without prior intention. "Citrikaraṇaṃ" means causing wonder.
"How is that?"—in what manner does this wonder arise unexpectedly? He asks about this matter with the words "How is that," and so forth.
"And this is a compound," and so forth.
Since this rule for the formation of suffixes applies to the domain of the sense of "as if" (*iva*), it is understood from this very indicator (*jñāpaka*) that a compound (*samāsa*) occurs.
But how is this an indicator? He says: "For there is not," and so forth.
This means that there is no general definition (*lakṣaṇa*) for a compound belonging to the domain of the sense of "as if."
Therefore, this very prescription of the suffix from that [base] is what is logically established as the indicator (*jñāpaka*) of its existence.

Alternatively, one might ask: "What is the reason that the existence of that [suffix] is established by means of an indicator? He replies with the words beginning with "for not of this" (*na hy asya*), etc., and concludes with "and thus it is precisely the object."
The meaning is that [the suffix] has precisely the sense of "as it were" (*ivārtha*). Regarding the phrase "by the mention of *anyatarasyām*" and so forth:
since the suffix *ṭhak* was already prescribed by the preceding rule (Pāṇini 5.3.108), it is the immediately following one;
the mention of *anyatarasyām* is for the purpose of inclusion (*samuccaya*).

Therefore, by the rule "a rule applies to what immediately precedes, or a prohibition applies to it" (Vyākaraṇa-paribhāṣā 19), that very [suffix] is obtained. Regarding "ima-tha": there exists another base, *ima*, which has the same meaning as *idam*; from that, the suffix *tha* is prescribed. Regarding "from the preceding": [this refers to the base].
The word *pūrva* denotes a constituent part. That which has a village headman (*grāmaṇī*) as its first [constituent] is *grāmaṇīpūrva*.
And it is understood that by means of this prohibition, the actual form [of the word] is being referred to.

When the word *pūga* is understood in its own form (*svarūpa*), there is no possibility of application [of the suffix] after a word preceded by *grāmaṇī*, because of the prohibition of the rule of "application to that which ends in" (*tadantavidhi*) for a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) that already possesses [the suffix] (Pāṇini 4.1.89).
In the example *lohaṣvajāḥ*, the suffix *kan* is applied.
Here, since the word *devadatta* is a constituent part of the preceding *grāmaṇī*, the suffix is not applied. [This applies to the category of] *āyudhajīvin*.
"In the Bāhīkas" means in the specific villages known as the Bāhīkas.
"Of the Kṣaudrakas" [is the meaning].
There was a certain group of weapon-bearers residing in the Bāhīka country named Kṣudraka; that very group is called the Kṣaudrakya.
[The term] "Mālavya" [is explained as follows].
There is a certain group among the Vāhīkas called Mālava, consisting of those who live by the profession of arms;
that very group is [referred to as] Mālavyaḥ.
Because of the presence of the phoneme *ṭ*, the suffix *ṅīp* is applied.
And thus, the meaning is that the phrase "not in the feminine" (*astriyām*) is not connected here. Regarding the phrase "in its particular [instance]":
the meaning is "because of the explanation. Regarding the phrase "among the Vāhīkas": [this refers to the usage].
The locative case is used in the sense of selection (*nirdhāraṇa*). [The example is:
"among the Vāhīkas, that group which subsists by arms.
Since selection occurs only among members of the same genus, the "group subsisting by arms" is understood to be specifically a Vāhīka group.

Alternatively, since the word *vāhīka* denotes a region, this locative case (*saptamī*) occurs precisely in the sense of location: "A guild of weapon-bearers dwells in a specific region of Vāhīka. [The statement] "In the case of *brāhmaṇa*, there is the mention of its specific [meaning]" applies here. Now, why does the mention of the word's own form (*svarūpa*) not occur? Precisely because of this prohibition. If it were a mention of the word's own form, the prohibition regarding *brāhmaṇa* would be purposeless.
For a prohibition presupposes a prior possibility of occurrence.

Since the word *brāhmaṇa* does not denote a community of weapon-bearers (*āyudhajīvisaṅgha*) among the Vāhīkas, what would be the purpose of prohibiting it [in that sense]? However, there are words such as *gopāla* (cowherd) and others which denote specific types of *brāhmaṇas*, and the communities of weapon-bearers denoted by those words do exist among the Vāhīkas. If no prohibition were made in this regard, then [the application of the term] might extend even to them.
Therefore, the prohibition is meaningful for the purpose of excluding that. The prohibition applies when a specific [sub-class] is being grasped.
Therefore: "In the case of a Brāhmaṇa, there is the apprehension of its specific [qualifications], but in the case of a Rājanya, there is simply no apprehension of its own form.
This is because the community of weapon-bearers denoted by that term exists among the Vāhīkas, and because of the rule stating, "The own form of a word is not a grammatical technical name (*saṃjñā*).
Regarding the phrase "by that," and so forth:
Why is this so? Because the letter *ṭ* has been added here for the sake of the suffix *ṅīp*; therefore, the term "not in the feminine" (*astriyām*) does not recur [from Pāṇini 4.1.113].
If that were to recur, the addition of the *ṭ*-marker would be purposeless, as a word ending in the suffix *ñyaṭ* would not occur in the feminine (and thus *ṅīp* would not be required).
Therefore, "not in the feminine" is discontinued; consequently, the suffix occurs even in the feminine.
In the words *kauṇḍībṛsī* and *kṣaudrakī*,

there is the elision of the letter *y* according to [Pāṇini 6.4.150]. Alternatively, if among the Vāhīkas there exists a community of weapon-bearers (*āyudhajīvisaṅgha*) denoted by the word *vṛka*, then, since the suffix *ñyaṭ* would otherwise apply, this rule for the application of a suffix should be understood as occurring in some other case— whether it be *āpta* (attained) or *anāpta* (not attained)— as in the expression *vṛkāv iva*.

In this context, the word *vṛka* denotes a genus (*jāti*). Regarding the phrase "and among them this is the traditional teaching" (*smṛti*), it is called a *smṛti* because by means of it the Trigarta-ṣaṣṭhas are remembered—that is, they are known. That [teaching] is as follows: "They call them the Trigarta-ṣaṣṭhas.

This very verse is composed by a trustworthy authority (*āpta*). Among these Trigarta-ṣaṣṭhas, the first and the fifth end in the suffix *aṇ* (as derived from *śiva*, etc.), while the remaining ones end in the suffix *iñ*.

Some read the fifth [suffix] as ending in an ataddhita suffix. For them, the *ccha* suffix occurs from the word *brāhmagupta* itself. But for what purpose are the *yaudheya*-type words recited here, since they were already enumerated in the fourth [section] for the purpose of prohibiting elision (*luk*), and it is those very same ones that are taken up here? This is true; however, the composition of the *gaṇas* by the author of the *gaṇapāṭha* is indeed diverse, and thus they are recited again. In the *parādi* group, the word *satvaccha* is recited.

And that [word] *satva* should be understood as a derivative formed by adding the suffix *matup* after the word *satvan*. Regarding the form *ābhijita*, the suffix *aṇ* is applied according to the rule "the offspring of *abhijit*" (Pāṇini 4.1.114), which is the general rule "the suffix *aṇ* is used before the sense of 'descendant' (*apatya*)," as stated in Pāṇini 4.1.83. The same applies in subsequent cases as well.
"It is intended that the *aṇ* suffix conditioned by *gotra* is to be understood.

How then does [the rule] "of a name of a genus" (*jātināmnaḥ*) continue to apply? By that [interpretation], only that which is a name of a genus ending in *aṇ* will be grasped. And that which is prescribed as an *aṇ* suffix for *gotra* is precisely what constitutes a name of a genus; for it is said: "A *gotra* is [also] a *caraṇa* [lineage]" (Mahābhāṣya).
Because it is designated as *āti* [by the rule] *bhā| 2|225),
[we have] "the moment of Ābhijit" (*ābhijitaḥ muhūrtaḥ*) and "the *sthālīpāka* offering for Ābhijit" (*ābhijītaḥ sthālīpākaḥ*).

In one case, [the suffix] *aṇ* is applied by [Pāṇini 4.2.3], and in the other, by [Pāṇini 4.2.24]. Thus ends the third quarter of the fifth chapter in the *Kāśikā-vivaraṇapañcikā*, composed by the venerable teacher Jinendrabuddhi, who is a disciple of the Bodhisattva. Now begins the fourth quarter of the fifth chapter. The term "from the nominal stem" (*pratipadikāt*) is understood [as the governing rule]. The mention of "foot" (*pāda*) and "hundred" (*śata*) serves as its qualifier; since a rule concerning that which ends in a qualifier applies to the whole ending in that qualifier, he says: "of that which ends in *pāda* or *śata*. The word "beginning with" (*ādi*) here signifies a constituent part.

Furthermore, it is not logical for the word "number" to be a constituent part of the words "pada" and "śata," because they exist separately and do not originate from one another. Indeed, it is not possible for something that exists separately and does not originate [from it] to be a constituent part of another word, just as the word "jar" is not a part of the word "cloth.
On the contrary, it is logical in the case of a composite whole, such as a cloth, where its cause—the threads and so forth—is said to be a constituent part occupying the same location.

Therefore, he says "of *saṃkhyā* and so forth" (*saṃkhyādeḥ*) etc., to show that this [term] is understood as referring to the nominal stem (*prātipadika*), and not to the words *pāda* and *śata*. This genitive case is characterized by immediate succession (*ānantaryalakṣaṇā*); for example, in the rule *gāpoṣṭakam* (Pāṇini 3.2.8), the suffix *ṭak* occurs after *go* and *āpa*, the sense being "immediately following.
And [the phrase] "in conjunction with that" (*tatsanniyogena ca*).
Because the letter *ca* has the sense of a restrictive conjunction (*sanniyoga*),
[the word] "of the final" (*antasya*) is understood through the paribhāṣā "of the final vowel" (Pāṇini 1.1.52).
"Again," and so forth.
That which exists because of a cause is "caused" (*naimittika*); according to Pāṇini’s rule *adhyātmāditvāt ṭhañ* (Vārttika 456), the suffix *ṭhañ* is applied.
That which is not caused is "uncaused" (*anaimittika*).
The repetition of the word "lopa" (elision) is for the purpose of ensuring that elision occurs even in this case.
Since elision is prescribed here along with the suffix *vun*, it does not depend on a subsequent cause (*paranimitta*) and thus becomes unconditional (*anaimittika*).
This refers to the elision [of the final vowel and consonant] by the rule *yasyeti ca* (Pāṇini 6.4.148).

Regarding the term "conditioned by what follows" (*paranimittaka*): because [the suffix] is prescribed when another element follows as a condition, there is the status of being like the original (*sthānivadbhāva*) by virtue of the rule *Pāṇini 1.1.57*. Since the elision (*lopa*) possesses the status of being like the original, it is prescribed that the word-form *pāc* [is present].
For the word *pāc* is taken as the original (*sthānin*) which is devoid of a vowel (*anacka*); however, its state of being vowel-less is lost once the status of being like the original is applied.

The intention is that because this [substitution] is not occasioned by a specific cause (*anaimittika*), the status of being "as if the original" (*sthānivadbhāva*) does not apply, and thus the substitution of *pad* occurs.
Regarding the phrase "two feet each": the reduplication occurs due to the sense of distributive repetition (*pīpsā*). Regarding the phrase "punishment is restraint": [this defines *daṇḍa*].

[Objection: But does this word *daṇḍa* not also apply to a staff (*yaṣṭi*) and so forth? [Reply: True; nevertheless, its application here is properly understood as "restraining" (*damana*), because it is precisely "restraining" that is conveyed by the suffix. [Regarding the statement] "giving is relinquishing": if this were so, then what? That which was cited as an example in the preceding rule—namely, *dattam* (given)—would only be appropriate if this present rule were for the purpose of providing an additional prescription and not an exception (*apavāda*). Therefore, there would be no need for this rule. To this he says: "It is for the purpose of excluding repetition" (*avīpsārtha*), and so forth.

By this [rule], the suffix *vuñ* is applied after *dāna* alone. However, when there is a repetition of *dāna* (i.e., in a distributive sense), it occurs again by means of the preceding rule. The phrase "it is an exception (*apavāda*) to *jātīya*" shows that just as the suffix *jātīya*, which is prescribed when expressing a manner (*prakāra*), applies to that which possesses the manner (*prakāravat*) and not to the manner itself, so too does this [suffix *vuñ*]. Otherwise, this exception to *jātīya* would not be logical, because of the difference in their respective domains. Now, for what purpose is the suffix *kan* not prescribed immediately after [the rule] *sthaulādi-bhyaḥ* (Pāṇini 5.3.69)? What would be achieved by that? [One might say: the mention of "expressing a manner" (*prakāravacana*) need not be stated for *kan*. But this cannot be maintained; for if it were so, [the distinction between the two suffixes would collapse].

For when there is a simultaneous desire to express both the types such as *sthūla-* and so on, and [the suffixes] such as *ajñāta-* and so on, [the suffix] *kan* would not occur because of its posteriority; since it is a different word (*śabdāntara*). Even if it were to occur, even so, in forms such as *sthūlaka*, there would be an acute accent (*udāttatva*) [on the first syllable]; however, here, since *kan* is prescribed, by virtue of its posteriority, once *kan* has been applied, the acute accent on the final syllable (*antodāttatva*) of *ka-* is established. Since the word *cañcat* (trembling) is not recited alongside *bṛhat* in the context of *sthālī* and other such words, that [suffix] would not apply there.
Therefore, an addition (*upasaṃkhyāna*)—that is, an explanation—must be provided.

In this regard, the following is the explanation: the particle *ca* ("and") from the preceding sūtra is carried over (*anuvartate*) here, and it serves the purpose of including what has not been explicitly mentioned (*anuktasamuccayārtha*).
And by that, it will apply even to *cañcadbṛhat* and others. Regarding the rule "in the case of *sthālī*, *aṇu*,
and *māṣa*," some explain these four as being part of the original context (*prakṛta*).
sthūlakaḥ (large), aṇukaḥ (minute), māṣakaḥ (bean-sized), iṣukaḥ (arrow-sized).

Others, however, say that the words "gross" (*sthūla*) and "subtle" (*aṇu*) are the primary subjects (*prakṛti*), while the phrase "among beans" (*māṣeṣu*) is an indication of a limiting condition (*upādhi*). Still others maintain that, due to proximity, the mention of "beans" is a qualifier for the word "subtle" itself. The first view alone is logical; for instance, [the term] "gross" and so forth [qualify] its specific variety.
"Black sesame seeds. Regarding the phrase "in the case of barley and rice":
*yava* (barley) is the base term, and *vrīhiṣu* (in rice) is its qualifier.

*Yavaka* is *vrīhi*. Regarding the rule "The [terms] *pādya* and *kāla* are [used] in the sense of 'white' when applied to *surā*," others, however, say that because of its immediate proximity, the word *avadāta* is a qualifier of *surā*, and does not function as a qualifier for *pādya* and *kāla*.

Regarding "gomūtrādācchādane" [the *Kāśikā* reads "gomūtre ācchādane"]: the word *gomūtra* is the base (*prakṛti*), and "in covering" (*ācchādane*) is its qualifier. A covering of the type of cow's urine is called *gomūtraka*.
Regarding "surāhau" [the *Kāśikā* explains this as "surāyā ahau"]: "surā" is the base form (*prakṛti*) and "ahau" is the qualifier.
A snake that has the color of wine is called "suraka."

Regarding the phrase "in *jīrṇaśāliṣu*": the word-forms *patra* and *mūla*, whether compounded or uncompounded, produce a suffix—namely, *patrakam* and *mūlakam*. Regarding the phrase "complete relation" (*aśeṣasaṃbandha*):
the meaning is that there is a pervasion (*vyāpti*) of all [parts], such as the divisions and so forth, by their own related whole.

Regarding the term "bhinnakam": it does not refer to that which has a connection through the division of its entirety, but rather that which has a connection through a single part; such is called *bhinnakam*.
In the word *bhinnam*, however, a connection of the entirety alone is understood.

If a jar or the like, being entirely pervaded by the action of breaking, is designated as "different" [from itself], [it is because of the rule] "in the sense of expressing a part" (*sāmivacane*). That by which a part is expressed is "that which expresses a part" (*sāmivacanam*).
[The example is] "half-made" (*sāmikṛtam*).

It is either a *bahuvrīhi* or a descriptive compound (*viśeṣaṇasamāsa*). The phrase "because it has already been expressed by the base form" provides the reason for the lack of necessity for the prohibition.
What is there to be made "non-final" (*anatyantagati*) by the suffix *kan*? Since that [state] is already understood by the word *sāmi* itself, there is no possibility for *kan* to apply at all;
therefore, the prohibition is purposeless.
Thinking that there is a rule prescribing the suffix *kan* even with the mere sense of "one's own," he says, "By what, then," and so forth.
This very statement of prohibition makes known: "Does *kan* occur in its own sense? Otherwise, the statement of prohibition would be purposeless.
[The word] *ardhakṛtam* [is used].
It is produced by the rim [of the wheel]. The word "follows" (*anuvartate*) is understood because it is *svarita*-accented. Thus, there is no prohibition.

By way of reversal, [the word] "bṛhatikā" [is formed]; [here] the short vowel occurs by [Pāṇini 7.4.13]: *ke'ṇaḥ*. [The compound] "avidyamānāni ṣaḍakṣīṇyasmin" is a *bahuvrīhi* [meaning] "that in which six eyes do not exist."
Then, by the rule *bahuvrīhau sakthyakṣṇoḥ* [Pāṇini 5.4.113], the suffix *ṣac* is applied.

From the word *rājan*, the locative case is used; having analyzed the compound as *rājani yathā* (as in the case of a king), the compound is formed according to [Pāṇini] 2.1.40. Thus, "the superlative suffixes (*tamap*) and so forth."
The rules beginning with *atiśāyane tamabiṣṭhanau* [Pāṇini 5.3.55] and ending with *prāk kṛtvasucaḥ* [Pāṇini 5.3.64] apply here.
"Ñya etc.
refers to [the suffixes] such as ñya in the rule *pūgāññyo'grāmaṇīpūrvāt* (Pāṇini 5.3.112).
"Prāgvṛñaḥ" refers to [the section] prior to the suffix vṛñ.
Because they are prescribed by the sūtra beginning with *pādaśatasya* [Pāṇini 5.4.1],
[the suffixes] such as *ām* and so forth are included;
that is, those beginning with *kimettiṅavyayaghāt* [Pāṇini 5.4.11].
"Prior to *mayaṭ*" refers to the rule [Pāṇini 5.4.21]. "Those ending in *bṛhatī* and those ending in a genus name (*jāti*)" refers to [Pāṇini 5.4.3].
Does [the rule] *bṛhatyā ācchadane* (Pāṇini 5.4.6) indicate this sūtra?
It also indicates *jātyantaśabdenāpi* (Pāṇini 5.4.9).
This plural-numbered reference is for the purpose of including that which is not prescribed by the sūtra beginning with *aṣaḍakṣā-* (Pāṇini 5.4.7). [The term] "by its position" (*sasthānena*).
The third case ending (*tṛtīyā*) is used in the sense of an instrument (*karaṇe*).
If that which ends in *sthāna* becomes meaningful through the meaning expressed by the word *sthāna*—that is, through a synonym for "equal"—then this suffix occurs, and not otherwise.
But how is equality expressed by the word *sthāna*? To this he says: "Equal" (*samānam*), and so forth.
One whose place is equal is called "having an equal place" (*sasthāna*).
And one who is of such a kind, in relation to whom another has an equal place, becomes similar to that [person].
Thus, [the term] "standing in the place of a father" (*pitṛsthānīya*) is used.

The term "pitṛsthāna" is a bahuvrīhi compound with elision of the final member, according to the rule *saptamyupamāna* (Pāṇini 2.1.40 vārttika 99), meaning "one whose place is like the place of the ancestors. The example given is "gosthāna" (cow-pen).
This is a genitive *tatpuruṣa* compound.
Is this not so? [The objection is: the base (*prātipadika*) ends with the word "sthāna," but it is not meaningful by virtue of having the same meaning as "sthāna.

Just as a suffix occurs after a base ending in "sthāna," so too, when the meaning has been presented by the word "svasthāna" within a *tatpuruṣa* compound, the suffix ought to occur after that "sthāna" which is meaningful by virtue of that [compound] meaning; for no distinction has been specified.

Furthermore, one might object: "In that case, isn't that *pratipadika* ending in *-stāna* equally meaningful by virtue of the meaning expressed by the word 'place' (*sthāna*)? To this, he replies: "The particle *iti* is for the purpose of indicating intention (*vivakṣārtha*).
For here, the particle *iti* is employed for the sake of indicating intention; by means of it, this meaning is obtained: "If there is an intention [to use the word] from that point.

When a suffix is produced after a base that is meaningful by virtue of the sense of a *bahuvrīhi*, there is an intention on the part of common usage, but not when it is meaningful by virtue of the sense of a *tatpuruṣa*.
Therefore, in order to produce the meaning of the word *sthāna* as the final member [of a compound], only a *bahuvrīhi* produces the meaning of the word *sthāna*, and not a *tatpuruṣa*.
Consequently, there is no over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).
The word *ca* is for the purpose of connecting [the preceding].

The word *cet* is for the purpose that there may be a connection between the fifth case-ending (*pañcamī*) and the sixth case-ending (*ṣaṣṭhī*). Otherwise, because the fifth case-ending is specified in relation to the suffix (*pratyaya*), there would be no connection between the fifth case-ending and the sixth case-ending.
Indeed, a connection with it cannot be made by means of a fifth case-ending.

But when the word *cet* is present, [the meaning] "if that [suffix] exists" is established as being meaningful through its position (*sthāna*), yet there is no actual grammatical connection (*sambandha*).
"Among two optional rules (*vibhāṣā*), the permanent rules (*nityavidhi*) [take precedence].

If these were not permanent, the preceding option would continue to apply in subsequent instances, and thus the mention of "option" (*vibhāṣā*) later on would be purposeless. Regarding the rule "not when there is no excellence of a substance" (*adravyaprakarṣe*):

But surely, there can be no excellence of a substance; for it is stated in the *Bhāṣya*: "Indeed, there is no excellence of a substance. Therefore, is this prohibition not purposeless? To this he replies with "Even though," and so forth.

Furthermore, the metaphorical attribution (*upacāra*) of the property of the contained to the container is observed, as in the expression, "The platforms are crying. Therefore, excellence (*prakarpa*), which is a property of the action or quality belonging to both the container and the contained,

when it is metaphorically attributed to the substance that serves as the container, becomes a property of the substance by virtue of being a property of the substance through that metaphorical attribution.
Therefore, this prohibition is made:
"only [the excellence] of action and quality," and so forth.
When the excellence of an action or a quality is not transferred to a substance—that is, when the excellence belongs only to the action or the quality—the suffix occurs only there.

If, however, it is applied metaphorically to a substance, then by the rule "the excellence of a substance," the word *kiṃtarām* is used. Since a thing possesses many specific qualities (*viśeṣa*), the question expressed by the word *kim* refers to which of those [qualities] is intended.
Regarding the form *pūrvāhṇetarām*: [this is derived] by the non-elision (*aluk*) of the case-ending according to Pāṇini 6.3.17.

Now, one might object: "The forenoon (*pūrvāhṇaḥ*) is time, and time is a substance (*dravya*); since a suffix [denoting degree] should not occur when there is excellence of a substance—because of the prohibition 'not when there is excellence of a substance' (Pāṇini 5.4.11)—this should not be possible. This is not a fault. For in this case, the excellence does not reside in the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadikārtha*), but rather in the meaning of the case-ending (*vibhaktyartha*), and that is merely a quality (*guṇa*). This is because the factors of action (*kāraka*s) consist of the nature of the potency (*śakti*) of a substance.
Alternatively, is it by the force of the statement? It occurs when there is an extension of time; for indeed, no suffix *gha* follows any other single vowel (*ekāra*) than one denoting time.
This is because the rule for the non-elision (*aluk*) of the locative case is prescribed [only] after a word denoting time.
Regarding "uccaistarām": "one who follows along by repeating [the words] is an *anugādī*";

the suffix *ṇini* is applied here because the root belongs to the *grahādi* class, or alternatively, it is used in the sense of necessity (*āvaśyaka*) or habitual disposition (*tācchīlya*), due to this very irregular derivation (*nipātana*). Regarding "vyāvakrośī": [it is derived from *vi-ava-kruś* with the suffix *ṇini*].

From the root *kraś* in the sense of "calling" (*āhvāne*) [Dhātupāṭha 856], the suffix *ṇic* is applied; there is the *guṇa* substitution for the light penultimate vowel, and from the form ending in *ṇic*, the suffix *añ* is added.
And by the paribhāṣā regarding the inclusion of *kṛt* suffixes (Pāṇini-vyākaraṇa-paribhāṣā 126), it is derived from the root together with its prefix (*sagatika*).

Therefore, in this case, the designation *pratipadika* applies only when there is a shared destination (*sagatika*), and not in the sense of mutual exchange of action (*karmavyatihāra*). Precisely because of this prohibition, despite the prohibitions regarding *vṛddhi*, only the initial *vṛddhi* occurs.
By the rule *ṭiṅḍhāṇañ* [Pāṇini 4.1.15], the suffix *ṅīp* is applied, resulting in *vyāvahāsī*.
From this, by the rule *ata upadhāyāḥ* [Pāṇini 7.2.116], there is vṛddhi.
"Thence" (*tataḥ*) means,
that is to say, from a word ending in the suffix *ṇaC*.
Since it is established that "affixes used in their own sense (svārthika) follow the gender and number of the base" (Jaiminīya-Paribhāṣāvṛtti 95),
