[the author] demonstrates that the mention of the word *strī* (female) serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*) by means of the phrase "In that case, then," and so forth.
The purpose of the indicator (*jñāpaka*) is stated by the words beginning with "by that" (*tena*).
The phrase "even though they transcend" means "even though they deviate."
By the force of the word "api" (also), the term "aṇ" (the suffix *aṇ*) is understood to follow.

If it were taught that for suffixes used in their own sense (*svārthika*), there is a deviation from following the gender and number of the base (*prakṛti*), then suffixes such as *kalpa* and others would occur in their own sense after bases like *guḍa* and so on which follow masculine gender and so forth; and in that case, they too would necessarily possess the masculine gender and number. Consequently, forms such as *guḍakalpā drakṣā* (a grape-vine resembling molasses) would not be possible. However, once this [deviation] is established, another gender also occurs.
By this, all of this becomes logically established.
By the word "etc. (*ādi*), there is the inclusion of such terms as *tailakalpāḥ*, *cāturvarṇyam*, *trailokyam*, and so forth. Regarding the term *sāṃrāviṇam*:
[the root] *ru* means "to sound" (*ru śabde*).

From this [root] *pā*, by [Pāṇini 3.3.44] *inuṇ* is added; by [Pāṇini 7.2.115] there is vṛddhi; and from that which ends in *inuṇ*, the suffix *aṇ* is applied. And that [suffix *aṇ*] occurs only after the prefix *sa-* (*sagati-*) as before.
By [Pāṇini 6.4.164], there is the preservation of the original form (*prakṛtibhāva*).
Regarding the word *sāṃkūṭinam*:
[the root] *kūṭa* [is used] in the sense of "burning" (Dhātupāṭha).
...as in [Dhātupāṭha] 1890), and "mṛjūṣ śuddhau" (Dhātupāṭha).

[1066], > [[Pāṇini 3.2.141]], *śamityaṣṭābhyo ghinuṇ*. Although *ghinuṇ* occurs when the letter *gh* is elided, nevertheless, the suffix *aṇ* does not follow from that [root]; this is because the particle *iti*, which serves to indicate the intended meaning, is understood to carry over from the rule *sthānāntādvibhāṣā* [[Pāṇini 5.4.10]]. Regarding the word *visārī*:
the suffix *ṇini* is applied as before.
Regarding "vaisāriṇaḥ":

the preservation of the original form (*prakṛtibhāva*) is as in the previous case. Regarding "repetition (*paunaḥpunyam*) is recurrence (*abhyāvṛtti*)," here, by association with that repetition, actions of the same kind performed by a single agent are implied; for this very reason, he says "of those having a single agent," and so forth.
For in the expression *ekakartṛkāṇām*, the quality (*guṇa*) added by way of enumeration (*upasaṃkhyāta*) refers only to that which is drawn along with the numbered object (*saṃkhyeya*).
For this very reason, the genitive case expressing distinction (*vyatireka*) occurs with the word for number.
Indeed, the counting of actions constitutes repetition (*abhyāvṛtti*).
"He eats five times" means that he performs five occurrences of the action.
"He eats many times."

If the mention of "number" (*saṃkhyā*) were not made, then just as the suffix occurs after number-words such as *pañca* ("five") and so on, it would likewise occur after words such as *bhūri* ("many") and so on; because of the mention of "number," it does not occur [after those]. [As stated: "Repetition (*abhyāvṛtti*) is possible only for an action (*kriyā*)," and so forth.

But is it not the case that repetition is also possible for substances (*dravya*) and qualities (*guṇa*)—as in "he is a staff-bearer again and again" or "he is stout again and again"? This is not so; here, by implication, there is the repetition of an action: "he becomes a staff-bearer again and again," "he becomes stout again and again."
Therefore, repetition is possible only for an action (*kriyā*), not for a substance (*dravya*) or a quality (*guṇa*).

In the example "again and again, a staff-bearer" (*punaḥ punar daṇḍī*), the action is understood through the force of the context; thus, the explicit mention of "action" (*kriyāgrahaṇa*) need not be made [in the rule].
This refers to the passage beginning with "of a single thing, once," and so forth.
By the word "one" (eka), only a single manifestation of action is denoted.

And repetition is not possible within a single manifestation of action; rather, it occurs across multiple manifestations of action. Thus it was stated previously: "of those [actions] having a single agent," and so forth.
Therefore, only the single performance of an action is counted, not its repetition.

Consequently, if the term "action" (kriyā) were not included, the suffix would not be obtained for counting actions from the word "one" (eka). Therefore, the inclusion of the term "action" must be made for the sake of what follows.
Regarding the term "five times cooked" (*pañcapākāḥ*):
if only "in the counting of actions" (*kriyāgaṇane*) were stated, this [term] would also apply here, for there is indeed a counting of actions here.

Reiteration (*abhyāvṛtti*) occurs among actions that take place at different times; however, in this case, the acts of cooking (*pākāḥ*) are counted as being of identical time. Therefore, that [general rule] is excluded.

But surely, even action (*kriyā*) does not exist here, since the suffix *ghañ* is prescribed for that property of the root-meaning called "accomplishment" (*siddhatā*)? This is not a fault; for even that accomplishment is indeed included by the mention of "action" in the rules concerning action, because the distinction between the property (*dharma*) and the possessor of the property (*dharmī*) is not intended to be expressed.

Otherwise, in examples such as *kārakasya gatiḥ* ("the going of the agent") or *kārakasya vrajyā*, the suffix *ṇvul* [prescribed by Pāṇini 3.3.10]—"after a verbal root meaning an action, when another action is intended, the suffixes *tumun* and *ṇvuṇ* are used"—would not apply. [This is stated in the passage beginning with] "if it were not so," and so forth.

The suffix shall occur after two kinds of words: after numerable words and after words expressing a number. For example: *śataṃ vārān bhuṅkte* (he eats a hundred times), which becomes *śatakṛtvo bhuṅkte*.
Here, by way of the relation "this is that," the word *śata* (hundred) refers to the numeral within the repetition of the action.
For this very reason, there is grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*).
To show that [the suffix] would not apply when "hundreds of times" (*śataṃ vārān*) is being enumerated, he says: "It would not occur here.
He asks why this is so and replies: "Because it functions solely with respect to enumeration (*saṃkhyāna*)."

The word *mātra* excludes the number [of times] and thus means "a hundred times. Regarding the term *caturbhukta*, there is the elision of the letter *s* by the rule *rāt sasya* (Pāṇini 8.2.24). The letter *c* is for the sake of the accent (*svarārtha*).

The intention is that the *prakṛti* (the base word) should have an udātta accent at its final syllable. However, the letter *c* in the suffix cannot serve the purpose of indicating an accent, because it is devoid of a vowel (*anacka*).

The function of the letter *c* as an indicator of an accent applies only with respect to the word *catuḥ*, which is the subject under discussion (*prakṛta*), and not to the two subsequent words; for those two are already udātta by nature.

The word *catuḥ*, however, is acutely accented on the first syllable by the *nitsvara* (the accent of a suffix marked with *n*) because it ends in the suffix *uran* according to [Pāṇini 5.1.87] *cateruran*. Regarding the form *sakṛdbhuktam*: the *s* of the suffix is elided by [Pāṇini 8.2.23] *saṃyogāntasya* ("there is elision of the final consonant of a conjunct").
The letter *c* is for the purpose of ensuring the acute accent on the final syllable.

If that [condition] were absent, however, because the word *eka* ends in the suffix *kan*—by the rule *iṇbhīkāpāśalyatimarcibhyaḥ kan* (Pāṇini 3.2.16)—it would be acutely accented on the first syllable (*ādyudātta*) due to the *nit-svara*; consequently, by the principle of *sthānivadbhāva*, the substitute (*ādeśa*) would also have been acutely accented on the first syllable. But because it possesses the marker *c*, it becomes acutely accented on the final syllable (*antodātta*).
Now, why does this not apply in the case of *ekaḥ pākaḥ* ("one cooking"), since there is indeed a counting of actions here? To this he says: "*ekaḥ pākaḥ*" and so forth.
Even when the word *bahu* is used, it refers only to a general sense, as it also functions in the sense of "manner.
In that case, it is logical that there should be no interval between the repetition of multiple actions, and this depends upon the context and other factors.
Furthermore, how could even the suffix *kṛtvasuc* function in this particular domain?

Therefore, the mention of *vibhāṣā* (optionally) need not be made. [Regarding the statement: "That which is presented in abundance is 'the subject under discussion' (*prakṛta*). But how is this specific distinction obtained, since the word *prakṛta* simply denotes that which is being presented? As for the inclusion of the word *vacana* (mention/usage) here—where one could have simply said "in the subject under discussion" (*prakṛte*)—the inclusion of *vacana* is for the purpose that the suffix *mayaṭ* should apply only in those cases where the usage of *mayaṭ* after a "subject under discussion" is observed in the world through a word ending in that suffix.

And in common usage, words ending in the suffix *mayaṭ*, such as *rannamaya* and others, express the abundance (*prācurya*) of the base substance; thus, the distinction is obtained precisely from the inclusion of the term "speech" (*vacana*).
Regarding the phrase "others, however," and so forth:
here, the suffix denotes a meaning entirely different from the meaning of the base.

By the word *prakṛta*, merely that which is under discussion (*prastuta*) is expressed; however, the distinction is that it does not mean "that which is under discussion" as qualified by abundance (*prācurya*). Regarding the phrase "in both ways" and so forth, the meaning is that the aphorism was composed for this purpose in either case. [The phrase] "it exists in the sense of a traditional lineage of instruction" (*upadeśapāramparye vartate*)...

This is because we observe the usage of the forms *iti ha smopādhyāyaḥ kathayati* ("Thus, indeed, the teacher used to say") and *iti ha sma pitā kathayati* ("Thus, indeed, the father used to say"). Regarding the rule "The fourth [case-ending] after an incapable [word]," the fourth case is used in the sense of *tādarthya* (being for the sake of that),

either by virtue of an *upasaṃkhyāna* (supplementary rule) or because of the indicator (*jñāpaka*) in the rule *caturthī tadarthārtha...* [Pāṇini 2.1.36], which implies that the fourth case occurs in that sense.
Since "there ought to be a dative case when [the suffix] denotes being for the sake of that (*tādarthye*)," the suffix is understood as being derived from a word ending in the dative case.
He shows that the suffix *ṣyañ* is used in its own sense (*svārthe*) by stating that "being for the sake of that" (*tādarthyam*) means "that very purpose.
But how can *ṣyañ* be used in its own sense? To this he says: "In the case of *cāturvarṇya*, etc. and so forth.

The addition of *ṣyañ* in the sense of the base itself (*svārthe*) was prescribed for the sake of establishing terms such as *cāturvarṇya*. But is this [term] not already included because it belongs to the *cāturvarṇyādi* group, and thus takes *ṣyañ* in its own sense?
[The answer is: "For the deity Agni" (*agnidevatāyai*).
This is a descriptive compound (*viśeṣaṇasamāsa*), meaning "that which is both Agni and a deity. [Regarding the word] "of the word" (*śabdasya*).

From the word *ap* (water), which denotes a collection of seven syllables, the suffix *yat* is applied in the sense of the base itself (*svārthe*). This is according to the rule "there is *yat* [after a word ending] in the second case plural" (*dvitīyābahuvacanasyāluk*),

meaning that after the word *ap* in the second case plural, when *yat* is added, the case-ending (*sup*) is elided by the rule "the *sup* [is elided] after verbal roots and nominal stems" (*supo dhātuprātipadikayoḥ*), resulting in forms such as *ṛtau* and so forth.
When the seasons are to be expressed, the suffix *kan* is added to the words *uṣṇa* and *śīta* to form *uṣṇaka* (the hot season) and *śītaka* (the cold season).
In other contexts, they remain simply *uṣṇa* and *śīta*.
[The rule applies] "when referring to the hair on an animal (*paśau*) that has been shorn."
When the word *lūna* (cut) and *viyāta* (shameless) produce the suffix *kan*, with "animal" as the referent, the forms are *lūnakaḥ paśuḥ* (a cut animal) and *viyātakaḥ paśuḥ* (a shameless animal).
Other than in reference to an animal, they are *lūnam* (cut) and *viyātam* (shameless).
[The rule] "the suffix *aṇ* [is applied] in the sense of 'skillful'" [is also mentioned].
The word *aṇu* has the sense of "subtle" (*nipuṇa*) and causes the suffix *kan* to be produced—thus, *putraka*. In other cases, it is simply *putra*.
Regarding the rule "the suffix *ka* is added after *snāta* when the completion of Vedic study is meant": [the examples are *snātaka* and *vedaka*].
The word *snāta* causes the suffix *kan* to arise when the completion of Vedic study is intended to be expressed.
One whose Veda is completed is called a *snātaka*. Why "upon the completion of the Veda"? [Consider: one who has bathed in a river (*nadyāṃ snātaḥ*).
Regarding the phrase "śūnya rikte":
the word *śūnya* produces the suffix *kan* when the sense of "empty" (*rikta*) is to be expressed; thus, *śūnyaka* means "trifling" (*tuccha*).
Elsewhere, it is simply "empty" (*śūnyam*).
Regarding the rule "dāna-kutsite":
the word *dāna* takes the suffix *kan* when it denotes something contemptible; thus, a contemptible gift is called *dānaka*, whereas otherwise it is simply *dāna*.
Regarding the phrase "tenu sūtre":
the word *tanu* induces the suffix *pratyam* when it means "in a sūtra"—as in *tanukam*;
elsewhere, it remains *tanuḥ*.
Regarding the rule "īyasaśca":
the suffix *kan* occurs after a word ending in the suffix *īyas*; for example, *śreyaskaḥ*. Regarding the rule "and toys for girls": [the suffix *kan* occurs].
Those things which are the playthings of young girls produce *kan* [the suffix *kan*]: *kandukaḥ* ("ball"). Regarding the phrase "dyed with lac and so forth":

is it not already established by the preceding rule that the red color applied by lac and such is impermanent? Indeed, when through a particular process (*yogaviśeṣa*) such stability is produced that it does not abandon its own substrate, then because of that permanence, the [previous] rule would not apply; therefore, this is stated for that purpose: "*upāyādhyasvatvañca*" ("and there is the state of being dyed by means of an agent").
It produces the suffix *ṭhak* from the word *upāya* and undergoes shortening [of the vowel], resulting in *aupayikaḥ*. "Vyāhṛtaḥ" means "spoken.
"Anyena" means...
By the sender;
for that speech was not previously sent. For by one who sends it first, there comes to be the message to be sent.

That by which a message is conveyed is called a "message-word" (*sandeśavāk*). Regarding the phrase "from the word *karman*": this indicates that the actual form of the word *karman* is what is being taken, and not the [grammatical object] as that which is most desired to be reached (*īpsitatama*). But surely, since the word *karman* is a technical term (*saṃjñāśabda*), it is more appropriate to take it as referring only to that which is most desired to be reached, rather than its own formal shape? This is not so; for here, from the rule beginning with *sthānāntāt* (Pāṇini 5.4.10), the particle *iti* is understood to carry over. By that, the following meaning is obtained: "if there is an intention to express that [form]."
Furthermore, in common usage, when a suffix arises after the word *karman*, it is due to the speaker’s intention [to denote the action], not because of that which is most desired (*īpsitatama*).

For it is not logical that the action (*karman*) could be expressed by the suffix *aṇ* produced from that [most desired object], since [the suffix] would then express a meaning already expressed [by another word]. However, it can be expressed by the suffix produced after the word *karman*. Therefore, it is appropriate to take the word itself [as the basis for the suffix].
Regarding the term *kārmaṇam*:
there is the preservation of the original form (*prakṛtibhāva*) by [Pāṇini 6.4.16], which states that *an* remains unchanged;
"in the same way" means exactly so.
Just as it has been set forth by speech whose meaning has been articulated—namely, "it should be done"—the sense is: "in that very manner.
Regarding the phrase "in the section on *aṇ*," etc., the meaning of the word *upasaṃkhyāna* is "presentation" (or "addition").

In this regard, the demonstration is as follows: since *prajñā* and so forth belong to the class of *ākṛtigaṇa* (open-ended groups), potters (*kulāla*) and others should be understood as included therein. Thus, by the rule [Pāṇini 4.3.117], the suffix *aṇ* will apply.

If that were the case, would it not also apply in the colloquial language (*bhāṣā*)? This is not a fault; for the term *vibhāṣā* ("optionally") is carried over from the sūtra [Pāṇini 5.4.20], *vibhāṣā bahoḥ*, and that is a restricted option (*vyavasthitavibhāṣā*) which will apply only in Vedic (*chandas*), not in the colloquial language.
"Sānnāya" [as in the *Sānnayya-kāśikā* and the *Padamañjarī*], and so forth.

The forms *sānnāya*, *anujāvara*, *anuṣūka*, *anuṣṭubh*, *cātuṣprāśya*, *rākṣodhva*, *vaiyāta*, *vaikṛta*, *vārivaskṛta*, *āgrāyaṇa*, *āgrahāyaṇa*, and *sāntapana* are desired both in the Vedic language (*chandas*) and in the common language (*bhāṣā*).
Therefore, there are *sānnāya* and the others.
The primary forms (*prakṛti*) of these [words] should be understood as occurring only in *prajñā* and so forth.

And here, in the case of *āgrāyaṇa* and *agrahāyaṇa*, the suffix is applied after the words *āgrāyaṇī* and *agrahāyaṇī* ending in long *ī*, rather than after other words ending in long *ā* such as *anujāvara* and so on. Furthermore, the word *sānnāyya* is included here for the purpose of its having a final acute accent (*antodātta*).

The word *rūpa* is established precisely by the rule of irregular derivation (*nipātana*) in *pāyyasānnāyya* (Pāṇini 3.1.129). Regarding the example "he drinks the medicine" (*oṣadhaṃ pibati*), the suffix is applied to the word *oṣadhi* when it refers to medicinal fruits and the like; however, this [suffix] does not denote a genus (*jāti*), because the defining characteristic of a genus—namely, that "a genus is that which is grasped through its form" (Kāśikā on 4.1.63)—is absent here.

"Plants grow in a field. In this context, the word *oṣadhi* (plant) applies to that class [of things] whose nature ends with the ripening of fruit. Regarding the statement "one who knows is wise (*prājña*)," one might object: "Since the suffix *ṇa* is already established by the rule *tad asyāstyasminn iti matup* (Pāṇini 5.2.94) to express possession—meaning 'he who knows has wisdom'—why is the suffix *aṇ* prescribed from the word *prajñā*? To refute this objection, he shows the specific distinction regarding the feminine gender, saying: "In the feminine, *prājñī*," and so forth.
"The term *vid* is understood as being in the present participle (*śatṛn*) form," and not [the rule] beginning with *Pāṇini 7.1.36*, etc.
"In the body of the ear."
That which exists in the body as the word *śrotra* becomes *śrautra*; elsewhere it is *śrotra*. [The example is] "juhvat."
From the word *juhvac* when it refers to a black antelope (*kṛṣṇamṛga*), the suffix *aṇ* occurs: *jauhvataḥ*. Otherwise, it remains *juhvad*. Others read "kṛṣṇamṛge" as a separate word.

The suffix *aṇ* occurs after the word *kṛṣṇa* when a deer is to be denoted—as in *kārṣṇo mṛgaḥ* (a black deer); otherwise, it means simply "black. In this recension, the suffix occurs after the word *juhvat* without distinction. [The commentary says: "But there is *satvan*."
The word *sat*, when ending in the possessive suffix *-mat*, becomes *sātvata* [meaning] "one who possesses beings" (*satvān*). This is an *ākṛtigaṇa* (an open class) beginning with *prajñā*.
To make it known that this is indeed an *ākṛtigaṇa*, the particle *ca* has been added for the purpose of including items not explicitly mentioned.

By that [rule], the suffix *aṇ* is established after words such as *kulāla* and *kukkuṭa*. But for what purpose is it prescribed again here? Why is it not simply prescribed in that very same place? Furthermore, this feminine suffix is compulsory; thus, once the suffix *ṭāp* has been applied, the desired form would be established by the rule "before a suffix beginning with a consonant, *i* is substituted for *ā* following *ka*" (Pāṇini 7.3.44). However, in cases where the elision (*luk*) of the suffix is performed, it would not be established—for instance, in the case of *pañcamṛttika*, meaning "bought for five clods of earth."

For in that case, when the suffix *ṭhak* (forming words like *ārhīya*) is elided by the rule "aṣyadrdhaparvadvigoḥ" [Pāṇini 5.1.28], the feminine suffix is also elided by the rule "luk taddhitaluki" [Pāṇini 1.2.49].

If the suffix *takan* were prescribed there, then because the feminine suffix *ṭāp* would be absent, the vowel *i* would not be heard; furthermore, there would be the fault of excessive complexity (*prakriyāgaurava*), since the form *ikak* is already prescribed by another rule. Such are the arguments beginning with "and so forth."

By the word "etc. (*ādi*), there is the inclusion of examples concerning the *apādāna* (ablative) and other case-roles (*kāraka*), as well as technical rules (*paribhāṣā*): for instance, "he comes from many" (*bahubhya āgacchati*) and "he comes many times" (*bahuśa āgacchati*), or "he comes a little" (*alpaśa āgacchati*), and "he places [it] many times" (*bahuśo nidadhāti*). In the expression "the master of many" (*bahūnāṃ svāmī*), the word "many" (*bahu*) does not denote the remaining factor (*śeṣa*) intended to express a specific *kāraka*.
Regarding the phrase "because of the inclusion of the word 'object' (*arthagrahaṇāt*)," and so forth:
if the word "object" were not included, the suffix would apply only after the words *bahu* and *alpa*.
However, since it is included, the suffix also occurs after synonyms.

"From that which has much or little meaning," and so forth. When a suffix is to be prescribed after that which has much or little meaning, an auspicious statement (*maṅgalavacana*) must be made. And here, by "auspicious statement," an explanation (*vyākhyāna*) is meant, because it is explained (*vyākhyāyate*) by means of it.
But how should the expression of auspiciousness regarding the cause be formulated? To this he says: "In which," and so forth.

Here is the explanation: the term "praise" (*praśaṃsā*) is understood to carry over here; a suffix must be employed in the sense of praise, and that [suffix] occurs in rites for prosperity (*abhyudayika*).
He gives much, not little—in this way, there is praise.

This very statement [is made] because in the world, in matters of giving during *ābhyudayika* (prosperity) rites, this [suffix] occurs frequently; otherwise, since its application would follow from the recurrence of the particle *iti*, it would not be understood as occurring in auspicious (*maṅgala*) contexts. Alternatively, here too, due to the recurrence of the particle *iti*, it occurs only in auspicious contexts and not elsewhere.
The letter *s* of the suffix *śas* does not receive the designation *it*; because there is no purpose for it. [End of section on] the case of opposition (*pratiyoga*).
Regarding the word *vihitā*:

since *prati* has the status of a *karmapravacanīya* by the rule "prati [is used] in the sense of a substitute (*pratinidhi*) and an exchange (*pratidāna*)," the ablative case is prescribed in its connection with it by the rule "the ablative [is used] after that [which denotes the source] when there is a substitute or an exchange. Thus, the meaning is that [the ablative] is prescribed. For example:
*pradyumnaḥ kṛṣṇataḥ prati*.
The meaning is "the representative of Kṛṣṇa.
Regarding the rule *ādyādibhyaḥ*:
this is the suffix *tasi* used in the sense of all case endings (*sārvavibhaktika*).
Regarding the rule *apādāne cā'hoyaruhoḥ*: the analysis of the compound is *ahīyarūhoḥ*.
In forms such as *hīyate*, the element *hīye* is an imitation (*anukaraṇa*) of a portion of the *yaṅ*-stem [of the root *hā*] when the suffix *lakāra* occurs in the sense of the object (*karman*).
The meaning is: that which does not belong to the agent (*hī*) or the object (*ruha*) is the *apādāna* (ablative case) in this context.
Regarding "exceeding" (*atigraha*) in the sense of "distress" (*vyathana*), the meaning is:
being perceived as distinct from worldly conduct by exceeding it.
Regarding the term *cāritreṇa*: conduct itself is *cāritra*; the meaning is that by reason of that, he is seen as distinct from others.
He states the conclusion: "He exists transcending all others."
The word *vyathana* is derived from the root *vyath*, meaning "to tremble" or "to move," with the suffix *lyuṭ*;
thus he says: "non-trembling means non-moving.
Regarding the term *kṣepe* (in the sense of reproach).
The word "is explained" (*udāhriyate*) is to be supplied as the ellipsis.
"Censure" (*kṣepa*) means reproach; and it is so called because of its association with the sin of being diminished.
Regarding the word *hīyamāne*: it means "from one joined with something inferior" and "from one joined with evil.

Now, one might ask: since this is already established by the inclusion of the term *kṣepa* (reproach) in the preceding rule, for what purpose is this stated? To this he replies: "when reproach is not intended."
The meaning is "in the statement of the truth.
The word *ṣaṣṭhī* refers to the sixth [case ending]; *vyāśraye* means "in the resorting to various positions (*pakṣa*)."
That is to say, having abandoned commonality with all, one takes recourse in a single side;
"side" (pakṣa) means acceptance as one's own. Thus, it is said that the gods were on the side of Arjuna.
The meaning is that they were on the side of Arjuna.
And from disease;
the remedy for disease is medical treatment (*cikitsā*).
Regarding "from dysentery" (*pravāhikāta*):
the meaning is "as a remedy for cholera" (*viṣūcikāpratīkāra*). Regarding "Pradyumna [is] from Vāsudeva":

the ablative case (*pañcamī*) is used by the rule "the ablative is used in the sense of a representative or an exchange" (*pratinidhipratidāne ca yasmāt*), and from that [base ending in the fifth case], the suffix *tasi* is applied.
The *taserikāra* (the letter *sa*) has the sense of "face-to-face" (*mukhamukha*).

Now, one might ask: "Is it not for the purpose that the letter *sa* should not receive the designation *it*? This is not so; for precisely because there is no purpose, it will not receive the designation *it*. [This is stated] as: "An addition must be made for words beginning with *ādi*."
The meaning is that an explanatory statement (*pratipādana*) must be made regarding the addition of the suffix *atas* after words beginning with *ādi*.

In this regard, the explanation is as follows: in the subsequent sūtra, the particle *ca* serves to include what has not been explicitly mentioned; by means of it, the suffix *atas* will apply after words beginning with *ādi*. The fact that *ca* has the sense of including what is unmentioned is evidenced by the rule "the first half-mora of that [word] is acute" (Pāṇini 1.2.32). For example: *grāmād āgacchati* ("he comes from the village").
The technical designation *apādāna* (ablative) is applied by the rule "That which is fixed as the point of departure is the *apādāna*" [Pāṇini 1.4.24],
as in the example "He fears from thieves" (*caurebhyo bibheti*). This is governed by the rule "The cause of fear for verbs meaning 'to fear'" [Pāṇini 1.4.25].
"He fails because of his study," as stated in [Pāṇini 1.4.26];
"he is deprived of his wealth."
The root *ohāk* means "in relinquishing" (*tyāge*) [Dhātupāṭha 1090].
The suffix *la* is in the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) because it denotes the object; *yak* is added, and by the rule beginning with *ghumāsthā* [Pāṇini 6.4.66], the substitution of *ī* occurs.

But surely there is no object (*karman*) that lacks an agent, because of the rule: "The object is that which is most desired by the agent" (Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.4.49); and in this case, the caravan is not the object—what then? Is it not the point of departure (*apādāna*)? This is not a fault; for in the definition of the term "object," the mention of the "agent" is intended as an indicator of independence (*svātantrya*).
Why is this so? Because it functions as a qualifier of the action.
And with respect to the agent, two things exist: independence and the technical designation of "agent."
In that context, it is not logical for the designation (*saṃjñā*) to function as an adverbial qualifier (*kriyāviśeṣaṇa*).
For whatever is its cause, by that alone it ought to be qualified.
And the designation "agent" (*kartṛ*) is not the cause of that [designation]; what then? It is independence (*svātantrya*), because that is the very nature of the agent.

When something possesses the status of being a cause (*kāraṇabhāva*) with respect to an action, yet the action is not further qualified by that object, then this is the meaning: that which is most desired (*īpsitatama*) by the action of an independent agent (*svātantrya*) receives the designation "object" (*karman*).
Even though it belongs to the caravan, Devadatta expresses it [as the object];
for if that were not the case, there would be no basis for the designation "ablative" (*apādāna*) either.
Therefore, Devadatta is the object (*karman*).
Only that which possesses the sense of the root *hā* (to abandon) ought to be the point of departure (*apādāna*).

In that case, even though it is the point of departure, because one intends to express its independence (*svātantrya*) with respect to the action of abandoning, Devadatta receives the designation of "object" (*karman*) precisely through that intention to express the action.

Now, for what purpose is the instruction given with the letter *ya*, rather than simply saying "of *hā* and *ruh*" (*hā-ru-hoḥ*)? To this he says: "The instruction of a modification" (*vikāra-nirdeśaḥ*), and so forth. That in which a form is modified is a "modification" (*vikāra*); and here, that [modification] is indeed the *ya*-suffix—as in *hīya*. For in that case, by the rule *dhu-mā-sthā-dīnām* (Pāṇini 6.4.66), the vowel *i* is prescribed [for the root *hā*], whereby the form of the root *jahāti* is modified.

Alternatively—*vikṛtiḥ* means a modification (*vikāraḥ*); the designation is by means of that modification. How so? It is for the purpose that there may be the understanding of the root *jahāti*, and not of *jihīti*; otherwise, there would be the inclusion of *jihīti* as well.
But when there is a designation by modification, only that which has such a form is included; thus, this undesirable consequence does not arise.
Regarding the phrase "it rises from the ground" (*bhūmita ujjihote*):
although the root *jihīti* is not explicitly mentioned here [in the rule], it certainly occurs because of its connection to the ablative case (*apādāna*).

Due to the marker *ṅ* in the root *hāṅ*, the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) is applied; by the rule *bhṛjāmit* (Pāṇini 7.4.76), the *it* substitution occurs for the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*), and by the rule *ata ekahalmadhye...* (Pāṇini 6.4.113), the *ī* substitution occurs for the vowel of the verbal base.

"How can a mantra be deficient in accent or phoneme?"—this refers to the intention expressed when it is said: "A prohibition is made regarding the root *jahāti*; therefore, [the suffix] does not apply to that. "'This is not the fifth case'":
because the fifth case (ablative) has not been prescribed [there], the suffix *-tasi* is used figuratively; thus it is said, "this is not the fifth case."
What then? It is by the third case-ending (tṛtīyā). Here too, because it is prescribed for the third case-ending, the suffix *tasi* is said to follow the word "third" (*tṛtīya*).

How is this so? It indicates that the suffix *tasi* here is not prescribed by this sūtra with the fifth case (*pañcamī*), but rather [it is prescribed] by the rule "also after [words] connected with *hīyamāna* and *pāpa*, [the suffix *tasi* is added] in place of the third case" (Pāṇini 5.4.47), while the phrase "after the third case ending" from the preceding rule "in the sense of *atigraha*, *avyathana*, and *kṣepa*, when [the word] is not the agent" (Pāṇini 5.4.46) is being carried over (*anuvartamāna*).

And that third case ending should be understood as expressing either the cause (*hetu*) or the instrument (*karaṇa*). By the word "having transcended" (*atikramya*), he shows that the prefix *ati-* here functions in the sense of transcendence (*atikrama*).
Regarding the term *acalanamadhyasthānam*:
the root *vyath* is listed in the Dhātupāṭha (764) with the meanings "to tremble" and "fear," but here it is said to function in the sense of "moving.

The instrumental case in *vṛttena* is used either to express the cause (*hetu*) or the instrument (*karaṇa*). In the expressions *vṛttena hīyate* ("he is deprived on account of conduct") and *vṛttataḥ pāpaḥ* ("wicked because of his conduct"), the instrumental case is used for the cause or the instrument in connection with the wicked person who is being deprived of his conduct.
"Why does this not become an example for the intention of censure (*kṣepa*)? To this he says: "And of censure," and so forth. Regarding the phrase "from *pravāhikā*":

the genitive case in the word *pravāhikā* is used in relation to the remedy (*pratīkāra*), and from that [genitive] the suffix *-tasi* is applied. Regarding the phrase "of a cause which has not existed in the form of an effect":
the "cause" (*kāraṇa*) is the primal matter (*prakṛti*); its very subsequent different state is the "effect" (*vikāra*).
The meaning is that it is "non-existent" (abhūta), i.e., unproduced (ajata), by way of that modified form.

But from what source is this specific distinction of "becoming what was not" (abhūtatadbhāva) obtained? It is obtained from the inclusion of the word *abhūta*; for here, "existence" (*bhāva*) means birth or being.
For if existence were merely being (*sattā*), the connection would be only with the roots *bhū* and *as*, and not with the root *kṛ*.
For that which is produced is not "existence" (sattā).

And when there is the inclusion of all three realms, it is logical to adopt only that meaning which, when grasped, possesses a connection with all three realms; and that is birth itself, not existence.
This distinction is obtained through the inclusion of the root *kṛ* ("to produce").

Regarding the phrase "existence as that essence" (*tadātmanā bhāvaḥ*): by the word *tat*, the modification (*vikāra*) is referred to; that very modification is the "essence" (*ātman*), meaning its own nature (*svabhāva*). Thus, "having that as its essence" (*vikārātman*) refers to the state of "becoming what was not previously so" (*abhūtatadbhāva*).

Furthermore, this is said to mean that for a cause which has already attained existence but had not previously assumed the state of modification, the subsequent attainment of the stage of modification is "becoming what was not previously so."

Therefore, where the original material (*prakṛti*) is not intended to be expressed, the suffix does not occur, as in the counter-example "he makes white" (*śuklaṃ karoti*). For when the original material is not intended here, such a transformation from non-existence to existence (*abhūtatadbhāva*) is not understood.
By the word *tat*, the intention to express the non-difference between the original material and its modification (*vikāra*) is conveyed.

Therefore, the suffix occurs only where the material cause (prakṛti) is intended to be expressed as non-different from that which it undergoes as a modification (vikāra); it does not occur, however, where the difference of the effect from its cause is intended to be expressed.
But where there is a difference—as in "he makes a cloth" (paṭaṃ karoti)—it does not occur there.
[This is stated in the rule: "The agent of the verb *sampadyate* is called the 'agent of transformation' (*sampadyakartṛ*)."

But how can there be a compound with a *tiṅ*-ending word, and how is there the elision (*lopa*) of the *tiṅ* suffix? This is all justified because it is a Vedic (sautra) usage, as such an indication exists. Alternatively, from the root *pad* preceded by the prefix *sam*, by virtue of this very irregularity (*nipātana*), the suffix *yat* is applied; this is a specific compound (*viśeṣasamāsa*) of that form. As for the *tiṅ*-ending [form], its mention in the commentary (*vṛtti*) is merely for the sake of illustrating the meaning; it is not, however, the actual analytical sentence (*vigrahavākya*).
When one ought to say "sampattiḥ," why is it stated as "sampadyakartari"? It is for the sake of variety, as in the example "śuklīkaroti.
Following the rule [Pāṇini 7.4.32], there is the substitution of *it* (short *i*), and by the rule [Pāṇini 7.4.26] "in the case of the suffix *cv-*," there is lengthening.
Because that which ends in *cvi-* is an indeclinable (*avyaya*), there is the elision of the case-ending *su*.

"In this case, the material cause (*prakṛti*) is not intended to be expressed," because only the modification (*vikāra*) is intended to be expressed. And where the material cause is not intended to be expressed, the transition from "not having been" to "becoming that" (*abhūtatadbhāva*) is not understood; therefore, the suffix does not occur.

"Obtained precisely through the capacity for becoming that which was not [previously]," and so forth. Is it by necessity that one who has existed in an unmodified form becomes a modifier—that is, becoming that [new] form, he becomes the agent of the act of becoming—or is it by implication? He becomes modified into another essential nature; thus, it is only by implication that he comes to possess the designation of "agent," not by necessity. With this intention, he says: "Let there be no [agenthood] in the case of becoming another *kāraka*."
Regarding the phrase "in a non-temple" (*adevagṛhe*) and so forth:

here, since a temple (*devagṛha*) does not previously exist as a place for the propitiation of a deity, but subsequently attains the nature of being such through its connection with the deity to whom offerings are made, this constitutes the grammatical operation of "becoming that which it was not" (*abhūtatadbhāva*). However, this applies to the locus (*adhikaraṇa*), not to the agent (*kartṛ*). For instance, even though it attains that other form, it does not receive the designation of "agent"; rather, it receives the designation of "locus" alone. Otherwise, the locative case (*saptamī*) would not be possible.

The letter *cvau* is for the purpose of pronunciation (*uccāraṇārtha*). The letter *c* is for the purpose of making the preceding base (*prakṛti*) have its final syllable accented (*antodātta*). There is elision of the letter *v* according to [Pāṇini 6.1.67]. Regarding the phrase "because of the connection with the qualifier" (*atra viśeṣaṇasaṃbandhāt*), and so forth:
All the qualifiers beginning with *abhūtatadbhāva* ("the becoming that which it was not") are carried over here from the preceding sūtra.

Therefore, because of the connection with all those qualifiers, the suffix is already established by the previous rule alone for words such as *aruṇa* and others; thus, that [suffix] is not prescribed here again. However, the mere elision (*lopa*) does not apply.
For this reason, the statement is made for that purpose.

If, however, the rule for the suffix were to apply by this [subsequent sūtra] alone, then in examples such as *durmanīkaroti*, the suffix would not occur; for there is a prohibition against the application of a suffix to a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) that possesses a specific marker when the rule concerns what ends with that stem (P.
1.1.72). By the preceding rule, however, the suffix occurs even after a form ending in that [marker], because in that case there is no nominal stem possessing the marker.
In forms such as *unmanīkaroti*, the suffix occurs after a *bahuvrīhi* compound. Thus, "the mention of the option (*vibhāṣā*) serves to introduce the suffix *cvi*."
Because it has the sense of conjunction (*samuccaya*).
Its having the sense of conjunction, however, is due to the fact that the particle [“ca”] has multiple meanings.

If this is so, why is the particle “ca” itself not used? Because of variety; because of the style of the author of the Sūtras. Now, why is the term *vibhāṣā* not employed for the sake of an option regarding the suffixes? To this he says: "But the option regarding the suffixes," and so forth. "That [option], however, occurs only in connection with the roots *kṛ*, *bhū*, and *as*."

Since the rule "with *kṛ*, *bhū*, and *as*" (Pāṇini 5.4.50) is indeed connected with that [previous rule] by way of its recurrence here, there must necessarily be a distinction between "limit-inclusive" (*abhividhi*) and "totality" (*kārtsnya*); otherwise, the commencement of two separate rules would be fruitless, as the result would be established by one alone. Furthermore, since that distinction is not known, he asks: "Is it limit-inclusive? and so forth, providing the example:
"As in this army," and so forth.

Now, in the case of the remaining substances, what is intended to be expressed is merely a connection with them through one part, not a transformation into the form of a modification through their entire essence—

as in the statement, "In the rainy season, all salt becomes identical with water. Here too, what is intended is merely a connection of all individual instances of salt with the nature of water through a transformation of one part.
But there is no transformation into a different form for a single substance in its entirety.

Regarding the phrase "but in its totality" (*kārtsnyam tu*) and so forth: where even a single substance undergoes transformation into a different form in its entirety, and not merely in part, there "totality" (*kārtsnya*) exists.

In that regard, if the first rule (*yoga*) were not commenced—wherein "wholeness" (*kārtsnya*) refers to the scope of a specific single substance—then the secondary application (*pratyayoga*) would not occur there, because of the absence of "pervasion" (*abhividhi*). On the other hand, if this [second rule] were not commenced—wherein all original bases (*prakṛti*) undergo modification by way of a single part—it would not occur.
Therefore, both must be commenced. [The phrase] "dependent on that" (*tadadhīnam*) means "subordinate to that" (*tadāyattam*).
"Dependent on that" means "subordinate to that.
By the word "that," the general category of the master is expressed;
by the word "subordinate" (adhīna), the general category of the one to be ruled is expressed.
In order to clarify the very point just mentioned, he says: "The meaning is 'that which has him as its owner'. That which has him as its owner is *tatsvāmikam*.
Here too, it is a *bahuvrīhi* compound because the external referent (*anyapadārtha*) is predominant.

And since the object to be ruled (*īśitavya*) is the referent of another word, it possesses the status of the primary element (*pradhānabhāva*); whereas the master (*svāmin*), being merely a secondary indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*) of that [object], possesses the status of a subordinate element (*guṇabhāva*). This is expressed in the phrase "the commonality of masters" (*svāmisāmānyam*), and so forth.

The commonality of the master (*svāmisāmānya*) and the commonality of the lord (*īśvarasāmānya*), as well as the commonality of the object to be ruled (*īśitavyasāmānya*)—this pair is expressed by the term *tadadhīna* (dependent on that). How so? Here, by the rule *adhir īśvare* [Pāṇini 1.4.96], the word *adhi* receives the designation of *karmapravacanīya*; when used in conjunction with it, the locative case is applied by the rule *yasmād adhikaṃ yasya ceśvaraḥ* [Pāṇini 2.3.9]. Since that sovereignty (*īśvara*) requires an object to be ruled (*īśitavya*), it follows by implication that the word *adhi*, when in conjunction [with a noun], denotes the object to be ruled.

This word *ādi* is recited among the *śauṇḍādi* group; when a compound is formed by [Pāṇini 2.1.40], the former member (*pūrvapada*) possesses the general sense of "owner" (*svāmin*), and the latter member (*uttarapada*) possesses the general sense of "that which is to be ruled over" (*īśitavya*). When the suffix *kha* is applied by the rule [Pāṇini 5.4.7] beginning with *avaḍakṣādi*, that very same meaning results, because that [latter member] has him as its owner. And it being thus, the general sense of "owner" and the general sense of "that which is to be ruled over" are expressed by the word *tadadhīna*.

In this context, the general sense of "owner" (*svāmisāmānya*) is the meaning of the verbal root (*prakṛtyartha*), whereas the general sense of "that which is to be ruled" (*īśitavyasāmānya*) is the meaning of the suffix (*pratyayārtha*); therefore, he says: "of words expressing a specific owner," and so forth. [The example is: "the kingdom belongs to the king" (*rājasādbhavati rāṣṭram*). By the preceding rule, only the suffix *sāti* occurs. Now, what is the purpose of the mention of *bahula* (diversity), since the term *vibhāṣā* (optionally) from rule 5.4.52 will indeed carry over, and thus the suffix will occur optionally? To this he replies: "By virtue of the mention of *bahula*, it is obtained even elsewhere."

Therefore, the intention behind the use of the term *bahulagrahaṇa* (the statement "in many cases") when the *vibhāṣā* (optionality) is under discussion is that it should apply elsewhere as well. Regarding the expression "the imitation of the indistinct (*avyakta*) is *avyaktānukaraṇa*":

although in an imitation the specific phonemes do not manifest in their formal shape, nevertheless, because the sound (*dhvani*) is similar, it is imitated by virtue of that mere similarity; thus, it too is called an "imitation. Why does it consist of two syllables? Because a suffix is added, provided that it does not become fewer than one syllable even after that addition.

If it were understood that *ḍāc* occurs after that which possesses a stem of at least two syllables (*dvyajavarārdhatā*) when the reduplication has not yet taken place, then forms such as *paṭat* would not be possible; for in these cases, there is no stem of at least two syllables in the middle portion. Having this in mind, he says: "And of that which... and so forth. But if this were the case, once *ḍāc* has occurred and the reduplication dependent upon it has been performed, the condition of having a stem of at least two syllables in the middle portion would arise; and since that condition exists, *ḍāc* would apply—thus a circular dependency (*itaretarāśraya*) would result. Are not operations involving circular dependencies inadmissible in the grammatical system? To this he replies: "In the sense of *ḍāc*, [the reduplication is] diverse (*bahulam*)" and so forth.

If this were a locative of reference (*parasaptamī*), this fault would arise; however, this is not a locative of reference, but rather a locative of domain (*viṣayasaptamī*). In the case of *paṭapaṭākaroti*: when the suffix *ḍāc* is intended to follow the word *paṭat* as its domain—that is, while it is present in the intellect but has not yet been produced—the reduplication of the word *paṭat* is first performed. Once that is done, and the condition of having "at least two syllables" (*dvyajavarārdhatā*) has arisen, the elision of the *ṭi* (the final syllable) occurs by *ḍāci* [Pāṇini 6.1.100], and the substitution of *ra* for the preceding *t* occurs by *paraḥ* [Pāṇini 8.3.1]. Thus, one says *damadamākaroti*.
The doubling of the word *vāma* is as before, followed by the suffix *ḍāc*.
Thus, "he makes it into a stone" (*dṛṣatkaroti*).
Here too, once the doubling has been performed, the word consists of two syllables with a minimum of one vowel, and thus the condition for the suffix is met.
This is not an imitation of an indistinct sound,
as in the case of "he makes it *śrat*.
This is indeed an imitation of an indistinct sound, but it is not more than two syllables long.
For even when reduplication (*dvirvacana*) is applied here, it results in a form ending in a single short vowel (*ekāj-vara*);
as in *kharaṭakharaṭākaroti*.
Here, the reduplication of the imitation-word *kharaṭat* occurs as before—just as it does for the imitation-word *paṭat*—and then the suffix *ḍāc* is added.
If only "from that which has two syllables and is not short" (*dvyajadrdhāt*) were stated, the suffix would not apply here, for in this case there is no state of being non-short after two syllables.
However, when the term "shorter" (*avara*) is included, it does apply even here.

For in that context, since the suffix must be applied from that which is shorter than the non-short portion of a word consisting of two syllables, it must necessarily be applied from everything other than that; otherwise, the inclusion of the term "shorter" would be entirely purposeless, and one would simply have said "from that which has two syllables and is not short."

Regarding the expression *paṭiti karoti*: by [Pāṇini 6.1.98], there is the substitution of a single subsequent form (*pararūpatva*) for the word *it*. If the suffix *ḍāc* were present here, then after that form ending in *ḍāc*, the verb *karoti* would have to immediately follow the word *param*; however, it does not follow *param*, and that is undesirable.

Now, for what purpose is the letter *ca* [in the rule]? Since the final acute accent (*antodāttatva*) has already been established by the accent of the suffix (*pratyayasvara*), one might ask why this is stated. To this he says: "The letter *ca*" and so forth.

When the form *paṭapaṭā asi* is established, once the *nighāta* (elision of accent) of the word *asi* has been applied by [Pāṇini 8.1.28], a single substitute (*ekādeśa*) with a circumflex (*svarita*) would result by [Pāṇini 8.2.6]: *svarito vānudātte 'padādau*. However, a circumflex is not desired here; for that reason, the letter *ca* is included. It should be understood as being "for its own sake" (*svārthika*).
Because there is no object distinct [from the action itself].

But by what means is the suffix *yak* added with its own inherent meaning (*svārthika*)? It is by this very rule of irregular derivation (*nipātana*). Now, since the word "karoti" (the root *kṛ*) follows from the rule "in connection with *kṛ*, *bhū*, and *as*" (*kṛbhvastiyoge*), for what purpose is the mention of *kṛñ*?

To this, [the answer is]: three verbal roots (*dhātu*) are under discussion; if the mention of *kṛñ* were not made there, then just as it occurs with *kṛñ*, it would likewise occur with *bhū* and *as* as well.
Therefore, the mention of *kṛñ* is for the purpose of excluding *bhū* and *as*. In the expression "of the number" (*saṃkhyāyāḥ*), the genitive case indicates a relationship of proximity.

By the phrase "ending in a secondary suffix denoting a quality" (*guṇāntāyāḥ*), he shows that the word "number" (*saṃkhyā*) is in the genitive case within this rule for the prescription of suffixes, by means of the expression "of the word denoting a number."

The word *anta* also has the sense of "part" (*avayava*). If it were taken in that sense here, there would be no connection with the word "number" (*saṃkhyā*), for a "part" which is a quality-word (*guṇaśabda*) is not applicable to a number-word. Thinking thus, [the author] shows that this word *anta* signifies "proximity," saying: "the quality-word at the end, i.e., in proximity.
By the word "wherein" (*yatra*), the base form (*prakṛti*) is indicated.
"‘Sā’ and so forth:
the meaning is that this *prakṛti* is denoted by a numeral followed by a word ending in a quality-term (*guṇa*). That which has a word for a quality at its end is thus described."

The phrase "from such as that" (*tādṛśāt*) and so forth means: from a word for number (*saṃkhyā-śabda*) that is of such a nature, or from a word for a quality (*guṇa-śabda*) situated in proximity. Now, one might object: in a word ending in a term expressing proximity, no distinction is determined as to whether the quality is prior or posterior to the number; and thus, even where it [the quality] is prior, the rule would still apply. This is not a fault; for this [suffix], when occurring in the sense of proximity, denotes that very proximity which has a fixed location and depends on something else (the number), and not mere proximity in general.

For example, a word denoting a part does not signify the mere part; what then? It signifies the part as qualified by its specific location—as in "he makes a double scratching. *Sapattra* means "with leaves"; *niṣpattra* means "from which the leaf has gone out.
*Atipīḍanam* means excessive pressing. [The phrase] "he makes them bent" (*nikuñcān karoti*) is used.
He whose family has been pointed out is "niṣkula";
here, the word *kula* refers to kinsmen.
"Accommodating the mind of the one to be propitiated":

the distressing of the mind—either by performing what is disliked by a master or the like, or by failing to perform what is desired—is suffering, which is opposition. That too is indeed a property of sentient beings. "The distressing of the mind of a master or the like."

The affliction of the mind through the performance of what is undesired by one's master and others, or through the non-performance of what is desired, is *duḥkha* (suffering), which is to say, opposition. That too is a property belonging solely to sentient beings. [In the expression] "he skewers the meat," the meaning is "he cooks. [In the expression] "he makes it Madra."

The meaning is that one performs the tonsure preceded by auspicious rites. Regarding the statement "it should be stated 'and from *bhadra*'," the meaning is that it must be explained that the suffix *ḍāc* occurs after the word *bhadra* as well.

In this regard, the explanation is as follows: from [Pāṇini 5.4.60], the letter *ca* is carried over (anuvartate), and it serves to include what has not been explicitly mentioned (*anuktasamuccayārtha*). By means of that, the suffix will apply even after the word *bhadra*. This [section] "Endings of Compounds" (*samāsāntāḥ*) is a governing heading (*adhikāra*).

The specific types of compounds, such as the *bahuvrīhi*, for which the suffixes are prescribed by the rules to be stated later—beginning with [Pāṇini 5.4.73]: "The suffix *ḍac* is added to a *bahuvrīhi* denoting a number, except after *bahu* and *gaṇa*"—are governed by this heading. Even where there is no explicit mention of the *bahuvrīhi* and so forth, the entire compound formation (*saṅghāta*) is indicated as the base (*prakṛti*).

Since [the rule] states, "After *sāman* and *loman* preceded by *ac*, *prati*, *anu*, or *ava*" (Pāṇini 5.4.75), the suffixes for compound-final elements (*samāsānta*) will be understood through the very force of that [rule] alone; so what is the purpose of mentioning "compound" (*samāsa*)? It is for the sake of those cases where both [conditions] are absent—such as in the rule "For *ṛc*, *pura*, *ap*, *dhu*, *pathin*, and *adhvan*, [the suffix *aC* is applied] except when followed by *akṣa*" (Pāṇini 5.4.74)—that the mention of "compound-final element" (*samāsānta*) is made.

This word *anta* also signifies "proximity. If it were taken here in that sense, then since the proximity [of the suffixes] is already established by their status as being subsequent to a base (*pratyaya-paratva*), the word *anta* would be redundant; considering this, he says: showing that this word *anta* is taken in the sense of "a constituent part" (*avayava*), he states "parts" (*avayavāḥ*) and, in order to provide a synonym for it, he says "portions" (*ekadeśāḥ*).

By taking the word *ekadeśa* (part) here as the basis prior to the rule for compound formation, it is implied that the suffixes to be mentioned occur first from the final member [of the compound], and the compound is formed afterwards. For they would indeed be parts of the compound only if they existed prior to the operation of compounding. Having first applied the compound-final suffixes (*samāsānta*), the compound is subsequently formed with that which ends in them.
And thus, since the designation of a compound (*samāsa-saṃjñā*) occurs together with them, it is established that the suffixes beginning with *ḍac* are constituent parts of the compound.
For this reason, it must be understood as follows:

for one who thinks that the suffixes beginning with *ḍac* should apply only after the compound has been formed, the statement that the author of the Vṛtti will make regarding the rule *na kapi* [Pāṇini 7.4.14]—namely, "when the final member of the compound has the sense of a compound and the suffix *kap* has been added, the compounding must subsequently take place"—would be contradicted.

But surely, when the suffixes such as *ḍac* and others have been applied to the final member (*uttarapada*) after the meaning of the compound has been established, the compound is subsequently formed with that which ends in those suffixes? Even in this view, the same fault remains; for in rules such as [Pāṇini 5.4.72], the references—such as "optionally, a compound-ending suffix occurs after a *tatpuruṣa* ending in the word *pathin* which follows the negative particle *nañ*"—would indeed be contradicted. This is not so; for the non-contradiction of those rules was already established under [Pāṇini 4.1.1], *ṅyāpprātipadikāt*. By the phrase "they are included by the mention of *tad*," the compound itself is referred back by the pronoun *tad*.
Since they are constituent parts of a compound, the designation of that [compound] is also applied to them;
therefore,
they are included by the mention of "compound" (*samāsa*).
Now, what is the purpose of the suffix when it is a constituent part of a compound? To this he says: "The purpose," and so forth. Examples are *adhirājam* and *uparājam*;
in these cases, respectively, there is an *avyayībhāva* compound in the sense of a case ending and in the sense of proximity.

Is it because [the term] ending in *ṭac* is included by the mention of the *avyayībhāva* compound in [Pāṇini 5.4.108], *anaśca*, that there is no elision (*aluk*) of the case-ending according to [Pāṇini 2.4.83], and the state of ending in *am* occurs? The compound "two cities taken together" (*dve purī samāhṛte*) is formed as a collective (*samāhāra*) according to [Pāṇini 2.1.51].

And that [compound] receives the designation of *dvigu* according to [Pāṇini 2.1.52]. Since [the word *pur*] ending in the suffix *akāra*—by virtue of being included in the mention of *dvigu* in [Pāṇini 5.4.74], *ṛkpūrabdhūḥpathām*—is one ending in *a*, the feminine suffix *ṅīp* is established according to [Pāṇini 4.1.21].

Regarding the term *kośaniṣadinī*: *kośa* and *niṣad* form a collective copulative compound (*samāhāra-dvandva*). By the rule *dvandvāccudaṣahāntāt samāhāre* [Pāṇini 5.4.106], the suffix *ṭac* is applied; since this is included by the mention of "copulative compounds" (*dvandva*) in that rule, the word *kośaniṣada* is formed. Then, by the rule *prāṇisthādāto lajanyatarasyām* [Pāṇini 5.2.128], the suffix *lañ* is applied to indicate "she who has this," resulting in *kośaniṣadila*. Finally, by the rule *ṛnnebhyo ṅīp* [Pāṇini 4.1.5], the feminine suffix *ṅīp* is added, yielding *kośaniṣadinī*. Regarding *ruāktvacinī*: [the analysis follows the same grammatical process].
This is the same as the previous case.

Regarding the words *vidhuraḥ* and *pradhuraḥ*: [they are formed] by the rule *pra-ādibhis tatpuruṣe* (Pāṇini 2.2.18), as in "one from whom the burden has departed" (*vigato dhuraḥ*) and "one who has gone beyond the burden" (*pragato dhuraḥ*). Thus, they are *prādi-tatpuruṣa* compounds.

As before, since the form *a-* is included here by the mention of the *tatpuruṣa* compound, the original accent (*prakṛtisvara*) of the first member is established by the rule *tatpuruṣe tulyārthatṛtīyā* [Pāṇini 6.2.2] and so forth. Furthermore, the first member is the particle *a-*, which is acute-accented on its initial syllable (*ādyudātta*). However, if the status of being a compound-final element (*samāsāntatva*) did not exist, the final syllable would be acute-accented due to the accent of the suffix (*pratyayasvara*).

Regarding the terms *uccairdhuraḥ* and *nīcairdhuraḥ*: *uccairdhūrasya* and *nīcairdhūrasya* are *bahuvrīhi* compounds. As before, the suffix *-a-* is applied; since this is included by the mention of *bahuvrīhi*, the original accent of the first member (*pūrvapada-prakṛti-svara*) occurs according to the rule: "In a *bahuvrīhi*, the first member retains its original accent" (Pāṇini 6.2.1).
In this case, the original accent (*prakṛtisvara*) of the first member is replaced by an acute accent on the final syllable (*antodātta*).

The words *sanutar*, *uccais*, *nīcais*, *śanais*, *ṛdhak*, *ṛte*, *yugapat*, *ārāt*, and *pṛthak*—these beginning with *sanutar*—are acute on the final syllable because they are listed among the *svarādi* group. Regarding *surājā* and *atirājā*: analyzing them as "a beautiful king" (*śobhano rājā*) and "an eminent king" (*atiśayito rājā*), respectively, the compound is formed according to *kugatiprādayaḥ* [Pāṇini 2.2.18].
Regarding the term *sugauḥ*: the compound is formed as before. Here, by rule [Pāṇini 5.4.92], the suffix *ṭac* would apply; however, due to this specific statement, it does not occur.
The compound "paramarājaḥ" and "paramagavaḥ" is formed according to [Pāṇini 2.1.61].
"Susakthaḥ" is likewise formed.
In the case of a *bahuvrīhi* compound, the suffix *ṣac* is applied after the words *sakthi* and *akṣi* when they denote a limb of one's own body (Pāṇini 5.4.113). Regarding the term *kiṃrājā*:
having analyzed it as "a censured king" (*nindito rājā*), a compound is formed according to [Pāṇini 2.1.64].
In the word *kiṃrāja*, the word *kim* is used in the sense of a question, not in the sense of censure; thus, it is a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*).

Now, one might object: since the rule *lakṣaṇapratipadoktayoḥ pratipadoktasyaiva grahaṇam* (Vyāḍi-Pāṇini 3) dictates that between a term defined by a general characteristic and one stated as a specific word-form, only the latter is to be understood, then the compound of *kim* prescribed by [Pāṇini 2.1.64] would be the one taken; thus, the inclusion of the word *kṣepa* ("contempt") would be redundant. If this is so, then by the inclusion of *kṣepa*, it is indicated that this *paribhāṣā* does not apply here. Consequently, the prohibition is established even in the case of a *bahuvrīhi*: *ninditā dhūrasya kindhuraṃ śakaṭam* ("a cart with a contemptible yoke"), *nirdhuraṃ śakaṭam* ("a cart without a yoke"). The example *arājā* ("non-king") is a *tatpuruṣa*.

"Anṛco māṇavakaḥ" (the boy who has no Ṛgveda verses) and "adhuraṃ śakaṭam" (a cart that is not yoked)—both of these are *bahuvrīhi* compounds. In both cases, the suffix *aC* is applied as in the preceding rules. In the case of "apatham" (a pathless place), the suffix *aC* is applied as in the preceding rules.

The neuter gender [of *apatham*] follows from the rule "apathaṃ napuṃsakam" (Pāṇini 2.4.30). In the expression "in a bahuvrīhi," the locative case is used by transposition (*subvyatyaya*) in the sense of the ablative. This refers to that bahuvrīhi compound which is formed by the rule "saṃkhyāvyayāsanna... (Pāṇini 2.2.25) and so forth;
its function is restricted solely to denoting a number (*saṃkhyeya*).

But what about cases where it occurs in the sense of *vā* (or), such as *dvitrāḥ* or *pañcaṣāḥ*, and where it occurs in the sense of *su-* (good/excellent), such as *dvidaśāḥ* or *tridaśāḥ*? In those instances, the rule would not apply. This is not a fault; for even there, it indeed occurs in the sense of a number (*saṃkhyeya*), since the meaning of *vā* and the meaning of *su-* are expressed precisely as being numbers. Similarly, *upadaśāḥ* means "near ten," and *upaviṃśāḥ* means "near twenty."

"Upaviṃśāḥ" means those near twenty; there is elision of "ti" by the rule "tiviṃśaterḍiti" [Pāṇini 6.4.142], and the single substitute for both *a* sounds occurs by the rule "akaḥ savarṇe dīrghaḥ" [Pāṇini 6.1.101]. "Āsannadaśāḥ" means those near ten.
"Near ten" is *adūradaśāḥ*; "more than ten" is *adhikadaśāḥ*; "two or three" is *dvitrāḥ*;
"five or six" is *pañcaṣāḥ*. In all these cases, the compound is a *bahuvrīhi* according to the rule beginning with *saṃkhyāvyayāsanna* [Pāṇini 2.2.24].
In the case of *citraguḥ*, [the rule] Pāṇini 1.2.48 prescribes a short vowel.

But surely, by the maxim of "that which is connected with *nañ* and *iva*" (Vyāḍipāda 65), because of the prohibition regarding *bahu* and *gaṇa*, the term *saṃkhyā* (numeral) will be understood as referring only to those compounds where a numeral is the final member (*uttarapada*), since it is understood to denote things similar to that. Thus, since there would be no possibility of application in cases such as *citraguḥ*, what is the purpose of including the mention of "numeral" (*saṃkhyā*)? This would indeed be so if the word *bahu* were exclusively a term for a thing to be numbered (*saṃkhyeya*); however, it also signifies "abundance" (*vaipulya*). Therefore, if the mention of "thing to be numbered" were not made, the mention of "having a numeral as the final member" would not apply [to *bahu*].
The terms *upabāhavaḥ* and *upagaṇāḥ* are bahuvrīhi compounds, as explained previously.
Regarding the phrase "here," etc.:
whether the suffix *ḍāc* is applied or not in the case of *upagaṇāḥ*, there is no difference in the resulting form.

Regarding the accent, however, [the following] is found: if *ḍac* were present, there would be an udātta on the final syllable; in its absence, due to the preservation of the original form (*prakṛtibhāva*) of the preceding member, it becomes udātta on the first syllable.
"Of a numeral," and so forth.
The meaning of the word *upasaṃkhyāna* is "explanation" (*pratipādana*).

The meaning is that the suffix *ḍac* must be prescribed after the final member of a *tatpuruṣa* compound when that member expresses a number. The demonstration of this is as follows: the particle *ca* is carried over from [Pāṇini 5.4.59], and it serves to include what has not been explicitly mentioned; by this, the suffix *ḍac* will apply to a *tatpuruṣa* compound whose first member is a numeral. [Question: "Is it for the sake of forms such as *niḥtraśa*? etc.
The word *ādi* (and so forth) indicates a class or type.
Regarding the form *nistriśāḥ*— [the forms *nistraśāni* and *nistraśaḥ* are also found in the original text]—
it is a *tatpuruṣa* compound according to [Pāṇini 2.2.18].

The addition of *ḍac* is for the purpose of making the final syllable udātta; otherwise, because the suffix is part of a compound, its accent would be overridden by the accent of the *bahuvrīhi*. Regarding the phrase "by virtue of semantic capacity" (*sāmarthyāt*):
that which has a connection with something else becomes its qualifier; and it is only with *dhur* that there is a connection with *akṣema*, not with the others.
Therefore, by virtue of proximity (*samarthyāt*), this qualification "not [in] the dice" (*anakṣe*) is understood as referring to that very [person], and not to the *ṛc* verses and so forth.
Furthermore, in the term "in the dice" (*anakṣe*), the locative case is used in the sense of the genitive through a substitution of case endings (*sub-vyatyayena*).
For this very reason, he says: "belonging to one who is not [involved with] the dice," and so on.

The connection with the axle (*akṣa*) is characterized by the relationship between part and whole; that which possesses this [connection] is "connected with the axle" (*akṣasambandhinī*). That [connection] does not exist in the case of the word *dhūḥ* (pole). Now, why is it not understood in this way: that [the suffix] does not occur when the axle is the expressed meaning (*abhidheya*)? It is impossible to understand it thus; for if it were understood in this way, the prohibition would apply only here: *dṛḍhā dhūr asyākṣasya* = *dṛḍhadhūrakṣaḥ* ("an axle with a firm pole").

But in this case, it would not apply to *akṣasya dhūḥ* as *akṣadhūḥ*. If that is so, then it is understood that [the rule] does not apply when *akṣa* is the preceding member (*pūrvapada*). Even so, it is impossible to understand [it in that way]; for if it were understood thus, the prohibition would apply only here—namely, in *akṣadhūḥ*—but it would not apply here in *dṛḍhadhūrakṣaḥ*.
As explained by the author of the *Vṛtti*, however, it applies in both cases.
Is it because the compound ends with that which is connected to the axle (*akṣa*)? Regarding the term *ardharcaḥ*:
"half of a *ṛc*" forms a compound by the rule *ardhaṃ napuṃsakam* [Pāṇini 2.2.2].
By the rule *adṛdharcā puṃsi ca* [Pāṇini 2.4.31], there is also neuter gender; thus we have *bahvṛcam*. [The form] *bahvṛcaḥ* is a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "one who has many *ṛc*s."
Regarding the term *lalāṭapuram*:
this is a genitive tatpuruṣa compound;
or alternatively, it is a compound formed according to [Pāṇini 2.1.56], beginning with the rule "that which fills the forehead" (*lalāṭaṃ pūrayati*).
Regarding the term *nāndīpuram*:

it is a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*). Although this form is established when the compound is made with the word *pura* ending in the vowel *a*, nevertheless, if the compound were made with the word *pūr* ending in a consonant, then the consonant would be heard [at the end of the compound]. It is for the purpose of preventing such a hearing of the final consonant that the word *pura* is used here.

The words *dvīpam*, *antarīpam*, and *samīpam* are formed as *bahuvrīhi* compounds meaning "in which water has gone twice," "in which water has gone within," and "in which water is joined," respectively. According to [Pāṇini 6.3.97], the vowel *i* is substituted [for the second member].
The term "rājadhūrā" is a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*).
[Similarly,] the term "mahādhuraḥ" [is a genitive compound].

In *bahuvrīhi*, there is the substitution of long *ā* [for the final vowel] by [Pāṇini 6.3.46], and the masculine form (*puṃvadbhāva*) is applied by [Pāṇini 6.3.33] and following rules. In the cases of *sthalapathaḥ* and *jalapathaḥ*, they are either genitive compounds (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*),
or locative compounds (*saptamīsamāsa*) due to the analytical split (*yogavibhāga*) of the rule [Pāṇini 2.1.40].

It is shown that for a *bahuvrīhi* compound ending in *ṛc* where the preceding member is a negative (*nañ*), the suffix is desired only when the referent is a *māṇavaka* (a young student), whereas for a *bahuvrīhi* ending in *ṛc* with multiple preceding members, it is desired only when the referent is a *caraṇa* (a Vedic school). This is indicated by the examples "anṛco māṇavako jñeyaḥ" ("the young student should be known as one who has no *ṛc*s") and so forth. Furthermore, it should be understood that because the term "optionally" (*vibhāṣā*) is carried over from [Pāṇini 5.4.72], this is to be recognized as a restricted option (*vyavasthitavibhāṣā*). Thus we have "anṛkkaḥ" and "bahavṛkkaḥ."
By [Pāṇini 5.4.154], the suffix *kapa* is applied;
by [Pāṇini 8.2.30], there is *kutva*—the change of the letter *ca* to *ka*. Thus, "pratisāmam" means that which has gone toward the *sāman* (prati-gataṃ sāma) is "pratisāmam."
It is either a *prādi-samāsa* (a compound with a prefix) or a *bahuvrīhi* (possessive compound) meaning "one to whom the *sāmānya* has returned. In the latter case,
the word *gata* is not employed in the compound because its meaning is already conveyed [by the prefix].

Alternatively, *sāmapratī* is an *avyayībhāva* compound according to [Pāṇini 2.1.6], *avyayaṃ vibhakti*, etc., meaning "in accordance with the truth" (*yathārthe*). Or, it is a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "that which has followed along with the *sāman*. Thus, it is *avasāmam*.

It is the same as the preceding [rule]. In examples such as *anuloma*, it is the same as the preceding; in examples such as *valoma*, it should be understood that they are formed by the *prādi* compounds and so forth, as previously described.

Regarding the rule "after *kṛṣṇa*, *udaka*, and *pāṇḍu* when they precede": the suffix *ac* is prescribed for that land (*bhūmi*) which has the words *kṛṣṇa*, *udaka*, or *pāṇḍu* preceding it. For example, a region where the ground is black is called *kṛṣṇabhūma*.
The suffix *ac* is prescribed after the word *udīcī* when it means "northern land" in this region, as in *udagbhūmaḥ*; and after *pāṇḍu* when it means "white land," as in *pāṇḍubhūmaḥ*.
Furthermore, the suffix *ac* is traditionally taught after the words *godāvarī* and *nadī*, provided that these two—*nadī* and *godāvarī*—follow a numeral.
The compound *pañcagodāvara* is an *avyayībhāva* formed by the collective sense (*samāhāra*) according to [Pāṇini 2.1.20]: "The collection of five Godāvarīs"; likewise, *pañcanada*.
Regarding the phrase "of the earth as well" and so forth: this is desired not only for the two rivers beginning with Godāvarī, but also for the word "earth" (*bhūmi*) when preceded by a numeral.
In all instances such as "dvibhūmaḥ" and so forth, [the compound] is a *bahuvrīhi*.
Regarding "tat" and so on: the teachers establish even forms such as "kṛṣṇabhūma" by means of a *yogavibhāga* (splitting the rule). A prohibition is made by the phrase "from non-observation."

"Kabarākṣam, gavākṣam"—these two are conventional terms (rūḍhi-śabda); one should not insist upon the meaning of their constituent parts here. The intention is that [if analyzed etymologically], "kabarākṣam" and "gavākṣam" would not be established as such.

It might be argued: "Is this not established by the negation of seeing (*darśana*)? For [the word 'eye'] means 'that by which one sees'; it does not mean 'seeing,' nor is it seen through a window, nor even through a lattice. To this he says: "By that also," and so forth.
This word *darśana* is well-known in common usage as referring to the eye, a member of a living being.
For instance, one employs the term *darśana* even for the eye when it is grasped.
Therefore? By virtue of common usage, the word *darśana* (seeing) is a synonym for the eye; that [usage] is relied upon here. [The rule] *akṣṇo'darśanāt* (Pāṇini 5.4.76):
"from *adarśanāt*. The word should be split as *a-darśanāt*. That by which one sees is *darśana*—namely, the eye.
The suffix *lyuṭ* is used in the sense of the instrument (*karaṇe*).
Thus, it results that [the word refers to] that which does not denote the eye.
He states this: "from a synonym of 'non-eye'."

Regarding the phrase "like the eye of cows" (*gavām akṣīva*): the word *akṣi* (eye) is used with the particle *iva* to indicate that it is metaphorical (*lākṣaṇika*), referring to something similar [to an eye],
because it does not denote the eye in its primary sense (*mukhyavṛtti*).

Masculinity [is established] from common usage. (*Bālamano ramā*) Now, he begins to state the specific compound-ending suffixes (*samāsānta*) for *tatpuruṣa* compounds: *tatpuruṣasyāṅguleḥ* (Pāṇini 5.4.86). From the previous rule, *ac* is understood by anuvṛtti from "after *prati*, *anu*, and *ava*," and the governing term *samāsānta* is in force. By this, it is understood that [the suffix] is a final constituent part of the compound. *Sūtra 5.4.76*: *tatpuruṣasyāṅguleḥ saṅkhyāvyayādeḥ*. Now, he begins to state the specific compound-ending suffixes (*samāsānta*) for *tatpuruṣa* compounds: *tatpuruṣasyāṅguleḥ*.
From the previous rule, *ac* is understood by anuvṛtti from "after *prati*, *anu*, and *ava*," and the governing term *samāsānta* is in force.
By this, it is understood that [the suffix] is a final constituent part of the compound.

Because of the governing rule "and the suffix *para*," even though the suffix *ac* follows the *tatpuruṣa* compound, it is still a constituent part (*avayava*) of that compound; therefore, in the expression *aṅguleḥ*, the genitive case denotes a constituent part (*avayava-ṣaṣṭhī*).

The term *aṅguleḥ* is a qualifier of the *tatpuruṣa*, and thus the rule applies to that which ends with it. This is what is meant by the statement "from a numeral or an indeclinable, etc. (*saṃkhyā-vyayādeḥ*).

The analysis of the compound is: "number and indeclinable" is *saṅkhyāvyaye*; that which has these as its initial members is [the compound]. In the example *dvyaṅgulam*, it is a *dvigu* compound according to the rule *taddhitārtha*.

In the case of *pramāṇe*, [the suffixes] *sad*, *daghna*, and *mātrac* are used; there is elision (*luk*) by the rule "in the sense of measure, after a *dvigu* compound, [the suffix *mātra* is always elided].

From the word *dvyaṅguli*, when the suffix *ac* is added, because that [suffix *ac*] is a *taddhita*, the vowel *i* is elided by the rule "when *yasya* follows, [the preceding *ī*, *ū*, or *ai* are also elided]" (*yasyeti ca*). Thus, we have *niraṅgulam*.

The compound is formed according to the rule *nirādayaḥ krāntādyarthe* ("*nir-* and others [form compounds] in the sense of 'having gone beyond' and so forth"). There is elision of the vowel *ac*. Regarding the phrase "even the restriction in a compound" (*samāse vyavasthāpi*), etc.:

"restriction in a compound" (*samāsavyavasthā*) means the regulation of compounds—such as that in some cases it must be a *bahuvrīhi* and in others a *dvandva*, and so on—which is to be understood solely from the rules of irregular derivation (*nipātana*), because there is no other basis for such differences in restriction.
By the word "even" (*api*), it should be understood that other operations, such as the elision of the suffix *ṭi*, are also to be known solely from the rules of irregular derivation.
For by the rule beginning with "saptamyarthavṛttayoḥ," a compound is prescribed for two indeclinables that denote the sense of the locative case and have the locus as their primary meaning.

Therefore, one should understand that this [particular form] occurs solely through irregular derivation (nipātana). Because of the word "api" [in the rule], the compound itself also exists only through irregular derivation.
In the word *ahardivam*,
the letter *n* is replaced by *r* according to [Pāṇini 8.2.69].
As for the phrase beginning with *nanu ca*:
For the employment of words has as its purpose the communication of meaning. Since the meaning has already been expressed by one synonym, the employment of a second is impossible.
The words *ahar* and *divā* are synonyms; therefore, how could there be a *dvandva* compound of these two? The sense is that it is not possible in any way.
Thinking that the usage of a word already stated for the purpose of indicating repetition (*vīpsā*) is not contradictory, he says: "In the sense of repetition," and so forth.
Since a *dvandva* compound arising in the sense of *ca* (and) would not otherwise apply in the sense of repetition, it is thus prescribed as an irregular formation (*nipātana*). One...
There is one type of *avyayībhāva*:
