that which occurs "in the sense of totality," according to the rule beginning with *avyayaṃ vibhakti* [Pāṇini 2.1.6].
In the word *sarajasam*, the substitution of *sa-* for *saha-* occurs according to [Pāṇini 6.3.81]. In the word *niḥśreyasam*,
it is a *prādi* compound.

Regarding "niśreyaskaḥ": this is a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "one by whom the highest good (*śreyaḥ*) is certain," with the suffix *kap* applied according to [Pāṇini 5.4.154]. Regarding "ṛgyajurunmugdhaḥ": [this refers to one who is confused regarding the Ṛgveda and Yajurveda].
One who, due to confusion, considers the *ṛc*s and the *yajus* [to be the same] is referred to as "ṛgyajuḥ" by means of a *bahuvrīhi* compound.
Then there is the *avyayībhāva*:
according to the rule beginning with "an indeclinable [is compounded] with that which denotes a case-ending" (*avyayaṃ vibhakti* 2.1.6), it is used in the sense of proximity.
Regarding the phrase "absence of *ṭi*-elision" and so forth:
in the word *upaśunaḥ*, the absence of *ṭi*-elision [which would otherwise apply by Pāṇini 6.4.144] occurs precisely due to this specific grammatical irregularity (*nipātana*).

Since the rule "of *āyu*, *magha*, and *van*, except before a secondary suffix" (Pāṇini 6.4.133) prescribes *samprasāraṇa* for these words only when they are not followed by a secondary suffix (*taddhita*), that very *samprasāraṇa* does not apply in the case of a secondary suffix; therefore, it occurs here precisely due to this specific irregularity.

Regarding the phrase "in the case of *caturoc-prakaraṇe*" and so forth: the meaning is that an addition (*upasaṃkhyānam*)—that is, a formal explanation—must be made concerning the vowel (*ac*) that follows the word *catur* which comes after the words *tri* and *upa*. This must be done by resorting to a split of the rule (*yogavibhāga*), just as was done previously.
"Three or four" is expressed as *tricaturaḥ*.
"Near four" is *upacaturāḥ*.
This is a *bahuvrīhi* compound formed according to the rule beginning with *saṃkhyāvyayāsanna-* (Pāṇini 2.2.25).

In this regard, since the suffix *ḍac* would otherwise apply by the rule "in a bahuvrīhi denoting a number, after *bahu* and *gaṇa*" (Pāṇini 5.4.73), the suffix *ac* is prescribed here. Examples are *brāhṛvarcasam* and *hastivarcasam*. These are genitive compounds (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*).
This word *varcas* signifies radiance.
"And it should be stated [that the suffix] occurs after the words *palya* and *rājan*" [as noted in the Kāśikā as *palyarājabhyām*].
The meaning is that this should be explained as having the sense that the suffix *ac* occurs after the word *varcas* when it follows the words *palya* and *rājan*.
And this explanation must be made by relying on a prior division of the rule (*yogavibhāga*). Regarding the example "deep darkness" (*avatamasam*): [it is formed from *ava*, *tamas*, and *ac*].

This is either a *prādi* compound meaning "devoid of darkness" (*avahīnaṃ tamasā*) or "darkness that has been removed" (*avahīnaṃ tamaḥ*). Likewise, "joined with darkness" (*saṅgataṃ tamasā*) or "darkness that is joined" (*saṅgataṃ tamaḥ*) constitutes the term *santamasam*.
[The word] *andham* is derived from the root *andh* with the causative suffix (*ṇic*), meaning "it makes blind"; thus, from that [causative form], it means "that which blinds."

And what is that which is both blind and darkness? It is called "blind darkness" (*andhatamasa*), because it makes the blind [even] darker; thus it is so described. "Worse than the lowest" (*āvasīya*) means "worse than the best" (*āśreyasa*).
*Āvaśīyaḥ*: having analyzed *āḥ śreyaḥ*, it is a compound according to the *mayūravyaṃsakādi* class. Regarding the phrase "and by its very nature" (*svabhāvācca*) and so forth:

although the word *āḥ* elsewhere denotes a specific time, nevertheless here, within the compound, it expresses the praise or eulogy of the object denoted by the second member, which is the domain of a benediction.
Why? Because of its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
The denotation of meaning by words is inherent;
in this case, the intrinsic nature itself is the reason.
"‘Āyavaśīyasam’ is a synonym for this very [term]. By the word "asya" (of this), the term *āśreyasam* is indicated. Regarding "anurahasam":
the word *rahas* refers to that which is not manifest (*aprakāśe*).

*Anugata-rahasaḥ*, *anugataṃ rahaḥ*, or *anugataṃ rahaḥ* is a *prādi-samāsa* (prepositional compound). Alternatively, it is a *bahuvrīhi* [compound] meaning "that in which privacy (*rahaḥ*) has followed. [The form] is *avarahasaṃ*.

*Avahīnam* is either a *prādi-samāsa* (compound with a prefix) meaning "secretly abandoned" (*rahase 'vahīnam*) or "abandoned in secret" (*rahe 'vahīnam*); or it is a *bahuvrīhi* (possessive compound) meaning "that in which there is a secret abandonment. Then, *taptarahasam* is a *viśeṣaṇa-samāsa* (descriptive compound) meaning "that which is both heated and secret."

That which has arisen in secret and is not perceived by anyone is called *taptarahasa*. It is "heated" (*tapta*) as if it were fire; just as that which is heated by fire is not perceived by anyone, so too is this. Regarding the term *saptamīsthāt*:
that which stands in the locative case is *saptamīstha*; the suffix *kap* is applied according to [Pāṇini 5.2.4].
And that which occurs in the sense of the locative case likewise becomes "situated in the locative"; thus he says, "it occurs in the sense of the locative.
[The example is] *pratyuraḥ*, meaning "that which has gone toward the chest.
[This is governed by the rule: *atyādayaḥ krāntādyarthe dvitīyayā* (Vārttika).
91) Thus ends the compound. Regarding the phrase "when extension (āyāma) is to be expressed": *āyāma* means length (*dairghya*).
This [word] ends in the suffix *-ā*, which expresses the sense of possession (*matvarthīya*).
The meaning is that "length" (āyāma) is what is to be designated.
Otherwise, there would be no grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) between [the terms] "that which follows" (*anugu*) and "going" (*yāna*).
"Going" (*yāna*) is length (*āyāma*).
Regarding the expression "anugavaṃ yānam" (the carriage follows the cows):
the meaning is that the carriage has arrived in the same manner as the cows.
Regarding the expression "gavāṃ paścāt" (behind the cows).
The compound *anugava* is an *avyayībhāva* according to the rule *avyayaṃ vibhakti* [Pāṇini 2.1.6] and others, used here in the sense of "behind" (*paścāt*).
As in the previous case, the word *go* undergoes shortening.
When the suffix is to be prescribed after the word *anu*, the specific form *anugavam* is taught as a *nipātana* (irregular formation) for the purpose of including well-known usage.
Therefore, when the word *bāhva* is equal in measure to cows (*go*), it occurs only in that specific context and not elsewhere. The sacrificial altar (*vedi*) is twice as large or thrice as large.
When the suffix *tāvat* is elided, the elision of the *ṭi* (the final vowel and following consonant) of the word *tāvat* is prescribed by rule;
this is indicated by the mention of "and a compound" (*samāsaśca*).
The forms *dvi* and *tri* are prescribed [as substitutes].
By the rule beginning with *yāvataḥ prakṛtau*, he demonstrates the purpose of this prescription.
The words *prakṛti* (base) and *vikṛti* (derivative) denote specific grammatical operations.

For among the specific types of action (*karmaviśeṣa*), one called "sacrifice" (*yāga*) is expressed by the word *prakṛti* (archetype), while another is expressed by the word *vikṛti* (ectype). Regarding the term *prādhvam*:
it is a *prādi*-compound.

In this case, the compound *prādhvam* is formed according to the rule *atyādayaḥ krāntādyarthe dvitīyayā* (Vārttika 91), which prescribes a compound with a word beginning with *pra-* when used in the sense of "having gone beyond," etc., together with a word in the accusative case.

The term *niṣkrāntamadhvanaḥ* means "having departed from the road," according to the rule *nirādayaḥ krāntādyarthe pañcamyā* (Vārttika 95), resulting in the form *atyadhvam*. This is equivalent to *prādhvam*.
Furthermore, in this context, the prefix (*upasarga*) is not intended merely as an indicator of motion (*gati*).

Why is this so? Because of the absence of the application of the suffix *kriyā*. [The term] "mātraco lopaḥ" refers to the elision of the suffix *mātraC* prescribed by the rule "pramāṇe dvayasac" (Pāṇini 5.2.37) and others.
[The example is] "niraṅgulam."
This is equivalent to "beyond the road" (*niradhvam*). "Beyond a finger's breadth" (*atyaṅgulam*)— this too is equivalent to "beyond the road."

The term *pañcāṅguliḥ* is a *bahuvrīhi* compound. Regarding the statement "the mention of *ahan* is for the sake of the *dvandva*," this is a desired interpretation (*iṣṭi*); it is not for the sake of the *tatpuruṣa*, because a *tatpuruṣa* is impossible in its primary sense.

In the sense of a *dvandva*, the substratum is with respect to each individual word-meaning. For instance, if the night possessing the qualities of the day is expressed by the word "day," or if the day possessing the qualities of the night is expressed by the word "night" through a figurative construction (*gauṇyā kalpanayā*), then a *tatpuruṣa* compound in apposition (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*)—namely, "day-and-night"—is indeed possible.
Therefore, this is the intended interpretation.

This much would have been said: "A copulative compound (dvandva) is desired. And here is the evidence for this—the rule [Pāṇini 2.4.28] which prescribes the substitution of the word *rātra* for the final member of a compound ending in *rātri*, as in the example *ahorātraḥ*.
Thus, there is the masculine gender.
By the rule *ahan* [Pāṇini 8.2.68], and by the supplementary rule (*vārttika* 924) *rūparātrirathantareṣūpasaṃkhyānam*,
the *n* is replaced by *r*, resulting in guṇa.
In the case of *sarvarātraḥ*,
[the compound] is a *tatpuruṣa* with a coreferential member (*samānādhikaraṇa*) according to [Pāṇini 2.1.49].
In the case of *dvirātraḥ*, it is a *dvigu* in the sense of a collective (*samāhāra*) according to [Pāṇini 2.1.51], and by [Pāṇini 2.1.23], it receives the technical designation of *tatpuruṣa*.
"Atirātra" means "beyond the night"; it is equivalent to "atyadhva" (beyond the path). "Nīrātra" means "without the night."

By the rule *rori* [Pāṇini 8.3.14], there is the elision of the *repha*; by the rule *akaḥ savarṇe dīrghaḥ* [Pāṇini 6.1.101], there is the lengthening of the vowel. [The author] will state the suffix *ṭac* in the rule *rājāhaḥsakhibhyaṣṭac* [Pāṇini 5.4.91]. Now, why is it not understood that the substitution occurs when a vowel (*ac*) has been added by another rule? It is impossible to understand it thus, because no vowel has been prescribed after the word *ahan* in any *tatpuruṣa* compound; how then could it be the cause for the substitution?

Now, is the vowel *ac* prescribed by means of a split in the rule (*yogavibhāga*) "ac" [Pāṇini 5.4.75]? Even so, this statement would be purposeless; for once the vowel *ac* has been applied, the substitution of *ah* is already established by the rule "allopaḥ" [Pāṇini 6.4.134].
Nor should it be thought that the elision of the suffix *ṭi* applies here; for that is precluded by the restrictive rule "na saṃyogādvaṃm" [Pāṇini 6.4.145].
Therefore, this is indeed an exception to the elision of *ṭi* specifically when a vowel follows.
This instruction is improper.

What, then, is that [reason]? It is the semantic capacity (*sāmarthya*), because of which the word *ahaḥ* is not accepted as being in the preceding position? To this he says: "Not from the word *ahaḥ*" and so forth.
[The example is] *dvyahnaḥ*.

The compound is formed by [Pāṇini 2.1.51] *dvayorahnorbhavaḥ* and so forth; the suffix *aṇ* is applied by [4.3.53] *tatra bhavaḥ*, and its elision is effected by [4.1.88] *tasya*. Regarding the form *ātyahnaḥ*:
the compound is formed in the same manner as *atyadhvan*.
Regarding "nirahnaḥ":
here too, the compound is like "niradhvan"?
[Answer: It is "sarvāhṇaḥ."
This is a descriptive compound (*viśeṣaṇasamāsa*). He will state a prohibition [to this effect] with the rule *uttarapadābhyāṃ ca* [Pāṇini 5.4.90]. Thus, the form *dvyahaḥ* [is derived].

By [Pāṇini 6.4.145], there is the elision of the *ṭi* suffix. Thus we have *puṇyāham* (or *puṇyāhaḥ*, according to the Kāśikā). Is it a qualifier? [In this case,] the compound is formed by [Pāṇini 2.1.56] and following rules. As for *ekāhaḥ*: [it is formed similarly].
In this case as well, [the rule] applies by "pūrvakālaika" [Pāṇini 2.1.48] and so forth.
But how is a prohibition obtained from the word *puṇya* when combined with "uttama" and "eka"? To this he says: "The word *uttama* signifies the final [member]," and so on;
because in the sūtra "ahaḥsarvekadeśa" [Pāṇini 5.4.87] and others, the word *puṇya* is prescribed at the end.

Regarding the word "agtyaḥ": although the word *uttama* (highest) is also present, here the term *antya* (last) is employed for the purpose of negation. Therefore, it expresses the word *puṇya* (meritorious).
Now, why was the term "merit" (*puṇya*) alone not employed, so that the sūtra would be more concise? To this he says: "The mention of 'merit' alone," and so forth.

Indeed, variety is desired by the author of the sūtras, and that is achieved when the term "supreme" (*uttama*) is included. Therefore, the term "supreme" was used for the sake of variety, rather than the term "merit."
Regarding the passage beginning with "some" (*kecit*):

some explain that when it was necessary to mention "merit" (*puṇya*), the mention of "supreme" (*uttama*) was made so that the negation might also be understood to apply to the word "supreme" itself, since it too is a countable entity. This occurs through metaphorical designation (*tācchabdyam*) based on proximity, as in the expression "the hamlet on the Ganges" (*gaṅgāyāṃ ghoṣaḥ*).
Therefore, their intention is that the word *uttama* (last) is capable of denoting the word *upottama* (penultimate) by virtue of proximity.

With the words "by that" (*tena*) and so forth, he demonstrates the purpose of the prohibition, which is the understanding of the word *upottama*. [The examples] "paramāhaḥ" and "uttamāhaḥ" are *karmadhāraya* compounds according to [Pāṇini 2.1.61].
[The example] "madrarājaḥ" [is a *tatpuruṣa* compound].
This is a genitive *tatpuruṣa* compound.
But how is it that when the word *rājan* is mentioned, the word *rājñī* is also included? To this he says: "by the maxim regarding the inclusion of gender," and so forth.
The maxim regarding the inclusion of gender is precisely this: "When a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) is mentioned, that which is qualified by gender is also included" (Vyāḍiparibhāṣā 29).

Regarding the phrase "of the light syllable" (*laghv-akṣarasya*): that whose purpose or objective is the formation of a long vowel by homogeneity (*savarṇa-dīrgha*) in the first member of the compound is so described.

Here, since the rule "the light syllable is placed first" would result in either *sakhi* or *ahan* being placed first, the fact that the word *ahan* is placed last serves the purpose of enabling the *savarṇa-dīrgha* with the word *rājan*.
However, the application [of the rule] does not indicate this in every case—that the suffix *ṭac* occurs only after a word ending in *a*, such as *rājan*.

It does not occur after a word ending in *ī*, because it is impossible for an *ī*-ending word to have a long vowel resulting from the combination of the *ī* with an *a* (as they are not homogeneous vowels). For example, in *pañcagavam*:
by the rule *taddhitārtha* [Pāṇini 2.1.50], a *dvigu* compound is formed in the sense of a collective (*samāhāra*).
In the case of *pañcaguḥ* as well, it is in the sense of a secondary derivative (*taddhita*). In *rājagavam*,
it is a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*).
By [Pāṇini 2.4.71], there is elision (luk) of the case-ending (sup).
In the form "rājagavīyati," there is elision of the case-ending (subluk), and by [Pāṇini 7.4.33], the substitution of *i* for the final vowel.
There is elision (*luk*) here, but it is that of the case-ending (*sup*), not of the secondary suffix (*taddhita*).
The locative case is used here in the sense of the ablative through a transposition of case endings.

Why is this so? Because of its grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the word *go* ending in the ablative. This is demonstrated by the statement: "If that word *uras* is a designation for 'forepart' (*agra*)."
Regarding the term "aāorasam":
it is a genitive compound (ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa).
The meaning is "the principal among the āpas" (waters).

"Hastyurasam" (the chest of an elephant), "rathorasam" (the interior of a chariot). Regarding "upānasam": it is a *prādi* compound meaning "that which has approached. Regarding "mahānasam": [it means] "a great fire-pit."
The term *mahādāna* is a *karmadhāraya* compound according to [Pāṇini 2.1.61] and other rules; likewise,
*amṛtāśmaḥ* and *piṇḍāśmaḥ* are examples of *viśeṣaṇa* (descriptive) compounds.
Likewise, "kālāyasaṃ" (black iron) and "lohitāyasaṃ" (red iron),
as well as "maṇḍūkasarasaṃ" (frog-pond) and "jalasarasaṃ" (water-pond),
are genitive compounds (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*).

Regarding the term "sadanaḥ": it is a compound similar to "mahānasavat" (like a kitchen). The meaning is "common to many," because the word *grāma* functions to denote a collection of inhabited regions (*janapada*).
"Kauṭatakṣaḥ": the compound is as before. "Atiāḥ":
a *prādi* compound. "Ākarśaāḥ": [the same].
In this case, *ā* is the object of comparison,
as in the example "ā ā loṣṭaḥ" (like a clod of earth).
Here, the word *ā* refers to the clod of earth, which is not a living being, and it does not function as the standard of comparison.
Regarding "vānarākhyā":
it is a compound formed according to the rule "upamitam vyāghrādibhiḥ" (Pāṇini 2.1.56).
Here, the word "vānara" refers to a living being. Regarding "uttarasaktham": [it is a compound formed according to the rule "pūrvāparaprathama..."].

The compound *uttaraṃ sakthnaḥ* is formed by the rule [Pāṇini 2.1.57] regarding the directions "east" and "west" (*pūrvāparādi*). Alternatively, it is a descriptive determinative compound (*viśeṣaṇasamāsa*) meaning "the northern thigh," as in the expression *mṛgasaktham*.
This is a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*). "The front thigh" (*pūrvasaktham*) is equivalent to "the back thigh" (*uttarasaktham*).
In the case of *phalakasaktham*,

the compound is formed by the rule beginning with *viśeṣaṇam* [Pāṇini 2.1.57]. In the cases of *dvināvam* and *trināvam*, the *dvigu* compound is formed by the rule beginning with *taddhitārthottarapada* [Pāṇini 2.1.51].
Regarding "dvināvadhanaḥ":
when the *bahuvrīhi* compound "one whose wealth consists of two ships" (*dve nāvau dhanaṃ yasya*) is formed, by that same rule, a *dvigu* is applied to the first two words before the final member.
[An example is] "pañcanāvapriyaḥ".
Is this the same as before? [The answer is] "dvināvarūpyam" and "dvināvamayam.
By that very sūtra, a *dvigu* compound is formed in the sense of a secondary derivative (*taddhita*).
As in the previous case, the suffixes *-rūpya* and *-mayaṭ* are applied.
*rājanauḥ* (king’s boat): this is a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*).
*pañcanauḥ* (five boats): here, the suffix *ṭhak*, which would otherwise be applied by rule 5.1.19, is elided by rule 5.1.28, *adhyardhapūrvam*, etc. *ardhanāvam* (half a boat).

But is it not the case that, according to the rule *paravalliṅgaṃ dvandvatatpuruṣayoḥ* [Pāṇini 2.4.26], the feminine gender should apply here? To this he says: "The gender of the final member does not occur," and so forth. As for *dvikhārī* and *trikhārī*, the shortening of the penultimate vowel (*upasarjana-hrasva*) applies as before.

In some places, the reading is *ardhakhārī*. Here, after the shortening of the penultimate vowel due to the word being a subordinate member (*upasarjana*) of a compound, the suffix *ṅīṣ* is applied because it is listed in the *bahv-ādi* group according to the rule *sarvato 'ktinnarthād ityeke* (Gaṇasūtra 51). Thus, "purchased for two *añjali*s" is *dvyañjaliḥ*.
As before, there is elision (*luk*) of the suffix for the word *arhīyas*.
In the example "devyañjalipriyaḥ," as before, there is a *dvigu* compound with the final member. "Hasticarma" and so forth are genitive (*ṣaṣṭhī*) compounds.

Regarding *sutrāmāṇam*: it is a *prādi-samāsa* (compound with a prefix) meaning "one who has an excellent protector" (*śobhanastrāmā*). The lengthening of the vowel in the first member of the compound is according to [Pāṇini 6.3.137]. It is in the second case singular. The lengthening of the penultimate vowel is by [Pāṇini 6.4.8] et seq., and the substitution of *ṇ* is by [Pāṇini 8.4.2] et seq. Regarding *anehasām*: [the analysis follows].

From the word *anehas*, which is masculine, the sixth case plural [is formed]. The remainder [of the rule] is that the term "optionally" (*vā*) is understood to carry over. By the word "optionally" (*vāvacana*), the preceding mention [*prāggrahaṇam*] is intended here; for by it, they are stated as alternatives, since a suffix (*pratyaya*) is thereby made known (*pratyāyyate*).
This is what is meant: "The term *prāk* (before) is understood to carry over from [Pāṇini 5.4.101], which states *khāryāḥ prācām*.
By the carrying over of the term *prāk*, he demonstrates what is intended to be established: *brāhma-sāma* and *devac-chandaḥ*.
In both cases, there is a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*). Regarding the rule "in the case of expressing a *jānapada* (country-dweller)":
here, the word *jānapada* has the state (*bhāva*) as its primary meaning.
For this very reason, the commentary (*vṛtti*) states: "If the status of being a *jānapada* is expressed by means of the compound."

For indeed, there are instances where a designation emphasizes the abstract state (*bhāva*) even without an abstract suffix (*bhāvapratyaya*), as in [Pāṇini 1.4.22]. But how can the status of being a *jānapada* (belonging to a country) be qualified by the word *brāhmaṇa*, given that there is only one mention of *brāhmaṇa* here, and by it the compound (*samāsa*) has already been qualified? This is not so; by means of *tantra* (repetition), two words *brāhmaṇa* are uttered. There, by one the compound is qualified, and by the other the status of being a *jānapada*. This refers to that *tatpuruṣa* compound in which the word *janapada* is the first member. As before, the compound is formed: *uparājam*, *pratirājam*.
The term *upaśaradam* is an avyayībhāva compound, just like *pratiśaradam*.
Regarding the word *avyātma*,
it means "with respect to the self" (*ātmani adhī*), used in the sense of a case ending.
Regarding the term *pratyātmam*:
as before, it denotes directness (*ābhimukhya*). By the mention of "river" (*nadī*), the actual form (*svarūpa*) is intended, not the name (*saṃjñā*).
If the name were intended, one would not have included [the specific terms] *paurṇamāsī* and *āgrahāyaṇī*.

But is this not for the purpose of restriction—that [the substitution] occurs only for *nadī* ending in long *ī*, namely *paurṇamāsī* and *āgrahāyaṇī*? This is not so; if this were the intended purpose, he would have simply said "paurṇamāsyāgrahāyaṇī. Therefore, it is a mention of accent (*svara*). In the case of *upanadi*, there is shortening by [Pāṇini 1.2.48]. In the case of *antagiram*.
The *avyayībhāva* compound occurs when the meaning of a case ending is [expressed] by being separated from a mountain (*giri*).
For the word *antaḥ* indeed functions in the sense of a case ending because it occurs in the sense of the locative case.
Why is the mention of *Senaka* not for the sake of providing an option? To this he says: "The option (*vikalpa*) indeed continues to apply."
Because it has the sense of "optionality" (vikalpa). Or rather, that [suffix] is used by means of this [word].
It was stated that the mention of *anyatarasyām* signifies optionality; that [term] is understood here from the rule *tadiha* (Pāṇini 5.4.109).

Why is that? Because the alternative interpretation (*vikalpa*) is established by that very [rule]. The mention of *senaka* was stated solely for the sake of honoring him, not for the sake of providing an alternative interpretation.
But is it not the case that "between two optional rules (*vibhāṣā*), the mandatory rules (*nityavidhi*) prevail"? (Kāśikā Paribhāṣā)

[Objection: "In this way, would not the mention of *Senaka* be for the sake of an option (*vikalpa*) in order to establish the obligatory nature (*nityatā*) of the preceding rule? [Response: This is not so; for if the preceding rule were indeed obligatory, the reading of words ending in *jhay* (consonants other than nasals and semivowels) in the list beginning with *śarat* would be purposeless, since [the desired form] would already be established by [Pāṇini 5.4.111], *jhayaḥ*.

Therefore, the mention of *Senaka* is not for the sake of an option; it is solely for the sake of honor (*pūjārtham*). [The phrase] "in the sense of a technical name (*saṃjñāyām*)" is an adjunct (*upādhi*) to the whole."

By this, he demonstrates that if the combination of base and suffix (*prakṛti-pratyaya-samudāya*) constitutes the name of something, then the suffix [ṇatva] occurs, and not otherwise— as in the example *druṇasaḥ*. Here, the substitution of *ṇ* [for *n*] occurs by the rule *pūrvapadāt saṃjñāyām agaḥ* [Pāṇini 8.4.3].
A female *vardhra* is a *vārdhrī*; he whose nose is like that is a *vārdhrīṇasaḥ*.
[This is] the prohibition of the masculine form (*puṃvadbhāva*) according to [Pāṇini 6.3.39]. He whose nose is like a cow’s is a *gonasaḥ*.
In this case, the insertion of *c* is for the purpose of subverting the accent of the *bahuvrīhi* compound; thus,
in "kharaṇāḥ" and "khuraṇāḥ," there is lengthening according to [Pāṇini 6.4.14].
His nose is black, thus "black-nosed" (*śitināsa*); his nose is like a snake, thus "snake-nosed" (*ahināsa*);
his nose is like a flame, thus "flame-nosed" (*arcanāsa*).

By [Pāṇini 6.3.63], there is shortening. The mention of *upasarga* (preverb) is for the purpose of indicating *pra* and the others; for there is no connection with an action directed toward the nose (*nāsikām prati*).
"The substitution of *gra* for *nas* after *vi* should be stated":
it should be stated that after the word *vi*, the word *gra* is the substitute for *nāsikā*.
The analysis [of the compound] is as follows: the suffix is *iva*. Regarding the phrase "the elision of *ṭi*, etc.," the word "etc.
(*ādi*) includes the word *su* as a qualifier of the object (*karman*).
"His morning is auspicious.
Here, "auspicious" is an adjective qualifying the action.
The meaning is: "his action at the time of morning is auspicious."

In the same way, it should be understood that "excellent" (*śobhana*) is an adjective qualifying the object (*karman*) in the subsequent cases as well. There is also a word *hala* ending in the vowel *a*; when a compound is formed with that, the form will be *hala*, but when it is compounded with the form ending in *ī*, it will be *halī*. Therefore, is the inclusion of the term *halī* redundant? It is not redundant, because they have different meanings.

Therefore, when the sense of "one who possesses great ploughs" (*mahaddhali*) is intended, the form *ahala* would not be established; for if *ahala* were formed as a compound with a word ending in long ā (as in *a-hala*), then—as in the previous case—the initial udātta accent would be desired by the rule *prakṛtyā bhāva-karmaṇoḥ* [Pāṇini 6.2.173], and consequently, the suffix *kap* would be improperly applied by the rule *na-āp-ī-tvā-kap* [Pāṇini 5.4.154]. Thus, the inclusion of the term *hali* is correct. "If that is so, then by the inclusion of the word 'nitya' (constant), it is indicated that this applies elsewhere as well"—this is understood on the principle that an increase in the wording of a rule results in an increase in its scope.

Why is the *cit* marker used in *duṣprajāḥ* and *durmedhāḥ* so that there may be an acute accent (*udātta*) on the final syllable? However, in cases such as *aprajāḥ*, there is no purpose for the *cit* marker; for by the rule itself [Pāṇini 6.2.172], the acute accent on the final syllable of the second member is already established. "Uncompounded" (*asamastaḥ*)—[this phrase is not found in the Kāśikā].
The meaning is that it is formed as a non-compound (*asamāsa*).
"Supreme own-dharma" (*paramasvadharmaḥ*).
"One's own" (*sva*) and "dharma" constitute *svadharma*; "supreme" (*parama*) and "one's own dharma" (*svadharma*) constitute *paramasvadharma*.
[Objection: "If that is so," and so forth.
If *dharma* were qualified by the term *kevala*, it would not be *paramasvadharma*, but rather *paramasvadhara*.
"From the isolated [word]? means "from the preceding word. This refers to the dharma being [derived] from the preceding word alone, without any companion;
it does not mean "from a collection of words."
The connection with the subject at hand is that "the supreme Dharma" (*paramo dharma*) [is the topic].

In this explanation, there is no possibility of [the application of] a three-word *bahuvrīhi* compound, for the word *paramo dharma* arises from a collection of words, not from a single one alone—namely, from the preceding member. The addition of the marker *cit* after the suffix *-an* is intended so that the original accent (*prakṛtisvara*) of the preceding member is set aside, and it may instead have an acute accent on its final syllable (*antodātta*). By the rule regarding *jambha*, the analysis (*vigraha*) should be understood as "one whose jaw is like grass" (*tṛṇamiva jambho 'sya*) or "one whose jaw is like Soma" (*soma iva jambho 'sya*).

[Objection: Should the analysis (*vigraha*) not rather be "grass is his bite" (*tṛṇaṃ jambho 'sya*) or "Soma is his bite" (*somo jambho 'sya*), for grass is not a bite, nor is Soma? [Response: But when the word *jambha* signifies the act of eating (*abhyavahāra*), the analysis must indeed be "grass is his bite" or "Soma is his bite," because grass and Soma serve the purpose of being eaten. In this context, the rule "when there is identity of form, [the compound] *tatra tenedaṃ* is a *bahuvrīhi*" is what is intended; since this very [term] functions in the sense of reciprocal action (*karmavyatihāra*), the long vowel [is applied] by the rule "in *keśākeśi*, etc. (Pāṇini 6.3.137).

Because the suffix *ic* is listed among the words beginning with *tiṣṭhadgu*, it receives the designation of *avyayībhāva*; and since a compound that is an *avyayībhāva* is designated as an indeclinable (*avyaya*), the elision of case-endings (*sub-luk*) occurs—this is the intended meaning. The addition of the indicatory letter *c* to *ic* serves a specific purpose.

For if the letter *ca* were not used here, then one would have read only the vowel *i* even in the *tiṣṭhadgu* group; consequently, there would be the inclusion of the vowel *e* as well. [Regarding the statement] "The dative case in *dvidaṇḍādibhyaḥ* is used in the sense of *tādarthya* (purpose)," and so forth: since the items beginning with *dvidaṇḍa* are indeed listed in the *pratipadika* (nominal stem) lists as ending in the suffix *ic*, it is impossible to prescribe the suffix *ij* for them again; moreover, even if it were prescribed, it would be useless. Therefore, this is not an ablative case, but rather a dative case in the sense of *tādarthya*.
By the statement "the suffix *ic* occurs for the sake of [denoting] 'two sticks' (*dvidaṇḍa*) and so forth," he demonstrates that [the compound] has that purpose (*tādārthya*).
To clarify the meaning of this very point, he says: "'it becomes such and so forth.
By speaking in this way, it is stated that 'the suffix occurs after *dvidaṇḍa* and so forth, but not after [the individual members] *dvi*, *daṇḍa*, and so forth.'"
In this way they are established; not otherwise.

Now, for what purpose are the bases (*prakṛti*) of these compounds taught in their pure, uncompounded forms within the list of nominal stems (*prātipadika*), and then a suffix prescribed after them? To this he says: "And because of the compounding of the whole," and so forth.

Having taught the bases in the list of nominal stems, only the suffix is prescribed after them; from that, a restriction would follow: by virtue of the compounding of the whole, they are restricted to those specific meanings in which they are well-known.
The meaning is that they exist in that very place.
Regarding the example "he strikes with two sticks" (*dvidaṇḍi praharati*): it means a striking in which there are two sticks.
"In this case, it is not valid"—

this means that the word-form *dvidaṇḍī* is not correct in this sense. Because the governing rule (*adhikāra*) pertains to *bahuvrīhi*, no suffix would be prescribed for a *tatpuruṣa* compound in any instance.
Is it because of its occurrence in a collective compound (*samudāya*)? But in some cases, it occurs even from a *tatpuruṣa* compound.

When there is elision of the suffix (*pratyaya-lopa*), the designation of *avyayībhāva* applies, and [the rule] would not otherwise obtain; therefore, he says: "by means of the characteristic of the suffix" (*pratyayalakṣaṇena*), and so forth. Regarding the statement, "there is a substitute (*ādeśa*) for the word *jānu*": how, then, is it known that this is a substitute and not a suffix (*pratyaya*)? If it were a suffix, he would have made the reference using the singular case-ending, as in *jānunaḥ*; however, the reference is made using the genitive dual ending.

Therefore, it is understood that this is a substitution (*ādeśa*) and not a mere grammatical relation (*pratyaya*). The use of the genitive dual ending is made for the sake of removing doubt, so that it may be understood without ambiguity that this is a genitive of location (*sthāna-ṣaṣṭhī*). If it were stated simply as "of the knee" (*jānunaḥ*), there would be doubt: is this a genitive or a ablative? [The rule specifies] "this becomes the substitute *anaṅ*."

How, then, is it understood that this is a substitute (*ādeśa*) and not an affix (*pratyaya*)? If this were an affix, the application of the marker *ṅ* would be purposeless; however, the marker *ṅ* is meaningful here for the sake of substituting the final phoneme. Therefore, it is understood from the very presence of the marker *ṅ* that this is a substitute, as in the example "kuṇḍodhnī."
When *anaṅ* has been applied, there is substitution of the subsequent form (*pararūpatva*) [by P. 6.1.97]. Then, [the suffix] *ṅīṣ* [is added] by [P.
4.1.25]. [Regarding this, it is said: "The mention of 'feminine' (*strīgrahaṇa*) must be made.
That by which the feminine is grasped through its necessary denotation is what is meant here by "the mention of 'feminine' must be made."
This is what is meant: the explanation should be formulated in such a way that *anaṅ* occurs when a feminine noun is the referent.

In this regard, the explanation is as follows: the term *vibhāṣā* (optionally) is carried over from [Pāṇini 5.4.130] *ūrdhvād vibhāṣā*; and since that is a *vyavasthita-vibhāṣā* (a restricted option), *anaṅ* occurs only in the feminine and not elsewhere.
The inclusion of the letter *a* at the beginning of *anaṅ* is for the sake of subsequent rules.
In this case, it is indeed established even without that [suffix]. Regarding the form *śāṅgadhanvā*:

when the suffix *anaṅ* is applied, there is the substitution of *yaṇ*, and by the rule *sarvanāmasthāne ca* [Pāṇini 6.4.8], there is lengthening. Regarding the statement "there is the substitution of *niṅ*":
its status as a substitute is understood from its being marked with the *ṅ*-indicator, just as in the previous case.

Regarding the term *yuvajāniḥ*: there is elision of *y* by the rule *lopo vyor vali* [Pāṇini 6.1.66]. There is the substitution of the masculine form by the rule *striyāḥ puṃvat* [Pāṇini 6.3.34]. "The substitute *ik* occurs."

How, then, is it known that this is a substitute (*ādeśa*) and not an affix (*pratyaya*)? Because of the indication by means of the genitive case in the word "of odor" (*gandhasya*). For if it were an affix, one would have used the ablative case in the form "from odor" (*gandhāt*) for the sake of clarity; however, the indication is by means of the genitive. Therefore, it is understood that this is a substitute.
"Regarding the phrase 'if [it were] smell,' etc.:
smell is of two kinds.
Smell as a quality (*guṇa*) is not exclusively restricted to other categories of entities."

In the case of "sugandha āpaṇikaḥ" (a merchant with a pleasant scent), the word *gandha* refers to the scent of a substance (*dravyagandha*), and that [substance] constitutes a part of the merchant. Therefore, so that [the rule] may apply to the scent as a quality (*guṇagandha*) and not to the scent of a substance, when the suffix *it* is to be prescribed for *gandha*, the inclusion of the term *tad* must be made. By the word *tat*, the meaning of the *bahuvrīhi* compound is indicated by implication.
A "part" (*avayava*) is a single portion or a specific aspect (*ekadeśa*) of that [whole] which constitutes its "exclusive side" (*tadekānta*);
by means of this, the grasping of that exclusive side must be performed.

What is meant is this: such an explanation must be made so that here, in the rule for *ittva*, there is not even a scent of the other word-meaning (*anyapadārtha*) being taken from a part; therefore, it must be resorted to.

In this regard, the explanation is as follows: the option (*vā*) from rule [Pāṇini 5.4.133] continues to apply, and that is a restricted option (*vyavasthitavibhāṣā*). Therefore, the substitution of *it* occurs only where the "fragrance" (*gandha*) constitutes a part of the meaning of the other member of the compound, and not otherwise. Alternatively, there is this word *gandha* which denotes a substance—as in the expression, "He sells fragrances" (*gandhān vikrīṇīte*).
There is that which expresses a quality, as in "the earth possesses fragrance" (*gandhavatī pṛthivī*).
In this context, it is the expression of a quality that is intended, not the expression of a substance.

Therefore, a word expressing a substance occurs in the plural only when referring to a substance—as in "he sells fragrances" (*gandhān vikrīṇīte*) or "fragrances are his merchandise" (*gandhāḥ paṇyam asya*).

Here, the indication is made by the singular form "gandhasya" alone. From this it is determined that this is a reference to a word expressing a quality (*guṇavacana*). Since it is a word expressing a quality, the quality "smell" (*gandha*) becomes a part of the referent of the other member of the compound; therefore, the substitution of *it* occurs only for a smell that is an absolute part [of that referent]. [The rule states: "There is elision as a compound-final suffix."

What, then, would be the consequence? Would the compound-final suffix (*samāsānta*) not occur? [The answer is: It would occur precisely from [the rule] beginning with *Pāṇini 5.4.68* (*na ṅisambuddhyoḥ*).
Since this word "final" (*anta*) denotes a constituent that occupies a fixed position when there is a compound-final suffix, it applies only to what is final.
And thus, it becomes a compound-final suffix only if it applies to the final member, and not otherwise.

But surely, since elision (*lopa*) is of the nature of non-existence, its being a compound-final member (*samāsānta*) is not tenable? To this he says: "by way of the substituend" (*sthānidvāreṇa*), and so forth. He shows that because the substituend—the vowel *a*—is a compound-final member, elision is also called a compound-final member through metaphorical designation (*upacāra*). Regarding the statement, "Words such as *kumbhapadī* are taught as whole complexes in which the word 'foot' (*pāda*) has been elided," if this is so, how is the following to be explained? To this he says: "In that case, thus," and so forth.

In this context, regarding those [words] beginning with *kumbhapadī*, which have undergone the elision of *pāda* and are recited [in the list], the meaning is that they should be explained in this manner;
that is, how it is that *kumbhapadī* and the others come into being.

But for what purpose are the entire compounds recited, rather than the individual words like *kumbhapada* and so on—[that is,] why not recite them as nominal stems (*prātipadika*) and then prescribe the elision of the word *pāda* following them? To this he says: "And of the recitation of the compound," and so forth.

If the elision of that [suffix] were stated for the word *pāda* occurring after words such as *kumbha*, then the restriction—that "only those composite forms in which the elision of *pāda* has already taken place should be recited"—would not be obtained.
Consequently, they would appear in all three genders, yet they are intended only in the feminine.
When there is a recitation of the composite forms, the suffix *ṅīp* occurs only when the feminine gender is the domain.

Regarding "not at another time" and "kumbhapadī": when the feminine suffix *ṅīp* is applicable by rule [Pāṇini 4.1.8], there is elision of the word *pāda*; then follows the suffix *ṅīp*. When that [suffix] is present, the substitution of *pad* occurs by rule [Pāṇini 6.4.130].
"Whatever [compound] here begins with a comparison," such as *kumbhapadī* (pot-footed), *jālapadī* (web-footed), and so forth;
"and that which has a numeral as its prior member," such as *ekapadī* (one-footed), *śatapadī* (hundred-footed), and so forth;
"in the case of its established form."

Since that which is preceded by a word of comparison is already established by the preceding rule, [the present rule] applies to that which is preceded by a numeral. Regarding the form *aṣṭāpadī*, it is recited there;
in that case, the irregular formation (*nipātana*) is for the purpose of lengthening the vowel.
Or rather, according to [Pāṇini 6.3.125], this [rule] is for the sake of excluding the meaning of "comparison. Regarding the form *dvidan*:

because the vowel *ṛ* is intended to trigger the operations of the *ugit* class, the augment *num* is applied by [Pāṇini 7.1.70]. Then, by [Pāṇini 6.1.68] and [8.2.23], there is the elision of the *hal* and *ṅī* suffixes, as well as the elision of the final consonant of the cluster (*saṃyogāntalopa*). Thus we have *sudantaḥ dākṣiṇātyaḥ*. Here, "excellence" (*śobhanatva*) is understood, not "age" (*vayaḥ*). This statement is made for the sake of excluding "age" and for the sake of cases where the preceding member is not a numeral.
Regarding the term "ubhayatodataḥ":
this is a teaching. This is not for the purpose of [conforming to] Vedic meter;
rather, it means "one whose teeth are like iron," thus "ayodatī" (iron-toothed).
This is the teaching.
Regarding the word *samadantī*: the suffix *ṅīṣ* is applied by the rule *nāsikodara* (Pāṇini 4.1.55) and so forth. The term *strīyām* ("in the feminine") has ceased to apply [here].
*Rokaḥ* means shining, radiance, or luster.
The root *ruc* (Dhātupāṭha 745) means "to shine.

With the suffix *ghañ* in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāve*), the substitution of *ku* for *c* and *j* before a suffix beginning with *ṇ* or *ya* (Pāṇini 7.3.52) applies, resulting in *roka*. Having derived the word *aroka* from the analysis "that which has no *roka*" (light/shine), he states its meaning: "without light" (*nirdīpti*). Regarding the phrase "produced by time and so forth": *ruca dīptau* (Dhātupāṭha 745); with the suffix *ghañ* in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāve*), the substitution of *ku* for [the letters] *c* and *j* before a suffix beginning with *ṇ* or *ya* (Pāṇini 7.3.52) applies. Having performed the etymological derivation of the word *aroka* as "one whose *roka* (light) does not exist," he says—showing its meaning—"without light" (*nirdīpti*). "[Produced] by time and so forth."

By the word "etc. (*ādi*), food and so forth are included. This is for the sake of avoiding an infinite regress. [Objection: On a mountain, which is the referent of another word (*anyapadārtha*), a primary hump (*kakuda*) is not possible; yet this is said—"the three-humped mountain" (*trikakut parvata*). In that case, by implication, the word *kakuda* applies to the mountain peak because of its similarity to the shape of a hump. Does this mean that the designation "three-humped" would apply to every such thing that has peaks shaped like humps? To this, [the author says] "And not," and so forth.
The word "it is said" (*ucyate*) connects with the subject under discussion.
Regarding the phrase "this is its name" (*saṃjñaiṣā*) and so forth:
by this, he demonstrates that for which this name is expressed by the term *trikakud*.
And this [result] is obtained because of the inclusion [of the term *nipātanāt*] from [Pāṇini 5.4.143], due to the continued application (*anuvṛtti*) of the mention of "technical name" (*saṃjñā*).

But surely, since the restriction of the meaning (*abhidheyaniyama*) is also obtained from that very same source, the mention of *parvata* need not be made? This is not so; for such is the style of the Teacher (*ācārya*) that he states the cause for the meaning even in cases where [the word] is already well-known and obligatory, as in [Pāṇini 3.1.116]; how much more so where there is no established usage! That [usage], however, is worldly (*laukikī*), as in "utkākut," "vikākut.
When the final [letter] has been elided, the substitution of *c* occurs by [Pāṇini 8.4.56].

But surely, by the elision [prescribed] in *nanu ca* (Pāṇini 1.1.54) and so forth, this should not occur; how then does it apply to the final [element]? It has been stated that the term "final" (*antya*) refers to a member (*avayava*) as well, and that it denotes a member located in a fixed position. In that case, if [the suffix] were to apply to the beginning (*ādi*), the status of being a compound-final element (*samāsānta*) would not be possible. Is this also like the previous case? Since [the suffix] *kap* is already established, it is for the sake of making it obligatory. For example: *bahudaṇḍikaḥ*.

Thus, there is the elision of *n*. Is "remainder" (*śeṣa*) to be understood in relation to the suffix *kap*—meaning that the remainder is that bahuvrīhi compound for which *kap* has not been prescribed—or is it to be understood in relation to the compound-final suffix (*samāsānta*)—meaning that the remainder is that bahuvrīhi compound for which a compound-final suffix has not been prescribed? In this regard, if the remainder were defined in relation to *kap*, then [the rule] would apply even to cases such as *anṛcaḥ*, *vyāghrapāt*, and *sugandhiḥ*; for in these instances, *kap* has certainly not been prescribed by anyone. Having observed this fault in defining the remainder in relation to *kap*, he shows that the remainder is defined in relation to the compound-final suffix, stating: "The remainder is that bahuvrīhi compound for which no compound-final suffix occurs."
How is it known that "the remainder" (*śeṣa*) refers to [the application of] the compound-ending suffixes (*samāsānta*)? It is because of the mention of the word "remainder.
For if "the remainder" were to refer to the suffix *kap*, the mention of the word "remainder" would be purposeless.

Indeed, by the very force of its introduction, the option will apply only to the domain of the remainder; otherwise, if this optional rule (*vibhāṣā*) were prescribed even for those cases where *kap* has already been enjoined by previous prescriptive rules (*vidhi-vākya*), the prescriptive rules themselves would become redundant.
Therefore, because of the mention of the term *śeṣa* (remainder), the remainder is understood as being dependent on a compound-ending (*samāsānta*).
In the case of *bahūkhaṭvakaḥ*, [the rule] *bahuvrīhau saṃkhyeye ḍaj asañjñāyām* [5.4.73] applies, and by *ṭaci* [6.4.143], the short vowel [is applied].
In the case of *bahukhaṭvaḥ* as well, [the rule] *na pūjanāt* [5.4.69] applies.
"How so? and so forth.

The intention is that if the "remainder" (*śeṣa*) were dependent upon the final member of a compound, then the suffix *kap* would not be established in cases such as *anṛkkaṃ sāma* ("a Sāman that does not contain Ṛg-verses") and *bahvṛkkaṃ sūktam* ("a hymn containing many Ṛg-verses").
[The rule] "it is desired in the case of a specific [restriction]" is stated.

That suffix *hrak* (the *a* of *hrasva*) is intended as a compound-ending (*samāsānta*) specifically for the word *māṇava* when it denotes a Vedic school (*caraṇa*), and thus the vowel *a* is prescribed there.
Nor is that specific rule prescribed only in that instance; rather, it applies to other domains—as well as to *sāman* and *sūkta*.
In those cases, the remainder [of the compound] following a *bahuvrīhi* depends upon the application of a compound-ending suffix.
And because of that, [the word] *priyapatha* [is formed], where the suffix *a* is applied as a compound-final (*samāsānta*) by the rule "ṛkpūrabdhūḥ" (Pāṇini 5.4.74), resulting in *priyamadhura*.

Now, for what purpose is the mention of the word *śeṣa* (remainder)? For, wouldn't those very [suffixes] which are prescribed after specific bases serve as exceptions (*bādhaka*) to them? This is not so; for it is the [rules] that have no other scope (*niravakāśa*) which will act as exceptions, whereas the compound-final suffixes (*samāsānta*) do have their own scope (*sāvakāśa*).

What is the scope [of the term *śeṣa*]? It is the bases (*prakṛti*) mentioned individually; that is the scope where, for specific meanings and specific compounds, suffixes forming compound-endings (*samāsānta*) are prescribed by being mentioned individually. When there is an occasion arising from those specific bases and both [the general and specific rules] would apply, the suffix *kap* would occur by virtue of its posteriority. Therefore, the mention of *śeṣa* must be made [to exclude these]. [The statement] "all application is prohibited" [is said].
But is it not the case that "a rule or a prohibition applies only to what immediately precedes"? (Vyāḍi)

[Objection: Does this not result in a prohibition of *kap* only for that which has the characteristic of being a "remainder" (*śeṣa*)? [Response: This is not a fault; for here *kap* is what is carried over (anuvartate), not the word "from the remainder" (*śeṣāt*).
Therefore, this will be a prohibition of *kap* alone.

Regarding the phrase "many are superior" (*bahavaḥ śreyāṃsaḥ*): the suffix *īyasun* is applied by [Pāṇini 5.3.57] *dvivacanavibhajyopapade*, and the substitution of *śra* is applied by [Pāṇini 5.3.60]. Furthermore, the shortening [of the vowel] does not occur.
By the rule *iti hrasvatvam prāpnoti* (Pāṇini 1.2.48), the shortening [of the vowel] would apply; however, that also does not occur.

Why does it not occur? He says: by the rule *īyaso bahuvrīheḥ* and so forth. Here, the intended meaning is not the removal of the feminine suffix (*strīpratyaya*) through the application of the "masculine-like" (*puṃvad*) rule; rather, because this is a section concerning shortening, there is an absence of that [shortening].

This is what is meant: just as when the masculine form (*puṃvadbhāva*) applies, the shortening of the vowel *ī* does not occur, so too the feminine suffix following *īyas* does not undergo such change. This is a prohibition of the *kap* suffix which would otherwise be required by the rule *nadyutaśca* [Pāṇini 5.4.153]. Although the root *vad* (from the Dhātupāṭha, no. 11), meaning "to speak" or "to praise," is used in the sense of salutation (*abhivādana*), it is nevertheless understood here specifically in the sense of praise; therefore, he says, "he who is *vanditaḥ* is one who is praised (*stutaḥ*)."

"Is this also like the previous case? It is a prohibition of the suffix *ka* that has already been obtained. Thus ends the fourth quarter of the fifth chapter in the *Kāśikā-vivaraṇapañcikā*, composed by the venerable master Jinendrabuddhi, who is a follower of the Bodhisattva. And thus the fifth chapter is completed. **The Sixth Chapter, First Quarter:** In this regard, some maintain that only suffixes (*vidhi*) express their own meaning (*svārtha*), and not the meanings of the word bases (*padārtha*). For example, in the rule "after *kuṭilikā*" [Pāṇini 4.4.18], the suffix *aṇ* being prescribed after the word *kuṭilikā* expresses its own meaning.

Which ones? Furthermore, some [grammatical operations] serve both their own purpose (*svārtha*) and the purpose of others (*parārtha*). For example: in the rule *padādibhyo ghañ* (P. 3.3.16), the suffix *ghañ* being prescribed serves its own purpose; however, as it continues to apply in subsequent rules due to the connection with the indicatory mark *svarita*, it serves the purpose of others as well. On the other hand, some governing rules (*adhikāra*) serve only the purpose of others and not their own purpose, such as the rule *taddhitāḥ* (P. 4.1.76). Now, is this [present governing rule] for its own purpose alone, or is the governing rule for both purposes, or is it for the purpose of others alone? To remove this doubt and demonstrate that it serves only the purpose of others, he says: "And [the word] *ekāc*" and so forth.
This is the governing statement (*grahaṇaka-vākya*), and its explanation begins with "from here onwards" (*ita uttaram*) and so forth.

By the maxim of the lion's glance (*siṃhāvalokita-nyāya*), the governing rules continue to apply even to what precedes; therefore, their cessation should be understood from the fact that they are not marked as *svarita*.

Furthermore, for whom is it to be understood that "the single-vowel [root] becomes doubled"? If this genitive were one of apposition with the root itself—as in "of the root which consists of a single vowel"—then doubling would apply only to roots like *pac* and the like, and not to roots like *jāgṛ*, for in those cases there is no single vowel. Thinking thus, he shows that this is not a genitive of apposition—meaning "of the root which is a single vowel"—but rather a genitive based on a part-whole relationship, meaning "of that part of the root which is a single vowel"; hence he says: "of a part of the root."

In the case of *jajāgāra*, the element *jāg* is reduplicated; in *papāca*, it is the word *pac*. In the former case, the rule *pūrvaḥ* [Pāṇini 7.2.115] applies for the *vṛddhi* strengthening, and in the latter, *aco ñṇiti* [7.2.116]. Regarding *iyāya*:

after the *vṛddhi* has been applied to the root *iṇ* (meaning "to go," Dhātupāṭha 1045) by [7.2.115], the vowel *i* is reduplicated due to its status as a *sthānivadbhāva* according to [1.1.59]; then the *āy* substitution occurs, and finally *iyaṅ* is applied to the reduplicated stem by [6.4.78]: *abhyāsasyāsavarṇe*.
"Āra":
[the root] *ṛ* means "to go" (Dhātupāṭha).

Regarding the reduplication of this [element] *ṛ*: there is the substitution of *at* by *urat* [Pāṇini 7.4.66], followed by the substitution of *rapara*, the lengthening by *dīrghaḥ* [Pāṇini 7.4.70], and the substitution of the long vowel for homogeneous sounds (*sarvarṇadīrghatva*).

Is this [term] *ekāc* a *tatpuruṣa* compound—meaning "that which is one and it is a vowel (*ac*)"—or is it a *bahuvrīhi*—meaning "that which has one vowel" (*eko 'c yasya*)? In that regard, if this were a *tatpuruṣa*, reduplication would apply only to roots beginning with *iṇ* (such as *iyāya* and *āre*), but it would not apply to roots like *pac* (as in *papāca*), because those consist of a combination of vowels and consonants (*ajjhal-samudāya*). Having considered this, he says: "This is a *bahuvrīhi* designation. A *bahuvrīhi-nirdeśa* is the designation—that is, the statement—or the mention or utterance of the meaning intended by means of a *bahuvrīhi*.

But how is it determined that this is a reference to a *bahuvrīhi* compound? It is from such indicative marks (*liṅga*) as [Pāṇini 7.4.60–61]: "The first consonant is the remainder" (*halādiḥ śeṣaḥ*).

But is there not also an indicative mark for a *tatpuruṣa*—namely, the prescription of lengthening for the reduplicated syllable of the root *iṇ* [in Pāṇini 7.4.69]? This is not so; for even in a *bahuvrīhi*, since the designation of the whole as if it were its parts (*vyapadeśivadbhāva*) applies, the prescription of lengthening for the reduplicated syllable of *iṇ* is indeed possible when it undergoes reduplication. However, in this *tatpuruṣa*, operations such as the "remainder of the initial consonant" (*halādiśeṣa*) are not possible, because reduplication of a collection of vowels and consonants (such as *pac-*) is impossible.
Therefore, the grammatical gender (liṅga) belongs only to the *bahuvrīhi* compound and not to the *tatpuruṣa*; thus, this is indeed a reference to the *bahuvrīhi*.

If this is so, since the *bahuvrīhi* alone has the external referent (*anyapadārtha*) as its predominant meaning, and since the *bahuvrīhi* denotes that pure external referent which is itself devoid of any qualifying attribute (*upalakṣaṇa*), then reduplication would apply only to that partless external referent which is qualified by a member [of the compound], and not even to that which serves as the qualifying attribute.
For a qualifying attribute does not participate in the grammatical operation.

For instance, when it is said, "Let the owner of brindled cows be brought," it is he who possesses the brindled cows who is brought, and not even the cows that serve as the defining attribute (*upalakṣaṇa*).
Therefore, showing that this is a *bahuvrīhi* compound where the quality is included in the cognition (*tadguṇasaṃvijñāna*), he says "In that case" and so forth:
"The aggregate is the meaning of the compound."

The meaning is that, together with that part which serves as a defining characteristic (*upalakṣaṇa*), the whole (*samudāya*) itself constitutes the referent of the other word (*anyapadārtha*). Regarding the phrase "and included within that," the meaning is "contained within that."
The word *ca* is used for emphasis;
the meaning is "precisely within. The particle *iti* indicates the reason.

Why? Because a constituent part (*avayava*) is included within the whole (*samudāya*), which is the meaning of the compound; therefore, reduplication (*dvirvacana*) occurs only for that which possesses a vowel (*sāckasya*). Even in common worldly usage, it is observed that when a characteristic mark is included within a compound, it serves a functional purpose; for example, when one says, "Bring the white-clad person," he is brought along with the white garment itself. In the case of *pac*, by the very same [vowel] through which the whole is a single-vowel (*ekāc*), its constituent parts—the word *ac* and the word *pa*—are also [single-vowels]; consequently, reduplication would also apply to each of those constituent parts individually.

Just as an arm becomes "possessing a hand" by that very limb which is the hand, so too Devadatta becomes "possessing a hand" by that same [limb]; likewise, within the verbal root *pac*, by whatever form the entire word *pac* is a single vowel (*ekāc*), by that very same [form] its constituent parts—the vowel *a* and the consonant *c*—are also [single vowels]. Consequently, reduplication (dvirvacana) would indeed apply to each of the constituent parts as well, because reduplication applies to a single-vowel base (*ekāc*) through a general designation.

And thus, if the doubling were performed separately for the monosyllabic wholes and their constituent parts, the form would become *anṣyaṭaṃ*; therefore, in order to avoid this undesirable result, he says "tatra" and so forth.
Among those monosyllabic wholes, the monosyllabic parts are not doubled separately;
rather, only the monosyllabic whole is doubled.
*Avayavaikāj* is a *karmadhāraya* compound;
*samudāyaikāc* is also a *karmadhāraya* compound.
But from where is this distinction obtained when there is a general designation? To this he says: "For instance" (*tathā hi*), and so forth.

Although both the whole (*samudāyin*) and the part (*avayava*) consist of a single vowel (*ekāc*), nevertheless, when reduplication (*dvirvacana*) is performed, it is proper that reduplication apply only to that [element] by whose reduplication the benefit of all [the vowels] is secured.
In this way, there is no abandonment of the grammatical rule (*śāstra*); for the operation prescribed by the rule is accomplished for all [the vowels] indeed.
This alone is the favor (*anugraha*): the accomplishment of the task prescribed by the treatise (*śāstra*).
When the doubling (*dvirvacana*) is performed upon the entire aggregate (*samudāya*), the favor accrues to all its parts.

Just as a tree moving moves along with its constituent parts, so too, when the aggregate is doubled by a single application of the rule, it is doubled together with its parts; for the aggregate cannot be doubled without its parts, since it is of the nature of those very parts.
However, the doubling of the constituent parts cannot be accomplished for all of them by a single application.

Nor does the doubling of one part result in the benefit of all. Why? Because the designation of "one vowel" (*ekāj*) for all of them is based on the reason that there is "only one vowel" (*eko 'j*); in that case, when a particular constituent part is designated as "one vowel" by means of a certain [vowel], then because that [part] is already occupied by that very [designation], it is impossible to designate another [part] as "one vowel."

Furthermore, when the reduplication of a single *ekāc* (monosyllabic) element is intended, then at that time, by that [rule], the reduplication would apply only to some one part of it, and not to the other, because the other lacks a vowel (*anackatvāt*). Here, one might argue: "Since all [parts] are designated as belonging to the 'single *ekāc*' [by the rule 6.1.1], the reduplication must be performed for all of them; however, that is not possible simultaneously, therefore it is performed for one [part] first."

[One might argue: "Once one [portion] has been doubled, another will be doubled by means of a subsequent application"? But this is not so; for since the syllable has already been doubled together with that very constituent part (*avayava*) upon which the doubling was previously performed, it is not proper to perform the doubling of it again with a different constituent part.
Indeed, doubling is performed on what has not yet been doubled, not on what has already been doubled; otherwise, there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*).
Furthermore, because of the rule *anabhyāsasya* [Pāṇini 6.1.8], it is simply improper to perform the doubling of another part when one part has already been doubled.
Therefore, it is not possible for all [the parts] to be accommodated by a reduplication of the constituent members.
In that case, there would be a loss of the grammatical rule (*śāstrahāni*) for that whose reduplication is not possible.
Thus, a reduplication of the members individually is incorrect.

Now, since a simultaneous doubling (*dvirvacana*) of these constituent parts is not possible, will it be performed alternately (*paryāyeṇa*) in another usage in order to avoid the previously mentioned fault? Even so, when there is a doubling of the element *pac-a* [in the derivation of *papāca*], then forms such as *papāca* would not be established. Furthermore, regarding the root *ṇijir* in the sense of "cleansing and nourishing" (Dhātupāṭha 1093), from this [root] we derive the present tense marker *laṭ*, then *jhi*, then *śap*; because it belongs to the *juhotyādi* class, there is *ślau* [substitution]; and by the rule *ślau* (Pāṇini 6.1.10), there is doubling.
In that case, if the reduplication is applied to the word *ni* alone, then by the rule "of the three *ṇij*s" [Pāṇini 7.4.75], a *guṇa* substitution occurs.

Now, in this context, the substitution of *ad* [by Pāṇini 7.1.4] is desired—specifically for the sake of obtaining the form *tenijatīti*—yet that substitution does not apply, because it is separated by the letter *j*.
For the designation *abhyasta* (repeated) does not belong to the letter *j*, but rather to the word *ni*; since *ni* is what is reduplicated, whereas the letter *j* is not.

Regarding the form *anenijuḥ*: here, the substitution *jus* for *jhi*, which is the substitute for *laṅ*, does not apply by virtue of [Pāṇini 3.4.109], *sijabhyastavidibhyaśca*, for the very same reason mentioned previously. Furthermore, in the case of *nenijat*, the prohibition of *num* by [Pāṇini 7.1.78] would not occur for that same reason.

Nor can it be argued that, by the force of the rule itself, the operation will take place even when there is an intervention; for when there is reduplication of the entire stem (*samudāya*), the rule still finds its scope of application.
But when there is reduplication of the letter *j* together with the vowel *i*, then forms such as *nenijati* would not even exist.
Therefore, reduplication of individual components is incorrect;
hence, the entire complex must be reduplicated.

Now, regarding the form *papāca*, how can there be reduplication (*dvirvacana*), given that it is stated [in Pāṇini 6.1.1]: "Of the first monosyllabic root, two [occurrences] [are made]" (*ekāco dve prathamasya*)? For here, the designation "first" (*prathama*) does not apply to a monosyllabic root. The word "first" is relative to something that is not first, because it is a relative term (*sambandhiśabda*); when there are several [roots], that from which no preceding one exists is "the first. However, that which is unique (being only one) does not receive the designation "first," and in this case, the monosyllabic root is indeed unique.

In that case, reduplication would not occur here [in *iyāya* and *āra*], but would only occur in forms such as *jajāgāra*; for how could there be reduplication in *iyāya* and *āra*, given that reduplication is prescribed for what consists of a single syllable (*ekāc*), whereas here there is no status of being a single syllable, because there is no basis for the designation "single syllable" for a non-vowel (*anac*) other than a vowel (*aj*)? To this, he says: "In the case of *papāca*, etc.
The designation is based on a connection with a vowel delimited by the number one; that which possesses this is "possessed of the designation" (*vyapadeśī*).
In verbal roots such as *jāgarti*, the element *jāg* and so forth [is such].
"By the rule *tena tulyaṃ vartate* [Pāṇini 5.1.114], it is treated as if it were the designated entity (*vyapadeśivat*); its state is *vyapadeśivadbhāva*.
By the word *api* (also) in the phrase *ekāctvam api*, it is implied that *advitīyatvam* (the state of being non-duplicated) is also included.

Therefore, just as in the case of *jajāgāra*, where there is a reduplication of the first single vowel *jāg-* because it is actually the first [vowel], so too in *papāca*, even though it is not actually the first [vowel] in the ultimate sense, there is a reduplication of the first single vowel *pac-* by virtue of *vyapadeśivadbhāva*."

In the case of *iyāya* and *āre*, even though there is no actual status as a single syllable (*ekāc*) or a second syllable, reduplication occurs by virtue of the principle of "designation-like behavior" (*vyapadeśivadbhāva*); just as in *aṭiṭiṣati*, where reduplication applies to the second syllable, the word *ṭi*, which is in fact a single syllable. Nor should it be said: "Because reduplication occurs by virtue of designation-like behavior even for that which is not actually first, such as *pac*."

In this regard, the rule *liṭabhyāsasyobhayeṣām* [Pāṇini 6.1.17] is an indicator (*jñāpaka*): even though there is no actual status of being a single vowel (*ekāctva*) or a second member (*dvitīyatva*), reduplication occurs for roots such as *ciṇ* and others by virtue of the designation *vyapadeśivadbhāva*.

Furthermore, the rule *atra abhyāsasya dīrghavidhānārtham* [Pāṇini 7.4.69] is an indicator. Here, according to the principle that "numbers from one up to ten denote the thing numbered (*saṃkhyeya*) and not merely the act of numbering," the word *dvi* here refers to the thing numbered.

And is that numberable [entity] the form of the word (*śabdarūpa*) or the act of utterance (*uccāraṇa*)? In this regard, if the form of the word were the numberable entity, then by the expression "two" (*dve*), two instances of the word-form *dvi* would be indicated as being brought about through cultivation (*bhāvyamānatayā*).

Consequently, there would be a relationship characterized by substitution (*sthāna*) between the element *ekāc* and the [doubling], and thus the position "doubling occurs in place [of the original]" (*sthāne dvirvacanam*) would be established. In that case, the genitive case in *ekācaḥ* would be a genitive of locus (*sthāna-ṣaṣṭhī*).
Furthermore, if the pronunciation were countable, then there would be no relationship between the original element (*sthānin*) and its substitute (*ādeśa*).
Pronunciation is a property inherent to the word.

If that [pronunciation] were the substitute, then the original element would possess the property of cessation; consequently, upon the cessation of the original element *śap*, the pronunciation itself would also not occur, because it is a property of that [original element].

Therefore, since reduplication (*dvirvacana*) is impossible if it were to occur in place of the thing to be enumerated (*saṃkhyeya*), the position that "reduplication is the double employment [of the same element]" (*dviṣprayogo dvirvacanam*) must be accepted.

In that case, in the rule *aikācaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.1.1), the genitive case is used for the object according to *kartṛkarmaṇoḥ kṛti* (Pāṇini 2.3.65); for that monosyllabic base is the object because it is most desired to be pervaded by the action of utterance.

If, in this context, the position that "reduplication occurs in place [of the original]" (*sthāne dvirvacanam*) were adopted, then in the form *jighāṃsati*, the change of *h* to *gh* (*kutva*) would not occur.

For when the entire complex [stem] ending in *san* is replaced by another entire complex ending in *san*, one might rely on that [substitute] as having undergone the grammatical operation; in that case, in forms such as *jīghāṃsati*, the substitution of *k* for *h* in the root *han* would not occur.
However, this is not the case when the entire complex ending in *san* is replaced by another entire complex ending in *san*.

Is this because of the doubt as to whether "this is the suffix" (*pratyaya*) or "this is the base" (*prakṛti*)? [For if] the *han* of the base-suffix were lost, then by the rule *pūrvapadāt saṃjñāyām agaḥ* (Pāṇini 8.4.3) and *hanterhaḥ* (Pāṇini 7.3.54), the substitution of *ha* for the *h* of *han* would not occur. Having observed this fault in the position that "doubling occurs in place of the original," he states "and there is a double application," etc., relying on the position that "doubling is the double application" (*dviḥprayoga*).
The word *ca* is used for emphasis;
the meaning is "only a double application."
The meaning is that there is no double application in the same position.

Now, one might ask: "How is it that this fault does not occur when there is doubling through double application? To this he says: "For the number refers to the repetition," and so forth. Repetition (*āvṛtti*) is utterance again and again.
Furthermore, that [suffix] is prescribed only for a verbal root (dhātu) that is established by a specific number;
thus, "by that" and so forth.

Since reduplication (*āvṛtti*) is prescribed for a verbal root (*dhātu*) that is already established, it is that very same word which, being established, is uttered twice; another word is not substituted in its place. Therefore, how could there be any occasion for the previously mentioned fault? If, then, this position—that reduplication is the dual employment (*dviṣprayoga*) [of the same word]—is rejected, then in the case of [Pāṇini 7.2.67], having cited *ādivān*, *āśivān*, *pecivān*, and *śekivān*, he will say:

"It is not correct [to say] that 'only after the single-substitute replacement (ekādeśa) of the root and the reduplication has occurred, and only after the elision of the reduplication (abhyāsalopa) has been performed, do these monosyllabic roots (ekācaḥ) fail to undergo reduplication'; for even when the single-substitute replacement of the root and the reduplication has not yet occurred, and even when the *aitva* and the elision of the reduplication have not yet been performed, these [roots] remain monosyllabic once they have undergone reduplication.

For if reduplication were by way of substitution (*sthāne dvirvacana*), then a different word altogether would be enjoined as beginning with multiple syllables, and thus those [roots] that have undergone reduplication would indeed possess multiple syllables; but this is not the case under the view of double utterance (*dviḥprayogapakṣa*).
For in that view, that very same word is uttered twice."

And this [root] does not lose its status as having a single vowel (*ekāctva*) even when pronounced a hundred times, much less when pronounced twice. As for the argument that he will later introduce examples such as *bibhidvān* to demonstrate what is excluded by the restrictive rule (*niyama*), that too is incorrect; for roots beginning with *bhid*, precisely for the reason stated above, retain their status as having a single vowel even after reduplication. Furthermore, as for his claim that the mention of the initial vowel (*ādigrahaṇa*) is for the sake of those with multiple vowels (*anekāc*), that too is incorrect; for by that very same reason, it is impossible for forms ending in long *ā* to have multiple vowels even after reduplication.
Therefore, the position that reduplication occurs in its proper place must also be accepted. Alternatively, it is explained in another way:
here, the two positions previously mentioned are both possible.

In this context, does one adopt the position that "doubling" (*dvirvacana*) means a double application (*dviṣprayoga*), or rather the position that doubling occurs in place (*sthāne*)? At this point of inquiry, he says: "And doubling is a double application. The word "and" (*ca*) indicates the sense that doubling also occurs in place. But surely, according to the rule *[[1.1.49]]*, it would be proper for there to be only the position of doubling in place; how then is the position of double application also tenable? To this he replies: "For the number refers to repetition," and so forth.

It has been stated previously that if another word is prescribed in place of that [original], then the position arises that "doubling occurs in place of the original" (*sthānin*) in relation to the substitute (*ādeśa*);
however, when the number of repetitions is prescribed, the other position prevails. This too has already been demonstrated.

Therefore, when the position of double application (*dviṣprayoga*) is intended to be accepted, the number of repetitions is prescribed as "two"; thus, that very same word is uttered twice, and no other word is substituted in its place.
Consequently, the position of reduplication through double application (*dviṣprayogadvirvacana*) must also be accepted.

Now, if this position—that there is doubling in place [of the original]—is also adopted, has it not been stated that in the case of *jighāṃsati*, the substitution of *gh* for the *h* of the root *han* would not apply? This is not a fault; for it is stated: "The substitution of *gh* for *han* occurs even when it is not part of a reduplicated syllable" (*avyāsācca* 7.3.55). And once another word has been substituted in place of that [original *han*], the root *han* no longer exists. Therefore, by the force of the explicit statement, the word *han* will be understood as referring to a form resembling *han* that constitutes a portion of the substitute.
However, the faults that might be suspected regarding these two positions have already been raised and refuted in the Bhāṣya itself;

they are not written here for fear of excessive prolixity. [Regarding the statement: "This is an exception (*apavāda*) to the first doubling"—but surely, by the rule *eka-aco dve prathamasya* (P. 6.1.1), the doubling of the first monosyllable is prescribed, whereas by the rule *ajāderdvitīyasya* (P. 6.1.2), the doubling of the second is prescribed. Therefore, how can this, which is stated for one case, be a sublater (*bādhaka*) of the other? Indeed, something becomes a sublater only when there is a possibility [of both rules applying]; yet there is a possibility that both might occur.

It might be argued: "This genitive case in *dhātoḥ* cannot logically connect with both the second [monosyllabic] and the first [monosyllabic], and therefore there is no possibility of both occurring. But this is not so; for the rule prescribing the doubling of the first is one sentence, while the rule prescribing the doubling of the second is another.

Since there is a division of sentences (*vākya-bheda*) here, why should the connection not be possible? Therefore, even when the doubling of the second has been performed, the doubling of the first is indeed still possible—so how can it be said that there is a sublation (*bādhana*)? This is not a fault.

In the case of *iha dvīpam* and *antarīpam*, by [Pāṇini 6.3.97] there is the substitution of *i* (ittva). By [Pāṇini 1.1.52], the substitution of *al* is obtained for that which ends in *ai*. However, by [Pāṇini 1.1.54], this is prescribed for the initial [element]. Just as, even when possible, a modification of a non-final element (*anantyavikāra*) sets aside a modification of the final element (*antyavikāra*), so too will the second doubling set aside the first doubling. If, then, the doubling of the first single vowel (*ekāc*) is set aside by this [rule], then the doubling of a consonant belonging to the first doubling would also be set aside.
Just as there is the application [of a rule] to that which is exactly as it is, so too does the cessation of doubling apply to that which is exactly as it is.

And to what kind of first doubling would there be such an application? To that which possesses a consonant (*savyañjana*). In that case, just as the doubling of a single vowel (*ekāc*) does not occur, would it likewise not occur for a consonant designated as "single-vowel" (*ekājvyapadeśin*)? This is not a fault; because this [sūtra] teaches the prohibition [at Pāṇini 6.1.3], it makes known that the cessation of doubling does not apply to a consonant.
For if there were difference [of the stems], the prohibition of reduplication would be purposeless, as there would be no possibility [of its occurrence]—
as in *aṭiṭiṣati* and *aśiśiṣati*. When the suffix *san* with the augment *iṭ* has been applied to the roots *aṭ* and *aś*, the forms *ṭiṣ* and *śiṣ* are reduplicated.

In the form *aririṣati*, after the suffix *san* has been applied to the root *ṛ*, and after the operations of *niṅ* (the substitution of *i*), *guṇa*, and the substitution of *ra* for *ṛ* have been performed, the syllable *riṣ* is reduplicated.
[Objection: "The status of being like the original (*sthānivadbhāva*) would apply. [Response:
By the rule [6.1.9], reduplication is prescribed for the entire form ending in *san*, and the augment *iṭ* is included therein.
Therefore, the intention is that this [the *iṣ*] is the cause for the doubling.

And if the status of being "as if in the original" (*sthānivadbhāva*) were to apply, then when doubling is performed on the *iṣ* devoid of the *repha*, and after the long vowel by position (*savarṇadīrghatva*) has occurred, the undesirable form *arīṣati* would result.
[The word] "the subject of the operation" (*kāryī*)...
