The repetition itself constitutes the "effect" (*kārya*); that which possesses this is the "possessor of the effect" (*kāryin*). It might be argued: "Even though he is the possessor of the effect, he is nevertheless the effect.
Or it might be argued: "Even though he is the possessor of the effect, he is nonetheless merely the cause with respect to the effect. To this, [the author] says: "And not," and so forth.
But how is this known—that the effect is resorted to as the cause? To this he says: "For thus" (*tathā hi*), and so forth.
The word *tathā* means "because" (*yasmāt*);
the particle *iti* indicates a manner.

Why? Because the prohibition being enjoined by the rule *kṅiti ca* (Pāṇini 1.1.5)—which states that there is no *guṇa* or *vṛddhi* when a *kṅit* affix follows—does not apply in cases such as *śayitā*. From this, it is understood that the recipient of the grammatical operation (*kāryin*) is not treated as a cause (*nimitta*). For if it were so treated, then since the root *śīṅ* has a *ṅit* marker, the prohibition of *guṇa* in *śayitā* (by the rule *kṅiti ca*) would apply, and likewise the prohibition of *vṛddhi* in *śāyaka* would apply.
[Objection: But surely, that without which something does not occur is its cause (*nimitta*), just as a cloud is the cause of rain.

Just as *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* do not occur without a condition (*pratyaya*), so too they do not occur without an effect (*kārya*). Why, then, is there no prohibition of *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* for the root *śīṅ* here? To this he says: "For [the rule] does not apply to that which possesses the effect," and so forth. The word "is resorted to" (*āśrīyate*) is to be supplied here. True, the effect is indeed caused by *śīṅ*, but its *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* are to be understood with respect to [the operation of] the suffix.
The particle *iti* indicates the nature of this immediate counter-argument.

How, then, is it known that "an effect is not taken as a cause"? For if that were the case, the prohibition of *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* [in the rule] *dīdhīvevīṭām* (P. 1.1.6) would be redundant; since the prohibition of those two *guṇas* would already be established by the rule *na dhātulopa ārdhadhātuke* (P. 1.1.4), which prohibits operations on an element whose cause is its own elision.
Regarding this, some maintain that the ablative case in *ajādeḥ* (P. 1.2.9) is derived from a *karmadhāraya* compound.

"Accāsāvādiśca ityajādiḥ; from that ajādi," thus they explain. By doing so, they intend this ablative case (*pañcamī*) to be derived from a *karmadhāraya* compound. If, then, this ablative case is indeed from a *karmadhāraya*, for them the mention of the word "second" (*dvitīya*) would be purposeless; because there is no possibility at all of a third [case] occurring.

For those for whom this is considered the sixth [alternative] regarding the *bahuvrīhi*, if the mention of "the second" (*dvitīya*) were not made, there would be no possibility at all of reduplication even for a third [element].

For those for whom this is considered the sixth [alternative] regarding the *bahuvrīhi*, if the mention of "the second" were not made, reduplication would apply even to a third [element]; therefore, the mention of "the second" is appropriate for the purpose of excluding that.

For those who maintain that this fifth case (*pañcamī*) follows from a *karmadhāraya* compound, the mention of the second [term] would be redundant; for by the rule *[[1.1.67]]*, it would apply only to the immediately preceding second term and not to the third, because the latter is separated. To address this, he says: "for them," and so forth. "Because of its inclusion therein" (*tadantarbhāvāt*):
because the parts are contained within the whole, there is "inclusion therein.
"Being constituent parts" (*avayavabhūtāḥ*).
Since the word *ādi* denotes a specific location or constituent part, this meaning should be understood as "becoming a constituent part of a specific location.
Regarding the form *andiviṣati*:
from the root *undī* in the sense of "moistening" (*dhātupāṭha* 1457), after the addition of the desiderative suffix *san* and the augment *iṭ*, there is reduplication of the syllable *diṣ*.

Regarding *aḍḍiḍiṣati*: in the case of the root *aḍḍa* (meaning "to attack," Dhātupāṭha 348), the *saṃyoga* (consonant cluster) begins with *da*. By the rule of *ṣṭutva*, the *da* becomes *ḍa*; however, this *ṣṭutva* is considered *asiddha* (non-existent) for the purpose of reduplication. Therefore, when the augment *iṭ* has been added in the *san* suffix, the word *viṣ* (derived from the modified form) is reduplicated, and only then does *ṣṭutva* apply.
Regarding *arciciṣati*: from the root *arca* (meaning "to worship," Dhātupāṭha 204), the word *ciṣ* undergoes reduplication.
Regarding *īcikṣiṣate*:

from the root *īkṣ* in the sense of "seeing" (*dhātupāṭha* 610), when the suffix *san* and the augment *iṭ* have been applied, there is reduplication of the syllable *kṣiṣ*. Then, by [Pāṇini 7.4.60] and [7.4.62], the substitution of *c* occurs.
Regarding *prāṇiṇiṣati*: [the same process applies].
The root *āsa* meaning "to breathe" (Dhātupāṭha 1069) and *ana* preceded by *pra* (Dhātupāṭha 1070).
Regarding the form *didrāsati*: the root *drā* means "wicked or contemptible motion" (Dhātupāṭha 1054).

"‘Some [hold that] after *aja* etc. and so forth. According to their view, the meaning of the sūtra is that those *n* sounds and others which follow *aja* etc. and constitute the first member of a conjunct consonant (*saṃyoga*) are not doubled.
What, then, is the purpose of following that [previous rule]? To this he says: "Of that," and so forth.

Since the letter *d* is indeed reduplicated, when the word ending in the fifth case (*pañcamyantā*) from the *karmadhāraya* compound is carried over [into the rule], there ought to be a prohibition of reduplication only for the subsequent letters beginning with *n*, according to [Pāṇini 1.1.58] *naḥ kye* [1.1.67]; this is because the mention of the term "indicated" (*nirdiṣṭa*) has the purpose of signifying immediate succession.
Although the letter *d* there is the initial member of the conjunction (*saṃyoga*) consisting of the letters *r* and *d*, it is nevertheless separated by the letter *n*.
Therefore, the letter *d* is also indeed reduplicated.

Regarding *indidrīyiṣati*: from the word *indra*, after [the addition of] *kyac* according to [Pāṇini 7.4.33], there is the substitution of *i* for the final vowel; then, from the form ending in *kyac*, the suffix *san* is added, followed by *iṭ*, and then the elision of the vowel *a* according to [Pāṇini 6.4.48]. Regarding *ubjijiṣati*.
The root *ubj* is listed as *ārjave* (Dhātupāṭha 1303).
When it is taught with the vowel *ba* as its penultimate letter (*bakāropadha*), then this prohibition must be stated;
however, when it is taught with the vowel *da* as its penultimate letter (*dakāropadeśa*), it need not be stated, because [the desired result] is already established by the rule *na ndrāḥ*.

"But then, the substitution of *ba* for the letter *da* must be prescribed so that forms such as *ubjita* and *ubjijiṣati* may occur. That too must be prescribed as an exception to the application of *baṭ*, *taṭ*, and *vam*; otherwise, forms such as *abhyudgaḥ* and *samudgaḥ* would not be established.

The reading with the letter *da* as the penultimate is indeed correct. Is it necessary to state the substitution of *ba*? That too need not be stated; for in that case, the substitution of *ba* is obtained precisely through the irregular derivation (*nipātana*) [Pāṇini 7.3.61].

Nor would this lead to the undesirable application of *ba* in forms such as *abhyudgaḥ* and *samudgaḥ*, because the irregular derivation applies specifically to cases where *ku*-tva (the substitution of *ka*) does not occur; it is understood to apply only where *ku*-tva is absent, and not in the domain of *ku*-tva.

Regarding the phrase "yakāraparasya" and so forth: the meaning is that this should be explained as having the sense that there should be no prohibition for that [suffix] after which a *yakāra* follows.

In this regard, some explain it as follows: the *repha* (the letter *r*) is *bahiranga* (external); since the *guṇa* substitution prescribed for the *aṅga* (stem) by the rules "guṇo 'rtisaṃyogādyoḥ" [Pāṇini 7.4.29] and "yaṅi ca" [Pāṇini 7.4.30] occurs when *yaṅ* is present, it is *bahiranga*, and the *repha* dependent upon it is likewise *bahiranga*. Consequently, it is not established as a basis for the prohibition, which applies to what is *antaraṅga* (internal).
Therefore, for that [root], the prohibition of reduplication does not occur.

If this is so, then in the case of *indidiṣati*, would the prohibition of the *num* augment also not apply? This is not a fault; for he will state this: "The instruction regarding the *upadeśa* form applies even when there is the scope of the *num* augment.
The Naiyāyikas, however, explain it otherwise as follows: [sūtra 6.1.3].

What was said by them? [It was: "Due to a conjunct (*saṃyoga*), the preceding *n* and so forth are not doubled, provided that the conjunct ends in *y*. Therefore, in the case of *arāyyate*, because the conjunct ends in *y*, the prohibition does not apply. Regarding "*arāyyate*": after applying the *guṇa* substitution by [Pāṇini 7.4.30] *yaṅi ca* and the replacement of *ra* by *ra*, there is reduplication of the word *rya*; then, by [Pāṇini 7.4.60] *halādiśeṣaḥ* and [7.4.83], the long vowel is applied.

But surely, because *ṛt* begins with a consonant, the suffix *yaṅ* should not apply to it; for that [suffix] is prescribed only for roots beginning with a consonant by the rule "of a one-syllable root" (*dhātor ekācaḥ*) [Pāṇini 3.1.22]? To this he says: "*arteḥ*" and so forth.
Regarding the word "*vyañjanasya*": when the single-syllable root *īr* is treated as having a consonant [as its initial], reduplication must be performed.

And that consonant is the letter *y*. When the suffix *iṭ* is applied, reduplication must be performed only for that which possesses a consonant, according to the rule "of a monosyllable" (*ekācaḥ*) [Pāṇini 6.1.1]. This refers to the suffix *san*.

When *iṭ* has been added, there is a single vowel (*ekāj*) in the third syllable. When reduplication (*dvirvacana*) is performed for that, the substitution of *i* occurs by [Pāṇini 7.4.79] *sanyataḥ*.
Then, depending on each preceding *iṇ*, the substitution of *ṣ* occurs for all the *s*s.
"Desires to scratch" (*kaṇḍūyiyiṣati*), "desires to find fault" (*asūyiyiṣati*).
The roots *kaṇḍūñ* and *asūñ* are listed among the *kaṇḍv-ādi* group; from that [group], by the rule [Pāṇini 3.1.27]: "Optionally for nominal stems used as verbal roots" (*vā nāmadhātūnām*).
The *sub-dhātu* is designated as the *nāmadhātu*.
For example, in the form *āyi-yi-ṣati*: from the word *ā*, with the suffix *kyac* added, and then the desiderative suffix *san* (*iṭ*) applied, there is reduplication of the syllable *yiṣ*.
Regarding "āśiśayiṣati":
there is reduplication of the syllable *āī*, shortening of the vowel, and the application of *halādiśeṣaḥ* [Pāṇini 7.4.60].
Regarding "at will" (*yatheṣṭam*).
"Whichever among the first [syllable] and the others is desired, for that the [designation] must be applied. This word *abhyāsa* (repetition) is well-known in common usage as signifying "reiteration.

Since that reiteration does not apply to the first [syllable], when the designation of *abhyāsa* is to be applied in specific rules, it is prescribed so that the designation may apply to the preceding [syllable], which would otherwise—given the rule for the subsequent [syllable]—be excluded.
The word *pūrva* (preceding) denotes a constituent part, as in the expressions "the front part of the body" or "the front part of the animal."

Parts belong to a whole, and although that whole is not explicitly mentioned here, nevertheless, because of the recurrence of the word "two" (dve) from [Pāṇini 6.1.1], it is understood that the meaning expressed by that very term is the "prior" one; thus he says: "The word 'two' which recurs in the nominative case," and so forth. But surely, while "two" recurs in the nominative case, the meaning here requires the genitive case; for otherwise, a connection with the word "prior" (pūrva) could not be demonstrated. To this he replies: "From its meaning," and so forth. That is to say, there is a change of case endings based on the sense.

Therefore, here the genitive ending in the sixth case signifies the sense of "conquering" (overcoming). Now, if instead the genitive here were characterized as expressing the relation between a part and a whole (*avayavāvayavi-lakṣaṇā*), as in the example "the branch of the tree," then—even if [the word] *dve* ("two") is supplied from the previous context so that the designation of *abhyāsa* ("reduplication") is prescribed for that which is prior to the two—this would result in the designation of *abhyāsa* also applying to that which is prior to those two which are prescribed in the section beginning with [Pāṇini 6.1.1]. Consequently, he says: "In that case," etc., and "the prior part."

The word *pūrva* also has the sense of "established order" (*vyavasthā*); therefore, the mention of the term *avayava* (member/part) is for the purpose of excluding that sense. In the case of *papāca*, once the designation *abhyāsa* (reduplication) is established, there is shortening of the reduplicated syllable by [Pāṇini 7.4.59] *hrasvaḥ*; then *halādiśeṣaḥ* [7.4.60]; and then, by the rule "the original *car* sounds become *car* sounds," there is the substitution of *c* for *p*. Regarding *pipakṣati*:
as before in *juhoti*, there is the substitution of *c* for the letter *h* [by 7.4.62], and for that *c*, there is the substitution of *k* [by 8.4.54] *cakāraḥ*.

Regarding the form *apipacat*: from the causative of the root *pac*, there is the substitution of *caṅ* for *liṭ*; the elision of the causative suffix (*ṇilopa*); the shortening of the penultimate vowel by the rule *ṇau caṅy upadhāyā hrasvaḥ* [Pāṇini 7.4.1]; reduplication; the substitution of *i* for the radical vowel by the rule *sanvallaghuni* [Pāṇini 7.4.93]; and finally, the lengthening of the vowel by the rule *ata upadhāyāḥ* [Pāṇini 7.4.94].

All these are the purposes for the designation of the "reduplicated syllable" (*abhyāsa*). In this context, the mention of both [the preceding and following elements] is made for the purpose of specifying the technical term (*saṃjñin*).

And as for that designation of the technical term *saṃjñin*, since the word "two" (*dve*) from [Pāṇini 6.1.1] is understood by way of *anuvṛtti*, the designation would indeed be established even without the mention of "both" (*ubhe*). Why, then, is the mention of "both" made while "two" is being carried over? To this he says: "While 'two' is being carried over," and so forth.
If the mention of "both" were not made, then the designation of *abhyasta* would apply to each one individually;
for even if it applies to them individually, it is still considered to have been applied.

For instance, when it is said, "one should bring two," by bringing each one individually, those two are brought. Therefore, the mention of "both" (*ubhe*) is for the purpose that the designation (*saṃjñā*) should apply to the collection as a whole, and not to each individual member.
Thus [it says] "when combined."

The meaning is "occurring together. Now, one might object: "Let this [designation] apply only where repetition (*abhyāsa*) is heard, but not where it is not heard; let it not apply in cases such as *īpsanti*, *īpsan*, and *aipsan*. To prevent this, would the inclusion of the term "both" (*ubhe*) be for that purpose? This is not so; for the mention of "repetition" (*abhyāsa*) is understood from the previous rule, and the connection is made thus: "Both receive the designation 'repeated' (*abhyasta*), provided that there is a repetition."
Furthermore, since the term *ubhe* (both) is absent [in the sūtra], it will apply only where the repetition (*abhyāsa*) is explicitly heard, and not elsewhere.
Therefore, the purpose for the inclusion of *ubhe* as shown by the author of the Vṛtti alone is logical.
[The example is] "dadati."
From the root *dā* (to give), there is the suffix *laṭ*, then *jhi*, then *śap*; by [Pāṇini 6.1.10], *ślau*, there is reduplication.

When the designation *abhyasta* (repeated) applies here, there is the elision of the long *ā* by [Pāṇini 6.4.112], *śnābhyastayor ātaḥ*. Then, by [Pāṇini 7.1.4], *ad abhyastāt*, there is the substitution of *ad* for *jhi*.
Thus we have *dadhātu* (or *dadhatu*, according to the Kāśikā).
[The rule] *loṭ*, *eruḥ* [Pāṇini 3.4.86] is stated so that "the accentuation of the entire complex" (*samudāya-udāttatvam*) may occur.
If the mention of *ubhe* were not made, the designation *abhyasta* would apply to each individual [element].
Consequently, even the initial acute accent (*ādyudātta*) prescribed by [the rule] *tasmāt* [Pāṇini 6.1.189] would apply to each individual [element].

Furthermore, because of the rule *athapi* [Pāṇini 6.1.158], there is no possibility of simultaneity; even so, could it occur by way of alternation? Therefore, the mention of both [terms] is for the purpose that the operation prescribed by *amyastānām ādiḥ* [Pāṇini 6.1.189] should apply to the entire aggregate, and not optionally to each individual part. Regarding the expression *jakṣityādayaḥ*: this example of *jakṣ* ending in *śtip* remains valid even when a *bahuvrīhi* compound is formed with the word *ādi*; it also holds when a *dvandva* compound is made—namely, when a *dvandva* is formed between *jakṣ* (which does not end in *an*) and the word *ādi*.

When both of these two [terms] just mentioned are used together in a sentence, then, if a *bahuvrīhi* were to be adopted there, if this *bahuvrīhi* were taken as one where the qualities are understood (*tadguṇasaṃvijñāna*), then there would be no inclusion of the roots *vevīṅ*; if, however, it were taken as one where the qualities are not understood (*atadguṇasaṃvijñāna*), then there would be no inclusion of *jakṣ*. Having seen this defect in resorting to the *bahuvrīhi*, he says—referring back to what has passed with the word "here" (*atrety-śabda*)—"and 'this root is *jakṣ*', etc. and so forth, thereby adopting one of the other two alternatives.
The root *jakṣ* has just been mentioned immediately prior; therefore, it is that very root which is referred back by the pronoun "this" (*ayam*).
The term "those beginning with this" (*ityādayaḥ*) means those for which this is the first; the meaning is "those beginning with *jakṣ*.
Furthermore, these extend from *jāgṛ* up to *vevīṅ*.
"This is the conventional designation for seven roots":
namely, the six beginning with *jāgarti* (as indicated by *jakṣiti*), and the seventh, *jakṣiti*, which is specified separately from them.

But surely, in forms such as *dīdhyate* and *vevyate*, the substitution of *ad* is already established by [Pāṇini 7.1.5], and the remaining operations pertaining to the abhyasta (repeated) class—such as the elision of the vowel *ā* and so forth—are also accomplished? However, those operations are simply not possible for *dīdhī* and *vevī*: first, the elision of the vowel *ā* is impossible because the vowel *ā* does not exist there; furthermore, the substitution of *jus* is impossible due to the absence of the suffix *jhi*; and the prohibition of *num* is also due to the fact that the suffix *śatṛ* is marked with *ṅ* and is ātmanepada. So, for what purpose is the designation *abhyasta* prescribed for these two? To this, he says: "In *dīdhyate*, *vevyate*, etc. and so forth.

By the rule "dīṣyad iti ca śatari" and so forth, he shows another purpose as well. Because these two roots are *ātmanepada*, the suffix *śatṛ* is not possible without a transposition (*vyatyaya*); therefore, the mention of *vyatyaya* is made. This word *ādi* (and so forth) indeed exists in the sense of restriction (*vyavasthā*) and also in the sense of manner (*prakāra*). If it were taken here in the sense of restriction, then only those [roots] read starting from "tuja pija hiṃsāyām" (Dhātupāṭha 1566, 1567) would be included.
Considering that, in this way, the long vowel would not occur for those [words] mentioned in the Sūtras as well as those recited in other groups, he says: "of *tu* and so forth" (*tujādīnām*), etc.
He states: "the word 'ādi' (and so forth) signifies a category (*prakāra*). Since that category is not explicitly specified, it is not known; therefore, he asks: "And what is the category?"
By the words "tujo dīrghatvam" and so forth, he demonstrates the sense of "manner" (*prakāra*).
The phrase "those who are such" means those who have attained the manner just described.
"The long [vowel] becomes correct.
By this, he shows that it is only the correctness of the already existing long vowel that is established by this rule,
and not that a previously non-existent long vowel is produced.
Regarding the word *tūtujānaḥ*: it is the perfect (liṭ) tense. And this is obtained by including the word "etc. (*ādi*), which expresses a variety of forms, through its suffix *-kan*.
Regarding "māmahānaḥ": the root *maha* is used in the sense of "worship" (*pūjā*) [Dhātupāṭha 7.30]; the remainder is as before. Regarding "dadhāna"—[this example is not found in the Kāśikā].
The root *ḍudhāñ* is used in the senses of "holding" and "nourishing" (Dhātupāṭha 1092).
Regarding the form *mīmāya*:
the root *ḍumiñ* is used in the sense of "throwing" (Dhātupāṭha 1250); this is the perfect tense (*liṭ*) with the suffix *ṇal*.
Regarding "dadhāra": the root *dhṛ* means "to hold" (Dhātupāṭha 900). Regarding "tūnāva":
*tu* is a verbal root found in the Vedic tradition (*sautro dhātuḥ*), as it is listed in the sūtra beginning with "turustuśamyama" (Pāṇini 7.3.95).
By the statement "and this [lengthening] of theirs," etc., that which is established as correct by this very rule is seen only in the Veda (*chandas*), not in the spoken language (*bhāṣā*).
Furthermore, even within the domain of the Veda, it occurs in the context of suffixes such as *kānac* and others, not in the context of suffixes in general.
Thus, "it does not occur elsewhere than that."
The meaning is that it does not occur other than in the aforementioned context.
The suffix *kānac* is seen after the root *tuj* in Vedic (*chandas*), but elsewhere—in secular language (*bhāṣā*) and even in Vedic when other suffixes such as *kānaj* follow—it does not occur.
And because this is so, its operation does not extend elsewhere.
By this [rule], the correctness of the long vowel *sata* alone is prescribed.
There is no other long vowel elsewhere for which its correctness could be prescribed by this [rule].
And this is understood from the word *ādi*, which expresses a class.
The form *tutoja* is a usage in the vernacular (*bhāṣā*).

If, then, this rule merely prescribes the correctness of a long vowel that already exists in Vedic (*chandas*), is this [rule] redundant because the substitution of a *su*-case ending has already been prescribed by [Pāṇini 3.1.85]? It is not redundant; for its purpose is to provide a detailed exposition (*prapañca*) of that very same point. The words [from Pāṇini 6.1.1 and 6.1.2] continue to apply here as well.
The genitive case in the word *dhātoḥ* expresses a part-whole relationship (*avayavayoga*).
For if there were grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), the connection between the first and the second [genitives] would not be tenable;
furthermore, it is because of the prohibition [contained in the rule] "of that which is not a reduplicated base" (*anabhyāsasya*).
For if there were grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), the prohibition would be meaningless, since it is impossible for a single-consonant root to possess repetition (*abhyāsa*).

Regarding the phrase "according to the application" (*yathāyogam*): this means that for a root beginning with a consonant (*hal-ādi*), the first single-consonant constituent is doubled, whereas for one beginning with a vowel (*aj-ādi*), the second is doubled; such is the meaning of "according to the application."
Regarding the form *prorṇunāva*:
from the root *ūrṇuñ* in the sense of "covering" (*ācchādane*, Dhātupāṭha 1039), there is reduplication of the syllable *nu* according to [Pāṇini 6.1.2].
However, for the letter *r*, reduplication does not occur because of the prohibition [stated in] *na ndrāḥ* [6.1.3].

[Objection: But surely, because the root *ūrṇu* belongs to the class beginning with *ij*, when the suffix *ām* is applied by [Pāṇini 3.1.36], the elision of *liṭ* occurs by [Pāṇini 2.4.81] (*āmaḥ*), and the subsequent application of *kṛñ* follows by [Pāṇini 3.1.40] (*kṛñ cānuprayujyate liṭi*). Consequently, the form will be *pro-ūrṇuvāñcakāra*; so how can there be *pro-ūrṇanāva*? To this he says: "The [substitution] of *ūrṇu* must be stated," and so forth. He shows that just as the *ām* suffix does not occur for the root *nau* due to its treatment as *nuvat*, the same applies to *ūrṇu*. As for the example *viśṛṇvire*: [it is explained as follows].
The root *śru* in the sense of "hearing" (Dhātupāṭha 942). By the rule *liṭastajhayoreśirec* [Pāṇini 3.4.81], *irec* is substituted;

by *liṭi dhātoranabhyāsasya* [Pāṇini 6.1.8] and *liṭ ca* [Pāṇini 3.4.115], the *liṭ* suffixes are treated as *sārvadhātuka*; then, by *sārvadhātukam apit* [Pāṇini 1.2.4], they receive the designation *apit*, and by *sārvadhātukārdhadhātukayoḥ* [Pāṇini 7.3.84], the substitution of *śnu* occurs along with the change to *śṛ*.
Finally, by *uraṇ raparaḥ* [Pāṇini 1.1.51] and *iko yaṇ aci* [Pāṇini 6.1.77], the *yaṇ* substitution takes place.

Regarding the form *sunvire*: the root is *ṣuñ* in the sense of "pressing" (*abhiṣava*; Dhātupāṭha 1247). Because the root itself is cited here, reduplication does not occur for the *vikaraṇa* suffix.

Some say that because the verbal root (*dhātu*) there is separated by a suffix (*vikaraṇa*), [the rule] does not apply; others say it is because of the Vedic character (*chāndasatva*), according to the principle: "All rules are optional in the Veda" (*sarve vidhayaśchandasi vikalpyante*).
And this is what is meant by: "Some say it does not apply because it is separated."
Others say it is because of its Vedic character (*chandasatvāt*), according to the principle: "All rules are optional in the Veda" (*sarve vidhayaśchandasi vikalpyante*).

And this is obtained from the inclusion of the term *bahulam* in [Aṣṭādhyāyī 3.1.85]. Having established this, [the Vārttika] states: "In the section on reduplication, optionally in the Veda" (*dvirvacanaprakaraṇe chandasi vā*).
Thus, this [form] is not to be produced: *nonāva*. [The derivation is as follows:

from the root *ṇu* "to praise" (*dhātupāṭha* 1035), there is the *yaṅ* suffix; reduplication; the *guṇa* substitution by the rule *guṇo yaṅlukoḥ* [Pāṇini 7.4.82], resulting in *nonūya*; then, with *nonūya* established, the elision of *yaṅ* occurs by the rule *yaṅo 'ci ca* [Pāṇini 2.4.74]; [then the suffix] *liṭ*.
Due to the prohibition [stated] in *amantre* [Pāṇini 3.1.35], [the ām-augment] does not occur.

Thus we have *sasnimikṣuḥ*. [The root] *miha* "to sprinkle" (Dhātupāṭha 992) is used here preceded by the prefix *sam*. From this, after the desiderative suffix *san*: (1) *ho ḍhaḥ* [8.2.31] changes *h* to *ḍh*; (2) *ṣṭunā ṣṭuḥ* [8.4.41] changes *ḍh* to *ṭ*; (3) the prohibition of *iṭ* by *ekācaḥ* [7.2.10] applies; (4) because the suffix is *kit* by *sanādyantā dhātavaḥ* [3.1.32], there is no *guṇa* substitution; (5) reduplication occurs; and (6) *ṣatva* is applied. When the form *sammimikṣa* is established, the *liṭ* suffix follows. Because of the prohibition in *amantre* [3.1.35], the *ām*-augment does not occur.
*Jhi*, for which *us* is substituted; then by *ato lopaḥ* [Pāṇini 6.4.48], the *a* is elided. Thus: *jāgāra*.
This is the *liṭ* (perfect) tense.
Regarding the form *dadāti*:

the *ślu* [substitution] occurs because of the statement "optionally" (*vā*); thus, in the alternative case, both *jajāgāra* and *dadāti* also occur. This is because of the rule "when *ślau* follows."

But surely, *ślu* is the non-observation of an affix (*pratyaya-adarśanam*), and that is of the nature of an absence (*abhāva-rūpam*). Since there can be no priority or posteriority (*paurvāparya*) in an absence, is it not incorrect to say "when *ślu* follows" (*ślau parataḥ*)? No, there is no fault; for since the original element (*sthānin*) has posteriority [relative to the preceding verbal root], one may rightly speak of priority and posteriority for *ślu* as well by way of that [original element], taking it in a figurative sense (*aupacārikam*). Regarding the phrase "they are introduced as uninflected (*nipātyante*) without distinction": this is because no specific distinction is mentioned.
Regarding the phrase "and the state of being without the augment *iṭ* (*aniṭ-tvam*)": [this refers to their introduction as such].

> Thus, the augment *iṭ* would apply; therefore, its absence is prescribed as a *nipātana* (irregularity). But surely, the rule for *iṅ* will be formulated for monosyllabic roots (*ekāc*) that have undergone reduplication (*dvirvacana*), whereas this [root] remains a monosyllable even before reduplication. Since it has not yet undergone reduplication, is it not improper to prescribe the absence of *iṭ*? This is not so; for in that rule, the mention of "having undergone reduplication" is intended as an indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*) for a monosyllable that is actually heard in the *liṭ* [perfect tense]. And since the state of being a monosyllable heard in the *liṭ* exists here, what is improper about it? [The term used is] "the parasmaipada."

Because *sah* is an ātmanepada verb, the parasmaipada ending would not be applicable; therefore, it is here treated as an irregular formation (*nipātana*). What, then, is the justification for this? He says: "the substitution of the remaining initial consonant" (*halādiśeṣaḥ*), and so forth.

If the rule of *halādiśeṣa* were to apply, then in that case one would have to perform the substitution of the vowel *ā* [for the final *h*], for when *halādiśeṣa* applies, there is no distinction made between an augment (*āgama*) and a substitute (*ādeśa*).
Regarding the mention of *ṇiluk*:

although the elision (*lopa*) of *ṇi* is already established by [Pāṇini 6.4.51], the explicit statement of *luk* is for the purpose of preventing the *vṛddhi* of the penultimate vowel (*upadhā*) by means of the technical designation of an affix (*pratyayalakṣaṇa*).

For if there were merely *lopa*, the *vṛddhi* of the penultimate vowel would occur by virtue of the affix being present; however, when there is *luk*, it does not occur because of the prohibition stated in [Pāṇini 1.1.63]. Furthermore, the term "vocalization" (*samprasāraṇa*) is prescribed as a technical name for an *ik* vowel that occupies the position of a *yaṇ*, and it applies to the meaning of the entire sentence.

Regarding this sentence-meaning characterized by the relationship between the original element (*sthānin*) and the substitute (*ādeśa*), expressed in the rule *igyaṇaḥ* [P. 1.1.44], it was stated there that "in the case of a restatement (*anuvāda*), a phoneme (*varṇa*) presents itself, but in the case of an injunction (*vidhi*), it is the sentence-meaning. Since this is an injunction, the presentation is of the sentence-meaning itself; thus he says: "In the place of *yaṇ*, etc. And [the suffix] *cāp* is prescribed by the rule *yaṅścāp* [P. 4.1.74].
"ibhyāputraḥ" [is formed] from "ibha-mātṛ" according to Pāṇini 4.1.66;
"kṣatriyāputraḥ" [is formed similarly].

In the case of *kṣatratrasyāpatyam* ("the offspring of Kṣatratra"), the suffix *dha* is applied by the rule *kṣatrād dhaḥ* [Pāṇini 4.1.138]. This is a mention of the suffix *ṣyaṅ*; since the technical rule regarding the mention of a suffix (*pratyayagrahaṇaparibhāṣā*) applies here, the inclusion of both the initial and final elements of the stem—namely, "that from which it is prescribed, beginning with that and ending with that"—would apply only in cases such as *kārīṣagandhīputra*, but would not apply here in the case of *paramakārīṣagandhīputra*.

For the suffix *ṣyaṅ* is prescribed after the word *kārīṣagandhi*, not after the word *paramakārīṣagandhi*. Therefore, in order to reject this objection, he says: "The mention of *strīpratyaya* (feminine suffix) [in Pāṇini 4.1.78] refers to *ṣyaṅ*. This is because it is prescribed under the governing rule [Pāṇini 4.1.3]. Furthermore, the femininity of *ṣyaṅ* is established through the principle of *sthānivadbhāva* (the substitute being treated like the original), and its status as a suffix is likewise established thereby; for otherwise, its status as a feminine suffix would not be tenable, since the view that it is a substitute (*ādeśa*) is adopted in that context.

If this were the inclusion of the feminine suffix (*strīpratyaya*), then what would follow? There would be no restriction regarding that which begins with it; for in that case, there would be the inclusion of even more [elements] than intended, or else an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). Indeed, if the restriction did not exist, just as we have here in *paramakārīṣagandhīputra*, so too would we have here in *atikārīṣagandhyāputra*. Therefore, he says: "And not when a feminine suffix follows," and so forth.

This is an exception (*apavāda*) made to the paribhāṣā concerning the mention of a suffix, namely: "Not when a feminine suffix follows, provided it is not a subordinate member" (*na strīpratyaye cānupasarjane*).

Therefore, where a feminine suffix (*strīpratyaya*) is not a subordinate member (*anupasarjana*), this paribhāṣā regarding the mention of a suffix (*pratyayagrahaṇa-paribhāṣā*) does not apply; consequently, there is no restriction that the compound must begin with that [feminine base]. Thus, in the case of *paramakārīṣagandhīputra*, the rule indeed applies. For here, the compound is formed by *paramā cāsau kārīṣagandhyā ca* according to Pāṇini 2.1.61 and so forth; the feminine suffix is the predominant element, and the masculine form (*puṃvadbhāva*) is applied by Pāṇini 6.3.34 and so forth. However, where the feminine suffix is a subordinate member (*upasarjana*), this paribhāṣā certainly remains in force because of the explicit statement "where it is not subordinate" (*anupasarjana*).
Therefore, in this case, the restriction beginning with "that" (tadādi-niyamaḥ) indeed applies.
Consequently, it does not occur here in the example *atikārīṣagandhyāputraḥ*. For in this instance, *atikrāntaḥ kārīṣagandhyām* is a *prādi-samāsa* (compound with prefixes).
In this context, that which has passed beyond is the principal (pradhāna), while Kāriṣagandhyā is the subordinate (upasarjana).

For this very reason, the shortening [of the vowel] occurs by virtue of Pāṇini 1.2.48. [Otherwise], there would be an over-extension (atiprasaṅga) regarding the rule for the vocalization (samprasāraṇa) of the vowels in "putra" and "pati" when they are at the beginning of a compound.
Here too, [the rule] would apply: *kārīṣagandhyāputrakulam*.

For in this way, the locative case in *putrapatyoḥ* expresses the immediate sequence of the element undergoing the grammatical operation (*kāryin*); consequently, it is indistinguishable whether the two elements are pure or whether they stand at the beginning of that [compound]. Even if, by some means, it were not to apply when standing at the beginning, even so, there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) to the end of that [compound] by virtue of the rule *tadanta-* (Pāṇini 1.1.72), such that it would apply here as well in the case of *karīṣagandhyāparamaputra*. When the three—the rule (*vidhi*), the element to be operated upon (*vidhāna*), and the possessor of the operation (*vidhibhāj*)—are in proximity, the operation applies to what stands between them.

And these [elements] are present here: the rule (*vidhi*) is *samprasāraṇa*; the subject of the rule (*vidhibhāk*) is *ṣyaṅ*; and the application (*vidhāna*) concerns the words *putra* and *pati*. Furthermore, because there is no deviation in this *tatpuruṣa* compound, the final member (*uttarapada*) which is brought into proximity is qualified by the words *putra* and *pati*. Someone might have the misconception that "since a rule applies within [the scope of] a qualifier, *samprasāraṇa* occurs when the final member ends in the word *putra* or ends in the word *pati*. To refute this, he says: "of *putra* and *pati*" (*putrapatyoḥ*), and so forth.

He thinks as follows: here, the *tatpuruṣa* compound, being indicated as the locus (*adhikaraṇa*) for the application of the suffix *ṣyaṅ* after the words "son" (*putra*) and "wife" (*patnī*), makes known that "son" and "wife" are constituent parts (*avayava*) of that *tatpuruṣa*. This is just like the case of "the branch on the tree.
When the tree is indicated as the locus of the branch, it makes known that the branch is a part of the tree; this is due to proximity (*pratyāsatti*).

In a *tatpuruṣa* compound where the element ending in *ṣyaṅ* occupies the position of a constituent member (*avayava*), it is only those two constituents of that very *tatpuruṣa*—namely *putra* and *pati*—that are intended to be included. It does not refer to the words *putra* and *pati* when they occur as subsequent members (*uttarapada*) in compounds such as *putrapati-*, for those are not constituents of the *pūrvapada* ending in *ṣyaṅ* within that specific *tatpuruṣa*.
However, this does apply to the words *putrakula-* and *patikulā-* which belong to other *tatpuruṣa* compounds.
Therefore, there is no over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) regarding cases beginning with "that" (*tadādau*).

Even at the end of that [compound], it does not occur at all; because here, in the case of the inclusion of the words *putra* and *pati*, there is freedom of choice regarding the relationship of qualifier and qualified between the latter member (*uttarapada*) and that which has been joined with it by a *tatpuruṣa* compound.

In that regard, if the latter member were qualified by the words *putra* and *pati*, then the rule for "that which ends in this" (*tadantavidhi*) would apply, on the grounds that a *tadantavidhi* occurs when there is a qualifier.

And here, the two [terms] are not qualified by that [suffix], but rather those two [terms] themselves are qualified by it. Consequently, since there is no rule for [a suffix] ending in that [term], this qualification applies only to the two [terms] taken alone; how then could there be the over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) of [the suffix] ending in them? But surely, if the son (*putra*) and the husband (*pati*) are qualified by the subsequent word (*uttarapada*), then by that [qualification] they would be understood as ending in that [subsequent word]; thus, only the final syllables of the subsequent word would be grasped, not the two [terms] alone. And in this way, there would be an over-extension to those beginning with that [term]? This is not so; for the words *putra* and *pati* cannot possibly end in a subsequent word. Because this word "end" (*anta*) denotes a constituent part (*avayava*).

Furthermore, the words *putra* and *pati* are not components (*avayava*) of a compound whose final member (*uttarapada*) is absent; rather, they are [components] of a compound, yet those two are not compounds themselves. Therefore, it is not understood in this way—that [the rule applies] to the words *putra* and *pati* when they stand at the end of a compound; rather, it applies to the words *putra* and *pati* alone, as independent final members.

By the rule *tadantavidhi* (Pāṇini 1.1.72), it is understood here that the *samprasāraṇa* applies to that which ends in *ṣyaṅ*. Consequently, in the case of *vārāhīputra*, the *samprasāraṇa* would also apply to the letter *v*; therefore, he says: “And when [the word] ends in *ṣyaṅ*,” etc.
He states the reason for this very point: “Of that which is being specifically indicated,” etc.
The mention of *samprasāraṇa* is for the sake of what follows.
It is indeed established even by the inclusion of the term *hikāra*.
We shall demonstrate that very purpose for the subsequent [rules] in that very place.

Indicating that same purpose for the subsequent [rules], he says: "The *samprasāraṇa*," and so forth. From the *Bālamanoramā*: "There is *samprasāraṇa* of the *ṣyaṅ* [suffix] in the case of *putra* and *pati* in a *tatpuruṣa* compound" (Pāṇini 6.1.13). *Ṣyaṅ-samprasāraṇa*.
By the paribhāṣā regarding the inclusion of that which contains the term [as its cause], "ṣyaṅ" is understood as including that which ends in it.

This is what he means by saying "of the prior member ending in ṣyaṅ. Although that rule occurs within the governing heading (adhikāra) for the "subsequent member" (uttarapada), the sense is that the status of being a "prior member" (pūrvapada) is obtained through the mention of the *tatpuruṣa* compound.
Regarding the phrase "of the two latter members":
this too is obtainable from the term *tatpuruṣa*.
Alternatively, by virtue of the governing rule (*adhikāra*) concerning the "latter member," the "former member" is implied.
The *Bālamanoramā* states: "In a *tatpuruṣa* compound, there is *saṃprasāraṇa* for the words *putra* and *pati*," and "there is lengthening of the *saṃprasāraṇa* vowel.
The intention is that this [rule] follows from the word "when there is elision of *ḍh* or *r*" (*ḍhralope*). [The phrase] "in the subsequent member" (*uttarapade*)...

The meaning is that this is because of the governing rule (adhikāra) stating "in a compound whose final member is not elided" (*aluguttarapade*). "The son of Kaumudagandhyā" is an analytical sentence (*vigrahavākya*).

*Kumudagandhi* means one whose scent is like that of the *kumuda* (white water-lily). This is a *bahuvrīhi* compound according to the rule: "A *bahuvrīhi* may be formed when the first member is either a locative case or a word denoting a standard of comparison (*upamāna*), and there is optionally the elision of the final member. Thus, it is a *bahuvrīhi*, with the elision of the latter part, the word *gandha*, from the first constituent *kumudagandha*.
Furthermore, the vowel substitution *it* (the long *ī*) is applied by the rule *upamānācca*.

In the sense of "the female offspring of Kumudagandhi," the suffix *aṇ* is applied by the rule *tasyāpatyam*. By the rule *aṇiño'nārṣayor*, this *aṇ* is replaced by *ṣyaṅ*. Then, by the rule *yasyeti ca*, the vowel *i* is elided.
The initial *vṛddhi* [substitution occurs]. The intention is that the word *kaumudagandhyā* [is formed] by the application of the suffix *cāp* after a *yaṅ*-intensive stem.
"Son of Kaumudagandhyā":
this is a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*).

When the case endings have been elided (*subluk*), the form *kaumudagandhyā-putra* remains; then, by the rule for the vocalization (*saṃprasāraṇa*) of the *ṣyaṅ* suffix, the letter *y* is changed to *i*.

The intention is that for *tasya* and its subsequent form [the penultimate vowel], the single substitute *ikāra* (short *i*) occurs by the rule *saṃprasāraṇācca*; then, the lengthening by the rule *saṃprasāraṇasya* results in the form *kaumudagandhīputra*.

However, the lengthening prescribed by the rule *halaḥ* does not apply here, because the consonant preceding the *saṃprasāraṇa* is not a member of the *aṅga* as determined by the cause of the *saṃprasāraṇa*. As for *kaumudagandhīpatiḥ*, the analysis (*vigraha*) is "the husband of Kaumudagandhyā."

The procedure is as before. Anticipating the possibility of an optional short vowel by the rule *iko hrasvo’ṅyo gālavasya*, he says: "By means of a restricted option (*vyavasthitavibhāṣā*), there is no shortening.
In this matter, however, the commentary alone is the refuge.

It might be argued as follows: *karīṣa* is the dried dung of cows, buffaloes, and so forth; that which has a scent like the scent of *karīṣa* is *karīṣagandhi*; the female descendant of that is *kārīṣagandhyā*; she who is both supreme and *kārīṣagandhyā* is *paramakārīṣagandhyā*; and her son is *paramakārīṣagandhīputra*. In this case too, the rule "there is vocalization (*saṃprasāraṇa*) of the suffix *ṣyaṅ*, and its lengthening" would apply—yet such a vocalization is impossible here.

Since the suffix *ṣyaṅ* is prescribed only after the word *kārīṣagandhi*, the preceding member of the compound *paramakārīṣagandhyā* does not end in *ṣyaṅ*; and because when a suffix is mentioned [in a rule], there is a requirement to include both that which begins with the element after which it is prescribed and that which ends with it, [the rule would not apply]. Therefore, he says: "And when it is a feminine suffix.
Since *ṣyaṅ* is prescribed in the feminine, it is a feminine suffix (*strīpratyaya*).

Furthermore, by the subsequent *paribhāṣā*—"In the case of a feminine suffix that is not a secondary member (*anupasarjana*), [the rule applies] to that which begins with it"—there is an absence of the restriction regarding the beginning of the word (*tadādiniyama*). Thus, even the word *paramakārīṣagandhyā* ends in *ṣyaṅ*. Consequently, when *saṃprasāraṇa* and lengthening (*dīrgha*) occur therein, the form *paramakārīṣagandhīputra* results; this is the intended meaning. This *paribhāṣā* is cited in the *Mahābhāṣya* on the present rule, "There is *saṃprasāraṇa* for *ṣyaṅ*. Regarding that, he states the purpose of the mention of "not being a secondary member" (*anupasarjana*) in the phrase "But in the case of a secondary member... (*upasarjane tu*).

*Atikārīṣagandhyaḥ* means "one who has surpassed Kārīṣagandhyā. In this compound, by the rule *atyādayaḥ*, the first member is compounded, and the feminine suffix is shortened as an *upasarjana*. His son is *atikārīṣagandhyaputraḥ*.

Here, the prohibition—"there is no restriction regarding the initial element when a feminine suffix is involved"—does not apply; for that prohibition operates only when the feminine suffix itself is an *anupasarjana* (not a subordinate member).

The meaning is as follows: since this *ṣyaṅ* feminine suffix here is indeed a subordinate member (*upasarjana*), the rule of "beginning with that" (*tadādiniyama*) applies; therefore, the word *atikārīṣagandhya* does not end in *ṣyaṅ*, and thus there is no vocalization (*saṃprasāraṇa*). Regarding the phrase "the neuter indication in *bandhunī*," etc., the meaning is that the neuter gender was used in the indication because it refers to the form of the word *bandhu*.
But what is the reason for explaining it in this way? He says: "This [term] is denoted by the masculine gender," and so forth.
Now, why was the reference not made using the masculine gender alone, as in *bandhau*? [One might object: "Lest it apply to synonyms.
For if it were done in this manner, it would follow that this reference is primarily concerned with the meaning (*arthapradhāna*), and consequently, it would also apply to synonyms.

It has been stated that when an instruction is primarily concerned with meaning (*arthapradhāna*), the technical definition of the formal word-form (*svarūpaparibhāṣā*) does not apply. Regarding the example beginning with *mātac*:

one might object that the word-form *mātac* simply does not exist, for this [suffix] is never found in usage as an independent entity; how, then, can a vowel-contraction (*samprasāraṇa*) be performed there? To this, he says: "Precisely because of this," and so forth.
Regarding the passage beginning with "tatra" and so forth:

if the accent of the *bahuvrīhi* compound were to apply by the rule "[6.2.1] yadi ca," then the employment of the marker *cit* would be purposeless. Therefore, lest that [marker] be purposeless, by the power of employing the marker *cit*, the accent of the *bahuvrīhi*—namely, the final acute (*antodātta*) prescribed for what is marked with *cit* by "[6.1.157] citaḥ"—is set aside.

But surely, the word *mātṛ* cannot possibly occur as a final member (*uttarapada*) in a *bahuvrīhi* compound, because by the rule *nadyutaśca* [Pāṇini 5.4.153], a suffix *kap* must necessarily be applied; how then can the vocalization (*samprasāraṇa*) of *ṣyaṅ* be justified there in the final member of the *bahuvrīhi*? To this he says: "And in the case of *mātṛ* and *mātṛka*," and so forth.
For if *kap* were obligatory, he would not have made a separate mention of *mātṛ* and *mātṛka*; yet he has done so.

Therefore, because it is mentioned separately, what is effected by the *vikalpa* (option)? The meaning of the word "also" (*api*) is that not only is the substitution of *māt* [for *yaj*] effected, but other things as well. This word "etcetera" (*ādi*) is connected only with *yaj*, and not with each of the others individually.

For if a connection with each one individually were intended, then after teaching *vac* in the sense of "speaking" (Dhātupāṭha 1063), one should have taught *ñiṣvap* in the sense of "sleeping" (Dhātupāṭha 1068); since the form would be established for *svap* as well by simply saying "of *vac* etc.," its separate mention would not be necessary.

But if this is so, would there not also have to be the inclusion of *svapi* in [Pāṇini 7.3.98]? This is not a fault; for it is possible to teach the *rud*-class roots beginning with *svapi*, and then formulate the rule simply as "and *svapi* after the five [roots].
Therefore, what was stated is correct: that it is connected only with *yaj*.
Because of its association with *svapi*, the letter *i* in *vac* serves to indicate the verbal root (*dhātu*), not for the purpose of qualification.
And because only the root *vac* belonging to the *brū* class is intended to be grasped here, he says: "The root *vac* is used in the sense of speaking, and it is also [the root] *brū*.
Regarding the word "spoken" (*uktaḥ*), the substitution of the subsequent sound (*parapadatva*) applies by rule 6.1.108.
Regarding "iṣṭaḥ":
the substitution of *ṣ* occurs by [Pāṇini 8.2.36] *vraśca* etc., and from that follows the substitution of *ṣṭu*.
Regarding "ūḍhaḥ": [the same applies].

By the rule *ho ḍhaḥ* [Pāṇini 8.2.31], there is the substitution of *ḍha*; by *ṣṭunā ṣṭuḥ* [8.4.41], there is the substitution of *ṣṭu*; by *ḍhralope pūrvasya dīrgho 'ṇaḥ* [8.3.13], there is the elision of the letter *ḍha*; and by *pūrvatrāsiddham* [6.3.111], there is the lengthening of the vowel. Regarding the form *uṣitam*, the substitution of *ṣ* is applied by the rule *śāsivasighasīnāñca* [8.3.60].
In *saṃvītaḥ* and *āhūtaḥ*, [the vowel] is long by [Pāṇini 6.4.2]: *halaḥ*. In *śūnaḥ*, there is the substitution of *ṇ* for the *ṣṭhā* (the suffix *kta*) by [Pāṇini 8.2.45].

Now, why does this not occur here: *vācam icchati* ("he desires speech") or *vācā tarati* ("he crosses by means of speech"), resulting in the suffix *ṭhak* [to form] *vācika* ("oral")? Even though the lengthening of the vowel in the root *vac* is performed by the rule *kvibvacipracchyāyatastukaṭaprujuśrīṇāṃ dīrgho'samprasāraṇañca* (Vārttika 288), nevertheless, because of the principle that "that which is modified in one part is not different from the original," the application [of the rule for verbal roots] would still follow; therefore, he says "of a verbal root" (*dhātoḥ*) and so forth.

Where a verbal root (*dhātu*) is not taken by means of the general term *dhātu*, but rather by its own specific name, there the grammatical operation is understood to apply only to that suffix which is prescribed after such a root by the rule *dhātoḥ*. And by making this specific formation (*nipātana*) of *bhrauṇahatya*, [the author] indicates that the formation is for the sake of [forming] a secondary derivative (*taddhita*). For if, when a root is mentioned by its own form, the operation were not understood to apply only to that suffix [prescribed after it], then this specific formation would be purposeless.
Because the reality [of the term] is established by this very rule [Pāṇini 7.3.32].

In the example "vācyati" and "vācikaḥ," although it is said that "those ending in *kvip* do not lose their status as verbal roots" (Vyāḍi-Pāṇinian Paribhāṣā 132), nevertheless, this suffix was not prescribed after a verbal root (*dhātu*) in that manner. For in one case, the suffix was prescribed after a nominal ending (*sup*), according to [Pāṇini 3.1.8], and in the other, it was prescribed after a nominal stem (*prātipadika*), due to the governing heading (*adhikāra*) of "from a nominal stem" (*prātipadikāt*) which includes those ending in *ṅī*, *āp*, and *prātipadika* (Pāṇini 4.1.1).

Therefore, because the root *vac* is taken here in its own form (*svarūpa*), the technical designation "kāryasaṃvijñāna" does not apply to its suffixes alone. [In the example] *gṛhītam*, the long vowel is applied by the rule *graho'liṭi* (Pāṇini 7.2.37).
[The example] *jarīgṛhrate*.
There is vocalization (*samprasāraṇa*) and reduplication.

The augment *rīk* is added by the rule "rīgṛdupadhasya" [Pāṇini 7.4.90]. This root *vayi* is indeed both *ātmanepada*—as in "aya vaya gatau" (Dhātupāṭha 474, 475)—and *parasmaipada*—as in "vetro vayiḥ" [Pāṇini 2.4.42]. In that case, one might ask: is the *ātmanepada* form taken here because of its association with roots like *grah*, which are not *ātmanepada*? To this, he says: "The root *vayi* in the perfect tense," and so forth.

And because of that, should not the following *liṭ* [perfect] suffix be treated as having the *kit* designation by the rule *asaṃyogālliṭ kit* [Pāṇini 1.2.5]? To this he says: "Of that," and so forth.
"If it were so" means:
if there were an inclusion of *vay-* for the substitute of *veñ*.

"Because *veñ* is recited among the roots beginning with *yaja*," and thus the intention is that its status as a *sthānivadbhāva* (substitute-like behavior) is established by the preceding rule alone, thereby making the *samprasāraṇa* (vocalization) accomplished. [The opponent replies:
"It cannot be so."
The word "to understand" (*vijñātum*) is to be supplied as the ellipsis. The meaning is that by this reasoning, it cannot be understood that the mention of *vay* is purposeless.
What is the reason? He says: "In the case of the *liṭ* [affix]," and so forth.

It might be argued: "Because of the contradiction between affirmation and negation, there will be affirmation alone in one place, not negation. To this he says: "In this case, just as... and so forth. It might be argued: "Because of the contradiction between affirmation and negation, there will be affirmation alone in one place, not negation. To this he says: "In this case, just as... and so forth. If, due to contradiction, they cannot coexist in one place, let there be alternation (*paryāya*); however, it does not follow that because the two have their fulfillment elsewhere, there must be only one of them.
"You mean that this meaning—that [the action] is not performed by another—is obtained," you say. "This is not a fault.
How is it not a fault? To this he says: "In the case of the *liṭ* [perfect tense]," and so forth.

The prohibition of *samprasāraṇa* for the letter *ya* in the rule "liṭi vayo yaḥ" is the *liṅga* (indicative mark) that the inclusion of *veñ* implies the inclusion of *vay*. For if there were no such inclusion, the application [of the rule] would be impossible, and thus the prohibition would be meaningless.
Furthermore, the fact that the inclusion of *vay* does not apply when there is a prohibition regarding *veñ*—as in the case of the rule "veñaḥ"—is also an indicative mark for this very point.

For if the mention of *veñ* were present, the prohibition would already be established by the rule *veñaḥ* itself; thus [the author] permits the meaning just mentioned by stating *panaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.1.38). If this is indeed the case, then for what purpose is the mention of *veñ*? To this he says: "This very... and so forth.
He explains that the mention of *vay* is for the sake of clarification,
as in the example "he pierces" (*vidhyati*),
where the suffix *śyan* is applied because the root belongs to the *divādi* class.

Regarding the form *uṣṭaḥ*: this ends in the suffix *tasa*; due to its belonging to the *adādi* (second) class, there is elision (*luk*) of the *śap* suffix. By the rule *vraścādi* (Pāṇini 8.2.36), there is the substitution of *ṣ* for *s*, followed by the substitution of *ṣṭu* for *ṣṭu*.
Regarding the form *vicati*: [it is derived from the root *viś*].

The suffix *śa* is applied because [the root] belongs to the *tud-ādi* class. In the form *vṛkṇa*, the substitution of *n* for *t* occurs as before, and there is the elision of *s* by the rule *skoḥ* (Pāṇini 8.2.29).
The phrase "the *niṣṭhā* suffix does not begin with a *jhal* sound" means that, for this reason, the substitution of *ṣ* for *s* does not take place here. This is the intended meaning.

For that [substitution] is prescribed for *jhal* and *ac*; this is because the term *jhal* is understood from the previous rule (Pāṇini 8.2.26). "But when *kutva* is to be applied, that [substitution] is indeed not established.

For it is not the case that, as in the instance of *ṣatva* and so on, the established status (*siddhatva*) of the substitute for the *niṣṭhā* suffix is stated here; such is not the case for *kutva*. Therefore, that [substitution] certainly takes effect.
Regarding "vṛścati":
the suffix śa is applied as before.
Regarding "varīvṛścyate": [the suffix yaṅ is applied].
The augment *rīk* is applied according to the rule "it should be stated that [the augment *rīk* occurs] after the root *ṛ*" (Vārttika 880).
Regarding the form *pṛṣṭaḥ*:
as before, there is the substitution of *ṣ*.
Since the suffix *naṅ* is prescribed by the rule *yajayāca* [Pāṇini 3.3.90] and others, why does vocalization (*samprasāraṇa*) not occur in the word *praśna*? To this he says: "*naṅi*" and so forth.
Regarding the form *bhṛṣṭaḥ*, the substitution of *ṣ* occurs as before.
Regarding "bhṛjjati," the suffix śa is applied as before.
Regarding "barībhṛjyate": [the same applies].
As before, [the rule] begins with "sakālasya" and so forth.

Now, one might object: "Should not its elision occur by the rule *skoḥ saṃyogādyor ante ca* [Pāṇini 8.2.29]? This is not so; for that [elision] is prescribed [only] when a *jhal* consonant follows or at the end of a word. Thus, [the form] is "uvayitha."

The augment *iṭ* is prohibited by the rule "after roots ending in *krādiniyama*, *iṭ* is obtained" (Pāṇini 7.2.62), but it occurs again due to the restrictive rule "after [roots] beginning with *krādiniyama*" (Pāṇini 7.2.63). Regarding the statement "there is no difference for the root *grah*":

because when there is vocalization (*samprasāraṇa*), the letter *r* is eliminated by the rule "remainder of the first consonant" (Pāṇini 7.4.60), the form of *grah* that results—namely *jagrāha*—is the same whether or not the vocalization occurs, even after the substitution of *u* for *ṛ*, the substitution of *ra-paratva*, and the application of "remainder of the first consonant" have been performed.
In the forms *jijyau* and *jijyatha*,
there is the elision of the vowel *ā* according to [Pāṇini 6.4.64].
"There is no difference whether there is a connection [with another rule] or not.

This means that if a connection intended for another purpose is undertaken, rather than for the purpose of the root *vṛścati*, then this statement does not apply to the meaning of *vṛścati*. Consequently, even though this statement for another purpose exists, the reduplicated form of *vṛścati* must certainly not undergo vocalization (*samprasāraṇa*). Is it not the case that when a statement to that effect is made by someone, vocalization is established in some manner? Such is the intention. Therefore, even if this connection were non-existent, the form that results—namely *vavraśca*—is exactly the same even when it exists; thus, there is no distinction regarding *vṛścati*.
This has been stated according to the opinion of the *vṛttikāra*.
However, according to the opinion of the *bhāṣyakāra*, he says: "In the beginning of the yoga," and so forth.

His intention is this: when a word is used in one sense while another meaning is being performed, that word may also have the sense of the root *vṛścati*; for *vṛścati* is included among the roots beginning with *grah*.

Furthermore, since this undertaking of yoga is for that very purpose, the *samprasāraṇa* must also occur through the practice of that [yoga]; thus, the word "tu" (but) shows a distinction from the opinion of the Vṛttikāra.

[The text says: "If, without performing the *samprasāraṇa*," and so forth. Now, one might object: "Will he not state the purpose of the mention of 'both'—namely, that even setting aside the *halādiśeṣa* (P. 7.4.60), the *samprasāraṇa* alone should take place? To this, [the author replies]: "How can there be any possibility of such a position? The intention is: [this would apply] if the yoga were devoid of the mention of "both."
"Now, regarding the letter *repha*, etc."—
the meaning is that this applies when the rule is accompanied by the mention of both [elements].
"Because of the status of the substitute as the original (*sthānivadbhāva*) for the substitution of *at* for *u*"— this refers to the following.

But by what [rule] does the status of being a *sthānin* (original element) apply? [It is by] Pāṇini 1.1.56: "That which is like the original (*sthānivadbhāva*) applies when there is an operation concerning an *ādeśa* (substitute). What, then, is that [element]? It is a suffix (*pratyaya*) following a vowel (*ac*), by reason of which the substitution of *at* for *ām* would occur. When it is understood that "the reduplication belongs to the *aṅga* (stem)," a suffix is necessarily resorted to by implication (*sāmarthyāt*), because without it there is no designation as an *aṅga*. Furthermore, the opinion of the author of the *Vṛtti* should be accepted; otherwise, since both [the stem and the suffix] are not explicitly mentioned there, the substitution of *samprasāraṇa* for the *v* would occur even after the *r* has been removed by the rule for "remainder of the initial consonant" (*halādiśeṣa*, 7.4.60), prior to the *samprasāraṇa*.

Consequently, the undesirable form *uvraśc* would result. Regarding the statement "there is no distinction between *pṛcchati* and *bhṛjjati*," it should be understood as being like the case of *grah*.

Regarding the phrase "akidartham" and so forth: what, then, is the reason that this [rule] must be explained as being for the sake of *kit* suffixes? To this he says: "In the presence of *kit*" and so forth. Because, when a *kit* suffix follows, after the *samprasāraṇa* has been performed, and given that there is a recognition of recurrence (*prasaṅga*) for that which has already undergone *samprasāraṇa*, then even without this specific statement, once reduplication (*dvirvacana*) has been performed, forms such as *ūcatuḥ* and others are indeed established.
Therefore, this [suffix] does not have the meaning of "ki," but rather has the meaning of "aki" itself.

Now, why is it said "of both" (*ubhayeṣām*), given that the term "of both" will follow by virtue of its connection with the indicatory mark *svarita*? Nor should one raise the objection that if there were such a following, the vocalization (*samprasāraṇa*) would also apply to the roots beginning with *vac* when followed by a suffix marked with *ṅ*; for if vocalization were to occur for *vac* and the others as well when followed by a *ṅ*-marked suffix, the division of the rule (*yogavibhāga*) would be purposeless.

Alternatively, the recurrence of *vṛc* and the others will occur according to the maxim of the frog’s leap (*maṇḍūkapluti*); so how could there be occasion for this fault? To this he says: “Precisely because of the governing rule (*adhikāra*),” and so forth. Since the inclusion of both [types of roots] would already be established by the governing rule alone, the fact that there is a further mention of “both” (*ubhayeṣām*) constitutes a repetition (*punarśruti*).
And the purpose of this repetition is this: where both a *samprasāraṇa* and something else would apply, let there be only the *samprasāraṇa*, and not the other.

Therefore, in the forms *vivyādha* and *vivyadhiṭha*, even though the rule for the "remainder of the consonant beginning with a *hal*" (P. 7.4.60) is subsequent, it is superseded and vocalization (*samprasāraṇa*) alone occurs. Otherwise, because the "remainder of the consonant beginning with a *hal*" would apply first due to its priority, the *yakāra* would be eliminated; once that was done, the *vakāra* would undergo vocalization, resulting in the undesirable forms *uvyādha* and *uvyadhiṭha*. [This applies] to the root *svāpi*.

Since the root *āplṛ* (meaning "to pervade," Dhātupāṭha 1260) could also be indicated by the single term *suparva*, he says—"the inclusion of the causative form of *svap*"—in order to dispel the suspicion that it might be that [other root].
And the inclusion of the causative form is understood from the mention of *caṅ*, for a *caṅ* affix cannot occur after a root ending in *ṇi*.
[The example is] *asūṣupat*.
The suffix *ṇic* is applied according to [Pāṇini 3.1.26]. Regarding the rule "here, the *samprasāraṇa* occurs prior to reduplication," it is because of its higher status (*paratva*).
In "svāpyate," the suffix *lakāra* denotes the object (*karman*);
in "svāpitam," it likewise denotes the object.

By [Pāṇini 6.4.52], there is the elision of the *ṇi* suffix. Now, one might object: does this not follow from the rule [Pāṇini 6.1.16] beginning with *grah*? Since the term *ṅitaḥ* (of that which has a *ṅit* marker) is understood as a governing element (*anuvartate*), and since there is no other *ṅit* suffix than *caṅ* in the case of *svāpi*, it would necessarily apply only to *caṅ* by virtue of its inherent capacity (*sāmarthya*); therefore, the explicit mention of *caṅ* should not be necessary. To this, he says: "The term *ṅit* alone," and so forth.

In the rule concerning *grah* and others, both elements—the mention of *kit* and the mention of *ṅit*—are present. When both are present without distinction, it is difficult for those of dull intellect to understand why only the mention of *ṅit* is understood to carry over (*anuvartate*) and not the mention of *kit*.
The intention is that this [long vowel] is employed for ease of comprehension by those of dull intellect. Regarding the term "svapnak":

why is there a long-vowel pronunciation (*dīrghoccāraṇa*) here, given that even if a short substitute were applied, the form *cekīyate* would still be established by the rule *akṛtsārvadhātukayoḥ* [Pāṇini 7.4.25], which prescribes lengthening? To this he says: "The long-vowel pronunciation," and so forth.

But how, when the rule *yaṅi ca* [Pāṇini 7.4.30] is stated, could the substitute apply in the case of *yaṅ*-luk (the elision of *yaṅ*)? It would apply by means of the *pratyayalakṣaṇa* (the treatment of an element as if its suffix were present).

Furthermore, is it not the case that the rule *atha pi* (Pāṇini 1.1.63), which provides for the application of suffixal characteristics (*pratyayalakṣaṇa*), is here prohibited? Even so, it is understood from this very fact of the long vowel pronunciation that [the rule] applies even when there is elision of *yaṅ* (*yaṅluk*); otherwise, that [long vowel] would be purposeless. [The example] *cekītaḥ* contains the suffix *tas*; the elision of *yaṅ* occurs by [the rule] *yaṅo 'ci ca* (Pāṇini 2.4.74). [The example] *sphātiḥ* is as follows:
> [[3.3.94]] The elision of *ya* after a *val* [root] [[6.1.64]]. Regarding the form *sphātībhavati*:

one might raise an objection, thinking that since the root *sphāy-* forms its past passive participle (*niṣṭhā*) with the suffix *kta*, and when the denominative suffix *cv-* is applied, this form arises by virtue of the rule *asya cvau* [[7.4.32]], how can the form *sphātībhavati* be correct? For in this case as well, if the substitution were applied to the past passive participle, it ought to be *sphītibhavati*. To such an objector, he replies: "This form *sphātībhavati* also," and so forth.

Is this also [the case] because of the word *sphāti*? When the suffix *ktin* has been applied and the substitution of *cv-* is made, then by the rule "also before *cv-*" (*cvau ca*, Pāṇini 7.4.26), the form remains that of the stem ending in *ktin*.
Therefore, this undesirable consequence does not arise. Regarding the phrase "there is a general inclusion":

when the vowel substitution (*āttva*) has been applied to both, and the initial *ṣ* of the former has been changed to *s* by the rule "the *ṣ* at the beginning of a root is replaced by *s*" (*dhātvādeḥ ṣaḥ saḥ*, Pāṇini 6.1.62), the forms are identical.

The technical rule *lakṣaṇapratipadoktaparibhāṣā* (Pāṇini 1.1.3) does not apply here, because both [the terms involved] are defined by rules (*lākṣaṇika*). Now, why does the substitution of *ṇ* for *t* in the *niṣṭhā* suffix not occur here according to [Pāṇini 8.2.43]? To this he says: "In the case of *samprasāraṇa*," etc. Is it not because of the principle that what precedes is treated as not having come into effect (*pūrvatrāsiddhatva*)? Since the *samprasāraṇa* is performed first, and once that has been done, the condition of having a *yaṇ* vowel (*yaṇvattā*) no longer exists, the substitution of *ṇ* for *t* does not take place.
Regarding the statement, "it is established as *prastya*":

one might object that if this were stated, there would also be vocalization (*samprasāraṇa*) of the syllable *pra*, and consequently the form would be *prastīta*. Why, then, is it said that it is established as *prastya*? [The author] considers that this fault does not arise because of the rule: "When there is a modification of a non-final element, [the substitution applies] to that which stands in the place of the final" (Pāṇini 1.1.54).
[The phrase] "so that it may also occur here" [is used].

Why does it not apply again? Because it is separated by the word *sam*. If the mention of *pūrva* (preceded by) were made, would the meaning of the word itself become such that it applies here as well? Or, with the intention of indicating that an increase in the wording suggests an increase in the meaning, he asks: "How so? Showing the first alternative, he says: "Of that which is preceded by *pra*."

Regarding the statement "a *bahuvrīhi* compound [is used] in the sense of the genitive (*ṣaṣṭhyarthe*)," since this word *pūrva* denotes a constituent part (*avayava*), the *bahuvrīhi* occurs in the sense of the genitive.
When the word *pūrva* denotes a constituent part, it is not possible for a verbal root (*dhātu*) to function as the external referent (*anyapadārtha*) of the compound.
For this prefix *pra* is not a constituent part of the verbal root (*dhātu*), but rather a constituent part of the combination of the root and the prefix (*dhātūpasarga*).
Therefore, it is logical that this very [prefix] constitutes the meaning of the other member of the compound; thus he says: "that which has *pra* as its prior member," and so forth.
[The phrase] "of its constituent part" refers to this.
The compound *tadavayavaḥ* is a genitive (*ṣaṣṭhī*) compound meaning "a member of that";
by the word *tat*, the entire complex of root and prefix is referred to.
Thus, there are two genitives with different referents (*vyadhikaraṇa*).

Regarding the phrase "of that which has *pra* as its prefix": the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) in [the term] *styaḥ* refers to the relationship between part and whole with respect to the constituent element *stya*; however, the genitive in *prapūrvasya* refers to the relationship with respect to the constituent element *yaṇ*. Thus, because they have different denotata, the two genitives in "of that which has *pra* as its prefix" (*prapūrvasya*) and "*styaḥ*" are in grammatical apposition (*vyadhikaraṇa*).

It might be argued that in the word *prasaṃstīta*, the verbal root *styā* cannot occur as a constituent part of the compound *pra-pūrva-samudāya*. To this he says: "In that regard," and so forth. "Fluidity and form" (*dravamūrttau*) means "fluidity and solidity" (*dravakāṭhinye*).
By this, he explains the meaning of the term *dravamūrtti*.
Here, the term *dravamūrtti* refers to a specific subsequent state called "solidity" (*kāṭhinya*), which follows the state of fluidity (*dravāvasthā*).
"And in the case of touch": touch is said to be a quality that accompanies form and the other [sensory objects]. "The water is cold."

But how, then, can there be grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) here, given that the word "cold" denotes a specific quality (*guṇaviśeṣa*), whereas words such as "wind" denote a specific substance (*dravyaviśeṣa*)? To this he says: "In the case of a mere quality," and so forth. Just as words such as "white" sometimes refer to the mere quality—as in "the white of a cloth"—but sometimes refer to the substance possessing that quality, either through the relation of identity (*abheda-sambandha*) expressed by "this is that," or by means of the suffix *matup* (possessive) being elided, as in "the cloth is white" (*śuklaḥ paṭaḥ*), so too is the word "cold."

The point is this: when [the word] applies to a substance (*dravya*) that possesses that [quality], then because both [the quality and the substance] are situated within a single substance, grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) is established. Regarding the form *saṃśyānaḥ*: the substitution of *n* occurs by the rule *saṃyogādeḥ* (Pāṇini 8.2.43) and so forth. "This is an option (*vibhāṣā*) in both cases."

Since [the rule] would apply to the case of liquid form and touch by the preceding rule, but not elsewhere, one might ask: what is the purpose of including the word "pūrva" (preceding), instead of simply saying "vibhāṣābhyavābhyām"? To this he says: "Of the inclusion of the word 'pūrva'," etc.
He explains why it does not apply here even when the word "pūrva" is included: "It is said, indeed," etc.

For this twofold compound is neither preceded by *abhi* nor preceded by *ava*; rather, it is preceded by *sam*. Therefore, because of the inclusion of the word "preceded" (*pūrva*) [in the rule], [the suffix] does not occur here.
Thinking that [the suffix] would indeed still apply even when the word "preceded" is included, he used the particle *kila* to indicate his lack of approval.
Demonstrating that very application (*prāpti*), he says: "In this case," and so forth.

Why does the option (*vikalpa*) not apply based on the collection of root and prefix that follows the word *sam*—since there is indeed an application [of the rule] because this [prefix *ava*] is preceded by *a-vi-va*? To this he replies: "Another effort must be undertaken.

Here the term *vibhāṣā* (optionally) is employed, and it is understood as a restricted option (*vyavasthitavibhāṣā*); therefore, the "another effort" consists in the fact that [the option] does not apply here.

"And another purpose for the inclusion of the word *pūrva* must be stated. What is that? It should be understood as follows: so that there may be an option (*vikalpa*) even in cases such as *abhisaṃśīnam*, *abhisaṃśyānam*, *avasaṃśīnam*, and *avasaṃśyānam*. And this [purpose] is explained under the rule *tathā* (Pāṇini 6.1.23) when the inclusion of *pūrva* is made, by means of the analysis beginning with "a *bahuvrīhi* compound in the sense of the genitive in the expression *prapūrvasya*. [This refers to] the root *śrā* in the sense of "cooking" (*pāke*).

The root *śrā* "to cook" is listed in the *adādi* class (Dhātupāṭha 1053) and also in the *ghaṭādi* class (Dhātupāṭha 810) for the purpose of assigning it the designation *mit*. Some also list it in the *curādi* class, while others list *śrai* "to cook" in the *bhvādi* class (Dhātupāṭha 919). Consequently, its inclusion here [in the present rule] would seem to apply without distinction to all of them; for indeed, this very form also belongs to the root *śrāyati* when its final vowel has been changed to *ā*.

Furthermore, due to the fact that this is a nipātana (an irregularly formed word), the paribhāṣā "the rule that applies to what is explicitly stated by its own technical definition takes precedence over a general rule" (Vyā|Pa|3) does not apply.
This is because [the rule] states "of both that which ends in ṇi and that which ends in aṇ," without specifying any distinction between them.

And so it has been said: "cooked in milk" (*śrāṇya-śṛta*). If the term *vibhāṣā* (optionally) were to carry over [from the previous rule], then even for *kṣīra* (milk) and *havis* (clarified butter), there would optionally be the forms *śrāṇam* and *śrapitam*; and in cases other than those two, the form *śṛtam* would also undesirably apply as an option. Therefore, he says: "This is a restricted option" (*vyavasthitavibhāṣā*).
Regarding the phrase "even when," etc.:
the operation of an instigator (*prayojaka*), such as commanding or requesting, is expressed by the word "instigator" (*prayojaka*) by applying a metaphorical designation of the cause to the effect.
For that [causative suffix] arises from a primary meaning (*prākṛta-artha*), since it is not included therein.

In that case, when a second *ṇic* is produced by the rule *tatprayojako hetuśca* (Pāṇini 1.4.55), even then this substitution is not desired for *kṣīra* and *havis*; precisely because of the understanding of the rule as having a fixed option (*vyavasthita-vibhāṣā*).
And so it has been said: "The form *śṛtam* applies to the root *śrap*, except in the case of *havis*."
The meaning is that the *ṇic* affix occurs after a root expressing a cause (*hetu*) in cases other than those [already mentioned].

Regarding the mention of the second [agent]: when there is only one [agent], then because it is desired, as in "the milk was cooked by Devadatta with Yajñadatta," the term "cause" (*hetu*) from the rule *tatprayojako hetuśca* (Pāṇini 1.4.55) includes the word "and" (*ca*), whereby the technical designation "agent" (*kartṛ*) is prescribed for both Devadatta and Yajñadatta; thus, the third case ending (*tṛtīyā*) appears in both instances to denote the agent. This refers to the word "cooked" (*śrapitam*).

When the causative suffix (*ṇic*) is applied to *śrā*, the augment *puk* is added by [Pāṇini 7.3.36], and the vowel shortening occurs by [Pāṇini 6.4.92]. When milk boiled itself (*kṣīraṃ svayameva śrāti sma*), and this action was then prompted by Devadatta, the first *ṇic* is applied by [Pāṇini 3.1.26]: "And when there is an instigator. When that [Devadatta] himself was prompted by Yajñadatta while causing [the milk] to boil, the second *ṇic* is applied. Then, by [Pāṇini 6.4.51], there is elision of the preceding *ṇic*. Subsequently, the past passive participle (*niṣṭhā*) is applied to the milk as the object of the prompted action, resulting in *śṛtam*.

When it is asserted that "both the causative (*ṇyanta*) and the non-causative (*aṇyant*) forms are irregularly derived (*nipātyete*)," it is appropriate that this irregular derivation applies even to the causative—provided one accepts the position that for some [grammarians] the root *śrāti* is also listed in the *curādi* group.

However, for those who do not accept its inclusion in the *curādi* group, how can this irregular derivation of the causative be justified? If someone were to object: "Even for them, this irregular derivation of the causative is justified because of the statement of the author of the *Bhāṣya*: 'The form *śṛtam* [is used] after the root *śrā*, except when the causative suffix *ṇic* is present,'" the author replies with the words beginning "This *śrāti*... and so forth.
