Even when an object has attained the state of being an agent (*karmabhāvāpanna*), if it is intended to be expressed independently for the sake of brevity, it is called a "self-agential object" (*karmakartṛ*). This is based on the principle that "the object becomes the agent.

It is a descriptive compound (*viśeṣaṇasamāsa*) meaning "that which is both an object and an agent. That which is its domain is the "domain of the self-agential object" (*karmakartṛviṣaya*). And this qualification—namely, that the root *pac* (to cook) has as its domain the self-agential object—should be understood as being mediated by the meaning [of the action].

Regarding its meaning: when it signifies the state of being the agent of the act of cooking (*pacyamāna-kartṛkatva*) as mere softening (*vikledana-mātra*), it is intransitive (*akarmaka*)—the root *śrā* functions thus.

But when it takes the causative suffix (*ṇic*), it expresses the original meaning of *pac*. "Original" (*prākṛta*) means that which exists in the base form (*prakṛti*). Furthermore, that which should be understood here is the meaning of the base form of *pac*, which has the cooker as its agent (*paktṛ-kartṛka*) and consists of softening, collecting, and so forth.
The meaning is that he states the common sense of the verb *pac* (to cook), which has Devadatta and others as its agent (*kartṛ*) and whose object is the act of cooking.

In that regard, it is desired that the term *śṛta* applies to both [forms]. That is to say, even in the case of the causative form *śrā-*, which has the same meaning as the non-causative *pac* when used in the sense of a reflexive object-agent (*karmakartṛ*), it is desired there;
and also in the case of the causative form which expresses the common sense of the verb *pac*, it is desired there as well.
In this regard, "the milk boiled by itself" is an example of the first [type],
and "the milk boiled by Devadatta" is an example of the second.

But has it not been stated in the Bhāṣya that "the form *śṛta* [is used] after the root *śrā*, except when there is a causal suffix (*hetu*)"? How then can both [the non-causal and the causal] be intended? The thought is this: regarding what was stated in the Bhāṣya—"the form *śṛta* after *śrā*, except when there is a causal suffix"—by the phrase "except when there is a causal suffix," a total exclusion of every causative (*ṇic*) is not intended; otherwise, this would be contradictory. For if the root *śrā* were not read in the Curādi class, and the form *śṛta* were thus prescribed (as a *nipātana*), how could one say "except when there is a causal suffix"?

It is an exclusion (*paryudāsa*)! If "other than that which has a causal suffix" (*anyatra hetoḥ*) were an exclusion, then the irregular derivation (*nipātana*) of *śṛtam* from the root *śrā-* would not be possible. For there is no other causative suffix (*ṇic*) following *śrāti* besides the one added in the sense of a cause (*hetu-ṇic*), since *śrāti* is not listed in the *curādigaṇa*. Therefore, that very [causative] for which the status of being a suffix expressing its own meaning (*svārthika*) cannot be established by any means is what the author of the Bhāṣya intends as the object of the exclusion.
Furthermore, that second *ṇic* which arises when there is an external prompter (*prayojaka*) is to be understood [as the one excluded].

However, that for which self-referentiality (*svārthikatva*) can be established by some means is not considered by the author of the Bhāṣya to fall within the scope of the exclusion; for him, this specific formation is indeed desired.

Moreover, that [second *ṇic*] upon whose occurrence the root *śrāti* expresses the primary meaning of "cooking" (*pacyartha*) is to be understood [as the one intended]; for since it has the same meaning as the root *pac* in its base sense, its status as self-referential can be figuratively designated.

Thus, even in this reading, this nipātana (irregular formation) is indeed appropriate for the root *śrā*, which belongs to the *curādi* class and is also *seṭ*. Regarding "pīnam," the substitution of *n* for the *ṣṭhā* suffix occurs by [Pāṇini 8.2.45]. Regarding "ityam api" and so forth...

By the word *api*, he shows that it is not only the option (*vibhāṣā*) mentioned in the preceding rule that is a fixed option (*vyavasthitavibhāṣā*), but this one as well. To the question, "What is established by this? he says: "By this," and so forth. He states an exception to the rule that [the suffix] does not occur after a verb with a prefix (*sopasarga*), namely: "of that preceded by *āṅ*," and so forth.
This substitution of *pī* for *andhu* and *ūdhas* is permanent;

it is indeed a rule of restricted option (*vyavasthitavibhāṣā*). This is because the word "optionally" (*vibhāṣā*) has ceased to apply, as evidenced by the fact that the word "optionally" is mentioned again in the subsequent sūtra.
Otherwise, one would not perform this very [operation], thinking that it will follow there as well.
For this very reason it is said: "Among two rules of different languages, those that are prescribed are obligatory," and "the rule *pyāyaḥ pī* is also drawn in by the word *ca*."
Otherwise, since *samprasāraṇa* is the subject under discussion, one might understand that *samprasāraṇa* applies to *pyā* even in the case of the suffixes *liṅ* and *yaṅ*.
However, when the word *ca* ("and") is present, the connection with the immediately preceding *pībhāva* (the substitution of *pī*) is easily determined.
The substitution *pī* is prescribed before the doubling (*dvirvacana*) has taken effect.
Someone might suspect that, because of this, it would result in the sublation of that [other cognition].
Therefore, in order to refute that suspicion, he says: "Because it is subsequent," and so forth.
For sublation would occur only if there were a contradiction; however, in this case, there is no contradiction.

Is it because of its subsequent occurrence? Or because, once the substitution of *pī* has been made, the principle of "non-repetition of what has already occurred" (*punaḥprasaṅgavijñāna*) applies? Thus, it is established that the reduplication takes place. As for the form *śuśāva*:
when the *liṭ* suffix *ṇal* follows, the semivowel is vocalized (*samprasāraṇa*), and then the *vṛddhi* and *ā* substitutions are applied.
As for *śiśāya*.
When there is no *samprasāraṇa*, then the *vṛddhi* and *ay* substitutions [apply],
as in *śuśuvatuḥ* and *śiśāyatuḥ*. When there is *samprasāraṇa*, then *uvaṅ* [applies], while in other cases *iyaṅ* [applies].
Regarding the term "not yet obtained" (*aprāptam*):
this is because [the rule] has not been prescribed by anything else.

As for the mention of "both" (*ubhaya*) in both instances of the rule *liṭabhyāsasyobhayeṣām* [Pāṇini 6.1.17], its purpose is stated as follows: so that when another operation might apply, it should be set aside and only the *samprasāraṇa* (vocalization) of the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*) should take place. This is the utility of including the word "both."

Furthermore, someone might have the misconception that this [rule] also sublates the alternative and thus there would always be vocalization (*samprasāraṇa*). Therefore, in order to dispel that, he says "And when," and so forth. Here, it is stated that the vocalization of *āya* is optional; if at some time there is no vocalization of the root, would it then apply to the reduplication? And consequently, the optional vocalization of *āya* would not have been established.

It might be argued: "This operation is prescribed optionally for the root *śak* when followed by the suffix *liṭ*, and since that [suffix] indeed follows it, [the rule should apply]. This is incorrect; for when there is a double application (*dvirprayoga*) in the case of reduplication (*dvirvacana*), only the action (*kriyā*) is differentiated, not the form of the verbal root (*dhāturūpa*). Therefore, how could there be a distinction between the preceding and following elements with respect to their connection to the grammatical operation? Consequently, when the operation does not apply to the root, it certainly does not apply to the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*) either. The rule *ṇau ca saṃścaṅoḥ* contains two locative case endings (*saptamī*) in different syntactical substrata (*bhinnādhikaraṇa*): "that which is a *ṇi*-affix following *sam* and *caṅ*, and that which is the root *āya* following a *ṇi*-affix. Thus, we have the form *śuśāvayiṣati*.

From the root *śvi* with the suffix *ṇic*, the desiderative suffix *san*, vocalization (*samprasāraṇa*), vṛddhi, and the substitution of *āv*; then reduplication of the syllable *śu*, resulting in *a-śu-śu-v-at* (the form *aśūśavat*).

In the case of *luṅ*, the suffix *caṅ* is applied after *cli*, followed by vocalization and so forth, the elision of the *ṇil* augment as before, the shortening of the vowel by *ṇau caṅi* [Pāṇini 7.4.1], reduplication, and finally the lengthening of the vowel by *ata upadhāyāḥ* [Pāṇini 7.2.116].

But surely, when the suffix *ṇic* is added to *āyati*, and then *san* is added after that, and finally *caṅ* [is applied], the internal (*antaraṅga*) operations—namely the *vṛddhi* and the substitution of *āy*—must occur first, followed by the *samprasāraṇa*. This being the case, when *san* follows *ṇi*, the form should be *śuśuyayiṣati*, and when *caṅ* follows, it should be *aśūśuyat*; so how is it that *śuśāvayiṣati* and *aśūśavat* are cited as examples? To this he says: "The *samprasāraṇa*," etc.
By the word "etc. (*ādi*), the substitution of *āy* is included.
Furthermore, in this case, the substitution of the preceding vowel (parapūrvatva) occurs by virtue of [Pāṇini 6.1.108], which relies on *samprasāraṇa*.
It is said that "by that [substitution] as well, the *vṛddhi* and other operations are superseded.

Now, even so, once the *vṛddhi* and the substitute have been applied, would not reduplication of the element beginning with *śā* apply, since no rule prevents it? Has not the status of being a *sthānivadbhāva* been prescribed for the causative suffix (*ṇau*)? To this, he says: "When *o* is followed by *pu*, *yaṇ*, or *j*, provided there is no *a* or *apara*," and so forth.
And where this is an indicator (*jñāpaka*), we shall demonstrate its application in the commentary on that very [sūtra]. Regarding *nicikyu*:
the substitution of *yaṇ* occurs by the rule *eranekācaḥ* [Pāṇini 6.4.82]. Regarding *nicāyya*: [the form is derived from the root *ci* with the suffix *lyap*].
This is the end [of the discussion].
The long vowel is pronounced for the sake of its being heard in the form *cikīrvān*;
this is the form [ending] in *kvasu*. [The rule] "and there is elision of the letter *a*" [applies here].
The vowel *a* which is a constituent part of the verbal root is elided by virtue of this irregular derivation (*nipātana*). Thus, we have *apāspardhethām*.
Regarding the *a* of *apa*, there is the substitution of a long homogeneous vowel (*savarṇadīrghatva*) by [Pāṇini 6.1.87] *āṭaśca*.
"He desires the division of objects"—

this should be understood as being obtainable through the force of the particle (*nipāta*). If, however, the absence [of the suffix] were observed in even a single instance, then another effort would have to be undertaken for that purpose.

For this is not established even by the word *śrātāḥ*, because of the use of the plural number in the Sūtra. Therefore, he says "of that" (*tasya*), and so forth. For those [grammarians] for whom the *samprasāraṇa* has been stated, since as many *yaṇ*s as are possible occur, the *samprasāraṇa* would apply to all of them; thus, this prohibition is commenced. Now, one might object: "By the maxim *alo 'ntyasya* [Pāṇini 1.1.52], it will apply only to the final [element], not to a non-final one? This is not so; for this maxim cannot be brought to bear here.
Because it is impossible for a *yaṇ* substitute to occur at the end of roots such as *vic*, *svap*, and *yaj*.

If that is the case, then by the rule "when there is no modification of the non-final [element], the operation applies to that which is in the vicinity of the final" (Vyāḍi-Pāṇini 63), the operation will apply to that which is in the vicinity of the final—namely, to that *yaṇ* which is in the vicinity of the final, and not to any other? This is not a universal maxim (*paribhāṣā*), because it lacks utility. As it has been said: "There are no purposes served by that maxim."

Therefore, this rule must be formulated as a *sūtra*. [Objection: But surely, the *samprasāraṇa* is characterized by a single grammatical operation (*ekayogalakṣaṇa*) for both the preceding and the following elements; therefore, if that [operation] has been accomplished for the following element, it has necessarily been accomplished for the preceding one as well. Now, it is impossible to effect the cessation of what has already been accomplished, nor is it logical to rely on what has not yet been accomplished as a cause (*nimitta*). Consequently, precisely because of this prohibitive statement, the operation is first performed for the following element; once that has been done, the [operation] which would have applied to the preceding element is prohibited.
Now, while the term *samprasāraṇa* is already being carried over [from the previous rule], for what purpose is *samprasāraṇa* mentioned again? To this he says: "*Samprasāraṇam*" and so forth.

If the mention of *samprasāraṇa* were not repeated, then according to the principle "a rule applies to or prohibits only that which is immediately preceding" (Vyākaraṇa-paribhāṣā 19), there would be a prohibition only of the *samprasāraṇa* under discussion [in the immediate context], and not of that occurring in a different location.

Therefore, the term *samprasāraṇa* is mentioned again so that the prohibition may apply even to that which is prescribed in a different context, even when it occurs in a separate location [of the rule].
For example: *yūno yūnā*.
Once the *samprasāraṇa* has been performed and the substitution of the preceding vowel (*parapūrvatva*) has been applied, [the form is established]. (Aṣṭādhyāyī 6.1.101)

But even if the term *samprasāraṇa* were mentioned again, would there not still be no prohibition in that case? For, since the long vowel resulting from *savarṇa-dīrgha* would, by virtue of the rule of *sthānivadbhāva* regarding a preceding operation, be separated by the letter *u*, [the condition for the rule would not be met]. To this he says: "Precisely by the force of mentioning *samprasāraṇa*," and so forth. The intention is that if *sthānivadbhāva* were to apply, the repeated mention of *samprasāraṇa* would be purposeless. Furthermore, having granted [the opponent's point], he states another refutation: "Or, even if [it were so]," and so forth.

Precisely by the force of the mention of *samprasāraṇa*, even though it is not explicitly heard here, that vowel (*aj*) which has attained the status of a *sthānin* through another rule will not be considered as creating an intervention merely by its presence; otherwise, the mention of *samprasāraṇa* would be rendered meaningless.

But is it not the case that, by virtue of the very *nipātana* (irregular derivation) rules "yūnaśca kutsāyām" [Pāṇini 4.1.165] and "vṛddho yūnā" [Pāṇini 1.2.65], there will be no *samprasāraṇa* (vowel substitution) for the word *yūnaḥ* or *yūnā*? Why then is the term *samprasāraṇa* mentioned again here for the purpose of excluding it? This is not so; for it has been stated that *nipātanas* can occur even without subverting other rules. Furthermore, this *nipātana* is understood to apply specifically to this context; thus, in forms such as *yūnaḥ*, *yūnā*, and *yūnī*, the *samprasāraṇa* would indeed occur.
[The example] is "ārevān."
The suffix *matup* is applied because [the word] possesses wealth (*rayi*).

When the semivowel substitution (*samprasāraṇa*) has been performed, the rule "the first vowel [of the two resulting from *samprasāraṇa*] becomes a single *guṇa*" (Pāṇini 6.1.87) applies, and by the rule "the *v* of *vaya* and *drū*" (Pāṇini 8.2.15), the substitution of *v* for *y* occurs. Since both *v* and *y* are semivowels (*yaṇ*), and since the prohibition of *samprasāraṇa* for the preceding [semivowel] *v* would have applied, this rule prohibits the *samprasāraṇa* of the *y* in the case of the *liṭ* [perfect tense].

In that case, since the *yakāra* is prohibited, it does not undergo *samprasāraṇa*; therefore, *samprasāraṇa* occurs for the *vakāra* of both the verbal root and the reduplication—the former by the rule *grahādi-sūtra* [Pāṇini 6.1.16] and the latter by the rule *liṭyabhyāsasyobhayeṣām* [Pāṇini 6.1.17].

Now, for what purpose is the mention of *liṭ* (the perfect tense), given that there is no possibility of the substitute *vay* occurring anywhere other than in *liṭ*, since the mention of *liṭ* follows from the rule *liṭanyatarasyām* [Pāṇini 2.4.40] in its formulation, and by the force of that very [mention], it will apply in *liṭ*? To this he says: "The mention of *liṭ* is for the sake of subsequent rules. The mention of *liṭ* is for the purpose that the prohibition [stated in] *veñaḥ* [Pāṇini 6.1.39] should apply specifically in *liṭ*. "The division of the rule (*yogavibhāga*) is for the sake of subsequent rules."

The separation of the rule (*yogavibhāga*) is for the purpose that, in what follows, the optional *samprasāraṇa* (vocalization) should apply only to the root *vyeñ*, and not to the root *jyā*. [The word] "of a root" (*dhātoḥ*) is understood from [Pāṇini 6.1.8]. And that [word "root"] is a qualifier of the diphthongs *ai* and *au* (*aic*), and by means of this qualification, there is an extension of the rule to include what ends in them (*tadantavidhi*). Thus he says: "that root which ends in *e*.
[The word] "in its original enunciation" (*upadeśe*).

The meaning is that [the word] occurs in the *gaṇapāṭha* at its first pronunciation, as in "cetā" and "stotā. Now, one might object: "Will this not already be excluded by the maxim regarding 'that which is taught by a rule' (*lakṣaṇapratipadokta*)? So what is the purpose of including the term 'upadeśa'? If this is so, then the inclusion of the term "upadeśa" indicates that this maxim is not universally obligatory (*anitya*).

By this, when even a phonetically conditioned (*lākṣaṇika*) *ā* is included in the rule *arti-hrī-...* [Pāṇini 7.3.36] and others, the augment *puK* is established even in forms such as *krāpayati*. [The term] *śit* means "that which has *ś* as its *it*.
Since the substitute *eś* (in place of *ta*) is a *śit*, when a prohibition is made regarding a *śit* suffix, the long-vowel substitution (*āttva*) does not apply even to *eś*.

Thinking that if the substitution of *ā* were applied here, the undesired form *jaglāya* would result through the principle of *sthānivadbhāva* (the substitute behaving like the original) when *glai* is reduplicated, he asks "How? and so forth.
The elision of the vowel *ā* occurs by the rule *glai-ādīnām* [Pāṇini 6.4.64].
The resolution is provided by the words "Not so" (*naivam*) and so forth.
Is it *ś* itself? When [the term] is understood as *śit*, there is indeed the inclusion of the letter *ś*.

In that case, by the paribhāṣā rule "when there is a mention of an initial [element], the operation applies to that which begins with it" (Vyāḍiparibhāṣā 127), a prohibition would have to apply to a suffix beginning with *śit*; however, *aiś* does not begin with *śit*. What then? It ends in *śit*, because it is pronounced as something ending in *śit*. Therefore, the prohibition does not apply here to *aiś*.

Is "aśiti" (not being followed by *ś*) a relative negation (*paryudāsa*) or a simple negation (*prasajyapratiṣedha*)? In that regard, if it were a relative negation, then something other than *ś* would have to be relied upon as the cause for the acute accent (*udātta*). And in that case, as long as it is not the cause for the acute accent, it ought to be acute; however, this is not so because it does not end in the vowel *ā*. Fearing that in examples such as "sugalaḥ," the suffix *kap*—which is conditioned by ending in *ā*—would not occur, he says "aśiti" and so forth.
What is established by this? He says: "By that," and so forth.

In the case of a *prasajya-pratiṣedha* (absolute negation), the substitution of *āt* is prohibited before a *śit* affix, but no specific cause (*nimitta*) is relied upon; thus, it becomes independent of any cause (*anaimittika*).

Consequently, the substitution of *āt* occurs even prior to the arising of the suffix, whereby the suffix characterized by having *ākāra* as its final element is established, resulting in forms such as *suglaḥ*.
The form is established.
By the word "ādi" (and so forth), there is the inclusion of *suglaḥ*, *suglā*, and others.
For in those cases, when feminine, the suffix *aṅ* is applied by [Pāṇini 3.3.106]: *ātaścopasarge*. [The root] *vyeñ* (in the sense of covering) [is also included]. (Dhātupāṭha 1007).

Now, why is it not understood that [the rule applies] to *aliṭ* (non-*liṭ* endings), since the *saṃhitā* is the same? This is not so; for if this were the case, the restriction would have been formulated as "in *liṭ*, [the root] *vyā*"—meaning that the substitution of *āt* occurs only in *liṭ* and not elsewhere. And by virtue of the established usage of the linguistic data (*lakṣya*), there will be a contrary restriction. Furthermore, in the case of the dual and plural, whether there is *samprasāraṇa*, the formation of the single substitute (*pūrvarūpa*), or the substitution of *āt*, there is no difference; thus, the example is given in the singular.

Regarding the phrase "saṃvivyayiṛtha": in the case of the suffix *thali*, the augment *iṭ*—which would otherwise be required by the rule for roots beginning with *valādi*—is prohibited by the rule *ekācaḥ* [Pāṇini 7.2.10]. Again, the restriction imposed by the rule for roots beginning with *krādi* applies, but that too is prohibited by the rule *acastāsvat* [Pāṇini 7.2.61]. When an option is again suggested by the rule *vā* [Pāṇini 7.2.63], the augment *iṭ* is applied invariably by the rule *iḍarttivyayatīnām* [Pāṇini 7.2.66]. Regarding the forms *visphāraḥ* and *visphālaḥ*:

The suffix *ghañ* is applied in the sense of an abstract action (*bhāva*), according to *Pāṇini* 3.3.18, or optionally in the sense of an instrument (*karaṇa*) or a locus (*adhikaraṇa*) by *Pāṇini* 3.3.121. [The roots are: *ḍukrīñ* "to exchange goods" (Dhātupāṭha 1473), *iṅ* "to study" (Dhātupāṭha 1046), and *ji* "to conquer" (Dhātupāṭha 561).
This rule is commenced for the sake of cases not taught elsewhere.
In forms such as *krāpayati*, once the vowel substitution (*ātva*) has taken place, the augment *puk* is added by *Pāṇini* 7.3.36, etc.

For what purpose is this stated? One might ask: why not simply derive forms such as *krāpayati* by adding the causative suffix (*ṇic*) to the roots *krap* (meaning "to move with contempt," DhP 771), *jap* (meaning "to speak clearly," DhP 397, 398), and *ā-plu* (meaning "to pervade," DhP 1260) when preceded by the prefix *adhi*; since verbal roots have multiple meanings, *krap* and the others could function in the sense of "buying" (*krīṇāti*) and so forth? It is replied: [this is stated] to exclude other possible applications of the causative suffix (*ṇic*) to the roots *krī* ("to buy") and the rest.

Now, why is it not understood that the root *īṅ* in the sense of "motion" (Dhātupāṭha 1143) is intended here for the root *kṛ*? It is said in reply: first of all, it cannot apply to *kṛ*, because of the governing rule (*adhikāra*) of "ec. For this very reason, the author of the Vṛtti has continued the term "ec. Or, [one might argue] that by the force of the explicit statement, its substitution as *āt* is already established simply by the rule for *vṛddhi*. This is not so; for [the rule] would then serve as a restrictive injunction (*niyama*), meaning that there is only the substitution of *āt* and not the substitution of *rapara*. This is not so either; according to the principle that "when both an original injunction (*vidhi*) and a restrictive injunction (*niyama*) are possible, the injunction alone is superior," only the root *krī* is intended to be included.
It does not apply to the root *kṛ*, because that [rule] serves a restrictive purpose (*niyamārthatva*),

whereas for the root *krī*, it serves a prescriptive purpose (*vidhyarthatva*). Furthermore, the inclusion of the root *iṅ* ("to go," Dhātupāṭha 1143) is also impossible, due to its association (*sāhacaryāt*) with *jayati*, which ends in a short vowel.

[Question: Is it the root ending in a short vowel that will be taken, and not the one ending in a long vowel? [Answer: Because of the subsequent contradiction regarding the word-form (*śabdapara-vipratiṣedha*).
It is accompanied by *ji* (to conquer), not by *krī* (to buy).
Or rather, the distinction is to be understood from the commentary (*vyākhyāna*), as in the example: "He prepares food" (*annaṃ sādhayati*).

The meaning is that he produces food. For here, the term *siddhi* (accomplishment) refers to a specific kind of knowledge regarding matters pertaining to the other world. He clarifies this meaning with the example: "The ascetic accomplishes [his goal]," and so forth.
Regarding the term "upasaṃhāraṇ" (bringing together), it means "accomplishing.
As for the question beginning with "Why does this not occur here? and so forth:

They think thus: "He who prepares food with the intention, 'I shall give it to Brāhmaṇas,' attains in another birth the fruit characterized by prosperity; therefore, since success regarding the goal of the next world exists here [in this world], there must be an exclusion (paryudāsa).
By stating that "the meaning of *sidhyati* here is 'accomplishment' (*niṣpatti*)," etc., he shows that its purpose pertains to this world.
"Food is the purpose of that [success]"—thus [it is said].
Because it is undertaken with reference to food;
"of that" means of food.
Regarding the phrase "but not success alone," one should connect it by changing the gender: "but not success alone pertaining to the next world. "Success" (siddhi) means accomplishment (niṣpatti).

The particle *iti* is used here in the sense of a reason. Why? Because the verbal root remains established. In this context, "establishment" does not refer to the other world; therefore, the substitution of *āt* is not excluded here.

It might be argued: "Even if the element (*dhātu*) does not directly serve the purpose of the next world, it certainly does so indirectly; therefore, a prohibition must indeed be applied. To this he says: "Directly," and so forth. If the meaning of the word *siddhyati* (is established) were such that its purpose for the next world is direct—that is, without mediation—then even in that case, the expression "pertaining to the next world" (*pāralaukika*) would not have fulfilled its function; consequently, it would apply even to that which serves the purpose of the next world only indirectly, lest the statement be rendered meaningless.

However, this [cognition], being directed toward an object established for the sake of the next world through a specific type of knowledge, has already fulfilled its purpose; therefore, it is simply unable to plunge into such a subject.
The meaning is that it cannot proceed with certainty regarding a subject of this kind.

Now, for what purpose is the mention of *siddhyateḥ* with the suffix *śyan*, rather than simply saying *sidheḥ*, since in this way the sūtra would be more concise? To this he says: “*siddhyateḥ*,” etc. Because of the continued application (*anuvṛtti*) of the rule [Pāṇini 6.1.44] *upadeśe*, the substitution of *āt* must occur even before the production of the suffix; therefore, at the time of prescribing the *āt* substitution, the condition of being followed by *lyap* is not possible. Consequently, he says “*lyapi viṣaye*” (in the domain of *lyap*), indicating that this is a locative of scope (*viṣaya-saptamī*).

Although *ec* was previously a qualifier of the subject (*prakṛta-viśeṣaṇa*), nevertheless, because this section concerns "instruction" (*upadeśa-ādhikāra*) and because *ec* is impossible for roots such as *mīnāti* at the stage of instruction, it is understood by implication to be a qualifier of the domain (*viṣaya-viśeṣaṇa*). Thus he says: "*ecaśca viṣaye*" ("and in the domain of *ec*").
He explains the meaning of "*upadeśe*" (in the [stage of] instruction) with the words beginning with "*prāk*" (previously), etc., as in "*pramāya*" (having measured).

The suffix *lyap* is applied by the rule *samāse 'nañ* [Pāṇini 7.1.37]. But what purpose is achieved by prescribing the substitution of *āt* (*āttva*) at the very stage of the original instruction (*upadeśāvasthā*), for the sake of which this *āttva* is performed at the stage of the original instruction? To this he says: "At the very stage of the original instruction," and so forth. [Otherwise], there would be the suffix *ac* prescribed by *erac* [Pāṇini 3.3.56] because the word ends in the vowel *i*, and the suffix *ghañ* [prescribed by Pāṇini 3.3.128] because it ends in the vowel *ā*, resulting in the forms *itvaraḥ* and *upadāyaḥ*.

Since the substitution of *āt* has been applied by the very rule of *upadeśa*, the condition for *ac* is established; thus, the general rule *ghañ* in the sense of "state" (*bhāve*) [Pāṇini 3.3.18] is indeed accomplished.
Then, by the rule *āto yuk ciṇ-kṛtoḥ* [Pāṇini 7.3.33], the augment *yuk* is added, resulting in the form *īṣadupādāna*.

In the state of instruction (*upadeśāvasthā*), when *āttva* has occurred, how is the suffix *yuc* established as an exception (*apavāda*)? [The answer is: "The mention of both of these by means of *yak* is recorded by the Teachers (*ācāryaiḥ*).
Now, why is this not understood as the mention of the root belonging to the *divādi* class by means of *śyan*? Precisely because of that very mention.
If it were intended here to specify only the *daivādika* [div] class, one would have made the specification "the *liṅ* with the suffix *anubandha* [ṅ]" (*anubandhena liṅ*).
Therefore, this specification for both [classes] is by means of the common, adventitious *yak*.
[The example is] "īṣatpramayaḥ."
The suffix *khal* is applied by the rule *īṣadduḥsuṣu* [Pāṇini 3.3.126];
the suffix *ac* is applied by the rule *erac* [Pāṇini 3.3.56]. Thus, the form *nimaya* occurs.
"But here, is [the desired form] established through the understanding of the option as being restricted (*vyavasthitavibhāṣā*) for the root *lī*? [The answer is:

"The mention of *lī* is merely illustrative; [the rule] is indeed established for the other two roots as well, because the mention of 'option' (*vibhāṣā*) connects with the preceding rule as well. Due to the understanding of the restricted option, the substitution of *ā* occurs invariably when the causative suffix *ṇiC* follows the roots in the senses of deceiving (*pralambhana*) and making timid (*śālīnīkaraṇa*)."
This is understood precisely from the rule regarding the established option (*vyavasthitavibhāṣā*):

"he causes to boast" (*ullāpayate*), "he causes to deny" (*apalāpayate*). The middle voice (*ātmanepada*) is applied by the rule *liyaḥ sammānana-śālīnīkaraṇayoḥ* [Pāṇini 1.3.70]. As for "he ate greedily" (*cikhāda*).

When the *guṇa* substitution is applied by the rule *pugantalaghūpadhasya* [Pāṇini 7.3.86], the vowel becomes *ā*. If *khād* also occurs in the sense of *khid*, then this grammatical rule (*yoga*) could be omitted; for from *khād* one would derive *cakhāda*, and from *khid* one would derive *cikheda*. [The example] is "apagāram apagāram."

The doubling [of the word] occurs by the rule *ābhīkṣṇye dve bhavataḥ* (Vārttika 887). This was not stated in that specific location (Pāṇini 6.1.48) for the purpose of ensuring that [the repetition] does not occur constantly. If this root *vā* (Dhātupāṭha 1050), meaning "to go" or "to blow," is used in the sense of "procreation," then the application of the rule can indeed be explained; for from *vāti* we will have *vāpayati*, and from *vīyati* we will have *vāyayati*. Regarding the phrase *hetubhaye*: he states that this is a genitive compound (*pañcamīsamāsa*) by saying, "the fear which arises from that."

What, then, is the fear from that? He says: "That [fear] of which... and so forth. Now, why does the augment *ṣuk* not occur in the case of the alternative view (*attva-pakṣe*)? For there is indeed an application here as well, based on the principle: "A form modified in one part is treated as non-different [from the original]" (Vyāḍiparibhāṣā 16). To this he says: "And that... and so forth.

For in the rule [Pāṇini 7.3.40], the instruction is made by joining *bhī* with *ī*—that is, *bhī-ī*—as a single ligature (*praśliṣṭa*), so that the *ṣuk* augment may apply only to what ends in the vowel *ī*, and not to that which ends in the vowel *ā*.

Likewise, there is the inclusion of *lī*; even under the alternative view that it undergoes *ātva*, the augment *nuk* does not apply by the rule "after *lī* and *lū*, *nuk* and *luk* optionally [are applied] when meaning 'melting' or 'flowing'" (Pāṇini 7.3.39).

That this is due solely to the mention of the elided *īkāra* has been explained incidentally. Regarding the phrase "because of the similarity of the root-meanings with the word *bhaya*," etc.: the meaning of the root *bhī* and that of *smi* are both similar, as they both consist in a modification of the mind.

Both of these are characterized by mental agitation; therefore, that which is common to both is their similarity (*sādṛśya*). Consequently, the meaning of the root *smi* (to smile) is expressed here by the word "fear" (*bhaya*).
For it is observed that words function with reference to something other than their primary meaning on account of similarity, as in the expression: "The boy is a lion."
But what is the reason for explaining it in this way? To this he says: "For not," and so forth.
The [rule] *[[6.1.56]]* is understood to carry over (*anuvartate*).
And this qualification is stated.
Furthermore, the root *smi* (to smile) does not have its primary meaning [of smiling] in the context of fear.

Therefore, it is understood that by some kind of semantic necessity (*sāmarthya*) or similarity, the very sense of the root *smi* is here denoted by the word *bhaya* (fear). [The forms] "ruṣṭā" and "draṣṭā":
when the augment *um* is applied, there is the substitution of *yaṇ*; then, by the rule *vraścādi* (Pāṇini 8.2.36), there is the substitution of *ṣ*.
"This [rule] is an exception (*apavāda*) to the *guṇa* substitution for a light penultimate vowel," and so forth.

Now, an exception occurs only when there is no possibility [of both rules applying simultaneously]; however, there is indeed a possibility that both might occur, in which case the augment *am* would apply after the *guṇa* has been performed. This is not so; for the *guṇa* is prescribed as a general rule (*sāmānya*), whereas the augment *am* is prescribed as a specific rule (*viśeṣa*). And a specific rule sets aside a general rule, just as in the example: "Let curd be given to the Brāhmaṇas, but buttermilk to Kauṇjinya."

Just as the specific injunction to give buttermilk (*takradāna*) overrides the general injunction to give curd (*dadhidāna*), so too here the substitution of *guṇa* is appropriately overridden by the *āgama*. Thus, in the forms *arukṣīt* and *adrākṣīt*: [by Pāṇini 8.3.59] there is the substitution of *ṣ*; [by 7.3.96] there is the augment *iṭ*; [by 7.2.3] there is *vṛddhi*; and [by 8.2.41] there is the substitution of *k*.
"Vṛddhi occurs when *am* is applied.
Now, why does *vṛddhi* not occur even earlier? To this he says: "But the former is sublated.

For just as the general rule for *guṇa* is sublated by the specific application of the augment *am*, so too is *vṛddhi*—which is likewise generally prescribed—sublated once *am* has been applied. However, because of the principle that "what is established [by a subsequent rule] prevails," that *vṛddhi* also takes place.

The augment *ām* does not occur when a *guṇa* [substitution] has been applied, because the cause [for the augment] has already been provided. Indeed, once the *ām* augment has been applied, it is not possible for the *upadhā* vowel to become light and thus undergo *guṇa*. Now, why does it not occur here in the case of *rajjusṛḍbhyām* and *devadṛgbhyām*? Even though there is the governing rule for verbal roots (*dhātu*), since it is said that "words ending in *kvip* do not lose their status as verbal roots" (Vyāḍipāda 132), one might expect the *ām* augment to apply by relying on the fact that the suffix *bhyām* is added to a form ending in *kvip*. To this, he says: "Of a verbal root," etc. Furthermore, what is the reason that the substitute [the whole word] is not desired [to be treated as a verbal root]? To this, he says: "For that too," etc.
Since the word *śiras* is also employed in the Vedic language (*chandas*), this substitution is not applied.

For if the substitution were to take place, the word *śiras* would not be used in the Vedic context, because the original term (*sthānin*) possesses the property of being subject to cessation [upon substitution].
However, if the phrase "optionally" (*anyatarasyām*) is understood to carry over here, then there is no fault even when the substitution occurs.
Regarding the word *śīrṣā*:
by [Pāṇini 6.4.7], there is a long vowel. In some places, it is read as *śīṣrṇā*; that should be understood as being in the instrumental case.
> [[6.4.134]] There is elision of the vowel *i*.

The form *śīrṣṇaḥ* is in the genitive singular. Here too, suffixes beginning with *śas* are taken as the cause [for the substitution], and the point is that these are not possible without a base (*prakṛti*).
When those [bases] have been prescribed by other rules, the substitutes such as *pada* and so forth are understood to be enjoined.

Nor does this rule result in the undesirable application of substitutes due to the non-mention of the original bases (*sthānin*), because when these [substitutes] are being enjoined, suffixes such as *śas* imply a corresponding nominal base (*prakṛti*) in the sense of "foot" and so on, which is derived from the same root. Thus he says: "*pāda-danta-nāsikā*" and so forth.
In the examples beginning with *pada*, the forms *padaḥ* and *dataḥ* end in *śas*.
*yūṣṇaḥ*, *doṣṇaḥ*, *yaknaḥ*, and *śaknaḥ* are in the nominative singular;
by [Pāṇini 6.4.134], there is the elision of the vowel *a*.
*Māsi*, *niśi*, and *āsani* are in the locative singular.
In the word *āsanī*, the elision of the vowel *a* does not occur optionally due to the rule *vibhāṣāṅiśyoḥ* [Pāṇini 6.4.136].
The remaining forms end in the third case singular.
The words *pādau* and *nāsike* end in the nominative dual.
Why do they continue [the application of] the term *anyatarasyām* (optionally)? To this he says: "Therefore, even *pāda* and the others," and so forth.

Because *pāda* and the others are also employed, they continue [the application of] *anyatarasyām*. With the intention that if the word *prabhṛti* were taken in the sense of a fixed limit (*vyavasthā*), the substitution would not be established for anything other than those beginning with *śas*, he says: "The word *prabhṛti* has the sense of 'kind' (*prakāra*).
[The example is: *doṣaṇī*.
Some say: in the dual number of the nominative case (*prathamā-dvivacana*), there is the substitution of *doṣan*, and for the suffix *auṅ* there is the substitution of *śī*.

Others, however, say: this is a word ending in the feminine suffix *ṅīp*, namely *doṣaṇī*; when the suffix *ṅīp* is to be applied, there is the substitution of *doṣan*, and then [the suffix] *ṅīp* is added by the rule *ṛnnebhyo ṅīp* (Pāṇini 4.1.5). [The form] *nasyam* [is derived as follows]:
the suffix *yat* is added in the sense of "beneficial" (*hitārtha*) to a word denoting a part of the body, according to the rule *śarīrāvayavādyat* (Pāṇini 5.1.6).
The word "nastaḥ" [is derived from] the suffix *tasi*. The word "naḥkṣudraḥ" [is derived from] *naḥ*.
The term *nāsikya* is a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "one whose nose is small. Regarding the expression "*nāsikyo varṇaḥ*" (a nasal sound),
the suffix *yat* is applied in the sense of "belonging to" (*bhavārtha*) according to Pāṇini 5.1.6, *śarīrāvayavāt*.

In the word *nāsikyaṃ nagaram*, the suffix *yat* is applied in the sense of "beneficial for" (*hitārthe*). In *siñcati*, the augment *num* is applied by [Pāṇini 7.1.59]. In *ṣoḍaśa*, [the substitution of ṣa for ṣaṣ occurs].

In the case of *ṣaḍvā daśa vā asya* ("six or ten of this"), a *bahuvrīhi* compound is formed by [Pāṇini 2.2.25] *saṃkhyāvyaya-*, etc., and the suffix *ṅac* is applied at the end of the compound by [Pāṇini 5.4.73] *saṃkhyeye ṅac*, etc. Regarding *ṣoḍan*:
it is a *bahuvrīhi* meaning "one who has six teeth," and the word *danta* is replaced by *datṛ* by [Pāṇini 5.4.141].

By the rule *ṣaṣa uttvaṃ datṛdaśadhāsūttarapadādeḥ ṣṭutvaṃ ca* (Vārttika 765), there is the substitution of *u* for *ṣaṣ*, and the substitution of *ṣṭu* (i.e., *ḍ*) for the initial letter of the subsequent member—namely, the letter *d*.
Thus, we have *ṣaṇḍaḥ*.
This is an underived (*avyutpanna*) nominal stem (*prātipadika*).

Regarding the word *ṣaḍika*: [the name] *ṣaḍaṅgulidatta* is one who has been shown compassion (*anukampita*). The suffix *ṭhac* is applied according to Pāṇini 5.3.78, *bahvaco manuṣyanāmnaṣṭhac*, because it is a human name with many syllables. Then, by Pāṇini 5.3.83, *ṭhājādāvūrdhvaṃ dvitīyādacaḥ*, there is the elision of the portion of the word *aṅgulidatta* starting from the second vowel. Now, one might object: since the term *dhātu* (root) is understood here as a carry-over from Pāṇini 6.1.8, *liṭi dhātoḥ*, what is the purpose of mentioning *dhātu* again here? In that case, this serves to indicate that the previous restriction (*tad*) has ceased to apply.

Indeed, if that [the status of being part of a verbal root] were to apply here as well, then this elision [prescribed by Pāṇini 6.1.64, *lopo vyor vali*] would also be understood to apply only to what is a constituent of a verbal root;

consequently, it would occur only in cases such as *knūyī* (DhP 4.85), with the suffix *kta*, yielding *knūtaḥ*, and *kṣmayī* (DhP 4.86), with the suffix *kta*, yielding *kṣmātaḥ*; however, it would not occur in cases such as *godharaḥ* or *pacerañ*.

But even so, the mention of "root" (*dhātu*) is indeed purposeless, because the term "instruction" (*upadeśa*) continues to apply, and there is no instruction for nominal stems (*prātipadika*). For what, then, is the instruction? It is the roots. This is not the case; by the inclusion of the word "instruction," the letter *ṣ* is qualified [by the context of] the governing rule on "instruction. And the letter *ṣ* of the root *ṣaṣ* is indeed an "instruction," because it is recited in the rule: "The substitution of *u* for *ṣaṣ*, and the initial letter of the subsequent member [becomes *ṣ*] after *datṛ* and *daśan*" (Vārttika 765). Therefore, the mention of "root" must be made.
Regarding "kaṣati": it is listed in the *bhvādi* class among the group of roots beginning with *kaṣa-sidha*, having the meaning of "to injure. Regarding "laṣati": [it is likewise].
Regarding the roots *laṣ* (desire) and *kānta* (to love) [Dhātupāṭha 888], there is the inclusion of the initial [ṣ].

Now, one might object: "Since this will not occur here by the very force of the original instruction (*upadeśa*), otherwise that instruction would be purposeless. This is not so; for there is another purpose for the original instruction. What is it? It is so that the mention of *keṣa* in rule [8.4.18] does not apply; thus, in forms such as *leṣatuḥ* and *leṣuḥ*, the substitution of *ṣ* may correctly take place.

But for what purpose are the *ṣa*-sounds taught [separately], rather than teaching the *sa*-sounds alone? Would it not be the case that in this way the *sūtra* would not need to be composed? To this he says: "of the substitute (*ādeśa*) and the suffix (*pratyaya*)" and so forth.
The "establishment of *ṣatva*" (*ṣatvavyavasthā*) means the rule regarding *ṣatva*.
This is for the purpose that the establishment of *ṣatva* should apply only to those [substitutes] beginning with *sah*, as prescribed by [Pāṇini 8.3.59].

Some [sounds] beginning with *ṣ* have been taught; otherwise, a separate effort would have to be made for the sake of the *ṣ*-ness of *sah* and so forth. And that [effort] would be cumbersome—this is the intended meaning.
Although there is no doubt regarding those beginning with *ṣ*, there certainly is regarding those beginning with *s*.

For here it is not known whether those [roots] which have been pronounced with the substitution of *s* for *ṣ* by the rule *ṣopadeśā eva santaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.1.64) are intended, or whether it refers to those that originally begin with *s*. Thus, being in doubt, he asks: "Which, then, are they?
[The answer is: "Those as they are recited. Those beginning with *ṣ* are to be understood as *ṣopadeśas* precisely as they are recited in proximity [to this context].
"Those which have 'a' or a dental [consonant] as their final member," and so forth.
Those whose final members (*para*) are 'a' or a dental are "those ending in 'a' or a dental. Here, the word *para* refers to a constituent part (*avayava*).

And since that status of being "final" (*ac-antyayoḥ paratvam*) is understood as being relative to other constituent parts [of a word], it is understood—due to proximity—to be relative to the letter *s*. This is indicated by the rule: *smi-svidi-svañji-svapayaś-ca* (Pāṇini 6.1.60).

Here, *ṣmiṅ īṣaddhasane* (Dhātupāṭha 948), *ñiṣvidā gātraprakṣaraṇe* (Dhātupāṭha 1188), *ṣvanja pariṣvaṅge* (Dhātupāṭha 976), and *ñiṣvap śaye* (Dhātupāṭha 1068) are mentioned by their own forms; for the letters *m* and *v* do not possess the quality of being final vowels or semivowels (*aj-dantyatva*).

Some read *svadi* in place of *svidi*, as in *smi-svi-svidi-svañji-svapayaśca*; for them, since the root *svad*—as in the Dhātupāṭha entry "*svada* [or *ṣvada*] in the sense of tasting" (*svadir api ṣopadeśa eva*)—is indeed a *ṣopadeśa* root, it is excluded by the rule:
"except for *sṛp*, *sṛj*, *stṛ*, *styai*, *sekṛ*, *sṛ*, and *vṛ*."

Excluding *gam* and *suplṛ* in the sense of "going" (DhP 982, 983), *sṛj* in the sense of "emission" (DhP 1178), *stṛñ* in the sense of "covering" (DhP 1252), *styai* in the sense of "sound and collection" (DhP 911, 910), and *sekṛ*, *ruokṛ*, *śrakṛ*, and *ślakṛ*—all of which have the meaning of "motion" (DhP 81, 82, 84, 85)—as well as *sṛ* in the sense of "going" (DhP 935), those other roots ending in *aj* (vowels) that follow these are *ṣopadeśa*.
Regarding the term *subdhātu* and so forth:
a *subdhātu* is one that ends in *kyac* and the like.

The root *ṣṭhiv* is listed as "in the sense of ejecting" (*nirasane*, Dhātupāṭha 560). Regarding the statement "*ṣvakka*, *vukka*, *makkatikka*, *ṭikka*, *ṭīkka*, *vagi*, *lagi*—these have their prohibition to be stated," the meaning is that this must be explained.

The explanation here is as follows: First, in the case of *subdhātu* (a nominal root), in forms such as *ṣoḍīyati*, the initial *ṣakāra* is not part of the verbal root itself; likewise, the *hrādi* group constitutes a suffixal element.
Furthermore, a suffixal element is something that initiates [a formation], and a *subdhātu* is initiated by a *kyac* affix following a form ending in a *sup* suffix.

Nor does it begin with the phoneme *ṣ* [as a separate initial sound], because it is not composed of a different phoneme; how then could it have *ṣ* as its initial? However, words such as *saha* and others are indeed commenced by phonemes beginning with *ṣ*, so it is logical that they have *ṣ* as their initial. As for *ṣṭhivu* as well, it does not [begin with *ṣ*] due to a specific grammatical exception (*nipātana*). What is that exception? It is the rule: "In place of the roots *ṣṭivu*, *klamu*, and *camu*, [the substitute *ṣ* occurs] before an affix marked with *ś*" (Pāṇini 7.3.75).

For whatever undergoes the substitution of *s* (satva), this [treatise] pronounces it as having already undergone that *s*-substitution in the specific rules (*pradeśa*), just as in the rule: "In place of *sthā* and *dhvṛ*, [there is *i* and *u*]" (Pāṇini 1.2.17).

It does not occur because it has been excluded by the rule "also after *ṣva* and *kka*, [the suffixes] preceded by vowels (*ac*) or dentals (*dantya*) [do not apply]. Since the letter *v* is both dental and labial (*dantyauṣṭhya*), it is not included by the mention of "vowels or dentals" (*ajdantyagrahaṇena*).

Alternatively, is it because of the word "or" (*vā*) [in the rule]? Then it will not apply to *ṣṭhivu* and *ṣvakk*; as for the letter *y*, however, it is not heard [in pronunciation] because it is mentioned as elided (*luptanirdiṣṭatvāt*).

Alternatively, the term *anyatarasyām* (optionally) is understood here as being carried over from a previous rule, and it is understood as a *vyavasthitavibhāṣā* (restricted option); therefore, [the substitution] does not apply to *sub*, verbal roots, and so forth. In the word *ṣaṣṭhīvati*, the long vowel is applied by the rule *ṣṭhivuklamucamāṃ śiti* [Pāṇini 7.3.75].
Regarding the word *ṣvakkate*:
the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) is applied because the root begins with an unaccented vowel (*anudāttettva*).

Now, as for the second letter of the root *ṣṭhiv*, is it intended to be *ṭha* or *tha*? If it were *ṭha*, then the form *ṭeṣṭhīṣyate* would be established, but *teṣṭhīvyate* would not be established; for, according to [Pāṇini 8.4.54], the closest substitute (*antaratama*) for the position of *tha* would be *ṭha* itself.

Now, if the letter *th* were used, then the form *ṭeṣṭhīvyate* would be established; however, the form *ṭeṣṭhīvyate* is not established because, due to the principle of closest proximity (*āntaratamya*), when the letter *th* is prescribed, only the letter *t* would result in its place. Therefore, he says: "of this [root] *ṣṭhivu*," and so forth, so that the two forms of the root may both be realized. Some disciples were instructed by the Teacher that "this is the letter *ṭh*."
Others, however, have been led to understand this point as follows: "This letter *tha* is heard as *ṭha* by virtue of being a *ṣṭu*-substitution.
Both of these [interpretations] serve a purpose.
Still others say: "The root *ṣṭhivu* is taught again among the *divādi* roots; therein, one [form] has the second letter *tha*, while the other has the letter *ṭha*."
"Regarding *teṣṭhīvyata*," this is a remainder (*śeṣa*). "This [application] of *subdhātu* is also not desired," for the same reason as before. "[The rule] *upasargādasamāse’pi*," and so forth.
In this context, the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) should be understood according to what precedes:

*nṛtī-nandi*, etc. *nṛtī* (in the sense of "movement of the limbs," Dhātupāṭha 1116); *ṭunadi* (in the sense of "prosperity," Dhātupāṭha 67); *nard* and *gard* (in the sense of "sound," Dhātupāṭha 56, 57); *nakka* and *vakka* [or *dhakka*] (in the sense of "destruction," Dhātupāṭha 1593, 1594); *naṭ* (in the sense of "throbbing" [or "shaking," *avaspandane*], Dhātupāṭha 1545), which is formed with the causative suffix *ṇic*; *nāthṛ* and *nādhṛ* (in the senses of "request, affliction, and benediction," Dhātupāṭha 6, 7); and *nṛ* (in the sense of "guiding").

(Dhātupāṭha 809, 1495) || One might have the misconception that this elision of *v* is prescribed for the root itself (*dhātu*) alone—thinking that the term "root" (*dhātu*) from [Pāṇini 6.1.8], *liṭi dhātoḥ*, continues here by the force of its observed recurrence (*dṛṣṭānuvṛtti*)—in order to dispel that, he says: "That which was introduced as 'of the root' (*dhātoḥ'), etc.
The form *didivān* is derived from the root *div* with the suffix *kvasu*.
Regarding *ūyī*: it means "to weave" (*tantusantāne*, Dhātupāṭha 483). Regarding *knūyī*:
it means "to sound" (*śabde*, Dhātupāṭha 485). [The word] *gaudera* [is derived from this].
> [[4.1.129]] For *ḍha*, there is the substitution of *ey*, and the elision of the letter *ya*.
Regarding "they might cook" (*paceran*):
there is the elision of the *u* of *sīyuṭ*.
"Jīveḥ" refers to the root *jīv* in the sense of "sustaining life" (Dhātupāṭha 562). "Riuvāveḥ" refers to [the same].
This is from the root *riuv* (meaning "to go" and "to dry up," Dhātupāṭha 1109).
In the word *āruomāṇam*,
the suffix *manin* is applied according to the Uṇādi rules.

But how can this be an illustration here, given that [the substitute] is subsequent? Is it not because of its strength, according to the rule *vārṇād āṅgaṃ balīyaḥ* (Vyākaraṇa-paribhāṣā 39), whereby it is more powerful? Should there not be the substitution of *ūṭh* here by the rule *chvoḥ śūḍ anunāsike ca* (Pāṇini 6.4.19)? To this he says: *uṇādayo bahulam*, etc.

Because the inclusion of the term *bahula* (in the rule) serves to allow for exceptions to all grammatical prescriptions, this undesirable consequence does not arise. When the elision (*lopa*) is applied after [the vowel], it must be pronounced with one and a half morae (*adhyardhamātra*) following the letter *pakāra*; for a vowel (*akāra*) consists of one mora, while a *visarjanīya* is less by half a mora. However, when the elision is applied before [the vowel], two morae must be pronounced, because the vowel *o* consists of two morae.
In that case, for the sake of brevity, it would be more appropriate to apply the elision only after [the vowel]; why then is it applied first? To this, he says: "First," and so forth.

But another [view] holds that the prior mention of the grammatical operation (*kārya*) is logical, followed by the mention of the cause (*kāraṇa*). Thus, he presents the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*): "Since the mention of *vy-*, etc., should have been made first, for what purpose is the mention of *lopa* (elision) made? This, however, is incorrect, because in the rule *lugaṇiñoḥ* [Pāṇini 2.4.58], the grammatical operation is also mentioned first.
Regarding the rule *verapṛktalopāt* [Pāṇini 6.1.67], etc.:

when the suffix *kvip* is applied to the roots *kaṇḍūyati* and *lolūyati*, the elision of the semivowel (*vali lopa*) would occur first. Why? Because it is more powerful (*paratvāt*) and, being obligatory (*nityatvāt*) due to its application regardless of whether the other rule has already taken effect or not (*kṛtākṛtaprasaṅgitvena*), the elision of the *apṛkta* suffix *vi* (*verapṛktalopa*) alone would occur first.

And while this [substitution] exists, because of the absence of the cause (*nimitta*), would there not be an absence of the *pratyaya-lakṣaṇa* (the grammatical operation conditioned by a suffix) based on the *varṇa* (the phoneme), such that the elision (*lopa*) after *val* would not occur? Therefore, the mention of "elision" (*lopa*) is made first—so that the elision after *val* may indeed occur first.
By mentioning "elision" first, this meaning is indicated: even when there is the elision of *ṛkta*, the elision after *val* must be performed first. As in the example:
*kaṇḍūḥ*.

> [[6.4.48]] There is elision of the vowel *i*. According to the rule *kvilugupadhātvacaṅgaparaniskutveṣu na sthānivat* (1.1.59 vārttika 2), the status of the *sthānivadbhāva* (the treatment as if the original element were present) does not apply to the vowel *a*; thus, there is no elision of the *v* sound (*vali lopaḥ*). Now, why is there no elision of the *vakāra* (the letter *v*) in *vraścakaḥ* and *vraścanaḥ* when followed by the *repha* (the letter *r*), which is a *val* sound? To this he says: *vraścādīnām*, etc.
If there were also elision (*lopa*) of these [consonants], the pronunciation of the letter *va* would be purposeless.
Therefore, by virtue of its being pronounced, there is no elision of the *va* in roots such as *vraśc* when followed by a *val* (semivowel or consonant).

It might be argued: "In forms such as *vṛścati* and *vavraśca*, the letter *va* should indeed be heard after the application of *samprasāraṇa* and *halādiśeṣa*; so how can the instruction [of the letter *va*] be considered useless? To this he says: "*vṛścati*," etc.

Just as there is the occurrence of elision (*lopa*) in cases such as *vraścaka*, so too is there [elision] in cases such as *vṛścati* even after operations such as *samprasāraṇa* have been performed; for that [elision] is considered non-existent (*asiddha*) due to its being "external" (*bahiraṅga*). In that context, *samprasāraṇa* is external because it depends upon a *ṅit* affix; the substitution of the first consonant for both in the reduplication (*halādiśeṣa*) is external because it depends upon the reduplication; however, the elision of *y* before *val* (*yalopa*) is internal (*antaraṅga*) because it depends upon the mere phoneme (*varṇa*).

Therefore, in every case, the elision of the letter *va* in the root *vraśca* would result. Yet, this [elision] is taught; thus, by the force of that teaching, it will not occur—this remains established. Regarding the phrase "of *vi*" (*veḥ*) and so forth: since there is no other *vi* besides those beginning with *kvip* that possesses the designation *apṛkta*, only those beginning with *kvip* are understood. But how is it justified to understand *kvip* and the others in a general sense when it is stated simply as "*vi*," given that these possess specific indicatory letters (*anubandhas*) such as *k* and so on? To dispel this objection, it is said: "setting aside the specific indicatory letters."

In the case of *brāhmaṇahā* and *bhrūṇahā*, [the substitution of *ha* for *ghna* occurs]. In *ghṛtaspṛk*, there is lengthening by [Pāṇini 6.4.13], and the substitution of *k* for *p* (i.e., *kutva*) occurs by [Pāṇini 8.2.62].
Regarding the term *ardhabhāk*, [the substitution of] *k* occurs by [Pāṇini 8.2.30].

In the case of *darvi-* and so forth, it can be stated that the elision does not occur precisely because of the inclusion of the word *bahulam* in [Pāṇini 3.3.1]; therefore, [the mention here] is for the sake of detailed exposition (*prapañca*).

Or, the mention of "unmixed" (*apṛkta*) is for the sake of variety. If the term *lopa* were understood here according to its technical (śāstrīya) meaning [as "non-perception"], then it would not be possible for it to be construed in grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with *hal*, which ends in the nominative case;
for the technical meaning of the word *lopa* is "absence of perception" (*adarśana*), and there is no such thing as the "perception of a consonant" (*hal*).
Nor can the ablative case in *hal-ṅy-ābbhyaḥ* be taken as establishing a genitive sense for the nominative *hal*.

Alternatively, by virtue of contextual implication (*sāmarthya*), the word *hal* may be transformed into a genitive form; thus, it can be conceived that the genitive form will be connected with the word *lopa*. [But] this is not possible because its purpose has not yet been fulfilled, as it is impossible for the nominative case to become a genitive. Having considered this, he says: "In this context," and so forth.
"It is called *lopa* because it is elided" (*lupyate*); the suffix *ghañ* is used in the sense of the object (*karman*).
By this, he demonstrates that the word *lopa* possesses meaning through its worldly sense.
"It is elided" (*lupyate*) means "it is obstructed" (*nirudhyate*).

Through the word *lopa*, which is meaningful by virtue of its worldly sense and functions as a karmasādhana (an object-oriented derivation), the relationship of qualifier and qualified between *ha* and [the word *lopa*] is established.
For by the word *lopa* (elision), the mere phoneme being elided is denoted;
and by the rule *sutisyapṛktam hal*,
that very [phoneme] is further specified.

Regarding the term "from a long vowel" (*dīrghāt*): this qualifies *ṅī* and *āp* alone, because they are possible [in that context] and do not deviate [from the condition]; it does not qualify a stem ending in a consonant (*halanta*), because such a case is impossible. For example: *ukhāsrat*, *parṇadhvat*.

The roots *ruāṃs* and *dhvaṃs* mean "to fall down" (*adhaḥpatana*; see Dhātupāṭha 754, 755). In the examples *ukhāyāṃ ruāṃsate parṇāni* ("the leaves fall into the pot") and *dhvaṃsate*, the suffix *kvip* is applied. By the rule *aniditām* [Pāṇini 6.4.24], there is the substitution of *c* for the final consonant, which here becomes the letter *t*.
Regarding the word *kumārī*: the feminine suffix *ṅīṣ* is applied by the rule *kumāri* [Pāṇini 4.1.20].
"Gaurī"—
[this is derived] by [the rule] Pāṇini 4.1.41, which prescribes the suffix *ṅīṣ*.
"Śāṅgaravī"— [likewise].
By [Pāṇini 4.1.73], the suffix *ḍāp* is applied;
thus, "kārīṣagandhyā. By [Pāṇini 4.1.74], the suffix *cāp* is applied after a reduplicated (*yaṅ*) stem.

"Only after a word ending in a consonant (hal) do the elision of *ti* and the elision of *si* occur. Now, [the author] indicates by means of the letter *e* in "after a stem ending in *ṅī* or *āp*" that this does not apply after a stem ending in *ṅī* or *āp*; for *ti* and *si* cannot follow a stem ending in *ṅī* or *āp*, since those two are prescribed only after a verbal root (*dhātu*).
For example: "abibhar bhavān" (you carried).
When the substitution of *r* for *ra* has been applied, there is elision of the *ti*. In the form "ajāgarbhavān," the *guṇa* substitution [is applied] by [Pāṇini 7.3.85].
The suffix *bhavān* is employed as an auxiliary (*anuprayoga*) for the manifestation of the word *ti*.

Regarding the form *abhinaḥ*: from the root *bhid*, there is the *laṅ* affix; by [Pāṇini 8.2.75] *daśca*, there is the substitution of *r*; by [Pāṇini 6.1.113], there is the substitution of *u*; and with the vowel *a* of *inam*, there is the substitution of the single substitute [guṇa] by [Pāṇini 6.1.84] *ād guṇaḥ*, followed by the substitution of the preceding form [pūrvarūpa] by [Pāṇini 6.1.109].
Regarding "grāmaṇīḥ": [the word] *grāmaṇī* is derived from the sense "he leads the village" (*grāmaṃ nayati*) by means of the suffix *kvip* according to the rule *satsūdviṣa-* (Pāṇini 3.2.61).

Regarding *niṣkauśāmbiḥ*: [it means] "one who has gone out from Kauśāmbī"; this is a *prādi*-compound (*pra-ādi-samāsa*), and the shortening of the vowel occurs according to the rule *pra-ādibhyaḥ* (Pāṇini 5.4.48).
Regarding "atikhaṭavaḥ":
it means "one who has transcended the bed," as in the previous examples; once the compound is formed, the vowel is shortened.
Regarding "abhaitsīt": [it is derived from the root *bhid* with the prefix *a-*].
By the rule *vadavraja* [Pāṇini 7.2.3], there is *vṛddhi*, and the augment *iṭ* is applied because it is an *apṛkta* suffix.

But is it not the case that since the term *si* is mentioned in a general sense, the mention of *sic* is also included; therefore, is this counter-example (*pratyudāharaṇa*) not inappropriate? To this he replies: "Of that which is accompanied by *tiṅ*" and so forth. Because of association with the word *tiṅ*, the mention of *si* refers only to *tiṅ* and not to *sic*; what is inappropriate about this?
Regarding the word *bibheda*:
here, the vowel *a* of the suffix *ṇal* is not a *hal* (consonant), but rather an *apṛkta* (single-letter) vowel; therefore, it is not elided. [Objection:
"This is already established by the rule for the elision of a final *saṃyoga*."
The phrase "such as 'rājā' etc. is the example, with "is" being the understood remainder [of the sentence]. Why, then, is it not established? To this he says: "rājā, takṣā," and so forth.

Just as in the case of *pacan*, because the elision of the final consonant of the conjunction (*saṃyogāntalopa*) is considered non-existent (*asiddha*), the elision of the *n* does not occur; likewise, it would not occur in cases such as *rājā* and *takṣā*.
The non-application (*asiddhatva*) of the elision of the final consonant of a conjunct (*saṃyogāntalopa*) is the indirect cause here.

For when that [elision] exists, the preceding element does not receive the designation "word" (*pada*) with respect to what follows it, due to the prohibition in [Pāṇini 1.4.17], *asarvanāmasthāne*. And when that [designation] is absent, the elision of *n* (*nalopa*), which is prescribed for a "word," would not occur; and if the elision of *n* did not occur, forms such as *rāja-* and so forth would not be established.

Regarding the term "datvam": it should be connected with the preceding phrase "it would not occur. For even the substitution of *d* for *t* would not take place, because the elision of a final conjunct (*saṃyogāntalopa*) is considered non-existent (*asiddha*), and thus the designation of a word (*pada-saṃjñā*) would not apply.

Alternatively—the elision of the final member of a conjunct (*saṃyogāntalopa*) does not apply here at all; for since the elision of the initial member of a conjunct (*saṃyogādilopa*), prescribed by the rule *skoḥ saṃyogādyor ante ca* [Pāṇini 8.2.29], serves as an exception (*apavāda*), that alone would take effect—as in the case of *kāṣṭhaṃ takṣṇoti* becoming *kāṣṭhatak*—and when that occurs, the substitution of *ru* and the visarga for the *s* of the case-ending would follow. So how could there be the substitution of *da*? Regarding the phrase "the substitution of *u*" (*uttvam*), it is understood that it would not occur, because even this [substitution] is rendered non-applicable due to the fact that the elision of the final member of the conjunct is considered as if it had not taken place (*asiddha*).
For one who has not yet acquired the designation [of being a *saṃyoga*], it would not apply;
this is because of the restriction [imposed] by the rule "after *r*, [the *s*] of a *saṃyoga*" (P.
8.2.24), since [the desired result] is already established by that very rule [P. 8.2.23].

Regarding the statement "because of the restriction [imposed] by *rātsasya* [Pāṇini 8.2.24]," this is because [the desired result] is already established by that very rule [8.2.23]. This [rule 8.2.24,
*rātsasya*], serves as a restrictive rule (*niyamārtha*) so that the elision (*lopa*) may occur only after *r* and *l*, and not after anything else.

Consequently, in the case of *tataścābibharbhavān*, the elision of the letter *t* would simply not occur. Therefore, since [the desired form] is not established by the "elision of a final consonant cluster" (*saṃyogāntalopa*), the elision of the final consonant (*halanta*) is prescribed.
For the sake of easily grasping this very point, the rule beginning with "if there were elision of a final consonant cluster" (*saṃyogāntasya lope hi*) and so forth is stated.
The introduction of the summary verse:
the word *hi* indicates the reason.
Why? Because if the elision of a final consonant (*saṃyogāntalopa*) were resorted to, grammatical operations such as the elision of *n* (*nalopa*) and so forth would not be established.

Furthermore—for you, who advocate for the elision of a final consonant in a conjunct (*saṃyogāntalopa*), there would be no elision at all of the *t* following the *r* in forms such as *abibhar-bhavān* and *ajagar-bhavān*.

Therefore, the elision of *su*, *ti*, and *si* is prescribed after a [stem] ending in a *val* (consonant). As for the rule "and when *hal* [follows]," it is understood that the word "occurs" (*vartate*) is required [to complete the sense].

If *hal* were not carried over [from the previous rule], then when *he kuṇḍa-su* is established, after *lopa* is applied, *ambhāva* would occur because it is subsequent; then, by the elision of the vowel *a* according to *ataḥ* [6.4.110] and the lengthening of the vowel by *supi ca* [7.3.102], the undesirable form *he kuṇḍam* would result—this is the intended meaning. As for the statement "the term *apṛkta* is not governed [here]," the sense is that if *apṛkta* were carried over here, then in *he kuṇḍa*, the elision would not occur because the designation *apṛkta* would be absent.

How, then, is it known that "uncombined" (*apṛkta*) does not carry over here? To this he says: "And thus," and so forth. The word *tathā* (and thus) indicates a reason. Because the term "uncombined" was employed in the preceding rule, it is understood that there is no carrying over of the term "uncombined" into this present section; for otherwise, since the term "uncombined" would have carried over from [Pāṇini 6.1.67], the term "uncombined" would not have been stated again in the preceding rule.
"If it belongs to the *sambuddhi* [case-ending]"—the meaning is:
"if it is connected with the *sambuddhi*.
By this, he shows that the word *sambuddheḥ* possesses a partitive genitive (*avayava-ṣaṣṭhī*).
In the cases of "he agne" and "he vāyo," [the rule] "guṇa for a short vowel" (Pāṇini 7.3.108) applies. In the cases of "he nadi" and "he vadhu," [the same applies].
The shortening [of the vowel] occurs by the rule *ambārthanadyorhrasvaḥ* [Pāṇini 7.3.107].
There is the elision of the *m* that is merely a consonant (*hal*),
because the term *hal* is understood as a governing word (*anuvṛtti*) from the preceding rule.

Regarding the question: "In the case of *he katarat*, once the single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) has been applied, why does the elision [of the final vowel] not occur by the rule *hrasvāt saṃbuddher hal* [P. 6.1.69]?"—the author replies with the words "*he katarat*" and so forth. Because in the rule *adḍ ḍatarādibhyaḥ* [P. 7.1.25], there is the mention of two *ḍ*s, the substitute is the syllable *adḍ*. Since it is marked with the *ḍ*-sign (*ḍit*), the *ṭi*-portion (the final vowel) is elided; however, because this elision occurs after the substitution has taken place, the condition of being a "short vowel" (*hrasva*) no longer exists, and thus the elision [prescribed by P. 6.1.69] does not apply. Now, one might ask: what is the purpose of including the mention of *eṅ* [in P. 6.1.69], since even in cases such as *he agne*, the elision would not occur by the rule *hrasvāt* alone, because it would have already taken place prior to the *guṇa* substitution for the vocative? To this, the author says: "*eṅgrahaṇam*" and so forth.

Because it is permanent (*nitya*) and because it is external (*para*), the elision (*lopa*) of the vocative (*sambuddhi*) is stronger; therefore, that [elision] should indeed occur first. Once that has been applied, since a consonant (*hal*) following a short vowel (*hrasva*) after the vocative is no longer possible, the elision would not otherwise apply. For this reason, the mention of *eṅ* is made. But surely, it could be understood as a qualifier of what is prescribed (*vihita-viśeṣaṇa*): "of a vocative prescribed after a short vowel"? This is not so; for this is a single ablative case (*pañcamī*). In that case, if it were understood as a qualifier of what is prescribed after a short vowel, it would also be understood as being after a stem ending in *eṅ*. And thus, it would also apply here: *he gauḥ*.

Therefore, the mention of *eṅ* must be made [in the rule]. This elision is prescribed for that which is the substitute *śi* by the rule *jas-śasoḥ śiḥ* [Pāṇini 7.1.20], as in *yā kṣetrā*, *yā vanā*. Once the elision of *śi* has been performed, *num* is applied by the rule *sarvanāmasthāne cāsambuddhau* [Pāṇini 6.4.8] according to the principle of "as if the original form were still present" (*pratyayalakṣaṇena*), and then the long vowel is applied by the rule *sarvanāmasthāne ca* [Pāṇini 6.4.8]; finally, the elision of *n* is applied by the rule *nalopaḥ prātipadikāntasya* [Pāṇini 8.2.7].

The inclusion of the term *bahulam* ("in many cases") when an operation is to be performed is for the purpose of allowing exceptions to all rules; thus it becomes established that "all rules are optional in the Veda" (Puṣpasūtra 56). Here, by means of the suffix (*pratyaya*), the verbal root (*dhātu*) is brought to mind, and it is that very root which is qualified by the short vowel (*hrasva*); furthermore, since the rule of "belonging to what ends in that" (*tadantavidhi*) applies, it is understood that a verbal root ending in a short vowel is the item to which the augment (*āgama*) is added. Therefore, he says: "of a verbal root ending in a short vowel," and so forth.
[The example is] *agnicit*.
The suffix *kvip* is applied by [Pāṇini 3.2.91].
Thus we have "Somasut. In both cases, a compound with an upapada is formed by [Pāṇini 3.2.90].
In *prakṛtya* and similar forms, there is a *prādisamāsa* (prepositional compound).

The substitution of *lyap* for *ktvā* occurs by the rule *samāse 'nañpūrve ktvo lyap* [Pāṇini 7.1.37]. Now, regarding the form *grāmaṇi brāhmaṇakulam*—meaning "the Brahmin family that leads the village"—once the shortening of the neuter vowel has been applied, why does the *tuk* augment, which depends on a short vowel, not occur? To this he says: "*grāmaṇi brāhmaṇakulam*" and so forth.

For the state of shortness (*hrasvatva*) is extraneous (*bahiraṅga*), as it depends upon a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) that functions in the sense of a neuter gender; whereas the *tuk* augment is intrinsic (*antaraṅga*), because it depends solely upon a phoneme (*varṇa*). According to the principle "that which is extraneous is considered non-existent (*asiddha*) with respect to that which is intrinsic" (Vyāḍi’s Paribhāṣā 42), the *tuk* does not apply here. The locative case in the rule "in *saṃhitā*" (*saṃhitāyām*) is a locative of occasion (*viṣaya-saptamī*).

Therefore, it should be understood that if the *saṃhitā* (euphonic combination) between the cause (*nimitta*) and the effect (*kāryin*) constitutes the domain [of the rule], then only in that case does the effect to be described occur, and not otherwise. Although this locative case [in the rule] "after *che*" (*che*) belongs to the letter *cha* accompanied by the vowel *a*, nevertheless, the letter *cha* alone is the cause for the *tuk* augment; the vowel *a*, however, serves merely for pronunciation (*uccāraṇārtha*).
This is established by the prohibition of the *ām* augment [in the rule] *etattadoḥ sulopo...* (Pāṇini 6.1.132).

If the letter *cha* accompanied by the sound *hrakāra* were the cause for the insertion of *tuk*, then, because *tuk* would be absent from *ṛcchet*, there would be no occasion for the heavy syllable (*gurumatva*) that would trigger the application of *ām*; thus, he would not have formulated the prohibition. [In the case of] "icchati," is it *tuk*? No, it is *cutva*.

In the previous rule concerning the substitution of *tu* for *st*, that which was to be inserted (*āgamī*) ended in a short vowel; therefore, someone might have the misconception that this very same [short-vowel-ending element] is the one to be inserted here. To dispel that error, he says: "only the short [vowel]," and so forth.

He thinks as follows: "The particle *ca* is used here for the purpose of drawing in [the term] 'short' (*hrasva*), so that only the short vowel may be the augment (*āgamī*) and not that which ends with it; otherwise, because of its being *svarita*-accented and its immediate proximity, that very [vowel] which was the augment in the preceding rule would be understood here as well, making the particle *ca* redundant. If only the short vowel were the augment, what desired result would be established such that this effort is made for its sake? To this he says: "By that," and so forth.

If the *tuk* augment were applied to that which ends in a short vowel, then in forms such as *cicchidatuḥ*, the *tuk* would be included by the term "reduplication" (*abhyāsa*), and consequently, it would be eliminated by the rule of *halādiśeṣa*. However, when the short vowel itself is the augment, this [augment] is not a consonant (*hal*) of the reduplication, and thus the fault does not arise at all. But how is it that when a short vowel is the augment, the *tuk* is nevertheless included by the term "reduplication"? To this he says: "A part of a part is not [considered a part of the whole]," and so forth.
The particle *iti* is used here in the sense of a reason (*hetau*).
Because a part of a constituent element is not a constituent element of the whole,
therefore, when the short vowel is the augment *tuk*, it is not included by the mention of "repetition" (*abhyāsa*).
Is this [the case] here—that a part of a part does not become a part of the whole? It should be understood that the intention is that the augment *tuK* is prescribed by the Sūtra.

For if a part of a part were not, without distinction, a part of the whole, then in the case of *śerate*, the augment *ruṭ*—which belongs to the *aṅga* (stem) ending in *sārvadhātuka* and which is a part of the substitute *jha* for *ātmanepada* endings (*ataḥ*)—would likewise not be a part of the whole *sārvadhātuka*.

In that case, by [Pāṇini 7.4.21], the *guṇa* substitution would not occur, because the *sārvadhātuka* suffix is separated by the augment *ruṭ*. [Objection: Since that [augment] is said to be a part (*avayava*), it would indeed separate that very [part], but it does not separate the whole (*samudāya*) at all.

Therefore, the intention of the author of the *Vṛtti* must be understood as stated previously. Why, then, is this so? Why is a part-of-a-part prescribed by a *satra* rule not considered a part of the whole? [Answer: Because of the force of the use of the particle *ca*, which serves to draw in the [previous mention of] the short vowel (*hrasva*).

Indeed, that *ca* (the particle "and") is for the purpose of carrying forward the term "short vowel" (*hrasva*); it is employed for this reason: lest, when a short vowel alone is the augment (*āgama*), there be an exclusion by the rule *halādi-śeṣaḥ* due to the fact that the augment *tuk* is not included by the mention of "reduplication" (*abhyāsa*).

For if even an augment belonging to a part were, by virtue of this sūtra, to become a part of the whole, then even when a short vowel is the augment, the *tuk* would have to be excluded by *halādi-śeṣa*, since its constituent parts would also be included by the mention of "reduplication"; thus, the *ca* for the purpose of carrying forward the "short vowel" would be rendered useless.
Therefore, this very limb of a limb (the hand) is not a limb of the whole (the arm), whereas another [limb] certainly is.
And this is logical;

for instance, that which is a limb of the arm—the hand—is indeed also a limb of Devadatta; otherwise, the usage "Devadatta has two hands" would not be possible. [Thus it is said: "In place of an *ik* vowel, a *yaṇ* substitute occurs."
Because of the similarity between the *ik* vowels and the semi-vowels (*yaṇ*), it should be understood that they correspond respectively (*yathāsaṃkhyam*).

Furthermore, regarding the vowel (*ac*) that is homogeneous (*savarṇa*), since the rule for lengthening (*dīrgha*) is established there by virtue of its own capacity, it is understood that the substitution of a semi-vowel (*yaṇ-ādeśa*) occurs when the vowel is non-homogeneous (*asavarṇa*). Why is the term "*ika*" used? It is so that in the example "vāg atra," the substitution of a semi-vowel (*yaṇ-ādeśa*) does not occur, because the desired form is already established through the rule for gutturalization (*kutva*).
What is an example where it is not *ac*? *dadhi karoti*.
Regarding the rule "of that which has a protracted vowel (*pluta*) preceding": that which has a protracted vowel before it is "that which has a protracted vowel preceding" (*plutapūrva*).

It must be stated—that is, explained. Here is the explanation: In the rule *iko yaṇ aci*, two rules are recited by means of *tantra* (simultaneous application).
