Therein, one is for the purpose of the *yaṇ* substitution, while the other will serve to block the long-vowel (*savarṇadīrgha*) substitution for an *ik* vowel preceded by a protracted (*pluta*) vowel. Consider the example: *bho idam*. When *bho + i + idam* is situated, the protracted vowel (*pluta*) is applied to the word *bho* in the sense of calling from a distance, according to the rule *guroranṛto 'nantasyāpy ekaikasya prācām* [Pāṇini 8.2.86]. Subsequently, when the condition for a long-vowel substitution (*savarṇadīrgha*) arises, the *yaṇ* substitution takes effect. Thus we have *bho'y idam*. Similarly, *kayete* and *yayete*.
When *ke + ete* remains as *ye + eta*, the substitution of *ay* occurs.

When *vāyau + avaruṇaddhi* remains as *vāyau + avaruṇaddhi*, the substitution of *āv* occurs. Since the term *yī* refers to the phoneme *y*, by the rule "when a grammatical operation is prescribed with reference to a specific element, it applies to that which begins with it" (*vyā.pa.* 127), it is understood that the operation takes place when the suffix begins with the letter *y*; therefore, he says: "when the suffix begins with the letter *y*."

Although the locus (sthānin) is not explicitly mentioned here, it should nevertheless be understood that the substitution *āv* occurs in place of the vowel *o*, and the substitution *āv* occurs in place of the vowel *au*.
How so? For whatever property was observed for the substitute *vānta* in the preceding rule (*yoga*), that same property follows here as well.
And what property was observed for the substitute *vānta* in the preceding rule? That the vowel *au* serves as its locus (*sthānitva*).

Since the substitution *au* (in *aukāra*) is also a substitute (*sthānin*), here too, the original substratum (*sthānin*) is understood to be the same as that of the *vānta* substitute (*au*), which continues [from the previous rule] without abandoning its own properties. Thus, in the case of *bābhravyaḥ*:

from the word *babhru*, in the sense of "descendant" (*apatya*), the suffix *yañ* is applied by the rule *madhubabhvrordvāhṛṇakauśikayoḥ* [Pāṇini 4.1.106]; then the *guṇa* substitution is applied by the rule *orguṇaḥ* [Pāṇini 6.4.140].
*Māṇḍavyaḥ*:
[the suffix] *yañ* is applied according to [Pāṇini 4.1.105].
*Śaṅkavyam*.

From the word *śaṅku*, [the suffix] *yañ* is applied by [Pāṇini 4.1.105]: "*tasmai guṇaḥ| māṇḍavyaḥ*" (The patronymic suffix *yañ* is added after *māṇḍūka*, *śaṅku*, and *vṛddhīcchandas*). Thus, [the form] *māṇḍavyaḥ*.
Regarding "śaṅkavyam":
[the suffix] *yat* is applied according to Pāṇini 5.1.5 and 5.1.2 from the word *śaṅku*.
Regarding "nāvyaḥ": [the suffix] *yat* is applied according to Pāṇini 4.4.91.
The suffix *yat* is applied [to the root *tṛ*] in the sense of "crossed by boat" (*nāvā taryate*) according to the rule *nau-vayo-dharma-viṣa-* [Pāṇini 4.4.91].
The form *raiyyati* is derived from the suffix *kyac* [applied to the root *rī*] according to the rule *rī-gatireṣaṇayoḥ* [Pāṇini 3.1.8].
"goyānam" is a genitive compound (ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa),
according to the rule "goryūto chandasi" and so forth.

The meaning of the word *vaktavya* (to be stated) should be understood as "to be explained. In this regard, the following is the explanation: a *yogavibhāga* (separation of rules) is made here of the rule *vānto yi*; by means of this, in the Vedic domain (*chandasi*), the substitution of *ava* occurs for the word *go* when followed by a diphthong (*yūti*). [Then there is the rule: *adhvaparimāṇe ca*.
The phrase *gauryūtau* (the word *go* before a diphthong) carries over from the previous rule.

In that case as well, the meaning of the word *vaktavya* is the same, and the explanation is also the same. This statement is general; therefore, it applies to the measurement of distance in common speech (*bhāṣā*). Since [the desired form] is already established by the preceding rule, this statement is for the purpose of restriction (*niyamārtham*).
Regarding the phrase "tannimittasya": by the word *tat*, the suffix beginning with *y* (the *yakāra*-pratyaya) is referred to; that which has this as its cause (*nimitta*) is thus described.
[The example given is] "lavyam."

Is it not the case that [the suffix] *yat* is prescribed by [Pāṇini 3.1.97]? Indeed, by depending on that very letter *v*, the substitution of *o* for *av* is prescribed by [Pāṇini 7.3.84], and thus it becomes caused by that [suffix]. In the example "avaśyalāvyam":

the suffix *ṇyat* is applied by [Pāṇini 3.1.125], there is a compound by [Pāṇini 2.1.72], and the letter *m* is elided according to the rule "one should drop the *m* of *avaśyam* before a *kṛtya* suffix" (Kāśikā 6.1.149).
In this case as well, the vowel *au* prescribed by the rule *ṇyato 'nāvaḥ* [Pāṇini 7.2.115] becomes conditioned by that [suffix].
[The mention of *dhātu* is used] so that the restriction does not apply to the nominal stem (*prātipadika*).
For if the mention of *dhātu* were absent, the restriction would apply to the nominal stem as well.

But surely, even for a nominal stem (*prātipadika*), this restriction would apply only to that which is caused by that [suffix], and not to that which is not so caused—this is the meaning that would follow. And in that case, the formulation of the preceding rule (*pūrvasūtra*) would be purposeless, as it would lack a scope of application. This is not a fault. For one who asks "Why [is it said] 'of a verbal root' (*dhātoḥ')? certainly does not desire the commencement of the preceding rule to be separate.
He thinks thus: "The single rule should be formulated as: 'Only of that which is caused by that [suffix]' (*tannimittasyaiva*)."

The intention is this: since there is a restriction regarding the nominal stem (*prātipadika*), if some fault were to arise, then the mention of "verbal root" (*dhātu*) being made for the purpose of avoiding that fault would be appropriate.
[The objection] "It would apply only in the case of *bābhravya*" is raised because [the suffix] is caused by that [nominal stem].
"But here it would not apply— [in the forms] *gavyam* and *nāvyam*—
because the *eC* [vowels] do not have that as their cause.
[This refers to the form] *upoyate*.

In the case of *veñ* with the prefix *upa*, when the suffix *ātvam* has been applied, the suffix *ātmanepada* is introduced by [Pāṇini 1.3.13], the suffix *yak* by [Pāṇini 3.1.67], and because it belongs to the *yajādi* class, there is *samprasāraṇa*. Then, by [Pāṇini 7.4.25], there is lengthening, which, together with the preceding *u*, results in *auyata* according to [Pāṇini 6.1.87].

When the same root takes the suffix *laṅ*, the *ātmanepada* endings and so forth are applied as before; the augment *aṭ* is added by [Pāṇini 6.4.72] because it begins with a vowel, and by [Pāṇini 6.1.87], there is *vṛddhi* (the substitution of *au*) for the *āṭ* and the following vowel.

This *au* and the preceding *o*—both of these have that [the *aṭ*] as their cause. The mention of "having that as its cause" (*tannimitta*) is for the purpose of ensuring that this does not apply to cases where these two vowels are not caused by that [augment].

But surely, the substitution of *yaṇ* is internal (*antaraṅga*) because it depends on a single phoneme, whereas the single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) is external (*bahiraṅga*) because it depends on both members of the compound; and since "that which is external is as if non-existent with respect to that which is internal" (*asiddhaṃ bahiraṅgam antaraṅge*), this [substitution] will not occur here precisely because it is non-existent? If that is so, then this teaches that this paribhāṣā does not apply here.
Consequently, in the case of *akṣadyūḥ*, even though the substitution of *ūṭh* is external, it is not treated as non-existent when the internal substitution of *yaṇ* is to be applied.

Otherwise, if this meaning were not made known, then when the suffix *kvip* is applied in the case of *akṣair dīvyati*, and the substitution of *ūṭh* is applied by [Pāṇini 6.4.19] (*cchvoḥ śūḍanunāsike ca*), the substitution of *yaṇ* would not take place because that [substitution of *ūṭh*] is considered non-existent (*asiddha*). In the word *lāyamāniḥ*, the sense is "the future state of what is being cut" (*lūyamānasyāyatyaṃ*); thus, the suffix *iñ* is applied by [Pāṇini 4.1.95] (*ata iñ*), and then [Pāṇini 7.2.117] applies the *vṛddhi* strengthening. This *vṛddhi* is caused by the *taddhita* suffix, and not caused by the suffix beginning with *yakāra*.

With the intention that "once [the rule] is established, a prescription being commenced will serve as a restriction even without the use of the particle *eva*," he asks: "What is the purpose of the particle *eva*?
Showing that the particle *eva* is employed for the sake of restriction according to what is desired, he says: "The restriction of the verbal root (*dhātu-avadhāraṇam*)," and so forth.

When the particle *eva* is uttered immediately after the word that is its cause, since the purpose of the particle *eva* is to restrict something other than that which is its cause, there occurs a restriction of the verbal root.
If there were no purpose for the particle *eva*, then the restriction to that cause alone—which is the cause of the verbal root—would also be understood as unintended.
Therefore, the purpose of the particle *eva* is so that there may be a restriction to the verbal root (*dhātu*) and not a restriction to its cause.
But what desired form is established when there is a restriction to the verbal root, such that it is so desired? To this he says: "For [it applies] to that which has that as its cause," and so forth.

For if there were a restriction to verbal roots (*dhātu*), then because that cause would not be restricted to them, [the suffix] would apply to non-roots as well—as in *bābhravya*—and to roots as well—as in *lavyam* and *avaśyalāvyam*. If the restriction were made to that cause, it would mean "only for a root is that cause [applicable]";
consequently, it would not apply in the case of *bābhravya*, because the word *babhru* is not a verbal root.

Therefore, the restriction of the verbal roots is intended as follows: "of these two roots, *kṣi* and *ji*. By the mention of *kṣi*, there is the inclusion of *kṣi* in the sense of decay (*kṣaye*; DhP 236), *kṣi* in the sense of dwelling and going (*vāsagatyoḥ*;
DhP 1407), and *kṣiṣ* or *kṣi* in the sense of injury (*hiṃsāyām*; DhP 1506). However, by the mention of *ji*, there is the inclusion of only *ji* in the sense of victory (*jaye*; DhP 561).

But surely, by the paribhāṣā "when there is the mention of a root without an *anubandha*, that with an *anubandha* is not included" (Vyāḍīya-paribhāṣā 53), the inclusion of *kṣiṣ* in the sense of "injury" (*hiṃsā*) would not be obtained? This is not a fault, because it will occur by way of *nipātana* (irregularity).

For what indeed cannot be obtained through *nipātana*? Just as some other operation not [otherwise] indicated by the rules might occur from that, so too might this one. The mention of the meaning (*arthagrahaṇa*) is so that [the suffix] may be applied even when the object (*karman*) is present; otherwise, since *śak* is intransitive (*akarmaka*), the *nipātana* would be understood to apply only to the abstract state (*bhāva*)—as in *kṣayyaṃ devadattena* ("it can be destroyed by Devadatta").
But it would not apply in the sense of the object—as in *kṣayyo vyādhiḥ* (a curable disease)—for a kṛtya suffix is not appropriate after roots that do not have an object.
However, by the inclusion of the word "artha" (meaning), the meaning of the kṛtya suffixes is indicated;
since kṛtya suffixes are prescribed for the object as well, it is understood through this irregular derivation (*nipātana*) that it applies there too, as in *krayyaḥ*.
In this context, the meaning of the suffix is the object (*karman*), because the *kṛtya* suffixes are prescribed in the sense of the object;
and the meaning of the base is exchange (*vinimaya*), because the root *krī* has exchange as its meaning.
Among these, the meaning of the suffix is primary, on the grounds that "the base and the suffix express the meaning of the suffix together."

The meaning of the base (*prakṛti*) is subordinate, serving as a qualifier for the meaning of the suffix (*pratyaya*). In this context, if the meaning of the suffix were indicated by the word *tad* because of its predominance, then the following would be the sense: "that whose object is something to be purchased (*kraya*) is 'tadartha'"; thus, when that [object] is to be expressed, the word *krayya* is prescribed as a grammatical irregularity (*nipātyate*). But this is incorrect; for in this case, there is no word denoting the meaning of "to be purchased" (*krayya-artha*) that could serve as the referent of the word *krayya*, since such a thing is not perceived.

Now, if it were understood in this way—that "that very object" is what is meant by "for that purpose"—even so, the inclusion of the term "for that purpose" (tadartha) would be redundant. For the word *krayya*, which ends in the suffix *yat*, necessarily denotes the meaning of that suffix.
Therefore, since the primary element is already indicated by the word "that" (*tat*), the inclusion of the term "for that purpose" is purposeless.

Therefore, considering that the meaning of the base (*prakṛtyartha*), although subordinate, is also indicated, he says: "In that which has that as its object—that which is for the purpose of buying—when that is to be expressed.

The phrase *tadartham* means "for the sake of that. By the expression "for the purpose of buying" (*krayārtham*), he shows that the meaning of the root *krī* ("to buy") is what is referred to by the word *tat*.
*Krayaṇa* is *kraya*, meaning "restriction" (*viniyama*).
In the expression *krayārtham*, it is also a dative compound: *krayāya idam* = *krayārtham*.
[The phrase] "that which is spread out for the purpose of purchase" (*krayārtha yaḥ prasāritaḥ*) [is meant].
The meaning is: that which has been offered for the purpose of exchange. "Our grain is to be bought" (*kreyaṃ no dhānyam*); "to be bought" (*kretavyam*) means it is to be taken up or accepted.
"And there is no meat" means that there is no grain presented here for the purpose of purchase. Regarding "of this [root] *vī*":

it refers either to the root *vī* listed among those meaning "motion," "procreation," and so forth, or to the substitute *vī* for the root *aj* prescribed by the rule *ajeḥ kyapi ca ghañapoḥ* [Pāṇini 2.4.56].
Regarding the statement "there must be an addition for *hyadayyā* and *āpaḥ*":
the word *upasaṃkhyāna* means "explanation" or "demonstration.
Thus, the meaning is that a demonstration of the forms *hyadayyā* and *hatya* must be provided.

In this regard, the following is the demonstration: the letter *ca* is employed here, and it serves the purpose of including what has not been explicitly mentioned (*anuktasamuccayārtha*). By means of it, the form *adadyāḥ* will also be possible. Now, for what purpose is the mention of both "preceding" (*pūrva*) and "following" (*para*)? For, by the rule *ādguṇaḥ* [P. 6.1.87], this ablative case (*pañcamī*) ending in *āt* will effect the status of a genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhītva*) for the locative case (*saptamī*) ending in *aci*; this is due to the statement [of P. 1.1.67]. Likewise, by the rule *āto dhātoḥ* [P.

6.4.140], this locative case (*saptamī*) ending in *aci* will effect the status of a genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhītva*) for the ablative case (*pañcamī*) ending in *āt*; this is due to the statement [of P. 1.1.66].

In that case, would [the substitution] not occur for both the preceding and the following even without the mention of "preceding and following"? To this he says: "The mention of 'preceding and following'," and so on.

What, then, is the reason why, in the absence of the mention of "preceding and following," the simultaneous substitution of both is not established? To this he says: "For of only one," and so on. He thinks as follows: this locative (*saptamī*) is already fulfilled in its purpose by the rule for the *yaṇ*-substitution and others; however, this ablative (*pañcamī*) is nowhere else fulfilled in its purpose. Therefore, it should be construed as a genitive (*ṣaṣṭhī*) in place of the locative.

In that case, if the mention of "prior" (*pūrva*) and "subsequent" (*para*) were absent, the *guṇa* substitution would apply to the vowel (*ac*) alone. Furthermore, in the rule [P. 6.1.88], since the ablative case in *āt* (in *ādguṇaḥ*) has already served its purpose in the formulation of the *guṇa* prescription, the locative case *ecī*—which has not yet fulfilled its function—would be interpreted as a genitive. Consequently, the *vṛddhi* substitution would result only for the vowel *a*.

Since both the fifth (ablative) and seventh (locative) case endings [in the rule] remain unfulfilled in their purpose, one might assume that a sixth (genitive) case ending is to be supplied alternately for each of them; thus, the *vṛddhi* substitution would occur only alternatively. Furthermore, as for the opponent's view that the fifth case will be construed as a sixth in relation to the seventh, and the seventh likewise as a sixth in relation to the fifth—thereby ensuring that the substitute occurs for both even without explicitly mentioning the "intervening" (*antara*) and "subsequent" (*para*) terms—to refute this, he says: "Not both," and so forth.

For that which possesses the property of cessation (*nivṛtti-dharma*) becomes the locus (*sthānin*), and it serves as the cause for the conceptualization of the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī-prakalpana*) regarding what is being heard. How could both the preceding and the following [elements] undergo cessation, and at the same time become the cause for the conceptualization of the genitive case? Precisely because of this impossibility—both of their non-cessation and of their becoming the cause—the seventh and fifth cases do not simultaneously effect the conceptualization.
Therefore, it must belong to one alone, not to both.

Now, what is the purpose of including the term *eka* (one), given that even without the inclusion of *eka*, only one [substitute] is possible in the rule *bhrasjo ropadhayo ram anyatarasyām* [Pāṇini 6.4.47]? Nevertheless, he says "one," etc., to show that even without *eka* here, only one will occur. For, because the augment *ram* has the marker *m*, by the rule *midacontyātparaḥ* [Pāṇini 1.1.47], it must occur after the final vowel (*ac*). And it is not possible for two instances of *ram* to occur after the final vowel of the root *bhṛjj*.
Therefore, even without the mention of "one" (*eka*), it is logical [to understand that the substitute is one];
for the rule states that "guṇa and so forth become one.

Furthermore, when there is a difference in the substituends (*sthānin*), it is possible for guṇa and so forth to be separate substitutes for each individual substituend; thus, if the mention of "one" were not present, there would be separate substitutes.
Therefore, the mention of the word "one" (*eka*) is for the purpose that the two substituends—the preceding and the following—should not occupy separate locations.

However, in the absence of the mention of "one," both [the substitute and the original] would result; in order to demonstrate this point along with its justification, he says: "For, due to the difference in the substituends," and so forth.

Because of the distinction in the substituends (*sthānin*) according to the rule *yatā* [Pāṇini 8.2.42], only two substitutes occur in cases such as *chinna* (from *chid-na*), and likewise, there would also be two substitutes in cases such as *khaṭvendra*. Since it is not understood what the meaning of this extension (*atideśa*) is when it is stated that "it is like the end and the beginning" (*antādivat*), he says "as... and so forth in order to clarify that understanding:
"this is the meaning of the extension."

The word *iti* refers back to what has preceded. An *atideśa* (extension) is that by which something is extended; this, moreover, is precisely the rule "as if internal and as if initial" (*antādivacca*), and the meaning of this extension is the sense of the rule just mentioned.
[The objection is: "This status of being 'as if internal and as if initial' is not desired in a rule that depends on a phoneme (*varṇa*).
How is this known? To this he says: "For instance," and so forth.

Regarding the rule *obhisa ais* [Pāṇini 7.1.9]: this is a grammatical operation dependent on the phoneme *ā*. When that operation is to be applied, in the case of *khaṭvābhiḥ*, the long vowel resulting from the substitution of a homogeneous vowel (*savarṇadīrghatva*) for the preceding [vowel] does not behave as if it were the original [short] vowel. Regarding the rule *ādguṇaḥ* [Pāṇini 6.1.87], which is dependent on the phoneme *ā*: when that operation is to be applied, in the case of *juhāva*, after the semivowel substitution (*samprasāraṇa*) of the root *hvayati* has been performed according to [Pāṇini 6.1.33], the single-substitute form (*pūrvarūpatva*) of the vowel *ā* does not behave as if it were the beginning [of the word].

The rule *eṅaḥ padāntādati* (Pāṇini 6.1.105) is one that depends upon the phonemes *eṅ*. When that [rule] is to be applied—in the case of *asmai + ā* becoming *asyai ā*—the augment *āṭ* [of the preceding *asme*] does not behave like the initial [element of the following word] according to *āṭaśca* (Pāṇini 6.1.87). Because that [initial-like status] is absent, there is no substitution of *āy* [for *ai*]. Consequently, by *lopaḥ śākalyasya* (Pāṇini 8.3.19), there is the elision of the *y*. Why, then, must it be stated that "in a matter depending on a phoneme, the final and initial do not [behave like the whole]"? It need not be stated. How so? Because it is an extension (*atideśa*) of non-identity (*atādrūpya*).

The property of having that same form (*tādrūpya*) is not extended here; furthermore, these [substitutes] have *rūpa* (the phonetic form) as their substratum, and therefore, because they do not possess that same form, they will not [behave like the original]. But for what purpose is this treatment as being "like the end and beginning" (*antādivadbhāva*) prescribed, given that the preceding and following elements were stated to be the substituends (*sthānin*) of the single substitution (*ekādeśa*), and that by the principle of "being like the substituend" (*sthānivadbhāva*) alone, the operation dependent upon them will occur? To this he says: "The preceding and following aggregate is the substituend of the single substitution.
How is this known? He says: "For that... and so forth.
For that by which something is replaced through a substitute (ādeśa) is its *sthānin* (original locus), as for example in [Pāṇini 2.4.52].

Here, in the case of *bhū* becoming *asti*, the entire complex (*samudāya*) is replaced by a single substitute; therefore, that complex alone is its *sthānin*, not the two constituent parts (*samudāyin*)—the preceding and the following elements.

It might be argued: "Since a part is included within a whole, when the whole is replaced by a substitute, the parts are also replaced. Therefore, do those two also possess the status of being *sthānin*s? To this, he says: "In that case," and so forth.
Both instances of the particle *iti* indicate a reason (*hetu*).

In that regard, the status of being a substituendum (*sthānitva*) belonging to the two parts within the whole is inferential; for when the whole is replaced by a single substitute, the replacement of those two parts is necessarily concomitant.
Indeed, the whole cannot be replaced without the replacement of its parts, because the whole is of the nature of those parts.
However, the status of being a substitute (*sthānitva*) belongs to the aggregate (*samudāya*).

This is because the genitive case ending denoting the locus of substitution (*sthāna-ṣaṣṭhī*) in the expression "of the preceding and the following" (*pūrvaparayoḥ*) is directly heard; and according to the principle that "between a directly stated [connection] and an inferred one, the directly stated connection is more authoritative" (*Cāndra-vyākaraṇa-pariśiṣṭa*, pāda 49), the grammatical operation prescribed for the substitute is based precisely on that which possesses the status of being a substitute as it is directly and explicitly heard by the rule *Pāṇini 1.1.56*. Since the status of being a substitute for the individual components is inferential and not directly perceived, the grammatical operation based upon them is not extended [to the substitute].

Consequently, an operation depending on that [original element] would not apply to the substitute by virtue of the *sthānivadbhāva* rule, yet it is desired that it should. For this reason, this *antavadbhāva* (the status of being like the end) is prescribed. In this context, does the statement "it is as if unestablished" (*asiddhavat*) effect the non-existence of the single-substitute (*ekādeśa*), or is it intended to demonstrate its functional incapacity? For even an established entity may be called "unestablished" because it lacks the capacity to perform the function of what is established, just as a son is called "sonless" because he lacks the capacity to perform the functions of a son.

In that regard, if by this [rule] the non-existence of the single-substitute (ekādeśa) were being effected, then in the case of *adhītya*, the *tuṅ* augment would not occur, for here there is no short vowel (*hrasva*), since it has been replaced by the single-substitute. Nor does the emergence of the short vowel occur once the single-substitute has been removed by the statement of *asiddha*; for when the killer of Devadatta is killed, Devadatta does not reappear. Having seen this defect in the first position, [the author], showing that the capacity for the grammatical operation is made known by the scriptural statement of the *asiddha* status of the single-substitute, says: "The meaning is that it does not perform its established function."

What is the meaning of "of that which is established" (*siddhasya*) and "accomplished" (*niṣpannasya*)? It means that even though the substitute (*ādeśa*) is established and accomplished, it does not perform its function; this is the sense of this statement.
With the words "the statement of non-establishment" (*asiddhavacana*), etc., he explains the purpose of the rule.

And when the substitution has been made, whatever operation follows as a consequence of that cause possesses the characteristic of the substitute (*ādeśalakṣaṇa*), because the substitute is its characteristic—that is, its cause or occasion.
The statement "asiddha" (not established) is for the purpose that its prohibition may take effect.
An *utsarga* is that which is emitted or set aside; here, it refers to the original element (*sthānin*).

That whose characteristic is an *utsarga* is "characterized by an *utsarga*" (*utsargalakṣaṇa*); the statement "asiddha" is for the purpose that this state [of being characterized by an *utsarga*] may occur.

Regarding the form *asicat*: from the root *sic* in the *luṅ* [aorist] tense, there is the substitution of *cl-* for *liṭ* by rule 3.1.53; then *aṅ* replaces *cli* by rule 3.1.44. Following the word *kim*, the *s* undergoes *rutva* (becoming *r*) by rule 6.1.113; then *utva* (becoming *u*) by rule 6.1.87; then *guṇa* (becoming *o*) by rule 6.1.87; and then *parapūrvatva* (the preceding vowel becoming the single substitute) by rule 6.1.109. As for the statement "because of being like the beginning with respect to what follows," etc.:
in the case of *asicat*, the single substitute [of *a* and *i*] is treated as if it were the beginning (*ādivadbhāva*) with respect to the following *a* by rule 6.1.85.
And this is the reason for not being considered *apādādi* (not beginning a word):
"Because it is *asiddha*, [the rule] does not apply.
For when it is *asiddha*, the letter *s* here remains the very first sound of the word; therefore, by the rule *sātpadādyoḥ* [Pāṇini 8.3.111], there is a prohibition against the substitution of *ṣ*.

Regarding "ko 'sya": this is the genitive singular of the pronoun *idam*. By [Pāṇini 7.2.102], the substitution of *a* occurs; by [Pāṇini 7.1.12], the form *syā* is substituted for *ṭā*, *ṅasi*, and *ṅas*; and by [Pāṇini 7.2.113], the *i* of this form is elided.
The remainder is as before.

This is an example of the prohibition of a rule characterized by an exception (*ādeśalakṣaṇapratiṣedha*). An example of the existence of a rule characterized by a general operation (*utsargalakṣaṇabhāva*), however, is "adhītya" and "pretya. Now, one might object: "The single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) is *bahiraṅga* because it depends on two words; whereas the *ṣatva* and *tuka* operations are *antaraṅga* because they depend on a single word. Therefore, by the very maxim 'that which is *bahiraṅga* is as if non-existent with respect to that which is *antaraṅga*' (Vyāḍi-Pāṇini 42), the [substitution] will be treated as non-existent here; thus, this statement is useless. If this is so, then that very maxim is restricted (*niyamyate*) in this context to the *ṣatva* and *tuka* operations.

Therefore, in the case of *akṣadyūḥ*, even though the substitution of *ū* is conditioned by external factors (*bahiraṅga*), it is not treated as non-existent (*asiddha*) when the internal substitution of *yaṇ* (*antaraṅga*) is to be applied.
Regarding the rule "in the case of *samprasāraṇa*" and so forth:

it must be stated that there is a prohibition against treating as non-existent (*asiddhatva-pratiṣedha*) that single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) which occurs in place of a *samprasāraṇa*, the locative suffix *ṅi*, and the augment *iṭ*.

Regarding the form *brāhṛhūṣu*: [the derivation is as follows: from the root *hvṛ* with the suffix *kvip* in the sense of "one who calls the Brāhmaṇas" (*brāhmaṇān hvayati*). Due to its inclusion in the *yajādi* group, there is vocalization (*samprasāraṇa*) according to Pāṇini 6.1.15; then, by 6.1.108, the preceding vowel takes the place of the subsequent one; and finally, by 6.4.2, there is lengthening. This is the locative plural.

In the word *parivīṣu*, it is the root *veñ* preceded by *pari*; the form arises after the application of [the suffixes] beginning with *kvip*, as previously described. In the expression *apacecchatram*, it is the first person singular of the imperfect (*laṅ*) of the root *pac*; there is the augment *iṭ*, the affix *śap* according to Pāṇini 3.1.68 (*kartari śap*), and the *guṇa* substitution according to 6.1.87 (*ādguṇaḥ*). In the examples *tavalkāraḥ* and *khaṭvalkāraḥ*:

How, then, is there the status of being followed by *r* (*laparatva*) in this case? To this he says: "In place of the letter *ḷ*" and so forth. This is obtained from the supplementary rule (*upasaṃkhyāna*), "The designation of homogeneity (*savarṇasaṃjñā*) should be stated for the letters *ḷ* and *ṛ*" (Vārttika 3), as well as from the inclusion of the *rapratyāhāra* in the rule *uraṇ raparaḥ* [Pāṇini 1.1.50].

For it has been stated regarding the traditional list of phonemes (*akṣarasamāmnāya*): "Among the phonemes beginning with *h*, the vowel *a* is for the purpose of pronunciation; however, in the case of the letter *ḷ*, it is declared that the nasalized (*anunāsika*) *a* bears the technical designation *it*."

In that context, when the *pratyāhāra* is formed starting from the letter *r* up to the letter *ṇ*, the substitution of *aṇ* prescribed for the place of the *ḷ*-vowel—which is included by the inclusion of the *ṛ*-vowel—becomes followed by *l* (*lapara*). A qualifier-qualified relationship (*viśeṣaṇaviśeṣyabhāva*) occurs only when there is both possibility (*sambhava*) and deviation (*vyabhicāra*); and these two, possibility and deviation, exist only in this verbal root (*dhātu*) and not elsewhere. Thus he says: "This very inclusion of *ej*," and so forth. [The example is] *praṣṭhauhaḥ*.

In the derivation of *praṣṭhavāh* from *praṣṭhaṃ vahati*, the suffix *ṇvi* is applied by [Pāṇini 3.2.64] *vahaśca*. Then, by [Pāṇini 6.4.132], the substitution *ūṭh* occurs, which is designated as *samprasāraṇa*; subsequently, by [Pāṇini 6.1.108], the preceding vowel (*parapūrvatva*) is formed, followed by *vṛddhi*.

The connection with the present context is that *vṛddhi* is prescribed as an exception (*apavāda*) to the rule regarding the single-substitute form (*pararūpa*) for the vowels *e* and *ai* before the vowel *eṅ*.

Now, why does the *vṛddhi* substitution not occur as an exception (*apavāda*) to the *pararūpa* [substitution] prescribed by the rule *atha>[[6.1.95]]* when the prefix *āṅ* follows? For this *vṛddhi* is commenced precisely when the *pararūpa* has not yet taken effect; thus, just as it subverts the *pararūpa* in the case of the suffix *eṅ*, it might likewise subvert the *pararūpa* in the case of *āṅ*. Consequently, would this not also apply here: *ā + itaḥ = etaḥ* and *upa + etaḥ = upetaḥ*? To this, he says: "The rule *omāṅośca*... and so forth. He states the reason for this very point: "That rule which is commenced when another rule has not yet taken effect is the subverter of that [other rule]. (Thus.)
Is it not logical that this *vṛddhi* is commenced when the *pararūpa* (single-substitute rule) has not yet applied to *eṅ*? It serves as its sublater (*bādhikā*).
However, this *vṛddhi* is commenced whether the *pararūpa* after *āṅ* has already applied or has not yet applied.
In the cases of *ā + itaḥ = etaḥ*, *pra + itaḥ = pretaḥ*, and *paretaḥ*, this *vṛddhi* is commenced whether the *pararūpa* after *āṅ* has already applied or has not yet applied.

In *ā-itaḥ* = *etaḥ*, *pra-itaḥ* = *pretaḥ*, and *paretaḥ*, [the substitution of] the subsequent form (*pararūpa*) applies when preceded by *āṅ*. However, in *upa-eti* = *upaiti*, this does not apply. Therefore, this *vṛddhi* (vowel strengthening) does not sublate the substitution of the subsequent form when preceded by *āṅ*. He states another solution with the principle beginning "Exceptions [operate] from above" (*purastādapavādāḥ*): "Exceptions from above sublate the rules immediately following them, not those that follow later" (Vyāḍipāda 9). This *vṛddhi* is an exception from above; for it, the rule for the subsequent form is the one immediately following. Therefore, only that is sublated by it, not the substitution of the subsequent form when preceded by *āṅ*, because that [subsequent form rule] is more internal (*antara*).
"From the sense-faculties," and so forth.
"To be stated" means that it is to be explained.

In this regard, the explanation is as follows: in the subsequent sūtra, the word "ca" (and) is for the purpose of prescribing an additional rule. By that, the *vṛddhi* [vowel substitution] will occur when the word *akṣa* is followed by the word *ūhinī*.
The meaning of the word "vaktavya" (to be stated) in the following cases should be understood in the same way, and the explanation should also be understood in this very manner.
*Akṣauhiṇī*: "Uha" means calculation (*ūha*). That which possesses this [calculation] is expressed by the possessive suffix *ini*.

By the rule *ṛnnebhyo ṅīp* [Pāṇini 4.1.5], the suffix *ṅīp* is applied, resulting in *akṣauhiṇī*. *Svairam*: The root *īr* (in the Dhātupāṭha, no. 1018) means "to go. "Going" (*īraṇa*) is *īra*; the suffix *ghañ* is used in the sense of an abstract action (*bhāve*). Thus, *svasya īraḥ* is *svairaḥ* (one's own movement). The adverbial form is *svairam*.
Is it because it functions as an adverb (*kriyāviśeṣaṇa*)? In the commentary (*vṛtti*), the term *svairam* is indicated in the neuter gender;
however, some action must be supplied here [to complete the sense].
Alternatively, it refers to a family (*kula*) whose master (*īra*) is himself (*svo*); that is, "a self-mastered family" (*svairaṃ kulaṃ*).
The neuter gender [of the word *napuṃsaka*] arises because it functions as the external referent (*anyapadārtha*) for "family" and so forth.
Regarding the form *svairī* (or *svairiṇī* according to the *Kāśikā*): the suffix *ṇini* is applied by [Pāṇini 3.2.78], meaning "one whose habit is to act according to one's own will."
The words *ūḍha* and *ūḍhi* end in the suffixes *niṣṭhā* and *ktin*, respectively.

Regarding the word *praiṣa*: it is derived from the roots *iṣa* (meaning "to go, to send, to take") [Dhātupāṭha 1127] or *iṣu* (meaning "to desire") [Dhātupāṭha 1351]. When the suffix *ghañ* is applied to these two roots preceded by the prefix *pra*, the form is *praiṣa*; however, when the suffix *ṇyat* is applied, the form is *praiṣya*.
Regarding "sukhārtaḥ," this is a compound according to [Pāṇini 2.1.32]. Regarding "īkṣata," this is the *laṅ* [aorist] from the root "īkṣa" meaning "to see" (Dhātupāṭha 610).
"Aikṣiṣṭa" is the form in the *luṅ* (aorist) tense; "aikṣiṣyata" is the conditional (*liṅ*) form.
The conditional (*lṛṅ*) form is *aubhīt*.

This is derived from the root *ubha* or *umbha* in the sense of "filling" (Dhātupāṭha 1319, 1320) in the *luṅ* tense, with the augment *iṭ*, followed by the augment *iṭ* according to Pāṇini 7.3.96: *astisico 'yukte*.
In *īṭi* [Pāṇini 8.2.28], there is the elision of *sic*. Regarding *aubjīt*: the root *ubj* means "to straighten" (Dhātupāṭha 1303).
Regarding the form *ādhrnot*:
from the verbal root *ṛṣu* meaning "to grow" (*dhātupāṭha* 1271), the suffix *śnu* is applied by [Pāṇini 3.1.73].
The letter *ca* [in the rule] is for the purpose of prescribing an additional [suffix].

The intention is that [the word *vṛddhi*] is not for the purpose of drawing [the previous rule] along with it, because its continued application is already established by its being marked with the *svarita* accent.

To clarify the meaning of the phrase "for the purpose of prescribing something additional" through another sentence, he says: "It is for the purpose of subverting the *pararūpa* [substitution] prescribed by the rule *usyomāṅośca*. The meaning is: it is for the purpose of subverting that *pararūpa* which would otherwise apply when *usi*, *omi*, and *āṅ* are present.
Indeed, the formulation of the rule twice indicates that there is a specific purpose. In this context, the second formulation serves to override what would otherwise be an overriding factor.
Consequently, having set aside both the *para-rūpa* (single-substitute form) that would result from Pāṇini 6.1.96 and that which results from 6.1.95, only *vṛddhi* (vowel strengthening) takes place.

Regarding *auruāiyat* and *auṅkārīyat*: from the words *uru* and *oṅkāra*, by [Pāṇini 7.4.33] the substitution of *it* occurs; then, after the suffix *kyac*, the *luṅ* [aorist] tense is applied. When the rule [Pāṇini 6.1.96], which prescribes the substitution of the subsequent form (*pararūpa*), would have been applicable as a sublater, the vowel *vṛddhi* alone takes place because the letter *c* in the sūtra serves the purpose of prescribing an additional rule. Thus we have *auḍhīyat*.

From the word *oḍha*, there is the suffix *kyac* followed by the *luṅ* tense; when the augment *āṭ* is applied, the rule *pūrvasya dīrgho 'ṇaḥ* [Pāṇini 6.1.95] would have applied as a sublater (*bādhaka*) resulting in a single substitute (*pararūpa*), but because the letter *ca* in the rule has the purpose of prescribing an additional operation, the *vṛddhi* substitution alone takes place. Thus we have *upācchati*. Regarding the root *ṛcch* [Dhātupāṭha 1296], which means "to go," "loss of sensory power," or "becoming solid": "a region from which people have departed" is a *pracchaka* region.

In this context, according to the rule "those particles beginning with *pra* which are connected with an action are designated as *gati* and *upasarga* with respect to that [action]," the word *pra* is designated as a *gati-upasarga* with respect to the root *gam*, but not with respect to the root *ṛcch*. Thus, this serves as a counter-example (*pratyudāharaṇa*).

[One might object: "The option provided by the rule *vā supyāpiśaleḥ* would apply here. By this, he demonstrates that the inclusion of the long vowel *ā* (the *tapara* marker) is for the sake of the subsequent rules.

Now, for what purpose is the mention of "root" (*dhātu*)? For relative terms necessarily bring to mind their correlative counterpart, just as words such as "son" do. Furthermore, since this prefix (*upasarga*) is dependent upon a root, is it not the case that the mention of the root is established by the very mention of the prefix? To this he says: "By the very mention of the prefix," and so forth. If the mention of the root were not made, then in the case of *parācchati*, the rule *ṛtyakaḥ* [Pāṇini 6.1.128] would apply because it is subsequent; thus, according to the opinion of Śākalya, there would be the substitution of a long vowel (*prakṛtibhāva*).
Therefore, the mention of "root" (*dhātu*) is made in order to exclude that *prakṛtivadbhāva* (the state of being like the original form) belonging to Śākalya.
But how, when the mention of "root" is made, is the exclusion of Śākalya’s *prakṛtivadbhāva* obtained? It is because of the reason of a formal split in the rule (*yogavibhāga*).

For when the mention of "root" exists, the rule is split as follows: first, "an augment *vṛddhi* occurs after a prefix"; then, "when there is a root," where the word "after a prefix" (*upasargāt*) from the previous rule continues to apply.
Then a second application [of the rule] is understood for the purpose of subverting what would otherwise obstruct [the formation].

Now, just as in the rule *atha* (Pāṇini 5.1.118), the mention of the term "preverb" (*upasarga*) is understood to include [all prefixes] beginning with *pra*, why should it not be understood in the same way here as well? Because it is impossible.

For in the rule *upasargāc chandasi dhātvarthe* (Pāṇini 5.1.119), since the presence of a verbal root (*dhātu*) is not possible [in that specific context], it is logical that the mention of "preverb" is intended to include [all prefixes] beginning with *pra*.

For it is incorrect to say that the application [of the suffix] is possible here in the root (*dhātu*). Since the term *dhātau* (in the root) is understood from a previous rule and the term *supi* (after a nominal ending) is also stated, and since there is no root that ends in a nominal suffix (*subanta*), this [suffix] is understood here as a qualifier referring to a portion of the root by virtue of its proximity. Thus he says: "In a root that has a portion consisting of a nominal ending," and so forth.
Regarding the form *upālkārīyati*:
how, when the rule is stated as "after *ṛ*" (*ṛtaḥ*), does the *vṛddhi* substitution apply to the letter *ḷ*? To this he says: "Of the letters *ṛ* and *ḷ*," and so forth.

Since the designation *savarṇa* (homogeneous) is prescribed for the sounds *ṛ* and *ḷ*, the letter *ṛ*, when being grasped, causes the letter *ḷ* to be included as well; therefore, the *vṛddhi* substitution also occurs there.

Regarding the statement, "The mention of Āpiśali is for the sake of honor," one might ask: why does it not serve the purpose of providing an option (*vikalpa*)? To this he replies: "The word 'or' (*vā*) is indeed already stated."

The intention is this: although both honor (*pūjā*) and optionality (*vikalpa*) are accomplished simply by the mention of the word *ācārya*, nevertheless, the word *vā* was employed in order to indicate that honor is the primary purpose of mentioning *ācārya*. Regarding the phrase "see the cow" (*gāṃ paśya*): how is this cited as an example, given that since the suffix is marked with the *ṇi*t (by *goto ṇit* [Pāṇini 7.1.90]), the subsequent rule would require *vṛddhi*? To this he says: "The word *dyo* also ends in the vowel *o*," and so forth.

Since the use of the *tapara* marker (the short *a*) is well-established in the specification of phonemes, the *tapara* designation in the rule *gotaḥ* is understood to indicate that which ends in the vowel *o*; consequently, even after the word *dyo*, a *sarvanāmasthāna* suffix is treated as having the *ṇit* quality.
If this is so, why does *vṛddhi* not occur here? To this he says: "By that," and so forth.

If the *sarvanāmasthāna* suffix following the word *dyo* were not to have the *ṇit* quality, then in the example *dyāṃ paśya*, the substitution of *āt* would find its scope [by P. 7.1.14], whereas in *gāṃ paśya*, that *āt* substitution would be superseded by *vṛddhi* due to its higher status [as a subsequent rule].

If, however, a sarvanāmasthāna suffix following even the word *dyo* were to be treated as having the marker *ṇit*, then in the case of *dyāṃ paśya*, the substitution of *vṛddhi* would indeed apply. Consequently, since this rule for *ātva* is prescribed when *vṛddhi* has not yet taken effect, it—being without any other scope (*anavakāśa*)—would block the *vṛddhi*. Therefore, the example *gāṃ paśya* is most appropriate.

Now, one might ask here: why does the substitution of *ā* for the vowel *au* not occur in the forms *acinavam* and *asunavam*, where, after the application of *guṇa* to the suffixes of the root *ci* and *su* in the *laṅ* tense with the ending *mip*, the *mip* is replaced by *am* according to the rule *tasthasthamipām* [Pāṇini 3.4.101]? To this he says: "In the case of *am*" (*ami*), etc.
Because of its association with *śas*, or because of the governing context of *sup*, this *am* is understood specifically as the *sup* suffix;
therefore, there is no occasion here for the substitution of *ā*.

But in the case of *citraguṃ paśya*, since the short vowel [of the *go*] has already been applied, there is no long *o* sound; therefore, by the prohibition of the status of being a substitute (*sthānivadbhāva*) according to [Pāṇini 1.1.56], the substitution of *ā* does not occur. Regarding *upelayati*:
the root *il* in the sense of "impelling" (Dhātupāṭha 1660) takes the causative suffix *ṇic*. Regarding *prokhati*: [the root is *ukh*].
Regarding the root *ukh* in *ukha-nakha* (Dhātupāṭha 1.28, 1.34), *ukh* is listed in the *bhū-ādi* group as having the meaning of "motion."

If they maintain that the rule *vā supi* [Pāṇini 6.1.89] continues to apply, then, since this would form a single syntactical unit (*ekavākyatā*) with that [rule], the substitution of the single subsequent form (*pararūpa*) would be applied optionally only to a verbal root ending in a *su*-affix; however, in the case of what is not a *su*-affix (*asu*), the single subsequent form would simply not occur at all. To address this, he says "And that," etc. For this fault would indeed arise if there were a single syntactical unit; but here there is no single syntactical unit—what then? There is a split of the sentence (*vākyabheda*).
Therefore, that [rule] being followed here effects an option only with respect to verbal roots (*dhātu*), whereas with respect to other elements, the subsequent form (*pararūpa*) invariably prevails.

In this regard, there are two statements: first, "When a verbal root beginning with *eṅ* follows a preposition ending in an *a*-vowel, provided that the root is not a member of a nominal stem (*asubanta*), a single substitute consisting of the subsequent form occurs for both the preceding and following sounds"; second, "When a verbal root beginning with *eṅ* follows a preposition ending in an *a*-vowel, provided that the root is a member of a nominal stem (*subanta*), a single substitute consisting of the subsequent form optionally occurs for both the preceding and following sounds.
Among these, by means of the first statement, the subsequent form is established as mandatory in cases such as *upelayati*, where the root is not a member of a nominal stem.

By the second [sūtra], however, *pararūpa* (the single substitute of the form of the subsequent element) is optionally prescribed for a verbal root (*dhātu*) that is a constituent part of a word ending in a case-suffix (*subanta*), as in cases such as *upeṅkīyati*.
The division of the rule (*vākyabheda*) is obtained through the principle of *tantra* (simultaneous application) from the enunciation of two sūtras in the form "eṅi pararūpam.

When both sūtras are being enunciated, although the word "ekah" [from 6.1.101] continues to apply [to the first], it is not connected [to the first sūtra] because of the requirement of the desired result; however, in the second [sūtra], it is indeed connected.
By this, the two statements previously mentioned are established:
"it must be stated," which means it must be explained.

In this regard, the following is the explanation: In the subsequent sūtra, the word *ca* (and) is for the purpose of adding further rules; by it, the substitution of the single form of the latter (*pararūpa*) will occur in cases such as *śakandhu* and others.
Furthermore, the meaning of the term *vaktavya* (to be stated) in the subsequent [sūtra] and its explanation should be understood in exactly this same way.
[This applies to the rule]: *eve cāniyoge*.
*Niyoga* means *niyojana*, which signifies "employment" or "application. *Aniyoga* (the negation of *niyoga*) means "impossibility" or "inapplicability.
In this context, within the word *eva*, the single-substitute form (*pararūpa*) is to be understood.

The word *eva* functions in the sense of non-restriction (*aniyama*). When it expresses that very same restriction as being unqualified by an action, then the *pararūpa* (substitution of the latter form) occurs; but when it is qualified by an action, then there is *vṛddhi* (vowel strengthening) alone.
Regarding the term *bimboṣṭhī*:
the suffix *ṅīṣ* is applied by the rule *nāsikodarauṣṭha* [Pāṇini 4.1.55].
Is this the sentence "tiṣṭha devadattauṣṭhaṃ paśya" (Stay, Devadatta, look at the lip)? No, it is not a compound (*samāsa*).
From the word *devadatta*, by [Pāṇini 6.1.69], there is the elision (*lopa*) of the nominative suffix *su*. Regarding the example *adyoḍhā* ("married today"):
it is *adya-oḍhā*.

Now, one might object: since the substitution of *guṇa* by [Pāṇini 6.1.87] has replaced *aṅ* with *āṅ*, is this not a proper example for *āṅ*? There is no fault, because the single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) resulting from *āṅ* and *māṅ* is included under the term *āṅ*.
For this was already stated previously: "When [a substitute] occurs in place of two things indicated by the genitive case, it receives the designation of either one.

Why, then, is there a separate mention of *āṅ*? Since the form *ādyoḍha*, etc., would already be established—first by lengthening according to *prāg āṅaḥ pūrveṇa saha* (P. 6.1.101) and then by *guṇa* substitution according to *tataḥ pareṇa saha* (P. 6.1.87)? It is not so established; because of the rule "the operation between a verbal root and a prefix is internal" (*antaraṅga*), the *guṇa* substitution of *ā* for *ā* + *u* must occur first. And that being the case, the *vṛddhi* substitution would result.
Therefore, the inclusion of *āṅ* must also be made [in the rule].
[This is because] it is stated that "here, the lengthening of a vowel before a homogeneous vowel (*akaḥ savarṇe dīrghatvam*) is superseded.

This is because the present rule is prescribed without qualification (*aviśeṣavihita*), whereas the lengthening of a vowel before a homogeneous vowel is prescribed as a general rule (*sāmānyavihita*).
It has been established that even a rule prescribed for a specific case (viśeṣavihita) can supersede a rule prescribed for a general case (sāmānyavihita). Regarding the form *bhindyuḥ*:

from the root *bhid* with the suffix *liṅ*, the *jhi* ending, the *yāsuṭ* augment, the *jus* substitution by [Pāṇini 3.4.108], the *śnam* augment, the elision of the vowel *a* by [Pāṇini 6.4.111], and the elision of the *sakāra* by [Pāṇini 7.2.79] (*liṅaḥ salopo'nantyasya*), we arrive at the form *bhindyā-uḥ*. In this state, the present rule effects the single-substitute *pararūpa* (the subsequent form). Regarding the form *aduḥ*: [the same process applies].

The *luṅ* [aorist] suffix after the root *dadāti*, with the suffix *jhi*; by the rule *ātaḥ* [Pāṇini 3.4.110], *jhi* is replaced by *jus*; by the rule *gātisthāghupābhūbhyaḥ sicaḥ parasmaipadeṣu* [Pāṇini 2.4.77], there is the elision (*luk*) of *sic*; when the form *adāt-us* is established, the present rule effects the substitution of the subsequent form (*pararūpatva*). Thus we have *koruāā* and *koṣitā*. Now, one might object: "In this single counter-example, the result will not occur by the very *paribhāṣā* ‘when a meaningful element is mentioned, that which is meaningless is not included’ (Vyāḍi’s Paribhāṣā 1). For the word *uruāā* as a whole is meaningful, whereas the constituent part *us* is not."

In the second case, however, it will not occur even by this *paribhāṣā*: "Between that which is stated by its own technical definition (*lakṣaṇa*) and that which is stated by its own word-form (*pratipadokta*), only that which is stated by its own word-form is to be taken, and not that which is derived through a definition" (*Vyā.pa.* 3). For [the form] there is derivative (*lākṣaṇika*); for instance, when the suffix *niṣṭhā* follows the root *vas*, after the semivowel-vocalization (*samprasāraṇa*) has been performed because it belongs to the *yajādi* group, we have *uṣitaḥ*. In that case, the substitution of the single substitute for the latter form (*pararūpa*) does not take place—so what is the use of the rule "not after a non-final [consonant]" (*apadāntāt*)? Thus...

The inclusion of the term *apadānta* (not being at the end of a word), which exceeds what is required by the context, indicates this meaning: that the single-substitute rule (*pararūpa*) applies to the letter *u* alone, regardless of specific distinctions such as whether it is meaningful or meaningless.
Consequently, the rule *usyapadāntāt* (Pāṇini 6.1.95) does not apply [to the *u* in *bhindyuḥ*].
For in the case of *bhindyuḥ*, the entire complex beginning with the suffix *yāsuṭ* is meaningful, but its constituent part, the letter *u*, is not.
It also occurs in the case of a word based on a technical definition (*lākṣaṇika*), as in *babhuṣaḥ paśya*.

From the root *bhā* in the sense of "shining" (Dhātupāṭha 1051), the suffix *kvasu* is applied after the *liṭ* tense marker; then *śas* is added. By [Pāṇini 6.4.131], there is vocalization (*saṃprasāraṇa*); by [Pāṇini 6.1.108], there is the formation of a single preceding form (*pūrvarūpa*). When the form *babhā usa as* is established, this rule effects the substitution of the subsequent form (*pararūpatva*). This should be understood as an example under the view that [the suffix] is *sārvadhātuka*.
In the view that it is a semi-vowel substitute (*ardhadhātuka*), the form is established simply by the elision of the phoneme *h*. It also occurs in the case of a [root] with an *anubandha*: *adhuḥ*.
Where, then, would it occur? In *babhūḥ*.

But surely, if [the rule] were meaningless, one might assume this purpose for the mention of "not at the end of a word" (*apadānta*): that there is indeed a purpose for it in the aforementioned sūtra. What is that? It is so that [the rule] may apply where it is not at the end of a word, but not here—so that in *daṇḍāgram*, [the substitution] does not occur. This is not so; if this alone were the intended purpose, then he would have placed it in the subsequent sūtra itself. However, because it is placed here, it is understood that its intent is precisely to establish the meaning as stated. Furthermore, by virtue of the governing context (*adhikāra*), it certainly serves the purpose of the subsequent rules as well.

In the form *koṣita*, the augment *iṭ* is applied by [Pāṇini 7.2.52] *vasatikṣudhoḥ*; then, by [Pāṇini 8.3.60] *śāsavasighasīnāṃ ca*, the substitution of *ṣ* occurs. Because that [substitution] is considered asiddha (not yet established), one should understand that the rule for *pararūpa* (the single substitute of the form of the subsequent vowel) would otherwise apply.
As for *cakre*, this is the form of the root *kṛ* in the perfect tense (*liṭ*).
Regarding the form *abibhayuḥ*:

from the root *ñibhī* in the sense of "fear" (*bhaye*, Dhātupāṭha 1084), in the *laṅ* tense with the *śap* suffix, there is *ślu* by [Pāṇini 2.4.75], followed by reduplication. Then, by [Pāṇini 3.4.109] *sijabhyastavidibhyaśca*, the *jus* replaces *jhi*; and by [Pāṇini 7.3.83] *jusi ca*, there is *guṇa*. In the case of *pace* and *yajai*, [Pāṇini 6.1.88] would require *vṛddhi*; therefore, the intention is that this very rule [of *ekādeśa*] serves as an exception (*apavāda*) to that [rule for *vṛddhi*] by establishing a single substitute (*pararūpatva*). Thinking that the word *āt* continues from [Pāṇini 6.1.84] *ādguṇaḥ*, he asks: "Why [is it said] 'from a short vowel' (*ataḥ*)?"
To show that the mention of the long vowel *ā* here is for the purpose of excluding [the short *a*], he says: "yānti, vānti.
Regarding "apace":
this is the first person singular of the middle voice in the *laṅ* [tense], with the augment *iṭ*; [the substitution of] *at* occurs by [Pāṇini 6.1.87].
But when there is another form [following], that quality is not obtained. This word *prathama* (first) refers to an object of denotation that depends on a specific arrangement;
for when others are observed, that which has nothing preceding it is the referent of the word *prathama*.

And here, because of the general indication "of the first two" (*prathamayoḥ*), it is not known which two "firsts" are being grasped; therefore, to ensure that understanding, he says: "The word *prathamā*," and so forth.
In this treatise, the word *prathamā* is a conventional term (*rūḍha*) for a specific case-ending; it is well-known as the first triad among the *sup*-suffixes.

For instance, in such rules as "optionally [the suffix] of the two preceding *prathamā*s" (Pāṇini 8.1.26) and "from the seventh, fifth, and first [cases]" (Pāṇini 5.3.27), that very specific case-ending is indicated by the word *prathamā*.
Therefore, because it is a conventional term, it is understood that here the word *prathamā* refers to that specific case-ending.

But surely, the word *prathamā* used here in this treatise is a technical term (*rūḍha*) for a specific case-ending (*vibhakti*) and is feminine in gender; moreover, its very femininity is doubtful? This is not so; from the very employment of the word *prathamā*, it is determined that this [term] is taken in the feminine gender. For if this were an employment of the masculine form, then, since this is the case, there would have been a mention of the suffix (*pratyaya-grahaṇa*). And if the mention of the suffix were intended, then one would have said simply "of *au* and *jas*" (*aujasoḥ*).

And even when this is stated, there is no possibility of including the vowel *au* belonging to the second [case], because here, due to association (*sāhacarya*) with the nominative (*jas*), only the *au* belonging to the first case will be understood. Therefore, it is beyond doubt that this is a reference to the feminine gender. Now, if this word "first" (*prathamā*) is conventionally established (*rūḍha*) in this treatise as referring to a specific case-ending, then in such a case, since it is a specific case-ending, it ought to be in the singular, as in "one" (*eka*); so how is there the dual "of the two first cases" (*prathamayoḥ*)? To this, he says: "Due to association with that," and so forth.

Because of its association with that specific case ending called "first" (*prathamā*), the second case (*dvitīyā*) is also referred to as "first"; consequently, due to its duality, the dual number alone is logical.
By this [use of the term] *prathamayoḥ*, he shows that this refers to the two case endings, not to the two [words] themselves—as in the examples *vṛkṣau* and *lakṣau*.

How is this illustrated? For, by the rule *para-rūpa* [Pāṇini 6.1.97], the single-substitute form of the subsequent vowel (*pararūpa*) ought to occur here. Indeed, that [rule]—being introduced when another suffixal element (*vibhaktyantara*) is present—just as it subverts the lengthening (*dīrghatva*) of a homogeneous vowel (*akaḥ savarṇe dīrghaḥ*), would likewise subvert the lengthening prescribed by *prathamayoḥ pūrvasavarṇaḥ*. To this, he says: "In the presence of a guṇa vowel," and so forth.
He provides the justification for this very point with the words: "Because it precedes," and so forth. The particle *iti* indicates the reason (*hetu*).

Why? Because of the principle: "Exceptions [apavāda] subvert the rules immediately preceding them, not those that follow" (Vyāḍipāda 9). Therefore, the *pararūpa* [substitution] subverts the lengthening (*dīrghatva*); for that [lengthening] is what immediately precedes it. However, the lengthening prescribed by the rule "the first two [cases] take the same sound as the preceding" (*prathamayoḥ pūrvasavarṇaḥ*) is not subverted, because of the reverse order. This is illustrated in the example "agnī" and so forth.

In the absence of the mention of "pūrva" (the preceding), when there is a substitution of a long vowel as the most similar (*antaratama*) for the *sthānin*—which is the combination of the preceding and following vowels in cases such as *agnī itaḥ*—there would have to be a substitution by that which is most similar to one of the two constituent parts. Here, there are two constituents: the preceding and the following. Since no restrictive rule is obtained to the effect that the substitution must belong to the preceding part alone—due to the lack of a rule establishing such a restriction—the substitution occurring alternately for those two might, in certain instances, be a *parasavarṇa* (homogeneous with the following). Therefore, the mention of "pūrva" is made in order to exclude that possibility.
The inclusion of the term *savarṇa* (homogeneous), however, is for the purpose of removing the contradiction (*vipratiṣedha*).

For if that were not present, while the word *dīrgha* (long) is being carried over [from the previous rule], a contradiction would arise in the case of *agnī*, since: if the preceding [vowel] is not long, then it is not long; and if it is long, then it is not preceding.
If the preceding [vowel] is not long, then it is not long; and if it is long, then it is not preceding.

And if by the word "prior" (pūrva) the prior form were intended, then the genitive case would have been used as in "of the prior" (pūrvasya) following the rule for long vowels; and in that case, the mention of "homogeneous" (savarṇa) could have been omitted. Or, if it is included, it should be understood as being for the sake of easy comprehension.

"The mention of 'long' [refers to] when the substituend has three morae," and so forth. When *agni* and *au* stand thus, if the mention of "long" were not present, the single substitute being applied would result in a three-moraic vowel due to the closest similarity (*āntaratamya*) to the substituend; for the substituend itself consists of three morae. To explain: in this case, the substituend is a composite consisting of the *ikāra* (the vowel *i*) of the word *agni*, which has one mora, and the *aukāra* (the diphthong *au*), which has two morae.

Therefore, for the purpose that—when a three-mora vowel (*trimātra*) is the substituend—a substitute that is the most similar (*antaratama*) and also three morae should not occur, the mention of "long" (*dīrgha*) is made.

For when the long vowel is mentioned, the substitute is qualified by it, and thus the undesirable consequence of a three-mora substitute does not arise; this is because the designation "long" (*dīrgha-saṃjñā*) is prescribed only for two-mora vowels. Regarding the phrase "therefore, from the long vowel homogeneous with the preceding" (*tasmāt pūrvasavarṇadīrghāt*):
by this, he shows that the word "therefore" (*tasmāt*) refers to the internal long vowel homogeneous with the preceding.
Regarding the phrase "of the *sakāra* which is a constituent part of *śas*":

by this, the genitive case in *śasaḥ* is a partitive genitive (*avayava-ṣaṣṭhī*) with respect to the *sakāra* that constitutes a part of *śas*. Alternatively, it is an adjective qualifying the meaning of the suffix, namely *puṃsi* (in the masculine): "if *śas* has been produced in the sense of a plurality of males."

Or, [the term "masculine"] is a qualifier of the base (*prakṛti*). If you ask, "From which word?"—it is from the word *pum* (masculine), as in the rule *paraḥ śas*. In that context, when the meaning of the suffix is qualified, this is the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) regarding the passage beginning with "all these": examples such as *vṛkṣān* and *agnīn* are appropriate, because the suffix *śas* is produced here when there is a plurality of males (*puṃsām*). As for the two examples *ṣaṇḍhakān* and *paṇḍakān*, they are inappropriate; for the suffix *śas* is not produced here in the sense of a plurality of males, but rather in the sense of a plurality of neuters (*napuṃsakānām*). Therefore, he says: "All these," and so forth.

By the use of the term "all," [the author] shows that not only words such as *vṛkṣa* (tree) express their own referent (*svārtha*) as qualified by the general property of masculinity (*puṃlliṅga*), but that the words *ṣaṇḍaka* and *paṇḍaka* do so as well. Furthermore, their own referent is a substance (*dravya*) such as a tree, delimited by the general property of masculinity. Thus, since all these [words] denote objects qualified by the masculine gender, the prima facie argument—that the suffix *śas* arising after them occurs only when there is a plurality of males—is refuted.

But when it is a qualifier of the base (*prakṛti*), then this prima facie argument holds: the example "vṛkṣān" and so forth is appropriate, for in that case the suffix *śas* follows a masculine word; however, the two examples "sthūrān" and "ararakān" would not be appropriate.

For instance, from the forms *sthūrāyā apatyāni* and *ararakāyā apatyāni*, the suffix *yañ* is applied [by Pāṇini 4.1.105], and when the elision [of the feminine suffix] is effected by [Pāṇini 2.4.64], there is also the elision of the feminine suffix itself by the rule *luk taddhitaluki* [1.2.49]. Thus, the suffix *aṇ* produced from these two feminine words, *sthūra* and *araraka*, follows feminine words; why then does it not follow neuter words? To this he says: "All these," and so forth.
For here the base itself, ending in the elision of the *taddhita* suffix, occurs in the sense of the suffix-meaning (*pratyayārtha*), and that suffix-meaning is qualified by the masculine gender.

Therefore, the prima facie argument—that not only words such as *vṛkṣa* (tree) express their own referent (*svārtha*) as qualified by the masculine gender, but that even the words *sthūrā* and *ararakā* do so—is refuted. If this is the case, then there is this fault in the position that the suffix-meaning (*pratyayārtha*) is the qualifier: [the example] *cañcā pumāṃsaḥ* ("male weavers' tools"). [The suffix] *kan* [is applied] by rule 5.3.96; then, by rule 5.3.98, there is elision (*lup*). When the suffix *śas* arises for the plural number of males from the word *cañcā*, which ends in *lup*, then in the expression *cañcāḥ paśya* ("look at the weavers' tools"), the substitution of *natva* (the change to *n*) would result. To this, he says: "But here," and so forth.

For here, the suffix *śas* has not been produced in the sense of a plurality of males (*puṃbahutva*); rather, it is in the sense of a plurality of females (*strībahutva*). Since even a male possesses that state [of being female] by virtue of being metaphorically designated as female (*strītva-atideśa*), the substitution of *n* does not occur here. The term "long" (*dīrgha*) is understood from the context; since that term is present here in the ablative case (*pañcamyanta*) by virtue of its meaning, one might think that even without the explicit statement "from that" (*tasmāt*), the substitution of *n* for *śas* would occur after a long vowel. With this intention, he says: "But here," and so forth.

For in this case, the suffix *śas* has not been produced after a plurality of masculine nouns (*puṃbahutva*); rather, it occurs after a plurality of feminine nouns (*strībahutva*), because even for a masculine noun, the status of being feminine is extended (*atideśa*) through its treatment as if it were feminine (*yuktavadbhāva*). Consequently, the substitution of *n* [for *ś*] does not take place here. The term "long" (*dīrgha*) is understood from the context; since that term is presented here in the ablative case by virtue of the sense, one might think that even without the explicit statement "from that" (*tasmāt*), the substitution of *n* for *śas* would occur only after a long vowel. With this intention, he asks: "What is the purpose of saying 'from that'? (*tasmāditi kim*)?
"Look at these cows grazing!
Here, by rule [Pāṇini 6.1.93], there is the substitution of *ā* (ātvam).

If the word *tat* were to refer back to the immediately preceding long vowel (*dīrgha*), then the substitution of *n* would be prescribed without distinction for any long vowel; consequently, it would also apply in the case of "Look at these cows grazing," since this *ā* is indeed a long vowel.

Therefore? There is no fault in that word; for the substitution of *ākāra* (ā) is not prescribed by the immediately preceding sūtra. In "khaṭve," there is the substitution of *śī* by [Pāṇini 7.1.18] "auṅa āpaḥ.
In "kuṇḍe," [the same applies].

In this case as well, by [Pāṇini 7.1.19], and when that has been applied, there is *guṇa* substitution by [Pāṇini 6.1.87]. The term *āt* (long vowel) does not carry over [from the previous rule]; therefore, this is a prohibition of the *pūrvasavarṇa* [substitution] after a long vowel only.
Now, how is the lengthening in *khaṭvā* [justified] by [Pāṇini 6.1.102]? The mention of "after a long vowel" (*dīrghāt*) is for the sake of clarity.

But would it not follow even in the absence of that [restriction], as in *vṛkṣāḥ*? This is not so; for if it were to apply here as well, then the word *ici* in the preceding sūtra would be rendered purposeless.

In that case, would there not be [the form] *agnaye*? There is no fault here because it is desired. For in this instance, by virtue of its higher status, only the *guṇa* substitution occurs according to *jasi ca* [Pāṇini 7.3.109]. Then, would it be for the sake of the subsequent rule so that the long vowel [substitution] occurs according to [6.1.106]? This is not so; because the mention of the option (*vā*) there is understood as a fixed option (*vyavasthitavibhāṣā*), the long vowel will occur only after a long vowel, not after a short one.
The rule *jasi ca* [Pāṇini 7.3.109] is also for the sake of clarity alone.

But surely, if this *jasi ca* did not exist, would there not be a prohibition even for the suffix *śas* in cases such as *yuvatīḥ paśya* ("see the young women") and *paddhatīḥ paśya* ("see the paths")? It will not occur because of an indicator (*jñāpaka*). Since Pāṇini makes the mention of the masculine (*puṃgrahaṇa*) in the rule *ato bhisa ais* [6.1.103], that indicates that the prohibition does not apply to *śas*.

For that mention is made solely for the purpose of excluding feminine forms, since in the neuter gender, the substitution of the long vowel homogeneous with the preceding one (*pūrvasavarṇadīrghatva*) is impossible.

If this prohibition were to apply even in feminine forms such as *yuvatīḥ paśya* ("look at these young women"), then, due to the absence of the long vowel resulting from the homogeneous substitution (*pūrvasavarṇadīrgha*), the substitution of *n* would not occur at all; so what would be the purpose of including the mention of "masculine" (*puṃs*)? [Objection: Then is the mention of *jas* for the sake of subsequent rules? [Response: This is not the case; because the mention of the option (*vā*) in that [subsequent rule] is understood as a restricted option (*vyavasthitavibhāṣā*), it will simply not apply elsewhere than in the case of *jas*. Regarding the form *mārutīḥ*: [the derivation is as follows: from *marud-devatā āsām* ("those whose deity is Marut"), the suffix *aṇ* is applied by Pāṇini 4.2.24. Then, the feminine suffix *ṅīp* is applied by Pāṇini 4.1.15, followed by the homogeneous long vowel substitution (*savarṇadīrgha*).

Regarding "vārāhīḥ" [as explained in the *Kāśikā* and *Padamañjarī*]: the suffix *aṇ* is applied by [Pāṇini 4.3.135], *varāhasya vikāraḥ*, and the feminine suffix *ṅīp* is added as before. Regarding "upānahī": [the same applies].

The suffix *ṅīṣ* is applied by [Pāṇini 4.1.41]. This rule is stated because the substitution of a long vowel homogeneous with the preceding one (*pūrvasavarṇadīrgha*) would otherwise apply; furthermore, the word "long" (*dīrgha*) is understood here from the previous context, for otherwise this rule would be purposeless. Now, what is the purpose of including the term "preceding" (*pūrva*), given that the subject under discussion is already established as "the preceding"? One might argue that the very same "preceding" mentioned in the original context will simply carry over here. To this, he says: "The inclusion of the term 'preceding'... and so forth.
The mention of "preceding" (*pūrva*) is for the purpose that [the substitute] should be of the same class as the preceding [vowel].
To show what is excluded by the particle *eva*, he says: "Let it not be the closest among those homogeneous with the preceding.
This is a *karmadhāraya* compound: that which is both homogeneous with the preceding (*pūrvasavarṇa*) and the closest (*antaratama*).

For if the mention of "the preceding" (*pūrvagrahaṇa*) were not present, that which is the preceding [mention of *pūrva*] would have to be carried over by that very [word]; and while that is being carried over, the mention of "homogeneous" (*savarṇagrahaṇa*), being connected to it, would also be carried over. And in that case, by this metarule (paribhāṣā) [P. 1.1.50], only that which is homogeneous with the preceding would be joined to the following.

But if this were so, what undesirable consequence would follow? If one were to argue that in cases such as *vṛkṣam*, a substitute of two morae (*dvimātra*) would result from a base (*sthānin*) of two morae, this is not the case; for if it were so, this rule would be purposeless, since [the desired form] is already established by [Pāṇini 6.1.102]. Therefore, he says: "In the case of *kumārim*, however," and so forth.

In the word *kumārī*, the vowel *ī* has two morae (*dvimātra*), while the suffix *am* contains the vowel *a* with one mora (*mātrika*). Here, the entire combination [of the stem and suffix] constitutes the substituendum (*sthānin*). In that case, if a homogeneous substitute (*pūrvasavarṇa*) were prescribed, it would have to be three morae (*trimātra*)—the most similar (*antaratama*) to the three-moraed substituendum. However, because of the inclusion of the word "preceding" (*pūrva*), the substitute becomes two-moraed (*dvimātra*), having the same nature as the preceding [vowel]. This is expressed by the rule "optionally in the Veda" (*vā chandasi*) and so forth.

If, then, the rule *yadi tarhi* [Pāṇini 6.1.106] continues to apply, would it not follow that when this [rule] forms a single syntactical unit with it, the substitution of the preceding vowel (*parapūrvatva*) would not be established in the colloquial language (*bhāṣā*)? This is not so; because that [rule] continuing here effects an option only in Vedic usage (*chandas*) through a division of the sentence as before, and not in the colloquial language. This substitution of the preceding vowel is prescribed for the purpose that the semi-vowel (*yaṇ*) replacement of the *saṃprasāraṇa* (vocalization) should not occur.
For if the *yaṇ* replacement were to take place here, then the prescription of *saṃprasāraṇa* would be rendered meaningless. Therefore...

"By the very force of the rule prescribing *samprasāraṇa*, the substitution of *yaṇ* will not occur; so why is this [substitution of *parapūrvatva*] prescribed? To this he says: "By the force of the prescription of *samprasāraṇa*" and so forth.

Because the substitution of *yaṇ* would not occur by the force of the prescription of *samprasāraṇa*, there would result the hearing of the separated form (*vigṛhīta*) without the application of the rules for *saṃhitā*. Therefore, so that this fault does not arise, the substitution of the preceding vowel with the following one (*parapūrvatva*) is prescribed. "Only by the rule 'optionally in the Veda' (*vā cchandasī*)" and so forth.

In this case as well, a split of the sentence (*vākyabheda*) should be understood as before; otherwise, it would not apply in the vernacular (*bhāṣā*). Regarding the form *yajyamānaḥ* (or *yajyamānau* according to the *Kāśikā*), the substitution of *yaṇ* occurs in the alternative where there is no preceding *para*.

But how, then, can there be the substitution of *yaṇ* here, since it ought to be the separate [vowels] that are taken up? For was it not just stated: "By the force of the prescription for *saṃprasāraṇa*, since the hearing of the separate [vowels] would otherwise result, the state of being preceded by the subsequent [vowel] is prescribed"? To this he says: "In the prescription of the state of being preceded by the subsequent," and so forth. For if the state of being preceded by the subsequent were not commenced, the hearing of the separate [vowels] would indeed result; [this is said] on the grounds that the *saṃprasāraṇa* [prescription] must not be rendered purposeless.

But when there is the condition of *parapūrvatva* (the substitution of the subsequent vowel for both), as in cases where *parapūrvatva* is intended—such as in *iṣṭam* and so on—is the *samprasāraṇa* meaningful there?
Therefore, in the alternative case where *parapūrvatva* does not occur, the *yaṇ* substitution indeed takes place.

Now, why does this not occur here: *śakahvau* [in the sense of] *śakahvartham*? For in this case, from the root *hvṛ* (to call) with the prefix *śaka*, there is the suffix *kvip*; because the root belongs to the *yajādi* class, there is vocalization (*saṃprasāraṇa*), followed by the substitution of the preceding vowel (*parapūrvatva*). Since that [resulting form] is included under the term "vocalized" (*saṃprasāraṇa*) by the rule *aglopiśca* [Pāṇini 6.4.94], which refers to those ending in a vocalized element, and because the single substitute for both the vocalized and non-vocalized vowels is designated as "vocalized," when the suffix *au* and the word *artha* follow, the substitution of the preceding vowel (*parapūrvatva*) would apply according to [Pāṇini 6.1.108]. To this, he says: "And when a vowel is internal," and so forth.

This vowel *ā* which is prescribed in place of the *ec* of the root *hve* is more internal (*antaraṅga*) and proximate to the *samprasāraṇa*, because both reside within the same verbal root. The vowel *au* and the vowel *ā* of the word *artha* are remote (*viprakṛṣṭa*).
They are remote both spatially and temporally, as it has been said: "in the case of *brāāhre*."
That which has a *samprasāraṇa* as its constituent part is external (*bāhya*) because it is not included therein;
and this is also due to time, as he says: "when it has subsequently occurred.
The meaning is that it is present at a time subsequent to the application of the rule for the *pūrvarūpa*.

In that context, between two vowels—one proximate and one remote—that vowel which is *antaranga* (internal) due to its proximity is the one to which this rule applies; since it has already achieved its purpose there, it does not subsequently apply to the remote vowel, such as the *au* in *aukārādi*.
