For example, in *agne'tra*, the *guṇa* substitution [of *e* for *a-i*] occurs by [Pāṇini 6.1.107]. Regarding the phrase "after *eṅ*" and so forth:
the meaning is that when *ṅasi* and *ṅas* follow, that vowel which is a constituent part (*avayava*) of those two [suffixes] is the one after which [the operation takes place].
In the example "agner āgacchati," there is the *guṇa* substitution [of *e*] by the rule "gher ṅiti" [Pāṇini 7.3.111].

Now, why does the correspondence of order (*yathāsaṃkhyam*) not apply here, since there are two *eṅ* vowels and also two [suffixes], *ṅasi* and *ṅas*, which would seem to require it? This is not a fault, for here an operation is not prescribed after *ṅasi* and *ṅas*; rather, it is prescribed in relation to that which is connected to them, and that [connection] is singular.

But even if there were a distinction based on the difference of the related elements (*sambandhī*), there would still be no fault; for here the particle *ca* is used in the sense of conjunction (*samuccaya*).

And such a conjunction occurs only if, after each individual *eṅ*, the substitution of the preceding vowel with the following one (*parapūrvatva*) takes place even when followed by *ṅasi* and *ṅas* individually; it does not occur otherwise.
Furthermore, the rule "iti ca" (Pāṇini 6.3.27) and "iti ca" (Pāṇini 3.1.125) indicates the absence of that [conjunction].
Or [it is understood] by the sign of the deviation from the general rule (*lakṣaṇavyabhicāra*).

By the subsequent placement of the genitive ending *ṅas*—which has fewer syllables—it is determined that there is no correspondence according to the order of enumeration (*yathāsaṃkhya*). [This is seen in the rule] "In place of two things indicated by the genitive," and so forth.

But what undesirable consequence would arise in cases such as *hotuḥ* if the substitution of *r* for *ṛ* (*raparatva*) were not applied? None at all; however, by logical necessity (*nyāyataḥ*), the substitution of *r* for *ṛ* would indeed apply, and therefore it must necessarily be performed.
To demonstrate that very same principle, it is stated: "In the place of two [sounds] specified by the genitive case.
The inclusion of the letter *t* in the term *ṛtaḥ* is for the purpose of excluding long vowels;
consequently, [the substitution] does not occur in rules such as *unyor graḥ* (3.3.29–32).

This *tapara* (the addition of *ṛ*) is also for the purpose of excluding the long vowel; for by the principle of closest proximity (*āntaratamya*), a two-moraic [vowel] would result in place of a two-moraic [original]. Now, one might argue that since "an *aṇ* being in the process of being substituted does not include its homogeneous counterparts" (Vyāḍipāda 35), there will be no inclusion of the homogeneous vowels; so what is the use of this *tapara* addition for the sake of exclusion? If that is so, then this serves to indicate that in this instance, an *aṇ* in the process of being substituted does include its homogeneous counterpart.

Therefore, in the forms *tenāmū* and *amūbhyām*, by the rule *adaso māt* [Pāṇini 8.2.80], a long *ū* is substituted in place of the long vowel [of *adas*]. It is said that "the mention of *khyatyāt* refers to the words *khi* and *khī*, as well as *ti* and *tī*, after they have undergone the substitution of *yaṇ*," because once the *yam* substitution has been applied, the form is identical and thus there is no distinction [between them].

Now, why is it that here only those forms of the words *khya* and *tya* ending in the vowel *ā* are not included? If you argue that this is because the simple words *khya* and *tya* cannot exist [as such], we say no; for if they do not exist in isolation, then let there be the inclusion of their derivatives—such as *mukhya*, *gosaṃkhya*, and so on, as well as *apatya*, *gārhapatya*, and so forth. This is not the case; for if it were so, the two grammatical rules [Pāṇini 7.1.92 and 4.1.33] would be untenable. [The word *sakha* is explained as: "one who exists together with a friend (*saha khena vartate*) is a *sakha*."

The term *sakhīyati* is a *bahuvrīhi* compound according to [Pāṇini 2.2.28], and the substitution of *sa-* for *saha-* occurs according to [Pāṇini 6.3.82]. The shortening of the vowel [to *i*] occurs according to [Pāṇini 7.4.33].
Regarding "sakhīḥ": by [Pāṇini 6.4.48] there is the elision of the letter *a*, and by [Pāṇini 6.1.66] there is the elision of the letter *y*. Regarding "lunam": [the same applies].
The substitution of *ṇ* for the final *t* of the *niṣṭhā* suffix occurs by the rule *lvādibhyaḥ* [Pāṇini 8.2.44].

Now, one might object: "But this is not the word *tī*; so how can it be cited as an example of that? To this he says: "The substitution of *ṇ* for the *niṣṭhā*," and so forth. Then, why does it not occur here: *atasakher āgacchati* ("he comes from the *atasakhi*") and *senāpater āgacchati* ("he comes from the *senāpati*"), since in these cases too there is the word *khi* and the word *ti*? To this he says: "Because of the mention of the modified form," and so forth.

This distorted formulation (*vikṛtanirdeśa*), made by applying the *yaṇ* substitution to the term *khyatyāt*, serves this very purpose: that [the suffix] should apply only where there is the *yaṇ* substitution. Since there is no *yaṇ* substitution here, it does not occur; otherwise, the distorted formulation would be meaningless. [Objection: But surely it would serve the purpose of brevity (*laghvartha*); for if it were stated as *khitikhītībhyaḥ*, there would be prolixity (*gaurava*). [Response: It is thought thus: if it were to occur even where there is no *yaṇ* substitution, then one should have said simply *khītībhyām*.

And even when this is stated thus, [the substitution] would not apply after those ending in short vowels—namely, from the word *khi* [in the form *sakhyaḥ*] by rule 5.1.126, *sakhyuryaḥ*, nor from the word *ti* [in the form *patyaḥ*] by rule 4.1.33? [This is because] it is established precisely by these two grammatical indications (*nirdeśa*); for here there is the mention of the words *sakhi* and *pati*, not of the words *sakhī* and *patī*.

For here, the word *pati* has no connection with sacrifice (*yajña*); nor is the suffix produced from the word *sakhi*, which is derived in such ways as "one who exists together with (*saha*) his own (*kha*)" capable of denoting the meaning of its base (*prakṛti*), because derivatives (*kṛt*), secondary formations (*taddhita*), and compounds (*samāsa*) are characterized by their denotative function. Therefore, the purpose of this modified mention is exactly as previously stated.

Now, why does that *yaṇ* substitution not occur here, [and] when would there need to be [the substitution of] *utva*? If it is argued that this is because it is barred by the *guṇa* [substitution] according to the rule *gher ṅiti* [Pāṇini 7.3.111], [we reply: no; because the technical designation *dhi* is prohibited by the rule *śeṣo dhyasakhiḥ* [Pāṇini 1.4.7]. To address this, he says: "Of the word *sakhi*," and so forth. And in this context, the reason is the prohibition: "There is no [application of the] rule of *tadanta* with a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) that possesses a specific marker" [Vyāḍi-paribhāṣā 89]. For what purpose is the word "of the following" (*parasya*) used? So that it might not apply to both the preceding and the following [sounds].
From this point forward, the phrase "of the preceding and following" (*pūrvaparayoḥ*) no longer applies. Regarding the rule "of that which has *u* as its indicatory letter" (*ukārānubandhakasya*):

if the word *ru* were the entire substitute for the whole [the preceding and following sounds], then in the case of *mahātaruvanam*, the substitution of *u* by the rule *haśi ca* (Pāṇini 6.1.110) would undesirably apply.
Furthermore, the addition of the indicatory letter *u* [in the rule *rori* (8.3.14)] would be rendered purposeless.

In this context, the letter *h* is used as a qualifier for this sūtra; however, within this aggregate (*samudāya*) which serves as the locus (*sthānin*), it becomes meaningless. Therefore, this [sūtra] refers to that which possesses the indicatory letter *u*. Now, one might object: since the substitution of *ut* (as in *r-ut-vam*) must be applied according to Pāṇini 6.1.113, the substitution of *ru* (from 8.2.66) is considered non-existent (*asiddha*); how then can the substitution of *ut* be prescribed for an *r* that does not exist? To this, he says: "The substitution of *ru* is also established by virtue of its basis (*āśrayāt*)."

If the substitution of *ru* were unestablished (*asiddha*), then the recourse to *ru* as the substitute would be purposeless; for there is no possibility of a *ru* characterized by the indicatory letter *u*.
Therefore, precisely because it serves as a basis [for other operations], the *ru* is not unestablished.
[The phrase] "of that too" refers to this.
Even where the substitution of *u* for *ru* after a vowel is prescribed, there is the protracted (*pluta*) vowel in the examples "suruāotā 3 atra" and "devadattā 3 atra," according to Pāṇini 8.2.84.

Here too, this is by virtue of Pāṇini 8.2.86: "In the opinion of the Easterners, the final syllable of a word ending in a heavy vowel (gurusaṃjñaka), provided it does not end in /ṛ/, becomes protracted even if it is not followed by another word."

Now, for what purpose is it stated that "after a non-protracted [vowel], before a non-protracted [vowel]" (*aplutād aplute*)? For when the letter *t* is added as a marker (*taparakaraṇa*) in the rule "after *h*, before *at*" (*hrato't*), would this not apply even when a protracted vowel follows a protracted vowel? To this he says: "of the protracted," and so forth. But surely the protracted vowel is already established in the rules concerning vowel-sandhi (*svarasandhi*), since this very rule—"protracted vowels and *pragṛhya* vowels remain in their original form before *āc*" (*plutapragṛhyā aci*)—teaches its preservation in its original state (*prakṛtibhāva*). He thinks thus: this very teaching of the preservation in the original state (*prakṛtibhāva*) must itself be the indicator (*jñāpaka*) [that the protracted vowel is otherwise not established].
Furthermore, even if it were somehow a *jñāpaka* (indicative evidence) regarding the domain of vowel-sandhi (*svarasandhi*), the substitution of *u* for *ru* would not be a vowel-sandhi.
Or, even if it were a *jñāpaka* regarding the domain of euphonic combination (*saṃhitā-kārya*), even then the substitution of *u* for *ru* would not be a euphonic combination operation.

For that by which letters are joined together is a euphonic combination operation, and letters do not become combined through the substitution of *u* for *ru*; this is because [the rule] still requires the application of *guṇa* and other operations such as *āṭ*. Since the word "preceding" (*pūrvatra*) is understood from the previous context, the substitution of *u* for *ru* is prescribed here precisely where it was not otherwise obtained.
The particle *ca* serves to carry forward [the condition] from rule 6.1.109, *aplutāt*.
Therefore, it does not apply here in the example: *suruāotā 3 vehi*. Regarding the term *prakṛtyā*, the third case ending is used in the sense of an instrument (*karaṇe*).
Regarding the term *antaḥpādam*:
this is a word ending in the locative case.

Having formed an *avyayībhāva* compound in the sense of a case ending, the locative case is then applied; for that locative, the substitution of *am* is made according to Pāṇini 2.4.84: *tṛtīyāsaptamyorbahulam*.
Regarding the passage beginning with "eṅaḥ":
a connection with the rule stating that "the *eṅ* ending in the ablative case remains in its original form" (*prakṛtyā bhavati*) is not possible.
Therefore, for the sake of the sense here, the mention of *eṅ* arises as a nominative case.
With the words "prakṛtiḥ" and so forth, he explains the word *prakṛti*.

For in common usage, the word *prakṛti* is employed in the sense of "intrinsic nature" (*svabhāva*), as in "nature is difficult to abandon"; it is also used in the sense of a "material cause," as in "milk is the *prakṛti* of curd. Here too, that same meaning is understood for it.
The indeclinable *antarā* functions as a locative.
For this very reason, the compound *antaḥpādam* is formed as an avyayībhāva.
Regarding the phrase "by the word *pāda*" and so forth:

how, then, is the inclusion of only the *ṛk*-verse quarter obtained, given that the word *pāda* is a general term? The thought is as follows: from rule 6.1.106, the mention of *chandas* (Vedic meter) is carried over here by the maxim of the frog-leap (*maṇḍūkapluti*), and by that means, the inclusion of only the *ṛk*-verse quarter is understood.

From the sūtra beginning with *atha* (Pāṇini 6.1.122), it is understood that the grammatical operation applies only to the Vedic language (*chandas*). For in this way, the mention of the term *sarvatra* ("everywhere") there becomes meaningful only if the preceding rule is intended for the Vedic language.
Having thus explained the meaning of the individual components, he states the meaning of the whole by means of the phrase "the letter *av*, the letter *ya*, etc. (*avakārayakāra*, etc.).
That in which the letters *va* and *ya* do not exist is described as such.
Regarding the phrase "by its own nature" (*svabhāvena*) and so forth:
when the word *prakṛti* is understood as referring to "own nature," then the meaning is this: the *eṅ* vowels exist by their own nature.

If one were to abandon its own nature (*svabhāva*), the operation of *saṃhitā* would not be possible. However, when the word *prakṛti* is understood as referring to the cause, then this is the meaning: "The *eṅ* exists by way of its causal self. The cause is the *eṅ*, which is the effect of the preceding [element] and so forth; it means that the *eṅ* exists by that very self, which is its own form. What is stated here is: prior to the operation of *saṃhitā*, the *eṅ* remains in that very form which it possessed.
To clarify these two points just mentioned, he says: "it does not undergo modification.

For it exists by way of its own nature (*svabhāva*) only if a state of modification characterized differently from that nature does not arise. Likewise, it exists even as the essence of the cause only if it does not arise into the state of being a modification.
The meaning is that it does not undergo transformation into the form of the effect.
Regarding the phrase "nor [is it] the cause and the effect," the "cause" (nimitta) refers to the letter *a* as qualified by posteriority (*paratva*).
For in that case, the original form (*prakṛtibhāva*) is prescribed by another rule;
the *eṅ* vowel is the subject of the operation, for it is that which possesses the operation of becoming its original form, as in:
"They yoked the horse in front."

In the middle of this *ṛc*-quarter, when there is the vowel *e*—whether in the word *te* or in the word *agre*—the *prakṛtibhāva* (non-application of sandhi) does not occur by [Pāṇini 6.1.109], nor does the substitution of *ay*. For example: *upaprayanto adhvaram*. Here too, because of the *prakṛtibhāva* of the *eṅ* vowel in the word *prayanta* immediately before the word *adhvara*, the *pūrvarūpa* (single-substitute) does not occur, nor does the substitution of *av*.

Likewise, in cases such as *sujāte aā*, one should understand that due to the preservation of the original form (*prakṛtibhāva*), the operation of *pūrvarūpa* (the single substitution of the preceding vowel) does not occur. In the example *ete 'rcayanti*,
in this word *ete*, the *eṅ* which is the phoneme *ekāra* occurs at the end of a word.
However, the *at* following that [the *eṅ*] occurs at the beginning of a word (*pādādau*), not in the middle of a word (*pādamadhye*).
For instance, in the phrase "te 'vadan," the *prakṛtibhāva* (non-sandhi) does not apply to the *eṅ* in the word *te*, because the *at* immediately following it is followed by the letter *v*.
"Avadan" means "they spoke";
it is the third person plural ending in the *laṅ* (imperfect) tense of the root *vad*.
"Te 'yajān" means "they sacrificed."
In this case as well, the *prakṛtibhāva* (non-application of sandhi) does not occur for the *eṅ* sound within the word *te*;
because the *at* immediately following it is followed by the letter *ya*,
as in *anvagni* and so forth.
Everything exists [in this view], yet the vowel *u* in the word *anu* does not become *eṅ*, nor does it undergo its original form (*prakṛtibhāva*).

Regarding the phrase "some" (*kecit*) and so forth: if they were to recite the rule as *nāntaḥpādam avyapare*, then in that case, the prohibition would apply only to what is preceded by another (*parapūrva*), but not to *ay* and *ava*; for is it not the case that the status of being preceded by another was just established for *eṅ*? To this he says: "In the case of those [who read] *saṃhitāyām*" and so forth.
If this prohibition were made with reference to a specific *saṃhitā* operation characterized by having another word preceding it (*parapūrvatva*), then this fault would arise.

However, when the prohibition is ordained with reference to any operation whatsoever prescribed under the heading of *saṃhitā*, then it is logical that there should be a prohibition of every single operation prescribed under that heading; such is their intention. [As in the example: "no avyāt."

From this [word *asmat*], when the second-person plural ending is applied, by [Pāṇini 8.1.21] the substitution of *ru* for *na*, by [6.1.113] the substitution of *u* for that *ru*, and then the *guṇa* substitution by [6.1.84], the form *naḥ* is obtained.

From the root *ava* in the sense of "protection" (*rakṣaṇe*) [Dhātupāṭha 600], in the optative (*liṅ*) with the augment *yāsuṭ* and the suffix *tip*, after the elision of the *ikāra* by [3.4.97] and the elision of the *sakāra* by [8.2.29], the form *avyāt* is obtained. Thus, [the phrase] *avadyāt*.
This word *avadya* ends in the fifth case singular. Regarding the form *avakramuḥ*, it is the perfect (liṭ) form of the root *kram* preceded by the prefix *ava*.

Others, however, explain it as being in the *luṅ* (aorist) tense: by [Pāṇini 3.1.44], there is *ślu*-elision of the suffix *cli*; by [Pāṇini 6.1.10], there is reduplication; and the substitution of *jus* is Vedic (*chāndasa*).
As for "avantu": this is the imperative (*loṭ*) of the root *ava*, with the substitution of *anta* for the suffix *jhi*, and the substitution of *u* for *e* according to [Pāṇini 3.4.76].

Regarding "avasyavaḥ": from the root *av*, by [Pāṇini 3.1.135] *asarvadhātubhyo 'sun*, the suffix *asun* is applied, yielding *avas*. From that, by [Pāṇini 3.1.8], the suffix *kyac* is applied; from that which ends in *kyac*, by [Pāṇini 3.2.170], the suffix *u* is applied; then *jas* is added; by [Pāṇini 7.3.109] *jasi ca*, *guṇa* substitution occurs, resulting in the vowel *o*; and by [Pāṇini 6.1.78], the substitution of *ava* takes place. Regarding "uro antarikṣam": there is the substitution of *utva* for the word *uras*; then by [Pāṇini 6.1.87] *ād guṇaḥ*, *guṇa* substitution occurs.

"It is taught that the word *uru* ending in *u*, when in the vocative case, becomes *uro*. This is because, after applying the *guṇa* substitution according to [Pāṇini 7.3.106], the form *uro* is obtained from the word *uru*. All these examples beginning with *āpaḥ* are imitations (*anukaraṇa*) that lack case endings, because the case endings produced after them have been elided by rules such as [Pāṇini 7.1.39]: *supāṃ suluk...*.
Here, *āpaḥ* is an imitation of the nominative plural ending.
"Juṣāṇo" is [the nominative] singular masculine ending;
"vṛṣṇo" is [the genitive].
The form *vaśiṣṭhe* is the nominative singular ending in *-e*;
it is the locative singular ending in *-e*.
This is a qualifier for the two words *amba* and *ambāle*.
[The compound] *ambikepūrve* is formed from the word *ambikā*, preceded by *ambike*; the compound is formed precisely because of this specific grammatical rule (*nipātana*).

Now, one might object: "Is not *ambe* an imitation of a vocative ending? And since that is the case, by the rule [Pāṇini 7.3.107], there ought to be the substitution of *e* (the *etva*) as an exception to the shortening; so how can there be *aitva* (the substitution of *ai*) in the form *ambe*? To this he replies: "Precisely because of this," and so forth.

Regarding the two words *ambāle* and *ambike*, this shortening is indeed appropriate; for he will state in the rule prescribing short vowels: "If [the word] consists of two syllables and has the sense of *amba*" (Vārttika 7.3.107). And [this applies] in cases such as *aṅga*.

By the use of the particle *iti*, the word *aṅga* mentioned previously is referred back. Regarding the rule "in the case of *tadādau cākāre*," both locative cases (*saptamī*) are in apposition (*samānādhikaraṇa*).
By the word "tat" (that), which refers back to what has preceded, he explains the meaning of the particle "iti": namely, "at the beginning of that.
This means at the beginning of the word *aṅga*.
[He says] "which is prior."
The term *eṅ* is connected [to the previous rule].

The particle *ca* (and) is used for the purpose of conjunction (*samuccaya*), so that when the vowel *a* at the beginning of the word *aṅga* is followed by *ap*, there may be the preservation of the original form (*prakṛtibhāva*) for the preceding *eṅ*.
In that case, when the vowel *a* of the word *aṅga* follows, the preservation of the original form would apply only to that *eṅ* which belongs to the word *aṅga* itself.
In this case, the *eṅ* vowels of the word *anaṅga* would not remain as they are when followed by the word *aṅga*. For example, in the phrase *prāṇo aṅge*,
the *eṅ* vowel in the word *prāṇaḥ* remains in its original form (*prakṛti*) before the vowel *a* of the word *aṅga*.
Regarding the rule "aṅga aṅge adīdhyat":

here, when the *eṅ* [vowels *e* or *o*] in the word *aṅga* occurs before the initial *a* of the word *aṅga*, there is the preservation of the original form (*prakṛtibhāva*) with respect to the beginning of the word *adīdhyat*. Regarding the rule "when followed by *ku* or *dha*":
this is a specification concerning the vowel *a*.
Why is it called *kudhau*? Because [the letter] *dh* follows [it], it is so designated.
In the syllable *dha*, the vowel *a* is for the sake of pronunciation.
"This is that Agni."

The word *agni* is derived from the root *aṅg* with the suffix *ni*, according to the rule *aṅgernir nalopaśca* (Pāṇini 6.4.20); thus, by the accent of the suffix (*pratyayasvara*), it is oxytone (*antodātta*). Since the *śas*-case ending is unaccented (*anudātta*), the vowel *a* [of the nominative singular] is likewise unaccented. Regarding the phrase "this is that sacrifice" (*ayaṃ so adhvaraḥ*):
the word *adhvara* is also oxytone by the accent of the nominal stem (*prātipadikasvara*), and consequently, the initial vowel *a* is unaccented.
"It is prescribed as having the acute accent on the first syllable" refers to the rule:
*ṛḍajjrendrāgravajraviprakuvracuvrakṣurakhurabhadrograbherabhelaśukaraśuklagauravanarerāmalāḥ* (Pāṇini 6.2.119).
"This is that" refers to this very [word].

This word *ayaṃ* is oxytone by the accent of the nominal stem (*prātipadika-svara*), and its first syllable is anudātta. [In the example] "yadrudrebhyo 'vapathāḥ," this word *avapathāḥ* is ādyudātta due to the accent of the augment *aṭ*. [Regarding the statement] "the word *ati* has ceased [to apply]": even if the word *iti* were to continue [from a previous rule], then [the suffix] would not apply in cases such as *gavaudana*; therefore, because it is not marked with the svarita accent, the word *ati* has ceased to apply.

In that case, would [the rule] not also apply to *hal* (consonants)? To this he says: "The word *aci* is repeated again. This is from [Pāṇini 6.1.77]. Furthermore, that repetition is to be understood according to the maxim of the frog-leap (*maṇḍūkapluti*).
For there is no repetition of the word *aci* in those rules that follow [6.1.108] and precede this rule.

And thus it was stated previously: "And this governing rule [applies] as far as [Pāṇini 6.1.108], namely, 'before a vowel' (aci). Examples are *gavāgram* and *gavājinam*, which may be either *bahuvrīhi* or *tatpuruṣa* compounds.
The compound *gavoṣṭram* is a *dvandva*.
Regarding the statement "this [compound] is also *ādyudātta*" and so forth:

here, if a *bahuvrīhi* were formed as *gāvo'gramasya*, two things would apply: the preservation of the original accent (*prakṛtisvara*) of the preceding member, and the substitution of *avaṅ*. In that case, because it is *antaraṅga* (more internal), the *avaṅ* substitution would occur first. And when it occurs, since it would replace the word *go*, which is *antodātta* by the accent rule for nominal stems (*prātipadika-svara*), the substitute *avaṅ* would necessarily also be *antodātta* due to the principle of *sthāny-ādeśa* (the substitute having the same accent as the original).

If that were the case, once the natural accent (*prakṛtisvara*) had been applied, the preceding member would result in being oxytone (*antodātta*); however, an initial acute (*ādyudātta*) is desired. Therefore, this substitute is prescribed as being *ādyudātta* by way of a specific rule (*nipātana*).
If this is so, then even in compounds such as *tatpuruṣa*, that same *nipātana*-accent would apply; to this he says: "But elsewhere," and so forth.
"Elsewhere" means in the case of *tatpuruṣa* and *dvandva* compounds.

The thought is: "This [suffix] is a substitute for the word *go*; therefore, only another word related to that [word *go*] is overridden by the accent of the *nipātana* (irregular formation), not the accent of the compound.

Consequently, in cases other than the *bahuvrīhi*—such as the *tatpuruṣa* and others—the accent of the *nipātana* is overridden by the oxytone accent of the compound. As for the statement, "The mention of *Sphoṭāyana* is for the sake of honor," what then is the reason that it does not serve to provide an option? To this he says: "For the term *vibhāṣā* (optionally) indeed continues to apply."

But for what purpose is *avaṅ* prescribed? Why not simply prescribe *aga* [the letter *a*]? For even there, it would be accomplished by means of the substitution of *hr*. It is indeed accomplished; however, by the rule *pūrvarūpaṃ prāpnoti* (Pāṇini 6.1.109), the formation of a single preceding form (*pūrvarūpa*) would result.

One might object: "When *ak* is prescribed, the word does not end in that [vowel]? No, because the augment (*āgama*) is included by the mention of that [word-final element]. Indeed, it cannot be said that the status of being a word-final (*padāntatā*) did not previously belong to the vowel *o*. Regarding the phrase "standing in the word *indra*": that which stands in the word *indra* is "standing in *indra*" (*indraśabdastha*). Furthermore, that which is a constituent part (*avayava*) standing in the word *indra* is to be understood as such.

By the previous [rule], the substitution of *vikalpa* (prolated vowel) is already established; since the rule for a permanent (*nitya*) application is obtained there simply by the force of the commencement [of the section], the explicit mention of "permanent" (*nitya*) is for the sake of what follows—namely, the prolation (*pluta*) in the example: *devadattā 3 atra tv asi*. Now, one might object: since the prolation is not yet established by [Pāṇini 8.2.1], how can the status of *parakṛti* (the subsequent operation) be prescribed for that which does not exist? To this, he says: "by virtue of its basis," and so forth.
"Taking as a basis" (āśrayaṇa) means "the basis" (āśraya).
What is this? It is the taking of the protracted vowel (*pluta*)—which is the subject of the operation—as the basis in order to prescribe the effect of *prakṛtibhāva* (non-modification).
Precisely for this reason, the protracted vowel is established here when *prakṛtibhāva* is to be performed; otherwise, its being taken as the subject of the operation would be purposeless.
Regarding the passage beginning with *agnī*:
the designation *pragṛhya* is applied here by the rule *īdūdeddvivacanam* [Pāṇini 1.1.11].
Now, for what purpose is the word *aci* [stated], since the word *aci* is already being carried over [from the previous rule]? To this he says: "While *aci* is being carried over," and so forth.

The vowel (*ac*) which is the cause of the substitution is mentioned again for the purpose that it may be understood as the cause for the *prakṛtibhāva* (non-application of grammatical operations) that follows it; for instance, in the case of *jānu-u asya rujati* becoming *jānū asya rujati*. Indeed, in the word *jānu*, neither the vowel *u* nor the subsequent *pra-gṛhya*-designated [vowel] possesses the status of being the cause for the long *savarṇa* vowel (*savarṇadīrghatva*) in respect to the vowel *a* that follows the *pra-gṛhya*-designated *u*.
And here [the rule] does not apply in the case of *jānv-asya rujati*.

Therefore, although the single substitute (*ekādeśa*) for the two preceding and following *u*-vowels is indeed included by the mention of the *pragṛhya* *u*-vowel—on the grounds that it behaves like [the vowels mentioned in] P. 6.1.85 and so forth—nevertheless, the *yaṇ* substitution still occurs when an *a*-vowel follows.
For even in this case, the *a*-vowel is not the cause of the single substitute.

If, however, the word *añ* were not repeated for the sake of excluding the specific [substitute], then the rule prescribing the *prakṛtibhāva* (non-substitution) for all *añ* suffixes would apply here as well. The designation *pragṛhya*, on the other hand, applies to an *u*-vowel preceded by an *a*-vowel according to [Pāṇini 1.1.14]. Regarding the phrase "the mention of *nitya*," etc.:

If the term *nitya* (invariable) were not carried over here, then because this rule would have fulfilled its purpose in cases such as *agnī itī*, the Śākala rules would apply by virtue of being subsequent in cases such as *vāyū atra*. Therefore, the term *nitya* is carried over here so that the *prakṛtibhāva* (original form) alone may occur. Regarding the mention of *āṅaḥ*: this is the inclusion of the vowel *ā* as qualified by the marker *ṅ*.

This is for the purpose that the rule should apply only to the particle *ā* used in the sense of "slightness" (*īṣadartha*), in connection with an action (*kriyāyoga*), or in the senses of "limit exclusive" (*maryādā*) and "limit inclusive" (*abhividhi*); it should not apply to the *ā* used in sentences (*vākya*) or in recollection (*smaraṇa*). If the original form (*prakṛtibhāva*) were not prescribed, then even if the nasalization (*anunāsikatva*) of *āṅ* were applied, the *svarasandhi* (euphonic combination of vowels) would still occur. Considering that the prescription of nasalization would otherwise serve only to make the substitute nasalized, he says: "And it does not remain in its original form."

Regarding the form *ātarat*: it is derived from the root *tṛ* with the prefix *ā*, in the *laṅ* (imperfect) tense; there is the augment *aṭ*, and with that *aṭ*, there is the lengthening of similar vowels (*savarṇadīrghatva*). As for the statement, "And a short vowel takes the place of its [the long vowel's] *ik*": if this were the case, the particle *ca* (and) need not be used for the purpose of carrying over (*anukarṣaṇa*) the rule *prakṛtyā* [Pāṇini 6.1.111], because the very fact of prescribing a short vowel would prevent the occurrence of vowel-sandhi (*svarasandhi*). Here, one might argue: "Because of the power of the prescription of a short vowel, let there be no vowel-sandhi only for those that are long. [Response: This is not so. Even in the case of short vowels, there would be no vowel-sandhi due to the power of the prescription of the short vowel itself. For example, in *agniḥ atra*, by the power of the prescription of the short vowel, there would be no sandhi even though the rule *iko yaṇ aci* [Pāṇini 6.1.77] applies. Therefore, the particle *ca* must be employed to carry over the rule *prakṛtyā*. Thus, in *agniḥ atra*, the visarga remains as it is because of the force of the word *prakṛtyā*. However, in *agniḥ karoti*, the visarga becomes *r* because the word *prakṛtyā* does not apply there. But in the case of *ātarat*, since the rule *iko yaṇ aci* applies, the *yaṇ* substitution occurs. Alternatively, the particle *ca* may be intended to indicate that the short vowel is also included within the scope of the rule *prakṛtyā*. That is to say, the meaning is: "The original form (*prakṛti*) is maintained, and furthermore, a short vowel takes the place of its *ik*. In this way, the particle *ca* serves to include the short vowel within the domain of the rule *prakṛtyā*. Consequently, in *agniḥ atra*, the visarga remains as it is because of the force of the word *prakṛtyā*. But in *agniḥ karoti*, the visarga becomes *r* because the word *prakṛtyā* does not apply there. And in *ātarat*, the *yaṇ* substitution occurs because the rule *iko yaṇ aci* applies. But in *agniḥ karoti*, the visarga becomes *r* because the word *prakṛtyā* does not apply there. And in *ātarat*, the *yaṇ* substitution occurs because the rule *iko yaṇ aci* applies. Or finally, the particle *ca* may be used to indicate that the short vowel is also included within the scope of the rule *prakṛtyā*. That is to say, the meaning is: "The original form (*prakṛti*) is maintained, and furthermore, a short vowel takes the place of its *ik*. In this way, the particle *ca* serves to include the short vowel within the domain of the rule *prakṛtyā*. Consequently, in *agniḥ atra*, the visarga remains as it is because of the force of the word *prakṛtyā*. But in *agniḥ karoti*, the visarga becomes *r* because the word *prakṛtyā* does not apply there. And in *ātarat*, the *yaṇ* substitution occurs because the rule *iko yaṇ aci* applies. Thus, the particle *ca* is indeed necessary. Otherwise, in *agniḥ atra*, the visarga would become *r* because the rule *iko yaṇ aci* applies. But in *agniḥ karoti*, the visarga becomes *r* because the word *prakṛtyā* does not apply there. And in *ātarat*, the *yaṇ* substitution occurs because the rule *iko yaṇ aci* applies. Therefore, the particle *ca* is required to indicate that the short vowel is also included within the scope of the rule *prakṛtyā*. In this way, the particle *ca* serves to include the short vowel within the domain of the rule *prakṛtyā*. Consequently, in *agniḥ atra*, the visarga remains as it is because of the force of the word *prakṛtyā*. But in *agniḥ karoti*, the visarga becomes *r* because the word *prakṛtyā* does not apply there. And in *ātarat*, the *yaṇ* substitution occurs because the rule *iko yaṇ aci* applies. But in *agniḥ karoti*, the visarga becomes *r* because the word *prakṛtyā* does not apply there. And in *ātarat*, the *yaṇ* substitution occurs because the rule *iko yaṇ aci* applies.
