However, for short vowels, it must indeed occur, for they do not become short [again].

As for the argument that this is unnecessary because there is no purpose [for it], that is not so; for even in the case of short vowels, a short vowel does indeed occur in order to prevent the application of vowel sandhi (svarasandhi).
Indeed, this grammatical treatise performs what has already been accomplished, like a rain-cloud; it does not perform what has not yet been accomplished, like a fire.

If that is so, then this is indicated by the particle *ca*: in certain cases, such as *īṣā-akṣa* and the like, there is only the preservation of the original form (*prakṛtibhāva*), and not shortening (*hrasvatva*).
Consequently, what was said—that in *īṣā-akṣa* and the like there is merely the preservation of the original form—need not be stated.

Why is the mention of Śākalya not intended to provide an option (*vikalpa*) alongside the substitution of *yaṇ*? To this he says: "Precisely because of the force of its initial formulation," and so forth.
The short vowel alone is the domain for the substitution of *yaṇ*, because a long vowel is prescribed by [Pāṇini 6.1.101] in the case of a homogeneous (*savarṇa*) vowel.
Furthermore, this short vowel is also prescribed by the Śākala rule.

Therefore, in this context, precisely because of the force of its commencement, an option between this rule and the *yaṇ* substitution is established; thus, the mention of the Teacher (Ācārya) is not for that purpose.
Regarding the phrase "of *sinn* and *nitya-samāsa*" and so forth:
although the locative case (*saptamī*) is but one, it is divided into two types due to a difference in perspective.
With respect to *sid*, it is a locative of posteriority (*parasaptamī*); with respect to *nitya-samāsa*, it is a locative of domain (*viṣayasaptamī*).

The term *sitsaka* is a *dvandva* compound consisting of *sica* and *nityasamāsa*. That which has this [suffix] is *sit*. A *nityasamāsa* is a compound prescribed under the governing rule (*adhikāra*) of "constant" (*nitya*).

This rule belongs to Śākalya, hence it is called *śākala*. From the suffix *aṇ* (by Pāṇini 4.2.111), there is the elision of the vowel *a* (by 6.4.148), and subsequently the elision of the consonant *y* (by 6.4.151).
The prohibition of Śākala is "śākalapratiṣedhaḥ. The word "vaktavya" means that it must be explained.

In this regard, the following is the explanation: from [Pāṇini 6.1.122], the mention of *vibhāṣā* (optionally) continues to apply, and that is understood as a restricted option (*vyavasthitavibhāṣā*). Consequently, the prohibition of the *śākala* rule will apply in the case of a suffix beginning with *s* and in eternal compounds (*nityasamāsa*).
Thus, we have the form *ṛtviyaḥ*.
The suffix *ghas* is applied by the rule *ṛtoraṇ* [Pāṇini 5.1.104–106], as in "whose season has arrived" (*ṛtuḥ prāpto'sya*). The compound is formed by the rule *vyākaraṇam* [Pāṇini 2.2.18].
For here, because the term *nitya* (invariable) is carried over from rule 2.2.17, this is an obligatory compound (*nityasamāsa*). Regarding the example *kumāryartham*:
"for the sake of the maiden" means "this [gift] belongs to the maiden."
The rule "there is a statement regarding compounding with the word *artha* and [the resulting form] takes all genders" (Vārttika 78) is also indeed a compulsory compound (*nityasamāsa*).

Since the application of Śākalya’s rule is prohibited in every case, the substitution of *yaṇ* occurs as a matter of course. This statement is made for the sake of the homogeneous vowels (*savarṇa*) and for the sake of excluding *anig* (the *ik* vowels);
otherwise, it would be established by the preceding rule alone.

If this rule is intended for the sake of homogeneous vowels (*savarṇa*), how then is *khaṭvaśryaḥ* given as an example? For in this case, there is no homogeneous vowel following the *ac*. This is not so; it is an example of what was stated [in the previous rule]: "and for the sake of non-elision" (*anigartham*). For this very reason, *akaḥ* is employed in the sūtra; otherwise, one would have to carry over *ikaḥ* from the preceding rule. When this connection exists, even in the case of a homogeneous vowel, the shortening and the absence of *prakṛtibhāva* (original form retention) are governed by this very rule due to its subsequent position; hence this example is presented. That which exists in the Ṛṣi—that is, in the Veda—is *ārṣa*; other than that is worldly (*laukika*), which is *anārṣa*.
"From the collection" means from the sentence. Why is this so? Because a sentence devoid of words is never employed.
And because a sentence consists of a collection [of words],
the term "having separated" means having made distinct.

"It is established in its own form" (*svarūpe vyavasthāpyate*)—as the *Kāśikā* reads "established in its own form" (*svarūpe 'vasthāpyate*). The meaning is that it is established as consisting of the word and the phoneme.
"As if not protracted" (*aplutavat*).
"It behaves like one who has not performed the *pluta* [protracted] vowel" means "like a non-*pluta*.
To show the basis of similarity by which it becomes like a non-*pluta*, he says: "the function of a *pluta," and so forth.
By this, it is shown that there is a prohibition of the *function* of the *pluta* with respect to its purpose, but not of the *pluta* itself.
Regarding "suślokā 3," there is a *pluta* (protracted) vowel according to [Pāṇini 8.2.84]. Thus,
it is "suślokā."

The single-substitute (ekādeśa) certainly occurs because the effect of a protracted vowel (*pluta*) has not been performed. Now, one might object: "But a single substitute should also not occur, since it too is an effect of a protracted vowel. This is not so; for if that were the case, the statement [of the rule] would be rendered purposeless. Therefore, by the very mention of the term *pluta*, there is a prohibition only of that specific effect which is prescribed for a protracted vowel, but not of every effect of a protracted vowel.
Nor has only a single portion been prescribed in this manner.
[Question: "What is the purpose of the use of the suffix -vat? [Answer:

The use of the suffix -vat would be for the purpose that there may be the actual hearing of the protracted vowel (*pluta*), since otherwise there would be a prohibition of every grammatical operation whatsoever.

Furthermore, even though there is a prohibition of the *prakṛtibhāva* (original form) for the effect as a whole, the *pluta* vowel must still occur by virtue of the scriptural injunction (*śruti*), because [the original form] has been set aside only partially.
Why is that? The intention is: why is the *pluta* itself not prohibited?
Having kept in mind the fault that will be stated regarding the prohibition of the *pluta*, he says: "When 'pluta' is being mentioned," and so forth.
"In that case, what is the fault?"—the sense is: "What fault arises when the *vat*-affix is applied? [The answer begins with] "In the case of relying on a *pragṛhya*," and so forth.

In what case does it have a *pragṛhya* as its basis? If there were a state of original form (*prakṛtibhāva*) based on a *pragṛhya*, then the hearing of that *pluta* vowel designated as *pragṛhya* would not occur if only the *pluta* itself were prohibited.
However, when the suffix *-vat* is employed, this prohibition applies to the grammatical operation (*kārya*) of the *pluta*, not to the *pluta* vowel itself.

Thus, although the *prakṛtibhāva* based on the *pluta* is prohibited, the *prakṛtibhāva* based on the *pragṛhya* remains unprohibited; consequently, since the single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) occurs, no fault arises.
Regarding "agnī":

by the rule *idūdeddvivacanam* [Pāṇini 1.1.11], the designation *pragṛhya* is applied; by the rule *guroranṛta* [Pāṇini 8.2.86], the *pluta* (protracted) vowel is applied. The phrase "when followed by a vowel" (*aci parataḥ*) indicates that the term "in the presence of" (*upasthite*) is no longer operative, because it is not marked with the *svarita* accent.
"Let there be *hī* three times.
The root *asu* means "to throw" (*dhātupāṭha* 1209); this is the imperative (*loṭ*) in the second person singular (*sip*).
By the rule *sehir apicca* [Pāṇini 3.4.87], *si* becomes *hi*; by transposition, there is *ślu* (reduplication).
The *pluta* (protracted) vowel occurs by the rule "In *kṣiyā*, *āśis*, and *praiṣa*, [the final syllable] is *pluta* when there is expectancy for a finite verb" (Pāṇini 8.2.104).
The phrase "for the purpose of excluding that which is proximate to it" is used because, in that case,
the state of not being treated as *pluta* would invariably apply by the preceding rule.
"In order to establish [the rule] for the sake of attainment" means that,
in that case, it has not been attained by anyone. "From the vowel *ī*," and so forth.

But how is this absence of *pluta* obtained even elsewhere than after the vowel *i*, even though it is desired there as well? It is because the particle *ca*, which recurs from [Pāṇini 6.1.127], has the sense of including what has not been explicitly mentioned. Regarding the phrase "because of having an *anubandha*," after which verbal root [is it intended]? Because of the context, it is precisely that one.

The verbal root *div* has an anubandha, whereas the nominal stem *divi* is without an anubandha; and it is the form without an anubandha that is employed in the sūtra. Therefore, according to the principle "when there is the mention of a form without an anubandha, [the mention] is not of the form with an anubandha" (Vyāḍīya-paribhāṣā 53), this is the mention of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*), not of the verbal root (*dhātu*).
Thus, "one who desires heaven" (*dyukāmaḥ*) is a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "one whose desire is for heaven" (*divi kāmo 'syeti*), or "one who desires heaven" (*divaṃ kāmayate*).
The suffix *ṇa* is prescribed [after the roots] *śīli*, *kāmī*, and *bhikṣācari* according to the rule *śīlikāmibhikṣācaribhyo ṇo vaktavyaḥ* (Vārttika 229).
Thus, "dyumān" means "one who possesses the sky" (*dyaur asyāsti*), according to Pāṇini 5.2.94.
Regarding "vimaladyu dinam":
it is a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "a day on which the sky is clear" (*vimalā dyaur asmin*).
Regarding "akṣadyūbhyām, akṣadyūbhiḥ": [these are examples of the same formation].

When the word *akṣa* is the upapada, the suffix *kvip* is applied to the root *div*, and by the rule *cchvoḥ śūḍanunāsike ca* [Pāṇini 6.4.19], the substitution *ūṭh* occurs. Now, what is the purpose of including the marker *t* (in *ūṭh*)? Even though it has been established by the inclusion of the marker *t* in the rule *ṛta ut* [Pāṇini 6.1.111] that "even when being taught (*bhāvyamāna*), the vowel *u* includes its homogeneous counterparts" (Cāndra-vṛtti-pāda 44), one might argue that here, by virtue of proximity (*antarya*), the substitute for the semi-vowel and the consonant—which have a duration of half a mora—will be only a short vowel (*mātrika*), and not a long one. To this, he says: "The inclusion of the marker *t*" and so forth.

Although *dīrgha* (long vowel substitution) does not apply by this [rule], *uṭh* would nevertheless apply by another rule in cases such as *dyubhyām* and *dyubhiḥ*; therefore, the addition of *ta* (the *tapara* marker) is for the purpose that this [*uṭh*] should not occur.
One might object: "But surely there is no possibility of *uṭh* applying at all; what then is the point of adding *ta* to exclude it? To this he replies: "*dyubhyām*, *dyubhiḥ*."
Regarding the passage beginning with "atra hi":

the scope (*avakāśa*) of *utva* is where there is no *kvip* suffix following a *jhal*-initial element—as in *vimaladyu dinam*; the scope of *ūṭh* is as in *akṣadyūbhyām*. In cases such as *dyubhyām*, where both would apply simultaneously, *ūṭh* would prevail due to its higher status in the order of rules; however, because of the inclusion of the long vowel marker *ṝ* (taparakaraṇa), *utva* alone occurs.

If, then, the addition of *t* (as in *tapara*) is made for the sake of excluding the *ūṭ* that has already been obtained, then how is it that—when the objection is raised by the opponent regarding the forms *dyubhyām* and *dyubhiḥ* under the rule *cachvoḥ śūḍanunāsike ca* [Pāṇini 6.4.19]—he will say: "Once *ūṭ* has been applied, the substitution of *u* by the rule *diva ut* [6.1.131] will take place because it is subsequent, and it will have the duration of one mora"? Does this mean that once *ūṭ* has been produced and established, a vowel *u* of one-mora duration will occur in its place? There is no contradiction.

For this passage, "when *ūṭh* has been applied," its connection is with the preceding section containing the objection (*codya*), and not with the other section containing the resolution (*parihāra*).

In that context, when the alternative view is presented—"some do not carry forward [the condition] *kṅiti* here"—the objection is raised: "How is it that in *dyubhyām* and *dyubhiḥ*, *ūṭh* is applied?"

In this regard, the intention of the objector is as follows: if the term *kṅiti* were not to follow [from the previous rule], then in the forms *dyubhyām* and *dyubhiḥ*, the substitution of *ūṭh* alone would have to be applied; consequently, once *ūṭh* had been applied, how could the forms *dyubhyām* and *dyubhiḥ* be established? For they ought to be *dyūbhyām* and *dyūbhiḥ*. To this objection, the resolution is that because of the specification of the short vowel (*t* in *ut*) in the rule *diva ut*, the duration will be that of one mātrā.

In this case as well, the intention of the objector is as follows: "The very purpose of the inclusion of *ta* (the long vowel marker) [in Pāṇini’s rule] is so that *ūṭh* shall not occur; otherwise, it would be useless, and therefore only *utva* should be applied, not the substitution of *ūṭh*. For those, however, who maintain that the term *kṅiti* is to be supplied [from a previous rule], for them the inclusion of *ta* is for the sake of clarity. Regarding the statement, "In some cases, the prefix *sam-* is desired even when there is no ornamentation," how is this desired meaning obtained? It is obtained from the indicative mark (*liṅga*) of the Teacher’s practice [as seen in the rule] beginning with 6.1.138. Regarding the phrase, "A collection (*samavāya*) is an aggregate (*samudāya*)."
From the root preceded by *sam-ava*, the suffix *ac* is applied in the sense of an abstract action (bhāva) according to Pāṇini 3.3.56 (*erac*).
Thus, *samavāya* means "a collection" (*saṅghāta*),
which is to say, "assembled together" (*samudita*).
The term *bhāve* [indicates] the locative case. Regarding the phrase "of that which exists" (*sataḥ*) and so forth:

for an object that has already acquired its existence (*labdhasattāka*), "another quality" (*guṇāntara*) is one distinct from the qualities previously arisen; that by which this other quality is deposited or produced is "the deposition of another quality" (*guṇāntarādhāna*). For what purpose is this? He says: "for the sake of excellence" (*ādhikyāya*) and so forth.
What is that? He says: "exertion" (*samīhā*).

Thus, that application of another quality (*guṇāntarādhāna*) by means of which an exertion or effort is performed for the sake of increasing an existing thing, for the growth of what has already grown, or for the maintenance of what is already grown—that is, so that its state of growth does not decline—is called *pratiyatna* (refinement).
It is said to be "modified."
The meaning is "that which has undergone transformation.
Regarding the phrase "of a sentence whose meaning is being understood in its own form":

since it is said that "words applied to wholes also function with respect to their parts" (*Vyāḍipañjikā*, Sūtra 85), the implied meaning—a portion of the sentence due to context and so forth—is expressed by the word "sentence" (*vākya*).

The explicit mention of even a meaning already implied for the sake of easy comprehension is called *vākya-adhyāhāra* (supplying an ellipsis). In the phrase "in the domain of cutting" (*lavana-viṣaye*), etc., this shows that "cutting" (*lavana*) is not a qualifier of the root *kṛ* (*kirati*) by way of being its denotation; rather, it is the state of being the object (*viṣaya-bhāva*) of that action.

But how is the suffix *ṇamul* used here, given that according to the grammatical rule "ṇamul is used [after a verb] when there is repetition" (*ābhīkṣṇye ṇamul ca*, Pāṇini 3.4.22), it is prescribed for meanings such as repetition?
And since that meaning is neither intended nor perceived here, he says: "The suffix *ṇamul* [is used] here," and so forth.
"It must be stated" means it must be explained.

The explanation there is as follows: "It will occur by virtue of the word *bahulam* (in various ways) from [Pāṇini 3.3.113] *kṛtyalyuṭo bahulam*. Regarding the phrase *hiṃsāyāṃ viṣaye* (in the domain of violence):
by this, he shows that violence is not a qualifier of the root *kṛ* (*kirati*) in terms of its expressed meaning (*abhidheya*), but rather as the domain of its sense."
Regarding the word *pratiskīrṇam*:

by [Pāṇini 7.1.100] *ṛta iddhātoḥ*, there is the substitution of *i* for the root vowel, followed by the replacement of that *i* with *ra*; by [8.2.42] *radābhyām* etc., there is the substitution of *ṇ* for the *t* of the *niṣṭhā* suffix; and by [8.2.77] *hali ca*, there is the lengthening of the vowel *i*.
By the words "in the same way" (*tathā*) and so forth, he demonstrates that the meaning of the root *kṛ* (from which *skṛ* is derived) pertains to the domain of injury (*hiṃsā*).
The word "anubadhnāti" means "he follows. Regarding the phrase "in that object" and so forth:

by this, he shows that "scattering" (*ālekhanam*) is not a qualifier of the root *kṛ* (to scatter) in its literal denotation, but rather qualifies its meaning by way of being its objective domain (*viṣayabhāvena*).

Regarding "apaskirate," the suffix *śa* is applied by [Pāṇini 3.1.77]; as before, there is the substitution of *i* for *k* and the substitution of *r* for *s*. By the phrase "having written" (*ālikhya*) and so forth, he demonstrates that writing constitutes the object-domain of the meaning of the root *kṝ* (to scatter).
"Having drawn" (*ālikhya*) means "having attracted" (*ākṛṣya*).

Since the act of drawing—which is accomplished by means of a four-footed animal or a bird—is mentioned in general terms, it would apply here as well [in the case of]: "He scatters a ball of boiled rice for eating. Therefore, he states this qualification of "drawing": "for the livelihood of joy," and so forth.
Joy (*harṣaḥ*) is delight (*pramodaḥ*).
*Jīvikā* means the means of sustaining life; *kulāya* means a dwelling or hermitage.

But what is the reason that the *ātmanepada* occurs after *harṣa*, yet not in this counter-example? To this he says: "Only in the cases of joy (*harṣa*), livelihood (*jīvikā*), and making a dwelling (*kulāyakaraṇa*)," and so forth. Now, one might object: since the rule is stated in the neuter gender (*napuṃsakaliṅga*), the [suffix] should occur only when the result (*phala*) is neuter, and not when it is of another gender; and it should occur only in the plural when the result is a class of medicinal herbs (*auṣadhajāti*), and not elsewhere, because the rule is stated in the plural.
How is it that in the expression *kustumburu*, there occurs both the masculine gender and the singular number? To this he says: "In the citation of the sūtra," and so forth.
The mention of the neuter gender is merely illustrative;
for in the sūtra, the plural number is likewise not restrictive.

And so it has been said: "In the *Sūtra* [or *Sūtranirdeśa*], the neuter gender is not intended to be significant—[as stated in the *Kāśikā* and *Padamañjarī*]: 'The gender and number are non-essential (*atantram*) because they are not intended to be significant (*avivakṣitatvāt*),' [this phrase is absent in the *Kāśikā*]. Regarding the term "*aparasparāḥ*":
it is a *dvandva* compound meaning "others and others" (*apare ca pare ca*).
With the intention that when the abstract suffix (*bhāvapratyaya*) is applied to the word *santata*, the form should be *sāntatya*, he asks "What is this? and so forth.
Showing that this abstract suffix is actually applied to the word *satata*, he says "The state of being *satata*," and so forth.
[He then asks] "In what sense is it *satatam*?"
He thinks as follows: "In this treatise, there is no rule for the elision of the *m* in *sama*.

Now, if *sātatya* were itself a *nipātana* (an irregular formation), then one might assume that it serves to indicate the meaning that the elision of the *m* of *sama* occurs when followed by the word *tata*; if that were the case, however, the form *santatam* would not be established. Therefore, he says: "*samastate vikalpena*" and so forth. The intention is this: by pronouncing the word *sātatya*, which is well-known through the rules of the ancient masters (*pūrvācārya*), he has also relied upon those very rules of the ancient masters.
Therefore, the elision of the letter *m* is prescribed here as being identical to that [elision of *y*].
And by doing this, the elision of the initial letters of words such as *avaśyam* and others before *kṛtya*-suffixes and the like is necessarily established.
Consequently, he demonstrates that very definition of the ancient masters with the words "one should elide" (*lumpet*), and so forth.
The word "final" (antya) is to be understood as the remainder [of the sense].
One should elide [the suffix] when followed by a word ending in a kṛtya suffix that contains the word *avaśyam*; the meaning is that one should perform the elision of its final [syllable]. [Thus:
*avaśyakartavyam* (that which must necessarily be done).

One should also elide the final letter of a word ending in the suffix *tumun*, when followed by the words *kāma* and *manas*: for example, *kartuṃ kāmo 'syeti kartukāmaḥ* ("one whose desire is to act") and *hartuṃ mano 'syeti hartumanāḥ* ("one whose mind is to take"). Furthermore, one may optionally elide the final letter of the word *sam* when followed by the words *hita* and *taya*: for example, *sahitam*, *satatam*, and *santatam*.
Thus ends the section on compound formation (samāsa).
One should elide the final letter of the word *māṃsa* where [the root] *pac* occurs— that is,
in this root *ḍupacaṣ* "to cook" (Dhātupāṭha 996)— provided it is qualified by the condition "of *yuṅ* and *ghañ*" (*yuṅghañoḥ*).
The meaning is: when the suffixes *lyuṭ* or *ghañ* follow, [the substitution of *pa* for *paca*] occurs in that which ends in *pac*.
Here too, the word "optionally" (*vā*) is connected.
Thus: *māṃspacanam*, *māṃsapacanam*.
*māṃspākaḥ*, *māṃsapākaḥ*.
This is a compound according to the rule "The genitive case [ending] in connection with a *kṛt*-derived word is also compounded" (Vārttika 86).
This elision occurs within the compound and, according to the intention of the ancient teachers (*pūrvācāryas*), also in *saṃhitā* (continuous phonetic junction).

Therefore, when the sentence is read with a pause (vicchidya-pāṭha), [the rule] "and its [s becomes ṣ]" does not apply. Since the *suṭ* augment is neither a substitute (*ādeśa*) nor part of an affix (*pratyaya*), it would not undergo the change to *ṣ*; thus, that too is established as an irregularity (*nipātana*).
By the example "cows frequent [this place]" (*gāvaḥ padyante*), he shows that the location is frequented.
Regarding the passage beginning with "in an untraversed place" (*asevite*):

Now, since the word *goṣpada* (cow’s footprint) is what is actually mentioned in the aphorism (*sūtra*), why is the example "in an untraversed place there are no cow’s footprints, etc. cited? To this he says: "in an untraversed place," and so forth.

Now, since the word *goṣpada* is what is mentioned in the aphorism, why is the example "in an untraversed place there are no cow’s footprints, etc. cited? To this he says: "in an untraversed place," and so forth.

And this [term] *asevitagohaṇa* is formed, yet the word *goṣpada* is not possible there; therefore, it is understood that the irregular derivation (*nipātana*) of *agoṣpada* applies to the sense of "not frequented.
"If this is so" means:
if the irregular derivation of *agoṣpada* is for the sense of "not frequented."
"There is no purpose served by this" refers to the inclusion of the term "not practiced.
How is [the goal] accomplished without that? To this he says: "Because of the negation of a cow's footprint," and so forth.
"This is indeed true.
This states the truth of what was previously said, beginning with "because of the negation of the cow's footprint," but it does not refer to the meaning of the phrase "there is no purpose by this.
If that is indeed true, then for what purpose is the term "cultivated" (*sevitam*) employed here? To this he says: "But where... and so forth.
In the negative compound *agoṣpada*, this *tatpuruṣa* by its very nature expresses a meaning similar to that of the subsequent member, just like *abrāhmaṇa*.

Consequently, when the *tatpuruṣa* "not a cow’s footprint" (*na goṣpadam agoṣpadam*) is formed, does this term *agoṣpada* apply only where there is the possibility of the act of treading? Even so, it is said to occur [elsewhere as well].
The word "even" (*api*) indicates that the term *agoṣpada* applies not only where there is the possibility of treading.
Why? Because here again the term "practiced" (āsevita) is included.
Since it occurs even there, he says: "For those which...
and "in this way."

The term *prakāra* (manner/type) is referred back as having the sense of "not being practiced" (*asevita*). For if the term "not practiced" were not included, its purpose would be redundant; therefore, this *bahuvrīhi* compound will be understood through the word *asevita*, which functions as an abstract noun (*bhāvasādhana*).

Since a *bahuvrīhi* compound—meaning "that in which practice does not exist"—can also apply to absolute non-existence, those forests where cattle are absolutely impossible are designated by the word *asevita*.
And thus, even in that case, it becomes "agoṣpadam" (not a cow's footprint). [The form] "goṣpadapūram" is derived by means of the suffix *ṇamul* according to [Pāṇini 3.4.32].

But is it not the case that "goṣpada" is a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*), whose meaning is "the footprint belonging to a cow," and not a measure? How, then, can examples such as "a field measuring only a goṣpada" be applicable to a measure? To this, he says: "Not here," and so forth.
For in this context, the term "goṣpada" is not employed solely for the purpose of conveying its own primary meaning;
rather, it is used to delimit the extent of the field and so on.
Therefore? Because the extent of the field and so forth is delimited—that is, measured—by it, it becomes a *pramāṇa*.
And here, by the word *pramāṇa*, length is not meant; what then? Merely delimitation.
Why is this so? By the force of the grammatical rule (*nipātana*).
For a placement (*nipātana*) takes up even an object that is not well-known [in common usage]. Regarding the phrase "for the sake of sustaining oneself" (*ātmayāpanāya*):
"sustaining oneself" (*ātmayāpana*) means the maintenance of life. That which is established for that purpose is called "foundation" (*pratiṣṭhā*).
Regarding the term *āsapada*: the augment *suṭ* is prescribed as a substitute for the word *pada* when it follows the prefix *ā*. Thus, we have *āpada*.

By [Pāṇini 1.4.89], *āṅ* has the status of a *karmapravacanīya*; in its connection with that [term], the fifth case (*pañcamī*) is applied by [Pāṇini 2.3.10], "the fifth case after *apa*, *āṅ*, and *pari*"; and by [Pāṇini 2.1.13], there is an *avyayībhāva* compound ending in that [fifth case]. If the word *āścarya* were prescribed as a *nipātana* (irregular formation) for something non-eternal and not a source of distress, then the same would apply to jars (*ghaṭa*) and so forth; wishing to avoid this fault, he says: "by way of non-eternality," etc. *Adbhuta* is said to mean "wonderful" (*citram*). That which is wonderful in the world is a marvel (*citram*); the state of being that is *adbhutatva*.

And since that [eating] does not exist elsewhere, impermanence becomes its object; for it is not possible for it to occur there [elsewhere] other than in that [specific place]. Therefore, by means of that which has become the object, its wonderfulness is characterized: "It would be a marvel if he were to eat."

According to the rule *anavakḷptyamarṣayorakiṃvṛtte’pi* [Pāṇini 3.3.145], the suffix *liṅ* is used in the sense of impossibility (*anavakḷpti*). Eating by someone at a specific time or occasion has never been seen before; therefore, in that case, "is it possible?"—that is considered a marvel. [The term] "part of a chariot" (*rathāvayava*) [is used].

By this [sūtra], he explains that the word *ādi* (and so forth) expresses a part. Now, one might ask: since the formation of the word *viṣkira* is established by the rule "the suffix *suṅ* is optionally applied after the root *kṛ* when followed by *vi* in the sense of a bird," what is the purpose of including the term *vikira* [in the sūtra]? To this he replies: "The inclusion of *vikira* is for the purpose that the word *vikira* be used only in the sense of 'bird' and not elsewhere. Words such as *pāraskara* and others are conventional (*rūḍhi*) terms that may be etymologically derived in some way or another; one should not be overly insistent on the meaning of their constituent parts. [In the case of] *pāraskara*, the suffix *ṭa* is applied according to the rule "he who makes the end (*pāraṃ karoti*) is *pāraskaraḥ*" (Pāṇini 6.1.157).
One who protects a chariot (*ratha*) is a *rathaspā*;
[this is derived] by [the rule] *ātonupasarge kaḥ* [Pāṇini 3.2.3].
From the root *kṛ*, meaning "to do what must be done" (*kārya karoti*), the suffix *ḍu* is applied, and there is a substitution of *kir* for *kārya*—thus, *kiṣkuḥ*.
The term *kiṣkindhā* is derived from the root *dadhāti* (to place) with the prefix *kim*, as before; there is reduplication of *kim* and elision of the preceding *m*.
Regarding the rule "of *tat* and *bṛhat*" (*tadbṛhatoḥ*), etc.:

after the words *kara* and *pati* respectively, when followed by *tat* and *bṛhat*, the suffix *suṅ* is applied if the deity is the meaning to be expressed, and there is elision of the final *t* of these two.

Regarding that: the rule *kiṃ-yattadbahuṣu* (Pāṇini 5.2.39) prescribes the suffix *añ*, as in *taskaraścauraḥ* ("a thief is a *taskara*") and *tatkaro 'nyaḥ* ("another who does that [is a *tatkara*]").
Similarly, *bṛhaspatir devatā* ("the deity Bṛhaspati is the lord of the great ones") and *bṛhatpatir anyaḥ* ("another who is the lord of the great").

Now, for what purpose is the condition (*upādhi*) "of a thief and a deity" (*cauradevatayoḥ*) introduced, since their inclusion would already be established by the mention of "proper names" (*saṃjñā*) alone? For are the words *taskara* and *bṛhaspati* not proper names of anything else? To this, he says: "The mention of 'proper name'... and so forth.

Regarding "prāttumpatau" and so forth: after the root *tupa* or *tumpa*, meaning "to satisfy" (*dhātupāṭha* 1309, 1360), when preceded by the prefix *pra*, the suffix *suṅ* occurs when "cow" (*go*) is the agent. Thus: *prastumpati gauḥ*.
The other [view] is indeed satisfied by what was stated in the Bhāṣya: "As for what was said.

If, then, *pāraskara* and so forth constitute an *ākṛtigaṇa* (a class defined by its general form), then the preceding rule should not have been recited starting from [Pāṇini 6.1.152], since that too would be included by this very [rule]. This is true; however, it should be recited for the sake of detailed exposition (*prapañca*). Regarding "with the exception of one" (*ekavarjam*): the meaning is "having excluded one."
The suffix *ṇamul* [is applied] by the rule "and after [a word ending in] the second case" (Pāṇini 3.4.53).
If this [rule] were intended as a governing heading (*adhikāra*), then only the accentuation belonging to the sixth book would be included;

those other accents found in the seven books of grammar, such as those governed by rules like "after [a word ending in] the seventh case" (4.4.108) and "before [the suffix] *kṛt* with an indicatory *ṇ*" (7.1.75), would not be included.
In this context, however, even those [other types of rules] are included.

For although it resides in only one part, it illuminates the entire treatise, just as a lamp illuminates a house; having considered this, he says, "This is a paribhāṣā. And it serves as a supplement to the constituent parts of the injunctions.
For a metarule (*paribhāṣā*) functions as a supplement (*śeṣabhāva*) to the operational rules (*kāryavākya*).
When a circumflex (*svarita*) or acute (*udātta*) accent is prescribed for a particular word-element, the remainder (*śeṣa*) therein becomes unaccented (*anudātta*).
This is what is meant by "pertaining to the domain of the rules for accents."
The analysis of the compound is: "its scope is the rule for accents.
Regarding the phrase "where there is another," this "otherness" is in relation to the *anudātta* (unaccented) tone.

Regarding the rule "In that case, a word (pada) is unaccented" (*tatrānudāttaṃ padam*): Now, is it not the case that the word *anudātta* [in Pāṇini 1.2.30] is established as denoting a specific quality (*guṇa*), whereas a word (*pada*) is defined by the vowels and consonants (*ac-ahal-lakṣaṇa*), and such is the meaning of the word *pada*? How, then, can there be grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) here? This is not a fault; for what is intended here is that a word whose vowel is unaccented is an "unaccented word. Thus, the word *anudātta* refers to the word (*pada*) itself. How so? Because it ends in the suffix *-a*, which expresses the sense of possession (*matvarthīya*).
"Those which belong to him are *anudātta*";
here, the suffix *ac* is applied because the group beginning with *arśas* is an *ākṛtigaṇa*.
It was stated that "with the exception of one," but that single [exception] is not known, being the one to be excluded; to make this clear, he asks: "Which one, moreover? and so forth.
That [vowel] for which an acute accent (*udātta*) is prescribed by rule is alone exempted from elision.
If even a short vowel were not exempted, then that prescription of the accent would be purposeless,
as in the cases "gopāyati" and "dhūpāyati."

Regarding the roots *gup* in the sense of "protection" (Dhātupāṭha 395) and *dhūp* in the sense of "torment" (Dhātupāṭha 396), by the rule *gupū-dhūpa-* [Pāṇini 3.1.28], they take the suffix *āya*. Consequently, by the rule *sanādyantā dhātavaḥ* [Pāṇini 3.1.32], these forms ending in *āya* receive the designation of "root" (*dhātu*). By the rule *dhātoḥ* [Pāṇini 6.1.156], the root-final syllable is udātta; thus, for a form ending in the suffix *āya*, the vowel *ā* of the final *y* receives the accent of the root. It is said that "the accent of the *śna* affix supersedes the accent of the root. This is because the accent of what remains after other rules have applied is stronger, as that which is taught later (satiśiṣṭa) possesses greater force.
Likewise, it is stated: "It should be said that a vowel remaining after elision (*sa-ti-śiṣṭa-svara*) is stronger" (Vārttika 6.1.174). For example:
*lunāti*, *punāti*.
The short vowel [of the root] is applied by the rule *pvādīnāṃ hrasvaḥ* [Pāṇini 7.3.80].
Furthermore, the *śnā* suffix is acutely accented on its first syllable by the accent of the suffix (*pratyayasvara*).
Thus, it is called "the accent of *śnā*" (*śnāsvaram*).

The word "is sublated" (*bādhate*) is understood [to follow]. Now, one might object: since [the suffix] is subsequent, the *vikaraṇa* suffixes must apply after the *tiP* and other affixes have been applied; therefore, because the accent of the *śnā* [suffix] remains when the accent of the *sārvadhātuka* [affix] is present, that [accent of the *śnā*] is "subsequently prescribed" (*satiśiṣṭa*). And thus, it would be logical that the accent of the *tasi* [suffix] is sublated by the accent of the *śnā* itself. [The author] thinks as follows: by the rule beginning with *[[Pāṇini 6.1.186]]*, which teaches that what follows *tasi* is a *lasārvadhātuka* [affix], it is indicated (*jñāpayati*) that even an accent prescribed for a *vikaraṇa* is sublated by the accent of a *sārvadhātuka* [affix]. For example: *lunītaḥ*, *punītaḥ*.
The substitution of *i* occurs by the rule *ī halyadhoḥ* [Pāṇini 6.4.113]. The connection is that [the rule] *tassvaramāmsvaraḥ* [Pāṇini 6.2.49] is sublated.
The reason for its being sublated is precisely its status as *satiśiṣṭa* (remaining when another rule applies).

In the example *lunītastarām*: from the word ending in *tas*, [the suffix] *tarap* is added by [Pāṇini 5.3.56] *tiṅśca*; then, from that which ends in *tarap*, the suffix *ām* is added by [Pāṇini 5.4.11] *kimetiṅvyayaghādām* and so forth.

But for what purpose is this rule of the single-exception word-accent (*ekavarjapadasvara*) prescribed? To this he says: "Of the *āgama*, etc. The word-accent of the *āgama* and so forth is prescribed as being unaccented (*anudātta*) with the exception of one [vowel], lest there be a separate accent for the *āgama* and the rest. [This is because] "the accent of an *āgama* subverts the accent of the base form (*prakṛti*)."
When this [elision] exists, the accent belongs to the single remaining word;
when it does not exist, the accent of the suffix and that of the augment would indeed be separate,
as in "catvāraḥ."
The natural accent (*prakṛtisvara*), moreover, is the acute accent on the first syllable.

For instance, the word *catuḥ* is derived from the rule *cateruran* (Pāṇini 5.1.78), which prescribes the suffix *uran*; thus, by the accent of the *nit*-suffix, it becomes acute-accented on its first syllable.
[This applies to] the form *anaṅvāhaḥ*.
The etymology of *anuḍuh* is likewise constructed as follows:

from the root *ana* (meaning "to breathe," Dhātupāṭha 1070), with the suffix *asun* (Dhātupāṭha 9.49), the word *anaḥ* ends in *asun*; thus, by the accent of a *nit* suffix, it is udātta on its first syllable. Then, [the word *anuḍuh*] is derived from the root *vah* (meaning "to carry") with the suffix *kvip*, preceded by *anas* (a cart) in the sense of "carrying a cart" (*ano vahati*). Here too, because it ends in *asun* according to the rule *uścānasaḥ* (Dhātupāṭha 9.49), the word *anaḥ* is udātta on its first syllable by the accent of the *nit* suffix.

Why then is there not [the application of] *kvip* in the case of *anovāhaḥ*? [The answer is: By the rule *uścānasaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.4.137), the suffix *kvip* is applied to the root *vah-* when *anas-* is the upapada; furthermore, the vowel *u* is substituted for the *a* of *anas*.

Since *vah-* belongs to the class beginning with *yaj-* (i.e., the *yajādi* group), there is vocalization (*samprasāraṇa*), followed by the formation of a compound with the upapada. By the rule *tatpuruṣe tulyārtha-* (Pāṇini 6.2.2) and others, the initial syllable of the first member retains its original accent (*prakṛtisvara*).
Therefore, even for *anuḍuh-*, which is derived in this same manner, there would be udātta on the first syllable.
A modification (*vikāra*) is a substitute (*ādeśa*).
"The *anaṅ* and the vowel [are applied] according to the original form (*prakṛti*).
Thus, the words *dadhi* and *asathi* are udātta on their initial syllable.

For instance, because the word *asthi* ends in the suffix *kthin*—according to the rule "from the roots *as* [in the sense of throwing] and *sañj*, the suffix *kthin*" (*Dhātupāṭha* 1209; *Daiva* 1.10)—it is acutely accented on the first syllable by the accent of the *nit* suffix. The word *dadhi* is likewise acutely accented on the first syllable because it ends in the suffix *kin*.

The suffix *kin* is applied to the root *dhā* by the rule "*ādṛgamahanajanaḥ kikinau liṭ ca*" (*Pāṇini* 3.2.171); when reduplication has occurred there and the vowel *ā* has been elided, the form *dadhī* results.

When *anaṅ* is substituted by [Pāṇini 7.1.75] *asthidadhi* etc., its accent must also be applied; for if this [rule] were not present, the words *asthi*, *dadhi*, and *anaṅ* would each have their own separate udātta accent. But since this rule exists, it belongs to *anaṅ* alone. [The phrase] "of the base" (*prakṛteḥ*) and so forth [is explained as follows].

Regarding the forms *gopāyati* and *dhūpāyati*: here, although the suffix *āya* (the initial vowel of which is udātta by virtue of being a pratyaya) follows the roots *gup* and *dhūp* (which would otherwise be antodātta by Pāṇini 6.1.156,

*dhātoḥ*), once the designation *dhātu* (verb root) has been applied to the words *gopāya* and *dhūpāya* by rule 3.1.32 (*tiṅ-śit-sārvadhātuka...*), the final syllable of these words would again be subject to the rule *dhātoḥ* (6.1.156), resulting in them being antodātta.

Is it thus separately? In the context of vowel accents (*svaraprasaṅga*), the accent of the verbal root (*dhātusvara*) applies only to the vowel *a* of the root, not to that of the roots *gup*, *dih*, or *pū*, nor to the vowel *a* of the suffix (*pratyaya*). For example, in the form *kartavyam*: although both the final acute accent (*antodātta*) of the root and the initial acute accent (*ādyudātta*) of the suffix would apply, only the initial acute accent of the suffix prevails, and not the accent of the root.

Now, why does the exclusion of a single vowel not occur without restriction? For no restrictive cause has been stated in this rule, and such an exclusion cannot be obtained without a restrictive cause? To this he says: "The subsequent, the permanent, the internal," and so forth. Where both the subsequent vowels and their opposites would apply, because the subsequent ones and so forth are stronger, there is an exclusion of those very [subsequent ones], while the others are set aside.

However, where even when there is a conflict between what is subsequent, what is constant, what is internal, and what is an exception, the desired result is not established, there the determination is made by that which is *satiśiṣṭa* (left over), for its superior strength has been stated.
Therefore, when there is the possibility of obtaining other accents that are *satiśiṣṭa*, only that which is *satiśiṣṭa* is employed, and not the other.
But how is there no determination in the case of what is *satiśiṣṭa*? To this he says: "For he who... and so forth.
How is this known? To this he says: "For thus," and so forth.
Regarding the word "gopāyati":
here, by the accentuation rule for suffixes (*pratyayasvara*), the initial syllable is acute (*udātta*) due to the suffix *āya*.

And although that accent is an exception (*apavāda*) to the accent of the verbal root (*dhātusvara*), once the designation of "verbal root" (*dhātusaṃjñā*) has been applied to a word ending in the suffix *āya*, it is again overridden by that root-accent, which is more residual (*satiśiṣṭa*). For example: *kārṣṇottarāsaṅgaputraḥ*.
One should first form a *bahuvrīhi* compound and then apply the *tatpuruṣa* compound.
Regarding the phrase "the accent of the *bahuvrīhi*":
this refers to what was stated in [Pāṇini 6.2.1], "In a *bahuvrīhi*, the original accent [of the prior member] prevails," and so forth.
Having taken the previous indicator (*jñāpaka*) as a premise, he says: "But the accent of the *vikaraṇa*," and so on.
Regarding the phrase "vibhaktisvarāt" and so forth:
by the rule "particles [beginning with *nañ*] are udātta on their first syllable" (Phiṭ-sūtra 4.80), the *nañ* is udātta.

When a *tatpuruṣa* compound is formed there, by the rule "in a *tatpuruṣa*, [the first member retains its original accent] when the meaning is similar" (Pāṇini 6.2.2), the word retains its original udātta accent.

But when the accent of the case-ending (*vibhaktisvara*) would apply by virtue of the accent of the negative particle (*nañsvara*), yet the accent of the negative particle is desired, therefore it must be stated that "the accent of the case-ending is stronger.
When it is stronger, what happens? To this he says: "In *atistaraḥ*, etc.
By the rule [Pāṇini 6.1.166], the acute accent (*udāttatva*) of the case-ending is prescribed.

Because of its greater strength, even that which is *satiśiṣṭa* (remaining after another rule has applied) is set aside by the accent of the negative particle (*nañ*). However, for the accent of a case-ending (*vibhaktasvara*), the scope is such as in *tiryañcaḥ* and *triṣu*.
This is expressed in the rule beginning with "and from an accent caused by a case-ending" (*vibhaktinimittasvarācca*), and so forth.

A vowel for which a case-ending (*vibhakti*) is the cause is called a "vowel conditioned by a case-ending" (*vibhaktinimittasvara*). This refers to the rule: "The [accent] of *ām* when a case-ending is its cause. The fact that *ām* has a case-ending as its cause follows from the continued application of the term *sarvanāmasthāna* (starting from Pāṇini 1.1.42) to the rule at 6.1.199.

By the words "that which is its udātta-ness," etc., he demonstrates the result of its greater strength. The scope for the accent caused by the case-ending is, for example, in the cases of *catvāraḥ* and *anaṅ vāha iti*. Regarding the phrase "for in a sentence," etc.:

The word *devadatta* has its initial syllable accented (*ādyudātta*) by virtue of the vocative accent; however, the word *go* is oxytone (*antodātta*) by virtue of the nominal stem accent (*prātipadika-svara*). Consequently, its replacement vowel /ā/—by the rule *tasya* [Pāṇini 6.1.93]—is also necessarily acute due to the status of the substitute (*sthānivadbhāva*). This remains so even when the single substitution (*ekādeśa*) with the case-ending occurs, because of the rule *ādguṇaḥ* [Pāṇini 6.1.87]. The word *abhi* is oxytone; for although the rules *nipātā ādyudāttāḥ* [Phiṭ-sūtra 4.80] and *upasargāścābhivarjam* [Phiṭ-sūtra 4.81] prescribe an initial acute accent for particles and prepositions, *abhi* is specifically excluded from that rule. Therefore, it retains its original nominal stem accent (*prātipadika-svara*).
The prefix *āṅ* is acute on its first syllable by virtue of the accent of a preposition (*upasarga*).
However, this word *aja*, being in the imperative mood (*loḍanta*), is grave (*anudātta*) due to the rule "a finite verb [is grave] after another finite verb" (*tiṅṅatiṅa*).

Since the word *śukla* is acute on its final syllable by virtue of the accent of a nominal stem (*prātipadika-svara*), when the single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) with the feminine suffix *ṭāp* is formed according to the rule "of that [which ends in a long vowel]" (*tasya*), it remains acute on its final syllable.

The same should be understood when the state of being "amipūrva" (preceded by am) has been established. Thus, because of the mention of the word *pada*, in each individual sentence, a distinct accent occurs for each individual word. If a word is unaccented (*anudātta*) with the exception of one [accent], then as long as the designation *pada* has not yet occurred, everything except that one [exception] must be unaccented. Consequently, in the case of *kauvalam*—the derivative meaning "a modification of *kuvalī*"—the suffix *añ* prescribed by [Pāṇini 4.3.140] would not apply.

Since this word *kuvala* is ādyudātta (accented on the first syllable) by the rule *grāmadīnāṃ ca* (Phiṭ-sūtra 2.38), even when the feminine suffix *ṅīṣ* is applied—despite the resulting loss of its status as a *pada*—it does not relinquish its initial accentuation. Thus he says: "And this is for the sake of defining the measure," and so forth.

Is "word" (*pada*) intended here in a secondary sense? No, in a primary sense; otherwise, since the governing topic (*adhikāra*) of "word" is already present, the repeated mention of "word" would be redundant.
Therefore, it should be understood that what is intended here by "word" is that which will subsequently receive the technical designation (*saṃjñā*) of "word."

If the term *pada* were not mentioned, it would not be known how many vowels (*ac*) are to be considered anudātta. However, when *pada* is mentioned, the meaning understood is that within a single *pada*, all the vowels that exist therein become anudātta; therefore, it is for the sake of this [specific] purpose, and not for the purpose of denoting a word ending in a case-suffix (*subanta*) or a verb ending (*tiṅanta*).
Therefore, since the [syllable] must already have been unaccented (anudātta) prior to the designation of the word (*pada*), the aforementioned undesirable consequence does not arise.

One might object: "Even if the term 'word' (*pada*) here does not denote the primary word, nevertheless, by virtue of the governing context of 'word,' that [primary word] is brought into proximity; thus, the defect remains as it was. To this, he says: "It effects the cessation of the governing context of 'word' (*padādhikāra*). That is to say, this mention of the word (*pada*) indicates a secondary sense and thereby sets aside the governing context of the primary word.
What is intended by that? He says: "by that," and so forth.
"And thus" means:
this being the case, even before the designation of the two words, the remaining [syllable] becomes unaccented at the very same time as the rule for the accent is applied.
To strengthen this very point, he says "garbhiṇī" and so forth.
The suffix *ini* is applied because she possesses a fetus (*garbha*); the feminine suffix *ṅīp* is added according to Pāṇini 4.1.5 (*ṛnnebhyo ṅīp*).
This word *garbha* is accented on the first syllable, like the word *kuvala*.

In that case, if the state of being *anudātta* (unaccented) were to occur for the suffix *ini* at the very same time as its *udātta* (accented) status, then—because the word *garbhiṇī* would begin with an *anudātta* vowel—the suffix *añ* would apply by the rule *anudātatāder añ* [Pāṇini 4.2.44]. To prevent this, its inclusion in the *bhikṣādi* group is appropriate.
However, once the designation *pada* has subsequently arisen, the remaining portion [of the stem] would have to be *anudātta*.
If that were so, the word *garbhiṇī* would be *ādyudātta* (accented on the first syllable).

Consequently, one who is afflicted by the *aṇ* [accent] would not recite [the word] in instances such as *bhikṣā*, yet he does recite it. From this it is understood: even prior to the designation of the word (*padavyapadeśāt*), at the very moment of the rule for the accent (*svaravidhi*), the remaining portion becomes unaccented (*anudātta*); this is the intended meaning.

But what is the reason that, once the designation "pada" has been obtained, when the remaining [syllables] are prescribed as *anudātta*, the word *kuvala* does not fail to be established; and how is it that the reading of *garbhiṇī* among the *bhikṣādi* group serves to block the suffix *aṅ* characterized by an initial *anudātta*, even before the designation of the two words as a *pada*? What is the indicator (*jñāpaka*) for the principle that the remaining [syllables] become *anudātta* at the very same time as the rule for accentuation? To this he says: "The words *kuvala* and *garbha*," and so forth.

If, when these two [words] have the acute accent on the first syllable (*ādyudātta*), the remaining portion were to become unaccented (*anudātta*) upon the application of the technical designation *pada*, then this would also apply to the word *kuvalī*. Consequently, the suffix *añ* would not occur in the sense of a derivative (*vikāra*) from the word *kuvalī*.

Since the word *garbhiṇī* has the acute accent on the first syllable, the suffix *añ* would apply to it; therefore, one would not need to list it among the *bhikṣādi* group (which prevents *añ*) to block that application. Yet it is listed there. From this, it is concluded that the remaining portion becomes unaccented even before the designation *pada* is applied. Regarding "Praskaṇva and Hariścandra": he whose *kaṇva* (a sage) is preeminent (*prakṛṣṭa*) is Praskaṇva.
"Hariscandra belongs to him," thus [he is called] Hariscandra. This is merely an etymological derivation; however, no meaning of the individual components exists here.
These two are conventional (rūḍhi) words in which the meanings of the parts have disappeared, and they refer only to a particular seer.

But surely, in the case of *hariścandra*, the augment *suṭ* is already established by the rule *hrasvāccandrottarapade* [Pāṇini 6.1.151]; so for what purpose is the mention of *hariścandra*? To this he says: "The mention of *hariścandra*" and so forth. Regarding *prakaṇva*:
it is called *prakaṇva* because Kaṇva has departed from it (*pragataḥ kaṇvo 'smāt*).

*Haricandra* means "one whose moon is like Hari. [The following are examples: *uñcha*, *mleccha*, *jañja*, and *jalpa*. These derive from the roots: *uchi* in the sense of "gleaning" (Dhātupāṭha 295); *mleccha* in the sense of "indistinct speech" (Dhātupāṭha 1662); *jaja* and *jaji* in the sense of "fighting" (Dhātupāṭha 242, 243); and *japa* and *jalpa* in the sense of "distinct speech" (Dhātupāṭha 397, 398). The absence of *kutva* (the substitution of *k* for *j*) in *jañja* is due to irregular derivation (*nipātana*).

Regarding the statement "The words *japa* and *vyādha* take the suffix *-aṇ*," therein the form ending in *-aṇ* is established by [Pāṇini 3.3.61] "After the roots *vyadh* and *jap*, when no prefix is present.
For the word *badha* [is derived] by [Pāṇini 3.3.76].
"The *dhātu-svara* (accent of the verbal root) applies to those two. [This refers to] the acute accent (*udātta*) [prescribed] by the rule *dhātoḥ* [Pāṇini 6.1.156].
[The example is] *vyadhaḥ*.
The root *vyadh* means "to pierce" (*dhātupāṭhaḥ* 1181).
Here too, by the rule *vyadhajapor anyatarasyām*, the suffix *aṅ* is applied; as before, the accent of the verbal root would have been obtained.
[The phrase] "at a specific time" (*kālaviśeṣe*).
In *kṛta*, *dvāpara*, and so forth;
and in "implements such as chariots.
By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), the inclusion of ploughs and other such items is intended.
Regarding the word "garaḥ": it is derived from the root *gṛ* in the sense of "swallowing" (*nigaraṇe*; Dhātupāṭha 1410). It ends in the suffix *ap* according to Pāṇini 3.3.57 (*ṛdorap*).
By the word "poison" (*viṣam*), he shows that the word *dūṣya* has its specific application [here].
"Only with the acute accent on the first syllable" is due to the accent of the verbal root.

Regarding the expression *vedavegaveṣṭabandhāḥ*: from the roots *vid* in the sense of "knowing" (DhP 1064), *vic* in the sense of "separation" (DhP 1442), *veṣṭ* in the sense of "wrapping" (DhP 255), and *bandh* in the sense of "binding" (DhP 1508)— from these, as appropriate, with prefixes such as *pari* and others preceding them, the suffix *kvip* is applied, and the compound is formed with *pra*.
"Except elsewhere, it has the acute accent on the middle syllable.

For the word *vartani* is derived from the root *vṛt* (meaning "to turn," Dhātupāṭha 758) by adding the suffix *ani*, following the rule *vṛteśca* (Dhātupāṭha 3.1.6), while the rule *artisṛghṛ...* (Dhātupāṭha 1.2) is still in effect. Therefore, by the accent of the suffix (*pratyayasvara*), it becomes acute-accented on the middle syllable.

Regarding the word *dara*: the root *dṛ* (meaning "to tear apart," Dhātupāṭha 1493) ends in the vowel *ṛ*; therefore, by the rule "a word ending in *ṛ* becomes an *ap*-stem [before certain suffixes]," it is an *ap*-stem.
This is according to the rule: "The suffixes *saN* and *yat* are used when there is censure regarding the state [of the action]."

*Sāmbaḥ* means "one who exists with his mother" (*sa-hāmbayā vartate*). Although the word *saha* would normally be acute-accented on its first syllable by the rule "particles are acute-accented on the first syllable" (*nipātā ādyudāttāḥ*), the rule here prescribes that when contempt for an action (*bhāvagarhā*) is expressed, it is instead acute-accented on its final syllable according to its original stem accent (*prakṛtisvara*). Thus, in the example *sāmbo bhikṣate*, the act of begging (*bhikṣaṇam*) is here intended as contemptible.
*Tapana* means *tāpa*. [The suffix] *ghañ* is applied to the root *tap* in the sense of "to heat" (*tapa santāpe*, Dhātupāṭha 985).
This rule is stated because the word would otherwise have received the acute accent on the first syllable by default.

Why is it said that *tāpa* [is used] in reference to the harassment of robbers toward the righteous, in the sense of reproaching their disposition? Consider: *sāmbastiṣṭhati tāpo mahān* ("Sāmba remains; there is great heat"). Here, *tāpa* refers to the summer heat.
These two [words] have the acute accent on the first syllable (*ādyudātta*) by the rule "the superlative and the ordinal.
These two end in the suffix *tamap*.

Because [the suffix] is *pittvāt*? Since the suffix would otherwise be unaccented (*anudātta*), the word *uc-* would receive an acute accent (*udātta*) by the rule "particles are acute on the first syllable" (*nipātā ādyudāttāḥ*, Phiṭ-sūtra 4.80). Thus, since an initial acute accent would result, the word *uttama-* is recited for the purpose of obtaining a final acute accent (*antodātta*).

The word *śas-* is also acutely accented on the final syllable by the accent of the nominal stem (*pratipadika-svara*); therefore, since a middle acute accent (*madhyodātta*) would otherwise result, it is recited precisely for the purpose of obtaining a final acute accent.
[The word] "everywhere" (*sarvatra*)—
In the sense of censuring a state of being, and in other cases as well: *bhakṣa-mantha*, etc. [The roots are:

*bhakṣ* in the sense of eating (*dhātupāṭha* 1557); *manth* in the sense of stirring (*dhātupāṭha* 42); *bhuj* in the sense of crookedness (*dhātupāṭha* 1417); and *diha* in the sense of accumulation (*dhātupāṭha* 1015).

Is it not the case that *bhakṣi* ends in a *ṇic* suffix because it belongs to the *curādi* class? Should it not then take the suffix *ac* by [Pāṇini 3.3.56] *erac*, rather than ending in *ghañ*? To this he says: “*bhakṣin*, even though ending in a *ṇic*,” and so forth. He states the reason for this very point: “*erac* does not apply to those ending in *ṇic*. Regarding the form *kumāryau*: the suffix *ṅīp* is applied by [Pāṇini 4.1.20], and the elision of the vowel *a* occurs by [Pāṇini 6.4.148].

"The word *kumāra* has its final syllable accented" is due to the accentuation rule for nominal stems (*prātipadika-svara*). In the same way, the state of having the final syllable accented should be understood in subsequent cases as well.
Regarding "ṅīp":
it is *anudātta* (unaccented) because it is marked with the *p*-sign (*pittvāt*).
Regarding the term *prāsaṅgyaḥ*:
the suffix *yat* is applied according to the rule *tadvahati* (Pāṇini 4.4.76) and others, as it belongs to the *prāg-dhita* group.
Regarding the phrase *prasaṅga-śabdaḥ* and so forth: [the analysis follows].

The word *prāsaṅga* is derived by adding the suffix *ghañ* to the root *ṣañj* (meaning "to attach," *dhātupāṭha* 987). While the rules *tatpuruṣe* [Pāṇini 6.2.2] and *tasya* [Pāṇini 6.2.139] are in force, the rule *anta udāttaḥ* [Pāṇini 6.2.144] prescribes that the final syllable is acute (*udātta*). Therefore, this word has an acute accent on its final syllable. The phrase "this is not so" is a negation of what was previously stated, namely, that "the acute accent is elided."
He asks, "Why is this not the case? and says: "For when there is a circumflex (*svarita*)," and so forth.
This is a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) because the remaining portion becomes unaccented (*anudātta*) at the very same time as the rule for the accent is applied.
Therefore, while the circumflex is being prescribed, the remainder must necessarily be unaccented.
That? From what [source] would there be the elision of the acute (udātta)? The meaning is: from nothing at all.
Regarding the phrase "this very [rule]," etc.:

since a counter-example for the mention of the grave (anudātta) is not possible in this manner, therefore the mention of the grave is for the purpose that the initial grave syllable should become acute; otherwise, its mention would indeed be entirely purposeless.

But what is the reason that the acute accent (*udātta*) is not established for the initial [vowel] which is originally grave (*anudātta*), such that the mention of "grave" (*anudāttagrahaṇa*) is made for its sake? To this he says: "For [the rule applies] to the final," and so forth. This should be understood as a mere restriction; the meaning is that it would apply only to the final [vowel], not to the initial.

But where is the mention of *anudātta* (unaccented) made for the sake of [indicating] the initial acute accent (*ādyudātta*)? He says: "mā hi dhukṣātām," and so forth. This is the *luṅ* (aorist) of the root *duh* (to milk), in the *ātmanepada*, with the suffixes *ātām* and *āthām*. Then, by Pāṇini 3.1.45, there is the substitution of *ksa* for *cli*. By Pāṇini 6.1.180 and following, the *lasārvadhātuka* suffixes are unaccented. By Pāṇini 7.3.72, there is the elision of the letter *a*. The vowel of *ksa* is acute by the accent of the suffix itself. By Pāṇini 8.2.32 and 8.4.54, there is the change of *gh* to *k* (*cartva*), and then the substitution of *ṣ* (*ṣatva*).

If the mention of *anudātta* (unaccented) were not present here, the initial *ā* of *ātām*, *āthām*, and *ā* would not be unaccented; however, when this [mention] exists, the initial *ā* would indeed be accented (*udātta*).
Furthermore, upon the use of the word *hi*, the prohibition of *nighāta* (elision of accent) by the rule *hi ca* [Pāṇini 8.1.34] would not apply.
For if *nighāta* were to occur, there would be no elision of the accent for the *tiṅ* ending.

The prohibition [of *vṛddhi*] by the rule *māṅprayoge 'ṭaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.4.74) must also apply here. For if the augment *aṭ* were present, because it is udātta, the remainder would be anudātta; and that being the case, the elision of the vowel *a* would occur for what is anudātta, not for what is udātta—as in the word *bhṛgavaḥ*.

The descendants of Bhṛgu are formed with the suffix *ṛṣyaṇ* by the rule *ṛṣy-andhakavṛṣṇi* [Pāṇini 4.1.114], and that suffix undergoes elision (*luk*) in the plural by the rule *atribhṛgukutsa* [Pāṇini 2.4.65].

Now, one might object: "In this case as well, when a case-ending (*vibhakti*) arises, there is the elision of the acute accent; therefore, shouldn't the same apply here? To this he says: "Prior to the arising of the case-ending," and so forth.
For in the prescription of the elision (*luk*) of a secondary suffix (*gotrapratyaya*), the case-ending is not accepted as the cause (*nimitta*).
Therefore? Even before the elision (*luk*) of the *gotra* suffix occurs, there is no subsequent application (*anuvṛtti*) here. [Examples: *baidī*, *aurvī*.

[In these cases,] from "the descendant of Vida" and "the descendant of Uru," the suffix *añ* is applied by [Pāṇini 4.1.104]: *anṛṣyānantarye bidādibhyo’ñ*. It is acutely accented on the first syllable due to the *ñit*-accent, and the feminine suffix *ṅīp* is applied by [Pāṇini 4.1.15]: *ṭiḍḍhāṇañ*. [The word] *ūrṇoti* [is derived as follows].

Because [the root] begins with *ad*, there is the elision (*luk*) of *śap*. In examples such as *bhaṅgura*, the final acute accent (*antodāttatva*) is prescribed as an exception to the accent of the suffix. However, in the case of *kuṇḍināḥ*, the accent follows the principle of *sthānivadbhāva* (the substitute behaves like the original).
This is a substitute for the word *kuṇḍinī*, and since that [word] is oxytone by the accent of the suffix (*pratyayasvara*), its substitute must also be oxytone. [The derivation is as follows:
from *kuṇḍa* with the sense "she possesses this," the suffix *ini* is applied; from that form ending in *ini*, the feminine suffix *ṅīp* is applied according to Pāṇini 4.1.5 (*ṛnnebhyo ṅīp*).

Then, for the meaning "many descendants of Kuṇḍinī," the suffix *yañ* is applied according to the *gargādi* group (Pāṇini 4.1.105), and there is elision (*luk*) of that [suffix] when many [descendants] are denoted.

The substitute for *kuṇḍinaja* and others is [taught] by the rule beginning with "when a *cit* suffix follows. But how is the final acute accent (*antodāttatva*) obtained for the entire combination of stem and suffix? It is explained as follows: here, in the expression "when a *cit* [suffix follows]," this genitive case refers to a part of the whole, being related to the aggregate.

The meaning is that the final syllable of the aggregate (samudāya) which is related to the *cit* member becomes udātta. Alternatively, the word *citaḥ* ends in the possessive suffix *ac*; thus, *citaḥ* means "that which has a *cit*"—the meaning is that the final syllable of such [an aggregate] becomes udātta.
By this, the fact that the final syllable of the aggregate consisting of both base and suffix becomes udātta is established.

If, then, *cita* ends in the suffix *-a* (the *matvarthīya* suffix *a*) expressing possession, then, by means of a transposition of case endings (*sub-vyatyaya*), the nominative will occur where the genitive would otherwise be expected. As for the example *bahupaṭavaḥ*: since they are "not quite clever" (*īṣadasamāptāḥ paṭavaḥ*), the suffix *bahuc* is applied according to [Pāṇini 5.3.68], *vibhāṣā supo bahuc purastāttu*.
Regarding "uccakaiḥ": the suffix *akac* is applied according to [Pāṇini 5.3.72], which states that *akac* is added after indeclinables and pronouns before the final vowel. Regarding "kauñjāyanāḥ":

from the word ending in *cphañ* (according to [Pāṇini 4.1.98], *cphañ* being added after *kuñja* and others), the suffix *ap* (which has arrived according to [Pāṇini 5.3.113]) is elided by [Pāṇini 2.4.62] and subsequent rules, which state that the *tadrāja* suffixes are dropped when occurring in the plural.
"‘For what purpose? This is a question from one who thinks that [the result] is already established by the preceding [sūtra].
‘Even the subsequent,’ and so forth."

For the letter *c* in the rule *cphaño hi cakāraḥ* (Pāṇini 5.3.113) has already served its purpose as a qualifier; the letter *ñ* also serves its purpose in [triggering] the *vṛddhi* vowel increase. If this were not stated, then, because it is subsequent [in the order of rules], the accentuation of the *ñit* suffix would apply.

Therefore, this [rule] is formulated so that even after setting aside that [previous rule], the final acute accent (antodāttatva) alone may occur; this is an exception (apavāda) to the accent of the affix. For example:
*ākṣikaḥ* and *śālākikaḥ*, where the affix *ṭhak* is applied in the sense of "he plays with that" (*tena dīvyati*). Also: *tiro 'vasthiṣṭhante*.
By [Pāṇini 7.2.99], *tisṛ* is substituted; by [Pāṇini 7.2.100], *ṛ* is replaced by *r*.
Regarding the rule beginning with *udāttasvaritayoḥ*:
since the word *tri* is oxytone by virtue of the accent of the nominal stem (*prātipadika-svara*), its substitute *tisṛ* is likewise oxytone.

In that context, the *ra* phoneme prescribed in place of the finally acute (*antodātta*) vowel *ṛ* is not an *udāttayaṇ*. Consequently, for the following *jas*, a circumflex (*svarita*) would be required by the rule "of an acute and a circumflex" (*udāttasvaritayoḥ*); therefore, this [present rule] is an exception (*apavāda*) to that.

Now, for what purpose is the mention of *jas*? If it is argued that it is so that [the suffix] might not occur even here in *tisṛka*, this could be the case: when the suffix *kan* is applied to the word *tri* to form a name (*saṃjñā*), and when the substitution of *tisṛ* occurs there by the rule "the addition of *kan* after *tisṛ*" (Vārttika 837), would it not then also occur in *tisṛka*? This is not so, because if the mention of *jas* were absent, the *nitsvara* (acute accent on the *ni*t) would serve as a sublater [of the application of *kan*].

If it is argued that the accent of *tisṛ* is not applied when another accent intervenes, and that just as it subverts the accent prescribed by the rule *anudāttau suppitau* [Pāṇini 3.1.4], so too it subverts the *nit*-accent, this is not so. For a rule subverts that which would otherwise apply when it is not yet applicable (*yena nāprāpte*). The accent of *tisṛ* is introduced while *anudāttau suppitau* is not yet applicable; however, the *nit*-accent applies both when it is applicable and when it is not.

Alternatively, according to the principle that "exceptions in the middle set aside preceding rules" (*vyā.pa. 10*), in the case of the *tisṛ* accent, the rule *anudāttau suppitau* [P. 3.1.4] will be set aside, but not the *nit*-accent. If it is argued that the mention of *jas* is for the purpose of excluding *śas* and the other cases, this too is not the case; for in the case of *śas*, there must necessarily be an acute accent on the final syllable by the rule *udāttayaṇo halpūrvāt* [P. 6.1.168]. As for all other plural endings beginning with consonants, they fall under the rule *tatra* [P. 6.1.179].
All other plural forms beginning with *hal* should have become udātta by [Pāṇini 6.1.179] and [6.1.180].
Furthermore, because the word *tisṛ* has the plural as its scope, the dual and singular do not exist for it.
In that case, even without the mention of *jas*, [the substitution] would apply only to *jas*; therefore, he says "the mention of *jas*" and so forth.

Some commentators and others maintain that if the mention of *jas* were not made, then even in a case such as *atitistrau*—formed by the *prādi*-compound *atisṛ* + *tisṛ*—the rule would apply; they desire the mention of *jas* to prevent this fault, for the purpose of including [the word] when it is compounded. The word *catuḥ* is acute on the first syllable because it ends in the suffix *uran* according to the rule *cateruran* (Pāṇini 5.1.78); for it is by this very rule that the acute accent on the final syllable is prescribed for it when followed by the nominative plural ending *śas*.

Now, why does this not occur here: *caturaḥ paśya* ("see the four")? Even when the substitute *catar* is applied, [the accent] would not apply due to the status of being a *sthānivadbhāva*. To this, he says: "*catar-ādeśa*" and so forth. Once the substitute *catar* has been made, the initial acute (*ādyudātta*) will be prescribed by way of a nipātana (irregular enunciation). That nipātana-accent is an exception to the accent [prescribed] for the case-ending *śas*; thus, because of the prescription of the initial acute via nipātana, this accent does not occur in *cyatannaḥ paśya*. Or rather, why not? When the substitution of *r* is made by [Pāṇini 7.2.100], there should certainly not be [an accent] for the vowel *ṛ*.

Even for the case of *akārasyāpi* [Pāṇini 6.1.108], since there is the status of being a substitute (*sthānivadbhāva*) for the *yaṇ* replacement [by Pāṇini 6.1.77], when there is an intervention by the vowel *ṛ*, the [substitution] must simply not occur.

But is it not the case that the status of being a substitute (*sthānivadbhāva*) is prohibited in rules concerning accent (*svara*) by the rule *na padāntadvirvacanavareyalopasvarasavarṇānusvāradīrghajaścarvidhiṣu* [Pāṇini 1.1.58]? This is not so; for it has been stated there: "In the case of accent, lengthening, and the elision of *y*, a substitute for an elided element (*lopājādeśa*) is not treated as the original" (Kāśikāvṛtti 1.1.59), and this [substitute] is not a substitute for an elided element. Would this [term] *sāv* be a reference to the nominative singular, or to the locative plural, or to both? If it were a reference to the nominative singular, then [the rule would apply] even in cases such as *tvāyā* and *tvayi*.
For when the substitution of *tvā* is applied by [Pāṇini 7.2.94] *bhavati hi yuṣmacchabdaya*, there is the state of being a single vowel (*ekāctva*) before the nominative singular case-ending.
This same fault would apply even if "both" were understood in a general sense.

However, this fault would not arise if the locative plural were intended; for in the case of *yuṣmāsu*, the word *yuṣmad* would not consist of a single vowel. Having considered all this, he says: "The term *sāu* refers to the locative plural."
Regarding "yādbhyām":
this is the instrumental case from the word *yāt*, which ends in the suffix *śatṛ*.
Regarding "rājñe": [this is the dative case].

O King, when the elision (*lopa*) has occurred after a word designated as *bha*, it becomes a monosyllable (*ekāc*); it is not [the case] in *rājasu* after the suffix *su*, because there it consists of more than one syllable (*anekāctvāt*). [Examples are] *vāktarā* and *vāktamā*.
Here, the suffixes *tarap* and *tamap* occur, but they are not case-endings (*vibhakti*).
Why then is the locative plural mentioned? He says: "Of the locative plural," and so forth.

In the phrase *tvayā tvayi*, the substitution *tvā* occurs by [Pāṇini 7.2.91] and [7.2.97]. For the remaining portion, the substitution of *y* occurs by [Pāṇini 7.2.89]: *yo'ci*. In the phrase *indro dadhīcaḥ*: [The remainder of the commentary follows: In *dadhīcaḥ*, the *i* of *dadhi* is replaced by *ai* before the suffix *aṅ* (the patronymic suffix *añ*), which is treated as having an indicatory *k* (*kit*). By [Pāṇini 6.4.150], the *i* of *dadhi* is replaced by *ai*. Then, by [Pāṇini 6.1.108], the *ai* and the following *a* are replaced by the single substitute *ai*. Subsequently, by [Pāṇini 8.2.39], the *ai* is replaced by *e*. Thus, *dadhya-aṅ* becomes *dadhyañ*. Finally, by [Pāṇini 7.1.2], the *ñ* is replaced by *c*, resulting in *dadhīcaḥ*. In *indraḥ*, the *r* of *indra* is replaced by *n* because it is followed by a word ending in a vowel (*aci*) that begins with a *s* sound (*sakāre*) and is not preceded by a preposition (*na saṃhitāyām*). This is according to [Pāṇini 8.3.22]: *raṣābhyāṃ no ṇaḥ samānapade*. Since the word *indra* is not preceded by a preposition, the rule applies, and the *r* is replaced by *n*. Thus, *indraḥ* becomes *indraḥ*. In *dadhīcaḥ*, the *r* of *dadhi* is replaced by *n* because it is followed by a word beginning with a *s* sound (*sakāre*) and is not preceded by a preposition (*na saṃhitāyām*). This is according to [Pāṇini 8.3.22]: *raṣābhyāṃ no ṇaḥ samānapade*. Since the word *dadhi* is not preceded by a preposition, the rule applies, and the *r* is replaced by *n*. Thus, *dadhn-aṅ* becomes *dadhnañ*. Finally, by [Pāṇini 7.1.2], the *ñ* is replaced by *c*, resulting in *dadhīcaḥ*. Thus, *dadhn-aṅ* becomes *dadhnañ*. Finally, by [Pāṇini 7.1.2], the *ñ* is replaced by *c*, resulting in *dadhīcaḥ*. This is according to [Pāṇini 8.3.22]: *raṣābhyāṃ no ṇaḥ samānapade*. Since the word *indra* is not preceded by a preposition, the rule applies, and the *r* is replaced by *n*. In the word *dadhyañc*, [the suffix] *kvin* is applied by the rule *ṛtvig-ādinā* (Pāṇini 3.2.59). There is the elision of the nasal (*anunāsika-lopa*), followed by the sixth case singular ending. Then, by the rule *acaḥ* (6.4.138), there is the elision of the vowel *a*, and by the rule *cau* (6.3.137), there is the lengthening of the vowel. Regarding the phrase "beginning with the third case," etc.:
if the term *sarvanāmasthāna* were employed [in the rule], then the suffix *śas* would not occur; for that [suffix] does not begin with the third case.
Even if the mention of "the third case and so on" were excluded, [the rule] would still apply even in the case of a *sarvanāmasthāna* [suffix]. For example:
*pratīcaḥ*. This is the same as the previous [example]. *Praṣṭhauhaḥ*.

The suffix *ṇvi* is applied by [Pāṇini 3.2.64], *ūṭh* is substituted by [Pāṇini 6.4.132], and *vṛddhi* is applied by [Pāṇini 6.1.89]. Regarding the phrase "the mention of *upadhā* in the rule concerning *ūṭh*," the meaning is that one must provide the following explanation: "That by which the *ūṭh* which has become the *upadhā* is grasped is called 'the mention of *upadhā*.'"

For what purpose? To this he says: "lest it should occur here. The explanation there is as follows: from the sūtra beginning with *antodāttāt* [Pāṇini 6.1.163], the term *anyatarasyām* (optionally) is understood to carry over here; and that is understood to be a restricted option (*vyavasthitavibhāṣā*). Therefore, since it must apply only when [the vowel] is the penultimate (*upadhā*), it is appropriate to take that very [penultimate] as the referent.
Thus, [we have] *akṣadyuvā*.
In *akṣair dīvyati*, the suffix *kvip* is applied; by the rule *cch-ś-ūṭ-anunāsike ca* [Pāṇini 6.4.19], the *uṭ* augment is added to the *v* of *div*, which is then replaced by *yaṇ*.
Regarding *ābhyām*:
this is the substitution of *at* for the stem *idam* belonging to the *tyadādi* class, followed by the elision of the form *id-* according to [Pāṇini 7.2.113].
Regarding the rule "atho ābhyām" (Pāṇini 8.3.47),
there is the substitution of *aś* [for *ābhyām*].
It is stated that "those ending in *ni* are included here."

This is also obtained through the previously established *vibhāṣā* (optional rule); for when that exists, it must apply only to those [prefixes] ending in *ni*. It is logical to include only them, and thus they alone are taken.
[The term used is] "after a word ending in *ni*."
When *śas* follows, *pāda* undergoes the substitution of *pada*.
Regarding the term *dataḥ*: here too, the word *danta* undergoes the substitution of *dad*.
Regarding "āsan": here, in the seventh case singular, the word *ās* undergoes this substitution *asat*. Regarding "udan".
In this case, the word *ap* undergoes the substitution of *udan*;
thus, from *adbhiḥ*,
the letter *p* becomes *t*, and by the rule of *jaśtva*, that *t* becomes *d*.
In *rābhyām*, the substitution of *āt* occurs by [Pāṇini 7.2.85]. In *aṣṭābhiḥ* and so forth,
the substitution of *āt* occurs by [Pāṇini 7.2.84].

Regarding the word "in eight" (*aṣṭasu*): one might object that here too the substitution of *āt* must necessarily occur, for there is no statement prescribing that [substitution] which indicates an option, nor is it the subject under discussion. To this he says: "This very [fact]," and so forth.

For if the substitution of *āt* were obligatory, the mention of the long vowel (*dīrgha*) here would be purposeless, as there would be nothing to exclude; and furthermore, the term *ṣaṭ* would apply to that which has already undergone the *āt* substitution. Therefore, the connection must be made thus: "This very mention of the long vowel (*dīrgha*) makes known [the optional nature] of 'eight' (*aṣṭan*)."
How, then, does [the author] make this known? He says: "For otherwise," and so forth.
The inclusion of the term "long" (*dīrgha*) is made for this purpose: so that this accent (*svara*) should not occur where there is no substitution of *āt* (for *aṣṭan*).

If the designation "six" (*ṣaṭ-saṃjñā*) were not applied to *aṣṭan* even when *āt* has been substituted, then—since the accent of *aṣṭan* would have its scope in that case while the designation "six" is absent—the accent of "six" (*ṣaṭ-svara*) would also apply there; it is with this in mind [that the term "long" is included].

Furthermore, if the mention of the long vowel (*dīrgha*) were not made, then because [the rule for *aṣṭan*] would have no scope [otherwise], when the accent does not apply to *aṣṭan* in the view where *ātva* (the substitution of *ā*) occurs, it would nonetheless apply in this other view as well.
Therefore, the mention of the long vowel is purposeful, as it serves to exclude that [undesired application].
