When *aṣṭan*, which has undergone *ātva*, is designated as belonging to the class of "six" (*ṣaṭ*), then in the form *aṣṭānām*, the augment *nuṭ*—prescribed by the rule *ṣaṭ-catur-bhyaś-ca* [Pāṇini 7.1.55]—is successfully established. [This applies to the roots] *tudati* and *nudati*.
The suffix *śa* is applied because [the roots] belong to the *tudādi* class.
In the forms "lunatī" and "punatī," there is the elision of the long *ā* by the rule "śnābhyastayor ātaḥ" (Pāṇini 6.4.112).
By virtue of the accent of the suffix (*pratyayasvara*), a word ending in the *śatṛ* suffix should be understood here as having the acute accent on the final syllable (*antodātta*).
Regarding the phrase "of that" (*tasya*) and so forth:
why, even though it is desired [by another rule], does it not occur? Because of the separation of the rule (*yogavibhāga*) by the word "not" (*na*) in [Pāṇini 8.2.3].

Regarding the phrase "bṛhanmahatoḥ" and so forth: the word *upasaṃkhyāna* means "addition" or "supplementation. Here is the supplementation: from the rule "ḍaāś chandasi" [Pāṇini 6.1.172], the term *bahulam* (diversely) applies by way of the "lion’s glance" (*siṃhāvalokita*) maxim; therefore, the suffix also occurs after *bṛhat* and *mahat*. This statement is made because [the desired form] would otherwise be obtained by [the previous rule] 8.2.4.
"This [word] ending in *tṛn* is ādyudātta (accented on the first syllable)"— this is due to the *nit*-accent. "Bahutitavā" [is an example].
"Bahutitavā" is a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "she who has many *titava*s. This word *titau* is oxytone (having the udātta accent on the final syllable) by [Pāṇini 6.2.175]. [The commentary states:
"The mention of the letter *n* must be made."
The meaning is that an explanation (*vyākhyāna*) must be provided for the inclusion of the letter *n* (*nakāragrahaṇa*).
In this regard, the explanation is as follows: here too, as before, the term "diversely" (*bahulam*) is understood to carry over.
By virtue of that, the [substitution] will not occur even after a *n* that stands in the place of an udātta vowel.

Alternatively, there is an elision (*praśleṣa*) of the letter *na* here [in the rule], as in *halpūrvāt* (Pāṇini 6.1.175). Thus, the meaning becomes: "from a *yaṇ* that is udātta, and from one that has an udātta *na*. By this, it will also apply after an udātta *na*, as in *vākpatnī*.

The word *pati* is oxytone by the accent of the nominal stem (*prātipadika-svara*). Therein, the substitution of the suffix -n (replacing the final vowel) occurs by [Pāṇini 4.1.34], and the feminine suffix -īp is applied by [Pāṇini 4.1.5]: "After stems ending in ṛ or nasal vowels, -īp is added. Regarding the form *brāhma-bandhū*: it is a bahuvrīhi compound analyzed as *brāhma-bandhu asyāḥ* ("she whose kinsman is a Brāhmaṇa").
Therefore, by [Pāṇini 4.1.66] *ūṅutaḥ*, the suffix *ūṅ* is applied;
and by the rule [Pāṇini 8.2.5] *tena saha ya ekādeśaḥ so'pyudāttaḥ*, that single substitute (*ekādeśa*) which occurs together with it is also acute (*udātta*).
"Is made svarita" means that it is rendered with the svarita accent. "When the first member of a compound is ku," and so forth.
In this context, the vowel *ū* is antodātta (accented on its final syllable) by the accent of the giver (*dātu*).

That [accent] remains as udātta by the rule *saḥ* (Pāṇini 6.2.139), according to the original accent (*prakṛtisvara*) of the base. Since the suffix *matup* would otherwise be anudātta due to its being *pit*, this rule is commenced.
Thus: "akṣaṇvatā."

The suffix *matup* is applied in the sense of "possessing" (*akṣamasyāsti*). By [Pāṇini 7.1.76], *anaṅ* is substituted; by [8.2.16], the augment *nuṭ* is added; and by [8.2.7], the preceding *n* is elided. Regarding the form *śīrṣaṇvatā*:
the word *śīrṣan* is derived from the stem *śiras*, which is prescribed as such in the Vedic language by [6.1.59]: *śīrṣaśchandasī*.

"The word *vasu* has its first syllable accented" means that it is derived by the rule "after the roots *bhṛ*, *mṛ*, *śī*, *tṛ*, *car*, *tṛ*, *tan*, *dhan*, *mi*, *masji*, [the suffix] *uḥ*" (DhP 1.92), while the condition from "in the sense of grain, [the suffix *uḥ*] is marked with the *niṭ* accent" (DhP 1.94)—specifically the mention of *niṭ*—is still in force; then, by the rule "also after *śṛ*, *svṛ*, *svid*, *hi*, *trap*, *yas*, *vas*, *han*, *klid*, *bandh*, and *man*" (DhP 1.95), it is formed.
Consequently, it becomes acutely accented on the first syllable due to the *niṭ*-accent.

Now, why does this not occur here: *marutaḥ asya santi* [“he has Maruts,”] resulting in *marutvān*? For the word *marut* also ends in the suffix *u* by the rule *mṛgrerutiḥ* (Pāṇini 4.1.85), and since it would be oxytone by the accent of the suffix (*pratyayasvara*), there is indeed an occasion for its application. If you argue that it does not apply because of the intervention of the letter *n*, we say no; for that [suffix] has been elided. Or, even if the elision of *n* is considered non-existent (*asiddha*) for the sake of establishing the accent, even so, according to the principle *svaravidhau vyañjanam avidyamānavat* (Vyāḍipāda 37), there is no intervention. To this, he says: “In the rule for accent,” and so forth.

How, then, is it known that this *paribhāṣā* is not resorted to? Because of the inclusion of *nuṭ*. This *nuṭ* augment is a part of *matup* itself; therefore, it is included by the mention of that very [suffix]. If this *paribhāṣā* were resorted to, then since the consonant *n* would be non-existent, the rule would be established simply by "after a short vowel" (*hrasvāt*), and one would not have made the inclusion of *nuṭ*; yet it has been made.
From this it is known that the technical convention (*paribhāṣā*) is not being relied upon here. "It must be stated" (*vaktavyaḥ*) means it must be explained (*vyākhyeya*).
This same meaning applies to the word *vaktavya* even in what follows.
However, the explanation should be made as before, by relying on the continued application of the term *bahulagrahaṇa*. Regarding the word *nām*:
this is the genitive plural form of the pronoun *tad* together with the augment *nuṭ*.
But what is the reason that the short vowel is qualified by the possessive suffix *matup*? To this he says: "For otherwise," and so forth.
That which exists at present is *sāmpratika*; [the suffix] *ṭhañ* is applied according to the rule for words beginning with *adhyātma*.
[The word] "of the three" (*tisṛṇām*).
Is this because of the prohibition of lengthening by [Pāṇini 6.4.4]? It is current; [the suffix] *ṭhañ* is applied according to the class beginning with *adhyātma*.
As for "of three" (*tisṛṇām*), is it because of the prohibition of lengthening by [Pāṇini 6.4.4]? Only the short vowel exists here as the current form.

But when there is a present [short vowel], it is not logical to resort to what occurred in the past. In this context, if the short vowel were not qualified by the possessive suffix *matup*, then [the rule] would not apply here in the case of *agnīnām*.
Once the lengthening prescribed by *nāmi* [Pāṇini 6.4.3] has been applied, [the rule for shortening] would not apply; because of the absence of a short vowel.

Therefore, for the purpose of ensuring that the short vowel occurs even when the suffix has previously undergone change, the short vowel is qualified by the possessive suffix *matup*. [Examples are] *dhenvām* and *śakaṭyām*.

If the inclusion of the suffix with the augment *nuṭ* were not made, then there would be the inclusion of the genitive case-ending *ām* as well; consequently, [the rule] would apply even in cases such as *dhenvām*.

However, this does not apply when *san* is included; for in its absence, since the words *dhenu* and *śakaṭi* are oxytone by virtue of their nominal stem accent (*prātipadika-svara*), once the final vowel has undergone the *yaṇ*-substitution, the resulting form becomes invariably oxytone according to [Pāṇini 6.1.174].
As for "of *trapūṇām*," the word *trapu* is acutely accented on the first syllable, just like the word *vasu*. [The commentary states: "The requirement that the word be oxytone is removed."

If this were to follow [the general rule], then in the cases of "five," "seven," and "four," [the final vowel] would not be acute; for in words such as *pañca* and *śabda*, the vowel is acute by the rule *nraḥ saṃkhyāyāḥ* (Phiṭ-sūtra 2.28). In the rule *nraḥ*, there is the inclusion of numerals ending in the letters *r* and *n*. Regarding the statement "the last [vowel] of those beginning with three is called *uttama* (highest)," the word *uttama* here is taken in its conventional sense (*avyutpanna*) rather than as a derivative term.

And that [suffix] is by virtue of its inherent nature (*svabhāva*), because it is stated to be the final member of a compound consisting of three or more elements. "That which is near to it is the *upottama* (penultimate).

The *avyayībhāva* compound is formed by [the rule] *avyayaṃ vibhakti* [Pāṇini 2.1.6] and so forth. This statement is for the sake of providing an option (*vikalpa*), since the preceding rule would have made [the accent] compulsory (*nitya*). [The word] *sau*.

Is there the inclusion of the nominative singular suffix *su*, or the inclusion of the locative plural suffix? If it were the inclusion of the locative plural, then in the forms *kebhyaḥ* and *tebhyaḥ*, [the rule] would not apply; for when the locative plural follows the words *ka-* and *ta-*, the property of ending in the vowel *a* is not established, since even if the substitution of *yatva* (for *tyad*-class stems) were applied, the rule "before a suffix beginning with *jhal* in the plural, *e* is substituted [for the final vowel]" (*bahuvacane jhalyet*) would cause the substitution of *e*.
However, if the nominative singular is included, it applies here as well.
Therefore, considering that its inclusion [in the list] only as the seventh case-ending is appropriate, he says: "that which ends in *a* in the nominative singular.

Since there is nothing to be prohibited immediately following this point here, he states: "that which has been prescribed for these [cases] does not take place," thereby making it understood that this prohibition applies to every vowel belonging to the sixth chapter (*ṣāṣṭhika*).

For example, in *suguḥ* ("one who has beautiful cows"), the shortening occurs by the rule *go-striyoḥ* [Pāṇini 1.2.48], and the final syllable of the second member (*uttarapada*) receives the udātta accent by the rule *antodāttam* [Pāṇini 6.2.172].
In the case of *śunā*, there is vocalization (*samprasāraṇa*) by [Pāṇini 6.4.133] *āyuvamaghonāmataddhite*. Regarding "the application is as before":
in the forms *śunā* and *ābhyām*, the application occurs by [Pāṇini 6.1.168] and the subsequent rules.
Regarding the term *paramaśunā*:
here, the final acute accent (*antodāttatva*) is due to the accent of the compound (*samāsasvara*), according to Pāṇini 6.1.169. As in the examples *rājā* and *paramarājaḥ*.
In this case as well, the application is as before:
"the root *añc* ending in *kvip*.
If that is so, then there should not be the elision of the *n* there; rather, the very form containing the *n* must be taken.
For what purpose is the inclusion of the nasal *ṇ* (in the root *añc*)? He says: "Of that," and so forth. For what purpose is this [mention] as well? He says: "Wherever this," and so forth.
But surely, in every case, there ought to be elision; how then can there be an absence of the elision of *n* (*nalopa*)? He says: "Not after *añc*," and so forth.
Regarding "prāñca": as before, it is derived from the root *pra-āp*. The suffix *kvin* is applied because of the sense "he goes forward" (*prāñcati*).
Regarding "prācā": there is elision and lengthening as in the previous case. Regarding "kruñcā": [the same applies].

The roots *kruñca* and *kruñca* are listed in the Dhātupāṭha (185, 186) with the meaning "crookedness" (*kauṭilya*) and "becoming small" (*alpībhāva*). Regarding the form *kruñc*, the absence of the elision of the nasal (*nalopa*) is due to its being an irregularly formed word (*nipātana*).
In the compound *paramakruñcā*, the final syllable is udātta by virtue of the accentuation rule for compounds (*samāsasvara*).
Regarding "extremely produced" (*paramakṛta*),
here too [the option] "or production" (*kṛtir vā*) applies.

The root *kṛtī* is listed as "in the sense of cutting" (Dhātupāṭha 1435). Regarding the forms *cikīrṣyam* and *jihīrṣyam*, this optional rule (*vibhāṣā*) is introduced because the prohibition [of the substitution of *ya* for *kyac*] by the rule *na gośvansāvavarṇa* (Pāṇini 6.1.176) would otherwise apply invariably. The mention of *tāsi* and the others is by way of a collective dvandva compound. [The phrase] "because it is not taught as having *ad*" refers to the fact that the root *kṛtī* is not taught with the augment *ad*.

That which is taught is "instruction" (*upadeśa*); the meaning is that which is pronounced first in the sentences of the scriptures and in the *khilapāṭha*. This [term] is "the instruction beginning with *a*" (*adupadeśa*).

The word "instruction" (*upadeśa*) is used here either as a noun denoting the object (*karmasādhana*) or as a noun denoting the action (*bhāvasādhana*), because otherwise there would be an impossibility of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with this [word *ad-*].
"lasārvadhātukam": a genitive compound (ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa). "adupadeśāt": [from a verbal root] taught with a short *a* as its penultimate vowel].

As before? By the word *upadeśa* (instruction), which functions as the object (*karman*), there is a *karmadhāraya* compound. The inclusion of the term *varṇa* (phoneme) serves to trigger the rule of "application to that which ends in it" (*tadantavidhi*) everywhere; thus, the meaning is "because of an instruction ending in the vowel *a*. [The example is] "the agent" (*kartā*).
From the root *kṛ*, there is the *luṭ* suffix, in the first person of the *ātmanepada*; for that, the substitutes *ḍā*, *rau*, and *ras* are applied.
In the singular, there is the elision of the *ṭi* (the final vowel and following consonant).
In the dual and plural, by the rule "ri ca" [Pāṇini 7.4.51], there is the elision of the *s*.
In forms such as *āste* and so forth, ending with *śete*, there is the elision (*luk*) of the *śap* suffix because they belong to the *ad*-class.
As for *vaste*:
the root *vas* means "to clothe" (*dhātupāṭha* 1023).
Regarding "sūte": the root *ṣūṅ* means "the delivery of the embryo by living beings" (Dhātupāṭha 1031). Regarding "śete": [the root *śī* means "to lie down"].
The *guṇa* substitution [is applied] by the rule "śīṅaḥ sārvadhātuke guṇaḥ" [Pāṇini 7.3.21]. Thus, [we have] *tudataḥ* and *nudataḥ*;
these two end in the suffix *tas*.
The same applies to *pacataḥ* and *paṭhataḥ*.

But surely, this *śap* is taught [in the grammatical system] as ending in a consonant (*vyañjana*), not as ending in the letter *n*; how then does its unaccented status (*anudāttatva*) occur here? To this he says: "of the *anubandha*" and so forth. "One-sided" (*ekānta*) means a single part; "not one-sided" (*anaikānta*) means that which is not a single part, meaning it is grasped by the inclusion of that [part]. The state of being not one-sided is "non-one-sidedness" (*anaikāntatva*).
For that reason, the suffix *śap* is taught as ending in the vowel *a*, and not as ending in a consonant.
The point is that by virtue of this, the state of being unaccented (*anudāttatva*) occurs in forms such as *pacate*;

however, its status as ending in the vowel *a* is due to the application of the principle of "behaving like that which possesses a designation" (*vyapadeśivadbhāva*) to the letter *ś* of the suffix *śap*.
Regarding the forms *pacamānaḥ* and *yajamānaḥ*, [the suffix] *śānac* is used.
But how is there an unaccented status here, given that there is an intervention by the letter *m*? To this he says: "If in this case," and so forth.

Is this augment *muk* applied to the mere vowel *a*, or to a stem (*aṅga*) ending in *a*? In that regard, if it were applied to the mere *a*, then since that [stem-final *a*] would already be included by the mention of "having an *ad*-upadeśa," the *lasarvadhātuka* suffix would follow immediately after the *ad*-upadeśa because there is no intervention; for one's own constituent part cannot be an intervening element.

Therefore, the elision (*nidhāta*) is established by virtue of its being *antaraṅga*. With the words "Now" (*atha*), etc., he demonstrates the second position, wherein the elision is not established, using the phrase "even so" (*tathāpi*).
The meaning is "even so.
The connection is with what will be stated later: "the *nighāta* (anudātta accent) of [the suffix] *la-sarvadhātuka* is established.
The connection for the word "unestablished" (*asiddha*) is also with the current topic, namely the suffix *muk*.
The particle *iti* is used here in the sense of a reason (*hetau*).

Therefore, the meaning is as follows: since the *muk* [augment] is not established because the *anudātta* accent of the *sārvadhātuka* suffix is *bahiraṅga*, for that very reason the *anudātta* nature of the *sārvadhātuka* remains even in this case.
The *muk* is *bahiraṅga*, however, because it depends upon many factors.

It takes as its basis a stem distinguished by the suffix *hrak*, as well as the specific suffix *āna*; it is a low-pitched (*anudātta*) accent applied to a portion of the stem that follows a verbal root taught with a vowel (*adupadeśa*), specifically before a *l*-sārvadhātuka suffix. Therefore, this [rule] is internal (*antaraṅga*).

And because it is a rule concerning accent (*svaravidhi*); for it has been stated that a rule concerning accent possesses internal validity (*antarangatva*) with respect to what is to be produced (*bhāvya*). Now, one might object: "In the first alternative (*pakṣa*), once *muk* has been applied, the *nighāta* (anudātta accent) would not be established, because of the inclusion of the *tapara* marker in the rule *adupadeśāt*, since once *muk* is applied, the duration of time is exceeded. This is not a fault; even if, when this is done, there is an excess of half a mora (*ardhamātrā*), it is nonetheless established by virtue of the mention of "original enunciation" (*upadeśagrahaṇa*), because at the time of original enunciation, only that which consists of one mora (*mātrika*) is uttered. [This applies] also to the *citsvara* (acute accent on a *cit* suffix), and so forth.

The scope for the *cit* accent is [in forms such as] *calanam* and *copanam* (by P. 3.2.148); the scope for the anudātta accent of roots beginning with *ās-* and *śī-* (by P. 6.1.196) is [in forms such as] *āste* and *śete*. Here, both would apply—[namely] *pacamānaḥ* and *yajamānaḥ*—but because it is subsequent, the anudātta accent of the *l-sārvadhātuka* suffix prevails, overriding the *cit* accent.

As for *cinutaḥ* and *cinvanti*, since the suffix *śnu* (by P. 1.2.4) is also treated as having the marker *ṅ*, how can this serve as a counter-example? To this he says: "This has the marker *ṅ*" and so forth.
By this [rule], the operation of the preceding [element] is extended, not that of the subsequent one.
And so it has been said: "But it is established by the extension of the operation of the preceding.
Therefore, the status of being *ṅit* applies toward the operation of the preceding, but not toward that of the subsequent; what here is not logically consistent?
Regarding the phrase "And here," etc.:

in cases such as *pacāvaḥ* and *pacāmaḥ*, if the lengthening [of the vowel] were applied by [Pāṇini 6.4.12], the rule would not apply. This would be the case if the term *upadeśa* (original instruction) were not included. However, since that term is present, even though the letter *śa* is taught as having only one mora (*mātrika*), the elision of the accent (*nighāta*) does not occur even if lengthening takes place at a later stage.

Regarding the phrase "let it not be here"—[the word] *hataḥ*; [the word] *hatha*: since the nasal is elided by the rule beginning with "anudāttopadeśa" (Pāṇini 6.4.37), the *lasārvadhātuka* suffix would follow what was taught (*upadeśa*) [as having a nasal]. If the mention of "what is taught" (*upadeśagrahaṇa*) were absent here, this case too would be subject to that rule. But because it is present, it does not apply; for the root *han* is not taught as ending in the vowel *a*.
What then? It ends in a consonant, as in *pacamānāḥ*. Furthermore, that is not a substitute (*lādeśa*), but rather an affix (*pratyaya*).
However, its belonging to all verbal roots (*sarvadhātukatva*) does not exist [here].
In the form *śiśye*, it is the ātmanepada form of the root *śīṅ*; the substitution of *yaṇ* occurs by the rule beginning with *eranekācaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.4.82).
By the rule *liṭ ca* [Pāṇini 3.4.115], this is an ārdhadhātuka suffix.
In the form *śiśyāte*,
it is the form of the *liṭ* [perfect] with the suffix *ātām*.
There is no lack of anudātta [accentuation] because the designation *asārvadhātuka* is prescribed [for the affix]. [Examples are:

*hyu te*, *yad adhīte*. [The roots] *hyuṅ* "to remove" (DhP 1082) and *iṅ* "to study" (DhP 1046) are used with the word *yat* so that the prohibition of *nighāta* [by the rule] *nipātaiyadyadi* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 8.1.30) may apply. [Another example is: *mā hi kārṣṭām*.
The purpose for the employment of *heḥ* and *māṅ* has already been stated previously.
Regarding the phrase "the other [form] has the udātta accent on the final syllable," this is due to the accent of the suffix (*pratyayasvara*).

"Another [form] has the middle syllable accented. This is due to the accent of the suffix itself. But surely, the suffix here begins with *val*, and *iṭ* is an augment; since augments are unaccented, this form ought also to have the final syllable accented. Why, then, is there accent on the middle? To this he says: "Because of the *cit* marker on *sic*," and so forth.

Since the lack of acute accent (*anudāttatva*) [of the suffix] is set aside by the application of the *cit* designation, the *cit-svara* (acute accent on the *cit* element) indeed occurs; thus, the middle-acute (*madhyodātta*) nature is appropriate.
Regarding the rule "the *sic* [suffix] is acute on the first syllable" (*sica ādyudātta*), etc.:

when the acute accent on the first syllable of *sic* is to be applied, it must be stated that the acute accent belongs to that *cit* affix which follows a *sic* that is present [but] lacks the augment *iṭ*.
"Let me not do [it]" (*mā hi kārṣam*).
This is for the purpose that, in the alternative case, the word should not become entirely unaccented (*sarvānudātta*).
For, when [the final vowel] is released from its acute accent (*udātta*) in the alternative case, the word indeed becomes entirely unaccented. "The mention of *sārvadhātuka*," and so forth.

Is this [the word] *aci*? It is a locative ending (*saptamyanta*) serving as a coreferential (*samānādhikaraṇa*) qualifier for the *lasārvadhātuka*. However, coreferentiality between a nominative ending and a locative ending is not logically possible.

Therefore, because of its connection with the term *aci*—characterized by the relationship of qualifier and qualified—it is said that the mention of *lasārvadhātuka* results in [the word *aci*] being understood as having a locative ending. This is stated in the rule: "From *svap* onwards, up to the marker *vṛt*."

Even though this is so, nevertheless, only those [roots] which are *ñiṣvap* "to sleep" (DhP 1068), *āsa* "to breathe" (DhP 1069), and *ana* "to breathe" (DhP 1070) are included here by the mention of *svapādi* ("beginning with *svap*"). As for the others, such as *jakṣ* and so forth, which possess the designation *abhyasta*, they invariably have the acute accent on the first syllable (*ādyudātta*) by virtue of the rule Pāṇini 6.1.189 (*abhyastānām ādiḥ*), because that rule is subsequent [to the present one].
[The example is: *hiṃsanti*.

The roots *tṛha* and *hiṃsi* are used in the sense of "injury" (*hiṃsāyām*) [Dhātupāṭha 1455, 1456]. Because they belong to the *rudhādi* class, the suffix *śnam* is applied; by [Pāṇini 6.4.111], there is the elision of the vowel *a*, and by [Pāṇini 6.4.23], there is the elision of the following *n*. Regarding the form *svapyāt*:
this is the optative (*liṅ*), and because it belongs to the *adādi* class, there is the elision of *śap*.

Regarding the form *svapitaḥ*: the augment *iṭ* is applied by [Pāṇini 7.2.76]. Although the accent would otherwise be determined by the accent of the suffix (*pratyayasvara*), this is set aside as an exception, and the acute accent is prescribed for the initial syllable of reduplicated (*abhyasta*) roots.
In forms such as *dadhati*, there is the elision of the long *ā* by [Pāṇini 6.4.112], *śnābhyastayor ātaḥ*; the designation "reduplicated" (*abhyastasaṃjñā*) is applied by [Pāṇini 6.1.5].
In the forms *jakṣati* and *jāgrati*, here too, by the rule [Pāṇini 6.1.6], the substitution of *at* for *jhi* occurs everywhere according to [Pāṇini 7.1.4]: *adabhyastāt*. Thus, we have *jakṣitaḥ*.
As before, [the word] *it* [is understood].

Now, for what purpose is the mention of *ādi* (beginning), since the word *ādi* continues from the rule "The beginning [of the root] optionally [takes *iṭ*] after *sic*" (Pāṇini 6.1.187)? To this he says: "While *ādi* is being carried over," and so forth.

For the previous mention of *ādi* was connected with the mention of *anyatarasyām* (optionally); therefore, when that [word *anyatarasyām*] does not continue, there would also be no continuation of that [word *ādi*].
Therefore, the word "ādi" (beginning with) is mentioned again for the sake of permanence. This is intended for cases beginning with non-vowels (*anaj-ādi*).
However, in the case of an *anudātta* (unaccented) vowel beginning with a vowel (*aj-ādi*), it is already established by the preceding rule, as in the examples *jihīte* and *mimīte*.

In this context, by the rule *tāsyanudāttet* [Pāṇini 6.1.180] and others, the *lasārvadhātuka* suffixes are unaccented (*anudātta*). Furthermore, by the rule *bhṛñām it* [Pāṇini 7.4.76], the *it* (the vowel *i*) is substituted for the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*). A certain person might have the misconception that the term "unaccented" (*anudātta*) here refers to a technical grammatical accent (*śāstrīya-anudātta*). To dispel that doubt, he says: "The term 'unaccented' (*anudātta*) is a *bahuvrīhi* compound. That is to say, it is called "unaccented" because there is no acute accent (*udātta*) in it.

But for what purpose is the mention of the *bahuvrīhi* compound? He says: "For the sake of elision (*lopa*) and the substitution of *yaṇ*. This is so that even when elision and the substitution of *yaṇ* have been performed, the initial syllable remains accented acute (*ādyudāttatva*). [Example: *mā hi sma dadhāt*.
Regarding the statement "he places here" (*dadhāty atra*),

the use of the particle *sma* is so that the *laṅ* (imperfect) may occur after *sma*, according to the rule *smottare laṅ*. In this case, if this were a technical (*śāstrīya*) designation, then once the *ikāra* had been elided by the rule *itaś ca* [Pāṇini 3.4.100] and the *yaṇ*-substitution applied, the word would not be accented acute (*udātta*), because there would be no technical *anudātta* (grave) to serve as its antecedent.

In this case as well, the designation as a *bahuvrīhi* applies; for here, an acute accent (*udātta*) is not present. Having introduced the rule *iṣīśībhyāṃ van* (Pāṇini 5.2.126), the rule *sarvanidhṛdhariṣvaliṣvaśivapaṭvapreṣvā asvatantre* (Pāṇini 5.2.127)—[variant reading: *sarvanidhṛṣvariṣvaliṣpaśipahrasvapadvapraheṣvā atantre*]—prescribes that the word *sarva* is a *nipātita* (irregularly formed) with an acute accent on the final syllable.
By means of that [rule], the property of having an acute accent on the first syllable (*ādyudāttatva*) is prescribed for it when followed by a case-ending (*sup*).

However, the prescription of the acute accent on the final syllable is so that [the form] may occur in a case such as *sārva-* in the sense of "a modification of everything" (*sarvasya vikāraḥ*), according to Pāṇini 4.3.134.
Regarding the phrase "even by means of the characteristic of an affix" (*pratyayalakṣaṇenāpi*), etc.:

how, then, can [the accent] be obtained even though it is desired, given that in the case of *sarvastoma* (by Pāṇini 2.4.71), there is elision by *lumat*, and consequently, by [Pāṇini 1.1.63], there ought to be a prohibition of the characteristic of an affix? This is not a fault; the word "and" (*ca*) is carried over from the preceding rule, and it has the sense of conjunction (*samuccaya*).
By that, this accent will occur even in a case where a prohibition would otherwise apply.

The phrase "sarvasvaro 'nakackasya" and so forth means that this *sarvasvara* (the accentuation of the whole word) which is prescribed [by rule 6.1.190] applies to that [word] when it is not accompanied by the augment *akac*; this is how the meaning should be explained. In this regard, the explanation is as follows: from rule 6.1.187, the term *anyatarasyām* ("optionally") is carried over here by the maxim of the frog-leap (*maṇḍūkapluti*), and that is a restricted option (*vyavasthitavibhāṣā*); therefore, it occurs when the word is not accompanied by *akac*. When the acute accent on the first syllable would otherwise apply by rule 6.1.190, the acute accent is prescribed for the words beginning with *bhī* and *hrī*, which precede the suffix. Regarding the expression "in that which has *l* as its *it*-designation": [this refers to the suffixes *laṭ*, etc., where *l* is the *it*].
That which has a *lakāra* bearing the designation *itsaṃjñaka* is described as such. In the word "cikīrṣakaḥ," the suffix *ṇvul* is added after a form ending in the desiderative (*san*) suffix.
In that context, when the vowel *i* is elided according to [Pāṇini 6.4.48], the preceding vowel *i* of the suffix *ṇvul* becomes udātta.

Regarding the term *bhaurikividham*, the suffix *vidhal* is applied by [Pāṇini 4.2.54]. "The region whose domain is the Bhaurikas" means it is the region of the Aiṣukāris; thus, *aiṣukāribhaktam* refers to the region whose domain is the Aiṣukāris.

The suffix *bhaktal* is indeed prescribed by the preceding sūtra alone. When the *liṭ*-accent (the acute accent on the final syllable) would otherwise apply, the rule prescribes optionally an acute accent on the first syllable (*ādyudāttatva*) when the suffix *ṇamul* follows.
Consequently, in the alternative case where this option is not exercised, the *liṭ*-accent still occurs.
Furthermore, roots consisting of more than one vowel (*anekāc*) trigger this optional application.
However, for those [roots] that consist of a single syllable, there is no distinction between them by virtue of this *lit*-accent or this [other accent],
as in *lolūyaṃ lolūyam* or *popūyaṃ popūyam*.
When the suffix *ṇamul* follows such a root, it is doubled according to the rule "there is reduplication when there is frequency" (*ābhīkṣṇe dve bhavataḥ*, Vārttika 887).

"And the *anudātta* [accent]" (Pāṇini 8.1.3) [prescribes] the *anudātta* nature of the reduplicated form (*āmreḍita*). Regarding the rule "in the case of *kartṛyaK*" (Pāṇini 6.1.195): that which is a *sārvadhātuka* suffix is expressed by the word *kartṛ*;
this is because the name of the signifier is applied metaphorically to the signified.

In this context, that *yak* which occurs when there is an agent is "kartṛyak. The compound [is formed] by means of a *yogavibhāga* (splitting of the rule) from [Pāṇini 2.3.36]: *saptamī*. An example is:
"The field reaps itself" (*lūyate kedāraḥ svayameva*).
Devadatta reaps the field; however, because the field is most desired to be pervaded by the action of reaping, it is the *karman* (object).

But when, for the sake of brevity, its very agency (*kartṛtva*) is intended to be expressed, then it becomes the agent; by the extended application (*atideśa*) of the rule *karmavat karmaṇā tulyakriyaḥ* [Pāṇini 3.1.87], there occurs the *yaṅ* suffix and the *ātmanepada* endings. Thus, "it is strewn" (*stīryate*).
[The root is] *stṛ* in the sense of "covering" (Dhātupāṭha 1252)—[or *stṛñ* in the sense of covering]—followed by the lengthening of the vowel by the rule *hali ca* [Pāṇini 8.2.77].

"When the non-acute accent (*nighāta*) has been applied to all suffixes other than those belonging to the *sārvadhātuka* class," [it follows that] "only the accent belonging to the root as taught in the *upadeśa* remains. This is due to the characteristic of the suffix (*pratyayalakṣaṇa*).

Now, how is it that here [in the case of roots like] *jan*, *san*, and *khan*—as in "it is born by itself," "it is earned by itself," and "it is dug by itself"—the substitution of *ā* (by rule Pāṇini 6.4.43) having been applied, these roots subsequently become vowel-ending (*ajanta*) after the application of the suffix, but not so during their original instruction (*upadeśa*)? To this he says: "of *jan* and the others," etc.
In the rule prescribing the substitution of *ā* for the roots beginning with *jan*, the phrase "being taught with an anudātta accent" (*anudāttopadeśa*) is understood to carry over.
Therefore, the substitution of *ā* for them must be regarded as occurring only at the stage of their original instruction.
"It is born by itself.

But how can it be its own object when the root *jan* (to be born) is intransitive? There is no fault here, because the root becomes transitive when the sense of causation (*ṇic*) is included within it. For example:
"The field is being reaped by Devadatta."

In this case, because the Ātmanepada is prescribed for the *śuddha* (pure) action, the agent (*kartṛ*) is not [the object of the passive]. While the term *anyatarasyām* [Pāṇini 6.1.188] is being carried over, the mention of *vā* (or) is for the purpose of providing an option regarding the recipient of the grammatical operation (*kāryin*).
By the mention of *anyatarasyām*, the operation itself is made optional; however, by the mention of *vā*, it is the recipient of the operation that is made optional.
Consequently, the augment *iṭ* and others are applied to the operation in turn.
In *lulavitha*,
the augment *iṭ* is applied according to the rule for roots beginning with *krī*.
In *yayātha*, [the same applies].

Regarding the form *vāsudevakaḥ*, there is an optional prohibition of the augment *iṭ* by the rule *acaḥ tāsvat thaly aniṭo nityam* [Pāṇini 7.2.61]. Now, consider the forms *gargāḥ* and *vidāḥ*. When the suffix *vun* is applied in the sense of "one who has devotion to Vāsudeva," and when elision (*luk*) occurs for plural endings according to *yañañoś ca* [Pāṇini 2.4.64], and when the suffix *kan* produced by *cañceva cañcaḥ* [Pāṇini 5.3.96] undergoes elision (*lup*) according to *kan* [Pāṇini 5.3.98], why does [the rule regarding the elision of the suffix] not apply here? For even when a suffix is elided, there is the possibility [of its effect persisting] by the rule *pratyayalope pratyayalakṣaṇam* [Pāṇini 1.1.62]. To this, he says: "In this case, the operation based on the suffix (*pratyayalakṣaṇa*) is not desired."

Why is that? Furthermore, why is it not desired [to apply] here? Because of the *jñāpaka* (indicative evidence) that will be stated in the rule beginning with "ityatra vakṣyamāṇāt" (from what will be stated here).

Alternatively, by the rule "atha vā" (or rather), whatever operation is prescribed for a stem (*aṅga*) within the governing heading on stems (*aṅgādhikāra*), by that very fact, the application of the rule regarding the presence of an affix (*pratyayalakṣaṇa*) shall not be accepted here due to the prohibition.
In this same way, the absence of the *pratyayalakṣaṇa* should be understood in subsequent cases as well.
Regarding the rule "yañi kani ca lupte":

due to the word *ca* ("and"), [the suffixes] *vid* and *dhañ* are also included. In the word "Devadatta," the suffix *kta* is applied in the sense of benediction (*āśis*) to the root *dā* (to give) by Pāṇini 3.3.174; then, by 7.4.46, the substitution of *da* for the root-initial *dā-* occurs.

The compound *dattaśabda* is formed with the word *deva* according to [Pāṇini 2.1.32]. In the phrase *sapiḥ āgaccha*, there is the elision (*luk*) of the case-ending according to [Pāṇini 7.1.23]: *svamornapuṃsakāt*.

Regarding "saptāgacchata," here too [the rule] "ṣaḍbhyo luk" (Pāṇini 7.1.22) applies. Regarding the words *pathin* and *mathin*, and so forth: while the suffix *ini* is being discussed in the rule "gameriniḥ" (Dhātupāṭha 6.57), the suffix *ini* is applied by the rule "manthaḥ" (Dhātupāṭha 6.62); thus the word *mathin* is derived. Because the mention of *kit* is carried over from the rule "parame kit" (Dhātupāṭha 6.61), there is the elision of the nasal in the root *manth*.
According to the rule *patastha ca* (Pāṇini 6.1.63), the word *pathin* also ends in the suffix *ini*; therefore, by the accent of that suffix, these two [words] are udātta on their final syllable.
In the form *panthāḥ*, there is the substitution of the vowel *a* at the end [of the stem], according to [the rule] 7.1.85.
By [Pāṇini 7.1.86] *ito't sarvanāmasthāne*, the vowel *i* is replaced by *a*; by [7.1.87], *th* is replaced by *nth*; thus: *pathaḥ paśya*. By [7.1.88], the *ṭi* (the final syllable) is elided.
When that has been done, [by 6.1.161], the word becomes antodātta (accented on the final syllable).
Regarding "pathipriyaḥ":

it is a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "one for whom the path is dear. The word "priya" is optionally placed at the end [of the compound] by the rule "vā priyasya" (Pāṇini 2.2.35). Regarding "kartavā" [the Kāśikā and Padamañjarī read "kartavai"]: ...

The suffix *tave* is applied according to [Pāṇini 3.4.14]: *kṛtyārthe tavaikenkenyatvanaḥ*. Why, then, is an effort made to exclude synonyms? To this he says: "with the exception of one," and so forth. Regarding "decay" (*kṣayaḥ*): this is a form of the root *kṣi*, meaning "to dwell" or "to go" (Dhātupāṭha 1407). Regarding "victory" (*jayaḥ*).
This form *jaya* is derived from the root *ji* in the sense of "to overcome" (*abhibhave*), as listed in the Dhātupāṭha (946, 947).

In the sense of the abstract action (*bhāve*), the suffix *ac* is applied according to Pāṇini 3.3.56 (*erac*), resulting in the form *jayaḥ*, as in the expression "the victory of the Brāhmaṇas. [The following are examples of nouns ending in *a*: *vṛṣaḥ*, *janaḥ*, *jvaraḥ*, *grahaḥ*, *hayaḥ*, *gayaḥ*.

The roots *vṛṣu* and *mṛṣu* mean "to sprinkle" (Dhātupāṭha 706, 707); *janī* means "to be born/manifested" (Dhātupāṭha 1149); *jvara* means "disease" (Dhātupāṭha 776); *graha* means "to seize/to take up" (Dhātupāṭha 1533); *hi* means "to go" (Dhātupāṭha 1257); and *kai* and *gai* mean "to sound" (Dhātupāṭha 916, 917). All of these end in the suffix *ac*.

This indicates that they are listed here because the accent [of the final syllable] is obtained through the rule for the *pacādi* group, even though the accent would otherwise have been determined by the *cit* suffix.

"nayaḥ, tayaḥ, ayaḥ, aṃśaḥ, vedaḥ, sūdaḥ, aśaḥ. Regarding these: *ṇīñ* "to lead" (Dhātupāṭha 901); *tāyṛ* "in the sense of continuity and protection" (Dhātupāṭha 489). In some places, instead of *tayaḥ*, *cayaḥ* is read; that should be understood as derived from the root *ci*. *iṇ* "to go" (Dhātupāṭha 1045).
Alternatively, [the word *sūda*] is derived from the roots beginning with *atha*, *vaya*, *maya*, and *caya* (Dhātupāṭha 474–478);

or from *aṃśa* in the sense of "resolution" (Dhātupāṭha 1918), *vida* in the sense of "knowledge" (Dhātupāṭha 1064), *ṣūda* in the sense of "protection" (Dhātupāṭha 1717), and *aśa* in the sense of "eating" (Dhātupāṭha 1523).
Thus, *sūdaḥ* ends in the suffix *kap* according to the rule *igupadhajñāprīkiraḥ kaḥ*.
Regarding what was stated as "these too," this is an exception (*apavāda*):
"guh. [The root] *guhū* means "to conceal" (*saṃvaraṇe*; Dhātupāṭha 896). [The suffix -a is applied] by the rule "śamaraṇau saṃjñāyām" (Pāṇini 3.3.57).

The root *śam* means "to pacify" (*upaśame*; Dhātupāṭha 1201), while *aṇa* and *raṇa* mean "sound" (*śabda*; Dhātupāṭha 444, 445). Except when used as a technical name (*saṃjñā*), these suffixes occur only after words that have udātta on the final syllable.
This applies to the meanings of "consent" (*sammata*) and "state or object" (*bhāva-karman*).
The term "ending in -śam or -raṇa" (śamaraṇāt) carries over from the previous rule.

When the meaning intended is that of a *sammat* (an agreed-upon technical term), the suffixes -śam and -raṇa are respectively udātta on their first syllable when they denote either a state (*bhāva*) or an object (*karman*). For example: *mantraḥ*.

Regarding the root *matri* in the sense of "speaking secretly" (*guptabhāṣaṇe*) [Dhātupāṭha 1679], some, however, read it as: "In the sense of consent (*sammata*), [the suffix] *manin* occurs for both the state (*bhāva*) and the object (*karman*); [the resulting form is] *mantra*.
Its meaning should be understood as "that which has become the subject matter of a secret counsel" (*mantre viṣayībhūta*).
[The word is] *śāntiḥ*.
From the root *śam* in the sense of "to pacify" (*dhātupāṭha* 1201), the suffix *ktic* is applied according to [Pāṇini 3.3.174], resulting in *śamaḥ*.
Similarly, from *kam* in the sense of "desire" (*dhātupāṭha* 443) and *yam* in the sense of "to cease" (*dhātupāṭha* 984), we derive *kāmaḥ* and *yāmaḥ*.
Regarding "ending in ghañ":
this is stated because [the rule] "the final syllable of a word ending in ghañ is udātta if it follows karṣa or a word ending in ātva" (Pāṇini 6.1.159) would otherwise apply.
Regarding "kalpa": [this is an example].
The root *kṛpū* means "capacity" (Dhātupāṭha 762).
Regarding the word *pādaḥ*: the root *pad* means "to go" (Dhātupāṭha 1169).

"‘The *vṛṣan* and so forth constitute an *ākṛtigaṇa* (a class defined by its form). It is precisely to indicate this status as an *ākṛtigaṇa* that the particle *ca* is employed. "‘If it is so’—that is, if there is elision (*lup*) of the suffix *kan*. Even though *kan* is elided, their initial acute accent (*ādyudāttatva*) is already established by the rule of *pratyayalakṣaṇa* (treating the suffix as present despite its elision); therefore, [the mention of the accent] would be purposeless—this is the intended meaning."
"‘This very [rule]’ and so forth:
for if *pratyayalakṣaṇa* (the presence of a suffix as a condition) were to apply in some cases regarding the rules for accentuation (*svaravidhi*), this statement would indeed have to be made;
yet it has already been established by means of *pratyayalakṣaṇa*, and thus [this rule] has been formulated."

Therefore, this indicates that the rule regarding the characteristics of a suffix (*pratyayalakṣaṇa*) would apply; this statement ought indeed to have been made. Since it is established by the rule regarding the characteristics of a suffix, yet it has been explicitly stated, therefore this indicates that the rule regarding the characteristics of a suffix does not apply here in the prescription of accents (*svaravidhi*).

The mention of "in some cases" (*kvacit*) and "but in others it occurs" (*kvacittu bhavati*) is for the purpose of illustration; for it has been stated under [Pāṇini 6.1.191] that "this accent is also desired by means of the *pratyayalakṣaṇa* rule.
With the words "And thus," etc., he states the purpose of this indication. He gives the example: "The boy is fire" (*agnirmāṇavakaḥ*).

The word "fire" serves as a point of comparison; for in that way it is understood as fire itself, and not as a name for the boy. Regarding "guptaḥ," [it is derived from] the root *gup* in the sense of "protection" (Dhātupāṭha 395).
Regarding "buddhaḥ":
The root *budh* is used in the sense of "understanding" (*avagamana*) [Dhātupāṭha 858].
Regarding the word *devaḥ*:
because it ends in the suffix *ac* added after the class beginning with *pac*, the word *deva* is oxytone (i.e., has its udātta accent on the final syllable).

Is *bhīma* also derived from the root *bhī* because it ends in the suffix *man*? It is derived by means of the suffix *man*, under the governing rule "iṣiyudhi" (DhP 7.31), with the specific rule "bhiyaḥ ṣug vā" (DhP 7.35) applying to form the word ending in the suffix *man*.
[The example is] "cintitaḥ" (thought).

In the case of *citi* [meaning] "to remember" (*dhātupāṭha* 1535), which belongs to the *cur*-class, there is the elision of the suffix *ṇi* according to [Pāṇini 6.4.52]. Regarding the form *rakṣitaḥ*:
[it comes from] *rakṣa* [meaning] "to protect" (*dhātupāṭha* 658).
"Trātaḥ" and "āptaḥ":
[derived from] *traiṅ* "to protect" (Dhātupāṭha 965) and *āplṛ* "to pervade" (Dhātupāṭha 1260). "Śuṣkaḥ":
[derived from] *śuṣa* "to dry up" (Dhātupāṭha 1183); by [Pāṇini 8.2.51], there is the substitution of *ka* for the suffix *kta*.
Regarding the word *dhṛṣṭaḥ*:
from the root *ñidhṛṣ* in the sense of "boldness" (*prāgalbhye*; Dhātupāṭha 1269), there is the substitution of *ṣ* for *s*.
Because the substitutions of *k* and *ṣ* are considered non-established (*asiddha*) in this context, it should be understood that the word here ends in a *niṣṭhā* suffix.

"The undertaking is for the sake of non-designation (*asaṃjñā*), because [the form] would already be established by the preceding rule if it were a designation (*saṃjñā*). Regarding "from *aśi*": the suffix *kta* is irregularly applied (*nipātyate*) in the sense of the agent (*kartari*) from the root *aśa* "to eat" (Dhātupāṭha 1523).
By the rule *gatyarthākarmaka* [Pāṇini 3.4.72], etc.;
by the rule *pūrvavat karmaṇi ktaḥ* [Kāśikā on Pāṇini 3.4.75];
and by the rule *tayoreva* [Pāṇini 3.4.70], etc.
Regarding "in the sense of a state" (*uttaratra bhāve*):
this refers to the rule *napuṃsake bhāve ktaḥ* [Pāṇini 3.3.114]. Regarding "empty" (*riktaḥ*): the root is *ricir* in the sense of "cleansing" or "purifying" (Dhātupāṭha 1441).

When the accent of the suffix (*pratyayasvara*) would otherwise apply, the optional acute accent (*udāttatva*) of the first syllable is prescribed by the rule beginning with *saṃjñāyām* [Pāṇini 6.2.145]. The scope (*avakāśa*) of that [rule, Pāṇini 6.1.205] is, for example, *dattaḥ*, *guptaḥ*.

The scope for this [application of the rule] is in the case of *asaṃjñā* (non-technical term), such as "an empty jar" (*rikto ghaṭaḥ*). However, when the word *rikta* is the name (*saṃjñā*) of something, then since both [rules] would apply, by the "prohibition of the preceding" (*pūrvavipratiṣedha*), it becomes invariably udātta on the first syllable according to [Pāṇini 6.1.205].
And a "prohibition of the preceding" need not be explicitly stated, because the word *para* signifies that which is desired. Regarding the word *juṣṭaḥ*:
the root *juṣ* (in the Dhātupāṭha, no. 1288) means "to delight in" or "to serve."

Regarding the word "arpitaḥ": from the root *ṛ* with the suffix *ṇic*, the augment *puk* is applied by the rule *artihro* [Pāṇini 7.3.36]. Regarding the phrase "some here," etc.: what then is the reason they continue to apply only the word *juṣṭa*? To this he says: "of the word *arpita*," etc.
What is the reason for this? He says: "Even when [the word] is oxytone," and so forth.
To demonstrate that very mantra which has an oxytone reading, he says: "In that [mantra], together with three hundred," and so forth.

Since its obligatory nature (*nityatva*) is already established by the very force of its initial formulation, the inclusion of the term "obligatory" (*nitya*) is for the sake of clarity and for the benefit of what follows. [The rule applies to] *yuṣmad* and *asmad* when they end in the suffix *madik*.
By deriving the suffix *madik* through the rule *yuṣyasibhyāṃ madik* (Pāṇini 5.1.50), the forms *yuṣmad* and *asmad* are produced;
by this, he demonstrates that *yuṣmad* and *asmad* are oxytone (*antodātta*) due to the accent of the suffix.

According to the rule *tava-mamau ṅasi* (Pāṇini 7.2.96), *tav* and *mam* replace the portions ending in *map* of *yuṣmad* and *asmad*; then, when the elision (*lopa*) of the remainder is performed by the rule *śeṣe lopaḥ* (Pāṇini 7.2.90), the substitution of the subsequent form (*pararūpatvam*) occurs by the rule *ato guṇe* (Pāṇini 6.1.94).

Because the substitute for *yuṣmad* and *asmad* possesses the status of the original (*sthānivadbhāva*), it is *antodātta* (accented on the final syllable). Thus, when a single substitution (*ekādeśa*) occurs together with a short vowel (*hrasva*) replacement, that too is necessarily *udātta* by the rule "that which is substituted for a vowel is like the original" (*sthānivadādeśo’nalvidhau*). When the accent of the case-ending (*vibhaktisvara*) has been obtained through this sequence, the following is stated: "tubhyam, mahyam. Here, the change to *-am* (*ambhāva*) occurs by [Pāṇini 7.1.28], and the substitutes *tubhyam* and *mahyam* take the place of *yuṣmad* and *asmad* respectively by [Pāṇini 7.2.95]: "In the dative singular (*ṅayi*), *tubhyam* and *mahyam* are the substitutes for *yuṣmad* and *asmad*."
For what purpose is this rule formulated as a separate *yoga*? To this he says: "The formulation of a separate *yoga," and so forth.

For if they were in a single *yoga*, since the two things to be operated upon (*kāryin*) and the two causes (*nimitta*) would be equal in number, someone might suspect that the correspondence of elements (*yathāsaṃkhya*) would apply here. Therefore, the formulation of a separate *yoga* is for the purpose of demonstrating the avoidance of such a correspondence.
Furthermore, because [the terms] lack the svarita accent, there would otherwise be no correspondence according to their respective order (*yathāsaṃkhyam*).
A certain person of dull intellect might harbor such a doubt; therefore, this separate rule (*pṛthag-yoga*) is composed in order to dispel it.
This too, like the previous case, is an exception (*apavāda*) to the accentuation of case endings (*vibhakti-svara*). [Examples: *kaṇṭham*, *oṣṭham*.
The secondary suffix (*taddhita*) expresses the sense of "being" (*bhāvārtha*).
Regarding the word *nāvyam*:
in the sense of "to be crossed by boat," the suffix *yat* is applied according to [Pāṇini 4.4.91], *nau-vayo-dharma-...*.

Since the substitution of *ava* [by Pāṇini 6.1.79] has been applied here, the consonant is non-existent for the purpose of a rule concerning vowels; therefore, the prohibition is made so that the [vocalization] does not apply to the preceding [vowel], as in the case of *lalāṭam*.

The suffix *yat* is applied according to Pāṇini 5.1.6 (*śarīrāvayavādyat*). From these roots—*īḍ* (in the sense of praise), *vad* (in the sense of salutation and praise), *vṛṅ* (in the sense of sharing), *śaṃs* (in the sense of praise), and *duh* (in the sense of filling)—the suffix *ṇyat* is added by Pāṇini 3.1.124 (*ṛhaloṇryat*). To the question, "In what case is this [rule] commenced? he says: "Because they have two indicatory letters (*anubandha*)," and so forth.

Now, as for the question, "How then is the suffix *ṇyat* applied in the word *vāryam*, given that it ought to be *kyap* by the specific rule `etistuśāsu` [Pāṇini 3.1.109]?"—to this he says: "*vāryam*" and so forth.

But surely, even for the root *vṛ* (to choose), there should be *kyap* alone, since it is referred to in general terms by the mention of "vṛ"? To this he says: "*kyabvidhau hi*" and so forth. [The term] "*ṇupratyayānta*" means ending with the suffix *ṇu*.
In that rule, the mention of *ṇu* follows from the recurrence [of the term] from "after a root ending in *stha*, *ṇu*" (Pāṇini 3.2.147).
Regarding the phrase "and when ending in *cānaś*" [the *Kāśikā* reads "when" (*yadā*)],
this refers to the rule "the suffix *cānaś* is used in the senses of habitual action, age, and ability" (Pāṇini 3.2.129).
"Now, regarding that which ends in *śānac*":
this refers to [the rule] "After *laṭ*, *śatṛ* and *śānac* [are added]" (Pāṇini 3.2.124), and so forth.
"When the *lasārvadhātuka* accent has been applied."
By the rule "tāsyanudāttet" (Pāṇini 6.1.180) and so forth;
[the form] "indhāne" [is used] because this [suffix] is unaccented (anudātta).
"By means of the accent called *udāttanivṛtti-svara*" refers to [Pāṇini 6.1.161]. Examples include "veṇuḥ" and so forth.

The scope of rule 6.1.204 is, for example, *cañcā* and *varghrikā*. The scope of this optional rule (*vibhāṣā*) is when the word *veṇu* is not an object of comparison (*anupamāna*), such as in the phrase "the bamboo in the forest is dry" (*veṇuḥ śuṣko vane veṇur iti vā*). However, when the word *veṇu* is used as an object of comparison—meaning "like a bamboo"—and serves as a proper name (*saṃjñā*) for someone, then by rule 6.1.204, its initial syllable is intended to be udātta-accented; and that result is obtained through the principle of prior exclusion (*pūrvavipratiṣedha*). The roots *kuha* (meaning "to cause wonder") [Dhātupāṭha 1901] and *śaṭha* and *āṭha* (meaning "to speak correctly") [Dhātupāṭha 1854, 1855] belong to the curādigaṇa (the tenth class).
Now, the roots *ślath*, *krath*, and *valath* have the meaning "to injure" (*hiṃsārtha*) [Dhātupāṭha 7.99, 8.1, 8.2]. Regarding the form *mā hi cīkaratām*:
by [Pāṇini 7.4.93], there is the substitution of *it* for the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*).
[The phrase] "when *aṭ* is prohibited" [is used].
If there is a prohibition of something, the accent of that very thing [which is being prohibited] would belong to the vowel of the verbal root;
thus, by the rule "hi ca," there would be the *nighāta* (elision of accent).
This refers back to the requirement that [the particle] must be prohibited.

If the prohibition of the *nighāta* (non-accentuation) were not established, then there would be an absolute absence of an acute accent (*udātta*) for that which ends in *caṅ*; for example, in *mā hi dadhat*, where *caṅ* is substituted for *cli* by [Pāṇini 3.1.49]. Also, in *udumbarāvatī*.
In *udumbarā asyāṃ santi*, the suffix *matup* is applied according to [Pāṇini 4.2.85], and the lengthening of the vowel occurs according to [Pāṇini 6.3.119].
In *śarāvatī*, it occurs according to [Pāṇini 6.3.120].
"What is the purpose of [specifying] *mataḥ*? [Consider the example: *gavādinī*.

If *mataḥ* were not stated, the mention of *pūrva* (‘preceding’) which is connected to it would also not be stated; consequently, it would follow that only the vowel *ā* of the technical term (*saṃjñāśabda*) would be acute.
The mention of *pūrva* is so that this [acute accent] may apply to that which immediately follows *matup*."

Let it not be the case here that [the suffix] *matup* applies after *sānumat*. By the rule "that which is taught by its own technical definition" (*lakṣaṇapratipadoktaparibhāṣā*, Vyāḍi-Pāṇini 3), it would apply only in cases such as *śyāmāvatī* and *udumbarāvatī*, but not in others. Because of the inclusion of the word "prior" (*pūrva*), it applies to that which is merely prior [to the suffix]. For example: *ajiravatī*, and so forth.
The suffix *matup* is as previously described;
since it is marked with the indicator *p*, it would have been *anudātta* (unaccented) by rule.
The remainder of the statement is that this [present rule] is an exception (*apavāda*) to that.

Now, when it is stated that [the suffix] occurs after *avatī*, one might ask why it does not occur after *rājavatī*; for even after the elision of *n* (*nalopa`) has taken place, this too ends in the word *avatī*. To this he says: "In the rule concerning vowels" (*svaravidhau*), and so forth. One might ask: how can this be an example, since the substitution of *vat* for *mat* is *asiddha* (not yet established), and thus here there is no ending in the word *avatī*? To this he says: "The substitution of *vat*, however," and so forth.
By the word "however" (*punaḥ*), he shows the distinction from the elision of *n*.
The elision (*lopa*) is not established as valid, whereas the substitution of *v* (*vatva*) is indeed established.
Why? Because of its basis (*āśraya*).
The meaning is that the "basis" refers to being adopted as the cause for an operation concerning accent (*svaravidhi*).

The rule that the word *avatī* is udātta at its final syllable relies upon the substitution of *vat* for *mat*; therefore, by virtue of that reliance, the [substitution] is established as valid. Otherwise, the statement would be purposeless, for there is nothing ending in the word *avatī* except when the substitution of *vat* has already been established. This [rule] is also an exception to the anudātta resulting from the *pit* designation, as in *ahīvatī* and so forth; [here], the long vowel is applied by [Pāṇini 6.3.120] and the substitution of *vat* by [Pāṇini 8.2.11]. Thus, "this is an exception to the accent resulting from the removal of the udātta."
Regarding the form *dadhīcaḥ*:

the suffix *kvin* is applied in the sense of "one who moves crookedly" (*dadhyañcati*), whereby, by the rule [Pāṇini 6.2.139], the vowel *a* of the root *añc-* becomes udātta due to the original accent of the final member of the compound.

When the case-ending is an aj-adi (beginning with a vowel) that is not a sarvanāmasthāna, the *a* is elided by [Pāṇini 6.4.138]. Consequently, the rule [Pāṇini 6.1.161] would require the substitution of the udāttanivṛtti-svara; this present rule is an exception to that.
Regarding the phrase "cāvataddhite" and so forth:

the meaning is that this rule prescribing the final acute accent (*antodāttatva*) for the root *añc* must be explained as having the sense that "this occurs when a *taddhita* suffix follows. This explanation is as follows: the term "optionally" (*anyatarasyām*) is understood from a previous rule; furthermore, that is a restricted option (*vyavasthitavibhāṣā*), and therefore [the accent] will not occur before a *taddhita* suffix. In examples such as "rājapuruṣaḥ," since various accents would otherwise apply to the constituent words of the compound, this [rule] is commenced, and its application is now declared.
First, regarding the word *rājan*: because it ends in the suffix *kanin* according to [Pāṇini 6.1.157] (*kanin yuvṛṣitakṣirāji*), it is udātta on its first syllable by virtue of the *nit*-accent.

Similarly, *puruṣa* is also derived as ending in the suffix *kuṣan* according to [Pāṇini 6.1.158] (*puraḥ kuṣan*). As for the word *brāhmaṇa*, derived from "this belongs to a brahmin" according to [Pāṇini 4.3.120], it ends in the suffix *aṇ* and is udātta on its final syllable by virtue of the accent of the suffix.

Is the word *kambala* derived from the root *kam* with the suffix *vuñ* according to *kamer buk* (Uṇādi 8.114), and by virtue of the rule *bṛṣādibhyaś cit* (Uṇādi 8.109)—which contains the term *bahula*—it is thus acutely accented on the final syllable due to the *cit*-accent?

The word *kanyā*, however, has a circumflex accent (*svarita*) on the final syllable; it is an irregularly formed (*nipātita*) word according to *adhnyādayaś ca* (Uṇādi 8.14). Alternatively, it may be derived from the root *kanī* [the root *kan* in the Dhātupāṭha] meaning "to shine, to be beautiful, or to move," with the suffix *ṇyat* according to *ṛhalor ṇyat* (Pāṇini 3.1.124); the absence of *vṛddhi* occurs due to this specific irregularity (*nipātana*).

By the accent of the suffix *tisi*, this becomes antasvarita (circumflex on the final syllable). Is it not so because the word *svana* ends in the suffix *aṅ* [by Pāṇini 3.3.62]? No; by the accent of the verbal root (*dhātu-svara*), it is ādyudātta (acute on the first syllable).

As for the word *paṭaha*: the term *paṭat* [is derived] from the root *paṭ* with the suffix *ac*; thus, the word *paṭaha* has its acute accent on the final syllable due to belonging to the *pṛṣodarādi* group.

The word *śabda* is acutely accented on its first syllable because it ends in the suffix *dan*, according to [Pāṇini 3.2.48] *śāśapibhyāṃ dadanau*. The suffix *nadaṭ* is listed among the *pacādi* group; by that, when the feminine suffix *ṅīp* is applied according to [Pāṇini 4.1.15] *ṭiḍḍhāṇañ*, and the subsequent elision of the vowel *a* is performed according to [Pāṇini 6.4.148], the word *nadī* becomes acutely accented on its final syllable due to the accent of the disappearance of the acute vowel (*udāttanivṛttisvara*). The word *ghoṣa* is acutely accented on its first syllable because it ends in the suffix *ghañ*, due to the accent of the suffix *ñit*.
The words *pṛṣat* and *samit* are oxytone by virtue of being nominal stems (*prātipadika-svara*).

Now, in the case of *rājapṛṣat* and *brāhmaṇasamit*, how can the final syllable be accented? For is it not the case that the end of the compound here does not possess the accent, while that which precedes it is separated from it by the letter *t*? To this he says: "In the rule for accentuation," and so forth;
and "even when ending in a consonant."
This is a qualifier of the compound (*samāsa*):

"having the udātta accent on the final syllable" (*antodāttatvam*). Within a compound, one should understand that the status of being "final" (*antatva*) belongs to the vowel that follows those vowels which precede it.
Therefore, it is said: "This is an exception to the accentuation of separate words.
For in a compound, the words would otherwise have their own individual accents;
if this were not stated, then the accentuation of distinct and separate words would consequently apply.
Therefore, this exception to that [rule] is now stated.

Thus ends the first quarter of the sixth chapter in the *Kāśikā-vivaraṇapañcikā*, composed by the venerable master Jinendrabuddhi, who is like a second Bodhisattva. Now begins the second quarter of the sixth chapter. Regarding the phrase "the mention of the *pūrvapada*," etc.:

it is indeed appropriate to prescribe here the preservation of the original form (*prakṛtibhāva*) for that [word] which would otherwise undergo a modification characterized by an unraised tone (*anudātta*). Now, such a modification does not apply to the *pūrvapada* as a collection of vowels and consonants; rather, to what then? To that which is circumflex (*svarita*) or acute (*udātta*).

In this context, if the mention of "the first member" (*pūrvapada*) were to apply only to the first member itself, then this statement would be entirely purposeless. Therefore, it is understood that the mention of "the first member" applies when the accent of the first member is either *udātta* or *svarita*. For indeed, by virtue of being located there (*tātsthyāt*), a term may denote that which is associated with it (*tācchabdyam*), as in the expression, "The platforms are crying," or "He remains in his own nature."

By this, he explains the meaning of "it becomes by its very nature. To clarify that very point through another sentence, he says: "The modification undergoes the state of being unaccented (*anudātta*).

But how does a modification characterized as unaccented arise, for the prevention of which this *prakṛtibhāva* (original state) is commenced? To this he replies: "For when there is the final acute accent (*antodātta*) of the compound," and so forth.
"This is an exception to the rule that the final syllable of a compound is udātta," because this [new rule] is formulated when that [previous rule] would otherwise have applied—
as in "kṛṣṇo mṛgaḥ" (a black deer).
Because of the suffix *kṛṣṇa* being *guṇa*;
"the first syllable is udātta" is due to the accent of the *ñit* suffix.
Regarding the passage beginning with "And there," etc.:
there, from the rule *stuvo dīrghaśca* (Dhātupāṭha 7.4), the mention of "long" (*dīrgha*) is carried over;
and from the rule *suśṛbhyāṃ nicca* (Dhātupāṭha 7.6)—where the variant reading is *sṛśṛbhyām ūrc*—the term "with the suffix *nic*" (*nicca*) is also carried over.
"By that, it is acute-accented (*udātta*)," meaning by the accent of the *nit* suffix;
[and] "the latter member of a *kṛt*-derivative," and so forth.

In the word *brāhmacārī*, the suffix *ṇini* is applied by the rule *vrate* (Pāṇini 3.2.80), forming an *upapada* compound. According to the rule *tatra* (Pāṇini 6.2.139), the word *brāhmacārī* is accented on the final syllable by the accentuation of the *kṛt* suffix. As for the word *snātaka*, it ends with the suffix *kan*. [The printed reading in the Kāśikā is *snāta-śabdaḥ*].

The word *kṣatriya* is derived as an irregular formation (*nipātana*) by the rule *kṣatriya~śchando'dīte* [Pāṇini 5.2.73]; therefore, it is acutely accented on the first syllable due to the *nit-svara* (the accentuation of a suffix marked with *n*).
As for the word *manuṣya*, it is said that "it has a svarita accent on the final syllable" because it ends in the suffix *yat* according to the rule *manorjātāvañyatau ṣukca* [Pāṇini 4.1.161].
"Regarding the mention of *udātta*," and so forth. Therein, the mention of *udātta* is understood as being carried over (*anuvartate*) from [Pāṇini 6.1.159].
"The mention of *svarita*" refers to the same.
From the rule *titsvaritam* (Pāṇini 6.1.185).
What is established by that? He says: "By that," and so forth.

The purpose of the continued application (*anuvṛtti*) of the terms "acute" (*udātta*) and "circumflex" (*svarita*) is this: that [the designation] should apply only where there exists either an acute or a circumflex accent.

For the word *sama* is derived from the root *sū* with the suffix *ḍamap* (Pāṇini 5.2.108); thus, when the *ṭi*-portion of the root is elided, because the suffix is marked with *p*, it becomes entirely unaccented. [However,] it is stated that "by the rule *yato ’nāvaḥ* (6.1.213), it is acutely accented on the first syllable. This is because the word *tulya* is derived with the suffix *yat* by the rule *nauvayodharmaviṣamūlamūlasītātulābhyas-taśca* (4.4.91)—that is, *tulya* means "measured by a balance" (*tulayā sammitam*).
As for the word *sadṛśa*, and so forth...

Regarding the rule *tyādādiṣu dṛśo'nālocane kañ ca* [Pāṇini 3.2.60], the supplementary statement (*upasaṃkhyāna*) *samānānyayośceti vaktavyam* (Vārttika 261) has been made; by that, the word *sadṛk* ends in the suffix *kan*. Consequently, by the rule *iti samānasya sabhāvaḥ* [Pāṇini 6.3.89], there is the substitution of *sa-* for *samāna-*. [The phrase] "the word *sadṛśa* also," and so forth, follows.
It is expected that [the rule] applies by means of the original accent of the final member of a *kṛt*-derivative compound.
[The phrase] "the suffix *ik*" [refers to *ikārapratyayaḥ* according to the *Kāśikā*].
In this regard, the suffix *ik* is understood through its recurrence from the rule *atra iḥ* (Pāṇini 4.2.85).
Regarding the word "kit":
because the term "kit" is understood from the rule *bhujeḥ kicca* (Dhātupāṭha 1.71),
the word *akṣa* is [understood here] as ending in a suffix.

In the rule *aśerdevane* (Dhātupāṭha 9.24), because the suffix *sa* is understood from the preceding rule *vṛtṛvadihanikamikaṣibhyaḥ saḥ* (Dhātupāṭha 9.21)— [the variant reading is *kamikaṣiyumucibhyaḥ* according to the Dhātupāṭha]—
the term *nabviṣayasya* means "that which has the neuter gender as its scope."
"And the state of having the middle syllable accented" and "and of the solitary nyagrodha"—
these are connected with the phrase "by means of an irregular grammatical form (nipātana)."
"Abrahmaṇaḥ": this is a negative compound (nañ-samāsa).
It is like "kubrahmaṇaḥ" and so forth, according to [Pāṇini 2.2.18].

"These indeclinables have the acute accent on their first syllable. This is because of the rule "Particles have the acute accent on their first syllable" (Phiṭ-sūtra 80), and because these words are particles (*nipāta*). Among them, the two words *na* and *ku* are particles because they are listed among the *ca*-group in the rule "The group beginning with *ca*, when not denoting a substance" (Pāṇini 1.4.57). As for the two words *nir* and *ati*, [they are particles] because they are listed among the *pra*-group in the rule "The group beginning with *pra*" (Pāṇini 1.4.58).
Regarding the passage beginning with *avyaye*:

when the original form (*prakṛtibhāva*) is to be applied to an indeclinable as the first member of a compound, this must be explained as having the sense that it occurs only for *nañ* and the other [negatives].

Here is the explanation: the term *anyatarasyām* ("optionally") is carried over from rule 6.1.218; and since that is a restricted option (*vyavasthitavibhāṣā*), it will apply only to *nañ*, *ku*, and particles (*nipāta*).
In the case of *svātvākālakaḥ*,
the preceding member (*pūrvapada*) is treated as an indeclinable (*avyaya*) according to [Pāṇini 2.1.72] and [1.1.40].
In examples such as *muhūrtasukham*, the accusative case ending is applied according to [Pāṇini 2.3.5].
"The word *sarvarātra* also ends in the suffix *ac*":

this is because, in the compound *sarvā ca rātriśca* ("the whole night"), the suffix *ac* is prescribed by the rule *ahaḥ sarvaika-* [Pāṇini 5.4.87] following the rule *pūrvakālaika-* [Pāṇini 2.1.48]. "In *ruha*, *ra* optionally becomes *la*":
here, the suffix *itan* is understood from the rule *hrasvyābhyāmitan* [Dhātupāṭha 6.12].
Regarding "paramakṛṣṇaḥ": here, the accentuation is solely that of the final member of the compound. Regarding "śambagādham":

it is called *gādha* because one stands firm (*gādhate*) upon it; from the root *gādhṛ* in the sense of "standing firm" and "desire for gain" (Dhātupāṭha 4)—[and according to some Dhātupāṭhas, also "in a book"]—it optionally takes the neuter gender by virtue of belonging to the *ardharca*-class (Pāṇini 2.4.31).
By the partial citation *artilūdhūsū*, the rule [Pāṇini 3.2.184] is indicated. The term *madhyodāttaḥ* means "having an acute accent on the middle syllable."
By the accent of the suffix (*pratyayasvara*):

the rule "aśū-pruṣi" refers to the sūtra *aśū-pruṣi-laṭi-kaṇi-ghaṭi-viśibhyaḥ kan* (Dhātupāṭha 8.125), which indicates that the suffix *kan* is applied after the roots *aśū*, *pruṣi*, *laṭi*, *kaṇi*, *ghaṭi*, and *viśi*. (Note: some versions of the Dhātupāṭha include *pluṣi*, *laṭi*, *kaṭi*, *khaṭi*, and *viśi*. It is the suffix *kan* that is intended here.

But is not length (*āyāma*) the measure, according to the statement, "Length, however, may be the measure"? And is the *tatpuruṣa* compound such as "deep as the shoulder" (*śambagādha*) not expressive of a measure? Rather, what does it express? It is the expression of a quantity (*iyattā*). To this he says: "The measure," and so forth. The state of being so much is "quantity" (*iyattā*); that by which it is delimited is the "delimitation of quantity" (*iyattāpariccheda*). That alone should be understood here as the "measure" (*pramāṇa*), and not merely length itself.

What is that? How so? Here, the word *pramāṇa* is taken as a verbal noun (*kriyā-śabda*) meaning "that by which something is correctly cognized" (*pramīyate 'nena*), and not as a conventional term (*rūḍhi-śabda*); this is because it must conform to the object to be defined (*lakṣya*). Therefore, everything by which a specific measure (*iyattā*) is delimited is a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
[This includes] "that which is manifested by accent" (*svaravyaṅgya*).
The meaning is that by this [rule] which prescribes the *prakṛtibhāva* (non-application of sandhi) regarding its vowel, that which is to be expressed (*vyaṅgya*) is illuminated (*dyotya*).
"Of these" (*eteṣām*) refers to *śambagādha* and so forth. "Portion" (*dāyaḥ*) means a share (*bhāgaḥ*), a part (*aṃśaḥ*).
One who takes the inheritance is an heir (*dāyāda*); [the suffix] *ka* is applied because it belongs to the class beginning with *mūlavibhuja* (Pāṇini 3.2.5). The activity of an heir is *dāyādya*.

What, then, is that? It is the very object given (dāya). For that inheritance, while being received by the heir, becomes the object of the action. And it is not the case that the term "udātta" applies to that [inheritance].

[This is derived] from the sūtra beginning with *mantre vṛṣa* [Pāṇini 3.3.96]. Now, one might object: "In the sūtra, the verbal root preceded by the prefix *ni-* is udātta; how then can [the suffix] occur after the simple [root]? To this he says: "Because of the word *bahulam*," and so forth.
If the genitive case is prescribed by [the rule] *svāmī-īśvara-adhipati-* [Pāṇini 2.3.39], etc.

Indeed, only the locative case (*saptamī*) should be prescribed, not the genitive (*ṣaṣṭhī*), because that [genitive] is already established by the rule *śeṣe* [Pāṇini 2.3.50]. To this he says: "But of that," and so forth. If only the locative were prescribed, then, because it is prescribed as a specific rule (*viśeṣavidhi*), it would be understood as superseding the genitive; however, it should not be understood in that way. Therefore, by this very [rule], the genitive characterized as a "remainder" (*śeṣa*) is permitted, but it is not prescribed as something previously non-existent. Consequently, since it is not prescribed by a specific rule (*apratipadavihita*), the compound indeed occurs.
Regarding the term "paramadāyādaḥ":

here, the first member of the compound expresses honor (*pūjā*), not inheritance (*dāyādya*). It is called *pratibandhin* because it obstructs—that is, it hinders—the accomplishment of an effect. The suffix *ṇini* is used here in the sense of habitual action (*tācchīlya*) or necessity (*āvaśyaka*).

"Once the descriptive compound (*viśeṣaṇasamāsa*) has been formed. Now, one might object: a descriptive compound occurs when there is grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*); yet this is not coreferentiality. How, then, does the first member of the compound function as a qualifier here? To this he says: "Going," and so forth.
When the going occurs after a short period of time, the accomplishment of the task is achieved.

Regarding the phrase "and [involving] hardship" (*kṛcchrayogi*): "hardship" (*kṛcchra*) means suffering. When a traveler proceeds on a journey involving such hardship, being struck by suffering, he does not reach the object to be attained; therefore, a journey that occurs over a long period of time or involves hardship becomes an obstacle to the accomplishment of the task. Regarding the term "deceit" (*vyāja*):
it means a disguise (*chadma*).
"By means of the word *mūtra*" means by way of the pretext of urine. "Ending with the suffix *ṣṭran*" means...
In the rule *ṣivimucyoṣṭerūcca* (Daiva 8.83)—which reads as *ṣivimucyoṣṭerū ca*—there is the carry-over (*anuvṛtti*) of the term *ṣṭran*.
Regarding the entry *mūtrayateḥ*: the root is *mūtra* (Dhātupāṭha 1909), meaning "to urinate."

The word *uccāra* also ends in the suffix *ghañ*; this is according to the rule beginning with "thāthādi," because it ends in *ghañ*. [This applies] to cases such as "caused by a wall (*kuḍya*) and so forth."
They occur when the cause is [the object], because of the metaphorical application of the name of the effect to the cause.
There is also the metaphorical application of the name of the effect to the cause, as in: "All this ancient karma is being experienced.
[The word] "from the root *kav*" [is used].
The root *ku* in the sense of "sound" (*dhātupāṭha* 1042) is [marked] as having an udātta accent on the first syllable by means of [Pāṇini 6.1.213].
"Others say that a word ending in the suffix *ḍak* is oxytone.
They study the rule "ḍark after the root *kav*" (*Daiva-ukta-sūtra* 8.20). Thus, we have *rajjuśāradam* and *dṛṣacchāradam* [the Kāśikā reads *dṛṣacchāradāḥ*].
This compound is formed through a separation of the rules (*yogavibhāga*).
"The word *śārada* here signifies 'fresh' (*pratyagra*). Fresh means new, that is to say, existing for a short period of time.
By this, he demonstrates that the word *śārada* has multiple meanings.

"An obligatory compound" (*nityasamāsaḥ*): because the *mahāvibhāṣā*, which is under discussion, is a restricted option (*vyavasthitavibhāṣā*). "Unimpaired" (*anupahatam*): [meaning it is not contradicted].
It is not affected by dust because it has been recently swept;
[the word] ends with the suffix *upratyaya*.

In the rule *sṛjerasuṃ ca* (Dhātupāṭha 1.100), because the suffix *u* is carried over from the preceding rule *bhṛmṛśītṛcaritsaritanidhanimimasjibhya uḥ* (Dhātupāṭha 1.92), [the word] ends with the suffix *adi*.

In the rule *dṛṇāteḥ ṣug hrasvaśca* (Dhātupāṭha 6.45), because the suffix *adi* is carried over from the preceding rule *śṛdṛbhaso'diḥ* (Dhātupāṭha 6.42), [the word] ends with the suffix *adi*. [Thus we have] *paramaśāradam*.
*Śārada* means "that which occurs in autumn.
This word is derived by the rule *sandhivelādyṛtunakṣatrebhyo'ṇ* [Pāṇini 4.3.16]. Regarding the phrase "words denoting a genus have restricted domains":
the analysis of the compound is "those whose domain (*viṣaya*) is restricted (*niyata*)."

However, the restriction to a specific object occurs only when there is a particular genus (*jāti*), because [the term] refers to those currently existing, such as the *adhvaryu* priests and others. According to the rule "and *gotra* [is a *jāti*] by virtue of being a *caraṇa*" (Pāṇini 4.1.63), [the names of these priests] possess the status of a genus (*jāti*) due to their being *caraṇas*. [This applies to] that which ends in the suffix *yat*.

Regarding [the rule] *Pāṇini 4.2.101*: "The word *kaṭha* is derived from the suffix *ac* (in the sense of the present participle) added after the verbal root *kaṭh*, according to the rule 'after the roots beginning with *pac*'.
This is derived from the root *kaṭh* (meaning "to live in hardship") as listed in the Dhātupāṭha (number 333).

Regarding the phrase "tadevam" (thus, therefore): because this word *kālāpa* ends in the suffix *aṇ*, it is consequently accented on the final syllable by the accentuation rule for suffixes (*pratyayasvara*). [The commentary states: "When the suffix *ṭhak* is present, it is accented on the final syllable."
By the rule *kitaḥ* [Pāṇini 6.1.159]. Regarding the example *pitṛsadṛśaḥ*:

the sixth case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) and the third case (*tṛtīyā*) are applied by the rules *tulyārthaiḥ* [Pāṇini 2.3.72] and *ṣaṣṭhī* [Pāṇini 2.1.31], respectively, resulting in a compound. It is stated that "the words *pitṛ* and *mātṛ* are prescribed as having the udātta accent on the final syllable within the *uṇādi* group."
In the rule *naptṛ-neṣṭṛ-tvaṣṭṛ-hotṛ-potṛ-bhrātṛ-jāmātṛ-pitṛ-duhitṛ* (Pāṇini 2.4.28), one might ask:

what is the purpose of including the word *sadṛśa* ("similar"), since in expressions such as *mātṛ-sadṛśa* and *pitṛ-sadṛśa*, the desired form is already established by the rule *tatpuruṣe tulyārthā-tena-ka-dvārā-ṭakṣṇaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.2.2)? To this he replies: "And for the sake of the genitive compound," and so forth. For when used in the sense of "equal to" (*tulyārtha*), the genitive case is also prescribed.

In that context, when the compound *mātṛsadṛśaḥ* is formed as a genitive (*ṣaṣṭhī*) compound, the mention of *sadṛśa* (resembling) is for the purpose of ensuring that this also occurs. However, since this [rule] is introduced, the mention of *sadṛśa* would have to be made even in the case of a third-case (*tṛtīyā*) compound; therefore, he says "here," etc.

In the examples *dāsyāḥ sadṛśaḥ* and *vṛṣalyāḥ sadṛśaḥ*, once the elision (*luk*) has been applied by [Pāṇini 6.3.21], the genitive compound is brought about by the mention of *tatsadṛśa*; for when there is no elision, a specific form exists [which would otherwise not be covered].

If the inclusion of the word *sadṛśa* here is intended for the sake of a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*), then a third-case compound (*tṛtīyāsamāsa*) should not be formed, because there would be no distinction [between the two]. This is not so; for even in that case, it must indeed be formed where the meaning is not that of the genitive, as in *vidyāsadṛśaḥ* ("similar to knowledge").
