For in this instance, the genitive sense does not exist; rather, it is the sense of the third case, meaning "similar by means of knowledge" (*vidyayā hetunā sadṛśaḥ*).

Regarding the word "here" (*atra*) and so forth: in that context, the word *dāsī* has its final syllable accented (*antodātta*) by the rule concerning the removal of the acute accent of the feminine suffix *ṅīp*.

Regarding *daśi sevane* (Dhātupāṭha 1786)—[the root *das* meaning "to nourish" according to the Dhātupāṭha]—the form is derived from the root *daṃś* with the suffix *ṭan*, by the rule *daṃśeṣṭaṭanau na ā ca* (Daiva 9.103), which prescribes the suffix *ṭan* and the replacement of the letter *n* with *ā*. The feminine suffix *ṅīp* is applied by the rule *ṭiḍḍhāṇañ* (Pāṇini 4.1.15), and the elision of the final vowel is governed by *yasyeti ca* (Pāṇini 6.4.148); thus, the acute accent (*udāttatva*) is applied by the rule *udāttayaṇo halpūrvāt* (Pāṇini 6.1.161). As for the word *vṛṣalī*, it ends in the suffix *ṅīṣ* by the rule *jāterastrīviṣayāt* (Pāṇini 4.1.63), and it is acutely accented on the final syllable due to the accent of the suffix (*pratyayasvara*). [The compound] *prācyasaptaśamaḥ* is as follows:

This is a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*). [The word] *prācya* "is acutely accented on the first syllable" because it ends in the suffix *yat*, according to the rule *yato 'nāvaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.1.207).

"The word *gāndhārī* is either ādyudātta (accented on the first syllable) or madhyodātta (accented on the middle syllable) because it belongs to the *kardama*-class," [as stated in] *kardamādīnāṃ ca* (Phiṭ-sūtra 3.10). Here, the term "and so forth" (*ādi*) from that rule continues to apply; thus, when the accent is prescribed for the first syllable, it becomes ādyudātta, but when it is prescribed for the second, it becomes madhyodātta. *Gamanīyam* means "that which is to be gone to";
*paṇyam* means "that which is to be traded."
Regarding the term *madravāṇijaḥ*: one who conducts business among the Madras is so called.
This is a locative compound (*saptamīsamāsaḥ*). [Locative compounds—Kāśikā].
[The word *mada* is derived] by means of the separation of the rules (*yogavibhāga*) in the sūtra *saptamī* (Pāṇini 2.1.39).

It is said to be "ending with the suffix *rak*" because it is etymologically derived by prescribing the suffix *rak* after the root *mad* according to the rule *sphāyitañci-* (Dhātupāṭha 3.8.31), etc. It "denotes that which has an equal measure" (the reading *tulyapramāṇaṃ* is found in the printed edition).
The analysis (vigraha) is: "that of which the measure is equal.
Why is this not considered a *svapadavigraha* (an analysis using its own constituent words)? For a sentence must be constructed in such a way that the meaning of the compound is understood;
[this is what is meant by] "merely eating" (*bhakṣāmātra*).

And the meaning of this is "of the same measure as this alms-food. Nor can this be explained by analyzing its own constituent words (*svapadavigraha*), because the word *mātra* functions to denote "equal measure"; for it occurs in that sense only within a compound, not in a sentence.
Therefore it has been said: "This word *mātra* refers to the domain of compound formation (*vṛtti*)," and so forth.
Here, "compound formation" (*vṛtti*) refers specifically to the compound (*samāsa*).
[The reading in the Kāśikā edition is: "That which does not end in an affix is udātta."

Because [the suffix] ṭāp shares a portion [of its status] with both the acute (*udātta*) and non-acute (*anudātta*), [it is said]: "In that regard, the words *sukha* and *priya*," and so forth. By the word *tat*, there is a reference back to *sukha* and *priya*; the cause of those two, *sukha* and *priya*, is that which produces pleasure in the future—that is, in another birth.
In that context, the words *sukha* and *priya* are employed.
For what reason is it explained in this way? He says: "For that is beneficial," and so forth.
The word *hi* means "for" (*tadā ca*).
In the case of a *tatpuruṣa* compound, the preservation of the original form (*prakṛtibhāva*) is prescribed.
For this *tatpuruṣa* compound denotes "beneficial" (*hita*) provided that the words *sukha* and *priya*, occurring as the prior members, refer to the cause of benefit in the subsequent member.
And what is "beneficial"? That which produces pleasure (*prīti*) in the future.

But how do the words *sukha* and *priya* denote their cause? Through the metaphorical attribution of the effect to the cause (*kāraṇe kāryopacārāt*), just as one says "the water of the reed-bed causes foot-disease. Now, for what purpose is the inclusion of the word "pleasure" (*prītau*) here, since pleasure is invariably concomitant with *sukha* and *priya*?
"Will it be so when *prīti* (pleasure) is being understood? To this he says: "In the case of *sukha* and *priya*, there is *prīti*" (*prītyetyādi*—this is the printed reading), and so forth.

Although the term *prīti* could have been established even without its explicit mention, since *prīti* is invariably concomitant with *sukha* and *priya*, the reason it is mentioned here is for the purpose of ensuring that it refers specifically to that *prīti* which is of an intensified degree.
[The words] "*brāhmaṇa*" and "*chātra*" [in the example] are oxytone due to the accent of the suffix."
The word *brāhmaṇa* ends in the suffix *aṇ*.
The word *chātra* ends in the suffix *ṇa*, according to the rule *chattrādibhyo ṇaḥ* [Pāṇini 4.4.62].
The word *kanyā* has a circumflex (*svarita*) accent on its final syllable.
Because [the word] *adhnya* and others are read in that very form in the *Daivata-pāṭha* (Pāṇini 6.2.193), as in "rājasukham" and "rājapriyam.

Although in these cases, because pleasure (*sukha*) and what is dear (*priya*) are never dissociated from delight (*prīti*), delight is understood; nevertheless, the delight that is characterized by excellence is not conveyed, and thus this serves as a counter-example. [The rule] "dhānyam-antaḥ-svaritam" [is stated].
[Is it] because it ends in *ṇyat*? [It is] by the accent of the *tit* suffix.

"The meaning is 'the husband of a *vṛṣalī*'"—that is to say, one who desires a *vṛṣalī*. By the rule "after *bhū*, [the suffix] *kvip* is used in the sense of a name or a specific state" (Pāṇini 3.2.179), the word *bhū* has its final syllable accented acute (*udātta*) by the accent of the verbal root.
In the same way, the word *vāk* [is derived from] the root *vac*. By the rule "kvip after *vac*, *pracch*, etc. (*Pāṇini* 3.2.178), there is the suffix *kvip*.
As for *cit*:

it is derived from the root *cit* in the sense of "perception" (*saṃjñāna*) [according to the Dhātupāṭha 3.9], by the rule "after roots ending in *i*, etc. (*Pāṇini* 3.2.178), there is the suffix *kvip*.

Under the governing rule *nṛtiśṛdhyoḥ kūḥ* (Dhātupāṭha 1.174), [the word] *didhiṣūḥ*—from the list *andūdṛmbhūjambūkaphelūkarkandhūdidhiṣūḥ* (Dhātupāṭha 1.176)—is formed with the suffix *kū*, and thus it has an udātta accent on the final syllable. From the root *śaki* in the sense of "doubt" (Dhātupāṭha 86), the suffix *akāra* is applied according to [Pāṇini 3.3.103]. However, some explain that this refers to the word *śaṅka* ending in the suffix *ghañ*. From the root *bādh* in the sense of "shaking" (Dhātupāṭha 5), preceded by the prefix *ā*, the suffix *ghañ* is applied to form *ābādhaḥ*.

*Atyarthamantikaṃ* means "very near. By [Pāṇini 5.3.63], when the suffix *iyasun* follows, the word *antika* undergoes the substitution *nedā*. "*Astitvādhyavasāyaḥ*" means "the determination of existence."
The meaning is "the certainty of non-existence.
In the phrase "gamanāśaṅkam," it is a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*).

It is neuter because it is an adverbial modifier (*kriyāviśeṣaṇa*), or because gender is dependent upon common usage (*lokāśrayatva*). Regarding the expression "one who was formerly wealthy" (*āḍhyo bhūtapūrvaḥ*): this refers to one who was previously wealthy.

Since the meaning is already understood through the compound, the word *bhūta* is not employed, just as the word *upasikta* ("sprinkled") is not used in the expression *dadhyodana* ("rice with curd").
Regarding the term *paramapūrvaḥ*: here, the compound is formed by [Pāṇini 2.1.61] and the following rules.
As for the statement, "In this case, the compound is 'that which is both supreme (*parama*) and prior (*pūrva*)'": [this is the analysis].
The particle *iti* is for the purpose of indicating the meaning.

The sense is that in this counter-example, there is a compound in the case of this sentence-meaning characterized by being honored— namely, "that which is both supreme (*parama*) and prior (*pūrva*)"—
but not in the case of "supreme being" (*paramo bhūtaḥ*).
The word *tu* is used for emphasis.

The meaning of the sentence—that this [term] is "the supreme former" (*paramo bhūtapūrvaḥ*), which characterizes a time that was previously supreme—is precisely within this compound; such is the sense.
For what reason? He says: "And thus," and so forth.
The word *ca* has the sense of *hi* (for/indeed).
This is not a compound.
This being so, this becomes merely an illustration (*udāharaṇa*), not a counter-illustration (*pratyudāharaṇa*), because the word *pūrva* denotes that which existed previously (*bhūtapūrva*).

As for the reading generally found in manuscripts here—“*paramaścāsau bhūtapūrvaśca* (‘that which is supreme and has existed before’), and not *paramo bhūtapūrvaḥ* (‘supreme and formerly been’)—it should be understood as an erroneous reading; for in both [possible] sentence constructions, the sense of ‘having existed before’ (*bhūtapūrva*) is understood. In the case of *savidha*, it is a *bahuvrīhi* compound according to Pāṇini 2.2.28 (*saha supā*), and the substitution of *sa-* for *saha-* occurs according to 6.3.82.

In this same way, one should understand that in *sanīḍa* and other such terms, there is also a *bahuvrīhi* compound and the substitution of *sa-*. Terms such as *madrasavidham* are genitive compounds (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*).

But surely, words such as *savidha* and so forth are derived in meanings such as "together with the object" (*saha viṣayeṇa*); how then can they function in the sense of proximity (*sāmīpya*)? To this he says: "The [words] beginning with 'together with the object' (*saha viṣayeṇa*)," and so on. By the word "etc. (*ādi*), there is the inclusion of [words] such as *sahanīḍena* ("with the nest") and *sahamaryādayā* ("with the boundary").

The particle *eva* (only) serves for restriction and excludes other denotable meanings; that is to say, [proximity] is merely the occasion for their derivation (*vyutpatti-nimitta*), not their actual denotation (*abhidheya*).

Regarding the statement, "But these [words] express proximity," here too the word *tu* (but) serves the purpose of restriction (*avadhāraṇa*). It means that they express only proximity to the object denoted by the base, and not the meaning of sentences such as "together with" (*saha*) or "in accordance with" (*vidhi*). As for the example, "vispaṣṭakaṭukaṃ" (distinctly pungent).

Regarding the word *kaṭuśabda* [from Pāṇini 5.3.87], it is stated: "The compound is formed by [the rule] *sup-supā*. Now, one might ask: why, in the case of *vispaṣṭakaṭukam*, is the analysis not performed according to *viśeṣaṇaṃ viśeṣyeṇa bahulam* [Pāṇini 2.1.57], and why is it not treated as a *karmadhāraya* compound? To this he replies: "For *vispaṣṭa* and so forth are used here," and so on.
For a *karmadhāraya* compound occurs only when there is grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*). But here, such coreferentiality does not exist.

Therefore, in this context, words such as "distinct" (*vispaṣṭa*) are qualifiers of the causal basis for the application (*pravṛttinimitta*) of a word like "pungent" (*kaṭuka*), namely pungency (*kaṭukatva*) and so forth, and not of the substance (*dravya*) possessing that quality.

By words such as *kaṭuka* ("pungent") and so forth, a substance possessing a quality characterized by pungency (*kaṭukatva*)—that is, a substance in which that quality exists—is denoted. Consequently, since there is no grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), a karmadhāraya compound is not possible.
Therefore, the compound must be formed according to the method already stated.

Regarding the term *vispaṣṭaḥ* [the word *vispaṣṭa*—Kāśikā]: it is derived from the root *spaś* (Dhātupāṭha 887), meaning "to afflict" or "to touch," in its past passive participle form (*niṣṭhā*). The word *spaṣṭa* is established as a *nipāta* by the rule *dasta-spaṣṭa-cchanna-jñaptāḥ* [or *vā dānta-śānta-pūrṇa-dasta-spaṣṭa-cchanna-jñaptāḥ*, Pāṇini 7.2.27]. A compound is formed with the prefix *vi-* [forming *vi-spaṣṭa*].
The same applies to the word *vicitra* and so forth.

The root *citra* in the sense of "making variegated" (*citrīkaraṇe*) belongs to the *curādi* class (Dhātupāṭha 1917). From this, the suffix *ghañ* is applied; thus, *viśeṣeṇa citram* (variegated in a special way) forms the compound *vicitra* by means of a *prādisamāsa*.
Regarding the phrase "by the accent of the indeclinable," this refers to the accent prescribed by the rule *tatpuruṣe tulyārtha-* (Pāṇini 6.2.2), etc.

Furthermore, the word *vi-* here has the sense of separation (*avayava*); and according to the rule "particles are udātta on their first syllable" (*phi-sūtra* 4.80), it possesses the udātta accent on its initial vowel.

Regarding the term *vicittaśabdam*: from the verbal root *citī* (meaning "to perceive," *dhātupāṭha* 39), the form *cittam* is derived through the addition of the past passive participle suffix (*niṣṭhā*).

"Vigata-citta" is a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "one whose mind has departed. Regarding the phrase "by the accent of the *bahuvrīhi*," the word *cittam* is derived from the root *citī* (meaning "to perceive" or "to know") with the addition of the *niṣṭhā* suffix.
"His mind is gone" (*vigata-citta*) is a *bahuvrīhi* compound.
Regarding the phrase "by the accent of the *bahuvrīhi*," it refers to that which is prescribed by [Pāṇini 6.2.1]:
"In a *bahuvrīhi*, [the first member retains its] original form (*prakṛtyā*)."
Regarding the phrase "the word *vyakta*," and so forth:

when the root *añj* preceded by the prefix *vi-* takes the *niṣṭhā* suffix, the *gatisvara* (accent of the prefix) is acute (*udātta*). In that case, the *yaṇ* substitute for the vowel *ī* is an *udāttayaṇ*; consequently, the following non-acute (*anudātta*) vowel *a* becomes a circumflex (*svarita*). Regarding the phrase "the word *sampanna*," and so forth.
The word *sampanna* is derived from the root *pad* with the prefix *sam* followed by the *niṣṭhā* suffix, and it denotes the agent (*kartṛ*).
Regarding the statement "the words *paṭu* and *paṇḍita* [are acute on the final syllable] by virtue of the accent of the suffix":

since the term "acute on the final syllable" (*antodātta*) was mentioned in the singular, one must effect a change in its grammatical number and connect it [to the current context] as "acute on the final syllable" (*antodāttāv iti*).
From the root *pāṭ* (to split), the suffix *u* is applied by the rule *phalipāṭinamijanīnāṃ guk paṭinākidhaśca* (Dhātupāṭha 1.103), and the word *paṭi* is the substitute; thus, *paṭuḥ*.
From the root *paḍi* (to go, Dhātupāṭha 281), the past passive participle (*niṣṭhā*) form is *paṇḍitaḥ*, meaning "skilled" (*kuśalaḥ*).

[The word] *kuśāl* is derived from the root *lā* in the sense of "taking" (*lā ādāne*, Dhātupāṭha 1058), with the suffix *ka* added according to [Pāṇini 3.2.3], forming an *upapada-samāsa*; the accent of the final member is its original one according to [Pāṇini 6.2.139].
Regarding the statement "the word *capala* has the *cit*-accent," this is understood to mean that it is oxytone.
How is this [word] *anta* oxytone by virtue of the *cit*-accent? To this he says: it is derived from the suffix *kala* according to [Pāṇini 4.2.80] *kalastṛpaśca*;
there, the mention of *cit* from [Pāṇini 4.2.82] *bṛṣādibhyaścit* is understood to carry over (*anuvartate*).
Therefore, by that *cit*-accent, it is oxytone.
The phrase "the word *nipuṇa*" and so forth; the term "ending in an udātta accent" is to be connected with what precedes.

Regarding "puṇeḥ": from the root *puṇ* in the sense of "to purify" (*puṇa karmaṇi śauce*, Dhātupāṭha 1333), the suffix *ka* is applied according to [Pāṇini 3.1.135]: *igupadhājñāprīkiraḥ kaḥ*. Regarding "the best of movements" (*gamanaśreṣṭham*):
the suffix *lyuṭ* is applied according to [Pāṇini 3.3.115], *lyuṭ ca*; this is a descriptive compound (*viśeṣaṇasamāsa*).
That which is most praiseworthy is *śreyaḥ*.
The substitution of *śr* [for *ṣṭh*] occurs by the rule *dṛṣṭannīyasunoḥ* [Pāṇini 5.3.60].
Regarding the term *vacanajyeṣṭham*,
here too [the same applies].
Following those same two suffixes, the word *praśasya* undergoes the substitution of *jy*.
Thus, in the forms *gamanakaniṣṭham* and *gamanakanīyaḥ*,
the word *yuva* and the word *alpa* undergo the substitution of *kan* following the suffixes *iṣṭhan* and *īyasun*, according to [Pāṇini 5.3.64].

But how is it that [the form] *śrajyakānām* occurs? The particle *iti* is used here in the sense of a reason (*hetu*). Because the mention here refers to the substitutes (*ādeśa*) [of *praśasya*, etc.]—and since those are prescribed before suffixes beginning with a vowel (*aj-ādi*), the occurrence of the bare forms is impossible—therefore, by implication (*sāmarthya*), the word ending in that [substitute] is understood as the subsequent member of the compound (*uttarapada*). Thus, [we have] *kumāraśramaṇā*.

According to the rule *prātipadikagrahaṇe liṅgaviśiṣṭasyāpi grahaṇam* (Vyāḍipāda 21), the word *kumārī* is compounded here. For it is only in this way that grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the feminine word *śramaṇā* is possible, and not otherwise.
[The word] *kumāra* is udātta on its final syllable.

[Is the word *kumāra*] derived from the root *krīḍāyām* (Dhātupāṭha 1877) by adding the suffix *ac* according to the rule *pacādyac*? [Regarding the phrase] "But some," etc.: how, then, is it obtained that [the term applies] without distinction when the paribhāṣā "that which is taught by a specific rule and that which is taught by a general definition" (Vyāḍi-paribhāṣā 3) exists? He thinks as follows: the letter *ca* is added here.
And that [particle] has the sense of conjunction for this very rule;
by it, [the application] occurs everywhere without distinction.
For in this way there is a conjunction, and not otherwise.

Those who maintain that the compound occurs only in the rule *ye tu* [Pāṇini 2.1.70] explain the particle *ca* here as having a conjunctive sense (*samuccaya*) with respect to the preceding rule. Regarding the example *pratigata enasā* ("one to whom sin has returned"), this demonstrates that the word *enas* forms a *tatpuruṣa* compound according to the Vārttika: *avādayaḥ kruṣṭādyarthe tṛtīyayā* (Vārttika 92).
Alternatively, it may mean *pratigatam eno yasya* ("he whose sin has returned").
By this [rule], it is a *bahuvrīhi* compound;
[thus] "kumārapratyenāḥ," where the lengthening [of the vowel] occurs by [Pāṇini 6.4.14].
But surely, the term "udātta" (acute) is not mentioned here in the sūtra; how then is the acute accent obtained? To this he says: "In this [sūtra], 'udātta'... and so forth.
What, then, is its functional force? To this he says: "The preceding member... and so forth. For it is not stated that there is an accent other than the natural accent (*prakṛtisvara*).
What then? It is simply the natural accent (*prakṛtisvara*); for the word *prakṛtyā* is understood [from the previous rule].

There, the connection is made as follows: "That accent which is obtained for the word *kumāra* by virtue of its being in its original form (*prakṛtibhāva*) becomes the accent of the initial [syllable].
And thus, by implication, an acute (*udātta*) accent is obtained.

For that very [word] has the accent of the base form (*prakṛtibhāva*) by virtue of being the word *kumāra*. When the rule *Pāṇini 5.1.81*, *taddhitārthe dvigoryap*, is being supplied, the suffix *yap* is applied by *Pāṇini 5.1.82*.
Then, there is the elision (*luk*) of the suffix *ṭhañ*.
Regarding the *prāgvatīya* [suffixes]:

"pañcakapalaḥ" means a sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) prepared on five potsherds (*kapāla*). Here, the suffix *aṇ* is applied by [Pāṇini 4.2.16], and its elision (*luk*) occurs by [Pāṇini 4.1.21] and subsequent rules.
"These are the compounds" refers to those beginning with *pañcakapāla* and ending with *daśaśarāva*. "Those in which there is the elision of a *kṛt* suffix" refers to these same cases.
Those for which the suffix *aṇ* has been elided are described as such.
In this context, the two words "pañca" and "daśa" are acute-accented (*udātta*) by the rule "praḥ saṃkhyāyāḥ" (Phiṭ-sūtra 2.28). Thus, [the form] is "pañcāśat."
The compound is formed in the sense of a secondary derivative (*taddhita*). The suffix *ṭhak* is applied by [Pāṇini 5.1.19], *ārhādagopucchāt*, and so forth;
subsequently, its elision (*luk*) occurs by [Pāṇini 5.1.28], *adhyardhapūrva*, and so forth.

The term *pañcaśarāvaḥ* is a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "that which has five bowls. Now, how does this apply here in the case of *pañcāratnyaḥ* and *daśāratnyaḥ*, since when the *yaṇ* substitution and the *guṇa* have been applied, the final member (*uttarapada*) no longer ends in a long vowel (*āt*)? To this he says: "*pañcāratnyaḥ*" and so forth.

Since the *yaṇ* and *guṇa* substitutions occur when a case-ending (*vibhakti*) beginning with a vowel follows, those two are *bahiraṅga* (external) operations here, whereas the accent (*svara*) is *antaraṅga* (internal); because [the accent] exists prior to the production of the case-ending, according to the principle: "That which is *bahiraṅga* is as if non-existent (*asiddha*) with respect to that which is *antaraṅga*" (Vārttika 42).
Therefore, even in the case of *pañcāratni*, the accent characterized by having a short vowel ending (*iganta-lakṣaṇa*)—which belongs to a *dvigu* compound—applies.
Alternatively, it is said: "by virtue of being as if the original element (*sthānivadbhāvāt*).

This means that when the preceding accent is to be applied, the *guṇa* substitution (which results in a long vowel) applies by virtue of being as if the original element, thus possessing the characteristic of ending in a short vowel (*iganta*).

But is it not the case that in rules concerning accent (*svaravidhi*), the status of being a substitute (*sthānivadbhāva*) is prohibited by the rule *na padānta* [Pāṇini 1.1.58]? This is not so; for it has been stated: "In the case of accent, lengthening, and the elision of *y*, a substitute for an elided element (*lopājādeśa*) is not treated as the original" (Kātyāyana Vārttika 1.1.59). Furthermore, the *yaṇ* and *guṇa* substitutions in the word *pañcāratnyaḥ* are not substitutes for an elided element. In this word, the stem *aratni-* ends in the feminine suffix *ṅīṣ*, because the word *aratni-* is listed among the *bahu*-group [of words] by the rule *kṛdikārādaktinaḥ* (Gaṇasūtra 50), or according to some, by the rule *sarvato 'ktinnarthād ityeke* (Gaṇasūtra 51).

Is it also here as before? [The answer is: It is a *dvigu* compound in the sense of a secondary derivative (*taddhita*), but there is the elision of the suffix *-mātra*. When the words beginning with *oṇa*, *gantā*, and so forth follow as the second members of the compound, although the original accent (*prakṛtisvara*) would invariably apply to the word *bahu* as well, this option is stated.
For example, in "bahuratniḥ":
[the formation] is as before, starting from the compound.
Regarding the term *bahumāsyah*:

as before, compounds such as *bahukapāla* and others are to be understood here as well; even in this case, when the sense of a secondary derivative (*taddhita*) has been expressed, the elision of the suffix *aṇ* is to be observed according to [Pāṇini 4.2.16].

"The word *bahu* has its final syllable accented" means that it is derived from the verbal roots *bahi* and *mahi* in the sense of "growth" (*vṛddhi*)— while the rule *ku-bhraś-ca* (Dhātupāṭha 1.107) is still in effect—
from the rule *laṅghibhrāṭrnalopaś-ca* (Dhātupāṭha 1.114), which prescribes the suffix *ku*. Thus, by the accent of the suffix, it has its final syllable accented.
"Where there is the substitution of *yaṇ*":
this refers to the case of *bahvaratniḥ*. This rule is commenced for the sake of excluding the meaning "many. An example is *pañcadiṣṭiḥ*.
This is equivalent to [the rule] "pañcāratni. The compound "sāṅkāśyasiddhaḥ" is formed according to [Pāṇini 2.1.41]. [The commentary states:
"Because the words sāṅkāśya and kāmpilya end with the suffix ṇya."

Because [the word *ūka*] has been derived by applying a suffix with four meanings (*cāturarthika*) characterized by the group beginning with *saṅkāśa*, according to the rule *vucchaṇ* [Pāṇini 4.2.79].
Regarding the phrase "the word *ūka*," and so forth:

under the governing rule *kṛdādhārārcikalibhyaḥ kaḥ* [Dhātupāṭha 3.18], the suffix *kak* is prescribed as *kid* by the rule *sṛdṛbhūśuṣimuṣibhya kak* [Dhātupāṭha 3.19, *kid* being the reading in the printed edition]; since this suffix is prescribed, it applies to the root *av* as well.
The word *tanoka* ends with the suffix *kak*;
by the rule *jvaratvara* [Pāṇini 6.4.20] and others, *ūṭh* is substituted for *vat*.
It is stated that "the word *nidhana*, formed from the root *ni-dhā* with the suffix *kyu*, has the udātta accent on the middle syllable."

This word *nidhana* [is derived] from the rule *kṛpṛvṛjimandi-nidhāñaḥ kyuḥ* (Dhātupāṭha 5.26). Since the printed reading is *nidhāñbhyaḥ*, one should apply the augment *num* according to Pāṇini 7.1.73 and understand the word as neuter in gender with respect to its phonetic form. Regarding the term *kyu*: the meaning is that this suffixal element (*pratyaya*) is designated by the technical name *kyu* when it takes the form of the word *nidhana*.

"The words *kumbhī* and *kalasī* end in the feminine suffix *ṅīp*"; by this, the intention is that they are oxytone (having the acute accent on the final syllable). However, their ending in the suffix *ṅīṣ* should be understood as being prescribed by the rule "from a genus-name not denoting a female" (*jāter astrīviṣayāt*, Pāṇini 4.1.63) and so forth.

"The word *bhrāṣṭra* ends with the suffix *ṣṭran*. This is stated while the rule "the suffix *ṣṭran*" (*daśapādī 8.2.79*) is in force; [and] under the rule "there is *vṛddhi* [of the root vowel] for *bhrasj*, *gam*, *nam*, *han*, *viṣ*, and *aś*" (*daśapādī 8.2.32*), [the form is derived]. A *dvandva* compound whose members are plural forms denoting *rājanya*s that are not in a compound is called a "plural *dvandva* of *rājanya*s. For example: "Āṣāḍhaka, Caitraka, and Raudhaka."
"Āāphalkāḥ," "caitrakāḥ," and "rodhakāḥ" form a *dvandva* compound.

In this context, the word *caitraka* functions as the prior member (*pūrvapada*) in relation to the word *rodhaka*, while the word *āāphalka* functions as the prior member in relation to the word *caitraka*. Consequently, both undergo the *prakṛtibhāva* (original form) rule.
For this very reason, he states "the word *āāphalka* and the word *caitraka*" and so forth, in order to demonstrate the accentuation of both of these.

"The word *śini* has its initial syllable accented" (*ādyudātta*). For it is derived as follows: while the suffix *ni* is being carried over from the rule "the suffix *ni* after the roots *vī*, *jyā*, and *jvar*" (*vījyājvaribhyo niḥ*, Dhatupatha 1.18), the rule "the suffix *ni* after *vah*, *śrī*, *śru*, *dru*, *glā*, *hā*, and *atvari*" (*vahiśriśrudruglāhātvaribhyo niḥ*, Dhatupatha 1.21) is prescribed; thus, it also applies to the root *śī*.
Furthermore, the shortening of the vowel occurs by virtue of that same rule's mention of the term *bahula* ("variously").
Therefore, it will be udātta by virtue of the *nit*-accent.
Regarding the phrase "in his descendants":
the meaning is "in those who are the descendants of that Śini, the Kṣatriya."
"Without distinction" means figuratively.
"The Haimāyanas."
The suffix *phak* is applied according to [Pāṇini 4.1.101].

Now, one might object: this word *rājanya* denotes the Kṣatriya caste, as it has been stated—“In the case of a descendant of a king, the mention of the caste [is required]” (Vārttika 392); thus, “one is a *rājanya* if he is a Kṣatriya. Furthermore, a *dvandva* compound that occurs among the Andhakas and Vṛṣṇis consists only of words denoting Kṣatriyas, because the Andhakas and Vṛṣṇis are Kṣatriyas.
And therefore, *dvaipyahaimāyanāḥ* is stated as a counter-example.

For this too is a *dvandva* compound consisting only of words denoting *rājanya*s (members of the royal order), since they reside among the Andhakas and Vṛṣṇis; thus he says, "the Andhakas and Vṛṣṇis," and so forth.

Since the inclusion of the *kṣatriya*s would be established by the mere mention of "among the Andhakas and Vṛṣṇis," what is the purpose of specifically employing the term *rājanya*? It is for the sake of ensuring that those who belong to a distinguished, consecrated lineage (*abhiṣiktavaṃśya*) are included.

The *santāna*—or lineage (*vaṃśa*)—of living beings is characterized by a single mark, whether by learning or by birth; however, in this context, that which is characterized by a single mark through birth is intended. That which exists therein is "of the lineage" (*vaṃśya*), according to [Pāṇini 4.3.54], because it belongs to the *dig-ādi* group. As for what might be said in that regard:
Are even the Dvaipya and Haimāyana [kings] Kṣatriyas belonging to the consecrated lineage? To this he says: "And these," and so forth.
Regarding the phrase "Saṅkarṣaṇa and Vāsudeva":
this is a dvandva compound consisting of the two words *saṅkarṣaṇa* and *vāsudeva*, both ending in the singular number.
"Vṛṣṇikumārāḥ"—
this is a *tatpuruṣa* compound.
"Kurupāñcālāḥ"— [likewise].
"Everything is here, yet because of the specific mention of the Andhakas and Vṛṣṇis, it does not occur; for there is no inclusion [of others] therein. Regarding "eleven" (*ekādaśa*):
it is a *dvandva* compound consisting of "one" (*eka*) and "ten" (*daśa*).

Regarding "twelve" (*dvādaśa*): the vowel substitution *āt* occurs according to the rule *dvy-aṣṭanaḥ saṃkhyāyām-abahuvrīhyaśītyoḥ* [Pāṇini 6.3.46]. The Teacher has stated that [in such a compound], the subordinate member (*upasarjana*) is the primary element.
One who dwells near is an *antevāsī*;
this designation is used figuratively.
Those which constitute the members of the *dvandva* compound denote the teacher as a subordinate element.

Therefore, because they denote pupils, the [pupils] themselves are expressed by the words "teacher" (*ācārya*) and "pupil" (*antevāsin*) through metaphorical transfer (*upacāra*), with the teacher as the subordinate element (*upasarjana*).

Even a single member of that [compound] is called "the pupil with the teacher as the subordinate element" (*ācāryopasarjanāntevāsī*) according to the property of being a member of a *dvandva* compound. For example:
"Āpiśali is the teacher."
"From this [root], *iñ* [is applied]" (Pāṇini 4.1.95).
Or else, "the students of Āpiśali himself are the Āpiśālās"; here, as before, the suffix *aṇ* is applied.
"Both ways," and so forth.
In both modes of etymological derivation, the student (*antevāsī*) is subordinate (*upasarjana*) to the teacher (*ācārya*).
For instance, when it is said "students of both kinds," the students alone are the primary referents, while the teacher is subordinate because he serves as their qualifier.

The word *āpiśala* is oxytone due to the accent of the suffix, as it ends in the *aṇ* suffix. [In the case of] *pāṇinīya*, the *aṇ* suffix is applied according to Pāṇini 4.2.114 (*tadadhīte*) following the rule 4.2.58 (*proktam*), and that suffix is elided. Thus, the word *pāṇinīya* is middle-accented (madhyodātta) by virtue of the accent of the suffix.

Regarding the term *pāṇinīyarauḍhīyāḥ*: *Rauḍhi* is the descendant of *Roḍha*, formed by the suffix *iñ* according to [Pāṇini 4.1.95]. The students of the teacher *Rauḍhi* are called *rauhīyāḥ*; although the suffix *aṇ* would have been applicable here by [Pāṇini 4.2.111], its application is prohibited by [Pāṇini 4.2.112] because the word consists of more than two syllables, and thus [the suffix *cha*] is applied by [Pāṇini 4.2.114]. Alternatively, *Rauḍhīya* refers to that which was taught by *Rauḍhi*. From that, the suffix *aṇ* is added in the sense of "one who studies that" [Pāṇini 4.2.58], and as before, there is elision (*luk*) of that suffix, resulting in *rauhīyāḥ*.
The word *rauḍhīya* is also oxytone (with the acute accent on the final syllable), as before.
[The suffix] *aṇ* is applied because it was taught by Kāśakṛtsna; those who study that [work] are the *kāśakṛtsnās*, with the elision (*luk*) of the suffix *aṇ* as before. Thus:
"the grammarians of the Vedic tradition" (*chāndasavaiyākaraṇāḥ*).

This is a copulative compound (*dvandva*) of pupils (*antevāsin*), but it is not one in which the teacher (*ācārya*) is subordinate. Here, only the pupils are denoted by the terms *chāndasa* and *vaiyākaraṇa*, and they do not have the teacher as a subordinate element. Those who study the Veda (*chandas*) are called *chāndasas*; those who study grammar (*vyākaraṇa*) are called *vaiyākaraṇas*.
In that context, those who study under a certain teacher are his pupils (*antevāsinaḥ*). Regarding the phrase "in the *Āpiśala* and *Pāṇinīya* treatises":
that which was proclaimed by Āpiśali is the *Āpiśala*.
That which was proclaimed by Pāṇini is "Pāṇinīya.
Since the suffix is prescribed in that treatise (*śāstra*) where it is primarily expounded, the Teacher (*ācārya*) is the primary referent, as he serves as its qualifier.
Here, his status as a teacher is relative to this specific treatise.

The status of being a teacher (*ācāryatā*) does not depend solely on having a pupil (*antevāsī*), but rather also on having a treatise (*śāstra*). "These two end in *aṇ*"—the meaning is that they are oxytone due to the accent of the suffix (*pratyayasvara*). It should be understood that even in subsequent cases, that which ends in *aṇ* is oxytone.

Regarding "sauvarṇiriñantaḥ" [the *Kāśikā* reads "sāvarṇiḥ"], the intention is that it is accented on the first syllable by virtue of the *ñit*-suffix accent. In the same way, it should be understood that subsequent forms ending in *iñ* are also accented on the first syllable.
The word *māṇḍūkeya* ends in the suffix *ḍhak*, according to [Pāṇini 4.1.119]: *ḍhak ca maṇḍūkāt*.
Regarding the form *āvanteḥ* and so forth:
since there are many descendants of Avanti, the suffix *ñyaṅ* is applied by [Pāṇini 4.1.171], and its elision (*luk*) occurs by [Pāṇini 2.4.62]: *tadrājasya* and so forth.
The suffix *aṇ* prescribed by [Pāṇini 4.2.69], "The country inhabited by the Avantīs," is applied;
then, by [Pāṇini 4.2.81], "Of that," there is elision (*lup*).
Thus: "the Avantīs, as well as the Aśmakas."
Just as [the suffix] *yañ* is applied in the case of *yathāvantayaḥ*, so too is it applied here in the case of *tathāśmakāḥ*.
In this instance, there are words denoting both *kṣatriyas* and [names of] countries (*janapada*).

When a secondary derivative (*taddhita*) is formed for the sense of "descendants" (*apatya*) and occurs in the plural, the suffixes prescribed in the four senses (*cāturarthika*) are applied after that [word] ending in the plural suffix to denote the place of residence.
Is there elision (*lup*) for that [suffix]? It has been applied; likewise also in the case of "the Ashmakas" (*āśmakāḥ*).
Only this much is extended by analogy.

The descendants of Aśmaka are numerous; by the rule *aśmakādibhyo 'ṇ* [Pāṇini 4.1.173], the suffix *iñ* is applied, which is then elided (*luk*) as before. By the rule for their residence, the suffix *aṇ* is applied, which is also elided as before. Some say that the word *Avanti* has its final syllable accented (*antodātta*) because it belongs to the *ghṛtādi* group.

Others say it is due to the accent of the *cit* suffix; for they explain that by the statement "the suffix *jhic* after the root *bhū*" (Pāṇini 3.2.178), the suffix *jhic* occurs after the root *ava* as well, owing to the frequentative use (*bahulavacanāt*).

The phrase "this is a *yuvan*-dvandva" means that this is a *dvandva* compound consisting of two words ending in suffixes designated as *yus*. Regarding "phailaḥ," the suffix *aṇ* is applied by [Pāṇini 4.1.118].
The word *śyāyarna* belongs to the *bidādi* group; therefore, when the feminine suffix is not intended, the suffix *añ* occurs, resulting in *bhavāḥ*. Regarding the word *strī*:
[the suffix] *ṅīn* is applied after the *añ* of the *śāṅgaravādi* group according to Pāṇini 4.1.73.
Regarding the term "Śyāparṇeya," [it is argued that] "the plural number is non-essential" because it is not intended to be significant.

By the words "by that" (*tena*) and so forth, he demonstrates the result of not intending the plural number. "The word *kapi* is udātta on the final syllable" is due to the accent of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*).
"By that," and so forth. Why? Because this word *kapi* ends in a *luK* elision; therefore, the plural number is indeed resorted to here. [The suffix] *ṛṣyaṇ*.
By the rule *ṛṣyaṇḍaka-* [Pāṇini 4.1.114] and so forth;
by the rule *yūni ya iñ* [Pāṇini 4.1.94];
and by the rule *ata iñ* [Pāṇini 4.1.95].
Regarding "pāñcālī": [the suffix] *añ* is applied by [Pāṇini 4.1.168]. From that which ends in this suffix, *ṅīp* is applied as before.
*Pāñcāleyī* [the *Kāśikā* reads *pāñcāleyaḥ*] is formed by the same suffix as before. The same applies to *vārcaleyī*.
Regarding *śākalyaḥ*:
Because it belongs to the *gargādi* group, the suffix *yañ* is applied.
The word *śākalya*, by virtue of the accentuation rule for words ending in *ñit*, has its first syllable udātta.
[The example is] "the Śaṇakas and Bābhravas."

Regarding the word *śaṇaka*, it is derived from the verbal root *śaṇ* in the sense of "making sound" (*kai gai śabde*; Dhātupāṭha 916, 917). Consequently, by the accentuation rule for suffixes (*pratyayasvara*), the word *śaṇaka* has its udātta accent on the final syllable. As for the words *bābhravaḥ* and *ārcābhinaḥ*.

The suffix *ṇini* is applied in the sense of "proclaimed" (*prokta*); from that, the suffix *aṇ* is added for the sense of "one who studies" (*adhyetṛ*), which is then elided by [Pāṇini 4.2.64]. In the same way, in subsequent cases as well, the elision of the suffix denoting "one who studies" after a suffix denoting "proclaimed" should be understood. "Mudgala belongs to the *kaṇva*-group."
The group beginning with *garga* (*gargādi-gaṇa*).
Regarding the phrase "of his offspring" (*tadapatyasya*),
[the example is] "the Maudgalas" (*maudgalāḥ*).

From the word *maudgalya*, [the suffix] *aṇ* is applied by [Pāṇini 4.2.111], and the elision of the vowel *a* occurs by [Pāṇini 6.4.148]. The elision of the letter *y* occurs by [Pāṇini 6.4.151]: "And [the final vowel] of a patronymic [is elided] when a secondary suffix (*taddhita*) beginning with a vowel follows. The word *ārcābhi* is oxytone (accented on the final syllable) due to the accent of the suffix.

Regarding the passage beginning with *kunte surāṣṭrasya*: [the word *surāṣṭra*] is derived from the root *kam* in the sense of "desire" (*kāntau*, Dhātupāṭha 443). As before, the suffix *ktic* is applied; due to the rule of "diversity" (*bahulavacanāt*), the vowel *u* is substituted for the radical *a*.
Thus, *kunti* means "a beautiful kingdom," and one who possesses such a kingdom is *surāṣṭra*.

"Many descendants of Kunti" (kunterapatyāni bahūni); "many descendants of Surāṣṭra"—here the suffix *aṇ* is applied by [Pāṇini 4.1.166] because these are words denoting a region (*janapada*). In both cases, there is elision (*luk*) in the plural by [Pāṇini 2.4.62], etc., due to the rule for *tadrāja* suffixes. Then, from "the country inhabited by the Kuntis," the suffix *aṇ* is added as a *cāturarthika* (fourfold) derivative by [Pāṇini 4.2.69], and this is elided by [Pāṇini 4.2.80] according to the rule "there is elision (*lup*) when it denotes that country. Thus, *kuntayaś ca surāṣṭrāś ca* becomes *kuntisurāṣṭrāḥ*.

Thus, among the many descendants of Kunti and Surāṣṭra, there arises this pair of country-names (janapada-dvandva) based on their residence. The word *kunti* is oxytone (accented on the final syllable) by the rule regarding the suffix *ci*. Hence, [the compound] is *kunti-surāṣṭrāḥ*.
The word *cinti* is also oxytone;
it too is derived from the root *citī saṃjñāne* (Dhātupāṭha 1535) with the suffix *ktic*.
Some derive the words *Avanti* and *Kunti* by adding the suffix *ktic* according to [Pāṇini 3.3.174],
while others say they end in the suffix *an* from the *pacādi* group.
[The former view holds that] they are formed from the root *taḍ* (Dhātupāṭha 280) meaning "joy," with the suffix *ac* added either to the root alone or preceded by the prefix *ava*.

The vowel *a* of the word *ava* is elided according to the rule: "Bhāguri desires the elision [of the *a*] of the prefixes *ava* and *api*" (Pāṇini 6.3.98). Furthermore, the suffix *yañ* is dropped according to the rule: "The *luk*-elision of *yañ* is performed" (Pāṇini 2.4.64).

Regarding the term *avimattakāmaviddhā*: from the root *mad* meaning "to rejoice" (*dhātupāṭha* 1208), with the prefix *vi-* and the suffix *niṣṭhā*, we derive *vimattaḥ*. *Avimattaḥ* is that which is not *vimattaḥ*. When the original form of the first member is maintained by the rule *tatpuruṣe tulyārtha-* (Pāṇini 6.2.2) and so forth, the word becomes acute on the first syllable due to the accent of the negative particle *nañ*.
By this partial statement of the sūtra, "bahvacaḥ" (Pāṇini 2.4.65), he indicates the full sūtra: "bahvaca iñaḥ prācāṃ yabharateṣu" (Pāṇini 2.4.66).
[He also mentions] "śalaṅku śalaṅkañca" (Pāṇini 2.4.67).
This is recited among the *naḍa*-class [of suffixes].
Its meaning is this: the word *śalaṅku* produces the suffix *phak* and undergoes the substitution of *śalaṅka*.
[The resulting form is] *bābhravadānacyutāḥ*.

*Bābhravaḥ* is the descendant of *Brābhrū*; it ends in the suffix *aṇ*. From the word *dānacyuta*, the suffix *iñ* is elided because it has more than two syllables, as previously stated. [The example] is "the Kaṭhas and Kālapas."
The word *kaṭha* is oxytone because it is derived with the suffix *ac* (in the sense of the present participle).
*Laukākṣi* is the descendant of Lokākṣa; his students are the *laukākṣāḥ*. [The rule applies to] "women and children" (*strīkumāram*).

From the word *satyāyati* [formed] by the suffix *ḍraṭ* (Pāṇini 5.1.165), the feminine suffix *ṅīp* is applied according to Pāṇini 4.1.15 (*ṭiḍḍhāṇañ...*). There, by the rule "the final vowel of the base is elided" (Pāṇini 6.4.148), the vowel *ā*—which is udātta due to the accentuation of the *pratyaya* (suffix)—is elided. Then, by the rule "the *ṅīp* is udātta" (Pāṇini 6.1.161), the word *strī* becomes udātta on its first syllable. [The compound is: "those who are students of that [work] are the *mīdāḥ*. Here, the suffix *aṇ* is applied according to Pāṇini 4.2.111 (*iñaśca*).
"Likewise, the Paippalādās": Pippalāda is the descendant of Pippala; his students are the Paippalādās.
"Vatsajarad."

According to the rule *vṛtṛvadihanikamikaṣibhyaḥ saḥ* (Dhātupāṭha 9.21)—which states that the suffix *sa* is added after the roots *vṛt*, *vad*, *hi*, *ni*, *kam*, *kaṣ*, *yu*, and *muc*—the word *vatasa* is derived from *vad* with the suffix *sa*. By this rule, the word *vatasa* has its final syllable accented (*antodātta*). [Pāṇini 6.2.104]. Then, there is a *dvandva* compound of those two: *jaradvatasa*. [The example given is] *sauśrutapārthavāḥ*.
The students of Suśruta are the Sauśrutās;
"the students of Pṛthu are the Pārthavas"— in both cases, the suffix *aṇ* [is applied] by [Pāṇini 4.3.120].

Regarding "jarāmṛtyu": from the root *jṛṣ*, by [Pāṇini 3.3.104] the suffix *aṅ* is applied, yielding *jarā*; it has an udātta accent on the final syllable due to the accent of the suffix (*pratyayasvara*). From the root *mṛ*, by [Dhātupāṭha 1.135] the suffix *tyuk* is applied, yielding *mṛtyuḥ*. Regarding the statement "the word *mahat* has an udātta accent on the final syllable."
Because that [term], being oxytone according to the rule *vartamāne pṛṣadbṛhanmahat* (Pāṇini 6.2.5), is listed as an irregular formation (*nipātana*) among the Uṇādi suffixes;
why then does it not apply here in the case of *mahato vrīhiḥ = mahad-vrīhiḥ*? To this he replies with the words beginning "of that" (*tasya*).
And this is obtained by means of the technical rule (*paribhāṣā*) "that which is taught by its specific form" (*lakṣaṇapratipadokta*; *Vyāḍīya-paribhāṣā* 3).

Now, for what purpose is the word *pravṛddha* recited here, since it ends in a *niṣṭhā* suffix, and [the desired result] would already be established by the rule to be stated later, *tṛtīyāsamāse* (Pāṇini 6.2.46)? To this he says: "*karmadhāraye 'niṣṭhā*" and so forth.
For in that very way, by that technical rule, this compound is formed by that [word] taught by its specific form according to Pāṇini 2.1.59.
In this context, the rule *karṣāpavādaniṣṭhā* [Pāṇini 6.2.46] prescribes the absence of the *prakṛtibhāva* (original form retention).

Furthermore, the compound *mahāpravṛddhaḥ* is not a *karmadhāraya* formed with a word ending in *niṣṭhā* (a past passive participle) as explicitly taught by the rule itself; for if the word *pravṛddha* were not included here, the *prakṛtibhāva* would not apply when that word follows. Therefore, its inclusion here is made.

And this *yoga* is an exception (*apavāda*) to the general rule regarding the accent of compounds (*samāsasvara*). [The example is: "He who takes away hunger is *kṣullaḥ*. Here, the suffix *kap* is applied according to [Pāṇini 3.2.3]. Then, by [Pāṇini 8.4.59], *t* is replaced by its homogeneous substitute (*parasavarṇa*). [The word is derived] from the rule "The suffix *ṣṭran* after all roots" (Dhātupāṭha 4.158); since *ṣṭran* is being carried over, it is derived according to [Dhātupāṭha 4.161]: "After the roots *uṣi* and *khan*, [the suffix *ṣṭran* is added] as *kit*. By the supplementary phrase "the sitting of a cow" (*goḥ sādaḥ*), he shows that the word *gosāda* is a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*).

And regarding the statement, "one places the cow" (*gāṃ sādayati*), by this too there is the status of having an *upapada* compound. Since the root *sū* has the meaning of "falling apart," when the word *go* is used as an *upapada* in the sense of the object, the form *gosāda* arises. Because the word *go* ends in the suffix *ḍoḥ*—according to the rule *gameḍoḥ* (Pāṇini 4.1.11)—it is oxytone (*antodātta*) due to the accent of the suffix. Here, the compounds beginning with *kurugārhapata* and ending with *paṇyakambala* are all [treated as such].
In this context, *kurugārhapata* and *ariṣṭaguru* are without case endings (*avibhaktika*).

However, the others—such as *asūta*, *jaratī*, and so forth—end in the nominative singular. That nominative case should be understood as standing in place of the genitive by means of a substitution of case endings (*sub-adhyatyaya*).
The plural number in "dāsībhārāṇām" is for the purpose of indicating a class;
therefore he says, "and of dāsābhāra and so forth.
[He also states] that "the word kuru ends in the suffix ku."

From the rule *kubhraśca* (Pāṇini 6.4.107), the term *ku* is carried over as an adhikāra; since [the word *gārhapata*] is derived by being formed with the suffix *kupratyaya* according to the rule *kṛgrorucca* (Pāṇini 3.1.109), [it follows that the form is established]. Regarding the statement "it should be stated that *gārhapata* [is the exception] for *kuru* and *vṛji*":

the meaning is that this must be explained as having the sense that the word *gārhapata* undergoes its original form (*prakṛtibhāva*) when the words *kuru* and *vṛji* are the preceding members (*uttarapada*).
In this regard, the explanation is as follows: first, for the word *kuru*, it will occur precisely because of its inclusion in the sūtra itself, namely *kurugārhapata* (Pāṇini 6.2.42).
Because the letter *ca* in the word *vṛji* here has the sense of an unmentioned inclusion (*anuktasamuccaya*),
[it follows that] "the word *vṛji* is udātta on the first syllable. [This is derived from] *vṛj* with the suffix *in*.
Because it has been derived according to the rule *igupadhāt kicca* (Pāṇini 3.1.135),
[the term] *riktaguruḥ* indicates that the word *riktaguru* is a coordinate compound (*samānādhikaraṇasamāsa*).
Similarly, by the example "asūtā jaratī" (an old woman who has not given birth), the word *asūtā-jaratī* [is explained];
and by "aślīlā dṛḍharūpā" (one of indecent form), the word *aślīla-dṛḍharūpa* [is explained].
The word *asūtā*, meaning "not born," is also acute-accented on its first syllable due to the accent of the negative particle *nañ*.
The same applies to the word *aślīla*.
It is not *ślīla*; it is *aślīla*.
[The suffix] *lac* is applied because [the base] belongs to the *ākṛtigaṇa* class beginning with *sidhma*.

Because of the continued application (*anuvṛtti*) of the suffix *la* from [Pāṇini 5.2.96] up to [5.2.97]; and because of the substitution of *l* for *k* due to its inclusion in the *kapilaka*-group, as stated in [Pāṇini 8.2.18]:
"The addition of the *kapilaka*-group and others should be made" (Vārttika 915), which prescribes the substitution of *l* for *k*.

But how is it known that a thing which possesses *śrī* (splendor/fortune) is denoted by the word *ślīla*? To this he says: "having a form that is not *ślīla* and is firm," and so forth. The meaning of the word *aślīla* is established as "that which is not *ślīla*. In that context, if the word *ślīla* did not have the meaning "that which possesses *śrī*," then in the phrase "having a form that is not *ślīla* and is firm," one would not be described as "devoid of *śrī*" (*niḥśrīka*); yet such a description is indeed used. Therefore, it is known that a splendid object is denoted by the word *ślīla*.
"It is beautiful by its configuration alone" means that it is beautiful by its configuration alone because of the firmness of that configuration and because it is devoid of beauty (*śrī*).
The word *mātra* serves to exclude [any other] excellence (*śrīmattā*).

By the phrase "devoid of loveliness" (*lāvaṇyarahitā*), he clarifies the meaning of "bereft of splendor" (*niḥśrīkā*). "Pārevaḍavā" means "like the submarine fire on the far shore" (*pāre vaḍavā iva pārevaḍavā*).
But by what means is there a compound here? For indeed, there is no grammatical rule (*lakṣaṇa*) for a compound in the sense of *iva*.
Nevertheless, how could it be that a compound might occur?
Even so, why does the elision of the case-ending not take place according to [Pāṇini 2.4.71]? To this he says: "Precisely because of its being a *nipātana*," and so forth.

By the statement "the offspring of Titili," he demonstrates here the derivation of a secondary suffix (*taddhita*) from the word *titilin* in the sense of offspring. [The Kāśikā reads: "or a student [of Titili]" (*chāttra*); this refers to one who belongs to the lineage of Titila (*taitila*). This is understood as "the descendant of Titila."

By this [rule] as well, in the sense of "belonging to them," the form *taitilāḥ* is derived; the elision of the *ṭi* (the *tila*) occurs by means of an addition (*upasaṃkhyāna*) as in the previous case. This is because [the base] ends in *yat*.
The word *avadyapaṇya* is derived from the irregular formation (*nipātana*) of a stem ending in *yat*,
and it is *ādyudātta* (accented on the first syllable) by virtue of [Pāṇini 6.1.213].
It is said: "It should be stated that *paṇyakambalaḥ* [is used] in the sense of a technical name (*saṃjñā*)"—the printed reading being *saṃjñāyāṃ vaktavyam*.

The meaning is that this rule must be explained as follows: the word *paṇyakambalaḥ* retains the original accent (*prakṛtisvara*) of its first member when it is a technical name. Regarding this, the explanation is as follows: from rule 6.2.28, the term *anyatarasyām* ("optionally") is carried over by the principle of the frog-leap (*maṇḍūkapluti*); furthermore, this is a restricted option (*vyavasthitavibhāṣā*).
Thus, the word *paṇyakambalaḥ* retains the original accent of its first member only when it is a technical name, and not otherwise.

"Except in other cases, there is only the acute accent on the final syllable of the compound. Now, one might object: "Since this word *paṇya* ends in a *kṛtya* suffix, according to the rule *tatpuruṣe* [Pāṇini 6.2.2] and so forth, when it is something to be bartered (*paṇitavya*), the original accent (*prakṛtisvara*) of the first member should indeed apply; so how can there be an acute accent on the final syllable of the compound? To this he says: "For in the case of what is explicitly stated," and so forth. That *kṛtya*-compound which is explicitly taught by the rule *dvitīyā-kṛtyāḥ* [Pāṇini 6.2.2], in that case the preservation of the original form (*prakṛtibhāva*) of the first member is prescribed.

Moreover, this is not a compound formed by a specific rule; rather, it is prescribed by the general rule "the qualifier [is compounded] with the qualified" (Pāṇini 2.1.57). Why is this so? Because the word *kambala* is a generic term (*jātiśabda*).
By this partial statement of the sūtra, "dvitīyākṛtyā," [the author] indicates the sūtra beginning with "tatpuruṣe tulyārtha.
The example is "dāsībhāraḥ" (the burden of a female slave);
the word *dāsī* has the accent previously mentioned.
The word *devahūtiḥ* is oxytone because it ends in the suffix *ac* (by Pāṇini 3.1.134). The word *oṣa-* is [oxytone] because it ends in the suffix *ghañ*.

Because this word is derived from the root *uṣ* in the sense of "burning" (*dāhe*, Dhp 6.96) with the suffix *ghañ*, and because it ends in the suffix *asi* according to the rule *candre māṅo ḍit* (Dhātupāṭha 9.88), which prescribes the suffix *asi* after the root *māṅ* when *candra* follows. (Note:
The reading in the printed Kāśikā is *candre mo'siḥ*.)
Because the suffix *asi* continues from the rule "In *mithuna*, as before, everything [is the same]" (*Daiva-ukta-sūtra* 9.82),
whereas the word *candra* ends in the suffix *rak*,
since it is derived by the rule beginning with "the roots *sphāyi*, *tañci*, etc. (*Daiva-ukta-sūtra* 8.31) as ending in the suffix *rak*.

"All of that is to be seen in the case of 'a load for a female slave' (*dāsībhāra*) and so forth," because [the phrase] "a load for a female slave" and the like constitute an *ākṛtigaṇa* (an open class). Regarding the term "for its sake" (*tadarthe*):
"this is for that" (*tasmai idam*); the word ending in the fourth case (*caturthyanta*), whose meaning is "that," is "for its sake" (*tadartha*). This is the meaning.
But how is the word *yūpa* (sacrificial post) acutely accented on the first syllable? To this he says: “*Kusuyubhyāṃ ca*,” and so forth.

While the term *paḥ* is being carried over from the rule “*pānīviṣibhyaḥ paḥ*” (Dhātupāṭha 7.2), the word *yūpa* is derived as ending in the suffix *pa* by the rule “*kusuyubhyāṃ ca*” (Dhātupāṭha 7.5)—[the printed reading is *kuyubhyāṃ ca*].
In that context, the term *nit* is carried over from the rule “*suśṛbhyāṃ nicca*” (Pañcapādī Uṇādi 3.26); therefore, it becomes acutely accented on the first syllable.

The lengthening [of the vowel] occurs because the mention of "long" (*dīrgha*) is carried over from the rule *stuo dīrghaśca* (Pāṇini 3.2.5). Regarding the phrase "ending in the suffix *kala*," the suffix *kala* is carried over from the rule *kalastṛpaśaca* (Uṇādi 8.107) within the context of *vṛṣādibhyaścit* (Uṇādi 8.109).
"The word *ratha* has its first syllable accented" (*rathaśabda ādyudāttaḥ*).

This is because the suffix *kthan* from the rule "after the roots *han*, *kuṣ*, *nī*, *ram*, and *kāś*, [the suffix] *kthan*" (*hanikuṣinīramikāśibhyaḥ kthan*, Pāṇini 3.2.149) is understood to apply here as well. Thus: "The word *ratha* has its first syllable accented."
This is because the suffix *kal* is understood from the rule *hanikuṣinīramikāśibhyaḥ kthan* (Daiva 8.107). Furthermore,
the word *ratha* has its initial syllable accented acute (*ādyudātta*),
because it ends in the suffix *kthan* according to the rule *hanikuṣinīramikāśibhyaḥ kthan* (Daiva 6.27).
"The word *vallī* is oxytone due to the accent of the suffix *ṅīṣ*";
however, it should be understood that the suffix *ṅīṣ* [is applied here] because [the word] belongs to the *gaura*-class [of feminine stems]. (Pāṇini 4.1.41)
Regarding the phrase "in the case of the relationship between the original material and its modification" (*prakṛtivikārabhāve*), etc.:

how, then, is this understood to apply to the relationship between the original material and its modification when it is stated in general terms? Because the option (*anyatarasyām*) from the preceding rule continues to apply here; and because that option is a fixed alternative (*vyavasthitavibhāṣā*), as indicated by the forthcoming evidence: "the words *mātṛ* and *pitṛ* are oxytone."
In forms such as *naptṛ* and *neṣṭṛ* (Pāṇini 6.1.190), because those two [words] ending in the suffix *tṛc* are irregularly formed (*nipātita*),

they are mid-tone (*madhyodātta*) by virtue of the accent of the *liṭ* suffix. Furthermore, in the case of [the word *devatā*], because it ends in the suffix *tal* according to Pāṇini 5.4.27 (*devāt tal*), [it is mid-tone].

But for what purpose is this [rule], since it would already be established by [Pāṇini 2.1.36]: *caturthī tadarthe*? For even the word *artha* becomes a subsequent member (*uttarapada*) meaning "for that purpose. To this he says: "*Only specific instances of 'for that purpose'," and so forth.
He thinks as follows: even the word *artha*, in a compound (*vṛtti*), expresses a specific [instance]. And this is logical.

Then, when it is said "for the sake of the mother" (*mātrartham*), a specific object whose form is distinguished from [the general category of] "mother" and so forth is understood as the meaning of "mother.
With the words "ādhāsaḥ" and so forth, he demonstrates the purpose of the indicator (*jñāpaka*). [The rule states: "The word *ā* is udātta-accented on its first syllable.
This is because it ends in the suffix *kvan*.

"The word *manuṣya* has a svarita accent on the final syllable," because it ends in the suffix *yat* according to [Pāṇini 4.1.161], "After *manu*, the suffixes *añ* and *yat* are applied, and there is also the augment *ṣuk*. "The remainder is udātta."
Furthermore, there are the words *go* and *tāpasa*.

Among them, because the word *go* ends in the suffix *ḍos* according to the rule *gameḍos* (Pāṇini 4.1.41), it is udātta on the final syllable by the accent of the suffix (*pratyayasvara*). The word *tāpasa*, on the other hand, ends in the suffix *aṇ*.
For that [word *tapasvin*] is derived by means of the suffix *aṇ*, according to the rules "from *tapas* and *saha* with the suffix *vin*" [Pāṇini 5.2.102] and "*aṇ* also" [Pāṇini 5.2.102].

Now, how can *gorakṣitam* be an example of this, given that in the expression "protected for the sake of cows" (*gobhyo rakṣitam*), the dative case is used in the sense of purpose (*tādarthye*), and in such a case there ought to be a subsequent member [of a compound] by virtue of the grammatical rule? To this he says: "Protected for the sake of cows," and so forth.
For here the intended meaning is not "protected for the sake of cows"; what then? One must supply the words "it is given, protected for the sake of cows."

Therefore, this fourth case ending (*caturthī*) is used in the sense of the recipient (*sampradāna*); how then could there be the sense of "for the sake of that" (*tādarthya*)? [The compound] "arranged in rows" (*śreṇikṛtāḥ*), and so forth, is a compound according to [Pāṇini 2.1.59].
[It is stated: "the word *śreṇi* has its first syllable accented acute (*ādyudātta*)."

It has an initial accent (*ādyudātta*). For, while the term *ni* is still in force from the rule *vījyājvaribhyo niḥ* (DhP 1.18), it is derived by the rule *vahiśriśruyudruglāhātvaribhyo nit* (DhP 1.21); therefore, it is ādyudātta.
[The word] *pūga* "multitude" is antodātta.

Is it because of the word "bahula" (in the rule *mudigro rgagau*, Pāṇini 3.2.166)? Since there is also the suffix *gak* after the root *pū*, it is consequently udātta on the final syllable by the accent of the suffix (*pratyayasvara*).
Thus, [the compound] *kṛtākṛtam*.

The compound is formed according to [Pāṇini 2.1.60]: *kṛtañca tad akṛtañca* ("that which is both done and not done"). It is "done" because one part has been performed; it is "not done" because at that very time another part remains unperformed. *Hīna* means abandoned; *ahīna* is that which is not abandoned. Regarding the statement, "the word *kaṣṭa* is oxytone."

Because it ends in the *ktapratyaya* suffix, [the word is accented] by the accent of the suffix (*pratyayasvara*). There is a prohibition of the augment *iṭ* by the rule "there is no *iṭ* after the root *kaṣ* when used in the sense of 'difficulty' or 'thicket'" (Pāṇini 7.2.22).
[The resulting form] is acutely accented on the first syllable by the accent of the *bahuvrīhi* compound.
For the word *tri* is oxytone by the accent of the nominal stem (*prātipadika-svara*).

In that case, when the original accent (*prakṛti-svara*) is applied according to [Pāṇini 6.2.1] "in a *bahuvrīhi*, the original accent [of the first member prevails]," the word *triśakala* becomes ādyudātta (accented on the first syllable) by the accent rule for *bahuvrīhi* compounds.
The word *grāma* is likewise ādyudātta.

Thus, while the suffix *man* is being carried over from the rule "a-ri-stu-su-hu-sṛ-dhukṣi" (Dhātupāṭha 7.26), the word is derived with the suffix *man* by the rules "avateṣṭilopaśca" (Dhātupāṭha 7.27) and "grasaterā ca" (Dhātupāṭha 7.28).
Regarding the phrase "kāntārātītaḥ": it means one who has passed beyond the wilderness (*kāntāra*), that is, one who has abandoned it.

The word *kāntārātīta* here is an example of a term expressing deficiency (*hīna*). Regarding the statement, "It should be stated that [the rule applies] when there is no prefix (*anupasarga*) and [the following word] ends in the second case," the meaning is that this should be explained as having the sense that a word ending in the second case, when followed by a *kta*-suffix without a prefix, retains its original accent (*prakṛtisvara*).

The explanation here also must be made by relying on the recurrence (*anuvṛtti*) of that very same [rule] containing the mention of "either one" (*anyatarasyām*) and its status as an optionally restricted rule (*vyavasthita-vibhāṣā*). Since the form would already be established by the rule *tatpuruṣe tulyārtha* (P. 6.2.2), and since the original accent of the first member (*pūrvapada-prakṛtisvara*) would be superseded by the general accent rule for *kṛt*-suffixes and the accent rule for *tha*, *tha-tha*, etc. (P. 6.2.143), this statement is intended to establish that [specific accent]. In the example *ahihatāḥ*, the compound is formed according to P. 2.1.32.
Regarding the statement, "The word *ahīn* is derived with an udātta accent on the first syllable":

the word *ahīn* is derived from the root *han* preceded by the prefix *āṅ*, following the rule *janighasibhyām iṇ* (Dhātupāṭha 1.58), while the rule *vāter ḍicca* is in effect; furthermore, by the rule *āṅi śrihanibhyāṃ hrasvaśca* (Dhātupāṭha 1.66), it is derived as ending in the suffix *iṇ* which is marked with the *ḍit* indicatory letter.
Regarding this, some maintain that it has the udātta accent on the first syllable.

They also carry forward the mention of the acute accent (*udātta*) from the rule *te 'samāne khyaḥ sa codāttaḥ* (Pāṇini 5.2.136). [The term *rakpratyayāntaḥ*] means "ending in the suffix *rak*," because it is derived as such by the rule *sphāyitañci-* (Dhātupāṭha 8.31) and others.
"Mahārāja ends with the suffix *ṭac*," because it is derived as ending in the suffix *rak* by the rule "sphāyitañci" (Pāṇini 6.1.27) and others. Thus,
"mahārāja ends with the suffix *ṭac*."
Because [the word *dātram*] ends in the suffix *ṭac* by the rule *rājāhaḥsakhibhyaṣṭac* [Pāṇini 5.4.91]. Regarding the form *dātralūnā*:

while the rule [3.2.181] is still in force, the word *dātra-* is derived as ending in the suffix *ṣṭran* by the rule *dāmnīśas* [3.2.182] and so forth; therefore, it is acutely accented on its first syllable (*ādyudātta*).
In all cases, the suffix *kta* is used in the sense of the object (*karman*) according to the rule *tayoreva kṛtyaktakhalarthāḥ* [Pāṇini 3.4.70]. Regarding the word *prakṛtaḥ*:
it is a compound formed by the rule *kugatiprādayaḥ* [Pāṇini 2.2.18].
Since the words beginning with *pra*—with the exception of *abhi*—are listed in the *ādyudātta* (initially accented) group as *nipātana*s, the word *pra* is therefore *ādyudātta*.

Regarding the term *abhyuddhṛtaḥ*: here, the [rule] does not apply to the immediately preceding word *abhi*. In this case, one should first form a compound of the word *ut* with the word ending in the *kta* suffix, and subsequently form a compound of the word *abhi* with the word *uddhṛta*.
Alternatively, because the mention of *sub* (the nominal suffix) has been withdrawn in rule 2.2.18, a compound may also occur even when there are multiple words involved.

Regarding the term "samudāhṛtaḥ," here too the [substitution] does not occur between *sam* and *ud*. This is because of the rule beginning with "of that which is preceded by a kāraka, when followed by *ti*," and so forth.

In the case of *dūrādāgataḥ*, when the *gati*-compound with the prefix *āṅ* has been formed, by this [rule] the original accent (*prakṛtisvara*) applies, whereby it becomes acute (*udātta*). Subsequently, the compound with the fifth case (*pañcamīsamāsa*) is formed according to [Pāṇini 2.1.39], *dūrādāgataḥ*, etc. When that is formed, while [the rule] *taddhitārthottarapada...* [6.2.139] is in effect, the rule *thāthaghañ...* [6.2.143], etc., prescribes that the final syllable of the second member (*uttarapada*) is acute. Since that [final acute] is prescribed in the presence of the *gati*-accent, it remains as such due to its being the subsequent rule (*śiṣṭatvena*).
> [[6.3.2]] Thus ends the section on *aluk*.

Now, how is the counter-example (*pratyudāharaṇa*) such as *samudghṛtaḥ* justified? For, according to the rule "when a *kṛt*-suffix is mentioned, that which is preceded by a *gati* [particle] is also included" (Vyāḍipāda 126), the *gati* here is indeed grasped by the mention of the *niṣṭhā* suffix; and thus, in the immediately preceding case of *samuddhṛta*, there is the word *sam*, and in *samudāhṛta* as well, there are the words *sam* and *ut*. To this he replies: "By virtue of the force of the mention of 'immediate' (*anantara*). By the mention of "immediate," this purpose is achieved: so that [the rule] does not apply in cases such as *samuddhṛtam*.

If this technical term (*paribhāṣā*) were to be adopted here, then in examples such as *uddhṛtaḥ*, since the rule "only the immediately preceding [verb] is [an upasarga]" would apply, the inclusion of the word *anantara* (immediately preceding) would be purposeless due to the absence of anything to be excluded. In the example *prakṛtaḥ kaṭaṃ devadattaḥ*, the suffix *kta* occurs in the sense of the agent according to [Pāṇini 3.4.71]. In the form *prakartum*, the suffix is *tumun*.
"‘Prakartā’ ends in the suffix *tṛn*. This refutes the suspicion that it might end in *tṛc*. [He states] "In order to override the accent of the *kṛt*-suffix," and so forth.

The rule *avyayasvarāpavādaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.2.139) would apply, resulting in the accent of the entire word (*kṛtsvara*); therefore, this statement is made to set that aside. In the case of *prajalpākaḥ*, the suffix *ṣākan* is applied by the rule *jalpabhikṣa* (Pāṇini 3.2.155).

Regarding the term *tṛjantaḥ*: this refutes the suspicion that [the word *mṛttikā*] might end in the suffix *tṛn*. Now, what is the purpose of including the mention of *ni*? If it is argued that it is so that [the rule] does not apply to cases such as *prakṛṣṭamṛṣṭamṛttikā* ("excellent clay"), that is not the case. For indeed, prefixes (*pra*, etc. receive the designations "motion" (*gati*) and "preverb" (*upasarga*) only with respect to that action (*kriyā*) with which they are connected (Pāṇini 1.4.59). Since this word *mṛttikā* is a proper name (*nāmadheya*), it does not denote an action; therefore, it cannot possibly have the designation "preverb" with respect to it. To address this, he says: "*kṛdgrahaṇam*" and so forth.

By the term *kṛti*, the time of the connection with the technical name (*saṃjñā*) is indicated. Consequently, the meaning "that which begins with *t* at the moment of receiving the *kṛt* designation" is established; thus, the mention of *kṛt* serves the purpose of referring to that which begins with *t* in the original instruction (*upadeśa*), because the time of the comprehension of the *kṛt* designation is identical to the time of the instruction. Therefore, he says "here," etc., to show that an effort is made for the sake of that which begins with *t* specifically in the instruction. If that mention of "instruction" were not made for the purpose of referring to that which begins with *t*, then [the form] *pralapitā* would not be possible there, because the status of beginning with *t* would be obstructed by the augment *iṭ*.

And because the designation "beginning with that" (*tādi*) applies precisely when [the suffix] is present—even if that status as "beginning with that" is subsequently sublated—it nonetheless remains valid.
Regarding the term *āgantuḥ*: the suffix *tan* is applied by the rule *sitanigamimasi-* (Dhātupāṭha 1.122). [The phrase] "the final syllable becomes udātta" means...

But how is it that the acute (*udātta*) accent is obtained here, since there is no mention of "acute" in this rule? For no entirely new accent is being prescribed here; what then? It is simply that which would have been obtained by the *prakṛtibhāva* (non-application of sandhi) according to [Pāṇini 6.2.139]. How does the word *prakṛtyā* (by its original form) carry over from that context? There, the connection is made as follows: "That which would have been obtained for the final syllable of a word ending in the suffix *tva*, that occurs for the final syllable.
And since that [original accent] is indeed acute, the acute is obtained by virtue of that corroboration (*sāmārthyāt*).
The inclusion of the word *yugapat* (simultaneously) is for the purpose of excluding successive application (*paryāya*).

Regarding *anvetavā* (the *Kāśikā* reads *ānvetavai*): from the root *i* preceded by the prefix *anu*, the suffix *tave* is applied according to Pāṇini 3.4.14 (*kṛtyārthe tavaikenkenyatvanaḥ*), and the *guṇa* substitution occurs. Regarding *paripātavā* (the *Kāśikā* reads *paripātavai*).
From *pari* preceding *vāti*, as in "he has blown around" (*parivāta*).
From *abhi* preceding *carati*, as in "he has practiced sorcery" (*abhicaritavai*).
"Acute on the final syllable" means by the accentuation of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*). "In the suffix *va*" means that which has the suffix *va* is so described.

Regarding the word *prāṅ* and so forth: the suffix *kvip* is applied by the rule *ṛtvig...* [Pāṇini 3.2.59] and others; and that suffix consists of the letter *v* alone, because the letters beginning with *k* are *anubandhas* (indicatory markers), and because they are not invariably present. By the rule *ugidacām* [7.1.70], the augment *num* is added; in the singular, the elision of the final consonant (*halṅyādi*) [6.1.68] and the elision of the final member of a conjunct (*saṃyogāntalopa*) [8.2.23] apply; and by the rule *kvinpratyayasya kuḥ* [8.2.62], the substitution of *ku* for the *n* results in the letter *ṅ*.

In the case of the dual and plural endings, the substitution of *ñ* for *ś* occurs by [Pāṇini 8.4.40], resulting in the letter *ñ*. This is then combined with the vowel *ā* of the prefix by [Pāṇini 6.1.101], yielding forms such as *parāṅ*, and so forth.
The word *parā* has its initial syllable accented (ādyudātta).

Therefore, the rule "optionally a svarita [occurs] when an unaccented [word] begins a pada" (Pāṇini 8.2.6)—as this is the reading found in the printed editions of the Nyāsa, Kāśikā, and Padamañjarī—does not apply.
Thus, we have *pratyaṅ*.

In this case, because the word *prati* ends in an *i*-vowel (*iganta*), the *parakṛti* substitution does not occur. But surely, once the *yaṇ* replacement has been applied, that [substitute] is no longer an *iganta*? This objection is flawed, because by virtue of the rule of *sthānivadbhāva*, the designation "ending in an *i*-vowel" will still apply even after the *yaṇ* replacement has taken effect. If it is argued that the rule of *sthānivadbhāva* is prohibited in the application of accent rules (*svaravidhi*), this is not so; for it has been stated: "In the case of accent, lengthening, and *yalopa*, the substitute for a deleted element (*lopājādeśa*) is not *sthānivat*, but any other substitute is indeed *sthānivat*" (Kāśikāvṛtti 1.1.59).
Regarding the word *udañcanaḥ*: it is formed with the suffix *lyuṭ*.
Here too, the original accent (*prakṛtisvara*) of the final member of the compound remains.
Regarding the rule *coraniganto’ñcatau* and so forth:

by the word *cau*, this indicates that the final acute accent (*antodāttatva*) which is prescribed by the rule *cau* [Pāṇini 6.1.216] is what is being characterized here. The scope of *cau* is, for example, *dadhīcaḥ*, where there is no movement (*gati*); the scope of *anigantasvara* (the accent for non-final roots) is where the letters *a* and *n* of the root *añc* are not elided, such as *parāṅ* and *parāñcāt*. In the case of *parācaḥ* and *parāca*, both rules would apply; therefore, by the principle of conflict (*vipratiṣedha*), the accent for non-final roots (*anigantasvara*) prevails.

In that context, the word "prohibition" (*pratiṣedha*) is to be supplied. This rule begins for the purpose of [excluding] vowels ending in *i* or *u* (*iganta*). [The examples are] "of the acute and circumflex" (*udāttasvaritayoḥ*), and so forth.

[The word *nirudātta*] is acutely accented according to the rule "prepositions [are acutely accented], except for *abhi*" (Phiṭ-sūtra 4.81). Therefore, the *yaṇ*-substitute that occurs in place of the vowel *a* of that [word] is an *udāttayaṇ*.

Therefore, by the rule *udāttasvaritayoḥ* [Pāṇini 8.2.4] and so forth, the vowel *a* following that *caṭi* becomes svarita. However, this does not occur in cases such as *adhyaṅ*, because the substitute (*ādeśa*) is udātta; for it is considered that the *yaṇ*-substitute is not an udātta-*yaṇ*.
This rule is an exception (*apavāda*) to the accentuation of compounds.
In the example "īṣatkaḍāraḥ," there is a compound according to [Pāṇini 2.2.7].
When this natural state (*prakṛtibhāva*) does not occur, then the udātta accent on the final syllable of the compound indeed takes effect;
as in "īṣadbheda" and similar cases, only the *kṛt-svara* (the accent of the *kṛt*-suffix) occurs.
The intention is that [the latter rule] prevails due to its higher status (*paratvāt*).

By the word "ādi" (and so forth), terms such as *īṣatkara* ("easy to do") and others are included. [The suffix] *khal* is applied by the rule *īṣadduḥsuṣu* (Pāṇini 3.3.126). "A measure of gold" means gold that possesses a measure;
however, in this context, the word-form denoting that [measure] is what is intended.
Regarding the term "dvisuvarṇadhana":

the word *suvarṇa* denotes a specific measure of gold. The compound *dvisuvarṇa* is formed according to [Pāṇini 2.1.50] *taddhitārtha*, meaning "that whose measure is two *suvarṇas*. Thus, it is a *tatpuruṣa* compound.
Regarding the rule *adhyardhapūrva* (Pāṇini 5.1.28) and so forth, there is elision (*luk*) [of the suffix], followed by a *karmadhāraya* compound with the word *dhana*.
Thus, the word *dvisuvarṇa* is oxytone by virtue of the accent of the compound.
As for the phrase "even in a *bahuvrīhi*," and so on:

Alternatively, *dvisuvarṇadhana* is a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "one whose wealth consists of two suvarṇas. Even that [compound] is merely optional due to its being subsequent [in the order of rules]; it is not a mandatory rule such as *bahuvrīhau prakṛtyā* [Pāṇini 6.2.1]. As for *prasthadhana*, this too is a *karmadhāraya*.
Or it may be a *bahuvrīhi* compound.
The word *prastha* denotes a measure, but not of gold; rather, it refers to grain and the like.
[Thus, the term is] "one whose wealth consists of gold."

If the mention of "measure" (*parimāṇa*) were not made, then the term *hiraṇya* being used here alone would also [trigger the rule]; for the word *kāñcana* denotes gold (*hiraṇya*). However, since that which denotes gold does not necessarily denote measure, this undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) does not arise. This rule is also an exception (*apavāda*) to the accentuation of compounds. [The sūtra states: "A recent contact (*aciro-paśleṣaḥ*)."
The meaning is "connected with a recent time.
To demonstrate this very meaning by means of a more well-known term, he says: "novelty" and "the first grammarian."

The compound "prathamavaiyākaraṇa" (the first grammarian) is formed by the rule *pūrvāpara* [Pāṇini 2.1.57] and so forth. In this context, that which constitutes "grammarian-ness" (*vaiyākaraṇatva*) is the state of being a student of grammar (*vyākaraṇa*).
By this, the student's connection with grammar for only a short period of time is understood.

By the phrase "an *abhinava-vaiyākaraṇa*," etc., he demonstrates in the example the state of having attained [the status] only recently. By the words "the first, which is primary," he shows that in this counter-example, the word *prathama* has a different meaning and, in that alternative case, there is an absence of recent attainment.
This rule is also an exception to the accentuation of a compound;

the same applies to the subsequent rules as well. The words *katara* and *katama* are derived by the rules "When selecting one out of two, *ḍatarac* [is added] after *kim*, *yat*, and *tad*" (Pāṇini 5.3.92) and "When asking about a genus among many, *ḍatamac* [is added]" (Pāṇini 5.3.93). Therefore, by the accent of the *cit* suffix, they are udātta on the final syllable. For example: *katarakaṭhaḥ*.
This is a *samānādhikaraṇa* compound according to [Pāṇini 2.1.63].
Why, then, is the mention of *karmadhāraya* not also intended for this purpose? To this he says: "But here," and so forth.

For, by the paribhāṣā regarding that which is taught by a specific rule (*lakṣaṇapratipadokta-paribhāṣā*) (Vyāḍi-paribhāṣā 3), only that *pratipada-samāsa* (compound formed by a specific rule) involving the words *katara* and *katama* is understood [to apply here].
And that [compound] is indeed a *karmadhāraya*.
Why? Because this compound is designated as such by its very specific formulation (*pratipadokta*);
therefore, the mention of the term *karmadhāraya* is not necessary for this purpose. For example: "an *āryabrāhmaṇa*" (a noble Brahmin).
The term "āryabrāhmaṇa" is a descriptive determinative compound (viśeṣaṇasamāsa) meaning "one who is both noble and a Brāhmaṇa.
It is stated that "the word *ārya* ends in the suffix *ṇyat*," because it is derived by applying the suffix *ṇyat* according to Pāṇini 3.1.124 (*ṛhalor ṇyat*).
Regarding the term *antasvaritaḥ*: by the accent rule for *tit* suffixes, [the final syllable would be circumflex];
