however, in the counter-example, there is simply the udātta accent on the final syllable of the compound, as in *rājabrāhmaṇam* (or *rājabrāhmaṇaḥ*, according to the Kāśikā).
As before? It is a compound.
In the counter-example as well, it is as before:
the word *rājan* is acutely accented on the first syllable because it ends in the suffix *kvan*.

"The formulation of a separate rule is for the sake of what follows," meaning that the subsequent rule should apply to the word *rājan* alone, so that it does not apply to the word *ārya*. [The example is: "the enemy of the king" (*rājñaḥ pratyenāḥ*).
> [[6.3.21]] Thus, there is no elision (*aluk*) of the case-ending. The word *nitya* refers to frequency (*ābhīkṣṇya*), not to immutability (*kūṭastha*).

Why is this so? Because it is stated [in Pāṇini's rule] that the suffix *kta* is used; and *kta* is prescribed after a verbal root (*dhātu*), and a verbal root denotes action (*kriyā*). Now, immutability is not possible for an action, because action is momentary (*kṣaṇika*).

However, with respect to its repetition (*paunaḥpunya*), the frequentative suffix (*ābhīkṣṇya*) is appropriate. As for the statement, "This is a compound with the second case ending according to [Pāṇini 2.1.27] *kālāḥ*," it is because of [the rule] *dvitīyā tu* [2.3.5].
Alternatively, [the word *nityam*] refers to the object (*karman*) itself;

for its designation as an object follows from the rule: "Time, state, and the distance to be traversed are designated as objects when [the verbs] are otherwise intransitive" (*kālabhāvādhvagantavyāḥ karmasaṃjñā hy akarmaṇām*, Mahābhāṣya 1.4.51).
[The commentary begins with: "The word *nitya*," and so forth.

By this [rule], *dhruva upasaṃkhyānam* (Vārttika 4.3.4), the word *nitya*, ending in the suffix *tyap*, is derived. Consequently, because the suffix *tyap* is unaccented due to its being marked with *p*, and because the root *ni-* is accented, the word becomes udātta on its first syllable.

As for the statement, "When *satata* is formed with the suffix *kta* in the sense of the object (*karman*), it is udātta on the final syllable by the rule *thāthādi-svara*," this reading is incorrect.

For when the suffix *kta* is applied in the sense of an object (*karman*), then by the rule *gati-kāraka-pūrvasyaiva ktasya kṛt-svaropasaṃkhyānam* (P. 6.2.49), there would have to be a *prakṛtibhāva* of the prefix *pra*, resulting in the word *satata* being udātta on its first syllable. Therefore, one should understand that the faultless reading in this context is: "When *satatam* is used in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāva*), then, by the accentuation rule for *thā-thādi* suffixes (P. 6.2.143), it is udātta on its final syllable.
For indeed, even the word *satata* is udātta on its final syllable by the *thā-thādi* accentuation rule (P. 6.2.143).
It has been stated that when this [suffix] is used in the sense of a state (*bhāva*), it does not take the accent of a *gati* particle.
However, when it is used in the sense of an action (*kramaṇi*), then by the accent of the *gati*, the word *satata* becomes exclusively udātta.
In the form *samahita*, the letter *m* of *sama* is elided according to the rule "samo vā hitatatayoḥ" (Vārttika 6.1.149).
Regarding the term *muhūrtaprahasitaḥ*:

here, the accentuation of the *thā-thādi* group (Pāṇini 6.2.144) applies to the word *prahasita*. Is *hasita* derived from the root *has* with the suffix *kta* in the sense of an intransitive action (*akarmaka*), or is it derived in the sense of the agent (*kartari*)?

Since the accent of the compound would otherwise be governed by the rule for the original accent of the second member (the *dvitīyā-pūrvapada-prakṛti-svara*), which would override [the *thā-thādi* rule], the *thā-thādi* accentuation is what actually prevails.

Therefore, the application [of the rule] occurs when that [word] follows immediately. The mention of "that which is designated by the seventh case" (saptamī-nirdiṣṭa) is carried over [from the previous rule].
By that, there is the inclusion of the meaning "artisan" (śilpin);
however, "village" (grāma) is taken as the actual form itself (svarūpa).

"Grāmanāpitaḥ": this is a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*), a rule that serves as an exception to the accent of the compound [prescribed by Pāṇini 6.1.223]. The same applies to the subsequent examples. "In a karmadhāraya," and so forth.
Regarding the term *rājanāpitaḥ*:

is this a *karmadhāraya* compound or a *ṣaṣṭhī-tatpuruṣa* compound? In that regard, when it is a *karmadhāraya*, the word *rājan* functions through metaphorical application (*upacāra*) toward the barber.
This metaphorical application is based on the attribution of royal qualities; therefore, by means of that very [application], the excellence of the subsequent member [of the compound] is established.
But how, then, is the barber referred to by the term *rājanāpita* through a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*)? To this he says: "Because of his suitability for the king," and so forth.
For he, due to his proficiency in his own craft, is suitable for the king;
therefore, he is called *rājanāpita* by means of a genitive compound.

In this view, the praise of the subsequent word should be understood as being due to its very fitness [to receive the accent]. By the words "the beginning" (*ādiḥ*) and so forth, he shows the limit of the governing rule concerning the beginning; and by the words "acute" (*udāttaḥ*) and so forth, he shows the limit of the governing rule concerning the acute accent. In the word *hārī*, the suffix *ṇini* is used in the sense of necessity (*avaśyaka*).
Because of its association with the word "seventh case" (*saptamī*), there is no apprehension of the actual form *ādhārī*.
For this very reason he says: "The word *parvan* denotes that which is charming.

In the case of the term *dharmye* as well, there is no apprehension of the word's own form (*svarūpa-grahaṇa*), because of the prohibition [stated] as *aharaṇe*. For this very reason he says: "denoting that which is righteous" (*dharmya-vācini*).
"Fixed by conduct" (*ācāraniyata*) means fixed in conduct; it is so called because it does not exist elsewhere.
It is fixed in conduct, or fixed by conduct; thus it is "fixed by conduct."

When that which must necessarily be performed due to the force of custom becomes fixed by custom, how then is such a duty fixed by custom called *dharma*? To this he says: "For *dharma* is that which is followed," and so forth.
"Followed" (*anuvṛtta*) means established (*vyavasthita*).
Regarding the word "therefore":
"not departed from dharma" means "conforming to it."
"By that" means by the Dharma. "Attained" means...
The meaning is "it is obtainable. In both senses, the suffix *yat* is applied according to Pāṇini 4.4.91 (*nau-vayo-dharmā-...*).
The particle *iti* and the word *hi* are used in the sense of a reason.

Since a specific mode of conduct is called *dharma*, that which does not deviate from that *dharma* is *dharmya*; or rather, that which is to be attained by means of it is *dharmya*. Therefore, that which is regulated by conduct is called *dharmya*.
"Thus ends the section on the seventh case (locative) compounds.

If this is so, does it not follow that there should be elision (*luk*) of the case-ending? To this he says: "And in the name of a cause," and so forth. However, in examples such as *yājñikāḥ*, it is a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*).

By the words "in some cases" (*kvacit*) and so forth, [the author] demonstrates that in examples such as *stūpeśāṇa*, there is a fixed rule of usage for terms like *śāṇa*. He shows that the final member of the compound expresses what is right or proper (*dhamrya*) by stating "of the sacrificers (*yājñika*) and so forth.
The phrase "he is established in this usage in some cases" is to be connected with the phrase "it must be given.
For the sacrificers and others are takers; they accept the deer, the things to be given, and so forth.
Regarding the term *stamberama*:

by the rule *stambakarṇayo ramijapoḥ* [Pāṇini 3.2.13], the suffix *ac* is applied; this is an *upapada* compound, and by the rule *gatikārakopapadāt kṛt* [Pāṇini 6.3.14], there is no elision (*aluk*) of the case-ending.
Here, in the word *stamberama*, the member *stamba* ends in the locative case, and the word *rama* does not denote the agent (*dharmivācin*).
Regarding the term "karmakaravarddhitaka":
here, the *karmakara* (laborer) is the one who takes [the object], for he accepts the *varddhitaka* (the surplus).
However, the word *varddhitaka* does not denote that which is subject to the rule (*dharmya*).
For this practice is not established anywhere that a *vardhitaka* (a type of sweetmeat) must be given to a laborer; rather,
[the term] *vāḍava* is derived from "this belongs to a mare (*vaḍavā*)" by applying the suffix *aṇ* according to [Pāṇini 4.3.120].
Regarding the phrase "from the infusion of the seed" (*bījaniṣekāt*): *garbhādhāna* (the conception of an embryo) is the infusion of the seed.
In this context, the term *vāḍava-agni* (the submarine fire) refers to *hārī*, for it indeed takes possession of what is to be given, which is the act of seizing (*haraṇa*).
The "taking" (*haraṇa*) is that which is prescribed by dharma.
In some cases, this practice is established as follows: "When a foal is conceived in a mare, one must provide suitable food and so forth for the nourishment of its body after the sowing of the seed.
Thus, the word *haraṇa* denotes that which is required by dharma.
Nevertheless, because of the prohibition "not in *aharaṇa*," this [suffix] does not apply.

Consequently, when the accent of the whole (*kṛtsvara*) would otherwise apply, the final member ending in the suffix *lyuṭ* becomes udātta on its final syllable according to [Pāṇini 6.2.150]. Now, one might object: "Since this accent is subsequent [to the *kṛtsvara*], it will simply prevail; so what is the purpose of the prohibition 'not in *aharaṇa*'? To this he replies: "Even though it is subsequent," and so forth.
With the words beginning with "tena," he demonstrates the purpose of the indication.
Regarding the term "vāḍavahāryam":
by the rule "ṛhaloṇryat" [Pāṇini 3.1.124], the suffix *ṇyat* is applied to the root *hṛ*, resulting in "hāryam"; furthermore, that very same [root] is what is being referred to.
*Vāḍavahāryam* means "to be carried away by a *vāḍava* (submarine fire).

In that context, if a prohibition against the "carrying away" (*haraṇa*) of the meaning just mentioned were not made for the sake of making it known, then—because it is subsequent—the final syllable of the second member would become circumflex (*svarita*) due to the accent of a *kṛt*-suffix, according to the rule *gatikārakopapadāt kṛt* [Pāṇini 6.2.139]. However, when this [prohibition] exists, this very accent of *hāri* occurs.

In cases such as *stūpeśāṇa*, where the first member of the compound ends in the locative case (*saptamyanta*), although the rule *tatpuruṣe tulyārtha-* [Pāṇini 6.2.2] would normally apply—thereby causing the original accent (*prakṛtisvara*) of the first member to prevail as an exception to *sthūlādibhyaḥ* [Pāṇini 6.1.223]—this word is instead stated to have its initial syllable acute (*ādyudātta*), as before. Furthermore, the first members are generally oxytone (*antodātta*). For instance, the word *stūpa* is derived from the root *stūp* (Dhātupāṭha 1672), belonging to the *cur*-class, with the suffix *ac*; thus, it is oxytone. When combined with the locative case ending, even though one part is modified, it remains oxytone.
> [[8.2.5]] Thus [it is said].

From the root *maki* in the sense of "adornment" (*maṇḍane*, Dhātupāṭha 89), by the rule *uṇādayo bahulam* [[3.3.1]], the suffix *uṇ* is applied; there is also the elision of the nasal (*na-lopa*), whereby the word *makuṭa* has its initial vowel as the udātta accent. From the root *hala* in the sense of "scratching" (*vilekhane*, Dhātupāṭha 837), the suffix *gha* is applied, because it is indicated that the suffix *gha* occurs after other roots beginning with a vowel by virtue of the application of the marker *ghi* in rule [[3.3.125]].
Therefore, the word *hala* has its acute accent on the final syllable (*antodātta*).

From the root *dṛ* in the sense of "tearing" (*vidāraṇe*) [Dhātupāṭha 1493], the word *dṛṣad* is derived by the rules *śṛdṛbhaso'diḥ* (Daiva 6.42) and *dṛṇāteḥ ṣug hyasvaśca* (Daiva 6.45); therefore, that word also has its acute accent on the final syllable. Words such as *yājñikānām* are genitive compounds (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*).

This [rule] is for the purpose that, when the accent of a compound (samāsa-svara) would otherwise apply, the first syllable of the preceding member (*pūrvapada*) which expresses "Hāri" should be acute.

In this context, the accent of the preceding and following members as they existed in their uncompounded state is not designated; for once the compound is formed, that [prior] accent no longer pertains to the actual usage.
Nor is there any possibility for it to apply once the compound has been formed.
This is explained for the purpose of demonstrating the meaning: "Since that [substitution] would have occurred by virtue of its being the original form (*prakṛtibhāva*), this [rule] is commenced.

For this very reason, it was not mentioned in the preceding rule either. "Yuktaḥ" means composed or concentrated; one who is intent upon a task is so called. As in the example: "goballavaḥ" (a cow-herder).

*Adhikāra-nāman* (the name of a supervisor): because he possesses this [quality], the suffix *va* is applied according to *vaprakaraṇe 'nyebhyo 'pi dṛśyate* (Vārttika 5.2.109); thus, *gavām ballavaḥ* (cow-herd) is a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhī-samāsa*).
Here too, although the accent of the compound itself would have applied, the rule ordains that the first member of the compound is acute (*udātta*).
Thus: *gomaṇindaḥ*.

In the expression *maṇiṃ dadāti* (he gives a jewel), there is no elision (*aluk*) of the case-ending according to Pāṇini 2.3.3 and 6.3.14; subsequently, *gavāṃ maṇida* forms a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*).
Since the accent of the compound itself would have applied here as well, this specific rule is established.
[The example is] *gosaṃkhyaḥ*.

Regarding the derivation of *gosaṃkhyā* from *gāṃ sañcaṣṭe* (he enumerates the cows), the suffix *ka* is applied [by Pāṇini 3.2.7]. Since an *upapada* compound (*upapadasamāsa*) is formed, and the accent of the suffix *kṛt* would normally apply by the rule *gatikārakopapadāt* (Pāṇini 6.2.139), this statement is made here to ensure that the preceding member (*pūrvapada*) is acute. Now, one might object: since the subsequent rule *thāthādisvaraḥ* (Pāṇini 6.2.143) applies, why is this statement necessary for cases such as *goballava*? Should not the *kṛt*-accent itself sublate the *yukta*-accent? If that is the case, then a "prior counter-exception" (*pūrvavipratiṣedha*) must be stated, because the word *para* (in the rule *parasmāt*) signifies "that which is desired."
Demonstrating that all such compounds as *goballava* and others denote one who is "engaged" (*yuktavācin*), he says: "*yukta iti samāhitaḥ*" and so forth.

By this, he shows that the form *yukta* is derived from the root *yuja* (Dhātupāṭha 1177) in the sense of "concentration" (*samādhau*) when the past passive participle suffix (*niṣṭhā*) is applied. The word *adhyakṣa*, when occurring in a compound, likewise denotes one who is "engaged. Since the preceding rule would have necessitated a constant initial acute accent (*ādyudāttatva*) there, this optional rule (*vibhāṣā*) is commenced. When the initial acute accent is set aside, the final syllable of the compound becomes acute (*samāsāntodāttatva*).
*gavām adhyakṣaḥ* is a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsaḥ*). In *pāpam*, there is a reference to the word-form itself (*svarūpagrahaṇam*);

in *śilpinī*, there is a reference to the meaning (*arthagrahaṇam*). For what purpose is the reference to the meaning made? [One might argue: "In the case of *grāmaśilpinī*, since the term *śilpī* is already established through its inclusion in the rule, it follows that the reference here also refers to the meaning. [Response: When the accent of the compound as a whole would otherwise be obligatory, this rule prescribes an option for the acute accent on the first member; thus, when that is set aside, the accent of the compound itself prevails.

Now, why does this not occur here in the case of *pāpasya nāpitaḥ* ("the barber of the wicked")? To this he says: "Because the word *pāpa* is mentioned by its specific form (*pratipadokta*). [The result is that] "therefore, it does not occur in a genitive compound. For when a compound is formed by its specific mention, by the maxim *lakṣaṇapratipadoktaparibhāṣā* (Vyāḍi-paribhāṣā 3), only that [specifically mentioned form] will be grasped, and not any other. It has been stated [in the Kāśikāvṛtti on Pāṇini 4.2.40]: "Except under the heading of *gotra*, when the term *gotra* is used elsewhere, the worldly sense of *gotra* is understood."
In common usage, this term is well known as referring simply to offspring; therefore, it is that very meaning which is intended here, and not the technical (paribhāṣika) sense.
"Antevāsī" means a pupil (śiṣya). In this context, by the inclusion of the word "antevāsī," the inclusion of the meaning [of the offspring] is well established.
Therefore, here too, only the meaning is grasped, not the formal essence (svarūpa).
In the case of *māṇava* and *brāhmaṇa*, it is indeed the formal essence [that is meant].
This *māṇava* is derived from *manu*; the substitution of *ṇa* for *na* occurs precisely by virtue of this irregular derivation (*nipātana*).
According to the view that "irregular formations (*nipātana*) are not subject to [general] rules" (*Puṣpasūtra* 99), the form *mānava* also occurs.
In the sense of "this is a Brāhmaṇa," we have *brāāhṛṇaḥ*.

As for the word *māṇavaka*, which is derived according to the rule "the suffix *aṇ* is traditionally taught as the general [suffix] for *manu* when denoting a contemptible or dull-witted offspring" (*Kāśikāvṛtti* 4.1.161), and the word *brāāhṛṇa* used in the sense of "the offspring of a Brāhmaṇa" (*brāāhṛṇasyāpatyam brāāhṛṇaḥ*), both are established by the very mention of the *gotra* [in the rule].
*Kṣepaḥ* means censure.
In the expression *jaṅghāvātsyaḥ*,
there is a compound (*samāsa*) according to [Pāṇini 2.1.4], *sup supā*.

How, then, is there a censure here? To this he says: "He who gives a *jaṅghādāna*," and so forth. A *jaṅghādāna* is said to be some gift prescribed by custom; one who intends, "I shall give that," becomes a *vātsya*. He who accepts [the status of] being a *vātsya* is thus censured as a "Jaṅghāvātsya."
Even though he was not a Vātsya by birth, he accepted the status of being a Vātsya in regard to the gift of his daughter;
for this word "Vātsya" belongs to the *gargādi* class [of gotra-forming suffixes].
Thus it is said: "The wife of Sauśruta."
*Sauśruta* is derived from *Suśruta* as his offspring, with the suffix *aṇ*; thus, one for whom the wife is predominant is *sauśrutaḥ*, [and] *bhāryāsauśrutaḥ*.

This is a compound formed by the rule: "In the section on coordinate compounds (*samānādhikaraṇa*), there is an addition [to the list] of *śākapārthiva* and similar compounds, and there is elision of the final member" (Vārttika 83).
By the phrase "by reason of Suśruta’s being characterized by the predominance of his wife," he demonstrates that this is a coordinate compound (*samānādhikaraṇa*) here.
By the statement "the offspring of Suśruta," it is also shown that *sauśruta* ends with the suffix *aṇ*. Regarding the rule "after *vaśā*, *brāhmaṇa*, and *kṛta*,
[the suffix] *yaḥ* [is applied]," the compound is formed by that very same supplementary rule (*upasaṃkhyāna*).

Here too, because the cow (*vaśā*) is the primary element, there is the elision of the offspring produced by the *brāhmaṇ* [as the secondary element]. In the expression "the initiations of the maiden" (*kumārī-dīkṣāḥ*),
the compound is formed according to *sup supā* [Pāṇini 2.1.4].
The same applies here to the term *kambalacārāyaṇīyāḥ*.

The treatise (*śāstra*) spoken by Dākṣi is called *dākṣa*. By the rule *iñaśca* [Pāṇini 4.2.111], the suffix *aṇ* is applied; then, by the rule *tadadhīte tadveda* [Pāṇini 4.2.59], another *aṇ* is applied, which is subsequently elided by the rule *proktālluk* [Pāṇini 4.2.64].

The word *cara* belongs to the *naḍādi* group; the descendant of *cara* is *cārāyaṇa*. That which was taught by him is *cārāyaṇīya*. By the rule *tad adhīte* (Pāṇini 4.2.59), as before, the suffix *aṇ* is applied.
*Pāṇinīya* is that which was taught by *pāṇini*; from that, as before, the suffix *aṇ* is applied for the student, and there is elision (*luk*) of that [suffix].
"Those desiring the acquisition of robes and so forth"—by the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), blankets, rice, and other such items are included.
Here too, the compound is formed according to *Pāṇini* 2.1.4: *sup supā*.
Or rather, by that very same supplementary rule (*upasaṃkhyāna*), [the compound] *kumārīdākṣāḥ* means "those who desire to obtain a maiden" (*kumārīlābhakāmā dākṣāḥ*). As for *bhikṣāmāṇavāḥ*,
the compound is formed as before.
A young brahmin who desires alms is a "begging-brahmin" (*bhikṣāmāṇava*). Regarding the term *dāsībrāhmaṇa*: it is a brahmin who desires a female slave; thus he is a "slave-desiring-brahmin."
Thus, in the case of *vṛṣalībrāhmaṇaḥ*,
the compound is formed even though it has not been explicitly prescribed, either by virtue of the word *bahulam* (in various ways) [Pāṇini 2.1.32],
or by the splitting of the rule (*yogavibhāga*) [of Pāṇini 2.3.18] beginning with *tṛtīyā*.
Regarding the term "dāsīśrotriyaḥ," it is equivalent to "dāsībrāhmaṇa. This rule is an exception (apavāda) to the accentuation of compounds. The word *aṅga* here signifies a cause.
That which initiates [the state] is called an "aṅga" (limb).
The plural form "aṅgāni" is used for the purpose of excluding the injunction regarding its essential nature. Intoxicating liquor, with the exception of *surā*, is designated as *maireya*.
"Guḍamaireyaḥ, madhumaireyaḥ"—
this is a *ṣṭhā* compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*).
[It means] "of the *maireya* liquor which is a modification of molasses, the molasses is a constituent part."
Because it is the cause of that [compound accent].

This rule is also an exception (*apavāda*) to the accentuation of a compound. The inclusion of the term "name" (*ākhyā*) is for the purpose of excluding a rule based on the word's own form (*svarūpavidhi*).

Now, one might object: "Will there not be no rule based on the word's own form simply because of the plural number? This is not so; for the plural number would indicate only the multiplicity of its meaning—that is, the word *bhakta* as occurring in a plurality of referents.

Moreover, when the injunction regarding the literal form [of the word] is set aside by the plural number, only those things such as food (*anna*) and so forth—which are synonyms for the meaning of the compound *bhakta*—would be understood, and not terms like *bhikṣā* (alms) which denote specific types of food.
However, when the term itself is taken up, the injunction regarding the literal form being set aside by the plural number results in the inclusion of its specific varieties.
Therefore, this [injunction] is for that purpose.
By the word *tat* (in the sūtra), the meaning of those things called "food" (*bhakta*) is indicated.

Examples such as *bhikṣākaṃsaḥ* ("a brass vessel for alms") and others are compounds formed with the fourth case ending according to [Pāṇini 2.1.36], *caturthī tadarthārtha...*. Now, one might object: "In that rule, the mention of 'material cause and its modification' (*prakṛti-vikṛti*) is required, and here there is no relationship of material cause and modification. This is true; however, this very statement is the indicator (*jñāpaka*) that, in the case of words denoting food, the fourth case is compounded with it even when there is merely the sense of being for that purpose (*tādārthya*).

Regarding the phrase "samaśanaṃ samāśaḥ": from the root *aś* meaning "to eat" (*aśū bhojane*, Dhātupāṭha 1523; *aśa bhojane*, DhP), with the prefix *sam-* and the suffix *ghañ* denoting the abstract state (*bhāve*), the mere act of eating is expressed.

By the word *mātra*, he effects the exclusion of the suffix *bhaktavya*. [The rule] "In this case, the preceding member is udātta" applies. The word *bhikṣā* is derived by adding the suffix *ap* to the root *bhikṣ* according to Pāṇini 3.3.103; the word *śrāṇā* is likewise derived from the root *śrai* (meaning 'to cook', Dhātupāṭha 919) with the suffix *kta*.
Therefore, both [words] are oxytone by virtue of the accent of the suffix (*pratyayasvara*).

By the rule "In a *bahuvrīhi*, [the first member retains its] original form" (*bahuvrīhau prakṛtyā* 6.2.1), they remain oxytone due to their original form (*prakṛtibhāva*). This rule is an exception (*apavāda*) to the general accentuation of a compound (*samāsasvarāpavāda*). This word, being a term of comparison (*upamāna*), is connected individually with each of the words beginning with *go*; otherwise, there would be no relationship of qualifier and qualified (*viśeṣyaviśeṣaṇabhāva*) between a singular ending and plural endings in grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*).
Alternatively, due to a transposition of case endings, this singular form should be understood as standing in place of the plural;
thus, "dhānyagavaḥ" [is formed],
with "ṭac" as the compound-ending suffix.
In this case, where the accent of the final member (*citsvara*) would otherwise apply, the rule prescribes that the first member of the compound bears the acute accent (*ādyudātta*).
This applies in compounds such as *bhikṣābiḍālaḥ* ("a cat-like beggar") and others,
according to the rule beginning with "even when the meaning is that of a standard of comparison" (*upamānārthaḥ*).
Whatever meaning of the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) is possible here in this example, that should be applied there.
Regarding the phrase "and according to what is well-known" (*yathāprasiddhi ca*):
whatever meaning of the standard of comparison is well-known in the world, that should be applied in that manner.

Regarding this, he says the following to show a mere indication of how to apply the purpose of the comparison: "The form of a cow" (*gavākṛti*) means the configuration of a cow; that which is arranged by that—meaning established and positioned by the specific configuration of a cow—is designated by the term *dhānyagava* (grain-cow), because it possesses a similar form.
In the same way, whatever similarity may be found elsewhere should be applied accordingly.
For example, just as there is a particular arrangement of the parts of a cow, so too that gold which has such [an arrangement] is designated by the term *hiraṇyagava* (gold-cow).

Just as cats are small in size, so too is the alms-food; or just as cats are found only in certain places and not everywhere, so too is the alms-food. In this way, such a similarity between the soup and the cat is to be understood. A blade of grass arranged in the shape of a lion is a "grass-lion."

"Just as *saindhava* is white, so too is *saktu*; thus [the compound] *saktusaindhava*. Likewise, *pānasaindhava*. [The word] "ak" is a mention of the suffix. In that context, by the paribhāṣā regarding the mention of a suffix (Nī.pā.vṛ. 31), it is understood that the mention refers to that which ends in it; therefore he says: "when the subsequent member (*uttarapada*) ends in the suffix *aka*."
Regarding the phrase "denoting a livelihood" (*jīvikāvācini*): "livelihood" (*jīvikā*) means "one who lives" (*jīvaka*); thus, the meaning is "that which denotes such a person.

The word *jīvikā* is included in the sūtra ending in the suffix *-a*, used in the sense of possession (*matvarthīya*), because it belongs to the class of words beginning with *harṣa* (the *harṣādi* group).

For this very reason, the author states in the commentary—“those whose livelihood consists of scraping teeth and so forth are called thus”—namely, "dantalekhakaḥ. [The suffix] *ṇvul* is added after the root *likh* with the prefix *danta-*, forming a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*). Furthermore, the genitive case is used according to Pāṇini 2.3.65, in the sense of the object (*karman*).
Regarding "avaskaraśodhakaḥ":

from the root *śudh* in the sense of "purification" (*śauce*; Dhātupāṭha 1191), the suffix *ṇvul* is applied after the causative (*ṇic*) form. In "ramaṇīyakārakaḥ" as well, [the suffix is applied] after the root *kṛ*.
Regarding the term *ramaṇīyakartā*:
the compound is as before;
here, by the rule [Pāṇini 6.2.139], the final syllable of the second member (*uttarapada*) retains its original accent (*prakṛtibhāva*).
Regarding the phrase "ikṣubhakṣikām" and so forth:
the suffix *ṇvuc* is applied to the root *bhakṣ* by the rule "paryāya-arhaṇa-utpattiṣu ṇvac" [Pāṇini 3.3.111].
In this case, the compound is formed solely by the general rule for compounds, "ṣaṣṭhī" [Pāṇini 2.2.8].
Here too, as before, the final syllable of the second member [of the compound] is udātta;
this rule is an exception to the *kṛtsvara* (the accentuation of the suffix).
The same applies to the subsequent rules.

Up to the rule *yuktārohādayaśca* [Pāṇini 6.2.81], this [rule] should be understood as an exception (*apavāda*) to the accentuation of the *kṛt*-suffix. Take the example *chatradhāraḥ*. Why, however, is this stated, given that while one who is "engaged" (*yukta*) is intended, he is not denoted by a word expressing that very state? [The answer is: because of the rule *niyukto’dhikṛtaḥ* [Pāṇini 6.2.66], which prescribes that the first syllable of the preceding member (*pūrvapada*) is acute-accented for one who is engaged—that is, attentive—to what must be done; therefore, it would not be established for one who denotes being "authorized" (*adhikṛta*).

Therefore, among those authorized for the umbrella and so forth, he who is intended as "appointed" (*niyukta*) is not necessarily intent upon the act of holding the umbrella for someone; thus, the compound *chatradhāra* ("umbrella-bearer") and the like is not accepted as being denotative of such a person in the rule *yuktārthavācinā ca* [Pāṇini 2.1.72]. By the phrase "appointed" (*niyukta*) and "authorized" (*adhikṛta*), he shows that this form *niyukta* is derived from the root *yujir* (Dhātupāṭha 1444) in its past passive participle (*niṣṭhā*) state. In the example *kāṇḍalāvaḥ* ("a reed-cutter"), only the status of being the agent (*kartṛtva*) with respect to the action of cutting reeds is understood, not the state of being authorized (*adhikṛtatva*).
Therefore, this [specific] accent does not occur. The statement "of that which is not preceded by *kṛñ*" (*akṛñaḥ*) is for the purpose of stating a prohibition regarding specific artisans (*śilpin*).

Regarding the word *tantuvāya*: from the verbal root *veñ* in the sense of "weaving" (*tantusantāne*; Dhātupāṭha 1006), the suffix *aṇ* is applied according to [Pāṇini 3.2.2], *hvāvāmaśca*, because he weaves threads (*tantūn vayati*). Then, by [Pāṇini 7.3.33], *āto yuk ciṇkṛtoḥ*, the augment *yuk* is added.
Regarding "ayaskāraḥ":
by the rule "ataḥ kṛkami" [Pāṇini 8.3.46] and others, the *visarjanīya* is replaced by *sakāra*. In the counter-examples, the accent remains that of the suffix (*kṛtsvara*) itself. As in "gopālaḥ."
The root *pā* is used in the sense of "protection" (*rakṣaṇe*; Dhātupāṭha 1056); the suffix *aṇ* is applied as before.
This new rule is commenced because its meaning is not already covered by the previous one; for it would have been established by the rule *niyukte* [Pāṇini 6.2.75] alone.

Regarding "Gorakṣa": [the root] *rakṣ* means "to protect" (Dhātupāṭha 658). Regarding "Pūṣpahārī": the suffix *ṇini* is applied to the root *har* according to Pāṇini 3.2.80 or 3.2.81 (*vrate*). Regarding "śabdārthaprakṛtau":
this is a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "that in which the word and its meaning constitute the primary matter."
"The standard of comparison is restricted.
Since the restriction follows from the particle *eva*, the limitation applies to whatever that particle follows.
And here, the particle *eva* follows the very nature of the word and its meaning; therefore, there is a restriction of the standard of comparison, and thus it is that which is restricted.

Regarding the term *uṣṭrakośī*: from the root *kruś* in the sense of "calling" (*āhvāne*; according to the Dhātupāṭha 856, and also "weeping" according to the Dhātupāṭha), the suffix *ṇini* is applied by the rule *kartaryupamāne* [Pāṇini 3.2.79]. Since the similarity is already expressed by the suffix *ṇini* itself, the word *iva* is not employed in the compound.
Regarding "dhvāṅkṣarāvī": [the root] *ru* means "to sound" (Dhātupāṭha 1034); the suffix *ṇini* is applied according to the preceding rule. Regarding "kharanādī": [the same applies].
The root *ṇad* is used in the sense of "indistinct sound" (*avyakte śabde*) [according to the Dhātupāṭha, 54]. Regarding the phrase "the mention of *upamāna*," etc.:
if the mention of *upamāna* were not made, then the distinction between the scope of the preceding rule and that of this one would not be known.
Even if another scope were to be inferred by virtue of the power of making a *yogavibhāga* (splitting of a rule), still the intended distinction of scopes would not be understood.

However, when the mention of "comparison" (*upamāna*) is made, the distinction between the objects of the two [types of cognition] is determined: the object of the former is the general property (*sāmānya*), whereas the object of this [latter] is the specific instance that serves as the standard of comparison (*upamāna*).
Therefore, the mention of "comparison" is for the sake of distinguishing their respective objects. As in the example: "one who acts like a wolf" (*vṛkavañcī*).
The root *vañc* is used in the sense of "deceiving" (*pralambhane*) [Dhātupāṭha 1703].
Regarding the term *vṛkaprekṣī*:
the root *īkṣ* is used in the sense of "seeing" (*darśane*) [Dhātupāṭha 610], preceded by the prefix *pra*.
In this case, the accent falls on the first syllable (*kṛtsvara*) alone.
Regarding the phrase "the base itself" (*prakṛtireva*), and so forth:

if the mention of *prakṛti* were not made, then one might understand [the rule] to mean that the compound has as its final member a *ṇini*-affix occurring after a word-meaning (*śabdārtha*). Consequently, even in cases such as *gardabhoccārī* ("one who makes the sound of a donkey") and *kokilābhivyāhārī* ("one who utters the cry of a cuckoo"), [the accent would undesirably apply], for here too there is a *ṇini* affix following a word-meaning consisting of a combination of verbal root and prefix (*dhātūpasargasamudāya*), and thus the final member of the compound would be that which ends in it.
Therefore, the term *prakṛti* (root) is employed here so that [the suffix] does not occur in this case; consequently, it does not apply here.
When *prakṛti* is included, [the rule applies] where the meaning is independent of a prefix (*upasarga*), because the root *gam* has the sense of "going" and the root *hṛ* has the sense of "carrying.
Alternatively, the suffix *ṇini* is not prescribed after that composite of word-meaning consisting of both root and prefix.

If the statement is for the sake of restriction (*niyamārtha*) since [the point] is already established by what precedes it—given that a rule (*vidhi*) being commenced when [the matter] is already established serves as a restriction—then why is the particle *eva* employed? To this he says: "The employment of the particle *eva*" and so forth. For if the particle *eva* were absent, there would be a restriction such that [the word] would exist only in the case of a simile (*upamāna*) as the primary nature of the word’s meaning; consequently, the primary nature of the word’s meaning alone would be restricted: "If it exists in the primary nature of the word’s meaning, it exists only in a simile, not in a non-simile.
And thus, it would not apply to a non-simile.
Therefore, the particle *eva* is employed so that there may be a determination through analogy;
for what reason? He says: "But in the case of the nature of word and meaning," and so forth.
The word *tu* (but) indicates a reason.
Therefore? In the case of the *prakṛti* (base form) of a word’s meaning, both the simile (*upamāna*) and the non-simile (*anupamāna*) are acute-accented on the first syllable.
For that reason, the particle *eva* is employed for the purpose of determining the simile.

For when there is a restriction to the simile, since the base form of the word’s meaning is not otherwise restricted, the acute accent on the first syllable of everything therein is obtained without distinction.
"Roaring like a lion" is an example of a simile (*upamāna*). "One who speaks voluminously" is [an example of] a metaphor (*rūpaka*).

In the case of *anupamānasya*, the suffix *ṇini* is applied in the word *puṣkalajalpī* by either [Pāṇini 3.2.80] or [3.2.81]. This rule is an exception (*apavāda*) to the accentuation of *kṛt*-suffixes (*kṛtsvara*). As in the example *kṛtījaḥ*.

In *kuṭāñjātaḥ*, the suffix *ḍa* is applied by the rule *saptamyāṃ janerḍaḥ* [Pāṇini 3.2.97]. This rule is also an exception (*apavāda*) to the accentuation of *kṛt*-suffixes (*kṛtsvara*). In the case of *dagdhajāniḥ*, the accentuation of the *kṛt*-suffix itself (*kṛtsvara*) occurs. Here, the word *nivasantaḥ* is understood as being derived from the *uṇādi* [list], formed by adding the suffix *jhac* to the root *vas* preceded by the prefix *ni*; this is according to the rule *jṛviśibhyāṃ jhac* [Dhātupāṭha 6.17], which remains in force, and the further rule *tṛbhūvahivasibhāsisādhigatimaṇḍijinandibhyaśca* [Dhātupāṭha 6.19]—where *vasi* is taken with the prefix *ni*—to form *nivasantaḥ*.
"Those who dwell" are *nivasantaḥ*. Some explain this as referring to the root *vas* with the suffix *-śatṛ*;
for example, "the village of the wrestlers" (*mallagrāmaḥ*).
This is a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*).
Regarding the example "the village of the gods" (*devagrāmaḥ*): the word *grāma* refers here to a collection of houses enclosed by a fence.
Therefore, the meaning is "having the gods as its owners.

By this, he demonstrates that the genitive case here is compounded when it expresses a relationship of owner and owned (*svasvāmibhāva*), and not when it expresses a relationship with an action or a dwelling (*nivāsa*). The intention is that otherwise, the word *deva* would only signify "dwelling" as the prior member [of the compound].
In the counter-example, "in which dākṣi and others dwell," etc., he shows that the prior member signifies "dwelling. This rule is an exception (*apavāda*) to the general rule for forming compounds.
The same applies to the subsequent rules as well.
Those *yoga*s (grammatical rules) beginning with the sūtra *na bhūtādhikasañjīva* [Pāṇini 6.2.91] should be understood as exceptions (*apavāda*) to the accentuation of compounds.
Examples such as *dākṣīghoṣaḥ* are genitive compounds (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*).

"Wherever [they may go]," and so forth. But how is this understood, given that "not dwelling" (*anivasantaḥ*) is the subject under discussion? To this he says: "Not dwelling," and "others," and so forth.

According to their opinion, those words which are designated as *nivāsana* (clothing) here remain acute-accented (*udātta*) even when they denote that in which one dwells. Regarding the passage beginning with "when [the word] ends in *śālā*":

by the rule *vibhāṣā senāsurā-* [Pāṇini 2.4.25], it is stated that a *tatpuruṣa* compound ending in *śālā* optionally takes the neuter gender. However, in this context, the feminine form of the word *śālā* is intended. In that case, someone might have the misconception that, just as the compound does not become neuter, the rule *yathāsamāsa-* [Pāṇini 6.2.123] would apply because it is subsequent, and thus the initial syllable of the second member (*uttarapada*) should be acute-accented.

Therefore, in order to exclude that [possibility], the passage beginning with "when inside a hall" (*yadā śālāntaḥ*) is introduced. That which is a neuter-gender *tatpuruṣa* compound ending in *śālā* but does not have *chāttra* or similar words as its prior member is the scope (*avakāśa*) for this [rule]: *chāttriśālā*, *ailiśālā*.

However, that which is a neuter-gender *tatpuruṣa* compound but does not have *chāttra* or similar words as its prior member is the scope for the rule "in the case of a neuter [compound] ending in *śālā*" (*śālāyāṃ napuṃsake*): *brāhmaṇaśālam*, *kṣatriyaśālam*.

In this case, two [rules] apply: [the rule for] *chāttriśālam* and [the present rule]. By the prior prohibition (*pūrvavipratiṣedha*), this very accent (*svara*) prevails. If the word *prastha* is derived [by adding the suffix *ka*] according to the Vārttika "The prescription of *ka* in the sense of *ghañ* is for the sake of *sthā*, *snas*, *pā*, *vyadh*, *han*, and *yudh*" (Vārttika 306), then the accent *thāthādi-svara* (Pāṇini 6.2.144) would apply.
If it is not so derived, then the final member of the compound takes the acute accent (*samāsāntodātta*).
Words such as *indraprasthaḥ* are genitive compounds (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*). Words such as *suhṛnagaram* are likewise genitive compounds.

Why is it not stated simply as "of the Easterners" (*prācām*)—for the statement "of the Easterners" would indeed be lighter than the statement "not of the Northerners" (*anudīcām*)? It cannot be so; for in the case of *madhyadeśanagaram* (the city of the Middle Country) and *virāṭanagaram* (the city of Virāṭa), [the rule] would not apply.

A prohibition is stated when the acute accent on the first syllable of the prior member (*pūrvapada*) is about to occur, but the compound itself does not come into being. Regarding the mention of *madrāśma*, etc.:
in both cases, there is the possibility of application whether the word consists of two syllables (*dvyac*) or three syllables (*tryac*).
Therefore, the statement [serves] both for the purpose of a compound (*saṅghāta*) and for the purpose of a separate word (*vigṛhīta*).
But how is the status of being both a compound and a separate word obtained? It is obtained by means of the *ekaśeṣa* (retention of one) formation, as indicated by the rule *madrāśma*.
Here, *madrāśmā* and *madrāśmānau* constitute an *ekaśeṣa*.

When *ekaśeṣa* (the retention of one member of a class) occurs, the prohibition of the word *madrá* alone, as well as the prohibition of the compound containing the word *madrá*, becomes logically consistent.

The phrase "the section concerning the initial acute accent" (*ādyudāttaprakaraṇam*) means that the section on the initial acute accent has been introduced. In that context, the meaning of the rule—that for words such as *divodāsa*, the initial syllable bears the acute accent in the Vedic language (*chandasi*)—is what must be explained. This is the sense.

However, in cases such as *vyākhyānāṃ tu* (Pāṇini 6.2.66), one should proceed by relying on the fact that any one of the *ca*s (*and*) occurring in this section has the sense of an unexpressed conjunction (*anuktasamuccaya*). Regarding "the entirety of qualities" (*guṇakārtsnye*):
the entirety of qualities is the absence of quality everywhere.
Regarding "all [of them]" (*sarvataḥ*).
The compound is a *samānādhikaraṇasamāsa* (appositional compound) according to [Pāṇini 2.1.48] *pūrvakālaika-* and so forth.
Here, the quality (*guṇa*) belonging to the whole is present everywhere;
however, since the word *sarva* applies to that [whole] rather than to its individual parts, there occurs the application of the entirety of the quality (*guṇakārtsnyasya vṛttiḥ*).

Regarding the term "paramatva" (supremacy): how, then, does the word *parama* apply here to the totality of qualities (*guṇakārtsnya*), given that it denotes excellence (*prakarṣa*) while excellence is one thing and the totality of qualities is another? To this, he says: "By pervading the substratum," and so forth.
The particle *iti* is used in the sense of a reason.

Because supremacy arises from pervading the entire substratum through excellence, and not otherwise; for its excellence is established only if it pervades the whole substratum. Therefore, in this context, the word "supreme" (parama) refers to the totality of qualities.

"Entirely golden, entirely silver. *Sauvarṇa* is a derivative of gold (*suvarṇa*), and *rājata* is a derivative of silver (*rajata*). Here, there is no totality of qualities; rather, what is meant is the totality regarding the modification of that which possesses the genus.

For all modified substances pervade their material cause (*prakṛti*); thus, "totality of substance" (*dravya-kārtsnya*) is intended here, and it is in this sense that the word "entirely" (*sarva*) is employed.
"‘The most pervasive of all, the pervader of all’—here [the term] refers to the completeness of qualities (*guṇakārtsnye*).

But how can there be a compound here, given that by the rule ‘*pūraṇagaṇasuhita-*’ (Pāṇini 2.2.11) and others, a genitive compound with a word denoting a quality (*guṇavacana*) is prohibited? Even if some way were found for the compound to exist, even so, once the compound is formed with the word *otatara*, would one not have to say *sarva-otataram*? To this he says: "The compound is with *tara* following a quality," and so forth.

This indicates that here, the elision of the *t* and the compound (*samāsa*) are both added as supplementary rules (*aupasaṃkhyānika*). This rule is an exception (*apavāda*) to the accentuation of compounds; the same applies to the subsequent rules.
> [[6.2.101]] Up to this point, an exception to the accent rules for compounds (*samāsasvara*) should be understood. *Añjanāgiri* and similar forms are genitive compounds (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*).

In the words *añjana* and *bhañjana*, there is lengthening by virtue of [Pāṇini 6.3.116]: "In the case of names, [the first vowel is long] before *vana* and *giri*. The words *śāpiṇḍi* and *mauṇḍi* end in the suffix *iñ*.
The word *cikhilliśabdaḥ* ends in the possessive suffix *ini*. The compound *vṛddhakumārī* is formed according to [Pāṇini 2.1.57]. The term *jaratkumārī* is likewise a compound.
The compound *jaratī cāsau kumārī ca* ("she who is both old and a maiden") is formed by the rule *pūrvakāla-* [Pāṇini 2.1.48] and others;

the masculine form (*puṃvadbhāva*) is applied by the rule *ubhayatra* [Pāṇini 6.3.42] and others. Now, one might object: the word *kumārī* refers to the first stage of life—for indeed, the suffix *ṅīp* is prescribed for it by [Pāṇini 4.1.20]—whereas the words *vṛddhā* and *jaratī* refer to the final stage of life. Therefore, how can there be grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) here? To this he replies: "The word *kumārī* is employed by taking as its ground for application (*pravṛttinimitta*) merely the state of not being united with a male."
Non-association (*asaṃprayoga*) means non-connection (*asaṃbandha*).
A word that functions as a constituent part of a collection whose activity and cessation pertain exclusively to that [general property] operates with respect to the universal (*sāmānya*).
For example, when the word *kumārī* ("maiden") is qualified by terms denoting specific stages of age such as "old" (*vṛddhā*), it then becomes coreferential (*samānādhikaraṇa*) with them.
The "distinction of age" refers to the final stage of life.
But how can a term expressing a specific [stage] apply to a general category? It is by virtue of the inclusion of the word "age" itself.
If the compound *vṛddhakumārī* (an old maiden) were to refer only to the first stage of life, the mention of "age" would be redundant.

In whichever case the word *kumārī* is employed as denoting the first stage of life, there the age is necessarily understood; so what is the purpose of explicitly mentioning "age"? Therefore, by the force of the mention of "age," it functions according to the manner described—that is, it operates with respect to the general category of age. For by the mention of "age," this [word] is removed from that specific instance and its function as a general term is adopted. And thus, "that age is what is grasped here."
That which, when occurring therein, stands in grammatical apposition with words expressing specific qualities—that is understood as "age.
By the word *ca* ("and"), something other than [the usual] youth and so forth is included; the meaning is that it refers specifically to childhood (*kumāratva*), not the first stage of life.
Thus, [the example] is "paramakumārī" (an extremely young girl).
In this case, it is "being honored" (pūjyamānatā) in brief; however, the state of being honored arises from being worthy of being seen.
The meaning is "a maiden worthy of being seen.
For here, the compound does not have the purpose of denoting age.
The word *nāpa* does not function as a secondary member (*uttarapada*) when it denotes the general category of age. Regarding the term *miśra*:
it means "mixed with another substance. For example, *guḍamiśram* ("mixed with molasses").

In the case of *śākapārthiva*, it is a compound with elision of the middle member (*uttarapadalopisamāsa*) according to the rule beginning with *śākapārthivādi* (Pāṇini 2.1.69). In the case of *śītodaka*,
it is a descriptive determinative compound (*viśeṣaṇasamāsa*).
In this case, the first member denotes water with quality as its subordinate element, and the second member likewise [denotes it] with genus as its subordinate element.

Thus, by means of that [compound], a single object is expressed through both genus and quality; therefore, this is a compound whose meaning is simply "water. Compounds such as *gargatrirātra* are genitive compounds (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*).
The aggregate of three nights is *trirātraḥ*. The compound suffix [ṭac] is applied by the rule "ahaḥ-sarvaikadeśa" (Pāṇini 5.4.87). Thus, [the form] is *atirātraḥ*.

The term *rātrim atikrāntaḥ* is a *prādi-samāsa* (compound with an indeclinable prefix). Similarly, compounds such as *gopālasabham* are genitive (*ṣaṣṭhī*) compounds; they take the neuter gender by the rule *sabhā-rāja-amanuṣya-pūrvā* [Pāṇini 2.4.23].

In the cases of *rājasabhā* and *brāhmaṇasabhā*, the neuter gender does not apply because of the prohibition in the phrase *amanuṣya-pūrvā*. Now, why does this not apply here in the case of *ramaṇīyā sabhā asya brāhmaṇakulasya* [forming] *ramaṇīyasabham*? To this he replies: "That which is explicitly stated," and so forth.

Regarding the technical rule (*paribhāṣā*) "that which is taught by its specific form" (*lakṣaṇapratipadokta*, Vyākaraṇa-paribhāṣā 3): that which is taught as a neuter gender by its specific form is what is understood here.
However, such a neuter status does not apply here;

rather, because the denoted object—the Brahmin family—is neuter, according to the principle that "gender and number follow those of the denoted object" (*abhidheyavalliṅgavacanāni bhavanti*, Vyākaraṇa-paribhāṣā 73).

Is that not so? It is not stated as a specific rule. *Lalāṭapuram* and the like are genitive compounds (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*). *Ariṣṭapuram* and *Gauḍapuram*—these two also are indeed genitive compounds. [Question: What is the purpose of including the word "prior" (*pūrva*)?

He thinks as follows: it should have been stated as "ariṣṭagauḍayoḥ"; for even if it were stated thus, the word *pura-* would still result in being oxytone (antodātta) when it is the final member (*uttarapada*) in the case of *ariṣṭa* and *gauḍa*.
[The author says: "So that it may also apply here.
If the mention of *pūrva-* were not made, then in a case such as *ariṣṭaṃ śritaḥ*, [the compound] *tasya puram* would be *ariṣṭaśritapura-*; [in that case, the rule would not apply].

The words *gauḍānām* and *bhṛtyāḥ* are [the examples for] the term *gauḍa*. However, when the inclusion of the word *pūrva* is present, a *bahuvrīhi* compound is obtained: "that compound in which *ariṣṭagauḍau* are the first members is *ariṣṭagauḍapūrvaḥ*.
By that [rule], even in cases such as *ariṣṭaśritapuram* and *gauḍabhṛtyapuram*, the final syllable of the *uttarapada* (final member) indeed becomes udātta.
Here too, the words *hariṣṭa* and *gauḍa* are placed first;

this [word] "first" (*pūrva*) refers to a constituent member [of a compound]. Compounds such as *kusūlabilam* are genitive compounds (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*). This rule is an exception to the accentuation rules for compounds.

In the same way, the subsequent rules prior to the application of *bahuvrīhau viāṃ saṃjñāyām* (Pāṇini 6.2.106) should be understood as exceptions (*apavāda*) to the accentuation of compounds (*samāsasvara*). For example, in *pūrveṣukāmaśamī*, there is a compound according to [Pāṇini] 2.1.50;
the same applies to *apareṣukāmaśamī*.

Regarding the term *pūrvakṛṣṇamṛttikā*: since it is both "prior" (*pūrvā*) and "black clay" (*kṛṣṇamṛttikā*), the compound is formed by the rule *pūrvāparā-* [Pāṇini 2.1.57] and so forth. The same applies to *aparakṛṣṇamṛttikā* and similar cases.
The word *ādhirāma* is formed by applying the suffix *aṇ* according to [Pāṇini 4.3.87]: "A treatise composed concerning Adhirāma is called *ādhirāma*.
Now, if the mention of the form is made in the case of *anurāṭa*, why does it not also occur in the case of *grāma* and the others? Because the reference is primarily concerned with the meaning.
For it has been stated that when a designation is primarily concerned with the word-form (*śabda*), there is a grasping of its own nature (*svarūpa*).
In this case, the designation *anarāṭ* alone is primarily concerned with the word-form, whereas in the case of *grāma* and so on, it is primarily concerned with the meaning (*artha*).
Now, for what purpose is the mention of "word" (*śabda*) made; why not simply say "direction" (*dig*)? To this he says: "The mention of 'word'... and so forth.
For if there were no mention of the word "direction" (dig), [the forms] *pūrvādhirāma* and *pūrvayāyāta* would not be possible.
Why, then, is the word *pūrva* used here as a term for time?
When there is a mention of the word "direction," it results in the inclusion of all words denoting direction.

Therefore, the word *śabda* is included so that the term for direction (*dik-śabda*) may also be understood even when it denotes time. Regarding the phrase "with the teacher as a subordinate element" (*ācāryopasarjana*), by the rule *supāṃ suluk...* (Pāṇini 7.1.39), the nominative singular replaces the locative singular; this is an adjective qualifying the pupil (*antevāsin*). Thus, the meaning is:
"when the subsequent member [of the compound] denotes a pupil who has the teacher as a subordinate element."
That whose primary element is the pupil and whose subordinate element is the teacher is called "ācāryopasarjanāntevāsī" (one for whom the teacher is subordinate and the pupil is primary).
A subsequent word which has the habit of expressing such a "teacher-subordinate-pupil" compound is termed "ācāryopasarjanāntevāsivāci.
For example: "pūrvapāṇinīyāḥ" (the former followers of Pāṇini).

The compound is formed by [Pāṇini’s rule] *pūrvāpara* (2.1.57) and so forth. The term *pāṇinīyāḥ* refers to the disciples of the teacher Pāṇini; here, the disciples are expressed primarily through the suffix, while the teacher is expressed as a subordinate element (*upasarjana*) because he serves as their qualifier. Thus, the final member of the compound denotes the disciples who have the teacher as a subordinate element. In the example *pūrvakāśakṛtsnāḥ*: these belong to Kāśakṛtsna, hence they are *kāśakṛtsnāḥ*; the suffix *aṇ* is applied according to the general rule (*autsargika*). In the example *pūrvapāṇinīyaṃ śāstram*: the "former" Pāṇinian treatise.

"Pāṇinīya" is that which was taught by Pāṇini; here, the compound has as its final member the word "śāstra" (treatise) with the teacher as a subordinate element (*upasarjana*), and not the word "antevāsī" (pupil) with the teacher as a subordinate element. Regarding the phrase "when there is vṛddhi of the final member":

*uttarapadavṛddhi* refers to the *vṛddhi* prescribed under the governing rule (*adhikāra*) concerning the final member; however, in this context, the final member itself is understood as being like that [vṛddhi].
To demonstrate this very point, he says: "of the final member, thus," and so forth.

But how, when it is stated "in the case of the increase of the subsequent member" (*uttarapadavṛddhau*), can this meaning be understood? To this it is said: the subsequent member (*uttarapada*) is marked with the *svarita* accent; by means of the *svarita*, a governing rule (*adhikāra*) is indicated. Therefore, having taken the governing rule "of the subsequent member," it is understood that the reference is first to that *vṛddhi* which has been prescribed for the subsequent member. This [rule] prescribes the final acute (*antodātta*) accent for the prior member (*pūrvapada*). And because it is a relative term, the prior member brings to mind the subsequent member.

Since the term *vṛddhi* alone cannot function as a final member (*uttarapada*), it follows by implication— due to its association with the word *vṛddhi*— that it indicates a final member that possesses *vṛddhi*. Consequently, within the governing rule concerning final members (*uttarapadādhikāra*), it is understood that this accent applies when the final member is one characterized by *vṛddhi*, as in the example *sarvapāñcālakaḥ*.
The compound [in *pūrvakālaika*] is formed by [Pāṇini 2.1.48] *pūrvakālaika* and so forth;
[the compound in] *pūrvapāñcālakaḥ* and so forth is formed by [Pāṇini 2.1.57] *pūrvāpara* and so forth.
[In these cases,] the suffix *vṛñ* is applied as a characteristic of a country (*janapada*).

While the rule [Pāṇini 4.2.121] is being carried over, by the application of [Pāṇini 4.2.124] and the mention of *janapada* (country) in [Pāṇini 4.2.125], the suffix *vañ* is applied. Thus, from the rule beginning with *su-sarvārdhād ḍhak* [Pāṇini 4.2.129], we derive *sarvapāñcālakaḥ*.
In this case, there is a vowel strengthening (*vṛddhi*) of the final syllable of the compound according to [Pāṇini 7.3.12]: *su-sarvārdhāj janapadasya*.
In cases such as *pūrvapañcālakaḥ*, however, [the rule] applies by [Pāṇini 7.3.13].
And this [rule] is prescribed under the governing heading (*adhikāra*) of "the final member" (*uttarapada*), because the term "of the final member" (*uttarapadasya*) recurs there.

But what is the reason that, under the governing heading of "the final member," it is understood that the term "final member" itself is indicated? To this he says: "Because of the indication of the governing heading," and so forth.

If the mention of the "subsequent member" (*uttarapada*) were intended to indicate that the governing rule (*adhikāra*) applies to the subsequent member, then it would have been stated that the substitution of *h* for *vuñ* occurs optionally when the subsequent member possesses only a *vṛddhi* vowel.
And in that case, it would also apply in forms such as *sarvabhāsaḥ* and *sarvakārakaḥ*.
However, if it is characterized as a governing rule (*adhikāra-lakṣaṇa*), then it does not apply; for it would have been stated that the substitution of *h* for *udātta* does not occur.

And likewise, [the form] *sarvabhāsaḥ* would also occur in the sense of "one who causes everything to shine. However, this does not occur under the rule for the technical designation (*adhikāra-lakṣaṇa*), because the *vṛddhi* [strengthening] is not prescribed by an *adhikāra* concerning the subsequent member of the compound. [In this case,] from the root *bhāsṛ* (meaning "to shine," Dhātupāṭha 624), one says "it shines" (*bhāsate*), hence *bhāsaḥ*, with the suffix *ac* according to the *pacādi* group.

One who acts is a *kāraka*; [the suffix] *ṇvul* is applied, resulting in *vṛddhi* by [Pāṇini 7.2.115], and that *vṛddhi* is not prescribed under the governing rule for the second member (*uttarapada*). [Thus,] "the status of being acutely accented on the first syllable (*ādyudātta*) is obtained by virtue of the accentuation of the first member (*pūrvapadakṛtisvara*)," according to [the rule] "In a *bahuvrīhi*, [the first member retains its] original form" (6.2.1), and so forth. Furthermore, in the case of *viāvevāḥ* from *vi ca te devāḥ*, it is a descriptive compound (*viśeṣaṇasamāsa*), and this is a *tatpuruṣa*.
In this case, there is only the udātta accent on the final syllable of the compound,
as in *viādevaḥ*.
Here, due to the original form (*prakṛtisvara*) of the first member of the compound, there is only the udātta accent on the initial syllable.

The word *viā* ending in the suffix *kvan* is acute on the first syllable by virtue of the *nit*-accent (*nitsvara*). Thus, in *viāmitraḥ*. As for the rule "In a bahuvrīhi compound, when *viā* denotes a name" (Pāṇini 6.2.106), this provides scope for the final acute of the preceding member—as in *viādevaḥ* and *viāyaśāḥ*.

The scope for the rule prescribing that the final syllable of the second member is udātta (accented) by [Pāṇini 6.2.165]—as in *kulamitram* and *kulājinam*—is present; however, in cases such as *vidyāmitraḥ* and *vidyājinaḥ*, both rules would apply, and thus [the latter] prevails by way of conflict (*vipratiṣedha*). Regarding the term *bandhuni*: the neuter gender is used with reference to the form of the word itself; otherwise, since the word *bandhu* is masculine, one would have specified it as *bandhau*. Examples are *gārgībandhuḥ* and *vātsībandhuḥ*.

From the words *garga* and *vatsa*, by virtue of belonging to the *gargādi* group, the suffix *yañ* is applied [Pāṇini 4.1.105]. From that which ends in *yañ*, the feminine suffix *ṅīp* is applied [Pāṇini 4.1.16].
Thus, the words *gārgī* and *vātsī* are udātta on the first syllable due to the accent of the *ñit* suffix.
Regarding the word *brāhma-bandhu*: [the analysis follows].
In this case, the original form (*prakṛtibhāva*) of the preceding member indeed occurs.

This word *brāhmaṇa* is derived by adding the suffix *manin*—while the rule *manin* (DhP 6.73) is still in effect—by means of the rule *bṛherno'cca* (DhP 6.74), which prescribes the suffix *manin* and changes the vowel to *a*; therefore, it is udātta on the first syllable.
[The example is] *gārgīpriyaḥ*.

The word *gārgī* also remains ādyudātta (accented on the first syllable) by virtue of its status as a *prakṛti* (base form). Regarding the example *prakṣālitapādaḥ*: from the root *kṣal* in the sense of "cleansing" (*śaucakarmaṇi*, Dhātupāṭha 1597), the suffix *ṇic* is applied, followed by the suffix *kta*. The word *prakṣālita* is ādyudātta according to [Pāṇini 6.2.49].

Regarding the term *pradhautamukham*: from the root *dhāv* in the sense of "movement" and "cleansing" (*dhātupāṭha* 601), the suffix *kta* is applied; by [Pāṇini 6.4.19] there is the substitution of *ūṭh*, and by [Pāṇini 6.1.89] there is the *vṛddhi* strengthening.
"If it is the word *mukha*," and so forth.
This word *mukha* can also denote one's own limb (*svāṅga*).
In that case, if it denotes a limb here, then by this [rule], there would be only the udātta accent on the final syllable of the preceding member.
In *mukte pakṣe*, the acute accent on the first syllable of the second member (*uttarapada*) occurs by [Pāṇini 6.2.167].

Here, because of the continued application of the option (*anyatarasyām*) regarding the rule for a *niṣṭhā* preceded by a prefix, when the final syllable is acute, then [Pāṇini 6.2.49] applies. Thus, there are three possible accents for the word *mukha* when it denotes a limb of one's own body (*svāṅga*).

By this [rule], there is the acute accent on the final syllable of the first member (*pūrvapada*); by the rule beginning with "uttarapadāntodāttatvam" (Pāṇini 6.2.167), there is the acute accent on the final syllable of the second member (*uttarapada*); and because of the preservation of the original form (*prakṛtibhāva*) by the rule beginning with "iti" (Pāṇini 6.2.49), the first member has the acute accent on its initial syllable. Regarding the phrase "if not" (*na cet*) and so forth:

if the word *mukha* here does not denote a limb of one's own body (*svāṅga*), then this is not the domain of the rule beginning with "iti" (6.2.167); thus, being exempted from that, the rule beginning with "iti" (6.2.49) applies.

Therefore, when the word *mukha* denotes one's own limb (*svāṅga*), there are two accents: the initial udātta of the first member and the final udātta of the whole compound. For example, in *prasecakamukhaḥ* (or *prasecakamukham*, as in the *Kāśikā*), only the original accent (*prakṛtisvara*) of the first member occurs.

The word *prasecaka* is derived from the root *sic* with the suffix *ṇvul* in the sense of the object (karmaṇi), according to Pāṇini 3.3.113; then a compound (*samāsa*) is formed according to 2.2.18. By the rule beginning with 6.2.2 (*tatpuruṣe tulyārthe*), there is the prakṛtibhāva of the indeclinable.
Thus, the word *prasecaka* has its initial syllable accented acute (*ādyudātta*).
[The example] is *śuṣkamukhaḥ*.

By [Pāṇini 8.2.51], there is the substitution of *kā* for the suffix *niṣṭhā*. By the accent of the suffix (*pratyayasvara*), the word *śuṣka* has its acute accent on the final syllable (*antodātta*). In a *bahuvrīhi* compound, by virtue of the preservation of the original form (*prakṛtibhāva*), it remains invariably acutely accented on the final syllable. *Varṇa* means "color" and so forth; that by which something is characterized (*lakṣyate*) is a *lakṣaṇa*, i.e., a "mark" or "sign. Thus, *varṇalakṣaṇa* means "color and mark."
In a *dvandva* compound, there is the state of being treated as a single entity (*ekavadbhāva*).

And here, the mention of "meaning" (*artha*) refers to both color (*varṇa*) and characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*), because the indication is primarily concerned with meaning. Examples are: *otakarṇaḥ* (having white ears) and *kṛṣṇakarṇaḥ* (having black ears).
The words *ota* and *kṛṣṇa* have their final syllables accented (*antodātta*).
To explain: the word *ota* is derived from the root *śitā varṇe* (Dhātupāṭha 742) with the addition of the suffix *ac* (belonging to the *pacādi* group).

The word *kṛṣṇa* is also formed by adding the suffix *nak* to the root *kṛṣ*, according to the rule *kṛṣervarṇe* (Daiva 5.37), while the rule *iṇsiñcidīṅyuṣyavibhyo nak* (Daiva 5.35) is being carried over.
Regarding "dātrākarṇaḥ":
while the rule [Pāṇini 3.2.181] is in effect, the suffix *ṣṭran* is applied by [Pāṇini 3.2.182], *dāmnīśas* etc.; therefore, the word *dātra* has its first syllable udātta.
Regarding "śaṅkūkarṇaḥ": [the same applies].

While the rule *kṛgrorucca* (Pāṇini 3.2.109) is being carried over, the word *śaṅku*, ending in the suffix *ku* according to *kharu-śaṅku-pīyu-nīlaṅguli-gu* (Pāṇini 3.2.120), is prescribed as having the udātta accent on the final syllable.

Under the governing rule *dhāpṛvasyajyatibhyo naḥ* (Pāṇini 3.2.178), and specifically under *kṛvṛcchasidrūpanyanisvapibhyo nit* (Uṇādisūtra 5.42), the word *karṇa* is derived; this refers to the sūtra *bhinnacchinnadruruāvasvastikasya* (Pāṇini 6.3.114). In examples such as *otapādaḥ*, the original accent (*prakṛtisvara*) of the first member of the compound remains.

Now, why does this not occur here in the case of *sthūlakarṇa* ("thick-eared")? For even by means of a thick ear, one is indeed characterized; therefore, is it not already established by the rule "because of being a characteristic" (*lakṣaṇāt*) alone? To this he says: "For the purpose of making known the classification of animals," and so forth.
The intention is that, for that reason, it does not occur in the case of *sthūlakarṇa*.
But how is the inclusion of a specific instance obtained when [the rule] is stated in general terms? It is obtained through the indicative power (*jñāpaka*) of the mention of *varṇa* ("color").

If it were intended here that only a general characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) should be understood, the mention of "phoneme" (*varṇa*) would not have been made; for a phoneme is indeed a characteristic, since it too is characterized [by its properties]. And yet, it has been mentioned. Therefore, this very fact indicates that what is understood here is a specific characteristic.
Furthermore, that which is distinguished from the [standard] explanation must be understood. Regarding the term *otapādaḥ*:

from the verbal root *i* in the sense of "coloring" (*varṇe*, Dhātupāṭha 742), the word *ota* is derived by adding the suffix *ac* (pacādyac); therefore, this word is oxytone (having the acute accent on its final syllable).

Regarding "kūṭaśṛṅgaḥ": from the root *kūṭ* in the sense of "burning" (Dhātupāṭha 1890)—or, according to others, in the sense of "tormenting" or "scorching" (Dhātupāṭha)—the suffix *ka* is applied by virtue of the rule [Pāṇini 3.1.135] for roots ending in *ig*. Consequently, the word *kūṭa* is also oxytone (having its acute accent on the final syllable). Regarding "śobhanakarṇaḥ": [this is explained as follows].

From the verbal root *śubha* and *śumbha*, meaning "to beautify" (*śobhārthe*) [as listed in the Dhātupāṭha at 1321 and 1322], the suffix *yuc* is applied according to Pāṇini 3.2.149. Due to the accentuation rule for *cit* suffixes, the word *śobhana* is also oxytone (having its final syllable accented). This application of the rule occurs because the original accent of the preceding member (*pūrvapada-prakṛti-svara*) is maintained.
In the same way, the subsequent *yoga*s [of Pāṇini 2.1.36] apply prior to the mention of the term *avyayībhāva*.

Therefore, in all counter-examples (*pratyudāharaṇa*), the original accent (*prakṛtisvara*) of the first member (*pūrvapada*) should be cited. For example: *kuñcikarṇaḥ* and *maṇikarṇaḥ*. From the verbal root list (*dhātupāṭha*): *kuci* (184) meaning "to sound loudly" [the root *kuc*]; and from *aṇa*, *raṇa*, *vaṇa*, *bhaṇa*, *maṇa* (444, 448), the word *maṇi* is listed under the *bhvādi* class. From these two roots, the suffix *in* is applied according to Pāṇini 5.2.117 (*sarvadhātubhya in*) and 5.2.119 (*igupadhāt kit*), with the suffix being *kit*. Thus, *maṇi* is derived.
By that [rule], the words *kuñci* and *kuñcimaṇi* have their first syllables acute-accented (*ādyudātta*). Regarding the word *gokarṇaḥ*:

The analysis of the compound is "one whose ears are like those of a cow" (*gaur-iva karṇo 'sya*). In this analysis, the word *go-* bears its stated accent; thus, [the resulting form] is *kharakarṇaḥ*.

The analysis of the compound begins with *kharasya* and so forth. Because it possesses *kha*, the suffix *ra* is applied according to the rule "In the section on *ra*, there is an addition for *kha*, *mukha*, and *kuñja*" (Vārttika 577); thus, the word *khara* has its udātta accent on the final syllable. The word *kaṇṭha* has its udātta accent on the final syllable because it ends in the suffix *ṭha* by the rule "*kaṇeṣṭhaḥ*" (Pāṇini 5.2.105). The word *pṛṣṭha* is prescribed as having its udātta accent on the final syllable by the rule "*ḍityapṛṣṭhagūthayūthaprothāḥ*" (Daiva-nighaṇṭu 6.37; Pañjikā-kośa 1.105).

With the suffix *van* continuing from the rule *iṇśībhyāṃ van* (Dhātupāṭha 8.126), the word *grīvā* is prescribed as having its final syllable accented (*antodātta*) by the rule *śevayahvajihvāgrīvāpvamāvāḥ* (Dhātupāṭha 8.128).

[The derivation is as follows: from the root *han* in the sense "to go excessively," there is the intensive (*yaṅ*) suffix; reduplication occurs; the augment *nuk* is added by the rule *nugato'nunāsikāntasya* (Pāṇini 7.4.85); *kutva* (the substitution of *gh* for *h*) occurs by the rule *ho ḍhaḥ* (Pāṇini 7.3.55); with the form *jaṅghanya* established, the suffix *ac* is added by the rule *pacādyac* (Pāṇini 3.1.134); the *yaṅ* suffix is elided; the feminine suffix *ṭāp* is added; and by the accentual rule for *cit* suffixes, the word *jaṅghā* has its final syllable accented.

Alternatively—the suffix *yaṅ* is elided by [Pāṇini 3.1.24] *hanteḷaṅgac ca*; then the feminine suffix *ṭāp* is added, and by the accent rule for *cit* suffixes (*citsvara*), the word *jaṅghā* has its final syllable accented acute (*antodātta*).

Or else, the word *jaṅghā* is derived as follows: by [Pāṇini 3.2.48] *hanteḷaṅgac ca*—where the suffix *ac* is applied and *jaṅgha* is the substitute for the root *han*—thus the word *jaṅghā* is etymologically explained.
The term *kaṇṭhādīnām* refers to a collective copulative compound (*dvandva*) of these parts, beginning with the throat.
Regarding the term *śitikaṇṭhaḥ*:

while the rule *sarvadhātubhya in* (Pāṇini 5.2.117) is in effect, the rule *kramitamiśāḍistambhāmata icca* (Pāṇini 5.2.121)—where *śiti-* is read as *śiti-śabdaḥ*—prescribes that the word *śiti* has its initial syllable accented (*ādyudātta*).
Thus, *nīlakaṇṭhaḥ* [is derived].
Regarding "nīla-varṇe" (Dhātupāṭha 522): [nīla-varṇe—DhP]. From this root, the suffix *ghañ* is applied; therefore, the word *nīla* is also udātta on its first syllable. Regarding "kharakaṇṭhaḥ":
the analysis (*vigraha*) is "one whose throat (*kaṇṭha*) is like that of a donkey (*khara*)."

The suffix *ra* is applied because of the supplementary rule (*vārttika* 577): "In the section on *ra*, [the suffix] should be added after *khama*, *mukha*, and *kuñja*. Consequently, *khara* is udātta on its final syllable. Regarding the term *uṣṭrakaṇṭhaḥ*:

it means "one whose throat is like that of a camel" (*uṣṭrasyeva kaṇṭho 'sya*). This is formed by adding the suffix *ṣṭran* while the rule *ṣṭran* (Dhātupāṭha 8.79) is in force, according to the rule *uṣikhanibhyāṃ kit* (Dhātupāṭha 8.82). From the root *uṣa* meaning "to burn" (Dhātupāṭha 696), the suffix *ṣṭran* is added, and it is also *kit*.
Therefore, the word *uṣṭra* has its first syllable accented (*ādyudātta*).
Regarding the term *kāṇḍapṛṣṭha*:
since it means "one whose back is a *kāṇḍa*," the word *kāṇḍa* is accented on the first syllable by the rule *nabviṣayasyānisantasya* (Phiṭ-sūtra 2.26).
Regarding the term *nākapṛṣṭham*:

because there is no *aka* (suffering) here, by the rule *na bhrāṭ* [Pāṇini 6.3.74] et cetera, there is an absence of *nalopa* (elision of *n*) due to the preservation of the original form (*prakṛtibhāva*).
Since the rule [Pāṇini 6.2.172] prescribes that the final syllable of the second member is udātta, the word *nāka* is udātta on its final syllable. As for *gopṛṣṭham*...
"His back is like that of a cow"—
here the word *go* (cow) has its [inherent] accent.
"The back of a goat" (*aja-pṛṣṭham*).

In the expression *ajasyeva pṛṣṭham asya* ("his back is like that of a goat"), the word *aja* is derived from the root *aja* meaning "to move" or "to throw" (*dhātupāṭha* 230) with the suffix *ac* (of the *pacādi* class). Because the word *aja* is listed among the *ajādi* group, the substitution of *ī* for *a* does not occur.
By the accent rule for *cit* suffixes, the word *aja* has its final syllable accented (*antodātta*).
Regarding "sugrīvaḥ":
since he has a beautiful neck (*grīvā*), the word *su-* is acute-accented on its first syllable according to the rule *nipātā ādyudāttāḥ* (Phiṭ-sūtra 4.80).
Regarding "nīlagrīvaḥ": [the same applies].

In the term *nīlagrīvaḥ*, [the word *nīla*] means "blue-colored" (*nīlavarṇe*; Dhātupāṭha 522). From this root, the suffix *ghañ* is applied; therefore, the word *nīla* has its first syllable accented acute (*ādyudātta*). Thus, [we have] *daśagrīvaḥ*.
In the word *daśagrīvaḥ*, the term *daśa* has its initial vowel udātta according to the rule *nraḥ saṃkhyāyāḥ* (Phiṭ-sūtra 2.28).
Regarding *āgrīvaḥ*:
[it means] "one whose neck (*grīvā*) is like that of a horse (*aśva*)."
The words *go* and *āśva* have the aforementioned accent.
Regarding the term *nārījaṅghaḥ*:
it means "one whose shanks are like those of a woman."
In the list beginning with *śṛṅgāra*, the forms *nṛ* and *nara* are recited [in the *Gaṇasūtra* 57] as *nṛnarayośca*; therefore, they have the acute accent on the first syllable (*ādyudātta*).

Regarding *tālajaṅghaḥ*: it means "one whose shanks are like palm trees. From the root *tal* (meaning "to establish" or "to stand," listed as number 1598 in the *Dhātupāṭha*) belonging to the *curādi* group, the suffix *ac* is applied according to the rule for the *vacādi* class.
Therefore, the word *tāla* has its acute accent on the final syllable.
Regarding *gojaṅgha*:
it means one whose shanks are like those of a doe (*eṇī*).
The word *eṇī* ends in the suffix *ṅīṣ* according to [Pāṇini 4.1.63], *jāter astrīviṣayāt*; therefore, it is udātta on the final syllable. Regarding the term *udgataśṛṅgaḥ*:

under the governing rule *gamādibhyaḥ* (Pañcapāda Uṇādi 1.122), the word *śṛṅga* is derived by applying the suffix *gan*, as prescribed by [Uṇādi 1.124], *bhṛñaḥ kinnuṭ ca*, and [Uṇādi 1.125], *śṛṇātehrasvaś ca*.

Therefore, this word is acute-accented on the first syllable. The word *udgata* is acute-accented on the final syllable by virtue of the rule [Pāṇini 6.2.143] regarding suffixes beginning with *tha*. [The example is] "having horns two fingers long" (*dvyaṅgulaśṛṅgaḥ*).

The term *dvyaṅgula* means "that whose measure is two fingers. It is a *dvigu* compound formed in the sense of a secondary derivative (*taddhita*). There is the elision of the suffix *mātrac*, which is prescribed by the rule *pramāṇe dvayasac* [Pāṇini 5.2.37] et seq., as well as the suffix *ac*, which is applied by the rule *pramāṇe lo dvigornityam* [Vārttika 558, 559 on Pāṇini 5.4.86]. Consequently, the word *dvyaṅgula* has its final syllable accented (*antodātta*).
"His horn is two finger-breadths [in length]" is expressed as *dvyaṅgulaśṛṅgaḥ*;
this is the same as the previous case.
Regarding the phrase "here" (*atra*) and so forth:
by the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), the inclusion of the two-finger measurement is intended.
As for "Ṛṣyaśṛṅga": [he is the one].
Regarding "one whose horn is that of a *ṛṣya*":
by the rule "and *adhry* etc.," the word *ṛṣya* is prescribed as having its initial syllable acute (*ādyudātta*).
Thus, [the form] is *meṣaśṛṅgaḥ*.

Regarding the phrase "one whose horns are like those of a ram" (*meṣasyeva śṛṅgo yasya*): from the verbal root *miṣ* in the sense of "shining" (*svardhāyām*) [Dhātupāṭha 1352], the suffix *pacādyac* is applied. Consequently, the word *meṣa* has its accent on the final syllable. Thus, in the compound *sthūlaśṛṅgaḥ*, [the first member retains its original accent].
The word *sthūla* has its final syllable accented acute (*antodātta*) by virtue of the accent of the nominal stem (*prātipadika-svara*). Regarding the word *ajara*:
"aging" is *jara*; [the suffix] *ap* is applied according to Pāṇini 3.3.57 (*ṛdorap*).
Therefore, this word has its initial syllable accented acute (*ādyudātta*) by virtue of the accent of the verbal root (*dhātu-svara*).
"One whose aging does not exist" is "amarah. "Mara" means death; [the suffix] *ap* is applied according to [Pāṇini 3.3.113].
Therefore, this [word] also has its initial syllable accented acute (*ādyudātta*), as before.
Regarding *amitraḥ*:
by the rule "from the roots *ami*, *ci*, *midi*, and *śasi*, the suffix *ktra* is added" (*daivam 8.86*), the suffix *ktra* is applied to the root *mide*.
Therefore, the word *mitra* has its udātta accent on the final syllable.
Regarding the word *amṛta*:
the root *mṛṅ* (meaning "to die," Dhātupāṭha 1403) [gives] *mṛta*, which means death.
Therefore, the word *mṛta* has its acute accent on the final syllable.
In the case of *brāhmaṇamitraḥ*,
the word *brāhmaṇa* has its acute accent on the final syllable because it ends in the suffix *aṇ*.
