In this case, the original accent (*prakṛtisvara*) of the first member alone remains. For example, in *aśatruḥ*:
the word *śatru* ends in the suffix *krun* [by Pāṇini 3.2.141] and, according to [Pāṇini 6.1.159], *ruśātibhyāṃ krun*, it is udātta on its first syllable.
This rule is an exception (*apavāda*) to the rule [Pāṇini 6.2.172], which prescribes that the final syllable of the compound is udātta.
The subsequent rules should likewise be understood as applying prior to [Pāṇini 6.2.121]. Regarding the word *sukarmā*:

by the rule *kṛ-dhṛ-ari-bhyaḥ manin* (Dhātupāṭha 6.73)—the reading in the Dhātupāṭha is simply *manin*; the reading in the Pañcapādī is *sarvadhātubhyaḥ manin*—and by the rule *sarvanāmasthāne ca* [Pāṇini 6.4.8], the vowel is lengthened.
Regarding the word *suprathimā*: *prathimā* is the state (*bhāva*) of being broad (*pṛthu*); [the suffix] *iman* is applied by [Pāṇini 5.1.121] *pṛthvādibhya imanij vā*;
[then, by Pāṇini 6.4.161] *ra ṛto halāder laghoḥ*, the vowel *ṛ* is replaced by the consonant *r*.
Regarding the word *supayāḥ*:
while the rule *asuN* (Daiva 9.49) is in effect, the word *payaḥ* is derived by the rule *pibatericca* (Daiva 9.50).
Consequently, this word is udātta on its first syllable.
The long vowel is applied by the rule *atvasantasya* [Pāṇini 6.4.14]. Regarding the word *suyaśāḥ*:

the root *aś* is used in the sense of "eating" (*aśa bhojane*, Dhātupāṭha 1523; the printed edition reads *aśū bhojane*). However, the word *yaśas* is derived from the root *aś* in the sense of "playing/shining" (*aśṛ devane*) with the suffix *yuṭ* [Dhātupāṭha 9.24; Pañcapādī Uṇādi 3.65; note that in both the Pañcapādī and Śarvavarman’s Uṇādi, the term *yūṭ* does not appear]. Thus, the word *yaśas* is etymologically explained through this very [root *aś*].

Therefore, this word has its first syllable accented acute (*ādyudātta*), and the long vowel is substituted as before. Regarding the form *suruāotāḥ*: while the rule *asun* (Pāṇini 3.2.188) is in effect, the rule *ruāūrībhyāṃ tuṭ ca* (Dhātupāṭha 9.62) applies.
Regarding *suruāt* and *sudhvat*:

the suffix *kvip* is applied after *ruān* and *sudhvan* by the rule *vasuruāṃsu* [Pāṇini 8.2.72], whereby *d* is substituted for *n*. Since that substitution is considered *asiddha* (not yet established), the condition of ending in *av* does not apply.
Thus we have *surājā* and *sutakṣā*.
O King, [the word] *takṣan* ends in the suffix *kanin*; [the word] *sulomā* [is derived] from the root *lū* with the suffix *manin*, [resulting in] *loma*.
Regarding the word *sudhā*:

from the root *uṣ* in the sense of "burning" (*dāhe*, Dhp 6.96), while the rule *mithune'siḥ* (Pāṇ. 3.2.42) is in force, the suffix *asi* is added; then, by the rule *uṣaḥ kit* (Pāṇ. 3.2.157), the suffix is marked with the *k*-indicator.

Now, how is it that in *suprathimā*, *suruāotāḥ*, *suruāt*, and *suvrat*, the first syllable of the subsequent member (*uttarapada*) is udātta-accented, given that according to the paribhāṣā "the mention of meaningful items [includes their substitutes]," only those [forms] that possess meaning are included here, yet these two [suffixes, *-iman-* and *-as-*, etc. do not possess meaning? To this, he says: "*an-in-as-man-*," and so forth.

By stating, "The mention of *ani*, *nas*, and *man*—whether they are meaningful or meaningless—triggers the rule of *tadantavidhi* (Vākyapadīya 1.129)," the author of the Vākya-kāra indicates that there is indeed the inclusion of even meaningless forms such as *ani*, *nas*, and *man*. Otherwise, this [statement] would merely serve to demonstrate the application of the rule of *tadantavidhi*. [This is further illustrated by the rule] "But in the case of *kap*, because it is subsequent," and so forth.

The scope of the rule *sormanasī* (Pāṇini 6.2.116) is, for example, *sukarmāḥ* and *suvayāḥ*. The scope of the rule *ayavakṣarayavakṣara-suvayāḥ* (6.2.173) is, for example, *ayavakaḥ* and *suyavakaḥ*, where the suffix *kap* [is applied] by rule 5.4.154. Here, both [rules] would apply simultaneously—as in *sukarmakaḥ* and *surucitaskaḥ*—and therefore the latter [rule, 6.2.173,] prevails by way of conflict (*vipratiṣedha*). In the word *kratuḥ* derived from the root *kṛ*, the initial syllable is udātta due to the *nit*-accent. The words *dṛśīka* and *pratīka* have their initial syllables udātta by the rule *adhyādayaśca* (6.2.194).

The word *pratūrti* is acutely accented on its first syllable by the rule regarding *gati* (prefix) accents, according to Pāṇini 6.2.50 (*sūpūrvasyatvarateḥ ktin*). [The Kāśikā notes that *pratūrti* is listed among the *kratv-ādi* group as *prapūrti*. The suffix *uṭh* is applied by the rule 6.4.20 (*jvaratvara*), etc.
The word *havya* is acutely accented on its first syllable by the rule 3.1.97 (*aco yat*) and 6.1.213.
In *bhaga*, the suffix *gha* is applied by the rule *khano gha ca*. For here, by the inclusion of the marker *ghit*, it is indicated that the suffix *gha* occurs after other roots as well.

Because the word *bhaga* belongs to the *vṛṣādi* group, it is *ādyudātta* (accented on the first syllable). [The commentator] says: "By the accentuation of the *nit* suffix, the words *aratha* and *anaratha* are also *ādyudātta*."

The word *āśa* is derived from the root *aś* with the suffix *kvan*, as established by the rule *aśipuṣi* (Pāṇini 3.2.151). The word *ratha* is likewise derived from the root *ram* with the suffix *kthan*, according to the rule *hanikuṣinīramikāśibhyaḥ kthan* (Uṇādi-sūtra 6.27).
It is stated that "the word *bāhu* has its final syllable accented acute (*udātta*) by virtue of the accent of the suffix."

Since the term *ku* is understood from the rule *kubhraśca* (DhP 1.107), and because the word is derived as ending in the suffix *ku* by the rule *arjidṛśikamyamipaśibādhāmṛjipasitugdīrghahakāraśca* (DhP 1.112)—[the variant reading *arjidṛśikamyamipaśibādhāmṛjitugdhugdīrghahakāraśca* is also found in the DhP]—the form *suhiraṇyaḥ* is established. In this compound, the word *hiraṇya* is udātta on its first syllable according to the rule *nabviṣayasyānisantasya* (PhSū 2.26). Furthermore, the word *vīra* is derived with the suffix *rak* after the root *sphāyi-tañci-* etc. (DhP 8.31).
Therefore, it has an udātta accent on the final syllable.
Alternatively, since [the word] is derived from the root *vīra* "to act with prowess" (Dhātupāṭha 1903) with the suffix *ac* (pacādyac),
[it is stated that] "vīrya ends in the suffix *yat*."
The suffix *yat* is applied according to Pāṇini 4.4.98 (*vīre sādhuḥ*) as a *prāg-dhita* suffix.

Alternatively, from this very root *vīra*, which belongs to the *cur-ādi* class, the suffix *yat* is applied by the rule *aco yat* (Pāṇini 3.1.97), resulting in the form *vīrya* ending in the suffix *yat*.
If this were the case, would not the rule *tatra* (Pāṇini 6.1.213) require the initial vowel to be udātta? To this he says: "In that case," and so forth.

How, then, is the inclusion of *vīrya* an indicator (*jñāpaka*)? To this he says: "In that case," and so forth. If [the word] were to have an acute accent on the first syllable, then it would already be established by [Pāṇini 6.2.119]. Consequently, one would not need to include *vīrya* here; yet it is included. Therefore, that very fact indicates that even for the word *vīrya* ending in *ya*, there is no acute accent on the first syllable.

In the absence of that [rule], by [Pāṇini 6.1.185], the final syllable alone becomes svarita. From the roots *kūla* (DhP 525, meaning "to cover"), *pāra* and *tīra* (DhP 1911, 1912, meaning "completion of an action"), *tūla* (DhP 527, meaning "to extract"), and *mūla* (DhP 529, meaning "foundation")—by the suffix *ghañ*, these words beginning with *kūla* have an udātta accent on the first syllable. From the roots *śul*, *hul*, and *patlṛ* (DhP 843, 844, 845, meaning "to go"), the suffix *ghañ* is applied; thus, *śālā* also has an udātta accent on the first syllable.

Regarding *strītvam* (femininity), it is due to the rule of irregular derivation (*nipātana*) at [Pāṇini 6.2.123]. Furthermore, because the word *akṣa* ends in the suffix *sa*—according to [Uṇādi-sūtra 9.21] *tṛvadihanikamikasibhyaḥ saḥ* (and according to Pañcapāṭha 3.62: *vṛtṛvadihanikamikaṣibhyaḥ saḥ*; and according to Pañcapāṭha 3.62: *vṛtṛvadinikamikaṣibhyaḥ saḥ*)—and also because of [Uṇādi-sūtra 9.24] *aśerdevane*, the word *akṣa* has its acute accent on the final syllable (*antodātta*) due to ending in the suffix *sa*.

Even that form of *akṣa* which is derived from the root *akṣ* with the suffix *ac* by [Pāṇini 5.4.76] *akṣṇo'darśanāt* when the compound-ending suffix (*samāsānta*) is applied, is also *antodātta* by virtue of the *cit*-accent; therefore, that too is included here.

From the root *ṣamu* in the sense of "completeness" (or *sama* in the sense of "non-deficiency")—as found in the Dhātupāṭha (829)—the suffix *ac* is applied according to the rule *pacādyac*. Consequently, *sama-* is udātta on its final syllable.
As for the word *sama-* that appears among the *sarvādi* group, it is listed there as anudātta; nevertheless, it is also included here.
The example is *upakūlam*.

The term *parikūlam* is an *avyayībhāva* compound according to the rule *avyayaṃ vibhakti* [Pāṇini 2.1.6], meaning "in the vicinity of the bank" (*kūlasya samīpam*). Furthermore, by the rule [Pāṇini 1.4.88], the word *pari* is designated as a *karmapravacanīya*.
In the case of *tena yoge* (Pāṇini 2.3.10), [the word] *kūlāt* is in the ablative case;
by *avyayaṃ vibhakti-* (Pāṇini 2.1.6), it forms an *avyayībhāva* compound.
In examples such as *suṣamam*, the substitution of *ṣ* occurs by *suṣamādiṣu ca* (Pāṇini 8.3.98); however, because that [substitution] is considered *asiddha*, this is simply the word *sama*.
"These are recited among the *tiṣṭhadgu* compounds," he says;
by this, he shows that these are *avyayībhāva* compounds according to [Pāṇini 2.1.17]. For example: *upakumbham*.
In these cases, there is simply the udātta accent on the final syllable of the compound:
*paramakūlam*, *uttamakūlam*. These are *bahuvrīhi* compounds meaning "that which has the highest bank" and "that which has the most excellent bank."
In this case, the original accent (*prakṛtisvara*) of the first member alone occurs.

As for the two *tatpuruṣa* compounds *paramakūla* and *uttamakūla*, they would not [be subject to this rule] precisely because of the governing heading of *bahuvrīhi*; therefore, the mention of *avyayībhāva* is inappropriate for the purpose of excluding them. Regarding the rule "from *pari* and so on" (*paryādibhyaḥ*), etc.:

the scope (*avakāśa*) of the rule "when *pari*, *prati*, *upa*, and *apa* are used with words denoting parts of days and nights that are excluded" (*paripratyupāpā vajryamānāhorātrāvayaveṣu*, Pāṇini 6.2.33) is where words such as *kūla* do not occur.

Regarding the rule *pariṃ trigartam*: the scope for [the accent] having the acute on the first syllable (*ādyudātta*) for words such as *kūla* and others occurs where *pari* and other such prefixes are present—as in *apakūlam*. However, in the case of *parikūlam*, both rules would apply; there, by the principle of conflict (*vipratiṣedha*), this very [rule for] acute on the first syllable prevails. This rule is an exception (*apavāda*) to the general accentuation of compounds (*samāsasvara*). The same applies to the subsequent rules prior to the sūtra beginning with *nācāryarāja* [6.2.133]. From the rule *vṛtṛvadihanikamikaṣibhyaḥ saḥ* (Uṇādi-sūtra 3.62), the suffix *sa* is added to the root *kam*; thus, *kaṃsa* has the acute on the final syllable (*antodātta*).
From the root *manth* in the sense of "churning" (*viloḍane*), [the suffix] *ghañ* is applied by [Pāṇini 3.3.19], whereby *mantha* has its first syllable udātta.
While the rule *pānīviṣibhyaḥ paḥ* (Pañcapādikā 3.23) is in effect, [the suffix] *pa* is added to the root *śṛ* by *suśṛbyāṃ nicca* (Pañcapādikā 3.26),
and due to the irregularity (*bāhulaka*), there is also the substitution of *ū* for *ṝ*.

Alternatively: from the verbal root *śūrpa* in the sense of "measuring" (*māne*, Dhātupāṭha 1612), the suffix *ghañ* is applied by [Pāṇini 3.3.18] *asamād ghañ*; thus, the word *śūrpa* has its initial syllable accented acute (*ādyudātta*).

The word *pāyya* is derived with the suffix *ṇyat* and is irregularly formed (*nipātyate*) by [Pāṇini 3.1.129] *pāyyasānnāyya...*; therefore, this [word *pāyya*] has its final syllable accented circumflex (*antasvarita*).
The word *kuṇḍa* has its accentuation already explained previously.

Regarding "dvikaṃsaḥ": it is a compound formed for the sake of a secondary derivative (taddhita) meaning "purchased with two *kaṃsas*"; then, because the rule [Pāṇini 5.1.25]—"after *prāgvatīya*, there is *ṭiṭhan* after numerals as prior members"—is accepted as applying to the final element of the compound (*tadanta-vidhi*), *ṭiṭhan* is applied; and that suffix is also elided by [Pāṇini 5.1.28], beginning with "when preceded by *adhyardha* or a numeral.
The same applies to "trikaṃsaḥ."
It is the same as the preceding case.
In the word *dvimantha*,
the suffix *ṭhak* is applied by the rule *ārhād agopucchasaṃkhyāparimāṇāt* [Pāṇini 5.1.19].
The remainder, beginning with the compound, is as before.
In the case of *dviśūrpaḥ*, the suffix *añ* is applied by the rule *śūrpād anyatarasyām* [Pāṇini 5.1.26];
the rest is as before.
Regarding the term "dvipāyya":
the suffix *yaṣṭhañ* is applied as before;
the remainder is as previously stated.

Regarding "dvikāṇḍam" [the *Kāśikā* reads *dvikāṇḍaḥ*]: since its measure consists of two sections (*kāṇḍa*), the suffixes *mātra*, *jā*, and so forth are applied by the rule "pramāṇe dvayasac" [Pāṇini 5.2.37]. Of these, there is elision by the rule "pramāṇe lo dvigornityam" (Vārttika 558, 559), and the compound is formed as before. Regarding "paramakaṃsaḥ": [it is formed similarly].
In this case, only the accent of the compound itself applies. Regarding the word *śāla*, its accent is as stated in [Pāṇini 6.2.120] under the rule for *kūlatīra*.
In the examples *brāhmaṇaśālam* and *kṣatriyaśālam*, the word *brāhmaṇa* is oxytone because it ends in the suffix *aṇ*;
however, the word *kṣatriya* is middle-accented because it ends in the suffix *gha* according to [Pāṇini 4.1.138]: *kṣatrād dhaḥ*.
Regarding the term *dṛḍhaśāla*:
this is a *bahuvrīhi* compound; therefore, it retains the original accent (*prakṛtisvara*) of the first member.
And because the first member ends in a past passive participle (*niṣṭhā*), it is oxytone (*antodātta*).

But surely, by the paribhāṣā "that which is taught by its specific form" (*lakṣaṇapratipadoktaparibhāṣā*), only that neuter gender which is specifically taught in the rule *vibhāṣā senā* [Pāṇini 2.4.25] will be understood. For in the case of *dṛḍhaśālam*, the neuter gender is not specifically taught; rather, it is taught by a general rule on account of the meaning to be expressed, according to the principle: "the gender and number are like those of the thing denoted" (*abhidheyavalliṅgavacanāni bhavanti*). So, what is the purpose of including the mention of *tatpuruṣa* here for the sake of excluding that? If this is so, then the mention of *tatpuruṣa* is for the sake of the subsequent rule.
By the rule *celakheṭakaṭukakāṇḍaṃ garhāyām* [Pāṇini 6.2.126], [the elision] should occur only in cases such as *dadhi ca tat kaṭukaṃ ca* → *dadhikaṭukam*,
as in *dadhikaṭukam udaiāt kaṭukam*.
However, that [elision] being performed for the sake of the subsequent rule also serves the purpose of making the meaning clearer (*vispaṣṭārthatva*).

The technical rule (*paribhāṣā*) regarding "that which is taught by its specific definition" (*lakṣaṇapratipadokta*) should not be relied upon here; for this very purpose, the example *dṛḍhaśāla* was presented as a counter-example (*pratyudāharaṇa*) to the mention of the term *tatpuruṣa*. [In the word] *kaṇṭha*, the suffix *ac* is applied according to Pāṇini 3.1.103 (*kliśyate*), whereby *kaṇṭha* has its final syllable accented (*antodātta*).
Thus, in *sauśamikakaṇṭham*: from *śuśamaḥ*—meaning "one whose tranquility (*śama*) is excellent"—the suffix *iñ* is applied according to Pāṇini 4.1.92.
Therefore, the word *sauśami* has its acute accent (*udātta*) on the first syllable.
Regarding the term *āhvakantha*:

the suffix *ka* is applied by [Pāṇini 3.3.106] to the root *hvayati* preceded by the prefix *ā*; thus, by [Pāṇini 6.2.143], the word *āhva* has its acute accent on the final syllable due to the rule for words beginning with *atha*.

Regarding the word *cappakaṇṭham*: from the root *cap* in the sense of "consoling" (*sāntvane*; Dhātupāṭha 399), the suffix *pa* is applied according to Pāṇini 3.1.135 (*pānīviṣibhyaḥ paḥ*), and because of the rule of "diversity" (*bahulavacanāt*), it is also applied after *cap*. Thus, the word *cappa* has its final syllable accented (*antodātta*). Although the accentuation of the second member [of the compound] was already established by the preceding rule, this present rule is commenced for the purpose of making the first member have an acute accent on its initial syllable (*ādyudāttatva*).
From the root *ci* with the suffix *kvip*, we have *cit*.

From the root *han* with the suffix *pacādyac*, we have *hanaḥ*. By means of irregular derivation (*nipātana*), there is elision of the suffixal *t* and the substitution of *ṇ* for *n*, resulting in *cihaṇaḥ*.

Regarding *mala* and *malla* in the sense of "holding" (*dhāraṇe*)—(Dhātupāṭha 493, 494)—from these two roots, the suffix *ra* is applied; due to a specific irregularity (*nipātana*) regarding the letter *l*, there is elision of the suffix marker (*talopa*) and the substitution of *ṇ* for *n*, resulting in *cihaṇa*.

Regarding *mala* and *malla* in the sense of "holding"—(Dhātupāṭha 493, 494)—from these two roots, the suffix *ra* is applied; due to a specific irregularity regarding the letter *l*, there is the substitution of *ḍ* for *l*, resulting in the words *maḍara* and *maḍaḍara*, which denote types of intoxicating liquor (*madya*).
That which has departed from comparison (*tulā*) is *vitula*; this [word] belongs to it, hence it is *vaitula*. Because it ends in the suffix *aṇ*, it is udātta on the final syllable.
It makes a sound "paṭat," thus it is *paṭatka*—derived from the roots *kai* and *gai* meaning "to sound" (Dhātupāṭha 916, 917)—and it is udātta on the final syllable.

Regarding the expression *cittamādatta*: from the root *lā* meaning "to take" (*dhātupāṭha* 1058), preceded by the prefix *ā*, this very form is derived through a specific grammatical irregularity (*nipātana*). What is it? It is *cittāla*. [The patronymic] "his descendant" is formed as *caittāli* according to Pāṇini 4.1.95 (*ata iñ*). He whose ear is that of Caittāli is *caittālikarṇaḥ*. This is a *bahuvrīhi* compound, which, by the accentuation rule for the original form of the first member (*pūrvapadaprakṛtisvara*), is acute-accented on the first syllable. For the first member is indeed acute-accented on its first syllable by the rule for suffixes ending in *ñi* (*ñitsvara*).
Others, however, read the form ending in *i* as *caittālikarṇi*, which is a collective compound (*samudāya*).

From the root *kuk* and *vṛk* in the sense of "seizing" (*ādāne*) [Dhātupāṭha 91, 92], with the suffix *kvip*, we have *kuk*. From the root *kuṭ* in the sense of "crookedness" (*kauṭilye*) [Dhātupāṭha 1366], with the suffix *ka* characterized by having a semivowel (*igupadha*), we have *kuṭaḥ*. Thus, from *kuk* and *kuṭaḥ*, we derive *kukkuṭaḥ*.
It is accented on the final syllable by the accent rule for compounds (*samāsasvara*).

From the root *ci* with the suffix *kvip*, we have *cit*; from *kaṇ* with the suffix *ac* (as in the *pac-ādi* group), we have *kaṇa*. *Cikkaṇa* is formed from *citaḥ* and *kaṇāḥ*, where the change of *t* to *k* occurs by way of irregular derivation (*nipātana*). Others read the form as *citkaraṇa*.
It is recorded in tradition that these words, beginning with *cihaṇa*, are names for types of thieves.

Now, what is the purpose of mentioning "the first" (*ādi*)? For [the word] "the first" (*ādi*) is already understood from the previous rule. To this he says: "While 'the first' (*ādi*) is understood," and so forth.
For the previous mention of "the first" was connected with the subsequent member of the compound;
here, however, the initial acute accent (*ādyudātta*) is desired for the first members of the compounds, such as *cihna* and others.

Therefore, for the purpose of ensuring that those words which constitute the prior members [of a compound] have an acute accent on their first syllable, the term "beginning" (*ādi*) is mentioned again. From the roots *velṛ*, *celṛ*, and *kelṛ* meaning "to move" (Dhātupāṭha 535, 536, 537), the suffix *ghañ* is applied in the sense of a technical name (*saṃjñā*), resulting in *cela*, which refers to "clothing.
From the root *khiṭa* meaning "to terrify" (Dhātupāṭha 302), the suffix *ghañ* is also applied in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāva*), resulting in *kheṭa*; this is a name for "grass.
By the accent rule for the suffix *ñit*, the words *cela* and *kheṭa* have an acute accent on their first syllable.
From the word *kaṭu*, the suffix *kan* is applied by [Pāṇini 4.3.145] when it denotes a name (*saṃjñā*). This is a quality-word (*guṇavacana*) with an udātta accent on the first syllable.
It has been stated that *kāṇḍa* likewise has the udātta accent on the first syllable. [The rule] "the reproach of sons and so forth is due to the similarity of things such as *cela*" applies here.
Just as a garment produced by a weaver of low birth is called *putracela* (son-cloth), so too a son born of a woman of low birth is called *putracela*.
Just as a reed (*kāṇḍa*) causes pain to living beings, so is such a being.
In that term, the word *putra* has its final syllable accented acute (*udātta*) by the accent of the suffix.

For the word *putra* is derived with the suffix *kya*, following the rule *amicimidiśasibhyaḥ kyaḥ* (Dhātupāṭha 8.86; Pañcapādikā 4.163), and by the rule *puro hrasvaśca* (Dhātupāṭha 8.87; Pañcapādikā 4.164)—[the variant reading *pūño hrasvaśca* in the Dhātupāṭha and *puvo hrasvaśca* in the Pañcapādikā]—it is thus derived as ending in the *kta* suffix.
The word *bhāryā*, however, has its final syllable circumflexly accented (*svarita*) because it ends in the suffix *ṇyat*, according to the rule *ṛhaloṇryat* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 3.1.124).

From the root *ṇaha* "to bind" (DhP 1166), preceded by the prefix *upa*, the suffix *kvip* is applied according to [Pāṇini 3.2.76]. By the rule beginning with [Pāṇini 6.3.116], there is lengthening of the first syllable (*upānah*). By [Pāṇini 8.2.34], the *n* is changed to *dh*, and by the rule of *carva*, that becomes *t*.
Thus, the word *upānat* is oxytone due to the accent of the kṛt-suffix.
In the sense of "that in which trees (*naga*) exist," the suffix *rap* is applied by way of irregular derivation (nipātana) according to [Pāṇini 4.2.128]. Consequently, the word *nagara* is oxytone.
The word *dadhi* is derived from the root *dadhāti* by means of the *kvin* suffix according to Pāṇini 3.2.171 (*ādṛgamahanajanaḥ kvi(n)*); therefore, it is acutely accented on its first syllable.
The word *uda* is formed from the root *śvayati* with the prefix *ud-* and the *kvip* suffix;
although the rule *kvibvacipracchi...* (Dhātupāṭha 10.2) would normally require lengthening, such lengthening does not occur here due to the presence of the term *bahulam* ("variously").
By [Pāṇini 6.3.57], there is the substitution of *u* for *ū*; by the accent rule for *kṛt*-suffixes (*kṛtsvara*), it is udātta on the final syllable.
The word *bhūta* is also udātta on the final syllable because it ends in a *niṣṭhā* suffix.
The word *prajā* ends in the suffix *ḍa* [by Pāṇini 3.2.99]; by the *kṛt*-accent rule, it is udātta on the final syllable.
Regarding the term *paramacela*:

here, honor (*pūjā*) is understood, not contempt (*garhā*). According to the rule *susūdāgṛdhibhyaḥ kran* (Dhātupāṭha 8.42; Pañcapādikā 2.25), while that rule is in force, the word *cīra* ends with the suffix *kran* by the rule *śusicimīnāṃ dīrghaśca* (Dhātupāṭha 8.43; Pañcapādikā 2.26); therefore, it is ādyudātta (accented on the first syllable). Thus, [the compound] *vastracīra*.
The compound is formed as before by the rule *vyāghrāditvāt*. From the root *vas* in the sense of "covering," the suffix *ṣṭran* is applied to form *vastra*; thus, it is udātta on its first syllable.
[The example is] "kambalacīra."

By the rule *ghṛtādīnāñca* (Pāṇini 6.2.192), the word *kambala* has its final syllable accented (*antodātta*). Regarding the root *pala* in the sense of "protection" (Dhātupāṭha 839) [and *pala* in the sense of "motion"], while the rule *kalaḥ tṛpaśca* (Uṇādisūtra 8.107) is in effect, the suffix *kala* is marked with the *cit* indicator by the rule *vṛṣādibhyaścit* (Uṇādisūtra 8.109); therefore, the word *pala* has its final syllable accented.

While the rule *roderṇiluk ca* (Uṇādisūtra 8.39) is in effect, the elision of the *ṇi* suffix occurs by virtue of the word *bahulam* ("variously") in the rule *bahulam anyatrāpi saṃjñācchandasoḥ* (Uṇādisūtra 8.40).

Under the governing rule *pānīviṣibhyaḥ paḥ* (Daiva 7.2) and the rule *stuvo dīrghaśca* (Daiva 7.4), as well as *suśṛbhyāṃ nicca* (Daiva 7.6)—[the variant reading is *suśṛmyāmūrca*—Daiva]—the word *sūpa* is derived with the suffix *pa*; therefore, it is udātta on its first syllable. Regarding the word *guḍa*: from the root *śo* in the sense of "making thin" (Dhātupāṭha 1270), the suffix *ka* is applied by the rule for roots ending in *ig* (Pāṇini 3.1.135); consequently, the word *guḍa* has the udātta accent on its final syllable. This is due to the presence of the term *bahulam* ("variously") in the rule *iṇbhīkāpāśalyatimarcibhyaḥ kan* (Daiva 3.21).

From the root *dhṛ* in the sense of "flowing" (*dhātupāṭha* 1096), the suffix *kta* is applied according to the rule *añcighṛsibhyaḥ ktaḥ* (Daiva 6.9); thus, *ghṛta* has its udātta accent on the final syllable. From the root *mud* in the sense of "joy," the suffix *ga* is applied according to the rule *mudigrorgaggau* (Daiva 3.66); thus, *mudga* has its udātta accent on the final syllable. The word *kūla* has the accent already stated; from the root *ṣūd* in the sense of "flowing" (*dhātupāṭha* 1717), the suffix *ka* is applied according to the rule *igupadhāt kaḥ* (Pāṇini 3.1.135); thus, *sūda* has its udātta accent on the final syllable. From the root *sthala* in the sense of "standing" (*sthāne*), the suffix *ac* is applied according to the *pacādi* group; thus, *sthalam* has its udātta accent on the final syllable.

The word *karṣa* is oxytone by the rule "the final syllable of a word ending in *dhan* preceded by *karṣa* or a word ending in *ā* is acute" (*karṣātvato dhaño 'nta udāttaḥ*). In examples such as *dākṣikūla*, the words *dākṣi* and *māhaki* end in the suffix *iñ* and are ādyudātta (acute on the first syllable).
The word *deva* has its initial syllable accented (*ādyudātta*) because it ends in the suffix *ac*, added by the rule *pacādyac*.
The word *bhājī* has its final syllable accented (*antodātta*) because it ends in the feminine suffix *ṅīṣ* according to the rule *jānapadādi-sūtra* (Pāṇini 4.1.42).
The word *dāṇḍāyana* ends in the suffix *phak* because it belongs to the *naḍādi* group (Pāṇini 4.1.99); therefore, it has its final syllable accented by the rule *kitaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.1.159).

But surely, the word *sthala* is employed in the Sūtra; how then can the word *sthalī* be cited as having its first syllable udātta when it serves as the final member of a compound? To this he says: "The mention of *sthala*, etc. *Rājyam* (sovereignty) means the state or activity of a king (*rājan*); because it ends in the suffix *ṣyan*, it has its first syllable udātta.
The words *brāhmaṇa* and *kṣatriya* have the accents already mentioned. [Examples include] *celarājya*, etc.

The scope for the accent [prescribed by] *celarājyasvarasyāvakāśaḥ*—namely, *bhāryācela-* and *brāhmaṇarājya-*—is that of the accent ordained by the rule *tatpuruṣe tulyārtha-* [Pāṇini 6.1.2] and so forth, as in *niṣkauśāmbiḥ*. Here, both [rules] would apply in cases such as *kucela-* and *kurājya-*; however, the accent of the indeclinable (*avyayasvara*) prevails by means of the prior prohibition (*pūrvapratiṣedha*). By the word "etc. (*ādi*), the inclusion of the accent for *vargyādi-* and others is intended. *Vargyādi-* and others are words ending in *digādi* and *yat*; among them, those consisting of two syllables are acute-accented on the first syllable by the rule *ye ca taddhite* [Pāṇini 6.1.213].

The remaining [words] have the final syllable as svarita according to Pāṇini 6.1.185. Regarding the word *vāsudeva*: the suffix *aṇ* is applied by the rule "ṛṣyandhaka... (Pāṇini 4.1.114) to denote the offspring of Vasudeva; thus, the word *vāsudeva* has an udātta accent on the final syllable.

Regarding the word *arjuna*: from the root *arj* meaning "to acquire" (Dhātupāṭha 224), with the addition of the causative marker *ṇic*, the suffix *unaṇ* is applied by the rule "ajerṇiluk ca" (Daiva 5.57).
Therefore, Arjuna is *madhyodātta* (middle-accented).
Regarding the phrase "and so forth" (*ityevamādayaḥ*), the word "etcetera" (*ādi*) includes those [names] which are recited after the word *pakṣa*. For example: *kaunaṭiputraḥ*.
The word *putra* has its vowel (*u*) stated to be udātta.
*Kaunaṭiḥ* is the descendant of *kunaṭa*; therefore, this [word] is udātta on its first syllable.
The words *dāmakamāhiṣaka* are also udātta on their first syllables because they end in the suffix *kan*.
Regarding the forms *gārgīputraḥ* and *vātsīputraḥ*:
from the words *gārgya-* and *vātsya-*, the suffix *ṅīp* is applied by the rule *yañaśca* [Pāṇini 4.1.16].
Consequently, the words *gārgī-* and *vātsī-* have their first syllable accented acute (*ādyudātta*) due to the accent of the *ñit* suffix.

In all these counter-examples within this section on *tatpuruṣa* compounds, ending-acute (*antodātta*) accentuation is to be understood [by rule 6.1.223]. Since the preceding rule would have resulted in the initial acute (*ādyudātta*) for the word *putra* even when following words such as *ācārya*, this prohibition is stated;
thus, the compound retains its ending-acute accent alone. This applies to cases such as those beginning with "when preceded by a name" (*ākhyāgrahaṇāt*).
The term "name" (*ākhyā*) is connected individually with each [term] beginning with "teacher" (*ācārya*).
Thus, when the mention of "name" is not excluded, there is the inclusion of synonyms and qualifiers for that teacher and so forth.
"The son of the teacher" (*ācāryaputraḥ*) is an example of the actual form [of the name].
"Upādhyāyaputraḥ" is an example of a synonym; "Śākaṭāyanaputraḥ" is an example of a specific instance;
and "Rājaputraḥ" is an example of the essential form.
"Son of Īāra" is an example of a synonym; "Son of Nanda" is an example of a specific attribute;
"Son of the Sacrificial Priest" is an example of the essential nature.
"Son of a priest" is an example of a synonym; "son of a *hotṛ*" is an example of a specific term;
and "son of a *saṃyukta*" is an example of a literal form.
"Son of a relative" is an example of a synonym;
"son of a maternal uncle" is an example of a specific term.
"Jñātiputraḥ" is an example of the general form;
"bhrātuṣputraḥ" is an example of a specific instance [where the vowel is lengthened];
and the substitution of *ṣ* [for *s*] occurs by the rule "kasyādiṣu ca" (Pāṇini 8.3.48).
In that regard, the word *ācārya* has its final syllable circumflex (*svarita*) by virtue of the *kṛt-svara* accent; for it is derived from the root *car* with the prefix *āṅ* and the suffix *ṇyat*.
The word *upādhyāya*, however, has its final syllable udātta by virtue of the *sthāthādi-svara* rule [Pāṇini 6.2.143]; it is derived from the root *iṅ* with the suffix *ghañ* [Pāṇini 3.3.21].
The word *rāja* has its acute accent on the first syllable (*ādyudātta*), because it ends with the suffix *kanin*.

The word *īśvara* has its acute accent on the final syllable (*antodātta*), because it ends with the suffix *varac* according to Pāṇini 3.2.175 (*stheśabhāsa-* etc.). The word *nanda* also has its acute accent on the final syllable, because it ends in a vowel (*ajanta*).
The word *ṛtvij* ends in the suffix *kvip* by the rule *ṛtvigdadhṛk* (Pāṇini 3.2.59);
it is accented on the final syllable by the accent of the kṛt-suffix (*kṛtsvara*).
The word *yājaka* ends in the suffix *ṇvul*; therefore, it is accented on the first syllable by the accent of the *lit*-suffix (*litsvara*).

The word *hotṛ* is acute on the first syllable because it ends in the suffix *tṛn*. The word *saṃyukta* is acute on the first syllable by the rule "a preceding verbal prefix [is acute]" (Pāṇini 6.2.49). From the root *syal*, meaning "to deliberate," with the addition of the causative suffix *ṇic* belonging to the curādi class and then the suffix *ac* (pacādi), the word *syāla* is acute on the final syllable.
From the root *jñā*, by [Pāṇini 3.3.174], the word *jñāti* has its final syllable accented (*antodātta*).

Regarding the word *bhrātṛ*, it is derived as ending in the suffix *tṛn* according to the rule "The suffixes *tṛn* and *tṛc* are added after the roots *śaṃs*, *kṣad*, etc. (Dhātupāṭha 2.1); therefore, it is accented on its first syllable (*ādyudātta*).

This word *saṃyukta* exists both as a conventional term (*rūḍhiśabda*) which refers to brothers-in-law, fathers-in-law, and so forth, based on a relationship established through marriage, and as a derivative term (*kriyāśabda*) which applies everywhere based on some kind of connection; here, the conventional term is intended.
Why is this so? Because of the separate mention of the wives of teachers (*ācāryānī*).

For if there were to be a mention of the term "action" (*kriyā*), then since [the prohibition] would already be established by the mention of "those associated" (*saṃyukta*), one would not have made a separate mention of the teachers and so forth.
For they too are indeed associated through a connection established by learning and the like.
Therefore, there is the inclusion of a conventional (*rūḍhi*) word.

Consequently, for that which is a verbal derivative (*kriyāśabda*) joined with a [conventional] word, the prohibition does not apply. From the root *cūr* "to burn" (Dhātupāṭha 1158), the past passive participle (*niṣṭhā*) is formed; thus, *cūrṇa-* is udātta on the final syllable.
In the case of *kariṇaḥ pāti* ("he protects the elephants"), by rule 3.2.3, the substitution of *va* for *pa* is optionally prescribed: *karipaḥ*, *karivaḥ*.
A word is accented on the final syllable by virtue of the *kṛtsvara* rule or the *thāthādi-svara* rule.

By the rule *maha itaṇ ca* (DhP 5.1.19), and because of the frequentative usage (*bahulavacanāt*), the suffix *itaṇ* also occurs after the root *śak*; thus we have *śākinam*, which is accented on the middle syllable due to the accent of the suffix (*pratyayasvara*).
According to the rule *śakādibhyo’ṭac* (DhP 5.2.2; Pañjikā 4.81), the suffix *aṭac* [or *aṭan* according to the Daivam and Pañjikā] is applied to *śaka* and others, resulting in *śakaṭam*.
That which carries it is a "cart-load" (śākaṭa);
it is accented on the final syllable by the accent of the suffix.
It is called *drākṣā* because it decays quickly; this is due to its inclusion in the *pṛṣodarādi* group.
This word is udātta on the final syllable.

From the roots *tusa*, *hyaṣa*, *hlaṣa*, and *rasa* (Dhātupāṭha 710, 711, 712, 713), the suffix *tan* is applied by virtue of the rule *bahulam* (Pāṇini 3.3.1). According to the rule *hasimṛgriṇavāmidamūlapūdhurvībhyastan* (Daurgasiddhi 6.7; Pañjikā 3.86)—[the Daurgasiddhi reads *hasimṛgriṇavamidamūlapūdhurvibhyastan*; the Pañjikā reads *hasimṛgaraṇvāmidamūlapūrvibhyastan*]—the suffix *tan* is added, and the vowel is lengthened by means of a *nipātana* (irregular derivation). Thus, *tūstam* is udātta on the initial syllable.

The rule "kvib-avaci-pracchi" (Pāṇini 3.2.178), among others (Vārttika 288), contains a *yogavibhāga* (separation of rules) for the suffix *kvip*, based on the principle that "the teaching of grammatical augmentations is not universal, either because of the word *bahula* or because it is non-eternal" (Vyāḍipāda 99).

Thus, from the root *du* (Dhātupāṭha 1256, meaning "to afflict"), the suffix *kvip* is applied; due to the *bahulavacana* (the rule of diversity), there is an absence of the *tuk* augment. Furthermore, by the same *bahulavacana*, the *mum* augment is added to the preceding member, resulting in *kundum*. From the root *māṅ* (Dhātupāṭha 1088, meaning "to measure"), the suffix *ka* is applied, and thus *kunduma* is derived with the udātta accent on the final syllable. According to the rule "uṣi-kuṭi-dali-kaci-khaji-bhyaḥ kapan" (Daiva-Uṇādi 7.9), the suffix *kapan* is applied; therefore, *dalapa* has the udātta accent on its first syllable.

By the rule *atyavicamitaminami* (Daiva 9.44), from the root *cam*, one forms *asacamasaḥ*; then, by the suffix *ṅīṣ* prescribed for feminine nouns denoting a genus (Pāṇini 4.1.63), one obtains *camasī*.
From the root *cak* in the sense of "satisfaction" (Dhātupāṭha 783), one forms *kavip* and then *cak*.
From the root *kanī* in the sense of "shining, beauty, and motion" (Dhātupāṭha 460; note: the Dhātupāṭha reads *kana*), one forms *kanaḥ* with the suffix *ac*.
Cakakaṇaḥ. Caulaḥ is the descendant of Cola; [the suffix] aṇ is applied by [Pāṇini 4.1.170], "cola-kerala-kuly-... and so forth. These are the items beginning with cūrṇa.
Regarding "mudgacūrṇam":
by the rule *mudi grorgaggau* (Daiva 3.66), *mudga* is oxytone.
Regarding "masūracūrṇam": [the same applies].
In *maserūran* (Pāṇini 4.2.95), *masūra* is udātta on the first syllable;
[as in] "matsyacūrṇam," *matsya* is udātta on the final syllable by the accent of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*).
"In this context, 'upagraha' refers specifically to that which ends in the genitive case.
By this, he shows the identity of meaning between the two sūtras.
But how is it that *upagraha* is understood as ending specifically in the genitive? To this he says: "By the usage of the ancient teachers (*pūrvācārya*)."

For the ancient teachers (pūrvācāryāḥ) indeed used the term *upagraha* as a synonym for the genitive case-ending (*ṣaṣṭhanta*). Therefore, by virtue of this usage by the ancient teachers, the word *upagraha* here is understood specifically as the genitive case-ending. This rule (*yoga*) is an exception (*apavāda*) to the accentuation rules governing compounds (*samāsasvara*); the same applies to the three subsequent rules as well. In the four rules beginning with "celakheṭakaṭukakāṇḍam" [Pāṇini 6.2.126], the six words beginning with *kāṇḍa* are included.

If it is thus established that these words have an acute accent on the first syllable by those very rules, then for what purpose is this [sūtra]? It is so that [the acute accent] may occur even elsewhere than where it is prescribed by those rules; and it is also for the sake of preventing [the acute accent] from applying to *prāṇiṣaṣṭha*. Regarding the example *darbhakāṇḍam*:
the word *darbha* ends in the suffix *bha* according to the rule *dṛdalibhyāṃ bhaḥ* (Pāṇini 5.2.151), and thus it has an acute accent on the final syllable.
Or, by the rule *tṛṇadhānyānāṃ ca dvyaṣām* (Phiṭ-sūtra 2.27), [the first syllable is acute]; thus,
in *śarakāṇḍam*,
the word *śara-* is also acutely accented on its first syllable by that very same rule *dvyaṣām*.
The word *kuśa* is likewise;
the word *tila* is also thus.
The words *palala* and *mūlaka* have the sounds as previously stated.

The root *nad* is recited among the *pacādi* group; therefore, because of its *ṭi*-designation, by [Pāṇini 4.1.15] the suffix *ṅīp* is applied after the word *nada*, resulting in the elision of the vowel [by Pāṇini 6.4.148], and by [Pāṇini 6.1.161] the *ṅīp* receives the udātta accent. Thus, the word *nadī* has its final syllable accented.
By the *Phiṭ-sūtra* "pāṭalā-pālaṅkāmbā-sāgara-arthānām" (Phiṭ-sūtra 1.2), the word *samudra* has its final syllable accented.
Regarding the term *rājasūdaḥ*:
the word *sūda* is listed after the six [categories].
Therefore, in this case, there is only the udātta accent on the final syllable of the compound.

And all those terms, such as *darbhakāṇḍa* and others, are genitive compounds (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*). Regarding the word *kuṇḍa*, it occurs here in the sense of a forest because of its similarity to a *kuṇḍa*.
Just as a bower (*kuṇja*) is a shelter for water and the like, so too is a forest;
therefore, the word *kuṇḍa* is used here for a forest by virtue of its resemblance to a bower.
For there is indeed the application of a term by virtue of similarity, as in the cases of "fire-gem" (*agni-maṇi*) and "fire-owl" (*agni-vaka*).
As for the expression "clay-bowl" (*mṛt-kuṇḍa*): here, the term *kuṇḍa* refers to a specific shape found in a modification of clay, not in a forest.

Therefore, only the udātta accent on the final syllable of the compound occurs. The term *bhagālam* is used here to capture the meaning (*arthagrahaṇa*); for the instruction is primarily concerned with the meaning, as it has been stated that when an instruction is primarily concerned with the meaning, there is no apprehension of the formal word itself (*svarūpagrahaṇa*).
And since the meaning is being captured, this grammatical operation is understood to apply to those words which express that meaning.
For this very reason, he says: "expressing *bhagāla*," and so forth.
Regarding the term *kumbhībhāgālam*:
the word *kumbhī* is oxytone because it ends in the feminine suffix *ṅīṣ*, according to the rule *jāter astrīviṣayādayopadhāt* [Pāṇini 4.1.63].
The words *bhagāla* and others are cited as being middle-accented.

Because the *Phiṭ-sūtra* (2.42), "In the case of two [words], many [words], and *guru*, [the first syllable is] acute," prescribes the acute accent for the vowel *ā* in these [words]. Regarding "śitipādaḥ":
the word *śiti* is acute on its first syllable by the *Phiṭ-sūtra* (2.33), "Of colors ending in *ta*, *ṇa*, *ti*, or *ni*.
Regarding "the words *aṃsau* and *oṣṭha*" and so forth...
Is it from the root *ama* (Dhātupāṭha 1720)? The word *asa*, ending in the suffix *san*, is derived according to [Pāṇini] 3.2.21 (*amaḥ san*).

The word *oṣṭha* also ends in the suffix *than*, according to [Uṇādi Sūtra] 6.29 (*uṣikuṣigarttibyasthan*). Therefore, because these two suffixes are *nit*, both words are udātta on their first syllable.
Regarding the term "darśanīyapādaḥ": the word *darśanīya* ends with the suffix *anīyar*. By [Pāṇini 6.1.217], it has the middle udātta accent.
Consequently, in this case, the original accent (*prakṛtisvara*) of the first member remains.
The same applies to the subsequent counter-examples as well.
But how is it that the word *kakuda* is not always polysyllabic (*bahvac*)? To answer this, he says: "There is elision [of the final syllable] of *kakuda* when it denotes a state," and so forth.
Regarding "śitilalāṭaḥ":

from the verbal root *lala* in the sense of "desire" (Dhātupāṭha 1687), the suffix *āṭ* is applied according to [Pāṇini 3.3.1], whereby the word *lalāṭa* has its acute accent (*udātta*) on the first syllable. Regarding "śitipādaḥ": [the same applies].
In the case of *śiteḥ pādaḥ*, the accent of the compound itself occurs.
The word *bhasat* is derived [in the sense of "the buttocks"] by the rule *śṛdṛbhasodiḥ* (Dhātupāṭha 6.42), whereby it ends in the suffix *di*;
consequently, this [compound] has an udātta accent on the final syllable, as in *prakārakaḥ* and *prahārakaḥ*.

The suffix *ṇvul* [is applied] in cases such as "prakāra"; the suffix *lyuṭ* in cases such as "prakaraṇa"; and the suffix *khal* [is applied] in cases such as "īṣatkara" according to the rule "īṣadduḥsuṣu."

In this case, where there is an indeclinable as the first member of the compound, the formation is a *tatpuruṣa* according to the rule "in a *tatpuruṣa*, [when the first member has] a meaning similar to 'equal' (tulyārtha)" [Pāṇini 2.1.49]. Regarding the term "from a *kāraka*," it should be understood that the genitive case is used for the object *kāraka* by the rule "the sixth case is used for the agent and the object when a *kṛt*-suffix follows" [Pāṇini 2.3.65].

For fuel (*idhma*) and the like undergo the status of the object (*karman*) because they are that which is most desired to be pervaded by the action of cutting. However, in cases such as *īṣatkaraḥ*, the compound is formed by [Pāṇini 2.2.19].
In that instance, the word *pra-* is acute-accented on its first syllable according to [Phiṭ-sūtra 4.81]: "And prepositions (*upasarga*), with the exception of *abhi*."
For the word *idhma* is oxytone because it ends in the suffix *mak*, according to the rule *iṣiyudhīndhi-* (Pāṇini 3.3.97).

[The root] *śo* (meaning "to sharpen" or "to thin") is listed as Dhp 1.145; from *śyatoti* (the reading *śyatoti* is found in the *Mudrita* manuscript) is derived *palāśa*. It is oxytone either by the accent of the whole compound (*kṛtsvara*) or by the accent of the *athādi* group (Pāṇini 6.2.143).

When the suffix *ṇic* is added to the root *śad*, the substitution of *t* for *ś* is applied by the rule *śaderagatau taḥ* [Pāṇini 7.3.42]; subsequently, with the suffix *lyuṭ*, the form *śātanaḥ* arises.
When the substitution of *l* for *ś* is applied to the root *śri* before the suffix *man* by the rule *śmani śrayater ḍan* [Daiva 1.161], the form *kalpanaḥ* arises.
The word *īṣat* has its final syllable accented (*antodātta*), because it is listed as such among the words beginning with *svarādi*.

*Sudurāvādya* are acute (udātta); this is because they are listed as such among the *prādi* group. "In all these cases, the accent belongs to the *lit* suffix"—that is to say, the preceding element [before the suffix] receives the acute accent.
"The genitive in *devadattasya* is a genitive characterized as a residual relation (*śeṣa-lakṣaṇā*).
This refutes the status of the genitive as one denoting the object (*karma-ṣaṣṭhī*).

For if it were a genitive of the object, Devadatta would be nothing other than a grammatical factor (*kāraka*), and in that case, the counter-example (*pratyudāharaṇa*) would not be logically possible.

Now, what is the purpose of including the term *kāraka* [in the definition]? If you say it is so that [the designation of *gati*] does not apply in cases such as *niṣkauśāmbiḥ* ("departed from Kauśāmbī"), this is not correct. For it has been stated: "Prefixes (*prādayaḥ*) which are connected with an action receive the designations of *gati* and *upasarga* in relation to that [action]" (Jainendra-vṛtti 99). Since the word *kauśāmbī* does not denote an action, how could *nis* receive the designation of *gati* in relation to it here? To this, he says: "The inclusion of the term *kṛt* is for the sake of clarity. If, then, the term *kṛt* is included, the rule regarding the elision of the final vowel of a *para-kṛt* suffix would not apply in a case such as *prapacatitarām*.
And in that case, would not the accent of the indeclinable (*avyaya*) prevail, overriding the accent of the compound (*samāsa*)? To this he says: *prapacatitarām*, etc.
For here, after the word *pacati*, the suffixes *tarap* and *tama* are added when there is a desire to express excellence.
Then, by the rule *praśabdasya samāsaḥ* [Pāṇini 2.2.18], the word *pra* forms a compound with the element ending in *tarap*.
But when the compound has been formed, the original accent (*prakṛtisvara*) of the first member applies by the rule *tatpuruṣaṃ tulyārtha* [Pāṇini 6.2.2] and others.

Subsequently, the suffix *ām* is added by the rule *kimettiṅavyaya* [Pāṇini 5.4.11]. Regarding the suffix-final *ām*, the accent of the affix (*pratyayasvara*) would be expected by the rule *āmaḥ* [Pāṇini 6.1.161]; however, since that occurs when the indeclinable accent is already present, it is *satiśiṣṭa* (occurring when another is already established). And it has been stated that what is *satiśiṣṭa* possesses greater force.

Therefore, although the original accent (*prakṛtisvara*) would apply when the term *kṛt* is included in this [rule] for the sake of *ām*, nevertheless, the accent of *ām* indeed prevails; for that [accent] is *satiśiṣṭa* (left remaining by the rules of successive application). Now, how then can there be a compound with that which ends in *tarap* and so on? And why should it not be so? Because of the rule: "The statement regarding the compounding of *gati*s, *kāraka*s, and *upapada*s with *kṛt*-derived forms occurs prior to the arising of case-endings" (Pāṇini-vārttika 88)? This is not a fault; for in this matter there are two views: one view holds that the compounding of *gati*s, *kāraka*s, and *upapada*s occurs only with *kṛt*-derived forms, and that [compounding] takes place prior to the arising of case-endings.

A compound occurs without distinction for words denoting direction (*gati*), agent (*kāraka*), or secondary member (*upapada*), but with *kṛt*-derived suffixes, it occurs prior to the production of case endings (*sup*); this is the second view.
In that regard, according to these two perspectives, a compound with a word ending in *tarap* or similar suffixes is indeed appropriate.
In that context, the mention of *kṛt* is connected to [the statement] "for the sake of clarity."
The meaning is that some teachers explain the inclusion of the term *kṛt* simply for the sake of clarity.
As for the phrase "but [it is used] for the sake of *deśya* and so forth," the word "but" (*tu*) serves to highlight the distinction from the previous explanation.

That which has "prapacatideśya" as its beginning is "prapacatideśyādi. By the word "ādi" (beginning), the term "prapacatideśīya" is included. That whose purpose or objective is "prapacatideśyādi" is "prapacatideśyādyartham."

"The mention of *kṛt* [suffixes] is observed. Thus, in the rule [Pāṇini 5.3.67], because [the word] *tiṅ* from [Pāṇini 5.3.56] continues to apply, the suffixes *deśya* and *deśīya* are added to the word *prapacati*. And when the prefix *pra-* forms a *gati*-compound with that which ends in those [suffixes], the mention of *kṛt* would not have been made [if it were not necessary].
Likewise, in cases such as *prapacatideśyaḥ* and *prapacativeśīyaḥ*, the original accent (*prakṛtisvara*) of the final member would also apply, yet this is not desired.
Therefore, the inclusion of the term *kṛt* is indeed observed here for the purpose of preventing [the application of the accent] in such instances.
Consequently, this [interpretation] is not for the sake of clarity.

The intention [of the rule] is that this [accentuation] should not apply in cases such as *prapacatideśya*. The word *vana* is udātta on its first syllable by the rule *nabviṣayasyānisantasya* (Phiṭ-sūtra 2.26).
The word *pati* is also [udātta on the first syllable] by the accent of the suffix;
it ends in the suffix *ḍati* according to the rule *pāterḍatiḥ* (Dhātu-pāṭha 1.27).
"Is *bṛhat* accented on the final syllable? and so forth.

Although the word *bṛhat* is prescribed as being exclusively accented on the final syllable by the rule "In the sense of the present tense, [the words] *pṛṣat*, *bṛhat*, *mahat*, *jagat*, and those ending in the suffix *śatṛ* [are treated as such]" (*Dhātupāṭha-Uṇādi* 65), nevertheless, in the case of *bṛhaspati*, it prescribes accentuation on the initial syllable.
[This is explained by the statement: "The suffix *ū* is an *auṇādika* [derivative] from the root *tan*."
By the rule *kaṣicamitaniṣanisarjikharjibhyauuḥ* (Pāṇini 5.1.82), the word *tanū* has its final syllable accented (*antodātta*).
By the phrase "it does not protect" (*na pāti na pālayati*), he shows that [the form] *asamānnapād* is derived as a nipātana from the root *pā* "to protect" (Dhātupāṭha 1056).
This is also shown by the phrase "it does not cause to fall" (*na pātayati*).

The elision of *n* (nalopa) would apply by [Pāṇini 6.3.73], but it does not occur because of the preservation of the original form (*prakṛtibhāva*) by [Pāṇini 6.3.74], *nabhrāṇnapāt*, etc. [The example is] "men seated in this [place] praise" (*narā asminnāsīnāḥ śaṃsanti*). By this, he shows that the word *śaṃsa* has the locus (*adhikaraṇa*) as its grammatical factor (*sādhana*). Likewise, by the word *śaṃsanti*, it also has the object (*karman*) as its grammatical factor.
Is it from the root *śaṃs* in the sense of "praising" (Dhātupāṭha 728)? [The suffix] *ghañ* is applied by [Pāṇini 3.3.19], *aṅ kartari ca kārake*. It ends in *a* because of [Pāṇini 3.3.57], *ṛdorap*.
Regarding the term *śunaḥśepaḥ*:
this is a *bahuvrīhi* compound.
Consequently, since the original form (*prakṛtibhāva*) of the first member would otherwise apply here, this specific rule is stated.
"Both have the acute accent on the first syllable.

In that regard, the word *āñ* is derived from the root *āp* with the suffix *kanin* according to the rule *ānnukṣan* (Daiva 6.55). The word *śeṣa* is derived from the roots *vṛṅ* and *śīṅ* with the suffix *asun* and the augment *puṭ* according to the rule *vṛṅśīṅabhyāṃ rūpasvāṅgayoḥ puṭ ca* (Daiva 9.61); thus, both of them have the acute accent on the first syllable.
Regarding the words *śaṇḍa* and *parka*:
from the root *śaḍi* in the sense of "sickness" (*rujāyām*) [Dhātupāṭha 279], the form *śaṇḍa* is derived with the suffix *ghañ*;
likewise, from the root *pṛcī* in the sense of "contact" (*samparke*) [Dhātupāṭha 1462], the form *parka* is derived in that very same manner.

"The word *tṛṣṇā* has its initial syllable accented" means that it is derived from the root *tṛṣ* with the suffix *niṣṭhā*; therefore, by [Pāṇini 6.1.205], it has an acute accent on the first syllable.
Regarding the word *vamba*:

it is derived from the root *lavi* (or *labi*) in the sense of "covering" (*avaruñchane*)—as found in the Dhātupāṭha (379)—by adding the suffix *ac* according to the rule *pacādyac*, and by this very irregular derivation (*nipātana*), the substitution of *va* for *la* occurs.
Regarding the word *viāvaya*.
The term *viāṃvayaḥ* is a *bahuvrīhi* compound.
In that case, by the rule *bahuvrīhau viāṃ saṃjñāyām* [Pāṇini 6.2.106], the word *viāṃ* has its final syllable accented (*antodātta*).
Regarding the phrase *tayoḥ*:
Regarding the words *vambavi* and *āyaḥśabda*, [the rule] states:
"The suffix *vic* is applied after the root *mṛ*" [reading *mṛñaḥ* in the *Kāśikā*; reading *mṛḍaḥ* in the *Padamañjarī*].
Following from *[[3.2.73]]* (*vijitya*), by the rule *[[3.3.130]]* (*dṛśyante*—Kāśikā), the suffix *vic* is applied.

The word *mṛtyu* has its final syllable accented (*antodātta*) because it ends in the suffix *tyuk*, according to the rule *bhujīmṛṅbhyāṃ yuktyukau* (Daiva-Uṇādi 1.135). Regarding the phrase "of dvandvas," and so forth...
Regarding the *dvandva* compounds mentioned here, their recitation is for the purpose of excluding those that are *devatā-dvandva* (dual compounds of deities).
For in the case of *devatā-dvandva*, the formation is already established by [Pāṇini 6.2.141].
Furthermore, [the rule] "when the second member begins with an *anudātta* vowel" applies.
The listing of *dvandva* compounds [is necessary].

For if their listing were not present here, then by the prohibition in [Pāṇini 6.2.142], the final syllable would be udātta. Thus, in "Indrāsomau," the substitution of *anaṅ* for the first member occurs by [Pāṇini 6.3.26]: "And in a *devatā-dvandva*."
Regarding the passage beginning with "ṛjrendra":

following the rule "from the roots vṛdhi and vap, the suffix ran" (Dhātupāṭha-Uṇādi 8.45), the word "indra" ending in the suffix *ran* is established as an irregular form (*nipātana*) by the rule "ṛjrendraḥ" (Uṇādi 8.46); therefore, it is acutely accented on the first syllable.
As for "soma," it ends in the suffix *man*.

The intention is that for this reason, it too has the udātta accent on its first syllable. Furthermore, its ending in the suffix *man* is established by deriving the suffix *man* from the root *ṣuñ* (meaning "to press") according to the rule *artti-stu-su-hu-ruc-vañcu-śvibhyaśca* (Dhātupāṭha 7.26). As for the statement, "Varuṇa ends in the suffix *unan*," [it refers to another derivation].

Regarding the rule *kṛvṛdāribhya unan* (Pāṇini 3.2.173), the word *bṛhaspati* is indeed listed among the group beginning with *vanaspati*; in that context, simultaneous acute accentuation (*ādyudāttatva*) is prescribed for both the preceding and following members of the compound, whereby there are two acute accents. Thus, in the expression *tenendrābṛhaspatī*, those [syllables] are acute.
The words beginning with *indra* [are included].
In the case of "plakṣanyagrodhau," there is only the udātta accent on the final syllable of the compound.
The same applies here to the word *agniṣṭomaḥ*.

This is a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*), and the present rule is an exception (*apavāda*) to the accentuation of compounds. [According to the rule,] the words *agni* and *vāyu* are udātta on their final syllable.

The word *agni* ends in the suffix *ni*, being derived from the rule "from *vī*, *jū*, and *ajū*, *ni*" (*daṇḍa-uṇādi* 1.18), while the suffix *ni* is applied by the rule "after *aṅg*, there is elision [of the root vowel]" (*daṇḍa-uṇādi* 1.20).

The word *vāyu* also ends in the suffix *uṇ*, according to the rule "from *kṛ*, *vā*, *pā*, and *aji*" (*daṇḍa-uṇādi* 1.86); thus, by the accent of the suffix, both words are oxytone (having the acute accent on the final syllable).

Now, what is the purpose of mentioning the term "subsequent member" (*uttarapada*), since the locative case in the phrase "in that which begins with an anudātta" (*anudāttādau*) itself would indicate that the word beginning with an anudātta is the subsequent member? To this, he says: "The mention of the subsequent member," and so forth.
For in this context, the *dvandva* compound is specified by the locative case, not the final member (*uttarapada*).
Consequently, the locative phrase "in that which begins with an unaccented vowel" (*anudāttādau*) becomes a qualifier of the *dvandva* itself—meaning "a *dvandva* beginning with an unaccented vowel.

However, if the term "final member" (*uttarapada*) were included, then when the locative is prescribed for the *dvandva*, the phrase "beginning with an unaccented vowel" would become a qualifier of the final member.

Therefore, the mention of the word "uttarapada" (the final member of a compound) is for the purpose that this [rule] should serve as a qualifier of the final member and not as a qualifier of the *dvandva* [compound] itself.
Regarding the phrase "anudāttādau" (beginning with an unaccented vowel):

if this qualification were absent, both the injunction (*vidhi*) and the prohibition (*pratiṣedha*) would apply to the *devatā-dvandva* [compound] without distinction; consequently, there would be no differentiation between their respective domains, and thus, because they would share the same domain, an option (*vikalpa*) would result.

If, however, the rule were simply *anudāttādau* ("when beginning with an unaccented vowel"), then the prohibition would apply only where the latter member of a dual compound of deities (*devatādvandva*) begins with an unaccented vowel; for all other cases, the general injunction would apply. Thus, there would be a distinction between the scope of the injunction and the prohibition. Therefore, the term *anudāttādau* is stated in order to clearly define this distinction of scope. [The word] *pṛthivī* "ends with the suffix *ṅīṣ*."
Because [the word] is listed among *gaura* and others;
and because of the rule "after *rud*, there is *ṇi*-elision" (*roderṇiluk ca*).

From the root *rudir* "to shed tears" (Dhātupāṭha 1067), after the causative suffix (*ṇic*), the suffix *rak* is applied by the rule "after *rud*, there is *ṇi*-elision" (*roderṇiluk ca*)—with the word *rak* being understood from the preceding sūtra "after *sphāyi*, *tañci*, etc. (Daiva 8.31). Consequently, *rudra* has its final syllable accented acute (*antodātta*).

Regarding the term *śukrāmanthinau*: the word *śukra* is formed with the suffix *ran* according to the rule *ṛjendra-* (Pāṇini 6.1.127), and by that rule, it is ādyudātta (accented on the first syllable). [The objection is: "In this case, the second member of the compound would be ādyudātta by virtue of the rule *kṛduttarapadaprakṛtisvara* (Pāṇini 6.2.139).
The sense is: "if this [present sūtra] were not commenced."

Regarding the statement, "the suffix *ath* is applied to the root *vas* when preceded by a prefix," since the suffix *ath* is understood from the rule "after the roots *śīṅ*, *śap*, *ru*, *gam*, *i*, and *vañc*" (*Dhātupāṭha* 6.38), the final member of the compound would be oxytone due to the preservation of the original accent of the final member of a *kṛt*-derived compound. [This would result in] "dūrādāgataḥ" (come from afar).

The suffix *kta* is applied to the root *gam*, the nasal is elided by the rule beginning with "anudāttopadeśa" (Pāṇini 6.4.37), a compound is formed with the word *āgata* by the rule beginning with "ātaścopasarge" (Pāṇini 3.1.136), and there is no elision of the *a* by the rule "gamah" (Pāṇini 6.4.40).
Regarding the form *śuṣkaḥ* (or *viśuṣkaḥ* according to the Kāśikā and Padamañjarī), the substitution of *ka* for *kta* occurs by the rule "śuṣka-dhṛṣṭau" (Pāṇini 6.1.27).

In both cases here, the suffix *niṣṭhā* [is applied]. Since the rule *tatra* (Pāṇini 6.2.49) would otherwise apply, this [present rule] prescribes the acute accent on the final syllable of the second member (*uttarapada*) as an exception to that. However, when the suffix *kta* denotes the agent (*kartari*), then by the accent of the *kṛt*-suffix (*kṛtsvara*), the second member retains its original form (*prakṛtibhāva*), and thus the acute accent on the final syllable is already established.

But surely, since *śuṣ* has "drying" (*śoṣaṇa*) as its object, how can it have a passive past participle (*niṣṭhā*)? There is no fault here, because the root, having the causative sense (*ṇyartha*) implied within it, becomes transitive. Thus, in the example *ātapaśuṣkam* (or *ātapaśuṣkaḥ*), the compound is formed according to [Pāṇini 2.1.32].

In this case, by the rule *tatpuruṣe tulyārtha* [Pāṇini 6.2.2] and others, the first member of the compound would take its original accent (*pūrvapada-prakṛtisvara*). Furthermore, since the first member here ends in the suffix *ac* (from the *pacādi* group), it is acutely accented on the final syllable by the rule for *kṛt* suffixes (*kṛtsvara*), as in *prakṣayaḥ* and *prajayaḥ*.

Regarding *erac* [Pāṇini 3.3.56]: One might ask, "Will not the final syllable of the second member (*uttarapada*) here be udātta by virtue of the rule *kṛduttarapadaprakṛtisvaratva* (the accent of the first member of a compound with a kṛt-derivative as the second member)? To this he says: "*kṣayo nivāse*" and so forth.

When the words *kṣaya* and *jaya* are udātta on the first syllable according to [Pāṇini 6.1.201] and [6.1.202], then by the accent of the kṛt-suffix (*kṛtsvara*), they would become udātta on the middle syllable. Examples are *pralavitram* and *prasavitram*.

By the rule *artilūdhūsūkhan- [Pāṇini 3.2.184]* and so forth, the suffix *itra* is applied. In this case, since the accent of the *kṛt*-suffix would apply, the accent of the suffix itself would prevail; consequently, the final member of the compound would be accented on the middle syllable (*madhyodātta*).
Regarding "govṛṣaḥ":

since the roots *pṛṣu*, *vṛṣu*, and *mṛṣu* mean "to sprinkle" (*secane*; Dhātupāṭha 705, 706, 707), there would be a compound according to [Pāṇini 2.2.19], and by [Pāṇini 6.2.139] the initial vowel of the second member would be udātta.
Regarding "sustutam": [the same applies].
By [Pāṇini 1.4.94] and [1.4.95], the words *sva* and *ati* receive the designation of *karmapravacanīya*.
"In this case, only the accent of the indeclinable (*avyaya*) occurs," according to [Pāṇini 6.2.2], *tatpuruṣe tulyārtha*, etc. As in the example *supītam*.
The substitution of *i* is applied by the rule *ghumāsthā* [Pāṇini 6.4.66]. Regarding the form *vṛkāvaluptam*: the root *lup* (meaning "to cut off") is found at number 1431 in the Dhātupāṭha.
Regarding "leaping like a hare":
the roots *cyuṅ*, *jyuṅ*, *pruṅ*, and *pluṅ* mean "to go" (Dhātupāṭha 955, 956, 957, 958).
Regarding "the lion's roar."

The word *nard* is listed as "to sound" in the Dhātupāṭha (56). The compound is formed according to Pāṇini 2.1.32 (*sarvatra*). The analytical explanation (*vigraha*) is "leaped upon by wolves," and so forth. Regarding the form *upahūtaḥ*:

it is the past passive participle (*niṣṭhā*) of the root *hveñ*; there is vocalization (*saṃprasāraṇa*) according to Pāṇini 6.1.15 (*vacisvapi* etc.), and lengthening according to Pāṇini 6.4.2 (*halapaḥ*).
Regarding the term *parijagdhaḥ*: by [Pāṇini 2.4.36], *jagdhi* is the substitute for the root *ad*;
and by [Pāṇini 8.2.40], *gh* is substituted for *d* following a *jhaṣ* consonant that is not followed by *dh*.

Regarding the rule "the suffix *kta* is used in the sense of the object" (*karmaṇi ktaḥ*): since the root *bhū* is intransitive, the formation of a past passive participle (*niṣṭhā*) in the sense of the object would not be appropriate. Consequently, someone might mistakenly think that in the word *sambhūtaḥ*, this *niṣṭhā* is used in the sense of the agent (*kartari*). To dispel that misconception, he says: "*sambhūtaḥ*. Because verbal roots have multiple meanings, here the root *bhū* functions in the sense of "attaining" (*prāptau*).
Furthermore, those roots whose meaning involves "attainment" (*prāpti*) necessarily become transitive (*sakarmaka*) through the very act of attaining.

For example, *ṇīñ* "to lead/bring" (Dhātupāṭha 901), and so forth. Therefore, in the case of *bhavateḥ sambhūtaḥ*, the suffix *kta* is applied to the root *bhū* in its sense of attainment, with reference to the object (*karman*).

What, then, is the reason that the suffix *kta* is desired after a verbal root expressing an object (*karman*)? He says: "In the rule *gati-r-anantaraḥ*, the term *karmani* (after an object) is understood to carry over. [Question: What follows from that? [Answer: He says: "And this [present rule] is for the purpose of setting aside that [previous rule].
For in the rule [Pāṇini 6.2.49], the term *karmani* indeed carries over.
And this sūtra is for the purpose of setting aside that very [rule] beginning with *tat* (Pāṇini 6.2.49).
In this way, it becomes a sublater of the accent of motion (*gatisvara*), provided that the suffix *kta* is prescribed in the sense of the object (*karman*).
By this rule, the final syllable of the subsequent member ending in that [suffix] is prescribed as udātta; it is not otherwise.
Therefore, the intention is that in the word *sambhūta*, the suffix *kta* is to be understood as having the sense of the object (*karman*). As in the example *dhanuṣkhātā*:
[the root] *khan* means "digging" (*avadāraṇe*) [Dhātupāṭha 878]; [here] the substitution of *ā* [for *an*] occurs by [Pāṇini 6.4.42]: *janasanakhanām*.
Thus is the compound [formed] according to [Pāṇini 2.1.32]. The same applies to forms such as *kuddālakhātā* and others.
The word *dhanus* has its first syllable accented acute by the rule *nabviṣayasyānisantasya* (Phiṭ-sūtra 2.26).
The word *kuddāla* has its middle syllable accented acute (*madhyodātta*) by the rule *laghāv ante* (Phiṭ-sūtra 2.42).

Regarding the term *hastimṛditā*: the root *mṛd* means "to crush" (Dhātupāṭha 1515); the word *hasti* is acutely accented on the final syllable because it ends in the suffix *ini* according to [Pāṇini 5.2.133].
Regarding "āsthāpitam": from the root *sthā* with the suffix *ṇic*, the augment *puk* is applied by [Pāṇini 7.3.36] *arti-hrī-*, etc. Regarding "parigṛhītam".
Regarding "niruktam": from the verbal root *vac* in the sense of "speaking" (Dhātupāṭha 1842), there is vocalization (*samprasāraṇa*) according to Pāṇini 6.1.15, etc., resulting in [the form] *ukta*.
Regarding "pratipannam": [it means] "understood."
The root *pad* (in the sense of "going," Dhātupāṭha 1169) undergoes the substitution of *n* [for *d*] by the rule *radābhyām* [Pāṇini 8.2.42].
Regarding the word *praśliṣṭam*:
the root *ṣliṣ* (in the sense of "embracing," Dhātupāṭha 1186).
Regarding the word *upadrūtam*: [the root] *du* and *dru* mean "to go" (*dhātupāṭha* 944, 945). Regarding the word *sthitam*:
the substitution of *ī* for *u* occurs by the rule beginning with *dyatisyati* (Pāṇini 7.4.40).
Regarding the term *saṃhitā*:
there is the substitution of *hi* for the root *dhā*. This statement is made because the accent of a *gati* [prefix] would otherwise apply.
Regarding *pravṛddham*, it is derived from the root *vṛdhu* in the sense of "growth" (Dhātupāṭha 759). Regarding *prayutāḥ*, the *Kāśikā* reads *prayuktāḥ*.
From the root *yu* in the sense of "mixing" (Dhātupāṭha 1033), we have the form *avahitam*. Here, as before, there is the substitution of *hi* for the root *dhā*.
As for the form *khaṭvārūḍhaḥ*:

In the case of *ruha-bīja-janmani* (Dhātupāṭha 859), the compound is formed according to [Pāṇini 2.1.26], following [8.2.40], [8.3.13], and [6.3.111]. When the rule [6.2.47] would have required the original accent (*prakṛtisvara*) of the first member, this specific reading is provided here: *kaviśastaḥ*.

The root *śas* is used in the sense of "injury" (*hiṃsā*) [Dhātupāṭha 727]. The compound is formed according to Pāṇini 2.1.32. For this [compound] as well, the original accent of the first member (*pūrvapada-prakṛtisvara*) applies by Pāṇini 6.2.48.
This refers to the rule "of *yāna* and so forth."
By the word "etc. (*ādi*), bulls and others are included.
The mention here of objects such as vehicles (*yāna*) is for the purpose of demonstrating the general or predominant usage of the term *pravṛddha* with respect to objects like vehicles and so forth;
however, it does not mean that *pravṛddha* becomes oxytone when applied to the two meanings of "vehicle" and "outcaste" (*vṛṣala*).
The purpose of the word *prayukta* in rules such as "in the case of *saktu*s only" (*saktūnām eva*) is to restrict the scope of the application (*viṣayaniyamārtha*).
To the question, "What will result from this? he says: "Even in cases other than those beginning with *yāna*" (*yānādibhyo 'nyatrāpi*), and so forth.
Some say, "[It is] for the purpose of restricting the scope."
For them, by this [rule], it should not occur except in the case of *yāna* and so forth;

for [the author] says, "This undertaking is for the purpose of excluding the technical term (*saṃjñā*)," since [the desired form] would already be established by the preceding rule in the case of a technical term.

"And the *pravṛddha* group should be regarded as an *ākṛtigaṇa* (an open-ended class). Why is this so? Because the particle *ca* is used here for the purpose of including what has not been mentioned, thereby indicating its status as an *ākṛtigaṇa*. To demonstrate what is established by its being an *ākṛtigaṇa*, he says: "a garment that has been sewn again," and so forth. [The root] *ṣivu* (meaning "to sew," Dhātupāṭha 1108) takes the augment *ūṭh* by [Pāṇini 6.4.19], *ṣṭhivuklamucamāṃ śitī ṅtvāṣṭhivuklamucamām ca*, and then the *yaṇ*-substitution occurs.

Regarding the term "punarniṣkṛtaḥ": the substitution of *ṣ* for the *visarjanīya* is according to [Pāṇini 8.3.41], "And [the *visarjanīya*] of that which has *i* or *u* as its penultimate letter, provided it is not an affix. The particle *iti* is used for the purpose of indicating the meaning.
Regarding the term "āpannaḥ": [it is formed by adding the suffix *kta*].
The meaning is "attained.

Regarding the term *suptapralapitam*: the roots *rap* and *lap* mean "to speak articulately" (*dhātupāṭha* 401, 402). Here, the state of being asleep (*suptatva*) has become the manner [of speaking]; by that, the pralāpita (incoherent speech) was produced. In this case, a compound (*samāsa*) occurs.
"Uttered by one who is insane":
here too, insanity has become the manner [of speaking], and thus it was "pralāpitaṃ," i.e., uttered. "Sung by one who is intoxicated."
In this case as well, negligence has reached its full extent; for that reason, he sang [the verse].
[The root] *gai* (in the sense of "sound") is found in the Dhātupāṭha (916, 917). By the rule *ghumāsthā* (Pāṇini 6.4.66) and others, the substitution of *i* occurs.
[The term is] *vipannaśrutam*.

In this case as well, the state of being "perished" (vipannatva) has attained the status of a subordinate member; thus, by the rule *sarvatra* [Pāṇini 2.1.32], a compound is formed. Therein, the word *supta* is oxytone due to the accent of the suffix (*pratyayasvara*).

If the word *pralapita* has the suffix *niṣṭhā* in the sense of the object (*karman*), then by the rule "the *gati* [preceding] another [word]" (Pāṇini 6.2.49), it is acute-accented on the first syllable due to the accent of the *gati*. If, however, it is in the sense of the action (*bhāva*), then by the rule for the suffixes beginning with *tha* (Pāṇini 6.2.143), it is acute-accented on the final syllable.

In this same manner, words such as *utpanna*, *āpanna*, and *vipanna*, which have arisen through similar formations, are also acute-accented on the final syllable by the rule for the suffixes beginning with *tha*.
However, the rule [6.2.49] does not apply here; for in that context, the term "in the sense of the object" (*karmani*) is understood as a governing requirement (*anuvṛtti*).

In this case, since the suffix *kta* cannot occur in the sense of the object (*karman*) after an intransitive root, the words *gīta* and *śruta*—like the word *supta*—are oxytone (accented on the final syllable). Now, how are these examples to be understood, given that this [rule] refers to the meaning "done by one who is in such a state" (*ityambhūtena kṛtam*), where "done" (*kāryam*) is what is expressed? This meaning is not possible here, because in words such as *pralapita*, the sense of being "done" is absent; for the root *kṛ* does not apply to the acts of prattling (*pralapanādi*) in the context at hand.
For the root *kṛ* (to do/make) functions specifically with respect to the manifestation of what was previously non-existent (*abhūtaprādurbhāva*), and not with respect to speaking and so forth.
To dispel the objection—"Why is it not produced by speaking and so forth?"—he says: "The term 'produced' (*kṛta*) refers to action in general," and so on.
For does the root *kṛ* function only with respect to the manifestation of what was previously non-existent? On the contrary, it also functions with respect to action in general.
And that general action exists even in the case of speaking; by means of that [general action], each instance of speaking and so forth becomes something performed.
This refers to the rule "the third case [is used] when there is an object" (*tṛtīyā karmaṇi*).
Regarding the phrase "the original accent of the first member [is maintained]":

by the words beginning with "yadi" (if), he demonstrates its lack of utility when the *niṣṭhā* suffix occurs in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāva*). The term "from a kāraka" (kārakāt) is understood to carry over [from the previous rule]. By the paribhāṣā concerning the mention of a suffix (pratyayagrahaṇaparibhāṣā), it is understood that the word ending in that suffix is what is being referred to. To this, he says: "ending in the suffix *ana*" (*anapratyayāntam*), and so forth.
In all instances such as "odanabhojanam" (the eating of rice), there is a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*).
The sixth case ending (*ṣaṣṭhī*), however, is characterized by its connection with a *kṛt* suffix and is used in the sense of the object (*karman*).
In examples such as "rājabhojanāḥ" ("those who eat for the king"), it is used in the sense of the agent (*kartṛ*).
The word "odana" has its initial syllable accented acute (*ādyudātta*) according to the rule "laghāvante" (Phiṭ-sūtra 2.42).
The subsequent member of the compound, such as *bhojana*, is acutely accented on its first syllable by virtue of the accent rule for the suffix *liṭ*.
The word *payaḥ* is acutely accented on its first syllable by the rule *nabviṣayasya* (Phiṭ-sūtra 2.42).
The subsequent member of the compound, such as *bhojana*, is acutely accented on its first syllable by virtue of the accent rule for the suffix *liṭ*.
The word *payaḥ* is indeed udātta on its first syllable by the rule *nabviṣayasya* (Phiṭ-sūtra 2.26).
The compound *candanapriyaṅgukā* is a dvandva; therefore, by the accent of the compound (*samāsasvara*), it is udātta on its final syllable.
[The word] *lepanam*.
The form *lipa* is from the root *lipa upadehe* (Dhātupāṭha 1433). The word *rāja* has its accent as previously stated. The word *ācchādana* is a form of the root *chada apavāraṇe* (Dhātupāṭha 1935).
By the single rule beginning with *karmaṇi ca yena*, he shows that the suffix *lyuṭ* occurs both to express an action (*bhāva*) and to express an object (*karman*).

Regarding the word *hastahāryam*: the word *hasta* ends in the suffix *tan* by the rule *hasimṛgriṇavāmidamipūdhurvībhyastan* (Dhātupāṭha 6.7; Pañcapādī 3.86), and because of this, it is udātta on its first syllable.
The word *hārya*, however, ends in the suffix *ṇyat* according to Pāṇini 3.1.124 (*ṛhaloṇryat*); by the accentuation rule for such suffixes (*titsvareṇa*), its final syllable is svarita.
Regarding the word *dantadhāvana*:
it is derived from the root *dhāv* (meaning "to move" or "to clean," Dhātupāṭha 601) with the suffix *lyuṭ* in the sense of an instrument (*karaṇe*).
The word *danta* is udātta on its first syllable by the rule *svāṅgaśiṭām* (Pāṇini Phiṭ-sūtra 2.29).
Regarding the term *nidarśanam*:
the suffix *lyuṭ* is applied to the root *dṛś* in the sense of an abstract action (*bhāva*).
Regarding "avalekhanam":
here too, [the root] *likh* is used.
"In all counter-examples," and so forth.
By this, he shows that this [rule] is an exception (*apavāda*) to Pāṇini 6.2.138: *gatikārakopapadānāṃ kṛt*. The mention of the suffixes *man* and *ktin* refers to the suffixes themselves.

In that context, by the paribhāṣā regarding the mention of a suffix (Pu. Pa. Vṛ. 44), it is understood that what ends in those suffixes is intended; thus he says: "that which ends in *man* and that which ends in *ktin*.
*Rathavartma* and so forth are genitive compounds (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*).
It has been stated that the word *ratha* ends in the suffix *kthan* and is udātta on its first syllable.
From the root *vṛt* (meaning "to turn," Dhātupāṭha 748), the suffix *manin* is applied;
thus, the word *vartman* is udātta on its first syllable.
The words *śakaṭa* and *payaḥ* are acute-accented on the first syllable because they end in a *nit* suffix;
the words *pāṇini* and *āpiśali* are so because they end in the suffix *iñ*;
and the word *kṛti* is also so because it ends in the suffix *ktin*.
This word *vyākhyāna* is derived instrumentally (*karaṇasādhana*) and ends in the suffix *lyuṭ*;
it is accented on the middle syllable by the rule regarding the accent of *kṛt*-suffixes (*kṛtsvara*).

As for the word *chandas*, it is formed by the addition of the suffix *asun* according to the rule *asarvadhātubhyo 'sun* (Pāṇini 5.4.50). [Note: The correct reading of the sūtra is *asan*, as indicated by the Daiva-nirukti.]
In that case, because it ends with the suffix *asun* by the rule "ac-ander-ādeś-ca cchaḥ" (Pāṇini 5.2.128), it is udātta on the first syllable.
It is called *ayana* because one goes (*ayanti*) by means of it; thus, it is the *ayana* of the *ṛcs*.
