In the expression "of the *ṛcs*," the genitive case is used in the sense of the agent (*kartari*).
The word *ṛgayana* has its first syllable (*ṛ*) acute by the rule of the "entire word" accent (*kṛtsvara*).
Regarding the examples beginning with *rājaśayanam*:
that in which one lies is a *śayana* (bed), and that in which one sits is an *āsana* (seat). With those two words, there is a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*) with the words *rājan* and *brāhmaṇa*.
The words *rāja* and *brāhmaṇa* have their vowels accented as stated [in the rules].
The words *śayana* and *āsana* are udātta on the first syllable by virtue of the suffix *liṭ*.
Here, as before, the genitive case is used for the agent (*kartṛ*) because it is connected with a word ending in a *kṛt* suffix.
The same applies here in the case of *go-sthāna-m-āsthānam*:
the words *go* and *āśva* have the accents already mentioned;
*sthānam*—derived from the root *sthā* with the suffix *lyuṭ* (meaning "that in which one stands")—is udātta on its first syllable by the accent rule for *lit* suffixes.
In expressions such as *brāhmaṇayājyaḥ*, the genitive case is used for the object according to the rule governing connection with a *kṛt* suffix.

Among those [words] listed under "sacrificers and so forth" (*yājakādi*) that end in the suffix *ṇvul*: those that are without prefixes—namely *yājaka*, *pūjaka*, and *snāpaka*—have the acute accent on their first syllable.
However, those with prefixes—namely *pariveṣaka*, *adhyāpaka*, *udvartaka*, and *utsādaka*—have the acute accent on the middle syllable by virtue of the accentuation rule for *kṛt* suffixes.
The words *hotṛ* and *bhartṛ* cause the suffixes *tṛn* and *an* to be employed.
As for those two which end in *tṛc*, their final acute accent is established by the rule regarding the accent of *kṛt* suffixes (*kṛtsvara*),
as in *gokrītaḥ*, *ākrītaḥ*, and so forth.
These two are compounds by the rule *kartṛkaraṇe kṛtā* [Pāṇini 2.1.31].
The word *krīta* is oxytone due to the accent of its suffix. "This rule is an exception (*apavāda*) to the accentuation of a *kṛt*-suffix."
In other cases such as *mankita* and *tanvī*, which follow from the word *krīta*, [the rule applies];

however, in the case of the word *krīta*, because of the rule *tṛtīyā karmaṇaḥ* [Pāṇini 6.2.48], there is the original accent (*prakṛtisvara*) of the first member. This is according to the statement: "The mention of *vyākhyāna*, *śayana*, *āsana*, and *sthāna* includes those whose meaning is 'absence' or 'object'."
Since this is already established by the rule *bhāvakarmavacanasyānantasya* [Pāṇini 6.2.150],
[the forms] *prakṛtiḥ*, *prahmatiḥ*—
in these cases, by the rule *tulyārtha* [Pāṇini 6.2.2] and so forth, the first member of the compound retains its original accent (*prakṛtisvara*).
These two are examples of the summary of accentual classes (*gatisamāsa*). Regarding the phrase "adhyayanāpuṇyam" and so forth:
the word *adhyayana* ends in the suffix *lyuṭ*, and by the rule concerning the accent of *kṛt*-suffixes (*kṛtsvara*), it is middle-accented (*madhyodātta*).
As for *puṇya*, it is initial-accented (*ādyudātta*) according to the rule "of that which falls within the scope of *na*" (*nabviṣayasya*, Phiṭ-sūtra 2.26).
"Veda" is derived from the sense "that by which [something] is known," using the suffix *ghañ*;

thus, the word "veda" has its first syllable accented (*ādyudātta*). This statement—"in a *tatpuruṣa* compound, when the meaning is 'equal to' (*tulyārtha*)"—and so forth, is said by relying on the position that "the *uṇādi* suffixes produce underived nominal stems (*avyutpanna-prātipadika*)."
Now, relying on the perspective of etymological derivation (*vyutpatti*), he says: "But in the case of the *uṇādi* suffixes," and so forth.
For in the view that favors derivation, the word *puṇya* is derived from the root *puñ* with the suffix *yaṇṇuk* and a short vowel, according to [Pāṇini 5.1.123]: *puño yaṇṇug hrasvaśca*.

In that context, if this [rule] were not commenced, then by the accent of the *kṛt* suffix (Pāṇini 6.2.139), the word *puṇya* would be acute-accented on the first syllable, as in the case of *adhyayanam* and similar forms.
Therefore, the intention is that this rule for the acute accent on the final syllable applies to that [compound]. In the case of "vedapuṇyam" (merit through the Veda),
the compound is formed by the division of the rule "tṛtīyā" [Pāṇini 2.1.30] according to the method of etymological derivation (*vyutpatti*).
And there is the accentuation of the *kṛt*-suffix belonging to the subsequent member.

In the view that [the word] is not derived (*avyutpatti-pakṣa*), the compound is formed by [Pāṇini 2.1.32], and by the accent rule for *kṛt*-suffixes (Pāṇini 6.2.139), the word *puṇya* has its initial syllable accented acute (*ādyudātta*). Regarding the example "māṣona" ("less by a māṣa"), the compound is formed with the third case ending according to [Pāṇini 2.1.31] and so forth.
The same applies in cases such as *kārṣāpaṇona*.

From the verbal roots *kaṣ*, *khaṣ*, *śiṣ*, *jaṣ*, *jhaṣ*, *śaṣ*, *vaṣ*, and *maṣ* (Dhātupāṭha 685–692), the suffix *ghañ* is applied; thus, the word *māṣa* has its initial syllable accented (*ādyudātta*).
From the rule *iṇ-siñ-jidīṅ-uṣyavibhyo nak* (Daiva 5.36), the suffix *nak* is applied; thus, the word *una* has its final syllable accented (*antodātta*).
A *kārṣāpaṇa* is an *apaṇa* [worth] one *kārṣa*.
By the accentual rule for compounds (*samāsasvara*), the word *kārṣāpaṇa* has its final syllable accented (*antodātta*).
One from whom the *kala* (defect) has departed is *vikala*.
In a *bahuvrīhi* compound, by virtue of the original accent of the first member (*pūrvapada-prakṛtisvaratva*), the word *vikala* has its initial syllable accented (*ādyudātta*).

Regarding the term *asikalaha*: while the rule *aca iḥ* (Dhātupāṭha 1.67) is in effect, the rule *khanikaṣyañjyasi* (Dhātupāṭha 1.68) and others [apply], whereby the suffix *siN* is accented. From the root *kal* (meaning "to go," Dhātupāṭha 1865), the suffix *ac* is added according to the *pacādi* class.

It is called *kala* because it measures (*kalayati*). Because it destroys what is measured (*kalaṃ hanti*), the suffix *ḍa* is applied according to Pāṇini 3.2.101 (*anyeṣv api dṛśyate*). Thus, the word *kalaha* has its final syllable accented (*antodātta*). Regarding the phrase "In this regard, some [say]" and so forth: The word *kalaha* is derived from the root *kalah* (DhP 1.469), which means "to quarrel. Alternatively, it is derived from the root *kala* (DhP 1.470), meaning "to sound," with the suffix *ap*. In this case, the vowel *a* is substituted for the root vowel by Pāṇini 6.1.158 (*ato guṇe*); however, since that rule is superseded by Pāṇini 6.1.97 (*ād guṇaḥ*), the substitution of *guṇa* does not occur here. Consequently, the word *kalaha* is derived from the root *kala*, and its final syllable is accented. Alternatively, it is derived from the root *kala* (DhP 1.470) with the suffix *ap*. [Objection: If [the word] *tadartha* means "its own form" (*svarūpa*), then in the case of the word *ūna* as well, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasajyeta*) of it being taken as its own form; and consequently, other words having that same meaning would not be included. To this, he says: "By the word *ūna* itself," and so forth. The word *ūna* demonstrates the distinction from other opinions.
For others believe that when "meaning" (*artha*) is mentioned, there is no inclusion of those [words] that are meaningless (*anarthaka*).
However, some say that it is so called because its purpose is the indication of meaning by means of the word *ūna* itself.
For it has been stated that when an indication is primarily concerned with the word-form (*śabda-pradhāna*), there occurs the apprehension of the word's own form (*svarūpa-grahaṇa*).
But here, the indication "deficient" (*ūna*) is one in which the meaning (*artha*) is primary.
They say that the word "tena" (by that) is for the purpose of indicating the meaning.
Therefore, the inclusion of those meanings occurs in that very [context]. The particle "iti" is used in the sense of a reason.

Since the meaning of those [words] is not included by the very word *ūna* (deficient) for the purpose of indicating the meaning, some here maintain that the term *artha* (meaning) in this context refers to the inclusion of the word-form itself.
Thus, in the example "dhānyārthaḥ" (grain-meaning), there is a compound according to [Pāṇini 2.1.30].

From the verbal root *dhā* in the sense of "wealth" or "grain" (*dhane dhānye*, Dhātupāṭha 1104), the suffix *ṇyat* is applied. Thus, *dhānya-* has its final syllable circumflexly accented (*svarita*).

Alternatively, *dhānya-* means "that which is good for wealth" (*dhane sādhu*); by the rule *prāgdhitādyat* [Pāṇini 4.4.75] and the subsequent rule [6.1.213], it is *dhānya-* with the first syllable acutely accented (*ādyudātta*).
In this context, the word *artha* is udātta-accented on its first syllable according to the rule *prāmīnāṃ ca* (Phiṭ-sūtra 2.38).

What is the purpose of including the mention of the third case (*tṛtīyā*)? If you ask, "Is it so that [the accent] might not apply in cases such as *anūnam* and *akalaha*?"—this is not the case. For here, by means of the *pratipadokta-paribhāṣā* (Vyāḍi-paribhāṣā 3), only that compound which is explicitly taught (*pratipadokta*) for words such as *artha* and *kalaha* is accepted. Therefore, what is the use of the mention of the third case for the purpose of excluding forms like *anūna-kalaha*? To this, he says: "*pratipadoktam*" and so forth.
The meaning is understood. Regarding the phrase "mixed with jaggery" (*guḍamiśrāḥ*): the compound is formed by [Pāṇini 2.1.31] and the subsequent rules, as before.

As for the word *guḍa*, it is derived from the root *guḍ* (Dhātupāṭha 1370), meaning "to protect," with the suffix *ka* added according to [Pāṇini 3.1.135] *igupadha*; thus, it is oxytone (accented on the final syllable).

By the rule *sphāyitañci* (Pāṇini 6.1.27), the suffix *ra* is prescribed; however, because of the word "in various ways" (*bahulavacanāt*), *ra* also occurs after the root *miś*. Consequently, the word *mitra* has its final syllable accented (*antodātta*).

The word *tila* is acutely accented on the first syllable by the rule *tṛṇadhānyānāṃ ca dvyakṣarāṇām* (Phitsūtra 2.27). [An objection is raised: since the forms *pramiśram* and *sanmiśram* would also result [from this rule], the term "without a prefix" (*anupasarga*) is included [in the sūtra] to exclude them. To this, he says: "In this case," and so forth.

Alternatively, one might ask: "How can a third-case compound (*tṛtīyāsamāsa*) expressed by the word *miśra* be understood when it is accompanied by a prefix (*sopasarga*)? To this he says: "In this [rule]," and so forth.

If the exclusion of prefixes (*anupasargagrahaṇa*) were made here, then since there would be no inclusion of the form with a prefix when the word *miśra* is mentioned elsewhere, the exclusion of prefixes here would be purposeless.
"By that," and so forth.
He demonstrates the purpose of the indication [of the rule] with the example:
"A king mixed with Brāhmaṇas" (*brāhmaṇamiśro rājā*).
The compound is formed by [the rule] beginning with *2.1.31* (*mayūravyaṃsakety-ādayaś ca*).
By the phrase "joined with those belonging to the Veda" (*brāhmaṇaiḥ saha saṃhitaḥ*), he demonstrates the euphonic combination (*saṃdhi*) in the counter-example.
With the words "having attained a single meaning" (*aikārtham āpannaḥ*),
he clarifies the very point just mentioned.
That which has a single, non-different object is *ekārtha*; the state of being that is *aikārthya*.
"Attained" (*āpanna*) means having reached that.
But how is it known that this is the meaning of the word *saṃdhi*? To this he says: "*Saṃdhiḥ*," and so forth.

*Paṇabandhaḥ* is a mutual agreement (*paribhāṣaṇam*), such as: "If you do this for me, then I too will do this for you. When there is a unity of meaning (*aikārthya*) resulting from such a mutual agreement, that is called *saṃdhi*.
Therefore, when there is *saṃdhi* in the counter-example, the meaning understood is: "The Brahmins have entered into a compact (*saṃhitā*) and attained a state of unity of meaning."
"Some, moreover, say" and so forth.
Some say that a *saṃdhi* (euphonic junction) is one in which a specific [consonant] is perceived; such a *saṃdhi* would occur only in that [specific instance].
Since this kind of *saṃdhi* does not exist in the counter-example, he says: "In this case, 'the two Brāhmaṇas with the king,'" and so forth.

Although there is proximity—that is, spatial nearness—between the king and the Brāhmaṇas, nevertheless, even when that exists, a distinction of form—a specific difference in physical appearance—is indeed perceived between the king and the Brāhmaṇas.
The particle *iti* is used here in the sense of a reason (*hetu*).
Since this is so, the king is cited as an example of one who is mixed with the Brāhmaṇas.
"In the examples [of *guḍamiśrā* etc.], there is indeed the attainment of non-distinction.
By this, he demonstrates the absence of *saṃdhi* (euphonic combination) in cases such as *guḍamiśrā*.

For just as grains and the like become mixed when dissolved, so too are these molasses; and their formal distinction (*mūrtivibhāga*) is not perceived. In that case, there is no attainment of non-distinction through *saṃdhi*.
"Non-distinction" (*avibhāga*) means the absence of distinction; its "attainment" (*āpatti*) means its acquisition.

When there is a "compact" (*sandhi*) consisting of a single purpose through a formal agreement (*paṇabandha*), then its absence should be understood in the examples [given], for that compact is characterized by a specific verbal agreement.

And such a compact does not exist in the case of insentient things like grains mixed with molasses, because it is a property belonging only to sentient beings. [This is stated] in the rule: "The secondary suffixes (*taddhita*) have the sense of 'to be accomplished' (*sampādya*) and so forth."

[The suffixes] are *taddhita* suffixes. Why? Because, by the paribhāṣā regarding the mention of a suffix (*pratyayagrahaṇaparibhāṣā*), it is understood that the rule applies to that which ends with [the suffix] (*tadantavidhi*). [This refers to the phrase] "in the prohibition of *guṇa*" (*guṇapratiṣedhe*).

The meaning of a sentence in which a secondary derivative (*taddhita*) is produced is prescribed as the ground for the application (*pravṛttinimitta*) of that secondary derivative—as it has been said: "That which assists is an established auxiliary (*aṅga*); that which is to be accomplished but does not assist is the principal (*aṅgin*).
These two, *aṅgin* and *guṇa*, are synonyms.
The negation of the *guṇa* is "negation of the auxiliary" (*guṇapratiṣedha*).

And this [word *guṇa*] is a qualifier of the negative particle (*nañ*); the meaning is that the negative particle applies when there is a negation of a quality (*guṇa*). Regarding the example "kārṇaveṣṭakikam" (made of earthen bricks):
the meaning is that it is beautified by two earthen bricks (*karṇaveṣṭaka*).
Regarding the rule *na karṇaveṣṭakikamakārṇaveṣṭakikam* (Pāṇini 5.1.18), following [5.1.99]:

here, in the sense of the sentence "it is completed by means of two ear-rings" (*karṇaveṣṭakābhyāṃ sampadyate*), the negative particle *nañ* functions as a negation of that quality which constitutes the ground for the application (*pravṛttinimitta*) of the secondary derivative (*taddhita*).
What, then, is this ground for application? It is the state of being produced by those [ear-rings].

Regarding "chaidika": the suffix *ṭhak* is applied according to the rule *ārhādagopucchādibhyaḥ* [Pāṇini 5.1.19], meaning "one who deserves cutting. Regarding "vatsīya": [the suffix *cha* is applied].
"cha after *prakṛti*" [Pāṇini 5.1.1];
"sāntāpikaḥ" [according to Pāṇini 5.1.101 and 5.1.18].
Regarding the term *vigārdabharathika*:
the suffix *ṭhañ* is applied according to the rule *tadarhati* (Pāṇini 5.1.62) in the sense of "deserving that";
the word *vi-* forms a *prādi*-compound [with *gārdabharathika*].
In this context, the word *vi-* in the term *gārdabharathika* functions to negate a quality (*guṇapratiṣedhe*).
Here, by the rule *tatpuruṣe tulyārtha-* [Pāṇini 6.2.2] and others, the original accent (*prakṛtisvara*) of the first member (*pūrvapada*) is maintained. The same applies in subsequent cases as well.

In what case does the negative particle (*nañ*) not [apply]? Even in this counter-example, that which is the preceding member (*pūrvapada*) must be cited as having its original accent (*prakṛtisvara*). For instance:

*agārdabharathikaḥ* ("other than a donkey-cart driver"). Here, the negative particle applies to "other than a donkey-cart driver" (*gārdabharathikāt anyaḥ*), and not to the negation of the state of being a donkey-cart driver; for this is a case of exclusion (*paryudāsa*).
Regarding the passage beginning with "The quality (*guṇa*) is the ground for the application (*pravṛttinimitta*) of the meaning of a secondary derivative (*taddhita*)," etc.:

the "meaning of a secondary derivative" refers to the sense of a sentence such as "one who is equipped with ear-rings" (*karṇaveṣṭakābhyāṃ saṃpādī*). In that context, whatever serves as the ground for the application of a word ending in a secondary derivative—such as "being equipped" (*saṃpāditva*) and so forth—is called a "quality. By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), qualities such as "being worthy of that" (*tadarhatva*) and others are included.
It includes that which ends in a *taddhita* suffix and that which has the sense of *alam*.
Regarding the phrase "the prohibition of that" (*tatpratiṣedhaḥ*) and so forth:
this rule applies in a compound where such a prohibition is stated.
How is the negation of that quality expressed? He says: "The face was not covered by the two ear-rings.

By all of this, he demonstrates that this is a rule regarding absolute negation (*prasajyapratiṣedha*) and not an exclusion (*paryudāsa*), showing that this rule does not apply in the counter-example *agārdabharathika*. [He gives another example:
"*pāṇinīyam*."
Regarding the rule *vṛddhāc chaḥ* (Pāṇini 4.2.125),
[the example] *apāṇinīyaḥ* is given;
here, the final member of the compound ends in a secondary derivative (*taddhita*) suffix used in the sense of "one who studies" (*adhyetṛ*).
The suffixes *taddhita* (secondary) that do not denote a derivative meaning such as "fit for" (*sampādya*), "worthy of" (*arha*), or "beneficial to" (*hita*) are those ending in *taddhita*.
Regarding the form *voḍhā*:
as before, the substitution of *dha* for *dh*, *ḍha* for *ḍh*, *ṣṭu* for *ṣṭ*, and the elision of *ḍh* must be applied; furthermore, by [Pāṇini 6.4.64], the substitution of *ū* for *o* is prescribed.

Regarding the word *avoḍhā*: here, the meaning [of the suffix] that has been elided is the *uttarapada*. Consequently, because of the exclusion of *taddhita* suffixes [from the definition of *uttarapada*], the final syllable of the *uttarapada* does not become udātta.

The original accent (prakṛtisvara) of the first member remains when it is an indeclinable (avyaya). This rule is an exception (apavāda) to the original accent of the first member; the subsequent rules should be understood in the same way.

This [term] occurs prior to the *bahuvrīhi* compound by virtue of the rule beginning with *prāgbahuvrīhāvidametat* (Pāṇini 6.2.161). Regarding the word *pāśyā*, it has the udātta accent on the final syllable due to the accent of the suffix (*pratyayasvara*). Regarding the word *adantyam*:
By [Pāṇini 6.1.213], there is the udātta accent on the first syllable.
Likewise, *akaṇryam* is also udātta on the first syllable in the same manner.
As for *pādyam*:
Regarding the rule *pādārdhābhyāṃ ca* [Pāṇini 5.4.25],
which states *dantyād anyad adanatyam*:
here, the negative particle *nañ* applies to something other than "tooth" (*dantya*), but it does not serve as a prohibition of that which ends in it.

Regarding the term *adeya*: in the rule [Pāṇini 5.1.67], the suffix *yat* is applied in the sense of "deserving" (*arha*), and by [Pāṇini 6.4.65], the vowel *i* is substituted for the final letter. Now, why does this not also apply here in the case of *vāmadevyam*, meaning "a Sāman seen by Vāmadeva"? To this, he says: "that which lacks an *anubandha*," and so forth.
The meaning has already been explained. Regarding "apacaḥ":
it is formed by adding the suffix *ac* to the root *pac*.
Regarding "avikṣipaḥ": [it is formed by adding the suffix *ghañ* to the root *kṣip* with the prefix *vi-*, with the vowel lengthening].
> [3.1.135] "One who has not been initiated does not cook," and so forth.

An initiated person (*dīkṣita*) and a wandering mendicant (*parivrājaka*) do not cook because it is prohibited by the scriptures, not because of incapacity. Therefore, in this context, a religious observance (*vrata*) is understood, not incapacity. Here, "abuse" (*ākrośa*) refers to the statement of a fault for the purpose of reviling.

The statement "so that it may apply even when [the compound] is not being formed" is intended for cases such as *adevadatto yajñadattaḥ*. Here, the words *devadatta* and *yajñadatta* are oxytone (accented on the final syllable) by virtue of the accent of the nominal stem (*prātipadika-svara*).
He who, being Devadatta, does not perform that particular action is thus reviled.
This should be understood to apply similarly in the case of the term *aviṣṇumitra*. Here, there is a mention of the suffixes *kṛtya*, *uka*, and *iṣṇuc*.
In that context, by the technical rule regarding the mention of a suffix (*pratyayagrahaṇaparibhāṣā*), the word ending with that suffix is brought to mind.
The words beginning with *cāru* are indeed nominal stems (*prātipadika*).
Regarding the phrase "it should not be done" (*akartavyam*): when it ends in the suffix *tavyat*, then the word *kartavya* has a circumflex accent (*svarita*) on its final syllable.
When it ends in *tavya*, it is then oxytone (acute on the final syllable).
Regarding the word *akaraṇīyam*:
because it ends in the suffix *anīyar*, the word *karaṇīya* is middle-accented (acute on the middle syllable) by the rule [Pāṇini 6.1.217] concerning the accent of the *rit* suffix.

Regarding the words *anāgāmṛkam* and *anapalāṣukam*: the suffix *ukañ* is applied by the rule *laṣapatapada* (Pāṇini 3.2.154). The words *āgāmuka* and *apalāṣuka* are oxytone (*madhyodātta*) due to the accent of the *kṛt* suffix.
Regarding the term *analaṅkariṣṇuḥ*: the suffix *iṣṇuc* is applied by [Pāṇini 3.2.136] *alaṃkṛñ* etc. The word *alaṅkariṣṇu* is oxytone (antodātta) due to the accent of the *cit* suffix.

The word *nirākariṣṇu* is likewise [an example]. Someone might have the misconception that, according to the paribhāṣā "when a suffix with one *anubandha* is mentioned... (Vyāḍiparibhāṣā 42), since the mention of *iṣṇuc* refers to a suffix with two *anubandhas*, it should not include *khiṣṇuc*. To dispel this doubt, he says: "In the mention of *iṣṇuc* [in the rule] 'after the root *bhū* in the sense of the agent' (Pāṇini 3.2.57), there is also the inclusion of *khiṣṇuc*, which has two *anubandhas*. This is connected to what will be stated later. He states the reason for this very point: "Because of the force of its being prescribed as beginning with the vowel *i*."

The sole purpose of prescribing *khiṣṇuc* with an initial *i*-vowel is so that it may be included here in the rule by way of a general reference; otherwise, it would be useless, because the suffix *bhavat* is udātta, and consequently, the *iṭ* augment following it would already possess an initial *i*-vowel. Regarding "acāruḥ" and so forth:
from the rule "from *dṛs*, *nij*, and *car*, the suffix *ñuṇ*" (*dṛsanijanicaribhyo ñuṇ*), the word *cāru* is ādyudātta (accented on its first syllable).
The word *sādyu* is oxytone because it ends in the suffix *uṇ* according to [Pāṇini 3.2.181] *kṛvāpājimisvidasi...* and so forth.
*Yaudhikaḥ*, meaning "one who acts with battle," is oxytone by virtue of [Pāṇini 6.1.159] *kitah*.
[This applies to the compound] *anaṅgamejayaḥ*.
By the rule regarding the accent of indeclinables (*avyaya*), the initial syllable would be udātta.
In this case, since the second [type of] *nañ*-compound would result in the final syllable of the compound being udātta, it would be a *nañ*-compound.
"In this case as well," and so forth.
Why? Because it is prescribed that a word following the negative particle *nañ* has its first syllable accented (*ādyudātta*).
In this case as well, by means of a second *nañ*-compound, there is an accent on the final syllable (*antodātta*).
The words *vartamāna*, *vardhamāna*, and so forth, have their final syllables accented because they end in the suffix *śānac*.
The word *vikāra-sadṛśa* has its final syllable accented acute (*antodātta*) by virtue of the accent of the compound (*samāsasvara*).

The word *gṛhapatika* has its initial syllable accented acute (*ādyudātta*) because it ends in the suffix *kan* [according to Pāṇini 5.3.87]. The word *vadānya* has its middle syllable accented acute (*madhyodātta*) by virtue of the accent of the suffix, according to the rule *vader ānyaḥ* (Dhātupāṭha 8.9). Regarding the mention of the suffix *tṛn*, this is a reference to the suffix; therefore, as before, there is the application of that which ends in it.
The words *annādi* and so forth are nominal stems (*prātipadika*). Regarding the term *akartā*:
the suffix *tṛn* here has the sense of habitual character (*tācchīlika*).
By that rule [Pāṇini 6.1.197], the word *kartṛ* has its first syllable accented (*ādyudātta*).
The word *anna* also [has its first syllable accented] by the rule "for that which falls under the domain of *na*" (Phiṭ-sūtra 2.26).

The word *tīkṣṇa* has its final syllable accented (*antodātta*) by the rules "the suffix *ksna* after roots ending in a consonant" (Dhātu-pāṭha 5.49) and "there is lengthening of the vowel in the root *tij*" (Dhātu-pāṭha 5.50).

While [the rule] *dāder dhātor haḥ* (Pāṇini 8.2.32) is in force, [the rule] *igupadhāt kit* (Uṇādi-sūtra 1.48) applies; by that, the word *śuci* has its first syllable accented acute (*ādyudātta*). Regarding the phrase "of the first and the ordinal numbers" (*prathamapūraṇayoḥ*):
in the case of "first," there is a reference to the word-form itself (*svarūpagrahaṇa*).
In the case of "ordinal numbers," those suffixes which are prescribed in the sense of ordinals are understood, because of their association with "first."

Alternatively, the inclusion of the term *pūraṇa* (ordinal) is intended; furthermore, the scope of the governing rule (*adhikāra*) is determined by the circumflex accent (*svarita*). Thus, with reference to [Pāṇini 5.2.48], there is the inclusion of those suffixes that have been prescribed under that heading. For example: *idamprathamaḥ*.
The first [form] has the udātta accent on the final syllable, because it ends in the suffix *amat* according to the rule *pratheramat* (Pāṇini 5.3.46).
The words beginning with *idam*, when included among the *tyadādi* group, are prescribed as having the udātta accent on the final syllable; for example: *idam dvitīyaḥ* and *idam tṛtīyaḥ*.
Because they end in the suffix *tīya* according to [Pāṇini 5.2.53]–[5.2.55], the words *dvitīya* and *tṛtīya* have the acute accent on the middle syllable.

In the case of "this is first by this" (*anena prathama idaṃ prathamaḥ*), the original accent of the preceding member (*pūrvapada-prakṛtisvara*) alone occurs, by virtue of the rule [Pāṇini 6.2.2]: "In a *tatpuruṣa* compound, [the accent of the first member remains] when it has the sense of 'equal' (*tulyārtha*)," and so forth.

Regarding the term *yatprathamaḥ*: it is a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "that which is first among these. In this case, by the rule *bahuvrīhau prakṛtyā* [Pāṇini 6.2.1], the original accent (*prakṛtisvara*) of the preceding member (*pūrvapada*) alone remains.
The same should be understood for the subsequent counter-examples within this section on *bahuvrīhi* compounds.

By stating, "the meaning is 'those for whom this is primary,'" he demonstrates that in the aforementioned counter-example, the word *prathama* denotes "primary" (*pradhāna*) and does not denote the number one; thus, he shows the absence of a plural sense. [He then provides] the phrase beginning with "of the final member," and so forth.

In this sūtra, the mention of "the first" (*prathama*) and "the ordinal" (*pūraṇa*) is made by way of indicating other case endings as the final members (*uttarapada*), not by way of indicating a *bahuvrīhi* compound.
Consequently, it is the final member itself that undergoes the grammatical operation, not the *bahuvrīhi* compound.
Therefore, when the suffix *kap* is produced, [the word] becomes oxytone according to Pāṇini 6.2.173.

Since the suffix *kap* is prescribed under the governing rule for compounds (*samāsādhikāra*), it occurs only at the end of the compound itself, not at the end of the final member (*uttarapada*). For the final member is not the compound; therefore, when the rule "the final syllable of the final member is acute" is stated, it does not apply to the suffix *kap*, but rather to what precedes it—as in the example *idamprathamakāḥ*.

The suffix *kap* is applied by [Pāṇini 5.4.154]. This rule is an exception to the original accent of the first member (*pūrvapada-prakṛtisvara*) prescribed by [Pāṇini 6.2.1], which states that in a *bahuvrīhi* compound, the accent of the final member prevails. In this same section on *bahuvrīhi* compounds, subsequent rules should be understood in the same manner. For example: *dvistanā*, *trisatanā*.

The words *dvi* and *tri* are oxytone by the accent of the nominal stem (*prātipadika-svara*). The root *stanagadī* (meaning "to sound" or "to cry out") belongs to the *curādi* class, ends in *a*, and forms its derivative with the suffix *ghañ*; thus, the word *stana* is ādyudātta (accented on the first syllable). [This explains the formation of] the compound *catuḥstanā*.
The word *catuḥ* is acute on the first syllable because it ends in the suffix *uran*, according to [Pāṇini 6.1.169] *careruran*.
The word *darśanīya* is acute on the middle syllable because it ends in the suffix *anīyar*, according to [Pāṇini 6.1.217].
As for the word *dviśirāḥ*:

The word *śiras* is udātta on its first syllable by the rule *nabviṣayasya* (Phiṭ-sūtra 2.26). In the examples *devamittraḥ* and *brāhmaṇamittraḥ*, the words *deva* and *brāhmaṇa* have the accents already mentioned. The word *mittra* is udātta on its final syllable, according to the rule *amicimidiśasibhyaḥ ktraḥ* (Dhātu-pāṭha 8.86).
Regarding the term *vṛkājina*:

since the distinction between the material cause (*prakṛti*) and its modification (*vikāra*) is not intended to be expressed here, the word *vṛka* is used in this context to refer to a modification of a wolf. Thus, *vṛkājinaḥ* means "one who has a wolf-skin."
The word *vṛka* has its first syllable udātta by the rule *prāṇināṃ kupūrvāṇām* (Phiṭ-sūtra 2.30).

Under the heading *śyāstyāhveñavibhya inac* (Dhātu-pāṭha 5.12), the substitution of *inaC* for the root *aj* is applied by the rule *ajeraja ca* (Dhātu-pāṭha 5.14); consequently, *ajina* has its final syllable udātta.
Regarding the term *kūlājinaḥ*:

*ku* is a particle (*nipāta*). With this as an upapada, from the root *lā* in the sense of "taking" (Dhātupāṭha 1058), the suffix *ḍa* is applied by [Pāṇini 3.2.101], and the lengthening of the first syllable occurs by [Pāṇini 6.3.137].
Consequently, *kūla-* has its final syllable accented (*antodātta*).
Regarding the word *kṛṣṇājina*:

under the rule *iṇsiñjidīṅuṇyavibhyo nak* (Dhātupāṭha 5.35), and specifically under the rule *kṛṣervarṇe* (Dhātupāṭha 5.37), the suffix *nak* is applied. Consequently, *kṛṣṇa* has its final syllable accented acute (*antodātta*).

Regarding "priyamittraḥ": it is *priya* because it pleases (*prīṇāti*), with the suffix *ka* applied according to [Pāṇini 3.1.135] *igupadhajñāprīkiraḥ kaḥ*. Thus, *priya* is udātta on its final syllable. Regarding "mahājinaḥ": [the analysis follows].
According to the rule *nṛt-māne-pṛṣat-bṛhat-mahat-jagac-chatṛ-vat* (Pāṇini 6.1.157), the word *mahat* has its final syllable accented (*antodātta*). Regarding the example *gauramukhaḥ*:

from the verbal root *gurī* (meaning "to lift up," Dhātupāṭha 1396), the suffix *ac* is applied. Even though it ends in that [suffix], because it is not included in the *prajñādi* group, the suffix *aṇ* is applied by the rule *parajñādibhyaśca* (Pāṇini 5.4.38). Consequently, *gaura* has its final syllable accented.

Having introduced the rule "After the root *dṛṇāti*, the suffixes *añ* and *alau* [the printed text reads *ajalau*] are applied, and there is elision of the final phoneme of the preceding word" (Pāṇini 5.2.19), it continues with "The suffixes *añ* and *alau* are applied after the root *khan*, and they are marked with the *ḍi*-sign; furthermore, *muṭ* is added, and it is udātta" (Pāṇini 5.2.20). Thus, the suffixes *añ* and *alau* occur after *khan*, and these two are marked with the *ḍi*-sign; moreover, *muṭ* is udātta.
Consequently, the word *mukha* has its first syllable udātta. For example: *bhadramukhaḥ*.
The word *bhadra* is derived by the rule *ṛjrendra* (Pāṇini 6.1.92);
therefore, *bhadra* is oxytone (having the acute accent on the final syllable).
[The example is] "the long-nosed *śalā*."

Here, by the word *mukha*, the region of the entrance of the hall (*śālā*) is meant. Regarding the phrase "here, a 'limb' (*svāṅga*) characterized by being non-fluid is taken," this refers to that definition of a "limb" characterized by being non-fluid, corporeal, and so forth, as established in [Kāśikāvṛtti 4.1.54]. Therefore, the intention is that [the rule] does not apply in the case of *dīrghamukhā śālā* ("a hall with a long entrance"). This prohibition is stated because the preceding [rule] would otherwise have resulted in the final syllable being udātta.
Regarding "uccairmukhaḥ":
the word *uccaiḥ* is recited among the particles (*svarādi*), and it is prescribed as having its final syllable accented (*antodātta*).
Regarding "prāṅmukhaḥ": [the same applies].
Regarding the word *prāk*: it ends in a *kvin* suffix and is udātta on its first syllable; therefore, by [Pāṇini 6.2.52], the original accent (*prakṛtisvara*) of the preceding member remains.
In the case of *pratyaṅmukhaḥ*, the original accent of the *kṛt*-derived final member prevails.
"Gomukhaḥ" and "mahāmukhaḥ"— it has been stated that the words *go* and *maha* have their final syllables accented. [The example] "sthūlamukhaḥ."
The root *sthūl* is listed in the Dhātupāṭha as *sthūla paribṛṃhaṇe* (1904) and belongs to the curādigaṇa; from it, the suffix *ac* (pacādyac) is applied.
Consequently, the word *sthūla* has its udātta accent on the final syllable.
[The example is] *muṣṭimukhaḥ*.

The word *muṣṭi* is derived from the root *muṣ* with the suffix *ktic*; therefore, the word *muṣṭi* is oxytone (having the acute accent on the final syllable). [The example is] "one with a broad mouth" (*pṛthumukha*).
Under the governing rule *kubhraśca* (Pāṇini 5.2.23), the suffix *ku* is applied by the rule *prathimradibhrasjāṃ saṃprasāraṇaṃ salopaśca* (Pāṇini-Uṇādi 1.29).
Consequently, *pṛthu-* is oxytone.
[The example is] *vatsamukhaḥ*.
By the rule beginning with *vṛtṛvadini* (Pāṇini 6.2.40), that [suffix] is applied; thus, *vatso* is udātta on the final syllable. Examples include *gomuṣṭi*, and so forth.

By this [rule], even that which would apply by virtue of the subsequent sūtra—characterized by having a word ending in a *niṣṭhā* suffix or the like as the prior member when it denotes a standard of comparison (*upamāna*)—is superseded.

The scope (*avakāśa*) for this prohibition is where there is no cow or similar object as the standard of comparison; for example, in *gaurmukhamiva yasya*, *muṣṭirmukhamiva yasya*, and *vatso mukhamiva yasya*, in all cases the cow and so forth are the objects of comparison (*upameya*), not the standards of comparison (*upamāna*).

The scope for the optional application (*vikalpa*) characterized by a prior member ending in a *niṣṭhā* suffix or the like as a standard of comparison, according to the subsequent sūtra, is where the standard of comparison is something other than a cow or the like—for instance, *siṃhamukhaḥ* (lion-faced) and *vyāghramukhaḥ* (tiger-faced).

In what case does the comparison [end] with *gava* and so forth? Where the first member [of the compound] is present, when both [conditions for accentuation] apply, this very prohibition—by means of the prior prohibition—sets aside the rule defining the upamāna (comparison). For example: *śāṅgarajagdhaḥ*. [The word] *śāṅgaraḥ* is derived from the root *guṇ* or *it*, by [Pāṇini 3.2.148] adding the suffix *ac*; then, because it belongs to the *prajñādi* group—which is an *ākṛtigaṇa*—the suffix *aṇ* is added. Thus, the word *śāṅgara* has its final syllable accented (*antodātta*).

Regarding "palāṇḍubhakṣitaḥ": from the verbal root *pala* in the sense of "going" (Dhātupāṭha 839), the suffix *āṇḍu* is applied according to Pāṇini 3.3.1; thus, the word *palāṇḍu* has its acute accent on the middle syllable. Regarding "surapītaḥ": [the analysis follows].
By the rule *susūdhāgudhibhyaḥ kran* (Pāṇini 6.1.42), the word *surā* has its first syllable udātta.
Regarding the term *māsajātaḥ*:

from the root *masī* in the sense of "measuring" (*parimāṇe*) [or "transforming" (*pariṇāme*) according to the Dhātupāṭha], the suffix *ghañ* is applied; thus, the word *māsa* has its first syllable udātta.

Regarding the term *saṃvatsarajātaḥ*: under the heading "after the root *aś*, [the suffix] *saran*" (*daśapādī-uṇādi* 8.50; cf. *daśapādī-pañcapādī-uṇādi* 3.70), there follow the rules "also after the root *vas*" (*daśapādī-uṇādi* 8.51) and "also when preceded by the prefix *sam*" (*daśapādī-uṇādi* 8.52).
Therefore, the word *saṃvatsara-* has its final syllable udātta [when used in the sense of] "born after two days" (*dvyahajātaḥ*) or "born after three days" (*tryahajātaḥ*).
It has been stated that the words *dvi* and *tri* have the udātta accent on their final syllable.
In the example "sukhajātaḥ," the suffix *ḍa* is applied according to [Pāṇini 3.2.101]: "After the root *khan*, when preceded by *su*."
Therefore, the word *sukha* has its udātta accent on the final syllable.
In the same way, the word *duḥkha* is also to be understood.
Therefore, the word *tṛpra* has its udātta accent on the final syllable.
Regarding the term *kṛcchrajātaḥ*:
according to the rule *kṛtecchaḥ krū ca* (Daiva 8.38; Pañcapādikā 2.21)—which reads *kṛteśchakrū ca* in the Pañcapādikā—the word *kṛcchra* has its udātta accent on the final syllable.

From the root *asu* (in the sense of "to breathe" or "to live," Dhātupāṭha 1209), the suffix *rak* is applied according to the rule *bahulamanyatrāpi* (Dhātupāṭha 8.40); therefore, *asram* is udātta on its final syllable.
According to the rule *vṛtṛvadahanikamikaṣibhyaḥ saḥ* (Dhātupāṭha 9.21)—[the variant reading being *kaṣiyumucibhyaḥ*—Dhātupāṭha]—the suffix *sa* occurs after *am* as well due to the word *bahula*.
*Aṃsaḥ* is udātta on its first syllable because it belongs to the *vṛṣādi* group.
Regarding the word *alaka*: it is derived from the root *alati* [Pāṇini 3.3.118], and then with the suffix *kan*, the word *alaka* ends in *kan*. Consequently, it is udātta on its first syllable.
By the rule *kṛvṛdāribhya unan* (Pāṇini 5.1.23), the word *karuṇa* has its first syllable accented acute (*ādyudātta*).

By the rule *rañjeḥ kvun* (Pāṇini 3.2.161), because of the mention of the term "variously" (*bahulavacanāt*), the suffix *kvun* also applies after the root *kṛp*. Consequently, *kṛpaṇa* also has its first syllable accented acute.
The word *soḍha* ends in the suffix *kta*;
therefore, it is udātta on its final syllable.
As before, the substitutions of *gha* for *ha*, *ḍha* for *dha*, and so forth, must be applied.
Regarding the term *pratīyam*:
it is a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "that in which waters (*āpaḥ*) have gone toward" (*pratigatāḥ*).

The suffix *a* is applied as a compound-final element (*samāsānta*) by the rule *ṛkpūrabdhūḥpathāmānakṣe* [Pāṇini 5.4.74], and the substitution of *i* for *ya* is applied by the rule *yasyeti ca* [Pāṇini 6.4.148].

Regarding the term *putrajātaḥ*: here, only the accent of the *bahuvrīhi* compound applies. According to Pāṇini 5.2.37 (*amicimidiśasibhyaḥ ktraḥ*) and Vārttika 3.4.164 (*puvo hrasvaśca*), the word *putra* has its final syllable accented (*antodātta*). Thus, [the accentuation of *putrajātaḥ* follows the rule].

But how is there the subsequent placement (*paranipāta*) of the word *jāta*, when by the rule "the past passive participle [*niṣṭhā*]" [Pāṇini 2.2.36], its prior placement (*pūrvanipāta*) should have occurred here? To this he says: "Because it belongs to the class beginning with *āhitāgni*" and so forth.

This word *putrajāta* is listed among the *āhitāgnyādi* group; therefore, by the rule "optionally in the *āhitāgnyādi* group" [Pāṇini 2.2.37], there is the subsequent placement of the word beginning with *jāta*.
[The example is] *vastracchannaḥ* ("covered with a cloth").
*Vastra* means clothing; it is so called because one is covered (*ācchādyate*) by it.
The word *vastra* has its vowel [the first syllable] accented as stated.

The word *channa* is derived from the root *chad* in the sense of "covering" (*apavāraṇe*) (Dhātupāṭha 1833); when this root takes the causative suffix (*ṇic*), it is formed with the past passive participle suffix (*niṣṭhā*) by the rule *vā dantaśānta-* (Pāṇini 7.2.27) and others.
Regarding the term "vasanacchannaḥ":
the suffix *lyuṭ* is applied to the root *vas* in the sense of covering (*ācchādana*).
Consequently, the word *vasana* is udātta on its first syllable.
Regarding the term "kuṇḍalakṛtaḥ":
this word *kuṇḍa* is udātta on its first syllable according to the rule "nabviṣayasya" (Phiṭ-sūtra 2.26).
[The example] "kuṇḍamitaḥ" [is also provided].

The root *māṅ* meaning "to measure" (Dhātupāṭha 1142) takes the augment *it* by the rule *dyatisyati* [Pāṇini 7.4.40]. Now, one might ask: why is there no prior placement (*pūrvanipāta*) of the word ending in a past passive participle (*niṣṭhā*) in these bahuvrīhi compounds, according to the rule *niṣṭhā* [Pāṇini 2.2.36]? To this he says: "In these," and so forth.
Because this has been established, the final acute accent (*antodāttatva*) is prescribed for words following those beginning with *jāti*.

From this very indicative mark (*jñāpaka*), it follows that a word ending in a *niṣṭhā* suffix does not undergo prior placement (as a first member of a compound). Otherwise, the rule prescribing its final acute accent (*antodāttatva*) would be untenable. Since the word *jāta* also ends in a *kta* suffix, this option is stated for it as well—despite the fact that by the preceding rule (*jātyādibhyaḥ parasya*), a word ending in *kta* following *jāti* and others would necessarily have its final syllable acutely accented. For example: *dantajātaḥ*. Here, the form *dantaḥ* is derived from the root *dan* according to the rule *hasimṛgriṇvamidami-* (Dhātupāṭha 6.7), etc.
Therefore, this [word] has its initial syllable accented (ādyudātta).
In the case of *stanajātaḥ*, the word *stana* has the aforementioned accent. In the case of *ayavo deśaḥ* and so forth...
In *yava-vrīhi-māṣāḥ*, the initial syllable is udātta by the rule "and for grass-grains with two vowels" (*tṛṇadhānyānāṃ ca dvy-aṣām*, Phiṭ-sūtra 2.27).
Regarding the rule "of the compound" (*samāsasya*), etc.: here, "compound" (*samāsa*) is the subject under discussion, as is "subsequent member" (*uttarapada*).

In that case, if this rule were to apply as an udātta accent on the final syllable of the *uttarapada*, then in the case of *anṛcaḥ* and *bahvṛcaḥ*, after the suffix *ac* (as in *ṛkpūrabdhūḥ* [Pāṇini 5.4.74]) has been added as a compound-final suffix (*samāsānta*), the rule would result in the final syllable of the word *ṛc*—which is the *uttarapada*—being udātta.

However, the udātta accent being prescribed for the end of the compound belongs to the letter *a* itself; for that [letter *a*] is a constituent part of the compound, since its application is governed by the heading *samāsasya* [Pāṇini 6.1.223].
Its status as a constituent part of the compound follows from its being prescribed under that heading.
Therefore, this final acute accent (*antodāttatva*) is desired for the member of the compound.
But how is that which is desired obtained? It is obtained because of the mention of "the preceding" (*pūrva*) in [Pāṇini 6.2.173].
For that mention of "the preceding" is made so that the final acute accent being prescribed by this rule may apply only to the *kap* suffix which is a member of the compound, and not otherwise.

If, however, this [rule] were to cause the final syllable of both members [of the compound] to be udātta, then—even without the mention of *kap* in the rule *pūrvapada*—the [udāttatva] would apply to the second member (*uttarapada*) that is preceded by *kap*, and not to *kap* itself; for *kap* is not a constituent part (*avayava*) of the second member. Consequently, the mention of *pūrvapada* would be purposeless. This was stated while accepting the view that "suffixes forming the end of a compound (*samāsānta-pratyaya*) are constituents of the compound itself, not of the second member. Now, relying on the alternative view that "they are also constituents of the second member," he says: "And the *samāsānta* suffixes," and so forth.

The word "and" (*ca*) implies that the latter member [of the compound] is also included; this connects with the previously mentioned rule that "this [compound] is desired to have its final syllable accented. The particle *iti* indicates the reason.
Alternatively, this final acute accent (antodāttatva) is intended for the second member (uttarapada) itself.
Why? Because the compound-final suffixes (samāsānta) become constituent parts of the second member;
therefore, in the case of *anūc* and *bahvṛc*, once the compound-final suffix has been applied, the final acute accent occurs, and that [accent] belongs to the second member.

The meaning is that it occurs only for that [suffix] which is a compound-final element (*samāsānta*), because it is a constituent part of the final member of the compound. In the case of a suffix ending in *s*, the udātta accent falls on the final syllable; and that [accentuation] would belong to the final member of the compound. The meaning is that it occurs only for that [suffix] which is a compound-final element, because it is a constituent part of the final member of the compound.

For if the *samāsānta* suffixes were not constituents (*avayava*) of the subsequent member (*uttarapada*), then the rule prescribing that the final syllable of the constituent of the subsequent member be udātta would not apply to the *samāsānta* itself. Indeed, when the *samāsānta* suffixes are constituents of the subsequent member, it is precisely that *samāsānta* which becomes udātta. But how is it that the *samāsānta* suffixes are constituents of the subsequent member? [They are so] because the *samāsānta* is prescribed before the subsequent member—which here refers to the meaning of the compound—and because the formation of the compound is subsequently prescribed with that which ends in the *samāsānta*.

For it will be stated in the rule *na kapi* [Pāṇini 7.4.14]: "This [word ending in a feminine suffix] also does not become *kapi*. When *kapi* is added after the compound has been formed with a word having *hrasva* as its final member, there must subsequently be a compound with that which ends in *kapi*; thus, the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) of the compound does not end in a feminine suffix.

And if a compound were to be formed with a word ending in a compound-final suffix (*samāsānta-pratyaya*), then, according to the principle "those that fall in the middle are included by the mention of the whole" (Vyāḍiparibhāṣā 21), the compound-final suffix would become a constituent part of the subsequent member (*uttarapada*).

If this is so, does it not follow that they cannot be members (*avayava*) of the compound? This is not the case; for even the member of a member is indeed a member of the whole aggregate. To illustrate: when it is said, "Let all the limbs of Devadattā be adorned," the fingers and other parts which are themselves members of Devadattā’s limbs are also adorned. Since the suffix *kap* would have been udātta (accented) on the final syllable by the preceding rule, this [present rule] prescribes that the preceding member itself is udātta when *kap* follows.
Examples include *akumārīkaḥ*, etc., where *kap* is applied according to [Pāṇini 5.4.154].
The word *kumārī* is oxytone by the rule regarding the "cessation of the acute" (*udāttanivṛtti-svara*).
The word *vṛṣalī* also [is oxytone] due to the feminine suffix *ṅīṣ* which characterizes a genus (*jāti*).
The word *brāhma-bandhū* likewise [is oxytone] because of the suffix *ūṅ*. [The phrase] "its end is short," etc., [explains the formation].

By this, he demonstrates that for the very *bahuvrīhi* compound ending in a short vowel, either the final member (*uttarapada*) or the entire compound itself constitutes the external referent (*anyapadārtha*). For example, in the phrase "a region devoid of barley" (*ayavako deśaḥ*), when the suffix *kap* follows, is it the word "barley" (*yava*) that ends in a short vowel, or is it the final member "devoid" (*ayava*), or is it the entire compound?

In that case, the syllable preceding the final *va*—namely the syllable *ya*—is acute (*udātta*). Other instances should be understood in this same manner. Now, as for the mention of "preceding" (*pūrva*): since the word "preceding" already continues [from the previous rule] by virtue of the rule at 6.2.173, why is it stated here again? To this he says: "While 'preceding' is continuing," and so forth.

For if a second mention of "preceding" were made, there would be a difference in application due to a split in the sentence (*vākya-bheda*); this is by the force of the repetition of "preceding. Otherwise, it would be purposeless.
In this regard, by one application [of the rule], the penultimate syllable preceding the final short vowel is prescribed as having the udātta accent;

however, by the other application, there is a restriction that the penultimate syllable preceding the final short vowel does not have the udātta accent. Consequently, in the case of the suffix *kap*, the penultimate syllable does not become udātta.

If there were no restriction by the rule beginning with "tena," then, because it is the final [element], would not the preceding [portion] be acute? Since there is no state of being acute for what precedes, the *kap* suffix would cause the preceding element to be acutely accented on its final syllable.
However, when the restriction by the rule "tena" (Pāṇini 6.2.172) is applied, this does not occur;
by that rule, only that which ends in *kap* becomes acutely accented on its final syllable.

And how that [substitution] occurs has been established right here by such rules as *yathā ca sa bhavati* (6.2.172). This [sūtra] is for the purpose that the placement of the accent (*svaravidhāna*) which follows a negative particle (*nañ*) according to those rules should apply even after the word *bahu*.

The term *nañvat* means "like *nañ*. The state of being much (*bahorbhāvaḥ*) is *bhūmā*; by applying the suffix *imanic* according to Pāṇini 5.1.122 (*pṛthv-ādi-bhya imanic ca*), there is the substitution of *bhū* for *bahu*.

The compound *uttarapadasya bhūme* is a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*). Now, for what purpose is this extension (*atideśa*)? Why not simply state: "after [words ending in] *nañ*, *su*, and *bahu*, when there is abundance (*bhūman*) in the final member"? Nor does such a formulation result in the restriction that this [rule] applies to *nañ* and *su* only when there is abundance in the final member; for this [extension] depends on possibility (*sambhava*). Just as in the rule *yathā eva hi* (Pāṇini 6.1.68), the mention of the long vowel (*dīrgha*) is a restriction based on possibility, applying only to *ṅī* and *āp* suffixes and not to consonants (*hal*).

In that case, this [accentuation] will also belong to *bahu* alone, and not to [the compound with] *nañ* or *su*; for a compound formation (*vṛtti*) is not possible when there is plurality of the meaning of the final member (*uttarapada*) for those two. If this is so, then even that rule prescribing the accent of a *bahuvrīhi* characterized by *nañ* which applies to a word standing in a different location (*videśastha*), this extension (*atideśa*) is made so that it may also apply by virtue of this [present] extension.
By means of this, the acute accent on the first syllable of the final member (*uttarapadādyudātta*) as prescribed by [Pāṇini 6.2.116] is also extended to *bahu*.
Thus: *bahumanāḥ*.

In this case, when there is a plurality of the final member [of the compound], the word *bahu* does not apply. Since the previous rule would have led to an over-extension (*atiprasakta*), it is prohibited by means of *guṇa* and so forth—as in "a rope with many qualities" (*bahuguṇā rajjuḥ*). The meaning is "having many parts. The root *guṇ* (Dhātupāṭha 1894), belonging to the *cur*-class, takes the suffix *ghañ*.
Therefore, the word *guṇa* has its initial syllable accented acute (*ādyudātta*).
By the rule *aśeḥ saraḥ* (Dhātupāṭha 8.50), the word *akṣara* has its final syllable accented acute (*antodātta*). That by which the *chandas* is measured is called *cchandomāna*.
In the word *chandomāna*, the term *māna* is acute-accented on its first syllable because it ends in the suffix *ghañ*. A *sūkta* is that which has been well-spoken;
it is a *prādi* compound.
By the rule *thāthādisvareṇa* [Pāṇini 6.2.143], the word *sūkta* has its final syllable accented acute (*antodātta*). An *adhyāya* is that from which one studies;
it is formed with the suffix *ghañ* by the rule *iṅaśca* [Pāṇini 3.3.21].
A chapter [ending with] *sūktavat* has its final syllable accented (*antodātta*). Regarding the term "preposition" (*upasarga*), it should be understood as an indication for *pra* and the others;
for there is no connection with an action in the case of *sv-aṅgam*.
However, the specific mention of "prepositions" was not made for the sake of variety.

This word *dhruva* occurs in the sense of a "part," as in [Pāṇini 1.4.24]; it also occurs in the sense of "having a single nature," as in *dhruvam asya śīlam* ("his character is constant"). Therefore, to show that it is understood here as referring to that which has a single nature, he says: "*Dhruvam* is said to be of one form," and so forth.
By the words "*satatam*" (constantly), etc., he demonstrates the constancy (*dhruvatva*) of the back (*pṛṣṭha*).
The word *pṛṣṭha* is accented on the final syllable (*antodātta*).
Because [the word *lalāṭa*] is derived from the root *pṛṣu*, *mṛṣu*, and *vṛṣu* in the sense of "to sprinkle" (Dhātupāṭha 705, 706, 707) with the suffix *thak*;
and in the compound *darśanīyalalāṭaḥ*,
the word *darśanīya* is oxytone according to Pāṇini 6.1.217.

From the root *lal* in the sense of "desire" (*ipsāyām*) [Dhātupāṭha 1687], the suffix *āṭ* is applied according to [Pāṇini 3.3.1]. Consequently, the word *lalāṭa* has its acute accent on the middle syllable. An example is: "a tree with spreading branches" (*praśākho vṛkṣaḥ*).

Is it because of the statement [in the *Śikṣā*], "Thus [it is said]"? [The word *śākhā*] is derived from the root *śo* (meaning "to thin out," *dhātupāṭha* 1145), with the suffix *kha*, the feminine suffix *ṭāp*, and the application of the *savarṇadīrgha* rule [Pāṇini 6.1.101].
Thus, the word *śākhā* has its final syllable accented (*antodātta*). [As in the example: "With arms raised, she cries out."
In this case, there is no single uniformity regarding the arms; hence the term *udhruvatva*.
For he does not emaciate himself with his arms perpetually raised upward alone, but rather at times even with his arms lowered.
[This is expressed by the word] *utparśuḥ*.
Regarding the rule *svṛśer āṇ śunau pṛ ca* (Pāṇini 5.2.27)—[the variant reading *āṇ śuno pṛ ca* is found in the Muñjakeśa recension]—the word *parśu* ends in the suffix *śun*.
Consequently, it is udātta on its first syllable. The phrase "in every compound" (*samāsamātre*) indicates by the inclusion of the word *mātra* that the *bahuvrīhi* is excluded.
Regarding the term *pravaṇe*:
when this is a *bahuvrīhi* compound, the analysis is "that which has an excellent (*prakṛṣṭa*) or primary (*prakṛta*) forest" (*vana*).
When, however, it is a *tatpuruṣa* compound, the analysis is "an excellent forest" (*prakṛṣṭaṃ vanaṃ*) or "a forest that has gone forth" (*pragataṃ vanaṃ*).
Regarding the term "nirvāṇa":

here too, when it is a *bahuvrīhi* compound, the analysis is "that from which the forest has departed" (*nirgataṃ vanaṃ asya*). When, however, it is a *tatpuruṣa* compound, the analysis is "departed from the forest" (*nirgato vanāt*), according to [Pāṇini 2.2.18].

Furthermore, what would happen if the mention of the compound (*samāsa*) were not made for the purpose of including all types of compounds? To this he says: "For [the suffix] would occur only in the *bahuvrīhi*.

[The suffix] *kyun* is added after the root *rañj* (Pāṇini 3.2.58; Dhatupāṭha 2.80). Is it because of the abundance [of usage]? It also occurs after the root *vanu* in the sense of "to beg" (Dhatupāṭha 1470).

By that, "vanam" (forest) is acute-accented on the first syllable. Regarding the word "antaḥ": it is prescribed as an indeclinable (nipāta) with the acute accent on the final syllable among the group beginning with "svarādi.

In the case of "antarvaṇo deśaḥ" (a region within the forest), it is either a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "that in which there is a forest," or a locative compound (*saptamī-samāsa*) based on its inclusion in the list of words beginning with "śauṇḍa" [Pāṇini 2.1.40], meaning "within the forest."
The substitution of *ṇ* [for *n*] occurs by the rule *pra-ni-r-antar-* [Pāṇini 8.4.5].

"The present rule is commenced for the sake of cases where there is no prefix (*anupasarga*). Why? Because in the case of a prefix, the result would already be established by the preceding rule. The word *antaḥ* is accutely accented on its first syllable because it ends in the suffix *tan*, according to the rule *hasi-mṛ-gṛ-iṇ-vami-dami-lū-pū-dhurvibhyas-tan* [Dhātupāṭha 6.7]. Since the preceding rule would have resulted in an oxytone accent even for *ni* and *vi*, this prohibition is stated.
"When the original accent (*prakṛtisvara*) of the first member has been applied":
when it is a *bahuvrīhi*, then the original accent applies by [Pāṇini 6.2.1];
but when it is a *tatpuruṣa*, then it applies by [Pāṇini 6.2.2], "In a *tatpuruṣa* compound, [the word] having the meaning of 'equal' (*tulyārtha*), etc. Examples are *parikūlam* and *paritīram*.
The words *kūla* and *tīra* have the aforementioned accents in rules such as Pāṇini 6.2.121.
Regarding the term *parimaṇḍalam*: that which is a circle (*maṇḍala*) on all sides (*paritaḥ*), i.e., everywhere, is *parimaṇḍala*.

From the root *maṇi* in the sense of "adornment" (*bhūṣāyām*) [Dhātupāṭha 321], the suffix *kala* is applied by virtue of the rule *kalastṛpaśca* (Pāṇini 3.3.107), which is an extension (*bāhulaka*), as well as by the rule *vṛṣādibhyaścit* (Pāṇini 3.3.109). Consequently, *maṇḍala* has its final syllable accented (*antodātta*).
[The commentary states: "This is a *bahuvrīhi* compound," and so forth.

When it is a *bahuvrīhi* compound, then—having "its bank on all sides" (*paritaḥ kūlam asya*) or "its shore on all sides" (*paritastīram asya*) as its analysis—it is consequently *maṇḍala* with an udātta accent on the final syllable.
"This is a *bahuvrīhi*" and so forth:
when it is a *bahuvrīhi*, then the analysis is "its bank on all sides" (*paritaḥ kūlam asya*) or "its shore on all sides" (*paritastīram asya*).
When, however, it is a *prādi*-compound (*prādisamāsa*), then it means "the bank is encompassed" (*parigataṃ kūlam*) or "the shore is encompassed" (*parigataṃ tīram*).
When, on the other hand, it is an indeclinable compound (*avyayībhāva*), then it means "around the bank" (*pari kūlāt*) or "around the shore" (*pari tīrāt*).
The indeclinable compound is formed by the rule [Pāṇini 2.1.12].

In the word *parikūlāt*, the fifth case ending (*pañcamī*) occurs due to its connection with a *karmapravacanīya* [particle], according to the rule *pañcamy apāṅparibhiḥ* [Pāṇini 2.3.10]. Its status as a *karmapravacanīya* is established by the rule *pareḥ* [Pāṇini 1.4.88].

It is appropriate that this final acute accent (*antodāttatva*) is prescribed for the bahuvrīhi compound, and also for the tatpuruṣa; for in those cases, it serves as an exception to the general rule of the final acute accent of a compound, whereby the original accent of the first member (*pūrvapadaprakṛtisvara*) would otherwise apply.

However, [the objection] is inappropriate regarding the *avyayībhāva* compound; for in that case, the desired accentuation is already established by the rule prescribing that the final syllable of a compound is udātta (*samāsāntodātta*). Indeed, has not the original accent of the first member (*pūrvapadaprakṛtisvara*) been prohibited for it by anything? To this he says: "Even in the case of the *avyayībhāva*," and so forth. Even when the *avyayībhāva* alternative applies, the original accent of the first member—which would otherwise be obtained by rules such as *paripratyupāpā* (Pāṇini 6.2.33)—is set aside by this present rule which prescribes that the final syllable be udātta. Therefore, what is inappropriate here?

Regarding the phrase "and that which has such an intrinsic nature" (*yaccaivaṃsvabhāvam*), etc.: that whose intrinsic nature consists in existing on all sides is grasped by the term *abhitobhāvi*, and not that which possesses an intrinsic nature contrary to that. Regarding the word *prakoṣṭham*: [it is derived] from the root *kuṣ* with the suffix *than*, according to the rule *uṣikuṣigārtibhyasthan* (Dhātupāṭha 6.29).
Therefore, the word *kroṣṭu* has its first syllable accented acute (*ādyudātta*). Regarding the term *pragṛham*: the suffix *kap* is applied according to [Pāṇini 3.1.144], *gehi kaḥ*.
Therefore, *gṛham* has its final syllable accented (*antodātta*). As for *pradvāram*,
by the rule "of that which falls within the scope of *nañ* and does not end in *ani*" (Phiṭ Sūtra 2.26), *dvāram* has its initial syllable accented (*ādyudātta*).
Regarding "prapadam": the word *pada* is acute-accented on its first syllable, just as in the case of *dvāra*. Regarding "prahastam": [the same applies].
By the rule *hasimṛgriṇvamidami* (Pāṇini 6.1.159), the suffix *stan* is applied after the root *has*; thus, the word *hasta* is udātta on its first syllable. Regarding the term *nirudaka*:

it is a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "from which water has departed" (*niṣkrāntam udakam asmāt*), or it is a *prādi-samāsa* (prepositional compound) meaning "departed from water" (*niṣkrāntam udakāt*).

Regarding the form *udakam*, [it is derived] from the root *kāy-* (to move) with the substitution of *ud-* for *udaka-* according to Pāṇini 6.3.57. Thus, *udaka-* is oxytone (acute on the final syllable).
Regarding the term *nirupalam*: [it means] "without stones."
In the rule *viṭapaviṣṭapaviśipolapāḥ* (Pāṇini 6.1.154), the word *upala* is prescribed as having its final syllable accented (*antodātta*).
Regarding the statement "others say *nirupalam*," [the suffix] *ka* is applied by the rule *upād dvyajajināṃ ḍaḥ* (Pāṇini 3.2.106).

By the rule *tenopalaśabdasthāthādi* (Pāṇini 6.2.143), [the word] is udātta on its first syllable. Regarding the examples "nirmakṣikam" and "nirmaśakam," the words *maśaka* and *makṣikā* are respectively udātta on the first syllable and udātta on the final syllable.

For in that context, [the rule] "Now begins [the section on] *pra* and so forth, prior to *śakaṭi*" (*Phiṭ-sūtra* 2.24), and "[Now begins] the second [section], prior to *prādi*" (*Phiṭ-sūtra* 3.50)—where "*second*" is understood to carry over—states:
"of these," and so forth.
If it is a *prādi*-compound, then the analysis (*vigraha*) is either "water has gone out" (*nirgatam udakam*) or "gone out from the water" (*nirgatam udakāt*).
But when it is a *bahuvrīhi*, then [the meaning is] "water has gone out from this.
Now, why does this [suffix] not also apply in the case of an *avyayībhāva*? To this he says: "In the case of an *avyayībhāva*, however," and so forth.
For in the cases of a *bahuvrīhi* and a *prādi*-compound, it is not established because they have the udātta accent on the final syllable of the compound.
For instance: [[6.2.1]] states that in a *bahuvrīhi* compound, the original accent (*prakṛtisvara*) of the first member is prescribed as an exception to the general accent rules for compounds.
This also applies to *prādi* compounds by the rule "in a *tatpuruṣa*, [the first member retains its accent] when meaning 'equal to' (*tulyārtha*)" [[6.2.2]], and so forth.
Thus, in the word *niṣkālakaḥ*.
The word *kāla* is acutely accented on its first syllable because it ends in the suffix *kan*.
Regarding the term *niṣkālikaḥ*: it is a *prādi* compound meaning "one who has gone beyond *kālikā*."

*Kālī* is oxytone because it ends in *ṅīṣ* according to the rule *jānapadādi-sūtra* [Pāṇini 4.1.42]. Even when the suffix *kan*, which denotes the same meaning (*svārthika*), is added, it remains acutely accented on the first syllable.
Regarding *niṣpeṣaḥ*:
the suffix *ghañ* is applied to the root *viṣlṛ* (meaning "to crush," Dhātupāṭha 1452).
Therefore, the word *peṣa* has its initial syllable accented acute (*ādyudātta*).

As for the word *tarīpa*, it has its final syllable accented acute (*antodātta*) according to [Pāṇini 3.2.3]: "The suffix *ka* is applied after the root *pā-* when preceded by *tarī-*, etc. (i.e., *tarī-pāti*).
By using the term "kutsita" (contemptible) in the phrase *kutsitastarīpaḥ*, [the author] shows that in the word *dustarīpa*, the prefix *duḥ* functions in the sense of contempt (*kutsā*).
Regarding the statement, "some say *nistarīpa*," they analyze it as *nirgataḥ tarīpaḥ* ("one from whom crossing has departed") and form it as a *prādi*-compound.
The connection is with the phrase "others read 'nistarīka'";
[the examples are] "nirajinam," and so forth.
It has been stated that *ajina* is oxytone (*antodātta*).
Regarding the rule beginning with *pareḥ*,
the words *hasta*, *pāda*, and *keśa* are acute on the first syllable (*ādyudātta*) by the rule *svāṅgaśiṭāmadantānām* (Phiṭ-sūtra 2.29).

The meaning is "of the pronouns" (*sarvanāman*). The word *karṣa* has its final syllable accented acute (udātta) by [Pāṇini 6.1.159]. Regarding the word *abhimukha*, the word *mukha* has the aforementioned accent.
The word *abhi* has its final syllable accented (*antodātta*).
Regarding the statement "this is a *bahuvrīhi*," and so forth:
when it is a *bahuvrīhi*, the analysis (*vigraha*) is "he by whom the face has been approached."
But when it is a *prādisamāsa*, then [the analysis is] "one who has approached the face" (*abhigato mukham*) or "one who has approached by means of the face" (*abhigato mukhena*).
Why does this not become an *avyayībhāva*? To this he says: "But in the case of an *avyayībhāva*" and so forth.
"This statement is for the sake of excluding the *bahuvrīhi*."
When *mukha* is permanent (*dhruva*), it then signifies something impermanent (*adhruva*) or something that is not a part of one's own body (*asvāṅga*).
This occurs even when *mukha* is used in a *bahuvrīhi* compound, as in the example:
"a hall facing [the east]" (*abhimukhā śālā*).

"Abhigatamukhā" is a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "one whose face has approached. In this case, the rule [Pāṇini 6.2.177] does not apply; for the word *mukha* does not denote a part of the body (*asvāṅga*). "The *avyayībhāva* compound also applies here"—the meaning of the word "also" (*api*) is that it is not only the *bahuvrīhi* and *tatpuruṣa* compounds that apply.
In that context, when it is a *bahuvrīhi* compound, the analysis (*vigraha*) is "that from which the face has departed" (*apagataṃ mukham asmāt*).
When, however, it is a *prādisamāsa*, it is "the departed face" (*apagataṃ mukham*). Furthermore, when it is an *avyayībhāva*, it is "apart from the face" (*apamukhāt*), meaning "excluding the face."
[The term *avyayībhāva* is established] by the rule [Pāṇini 2.1.12].

But how does the *avyayībhāva* compound necessitate [this specific accent], since it is already established by the fact that a compound has its final syllable accented (*samāsāntodātta*)? To this he says: "For even there," and so forth. The phrase "the original accent" (*prakṛtisvaratvam*) is to be supplied here.

In that case as well, the rule *paripratyupāpā* [Pāṇini 6.2.33] and so forth has stated that the initial member of the compound retains its original accent (*prakṛtisvaratva*), which is an exception to the general accentuation rules for compounds.
Therefore, the *avyayībhāva* compound also serves as a motivation [for this rule].
"The division of the *yoga* (sūtra) is for the sake of what follows."
In the subsequent sūtra, the term *ap* alone should be understood as recurring, and not *agni*.
This rule is an exception to the original accent (*prakṛtisvara*) even when preceded by an indeclinable (*avyaya*).

The same applies to the subsequent rules prior to the rule "in a *bahuvrīhi* compound with *paddanmūrdha* following *dvi* or *tri*" (Pāṇini 6.2.197). In a *dvandva* compound denoting a collective (*samāhāra*), the words beginning with *sphic* and ending with *nāman* [take the final acute accent].
"And names of ploughs" refers to those beginning with *hala*,
such as *apasphiga* and *apapūta*.
This is either a *prādi*-compound or a *bahuvrīhi* compound.
The words *sphig* and *pūta* have the acute accent on the first syllable according to the rule *svāṅgaśiṭāmadantānām* (Phiṭ-sūtra 2.29).
However, some maintain that the word *sphiga* has the acute accent on the final syllable because it belongs to the *dhṛtādi* group (Phiṭ-sūtra 1.21).

By the rule *rāsnāsāsnāsthūṇāvīṇāḥ* (Pāṇini 6.1.157), the word *vīṇā* is prescribed as having its first syllable udātta. From the root *añjū*, the suffix *asun* is applied; by that, *añja* has its first syllable udātta.

Under the governing rule *śīṅ-kruśi-ruhi-jikṣi-sṛ-dhṛ-bhyaḥ kvanip* (with the variant reading *kvan* in the Mugdhabodha), and under the rule *adeḥ dhak ca* (with the variant *adeḥ dhaś ca* in the Daiva), the suffix *adhvan* is formed;
therefore, this word is udātta on its first syllable.
Regarding the rule *upasargādadhvanaḥ* and so forth:

while the suffix *ac* is being carried over from the rule *ac-pratyanvavapūrvāt sāmalomnaḥ* (Pāṇini 5.4.75), the suffix *ac* is prescribed as a compound-final element (*samāsānta*) by the rule *aṇajau* (Pāṇini 5.4.85).

Consequently, because that *ac* suffix [which functions as the final member of the compound] is marked with the *cit* indicator, its status as having the udātta accent on the final syllable is established by that very fact.

But is it not the case that the suffix added at the end of a compound (*samāsānta*) is compulsory? Why, then, is it said that "when the suffix at the end of a compound does not exist"? To this he says: "And [the suffix] is non-compulsory," and so forth.

If the suffix added at the end of a compound were compulsory, the mention of the word *adhvan* (path) here would not have been made; for the acute accent on the final syllable would already be established by the fact that the suffix *ac* is marked with the letter *c*. Yet it has been mentioned, and therefore this very fact indicates: "The rule regarding suffixes added at the end of compounds is non-compulsory.
By this, usages such as *tatropāsitalokabhartari* become justified.

From the rule *pluṣikuṣiśuṣibhyaḥ ksiḥ* (Pāṇini 4.11), [we derive *pluṣi*, *śuṣi*, and *kuṣi*]. Regarding the form *anujyeṣṭhaḥ*: by the rule *anujyeṣṭhaḥ* (Pāṇini 5.3.62), when the suffix *iṣṭhan* follows, the substitute *jy* replaces *vṛddha*. The word *jyeṣṭha* is udātta on its first syllable due to the *niṭ* accentuation of the suffix *aṇ*.
Regarding the term *anumadhyamaḥ*:
according to [Pāṇini 4.3.8], it is a *madhyama* compound; by the accent of the suffix (*pratyayasvara*), it is oxytone (*antodātta*).
It is a *prādi-samāsa* (prepositional compound) in which the meaning of the first member is predominant.

For here, that which follows the eldest and the middle one is expressed primarily through a *prādi* compound, while the terms "eldest" (*jyeṣṭha*) and "middle" (*madhyama*) are subordinate. Therefore, this is a compound in which the meaning of the first member is predominant,
as in the expression "anukanīyān" (one younger than the youngest).

When the suffix *īyasun* follows, the word *yuva-* undergoes the substitution of *kan-* according to [Pāṇini 5.3.64]. The word *kanīya-* is acutely accented on its first syllable due to the *nit*-accent.
Thus: "the elder who has followed is *anu-jyeṣṭhaḥ*."
This [compound] has the meaning of the final member as its predominant sense;

therefore, the word *jyeṣṭha* possesses the quality of denoting the predominant element. From the root *pṛ* in the sense of "protecting" or "filling" (DhP 3.1489), the suffix *kuṣan* is applied by the rule *puraḥ kuṣan* (Daiva 9.14).
Consequently, the word *puruṣa* is udātta on its first syllable.

The term *anvādiṣṭa* means "prescribed as secondary" (*anvācita*). For example, in the command "Go for alms and bring the cow," the bringing of the cow is secondary; or as in the rule *kartuḥ kyaṅ salopaśca* [Pāṇini 3.1.11], where the elision of the suffix *sa* is secondary.

"Recounted after having been told" (*kathitānukathita*) means: that which is told after [something] has already been told is "recounted after having been told. Alternatively, that which is told after first telling something else is called "recounted after having been told."

Regarding the phrase "anupuruṣaḥ," it means "a person who follows. That person who exists behind [another] is thus called *anupuruṣaḥ*. Regarding the term "*akṛtpade*": *akṛt* and *pada* together form *akṛtpade*; this is a nominative dual ending.

Regarding the term *atyaṅkuśo nāgaḥ*: the word *aṅkuśa* is derived from the root *aki* (meaning "to mark" or "characterize," Dhātupāṭha 1024) according to the rule *sānasiparṇasi-* (Pāṇini 3.2.28), followed by the suffix *ac* (pacādyac), and the feminine suffix *ṭāp*. Thus, it becomes *aṅkuśā*. [The formation follows Pāṇini 8.2.5].
Therefore, it is *kaśāntodāttā*. According to [Pāṇini 3.3.125], *atipadā śakvarī*, the suffix *gha* is applied to the root *pad*.
For by the inclusion of *ghit* [in the rule], it is made known that *gha* occurs even from something other than [the end of] a word; therefore,
the word *atikārakaḥ* has its final syllable accented (*antodātta*).
The suffix *ṇvul* is added to the root *kṛ*.

Here, by the rule "In a *tatpuruṣa* compound, [the first member retains its accent] when meaning 'equal' (*tulyārtha*)" (Pāṇini 6.2.2), the first member takes the accent of an indeclinable (*avyaya*).
[The form *atikaraṇī* is derived] with the elision of the verbal root (*dhātulopa*) according to the rule "After *ati*, there is elision of the root" (Pāṇini 6.4.149).
It should be stated that where there is elision of a verbal root (*dhātu*), the final syllable of the word following *ati* becomes udātta.
For what purpose? He says: "In this case," and so forth.
If it were not stated that the elision of the root *at* [triggers this], then this would also apply here: *śobhano gārgyaḥ* → *atigārgyaḥ*.
For in this case, the final member [of the compound] following *ati* would not end in a *kṛt* suffix;
and here it would not occur in the form *atikārakaḥ*,
meaning "one who has surpassed the agent," because it is a *prādi*-compound according to the rule *nirādayaḥ krāntādyarthe pañcamyā* (Vārttika 94).
For here, the word *kāraka* ending in a *kṛt* suffix is the final member (*uttarapada*).
In that case, if it were not stated that [the rule applies] "when there is elision of a verbal root (*dhātulopa*)", then it would not apply here either.
However, since it is stated thus, it does apply here as well, for there is indeed an elision of the verbal root *kram*.

"Omission," moreover, is the non-appearance of that which is not being used because its meaning is already understood within a compound. Regarding "treasure" (*nidhāna*) and "non-revelation" (*aprakāśatā*):
it is not a non-treasure (*anidhāna*). Regarding "rootless" (*nirmūla*) and "completely" (*nyakṣam*).
From the root *mūla* in the sense of "establishing" (*pratiṣṭhāyām*)—according to Dhātupāṭha 529—the suffix *ac* is applied by the rule *pacādyac*.
Therefore, the word *mūla* has its udātta accent on the final syllable.

Regarding the word *akṣa*, under the governing rule *vṛtṛvadihanikamikaṣibhyaḥ saḥ* (Dhātupradīpa 9.21)—where the variant *kamikaṣiyumucibhyaḥ* is also cited—and specifically by the rule *aśerdevane* (Dhātupradīpa 9.24), it ends in the suffix *sa*; thus, the word *akṣa* also has its udātta accent on the final syllable.
Regarding the word *nitṛṇam*:
by the rule *nabviṣayasya* (Phiṭ-sūtra 2.26), *tṛṇam* is udātta on its first syllable. "This is a *bahuvrīhi*," and so forth.
When it is a *bahuvrīhi*, the analysis (*vigraha*) is "from which the roots have gone out" (*nigatāni mūlāny asya*). When it is a *prādisamāsa*, it is "the root has gone out" (*nigataṃ mūlam*).
Why does this not become an *avyayībhāva*? To this he says: "But in the case of an *avyayībhāva*," and so forth.

In the case of a *bahuvrīhi* compound, however, the rule "in a *bahuvrīhi*, [the first member] retains its original accent" (6.2.1) and so forth prescribes that the first member retains its natural accent (*prakṛtisvara*), which is an exception to the general rule of the final syllable of the compound being accented. Similarly, in the case of a *tatpuruṣa* compound, the rule "in a *tatpuruṣa*, [the first member retains its accent] when it has the sense of 'equal to'" (6.2.2) and so forth applies. Therefore, for these two types of compounds, the accentuation of the final syllable would not be established without this specific statement.

In the case of an *avyayībhāva* compound, however, the desired result is already established by the general rule of the final syllable of the compound being accented, for no exception to that rule has been stated there.
In the case of *nivāgvṛṣalaḥ* and *nidaṇḍaḥ*,
the original accent (*prakṛtisvara*) of the first member remains.
The word *vāk* is derived with the suffix *kvip* according to the rule *kvibvacipracchi* (Pāṇini 3.2.178), and thus it is accented on the first syllable (*ādyudātta*).
From the root *damu* in the sense of "to pacify" (*damu upaśame*, Dhātupāṭha 1203), [the suffix] *ṅa* is applied by the rule *ñamantāṅṅaḥ* (Pāṇini 3.2.167).
Consequently, the word *daṇḍa* is also oxytone.
As for the word *ni*, it expresses the sense of "placing down" (*nidhāna*).
The meaning is that it expresses the state of non-manifestation (*aprakāśatā*).
But how does the word *ni-* here express the sense of "placing" (*nidhāna*)? To this he says: "For *pra* and the others," and so forth.
By the term "vṛtti" (*vṛttiśabda*), the compound formation (*samāsavṛtti*) and so on are intended here.
