For particles such as *pra* and others, by their very nature, express an action together with its means (*sādhanā*) within the scope of their derivative usage (*vṛtti*).

Therefore, in this case of compound formation (*samāsa-vṛtti*), there is an action consisting of non-manifestation which is denoted by the word *ni-dhāna*; that action has speech (*vāk*) as its means and the staff (*daṇḍa*) as its means, and the particle *ni* expresses it. This rule is an exception (*apavāda*) to the original accent (*prakṛti-svara*) of the first member of the compound.
For example: *pratyaṃśuḥ*.
It is a *prādi* compound.
Under the heading "and *ku*, *bhadra*, etc. (*kubhraśca*), the word *aṃśu* is prescribed as a *nipāta* by the rule "*mugayvādayaśca*" (*da|u|1|121*).
Consequently, it is oxytone.
The suffix *ghan* is applied after the root *jan*;
therefore, the word *jana* has its initial syllable udātta.
The word *rājan* also [has its initial syllable udātta] because it ends in the suffix *kanin*.

Regarding the passage beginning with "the word *rāja*": when the suffix *ṭac*—prescribed by the rule *rājāhaḥsakhibhyaṣṭac* [Pāṇini 5.4.91]—is absent due to its optional nature (*anityatva*), then the word *rāja* serves as the purpose for this recitation. But why does it not serve as the purpose when that compound-final suffix (*samāsānta*) is present? To this he says: "For when that [suffix] exists," and so forth.

The fact that the suffix *tva* is not applied [to form *anityatva*] has already been made known by the rule for the addition of compound-final suffixes (*samāsāntavidhi*). Furthermore, the inclusion of the word *rājan* in this list makes it known that the application of compound-final suffixes is not mandatory (*anityatva*). From the root *uṣ* "to burn" (Dhātupāṭha 696), the suffix *ṣṭran* is added.

Therefore, the word *uṣṭra* has its initial syllable accented (*ādyudātta*), derived from the root *uṣ* (meaning "to heat," or *khiṭ* meaning "to terrify" according to the Dhātupāṭha, no. 302) with the suffix *ṇvul*. For that same reason, the word *kheṭaka* also has its initial syllable accented.
Furthermore, the word *ajira* is established as having the suffix *kirac* by the rule beginning with *ajira-śiśira-* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 6.4.27).

Therefore, it has the udātta accent on the final syllable. From the root *dru* meaning "to move with contempt" (Dhātupāṭha 1054), preceded by the prefix *ā*, the suffix *aṅ* is applied according to [Pāṇini 3.3.106]. Due to this irregular formation (*nipātana*), the first member ends in *r*. Consequently, because its status as an indeclinable (*avyaya*) is lost, the original accent of the first member (*pūrvapada-prakṛtisvara*) does not apply; thus, *ārdra* becomes udātta on the final syllable.
The suffix *lyuṭ* is applied to the root *śru* in the sense of "hearing" (*śravaṇe*; Dhātupāṭha 942).
Consequently, the word *śravaṇa* is udātta on its first syllable due to the accent of the *lit* suffix.

Based on the rule *vṛtestikan* (Daiva 3.28), the suffix *tikan* is applied—along with the feminine marker *ṭāp*—to the roots *kṛ*, *bhid*, and *lit* according to the rule *kṛtibhidilatibhyaḥ kit* (Daiva 3.29).

Therefore, the word *kṛttikā* has its initial syllable accented (*ādyudātta*). From the root *ṛdh*, either by the suffix *ac* or *ghañ*, the word *ardha* has its final syllable accented (*antodātta*) or its initial syllable accented (*ādyudātta*).

Regarding *pura-agragamane* (Dhātupāṭha 1346): from this root, the suffix *ka* is applied according to [Pāṇini 3.1.135] because it has a penultimate *i*. Consequently, the word *pura* is oxytone (*antodātta*).
[The compound *purāṃsā* is explained as] "one whose rays (*aṃśavaḥ*) have gone forth (*pratigatāḥ*)," and so on.

In this case, within a *bahuvrīhi* compound, the original accent of the first member (*pūrvapada-prakṛtisvara*) occurs—as in "upadevaḥ. This is a *prādi-samāsa* (compound with prefixes). The word "deva" is oxytone (*antodātta*) because it ends in the suffix *ac* added after the root *div* according to Pāṇini 3.1.134.
Regarding the word *upasomaḥ*: by the rule *ati-su-hu-sṛ-...* (Pāṇini 6.4.149), the suffix *man* is applied; consequently, the word *soma-* has its initial syllable accented acute (*ādyudātta*).
From the roots *huḍṛ* and *huḍṛ* meaning "to move" (*dhātu-pāṭha* 352, 353), the suffix *ac* is applied according to the *pacādi* group;
thus, the word *hoḍa* has its final syllable accented (*antodātta*).
It has been stated that the word *ajina* has its final syllable accented, and this [mention of *hoḍa*] is for the purpose of excluding the two types of *aja*.
The word *gaura* is ādyudātta (accented on the first syllable) because it ends in the *yaṅ* suffix derived from *prajña*.
The time joined with the asterism Tiṣya is called *taiṣa*;
here, the *y* is elided by the rule *sūryatiṣya* [Pāṇini 6.4.149].
Neither *naiṣa* nor *taiṭāva* have a final vowel [that is grave].
Therefore, it has an udātta accent on the final syllable.
From the root *raṭ* in the sense of "speaking" (*raṭa paribhāṣaṇe*, Dhātupāṭha 297), the suffix *ac* is applied.

Because *ra* and *la* are identical, the *repha* [the sound *r*] is replaced by *lakāra* [the sound *l*]. From the root *luṭ* in the sense of "agitating" (*luṭa viloḍane*, Dhātupāṭha 314), the suffix *pacādyac* is applied.

By that rule, *laṭa* and *loṭa* are also udātta on the final syllable. Furthermore, according to the rule *śavayahvajihvāgrīvāpvāmīvāḥ* (Daivamudgala 8.128), *jihvā* is prescribed as being udātta on the final syllable. Also, by the rule *iṇsiñji* (Daivamudgala 5.35)—[referring to *iṇ*, *siñ*, etc.]—[the formation of *jihvā* follows].

With reference to this [section], by the rule *kṛṣervarṇe* (Daiva-kośa 5.37), the suffix *nak* is added to the root *kṛṣ*, followed by the feminine suffix *ṭāp*. Through the rule for the lengthening of homogeneous vowels (*savarṇadīrghatva*), and by the rule *ekādeśa udāttenodāttaḥ* (Pāṇini 8.2.5), the word *kṛṣṇā* has its final syllable accented. By the rule *adhnyādayaśca* (Daiva-kośa 8.14), the word *kanyā* is prescribed as having its final vowel circumflex-accented (*svarita*).

Regarding *guḍa* [the root *guḍ* meaning "to protect" in the Dhātupāṭha, no. 1370]: from this, the suffix *ka* is applied according to Pāṇini 3.1.135 (*igupadhajñāprīkiraḥ kaḥ*). By that rule, *guḍa* has its udātta accent on the final syllable.
The words *kalpa* and *vāha* have their udātta accent on the final syllable because they belong to the *vṛṣādi* group. [The example is] *susthaṇḍilaḥ*.
*Sthaṇḍila* means "that in which a firm place (*sthāna*) exists";
it is accented on the first syllable because it belongs to the *pṛṣodarādi* group.
[The commentary says: "With well-rounded buttocks."
The word *sphiga* has its initial syllable accented (*ādyudātta*).
Regarding the term *supratyavasita*: the word *pratyavasita*, by the rule [Pāṇini 6.2.143] concerning suffixes beginning with *tha*, is accented on the final syllable (*antodātta*).

But surely, even when a compound is formed with the word *su*, the final acute accent (*antodāttatva*) will occur by the rule *thāthādisvara* itself; so for what purpose was this example cited? The intention is as follows: since this [present rule] is formulated for a different purpose, it is appropriate that the final acute accent here also be determined by this very rule due to its superior status. If the word *su* here functions only in the sense of praise (*pūjā*), then for what purpose is "contempt" (*avakṣepaṇa*) mentioned? To this he says: "The meaning of the sentence, however, is contempt. He states the reason for this very point: "Because it is expressed in that way [as such] without being false (*asūṇyā*)."
In this case, since a sentence such as "May you have good ground" is employed out of malice (*asūyā*), there is indeed a disparagement of the very meaning of the sentence. However,
in the phrase "in well-grazed [pastures]," the expression is made with the desire to highlight a quality (*guṇodbhāvanecchā*), not out of malice.
Therefore, there is no elision [of the initial vowel], but rather only the honorific treatment (*pūjā*) applies. Regarding the term *utpucchaḥ*:
the word *puccha* is acute-accented on its first syllable by the rule *nabviṣayasya* (Phiṭ-sūtra 2.26).
Thus, this is an optional rule (*vibhāṣā*) that applies in both cases.
When the word *utpuccha* does not end in the suffix *ac*, then there is the udātta accent on the final syllable of the compound.

When, however, by the exception to the rule for the udātta of the final syllable of a compound—namely, by [Pāṇini 6.2.2] *tatpuruṣe tulyārtha* and so forth—the original accent (*prakṛtisvara*) of the first member, which is an indeclinable, applies, then this option (*vibhāṣā*) is provided because that [rule] would otherwise have precluded the application of this final-udātta accent.

However, when there is the intention to express the meaning "he raises his tail," after applying the suffix *ṇiṅ* according to [Pāṇini 3.1.20], and then adding the suffix *ac* (as in the *pacādi* group) to the resulting form *utpucch*, the word-form *utpuccha* arises; at that point, since the rule [Pāṇini 6.2.143] regarding the *thā-tha-ādi* suffixes would invariably result in an udātta accent on the final syllable, this option is introduced. Thus, this is an optional rule (*vibhāṣā*) with respect to what was previously established. For example: *utpacchaḥ* ("one whose tail is raised").
The accent remains that of the original *bahuvrīhi* compound itself. [Regarding the rule] "from *dvi* and *tri*":
the ablative case is used according to [Pāṇini 2.3.29], which characterizes a connection with a direction (*digyoga*).
[Regarding the rule] "in *pād*, *dan*, and *mūrdhan*": [the same applies].
The locative case [in *yasya ca bhāvena bhāvalakṣaṇam* (Pāṇini 2.3.37)] is used for the indication of an action (*bhāvalakṣaṇā saptamī*).
The *bahuvrīhi* compound is the object of the operation;
therefore, he says: "by these two, namely *dvi* and *tri*," and so forth.

In the words *dvipāt* and *tripāt*, the vowel *a* is elided by [Pāṇini 5.4.138] and [5.4.140]. Since the word *pāda* is accented on the first syllable because it ends in the suffix *ghañ*, the word *pād-* likewise remains accented on the first syllable.
Regarding the word *dvijan*: by the rule *vayasi dantasya* (Pāṇini 5.4.141), the substitute *datṛ* is applied. It has been stated that the word *danta* is udātta on its first syllable.
Therefore, by virtue of the *sthānivadbhāva* rule, even the substitute for the dative case remains udātta on the first syllable.
Regarding the word *dvimūrdhā*: the word *mūrdhan* is derived with the suffix *ran* according to the rule "ān, nukṣan, pūṣan, plīhan," etc. (Dhātupāṭha 6.55).
Therefore, it is acutely accented (*udātta*).
[The word] "mūrdhan" and so forth;
[the rule] "ṣo" is from Pāṇini 5.4.115. [Note: *mu* refers to the commentary.]
[In the reading] "iti," the suffix *ṣ* as a compound-final (*samāsānta*) would have applied, but it was not applied.
Therefore, in this context, the word *mūrdhan* ends precisely in *n*.
But what is the reason that the word *mūrdhañ* is employed here without the compound-final suffix having been applied? To this he says: "Of that," and so forth.

If [the term] were employed with the compound-final suffix (*samāsānta*) already applied, then the word would have an acute accent on the final syllable (*antodāttatva*) only when that suffix is present, but not when it is absent. Therefore, the purpose of specifying the form without the compound-final suffix is so that the acute accent on the final syllable may occur even when the suffix is not present. [Objection: But surely a compound must always possess a compound-final suffix; how then could it be absent? To this, he says: "This very... and so forth.

The very fact that the word *mūrdhan* is employed here without the application of a compound-final suffix (*samāsānta*) for the sake of accomplishing this specific purpose is itself the indicator (*jñāpaka*) that the compound-final suffix is not obligatory (*anitya*). Consequently, the usage of forms such as *dvimūrdha* becomes justified.
If, however, the word *mūrdhan* is taken here without the compound-final suffix, then it follows that when the suffix is subsequently applied, the word should not be oxytone (*antodātta*).

Because that which has undergone the addition of a compound-final suffix (*samāsānta*) is a distinct word, he says "even though" and so forth. For here the *bahuvrīhi* is the subject of the operation, and the compound-final suffix is a part of that [compound].

That of which a part exists is a "possessor of a part" (*ekadeśin*); that *bahuvrīhi* is the possessor of a part for that compound-final suffix, and its state of being such is "the state of being a part-possessor" (*tadekadeśitva*).

By this, demonstrating that the compound-ending suffix (*samāsānta*) is a constituent part of the *bahuvrīhi*, he refutes the notion that the word with the compound-ending suffix applied is a distinct word altogether.

Thus, since the *bahuvrīhi* is the primary element to undergo the operation here, and the compound-ending suffix is merely a part of it, therefore even when the compound-ending suffix is applied, the final acute accent (*antodāttatva*) certainly occurs in the alternative case,
as in "kalyāṇamūrdhā" (one who has a beautiful head).
The word *kalyāṇa* is udātta on its first syllable by the rule *nabviṣayasya* (Phiṭ-sūtra 2.26).
Regarding the phrase "the head of two," here the udātta accent on the final syllable of the compound occurs invariably. Regarding the word "thigh" (*saktham*).

By the rule *bahuvrīhau sakthyakṣṇoḥ svāṅgāt ṣac* [Pāṇini 5.4.113], the word *sakthi* is understood here as that which has the suffix *ṣac* as its compound-ending (*samāsānta*). Regarding the term *akrāntāt*: that which has the word *kra* as its final member is called *krānta*.
It is not "krānta," but "akrānta. Regarding the term "gaurasaktha":
the word *gaura* is oxytone (accented on the final syllable) because it ends in the suffix *aṇ* added after *prajñādi*.
Regarding the term *ślakṣṇasakthaḥ*:
while the rule *kṛtyaśūbhyāṃ ksnah* (Dhātupāṭha 5.49) is in effect, the word *ślakṣman* ends in the suffix *ksna* according to *śliṣer accopadhāyāḥ* (Dhātupāṭha 5.51).
Consequently, it is udātta on its final syllable.

Regarding the term *cakrasakthaḥ*: according to the rule *karoteḥ kinn dve ca* (Pāṇini 6.1.156; Daiva 8.103)—which states that the word *cakra* is derived from the root *kṛ* with the suffix *kin* and the reduplication of the syllable—the word *cakra* has its first vowel udātta (accented). In this context, by the word "para" (the latter), it is specifically the word *saktha* that is intended. This is due to proximity (*pratyāsatti*), for it is the word *saktha* that is proximate because it was present in the preceding sūtra.

If this were so, the mention of the word *para* would be purposeless, for the word *saktha* alone would continue to apply here. This is not the case; since the mention of *bahuvrīhi* also continues to apply here, one might suspect that its initial syllable would likewise be udātta.
In the example *añjisaktham*, the word *añji* is udātta on its final syllable by the accent of the nominal stem (*prātipadika-svara*).
Furthermore, even if the suffix *ini* is applied in the sense of possession (*matvartha*) to the word *añjas*, it would still be oxytone (having the acute accent on the final syllable),
as in the example *lomaśasaktham*.
This is because the word *lomaśa* is oxytone due to its ending in the suffix *śa* [according to Pāṇini 5.2.100].
Regarding the word *ṛjubāhuḥ*:

under the governing rule *kubhraśca* (Dhātupāṭha 1.107), the words *ṛjubāhu* ending in the suffix *ku* are formed by the rule *arjidṛśikamyamipaśibādhāmṛjipasitugdhugdīrghahakārāśca* (Dhātupāṭha 1.112).
Therefore, they are oxytone (having the acute accent on the final syllable).

Regarding the expressions "vākpatiḥ" and "citpatiḥ," these are genitive compounds (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*). In these cases, the final member of the compound (*uttarapada*) is accented on its first syllable, due to the inclusion of the term "optionally" (*bahulagrahaṇa*) [in Pāṇini’s rule].

For, since the term *vibhāṣā* (optionally) was already under discussion, this was introduced for the purpose of showing what is accomplished by means of the term *bahulam* (variously). Thus: "From that, there is a various transposition.
Since the grammatical operation is accomplished by this use of *bahulam*, therefore a various transposition occurs.
Now, was it not already established previously that there is a transposition of vowels? True, that is so; however, this is merely an elaboration of that very point.
Regarding the phrase "the first member is cited as an example," such as *vākpati* and *citpati*:
here, by the mention of the word "first" (*para*), the subsequent member (*uttarapada*) is indicated.
"In the section concerning the acute accent on the final syllable" refers to [Pāṇini 6.2.144] *antaḥ* and the following rules.
"In the section concerning the acute accent on the final syllable of the first member" refers to the same.
In rules such as *antaḥ* [Pāṇini 6.2.92] and *sarvaṃ guṇakārtsnye* [Pāṇini 6.2.93], etc.,

[the term "beginning" (*ādi*) refers to the beginning of the compound]. Regarding the phrase "in the section on the acute accent on the first syllable of the prior member" (*pūrvapadādyudāttaprakaraṇe*), the first syllable is acute— as in *saptamīhāriṇau dhamya'haraṇe* [Pāṇini 6.2.65], etc.

"All such [cases] are included" means by virtue of the inclusion of the term *bahulam* (in various ways). The intention is that, although the rule of optionality (*vibhāṣā*) was already in force, the term *bahulam* was employed here for that purpose.
Since the vowels of the preceding and following words for the *tricakra* and so forth have already been stated previously, they are not mentioned again here.

Thus ends the second quarter of the sixth chapter in the *Kāśikā-vivaraṇapañjikā*, composed by the venerable master Jinendrabuddhi, who is like a Bodhisattva. Now begins the third quarter of the sixth chapter: "Released from a little" (*stokānmuktaḥ*), "released from a small amount" (*alpānmuktaḥ*).
[The fifth case ending is applied] by the rule *karaṇe stokālpakṛcchrakatipayasyāsatvavacanasya* (Pāṇini 2.3.33), and [the compound is formed] by the rule *karaṇe ca* (Pāṇini 2.1.39).

But surely, the term *samāsa* (compound) will be understood as a governing word (*anuvartate*) from [Pāṇini 6.2.178]; and since in a compound the subsequent member (*uttarapada*) is invariably present, one might think that the subsequent member is obtained even without explicitly mentioning "subsequent member. With this intention, he asks: "What is meant by 'subsequent member'?

He gives the example: *niḥstokaḥ*. This is a *prādi*-compound according to the rule: "Words beginning with *nis*, etc., form compounds with a word in the fifth case when meaning 'gone beyond' (*krānta*), etc. (Vārttika 94).

He thinks as follows: if the mention of the word *uttarapada* (subsequent member) were not made, one would obtain only this much—that there is no elision (*aluk*) of the ablative case after those words such as *stoka* when they occur in a compound, whether they function as the subsequent member (*uttarapada*) or the prior member (*pūrvapada*). However, the specific distinction that [the rule applies] only when *stoka* and so on occur before a subsequent member would not be established. Consequently, in the example *niḥstoka*, there would also be no elision;
for here too, the ablative case follows a word such as *stoka* that resides within a compound.

Even so, this mention of the "subsequent word" (*uttarapada*) need not be made at all. By the maxim *lakṣaṇapratipadoktaparibhāṣā* (P. 1.1.3), only that fifth case (*pañcamī*) which is prescribed by specific rules such as *stokādibhyaḥ karaṇe ca* (P. 2.3.33) is to be understood; however, that fifth case which is prescribed by the general rule *apādāne pañcamī* (P. 2.3.28) is not to be understood.

Furthermore, one must necessarily rely on the technical rule (*paribhāṣā*) that "the specifically prescribed [rule] takes precedence over the general rule" (*salakṣaṇa-apratipadokta-paribhāṣā*). Otherwise, in the case of *stokāpeta* (meaning "departed from a little"), there would also be non-elision (*aluk*) of the case-ending; whereas in this situation, in the case of *niḥstoka*, the non-elision would not even be applicable, because here the ablative case is not prescribed by a specific rule (*pratipad-vihita*) following the word *stoka*, but rather is prescribed by a general rule (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa-vihita*). Therefore, what is the purpose of including the mention of the "subsequent member" (*uttarapada-grahaṇa*) for the sake of excluding that [non-elision]? To this he says: "For another purpose," and so forth.
This mention of the "subsequent member" is for the sake of [preventing the substitution of] *ānaṅ* and other such changes.
And if this [condition] were absent? In the rule *hotṛpotṛbhyām*, just as the shortening occurs for the first member (*pūrvapada*), so too would it occur for the second member (*uttarapada*).
Likewise, by the rule *tathā* (Pāṇini 6.3.61), just as the shortening occurs here in *grāmaṇiputraḥ*, so too would it occur here in *grāmaṇīḥ*.
Now, if the shortening were to occur even when there is no following word (*anuttarapada*), then just as the shortening occurs here in *grāmaṇiputraḥ*, so too would it occur here in *grāmaṇīḥ*.
Now, if there were shortening even when not followed by a subsequent word (*anuttarapada*), then just as the shortening occurs here in *grāmaṇiputraḥ*, it would likewise occur here in *grāmaṇīḥ*.

Furthermore, if there were shortening even when not followed by a subsequent word, then just as the rule "there is shortening of the neuter nominal stem" (*hrasvo napuṃsake prātipadikasya*) applies, it would likewise apply here in *grāmaṇīḥ*.

Now, one might object: "If a short vowel were to occur even when there is a following member (*uttarapada*), then the rule *hrasvo napuṃsake prātipadikasya* [Pāṇini 1.2.47] would be purposeless, since the desired result would be established by this very [present rule]. [The author replies: It is not purposeless, because it serves the purpose of applying to bases that do not end in a nasal (*aniganta*) and for the sake of making the operation obligatory (*nitya*). Furthermore, if the mention of "following member" (*uttarapada-grahaṇa*) were absent, [the rule would apply] even after a *kṛt* suffix. If that is so, then for whatever purpose this is intended, it should have been formulated within that specific rule itself; why is it done here? To this he says: "In order to prevent elision (*aluk*) here as well," and so forth.
The particle *iti* is used here in the sense of a reason (*hetau*).
First of all, this mention of the term "subsequent" (*uttara*) is certainly necessary for another purpose;
however, when it is applied here, this specific distinction is made: even in the case of *niḥstoka*, the non-elision (*aluk*) is prevented.

Therefore, the technical rule (paribhāṣā) stating that "the specific mention of a term [in a sūtra] prevails" (vya|pa|3) need not be resorted to. Now, from what source do these two governing scopes (adhikāra) derive? To this he says: "The governing scope of *aluk*, etc.

Since one thing to be enjoined (vidheya) sets aside another thing to be enjoined, when *ānaṅ* is being enjoined, it sets aside *aluk* in the case of the subsequent member (*uttarapada*). Therefore: "The governing scope of *aluk* extends prior to *ānaṅ*."

The section concerning the subsequent member (*uttarapadādhikāra*) extends "prior to the section concerning the base (*aṅgādhikāra*). When an operation is prescribed with respect to a subsequent member, because that [subsequent member] is a relative term, the preceding member is the locus of the rule.
Therefore, the base (*aṅga*), being understood as the locus of the rule, sets aside the section concerning the subsequent member.

For that which is the grammatical operation (kārya) pertaining to a base (aṅga) is prescribed when a suffix (pratyaya) follows, not when a subsequent member of a compound (uttarapada) follows. This is because the designation "base" (aṅgasaṃjñā) does not apply to a subsequent member of a compound.
Alternatively, because of the locative indication in the term "uttarapade," the substitution of ānaṅ must occur only when the subsequent member is immediately following.
If, moreover, there were no elision (*aluk*) of the case-ending here, then because of the intervention, there would be no immediate succession (*ānantarya*).
Nor can it be assumed that even with an intervention, *ānaṅ* would occur by virtue of the power of the rule;
for if that were so, the mention of "as specified" (*nirdiṣṭagrahaṇa*) in [Pāṇini 1.1.66]—which is intended to ensure immediate succession—would be sublated, and an undesired form would result.
Furthermore, it is not logical for a grammatical rule (*praklṛpti*) in a treatise to have an undesirable result.
Therefore, the governing heading for *aluk* (non-elision) extends prior to *ānaṅ*.

Since a *aṅga* (stem) cannot exist when followed by an affix (*pratyaya*), that [elision] does not occur when followed by a subsequent word (*uttarapada*); hence, the governing heading for the subsequent word (*uttarapadādhikāra*) extends prior to the governing heading for the stem (*aṅgādhikāra*). The words beginning with *stoka* are not listed among the groups of nominal stems (*prātipadika-gaṇa*).

Therefore, showing that only those [words] recited in the Sūtra itself should be accepted here, he says: "stokāntikadurārthakṛcchrāṇi" and so forth. Now, why are *stoka* and the others not taken from the Sūtras such as "and in the case of an instrument" (*karaṇe*, Pāṇini 2.3.33)? He thinks as follows: since it would have been sufficient to say "from *stoka* and the others after the suffix *ṅasi*" (*ṅaseḥ stokādibhyaḥ*), the mention of the longer term "of the fifth case" (*pañcamyāḥ*) indicates this: "those *stoka* and the others which, when included, result in the inclusion of a greater number of examples (*lakṣya*) are to be accepted."

When these very terms—*stoka*, *antika*, *dūra*, and *arthakṛcchra* (note: "dūrārtha" does not appear in the printed reading of the Nyāsa)—are taken [as the basis for the rule], there is a more extensive inclusion of examples of the target forms, because of the inclusion of the word *artha* therein; this is not the case with the others. Therefore, it is logical that only these should be included. But how is it that elision (*luk*) applies here? To which [case] would it apply, such that this prohibition is made when it has already occurred? To this he says: "When the compound has been formed," and so forth.

When the compound has been formed, [the rule] *tasya* (Pāṇini 1.2.46) establishes its status as a nominal stem (*prātipadika*). Consequently, since the elision (*luk*) of the case-ending (*sup*) would apply by the rule *ataḥ* (Pāṇini 2.4.71), this prohibition is stated.

But what is the reason that the non-elision (*aluk*) of *stoka* and the others is illustrated only when they end in the singular number, and not when they end in the dual or plural? To this he says: "Of those ending in the dual and plural," and so forth.
For in a derivative formation (*vṛtti*), qualifying words abandon numbers such as singularity and instead attain the number of undifferentiated unity (*abhedaikatvasaṃkhyā*).

Furthermore, that [number] is merely the general state of being numbered, without the specific number being grasped; since it is thus, a compound does not occur at all with words ending in the dual or plural numbers, because the intended meaning is not expressed.
For *kṛt*, *taddhita*, and compound formations are characterized by their expressive power (*abhidhāna*).
"By that," and so forth.

Since, for this reason, compounds of words such as *stoka* ending in dual or plural numbers do not occur, there is never a single word-form (*ekapadya*) nor a single accent (*eka-svarya*) in expressions such as *stokābhyāṃ muktaḥ* ("released from two small [quantities]") or *stokebhyo muktaḥ* ("released from many small [quantities]").
For the word *muktaḥ* following the word *stokābhyām* is indeed another word, entirely distinct; likewise, the word *muktaḥ* following *stokebhyaḥ* is another.
Furthermore, the accent here is also manifold.

For instance: the word *stokābhyām* is middle-accented (*madhyodātta*) by the accent of the nominal stem (*prātipadika-svara*), while *muktaḥ* is end-accented (*antodātta*) by the accent of the suffix (*pratyaya-svara*). Thus, in the case of *stokebhyo muktaḥ* as well, one should understand that there is a diversity of accents.
However, in the original example provided, once the compound (*samāsa*) is formed, it becomes a single word (*ekapada*), and consequently, there is only a single accent.
For instance, by the rule *thāthādi* (Pāṇini 6.2.143), there is here an udātta accent on the final syllable.

If a compound were not permitted for words ending in dual or plural numbers, then how would [the forms] *goṣucaraḥ* and *varṣāsujaḥ* be formed in this case? It is because the intended meaning is expressed.
Non-expression was stated as the reason for the prohibition in the case of a *samāsa*; however, in this instance, the expression of the intended meaning—namely, the plural—is indeed present.
Where the number of non-different unity arises, there is no denotation of a specific number; however, in this case, the number of non-different unity does not arise.
Consequently, because the intended meaning is being expressed, the number of non-different unity is not applicable.
To illustrate: in the expression *goṣucaraḥ*, the word *go* refers to water (*apsu*), and in denoting water, it denotes it as qualified by the number of plurality, just like the word *āp*.

Regarding the term *varṣāsuja*: the word *varṣā* (rainy season) also refers to a specific period of time characterized by the number "plurality. Therefore, since plurality is already established by the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) itself, the number "oneness of non-difference" does not arise here. If it were to arise, however, the number "plurality" would be set aside; consequently, the intended meaning of the nominal stems of both the word *go* (cow) and the word *varṣā* would not be understood in this context.

Therefore, so that there may not be a failure to understand the intended meaning in the case of the words *go* and *varṣā*, the number one (ekatva) associated with non-difference (*abheda*) does not arise here.

Consequently, because the intended meaning is expressed, a compound is indeed valid in cases such as *goṣucaraḥ* ("moving among cows") and *varṣāsujaḥ* ("born in the rains"). [Regarding this, it is said: "An addition must be made for the term *brāhmaṇācchaṃsin*."
The meaning is that an addition (*upasaṃkhyānam*)—that is, a formal explanation (*pratipādanam*)—must be made for this word *brāhmaṇācchaṃsī*.
What, then, is not established here? It is the fifth case ending (*pañcamī*).

In this context, the word *brāhmaṇa* denotes a specific portion of study; one who recites (*śaṃsati*) or narrates (*kathayati*) that is a *brāhmaṇācchaṃsī*, where the suffix *ṇini* is used in the sense of habitual action (*tācchilika*).
Here, when the second case ending would have been required by the rule *brāhmaṇaśabdāt* (Pāṇini 2.3.2), the fifth case ending is to be added as an exception.
However, this is already established by the rule *aluk punaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.3.14).
But when one intends to express that [the person] recites a portion or the meaning drawn from the *Brāhmaṇa*, then even the fifth case ending need not be added as an exception.
> [[2.3.28]] This is because it is established in exactly that way.

But how, then, is the derivation performed here by means of the sense of the fifth case (ablative), which is non-existent [in this context]? To this he says: "A specific kind of officiating priest" (*kratvigviśeṣa*), and so forth.
*Rūḍhi* means common usage; that is to say, a conventional designation (*saṃjñā*).
By the word "tasyāḥ" (of her), only the conventional meaning (*rūḍhi*) is referred to, and not the term "brāhmaṇācchaṃsī," which is itself a conventional term.

A conventional term denotes a specific officiating priest (*ṛtvij*), for it has been established as a technical name (*saṃjñā*) for that very person. Therefore, even for that [term], an etymological derivation (*vyutpatti*) is performed through its component meanings, whether they exist or do not exist.

In this regard, if the intended meaning is "he recites the Brāhmaṇa," then, because there is no source (apādāna) for the sense of the ablative case, the derivation is performed by means of the non-existent sense of a part (*avayava*).

However, when the intended meaning is "he recites [something] from the Brāhmaṇa" or "having taken a portion from the Brāhmaṇa," then, because the sense of the ablative exists, the compound is formed by the rule *ojasā kṛtam* etc. (Pāṇini 2.1.32). [The Vārttika] states:
"There should be an addition [to the rule] regarding *añjas*."
Is there not an absence of *luk* (elision) for the third case ending after the word *añjas*? The meaning is that an *upasaṃkhyāna*—that is, a supplementary rule—must be formulated.

The formulation here is as follows: in [Pāṇini 6.3.5], the particle *ca* (and) serves to include what has not been explicitly mentioned; therefore, by this, there is an absence of *luk* for the third case ending following the word *añjas*. Furthermore, we shall provide another formulation for this later on, as in the example *puṃsānujaḥ* ("born after a male").
The meaning is that here too, in the case of *puṃsānujo januṣāndhaḥ*, the non-elision (*aluk*) of the third case ending must be established.
The establishment is as before:
one who is younger than a male (*puṃsā*) by reason of being a male (*pumsā hetunā*) is "younger than a male" (*puṃsānujaḥ*).
"Blind from birth" (*januṣāndhaḥ*) means one who is blind by reason of birth (*januṣā hetunā*).
The compound is formed through the application of a *yogavibhāga* (splitting of a rule) to the sūtra *tṛtīyā* [Pāṇini 2.1.30].
*Januḥ* is a synonym for "birth. Similarly, there is the term "one who knows with the mind" (*manasājñāyī*).

The suffix *ṇini* [is applied] by [Pāṇini 3.2.146] *tacchīlaḥ*; the augment *yuk* is added by [Pāṇini 7.3.33] *āto yuk ciṇkṛtoḥ*, and there is a compound with an upapada. Here, the term "pūraṇa" (ordinal) is marked with a circumflex accent (*svarita*), and through the circumflex accent, the governing scope (*adhikāra*) is understood.

Consequently, with reference to the mention of "pūraṇa"—that is, having the mention of "pūraṇa" as the governing heading—only those suffixes prescribed as "pūraṇa" suffixes are included by the mention of "pūraṇa," and not the word-form itself.

The phrase "in the subsequent member" (*uttarapade*) [6.3.1] is also understood here; therefore, by the paribhāṣā concerning the mention of an affix (Bhāṣya on Pāṇini 1.1.72), it is understood that the operation applies when the subsequent member ends in an ordinal affix. Having considered this, he says: "when the subsequent member ends in an ordinal affix," and so forth.
Regarding the word *pañcamaḥ*:
from "the filler of five" [Pāṇini 5.2.48], the affix *ḍaṭ* is applied, and of that [affix, the *ṭ* is elided] [Pāṇini 5.2.49].
Regarding the term *ṣaṣṭhaḥ*:
it means "the completer of six," according to [Pāṇini 5.2.51], with the substitution of *ṣṭu* for *ṣṭu*.

In expressions such as *ātmanāpañcamaḥ* ("with himself as the fifth"), by what rule is the instrumental case (*tṛtīyā*) applied? For here there is no sense of the instrumental, such as an instrument (*karaṇa*) and so forth; indeed, an instrument and the like are *kārakas* (factors of action), and a *kāraka* exists only in relation to an action (*kriyā*). Yet, no action whatsoever is evident here. To this, he says: "In the prescription of the instrumental case," and so forth.

"Let it be so; but how can there be a third-case compound (*tṛtīyāsamāsa*) here, for there is no defining characteristic of a compound in this case? To this he says: "In the rule for the application of the third case," and so forth. "Let it be so; but how can there be a third-case compound, for there is no defining characteristic of a compound in this case? To this he says: "And [the word] 'third case' (*tṛtīyā*)," and so forth. Alternatively, showing that the third case here is indeed by rule *Pāṇini 2.3.18* and the compound is by rule *Pāṇini 2.1.32*, he says: "Or by oneself (*ātmanā*)," and so forth.
In this case, this third case ending (*tṛtīyā*) is used for both the agent (*kartṛ*) and the instrument (*karaṇa*), as in "the fifth [note] produced" (*kṛtaḥ pañcamaḥ*).
Once the compound has been formed, the word *kṛta* is not employed, because its meaning is already included within the compound (*vṛtti*). As for the phrase beginning with "How," etc.:
The sense here is that it ought to be "the self as the fourth" (*ātmanā caturthaḥ*).
The rebuttal beginning with "this is a *bahuvrīhi*" is as follows:
for if this were a *tatpuruṣa* compound, it would have to be "the fourth by means of the self" (*ātmanā caturthaḥ*), yet this is not a *tatpuruṣa*.
What then? It is a *bahuvrīhi* compound.
And since that [compound] occurs only when two words end in the nominative case (*prathamā*), there is no occurrence of the undesired consequence.
But surely, a *bahuvrīhi* is said to denote an external referent (*anyapadārtha*), and an external referent is something distinct [from the members of the compound]?

Just as in the case of "one who has brindled cows" (*citragu*), where there is no distinct external referent for the compound, is there not likewise no such distinct external referent here? This is not a fault; even though the external referent is non-distinct, it exists by virtue of the principle of "behaving like that which possesses a designation" (*vayapadeśivadbhāva*).
For example: "the stone statue with a beautiful body" (*śobhanaśarīraḥ śilāputrakaḥ*). Regarding the term *yudhiṣṭhiraḥ*:
[it is formed] by the rule [Pāṇini 2.1.69] for the compound, and by the rule [Pāṇini 8.3.95] for the substitution of *ṣ*.

Now, regarding the form *gaviṣṭhira*, how is there an absence of elision (*aluk*)? For the word *go* is neither stem-final in *hal* nor does it end in *a*. One might argue: "When *go + i + sthira* is established, since the substitution of *ava* is internal (*antaraṅga*), the word will become stem-final in *hal* and thus [the elision] will occur. But this is not so; for it is said: "The external (*bahiraṅga*) elision (*luk*) subverts even internal rules" (Vyāḍi-Pāṇini 128), and this must necessarily be accepted.

Otherwise, in cases such as *nadīkukkuṭikā* (a hen by the river) and *bhūmipāśaḥ* (a snare on the ground), when the *yaṇ* substitution is applied, would there not result the non-elision (*aluk*) of the case-ending? To address this, he says: "But in the case of *gaviṣṭhira*, etc. [The rule] "after *han*, *mat*, and *div*" is for the purpose of excluding [the application of] technical names (*saṃjñā*).
"It should be stated" means it should be explained;

and that explanation will be provided later. Alternatively, it may be provided here as well: the mention of "end" (*anta*) need not be made here, because even without it, once the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) is brought to mind by the locative case, the status of having *hal* (consonants) or ending in a vowel is already obtained. Therefore, the mention of "end" is made here in addition [to what is necessary]. This addition, being made, indicates this: that this *aluk* (non-elision) occurs because of something additional.

Therefore, there is non-elision (*aluk*) in certain instances of *asaṃjñā* (non-technical names), as in *dyudispṛk*, *divispṛk*. By [Pāṇini 8.2.62], *kvinpratyayasya kuḥ*, the letter *ś* is replaced by *kh*; by [8.2.39], *jhalāṃ jaś jhaśi*, that *kh* becomes *g* (the *jaś*-substitute); and by [8.4.56], *khari ca*, that *g* also becomes *k* (the *car*-substitute).
And here the meaning is this: it touches the earth, it touches heaven.

For it has been stated thus in the Bhāṣya: "This locative case is to be understood as having the sense of the accusative, as in 'it touches the earth' and 'it touches heaven,' resulting in the forms *bhūmispṛk* and *divispṛk*.
But how can it have the sense of the accusative? Precisely from the statement of the author of the Bhāṣya.
Alternatively: one who touches the heart touches it in the heart; one who touches heaven touches it in heaven. In this case, the locative case will apply by the rule *adhikaraṇe* [Pāṇini 2.3.36].

Although the term *ākhyā* (name) was already under discussion, its mention again as *saṃjñā* (technical name) is for the sake of clarity. The portion to be given to the king by merchants, farmers, and herdsmen, which is based on protection, is called *kāra*; the name of that is *kāranāman*.
In examples such as *kūpeśāṇam*, there is a compound formed by the rule *saṃjñāyām* [Pāṇini 2.1.43].

Regarding the term *haledvipadikā*: two feet each are to be given, hence it is called *dvipādikā*. By the rule *pādaśatasya* [Pāṇini 5.4.1], the suffix *vun* is applied; by the rule *alo 'ntyasya lopaḥ* [Pāṇini 1.1.52], there is elision of the final letter, and by the rule *pādasya lopaḥ* [Pāṇini 5.4.138], the word *pāda* is replaced by zero.
With the words *kāraviśeṣasya* and so forth, he demonstrates that this sūtra serves as a restrictive rule (*niyamārtha*).

"Variations of restriction" (*niyamavikalpāḥ*) means specific types of restrictions. By the rule beginning with "and when the name of the cause" (*kāraṇāmni ca*), he demonstrates the nature of those variations of restriction.

Furthermore, these variations of restriction are obtained here from the inclusion of the words "when the name of the cause," "of the ancients" (*prācām*), and "beginning with a consonant" (*halādau*) within the restrictive statement.
If the first restriction were not intended, then he would not have said "in the name of the cause" (*kāraṇāmni*).

Likewise, if the second restriction were not intended, then he would not have said "of the easterners" (*prācām*). Similarly, if the third restriction were not desired, then he would not have said "beginning with a consonant" (*halādau*).

Now, for what purpose is the mention of "name" (*nāman*), rather than [relying on] the previous rule (*pūrvayoga*)? Does the mention of "designation" (*saṃjñā*) not continue [from that rule]? The mention of "name" in the previous rule is for the sake of indicating that the condition of being a "designation" is generally applicable; by means of that, in cases such as *ahmadispṛk* and *divispṛk*, the non-elision (*aluk*) is established even when it is not a designation. Regarding the statement, "it should be stated that [the elision does not occur] after the word 'anta'":
the meaning is that this should be explained as having the sense that there is no elision of the locative case (*saptamī*) following the word *anta*.
In this regard, the following is the explanation: the particle *ca* (and) is carried over from the preceding rule (*pūrvayoga*), and it serves to include what has not been explicitly mentioned.

By means of that, the elision (*aluk*) of the locative case occurs even after the word *anta*. As for the term "limb" (*svāṅga*), that which is defined by the technical definition (*paribhāṣā*) beginning with "not liquid" (*adrava*) is what is understood here.
Thus, *kaṇṭhekālaḥ* ("the one whose throat is black") is a *bahuvrīhi* compound.

The *bahuvrīhi* compound is indeed formed even for words that have different grammatical referents (*vyadhikaraṇa*). Is the rule "having a common referent" (*samānādhikaraṇa*, Vārttika 97) mandatory? No, it is merely indicative;
as in the example "skilled at dice" (*akṣaśauṇḍaḥ*).
Thus ends the compound (*samāsa*).
In *aṅgulitrāṇajaṅghāvalaḥ*, there are two locative *tatpuruṣa* compounds. The rule *svāṅgāt* [Pāṇini 6.3.11] has ceased to apply; this is a general prescription.
[The word] "in a binding" (*bandhe*) [is used].
This form [of the root] *badhnāti* is used;
by the rule *it* (Pāṇini 6.3.19), they will state a prohibition regarding *badhnāti* in a *tatpuruṣa* compound.

In that case, the specific scope [of the prohibition] is not known—namely, in which *tatpuruṣa* compounds is there a prohibition? Therefore, for the sake of understanding that, he says: "The word *bandha* is understood as ending in the suffix *dhañ*."

*Bandhanam* means "binding"; the suffix *ghañ* is used here in the sense of an abstract action (*bhāve*). By this, it is shown that there is an option (*vibhāṣā*) for the root *bandh* when followed by a suffix ending in *ghañ*, whereas there is a prohibition (*pratiṣedha*) when another suffix follows.

But how is it known that this [word] ends in the suffix *ghañ*? Because it has the acute accent on the first syllable (*ādyudāttatvāt*). For example, in the word *hastebandhaḥ*, it is either a *tatpuruṣa* or a *bahuvrīhi*.
Regarding the phrase "in both cases":

how is this option (*vibhāṣā*) applicable both when [the suffix] has been applied and when it has not been applied? To this he says: "For, from a word denoting one's own limb," and so forth. Examples are *stamberamaḥ* ("an elephant") and *karṇejapaḥ* ("a slanderer").
The suffix *ac* is applied by the rule *stambakarṇayo ramijapoḥ* (Pāṇini 3.2.13), and the compound is a *tatpuruṣa* by the rule *upapadam atiṅ* (Pāṇini 2.2.19).
"one who wanders in Kuru," "one who wanders in Madra.
When the option (*vibhāṣā*) is under discussion, the use of the term *bahula* ("diverse" or "various") is for the purpose of including certain meanings such as "wandering" (*pravṛtti*) and so forth.
Consequently, the non-elision (*aluk*) occurs only in certain instances—such as in the case of *stamberamaḥ* ("an elephant") and others.
In some cases there is no application at all—as in *kurucara* and so forth.
In some cases both [the suffixes] apply—as in *sarajim*, *sarojam*, and so forth.
In some cases something else entirely applies—as in *brāhmaṇācchaṃsī* and so forth.

The non-elision (*aluk*) prescribed for the seventh case also occurs for the fifth case. Likewise, the non-elision prescribed when a *kṛt*-derived word is the final member of a compound also occurs with a *taddhita* suffix—as in *apsavya*, meaning "born in the waters.

Here, the suffix *yat* is applied because [the stem] belongs to the *digādi* group, resulting in the *guṇa* substitution [of *as* to *o*], and then the *vānta* replacement [of *o* to *au*]. Thus, in all such cases, the rule is established by the mention of *bahulam* ("diversely"); hence there are additions such as "the inclusion of *brāhmaṇācchaṃsin*."

As for what has been stated and what will be stated—namely, “In the case of *apa*, *yoni*, and *yātumat*, there is no elision (*aluk*) of the locative case-ending” (Vārttika 721), and so forth—all that need not be stated.

If this is so, then since everything would be established by this very rule even in cases such as *stokānmuktaḥ* (“freed with little difficulty”), the rule “*pañcamyāḥ stokādibhyaḥ*” (Pāṇini 6.3.2) would not need to be stated? This is true; however, that [rule] should be understood as an elaboration (*prapañca*) of this very point.
And this being the case, the grammatical illustrations (*lakṣya*) are well-comprehended.
And so it has been said: "Those very objects are well-grasped whose characteristic (lakṣaṇa) and elaboration (prapañca) [are understood]. Regarding the form *prāvṛṣijaḥ*:

there is elision of the suffix *ṭi* by [Pāṇini 6.4.143], and a compound by [Pāṇini 2.2.19] since it is not a subordinate term (*apapada*) and does not end in a finite verb (*atiṅ*). The term *gha* refers to the inclusion of the suffixes *tarap* and *tamap*; *kāla* refers to a word denoting time; and *tana* refers to the substitute *tana* for *ṭau* and *ṭaulo*, which includes the augment *satuṭ*. The example is *pūrvāhṇetarām*.

Having analyzed *ahnaḥ pūrvam* [as a genitive tatpuruṣa], there is a partitive compound (*ekadeśisamāsa*) by [Pāṇini 2.2.1] *pūrvāparaprathama...*. The suffix *ṭac* is applied as a compound-final element (*samāsānta*) by [Pāṇini 5.4.91] *rājāhaḥsakhibhyaṣṭac*. Then, the substitution of *ahan* for *ahar* occurs by [Pāṇini 5.4.88] *ahno'han etebhyaḥ*. Finally, the substitution of *ṇa* for *n* occurs by [Pāṇini 8.4.7] *ahno'dantāt*.

"Among these two, this one is more of a morning than the other; that is, it is a 'morning-other' (pūrvāhṇetara) to an excessive degree. The suffix *tarap* is applied according to the rule beginning with "dvivacana" [Pāṇini 5.3.57].
Thus we have "pūrvāhṇetamām."

By the rule *atiśāyane* [Pāṇini 5.3.55], the suffix *tamap* is applied. When the word becomes a *prātipadika* by the rule *taddhita-āśraya-liṅga-vacane ca* [Pāṇini 1.2.46], the elision of the case-ending (*subluk*) would apply; however, this is prohibited in one alternative. Thus we have *pūrvāhṇetane*.

In the sense of *pūrvāhṇetare*, the suffixes *ṭa* and *ṭala* are applied along with the augment *tuṭ* by the rule *pūrvāhṇāparāhṇābhyām ṭaṭulau* [Pāṇini 4.3.24], and the substitution of *aṭan* for the *yuvan* and *yuvas* stems occurs by the rule *yuvoranākau* [Pāṇini 7.1.1].

Regarding the term *rātritarāyām*: the analysis (*vigraha*) is "in this night and in that night, [the one] which is excessively [long] among these two nights. Now, one might object: since the rule "when a suffix is mentioned, it refers to that which begins with what the suffix follows and ends with that suffix" (Paribhāṣā 44) implies that the mention of the suffix includes the word ending in it, examples should have been cited where the subsequent member (*uttarapada*) ends in a suffix having the technical name *gha* or ends in the suffix *tanap*. Why, then, was it cited here for the suffix alone? To this he replies: "In the governing context (*adhikāra*) of the subsequent member," and so forth.
He asks, "From where, then, does this [distinction] come? and says: "Because of the mention of *lekha*," and so forth.
In the rule [Pāṇini 4.3.72], there is a separate mention of the word *lekha* and of the suffix *aṇ* ending in *lekha*.

In that context, if—in the governing rule concerning the subsequent member (*uttarapada*)—the inclusion of the internal element (*tadantavidhi*) were intended when a suffix is mentioned, then one would not have mentioned *lekha*; for its inclusion would already be established by the mention of *aṇ* alone. Yet, it is indeed mentioned.

Therefore, from the mention of the *lekhā* [in the rule], it is understood that "when a suffix (*pratyaya*) is mentioned within the governing scope of a subsequent term (*uttarapada-adhikāra*), the inclusion of that which ends with it (*tadantavidhi*) is not intended" (Puṣpamālā 26).
This is indicated by the phrase "by that" (*tena*),
because the inclusion of that which ends with it is not desired here.

"Regarding the statement 'Time is not a grasping of its own nature,' this is because it is mentioned by name; for that is precisely its purpose. [The term used is] 'one who lies in the sky' (kheśayaḥ)."
[[3.2.15]] Thus, [the suffix] *itac* [is applied]. For example:
*grāmevāsaḥ*. "Vāsaḥ" means dwelling; [the suffix] *ghañ* is used in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāve*).

"In *grāmevāsī*," the suffix *ṇini* is used either in the sense of habitual character (*tācchīlika*) or in the sense of a religious observance (*vrata*). In "*pūrvāhṇaśayaḥ*," [the suffix is likewise applied].
But surely, when there is the apprehension of the word-form itself, "kālaśaya" should be cited as a counter-example; yet this is not an apprehension of the word-form at all.
What then? It is an apprehension of the meaning.
For this very reason, it is stated in the Vṛtti: "of that which does not denote time."

How, then, is the inclusion of the word "meaning" (*artha*) obtained? Because the term "name" (*nāman*) from the preceding sūtra is understood to carry over here. If that is so, then the phrase from [Pāṇini 2.4.28], *na kāla-samaya-vellā-velāsu*, would be carried forward, and we would connect it with the negative particle *nañ*—that is, "not after a name of time. In that case, the meaning would be: "In the rule *nen-siddha-badhnātiṣu ca* (or, as the older printed reading has it, *nen-siddha*), it need not be stated 'not' (*na*); for this very 'not' (*na*) will be carried forward [from the previous sūtra]. This cannot be maintained.

If it were stated as "na śayavāsavāsiṣu," this prohibition would be understood as applying only to the elision of the short vowel (*hrasva-luk*), because that alone is the subject under discussion here as something to be enjoined. Therefore, the term "time" (*kāla*) must be included so that the prohibition applies specifically to time.
The word "vaktavyam" (it should be stated) means "it should be explained."

The explanation has already been provided previously. This is a prohibition of the *aluk* (non-elision) that was otherwise applicable by the rule "in a compound where the second member ends in *in*" (*innanta uttarapade*).

But surely it has been established that "in the governing context of the second member (*uttarapadādhikāra*), when a suffix is mentioned, the inclusion of that which ends in it (*tadantavidhi*) is not accepted"? How, then, can the second member ending in that [suffix] be understood here? For a suffix *in* occurring after a locative case-ending is impossible.
The secondary suffix *in* is indeed of two kinds: *kṛt* and *taddhita*.

Among these, since a *kṛt* suffix is produced from the verbal root itself, it is impossible for the suffix *in* to follow a locative case ending. Thus, the secondary suffix *in* is indeed of two kinds: *kṛt* and *taddhita*.

In that case, since [the suffix] arises from the verbal root (*dhātu*) itself, it cannot possibly follow a locative case ending (*saptamī*). Nor can there be any secondary derivative (*taddhita*), for even if such a derivative were to arise from a base qualified by the locative, it likewise could not possibly follow a locative case ending. Therefore, it is correct to state that this refers only to that which ends in *in*.
Regarding "sthaṇḍilavartī":
the suffix *ṇini* is applied by [Pāṇini 3.2.80] *vrate*; the compound is formed by [Pāṇini 2.2.19]. Regarding "sāṅkāśyasiddhaḥ": [the suffix *kṛt* is applied].
The compound is formed by [Pāṇini 2.1.41] and so forth. Regarding the term *cakrabaddhaḥ*:
the word *baddha* ends in a niṣṭhā suffix; the compound is formed by the application of a *yogavibhāga* (separation of rules) from [Pāṇini 2.1.40], which governs the locative case.
By the word *bandha*, [the compound] "cakrabandha" is meant;
the compound is formed according to [Pāṇini 2.1.40] *siddha* and so forth. It should be understood that this [word *bandha*] ends with the *ac*-suffix belonging to the *pacādi* group.

Now, why is the word-form *bandha*, ending in the suffix *ghañ*, not accepted here? To this he says: "In the case of [a word] ending in *ghañ*," and so forth. This is also a prohibition of the non-elision (*aluk*) that would otherwise apply by the rule "in a *tatpuruṣa*" (Pāṇini 6.3.13) and subsequent rules.
Regarding *samasthaḥ*:

from *samam tiṣṭhati*, the suffix *ka* is applied, resulting in the elision of the vowel *a* by the rule "after *sama*, [the *a* of] *sthā* is elided" (Pāṇini 6.4.64). As for "Kṛṣṇo 'syākhareṣṭhaḥ" (O Kṛṣṇa, you are the one who stands on the mountain peak)—this is the reading found in the Vārāṇasī edition of the Kāśikā, whereas the printed edition reads "Kṛṣṇo 'syākhareṣṭhā."

Regarding the phrase *kṛṣṇobhyāreṣṭhaḥ*—the reading in the *Kāśikā* is *saṃ-pā-pāṭhaḥ*—the suffix *kvip* is applied according to [Pāṇini 3.2.77] *sthaḥ kaḥ ca*. As for the example *caurasya kulam*, this is intended solely to convey an expression of reproach (*ākrośa*); it is not intended to express an actual relationship with him.
"It is to be spoken" means it is to be explained;
however, the explanation has already been provided.

Regarding the term *paśyatoharaḥ*: [the word] *paśyataḥ* takes the genitive case by [Pāṇini 2.3.38]. [The word] *haraḥ* means "one who steals"; it is formed with the suffix *ac* (specifically *pacādyac*) added to the root *hṛ*.

Regarding the form *amuṣya*: the substitution of *yat* for *adas* occurs by [Pāṇini 7.1.102], followed by the substitutions of *ut* and *matva* (i.e., *u* and *ma*) by [Pāṇini 7.1.103]. Since the substitution of *ut* is considered *asiddha* (non-existent) for the purposes of the following rule, the genitive suffix *ṅasi* is replaced by *syā* by [Pāṇini 7.1.12]. Similarly, one forms *amuṣyakulikaḥ*.

The meaning is that just as in the case of *amuṣyaputrikā*, the suffix *vuñ* is applied because it begins with *bhṛgu* (according to Pāṇini 4.1.132), so it is here as well. Regarding the term *devānāmpriyaḥ*:
it is called *priya* because it pleases (*prīṇāti*), and thus the suffix *kap* is applied [by Pāṇini 3.1.135], followed by the substitution of *iyaṅ*.

Regarding "Śunaḥśepaḥ": there is vocalization (*samprasāraṇa*) according to [Pāṇini 6.4.133], *āyuvamaghonāmataddhite*. "Knowledge and birth" is *vidyāyonī*; those whose relationship is produced by these two are "those connected by knowledge or by birth" (*vidyāyonisambandhāḥ*).
The word *kṛta* is not employed in the compound because its meaning is already understood, just as the word *miśra* ("mixed") is not used in the expression *guḍadhānāḥ* ("molasses and grains").

"Regarding the rule *ṛto vidyāyonisambandhebhyastatpūrvottarapadagrahaṇaṃ kartavyam* (the substitution of *ṛt* for *ṛ* should be performed in compounds denoting relations of learning or parentage by taking both the preceding and following members): by the word *tat* (that), both types of relations—those of learning and those of parentage—are indicated; the meaning is that one must perform an explanation (*grahaṇam*) by which [the substitution] is grasped—that is, such an analysis must be made by which they are grasped."

What, then, is that commentary? For what purpose should it be composed? To this he says: "Only when denoting a relationship through learning or birth," and so forth. Herein lies the commentary: in this great composition of sūtras, which has been expanded by the gestures and insights of the teachers, the intentions of the masters are indicated. This great sequence of sūtras—beginning with "The suffix *ṛt* [is applied] after words denoting a relationship through learning or birth"—would have been stated as "after what is not a relationship through learning or birth" (*avidyāyonisambandhāt*) if the non-elision (*aluk*) were intended when the subsequent member denotes such a relationship.

Alternatively, [the author] would not even have mentioned the mention of a relationship (*sambandhagrahaṇa*); for there is no word ending in *ṛkārānta* that denotes either knowledge (*vidyā*) or a womb (*yoni*) which is unrelated [to its possessor]. In that case, even without the mention of a relationship, it would be understood that [the suffix is applied] to words denoting a relationship of knowledge or a womb; so what is the use of mentioning the relationship? Therefore, it is observed from this extensive series of sūtras that the Teacher intends this elision (*aluk*) when the subsequent member (*uttarapada*) denotes a relationship of knowledge or a womb. [The example is] "of the Hotṛ" (*hotuḥ*).

The substitution of *u* [for *ṛ*] occurs by the rule *ṛta ut* [Pāṇini 6.1.107], followed by the substitution of *ra* [for the *ṛ*] by *raparatvam*, and the elision of the *s* by *rātsasya* [Pāṇini 8.2.24]. [The sūtra states: "In a *dvandva* compound of words ending in *ṛ* that denote a relationship based on knowledge (*vidyā*) or biological origin (*yoni*), etc.

Now, why is it not understood as: "In a *dvandva* of words ending in *ṛ*, the substitute *ānaṅ* occurs"? It is impossible to understand it in this way; for in that case, it would also apply here: *pitṛpitāmahau*.
The letter *ṅ* is for the purpose of indicating that the substitute applies to the final sound.

For here, the instruction of phonemes is either for the sake of a grammatical operation (*kāryārtha*) or for the sake of being heard (*śravaṇārtha*). Now, this letter *n* is not heard anywhere; since it must be elided everywhere by the rule "there is elision of *n* at the end of a nominal stem" (*nalopaḥ prātipadikāntasya*, Pāṇini 8.2.7), nor is any grammatical operation observed to apply to it. So, for what purpose is the pronunciation of the letter *n*? To this he says: "The pronunciation of the letter *n*" and so forth.

If the letter *n* were absent, only an *aṇ* vowel would remain in place of the vowel *ṛ*; consequently, by the rule "an *ṛ* is replaced by *ra* followed by *r*" (*uraṇ raparaḥ*, Pāṇini 1.1.50), the substitution of *rapara* would occur.

But when the letter *n* is present, this *aṇ* alone is not what remains; rather, both *aṇ* and *anaṅ* remain. Thus, there is no contingency of the substitution of *ra* (raparatva). For the substitution of *ra* does not occur where both *aṇ* and *anaṇ* remain, as in the case of "saudhātakir" according to the rule *sudhātur akaṅ ca* [Pāṇini 4.1.97].
Therefore, in this context, the letter *n* is pronounced for the purpose of preventing the substitution of *ra*.

Now, as for the forms *pitāputrau* (father and son) and *mātāputrau* (mother and son), how is there the substitution of *ānaṅ* here, given that there is no *dvandva* compound of words ending in the vowel *ṛ*? To this he says: "The word *putra* is understood to follow from here.
The intention is that the word *putra* is carried over (*anuvartate*) from [Aṣṭādhyāyī 6.3.22] to this point.

If, however, the word *putra* (son) continues [from the previous rule], then would not an option (*vibhāṣā*) also apply to *putra* in the case of [Pāṇini 6.3.24]? This is not a fault; it continues by way of the "frog-leap" maxim (*maṇḍūkapluti-nyāya*).
For this very reason, it was stated that "here" (*atrety uktaṃ*), meaning that it continues in that very place and not in the subsequent one, for the sake of demonstration.

[Objection: Even so, when the word *putra* follows as the second member (*uttarapada*), the substitution of *anaṅ* would apply to the mere first member (*pūrvapada*) alone; for here the thing to undergo the operation (*kāryin*) is not explicitly specified, and by the term *uttarapada*, only the first member is implied. Furthermore, one cannot argue that "by the statement *ṛtaḥ*, it will apply to the vowel *ṛ*"; therefore, is it not the case that the single statement *ṛtaḥ* here qualifies the *dvandva* compound, rather than the thing to undergo the operation? [To this, the author] says: "*ṛta iti ca*" (and "after *ṛ*"). The connection here is that [the word *ṛtaḥ*] continues from [Pāṇini 6.3.23].
Since *ṛtaḥ* continues from that rule, it will serve as a qualifier of the thing to undergo the operation.

Is it not so that what is indicated by the fifth case (*pañcamī*) is here intended as having the meaning of what is indicated by the sixth case (*ṣaṣṭhī*)? This is not a fault; the word *putre* (locative) will function as a genitive for the fifth-case word *ṛtaḥ*, according to Pāṇini 1.1.66. But even so, there is still a contradiction; for if the word *putra* is the final member (*uttarapada*) of a compound, how then can there be a *dvandva* of words ending in *ṛ*, since a *dvandva* of words ending in *ṛ* cannot have the word *putra* as its final member? This is not the case; for that *dvandva* of which *ṛtaḥ* is the qualifier is indeed different.

What contradiction is there in the fact that for another [word], the word *putra* (son) is the final member (*uttarapada*)? The statement is made for the sake of imitation and to indicate a connection through the source of ignorance (*avidyāyonisambandha*). But surely, since the mention of "dvandva" (copulative compound) continues from the rule *ānaṅ ṛto dvandve* [Pāṇini 6.3.24], why is "dvandva" mentioned again here? To this he says: "While 'dvandva' is being carried over," and so forth.

The previous mention of the term *dvandva* was for the purpose of identifying a specific type of compound; this one, however, is for the purpose of [denoting] well-known association—that is, so that there may be the inclusion of those whose association is well-established in both common usage and the Veda. Now, even if the term *dvandva* is mentioned again, how is this meaning obtained? To this he says: "In the case of those that are extremely associated," and so forth. This is stated in reference to the rule *dvandvaṃ rahasyamaryādāvacanavyutkramaṇayajñapātrātmanāmasu* (Pāṇini 2.4.2).
"It is prescribed that the term 'dvandva' (copulative compound) is applied to those things known in common worldly usage as being invariably associated.
By this, he shows that the following meaning is obtained:
"And in the Veda, those which are indicated as occurring together."

*Sahavāpaḥ* means *sahadānam* (joint offering). Those specified therein are called *sahavāpanirdiṣṭāḥ*. Who, then, are those connected to a single oblation (*ekahavis*)? They are to be understood as those who are specified as recipients (*sampradāna*) with respect to a single oblation being offered in a single mantra, such as: "I offer the goat-oblation to Indra and Varuṇa. Regarding the phrase "both [cases] in the tri-," etc.:
when both the first member and the second member [of a compound] are present, a prohibition must be stated—that is, explained—for the substitution of *ānaṅ* for *vāyu*.

In this regard, the following is the explanation: from [Pāṇini 6.3.24], the mention of *vibhāṣā* (optionally) continues, and that is a restricted option (*vyavasthitavibhāṣā*). Therefore, when *vāyu-* is the second member or the first member [of a compound], [the substitution] will not occur. This vowel *ī* is prescribed as an exception to the substitute *ānaṅ*. The letter *t* is for the sake of pronunciation. [The words] *agneḥ* [from 6.3.26] and *devatādvandve* [from 6.3.25] continue [to apply].

The phrase "iti nivṛttam" (thus it is excluded) applies here. Due to its association with the word *vṛddhi*, the term refers to a compound whose second member (*uttarapada*) has undergone the *vṛddhi* strengthening.
For this very reason, he says: "when the second member has undergone *vṛddhi*."
Regarding the term *āgnivāruṇīm*:
when the suffix *aṇ* is applied by default, the feminine suffix *ṅīp* is added according to [Pāṇini 4.1.5], *ṭiḍḍhāṇañ*.
Here too, the letter *t* serves merely for pronunciation. [The rule] "in a *devatā-dvandva*, when there is a final member" applies.
The meaning is: "when that which is the final member (*uttarapada*) in a *devatā-dvandva* [compound] follows. This is an exception (*apavāda*) to *ānaṅ*.

Now, if it is asked for what purpose the vowel *a* is pronounced [there], one might suggest it is for the sake of protecting the letter *s* from receiving the technical designation *it*; but this is not so. He says—"the pronunciation of the vowel *a*" and so forth—because there is no purpose [for it], the designation *it* will simply not occur.

If the letter *a* were not present, then by relying on the internal case-ending (*vibhakti*), the designation "word" (*pada*) would apply; consequently, the substitution of *ru* for the *s* [by Pāṇini 8.2.66] would occur, and for that *ru*, the substitution of *visarjanīya* [by 8.3.15] would follow, and for that *visarjanīya*, the substitution of *upadhmānīya* [by 8.3.37] would occur when followed by *k* or *p*.

However, when the letter *a* is pronounced, this does not happen. How so? The purpose of employing the modified *s* (i.e., *sa*) through the pronunciation of the letter *a* is precisely this: so that the unmodified form may be used, as in examples such as *dyāvā divasam*.
This is the statement: here in the sūtra, the mention of the *dvandva* compound and the mention of the "subsequent member" (*uttarapada*) both carry over.
Since the substitution of *dyāvā* would not apply in a sentence (*vākya*), he asks, "How [is this so]? and so forth.
[The answer is: "An effort must be made in this regard."

In this regard, the effort is as follows: since the term *bahulam* ("in many cases") is understood to carry over from [Aṣṭādhyāyī 6.3.14], the substitution *dyāvā* will occur even in a prose sentence within the Veda (*chandas*).

Alternatively, the particle *ca* ("and") is inserted here; because its purpose is to include what has not been explicitly stated, the rule will apply. Furthermore, the word *dyāvā* itself will carry over simply by virtue of being marked with a circumflex accent (*svarita*); therefore, there is no need for the particle *ca* to draw that word forward.

Alternatively, there exists another verbal root *dyāv-* which has the same meaning as the word *dik-*, and this is its usage here. However, the mention of the substitute *div-* is for the purpose of precluding the usage of that other form. [The statement] "it is an exception to *ānaṅ*" does not appear in the *Kāśikā*; the same applies to the two subsequent rules. Thus: *uṣāsānaktam*.

The analysis of the compound is *uṣāśca naktam ca* ("both dawn and night"). Here, three possibilities are considered: in the word *striyāḥ*, is there a reference to a suffix (*pratyaya*) by means of the word "strī," or a reference to the meaning (*artha*), or a reference to the word-form (*śabda*) itself?

In that regard, if the word *striyāḥ* is intended as a reference to a feminine suffix (*strīpratyaya*)—that is, if it is marked with an accent (*svarita*)—then, according to the rule *svaritenādhikārāvagatiḥ* (P. 1.3.11), the governing scope (*adhikāra*) is understood; thus, those suffixes prescribed under the heading of "feminine" (*stryadhikāra*) are taken, as in the case of [the rule] P. 4.1.48.
Now, if by the word *strī* (woman) a substance (*dravya*) qualified by femininity is denoted, then there is the inclusion of the word *artha* (meaning).

But if by the word *strī* a word (*śabda*) expressing the meaning "woman" is denoted, then there is the inclusion of the word *śabda*. In that case, according to the first alternative, this is the meaning of the Sūtra: a feminine suffix (*strīpratyaya*) following a word that has been used in the masculine (*bhāṣitapuṃska*), provided it is not *ūṅ*, becomes like the masculine (*puṃvad*) when there is a subsequent member (*uttarapada*); that is to say, it is replaced [by the masculine form]. In that instance, the genitive case in *striyāḥ* is used in the sense of the nominative.

But how, by the rule *puṃvat*, can the exclusion of that which has a feminine referent be understood? It is through the supply of the remainder of the sentence (*vākyaśeṣa*), namely, "it becomes" (*bhavati*). And in this view, in the case of *paṭubhāryaḥ* (one whose wife is clever), where the feminine suffix has been excluded due to the subsequent member [of the compound], when the *yaṇ*-substitution must be applied to the preceding [vowel]—and since there would be the status of being "as if occupying the original place" (*sthānivadbhāva*) according to Pāṇini 1.1.57—the *yaṇ*-substitution would indeed occur.

And here—regarding the forms *gārgya-vṛndārikā* and *garga-vṛndārikā*, while the rule *tadrājasya bahuṣu tenaivāstriyām* [Pāṇini 2.4.62] is in force, the elision (*luk*) of the suffix *yañ* [by 2.4.64] does not apply.

For by means of the masculine treatment (*puṃvadbhāva*), the feminine suffix is removed, but not the meaning of femininity; and since that meaning has not been removed, why would the suffix *yañ* not be heard? Such are the objections regarding the view that the suffix is the primary element, which have been stated at length in the Bhāṣya. Here, they are not mentioned for fear of excessive prolixity.

In the view that it refers to the meaning (*arthapakṣa*), however, when a subsequent word follows, the masculine meaning of the feminine word *strī*—which has a corresponding masculine form (*bhāṣitapuṃska*) and does not end in the suffix *ūṅ*—is extended (*atidiśyate*). In the rule "from a word having a masculine counterpart" (*bhāṣitapuṃskāt*), the ablative case is used in the sense of the genitive; thus, the feminine meaning becomes like the masculine. And once the masculine meaning has been extended, the word expressive of that [masculine] meaning comes into operation.

In this view, the mutual exclusion (*vipratiṣedha*) between the shortening [of the vowel] prescribed by *[[6.3.66]]* and this masculine-like treatment (*puṃvadbhāva*) does not occur, because their domains (*viṣaya*) are distinct. To explain: the shortening applies to the word-form (*śabda*), whereas the masculine-like treatment applies to the meaning (*artha*). Consequently, in the case of *kālimmanyā*, the shortening prescribed by *[[1.4.2]]* would not apply; yet such a mutual exclusion is desired. Thus, the mutual exclusion of the masculine-like treatment does not obtain, due to the difference in their domains.

For instance, there is shortening of the word (*śabda*) and the masculine-like treatment (*puṃvadbhāva*) of the meaning (*artha*). Consequently, in the case of *kālimmanyā*, the shortening [prescribed by] Pāṇini 6.3.43 would not apply, yet a conflict (*vipratiṣedha*) is intended. To explain: the scope of the masculine-like treatment is where the final member (*uttarapada*) does not end in *-khid*—as in *darśanīyabhārya*; the scope of shortening is where the masculine-like treatment does not apply—as in *kālimmanyaḥ pumān*. In the case of *kālimmanyā strī*, both rules would apply; therein, because it is subsequent, shortening occurs.
Thus, considering the first two positions to be flawed, he resorts to the third position and says: "Is it a word whose masculine form has been mentioned? and so forth.

He says this because he considers that if any word whatsoever were taken here without qualification as one whose masculine form has been mentioned, then even in the case of *droṇībhārya*, there would be the substitution of the masculine form (*puṃvadbhāva*). Therefore, he says: "In a common [denotation] based on form," and so forth;
that is, "when there is a single ground for application."

By this, he clarifies the meaning of the phrase "when the form (ākṛti) is the same. That by which a thing is "formed" (*ākriyate*)—that is, grasped or delimited—is the ground for the application (*pravṛttinimitta*) of a word, such as a genus (*jāti*) and so forth; this is what is expressed here by the word *ākṛti*.

With the intention that if only the words "from a word that has been used with the masculine gender" (*bhāṣitapuṃskāt*) were stated, this specific qualification "when the form is the same" could not be obtained, he says: "This being so," and so forth.
The word "tat" (that) is used here as an introductory particle for the statement.
The meaning of this speech is as follows: "In what manner does it exist? It does not exist in any such manner at all. This is the sense.

If, in the case of a *bahuvrīhi* compound such as *bhāṣitapuṃska-śabda*, the word "word" (*śabda*) were taken as the external referent (*anyapadārtha*)—that is, [if one were to ask]: "By which word has the masculine been expressed? That [word] is a *bhāṣitapuṃska* word"—then this distinction, namely "in the same form" (*samānāyām ākṛtau*), would not be obtained. For every single word, having expressed a masculine in some form, expresses a feminine in another form; thus, [the distinction would be lost]. However, when the meaning (*artha*) is accepted as the external referent, this very distinction is indeed obtained. Having considered this, he says: "In which meaning the masculine has been expressed," and so forth.

What is the basis for the application (*pravṛttinimitta*) of a word—be it a genus (*jāti*) or the like—that is the "referent of another word" (*anyapadārtha*). By which word, then, is the masculine gender expressed therein? It is understood that it is expressed by that very same [word] which serves as its basis for application, due to proximity (*pratyāsatti*). Otherwise, the mention of the term *bhāṣitapuṃska* would be meaningless, as there would be nothing to be excluded. In every case, the masculine is expressed by some word or other regarding the meaning that is to be denoted.

Finally, even by the word "bhāṣitapuṃska" (having a masculine counterpart), that base (*prātipadika*) which expresses the meaning of such a word is also called "bhāṣitapuṃska" in a figurative sense, because it possesses the property of denoting [that meaning]. Furthermore, by proximity, it should be understood as that very [base] whose meaning serves as the ground for application (*pravṛttinimitta*), and by means of which a man is spoken of. And that which denotes the ground for application of a word having a masculine counterpart necessarily speaks of a man with respect to one ground for application, and then speaks of a woman [with respect to that same ground].

As in the root examples—"words such as *darśanīya*," etc.—by means of the word *samāthryādi*, when the form (*ākṛti*) is the same, this specific distinction is obtained: "the masculine has been expressed. If *anūṅ* were an exclusion (*paryudāsa*), then *anūṅ* would mean "other than *ūṅ*"; consequently, by the rule of "that which is connected with *nañ* or *iva*" (Vyāḍi-Pāṇini 65), since there would be a reference to suffixes similar to it, such as *ṭāp* and others, the substitution for the masculine (*puṃvadbhāva*) would apply only to that which ends in those [suffixes]. Thus, in cases such as *aiḍaviḍavṛndārikā* and *dāradavṛndārikā*, [the masculine substitution] would not occur.

The feminine *iḍaviḍī* is the offspring of *iḍaviḍ*, and thus the suffix *añ* is applied by [Pāṇini 4.1.168], *janapadaśabdāt kṣatriyād añ*. The feminine *daratī* is the offspring of *darad*, and thus the suffix *aṇ* is applied by [Pāṇini 4.1.170], *dvyañmagadha...*. By [Pāṇini 4.1.177], *ataś ca*, there is elision (*luk*) of these two suffixes. Consequently, in the compounds *iḍaviṭ cāsau vṛndārikā ca* and *darat cāsau vṛndārikā ca*, the compound is formed by [Pāṇini 2.1.62], *vṛndārakanāgakuñjaraiḥ*. In this case, the substitution of the masculine form (*puṃvadbhāva*) does not apply by [Pāṇini 6.3.42], *puṃvat karmadhāraye...*.
Because there is no other suffix similar to *ūṅ*, otherwise the word *aiḍaviḍa* would not exist from the word *aiḍaviḍī*, nor would the word *dārada* exist from the word *dāradī*.

However, this is possible if it is a *prasajya-pratiṣedha* (prohibitive negation), for even here the absence of *ūṅ* exists. Having considered this, and showing that this is indeed a *prasajya-pratiṣedha*, he says: "the absence of *ūṅ* is *anūṅ*," [referring to the rule] "*anūṅ* after a word that has been mentioned with a masculine form."

If this were not a compound, but rather [the analysis] *na bahuvrīhiḥ*, then the meaning would be as follows: "When a word denoting a feminine sense follows a word that has a corresponding masculine form (*bhāṣitapuṃskāt*), provided it lacks the suffix *ūṅ*, it becomes like the masculine (*puṃvat*) when followed by a subsequent member (*uttarapade*)."
