And this being the case, it follows by implication that the word *strī* (female), which denotes a specific meaning, is replaced by a word *puṃs* (male) that denotes that same specific meaning; from this, an undesirable consequence (*aniṣṭaprasaṅga*) arises: there are birds named *aṅgāraka*, and their females are named *kālikā*. When the compound *etāśca kālikāvṛndārikāśca* is formed, the word *etad* would be considered *bhāṣitapuṃska* (having a corresponding masculine form). Consequently, for the subsequent word *kālikā*, which does not end in *ūṅ*, the word *aṅgāraka*—being semantically the most similar (*antaratama*)—would have to undergo replacement by a masculine word-form, because no other more similar [masculine] form exists.
Consequently, this [compound] would have to be *aṅgārakavṛndārikā*; however, *etatkālikāvṛndārikā* is what is intended.

If it were a *bahuvrīhi*, there would be no undesirable consequence, because in that case, a word that has a corresponding masculine form (*bhāṣitapuṃska*) and does not end in the suffix *ūṅ* must undergo the substitution of the masculine form (*pūṃvadbhāva*). Yet, the word *kālikā* does not have a corresponding masculine form. Having considered all this, he says—showing that this is indeed a *bahuvrīhi*—"In which feminine word [the first member] has a corresponding masculine form and does not end in *ūṅ*" (Pāṇini 6.3.34).
[The phrase] "if this is a *bahuvrīhi*" is not found in the *Kāśikā*.

This being the case, does [the rule] *evaṃ sati* (Pāṇini 2.4.71) not result in the elision (*luk*) of the fifth case ending? To this he says: "Because of the irregularity (*nipātana*)," and so forth. Now, one might object that since this sentence is ungrammatical (*alaukika*), the argument "because of the irregularity" is no solution at all; for an irregularity (*nipātana*) pertains to ordinary usage (*laukika*). If that is so, should there not likewise be no elision here either? If it is determined that elision will occur, then let it also be determined that non-elision occurs. [The example is: *darśanīyabhāryaḥ*.
The term *darśanīyabhāryaḥ* is a *bahuvrīhi* compound;
by [Pāṇini 1.2.48], the final vowel of the second member (*uttarapada*) is shortened.
Here, "the state of being beautiful" (*darśanīyatva*) is the specific quality within the general category that serves as the ground for the application (*pravṛttinimitta*) of the word *darśanīya*.
Taking up that very same meaning, this word applies to both the masculine and the feminine—as in "Devadatta is handsome" (*darśanīyo devadattaḥ*) and "the wife is handsome" (*darśanīyā bhāryā*).

Why is this so? Because when the generic form (*ākṛti*) is the same, the word *darśanīya* is one whose masculine form has been expressed (*bhāṣitapuṃska*); it applies to the feminine as well, yet the suffix *ūṅ* does not arise from it.
Therefore, when the feminine word *bhāryā* follows as the second member of a compound, this word *strī* (in the form of *darśanīyā*) assumes the same form as the masculine word.
The reading in the printed edition is "puṃśabdasyaiva" (only of a masculine word). In this same manner, it should also be applied to cases such as "ślakṣṇacūḍaḥ. Regarding "grāmaṇidṛṣṭiḥ":
here all the conditions are present, yet the word *grāmaṇī* does not refer to a female; rather, it is neuter, and therefore the substitution of the masculine form (*puṃvadbhāva*) does not occur.
Regarding the term "droṇībhārya":
the word *droṇa* denotes a male, but not because it shares the same basis for application (*pravṛttinimitta*).
Why? Because it applies to a male possessor of a measure by taking a specific measure as its basis for application.
However, depending upon a specific genus (*jāti*), it applies to a female animal such as a cow;
where cows eat, that trough is called *gavādanī* by means of the word *droṇī*.
Therefore, the word *droṇa* is not one that has been previously mentioned as masculine within the same form (*ākṛti*).
"Regarding the passage beginning with *katham* and so forth:

if *puṃvadbhāva* (the substitution of the masculine form) is prescribed for that which has been mentioned as masculine when the *ākṛti* (form/external appearance) is the same, then in cases such as *garbhibhāryaḥ*, *puṃvadbhāva* would not apply.
The intention is that words such as *garbhin* and others have different *ākṛtis* even though they are mentioned as masculine."
For when there is a connection with a specific internal object that has not become a constituent part [of the body], a woman is called "pregnant" (*garbhiṇī*);
whereas when there is a connection with a specific internal constituent part, a grain of rice (*vrīhi*) is called "pregnant" (*garbhī*).
Therefore, the ground for the application (*pravṛttinimitta*) of the word *garbhin* differs according to whether it refers to a man or a woman.
The grounds for the application (*pravṛttinimitta*) of the two words *prasūta* and *prajāta* are also distinct due to their respective actions.
When these two refer to a woman, they function by taking the release of the fetus as their ground for application; when referring to a man, however, it is the implantation of the embryo.
Thus: "An effort must be made in this matter."
Some explain that an addition (*upasaṃkhyāna*) must be made;
others, however, say that a split of the rule (*yogavibhāga*) should be made as "the feminine [stem] like the masculine.

Or else, by the statement "effort must be made here," he shows this: even though there is a difference in the state of being an embryo (*garbhatva*) between a woman and rice (*vrīhi*), nevertheless, that difference should not be relied upon.
However, in that case, having set aside the distinction between the parts and the whole, one must rely solely on the general connection with some specific object existing within.
Therefore, with respect to that, the ground for the application (*pravṛttinimitta*) of the word *garbhin* as it occurs in reference to both a woman and rice is exactly the same.

In this way, even in the case of the words *prasūta* and *prajāta*, having abandoned the distinction between the act of conceiving and the act of releasing [the offspring], the mere connection with "one who possesses offspring"—expressed as "this one has offspring" (*apatyavān*) or "this one has offspring" (*apatyavatī*)—is what is intended; such is the interpretation that must be made.
Regarding the term *brāhṛbandhūbhāryaḥ*:
from the word *brāhṛbandhū*, the suffix *ūṅ* is applied according to [Pāṇini 4.1.66] *ūṅutaḥ*. Regarding the term *kalyāṇīpañcamāḥ*: [the same applies].

The suffix *ap* is applied by the rule *ap pūraṇī-pramāṇyoḥ* [Pāṇini 5.4.116], forming a compound ending in *ap*. From "the ordinal of five" (*pañcānāṃ pūraṇī*), the suffix *ḍaṭ* is added; this is replaced by *ṅīp* according to *ṭiḍḍhāṇañ* [Pāṇini 4.1.15], resulting in the form *pañcamī*. Regarding the statement "the mention of the principal ordinal (*pradhānapūraṇī*) must be made": that explanation by which the principal ordinal is grasped is called "the mention of the principal ordinal. This must be done so that the prohibition applies to that which is a principal ordinal, and not to one that has become non-principal.

In this regard, the following is the explanation: Here, by the rule *dvandve ghi* [Pāṇini 2.2.32], the word *priya* and others would normally be placed first in a *dvandva* compound; however, the fact that they appear last indicates, through the sign of a deviation from the general rule, that this prohibition applies only in certain instances and not universally. Therefore, it occurs only where the ordinal number (*pūraṇī*) is the predominant member, and not elsewhere. Consequently, wherever it does occur, it is logical to understand that very predominant ordinal number as being intended.

Wherein does the predominance of the *pūraṇī* (ordinal) reside? It resides where it is included within the compound as the expressed meaning (*abhidheya*), as in the counter-example just mentioned. For in that case, the analysis (*vigraha*) is by means of a constituent part; yet the whole (*samudāya*), being non-different from its distinct parts, is simply the meaning of the compound itself.
Regarding the word "therein" (*tatra*):
just as the first, second, third, and fourth [lunar days] are designated, so too is the fifth.
For example, one says, "the fortnight has the auspicious fifth day."

In this case, however, the compound *anyapadārtha* (the meaning of another word) is the primary element, just as in *anyapādrathaḥ* (a chariot with its parts hidden), where the chariot itself is the principal referent and the fifth night is merely subordinate.
In this view, the *anyapadārtha* is indeed inferable (*anumeya*), but not directly denotable (*abhidheya*).
Just as in the word *vṛkṣa* (tree), the roots and other parts are not the direct denotation, so too, because it is not directly denoted, the *anyapadārtha* is not the primary element.

Now, why does the *samāsānta* suffix not occur here? To this he says: "In the case of *appaūraṇīpramāṇyo*," and so forth. Now, how is there the substitution of the masculine form (*puṃvadbhāva*) in examples such as *dṛḍhabhaktiḥ* (firm devotion) and *śobhanabhaktiḥ* (beautiful devotion), given that there ought to be a prohibition because [the word *bhakti*] belongs to the *priyādi* group? To this he says: "In cases such as *dṛḍhabhaktiḥ*," and so forth.

This should be resolved by noting that since the intention is for the preceding member (*pūrvapada*) to denote something other than a female, the target forms (*lakṣya*) such as *dṛḍhabhaktiḥ* are established.
The meaning is that what is loathsome must be avoided.
Here, the word *dṛḍha* (firm) is employed with the intent of precluding lack of firmness (*adāḍharya*).
In this injunction intended to preclude lack of firmness, the mention of a specific gender (*liṅga-viśeṣa*) is indeed of no assistance whatsoever.
Therefore, femininity is not intended here.

Consequently, the intention is that this is an employment of the word *dṛḍha* in a non-feminine gender. This undertaking [of the rule] concerns a meaning that does not occur in a subsequent word (*anuttarapadārtha*). [The word] "therefore" (*tataḥ*).

Because of the designation *vibhakti* [of the word] by the rule *tasya* (Pāṇini 5.3.1), the substitution of *at* for the words beginning with *tyad* occurs; then the feminine suffix *ṭāp* is applied, and by this [present rule], the masculine form (*puṃvadbhāva*) is substituted. Regarding the word *tatra*:
the remainder is as before.
Regarding the rule beginning with *tasilādiṣu*:

if it were stated simply as *tasilādiṣvākṛtvasucaḥ*, then in some cases where *puṃvadbhāva* (masculine-like treatment) is desired even for those not included among the *tasil*-class suffixes, it would not be obtained. Conversely, in other cases where it is included among the *tasil*-class, it would be undesired even though it is required. Such being the case, an undesirable result would follow.
Therefore, an enumeration must be made.
Among those, examples for *tataḥ* and *tasi* have been stated.

Now, the remaining ones are being explained: this is clever (*paṭu*), this is clever; of these two, that which is more clever—by the rule beginning with "dvivacana" [Pāṇini 5.3.57], the suffix *tarap* is applied, resulting in *paṭutarā*.

This [word] *paṭvī* is [formed] with the suffix *ān* by the rule *atiśāyane* [Pāṇini 5.3.55], followed by *tamap*; thus, *paṭutamā*. When it denotes one who was previously clever, the suffix *ṅīp* is applied [by Pāṇini 4.1.41], resulting in *paṭucarī*. When it denotes a type of cleverness, the suffix *jātīyar* is applied [by Pāṇini 5.3.69], resulting in *paṭujātīyā*.
Slightly incomplete *paṭvī* (clever) becomes *paṭukalpā*, *paṭudeśyā*, or *paṭudeśīyā* [by Pāṇini 5.3.67].

When *paṭvī* means "praiseworthy," it becomes *paṭurūpā* [by Pāṇini 5.3.66, which prescribes the suffix *rūpap* for praise]. When *paṭvī* means "despicable," it becomes *paṭupāśā* [by Pāṇini 5.3.47, which prescribes the suffix *pāśap* for what is despicable].
The suffix *thyan* is prescribed after the word *ajā* [in the sense of "good for"] by the rule *ajāvyoḥ thyan* (Pāṇini 5.1.8), as in *ajathyā*.
The suffix *thyan* is recited before the suffixes beginning with *tasil* [i.e., in the section on adverbial suffixes].
[It is used] in the sense of "in every way" or "by all means," according to the rule *sarvaprakāreṣu thā* (Pāṇini 5.3.23).
In that night, at that time—[[5.3.15]].
In this night, here—*etahiṃ*—by *idamorhil* [[5.3.16]].
There, for *idam*, the substitution *itaḥ* applies by *tatremaḥ* [[5.3.4]]; [thus] a praiseworthy female wolf is *vṛkatiḥ*.

*Praśastā jyeṣṭhā jyeṣṭhatātiḥ*: by the rule *vṛkajyeṣṭhābhyāṃ tiltātilau ca chandasi* [Pāṇini 5.4.41], the suffixes *til* and *tāti* are applied. Having formed these two, they are recited after the suffix *asu*. This is the opinion of the author of the Bhāṣya that an enumeration (*parigaṇana*) must be made among the suffixes beginning with *tasil*, but it is not the opinion of the author of the Sūtras.
Furthermore, if there were no enumeration, nothing undesirable would result.

For those *tasil*-type suffixes not included in the list where *puṃvadbhāva* (the substitution of the masculine form) is desired, it will occur because the particle *ca* in that sūtra has the sense of including what is not explicitly mentioned (*anuktasamuccaya*).

As for those *tasil*-type suffixes included in the list where it is not desired, the rule will not apply because of the separation of the yoga (*yogavibhāga*) in the statement "na" [Pāṇini 6.3.37]. Indeed, there is also a fault in the case of enumeration: from the word *dāra*, with the suffix *kap*, in the form *dāradikā*, the application of *puṃvadbhāva* would not be obtained, because the suffix *kap* is not included in the enumeration.

Regarding the rule "śasi bahvalpārthasya": when the suffix *śas* follows, the *puṃvadbhāva* (masculine-like behavior) of words meaning "many" (*bahu*) and "few" (*alpa*) must be stated; that is to say, it must be explained.
This explanation, however, should be made by relying on the fact that the particle *ca* in that very [rule] has the sense of including what has not been explicitly mentioned (*anuktasamuccaya*).
"Before a *taddhita* suffix beginning with a vowel," and so forth.
"Hāstikam":
[the suffix] *ṭhak* is applied by [Pāṇini 4.2.47].

If the masculine treatment (*puṃvadbhāva*) were not applied here, then, after the elision of the *ī* by rule Pāṇini 6.4.148, the elision of the *ṭi* (the first vowel) by rule 6.4.144 would not take place due to the status of the preceding element as a substitute (*sthānivadbhāva*) according to rule 1.1.57. However, when the masculine treatment is applied, this becomes simply the word *hasti*.

But is it not the case that the masculine-like substitution (*puṃvadbhāva*) is established here by the rule *ṭhakchasoḥ* (Pāṇini 7.3.51) alone? It is not established; it is not established because, due to association with *chas*, only that *ṭhak* which is prescribed by the rule *bhavataṣṭhakchasau* (Pāṇini 4.2.115) is understood there, and not every *ṭhak*. [The question begins with] "How," etc.

If the prohibition of *puṃvadbhāva* (masculine-like behavior) were applied when the suffix *ḍha* follows, then after the suffix *ḍhak* is added in the sense of "this has Agnāyī as its deity" (*agnāyī devatāsya*), the form would have to be *āgnāyeya*; how then could it become *āgneya*? This is the intended objection. When there is the intention to express "the female of Agni," the word *agni* takes the suffix *ṅīp* by [Pāṇini 4.1.37], and with the substitution of the final vowel for *ai*, the form *agnāyī* arises.
"An effort must be made here."

But by whom should this effort be made? It is by one who desires the supplementary rule (*upasaṃkhyāna*) "bhasyāḍhe taddhite" (Vārttika 731), and not by one who places the letter *c* in the subsequent sūtra for the purpose of an unexpressed conjunction (*anuktasamuccaya*). For the latter says: "The letter *c* conjoins the *puvadbhāva* only where it is intended, and not elsewhere."
What, then, is this effort? Someone says: "The mention of *apatya* (offspring) must be made as a qualifier of the suffix *ḍha*—namely, 'that which is *ḍha* when [denoting] offspring.

By this, the following meaning results: the *pūrvavadbhāva* (masculine-like behavior) of the suffix *ḍha* occurs when it denotes its cause (*taddhetau*), with the exception of a suffix whose meaning is offspring.

Now, in the case of *āgneyaḥ sthālīpākaḥ*, the suffix *ḍha* does not have the meaning of offspring; rather, it has the meaning "this is its deity" (*sāsya devatā*). Therefore, in this instance, *pūrvavadbhāva* indeed occurs.

But another says: "In the rule *bhasyāḍhe taddhite* (Vārttika 731), the two locative cases are in different grammatical relations (*vyadhikaraṇa*). Furthermore, the negative particle (*nañ*) here signifies 'a small amount,' just as a gruel that has little salt is called 'saltless' (*alavaṇā*). In that case, the meaning is this: "The substitution of the masculine form (*puṃvadbhāva*) for a *bha*-stem before a *taddhita* suffix should be stated when the suffix *ḍha* follows, provided it signifies a small amount."
Therefore, in the case of *āgneyaḥ* and *sthālīpākaḥ*, the substitution of the masculine form (*puṃvadbhāvaḥ*) occurs;
however, in cases such as *śyaineyaḥ* and *rohiṇeyaḥ*, it does not occur.
This is due to the rule beginning with "ṭhakchasośca" and so forth.

Now, what is the purpose of including the mention of *ṭhak*? For, once the single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) for *ṭha* has been made, the desired result is already established by the rule *bhasyāḍhe taddhite* (Vār. 731). [The answer is: It is for the sake of ensuring that the operation takes place while the suffix is still in its *ṭha*-state. What follows from this? The suffix *ka*, prescribed by *isusuktāntāt kaḥ* (Pāṇ. 7.3.51), becomes established; otherwise, if the masculine-like treatment (*puṃvadbhāva*) were to occur after the single-substitute had been made, then just as the single-substitute does not occur in *māthitika*, it would likewise not occur in *bhāvatka*.

"Bhāvatkāḥ" and "bhavadīyāḥ" are formed by the suffixes *ṭhak* and *cha*, according to [Pāṇini 4.2.115]. In "etāyate" and "śyetāyate," the feminine suffix *ṅīp* is applied to the words *eta* and *śyeta* by the rule [Pāṇini 4.1.39], "From a non-udātta-final color word ending in *t* with *t* as its penultimate letter, *na* replaces *t*"; thus, the *t* is replaced by *n*. (Note: The printed reading is "eta-ota-śabdābhyām").

"He behaves like a female elephant" (*enīvācarati*), "he behaves like a hawk" (*śyenīvācarati*). [The suffix] *kyaṅ* is applied by the rule "The suffix *kyaṅ* is added after a word denoting the agent, and there is elision of the final syllable" (*kartuḥ kyaṅ salopaśca* 3.1.11). Lengthening occurs by the rule "In place of [the short *i* of] a non-*kṛt* or non-*sārvadhātuka* suffix" (*akṛtsārvadhātukayoḥ* 7.4.25).

Regarding the example "He considers her beautiful" (*ayamasyāṃ darśanīyamānī*)—[the Kāśikā reads: *darśanīyamānī ayamasyāḥ*]—it means that he considers this woman to be beautiful (*darśanīyām imām manyate 'yam iti*).
The suffix *ṇini* is applied by [Pāṇini 3.2.82] *manaḥ*.

Thus, "she thinks this one is beautiful" (*darśanīyamānanīyā asyāḥ*). Because she thinks, "This woman is beautiful," the suffix *ṇini* is applied as before, and the feminine suffix *ṅīp* is added by [Pāṇini 4.1.5] *ṛnnebhyo ṅīp*.
[4.1.5] Thus [the suffix] *ṅīp* [is applied].

But what is the reason for citing an example of *puṃvadbhāva* (masculine-like substitution) when the word *mānin* is the final member (*uttarapada*), even though the rule "when there is a feminine word in grammatical apposition" (*striyāṃ samānādhikaraṇe*) is still in force—given that this would normally apply only to non-feminines and not when in apposition? To this he says: "`The mention of *mānin*" and so forth.
How is this known? To this he says: "`But here..."* and so forth.

If the final member [of the compound] occurs in the feminine and is in grammatical apposition (*samānādhikaraṇa*)—as in examples such as *darśanīyamāninī* ("one who considers herself beautiful")—then why is this so? Because it is already established by the rule *striyāṃ puṃvat* (Pāṇini 6.3.34), the mention of *mānin* here is for the purpose of excluding the feminine. From this, it is understood that the rule applies even when there is no apposition; otherwise, it would be redundant. This is a prohibition of the masculine-like form (*puṃvadbhāva*) which would have been obtained by the preceding method.
In the expressions *pācikābhāryaḥ* and *kārikābhāryaḥ*,

the suffix *ṭāp* is added to the words *pācaka* and *kāraka* ending in the suffix *ṇvul*. The substitution of *it* [for the vowel preceding *k*] occurs by the rule *pratyayasthāt kātpūrvasyāta idāpyasupaḥ* [Pāṇini 7.3.44].

In this case, there is the possibility of application by the rule *striyāḥ puṃvat* [Pāṇini 6.3.33] and others, as in the examples *madrikābhāryaḥ* and *vṛjikābhāryaḥ*. Here, [the words] *madrī* and *vṛjī* mean "born among the Madras" and "born among the Vṛjis," respectively; the suffix *kan* is applied according to the rule *madravṛjyoḥ kan* [Pāṇini 4.2.130].

Here too, there is an application [of the rule] by "the feminine [stem] like the masculine" (*striyāḥ puṃvat*) and so forth [Pāṇini 6.3.34]. In the examples "madrikākalpā" and "vṛjikākalpā," there is an application by the rule beginning with "hereafter" (*atra*) [Pāṇini 6.3.35].
In examples such as *madrikāyate*, there is the application [of the suffix] according to Pāṇini 6.3.36.
Regarding *vilepikāyā dhamryam*:
from the root *lip* in the sense of "smearing" (*upadehe*; Dhātupāṭha 1433), the suffix *ṇvul* is applied.
Regarding the term *vailepika*:
the suffix *aṇ* is applied by [Pāṇini 4.4.48], *aṇ mahiṣyādibhyaḥ*.

Here, there is an optional application of the rule [Pāṇini 6.4.149], *bhasyāḍhe taddhite*, which prescribes the substitution of *ya* for the final vowel of the base when followed by a non-ādi taddhita suffix.

Regarding the rule "kopadhapratiṣedhe" (the prohibition concerning [stems] having *k* as their penultimate letter), etc.: in this prohibition of stems with *k* as a penultimate letter, the mention of the suffix *vu* must be made.
This is so that the prohibition may apply only where the penultimate letter *k* is connected to a *taddhita* suffix or connected to the suffix *vu*.
Let it not be the case that [the form] *pākabhāryaḥ* would arise here. This word *pāka*, ending in the suffix *kan*, is prescribed by the rule *arbhakapṛthukapākā vayasi* (Pāṇini 5.3.50).
If the mention of *vu* were absent here, the prohibition would apply even in this instance.

If the mention of *taddhita* and *vu* is made [in the rule], then that which will be stated under [Pāṇini 8.2.1]—namely, that in the case of *śuṣkajaṅgha*, because [the substitution] under [Pāṇini 8.2.51] is not established (*asiddha*), the prohibition [stated in] *na kopadhāyāḥ* [6.3.36] does not apply—and thus the purpose of the section on non-establishment (*asiddhādhikāra*) is fulfilled; this is untenable. For even if [the rule] *śuṣaḥ kaḥ* were not established, there ought to be the prohibition [stated in] *na kye* [1.4.15] here, since there is no connection with a *taddhita* suffix in this instance.
Is the letter *ka* not also related to *vu*? There is no fault, because it is so designated by relying on a difference in philosophical perspective (*darśana-bheda*).

For this has been stated by relying on the view of the author of the Vārttika. That [view], however, he will explain by relying on the perspective of the author of the Ślokavārttika, who follows the view of the author of the Sūtras. But how can there be the application of the masculine form (*puṃvadbhāva*) for a technical term (*saṃjñā-śabda*), since the rule for masculine form is stated to apply to words that have already expressed the masculine (*bhāṣita-puṃska*), and a technical term that functions as a feminine does not express the masculine, because technical terms reside in a single substance (*ekadravya-niveśitvāt*)? This is not so; for...

Is this restriction not [applicable] because technical terms (*saṃjñāśabda*) reside in a single substance? This is not so; for it is not the case that a restriction must exist such that technical terms can only reside in a single substance. To illustrate:

words such as *Devadatta* are observed to be used in common worldly usage as designations for a single entity, despite being connected to multiple substances, actions, and so forth; the same is true for words like *sva* (self/possessive) in the technical treatises (*śāstra*).
As for those technical terms that do reside in a single substance, this prohibition is not made with respect to them; thus, the objection is without merit.

Now, it may be granted that proper names (*saṃjñāśabda*) can apply to multiple objects, yet they are "masculine when spoken" (*bhāṣitapuṃska*) with respect to a single form. How then is there any basis for their application (*pravṛttinimitta*), given that they are arbitrary words (*yadṛcchāśabda*)? This too is without substance; for even among them, some indeed possess a basis for application, such as the word *saptaparṇa* ("seven-leaved"). Even where this is absent, they still function toward the denoted object by taking their own form (*svarūpa*) as the basis for application.

In that case, since the basis for application (*pravṛttinimitta*) is not different, why is it incorrect to say that those by whom "man" (*pumān*) is expressed are "those who express the masculine" (*bhāṣitapuṃskāḥ*)? [Consider] the example *dattābhryaḥ*.
Here, the word *dattā* is one that expresses the masculine in reference to that very same action of giving (*dānakriyākṛti*).
[And consider] *guptābhāryaḥ*.
Here too, the word *guptā* functions either as the cause for its application (*pravṛttinimitta*) in the sense of the action of hiding, or in its own form (*svarūpa*).

Both are words that have been previously used in the masculine (*bhāṣitapuṃska*), as in "she acts like one who is hidden" (*guptāyate*) or "she acts like one who is given" (*dattāyate*). How can these two be presented as examples of the prohibition [of *puṃvadbhāva*], since even if *puṃvadbhāva* were applied, both forms would be established by the lengthening [of the vowel] according to Pāṇini 7.4.25, "There is lengthening for [stems ending in] a short vowel before a non-Ṭi affix and before a sārvadhātuka affix"? The intention is this: the rule "A grammatical operation conditioned by a technical name (*saṃjñā*) is not mandatory" (Vyāḍiparibhāṣā 64). Therefore, if there were no prohibition of *puṃvadbhāva*, the absence of lengthening would be inferred [as the intended result].
In that view, forms such as *dattayate* and *guptayate* would also be possible.

Although the rule *na kopadhāsaṃjñāpūraṇīnām* [Pāṇini 6.3.37] could have been formulated as a single *yoga*, the division of the rule (*yogavibhāga*) was made for the purpose of indicating that this prohibition is not universally obligatory (*anityatva*). Consequently, what was stated—namely, "In the prohibition regarding words ending in *ka*, the mention of *taddhita* suffixes and *vuñ* must be made" (Vārttika 733)—need not be done. [This applies to] suffixes *ña*, *ṇa*, and *ka* when they cause *vṛddhi*.
Regarding the term *ruāaudhnībhāryaḥ*: [the word] *ruāaudhnī* is derived by adding the suffix *aṇ* according to [Pāṇini 4.3.53],
and then the suffix *ṅīp* is added according to [Pāṇini 4.1.15].

The same applies here in the case of *māthurī-bhāryaḥ* ("one whose wife is from Mathurā") and *madhyama-bhāryaḥ* ("one whose wife is middle-aged"). In *madhyama-bhāryaḥ*, the suffix *map* is applied according to [Pāṇini 4.3.8]: *madhye bhavā*.
Regarding "kāṇḍalāvabhāryaḥ":
[the word] *kāṇḍalāva-* is formed from *kāṇḍam lunāti* by the addition of the suffix *ṅīp* as previously explained.
Regarding "tāvadbhāryaḥ": [the word] *tāvadbhārya-* is formed similarly.

From the word *tāvat*: "that which has this as its measure" (*tat-parimāṇam-asyāḥ*). By the rule *yattadetebhyaḥ parimāṇe vatup* (Pāṇini 5.2.39), the suffix *vatup* is applied; by *taddhiteṣvacāmādeḥ* (6.1.107), the vowel at the beginning of the stem is lengthened; and by *ṭiḍḍhāṇañ* (4.1.15), the feminine suffix *ṅīp* is added. Thus, one whose wife is *tāvatī* is called *tāvadbhāryaḥ*. If the term *vṛddhinimittasya* were understood here as referring to a *tatpuruṣa* compound, then a prohibition would apply even in this case, because the suffix *vatup* is indeed the cause (*nimitta*) for the vowel *ā*, which is a *vṛddhi* substitute. However, there is no fault if it is understood as a *bahuvrīhi* compound; for in the case of *vatup*, the letter *ñ* and so forth are not the cause of the *vṛddhi* substitution.
Regarding the word *kāṣāyī*: [the suffix] *aṇ* is applied according to the rule *tena raktam* (Pāṇini 4.2.1). Regarding the word *lauhī*: [the suffix *aṇ* is applied according to the same rule].
By [Pāṇini 4.3.154], *añ* is applied; as before, *ṅīp* follows.
Thus, "khādireṣaḥ. By [Pāṇini 4.3.141], either *añ* or *aṇ* is applied.
"One whose pole is made of *khadira* wood" is *khādireṣā*. Regarding "long-haired" (*dīrghakeśī*):
the suffix *ṅīṣ* is applied by [Pāṇini 4.1.54], "The suffix *ṅīṣ* follows a word denoting a limb of one's own body that is an *upasarjana* and does not have a conjunct as its penultimate letter.
Regarding "sixfold" (*ṣaṭvī*).
From the word *paṭu*: the suffix *ṅīṣ* is applied by [Pāṇini 4.1.44], *voto guṇavacanāt*. Regarding *akeśabhāryaḥ*:
since the suffix *ṅīp* is prohibited for *akeśā* (meaning "one who has no hair") by [Pāṇini 4.1.57], only the suffix *ṭāp* occurs. Regarding *kaṭhībhāryaḥ*: [the same applies].

From the word *kaṭha*, the suffix *ṅīṣ* is applied according to [Pāṇini 4.1.63]: "The suffix *ṅīṣ* is added after a word denoting a genus (*jāti*), provided it does not refer to a feminine and its penultimate vowel is not *ay*. Its status as a genus is established by the definition: "A lineage (*gotra*) together with Vedic schools (*caraṇa*") [is also a genus]. "This," and so forth.

The prohibition of that *puṃvadbhāva* which is introduced by the supplementary rule (*vārttika*) "in a taddhita suffix beginning with a vowel and having an indicatory letter *ḍ*" (Vā. 731) is not intended here.

For the intention is that, in order to set aside this prohibition, a *yogavibhāga* (splitting of the rule) must be made in the subsequent sūtra [Pāṇini 6.3.34] as "puṃvat" [and so on]. [Objection: But surely the *puṃvadbhāva* is already established in a *karmadhāraya* by the rule "the feminine becomes like the masculine" (6.3.33), etc., and in the case of the words *jātīya* and The object of a negation is expressed by the word "negation" (pratiṣedha) due to association. It is so called because negation is its meaning or purpose.
The meaning is that in whatever context a negation is stated, the transformation into the masculine form (puṃvadbhāva) is the purpose.
Alternatively, the word *artha* here functions in the sense of "cessation" (*nivṛtti*), as in the expression "smoke for the sake of mosquitoes" (*maśakārtho dhūmaḥ*).

Therefore, the meaning is this: "this undertaking is for the purpose of the cessation of the prohibition. Regarding the phrase "only [if it follows] what has a corresponding masculine form" (*bhāṣitapuṃskādityeva*):

if the rule *bhāṣitapuṃskādanūṅ* (Pāṇini 6.3.33) were not being carried over [into this sūtra], then this statement would be intended for the sake of forms that do not have a corresponding masculine (*abhāṣitapuṃska*) and for those that do not take the suffix *ūṅ* (*anūṅ*), rather than for the purpose of a prohibition.
And in this way, the substitution of the masculine form (*puṃvadbhāva*) would also apply in cases such as *khaṭvāvṛndārikā* and *brāhmaṇabandhūvṛndārikā*.

Therefore, one must carry forward the condition "provided there is no *ūṅ* following a word that has a corresponding masculine form" (*bhāṣitapuṃskādanūṅ*). Regarding the rule "of *kukkuṭa* and so forth," etc.:

since the final syllable of the subsequent member (*uttarapada*) does not end in a feminine suffix and because there is no grammatical coreferentiality (*asāmānādhikaraṇya*), the substitution of the masculine form does not apply; thus, this is added as a supplementary rule (*upasaṃkhyāna*).
By the phrase "or rather not" (*na vā*), he rejects the proposed addition (*upasaṃkhyāna*). It need not be stated. Why? Because what is intended is a prior member that is not feminine.
The intention is that a prior member in a non-feminine gender is intended. To clarify the meaning of this very point, he says: "without being feminine," and so forth.
For here, what is intended to be expressed is the exclusion of other classes, such as peacocks and the like.
In a teaching whose purpose is the exclusion of other classes, the employment of a specific gender is indeed of no assistance;
for the exclusion of other classes can certainly be accomplished even without it.

For instance, when "deer meat" (*mṛgamāṃsa*) is mentioned, even without the employment of a specific gender, the exclusion of other classes is established: namely, that this is meat belonging to the deer species, not belonging to any other species.

Therefore, the feminine gender here is not intended because it is irrelevant; thus, the meaning is that in cases such as *kukkuṭāṇḍa* ("hen's egg"), the meaning of the first member is intended by way of the commonality of the genus (*jātisāmānyena*), as the feminine gender is not specifically prescribed.
Consequently, the point is that words such as *kukkuṭa*, which are inherently non-feminine, are compounded here with words such as *aṇḍa*.

What, then, is this "prior member" (*pūrvapada*)? It is a mere substance (*dravya*) delimited by a genus such as "cock" (*kukkuṭa*) and so forth. Regarding the phrase "due to *puṃvadbhāva*" and so on:

here, it has already been explained that in the presence of a suffix marked with *kh* (i.e., *khid*), shortening occurs by way of *vipratiṣedha* (conflict of rules) because of *puṃvadbhāva*. However, it is now being explained in the context of suffixes beginning with *gh*.

The scope for the rule "the *ṅī* [suffix] becomes short before the suffixes *gha*, etc. is, for example: *nartakitarā*, *nartakitamā*, *nartakirūpā*, *nartakikalpā*; the scope for the rule regarding the masculine form (*puṃvadbhāva*) is, for example: *darśanīyatarā*, *darśanīyatamā*, *darśanīyarūpā*, *darśanīyakalpā*. In the case of *paṭvitarā*, *paṭvitamā*, *paṭvirūpā*, *paṭvikalpā*, both rules would apply; however, by the principle of conflict (*vipratiṣedha*), the shortening occurs.

The rule *ke'ṇaḥ* [Pāṇini 7.4.13] provides scope for the short vowel in the case of *nartakikā*; the rule *prāgivāt kaḥ* [Pāṇini 5.3.70] providing scope for the masculine base form (*pūrvadbhāva*) in the sense of "unknown" and so forth, as in *dāradikā*. Here, when the suffix *ka* follows the word *darat*, the word *darada* becomes masculine by virtue of the rule *tasalādiṣvākṛtvāsucaḥ* [Pāṇini 6.3.35]. Consequently, when the feminine suffix *ṭāp* is applied, both rules—*pratyayasthāt kāt* [Pāṇini 7.3.44] and the present rule—apply simultaneously.
Regarding the term *paṭvikā*:
here, by way of a conflict between rules (*vipratiṣedha*), the shortening will take effect.

But by what rule would there be the substitution of the masculine form (*puṃvadbhāva*), since the enumeration was made for the suffixes beginning with *tasil*, and the suffix *kap* is not included in that enumeration? To this, one should ask the author of the Bhāṣya, who provides the enumeration, and not the author of the Sūtra.
In order to demonstrate that in the previous [rule] a *prasajya-pratiṣedha* (prohibitive negation) was relied upon for the sake of establishing the result, he says "here," and so forth.
Regarding the phrase "there, of the *tadrāja* suffix," and so on:
from the two words *iḍaviṭ* and *pṛthu*, the suffix *añ* is prescribed by [Pāṇini 4.1.168], and that *tadrāja* suffix undergoes elision (*luk*) by [Pāṇini 4.1.175].
The suffix *aṇ* is prescribed by the rule beginning with *darad-uśij-ity-etābhyām* (Pāṇini 4.1.170).

Having analyzed the compound as "she who is both *iḍaviṭ* and *vṛndārikā*," the term *viśeṣaṇa* (and so forth) applies; by the phrase "*atraiḍaviḍādayaḥ*" (note: this phrase is not found in the Kāśikā), the word *ādi* includes *dāradaḥ*, *pārathaḥ*, and *auśijaḥ*. Because words denoting lineages (*gotra*) such as *celaṭ* and *abrāu* have a derogatory sense, the compound is formed according to *kutsitāni kutsanaiḥ* (Pāṇini 2.1.52).

[The form *brāuvaḥ*] is derived by the rule *matahataśabdābhyām tu* [Pāṇini 2.1.57]. The suffix *celaṭ* is listed among the *pacādi* group; the letter *ṭ* is for the purpose of forming the feminine with *ṅīp*. If this [word *brāuvaḥ*] ends in the *ac* suffix of the *pacādi* group, then, that being the case, the substitution of *vac* and the application of *guṇa* would result by the rule *brāuvo vaciḥ* [Pāṇini 2.4.53]. Why does this not occur? To the one who raises this objection, he replies: "The substitution of *vac* and the *guṇa* do not occur because of *nipātana* (irregularity)."
Regarding the examples "āmalakītarā" and "kuvalītarā":

the words *āmalaka* and *kuvala* are invariably feminine when referring to the tree, but they are neuter when referring to the fruit; thus, both are "not having been previously masculine" (*abhāṣitapuṃska*). From these two, the suffix *ṅīṣ* is applied because they belong to the *gaurādi* group. The rule "after a word that has been previously masculine, provided it does not end in *ū*" (Pāṇini 4.1.37) is no longer operative here.

Regarding the question, "And what is the remainder (*śeṣa*)?"—if the remainder were that for which shortening was not prescribed by the preceding rule, then that which has been mentioned as having a masculine counterpart (*bhāṣitapuṃska*) and that which has been mentioned as having a masculine counterpart despite having a different form (*bhinnāyām ākṛtau bhāṣitapuṃska*), such as *naicāc*, would also be considered a remainder. Consequently, in cases such as *āmalakītarā* and *droṇītarā*, there would also be an optional shortening. With the intention of showing that shortening is not prescribed here by the preceding rule, he says: "The feminine stem (*aṅ*) which is a river-name (*nadī*), and that which ends in the suffix *ṅī* and consists of a single syllable (*ekāc*)."

By this, it is shown that here the status of being a "remainder" (śeṣatva) is relied upon on the basis of what has been heard [in the rule], and not with reference to that for which a short vowel has not been prescribed. But how is this obtained? From the mention of the word "remainder" (śeṣa). Even without the mention of the word "remainder," the shortening would apply optionally only to the remainder.

For instance, if the short vowel were optionally allowed for a feminine stem ending in *ṅī* that has more than one syllable even when it expresses the masculine (*bhāṣitapuṃska*), then the author would have used the term *anyatarasyām* ("optionally") in the very preceding rule.

Since the reason here is that the optional shortening applies only to those cases where the short vowel was not previously prescribed by the preceding rule, it can be concluded that even without the mention of "the remainder" (*śeṣa*), the shortening would apply only to the remainder. Why, then, is the mention of "the remainder" made? It is made so that "the remainder" may be understood in relation to the vowel *ac* that is heard in the preceding sūtra, *ṅyo 'nekācaḥ* [Pāṇini 6.3.43].

In the case of *camalakītarā* and *drīṇītarā*, the status of being a remainder (*śeṣatva*) with respect to what is heard [in the rule] is not tenable; for [the suffix] *ṅīp* consists of more than one vowel (*anekāctvāt*).
Therefore, there is no occasion here for the shortening [of the penultimate vowel]. Thus, it is *strītarā*.

Regarding *styāyateḍaṭ*: because the suffix is marked with *ḍ*, there is elision of the *ṭi* portion [by Pāṇini 6.4.143], and elision of the *val* portion [by Pāṇini 6.1.66]. Because the suffix is marked with *ṭ*, the feminine suffix *ṅīp* is applied. "It must be explained" means that it must be commented upon.

In this regard, the explanation is as follows: because the mention of "either one" (*anyatarasyām*) is understood as a fixed option (*vyavasthitavibhāṣā*), the [suffix] will not apply after a *kṛt*-derived word ending in a feminine noun. Thus, in the case of *lakṣmītarā*:

the word *lakṣmī* is derived from the suffix *ī* added to the roots *avi*, *tṛ*, *stṛ*, and *tantri* (Dhātupāṭha 1.82), with the augment *muṭ* added to *lakṣ* (Dhātupāṭha 1.84), resulting in a word ending in the suffix *ī*.

This [suffix] *kṛt* becomes *nady*. In the case of *śreyasitarā*, the substitution of *śra-* for the word *praśasya* occurs by Pāṇini 5.3.60 when the suffix *īyasun* follows, and the feminine suffix *ṅīp* is applied by Pāṇini 4.1.5. In the case of *viduṣītarā*, [the same applies].

The substitution of *śatṛ* for the *laṭ* of the root *vid* (to know) occurs; for that [suffix], the substitution of *vas* takes place by Pāṇini 7.1.36, followed by the replacement of the preceding vowel with the subsequent one by 6.4.131, and as before, the feminine suffix *ṅīp* is applied.
It must be stated that "the masculine form (*puṃvadbhāva*) also applies in this case," so that forms such as *śreyastarā* and *vidvattare* may occur according to the alternative view.
Regarding the term *vidbattara*:
by the rule *vasuruāṃsu* [Pāṇini 8.2.72], the *s* is replaced by *d*; then, by the rule *khari ca* [Pāṇini 8.4.54], the *d* is replaced by *t*.
With the words "due to connection with excellence" (*prakarṣayogāt*) and so forth, he rejects the proposed addition (*upasaṃkhyāna*).
In the derivation and application of words, the proximity of the actual object is not the primary cause; rather, it is the speaker's intention (*vivakṣā*) alone.

And it is not the case that, because of its prior connection with excellence, femininity was intended [to be expressed]. Therefore, the suffix of excellence (*atiśāyika*) must be applied to a word that does not already end in a feminine suffix.
However, when a feminine suffix is added to a word ending in a superlative suffix, the forms such as *śreyas-tarā* are established.

But has it not been stated that the mention of *ṅī* and *āp* is for the purpose of prescribing a *taddhita* suffix after a word ending in those [feminine suffixes]? How then can a *taddhita* suffix expressing excellence (*prakarṣa*) be applied to a word ending in a feminine suffix other than those? This is not so; that statement was made with the intention of simultaneously intending both the feminine gender and the meaning of the *taddhita* suffix in this context. However, it was not made with reference to a case where the feminine gender is not intended before its connection with the sense of excellence—so why would it not be appropriate here? For example: *mahādevaḥ*, *mahābrāhmaṇaḥ* (formed as a *karmadhāraya* compound by rule 2.1.61 et seq.), and *mahābāhuḥ*.
This is a *bahuvrīhi* compound.
Having set forth the opinion of another by means of the words "because it has been stated as a defining characteristic" (*lakṣaṇoktatvāt*) and so forth, he refutes it.

It might be argued as follows: "The compound is brought to mind by the subsequent member (*uttarapada*), for a compound exists only when there is a subsequent member. And that compound—by the paribhāṣā 'that which is taught by a specific rule [takes precedence over] that which is taught by a general rule' (Vyā|Pa|3)—is understood to be only that which is directly prescribed by a specific rule, such as *mahato yaḥ pratipadoktaḥ* (Pāṇini 2.1.61), and not a compound that is derivative (*lākṣaṇika*) or taught by a general rule, such as *mahatputraḥ*. Therefore, since this [compound] is prescribed by the general rule *ṣaṣṭhī* (Pāṇini 2.2.8), it will not [be subject to the aforementioned restriction]."
If this were so, then [the substitution] would not occur even in a *bahuvrīhi* compound, because that too is based on a secondary (figurative) meaning (*lākṣaṇika*).
Regarding the phrase "for that purpose" and so forth:
the mention of "coreferential" (*samānādhikaraṇa*) must be made so that the substitution of long *ā* (*ātva*) may occur even in a *bahuvrīhi*.
In that regard, this technical designation (*paribhāṣā*) does not apply.

If it were to apply, the term "samānādhikaraṇa" (having a common substratum) would be redundant; for the specific compound prescribed by the rule *mahataḥ* is already one whose constituent members share a common substratum. And since that designation does not apply, the substitution of *āt* occurs even in the case of a *bahuvrīhi*.

However, if the term *samānādhikaraṇa* (co-referential) were not included [in the rule], then this paribhāṣā would have to apply here [to the present case]. Consequently, just as it does not apply in the case of *mahat-putra*, it would likewise not apply in the case of the *bahuvrīhi* compound *mahābāhu*. Someone might have the misconception: "In examples such as *amahān mahān saṃpannaḥ* or *mahadbhūtaś candramāḥ*, where the word *mahat* ending in the suffix *cv-* occurs in its true sense, the word *bhūta* also applies there; therefore, since there is co-referentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), it ought to be subject to that [paribhāṣā]. To dispel this, he says: "*amahān mahān*," etc.

Regarding the term *mahadbhūtaḥ*: from the word *maha-* [the suffix] *cvi* is applied by the rule "in the sense of becoming that which was not previously so" (Pāṇini 5.4.50), etc.; because of the rule "after that [which ends in *cvi*, the preceding element becomes the first member]" (Pāṇini 1.4.61), it receives the designation *gati*; and thus, by the rule "with a *gati* [word, there is compound formation]" (Pāṇini 2.2.18), a compound is formed with the word *bhūta*.
Regarding the phrase "because of its being secondary," etc.
For in the world, when a word is uttered and both a primary and a secondary meaning are possible, comprehension occurs only with respect to the primary meaning, not with respect to the secondary one.
To illustrate: when it is said, "Let the cow be brought," only that which possesses a dewlap and so forth is brought, not a *bāhīka* (a person from the Punjab).
Therefore, here too, when the word "great" (*mahat*) is uttered, comprehension occurs only with respect to the primary sense of greatness, not the secondary one.

In this context, the meaning of "great" (*mahat*) is figurative (*gauṇa*). Because it denotes that [figurative sense], the word *maha-* itself is also figurative, and thus the substitution of *āt* does not occur. Now, one might object: "The moon is indeed 'great' when endowed with greatness; therefore, it is incorrect to say that the meaning of 'great' is figurative. This is not so. For in every instance, a thing whose prior state has been set aside and whose subsequent state is metaphorically attributed is expressed by means of a suffix ending in *cvī*. Therefore, here too, the moon—which had a prior state of non-greatness—is expressed by the word *maha-*, and is said to possess a subsequent state characterized by metaphorical greatness; thus, its figurative nature is logical.

If, because the word *mahat* is used in a secondary sense (*gauṇa*), the substitution of *āt* does not occur here, then the masculine-like form (*puṃvadbhāva*) would likewise not occur, as in the case of "the great Brāhmaṇī woman who was previously small has become great" (*amahatī brāhmaṇī mahatī saṃpannā mahadbhūtā*).

[Objection: In the case of the secondary (*gauṇa*) application of the word *go*, would there not be [the absence of] both the substitution of *ā* (*āttva*) and the designation *vṛddhi*? For instance, in the sentence *gaur vāhīkaḥ tiṣṭhati* ("The Vāhīka is standing like a cow"), the designation *vṛddhi* would not apply [to the *o* of *vāhīka*]. Furthermore, since the suffixes called *sarvanāmasthāna* following the secondary word *go* would lack the marker *ṇit*, in the sentence *gāṃ vāhīkam ānaya* ("Bring the Vāhīka who is like a cow"), the substitution of *ā* (*āttva*) would not apply [by Pāṇini 6.1.93]. [Reply: This is not a fault. First, as for the masculine treatment (*puṃvadbhāva*), it will occur through a division of the rule (*yogavibhāga*) in the sūtra *striyāḥ puṃvat* (Pāṇini 6.3.33).

A separation of the rule (*yogavibhāga*) must necessarily be made for the sake of forms such as *garbhibhārya* ("one whose wife is pregnant") and for forms such as *mahāghāsa* ("great fodder"); when that [separation] is performed for another purpose, it will also serve this purpose. [Objection: But even if the separation of the rule is performed, the substitution of the masculine form (*puṃvadbhāva*) does not apply here, because the sense of "great" (*mahat*) is secondary (*gauṇa*), and because the separation of the rule has its utility elsewhere. [Response: In that case, in the sūtra beginning with *ṅy-āp-prātipadikāt* (Pāṇini 4.1.1), a second separation of the rule, *puṃvat*, is prescribed; that will apply to the secondary sense.
Nor does the fault of the absence of the *vṛddhi* substitute apply here; for from which sentence is that [fault derived]? In that case, a figurative sense (*gauṇatva*) is perceived.
However, the meaning of a word is strictly its primary sense (*mukhya*), and the meaning of the sentence is not taken into account at the time of the grammatical formation (*saṃskāra*) of the word.
This is illustrated by the rule "in the state of being a great vowel" (*mahādāttve*), and so forth.

The rules prescribing the acute accent (*āttva*) and the *puṃvadbhāva* (masculine stem substitution) apply only when there is grammatical coreferentiality (*samānādhikaraṇa*); they do not apply when there is a lack of coreferentiality (*vyadhikaraṇa*).
Therefore, even in the case of a non-coreferential subsequent member (*uttarapada*) such as *ghāsa*, an extension (*upasaṃkhyāna*) must be made for the acute accent of *mahat*.
The term "extension" (*upasaṃkhyāna*) here means "formulation" (*pratipādana*).

In this regard, the following is the demonstration: even in the rule at [Pāṇini 6.3.46], he will perform a *yogavibhāga* (separation of rules) by stating "āt. By means of that, the substitution of *āt* will occur in cases such as *mahāghāsaḥ* ("food for many") and so forth.
Furthermore, that *yogavibhāga* must necessarily be made for the sake of forms such as *aṣṭākapālam*; when it is performed for one purpose, it also serves this present purpose.
This is what is meant by the statement beginning with "and the mention of the masculine form," etc.

The phrase "in the case of words distinguished by *ghāsa* and *karīṣa*" is required [as a condition]. The statement regarding the substitution of the masculine form (*puṃvadbhāva*) must be explained, and that has already been done previously.
[Examples include] "aṣṭanaḥ kapāle" and so forth.
Here too, the meaning of the word "supplementary statement" (*upasaṃkhyāna*) is its demonstration;
and that demonstration has already been made [in the form of the example] "an eight-potsherd offering" (*aṣṭākapālam*).

The compound *aṣṭasu kapāleṣu saṃskṛtam* ("prepared in eight potsherds") is formed by [the rule] *taddhitārtha-* (Pāṇini 2.1.50) and so forth; then the suffix *aṇ* is applied by [the rule] *tadasmin-* (4.2.16), and that suffix is elided by [the rule] *taddhiteṣvacāmādeḥ-* (7.2.117) and *yasyeti ca* (6.4.148). Thus we have *aṣṭakapālaṃ brāhmaṇasya*. "Aṣṭakapālam" is a collective dvigu compound meaning "a collection of eight potsherds."
In this case, because [the word] belongs to the *pātra* group (Pāṇini 4.1.44), the feminine suffix is not applied;
consequently, by [Pāṇini 4.1.21], the suffix *ṅīp* does not occur. [The rule] "and in *go* when joined [with another word]" (*gavi ca yukte*), etc., applies.

And when the word *go* occurs as the final member of a compound (*uttarapada*) and its meaning is understood, the substitution of *āt* for the vowel of the word *aṣṭan* must be prescribed; and that prescription has already been made [by Pāṇini 6.3.129] in the example:
"with a cart drawn by eight oxen" (*aṣṭāgavena śakaṭena*).

The compound *aṣṭāgavaḥ* (meaning "eight oxen are yoked to this") is a three-membered *bahuvrīhi*. The word *yukta* ("yoked") is not explicitly used in the formation of the *dvigu* because its meaning is already implied, just as the word *upasikta* ("sprinkled") is omitted in the expression *dadhyodanaḥ* ("curd-rice"). If this is indeed a *bahuvrīhi*, then the suffix *ṭac*—prescribed by [Pāṇini 5.4.92]—would not apply as a compound-final suffix (*samāsānta*), because that rule falls under the governing heading (*adhikāra*) for *tatpuruṣa* compounds. [Objection: Let it not be so; let there be no *ṭac*. [Response: It will occur nonetheless. By means of a formal split (*yogavibhāga*) in the rule [Pāṇini 5.4.75], *ac pratyanvavapūrvāt*, where the term *ac* is separated [from the rest of the rule], the suffix will apply. This is seen, for example, in *kṛṣṇabhūmaḥ* ("black-soiled land") and *padyanāma* ("having a name ending in -pad"), and so forth.
Alternatively: "aṣṭagava" is a collection of eight cows (*aṣṭānāṃ gavāṃ samāhāraḥ*); that which is joined with eight cows is "aṣṭāgava.

Nor does it follow that the word "yukta" (joined) must be explicitly used, because a single part of a compound may be employed [to represent the whole], just as *Satyabhāmā* is called *Bhāmā*, *Bhimasena* is called *Bhīma*, and *Balabhadra* is called *Bala*.
In the case of "ekādaśa" (eleven) as well, the substitution of *ā* for *e* should be understood to occur by that same rule of separation (*yogavibhāga*).

And the evidence for the analysis of the rule (*yogavibhāga*) is the mention in [Pāṇini 5.3.49]: *prāgekādaśabhyaḥ*. As for the statement, "The inclusion of the marker *t* is for the sake of clarity," one might ask: why is it not intended to exclude those vowels that belong to different time-periods (*bhinnakāla*)? It is because a vowel being taught (*bhāvyamāna*) does not include its homogeneous counterparts (*savarṇa*).

If that is so, why does there not occur the apprehension of [the sounds] as being distinguished by different qualities (*guṇa*)? Because qualities do not serve to differentiate [phonemes]. In this case, there is no application of the rule for the designation of enumerated items (*saṃkhyātānudeśa*).

For if it were so, there would be a prohibition regarding the substitution of *aṣṭan-* [with *aṣṭā-*, etc. before *aśīti-*, and thus that [prohibition] would be rendered purposeless. For when the substitution of *ā* is prohibited, the long vowel resulting from the homogeneity rule (*savarṇadīrgha*) must necessarily take place.

Since the word "aśīti" (eighty) has fewer syllables, it ought to have been placed first according to the rule; however, by its placement as the latter member, which serves as a sign of deviation from the general rule (*lakṣaṇavyabhicāra*), it is indicated that there is no application of the principle of numerical correspondence (*saṃkhyātānudeśa*).
Regarding "dvādaśa" (twelve):
it is a *dvandva* compound consisting of "two" and "ten."

Alternatively, [the compound] "eleven" (*ekādaśa*) is a *tatpuruṣa* compound with elision of the final member, formed according to the rule in the section on compounds with a common referent (*samānādhikaraṇa*): "An addition is made for *śākapārthiva* and similar compounds, and there is elision of the final member" (Vārttika 83). This should be understood to apply similarly to forms such as "twenty-two" (*dvāviṃśati*).
As for "born of two mothers" (*dvaimātura*), [it is likewise explained].

Having analyzed *dvayormātroḥ apatyam* (the offspring of two mothers), there is a compound for the sake of a secondary derivative (*taddhita*) meaning. From that, by the rule *mātur utsaṃkhyāsambhadrapūrvāyāḥ* [Pāṇini 4.1.115], the suffix *aṇ* is applied; furthermore, the letter *u* is the substitute for the final syllable. Regarding *dvitrāḥ*: having analyzed *dvau vā trayo vā* (two or three), there is a *bahuvrīhi* compound by the rule *saṅkhyāvyaya* [Pāṇini 2.2.25] et cetera. By the rule *bahuvrīhau saṃkhyeye* [Pāṇini 5.4.73] et cetera, the suffix *ḍac* is added as a compound-final element (*samāsānta*), and there is the elision of the *ṭi* vowel.
Regarding the term "dvidaśāḥ": as before, it is a *bahuvrīhi* compound with the suffix *ḍac*. Its analytical explanation (*vigraha*) is "twice ten."
This compound is used in its primary sense;
for here, the repetition related to ten, which is indicated by the word "ten," is counted by the word "two. Therefore, the meaning should be understood as "two tens" (twenty).
Since a compound is capable of conveying the meaning of the case-ending (*subartha*), the case-ending is not employed in the formation of the derivative (*vṛtti*).
Thus, "dvyaśītiḥ" (eighty-two):
[this is] either a *dvandva* as before, or a *tatpuruṣa* with elision of the final member (*uttarapadalopin*).
Regarding the phrase "before one hundred" (*prāk śatāt*) and so forth:

the meaning is that this rule must be explained as follows—when a word expressing a number less than one hundred is the subsequent member (*uttarapada*), the substitution of *ā* for the final vowel of *dvi* and *aṣṭan* occurs.

The explanation for this is as follows: the mention of the option (*vibhāṣā*) which will be stated in the rule *vibhāṣā catvāriṃśataḥ* [Pāṇini 6.3.48] applies here as well by the logic of the "lion's glance" (*siṃhāvalokita-nyāya*), and that is a restricted option (*vyavasthita-vibhāṣā*).

Therefore, the rule will apply when the subsequent member (*uttarapada*) expresses a number beginning with "hundred" (*śata*) and so on, but it will not apply when [the subsequent member] itself denotes "hundred" and so forth. In this way, it should be understood that in the two subsequent rules as well, the operation takes place for numbers prior to "hundred. The inclusion of the word "all" (*sarva*) is for the purpose of ensuring that the rule applies even to *dvi* and *aṣṭan*; otherwise, according to the principle "a rule or a prohibition applies only to what immediately precedes" (Vyāḍipāda 19), it would apply only to *tri*.

If it is argued that the rule *dvyaṣṭanaḥ* will also follow here by the logic of the frog’s leap (*maṇḍūkapluti*), and therefore this fault does not arise; [we reply: in that case, the inclusion of the word *sarva-* is for the sake of clarity. [This is a minor point. [Regarding the examples] *hmayyaḥ*:
[it is derived from *hima-*, with the suffix] *-yat* [added] *prāgdhitāt* (Pāṇini 4.4.75).
Regarding "hārdam":
by [Pāṇini 4.3.120], the suffix *aṇ* is applied before *prāgdīvya*.
Regarding "hmallāsaḥ": [the same applies].
*Lāsana* means *lāsa*; the suffix *ghañ* is used in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāva*).
It is a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*) according to the rule: "The sixth case [ending] is compounded when connected with a word ending in a kṛt suffix" (Vārttika 86).
Thus, it refers to the form *lekha*, which ends in the suffix *aṇ*.
And this is understood from the statements of authoritative authorities such as Kātyāyana and others.

Kātyāyana stated: "When a term is mentioned [in a rule], it should be understood as referring to its own form (svarūpa); why? Because of the mention of writing. The author of the Bhāṣya also stated: "In every case where there is a governing rule concerning a subsequent member (uttarapada-adhikāra), when a suffix (pratyaya) is mentioned, it should be understood as referring to its own form; why? Because of the mention of writing."
And how is this pair of statements justified? It is so if there is an inclusion of the word *lekha* ending in the suffix *aṇ*, and not otherwise.
Now, why is the inclusion of the word *lekha* ending in the suffix *ghañ* not understood? To this he says: "But in the case of *ghañ*" and so forth;
"this very [point]" and so forth.

Since the inclusion of that which ends in *aṇ* would already be established by the very mention of *aṇ*, the separate mention of it serves to indicate this: that in a governing rule concerning a subsequent member (*uttarapadādhikāra*), when there is a mention of an affix (*pratyayagrahaṇa*), that which ends in the affix is not included.

Therefore, in this case—both in the mention of *aṇ* and in the mention of affixes such as *gha* in the rule *gharūpādi* (Pāṇini 6.3.42)—only the affix itself is taken, and not the application of the rule regarding what ends in it (*tadantavidhi*). This is the sense. Regarding the word *sauhārdyam*:
it is a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "one whose heart (*hṛdaya*) is beautiful (*śobhana*)."
Then follows the rule for *ṣyañ*:
"By the word *hmadaya*, etc.

Here, when the word *hmacchabda* is synonymous with the word *hmadaya*, if the word *hmacchabda* is employed, the form will be *hmacchoka*; if the word *hmadaya* is employed, it will be *hmadayaśoka*. Therefore, since this is already established by that very alternative base (*prakṛti*), this optional rule (*vikalpa*) need not be formulated.
Why is this done? It is done for the sake of elaboration (*prapañca*); that very established usage is stated by means of this sūtra. Regarding "padājiḥ":
the root *aj* [is used] in the sense of "going" and "throwing" (Dhātupāṭha 230).

Regarding the word *padāti*: from the root *at* meaning "to go continuously" (Dhātupāṭha 38), the Uṇādi suffix *iṇ* is applied according to the rule "after *aj* and *ati*, and with the word *pāda*" (*ajyatibhyāṃ ca pāde ca*). Thus [the form *padāti* is derived].

In this case, because the mention of the root *iṣ* is carried over from the rule *janighasibhyāmiṇ* (Dhātupāṭha 1.58), when the *iṇ* suffix is an *auṇādika* one, why does the substitution of *vī* not occur there by the rule *ajer vy-ghañapoḥ* (Pāṇini 2.4.56)? To this he says: "In that case," etc., ending with "padagaḥ."

Regarding the rule *antātyantādhvadūrapāra* (Pāṇini 3.2.48) and others, it is stated: "It should be stated that the section on the suffix *ḍa* is seen elsewhere as well" (Vārttika 256). By this, the suffix *ḍa* is applied to the root *gam* even when the word *pāda* is the upapada, as in *padopahataḥ*.
The compound [in this rule] is formed according to Pāṇini 2.1.32, whereas in the preceding case it was an upapada-compound.
This substitute ends in the vowel *a*,
and it is taught with the elision (*luk*) of the first case ending.
Regarding the passage beginning with "this word *pāda*" and ending with *[[6.1.159]]*:

when the rule [6.1.168] would result in the final syllable being udātta, the initial udāttatva of the word *pāda* is prescribed because it belongs to the *vṛṣādigaṇa*. Consequently, when the substitute *pada* is prescribed in its place, would it not necessarily be initial-udātta due to *āntaratamya* (phonetic proximity)? Yet, it is desired to be final-udātta. Therefore, it is treated as a nipātana (irregular form) that is final-udātta even at the stage of the original instruction (*upadeśāvasthā*).
By the words "by that" (*tena*) and so forth, he demonstrates the purpose of the prescribed final acute accent (*antodātta-nipātana*).
By the examples "foot-soldier" (*padājiḥ*) and "pedestrian" (*padātiḥ*), he also demonstrates the purpose of including the term "original instruction" (*upadeśagrahaṇa*).

If, after the current accent has been applied by [Pāṇini 6.2.139], the final acute nature of the word *pada* is prescribed as an exception (*nipātyate*), then that [prescribed accent] would be "later-remaining" (*satiśiṣṭa*). Consequently, in the cases of *padājiḥ*, *padātiḥ*, and *padagaḥ*, the accent of the kṛt-affix (*kṛtsvara*) would be superseded, because a later-remaining accent is more powerful.

However, in the stage of the *upadeśa* (the original grammatical instruction), when the rule for the enclitic accent (*antodāttatva-nipātana*) applies, the accent of the whole word (*kṛtsvara*) alone remains as the finally established one.

Therefore, by that [rule], the compound itself becomes oxytone (*antodātta*), and not the individual word *pada*. [The form] *padyāḥ* [is derived] by [the application of] Pāṇini 4.4.83, which prescribes the suffix *yat*.

Regarding "pādyam": from the word *pāda*, when the suffix *yat* is being applied by the rule *tādarthye yat* [Pāṇini 5.4.24], which is still in force, the suffix *yat* is added by the rule *pādārghābhyāñca* [Pāṇini 5.4.25]. Regarding "padbhāve" and so forth...

When the substitution of *pad* is to be applied in the sense of "he moves" (*carati*) after the suffix *asman*, the meaning is that an *upasaṃkhyāna*—that is, a supplementary rule—must be formulated for that substitution of *pad*. In this regard, the formulation is as follows: it is established by means of a split in the *yoga* (i.e., *yogavibhāga*), or alternatively, it is established because the reading "pādaḥ pañc" occurs specifically within the *parpādi* group [of words].
"Of a limb of the body" [the *Kāśikā* reads "of a word denoting a limb of the body"] and so forth.
But how is this obtained? Some say: by implication (*sāmarthyāt*), the word *pāda-* is understood in the preceding sūtra to mean a "limb of the body.
Among those [compounds], the three beginning with *ājya-* have the sense of "going," while the fourth has the sense of "striking."
In those [rules] beginning with *gamanādi*, the status of being an instrument (*karaṇabhāva*) is possible only for the word *pāda* when it denotes a limb of a living being, and not for anything else.

Therefore, in that context, the word *pāda* is understood as denoting a limb of a living being; and here too, it is logical that the same [meaning] continues—that is, the word is taken to denote a part of the body.

If this is so, then would there also be a reference to a part of the body in the rule *ṛcaḥ śeṣe* [Pāṇini 6.3.55]? This is not a fault, because it is impossible for a word denoting a part of the body to be connected with a *ṛc*.
The word *pāda* will be understood here as denoting a "fourth part.

Regarding the phrase "by that" (*tena*) and so forth: since the word *pāda* is taken here in the sense of a limb of the body, therefore, in a rule such as *paṇapādamāṣa* (Pāṇini 5.1.34), the word *pāda* does not undergo the substitution of *pad*; for that [word in the rule] does not denote a limb of the body, but rather denotes a measure (*parimāṇa*).

Whence is this [known]? From the association with words denoting measure such as *paṇa* and others, as in "worth two *pādas*, worth three *pādas*" (*dvipādyam*, *tripādyam*), where the suffix *yat* is applied in the sense prescribed by [Pāṇini 5.1.37]. [And] "worth a *padī*. (*paddhimam*)
This is a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*).
In the word *patkāṣiṇaḥ*,
the suffix *ṇini* is applied according to [Pāṇini 3.2.78], forming an *upapada* compound.
Regarding the term *paddhati*:
it is called *paddhati* because it is struck (*hanyate*) by the two feet (*pādābhyām*).

This is a compound formed with the word *hati*, which ends in the suffix *ktin*, according to [Pāṇini 2.1.32]. Regarding the term *śe*: here, there is the inclusion of the sound *śa* which constitutes a portion of the *śas* suffix belonging to the secondary derivative (*taddhita*); this is because a foot of a verse (*ṛkpāda*) cannot possibly follow [the word *paddhati*].

But surely, in the case of *pāde śete* ("he lies on his foot"), when the suffix *ac* is applied by [Pāṇini 3.2.15] *adhikaraṇe śeteḥ*, the form *pādaśaḥ* is possible, since the sound *śa-* is connected with the root *śī-*? This is not so; for the suffix *ac* cannot occur when *ṛkpāda-* is the governing word (*upapada*), because lying down is impossible there, or because of non-usage (*anabhidhāna*). Even the suffix *śa-* that is prescribed [by Pāṇini 5.2.100] *yaḥ* is not at all possible after *ṛkpāda-*, because of non-usage in that context.

And because it is not recited among *loman* and the others. A genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*) is formed with the two words *ghoṣa-śabda* and *śabda-śabda*; and with the word *miśra*, a third-case compound (*tṛtīyāsamāsa*) is formed by [Pāṇini 2.1.31] and following rules.

Regarding the statement "it should be stated that [the substitution applies] when *niṣka* follows," the meaning is that this should be explained as having the sense that when the word *niṣka* is the subsequent member (*uttarapada*), the word *pāda* undergoes the substitution of *pad*.
In this regard, the explanation is as follows: the particle *ca* is carried over from [Pāṇini 6.3.54], and it serves the purpose of including what has not been explicitly mentioned.

Alternatively, a *yogavibhāga* (separation of rules) is made in the sūtra by means of the word *vā*; by this, the rule will also apply when *niṣka* is the subsequent member of the compound. Thus: "He whose son is named Udameghi is called Udamegha. Since the father is not well-known, the phrase "he whose son is Udameghi" is stated in order to identify Udamegha by means of his offspring.
By this, he shows that one whose offspring is Audameghi should be understood as Udamegha himself.
Likewise, in the case of "he whose son is named Audavāhi is Udavāha," it should be understood in the same way.

*Udamegha* is a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*). Alternatively, it is a middle-term-elided *tatpuruṣa* belonging to the class beginning with *śākapārthiva* (Pāṇini 2.1.69), meaning "a cloud full of water. *Udavāha* means "one who carries water" (*udakaṃ vahati*). [3.2.1]
"Vaktavyaḥ" means "to be explained.

Regarding this, the explanation is as follows: here too, that same particle *ca* (and) is understood by way of recurrence (*anuvartate*), serving to include what has not been explicitly stated; and there is nothing else to be included.
In this context, the word "water" (udaka) includes the very absence of water when it functions as a technical name (saṃjñā).
Of what does it include [the absence]? Of that for which [the designation] would otherwise not apply.
For what would it not apply? For that which has become a final member of a compound (uttarapada).

Therefore, in a compound name (*saṃjñā*), this substitution of *uda* for the word *udaka* occurs even when it is the final member [of the compound]. Examples are *lohitodaḥ* ("Red-water") and *kṣīrodaḥ* ("Milk-water"), which are *bahuvrīhi* compounds. If the word *eka* were understood here as signifying "alone" (*mukhya*), then its inclusion would be purposeless; for never do two or more consonants occur at the beginning [of a word], such that the mention of *eka* would be made for the sake of excluding them.

Therefore, this word *eka* signifies "without a companion" (*asahāya*). Even so, if one were to take as the basis any undistinguished single consonant (*hal*) that is without a companion—such that the subsequent member of the compound begins with it—then the term *ekahalādy-uttarapada* would apply even to the word *udakasthāna*.
For here too, the letter *s* is indeed a single consonant (*ekahal*) without a companion.

If multiple phonemes were pronounced simultaneously, or if pronounced phonemes did not perish, then even that which has an accompaniment might possess the status of being "initial. But this is not the case; for phonemes are not pronounced simultaneously, and they perish as soon as they are pronounced. Therefore, there is nowhere at all any such thing as having multiple consonants as its beginning, for the purpose of excluding which it is stated [in the rule] "when preceded by a single consonant" (*ekahal-ādi*).
And this has been stated:

"Is it not the case that, by this very statement, it is intended that [the term] refers specifically to those beginning with a single consonant? Having taken all of this into account, he says—beginning with "a single [consonant] without a companion"—in order to demonstrate that very specific [category]:
"that which is preceded by a single consonant" (*ekahalādi*) means that of which a single consonant (*hal*), even if it is of a different class (*atulyajātīya*), is the initial element.

If that which depends upon a single consonant (*ekahal*) were to depend on one of its own kind even when it is not immediately contiguous, then [the rule] would never apply; for there exists no such subsequent member (*uttarapada*) that expresses something requiring completion, yet this [rule] is stated. Therefore, by the authority of the statement, it is understood that here the word *eka*—which denotes "without assistance"—intends that which exists without an immediately contiguous consonant of the same class (*tulyajātīya*).
That which has such a consonant as its initial is called *ekahalādi*.
And the word *sthāna* [in the rule] is not excluded by the mention of "beginning with a single consonant" (*ekahalādi*) in the rule *halas ti* (Pāṇini 6.4.129), which applies to such a word.
Regarding the phrase "that which is to be filled": that which is to be completely pervaded by a substance such as water is called "to be filled" (*pūrayitavya*).
The suffix *ṇini* is used here in its *tācchīlika* (denoting habitual action) sense, as the meaning is "one whose habit is to speak that. Barley-meal mixed with liquid substances is called *mantha*.

In this context, if the word *mantha* is an unanalyzed (*avyutpanna*) nominal stem (*prātipadika*), then the compound "water-mixture" (*udakamantha*) is formed by the rule of splitting the sūtra "the third case" (*tṛtīyā*, Pāṇini 2.1.30).
Alternatively, if it is analyzed—meaning "that which is stirred" (*mathyate*) is *mantha*—then the compound is formed by the rule "with a word ending in the seventh case" (*saptamī*, Pāṇini 2.1.40).

The compound [in *sakatvodanābhyām*] is formed by [Pāṇini 2.1.34]. [In *binduvajravīvadhaiḥ*], [the term *bhārahāra*] is formed by [Pāṇini 2.2.8, *ṣaṣṭhī*], and [the term *gāha*] is formed by [Pāṇini 2.2.19, *gāhaprakṛtīnām anantatvam*]. Regarding *grāmaṇiputraḥ*:
[the word *grāmaṇi*] is derived from the root *nī* (to lead) with the suffix *kvip* by [Pāṇini 3.2.61, *satsūdviṣadruhaduhayujavidabhidacchidajinīrājām upasaṃkhyānam*].
The substitution of *ṇ* [for *n*] occurs by the rule *agragrāmābhyāñca nayateḥ* (Kātyāyana-Vārttika 5064).
Thus we have *gārgīputraḥ*.

From the word *gārgya*, the suffix *ṅīp* is applied by the rule *yañaśca* (Pāṇini 4.1.16), followed by the elision of the vowel *a* by *yaṅo 'ci ca* (Pāṇini 6.4.148) and the elision of the letter *y* by *halastaddhitasya* (Pāṇini 6.4.150).

Now, why is the mention of Gālava not intended solely for the sake of the alternative option (*dikalpārtha*)? To this he says: "In the case of *anyatarasyām*," and so forth. Regarding the example *kārīṣagandhīputraḥ*:

it is a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*) meaning "the son of Karīṣagandhyā. There is vocalization (*samprasāraṇa*) by the rule beginning with "vocalization of *ṣyaṅ*" [Pāṇini 6.1.13], followed by the substitution of the preceding vowel [Pāṇini 6.1.108], and the lengthening of the vocalized vowel by the rule "after a consonant" [Pāṇini 6.4.2].
Regarding the phrase "of those that undergo *iyaṅ* and *uvaṅ*" and so forth:
those for whom *iyaṅ* and *uvaṅ* are to occur are described as such.
An example is "śrīkulam."
The example for that which undergoes the substitution of *iyaṅ* is "bhrūkulam";
likewise for that which undergoes the substitution of *uvaṅ*.

"Kaṇḍībhūtam, vṛṣalībhūtam"— these are examples of *avapyaya* (the state of becoming what one was not). The suffix *cvi* is applied to the words *kāṇḍa* and *vṛṣala* by the rule *abhūtatadbhāve* [Pāṇini 5.4.50], and the substitution of *i* for the final vowel occurs by the rule *cver dīrghāt* [Pāṇini 7.4.32].
Regarding the term *bhrūkuṃsaḥ*:
it is a descriptive compound (*viśeṣaṇasamāsa*) consisting of *bhrū* (eyebrow) and *kuṃsa* (a deceptive person).
The same applies to the term *bhrukuṭiḥ*.

"It should be stated" means it should be explained. In this regard, the explanation is as follows: by virtue of belonging to the *pṛṣodarādi* group, the vowel 'a' will occur in words such as *bhrukuṃsa*. "Uniformity" (*ekarūpyam*).
The suffix *rūpya* is applied by the rule *hetumanuṣyebhyo 'nyatarasyāṃ rūpyaḥ* [Pāṇini 4.3.81].
Regarding the form *ekamaya*,
the suffix *mayaṭ* is applied by the rule *mayaṭ ca* [Pāṇini 4.3.82].
Regarding "ekatvam, ekatā":
by the rule *Pāṇini 5.1.119*, the suffixes *tva* and *tal* are applied.
This is the example when the word *eka* refers to a number (*saṃkhyā*).

When it is the latter *saṃkhyeya* [in the sense of "one who possesses a number"], then it is already established by the rule *tva-talorguṇavacanasya* (Vārttika 730) through the application of the masculine form (*puṃvadbhāva*).

But has it not been said that it expresses a quality (*guṇa*)? It is called *guṇavacana* because it denotes a quality; and that which, having denoted a mere quality, expresses a substance qualified by that quality, is what is termed *guṇavacana*.

For example, one says "a black cloth" or "a white cloth. However, this word *eka* (one) never denotes a quality (*guṇa*) distinct from a substance (*dravya*), because it always refers to a substance that is the object of enumeration (*saṃkhyeya*). [Objection: If that is so, how can there be this substitution of the masculine form (*puṃvadbhāva*)? [Response: This which is stated is incorrect. For, while it is said that words such as *eka* denote the object of enumeration by relying on conventional usage (*prasiddhi*), it is not accepted that their application lies in the act of counting (*saṃkhyāna*) itself. Indeed, in the rule [Pāṇini 1.4.22], the word *eka* is employed in the sense of number (*saṃkhyā*) alone, not in the sense of a substance that is the object of enumeration.

Regarding the phrase "of that which is qualified by gender" (*liṅgaviśiṣṭasya*), etc.: since the masculine form of the word *eka* is inherently short-voweled at its end, its mention does not serve as a purpose [for the rule]; rather, it applies only to that which is qualified by the feminine gender.
For it is only for that [feminine form] that the prescription of shortness becomes meaningful.

[Objection: But surely, even for this word *eka*, the prescription of shortness for its vowel *e* is meaningful; so why is it said that "the inclusion of the word *eka* qualified by gender" is the purpose? To this, he says: "When [a term] is apprehended as a vowel," and so forth.
There is freedom of choice regarding the relationship between qualifier and qualified. As it has been stated: "Because the relationship between qualifier and qualified is according to one's wish."

In that case, if the vowel (*aj*) were qualified by the word *eka* being mentioned—meaning "that which is the *aj* of the word *eka*"—then the prescription of shortness for the vowel *e*, as a constituent of the word *eka*, would be meaningful.

Furthermore, this would necessitate the inclusion of the masculine form of the word *eka*. However, in this context, the vowel is not qualified by the word *eka* being mentioned; for the shortness of the vowel *e* is not desired here.

A grammatical formulation in a treatise that does not serve a desired purpose is not logical (Bhāṣya on Pāṇini Sūtra 1.1.56). Therefore, in this context, the word *eka* is qualified by the vowel (*āc*).
By that [qualification], there is the inclusion of the form [ending] in a gender-marker (*liṅga*).
