The short vowel (*hrasva*) applies to the word *eka*; and what is qualified by the vowel? The meaning is: "that which ends in a vowel" (*ajanta*).

In that case, the shortening must apply only to the final vowel, and that [shortening] is meaningful only for a word ending in *ṭāp*, not for a masculine form; for when shortening is prescribed for what is already short, no purpose whatsoever is achieved. The particle *iti* indicates the reason (*hetau*).

Precisely because the single word *eka* is qualified here by the mention of *āc* (vowels), this necessitates the inclusion of the word *eka* as qualified by gender (*liṅgaviśiṣṭasya*). In the example "the son of Revatī" (*revatiputraḥ*), it is a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsaḥ*).
The same applies in cases such as "son of Rohiṇī" (rohiṇiputra).
One who gives a maiden is a "giver of a maiden" (kumāridā);
one who gives the earth is an "earth-giver" (urvidā).
"Phālgunī," and so forth.

"Phālgunī" is both *phālgunī* and *paurṇamāsī*, thus forming the compound *phālgunī-paurṇamāsī* according to the rule beginning with *viśeṣaṇam* [Pāṇini 2.1.57]. The same applies to the expression *jagatīcchandaḥ*. Furthermore, there are examples such as *śilavaham* and *śilaprastham*.

In the cases of *śilāvaham* and *prasthaśabdābhyām*, the compound is formed by [Pāṇini 2.2.8] *ṣaṣṭhī* ("the sixth [case]"). In *lomakāgṛham* and *lomakāṣaṇḍam*, the compound is likewise formed here by the word *lomakā* with the words *gṛha* and *ṣaṇḍa*.
Regarding the phrase "with goat's milk" (*ajakṣīreṇa*),
here too there is a [compounding] of the word *ajā* with the word *kṣīra*.
[In the case of] *ūrṇamṛt* (or *ūrṇamṛdā*, as in the Kāśikā).
"Ūrṇāmṛdvā-pada-mañjarī. Here, "ūrṇāmṛt" means wool-soft (*ūrṇā-sahitā mṛd*).

This is a compound with elision of the second member (*uttarapadalopa*), belonging to the *śākapārthiva* class. It is said that "because [the literal sense] is impossible as a proper name (*saṃjñā*), these examples exist only for the sake of the Vedic language (*chandaḥ*)."

By the word *eva* (only), the exclusion of "name" (*saṃjñā*) is effected. For when the suffix *tva* is applied, and the feminine marker (*ṅī*), long vowel (*ā*), and *hrasva* (shortening) have been performed, no name is understood for anything. Therefore, because it is impossible [for the rule] to apply to a name, the examples are only of words; as in "built with bricks" (*iṣṭakacitam*).
The compound [in *iṣīkatūla*] is formed by [the rule] *kartṛkaraṇe* (Pāṇini 2.1.31) and so forth.
The term *iṣīkatūlam* is a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*).

Regarding the term *mālabhāriṇī*: the suffix *ṇini* is applied in the sense of habitual action according to Pāṇini 3.2.78, resulting in the compound [mālā-bhārin] by Pāṇini 2.2.19. It is stated that "there is also the inclusion of that which ends in such a suffix, as in the case of *iṣṭakā* and others."
The intention is that this is because the term *bahulam* (optionally) is understood to carry over [from the previous rule]. Regarding the examples *kālīmanyā* and *hariṇīmanyā*:

from the analysis *kālīm ātmānaṃ manyate* and *hariṇīm ātmānaṃ manyate*, the suffix *khaś* is applied by [Pāṇini 3.2.83], followed by *śyan* due to the root belonging to the *divādi* class; by this [present rule], there is shortening (*hrasvatva*), and by the subsequent sūtra, the augment *mum* is added.
In this case, the shortening of the vowel ending in *ā* must be accepted; otherwise, it would also apply in the case of *vāṅmanya*.

To one who might think that when the rule for shortening applies to a stem ending in *a*, the suffix *mum*—being applied later—would cause the stem to no longer end in *a*, thereby making the shortening inapplicable, the author says: "The shortening is not barred by *mum*.
He states the reason for this very point in the passage beginning with "Otherwise, indeed," and so forth.
That by which the short vowel is taught—that is, prescribed—is the rule for shortening, namely the statement: "In the case of a word ending in *khit*, provided it is not a part of a compound."

For if the *mum* were to sublate the short vowel, then this rule prescribing the short vowel would become devoid of scope (*anavakāśa*), and consequently, it would be rendered entirely purposeless. Therefore, so that this fault does not occur, the short vowel is not sublated by the *mum*. Thus, due to the absence of conflict, both occur: the short vowel and the *mum*.

But how is the sublation (*bādhā*) of *mum* by the short vowel (*hrasva*) suspected? Or how is the short-vowel rule (*hrasva-śāsana*) considered to have no scope (*anavakāśatva*), given that *mum* is prescribed without distinction for any *aj*-ending stem before a *khit* suffix? How is the sublation of *mum* suspected? Or how is the short-vowel rule considered to have no scope, since *mum* is indeed prescribed without distinction for any *aj*-ending stem before a *khit* suffix?

But how is it that the sublation (*bādhā*) of *mum* by the short vowel (*hrasva*) is suspected? Or how is the short-vowel rule (*hrasva-śāsana*) considered to have no scope (*anavakāśatva*), given that *mum* is prescribed without distinction for any *khit* suffix ending in a vowel? Furthermore, the shortening occurs by implication (*sāmarthyāt*) for a long vowel, for the prescription of shortness for what is already short is not purposeful. Thus, since *mum* has already served its purpose in cases such as *stanandhaya*, would it not be sublated by the short vowel as an exception (*apavāda*) in cases such as *kālimmanyā*? The [author] thinks thus: [The short vowel is taught] so that *mum* may be prescribed even within the domain of the exception.

The substitution of *mum* must necessarily be applied; otherwise, how could there not be the form *kālimmanyā*? Furthermore, if *mum* were to apply even in cases where an exception (*apavāda*) is intended, it would be possible for that exception to be sublated.
And it is precisely for this reason that *mum* applies even in the domain of exceptions, because it possesses no other scope [of application].

Now, how is there a mention here of that which ends in *khi*, given that it has been established [in the Paribhāṣā]—"In the governing context of a subsequent member (*uttarapada*), when a suffix (*pratyaya*) is mentioned, there is no inclusion of that which ends in it" (PuPaPā 26)? To this he says: "The very phrase 'of that which is not an indeclinable' (*anavyayasya*)," and so forth.

If only the suffix *khi* were taken here and not that which ends in it, then the prohibition "of that which is not an indeclinable" would be purposeless. For a suffix ending in *khi* cannot occur after an indeclinable; since its prescription is only after a verbal root (*dhātu*).

Consequently, because it would otherwise be meaningless, the phrase "of that which is not an indeclinable" (*anavyayasya*) would not have been stated. And it has been said: "Therefore, this very [statement] indicates that here there is the inclusion of a form ending in *khid*. Regarding the word *aruntudaḥ*: from the sense "one who pierces the vital parts" (*aruṃ tudati*), the suffix *khaś* is applied by the rule *viṣvaruṣostudaḥ* (Pāṇini 3.2.35). There is the elision of the final consonant of the conjunct (*saṃyogāntalopaḥ*). Because it belongs to the *tud*-class, the suffix *śa* is applied; then, by the rule *ato guṇe* (Pāṇini 6.1.97), the subsequent form (*pararūpatva*) is substituted.
Regarding "dviṣantapaḥ":
[the suffix] *khac* is applied according to Pāṇini 3.2.39 (*dviṣat-tapobhaye*), and shortening occurs according to 6.4.94 (*khaci hrasvaḥ*).
Regarding "vidvanmanyaḥ": [the suffix *khaś* is applied].

Regarding the form *vidvāṃsam*, [the suffix] *khaś* is applied by the rule *vidvāṃsamātmānaṃ manyata iti* (Pāṇini 3.2.83). Then, by the rule *vasuruāṃsudhvaṃsvanaḍuhāṃ daḥ* (Pāṇini 8.2.72), the letter *s* is replaced by *d*, and by the rule *naśca* (Pāṇini 8.4.45), that *d* is replaced by *n*.

Now, for what purpose is the inclusion of the word "end" (*anta*)? Since the rule *yena vidhistadantasya* (Pāṇini 1.1.72) would ensure that the operation applies only to that which ends in [the specified element], he says: "The inclusion of the word 'end'... and so forth.

The term *kṛtājantakārya* means one for whom the operation pertaining to that which ends in a vowel (*ajanta*) has been performed; the mention of the word *anta* (end) is for the purpose that such a person should have this understanding (*pratīti*).

For by the mention of *anta*, the meaning is indicated that the suffix *mum* is to be applied at the end, that is, at the conclusion of another grammatical operation. Therefore, once the vowel-ending operation—namely, the substitution of *as*—has been performed, the suffix *mum* subsequently occurs.

[Objection: But surely this point has already been established with its supporting reasoning by the statement, "the *mum* [augment] does not subvert the rule for shortening (*hrasva*)," so what is the purpose of including the mention of "ending" (*anta*) here? [Response: This is not so. For by that [previous rule], it was merely established that the rule for shortening is not subverted by the *mum* augment because the former is without scope (*niravakāśa*); however, the meaning that "the *mum* occurs after a word ending in a *kṛt* suffix" was not established. Consequently, once the *mum* is applied, the shortening would undesirably apply even to a word that no longer ends in a vowel (*anajanta*).
What is the fault in this? It is that there would be no occurrence of the shortening of a word ending in a *kṛt* suffix followed by a *khid* suffix.
Just as in the case of *kālimmanya*, where once the suffix *mu* has been applied, shortening occurs even though the stem does not end in *an*, so too would it occur in the case of *vāṅmanya*.

Therefore, the mention of the word "end" (*anta*) must be made. In this context, if only the rule "and like a suffix" (*pratyayavat ca*) were stated, then in *gāmmanya*, the substitution of *ā* (by P. 6.1.93) would not occur; and here in *strīmmanya*, the homogeneous preceding vowel (by P. 6.1.107) would not occur; and here in *narammanya*, the guṇa substitution for the word *nṛ* (by P. 7.3.110) would not occur.

In the case of an extension of a general rule (*sāmānyātideśa*), because a specific rule (*viśeṣa*) is not extended, this statement would apply solely for the sake of *iyaṅ* and *uvaṅ*. This is because *iyaṅ* and *uvaṅ* are prescribed after a suffix beginning with a vowel (*ajādau pratyaye*) by virtue of the general category of "suffix" alone; thus, they occur even when there is an extension of a general rule. When it is stated "and like the *am*-suffix," the *āttva* (substitution of *ā*) and other such operations take place, since the *am*-suffix is also intended for them. Having taken all of this into account, he says: "and like the *am*-suffix."

He explains this very point with the words: "and like the second singular. But how is this meaning obtained, given that there is only one mention of *am*, and by that the augment (*āgama*) is indicated; thus, [the rule] "like a suffix" (*pratyayavat*) would become unintended? Or, if the suffix were qualified by that [mention], the augment would not be indicated. Therefore, he says: "For *am*... and so forth.
The intention is that since the single mention of *apaya* being undertaken accomplishes both of these, this meaning is thereby obtained.
[Examples are] *śriyammanyaḥ* and *bhrūvammanyaḥ*;
here, the suffixes *yaṅ* and *vaṅ* are applied by the rule *aci śnudhātu* [Pāṇini 6.4.77].
Regarding the expression "lekhābhrūmmanyaḥ": the augment *mum* is applied by the preceding rule. Now, concerning the passage beginning with "atheha" and so forth:

Having begun by stating, "one considers oneself to be *śrī* (fortune) or a member of the Brāhmaṇa caste," and having introduced the subject, when the suffix *khaś* is applied, how should the form be? Should it be *śriyammanyamati*, or rather *śrimanyam*? How is it that these two alternatives are even conceivable, such that he asks this question? It is because we observe that words function in two ways.

For instance—of some words, application to another object is observed even without abandoning their own gender, as in the case of the word *bhūta* in the expression *bhūtam iyaṃ brāhmaṇī*; of others, that [application] is observed even with the abandonment of their own gender, as in the case of the word *praṣṭha* in the form *praṣṭhī*.

In this regard, when the word *śrī* exists in a Brāhmaṇa family and does not abandon its own gender, it should then be *śriyammanya*; however, if it abandons its own gender and takes on the neuter gender, then, after the elision of the suffix *am* by the rule *svamornapuṃsakāt* [Pāṇini 7.1.23] and the shortening of the vowel by the rule *hrasvo napuṃsake prātipadikasya* [Pāṇini 1.2.47], it should become *śrimanya*. Thus, both of these two alternatives are possible.
Therefore, since both alternatives are possible, it is not known how it ought to be; hence, the question is raised for the sake of determining that.

[The *Bhāṣya* establishes: "It must be *śrimanyam*. [The *Kāśikā* reads: "it is established" (*sthitam*). Now, one might object: this word *śrī* is feminine, and even when occurring in other meanings, it functions without abandoning its own gender; likewise, usage is observed such as "May *śrī* be my head," and "May *śrī* be my fame. So then, why is it established in the *Bhāṣya* as *śrimanyam*? To this he says: "In that case," and so forth.

Just as words such as *praṣṭha* and others, when applied to a woman due to her connection with a man, function retaining their own original gender—as in *praṣṭhī*, *pravarī*, and *gaṇakī*—so too, according to the opinion of the author of the Bhāṣya, the word *śrī* here functions while referring to a family (*kula*).
Therefore, according to that view, once the suffix *am* has been elided by the rule *svamornapuṃsakāt* [Pāṇini 7.1.23], the form is *śrimanyam*.

But surely, this [rule] is not commenced when the elision (*luk*) has already applied, just as it subverts the elision prescribed by *Pāṇini 2.4.71*, so too would it subvert the elision prescribed by *Pāṇini 7.1.23* (*svamornapuṃsakāt*)? Furthermore, since the elision (*luk*) depends on a single word, it is "internal" (*antaranga*), whereas the augment *am* is "external" (*bahiranga*) because it is the opposite; therefore, according to the principle that "the external is not established when the internal is to be applied" (*Vyāḍiparibhāṣā* 42), the external augment *am* does not exist at all when the internal elision is to take effect—so how could there be an elision here? This is not a fault.

"Exceptions in the middle sublate preceding rules, not subsequent ones" (Vyāḍiparibhāṣā 10). Thus, this augment [ṇiC] will sublate the elision (*luk*) prescribed by "of the neuter, *kha* and *su*" (Pāṇini 7.1.23), but not the one prescribed by "after *am*, [the case-ending]" (Pāṇini 2.4.71).
Furthermore, the paribhāṣā regarding external elements (*bahiraṅga-paribhāṣā*) cannot be invoked here, for a fault would arise in this case: namely, in the word *aruntuda*.
If, however, one were to resort to that [the *mum* augment], the elision of the final consonant cluster (*saṃyogāntalopa*) would not occur;

for when the internal operation (*antaraṅga*) of the elision of the final consonant cluster is to be performed, the external *mum* augment is considered non-existent (*asiddha*), and thus the status of being a "final consonant cluster" (*saṃyogāntatā*) cannot be established.
Therefore, although its cause is present, this [rule] is not resorted to here.
For its defects are indeed of this nature. Regarding the term "vācaṃyamaḥ":

it means "one who restrains speech" (*vācaṃ yacchati*). By the rule *vaci-yamo vrate* [Pāṇini 3.2.40], the suffix *khac* is applied. In that case, the word *vāk* is irregularly derived with the suffix *ām*.
Regarding the word *purandara*:
by the rule *pūḥsaravayordārisahoḥ* [Pāṇini 3.2.41], the suffix *khac* is applied; by the rule *khaci hrasvaḥ* [Pāṇini 6.4.94], shortening occurs.
Here too, the fact that the word *pūḥ* ends in the suffix *am* is treated as an irregularity (*nipātana*).
The letter *ca* has the sense of including what has not been explicitly mentioned (*anuktasamuccayārtha*).
By this, the entire rule *astusatyāgada-saya kāre* (Vārttika 744) need not be stated. By the expression *satyaṃ karoti*, he indicates the suffix *aṇ* [by Pāṇini 3.2.1] when there is an object;
by the expression *satyasya kāraḥ*, he also indicates the suffix *ghañ* [by Pāṇini 3.3.18].
In the same way, in the case of *agadaṅkāraḥ*, the suffixes *aṇ* and *ghañ* should also be understood; thus,
*astuṅkāraḥ* [is formed],
where *ghañ* denotes the abstract state (*bhāve*).
The word *astu* is an indeclinable particle (*nipāta*) resembling a case ending; it occurs in the sense of acceptance (*abhyupagama*).
The expression "the making of *astu*" refers to the act of expressing acceptance.
[Similarly,] there is the expression "the making of *bhakṣam*."
The suffix *ghañ* is used in the sense of the action (*bhāve*).
In the expression "dhenurbhavyā" (a cow that is to be),
the *kṛtya* suffix is used in the sense of the agent (*kartari*) according to the rule beginning with "bhavyageya" (Pāṇini 3.4.68).
"Dhenubhavyā" means she who is both a cow (*dhenu*) and auspicious (*bhavyā*).
Regarding the term "lokampṛṇaḥ":

from the root *pṛṇ* meaning "to satisfy" (Dhātupāṭha 1329), the word "lokampṛṇa" is formed by adding the suffix *ka* according to the rule for the class beginning with *mūlavibhuja*. Thus, it means "one who fills the world."
Regarding the term *anabhyāśamityaḥ* [the printed reading is *anamyāśamityam*]:
it means that which is to be reached (*ityam*) from afar (*anabhyāśam*), that is, it is to be gone to; thus it is *anabhyāśamityaḥ*.
*Indhana* is *indh*, with the suffix *ghañ* in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāve*).
"Indra is the kindler of the frying pan;
the kindler of fire is the kindler of Agni.
[And] "Timiṅgila."

The root *gṛ* is used in the sense of "swallowing" (*nigaraṇe*; Dhātupāṭha 1410). [The word] *timiṅgila* means "one who swallows a *timi*," as explained previously. Why [is it formed thus]? Because of the substitution of *i* for the *ṛ* of a root according to Pāṇini 7.1.100 (*ṛta iddhātoḥ*), the substitution of *ra* [for the *ṛ*] by Pāṇini 6.4.77 (*uraṇ raparaḥ*), and the substitution of *la* [for *ra*] by Pāṇini 8.2.21 (*aḍvyavāye 'pi*); thus, we have *giligila*.
"He swallows what is swallowed," as before; [the suffix] *ka*, and the shortening of the vowel (*ittva*) and so forth. Regarding the rule "and in *gilagila*":
he swallows what is swallowed, thus he is a *gilagila*.
Because of the particle *ca* in this rule [Pāṇini 3.3.106], which serves to include what has not been explicitly mentioned, who [is the agent]?
Even in the previous case where *ka* was prescribed, there is no fault.
This must be stated when the intended meaning is "a *gilagila* of fish" (one that swallows fish).

Now, "timiṅgila" means that which swallows a *timi* (whale); when the sense of "swallowing a *timiṅgala*" is intended to be expressed, it is already established by the preceding rule, so this [present] rule is unnecessary.
As for "uṣṭraṅkaraṇam" and "bhadraṅkaraṇam," these are genitive compounds (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*).
Regarding the term "putraṭ":
the letter *ṭ* is for the purpose of [introducing] the feminine suffix *ṅīp*.
However, some read the word "putra" in the list beginning with Śāṅrgarava.
This supplementary rule (*upasaṅkhyāna*) need not be made regarding them, [based on the principle] that "it is seen elsewhere as well.
By this, he confirms the inclusion of the word *putra* among the *śārṅgarava*-class [of stems]. [The phrase] "when the suffix *ñya* follows" [is used].
From which subsequent word does the suffix *ña* [occur]? That is what was stated. Regarding the example "śyainampātā":
falling is *pātaḥ*, with the suffix *ghañ* in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāve*); thus, the flight of a hawk is *śyenapātaḥ*.

The compound is formed by the rule *kṛdyogā ca ṣaṣṭhī samasyate* (Vārttika 86), which states that the genitive case ending used in connection with a *kṛt*-derived word may be compounded. [Pāṇini 2.2.58] states: "When a *kṛdanta* word follows as the second member... But how is the inclusion of the suffix itself (*tadantavidhi*) obtained here, given that it has been established: "In the governing context of the second member (*uttarapada*), when a suffix is mentioned, there is no inclusion of what ends with that suffix" (Puṣpabhūti-pāda 26)? This is because a *kṛt* suffix cannot possibly follow immediately after the word *rātri*. If you argue that the inclusion of the suffix is not understood here, that is incorrect; for it is indeed possible for a *kṛt* suffix to follow immediately after *rātri*.

In the expression *rātrir ivācarati* ("he acts like night"), the suffix *kvip* is applied by the rule *acāre sarvaprātipadikebhyaḥ kviv vā* (Vārttika 187). Then, by the rule *dhātusajñā* (Pāṇini 3.1.32), it receives the designation of "root" (*dhātu*). From this root, the suffix *tṛc* is added, followed by the augment *iṭ*, and the substitution of *guṇa* and *āy*. Thus, we obtain the form *rātrayitṛ*. Now, if this is the case, would the operation apply only when the *kṛt* suffix follows immediately [after the first member], and not when it occurs at the end of that member? This is not a fault; for the term *anta* ("end") is understood to carry over from the rule *ṣyaṣṭhan* (Pāṇini 6.3.67). Therefore, it is understood that the grammatical operation applies specifically when [the word] ends in that [suffix]. If this is so, then even for the word *rātri* ending in *kvip*—which is itself a *kṛdanta*—the operation would apply when it is the prior member of a compound with a subsequent *kṛdanta* word.
Let it be so.
But if it is not accepted, then the rule of restricted option (*vyavasthitavibhāṣā*) must be admitted.
Or else, because the word "night" (*rātri*) is used in a figurative sense (*gauṇatva*), the [suffix] will not apply.
Furthermore, its secondary nature (*gauṇatva*) arises because it has deviated from its primary meaning, as in the case of the word *go* in the expression "the Vāhīka is an ox.
[In the word] *rātriñcaraḥ*:
[it is derived] from *rātrau carati* by [Pāṇini 3.2.16], with the suffix *ṭa*, forming an *upapada* compound.
Regarding the term *rātrimaṭaḥ*:

it is called *aṭaḥ* because he wanders (*aṭati*), formed with the suffix *ac* according to Pāṇini 3.1.134. The compound *rātryaṭaḥ* (or as printed in some editions, *rātrāvaṭaḥ*) is a compound formed by the rule of *yogavibhāga* ("separation of rules") from Pāṇini 2.1.40, which states that a word ending in the locative case may be compounded with another word.
Regarding the phrase "this option applies where [the suffix] *khit* is both applicable and inapplicable":

one might object—surely there is also a case with *khit*, namely *rātrimmanyam*, for here [the suffix *mum*] necessarily applies by [Pāṇini 6.3.67]; yet in cases such as *rātriñcaraḥ*, it does not apply at all. Thus, since this option is appropriate when [the suffix] is both applicable and inapplicable, he says: "For when *khit* follows, *mum* occurs invariably.
The intention is that this is by way of a prior counter-exception (*pūrvavipratiṣedha*).
For here, the *pūrvavipratiṣedha* (the rule of priority) is resorted to: when a *khit* suffix follows, the *mum* augment necessarily occurs by the preceding rule.

Thus, this statement finds its scope (*avakāśa*) only in *kṛt*-affixes other than *khit*. And since it does not apply to anything [else] there, it is correct that this is an optional rule (*aprāptavibhāṣā*) for what was not otherwise established. The mention of the suffix with its *anubandha* (indicatory letter) here is intended so that it would not apply in cases such as *pāmanaputraḥ*.
The suffix *na* is applied by the rule "pāmādy-ādibhyaḥ" [Pāṇini 5.2.100].

A genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*) is formed between that which ends in this suffix and the word *putra*. Now, if the inclusion of the *anubandha* (indicatory letter) were being made, why does [the suffix] not apply in the case of *straiṇārtham*—derived from *striyā ayam iti* ("this belongs to a woman") by the rule "stripuṃsābhyām" [Pāṇini 4.1.87], resulting in *nañ*-strengthened *straiṇaḥ*, and then *straiṇaś cāsāv arthaś ca* ("that which is both *straiṇa* and an object")? Because of the inclusion of the *nañ* that functions as the prior member (*pūrvapada*).

Whence is this [known]? Because the subsequent member (*uttarapada*) is a relative term; for a subsequent member exists only in relation to a preceding member (*pūrvapada*). Therefore, by virtue of the governing rule concerning the subsequent member, the negative particle *nañ* is understood here as being the preceding member.
Alternatively, the term *vibhāṣā* (optionally) continues to apply; because it is understood as a *vyavasthita-vibhāṣā* (a restricted option), [the substitution] will not occur.

If this is so, then in the case of *pāmanaputra*, it likewise will not occur for that very reason; thus, would there not be no purpose in mentioning the form with the *anubandha* (*n*)? In that case, the mention of the form with the *anubandha* is for the sake of clarity.
Furthermore, when it is stated as *nasya*, there is no distinction made on account of brevity.
"It must be stated that the rule applies to verbal suffixes (*tiṅ*) in the sense of 'contempt' (*avakṣepa*).
Contempt means censure.

Since the elision of the *n* is prescribed for the following member (*uttarapada*), it does not apply when that member ends in a verbal suffix; therefore, an extension of the rule must be made for that case.

But surely there already exists a particle expressing negation, according to the statement: "The particles *a*, *mā*, *no*, and *naḥ* are words of negation. Consequently, since the use of a verbal suffix (*tiṅ*) will occur in connection with that very [negation] when it expresses contempt (*avakṣepa*), what is the purpose of this supplementary rule (*upasaṃkhyāna*)? [Objection: In that case, the use of a verbal suffix after the negative particle *nañ* would also result when it expresses contempt.
Therefore, a supplementary rule must be formulated to prevent the occurrence of the form where the *n* of *nañ* has been elided when expressing contempt.
The word *upasaṃkhyāna* means "explanation" or "demonstration."
In this regard, the following is the demonstration: the word *ca* is carried over from [Pāṇini 6.3.69], and its purpose is to include what has not been explicitly mentioned.

Therefore, even in the case of a verbal suffix (*tiṅanta*), when contempt (*avakṣepa*) is implied, the elision of the *n* of *nañ* will occur. As for the statement, "It would apply only to *nañ*," this is because of the locative indication in *aci* (Pāṇini 6.3.68), according to the principle [of Pāṇini 1.1.66].

If the augment *nuṭ* were applied to the negative particle *nañ*, there would be the undesirable consequence of the appearance of the sound *r*. However, when the term *grahaṇa* is employed [in the rule], according to the principle that "when both [the fifth and sixth case endings] are indicated, the indication by the fifth case is stronger" (*Śākaṭāyana-paribhāṣā* 97), the operation occurs only for the subsequent member (*uttarapada*); therefore, the undesirable consequence does not arise. Now, one might object: if *nuṭ* were applied to *nañ*, would not the prescription for the elision of *n* (*nalopa*) be purposeless? It is not purposeless; its purpose is to ensure that the nasal *n* is not heard at the beginning of words such as *abrāhmaṇaḥ* and *avṛṣalaḥ* when they are followed by vowels other than *a* (i.e., in *an-aj-ādi*). Thus, the rule for eliding *n* is necessary.

If the word *tasmāt* is stated for the purpose that the augment *nuṭ* should not occur [after *nañ*], then it need not be mentioned at all; for is this *nuṭ* not already being applied at the beginning [of the compound]? To this he says: "For if [the augment] were applied at the beginning. If *nuṭ* were applied at the beginning, then the *nuṭ* prescribed by the rule *ṅamo hrasvād aci ṅamuṇ nityam* [Pāṇini 8.3.32]—which applies to a word ending in a *ṅam* sound—would result, and thus that same undesirable consequence would follow.
Therefore, *nuṭ* must indeed be applied [only after *nañ*].

In this case, however, the mention of *tasmāt* (from that) is for the purpose of ensuring that [the rule] does not apply to the negative particle (*nañ*) itself when it is being formed. Regarding *nabhrāj*: from the root *bhrājṛ* (meaning "to shine," Dhātupāṭha 181), the suffix *kvip* is applied by the rule *bhrājabhrāsa-* (Pāṇini 3.2.177). By the rule *vraśca-* (Pāṇini 8.2.36), the letter *j* is changed to *ṣ*; this undergoes *jaś*-ness, becoming *ḍ*; and this also undergoes *car*-ness, becoming *ṭ*. Regarding *napāt*: [it is derived from *na* + *pāt*].

Since it is a neuter, when the designation *sarvanāmasthāna* does not apply, does the augment *num*, characterized by having *u* as its penultimate letter, not occur? It does not occur; thus, in the form *navedāḥ*, there is lengthening according to [Pāṇini 6.4.14].
"In 'those who are virtuous among the good' (satsu sādhavaḥ satyāḥ)," by this [reference to Pāṇini 4.4.98], he shows that the suffix *yat* is applied before the word *sat*,
and that "the suffix *ki* is derived from the *uṇādi* [list]."
The suffix *kip* is applied by the rule *igupadhāt kit* (Pāṇini 3.1.135). Regarding the term *kṣiyaḥ*:
there is the root *kṣiṣ* in the sense of "harming" (Dhātupāṭha 1506), as well as *kṣīṣ* [Dhātupāṭha], and the root *kṣi* in the senses of "dwelling" and "going" (Dhātupāṭha 1407).
"Or from the root *kṣar*," as in "the root *kṣar* means 'to move' (Dhātupāṭha 851);
[with this root] *nakṣatra* is derived as an irregular form (*nipātana*)."

What is elided here? If it is from the root *kṣi*, then there is the suffix *tra* and the substitution of *a* for the vowel *i*. If it is from the root *kṣar*, then likewise there is the suffix *tra* and the elision of the letter *r*.
"That in which there is no pleasure (*aka*) is 'Nāka'. Here, *kama* is said to mean happiness.
"Na-aka" means "not suffering. Because there is no suffering (aka) in this place, it is "nāka," which is heaven (*svarga*).
Etymological words (*rūḍhiśabda*) are analyzed in whatever way possible. "Eka-ādi" is a *bahuvrīhi* compound.
Regarding "ekānnaviṃśatiḥ":
first, one should form a compound of the word *nañ* with the word *viṃśati*, and then a third (possessive) compound should be formed.

But for what purpose is this augment *āduk* applied at the end of the preceding member (*pūrvānta*), rather than being applied at the beginning of the following member (*parādi*) as *āduṭ*? In that case, the further advantage is that the mention of the augment as having two forms (*dirdaśa*)—as in the rule *ekasya ca*—need not be made.

For if [the augment] were placed at the beginning of the subsequent element (*parādau*), it would simply be an augment (*āgama*) like *naÑ*; and since it is the subject under discussion, it would be understood as such. In that case, the meaning of the sentence would be: "The word *eka* and so forth becomes its own base (*prakṛti*) together with *naÑ*, and *āduT* is its augment. Thus, the desired result would be established. To this he says: "This is a final element of a word" (*pūrvānto'yam*), and so on.

For in the rule [Pāṇini 8.4.45], the phrase "final element of a word" (*padāntāt*) is carried over from [Pāṇini 8.4.37]. In that context, if [the augment] were placed after [the base], it would not be the final element of a word; consequently, the optional nasalization (*anunāsika-vikalpa*) conditioned by being the final element of a word would not occur, yet it is desired.

Therefore, the suffix *āduk* is added so that [the desired form] may occur through optional application (*vikalpena*). Now, for what purpose is *āduk* added? Why not simply say *ādu* instead? Even if *āduk* were used, would the long vowel not be established by the rule "a long vowel replaces two homogeneous vowels" (*akaḥ savarṇe dīrghaḥ*)? It is not established; the rule "the subsequent form" (*pararūpatvam*) would apply [by *ato guṇe*]. That will not occur due to the functional force (*sāmarthya*) of the explicit utterance of the letter *u*. For if the subsequent form were to occur here, he would have prescribed merely *duk*. In that case, would even the substitution of a long homogeneous vowel not occur due to the functional force of the utterance of the letter *a*? This is not so.

For instance: that rule for which the instruction would otherwise be purposeless is the one that is sublated (*bādhyate*). However, a rule whose very cause [for application] is that [instruction] is not itself sublated.

Furthermore, the pronunciation of the letter *a* is purposeless with respect to the state of being another form (*pararūpatva*), whereas it is indeed the cause with respect to the long vowel resulting from the combination of similar vowels (*savarṇadīrghatva*).
If this is so, then this [substitution] is indeed *adug*.
For the *saṃhitā* [reading] is the same: "the suffix *ḍa* is applied after the root *gam*.
This is because of the statement: "In the section on *ḍa*, it is seen elsewhere as well" (Vārttika 256). Regarding "sāāttham":
it is a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "together with Āttha" (*sahāātthena*).
Regarding the forms *sahayudhvā* and *sahakṛtvā*:

while the rule *dṛśeḥ kvanip* [Pāṇini 3.2.94] is still in effect, the suffix *kvanip* is applied by the rules *rājani yudhi kṛñaḥ* [3.2.95] and *sahe ca* [3.2.96]. This results in an upapada compound (*upapadasamāsa*). Then, by the rule *sarvanāmasthāne* [6.4.8], the vowel is lengthened. But what is the reason that the substitute *sā* is prescribed as having an acute accent (*udātta*)? To this he says: "For [the root] possesses both acute and grave accents," and so forth.
According to the rule *nipātā ādyudāttā bhavanti* (Phiṭ-sūtra 4.80), the word *saha* is indeed udātta in its first syllable, while the remainder is anudātta.
Consequently, it possesses both udātta and anudātta accents; therefore, by the principle of proximity (*antaryataḥ*), the substitute *sa-* would become svarita in its place.
To prevent this defect, it is prescribed as an udātta nipāta.
If this is so, would not an acute accent (*udātta*) likewise result in the case of an *avyayībhāva* compound? To this he says: "And that is the accent of a particle," and so forth;
"where," and so forth;
[namely] in a *bahuvrīhi* or a *tatpuruṣa*.
> [[6.2.1]] Thus, this is an exception to the rule that the final member of a compound is udātta with respect to the word *saha*; rather, the original accent (*prakṛtisvaratva*) prevails.

This also applies to the *tatpuruṣa* compound by the rule "in a *tatpuruṣa*, [the first member retains its accent] when meaning 'equal to' (tulyārtha)," etc. Therefore, in that very case, the accent of the particle (*nipātasvara*) would necessarily apply.

In the case of an *avyayībhāva* compound, however, since no rule has prescribed the original accent (*prakṛtisvara*) as an exception to the rule that the final member of a compound is udātta, it must necessarily be udātta by virtue of that very rule regarding the final syllable of the compound. Therefore, it is indeed sublated by that [rule]. For example: *seṣṭi*, *sapaśubandham*.

In the case of *iṣṭyanto* and *paśubandhāntaḥ*, the compound is formed by the rule *avyayaṃ vibhakti-* [Pāṇini 2.1.6] et cetera, with the sense of "ending in. Here, because it is subsequent, the accent of the first member (*satiśiṣṭa*) applies; thereafter, the compound receives an udātta accent on its final syllable. Since that [final accent] remains even when the accent of the particle (*nipātasvara*) is present, it is called *satiśiṣṭa*; therefore, it sublates the accent of the particle, for a *satiśiṣṭa* accent possesses greater strength. [The word] *sakalam*.

*Kalā* means a specific division of time; the text associated with that is likewise so called. That which exists together with *kalā* is *sakala*. In this same way, the term *samuhūrta* is also to be understood.

Regarding the term “*sasaṃgraham*”: this example was written by contemporary scribes out of negligence, for in that case, the substitution of *sa* [for *sam*] is established by the rule *[[Pāṇini 6.3.81]]*. To this he says: “In that case,” and so forth. But how is it that [the substitution] does not apply here, given that the words *kāla* and *muhūrta* are present? [The answer is: they occur here in the text by virtue of association (*sāhacarya*). He thinks as follows: the fact that those two [words] refer to the subject matter of the treatise is understood through the context and other such factors within the sentence.

But time itself is the primary thing to be expressed, as in "a *khārī* containing six *droṇas*" and so forth; here, a *bahuvrīhi* compound is formed by [Pāṇini 2.2.28] "with that" (*tena saha*) and so on. Regarding the statement: "Of two things used together, that which is subordinate is the second."
Because when there is a conjunction of a primary and another [secondary] element, the word "second" (*dvitīya*) is applied only to that which is not primary.

To illustrate: when a master and a servant are joined together, it is the servant alone who is called the "second" in relation to the master, but the master is not called the "second" in relation to the servant.
Thus, "that which is narrated is a narrative" (*upākhyāyate yaḥ sa upākhyaḥ*).
By rule [Pāṇini 3.3.106], the suffix *ka* is applied; and that [suffix] occurs in the sense of "becoming" by rule [Pāṇini 3.3.113] in the objective case (*karman*). Thus, we have the example:
*sāgniḥ kapotaḥ* ("a pigeon that has become possessed of fire").
As before, this is a *bahuvrīhi* compound.

Here, the pigeon is conjoined with fire; for their association is well-known in the world. In that case, fire is subordinate. Thus, fire conforms to the pigeon—wherever the pigeon is, fire must necessarily be there—but it is not the case that wherever fire is, the pigeon is there; therefore, the pigeon does not conform to fire, and by that, the pigeon possesses primacy.
Furthermore, Agni and the others are indeed secondary.
Regarding the phrase "Agni and the others," the word "and others" (ādi) here includes Piśācas and so forth.

"In that case, [is it not so] that they are perceived by direct perception (pratyakṣa) somewhere? No; rather, they are inferred through [signs] such as pigeons which are invariably concomitant with them, and thus they become indefinable. Regarding the phrase "not denoting time" (*akālavācini*):
by this, he shows that here the term "time" (*kāla*) does not refer to the word-form itself, but rather to words such as *pūrvāhṇa* ("forenoon") and so forth, which denote specific divisions of time.
How is this further determined? From the inclusion of the phrase "another work" (*granthāntara*) in the rule [Pāṇini 6.3.79].
For by this [rule], a prohibition would apply when a word denoting time occurs as the subsequent member (uttarapada); [the author] says "let that not be so.

In that regard, the mention of *granthānta* is made; for if here there were a mention of the form *kāla* itself, then by that very [rule], the substitution of *sa-* in *sakalam* and *samuhūrtam* would be established, and thus the mention of *granthānta* there would be purposeless.
Regarding "sacakram":
by the rule "an indeclinable [compounded] with a case-ending" (Pāṇini 2.1.6) and so forth, this is an *avyayībhāva* compound denoting simultaneity. Regarding "sadhuram": [the same applies].
The suffix *a* is applied as a compound-final (*samāsānta*) by the rule *ṛkpūrabdhūḥ pathāmānakṣe* [Pāṇini 5.4.74].
Thus, we have *sahapūrvāhṇam*.

By that same rule, when there is completeness (*sākalya*), the *avyayībhāva* compound is formed. If this term *upasarjanasya* were a qualifier of the word *saha*, then there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).
Since no specific distinction is made here either, the forms *sahayudhvā* (having fought together) and *sahakṛtvā* (having acted together) would also result.

Furthermore, in this case as well, the word *saha* is a subordinate member (*upasarjana*), because it is indicated by the first case ending according to [Pāṇini 2.2.19], and because it lacks predominance. Moreover, the qualification would be redundant; for in every compound, the word *saha* is invariably a subordinate member.

And here, the compound is brought into proximity by its final member (*uttarapada*). Why? Because in a compound, the final member exists; therefore, thinking that this [term *upasarjana*] is a qualifier of that very [final member], he says: "that of which every member (*sarva-avayava*) is subordinate (*upasarjana*).

That is what is meant by the expression: "that whose every constituent part is subordinate. This is because the property of the whole is designated in such a way through the property of its parts, just as one says, "this city is prosperous" (referring to its inhabitants).

If it were the case that for some compound, one constituent part is a subordinate element (*upasarjana*) while another is not, yet that [non-subordinate] part is also called a subordinate element, then the fault of over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) would remain as it was; therefore, the term "all" (*sarva*) is used.
But what is this compound whose every constituent part is a subordinate element? It is the *bahuvrīhi*. [Objection:

Is it not the case that the *dvandva* also has all its parts as subordinate elements, and thus its inclusion [under the rule] would follow? This is not a fault; for in that [case of the *dvandva*], the state of being a subordinate element is applied only to the word that is used in a subordinate sense along with another.
Alternatively—since both types of application are possible in this treatise, even the worldly [term] is included here as a subordinate element (*upasarjana*).

Therefore, it is understood that the word *upasarjana* intends to refer to that whose every constituent part has become subordinate, whether by virtue of being a technical subordinate element of the treatise or a worldly subordinate element.
And such is not the case with a *dvandva* compound.

The status of being a subordinate element (*upasarjana*) for its constituent parts is due solely to the technical definition in the grammatical treatise (*śāstra*), and not according to common worldly usage.

However, the *bahuvrīhi* compound [is so designated] even by worldly usage. Therefore, it is precisely that [the *bahuvrīhi*] which is captured by the mention of the term "subordinate element" (*upasarjana*).
Regarding the phrase "of its part" (*tadavayavasya*): by this, he shows that the genitive case in *upasarjanasya* is a partitive genitive. The example is "one who has a son" (*saputraḥ*).
As before, there is a *bahuvrīhi* compound:
"one who has eaten together" (*sahabhuk*) and "one who has acted together" (*sahakṛt*).
This is a *tatpuruṣa* compound in which the meaning of the final member is predominant.

Now, why does this not occur here: *sahakṛtvapriyaḥ* or *priyasahakṛtvaḥ*? For in these cases as well, the word *saha* is a constituent part (*avayava*) of a *bahuvrīhi* compound. To this he replies with the words beginning with "here" (*iha*).
Regarding the rule *vā priyasya* (Pāṇini 2.2.36), the word *priya* may optionally be placed first.

Furthermore, because the section concerning the "subsequent member" (*uttarapada*) applies here and a *bahuvrīhi* is being relied upon, that which is the subsequent member in a *bahuvrīhi*—namely, the word *kṛtva*—must follow the word *saha*. Therefore, [the forms] must be *sahakṛtvapriyaḥ* and *sahakṛtva-priyaḥ*.

And here, in this *bahuvrīhi* compound, that which is the final member (*uttarapada*) does not follow immediately after the word *saha*, because it is separated by another word; therefore, the substitution of *sa-* [for *saha-*, as prescribed by Pāṇini 6.3.95] does not occur. By means of the preceding rule [Pāṇini 6.3.78], the over-extension of the substitution of *sa-* is prevented through the application of the original form (*prakṛtibhāva*). Although it would have sufficed to say "not" (*na*), the use of the term "original form" (*prakṛtyā*) is for the sake of stylistic variety. In the examples "sagarbhaḥ" (having a common womb) and "sapūthyaḥ" (belonging to the same herd), one analyzes the compounds as "common womb" (*samāno garbhaḥ*) and "common herd" (*samānaṃ yūtham*), and then forms them as *karmadhāraya*s according to [Pāṇini 2.1.58] and the subsequent rules.
Regarding "sādharmyam":
it is an abstract suffix (*bhāvapratyaya*) applied to a *bahuvrīhi* compound.
Regarding "sajātīyaḥ": [it means] that which belongs to the same class.
In this case as well, the suffix *cha* is applied by the rule *bahuvrīher eva* [Pāṇini 5.4.9]. Regarding the form *sasthānīyaḥ*:
the suffix *cha* is applied by the rule *sthānāntād vibhāṣā saṃsthānena cet* [Pāṇini 5.4.10]. Regarding the form *sajyoti*.
The compound *samānajyotiḥ* is a *bahuvrīhi*, meaning "one whose light is the same. In this same way, compounds such as *sajanapadaḥ* and others are to be understood.
It must also necessarily be so in the case of a *tatpuruṣa* compound, because there is no adoption of any specific distinction [to the contrary].
In the case of *sanāmā*,
the long vowel is applied by the rule *sarvanāmasthāne ca* [Pāṇini 6.4.8] and so forth. In the case of *savayāḥ*:

Here too, there is lengthening by the rule *atvasantasya* [Pāṇini 6.4.14]. This word *caraṇa* refers to persons and so forth by taking its basis in the act of study (*adhyayana*). One who practices the *Brāhmaṇa* is a *brāhma-cārī*; the suffix *ṇini* is applied here by the rule *vrate* [Pāṇini 3.2.80]. Thus we have *sabrahmacārī*.
As before, this is a *karmadhāraya* compound.
The intended meaning of the term *sabrahmacārī* is "one who practices the vow (*vrata*) together with [another] regarding the *brahma*.
To show how this meaning is applicable here, he says: "*Brahma is the Veda,*" and so forth.
The vow for the purpose of studying that [Veda] is also called "Brahma" because it is for its sake; this is a designation based on the purpose, just as a pillar intended for Indra is called "Indra.
And he who practices that [vow] is one who accomplishes it, meaning he observes it.
But by what is this [Veda] equal? To this he says: "It is equal to that very [one]," and so forth.
"To that very one" refers to the Veda, which is called *brāhmaṇa*. The particle *iti* is used in the sense of a reason.

Since he performs the vow which has acquired the designation "Brāhmaṇa" through metaphorical usage, and because of the identity with a Brāhmaṇa, he who is equal [to him] is a *sabrahmacārī*. Thus, the meaning of the term *sabrahmacārī* is: one who performs the vow within the same *brahman* (sacred knowledge).
For if he were to perform the vow within a different *brahman*, then there would be no equality.
Nevertheless, even if one does not observe the vow called *brāhma*, one would still not be a practitioner of the *brāhma*.

Therefore, he who is a practitioner of the *brāhma* while the *brāhma* is common [to all] necessarily becomes a practitioner of the vow while the *brāhma* is common. Thus, the meaning of the term "one who practices the *brāhma*" (*sabrahmacārī*) is established as "one who practices the vow while the *brāhma* is common."

Alternatively, in this view, there is a reference by way of metaphorical designation (*upacāra*) to that very vow (*vrata*) which has received the name "Brāhmaṇa. In the phrase "in the same Brāhmaṇa," the word *brāhmaṇa* refers to the Veda; for [the Veda] differs according to each individual Veda. The vow undertaken for the purpose of studying that [Veda]—he who performs the vow when the Veda is to be studied is called a "sabrāhmacārī" (one who studies the same Veda).

In the *Bālamanauramā*, under the section on *jyotis*, *janapada*, *caraṇa*, and *brāhmaṇa* (Pāṇini 2.1.50), sūtra 6.3.96 states: "The mention of *jyotis* and *janapada* is for the purpose of excluding *chandas*.
Thus, [the term] *sajyotis*.
The analysis of the compound is "that which has the same light" (*samānaṃ jyotir yasya*). The same applies to *sajanapada* and so forth:
*sarātriḥ*, *sanābhiḥ*, *sanāmā*, *sagotraḥ*, *sarūpaḥ*, *sasthānaḥ*, *savarṇaḥ*, *savayāḥ*, *savacanaḥ*, and *sabandhuḥ*.

In the *Bālamano-ramā*: "In the case of a Vedic school (*caraṇa*), when [the word] *brāhma* is the first member. (Pāṇini 6.3.96). The words "of *samāna*" and "that" (*sa*) are carried over [from previous rules].
The term "in the subsequent member" (*uttarapade*) is also supplied as a governing heading.
Regarding this, it is said: "When *caraṇa* follows as the second member [of a compound], *samāna* becomes *sa*. The locative case in *caraṇe* connects with *samānasya*;
the meaning is "when [the word] exists within *caraṇa*."
He states the conclusion: "when the *caraṇa* is understood as being identical.
Therein, he explains the word *caraṇa*: "*caraṇa* means *śākhā* (branch).
The basis for this is indeed Vedic usage.
He speaks in order to etymologically explain the term *brāhmacāri*: "The Veda is *brahma*.
According to Amarasimha, "The Veda, reality, and austerity are *brahma*.
[The compound means] "for the sake of practicing that."
The meaning is that the *caraṇa* of that *veda* is its study (*adhyayana*), and by the word "brahmin" (*brāhma*), the vow (*vrata*) is also intended to be expressed.
The phrase "by way of figurative usage" (*gauṇyā vṛttyā*) is to be supplied as the remainder [of the sentence]. Thus, it is one who practices that [study and vow] who is so called.
The word *brāhmacārī* means "one who performs" or "practises" that vow;
[it is formed] with the suffix *ṇini* according to the rule *supyajātau*.
[In this formation,] *samāna* becomes *sa*.

The meaning is that when it is a *karmadhāraya* compound in the form "one who practices the Veda equally" (*samāno brāhmacārī*), the word *samāna* undergoes the substitution of *sa-* by the aforementioned rule, resulting in the form *sabrāhmacārī*. Furthermore, this "equality" is to be understood through the medium of the Veda;
thus, the resultant meaning is "one who practices the vow for the purpose of studying the same Veda."

In the Bhāṣya, however, it is stated that when the meaning is "he observes the same vow (*vrata*) as [another]," the suffix *ṇini* is applied to the root *car*, and the word *vrata* is elided here by nipātana. Regarding the term *satīrthya*:
as before, one should form the *taddhita* suffix after first constructing a *karmadhāraya*.

One who dwells at the same sacred site (*tīrtha*) is a *satīrthya*. [Regarding *sadṛk*]: one who perceives oneself as equal is *sadṛk*; this is an *upapada* compound, and the substitution of *k* for *d* occurs according to Pāṇini 8.2.62.

But how can *kañ* and *kvin* apply here, given that those two suffixes are prescribed when words from the *tyadādi* group are present as upapadas, and the word *samāna* is not listed among the *tyadādi* group? To this, he says: “*tyadādiṣu*,” etc.

The meaning is that one must explain the rule by adding the phrase “and when *vṛkṣa* [is the second member],” so that the substitution of *sa-* for *samāna-* occurs when the word *vṛkṣa* is the subsequent member (*uttarapada*).

In this regard, the explanation is as follows: because of the previous separation of the *yoga* (sūtra rule), the suffix *kṣa* will also apply after the root *dṛś*. For this very reason, the author of the *Vṛtti* stated there [at 6.3.83]: "Forms such as these become established. But by what rule is the suffix *kṣa* prescribed for the root *dṛś*, such that the word *dṛkṣa* can serve as a final member (*uttarapada*)? To this he says: "The suffix *kṣa* is also [prescribed] for *dṛś*" and so forth.

"In that very [place]" means in the sūtra beginning with "tyadādiṣu" (Pāṇini 1.1.74). Now, what is the purpose of including the mention of *vatup*, since a *vatup* following a word identical in form [to the base] is not possible at all? For that [suffix] is prescribed only after words such as *yat* and so on, by the rule "yattadetebhyaḥ parimāṇe vatup" (Pāṇini 5.2.39)? To this he says: "The mention of *vatup* is for the sake of what follows. The letter *ś* is for the purpose of making [the suffix] a substitute for the whole [base].

"That which one sees as being like this" is *īdṛk* or *īdṛśaḥ*. "Like the former" is *pūrvavat*. [The suffixes] *-kañ* and *-kvan* [are added]: "that which one seeks as being like what? is *kīdṛk* or *kīdṛśaḥ*.

The analysis (vigraha) has been performed merely for the sake of etymological derivation; the meaning of the individual components as presented in the analytical sentence does not exist here. For instance, by the words "such" (īdṛg) or "of such a kind" (īdṛśa), the sense of "equal to this" is understood from the whole alone.
Regarding "of what kind" (*kīdṛk*) and "of what sort" (*kīdṛśa*), [the suffix *dr̥ś* is applied] here also in the sense of "equal to what"?
Regarding "what is its measure? (*kiṃ parimāṇam asya*), [the suffix *yat* is applied] as *kayāna*;
regarding "this is its measure," [the suffix *yat* is applied] as *iyān*.
By the rule *[[5.2.40]]*, there is the substitution of *gh* for *vatup*; when the replacement of *iy* has been made for that [suffix], there is the elision of the vowel *i* by the rule *[[6.4.148]]*.

[Objection: But surely, by this rule, the replacement of *iy* is prescribed for the *v* of *vatup*, not for *vatup* itself. What then is prescribed for *kim* and *idam*? [Response: It is thought thus: *vatup* is understood from this statement regarding its replacement; for there is no other defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) for *vatup*. And it is not possible to understand a replacement of *gh* for a *vatup* that does not exist. [The author says: "And it should be stated: 'and before *dṛkṣa*'" (*dṛkṣe ceti vaktavyam*).
The meaning is that this rule, which states that the substitution of *āt* occurs for a pronoun when the word *dṛkṣa* follows, must be explained.

The explanation here is as follows: from the subsequent sūtra, the particle *ca* ("and") is carried over to this rule by the maxim of the "lion's glance" (*siṃhāvalokita-nyāya*), and it serves to include what has not been explicitly mentioned.
By this means, the substitution will also occur when the word *dṛkṣa* is the following member of a compound.

Now, for what purpose is the long vowel (*dīrgha*) prescribed? Why not simply prescribe the short vowel (*hrasva*) instead? For even with a short substitute, the desired form would be established by the rule of *savarṇa*-lengthening (*savarṇadīrghatva*). No; because [if a short vowel were used], the rule for *pararūpa* (the single substitute of the subsequent form) would apply. Nor can it be argued that it will not occur due to the force of the explicit utterance of the vowel *a*; for the prescription of *a* is intended to exclude the letter *da*. Indeed, if there were a rule for elision (*lopa*), there would be unnecessary complexity (*gaurava*). Furthermore, in forms such as *tvādṛk* and *tvādṛśa*, the long vowel would not be heard.

Therefore, only the long vowel [of *viṣvañc*] is to be prescribed. Regarding the form *viṣvadraṅ*: from the root *añc*, the suffix *kvin* is applied by the rule *ṛtvig-ādi-sūtra* (Pāṇini 3.2.59); then the *num* augment is added by *ugidacām* (7.1.70); the elision of the final consonant (*hal*) and the *ṅī* suffix occurs by *halṅyāb-bhyo dīrghāt sutisyapṛktaṃ hal* (6.1.68), followed by the elision of the final consonant of the *saṃyoga* cluster; finally, the change to the guttural *k* (*kutva*) occurs by *coḥ kuḥ* (8.2.30).
Regarding the statement "the words *adri* and *sadhri* are nipātana forms with udātta accent on the final syllable," and so forth.

In the case of *viṣvadṛṅ*, when the substitution of *adri* is made by this [rule], and in the case of *sadhyraṅ*, when the substitution of *sadhryac* for *saha* is made, the rule *[[6.2.139]]* would result in the final syllable of the second member being udātta by virtue of the natural accent (*prakṛtisvara*). However, a circumflex (*svarita*) accent is desired.

Therefore, in order to prescribe the udātta accent on the final syllable of the second member here, the udātta nature of the finals of *adri* and *sadhryac* is specifically prescribed (as an irregularity).
Consequently, the remainder becomes anudātta.
In that case, once the substitution of *yaṇ* has been applied, the svarita accent of the subsequent member (*uttarapada*) is established by [Pāṇini 8.2.4].
Now, what is the purpose of mentioning the suffix *vap*? For, when it is stated "in *añcatu*," the grammatical operation should apply only when the bare form *añcatu* is the subsequent member;
yet it is only when ending in the suffix *vap* that *añcati* constitutes the subsequent member.
Regarding this, he says "the mention of the suffix *v*," and so forth.

The mention of the suffix *v* is for the purpose that, in other instances where there is a mention of a root (*dhātu*), there may be the comprehension—that is, the understanding—of the entire collection [beginning] with the root-initial as being the base (*prakṛti*).
By this, the following meaning is made known: when there is a mention of a root elsewhere than this, not only the root alone is grasped, but rather the word beginning with the root.

Therefore, in the case of *ayaskṛtam* and *ayaskāraḥ*, the substitution of *s* for the elided *r* (visarjanīya) is established by the rule *ataḥ kṛkami* [Pāṇini 8.3.46]. If, however, this meaning were not understood, then there would be the inclusion of the root *kṛ* alone; consequently, the rule would apply only where the root *kṛ* is used in its isolated form, devoid of suffixes—as in *ayaskṛt*. In this instance, the augment *tuK* belongs to the root *kṛ* itself because it is part of its stem (*bhaktatvāt*); since it is included by that very [inclusion of the root], the usage would be of the root *kṛ* alone.
Regarding "aācī":

[the root] *añc* takes the suffix *kvip* because it means "she bends toward" (*āmañcati*); the feminine suffix *ṅīp* is added by the rule "and there is an addition for *añc*" (Vārttika 336); the vowel *a* is elided by the rule "of *ac*" (Pāṇini 6.4.138); and the lengthening occurs by the rule "in the presence of *ca*" (Pāṇini 6.3.137).
Regarding "viṣvagyuk": [it is derived from *yuj* with the prefix *viṣvak*].
The suffix *kvip* is applied [to the root *añc*] in the sense of "he connects in all directions" according to the rule *satsūdviṣa-* (Pāṇini 3.2.61).
Thus, we have *viṣvagañcanam*.
The suffix *lyuṭ* is applied according to the rule *lyuṭ ca* (Pāṇini 3.3.115).
Regarding the phrase "in Vedic usage" (*chandasi*) and so forth:

the meaning is that this rule should be explained as having the sense that, in the domain of Vedic usage, when the feminine gender is to be expressed, the substitution of *madra* occurs diversely (*bahulam*). In this regard, the explanation is as follows: the term *vibhāṣā* ("optionally") is understood to carry over from [Pāṇini 6.3.88], and that is a restricted option (*vyavasthitavibhāṣā*).

Alternatively, the word *ca* here serves to include what has not been explicitly mentioned; by virtue of this, in the domain of Vedic usage (*chandas*), the substitution of *adra-* occurs for *viṣvañc-* and so forth even in other instances, while in some cases it does not occur at all.

Now, one might ask: "Is the word *ca* intended to draw back the term 'pronoun' (*sarvanāman*) from the previous rule? This is not the case; for the recurrence of the term 'pronoun' will occur simply by virtue of its being marked with a circumflex accent (*svarita*).
[The examples follow: *viāācī*, etc.

When *vi-*, *āghṛta-*, or *kiṃśabda-* are used as upapadas [to the root] *añc*, the suffix *kvin* is applied as before, and the grammatical operations such as the addition of the feminine suffix *ṅīp* also take place. In the form *sadhrīcā*:

as before, there is the elision of the vowel *a*, and the lengthening of the preceding vowel. In the form *sadhamādaḥ*: it means "that which exists together with intoxication" (*māda*). This is a *bahuvrīhi* compound according to the rule beginning with *tena saha* (Pāṇini 2.2.28). The word *māda* ends in the suffix *ghañ*.

But should it not be *ap* by [Pāṇini 3.3.67]? This is not a fault; for in that rule [3.3.62], the option (*vā*) from the preceding sūtra is understood, and that is a restricted option (*vyavasthitavibhāṣā*).
Therefore, in the Vedic language, only the suffix *ghañ* will occur.
Or else, it is because of this very specific formulation [of the sūtra].
Regarding "sadhasthaḥ" [the printed reading in the Kāśikā is "sadhasthāḥ"; the printed reading in the Saṃkṣiptasāra commentary is "sadhasthā"]:
[it means] "one who stands together," formed with the suffix *ka* according to [Pāṇini 3.2.4]. Regarding "dvīpam": [it means] "that which has water on both sides."
The term *dvirgata* is a *bahuvrīhi* compound whose analysis (*vigraha*) does not contain its own constituent members, as in: "water has gone twice in this.
For example, *sumukhī* ("fair-faced") means "she whose face is beautiful. In this case, the suffix *a* is added at the end of the compound by the rule *ṛkpūrabdhūḥ* [Pāṇini 5.4.74].
"Antarīpa" means that water is contained within it;
"sapīpa," "vīpa," and "nīpa" mean that water has come together, gone away, or flowed out from it.
[The word] "vaktavyam" (it should be stated) [is used].
The meaning is that it must be explained.

This same meaning applies to the word *vaktavya* (to be stated) in subsequent sections as well. However, here too, the explanation is as before: it is obtained through the continued application of the term *vibhāṣā* from the rule *vibhāṣodare*, because [the rule] is a *vyavasthitavibhāṣā* (an option restricted by specific conditions).

We shall provide another explanation here as well, beginning with the words "with respect to the word *ap*. In this context, prepositions (*prādayaḥ*) are designated as either verbs (*gati*) or prefixes (*upasarga*) only with respect to that [word] toward which they are connected with an action (*kriyā*). However, the status of being an action is not possible for the word *ap*, because it denotes a substance (*dravya*).
Therefore, for that [word], there is no designation as an *upasarga* (preverb) for anything else.
Yet, this mention of *upasarga* is made;

by its force, it is understood that the mention of *upasarga* serves as an illustration (*upalakṣaṇa*) for cases where the status of being an *upasarga* is observed elsewhere than after words beginning with *pra*.

If this is so, the mention of the word *anta-* should not be made; for just as the words beginning with *pra-* are indicated by the mention of "prepositions" (*upasarga*), so too is the word *anta-*, since its status as a preposition is indeed observed in rules concerning the suffix *aṅ* and the substitution of *ṇ*. If that is the case, then the mention of *anta-* serves to indicate that the substitution of *īt* (long *ī*) conditioned by the mention of "prepositions" is non-obligatory (*anitya*). By this, forms such as *samāpam*, *parāpam*, and *prāpam* are established. Regarding the term *anūpa*: the analysis is "that in which waters have followed" (*anugatā āpo 'smin*). As before, there is a compound-ending suffix (*samāsānta*), and [the vowels] undergo coalescence (*savarṇadīrgha*).

Now, for what purpose is the long vowel pronounced, since even with a short vowel, the form *anūpa* would be established by the rule *akaḥ savarṇe dīrghaḥ*? To this he says: "The pronunciation of the long [vowel]," and so forth.
If the long vowel were not pronounced, the lengthening would occur only in *saṃhitā*, not in *avagraha*.
Therefore, the long vowel is pronounced so that it may also occur in *avagraha*, as in the example: *anyāśīr anyadāśīḥ*, and so on.

By means of a specific analysis of the compound, he demonstrates that in all cases there is a descriptive determinative compound (*viśeṣaṇasamāsa*), as in the phrase "not established by another, [but] established by another" (anyenāsthito 'nyadasthitaḥ),
which is a compound according to [Pāṇini 2.1.32].
[He also mentions] "the addition of the suffix *dṛk* without distinction," and so forth.

When the suffix *cha* follows a word denoting an agent (*kāraka*), the augment *duK* is to be applied without distinction—that is, universally. However, in the case of the other seven subsequent bases beginning with *āśis*, the [augment] is not desired nor intended for those standing in the genitive or instrumental cases.
What, then, is the indicative mark (*liṅga*) for this meaning, by which it is determined? To this, he says: "And of this," and so forth.

Since the rule would have been established simply by stating "of that which stands in the sixth or third case," the repetition of the negative particle *nañ* is a sign (*liṅga*) that this prohibition is not universal (*anitya*).
Consequently, in some instances, the augment *dug* occurs even for that which stands in the sixth or third case within a compound. Regarding the term *anyārtha*:

this is a compound formed according to [Pāṇini 2.1.36], *caturthī tadarthārtha*, meaning "this is for the sake of another" (*anyasmai idam*). Regarding the term *kadaja*: [this is a compound formed according to Pāṇini 2.1.37].
The compound *kūṣṭra* is a *tatpuruṣa* according to [Pāṇini 2.2.18] (*kutsito 'jaḥ*), whereas *kūṣṭro rājā* is a *bahuvrīhi*.
Regarding the phrase "in the case of the substitution of *kad*" and so forth:
although the substitution of *kad* is prescribed when a word beginning with *aj-* follows as the second member (*uttarapada*), it does not apply when the word *tri* is the second member.

Therefore, when *tri* is the final member of a compound, an addition (*upasaṃkhyāna*) must be made regarding the substitution of *ka* for the word *ku* that precedes it—that is, its formal presentation must be provided. Here is the presentation: the letter *ca* is employed in the subsequent sūtra, and it serves the purpose of including what has not been explicitly mentioned.
By this means, the substitution of *ka* will also occur when *tri* is the final member of the compound. This rule is intended for cases other than those beginning with a vowel (*anaj-ādi*).
The same applies in subsequent cases as well. This undertaking is for the purpose of expressing slight deficiency. Regarding the term *kāpatha*:
a "bad path" (*kutsitaḥ panthāḥ*) is *kāpatha*; the suffix *a* is applied at the end of the compound by the rule *ṛkpūrabdhūḥpathāmānakṣe* (Pāṇini 5.4.74).
Regarding "kākṣaḥ":

it is a *tatpuruṣa* compound meaning a "bad eye" (*kutsita-akṣa*). Alternatively, it is a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "one whose eyes are bad"; in this case, the suffix *ṣac* is applied according to Pāṇini 5.4.113, *bahuvrīhau sakthyakṣṇoḥ svāṅgāt ṣac*, which serves as the final member of the compound. "Slightly sweet" is expressed as *kāmadhuram*.
Thus ends the compound [2.2.18].

It has been stated that the statement "the word *ku* signifies evil" (*pāpa*) is merely a general indication based on common usage (*prāyika*). Regarding its being general, this very mention of the substitution of *ka-* (*kādeśa*) serves as the indicator (*jñāpaka*).
Regarding the word *kāmlam*:

one might ask, "In this case, should there not be the substitution of *kad-* by the rule *koḥ kattatpuruṣe* [Pāṇini 6.3.101]? To this he replies: "Even when beginning with a vowel," and so forth. This is an optional rule (*vibhāṣā*) because the sense of "slightness" (*īṣadartha*) has been removed.

But surely, since [the suffix] is not prescribed by anything for the sense of "not slightly" (*anīṣad*), whereas it is already prescribed by the preceding rule for the sense of "slightly" (*īṣad*), it is logical that this [present rule] should be an option (*vibhāṣā*) in both cases. To this he says: "But in the sense of 'slightly,' by way of a prior counter-exception" (*pūrvavipratiṣedhena*), and so forth.

The scope (*avakāśa*) of P. 6.3.105 is *īṣanmadhuram* (slightly sweet) and *kāmadhum*; the scope of the rule "optionally before *puruṣa*" (*vibhāṣā puruṣe*) is *kutsitaḥ puruṣaḥ* (a contemptible man), which becomes *kāpuruṣaḥ*. Here, however, both rules would apply simultaneously: *īṣatpuruṣaḥ* (a slightly deficient man), which becomes *kāpuruṣaḥ*.

In this context, by the very phrase "in some cases" (*atreṣadarthe*), there occurs a reversal of the previous [rule]. Some say that this is understood through the application of the "lion's glance" (*siṃhāvalokita*) maxim to the upcoming mention of the term *bahulam* (variously) here, which implies that "the suffix *valac* is intended, not the nominal stem.
Others say it is because of the association with the suffix *matup*, which will be mentioned immediately thereafter. The word "etcetera" (*ādi*) expresses a class or type.

If the word "ādi" (and so forth) were taken here in the sense of restriction (*vyavasthā*), then only those words that are recited in the list would be correct, and no others. But when the word "ādi" is taken in the sense of "manner" or "type" (*prakāra*), then even those not recited in the list attain the status of being correct. Having considered all this in his mind, the author shows that this word "ādi" signifies "manner" by stating: "Words of the *pṛṣodara* type," and so on.
Here, "manner" (*prakāra*) means similarity (*sādṛśya*).
Therefore, in order to demonstrate this, he says: "In those [words]," and so forth.

Just as in the word *pṛṣodara* the operation of elision is seen even though it is not prescribed by the grammatical treatise (*śāstra*), so too elsewhere operations such as elision are seen even though they are not prescribed by the treatise;
and these are of the same class as *pṛṣodara*.
Regarding the phrase "yathopadiṣṭam" (as taught):
the term *yathā* forms an avyayībhāva compound with the sense of repetition (*vīpsā*) according to [Pāṇini 2.1.7], *yathā’sādṛśye*.
For this very reason, he provides its explanation: "those which have been taught," and so forth.
The activity consists of the pronunciation of the directions [of the phonemes].
The meaning is that they have been taught and pronounced.
By whom, then, were they taught? By the learned (*śiṣṭa*).
Furthermore, the cultured (śiṣṭas) are to be known by their conduct, residence, and so forth.
"Those [words] are to be accepted as such" means that they are to be accepted as correct (sādhu) exactly as they were employed by them.

If the learned (śiṣṭas) are the authority regarding words, then what is the use of this Aṣṭādhyāyī? For would not the correctness of words be understood from the very speech of the learned? It is replied: the Aṣṭādhyāyī is for the purpose of identifying who the learned are.

One who is studying the *Aṣṭādhyāyī*, upon seeing someone else—who has not studied the *Aṣṭādhyāyī*—employing words prescribed in this *Aṣṭādhyāyī*, determines: "This person is an *āpta* (an authoritative person). Now, that person has not studied the *Aṣṭādhyāyī*, yet he employs those words which have been derived therein; therefore, one concludes: "Surely he knows others as well. Thus, the *Aṣṭādhyāyī* serves for the purpose of identifying the *āptas*. Regarding the phrase "and so on for others":
when the words *kapi* and *āma* are used as upapadas, the suffix *kap* is applied to the root *sthā* [by Pāṇini 3.2.4].
The letter *sa* is changed to *ta*,
and the word *mahī* is also shortened,
resulting in "dakṣiṇatāram."
This is a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*).
There is a change to the masculine form (*puṃvadbhāva*) according to the rule: "In all derivative formations (*vṛtti*), the masculine form should be stated for pronouns" (Vārttika 104).
Alternatively, this is a genitive compound of the word *dakṣiṇa* with the word *tīra*. [The phrase] "in the address of speech" (*vācovāde*).

When the word *vāda* follows as a subsequent member (*uttarapada*) to the word *vākya*, the substitution of *ḍa* occurs for the [final] syllable. Furthermore, when the suffix *iñ* follows, the substitution of *val* occurs for the subsequent member *vāda*. Thus:
"one who speaks words" (*vācaṃ vadati*) becomes *vāgvāda*; his descendant (*tasyāpatyam*) is formed by the rule *ata iñ* (Pāṇini 4.1.95) as *vāṅvaliḥ*.

"ṣaṣa utvam" and so forth: the substitution of *u* for the vowel of the word *ṣaṣ* occurs when the words *datṛ* or *daśan* follow as the second members of a compound; furthermore, there is the substitution of *ṣṭu* for the initial sound of the second member.
[The example is] a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "one whose teeth (*danta*) are six."
By the rule *vayasa dantasya datṛ* [Pāṇini 5.4.141], there is the substitution of *datṛ*—thus, *ṣoḍan*.
The term *ṣoḍaśa* is a *dvandva* compound meaning "six and ten. Regarding the phrase *dhāsu vā*: [it means that the substitution is optional when followed by words beginning with *dhā*].
This option applies only to the substitution of *u* for *v*; however,
the substitution of *ṣ* for *s* occurs invariably,
as in the forms *ṣoḍhā* and *ṣaṅdhā*.
By [Pāṇini 5.3.43], the suffix *dhā* is applied.
Now, for what purpose is the plural designation "in *dhāsu*" (*dhāsviti*) employed? To this he says: "The plural designation," and so forth.
"[In the word] *ṣaṅdhā*."

The suffix *kap* is applied according to [Pāṇini 3.2.3], "after the roots *dhā* or *dhe*, in the feminine. From the root *dāśṛ* ‘to give’ (DhP 882), from *ṇaśa* ‘to disappear’ (DhP 1194), and from *dambhu* ‘to deceive’ (DhP 1270)—in the sense of the object (*karman*)—the suffix *ghañ* is applied, resulting in *dāśaḥ*, *nāśaḥ*, and *dambhaḥ*.
In the case of the word *duḥśa*, when it forms a *prādi*-compound with words such as *dāśa*, etc., we have *dūḍāśaḥ*, *dūṇāśaḥ*, and *dūḍabhaḥ*.
Regarding the rule "there is elision of the nasal of *dambh*" (*dambheranunāsikalopaḥ*), etc.:

the mention of *dambh* with its nasal elided in the rule "in the case of *dāś*, *nāś*, *dabh*, and *dhyai*" (*dāśanāśadabhadhyeṣu*) is a *nipātana* (an irregularity); from that very fact, the elision of the nasal of *dambh* occurs here.
Those whose fasting consists of fat are "fat-fasting" (*pīvopavasanāḥ*); likewise, "milk-fasting" (*payopavasanāḥ*).
In both cases, there is the elision of the letter *s*.

Regarding the phrase "addition of a phoneme" (*varṇāgama*), he states this verse beginning with "addition of a phoneme," etc., because in the science of etymology (*nirukta*), the correctness of those words that are derived is accepted precisely on the grounds of their belonging to the *pūṣodara*-class and similar groups.

*Varṇāgama* (the addition of a phoneme) is the arrival of a previously non-existent phoneme—the acquisition of a phoneme such as *na* that was not there before—as in *ko jīryate kuñjaraḥ*. Here, the augment *nuk* is applied to the word *ku*.

*Varṇaviparyaya* (the transposition of phonemes) is the exchange of the positions of phonemes; for example, from the root *hisi* (meaning "to injure," Dhātupāṭha 1456), the word *siṃha* ("lion") is derived by adding the suffix *ac* (of the *pacādi* class), wherein there is a transposition of the positions of the phonemes *ha* and *sa*.

Change of phoneme (*varṇavikāra*) is the transformation of one phoneme into another form, as in *ṣoḍan*. Here, there is the transformation of the phoneme *kha* into the form of *u*, and the transformation of the phoneme *da* into the form of *ḍa*.
*Varṇanāśaḥ*—the elision of a phoneme (*varṇa*), as in *pṛṣodara*;
here there is the elision of the letter *t*.

*Arthātiśayaḥ*—a specific meaning, a different meaning from the conventional one; by means of that, there is a connection (*yoga*) with a verbal root (*dhātu*), as in *mayūra*, [derived] from "he roams among the great" (*mahatām rauti*).
In this case, there is an exceeding connection with the meaning "delight" (*ramaṇa*).

This is the fivefold *nirukta*, so called because the meaning is definitively stated (*niścayena ucyate*) by it. Regarding the example "that which occurs in two days": when the sense of "occurring" (*bhava*) is intended, a compound is formed by [Pāṇini 2.1.50] *taddhitārtha*. From that, the suffix *ṭhañ* is applied by [4.3.11]; its elision is effected by [4.1.88] *dvigor lṛganapatye*; the compound-final suffix *ṭac* is added by [5.4.91] *rājāhaḥsakhibhyaṣ ṭac*; and the substitution of *ahn* for *ahan* is applied by [5.4.88] *ahno 'hna etebhyaḥ*.
In the case of *drahni*,
the elision of the vowel *a* is optional by virtue of the rule *vibhāṣā ṅiśyoḥ* [Pāṇini 6.4.136]. In the case of *dvyahnaḥ*, [the elision is obligatory].
"Guṇa is substituted [for the first vowel] when followed by a vowel" (Pāṇini 6.1.84). *Vyahnaḥ* is a *prādi-samāsa* (compound with a prefix);
the remainder is as before.

Regarding the term *sāyāhnaḥ*: this is a *ekadeśisamāsa* (partitive compound). Here, the following objection might be raised: "Indeed, a compound is prescribed by the rule *pūrvāparādharottaram* [Pāṇini 2.2.1] and so forth, but the word *sāyam* is not listed therein; how then is the compounding of the word *sāyam* with the word *ahar* possible here? To refute this, he says: "*The partitive compound applies even to words other than 'pūrva' and the rest,*" and so on.

By the rule *tatpuruṣe* [Pāṇini 5.4.88], the substitution of *ah-* is prescribed; and by the phrase *etebhyaḥ*, the terms beginning with "number" (*saṃkhyā*) and "indeclinable" (*avyaya*)—which were introduced in the rules *tatpuruṣasyāṅguleḥ saṃkhyāvyayādeḥ* [5.4.86] and *ahaḥsarvaikadeśasaṃkhyātapuṇyācca rātreḥ* [5.4.87]—are referred back. In that context, if only words such as *pūrva-* were compounded with a part-whole (*ekadeśin*), then the word *sāyam* would not be referred back by the phrase *etebhyaḥ*; for it is not enumerated among the "numbers" and so forth.

Furthermore, if [the rule were restricted], the substitution of *ah* for the word *sāyam* would not occur; and thus, because the word *ahan* preceded by *sāyam* would be absent, its inclusion here would not be made, yet it is indeed included. Therefore, this very inclusion of the word *ahan* preceded by *sāyam* indicates that a *ekadeśisamāsa* (part-whole compound) occurs even with words other than those beginning with *pūrva*.
By this, the form *madhyāhnaḥ* (midday), derived from *madhyamahnaḥ*, is established.
Regarding "pūrvāhṇe":
the substitution of *ṇ* [for *n*] occurs by the rule "ahno 'dantāt" [Pāṇini 8.4.7].

Although it would have been sufficient to state simply "saṃkhyā-visāyebhyaḥ," the inclusion of the additional word "pūrva" is for the purpose of indicating that this specific operation takes precedence over others.

By this [rule], the elision of the letter *m* in the word *sāyāhne* is established. Regarding the rule *ḍhralope*, is this a *tatpuruṣa* compound or a *bahuvrīhi*? If it were a *tatpuruṣa*—meaning "the elision (*lopa*) of *ḍha* and *ra*" (*ḍhralopa*)—then the status of being "preceding" (*pūrvatva*) would not be possible for the vowel *a*; because elision (*lopa*) is of the nature of non-existence (*abhāva*), and in the case of non-existence, priority and posteriority (*paurvāparya*) are impossible.
