Furthermore, even if "priority" (*pūrvatva*) is asserted by relying on the sequence [of sounds] through the medium of their positions—as in *karaṇīya*, where one might observe the fault that once the *repha* of *apayanīya-ra* is elided, the preceding vowel would become long—the author states "in which there is the elision of the letter ḍ and the letter r," etc., showing that this is a *bahuvrīhi* compound.
A *bahuvrīhi* certainly occurs even with non-co-referential (*vaiyadhikaraṇya*) members when the meaning is clear, as in the example *kāṇṭhekāla*.
[The example] is *līḍham*.

Regarding the word *liha*: from the root *lih* in the sense of "tasting" (*dhātupāṭha* 1066), the suffix *niṣṭhā* is applied; then the following rules must be applied: *ho ḍhaḥ* [Pāṇini 8.2.31], *jhaṣastathordho'dhaḥ* [8.2.40], *ṣṭunā ṣṭuḥ* [8.4.40], and *ḍho ḍhe lopaḥ* [8.3.13]. Thus, the form *mīḍham* is derived from the root *miha* in the sense of "to sprinkle" (*dhātupāṭha* 992).
Regarding "upagūḍham": [the root] *guhū* means "to conceal" (Dhātupāṭha 896).
Regarding "mūḍhaḥ": [it is derived from the root *muha*].
The root *muh* is listed as number 1198 in the Dhātupāṭha with the meaning "to be bewildered.
The word *nīraktam* is a compound formed according to [Pāṇini 2.2.18], and the elision of the *r* is applied by [Pāṇini 8.3.14]: *ro ri*.

Now, for what purpose is the mention of "prior" (*pūrva*)? Since the rule *ḍhralope* (Pāṇini 6.3.111) is indicated by a locative case, even without the mention of "prior," the operation would apply to the prior [element] by virtue of the rule *tasmād ity uttarasya* (Pāṇini 1.1.67). To this he says: "The mention of 'prior' (*pūrvagrahaṇam*)" and so forth.

If the mention of "prior" were absent, because of the governing context of "the subsequent member" (*uttarapada*), the operation would apply only when there is a subsequent member—as in *nīraktam* and the like—but it would not apply when there is no subsequent member—as in *līḍham* and the like.

Although, because the elision of *ḍh* is impossible when there is a subsequent word (*uttarapada*), the lengthening would apply even in the absence of a subsequent word by virtue of the authority of the rule itself, the elision of *r* (in *ra-lopa*) does not apply when there is no subsequent word, since the elision of *r* is possible only when there is a subsequent word. Therefore, the mention of "the preceding" (*pūrva*) is made so that the lengthening of the *aṇ* vowel belonging to the preceding member alone may occur even in the absence of a subsequent word— as in the example *ātṛḍham*.
The roots *tṛhū* and *tṛṇhū* have the meaning "to injure" (*hiṃsārtha*) (Dhātupāṭha 1348, 1350).

Regarding the reading *ādṛḍham* found in some places: this is said to be the form of the past passive participle (*niṣṭhā*) of the root *dṛh*, *dṛhi*, or *dṛhi* in the sense of "growth" or "strengthening" (Dhātupāṭha 733–736), yet this is not tenable; for since *dṛh* is marked with *seṭ* (indicating the presence of the augment *iṭ*), it ought to take that *iṭ*.
Furthermore, even if it were somehow not to occur, it would still have to become *gha* by the rule *evamapi* (Pāṇini 8.2.32).

If it is argued that both [the substitution of *gha* and the lengthening] will not occur because of the specific instruction *sthūlabalavadvivakṣāyām* (Pāṇini 7.2.20), then for that very reason, the lengthening would also not occur.
Some explain the absence of the augment *iṭ* here on the grounds that the teaching regarding augments is non-eternal (*anitya*).
In the rule beginning with *vā druha* [Pāṇini 8.2.33], because of the separation of the yoga (*yogavibhāga*) by the word *vā*, there is optionally an absence of the substitution of *gh*.
Thus we have *āvṛḍham*.
[The root] *vṛhū* means "to lift up" (Dhātupāṭha 1347). [Examples: *ūḍhaḥ*, *ūḍhavān*.

Because [the root] belongs to the *yajādi* class, there is vocalization (*samprasāraṇa*) according to Pāṇini 6.1.15, followed by the substitution of the subsequent vowel (*parapūrvatva*) and lengthening (*dīrghatva*).
In that case, if the mention of the specific letter (*avarṇagrahaṇa*) were not present, the substitution of *u* for *ū* would also apply to the long vowel *ū*.

But surely, because it is subsequent to the semi-vowel vocalization (*saṃprasāraṇa*) and the other operations, the *au*-substitution ought to occur; and thus it is stated in the Bhāṣya: "Since both [rules] are obligatory, the *au*-substitution must occur by virtue of its posteriority. Once the *ā*-substitution has been made, there is semi-vowel vocalization; once the semi-vowel vocalization has been made, there is the substitution of the preceding vowel for the one following the vocalized sound (*saṃprasāraṇapara-pūrvatva*), because the operation has already been effected. Consequently, the *au*-substitution will not occur again. Therefore, the *au*-substitution must indeed take place, and after that, the semi-vowel vocalization and the rest.
And since nothing undesirable follows from this, there is no purpose in the mention of the specific letter (*varṇagrahaṇa*).
Thus, by employing the mention of the *varṇa* (phoneme), he makes this known: "In certain instances, *samprasāraṇa* and the operation dependent upon it are stronger.
By this, what was stated—"*Samprasāraṇa* and the operation dependent upon *samprasāraṇa* are stronger" (Pu. Pa. Vṛ. 103)—is justified.
[The question is: "What is the purpose of the mention of *varṇa*?"
The intention is that even when there is only this much—namely, *odasya*—forms such as *soḍhā* and *soḍhum* are indeed established.

Regarding the phrase "even when [the substitution] has been performed," etc.: from the root *vah* preceded by *ut*, in the conditional (*lṛṅ*), there is *cli*. By [Pāṇini 3.1.44], *tas* becomes *tām* and *thas* becomes *tam*. Then, before the augment *aṭ* is applied, because the substitution of *ḍha* and so forth is considered non-existent (*asiddha*), the vowel lengthening (*vṛddhi*) occurs by [Pāṇini 7.2.3] "for *vad*, *vraj*, etc."; after that, the substitution of *ḍha* and so forth takes place.

Now, if there were no mention of the *varṇa* (phoneme), then the substitution of *o* (*auttvam*) being prescribed for the short *a* (*mātrika*) would not apply to the long [vowel], because [the rule] would apply only to the mere phoneme due to the mention of *varṇa*. Thus, forms such as *udavoḍhām* and *udavoḍham* would not be established. [Objection: But surely, by the rule *na vibhaktau tusmāḥ* [Pāṇini 1.3.4], the short *a* being mentioned will also include the long *ā*; so what is the use of mentioning *varṇa*? To this, he says: "Even from that, the subsequent [element]" (*tādapi paraḥ*), and so forth.

In this regard, even in the rule [Pāṇini 1.1.70], *tādapi parastaparaḥ*, this compound is also adopted for the purpose that the designation *vṛddhi* should not apply to the vowel *e* occurring in three-mora or four-mora forms such as *khaṭvaiḍakaḥ* and *khaṭvaitikāyanaḥ*. In that case, if there were no mention of the term *varṇa* (phoneme), because of the *tapara* status of the letter *a*, the long vowel *ā* would not be included; consequently, its substitution by *ū* would not take place. Therefore, the mention of *varṇa* must be made so that the rule applies to the entire phoneme *a* (both short and long).

Furthermore, it should be understood that this very mention of the vowel *a* (*varṇagrahaṇa*) is the indicator (*jñāpaka*) for the compound *tādapi parastaparaḥ*. In forms such as *sāḍhva*, the absence of *auttvam* (the substitution of *au* for *a* and *u*) is established by nipātana (irregular prescription).

The [substitution] resulting from *dīrghas tu* (Pāṇini 6.3.111) and so forth is already established. The term *uttarapade* (in the following word) is understood [from Pāṇini 6.3.1]; and since an "uttarapada" occurs only within a compound (*samāsa*), there must necessarily be *saṃhitā* (euphonic combination) therein even without an explicit statement. Therefore, regarding the grammatical operations to be described when an "uttarapada" follows, this governing rule (*adhikāra*) is not applicable for that purpose; rather, this governing rule is intended solely for those operations which apply when an "uttarapada" does not follow.

Therefore, showing the utility of this [principle]—that when an operation is prescribed by a certain rule for a word ending in a suffix (uttarapada), that same rule applies even when the word does not end in such a suffix, thereby overriding other rules—he says: "He will state: 'A word of two syllables ending in /t/ [receives ṣatva], except for a finite verb (tiṅ),' etc.

Examples include "vidmā hi tvā" and so forth. In "vidmā," the suffix *mas* of the imperative (*loṭ*) undergoes the elision of its *s* according to Pāṇini 3.4.98; furthermore, due to the root belonging to the *adādi* class, there is the elision of the *śap* augment. A "characteristic" (*lakṣaṇa*) is that by which the connection with a particular master is indicated; it is a mark.
Regarding the term "dātrākarṇa": "dātra" means a sickle; by way of similarity, a mark having that shape is so called. He who has a sickle [shaped mark] on his ear is "dātrākarṇa."
In the same way, it should be understood that in what follows as well, it is a *bahuvrīhi* compound.
That which has two qualities (*guṇa*) is "twofold" (*dviguṇa*). A mark (*cihna*) having that appearance is also "twofold."
The word *guṇa* here signifies "binding.

The combination of two fingers is *dvyaṅgula*; the compound ending [is formed] by the rule *tatpuruṣasyāṅguleḥ* [Pāṇini 5.4.86], and thus even a mark in the shape of two fingers is called *dvyaṅgula*. [The author states:
"In this context, the term is understood to mean a 'mark' (*lakṣaṇa*)."

How is this so? If, by the mention of "characteristic" (*lakṣaṇa*), it were meant that whatever is characterized here in a general sense—be it by anything at all—is to be understood as the "characteristic," then he would have simply said "of the mark" (*cihnasya*). In that case, the sūtra would indeed be more concise. Therefore, since the mention of "mark" (*cihna*) ought to have been made, the fact that the term "characteristic" (*lakṣaṇa*) was used instead indicates that he intended to establish the following point: that what is to be grasped here is a specific kind of characteristic, and not a characteristic in its mere generality. And thus it has been said: "The intentions of the Teachers are indicated here by a hint, by an opening [of the meaning], or by an extensive composition of sūtras."

But surely, by the mention of "characteristic" (*lakṣaṇa*), it is understood here that a specific characteristic is intended, rather than a characteristic in general; however, since that specific distinction has not been shown by the author of the commentary (*vṛttikāra*), how is it to be determined? It is from the acceptance [of the rule] by the Teachers (*ācāryas*).
For example, in the case of "one with beautiful ears" (*śobhanakarṇaḥ*):
although this too is characterized [by the presence of a compound], such a type of characteristic is not what is meant here.
Nor is "beauty" recognized in the world as a *lakṣaṇa* (defining characteristic); thus, this serves as a counter-example. Regarding the root *ṇaha* "to bind" (Dhātupāṭha 1166):

from *upanahrati*, [the word] *upānat* is formed. By virtue of belonging to the *sampadādi* group, the suffix *kvip* is applied. Then, by the rule *naho dhaḥ* (Pāṇini 8.2.34), *dha* replaces *na*; subsequently, there is the substitution of the voiced stop (*jaśtva*) and the retroflex stop (*cartva*). From *parinahrati*, [the word] *pariṇat* is formed.

The substitution of *ṇ* [for *n*] occurs by the rule "after a prefix, except in a compound" (Pāṇini 8.4.14). From the root *vṛt* with the prefix *ni*, the form *nīvṛt* is derived by adding the suffix *kvip* according to Pāṇini 3.3.130.
In the same way, it should be understood that *kvip* alone [is applied] in subsequent cases as well.
From the root *vṛṣu* (meaning "to sprinkle," Dhātupāṭha 706), [the word] *prāvṛṭ* is derived in the sense of "it rains.
The retroflex *ṣ* undergoes *jaś*-tva, becoming *ḍ*; then, by *cari*-tva, that *ḍ* becomes *ṭ*.

The root *vyadh* means "to pierce" (*dhātupāṭha* 1181). From the sense "he pierces the vital points (*marmāṇi*)," the term *marmāvit* is derived; by the rule [Pāṇini 6.1.16] governing the *grah*-class, there is vocalization (*samprasāraṇa*).

The root *ruc* means "to shine" (*dhātupāṭha* 745)—[the Dhātupāṭha also notes it means "to please"]—and from *nirocanam*, the term *nīruk* is formed; by the rule [Pāṇini 8.2.30], there is the substitution of *k* for *c*.

"Ṛtīṣaṭ" means "one who endures distress. Regarding the word "ṛtīṣaṭ," the substitution of *ṣ* for *s* occurs because of the rule *saheḥ pṛtanartābhyāñca* (Pāṇini 8.3.109); this is either due to a split in the rule (*yogavibhāga*) of the term *saheḥ*, or because the particle *ca* has the sense of an inclusive conjunction (*anuktasamuccaya*).
"Parītat" means "one who extends around."

When the elision of the nasal (*anunāsika-lopa*) has been performed, the augment *tuk* is applied. But by what rule here is the elision of the nasal effected? To this he says: "In the case of the root *gam* followed by the suffix *kvip*," and so forth. It is intended [to apply] only when preceded by a preverb (*gati*) or a kāraka. For that purpose, the term "optionally" (*vibhāṣā*) is understood to carry over from rule 6.3.106; and that should be understood as a restricted option (*vyavasthita-vibhāṣā*). Thus we have the form *koṭarāvaṇam*.
This is a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*). The substitution of *ṇ* [for *n*] occurs by the rule "vanaṃ purugā" (Pāṇini 8.4.4) and so forth. Regarding "Viśvāvasuḥ":
it is a possessive compound (*bahuvrīhi*) meaning "one whose wealth (*vasu*) is universal (*viśva*)."

Regarding the term *viśvārāṭ*: it means "one who rules over the universe" (*viśvasmin rājate*). The suffix *kvip* is applied by the rule *satsūdviṣa* [Pāṇini 3.2.61]. By the rule *vraścādi* [Pāṇini 8.2.36], the substitution of *ṣ* occurs. For that *ṣ*, by the rule *jhalāṃ jaś ante* [Pāṇini 8.2.39], the substitution of a *jaś* sound occurs—namely, the letter *ḍ*. Furthermore, for the letter *ḍ*, the substitution of a *car* sound occurs—namely, the letter *ṭ*. Regarding the phrase "where this form of it [occurs]": where, then, does this form occur? It occurs where there is the designation of a *pada* (word); for the application of the *ṣ* and other such substitutions is prescribed within the governing context (*adhikāra*) of *pada*.

Regarding "viśvarājau" and "viśvarājaḥ," there is no designation as a *pada* here, due to the prohibition [by Pāṇini 1.4.17] stating "not before a case-ending that is not a *sarvanāmasthāna*. In "vrīhimatī" and similar forms, the suffix *matup* occurs as previously explained. However, in "valayavatī," [the suffix *matup* is applied] by [Pāṇini 5.2.94]. This rule is commenced because the meaning "many" (*bahvartha*) is not intended here.
Regarding "śarāvatī":
[the suffix] *matup* is applied according to [Pāṇini 4.2.85]. Regarding "ṛṣīvahaḥ" (or "ṛṣīvaham" according to the Kāśikā):
this is a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*).

The word *vaha* ends in the suffix *ac* (by the rule *pacādyac*). Regarding the phrase "not for *pīlu* and so forth," the meaning is that this rule prescribing the lengthening of the vowel *i* (*iko dīrgha*) must be explained as having the sense that it does not apply to *pīlu* and the others.

In this regard, the explanation is as follows: here too, that same mention of "mostly" (*bahula*) applies as before; therefore, by virtue of that, the lengthening of the vowel will not occur for some other words besides *pīlu*. As for the rule regarding "after a prefix" (*upasargāt*): a suffix *ghan* alone cannot occur [after a prefix]; therefore, it is understood that the grammatical operation applies when the word ending in *ghan* is the subsequent member of a compound. Thus he says: "when the subsequent member ends in *ghan*" and so forth. Regarding the example *vīkledaḥ*:

the root *klid* (in the sense of "becoming wet") is listed as 1242 in the Dhātupāṭha (and *klidū* is also found there); the suffix *ghan* is applied according to Pāṇini 3.3.19, *akartari ca kārake*, etc.
Regarding the word *vīmārgaḥ*: the root *mṛj* means "to cleanse" (Dhātupāṭha 1066); by [Pāṇini 7.2.114] and [Pāṇini 7.3.52], the substitution of *k* occurs (*kutvam*). Regarding the word *prasevaḥ*.
The root *ṣivu* means "to weave" (*tantusantāne*, Dhātupāṭha 1108).
Regarding the word *kṛtrima*:
that which is produced by means of an instrument (*karaṇa*) is *kṛtrima*.
The meaning is that it is produced by human activity and so forth.

Regarding the word "niṣāda": according to the root list (dhātupāṭha 854), the root *ṣadlṛ* means "to perish," "to go," or "to sink. It is called a *niṣāda* because sin (*pāpa*) sinks (*niṣīdati*) into it.
The suffix *ghañ* is applied by [Pāṇini 3.3.121] *halaśca*. Regarding the word *nīkāśaḥ*:
the root *kāsṛ* means "to shine" (Dhātupāṭha 647).
This word *kāśa* ends in the suffix *ac* (from the *pacādi* group) and does not end in *ghañ*.
The intention here is that [the desired form] is already established by the preceding rule alone.

Regarding the statement found in some texts—"Since it is already established by the preceding rule, this is for the sake of restriction (niyamārtha), meaning that in the word *kāśa*, the suffix *ika* occurs only after this [specific stem] and not after any other"—this is untenable; for while the preceding rule prescribes the long vowel (*dīrgha*) before the *ghañ* suffix, this word *kāśa* ends in the *ac*-suffix added after the root class beginning with *pac* (*pacādyac*). If, on the other hand, it is argued that because of the mention of "diversely" (*bahulagrahaṇa*), the form is already established even when ending in *pacādyac*, and that for that very reason of "diversely," the suffix *ika* will not occur after any other [stem], then this sūtra need not be composed at all.

And that which is being performed should be understood as being for the purpose of elaborating upon the preceding [rule]. Regarding the statement "the substitute beginning with *t* for this [root] *dā*":
by this, it is understood that in the relationship between the original element (*sthānin*) and the substitute (*ādeśa*), the genitive case in *daḥ* [expresses the sense of "for" or "in place of"].
[The example is] *vīttam*.
This is the form of the past passive participle (*niṣṭhā*) of the root *dā*.

Now, one might object that a substitute beginning with *t* cannot possibly occur here as a subsequent element; for instance, the *t* [prescribed] by the rule *yastāvat...* (Pāṇini 7.4.47) is applied to the final letter according to the statement *saḥ...* (Pāṇini 1.1.52), and since that is separated by other phonemes, a *t* occurring immediately after it as a subsequent element is not possible. Furthermore, even the substitution of *t* for *d* prescribed by the rule *khari ca* (Pāṇini 8.4.54) is likewise impossible.

Since the substitution of *c* for *t* (*cartva*) would be non-existent due to its being considered unestablished (*asiddha*) when lengthening is to be performed, he says: "From a prefix, *t* is substituted for *d*" (*aca upasargāt taḥ*), and so forth.
"Resorting" (*āśrayaṇa*) means taking as a basis or accepting.

In the rule for the word *dā*, the substitution of an affix beginning with *t* is resorted to by stating that a prefix ending in *i* undergoes lengthening when that [affix] follows; for otherwise, an affix beginning with *t* could not possibly follow.
Therefore, because the rule is based on the presence of the suffix *ni*, it is established that the substitute begins with the letter *t*. Thus,
[the form] is *nitīrṇam*.

From the root *tṛ* in the sense of "floating" or "crossing over" (*dā|pā|969*), there is the substitution of *i* for *ṛ* by [Pāṇini 7.1.100] *ṛta id dhātoḥ*; then, by [Pāṇini 8.2.77] *hali ca*, there is lengthening;
and by [Pāṇini 8.4.2] *aṭkupvāṅnumvyavāye 'pi*, there is the substitution of *ṇ* for *n*. Thus, we have *sudattam*.

Regarding the rule *do dadghoḥ* [Pāṇini 7.4.46], it is stated: "In the sense of the beginning of an action (*ādikarman*), the forms *avadattam*, *vidattam*, *prādattam*, *sudattam*, *anudattam*, and *nidattam* are desired. By this desired rule, there is the substitution of *dad* for the root *dā*. Thus, we have *aṣṭāvakraḥ*; this is a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "one whose eight parts are crooked" (*aṣṭau vakrāṇy asya*). And [we have] *aṣṭākapālam*.
The suffix *aṇ* is applied according to the rule *aṣṭasu kapāleṣu saṃskṛtam* (Pāṇini 4.4.3), and that suffix is elided by the rule *dvigor lug anapatye* (Pāṇini 4.1.88).
Thus, we have *aṣṭāhiraṇyā*;
this is a *bahuvrīhi* compound.
"When the foot has been elided," according to [Pāṇini 5.4.138];
"when joined with *go*," and so forth.

"It is to be stated" means that this is what is to be explained. In this regard, the explanation is as follows: the particle *ca* (and) is employed here, and it serves the purpose of including that which has not been explicitly mentioned.
Therefore, when *go* is joined [with another word], even in the *bhāṣā* (colloquial) register, the long vowel occurs for *aṣṭan*. Regarding the example *ekacitīkaḥ*:

it is a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "one whose layer (*citī*) is one"; then, by the rule *striyāḥ puṃvat* [Pāṇini 6.3.34] and others, there is the substitution of the masculine form, followed by the suffix *kap* [Pāṇini 5.4.154]. [The commentary states]: "This is a governing rule (*adhikāra*)," because it is connected with a circumflex accent (*svarita*) as its indicator.

In this regard, some maintain that this governing rule (*adhikāra*) regarding the "stem" (*aṅga*) is appropriate prior to the modifications [introduced by] the *abhyāsa* (reduplication). For if this were so, the mention of *luk* (elision) would not need to be made in the sūtra [P. 7.4.82], because even in the case of *yaṅ-luk*, the *guṇa* substitution would be established by means of the *pratyaya-lakṣaṇa* (the application of rules conditioned by an affix). However, if this governing rule for the stem were to extend until the conclusion of the seventh chapter, then the mention of *luk* would necessarily have to be made; otherwise, the *guṇa* would not be established in *yaṅ-luk* due to the prohibition [contained in P. 1.1.63]. This is their intention.

The author of the *Vṛtti*, however, [argues as follows]: If this section on the substitution of *aṅga* were to apply prior to the modifications resulting from practice (*abhyāsa*), then in the case of *vavraśca*—where the root *vṛśc* takes the suffix *liṭ* and reduplication has been performed—the substitution of *samprasāraṇa* would occur by means of a prior prohibition (*pūrvapratiṣedha*) even before the application of *halādiśeṣa*. By the force of the statement "of both" (*ubhayeṣām*), the *samprasāraṇa* would override even the subsequent *halādiśeṣa*. Consequently, after the formation of the single substitute by *pūrvarūpa* according to [Pāṇini 6.1.108], the substitution of *at* by *urat* [7.4.66], the replacement of *a* by *r* (*raparatva*), and the application of *halādiśeṣa*, the *samprasāraṇa* of the letter *v* would also undesirably follow.

Up until the completion of the seventh chapter, since there is again the governing rule (*adhikāra*) regarding suffixes (*aṅga*), the suffix is relied upon as the cause for the rule *uraṛ* [Pāṇini 7.4.66]. Because it has a subsequent cause (*paranimittatva*), the *samprasāraṇa* of the vowel *u* in the case of *uradat-tvasya* is prohibited by the rule *samparasarāṇam* [Pāṇini 6.1.36] with respect to the substitution of the semivowel *v*.

If the governing scope (*adhikāra*) of "stem" (*aṅga*) were to apply prior to the rules concerning modifications of the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa-vikāra*), then, because it would not have a subsequent cause (*apara-nimitta*), the status of being "as if occupying the original position" (*sthānivadbhāva*) would not apply to the substitution of *u* for *ṛ* (by P. 6.4.19). Consequently, due to the absence of that prohibition [stated in] P. 6.1.37, the *samprasāraṇa* of the letter *v* would indeed occur;
as a result, the undesirable form *uvraśc* would arise.

Therefore, considering that it is logical for the governing scope of "stem" to extend until the end of the seventh chapter rather than ending prior to the rules on reduplicated syllable modifications, he says: "until the completion of the seventh chapter."

However, after the completion of the seventh chapter, an operation (*kārya*) is prescribed under the governing rule *padasya* [Pāṇini 8.1.16]; therefore, the governing heading for the *aṅga* does not continue there. From the root *hveñ* (meaning "to contend" and "to call out"—Dhātupāṭha 1008), the past passive participle suffix (*niṣṭhā*) is applied; because it belongs to the *yajādi* group, *samprasāraṇa* occurs.

Regarding the word "jīnaḥ": from the root *jyā* in the sense of "loss of vitality" (Dhātupāṭha 1499), there is vocalization (*samprasāraṇa*) by the rule [Pāṇini 6.1.16], and the substitution of *ṇatva* for the final *t* by the rule [Pāṇini 8.2.44]. Regarding the word "saṃvītaḥ": [it is derived from the root *vye* with the prefix *sam-*].

The root *vyeñ* in the sense of "covering" (*saṃvaraṇe*; Dhātupāṭha 1007) undergoes *samprasāraṇa* according to Pāṇini 6.1.15, resulting in the forms *niruta* and *duruta*. The root *veñ* in the sense of "weaving" (*tantusantāne*; Dhātupāṭha 1006) likewise undergoes *samprasāraṇa* as before.
If the governing context were "non-member" (*asatyaṅga*), then for a *hal* (consonant) that is a part of the prefix *ni-* or *dur-*, the long vowel would apply even to the subsequent *samprasāraṇa*.

However, since the governing context is "member" (*aṅga*), it is understood that the lengthening applies to the entire member (*aṅga*) which ends in that *samprasāraṇa* following a *hal* that is a part of the member;
thus, there is no occasion for the application of lengthening here, because the *samprasāraṇa* does not follow a *hal* that is a part of the member.
Regarding the word *agnīnām*:

by the rule *hrasvanadyāpo nuṭ* [Pāṇini 7.1.54], [the suffix *nuṭ* is applied]. As in: "Look at the *krimiṇaḥ* (those afflicted with worms); look at the *pāmanaḥ* (those afflicted with skin diseases)."

The suffix *na* is applied by the rule *lomādi* (Pāṇini 5.2.99) because of the sense "there are worms (*krimayaḥ*) in this" or "there are scabs (*pāmānaḥ*) in this"; from that, the feminine suffix *ṭāp* is added, followed by the second case singular ending.
By the rule [6.1.107], there is the substitution of the single preceding form (*pūrvarūpatvam*).

If the phrase "of the base (*aṅgasya*)" were not supplied as a governing heading (*adhikāra*), then even in these cases, the lengthening of the vowel would occur for the words *krimi-* and *pāma-* when followed by a *nāmi* (a strong case ending beginning with a vowel).

However, there is no fault in the context of the definition of a "stem" (*aṅga*). For here, the words *krimi* and *pāman* do not possess the status of a stem (*aṅgatva*) when followed by a *nām* suffix; rather, they have it when followed by the suffix *nap*, as in *brāhmaṇabhissā* and *odanabhissiṭā*.
The words *bhissā* and *bhissiṭā* end in the feminine suffix *ṭāp*;
therein, one denotes boiled rice (*odana*), while the other denotes its burnt form.
In those two cases, there is respectively a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*) of the words *brāhmaṇa* and *odana*.

In that context, if the governing rule for "limbs" (*aṅga*) were not present, the substitution of *ais* for *bhis* would undesirably apply even after the words *brāhmaṇa* and *odana*, which are not "limbs."

But surely, according to the rule "when there is the apprehension of that which has meaning, not of that which is meaningless" (*vyā.pa.* 1), just as there will be no lengthening in examples such as *krimiṇām paśya* ("look at the worms") and *pāmanām paśya* ("look at the scabies-afflicted"), so too there would be no substitution of *ais* in *brāhmaṇabhissaudanabhissiṭa*, since neither the *nām* nor the *bhis* here possesses meaning. Why, then, is the governing heading for "stem" (*aṅga*) required to exclude those cases? To this he says: "The governing heading for 'stem' (*aṅga*)," and so forth; and "the lengthening of *nām*," and so forth. By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), the substitution of *ais* [by Pāṇini 7.1.9] is included.
The particle *iti* is used here in the sense of a reason (*hetu*).

Because, even though there is no governing rule for the suffix *aṅ*, the lengthening [of the vowel] by the rule *halaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.4.2)—as it occurs in forms such as *hūtaḥ* and *jīnaḥ*—would likewise apply in cases such as *nīrutam* and *durutam*.
Similarly, the lengthening by the rule *san-liṭor jeḥ* (Pāṇini 6.4.16)—as it occurs in *cikīrṣati*—would likewise apply in cases such as *dadhi sanoti* and *madhu sanoti*.

> [Pāṇini 6.4.67] `vānyasya saṃyogādeḥ` [6.4.68]: Just as the substitution of *e* occurs in *gleyāt*, it would likewise occur in *niryāyāt* and *nirvāyāt*. Therefore, the governing context (*adhikāra*) of "stem" (*aṅga*) must necessarily be established for such purposes.

Being established for other purposes, it also regulates the lengthening of the vowel in *nām* (the genitive singular ending) by excluding it from other domains and restricting it to its intended domain.

Therefore, this technical rule (*paribhāṣā*) need not be resorted to for that purpose. The point is that a technical rule is indeed resorted to only when there is no other way. Now, one might object: because of the statement [P. 1.1.49], the term *aṅgasya* is a genitive of location (*sthāna-ṣaṣṭhī*); consequently, in the rule *ato bhisa ais* [P. 7.1.9], how could this word ending in a genitive be in grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the word *aṅgasya* which ends in a genitive [in P. 1.1.49]? For they possess different case endings.

And if that were the case, then in the word *satyakārāntāt* (from [the rule] ending in *satyakāra*), the substitution of *ai* for *bhī* in the subsequent word *bhissā* would result; furthermore, in the rule *ūdupadhāyā gohaḥ* [Pāṇini 6.4.89], because the genitive case in *gohaḥ* is understood as a "genitive of the locus" (*sthāna-ṣaṣṭhī*)—as concluded by the mention of *ali* at the end [of Pāṇini 1.1.52]—and due to the force of the inclusion of the term *upadhā*, the substitution of *ū* would apply to the final letter of *goh*.

Regarding the rule *upadhāmātrasya ca* (P. 6.4.34), even here, because the genitive case in *śāsaḥ* is understood as a genitive of location (*sthāna-ṣaṣṭhī*), and because the final letter is subsequently restricted [to the substitute], and by the force of the continued application of the term *upadhā*, one might think that the substitution of *it* applies to the final letter of *śās* as well as to its entire penultimate portion. To set aside this objection, he says: "This genitive in *aṅgasya* expresses a general relation," and so forth.
"General relation" means a mere relation without further specification.

In that regard, having proceeded by taking up a general relation (*sambandhasāmānya*)—which does not depend on specific particulars—for the sake of encompassing numerous relations, it settles upon specific instances as appropriate within subsequent *lakṣya* sentences whose meanings are distinct. In some cases, its application occurs through a formal connection (*sthānayoga*), as in [Pāṇini 6.4.36] and so forth; in other cases, it concerns the relationship between a cause and its effect (*nimittanimittisambandha*), as in [Pāṇini 7.1.1] and so forth.

For just as the single genitive case ending in *devadattasya*, having been introduced by the sixth [case] distinction, becomes differentiated by various types of relations among kinsmen, limbs, and so forth, and accordingly presents itself in specific relations such as that of produced and producer—as in *devadattasya putraḥ* ("Devadatta’s son"), *pāṇiḥ* ("hand"), or *kambalaḥ* ("blanket")—so too does this [genitive] in *aṅgasya*.

In that regard, in a sentence such as *yasmin...* (Pāṇini 6.4.34) and so on, where a specific related entity exists—whether it be a limb (*avayava*) or something else—the genitive should be understood according to the appropriate relation with the limb or other such entities.

The genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) occurs in that place where [something] is not found, as in *itayavam-ādau* (P. 6.4.36). But how is it understood that this is a genitive expressing a general relationship (*sambandhasāmānye*), given that it has been stated [in P. 1.1.49] that "the genitive denotes the place of substitution" (*ṣaṣṭhī sthāneyogā*)? He thinks as follows: not every genitive denotes a relationship of substitution; rather, it is that for which a characteristic such as *kalādi* is prescribed. Otherwise, the explicit mention of the word "place" (*sthāna*) in the rule *udīcām ātaḥ sthāne* (P. 7.3.46) would be purposeless.
Therefore, it has been stated that only that specific genitive which has "parts" (*kalā*) and so forth as its sign is used in the sense of "substitution" (*sthāneyoga*).
Since this [genitive] does not have "parts" and so forth as its sign,
it cannot be considered a case of substitution.
Regarding the phrase "Or rather" (*atha vā*), etc.:
that which is governed is the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) *aṅga* itself, and not this specific word-form *eṅsya*.
The word *mātra* is used for the purpose of excluding the meaning of the case ending.
Therefore he says: "the meaning of the case-ending is not intended to be expressed.
That is, that in which the meaning of the case-ending is not intended to be expressed is merely the object (artha-mātra); thus it is said.
And since this is so, [the rule] "the sixth case-affix is used in connection with 'sthāne'" applies.
This technical rule (*paribhāṣā*) does not apply here.
For this rule was formulated for the purpose of excluding other relations when there is the possibility of multiple relations.

Therefore, it applies as a restrictive rule only where a relation is intended to be expressed; but here no relation is intended to be expressed by the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*), its employment being solely for the sake of formal reference.
Indeed, since a designation must necessarily be made by some case-ending or another, the genitive case has been employed here.

But is it not the case that "the governing force (adhikāra) is indicated by the circumflex accent" (*svarita*), and that this is a property of the word (*śabda-dharma*), not a property of the meaning (*artha-dharma*)? How then can a meaning devoid of the circumflex accent be subject to the governing force? This is not a fault; for the meaning conveyed by the word *aṅga* is itself essentially of the nature of a word.
For instance, it is because the technical name *aṅga* is prescribed for the word beginning with that [element] after which the suffix is introduced.

"Later on, it is modified according to the requirements," and so forth. This is due to the force of the meaning (*arthavaśāt*): in some cases by means of the genitive case-ending itself, and in other cases by means of another case-ending. For example: *āḍhyasya dhanino devadattaḥ* ("the wealthy Devadatta"), *uccānyasya gṛhāṇi* ("his houses are high"), and *āmantrayasvainam devadattam* ("invite this Devadatta").

Therefore, in the rule *ato bhisa ais* [Pāṇini 7.1.9], when there is a modification of the case-ending into the ablative form, the resulting sense becomes: "the substitution of *ais* for *bhis* occurs after a stem (*aṅga*) ending in the vowel *a*. Thus, the intended meaning is established.

By the word "ādi" (and so forth), the rule that "the *ṅas* following *yuṣmad* and *asmad* becomes *aś*" is included. From the word "api" (also), the genitive of part (*avayava-ṣaṣṭhī*) and others are also fully accounted for.

However, in the previous explanation regarding the rule "ato bhis ais" [Pāṇini 7.1.9], this genitive "ataḥ" should be understood as expressing the relationship between cause and effect (*nimitta-nimitti-sambandhe*).

In this regard, the meaning of the Sūtra is as follows: "Of a stem (*aṅga*) ending in *a*, when *bhis* follows, *ais* occurs in its place. Therefore, it does not apply in cases such as *brāhmaṇabhiḥ*.
For what is the *bhis* of the stem? That which is its cause (*nimitta*).

What, then, is its cause? It is the *bhis* [case-ending] when it is understood that "in this [element], there is a member (*aṅga*) which has become something else. And in what does this occur? In a suffix (*pratyaya*). Furthermore, since in forms such as *brāhmaṇibhiḥ*, the suffix is *bhis*, how could there be any occasion for *ais* to apply to it? This refers to the mention of *aṇ*, the mention of *samprasāraṇa*, and the mention of *dīrgha*; all three of these continue to apply [from the preceding rules].
But from where does the mention of *aṇ* (the suffix *a*) come? It comes from [Pāṇini 6.3.111].

But has that not been excluded by the mention of *ig* (the suffix *i*) in [Pāṇini 6.3.123]? How then can it be carried over here? This is not a fault; for by the mention of *ig*, only *aṇ* is qualified—namely, "an *aṇ* which is not *ig*.
Therefore, because there is no contradiction, the mention of *aṇ* is not excluded by the mention of *ig*.
Now, if the mention of *iK* (short vowels) is intended to qualify the mention of *aṇ* (all vowels), then in forms such as *avācā* and *svarācā*, lengthening would not occur.
[To this we reply: In the rule *cau* [Pāṇini 6.3.137], only the mention of *aṇ* will be carried over (*anuvartate*), while the mention of *iK* has ceased; thus, there is no fault.
Alternatively, even though the mention of *aṇ* is excluded by the mention of *iK*, it nevertheless carries over here according to the maxim of the frog-leap (*maṇḍūkapluti*).

Now, one might think: "Just as the rule *śeṣe* [Pāṇini 4.2.91] is both a prescriptive rule (*vidhi*) and a governing heading (*adhikāra*), so too is this rule *ḍiti* [Pāṇini 6.4.1]. Consequently, since forms such as *hūtaḥ* and *jīnaḥ* would be established by this very rule, the statement *halaḥ* [Pāṇini 6.4.2] is purposeless; therefore, it should not even be composed. Thinking thus, he asks:
"What is the purpose of *halaḥ*?"—that is to say, for what reason is this sūtra being commenced?
Regarding the phrase "utaḥ, utavān":
if this sūtra did not exist, then when it is stated that "the long vowel occurs for a base (aṅga) ending in a *saṃprasāraṇa*," the lengthening would apply here as well.

For even this [base] is a base ending in a *saṃprasāraṇa* by virtue of the principle of "behaving like that which possesses the designation" (*vyapadeśivadbhāva*). Therefore, the sūtra "halaḥ" must be formulated.
Regarding the forms *viddhaḥ* and *vicitaḥ*:

the root *vyadha* means "to strike" (Dhātupāṭha 1181), and *vyaca* means "to deceive" (Dhātupāṭha 1293). The suffix *niṣṭhā* is applied, and by the rule [Pāṇini 6.1.16] beginning with *grah*, there is vocalization (*samprasāraṇa*).
Because the rule for lengthening applies to a stem that ends in a vocalized element, the lengthening does not occur here.

Although it might be understood from the rule *grahijyāvayivyadhivaṣṭivicati* [Pāṇini 6.1.16]—which mentions *grahi* as an example—that the long vowel does not apply to the *samprasāraṇa* of a consonant-final element, nevertheless, explaining this matter by means of such an indicator (*jñāpaka*) would result in excessive cognitive burden (*pratipattigaurava*). To avoid this, it is stated that the term applies to "that which ends in a *samprasāraṇa*. Regarding the word *tṛtīyaḥ*:
the suffix *tīya* and the *samprasāraṇa* substitution are applied according to [Pāṇini] 5.2.54 and 5.2.55.

Does every *mātrā* exist, or is there no *aṇ*? Why is there no *aṇ*? Because [the rule] *ḍhralope* (Pāṇini 6.3.111) follows here the mention of *aṇ*, and in that context, the pratyāhāra is understood by means of the preceding *ṇ* alone; since the vowel *ṛ* is not included therein, this indeed serves as a counter-example.
[The phrase] "or by the third," etc., means:
alternatively, the term *aṇ* has simply ceased to apply.

Nevertheless, the lengthening does not actually occur here, due to the specific grammatical rule (*nipātana*): "The third case ending is used for the agent and the instrument" (Pāṇini 2.3.18). Three possible meanings for the word *halaḥ* are conceivable: first, that the lengthening occurs for a stem (*aṅga*) ending in a semivowel (*samprasāraṇa*) that follows a consonant (*hal*); second, that the lengthening occurs for a semivowel (*samprasāraṇa*) following a consonant (*hal*) which is a member of the stem (*aṅga*); and third, as shown by the author of the *Vṛtti* itself.
If the first alternative were adopted, then lengthening would also apply in cases such as *niruttam* and *duruttam*.
This is indeed a valid reply: even here, the *aṅga* (base) ends with a semivowel resulting from *samprasāraṇa*.
If, on the other hand, the second [consonant] were [the cause of the *samprasāraṇa*], then [the rule] would apply in cases such as *viddhaḥ* and *vicitaḥ* as well;
for in those cases too, there is a *samprasāraṇa* following a consonant (*hal*) that is part of the *aṅga*.

Now, one might argue that [the lengthening] will not occur because of the specific grammatical indications (nirdeśa) in the rules *atha* (Pāṇini 4.4.83) and *grahijyāvayivyadhivaṣṭivicati* (Pāṇini 6.1.16). Consequently, by means of such an indicator (jñāpaka), there would indeed be a burden on the understanding regarding the absence of lengthening in such cases.
Therefore, with the desire to avoid this very fault, the author of the Vṛtti has presented a third meaning.

Even here, this objection is raised: "But surely this meaning of the rule is not tenable at all, because the term 'of the aṅga' (*aṅgasya*) is already present as a single, established reference to the *aṅga*."
And that [term *hal*] must either be a qualifier of [the term *saṃprasāraṇa*], or it must be for the purpose of understanding the operation as applying to the *aṅga*.

In that regard, if the first alternative is adopted, then because [the rule would apply to] an *aṅga* qualified by the *aṅga*, the lengthening would not be obtained for an *aṅga* ending in *saṃprasāraṇa*. If, on the other hand, the second [alternative] is adopted, then *hal* would not be qualified.
Therefore, a second mention of the word *aṅga* ought to be made;
for it is not possible to convey both of these [meanings] by means of a single [mention].
Thus, in order to refute this objection, he says "the mention of *aṅga*" and so forth, relying on the principle of repetition (*āvṛtti*).
For even a single entity, when repeated, serves multiple purposes;
just as a single vessel is used for the act of eating by many people who do not eat simultaneously, so too is this mention of the *aṅga* (base) repeated.

In that regard, through the non-repetition [of the rule], the *hal* (consonant) is qualified, whereas through the repetition, the lengthening of the *aṅga* occurs; thus, the comprehension of the meaning is achieved in both ways. The forms "tisṛ" and "catasṛ" are given as a reference after applying the elision (*luk*) of the genitive dual ending according to Pāṇini 7.1.39, *supāṃ suluk*.
In the forms *tisṛṇām* and *catasṛṇām*,
the substitutes *tisṛ* and *catasṛ* occur [by Pāṇini 7.2.99].
But surely, in this case, there is no possibility for the lengthening [of the vowel] at all?

Why [is this] by way of prohibition? For in this case, once the two substitutes have been applied, both would apply: the augment *nuṭ* and the substitution of *r* according to [Pāṇini 7.2.100]. Therein, because the substitution of *r* occurs due to its higher status, the stem (*aṅga*) no longer ends in *an*.
Since a stem ending in *ac* ought to undergo lengthening—and because the rule *acaśca* [1.2.28] is brought to mind by the mention of "lengthening" (*dīrgha*)—he says: "This very... and so forth.

If the substitution of *r* were to occur here, this prohibition would not have been made; yet it has been made. Therefore, this prohibition indicates that—by means of a prior conflict (*pūrvavipratiṣedha*)—the augment *nuṭ* occurs [after a stem ending in *ṛ*, even when the conditions for the rules at Aṣṭādhyāyī 7.2.100 apply].

By this, it is stated: "The augment *nuṭ* occurs by prior conflict in preference to the *num* augment, the *aci-r-ṛt* rule, and the *jvadbhāva*. The expression "in both ways" (*ubhayathā*), where one might simply say "optionally" (*vā*), is for the sake of stylistic variety. Some do not carry forward the phrase "in the Veda" (*chandasi*) from that rule.
They think as follows: "If this rule were intended for Vedic usage alone, he would have made it a single rule, [Pāṇini 6.4.7]: *chandasi nṛ cobhayathā*.
For the particle *ca* there serves to draw forward [the terms] *tisṛ* and *catasṛ*.

Since the matter is established by that single rule alone, the fact that he makes a separate rule leads to the conclusion that this rule applies to the spoken language (*bhāṣā*) as well. This [separate] formulation is for the sake of excluding words ending in *-ac*."

The word *na* ends in the sixth case singular (*ṣaṣṭhy-ekavacana*). Because this is a sūtra formulation, the elision of the letter *y* is not treated as non-existent (*asiddha*), and thus [the rule] is applied according to Pāṇini 6.1.87. Since *na* is a mention of a specific phoneme (*varṇagrahaṇa*), and because in all cases involving a mention of a phoneme the rule of "specification by the final element" (*tadantavidhi*) is invoked, it is understood that the penultimate vowel (*upadhā*) of a stem (*aṅga*) ending in *n* undergoes lengthening. Therefore, he says: "of a stem ending in *n*" (*nakārāntasyāṅgasya*). The example is "pañcānām."
Thus, there is the elision of the letter *n*. Here, by the mention of "long" (*dīrgha*), the presence of the paribhāṣā *acaśca* [Pāṇini 1.2.28] is brought about;
furthermore, due to the governing rule [of the preceding section], the term "penultimate" (*upadhā*) is also implied.
[The phrase] "*ṣapūrvasya*" [refers to that which is preceded by *ṣ*].

The term *ṣapūrva* is a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "that which has *ṣa* as its predecessor. In this context, if the *upadhā* (penultimate letter) were taken as the referent for the external object (*anyapadārtha*) of the compound, the masculine designation *ṣapūrvasya* would be untenable; therefore, he states "of the vowel (*acaḥ*) preceded by *ṣa*" and so forth, indicating that the vowel is here taken as the referent for the external object. The word *upadhāyāḥ* is a coreferential (*samānādhikaraṇa*) qualifier of the vowel.

Regarding "ṛbhukṣāṇām": *ṛbhukṣas* is in the nominative singular; since the term *pathimathyṛbhukṣām* [Pāṇini 7.1.85] is being carried over, the substitution of *at* occurs by [Pāṇini] 7.1.86 (*ito'tsarvanāmasthāne*).
The mention of "pūrva" (the preceding) is for the sake of the subsequent rule.

But here, if only "vā ṣo nigame" were stated, lengthening would indeed be indicated optionally by [Pāṇini 6.4.7], which prescribes lengthening for a vowel following a *ṣ*. The letter *a* after the *s* is for the sake of pronunciation (*uccāraṇārtha*). It is described as such because it ends in *s* (*sa-anta*). This reference "sānta" is without a case ending (*avibhaktika*), because the sixth case ending that arose there has been elided.
"Of that which ends in *s*, the conjunction [is dropped], and [the final letter] of *mahat* is also [dropped].
In this rule as well, the word "nakāraḥ" (the letter *n*) is required [from a previous context].

Both "of that which ends in *s*" (*sakārāntasya*) and "of *mahat*" (*mahataḥ*) are genitives denoting parts (*avayava-ṣaṣṭhī*); the meaning is: "that *n* which is a constituent part of the conjunction ending in *s*, and that which is a constituent part of the word *mahat*."
By this, he shows that both "preceded by *sa*" (*sānta*) and the word "great" (*maha*) are qualifiers of the letter *n*. [The rule] "of its penultimate vowel" (*tasyopadhāyāḥ*):
by the word "its" (*tasya*), the letter *n* is referred back.
The meaning is "of the penultimate (upadhā) belonging to that *n*.
By this also, he indicates that the *n* is a qualifier of the penultimate.

But what is the relationship between the *n* and the penultimate, by virtue of which it is designated as "belonging to that" (*tasya*)? It is the relationship of cause and effect (*nimitta-naimittika-bhāva*).

For, with respect to the final *n*, when there is the state of being a penultimate (*upadhā*), the letter preceding that final *n* becomes the penultimate. Therefore, the *n* is the cause (*nimitta*), and the penultimate is the effect (*naimittika*).
Alternatively, the relationship is characterized by proximity; thus, the meaning is "of the penultimate situated near the *n*."

Regarding the word *śreyān*: [it is derived from] "this is praiseworthy, this is praiseworthy; between these two, this is more praiseworthy. By [Pāṇini 5.3.57], the suffix *īyasun* is applied; by [5.3.60], the substitution of *śr* occurs; by [6.4.163], due to the preservation of the original form (*prakṛtibhāva*), the elision of the penultimate vowel (*ṭilopa*) does not take place; and by [6.4.148], the elision [of the final consonant] also does not occur.
Then, by [7.1.70], the augment *num* is added, and by [6.1.66] and [8.2.23], the elision of the *hal-ṅyādi* and the final consonant of the conjunct (*saṃyogāntalopa*) respectively apply.
In the words *śreyāṃsi* and *payāṃsi*, the substitution of *śi* for the *jas* ending occurs as before, and by the rule *pūrvavajjasaḥ śibhāvaḥ* [7.1.72], the augment *num* is applied.

But how can there be the status of being a penultimate (*upadhā*) for the vowel preceding the *n* here, given that the rule *alontyātpūrva upadhā* [1.1.65] prescribes the designation *upadhā* for that which precedes the final *al* (vowel) among the contiguous *al*s? [The answer follows: It is established that the *upadhā* is that which precedes the final *al*.

And here, the letter *na* is not the final one; what then? The letter *sa*. This is not a fault; for "finality" is relative. That is to say, the letter *na* is the final among those letters which precede the letter *sa*.
Therefore, the letter preceding that becomes the *upadhā*.

If this is so, then in the case of *takṣakaḥ* (protector), would there not also be [vṛddhi] from the letter *s*? Since the letter *k* is the final among those letters preceding it, the vowel *a* preceding that would be the *upadhā*; and consequently, by the rule "of the *upadhā* ending in *a*" (*ata upadhāyāḥ*, Pāṇini 7.2.116), there would be *vṛddhi*. This is not the case; for the *vṛddhi* is prescribed for that vowel *a* which is the *upadhā* of the *aṅga*. And here, the vowel *a* is not the *upadhā* of the *aṅga*; therefore, it will not occur. This cannot be said, because the vowel *a* is a constituent part (*avayava*) of the *aṅga*.

In cases such as *pācaka*, because it is a part of the base (*aṅga*), the letter *a* is called the "penultimate" (*upadhā*) of the base; therefore, does not the *vṛddhi* substitution necessarily apply? This is not a fault. For in the rule [Pāṇini 7.2.116], the phrase "before a suffix marked with Ñ or Ṇ" (*ñṇiti*) from [7.2.115] is understood as a governing term (*anuvartate*). By this, the penultimate vowel is qualified: "that which is the penultimate vowel when a suffix marked with Ñ or Ṇ follows. In that context, according to the principle "that by which there is no intervention [is considered contiguous even] when there is intervention, on account of the authority of the statement" (Vyāḍīya-paribhāṣā 49), an intervention by only one phoneme is accepted, but not by multiple ones.
In the case of *takṣakaḥ* and *rakṣakaḥ*, there is an intervention by multiple phonemes; therefore, the undesirable consequence of lengthening (*vṛddhi*) does not occur.

However, in this rule (*sūtra*), the penultimate vowel (*upadhā*) is qualified by the term "sarvanāmasthāna"; what then? It is qualified by the term "consonant cluster" (*saṃyoga*). Thus, [the meaning is]: "when a consonant cluster precedes a *sarvanāmasthāna* suffix.

Consequently, wherever a *sarvanāmasthāna* follows immediately after a consonant cluster, even if there is an intervention between the penultimate vowel and the *sarvanāmasthāna* consisting of multiple phonemes, lengthening nevertheless occurs.

For this very reason, even if there is an intervention between the penultimate vowel (*upadhā*) and the *sarvanāmasthāna* [case ending] consisting of multiple syllables, lengthening (*dīrghatva*) still occurs.
Precisely because the *sarvanāmasthāna* qualifies the *saṃyoga*, there is no lengthening in forms such as *haṃsau* and *haṃsāḥ*;
for in these cases, the *sarvanāmasthāna* does not follow immediately after the *saṃyoga*, due to the intervention of the vowel *a*.

Now, why does this not occur here: *haṃsam ācaṣṭe* ("he describes a swan")? [Why not apply] the suffix *ṇic* by the rule *tad ācaṣṭe* (Vārttika 201)? [And why not apply] the elision of the *ṭi* by the rule *ṇāviṣṭhavad* (Vārttika 813), which prescribes the operations of the *iṣṭhan* suffix for the nominal stem (*prātipadika*)? Thus, from the root *haṃsayati*, with the suffix *kvip*, we would have *haṃ* (as in *haṃsau*, *haṃsaḥ*)? [Answer: Because of the continued application of the word "optionally" (*vā*) from the rule *ity ato vā* (Pāṇini 6.4.9). And even if this were so, there is no contingency of an option applying everywhere, because it is a "restricted option" (*vyavasthita-vibhāṣā*). By this same principle, one should understand that in the case of the form *suhin*, *suhimsau*, *suhimsaḥ*—derived from the root *hisi* (meaning "to injure," Dhātupāṭha 1829) with the suffix *kvip*—there is an absence of lengthening.

As for the one who says: "The *num* [augment] is obligatory by the rule *idito num dhātoḥ* [Pāṇini 7.1.58]; because of the statement that in the prescription of *num* it is as if it were part of the original instruction (*upadeśivat*), there is no separate establishment (*pṛthaksiddhatva*) of the *num*. In this case, however, there is an inherence (*samavāya*) connection between established entities, not a conjunction (*saṃyoga*).

Therefore, due to the absence of conjunction, lengthening does not occur here according to his view; likewise, by that same logic, the elision of a final consonant in a cluster (*saṃyogāntalopa*) would also not occur in the word *suhṛn*."

The conjunction (*saṃyoga*) well-known in the Vaiśeṣika treatise is not what is intended here; rather, it is precisely that conjunction well-known in this very science as defined by the lack of interval between consonants (*hal*), according to the rule *halo 'ntarāḥ saṃyogaḥ* [Pāṇini 1.1.7]. Since that [conjunction] certainly exists here, the [opponent's] rebuttal is without merit. [The word] "great" (*mahān*).

By the rule of formation (*nipātana-sūtra*) "In the present tense, *pṛṣat*, *bṛhat*, and *mahat* [take the suffix *śatṛ*], and it is treated like the *śatṛ* suffix" (Pāṇini 6.1.170), there is the application of *num*—the grammatical operation for stems ending in *ugit*—due to that extended designation (*atideśa*) as being like the *śatṛ* suffix.
Why [is the condition] "ending in *s* or being *mahat*" stated? [Consider: *bṛhanti*. Regarding the word "āpaḥ":
since the word *ap-* denotes plurality, the singular and dual numbers are not possible; therefore, the plural number is presented.
Regarding the term *bahvāmpi*:

it is a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "those in which there are many waters. Since the application of a grammatical rule to that which ends in such a compound is desired, the lengthening of the vowel occurs even for that which ends in such a form.

For instance, regarding the rule *tathā hi* [Pāṇini 1.1.72], when the question "What, then, are the purposes here? is asked, this purpose is stated: *mahadapasvasṛnaptṛneṣṭṛtvaṣṭṛ*. But how can the rule of "specification by the final element" (*tadantavidhi*) be obtained even though it is desired, given that "specification by the final element is prohibited when a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) is accompanied by a term used for its own mention" (Vyākaraṇa-paribhāṣā 89)? This is not a fault; the particle *ca* ("and") is carried over from the rule *sarvanāmasthāne cāsambuddhau* [Pāṇini 6.4.8], and it serves the purpose of including what has not been explicitly mentioned. By means of that, the lengthening will apply even to that which ends in such a stem.
Regarding the statement "some": it has been said that some do not accept [this]. According to their view, the form *bahvīpī* arises in this way.

Why, then, is the compound-final suffix *ā* not applied here by the rule *ṛkpūrabdhūḥpathāmānakṣe* [Pāṇini 5.4.74]? To this he says: "In that regard, the rule for the compound-final suffix is not mandatory," and so forth.
And this technical rule (paribhāṣā) is indicated by the mention of the word *adhvan* in [Pāṇini 6.2.187];
how that mention of *adhvan* serves as an indicator has been explained there.

But even so, the form *bahvām* is not at all possible; for when *bahu-śas* is established, this [rule] would cause the substitution of a long vowel (*dīrghatva*), while by the rule *napuṃsakasya jhalacaḥ* [Pāṇini 7.1.72], the augment *num* would also apply. Between these two, because it is "ever-applicable" (*nitya*)—since it applies regardless of whether the other has already occurred—and because it is "subsequent" (*para*), *num* must be applied first. Once *num* has been applied, since the penultimate vowel (*upadhā*) no longer possesses the quality of being short (*adīrghabhāvinī*), the substitution of the long vowel would not apply. To address this, he says: "Even though it is ever-applicable," and so forth. By the word "even" (*api*) in the phrase "even though it is ever-applicable," it is implied that it also applies despite being subsequent.

But how is it that lengthening (*dīrghatva*) is observed without first applying the *num* augment that is desired [by rule 7.1.72]? This is because of the continued application (*anuvṛtti*) of the term "preceding" (*pūrva*) from the previous rule. Its purpose is this: that even when another operation would apply, lengthening alone must be performed first. However, another says: the *num* is prescribed by rule 7.1.72; and "neuter" (*napuṃsaka*) is a property of the meaning (*artha-dharma*). Since there is no grammatical operation (*kāryābhāva*) regarding the meaning in this science of word-grammar (*śabdānuśāsana*), the word expressing the neuter meaning must be relied upon in the prescription of *num*.

Furthermore, the application [of the rule] must follow in order to apprehend that sound (*śabda*); thus, *num* is considered "external" (*bahiraṅga*). However, this long vowel (*dīrgha*), being prescribed by directly uttering the word *ap*, is performed only for that which is actually uttered; because it has a smaller basis (*alpa-āśrayatvāt*), it is "internal" (*antaraṅga*). Consequently, the long vowel would apply first, and *num* afterwards.
But this is incorrect, for according to this logic, the form *bahvām* would not be established.
Some also maintain this: since this principle is general, here too the long vowel must occur first, followed by the *num* augment;
however, there is no fault in the previous solution. For those who desire that *bahvī* and so forth [be formed with a long vowel], they do not carry over the mention of "first" (*pūrva*) here.

Regarding "kartāraḥ": the suffix *tṛn* is applied in the sense of habitual action (*tacchīla*) and so forth, according to Pāṇini 3.2.135; thus, the *guṇa* substitution occurs. Regarding "janāpavādān": [this refers to] the censure of people.
The use of a word ending in the accusative case is intended to demonstrate that [the verb] ends in the suffix *tṛn*.

For when a word ending in *tṛn* is employed, the genitive case is prohibited by the rule "na lokāvyayaniṣṭhā" (Pāṇini 2.3.69) and so forth; consequently, only the accusative case occurs. A singular number has not been cited as an example.

In that context, since the substitution of *anaṅ* [by Pāṇini 7.1.94] has been applied, the lengthening [of the vowel] is established by the rule beginning with "and in the case of a sarvanāmasthāna" [6.4.8].
The use of the genitive form "of the mat" (*kaṭasya*) is for the purpose of making the *tṛc* suffix manifest;
when that [suffix] is employed, the genitive case occurs in the sense of the object by the rule "the agent and the object [take the sixth case] before a *kṛt* suffix" [2.3.65].

Now, just as in the rule *atha yathā* [P. 6.4.154], where the form *tuḥ* is used to include both *tṛn* and *tṛc* because they share the same form, and not by distinguishing between them—why is it not done here as well? If it is argued that this is for the purpose of preventing the inclusion of the word *tṛ* which undergoes the substitution of *ar* [by P. 6.4.127], this is not a valid purpose; for by the *arthavat-paribhāṣā* itself, its inclusion will not occur. Thus, the separate mention of *tṛn* and *tṛc* is intended to indicate the non-universality (*anityatva*) of this *paribhāṣā*.
By this, the rule "the mention of *ani*, *na*, *as*, and *man* applies both when they have meaning and when they are meaningless" (Vyākaraṇa-paribhāṣā 129) becomes justified.
Alternatively, it is for the purpose of indicating that "in the case of a general designation, sometimes only a specific instance is intended.

Therefore, in the rule [Pāṇini 6.3.37], although there is a general statement, only the *k* belonging to the *vuñ* suffix is understood, not the letter *k* in its entirety. Now, what is the purpose of including *naptr* and the others, since some of them are derived from roots ending in *tṛc* (*tṛj*), while others are derived from roots ending in *tṛn* (*tṛn*)?
Is this not already established by the very mention of *tṛ* and *tṛc*? To this he replies: "Of *naptr* and so forth," and so on.
Some scholars maintain that *naptr* and the others are primary nominal stems (*prātipadika*) derived [from roots], while others hold them to be underived.
In this regard, the derivation is as follows: from the root *nam*, the suffix *tṛc* is applied, and the substitution of *p* for the letter *m* is prescribed.
*Neṣṭṛ*: from the root *nī*, with the suffix *tṛc* and the augment *ṣuk*.
*Tvaṣṭṛ*: from the root *tviṣ*; in that same context, there is the substitution of the vowel *a* for the penultimate [radical], and it is also *aniṭ* (lacking the *iṭ* augment).
*Kṣitṛ*: from the root *kṣad*, with the suffix *tṛc*.
The words *hotṛ* and *potṛ* are derived from the roots *hu* (to sacrifice) and *pū* (to purify) respectively; they are formed with the suffix *tṛn*.

The word *praśāstṛ* is derived from the root *śās* (to command) with the suffix *tṛn*; according to Pāṇini 3.2.135 (*tṛntṛcau śaṃsikṣadādibhyaḥ saṃjñāyāṃ cāniṭau*), the suffixes *tṛn* and *tṛc* are added to the group of roots beginning with *śaṃs* and *kṣad* when a name is to be formed, and there is no *iṭ* augment.

Since the suffix *tṛn* is one that lacks the *iṭ* augment, in the view that these words are not etymologically derived (*avyutpatti-pakṣa*), they would not be included by the mention of *tṛn* and *tṛc* because they lack those specific suffixes. Therefore, they are mentioned separately for the purpose of this rule (*vidhy-artha*).

But according to the view that [the rule] is for the purpose of derivation (*vyutpatti*), since the form is already established from a stem ending in *tṛn* or *tṛc*, the rule is for the sake of restriction: "Let this [substitution] apply only to these specific words which are technical names (*saṃjñāśabda*); let it not apply to other such words that are technical names.

Consequently, it does not occur in forms such as *mātarau* or *mātaraḥ*. Now, if it is asked: "By what rule is the *ṇ*-substitution effected in the word *praśāstṛṇām*?"—if one suggests it is by the rule *raṣābhyām* [Pāṇini 8.4.1] and so forth—that is not correct; because the rule *raṣābhyām* is stated, and yet neither a *r* nor a *ṣ* exists here [in *praśāstṛ*].
Thus, this instruction makes it known that the substitution of *ṇ* occurs not only where specifically prescribed, but elsewhere as well.

By this, the substitution of *ṇ* in forms such as *mātṛṇām*, *pitṛṇām*, *grāmaṇīḥ*, and *agraṇīḥ* becomes established. Consequently, the requirement to state the Vārttika "it should be stated that [the rule for] *ṇ* after *ṛ* and *ṣ* applies also after a vowel (*ṛvarṇāt*)"—is no longer necessary. Furthermore, according to the principle "the mention of *ani*, *as*, and *man* causes the application of the rule to what ends with those elements, whether they are meaningful or meaningless," the mention of *in* here includes that which ends in *in*.
The feminine suffix *ṣin* occurs even after other [roots] when they are used alone.
For instance: the form *han* here is the root *han* with the *kyap* suffix; however, the *kyap* suffix is not seen after the root *han* alone.
The other two [forms], moreover, are masculine.
The suffix *śi* is prescribed for the two endings *jas* and *śas* following a neuter stem.

Therefore, because of their semantic connection (*sāmarthya*), it is understood that the rule applies to those [stems] ending in those [suffixes]; thus he says: "of stems (*aṅga*) ending in *in*, *han*, *pūṣan*, *aryaman*, and so forth.
For example: *bahudaṇḍīni*.

The suffix *ini* is used here in the sense of possession (*matvarthīya*), as in "they have a staff" (*daṇḍa eṣām asti*). Then there is the *bahuvrīhi* compound "those who have many staff-bearers" (*bahavo daṇḍino yeṣām santi*). From that, the case endings *jaś* and *śas* are applied, and for these two, as before, there is elision (*śibhāva*), by which [the preceding vowel] becomes long.

If it is argued that because of the mention of the term *pratyaya* (suffix), the paribhāṣā—"When a suffix is mentioned, there is the inclusion of that which begins with the element from which that suffix is prescribed, as well as that which ends in it"—applies, then lengthening should occur only in *daṇḍinī*, and not in *bahudaṇḍinī*; this is not so, for this paribhāṣā applies only where there is the mention of a suffix alone, whereas here there is not the mention of a suffix alone, but rather the mention of both suffix and non-suffix.

Otherwise, [the forms] *vāgmīni* (from *vāc* + *in*) meaning "those who possess speech," and *rūāgviṇī* (from *rūāj* + *in*) meaning "those who possess sovereignty," and so forth, would not be possible.
Therefore, that paribhāṣā does not apply here.
[The example is] *bahuvṛtrahāṇi*.

They have killed Vṛtra; by the rule *brahmabhrūṇavṛtreṣu kvip* [Pāṇini 3.2.87], the suffix *kvip* is applied. Those [days] in which there are many slayers of Vṛtra (*vṛtrahan*) are called *bahuvṛtrahāṇi*.
The substitution of *ṇ* occurs by the rule *prātipadikāntanumvibhaktiṣu ca* [Pāṇini 8.4.11]. Those [days] in which there are many Pūṣans are called *bahupūṣāṇi*.

Those words in which there are many *aryaman*s are called *bahvaryamāṇi*. Is it not the case that lengthening (*dīrghatva*) is already established by [Pāṇini 6.4.8]? If so, what is the purpose of this new rule? To this he says: "Since [the result] is already established, the commencement [of the rule]" and so forth. This commencement is appropriate for the purpose of restriction (*niyamārtha*). However, even when this rule for restriction is commenced, in the word *bhrūṇahanī*, lengthening would still occur by [Pāṇini 6.4.15]; likewise, this restriction is commenced with respect to the *sarvanāmasthāna* case-ending *śi*.

In this regard, just as a restriction (*niyama*) being initiated for a specific base (*prakṛti*)—such as *pratāmau* and *pratāmaḥ*—does not apply to other bases, so too a *śit* suffix being initiated when characterized by the technical name "pronoun" (*sarvanāman*) would occur only in the case of a "pronoun-sthāna" (*sarvanāmasthāna*) and not elsewhere; for a restriction depends upon its own homogeneous class (*tulyajātīya*). Consequently, since there would be no restriction in the case of what is not a "pronoun-sthāna," lengthening (*dīrghatva*) would indeed occur; therefore, he says the verse beginning with "the rule for lengthening" (*dīrghavidhiḥ*).

Having restricted—that is, having established the limitation of—that which is taught in this treatise regarding the lengthening of vowels for stems ending in *in* and others; where has it been restricted? In the presence of *suṭ*.
Is this an indication of all *sarvanāmasthāna* suffixes? It is a comprehensive inclusion (*saṅgraha*).
The meaning is "in a *sarvanāmasthāna* [suffix]. What should one do after that? To this he says: "In *śi*, a restriction," and so forth.
Having made a restriction regarding the *sarvanāmasthāna*, one should again make a restriction regarding *śi*.

The particle *eva* has the sense of restriction (*avadhāraṇa*), but its position is displaced; it should be understood immediately after the word *vidadhyāt*. *Suviddhān* means "very wise. But how can two restrictive rules be established by a single rule (*yoga*)? It is thought thus: this rule (*yoga*) should be divided into two rules. One rule is *inhanpūṣāryamṇām*, and then the second is *śau*.
And here, the mention of "all names" (*sarvanāman*) is understood to carry over.
Among those, the first rule—concerning the prescription of lengthening for *idam* and the others—is demonstrated by the phrase "having restricted that rule by means of *suṭ*.
The second, however, is shown by the phrase "it would again establish a restriction in the case of *śi*."
In that regard, lengthening (*dīrghatva*) would occur by means of the preceding rule;

however, lengthening is restricted by either [Pāṇini 6.4.8] or [Pāṇini 6.4.15]—namely, that lengthening occurs for stems ending in *-in* and so forth only before a *sarvanāmasthāna* (strong case) ending, and not elsewhere.
Consequently, there is no lengthening in the locative case, as in *vṛtrahaṇi* and *bhrūṇahanī*.

But by the second [rule], *śi* is restricted; even there, the long vowel occurs only before *ś* in a *sarvanāmasthāna*, and not elsewhere. Thus, while two restrictions are being established by the two rules, he says "in *bhrūṇahani*" (*bhrūṇahan-śi*) in order to demonstrate the result that is achieved.
"So that this [form] would not be corrupted.

This means that when these two rules have been applied in this manner, this word-form *bhrūṇahanī* of Pāṇini’s would not be corrupted; that is, it would not become possessed of the defect of being *asiddha*. The particle *iti* is used here in the sense of a reason.

Since, when these two rules are applied by means of these two *yoga*s, the form *bhrūṇahanī* would not be faulty, therefore [the author]—having restricted that long-vowel rule which applies here starting from the suffix *in*, and having established the restriction for *suṭ* and *śi*—would then re-enjoin it. However, the second occurrence of the particle *iti* indicates that the word *bhrūṇahanī* here denotes its own formal identity (*svarūpa*). Having thus avoided the lengthening in *bhrūṇahanī* by means of the two *yoga*s, he says "In *śās*... and so forth, in order to avoid it within a single *yoga*.

I shall explain—teach—that other means by which, when there is a single *yoga*, one does not incur the fault of being a "feticide" (*bhrūṇahan*) nor [the plural] "feticides" (*bhrūṇahanī*). What, then, is this means? He says: "having turned back," and so forth.
By the single compound *suṭi*, the term *sarvanāmasthāna* is indicated;
having set aside that which was under discussion as "*sarvanāmasthāne*," [the word] "*aviśeṣe*" [is used].

"No distinction exists in this" means it is "without distinction" (*aviśeṣa*); in that state without distinction—that is, in mere cognition (*pratyayamātra*) where no distinction is supported—apply that rule (*niyama*) as "the *śau* [suffix] alone. Or, the meaning is: apply the rule in this manner.
The word "or" (*vā*) indicates that this is an alternative solution to the objection.

Does the word *api* not also serve to show that there is no fault even when another alternative (*pakṣāntara*) is adopted regarding the term *bhrūṇahanī*, because the lengthening [of the vowel] is restricted specifically to the suffix *śā*? That is, if lengthening occurs for *in* and the others, it happens only when the suffix *śā* follows, and not otherwise. By the phrase "having set aside *suṭ*," the cessation of the technical governing rule (*adhikāra*) is indicated.

But when that [technical designation] has ceased, if one were to resort to a worldly authority characterized by mutual expectancy, then—as before—the lengthening would certainly occur in the case of *bhrūṇahanī*. Therefore, in order to exclude such a worldly basis, he says "without due consideration";
this is to be connected with the word *suṭ*.

The meaning is that it depends upon a *sarvanāmasthāna* [suffix]. Thus, when the mention of *sarvanāmasthāna* has ceased and is no longer required, this restriction—that "after [the vowel] *ś*, [the penultimate short vowel becomes long]"—restricts the suffix in general; it does not, however, restrict only those of the same class, namely the *sarvanāmasthāna* suffixes.
Consequently, the long vowel does not occur not only elsewhere than in a *sarvanāmasthāna*, but also in forms such as *bhrūṇahanī*.

If, then, the restriction [of lengthening] applies to *śau* by depending on the condition [of being a *sarvanāmasthāna*] while disregarding the domain of *sarvanāmasthāna*, then—since the lengthening would thus be restricted to *śau* alone—it would not occur in *bhrūṇahanī* (as in the example given), nor would it occur in the formation with *ky-aṅ* according to Pāṇini 7.4.25 (*ācāre ky-aṅ*). Consequently, when *ky-aṅ* is prescribed by Pāṇini 3.1.11 (*kartuḥ ky-aṅ sa-lopaś-ca*) in the sense "he acts like one who kills a fetus," the undesired form *bhrūṇahaya-te* would result. To this, he says:
"Of the prescription of lengthening," and so forth.

> [[6.4.7]] From this point on, the term *upadhā* (penultimate vowel) continues to apply; therefore, this restriction does not apply to every rule for lengthening, but rather specifically to the rule for lengthening the *upadhā*.

Now, the rule `akṛtsārvadhātukayoḥ` [[7.4.25]] is not a rule for lengthening the *upadhā*; what then? It is a rule for lengthening vowels ending in *ac*. Consequently, this [restriction] indeed applies here.
"Ah! There is no fault even in the rule for the lengthening [of the vowel].
This means that there is no fault when the suffix *kyaṅ* begins with the letter *y*.
The particle *hanta* occurs at the beginning of a statement or in the sense of addressing someone.
Others, however, read: "There is no fault even in the rule prescribing lengthening in *hanti*.

They explain it as follows: *hanti* means "in *hanti*"; the compound is formed by the analytical division (*yogavibhāga*) of the rule *pañcamī* [Pāṇini 2.1.36]. This is the locative singular form *tasmin* [meaning] "in that," i.e., in *hanti*.
Regarding the statement "the suffix beginning with *y* which follows the root *han*":
there is no fault in that rule concerning the prescription of the long vowel. The letter *ca* [in the sūtra] serves both for the previous resolution and for what is to be stated hereafter.

Precisely for this reason, there is no fault regarding the suffix *ya* beginning with *y* when added to the root *han* after the augment *upadhāniyam*. To illuminate this point—that even though the term "sarvanāmasthāna" is currently being carried over [from the previous rule], and even in the absence of a formal split of the rule (*yogavibhāga*), lengthening does not occur in the case of *bhrūṇahanī*—he says: "*suṭ api vā*" and so forth.
Here, the word *vā* indicates an alternative position.

The word *api* is displaced; it should be understood as following immediately after the phrase "in the negation of what is not the original subject. Here too, this term *suṭ* is to be understood as an indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*) for all *sarvanāmasthāna* suffixes.
There is no scope for this [rule].
There is no room for the objection that "the object of exclusion (*vyavacchedya*) is the domain of exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*).
Why? Because [in this context] "non-contextual" (*aprakṛta*) refers to something other than the *sarvanāmasthāna*.
Any suffix other than the *sarvanāmasthāna* is non-contextual; the prohibition of lengthening (*dīrghatva*) with respect to that is "prohibition of the non-contextual" (*aprakṛtapratiṣedha*).

*Aprakṛtapratiṣedhaḥ* means the negation of that which is not the subject under discussion (*aprakṛta*). The compound is formed by the rule *saptamī* [Pāṇini 2.1.40], through a split of the sūtra (*yogavibhāga*). Thus, it is "in the case of the negation of that which is not the subject under discussion."
This is a locative of domain (*viṣayasaptamī*). This is the meaning of the constituent parts (*avayavārtha*) of the first half [of the verse].

Now, the collective meaning (*samudāyārtha*) is stated: Alternatively, even though the term *sarvanāmasthāna* continues to apply, there is something to be excluded by the restriction (*niyama*) "in that case, [the suffix] *śi*" (P. 7.1.20); thus, being without scope (*anavakāśa*), it operates—that is, it functions—by virtue of its own capacity (*sāmarthyāt*) in a domain where the prohibition has not yet been applied, even though it ought to be applied.
By the word *api* ("also"), [the rule applies] elsewhere as well, in the case of a *sarvanāmasthāna*. But how is there scope [for this]? He says: "For that which... and so forth.
The genitive in *yasya* is in relation to *śau*.
The word *hi* has the sense of "because. For the *sarvanāmasthāna* suffixes are of two kinds: *suṭ* and *śi*.

Of these two, the former belongs to feminine and masculine [bases], not to the neuter; this is because of the rule: "After a neuter [base], [the *sarvanāmasthāna* suffixes] are strong" (Pāṇini 1.1.43).
What, then, is the case for the neuter? It is [the same] as before, because its [neuter status] is prescribed precisely for that [condition].
In this regard, the restriction "śau" (in the case of the *sarvanāmasthāna* ending *śi*) is made with respect to that which is related to *śi*; however, this does not apply when *suṭ* follows.
The meaning is that when *sarvanāmasthāna* followed by *suṭ* occurs, that [word] is no longer neuter.

By this, it is declared that *suṭ* belongs to a *sarvanāmasthāna* that is not connected with the neuter. Therefore, there would be nothing to be excluded (*viniyamyam*) in that case. Why? Because *suṭ* is a *sarvanāmasthāna* that is not connected with the neuter; for that reason, in that *sarvanāmasthāna* which is not connected with the neuter, there is no rule to be excluded—that is, nothing to be set aside—of the restriction "śi" [is the substitute for the neuter]. Indeed, a restriction is appropriate only when it is applied to that which is connected with the neuter.
If this [rule] were restricted only to that *sarvanāmasthāna* which is connected with the neuter, it would exclude [the application of the rule] from those of a similar class;
