however, there is no *sarvanāmasthāna* other than the nominative-accusative dual (*śi*) that is connected with the neuter, and therefore there is nothing of a similar class to be excluded.
Consequently, because of the restriction regarding *śi*, that [general rule] would have no scope of application.
Therefore, it also functions in the negation of what is not the primary subject.
By the rule "of the nasalized [root] *han*" (*hanteranunāsikasya*) and so forth, he explains the meaning of all three verses according to their relative importance.
Therein, by the rule "of the nasalized *han*" (*hanteranunāsikasya*) and so forth, the meaning of the verse "In the case of *bhrūṇahan*, likewise for him there would be no fault" has been explained.

By the words "yogavibhāgaḥ" (the splitting of the rule), [the author] explains the first half of the second verse, beginning with "dīrghavidhirya ihenprabhṛtīnāṃ taṃ viniyamya suṭi. By the words "tataḥ" (then), he explains the latter half of that same verse, beginning with "niyamaṃ punareva vidadhyāt. And by the words "sarvanāmasthāna," he explains the first half of the second verse.
The phrase beginning with "yastu" refers to the second half [of the verse];
the phrase beginning with "atha vā" refers to the statement "or even *suṭ* would have no scope for the base (*prakṛti*).
The term "sāmarthyāt" means "by virtue of the contextual force."
The lack of scope [for the previous rule] is due to its capacity [to override].
By the phrase "a restriction without qualification," the [rule] "the restriction applies to *ś* when there is no prohibition of the original form" is superseded.
"Without qualification" means generally; that is to say, it does not apply only to the specific case under discussion, but rather to suffixes in general.

However, for one who explains this rule as having the purpose of excluding the non-contextual (*aprakṛta*) alone, his statement contradicts the author of the *Vṛtti*’s own words, namely "without distinction" (*aviśeṣeṇa*). For a restriction (*niyama*) occurs without distinction only if it applies everywhere—both to the contextual (*prakṛta*) and the non-contextual (*aprakṛta*)—regarding the suffix (*pratyaya*) in general. But if, setting aside the contextual, it were to apply only to the non-contextual, then it would indeed be with distinction, not without distinction.

If this restriction were applied without distinction, then by this very rule, length (*dīrghatva*) would be excluded everywhere; therefore, this rule *sau ca* [Pāṇini 6.4.13] should be understood as having a prescriptive (*vidhi*) purpose. It has been stated that, by implication, the restriction applies without distinction.

Thus, demonstrating that implication, he explains the meaning of the statement "for that which has a restriction in the case of *śi*" with the words beginning with "for in the word *śi*," and so forth.

In this context, the restriction (*niyama*) is applied to the sound *ś* because the *sarvanāmasthāna* [suffixes] belong to the neuter and not to the feminine or masculine; for it is prescribed that the substitutes [beginning with] *j* and *ś* occur after the neuter. By stating, "And there is no other *sarvanāmasthāna* for it," he demonstrates that the *sarvanāmasthāna* suffix *suṭ* is connected with the neuter.
The particle *iti* is used here in the sense of a reason (*hetau*).

Since this restriction (*niyama*) is thus enjoined—that [the substitution of *n*] occurs before a *sarvanāmasthāna* ending in *śi* that is connected with a neuter—does another [ending] of the same class exist? For there is no other *sarvanāmasthāna* [ending]. Therefore, because there is no possibility of excluding anything of a similar class, the restriction applies without distinction.
Regarding the passage beginning with "But there" (*tatra tu*):
the word *tu* (but) serves to emphasize and its position is displaced; it should be understood immediately after the word *na* (not).
In this rule being formulated, the qualification "of the neuter" (*napuṃsakasya*)—which applies to the suffixes *in* and others—is not at all resorted to.
And if that [qualification] were not relied upon, this meaning would result: "In the case of *in* and the others, the long vowel occurs only before *śas*, and not elsewhere.
Consequently, even for a non-neuter [stem], as in *bhrūṇahanī*, the long vowel would not occur because it has been excluded by the restrictive rule.

If, however, the specific qualification "of neuters" (*napuṃsakasya*) were relied upon for them, then the meaning would be: "In the case of neuter stems beginning with *in*, the long vowel occurs only before *śas*, and not elsewhere."
Consequently, the restriction would apply only to the neuter gender.

What is the fault in that? In the case of *bhrūṇahani brāhmaṇakule*, the long vowel would be excluded, but in *bhrūṇahani brāhmaṇe*, it would not. Therefore, with a desire to avoid that fault, this qualification "of the neuter" (*napuṃsakasya*) is not adopted.

If this is so, then what was stated—that "the restriction (*niyama*) regarding *śi* has no scope" (*anavakāśaḥ śau niyamaḥ*)—is not tenable. For if this qualifier were not resorted to, then for those neuter nouns that do not have a qualifier, there would be a restriction regarding the *sarvanāmasthāna* case-ending *śi* when it relates to something other than a neuter. And since such [neuter] nouns also possess other *suṭ* and *sarvanāmasthāna* endings, then, given that there exists a domain for excluding members of the same class, how could the restriction be said to have no scope? This is not the case.

Although their neuter gender is not explicitly adopted as a qualifier at the time of formulating the restrictive rule (*niyamavidhāna*), nevertheless, because the suffix *śi* is prescribed specifically for the neuter, the neuter functions as the cause (*nimitta*) and *śi* functions as the effect (*nimittin*). Thus, by virtue of this relationship characterized as that between cause and effect, the status of being a "sarvanāmasthāna" suffix belonging to the neuter is indeed established for *śi*. Furthermore, since no other *sarvanāmasthāna* suffix exists that belongs to the neuter, it is logically sound to say: "The restriction regarding *śi* is of no occasion (*anavakāśa*)."

But surely, the term *napuṃsakasya* (of the neuter) is neither under discussion nor explicitly mentioned here; therefore, since there is no possibility of relying upon it, this [objection] is not appropriate for its exclusion. Why, then, is *napuṃsakasya* not relied upon in that context? To this he says: "But in the prescription of the technical name *sarvanāmasthāna*," and so forth. The word *tu* (but) indicates a reason (*hetu*). Since the technical name *sarvanāmasthāna* is prescribed by the rule *vi-bhakty-ām* [Pāṇini 1.1.42] for the word *vi* produced by a neuter [stem], therefore, with respect to the prescription of the technical name *sarvanāmasthāna*, the neuter becomes the cause (*nimitta*).
Thus, in this way, the function of the rule prescribing the technical name *sarvanāmasthāna* for the neuter is the adoption of the presence of the cause (*nimitta*).
Therefore, wherever the term *śi* is designated by the technical name *sarvanāmasthāna*, it must necessarily be accompanied by a neuter [stem].
Here, however, because of the continued application (*anuvṛtti*) of the mention of *sarvanāmasthāna*, there is the inclusion of the term *śi* as that which bears the technical name *sarvanāmasthāna*.

Then, by implication, the neuter [ending] is present; the intention is that its adoption is therefore possible. Since the preceding restrictive rule does not allow for lengthening (*dīrghatva*) before *su*, this [present sūtra] is commenced for the purpose of prescribing it. The particle *ca* serves to carry over the items beginning with *in*. [As stated: "When the lengthening has been effected here, the augment *num* is applied."

But how is this obtained, given that [the rule for *num*] would apply both when [the suffix] has been added and when it has not? Furthermore, since it is subsequent, one might expect *num* to occur first; to this he says, "If indeed," and so forth.

Here, when the term *acaḥ* (from Pāṇini 1.2.28) is brought to mind by the mention of *dīrgha* (long vowel), a long vowel is prescribed for the penultimate (*upadhā*) vowel characterized by the augment *aj*. And if *num* were to be applied first—on account of its being subsequent and its being obligatory—the status of the vowel as a penultimate (*upadhātva*) would be destroyed.

Therefore, by the force of the statement, the vowel is long first, and then the augment *num* is added. Thus we have *supayāḥ*, *suyakṣāḥ*, and *suśrotāḥ* [the Kāśikā reads *suśrotāḥ*]. While the rule *asuN* (Dhātupāṭha 9.49) is in effect, the forms are derived respectively from the roots *pā* (*pibateḥ*), *yaś* (*aśeḥ*), and *ru* (*ruāuḥ*) by means of the suffixes *asuN* with the respective additions: *pibatericca* (Dhātupāṭha 9.50), *aśerdevane yuṭ ca* (Dhātupāṭha 9.51), and *ruāuribhyāṃ tuṭ ca* (Dhātupāṭha 9.62). Thus, the words *payas*, *yaśas*, and *śrotas* are formed ending in the suffix *asuN*.

Regarding the forms *piṇḍagraḥ* and *carmavaḥ*: the roots *grasu* and *glasu* mean "to eat" (Dhātupāṭha 630, 631), and *vasa* means "to cover" (Dhātupāṭha 1023). The suffix *kvip* is applied according to Pāṇini 3.2.178: *anyebhyo 'pi dṛśyate*.

[Objection: But surely, by the paribhāṣā "that which has a meaning" (arthavat-paribhāṣā), only that which possesses a meaning is taken here, as in the examples from the root [sūtra], because words such as *payaḥ* end in the suffix *asun* and are thus meaningful through the sense of the suffix; whereas this is not the case in the two counter-examples, where the long vowel is part of the verbal root and, since another [suffix] is attached, it is meaningless—so how is the prohibition "not after *adā*" applicable? To this he says: "Even if it is meaningless," and so forth. How is this obtained? To this he says: "The mentions of *ani*, *ina*, *as*, and *man*," and so forth.

Now, how is there lengthening (*dīrghatva*) here? [In the derivation: one desires what possesses cows (*gomantam icchati*), hence *gomatyati* by *supa ātmanaḥ kyac* [Pāṇini 3.1.8]; then the suffix *kyac* is elided, resulting in *gomān*. But why should it not be so? Is it because of the prohibition [by the rule] *na dhātoḥ* [6.4.145]? Or is it because [the base] is a verbal root (*dhātu*) due to the rule *asya* [6.4.132]? This is not the case; the prohibition *na dhātoḥ* applies only to that which is immediately preceding [the suffix], not to that which is separated.
Alternatively, the letter *c* is added here, and it serves to include what has not been mentioned; therefore, in this instance, the operation will take place even for a verbal root.

Now, what is the purpose of including the term *anta* ("end"), given that the rule *ataḥ* (Pāṇini 6.4.1) continues to apply? In that context, since the stem (*aṅga*) under discussion is qualified by the words *anu* and *asa*, and because a rule involving a qualifier applies to that which ends with it (*tadantavidhi*), even without the inclusion of *anta*, the lengthening would occur for that which ends in those [words]. To this, he says: "The inclusion of *anta*," and so forth. *Upeśa* refers to the *lakṣaṇavākya*s (the rules), the *gaṇapāṭha*, and the *prātipadikapāṭha*.
It is called *prayoga* because it is employed; the suffix *ghañ* is used here in the sense of the object (*karman*).
The compound *upadeśaprayoga* means "usage in the instruction" (*upadeśe prayoga*). The compound is formed by the rule of *yogavibhāga* (separation of rules) from *saptamī* [Pāṇini 2.1.40].

Therefore, the meaning of this sentence is as follows: the mention of the word *anta* ("end") is for the purpose that there may be the inclusion of even a single portion of a word-form that is employed in the instruction, so that it might be grasped in its entirety.

But if there were no mention of "extremes" (*anta*) in the instruction, why would there not be a grasping of only a portion of the application (*prayoga*), such that the mention of "extremes" is made for the sake of including that [entirety]? To this he says: "For otherwise," and so forth.
What is the reason why it would not [occur]? To this he says: "In the instruction, which is the cause for the determination of form," and so forth.
*Nigraha* means grasping; that is to say, ascertainment (*niścaya*).

The "determination of form" (*rūpanigraha*) is the ascertainment (*nigraha*) of the nature of form (*rūpa*), that is, of the word; the "cause of the determination of form" (*rūpanigrahahetu*) is the cause of that [ascertainment].
The mention of "instruction" (*upadeśa*) is merely illustrative;
for even worldly usage is included.
For the form of a word is determined either from its grammatical instruction (*upadeśa*) or from common usage (*laukika-prayoga*).
And this suffix *matup* is not heard with a long vowel (*ā*) in common usage, nor is it so in its grammatical instruction; therefore, it is not ascertained as having a long vowel.
Consequently, because it is not so ascertained, it is not included [in the rule].

And since there is a mention of "extremes" (*antagrahaṇa*), by the force of that mention of extremes, when it is understood that only the extreme [end] is being mentioned, it follows that there is also the inclusion of that which constitutes a portion of the usage within the instruction (*upadeśa*); thus, the inclusion of the suffix *matup* is justified. Regarding the rule: "When the suffix *kvip* follows, and when a suffix beginning with a *jhal* consonant and marked with *k* or *ṅ* follows," here the term "*kṅiti*" is connected only with "beginning with a *jhal* consonant" (*jhalādau*), and not with the suffix *kvip*; for the relationship between a qualifier and the qualified (*viśeṣya-viśeṣaṇa-bhāva*) occurs only where there is both possibility and deviation [between the two terms].

However, both *kittva* (the property of having a *k*-marker) and *ṅittva* (the property of having a *ṅ*-marker) occur before suffixes beginning with *jhal*, as they are both possible and non-deviating [in that context], but not before *kvip*. For instance, *kittva* is never absent before *kvip*, whereas *ṅittva* is impossible there.
As in: *praśān*, *pratān*, *pradān*.

From the roots *śam* (meaning "to pacify," Dhātupāṭha 1201), *tam* (meaning "to desire," Dhātupāṭha 1202), and *dam* (meaning "to pacify," Dhātupāṭha 1203)—preceded by the prefix *pra*—the suffix *kvip* is applied, and according to [Pāṇini 8.2.64], the substitution of *n* for *m* occurs.
Thus, the form *śaṃśāntaḥ* is derived.

From the root *śam* with the *yaṅ* affix: reduplication; then by [Pāṇini 7.4.85], *nuk* is added because the root ends in a nasal; then by [Pāṇini 2.4.74], there is elision (*luk*) of the *yaṅ*; then *laṭ* (present tense), *tas* (third person dual); for that [affix], by [Pāṇini 1.2.4], it is treated as having the marker *ṅit*; and by "and *carkarīta*" (Dhātupāṭha 1081), because it is read among the roots beginning with *ad* (the *ad*-class), there is elision of *śap*. The rule "of the penultimate vowel" (*upadhāyāḥ*) has ceased to apply; for this very reason, it was not mentioned in the *Vṛtti*. What fault would there be if that [rule] were still in effect? The lengthening of a consonant would also undesirably follow.

For in cases such as *cikīrṣati* and *tuṣṭūṣati*, just as [the substitution] of a vowel (*ac*) occurs by virtue of the rule "of a vowel" (*acaḥ* 1.2.28), so too [the substitution] of a non-vowel (*anac*) would occur by virtue of the rule "of the penultimate" (*upadhāyāḥ*).

If this were the case, then in the roots *han* and *gam*, there would be no lengthening of the penultimate vowel before a vowel-initial suffix; of what, then, would it apply? Would it apply to the final letter by virtue of the rule "of the final [letter]" (*antyasya* 1.1.52)? This is not so; for here, by the mention of "lengthening" (*dīrgha*), we shall qualify that which was brought forward by the rule "of a vowel" (*acaḥ* 1.2.28) with respect to *han* and *gam*: "there is lengthening of a vowel, provided that it belongs to *han* or *gam*."

If this is so, would it not also apply to the reduplication (*abhyāsa*)? No; because the rule for doubling is prescribed only for that which has already undergone lengthening. Why is this so? Because the doubling occurs first, and the lengthening follows as a subsequent operation—as in the form *tuṣṭūṣati*.
"Consonants preceded by *ś* are the remainder [of the preceding rule]" (Pāṇini 7.4.61).

Regarding the form *cikīrṣati*: there is the substitution of *i* for the root vowel *ṛ* according to "The *ṛ* of a root is replaced by *i*" (7.1.100); then there is the substitution of *r* as the subsequent element (*raparatva*); then the lengthening according to "And before a consonant" (8.2.77); and finally, the substitution of *c* for the semivowel in the reduplicated syllable according to "Of the reduplicated syllable" (7.4.62).

In the case of *jighāṃsati*, by [Pāṇini 7.3.55], there is the substitution of *gh* for the *h* of the root *han*; the reduplication undergoes the same change as before, resulting in *jh*; and by [Pāṇini 8.4.54], that *jh* becomes *j*. In the case of *adhijighāṃsate*:
By the rule *iṅśca* [Pāṇini 2.4.48], *gam* is the substitute for *iṅ*; by the rule *pūrvavatsanaḥ* [Pāṇini 1.3.62], the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) is applied. Thus we have *sañjigāṃsate*.
Here too, by the rule *pūrvavatsanaḥ* [Pāṇini 1.3.62], the *taṅ* (middle endings) are used.
Regarding the root *gam* followed by the suffix *hrasranantāt*: the ātmanepada is prescribed by the rule *samo gamyucchi* [Pāṇini 1.3.29] and others;
the same applies to the root *iṅ* by the rule *anudāttaṅitaḥ* [Pāṇini 1.3.12] and others.

If it is stated that this refers to *gam* as a substitute for *iṅ*, then how is it that in the Vedic passage *svargaṃ lokaṃ samajigāṃsat* ("he desired to go to the heavenly world"), where *gam* is not a substitute for *iṅ*, the lengthening of the vowel is observed? To this he says: "In the Veda, even when it is not a substitute for *iṅ*," and so forth.

Regarding the form *samajigāṃsat*: this is the aorist (*luṅ*) of the root *gam* with the desiderative suffix (*san*). The augment *iṭ* does not apply here by the rule *gameriṭ parasmaipadeṣu* [Pāṇini 7.2.58]; rather, this is because of the word-splitting (*yogavibhāga*) in the rule *na vṛdbhyaś caturbhyaḥ* [Pāṇini 7.2.59], where the negative particle *na* is separated.
By the words "here" (*iha*) and so forth, he refutes what was stated [in the Vārttika]: "of *gam* when it is the substitute for *iṅ*" (Vārttika 775).
The first rule is *sani*; however, the intention is that a second rule, *hanigamyoh*, must be formulated in order to prescribe the lengthening [of the vowel] for the roots *han* and *gam*.
But how is it that, when these two rules are formulated, the lengthening of the vowel is established only for that which ends in a vowel (*ajanta*)? To this he says: "In that case," and so forth.
"[Of that which is being grasped]" (*gṛhyamāṇasya*).
In connection with a *kṛt* suffix, the sixth case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) is used for the object.
Regarding the word "viśeṣaṇe":
here, the suffix *lyuṭ* is used in the sense of an abstract action (*bhāva*).
The mention of *ac* (vowel) is for the purpose of exclusion (*vyavaccheda*).

Where short (*hrasva*), long (*dīrgha*), and protracted (*pluta*) vowels are taught, the rule *acaśca* [Pāṇini 1.2.28] applies; there, a long vowel occurs for the *aṅga* (stem). Of what kind of *ac*? Thus, when the *aṅga* being grasped by the *ac* is qualified and thereby excluded, the lengthening of the final [vowel] alone is established even without the mention of *ac*, as in the case of *akṛtsārvadhātukayoḥ* [Pāṇini 7.4.25].
Therefore, because it is redundant, it should not be made at all.
For what purpose is that performed? To this he says: "That is performed.

*Pravartana* (setting into motion) is *pravṛtti*, which is activity (*vyāpāra*). Its "difference" (*bheda*) is its manifoldness (*nānātva*). And since a difference in activity is not possible when there is only a single [repetition], repetition must be admitted.

But surely, when the rule *acaśca* [Pāṇini 1.2.28] is present, there are two occurrences of the term *aj*; why then is its repetition (*āvṛtti*) resorted to? This is not so; for in the absence of the mention of *aj*, the rule *acaśca* [1.2.28] would apply.

However, since the mention of *aj* is present here, *acaśca* [1.2.28] does not apply because its locus has been specifically specified. Just as in the case of *ato dīrgho yañi* [6.1.101], the paribhāṣā regarding *ik*—by means of its different scopes such as "of a stem ending in *aj*" and so forth—qualifies both the stem (*aṅga*) and the root *gam*.
Therefore, this need not be stated.

Because this intended meaning is not established by the mention of *aj* alone; for no other root *gam* besides the substitute *iṅ* is possible in place of an *ac*. [The phrase] "by the addition of *tan*" refers to the rule *tanipatidaridrāṇām* (Kātyāyana-vārttika 5059 on Pāṇini 7.2.49).
The mention of *śtip* is for the purpose of excluding the *yaṅ*-luṅ (the absence of the *yaṅ* suffix).
Otherwise, by the paribhāṣā regarding the mention of a root-stem (*prakṛtigrahaṇa-paribhāṣā*, Vyā.pa. 77), the option might apply even to that which ends in such a stem—as in *tantan-sati*.
And in the *Bālamano-ramā*, regarding the two [sūtras] 329 and 6.4.17, the word "ā" is in the nominative case with its case-ending elided.
The intention is that this is because of the continued application (*anuvṛtti*) of [the rule] from the sūtra "jahāteśca" (6.4.116).
Regarding "cādidītāviti":
the sense is that both [rules]—from "iddaridrasya" and from "ī halyaghoḥ"—are drawn back here by the particle *ca*.
[The forms are: *jahitāt* / *jahītāt*, *jahitam* / *jahītam*, *jahita* / *jahīta*.
*ajahāt*, *ajahāḥ*, *ajahām*.
[The commentator] says: *ajahāt*. *ajahitām*, *ajahītam*, *ajahuḥ*.
*ajahā* means "he abandoned. *Ajahitam*—*ajahītam*, *ajahita*, *ajahīta*.
*Ajahāma*, *ajahiva*, *ajahīva*, *ajahima*, *ajahīma*.
Regarding the rule *tanoter vibhāṣā* (Pāṇini 6.4.17): "There is optionally [lengthening] for the root *tan*. The intention is that this follows from the recurrence (*anuvṛtti*) of the two rules:
*upadhāyā dīrghaḥ* (from 6.4.7) and *ḍhralope* (from 6.3.11). Thus, the sense is that there is optional lengthening of the penultimate vowel (*upadhā*) of the root *tan*.
Regarding the phrase "before a *jhal* beginning [affix] with *san*":
the term "before a *jhal* beginning" (*ajjhane*) is understood to carry over from that [previous rule]. The point is that this is established as such in the *Bhāṣya*.
Regarding the phrase "in the sense of apprehension":
the meaning is that the suffix *saN* occurs in its own sense after a verbal root that denotes an action which is the object of apprehension. An example is *ā mumūrṣati*.
The meaning is that he becomes apprehensive of death. "The bank wishes to fall" means that it becomes apprehensive of falling.

"*Tani-patī*" is the form when there is the augment *iṭ*. Regarding the absence of *iṭ* after the root *pat*, he says: although [the substitution of long *ī*] would have been obligatory by the rule "*anunāsikasya kvijhaloḥ*" (Pāṇini 6.4.15) and so forth, this statement is for the sake of making it optional. "[Of the penultimate vowel]" (*upadhāyāḥ*).
Why is this so? Because of the application of the rule *acaśca* [Pāṇini 1.2.28], the penultimate vowel alone possesses the status of being an *ac*;
therefore, in the form *kramitvā*, the augment *iṭ* is applied according to the rule *kramaśca ktvi* [Pāṇini 7.2.36].
Regarding the term "prakramya":
by the rule *samāse 'nañpūrve ktvo lyap* [Pāṇini 7.1.37], the suffix *lyap* replaces *ktvā* in a compound that does not begin with the negative particle *nañ*.
Now, one might object that lengthening (*dīrghatva*) is an internal (*antaranga*) operation because it depends upon the suffix *ktvā*.
But why is the substitution of *lyap* considered *bahiraṅga* because it depends on multiple words, namely the compound (*samāsa*)?

In that case, since it is *antaraṅga*, why does the lengthening [of the vowel] before an affix beginning with *jhal* not occur even prior to the substitution of *lyap*? To this he says: "Even though it is *bahiraṅga*," and so forth.

In this regard, it has been established by implication that "the external substitution of *lyap* subverts internal rules. If the rule were applied to the mere letter *ch* alone, then when the suffix *kta* is added to the root *pracch* (Dhātupāṭha 1413, meaning "to desire to know"), the substitution of *ś* for the mere letter *ch* would occur after the *tuk* augment—by virtue of its being an internal operation under [Pāṇini 6.1.71] *cche ca*—resulting in the undesirable form *pṛṣṭa*.

But if there were a mention of [the root] *pracch* with its *tug* augment (*satukka*), then because it would be included among the roots ending in a consonant (*sthānī*), it would be replaced by the *tug* substitute; thus, considering that such an undesirable consequence (*doṣaprasaṅga*) would not occur, the mention of *pracch* with its *tug* augment is made. This is shown by the words: "of this *cha*, which has its *tug* augment.
That it is mentioned with its *tug* augment is understood from the fact that the marker *ṅ* is applied in the rule *yajayācayatavicchapracchirakṣo naṅ* [Pāṇini 3.3.90].

For this is the purpose of making [the suffix] *ṅit*: so that in the case of *viśnaḥ*, the rule *pugantalaghūpadhasya* (Pāṇini 7.3.86) might not apply to cause *guṇa*. If, however, only the letter *ch* were accepted here as the substitute, excluding the augment *tuk*, then once *tuk* had been applied and the letter *ch* alone were changed to *s*, there would be no *guṇa* simply because the penultimate syllable would be heavy (*gurūpadha*); thus, the designation *ṅit* would be redundant.

Some explain that when the addition of *tuk* has been made, the substitution of *śakāra* is applied only to that which already possesses *tuk*; consequently, since a light penultimate vowel (*laghvī upadhā*) arises, *guṇa* would apply, and thus the application of the *ṅit* marker is performed for the purpose of prohibiting that. However, this is incorrect. Some explain that when *tuk* has arisen, *guṇa* would apply, and thus the application of the *ṅit* marker is performed for the purpose of prohibiting that; however, this too is incorrect.

Some explain that the addition of the marker *ṅ* is performed for the purpose of preventing the occurrence of *guṇa*, on the grounds that *guṇa* would otherwise apply when the suffix *sat* has been added. However, this is incorrect; for even when the substitute (*ādeśa*) with *sat* has been applied, the base (*aṅga*) becomes finalized (*niṣṭhita*), as it is then fit for usage.

In that case, by the paribhāṣā "When an operation has already taken place upon a base, another operation upon that same base does not apply to what is already finalized" (Vyāḍiparibhāṣā 38), *guṇa* will not occur.

Therefore, even when the suffix *satuk* is applied, the designation *ṅit* would be entirely purposeless; how then could it be determined that the form with *tuk* is what is intended to be included? If this is so, then [the inclusion of the form with *tuk*] is determined by the rule "In response to a question, when *nañ* is used" (*nanau pṛṣṭaprativacane* 6.2.120). For if the form without *tuk* were intended, it would have been stated as "in response to a question" (*pṛṣṭa*) as previously explained. However, the designation *ṅit* for *nañ* is for the purpose of indicating the maxim: "The teaching regarding augments is not universal" (*anityam āgamaśāsanam*).
For if that [suffix] were non-nasal (anitya), then when it is absent, the *guṇa* substitution would undesirably apply in the absence of the marker *ṅ*.

Now, a rule may serve as an indicator (*jñāpaka*) even when there is no apparent purpose, provided there is indeed a purpose for applying that marker *ṅ*. What is that purpose? Is it so that the *samprasāraṇa* of the root *pracch* might occur by the rule *grahādibhyaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.1.16)? This is not the case; for the *samprasāraṇa* of *pracch* is not desired before the suffix *naṅ*.
How is this known? From the grammatical indication in [Pāṇini 3.2.117].

Is this [the purpose of] the addition of the marker *ṅ*? It is indeed an indicator (*jñāpaka*) for the rule "the teaching regarding augments is not eternal" (*anityam āgamaśāsanam*, Vyāḍi-pāṭha 99). But if there is a mention of even that which has the augment *t* (*satukka*), how can there be a substitute for that which has the augment *t*, given that by the statement "[1.1.52] *alo 'ntyasya*" [a substitute applies] only to the final [sound]? This is not so; because of the force of mentioning that which has the augment *t*, it will not [apply to the final sound]. Even so, it would apply to the stem (*aṅga*) ending in that [which has the augment *t*].
"Substitutes apply to that which is being specified" (Vyākaraṇa Mahābhāṣya, Pāda 1, Sūtra 106); therefore, [the substitution] will not apply to that which ends in such [a root].

In the case of *praśnaḥ* and *viśnaḥ*, the suffix *naṅ* is applied by [Pāṇini 3.3.90] *yajayāca* etc., to the roots *praccha* "to desire to know" (Dhātupāṭha 1413) and *viccha* "to go" (Dhātupāṭha 1423). [The objection is raised: "[But this cannot be,] because it is antaranga," and so forth.

Since the *tug* augment is prescribed for a short vowel by the rule *che ca* [Pāṇini 6.1.73], it is dependent upon a phoneme (*varṇa*) and is therefore *antaranga*. The letter *ś*, however, depends upon the *aṅga* (the stem). In that case, the *aṅga* itself is *bahiraṅga* because it depends upon the suffix;
how much more so, then, the letter *ś* which depends upon that?

But is it not the case that, by the rule *vārṇādāṅgaṃ balīyaḥ* (Vyāḍiparibhāṣā 39), the śakāra itself is stronger? This is not so; for this paribhāṣā applies where both an āṅga (an operation dependent on a suffix or stem) and a vārṇa (an operation dependent on a phoneme) would apply simultaneously based on a single cause. For example, in the word *iyāya*, based on the very same vowel *ā*, both the substitution of *yaṇ* for the *ikāra* of the reduplicated syllable [by P. 6.1.77] and the substitution of *iyaṅ* [by P. 6.4.78] would apply.

In that case, when both [rules] apply simultaneously in one instance, the rule *vārṇād āṅgaṃ balīyaḥ* (Vyāḍiparibhāṣā 39) presents itself, and thus the operation of the *aṅga* (the stem) occurs first. However, here, even before the suffix *naṅ* has arisen, *tuk* would apply by depending on the letter *ś*. Once *naṅ* has been prescribed at a later time, the letter *ś* depends upon that (*naṅ*); therefore, because they have different bases (*bhinnāśrayatva*), this [paribhāṣā] does not apply.
[The word in the sūtra is] *sedeḥ*.

Regarding the root *ṣivu* in the sense of "weaving" (*tantusantāne*) [Dhātupāṭha 1108]: the suffix *na* is applied according to the rule "after the roots *dhā*, *pṛ*, *vas*, *ji*, and *at*, the suffix *na* is added" (Uṇādisūtra 5.39). Since this suffix *na* is prescribed after the group of roots beginning with *dhā* by virtue of the term "variously" (*bahulavacanāt*), it also occurs after the root *ṣivu*.

According to some, by the rule *siveṣṭer ūc* (Pāṇini 6.4.19)—which prescribes the substitution of *ū* for the vowel of the root *iṣ*—the letter *n* is prescribed for the derivation of the word *sūna*, due to the force of the long-vowel pronunciation [in the rule]. In that case, *guṇa* does not occur. However, for those who explain this sūtra as being solely for the derivation of the word *syona*, the long-vowel pronunciation would be purposeless;
for there is no difference whatsoever whether *guṇa* is applied to a short vowel or a long one.
"Is it because the *uṭ* is applied before the *guṇa* of the light penultimate vowel? "Because it is *antaraṅga* (internal).
The reason that will be stated [later] should be understood here as well.
The *guṇa* substitute depends specifically upon a suffix characterized as beginning with a vowel (*iglakṣaṇa*) that is related to the stem and has a light penultimate vowel (*upadhā*).
However, the substitute *ūṭh* depends merely upon the letter *v*, which is related to the stem and characterized by a suffix beginning with a nasal (*anunāsika*).
Therefore, *guṇa* is extrinsic (*bahiraṅga*).

The substitution of *ūṭ* is internal (*antaraṅga*). Therefore, because it is internal, *ūṭ* is applied even before the *guṇa* substitution of the light penultimate vowel. Once that has been done, the *yaṇ* substitution is applied because it is also internal; thus, it is performed prior to the *guṇa* substitution of the light penultimate vowel—this is the connection with the subject at hand.
The internal nature (*antaraṅgatva*) of the *yaṇ* substitution, however, arises from its dependence on a phoneme (*varṇa*).

Now, one might object: since the rule "that which pertains to an affix (*āṅga*) is stronger than that which pertains to a phoneme (*varṇa*)" (Vyāḍiparibhāṣā 39) establishes that the *āṅga* *guṇa* alone is stronger, why is it not applied before the *yaṇ* substitution? To this he replies: "Because they have different bases," and so forth. For it has been stated that this [paribhāṣā] applies only where both rules—one pertaining to an affix and one pertaining to a phoneme—would apply by depending upon a single and the same cause.
But here, the substitution of *yaṇ* depends on *ūṭ*, whereas the *guṇa* substitution depends on the *ārdhadhātuka* suffix; thus, there is a difference in their substrata (*bhinnāśrayatva*).
Consequently, this paribhāṣā does not apply.
[The example is] "śabdaprāṭ."

In the word *śabdampṛcchati*, the suffix *kvip* is applied by the rule "kvibvacis" (Vārttika 288), and there is lengthening of the vowel; by the rule "vaścādi" (Pāṇini 8.2.36), the letter *ś* is changed to *ṣ*; that *ṣ* is further changed to *ḍ* by the rule for *jaś*-substitution (*jhalāṃ jaśo'nte*), and that *ḍ* is changed to *ṭ* by the rule for *car*-substitution (*khari ca*). Thus we have *goviṭ*. In the word *goviṭ*, [the suffix *kvip* is applied] to the root *viccha* (meaning "to go," Dhatupāṭha 1423) in the sense of "one who seeks cows" (*gāṃ vicchati*).
By the rule *kvip ca* [Pāṇini 3.2.76]. Likewise, in the cases of *akṣadyūḥ* and *hiraṇyaṣṭhīvūḥ*, [the suffix] *kvip* is applied after the roots *div* and *ṣṭhiv*.
Now, one might object that the substitution of *yaṇ* is internal (*antaraṅga*) because it depends on individual phonemes.

But the substitution of *ūṭ* is *bahiraṅga* because it depends upon an affix; therefore, according to the principle "that which is *bahiraṅga* is considered non-existent (*asiddha*) with respect to that which is *antaraṅga*" (Vyāḍiparibhāṣā 42), the substitution of *yaṇ* should not occur here? To this he says: "That which is *bahiraṅga* is non-existent with respect to that which is *antaraṅga*" and so forth. This [paribhāṣā] is prohibited where there is immediate succession (*ānantarya*) between two vowels, according to the rule: "When there is immediate succession of vowels, the status of being *bahiraṅga* is not established" (Vyāḍiparibhāṣā 44). The meaning of this is: when there is immediate succession of vowels, the *bahiraṅga* paribhāṣā does not apply—that is, it does not take effect.
The proof for this point is as follows: the statement that [the substitution] is *asiddha* when the *tuk* augment is to be applied by [Pāṇini 6.1.86].

The sole purpose of that [rule] is so that, in the case of *adhītya*, the *tuk* characterized by a short vowel may occur because the *savarṇadīrgha* (long vowel resulting from homogeneous vowels) is treated as *asiddha*.

And if the *bahiraṅga-paribhāṣā* were to apply even in the absence of *jānantarya* (immediate proximity), then—since the *tuk* augment would be *antaraṅga* because it depends on a single word, while the *ekādeśa* substitution would be *bahiraṅga* because it depends on two words—the *ekādeśa* would be considered non-existent (*asiddha*) when the *antaraṅga* *tuk* is to be applied. In that case, what would be the purpose of the rule stating "non-existent" (*asiddhavacana*)? It is stated for the sake of making known that the *bahiraṅga-paribhāṣā* does not apply when there is *jānantarya*.

In the word *hiraṇyaṣṭhyūḥ*, the substitution of *s* [for *ṣ*] does not occur by rule 6.1.64, because of the statement: "A prohibition must be stated for *sub*, verbal roots, *ṣṭiv*, *ṣvaṣk*, and *tīn*" (Vārttika 671).
In *pṛṣṭaḥ*, there is vocalization (*samprasāraṇa*) by rule 6.1.16 (beginning with *grah*), and as before, the substitutions of *ṣ* and *ṣṭu* occur.
Regarding the form *dyubhyām*, [the rule] Pāṇini 6.1.131 applies.

Those who do not carry forward the condition *kṅiti* (before a suffix marked with K or Ṅ) from that rule must hold that this operation should apply elsewhere as well; otherwise, they would consider that forms such as *dyubhyām* and *dyubhiḥ* could not be established. Therefore, he asks: "How is it that we have *dyubhyām* and *dyubhiḥ* when *ūṭh* has been applied?"

When *ūṭh* is substituted, does nothing happen? The meaning is that it is accomplished. Regarding the statement, "Because of the *t* in *uditi*, there will be a duration of one mātrā," the addition of the *t* (the *tapara* marker) in [Pāṇini 6.1.131] need not have been made.

For although it is stated that "an *ukāra* being produced (*bhāvyamāna*) includes its homogeneous counterparts" (*Cāndra Vyākaraṇa* 1.4.44), nevertheless, due to the closest similarity (*āntaratamya*), the *ukāra* will have a duration of one *mātrā*, corresponding to the consonant which has a duration of half a *mātrā*.

It is not long; so what is the purpose of the addition of the *tapara* marker (*t* after *u*) for the sake of excluding that [long vowel]? It is done so that even by another rule (*lakṣaṇāntara*), whatever long vowel might otherwise result, that shall not occur.

In this case, by the rule itself [Pāṇini 6.1.131], because of the *tapara* designation (*t*), the duration will be one mātrā; otherwise, if [the substitution] were long by [Pāṇini 6.4.19], then the inclusion of *tapara* in [Pāṇini 6.1.131] would be fruitless, as there would be nothing to exclude. Alternatively, the phrase "when *ūṭ* has been applied" is connected with the subsequent paragraph of the refutation. In that context, the meaning is: let *ūṭ* indeed be applied generally, both before *kṅit* and before *akhit*.

Even if that [substitution] were applied there, by the principle "that which is modified by a single substitution is treated as non-different from the original," the short vowel would occur in its very place by virtue of the rule *taparakaraṇam* [Pāṇini 1.1.70].
For this is precisely its purpose: that the substitute for *ūṭh* should be one consisting of a single *mātrā*, so that by reason of proximity (*āntaratamya*), a long vowel does not occur.

And according to this interpretation, the statement—"The inclusion of the *tapara* marker in *diva ud* is for the sake of excluding *ūṭh*; otherwise, in forms such as *dyubhyām* and *dyubhiḥ*, *ūṭh* would apply because it is subsequent"—is contradicted.

For in that case, the relationship of original and substitute (*sthānyādeśabhāva*) between *ut* and *uṭha* is not tenable; what then? It is a relationship of sublated and sublator (*bādhyabādhakabhāva*). For it is described as follows: the inclusion of the *tapara* marker [in the rule for *ut*] is for the purpose of excluding and subverting *uṭha*. For if that were absent, *uṭha* would apply by virtue of its posteriority; therefore, the *tapara* marker is included in order to subvert it.
There is no contradiction in this, because even though it sets aside the subsequent *ūṭh*, the vowel *u* is used here so that it may take the designation *mātrika*.
Those who maintain the relationship of original element (*sthānin*) and substitute (*ādeśa*) explain the text in this way:
"For the purpose of excluding *ūṭh*" means for the purpose of excluding the *ūṭh* that constitutes the original element.
The purpose of including the *tapara* (the long vowel marker) is so that, once the substitution of *ūṭh* has been made, there may be the cessation of that which stood in the place of *ūṭh*.
[Objection: Since it is subsequent, *ūṭh* would apply; and in this case, it is prescribed.
[Response: The word "possessing the audible form" (*śrutimān*) must be supplied as an ellipsis.
This is what is meant: here, since the *ūṭh* is prescribed by a subsequent rule, it would indeed result in its presence (*prāpti*), whereas its cessation (*nivṛtti*) is desired.
Therefore, the vowel *t* is added as a marker (*taparatva*) for the sake of its cessation.
Even when the substitute is prescribed without the vowel *t* as a marker (*atapara*), the cessation of *ūṭh* still occurs; for the original element (*sthānin*) possesses the property of cessation.
And it is said that the inclusion of *ta* (the long vowel marker) in the rule [Pāṇini 6.4.19] is for the purpose of excluding [the substitution of *ū*].
In this regard, by the force of the statement, it is understood that the inclusion of *ta* is for the sake of that exclusion in which a specific distinction arises.
Consequently, by implication, this has been stated: the inclusion of *ta* is for the purpose of providing a short substitute for *ū*.

For when a substitute followed by *t* (*tapara*) is applied, a specific distinction arises from the cessation of the *ūṭh* vowel that occurs; this is not the case when it is not followed by *t* (*atapara*).
If a substitute not followed by *t* were applied, then by the principle of closest proximity (*āntaryāt*), a long vowel would simply result from a long vowel—so where would the distinction lie?

Furthermore, what desired result is achieved when the mention of *kṅit* is removed, such that some do not carry forward the term *kṅiti* here? To this he says: "In the rule *chaśāṃ ṣaḥ*," and so forth.

When the mention of *kṅit* has been removed, by this [rule] a *ṣ* is prescribed for *ch*, *ś*, and *ṣ* without distinction, both in the presence of *kṅit* and in its absence; consequently, the mention of *ch* in the rule *vraścādiḥ* (Pāṇini 8.2.36) would not need to be made.

Since the substitution of *ṣ* for *ś* would already account for all instances of that substitution, the inclusion of the letter *ch* in the rule *vraśca-* (Pāṇini 8.2.36) must indeed be made for the purpose of substituting *ṣ* for *ś*. Now, how is the form *praṣṭhā* established, given that if the augment *tuk* were applied, the substitution of *ṣ* for the mere letter *ch* would result in the undesirable form *praṭṣṭhā*? This is not a fault, for they maintain that in the rule *vraśca-* (8.2.36), the letter *ch* is to be understood as including the augment *tuk*. Otherwise, it would apply in cases such as *ūḍidam-pada-ādy-ap-ukta-alvam-asthānivat* (1.1.46).
In that regard, although forms such as *akṣadyūḥ* are established by applying the elision (*lopa*) of the *va*-sound according to the rule *vali lopaḥ*, forms such as *jūḥ* would not be established.

For if it possessed the property of being *ṭit*, then by the rule *jvaratvarasrivyavimavāmupadhāyāśca* (Pāṇini 6.4.20), there would be two instances of *ūṭ*: one preceding the *va*-sound and another following the vowel *a*. Therefore, the *ūṭ* should be accepted as having the property of being *ṭit*, and not [the suffix] itself.

Thinking that if this *ṭhi*-ness (*ṭhittva*) were to have no purpose, it would be redundant, he says—beginning with "The making of *ṭh* for *ūṭh*"—in order to demonstrate the purpose of the *ṭh*-ness of the substitute *uḍ*.
By stating this, the mention of [the rule] *brāūvatā* (P. 6.1.89) also becomes a reference to something that is *ṭhit* (marked by *ṭh*).
For in this way, the purpose of making *ṭh* for *ūṭh* is established as being for the sake of qualification, provided that there too the reference is indeed to what is *ṭhit*, and not otherwise.
If the marker *ṭ* were not applied here, then it need not have been applied in rule 6.1.89 either; for an *ū* vowel possessing the marker *ṭ* is impossible in some instances.
If it were stated in this way, then *vṛddhi* would also occur in forms such as *prauha-te* and *prohata*.
Therefore, the marker *ṭ* is applied for the sake of specification.

However, the sound of the letter *ṭh* is not heard [in that rule], because the rule is stated using the form with *c* substituted for *t* (*kṛtacartva*). If, then, this were a *ṭh*-marker, then in the rule *ṭeḥ* (P. 6.4.143), only those [bases] ending in *ṭh* would be included; as a result, the rule *ata upadhāyāḥ* (P. 7.2.116) would not apply there, and consequently, the vṛddhi substitution in *praṣṭhauhaḥ* would not occur. To address this, he says: "This *ūṭh* in *vāha ūṭh* (P. 6.4.132) also... and so forth.
Just as before, the sound of the letter *ṭh* is likewise not heard.

*Bālamano ramā*: "In place of *dhvas* and *as*, there is *et* before *dhau*, and the elision of the penultimate vowel. (Pāṇini 6.4.19). *Ghu* and *sa* form a *dvandva* compound. The analysis of the term is *et-hau*.

Now, when *as* is established [by *aster bhūḥ*], one might ask: since the rule *hujhalbhyo herdhiḥ* (P. 6.4.101) prescribes the substitution of *dhi* for *hi*, and since the rule *dhvasoḥ* (P. 6.4.119) prescribes the substitution of *e* for the *s* of *as*, the former would be superseded by the latter due to its posteriority; thus, because the *s* has been replaced by *e*, the *as* is no longer followed by *hu* or *jhal* sounds, so how can there be the substitution of *dhi*? To this he replies: "Because it is *ābhīya*. And so, when *a-e-dhi* is established, he says: "By the rule *śnasoh*... (P. 6.4.112).

Now, when *āśiṣi* and *as* are present, one might object that *ettva* (the substitution of *e*) would apply by virtue of its higher status, thereby subverting *tātaṅ*. To this he says: "In the case of *tātaṅ*, there is no *ettva*.

Why? To this he says: "By the subsequent [rule]. Now, once *tātaṅ* has been applied, since it possesses the status of a *sthānivat* (substitute for the original), and because of the presence of that [suffix], why does *ettva* not apply by the rule *dhvasoḥ*? To this he says: "When [an operation] has occurred once" (*sakṛdgatau*).

The meaning is as follows: *sakṛt* means "once"; *gatau* means "in the case of application"; *vipratiṣedhe* means "when there is a conflict"; and when one [rule] has been sublated, it does not apply again—that is the sense. He states the specific rule for the *laṅ* in the *tip* ending with the words *astisicaḥ*: after the elision of the *ik* vowel and the addition of *āṭ*, which causes vṛddhi, the augment *īṭ* is applied by the rule *astisicaḥ*.

One might object: "In forms such as *āstām*, since the augment *āṭ* applies later [in the order of rules], the elision of *a* by the rule *śnasor allopaḥ* would occur first; consequently, because the root would no longer begin with a vowel (*ajādi*), how could *āṭ* apply? To this, he replies: "Because the elision of *a* in *śnasor allopaḥ* is considered *abhīya* (not yet established).

Regarding the form *āstām*: once the augment *āṭ* has been applied here, the letter *t* is used in the rule *śnasor allopaḥ* as a *tapara* marker in order to prevent the subsequent elision of that *āṭ*.

In reality, however, because [the substitution] is *asiddha* by virtue of being an *ābhīya*, the elision (*lopa*) does not occur; thus, it is clear from the *Bhāṣya* that the inclusion of the *tapara* (long vowel marker) in the rule *śnasorallopaḥ* is redundant. [Examples:
*āsann* [from *āsan*], *āsīḥ*, *āstam*.
He sat; I sat; you (singular) sat; we (plural) sat.
Regarding the optative (vidhiliṅ), he says "syāt" (it may be);
[and similarly] "syātām," "syuḥ," and so forth.
Regarding the benedictive (āśīrliṅ), considering that it belongs to the *ārdhadhātuka* category and thus undergoes the substitution of *bhū* for *as*, he says "bhūyāt."

In the *Laghu-kaumudī*, however, considering that the suffix *sic* is elided by the rule "gātisthāghupābhūbhyaḥ sicaḥ parasmaipadeṣu" (*Pāṇini 2.4.77*) when there is the substitution of *bhū* [for *as*], it says "abhūt.
In that context, having raised the doubt regarding the augment *īṭ* by the rule "astisico 'pṛkte" (*Pāṇini 7.3.96*), it says "sico 'steśca" [referring to *Pāṇini 7.3.98*].
The intention is that since the substitution of *bhū* has occurred here, the root *as* is not heard, and therefore the augment *īṭ* does not apply.
From the *Bālamanoramā*: "cchvoḥ śūḍanunāsike ca" (Pāṇini 6.4.19).
This is a dual genitive case from the dvandva compound of *cch* and *v*.
The letter *ca* (the letter *k*) is indicated here by the letter *ca* [in the sūtra] due to the substitution of *ścu* for *tuka*.
The word *śūṭha* is a compound;
it is the nominative case from the collective dvandva of *ś* and *ūṭh*. By the use of the particle *ca*, the phrase *kvijhaloḥ kṅiti* is understood to follow.
Thus he says: "of *satukka*," and so forth.
For example, the word *viśnaḥ* is a question-word (*praśna*).

When the suffix *naṅ* is applied to the roots *vicch* and *pracch* according to the *uṇādi* rules, the augment *tuk* is inserted because it is an internal operation (*antaraṅga*); once *tuk* has been applied, the letter *śa* is substituted for the *cha* that possesses the *tuk* augment.
He provides an example of *ūṭh* for the letter *v*: *khaunāti*.

When the form *khav-nā-ti* is established, *ūṭh* is substituted for the letter *v*; the intention is that the vowel *ṬH* (indicating a long vowel) triggers the *vṛddhi* substitution according to the rule *etyedhatyūṭhsu*. Thus we have *khaunītaḥ*, *khaunanti*, and so forth.
Since *khav-nā-hi* is established, one might suspect the substitution of *śānac* by the rule *halaḥ śnaḥ śānajjhau*; therefore, he says: "Because of the posteriority of *śānac*.
Regarding *heṭha ca*:
the meaning is that the root *heṭh* also occurs in the sense of "the manifestation of what has existed" (*bhūtaprādurbhāva*).

The root *grah* means "to seize" or "to take. It has a short vowel (*a*) as its penultimate letter. Because it is marked with a circumflex accent (*svarita*), it belongs to both classes (parasmaipada and ātmanepada).
It causes one to recall the rule regarding *saṃprasāraṇa* (vowel substitution) when a *ṅit* or *kit* affix follows—namely, Pāṇini 6.1.16 (*grahijyā...*).

Thus, in the forms *gṛhṇāti* and *gṛhṇīte*, because the affix *śnā* is *ṅit*, the *repha* (the letter *r*) undergoes *saṃprasāraṇa*, resulting in the single substitute of the preceding form (*pūrvarūpa*); this is the intended meaning.

When the *ṇal* suffix is applied, the reduplication (*dvitva*) occurs; then, by the rule "the reduplicated syllable of the *liṭ*" (*liṭabhyāsasya*), there is vocalization (*saṃprasāraṇa*), followed by the substitution of *u* for *ṛ* (*uradatta*), the substitution of *ra* for the vowel *ṛ* (*raparatva*), the retention of the first consonant of the reduplicated syllable (*halādiśeṣa*), the elision of the reduplicated consonant (*abhyāsacutva*), and finally the vṛddhi strengthening of the penultimate vowel. Thus, *jagrāha*. In the case of the *atus* and other endings beginning with a *kṅit* suffix, because the rule "for *grah*, *jyā*, etc. (*grahijyē*) applies later in the sequence, vocalization is performed first, followed by reduplication and the subsequent operations. Thus, *jagṛhatuḥ*, *jagṛhuḥ*.
jagrahitha, jagṛhathuḥ, jagṛha; jagrāha-jagraha, jagṛhiva, jagṛhima.
*Jagṛhe*, *jagṛhāte*, *jagṛhire*;
*jagṛhiṣe*, *jagṛhāthe*, *jagṛhiḍhve* (or *jagṛhidhve*);
*jagṛhe*, *jagṛhivahe*, *jagṛhimahe*. The substitution of *v* for the final consonant of *ri*, *u*, *ā*, *vi*, and *mā* is already established by the rule itself.
However, [the substitution] does not succeed for the penultimate vowel (*upadhā*); therefore, these [roots] are included for that purpose.

But in the case of *jvara* and *tvara*, the substitution for the letter *v* also does not succeed by the preceding rule; because [in those cases], there is an intervention by the letters *a* and *r*, as well as by a *kvip* suffix beginning with a *jhal* consonant.
Therefore, they are included for the sake of the letter *v* in those two roots and for the sake of the penultimate vowel.

"jūḥ, jurau, juraḥ. Regarding the root *jvara* (meaning "to suffer from fever," Dhātupāṭha 776), when the suffix *u* is applied, the semivowel *v* and the penultimate vowel undergo *pūrvarūpa* (the single-substitute form of the preceding and following sounds) according to [Pāṇini 6.1.108]. Thus, we have "jarttiḥ."
The suffix *ktin* [is applied]:
thus, *tūḥ*.
From the root *ñi tvara* (meaning "to hasten" or "to be in agitation," Dhātupāṭha 775), we have *tūrṇaḥ* [the form *tūrttiḥ* does not appear in the Kāśikā; the form given is *tūrṇaḥ*].
The substitution of *na* for the final *t* occurs by the rule *radābhyāṃ niṣṭhāto naḥ* [Pāṇini 8.2.42].
Regarding the form *srūḥ*:
the root *sru* [meaning] "flowing" or "drying up" is found in the Dhātupāṭha as number 1109.
The lengthening occurs by way of substitution:
*ruāvau*, *ruāvaḥ*.
[This is] due to the *uvaṅ* substitution prescribed by the rule *aci śnudhātu* (Pāṇini 6.4.77), etc.

"Ūḥ"— [the root] *ava* is used in the sense of "protection" (*rakṣaṇa*) [and also in the senses of beauty, affection, satisfaction, understanding, entry, hearing, sound, one's own, requesting, action, desire, splendor, obtaining, embracing, harming, giving, a share, and increase— Dhātupāṭha 600]. "Mūḥ"— [the root *mū*].

In the *dhātupāṭha* entry *mava bandhane* (599), the suffix *ūṅ* is prescribed here for the penultimate vowel (*upadhā*) associated with roots such as *jvara*. The penultimate (*upadhā*) is defined as the letter preceding the final letter, and "final" status is required [for that reference]. For instance, in the forms *śreyān* and *śreyāṃsau*, the letters preceding the *sakāra* are those whose last is the *nakāra*; the letter preceding that *nakāra* is the penultimate (*upadhā*). Similarly, regarding roots like *jvara*, the letters preceding the final letter of those two [initial] letters constitute the penultimate (*upadhā*), and that [penultimate] belongs to *jvara* and the others.

Because it is a part of that [root], one might mistakenly think that the *ūṭh* substitution must also occur for that *upadhā*. To dispel this error and to demonstrate which *upadhā* is to undergo the *ūṭh* substitution, he says: "In the case of *jvara* and *tvara*, the *upadhā* following the letter *v*," and so forth. That *upadhā* for which the *ūṭh* substitution is to occur is what is intended by the term *upadhā* here.

Furthermore, why does *ūṅ* occur for the penultimate vowel (*upadhā*) as shown by the author of the *Vṛtti*, and not for any other? [The answer is: because the penultimate vowel is qualified by the suffixes *kvip* and those beginning with *jhal* that have a *kṅit* marker.

Here, the penultimate vowel is qualified by the *kvip* suffix and by those beginning with *jhal* that have a *kṅit* marker—meaning that for roots such as *jvara*, when a *kvip* suffix or one beginning with *jhal* follows, *ūṅ* occurs for that penultimate vowel.

In this context, according to the principle "that which cannot be separated [by more than one letter] applies even when there is an intervention" (*Vyāḍiparibhāṣā* 46), *ūṅ* occurs only for that penultimate vowel of which an intervention by a single letter is possible, as stated by the author of the *Vṛtti*; thus, we have *mūrchā*.
The root *murch* is listed as "murchā mohasamucchrāyayoḥ" (Dhātupāṭha 212).

Regarding the form *hūrchā*: the root *hurchā* is listed as "hurchā kauṭilye" (Dhātupāṭha 211). But how does the elision of the letter *ch* occur here, given that the letter *ch* is not included in this rule (*sūtra*)? Furthermore, even the [root] under discussion has a *tuk* augment, yet there is no *tuk* here; for is a *tuk* ever prescribed for the letter *repha* before *ch*? To this he says: "When there is elision of *ra*, [the *ch* of] that which has *tuk*... and so forth.

It was declared that the *cch* in the preceding rule (*sūtra*) is *svarita* so that it might carry over (*anuvṛtti*) into subsequent rules; however, since a *ra* followed by *tuk* is not possible, [the *cch*] carries over there only as devoid of *tuk* by virtue of its association. Alternatively, in the preceding rule there is a mention of two *cch*s: one with *tuk* and the other devoid of *tuk*.
Furthermore, because the grammatical tradition (āgama-śāsana) is non-eternal, it is possible that the letter *cha* was omitted.

This being the case, what was stated—that the *ṅit* designation of the suffix *naṅ* is for the purpose of prohibiting *guṇa*—becomes logical. Thus, although both *cha*s were present in the preceding rule (*pūrvasūtra*), nevertheless, one followed by *repha* and accompanied by *tuk* cannot occur.

Only that which has been grasped as a distinct entity persists, as in the forms *tūḥ* and *dhūḥ*. [The roots] *turvī*, *thurvī*, *durvī*, and *dhurvī* have the meaning "to injure" (*hiṃsārthaḥ*) [according to the Dhātupāṭha, 570–573]. It should be understood that "it is as if unestablished" (*asiddhavat*).
This word *siddha* signifies that which is fully accomplished, as in the expression "the rice is cooked" (*siddha odanaḥ*).

It is not [merely] accomplished; rather, because it shares the property of not performing its function—just like that which is unaccomplished—it is treated as if it were unaccomplished (*asiddhavat*).

What, then, is that [which is primary]? Some say it is the *kārya* (the grammatical operation), because it is the most important; for the treatise (*śāstra*) exists for the sake of the operation, and thus, in relation to the treatise, the operation is primary by virtue of its pervasiveness (*vyāpti*). Furthermore, because the treatise is taken as the limit (*avadhi*), it is logical that the treatise itself is treated as non-existent (*asiddhavat*); otherwise, some specific operation would have been taken as the limit. Now, for what purpose is the mention of *ā bhāt* (up to the word *bhāt*)? Since the mark of the circumflex accent (*svarita*) applies, even without the mention of *ā bhāt*, the rule "as if not established" (*asiddhavat*) will continue to apply until the end of the chapter (*pāda*). To this he says: "The phrase 'up to *bhāt*' is an indication of the scope (*viṣaya-nirdeśa*)."

If the mention of *ā bhāt* were not present, it would not be known—*in what?*—that this section (*prakaraṇa*) is to be treated as *asiddha* when something is to be performed. Therefore, the mention of the scope (*viṣayanirdeśa*) is made by saying *ā bhāt*; that is, for the sake of fully understanding the meaning: "when whatever is about to be stated up to the technical term *bha* is to be performed, [the preceding] becomes as if non-existent (*asiddhavat*). If this is so, then since the word *atra* (here) serves to indicate the scope of this very matter, and that scope has already been indicated by *ā bhāt*, why is it said "*atra*" and so forth? To this he replies with the words "*atra*" etc.

That which has the same substratum as its cause is "samānāśraya"; the state of being such is "samānāśrayatva. The mention of *atra* (here) is for the sake of establishing—that is, for the thorough understanding of—that state; the completion of the sentence is: "if that [cause] exists here. By the word *tat*, that for which the status of being as if unestablished (*asiddhavat*) is prescribed is indicated.

By the word *atra* ("here"), it is meant that where there is the non-appearance (*abhāva*) of something else [namely, a grammatical operation prescribed by the treatise], that very thing becomes the basis for the application of the rule.

This is connected with what will be stated later as *asiddhavat* ("as if unestablished"). By the word *tat* ("that"), there is a reference to that which is prescribed as having the non-appearance of a grammatical operation.
That which has that as its basis (āśraya) and its cause (nimitta) is "dependent on it" (tadāśrayam).
The particle *eva* is for the purpose of restriction;
the meaning is that only that [element] becomes as if unestablished (*asiddhavat*).
"But that which has a different substratum (*vyāśraya*) does not behave as if it were unestablished" (*asiddhavat*).

By means of the particle *eva*, he shows what is excluded [by this rule]. The meaning is: that whose substratum (*āśraya*) is distinct from—that is, a different entity than—that upon which the scriptural operation (*kārya*) is prescribed on account of its appearance; such a thing is so described.
By the use of the particle *iti*, the meaning explained immediately prior is referred back.
Here, the inclusion of the word *atra* is for the purpose of establishing that they share the same locus (*samānāśrayatva*); thus, this is the resulting meaning of the rule.
To the question, "For what purpose, then, does it become as if unestablished (*asiddhavat*)?", he says: "The statement 'asiddhavacana'... and so forth.
By the word *utsarga*, the original element (*sthānin*) is indicated here, on the grounds that it is set aside by the substitute (*ādeśa*).
Alternatively, it is called *utsarga* because of its similarity to a general rule;
just as a general rule, having been applied universally, is withdrawn from a particular case, so too is the original element withdrawn by means of the substitute.

That which has an *utsarga* (general rule) as its *lakṣaṇa*—that is, its cause—is called *utsargalakṣaṇa*. That which has an *ādeśa* (substitute) as its *lakṣaṇa*—that is, its cause—is called *ādeśalakṣaṇa*. The statement "asiddha" (not yet established) is for the purpose that the affirmation and negation of these two should occur respectively;
for example, *edhi* and *śādhi*. These are examples of the affirmation of a state characterized by an *utsarga*.

Regarding the roots *as* (Dhātupāṭha 1065) and *śās* (Dhātupāṭha 1075, meaning "to instruct"): in the imperative (*loṭ*), second person singular (*sip*), there is the substitution of *hi* by [Pāṇini 3.4.87] *sehrappric ca*; due to the root belonging to the *adādi* class, there is the elision of *śap*; and by [Pāṇini 6.4.111] *śnasorallopaḥ*, there is the elision of the vowel *a*.

As for the question of whether the substitution of *ghi* (by which the penultimate vowel becomes long) applies first because it is subsequent and obligatory: no, because the substitution of *e* for the final vowel and the elision of the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsalopa*)—prescribed by [Pāṇini 6.4.119] *dhvasoreddhāvabhyāsalopaśca*—take effect first.

Is it not because the substitute *śā* [for *hi*] is also eternal? According to the rule *śā hau* [Pāṇini 6.4.35], the substitution of *śā* occurs prior to the *ghi*-designation. Consequently, for those two—the substitution of *e* and the absence of *śā*—the *dhi*-treatment characterized by a stem ending in a *jhal* consonant (as per Pāṇini 6.4.101) would not apply, due to the absence of its cause.
However, it does occur because [the former operation] is considered *asiddha* (non-existent) [relative to the latter].
Thus we have *āgahi* and *jahi*.
An example of the prohibition [of *śap*] by way of its specific grammatical form (*ādeśalakṣaṇapratiṣedha*) is as follows:

*agāhi*. From the root *gam*, preceded by the prefix *āṅ*, there is the imperative (*loṭ*), the suffix *sip*, which undergoes the substitution *hi*; then, by [Pāṇini 7.4.78], there is the elision (*luk*) of *śap*, and by [Pāṇini 6.4.36], "the nasal is elided" (*anudāttopadeśa...*) etc., there is the elision of the nasal.

In *jahī*, from the root *han*, the same process applies as before starting with the imperative; due to belonging to the *adādi* class, there is the elision of *śap*, and by [Pāṇini 6.4.36], there is the substitution of *ja* for *ha*.

Now, in this case, after the elision of the nasal (*anunāsikalopa*) and the substitution of *ja*, the elision of the suffix *hi* would apply by [Pāṇini 6.4.105]; however, because it is considered non-existent (*asiddha*), it does not take effect. Regarding the form *abhāji*: from the root *bhanj* in the sense of "crushing" (Dhātupāṭha 1453), in the *luṅ* tense, the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) is used for the passive/objective sense. By [Pāṇini 3.1.66], *ciṇ* replaces *cl* in the passive and intransitive senses; then, by [Pāṇini 6.4.104], there is the elision of the *t* of the suffix; finally, by [Pāṇini 6.4.33], there is the elision of the nasal.

Even though it shares the same base (*samānāśraya*), when a grammatical operation (*śāstrīya*) requiring augmentation is to be performed, its status as *asiddha* does not occur due to the rule stating "up to and including *ābhāt*.
In the word *rāgaḥ*, the suffix *ghañ* is applied after the root *rañj*, and by [Pāṇini 6.4.27], the nasal is elided.

Even for that [substitution], although it shares the same locus (*samānāśraya*), its status as *asiddha* does not apply when the seventh-strengthening (*sāptamikī vṛddhi*) is to be performed, because of the statement "it is not *asiddha* up to [the rule concerning] *ābhāt*. For example, in the forms *papuṣaḥ*, *cicyuṣaḥ*, and *luluvuṣaḥ*—derived from the roots *pā* (to drink), *ci* (to gather), and *lū* (to cut) with the suffix *kvasu* after the perfect tense (*liṭ*), followed by reduplication—is it not the case that this [strengthening] depends on a different locus (*vyāśrayatvāt*)? [Answer: No. Because the reduplication occurs first, and the strengthening (*vṛddhi*) applies subsequently, there is no dependence on a different locus. Furthermore, since the *kvasu* suffix is introduced immediately after the verbal root, the reduplication is applied directly to that which has already received the *kvasu* suffix; thus, the strengthening is indeed dependent on the same locus. Therefore, the rule "it is not *asiddha* up to *ābhāt*" prevents it from being treated as *asiddha*. Consequently, the strengthening takes place. Thus, the forms *papuṣaḥ*, *cicyuṣaḥ*, and *luluvuṣaḥ* are established.

In the forms *pāte* and *cinoteḥ*, derived from the roots *pā* (to drink) and *ci* (to gather) respectively, the suffix *kvasu* occurs in the perfect tense (*liṭ*), followed by reduplication. Because that [reduplication] depends on different bases (*vyāśrayatvāt*), the elision of the vowel *a* (by Pāṇini 6.4.64) does not count as "asiddha" when the substitution of *yaṇ* (by 6.4.82) and the substitution of *uvaṅ* (by 6.4.77) are to be applied.

Now, one might object: "Is this not already established by the rule *usyapadāntāt* (6.1.96), which provides the single-substitute form (*pararūpa*)? This is not so; for in that rule, the word *hrasva* is understood in its primary, etymological sense (*pratipadokta*), whereas here the forms are merely derivative (*lākṣaṇika*).
But how, then, is there a case of having different bases (*vyāśrayatva*) here? He says: "For [the elision of *ā*], etc.
The word *hi* has the sense of "because" (*yasmāt*), and the particle *iti* has the sense of "therefore" (*tasmāt*).

But even so, according to the principle that "that which is external (*bahiraṅga*) is as if non-existent (*asiddha*) when compared to that which is internal (*antaraṅga*)," since the external *samprasāraṇa* would be as if non-existent with respect to the internal operations such as the elision of *ā* (*āllopa*), those [operations] such as *āllopa* would not apply at all. For in that case, the portion ending in *-vas* precedes the case-ending (*vibhakti*), and thus the elisions and so forth depend upon that; whereas the *samprasāraṇa* depends upon the case-ending, while the [elisions] are internal because they depend upon the base (*prakṛti*), and [the *samprasāraṇa*] is external because it depends upon the suffix (*pratyaya*). To this he says: "The external is as if non-existent," etc.
"This too" refers to...
The neuter gender in the word *nirveśaḥ* is used in view of the expression *etad api*.
With the words *eṣā hi*, etc., he states the reason why this paribhāṣā does not apply:

this paribhāṣā operates where there is a simultaneous presentation (*yugapad-upasthāna*) of both an internal (*antaraṅga*) and an external (*bahiraṅga*) rule, in order to render the external rule as if non-existent (*asiddhatā*) when the internal rule is to be applied.
And this technical rule (*paribhāṣā*) is "pertaining to the domain of the *ābhāt* rules" because it is made known by the rule *ābhāt* [P.

6.4.132]. Therefore, while this [rule] is to be applied, since the substitution of *samprasāraṇa* for *vasu* [P. 6.4.131] and the elision of *ā* [P. 6.4.64] and so forth are treated as "not established" (*asiddha*) by the rule *asiddhavadatrā bhāt* [P. 6.4.22], there is no simultaneous presentation of the internal (*antaraṅga*) and external (*bahiraṅga*) operations; thus, [the present rule] does not apply. Since that [rule] does not apply, there is no "non-establishment" (*asiddhatva*) of the external *samprasāraṇa*.
Therefore, the elision of *al* (*allopa*) and so forth indeed occur. Regarding the statement "vug and yuṭ," etc.:
the meaning is that this should be explained as having the sense that these two, *vuk* and *yuṭ*, are established when *uvaṅ* and *yaṇ* are respectively to be applied.

In this regard, the explanation is as follows: here, the mention of *vat* (the suffix *-vat* indicating extension) need not be made; even without it, the extension is already established, just as in the case of [Pāṇini 6.1.86] and "that which is previously taught is as if non-existent" [Pāṇini 8.2.1].
Why is it done in some cases? It is for the purpose that its own substratum (*svāśraya*) may also be established.
By means of this, *vuk* and *ṛṭ* will be established even in the presence of *uvaṅ* and *ayaṇ*.
For example: *babhūva*.

By the rule *bhavateraḥ* [Pāṇini 7.4.73], there is the substitution of *ā* for the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*), and by *bhuvo vug luṅ-liṭoḥ* [Pāṇini 6.4.88], the augment *vuk* is added. In that context, if [the former] were considered asiddha (non-existent), then *uvaṅ* would apply by the rule *aci śnu-dhātu-...* [Pāṇini 6.4.77]; however, because it is treated as established (*siddha*), it does not occur.
Thus we have *upadidīye*.

Regarding the root *dīṅ* in the sense of "perishing" (*kṣaye*; Dhātupāṭha 1134), [in the case of] the *liṭ* [perfect tense], the substitution of *i* occurs by the rule *liṭastajhayoḥ* [Pāṇini 3.4.81], and the augment *yuṭ* is added by the rule *dīṅo yuḍaci kṅici* [Pāṇini 6.4.63].

If that [augment *yuṭ*] were also considered asiddha, then the substitution of *yaṇ* would occur by the rule *eranekāco'saṃyogapūrvasya* [Pāṇini 6.4.82]. Because it is established (*siddhatvāt*), however, this does not happen.

Does *ā* signify "up to and including" (*maryādā*) or "including" (*abhividhi*)? If the first alternative is adopted, then the status of being "unestablished" (*asiddhatva*) for that which falls under the heading of *ā* would not apply.

Consequently, since the technical rule (*paribhāṣā*) "that which is external is unestablished with respect to that which is internal" (*asiddhaṃ bahiraṅgam antaraṅge*) would not be applicable—because it would lack scriptural authority (*anābhācchāstrīyatva*)—the semi-vowel vocalization (*samprasāraṇa*) of *vasu* and the elisions (*allopādi*) would not be considered unestablished.

Even so, when there is a simultaneous presentation of both the *samprasāraṇa* of the suffix *vasu*, which is *bahiraṅga*, and the elisions (*alopa*) and other operations, which are *antaraṅga*, would not the *antaraṅga* operations such as elision fail to apply in forms like *papuṣaḥ*, *cicyuṣaḥ*, and *luluvaṣaḥ*—since that Paribhāṣā, being operative, would render the *bahiraṅga* *samprasāraṇa* of *vasu* as if it were non-existent (*asiddha*), and [the rule for] *antaraṅga* operations would [otherwise] take precedence? To this [objection], [the author says]: "From here..."

Having observed the fault in the view of *maryādā* (limit), he resorts to the second alternative and says: "The word *ā* [in the rule] is used in the sense of *abhividhi* (inclusiveness). This has already been explained. Since no other element containing the sound *śn* is possible, even though the *m* of *śnam* is not heard, it is understood by implication that the reference is to *śnam* itself; therefore, he says: "*śnam* is this [element] with its *u* elided. That is to say, it is so called because its *m* has been discarded (*utsṛṣṭa*) or abandoned (*parityakta*).

Regarding the passage beginning with *anakti*: the root *añj* (DhP 1458) means "to manifest, to smear, to shine, or to go"; *bhañj* (DhP 1453) means "to crush"; *his* (DhP 1456) means "to injure. Because this [root *his*] has an indicatory letter *u* (*udid*), the augment *num* is applied. Because it belongs to the *rudh*-class, the suffix *śnam* is added.

This inclusion of the letter *ś* [in the rule] is done for the purpose that [the substitution] should not occur in forms such as *nanditā* and *nandakaḥ*. However, this is unnecessary; for by the metarule (*paribhāṣā*) "between a suffix and a non-suffix, the suffix alone is to be understood" (Vyāḍiparibhāṣā 72), it will not apply here.

And because of an indicator (*jñāpaka*): the fact that he recites the words *nandin* and *nandana* in the *kṣubhnādi* group indicates that the elision of the letter *n* in *nandi* does not occur. Furthermore, this indicator is intended generally; therefore, it will not apply in cases such as *nanditā* and *nandaka*.
Consequently, with the intention that one should simply state "there is no elision of *n*," he asks: "Why is there the mention of [the word] containing the letter *ś*?"
Regarding "yajñānām" and "yatnānām":
[the suffix] *naṅ* is applied by [Pāṇini 3.3.90] *yajayāca*, and from that which ends in it, the genitive plural is formed with the augment *nuṭ*.
If the inclusion of the letter *ś* were not made, then in those cases there would certainly be the elision of the nasal (*nalopa*).

It might be argued: "Once the lengthening (*dīrgha*) has been applied, the designation *an* will no longer exist, so [the rule for] *nalopa* will not apply. To this, he says: "And when a *sup* [suffix follows]" (*supi ca*), etc. The meaning of "and when a *sup* [suffix follows]" (*supi ca*, Pāṇini 6.4.102) is that the long vowel (*dīrgha*) is a substitute for a short vowel (*aj-ādeśa*). When the elision of the *n* (*nakāra-lopa*)—which is a preceding operation (*pūrva-vidhi*)—is to be performed, by virtue of the status of being a *sthānivadbhāva* (Pāṇini 1.1.57), that [long vowel] assumes the form of its original. Consequently, even if the lengthening (*dīrghatva*) is subsequently applied, if the inclusion of the element qualified by the *śakāra* were not made, then the elision of the *n* (*nalopa*) would indeed occur here. This is because the rule applies whether the lengthening has already been performed or not (*kṛtākṛta-prasaṅgitvāt*).

However, once the elision of the letter *n* has been performed, the lengthening does not apply because it is prescribed as being conditioned by that [elision]; therefore, it is considered non-eternal (*anitya*).

But is it not the case that the status of being "as if in the place of the original" (*sthānivadbhāva*) was stated only for a rule concerning what precedes (*pūrvavidhi*), and this is not a rule concerning what precedes? This is not a fault; for this too is indeed a rule concerning what precedes, since the compound *pūrvavidhiḥ* is understood there as "a rule [conditioned] by what precedes" (*pūrvasmād vidhiḥ*).

Now, even though the inclusion of [the substitute] containing the letter *ś* has been made, why does [the rule] not apply here in the cases of *viśnānām* and *praśnānām*, since the letter *n* here also contains the letter *ś*? To this he says: "In the case of *viśnānām* and *praśnānām*, etc.

For here, by the maxim *lakṣaṇapratipadoktayoḥ pratipadoktasyaiva grahaṇam* (Paribhāṣā 3), there is the inclusion of the word *śna* as it is directly specified (*pratipadokta*), and not of that which is derived through a grammatical rule (*lākṣaṇika*). In the forms *viśnānām* and *praśnānām*, the word *śna* is produced only after the substitution of *ś* [for *s*] by [Pāṇini 6.4.19]; and that [word *śna*] is derivative (*lākṣaṇika*).
Therefore? From that point onward, elision does not occur.

Since the application of the term "elision" (lopa) is established by its recurrence through the "frog-leap" (maṇḍūkapluti) principle from the rule [P. 6.4.21], the fact that "elision" is mentioned again is for the purpose of dividing the grammatical rules (yogavibhāga).

"Śnān na" is one rule (yoga); here, "na" is an indeclinable reference, and the mention of "lopa" (elision) is carried over from the previous context. Therefore, the meaning is this: there is elision of the letter *n* that follows a suffix ending in *śn*. Then, "lopaḥ" is the second rule; from the preceding "śnān na," the word "na" is carried over [to this rule] so that the elision of the letter *n* may occur in the desired instances.

By this, the elision of *n* (nalopa) is established in cases such as *laṅgika*, *kampin*, and others, regarding affliction, bodily transformation, and so forth. Regarding the phrase *iditaḥ*: those [roots] which have *it* as an indicatory letter (*it*) are called *idita*. The expression *aniditaḥ* (those not having *it*) is a singular form used by transposition (*subvyatyaya*) in place of the genitive plural; and that [term] qualifies "those not having *it*" (*aniditām*). Since a rule involving a suffix applies to that which ends with it (*tadantavidhi*), he says: "of those ending in a consonant" (*halantānām*), and so forth. Regarding "of the *n* of the penultimate" (*upadhāyā nakārasya*): the word "penultimate" (*upadhā*) is a qualifier of the *n*.
"Ruāstaḥ, dhvalastaḥ. [The roots] *ruānsu* and *dhvansu* [mean] "to fall down" (*adhaḥpatane*) [Dhātupāṭha 754, 755]. The past passive participles (*niṣṭhā*) are "ruāsyate" and "dhvasyate."
The *lakāra* (verbal suffix) is used here either in the sense of the agent (*bhāva*) or the object (*karman*).
These two examples— *sanīruāsyate* and *danīdhvasyate*—
are formed with the *yaṅ* affix.

By the rule *nīg vañcu* [Pāṇini 7.4.84], the augment *nīg* is added to the reduplicated stem. Regarding the form *nandyate*: the root is *ṭu ṇadi samṛddhau* (Dhātupāṭha 67) [or *ṭu nadi*]. Regarding the form *nānandyate*.
By the rule *yaṅantam* (Pāṇini 7.4.83), there is lengthening of the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*); thus:
*nenīyate*.
In the case of *nayati*, there is guna of the reduplicated syllable according to [Pāṇini 7.4.82], *gaṇo yaṅlukoḥ*. Regarding *nahrate*: the root is *ṇaha* in the sense of "binding" (Dhātupāṭha 1166).

Regarding the phrase "laṅgikampyoḥ" and so forth: because *laṅgi* and *kampi* have an indicatory *it*, the elision of the nasal (*nalopa*) would not otherwise apply; therefore, an extension (*upasaṃkhyāna*) must be made for these two, namely for the meanings of "affliction" and "bodily transformation.
*Upasaṃkhyānam* means "explanation" or "establishment [of a rule]."
In the subsequent [sūtra] as well, the meaning of the word *upasaṃkhyāna* is "explanation" (*pratipādana*). And that explanation has indeed already been provided.
*Upatāpa* means "disease."
