"Alteration of the body" (*śarīravikāra*) means the body's becoming otherwise. Furthermore, in this context, it refers to affliction (*upatāpa*) and the like; otherwise, since the meaning would already be established by the term "affliction" alone, the inclusion of "alteration of the body" would be purposeless.
[The word is] "clinging" (*vilagita*).
The roots *agi*, *vagi*, and *lagi* have the sense of "motion" (*gaty-artha*) [Dhātupāṭha 146, 147, 145].

The elision of the root *laṅg* is prescribed so that there may not be such usage as *vilaṅgitaḥ* in the sense of "affliction" (*upatāpa*), and not for the sake of establishing the form itself; for that form is already established from the other root *lage* in the sense of "clinging" (*saṅga*) [Dhātupāṭha 786].
"Rañjer ṇau," etc. This statement is for the purpose of excluding the augment *iṭ*. *Mṛgaramaṇam* means the sporting of deer.
Regarding the example "he causes the deer to hunt":
the meaning is that he employs the deer while they are sporting.
[This is explained by the rule: "The addition of *rajan*, *rajaka*, and *rajaḥ* should be enumerated."
Here, the matter is further explained:

in the rule *[[6.4.27]]*, the particle *ca* (and) has the sense of including what has not been explicitly mentioned; therefore, when words such as *rajaka-* are to be derived, there is elision of the nasal (*n*) after the root *rañj-* when followed by suffixes such as *ṣvun*.
Thus, the form *rajakaḥ* is obtained.
The word "rajanam" is derived from the suffix *lyuṭ*. The word "rajaḥ" [is derived from the root *raj*].
The suffix *asun* is applied [to all verbal roots] by the rule *sārvadhātubhyo 'sun* (Pāṇini 3.2.49). Regarding the word *rāgī*,
the suffix *ghinuṇ* is applied according to the rule *sampṛcānvādisūtreṇa* (Pāṇini 3.2.142), and the substitution of *k* for *c* and *j* occurs by the rule *cajoḥ ku ghiṇṇyatoḥ* (Pāṇini 7.3.52).
Is it established by the rule of irregular formation (*nipātana*) stating "abandon passion, resort [to virtue]" (*tyaja rāgaṃ bhaja*)?

Because here, in the rule for *sampṛc* and others (Pāṇini 3.2.142), the author makes the reference after having applied the elision of the nasal of the root *rañj*, this indicates that the elision of the *n* occurs before an affix marked with *gh* or *ṇ*.

But is it not the case that the elision of the *n* is already accomplished by the rule itself (Pāṇini 6.4.26) when the suffix *śap* follows? That is not so; for just as in the rule "and from *indh* and *bhavati*" (Pāṇini 1.2.6), the root *indh* is referred to by means of an adventitious *i*, so too here it is referred to by an adventitious *a*, and not by the suffix *śap*.

For in the rule *indhibhavatibhyāṃ ca* [Pāṇini 1.2.6], there is no singular mention; otherwise, the elision of the nasal vowel (*anunāsikalopa*) would apply by the rule *aniditām* [Pāṇini 6.4.24]. Regarding the roots *daṃśa* (to bite, DhP 989) and *ṣvanj* (to embrace, DhP 976), we have the form *pariṣvajate*. Here, the substitution of *ṣ* occurs according to the rule *upasargāt sunoti* [Pāṇini 8.3.65] and others. Now, for what purpose is a separate rule (*pṛthagyoga*) formulated? Why is the mention of the root *rañj* not made in the preceding rule itself? To this, he says: "The formulation of a separate rule," and so forth.

In the subsequent sūtra, the recurrence of *rañji* alone is intended so that [the suffix] does not apply to *daṃśa* and the others. "That by which one is colored is *rāga*"—here, the suffix *ghañ* is applied according to *halaśca* [Pāṇini 3.3.121].
The same applies to *raṅga*. *Java* means speed, a particular kind of motion.
"And the absence of vṛddhi.
Regarding the rule "ata upadhāyāḥ":
once the elision of *n* has been performed, the rule "ata upadhāyāḥ" would require the application of vṛddhi; therefore, its absence is prescribed as an irregularity (nipātana).

But is it not the case that the prohibition of *vṛddhi* is already established by this very rule [1.1.4]? Why, then, is the absence of *vṛddhi* prescribed as a *nipātana* (irregularity)? To this he says: "Because of the context of *ik*" (*ikprakaraṇāt*), and so forth.
In that context, the term "*ik*" is carried over from [1.1.3]; therefore, there is a prohibition of *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* characterized by an *ik* vowel.
However, this *vṛddhi* is not characterized by an *ik*, but rather is characterized by the penultimate vowel (*upadhā*).
And this *vṛddhi* characterized by the presence of the suffix *upadhā* is not [the same as] that characterized by the suffix *ig*, because its locus has been specifically indicated;
therefore, there is no prohibition of it here. As in the example: *gosyadaḥ*.
The suffix *dhañ* is used in the sense of a state (*bhāva*).
In the example "the speed of cows" (*gosyadaḥ*), there is a compound according to the rule "the genitive case [ending] connected with a *kṛt*-derived word is compounded" (*kṛdyogā ṣaṣṭhī samasyate*).
[Similarly, one has] "the flow of oil" (*tailasyandaḥ*).
The meaning is "the flowing of oil.

[The root] *syandū* is used in the sense of "flowing" (*ruāvaṇe*) according to the Dhātupāṭha (761). Regarding the form *avodaḥ*, it is formed by [the rule] Pāṇini 6.1.87, which applies when combined with a prefix (*upasarga*).
The prohibition [of guṇa] by the rule *na dhātulopaḥ* [Pāṇini 1.1.4] and so forth does not apply here, because the guṇa is not characterized by the elision of a root-vowel (*aniglakṣaṇatvāt*).
It is said, "and the guṇa is introduced as an irregularity (*nipātyate*).
But surely the guṇa is already established by the rule *pugantalaghūpadhasya* [Pāṇini 7.3.86]?
Why is that [suffix] elided? To this he says: "There is no elision of a root," and so forth.
"[The suffix *man* is *auṇādika*" means:

by the rule *ṛtistusu-hu-sṛ-dhṛ-kṣi-kṣu-bhā-yā-vā-pada-yakṣi-nībhyo man* (Dhātupāṭha 7.26), which prescribes *man* after roots such as *ṛti*, etc., it occurs after *und* as well due to the word *bahulam* ("variously")."
Regarding the word *śranteḥ*:

this is the prohibition of the elision of the nasal (*nalopa*) which would otherwise apply by the rule *aniditām* [Pāṇini 6.4.24] to the root *śranth*, meaning "to loosen" or "to gladden" (Dhātupāṭha 1510).
From this very prohibition, it is understood that this nasal *n* is indicated as being *it* (having an indicatory *i*).

Now, why was it not simply stated as *nāñceḥ iṭi*? Even if this were stated, the prohibition would apply only in the sense of honor (*pūjā*). For indeed, the augment *iṭ* is prescribed after the root *añc* only in the sense of honor. It is impossible to say so, because by the rule *ktvāniṣṭhayornityam* [Pāṇini 7.2.53], the augment *iṭ* is invariably prescribed for the suffixes *ktvā* and *niṣṭhā*. As for the suffix *ktvā*, the addition of the augment *iṭ* is optional by the rule *vibhāṣā seṭ* [Pāṇini 7.2.56]; that [augment] occurs even in the sense of honor. If it were stated in that way, then when the suffix *ktvā* does not have the augment *iṭ* in the sense of honor, the prohibition would not apply—as in the example *gurumaṅktvā* ("having honored the teacher").

The negative particle *na* is this prohibitive statement for the sake of what follows. In this context, if it were stated simply as "after *añc*, when not expressing worship," the desired form would indeed be established, as in: *añcitā asya guravaḥ* ("his teachers are respected").
The suffix *kta* is applied by the rule *matibuddhipūjārthebhyaśca* (Pāṇini 3.2.188).
The genitive case is applied by the rule *kartṛkarmaṇoḥ kṛti* (Pāṇini 2.3.65).
[In this formation] there is a prohibition of the augment *iṭ* by the rule *yasya vibhāṣā* (Pāṇini 7.2.15).
Because the rule *añceḥ* [Pāṇini 7.2.56] prescribes the optional introduction of *iṭ*, [the form] *skantvā* arises;
[this is] from the root *skandira* "to move" or "to dry up" (Dhātupāṭha 979), with the addition of *iṭ* in the alternative case by the rule *svarati* [Pāṇini 7.2.44], etc.

"Because of the prohibition of *kittva*, there is no elision of *n*. For by the rule "of those [roots] not having *i* or *u* as *it*" (Pāṇini 6.4.24) and so forth, the elision of *n* is prescribed when a suffix marked with *k* or *ṅ* follows. However, for the *ktvā* suffix that has an *iṭ* augment, the prohibition of *kittva* is established by the rule "after a root ending in *iṭ*" (Pāṇini 1.2.18). Consequently, in the alternative where the *iṭ* augment is present, the absence of *n*-elision follows simply from the absence of *kittva*; therefore, that [case] does not motivate this particular grammatical rule (*yoga*).
The intention is that, for this reason, no example of the suffix *ktvā* has been shown [by him]. Regarding "naṣṭvā, naṃṣṭvā":
the substitution of *ṣ* [for *ś*] occurs by the rule Pāṇini 8.2.36 (*vraścādi*), followed by the substitution of *ṣṭu* [for *ṣṭu*].
Then, by [the rule] Pāṇini 7.1.60, the augment *mum* is inserted.

The term *ja* here is a reference to a phoneme (*varṇagrahaṇa*). Since in the case of a reference to a phoneme, the rule of "specifying that which ends with it" (*tadantavidhi*) applies everywhere even without explicitly mentioning the word "end," the inclusion of the word "end" (*anta*) here is for the sake of clarity. As for what some say—that the mention of the "end" is intended to prohibit the elision (*lopa*) of the *n* even when it is not a penultimate letter (*anupadhā*), as in the examples *bhaktvā* and *bhaṅktvā*—that is not correct.
For by what rule would the elision of a *n* that is not a penultimate letter ever apply, such that it would need to be prohibited in certain cases?
It has been stated that the elision (*lopa*) of a penultimate *n* (*upadhānakāra*) occurs; however, this [final] *n* is not a penultimate *n*.

If that is so, then it indicates that the elision of *n* occurs in some instances even outside the scope of a grammatical rule (*vidhi*). By means of this, the forms "magnaḥ" and "magnadān" are established.

Consequently, this statement—"they desire the augment *num* before the final letter of the root *masj*"—need not be stated for the sake of the elision of the *anuṣaṅga*. For if this were not stated there, then in that alternative where the elision does not occur by means of the suffix *ktvā*, the elision of *s* [by Pāṇini 8.2.29] would also not take place, because the root would not begin with a non-conjunct consonant (*asaṃyogādi*).
Therefore, this must indeed be stated: "they desire the augment *num* before the final letter of *masj*."

Furthermore, since it is impossible for a *nakāra* that is not penultimate (*anupadhā*) to undergo elision, the mention of "the end" (*anta*) would not be appropriate for the purpose of ensuring that the prohibition of elision applies specifically to a *nakāra* that is not penultimate. The particle *ca* serves to carry forward the optionality (*vibhāṣā*) from [Pāṇini 6.4.32]. The form *abhāji* has already been explained previously.
"This elision of the letter *n* has not yet occurred," because the rule for the elision of *n* applies only before suffixes marked with *k* or *ṅ*, whereas the suffix *ciṇ* is not marked with *ṅ*.
Therefore, since there is no [suffix] to be prohibited, the word "not" (*na*) does not carry over.
Therefore, the intention is that this is indeed a mandatory rule (*vidhi*). Regarding the form *anvaśiṣat*:
by [Pāṇini 3.1.56], there is the substitution of *aṅ* for the suffix *cli*; thus we have *anvaśiṣat*.
As for the examples *aśiṣva* and *aśiṣma*, the *śap* suffix is elided because the root belongs to the *adādi* (second) class.

Regarding "śāsati": by [Pāṇini 6.1.6], it receives the designation *abhyasta* (repeated), and by [Pāṇini 7.1.4], the suffix *jhi* is replaced by *at*. Regarding "śaśāsatuḥ" and "śaśāsuḥ": [these are derived from the same root].
The forms are *liṭatusus*.
Regarding the rule "kvau ca śāsaḥ":
the meaning is that one must explain this as having the sense that the substitution of *i* for [the final letter] of the root *śās* occurs when *kvip* follows.

In this regard, the explanation is as follows: although the substitution of *it* (the long vowel *ī*) was prescribed here earlier than the elision of the *kvip* suffix—because it applies both to what has been formed and what has not been formed due to its being eternal (*nitya*)—nevertheless, even though that [suffix] has been elided, the substitution of *it* will still occur by virtue of the rule regarding "characteristics based on an affix" (*pratyayalakṣaṇa*).
However, the statement "there is no operation based on an affix when it depends on a phoneme" (*varṇāśraye pratyayalakṣaṇaṃ nāsti*) is merely a general rule (*prāyika*).
For instance, even in cases depending on a phoneme, [an operation based on an affix] sometimes does occur.

For example, in the form *atṛṇeṭ*, there is the augment *īm* by [Pāṇini 7.3.92] *tṛ ha im*. Alternatively, this shortening of the vowel (*itva*) does not occur at all because it depends solely on the phoneme (*varṇāśraya*).
How so? Here, by the mention of the term *aṅga*, the suffix (*pratyaya*) is brought to mind;

it is then qualified by the mention of *hal*. For this very reason, it is stated in the commentary (*vṛtti*): "before a suffix beginning with *hal* that has *k* or *ṅ* as an indicatory letter" (*halādau kṅiti*).

Therefore, although the suffix *kvip* consists of phonemes (*varṇa*), it is nevertheless not relied upon as having the nature of phonemes; rather, it is relied upon as having the nature of a suffix. In the case of *āryaśīḥ*, once the substitution of *ru* for the *s* has been made, the lengthening occurs by [Pāṇini 8.2.76]: "There is lengthening of the penultimate vowel before *r* and *v*. Now, one might ask: why does the substitution of *it* (the short *i*) not occur in the forms *āśāste* and *āśāsyamānaḥ*? To this he says: "From which *śās*" and so forth. There are two roots *śās*: one is *parasmaipada* (active), and the other is *ātmanepada* (middle). Of these, the reference is specifically to that *śās* from which the suffix *aṅ* is prescribed.

And that [suffix] is prescribed by the rule *sattiśāstyarttibhyaśca* [Pāṇini 3.1.56] for the root *śās* in the sense of "instruction" (*anuśiṣṭi*) from the Dhātupāṭha (1075). In that context, the term *parasmaipadeṣu* [Pāṇini 3.1.55] is understood to carry over, because this [root] can only occur with the *parasmaipada* endings. But how is it understood that, despite being mentioned in a general way, it refers specifically to the *parasmaipada* forms? It is through association (*saṃsarga*).

For when there is an association, a specific determination occurs; thus, when it is said, "Let the cow with the calf be brought," the understanding arises that it is specifically a mare, due to its association with the calf.

In this case, the *aṅ* augment is employed as a cause for the root *śās*. Therefore, due to its association with that [augment], the root *śās* is understood specifically as one that takes the *parasmaipada* (active voice) endings.

[Objection: But is it not the case here that the *aṅ* alone is not taken as the cause? What then? The *hal* (consonant) is also included, and that [consonant] can belong even to roots that take the *ātmanepada* (middle voice). So, how is there an understanding of the *śās* qualified by its association with the *aṅ*? [Response: This is not so. When both a common and an uncommon related element are present, the cognition arises only with respect to that whose uncommon related element is proximate.
For instance, when it is said, "Let the cows be tied up among the old and the young," only mares (*baḍavā*) are understood [to be meant].

Therefore, even though both *aṅ* and *hal* are mentioned, it is logical that only that after which *aṅ* is prescribed should be taken. If, then, this refers only to that after which *aṅ* is prescribed, then in cases such as *yathāśāste* ("as he prays") and *āśāsyamāna* ("being prayed for"), [the suffix] would not occur; likewise, it would not occur with the *kvip* suffix either? To this, he says: "*In the case of the *kvip* suffix,*" etc., and "*kṣiyāsīḥ,*" etc.
Alternatively, one should simply state that the *kvip* suffix does not occur after this [root] either.
The word "or" (*vā*) is used for the sake of an alternative view.

Now, what is the purpose of the letter *ta*? If it is argued that it is so that a long vowel (*dīrgha*) might not occur by virtue of being the closest [substitute], this is not the case; for by the rule "an *aṇ* being taught [as a substitute] does not include its homogeneous counterparts" (*vyā.pa.* 35), such a substitution will not take place. If that is so, then [the *ta*] is for the sake of clarity.

Now, why does this not serve to eliminate doubt? If it were stated as *śāsa yaṅṅaloḥ*, there would be doubt: "Is this vowel *i* (ikāra) indicated here after it has undergone the *yaṇ* substitution, or is it the vowel *ī* (īkāra), or perhaps the consonant *y* (yakāra)? There is no such doubt, because he provides the specific indication *yadayam* [Pāṇini 1.2.53]. From that, it is determined: "This is the vowel *i* (ikāra), not the vowel *ī* (īkāra), nor the consonant *y* (yakāra). If the term *upadhāyāḥ* [Pāṇini 6.4.24] is understood to carry over here, then just as in the preceding rule [the word] *śāsaḥ*...

[6.4.34] Thus, since the genitive case here functions as a partitive genitive (*avayava-ṣaṣṭhī*), would it not be the same in this instance as well? If that were so, this substitution would apply only to the *upadhā* (the penultimate vowel), whereas it is intended to be a replacement for the whole (*sarvādeśa*). Having considered this, he says: "The mention of *upadhā* is withdrawn. For that mention of *upadhā* was connected with the mention of *kṅit*, and here the mention of *kṅit* has been withdrawn. Therefore, the [genitive] "of the *upadhā*" [from 6.4.24] is also withdrawn.

"The [term] *kṅiti* has also ceased to apply," because the term *kṅit* is mentioned again in the rule beginning with *anudāttopadeśa* (Pāṇini 6.4.37). By the words "by that" (*tena*) and so forth, he shows what is achieved when the application of *kṅit* has ceased: if the term *kṅiti* (Pāṇini 6.4.24) were to carry over here, then in the alternative where *hi* does not have the designation *apit* according to *vā chandasi* (Pāṇini 3.4.88), the designation *ṅit* would not exist due to the statement *na dhātulopa ārdhadhātuke* (Pāṇini 1.1.4); consequently, the substitution of *ś* for *s* would not occur.
But when the mention of *kṅit* has ceased, it indeed occurs even in the alternative view where [the suffix] is not *pit*.

One might argue: "By understanding this as a fixed option (*vyavasthitavibhāṣā*), the *hi* following *śās* will not be *pit*; therefore, there is no need to remove the mention of *kṅit*. To this, he says: "As for 'śādhī'... and so forth.
If the *hi* following *śās* were not optionally *pit*, then in the form *śādhi*, because it would be "taught later" (*satiśiṣṭa*), it would be exclusively oxytone by the accent of the suffix.
In the Vedic language (*chandas*), even an initial acute accent (*ādyudātta*) is desired.
And that [accent] occurs through the accent of the verbal root (*dhātusvara*) when the suffix *hi* possesses the property of *pit*; it does not occur otherwise.
Therefore, the status of *pit* must necessarily be prescribed for *yakṣe* in the Vedic language.

Now, why was it not stated simply as *ā hau*? For would not the form *śādhi* be established by the rule *akore’pi hi* (Pāṇini 6.1.93), which prescribes the substitution of *s* for *ś*, followed by the long vowel by the rule for homogeneous vowels (*savarṇadīrgha*)? It is not established; because by the preceding rule (Pāṇini 6.4.74), the substitution of *i* for the penultimate (*upadhā*) would occur.

Nor is it proper for this [new rule] to be an exception (*bādhaka*) to that [preceding rule]; for an exception occurs only when there is no possibility [of both rules applying together], yet here there is the possibility for both to exist.
Therefore, even if the substitution of *i* for the penultimate were prescribed by the previous rule, it would certainly still take place.
Regarding the term *hanter*:

the mention of *sip* is for the purpose of excluding the *yaṅluṅ* (the elision of the *yaṅ* suffix); thus we have *jaṅghahi*. As for the term *anunāsika*, this is a mention without a case-ending (*avibhaktika*), having applied the elision (*luk*) of the sixth case plural;
therefore, he says: "of those ending in an *anunāsika*."
When [the rule] "6.4.15" would otherwise require lengthening, this elision (lopa) is prescribed.
Once this elision has taken place here, lengthening does not apply, because its cause has been removed.

Regarding the forms *yami*, *rami*, *gami*, *nami*, *hani*, and *manyatayaḥ*: *Yama* is in the sense of "ceasing" (*uparame*; Dhātupāṭha 984); *ramu* is in the sense of "sporting" (*krīḍāyām*; Dhātupāṭha 853); *ganlṛ* and *sṛplṛ* are in the sense of "going" (*gatau*; Dhātupāṭha 982, 983); *ṇama* is in the sense of "bowing" (*prahvatve*; Dhātupāṭha 981; according to the Dhātupāṭha, also in the sense of sound); *hana* is in the sense of "injury" and "going" (*hiṃsāgatyoḥ*; Dhātupāṭha 1012); and *mana* is in the sense of "knowing" (*jñāne*; Dhātupāṭha 1176). Regarding the suffix *vati*:
*vana* and *ṣaṇa* are in the sense of "acquisition" (*sambhaktau*; Dhātupāṭha 463, 464). The prohibition of the augment *iṭ* is applied by the rule beginning with *titutratatha* (Pāṇini 7.2.9).
By the mention of *ktin*, he shows that an example for the root *van* is possible only with *ktin*, and not elsewhere. Why so? He says: "But in the case of *ktic*," and so forth.
For he will state a prohibition [by the rule] *ktici ca* (Pāṇini 6.4.39).

As for those other suffixes beginning with *jhal*, they too ought to have the augment *iṭ*; therefore, because they lack the quality of beginning with *jhal*, they do not serve as causes for the elision of the nasal in the root *van*. By the principle of elimination (*pāriśeṣya*), the elision of the nasal in *van* must occur only before the suffix *ktin*. The statement "he will explain the substitution of *ā* for *san*" implies that this [suffix] is not an example of the elision of the nasal.
Furthermore, the substitution of *āt* will be stated [by Pāṇini] in the rule beginning with "janasanakhanām" (Pāṇ.
6.4.42). Regarding the form "kṣataḥ":
the root is "kṣaṇu hiṃsāyām" (Dhātupāṭha 1465).
Regarding "ṛtaḥ": from the root *ṛṇu* meaning "to go" (Dhātupāṭha 1467). Regarding "tṛtaḥ":
from the root *tṛṇu* meaning "to give" [or "to eat"] (Dhātupāṭha 1468).
Regarding "ghṛtaḥ":

[it is derived from] "ghṛṇu" in the sense of "to shine" (Dhātupāṭha 1469). Regarding "vataḥ": [it is derived from] "vanu" in the sense of "to beg" (Dhātupāṭha 1470). Regarding "mataḥ": [it is derived from "man" in the sense of] "to think."
The root *manu* in the sense of "to understand" (Dhātupāṭha 1471) [is used in the forms] *atata*, *atathā*;
these are the third person singular and second person singular forms of the Ātmanepada in the Imperfect (*luṅ*) tense derived from the root *tan*.
By [Pāṇini 2.4.79], there is the elision (*luk*) of *sic*. Thus: *śāntaḥ*, *tāntaḥ*, *dāntaḥ*—these are the forms of the roots *śam*, *tam*, and *dam*.
These [roots] are not taught with an anudātta (low-pitched) vowel.
Regarding the phrase "and here," etc.:

when the suffix *ktin* is added to the roots *gam* and *ram*, they would become udātta on the first syllable by the rule for *nit*-suffixes; since they would thus lack the status of being anudātta, the elision [of the root-final *m*] would not occur if the term "in the original teaching" (*upadeśa*) were not included. However, because this term is present, the elision does take place.

Furthermore, if the mention of "in the original instruction" (*upadeśagrahaṇa*) were not made, the term *śāntaḥ* (appeased) would also [be subject to this rule]. For in the case of the root *śam*, once the accent of the suffix has been applied according to Pāṇini 6.1.158, the remainder becomes unaccented (*anudātta*), and thus [the word] would be unaccented.

However, because of the mention of "in the original instruction," it does not occur; for in its original instruction, the root *śam* is not unaccented. This rule is commenced for the sake of excluding roots beginning with a consonant (*ajhalādi*).

Regarding "prayatya": when the prefix *pra-* has been compounded, [the rule] "in a compound not preceded by *nañ*, *lyap* replaces *ktvā*" (Pāṇini 7.1.37; 6.1.71) applies. Regarding "yantī" and so forth:
the suffix *ktic* is applied according to the rule "the suffixes *ktic* and *kta* occur after a root to form a name" (Pāṇini 3.3.174).
And here, the rule regarding "those taught with an anudātta [vowel]" and so forth continues to apply; therefore, in the case of *kāntiḥ* and *śāntiḥ*, the prohibition of lengthening does not occur.
However, there is no possibility at all for the elision of the nasal (*anunāsika-lopa*) here, because these are taught with an udātta vowel.
By the statement beginning with "when the elision of the nasal is prohibited," he explains the purpose of including the mention of "lengthening" (*dīrgha*).

But surely, since it is understood that what is prescribed in this context does not apply by virtue of the specific context (*prakaraṇa*), even without the mention of "long" (*dīrgha*), the prohibition will apply to long vowels as well; so what is the purpose of mentioning "long"? In that case, this [mention of "long"] teaches the following *paribhāṣā*: "A rule or a prohibition applies to the immediately preceding [element]" (*Vyāḍīya-paribhāṣā* 19). This [mention] is also undertaken for the sake of cases where the vowel is neither *ac* nor *jhal*, such as in *adhvagato harayaḥ*.
[The derivation is as follows: from *adhvan* with the suffix *kvip* in the sense of "going on a path" (*adhvānaṃ gacchanti*), followed by the suffix *jas* after that [form ending in *kvip*].
Regarding the phrase "of *gam* and so forth" (*gamādīnām*), etc.:
the meaning is that one must explain this as having the sense that "the elision of the nasal (*anunāsika*) of *gam* and so forth occurs before a *kvip* suffix.

In this regard, the explanation is as follows: the particle *ca* ("and") is carried over from the preceding rule, and it serves to include what has not been explicitly mentioned; by means of it, the rule will apply to *gam* and its class, and not to *gam* alone.
Regarding "saṃyata": [it is derived] from the root *yam* preceded by the prefix *sam*, with the suffix *kvip*.
Regarding "paritata": [it is derived from the root *tan* preceded by the prefix *pari*].
From the root *tan* preceded by *pari*, the vowel is lengthened according to [Pāṇini 6.4.15],
etc.; and from the rule "and *ū*," etc.,
the nasal is elided due to the presence of the particle *ca*.
In some places, the rule is read as *ūṅ ca*; in that case, the purpose of the letter *ṅ* must be considered.
This will be accomplished here by the *alo’ntyaparibhāṣā* (the paribhāṣā concerning the final letter) alone.
[The example is] *agregūḥ*.
In the case of *gameḥ* and *bhrameḥ*, when the nasalization (*anunāsika*) has been elided, the vowel *a* is replaced by *u*. Regarding the word *abjāḥ*:
it is a compound with an upapada meaning "born in the waters" (*apsu jāyate*); the substitution of the *ja*-class sound (*jaśtva*) for the letter *p* results in the letter *b*.
Regarding *goṣā*: [it is derived from *go-sā*].
The root *ṣaṇ* in the sense of "giving" (Dhātupāṭha 1464) [is used in the word] *vijavā*.
Or [it is derived from] *jan* in the sense of "birth" (Dhātupāṭha 1105) or *janī* in the sense of "manifestation" (Dhātupāṭha 1149).
[The compound] *agregāva* (the Kāśikā reads *agrejāvā*) [is formed accordingly].
Thus, there is no elision (*aluk*) of the locative case ending in *saptamyāḥ*.

Now, for what purpose is the mention of "nasalized" (*anunāsika*) [in this rule], given that the mention of "nasalized" continues from the previous rule beginning with *anudāttopadeśa-* (Pāṇini 6.4.37)? To this he says: "While the mention of 'nasalized' is still in force," and so forth.

For that previously mentioned mention of "nasalized" is connected with the mention of "those taught as having an anudātta accent"; therefore, when that [mention of the anudātta] recurs, its [mention of the nasalized] would also recur.

Therefore, this mention of *anunāsika* (nasal) is made so that it may apply to the mere nasal [sound]. Now, what is the purpose of the long (*dīrgha*) pronunciation here? One might say that the short (*hrasva*) alone should be stated; for even if the short is used, the rule *ataḥ kṛ-k-ti* [P. 6.1.101] would still result in the desired form through the substitution of a long vowel for homogeneous vowels. One should not raise the objection that the desired form is not achieved because the subsequent form (*pararūpa*) would apply [by P. 6.1.97]; for this is precluded by the force of the prescription of the letter *a*. If indeed the subsequent form were to apply by the rule *ato guṇe*, then the author would have prescribed the elision (*lopa*) itself in the present context. Therefore, the short vowel alone should be employed.

This is not the case; for if [the short vowel] were present, when the suffix *vanip* is prescribed after the root *ghuṇ* (meaning "to whirl," *bhramaṇe* according to the Dhātupāṭha), the form *dhvāvā* would not be established. Therefore, the prescription of the long vowel alone is appropriate. [The word *san*] is understood from the previous rule as being qualified by both *jhal* and *kṅit*, respectively. However, it is not possible to qualify the suffix *san* with the mention of *jhal* in the current sūtra, because a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) is subordinate (*aprādhāna*), whereas that which is qualified (*viśeṣya*) is primary (*pradhāna*).
Furthermore, this compound *sañjhaloḥ* is a *dvandva*.
In that regard, because all the pairs of terms are equally primary, a mutual relationship of principal and subordinate cannot be established.
Furthermore, the inclusion [of the term *sarva*] is for the sake of including those [terms] ending in *aṅ*.
"In this case," and so forth.

Why? Because the augment *iṭ* occurs after the root *san*, therefore a *san* beginning with a *jhal* consonant can follow that very [root]. It is for this purpose alone that the mention of *san* is made, and not for the sake of the roots *jan* and *khan*; for a *san* beginning with a *jhal* cannot follow those two, as they are invariably accompanied by *iṭ*. If this were so, since the purpose would already be served by *san* following *san*, the substitution of *ā* would not occur; furthermore, in other cases such as the *niṣṭhā* suffixes and others beginning with *jhal* which are *kṅit*, there would be elision of the *n* by the rule *anudāttopadeśa-* (Pāṇini 6.4.37). To this, he says: "In other cases," and so forth.

What is the scope for the reading of *sanoti*, *tanoti*, and so on, as distinct from [the rule] "The operations beginning with *tanādika* apply" (Pāṇini 2.4.79) and others? And what is the scope for the mention of *san* in the rule prescribing *āttva* (the substitution of *ā* for *o*)—namely, in the forms *san* and *siṣāsati*? In the case of *sātaḥ* and *sātavān*, both [rules] would apply. Here, by means of *vipratiṣedha* (conflict of rules), *āttva* occurs, overriding the elision of the nasal (*anunāsikalopa*). [Objection: But a conflict of rules (*vipratiṣedha*) occurs only when both [rules] are established. However, here, by the rule "In this context, that which precedes is as if unestablished" (Pāṇini 6.4.22), both are unestablished. So, how can there be a conflict? To this, he says: "ghumāsthāgā... and so forth.

How does this serve as an indicator (*jñāpaka*)? The purpose of the mention of *hal* [in Pāṇini 6.4.64] is precisely this: that the substitution of *ī* should occur when a consonant (*hal*) follows, but it should not occur here in the examples *godāḥ* and *kambaladaḥ* (derived from *go-dā-*, *kambala-dā-*). If there were a conflict (*vipratiṣedha*) in this case, then [the author] says: "ghu-mā-sthā-gā... and so forth. How does this serve as an indicator? The purpose of the mention of *hal* is precisely this: that the substitution of *ī* should occur when a consonant follows, but it should not occur here in the examples *godaḥ* and *kambaladaḥ*. If there were no conflict in this case, the mention of *hal* would be purposeless.
"Let it be that *ittva* (the substitution of *i*) occurs; since it is not established [by other rules], the elision (*lopa*) will take place.
However, the Teacher perceives that in this context there is a conflict of rules (*vipratiṣedha*), which is why he employs the mention of "consonant" (*hal*).
For if the mention of "consonant" were absent, *ittva* would apply even before vowel-initial suffixes; consequently, *ipaṅ* would be applied, resulting in an undesirable form.

Therefore, since the mention of *hal* (the consonant) is for the purpose of excluding what is undesirable (*aniṣṭanivṛttyarthatvāt*), its status as an indicator (*jñāpakatvam*) is not tenable? This is not a fault; because [the substitution] *īt* is indeed *asiddha*, the substitute *iyaṅ* will not occur. In that case, the mention of *hal* would be for the sake of establishing a fixed order (*vyavasthārtham*). For if it were absent, then because *īt* is *asiddha*, there would be the elision of *ā* (*āllopa*); and because the elision of *ā* is *asiddha*, there would be *īt*. Thus, there would be a circularity (*cakravat*) in the established order. This too is without purpose. If the mention of *hal* were for the sake of establishing a fixed order, he would not have mentioned *hal* at all.

Having stated the substitution of *i* for [the final vowel] without distinction, one would then establish an exception (*apavāda*) for its elision (*lopa*) when followed by a root beginning with a vowel.

Why then is it that this rule [Pāṇini 6.4.64] applies? Consequently, by [Pāṇini 6.4.66], there occurs the elision of the vowel *ā* in the case of the roots *dhū*, *mā*, *sthā*, *gā*, *pā*, *hā* (jahāti), and *sā*, provided that an affix follows which begins with a vowel and is marked with *k* or *ṅ*.

For what purpose is this? If *īttva* (the substitution of *ī*) for *gh* and other letters were taught to apply merely before an affix (*pratyaya*), then [by the rule] "before an affix beginning with a consonant (*jādi*) that has *k* or *ṅ* as an indicatory letter (*kiṅti*), provided it is not a word-final (*apadāt*)", there would be *īttva* by [Pāṇini 6.4.68] *īt* for *gh* and others when followed by a *kiṅt* vowel (*anaci*). Then [by 6.4.67] *dānyasya saṃyogādeḥ* [and subsequent rules], *īttva* would occur. Since this is already established by a much simpler formulation (*lagīyasā nyāsena*), the fact that the Teacher includes the mention of *hal* (consonant) indicates that he intends to show: "In this case, a conflict of rules (*vipratiṣedha*) occurs. This introduction is for the sake of cases such as *asat* and those beginning with *hal*.
"It is born, it is produced"—
here the verbal suffix (*lakāra*) denotes the abstract state (*bhāva*).
"It is born repeatedly" (*jājāyate*).
Furthermore, by [Pāṇini 7.4.83], there is lengthening of the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*),
as in *jañjanyate*. By [Pāṇini 7.4.85], there is the augment *nu*, as in *sāyate* and *sanyate*.

The *lakāra* (verbal suffix) is used either in the sense of the abstract state (*bhāve*) or the object (*karmaṇi*). Someone might have the misconception that, even when the *śyan* affix follows the root *jan*, there should optionally be the substitution of *ā* (by Pāṇini 6.1.59). To dispel this error, he says: "In the case of *jan* with *śyan," etc. Since *jan* belongs to the *divādi* class, when *śyan* is prescribed, both [possibilities] would apply: the optional substitution of *ā* by [Pāṇini 6.1.59] and the replacement of *jan* by *jā* by [Pāṇini 7.3.79]. In that situation, because the substitute *jā* is an *anavakāśa* (irreducible/inevitable) rule, that alone occurs invariably.

Therefore, in the case of *śyani*, it always occurs as *jāyate* and never as *janyate*. The mention of *asya* is for the purpose that the elision (*lopa*) of the suffix *ktic*—which was previously mentioned—should not apply here, so that the elision of *n* may occur even when [the suffix] is separated [from the root].
Now, even though *asya* is mentioned, why does the elision of *ktic* not occur? It is because of the force (*sāmarthya*) of the mention of *asya*. [Objection:

Then what is the purpose of mentioning *anyatarasyām*, since the term *vibhāṣā* (optionally) continues to apply from [Pāṇini 6.4.46]? [Response: He says: "The mention of *anyatarasyām*," and so forth.

But how is the cessation of the inclusion of the term *vibhāṣā* suspected, such that the term *anyatarasyām* is employed for the sake of clarity? To this he says: "For [it is] connected with the letter *ya*" (*yakārasambandhaṃ hi*), etc. That inclusion of *vibhāṣā* is connected with the suffixes beginning with *ya*.

Furthermore, one might have the suspicion that once the word "ye" has ceased to apply because another cause [the suffix *ktic*] has been introduced, the mention of the option (*vibhāṣā*) also ceases upon its cessation; therefore, for the sake of clarity, the mention of "anyatarasyām" is made again. Regarding "cikīrṣitā," the suffix *tṛc* follows a desiderative form.
Regarding "bhavati, bhavataḥ."
Is it because of the governing rule (*adhikāra*) "in an *ārdhadhātuka* suffix"? [The answer is: In this case, the elision of *śap* does not occur in an *sārvadhātuka* suffix.

If the governing rule for *ārdhadhātuka* were established for the purpose that the elision of *śap* should not occur here, then it need not be established; for the elision of *śap* will not occur simply by virtue of an indicator (*jñāpaka*). The Teacher’s practice indicates that "the elision of *śap* does not occur by this [rule]," since he prescribes the elision (*luk*) of *śap* in the rule *adi-prabhṛtibhyaḥ* [Pāṇini 2.4.72]. To this, he says: "*Adiprabhṛtibhyaḥ*," etc. The particle *iti* is used in the sense of a reason (*hetu*).

For an indicator (jñāpaka) exists only when there is a purpose; and there is indeed a purpose for the statement regarding the elision of *śap* after roots beginning with *ad* and others. What is that? It is so that the *guṇa* substitution does not occur in the form "vittaḥ."

If there were elision (*lopa*) in the case of *vittaḥ*, then by the rule *pratyayalakṣaṇa* [Pāṇini 1.1.62], there would be *guṇa* substitution according to *pugantalaghūpadhasya* [Pāṇini 7.3.86]. However, in the case of *mṛṣṭaḥ*, when elision occurs [by *ślu*] according to [Pāṇini 7.2.114], it does not take place because of the prohibition of *pratyayalakṣaṇa* by [Pāṇini 1.1.63]. Therefore, the prescription of the elision of *śap* after roots such as *ad* and others must be for the purpose of prohibiting *pratyayalakṣaṇa*; thus, it is not an indicator (*jñāpaka*) for the absence of elision of *śap*.
Regarding "bebhiditā":

there is the elision of the *yaṅ* suffix. In the case of "bebhid-y-ate," [the substitution] does not occur before the *śap* augment of the *sārvadhātuka* suffix. Regarding "kāraṇā": [this is formed with the suffix *lyuṭ*].
The [augment] does not occur before the *śap* [suffix] when it is a *sārvadhātuka* [affix], as in:
*papatuḥ*, *papuḥ*;
*vavatuḥ*, *vavuḥ*.

*atus* is the suffix. By [Pāṇini 6.4.64], *pāter vā teś ca*, there is the elision of the vowel *a*. In the forms *dīyate* and *dhīyate*, the *ya*-suffix is applied because they belong to the *ārdhadhātuka* class.

"Adātām? Adhātām? [These are] in the *luṅ* [aorist]; by [Pāṇini 3.4.101], *tasthastha*, the *tas* [suffix] becomes *tām*; and by [Pāṇini 2.4.77], *gātisthā* etc., there is the elision (*luk*) of *sic*.
"Snāyāt, sneyāt. [These are] in the *liṅ* [optative].

The suffix *liṅ* occurs in the sense of benediction (*āśis*). By the rule *tasya* [Pāṇini 3.4.116], it receives the designation *ārdhadhātuka*. The augment *yāsuṭ* is added, and by the rule beginning with *skoḥ saṃyogādyoḥ* [Pāṇini 8.2.29], there is the elision of the *sakāra*.

Regarding the statement "it does not occur in the *liṅ* of benediction (*āśīrliṅ*)": what is other than the *liṅ* of benediction? It is the *liṅ* of the optative (*vidhyādi-liṅ*). In that case, it does not occur; because that [optative *liṅ*] possesses the designation *sārvadhātuka*.
Therefore, in that context, it becomes "snāyāt" (he should bathe);
here, by [Pāṇini 7.2.79], there is the elision of the letter *s*.
"Kāriṣīṣṭa" (he should be made).

In the sense of benediction (*āśis*), the *liṅ* [is used]; by [Pāṇini 1.3.13], the *ātmanepada* suffix *sīyuṭ* is applied; by [Pāṇini 3.4.107], *suṭ* is added; and due to the *ciṇvad-bhāva*, there is *vṛddhi*.
Thus, "kriyeta" is the *liṅ* of the potential mood (*vidhyādi*) and so forth.

As before, there is the *ātmanepada* suffix; the *yak* affix is added before the *sārvadhātuka* [suffix]; by the rule "with *sīyuṭ* and *īṭ*" (Pāṇini 6.1.87), which is subsumed under 6.1.66, there is the elision of the *yak* vowel; and by the rule "for *ṛ*, *riṅ* is substituted before *śa*, *ya*, *liṅ*, and *kṣu*" (Pāṇini 7.4.28), the substitution of *riṅ* occurs. In this context, he demonstrates the fault that might arise from the treatment as *ciṇvadbhāva* by means of the phrase "of that which ends in *yak*" (*yagantasya*), etc. If, in this case, there were a *vṛddhi* [vowel lengthening] due to *ciṇvadbhāva*, then consequently the suffix *yuk* would be applied by the rule "after an *ā*-stem, *yuk* is added before *ciṇ* and *kṛt* suffixes" (Pāṇini 7.3.33).
"Thus, [there is] elision and the elision of *ya*," and so forth.
This is a summary verse regarding the purpose of the section on *ārdhadhātuka* suffixes;
its meaning is already explained.

Now, one might ask: "In this context, will not the *ram* [augment] be prescribed by the rule *bhrasjo ropadhayo ram anyatarasyām* [Pāṇini 6.4.47], and the *yuṭ* [augment] by the rule *ārddhadhātukasya...* [Pāṇini 6.4.63], both within the governing heading (*adhikāra*) for *ārddhadhātuka* suffixes? Why then are those two not mentioned there as the purpose [of the present rule]? The thought is as follows: the substitution of *ram* for the root *bhrasj* does not necessitate the governing heading for *ārddhadhātuka* suffixes; rather, that root is listed among the *tud*-class roots. Consequently, when a *sārvadhātuka* suffix follows, it ought to take the *śnā* augment. When *śnā* is present, by the principle of priority (*pūrvavipratiṣedha*), there must be vocalization (*samprasāraṇa*) according to the rule *grahijyāvayi...* [Pāṇini 6.1.16].

Furthermore, it does not even cause [the augment] *yuṭ* to be applied, because since the root *dīṅ* belongs to the *divādi* class, there must be the affix *śyan* in the *sārvadhātuka* [context]. Consequently, due to the absence of being an initial vowel (*ajādi*), the augment *yuṭ* simply does not occur.

When the term "in the *ārdhadhātuka*" is intended to refer to the *ārdhadhātuka* in general, then, since priority and posteriority are impossible in a general sense, this is a locative of occasion (*viṣayasaptamī*).

When there is the manifestation of an *ārdhadhātuka* suffix, then [the locative case] is a "locative of sequence" (*parasaptamī*). We have already established, by means of an indicator (*jñāpaka*), under the rule *na dhātulopaḥ* [P. 1.1.4], that this [locative] functions both as a locative of sequence and as a locative of scope (*viṣayasaptamī*). Anticipating the following objection—"If *ram* were to take the place of the *repha* (r) and the *upadhā* (u), then its status as a *mit* would be purposeless; or, if this augment *ram* follows after a vowel other than [the *upadhā*], then the *repha* and the *upadhā* would undergo elision"—he says: "*ropadhayoḥ*" and so forth.
Because of the mention of *mit* [in Pāṇini 1.1.47], it must necessarily follow after the final vowel; otherwise, that [mention] would be purposeless.

In that case, if there were the hearing of the *repha* (the letter *r*) and the *upadhā* (the penultimate vowel), the genitive indication "of those having *r* as their *upadhā*" (*ropadhayoḥ*) would be meaningless. Therefore, the genitive indication itself teaches the exclusion of those two.

This is precisely the purpose of that [genitive case]: so that the property which is the cessation (*nivṛtti*) of that which is being designated by the genitive may occur. For there is no other purpose for the designation by the genitive. Therefore, because of the status of *mit*, the augment *ram* occurs immediately after the final vowel.
By the force of the mention of the genitive case [in Pāṇini’s rule], those [roots] having *r* as an upadhā undergo the cessation of the properties of the substituend. For example,
in the form *bhraṣṭā*,
from the root *bhrasj* "to cook" (Dhātupāṭha 1284), the substitution of *ṣ* occurs by the rule concerning *vraśc* and others (Aṣṭādhyāyī 8.2.36).

Regarding the term *bhrajjanam*: the substitution of the *jaś*-class sound (*jaśtva*) for the letter *s* results in *d*; furthermore, the substitution of the *ścutva* sound for that *d* results in *j*.
Now, why does this not occur here in the forms *bhṛṣṭaḥ* and *bhṛṣṭavān*? To this he replies: "In *bhṛṣṭaḥ*, *bhṛṣṭavān*, etc. [the rule does not apply].

The scope for *bhṛṣṭā* (the form with *ṣṭ*) is the occasion for the rule of *bhṛṣṭā*, while the scope for *samprasāraṇa* (vowel substitution) is the occasion for the rule "he fries" (*bhṛjjati*). Here, both would apply in the case of *bhṛṣṭā* and *bhṛṣṭavān*; however, by the rule on *grah* and so forth (Pāṇini 6.1.16), only *samprasāraṇa* occurs due to a prior conflict (*pūrvavipratiṣedha*). And this prior conflict is obtained because the word "para" (in the rule) implies that which is desired. As in the example: *barībhṛjyate*.
Furthermore, by the rule *rīgṛdupadhasya* [Pāṇini 7.4.90], the augment *rīk* is added.

For the mention of "optionally" (*anyatarasyām*) that was introduced from the rule *atra upadeśe* [Pāṇini 6.4.45] is connected with *san* and the others; however, in this case, *san* and the others are excluded.

Therefore, upon the cessation of that [suffix], the cessation of this [element] might also be suspected. Furthermore, because the subsequent rule (*anantarya-yoga*) serves another purpose, there would be no point in including the mention of "either one" (*anyatara*) therein.
Now, why was it not stated as *bhrasjo bhraj*? It is impossible to state it in such a manner.

If this is argued: "When a verbal root is mentioned [in a rule], it includes the root even when followed by the suffix *yaṅ* in its elided (*yaṅluk*) form" (Vyākaraṇa-paribhāṣā 77), then when an *ārdhadhātuka* suffix arises after a *yaṅluk* form, would the substitution of *bharj* for the reduplicated root *bhrasj* not apply? This is not a fault; we shall qualify *bhrasj* by the mention of its original form (*upadeśa*), [interpreting the rule as]:

"that which is *bhrasj* in its original form. Alternatively, an indication using the *śtip* marker will be made here: "of *bhṛjjati*, [the substitute is] *bhajam*"; by that means, there will be no inclusion of the *yaṅluk* form.

Does this [rule] not also apply here in the case of *bhujjayate*, since the root *bhrasj* occurs in the original instruction (*upadeśa*)? This is not so; for in this case, by the rule of "priority" (*pūrvavipratiṣedha*), there must be vocalization (*samprasāraṇa*), as in the form *bhṛṣṭa*.
If that is so, then it was not stated in that way for the sake of variety. [Examples: *dhinutaḥ*, *kṛṇutaḥ*.

The roots *hivi*, *divi*, and *dhivi* mean "to breathe" (*prāṇana*), and *kṛvi* means "to injure" or "to do" (*hiṃsākaraṇa*) (Dhātupāṭha 591, 592, 593, 598). Because they are marked with the *it*-sign (*idit*), the augment *num* is applied. In the present tense (*laṭ*), with the suffix *tas*, the suffix *u* is added by [Pāṇini 3.1.80], and the letter *a* is substituted for the final vowel. By this rule, that [final *a*] is elided. Now, what is the purpose of including the letter *t* in the rule? One might ask: why should it not apply to the root *dhā* (as in *dhā-tas*)? But surely it will serve as a restrictive rule (*niyamārtha*) according to [Pāṇini 6.4.64]: "The elision of *ā* occurs only before an affix beginning with a vowel that has the *it*-sign and is marked with *k* or *ṅ*. This is not so; for a contrary restriction (*viparīta-niyama*) could also be possible: "The elision of *ā* occurs only before an affix with the *it*-sign and marked with *k* or *ṅ*, and not before any other."
And thus, [the rule] would not apply in the case of *cikīrṣitā*.
Therefore, the inclusion of *t* (in *tapara*) is for the purpose of removing the possibility of a contrary restriction;
or it is for the sake of clarity.

Regarding the rule *vṛddhirād-aic* [Pāṇini 1.1.1] and so forth, up to *vṛddhireci* [Pāṇini 6.1.88], and the rule *vṛddhi-dīrghābhyām* [Pāṇini 1.1.3] and so forth, up to *ato dīrgho yañi* [Pāṇini 7.3.101]:

the scope of the former is exemplified by *kārayati* and *hārayati*; the scope of the elision of *at* (*ato lopaḥ*) [Pāṇini 6.4.48] is exemplified by *cikīrṣitā* and *jihīrṣitā*. In the case of *cikīrṣakaḥ* and *jihīrṣakaḥ*, both rules would apply; however, the elision of *at* alone occurs by virtue of a prior conflict (pūrvavipratiṣedha). The scope of the rule *aci śnu-dhātu-bhruvāṃ y-v-or iyaṅ-uvaṅau* [Pāṇini 6.4.77] is exemplified by *cīyate* and *lūyate*; the scope of the elision of *at* is the same as before. In the case of *cikīṣryate* and *jihīṣryate*, both rules would apply; however, the elision alone occurs by virtue of a prior conflict. As for the form *bebhiditā*: [this is derived from the root *bhid* with the desiderative suffix *san* and the periphrastic future suffix *tṛc*].

When an *ārdhadhātuka* suffix beginning with *tṛc* follows, there is elision of the sound *ya* that precedes it. Is this [the word] "yasya" a reference to a single phoneme (*varṇa*), or is it a reference to the combination of the phonemes *yakāra* and *akāra*? If the first alternative were adopted, then [elision] would also occur in forms such as *ūrṣyitā* and *mavyitā*; therefore, adopting the second alternative, he says: "The term 'yasya' refers to the entire cluster. Why is this so? Because of the specific formulation [of the rule].
If there were a reference to individual phonemes (*varṇa*), then one would have said simply "of a consonant" (*yo halaḥ*).

If, then, there is a reference to a cluster (*saṅghāta*)? In that case, [the rule] Pāṇini 1.1.52 would apply to the final [element of the cluster]; therefore, he says: "In that case, [the rule] *alo'ntyasya*," and so forth.
Why does [the rule] not apply? He says: "The elision of *at*" (*ato lopaḥ*), and so forth.

The elision of the final [element] even by the previous rule (*alo’ntyasya*) was already established; however, because of the force of its formulation here, it applies to the whole. He states another resolution with the words "or by the rule *halaḥ*," etc.

The mention of *halaḥ* is in the ablative case; when it is stated that "the *yaśabda* which follows *hal* is elided," then by the statement of [Pāṇini 1.1.54], the elision of the *yakāra* occurs by this very rule.
But for the root *ak*, it is by the rule [Pāṇini 6.4.48].
Thus we have *īrṣyitā* and *mavyitā* (the reading *bhavyitā* is found in the Nyāsa).
In the Dhātupāṭha, *sūkṣya*, *ikṣya*, and *īṣrya* are listed as having the meaning "to envy" (509, 510, 511), and *mavya* means "to bind" (508).

In this case, since the word *yaśabda* does not consist of a composite (*saṅghāta*), the elision (*lopa*) does not take place. In the form *lolūyitā*, there is a *guṇa* substitution by the rule *guṇo yaṅlukoh* [Pāṇini 7.4.82]. The term *kya* is a general reference to both *kyac* and *kyaṅ*, as the specific markers (*anubandha*) have been dropped and no distinction is made between them.

"He practices himself as if he were fuel. Here, the word "vā" (or) functions as a conjunction (*samuccaya*) and conveys the sense that he acts "like fuel. Regarding the phrase "according to what is appropriate":

When the intended meaning is "he desires fuel for himself," then [the suffix] *kyac* [is applied] according to Pāṇini 3.1.8; when the meaning is "he treats himself as if he were fuel," then *kyac* is applied according to 3.1.10; and when the meaning is "he behaves like fuel," then *kyaṅ* is applied according to 3.1.11, which states: "The suffix *kyaṅ* is applied after a word denoting the agent, and there is elision of the final phoneme. Such is the meaning of the term *yathāyogam* ("according to what is appropriate"). Regarding the term *ṇeḥ*:
having set aside the distinctive markers (*anubandha*) of both *ṇiṅ* and *ṇic*, the reference is to the common element *ṇi* alone. Thus, it is the general category of *ṇi* that is being grasped.

Since all [other] objects [of application] are already occupied by *iyaṅ* and the others, this *ṇi*-elision has no scope; therefore, it is understood as an exception (*apavāda*) to them. For this reason, he says: "*iyaṅ-yaṇ*" and so forth. Regarding the examples "atatakṣat" and "ararakṣat": from the roots *takṣ* and *rakṣ*, there is the causative suffix *ṇic*; from that which ends in *ṇic*, the aorist (*luṅ*) suffix is applied. By the rule "after *ṇi*, *śri*, *du*, and *ru*, [the suffix *cli* becomes *caṅ*]" (*Pāṇini 3.1.48*), the suffix *cli* is replaced by *caṅ*. Because of the *ṅit*-characteristic, there is no possibility for *guṇa* substitution at all, and thus the substitute *iyaṅ* would apply.
Therefore, there is an exception (apavāda) for that [doubling], namely the elision of the *ṇi* suffix:
*āṭiṭat*, *āśiśat*. When the *ṇic* and other affixes have been applied first to the roots *aṭ* and *śi*, the words *ṭi* and *śi* are doubled by [Pāṇini 6.1.2].
In this context, this [rule] is an exception (*apavāda*) to the substitution of *yaṇ* that would otherwise be obtained by the rule *eranekācaḥ* [Pāṇini 6.4.82]; for example,
in *kāraṇā* and *hāraṇā*,
it is an exception to the *guṇa* substitution that would otherwise be obtained by the rule *āt-aḥ* [Pāṇini 7.3.84].

In the words *kārakaḥ* and *hārakaḥ*, [the suffix *ṇvul* is applied] after [the roots *kṛ* and *hṛ*] by rule Pāṇini 3.1.133; here, [the vowel substitution] is by rule 7.2.115, which effects *vṛddhi*. In the forms *kāryate* and *hāryate*, [the suffix *ṇic* is applied].
In this context, [the rule] *akṛtsārvadhātukayoḥ* [Pāṇini 7.4.25] prescribes a long vowel; likewise,
in the case of *jñīpsati*, [the rule] *jñīpsyamānaḥ* [Pāṇini 6.4.16] prescribes a long vowel.

In the case of *jñā* with the causative suffix (*ṇic*), the augment *puk* is applied by [Pāṇini 7.3.36] *arti-hrī-...*. Since *jñā* is listed among the roots beginning with *ghaṭ* in the Dhātupāṭha (811) as "in the senses of killing, pleasing, and perceiving," the designation *mit* is assigned to it by the rule *ghaṭādayo mitaḥ* (Gaṇasūtra on Dhātupāṭha 817). Consequently, shortening occurs by [Pāṇini 6.4.92] *mitāṃ hrasvaḥ*, and the elision of the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa-lopa*) occurs by [Pāṇini 7.4.58]. Thus, we have the forms *kārayitā* and *hārayitā*.
Because of the statement "when there is no *iṭ*," this [shortening] does not take place here.

The rule *aniṭi* could have been omitted. How so? [One might argue] that the rule *[[P. 6.4.52]]* would serve as a restrictive rule (*niyamārtha*), meaning: "only before a *seṭ* suffix in the case of the *niṣṭhā* [suffixes], and not elsewhere"? This is incorrect, for a contrary restriction might also be suspected: "*only before a *seṭ* suffix in the case of the *niṣṭhā*. And if that were the case, the elision of the *ṇi* [augment] would indeed occur in the word *kārayitā*.
Therefore, the term "aniṭi" is stated in order to dispel the suspicion that the rule might apply in the reverse manner. [Examples: "gaṇitam" (calculated), "lakṣitam" (marked). [Roots:
"gaṇa" in the sense of counting (Dhātupāṭha 1853); "lakṣa" in the senses of seeing and marking (Dhātupāṭha 1538). [Example:
"saṃjñapitaḥ paśuḥ" (the animal has been slaughtered).

Now, one might ask: "If, because of the rule 'seṭi' (P. 1.2.19), [the elision] should not occur here by this [present rule], then why does it not occur by the preceding rule? To this he says: "By the force of the inclusion of *seṭ*," and so forth. For if the elision of *ṇi* were to occur by the preceding rule even when the affix is *aniṭ*, then the inclusion of *seṭ* would be purposeless; one could simply have said "in the case of *niṣṭhā*" (*niṣṭhāyām*). Indeed, the meaning of *seṭ* would be established simply by the force of the rule's formulation. Therefore, by the force of the inclusion of *seṭ*, the elision of *ṇi* does not occur even by the preceding rule in examples such as *saṃjñāpitaḥ paśuḥ*.
But how is it that here [in *jñapta*] there is no occurrence of the suffix *iṭ*? To this he says: "In the rule *sanīvantardha*, etc.
and "Now (*atha*), etc.

In the rule *atha* (Pāṇini 7.2.15), the term *ekāc* from the rule *ekāca upadeśe'nudāttāt* (Pāṇini 7.2.10) is understood to carry over. Consequently, because the root *jñap* has more than one vowel (*anekāctva*), the prohibition [of *iṭ*] does not apply; thus, the augment *iṭ* must occur before the suffix of the past participle (*niṣṭhā*).

Therefore, the inclusion of *se* would be purposeless, as there is nothing to be excluded. [Objection: But surely the inclusion of *se* will be for the sake of preventing [the rule] from applying in the case of *jñaptaḥ*? [Response: This is not so; even if the inclusion of *se* were made, by the rule *nipātānām* (Pāṇini 6.3.139), the elision of *ṇi* must necessarily occur here. If, then, the inclusion of *se* is purposeless, for what purpose is it made? To this he says: "It is made," and so forth.

The inclusion of the term *seṭ* (having the augment *iṭ*) was made so that the elision of *ṇi* (*ṇilopa*) would occur after the augment *iṭ* has been applied to the *niṣṭhā* suffix; [otherwise], the elision of *ṇi* would have occurred first.

But what fault would there be if *ṇi* were elided before *iṭ* had been added, such that the prior application of the augment *iṭ* is desired to prevent it? To this he says: "For if [it were] not done," and so forth.

Since it is established that [the suffix] *ṇic* is applied when there is no *siṅ* (the augment *iṭ*), the elision of *ṇic* (*ṇilopa*) would apply, as would the augment *iṭ*. In that case, because the rule applies whether [the condition] has already occurred or not yet occurred (*kṛtākṛtaprasaṅgitva*), the elision of *ṇic* must take effect first. Once the elision of *ṇic* has occurred, by the principle that "that which is modified in one part is not different from the original" (*ekadeśavikṛtanyāya*), this very root *kṛ* remains; consequently, the prohibition of *iṭ* by the rule *ekāca upadeśe'nudāttāt* [Pāṇini 7.2.10] would apply, and thus the form *kāritam* would not be established. Therefore, the mention of *siṅ* must be made. [The view is expressed: "In the case of roots beginning with *iṅ*, the elision of *ṇic* is prescribed as an irregularity (*nipātana*)."

The word *janitā* ends in the suffix *tṛc*; since there is a prohibition [of *iṭ*] by the rule "before a suffix beginning with a vowel that does not take *iṭ*" (*aniṭi*), *iṭ* would not apply before a suffix beginning with *iṭ*, and therefore it is treated as an irregularity (*nipātana*). As for its being like the previous day (*hyasvat*), it is established by the very rule "the short vowel of roots marked with *mit*" (*mitāṃ hrasvaḥ*) [Pāṇini 6.4.92], because of the designation *mit* given to the root *jan* by the list of gaṇas (Gaṇasūtra on Dhātupāṭha 817). In the case of *śamitaḥ*, the shortening is as before; then, by the rule "guṇa is substituted for *iK* before a suffix beginning with a vowel" (*pūrvasya guṇaḥ*) [Pāṇini 7.3.110], *guṇa* is applied, followed by the elision of the case-ending *su* by the rule "after a consonant, a long vowel, or *ī*, the case-endings are dropped" (*halṅyādinā*) [Pāṇini 6.1.66], and the *visarga* replaces the *repha*.
"This [word] ends in the vocative case within a *tṛc* [suffix].
Someone might suspect that this [word] ends in a past passive participle (*niṣṭhā*), and therefore this was said in order to dispel that doubt.
"Śamayitaḥ" is also the vocative case ending in a *tṛc* suffix. "[He] caused [it] to be done" (*kārayāñcakāra*).

By the rule *kāspratyayāt* [Pāṇini 3.1.35] and others, there is the elision of *liṭ* by the rule *āmaḥ* [Pāṇini 2.4.81]. By the rule *kṛñ ca* [Pāṇini 3.1.40], there is the subsequent application (*anuprayoga*) of the root *kṛ*, followed by reduplication and the grammatical operations pertaining to the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsakārya*). Thus we have *gaṇḍayantaḥ* and *maṇḍayantaḥ*. The root *gaḍi* (Dhātupāṭha 777; alternatively *gaḍa* in Dhātupāṭha 65.361, meaning "to moisten") and *maḍi* (Dhātupāṭha 321, meaning "to adorn") take the causative suffix *ṇic*. Since *gaḍi* belongs to the *ghaṭādi* group, the vowel becomes short (*mittva*) as previously explained.

While the rule *jṛviśibhyāṃ jhac* (Dhātupāṭha 6.17) is being carried over, the suffix *jhac* is applied by the rule *tṛbhūvahivasabhāsisādhigamimaṇḍijinandibhyaśca* (Dhātupāṭha 6.19), resulting in the substitution of the final letter.
Thus, we have *spṛhayāluḥ* and *gṛhayāluḥ*.

The roots *spṛh* (desire) and *gṛh* (seizing), both belonging to the curādigaṇa and ending in long vowels, undergo the elision of the suffix *ak* according to Pāṇini 6.4.48. Because that elision is treated as *sthānivat*, there is no guna substitution for the light penultimate vowel.

The suffix *āluc* is applied by the rule *spṛhi-gṛhi-* (Pāṇini 3.2.158). Thus, in the form *spṛhayāyyaḥ*, the suffix *āyya* is added according to the rule *tanu-dakṣi-spṛhi-gṛhibhya āyyaḥ* (Pañcapādikā 3.96).

Regarding the word *stanayitnu*: the root *stan* (meaning "to sound," as listed in the Dhātupāṭha 1859–1860) belongs to the curādigaṇa and ends in a short vowel. Because of the status of the elided *a* as *sthānivadbhāva*, the rule [Pāṇini 7.2.116] does not apply, and thus the vṛddhi substitution does not occur.
The suffix *il* (*itnuc*) is applied according to Pāṇini 3.2.168: *stanihmaṣipuṣigadimadibhyo ṇeritnuc*.

Thus we have the forms *poṣayiṣṇavaḥ* and *pārayiṣṇavaḥ*. Regarding *poṣayiṣṇavaḥ*: from the root *puṣ* (DhP 700) meaning "to nourish," the causative suffix *ṇic* is added because it functions as a causal verb (*hetumāṇṇic*). Regarding *pārayiṣṇavaḥ*: from the roots *pāra* and *tīra* (DhP 1911, 1912) meaning "completion of an action," the causative suffix *ṇic* is added as they belong to the *curādi* group, after which the suffix *iṣṇuc* is applied by Pāṇini 3.2.137.

Now, why was it not stated simply as "na" (not)? For if the prohibition of the *ṇi*-elision were established, the *guṇa* substitution alone would occur; in that case, the *ayādeśa* (substitution of *aya*) would take place by [Pāṇini 6.1.78]. Moreover, the rule would thus be more concise. Considering that if "aya" were stated, the rule would become heavy due to the addition of a syllable (*mātrā*), he says: "When 'na' ought to have been said," and so forth. If "na" were stated, then because of the absence of *guṇa* in the rule [Pāṇini 6.4.56], "lyapi laghupūrvāt," the *ayādeśa* would not occur. Therefore, the mention of the *ayādeśa* is for the sake of the subsequent rule: "laghupūrvāt."
The term *laghu* (light) is the first member of a *bahuvrīhi* compound, meaning "that from which [the preceding syllable] is light.
The referent of the other member (*anyapadārtha*) is the phoneme (*varṇa*).
Examples are: *praṇamya*, *pratamayya*, *pradamayya*, and *praśamayya*.

In this case, because *nam* and the others belong to the *mit* class, as before, when shortening has been applied, the letter *m* is preceded by a light vowel. Thus, in the example "having gone after causing to split" (*pravebhidayya gataḥ*),
the suffix *ṇic* is added to the root *bhid* following the *yaṅ* intensive suffix.
By [Pāṇini 6.4.49], there is elision of the letter *y*.
Here too, the letter *d* is preceded by a light vowel.
Thus: *pragaṇayya*.
The root *gaṇ* is listed as number 1853 in the Dhātupāṭha, belonging to the *curādi* group. As before, there is elision of the penultimate vowel (*allopa*).

Here too, the letter *ṇ* is preceded by a light vowel. Now, one might object: "Only short vowels and the like are considered 'within the *ābhīya* [section]' according to the technical rules, as is the case with the *ayādeśa* substitute. Since the rule *asiddhavadatrā bhāt* (Pāṇini 6.4.22) treats these short vowels and so forth as if they were non-existent (*asiddha*) within the *ābhīya* section, it would follow that the condition of being 'preceded by a light vowel' cannot apply to the letter *m* and the others. To this, he replies: "Of the shortening, the elision of *y*, and the elision of *a*" (*hrasvayalopāllopānām*), and so forth.

How is there a lack of a common locus (*asamānāśrayatva*)? To this he says: "For *hrasva* and so forth," and so on. Now, what is the purpose of including the mention of "the preceding" (*pūrva*), instead of simply saying "of the light syllable" (*laghoḥ*)? It is impossible to speak in such a way; for if it were stated thus, the meaning of the sentence would be that the substitution of *lyap* for *ṇi* occurs after a light syllable. And in that case, [the rule] would not apply in examples such as *pratamayya*, because of the intervention by a consonant (*hal*).

Where, then, would [the rule] apply? In cases such as *pragaṇayya*. But surely, even here, once the elision (*lopa*) of the *a* has occurred, a *ṇic* following a light syllable is indeed possible; therefore, by the force of the statement, one might resort to the presence of an intervening element? This is not so; rather, by the force of the statement, one must resort to the notion of what existed previously (*bhūtapūrvagati*). Why is this obtained—that by the force of the statement one should resort to an intervening element, and not to the notion of what existed previously? Because if the notion of what existed previously were resorted to, [the rule] would apply only in cases like *pragaṇayya*, but it would not apply in cases like *praṇamayya gataḥ*.
Therefore, the inclusion of the prefix *pra-* must be made. Regarding the term "having caused to reach" (*prāpayya*):
both roots are intended—namely, *āplṛ* in the sense of "attaining" (Dhātupāṭha 1839) and *āplṛ* in the sense of "pervading" (Dhātupāṭha 1260).
The former belongs to the *curādi* class, while the latter belongs to the *svādi* class.

Now, why does [the substitution] not occur in *adhyāpya gataḥ*? For here too, once the substitution of *ā* for *iṅ* has been made by rule 6.1.48, would not the subsequent *ṇi* be followed by *puK* by rule 7.3.36 (*arti-hrī-...*)? To this he says: "of the substitute of *iṅ*" and so forth. If that were so, then in *apa ācaṣṭe*, when *ṇiC* is applied to the word *ap*, forms such as *prāpayya* would not occur; let them not occur by this [rule] precisely because they are *lākṣaṇika* (derived). They will be accounted for by the preceding rule. But surely, once the single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) has taken place, [the condition of] having a non-light (*alaghu*) vowel before [the *ṇi*] is absent, so it should not apply? There is no fault, because the single-substitute is considered *asiddha* (non-existent) [for the purposes of this rule].

How so? According to the rule "that which is *bahiraṅga* is unestablished (*asiddha*) with respect to that which is *antaraṅga*" (Vyākaraṇa-mahābhāṣya, Pāda 42), the substitution of *ekādeśa* (the single substitute for *u* and *i*) is *bahiraṅga* because it depends upon two words (*dvipadāśrayatva*). The substitution of *ay* (for *i* and *a*), however, is *antaraṅga* because it depends upon only one phoneme (*ṇimātrāśrayatva*). Regarding the roots *yu* (meaning "to mix," Dhātupāṭha 1033; meaning "to mix" and "not to mix"—Dhātupāṭha) and *pluṅ* (meaning "to move," Dhātupāṭha 958), this statement is made for the sake of lengthening (*dīrghārtham*) when *tuk* is about to be applied. The word "in the Veda" (*chandasi*) is no longer in force.

Regarding the term *kṣiyaḥ*, by the rule "when there is a mention of a root without an *anubandha*, [it does not include] one with an *anubandha*" (*Vyāḍiparibhāṣā* 53), there is the inclusion of the two roots *kṣi* "to perish" (*Dhātupāṭha* 236) and *kṣi* "dwelling and going" (*Dhātupāṭha* 1407), but not of *kṣiṣ* "to injure" (*Dhātupāṭha* 1506) [or *kṣīṣ*]. The meaning of the *kṛtya* suffixes is "the state of being" (*bhāva*) and "the object" (*karman*), because of the statement: "The *kṛtya*, *kta*, and *khal-artha* suffixes occur only in those two senses" (*Pāṇini* 3.4.70). The phrase "other than those two" refers to cases other than *bhāva* and *karman*.
In the case of the agent and the locus:
"ākṣīṇaḥ" (not diminished). The substitution of *ṇ* for the *ṣ* of the suffix *niṣṭhā* occurs by [Pāṇini 8.2.46]: "After the root *kṣi*, when it is long."

"How is [the suffix] *kta* used in the sense of the agent (*kartari*) here? This is the suffix *kta* applied to the root *kṣi* (to perish) in the sense of the agent," according to the rule beginning with "roots meaning 'to go' etc. (Pāṇini 3.4.72).
As in: "This has perished for Devadatta."
By [Pāṇini 2.3.68], the sixth case is used in the sense of the agent (*kartṛ*). Regarding the term "locus" (*adhikaraṇe*):
its connection is with the present context, namely that this suffix *kta* is used in the sense of the locus.

"Prakṣīṇam" means that in which something has been destroyed; it refers to a substance serving as the locus (*adhikaraṇa*). Regarding the phrase "it is [used] in the sense of the action (*bhāva*"), its connection is also to be understood as before.

One does not cite it as an example for the passive (karmaṇi), because the root *kṣi* is intransitive (*akarmaka*). [The form] "kṣitāyuḥ" is formed with the suffix *kta* in the sense of the agent (kartari), as before;
the same applies to the subsequent cases as well.
Regarding the word *kṣitakaḥ*:
the suffix *kan* is used here in the sense of compassion (*anukampā*). In cases other than those involving abuse (*ākrośa*) or dejection (*dainya*), the former [suffix] occurs invariably.

Why does it say "not having another meaning" (*anyadarthe*)? [Consider: *kṣitam jālmasya* ("the ruined state of the rogue"), *kṣitakam asya tapasvinaḥ* ("the ruined thing of this wretched man"). Because of the rule *syasicsīyuṭtāsiṣu* (Pāṇini 6.4.62), where the locative case indicates the counter-correlative (*pratiyogin*), it is understood that the suffix *vat* is applied after a word in the locative case meaning "like that," just as in the example: *mathurāvat pāṭaliputre prakāraḥ* ("the manner in Pāṭaliputra is like that in Mathurā").

By the phrase "in the domain of the abstract state (*bhāva*) and the object (*karman*)," he shows that the locative in the rule *bhāvakarmaṇoḥ* (Pāṇini 3.1.66) is a locative of domain (*viṣayasaptamī*).

Those [suffixes] whose objects are the abstract action (*bhāva*) and the object (*karman*) are described as such. Which, then, are the *syādi* suffixes that have the abstract action and the object as their objects? They are those *syādi* suffixes which occur when the abstract action and the object are intended to be expressed by means of the *lādeśa* (the substitutes for *liṅ*).
Here, the particle *ca* is used in the sense of a restrictive conjunction (*sanniyoga*). By this, [it is established that] when there is the state of being like *ciṇ* (*ciṇvadbhāva*), and so forth.

Regarding the word "of whom" (*kasya*): augmentations (*āgama*) occur for that which is indicated by the genitive case, whereas *syat*-suffixes here are indicated by the locative case; since no other element to which an augmentation could apply is heard [in the rule], this is the question.
Although they are indicated by the locative case, and no other element to which an augmentation could apply is heard, this is the question.

Although they are indicated by the locative case (*saptamī*), nevertheless—just as *hanti*, even when indicated by the ablative case (*pañcamī*) in the rule *yathā* (Pāṇini 3.1.76), gives rise to a suffix and, while experiencing a connection with the place [of its application], comes to be understood as having a genitive ending (*ṣaṣṭhyantatā*)—so too do *sy-* and the others come to be understood as having a genitive ending when they experience a connection with an augment (*āgama*). With this intention, he says: "In the case of *syasic*," etc.
He states the reason for this very point: "For those [suffixes] are the subject under discussion (*prakṛta*)," etc.

The *iḍā* is characterized by its being mentioned in the traditional scripture (*āgama*); therefore, it must necessarily be something derived from scripture (*āgamī*). In that case, should the status of being scripturally derived be postulated for what has not been heard [in the specific context] and then applied to that very thing, or should it apply to the very elements under discussion, such as *sy-* and so on? What is logical? It is logical that it is prescribed for the very elements under discussion; for the postulation of what has not been heard is more cumbersome. [Objection: But the *aṅga* (the base) is also under discussion; why is it not applied to that? To this, he says: "Of the *aṅga*" and so forth.
It is not applied to the *aṅga*, because it would contradict the intended object (*lakṣya*).
If [the substitution] were to apply to the *aṅga*, then once *iṭ* is added, an undesirable result would arise due to the conflict with the observed forms (*lakṣya*).
For it is improper to assume a construction in the grammatical treatise that does not serve its intended purpose.

Therefore, so that there may be no contradiction with the observed forms, even though the *aṅga* is also under discussion, the operation is nevertheless performed only for *sy-* and the others, and not for the *aṅga*.
In this regard, two alternatives are possible: either that which is an operation caused by *ciṇ*—that which is specifically prescribed for *ciṇ*—is extended [by analogy];
or rather, whatever is observed in *ciṇ*, whether it be caused by *ciṇ* or not caused by *ciṇ*, is [extended] in a general sense.
If the former alternative were adopted, then the augment *yuk* would apply by the rule "āto yuk ciṇkṛtoḥ" [Pāṇini 7.3.33].

And by the rule *viṇṇamulordīrgho 'nyatarasyām* [Pāṇini 6.4.93], there is the substitution of a long vowel; these two alone would be the operations pertaining to the *aṅga* (the stem) in the case of *ati-viś*, not others such as *vṛddhi* and so forth, for those are not specifically prescribed (*āhatya*) for the *ciṇ* affix.
"Specifically" (*āhatya*) means "having been explicitly stated" (*uccārya*).

For that which is prescribed by taking the *ciṇ* affix as its direct cause is prescribed directly with respect to the *ciṇ*; however, the *vṛddhi* substitution and so forth are not prescribed in this manner.
If [the objection is raised]: "If the second alternative is taken, then this undesirable consequence does not arise, because *vṛddhi* and the rest are also observed in the context of *ciṇ*;

if that which is observed in *ciṇ* is extended [by analogy], then the substitutes for *han*, *ṇi*, and *ṅī* would also apply, since they too are observed there," [the author] says "But what [are they]? and so forth, with this intention.

Thinking, "I shall resolve later whatever fault there may be in the second alternative," and showing that what was observed as an effect in the case of *ciṇ*—whether it be the cause itself or something else—is here indicated in a general sense, he states a summary verse regarding the purposes of this rule, beginning with "vṛddhiściṇvat.
In the example *cāyiṣyate*, the purpose is *vṛddhi* (vowel lengthening). This is derived from the root *cinoti* in the periphrastic future (*luṭ*), with the suffix *syap*.

This is the *ātmanepada* form. Now, here, due to the status of being like *ciṇ* (*ciṇvadbhāva*), a vowel lengthening (*vṛddhi*) occurs, just as [the rule] "in *ciṇ*" (*ciṇi*, Pāṇini 7.2.115) prescribes lengthening for the root *ac*. Thus, in the subsequent cases as well, one should apply the extension (*atideśa*) by connecting the term *ciṇvat* with each [rule] individually, as appropriate. For example: *acāyiṣyate*.
This is from the *luṅ* tense; the rest is as before.
And there is a purpose [for this rule] in the case of *dāyiṣyate*:
the long vowel that is prescribed for roots ending in a short vowel (*mit*) before the *ciṇ* affix would also apply here.
Furthermore, there is a purpose in the cases of *śamiṣyate* and *śāmiṣyate*.

The root *śam* receives the designation *mit* by the rule *janijṛṣknasurañjo'mantāśca* (Dhātupāṭha 817); and since it is taught as such in the context of [the rule] *sa ca ṇyantaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.1.49), it is considered to end in a vowel (*ajanta*) at the time of its original enunciation (*upadeśe*). As for the substitution of *k* for *h* in the root *han* which will be prescribed by the rule *ho hanteñcinneṣu* (Pāṇini 7.3.54), that purpose applies in the form *ghāniṣyate*;
however, in the form *haniṣyate*, the augment *iṭ* is applied by the rule *sārvadhātukārdhadhātukayoḥ* (Pāṇini 7.3.84).
These purposes indeed exist; however, when this *iṭ* is applied, the elision of *ṇi*—as in the rule "śamiṣyate" (Aṣṭādhyāyī 6.4.51)—is not established because [the root] is considered *seṭ*.
Therefore, he says: "And the *iṭ* is as if non-existent," and so forth.
By the rule "asiddhavad atrā bhāt" (Aṣṭādhyāyī 6.4.22), this *ciṇvadiṭ* is treated as non-existent; therefore, the elision of *ṇi* will take place.

It might be argued: "In the case of roots such as *cinoti* which are taught with an anudātta vowel, it is correct that the *iṭ* prescribed by this rule for the subsequent *sya*-affixes and so on should be considered asiddha (non-existent). However, in the case of roots like *śam*, which are taught with an udātta vowel, since [the *iṭ*] follows them, the *iṭ* caused by the *val* suffix—by the rule *ārdhadhātukasyeḍvalādeḥ* [Pāṇini 7.2.35]—must occur, and that [original *iṭ*] is indeed established. Therefore, the same fault remains. To this, he says: "And this is permanent (*nitya*)," and so forth.
A rule that applies whether or not another rule has already taken effect is called permanent (*nitya*). Relying on this principle, this *ciṇvat-iṭ* is permanent.
For even when *valāditva* (the state of having *val* as the initial) has been applied, it is prescribed [as such]; thus,
"that which has *val* as its cause" means that for which *val* is the cause or the reason— it is described in that way.
That which possesses an obstacle (*vighāta*) is called *vighātī*.
An obstacle is non-occurrence due to the absence of a cause.

Thus, because [the root] is eternal, this very *ciṇvad-iṭ* must occur even after roots with the acute accent (*udātta*); and since this [augment] is considered "as if not having taken place" (*asiddha*), there is no contingency of the elision of the *ṇi*-affix not occurring.
Regarding the form *grāhiṣyate*:
the purpose [of the rule] is the *vṛddhi* substitution according to Pāṇini 7.2.116.
