When the form *śaṃśamī* is thus established and the suffix *ciṇ* follows it, then, if the lengthening of the vowel is optionally applied, the form *aśaṃśamyaśaṃśāmī* results.

But when the suffix *ṇamul* is present, as in *śaṃśamaṃśaṃsam*, *śaṃśāmaṃśaṃśāmam*, and so on—there, because of the inclusion of "long" (*dīrgha*) in the rule [Pāṇini 6.1.101], the status of being a *sthānivat* does not apply to that *ṇi* which is elided when the suffix *ṇi* is added, nor to the vowel *a* of the *yaṅ* reduplication; this is due to the prohibition stated in [Pāṇini 1.1.58]: *na padānta...*. Consequently, the long vowel is established even in the absence of an intervening element.

It might be argued: "When an optional short vowel (*hrasva-vikalpa*) is prescribed, in that case where there is no short vowel, would not the long vowel remain in its own form? To this, he says: "But when an optional short vowel [is prescribed]," and so forth.

For when a short vowel is to be prescribed, the status of being a *sthānivadbhāva* (the substitute behaving like the original) is not prohibited by anyone. In that context, when an optional short vowel is prescribed, the *sthānivadbhāva* of the elision of the *ṇi* suffix and of the *yaṅ* affix would certainly still apply.
Consequently, due to the status of the substitute (*sthānivadbhāva*), the optional shortening would not occur.
For the shortening of *mit* bases is prescribed when a *ṇi* follows that is itself followed by *ciṇ* or *ṇamul*;
however, the *ṇi* in this case is not followed by *ciṇ* or *ṇamul*, because it is separated from the *mid* base by the preceding *ṇi*.

Furthermore, that which has *mid* as its marker (*aṅga*) within the causative suffix *ṇi* is not preceded by *ciṇ* or *ṇamul*, because it is separated from the subsequent *ciṇ*. Therefore, this [present] rule does not apply to it; consequently, the optional shortening would not occur by this rule. By the preceding rule alone, the shortening would be obligatory, and thus the lengthening would not take place. [This is addressed in the commentary beginning with] "In the case of a causative ending in *ṇi*," and so forth.
That which has *ṇi* and *ṇi* as its interior (*anta*)—that is, its proximity—is *ṇiṇyanta*.
Alternatively, *ṇi* and *ṇi* together form *ṇiṇi*; that which has this as its end (*anta*) is *ṇiṇyanta*. In this latter case, the word *anta* signifies a constituent part.
"But in the case of the *yaṅ* [intensive] with the *ṇic* suffix, there is simply no establishment [of the long vowel].

The term *yaṅṇyanta* is also derived in two ways, as previously [explained]. Of what is there non-establishment? It should be understood that, by virtue of the context, it refers to the long vowel (*dīrgha*).

By the word "eva" (only), he shows this: [the lengthening] might occur by some means in the case of the causative (*ṇic*) suffix, but in the case of the intensive (*yaṅ*) with the causative suffix, there is simply no accomplishment;
the meaning is that there is no accomplishment by any means whatsoever.
How, then, is there accomplishment in the case of the causative with the causative suffix? By resorting to the general category of the causative (*ṇij-āti*).

For when there is the intention to express the genus (*jāti*), although there is indeed the status of being a *sthānivadbhāva* for the elision of the *ṇic* suffix, nevertheless there is no intervention; because the genus is a single entity, an intervention by that very same [genus] is not possible. Thus, due to the absence of intervention, the lengthening of the vowel is established in the case of a root ending in *ṇic*.

Alternatively, he demonstrates this very point by means of the particle *eva*: "In the case of the *ṇi*-ending [denominative], the long vowel is established because the rule *pūrvaṃ ṇicam āśritya* (Pāṇini 7.2.116) prescribes *vṛddhi*; however, its cessation occurs through the substitution of a short vowel, but it is not the case that it does not exist at all.
In the case of the *yaṅ*-ending, however, there is an absolute absence of the establishment of the long vowel, because *vṛddhi* is impossible therein.
This might be argued: even if the long vowel were prescribed as an option, the long vowel would still not be established here.

Because the elision of *ṇi* and *yaṅ* is considered as if not yet established (*asiddhavat*) by the rule "asiddhavadatrā bhāt" [Pāṇini 6.4.22], he says: "Because they have different bases," and so forth.
But how is there a difference of basis? He says: "For in the case of *ṇi*," and so forth.

The mention of "optionally" (*anyatarasyām*) is for the sake of clarity; for it is possible to carry forward the word "optionally" from the rule "śakyate" [Pāṇini 6.4.91] by means of the "frog-leap" (*maṇḍūkapluti*) method. Examples are: *dviṣantapaḥ*, *parantapaḥ*.

In the word *purandaraḥ*, the suffix *khac* is applied by [Pāṇini 3.2.39] *dviṣatparayostāpe*, followed by the augment *mum* by [Pāṇini 6.3.67]. Furthermore, in the same word, the suffix *khac* is applied by [Pāṇini 3.2.41], and the augment *mum* is introduced by the irregular rule (*nipātana*) [Pāṇini 6.3.68] *vācaṃyapurandarau ca*.

The inclusion of the term *hrasva* (short vowel) is for the sake of clarity; however, it is possible to carry forward the mention of *hrasva* from [Pāṇini 6.4.92] *mitāṃ hrasvaḥ* by means of the "frog-leap" (*maṇḍūkapluti*) maxim. Regarding *prahlanna*: the root *hlādī* is listed in the Dhātupāṭha as meaning "to feel pleasure" (No. 27). The substitution of *n* for *d* occurs according to [Pāṇini 8.2.42] *radābhyām* and so forth. *Prahlādayati* is formed with the causal suffix *ṇic*. Regarding *uraśchadaḥ*: [this is a compound formed with the suffix *ac*].

The root *chad* means "to cover" (*apavāraṇe*) [Dhātupāṭha 1935]. With the causative suffix *ṇic*, the suffix *gha* is applied according to [Pāṇini 3.3.118]. Having analyzed the compound as *uraśchadaḥ* ("a covering for the chest"), the compound is formed by the rule "the genitive case is compounded when connected with a *kṛt*-derivative" (Vārttika 86). Now, one might object: since the elision of the *ṇic* suffix is considered "non-existent" (*asiddha*) by the rule "in this context, it is as if non-existent" (Pāṇini 6.4.22), or because of the status of the substitute (*sthānivadbhāva*) by the rule "that which takes the place of something is like the original" (Pāṇini 1.1.57), there cannot exist a penultimate vowel (*upadhā*) characterized by a short vowel (*hrasva*) which would trigger the application of the suffix. So, how does the shortening take effect? To this he says: "of the elision of the *ṇic*," and so forth.

If, in this case, either the non-application of the rule due to the *asiddha* status of the elision of *ṇi* or the treatment as a *sthānivadbhāva* were to occur, then the explicit statement [of the sūtra] would be purposeless.
Therefore, by the force of that explicit statement, neither of these two applies; consequently, the penultimate vowel (*upadhā*) becomes short.
Regarding this, it is said: "It should be stated that [the shortening occurs] when the prefix consists of two or more syllables."
But surely, where there are three or more, two are also present; therefore, would this not be established by the rule *advyupasargasya* alone? To this he says: “For the subsequent,” and so forth.
Although two are indeed present among three or more, nevertheless they are not denoted here by the word *dvi*; for the subsequent number subverts the designation made of the preceding number.
How is this known? To this he says: “For not,” and so forth.

If a subsequent number did not cause the cessation of the designation established by a preceding number, then even one who has three sons would be called "one who has two sons" in common usage; yet he is not so called.

For instance, when it is said, "Let the man with two sons be brought," it is not the man with three sons who is brought, but rather only he who has exactly two sons. Furthermore, the meaning of the statement beginning with *addhiprabhṛti* is to be explained as follows: the shortening of the vowel occurs for the substitute *chādi* following the prefix *addhi*. This is the intended sense.

In this regard, the explanation is as follows: here the word *dvi* (two) serves to indicate "many" (*aneka*); that is to say, it refers to a root with many prefixes (*upasarga*). Furthermore, the expression *advyupasargasya* is a simple negation (*prasajya-pratiṣedha*).
Consequently, the meaning is this: when the suffix *gha* follows, the penultimate vowel (*upadhā*) of a root belonging to the *chādi* group, which has many prefixes, does not undergo shortening.
But by what means is the prohibition of the short vowel [of the root] that has been obtained effected by this [rule]? Precisely from this prohibition, a prescriptive statement is inferred.

Or, through a split of the *yoga* (yogavibhāga), [the rule] "chāder ghe" is established. And if the word "dvi" here is intended as an indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*) for "more than one," and a split of the *yoga* is indeed accepted, then there is no fault even in the case of an exclusion (*paryudāsa*).

How so? "Different from that which has two prefixes" means one that has more than two prefixes; "different from that which has two prefixes" means one that has a single prefix. For such [a word], shortening occurs. Why is this [rule] stated? Is it not already established by the rule *chāder ghe*? Since it is already established, the restatement is for the purpose of restriction (*niyamārtha*): [shortening] occurs only when there is a single prefix, and not otherwise. If this were the case, would it not fail to apply in the example *uraśchadaḥ*? This is not a fault, for if it were so, the division of the rule (*yogavibhāga*) would be purposeless.

Since a restrictive rule (niyama) depends upon that which is of the same class, this restriction being applied to [the word] with a prefix (sopasarga) serves to exclude shortening only for that which has a prefix, not for that which lacks a prefix.
Therefore, in the case of *uttaraśchadaḥ*, the rule indeed operates. Furthermore, the letter *ca* is for the purpose of drawing forward (*anukarṣaṇa*) the initial [word] *chadiḥ*.
Thus: *chadiḥ*.
The suffix *isi* is applied according to the rule *aciśucihusṛpicchādicchadibhya isiḥ* (Dhātupāṭha 9.30). Regarding the word *chadma*,
the suffix *manin* is applied according to the rule *sarvadhātubhyo manin* (Pāṇini 5.2.127).
Regarding the word *chattra*:

the suffix *ṣṭran* is applied by the rule *sarvadhātubhyaḥ ṣṭran* (Dhātupāṭha 8.79). There is a separation of the yoga (*yogavibhāga*) so that [the suffix] may also apply after multiple prefixes, as in *samupāticchadiḥ*. Regarding the phrase *anaṅi*: this prohibition applies when a suffix beginning with a vowel (*ajādi*) follows; therefore, it is understood that the grammatical operation applies only when a suffix beginning with a vowel follows that which is equivalent to *an*. Thus he says: "when a suffix beginning with a vowel (*ajādau pratyaye*) follows."
In the forms *jadhnatuḥ* and *jadhnuḥ*,
there is the substitution of *k* [for *h*] according to [Pāṇini 7.3.55].
In the forms *jajñatuḥ* and *jajñuḥ*, [the same applies].

The root *jan* in the sense of "procreation" (*dhātupāṭha* 1105) belongs to the *jauhotyādi* class and takes the *parasmaipada* endings; by [Pāṇini 8.4.40], the change to *ścu* (i.e., *j* to *jñ*) occurs, resulting in *jajñe*.

The root *jan* in the sense of "manifestation" (*dhātupāṭha* 1149) belongs to the *divādi* class and takes the *ātmanepada* endings; by [Pāṇini 3.4.81], the substitution of *eś* for the suffix occurs.

Regarding the form *jakṣatuḥ*: the root *ad-* takes the substitute *ghas-* by the rule *liṭanyatarasyām* [Pāṇini 2.4.40]; the *gh* is changed to *k* by *khari ca* [8.4.54]; and the *ṣ*-quality (*ṣatva*) is applied by *śāsivasidhasīnāñca* [8.3.60]. Alternatively, this is the form of the root *ghas-lṛ adane* (Dhātupāṭha 715).
Regarding the form *akṣan*:

it is the *luṅ* [aorist] tense. By the rule *luṅsanorghaslṛ* [Pāṇini 2.4.37], there is the substitution of *ghaslṛ* for the root. By the rule *mantre ghasahvara* [Pāṇini 2.4.80] and others, there is the elision (*luk*) of the *liṭ* suffix; *jhi* is replaced by *ant*, and there is the elision of the final consonant of the conjunct (*saṃyogāntalopa*). The remainder is as before.
Regarding "adhasat" and "agamat," the suffix *aṅ* is applied by the rule [Pāṇini 3.1.55] for roots beginning with *puṣ*. Regarding "vitatnire":

even if the elision of the penultimate vowel (*upadhālopa*) were considered *asiddha* (non-existent) here, nevertheless, due to the force of the rule prescribing that elision, the substitution of *i* and the elision of the reduplicated syllable do not occur by virtue of the rule [Pāṇini 6.4.120], "In the interior of a single consonant following a short *a*," etc.

In the form *paptima*, the suffix *liṭ* is present; the augment *iṭ* is applied according to the rule for roots beginning with *krī*. Regarding the change of the letter *t* to *dh*, it is by [Pāṇini 8.2.40].
"Regarding 'jaśtvaṃ dhakārasya' (Pāṇini 8.4.53),
it means 'when the compound has been formed.'"
By [the rule] beginning with 2.1.58, etc., [it is stated]:
"The substitution of *sa* for *samāna*.
This is by [the rule] beginning with 6.3.84: "In the Vedic language (*chandas*), [the substitution of *sa* occurs] for *samāna*," etc.

If the elision of the *upadhā* vowel were performed prior to reduplication, then, due to the absence of being a single-syllable (*ekāc*) word, reduplication would not apply. To this, he says: "Because it is Vedic," and so forth. The form "bandhām" is a Vedic usage.

In this regard, by virtue of the rule *tatra* [Pāṇini 7.4.78], the scope [of the operations] is manifold. Therefore, although—on account of its higher status (*paratva*) and because it is obligatory (*nitya*)—the elision of the penultimate vowel (*upadhā-lopa*) would logically occur prior to reduplication (*dvirvacana*), nevertheless it is not performed in that manner. The intended meaning is that it is not carried out before the reduplication.

Regarding *bapsati*: for the root *bhakṣ* (to eat), there is the substitution of *at* for the suffix *jhi*; there is the elision (*ślu*) of the suffix *śap*; by the rule *ślau* [Pāṇini 6.1.10], there is reduplication; the operations pertaining to the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*) are performed; when the penultimate vowel (*upadhā*) has been elided, there is the substitution of *p* for *bh* by the rule of *cartva*.
Regarding *basti*: [the same process applies].

"Also *rūpa*. Regarding the phrase "beginning with a consonant" (*hal-ādeḥ*): from where, then, is the mention of "consonant" (*hal*) derived, by which the word *hi* is qualified? If it is argued that it comes from the immediately preceding rule, no; for that [rule] is indicated in the locative case, whereas here the requirement is one indicated in the genitive case. The fifth-case form *hujhalbhyaḥ* will effect the conversion of the seventh-case form *hali* into a genitive.
There is no fault, because of the statement [of Pāṇini] "iti vacanāt" (P.
1.1.67). In the case of "bhindhi," there is the elision of the vowel *a* by [the rule] "iti akāralopaḥ" (P. 6.4.111).
"Krīṇīhi":
by [Pāṇini 3.4.87] *sehrrapicca*, there is the substitution of *hir*; by [Pāṇini 6.4.113], there is the substitution of *it* for *i*.
"Juhutām."
In the imperative (loṭ), *tas* becomes *tām*:
"rudihi," "svapihi.
Due to its inclusion in the *adādi* class, there is elision (*luk*) of the *śap* suffix; [by Pāṇini 7.2.76], the augment *iṭ* is applied.

Now, why does this not occur here—namely, *juhutāt* *tvam*? He says: "here," and so forth. The scope for the substitution of *dhi* is in non-benedictive forms, such as *juhudhi*. The scope for *tāt* is in benedictive forms, such as *jīvatāt* *tvam*. When both [substitutions] would apply simultaneously in the benedictive *loṭ* mood, *tāt* alone occurs by virtue of its higher status in the order of rules (*paratva*).

Now, even when that [substitution] has been performed, because of its status as a *sthānivadbhāva* (as if it were the original), why does reduplication (*dhibhāva*) not occur again due to the principle of "re-occurrence" (*prasaṅgavijñāna*)? To this he says: "In that case," and so forth.

If this is so, then in forms such as *bhindhaki* and *chindhaki*, since reduplication would apply by virtue of being subsequent (*paratva*), would the augment *akac* not occur for the very reason just mentioned? To this he says: "In *bhindhaki*, *chindaki*, etc.

For when a word-meaning (*padārtha*) is understood as an individual instance (*vyakti*), the rule "when there is a conflict between two rules, that which is sublated once is sublated forever" (*Vyāḍipāda 40*) applies.

And this was established in the section beginning with "Because of the understanding of recurrence, [the rule] is established" (Vyāḍi-Pāṇini 41). For Pāṇini, however, both views are accepted; depending on the requirements of the linguistic data (*lakṣya*), one or the other is resorted to in specific instances. In that regard, because the individual (*vyakti*) is taken as the referent (*padārtha*) in the prescription of *tātaṅ*, the principle "once a conflict has been resolved by a prohibition, what was prohibited remains prohibited" applies; whereas in the prescription of *akac*, because the genus (*jāti*) is taken as the referent, the principle "because of the understanding of recurrence, [the rule] is established" applies.
Regarding "bhindhaki":

the suffix *akac* is applied by the rule beginning with "avyayasarvanāmnām" [Pāṇini 5.3.71]. In that context, the term "tiṅaśca" [Pāṇini 5.3.56] is understood as a governing rule (*anuvartate*). Regarding "śruṇudhī": [this is formed from the root *śru* with the imperative suffix *hi*].
By [Pāṇini 3.1.74], the suffix *śnu* is applied, and there is the substitution of *śṛ* for the root.
Regarding the form *pūrdhi*:
the root is *pṛ* in the sense of "protecting" and "filling" (Dhātupāṭha 1086); by [Pāṇini 7.1.102], *u* is substituted [for the radical vowel]; and by [Pāṇini 8.2.77], the vowel is lengthened.

In the phrase *uparuṇaskṛdhi*, when *uru asmākaṃ kṛdhi* is established, the substitution of *naḥ* for *asmad-* occurs by [Pāṇini 7.1.28]; then, by [Pāṇini 8.4.27], the *ṇa*-substitution (*ṇatva*) applies; the *s* becomes *r* (*rutva*), which becomes a *visarjanīya*; and that *visarjanīya* becomes *s* by [Pāṇini 8.3.46] and following rules.
Regarding the form *apāvṛdhi*:
it is a form derived from either the root *vṛṅ* or *vṛñ*.
For even from *vṛṅ*, the Parasmaipada ending occurs in Vedic usage by virtue of the rule *chandasyubhayathā* (Pāṇini 3.4.117).

Now, regarding the word *śṛṇudhi*: why does elision (*luk*) not occur here by the rule "also after an *u*-ending suffix that is not preceded by a conjunct consonant" [Pāṇini 6.4.106]? To this he says: "In *śṛṇudhi*, etc.
The sense is that if elision were to occur here, there would be the undesirable consequence of the loss of the syllable *dhi*.
Furthermore, in the word *apāvṛdhi*, there is lengthening [of the vowel] by the rule [Pāṇini 6.3.137].

But surely, in *śrudhi* there ought to be the substitution of *śṛ* by [Pāṇini 3.1.74] along with the *in* suffix, and in *pūrdhi* there ought to be the *śnā* suffix because it belongs to the *kry-ādi* class; in *uruṇaskṛdhi* there ought to be the *u* suffix by [Pāṇini 3.1.79]; and in *apāvṛdhi*, if it is from the root *vṛṅ*, then because it belongs to the *kry-ādi* class there ought to be the *śnā* suffix, and if it is from *vṛñ*, then because it belongs to the *svādi* class there ought to be the *śnu* suffix. Thus, these forms would not be established? To this he says: "ato 'nyatara" and so forth.

From this example, "śṛṇudhi," by the rule *śap* [Pāṇini 3.1.68], the affix *śap* is applied; for that as well, by the rule *tasyāpi* [Pāṇini 7.4.78], there is elision (*luk*). Regarding the phrase "optionally in the Veda" (*vā chandasi*) and so forth:

by the rule *apit* [Pāṇini 1.2.4], the status of having the marker *ṅ* (*ṅittva*) is prescribed for a sārvadhātuka affix that does not have the marker *p*. In the domain of the Veda, by the rule *herdhi* [Pāṇini 6.1.106], the fact that the substitute *dhi* lacks the marker *p* (*apittva*) is made optional.
Consequently, in one alternative, that [substitute] does not possess the status of having the marker *ṅ*.

Now, [one might ask]: how is *rārandhi* formed in the *parasmaipada*, given that this root *ram* is *ātmanepada* by nature? Or why is there no audible *śap* suffix here? And how is there lengthening of the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*), and how is it that the elision of the letter *m*—prescribed by the rule *anudāttopadeśa...* (Pāṇini 6.4.37)—does not occur? To this, he says: *rārandhi*, etc. By stating *śapaḥ śluḥ*, Bhoja implies that there is reduplication according to the rule *ślau* (Pāṇini 6.1.10). The absence of the elision of *m* is established because the suffix is not marked with the *ṅit* indicatory letter; thus, its non-occurrence does not require further effort. This is the intended meaning.
"Of the root *yam*, [there is] *śap*"—
this is by the rule "In the Veda, diversely" (*bahulaṃ chandasi*).
"Of the root *yu*, [there is] *ślu* for *śap*."

By this [rule], namely *ciṇa uttarasya pratyayasya* (P. 6.4.74), [it is meant that] "of the suffix following *ciṇ*. Now, how is it obtained that this refers to a suffix? By the rule *pratyayalope pratyayalakṣaṇam* (P. 1.1.62), because the suffix is brought into proximity by that. If there is elision (*luk*) of the suffix following *ciṇ*, why does it not occur in cases such as *akāritarām* and *akāritamām*, where the suffixes *tarap* and *tamap* follow? To this he says: "*akāritarām*" and so forth.

Regarding that elision (*luk*) of the suffix *ta*, when the elision of *tarap* and *tamap* is to be applied, there is non-attainment (*asiddhatva*) by the rule "in this [section], [an operation] is as if not accomplished, up to the end of the *ābhāt*" (Pāṇini 6.4.22).

Therefore, because they are separated by the word *ta*, the *tarap* and *tamap* do not immediately follow *ciṇ*; thus, their elision does not occur. Now, one might object: since the rule concerning non-attainment applies one thing in place of another, it is not logical for the same thing to be considered non-attained in that very same context. To this he says: "This [rule] regarding the elision of *ciṇ*" and so forth.

Although this rule, "there is elision of *ciṇ*" (*ciṇo luk*), is heard as non-distinct [in its formulation], it is differentiated by the distinction between the domain of the rule (*lakṣaṇa*) and the object of the rule (*lakṣya*); for, on the basis that the rule is differentiated with respect to each individual instance when the word-meaning is an individual (*vyakti*), its status as "not yet established" (*asiddhatva*) is indeed justified when such a distinction exists. When the forms *akāri* and *ahārī* have been established, if one intends to express excellence, the suffixes *tarap* and *tamap* are applied by the rule "also after a verbal suffix" (*tiṅaśca* 5.3.56). After adding the suffix *ām* to those forms ending in them by the rule "after that which ends in *ām*" (*tadantāt* 5.4.11), the forms *akāritamām* and *akāritamām* result. Regarding the word *gaccha*:
it is the imperative (*loṭ*) of the root *gam*, and the substitution of *ch* occurs by the rule "after *gam*" (*gam-chaḥ* 7.3.77).
"Run" (*dhāva*).

[The root] *dhāv* is used in the sense of "motion" and "purification" (Dhātupāṭha 601); alternatively, it is the substitute *dhāv* for the root *sṛ*, according to Pāṇini 7.3.78 (*pāghrādhmādheṭdrśaḥ paśyārthāśca*).
"Join," "ascend."
Because [the root] begins with a vowel, there is *luk* elision of the suffix *śap*.
In the forms "lunīhi" and "punīhi," there is shortening according to Pāṇini 7.3.80 (*pvādīnāṃ hrasvaḥ*), and the substitution of *ī* according to Pāṇini 6.4.113 (*ī halyadhoḥ*).

[Objection: "But if [the substitution] has already been performed, then because the word would not end in the letter *n*, [the rule] will not apply; so what is the purpose of including the *tapara* (long *ī*) marker for the sake of its exclusion? To this he says: "For the sake of *ītva*," and so forth. However, due to its being *asiddha* (not yet established), it is as before. Regarding the phrase "the *u* which is not preceded by a conjunct consonant" (*asaṃyogapūrva*):
that from which no conjunct consonant (*saṃyoga*) precedes is described in that way.

By this, he shows that the mention of "not preceded by a conjunct" (*asaṃyoga-pūrva*) is a qualification of the letter *a*. Such an *u* (as in *ku*) is a qualifier of the suffix; and since a rule involving a suffix applies to that which ends with such a qualified element, he says "from that which ends in that" (*tadantāt*), and so forth.

But for what purpose is the application of the suffix to that which ends in it (*tadantavidhi*) accepted? [One might say: "Let it be so for the sake of [forms like] *sunvaḥ* and *cinvaḥ*; this may be the purpose. However, there is this fault: [the rule] would not apply in cases such as *tanu* and *kuru*, because here the suffix is merely the letter *u*, and not something ending in it. To this, [the author replies]: even here, by the principle of "behaving like that which possesses a designation" (*vyapadeśivadbhāva*), the suffix does possess the status of being "that which ends in it," and thus there is no fault.
In the case of *kuru*, after applying guṇa and changing the vowel to *r* (raparatva), the substitution of *u* occurs by the rule *ata utsārvadhātuke* [Pāṇini 6.4.110].
Thus, *taruṇuhi*.

In the rule "the suffix *śnu* [is used] after the root *takṣ* in the sense of 'making thin'" (Pāṇini 3.1.76), there is the term "*chandovāvacanam*" ("the statement that it is optional in the Veda"). Here, by the metaphorical application of the name to the named (*abhidhāne'bhidheyopacārāt*), the word *vā* is intended to express the meaning "optionality" (*vārtha*). It is called *vacanam* because "it is spoken" (*ucyate*) or "explained" (*vyākhyāyate*) by means of it. *Vāvacanam* is the statement of optionality (*vārthasya vacanam*). The compound *chandovāvacanam* is formed as "the statement of optionality in the Veda" (*chandasi vāvacanam*), according to the analysis of the rule (*yogavibhāga*) "the seventh case [is compounded]" (Pāṇini 2.1.40). Thus, it is a compound.

"It should be stated that 'in the Vedic language (chandas), [the rule] is optional. This means that it must be explained that this rule applies optionally within the domain of the Vedic language. Regarding this, the explanation is as follows: the mention of *anyatarasyām* ("optionally") in the subsequent sūtra is a supplement (*śeṣa*) to both rules, and it is a restricted option (*vyavasthitavibhāṣā*).
Therefore, this rule applies optionally in the domain of the Vedic language (*chandasi*), as in the forms *dhinuhi* and *kṛṇuhi*.

[The roots] *hivi*, *divi*, and *dhivi* are for the sense of "pleasing" (Dhātupāṭha 591–593); *kṛvi* is for "injuring" and "doing" (Dhātupāṭha 598). Because they are marked with the indicatory letter *it*, the augment *num* is added by [Pāṇini 7.1.58], followed by the suffix *u* (the *upratyaya*) by [Pāṇini 3.1.80], and the final vowel *a* is substituted [for the root-final *i*]. That *a* is then elided by [Pāṇini 6.4.48: *ato lopaḥ*]. As for the statement, "this *u* which is not preceded by a conjunct consonant," [it refers to the following].

By the phrase "of this" (*asya*), he shows that the *u* under discussion is being referred back. Now, since the word "from this" (*ataḥ*) [from Pāṇini 6.4.106] is understood as a governing term (*anuvṛtti*), the elision will be understood to apply to the *u* alone; so what is the purpose of the word "of this"? If you argue that the word "of this" is for the sake of establishing the genitive case, we say no; for the locative *mvoḥ* itself, having already served its purpose in the preceding rule, will cause the fifth-case form *utaḥ*—which has already fulfilled its function in the previous yoga—to be interpreted as a genitive, according to the statement [Pāṇini 1.1.66]: "In the absence of another rule, the first case ending is used in place of the sixth. This might be the case.

If this [term] *mvoḥ* is understood as a locative (*saptamī*), then it is not yet understood whether it is a genitive (*ṣaṣṭhī*) or a locative. Therefore, it is stated that "of this" (*asya*) is used to establish it as a genitive. Regarding the phrase "while *luk* is being supplied," etc.: if *luk* were applied to the very same element under discussion, then *luk* would apply to the entire suffix, not just to the final one; for the technical term *luk* has been prescribed for the non-appearance of a suffix as a whole, and not for the non-appearance of a portion of a suffix.

But if the *luk* elision is applied to the whole suffix, would not the forms *sunvaḥ* and *sunmaḥ* fail to be established? There is no such fault because of the inclusion of the term *lopa* (elision).
For in that case, by the rule "the elision of the mere *ru*-sound" [Pāṇini 1.1.52], only the *ru* is elided.
Therefore, the mention of *lopa* is for the purpose of eliding the final sound.

Furthermore, in the case of *kiṃ kurvāṇaḥ*, when there is elision (*luk*), the *guṇa* substitution would not occur, because of the prohibition of the application of suffixal characteristics (*pratyayalakṣaṇa*) by [Pāṇini 1.1.63].

However, when there is elision (*lopa*), it does occur. Therefore, the mention of "elision" (*lopagrahaṇa*) must also be made for the sake of the *guṇa*. [This refers to the rule] "of the suffix *u* after the root *kṛ*."

[Objection: But surely, by the particle *ca*, the vowel *u* was drawn forward from the preceding sūtra, according to the rule: "That which is drawn forward (*anukṛṣṭa*) by *ca* does not recur in what follows" (Vyākaraṇa-paribhāṣā 76). How, then, can the elision of *u* be obtained? [Response: It is not so; for in the preceding sūtra, the proximity of the vowel *u* is already established by the very expression *asya* ("of this"). Therefore, the drawing forward of that *u* by the particle *ca* should be understood as being solely for this purpose. By the phrase "of the elision of *u*" (*ukāra-lopasya*), etc., he demonstrates the occurrence of lengthening in the case of *kurvaḥ* and *kumam* along with its justification, and shows its prohibition by the rule [Pāṇini 8.2.79].
The inclusion of the word *nitya* ("always") is for the sake of clarity.

Indeed, by the very force of its commencement, the rule will be understood as permanent (*nitya*). The particle *ca* is for the purpose of drawing in [the mention of] elision (*lopa*). Regarding the phrase "ending in the suffix *u*" and so forth: that which has the suffix *u* at its end is described as such.

And the root *kṛ*, when ending in the suffix *u*, does not deviate from being a *sārvadhātuka* [suffix]; with this intention he asks: "What is the purpose of mentioning *sārvadhātuka*? [He replies: "Even in the case of what occurred previously," and so forth.

If the term *sārvadhātuka* were not included [in the rule], then the substitution of *u* for the vowel of the root *kṛ*, which is prescribed when followed by an affix marked with *k* or *ṅ* (*kṅit*), would apply only where a *sārvadhātuka* affix follows—such as in *kurutaḥ* and *kurvanti*. However, in the case of *kurvit*, once the suffix *hi* has been elided (*luk*), there is no longer a *kṅit* affix present; consequently, due to the prohibition of *pratyayalakṣaṇa* (the treatment of an elided suffix as if it were still present) by [Pāṇini 1.1.63], the substitution would not take place.
Therefore, the inclusion of the term *sārvadhātuka* is for the purpose that the substitution should occur even when the *sārvadhātuka* affix existed previously.

Now, what is the purpose of adding the *t* (tapara) marker? For even though the vowel *u* when being taught (*bhāvyamāna*) includes its homogeneous counterparts (*savarṇa*), nevertheless, by virtue of proximity (*āntaratamya*), that which stands in place of a one-mora (*mātrika*) vowel will itself be one-mora. To this he says: "The addition of the *t* marker," and so forth. For if the *t* marker were not present, then by relying on the suffix *u*, after the *guṇa* substitution [by P. 7.3.84] has been made and the substitution of *r* [for the final element] has occurred, there would be a *guṇa* substitution for that *u* [which results from the *utva* change] by [P. 7.3.86].

Therefore, the addition of *ta* (the *tapara* marker) is made so that there may be the hearing of only the short vowel, and not that long vowel which would otherwise result from another rule. In the word *rundhaḥ*,
the substitution of *dha* for *ta* occurs by [Pāṇini 8.2.40].
Regarding the form *staḥ*:

due to its belonging to the *adādi* class, there is the elision (*luk*) of the *śap* suffix. Now, as for this reference *śnasoh*, since the lengthening [of the vowel] occurs by rule 6.4.111, should it not have been referred to as *śnasoḥ* after that lengthening had taken place? To this he says: "In the reference *śnasoh*, the *ā*-vowel undergoes the substitution of a single subsequent form (*pararūpa*)," and so forth.

What is the purpose of including the long vowel *ā* (the *tapara* marker) here? If you argue that it is so that [the augment] *āṭ* does not apply in forms such as *āstām* and *āsann*, this is not correct. For in this case, when the *laṅ* suffix is applied, at the stage of the root *lā*, the substitution for *l* is performed first because it is an *antaranga* (internal) operation, prior to the addition of the augment *āṭ*.
Once that has been done, the *vikaraṇa* (verbal suffix) supersedes the augment *āṭ* because it applies whether the latter has been added or not (*kṛtākṛta-prasaṅgitva*).
Furthermore, the augment *āṭ* is considered non-permanent (*anitya*) because its application depends on the presence of a different sound (*aśabdāntara-prāpti*).

For instance, once the *vikaraṇa* suffix has been applied, it must belong to the stem (*aṅga*) ending in that *vikaraṇa*; whereas if it has not been applied, it belongs to the verbal root alone. Even though, once the *vikaraṇa* is applied, both the augment *āṭ* and the elision of the vowel *a* are obligatory because they apply whether [the other] has been performed or not, nevertheless, the elision of the vowel *a* is carried out first because it is subsequent. Once that has been done, since it is considered non-existent (*asiddha*), the augment *āṭ* applies; and precisely because that [elision] is non-existent, the elision will not occur. So what is the purpose of the inclusion of *t* (in *tapara*)? This indicates that "the non-existence (*asiddhatva*) prescribed by grammatical rules is not absolute."

Therefore, the statement "the *vuṅ* and *yuṭ* augmentations are established in place of *uvaṅ* and *ayaṇ*" need not be stated; [it follows naturally]. In the case of "lunate," there is the substitution [of *yaṇ*] according to [Pāṇini 7.1.5];
in the case of "lunatām," [there is the substitution of *guṇa*].
The imperative? [It is] "āmetah" according to Pāṇini 3.4.90. "Alunata" is the imperfect (laṅ).
Regarding *mimate*:
from the root *māṅ* in the sense of "measuring" (*māne*, Dhātupāṭha 1088; or *māne śabde ca*, Dhātupāṭha)—the substitution of *i* for the reduplicated syllable occurs by [Pāṇini 7.4.76] *bhṛñām it*.
Similarly, in *sañjihate*, this applies to the root *ohāṅ* in the sense of "going" (*gatau*, Dhātupāṭha 1089).
In "bibhrati," there is the status of being a pūrvādi (a root beginning with a vowel). In "alunāt," [there is the substitution of *u* for *ṛ*].

[Objection: But surely, if this [rule] *kṅiti* did not exist, then by the rule for *ī*-substitution (*ītva*), this [shortening] ought to occur; so how could there be occasion for elision (*lopa*)? [Response: This is not so; for even the substitution of *ī* must be understood as following from the condition *kṅiti*. In that case, if "in the presence of *kṅit*" (*kṅiti*) were not carried over [from the previous rule], then elision would indeed occur.

[Objection: For what purpose is the mention of *āt* (the long vowel *ā*)? One might simply say "of the *a* of *śnā* and the reduplicated stems" (*śnābhyastayor ataḥ*); in this way, it would be lighter by one syllable. [Response: To this he says: "The mention of *āt* is for the sake of clarity.
Even when the designation 'reduplicated stem' (*abhyasta-saṃjñā*) applies—as in the case of the root *jāgarti*—there is no elision of the *ṛ* vowel: [we have] *jāgrati*."

And this [rule] is obtained because of the association with that which ends in *śnā* ending in *a*, since only the reduplicated (*abhyasta*) form ending in *a* is intended to be included: namely, *lunītaḥ*, *punītaḥ*; *lunītha*, *punītha*;
and *mimīte* (from the suffix *tasthasau*).
The third person singular middle voice form is *mimīṣe*. [In this form,] the substitution of *s* for *thās* is applied by Pāṇini 3.4.80.
"mimīdhvam"— the ending *dhvam*; "lunanti, punanti"— [the endings] *anti* and *anti*.

[The suffix] *jhi* is the condition. Now, one might object: "Even if *ittva* (the substitution of *i*) were to apply even when [the following suffix] begins with a vowel (*ajādau*), the elision (*lopa*) would be without scope (*anavakāśa*); therefore, because it is without scope, the elision would sublate the *ittva*. So what is the purpose of the mention of *hali*? This is not so; for if the mention of *hal* were absent, both [operations] would apply by virtue of the general rule.
[Consequently,] the elision of *ā* (*āllopa*) would undesirably apply to those [roots] designated as *ghu*.
Therefore, it must be stated that [the rule applies] "before a consonant" (*hali*). Thus,
in the case of *dattḥ*,
there is the substitution of *c* for *t* by the rule *khari ca* [Pāṇini 8.4.54].
Regarding "dhattaḥ":

when reduplication is applied to the root *dhā*, the initial *d* becomes *dh* by virtue of the substitution of *bhaṣ* for the abhyāsa (reduplicated syllable) according to [Pāṇini 8.4.54], and subsequently, after the elision of the vowel *ā* from the root, the *jaś*-substitution and *cartva*-substitution take effect. Regarding "daridrati":
by [Pāṇini 6.1.6], the designation *abhyasta* (repeated) is applied; consequently, the elision of the vowel *ā* occurs by virtue of the characteristics of the *abhyasta*.

"It must be stated" means it must be explained. Here is the explanation: by carrying forward the mention of *lopa* (elision) from [Pāṇini 6.4.111] according to the "frog-leap" (*maṇḍūkapluti*) maxim, one should set aside the specific conditions *sārvadhātuke*, *hali*, and *kṅiti*, and instead prescribe the substitution of *it* and elision for the root *daridrā* in a general sense.
And this being the case, those two [rules] do not result in confusion, because the mention of "in either one" (*anyatarasyām*), which will be stated later, is supplementary to both rules.
And that is a restricted option (*vyavasthitavibhāṣā*). Therefore, wherever it is intended that something should occur, it will occur only there and not elsewhere.

"And [the rule] 'siddhaśca pratyayavidhau' (and it is established in the formulation of an affix). This means that it must be performed in such a way that it is *siddha*—that is, already accomplished—at the time of the formulation of the affix (*pratyayavidhau*), i.e., at the moment the affix is being prescribed. What is meant by this is: the elision (*lopa*) must be carried out even while the *ārdhadhātuka* affix has not yet arisen, provided that it is present as the object of the operation.

In this way, the rule for the formation of the suffix (*pratyayavidhi*) becomes established, and not otherwise. By the inclusion of the phrase "and [the elision] is established in the formation of the suffix" (*siddhaśca pratyayavidhau*), what is the result? That result is demonstrated by the passage beginning with "characterized by having *ā* as its final phoneme" (*ākārāntalakṣaṇaḥ*).
If the elision were performed once an *ārdhadhātuka* suffix had arisen, then the suffix *ṇa* would apply by the rule *śyādvyadhāruāu* (Pāṇini 3.1.141), because the root *daridrāti* ends in *ā*.

Furthermore, if the *yuk* augment were applied by the rule *āto yuk ciṇ-kṛtoḥ* [Pāṇini 7.3.33], the undesirable form *daridrāya* would result. However, when it is stated that "the [base] is established prior to the prescription of the suffix," the elision occurs even before the suffix arises; because of that elision, the base no longer ends in an *ā*, and thus the suffix *ac* (as in *pac-ādi-ac*) applies. By this means, the desired form *daridraḥ* is established.
With the verse beginning "There is no elision in *daridrāyaka*," etc., [the author] shows where elision is not desired in an *ardhadhātuka* suffix, or where it is desired optionally by some.
In the case of *daridrāyaka*, when the word ending in the suffix *ṇvul* is intended to be established, elision is not desired;
thus, from the root *daridrāti*, one forms *daridrāyāka*.
The reasoning is as before. Regarding the term "daridrāṇe," here too, when the suffix *lyuṅ* is applied, the elision of *n* is not desired.
"Some say 'didaridrāsati'";
when the suffix *san* is applied, there is reduplication and the operations pertaining to the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*).
Or, "didaridriṣati."

In the rule *sanīvantardha* [Pāṇini 7.2.49], the augment *iṭ* is optional due to the supplementary rule (*upasaṃkhyāna*) stating "of *tan*, *pat*, and *daridrā*. The phrase "in the adyatani" means in the *luṅ* tense; "adyatani" is the designation used by the ancient grammarians for the *luṅ*.

Regarding the form *adaridrāsīt*: by the rule *yamaramanamātāṃ sak? ca* [Pāṇini 7.2.73], the augment *s* and the augment *iṭ* are applied; then by *asti sico'pṛkte* [Pāṇini 7.3.96], the augment *iṭ* is added to the root *as*; and by *iṭa īṭi* [Pāṇini 8.2.28], there is the elision of the *sic*. Now, one might object: since the vowel *ā* is elided by *ato lopaḥ* [Pāṇini 6.4.140], the form should have been cited as *daridra*, so how is it cited as *daridrasya*? To this he says: "The citation is *daridrasya*" and so forth.

Because of the statement "the sūtras are like Vedic" (Aṣṭādhyāyī 6.3.63), the shortening here is Vedic due to the use of the word *bahulam* ("variously"). The inclusion of the letter *t* [in the term *tapara*] is for the sake of clarity;

since a long vowel is not included among its own class (*savarṇa*) when it is being taught (*bhāvyamāna*), a long vowel will not occur. [The rule applies] "when a sārvadhātuka suffix beginning with a consonant (*hal*) follows that has the markers *k* or *ṅ*."
Although these specific details were already excluded in the preceding [sūtra], the intention here is that they nevertheless carry over by way of the "frog-leap" maxim (*maṇḍūkapluti-nyāya*).
Regarding the form *bibhītaḥ*: the root is *ñi bhī* in the sense of "fear" (Dhātupāṭha 1084); because it belongs to the *juhotyādi* class, there is *ślu*-elision of the *śap* suffix.
Only when followed by *hal* and so forth—as in *bibhyati*.
Precisely because of the force of the rule prescribing the substitution of *it*, the *yaṇ* substitute [from Pāṇini 6.4.82, *eranekācaḥ*] would not otherwise apply.
Only when followed by a *sārvadhātuka* suffix—as in *bhītaḥ* and *bhītavān*.

Why specify "before an affix marked with K or Ṅ"? [Consider: *bibheti*. This substitution of *i* is introduced as an exception to the substitution of *īt*; because the phrase "optionally" (*anyatarasyām*) is understood to carry over, that [substitution of *īt*] also occurs in the alternative case. [This rule applies] only when a sārvadhātuka affix follows—[as in] *hīnaḥ*, *hīnavān*.

In this regard, some reject the continued application (*anuvṛtti*) of the rule *sārvadhātuke* [Pāṇini 6.4.110]. How so? They argue: "When a consonant (*hal*) follows, the substitution of *ī* and *u* (īttva-ettva) would apply, as would reduplication (*dvirvacana*). In that case, if the substitutions of *ī* and *u* were to occur by virtue of their being subsequent rules, then the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*) would end in the vowels *i* and *e*. Therefore, the term 'reduplicated' (*abhyasta*) must be understood as continuing from the previous context; and since that term continues, the continued application of *sārvadhātuka* is redundant. This, however, is incorrect, because [the reduplication] is an internal operation (*antaraṅga*).

By the very fact of reduplication (*dvirvacana*), the substitution of *it* and *et* ought to occur first; how then could there be any possibility of the reduplicated syllable ending in an *i*-vowel? For reduplication is *antaraṅga* (internal) because it depends on fewer factors—it depends merely on the root itself. In contrast, the substitutions of *it* and *et* are *bahiraṅga* (external) because they depend on more factors; this dependence on many factors arises because those two are prescribed for the stem (*aṅga*) when followed by a *sārvadhātuka* suffix beginning with a consonant (*hal*) that has the markers *k* or *ṅ*.
Is it because of the specific mention of *jahāti*? [The form] *jihīte* does not arise from the root *hā* (*jihī-*).
"The formulation of a separate rule is for the sake of subsequent rules.

This means that the rule *āca hau* [Pāṇini 6.4.117] should apply only to *jahāti*, and not to *bibheti*. The letter *c* is for the purpose of carrying forward (*anukarṣaṇa*) both the optionality of *ittva* (the substitution of *i*) and the mention of *anyatarasyām*. The mention of *abhyāsalopa* ("elision of the reduplicated syllable") is for the sake of those roots designated as *dhut*; it is not for the sake of the root *as*, because the reduplication of *as* is impossible.
"Dehi" and "cehi"—
these are the forms derived from the roots *dā* and *dhā*.
However, examples of other roots designated as *ghu* are not possible here, because they are separated by the *vikaraṇa* suffix *hi*.
And because [the forms] are impossible according to their respective applications:

there, the particle *hi* intervenes between the root *do* and the suffix *śyan*; however, for *dāṇ* and *dheṭ*, there is the suffix *śāp*; furthermore, because *deṅ* is marked with the *ātmanepada* (middle voice) indicator, the occurrence of *hi* is impossible.
Thus, [the form] is *edhi*.

When the substitution of *ai* for the *s* has been made, because that [substitution] is considered non-existent (*asiddha*), the replacement by *dhi* occurs according to the rule *hujhalabhyo herdhiḥ* (Pāṇini 6.4.101). But surely, by the rule *alo 'ntyasya* (Pāṇini 1.1.52), there ought to be elision of only the final letter; so how does the elision of the entire reduplicated syllable occur? To this he says: "This [root] begins with *ś*" and so forth. In the rule *lopaśca*, two *ś*s are specified.
In that context, one [element] is related to the elision (*lopa*), while the second is related to the case-ending (*vibhakti*).
Since it is declared that the *it* designation applies to that which is related to the elision, this elision is optional (*śit*).
Consequently, the elision of the entire reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*) takes place.

The mention of *hau* can be understood as being carried over from the rule *ā ca hau* [6.4.117] by means of the "frog-leap" (*maṇḍūkapluti*) maxim. Since that [previous rule] is connected with the mention of *anyatarasyām*, one might suspect that upon its recurrence, the term *anyatarasyām* would also recur; therefore, the word *hau* is stated in order to prevent that. Because the particle *ca* has the sense of conjunction (*sanniyoga*), both elision (*lopa*) and the substitution of *et* (the *ēt* augment) take place. [This applies when the vowel is] "between two single-consonant sounds" (*ekahalmadhye*).
This word *eka* signifies "without a companion.

*Ekaśca ekaśca* becomes *ekau*; *ekau ca tau halau ca* becomes *ekahalau*. Thus, *ekahalormadhye* is a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*) consisting of a dual-ending term. For a space between two consonants is indeed possible, but not between a single one.
In this context, if the substitute for *liṭ* were not qualified, then forms such as *nematuḥ*, *nemuḥ*, *sehe*, *sehāte*, and *sehira* would not be possible.
Having kept in mind that here too the beginning of the *aṅga* is subject to substitution, he says "when *liṭ* follows," etc., in order to qualify the substitute for *liṭ*.
The meaning is: when a substitute is prescribed when *liṭ* follows, that [substitute] does not belong to the beginning of the *aṅga* to which it is applied.
Regarding the word "tasya" (of that):
it means "of such a limb" (aṅga).
Furthermore, the word "tasya" is connected with the phrase "the vowel 'a' which belongs to that limb."
And this is a genitive of part (*avayava-ṣaṣṭhī*); the meaning is "of that which is such a member, namely the vowel *a* which is its constituent part.
This is the explanation of the rule "in the middle of a single consonant" (*eka-halmadhye*), namely: "in the middle of two non-accompanied consonants" (*asahāyayor haloh*).
The word "that" (*tasya*) refers back to the vowel *a* mentioned immediately prior.
The meaning is "of that limb, part, or form. And this is a genitive of location (*sthāna-ṣaṣṭhī*): in place of that, the vowel *e* becomes the substitute—as in *reṇatuḥ* and *reṇuḥ*.
Regarding "aṇa raṇa" (Dhātupāṭha 444, 445), it is recited that "raṇi means sound. Regarding "yematuḥ, yemuḥ," [this is from] "yama uparame" (Dhātupāṭha 984).
"dematuḥ, demuḥ"— from the root *damu* in the sense of "to pacify" (Dhātupāṭha 1203). "rarāśe" [the Kāśikā reads *rarāse*].
The root *rāśṛ* in the sense of "sound" (*rāśṛ śabde*; Dhātupāṭha 626) is ātmanepada. [Examples are: *śaśramatuḥ*, *śaśramuḥ*.

The root *śramu* is used in the senses of "exertion" and "weariness" (*śramu tapasi khede ca*; Dhātupāṭha 1204). However, some read *tatakṣatuḥ* and *tatakṣuḥ* as counter-examples under the assumption that there is a single *hal* (consonant) [in *pakṣ*]; but this is incorrect, because the term *kṅiti* is understood [from the previous rule], and the *liṭ* affix following *pakṣ* does not possess the *kit* designation in any case.
Is it because of the prohibition [of the suffix -an] by the rule "asaṃyogāt"?
[The forms would then be] *tatsaratuḥ* and *tatsaruḥ*. [The root is] *tsara* in the sense of "going by stealth" (Dhātupāṭha 554).
"Cakaṇatuḥ, cakaṇuḥ"—
these forms [are derived from] the roots *aṇ*, *raṇ*, *vaṇ*, *bhaṇ*, *kvaṇ*, and *kaṇ*, which have the meaning "to sound" (Dhātupāṭha 444,
445, 446, 447, 449, 450). Among these, the root *kaṇati* is listed in the *bhvādi* class.
Regarding the forms *jagaṇatuḥ* and *jagaṇuḥ*:
the root *gaṇa* (meaning "to count") is listed among the roots of the *curādi* class (Dhātupāṭha 1853).

Now, one might object that because it belongs to the *curādi* class, when the causative suffix *ṇic* is applied, the suffix *ām* must necessarily be added according to Pāṇini 3.1.35. However, there is no fault here, because it is held that "the *curādi* roots are not invariably transitive" (*anityaṇyantāścurādayaḥ*).
The fact that these roots are non-causative (aṇyantatva) will be made known in the seventh [chapter].
Regarding "babhaṇatuḥ": the root *bhaṇ* is recited in the Bhvādi class with the meaning of sound alone. Regarding "nematuḥ": [the root *nī* is used].
The root *ṇam* [is used] in the sense of bowing and sound (Dhātupāṭha 981).
By the rule *ṇo naḥ* [Pāṇini 6.1.65], there is the substitution of *na* for *ṇa*.
Thus: *sehe*.
In the root *ṣaha* (meaning "to endure," Dhātupāṭha 852), the substitution of *s* occurs according to [Pāṇini 6.1.64].

But how is it that, even when the substitution of *n* and the substitution of *s* have occurred, the substitutes for the *liṭ* [perfect tense] and so forth do not take effect? To this he says: "The substitutions of *n* and *s* are non-contingent" (*anaimittike natvasatve*), etc.

For, since no specific cause (*nimitta*) is relied upon in the prescription of the substitutions of *n* and *s*, these two occur as non-contingent; consequently, they must take effect prior to the very production of the *liṭ*.
Therefore, that which is the *aṅga* (base) starting with that [augment] does not become something whose initial element is the substitute for *liṭ*.

If, then, the substitute for *liṭ* were indeed qualified [by the base], the *aṅga* would remain unqualified; consequently, this rule would undesirably apply even in cases such as *pakvaḥ* and *pakvavān*, since the substitute applied to the root *pac-* when *liṭ* follows is also not preceded by anything here? This is not so; for the substitution of *et* is stated in conjunction with the elision of the reduplication (*abhyāsa-lopa*). Therefore, it must occur only where there is the elision of the reduplication.
And there is no elision of the reduplication here, because it is impossible [for it to occur].
Well then, would it not occur here in *pāpacyate*? This too is no fault; here, by the rule *para* (Pāṇini 7.4.83), the long vowel will take effect.
Shortening and the replacement by a single consonant (*halādiśeṣa*) are general rules (*utsarga*), while the lengthening and the substitution of *e* (*ettva*) are exceptions (*apavāda*) to them.

In this regard, the scope for lengthening (*dīrgha*) is, for example, *bābhāsyate*; the scope for the substitution of *et* is, for example, *pecatuḥ* and *pecuḥ*. Here, however, both rules would apply in the case of *pāpacyate*. Since there is a conflict between an exception (*apavāda*) and a prohibition (*vipratiṣedha*), lengthening will occur by virtue of its being the subsequent rule. Now, why does the substitution of *et* not occur in *babhaṇatuḥ* and *babhaṇuḥ*? If it is argued that [the substitution of *et* does not apply] because the substitution of *jaś* has already been performed according to Pāṇini 8.4.54, and thus [the root] begins with a substitute [consonant], we say: no; because when the substitution of *et* is to be applied, the substitution of *jaś* is considered as if non-existent (*asiddha*). Therefore, the substitution of *et* must indeed take place.

However, since there would be no scope for the rule *kuhoścuḥ* [P. 7.4.62]—which effects the substitution of *c* and *u*—in cases such as *cakaṇatuḥ*, *cakaṇuḥ*, *jahasatuḥ*, and *jahasuḥ* (where *jaś*-substitution has already occurred), he says "here," etc.
How is it known that there is no status of being *asiddha*? He says: "And thus," etc.

Only then does the substitution of *e* and *o* for the roots *phal* and *bhaj* in the rule *tṛphalabhajatrapaśca* [P. 6.4.122] become possible, provided that the *jaś*- and *cu*-substitutions are not *asiddha*; otherwise, it would not.
Is it not the case that because [the rule] begins with *anādeśa*, the substitution of *et* is already established by this very [rule]? That is not tenable.
Therefore, because the substitution of *et* is prescribed for the roots *phal* and *bhaj*, it is understood that here the rules for *jaśtva* and *cattrva* are not considered *asiddha*.
This is expressed in the phrase "and when there is no difference in form," and so forth.

The statement that "an *ādeśa* (substitute) is not accepted here when there is non-difference from the *sthānin* (original element) in terms of its phonetic form" is supported by the prohibitory rule regarding *śas* and *did* in [Pāṇini 6.4.126].

Furthermore, by the rule [Pāṇini 8.4.54], which states that the *jaś* sounds of the original element (*prakṛti*) are replaced by *jaś* sounds and the *car* sounds by *car* sounds, the *ś* of *śas* remains *ś*, and the *d* of *dad-* also remains *d*; thus, both of these remain as they were even before the substitution.

In this regard, if the substitute (*ādeśa*) were also accepted here as being identical to the original form (*sthānin*), then, precisely because it would be the same as the original, the rule would not apply, and consequently, the prohibition of *et*-vocalization for the [suffixes] *śas* and *idi* would not need to be prescribed. Yet, it has been prescribed; therefore, this very statement of the prohibition makes known that when there is no difference in form, the substitute is not accepted here.
If it were indeed accepted, what would happen? To this he says: "Otherwise, however," and so forth.

Otherwise, even that substitute which, due to non-difference in form, is identical in form with the original (sthānin), would be subject to this rule here. Consequently, just as the substitution of *et* does not occur for forms such as *cakaṇatuḥ*, it would likewise not occur for *pecatuḥ*, *pecuḥ*, and so forth, which have *j* and *c* sounds as their original bases (*prakṛti*). By "those whose original bases are *j* or *c*" is meant those whose original bases are *jaś* or *car* sounds. For example: *ahaṃ papaṭha*, *ahaṃ papaca*.

In this case, because [the suffix] is treated as if it were the original (sthānivadbhāva), it is *pit* (having a *p* marker); therefore, it lacks *kit*-ness (*kittva*), and consequently, neither the substitution of *et* nor the elision of the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsalopa*) occurs.

Nor does *vṛddhi* (vowel strengthening) occur, because in one view there is an absence of *ṇit*-ness according to Pāṇini 7.2.116. However, in the view where it possesses *ṇit*-ness, since *vṛddhi* would take precedence and supersede [the other operations], the substitution of *et* and the elision of the reduplicated syllable should not occur. Thus, the example is given specifically under the view that it lacks *ṇit*-ness (*aṇittvapakṣa*).

Regarding the word "dambheḥ": what is the reason that the substitution of *e* for the vowel of the root *dambh* does not occur, given that the rule "the substitute [of the root] is the body of the stem (*aṅga*) when *liṭ* follows" applies, and once the elision of the nasal has been performed by the rule beginning with "aniditām" (Pāṇini 6.4.24), the vowel *a* remains precisely within the middle of a single consonant (*ekahalmadhya*)? To this, he says: "of the elision of *n*" (*nalopasya*), and so forth.

In the rule *granthi-śranthi-dambhi-svañjīnām* (Vārttika 17), it is stated that the *liṭ* suffix following the root *dambh* is *kit*. When that is the case, the elision (*lopa*) of the penultimate vowel (*upadhā*) would not occur because of the rule *asiddhavad atrā bhāt* (Pāṇini 6.4.22), which renders such an operation as if non-existent (*asiddha*). Therefore, the substitution of *e* for the vowel of *dambh* must be stated;
that is to say, it must be explained [as a necessary addition].

In this regard, the following is the explanation: In the rule *śnasorallopaḥ* [Pāṇini 6.4.111], it is indicated that the unestablished status (*asiddhatva*) of a grammatical operation is not invariably so; by this, when the substitution of *e* for the root *dambh* is to be applied, the elision (*lopa*) does not remain unestablished, and consequently, the substitution of *iṭ* for *dambh* will take place.

Alternatively, in the rule *ata ekahalmadhye* [Pāṇini 6.4.120], a split of the yoga (*yogavibhāga*) should be made after the word *ataḥ*; by this, wherever the substitution of *e* is desired, it will occur there.

And by adopting this view, even the supplementary rule (*vārttika*) "the substitution of *et* for the *liṭ* [augment] of the roots *naś* and *man*" (Vārttika 793) need not be added, since it is established by means of a word-splitting (*yogavibhāga*) alone.
It should be understood everywhere that the word "to be stated" (*vaktavya*) has the meaning "to be explained. As in the example:
"aneśam."
The substitution of *am* for *mi* occurs by the rule *tasthasthamipām* [Pāṇini 3.4.101].

Now, one might ask: why does the substitution of *ī* not occur in the word *menakā* according to the rule *pratyayasthāt* [Pāṇini 7.3.44]? To this he says: "In the case of *kṣipakā* and so forth," etc.
It will be stated that the substitution of *ī* is prohibited in the case of *kṣipakā* and other such words.
And its insertion occurs in *kṣipakā* and similar forms; therefore, the shortening (*ittva*) is not performed.
Regarding the term "in *cānaś*":
[the rule] *tacchīlyavayovacanaśaktiṣu cānaś* (Pāṇini 3.2.129) applies, and thus the substitution of *muk* is not performed.

By [Pāṇini 7.2.82], the substitution of *muk* would have been required, but it does not occur because "the teaching regarding augments is not obligatory" (Vyāḍipāda 95). Alternatively, due to its Vedic character— since "all rules are optional in the Veda" (Bhāṣyapāda 99)—
it is said that "the shortening is Vedic."

By the rule *ṅyāpoḥ saṃjñācchandasorbahulam* [Pāṇini 6.3.63], the shortening of the vowels *ṅī* and *āp* is prescribed; due to the mention of "optionally" (*bahulam*), this applies even in cases such as *periran*. Here, from the root *pac*, we have the optative suffix *liṅ*, the augment *sīyuṭ*, the replacement of *jh* by *ran*, and the addition of *śap*. Thus, one would expect *paceiran*; however, once the substitution of *e* for *a* (by *ādeca upadeśe'śiti*) and the shortening of the vowel have been applied, the form becomes *peciran*. As for *teratuḥ* and *teruḥ*: [the process is similar].
The *guṇa* substitution [of *o* for *av*] applies by the rule *ṛcchatyṛtām* [Pāṇini 7.4.11].
Thus we have *phelatuḥ* and *pheluḥ*.
These derive from the roots *phala* in the sense of "accomplishment" (*niṣpatti*) [Dhātupāṭha 530] and *ñi phalā* in the sense of "falling apart" (*viśaraṇa*) [Dhātupāṭha 516].
Regarding the phrase "for the sake of the guna of *tṛ*":
he will state a prohibition [in Pāṇini 6.4.126] beginning with "not after *tṛ*.
Therefore, this statement concerning *tṛ* is for the purpose that the rule should apply even to that which has already been established as having undergone *guṇa*.
Regarding the statement, "It should be stated that [the rule] also applies to *śranthi*":

the meaning is that this must be explained as having the sense that the substitution of *e* for the vowel of the root *granth*—given in the Dhātupāṭha as *grantha śrantha sandarbhe* (1511, 1512)—also occurs.

The explanation here is as follows: the particle *ca* ("and") is used in the sense of *atraciye* (inclusion), and it serves to aggregate what has not been explicitly mentioned; therefore, the rule will apply to *śranthi* as well.

In the forms *śrethatuḥ* and *śrethuḥ*, the elision of the nasal (*nakāra*) occurs because the *liṭ* [perfect tense marker] is treated as having the *kit* designation by means of a supplementary rule (*upasaṃkhyāna*), as in the previous cases. The statement regarding the root *jṛ* (meaning "decay of age," *vayohānau*; Dhātupāṭha 1494; *jṛ-mu* according to the *mūlapāṭha*) is for the purpose of [preventing] *guṇa*. It is also intended to provide a substitute for *bhram*, and for the sake of [applying the rule] to roots situated between multiple consonants (*anekahalmadhya*). Furthermore, it is for the sake of [the form] *traseḥ* when it occurs between multiple consonants. Thus, we have the form *jajaratuḥ*.
The quality [of the suffix] is as previously stated. Because of the use of the plural number, the sense of "and so forth" (*ādi*) is understood.
Therefore, he says: "of *phaṇa* and the others," etc. [The roots are:
*phaṇa* "to move" (DhP 821), *rājṛ* "to shine" (DhP 822), and *ṭu bhrājṛ*, *ṭu bhrāśṛ*, *ṭu bhlāśṛ* "to shine" (DhP 823–825).
The seven roots beginning with *phaṇ*—namely *syam*, *svan*, *dhvan*, and *śabd* (as listed in the Dhātupāṭha, 826–828)—excluding *dhvan*, [are the subject].
Among them, the rule is stated for the first root (*syam*) to provide an option where [the ātmanepada] was already obligatory, and for the others where it was not yet applicable.

In that regard, concerning the four [cases] beginning with the king (*rājan*), regarding the substitution of *et* for the vowel *a*, what was stated under [Pāṇini 6.4.123]—namely, "the form *ataḥ* (of *at*) is present here"—is to be understood according to the possibility of its application. Here, if by the word *guṇa* the very same vowel *a* is meant for which the substitution of *et* was prescribed, then the meaning is this: "it does not occur for the *guṇa* substitute of the vowel *a*."

Thinking that, if this were so, the rule for *ettva* (the substitution of *e* and *o*) would have no scope at all, [the author], keeping this in mind, shows that here it is not the vowel *a* itself that is called "guṇa," but rather that which is produced by the word "guṇa. Thus he says: "And of that which is produced as 'guṇa,'" and so forth. The meaning is: the *ettva* substitution does not occur for that *a* which belongs to the word-form produced after pronouncing the word "guṇa. Furthermore, its connection with that [word-form] should be understood according to the circumstances, either because it occupies the place of that [original *a*] or because it is a constituent part of it.

Thus, in this way, for that which is produced by a word denoting a quality (*guṇa*), the non-existence of a related element is the cause for a prohibition, whereas its existence is the cause for an injunction; such is the distinction between the domains of injunction and prohibition. Regarding the form *viśaśasatuḥ*:
the root *śasu* is used in the sense of "injuring" (*hiṃsāyām*) [Dhātupāṭha 727].
Regarding "dadade":
the root *dada* in the sense of "giving" is found in the Dhātupāṭha (17).
Regarding "vavamatuḥ": [the root *vam*].
Regarding the roots *ṭu vama* in the sense of "vomiting" (Dhātupāṭha 849) and *viśaśaratuḥ*,
the root *śṛ* is used in the sense of "injury" (Dhātupāṭha 1488).
He demonstrates the meaning of what was stated in the passage beginning with "of that which is produced from a word denoting a quality" by means of these examples.
In the form *viśaśaratuḥ*, this sound *ari* is produced from a *guṇa* sound; for the vowel *a* connected with it is a constituent part (*ekadeśa*) of that [guṇa]. [The example] is *lulavitha*.
In this case as well, the vowel *o* is produced by the term "guṇa," because the *a*-sound associated with it occupies its place [in the resulting form].

Now, one might object: "In the example *viśaśaratuḥ*, only the sound *ā* is produced by the term 'guṇa,' not the sound *ār*! This is not so; for the *r*-sound is a constituent part (*bhakta*) of the guṇa.

Thus says the Bhāṣya: "When there is guṇa, there is *ar*; when there is vṛddhi, there is *ār*—that which is accompanied by the *r*-sound receives the technical designations 'guṇa' and 'vṛddhi'. And: "The substitute *t* occurs."
The rule ending with *nānubandhakṛtamanekāltvam* (Vyāḍiparibhāṣā 14) applies here; because [the substitute] is single-letter (*ekāl*), since the letter *k* is an *anubandha*.

Is it because the letter *u* is an *anubandha*? The nominative singular suffix *su* is understood [as the subject], therefore it indeed occurs in the locative plural—as in *arvatsu*—[where the substitution does not apply].
And if it is argued that "it does not follow after the negative particle (*nañ*)"? That which was under discussion [in the previous rule] is connected here as well.

Regarding the word *arvantau*: because the vowel *ṛ* in *ṛt* is for the purpose of triggering the operation of the *ugit* designation, the augment *num* is applied by [Pāṇini 7.1.70] *ugidacām*. Thus, we have *arvati*.
The suffix *ṅīp* is applied by [Pāṇini 4.1.45].
Regarding the form *ārvatam*:
when there is a desire to express the sense of "offspring," the suffix *aṇ* is applied.

But surely, by the logic of the *nañ-iva-yukta* rule (*vyā.pa. 65*), because of similarity, [the suffix] *su* must occur only after another case-ending (*vibhakti*)? This is not so; this is a *prasajya-pratiṣedha* (absolute negation). For this very reason, the author of the *Vṛtti* stated: "If it is *su*, then [another] *su* does not follow it. Otherwise, he would have said: "If there is something other than *su* which is a *sup*, then [another *su*] follows it."

Or even if it is a *paryudāsa* (an exclusion)? Even so, there is no fault; for the rule regarding the *nañ* (negative particle) and its connection [to a following word] is non-eternal (*anitya*). Its non-eternality is understood from the inclusion of the term "case-ending" (*vibhakti*) in the sūtra at [Pāṇini 6.3.132]. For if that rule were eternal, then by the exclusion of the nominative (*prathamā*), it would apply only to case-endings, and thus he would not have included the term "case-ending."

Even by doing so, it indicates that this technical designation (*paribhāṣā*) is not eternal. In the word *madhavā*, the nominative case is used in place of the genitive due to a transposition of cases;
thus we have *madhoḥ*.
By the rule *āyuvamaghonām* [Pāṇini 6.4.133], there is Samprasāraṇa of the vowel, followed by the substitution of the preceding sound for the following one [6.1.87].

But surely, if one intends to express the possessive sense (*matvartha*) as "he who has *magha*," this word *maghavan* would end in the suffix *vanip* according to the rule *chandasi vanipo vaktavyaḥ* (Vārttika 582).

In that case, once the *vanip* suffix undergoes vocalization (*samprasāraṇa*) and the term receives the designation *bha*, there would have to be an elision according to [Pāṇini 6.4.148], and consequently the undesirable form *madhunaḥ* would result. This is not so; for this is indeed a different, underived nominal stem (*prātipadika*), since its usage is observed even in the neuter gender (*bhāva*).

Furthermore, even if it were to end with the *vanip* suffix, there would still be no fault; for by virtue of the rule of "diversity" (*bahulavacanāt*), the elision prescribed by [Pāṇini 6.4.148] "of that which ends in *i*" will not occur.
Thus, [the form] "maghonī" is derived by applying [Pāṇini 4.1.5]:
"the suffix *ṅīp* after stems ending in *ṛ* or *n*."
Regarding "māghavanam": the suffix *aṇ* is applied as before; by [Pāṇini 6.4.67] "an," there is the preservation of the original stem form (*prakṛtibhāva*). Regarding "pādaḥ": [the same applies].
"The word *pāda* is taken as having its vowel *a* elided.

Now, why is the form *pād* not taken here—the form that results from the root *pādayati* when the suffix *kvip* is applied? Because such a form is impossible. For [the suffix] *kvip* would have to be applied by the rule *pāghrādhmādheṭdṛśaḥ śaḥ* (Pāṇini 3.1.137), and that is not possible because of the explicit statement "it is seen" (*dṛśyate*).

In cases where the usage of a word ending in *kvip* is observed in the world, the term "is seen" (*dṛśyate*) is employed there for the purpose that it might occur exactly as such; however, no usage of *pādayati* ending in *kvip* is observed. Since the vowel *ā* is elided only in a compound of the word *pāda*, [the author] says "of the stem ending in that" (*tadantasyāṅgasya*), etc., because by implication (*sāmarthyāt*) the operation is understood to apply to the stem ending in that.

If, then, this substitution *pad* were understood as applying to a stem (*aṅga*) ending in the word *pād*, then— since [by rule 1.1.72] it would apply to the whole of that which ends in it— he says "And that," etc. "Dvipadaḥ" is a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "one who has two feet."
> [[5.4.140]] There is elision of the vowel *i*.
Regarding the form *dvipadikām*:
[it means] one who gives two feet at a time; the suffix *vun* is applied by the rule beginning with *pādaśatasya* [[5.4.1]].

Regarding the term *vaiyāghrapadyaḥ*: it is a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "one whose feet are like those of a tiger. By [Pāṇini 5.4.138], there is the elision of the vowel *a*; then, because he is the descendant (*apatyam*) of Vyāghrapada, the suffix *yañ* is applied due to his inclusion in the *gargādi* group. According to the technical rule concerning the mention of a suffix (*pratyayagrahaṇaparibhāṣā*), it is understood that the grammatical operation applies to that which ends in the suffix; thus he says: "of that which ends in *vasu*, etc. Regarding the word *viduṣaḥ*.
In *pecaṣaḥ*,

the suffix *kvam* is applied to the root of the perfect tense (*liṭ*) by [Pāṇini 3.2.107], and the substitution of *et* for the radical vowel and the elision of the reduplication occur by [Pāṇini 6.4.120] and subsequent rules. In *papuṣaḥ*, the same applies.
Thus, there is the elision of the vowel *ā*. Now, one might object:

"When the elision of *ā* is to be performed, the *samprasāraṇa* (vowel substitution) is considered non-existent (*asiddha*); therefore, how can there be an elision of *ā* here? To this he replies: "When the elision of *ā* is to be performed," and so forth.

The elision of *ā* occurs after the *samprasāraṇa*, and that [elision] occurs in the presence of a case-ending (*vibhakti*). Thus, because they rely on different bases (*vayāśrayatva*), there is no state of being non-existent (*asiddhatva*).

But surely, according to the rules "when a [suffix] with one *anubandha* is mentioned, there is no inclusion of one with two *anubandhas*" (Vyāḍi-Pāṇini 52), or "when a [suffix] having that *anubandha* is mentioned, there is no inclusion of one not having that *anubandha*" (Vyāḍi-Pāṇini 54), there ought to be no mention of *kvasu* here. How then does the *samprasāraṇa* occur in forms such as *papuṣaḥ* and *pecuṣaḥ*? To this he says: "In the mention of *vasu*, etc. This, however, is to be understood from the addition of the *anubandha* *ū* to the *vasu* which is the substitute for the *śatṛ*. For this is the very purpose of the *anubandha* *ū*: so that there may be a general inclusion [of the suffix] here.

Is it not for the sake of the *ugit* designation? It might be so; but this is not the case, because the effect of being *ugit* is already established through the rule of *sthānivadbhāva*. Regarding the term "of *vāh*":
this *vāh* ends in the suffix *ṇvi*, and that *ṇvi* is prescribed only after this root when it is accompanied by an upapada.
Therefore, by implication (*sāmarthya*), it is understood that the rule applies to that which ends in it; thus he says: "of that which ends in such as *vāh*," and so forth.
Regarding the statement "this [is] *ūḍ*":
the vowel *ū* here is for the purpose of specification, according to the rule *idayamūkāraḥ* (Pāṇini 6.1.89).

"It becomes a *samprasāraṇa*. From where is this specific term *samprasāraṇa* obtained? From the preceding rule (*pūrvasūtra*), due to the continued application (*anuvṛtti*) of the word *samprasāraṇa*.

For what purpose, then, is *samprasāraṇa* restated? It is for the sake of restricting the substituend (*sthānin*). If this were not restated, it would have to occur only in place of a *yaṇ*, as in the case of *praṣṭhauhaḥ*.
While the rule *praṣṭhaṃ vahati* (Pāṇini 3.2.62) is being carried over, the suffix *ṇvi* is applied by the rule *vahaśca* (Pāṇini 3.2.64).

Now, for what purpose is the augment *ūṭh* inserted? The intention is that the sūtra should simply be formulated as *vāha*. [The objection is: "Once the *samprasāraṇa* has already been performed... [the augment would be unnecessary].
From the preceding rule? Because the mention of *samprasāraṇa* continues [from that rule].
[The phrase] "and in the case of *guṇa*" is connected with the word "when it has been formed" (*kṛte*).

Even though the suffix *ṇvu* has been elided by [Pāṇini 7.3.86], the *guṇa* substitution occurs by virtue of the *pratyayalakṣaṇa* rule (the rule that the effect of a suffix persists even after it is elided).

Now, one might object: "According to the principle *aṅgavṛtte punaraṅgavṛttāvavidhiḥ niṣṭhitasya* (Vyākaraṇa-paribhāṣā 38), once the *samprasāraṇa* has taken place, the *guṇa* should not occur because the word-form is already established (*niṣṭhita*). [The reply is: There is no fault here, because of the explicit statement [*niṣṭhitasya*]. This very statement serves as an exception to the aforementioned paribhāṣā.
For the "completion" (niṣṭhā) of a word is its finality, and that occurs only when the word becomes fit for usage.
And as long as the grammatical refinement (*saṃskāra*) of the *guṇa* and so forth has not been performed, it does not become fit for usage.
Therefore, even though the *samprasāraṇa* has already taken place, the *guṇa* substitution certainly occurs; in this regard, it might be argued as follows:

If [the suffix] ūḍ were not applied, then forms such as *śālivahaḥ* (one who carries rice) and *dityūhaḥ* (a cart that carries a Diti) would not be established—since the suffix *ṇvi* is prescribed after the root *vah* when words like *śāli* and *diti*, which end in a vowel other than *a*, function as the upapada. Therefore, he says: "And when the upapada ends in a vowel other than *a*," and so forth.

By the rule *vahaca* [Pāṇini 3.2.64], because the term *chandas* (Vedic) is understood to carry over from the preceding rule [3.2.63], the suffix *ṇvi* is prescribed only for Vedic usage. In the Veda, rules are prescribed for observed purposes; thus, the suffix *ṇvi* is seen after the root *vah* only when the upapada (governing word) is *praṣṭha* and so on, which end in *a*, but not when the upapada is *śāli* and so on, which do not end in *a*. How, then, is the *paribhāṣā* (metarule) regarding "that which is external" (*bahiraṅga*) indicated by this? To this he says: "For in that case," and so forth.

Furthermore, the status of being *bahiraṅga* belongs to the *samprasāraṇa* (vocalization) because its operation depends upon the designation *bha*, which is caused by the subsequent suffixes such as *bāhu* and others.
The *guṇa* substitution, however, is internal (*antaraṅga*), because it applies before the suffix has been introduced.

What, then, is the purpose of making known this *paribhāṣā*? It is for the sake of establishing the correctness of forms such as *pacāvedam* and *yajāvedam*. Thus, the *aitva* (the substitution of *ai*) does not occur here by virtue of its being an internal rule, because the *guṇa* substitution is an external (*bahiraṅga*) rule.

The status of being "external" (bahiranga) belongs to [the substitution of] *ai* because it depends upon two words; however, the status of being "internal" (antaranga) belongs to [the substitution of] *i*, due to the opposite being the case. In the form *yūnaḥ*, once the semivowel-vocalization (*samprasāraṇa*) has been performed and the substitution of the preceding vowel with the following one (*parapūrvatva*) has occurred, there is the application of the long vowel by class (*savarṇadīrghatva*).
In the word *śauvam*,
there is the elision of the *ṭi* suffix by [Pāṇini 6.4.144].
In the word *yauvanam*, [the same applies].

In the case of *yūno bhāvaḥ*, the suffix *aṇ* is applied by [Pāṇini 5.1.130]. Due to the preservation of the original stem form (*prakṛtibhāva*) by [Pāṇini 6.4.167], the elision of the final syllable (*ṭilopa*) and the elision of the penultimate vowel (*allopa*) by [Pāṇini 6.4.143] do not occur.

Regarding *māghavanam*—derived from *maghavā devatā asya*—the suffix *aṇ* is applied by [Pāṇini 4.2.24], and the preservation of the original stem form occurs as before. To derive *śauvam*, he says: "The modification of a dog," and so forth.

Even for the word *yuva*, which ends in the suffix *ti*, the substitution of *samprasāraṇa* would apply because of the rule "when a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) is mentioned, that which is qualified by gender is also included" (Vyāḍiparibhāṣā 29).
