Furthermore, even for *madhavan*, once the replacement of *tri* has been made, the [substitution] would apply to that which ends in *t* as well, according to the principle "that which is modified in one part is not different from the original" (Vyāḍiparibhāṣā 16). Why, then, does this not occur? To this he says: "of those beginning with *āt*" and so forth.
Regarding the phrase "for that purpose":
this is so that [the rule] may apply only to those ending in *n*, and not to those not ending in *a*.
As for the statement "the word *ana* is the remainder for both," [it means that *ana* applies to both cases].

Since the term *ana* is a remainder (*śeṣa*) and a constituent part (*avayava*) of both [the suffixes] *yañ* and *aṇ*, there is no extension (*atideśa*) of the *samprasāraṇa* remainder by means of *ana*. This statement is for the purpose that the elision of *al* (*al-lopa`) should not be prevented by the status of being the original base (*prakṛtibhāva*) according to [Pāṇini 6.4.167] *an*. [Examples:
*aukṣṇaḥ*, *tākṣṇaḥ*. From the words *ukṣan* and *takṣan*, the suffix *aṇ* is applied in the sense of offspring (*apatya*).

Regarding *bhrauṇādhnaḥ*: "one who has killed a *bhrūṇa*" (an embryo). By the rule *brāhṛbhrūṇavṛtreṣu hanaḥ* [Pāṇini 3.2.87], which is the rule *brāhṛbhrūṇavṛtreṣu kvip*, the suffix *kvip* is applied; from that form ending in *kvip*, the suffix *aṇ* is added by [Pāṇini 7.3.54], resulting in the substitution of *ku* for *han*. Regarding *dhārtarājñaḥ*: [it is formed similarly].
From the bahuvrīhi compound *ghṛtarājaśabda*, [the suffix] *aṇ* is applied;
thus we have *sāmanaḥ* and *vaimanaḥ*.
According to [Pāṇini 4.3.120], the suffix *aṇ* is applied, yet [the commentator notes that] "neither of these two occurs."
Because the preservation of the original form (*prakṛtibhāva*) is prescribed with reference to both *allopa* (the elision of *a*) and *atilopa* (the elision of *i*).
For example, in the word *tākṣṇyaḥ*:

when the suffix *ṇya* is applied by the rule *kurvādibhyo ṇyaḥ* [Pāṇini 4.1.151], the suffix *ṇya* is added because it is characterized by the presence of the word *senānta* [by the rule *senāntalakṣaṇakāribhyaśca* 4.1.152], and then the preservation of the original form occurs by the rule *na karmavyatihāre* [6.4.168]. Furthermore, regarding the word *śīśabda*.
This indicates that the term *śas* prescribed by [Pāṇini 7.1.19] is what is being referred to here, and not the term *śi* prescribed by [Pāṇini 7.1.20].
How, then, is this known? Because the designation *bha* does not apply to the term *śi*. [The example is] *pratidīvnā*; the lengthening is according to [Pāṇini 8.2.77]: *hali ca*.

Now, for what purpose is the inclusion of the word *anta* (end)? Why not simply say *damaḥ*? Since a rule involving a specific combination of the letters *va* and *ma* would result in a *tadantavidhi* (application of a rule to that which ends with those letters) even without the inclusion of *anta*, would the *tadantavidhi* not be obtained anyway? This is true; however, the inclusion of *anta* is for the sake of clarity. [The statement] "the term *ac* is taken as the root *añc* with its nasal *n* elided"—from where is this known? Why is it not taken as a *pratyāhāra* (a technical abbreviation)? It cannot be taken as a *pratyāhāra* because of the continued application (*anuvṛtti*) of [the rule] *allopaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.4.134).

If there were the inclusion of a *pratyāhāra* (abbreviated term), then [the vowel] *a* would be qualified by it; and in that case, the inclusion of the *pratyāhāra* would be purposeless, for the vowel *a* never deviates from being a vowel (*ac*). But is it not the case that "stem" (*aṅga*) is the subject under discussion (*prakṛta*), and that is what is qualified by the *pratyāhāra*, such that [the meaning would be] "of a stem ending in a vowel"? No; if that were so, the meaning of the rule would be: "there is elision of *l* of a stem ending in a vowel."
And thus, the elision [prescribed] by *tathā ca* (Pāṇini 6.4.148) would be purposeless, since the result is already established by this very rule.
Furthermore, the citation beginning with *api ca* (Pāṇini 4.2.101) serves as an indicative mark (*liṅga*) here that there is no inclusion of a *pratyāhāra*.
For if there were an inclusion of a *pratyāhāra*, the mention of *añceḥ* here would not occur, because this member (*aṅga*) does not end in the vowel *a*.

Precisely because of this indication, even the suffix *ac* (of the *pacādi* class) is not accepted [as the relevant element]. For this [form] "dadhīcaḥ" does not have an *aṅga* (stem) ending in *ac*. Thus, "dadhīcaḥ."
In *dadhyañcati*, the suffix *kvin* is applied by [Pāṇini 3.2.59], and the nasal is elided by [Pāṇini 6.4.24]; the lengthening occurs by [Pāṇini 6.3.137]. Regarding *kīlālapaḥ*:
since *vic* was already applicable by [Pāṇini 3.2.73], *vic* is applied by [Pāṇini 3.2.74]. Regarding *niyeḥ*.

Regarding *kvip*: [the substitution of] *iyaṅ* [occurs]. This designation *āṅ* was established by the ancient teachers for the singular instrumental case ending. [The rule] "it is seen elsewhere than after *āṅ*" is understood from the mention of the plural "in mantras."

By the use of the plural number, this meaning is indicated: that this reference has many objects. And it becomes one with many objects only if *āṅ* occurs elsewhere as well, and not otherwise—as in the example "ātmānyāsamañjasam."
In the singular of the seventh case (locative). Here, there is elision of the initial [vowel]. The inclusion of the word "initial" (*ādi*) is for the sake of what follows.

But here, due to the recurrence (*anuvṛtti*) from the preceding sūtra of the word "ātaḥ" [Pāṇini 6.4.140], it can be understood—even without the mention of the word "ādi"—that the elision of the initial [vowel] alone occurs. Regarding the form *viṃśakaḥ*:

by the rule *viṃśatitriṃśadbhyāṃ ḍvunasaṃjñāyām* [Pāṇini 5.1.24], the suffix *ḍvun* is applied; when the syllable *ti* is elided, the substitution of the subsequent form (*pararūpa*) applies by the rule *ato guṇe* [Pāṇini 6.1.97]. Regarding the phrase *viṃśaṃ śatam*: [this is formed in the same manner].
Because twenty is added to this, the suffix *ḍa* is applied according to [Pāṇini 5.2.46]: *śad-antar-viṃśateś-ca*.
Thus we have *viṃśaḥ* and *ekaviṃśaḥ*.
To denote the ordinal position of that, the suffix *ḍaṭ* is applied according to [Pāṇini 5.1.47].

The inclusion of the word *ti* (the suffix *ti*) is for the purpose of preventing [the application of the suffix] to *anatya*. For example, in the case of *kumudvān* and so forth, the suffix *ḍmatup* is applied according to Pāṇini 4.2.86: "After *kumuda*, *naḍa*, and *vetasa*, the suffix *ḍmatup* is used in the four senses.
In the case of *upasarajaḥ*: [the suffix is applied].
Similarly, in the case of *mandurajaḥ* as well,
the shortening of the first member occurs by [Pāṇini 6.3.63].
As for *tiṃraśakaḥ*:

As before? [The suffix] *ḍvun*. But surely, since the rule *bhasya* [Pāṇini 6.4.129] continues to apply, and since the designation *bha* does not apply to what precedes when the suffix *ḍmatup* or the suffix *ḍa* is prescribed after a verbal root—because both [suffixes] do not begin with a vowel (*aj-*) and because they are not *asva* (containing *s*), as appropriate—how then can there be elision (*lopa*) here? To this he says: "*ḍityabhasyāpi*" and so forth.
If the elision of *ṭi* were not to occur, then the fact that [the suffix] is marked with *ḍ* would be purposeless.

Now, why is it not understood in this way? If that were so, then the mention of the root *jan* after the rule [Pāṇini 6.4.48]—which prescribes the elision of the *ṭi* suffix—would be untenable. Therefore, from this very mention, it is concluded that the letter *ḍ* of the verbal suffix (*pratyaya*) receives the designation *it*. And if that designation did not exist, and the elision of the *ṭi* were not to occur, then that designation would be rendered purposeless.

If there were no elision of the letter *ḍ* even in the case of the suffix *ḍmatup*, then the designation of that [name] would not be understood by means of that which ends in it; and in that context, the rule [Pāṇini 4.2.67] applies.

Therefore, in that case as well, the letter *ḍ* must necessarily have the technical designation *it*, and by virtue of that, there is elision of the *ṭi* (the final vowel and following consonants) due to its power. Thus: "Sātvataḥ"—[this is derived from] "the offspring of Satvata," with the suffix *aṇ*.
"‘The elision of the *ṭi* of *anta*’ and so forth.
But what is the reason that [the desired form] is not established, such that an additional rule (*upasaṃkhyāna*) must be made? To this he says: "In this case, those which end in *in*" and so forth.
As for those ending in *an*, the status of the base (*prakṛtibhāva*) is obtained by the rule *an* [[Pāṇini 6.4.167]]; thus, the connection is with what has been previously stated.
The term *sābrāhmacārī* is formed with the suffix *aṇ* according to [Pāṇini 4.3.120].
The term *pīṭhasarpiṇaḥ* is likewise formed.
The word "these" (imaḥ) is connected with what precedes. Regarding "Paiṭhasarpāḥ," the suffix *aṇ* is applied by [Pāṇini 4.3.120].
Regarding the term "pīṭhasarpiṇaḥ," it is connected with the subject at hand by the word "ima" (these). [The variant] "paiṭhasarpāḥ" [is also used].

As before, regarding the term *kālāpāḥ*: since the sense has already been explained as before, the suffix *ṇini* would have applied by [Pāṇini 4.3.104], *kalāpivaiśamyāyanāntevāsibhyaśca*, because they are pupils of Vaiśampāyana; however, this is set aside by that exception [4.3.108]. Then, by [4.2.59], the suffix *aṇ* is applied, which by [4.2.64] undergoes elision (*luk*), and by [4.2.66], it is restricted to the sense of those who study or know [the text].

Regarding the term *kauthumāḥ*: [the suffix] *aṇ* is applied according to [Pāṇini 4.3.120]. [The phrase] "the treatise composed by them is [called so] by metaphorical designation" (*tatkṛto grantha upacārāt*), and so forth, [is used].
However, since that [usage] is produced by metaphorical designation (*upacāra*), there is no restrictive basis for it here.
For when something is produced by metaphorical designation, such a designation occurs, as in: "All this ancient karma, whether auspicious or inauspicious, is experienced.

Now, why is metaphorical designation resorted to, rather than simply forming a *taddhita* suffix when there is a desire to express a secondary meaning (*śaiṣika-artha*) such as "in this" (*atra*) and so forth? To this he says: "In the case of secondary meanings," and so on.

The words *taitili* and *jājali* are designated as *vṛddha* (possessing a long vowel in the first syllable); because they are *vṛddha*, the suffix *cha*—which is prescribed for secondary derivatives (*śaiṣika*) by the rule "after those [words] that are *vṛddha*" (Pāṇini 4.2.114)—would apply. If that were the case, the forms *taitilāḥ* and *jājalāḥ* would not be established. Therefore, so that this fault does not occur, the usage of the term *upacāra* (metaphorical designation) is resorted to. By the word "thus" (*evam*), he demonstrates the previously mentioned etymological derivation in order to preclude the application of the suffix *cha*.

The etymology of the word *lāṅgali* should be understood in the same way: the teacher is *Lāṅgali*, and by metaphorical designation, the treatise composed by him is also called *lāṅgala*. Thus, [the plural] "the *lāṅgalas*" [is used].
In all three examples beginning with *śikhaṇḍaḥ*, the suffix *aṇ* [is applied] by [Pāṇini 4.3.120].
As for *āśmaḥ*,
here too the suffix *aṇ* [is applied] by [Pāṇini 4.3.134].

Regarding "other than *āśmana*": here too, by virtue of the rule [Pāṇini 4.3.120], when there is the expression of meaning, [the suffix] applies; likewise, in the case of *cārma*, by that same rule [4.3.120], only the suffix *aṇ* is applied. Thus: "other than *carman*."
"A modification of leather" (*carmaṇo vikāraḥ*). Regarding "belonging to a dog" (*śauvaḥ*), the augment *ai* is applied by [Pāṇini 7.3.4]:
"And in the case of *dvāra* and so forth."

Since *sāyamprātika* and similar forms are not recited among the *prātipadika*s (nominal stems), he asks: "What, then, are *sāyamprātika* and the others? By the phrase "types of *sāyamprātika*," he shows that the word *ādi* (and so forth) expresses the sense of "type" (*prakāra*). But surely, by the rule *sāyañciram* [Pāṇini 4.3.23], there ought to be the suffixes *ṭa* and *ṭyaL* after indeclinables; how then can there be the suffix *ṭhañ*? To this he says: "*ṭa* and *ṭyaL* are not desired," because such forms are not established by usage (*anabhidhānāt*).
And here, throughout [the following rules], the meaning is the establishment of the term *upasaṃkhyāna* (supplementary addition).

In this regard, the establishment is as follows: from the sūtra beginning with *mantra-ṣu* (Pāṇini 6.4.141), the mention of *ādi-* (beginning with) is carried over (*anuvartate*), and the mention of *taddhita-* (secondary suffix) has been made for this very purpose.
When that is carried over, the meaning becomes: "The elision of *ṭi* occurs after words ending in *nām*, etc., when a *taddhita* suffix follows."
By the word "and so forth" (ādi), [terms such as] *sāyamprātika* and others are included;
thus, the elision of the *ṭi* suffix is established in all such cases.
[The objection is: "In examples such as these, the elision of the *ṭi* is not observed."
By this [sūtra], he demonstrates that words such as *ārātīya* and others do not possess the suffix *yat*.

Now, regarding the word *śāāta*, how is the suffix *aṇ* applied, given that by the rule *kālaṭṭhañ* [Pāṇini 4.3.11], the suffix *ṭhañ* ought to occur? This is not so; in the rule *kālaṭṭhañ* [4.3.11], a *yogavibhāga* (splitting of the rule) must be made as *kālāt*. By this, the suffix *aṇ* occurs after the word *śāā* according to the prescribed application. Nor is the suffix *ṭhañ* barred by the *yogavibhāga*; for there is the irregular formation (*nipātana*) in the rule *yeṣāñca virodhaḥ śāātikaḥ* [Pāṇini 2.4.9].
Therefore, the suffix *ṭhañ* also occurs in this case.

However, the suffixes *ṭau* and *ṭaulau* are not desired after the word *śāta*, precisely because of the lack of conventional usage (*anabhidhāna*). Now, why does the substitution of *ka* for *ṭhañ*—by the rule "after [stems ending in] *iṣ*, *uṣ*, *uk*, and *t*, there is *ka*" (Pāṇini 7.3.51)—not occur in the form *śātikaḥ*? It is precisely because of this very [absence of the desired form in the] grammatical instruction. [The example] *dvyahaḥ* [is as follows].

The compound is formed by [Pāṇini 2.1.51], and the suffix *ṭac* is added as a compound-final element (samāsānta) by [Pāṇini 5.4.91]: "After *rājan*, *ahan*, and *sakhi*, the suffix *ṭac* [is applied].

Here, the substitution of *ahna-* for *ahan* would have been required by [Pāṇini 5.4.88]: "For *ahan*, [the substitute] *ahna-* [occurs] after these [words]," but that does not take place because of the prohibition [in Pāṇini 5.4.89].
Thus, we have *dvyahīnaḥ*.

While the rule *taddhitārthe 'samāyāḥ* [Pāṇini 5.1.84] is in effect, [the suffix] *kha* is applied by [the rule] *ahnaḥ khaḥ* [Pāṇini 5.1.87]. But why is the suffix *kha* used here in the word *ahīna*? To this he says: "The suffix *kha* should be stated for the collective sense of *ahan*. Now, since *ahan* ends in the letter *n*, the elision of the *ṭi* portion would be established by the preceding rule alone; so what is the purpose of this new beginning? To this he says: "Since [it is] already established," and so forth.
Regarding the term *āhnikam*:
the suffix *ṭhak* is applied according to the rule for the secondary suffix *ārhīya*.

If this rule were commenced for the purpose of restriction (*niyama*) when [the desired form] is already established, then the inclusion of the word *eva* would be redundant; for even without it, it would be understood that an operation commenced when something is already established serves the purpose of restriction. To this he says: "The use of the particle *eva* is for the sake of clarity."

Now, in order to dispel the suspicion that there might be a reversed restriction, he asks: "Why does it not occur? and says: "Of the day itself," and so forth. If there were a reversed restriction such as "only after *ahn* [comes] *ṭa* and *kha*," then in that case, there would be no possibility at all for the elision of the *ṭi* [portion] in another [word] before *kha*. The intention is that the rule prescribing the status of being like the original base (*prakṛtivadbhāva*) in "ātmādhvāno khe" (Pāṇini 6.4.169) would be rendered useless. [The example is] "bābhraṣyaḥ."

In the case of *māṇḍavyaḥ*, the suffix *yañ* is applied after the word *babhru* in the sense of offspring, according to [Pāṇini 4.1.106]: *madhubabhvror brāhmaṇakauśikayoḥ*. Here too, it is due to its inclusion in the *gargādi* group.
By [Pāṇini 6.1.79],
there is the substitution of *ava*; in examples such as *śaṅkavya*, by [Pāṇini 5.1.5] in this sense,
and by [Pāṇini 5.1.2], we have *aupagavaḥ* and *kāpaṭavaḥ*.
Here too, the suffix *aṇ* is used in the sense of offspring;
since it is a *taddhita* suffix, the feminine suffix *ṅīṣ* is applied by the rule "after a word ending in *u* that denotes a quality" (*voto guṇavacanāt*, Pāṇini 4.1.44), resulting in *paṭvī*.
Regarding the statement "it should have been said 'from *u* to *o*" (*orot*), and so forth.
The intention is that by speaking thus, the sūtra becomes concise.

Regarding the term "svāyambhuva": from the root *bhū* with the prefix *svayam*, the suffix *kvip* is applied to form *svayambhū*; then, the suffix *aṇ* is added in the sense of "proceeded from" (*ita*) to *svayambhū*.

Because a grammatical operation (*vidhi*) preceded by a specific technical name (*saṃjñā*) is not invariably applied, the *guṇa* substitution does not occur here; and since that is absent, only the *uvaṅ* substitution is performed—as in *kāmaṇḍaleyaḥ* and *śaitabāheyaḥ*, [formed] by the suffix *ḍhañ* according to [Pāṇini 4.1.135]. The same applies in the case of *jāmbeyaḥ*.

Regarding "Mādrabāheya": from the word *madrabāhu*, by the rule *bāhv-antāt saṃjñāyām* [Pāṇini 4.1.67], the suffix *ūṅ* is applied; from that which ends in this [suffix], [the suffix *ḍhak* is added] by [Pāṇini 4.1.120]. Regarding "Kādraveya": [it is formed similarly].

[Is this] from [the word] *kadrūka-māṇḍūka* by means of the suffix *ūṅ* according to Pāṇini 4.1.71–72 (*kadrūkamaṇḍalvośchandasi saṃjñāyām*), and then the suffix *ḍhak* as before? In this regard, does this refer to the inclusion of the letter *y*, or to the vowels *i* and *u*? Here, if this were an inclusion of the letter *y*, one would not have to repeat the mention of *ya* in the subsequent sūtra; for that very [term] would carry over there by anuvṛtti. Therefore, this is an inclusion of the vowels *i* and *u*.

In this context, since the mention of the *varṇa* (vowel) applies the rule of "that which ends with it" (*tadantavidhi*) everywhere, the rule of "ending in that" is understood; having kept this in mind, he says: "of that which ends in *i-varṇa* or *u-varṇa*" and so forth. [The examples] are *dākṣī* and *plākṣī*.
From the words *dākṣi* and *plākṣi*, the suffix *ṅīṣ* is applied by [Pāṇini 4.1.65].

In the case of *sakhī* as well, [the form is established] by the irregular derivation (*nipātana*) [Pāṇini 4.1.62]: "In the common language, [the word] *sakhi* [is used in the sense of] friends. Now, one might ask: "Is this not already established here even by the rule for long vowels of the same class (*savarṇadīrgha*)? Why, then, is elision (*lopa*) prescribed here? To this, he says: "For, if there were the long vowel of the same class," and so forth. [The analysis is as follows:

"She has surpassed her friend" (*atikrāntā sakhīm enām*) forms a *bahuvrīhi* compound according to the Vārttika "After prepositions, [there is elision] of that which is derived from a verbal root" (Vārttika 101), along with the elision of the final member of the compound and the shortening of the *upasarjana*.

In that case, if the rule for lengthening by homogeneity (*savarṇadīrghatva*) were applied instead of elision (*lopa*), then the single substitute for the *ī* of *sakhi* and the *ā* of *kāra* would, by the principle of "behaving like the final" (*antavadbhāva*), be subject to the prohibition of the designation *ghi* by the rule *śeṣo dhyasakhi* [Pāṇini 1.4.7]. Consequently, in the form *atisakheḥ āgacchati*, the *guṇa* substitution required by *ghe ṅiti* [Pāṇini 7.3.111] would not occur. Even though the resulting form would be indistinguishable from the one with elision once the shortening of the secondary member (*upasarjana*) has taken place, it would nevertheless be considered derivative (*lākṣaṇika*).
Therefore, by the paribhāṣā "that which is taught by its specific technical definition" (vyā|pa|3), that [suffix] is not taken; thus, the prohibition does not apply.
Consequently, only elision (lopa) should be performed.
In the three examples beginning with *dauleyaḥ*, the suffix *ḍhak* is applied in the sense of offspring according to [Pāṇini 4.1.122]: *itaśṭacāniñaḥ*.
In the case of "kumārī," the suffix *ṅīp* is applied by [Pāṇini 4.1.20].
In the case of "gaurī," [the same applies].
The suffix *ṅīṣ* is applied by [Pāṇini 4.1.41],
resulting in "Śāṅgaravī. The suffix *ṅīn* is applied by [Pāṇini 4.1.73] to the *aṇ* suffix following "Śāṅgarava" and others.
"Bālākiḥ saumitriḥ": [the suffix] *iñ* is applied after *bālaka* and *sumitrā* because they belong to the *bahv-ādi* group. "In the rule beginning with 'yasya'... [and so forth].
By the word "ādi" (and so forth), the subsequent rule is included.

"Vaktavyaḥ" means it should be explained. In this regard, the explanation is as follows: from the sūtra [Pāṇini 6.4.136], the term *vibhāṣā* (optionally) is carried over by the maxim of the frog-leap (*maṇḍūkapluti*), and that is a restricted option (*vyavasthitavibhāṣā*).
By this rule (*sūtra*) and by the subsequent rule (*sūtra*), both [the operations] are prohibited;

thus, in the forms *kāṇḍe* and *kuḍye*, according to *auṅa āpaḥ* [Pāṇini 7.1.18] and *śī* [Pāṇini 7.1.19], there is the substitution of *śī*. In that case, the elision of the vowel *a* (as prescribed by *yasyeti ca*) would apply.

Regarding the word *saurye*: by the rule [Pāṇini 4.3.112], the suffix *aṇ* is added to the word *sūrya*; from that form ending in *aṇ*, the substitution of *śī* occurs for the case-ending *auṅ*. In that situation, the elision of the vowel *ā* would apply by this [present] rule, and the elision of the consonant *y* would apply by the subsequent rule. [This is addressed by the rule] beginning with *iyaṅvaṅbhyām*.

The scope for *iyaṅ* and *uvaṅ* is, for example, *śriyau*, *śriyaḥ*, *bhrūvau*, *bhravaḥ*; the scope for elision (*lopa*) is, for example, *kāmaṇḍaleyaḥ*, *mādrabāheyaḥ*. In the case of *vātsapreyaḥ* and *laikhābhreyaḥ*, both [rules] would apply, and by the principle of conflict (*vipratiṣedha*), elision takes place.

[The word] *vatsaprīḥ* ends in the suffix *kvip*. If, in this context, the term *bha* were to qualify *sūrya* and the others—meaning "of *sūrya* and so on when they bear the designation *bha*"—then in forms such as *saurī* and *balākā*, elision would not occur.

For the word *sūrya* here is not designated as *bha*; what then? Having established in the mind that it is another distinct word ending in *-an*, [the author] shows that the letter *y*—whose difference in form has not been relied upon—is specified by its relations with the related words such as *sūrya* through elision (*lopa*). Thus he says: "of these, namely *sūrya*, *ati*, *vyāghra*, *agastya*, and *matsya*," and so forth.
"Of the *bha*" means:
of that which bears the designation *bha*.
There is elision of a *yakāra* that serves as a penultimate (*upadhā*) provided that this *yakāra* belongs to the group beginning with *sūrya*—this is the intended meaning here.
However, those words beginning with *sūrya* are not qualified by being in the *bha*-state.
Therefore, even when they do not bear the technical designation of *bha*, there is still elision of that penultimate *yakāra*, provided that this *yakāra* belongs to the group beginning with *sūrya*.

"Regarding the statement *saurī balākā*: is it not the case that here, because the elision of the vowel *ā* depends on two different bases (*vyāśrayatvena*), it is not considered *asiddha*, and thus it has been stated that the penultimate (*upadhā*) is not the vowel *i*? To this he says: "The elision of *ya* when *aṇ* follows," and so forth.
For in this instance, there are two instances of the elision of *ya*: one occurs when *aṇ* follows, and the other occurs when the vowel *ī* follows.

In this regard, the first [case] depends on different bases (*vyāśraya*); for instance, elision (*lopa*) occurs depending on the *aṇ*, whereas the elision of *y* (*yalopa*) depends on the vowel *ī*. Therefore, because they depend on different bases, it is correct that the former is not considered "unestablished" (*asiddha*) with respect to the latter. The other, however, occurs depending on the vowel *ī* alone; thus, since they share the same basis (*samānāśraya*), the former is indeed "unestablished," and consequently the penultimate vowel (*upadhā*) remains as *i*. He demonstrates the meaning of the rule, beginning with "of a *bha*-stem ending in *aṇ*," through the examples.
Regarding "taiṣam, taiṣī":
[the suffix] *aṇ* is applied by [Pāṇini 4.2.3], and *ṅīp* is applied by [Pāṇini 4.1.15].
[The phrase] "when *aṇ* has been applied due to [his] being a seer (*ṛṣi*)" means:
By the rule *ṛṣy-andhaka-* [Pāṇini 4.1.114] and others, we have *matsyacarī*.

[The word *matsya*] was previously a fish; thus, by [the rule] *pūrvapadāt saṃjñāyām agaḥ* [Pāṇini 5.3.53], the suffix *ṅīp* is applied as before. Here, the letter *y* is related to the word *matsya*, which bears the technical designation *bha*; however, since this *y* is not an *upadhā* (penultimate vowel) of that which bears the *bha* designation, the elision [of the penultimate vowel] does not take effect.

Now, for what purpose is the mention of *ya* (the letter *y*), since even without the mention of *ya*, the elision of the *y* that has become an *upadhā* would be understood when the *upadhā* is specified by means of the sun (*sūrya*) and so forth? For indeed, among those [words], the *y* itself is the *upadhā*, not any other phoneme. To this he says: "The mention of *ya* is for the sake of what follows. The meaning is that it "should be stated," i.e., it must be explained. This explanation here also should be made by resorting to the option (*vibhāṣā*) as was done previously.
In the case of *mātsyam*, the suffix *aṇ* is applied according to [Pāṇini 4.3.120]. In the case of *saurīyam*, [the suffix *cha* is applied].
From *aṇanta* [ending in the suffix *aṇ*]? Thus: *āgastīyam*, *sauryam*.
From *sūrya* and *devatā*, [the form] *sauri* is derived by the rule *tasya devatā* (Pāṇini 4.2.23), which prescribes the suffix *aṇ*.
From *agastya*, [the form] *āgastyaḥ* is derived; here, the suffix *ṛṣyaṇ* is applied in the sense of "offspring" (*apatya*).

Regarding the term "nakṣatrāṇi": it means that which possesses a connection with the nakṣatras (asterisms). Regarding the phrase "of the word beginning with the letter 'ka'": [it refers to the word *kṛttikā*].
The meaning is "of the letter *ka* and the letter *a*.

Regarding the phrase "and [the rule for] initial acute accent": since the final syllable would have been acute by the accent of the suffix (*pratyayasvara*), this statement is made to ensure that the initial syllable is acute.
The word "antitaḥ" [is formed] with the suffix *tasi* according to [Pāṇini 5.4.45];
[the form] "tādeśca" [is derived from Pāṇini 6.2.173].
The meaning is "of the word *tika*"; by the word "and" (*ca*), [it includes] *kā* as well.
Thus: "*antamaḥ*."
The suffix *tamap* is used in the sense of superlative (*atiśāyana*) according to Pāṇini 5.3.55.
Regarding the form *antiṣat*,
the suffix *kvip* is applied by the rule beginning with 3.2.61 (*satsūdviṣa*).
Regarding the phrase "and those which":
it is connected with the word "are seen" from the preceding context.
Regarding the word "the last": [it refers to the final cognition].
Whether [the suffix] *ya* is applied by rule 4.4.110 or by rule 4.4.98,

some maintain that all rules prescribing elision apply only in the Vedic language (*chandas*). This is because the term "secondary derivative" (*taddhita*) is understood to have ceased its application,
as indicated by the inclusion of the word "secondary derivative" in the subsequent sūtra.
Therefore, this is the rule: "it is indeed so. Regarding "Gārgī" and so forth:
from words such as *Garga* ending in *yañ*, the suffix *ṅīp* is applied by the rule *yañaśca* [Pāṇini 4.1.16].
Regarding "kārikeyī":
[it is formed] from that which ends in [the suffix *ka*], by the rule *ṭiṅḍhāṇañ* [Pāṇini 4.1.15], the feminine suffix *ṅīp* is applied.
Regarding "vaidhī": [it is formed] in the same manner.

The suffix *ṅīṣ* is applied by [Pāṇini 4.1.48]. Regarding the form *gārgakam*: the suffix *vuñ* is added to the word *gārgya* by [Pāṇini 4.2.39] et seq., whereby the *yañ* suffix is elided. Regarding the form *sāṅkākhyakaḥ*.
Regarding the term *kāmpilyaka*:

as before, from the words *saṅkāśa* and *kampila*, the suffix *ṇya* is applied by [Pāṇini 4.2.79] *duñ-chaṇ-...*, etc.; then, from that which ends in *ṇya*, the suffix *vuñ* is applied in the sense of a secondary derivative (*śaiṣika*) such as "born there" and so forth, by [Pāṇini 4.2.121].

Now, for what purpose is the mention of *taddhita* (secondary suffix) [in the rule]? Will the mention of *taddhita* not continue to apply here by [Pāṇini 6.4.144]? To this he says: "The mention of *taddhita*, etc."

In the case of *somī devatāsyeti*, the suffix *ṅīp* is applied by [Pāṇini 4.1.15] *ṭiṅḍhāṇañ*. In that context, the mention of *taddhita* is for the purpose that the elision of the *y* of the non-patronymic [suffix] should occur according to [Pāṇini 6.4.150] *parato'napatyayakārasyāpi*. Otherwise, if that same *taddhita* mentioned in the previous context were to be carried over (*anuvarteta*) here, then the mention of *īd* connected with it would also be carried over.
And thus, both being carried over here, they would also be carried over into the preceding rule.

And thus, since [the result] is already established by the previous rule alone, this present undertaking must be for the purpose of restriction (*niyamārtha*) regarding both cases: namely, that the elision (*lopa*) occurs only when the secondary derivative suffix (*taddhita*) begins with *ī* or *ti*, and only when it is not a patronymic (*anapatya*), as well as when it is a patronymic. In this way, just as there will be no elision in the case of a non-patronymic such as *sāṅkaśyaka*, so too there would be none in the case of *saumī iṣṭiḥ*; for [the elision] has been excluded by the restriction.
However, when the term "secondary derivative" (*taddhita*) is included here, it is declared that the inclusion of "secondary derivative" in the preceding rule is hereby withdrawn.
By that same rule (*parvayoga*), the elision (*lopa*) of the *yakāra* of a *taddhita* suffix—whether it denotes non-descendance or descendance—is prescribed without distinction.

The mention of *taddhita* is for the purpose that the elision should also occur in cases such as *saumī iṣṭiḥ*. Now, if this restriction—that it is a *taddhita* in both instances—were to apply, then the purpose of the two rules would be rendered redundant.

One should formulate the rule as a single *yoga*: "After *hala*, [the suffix] *āpatya* is not elided. Why? Because by the force of commencing two separate *sūtras*, only one of them will be understood to carry over (*anuvṛtti*) here, but not both.

In this case, however, there might be this doubt: does the mention of *taddhita* carry over here, or the mention of *id*? Here too, it is the mention of *taddhita* that carries over, not the mention of *id*; because of the [traditional] commentary (*vyākhyāna*).
In cases of doubt, this principle applies: "The specific meaning is understood from the explanation; for there is no rule [that is not valid] because of doubt" (Puṣpikā-vṛtti 120).

And when the term *taddhita* is being carried over here alone, this restriction will apply only to the domain of *taddhita* suffixes, and not to the domain of *īd*. Thus, even if the term *taddhita* were not mentioned again here, since there would be no such restriction, the elision (*lopa*) is indeed established by the preceding rule even in the case of *saumī iṣṭiḥ*.

Why was this stated—that the mention of *taddhita* [in Pāṇini 6.4.151] is for the sake of elision even when there is no offspring? The intention should be understood as follows: this is stated so that the elision may be easily understood. Consequently, the meaning here becomes this: the mention of *taddhita* is for the purpose of avoiding complexity in comprehension. [The example is] *gāgryāyaṇaḥ*, [formed] by [the suffix] *phak* according to [Pāṇini 4.1.101].
Regarding the term *kārakeyi*:

it means "the offspring of a *kārikā*. From the rule *strībhyo ḍhak* [Pāṇini 4.1.120], we derive *kārikā + ḍhak*; then, for its offspring, from the rule *ata iñ* [Pāṇini 4.1.95], we derive *kārikeyi*. This undertaking is for the sake of something other than a *taddhita* suffix. The term *kya* is a general designation for both *kyac* and *kyaṅ*.
In the form *gārgīyati*, there is the substitution of *it* [for the final vowel] by [Pāṇini 3.1.8] and [7.4.33]. Thus,
we have *gārgīyaḥ*.

The suffix *kyaṅ* is applied by the rule *kartuḥ kyaṅ salopaśca* [Pāṇini 3.1.11], and the lengthening of the vowel occurs by the rule *akṛtsārvadhātukayoḥ* [Pāṇini 7.4.25]. Thus we have *gārgībhūtaḥ*. The suffix *cvi* is applied by the rule *abhūtatadbhāve* [Pāṇini 5.4.50], and the change to *i* occurs by the rule *cver dīrghaḥ* [Pāṇini 7.4.32]. Regarding the phrase *bilvakādibhyaḥ*: [the suffix *kan* is added].
The designation is by means of an adventitious form:
*bilvakīyā*.
Here, the suffix *cha* (forming *-īya*) is applied according to Pāṇini 4.2.90 and 4.2.91 as a *cāturarthika* suffix, with the augment *kuk*.

Regarding the term "bailvakāḥ": [the suffix] *aṇ* applies before the word *dīvyati* (Pāṇini 4.1.83). Now, what is the purpose of including the mention of *cha*, since the forms such as *bilvakī*—to which the augment *kuk* has been added—are already included, and the suffix *cha* can occur after them; thus, even without the mention of *cha*, the elision of *cha* itself ought to take place? To this, he says: "The mention of *cha*" and so forth.
If the mention of *cha* were not made, then by the *sanniyogaśiṣṭa* paribhāṣā (HA BHĀ 14), when the letter *cha* is withdrawn, there would be the withdrawal of *kuk* as well.
And this very mention of *cha* is the indicator (*jñāpaka*) for that paribhāṣā.
Now, for what purpose is the mention of *luk* [made], since the elision (*lopa*) is already prescribed in the context? To this he says: "The mention of *luk*, etc."
The inclusion of the letter *y* should be understood as an indicator for a portion [of the rule].

For that [letter *y*] is connected with the rule "there is elision of the penultimate" (*sa hi lopa upadhāyāḥ*); while that [rule] continues to apply, the rule "when *y* is the penultimate" (*ya upadhāyāḥ*) would also continue to apply, and once the substitution of *iy* has been made for *cha*, it would apply to the letter *y* alone.

Furthermore, even if the term "penultimate" (*upadhāyāḥ*) were not to continue to apply, [the substitution] would still apply to the vowel *i* alone by the rule "in place of the final element" (*alo 'ntyasya*).
Regarding the phrase "the mention of *luk*": *luk* is the technical term (*saṃjñā*) for the non-appearance of an entire suffix, and not for the non-appearance of a portion of a suffix.
When there is the mention of *luk*, the elision (*luk*) of the whole [suffix] is established.

For that *ratha* [is used] because of the inclusion of the elision (*luk*). As for "tuḥ," it is a general reference to both *tṛn* and *tṛc*, having set aside the distinctive indicatory letters (*anubandha*). As for "kariṣṭhaḥ."
The suffix *tṛn* is applied after a verbal root;
the suffix *iṣṭhan* is applied after that [form] to express excellence, and there is the elision of the word-element *tṛ*. Thus, "vijayiṣṭhaḥ" (most victorious).
The suffix *tṛn* is applied to the root *ji* preceded by the prefix *vi*;
thus, "vahiṣṭhaḥ.
Here too, the suffix *tṛn* is applied to the root *vah*.
The suffix *iṣṭhan* follows that [comparative suffix]; by the rule *ho ḍhaḥ* [Pāṇini 8.2.31], the substitution of *ḍha* for *ha* occurs.

When the elision (*lopa*) of the word *tṛ* is to be performed, [the former operation] is considered as not having taken effect (*asiddha*) according to [Pāṇini 6.4.22]. Therefore, only the preceding elision is carried out. Once that has been done, the substitution of *ḍha*, which is prescribed when a *jhal* sound follows or at the end of a word, does not take effect due to the absence of its cause. Thus we have *dohīyasī*.
The suffix *īyasun* is added after a word ending in *tṛc* [by Pāṇini 5.3.57], and by [Pāṇini 4.1.5] the feminine suffix *ṅīp* is applied.

Here too, when the elision (*lopa*) is to be performed, the rule "for a root beginning with *da*, *dha* is substituted" [Pāṇini 8.2.32] is also considered asiddha; therefore, the elision occurs first. When that has occurred, the substitution of *dha* does not take place as before. Now, why does this elision not apply to the final letter according to [Pāṇini 1.1.52]? To this he says: "of the whole," and so forth.
He states the reason for that very point with the words "of the final," and so forth.
If [the elision] were to apply to the final [sound], the statement would become redundant; for it would already be established by the rule "of the final *ṭi*.
Therefore, since there is no purpose in stating the elision of the final [sound], this statement is understood to have the purpose that the elision of the entire word *tṛ* should occur.

If, then, for the sake of eliding the sound *tṛ*, the rule for elision (*lu*) were simply prescribed immediately after [the suffix], then in that case, the elision of the entire suffix would be easily understood, since elision (*luk*) is prescribed as the non-appearance of a suffix. To this he says: "But as for this term ‘*luk*’," and so forth.
What, then, would be the fault in that case? To this he says: "For thus," and so forth.

If the term *luk* were to be carried over (*anuvartate*) here, then—on the principle that "the external elision (*luk*) subverts even internal rules" (Vyāḍipāda 128)—the elision would have to occur first. Consequently, there would be a prohibition of the designation of the element as a suffix (*pratyayalakṣaṇa*) by [Pāṇini 1.1.63]. As a result, in forms such as *kariṣṭhaḥ* and *vijayiṣṭhaḥ*, the *guṇa* substitution conditioned by an *ārdhadhātuka* suffix would not take place.
Therefore, so that this fault does not arise, the term *luk* is indeed carried over here.
Now, what is the purpose of mentioning the suffix *imanij*? For it is impossible for *imanij* to follow after the word *tṛ*.

Nevertheless, that [suffix] is prescribed by these two rules, [Pāṇini 5.1.122 and 5.1.123]; yet, is there nothing ending in the word *tṛ* [to which it applies]? It is not recited among the *pṛthv-ādi* or *dṛḍh-ādi* groups, nor is there any word denoting a phoneme [ending in *tṛ*]. Therefore, he says: "But the other two," and so forth; [and] "as if it were *iṣṭhan*."

The masculine form (*puṃvadbhāva*) has been stated for the suffix *iṣṭhan* [by Aṣṭādhyāyī 6.3.35]; the substitution of *ra* [for *ra*] occurs by [Aṣṭādhyāyī 6.4.161]; the elision of the final vowel (*ṭilopa*) occurs by [Aṣṭādhyāyī 6.4.143]; the elision of the subsequent sound beginning with *yaṇ* (the semivowel) and so forth, along with the *guṇa* substitution of the preceding sound, occurs by [Aṣṭādhyāyī 6.4.156]; the elision [of the suffix] occurs by [Aṣṭādhyāyī 5.3.65]; and the suffix *kan* occurs by [Aṣṭādhyāyī 5.3.64]. By [Aṣṭādhyāyī 6.4.157], the substitutes *pra* and so forth are applied. Just as these operations take place when *iṣṭhan* is present, so too should they occur when *ṇa* is present; therefore, one must state that "the operation of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) applies as if it were *iṣṭhavat* when *ṇa* follows."
The mention of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) could have been omitted, because no other [operation] could possibly be extended [to it].

Here, the suffix *vat* has the sense of "similarity"; therefore, since no operation other than that which is intended for the element following the superlative suffix *iṣṭhan* can be extended, the mention of the nominal stem need not be made for the purpose of excluding that [other operation]. Why then is it stated? It is stated for the sake of clarity.
Some, however, say that the mention of the *prātipadika* (nominal stem) need not be made for the purpose of preventing the extension (*atideśa*) of the operations of the suffix.

Why then is it done? It is done for the sake of clarity. Others, however, say that the mention of the *prātipadika* is for the purpose of preventing the extension of the operations of the suffix; therefore, in the case of *bahum ācaṣṭe* → *bahayati*, the suffix *ṇic* [prescribed by Pāṇini 3.1.25] does not occur [by virtue of the present rule]. This is incorrect; for in the rule *iṣṭhavad* [Pāṇini 6.4.157], the suffix *vat* is prescribed after a locative form, since a locative is heard in the word *ṇād* which serves as the correlate (*pratiyogin*).
What is prescribed for the *iṣṭhan* suffix is extended [to the present case], but not what is prescribed for the *iṣṭha* suffix as well.
Nor is it that whatever operation applies to the *yiṅ* suffix applies to the *iṣṭhan*; rather, it is only what applies to the *iṣṭhan* itself.
Since there is no possibility of its application here at all, what is the purpose of mentioning the "prātipadika" (nominal stem) in order to exclude it? [The example is] "enīm."

From this word [eta], by the rule "after a vowel that is anudātta and has t as its penultimate letter" (Pāṇini 4.1.39), the suffix ṅīṣ is applied and the letter t is replaced by n, resulting in *etā*. In the form *etayati*,
once the causative suffix ṇi is added, both the suffix ṅīṣ and the letter n are eliminated through the process of *puṃvadbhāva* (masculine-like substitution).

But surely, since the suffix *ṇi* is here separated by the suffix *ṅīṣ*, the extension (*atideśa*) of the property of being a *ṇit* would not apply when there is such an intervention? This is not a fault; for even in the case of the suffix *iṣṭhan*, the masculine form (*puṃvadbhāva*) of the nominal stem occurs precisely when there is intervention by the suffix *ṅīp*. Therefore, here too, despite the intervention, it will be exactly like that. [The form] *rūpaviṇam* is derived with the suffix *vini* according to [Pāṇini 5.2.121].
In the case of *ruājayati*, the *vṛddhi* substitution does not occur because of the rule "A rule conditioned by a technical designation (*saṃjñā*) is not universally obligatory" (Vyāḍi-Patañjali 64).

Furthermore, according to the principle "When a grammatical operation has already taken effect on a base (*aṅga*), another operation on that same base does not apply to what is already established" (Vyāḍi-Patañjali 38), [the *vṛddhi* would not apply];
however, in forms such as *prāpayati*, it does indeed occur because the [base] is not yet established [as a completed form].

In this context, the suffix *puk* is applied by the rule *artihro* [Pāṇini 7.3.36]. Now, one might object: "In the recension of Bhāradvāja, forms such as *prādayaḥ* would not be established; rather, there would be elision (*luk*) in *rujāyati*, *vasayati*, and in *kanayati* from the root *kan*. To this he replies: 'Both of these are merely illustrative examples,' and so forth. Thus, in the recension of Bhāradvāja and for others, this has been shown to serve a specific purpose, but it is not intended as an exhaustive enumeration of examples."

Why is it that this alone is the purpose? Because even the *pra*-class [prefixes] are intended [to function here]. But is it not the case that [the rule] "after a nominal stem (*prātipadika*), [the suffix *ṇic* is added] in the sense of the meaning of a verbal root (*dhātvartha*), diversely (*bahulam*), and like the superlative (*iṣṭhan*)" is recited specifically in the *curādi* group [of roots]? Why, then, is the treatment of the suffix *ṇic* as being like *iṣṭhan* stated here again? Some say it is for the sake of elaboration (*prapañca*) upon that very point;
others say that it should have been stated in the [curādi] group itself.

Others maintain that the phrase "this other one" is intended to demonstrate an alternative interpretation. Although the word *lopa* was previously employed as an abstract noun (*bhāvasādhana*), here it is taken as an object noun (*karmasādhana*), because of the specific mention of "that which follows *yaṇ*" (*yaṇādi-param*). For if it were an abstract noun, the genitive case would have applied according to the rule *kartṛ-karmaṇoḥ kṛti* [Pāṇini 2.3.65]. However, since it is an object noun, the object is expressed by that very term, and thus the nominative alone is appropriate. Thinking this, and demonstrating that the word *lopa*—which is synonymous with the word *karman*—functions as an object noun, he says: "That which follows *yaṇ* and so forth is elided."

But how, then, can that very same [word] which is a *bhāva-sādhana* (denoting an action or state) be established as a *karman-sādhana* (denoting an object)? Who, indeed, says "of that very same"? For the word *lopa*, recurring with every sūtra, is distinct [in each instance].

But surely, when [the suffix] *yaṅ* and so forth have been elided, by virtue of the grammatical capacity (*sāmarthya*), the *guṇa* substitution will be understood as applying only to that which precedes it; so for what purpose is the mention of "preceding" (*pūrva*)? To this he says: "The mention of 'preceding' is for the sake of clarity. Furthermore, what is the reason that the suffix *iman* is taught only after words such as *priya*, *uru*, *guru*, and *dīrgha*, and not after others? To this he says: "*Priya-uru-bahula-guru-dīrghāḥ*" and so forth.
The meaning of this statement is that the suffix *iman* is possible only after words beginning with *priya*, and not after others.

Otherwise, even if *priya* and the others were listed among *pṛthu* and the rest, or if they were words denoting color (*varṇa*), then why would *imanic* not be illustrated by them? In that case, the illustration for *imanij* here would be *teṣām* (of those), where the vowel *a* is not the cause [for the application of the suffix]. Regarding the phrase "after *bahu* and the subsequent ones":

by this, he shows that the first *bahu* is in the ablative case (*pañcamyanta*), and by the word *tasya* (of that) combined with *bahoḥ*, he shows that the second *bahu* is in the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhyanta*).
The form is *bhūyān*.
> [[1.1.54]] Thus, there is the elision of the vowel *i* alone.
Now, for what purpose is the word *bahoḥ* mentioned again? He says: "The mention of *bahoḥ* again," and so forth.

For if the mention of *bahoḥ* were absent, the status of the word *bahu* as a substituendum (*sthānin*) would not be understood; because [the rule] is stated with a word ending in the fifth case (*pañcamyanta*).
Therefore, for the sake of establishing that [the substitute] occupies the position [of the original], the word *bahoḥ* is stated again.
Regarding the phrase "otherwise," etc.:
if *bahoḥ* were not stated, then the substitution of *bhū-* would apply only to the suffixes, because of the rule [Pāṇini 7.3.89]: *bahorlopo bhū ca bahoḥ*.

[Objection: Surely, by the very fact of their separate mention, the [substitution of] *pratyayas* will not occur; otherwise, one would have said "bhūlopau" (the two: *bhū* and *lopa*). [Reply: This is not so; for there is another purpose for the separate mention. What is it? So that they may be substitutes for distinct positions (*pṛthaksthānaka*), and not for the initial [element]. If it were stated as "bhūlopau," then, according to [Pāṇini 1.1.54], *bhū* and *lopa* would optionally be substitutes for the very first phoneme.

Therefore, the separate statement of the two rules would be for the purpose that they should have distinct locations; hence it was rightly said: "Otherwise, the substitution of *bhū* would apply only to the suffixes. Here, the particle *ca* serves the purpose of conjunction (*sanniyoga*). [The rule] "the augment *yiṅ* is an exception to elision" [is also stated].
Because its commencement does not occur until that [suffix] has been reached;
for it is said, "In this case, the *it* is for the purpose of pronunciation," since there is no other purpose.
The letter *ca* serves to carry forward (anukarṣaṇa) the rule "and *bhū* for *bahu*" [from Pāṇini 6.4.158]. Regarding "jyāyān":
by [Pāṇini 5.3.61] "and *jya*," there is the substitution (*ādeśa*) of *jya*. [Regarding the form *jyāyān*:
"there is elision (*lopa*) and *yiṭ*," and so forth.

The intention is as follows: if, in this case, the elision (*lopa*) is not separated from the augment *yiṭ*, then by that very [elision], the form *jyāyān* is established; therefore, one should not state "from the beginning" (*āt*). But how is it established by elision when "from the beginning" is not stated? To this he says: "For when there is elision," and so forth.

Now, what is the purpose of pronouncing the long vowel (*dīrgha*), since by the principle of closest proximity (*antaratama*) alone a long vowel will result from a long vowel? This is not so; for it is said that "an *aṇ* being taught (*bhāvyamāna*) does not include its homogeneous counterparts" (*vyā.pa.* 35). Thus, [the rule] must be formulated.

The meaning is that this must be explained. Here is the explanation: the mention of *vibhāṣā* (optionally) in the subsequent sūtra is also connected here, and that is a *vyavasthita-vibhāṣā* (restricted option); therefore, it will apply only to the roots beginning with *pṛthu*. If this is so, then the rule *halāder laghoḥ* need not be formulated, as [the desired forms] will be obtained through the *vyavasthita-vibhāṣā* for both [roots] beginning with a consonant and those having a light vowel? True, this is so; however, it is formulated for the sake of clarity.

The phrase "therefore, it does not occur here" and so forth means that if the enumeration were not made, then even in cases such as *kṛtayati*, the treatment of the suffix as being like *iṣṭhan* would indeed apply. Regarding *ruājiṣṭhaḥ*, here, by virtue of the treatment of the base as it was (*prakṛtivadbhāva*), the elision of the *ṭi* portion does not take place.

But surely [it might be argued]: "It will subvert the elision of the *ṭi* (P. 6.4.155), because this rule is commenced when that [elision] has not yet taken effect"? This is not so. There are two types of *ṭi*-elision: one belonging to that which ends in the suffixes *vin* or *mat*, and another belonging to what remains once the *luk* has been applied. In that case, since the *luk* is commenced when the *ṭi*-elision belonging to the element ending in *vin* or *mat* has not yet taken effect, it is logical that the latter should subvert the former. However, as for the *ṭi*-elision belonging to the remainder, since it is impossible for the *luk* to have taken effect prior to it, how could this [new] rule, being commenced while that [elision] is still unobtained, subvert the elision whose application arises only subsequently?
Therefore, this [rule] must indeed be commenced.
"By nature, a Kṣatriya [is brave]," and so forth.

Why should this be stated? It need not be; for how then [is it understood]? The rule *turiṣṭhemeyastu* (Pāṇini 6.4.154) has been set aside. This state of being "like the base form" (*prakṛtivadbhāva*) is to be prescribed generally, and the word *vibhāṣā* ("optionally") continues to apply, and that is a restricted option (*vyavasthitavibhāṣā*).

Therefore, it will occur everywhere where it is intended, but it will certainly not occur where it is not intended. If it is argued that, in this way, the prescription of *prakṛtibhāva* (the preservation of the original form) beginning with [Pāṇini 6.4.164] would be purposeless, we say: no; for it serves the purpose of detailed exposition (*prapañca*). For example: *rājanyakam*.
Regarding "the offspring of a king" (*rājño'patyam*):
from the rule *rājaruṣasurādyat* [Pāṇini 4.1.137], and subsequently by the rule *tasmātsamūherthe* [Pāṇini 4.2.39] and so forth, the suffix *vuñ* is applied here.
Thus, "humanity" (*mānuṣyakam*).

Regarding the form *manorapatyam* ("the offspring of Manu"): according to those who hold that the suffix *yat* is applied in the sense of "offspring" by [Pāṇini 4.1.161], when the suffix *vuñ* is applied by the preceding rule, elision would result; this is prevented by the application of *prakṛtibhāva* (the preservation of the original form).

However, for those who maintain that *yat* is applied merely in the sense of a genus (*jāti*) and not in the sense of "offspring," there is no need for *prakṛtibhāva*; for since it is not the *yat* of the "offspring" suffix, elision will not occur anyway. Examples are: *sāṅkūṭinam*, *sāṃrāviṇam*, and *sāmmārjinam*.

From the roots *kūṭa* (burning, DhP 1890), *ru* (sound, DhP 1034), and *mṛjū* (cleansing, DhP 1066)—with the suffix *inuṇ* added in the sense of "pervasion" or "state" according to Pāṇini 3.3.44—the forms *sāṃkūṭin*, *sāṃrāvin*, and *sāṃmārjin* are established. Then, by applying Pāṇini 5.4.15, the suffix *aṇ* is added in the sense of the word itself (*svārthe*). Regarding the form *maidhāva*:

the suffix *vini* is applied according to Pāṇini 5.2.121 et seq., and from that form ending in *vini*, the suffix *aṇ* is applied in the sense of "descendant" (*apatya*) before the scope of Pāṇini 4.1.83. This rule is commenced for the purpose of expressing "descendant"; for in cases where there is no descendant, the desired form is already established by the preceding rule.
"Because these [suffixes] have no limit. This is also an introduction for the purpose of deriving patronymics (apatya), as in "Śāṅkhinaḥ.

From the words *śaṅkha*, *madra*, and *vajra*, the suffix *ini* is applied in the sense of possession (*matvartha*); from that which ends in it, the suffix *aṇ* is applied as before. "In the absence of a patronymic" (*anapatye*).
It has ceased.
The rule applies generally to this [section]:
"sāmanaḥ," "vaimanaḥ."
> [[4.3.120]] The suffix *iṭ-aṇ* [is applied]. Regarding the example "sautvanaḥ":

from the root *ṣuñ* (meaning "to press," Dhātupāṭha 1247), the suffix *ṅvanip* is applied by rule [[3.2.103]], followed by the substitution of *samprasāraṇa* by rule [[6.1.71]]. Regarding "sāmanyaḥ" and "vemanyaḥ": [these are derived similarly].

The suffix *yat* is applied by [Pāṇini 4.4.98]. Regarding "ātmanīna," the suffix *kha* is applied by [Pāṇini 5.1.9]: "After *ātman*, *vija*, *jana*, and a word ending in *bhoga*, [the suffix *kha* is added].
Regarding "adhvanīna," [the suffix *kha* is applied after the word *adhvan*].
Here too, the suffix *kha* is applied by the rule *advane yat-khau* [Pāṇini 5.2.16].

Regarding the term *pratyātmam*: the compound *avyayībhāva* is formed in the sense of "towards" (*yathārthe*) according to the rule *avyayaṃ vibhakti-* [Pāṇini 2.1.6], meaning "towards the self" (*ātmānaṃ prati*).

From that [suffix], by [Pāṇini 5.4.108] *anaśca*, the suffix *ṭac* is applied. Regarding *prādhvam*: it is a *prādi*-compound meaning "gone forth on a path" (*pragatamadhvānam*), and [the suffix] *ac* is applied by [Pāṇini 5.4.85]. Regarding *cārmaṇaḥ*.

Regarding the meaning "the chariot has turned back" (parivṛtto rathaḥ), [it is stated] that "it should be stated that [the suffix] optionally applies after a word denoting 'beneficial' (hitanāman). The sense of this is to be explained as follows: there is a prohibition of [the suffix] *va* for the word *hitanāman*. This is the meaning.

In this regard, the explanation is as follows: here too, that very term *vibhāṣā* (optionally) is understood to carry over, and it is a restricted option (*vyavasthitavibhāṣā*). Therefore, there will be an optional prohibition regarding names ending in *hita*. If this were a single rule alone, would it then serve the purpose of a restriction (*niyamārtha*) or the purpose of an injunction (*vidhyartha*)? If the word *apatye* (in the sense of offspring) is understood to carry over, then since the original form (*prakṛtibhāva*) has already been prohibited by the immediately preceding rule, the elision of the suffix *ṭi* is established by [Pāṇini 6.4.144] itself. Since it is already established, this [present rule] must serve the purpose of a restriction: "so that [the elision] occurs only when the sense of 'offspring' refers to a genus (*jāti*)."

And likewise, when the suffix *aṇ* is prescribed by [Pāṇini 4.3.120], forms such as *brāhmaḥ garbhaḥ*, *brāhmaṃ astram*, *brāhmaṃ haviḥ*, and *brāhmī oṣadhiḥ* would not be established, because the *aṇ* [prescribed] for offspring (*apatya*) would be absent.
Now, if the term "offspring" (*apatya*) is removed [from the rule], then it will serve solely as a prescriptive injunction (*vidhi*).

For in the previous rule, the preservation of the original stem-form (*prakṛtibhāva*) was prohibited in the case of offspring; consequently, since the preservation of the stem-form would have been obtained by [the rule] *an* [6.4.167], the word *brāhma* in the sense of "not born of a Brāhmaṇa woman" (*ajāta-brāhmaṇī*) is treated as an irregular formation (*nipātana*) for the purpose of eliding the *ṭi* [portion].

And if this [suffix] were for the purpose of an injunction (*vidhi*), then while forms such as *brāhmaṇo garbhaḥ*, *brāhmaṇastram*, and *brāhmaṃ haviḥ* would be established, the form *brāhmaṇī oṣadhiḥ* ("a Brāhmaṇa woman is a medicinal herb") would not be established, because of the prohibition by the rule "not when [denoting] a genus" (*ajātau*).

Furthermore, since the preservation of the original stem (*prakṛtibhāva*) is prohibited by the rule "in the case of offspring and a genus" (Pāṇini 6.4.170), the elision of the suffix *ṭi* occurs by the rule "thereafter" (Pāṇini 6.4.144), resulting in *brāhmaṇo nāradaḥ*. Likewise, here too it would result in *brāhmaṇaḥ* in the sense of "the offspring of a Brāhmaṇa."

Having thus observed the undesirable consequence (doṣaprasaṅga) arising from a single application (*ekayoga*), and desiring to avoid it, he says: "In this case, a division of the rule (*yogavibhāga*) is made. If, upon the division of the rule, the elision of *ṭi* is prescribed only for "offspring" (*apatya*) due to its continued application (*anuvṛtti*), then—since [the desired form] is already established as before—the prescription would serve merely as a restrictive rule (*niyamārtha*). Consequently, that same defect which was previously stated regarding the position of non-restriction (*aniyamapakṣa*) would remain exactly as it was;
and thus, the making of the division of the rule would be purposeless.

Therefore, even though the scope of the rule concerns offspring (*apatya*), by the power of making a *yogavibhāga* (splitting the rule), the form *brāhmaḥ* is derived as something other than offspring.

Thus, through this derivation of *brāhmaḥ* even when not denoting offspring, the forms *brāhmo garbhaḥ*, *brāhmatram*, and *brāhmaṃ haviḥ* are established. Following that, the second rule begins: *ajātau* ("when not denoting a genus").

Since the preservation of the original form (*prakṛtibhāva*) is prohibited by [Pāṇini 6.4.170], the elision of the *ṭi* suffix by [Pāṇini 6.4.144] would otherwise apply; therefore, the phrase "in the sense of offspring" (*apatye*) is used for the purpose of preventing that.
By this, he explains that the term "offspring" (*apatya*) is carried over (*anuvartate*) into this second rule.
Furthermore, the expression "not when denoting a genus" (*ajātau*) is a prohibitive negation (*prasajyapratiṣedha*).

In this context, the connection of the genus (*jāti*) is with the sense of "offspring" (*apatya*), whereas that of the negative particle (*nañ*) is with the verb *bhavati*. Demonstrating that very meaning in the commentary (*vṛtti*), he says: "When the suffix *aṇ* occurs in the sense of offspring denoting a genus, as in the word *brāhmaṇa*, the elision [of the final vowel] does not take place.
The meaning is that when offspring qualified by a genus is intended to be expressed, and the suffix *aṇ* follows—as in the case of *brāhmaṇa*—the elision of the *ṭi* (the final vowel) does not occur.

"Regarding *apatya* (offspring) alone—as in ‘*brāhmau oṣadhiḥ*’ (the Brāhmaṇa herb). By means of this counter-example (*pratyudāharaṇa*), he demonstrates that through the division of the rule (*yogavibhāga*), even the form ‘*brāhmau oṣadhiḥ*’ is established when there is a desire to express merely the genus (*jātimātra*). “If this is so,” [he asks]. If the suffix *ṇakāra* is indeed present here, then what is the purpose of this [rule]? The meaning is that it has no purpose whatsoever.
What is the reason? He says: "For [the rule] 'naḥ taddhite' (Pāṇini 6.4.144) [already applies]," and so forth.

For a *nipātana* (irregular formation) is undertaken for that purpose which is not obtained through a general grammatical rule (*lakṣaṇa*). But here, [the desired form] is already established by the rule "naḥ taddhite. Indeed, no *prakṛtibhāva* (non-elision of the final vowel) has been stated for the suffix *ṇa*; therefore, this *nipātana*—which would cause the elision of the *ṭi* (the final vowel)—being undertaken there, would be meaningful. For *prakṛtibhāva* has been stated for a stem ending in *aṇ*, but not for one ending in *ṇa*.
He accepts the point just stated and asks, "If this is true, for what purpose is this [rule]? He replies with "for the sake of indication" (*jñāpakārtham*), and so forth.
Regarding "those formed by *aṇ*" (*aṇkṛtāni*) and so on:
operations performed by *aṇ* are "formed by *aṇ*" (*aṇkṛtāni*). The compound is formed by the division of the rule (*yogavibhāga*) "the locative case" (*saptamī*, Pāṇini 2.1.40).

Alternatively, the compound is formed by *aṇ* [the suffix *a*] according to the rule "The agent and the instrument [are compounded] with a word ending in a *kṛt* suffix, diversely" (*kartṛkaraṇe kṛtā bahulam*, Pāṇini 2.1.31). [An objector asks:
"What is the purpose of making this known? To this he replies: "By that," and so forth.

[In the case of] *curāśīlā* ("she whose habit is stealing") and *tapaḥśīlā* ("she whose habit is austerity"), the suffix *ṇa* is applied according to the rule "After *chattra* and others, *ṇa*" (*chattrādibhyo ṇaḥ*, Pāṇini 4.4.62), and the feminine suffix *ṅīp* is added to that which ends in *ṇa*.

Because the meaning of the rule "the suffix *ṇa* [is applied] in the sense of having that as one's characteristic" (*tācchīlike ṇaḥ*) has already been made known, [one might ask]: why is the suffix *ṇa* not applied after the word *daṇḍa* by the rule "the suffix *ṇa* is applied to denote 'this is the weapon used in this sport'" (*tadasyāṃ praharaṇam iti krīḍāyāṃ ṇaḥ*) [Pāṇini 4.2.57], resulting in *dāṇḍā*? If the operation of the suffix *aṇ* were intended for words denoting a characteristic (*tācchīlaka*), why would it not be explicitly stated that *aṇ* is applied after words such as *chattra* and others? In that case too, the purpose [of the rule] would be that an irregular formation (*nipātana*) need not be prescribed. You have spoken correctly; however, the suffix *aṇ* was used for the sake of variety, as in the form *kārmaṇam*.
The suffix *aṇ* is applied according to [Pāṇini 5.4.36]: *tadyuktāt karmaṇo’ṇ* ("the suffix *aṇ* after a word denoting an action connected with that").

Thus, "connected with ritual action" (*karmaṇā yuktam*) is *kārmaṇam*. Regarding the phrase "the step of the ox" (*aukṣaṃ padam*), the suffix *aṇ* is applied according to [Pāṇini 4.3.120]. It is said: "By metaphorical usage, the text (*grantha*) is also called 'Atharvan'."
However, the sole basis for such metaphorical designation is the fact that it was taught by them;
as in the cases of "an Atharvaṇika" and "Bhrūṇahatyam."

Regarding the form *brahmahā* in the sense of "one who has killed a Brahmin," [the suffix] *kvip* is applied by the rule *brāhmaṇabhrūṇavṛtreṣu kvip* [Pāṇini 3.2.87]; from that [base ending in *kvip*], the suffix *ṣyañ* is added.
By the rule *harastoraciṇṇaloḥ* [Pāṇini 7.3.32], the letter *t* is already established; why then is it specifically prescribed here? To this he says: *inantastoraciṇṇaloḥ*, etc. [The principle is:
"When there is a mention of the actual form of a verbal root (*dhātu*), the grammatical operation is understood to apply only to a suffix belonging to that [root]. (Jainendra-vṛtti 31).
The meaning is that the grammatical operation is understood to apply to that suffix which is prescribed [by a rule] following the word "dhātoḥ" (Pāṇini 6.1.156).

Now, the suffix *ṣyañ* is not a suffix prescribed after a verbal root (*dhātu*); what then? It is a suffix prescribed after a nominal stem (*prātipadika*). Therefore, the substitution of *t* [for *s*] by the rule "tena" (Pāṇini 7.3.32) would not apply there; hence, it is treated as an irregular formation (*nipātana*). But how is this understood—that when the form of a verbal root itself is mentioned [as a condition], the grammatical operation applies to a suffix following that root? This is not so; for in the case of the rule "na" (Pāṇini 7.3.59), the prevention of the change to *k* can be achieved even through the division of the *yoga* (separation of rules).
In the case of *bhrauṇaghnaḥ* and *vṛtraghnaḥ*,
the suffix *aṇ* is applied in the sense of offspring (*apatya*).
When the suffix *añ* is applied to the word *ikṣvāku* by the rule *ikṣvāku-śabdād yañ* (Pāṇini 4.1.168), then the word *aikṣvāka* is acute-accented on the first syllable due to the *ñit*-accent.

But when the secondary suffix *aṇ* [is applied] by the rule *kopadhāt* [Pāṇini 4.2.131], then [the word] is oxytone. Now, one might object: "In a rule of this kind, the inclusion of one form does not result in the inclusion of the other; therefore, both forms, differing in accent, must be explicitly mentioned—as in *eākaḥ* and *aikṣvakaḥ*.
To refute this objection, he says: "By means of a pronoun for all accents," and so forth.
The pronunciation of accents such as the acute (*udātta*) and others without distinction is called *ekaśruti*.

And just as the term *sarvanāman* [in Pāṇini’s rule] 1.1.27, "That which is a name for all [things] is *sarvanāman*," indicates specific instances such as *upagu* and so forth without distinction, so too does *ekaśruti* indicate specific accentual distinctions such as the acute and others.

Thus, this word *aikṣvāka* is recited here neither with an initial acute nor with a final acute; however, when it is recited in this manner, a specific accent arises for it due to a specific suffix—namely, when the suffix *añ* is applied, then it has a final acute.
"Thus, this is an exception to the substitution.
By the rule [Pāṇini 7.3.2], *kekayādi*, the substitution of *iy* would apply; however, its exception (*apavāda*) is the prescribed elision (*lopa*).
[By Pāṇini 6.1.97] there is the substitution of the subsequent form (*pararūpatva*).
"Now, for what purpose?"—with this intention he asked, and in order to reveal that very intention himself, he says: "Then, when *añ* has been applied," and so forth.
"Established."
Because there is no difference between the form and its essential nature.
By the rule "and for the sake of eliding *ya*" (*yalopārthaśca*), he demonstrates the *guṇa* [substitution] that occurs when [the word] is listed among the *bidādi* group;
and by "among the *yaskādi* group," etc., [he shows another].

For in that context, the purpose of the recitation is so that the elision (*luk*) of the many *gotra*-suffixes may occur. And since that elision is already established by the rule [Pāṇini 2.4.64] when they are included among the *bidādi* group, there is no need for their inclusion among the *yaskādi* group. For example: "the Maitreya community" (*maitreyaḥ saṅghaḥ*), and so forth.
By this, he demonstrates the fault that arises from including [the word] in the *bidādi* group.

If it were included in the *bidādi* group, all this that you have stated would be consistent; however, if it were derived from the word *maitreya* ending in the suffix *añ*, then by the rule "saṅghāṅkalakṣaṇa" [Pāṇini 4.3.127], the suffix *aṇ* would apply, resulting in the undesired form *maitreya*, rather than the desired *maitreyaka*.
If, on the other hand, it were derived from the word ending in the suffix *ḍhañ*, then by [the rule] "ḍhañ" [Pāṇini 4.3.126], the desired form *maitreyaka* is established.
In the word “*hiraṇmayaḥ*,” the suffix *mayaṭ* is applied according to [Pāṇini 4.3.143]. In the words “*ṛtvyam*” and “*vāstvyam*,” the suffix *yat* is applied according to [Pāṇini 4.4.110].
The suffix *aṇ* [is applied] by [Pāṇini 4.3.120], which states "vāstva-". The same applies to the word *mādhvī*.

Regarding the term *hiraṇyayaḥ*: the suffix *mayaṭ* is applied as in the previous case. Thus ends the fourth quarter of the sixth chapter in the *Kāśikā-vivaraṇapañjikā*, composed by the venerable master Jinendrabuddhi, who is a teacher representing the Bodhisattvas. [The Seventh Chapter, First Quarter] In this [chapter], for the sake of brevity in the treatise, the two suffixes *yu* and *vu* are taught; in place of these, the substitutes *an* and *āk* are prescribed.

For if the substitution of *yu* and *vu* were prescribed wherever they are taught [in the grammatical system], then there would be prolixity (*gaurava*) in the treatise, because those two consist of a large collection of phonemes. Here, however, this is a reference to the suffixes *yu* and *vu* which have a nasal as their *yaṇ*-substitute; and such unmarked (*ananubandhaka*) forms of *yu* and *vu* do not exist in the treatise. Therefore, by virtue of the contextual capacity (*sāmarthya*), one understands that these two are to be understood in a general sense, setting aside the specific markers (*anubandha*). Thus he says: "of these two, *yu* and *vu*, whose specific qualifiers have been discarded."
The connection with the upcoming phrase "this is the inclusion" (*idaṃ grahaṇam*) is as follows:
those two [suffixes] are described as such because they have discarded—that is, abandoned—their respective qualifiers, such as the letter *la* and so forth.
By this, he shows that the term *yuvu* is a general reference for *lyuṭ* and the other suffixes.

If, in this context, there were a general inclusion of the term *yu* without qualification, then in forms such as from the root *yu* (DhP 1033)—meaning "to mix" (*yu miśraṇe*; or *yu miśraṇe'miśraṇe ca* according to some DhP recensions)—the forms *yutaḥ*, *yutavān*, and *yutvā*; or from the root *dīv* (DhP 1107)—meaning "to play," etc.—the forms *dyūtaḥ*, *dhūtavān*, and *dhūtvā*; or even in cases like *ūrṇāyuḥ* and so forth, the vowels *a* and *ā* would [erroneously] be substituted for the semivowels (*yaṇ*). Therefore, in order to avoid this over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*), he says: "*anunāsikayaṇoḥ*. This is a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "that which has an *anunāsika* [nasal] and a *yaṇ* [semivowel]."
For there are *yaṇ* sounds that are both nasalized (*sānunāsika*) and non-nasalized (*niranunāsika*). Among these, this [rule] applies to those two *yaṇ*s that are nasalized.
Furthermore, in order to show that the nasalized *yaṇ*s, namely *yu* and *vu*, are indeed suffixes (*pratyaya*) and not non-suffixes, he says: "of the two suffixes" (*pratyayayoḥ*).

Others, however, explain that the word "of the two suffixes" was stated for the purpose of excluding non-suffixes; but that is incorrect, because the exclusion of non-suffixes is already established by the very phrase "of the nasalized *yaṇ*s" (*anunāsikayaṇoḥ*).

In this context, it is understood that the *yū* (the vowels *i* and *u*) and the *vu* (the diphthongs *e* and *o*) that are nasalized (*anunāsika*) and semivowels (*yaṇ*) exist as suffixes (*pratyaya*) in the grammatical treatise (*śāstra*).

Therefore, those *yū* and *vu* which are nasalized and semivowels are indeed suffixes and not non-suffixes; thus, the term "of the two suffixes" (*pratyayayoḥ*) is stated for the purpose of demonstrating this possibility. Furthermore, since the nasalized semivowels are being taken as suffixes, this genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) should be understood as having the sense of a relationship characterized by the term "of the stem" (*aṅgasya*).
The connection is that "of you two who are related to the *aṅga*.
Furthermore, this [connection] is characterized by the relationship between the cause (*nimitta*) and the effect (*nimittin*).
For the acquisition of its own existence (*ātmalābha*) by the *aṅga* is caused by the suffix; thus, the *aṅga* is the cause-possessor (*nimittin*), and the suffix is the cause (*nimitta*).
By the statement "yoraṇo vorakaḥ," he expresses the relationship between the substituend (*sthānin*) and the substitute (*ādeśa*) in their respective order;
[and by] "nandyādibhyo lyuḥ."
By the rule *nandigrahi* [Pāṇini 3.1.134] and others,
we have the forms *nandanaḥ* and *ramaṇaḥ*. [The roots are] *ṭu nadi samṛddhau* (Dhātupāṭha 67) and *ramu krīḍāyām* (Dhātupāṭha 853).

The suffix *ṇic* is applied when there is a cause [for action]; from that which ends in *ṇic*, the suffix *layu* follows. Regarding the form "sāyantanaḥ," it is derived by the rule "from *sāyam* and so forth, the suffixes *ṭa*, *ṭyaP*, etc. (Pāṇini 4.3.23).
By the rule *sāyaṃ-ciraṃ* [Pāṇini 4.3.23] and others,
a secondary suffix (*taddhita*) is applied in the sense of a derivative (*śaiṣika*) such as "born at" and so forth,
as in *vāsudevakaḥ* and *arjunakaḥ*.

The offspring of Vasudeva is Vāsudeva; from the word *vāsudeva*, by applying the suffix *vun* according to Pāṇini 4.3.98 (*vasudevārjunābhyāṃ vun*), we get *vāsudevakaḥ* and *arjunakaḥ*. [In the case of] *ūrṇāyuḥ* (woolly), because there is no nasalization (*anunāsika*) of the semi-vowel (*yaṇ*) therein, the rule does not apply.
But what is the reason that in such cases the semi-vowel lacks nasalization? To this he says: "of such cases," and so forth.
"The followers of Pāṇini accept [the quality of] nasality as a formal postulate.

This means that it occurs only where nasality is postulated by them, and not elsewhere. And nasality is not postulated by them for forms such as *yus* and so on, because they follow the requirements of the linguistic data (*lakṣya*).
Therefore, the *yaṇ* substitution does not apply to the nasalization of those [sounds].
By the word "etc. (*ādi*), rules such as Pāṇini 5.2.140 and others are included.

Now, one might object: in the rule *ahaṃśubhamoryus* (Pāṇini 5.2.138), the suffix will not undergo this change simply because of the presence of the marker *s*. Indeed, the marker *s* is for the purpose of designating a *pada*; and the *pada* designation is for the sake of the *anusvāra*, so that when that designation is present, the *anusvāra* may occur by the rule *tasyāṃ satyām* (Pāṇini 8.3.23).

And if there were no substitution here, then the addition of *s* (in *si*) would be purposeless; for an *anusvāra* does not occur when a non-substitution (*anādeśa*) has been made, because of the continued application of the rule "before a consonant" (*halī*) from [Pāṇini 8.3.22]. When a substitution is made, it does not occur, because the condition of being preceded by a consonant (*hal-ādi*) is absent. This is not so; by the force of the explicit statement, the *anusvāra* would occur even before vowels beginning with *a*. Furthermore, there is another purpose for adding *s*: it serves to establish the technical designation (*saṃjñā*) of a "word" (*pada*).
The purpose of that [marking] is to set aside the designation *bha*.

If the designation *bha* were applied, then by the rule "in the case of *bha*, there is elision of the *ṭi* [of what ends in *an*]" (*adhyayānāṃ bhamātre ṭilopaḥ*), there would be elision of the *ṭi* whenever *bha* occurs. Alternatively, the addition of the *s* (in *yus*) would be for the sake of the *avagraha* (word division) in the Pada-pāṭha; so how could it be purposeless? In this context, regarding the mention of *yuvoḥ*, one must resort to either a collective *dvandva* compound or a *itaretarayoga* (copulative) *dvandva*. If the former view is adopted, then when the genitive singular is formed, because it is neuter according to the rule "that [compound] is neuter" (*sa napuṃsakam*), the augment *num* must be applied by the rule "after a neuter [stem ending in a vowel], *num* is added before the endings beginning with a vowel or a soft consonant" (*napuṃsakasya jhalacaḥ*). Consequently, the mention [in the sūtra] would have to be *yuvunoḥ*.

But in the other view, once the substitution of *yaṇ* for the following *o* has been applied, there would result the hearing of a second *v* in the form *yuṣvoḥ*. To refute this objection, he says: "In this case, the mention is *yuvoḥ*," and so forth. "The teaching regarding augments (*āgama*) is not eternal. This means that the teaching (*śāsana*), i.e., the prescription (*vidhāna*) of augments, is not eternal; why? Because in some instances they are absent.

Alternatively—*āgama-śāsana* refers to that grammatical treatise (*śāstra*) by which *āgamas* (augmentations) are taught or prescribed; that [treatise] is non-eternal (*anitya*), because its effect (*kārya*) is not found to be eternal. Furthermore, the non-eternality of the *āgama-śāsana* is understood from the inclusion of the word "or" (*vā*) in the rule *an-ityatā punar-āgama-śāsanasya* (Pāṇini 7.3.70). For that [inclusion] is made for the purpose that, in forms such as *dadat* and *dadāt*, the elision of the *ghu*-marker (*gho-lopa*) should not occur eternally.

Furthermore, if the teaching regarding augments were eternal (*nitya*), the mention of the word "vā" (optionally) would be purposeless. Suppose the elision (*lopa*) were eternal; even so, once the augment *aṭ* has been applied by [Pāṇini 6.4.71], forms such as *dadat* and *dadāt* are indeed established. However, if the teaching regarding augments were non-eternal (*anitya*), then due to the absence of the augment *āṭ*, the form would not be established.
Consequently, the alternative formulation becomes meaningful:
"or [the word] has neuter gender," and so forth.
Alternatively, there is simply no neuter gender here at all.
What is the reason? [The author] says: "Gender is not to be taught," and so forth.
Since gender is a worldly matter (*lokadharma*), the world itself is its authority.
Therefore, because it is established through the world alone, it is not to be taught; it is not to be prescribed.

In this context, the word *liṅga* refers to the treatise (*śāstra*) itself because of its subservience to that purpose. The meaning of gender (*liṅgārtha*) is not to be taught by the treatise; it need not be prescribed, because the gender to be established by it is based on common usage (*lokāśrayatva*).
By this, he demonstrates the rejection of rules such as "that [stem] is neuter" (Pāṇini 2.4.17).
