And since that [suffix] has been rejected, its neuter status does not occur by way of it; so how could there be the contingency of the *num* augment? As for the statement, "But in the case of mutual dependence (*itaretarapakṣe*), there is elision of a phoneme due to its being Vedic (*cchāndasatvāt*)," this refers to the fact that "the Sūtras are like the Vedas" (*chandovat sūtrāṇi bhavanti*);
thus, it is Vedic usage.

Therefore, just as in the case of *niṣkartāram adhvaraḥ*, there is the elision of the letter *n* [of the prefix *nis-*], so too here the elision of the letter *v* should be understood. Furthermore, the letters beginning with *pha* are taught in this treatise for the sake of brevity (*lāghava*); consequently, substitutes such as *āyan* and others are prescribed for them.

It should be understood that those being prescribed apply to the mere consonant (*hal*) beginning with *pha*. Why is this so? Because of the mention of *ghām* at the end [of the sūtra] without an inherent vowel (*anacka-nirdeśa*); otherwise, one would have said *ghānām*.

Elsewhere, however, the adventitious letter *a* is merely for the sake of pronunciation. For this very reason, since only the consonant portion of *pha* and so on—occurring at the beginning of an affix—is taken as the substituendum (*sthānin*), the paribhāṣā regarding "that which lacks an anubandha" (Pāṇini 1.1.68) does not apply here; for in all such cases, *pha* and the others are indeed without anubandhas. This paribhāṣā applies only where both conditions are possible, as in the example *nāḍāyanaḥ*.

> [[4.1.99]] The suffix *phak* is used in the sense of offspring (*apatya*). In the subsequent examples as well, except where the substitution of *īya* is illustrated, it should be understood as being used in the sense of offspring. For example:
*sauparṇeyaḥ*, *vainateyaḥ*.

The suffix *ḍhak* is applied after the words *suparṇa* and *avinata*, as in the example "āṭhakulīnaḥ. One might ask: does this not contradict the rule "after a word that does not have another word as its prior member, the suffixes *yañ* or *ḍhakañ* are optionally applied" [Pāṇini 4.1.140], since that rule specifies "when there is no prior member"? To this we reply: by the rule "the suffix *kha* is applied after *kula*" [Pāṇini 4.1.139], the suffix *kha* occurs even when there is a prior member.

"Gārgīyaḥ, vātsīyaḥ. From the words *gārgya* and *vātsya*, which end in the suffix *yañ*, when the sense "belonging to him" (*tasyedam*) is intended, the suffix *cha* is applied; by [Pāṇini 6.4.148] there is the elision of the vowel *a*, and by [Pāṇini 6.4.151] there is the elision of the letter *y*. "Phakkati, ḍhaukate. [These are examples of the denominative suffix *kyac*.]

The forms of these [roots] are as follows: *phakka* in the sense of "going downwards" (*nīcairgatau*; Dhātupāṭha 116), *ḍhokṛ* in the sense of "going" (*gatau*; Dhātupāṭha 98), *khanu* in the sense of "digging" (*avadāraṇe*; Dhātupāṭha 878), *chidir* in the sense of "cutting" (*dvaidhīkaraṇe*; Dhātupāṭha 1440), and *ghūṇa* and *ghūrṇa* in the sense of "wandering" (*bhramaṇe*; Dhātupāṭha 437, 438).
The forms *ḍhaukati* and *ghūrṇati* take the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) because they are marked with an indicatory vowel *ṅ* (indicating that they are *anudāttet*).
The examples are *ūrudadhnam* and *jānudadhnam*.

The suffix *dadhnac* is applied in the sense of "the measure of this" (*ūrū pramāṇam asya*) by the rule *pramāṇe dvayasac* [Pāṇini 5.2.37] and others. In this context, suffixes such as *āyan* and so forth, being prescribed under the governing heading (*adhikāra*) of "stem" (*aṅga*), are *bahiraṅga* because they occur in dependence upon both the stem and the suffix. However, the acute accent (*udātta*) of the suffix is *antaraṅga*, because it occurs in dependence on the suffix alone, without regard for the stem.

Therefore, as long as the *āyan* and other suffixes have not yet occurred, the substitution must necessarily be acute-accented (*ādyudātta*) by virtue of the rule for suffixes; once that has been effected, the substitutes would occur in cases such as [Pāṇini 5.3.102] and [4.2.114], where no indicatory letter (*anubandha*) is prescribed for the sake of accent, and thus an indefinite accent would result. To refute this objection, he says: "In this case, these *āyan* and others," and so forth. The intention is this: even the *āyan* and others are indeed *antaranga* (internal).

If [the word *bahiraṅga*] were connected here with the rule *yadi hi* (P. 6.4.1), then those [suffixes] would indeed be considered *bahiraṅga* in relation to the base (*prakṛti*) and the suffix (*pratyaya*). However, it is not connected here, because there is no purpose for it.

For instance, would the purpose be this: that the substitutes *āyan*, etc., should apply to *pha*, etc., when they are preceded by suffixes that are the cause of the *aṅga* (the base), but should not apply to others? [That is not the case.]
And this is obtained by implication alone, even without the heading concerning the subsidiaries (*aṅga*).
For among the [suffixes] beginning with *kyap*, there is no such suffix which does not serve as a cause for a subsidiary.
Therefore, because there is no purpose [for it], the term "of the subsidiary" (*aṅgasya*) is not connected [to this rule].

Therefore, substitutes depend only on the locus (*sthānin*) and not on the original base (*prakṛti*); thus, they too are indeed *antaranga*. Consequently, because of their priority, those [substitutes] such as *ayana* and so forth must first occur at the time of the instruction of the suffix (*pratyayopadeśakāla*), and subsequently, by virtue of the acute accent (*udātta*) on the beginning of the suffix. Thus, since *ayana* and the others occur precisely at the time of the instruction of the suffix, the acute accent on the beginning of the suffix takes effect once they have been applied. Regarding this, he provides a further indicator (*jñāpaka*) with the words "And thus," and so forth.
And such is the meaning.
What is the purpose of making *ghac* marked with the *cit* designation? It is so that the final syllable may be udātta according to [Pāṇini 6.1.157] *citaḥ*.

And if *ayann* and the others occur precisely at the stage of the presentation of the suffix (*pratyaya-upadeśāvasthā*), then the application of the *cit* marker to *ghac* becomes meaningful; not otherwise.

Otherwise, if these [substitutions] were to occur after the time of the instruction [of the accent], then since the acute accent occurs precisely where there is no *cit*-marking, it would have to occur in that very same place even when the letter *dh* and the vowel *ā* are present despite the *cit*-marking; thus, the *cit*-marking would be rendered useless.

Therefore, from the presence of the *cit*-marking, it is understood that these substitutes for *āyan*, etc., occur at the very time of the instruction of the suffix, and only afterwards does the acute accent of the suffix apply—this is the intended meaning.

But surely these [phonetic qualities] are prescribed for the consonant (*vyañjana*), and that consonant is without vowel (*asvara*); moreover, it must necessarily be accompanied by some vowel, because a vowel devoid of qualities such as the acute accent (*udātta*) and so forth is impossible.

In that case, because the substitute (*sthānin*) lacks a vowel, there is no closest similarity (*āntaratamya*); thus, since the paribhāṣā "the closest similar [substitute]" (P. 1.1.50) does not apply, these [suffixes] would necessarily have indeterminate accents. Consequently, if they did not possess the *cit* designation, then when these suffixes—prescribed subsequently—receive an initial acute accent (*ādyudātta*), that very accent would result, because it would be the "later-prescribed" (*satiśiṣṭa*) accent. Therefore, the *cit* marker is applied to the *ghac* suffix so that, even overriding that later-prescribed accent, the final acute accent (*antodāttatva*) may occur. Hence, one must consider: how can this [application of *cit*] serve as an indicator (*jñāpaka*)?

Now, why do substitutions not occur in cases such as *śameḥ khaḥ* (Pāṇini 3.1.104) resulting in *śaṅkhaḥ*, and *ṣaṇo ḍhaḥ* (Pāṇini 5.2.104) resulting in *ṣaṇḍhaḥ*? To this he says: "*śaṅkhaḥ, ṣaṇḍhaḥ*" and so forth.

Furthermore, it should be understood that even the technical designation (*itsaṃjñā*) [of the letter *ṭ*] by the rule *cūṭū* (Pāṇini 1.3.7) does not occur here precisely because of the word *bahula* ("diversely").
[This applies to] *ṛterīyaṅ* and the following rules.
The fact that he teaches the suffix *īyaṅ* in the rule "ṛterīyaṅ" [Pāṇini 3.1.29] indicates that āyan and other such suffixes do not apply to verbal roots and suffixes.
For if they did exist, he would have said "ṛteśchaṅ."

Is it not the case that when a rule is commenced for something already established, it serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*)? And yet, *chaṅ* is not established [by such a rule], for if *chaṅ* were present, the augment *iṭ*—characterized by beginning with a consonant (*valādi*)—would necessarily follow; and consequently, because the original form would no longer be the initial element (*anāditvāt*), the substitution (*ādeśa*) would not take place. This is not so; because, due to its being an internal operation (*antaraṅgatvāt*), the substitution must indeed occur first.
Its status as an internal operation is due to the fact that it is prescribed at the very stage of the original instruction (*upadeśāvasthā*).
Once the substitution has been made, there is no occasion for *iṭ* because the condition of beginning with a consonant (*valāditva*) no longer exists.
This statement of his serves as an indicator (*jñapaka*) for rules such as "after the root *ej*, the suffix *khaś*.
The word "but" (*tu*) is intended to demonstrate the distinction from words such as *śaṅkha* and *ṣaṇḍha*.

Where this *itsaṃjñā* (the designation "it") does not exist—as in the case of *śaṅkha* and so forth—since there would be the contingency of substitution (*ādeśaprasaṅga*), the statement "bahulam" (diversely) is introduced for the purpose of excluding that. Thus, the option (*vāvacana*) is presented [in Pāṇini 3.1.29]. However, in cases such as [Pāṇini 3.2.28], since the *itsaṃjñā* must apply by [Pāṇini 1.3.8], there is no contingency of substitution at all. Therefore, the statement "bahulam" is not required there to prevent that [substitution]; rather, the option "vā" should be introduced in the rule "ṛterīyaṅ" (Pāṇini 3.1.29). This is the intended meaning.
By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), rules such as *priyavaśe vadaḥ khac* [Pāṇini 3.2.38] and *khac* [3.3.118] are included.

It might be argued: "The prescription of the substitutes *kh* and *gh* is without scope; therefore, since the designation *it* would be sublated by that [prescription], how could it apply here? To this he says: "In a taddhita suffix," etc.

The prescription of the short vowel [in *khac*] by [Pāṇini 6.3.66] and the prescription of *kutva* [the change of *kh* to *k*] by [7.3.52] are the indicators (*jñāpaka*). For if the designation *it* were sublated by the prescription of the substitute, those [rules] would not be possible; for a suffix marked with *kh* or *gh* is absolutely impossible [if the *it*-designation were blocked].
Regarding the rule "āyannīnornakārasya" and so forth:

since the letter *n* occurs at the end of the suffixes *āyan*, *īn*, and *ūn*, it would incur the designation *it* by [Pāṇini 1.3.3]. Once that designation is applied, by [Pāṇini 1.3.9], forms such as *nāḍāyanaḥ* and *āḍhakulīnaḥ* would not be established.
Therefore, when the designation *it* is about to apply to the *n* of *āyan*, *īn*, and *ūn*, a counter-exception must be made.
This might be the case:
[one could argue] that the designation *itsaṃjñā* will not occur simply because there is no purpose for it? To this he says: "For the sake of the *nit*-designation," and so forth.
That, moreover, results in the acute accent (*udātta*) by rule P. 6.1.197.

Furthermore, the counter-argument here is that the addition of the indicatory letter *n* (nakārānubandha) to the suffix *phin* in the rule *prācām avṛddhāt phin bahulam* [Pāṇini 4.1.160] serves a specific purpose: namely, that because it is marked with *n*, it should be accented on its first syllable (*ādyudāttatva*) due to its being *nit*. In that case, if the *n* of the suffixes *āyan* and *īn* were also subject to the designation *it*, then since the initial accent would already be established by their status as *nit*, the marking of *phin* as *nit* would be rendered purposeless.

[Objection: Is it not the case that the mention of *nanu* [in Pāṇini 4.1.149] is for the purpose of including the general term *nanu*, so that in its absence, by the paribhāṣā "the one without an *anubandha* is understood," only this [suffix *phiñ*] would be grasped and not *phiñ*? [Reply: This is not so; for there, because of the continued application of the word *bahulam* in the rule *vṛddhāṭ ṭhak sauvīreṣu bahulam* [Pāṇini 4.1.148], the inclusion of *phiñ* alone is intended, not *phin*. Therefore, this very addition of the marker *n* to *phin* is indeed an indicator (*jñāpaka*) of the absence of the *it*-designation [for the *ph*].
And this [mention of] the *yogapakṣa* is an indicator (*jñāpaka*) that the *it*-designation does not apply to the *n* which belongs to a substitute (*ādeśa*) prescribed by this rule (*yoga*).

By this, it is established that even for the *n* in *inu*, the absence of the *it*-designation does not occur. "The term *pratyaya* (suffix) is understood as a carry-over" means from the immediately preceding rule.

If this were so, then because they are taught in a single grammatical connection (*ekayoga*), the inclusion of the word "beginning" (*ādi*) would also carry over; consequently, in the rule *śayāntaiḥ*, [the suffix] would not apply, since the letter *c* is not at the beginning. To this he says: "The inclusion of 'beginning' has ceased. He thinks as follows: the continued application (*anuvṛtti*) of words is indeed dependent upon their being marked with a *svarita* accent. And that *svarita* quality is a property of formal agreement (*pratijñā*), according to the principle: "The followers of Pāṇini agree upon the *svarita*. That *svarita* quality occurs only where it is formally agreed upon by them, and not elsewhere.
Therefore, it is not contradictory for one [term] from among those taught in a single *yoga* (sūtra) to continue [into subsequent rules].
And here, it is only the *pratyaya* (suffix) that is declared to have the *svarita* accent, not the mention of the word *ādi* ("beginning with").
Consequently, even though they are taught in a single *yoga*, the term *pratyaya-grahaṇa* continues [to apply].
"The mention of 'ādi' (beginning) is withdrawn," meaning "this substitute [ant] occurs in place of the end. Thus,
the substitute must be performed together with the vowel *a*.
The letter *a* [is used] for the purpose that there should not be the designation *it*. This applies in cases such as *jarantaḥ* and *veśantaḥ*.
In forms such as *kurvanti*, the designation *it* does not occur precisely because of the prohibition [stated in] 1.3.4.

But then, by the rule *atha tu* (P. 3.3.1), would [the substitution] not occur in forms such as *jarantaḥ* and *veśantaḥ*? Furthermore, the pronunciation of the vowel *a* is either for the purpose of easy articulation (*uccāraṇārtha*) according to the principle that "the letter *a* is for the sake of pronunciation" (P. 1.3.4), or for the purpose of indicating the non-eternality (*anityatva*) of that rule. Consequently, in rules such as *tena kimo't* (P. 5.3.12), the letter *t* receives the designation *it*.
Regarding "kurvanti," the substitution of *u* occurs by the rule "ata utsārvadhātuke" [Pāṇini 6.4.110]. Regarding "śayāntai," [the same applies].

From *śīṅ* [Pāṇini 3.4.7], [Pāṇini 3.4.94] applies the augment *āṭ*; the final vowel becomes *e* [Pāṇini 3.4.82]; while *eta ai* [Pāṇini 3.4.93] is being carried over, *vaito'nyatra* [Pāṇini 3.4.96] applies the substitution of *ai*. Regarding the form *ujjhitā*: from the root *ujjha* meaning "to abandon" (Dhātupāṭha 1304), the suffix *tṛc* is applied.

The suffix *anaṅ* is applied by [Pāṇini 7.1.94] *ṛduśanas*, etc., and the lengthening of the vowel occurs by [Pāṇini 6.4.8] *sarvanāmasthāne ca*. Regarding the form *ujjhitum*, it is the infinitive suffix *tumun*.
"It must be abandoned"—
this is the suffix *tavya*.
"In this case too," and so forth.

But surely, because it is *antaraṅga*, the acute accent on the beginning of the suffix (*pratyayādyudātta*) ought to occur first, and only afterwards the substitution (*ādeśa*)? It is not so; for the final substitution (*antādeśa*) is also *antaraṅga*. Its status as *antaraṅga* should be understood in the same way as that of [the suffixes] *āyan*, *ādin*, and so forth. Since both are *antaraṅga*, does the final substitution occur first, and afterwards the acute accent on the beginning of the suffix?

Regarding this very point, he states the proof: "And thus," and so forth. This has been explained by the commentary on the statement: "In this way, the addition of the *cit* marker to the suffix *ghac* [in Pāṇini 4.4.117] would be rendered purposeless. Because of the acute accent (*udātta*) on the beginning of the suffix, when the substitution of the final syllable (*anta-adeśa*) occurs previously, there is an acute accent on the middle syllable in the word *dviṣanti*; otherwise, there would be an acute accent on the final syllable.

And since that [substitution] is undesirable, the substitution of the final letter (anta-ādeśa) is performed first. This undertaking is for the sake of non-reflexive endings (*anātmanepada*); for in the case of reflexive endings (*ātmanepada*), it would already be established by the subsequent rule. In the form *dadati*, there is the elision of the long *ā* by the rule *śnābhyāstayorātaḥ* [Pāṇini 6.4.112].
In *dadatu*,
the *loṭ* [imperative] suffix undergoes the substitution of *u* by [Pāṇini 3.4.86] *eruḥ*.
In *jakṣati* and *jāgrati*, the designation *abhyasta* (repeated) applies by [Pāṇini 6.1.6].

The examples beginning with *jakṣiti* are appropriate, but those beginning with *dadati* are inappropriate. Here, immediately after the letter *jh* acquires its own existence (*ātmalābha*), the substitution of *at* must occur because it is internal (*antaraṅga*). Following that, there is the *ślu* replacement of *śap*, then reduplication by the rule *ślau* [P. 6.1.10], and then the designation *abhyasta*. At that point, since the original element (*sthānin*) *jh* no longer exists, the substitution of *at* does not apply. Nor can it be argued that it will occur through the status of being "as if the original" (*sthānivadbhāva*);
for in this case, there is no *sthānivadbhāva* because it is not a rule conditioned by an *al* (phoneme).

Nor is it reasonable to assume that the substitution of *ad* will occur by superseding the substitution of the final letter (*antādeśa*) on the grounds that [the former] lacks scope; for that [substitution of *ad*] already finds its scope in cases such as *jakṣ*, where the designation *abhyasta* is acquired precisely at the stage of the original instruction (*upadeśāvasthā*). To refute this objection, he says: "This is an exception (*apavāda*) to the substitution of the final letter.
This substitution of *ad* is introduced as an exception to the substitution of the final letter, which would otherwise apply universally everywhere.
Furthermore, a general rule does not apply to that which is the domain of an exception.
As it has been said: "Exceptions operate first, and general rules afterwards; having excluded the domain of the exception, the general rule operates" (Puṣpapañjikā 56).
For this very reason, then, the substitution of *jus* would not occur.

Just as the substitution of *ad* for *han*, which applies generally, is superseded by the specific rule introducing the substitution of *abh* as an exception (*apavāda*), so too is it with the substitution of *jut*. Thus he says: "But it is superseded by the substitution of *jus*. Because the substitution of *jus* is without scope (*anavakāśa*), the substitution of *ad* is superseded; as in the example *adaduḥ*.

In *laṅ*, the suffix *jhi* is replaced by *jus* according to *sijabhyastavidhibhyaśca* [Pāṇini 3.4.109]. Regarding *ajāgaruḥ*: although the root *jāgarti* would otherwise undergo *guṇa* substitution, that is prohibited by another rule, *aviciṇṇalṅitsu* [Pāṇini 7.3.85]; nevertheless, *guṇa* is applied here by the rule *jusica* [Pāṇini 7.3.83].

"In this case as well, when the substitution has been made, the acute accent (udātta) falls on the beginning of the suffix"—this is the meaning [of the rule]. Consequently, words such as *punataḥ* become middle-accented (*madhyodātta*).

However, if the reverse were the case, then because the acute accent on the beginning of the suffix would apply first due to its being an internal operation (*antaraṅga*), the substitution of *ā* for the mere consonant being prescribed would result in an indefinite accentuation.

In that case, if it were *anudātta*, then the word beginning with *punataḥ* would incur the fault of having its final syllable accented (*antodāttatā*). When it is *svarita*, however, a middle *svarita* accent or a middle *udātta* accent is desired.

Now, one might object: the initial accentuation of the suffix (*pratyayādyudāttatva*) is *antaraṅga* because it depends solely on the suffix, whereas the substitute (*ādeśa*) is *bahiraṅga* because it depends upon both the base (*prakṛti*) and the suffix.

According to the rule *antaraṅgabahiraṅgayor antaraṅgaṃ balīyaḥ* (Vyāḍi-paribhāṣā 94), it would be proper for the acute accent on the beginning of the suffix to occur first, and the substitution (*ādeśa*) only afterwards; so how can it be said that "the acute accent on the beginning of the suffix occurs after the substitution has been made"? This is not so, for it has been stated: "The instruction should be treated as if it were original (*upadeśivat*). Furthermore, the substitution is permanent (*nitya*), because it applies whether [the accent] has already occurred or not; whereas the acute accent on the beginning of the suffix, once the substitution has been made, is non-permanent, since another form of the word (*śabdāntara*) is obtained.

Likewise, when the substitution of *ad* for *hrakṛta* has not yet occurred, the substitution of *i* for *jhi* would apply; whereas once the substitution of *ad* for *sva* has occurred, the substitution of *ā* applies. According to the rule, "A grammatical operation that applies upon the occurrence of another word-form is non-eternal" (*Vyāḍipāda* 106), and by the principle, "Between an eternal and a non-eternal operation, the eternal is stronger" (*Vyāḍipāda* 93), this [substitution of *ā*] possesses greater force.

Therefore, because these two are both strong due to their eternality, the substitution of *ad* must occur first on account of its priority, and subsequently, the acute accent (*udātta*) of the initial syllable of the suffix.
Therefore, it has been well said: "When the substitution [of *śn*] is made, the acute accent (*udātta*) falls on the beginning of the suffix. Regarding "cincete":
this is the present tense (*laṭ*), and the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) occurs because of the *svarita* accent.
Regarding "cinvatām": [this is the imperative].
In *leṭ*, there is the substitution of *at* for *jhaḥ* by [Pāṇini 3.4.97], and *āma* replaces *taḥ* by [3.4.90]. Regarding *acinvata*:
this is *laṅ*; with the augment *aṭ* added, the substitution of *yaṇ* occurs by [6.1.77].
In *punate* and *lunate*,
the vowel *ā* is elided as before;
[the forms] *cyavante* and *plavante* [are likewise].

In this case, once the *śap* suffix has been applied, the letter *jha* does not follow an *aṅga* (verbal base) that ends in a non-*a* vowel. Now, one might object: "Since it is subsequent, should not the substitution of *ad* occur first, and only afterwards the *vikaraṇa*? To this, he says: "Because of its necessity (*nityatva*), it is not that" and so forth.
Its necessity, however, arises from the fact that it applies regardless of whether [the other rule] has already taken effect or not.

For the *vikaraṇa* applies whether the substitution of *at* has been made or not; however, when that [substitution] has been made, there is no occurrence of the state of being *at*, and thus this [rule] is non-eternal (*anitya*). Regarding the phrase "by that which does not end in *a*" and so forth:
why is the suffix not qualified by the stem (*aṅga*) that does not end in *a*? Thinking thus, he says "here" and so forth.
If the suffix were specified as *jha*, then [the rule] would also apply here in the case of *śayāntam*, because even here the suffix *jha* follows an *aṅga* that does not end in *an*.
If it is argued that [the rule] does not apply because it is separated by *āṭ*, we say no; for since *āṭ* is a part (*bhakta*) of that [suffix], a separation by a portion of it is not logical.
However, if *jha* is specified, there is no fault, because [the suffix] is indeed separated by *āṭ*.

The *hrāṭ* [augment] is a part of the whole (*samudāyabhakta*); it would not obstruct the whole itself, but it certainly obstructs the individual constituent (*avayava*). For indeed, one part is never observed to be non-obstructive of another part.

Although it could have been stated as "after *taṅ*, after *yan*, after *anataḥ*" or "after *jha*, after *anataḥ*", the formulation "in the *ātmanepada*s, after *anataḥ*" is for the sake of variety. [The meaning is: "the augment *ruṭ* occurs after the *āt* that is a substitute for *jha*."

But is it not the case that there is no explicit mention of *āt* here? Even that which is under discussion (the subject of the rule) ends in the nominative case, whereas the meaning here is expressed by a genitive indication (*ṣaṣ�ṭhī-nirdeśa*). Therefore, how can it be understood that the augment *ruṭ* occurs after the *āt* that is the substitute for *jha*? This is not so; because of the rule *śīṅo 't* [Pāṇini 1.1.6], this fifth-case [ablative] form *śīṅaḥ* will be treated as if it were a sixth-case [genitive] in relation to the first-case [nominative] form *at*. Thus, there is no fault. Regarding the form *śerate*: [it is derived] by the rule *śīṅaḥ sārvadhātuke guṇaḥ* [Pāṇini 7.4.21].

But surely, in this case, the *sārvadhātuka* suffix is separated by the *ruṭ* augment; so how can there be *guṇa* substitution? Is it not the case that this [augment] does not belong to the *sārvadhātuka*? How then could it not be an intervening element? [Answer: It is not an intervening element because it is part of the word-element *ac*, which itself is a constituent of the *sārvadhātuka*; thus, it is included by the mention of that [element *ac*], but not by the mention of the *sārvadhātuka* as a whole. For a constituent of a constituent is not a constituent of the aggregate.
For instance, it was stated under [Pāṇini 6.1.73] *che ca*: "A part of a part is not a part of the whole. This is not a fault; even a part of a part is indeed a part of the whole.
For example, when it is said, "Let Devadatta be adorned," those parts of Devadatta such as his hands and feet, and even their parts such as the fingers and so forth, are adorned.

Therefore? Since the augment *ru* is a part of the letter *ac* which is itself a part of a *sārvadhātuka* [affix], that *ru* is also considered a part of the *sārvadhātuka*; thus, it is included by the mention of that [term], and consequently there is no intervention. As for what was stated regarding the rule *che ca* [Pāṇini 6.1.71]—that "a part of a part does not become a part of the whole"—that was said with reference specifically to the *tug* augment prescribed by that sūtra, on the grounds that even though the *tug* is a part of a part, it is not included by the mention of the whole. Why, then, is it not included? Because of the force of the attraction (*anukarṣaṇa*) of the short vowel (*hrasva*).

For in that rule, the word *hrasva* (short vowel) is drawn forward by the particle *ca*—so that the status of being an augment (*āgama*) may belong to the short vowel alone, and not to that which ends in a short vowel. If the status of being an augment belonged to that which ends in a short vowel, then in forms such as *cicchidatuḥ* and *cicchiduḥ*, the augment *tuk* would be included by the mention of the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*), and its removal would consequently occur through the rule *halādiśeṣaḥ*. Furthermore, if a part of the *tuk* prescribed by that rule were not included by the mention of the whole [reduplicated syllable], then even if the status of being an augment belonged to the short vowel alone, its removal by *halādiśeṣa* would still occur; for the *tuk* which is a part of the short vowel would be included by the mention of the reduplicated syllable.
Furthermore, the inclusion of the short vowel [in the rule] would be purposeless.

Now, for what reason is *ruṅ* prescribed for the substitute *ad*, rather than being prescribed for *jhak*? In that case, the meaning would be this: the genitive case in *ataḥ* would not need to be supplied, because *jhaḥ* is already present as a genitive form in the context. To this he says: "This *ruṅ*," and so forth.

If the letter *k* were taken as an *anubandha* (indicatory letter) and the substitute were made to end with the preceding element (*pūrvānta*), then in the form *śerate*, the *guṇa* substitution would not occur, because the root would no longer end in *i*.

Therefore, so that this fault may not occur, the augment *ruṭ* is made to follow the initial [of the suffix]. But even if it is made to follow the initial, if it were to belong only to the letter *jha*, what undesirable consequence would there be? To this he says: "If," and so forth.
If *ruṭ* were to belong only to the letter *jha*, then the substitution of *ad* would not take place.

Consequently, just as in the case of *śayānte*—where, because it is separated by the augment *āṭ*, the substitution of *ad* does not occur—so too it would not occur in *śerate*, since it is separated by *ruṭ*.

Therefore, for the sake of avoiding this fault, some explain that the augment *ru* is prescribed specifically for [the letter] *a*, and not for the letter *jha*; however, this is incorrect. If the augment *ru* were applied to the letter *jha*, it would become a part (*bhakta*) of that very [letter]; so how could there be an intervention by it? For one does not intervene by means of one's own constituent part.

Therefore, this is an incorrect explanation and is explained otherwise: [the phrase] "there would be no substitution of *at*" requires the word "of *jh*. Thus, the meaning becomes this: if the augment *ruṭ* were to belong to *jh* alone, then the substitution of *at* would not apply to that very [element]. To what, then, would it apply? It would apply to that very *ruṭ*; for according to the rule [Pāṇini 1.1.54], even though it consists of more than one phoneme (*anekāl*), it does not become a substitute for the whole [stem], because it would result in the *ruṭ* being rendered meaningless.

If it is argued that *ruṭ* will not occur because of the force of the rule [itself], this is not so; the prescription of *ruṭ* would be for the sake of the subsequent rule. [In the rule] "rujāgamo yathā syāt" (so that the augment *ruj* may occur) under [Pāṇini 7.4.78], it would not be established by the suffix *aṭ* in the case of forms such as *ahṛt*, *adrākṣīt*, and *aśrauṣīt*.

Therefore, the purpose of the rule for *ru* is the hearing of the suffix *jha*. To exclude this defect, *ru* is prescribed for the substitute [of *jha*], and not for the original *akāra*. The mention of the *anubandha* "śīṅ" is for the sake of excluding the *yaṅ*-lopa (the elision of *yaṅ*), as in *vyatiśeśyata*. [Examples are] *saṃvidrate*, *saṃvidate*.
The root *vid* means "to know" (*dhātupāṭha* 1064).
The middle voice (*ātmanepada*) is applied according to the rule *samobhyṛcchi* [Pāṇini 1.3.29], and because it belongs to the *adādi* class, there is elision of the *śap* suffix.
Thus we have the forms *saṃvidratām* and *saṃvidatām*.
In the imperative (*loṭ*), once the substitution of *et* for *i* has been applied, the suffix *ām* is added by the rule *āmetaḥ* [Pāṇini 3.4.90]. [The question is:
"Why is there a mention of *vetti* as having the *luk*-suffixation?"

He thinks as follows: "By the general mention of *vidhi* (the suffix *vid*), let there be the inclusion of all [roots] having that suffix; for in this way the rule (*sūtra*) becomes concise. Even if all roots having the suffix *vid* were included, the operation will occur only after those with the *luṅ*-class suffix (*lug-vikaraṇa*), and not from any other, because of the intervention by the suffix (*vikaraṇa*). If the inclusion of *vid* roots were without distinction, would it apply even to the root *vid* in the sense of 'investigation' belonging to the *raudhādika* class? It would, for here the suffix is not an intervening element, since it is contained within the body of the root. To this, he says: "In this case," and so forth.
Regarding the forms *vinte*, *vindāte*, and *vindate*:
because the root is marked with an anudātta vowel, the ātmanepada suffixes are applied according to Pāṇini 1.3.12.
However, in this context, *vindate* is cited as a counter-example in the plural form.

The presentation of the singular and dual forms is for the purpose of demonstrating that this is the form of the root *vid* in the sense of "investigating" (*vicāraṇā*). Otherwise, if only "vindate" were stated, someone might mistakenly think that this is the singular form of the root *vid* in the sense of "obtaining" (*lābha*). Due to the mention of the *śtip* affix, [the substitution] does not occur when there is the elision of *yaṅ*: as in *saṃvevidate* and *vyativevidate*.
Regarding the form *aduhya*:
the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) occurs because of the rule for the root *svarita*.

Now, one might object: "Since the term *vibhāṣā* (optionally) continues to apply, forms such as *aduhyata* are already established; what is the purpose of the statement 'bahulam' (diversely)? To this, he replies with the words beginning "Because of the statement *bahulam*."
For by following the rule of *vibhāṣā*, only an option (*vikalpa*) is obtained, and it does not apply elsewhere;
however, because of the statement "frequently" (*bahula*), it does apply elsewhere as well.
Therefore, the sense is that when *vibhāṣā* is the subject under discussion, there is the principle of "frequent occurrence."

Regarding the form *adṛśran*: it is the *luṅ* (aorist) of the root *dṛś*, with *an* as the substitute for *jhi*. By the rule *irito vāṭ* [Pāṇini 3.1.57], *cleraṅ* is applied, and *ruṭ* is added to it. Then, by *itaśca* [3.4.100], there is the elision of the *ikāra*; and by *saṃyogantasya* [8.2.23], there is also the elision of the *takāra*. By *pararūpatvam* [6.1.97], the subsequent single substitute is formed. Now, why does not *guṇa* occur here by the rule *ṛvṛśoraṅi* [7.4.16]? If you say it is because of the prohibition [by *na dhātulopa ārdhadhātuke* 1.1.4], that is not so; for that [prohibition] is prescribed only when a *ṅit* affix follows.

If it is argued that a prohibition applies by depending on the *ṅit* suffix of the *sārvadhātuka*, [the author] says no; for one might object that "a single substitute (*ekādeśa*) is treated as the original (*sthānivat*) in a rule concerning what precedes it," and in response to such an objection, he states: "There is *guṇa* for *ṛ* and *ṛś* before *aṅ*. The inclusion of the word *bahula* (variously) is for the sake of clarity, for it is possible to carry forward the application of *bahula* by means of the "frog-leap" maxim (*maṇḍūkapluti-nyāya*). The two [suffixes] which lack the letter *k* are *tavak* and *mak*.
"By these" refers to them.

This is the substitution of *at* for *adas* (i.e., *adaḥ* becomes *ataḥ*). Then, by the rule "in the plural, when followed by a *jhal* consonant, *e* is substituted" (*bahuvacane jhalyet*), the substitution of *e* occurs; subsequently, by the rule "the elision of *i* and *u*" (*iṇaḥ ṣaḥ*), there is the elision of the form *i*.
Thus we have *amībhiḥ*.
Once the substitution of *e* for *adas* has been made, the substitution of *it* occurs by the rule "for *e*, *īt* is substituted in the plural" (*eta īdavahuvacane*), and the *d* is changed to *m*.
Regarding "imakaiḥ":

the suffix *akac* is applied by [Pāṇini 5.3.71] *avyayasarvanāmnām akac prāk ṭeḥ*, and the substitution of *m* for the letter *d* is applied by [Pāṇini 7.2.109] *daś ca*. Regarding "amukaiḥ": [the same process applies].
Having applied the substitution of *u* for *o* by the rule *adaso'sordādu do maḥ* [Pāṇini 8.2.80], one might ask:

why was it not simply stated as *nedamadasoḥ* (not after *idam* or *adas*)? What is the purpose of the word *akoḥ*? If it is argued that if *akoḥ* were not mentioned, the prohibition would apply even to the forms containing the letter *k* (such as *akac*), the answer is: this is not so. For when the prohibition is stated for *idam* and *adas*, what possibility is there for it to apply to those forms containing *k*, since they are different words? It is said—starting with *akorityetat*—that the purpose of the indicator (*jñāpaka*) is that the designation of pronoun (*sarvanāman*) applies to *sarva* and the others even when they take the suffix *akac*, and the designation of indeclinable (*avyaya*) applies to *svar* and the others.

Now, why was it not stated as "kādidamadasoḥ" (the *kā* [suffix] follows *idam* and *adas*)? In that case, since the desired result would already be established by the previous rule (*Pāṇini 7.1.27*), this new formulation would serve as a restrictive rule (*niyama*): "Of the *bhis* suffix related to *idam* and *adas*, the *ais* substitution occurs only when it follows *kā*. If understood in this way as a restriction, everything intended would indeed be established, and the sūtra would be more concise. True, this is so; however, with such an arrangement of the sūtra, the principle "that which falls within a certain scope is included by the mention of that scope" (*tanmadhyapatitastadgrahaṇena gṛhyate*) would not have been indicated.
Even a reversed restriction might be suspected by those of dull intellect—that [the substitution] occurs only for *idam* and *adas*.

In that case, this would be the meaning of the restriction: "For the *ka*-sound which belongs only to *idam* and *adas*, the following *bhis* becomes *ais*. Consequently, [the substitution] would not occur in *viākaiḥ* or *sarvakaiḥ*, because it has been excluded by the restriction.

And in this case, there would indeed be the forms "ebhiḥ" and "amībhiḥ," because [the rule] has not been restricted by a fixed limitation. Therefore, let it remain exactly as in the original formulation: "atijarasinā," and so forth.
As before? When the compound has been formed and shortening has occurred, the substitution of *jaras* takes place. "Some" refers to those who follow the opinion of the author of the *Sūtras*.
If *hrasvasya guṇaḥ* were not intended by the author of the Sūtras as being correct, he would have simply prescribed the substitute *ṭa* for *ṭā*.

Even so, once the substitution of *et* has been applied, forms such as *vṛkṣeṇa* are established. If it is asked how this substitution of *et* occurs, the rule for *et* will be formulated through a split of the yoga (*yogavibhāga*).

This is the sequence: first, "bahuvacane jhalyet" [Pāṇini 7.3.103], then "osi ca" [7.3.104], and then "āṅi ca" [7.3.105]. In this context, a *yogavibhāga* (separation of rules) must be made for the term "āṅi": when the suffix *āṅ* follows, the substitution of *e* occurs for the final vowel of the stem—as in *vṛkṣeṇa*, *plakṣeṇa*; thereafter, the rule "āpaḥ" [7.3.106] applies.

But surely, if the substitution of *na* does not occur, then the elision of the form *idam* before a consonant (*hal*) would apply, and consequently, forms such as *anena* would not be established? This is not a fault. In the rule [Pāṇini 7.2.113], the term *anyatarasyām* from [Pāṇini 7.2.101] is understood to carry over; and that is understood as a restricted option (*vyavasthitavibhāṣā*). Therefore, when the substitution of *na* has been made, the elision of the form *idam* does not take place. Thus, by means of the substitution of *na* itself, forms such as *vṛkṣeṇa* are established.

Therefore, that [substitution] alone should be performed, not the substitution of *in*; and since that has been done, it is understood that the form *ati-jarasi-na* was certainly intended by the author of the Sūtra as correct, for the sake of whose establishment he made the substitution of *in*.
Otherwise, if the correctness of *ati-jarasāt* were not desired, why would he have prescribed the substitution of *ad* for the *ṅasi* case-ending?
Even in that case, by the rule "a long vowel replaces a homogeneous vowel" (Pāṇini 6.1.101), forms such as *vṛkṣāt* and so forth would be established just as well.

But surely, since [the rule] *ako 'ki dīrghaḥ* [Pāṇini 6.1.101] is an exception to *akaḥ savarṇe dīrghaḥ* [Pāṇini 6.1.101], would not *pararūpa* (the single substitute of the following form) apply? How is this established? This is not so; by the force of the explicit utterance of the letter *a*, *pararūpa* will not occur; otherwise, he would have prescribed the letter *t* alone.

For here, when the letter *t* is substituted for the letter *a* by *ato guṇe* [Pāṇini 6.1.97], and the final consonant is elided by *saṃyogāntasya lopaḥ* [Pāṇini 8.2.23], forms such as *vṛkṣāt* are indeed established.

For here, when the letter *t* is substituted for the letter *a* by *ato guṇe* [Pāṇini 6.1.97], and the final consonant is elided by *saṃyogāntasya lopaḥ* [Pāṇini 8.2.23], forms such as *vṛkṣāt* are indeed established.

Therefore, since the substitution of the single form (*pararūpa*) would not occur by the force of the utterance of the vowel *a*, the substitution of *āt* must be prescribed; why then prescribe the substitution of *āt*? Since the substitution of *āt* has indeed been prescribed, it is concluded that the author of the Sūtras certainly intended the correctness (*sādhutva*) of the form *atijarasāt*, for which purpose he prescribed the substitution of *āt*.
Following the opinion of the Sūtra-author in this way, some maintain the correctness of both *atijarasinā* and *atijarasāt*.
[The phrase] "But as... and so forth [is explained as follows].

For in the Bhāṣya, within the textual sequence beginning with "Now, for what purpose is the substitute *in* stated? Why should not the substitute *na* alone be stated?", the substitute *in* is rejected and the substitute *na* alone is established. And within the textual sequence beginning with "Now, for what purpose is the substitute *āt* stated? Why should not *ad* be stated?", the substitute *āt* is rejected and the substitute *ad* alone is established. Furthermore, if the correctness of forms such as *atijarasinā* and *atijarasāt* were intended, the author of the Bhāṣya would not have rejected the substitute *in* and the state of being *āt*.

Indeed, when there is a purpose [for a rule], its rejection is not logical; yet, a rejection of those two has been made. Therefore, it is understood that "this is not intended. Regarding the term *ṅeḥ*: this is the inclusion of the singular dative case-ending. Why is the inclusion of the singular locative case-ending not [intended]? For if there were an inclusion of that, then [rules such as] *atyantasaṃyoge*, *bhāve apavarge*, and *kārakamadhye* would not be established.
Therefore, because this is not the mention of the locative singular among these [preceding] mentions,
it is determined by the method of elimination (*pariśeṣya*) that the dative singular is what is being referred to.
Furthermore, due to the indicative mark (*liṅga*) in the rule *iti nirdeśāt*, this very same [dative singular] also carries over (*anuvartate*) in the subsequent [rules].

Regarding the form *vṛkṣāya*: the long vowel [in place of the short *a*] is applied by the rule *supi ca* [Pāṇini 7.3.102]. Now, one might object: since the technical rule (*paribhāṣā*) *sannipātalakṣaṇo vidhir animittaṃ tadvighātasya* (a rule conditioned by a specific phonetic combination does not become the cause for the destruction of that very combination) applies here, the rule for *ya*—being conditioned by a particular phonetic combination—cannot logically serve as the cause for the destruction of the vowel *a*; so how can there be lengthening? To this, he says: "conditioned by a combination," etc. Furthermore, the non-eternality (*anityatva*) of this rule has already been established previously.
Now, for what purpose is the pronunciation of the letter *ṅ*? It is so that there may not be the inclusion of the vowel *e* alone.
If it were otherwise, [the rule] would apply even in cases such as *pace* and *yaj-e*.

But surely, once the single-substitute form (*pararūpa*) has been applied by [Pāṇini 6.1.97], this [substitution] will not occur because the cause for it is absent? This is not so; for this substitution is prescribed when the *guṇa* substitution for *hrasva* (short vowel) has not yet taken effect. Just as it subverts the *pararūpa* in the case of *vṛkṣāya*, it would likewise subvert it in cases such as *pace* and *yaj-e*. If it is argued that it will not occur here because of the mention of the specific *ikāra* (the vowel *i*), [we reply: no, for even this *ikāra* is mentioned specifically. It becomes a specifically mentioned *ikāra* due to the citation in [Pāṇini 3.4.79].
Therefore, the letter *ṅ* must be added for the sake of specification. In the case of "bhavate," the substitution of *yat* for the pronoun stems beginning with *tyad* does not occur.

Because of the rule "the pronouns beginning with *tyad* end in *d* up to *dvi*" (Vārttika 7.2.102), the word *bhavat* lacks the status of being a *tyadādi* pronoun; consequently, it does not undergo the change to an *a*-stem ending.

The objection beginning with "atho atra" is as follows: when *atra* is present, and after the substitution of *aś* by [Pāṇini 2.4.32] *idamo'nvādeśe*, the single-substitute long vowel (*ekādeśa*) prescribed by [Pāṇini 6.1.97] *akaḥ savarṇe dīrghaḥ* would apply, even overriding the subsequent *smai*-substitution because it is obligatory (*nitya*). Its obligatoriness, moreover, stems from the fact that it applies regardless of whether the other rule has already taken effect or not (*kṛtākṛtaprasaṅgitvāt*).

And once the single-substitute (ekādeśa) has been applied, because the word would no longer end in *an*, the substitution of *smai* would not obtain. The refutation begins with "In that case" (*tatra*), etc.: when the single-substitute is about to apply, the substitution of *smai* is prescribed first because it is an internal operation (*antaraṅga*), and the single-substitute follows later.

The status of *smai* as internal (*antaraṅga*) is due to its being based on a single word (*ekapada*), whereas the status of the single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) is external (*bahiraṅga*) because it is based on two words (*dvipada*). The placement of *smai* at the end, when the rule for the prior placement of the shorter word (*ṅeralpāctarasya*) would have applied, is for the sake of variety. This statement serves to provide an option for *smāt* and *smin*, which would have been obligatory by the preceding rule.

But is it not the case that only nine words beginning with *pūrva* are recited in the sūtras [Pāṇini 1.1.34, 1.1.35, and 1.1.36]? Therefore, the mention of "nine" (*nava*) is redundant. This is not so; for here, the words *pūrva* and so on are not taken as they are recited in the sūtras, but rather as they are recited in the *gaṇa* list. Why is this so? Because the designation of "pronoun" (*sarvanāman*) applies to those words as recited in the sūtras only when followed by the suffix *jas*, and not in the cases of *ṅasi* and *ṅi*. The term "*sarvanāmnaḥ*" from [Pāṇini 7.1.14] is understood here [in 7.1.15]. What is the purpose? So that [the substitution of *sva* for *sma*] does not occur in examples such as *vidyamāne sve yajate* ("he sacrifices while his own [property] exists") or *svād bibheti* ("he fears his own").

Therefore, only those [words] such as *pūrva* that are recited in the *gaṇa* (list) are understood here; for if the mention of *nava* were not made there, [the suffixes] would apply even to *tyad* and the others.
Consequently, the mention of *nava* must be made. [Regarding the rule] "of *yuṣmad* and *asmad*":
it means "when distinguished by the sixth case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) and so forth."
The analysis of the compound is as follows: *ṣaṣṭhī-caturthī-dvitīyā-sthau* means "those which stand together with the sixth, fourth, and second [cases].
This refers to those [words] qualified by the sixth case and so forth.
An analysis such as "those which stand when the sixth, fourth, and second cases follow" is not possible, because it would contradict the governing rule (*adhikāra*) of the term *pada*.

The term *padaḥ*, which is understood from the previous rule, is modified by the dual number (*dvivacana*) and serves as a qualifier for the expression "standing in the genitive, dative, or accusative" (*ṣaṣṭhī-caturthī-dvitīyā-sthayoḥ*). For the substitution of *ṣ* does not occur when followed by the genitive and other such case-endings; even though it exists in the case of *bhyām* and so forth, it is absent elsewhere, such as in the accusative and other cases.
The purpose of including the term *sthā* will be explained in the rule itself. This [sūtra] is commenced because the [substitution of] *vṛddhi* would otherwise apply by [Pāṇini 7.3.102].
In the expression *auṅaḥ*, there is a general inclusion of both the dual endings of the nominative (*prathamā*) and accusative (*dvitīyā*).
In the expression *āpaḥ*, there is an inclusion of the feminine suffixes *ṭāp*, *ḍāp*, and *cāp*.

Regarding "khaṭve": the suffix *ṭāp* [Pāṇini 4.1.4] applies because the word begins with a vowel and ends in *a*. The presentation of the auxiliary verbs (*anuprayoga*) "tiṣṭhati" and "paśya" in their respective order is intended to demonstrate that they end in the nominative and accusative cases respectively; otherwise, since the form would be identical in both instances as "khaṭve," there would be doubt regarding the specific case endings such as the nominative. Regarding "bahurāje."
The term *karīṣagandhī* is a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "one whose scent is like that of dried cow-dung," with the suffix *ic* applied according to Pāṇini 5.4.137.
From this, the patronymic suffix *aṇ* is added to form *kāriṣagandha*, which undergoes the substitution of *ṣyaṅ* for *aṇ* and *iñ* according to Pāṇini 4.1.78,
and finally the feminine suffix *cāp* is applied according to Pāṇini 4.1.74.
Regarding the phrase "this [vowel] *au*," and so forth:

in the rule for the application of *śī*, the meaning is that this vowel *au* is the substitute (*sthānin*) which is grasped as having the marker *ṅ*— that is, it is taken as being accompanied by the indicatory letter *ṅ*.

That which has *ṅ* as its indicatory letter (*ṅit*) is called *ṅit*. According to our grammarians, the vowel *au* does not exist in the technical treatise (*śāstra*). Therefore, what kind of form is this? The word *kim* is used here in the sense of censure.
The meaning is that this manner of composing the sūtra is contemptible.
Its contemptibility, however, arises from the inclusion of something that is non-existent.

By way of demonstrating the purpose for attaching the letter *ṅ*, he states "for the sake of the general meaning" (*sāmānyārthaḥ*) in order to refute the contemptibility of the composition of the sūtra.

If the syllable *hrau* were taken as the substituendum (*sthānin*) without its indicatory letter (*anubandha*), then, according to the rule "when a form without an indicatory letter is mentioned, that which possesses an indicatory letter is not included" (Vyāḍi-Pāṇini 53), the dual of the second case would not be grasped. On the other hand, if the letter *ṭ* were attached as an indicatory letter to *tsa*, even so, the dual of the first case would not be grasped. Therefore, the letter *ṅ* is appended so that there may be the inclusion of both [the first and second case duals] by way of their commonality.

But surely, the letter *yaṣ* [the *ya* and *ṣ*] in the dual ending of the second case (*au*) is not an *anubandha* (indicatory letter) belonging to that [suffix] alone; to what, then, does it belong? It belongs to the entire group (*samudāya*). For those *anubandhas* which serve the purpose of indicating [a grammatical operation] are understood to be *anubandhas* of the group as a whole, such as the *ṅ* in *mahiṅ* and the *p* in *sup*. Therefore, when there is a mention of a suffix without an *anubandha*, since both [the *ya* and *ṣ*] are *anubandhas*, will there not be a general inclusion [of both endings]? What is the use of the *ṅ*? This is not so; for even when they function as *anubandhas* of the group, their status as *anubandhas* of the individual components is also admitted.
For being an *anubandha* (indicatory letter) of a composite whole does not contradict being an *anubandha* of a suffix.
An *anubandha* is indeed said to be designated as *hat* (the "killer"), and it is established that the final letter of a *hal* (consonant) receives the designation *it*.
And just as the letter *ṭ* in *auṭ* is the final member with respect to the composite whole, so too is it the final member with respect to the suffix.

Therefore? When the technical designation *it* has been prescribed for that [suffix], just as it is an *anubandha* (indicatory letter) with respect to the entire complex, so too is it with respect to the suffix.

If it is argued that its status as an *anubandha* of the suffix is untenable due to a lack of purpose, we say no; there is indeed a purpose here: namely, that the second dual suffix should possess an *anubandha*.

If, then, it is accompanied by an indicatory letter (*anubandha*), then even though the letter *ṅ* is attached, there would be the apprehension of only the dual number in the nominative case—according to the rules "when there is the mention of that which has a specific indicatory letter, there is no [apprehension] of that which does not have that indicatory letter" (Vyāḍiparibhāṣā 54) and "when there is the mention of that which has one indicatory letter, there is no [apprehension] of that which has two indicatory letters" (Vyāḍiparibhāṣā 52); for in that [nominative dual], the *ṅ* alone is the single indicatory letter.

But in the dual number of the accusative case, there is also the letter *ṭ* as well? This is not a fault, because by the force of the pronunciation of the letter *ṅ*, the dual number of the accusative case will also be apprehended.

Since the first dual ending alone would have been understood even without the letter *ṅ*, the letter *ṅ* is taught for the sake of generalization (*sāmānyārtha*). If, despite the presence of *ṅ*, only the first dual were understood, then the letter *ṅ* would be useless.

But how can this letter *ṅ* receive the technical designation *it*, given that the rule "the final consonant (*hal*) in an original enunciation (*upadeśa*)" prescribes the *it*-designation, and this [letter *ṅ*] is not the final one in the enunciation? Or, let it be that it receives the *it*-designation; however, then the *ṭ* of *auṭ* would not [be an *it*]. How could there be two finals in a single enunciation? This is not a fault, because of the explicit mention of *auṅ*.

This substitution *auṅ* is understood to apply to both instances of the vowel *au*; and its instruction (*upadeśa*) exists, just as in the rule "for *cakṣiṅ*, [substitute] *khyāñ*" (Pāṇini 2.4.54), where the letter *ñ* is final in the instruction. Just as that [letter *ñ*] receives the designation *it*, so too does the letter *ṅ*.

As for the letter *ṭ*, however, its designation as *it* and its subsequent elision have already been performed in due order; thus there is no fault. Furthermore, it should be understood that this very substitute vowel *au* is taken as the substituendum (*sthānin*) for the word *śobhāṣasya*.

With the words "And of that" (*tasya ca*) and so forth, he demonstrates the fault that arises from the attachment of the letter *ṅ*. "Attachment" (*āsañjanam*) is the inclusion of the letter *ṅ* as an *anubandha* (indicatory letter).

Regarding the expression "the operation when there is *ṅ*" (*ṅiti yat*), the compound "the operation of *ṅ*" (*ṅitkāryam*) is formed by splitting the rule [Pāṇini 2.1.39] "The locative case" (*saptamī*) into separate rules (*yogavibhāga*).
Therefore, that [operation] must be performed: the augment *āṭ* by the rule *yāḍāpaḥ* [Pāṇini 7.3.113].

If this *ṅ* is attached for the sake of a general purpose, then, given that attachment of the *ṅ*, whatever operation applies to a *ṅit* [element] would, according to your—the Sūtrakāra’s—view, become applicable (*prasakta*) to *śī*. That is the fault.
If the augment *yāṭ* were applied by the rule *yāḍāpaḥ* [7.3.113], the form *khaṭve* would not be established.

Therefore, how could *śyām* and so forth be [treated as] *ām-vṛddhi* [cases]? And why would they not be so? Because they are not *nadī*s (feminine stems ending in /ī/ or /ū/). And why are they not *nadī*s? Because that word (*śyām*) is designated as feminine (*stryākhya*). This is not the case; for just as words such as *khaṭvā* denote the feminine, so too does the word *śī*. Thus says the author of the *Liṅgakārikā*: "That which ends in /ī/ or /ū/ and is monosyllabic, as well as *śarat*, *darat*, *ṛṣat*, and *prāvṛṣ*. Therefore, because it denotes the feminine, this too is indeed designated as a *nadī*; for there is grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the [word] *strī* (feminine).
The word *śī*, occurring in the *śruti* (the original phonetic form), receives the designation *nadī*.
*Śruti* refers to the very form itself. [This applies] in the case of [the rule] "when there is the marker *ṅ*" (*ṅittve*), and so forth.
In the rule *yāḍāpaḥ* [Pāṇini 7.3.113], the term *ṅit* is understood by anuvṛtti from the preceding rule *dherṅiti* [Pāṇini 7.3.111].

In this context, *ṅit* is not a bahuvrīhi compound meaning "that which has *ṅ* as its *it*" (i.e., whose indicatory letter is *ṅ*); rather, it is a tatpuruṣa compound: *ṅ* itself is the *it*, thus *ṅit*.

Therefore, when the vowel *au* is accepted as being *ṅit*, a wise person should understand that in this designation *ṅiti*, there is a reference to the mere phoneme *ṅ* which bears the technical name *it*.

The word *mātra* is used there for the purpose of excluding anything other than that. If, in the rule *ṅiti*, there is a reference to the letter *ṅ* alone as a mere phoneme (*varṇamātra*) and not to a suffix (*pratyaya*) having *ṅ* as its indicatory letter (*anubandha*), then why does the operation conditioned by *ṅit* not occur in [the case of] *śyā*? To this he says: "When a phoneme," and so forth. When an operation is prescribed when a phoneme follows, one should understand it to apply to that which begins with that phoneme, according to the metarule (*paribhāṣā*): "In a reference to a beginning element (*algrahaṇa*), the operation applies to that which begins with the element for which the rule is stated" (Vyāḍiparibhāṣā 127).
Consequently, the augment *yāṭ* should apply only where the letter *ṅ* occurs at the beginning and is designated as having the technical name *it*; it should not apply to [the root] *śyai*.
For in this case, the letter *ṅ* does not occur at the beginning; where, then, does it occur? At the end.
Thus, this rebuttal has been stated by accepting the status of *ṅit*.
Now, without accepting that [the suffix] has the marker *ṅ*, he states another solution, beginning with "And this is a phoneme" (*varṇaścāyam*):
the word "and" (*ca*) has the sense of "or";
that is to say, "or this is a phoneme."
The term *auṅ* here consists of the vowel *au*; it is employed for the purpose of qualifying the suffix (*pratyaya*), and not as a suffix itself.

Since the context is governed by the heading (*adhikāra*) of "stem" (*aṅga*), the suffix—which is understood through the force of the rule—that follows a stem ending in *ā*, is qualified by the syllable *au*. And by means of this qualification, the rule of "ending in that" (*tadantavidhi*) applies.
Consequently, the following meaning arises: "of this suffix when it ends in *au*."
The status of having the vowel *au* as its final element is due to the principle of "behaving like that which possesses a designation" (*vyapadeśivadbhāva*).
Furthermore, this letter *ṅ* is not an *anubandha* (indicatory letter); rather, it is for the sake of ease of pronunciation, just as the letter *d* is in the rule *ṛdorap* [Pāṇini 3.3.57].
And since the vowel *au* is thus grasped by virtue of its form as a phoneme, the substitution of *śī* is established for both instances of the vowel *au*.

For when there is the mention of a *pratyaya* (suffix), the *paribhāṣā* "niranubandhakagrahaṇe" (Vyāḍīya-paribhāṣā 53) applies; however, here there is no mention of a *pratyaya*. What then? There is the mention of a mere phoneme (*varṇa*). But surely both of these [the suffixes *kta* and *ktavatu*] are *pratyayas*; why then does that rule not apply? True; although they are indeed *pratyayas*, nevertheless, in this grammar (*śāstra*), the vowel *o* is not employed in the form of a *pratyaya*. What then? It is employed in the form of a phoneme. Therefore, that *paribhāṣā* does not apply here.
Without accepting that [the letter] has the *ṅit* designation, he states another solution, beginning with "This is a technical description" (*nirdeśo 'yam*).
Here in this grammar, the letter *ṅ* is not employed as an *anubandha* attached to the vowel *au*.
However, according to the ancient teachers, both of these [terms] are recited in their sūtras as being *ṅit* when they denote the dual number.
For indeed, the reading of the rule there is "āṬjau ca auṅ.
Therefore, this reference is made in accordance with that rule so that its inclusion might occur here.
Consequently, due to the absence of the marker *ṅ*, there is no occasion for the operation dependent on a *ṅ*-marker.
For here, the operations concerning *anubandhas* (indicatory letters) are not performed in accordance with the rules of the earlier teachers or the *sūtras*.
Thus, there is no fault even if [the root] has the property of being marked by *ṅ*.
Furthermore, the meaning of the word "even" (*api*) is: what then to say of cases where the property of being marked by *ṅ* does not exist at all?
This is what is meant: when the status of being *ṅit* is accepted, one should understand that the mention of the letter [in the rule] is merely for the sake of pointing out the phoneme.

By the statement, "Whatever [operation] would apply to a letter, one should know that it applies to that which begins with it," a solution is provided to avoid the contingency of the *ṅit* designation [applying to the whole word].

By the phrase "because this is a letter" (*yasmād varṇaś cāyam*) and by the phrase "this is a reference [made] by the preceding rule" (*nirdeśo 'yaṃ pūrvasūtreṇa vā syāt*), the fact that the vowel *o* possesses the status of being *ṅit* is established.
For that reason, there is no fault even though the marker *ṅ* is present.

How much less so where the marker *ṅ* is entirely absent? [The form] "dadhinī" [is derived] by [the application of] *num* according to [Pāṇini 7.1.73]. [In the case of the plural,] *vas* and *nas* are substituted for the plural endings.
Regarding the phrase "of the two [forms] mentioned":

this means of the forms of *yuṣmad* and *asmad* characterized by the sixth case-ending (*ṣaṣṭhī*) and so forth. The statement "the word *aṣṭan* is understood as having the vowel *ā*" intends that where there is *ātva* (the substitution of *ā*), there should likewise be *auśtva* (the substitution of *auś*).
Regarding "aṣṭau tiṣṭhanti":
when the substitution of *āt* has been applied, the substitution of *auś* occurs,
resulting in "aṣṭa tiṣṭhanti."
Because the substitution of *āt* is absent here, the substitution of *auś* does not occur.

But how is there an absence of *āt* here, given that in the rule prescribing *āt*, there is no indicator of an option—such as the mention of *anyatarasyām*—in its absence? To this he says: "This very [is the purpose]," and so forth.
The purpose of stating the form with *āt* applied is precisely this: that the substitution of *auś* should occur only where *āt* occurs, and not elsewhere.

And if the substitution of *āt* were permanent (*nitya*), then the mention of the form with *āt* applied (*kṛtātva*) would be purposeless, as there would be nothing to exclude; one would simply have said "of *aṣṭan*. Since such a concise mention is possible, the fact that this more cumbersome mention of the form with *āt* applied is made indicates that the substitution of *āt* is optional (*vikalpa*).
Although this point was already indicated under [Pāṇini 6.1.172], it is nevertheless indicated here again for the benefit of those who are prone to forgetfulness.

If it is argued that [the form] *aṣṭaputraḥ* and *aṣṭabhāryaḥ* should not occur here because [the substitution] is barred by the elision (*luk*) prescribed by [Pāṇini 6.4.143], we say no; for in that case, one would also not obtain the forms *aṣṭau tiṣṭhanti* and *aṣṭau paśya*, since they too would be barred by the elision prescribed by [Pāṇini 7.1.22]. However, since the substitution of *auś* is an exception (*apavāda*) to elision, it prevails here, setting aside the elision and taking its place.

"In that case, let that very same [rule] apply even in the preceding instance for this very reason? To this he says: "This is an exception (*apavāda*) to the rule *ṣaḍbhyaḥ luk* [Pāṇini 7.1.22]. He provides the justification for this very point with the words beginning "nāprāpte" (when [the previous rule] has not already applied).
The rule *ṣaḍbhyaḥ luk* applies in a non-compound (*asamāsa*), as in "aṣṭau tiṣṭhanti" and so forth, and also in a compound, as in "aṣṭaputra" and so forth.

Therefore, in the case of *nāprāpte aṣṭabhāryaḥ*, there must be elision (*luk*) of the case-ending (*sup*) alone; thus, the substitution of *auś* does not occur. Regarding the phrase "the inclusion of that which ends in this" (*tadantagrahaṇam*), etc.: how, then, is even what is intended obtained? It is obtained by the statement: "In the governing context of the *aṅga* (stem), [the rule applies] to that [stem] and to its subsequent member" (*Puṃvadbhāva-vṛtti* 85).
Alternatively—this reference "from eight" (*aṣṭabhyaḥ*) is understood to be a designation where the meaning is primary, because of the use of the plural number.
For if the designation were one where the word-form itself is primary, he would have said "from *aṣṭan*" (*aṣṭanaḥ*).
And since the status of being followed by *jaś* and *śas* is understood through the word as the medium of the meaning, the [substitution] occurs from the bare stem *aṣṭan* alone.

For even when [the word] does not end in that [suffix], the two suffixes *jaś* and *śas* occur after the word ending in that [suffix], by means of the word itself through implication (*artha*). If the inclusion of "ending in that" (*tadanta*) were intended here, then it would also apply in the case of *priyāṣṭan*. Therefore, he says: "*priyāṣṭanaḥ*" and so forth.
It is a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "those for whom there are eight dear ones."
But surely, the substitution of *āt* is optional (*vikalpa*).

In that case, when there is no *āt*, let there be no *au*; but when there is *āt*, it must certainly occur. There is no fault here, for by the rule of "optionally fixed" (*vyavasthitavibhāṣā*), the *āt* will not occur. Thus, [we get] "pañca," "sapta"—[in these cases], by [Pāṇini 8.2.7], there is the elision of the nasal (*nalopa*).
"Is it because of the six subsequent [suffixes]? It also occurs after those at the end.
Here, the preceding reason must be stated:
"But where," and so forth.
This inclusion of the word "artha" (meaning/object) is understood from the use of the term *bahula* (in various cases).
That *artha* is of two kinds: primary (*pradhāna*) and non-primary (*apradhāna*).
Regarding this, according to the rule *pradhāne kāryasaṃpratyayaḥ* (Vārttika on Pāṇini 1.4.1), the operation occurs only where the *artha* is primary, and not where the *artha* is non-primary.

And this reason should be understood to apply even in the absence of the substitution of *auś* in the case of *priyāṣṭānām*. [The example] *priyaṣaṣaḥ* is a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "those for whom six beloved ones exist."

In this case, the meaning of the other word (*anyapadārtha*) is predominant, whereas the six meanings are subordinate and thus not predominant there. Although *su* is the locative plural, it is nevertheless understood as the nominative singular because of its association with *am*, the accusative singular.

Regarding the example *tad-brāhmaṇa-kulam*, since [the rule for] *tyadādyatva* (the substitution of *a* for the initial of *tyad* etc. is subsequent, one might think that *tyadādyatva* must necessarily occur first. However, once *tyadādyatva* has been applied, elision (*luk*) would not apply, because there would be the contingency of the *ambhāva* (substitution of *am*) by the rule *ato 'm* [Pāṇini 7.1.24]. Therefore, it must be stated that elision occurs prior to *tyadādyatva*. To this he says: "In the case of *tad-brāhmaṇa-kulam*, etc. The scope for elision (*luk*) is in examples such as *dadhi* and *madhu*; the scope for *tyadādyatva* is in examples such as *brāhmaṇa*. In the present case, *tad-brāhmaṇa-kulam*, both rules would apply. Elision takes place by means of a *pūrvavipratiṣedha* (prior counter-exception).

Nor should a prior contradiction be asserted; for the word "para" (subsequent) denotes that which is desired [as the final]. As for the phrase "or because of eternality," the word "vā" (or) is used in the sense of conjunction.
Although both elision (*luk*) and the substitution of the *tyadādi* forms would apply, nevertheless, elision alone is understood to be the constant (*nitya*).
Why? Because of the logical force (*sāmarthya*).
For this very reason, another argument was stated in the rule: "The *tyadādi* substitution is superseded by elision."

Thus, another reason for this matter is possible: if the elision (*luk*) is compulsory (*nitya*), [the substitution] occurs, but not otherwise. Furthermore, its compulsion arises from the fact that it applies whether [the elision] has been performed or not. For if the substitution of *yat* for the pronouns beginning with *tyad* were stated to apply when a case-ending (*vibhakti*) is present, it would not take effect once the elision has occurred, because the case-ending is absent. Nor is its application by means of the "characteristic of an affix" (*pratyayalakṣaṇa*) appropriate, due to the prohibition in [Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.1.63]: "That which is taught in relation to an affix does not take place when an affix has been elided."
[The objection: "Once *tyadādyatva* (the substitution of *t-*, *y-* etc. has been applied, *luk* (elision) applies; but even when it has not been applied, it also applies.

Now, once *tyadādyatva* has been applied, there is no possibility for *luk* at all, because the rule *ato'm* [Pāṇini 7.1.24] prescribes an exception (*apavāda*). Therefore, that [application of *luk*] is also indeed non-eternal (*anitya*)? To this he says: "For *luk*... and so forth.

In the absence of the rule *ato 'm* [Pāṇini 7.1.24], even a base (*aṅga*) ending in the vowel *a* would have been a cause for elision (*luk*); however, because this present rule arises and prescribes an exception (*apavāda*), it becomes a non-cause for that elision.
"Subversion" (*vighāta*) consists precisely in bringing about the absence of the cause for elision;
it does not, however, consist in [the application of] the substitution of *yat* and so forth [as prescribed by *tyadādīnām atve*].
The phrase "the status of *luk* as a cause is obstructed" is to be connected [to the preceding].

If there were no other rule (*lakṣaṇāntara*) prescribing an exception (*apavāda*) such as *ato 'm* (Pāṇini 7.1.24), then once the substitution of *tyadādi* elements had taken place, a stem ending in *a* would indeed be the cause for *luk*.
However, that very cause for *luk* is obstructed by the exception *ato 'm* itself, and not by the substitution of *tyadādi* elements.
If this is so, why does elision (*luk*) not become non-eternal? To this he says: "And of that which," and so forth.

Furthermore, the fact that this is a separate rule (*lakṣaṇāntaratva*) from the rule for the substitution of *am* should be understood with respect to the rule for the substitution of *at* in the words beginning with *tyad*. This [rule] is an exception (*apavāda*) to the elision that would otherwise apply by the preceding rule. The inclusion of the marker *t* (in *ataḥ*) is for the sake of ease of pronunciation; it is not for the purpose of excluding the long vowel.

Because of the absence of length. Its absence, however, follows from the prescription of the short vowel in the rule "The neuter stem [ending in a long vowel] becomes short" (Pāṇini 1.2.47). Now, for what purpose is the substitution of *am* stated, rather than simply the substitution of *m*? It cannot be so; for if the substitution of *m* were made for the *a* of the second singular case ending by the rule "In place of [the final phoneme of a word], there is *m*" (Pāṇini 1.1.54), then the elision of two *m*s would result; since one of them would have been removed by the elision of a word-final consonant cluster (*saṃyogāntalopa*).

Nor does the lengthening prescribed by *supi ca* [Pāṇini 7.3.102] for a case-ending (*sup*) beginning with *yañ* apply here; this is because of the rule: "A grammatical operation conditioned by a specific configuration is not the cause of the destruction of that very configuration" (*sannipātalakṣaṇo vidhir animittaṃ tadvighātasya*, Vyāḍīya-paribhāṣā 12).

For the prescription of the letter *m* occurs upon the configuration of the stem ending in *a*; how then could that be the cause for the destruction of the vowel *a*? If this is so, then by applying the substitution of *am* when the substitution of *m* ought to have been applied, the author indicates that this paribhāṣā is indeed obligatory.

Therefore, by means of this [reference], the substitution of *jaras* in the forms *tenātijarasāt* and *atijarasaiḥ* is established. This reference contains two forms of *ḍa*: one is connected with *ḍatara*, while the second is connected with the substitute (*ādeśa*). Furthermore, these terms beginning with *ḍatara* are understood as falling within the group of words beginning with *sarva*; they do not refer to suffixes such as *ḍatarac* prescribed in rules like "of two, one: *ḍatarac*" (Pāṇini 5.3.92). Why is this so? Because of the prohibition in the rule "not after *itarat* in the Veda" (Pāṇini 7.1.26).
For if the term *pratyaya* (suffix) were not mentioned, since there is no possibility [of the application] from any other word, the prohibition would be meaningless.

Among those [words], namely *ḍatara* and so on, the last three are nominal stems (*prātipadika*), while *ḍatara* and *ḍatama* are suffixes (*pratyaya*). In that case, by the paribhāṣā regarding the mention of a suffix (Pāṇini 1.1.72), there is the inclusion of those ending in them. Thus, for example, "katarat."
"From among two [things], when there is a selection from *kim*, *yat*, or *tad*, the suffix *-atarac* is applied" (Pāṇini 5.3.92);
thus, "which one? (*katamat*).
"Or, when there is an inquiry regarding a class among many, the suffix *-atamaj* is applied" (Pāṇini 5.3.93).
Regarding the phrase "In the case of *katarat tiṣṭhati*," and so forth:

for if the designation *ṅit* were not applied, then in the case of *katarat tiṣṭhati*, the rule [Pāṇini 6.1.102] would apply while [6.1.101] is still in force, resulting in a long vowel (*dīrgha*). Therefore, the designation *ṅit* is applied so that this [long vowel] does not occur. When this is done, the contingency of lengthening does not arise, because the *ak* portion has been removed by the elision of the *ṭi*.

But what is the reason that the purpose of making the first singular [case-ending] *ṅit* is stated to be the absence of lengthening (*dīrgha*), and not that of the second singular? To this he says: "In this case, however," and so forth. For since the substitute in place of *ām* would, by virtue of the rule *sthānivad ādeśo 'nalvidhau* (Pāṇini 1.1.56), be treated like its original, the form *katarat* would also be established through the application of *pūrva-vidhi* (the substitution of *at* for *ām*). Therefore, in that case, the absence of lengthening is not cited as the purpose of making it *ṅit*. [The questioner asks: "Why is not the substitution of *t* alone made?"
If length (*dīrghatva*) is not desired here, then only the substitution of *t* should be applied.
In that case as well, the meaning is this: the addition of the marker *ṅ* need not be made for the purpose of excluding length.
[Examples include] "he katarat" and so forth.

If the substitution of *t* were indeed made, then by virtue of its status as a *sthānivadbhāva* (acting like the original), the form would possess the nature of a vocative (*sambuddhi*), and consequently, the elision [of the final vowel] prescribed by Pāṇini 6.1.69 would apply. Therefore, so that this [elision] does not occur, the substitution of *t* is not made. Regarding the rule beginning with *apṛktaśca* [Pāṇini 6.1.68], if the mention of *apṛkta* (uncombined suffix) were to carry over into the elision of the vocative, then there would be a fault in the case of *he kuṇḍa*.

When the section on *apṛkta* [suffixes] has concluded, there is a fault regarding forms such as *ḍatara*, namely in the vocative *he katarat*. Therefore, because the *ḍit* marker is employed, once the elision of the vowel *a* has been performed, the elision of the suffix does not occur due to the absence of a *hrasva* (short vowel), nor does lengthening take place. This is a prohibition against the application of the substitute *adḍ* which was previously applicable. Now, why is it not stated immediately after the rule *ato'm* [Pāṇini 7.1.24] that "in the Veda, [the suffix becomes] *itarāt*"? For in that case, the prohibition *na* would not have to be formulated, as the substitution of *am* would serve as an exception (*apavāda*) to the substitution of *adḍ*. To this, he says: "Immediately after *ato'm*," and so forth.

"‘For the purpose of splitting the rule (yogavibhāga)’ means that there should be a split of the single rule [into two]. But for what purpose is the splitting of the rule desired? To this he says: ‘For from one [of the two]... and so forth."

For a negation is intended to apply everywhere from the word *eka*; and that [negation] is obtained through the separation of the rule (*yogavibhāga*) by means of the word *na*. Therefore, the separation of the rule is desired. And that is established according to the original formulation (*yathānyāsa*); it is not otherwise. Thus it is stated: "Not after another [than *eka*], in the Vedic language" (*netarācchandasī*). If there is elision of the final syllable (*antyalopa*) by [Pāṇini 7.2.90], then this statement is made because its occurrence would otherwise be expected.
