Now, if there is elision of the *ṭi* (the final vowel and following consonant), then since the case-ending would otherwise be audible, this statement is for the purpose of prescribing the substitutes:
"your own" (*tava svam*) and "my own" (*mama svam*).
By the rule *tada-mamau ṅasi* [Pāṇini 7.2.96], the substitutes *tava* and *mama* occur in place of *yuṣmad* and *asmad* ending in *map*.

When the elision of the *da* and *ka* sounds has been performed by [Pāṇini 7.2.90], the substitution of the subsequent form (*pararūpa*) applies by [Pāṇini 6.1.97]. "The inclusion of the marker *ś* is for the sake of making it a substitute for the whole" (sarvādeśārtha).
If the marker *ś* were not present, the substitute *a* would apply to the vowel *ā* by [Pāṇini 1.1.54].

Now, one might object: "Since there is no purpose in mentioning the letter *a* when [the substitute] *ākāra* is being stated, even without the addition of the marker *ś*, it will become a universal substitute (*sarvādeśa*), or else it will be a final substitute (*antādeśa*).

In that case, since there are two *a*-sounds, the desired result would be established by the substitution of the subsequent form (*pararūpa*) according to the rule *ato guṇe*. To this, he says: "Otherwise, however" (*anyathā hi*), and so forth.

Otherwise, if the marker *ś* were not present, then for the sake of establishing—that is, bringing about—the designation "substitute" (*ādeśa*), it would apply only to the initial sound (*ādi*), because of the rule *ādeḥ parasya* (Pāṇini 1.1.54).

It might be argued: "If some purpose were accomplished through the application of the designation 'substitute' (ādeśa), then it would be so; however, the word *ādi* is used for that very purpose, yet no such purpose is accomplished from it. Therefore, [the designation] is indeed improper. To this he says: "And therefore," and so forth. The word *ca* indicates a reason (*hetu*).
The term *liṅ* expresses possibility (*sambhāvanā*).
Consequently, because the designation "substitute" (ādeśa-vyapadeśa) would be established [by that rule], the operation prescribed by *yo'ci* [Pāṇini 7.2.82] would not occur.

For this [operation] is ordained only where there is no substitute in the case of a case-ending (*vibhakti*), due to the governing rule *anādeśe* [Pāṇini 7.2.86]. Therefore, since the designation "substitute" is established for a purposeful [element], it would apply only to the initial sound (*ādi*); and as a result, this form would not be established.

Therefore, the letter *śa* must be applied for the sake of all the initial vowels. [Regarding the statement] "The term *ṅe* is a citation without a case ending," this is because the genitive case has been elided by the rule *supāṃ suluk* [Pāṇini 7.1.39].
The expression *prathamayoḥ* is a genitive dual; *prathamā* and *prathamā* are "the two *prathamās*," and [the compound refers to] those two *prathamās*.

Since the indication by the genitive case is identical in both instances, someone might have the misconception that the mention of *sv-au-kāra* refers to the two initial suffixes; therefore, in order to dispel that, he says: "of the two case-endings. To clarify this very point, he says: "of the first and second [cases].
But how, then, is the second [case] referred to by the word "first"? Because of its proximity to the first [case] in the grammatical instruction (*upadeśa*).
For indeed, a term may denote that which is proximate to it, as in the expression "a hamlet on the Ganges" (*gaṅgāyāṃ ghoṣaḥ*).
Now, how is this determined—that this is a reference to the two case-endings (*vibhakti*) and not to the two suffixes (*pratyaya*)? It is from an indicative mark (*liṅga*).
That indicative mark, moreover, is the prescription of the substitution of *at* [for *as*] in the rule "and in the second case" (*dvitīyāyāṃ ca*, Pāṇini 7.2.87).
This is stated for the purpose of providing an instruction (*ādeśa*); for if there were no instruction, the rule *yuṣmadasmadoranādeśe* [7.2.86] would not apply otherwise.

But is it not the case that the statement *dvitīyāyāñca* [7.2.87] is intended to block the substitution of *ya* by the rule *yo'ci* [7.2.89]? This is not so; if that were the intention, he would have prescribed the letter *y* itself as a qualifier for the dual number in that context—either stating *yo'cyadvitīyāyām* or *yo'cyanaci*.

Therefore, the prescription of *āt* (the substitution of *ā*) in the second case is precisely the indicator (*jñāpaka*) of the necessity of including the mention of "case-ending" (*vibhakti*) in the rule.
"From those two, *tabhyam* and *mahyam*": for *yuṣmad* and *asmad* ending in *m*, *tabhyam* and *mahyam* are the substitutes.
"Thou, I."

"Yuvām, āvām?"—here, by the rule "yuvāvau dvivacane" [Pāṇini 7.2.92], *yuva* and *āva* are substituted; then, by the rule "prathamayor ca" [Pāṇini 7.2.88] and others, the substitution of *a* occurs. "Yūyam, vayam"—[these are formed similarly].
In the forms *tvām* and *mām*,
the substitution of *ā* occurs by the rules *tvamāvekavacane* [Pāṇini 7.2.97] and *dvitīyāyāñca* [Pāṇini 7.2.87].

Now, for what purpose is the designation *am* stated, rather than simply the letter *m*? Since that [letter *m*] would belong to the beginning [of the suffix] due to being a single phoneme (*ekāl*), its application to the following [word] would be established by the elision of a conjunct consonant (*saṃyogāntalopa*). If it is argued that it is not established because of the elision of the *ṭi* [portion] according to Pāṇini 6.4.143, this is not a fault; for even if the elision in the *seṣa* [rule] were an elision of *ṭi*, it would still be established because those [suffixes] ending in *am*—such as [the one under discussion]—end in the vowel *a*. Furthermore, they must necessarily be prescribed as ending in *a* so that they may have the final acute accent (*antodāttatva*).

Furthermore, when *m* is substituted [for *na*], lengthening would not apply by the rule *suci ca* [Pāṇini 7.3.102]; this is because of the maxim: "When an operation has already taken place within a stem, a further operation regarding that same stem does not apply to what is already established" (*aṅgavṛtte punaraṅgavṛttāvidhirniṣṭhitasya*). If that is so, then the prescription of the substitute *am* is for the sake of variety.

Alternatively, *m* alone is the substitute, while the vowel *a* is merely for the purpose of pronunciation; for otherwise, it would not be possible to pronounce the letter *m* at the beginning or end of this grammatical instruction without first employing the vowel *a*.
Regarding the rule *ṅe-su-toḥ*:

although it would have been sufficient to say *ṅe-prathamayoḥ*, the statement as it stands is for the sake of variety (*vaicitrya*). Since the substitution of *ām* was already established by the preceding rule, [the substitution] of *śas* is not prescribed here. [Example: *yuṣmān brāhmaṇān*.

"asmān," "brāhmaṇān"—here, by [Pāṇini 8.2.37], the letter *a* is replaced by *na*; then, there is the elision of the final consonant due to being a *saṃyoga*, and as before, the acute accent (*udātta*). Now, one might object: do these two examples not already succeed through the substitution of *am*, the substitution of *āt* [by 6.1.102], and the lengthening [by 6.1.103], without even this rule for *natva*? This is not so; for in these cases, the lengthening of the homogeneous preceding vowel (*pūrvasavarṇadīrghatva*) does not apply, because it is superseded by the rule for the substitution of *am* (which precedes the case-ending). Thus: "yuṣmabhyam," "asmabhyam."

By [Pāṇini 7.2.90], there is elision of the final [sound]. If this were the substitute *bhyam*, then when that [substitute] is prescribed and the remaining [portion] is elided, the substitution of *e* by [Pāṇini 7.3.103], "in the case of a plural ending beginning with *jhal*, *e* is substituted," would apply; consequently, an undesirable form would result. To address this, he says: "When the substitute *bhyam* has been made," and so forth. "Occurrence" (*vṛtta*) means existing. An operation that exists within a stem is an "operation occurring in a stem" (*aṅgavṛtta*). When such an operation occurring in a stem has taken place, and subsequently another operation occurring in a stem presents itself, there is a non-prescription (*avidhi*) of that [second] operation. That is to say, it does not take effect.

By the term "of that which is completed" (niṣṭhitasya), that subsidiary (aṅga) whose related action is not prescribed is specified. "Completed" means finished, i.e., a subsidiary ready for performance. The meaning is that the non-prescription of the action applies to what is related to that [completed subsidiary], and not to what is related to anything else.
Regarding the phrase "some" (*kecit*) and so forth:
when the final [vowel] of those [elements] is elided, the substitution of the subsequent form (*pararūpatva*) occurs by [Pāṇini 6.1.97].
Regarding the phrase "but for those who" (*yeṣām tu*) and so forth...

Regarding those for whom the elision of the final [vowel] is performed by the rule *yaiḥ* (Pāṇini 7.2.90), there is a difference of opinion: some of them desire the substitution of *bhyām*, while others desire the substitution of *abhyam*. However, according to the view of those for whom there is elision of the remainder (*śeṣelopas*)—that is, elision of the *ṭi* suffix—it is precisely this substitution of *abhyam* that occurs, not the substitution of *bhyām*; otherwise, the form *yuṣmabhyam* would not be established. This is the intended meaning. If, then, there is elision of the remainder—that is, elision of the *ṭi* suffix—then in that case, wouldn't the word *abhyam* have its final syllable accented acute (*antodāttatva*) by the rule *titsvaritam* (Pāṇini 6.1.161)? To this he says: "And the accent of the cessation of the acute" (*udāttanivṛttisvaraś ca*), and so forth.
The proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣavādin*), thinking that the mention of "the end" (*anta*) continues from the rule *udāttanivṛttisvara* [P. 6.1.159], raised an objection.

The proponent of the final view (*uttarapakṣavādin*), however, thinking that "the mention of the end" has ceased there and that, due to the proximity of the order of pronunciation, it is proper for the acute accent (*udātta*) to belong only to the beginning (*ādi*), offered a resolution. This [rule] is an exception (*apavāda*) to what was previously obtained by the suffix *bhyām*. The *ca* is for the purpose of carrying over the substitute [from the previous rule], or it serves as a conjunction (*samuccaya*) with respect to *bhyas*.
Regarding the statement "ṅaseśca":

although it could have been stated simply as "ṅasaḥ," the formulation "ekavacanaktā" is for the sake of stylistic variety (*vaicitrya*). As for the remark "the genitive plural *sāma* with the inserted *suṭ* is understood," this is because no other word form *sāman* can possibly follow the words *yuṣmad* and *asmad*.

"Come" (*āgata*) means arrived; that which is [accompanied] by *suṭ* in such a way is called "that which has *suṭ* come" (*āgatasuṭ*). In the sentence beginning with "Now" (*atha*), the masculine gender of the term "that which has *suṭ* come" (*āgatasuṭkaḥ*) should be understood in relation to the suffix *ām*. Anticipating the objection—"For what purpose is 'that which has *suṭ* come' accepted?"—he provides the answer: "Indeed not," etc. In the rule at [Pāṇini 7.1.52], the word *āt* (from [Pāṇini 7.1.50]) is understood to carry over; therefore, *suṭ* is prescribed after a pronoun ending in the vowel *ā*.
The state of having the vowel *a* as their final sound occurs for the pronouns *yuṣmad* and *asmad* when there is elision of the final [suffix] by [Pāṇini 7.2.90].

Furthermore, even when the replacement by *ākam* has been performed through the elision of the remainder (*śeṣe lopena*), [the condition for that rule] must apply. Therefore, at the time of prescribing the replacement, the case-ending *su* does not exist.

Consequently, the purpose—that the substitution should apply to the form including *suṭ*—is not achieved; therefore, with the intention of stating something else, he says "of that very [form]," and so forth.

If the form without *suṭ* were taken, then by the rule "substitutions apply to that which is explicitly mentioned" (*nirdiśyamānasyādeśā bhavanti*), the substitution would apply only to the form without *suṭ*.

In that case, once the relationship between the original element (*sthānin*) and the substitute (*ādeśa*) has been established, by what means could there be the removal of the *suṭ* that occurs subsequently? Yet, its removal is indeed desired.
Therefore, the augment *samuṭ* is added so that there may be the cessation (*nivṛtti*) of that [augment] even when it is about to occur.

Now, one might object: the *suṭ* augment does not apply at all to the suffix *am* following the words *yuṣmad* and *asmad*, because the *suṭ* is prescribed for a pronoun (*sarvanāman*) ending in the vowel *a*; however, in the case of *yuṣmad* and *asmad*, the substitution of *tyadādi* [for the final consonant] does not take place. Since the *tyadādi* rule applies only to those [pronouns] up to *dvi*, the absence of the *tyadādi* substitution means that the elision of the remainder (*śeṣalopa*)—which would result in the form ending in *a* through the elision of the *ṭi*—is impossible.

Therefore, does the removal of the *suṭ* even though it is yet to arise not constitute a valid purpose? To refute this objection, [the author], having established that "the elision of the final [sound] occurs in the remainder" (*śeṣe lopaḥ*), says: "For when [it is] made," and so forth. Now, if the term *samuṭka* (along with *suṭ*) were being employed, how could this [substitution] be removed? For the removal of what is applicable from another rule is effected by a rule; and at the time of prescribing the substitute, there is no occasion for the application of *suṭ*. To this he says: "And because it is included within the original element (*sthānin*)," and so forth.

If the occurrence of *suṭ* were possible at the time of the prescription of the substitute, then that which is yet to come (*bhāvī*) would not be excluded; however, it is not possible at the time of the substitution.

Therefore, because the future *suṭ* is included within the substituend by virtue of the mention of "with *suṭ*" (*sasuṭka*), that which is applicable at the stage where its [the *suṭ*'] acquisition occurs is what is excluded. Otherwise, its inclusion within the substituend would be purposeless.

It might be argued: "If there is elision of the final [letter] by [Pāṇini 6.4.143], then the mention of *samuṭaka* is meaningful; but when there is elision of the *ṭi* by the rule for the remainder (*seṣe lopaḥ*), then why is that meaning not accepted? This is because that [latter case] is untenable.
The untenability arises from the absence of a grammatical rule [for it].
Since this very [rule, 6.4.143], which prescribes the elision of the final letter, is the only rule available for this, it alone has been adopted.

If this is so, when the final [vowel] is elided in *yuṣmad-brāhmaṇībhyām gacchati*, would not the suffix *ṭāp* apply by the rule *ajādyataṣṭāp* [Pāṇini 4.1.4]? This contingency for *ṭāp* does not arise because of the statement: "The words *yuṣmad* and *asmad* are devoid of gender. [Objection: But even so, would not the long vowel be established by the rule *akaḥ savarṇe dīrghaḥ* [Pāṇini 6.1.101]? [Response: No; it is indeed established. By the phrase "the pronunciation of the long [vowel]" and so forth, [it is shown that] even though [the rule applies], it is not accomplished [by that specific rule alone]. No; it is accomplished.

If it is argued that, by the rule *ato guṇe* [Pāṇini 6.1.97], the substitution of the subsequent form (*pararūpatva*) would apply as an exception (*apavāda*), we say no; this is because of the functional force (*sāmarthya*) of the explicit utterance of the vowel *a*. If the substitution of the subsequent form were to occur by *ato guṇe*, then the utterance of the long vowel *ā* would be purposeless; one could have simply said *kam*. Therefore, he says: *akami tu*, etc.
The word *tu* has the sense of a conjunction (*samuccaya*) with respect to the utterance of the long vowel.
The particle *iti* is used here in the sense of a reason (*hetau*).

For if there were no purpose for the pronunciation of the vowel *a*, one could simply say: "It will not occur because of the power of the pronunciation of *a*. However, there is indeed a purpose for it. What is that? [It is so that] the substitution of *e* (by Pāṇini 7.3.103: *brūhuvacane jhalyet*) does not take place. Therefore, even though the vowel *a* is pronounced, [if it were not for this rule], the substitution of the single subsequent form (*pararūpatva*) by [Pāṇini 6.1.97] would occur instead of the long vowel of homogeneous quality (*savarṇadīrghatva*).
Therefore, for that purpose, the long vowel is pronounced. Regarding "tasyau":
by [Pāṇini 7.4.61], there is the retention of the remaining consonant (*khayaḥ śeṣaḥ*).
Regarding "jaglau": [the same rule applies].
The substitution of *c* is applied by [Pāṇini 7.4.62] *kahoścuḥ*.

Here, when the suffix *ṇal* follows roots such as *pā*, three operations simultaneously present themselves: reduplication (*dvirvacana*), the single-substitute replacement (*ekādeśa*), and the change to *au* (*autva*). Since it is impossible for these operations, having thus presented themselves, to apply simultaneously, a sequence (*krama*) is necessarily resorted to by implication (*sāmarthyāt*).
In this regard, he says "here" (*atretyādi*) in order to show the sequence in which those operations must be performed. By the word "here," examples such as *papau* and others are intended.

If the single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) were applied before the reduplication (*dvirvacana*), then after the single-substitute had been made by [Pāṇini 6.1.88], there would be no distinction between the cause (*nimitta*) and the effect (*nimittin*); consequently, the reduplication prescribed for what precedes when a *liṭ* suffix follows would not apply. To preclude that, it is stated: "the status of being a substitute (*sthānivadbhāva*) applies to the reduplication."

But by what [rule] does the status of being a substitute (*sthānivadbhāva*) apply here? Is it by [Pāṇini 1.1.56]: "That which is taught concerning a substitute shall be like the original"? No, that is not so. For even when there is a cause for reduplication (*dvirvacana*), the reduplication of the preceding element would not be obtained when something else follows; therefore, this was stated in order to exclude that [objection]: "The status of being a substitute applies to reduplication.

But by what [rule] does the status of being a substitute apply here? Is it by [Pāṇini 1.1.56]? No, that is not so. The status of being a substitute is taught for the preceding element when a vowel (*ac*) that is the cause of reduplication follows, but we do not see any following vowel here that is the cause of reduplication.

On this point, some say: the mention of "vowel" (*ac*) is an *upalakṣaṇa* (an elliptical indication). This statement was made by relying on the following meaning of the rule: "Whatever substitute is seen for a vowel (*ac*) becomes like the original (*sthānivat*) when reduplication (*dvirvacana*) is to be performed. Here, although it is not followed by a vowel at present, at the time the single substitution (*ekādeśa*) was made, that which followed the vowel was relied upon as the cause (*nimitta*).
Therefore, the status of being like the original must apply.

Others, however, say: "It should be stated that 'a single-substitute [element] is like the original (sthānivat) for the sake of a preceding operation'"; thus, the status of being *sthānivadbhāva* is established by this desired rule.
Or, according to others, the status of *sthānivadbhāva* arises from the division of the sūtra (*yogavibhāga*) [Pāṇini 1.1.57].
But how is the sequence of these operations perceived? To this he says: "From the single-substitute," and so forth.

When *pā + a* is established, the rule *akaḥ savarṇe dīrghaḥ* [Pāṇini 6.1.101] applies, as does the substitution of *au*. In this regard, the single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) rule has scope in cases such as *daṇḍāgram*, whereas the substitution of *au* has no scope anywhere. Therefore, because it is the one without scope, the substitution of *au* is performed first. Once that is done, the rule for *vṛddhi* (vowel strengthening) and the rule for doubling (*dvirvacana*) apply. Between these two, the *vṛddhi* takes effect because it is subsequent. Indeed, the doubling has scope in cases such as *papāca*, while the scope for *vṛddhi* is in cases such as *khaṭvaiḍaka*.

Therefore, when the augmentation has been applied, the reduplication occurs subsequently by virtue of the *sthānivadbhāva* (the status of being as if occupying the original position) according to the rule "of *ṇal*. The explicit pronunciation of the letter *ṇ* is for the purpose of ensuring that this is understood as the mention of the suffix (*pratyayagrahaṇa*).
For, when the letter *ṇ* is pronounced in *ṇal*, the suffix *ṇal* is indeed included in the reference.

And if *asatya-l* were stated [instead], since the suffix *satyal* would not exist, it would have to be understood as a reference to a *pratyāhāra* (abbreviated term). The explicit utterance of the letter *l* is for the purpose of preventing the inclusion of the suffix *ṇa* prescribed by rules such as *śyādvyadha-* [Pāṇini 3.1.141].
Now, does the term *ekavacanasya* [from Pāṇini 7.1.32] continue to apply? If so, it is merely for the sake of ease of pronunciation, as in: "May you live! (*jīvatād bhavān*).

By the rule *loṭ* [3.3.173], the suffix *tip* is applied; by *śap* [3.1.68], the *śap* augment is added; by *eruḥ* [3.4.86], the substitution of *u* occurs; and for that word ending in *tu*, the substitution *tāt-aṅ* is applied.

Thus: *jīvatāt tvam*. By *sip* [3.4.78], the suffix *sip* is applied; by *sehrrapicca* [3.4.87], the substitution *hi* occurs; and for that *hi*, the substitution *tāt-aṅ* is applied. Thus: *jīvahi tvam*.

In the example *jīva tvam*, there is the elision (*luk*) of the imperative suffix *hi* by [Pāṇini 6.4.105]. Now, why does the elision not also occur in *tvam* in the form *jīvatāt*? For, by the principle of "behaving like the original" (*sthānivadbhāva*), the substitute *tāt* would be included under the term *hi*, and thus [the *hi*] should be elided. [The answer is: because the word *hi* is mentioned again in [6.4.105], even though the word *hi* is already being carried over (*anuvartamāna*) from [6.4.101]: *hujhalbhyo herdhiḥ*.

This is its purpose: so that *hi* may undergo *luk* only when it remains in its own form. Let it not happen that another word beginning with *hi*, which is [substituted] by virtue of being a *sthānivadbhāva*, would be included under the mention of *hi*.
Now, if it is argued on the basis of the rule "ṅicca" [Pāṇini 1.1.53], why does the substitution of *tātaṅ* not apply to the final letter? To this he says: "The making of it ṅit," and so forth.
For the purpose of prohibiting the formation of a plural: [one should say] *bhavantaḥ* in the case of *bhavān*.
For the purpose of prohibiting the *vṛddhi* substitution: [one should say] *mṛṣṭāḥ* in the case of *mṛṣṭāt*. The particle *iti* is used in the sense of a reason.

Since the addition of the marker *ṅ* is for the purpose of prohibiting *guṇa* and *vṛddhi*, therefore *tātaṅ* becomes a substitute for the whole [stem]. For if it had no other purpose, *tātaṅ* would indeed replace only the final letter; however, it does have another purpose, namely the prohibition of *guṇa* and *vṛddhi*.

When that [condition] exists, should the substitution apply to the final letter by the rule *ṅicca* (Pāṇini 1.1.53), or to the whole word by the rule *anekāl śit sarvasya* (Pāṇini 1.1.55)? In this case, because the latter rule is subsequent, it is proper that it should apply as a substitute for the whole. Therefore, by the rule *anekāl śit sarvasya*, it should apply to the whole; thus, it becomes a substitute for the entire word.

But surely, since the substitute *tātaṅ* for [the suffix] *thās* possesses the status of being *pit* by virtue of the rule *sthānivad ādeśo ’nalvidhau*, then just as *iṅ* occurs in *bravītu* by the rule *hali piti sārvadhātuke yat* (Pāṇini 6.1.69), so too in *brūhi tādbhavān* there ought to be the augment *iṭ* by the rule *aṇīṭ* (Pāṇini 7.2.80)? To refute this objection, he says: “And because of its *ṅit*-ness,” and so forth.
“Of this” refers to *tātaṅ*. For what reason is [the *pit*-status] set aside? He says: “And because it is *ṅit*,” and so forth.
The word "ca" (and) indicates the reason.

Since the *ṅit*-ness of the substitute *tāt* was not applicable when its *pit*-ness was already in force, the *ṅit*-ness is now introduced; for by means of this *ṅit*-ness, the *pit*-ness is set aside. Thus, it becomes *ṅit* provided that the *pit*-ness obtained through the principle of "acting like the original" (*sthānivadbhāva*) is removed.
"By that," and so forth. Since *pittva* (the state of having *pit* as an exponent) is thus excluded, therefore the *īṅ* [augment] does not occur based on *pittva*. "May you go to the village."

"Go, you!"— here the *loṭ* suffix is used in the sense of an injunction (*vidhi*) and so forth, according to Pāṇini 3.3.62 (*loṭ ca*). Although this reference "of the root *vid*" is a general indication, it is nevertheless understood to refer specifically to the root meaning "to know" (*jñāna*), for only that [root] can occur immediately followed by the suffix *śatṛ*, and not the other roots *vid*.
In that context, for the roots *vid* meaning "existence" and "deliberation," the suffix *śatṛ* is simply impossible, as they take the *ātmanepada* endings.

However, for the root *vid* meaning "to obtain," since it takes both sets of endings (*ubhayapadī*), that suffix is possible; yet it is not the one immediately following [the root], because it is separated by the *śap* affix.

For the root *vid* meaning "knowledge," however, there is no separation caused by the *vikaraṇa* [affix] *śap*, because its *vikaraṇa* is elided (*lugvikaraṇa*); therefore, only that [root] is intended, as he says: "*vida jñāne*" ("*vid* in the sense of knowing").

Regarding the word "vidvān": by virtue of its being marked with the *ugit* designation, the augment *num* is applied, and the vowel is lengthened according to [Pāṇini 6.4.10]. The phrase "optionally" (*anyatarasyām*) is understood to carry over from the preceding rule.
Therefore, forms such as *vidan*, *vidantau*, and *vidantaḥ* also occur in that alternative view. Since this is already understood, it was not explicitly stated in the commentary (*vṛtti*).

Now, one might ask: for what purpose is the marker *u* (the *anubandha*) attached? If it is argued that it is so that the operations of an *ugit* stem—such as the addition of the suffix *num*—may take place, [the answer is] no; because that is already established by the principle of *sthānivadbhāva* (the substitute being treated like the original). To address this, he says: "By virtue of *sthānivadbhāva*," and so forth.
Regarding the phrase "kvaso 'pi":
by the word *api* (also), this [suffix] is included as well.
If the letter *u* were not present, only *kv-as-* would be understood in its general sense, and no other.

Now, the rule *atha* (Pāṇini 6.4.131) is indeed formulated for the purpose of including this very [suffix], and not for *kvasu*; but even if the letter *u* were present, would not a general inclusion be impossible? For, due to the exclusion of that which has only one indicatory letter (*ekānubandhaka-paribhāṣā*), there would be an inclusion of this [suffix] alone, and not of *kvasu*. To this he says: "In the case of the inclusion of that which has only one indicatory letter," and so forth. This is a metarule (*paribhāṣā-sūtra*). It does not apply here.
The meaning is that it does not remain present. Why is this not the case? To this he says: "And such being the case," and so forth.
The meaning is: "and this being so."

If the technical rule (*paribhāṣā*) concerning that which has a single indicatory letter (*ekānubandha*) were to apply even when the letter *u* is present, then the inclusion of *u* would be purposeless.
Even without it, by stating simply "there is vocalization (*samprasāraṇa*) of *vas*," the inclusion of this [root] alone would indeed be obtained.
Therefore, by virtue of the power of including the letter *u*, this technical rule does not apply. [This refers to the condition] "not preceded by the negative particle (*nañ*)."
"Is it not *nañ*? "It is not *nañ*. "Not preceded by *nañ*": that which has [the word] *anañ* preceding it is *anañpūrvaḥ*.
Regarding "by its own nature" (*prakṛtyā*) and so forth:
the suffix *ktvā* is applied according to Pāṇini 3.4.21, *samānakartṛkayoḥ pūrvakāle*, and the compound is formed according to 2.2.18; then, the augment *tuk* is added according to 6.1.71.
Regarding "pārātaḥkṛtya":

the suffix *ktvā* is applied by [Pāṇini 3.4.61], "When a word ending in a *taddhita* suffix denoting one's own limb follows, [the suffix *lyap* is used] for the roots *kṛ* and *bhū*"; then a compound is formed by [Pāṇini 2.2.210], "The words beginning with the third case may optionally form a compound.
Regarding "nānākṛtya": [the same analysis applies].
The suffix *ktvā* is applied by the rule *nādhārthapratyaye cvyarthe* [Pāṇini 3.4.62], and the compound is formed as before,
resulting in *kṛtvā* and *hrutvā*.
This is the counter-example.
In this case, although the word *kṛtvā* exists without the negative particle *nañ*, a compound is not formed, and thus there is no *lyap* substitution. For example: *paramakṛtvā*, *uttamakṛtvā*.
[The compound is formed] by the rule beginning with *sanmahat* (Pāṇini 2.1.60).

But how, then, is this compound formed? And why should it not be so? Is it because of the absence of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*)? This is incorrect; for the suffix *ktvā* is prescribed when the agent is expressed, and that very agent is qualified by the two words "supreme" (*parama*) and "most excellent" (*uttama*). So how can there be an absence of coreferentiality? Now, if you argue that coreferentiality is absent because those two words are taken as adverbs (*kriyāviśeṣaṇa*), even so, the compound is still valid. This is because the term "diversely" (*bahulam*) is understood to carry over from [Pāṇini 2.1.57], whereby a compound occurs even in the absence of coreferentiality.

"But surely these two compounds do not have *nañ* as their prior member; how then is this counter-example appropriate? To this he says: "Not *nañ*," and so forth. This term "not *nañ*" (*anañ*) is not a simple negation (*prasajyapratiṣedha*); rather, it is an exclusion (*paryudāsa*). That which is other than *nañ* is "not *nañ*. In that context, according to the maxim of "that which is joined with *nañ* as if it were *nañ* itself" (*vyā|pa|65*), that indeclinable which is other than *nañ* and similar to *nañ* is understood here as "not *nañ*."

For that reason, both of these—namely, the negative particle *nañ* as an indeclinable (*avyaya*) and [the compound] beginning with *parama* as a non-indeclinable (*anavyaya*)—are not [simply] *nañ*. There is no similarity between them and the indeclinable *nañ*, because they are respectively characterized by absolute non-difference and by being non-indeclinables. Therefore, just as the counter-examples *akṛtvā* and *ahatvā* are logically appropriate, so too are *paramakṛtvā* and *uttamakṛtvā*.

If, then, "anañ" is understood as including that which is similar to the negative particle *nañ*—in which case forms such as *snātvākālakaḥ* and *pītvāsthirakaḥ* would also [be subject to the rule] because here too there is a preceding member similar to *nañ*, since the suffix *ktvā* is an indeclinable (*avyaya*)—he says: "*snātvākālakaḥ*" and so forth. These compounds are listed in the *mayūravyaṃsakādi* group for the purpose of receiving the technical designation of a compound (*samāsa*); therefore, by virtue of this specific grammatical convention (*nipātana*), the substitution of *lyap* does not occur.
Regarding the phrase "or rather," and so forth:

If the locative case *saptamī* is understood as a locative of location (*adhikaraṇa-saptamī*) in the rule "in a compound" (*samāse*), then there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of the substitution of *lyap* for *ktvā* even in cases such as *snātvākālaka*.
For, if it were a locative of location, the meaning would be this: "In a compound that does not have *nañ* as its prior member, *lyap* occurs for that *ktvā* which exists [there].

And this being the case, since there would be no restriction to a specific position within the compound, just as *lyap* would occur for a *ktvā* standing at the end of the compound, so too would it occur for one in the middle.

Therefore, this is not a locative case in the sense of location (*adhikaraṇa-saptamī*); what then? It is a locative case in the sense of selection (*nirghāraṇa-saptamī*). And in that view, the word "in a compound" (*samāse*) is used in the singular to denote a class, just as in the rule "in a kāraka" (*kārake*, Pāṇini 1.4.23).
Alternatively, it should be understood that the singular number takes the place of the plural by means of a transposition of case endings (*sub-vyatyaya*), according to [Pāṇini 3.1.85].

Regarding the phrase "by that" (*tena*), and so forth: since this locative case (*saptamī*) is used in the sense of selection (*nirdhāraṇa*), it refers specifically to a compound ending in *ktvā*, and not to a member of a compound—such as "having bathed" (*snātvā*).

For selection occurs only among members of the same class; just as when it is said, "Among cows, the black one is the most abundant in milk," it is understood that a cow alone is being selected, so too here, when it is stated "a compound not preceded by a negative particle (*anañpūrva*)," it is understood that among compounds not preceded by a negative particle, that very compound which ends in *ktvā* is what is being selected.

Therefore, since only a compound ending in *ktvā* is being referred to, it alone must undergo the substitution of *lyap*; however, in compounds such as *snātvākālaka*, there is no compound ending in *ktvā*.
Although *snātvākālaka* and similar forms are indeed compounds, they do not end in *ktvā*, and thus the substitution of *lyap* does not apply.
Furthermore, that compound is understood to end in *ktvā* by means of the rule of "reference to what ends in that" (*tadantavidhi*) according to [Pāṇini 1.1.72].

When a *kṛt* suffix is mentioned [in a rule], one cannot claim that it includes a suffix preceded by a *gati* or a *kāraka*—either by the principle that "when a suffix is mentioned, it includes what precedes it" (*bhāṣya-pāṭha-sūtra* 7) or by the paribhāṣā "when a *kṛt* suffix is mentioned, it includes what precedes it" (*vyāḍi-paribhāṣā* 126)—because the *ktvā* suffix does not arise after a compound.

In that case, if one were to accept the inclusion of the suffix-ending form by the *kṛt*-paribhāṣā, the rule would not apply in the example *nānākṛtya*; for this [compound] is not preceded by a *gati* or a *kāraka*.
But here one might think: [the word] *prakṛtya* [is formed by adding] *lyap* after *prakṛti*.

For even here, there is the understanding that "as" (*asi*) is both a verbal root (*gati*) and a preceding constituent (*kāraka*), and since the rule [Pāṇini 1.4.72] is understood to apply by extension (*tadantavidhi*) to all such cases, [the author], thinking that [the suffix] occurs everywhere, says: “And that,” etc. He provides the justification for this very point with: “And thus,” etc.

Why? Because by this [sūtra], a compound ending in *ktvā* is understood; and having done so, it is stated that "it must not be preceded by *nañ*. For if, by this [rule], there were a general application of the rule for suffixes ending in a specific element (*tadantavidhi*), then the case of a compound preceded by *nañ* would also follow as a possibility.
Therefore, for the purpose of excluding that [undesired application], it is rightly stated: "provided it is not preceded by *nañ*. If, by the paribhāṣā regarding the mention of *kṛt*-suffixes (P.
2.2.19), a compound ending in *ktvā* were to be understood, then only those preceded by a *gati* or a *kāraka* would be included.
And thus, when only those preceded by a *gati* or a *kāraka* are included, there is no possibility at all for a compound preceded by *nañ*.
"Is *nañ* not a *gati* nor a *kāraka*?

For this reason, just as there is no application [of the rule] in the case of *paramakṛtvā* because the word *parama* is neither a *gati* nor a *kāraka*, so too it is in the case of *akṛtvā* because *nañ* is neither a *gati* nor a *kāraka*. Consequently, since there would be no such application, the phrase "provided it is not preceded by *nañ*" (*anañpūrve*) need not have been stated; yet it has indeed been stated.

Is this because of the statement "provided it is not preceded by *anañ*"? It is established that by the rule *yena vidhis tadantasya* (Pāṇini 1.1.72), a compound ending in *ktvā* is understood here, and not by the technical maxim regarding the mention of a *kṛt*-suffix. In the case of *pradhāya*, since it is an internal (*antaraṅga*) operation, the substitution of *hi* for the root *dhā* (by Pāṇini 7.4.42) would apply.
In the case of *prasthāya*, the substitution of *i* for the final vowel (by Pāṇini 7.4.40) would likewise apply.
Regarding "prakhanya":
by the rule *janasanakhanām* [Pāṇini 6.4.42], there is the substitution of ā for the vowel.
Regarding "praṇabhya": [the same applies].
In *āpṛcchya*, the vowel is lengthened by [Pāṇini 6.4.15].
In *āpṛcchya*, the substitution of *ś* occurs by [Pāṇini 6.4.19].
In *pratidīvya*, [the same applies].

By that very [rule], there is the augment *iṭ* [in the form] "prapaṭhiṣati"; [the augment] *iṭ* is applied by [Pāṇini 7.2.35]: "The *iṅ* of an *ārdhadhātuka* suffix beginning with a consonant [is added]."
Their status as *antaraṅga* (internal) is due to their dependence on a single word;
however, the substitution of *lyap* is *bahiranga* (external), because it depends upon a compound that relies on multiple words in a state of semantic connection (*samartha*).
To one who might object, "If [suffixes] such as *hi* were applied first, forms such as *pradhāya* would not be established," he replies with the words beginning with "*pradhāya*."
"This has already been explained" refers to the rule *ado jagdhir lyapti kiti* [Pāṇini 2.4.36].
Now, what is the purpose of including the mention of "pūrva" (the preceding)?

Could it not be said that [the term] is *anañ*? It cannot be so; for if it were called *anañ*, this would be a *bahuvrīhi* compound—meaning "that in which *nañ* is non-existent"—namely, where that *nañ* is absent.
Consequently, even in this case, [the suffix] would not apply: *straiṇīkṛtya*.
Here, *straiṇam* means "belonging to a woman" (*striyā idam*); [the suffix] *nañ* is applied by the rule *strīpuṃsābhyāṃ nañsnañau bhavanāt* [Pāṇini 4.1.87].
From that [word] ending in *tad*: by the rule "abhūtatadbhāve" (Pāṇini 5.4.50) and so forth, the suffix *cvi* is applied; by "īttvam" (Pāṇini 7.4.32), the substitution of *ī* occurs;
and by "iti samāsaḥ" (Pāṇini 2.2.18), the compound is formed.
However, when the term *pūrva* is employed, the word *pūrva* denotes the initial constituent member.
Therefore, where the negative particle (*nañ*) has become part of a compound and so forth, there *lyap* should not occur; yet in the case of *straiṇīkṛtya*, it does indeed occur.
For here the negative particle is not a constituent part (*avayava*) that has become part of a compound and so forth; what is it then? It is situated in the middle.
The purpose of the *lit* marker [in *kṛ*] is so that, in the case of *pratikīrṣya*, the preceding syllable may have the acute accent (*udātta*) due to the *lit* suffix.

In examples such as *prakṛtya* and so forth, the inclusion of the *liṭ* marker for the sake of the acute accent (*udātta*) is not justified, since the acute accent of the preceding syllable is already established by the accent of the verbal root (*dhātusvara*). Therefore, it is only when the verbal root consists of multiple syllables that the *liṭ* marker serves its purpose. [Examples: *paridhāpayitvā*, *pratyarpayitvā*. From the roots *dhā* and *ṛ*, there is the causative suffix *ṇic*; then, by [Pāṇini 7.3.36] *artihyī* etc., the augment *puk* is added; then, by [Pāṇini 7.3.86] *pugantalaghūpadhasya*, *guṇa* substitution occurs; then the suffix *ktvā*; then the augment *iṭ*; and finally the substitution of *ay* for *e*.
Regarding the word "uddhṛtya": [the root] *hr̥ñ* means "to take away" (*harane*; Dhātupāṭha 899). By the rule [Pāṇini 8.4.62], the letter *h* is replaced by *dh*.
[The phrase] "optionally in the Veda" (*vā chandasi*) [is applied].

It should be stated that *ktvā* also occurs in the Vedic language (*chandasi*). This statement is made so that [the suffix] may apply even when there is no compound—as in *ācārya tān devān gataḥ*. Regarding the form *panthāḥ*: from the stem *pathin*, the nominative singular suffix *su* is added; by *pathimathyṛbhukṣāmāt* [Pāṇini 7.1.85], the final vowel is replaced by *ā*; by *ito'tsarvanāmasthāne* [Pāṇini 7.1.86], the *i* is replaced by *at*; and by [Pāṇini 7.1.87], *nth* is substituted for the final portion.
The meaning is that this rule, beginning with *supām*, must be explained as having the sense that substitutes for case endings (*sup*) occur in place of case endings (*sup*).

The explanation here is as follows: the word *api* ("also") is carried over from the preceding rule, and it serves to include what has not been explicitly mentioned; by means of it, other case endings (*sup*) also become [substitutes] for case endings (*sup*). An example is:
*dhuri dakṣiṇāyāḥ*.
In place of the singular locative case, there occurs either the singular ablative or the singular genitive.
Regarding the phrase "of the *tiṅ*s," etc.,
the meaning is that this form of the sense— that *tiṅ* endings occur in place of *tiṅ* endings— must be explained.
The explanation, however, should be stated as before:
in the case of *ādre carman*,
there is elision (*luk*) of the locative singular ending after the word *carman*.
Regarding the word "yat": here too, [the correlative] "tat" is understood from the word "yat.
"Dhītī" and so forth.

After the words *dhīti*, *mati*, and *suṣṭuti*, the third-case singular ending [ṅi] becomes the vowel *i* which is homogeneous with the preceding vowel; by the rule *ubhayor akaḥ savarṇe dīrghatvam* [Pāṇini 6.1.102], there is lengthening of both [vowels].
Regarding the word *ubhā*:
from the word *ubha*, the first-case dual ending [au] becomes *ā*.
This is a single-substitute (ekādeśa) [by Pāṇini 6.1.102]:
"I do not despise that Brāhmaṇa.
This is the nominative singular from both the word *tat* and the word *brāhmaṇa*.
When followed by *niśabda*, the substitution of *na* for *ta* occurs according to [Pāṇini 8.4.45]. Thus we have *yuṣme* and *asme*.
Furthermore, for the *jas* following the words *yuṣmad* and *asmad*, this substitution *śe* applies according to [Pāṇini 7.1.27].

The suffix *śakāra* (the letter *ś*) serves the purpose of indicating that all [substitutes] apply. Now, one might ask: why do the substitutes *yūyam* and *vayam* not occur here by the rule *yūyavayau jasi* [Pāṇini 7.2.93]? To this he says: "the substitute *yūyam*" and so forth. Examples are *uruyā* and *dhṛṣṇuyā*.
The substitution of *yā* occurs for the third-case singular ending following the words *uru* and *dhṛṣṇu*.

Regarding the form *nābhā*: from the word *nābhi*, the substitution of *ḍā* occurs for the seventh-case singular; the letter *ḍ* is for the purpose of eliding the *ṭi* (the final vowel and following consonant).
Regarding "anuṣṭhā": from the word *anuṣṭubh*, there is the substitution of *ḍā* for the third case singular ending. Regarding "sādhuyā": [it is formed from *sādhu* with the suffix *-yā*].

From the word *sādhu*, the substitution of *yāj* occurs for the third case singular ending. The letter *c* is for the purpose of making it udātta at the end. [This is stated] because the elision (*luk*) of the nominative singular suffix (*su*) would otherwise apply.
The remainder [of the sentence] is that the substitute *yāj* is prescribed by this rule. However, the elision (*luk*) would have been applicable by the rule *svamornapuṃsakāt* [Pāṇini 7.1.23].
[The form] is *vasantā*.

After the word *vakanta*, this substitution of *ali* occurs for the seventh case singular (*saptamyekavacana*). The inclusion of the marker *l* is so that the preceding element may receive the udātta accent due to being a *lit* suffix.
[The term] "addition" (*upasaṃkhyānam*) [is used].
The meaning of this is "establishment. In what follows as well, the word *upasaṃkhyāna* has the meaning of "establishment.
However, this establishment should be carried out by relying on the word *api*.
In *urviyā* and *dārviyā*,
the third case singular ending is replaced by *iy* after the words *uru* and *dāru*. In *sukṣetriyā*, [the same applies].

From the word *sukṣetrin*, which ends in the suffix *ini* used in the sense of possession (*matvarthīya*), there is the substitution of *ṅi* for the following third-case singular ending. The letter *ḍ* is for the purpose of eliding the *ṭi* (the final vowel and following consonant);
the letter *c* is for the purpose of making the word have an udātta accent on its final syllable.
Regarding "sarasī":
this is the substitution of the vowel *ī* for the locative singular ending after the word *saraḥ*.
Regarding "prabāhavā": [this is the substitution of *ā* for the dual ending].

From the word *prabāhu*: there is the substitution of *aṅ* for the third-case singular ending; by the rule *gheṅiti* [Pāṇini 7.3.111], there is *guṇa*, and then the substitution of *ava*. Now, it has been stated: "One should know that when a marker (*ṅit*) is used, it indicates merely the mention of the phoneme; whatever applies to that phoneme should be understood as applying to the beginning of the word. But here, the letter *ṅ* is not at the beginning; so how can there be *guṇa*? There is no fault, because it will occur by virtue of the power of the marker being applied (*ṅit-karaṇa-sāmarthyāt*). [The form] is *svapnayā*.
From the word *svapna*, by [Pāṇini 7.1.2] (*supo dhātuprātipadikayoḥ*), there is the replacement of the third case singular ending with *ā*. The letter *ca* is for the sake of the accent.
Thus: *nāvayā*.

Why [is it] from the word *mau*? It is because the third person singular ending (*ṅe*) undergoes the substitution *ay*. The letter *r* is for the purpose of making the penultimate vowel acute according to [Pāṇini 6.1.217]. By stating "the substitute *am* is understood as the substitute for *mip*," he dispels the doubt that it might be the second person singular ending.
There is no inclusion of the second person singular ending; for in the Veda, one follows the forms exactly as they are observed.

Or, because of the recurrence of the word *api*, when that [word] recurs, this connection is made: "the substitution of *ama* and *ma* occurs; by virtue of the word *api*, it is also heard in some instances," as in "vadhīm."

In *hanterluṅ*, the suffix *sic* is applied by [Pāṇini 3.1.44], which becomes *am* by [Pāṇini 3.4.101] et seq., and this is replaced by *ma*; the vowel *a* is for the sake of pronunciation. By [Pāṇini 2.4.43], *han* is replaced by *vadh*. Is there not the augment *iṭ* by [Pāṇini 7.2.35] et seq.? No; by [Pāṇini 7.3.96], *iṭ* is added, and then the *sic* is elided by [Pāṇini 8.2.28]. Due to the rule of homogeneous long vowels (*savarṇadīrgha*), we obtain *avadhīt*. Regarding *kramīm*: the root *kramu* means "to step" (Dhātupāṭha 473). Everything else is as before.
The distinction here is this: by [Pāṇini 7.2.36], the augment *iṭ* is applied; thus, while one might expect forms such as *avadhiṣam* or *akramiṣam*, [the rule] states:
"The inclusion of the marker *ś* is for the purpose of making the replacement total."
If that [the letter *ś*] were absent, what would happen? The sense is: "it would be so.

Now, one might object: "Since there is no purpose in pronouncing the letter *m* when the letter *m* itself is to be expressed, the substitution will occur for the whole even without the letter *ś*. To this he says: "Of the letter *m*" and so forth.
For there is indeed a purpose in prescribing the letter *m*.
What is that? [It is] "it follows"; let it not be so. If this purpose exists, and the letter *ś* were not employed, then [the substitution] would apply only to the final [element], and not to all.
Therefore, the letter *ś* must be employed for the sake of making it a substitute for the whole. As in the example "aduhya."

In *duhyāt*, because the root belongs to the *adādi* class, there is elision of *śap*; then the substitution [of *sīyuṭ*] by [Pāṇini 3.4.103]; then the augment *ruṭ* by [Pāṇini 7.2.76]; upon the elision of the letter *t*, the two *a*s undergo the substitution of a single long vowel (*pūrvarūpa*) by [Pāṇini 6.1.107]. Thus: *duhyāt*. In *duhyām*: this is the imperative (*loṭ*). The third person plural suffix is *jha*; the *ṭi*-portion is replaced by *e*; the suffix is replaced by *ām*; for the substitute *ām* (which takes the place of *jha*), the augment *ruṭ* is added; there is elision of the preceding *śap*; upon the elision of the letter *t*, the rule "a long vowel replaces a homogeneous vowel" [Pāṇini 6.1.101] applies. Thus: *duhyām*.
In "śaye," [the suffix] *laṭ* (present indicative) ending in the singular, with the elision of *śap* according to Pāṇini 3.1.68. In "duhām," [the suffix is] *loṭ*.
The imperative (*loṭ*) ending in the singular; the substitution of *e* for the final vowel (*ṭi*), and the addition of *ām* by the rule *āmetaḥ* [Pāṇini 3.4.90]. Regarding the form *dugdhām*:

the substitution of *dh* for the initial *d* of the root by *dāderdhātorghaḥ* [Pāṇini 8.2.32], the substitution of *ṣ* for *dh* by *ṣṭunā ṣṭuḥ* [Pāṇini 8.2.40], and the substitution of *g* for *dh* by *jhalāṃ jaś jhaśi* [Pāṇini 8.4.53].

Regarding the phrase "because of the inclusion of *api*" and so forth: from the rule *ktvādi chandasi* [Pāṇini 7.1.38], the word *api* is understood to carry over (*anuvartate*). There, the connection is made as follows: "there is elision (*lopa*), and there is also hearing (*śravaṇa*)"; by this, [the elision] does not occur in the case of *kuruta*.
Once the *guṇa* substitution has been applied to the root *kṛ*, the substitution of *ut* occurs by the rule *ata utsārvadhātuke* [Pāṇini 6.4.110].

Even though there is occasional hearing [of this form] due to the recurrence of the word *api*, for that very reason [it does not occur] in the *parasmaipada*; so what is the purpose of mentioning the *ātmanepada*? If this is the case, the mention of the *ātmanepada* is for the sake of clarity. Regarding the form *vārayadhvāt*:

it is derived either from the root *vṛñ* or *vṛṅ* with the causative suffix *ṇic*, or from the root *vṛñ* "to cover" (Dhātupāṭha 1813) with the *curādi* suffix *ṇic*. From this, the imperative (*loṭ*) is formed; its ending is *dhvam*, which becomes *dhvāt*. Thus: *vārayadhvam*.

When *ṭerettva* has been applied, there is the substitution of *am* by [Pāṇini 3.4.91]. Regarding the rule "of the middle person plural of the *loṭ* [mood]": why then does this not apply to the singular of the first person? It is because in the Vedic language one follows what is actually observed, or because of the continued application of the word *api*. Thus: *kṛṇutāt*.

From the root *kṛvi* in the sense of "injuring" or "doing" (Dhātupāṭha 598), because it is marked with *it*, there is the augment *num*; then the suffix *u* is added by [Pāṇini 3.1.80], the letter *a* is substituted for the final, and the elision of the *a* occurs by [Pāṇini 6.4.48]. Regarding the form *saṃsṛjatāt*:
the suffix *śa* is applied to the root *sṛj* because it belongs to the *tudādi* class.
Regarding "gamayatāt":
there is the *ṇic* suffix, and by [Pāṇini 6.4.92], "the short vowel for roots marked with *mit*. Regarding "of *śṛṇoti*": by [Pāṇini 3.1.74], there is the *śnu* suffix and the substitution of *śṛ*.
In the case of *pitsu*, because of the absence of the *ṅit* designation, there is *guṇa*.
Thus: *sunota*. [The suffix] *śnu* [is applied] by [Pāṇini 3.1.73]: *svadibhyaḥ śnuḥ*.
In the word *dadhātana*,

there is reduplication by [Pāṇini 6.1.10] *ślau* following the root *dhā*. Here too, because the preceding [reduplicated syllable] lacks the *ṅit* designation, the elision of the long *ā* by [Pāṇini 6.4.112] *śnābyastayorātaḥ* does not occur.

In the word *dhatta*, by [Pāṇini 8.2.38], the letter *dh* replaces the vowel *a* of the reduplicated syllable. When the vowel *a* of the root has been elided, by [Pāṇini 8.4.53], the substitution of the voiced unaspirated stop (*jaś*) occurs, resulting in *ḍ*. Then, by [Pāṇini 8.4.54], the substitution of the voiceless unaspirated stop (*car*) occurs for that *ḍ*, resulting in *t*.

Regarding the word *jujuṣṭana*: from the root *iṣ* meaning "to desire," the suffix *śa* is applied as before, and there is its elision (*luk*) according to [Pāṇini 7.4.78]. Thus, it means "those who desire. Regarding the phrase *yadicchata*.
The *ca* (and) serves here to draw forward the word *tasya* (of that). Regarding the term *idantaḥ*:
the letter *t* is for the sake of avoiding ambiguity.

For if the letter *t* were not present, once the *yaṇ*-substitution had been applied, the form would have to be *yantaḥ*; in that case, there would be doubt—whether this refers to something ending in *yakāra* (the consonant *y*) or something ending in *ikāra* (the vowel *i*).
"Idanta" means that which has "id" as its end. The word "masi" is the referent of the compound (anyapadārtha).
This is a citation of the form "masi" ending in *s*, without a case-ending; the nominative singular ending is elided according to Pāṇini 7.1.39 (*supāṃ suluk* etc.).
The vowel *i* is for the purpose of pronunciation.
The word *bhasi* ends in the vowel *i*; this meaning is clarified by the rule beginning with "of *mas*, which ends in *s*" (*masaḥ sakārāntasya*).
By the phrase "ending in *s*," he demonstrates that [the substitution] does not occur for that which ends in *a*, as in the case of the mantra *mantraṃ vocema*.

But how, when there is the inclusion of that which ends in *s*, does it apply to that which does not end in *s*? Because that which has undergone a partial modification is not different [from the original].
If this is so, why does it not occur? Because in the Vedic language (*chandas*), one follows exactly what is observed, or because of the governing rule (*adhikāra*) of the word "also" (*api*).

Regarding the form *vocema*: it is the first person plural (*mas*) of the optative (*liṅ*) in the sense of benediction (*āśis*) derived from the root *vac*. The augment *yāsuṭ* is applied because of the rule *liṅyāśiṣi* (Pāṇini 3.4.116). The suffix *aṅ* is applied by the same rule (*liṅyāśiṣi*). Then, the substitution of *iy* for *at* occurs by the rule *ato yeyaḥ* (Pāṇini 7.2.80). The augment *um* is added to the root *vac* by the rule *vaca um* (Pāṇini 7.4.20). Because the suffix is treated as *sārvadhātuka*, the *u* of *vac* is replaced by *guṇa* (the vowel *o*) according to the rule *ādguṇaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.1.87). Finally, the *s* of the suffix is elided by the rule *ato dīrghau yañi supi* (Pāṇini 7.3.101), which prescribes the elision of the *s* of the first person plural (*uttama*) when preceded by a short *a*, and the *s* of the *yās* portion is also elided by the rule *lopaścāsyānyatarasyām* (Pāṇini 7.2.79). Thus, the form *vocema* is established.
"The augment *i* occurs. But how is this an augment? And why might it not be so? Because the characteristic marks (*liṅga*) of an augment are absent.

The properties of being *ṭit*, *kit*, or *mit* are the marks of an augment; here, not even one of these exists. Therefore, this is not an augment, just as in the case of the substitution of *bhū* [by rule 2.4.52].

If this is so, then by the rule "na yvābhyāṃ padāntābhyāṃ pūrvau ca tābhyāmaic" [Pāṇini 7.3.3], the augment *aij* would not occur. If you argue that its status as an augment is determined by the mention of the word *pūrva* (preceding), then let its status be determined here as well by the mention of the word *anta* (end). For just as the word *pūrva* denotes a part and expresses a part located in a specific position, so too does the word *anta*; thus, the two cases are identical.
"And that becomes its end (*anta*).

*Anta* means a part, a portion, or a member. For this very reason, he says that it is included by the mention of "that" (*tad-grahaṇena*), stating: "The purpose of mentioning 'that' is the cessation of separate accents (*pṛthak-svara-nivṛtti*) and the occurrence of the *nighāta* (elision) according to [Pāṇini 8.1.28]: *tiṅṅatiṅā*."
It is not stated as "masa-ik," for the sake of avoiding ambiguity.
If it were stated in this way, there would be doubt: whether it is the augment *ik* or the pratyāhāra [denoting the vowels]. [Examples are:
*dīpayāmasi*, *jambhayamasi*.

The roots *dīpī* and *dṛptau* (Dhātupāṭha 1150), and *jabhi* and *jṛbhī*, meaning "to bend the limbs" [from the Dhātupāṭha 388, 389]—from these two, when followed by the causative suffix (*ṇic*), the present tense marker (*laṭ*) is applied, and according to Pāṇini 7.1.61, there is elision (*lup*).
In some places, the reading is *bhañjayāmasi*;
this should be understood as derived from the root *bhañjo* (Dhātupāṭha 1453), "to crush," with the causative suffix (*ṇyac*) added. Regarding the form *dattvāya*: [this is explained as follows].
The substitution of *dad* is applied by the rule *do dad ghoḥ* [Pāṇini 7.4.46].
Regarding the phrase *ktvāpi chandasi* and so forth: the intention is that if this were stated, the mention of *ktvā* would not need to be repeated twice.

"The word *samāsa* (compound) is understood here" means that it is carried over from [Pāṇini 7.1.37], which states "in a compound not preceded by *nañ*. If this were stated immediately after that rule, there might be the suspicion that the mention of "compound" (*samāsa*) continues to apply there as well; therefore, the intention is that this is not stated immediately after it, in order to prevent its continued application. [The example is] *iṣṭvīnam*.
By the rule *vacyādi* [Pāṇini 6.1.15], there is vocalization (*samprasāraṇa*).
Thus, *pītvīnam*.
By the rule *dhumāsthā* [Pāṇini 6.4.66] and so forth, there is the substitution of *it*.

This [result] is obtained either from the particle *iti* (in *etad-iti-karaṇāt*), from the sense of "and so forth" (*ādy-artha*) inherent in the word *ca*, or from the fact that *ca* has the function of including what has not been explicitly mentioned (*anukta-samuccaya*).

Since the rule would be established by the inclusion of either one of these two, the inclusion of both is for the sake of stylistic variety (*vaicitrya*). In the forms *snātvī* and *pītvī*, the substitution of *ī* is prescribed in place of the long vowel *ā*.

But surely, words such as *snātvyā* are not recited in the list of nominal stems (*prātipadika-gaṇa*); how then are they to be understood? And how can they be indicated by the word "etcetera" (*ādi*)? To this he says: "This word 'etcetera' has the sense of 'type'. Words of this type—those similar to these—are to be understood as *snātvyā* and so forth. The form *jaseḥ* is a designation used by the ancient teachers; for the ancient teachers indeed analyzed [the suffix] as *jasiḥ*.

The objection beginning with "In the case of [the rule] *ye pūrvāso ye parāsaḥ*," and so forth, concerns the view that the word-referent (*padārtha*) is a universal (*jāti*). In that context, when two rules of equal strength have their purposes fulfilled elsewhere and thus come into conflict, there arises the possibility of non-application due to mutual obstruction. To address this, it is stated: "In the case of a conflict (*vipratiṣedha*), the subsequent [rule] prevails; once that has been applied, if the preceding [rule] also applies, it too shall take effect. Thus, the view that the word-referent is a universal is the domain for understanding the principle of "re-occurrence" (*punar-prasaṅga*).
The resolution is provided by the word "sakṛt" (once), and so forth.

Thus, since the purpose of the word-meaning has been accomplished elsewhere, when both rules would otherwise apply alternately to such a subject matter, this restrictive rule (*niyama*) is initiated: "In case of conflict (*vipratiṣedha*), the latter alone takes effect, not the former.
Consequently, because there is no cognition of a recurrence (*punar-prasaṅga*), the substitution of *ś* is not repeated once it has been superseded.

What has been sublated does not persist when there is a subsequent application; it cannot come into being again. Regarding the phrase "in *ātmaprīti*," this is a locative case denoting the object (*viṣaya-saptamī*).
For this very reason, he says: "when *kyac* follows in the sense of *ātmaprīti*."
That *kyac* suffix for which "self-love" (*ātmaprīti*) is the object is described as such. Regarding the form *āśyati*:

from the sense "he desires food for himself," the suffix *kyac* is applied by the rule *supa ātmanaḥ kyac* [Pāṇini 3.1.8]; thus we have *āś-ya*. Then, by the rule *ato guṇe* [Pāṇini 6.1.97], the substitution of the single substitute (the *guṇa* vowel) occurs.
The same should be understood for cases such as *kṣīrasyati* and so forth.

In all instances, the suffix *kyac* is applied when the object of desire is one's own pleasure (*ātmaprīti*). For whoever desires food and other things for himself necessarily desires them for the sake of his own pleasure.

If this is so, since the suffix *kyac* is prescribed after a word expressing desire (*icchā*) and will thus apply everywhere where there is a matter of one's own pleasure, why is it stated "in the sense of desire" (*icchyām*)? The inclusion of the phrase "in one's own pleasure" (*ātmaprītau*) is for the purpose of encompassing well-known usage; by means of this, the suffix occurs only where it is employed in common worldly usage regarding one's own pleasure, and not elsewhere. Consequently, forms such as *aśvīyati* (desiring a horse) and *kṣīralavaṇīyati* (craving milk and salt) become logically justified. As for the form *aśvīyati*: [it is derived from *aśva* with the suffix *kyac*].
The suffix *kyac* is applied according to [Pāṇini 3.1.10], and the substitution of *i* for the vowel [of the root] occurs according to [Pāṇini 7.4.33].

Regarding the phrase "in the case of *ā* and *vṛṣi*" and so forth, the meaning is that this should be explained as having the sense: "the suffix *asuc* occurs after *ā* and *vṛṣi* when there is a desire for sexual union."
Regarding the phrase "of milk and salt" (*kṣīralavaṇayoḥ*) and so forth:
it depends on the word "should be stated" (*vaktavyam*).
The meaning is that this form of the sense—"there arises a longing for milk and salt" (*kṣīralavaṇayor lālasāyām asug bhavati*)—is what must be explained.
The explanation has already been provided:
"It does not occur even in the case of one's own pleasure.
This is because one desires for oneself what is beneficial (*āyāti*) and thus seeks it (*āyāyati*).

*Lavaṇīyati*. Regarding the term *tṛṣṇātirekaḥ*: the excess (*atireka*) of thirst means its surplus, its intensity, or its abundance—this is the meaning. This statement is made because [the suffix *nuṭ*] would otherwise apply by the rule *hrasvanadyāpo nuṭ* [Pāṇini 7.1.54].

"The form *ām* is understood here as the genitive plural (*ṣaṣṭhībahuvacana*). In this context, several instances of *ām* are possible: the genitive plural [by Pāṇini 7.1.54], the *ām* [by Pāṇini 5.4.11] after words ending in *kim*, *tiṅ*, indeclinables, or verbal roots when expressing excellence of a substance, and the *ām* [by Pāṇini 3.1.35].

If there were to be the inclusion of all these [augment rules], then for all of them, the *nuṭ* augment prescribed by "hrasvanadyāpo nuṭ" [Pāṇini 7.1.54] would apply. In that case as well, this very mention of *am* (the genitive plural ending) is understood to follow; since it is desired only for the genitive plural, that alone is taken. Thus he says: "Because of its posteriority," and so forth. The scope of *suṭ* and *nuṭ* is the genitive plural, whereas for *āṭ* and the others, it is the singular and so on of the four cases beginning with the dative. Since they are subsequent, *āṭ* and the others take effect by virtue of the rule "ṅerāmnadyāmnībhyaḥ" [Pāṇini 7.3.116].
In that regard: by [Pāṇini 7.3.112], *āṭ* is added—resulting in *kumāryām*; by [Pāṇini 7.3.113], *yāṭ* is added—resulting in *khaṭvāyām*;
and by [Pāṇini 7.3.114], *syāṭ* is added with the shortening of the vowel—resulting in *sarvasyām*.
If that is so, why are those [suffixes] prescribed after a verbal root ending in *gh* and those prescribed after the *liṭ* [tense] not included? To this he says: "And which...? and so forth.
Of those two, one is prescribed after a verbal root ending in *gh*, and the other after a verbal root (*dhātu*).
However, a verbal root ending in *gh* does not have the technical designation "pronominal" (*sarvanāman*), nor does a verbal root (*dhātu*) [have that designation].
Since those two [suffixes] cannot occur after a pronoun (*sarvanāman*), they are not included [in this context].

Now, if it is argued that their inclusion here is unjustified on the grounds that they cannot occur after a pronoun, even so, it is justified for the sake of the subsequent rule; for those two do indeed occur after a stem ending in *haras* or *svan*: *pacatitarām*, *pacatitamām*, *cikīrṣāñcakāra*, and *kārāyāñcakāra*. To this he says: "Or, because they have an indicatory letter (*sānubandhaka*), those two are not included.
The intention is that this is according to the maxim regarding suffixes without an indicatory letter (*niranubandhaka-paribhāṣā*).

In that regard, the suffix *ghā* has the phoneme *ā* as its *anubandha*, whereas the other [suffixes] have the phoneme *a*. Thus it has been stated: "The suffix *ām* is not designated as *am* because it does not end in the vowel *a*.
As for the phrase "for the sake of what follows," and so forth:
[The rule] "it" [Pāṇini 7.1.53] is stated so that [the suffix] *ām* may follow.

Why is this not a locative indication (*saptamīnirdeśa*), such as "even after this [stem], when *ām* follows"? For there is indeed a purpose here: so that *suṭ* may occur for a pronoun (*sarvanāman*) when *ām* follows? To this he says: "But here," and so forth.

Regarding the statement "when both [case endings] are specified, the specification of the fifth [ablative case] is stronger" (Śākalya-Pariśiṣṭa 97), by this rule [Pāṇini 1.1.67], the ablative *sarvanāmnaḥ* causes the locative *ām-i* to be interpreted as a genitive; thus, *suṭ* must be applied to *ām* itself, and so there is no purpose for the specific mention here. This being the case, the following statement is made: "of three" (*trayāṇām*).
The lengthening of the vowel occurs by [Pāṇini 7.3.102]: *supi ca*.

But surely this is already established by the specific rule (*nipātana*) "there is *guṇa* substitution for the three roots beginning with *ṇij* before *ślau*" [Pāṇini 7.4.75]; so for what purpose is this [present rule] commenced? Since it is already established in this way, its commencement serves to indicate: "specific rules (*nipātanas*) do not necessarily override other rules" (*abādhakāny api nipātanāni bhavanti*). By this, forms such as *purātanam* are established; otherwise, they would not be established because they would be overridden by the specific rule "in the case of words taught by ancient sages" [Pāṇini 4.3.105]. [The rule further states: "it is also desired for the three [roots] in the Veda."

And this [option] is obtained either by virtue of the governing rule (*adhikāra*) beginning with "etaccāpi," or by the rule: "In the Vedic language (*chandasi*), all grammatical operations are optional" (*sarve vidhayaśchandasi vikalpyante*). Regarding "of the young girls" (*kumārīṇām*):
the suffix *ṅīṣ* is applied according to Pāṇini 4.1.20.
Regarding "of the fair-complexioned women" (*gaurīṇām*): [the same applies].
The suffix *ṅīṣ* is applied by [Pāṇini 4.1.41].
Regarding "śāṅrgaravīṇām," the suffix *ṅīn* is applied by [Pāṇini 4.1.73]: "After *śāṅrgarava* and others, *ṅīn* replaces *aÑ*."
Regarding the word "lakṣmīṇām":
following the rule *avitṛstṛtantribhya īḥ* (Pāṇini 3.2.158), the rule *lakṣermuṭ ca* (Pāṇini 3.2.160) applies, whereby the suffix *ī* is added and the augment *muṭ* is inserted.
Regarding the term *brāhṛbandhūnām*: it is a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "those whose relatives (*bandhu*) are *brāhṛ*s. The suffix *ūṅ* is applied according to Pāṇini 4.1.66, *ūṅutaḥ*.
Regarding "khaṭvānām": [the suffix] *ṭāp* is applied by [Pāṇini 4.1.4], "The feminine suffix *ṭāp* is added after a stem beginning with *aja-* and ending in short *a*.
Regarding "bahurājānām": [the suffix *ṅīp* is applied].
The suffix *ḍāp* is applied by the rule *ḍābubhābhyāmanyatarasyām* [Pāṇini 4.1.13], as in the form *kārīṣagandhyānām*. [This is derived as follows:
from *kārīṣagandhi*, the suffix *aṇ* is applied to denote "the offspring of."

For that [word], there is the substitution of *ṣyaṅ* by the rule *aṇiñoranārṣayoḥ* [Pāṇini 4.1.78], and the feminine suffix *cāp* by the rule *yaṅścāp* [4.1.74]. In the form *pañcānām*, there is lengthening by the rule *pañcānām* [6.4.7], and the elision of *n* by the rule *nalopaḥ prātipadikāntasya* [8.2.7].
In the form *ṣaṇṇām*:

By [Pāṇini 8.2.39], the *ṣakāra* becomes *ḍakāra*; by [8.4.45], the *ḍakāra* becomes *ṇakāra*; and by [8.4.41], the *nakāra* becomes *ṇakāra*. One might ask: "Why is the technical name *ṣaṭ* not prescribed for a numeral ending in *repha* (r) as well, according to [1.1.24]? If that were so, the mention of *cu* and *tu* would not need to be made here. To this he says: "Of that which ends in *repha*" (*rephāntāyāḥ*), etc. The meaning has already been explained.
"Because of the use of the plural number," and so forth.

For if there were a reference to the word as the primary element (*pradhāna*), then in the case of the *itaretarayoga* (mutual conjunction) alternative, one would have made the reference in the dual number as "ṣaṭ-catur-bhyām. However, in the case of the *samāhāra* (collective) alternative, one would have used the singular number as "ṣaṭ-caturaḥ. Yet, the reference has been made using the plural number. Therefore, because of this indication by the plural number, there is a reference specifically to the words named *ṣaṣ* and *catuḥ* when they have number as their primary meaning.

And this is its purpose: wherever the number is predominant, [the suffix] occurs even after that which ends in it. For when the reference is made with the number as the primary element, this [suffix] occurs upon the inclusion of the meaning; and since the status of being "subsequent" (*paratva*) to *ām* is understood through the word itself, it therefore occurs both after the simple words *ṣaṣ* and *catur*, and after those that end in them.
Even after that [suffix], the condition of being followed by *ām* occurs precisely by way of the word;
this is shown in the passage beginning with "but when it has become a subordinate element" (*upasarjanībhūtāyās tu*).
Furthermore, because of the use of the plural number in the reference, this refers to the meaning of number (*saṃkhyārtha*).
And that referent is of two kinds: primary (pradhāna) and non-primary (apradhāna).

Among these, when there is a comprehension of the action with respect to the primary referent, the [suffix] occurs even after a compound ending in that [numeral], provided that the numeral is primary therein—as in *priyaṣaṣaḥ* and so forth. However, where the numeral has become a subordinate member (*upasarjana*), it does not occur—as in *priyaṣaṣām*.

For here, the meaning of the other word (*anyapadārtha*) is predominant, while the number is subordinate. In the example *priyapañcānām*, once the elision (*alopa*) [of the case-ending] has occurred by [Pāṇini 6.4.134], the substitution of *ś* [for *n*] occurs by [Pāṇini 8.4.40]. The genitive case in *śrīgrāmaṇyoḥ* is characterized by its relation [to the preceding word].
"The statement 'for the sake of eternity' refers to the word *śrī*, and not to the word *grāmaṇī*;
for that [latter] is used solely for the purpose of attainment."

For just as in the spoken language (bhāṣā), when the designation *nadī* applies, the rule *hrasvanadyāpo nuṭ* [Pāṇini 7.1.54] is established, so it is also in the Vedic language (*chandas*). Therefore, this [mention of *chandasi*] is for the purpose that [the application of *nuṭ*] should be constant. If this were not present, it would apply only when the designation *nadī* occurs, and not at other times.

Regarding the passage beginning with "yadā sūtāśca": by this, he demonstrates the following—when the word *sūta* is formed as a *karmadhāraya* compound with the word *grāmaṇī*, then the resulting term *sūtagrāmaṇī* does not end in a short vowel (*hrasva*), nor does it end in *nadī*, nor does it end in *ā*; consequently, the [application of the feminine suffix] would not be obtained, yet it is desired. Therefore, this statement is made so that it may occur accordingly.

When the compound *sūtagrāmaṇī* is a dvandva subject to the rule "every dvandva may optionally be treated as a singular" (*sarvo dvandvo vibhāṣayaikavadbhavati*), then, because it is neuter by virtue of [Pāṇini 2.4.17], the shortening of the stem-final vowel is applied according to "the stem-final vowel is shortened in the neuter" (*hrasvo napuṃsake prātipadikasya*). Subsequently, a single remainder (*ekaśeṣa*) is formed from many instances of the word *sūtagrāmaṇī*, and then the genitive plural is prescribed. In that case, since the desired form is already established simply by the fact that the stem ends in a short vowel, there is no purpose for your stated rule. [The phrase] "from that which occurs at the end of an *ṛk*-verse quarter" [is used].
In the Vedic language (chandas), only a quarter-verse of a *ṛc* is possible, not a quarter-verse of a *śloka*; therefore, the term "quarter-verse of an *ṛc*" (*ṛkpāda*) is employed.
Regarding the forms *kuṇḍitā* and *huṇḍitā*:

from the roots *kuḍi* (meaning "to burn," Dhātupāṭha 270) and *huḍi* (meaning "to heap together," Dhātupāṭha 269), the suffix *tṛc* is applied, followed by the augment *iṭ*, and then *anaṅ* is substituted according to Pāṇini 7.1.94 (*ṛduśanaspurudaṃso’nehasām ca*). Does this *num* augment apply at the very stage of the root’s instruction (*dhātūpadeśāvasthā*)? To this he says: *kuṇḍā*, *huṇḍā*, etc. If the *num* were to occur after the suffix has arisen, then at the time of the suffix’s application, because the roots *kuḍi* and *huḍi* would not be heavy (*agurutvāt*), the suffix *ktin* alone would be applicable, and not the suffix *a* (which results in the forms *kuṇḍā* and *huṇḍā*). Therefore, [the rule for *num*] must be applied while the root is still in its state of instruction.

Therefore, for that reason, it is determined that the augment *num* occurs precisely at the stage of the instruction of the verbal roots (*dhātūpadeśāvasthā*). But how is it determined that *num* occurs at the stage of the instruction of the verbal roots, given that the term "instruction" (*upadeśa*) is not explicitly mentioned here? To this he says: "For instance," and so forth.

In the rule *dhinvikṛṇvyora ca* [Pāṇini 3.1.80], which prescribes the suffix *u*, the mention of the roots *dhinv* and *kṛṇv* accompanied by *num* is intended so that they may be understood as being inherently possessed of *num*.

In this way, the addition of *num* occurs for those [roots] that have *num* attached, provided that *num* occurs precisely at the stage of the original instruction (*upadeśāvasthā*); it does not occur otherwise.
Therefore, from the evidence (*jñāpaka*) of the mention of roots "with *num* attached," it is understood that *num* must occur only at the stage of the root's original instruction.
For this is its purpose: so that *num* may be understood as occurring only at the stage of the original instruction.
For that [augment] is not applied for the sake of *num*; rather, it becomes *num*.
Its purpose is this: so that *num* may be understood as occurring precisely in the state of the original instruction (*upadeśāvasthā*).

For that [augment] *num* is not applied for the sake of that [specific purpose]; rather, *num* must occur there by the force of the grammatical rule itself (*lakṣaṇavaśāt*) in the case of "dhinvikṛñcyora ca" (Pāṇini 3.1.80). Since the mention of the root *gṛ* is accompanied by *num*, how can that be an indicator (*jñāpaka*) for this meaning? This is not so; for the mention of *ik* in "na hi" (Pāṇini 3.1.80) is not a general indication, because due to the presence of the term "variously" (*bahulam*) in "rogākhyāyāṃ ṣvul bahulam" (Pāṇini 3.3.108), it occurs only in certain instances and not everywhere. And thus, mentions such as "evaṃ ca" (Pāṇini 3.1.5) and others become logically consistent.

Therefore, in the rule *dhinvikṛṇvyoḥ* [Pāṇini 3.1.80], this is not a reference by means of the vowel *i*; what then? It is a reference by means of the vowel *i* used for the purpose of pronunciation, just as in the rule *indhibhavatibhyām* [Pāṇini 1.2.6] there is a reference by means of the vowel *i*; otherwise, the elision of the nasal (anunāsika) would occur according to the rule *aniditām* [Pāṇini 6.4.24].

Furthermore, there is indeed the mention of the long *ī* in the rule *dhinvikṛṇvyoḥ* (Pāṇini 3.1.80). Even so, if it were not intended to convey the meaning that the augment *num* occurs precisely at the stage of the root's formal instruction (*dhātūpadeśāvasthā*), then, for the sake of brevity—since the teaching of augments is not subject to the restriction of being "not otherwise" (*anitayatvāt*)—the author would have made the mention without adding *num*, just as was stated in the case of the singular collective compound (*dvandvaikavadbhāva*) under [Pāṇini 7.1.1].
Therefore, the inclusion of the term *grah* accompanied by *num* is itself an indicator (*jñāpaka*), and this is also understood from the mention of the word "root" (*dhātu*).
In order to show that the augment *num* occurs only at the stage of the original enunciation (*upadeśāvasthā*), he says: "And the mention of 'root' (*dhātugrahaṇam*)," and so forth.

The time when the designation "root" (*dhātusaṃjñā*) becomes active is the time of the enunciation of the root; it is for the purpose of [establishing] that *num* occurs only there that the mention of "root" is made here.

Therefore, from this mention of "root" as well, it is understood that *num* occurs only at the stage of the original enunciation, for there is no other purpose for the mention of "root"—this is the intended meaning.

"But would there not be the nasalization (*num*) by the rule *idito num dhātoḥ* for the two [roots] *tās* and *sic* in the forms *bhettā* and *abhaitsīt*, since they contain the *it*-marker *i*? Should the mention of 'dhātu' (root) be for the purpose of preventing this? To this he says: "In the case of *tās* and *sic*" and so forth.
