If the operation of the *it*-marker were to apply to *tās* and *sic*, then their nasality would have to be formally declared (*pratijñāta*) for the sake of assigning the technical designation *it* to the vowel *e*; however, since there is no such purpose, it is not so declared.

Furthermore, since the vowel *i* in these two [roots] is read as being without a nasal (*niranunāsika*) and designated as merely for the purpose of pronunciation (*uccāraṇārtha*), there is no possibility at all for the application of *num*; so why is the mention of "root" (*dhātu*) used to exclude that? [Objection: But in forms such as *araṃsta*, *amaṃsta*, *mantā*, and *saṃganta*, the rule *aniditām* [Pāṇini 6.4.24] would otherwise cause the elision of the nasal; therefore, the status of *tāsi* and *sici* as having an indicatory *it* (*idit*) is for the sake of preventing that. Why then is it said that there is no operation of an *idit* for *tāsi* and *sici*? To this he says: "*araṃsta, amaṃsta*" and so forth.
> [Regarding] 1.2.14, this is the purpose of prescribing *kittva* (the status of being marked with *k*): so that there may be the elision of the nasal (*anunāsikalopa*) in the case of *āhatā*.

If the elision of the nasal in the form ending in *sij* were to occur by relying on the *ṅittva* (marked with *ṅ*) of the *sārvadhātuka* suffix, then the prescription of *kittva* would be useless due to the absence of a purpose. This is not so; for there is another purpose for the prescription of *kittva*: so that the elision of the nasal in *sij* may occur by the rule "anudāttopadeśa" (6.4.37) etc.; and so that, by the rule "aniditām" (6.4.24) etc., it does not occur for a form ending in *sij* when followed by a *sārvadhātuka* suffix.

What, then, is the distinction here: [the rule] "optionally before a *ṅit* *sārvadhātuka* affix" or "before a *kit* *sic*"? This is the distinction: when the *sic* affix shares the same locus [as the cause of the elision], the elision of the nasal (*anunāsikalopa*) is considered non-existent (*asiddha*), and thus the elision of the vowel *a* (by P. 6.4.48) does not occur. However, in the case of a *sārvadhātuka* affix, since the elision of the penultimate vowel (*upadhālopa*) is not considered non-existent due to having a different locus, the elision of the vowel *a* would indeed take place.

There is no such distinction here. Therefore, in the rule for elision (*lopavidhi*), the term "upadeśa" (in the state of being taught) is understood to carry over from the sūtra beginning with *anudāttopadeśa* [Pāṇini 6.4.37]. Consequently, it is understood that the elision applies to that base (*aṅga*) which ends in the vowel *a* at the time it is taught as an *ārthadhātuka* suffix. Now, in the case of *āha*, this base does not end in the vowel *i* at the time it is taught. For this reason—and by virtue of the power of the prescription of the *kit* designation in the rule *tadaśiṣyaṃ saṃjñāpramāṇatvāt* [Pāṇini 1.2.53]—there is no elision of the nasal *n* in forms such as *aramsta*. Thus, it has been demonstrated that the *idit*-operation does not apply to the suffix *sic*.
Now, in order to demonstrate that even for the root *tās* there is no absence of nasal elision—that is, the operation of the *idit* designation does not apply—he says "mantā," and so forth.
The connection with the subject at hand is that the elision of the letter *n* does not occur.
It is by the rule beginning with *aniditām* [Pāṇini 6.4.24] that the elision of the penultimate *n* is prescribed.

And in the case of *maktā*, the letter *n* does not become an *upadhā* (penultimate vowel), because the elision of the *ṭi* suffix is considered non-existent (*asiddha*). Therefore, even for the root *tās*, the grammatical operation pertaining to roots marked with the indicatory letter *it* (*idit-kārya*) does not apply. Consequently, it is rightly stated: "The operation of *idit* does not exist for the roots *tās* and *sic*."

Now, why does the addition of the augment *num* not result in the operation [prescribed] for an *idit* [root]? Because it is undesired. Indeed, it is not proper to assume an undesired grammatical effect in the treatise.

If, then, the vowel *i* in the root *tās-* is for the sake of pronunciation (*uccāraṇārtha*), how then is this not in contradiction with what was stated under [Pāṇini 7.1.58]: "The addition of the marker *it* is for the purpose of preventing the elision of the nasal"? It has been explained right there how there is no contradiction.

Now, why does *num* not occur for roots such as *bhidir*? Is it not the case that these also have the vowel *i* designated by the technical term *it*? To this he says: "In the case of *haritām*" and so forth.

For *bhidir* and the others have *ir* [as their penultimate], not *id*; because, according to the supplementary rule (*vārttika*) "the addition of *ira*" (Pāṇini 1.3.7), the designation *it* applies to the entire cluster containing the letter *r*, and not to each individual constituent part.

In this context, what occasion is there for the *it* designation to apply to the *i* that is being released [from its status as an *it*]? It might be argued: "By rule 1.3.2, the *i* has the designation *it*; by rule 1.3.3, the *r* has the designation *it*; therefore, they indeed possess the status of being *its*. To this he replies: "Even of a part... The meaning is already explained. The roots beginning with *muc* are listed in the *tudādi* class, starting from *muclṛ mokṣaṇe* (Dhātupāṭha 1430) up to the end of the class.
Regarding the form *moktā*: the suffix *tṛc* is applied; the prohibition of *iṭ* is by rule 7.2.10 (*ekācaḥ*), and the substitution of *k* for *c* is by rule 8.2.30 (*co kuḥ*).

"What, then, are *tṛmph* and the others? He thinks as follows: among the roots beginning with *tṛmph*, those beginning with *tṛph* are also listed in the root list (*dhātupāṭha*) without the nasal augment (*anunāsika*), such as "√*tṛph* √*tṛnph* in the sense of satisfaction" (DhP 1307, 1308).

If those were also included by the mention of *tṛph* and so on, then forms such as *tṛphati* would not be possible; therefore, he says: "Those that are listed there with the nasal augment are *tṛmph* and the others."

This word "ādi" (beginning) has the sense of "type" (*prakāra*); and "type" means similarity. Therefore, the intention is that those [roots] which are similar to *tṛmphati* along with its *anuṣaṅga* (nasal augment) are indicated by the inclusion of the term "ādi.

Regarding the phrase "sānuṣaṅgāḥ": the letter *n* is the *anuṣaṅga*; those which exist together with it are "similar," and it is these very ones that are indicated by the inclusion of the term "ādi"—this is the intended meaning.
Regarding the term *sānuṣaṅgāḥ*: the letter *n* is the *anuṣaṅga*; those which exist together with it are *sānuṣaṅgāḥ*.

If, then, those that are recited as having the *anuṣaṅga* are *tṛmph* and the others, and when *num* is applied to them and the subsequent *anusvāra* is formed, followed by the *parasavarṇa* substitution for that [anusvāra], would there not result the hearing of two *n*s? To this, he says: "Of these," and so forth.
For *num* is prescribed after the elision of the letter *n* has already taken place.
The intended meaning is that, therefore, no fault arises at all.
Now, one might ask: "Why is that *num* not elided as well? To this he says, "And that," and so forth.
He considers that if that too were elided, the prescription of *num* would be entirely purposeless.
The purpose of the word *upasaṃkhyāna* (supplementary addition) is to provide an explanation.

In this regard, the explanation is as follows: the term *dhātoḥ* (after a verbal root) from [Pāṇini 7.1.58] is carried over; then the rule is split (*yogavibhāga*) into two parts, beginning with *śe*. By means of this, the augment *num* will apply even to roots such as *tṛmph* and others. [Objection: Would the mention of *muc* and others in the rule be redundant, since the desired result would already be established by the portion *śe*? [Response: It is not redundant, because the portion *śe* is intended to indicate that its scope does not extend to all cases.
Thus, this over-extension does not occur.

Why then are *tṛmph* and the others not listed among the *muc*-class roots? It is for the purpose that the augment *num* should not apply to those which are listed here without the nasal (*niranuṣaṅga*). Regarding the form *maṅktā*:

from the root *ṭumasjo śuddhau* (Dhātupāṭha 1415), with the suffix *tṛc*, the absence of *iṭ* as before, and the change of *j* to *g* (*kutva*), the augment *num* is placed before the final *j*. Then, by the rule *skoḥ* [Pāṇini 8.2.29], there is the elision of the *s*, followed by the substitution of the corresponding homogeneous letter (*parasavarṇa*) for the *anusvāra*.
Regarding the form *neṣṭā*:
when the augment *iṭ* is not present, this *num* [augment] applies; then, by the rule *vraścādi-* (Pāṇini 8.2.36), there is the substitution of *ṣ*, and subsequently *ṣṭu*-hood (*ṣṭutva*).
In the alternative where *iṭ* is present, because the root does not begin with a *jhal* consonant, the *num* augment does not occur—hence the form is *naśitā*.
"Immersing, destroying"— here,

by the rule *lyuṭ* [Pāṇini 3.3.115], there is the substitution of *jaś* (the rule *jaśtva*), whereby the *s* becomes *d*, and by the rule of *catva*, that *d* becomes *j*. "Of the root *masji*" and so forth.

If *num* were to follow the final vowel of the root *masj*, then because it would not be preceded by a conjunct consonant (*asaṃyogaditvāt*), the elision of *m* would not apply; furthermore, because it would not end in *u* (*anupadhatvāt*), the elision of *n* would not apply either, yet that [elision] is desired. Otherwise, forms such as *magno* and *mānavān* would not be established. Therefore, the Teachers desire that *num* be inserted before the final letter of *masj*. But how is this desired meaning obtained? It is obtained from the indicative mark of the non-deviation of the rule regarding the prior placement of the shorter word in the compound *naśer alpa-actarasya*.

For by indicating independence from a formal definition (*lakṣaṇa*), he suggests that even this [definition] is not required here. And since that [definition] is not required, the rule is applied only where, in accordance with the object to be defined (*lakṣya*), the desired result is achieved once the augment *num* has been added to the root *masj*. Consequently, the *num* is established as occurring before the final syllable of *masj*.
In the word *magnaḥ*, the substitution of *ṇatva* for *n* is applied by [Pāṇini 8.2.45]. In the word *randhayati*,
the root *radh*— meaning "to injure" or "to accomplish"— takes the causative suffix *ṇic*.
The word *rabbhaka* is formed with the suffix *ṇvul*;
the word *sādhurandhī* is formed with the suffix *ṇini* according to [Pāṇini 3.2.78].
In the expression *randhaṃrandham*,

the suffix *ṇamul* is applied according to Pāṇini 3.4.22 (*ābhīkṣṇye ṇamul*) because of the sense of repetition; furthermore, the doubling of the word occurs according to the Vārttika 887 (*ābhīkṣṇye dve bhavataḥ*).
In the case of *randho vartate*, the suffix *ghañ* is applied in the sense of the action (*bhāve*).

Now, in forms such as *randhayati*, since the rule [Pāṇini 7.2.116] applies later, *vṛddhi* would be expected; why, then, does it not occur? To this he says: "Even though it is subsequent," and so forth.
Furthermore, we infer its permanence (*nityatva*) from the fact that it applies whether [the condition] has been performed or not.

For that [augment *nuṭ*] applies both when the increase (*vṛddhi*) has been performed and when it has not; thus it is permanent. But the increase, once *nuṭ* has been applied, does not apply because the vowel *a* is no longer penultimate; therefore, it is non-permanent.
[The example is] "raddhā."

By the rule *iti takārasya dhakāraḥ* (8.2.40), the letter *t* is replaced by *dh*; then, by the rule of *jaśtva*, the *dh* of the root becomes *d*. A prohibition of the *num* augment, which would otherwise have been required by the preceding rule, is now stated. Thus, in forms such as *radhitā*, the augment *iṭ* is applied by the rule *iti iṭ* (7.2.45).
Regarding the forms *rarandhiva* and *rarandhima*:

the augment *iṭ* is applied by the rule *krādiniyamāt* [Pāṇini 7.2.13], and the substitutions of *va* and *ma* for *vas* and *mas* are applied by the rule *parasmaipadānām* [Pāṇini 3.4.82]. Now, one might object: this root *radh* is recited as ending in a non-conjunct consonant (*asaṃyogānta*); therefore, since it would be *kit* by the rule *asaṃyogālliṭ kit* [Pāṇini 1.2.5], the elision of the nasal (*n*) would apply by the rule *aniditām* [Pāṇini 6.4.24]. Why does that not occur? To this he replies: "When *num* has been applied," and so forth.

It has been stated that "the augment *num* occurs only in the stage of grammatical instruction (*upadeśāvasthā*). Therefore, since *num* is applied only in the stage of instruction, the condition of being "ending in a consonant cluster" (*saṃyogāntatva*) arises; thus, because the status of being a *kit* suffix no longer exists, there is no elision of the nasal (*nalopa*). [The author] asks: "Now, how should it be in the case of the suffix *kvasu*?
Does it become *rarādhvān*, or rather *redhivān*? Thus he questions.

Another says: "From *redhivāt*. [The suffix] *kvasu* is applied by [Pāṇini 3.2.107], followed by reduplication; then, by [Pāṇini 6.4.120] and the following rules, there is the substitution of *et* for *at* and the elision of the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsalopa*); then, by [Pāṇini 7.2.67], there is the augment *iṭ*; and finally, by [Pāṇini 6.4.10], there is the lengthening of the vowel.
[The question] "How? and so forth [is raised].

He thinks as follows: "When *iṅ* occurs, there must be *num*; and when *num* is present, the condition of being between two single consonants (*ekahalmadhyatā*) no longer exists. Consequently, after the substitution of *etva* and the elision of the reduplication (*abhyāsalopa*), there must be a restoration (*pratyāpatti*). Thus, once the reduplication has been performed, the root is no longer a single vowel (*ekāṇ*), and therefore *iṭ* should not occur. Therefore, it is correct that [the form] should be *rarandhvam*."

But for the other [view], even though *num* has been applied, there must be elision (*lopa*) by [Pāṇini 6.4.107]; consequently, the state of being between two single consonants (*ekahalmadhyatā*) is not established. How, then, could there be the restoration (*pratyāpatti*) of the substitution of *et* and the elision of the reduplication? To this he says: "When the substitution of *et* and the elision of the reduplication have been performed," and so forth.
For monosyllabic roots that have undergone reduplication, the suffix *iṅ* is prescribed for *kvasu*;
"thereafter, the augment *num* is added."

Is it not because of its being prescribed [by rule]? Since the elision (*lopa*) is based on its being *aupadeśika* (originally taught), when the *num* augment has been applied, the status of being *kit*—which is *ātideśika* (derived by extension)—is impossible due to the presence of a *saṃyoga* (consonant cluster).

Regarding the words "Now" (*atha*) and so forth: since the [augment] *iṭ* would already be established by the preceding rule when it is stated "not before *iṭ*" (*neṭi*, Pāṇini 7.2.4), this [subsequent rule] will serve as a restriction (*niyama*), meaning that [the *iṭ* augment occurs] only before the *liṭ* [affixes] beginning with *iṭ*, and not before any other [affixes] beginning with *iṭ*.
Therefore, [the augment iṭ] occurs in forms such as *rarandhiva* and *rarandhima*, but not in forms such as *radhita*.

Consequently, why was it not stated that [the augment iṭ is applied] "after [a root ending in a consonant] before the liṭ"? For if this were so, the desired result would be achieved and the sūtra would be more concise; this is the intended meaning.
[The phrase] "only after the liṭ" [is used].
He demonstrates the nature of the restriction (*niyama*).
By the phrase "not elsewhere" (*nānyatra*), that which is excluded by it is also indicated.
To show the reason why the restriction is not established, he says: "the opposite," and so forth.
The phrase "only after [a root] ending in *iṭ* in the case of *liṭ*" is a statement of the nature of the reversed restriction (*viparītaniyama*).
By the words "not elsewhere," he also demonstrates that which is excluded by that restriction.
Why is the restrictive rule not accepted in the reverse manner? To this he says, "For instance" (*tathā hi*), and so forth.

According to the restriction that [the augment *iṭ*] occurs only before *liṭ*, the *liṅ* [augment] beginning with *iṭ* is excluded; thus, [the augment] occurs only before *liṭ* when it begins with *iṭ*, and not when it does not begin with *iṭ*.
Consequently, because it does not begin with *iṭ*, the *num* augment would not occur in the form *rarandha*.
In the case of *radhita*, it would indeed belong to the former [root] because it is not excluded by a restrictive rule (*niyama*).
Therefore, in order to avoid that fault, no restrictive rule is applied. Regarding *ārebhe*:

from the root *rabha* in the sense of "undertaking" (*rābhasye*; Dhātupāṭha 974), the perfect tense (*liṭ*) is formed; because the root is marked with an indicatory vowel *a* (anudāttet), the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) is used.

By [the rule] *it-e-śū*, as before, there is the substitution of *e* for *i* and the elision of the reduplication (*abhyāsa-lopa*). "The formulation of a separate rule (*pṛthagyoga*) is for the sake of what follows" means that by the subsequent sūtra,
the operation should apply only to *labh*,
and not to *rabh*.
If the single rule *rabhilabhyoraśavliṭoḥ* were formulated, then the term *rabhi-* would carry over into the subsequent rules;
consequently, its operation would also undesirably apply there. Regarding the phrase "in a suffix beginning with *ya*":

by this, he shows that the locative case in *yi* is a locative of occasion (*viṣayasaptamī*). He demonstrates that the augment *num* occurs even before the suffix beginning with *ya* has actually arisen—that is, while it is still in the state of being merely a potentiality (*vavayabhūta*).
By the words "prāk" (before) and so forth, he explains what is achieved when the locative of scope (*viṣaya-saptamī*) is in effect.

For if it were the locative of proximity (*parasaptamī*), the suffix *pratyaya* would have to occur first, followed by *num*, and consequently, the suffix *yat* prescribed by [Pāṇini 3.1.98] "after a root with *a* as its penultimate letter" would apply. However, when it is the locative of scope, since the state of having *a* as a penultimate letter is destroyed by the *num* that arises beforehand, only the suffix *ṇyat* prescribed by [Pāṇini 3.1.124] "after roots ending in *ṛ* or *h*, and after *hal*" applies.

But what is the reason, or rather, what is the distinction [between the two], since in both cases the form is exactly the same? For if that were so, there should not be *vṛddhi* even when the suffix *ṇyat* is applied; and thus it was stated previously: "Even though *vṛddhi* is subsequent, it is superseded by the former because of its status as *nitya*. To this he says: "In that case," and so forth.

In that case, when *ṇyat* is present, because of the rule "the suffix *ti* is *svarita*" (Pāṇini 6.1.185), there is the accent of the base (*prakṛtisvara*); therefore, the example *ālambhyaḥ* has the final syllable as *svarita*.

However, since the initial syllable is udātta by the rule *yati tu* [Pāṇini 6.1.213], there is a distinction in that the udātta quality is also maintained through the application of *prakṛtibhāva* (the preservation of the original form).
Regarding the word *labhyam*:
this ends in the suffix *yat*.

Regarding the phrase "having thus touched," here too the suffix *lakāra* is used either in the sense of the abstract action (*bhāve*) or the passive (*karmaṇi*). It is stated that "the elision of the *anuṣaṅga* is performed."
By the rule beginning with *aniditām* [Pāṇini 6.4.24], etc. Regarding the term *praśaṃsāyām*:
it means "having perceived" in the sense of praise;
that is to say, "highly praiseworthy."
"Upalabhyam" means "that which is to be attained. In the term "īṣatpralambhaḥ," the suffix *khal* is applied according to the rule "īṣadduḥsuṣu" (Pāṇini 3.3.126).
[Similarly] there is "duṣpralambhaḥ."
The substitution of *ṣ* [for *s*] is according to the rule beginning with *idudupadhasya* [Pāṇini 8.3.41].
In the word *vipralambhaḥ*,
the suffix *ghañ* is used in the sense of an abstract action (*bhāva*).
But surely, is this not already established by the rule *labheśca* [Pāṇini 7.1.64]? What, then, is the purpose of this new beginning? To this he says: "Even though it is established," and so forth.
"It does not occur elsewhere" is what is to be excluded by that [rule].

However, a contrary restriction—namely, that [the augment] occurs only after a prefix when followed by *khal* or *ghañ*—is not possible here, because of the technical indication in [Pāṇini 1.3.69]. [This refers to the term] "of that which is preceded by a prefix."

The meaning is "of that which is connected with a prefix," as in *sulābhaḥ*. Here, the word *su-* has the sense of abundance (*ādhikya*), not the sense of ease (*akṛcchra*), as in: "What indeed is well-sprinkled (*suṣikta*) here for you?
[And] as in *durlābhaḥ*.
The word *duḥ* has the sense of censure (*nindā*), not the sense of difficulty (*kṛcchra*), as in the example *durbrahmaṇa*. Therefore, only the suffix *ghañ* occurs, and not *khal*.
[The author] states: "Considering *sudurmryā* to be in the instrumental case, the mention of the word *kevala* is made."

Regarding the phrase "sudibhryām": when the third case ending is accepted, the meaning that results is this: the augment *num* does not occur for the root *labh* when it is preceded by the prefix *su* and *du*.
It is indeed the case that a root can be preceded by a prefix even when separated [by other elements].

In that case, if the word *kevala* were not included, there would be a prohibition even in the instances "easy to deceive" (*supralambhaḥ*) and "difficult to deceive" (*duṣpralambhaḥ*). Therefore, since the third case [the locative] has been accepted, the inclusion of the word *kevala* is made.
Now, at the point of the question—"Why then is the inclusion of *kevala* not made in the fifth case?"—he says: "For in the fifth case," and so forth.

Regarding the fifth [alternative]: since the mention of the word "nir" is intended to signify immediate sequence (*anantarya*), there ought to be a prohibition only for what is immediately following. However, in this case, there is an intervention by the prefix *pra*; therefore, the very contingency (*prasaṅga*) does not arise. So, what is the purpose of the mention of the word "kevala"? If that is so, then the mention of "kevala" should certainly not be made, as one might simply accept this [use] as being governed by the fifth [alternative]. This is not the case; this was stated with two counter-examples in mind—*supralambhaḥ* and *duṣpralambhaḥ*. For in those cases, because of the intervention, the contingency would indeed not arise even without the mention of "kevala. Thus, the mention of "kevala" is necessary to exclude such instances.

Regarding the phrase *atisulabham*: when the word *abhi* is also considered a prefix (*upasarga*), then a prohibition would apply even when [the rule] refers only to a simple [root], because there is no intervention. Therefore, since the mention of "only" (*kevala*) must be made in all cases, and since there is no purpose for the transposition of the words, it is proper to recognize this as the third [case]. Someone might have the misconception that in *atisulabham*, the root *labh* is preceded by the prefix *su* along with the prefix *ati*; therefore, a prohibition [of the elision of the penultimate vowel] should occur. To dispel this, he says: "In *atisulabham*," and so forth.
Furthermore, the status of *ati* as a *karmapravacanīya* follows from the rule prescribing that designation at Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.4.95.

For that which has the designation *karmapravacanīya*, there is no designation *upasarga*; this is because of the governing principle of "one designation" (*ekasaṃjñādhikāra*), whereby the designation *upasarga* is sublated by the designation *karmapravacanīya*. But how, then, can the "isolated" (*kevala*) status of that very same word be established when it is a *karmapravacanīya*? It is thought thus: [the term] *kevala* [is used] because of the mention of the word *sva*; it excludes only what is of the same class (*tulyajātīya*), not what is of a different class (*vijātīya*). Thus, it excludes only another *karmapravacanīya*, not an *upasarga*.

For instance: "The two [roots] enter [the domain of the suffixes] only when accompanied by something of a different class, such as *karkaṭa* and so on. For this very reason, by the phrase "when devoid of other prefixes," it is shown that the inclusion of the word "only" (*kevala*) serves the purpose of excluding those of the same class.

If, however, the inclusion of "only" were capable of excluding everything—both those of the same class and even those of a different class—then the mention of "prefixes" would be redundant; one should have simply said "devoid of anything else" (*anyarahitābhyām*).

Therefore, exclusion can be effected by the apprehension of that which is of a different class (*vijātīya*) alone; in that case, the mention of the prefix (*upasarga*) would be purposeless, and one should have simply said "by those [words] devoid of any other. Consequently, even when accompanied by something of a different class, they are indeed "alone" (*kevalau*); this is very easy to establish. Thus, even with the word *su* accompanied by a *karmapravacanīya*, there is indeed a prohibition for that which is preceded by a prefix (*upasṛṣṭa*). But how is it in cases where the function of the word *ati* is other than honor (*pūjā*) or transgression (*atikramaṇa*), since in those instances the designation *karmapravacanīya* does not apply to *ati*? To this he says: "But when," and so forth.

Even in the statement of the fifth [case], the inclusion of the word *kevala* ("only") must be made for this very purpose; otherwise, since there would be no intervention here, the prohibition would apply—this is the intended meaning. Now, one might object: "Should the word *kevala* be included for the sake of [the form] *prasulambha*? This is not so; for it has been stated in the Bhāṣya: "This usage does not exist. Regarding the form *alābhi*: it is the *luṅ* [aorist] tense; by the rule *ciṇbhāvakarmaṇoḥ* [Pāṇini 3.1.66], the suffix *ciṇ* is applied, and by [the rule] *ciṇo luk* [Pāṇini 6.4.104], there is the elision (*luk*) of the *takāra*.

"Of that which is not preceded by a prefix" (*anupasṛṣṭasya*) means "not connected with a prefix. The term *ugit* is a reference to a *pratyāhāra* (abbreviated linguistic sequence): those [suffixes] whose beginning is *u* or *i* are called *ugit*. This is a qualifier of the *aṅga* (stem), and therefore he says: "of *aṅgas* ending in *ugit* suffixes.

This must be a reference to the *pratyāhāra* *ac*, or else it must be the root *añc-* with its *n* elided. If it were a reference to the *pratyāhāra* *ac*, then one would not have to repeat the mention of *ac* in the rule [Pāṇini 7.1.72], for that [mention] is a reference to the *pratyāhāra*, not to the root *añc-*, due to its association (*sāhacarya*) with *jhal* sounds.
Therefore, considering that this is the inclusion of the root *añc*, he says "of *añc*" and so forth. In the word "bhavān," there is lengthening [of the vowel] according to [Pāṇini 6.4.14].

Regarding the word *śreyān*: from the word *praśasya*, [the suffix] *īyasun* is applied by [Pāṇini 5.3.57], the substitution of *śr* occurs by [Pāṇini 5.3.60], and due to the preservation of the original form (*prakṛtibhāva*) by [Pāṇini 6.4.163], there is no elision of the *ṭi* (the final vowel and following consonant). Then, by [Pāṇini 6.1.87] and [Pāṇini 6.4.10], the vowel is lengthened. Now, one might object: "In this case, the stem (*aṅga*) is not *ugit*; rather, it is the suffix. This is not so; for the stem itself is indeed *ugit*.

How so? A whole is indeed related even to a part of a part; for example, in the expression "Devadatta’s finger," there is a relationship between Devadatta and the finger, which is a part of the hand, which itself is a part of Devadatta. Therefore, here too, since the *it*-named element is a part of the suffix (*pratyaya*), it is also related to the base (*aṅga*); thus, the base is indeed one ending in an *uṅid* vowel. [The word] "prāk" [is used].

From the root *añc* with the suffix *kvip* by [Pāṇini 3.2.59], the augment *num* by [6.1.66], and the elision of the final consonant of the cluster (*saṃyogāntalopa*) by [8.2.23], there is the substitution of *k* for *c* (i.e., *ṅ*) by [8.2.62]—thus the *n* becomes *ṅ*. Hence:
*prāñcau*, *prāñcaḥ*. Then, by the substitution of *c* for *j* (i.e., *cutva*), the *n* becomes *ñ*. Thus: *prāñcau*, *prāñcaḥ*.

Now, for what purpose is the inclusion of *añcati*? Since the augment *num* would already be established for it simply by virtue of its being marked with the *it*-sign (*gittvāt*), he says: "The inclusion of *añcati*, etc. [Examples: *ukhāruāt*, *parṇadhvat*.

[The roots] *ruāṃs* and *dhvans* mean "to fall down" (Dhātupāṭha 754, 755; [meaning "to sink down"—Dhātupāṭha]). [It means] "it sinks into a pot" (*ukhāyāṃ ruāṃsate*) and "the leaves fall" (*parṇāni dhvaṃsate*).

The suffix *kvip* is applied by [Pāṇini 3.2.76] *kvip ca*; there is elision of the nasal (*nalopaḥ*); the *s* is replaced by *d* by [Pāṇini 8.2.72] *vasuruāṃsudhvaṃsvanaḍuhāṃ daḥ*; and that *d* becomes *t* by [Pāṇini 8.4.56] *jhalāṃ jaś jhaśi*, resulting in the letter *t*. Regarding the question "Why [is it said] 'not after a verbal root' (*adhātoḥ*)?", the intention is that because the mention of *añcati* itself serves as a restrictive rule (*niyamārtha*), the suffix does not apply after a verbal root.

Thinking that this "not after a verbal root" (*adhātoḥ*) is not a simple prohibition (*prasajyapratiṣedha*), but rather an exclusion (*paryudāsa*), he says: "[It is stated] so that it may also apply to that which was previously not a verbal root."
The proponent of the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣavādin), considering this "not of a verbal root" (*adhātoḥ*) to be an absolute negation (*prasajyapratiṣedha*), raised an objection.
The proponent of the established conclusion (siddhāntavādin) refuted it by means of a relative exclusion (*paryudāsa*),
citing the example "gomatyati."
From the word *goman*, [the suffix] *kyac* is applied by the rule *supa ātmanaḥ kyac* [Pāṇini 3.1.8].
Then, by the rule *gomatyaterapratyayaḥ*, the suffix *apratyaya* is added.
An *apratyaya* is a suffix that is not a [verbal] suffix; this, moreover, is *kvip*. By the rule *aci śnudhātubhruvāṃ yvoriyaṅuvaṅau* [Pāṇini 6.4.77], there is lengthening—thus, *gomān*.
Why is it that this [rule] would not be established here if the mention of *dhātu* were absent? To this he says: "For here," and so forth.

If the mention of *dhātu* were absent, then because of the restriction resulting from the mention of *añcati*, it would not apply in cases such as *ukharaudri* and the like; likewise, it would not apply here either.

However, this too is indeed a *dhātu*, for even though it is a *dhātu*, when it ends in *kvip*, it does not abandon its status as a *dhātu*, according to the principle: "Those ending in *kvip* do not lose their status as *dhātus*" (*Vaiyākaraṇabhūṣaṇasāra* 132).
Therefore, the mention of "non-root" (adhātu) is made so that there may be the inclusion of that which was a non-root in another state.
Now, how is there lengthening in the word *gomān*? And why would it not occur? The prohibition "of a non-root" applies, but not to that which ends in /ā/.

What is the purpose of "of a non-root" here? *Piṇḍagraḥ* ("one who eats a lump") and *carmavaḥ* ("one who wears a hide") are presented as counter-examples specifically for [stems] ending in /as/, not for those ending in /ā/.

Alternatively—the letter *ca* is added there, and it serves to include what has not been mentioned; by means of that, in certain instances, the suffix *ayi* will occur after a verbal root, as in *paryāyi* and *śreyāṃsi*. [In these cases] the lengthening occurs by [Pāṇini 6.4.10].
[The forms] *bahupurī* and *bahudhurī* [are derived similarly].

"Bahvyaḥ puraḥ, bahvyo dhuro yeṣām" is a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "those which have many cities or many yokes. The suffix *a*, prescribed by the rule "ṛk-pur-ab-dhūḥ-pathām āna-kṣe" [Pāṇini 5.4.74], does not apply here; this is because the application of suffixes at the end of a compound (*samāsānta*) is considered non-universal (*anitya*). Thus, we have "vimaladivi."

Those [words] for which the sky (*dyu*) is pure (*vimalā*) are "vimaladivi. In *vimaladivi*, the letter *va* is neither a dental (*dantya*) nor a labial (*oṣṭhya*), because it is recited as a *jhal* sound preceding a *jhal*. [The word] is "four" (*catvāri*).
Regarding the rule *ityām* [Pāṇini 7.1.98]:

here, when a neuter stem ending in a consonant (*jhal*) that possesses an *uk* or *ik* vowel has the augment *num* applied by the rule *ugidacām* [7.1.70], a second *num* would also appear. For it is possible for one element to be "subsequent" (*para*) at the time of its own application, just as in the case of *pacati*, where both the *lakāra* (the verbal suffix) and the *vikaraṇa* (the class marker *śap*) follow from the same root.

In the case of *tudanti* and *nadanti*, once the *num* augment has been applied and converted to an *anusvāra*, and that *anusvāra* has been changed to its homogeneous sound (*parasavarṇa*), would there not result the hearing of two *n* sounds? Let it be so; for regarding the perception of one or many consonants following a *hal*, no distinction can be asserted.

However, in this case, there is indeed a distinction: in *kurvanti* and *kṛṣanti*, once the *num* augment has been applied and changed to *anusvāra* and *parasavarṇa*, because the preceding [consonant] is not followed by a *jhal* sound, the *anusvāra* and *parasavarṇa* do not apply; consequently, by the rule *aṭ-ku-pv-āṅ-num-vyavāye’pi* (Pāṇini 8.4.2), the substitution of *ṇ* for *n* would occur.

However, when there is a single *num*, once its *anusvāra* has been changed to a *parasavarṇa*, the contingency of *ṇatva* does not arise, because the *parasavarṇa* substitution is considered asiddha (non-existent for the purposes of subsequent rules).

Therefore, he states—beginning with "of that which ends in a consonant preceded by a vowel having the marker u (*ugit*)"—that a prohibition must be stated regarding the *num* characterized by the presence of an *ugit* vowel.

The scope for the *num* augment characterized by [the rule] "ending in a *jhal*" is, for example, the neuter form *sarpīṃṣi*; the scope for the *num* characterized by [the rule] "ending in an *ugit*" is, for example, non-neuter forms such as *gomān* and *yavamān*. When both [rules] would apply to a neuter word ending in an *ugit* that also ends in a *jhal*, this very *num* must occur by virtue of its higher priority (*paratva*). Once that has occurred, the *num* characterized by the *ugit* rule does not occur again, because of the principle: "In the case of a conflict between two rules, once a matter has been decided, it remains decided" (*vyāpa* 40). Thus we have the form *bhūyāṃsi*.
From the word *bahu*, the suffix *īyasun* is applied; by [Pāṇini 6.4.158], there is the elision of the vowel *i*, and *bahu* undergoes the change to *bhū*.
[The forms] *kurvanti* and *kṛṣanti* [are derived] from the present participle (*śatṛntāt*); by [Pāṇini 7.1.20], there is the substitution of *śi*.
Regarding the phrase "bahūrji" and so forth:
the prohibition of the suffix *nuc* must be stated—that is, explained—in the case of *bahūrji*.

This is the explanation: the term *vibhāṣā* (optionally) from rule 7.1.69 is understood to carry over here, and since that is a restricted option (*vyavasthitavibhāṣā*), the suffix does not occur in the word *bahūrji*.

[Is this] from the root *ūrja* (Dhātupāṭha 1549), meaning "to possess strength" or "to give life," [as noted in the Dhātupāṭha as "to possess strength and to give life"]? From this, by the rule *bhrājabhrāsa-* [Pāṇini 3.2.177], the suffix *kvip* is applied. Those Brāhmaṇa families which possess many *ūrja*s or strengths are called *bahūrji*.
Regarding the phrase "before the final letter":

some maintain that the augment *num* should be inserted before the final letter *j*, resulting in *bahūrñji*. Because of the mention of the word "in a case-ending" (*vibhaktau*), the term "in a sarvanāmasthāna ending" [from Pāṇini 7.1.70] is no longer applicable here.

"What is the purpose of *ac*? He thinks thus: "The mention of *ac* is made so that [the rule] does not apply when a consonant begins [the following word], as in *trapubhyām* and *trapubhiḥ*; however, this is not a valid reason. Let there be *num* here; the elision will occur by the rule *na ṅisambuddhyoḥ* (Pāṇini 8.2.7).
The other, having understood his intention, says: "It is for the sake of the subsequent rules."
> [The mention of] *aj-* is for the purpose that [the rule] should apply when a vowel (*ac*) begins [the following word], so that it does not apply here in the case of *asthibhyām* and *asthibhiḥ*.
With the intention of asking, "What is the purpose of this *karaṇa* (instrumental cause) here? Therefore, let that very thing be stated," he says: "If it is thus," and so forth.
The other, having understood the intention, says: "But here, as for the purpose of the *karaṇa*," and so forth.

Regarding the word *trapu*: if the condition "when followed by a vowel" (*acīti*) were not stated, then the augment *num* would also occur here when the nominative singular is formed in the vocative. Therefore, so that *num* does not occur in this case, the condition "when followed by a vowel" is stated.

It might be argued: "Let *num* indeed occur; once the suffix *su* is elided by the rule *svamornapuṃsakāt* [Pāṇini 7.1.23], the elision of the *n* will take place by the rule *nalopaḥ prātipadikāntasya* [Pāṇini 8.2.7]. To this he replies: "Not in the case of the *ṅi* or the vocative," and so forth. And then: "But surely," and so forth.

The particle *eva* here is displaced in its order and should be understood immediately after the negation. It establishes that [the existence of case-endings] does not exist, following the negation in the rule: "Is there even a figurative (*aupacārika*) existence of case-endings? (Pāṇini 1.1.63). For the existence of case-endings is indeed twofold: primary (*mukhya*) and figurative (*aupacārika*).
In that regard, the primary [existence] belongs to the case-ending (*vibhakti*) as it is actually heard; however, the other [secondary existence] pertains even to one that has been elided (*luptā*).

Because the function (*kārya*) exists, the existence of the case-ending is also spoken of figuratively (*upacāreṇa*), just as it is said, "past action exists" (*astyatītaṃ karma*); there, because the capacity for yielding a fruit (*phaladānasāmarthya*) deposited by the past action exists, that action is said to exist. Thus, in this instance, since the case-ending is elided according to [Pāṇini 7.1.23], primary existence does not exist.
Because of the prohibition of the *pratyayalakṣaṇa* rule by [Pāṇini 1.1.63], even the figurative (*aupacārika*) [presence of a suffix] does not exist at all.

In that case, what occasion is there for the *num* augment—which is prescribed when a case-ending (*vibhakti*) follows—to apply in *he trapo*, where a case-ending is entirely absent? It simply does not apply; therefore, this is not the purpose of including the mention of *ac*.
"This very [point]" and so forth.

For if, in this case, there were a prohibition [of the rule] characterized by the elision of an affix (*pratyayalopalakṣaṇa*), the mention of *aj* would be purposeless. Why? Because this very mention of *aj* indicates that here, in the case of a neuter stem ending in *i*, there is no prohibition characterized by the elision of an affix with respect to the vocative (*sambuddhi*). By the words "And thus," etc., he states the purpose of this indicator (*jñāpaka*). While the phrase "the group [of rules] concerning the vocative" (Pāṇini 7.3.106) is in effect, that *guṇa* which occurs by the rule "guṇa for a short vowel" (Pāṇini 7.3.108) should be understood [to apply here].
Regarding the phrase "taumburavaṃ cūrṇam" (powder of *tumburu*):
the derivative from *tumburu* is formed by [the suffix] *aṇ* [Pāṇini 4.2.70], followed by [the substitution of *vṛddhi*] [Pāṇini 6.4.146].
In some places, he recites two verses beginning with: "Let there not be [substitution] for an *ik* vowel before a consonant; let there be elision, but how then the accent? and so forth.

Regarding [Pāṇini 7.1.73], for what purpose is the term *aci* stated here? Why not simply say *iko vibhaktau*? He states the purpose: "So that [the substitution] does not occur before a consonant. It is understood from the context that this refers to the augment *num*. The mention of *ac* is made so that [the substitution] does not occur in cases such as *trapubhyām* and *trapubhiḥ*, where a consonant begins the case-ending.

If this is so, there is no need for that [augment]; let the *num* augment apply to the consonant-initial [forms], and its being heard does not follow as a consequence. Why? Because the elision of *n*, by the rule "elision of *n* at the end of a nominal stem" (*nalopaḥ prātipadikāntasya* 6.4.7), will take place.

But how is the accent in forms such as *pañcatrapubhyām* and *pañcatrapubhiḥ*? It is because [the word] is a compound in the sense of a secondary derivative (*taddhita*), according to the rule "purchased with five *trapus*" (*pañcabhistrapubhiḥ krītābhyāṃ krītairvā* 2.1.51).

By the rule *dvigu* [Pāṇini 2.1.52], the designation *dvigu* is applied; by the rule *ārhādagopuccha* [5.1.19] et cetera, the suffix *ṭhak* is added; its elision (*luk*) occurs by the rule *adhyardhapūrvadvigorlugasaṃjñāyām* [5.1.28]; then, after the case-ending (*vibhakti*), the *num* augment is inserted, followed by the elision of the letter *n*. Because that [elision of *n*] is considered non-existent (*asiddha*) by the rule *nalopaḥ supsvara-saṃjñātugvidhiṣu kṛti* [8.2.2], the original accent of the first member (*pūrvapadaprakṛtisvara*) does not apply by the rule [6.2.29];
furthermore, because it does not end in a vowel other than *i* (*aniganta*), the acute accent on the initial syllable would instead apply by the rule *bhraḥ saṃkhyāyāḥ* (Phiṭ-sūtra 2.28).
The term "bhraḥ" includes those ending in *n* and *r*. [This applies to rules] such as "a consonant before *ṣa*" (*kharo ṣai*).
The word "vai" is used in the sense of intolerance.
When the augment *num* is heard in the word *pañcatrapuṇaḥ*, the accent occurs. [Question:
"Will it not occur when [the augment] is elided?
[Answer: The meaning is that it will indeed occur.
But what is the reason that the accent occurs when the *num* suffix is being heard? Because, in a rule governing accent, a consonant is as if non-existent.
Or rather, does this *num* belong to the whole [word]? It is not able to obstruct the status of the constituent part, the word *trapu*, as having an *ī*-ending.

In this case, then, when a compound is formed from two *brāhmaṇa* families that have surpassed wealth—using the rule *atirābhyām* [Pāṇini 2.2.18]—and when the shortening of the stem in the neuter has been applied by the rule *hrasvo napuṃsake prātipadikasya* [Pāṇini 1.2.47], if the augment *num* were to occur before a consonant-initial suffix, then upon its elision, the substitution of *ā* (ātvam) prescribed for a consonant-initial suffix by the rule *na lopasyāsiddhatvāt* [Pāṇini 7.2.85] would not apply because of the intervention of *num*. [Objection: Since *num* is part of the whole, it should not intervene between the whole and the suffix; however, it certainly does intervene with respect to the individual parts.

Likewise, in the case of *priyatisṛ*—formed as a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "one who has three beloveds"—if *num* were to occur before a consonant-initial [suffix], then by rule [Pāṇini 7.2.99], the substitution of *tisṛ* would not apply because the word *tri* is separated [from the suffix] by *num*, which is a part of the whole (*samudāyabhakta*). This is not so; for it is said: "The state of *rāy* and the state of *tisṛ* [occur] even when there is separation by *num*.
The word "it happens" (*bhavati*) is to be supplied.
The ablative in "because of separation" (*vyavadhānāt*) is used with the elision of the suffix *lyap* (as in *lyablope*), just as in the expression "he looks from the palace" (*prāsādāt prekṣate*).
The meaning is "they ascend the palace.
Thus, the sense is this: even when there is an intervention by the suffix *num*, the substitution of *ā* for *rāi* and the change to *tisṛ* occur.

Why do these two operations occur despite the intervention? Because in the rule [Pāṇini 7.2.85], one adopts the view that the qualifying condition (*viśeṣaṇa*) is the specific prescription, namely: "in that case, [the operations apply] in whatever case-ending is prescribed after the word *rāi*, and in whatever case-ending is prescribed after the word *tri*."

Alternatively—what is the need for considering the intervention [of the augment *ṇi*]? For those two [the *ṇatva* and *num*] will indeed occur simply because of their posteriority (*paratva*). But once they have been applied, according to the rule "In the case of a conflict between rules applying simultaneously, that which is sublated remains sublated" (Vyāḍipāda 40), would the *num* not occur again?
No; for it has been stated that even the *num* occurs despite the intervention, by not accepting the posteriority of the *num*.
It is precisely for this reason that the word "also" (*api*) is employed to indicate an alternative view.
And as it occurs when there is an intervention, that has already been stated.
If that is so, then the mention of *ac* is for the purpose of [establishing] a conflict (*vipratiṣedha*) between *num* and *nuṭ*; thus, once *nuṭ* has been applied, *num* is not applied.

The scope of [Pāṇini 7.1.54] *hrasvanadyāpo nuṭ* is, for example, *agnīnām* and *vāyūnām*; the scope of [7.1.54] *iganta-numaḥ* is, for example, *trapuṇe* and *jatune*. In the case of *trapūṇām* and *jatūnām*, both rules would apply. By the "priority-exception" (*pūrvavipratiṣedha*), the augment *nuṭ* occurs. Once *nuṭ* has been applied, [the rule] *nāmi* [6.4.3] would require lengthening of the vowel, but this would not occur if [the *num* augment were applied instead], because the stem would no longer end in a vowel (*anajantatvāt*), as in the case of *varmaṇām*. Furthermore, this priority-exception is only possible if there is the mention of the vowel (*aj-grahaṇa*). If *nuṭ* were applied first, *num* would not apply, because the stem would not begin with a vowel (*anajāditvāt*).
Even when *num* has been applied, *nuṭ* does not occur because there is no [stem] ending in a short vowel; thus, since both rules are equally applicable, a conflict (*vipratiṣedha*) is established.

If the mention of *ac* (the vowel) were not made, then even after *nuṭ* has been applied—or even if it has not been applied—*num* would have to occur before both consonant-initial and vowel-initial suffixes, and thus it would be obligatory (*nitya*).
Once *num* has been applied, however, because the stem no longer ends in a short vowel, *nuṭ* would not occur, and thus it would be non-obligatory (*anitya*).

Since the permanent (*nitya*) and the non-permanent (*anitya*) rules do not possess equal force, the contradiction is untenable; therefore, by virtue of its permanence, the augment *num* alone must occur. Consequently, the mention of the vowel *a* (*aj-grahaṇa*) is for the purpose of [establishing] this contradiction. To this, he states another solution: "The augment *nuṭ* should be prescribed."
For the sake of brevity;
the purpose of the *nuṭ* augment is a prior counter-exception (*pūrvavipratiṣedha*). It is stated that [the suffix] *anudāt* is used in the sense of being for the sake of that (*tādarthya*).

Even if the mention of *ac* were not made, by the rule of mutual exclusion (*vipratiṣedha*), only *num* would apply; therefore, one must necessarily state that *nuṭ* occurs by way of a prior exclusion (*pūrvavipratiṣedha*), according to the maxim: "By a prior exclusion, *nuṭ* takes precedence over *num*, *aci-ra*, and *ṛj-vad-bhāva*" (Vārttika 11 on Pāṇini 7.1.96).
Even if the mention of *ac* were made, this prior exclusion must still be stated.

If that [operation] were not performed, would *nuṭ* not occur by that very same effort? Why then two efforts? Therefore, is the mention of *ac* (the vowel) useless? But surely the word "para" (subsequent) denotes what is desired; because it denotes what is desired, it will occur, so enough with the effort! This is incorrect; one must necessarily enumerate a prior exception (*pūrvavipratiṣedha*), otherwise it would not even be known which of these is desired and which is undesired.

But is it not the case that in the word *trapūṇām*, once *nuṭ* has been applied by the rule of prior contradiction (*pūrvavipratiṣedha*), should the mention of *ac* (the vowel) be made so that *num* does not occur? This is not necessary; let *num* occur here, and its elision will take place. If it is argued that because the elision of *n* (*nalopa*) is considered non-existent (*asiddha*) for the purpose of applying the rule for lengthening (*dīrghavidhi*), the lengthening prescribed by *nāmi* [Pāṇini 6.4.3] would not apply because the stem would no longer end in a vowel (*anajanta*), we reply: let it not be by that rule, but it will be accomplished by the rule *sarvanāmasthāne cāsambuddhau* [Pāṇini 6.4.8].

In that case, would not the lengthening [of the vowel] fail to occur in *śucīnām* due to the restriction [*niyama*] in [Pāṇini 6.4.12]? This is not so; for by the paribhāṣā "that which is taught in a specific rule [takes precedence over that which is arrived at through a general definition]" (*lakṣaṇapratipadoktaparibhāṣā*), that restriction applies only to a form ending in *in* that is taught as such in a specific rule (*pratipadokta*). Since this [form *śucinām*] becomes an *innanta* only after *num* has been applied, it is merely derivative (*lākṣaṇika*) and is therefore excluded by the said restriction. Once the mention of *aj* has been thus refuted, he says, "But it is for the sake of what follows," in order to demonstrate the purpose of the mention of *aj* in the subsequent rules.
The word *tu* (but) is used here in the sense of *tarhi* (then).
The word *tarhi* introduces an alternative position.
If this purpose is not tenable, then the mention of the vowel *aj* must be made for the sake of what follows.
"But here, let the purpose of the instrument be stated? To this he says: "In this [world]," and so forth.
The word "api" (also/even) is not employed here because its meaning is already implied.
He asks: "There is a purpose here as well; what, then, is it? To this he says: "Shame."
The mention of *ac* (a vowel) is for the sake of ensuring the correctness of the example *he trapo*.

If the mention of *ac* were not made, it would not be made known that the rule regarding the "marking of the elision of an affix" (*pratyayalopalakṣaṇa*) applies here; consequently, in the case of *he trapo*, when the vocative suffix is elided, the *guṇa* substitution prescribed for the vocative would not take place. However, when the mention of *ac* is present, the "marking of the elision of an affix" does apply even here. Therefore, the mention of *ac* must be made for this purpose, as well as for the sake of subsequent rules, such as "a neuter [stem] ending in an *ik*" (*igantaṃ napuṃsakam*).
The term *napuṃsakasya* (of the neuter) and *ekah* (one) are understood to carry over [from the previous rule].

Although that [term] was originally presented in the genitive case, nevertheless, for the sake of this meaning, there occurs a change of case-ending (*vibhaktivipariṇāma*), whereby it becomes nominative.
Thus, "it becomes like the masculine" (*puṃvadbhavati*).
To clarify the meaning of this, he says "yathā" and so forth.

But how can an extension of the prohibition (*pratiṣedhātideśa*) be stated by means of the expression "it becomes like the masculine" (*puṃvadbhavati*)? He thinks as follows: in the masculine, in the case of [stems] beginning with *ajā-* in the third case and so on, no grammatical operation (*kārya*) is prescribed that could be extended to the neuter.

Therefore, since an operation dependent on the neuter gender does not exist in the masculine, this must be understood as an extension of a prohibition (*pratiṣedhātideśa*). Even so, there would be an extension of the absence of *num* alone—which is the subject under discussion—in one alternative case, while for the short vowel (*hrasva*), there would be no such extension because it is not the subject under discussion. Consequently, operations dependent on the short vowel—namely *guṇa*, the absence of *nābhāva*, *nuṭ*, *aut*, and *āttva*—would undesirably apply. For instance, by rule [Pāṇini 7.3.111], *aut* and *āttva* would apply, resulting in *grāmaṇyāṃ brāhmaṇakulam*. This is not the case; for if only the absence of *num* were extended, the extension itself would be purposeless. It would be sufficient to simply prohibit *num* according to the opinion of Gālava.
Therefore, because the transfer [of properties] lacks the capacity [to apply to the feminine], the absence of shortness (*hrasvatva*) is also transferred:
*grāmaṇībrāhmaṇaḥ*, *grāmaṇibrāhmaṇakulam*.
This was stated for the purpose of showing that [the word] has been used as masculine; it is not, however, an actual example [of the rule].
An example of this is: *grāmaṇyā brāhmaṇakulena*.
Here, due to the *puṃvadbhāva* (masculine-like treatment), neither the shortening of the vowel nor the insertion of *num* occurs.
[Otherwise,] there would have been shortening by the rule *eranekācaḥ* [Pāṇini 6.4.82] and the substitution of *nā* by the rule *na āp* [Pāṇini 7.3.120].
Regarding the term *grāmaṇīnām*:
when the augment *nuṭ* is applied by means of a prior counter-exception (*pūrvavipratiṣedha*), the lengthening [of the vowel] occurs by the rule *nāmi* [Pāṇini 6.4.3].
The instrumental singular form of the word *nnucis* has not been cited as an example; this is because there is no difference [in the resulting form].
Whether or not the substitution of the masculine form (*puṃvadbhāva*) occurs, there must be the substitution of *nā* [for *na*] by rule 7.3.120.
In the case of *śucaye*,
if the masculine form is applied, the augment *num* does not occur, and by rule 7.3.111, the *guṇa* substitution takes place.
Regarding "śucine":
when there is no substitution by the masculine form (puṃvadbhāva), the augment *num* is applied. As in "grāmaṇinī brāhmaṇakule" ("a village headman in a Brāhmaṇa family").
Due to the absence of *puṃvadbhāva* (the substitution of the masculine form), the short vowel and the *num* augment occur here,
as in "trapuṇe" and "jatune.
Since these two words are exclusively neuter at all times, they lack the quality of having been previously used in the masculine (*bhāṣitapuṃskatva*).
Therefore, because the absence of the masculine form does not exist here, the augment *num* indeed occurs.
[Question: "Why does it not occur in this case?
[Answer: In the case of a *bahuvrīhi* compound whose constituent word has been previously used in the masculine (*bhāṣitapuṃska*), the external referent (*anyapadārtha*) is the word itself.

This word *pilu* first functions as a masculine tree-name; when there is the intention to express "the fruit is a modification of the *pilu*," the suffix *añ*—which would have been introduced by [Pāṇini 4.2.70] *orañ*—is elided by [Pāṇini 4.3.163] *prāgdīvyato’ṇ*. At that point, since it refers to a neuter fruit, it becomes a word that has been "spoken of as masculine" (*bhāṣitapuṃska*). Yet, no specific distinction is mentioned here [in the rule regarding the application of the masculine form]. Therefore, the question arises from one who thinks that the substitution of the masculine form (*puṃvadbhāva*) must necessarily apply here. The answer is: "When the configuration (*ākṛti*) is the same. To clarify the meaning of this very statement, he says: "When the cause for the application of the word (*pravṛttinimitta*) is identical."

In this context, the phrase "the masculine form of that [word] is prescribed" (*tasya puṃvadbhāvo vidhīyate*) is to be supplied as an ellipsis. That by which things are formed (*ākriyante*), derived, and delimited is "form" (*ākṛtiḥ*). Here, what is intended by "form" is the cause for the application of a word; it does not mean spatial configuration (*saṃniveśa*), nor merely a genus (*jāti*).
Therefore, when the basis for application (*pravṛttinimitta*) is identical, the masculine form is prescribed for that which has already been used in the masculine.

And so, in the case of the words *grāmaṇī* and *śuci*, the masculine form is cited as occurring in a compound when the basis for application is the same; for instance, the basis for application for the word *grāmaṇī*—whether it occurs in the masculine or the neuter—is the agency toward leading the village, which is uniform in form.
For the word *śuci* as well, the quality of purity (*śucitva*) is the basis for application, and this applies to that very same [quality]. Is it not so?
Is the form (*ākṛti*) here also the same? To this he says: "But here," and so forth.
The word "but" (*tu*) demonstrates the distinction from words such as *grāmaṇī*.
By this, he shows that the word *pīlu* possesses the quality of having been used in the masculine (*bhāṣitapuṃskatva*) despite having a different form.
The form of a tree is the genus "tree";
the form of a fruit is the genus "fruit.
Thus, when the form is the same, the masculine gender is prescribed for that which has been expressed as masculine.

However, because the word *pīlu* is not mentioned in the list (*samāmnāya*) as having a masculine form when referring to a genus (*ākṛti*), its transformation into the masculine form (*puṃvadbhāva*) does not occur.
Regarding the phrase "this being so" and so forth:
as for what was stated—that "in the list [of words] referring to a genus," etc.—how can this take such a form of meaning? The meaning is: it cannot be so in any way.
The intention is that [the rule] "when the form (*ākṛti*) is the same" does not specify a particular [instance].
By the phrase "because of the mention of 'having been spoken of as masculine' (*bhāṣitapuṃska*)," etc., he demonstrates how this very [result] comes about.
This would not be possible if another word-meaning were resorted to in place of the word itself.

And here, it is not the word (*śabda*) that is relied upon as the meaning of the other member of the compound; what then? It is the *artha* (referent). Moreover, it is not every referent, but rather—due to proximity—it is understood to be that very thing which is the ground for the application (*pravṛttinimitta*) of a particular word; it is precisely that which is called "having been spoken with the masculine gender" (*bhāṣitapuṃska*). Otherwise, every referent whatsoever would be "having been spoken with the masculine gender," because even the word *artha* itself could potentially have been spoken with the masculine gender.

In this context, if any word whatsoever that has been used to denote a masculine were accepted here [as "bhāṣitapuṃska"], then the mention of "bhāṣitapuṃska" would be purposeless, as there would be nothing to exclude. Therefore, only that word which expresses the neuter and for which a masculine form is intended to be prescribed here—provided that the same basis for application (*pravṛttinimitta*) was expressed by the masculine—is understood here as "bhāṣitapuṃska. This is what is meant by the phrase "by connection with that," and so forth.

Because of its connection—that is, its relation—with that meaning characterized as the ground for the application of the term, even that which is expressed in the neuter gender is called "bhāṣitapuṃska" (having a corresponding masculine form).
For indeed, through such a connection, a thing receives the designation of the other; as in the example, "Bring in the sticks" (*yaṣṭīḥ praveśaya*).

Furthermore, the "connection" here is characterized by the relationship between the inherent and the inherent-in-it (*samavāya-samavāyin*); it is because the meaning that serves as the ground for the application of the word is inherently related to the neuter [gender].

Regarding the phrase "that which [denotes] it" and so forth: that form of a word which denotes that neuter gender is also called *bhāṣitapuṃska* because of its connection with a neuter that has a corresponding masculine form (*bhāṣitapuṃskena*). Furthermore, the "connection" between these two is the relationship of signifier and signified (*vācyavācakabhāva*).

In this regard, although in the Sūtra the meaning (*artha*) is presented by means of a word that has been stated to have a masculine form (*bhāṣitapuṃska*), nevertheless, because an operation cannot apply to a meaning, this rule of "masculine-like behavior" (*puṃvadbhāva*) is prescribed for that very word which has been stated to have a masculine form according to the manner described. And thus, when it is being prescribed, it is understood by implication that it applies to that word which has been stated to have a masculine form within the same general form (*ākṛti*). For a neuter word that expresses a thing connected with a cause for the application of a word stated to have a masculine form is necessarily stated to have a masculine form within the same general form.

Just as with the word *grāmaṇī* and the word *śuci*, when the word *pīlu* is used to denote a male, it does not refer to that [male] which is connected to the tree-shape—the basis for its application—but rather to that which is connected to the shape of the fruit. What then? It refers to the connection with the form of the fruit.

Therefore? Since the word *pīlu* is not a word that has been taught as masculine (*bhāṣitapuṃska*) when applied to the same form (*samānāyām ākṛtau*), its transformation into the masculine form (*puṃvadbhāvaḥ*) does not occur. In the case of *kīlālapā*, the suffix *vic* is applied according to [Pāṇini 3.2.74]: *ato maninkvanibvanipaśca*.

This word *kīlālapā* is one that has been stated as masculine (*bhāṣitapuṃska*) within a common form (*samānākṛtau*), since it occurs in both genders by taking "the state of being a drinker of *kīlāla*" (*kīlālapātva*) as its basis for application (*pravṛttinimitta*).

However, because it does not end in a short vowel (*iganta*), the substitution of the masculine form (*puṃvadbhāva*) does not occur; consequently, the shortening of the vowel (*hrasvatva*) certainly takes place.
When that [shortening] has occurred, the substitution of *in* for *ā* according to Pāṇini 7.1.12 (*tasyāpatyam*) results in the form *kīlālapena*.

If, however, there were *puṃvadbhāva* (masculine treatment) here, then the short vowel would not occur; consequently, when the elision of the vowel *a* is performed by [Pāṇini 6.4.140], the form would become *kolālāpā*. When *num* is about to be applied by [Pāṇini 7.1.73], *anaṅ* is prescribed for *asṛj* and others. The letter *ṅ* is for the purpose of indicating that the substitution applies to the final sound;
the vowel *a* is for the purpose of pronunciation.
Furthermore, these words beginning with *asthi* are acute-accented on the first syllable by the rule *nabviṣayasyānisantasya* (Phiṭ-sūtra 2.26), while the remainder is unaccented (*anudātta*).

In that context, since the substitution *anaṅ* being prescribed would, by virtue of its status as a *sthānivadbhāva*, inherit the unaccented quality of its original, it is stated that it is [instead] acute-accented—namely, by the rule *nabviṣayasya*.
This means "belonging to the domain of the neuter."
Regarding "asthnā": after the substitution of *anaṅ* [by Pāṇini 7.1.75], there is the elision of the vowel *a* [by Pāṇini 6.4.134]. Regarding "etaiḥ" and so forth.

But how is this obtained, given that the base subject [of the rule] is qualified by "bones" (*asthi*) and so forth, and it is understood through the principle of *tadanta-vidhi* (application of a grammatical operation to that which ends with the qualifier)? Or, even if there is *tadanta-vidhi* because of the statement, "In the context of a member (*aṅga*), [the term refers to] that which has 'sat' as its subsequent member" (Puṣpasūtra 85), nevertheless—even if that were the case—the inclusion of that which ends in "bones" and so forth as being neuter would not be tenable, because the term "neuter" (*napuṃsakasya*) is understood as a governing word (*anuvṛtti*) from the previous rule? This is not a fault; for here the member (*aṅga*) is not qualified by the neuter gender, but rather, because they are explicitly mentioned, it is "bones" and the others that are qualified.

And thus, even when that which ends in those [suffixes] occurs as a member (*aṅga*) in another gender, the neuter status of *asthi* and the others still exists. Consequently, it is logically established that those words beginning with *asthi* which function as neuter are included even when they occur at the end of a compound in a non-neuter gender. If, then, there is an inclusion of what ends in those suffixes, how is the rule not unestablished for the simple words themselves? This is not a fault; because of the principle of "behaving like that which is designated" (*vyapadeśivadbhāva*), the rule will not apply to the simple words.

The *paribhāṣā* "the treatment as if possessing a designation applies to that which is not a nominal stem" (Śākalya-pariśiṣṭa 65) does not apply here at all, as its scope is restricted to the domain of affixation rules. Why is the neuter gender used as a qualifier for "bones" (*asthi*) and so forth? It is so that [the rule] should not apply when those words, such as *dadhi*, although they exist [in the neuter], function in another gender—for instance, in the case of a certain person named Dadhi, as in "by that Dadhi" (*tena dadhinā*). By the phrase "from which [an affix] is prescribed" and so on, he shows that the word "also" (*api*) serves the purpose of including everything without exception. "By the bones" (*asthibhiḥ*).
When *anaṅ* is substituted, there is the elision of *n*.
As in the example "having cut out the heart," *anaṅ* is substituted for *śas*.
Regarding "akṣaṇvatā":
here too, the application of the suffix *matup* is the same as in [Pāṇini 5.2.94].
This word ends in the accusative case.

Regarding the term *anastha*: that which has no bone (*asthi*) is *anaṅ*. The lengthening [of the vowel] occurs by the rule *sarvanāmasthāne ca* (Pāṇini 6.4.8). The letter *ca* is for the purpose of drawing in [the word] *chandasi* [from the previous sūtra].

In the case of *akṣī te*, when *akṣi* is followed by the dual ending *au*, the substitution of *śī* occurs by the rule *jaśśasoḥ śiḥ* (Pāṇini 7.1.19). Once the long vowel *ī* is produced, the lengthening by *prathamayoḥ pūrvasavarṇaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.1.102) occurs; although [this lengthening] is prohibited by *na samprasāraṇe* (Pāṇini 6.1.105), it nevertheless takes place here due to its being Vedic (*chāndasatvāt*).

Is this not already established by the rule for lengthening (*dīrghatva*) when [the vowel] is homogeneous (*savarṇa*)? Although the form is established, the acute accent (*udāttatva*) is not established.
By this [rule], an acute *ī* is prescribed.
Alternatively, even the form itself is not established.

Because [the rule for] *pūrvasavarṇa* (the substitution of a homogeneous long vowel) has higher priority, once the *num* augment has been applied first, the *savarṇadīrgha* (lengthening by a homogeneous vowel) would not occur at all. Now, why does the *num* augment not apply in the case of *akṣī* according to [Pāṇini 7.1.73]? To this he says: "In the case of *akṣī*, etc. The scope (*avakāśa*) of *num* is in forms such as *trapuṇe* and *jatune*; the scope of the vowel *i* (in 7.1.73) is in forms such as *akṣībhyām*. When both are applicable in the dual of the nominative, the vowel *ī* alone occurs because it is subsequent in the order of rules.

Now, since the substitution of *ī* has been made, does the rule for *num* not apply again because of the principle of "recognition of recurrence" (*punar-prasaṅga-vijñāna*)? Why does it not occur? To this he says: "because it has already taken effect once" (*sakṛdgata*). [In the forms] *udatta*, *dadattau*:

there is elision of the vowel *ā* by the rule *śnabhyastayor āttaḥ* [Pāṇini 6.4.112]. [The forms] *akṣiti*, *jāgarti*, etc., receive the designation of "reduplicated" (*abhyasta*) by the rule *adabhyastāt* [Pāṇini 7.1.4] and *jāgro 'viciṇṇalṅitsu* [Pāṇini 7.3.85].

But how is this prohibition of *num* to be understood, given that according to the rule "for an infinite [element], there is either an injunction or a prohibition" (*Vyāḍipāda* 19), a prohibition of the vowel *ī* would be appropriate? To this he says: "The *ī* following *śatṛ*," and so forth. A prohibition applies to that which has been enjoined by another rule, but the vowel *ī* following *śatṛ* has not been enjoined by anything.
The term "of the stem" (*aṅgasya*) is understood [from the previous rule], and no other operation than *num* is possible for *śatṛ*.

Therefore, by implication, the prohibition of *num* (the augment *n*)—even for that which is separated [by other elements] according to the rule "after *ug*, *i*, and *v*" (*ugidacām* 7.1.70)—is understood. Since the suffix *śatṛ* alone does not occur in the neuter gender, it is understood that the option applies to a neuter base ending in *śatṛ* that follows an abhyasta (repeated) *aṅga*; thus he says: "after an abhyasta *aṅga*" and so forth. In the example "that family" (*tadunti kule*), the feminine suffix *śī* is applied by the rule [7.1.19].
In the example "the Brahmin woman piercing" (*tudatī brāhmaṇī*), [the same applies].

The suffix *ṅīp* is applied by [Pāṇini 4.1.6], as in "a Brāhmaṇī woman who goes" (*yāntī brāhmaṇī*). Because it begins with a vowel, there is elision of the *śap* affix; the suffix *ṅīp* is applied by [Pāṇini 4.1.6], as in "a woman who will act in her family" (*kariṣyantī kule*).
The substitution of *śatṛ* [for *lṛṭ*] occurs by the rule *lṛṭaḥ sadvā* [Pāṇini 3.3.14], and the augment *iṭ* is added by *ārdhadhātukasyeḍvaḷādeḥ* [Pāṇini 7.2.35].

Regarding the objection beginning with "because it is *antaraṅga* here," etc.: when the suffix *śatṛ* follows an *a*-ending *aṅga*, and the vowel *ī* [of the feminine suffix] is present, should the *num* augment be applied, or should the single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) be applied? Here, because it is *antaraṅga*, the single substitute is the subsequent form (*pararūpa*) by *ekādeśaḥ parasya* [Pāṇini 6.1.97].

Furthermore, its status as *antaraṅga* (internal) is due to its dependence on vowels (*varṇa*), whereas *num* is *bahiraṅga* (external) because it depends on many factors. For [the substitution of] *śī* and *nadi* depends upon a base (*aṅga*) ending in the letter *a* followed by the suffix *śatṛ*. The rule *vārṇād āṅgam* (Vārttika 39) does not apply here, because the times of application differ: for *num* applies only when *śī* or *nadī* follows, whereas the single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) occurs prior to that.
It was stated previously that "where there is simultaneous application of a vowel and an affix, this [rule] applies.
Because there is no separation (*vyapavarga*), one can say, "of the *śatṛ* following an affix ending in a vowel.
For indeed, such linguistic usage as "this is after that" or "this is before that" occurs only when there is a distinction; not otherwise.

It might be argued: by the rule *Pāṇini 6.1.85*, through the absence of the "as if prior" (*pūrvavat*) and "as if posterior" (*paravat*) designations, a single substitute (*ekādeśa*) is both as if the end with respect to what precedes it and as if the beginning with respect to what follows it; thus, because the single substitute is the end with respect to the preceding element and the beginning with respect to the following element, is it not indeed correct that the suffix *śatṛ* which follows an *aṅga* ending in an *avarṇa* [should be treated as such]? To this he says: "In the case of relying on both," and so forth.
Here, both the *aṅga* ending in the letter *h* and the suffix *śatṛ* are relied upon.
This refers to the phrase "in the case of relying on both," and so forth.

In this case, both the member ending in *hrak* and the suffix *śat* are dependent [on the same element]. According to the rule "When there is dependence on both sides, the treatment as either the final or the initial does not apply" (Vyākaraṇa-paribhāṣā 51), the status of being like the final or the initial does not obtain.
For it is not possible for one and the same thing to simultaneously be treated as the final with respect to what precedes it and as the initial with respect to what follows it.

For instance: if [the suffix] *śatṛ* were like the final element (*pratyantavat*) with respect to what precedes it, then the form of *śatṛ* would not be established; if, on the other hand, it were like the initial element (*ādivat*) with respect to what follows it, then the status of the stem (*aṅga*) as ending in the vowel *a* could not be assumed. Yet, this rule is stated: "The augment *num* occurs after [stems ending in] *ā*, *śī*, and *nadī*. Furthermore, a *śatṛ* suffix never occurs immediately after a stem that actually ends in the vowel *a*. In this regard, by the authority of the grammatical statement, one resorts to the notion of what was previously so—that is, a *śatṛ* which formerly followed a stem ending in *a*.
Therefore, he says: "by way of having been previously so," and so forth.

For if one were to rely on the principle of having previously existed (*bhūtapūrvagati*), there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) in cases such as *avatī* and *dhnatī*; for here too, was there not previously a *śatṛ* [suffix] following an *aṅga* ending in the vowel *a*? To this he says: "In this regard, some state a resolution (*samādhi*).
*Samādhi* means a refutation (*parihāra*).
And the refutation is: "It is a part (*avayava*) of the *śatṛ*."
The letter *t* is a constituent part (*avayava*) of the suffix *śatṛ*.

In this context, the word *śatṛ* refers [to that *t*], just as in the expression "the cloth is torn" (*paṭo dandaḥ*), the word "cloth" (*paṭa*) refers to a part of the cloth; for words that apply to wholes sometimes also apply to their parts.

And since that *t*, which is a part of *śatṛ*, follows a stem (*aṅga*) ending in an *a*-vowel once the single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) has been applied, the objection raised by the statement "because the single-substitute is internal (*antaraṅga*)" and so forth is thereby refuted.

But then, would there not be *num* for a *takāra* that lacks a vowel (*anacka*), or would there be *num* for *ru* as well? And why would it not be so? Because of the rule: "When [the augment] *num* follows, *ru* is substituted [for *r*]" (Pāṇini 1.1.47). Let it not be for the *takāra*; it will apply to that which ends in it.
And we shall explain the meaning of the sūtra in this way: *num* occurs for a stem (*aṅga*) that ends in that which is a portion of *śatṛ* following a stem ending in an *avarṇa*.
And we shall repeat the mention of *aṅga* twice: [first] to mean "does *num* occur for that *aṅga* which ends in a portion of *śatṛ* that follows a stem (*aṅga*) ending in a vowel"?

And we shall repeat the mention of *aṅga* [a second time] for the purpose of qualifying the portion of *śatṛ*, and for the purpose of ensuring the application of the operation pertaining to the *aṅga*.

But how is it that [the suffix] *tudati* and so forth have the designation "stem" (*aṅga*) with respect to the letter *t*? For the designation "stem" applies to that which begins from the element after which a suffix is prescribed when a suffix follows; and the letter *t* is not a suffix. Furthermore, if the designation "stem" does not exist, then the statement—"that portion of *śatṛ* which follows a stem ending in an *a*-vowel"—is untenable. This is not a fault. For just as the word *śatṛ* refers to the entire portion of *śatṛ*, so too the word "stem" (*aṅga*) refers to the portion preceding the letter *t*. What, then, is that stem? It is that of which the portion ending in *śatṛ* is a member.
For it is after *śī* and *nadi* that the designation *aṅga* is prescribed [by Pāṇini].

Why, then, does this not also apply here in the cases *adatī* and *dhnatī*, since even here the element *śatṛ* follows an *aṅga* ending in the vowel *a*? If it were to apply here as well, the qualifier *āt* (ending in *ā*) would be redundant; one should simply have said *śīnadyoḥ*.
And wherever an *aṅga* ending in *śatṛ* occurs after *śī* or *nadi*, there the element *śatṛ* necessarily follows an *aṅga* ending in the vowel *ā*.

Why [is this so]? Because of the force of employing the qualifier "ātaḥ" (from ā), a specific inclusion is understood: that which follows the *śatṛ*-affix element *a*—namely, the *a* that precedes it—and which is itself the subsequent *śatṛ*-affix element; thus, there is no occasion here for the application of *num*.
[The rule] "when *śī* and *nadī* follow an *aṅga* ending in an *a-varṇa*" also functions here as before, with the word *aṅga* referring to a constituent part of the *aṅga*.

But is it not the case that in forms such as *tudanti*, the suffixes *śī* and *nadyau* cannot possibly follow an *aṅga* ending in the vowel *a*, because of the intervention of the letter *t*? To this he says: "In that case, by whatever... and so forth. The meaning has already been explained. Now, while *num* is still in force from the previous rule, for what purpose is *num* mentioned again? [The answer is: No, for both *na* and *vā* are understood from the context.

In that context, even an unintended consequence would be understood if the mention of *num* were omitted: namely, that the optional *num* [prescribed] for feminine bases ending in long *ī* and *nadī* does not apply to those ending in a vowel (*avarṇa*).
What would be the result? In forms such as *kurvatī* and *tanvatī*, the optional *num* would apply, but in *kariṣyantī*, it would not.

Furthermore, by what means is the prohibition of *num*—which was already applicable—stated for bases ending in long *ī* and *nadī*? This very fact indicates that there is indeed an optional *num* for bases ending in the root *as* (the verb "to be") and for *nadī* bases.

However, when the mention of *num* is made, this is understood as a mandatory injunction (*vidhi*), and thus there is no fault. Regarding the forms *īdṛṅ* and *kīdṛṅ*: by the rule *tyadādiṣu* [Pāṇini 3.2.60], the suffix *kvin* is applied; then, by the rule *īśkī* [Pāṇini 6.3.90], the substitutes *ī* and *kī* are applied; then, by the rules *halṅyābbhyo dīrghāt* [6.1.68] and *saṃyogāntasya lopaḥ* [8.2.23], the elision of the final consonant occurs; finally, by the rule *kuhoścuḥ* [8.2.30], the substitution of *c* for the guttural (*kutva*) takes place.
