This results in *yāvṛṅ* and *tādṛṅ*.
The substitution of *āt* [for *samāna-*] occurs by rule [Pāṇini 6.3.91]. Thus, "sadṛṅ" (resembling);
here, the substitution of *sa-* for *samāna-* occurs by rule [Pāṇini 6.3.88], which states that *sa-* is substituted before the suffixes *dṛk*, *dṛś*, and *vat*. "Dyauḥ" (the sky).

When *aut* has been applied, the substitution of *yaṇ* occurs. Here, in the case of *akṣadyūḥ*—derived from *akṣair dīvyati* with the suffix *kvip*—the substitution *uṭh* [by Pāṇini 6.4.19] applies because it is internal (*antaraṅga*) and dependent on that [suffix]. Since the form remains non-different due to the principle of "change in one part" (*ekadeśavikṛtanyāya*), this is indeed the word *div*, and thus the substitution of *aut* for the final *ū* would be expected. Why, then, does it not occur? To this he says: "The base *div* is a nominal stem," and so forth.

This verbal root *div* certainly exists, and there also exists an underived nominal stem (*prātipadika*). Among these, the verbal root possesses an indicatory letter (*anubandha*), and thus it undergoes the grammatical operation prescribed for roots ending in an *u*-vowel (by Pāṇini 7.2.56).
The nominal stem, however, is devoid of an indicatory letter; indeed, no grammatical operation based on an indicatory letter applies to it.

In this context, by the paribhāṣā "that which has no suffix following it" (Pāṇini 1.4.56), a verbal root (*dhātu*) is understood here. Consequently, in the case of *annadyu*, the undesirable application of the substitution of *ā* for *at* does not occur.

The letter *t* is for the sake of ease of pronunciation (*mukhasukhārtha*). When the elision of *hal* and *ṅi*-stems etc. is about to take place, as well as the elision of *n*, the substitution of *ā* is prescribed.

In the word *panthāḥ*, there is the substitution of *na* by [Pāṇini 7.1.87], and the substitution of *at* by [Pāṇini 7.1.86] because it is a *sarvanāmasthāna* case ending. Now, one might object: since the original (sthānin) is a nasalized *n*, and given that [Pāṇini 1.1.70] allows for the inclusion of homogeneous sounds (*savarṇa*), the substitute *a* ought to be nasalized as well, due to the principle of closest proximity (*āntaratamya*).
"Why is this [substitute] being cited here as pure (*śuddha*)? To this he says: "Even when the original locus (*sthānin*) is nasal," and so forth.
He states the reason for this very point: "That which is being taught (*bhāvyamāna*)," and so forth.

If, moreover, there were no inclusion of homogeneous sounds (*savarṇa*) by means of an *aṇ* sound even when it is taught with a following *t* (i.e., *tapara*), then in the rule *viṅvanoranunāsikasyāt* [Pāṇini 6.4.41], the substitution would not occur; likewise, in the rule *tathoḥ* [Pāṇini 6.4.42], the nasalized vowel *ā* would not exist.
If that is so, then this *ā* is not intended to include its homogeneous counterparts (*tapara*); what then? It is the letter *d*.
The *d*, however, is for the sake of ease of pronunciation (*mukhasukhārtha*), and because it has undergone a change of place of articulation (*cartvabhūtatva*), it is not heard.

One might argue: "Even though an *aṇ* being taught (*bhāvyamāna*) does not include its homogeneous counterparts (Pāṇini 1.1.69), thus there will be no inclusion of the homogeneous letters; nevertheless, since it is pronounced as qualified by nasality (*anunāsika*), is it not proper that it should be associated with the nasalized [vowel] alone? To this he says: "For it is pure," and so forth.
This *hr* is said to be pure (*śuddha*) and non-nasal (*niranunāsika*); therefore, it is purely [the letter *h*] and not characterized by nasality.

Now, for what purpose is this stated as long (*dīrgha*), rather than being made short (*hrasva*)? For in this case too, the long vowel would be established by the rule *akaḥ savarṇe* [Pāṇini 6.1.101]. It is not so established; for by the rule *ato guṇe* [Pāṇini 6.1.97], there would be the substitution of the single subsequent form (*pararūpatva*). If it is argued that this will not occur due to the force of the explicit utterance of the letter *a*, we say no; for there is another purpose for the utterance of the letter *a*.

What is that? [The objection is: "There would be no hearing of the letter *na*. For if elision (*lopa*) were performed, there would be prolixity (*gaurava*); therefore, the long vowel is prescribed. Now, while the term "after *āt*" (*āt*) is being carried over [from 7.1.85], what is the purpose of stating "after *ad*" (*ad*)? If it is argued that it is so that the short vowel may be heard, this is not so; for once the shortening has occurred, when the suffix *su* follows, the substitution of a long vowel by the rule "a long vowel replaces [a homogeneous] *ak* with a homogeneous vowel" (6.1.101) must take place according to "anyatra" (6.4.7). Thus, how could there be the hearing of the short vowel? To this he says: "While 'after *āt*' is being carried over," and so forth.

What is its purpose (*prayojana*)? It is that which has the preceding *ṣat* as its purpose; thus it is said. But how does this have the preceding *ṣat* as its purpose? To this he says: "ṛbhukṣaṇam," etc.
If only the long vowel were prescribed in the present context, then in the case of *ṛbhukṣam indram*, there would be no hearing of the short vowel.

But [the objection] that it occurs optionally because of the rule for long vowels in *hrasvavidhāne tu* (Pāṇini 6.4.9)? Some say that the addition of *ta* (the *tapara* marker) both in the original element (*sthānin*) and the substitute (*ādeśa*) is for the sake of ease of pronunciation;
others say it is for the sake of excluding the long vowel in forms such as *pathīḥ*.

From *panthānamicchati* [by *pathin-āśiṣoḥ kyac* 3.1.8], there is lengthening by *akṛtsārvadhātukayoḥ* [7.4.25]—thus *pathīyati*. From *pathīyateḥ* with the suffix *kvip*, there is elision of the final vowel by *verapṛktasya* [6.4.48], and then the elision of the *yakāra* by *lopo vyorvali* [6.4.50]—thus *pathīḥ*. As for the two [suffixes] *thaḥ* and *nthah*, both the original base (*sthānin*) and the substitute (*ādeśa*) are devoid of vowels. As for the vowel *a* that is heard in the form *an-tha*, it is merely for the sake of pronunciation (*uccāraṇārtha*).

Even though the substitute (*ādeśa*) consists of multiple *al* sounds, according to the rule "substitutes apply to that which is being specifically indicated" (*nirdiśyamānasyādeśā bhavanti*, Vyāḍiparibhāṣā 106), it is understood that the substitute applies only to the letter *th*, and not to the entire [stem]. This is the meaning of the rule beginning with "in the place of a sarvanāmasthāna" (*sarvanāmasthāne*).

> [[1.4.18]] *pratyatra* > [[1.4.17]] From this point onward, while the term *asarvanāmasthāne* (not being a case-ending that follows a pronoun) is understood as a governing rule (*anuvartamāna*), the technical designation *bha* is prescribed. In that context, if the elision of the *ṭi* suffix in words such as *pathin* were to occur when followed by a *sarvanāmasthāna*, then those words would not possess the *bha* designation; conversely, if they were to possess the *bha* designation, then a *sarvanāmasthāna* could not follow them. Thus, there is a contradiction characterized by mutual exclusion between the *bha* designation and the presence of a *sarvanāmasthāna*.

Therefore, although the mention of *sarvanāmasthāna* continues for the sake of what follows, it is nevertheless not connected here. The letter *ṅ* in *asuṅ* is for the purpose of indicating that it replaces the final letter;
the letter *u* is for the purpose of the operations applicable to bases ending in *ugit*.
[The example is] "pumān."

The augment *num* is applied by the rule *ugidacām* [Pāṇini 7.1.70], followed by lengthening according to *sarvanāmasthāne cāsambuddhau* [6.4.8], and the elision of the final consonant (*saṃyogāntalopa*) and the following vowel (*halṅyābbhyo dīrghāt sutisyapṛktaṃ hal* [6.1.68]).
Regarding the example *paramapumān*:

once the compound *paramaścāsau pumāṃśca* has been formed by rules such as *viśeṣaṇaṃ viśeṣyeṇa bahulam* [2.1.57], the substitution *asuṅ* must not yet take place as long as the case-ending (*vibhakti*) has not arisen, because that substitution is dependent upon the latter.

But since the accentuation of the final syllable of a compound does not depend on anything else, it is *antaraṅga* (internal); therefore, the final-accentuation occurs even before the case-ending. When the case-ending has subsequently arisen, the augment *asuṅ* would occur in place of a consonant that lacks an accent; consequently, it would have no fixed accent. Thus, an undesired accent would result, whereas the final syllable of the second member is intended to be oxytone (*antodātta*), yet it would instead result in being ādyudātta (accented on the first syllable). [The sūtra] begins with "for that purpose," etc.

The word *artha* signifies "cessation," as in the expression "smoke for the sake of mosquitoes" (*maśakārtho dhūmaḥ*). For that purpose—that is, for the sake of the cessation of that undesirable [suffix] by its own force—the statement "like the original form" (*upadeśivad-vacanam*) must be made, so that the augment *asuṅ* may occur precisely in the state of the original form (*upadeśāvasthā*), prior to the arising of the case-ending (*vibhakti*) when the compound is not yet formed. Thus, once *asuṅ* has been applied first and subsequently the accentuation of the final member of the compound (*samāsāntodāttatva*) is applied, the word *paramapumān* becomes oxytone (having the acute accent on its final syllable).

If this were so, the word *pumān* would also have its final syllable accented acute (*antodātta*), because the substitution of *asuṅ* occurs precisely at the stage of the original instruction (*upadeśāvasthā*). Should it not then follow that the accentuation of the nominal stem (*prātipadika-svara*) would apply later? To this he says: "But this word *pumān*," and so forth. This word *puṃs* is derived from the root *pū* with the suffix *muksun*—according to [Pāṇini 3.2.177], which states "after the roots *pū* and *mā*, the suffix *muksun* is added and the vowel is shortened"—thus it is formed by the addition of the suffix *muksun*.

By that *ṇit*-accent, this [suffix] becomes udātta on the first syllable, not udātta on the final syllable. Alternatively, by this [sūtra], the designation *ṇit* is assigned: "A *sarvanāmasthāna* suffix following *go* is *ṇit*," meaning it receives the technical name *ṇit*; or else, the letter *ṇ* of the *sarvanāmasthāna* suffix following *go* is made to have the designation *it*, meaning that the letter *ṇ* of the *sarvanāmasthāna* suffix following *go* becomes an *it*.

Either a substitute (ādeśa) is prescribed—meaning that a substitute bearing the indicatory letter *ṇ* takes the place of a *sarvanāmasthāna* following a word ending in *go*; or an extension (atideśa) is made—meaning that [the suffix] becomes *ṇit*, i.e., it behaves as if it were *ṇit*. Even without the suffix *vat*, the sense of "behaving like" (*vatyartha*) is understood, as in the rule for *gāṅ-kuṭādi* (Pāṇini 1.2.1). In the first case, since a technical term (*saṃjñā*) when uttered denotes the thing named (*saṃjñin*), then in the rules concerning *ṇit* suffixes, because of its artificial nature (*kṛtrimatva*), only this specific *sarvanāmasthāna* would be understood, and not those such as *ṇvul* and others.

In the second [view], however, the letter *ṇ* would bear the designation *it*, which would result in the application of the term "sarvanāmasthāna" [to that suffix]. In the third [view], on the other hand, since a *sarvanāmasthāna* with the marker *ṇit* is never observed anywhere, those very substitutes such as *ṣvu*, *lā*, and so forth, would themselves result as the replacements; these are the defects in the first three positions which must be addressed respectively.

In that case, there would be a burden of effort in providing a remedy; however, under the view of *atideśa* (extended application), nothing at all needs to be remedied. Therefore, that [view] alone is correct.
Relying on that very point, he says: "From the word *go*" and so forth.
By explaining the meaning of the phrase "it becomes *ṇit*" through the words "the operation of *ṇit*" and so on, he declares that this is an *atideśa* of the operation.
In the word *gaur*, there is the substitution of *vṛddhi* and the application of the rule for [stems] marked with the indicator *ṇit*.
In the case of *citraguḥ*,
when the *bahuvrīhi* compound has been formed, the short vowel [substitution] applies by [Pāṇini 1.2.48].

In that case, if the marker *t* were not present, then by the rule "In the context of *aṅga*, [the operation applies] to that [element] and to what follows it" (*PuPāVṛ* 85), one would have to accept the application of the rule regarding the final element of a compound (*tadantavidhi*). Consequently, by means of the status of being a substitute (*sthānivadbhāva*), this *aṅga* would end with the word *go*, and thus the status of being a *ṇit* would apply.
However, when the marker *t* is present, there is a restriction to that specific duration [of the vowel], and therefore [the *ṇit* status] does not occur, because the durations are different.
Furthermore, since the mention of *aṇ* has been removed in the rule *Pāṇini 1.1.70*, the restriction to that specific duration applies even to vowels that are not *aṇ*.
Regarding the phrase "How so? and so forth:

even though the *tapara* marker is present, [the rule] "guṇa for a short vowel" (Pāṇini 7.3.108) and "also before *jas*" (Pāṇini 7.3.109) would apply when the guṇa is effected for the vocative *jas* ending, resulting in the forms *he citrago* and *he citragava*.
The intention is that this occurs because [the guṇa] shares the same time [of application].

But will this not be avoided by the *lakṣaṇapratipadokta* maxim (P. 1.1.3)? This is not so; for that maxim does not apply where there is the operation of *sthānivadbhāva*, since if *sthānivadbhāva* were present, the application of the maxim would be redundant.
The phrase "but when the operation of the *aṅga* has taken place" (*aṅgavṛtte punaḥ*) and so forth is the solution [to the objection regarding *citrago*].
However, this is the solution for *he citrago*, and not for *citragavaḥ*, because [the latter] is not yet finalized (*aniṣṭhitatvāt*).

For once the substitution of *ava* has been made, the word will attain its final form (*niṣṭhitatva*) here, and not merely through the *guṇa* [substitution], because that alone is unfit for usage. Therefore, being dissatisfied with this solution because it is not universally applicable (*avyāpakatva*), he states another solution beginning with "Or rather" (*atha vā*). It might be argued: "In this case as well, the *sarvanāmasthāna* suffix related to *go* occurs through a relationship characterized by immediate succession (*ānantarya*). To this he says: "And that which... and so forth.

If the term *sarvanāmasthāna* were understood here as being related to the word *go* by way of immediate proximity (*ānantarya*), then the recourse to the genitive case would be purposeless; rather, the ablative case alone should have been employed, since there is no purpose for deviating from the sequence [of grammatical relations].

Therefore, by the force of employing the genitive case, it is stated that "the *sarvanāmasthāna* which occurs when there is oneness and so forth of the meaning of the word *go* is the *sarvanāmasthāna* of *go*. Furthermore, that [oneness and so forth] is to be understood as belonging to the word *go*.

By the word "etc. (*ādi*), the inclusion of duality (*dvitva*) and so forth is intended. One might ask: even in the case of the word *citragu*, does that which is a *sarvanāmasthāna* [suffix] apply to the oneness and other numbers of the meaning of the word *go*? To this he says: "From the word *citragu*" and so forth. If the status of being a *ṇit* were prescribed for every *sarvanāmasthāna* suffix related to *go*, then the use of the *tapara* marker would be purposeless; for that marker is employed so that [the rule] does not apply in cases such as *citraguḥ*.

And there is no application [of the rule] here, for in this case the *sarvanāmasthāna* suffix is not related to "cow" (*go*), but rather to the meaning of another word; thus he says: "But the inclusion of *t* [in the technical term *tṛtīyā*]" and so forth.
"Some" and so forth.
But for what purpose do they recite it in this way? To this he says: "The word *dyo* also," and so forth.

As for those who do not read "gotaḥ" here, for them the status of being a *ṇit* for the *sarvanāmasthāna* suffixes following the word "dyo" would not be established; therefore, he says: "This very [term] 'gotaḥ'," and so forth.
But how can this be understood as an indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*) of that which ends in the vowel *o*? To this he says: "In the case of the mention of phonemes," and so forth.

For it is well known that in rules such as "[1.1.1] *tādau ca nityam*" and "[1.1.2] *adeṅ guṇaḥ*," a phoneme is mentioned with a following *t* (i.e., *tapara*), and thus the use of *tapara* is established in the mention of phonemes.

Therefore, here too, because of the mention of the *tapara* (the vowel with a following *r*), the term "ending in *o*" (*gotaḥ*) should be understood as an indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*) for vowels ending in *u*. From this statement, it is understood that the employment of the *tapara* is solely for the purpose of indicating the phoneme, and thus it serves as an indicator for vowels ending in *ū*. The phrase "or there is the operation of *ṇit*" means that since the operation of *ṇit* is optional, it is stated that it may optionally be *ṇit*; he shows by this that it is not a total prohibition of the status of being *ṇit*.
The point is that the status of being *ṇit* established for *ṇal* at the stage of its *upadeśa* cannot be set aside even by a hundred such statements.

[Thus we have] "cakāra" and "cakara. When there is the status of *ṇit*, then by [Pāṇini 7.2.115] there is *vṛddhi*; otherwise, there is the *guṇa* substitution conditioned by the *ārdhadhātuka* suffix.
Regarding the forms *papāca* and *papaca*:

when there is the status of being marked with Ñ (ṇittva), then by [Pāṇini 7.2.116] *akata upadhāyāḥ*, there is vṛddhi; otherwise, its absence occurs. The term *asambuddhau* is a paryudāsa (an exclusion): *asambuddhi* means other than the vocative (*sambuddhi*).
For example: *he sakhe*.

The *guṇa* substitution [is applied] by the rule *hrasvasya gaṇaḥ* [Pāṇini 7.3.108]. Although the status of being a *ṇit* suffix would have been obtained by the preceding rule, *anaṅ* is prescribed here.
The letter *ṅ* in that term is for the purpose of indicating that it replaces the final phoneme;
the vowel *a* is for the purpose of pronunciation.
In the word *sakhi*,

[the vowel] becomes long by [Pāṇini 6.4.8], the suffix *su* is elided by [Pāṇini 6.1.68], and the *n* is elided by [Pāṇini 8.2.7]. The mention of *anaṅ* [in Pāṇini 7.1.93] is for the purpose of ensuring that the elision of *su* occurs when the vowel *ā* is to be substituted [by 7.1.92].

If the vowel *a* were prescribed [as the substitute], its elision would not occur, as in the case of *panthāḥ*. When the *guṇa* substitution [of *o*] for that which ends in *ṛ* (by Pāṇini 7.3.110) has been applied, and when the elision of *hal*, *ṅī*, etc. (by 6.1.68) has been performed for the others, and when the rules for *ru*-tva, *visarjanīya*, and the lengthening of a final *s* have become applicable, it is stated: "In the case of *uśanas*, even in the vocative, [the form with *o*] is desired as an alternative."

How so? The letter *ca* is employed here, and it serves the purpose of including what has not been explicitly mentioned. By that means, the substitution of *anaṅ* will occur for *uśanas-* even when it is in the genitive case (*tadbuddhau*).
If this were the case, would it be obligatory? No; because of the governing rule [Pāṇini 7.1.91], it will occur only optionally.

"And for others, [the rule] is always [applicable] because of the knowledge of the *vyavasthita-vibhāṣā* (restricted option). It is also desired that 'the prohibition of the elision of *n*' (*nalopa-pratiṣedha*) applies even in this alternative view. How is this obtained? For in that context, from the rule *svarito vānudātte padādau* [Pāṇini 8.2.6], the word *vā* ("or") is understood to carry over; by that very fact, it is understood thus: "In the case of the genitive singular ending (*ṅi*) and the vocative (*sambuddhi*), either the elision of *n* occurs or its prohibition. And through the knowledge of the *vyavasthita-vibhāṣā*, the elision of the *n* of the vocative of *uśanas* will optionally take place.
"But for others, there will never be an elision.
With the words "And so it has been said," etc., he confirms the meaning just mentioned by means of a scriptural statement. "That which ends in *s*," etc.
When *anaṅ* is not applied,
[the form is] "nāntam," but there is no elision of the *n*.
Regarding the term "adanta" (ending in 'a'):
when the elision of 'n' (nalopa) is performed,
the inclusion of the marker 't' (taparakaraṇa) is for the purpose of removing ambiguity.

For if that [suffix *tun*] were not present, once the substitution of *yaṇ* for the following vowel had been applied, there would be doubt: "Is this the inclusion of a word ending in the vowel *ṛ*, or rather of one ending in the letter *r*? [The answer is: "The word *kroṣṭu* ends in the suffix *tun* and is a technical name (*saṃjñāśabda*).

This is because it is derived from the root *kruś* ("to call out," or according to the Dhātupāṭha, "to call out and to weep") by means of the suffix *tun*—as established in the rule "from the roots *si*, *tan*, *gam*, *mi*, *mas*, *sic*, *vyadh*, *añc*, and *kṛś*, the suffix *tun* is added" (Dhātupāṭha 1.122)—and because this is a technical name for a jackal (*jambuka*).
Regarding the rule *tṛjvadbhavati*:
it is called *tṛjvat* because it behaves similarly to the suffix *tṛc*.
He will explain that "this is an extension of form (*rūpātideśa*)."

In this regard, when it is stated that "it becomes like *tṛj*," someone might have the misconception that the form of the word *tṛc* itself is being extended [to the other]. Therefore, in order to dispel that, he says: "the form which belongs to that which ends in *tṛj*," and so forth.

And this is obtained from the rule: "When there is a mention of an affix (*pratyaya*), the inclusion is of that which begins with the element after which it is prescribed and ends with that affix" (Paribhāṣā 44).

Although various ways in which there is no fault even in the extension (*atideśa*) of the rule (*śāstra*) have been demonstrated in the *Bhāṣya*—since that [extension of the rule] has been established as being free from defect—and although the extension of the operation (*kāryātideśa*) has also been explained as being almost faultless because it is not distinct from the extension of the rule; nevertheless, since the extension of the rule and the extension of the operation have form (*rūpa*) as their object, there is an absence of qualities (*guṇa*) in the form.
For form is primary, because it is that which is to be refined by those two.
Therefore, he says "this is an extension of form" (*rūpātideśo'yam*), and so forth, stating that this extension of form is logical.

If, then, the form of that which ends in *tṛc* is extended to the word *kroṣṭṛ*, then would not any form whatsoever ending in *tṛc*—such as *vaktṛ*, *paktṛ*, and so forth—also result? To this he says: "And because of proximity," and so on. Here, there exists the form of a different root ending in *tṛc*, such as *pacati* and others, as well as that of the root *kruś*. Is the form of a root ending in *tṛc* that has not been heard [in this context] being extended, or rather that of the heard root *kruś*? In that case, it is precisely the form of the heard one that is to be extended.
Is it by the force of the pronunciation of the letter *ca* that the vowel is also understood? The sense is that otherwise, one would have simply said "like *tṛ*" (*tṛvat*).
[The example is] "kroṣṭā."
When the substitution of *tṛjvat* has been applied, the suffix *anaṅ* is added by the preceding rule (*sūtra*). Thus, in the forms *kroṣṭārau* and *kroṣṭāraḥ*,
there is *guṇa* substitution, followed by the replacement of the vowel with *r* (*raparatva*), and finally lengthening (*dīrgha*) by the rule beginning with *apṭṛ* (*sūtra* 6.4.11).
In the word *kroṣṭūn*, there is lengthening by [Pāṇini 6.1.102] and the substitution of *n* for *t* by [Pāṇini 6.1.103]. In the word *kroṣṭrībhiḥ*, [the same rules apply].

When the substitution of *tṛjvat* has been applied, the *yaṇ* replacement [of *ṛ*] occurs. But by what rule is the long *ī* added to the word *kroṣṭu*, once *tṛjvat* has been applied? If one suggests it is by the rule *ṛnnebhyo ṅīp* (Pāṇini 4.1.5), that is not correct, because it would result in the word being unaccented (*anudātta*). Therefore, he says: "Some [grammarians] [apply] the word *kroṣṭu*," and so forth.
[The example is: "bought with five *kroṣṭrīs*."

The compound is formed according to [Pāṇini 2.1.51]. By the rule [Pāṇini 5.1.19], *ārhādagopucchād ṭhak*, the suffix *ṭhak* is applied; by [Pāṇini 5.1.28], *adhyardhapūrvād dvigor lug*, the *luk* elision applies; and by [Pāṇini 1.2.49], *luktaddhitaluki*, there is the elision (*luk*) of the feminine suffix. For those who apply the *tṛjvadbhāva* (the substitution of the form of the suffix *tṛc*) when that *ṅīṣ* suffix has been elided, the *tṛjvadbhāva* does not occur; therefore, it says "prativiṣeyam. The meaning is that a counter-measure (*pratividhāna*) must be taken.

In this regard, the following is the rebuttal: the particle *ca* (and) is used here, and it serves the purpose of including what has not been explicitly mentioned; therefore, [the suffix] will apply even when the feminine suffix (*strīpratyaya*) has been elided.

If so, how can the vowel *ī* apply for those who do not read [the word *kroṣṭu*] in the *gaura*-group? To this he says: "In the *gaura*-group," and so forth. For them, there is nothing at all to be rebutted in the case of the form *pañcakroṣṭubhiḥ*; because they do not rely on a subsequent feminine suffix as the cause [for the application of the *ī* vowel].

But surely, since the feminine suffix (*strīpratyaya*) has been elided for them as well, the designation "stem" (*aṅga*) does not exist; and in the absence of that stem-designation, the substitution of *tṛṇvat* prescribed for a stem would not apply? This objection must indeed be addressed. It is not so; for even when the feminine suffix is elided, the designation "stem" still occurs by virtue of the rule *pratyayalakṣaṇena*.

As for the prohibition [stated in Pāṇini 1.1.63], it applies only to an operation prescribed within the governing context of "stem" (*aṅgādhikāra*). And the designation "stem" itself is not prescribed within the governing context of "stem."

Regarding the phrase "when the extension [of the designation] has been made" (*kṛte 'tideśe*), etc.: because of the continued application (*anuvṛtti*) of the rule *iko 'ci vibhaktau* [Pāṇini 7.1.73], once a case-ending (*vibhakti*) has arisen and the designation "stem" (*aṅga*) dependent upon that [ending] has been established, the extension of the word *kroṣṭṛ*—which is currently functioning as feminine—is performed. When that [extension] has been made, since it ends in the vowel *ṛ*, the suffix *ṅīp* is applied by the rule *ṛnnebhyo ṅīp* [Pāṇini 4.1.5].
But surely, when the suffix *ṅīp* is applied, the word *kroṣṭrī* would not be established as having its final syllable accented (*antodātta*)? To this he says: "In that case," and so forth.

Since the word *kroṣṭrī* is prescribed as being *antodātta*, the *yaṇ* substitute occurring in place of the vowel *ṛ* belonging to the element *tṛ* becomes an *udāttayaṇ*. Consequently, while the rule [Pāṇini 6.1.173] is in effect, by [Pāṇini 6.1.174], the word *kroṣṭrī* becomes *antodātta*. [The rule] Pāṇini 4.1.3 does not apply here; therefore, this is an optional rule (*vibhāṣā*) for a case where [the accent] was otherwise not obtained. [The form] is *kroṣṭunā*.
By [Pāṇini 7.3.120], the substitution of *nā* occurs;
by [Pāṇini 7.3.111], there is *guṇa* (vocalization) in "kroṣṭave."

Regarding "kroṣṭuḥ": by [Pāṇini 6.1.107] *ṛta ut*, the substitution of *u* occurs; then there is the substitution of *ra* for the *ṛ*; and by [Pāṇini 8.2.24] *rāt sasya*, there is the elision of the *s*.
Regarding "kroṣṭoḥ": [the same process applies].

Is there the substitution of the prior form (*pūrvarūpatva*) by the rule *pūrvavadguṇaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.1.102)? [In the case of] *kroṣṭari*, there is the substitution of *guṇa* by the rule *kroṣṭari* (Pāṇini 7.1.95). [In the case of] *kroṣṭau*.
By [Pāṇini 7.3.119], the substitution of *at* and the substitution of *aut* [are applied].

Regarding the phrase "due to the treatment as *tṛc*" (*tṛjvadbhāvāt*), and so forth: the scope of the treatment as *tṛc* is exemplified by *puṃsi kroṣṭroḥ*; the scope of *num* is exemplified by *trapuṇe*, *jatune*. When both would apply simultaneously—as in *priyakroṣṭune vanāya*—*num* occurs by virtue of the "prior rule taking precedence" (*pūrvavipratiṣedha*).

The scope for *nuṭ* is in forms such as *agnīnām* and *vāyūnām*; the scope for the substitution of *tṛjvat* is the same. When both would apply in a case such as *kroṣṭṝṇām*, *nuṭ* occurs by means of a "prior conflict" (*pūrvavipratiṣedha*). This prior conflict is obtained because the word *para* (in the rule *paranityāntaraṅgāpavādānām uttarottaraṃ balīyaḥ*) signifies that which is desired [by the author]. The term *sarvanāmasthāne* from [Pāṇini 7.1.86] is reiterated here, not *tṛtīyādiṣu* from [7.1.97].
Since *āgamas* (augmentations) are inherently *anudātta* (unaccented) according to the principle "āgamā anudāttā bhavanti," this statement is made to ensure they are *udātta* (accented).

"In this case, the rule of *tadanta-vidhi* (extension to that which ends with the specified element) is intended," because of the statement: "In the context of the *aṅga* (stem) designation, [the term refers] to that [element] and what follows it as its final member" (Pāṇini-vārttika 85). Thus, we have *priyacatvāḥ*.
This is a *bahuvrīhi* compound.

Although the rule "the addition of [the rule for] pronouns and numerals" (*sarvanāmasaṃkhyayor upasaṃkhyānam*) would require the numeral to be placed first, the rule "optionally for the word *priya*" (*vā priyasya*) causes the word *priya* to be placed first. This statement is made because the suffix *ām* would otherwise have been required by the preceding rule; thus: "O *priyacatvaḥ*! (O you who possess four dear things).
Regarding "he priyānaḍvān":

here, since the vocative case does not occur for the word *catuḥ* alone, this is an example of [the suffix] ending in *-dat*. Although the vocative can occur for *anajuh* alone, nevertheless, the rule of extension (*tadantavidhi*) is intended here; therefore, it is an example of [the suffix] ending in that [word]. Regarding "kirati" and "girati": [these are examples of the suffix *śnu*].
The root *kṛ* is used in the sense of "scattering" (*vikṣepe*; Dhātupāṭha 1409), and *gu* is used in the sense of "swallowing" (*nigaraṇe*;

Dhātupāṭha 1410). Regarding the word *āstīrṇam*: the root *stṛ* is used in the sense of "covering" (*ācchādane*; Dhātupāṭha 1484; note that *stṛñ* is also listed in the Dhātupāṭha). By [Pāṇini 8.2.42], there is the substitution of *na* for the final consonant; by [8.4.1], there is the substitution of *ṇa* for the preceding *ra*; and by [8.2.77], there is the lengthening of the vowel before a consonant.
Regarding the word "viśīrṇam":
the root *śṛ* means "to injure" (Dhātupāṭha 1488).
[The phrase] "of the mothers, of the fathers."
The vowel lengthening [occurs] by the rule *nāmi* [Pāṇini 6.4.3].
Even though the word ends in the vowel *ṛ*, this [lengthening] does not apply here because it is not a verbal root (*adhātu*).

Now, one might object: "By the maxim regarding that which is taught by a rule versus that which is taught by its own form (*lakṣaṇapratipadokta-paribhāṣā*), this will not occur here; so what is the purpose of including the term 'verbal root' (*dhātu*) to exclude it? To this he says: "Even of that which is taught by a rule," and so forth.
For what purpose, then, is the inclusion of that which is defined by its technical characteristics (*lākṣaṇika*)? He says: "when one desires to act" (*cikīrṣati*), and so forth.

But how is it possible for the inclusion of that which is defined by its characteristics to be obtained here, even though it is not explicitly intended? Precisely because of the indicative mark (*jñāpaka*) provided by the mention of "root" (*dhātu*). For this is its purpose: [to ensure that the rule does not apply] in cases such as *mātṛṇām* and *pitṛṇām*.

If there were no inclusion of the derivative (lākṣaṇika) form here, then in cases such as *mātṛṇām* and *pitṛṇām*, [the rule] would not apply precisely because they are derivative; thus, the mention of "dhātu" (root) would be purposeless.
Therefore, in this context, the derivative form is also included.
Consequently, in forms such as *cikīrṣati*, even when the lengthening [of the vowel] occurs by [Pāṇini 6.4.16], the [application of the rule] indeed takes place.
The addition of *t* (in *tapara*) is for the sake of removing ambiguity.

If it were stated simply as "ra," a doubt would arise: is this a reference to the phoneme *r*, or is it the *yaṇ*-substitute for *ṛ*? It has been stated that the substitution of *i* occurs for a verbal root ending in *ṛ*.
However, this would not apply to the *ṛ* that constitutes the penultimate (*upadhā*) of a root, yet it is desired; therefore, this [addition of *t*] is for that purpose.

Regarding the word "kīrtayati": the root *kṛt* in the sense of "proclaiming" (*saṃśabdana*) belongs to the *curādi* class and is formed with the causative suffix *ṇic*. Now, one might object: since the vowel substitution for *i* (ittva) will occur by the rule of irregular derivation (*nipātana*), "ūti, yūti, jūti, sāti, heti, and kīrti" [Pāṇini 3.3.97], why is this specific grammatical rule (*yoga*) formulated? This is not so; for that irregular derivation would apply only in the domain of the suffix *ktin*.

If that is so, one might argue: "In the previous rule (*pūrvayoga*), we shall qualify the vowel *ṛ* by means of the verbal root (*dhātu*), while here [in the present rule] it refers to that which is situated therein (*tatstha*). This too is not correct; for if that were the case, the rule would also apply in instances such as *ṝkārīyati*, where one desires the sound *ṝ*.
Therefore, this must be stated:
although it could have been said simply as "and after a *kṛt* suffix" (*kṛtaśca*), the statement "and after a penultimate vowel" (*upadhāyāśca*) is for the sake of stylistic variety (*vaicitrya*).

If it were said "and after *kṛta*," would [the substitution] apply to the letter *t*? No, this is not the case; for in the preceding sūtra, "after *ṛ*" (*ṝtaḥ*) was introduced as a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*). It is not possible to intend that very same term as the qualificand (*viśeṣya*).
Consequently, the commentary (*vṛtti*)—which states, "there is the substitution of *i* for the *ṛ* that is the penultimate vowel (*upadhā*)"—would be contradicted.
For in this [commentary], the *ṛ*-vowel is shown to be the qualificand.

Therefore, just as this [element] is sometimes a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) of the member (*aṅga*), so too the word "ṛtaḥ" is a qualifier in the preceding sūtra, but here it is the qualificand (*viśeṣya*). When the substitution of *it* (short *i*) would have been required by the rule *ṛta iddhātoḥ* [Pāṇini 7.1.100], the substitution of *ut* is prescribed [instead]. For example:
*pūrttaḥ* (or *pūrttāḥ*, according to the Kāśikā and Padamañjarī). [The root is] *pṛ?* meaning "protection" and "filling" (Dhātupāṭha 1086), with the suffix *kta*.
Because it is prohibited by the rule beginning with *na dhyākhyā* [Pāṇini 8.2.57], the substitution of *ṇatva* for the *ṣṭhā* does not occur.
Regarding *vuvūrṣati*:
the root is *vṛ* (meaning "to choose") from the Dhātupāṭha (1490).
Regarding "mumūrṣati":
the root *mṛ* is used in the sense of "killing" (*hiṃsāyām*) [Dhātupāṭha 1492].
Regarding "susvūrṣati": [the root *sū*].
The root *sthṛ* is listed in the Dhātupāṭha (932) as meaning "sound" and "affliction. According to [Pāṇini 6.4.16], there is lengthening of the vowel, and thus its ending is the vowel *ṛ*.

Now, how is it that the substitution of *u* occurs here in the cases of *vṛṅ* (Dhātupāṭha 1509, meaning "to choose") and *vṛñ* (Dhātupāṭha 1254, meaning "to cover"), as in *prāvuvūrṣate* and *prāvuvūrṣati*? For in these instances, the *ṛ* is not preceded by a labial; rather, it is preceded by a dental and a labial (*dantyauṣṭhapūrva*). To this, he says: "Even that which is preceded by both a dental and a labial is considered 'preceded by a labial,'" and so forth.
For that which is produced in the place of articulation of both [sounds] receives the designation of either one.
Therefore, that which is both dental and labial remains indeed labial. That which is preceded by something dental and labial is precisely preceded by something labial.
Now, why does [the substitution] not occur in the word *samīrṇam*, since here too there is the quality of being preceded by the tip of the lips? To this he says: "For here, the lip... and so forth.

For here, although the *oṣṭha* (lip) is also a member of a word (*aṅga*), it is the member of the *aṅga* that is understood in this context due to proximity (*pratyāsatti*), not the member of a prefix (*upasarga*). Proximity, moreover, exists because the [term] *aṅga* is the subject under discussion; however, there is no proximity for the prefix, as the case is the reverse.

Regarding the rule beginning with *ittvottvābhyām*: the scope for *ittva* and *uttva* is, for example, *āstīrṇam* and *pūrta*; the scope for *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* is, for example, *cayanam* and *cāyaka*. Here, both would apply—namely *āstaraṇam*, *āstārakaḥ*, *niparaṇam*, and *nipārakaḥ*—but in these cases, *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* take effect by virtue of the rule of conflict (*vipratiṣedha*). [Examples of the latter are] *taturiḥ* and *jaguriḥ*.

From the roots *tṛ* and *gṛ*, either of the two suffixes *kikin* is applied by the rule *ādṛgamahanajanaḥ kikinau liṭ ca* [Pāṇini 3.2.171]. Thereafter, due to the status of being a substitute (*sthānivadbhāva*) according to the rule *ut* [Pāṇini 1.1.59], the forms *tṛ* and *gṛ* are reduplicated; then, by the rule *urat* [Pāṇini 7.4.66], the vowel substitution *at* occurs, resulting in *papritamam* and *vavritamam*.
From the roots *pṛ* and *vṛ*, either of the two suffixes *kikin* is applied, according to their respective positions.
From what ending in the suffix *kip*? From [a word] by means of the suffix *tamap*, according to the rule "The suffix *tamap* is used in the sense of excellence" (Pāṇini 5.3.55), and so forth.
Thus ends the first quarter of the seventh chapter in the *Kāśikā-vivaraṇapañcikā*, composed by the venerable master Jinendrabuddhi, who is like a Bodhisattva.

— — — Now begins the seventh chapter, second quarter. When [the rule] *guṇa* [Pāṇini 1.1.3] was about to apply, this statement is commenced. The two terms *sici* and *parasmaipadeṣu* are both locative absolutives (*parasaptamī*); therein, the "subsequent" status (*paratva*) of *sic* is in relation to the stem (*aṅga*), whereas for the *parasmaipada*s it is in relation to *sic*. [The phrase is] *parasmaipadapare*.
Why is it called *parasmaipada*? It is so designated because it is directed toward another (*para*).

Regarding the term "ending in an *ik*" (*igantasya*): since the rule "guṇa and vṛddhi substitutions apply to an *ik*" (*iko guṇavṛddhī*, P. 1.1.3) is present [by context], the stem (*aṅga*) is qualified by that; and because of this qualification, the principle of "specification by the final letter" (*tadantavidhi*) applies. Thus he says: "A vṛddhi substitution occurs for a stem ending in an *ik*."
Regarding the forms *acaiṣīt* and *anaiṣīt*:

from the roots *ciñ* (meaning "to pile up," DhP 1251) and *ṇīñ* (meaning "to lead," DhP 91), the suffix *luṅ* is applied for the past tense. There is a prohibition of the augment *iṭ* by the rule *ekācaḥ* (Pāṇini 7.2.10). The augment *aṭ* is added. While the previous rule [3.4.99] is still in force, the elision of the final *i* occurs by *itaśca* (3.4.100). The augment *iṭ* is added by *astisico'pṛkte* (7.3.96). While the rule *iṣkoḥ* (8.3.57) is in force, the substitution of *ṣ* occurs by [8.3.59]. Regarding the forms *alāvīt* and *apāvīt*: [the same process applies].

As before, the *luṅ* [suffix] is applied; does the augment *iṭ* apply by the rule *ārdhadhātukasyeṅvalādeḥ* [Pāṇini 7.2.35]? As before, there is the augment *iṭ*, and by the rule *iṭa īṭi* [Pāṇini 8.2.28], there is the elision of *sic*. The example *akārṣīt* is easily understood.

But surely, in this case, the *guṇa* substitution ought to occur because it is internal (*antaraṅga*). Its internality, moreover, follows from its dependence on the *ārdhadhātuka* suffix; whereas the *vṛddhi* is external (*bahiraṅga*) because it depends upon the specific *guṇa* [substitution] conditioned by the *sic* suffix followed by a *parasmaipada* ending. To this, he says: "Even though it is internal," and so forth. If the *guṇa* were to occur due to its internality, then this statement would be purposeless.
Therefore, by the force of the explicit rule, even the external *vṛddhi* subverts the *guṇa*.

If this is so, then just as by the force of the statement (*vacana-sāmarthya*) *vṛddhi* sets aside *guṇa* even though it is *antaranga*, it would likewise set aside the substitution of *uvaṅ*; consequently, forms such as *nyanuvīt* and *nyadhuvīt* would not be established? To this, he says: "In *nyanuvīt*, *nyadhuvīt*, etc. For where there is no prohibition of *vṛddhi*, there that [substitution] proceeds by the force of the statement, overriding other rules.
But here, since the suffix is marked with *ṅit*, *vṛddhi* is prohibited by the rule *ṅicca* (Pāṇini 1.1.5); and once it is prohibited, it is not capable of setting aside the substitution of *uvaṅ*.

Since that [vṛddhi] has been prohibited, the substitution of *uvaṅ* is applied by the rule "aci śnudhātu" [Pāṇini 6.4.77]. But as for the *ṅit*-character here, would it not follow that—just as in the case of the two roots "ṇū stavane" (DhP 1397) and "dhū vidhūnane" (DhP 1398), which are read among the *kuṭādi* group so that, by the rule "gāṅkuṭādibhyaḥ" [Pāṇini 1.2.1], the *guṇa* is barred by the *vṛddhi* due to their specific capacity (*sāmarthya*)—the prohibition too would likewise be barred? This is not so; for the *vṛddhi* is commenced when the *guṇa* is not yet applicable, whereas the prohibition applies both when the *guṇa* is applicable and when it is not.

In that case, it is logical that there should be a sublation of the *guṇa* [vowel] itself by that [rule], and not of the prohibition, by which neither non-attainment nor anything else occurs—namely, in the forms *acyoṣṭa* and *aploṣṭa*.

[The roots] *cyuṅ*, *chuṅ*, and *jyuṅ* do not exist [in the *Dhātupāṭha*]; rather, the *Dhātupāṭha* states: *iyuṅ*, *pruṅ*, and *pluṅ* mean "to go" (955, 956, 957). This word *anta* signifies a part (*avayava*), as in *vastrānta* ("the edge of a garment") or *vasanānta* ("the hem of a cloth").

Furthermore, the word *anta* has the sense of "proximity," as in the expression: "one should follow a dear person as far as the edge of the water" (*udakāntam*), which means "as far as the vicinity of the water.

If, in this context, the word *anta* were taken to mean "a part" (an avayava), then the inclusion of the term *anta* here would be redundant. Is it not the case that the purpose of employing it is so that the rule may apply to those words ending in the letters *r* and *l*?
And this is established by the rule itself [Pāṇini 1.1.72].
Therefore, thinking that only those words denoting proximity are to be understood, he says: "The *repha* and *lakāra* are the two ends that are proximate.
If, then, that which has *la* and *ra* as its proximate ends is indicated by this [rule], would not that which undergoes *vṛddhi* fail to be indicated?

And thus, by the rule *evañca* [Pāṇini 1.1.52], [the substitution] would apply to the final [element]; however, since there is no *ik* vowel subject to *vṛddhi* that is both final and situated near the letter *a*, he says: "Precisely for this reason, [the substitution occurs] in place [of the *a*]. He thinks as follows: because the letter *a* is explicitly mentioned (*śruta*), it is understood that the *vṛddhi* occurs in place of the *a* itself. Examples include *akṣārīt* and so forth.

These are the forms derived from the roots *kṣara* (meaning "to move," Dhātupāṭha 851), *tsara* (meaning "to go by stealth," Dhātupāṭha 554), *jvala* (meaning "to blaze," Dhātupāṭha 804), and *hvala* and *hrala* (both meaning "to move," Dhātupāṭha 805 and 806).

By stating, "This is an exception (*apavāda*) to the optional rule [Pāṇini 6.1.11] *ato halāder laghoḥ*," he demonstrates that this grammatical rule (*yoga*) serves a restrictive purpose (*niyamārtha*).
"nyakhorīt, nyamīlīt," and so forth.
[The roots] *khur* "to cut" (Dhātupāṭha 1342, vādyāṃ) and *mīla*, *śmīla*, *smīla*, *śmīla* "to close the eyes" (Dhātupāṭha 517–520). [Examples:
"mā bhavānaṭīt, mā bhavānaśīt."

The roots *aṭ* and *paṭ* mean "to go" (Dhātupāṭha 295, 296), and *aś* means "to eat" (Dhātupāṭha 1523). The connection with the prohibitive particle *māṅ* is for the purpose of prohibiting the augment *āṭ* according to Pāṇini 6.4.74.
The word "bhavān" is used here to dispel doubt, as there would otherwise be no distinction from other instances.
Regarding "avabhrīt":
[the roots] *abhra*, *vabhra*, *mabhra*, and *cara* have the meaning of "motion" (*gatyarthāḥ*) [Dhātupāṭha 556–559].
Regarding "āllīt": [this is derived from the root *lī*].
The roots *āla* and *alla* mean "to go quickly" (*āśugamana*) [Dhātupāṭha 549, 550].

[The rule does not apply] "in those cases where [the suffixes] are not immediately adjacent," because they are separated by the letters *bh* and *l*. This new formulation is intended for cases where the suffix does not end in *i*.

Now, for what purpose is the inclusion of the term *vadivrajī*? Since the *vṛddhi* [substitution] would be established simply because [the roots] end in a consonant (*halanta*), he says: "For the purpose of subverting the optional rule," and so forth.
He will state an option in [Aṣṭādhyāyī 7.2.7], *ato halādeḥ*; [this inclusion ensures that] there may be a subversion of that [optional rule]. As in: *apākṣīt*.
The root *ḍupacaṣ* is listed as "in the sense of cooking" (Dhātupāṭha 996); by [Pāṇini 8.2.30], there is the substitution of *k* for *c*. Regarding the form *abhaistīt*:

the root *bhidir* is listed as "in the sense of splitting" (Dhātupāṭha 1439); by [Pāṇini 8.4.54], there is the substitution of *t* for *d* due to the rule of *cartva* (the replacement of a dental by a retroflex before a *khari* sound).
"He obstructed" (*arautsīt*).
[The root] *rudh* is used in the sense of "obstructing" (*āvaraṇe*; Dhātupāṭha 1438).
"In this," and so forth.

"Vadivrajyoḥ" is one rule, and "acaḥ" is the second; thus, when there is this division of rules (yogavibhāga), the desired result is indeed accomplished even without the inclusion of the term "halanta.
[The question] "How?
is asked by one who finds this difficult to conceive.
He demonstrates how [the desired forms] are established through the division of the rule (*yogavibhāga*) by means of the phrase "of *vadi* and *vraj*" and so forth.

In that regard, in the first application of the rule, the word "*ataḥ*" (from *at*), which is the substitute, is carried over from the preceding sūtra. By this, only *avādīt* and *avrājīt* are established.

Then, regarding the second rule, *yad aceti*, since the relationship between qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) and qualified (*viśeṣya*) is optional, the vowel (*aj*) is qualified by the member (*aṅga*) under discussion—that is, the vowel which belongs to the member. Consequently, a *vṛddhi* substitution occurs for a vowel situated anywhere within the member when *sic* follows;
thus, forms such as *apākṣīt* are also established.
If this is so, then a *yogavibhāga* (separation of rules) alone should be made; what is the use of including the mention of *hal*? To this he says: "This very [point]," and so forth.
For what purpose is the inclusion of the entire collection of *hal*s, such that this effort is made for its sake? To this he says: "In this case as well," and so forth.
"He desired" (*arāṅkṣīt*).
The root *rañj* means "to color" (Dhātupāṭha 1167).
Regarding the form *asaṅkṣīt*,
the root *sañj* means "to adhere" (Dhātupāṭha 987).

But surely, it is taught that *vṛddhi* occurs for an *ac* (vowel) of the *aṅga* when *sic* follows; yet here, no *ac* belonging to the *aṅga* can possibly occur immediately before *sic*, for which this *vṛddhi* would be prescribed. Furthermore, in the case of an *aṅga* ending in *hr*, there ought to be elision (*lopa*) by [Pāṇini 6.4.48]. Nor can it be argued that *vṛddhi* will supersede the elision of *at* on the strength of this specific rule; for if *vṛddhi* were to apply only to an *aṅga* ending in *hr*, the mention of the *pratyāhāra* (*ac*) would be useless, and one should have simply said "of *at*" (*ataḥ*).

Alternatively—that too is possible; indeed, it is possible for a word ending in *a*, such as *yāvat* and others. However, there is no distinction for that [word] whether the *vṛddhi* occurs or does not occur.
Furthermore, for a word ending in an *ik* vowel, the substitution of *vṛddhi* has already been prescribed by rules such as "there is *vṛddhi* before *sic*" (Pāṇini 7.2.1).

Moreover, for diphthongs (*sandhyakṣara*), there is no [substitution of *vṛddhi*] at all, because of the rule prescribing the substitution of *ā* (Pāṇini 6.1.45). If it is argued that [the substitution of *vṛddhi*] does exist in forms such as *udavoḍhām* and *udavoḍham*, we say no; because the elision of *ḍh* (*ḍhalopa*) is considered non-existent (*asiddha*).

Now, is there not some vowel that is immediately followed by a *sic* suffix ending in a *parasmaipada* [ending]? This statement is indeed made. Therefore, according to the principle "that by which there is no intervention [is considered as if] even when there is intervention, due to the authority of the rule" (*Vyāḍīya-paribhāṣā* 46)—just as the *vṛddhi* substitution occurs in forms such as *apākṣīt*, so too will it occur in forms such as *arāṅkṣīt*; thus, there would be no purpose for the mention of *hal*. To this, he says: "Otherwise, however," and so forth.
For in every case, there is an intervention by at least one phoneme.
In examples such as *arāṅkṣīt*, [the rule applies] by means of a collection of consonants (*hal-samudāya*);

it does not apply in cases such as *apākṣīt*. If the mention of "consonant" (*hal*) were not present, then according to the principle just stated, the rule would apply only where there is an intervention by a single phoneme—as in *apākṣīt*—and would not apply where there is an intervention by more than one phoneme—as in *arāṅkṣīt*. For instance, in *pipaṭhiṣīṣṭa* and similar forms, [the rule] does not apply because of the intervention of two vowels (*ac*).
However, when "consonant" (*hal*) is mentioned, the rule applies even when there is an intervention by a collection of consonants, due to the force of the mention of "consonant."

Regarding the forms *udavoḍhām* and *udavoḍham*, why does the *vṛddhi* substitution not occur for the root *vah* after the elision of *ḍh*—on the grounds that the preceding element is not one ending in a consonant (*ahalanta*)? If someone were to object thus, one should reply: "The *vṛddhi* is indeed applied here; however, its subsequent change to *ū* is what is being prescribed. To demonstrate this, he says: "*udavoḍhām*" and so forth.
By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), the beginning of the verbal roots and other such elements are included.

From the root *vah* preceded by *ud*, the *luṅ* suffix is applied; for the two [suffixes] *tas* and *thas*, the substitutes *ta* and *mā* are applied respectively according to the rule "tasthasthamipām" [Pāṇini 3.4.101]. Then, there is the *vṛddhi* strengthening conditioned by a consonant-final [root]; the substitution of *ḍha* for *ha* occurs by the rule "ho ḍhaḥ" [8.2.31]; the elision of *sic* occurs by the rule "sici vṛddhiḥ parasmaipadeṣu" [7.2.1]; the substitution of *ṣ* for *t* occurs by the rule "jhaṣastathordho'dhaḥ" [8.2.40]; and the substitution of *ṣṭu* for *ṣṭa* occurs by the rule "ādeśapratyayayoḥ" [8.3.59]. Finally, the substitution of *ū* for *o* occurs by the rule "otaḥ śyani" [6.4.68]. Regarding this, one might ask: why does *vṛddhi* not occur again after the substitution of *ū* for *o*? To this, he says: "When that has been performed, again... and so forth.

For in this case, there is only one rule for *vṛddhi*, and since the *vṛddhi* has already been effected by that [rule] beforehand, the rule for *vṛddhi*—having its purpose already fulfilled—does not operate again; thus, there is no further *vṛddhi*.
If so, how is it that in the word *sauḍhāmitri*, once *aut* has been applied, *vṛddhi* still occurs? To this he says: "But where," and so forth.

Where *vṛddhi* has already been effected previously, there the rule for *vṛddhi* does not operate again because its purpose has been achieved, and thus no further *vṛddhi* occurs; however, in the case of *soḍhāmitri*, *vṛddhi* had not yet been effected.

Therefore, because the purpose has not yet been fulfilled, the rule for *vṛddhi* (vowel strengthening) operates, and thus *vṛddhi* indeed occurs. And that *vṛddhi* occurs for the vowel *o*, not for the vowel *a*; for at the time of prescribing *vṛddhi*, it is the vowel *o* alone that is present as the recipient of *vṛddhi*. From the root *sah* with the suffix *niṣṭhā* (the past passive participle suffix *-ta*), after the substitution of *ḍha* and other changes have been applied, the form *soḍha* arises. From *soḍha-amitraḥ* ("one by whom the enemy was endured"), [the derivative] *soḍhāmitraḥ* is formed. Then, from "his descendant" (*tasyāpatyam*), the suffix *iñ* is added according to Pāṇini 4.1.95 (*ata iñ*). Subsequently, *vṛddhi* is applied according to Pāṇini 7.2.117 (*taddhiteṣvacāmādeḥ*).

Since the status of being "that which ends in" (*tadanta*) is already established by [Pāṇini 1.1.72], the inclusion of the word *anta* ("end") is for the sake of removing ambiguity. If it were stated simply as *halo'caḥ* ("of a consonant, [there is] a vowel"), an ambiguity would arise: does the vowel-vṛddhi apply to a stem (*aṅga*) ending in a vowel, or to a vowel that follows a consonant? The vṛddhi that was applicable as ending in a consonant is prohibited by this [sūtra], on the principle that "a rule or a prohibition applies only to what is immediately preceding" (*anantarasya vidhirvā bhavati pratiṣedho vā*). Examples: *adevīt*, *asevīt*.
The root *div* meaning "to play" and so forth (Dhātupāṭha 1107), and *ṣivu* meaning "to weave" (Dhātupāṭha 1108;
according to Dā|Pā|). When the *vṛddhi* substitution is prohibited, the *guṇa* substitution applies by Pāṇini 7.3.86 (*pugantalaghūpadhasya*). Thus we have the forms *akoṣīt* and *amoṣīt*.
The roots *kuṣ* in the sense of "extracting" (Dhātupāṭha 1518) and *muṣ* in the sense of "stealing" (Dhātupāṭha 1530).

Here, the objection is raised: "But surely, in this case, because this [rule] is *antaraṅga*... [In the Kāśikā: "But surely, even here, because this is *antaraṅga*..."]. The resolution is: "This is not so."
Both of these points have already been explained. Regarding "he took" (*agṛhīt*):
the root *grah* means "to take" (Dhātupāṭha 1533).
Regarding "he was afraid" (*asyamīt*).
From the root *sthāmu* (meaning "to sound" or "to roar," Dhātupāṭha 826), [the form] *avamīt* is derived.
From the root *ṭu vama* (meaning "to vomit" or "to eject," Dhātupāṭha 849),
[the form] *adyatīt* is derived.

In the phrase "vyayavittasamutsarge" (Dhātupāṭha 1932), [the form] "akṣaṇīt" occurs. [The root] "kṣaṇu" is used in the sense of "injury" (Dhātupāṭha 1465); [the form] "āsīt" is from the root "ās" in the sense of "breathing" (Dhātupāṭha 1069).
Regarding "ajāgarīt": *jāgṛ* means "to wake" or "the cessation of sleep" (Dhātupāṭha 1072).

Regarding "aunayīt" and "ailayīt": *ūna* means "diminution" (Dhātupāṭha 1888) [or "avoidance" according to the Dhātupāṭha], and *īla* means "impelling" (Dhātupāṭha 1660); [for *ila*, it belongs to the *curādi* class with the suffix *ṇic*].

By the rule *na ayati* [Pāṇini 3.1.51] and others, the *caṅ* suffix is prohibited, and thus only the *sic* suffix occurs. Then, by *āṭ* [Pāṇini 6.4.72], the augment *āṭ* is added, and by *āṭaśca* [Pāṇini 6.1.87], there is *vṛddhi*.
Thus we have *āyīt*. The root is *ṭu ośvi* (meaning "to move" and "to increase") from the Dhātupāṭha (1010).
"Did he sing well (*aragīt*) or not sing well (*alagīt*)? [The roots *rañj* and *lag* are used in the sense of attachment; *rañj* is also listed in the *Dhātupāṭha* as meaning "doubt.
[He said: "He sang poorly (*asthāgīt*)."
Regarding "sthage saṃvaraṇe" (Dhātupāṭha 790) [and "ṣṭage" in the Dhātupāṭha], it says "akakhīt.
Regarding "kakhe hasane" (Dhātupāṭha 784), it is said: "And because that [root] does not take the augment *iṭ*, it is not prohibited [from taking *aṭ*]."
The prohibition applies to the *vṛddhi* substitution that follows immediately after the final consonant, not to the preceding one.

Now, for what purpose is the mention of *ṇi* [in the rule], since by virtue of being *antaraṅga* (internal), *guṇa* ought to occur here first; once *guṇa* has been applied, the *ay* replacement would follow, and then the prohibition of *t* and *th* would occur simply because of the word ending in *y*? To this he says: "And not," etc.
This status of being *antaraṅga* was stated while assuming the presence of *sic*.
Now, in order to show that internal status (*antaraṅgatva*) itself does not exist in the case of *sic*, he says "yadi" and so forth.

What is the reason that the mention of *ṇi* would be purposeless? To this he says: "of the *guṇa* and *āyādeśa*. If, then, there is no internal status in *sic*, does this not contradict what was stated: "this *vṛddhi* sets aside even the *guṇa* by virtue of its explicit statement"? There is no contradiction, because such a statement is made through superimposition (*adhyāropa*).
"Then," and so forth. Here, the intention is that which is about to be stated.

Regarding the question, "What is the purpose of including the root *jāgṛ*?", when asked why the inclusion of *jāgṛ* need not be made, he says—"In the case of *jāgṛ*, except before *av* and *ciṇ*"—in order to reveal the underlying intention with which he asked the question.

Just as in forms such as *jāgarayati*, the rule [Pāṇini 7.2.115] which would otherwise require *vṛddhi* is superseded by the *guṇa* substitution for the root *jāgṛ*, so too will it supersede the *vṛddhi* that would apply before the suffix *sic*; for the rule prescribing *guṇa* is an exception (*apavāda*) to the rule for *vṛddhi*. For example, in *agūṇe kata* and so forth: since the *guṇa* has not yet been applied, the *vṛddhi* that would otherwise apply before *sic* is superseded by the *guṇa*, because the rule for *guṇa* has not yet fulfilled its purpose.

And that [substitution] will not be sublated by this rule; what then? A prohibition is prescribed for that *vṛddhi* which would subsequently apply after the *guṇa* has been effected and the substitution of *r* for *ṛ* has occurred (by P. 7.2.2). That [substitution] cannot be sublated by the *guṇa*, for the rule "na hi" (P. 7.3.85) is not able to operate again, since its purpose has already been fulfilled. Nor is there any other characteristic of *guṇa* that could sublate the subsequent *vṛddhi*.
In that regard, if the mention of "jāgṛ" were not made, then by the rule *vṛddhir ādaic* [Pāṇini 1.1.1], vṛddhi would occur.
The objector says, "Now," and so forth:
if vṛddhi were to occur again even after guṇa has been applied, then the prescription of guṇa in the domain of vṛddhi would be purposeless.

Therefore? Because of the force of the prescription of the *guṇa* substitution, even when the *guṇa* has been applied and the replacement by *ra* (*raparatva*) has occurred, the subsequent rule [Pāṇini 7.2.2] which would cause *vṛddhi* to apply is prohibited, as in the case of *jāgarayati*. When the *guṇa* has been applied and the replacement by *ra* has occurred, the *vṛddhi* that would otherwise apply at a later stage—namely, that which follows from [Pāṇini 7.2.116]—does not take place either; for it has been superseded by the *guṇa*.
"And so," etc.

By the force of the prescription of *guṇa*, even the *vṛddhi* that would occur at a later time is sublated; for otherwise, once the *guṇa* has been applied and the substitution of *r* (*raparatva*) has taken place, the *vṛddhi* that would occur at a later time by the rule "ata upadhāyāḥ" would also not take place, because it too would have been sublated by the *guṇa*.
The phrase "And thus," etc., confirms that very point: that by the force of the prescription of *guṇa*, even the *vṛddhi* occurring at a later time is sublated by the *guṇa*.

And thus, the prohibition regarding *ciṇ* and *ṇal* becomes meaningful only if the *vṛddhi* that would occur at a later time is also sublated; otherwise, once *guṇa* has been applied and *raparatva* (the substitution of *r* for *ṇ*) has occurred, *vṛddhi* would have to take effect by rule 6.1.88 (*aci śnu-dhātu-...*).
The prohibition made regarding *ciṇ* and *ṇal* would then be rendered useless. Therefore, it is established that even the *vṛddhi* occurring at a later time is sublated by *guṇa*.
And thus, it would indeed have been possible not to include the mention of *jāgṛ*.
When the mention of *jāgṛ* has been rejected in this manner, the other says: "That [mention] is made," and so forth.

For the sake of clarity for one who is unable to understand in such a way, the mention of *jāgṛ* is made. This statement is intended as an option (*vikalpa*) when the occurrence of *vṛddhi* is otherwise mandatory.
Since the prohibition [of *ṇic*] by the rule *neṭi* [Pāṇini 7.2.4] would otherwise apply, this [sūtra] is commenced for the purpose of providing an option:
*akaṇīt*, *akāṇīt*.
The root *aṇa*, *raṇa*, *vaṇa*, *kaṇa*, *bhaṇa*, *kvaṇa* is listed in the *Bhvādi* class [of roots, Dhātupāṭha 444–446, 449, 447, 450].
Regarding "araṇīt" and "arāṇīt," the root *raṇ* is also used in that very context. Regarding "nyakuṭīt," the root *kuṭ* is used in the sense of "crookedness" (*kauṭilye*; Dhātupāṭha 1366).
Regarding the form *nyapuṭīt*:

since the root *puṭ* is listed as "saṃśleṣaṇe" (Dhātupāṭha 1367), one might object that because it belongs to the *kuṭādi* group, it possesses the *ṅit* designation; consequently, by [Pāṇini 1.1.5], the prohibition [of guṇa] will apply, so this [rule] would not be for the purpose of restriction. Therefore, is it necessary to state "from *ataḥ*"? To this he says: "If this 'from *ataḥ*' were not present," and so forth.

If the word "ataḥ" (of this) were not stated, then [the rule] "avaśyam" [P. 7.2.3] would necessarily have to be supplied as a governing term (*anuvartate*). Otherwise, because no specific locus (*sthāna*) would be specified, the optional substitution of *vṛddhi* would apply only to that which is light (*laghu*), such as in *adevīt* and the like; however, in cases such as *akāṇīt*, the *vṛddhi* would not apply to the letter *a*. But when the reference to the vowel *a* (*aj-grahaṇa*) is continued [from the previous rule], this *vṛddhi* applies specifically to what is characterized by *a* (*aj-lakṣaṇā*), and not to what is characterized by *i* (*ig-lakṣaṇā*), because its locus is explicitly specified.

For where the substitute (*sthānin*) is not specifically mentioned, that is the domain of the *vṛddhi* characterized by *ik*; however, it is not the case that wherever the substitute is mentioned, that too [is such a domain]. Consequently, the prohibition [stated in] *Pāṇini 1.1.5* would not apply there, because of the governing rule (*adhikāra*) of *ikaḥ*. Therefore, in order to prevent optional *vṛddhi* in forms such as *nyakuṭīt* and *nyapuṭīt*, it must be stated that [the rule applies] "after *at*" (*ataḥ*). As in the examples *atakṣīt* and *arakṣīt*.

The roots *takṣū* and *tvakṣū* mean "to make thin" (Dhātupāṭha 655, 656); *rakṣa* means "to protect" (Dhātupāṭha 658). Here, it is stated that there is a *vṛddhi* [strengthening] of the vowel *a* immediately following the suffix *sic*. Is there not any instance where *sic* is not immediate? Indeed, such a case is possible. In that regard, according to the principle "that by which there is no intervention [is considered immediate], even when there is intervention, because of the authority of the statement" (Vyākaraṇa-paribhāṣā 46), the *vṛddhi* must occur even when there is an intervention.

"Just as the substitution occurs for the short *a* in *akāṇīt*, should it not likewise necessarily occur by way of *vṛddhi* for the short *a* in *acakāsīt*? With this intention, he asks: "Now, why does it not occur here in *acakāsīt*?
[The root] *cakāsṛ* [is used] in the sense of "shining" (*dīptau*; Dhātupāṭha 1074).
The response begins with "By which," and so forth.

"‘halā vyavadhānam āśritam’ (consonantal intervention is resorted to). The intention is that this follows from the continued application (*anuvṛtti*) of the rule "of that which ends in a consonant" (*halanta-*). To the question "Why [is there the mention] of *laghoḥ* (of a light syllable)?", he—who intends to refute the inclusion of the term *laghu*—says "Now, furthermore," and so on.

If it were assumed in this way that consonantal intervention is resorted to by the authority of the statement itself and not vocalic intervention, then it should have been stated as "ato laghoḥ" (after *a*, when followed by a light syllable); otherwise, it would apply even in cases such as *hratakṣīt*, for here there is consonantal intervention, not vocalic.

Now, if it is further postulated: "That by which there is no intervention [is considered non-intervening] even when there is intervention, on account of the authority of the statement" (*Vyā.pa.* 46), then one would rely on intervention by only a single phoneme (*varṇa*) and not by several; thus, the purpose of the word *laghoḥ* [in Pāṇini 7.3.86] would be lost. If this were so, would [the rule] not apply in cases such as *atakṣīt*, where there is intervention by more than one phoneme? To this, he says: "*tat kriyate*" and so forth. He will state [later] the augment *iṭ* for the *ārdhadhātuka* affixes beginning with a consonant (*valādi*), according to [Pāṇini 7.2.35]: *ārdhadhātukasyeḍvalādeḥ*.
Where there is no prohibition based on the root's inherent nature (*prakṛti-lakṣaṇa*), it is in those cases that this [rule] effects a prohibition.
Regarding the purpose of the preceding section on prohibitions, he will explain it in the rule concerning the restriction for roots beginning with *krī* (Pāṇini 7.2.13).

However, in the case of forms such as *īśitā*, because the augment *iṭ* is present due to another suffix, this rule declares the absence of that very prohibition which would have been triggered by the root's nature according to Pāṇini 7.2.10 (*ekāca upadeśe 'nudāttāt*).

Regarding "īāraḥ": from the root *īś* meaning "to rule" (Dhātupāṭha 1020), the suffix *varac* is applied according to Pāṇini 3.2.175 (*stheśabhāsa...* etc.). Regarding "dīpraḥ": [it is derived from the root *dīp*].
The root *dīp* is listed as *dīpī dīptau* (Dhātupāṭha 1150); by the rule *namikamyi* etc. (Pāṇini 3.2.167), the suffix *ra* is applied. Regarding the word *bhasma*:
the root *bhas* is listed as *bhasa bharsanadīptyoḥ* (Dhātupāṭha 1100).

In the case of *ityādau* [and so forth], the suffix *manin* is applied according to [Pāṇini 3.2.75]. Regarding the word *yācñā*: it is derived from the root *ṭu yācṛ* in the sense of "begging" (Dhātupāṭha 863).

The suffix *naṅ* is applied by the rule *yajayāca* [Pāṇini 7.3.66]. Regarding what was stated—that there is a purpose for the mention of *vara*, *man*, and so forth—it should be understood that this is an exhaustive enumeration (*parigaṇana*). Against one who might object: "If an exhaustive enumeration is made as 'in *vara*, *man*, and so forth,' then the prohibition would not apply in cases such as *ṣaṇḍaḥ* (from the root *ṣaṇu* 'to give,' with the suffix *ḍa* by *ñamantāḍḍaḥ* [Pāṇini 5.1.104]) and *śaṅkhaḥ* (from the root *śama*, with the suffix *kha* by *śamaḥ khaḥ* [Pāṇini 5.1.113])," the author says—intending to show that this is not an exhaustive enumeration—"the mention of 'in *vara*, *man*, and so forth' is merely an illustration."

Regarding the passage beginning with "atha tatra" and so forth: the meaning is that by applying the *ḍa*-suffix according to the *auṇādika* [list of primary suffixes], the objection concerning the inclusion [of the word] within the enumerated categories is resolved. This is stated for the purpose of demonstrating an example of its derivation.

Here too, it is connected with the phrase "this is not an exhaustive enumeration. An example of the possibility of a prohibition is being illustrated; this is stated for the purpose of demonstrating those cases where a prohibition of *kṛt* suffixes is possible.

The phrase "in *vama* and so forth" was stated for the purpose of illustrating those cases where the prohibition of *iṭ* is possible after a *kṛt* suffix; it is not, however, an exhaustive enumeration (*parigaṇana*).
[Examples are] *rurudiva*, *rurudima*.
Here, because of the mention of *kṛt*, the prohibition does not apply to the *iṭ* of the *ārdhadhātuka* suffix. [Regarding the rule] "after an unaccented [root vowel]... (*anudāttāt*).
This is a *bahuvrīhi* compound: "anudātta" means "that which has no udātta.
This word "anudātta" is etymologically descriptive (*anvartha*). For if the technical term "anudātta" were taken in its strict grammatical sense, only monosyllabic roots would be included.
Furthermore, the declaration that other roots are *anudātta* (unaccented) would be purposeless.
And here, the mention of "single-vowel" (*ekāj*) is a qualifier of "in the original instruction" (*upadeśe*). Thus: "in the original instruction."
The meaning is "in the list of roots" (*prakṛtipāṭha*).

Regarding the rule "and [a root] that is unaccented" (*anudāttaśca*), the term "in the original instruction" (*upadeśe*) is required; thus, he shows that the mention of "original instruction" qualifies both [the preceding and the following].
Its purpose will be revealed in the counter-examples with the words,
"those who recite them thus in the list.
By this, he shows that they are to be understood solely from their inclusion in the list (gaṇapāṭha).
With the words "ta eva" (those very ones) and so forth, he states the second reason for thorough knowledge.
What, then, are those *aniṭ*-karikās? He says: "aniṭsvarāntaḥ" and so forth. Let it be seen—that is, let it be understood—that whatever root ends in a vowel (*ajanta*), all such roots are *aniṭ*.

*Aniṭ* is a *bahuvrīhi* compound, meaning "that to which the augment *iṭ* does not belong. He states an exception (*apavāda*) to the general rule (*utsarga*) that "those ending in vowels are *aniṭ*" with the words beginning with "But these," and so on. They declare that these roots—beginning with those ending in *a*, etc., which are about to be mentioned—are *seṭ* (possessing the augment *iṭ*).

Those which exist together with *iṭ* are called *seṭ*. Who says this? Those who know that [distinction], meaning those who know what is *seṭ* and what is *aniṭ*. "Ending in *a*" (*adantam*) is a bahuvrīhi compound; it means that whose final letter (*anta*) is the short vowel *a* (*akāra*) followed by *t* (as a marker).
The inclusion of the long vowel marker (taparakaraṇa) is for the purpose of excluding the long [vowels].
"Ending in ṝ" (ṝdanta):
this also is a bahuvrīhi compound.
The addition of the long *ṝ* (tapara) is for the sake of avoiding ambiguity.
If it were simply stated as "rantam," there would be doubt: is this a reference to the letter *r*, or to the vowel *ṛ*? [Therefore, the rule says:
"And of the *ṛ*-sounds" (*ṝtām ca*).
The genitive case in *ṝtām* is used in the sense of selection (*nirdhāraṇa*).
Among those [roots] ending in the vowel *ṛ*, they declare that *vṛṅ* and *vṛñ* take the augment *iṭ*.
The inclusion of the long vowel *ṝ* (the *tapara* designation) is for the purpose of excluding other vowels.
For it is understood from the previous mention of the ending in *ṛ* that a short vowel is intended here; [as in the rule] "in the case of *i*, *āṬ*, *īṄ*,
and vowels," the locative case is used in the sense of selection (*nirghāraṇa*).
Among those ending in *ivarṇa*, they declare that *iāṭ* and *iṅ* are *seṭ* [roots]:
*ṭu o iā* "in the sense of motion and growth" (Dhātupāṭha 1010) and *ḍīṅ* "in the sense of moving through the air" (Dhātupāṭha 968).
Then there are also *śīṅ* and *śriñ*.
The word *atha* here signifies immediate succession. Following these two previously mentioned [roots], they also declare *śīṅ* and *śriñ* to be *seṭ* (possessing the augment *iṭ*).
[These are] *ghīṅ* "in sleep" (Dhātupāṭha 1032) and *śriñ* "in service" (Dhātupāṭha 897).
Regarding the term "gaṇastham":
this is a description of its own nature (*svarūpakhyāna*), not a qualification intended for the purpose of excluding the *gaṇa* [suffixes], because such exclusion is impossible.
Regarding the term "ūntam": [this refers to those ending in *-ūn*].
Roots such as *lūñ* in the sense of "cutting" (*Dhātupāṭha* 1483) and *pūñ* in the sense of "purifying" (*Dhātupāṭha* 1482), and so forth.
Regarding the term *uttānām*,
this is a genitive of selection (*nirdhāraṇa-ṣaṣṭhī*).

*ru* in the sense of sound (*dhātupāṭhaḥ* 1034); *snu* in the sense of causing to flow (*dhātupāṭhaḥ* 1038). "And likewise *kṣuva* and *ūrṇoti*" and so forth: *ṭu kṣu* in the sense of sound (*dhātupāṭhaḥ* 1036); *ūrṇuñ* in the sense of covering (*dhātupāṭhaḥ* 1039); *yu* in the sense of mixing (*dhātupāṭhaḥ* 1033) [in the sense of both mixing and not mixing—*dhātupāṭhaḥ*]; *ṇu* in the sense of praise (*dhātupāṭhaḥ* 1035); *kṣṇu* in the sense of sharpening (*dhātupāṭhaḥ* 1037).
Regarding the form *āvadhiṣṭa*:

it is the *luṅ* (aorist) of the root *han* preceded by the prefix *āṅ*. The middle voice (*ātmanepada*) is applied by the rule *āṅoyamahanaḥ* [Pāṇini 1.3.28]; the substitution of *vadh* for *han* occurs by the rule *hanastaḥ* [Pāṇini 6.4.36]. Furthermore, it is recited with a final short *a* (*adanta*) so that there may not be *vṛddhi* (vowel strengthening) in the case of *avadhīt*.

The *iṭ* augment is elided by [Pāṇini 6.4.48], which prescribes the elision of the vowel *a*. Now, for what purpose is the root *ūrṇoti* taught as having an udātta accent? If it is argued that it is so that the prohibition of *iṭ* may not apply, this is not correct; for the prohibition of *iṭ* is stated to apply to monosyllabic roots (*ekāca*), and this root does not possess monosyllabism. Therefore, he says: "The state of being like *ṇu* (*ṇuvadbhāva*) must be stated for *ūrṇu*. This means "monosyllabism" [is to be understood]. Furthermore, there is an absence of the *kutva* substitution even at the end of a word, because *kutva* is not invariably obligatory.
The fact that [the word] *anitya* is not fixed, however, is to be understood from the indications [of the sūtras] *bahvac-pūrvapadāt* (Pāṇini 4.1.64) and *alpāctaram* (Pāṇini 2.2.34).
The word *iti* has the sense of "in this manner.
The word *nipuṇam* means "skillfully."
"Correctly" means "without error";
this is an adverbial modifier.
[The word] "combined."
The meaning is that they are established separately from the collection of verbal roots (dhātu-rāśi) which are mixed with both acute (udātta) and grave (anudātta) accents.
Regarding the word "tataḥ" (then):
it refers to the time subsequent to the collective enumeration of the verbal roots ending in vowels.
"Understand even those ending in a consonant (*halantān*)," meaning "comprehend.
"The root *śaki*" and so forth;
[the entry] "*śaklṛ* in the sense of capability" (Dhātupāṭha 1261).
Regarding the passage beginning with "ghasiśca" and so forth:

[An objection is raised]—"But surely, when there is a formal mention (*svarūpagrahaṇa*) of *had* and so on as the initial element, then by the principle of *sthānivadbhāva*, the non-causative nature (*aniṭtva*) of the substitute *ghas*—which is prescribed for its place by the rule *luṅsanorthaslṛ* [Pāṇini 2.4.37]—is already established. So for what purpose is *ghas* mentioned separately? To this he replies: "*Ghas* is a separate root.
For this is indeed a different verbal root altogether, read in the list of roots (*dhātupāṭha*) under the *ad*-class as *ghaslu adane* (No. 715); this is its mention here, not that of the substitute.
Regarding "prasāraṇī": *prasāraṇa* means *samprasāraṇa*; that which possesses this is called *prasāraṇī*.
Regarding "vasitā": [it refers to one who has attained mastery].

The root *vas* in the sense of "covering" (*ācchādane*) is [listed as] 1023 in the Dhātupāṭha; however, for the root *vas* in the sense of "dwelling" (*nivāse*), vocalization (*samprasāraṇa*) is prescribed by the rule *vācyadi-* [Pāṇini 6.1.15].
By this, he shows that the root *vas* has the sense of "dwelling" (*nivāsa*) and is *prasāraṇī*, but not in the sense of "covering" (*ācchādana*).
[He cites] "rabhiśca" and so forth:
*rabha* in the sense of "impetuosity" (Dhātupāṭha 974), *yabha* in the sense of "sexual intercourse" (Dhātupāṭha 980), and *ḍu labhaṣ* in the sense of "attainment" (Dhātupāṭha 975).

Regarding the passage beginning with "yamiñaṃ manteṣu": the term "ñam" is a collective reference (*pratyāhāra*) starting from the letter *ñ* and ending with the letter *m* in the word *ama*. [The relevant roots are: *yama* (to cease) [DhP 984], *ramu* (to sport) [DhP 853], *mana* (to know) [DhP 1176], *ṇama* (to bow and to sound) [DhP 981], *hana* (to injure and to go) [DhP 1012], and *gam-lṛ*, *sṛp-lṛ* (to go) [DhP 982, 983].
Regarding the phrase "it is recited in the *śyan* [section]": by virtue of association (*sāhacarya*), the root beginning with *div-* (the *divādi* class) is indicated;
the meaning is that it is recited in the *divādi* section.
Regarding the phrase "of those expressing a prohibition":

those whose nature (*śīla*) is to express a prohibition are so described. For indeed, it is the verbal roots themselves, accompanied by the mark of the low-pitched vowel (*anudātta*), that convey the prohibition; thus they are called "expressing a prohibition.

Alternatively, they are called "expressing a prohibition" because they cause [the learner] to speak—that is, to understand—the prohibition of *iṭ* as applying to themselves, according to the Teacher's instruction.

And in this context, the connection should be made as follows: among those roots ending in *ñ* which express a prohibition, *yam* is intended to be *aniṭ* (lacking the *iṭ* augment) in the middle [of that group].
[This applies to] "and *rami*" and so forth.
Alternatively, in the phrase "of those expressing a prohibition," the word "in the opinion of" (*matena*) should be supplied.
