In this context, the connection should be made as follows: according to the opinion of those teachers who advocate the prohibition of *iṭ*, the root *yam* alone is desired to be without *iṭ* when followed by suffixes ending in *ṇ*.
Regarding the word "of *man*" (*manuteḥ*):
this refers to the root *man* in the sense of "understanding" (*avabodhane*), which belongs to the *tanādi* class (Dhātupāṭha 1471).
"Dihiḥ," and so forth. [The roots are:

*diha* "to increase" (DhP 1015), *duha* "to fill" (DhP 1014), *miha* "to sprinkle" (DhP 992), *ruha* "to be born, to appear" (DhP 859), *vaha* "to carry" (DhP 1004), *ṇaha* "to bind" (DhP 1166), *daha* "to reduce to ashes" (DhP 991), and *liha* "to taste" (DhP 1016).
[The phrase] "those whose doubts have been dispelled" (*muktasaṃśayāḥ*).
"Those in whom or by whom doubt has been abandoned (mukta = tyakta) are so described. Regarding the phrase "declared after having analyzed":
the meaning is that they have been declared by establishing them through the distinction between those roots that take the suffix *iṭ* and those that do not (*aniṅ*).
In the forms *degdhā* and *dogdhā*, the following rules must be applied:

the substitution of *dh* for the initial *d* of a root according to Pāṇini 8.2.32; the substitution of *dh* according to 8.2.40; and the substitution of the voiced unaspirated stop (*jaś*) according to 8.4.53. Similarly, in *meḍhā* and *āroḍhā*.

By [Pāṇini 8.2.31] *ho ḍhaḥ*, there is the substitution of *ḍha*; as before, there is the substitution of *ḍha* [by 8.2.39]; by [8.4.40] *ṣṭunā ṣṭuḥ*, there is the substitution of *ṣṭu*; and by [8.3.13], there is the elision of *ḍ*. Thus, "voḍhā" [is formed]. As before, there is the substitution of *ḍha* and so on; then, by [6.3.112], there is the substitution of *ū*.
Regarding *naddhā*: by the rule *naho dhaḥ* [Pāṇini 8.2.34], there is the substitution of *dha* for *nah*; as before, there is the substitution of *jaś* and *car* sounds. Regarding *tannāntare*.

In the *Āpiśala-vyākaraṇa*, it is stated: "There is an option for *sah* before suffixes beginning with *t*. By the rule *tīṣasaha* [Pāṇini 7.2.48] and others, an option for *sah* before suffixes beginning with *t* has been prescribed.
"Even *muh* is recited [in the rule] beginning with *rādhādi*"—
by this, he shows that there is an option (*vikalpa*) for *muh* according to [Pāṇini 7.2.45]. "Therefore, those two are accompanied by doubt and accompanied by option."
By this he shows that those two are "doubtful" by virtue of being of the nature of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), and not by virtue of being of the nature of uncertainty (*saṃdeha*).
"The other two" refers to *rihi* and *luhi*.
"Are accepted by some"—
that is, by Āpiśali and others.
"In their very own form, they are accompanied by doubt."
"By its own nature" means by its intrinsic essence (*svabhāva*). "With doubt" means accompanied by uncertainty; for the term *saṃśaya* here refers to uncertainty (*sandeha*).

But there is doubt because [the word] is not listed among the verbal roots (dhātu), and yet it is accepted by some. Of these two, one is accepted as occurring in the sense of "injuring" (hiṃsā), while the other occurs in the sense of "being firm" (gādhrya).
Regarding "diśiṃ dṛśim" and so forth:

*diś* (in the sense of "bestowing," Dhātupāṭha 1283), *dṛśir* (in the sense of "seeing," Dhātupāṭha 988), and *daṃś* (in the sense of "biting," Dhātupāṭha 981); furthermore, the word *atha* is for the purpose of filling out the meter.

*mṛś* [in the sense of] touching (*āmadrdane*; Dhātupāṭha 1425); *spṛś* [in the sense of] contact (*saṃsparśe*; Dhātupāṭha 1422); *ruś* and *riś* [in the sense of] injury (*hiṃsāyām*; Dhātupāṭha 1419, 1420); *krūś* [in the sense of] calling out and weeping (*āhvāne ca rodane*; Dhātupāṭha 856); *viś* [in the sense of] entering (*praveśane*; Dhātupāṭha 1424); *liś* [in the sense of] becoming small (*alpībhāve*; Dhātupāṭha 1179). Regarding the term *purāṇagāḥ*:
*purāṇam* means grammar (*vyākaraṇam*), so called because it is ancient; those who sing—that is, study—that [grammar] are the *purāṇagāḥ*.

"In the recensions" (*pāṭheṣu*) means in the recensions of the *aniṭ*-verses or in the lists of verbal roots (*dhātupāṭha*). "Not others" (*netarān*) refers to [roots] such as *spaśa* (in the sense of "afflicting" and "touching," DhP 887).

Regarding the word *deṣṭā*: the substitution of *ṣ* occurs by the rule [Pāṇini 8.2.36] concerning the *vraśc-* group. Since the prohibition of the *iṭ* augment for roots beginning with *mṛś-* is established by the rule [Pāṇini 6.1.58] "of the anudātta," how does he show something additional? He says: "*rudhiḥ sarādhiḥ*" and so forth.
It is "sarādhi" because it exists together with *rādhi*.
[The roots] are *rudhir* in the sense of "obstructing" (Dhātupāṭha 1438) and *rādha* and *sādha* in the sense of "accomplishment" (Dhātupāṭha 1162, 1163).
[According to the rule] "from *rādha* when intransitive, in the sense of increase... [the suffix *iṇ* is applied].
The inclusion of both [roots] is intended, as there is no distinction [between them]:

*yudha* in the sense of "striking" (Dhātupāṭha 1190), *śudha* in the sense of "purification" (Dhātupāṭha 1191), *budha* in the sense of "understanding" (Dhātupāṭha 1172), *vyadha* in the sense of "piercing" (Dhātupāṭha 1181), and *sidhu* (or *ṣidhu*) in the sense of "accomplishment" (Dhātupāṭha 1192).
[The phrase] "not the others" [is used].
"Indhi and so forth.
The phrase "of the two with and without the *śap* suffix" means "of the two roots having the *śap* suffix.
These are the two roots *budh* in the sense of "awakening" (Dhātupāṭha 875) [and *budhir*—Dhātupāṭha] and *ṣidhu* in the sense of "motion" (Dhātupāṭha 47) [and *vidha*—Dhātupāṭha].

Regarding the phrase "even in the case of the *niṣṭhā* suffix," etc.: now, why is the prohibition of the root *budh* belonging to the *bhūvādika* class suspected here? [Is it not] because it is already prohibited by virtue of being marked with an *u* (as in *sidh*), since the rule "or when marked with *u*" (*uditto vā*) prescribes an option for the *ktvā* suffix? [One might argue that] since there must be a prohibition in the case of the *niṣṭhā* suffix according to [the rule] "before *niṣṭhā*" (*niṣṭhāyām*), the suspicion of a prohibition is indeed appropriate.

However, regarding the root *budh*, there is no cause for any suspicion of a prohibition in the case of the past participle (*niṣṭhā*). This is because [the following objection] exists: here, since the two roots *budh* belonging to the *bhūvādi* and *divādi* classes are identical in their meaning, a learner who has conceived a delusion due to this identity of meaning might think: "This is one and the same root; its recitation in both classes is for the sake of the two different *vikaraṇas*. Since it is stated that *iṭ* is added to it in the *ārdhadhātuka* context, and by this rule (*Aṣṭādhyāyī* 1.2.19) there is also a prohibition of *iṭ*, then because the injunction and the prohibition share the same object, there would be an option (*vibhāṣā*) regarding the addition of *iṭ* due to the possibility of either application. Consequently, by the rule *budha-yudha-ruṣa-rima-niṣṭhāyām* (1.2.15), there would be no prohibition of *iṭ* in the past participle. [The answer follows: ...therefore, in the case of the past participle, there is no prohibition.

Some think that [the augment] must necessarily occur. Why? Anticipating that view, this was stated: "even in the case of the final form," and so forth. He thinks as follows: the root *budh* belonging to the *bhū* class (Bhvādi) is one for which the rule for *iṭ* applies, while the root *budh* belonging to the *div* class (Divādi) is another for which the prohibition of *iṭ* applies; therefore, because the scope (*viṣaya*) of the injunction and the prohibition is distinct, the optionality (*vibhāṣā*) regarding the presence of *iṭ* is not tenable.

Now, how is it stated that there is no prohibition of the *niṣṭhā* [suffixes *kta* and *ktavatu*] for the root *sidh*? Is it because of its being marked with *u* (*udid*) by the rule *yāsisīṣṭhāḥ* [Pāṇini 7.2.56]? Or is it because of the optionality of *iṭ* [augment] in the *niṣṭhā* by the rule *vibhāṣeṭ* [Pāṇini 7.2.15], whereby a prohibition would necessarily apply to the *niṣṭhā*? The thought is this: the status of *sidh* as being marked with *u* (*udit*) is certainly not based on the Vedic tradition (*anārṣa*). If it were *udit*, its inclusion in the *Bhvādi* class would be purposeless;

for whatever form is to be derived from it is already established by the root *ṣidhū* [listed as 48 in the Dhātupāṭha, defined as "in the sense of a treatise" (*śāstre*) and "in the sense of auspiciousness" (*māṅgalye ca*)].
However, since it is established that this root has the marker *u* (ūdittva), its recitation [in the Dhātupāṭha] is meaningful for the sake of establishing this very point.

For this cannot be established by the rule "ṣidhū śāstre" [DhP 3.20], because by virtue of its being marked with *u*, the prohibition of *iṭ* applies in the case of the *niṣṭhā* suffixes according to the rule "svaratisūtisūyatidhūñūdito vā" [Pāṇini 7.2.44]. Thus, by the rule "vibhāṣiteṭaḥ" [Pāṇini 7.2.15], there is a prohibition of *iṭ*.
Therefore, since [the form] is already established by the very recitation in the *bhū* class and so forth, the designation *udit* for the root *sidh* is certainly not of Vedic origin (*anārṣa*).
[Examples include: "after *śiṣ*, *piṣ*" etc.; *śiṣlṛ* "in the sense of perishing" (DhP 1451);
*piṣlṛ* "in the sense of crushing" (DhP 1452); *śuṣa* "in the sense of drying up" (DhP 1183); *puṣa* "in the sense of nourishing" (DhP 1182); *tviṣa* "in the sense of shining" (DhP 1001).

The roots *jiṣu*, *viṣu*, and *miṣu* in the sense of "to sprinkle" (*secane*) [Dhātupāṭha 697, 698, 699], and *śriṣu*, *śliṣu*, *praṣu*, and *pluṣu* in the sense of "burning" (*dāhe*) [Dhātupāṭha 701–704]—both groups are included. *Tuṣa* in the sense of "contentment" (*tuṣṭau*) [Dhātupāṭha 1184; note: some lists read *prītau* or *tūṣa*] and *duṣa* in the sense of "defilement" (*vaikṛtye*) [Dhātupāṭha 1185], *dviṣa* in the sense of "dislike" (*aprītau*) [Dhātupāṭha 1013], and *kṛṣa* in the sense of "plowing" or "scratching" (*vilekhane*) [Dhātupāṭha 1286] belong to the *bhūvādigaṇa* and *tudādigaṇa* respectively. [This applies to the form] *puṣyati*.
The mention of *śyan* is for the purpose of excluding the *bhauvādika* and *kaiyādika* [roots];
however, in the case of roots such as *śuṣ*, it is for the purpose of avoiding a break in the meter. [Examples:
*kraṣṭā*, *karṣṭā*.
As before, there is no arrival [of the suffix] due to the optionality;
this refers to "tapiṃ tipim" and so forth.
Regarding "tapa santāpe" (Dhātupāṭha 985) and "tapa aiśvarye" (Dhātupāṭha 984)—the latter meaning either sovereignty or burning—both are included.

The roots *tipṛ*, *tepṛ*, and *ṣṭepṛ* have the meaning "to flow" (*kṣaraṇa*) [Dhātupāṭha 362, 363, 365]; *āplṛ* means "to pervade" (*vyāpti*) [Dhātupāṭha 1260]; *ṭu vap* means "the continuous succession of seed and thread" (*bījatantusantāna*) [Dhātupāṭha 1003; note: *ḍu vapa* is also listed as "the continuous succession of seed and thread" and "cutting" (*chedana*) in the Dhātupāṭha]; *ñi ṣvap* (or *ṣvapa*) means "to lie down" (*śaya*) [Dhātupāṭha 1068]; *lipa* means "to smear" (*upadāha*) [Dhātupāṭha 1433]; *luplū* means "to cut" (*chedana*) [Dhātupāṭha 1431]; and *tṛpa* means "to satisfy" (*pīṇana*).
(Dhātupāṭha 1195) *hṛpa* "to rejoice and to release"; (Dhātupāṭha 1196) [*harṣa-mohana-yoḥ*—Dhātupāṭha]; (Dhātupāṭha 982, 983) *gamḷṛ* and *sṛpḷṛ* "to go.
Regarding the phrase "with a low tone," the meaning is "with an unaccented (*anudātta*) tone."

The roots *śap* in the sense of "cursing" (*ākrośe*; DhP 1000) and *śap* in the sense of "reproaching" (*upālambhe*; DhP 1168)—both are included here. The root *chupa* in the sense of "touching" (DhP 1418) and *kṣip* in the sense of "impelling" (DhP 1285).

The fact that *tṛp* and *dṛp* are marked with an anudātta vowel is for the purpose of introducing the augment *am*, so that by the rule *anudāttasya* [Pāṇini 6.1.58], the augment *am* may optionally occur.
Why is this not for the purpose of prohibiting *iṭ*? To this he says: "But *iṭ* [is applied] to these two," and so forth.
"Those two which are *tṛp* and *dṛp* among the *tud*-class roots" refers to these two:
*tṛpa* and *tṛmpa* in the sense of "satisfaction" (*tṛptau*)—[as listed in the Dhātupāṭha as 1307 and 1308]—and *dṛp* in the sense of "affliction" (*upakleśe*)—[as listed in the Dhātupāṭha as 1313].

Regarding the passage beginning with *adiṃ hadim*: *ad* (in the sense of eating, Dhātupāṭha 1011); *had* (in the sense of voiding excrement, Dhātupāṭha 977); *skand* (in the senses of moving and drying up, Dhātupāṭha 959); *bhid* (in the sense of splitting, Dhātupāṭha 1439); *chid* (in the sense of cutting into two, Dhātupāṭha 1440); *kṣud* (in the sense of crushing, Dhātupāṭha 1443); *śad* (in the sense of falling off, Dhātupāṭha 855); *sad* (in the senses of dissolving, going, and sinking down, Dhātupāṭha 854); and *ṣvid* (in the sense of perspiration of the limbs).
(Dhātupāṭha 1188) *pada* "to go" (Dhātupāṭha 1169);

*khida* "in dejection" (Dhātupāṭha 1170), *khida* "in exchange" (Dhātupāṭha 1282); *vida* "in existence" (Dhātupāṭha 1188); *pada* "to go" (Dhātupāṭha 1169); *vida* "in deliberation" (Dhātupāṭha 1450).
[The mention of] *ñiṣvidā* "is intended so that there may not be the inclusion of this [root]."
Regarding the root *ñiṣvidā* in the sense of "moistening and releasing" (*snehanamocanayoḥ*) from the Dhātupāṭha (744):

the phrase "for the purpose of excluding other conjugational suffixes" (*anyavikaraṇanivṛttyarthaḥ*) means that it serves to exclude the *śnu*-suffix of the root *vida* in the sense of "knowing" (*vida jñāne*, Dhātupāṭha 1064), as well as the *śap*-suffix of the root *vidlṛ* in the sense of "obtaining" (*vidlṛ lābhe*, Dhātupāṭha 1432).

Regarding *vida* [in the sense of] "feeling," "narrating," and "separation" (*dhātupāṭha* 1708), and regarding the *curādika* root *cetana* [in the sense of] "feeling," "narrating," and "separation" (*dhātupāṭha*), there is no possibility [of the application of the suffix] because they consist of more than one vowel (*anekāctva*).
[The examples are] *paciṃ*, *vacim*, and so forth.
*Ḍu pacaṣ* means "cooking" (*dhātupāṭha* 996).
In the *Dhātupāṭha*, both "vac" (meaning "to speak") [1063] and "vruva" are included by the rule "vruvo vaciḥ" [Pāṇini 2.4.53];
thus, the instruction in the *Sūtra* is indeed valid for both.

*vicir* in the sense of separation (*pṛthagbhāve*) [DhP 1442]; *vicir* in the sense of discrimination (*vivecane*) [DhP 1094]; [*vijir* in the sense of separation—DhP—]; *rañj* in the sense of coloring or passion (*rāge*) [DhP 999]; *pracch* in the sense of the desire to know (*jñīpsāyām*) [DhP 1413]; *ṇijir* in the sense of purification and nourishment (*śaucapoṣaṇayoḥ*) [DhP 1093]; *ṣicir* in the sense of flowing or sprinkling (*kṣaraṇe*) [DhP 1434]; [*ṣica*—DhP—]; *mucḷ* in the sense of releasing (*mokṣaṇe*) [DhP 1430]; *bhaj* in the sense of service or devotion (*sevāyām*).
(dhātupāṭhaḥ-998), *bhanj* ‘to crush’ (dhātupāṭhaḥ-1453), *bhrasj* ‘to cook’ (dhātupāṭhaḥ-1444), *yuj* ‘to concentrate’ (dhātupāṭhaḥ-1177)—there is the inclusion of both [roots].
*ruj* ‘to break’ (dhātupāṭhaḥ-1416), *sañj* ‘to adhere’ (dhātupāṭhaḥ-987), *masj* ‘to cleanse’ (dhātupāṭhaḥ-1415).
*bhuja* ‘to protect and to eat’ (dhātupāṭhaḥ-1454), *bhuja* ‘crookedness’ (dhātupāṭhaḥ-1417)—there is the inclusion of both as well.
*ṣvañj* in the sense of embracing (*pariṣvaṅge*; Dhātupāṭha 976).
The mention of the form with the nasal elided is for the purpose of avoiding the disruption of the meter.
*sṛj* in the sense of emission (*visarge*; Dhātupāṭha 1414).
The root *mṛj* in the sense of "cleansing" (*śuddhi*) belongs to the *adādi* class (Dhātupāṭha 1066).

There is also a root *mṛj* in the sense of "purification and adornment" (*śaucālaṅkāra*) belonging to the *curādi* class (Dhātupāṭha 1848), which is the same as *mṛjū*. When this [curādi root] lacks the causative suffix *ṇic*—as in the case where it follows the rule *ā dhuṣādvā* (Dhātupāṭha 1805)—then it is certainly possible to include it [in the present discussion]. However, when the suffix *ṇic* is present, then because the root has more than two syllables (*anekāctva*), the prohibition of *iṭ* does not apply.
With the words "This root *mṛj*" and so forth, he rejects the view that its purpose here is for the sake of prohibition;
with the words "There is also the augment *am* for this" and so forth,
he [rejects] the view that its purpose is for the sake of the augment *am*.
Regarding the passage beginning with "tadiha" and so forth:
since these two purposes are indeed not possible, the purpose for its recitation must be considered here.
On this point, some say: "Even though this insertion (*āgama*) is not observed, it must nevertheless be performed; otherwise, its recitation would be meaningless."

For it is not the case that something must simply not exist because it is not perceived; otherwise, the rule *yathālakṣaṇam aprayukteṣu* would remain unapplied. Others, however, explain: [the form] *mājaṃ* is derived from the root *mṛj-* without an upapada, followed by *kvip*, and then the suffix *añ* is applied according to *vikārāvayavavivakṣāyām* (Pāṇini 4.3.134) so that the form may be obtained—this they claim is the purpose [of the rule]. But this is incorrect; for since the root is monosyllabic (*ekāc*), the suffix *mayaṭ* ought to apply invariably.

For instance, regarding the rule *[[Pāṇini 4.3.144]]*, one might ask: "What is the purpose of including the term *nitya* (always), since the operation will necessarily occur by the very force of its formulation? To this, it is said: "This is done for the sake of those who desire that *mayaṭ* always [be applied] after a monosyllabic base, as in *tvaṅmayaṃ* and *vāṅmayam*.
Regarding the phrase "some," etc.: who are these? They are some who, seeing no purpose [for the inclusion of *nitya*], read *viji* in place of *mṛj*.
He asks, "What is the reason? and says: "For in the *nijādi* [group]," and so forth.

Since the root *viji* is recited among the *nijādi* roots in the sense of "separation" (*vijir? prathagbhāve*; Dhātupāṭha 1094), and since it is desired to be without the augment *iṭ* (*aniṭ*), they have removed *bhṛj* and recited *viji* in its place.
How is it known that this [root] is desired to be *aniṭ*? He says: "And thus," and so forth.

Regarding the phrase "in another tantra" [with the variant reading "in another book"]: this refers to Āpiśali’s grammatical treatise (*vyākaraṇa*). Now, in the reading *sujivijī*, why is there not an inclusion of the root *ovijī* in the sense of "fear and trembling" (Dhātupāṭha 1289)? Because it is marked with the *īt* indicatory letter (*īdit*).

For that [designation] is indeed made for this purpose: so that there may be the prohibition of *iṭ* by the rule "after a root marked with *ā*, there is no *iṭ* in the case of the *niṣṭhā* suffix" (Pāṇini 7.2.14). If its inclusion here were also intended, then since the result would already be established by this very [rule], the marking with *it* would be purposeless—as in the form *avadhīt*.

By the rule *luṅi ca* [Pāṇini 2.4.43], there is the substitution of *vadh* for *han*, which ends in a short vowel (*adanta*). That substitution is one of an unaccented (*anudātta*) element by virtue of the status of being a substitute (*sthānivadbhāva*). Since there is no unaccented monosyllabic root in its original form of instruction (*upadeśa*), the prohibition does not apply.
But how does this [term] become a single syllable (*ekāj*)? To this he says: "For the purpose of precluding *vṛddhi*," and so forth.
If the word *vadhi* ending in *ṛ* were not taught, then by the rule [Pāṇini 7.2.7], *vṛddhi* would optionally occur.
But since it ends in *at*, [the substitution] does not take place; for in that case, one relies on the intervention of [the letter] *ya*.

However, when it ends in a vowel (adanta), even by virtue of the *sthānivadbhāva* rule regarding the elision of the letter *a* in the case of the root *vadh*, there is an intervention [between the suffix and the root] not only by a consonant (*hal*) but also by this [elided *a*].

Furthermore, as for the *vṛddhi* substitution conditioned by ending in a consonant (*halanta*), that too simply does not occur when it ends in a vowel, because due to the *sthānivadbhāva* of the elision of the letter *a*, it no longer ends in a consonant.
Therefore, the root *vadh* is taught with a final vowel for the sake of its grammatical treatment (*vṛtti*).

Objection: Even if it is taught as ending in a vowel (adanta), nevertheless, since it would be designated as "having a single vowel" (ekāj) by virtue of the rule of *sthānivadbhāva*, the prohibition [of vṛddhi] ought indeed to apply. Response: That is not so; for if that were the case, the mention of "single vowel" (ekāj) would be purposeless. To explain: because roots such as *jāgṛ*, *adarśi*, and *acakāt* are udātta, the mention of "single vowel" does not apply to them. Furthermore, derivative verbal bases (dhātus) formed with suffixes such as *san* and others do not possess the status of being "taught" (*upadeśatva*), because the entire complex is derived (*lākṣaṇika*).

Furthermore, there is no other monosyllabic (ekāj) verbal root that is taught as being unaccented (anudātta) which would necessitate the inclusion of the term "monosyllabic" (ekāj-grahaṇa). Nor does the status of being a substitute (sthānivadbhāva) apply when this designation is to be made, because it is not a rule concerning an *al* element (alvidhi).
[This is stated] so that "it may occur here."

If the acceptance of this instruction were not present, the meaning of the sūtra would simply be that the augment *iṭ* does not occur after a root consisting of a single vowel (*ekāc*) that begins with an anudātta vowel; and in that case, the augment *iṭ* would not occur in forms such as *laviṣyati* and *paviṣyati*. This is because, once the accent of the suffix has been applied and the remaining parts have become anudātta, the root itself becomes anudātta. However, in cases such as *kartā kaṭān* (he will make mats) and *kartum icchati* (he wishes to make), the augment *iṭ* must indeed occur; for when the suffixes *tṛn* and *tumun* are added, the root becomes udātta due to the *nit*-accent.

But when there is the inclusion of the term "in the original enunciation" (*upadeśa*), the initial state is thereby qualified; thus, the undesirable consequence (*doṣaprasaṅga*) does not occur at all. Even though *lunāti* and *punāti* are unaccented (*anudātta*) at a later stage, they are indeed accented (*udātta*) precisely in the state of the original enunciation.
Likewise, even though *karoti* is accented at a later stage, it is indeed unaccented in the state of the original enunciation.

Now, although the word *bibhits* is not included in the list of roots under discussion, nor does it consist of a single vowel (*ekāctva*), nevertheless, both of these conditions apply to the root *bhid*.

Furthermore, the view that "doubling consists in the double usage [of the same element]" is also adopted there; thus, it is the root *bhid* itself that is doubled. And because that [root] is qualified by both [the aforementioned] specifications, the prohibition is indeed established. This [sūtra] is commenced for the sake of the acute accent (*udātta*). For example: *lūnaḥ*.
The substitution of *n* [for *t*] occurs by the rule *lvādibhyaśca* [Pāṇini 8.2.44]. Regarding the form *tīrṇaḥ*,
here too [the substitution of *n* for *t* occurs] by the rule *radābhyām* [Pāṇini 8.2.42].

Regarding the passage beginning with "some" (*kecit*), [it concerns] the rule *glājisthaśca ksnuḥ* (Pāṇini 3.2.139). Since there is the statement "and *bhū*" (*bhuvaśca vaktavyam*)—referring to the sūtra *bhuvaśca*—when the suffix *ksnu* is applied to the root *bhū* and the marker *g* is added, the prohibition of the augment *iṭ* prescribed for markers marked with *g* would not apply. Consequently, the form *bhūṣṇuḥ* would not be established.

Therefore, some maintain that in the word *bhūṣṇu*, the prohibition of the augment *iṭ* applies; they explain that in the rule *śrayukaḥ kiti*, the letter *g*—which has become a *car* sound—is included by means of the mention of the double *k* (*kk*), as in the case of *ābhūti* and *vyāṅ*.

If the *g* sound, having become a *c* sound (*cartva*), were joined [as in *praśliṣṭa*], then, since the rule *haśi ca* (P. 6.1.114) would require the *ru* sound to become *u* after the application of *rutva* by the rule *ato ror aplutād aplute* (P. 6.1.113)—given that the change to *c* (*cartva*) is considered non-existent (*asiddha*)—would not the substitution of the visarga (*visarjanīya*) be required instead? Consequently, the grammatical formulation *śrayukaḥ kiti* (P. 7.2.11) would be untenable. To refute this objection, he says: "Because the formulation is based on the *sūtra*," and so forth.
They explain that the change to *u* for the *ru* sound was not applied because they do not rely on the non-existence (*asiddhatva*) of the change to *c*, and thus the visarga is applied.
But for what purpose do they maintain that the suffix *ksnu* has the property of being *kit*, such that this explanation must be provided? It is for the sake of establishing the word *sthāsnú*.

For they think as follows: if *ksnu* were *kit*, then by the rule *dhumāsthāgāpājahātisām aṭ* (Pāṇini 6.4.66), the substitution of *ī* for the root *sthā* would occur; consequently, the form *sthāsnú* would not be established.
[This is addressed] in the passage beginning with "In the rule *glājisthaśca ksnuḥ*," and so forth.
For when [the suffix] *kṣnu* has the marker *g*, it is explained in this way solely for the purpose of prohibiting [the substitution of] *aṭ*; yet it does not possess the marker *g*.

What then? It possesses the marker *k* alone. Nor does the presence of the marker *k* entail the presence of the marker *i*, because in the rule [Pāṇini 6.4.66], *sthā-ād-aṭi*, the vowel *a* has been elided (praśleṣa) from *sthā*.

The purpose [of the vowel *a*] is so that the suffix *ksnu*, when added to the root *sthā*, remains an *ā*-stem (ending in *ā*) and does not become an *ī*-stem. For if the vowel *a* were not elided (*apraśleṣa*), the substitution of *ā* for the root *sthā* would serve as an exception (*apavāda*) to the rule for *ī*-substitution; thus, because it would be superseded by that [substitution of *ā*], the *ī*-substitution would not take effect. Therefore, since the word *sthāsnu* is established through the presence of *kit* and the elision of the vowel *a*, this objection amounts to nothing.

The meaning is that this explanation is without substance. Regarding the word "tīrṇam" (crossed), one might ask: what is the reason that [the rule] would not apply here even if the mention of "upadeśa" (original instruction) were absent, given that the root *tṛ* is recited as ending in *u*? To this he says: "For if there were *it*-ness," and so forth. If *it*-ness were applied by the rule "ṛt- id dhātoḥ" [Pāṇini 7.1.100], the status of ending in *u* would be destroyed; thus, if the mention of "upadeśa" were absent, [the rule] would not apply. But when that [mention of "upadeśa"] exists, it does apply.
Even though the root *tṛ* does not end in *ru* at a later stage, it is nevertheless taught [as such] in the original instruction (*upadeśa*).
"Let it not be so," and so forth— this is the challenger (*codaka*).
"Of what, then? and so forth is the respondent;
"It has been done" (or "It was made," as printed) is the questioner;
"If that is so" and so forth is the respondent.
"Because of the status as a substitute" (*sthānivadbhāvāt*). Furthermore, it is not a rule concerning vowels (*alvidhi*) because of the inclusion of the *pratyāhāra* "uG.
"Therefore," etc.
He says: Since this prohibition in the word *tīrṇa* would not apply if the mention of *upadeśa* were absent, therefore the term *upadeśa* must be understood as carrying over [from the previous rule].
"And such being the case," etc.; the meaning is: while *upadeśa* is being carried over.
"The [suffix] would also apply here in the case of *jāgarita*,
because the root *jāgṛ* ends in the vowel *u* at the stage of its formal instruction (*upadeśa*).
"For that purpose" means:
In the rule beginning with *jāgarita*, [the mention of] "artha" is for the purpose of removing the application of the prohibition of *iṭ*; this is because the word *artha* signifies cessation.

If, however, the term *ekācaḥ* from [Pāṇini 7.2.10] is understood to carry over [to this rule], then in forms such as *proṛṇutaḥ* and *proṛṇutavat*, the prohibition of *iṭ* would not apply, since the root *ūrṇu* has more than one vowel (*anekāctva*)? To this, he says: "*ūrṇoḥ ṇuvat vācyaḥ*," and so forth.

The meaning of this *kārikā* has already been explained previously, so it is not explained again here. Since the augment *iṭ* would apply to the root *grah* when followed by the desiderative suffix (*san*), and since the root *guh* also contains the vowel *ū* (an *ūdittva*), the option prescribed by the rule *svarati* [Pāṇini 7.2.44] would also apply; therefore, this [present rule] is commenced. The particle *ca* serves to carry forward the term *ukaḥ* [from Pāṇini 7.2.11].

But is it not the case that, according to [Pāṇini 1.2.9], the *san* suffix after roots ending in long *ū* is only *kit*? In that case, the prohibition is already established by the preceding rule (1.2.8); what then is the purpose of the particle *ca*, which serves to carry over (*anukarṣaṇa*) the term *kit*? This is not so; for without the prohibition of *iṭ*, the status of *san* as beginning with a *jhal* consonant is not established, and how then could it be *kit*? By this [rule], however, once *iṭ* is prohibited, the status of *san* as beginning with a *jhal* consonant arises, and subsequently, the *kit* status is for the purpose of prohibiting *guṇa*; such is the sequence. [Thus we have] "jighṛkṣati."

In the case of *rudavida* [1.2.8] and so forth, since the suffix *san* is marked with *k* (indicating it is *kit*), there is vocalization (*samprasāraṇa*) by the rule *grahādi* [6.1.16]; then, by *ho ḍhaḥ* [8.2.31], there is the substitution of *ḍha*; by *jhaṣastathordho'dhaḥ* [8.2.40], there is the substitution of *dha*; by *iṇkoḥ* [8.2.57], there is the substitution of *ṣ*; and by *ekāco vaśo bhaṣ* [8.2.37] and following rules, through the *bhaṣ*-bhāva, the letter *ga* becomes *gha*. Then follows reduplication and the operations pertaining to the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsakārya*). Thus, one obtains *judhukṣati*.

In the case of *rudavida* [1.2.8] and so forth, when the suffix *san* is *kit*, there is *samprasāraṇa* by the rule *grahādi* [6.1.16]; then *ḍhatva* by *ho ḍhaḥ* [8.2.31], *katva* by [8.2.41], reduplication, and the operations pertaining to the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsakārya*). Thus we have *jughukṣate* [the *Kāśikā* and *Padamañjarī* read *judhukṣati*].
The root *guhū* means "to conceal" (Dhātupāṭha 896); the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) is applied by the rule *pūrvavatsanaḥ* [1.3.62].

Regarding the form *rurūṣati*: [the vowel lengthening occurs] by [Pāṇini 6.4.16]. Now, if the particle *ca* were to carry forward (*anukṛṣyate*) only one [root], then *śri*, which is also prescribed in the same grammatical rule (*ekayoganirdiṣṭa*), would likewise be carried forward. To address this, he says: "*śrisvṛyūrṇurabhajñapi*," and so forth.

Since the rule *sanīdantargha* [Pāṇini 7.2.49] will prescribe the optional application of the augment *iṭ* for the root *śri*, its recurrence here would be purposeless; therefore, it is not carried over. In the forms *sakṛva* and *cakṛma*, the substitutes *vas* and *mas* are replaced by *vam* according to the rule *parasmaipadānām* [Pāṇini 3.4.82]. The phrase "only *krādayaḥ*" [refers to the fact that these roots belong to the *kry-ādi* class].
He demonstrates the nature of the restrictive rule (*niyama*).

However, one should not suspect the reverse restriction—that "only after *liṭ* are *krādi* roots *aniṭ*"; for this is precluded by such indications as [Pāṇini 4.3.38] and [5.1.80]. But by what means is the prohibition of *iṭ* for them already established, such that the formulation of a new rule, when [the result] is already established, is said to be for the purpose of a restriction? To this he says: "Of those taught with an anudātta accent," and so forth.
The roots beginning with *kṛ*—other than *vṛṅ* and *vṛñ*—are taught with an anudātta vowel; for these alone, the prohibition based on the root (prakṛti) is established by [Pāṇini 7.2.10] *acaḥ* etc.
However, for *vṛṅ* and *vṛñ*, the prohibition is based on the suffix (pratyaya) by [Pāṇini 7.2.11] *śrayukaḥ kiti*, and not based on the root, because those two are udātta.
"That," etc. [refers to the following].

Since the prohibition of those [roots] based on their nature (*prakṛti*) and their basis (*āśraya*), as applicable, is already established, the meaning is that this restriction (*niyama*) applies to both types of prohibition when they have been employed.
Here, the restriction should be understood as a prohibition of roots such as *kṛ* and others, specifically by excluding them from other verbal roots (*dhātu*).

But how is it possible for this to serve as a restrictive rule (*niyamārtha*) regarding the suffix *thali* after the root *vṛñ*, given that a restriction only occurs when there is a prior general prohibition (*pratiṣedha*)?
This is a prohibition of the suffix *thali*. For in this case, a prohibition based on the root (*prakṛti*) is not established, because [the root] is acute-accented (*udātta*).
Nor is it based on the suffix (*pratyaya*), because *thali* lacks the *kit* designation.

Therefore, is it not more logical that [the rule] serves solely to prohibit *iṭ* after *thal* following the root *vṛñ*, rather than serving as a restrictive rule (*niyama*)? To this he says: "For *vṛñ*... and so forth.
*Vyavasthā* means restriction (*niyama*).

Because of the formal derivation (*nipātana*) [of the form *vavritha*] by [Pāṇini 7.2.64], the prohibition of *iṭ* after *thal* must apply to *vṛñ* only in the Vedic language (*nigama*), and not in the common language (*bhāṣā*).

Since the established rule is thus, this prohibition does not apply to the root *vṛñ*; otherwise, the specific grammatical prescription (*nipātana*) for the form *vavartha* would be rendered meaningless.

Therefore, because there is no prohibition [of the *iṭ* augment] for *vṛñ*, it is an absolute conclusion that this sūtra is understood to serve solely as a restrictive rule (*niyamārtha*) even for *vṛñ*. As for the statement beginning with "but in the case of *stu*, *dru*, *sru*, *śru*, and *vṛ*" and so forth...
The word *api* (also) is for the purpose of showing that even that *iṭ* which would otherwise apply by virtue of the rules governing *ārdhadhātuka* affixes is not desired.
But how can it be obtained even though it is [otherwise] desired? Because the section containing prohibitions (*pratiṣedhakāṇḍa*) is stronger.
And here, it would have been more appropriate to place this section of prohibitions immediately after the rule *na vṛdbhyaś catubhyaḥ* [Pāṇini 7.2.59].
In this way, there would be no need to resort to a double negation.

The purpose of the negation that is made here at the beginning is as follows: it is understood as a negation of the mere *iṭ* augment when no specific rule for its application has been established. When the negation is performed at the outset, this becomes an exception (*apavāda*) to the mere *iṭ* without depending on any specific [rule].
Consequently, the negation of every *iṭ* that might otherwise have occurred is established.

But another says: since the word *na* from [Pāṇini 7.2.4] "neṭ" is understood as a governing rule (*anuvartamāna*), by the force of the repetition of the term *iṅ*, and by the force of the repetition of the prohibition, the prohibition is understood to apply only to the root *iṇ*. Thus, it must be stated that "it should be said: 'of the root *kṛñ* when not preceded by *suṭ*'"; the meaning is that this should be explained as having the sense that the prohibition of *ṣat* applies to the root *kṛ* when *suṭ* is absent.

For what purpose? So that the augment *iṭ* may apply to [the root] together with the suffix *suṭ*. Regarding this, the following is the explanation: by the rule at [Pāṇini 2.2.32], without having effected the prior placement (*pūrvanipāta*) of any one of the items beginning with *stu* that bear the technical name *ghisamjñaka*, this [rule] indicates: "In this case, the characteristic for prior placement deviates; it does not operate within its own scope, and this [augment] is likewise. Therefore, when the root *kṛ* is accompanied by *suṭ*, [the rule] does not operate there.
In the forms *sañcaskariva* and *sañcaskarima*,
while the rule for *suṭ* from [Pāṇini 6.1.137] is being carried over, *suṭ* is applied by [Pāṇini 6.1.136].
Furthermore, the rule [Pāṇini 7.2.63], *ṛto bhāradvājasya*, is also intended to apply only to that which does not have *asu* or *yaṭ*.

The word "of *kṛñ*" (*kṛñaḥ*) is connected [to the rule]. But how is it understood that this applies only to the form without the augment *suṭ*? Listen to how it is so understood: for from the rule [Pāṇini 7.2.56], the word "or" (*vā*) is carried over by the maxim of the frog’s leap (*maṇḍūkapluti*), and that is a restricted option (*vyavasthitavibhāṣā*); therefore, it occurs only for the form without *suṭ*. Regarding the form "śūnaḥ":
there is vocalization (*samprasāraṇa*) by the rule [Pāṇini 6.1.15] beginning with *vaci-*, and lengthening by [Pāṇini] 6.4.2, "after a consonant" (*halaḥ*).
Regarding the word *lagnaḥ*:
is it not the case that the substitution of *k* [for *g*] applies here because of the rule *natvasyāsiddhatvāt* (Pāṇini 8.2.30)?
Regarding the word *uḍḍīnaḥ*.
The root *ṅīṅ* means "to go through the air" (*vihāyasā gatau*; Dhātupāṭha 1135).

Now, since *ṅīṅ* is marked with an acute accent (*udātta*), the augment *iṭ* would apply to its past passive participle (*niṣṭhā*); therefore, a prohibition of that must be stated. For one who might think that the undesirable form *uḍḍayita* would result, [the author] says "of *ṅīṅ*" and so forth. [This refers to the rule] "of those ending in *o* or *iṭ*" (*oditām*).

The meaning is "of *svā* and the others. This is because of the statement, "the roots beginning with *svā* are marked with the *o*-diacritic. The roots beginning with *svā* are *ṣūṅ* "to release the embryo of a living being" (Dhātupāṭha 1031), and so forth.
How does this serve as an indicator (*jñāpaka*)? He says: "For that," and so forth.

Among the roots beginning with *hr-* (those marked with *h*), the reading of that [root] has this purpose: so that the substitution of *n* may occur for the *t* of a *niṣṭhā* suffix following a root marked with *u*.
One might object: "Even when the augment *iṭ* is applied, the substitution of *n* will still take place. To this he says: "And the substitution of *n*," and so forth.

In this context [of Pāṇini 1.1.67], because the term *nirdiṣṭa* (specified), which signifies immediate proximity (*ānantarya*), is understood to carry over [from the previous rule], the substitution of *na* for the *t* of the *niṣṭhā* suffix is prescribed only when it follows immediately after a root marked with the indicatory vowel *o* or *i*.

In that case, if the augment *iṭ* were to follow a *niṣṭhā* suffix preceded by the affix *ṅīṅ*, then even though the root is marked with *o* or *i*, the substitution of *na* would not occur because the *t* would be separated from it by the *iṭ*.

If it were not so, the reading of [the suffix] *ṅīṅ* among those vowels marked with the indicatory letter *u* (nityodita) would be purposeless, yet that reading does exist. Therefore, is it not this very reading that serves as the indicator? This is not the case; for in this way, the Paribhāṣā concerning immediate sequence (*ānantarya*) would be sublated, and the grammatical treatise (*śāstra*) would yield an undesirable result, which is improper. Indeed, there is no formulation in the treatise intended for an undesirable purpose.

Therefore, one must accept that procedure by which the Paribhāṣā concerning immediate sequence is not sublated, the treatise does not yield an undesirable result, and the reading of *ṅīṅ* among the *nityodita* vowels becomes fruitful.
Furthermore, the inclusion of *ṅī* and *ṅīṅ* among those marked with the *u*-diacritic (*udit*) serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*).

There is another method: the term *audit* in [P. 8.2.45] will be repeated for the sake of the double application of this technical rule (*paribhāṣā*) [P. 1.1.67]. Regarding its second application, this is its purpose: so that the substitution of *n* may occur only for the immediately following *t* of the past participle suffix (*niṣṭhā*) after roots ending in *ṅī* or *ṅīṅ*. For if there were an augment *iṭ* after the *niṣṭhā* of roots ending in *ṅī* or *ṅīṅ*, the substitution of *n* would not take place because it would be separated by the *iṭ*.
Nor can it be argued that [the rule] will apply even when there is an intervention, on the strength of its recitation [in the sūtra];

for if that were so, the double occurrence of this paribhāṣā would be purposeless. This, however, is incorrect; therefore, the recitation of ṅīṅ among the vowels ending in "o" (oditām) is indeed an indicator (jñāpaka).

The mention of *i* could have been omitted; for by the very fact of designating [the roots] as *odit*, there will be no *iṭ* in the *niṣṭhā* [past participles], since the *odit* designation is made for the purpose of causing the substitution of *n* [for *t*], and that substitution is prescribed immediately after the *niṣṭhā*. If there were an *iṭ* after that [root] followed by the *niṣṭhā*, the *odit* designation would be useless. Therefore, the mention of *i* should be understood as being for the sake of variety. [Examples: *vidhūtaḥ* [from the root *dhūñ* "to shake" (DhP 1836)];
*gūḍhaḥ* [from the root *gūhū* "to conceal" (DhP 986)].

When the substitutions beginning with *ḍha* have been applied, a long vowel occurs by [Pāṇini 6.3.111], etc. Why is there no prohibition here in the case of *patita-patita*? For is not the root *pat-* optionally marked with the *iṭ* augment? Because of the supplementary rule (*upasaṃkhyāna*) "an addition for *tan*, *pat*, *dṛ*, and *drā*" under [Pāṇini 7.2.49] *sanīvantardha*, which provides for the optionality of the *iṭ* augment. To this he replies: "In the case of *dvitīyā-śrita*, etc. He will state the optionality immediately after the section on abstract action (*bhāva*) and passive (*ādika-rma*). Therefore, elsewhere—specifically in the active (*kartṛ*) and passive (*karman*) voices—this prohibition is understood to apply. Thus, the form *āstaḥ*.
The root *ās* is used in the sense of "breathing" (*prāṇana*) [Dhātupāṭha 1069].
Regarding the term *vāntaḥ*:
the root *ṭu vam* is used in the sense of "vomiting" (*udgiraṇa*) [Dhātupāṭha 849].
Thus, there is a long vowel [by rule 6.4.15].

[The question] "What is the purpose of making this *yogavibhāga* (splitting of the rule)? is answered by [the rule]: "And optionally [the augment *iṭ* is applied] after roots beginning with a vowel, in the sense of the abstract action (*bhāva*) and the beginning of an action (*ādikarman*)."

If a single rule (*ekayoga*) were made, then there would be no prohibition for cases other than the abstract state (*bhāva*) and the passive (*ādikarman*); anticipating this objection, he says: "And from the beginning," and so forth. If there were a single rule stating "And optionally from the beginning in the case of the abstract state and the passive," then once the optionality had been prescribed for the abstract state and the passive, the prohibition "[7.2.15] *na duhasnunamām ayami...* [etc. would apply to other cases such as the agent (*kartṛ*). Therefore, the making of a split rule (*yogavibhāga*) would be purposeless.
With the words "For the sake of providing an indication" (*jñāpanārtham*), etc., he refutes this charge of purposelessness.
"In the case of whichever qualifier there is an option, [it applies] to that same qualifier.
In both instances, this is a *bahuvrīhi* compound. Here, "qualifier" (*upādhi*) means a distinguishing attribute (*viśeṣaṇa*).
And for this purpose, the condition (*upādhi*) must be understood as follows:

if, when there is an option (*vibhāṣā*) with respect to a certain condition, there were also a prohibition (*pratiṣedha*) of that very condition, then he would not have made the division of rules (*yogavibhāga*).

For even by a single rule (*ekayoga*), once the option has been prescribed for the states of being (*bhāva*) and the passive (*karma*), the prohibition "in other cases than those" (Pāṇini 7.2.15) would certainly be obtained; yet a division of rules has been made. Therefore, by this act of making a division of rules, it is indicated: "where there is an option with respect to a condition, there is a prohibition of that condition."

By the words "by that" (*tena*) and so forth, he demonstrates the purpose of the indicator (*jñāpaka*). Here, because of the association with the *tud*-class root *vid* meaning "to find," which is marked by the suffix *vi*, there is the inclusion of the *tud*-class root *vid* meaning "to obtain. Furthermore, the prohibition [of the augment *iṭ*] applies only to that [specific root] and not to any other.

If it is signaled that "the optionality [of a grammatical operation] applies to whatever condition [it is prescribed for], and the prohibition applies to that same condition," then since the suffix *ktvā* in the rule *jṛvraścoḥ ktviḥ* (P. 7.2.55) is optional when referring to an abstract action (*bhāva*), the prohibition of *iṭ* in the past participial suffix (*niṣṭhā*) would apply only when referring to an abstract action (by P. 7.2.15), and not in the case of the agent (*kartṛ*) or the object (*karman*). This is not a fault; for a property (*dharma*) must be relied upon as a differentiator.
Now, neither in the case of the suffix *ktvā* nor in the case of the suffix *niṣṭhā* is a distinct denotable meaning (*abhidheya*) relied upon as the cause [for the application of the rule].
Therefore, the prohibition indeed applies here.

The indicator here is the reference to [Pāṇini 5.1.79]. In the forms *bhinnam anena* ("broken by this") and *meditam* ("melted"), there is guna-vowel substitution because the prohibition of *kittva* (the status of having a *k*-marker) applies by the rule beginning with [Pāṇini 1.2.19], *niṣṭhā śīṅ*.

Regarding the word "praminnaḥ": the prefix *pra-* indicates the inception of an action (*ādikarma*). Regarding the term "inception of an action" (*ādikarma*): [it refers to the initial stage of an action].
Regarding the phrase "the moment of the initial action" (*ādibhūtakriyākṣaṇa*):
when that [moment] is intended to be expressed as having already occurred (*bhūtatva*), the suffix *kta* is applied to the agent (*kartṛ*) case-factor by the rule *ktaktavatū niṣṭhā* (Pāṇini 1.1.26).

To establish forms such as *śakto ghaṭaḥ kartum* ("the jar is capable of being made") and *śakito ghaṭaḥ kartum* ("the jar has been rendered capable of being made"), a formal split of the yoga-rule (*yogavibhāga*) must be made here, namely: *vibhāṣā*.

In this context, the term "from the beginning" (*āditaḥ*) from [Pāṇini 7.2.16] should not be carried over; rather, it is precisely the term "of the state and the beginning of an action" (*bhāvādikarmaṇoḥ*) that must be carried over into the second rule. Regarding the form *kṣubdhaḥ*:
the absence of the augment *iṭ* is prescribed as a formal anomaly (*nipātana*) for the root *kṣubh* "to shake" (Dhātupāṭha 1239).
"If it is called 'churned' (*mantha*)," [means]:
if the "churned" is denoted by the collective whole—
whereby "churned" refers to barley flour mixed with liquid substances.
"Kṣugdho manthaḥ" means the churning-stick has moved. "Kṣubhitaṃ mantreṇa" means [disturbed] by the mantra.
In this context, churning itself is not being denoted; rather, what is meant is the motion that accomplishes it.

Now, if the word *mantha* (churning) is being denoted, then the word *kṣubdha* is prescribed as a nipātana (irregular formation), as in: "the mountain torrent is agitated" (*kṣubdhā girinadī*), "the army is agitated" (*kṣubdhā senā*), "the ocean is agitated" (*kṣubdhaḥ samudraḥ*), and so forth. Why would this not be appropriate? To this he says: "the mountain torrent is agitated," and so on.
He shows that [the word *kṣubdha*] is applied to mountains, rivers, and so forth, because of their similarity to a churned substance (*mantha*) in motion.

Just as the state of being agitated (*kṣubdhatva*) is the means for the movement of a churned substance, so too the mountain, river, and other objects are designated by the word *kṣubdha* because they are the means for movement due to their similarity to a churned substance. This is just as a *vāhīka* is called by the word "cow" due to his similarity to a cow.
Examples are "swāntam" and "dhvāntam."

In the roots *svan* and *dhvan*, meaning "to sound" (*dhātupāṭhaḥ* 827, 828), the absence of the augment *iṭ* is prescribed as an irregularity (*nipātana*). This should be understood to apply similarly to the subsequent examples as well.
"A mind that is undistracted and unperturbed regarding external objects is called *svāntam*";
thus [the word] is long.
[The phrase] "resounded by the mind" (*svanitaṃ manasā*).
The act of sounding has the mind as its agent; it is not the mind itself.
Regarding the phrase "it was sounded by darkness," here too the act of sounding has darkness as its agent; it is not darkness itself.

Regarding the word *lagna*: [the root] *lag* is used in the sense of "clinging" (*lage saṅge*) and "fear" (*rage śaṅkāyām*) according to the Dhātupāṭha (785, 786). The substitution of the nasal *ṇ* for the final consonant is prescribed as a grammatical irregularity (*nipātyate*). [The phrase] *svaraś cet* means "if it is a vowel."
In this context, the word *svara* refers to sound (*dhvani*).
Regarding the term *phāṣṭam*:
[it is derived from] the root *phaṇa* meaning "to go" (Dhātupāṭha 821).
As before, there is lengthening and the substitution of *ṣṭu*.
What, then, is this so-called "lack of effort"? To this he says: "That which is uncooked," and so forth.
"Uncooked" means unripened.
"Un-grounded" (apiṣṭam) means not pulverized.
"Contact with water" (udakasamparkaḥ) means conjunction with water. By the word "mere" (mātra), there is an exclusion of squeezing and so forth.
"Vibhaktarasaṃ" means having distinct flavors;
"īṣaduṣṇaṃ" means lukewarm.
"Because it is accomplished with little effort, it is perceived without exertion.
Exertion (*āyāsa*) is an excess of effort; that which does not possess this is "accomplished with little effort," meaning it is without exertion (*anāyāsa*).
Therefore, in this context, the object characterized by being uncooked and so forth is perceived without exertion because it is accomplished with little effort.

Therefore, by this [rule], the suffix *kāṣṭha* is applied as an irregular formation (*nipātana*) to that specific object which is characterized by ease, but not to "ease" itself. This shows that it is not applied everywhere else simply because something is characterized by ease.
And this meaning is obtained through the force of the irregular formation.

How is it so? Just as some [grammatical operations], such as the substitution of *iḍ* and so forth, are obtained due to the capacity for falling [into application], so too is it in the case of a specific meaning.
"Certainly" (*bāḍham*):
here, as before, there is the grammatical operation of changing *t* to *ḍh*, and so on. "The state of being shameless is *vaiyātyam*"—thus [it is formed].

*Yātam* means going or reaching. One whose conduct (*yātam*) is distorted (*virūpam*) because it concerns an improper path is called *viyāta*, meaning ill-mannered or undisciplined. The state of being that is *vaiyātyam*. The suffix *ṣyañ* is applied according to Pāṇini 5.1.123, as it belongs to the *brāhmaṇādi* group. [The form] is "ṣuṣṭaḥ."
The root *dhṛṣ* is listed as *ñi dhṛṣā pragalbhye* (Dhātupāṭha 1269). Regarding the form *viśastaḥ*:

since the root *śas* is listed as *śasu hiṃsāyām* (Dhātupāṭha 727), and because the optionality of the augment *iṭ* is prescribed for *śas* by the rule *udito vā* (Pāṇini 7.2.56), the prohibition of *iṭ* is already established by the rule *na vṛdbhyaś caturbhyo’ṅi* (Pāṇini 7.2.59); thus, the connection [of this example] is already proven.

If, then, the prohibition is already established, for what purpose is the statement? He says: "For the sake of restriction," and so forth. [The purpose is] so that [the suffix *ṇic*] occurs only when there is audacity (*vaiyātya*), and not otherwise. Now, one might ask: since the optionality [of *ṇic*] is obtained by the rule "after the root *dhṛṣ*, it is optional in the sense of becoming (*bhāva*) and acting (*ādikarman*)" (Pāṇini 7.2.17), why is this statement not intended to make it obligatory (*nitya*)? To this he replies: "In the sense of becoming and acting, [it is] excluded," and so forth.
And here, the reason is the inherent nature of the power of intimidation;
[as expressed by] "intimidated" (*dharṣitaḥ*). "Intimidated" (*dharṣitaḥ*).

As before? When *kittva* is prohibited, there is *guṇa*. By indicating [the word] with the suffix *matup*, he shows that in the sūtra the word *bala* ending in the possessive suffix *-a* is cited, because it belongs to the *arśa-ādi* group. Regarding "of *dṛṃhi*":
this refers to the root *dṛhi* in the sense of "growth" (Dhātupāṭha 834).
Or rather: "There is another root-form *dṛhi*," as some [maintain] based on the recitation [of the Dhātupāṭha]: "√dṛh, √dṛhi, in the sense of strengthening" (Dhātupāṭha 733, 734). [The objection is:
"Because of the absence of the letter *n*."

"Because there is no instruction for the letter *n*, and because it is not marked with *i* or *t*, the letter *n* does not exist [in this context]. Now, for what purpose is the elision of the letter *h* prescribed as a *nipātana* (irregularity)? Why not simply prescribe the letter *ḍh* itself? For once *ḍh* is substituted for the following [letter], and *ṣṭu* is applied, and then the rule "when *ḍh* follows *ḍh*, there is elision" is applied, the form *dṛḍha* is established. In this case too, the objection might be: "There is no need to prescribe the substitution of *ḍh* for the following [letter], since it is already established by the *ṣṭu* rule alone? To this he says: "The prescription of the elision of the consonant (*halopa-nipātana*)," and so forth.

If the substitution of *ḍha* for *ha* were prescribed as a *nipātana*, then by the rule "that which is taught later is not established for that which precedes" (*pūrvatrāsiddham*), [the substitution of *ḍha*] would be considered unestablished (*asiddha*) with respect to [the application of] P. 8.2.1; yet it is intended to be established. Therefore, the elision of *ha* (*halopa*) is prescribed as a *nipātana* in order to prevent its being unestablished with respect to what precedes, rather than the substitution of *ḍha*. But what is the fault in its being unestablished, such that—in order to avoid it—the elision of *ha* is prescribed as a *nipātana* to prevent its being unestablished with respect to what precedes, rather than the substitution of *ḍha*? To this he says: "In the case of the elision of *ḍha*" (*ḍhalope*), etc.

For if the letter *ḍha* were prescribed as a *nipātana*, then [the rule] Pāṇini 8.3.13 would have to be applied; however, if that were the case, then in forms such as *draḍhimā*, the substitution of *ra* [for *ḍha*] by Pāṇini 6.4.161 would not occur, because the elision of *ḍha* would be considered non-existent (*asiddha*) by Pāṇini 1.4.11, and once the designation of "heavy" (*guru-saṃjñā*) has arisen, the designation of "light" (*laghu-saṃjñā*) is sublated.
Regarding the form *draḍhimā*:
the suffix *iman* is added by Pāṇini 5.1.123, and the elision of the final syllable (*ṭi-lopa*) occurs by Pāṇini 6.4.154.
Regarding the word *draḍhīyān*:
the suffix *īyasun* is applied according to [Pāṇini 5.3.57], *dvivacanavibhajyopapade tarabīyasunau*.
Regarding the word *draḍhayati*: [it is derived from the root *dṛḍha* with the causative suffix *ṇic*].

Regarding *draḍhayati*: from the sense "he makes firm" (*dṛḍham ācaṣṭe*), the suffix *ṇic* is applied by the rule *tat karoti tad ācaṣṭe* (Dhātupāṭha Gaṇasūtra 187). By the rule *ṇāviṣṭhavad bhāvaḥ kāryaṃ prātipadikasya* (Vārttika 813), which prescribes the treatment as if it were the superlative suffix *iṣṭhan*, the elision of the *repha* and the *tilopa* occur. Thus, in the form *paridraḍhayya gataḥ*, the suffix *ṇic* is applied in the sense "he makes firm" (*dṛḍham ācaṣṭe*).

When the *rabhāva* (substitution of *ra*) has been applied to the causative (*ṇyanta*), it is joined with *pari*; from that, the suffix *ktvā* is added, followed by a *prādi*-compound. By the rule *samāse 'nañpūrve ktvo lyap* [Pāṇini 7.1.37], *lyap* is substituted for *ktvā*. Thus we have "pāridraḍhī kanyā" (a girl who has become very firm).
From the word *paridraḍha*, the suffix *iñ* is applied, and then *ṅīṣ* is added by the rule *ṭiḍḍhāṇañ...* [Pāṇini 4.1.15].
"The suffix *ṣyaṅ* would apply" refers to [Pāṇini 4.1.78],
"after [stems ending in] *aṇ* or *iñ*, when they are not Vedic (*anārṣa*) and have a heavy penultimate syllable (*gurūpottama*)," and so forth.
"Dṛṃhitam" means "strengthened."

The counter-example for *dṛṃhi* is *dṛhitam*, derived from *dṛh*. The phrase "the same as the preceding" is used because the absence of *iṭ* and other features due to the irregular derivation (*nipātana*) are identical in both cases.

For just as in the previous sūtra, when the suffix *kta* is applied, the elision of the letters *ha* and *na*, the absence of the augment *iṭ*, and the substitution of *ḍha* for the following letter were all established by way of *nipātana* (irregular derivation), so too here everything is established by *nipātana*. "The *nipātana* of *vṛṃhi*" refers to the root *vṛhi* (meaning "to grow") [listed as *bṛhi* in the Dhātupāṭha, no. 736].

"And if *vṛhi* is a separate root, then [the rule] applies to that as well"—this connects with the statement "this is a *nipātana*. As for the existence of a separate root, some have stated it is *vṛha* (or *bṛha*) in the sense of "growth" (*vṛddhau*), as found in the *Dhātupāṭha* (root list, no. 735).
"That very purpose" means the removal of the status of being "not established" (*asiddha*) in the preceding rule. An example is *parivrajhayati*.

In this case, when the letter *ḍh* is elided, the *repha* (the sound *r*) would not occur as it did before; for example, in the form *parivraḍhayya gataḥ*. However, these faults arise when the elision of the *hal* (consonant) is applied.
"He speaks of one who is *parivṛḍha*," and so forth.

But how is it that when the analysis (*vigraha*) is made with the word *parivṛḍha*, the derivation of the causative suffix (*ṇic*) is understood to arise from the root *vṛ* itself? To this he says: "Of *saṃgrāmayati*," and so forth.

Since the causative suffix (*ṇic*) is already established by the rule "From a nominal stem, in the sense of a verbal root, abundantly, as if it were an *iṣṭhan* suffix" (Dhātupāṭha, Gaṇasūtra 186), the inclusion of the form *saṃgrāma*—which is accompanied by a prefix—in the [Dhātupāṭha] list is for the purpose of restriction: so that the derivation of the causative suffix may occur only from *saṃgrāmayati* when it is accompanied by a prefix, and not elsewhere.

Thus, since the derivation of the causative suffix (*ṇic*) is desired only from the root *saṃgrāmayati* when it is accompanied by a prefix, and not from any other, therefore—even if the analytical explanation (*vigraha*) is made as "he causes [someone] to be powerful" (*parivṛḍham ācaṣṭe*)—nevertheless, when the suffix *ṇic* is derived from the word *vṛḍha*, the *lakāra* (verbal suffix) that occurs belongs only to that which begins with the element from which the *ṇic* was prescribed, according to the technical rule regarding the mention of a suffix (*pratyayagrahaṇa-paribhāṣā*). This is because the designation of "root" (*dhātu-saṃjñā*) is prescribed for that which begins with such an element, by the rule *Pāṇini 1.3.32*.

Because of that, since there is no inclusion [of the word *parivṛḍha*] by the mention of "another *tiṅ*-ending" (*pareḥ tiṅ-antasya*), [the rule applies] to a *tiṅ*-ending word following that [word] which does not end in *taṅ*. Thus, in the case of *parivṛḍhayati*, the *nighāta* accent is established by [Pāṇini 8.1.28].
However, if the suffix *ṇic* were derived from the word *parivṛḍha*, then the *lakāra* (the verbal ending) would not be subject to *nighāta*.
Furthermore, when the suffix *ṇic* is derived from the word *vṛḍha* and not from the word *parivṛḍha*, then the *ktvā* suffix also occurs after the word *vṛḍha* followed by the *ṇij*-ending.

By that [rule], when the compound *pari-vṛḍhena* is formed with the word *vṛḍha* ending in a *kta*-suffix according to Pāṇini 2.2.18, the replacement by *lyap* in the form *parivṛḍhayya* becomes established. However, if the suffix *ṇic* were derived from the word *parivṛḍha*, the *ktvā*-suffix would also be produced from the word *parivṛḍha* itself after it has taken *ṇic*; consequently, no compound could occur there. This is because, according to Pāṇini 2.2.18 (*kugatiprādayaḥ*), prefixes such as *ku*, *gati*-words, and *prādi*s are compounded with another word that is semantically related (*samartha*), and in this case, there is no other word ending in a *kta*-suffix following *pari*.

For this is indeed a single word ending in a *kta* suffix together with the prefix *pari*; since the prefix *pari* is included within that very [word], the substitution of *lyap* by the rule beginning with "asati ca samāse" (Pāṇini 7.1.37) would not otherwise apply. Thus:
*parivṛṃhitam*.
The counter-example for *vṛṃhi* is "parivṛhitam," which is derived from *vṛh*. The example "kaṣṭaḥ" is derived from *kaṣ*.
In the group of verbal roots meaning "to injure," such as *kaṣ*, *śiṣ*, and so forth, the root *kaṣ* is recited.

What, then, is meant by "hardship" (*kṛcchra*)? To this he says: "Hardship is suffering. If this is so, then since a prohibition is being stated regarding suffering—which is a property of living beings—it would not apply to fire and the like? To this he says: "The cause of that [suffering], such as fire and so forth, is also called 'hardship'."

This is due to the metaphorical application of the name of the effect to the cause, as in the expression "the water of the Naṅvala river is a foot-disease. However, this must be considered: is it appropriate to employ a secondary (gauṇa) sense when the primary (mukhya) sense is available, or not? If, however, the word *kṛcchra* is derived from the root *kṛcchrayati*—formed by adding the suffix *ṇic* and then the suffix *ac* according to Pāṇini 3.1.134—such that it is etymologically explained as "that which causes difficulty," then the word *kṛcchra* applies primarily to fire and other such things as well, and thus there is no need for further deliberation. Furthermore, under this etymology, it is not contradictory to say that even the cause of that [fire], such as firewood and so forth, is called *kṛcchra*.
For that which causes distress necessarily becomes the cause of suffering. "Declaration" means "proposition";
the meaning is the manifestation of one's own intention through words.
"Grasping by way of generality" means...
Because no specific distinction is stated.

If the root *ghuṣ* is indeed listed in the *curādi* group as "ghuṣir aviśabde" [or "ghuṣir viśabde"], then it must take the *ṇic* suffix; yet, whether the *iṭ* augment is present or absent for that which ends in *ṇic*, there is no difference whatsoever. For instance, when the *iṭ* is present, after the elision of *ṇic* by [Pāṇini 6.4.51], the form becomes *ghoṣitam*; and even when the *iṭ* is absent, because there is no elision of *ṇic*, the resulting form is exactly the same.
Furthermore, there is no possibility for the prohibition of *iṭ* after that [root], because of the governing rule *ekācaḥ* [Pāṇini 7.2.10].

For the root *ghuṣir* belonging to the *bhūvādigaṇa* (Dhātupāṭha 653), there is simply no occurrence of the sense of "making sound" (*aviśabdane*); this is due to the inherent nature of the word's expressive power (*śabdaśaktisvābhāvyāt*). Therefore, what would be the point of a prohibition against "making sound"? To this, he says: "The prohibition of making sound," and so forth.

And if the *ṇic* were eternal (*nitya*), then, according to the manner described, the prohibition would be purposeless; consequently, it should not have been made at all. Yet it has been made; therefore, this very prohibition indicates that the *ṇic* added to roots such as *cur* for the sake of expressing a specific meaning is non-eternal (*anitya*). The example "jughuṣuḥ" illustrates the purpose of asserting its non-eternality.
For if impermanence did not exist, it would have to be said that "they caused it to be proclaimed. Regarding the word *arda*:
"arda" [is used] in the senses of "going" and "begging" (Dhātupāṭha 55). Regarding "far away" (*vidūram*):
it is called *vidūram* because it is "distant" (*dūram*) in a special or excessive sense; other than that is "not far away" (*avidūram*).
Furthermore, that which is proximate and not distant— that is, not excessively remote— should be understood as such.
Regarding the expression "the state of that is *ādidūryam*," the suffix *ṣyañ* is applied according to [Pāṇini 5.1.123] because it belongs to the *brāhmaṇādi* group.

But surely, since the suffix expressing the abstract state (*bhāvapratyaya*) following a *tatpuruṣa* compound that begins with the negative particle *nañ* is prohibited by the rule "not after [a word] preceded by *nañ*" (Pāṇini 5.1.121), the suffix *ṣyañ* should not occur here? To this he says: "Precisely for this reason," and so forth.

Furthermore, the status of being "subsequent" (*uttaratvam*) for the abstract suffix should be understood in relation to the suffixes *tva* and *tal*. In the word "study" (*adhyayanam*), the suffix *lyuṭ* is applied according to the rule "the *kṛtya*, *lyuṭ*, and others are used diversely" (Pāṇini 3.3.113).
"It is studied" (adhīyate) is "study" (adhyayanam); thus, the word *adhyayana* is used in the sense of the object (*karmasādhana*).

For if it were used in the sense of the action itself (*bhāvasādhana*), the construction "the quality performed by Devadatta" (*vṛtto guṇo devadattena*) would not be possible; rather, it would have to be "the performance of the quality by Devadatta" (*vṛttaṃ guṇasya devadattena*).
Furthermore, this [word] serves as a qualifier for the past participle (*niṣṭhā*).

The meaning is: "in the case of the suffix -niṣṭhā which denotes that [the Veda] is to be studied. Regarding the phrase "and there is the elision of the ṇi," the elision of the ṇi is prescribed for the purpose of prohibiting the application of the *pratyayalakṣaṇa* (the rule regarding the treatment of a suffix as present).

For if there were elision (*lopa*), the *guṇa* substitution would occur by virtue of the condition "as if the suffix were present" (*pratyayalakṣaṇa*). But when there is elision by *luk*, the *guṇa* would not occur because of the prohibition of the condition "as if the suffix were present" according to [Pāṇini 1.1.63].
Thus, it is said: "the *guṇa* has already taken effect."

A certain specific quality of study is what is referred to here by the term *guṇa*. This is because we observe the use of the past passive participle (*niṣṭhā*) in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāva*), as in the examples "the *vṛtta* of the *guṇa*" and "the *vṛtta* of the *pārāyaṇa*," where it is said that this [verb] *vṛt* is intransitive.

For the past passive participle (*niṣṭhā*) occurs in the sense of the abstract action (*bhāva*) for intransitive verbs, but not for transitive ones. Regarding the phrase "it [occurs] in the sense of the causative" (*sa ṇyarthe*), etc.:

when that [verb] has the causative meaning internalized (*antarbhāvita-ṇyartha*), then the root, functioning in the sense of the causative, becomes transitive—as in the case of the root *vṛdh* in the verse, "May the beautiful hymns cause you to grow."
How is this understood? To this he says: "produced by that," and so forth.
Nor should it be said that these are intransitive;
for "roots become transitive when accompanied by prepositions," and thus, due to being accompanied by a preposition, the root *vṛt* is transitive here.

But how is the sense of the causative (*ṇyartha*) understood [in the word *vṛtti*], given that it does not function as a causative? If its transitivity here were due to its being accompanied by a prefix (*sopasargatvāt*), and not because it functions as a causative, then just as the causative sense is not perceived in the phrase "Devadatta has experienced the fruit of his actions" (*anubhūtaḥ karmaphalo devadattena*), so too it would not be perceived in the phrase "produced by him" (*tena nirvṛttaḥ*). Yet it is indeed perceived; therefore, the transitivity of the word *vṛtti* arises precisely because it functions as a causative. And when it functions as a causative, then, with respect to the activity of the instigator (*prayojaka-vyāpāra*), its agent undergoes the state of being the object (*karmabhāva*).
By that prompted action, [the root] becomes transitive.
"In the same way here as well," and so forth:

because even though it is intransitive, it does not become transitive merely by its own nature, but rather while functioning in the sense of the causative (*ṇyartha*), therefore, in the case of *vṛtto guṇo devadattena*, the suffix *kta* will likewise occur with respect to the object precisely when [the root] functions in the sense of the causative.

Consequently, the irregular formation (*nipātana*) would be purposeless, because the desired form is established even without it. If one asks how this is so: when the suffix *kvā* is applied after the root *vṛt*, there is an option for the substitution of *iṅ* according to Pāṇini 7.2.56; however, in the case of the *niṣṭhā* suffix, the aforementioned substitution is prohibited by Pāṇini 7.2.15.
If this is so, for what purpose is that [suffix] used? To this he says: "That is performed," and so forth.

Sometimes the sense of the causative (*ṇyartha*) is expressed by the verbal root itself through the inclusion of the causative meaning; in that case, if the irregular formation (*nipātana*) were not applied, it would follow that the word could also be used in the sense of "studying" (*adhyayana*).
Therefore, some maintain that it is for the sake of excluding that [meaning].
"But others," and so forth.

Others, however, also maintain that *guṇa* is derived from the root *vṛt*; thus, both for the causative form (*ṇyant*) and the non-causative form (*aṇyant*), one says "the quality has functioned" (*vṛtto guṇaḥ*).

According to his opinion, the elision (*nipātana*) should not be performed at all; if it were to be performed, it should be understood as being for the sake of variety (*vaicitryārtha*). For example: *dāntaḥ*, *śāntaḥ*. [The roots] *śamu* and *damu* are used in the sense of "pacification" (*upaśama*) [as listed in the Dhātupāṭha, sūtras 1201 and 1203].

The long vowel [is applied] by the rule *hetumaṇṇic* [3.1.25], after the elision of *ṇi* and the prohibition of *iṭ* have been performed. Now, one might object: "But surely, because of the status of the elided element as if it were still present (*sthānivadbhāva*), the [longening] should not apply when there is an intervention? This is not so; for when an elision occurs by means of a specific grammatical injunction (*nipātana*), that elision cannot be designated as having a subsequent cause (*paranimitta*). Therefore, how could there be the status of being as if present (*sthānivadbhāva*)? Furthermore, the status of being as if present is prohibited in the rule prescribing the long vowel by the sūtra *na padānta* [1.1.57]. Thus we have *damitaḥ*, *śamitaḥ*.
The short vowel [of the suffix] is applied by the rule *mitāṃ hrasvaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.4.92).
Regarding the word *pūrṇaḥ*:
the root is *pūrī* in the sense of "to fill" (*āpyāyane*; Dhātupāṭha 1803).
The roots *div* and others, as well as *cur* and others [belong to the respective classes].
Regarding the form *dasta*:
[it is derived from] *tasu* "to throw up" (Dhātupāṭha 1212) [or "to diminish" (Dhātupāṭha)] and *dasu* "to bite" (Dhātupāṭha 1213).
In this case, the shortening of the vowel in the prefix *upa* is also prescribed as a nipātana (irregular formation).
Thus: *spaṣṭacchannaḥ*.
[The roots are] *spaś* in the sense of "afflicting" and "touching" (Dhātupāṭha 887) and *chad* in the sense of "covering" (Dhātupāṭha 1935).

Here, the shortening of the vowel in the penultimate position (*upadhā*) is also treated as an irregularity (*nipātana*). Thus, we have *jñapta*. The root *jñap* belongs to the *curādigaṇa*, as per the Dhātupāṭha entry: "√*jñap* [is used] in the senses of killing, pleasing, and sharpening" (DhP 1624); alternatively, it belongs to the *ghaṭādigaṇa*, as per the Dhātupāṭha entry: "√*jñā* [is used] in the senses of killing, pleasing, and sharpening, and it takes the augment *mic*" (DhP 811). From these roots, the causative suffix *ṇic* is applied.

"Regarding the statement *iṭ-pratiṣedho ṇiluk-ca*: by virtue of the word *ca* ('and'), in some instances the shortening of the penultimate vowel (*upadhā-hrasvatva*) is also prescribed as an irregularity (*nipātana*). [The roots] *ruṣa* in the sense of 'anger' (Dhātupāṭha 1670) and *ama* in the sense of 'motion and so forth' (Dhātupāṭha 465)—and not the *curādika* root *ama* in the sense of 'disease' (Dhātupāṭha 1720)—are intended here; this is because of the governing rule *ekācaḥ* (Pāṇini 7.2.10)."
The root *tvar* meaning "haste" (Dhātupāṭha 775) is preceded by the prefix *sam*.
The previously mentioned root *dhuṣ* is preceded by the prefix *pra*.
The previously mentioned root *svan* is preceded by the prefix *āṅ*.
In "āsvāntaḥ," there is a long vowel as before;
in "tūrṇaḥ," likewise.
The substitution of *ūṭh* occurs by the rule *jvaratvarasrivyavimavām upadhāyāḥ* [Pāṇini 6.4.20].

Regarding the phrase "preceded by *sam*" (*sampūrva*) and so forth: the scope of the root *ghuṣir* (listed as number 653 in the Dhātupāṭha, meaning "to sound") applies when it is not preceded by *sam* and is combined with the word *avi*—as in *ghuṣṭā rajjuḥ* ("the rope is sounded") and *ghuṣṭau pādau* ("the feet are sounded").

And the scope for this rule [of *sam-ghuṣir aviśabde*] exists when the prefix *sam-* is present and there is verbal expression (*viśabdana*): one says "he uttered a resonant sentence" (*saṃghuṣitaṃ vākyam āha*) or "he uttered a resonant speech" (*saṃghuṣṭaṃ vākyam āha*). When the prefix *sam-* is present but there is no verbal expression (*aviśabdana*), since both [rules] would otherwise apply, this [present rule] takes effect by virtue of its posteriority: "the two teeth are resonant" (*saṃghuṣṭau dantau*) or "the two teeth are resonated" (*saṃghuṣitau dantau*).
Regarding the phrase "of that preceded by *āṅ*" (*āṅpūrvasya*), etc.:
the scope for the prohibition of the suffix *iṭ* in the case of *svan* is provided by the rule *kṣubdhasvānta* (Pāṇini 7.2.18).

When it does not have the prefix *āṅ* and denotes the mind (*manas*), there is scope for the rule *svāntaṃ manaḥ*; when it has the prefix *āṅ*, there is the denotation of non-mind (*amana*). For example:
*āsvantaḥ devadattaḥ* (Devadatta is breathless) and *āsvanitaḥ devadattaḥ* (Devadatta is breathless).
When it has the prefix *āṅ* and denotes the mind, there is scope for the rule *svāntaṃ manaḥ*; when it has the prefix *āṅ*, there is the denotation of non-mind.

"‘*āsvantaḥ devadattaḥ*, *āsvanitaḥ devadattaḥ*. When preceded by the prefix *āṅ*, if it denotes silence (*mauna*), this very option applies because it is subsequent [in the rules]: *āsvāntaṃ manaḥ*, *āsvanitaṃ manaḥ*. Regarding ‘*cāyateḥ*’: *cāyṛ* [is used] in the senses of honoring and perceiving” (Dhātupāṭha 880).
This rule is formulated for one who does not understand that the root *ci* (to gather) has the sense of "worship" (*pūjā*) when preceded by *apa*;
it is not, however, formulated for one who does understand this.
For instance, [the former] will say *apacita* from *ci*, while [the latter] will say *avacāyita* from *cāyati*.
"It is to be stated" means it is to be explained.
Regarding this, the explanation is as follows: the particle *ca* (and) is inserted here.

And that [particle *ca*] has the sense of an unexpressed conjunction (*anukta-samuccaya*). By that, the form *apacitiḥ* is also derived as a nipātana (irregular formation). And regarding this nipātana, it must be stated that when the suffix *ktin* follows the root *cāy*, the substitution of *ci* occurs invariably. Since the root *hvṛ* (meaning "crookedness," Dhātupāṭha 931) is anudātta, the prohibition of the augment *iṭ* already applies; therefore, this statement is for the purpose of prescribing the substitute. Thus, the absence of the substitute *hyu* is prescribed as a nipātana.

This refers to what was obtained by the preceding sūtra. The mention of the plural number is so that the irregular formation (nipātana) occurs only in the plural; therefore, in other cases, one has only *aparihyutaḥ*, *aparihyuḥ*, and *aparihyutau*. [The commentary states: "The augment *iṭ* and the guṇa substitution are irregularly formed."
Because of the word "and" (*cakārāt*), there is also the absence of the substitution of *hyu* for these [roots]. Regarding the statement beginning with "*grasu*, *skanbhu*, *stanbhu*," etc.:

*grasu* and *glasu* mean "to eat" (Dhātupāṭha 630, 631); *skanbhu* and *stanbhu* are Vedic roots (sautra-dhātu), as they are included in the rule *stambhustumbhuskambhuskumbhuskuñbhyaḥ śnuśca* (Pāṇini 3.1.82). Examples are *skabhitam* and *stabhitam*.
By the rule *aniditām* [6.4.24], there is the elision of the nasal (*n*).
Thus we have *stabdha*, as in *stabdhab*, *stabdham*.
By [8.2.40], there is the substitution of *dh*; by [8.4.53], there is the substitution of the voiced unaspirated stop (*jaś*).
Regarding the term *uttabhitam*:
by [Pāṇini 6.4.61], there is the substitution of the preceding vowel with its homogeneous counterpart (*pūrvasavarṇa*).
This is because the word *stabhita* does not occur when preceded by any other prefix.
If it were so, the formation of the root with the prefix *ut-* would be purposeless;
for it is said, "from *cat* and *kas*"—
where *cat* (DhP 865, 866) means "to beg" (*cade yācane*) and *kas* (DhP 860) means "to go."

Now, one might object: "In the Sūtra, the plural form *vikastāḥ* is heard; therefore, how can this [word] be cited from the Vṛtti in the singular form *vikastaḥ*? To this he replies: "The formation is with respect to plurality; *vikastāḥ* is the plural.
In the Sūtra, *grasita* and the others are formed as a Dvandva compound; therefore, the plural is used in reference to that [compound].
In the commentary (*vṛtti*), however, this word *vikasta* is not compounded;
nor is the plural number intended for its meaning, which is why it is cited in the singular.
[The phrase] "in others" (*apareṣu*).
