Regarding [the rule] "in the case of *viśastṛ* and so forth":
the intention is that the plural number was not employed there because the plural sense is absent, since the case endings are specified individually.
[The forms] *śaseḥ*, *vipūrvasya śaṃseḥ*, and *śāseḥ* [are derived from the following roots]:
*śasu* in the sense of "harming" (Dhātupāṭha 727), *śaṃsu* in the sense of "praising" (Dhātupāṭha 728), and *śāsu* in the sense of "instructing" (Dhātupāṭha 1075). [Examples include:
*tarītāram* and *varītāram*.
The vowel lengthening [is applied] by the rule *vṛto vā* [Pāṇini 7.2.38].

Regarding the form *varūtrīḥ*: the suffix *ṅīp* is applied by the rule *varūtrī* [Pāṇini 4.1.5]; from that which ends in this suffix, the nominative singular case ending *jas* is added; then, by the rule *jasi ca* [Pāṇini 6.1.106], there is the long vowel of the homogeneous preceding sound (*pūrvasavarṇadīrgha*).
Regarding the statement "in the case of *jas*, there is the pronunciation of the preceding homogeneous vowel," and so forth:

[an objection is raised]—"But once the *yaṇ* substitution has been applied, the form should be *varūtryaḥ*; how then does *varūtrayaḥ* come to be? To this he says: "It is Vedic (*chāndasa*)," and so forth.
For, by virtue of being Vedic, when shortening (*hrasvatva*) has been applied, the rule *jasi ca* [Pāṇini 7.3.109] prescribes *guṇa* as an exception (*apavāda*) to the *yaṇ* substitution.

"Prapañcārtham" means "for the sake of detailed exposition. For it is said in the Dhātupāṭha (1651), "The root *pac* signifies expansion," and thus from that very root ending in *ā*, the form *prapañca* is derived.
The term *prapañca*, however, has the sense of "making clear. For an explanation given in detail becomes clear.
Now, why is there not a grammatical derivation (*nipātana*) for the sake of establishing the word *varūtrī*? To this he says: "For the word *vaktr*" and so forth.

Regarding the words beginning with *jvalate*: *jvala* means "to blaze" (Dhātupāṭha 831), *kṣara* means "to move" (Dhātupāṭha 851), *ṭu vama* means "to vomit" (Dhātupāṭha 849), and *ama* means "motion and so forth" (Dhātupāṭha 465).
The use of the particle *iti* is for the purpose of illustration; that is, the particle *iti* is used to indicate other similar types as well.
What is established by this? He says: "Therefore, in some cases," and so forth.
The particle *ca* serves the purpose of drawing forward [the preceding rule] by the phrase *chandasi* (in Vedic). Because it is drawn forward, it is not connected with what follows;
consequently, the subsequent prescription applies without distinction, as in the examples: *āste*, *śete*, *vaste*.
The roots *ās* "to sit" (Dhātupāṭha 1021), *śīṅ* "to sleep" (Dhātupāṭha 1032), and *das* "to cover" (Dhātupāṭha 1023) [are included].

Due to their belonging to the *adādi* class, there is elision (*luk*) of the *śap* suffix according to Pāṇini 3.1.68. Because of the mention of the term *ārdhadhātuka*, the substitution of *iṇ* for the *sārvadhātuka* suffix does not occur here.

But is it not the case that this rule, *[[Pāṇini 7.2.76]]*, is understood as being for the purpose of restriction—namely, "the augment *iṭ* occurs after the roots beginning with *rud* only before a *sārvadhātuka* suffix, and not after others"?
One should not entertain the suspicion of a contrary restriction, such as "after the roots beginning with *rud*, [the augment *iṭ* occurs] only before a *sārvadhātuka* suffix.
For if such a restriction were to exist, then the augment *iṭ* would not apply to the suffix *san* following a root beginning with *rud*, because it would have been excluded by the restriction.

Furthermore, in the rule *rudavidamuṣagrahi...* [Pāṇini 1.2.8], the mention of the root *rud* would be redundant, because the status of being *kit* is already established by the rule *...* [Pāṇini 1.2.10].

Therefore, there is no suspicion here of a reversed restriction (i.e., that the rule might mean "the suffix is *kit* only after *rud* etc."). One might argue: "The restriction will be 'the *sārvadhātuka* suffix is *kit* only after *rud* etc., and not after others'; thus, there is no need for the mention of *ārdhadhātuka* for the purpose of excluding the *sārvadhātuka*. To this, he says: "After *rud* etc. and so forth.

When this rule [Pāṇini 7.2.76] is understood as having the purpose of restriction (*niyamārtha*), some dull-witted student might conceive of a contrary restriction. In that case, while one is attempting to understand the intended restriction according to the principle just mentioned, there would be "cognitive complexity" (*pratipattigaurava*). The particle *iti* is used here in the sense of a reason (*hetau*).

Since cognitive complexity arises when this rule [7.2.76] is understood as having the purpose of restriction, for that very reason, why is the mention of *ārdhadhātuka* not made? It is so that it should not be necessary.

If [the augment] *iṭ* were to belong to the root (*dhātu*), then the prohibition of *iṭ* for the affix by the rule "after a monosyllabic root that is unaccented in its original enunciation" (Pāṇini 7.2.10) would be purposeless, because there would be no possibility of its application;

this is also because of the specific statement "the past participles [are used after] *śīṅ*" (Pāṇini 1.2.19). For if the augment *iṭ* were added to the root, it would not be possible for the affixes *ktvā* and *niṣṭhā* to be considered "with *iṭ*" (*seṭ*).

In that case, why is it not for the purpose of preventing [the substitution] from occurring in the nominal stem and suffix in forms such as *vṛkṣātva* and *vṛkṣatā*? It cannot be for this purpose either, because the term "dhātoḥ" (of a verbal root) is understood to carry over from the rule "ṛta iddhātoḥ" [Pāṇini 7.1.100].

But even so, [the substitution] would still apply in cases such as *lūbhyām* and *lūbhiḥ*, because here the status of being a verbal root (*dhātutva*) is not destroyed by the nominal stem (*pratipadika*) status of the base, on the grounds that "forms ending in *kvip* do not abandon their status as verbal roots" (Vyāḍi-Pāṇini 132). Therefore, is it not proper to include the term *ārdhadhātuka* for the purpose of preventing this from occurring here? This is not the case; for in rule 7.1.100, the word *dhātu* is understood as referring to its own form (*svarūpa*).
Consequently, here too, the word *dhātoḥ*, which is being carried over [from a previous rule], is carried over in that very same sense.

Because the *iṭ* augment is prescribed for that which is ordained by the rule "of the root" (*dhātoḥ*), there is no possibility of the application of *iṭ* in cases such as *lūbhyām* and *lūbhiḥ* if the term "ārddhadhātuka" were not included [in the rule].

The same applies to forms such as *jugupsate*; for here the suffix *san* is not prescribed by the rule "of the root," but rather by specifically taking up the roots *gup* and others in their own form.
Therefore, it should be understood that the inclusion of the term "ārddhadhātuka" is not intended for the purpose of excluding those cases.

In the rule *ṛta iddhātoḥ* [Pāṇini 7.1.100], there would be the inclusion of the word *dhātu* as its own form (*svarūpa*). In that case, the qualification *ṛtaḥ* would not be applied to it, because that [qualification] is impossible within the word *dhātu*. Therefore, it is understood that the qualification applies to its meaning; this is the conclusion.

Alternatively—in that context, two [types of] *ārdhadhātuka* are included by means of ellipsis (*tantra*): one consisting of a word denoting meaning (*arthapada*), and the other consisting of a word denoting its own form (*svarūpapada*). Therein, the former is useful in that [rule], while the latter is useful here; thus, there is no fault whatsoever. Therefore, the mention of *ārdhadhātuka* is solely for the purpose of avoiding the burden of comprehension (*pratipattigaurava*).
What is the purpose of mentioning *iṭ* here, given that the mention of *iṅ* continues from [Pāṇini 7.2.8]? To this he says: "While *iṭ* is being carried over," and so forth.
For that mention of *iṭ* is connected with the prohibition; therefore, if that were to continue, its [prohibition] would also continue.
To prevent that, the mention of *iṭ* is made once again.

But surely, a prohibition can only occur when there is a possibility of application; and since no *iṭ* is obtained for an *ārdhadhātuka* suffix beginning with *val* by any other rule, this must be understood as an injunction (*vidhi*) due to the absence of any prior application, not a prohibition (*pratiṣedha*). This is not so; from this very statement of a prohibition, an injunction is also inferred.
Surely there is an injunction of *iṭ* for an *ārdhadhātuka*, since [the grammarian] teaches a prohibition of it for those beginning with *val*.

Why is there a reiteration of *iṭ* here? This [repetition] should be understood as an injunction (*vidhi*). Since the augment *iṭ* is already established for these two roots—*ṣṇu* (listed as 1038 in the Dhātupāṭha) meaning "to flow forth," and *kramu* (listed as 473 in the Dhātupāṭha) meaning "to step"—this statement is for the purpose of restriction (*niyama*), so that it may apply only in the domain of non-middle-voice (*anātmanepada*) forms, and not elsewhere.

But is it not the case that because the root *snai* ends in a consonant (*ugantatvāt*), there is a prohibition [of *iṭ*] when a *kit* suffix or the desiderative (*san*) follows? Could its statement not also be for the purpose of providing an option (*vidyartham*)? This is not so; for the rule *ārdhadhātukasyeḍvalādeḥ* [Pāṇini 7.2.35] is understood to be in force. Therefore, this present rule is understood to apply specifically to the domain where that [general] application would otherwise occur. Furthermore, the desiderative (*san*) and the *kit* suffixes are not the domain of that application, because they constitute the domain of exceptions (*apavāda*) to it.

The term *ātmanepada-nimitta* is in the nominative dual. To show that this qualifies the roots *snū* and *kram*, he says "provided that" (*na cet*), etc. He asks: "And where, then, are these [roots] the cause for the *ātmanepada*?"

Does [the rule] apply even where those two possess merely the fitness for the *ātmanepada*, and thus they are causes for the *ātmanepada*? Or does it apply only where the *ātmanepada* actually occurs based upon them? He asks this with the words "where," etc. Here is the explanation: "Where the *ātmanepada* based upon them is possible, there they are the causes for the *ātmanepada*.

What, then, is that [where it occurs]? He says: "In the case of the action (*bhāva*), the object (*karman*), the agent as object (*kartṛkarman*), and the reciprocal action (*karmavyatihāra*), and in sequence."
For in these cases, the *ātmanepada* [middle voice] occurs by virtue of the sequence of the bases (*āśraya*).
By the word "etc. (*ādi*), the inclusion of creation (*sarga*) and so forth is intended.
"Cause" (*nimitta*) means the instrumental factor (*kāraṇa*).
Furthermore, that which does not perform an action cannot be a cause.

However, where even though it does not perform an action, there is the designation of "cause" with respect to a grain-storing jar (*kusūla*) or seeds and the like, in those cases, such usage is figurative by virtue of its suitability (*yogyatā*).

Therefore, wherever the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) occurs based on the sequence [of the verbal root], it is understood that in those instances—such as in the case of the abstract action (*bhāva*) or the object (*karman*)—those two constitute the primary causes for the middle voice.
Regarding the phrase "by that" (*tena*) and so forth:
because it is thus, wherever the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) occurs by depending on those two, those two constitute the cause for the middle voice.
Therefore, this prohibition applies when the middle voice is present, not when it is absent.
Since [the suffix] does not occur in the *ātmanepada*, it is not possible for those two [roots, *snū* and *kram*] to possess the primary status of being causes for the *ātmanepada*.

Consequently, in forms such as *prasnavitā*, *prasnavitum*, *prasnavitavyam*, *prakramitā*, *prakramitum*, and *prakramitavyam*, although *snū* and *kram* acquire the designation of "cause" for the *ātmanepada* because they are eligible for it, nevertheless, the prohibition does not apply. For here there is no primary causality for the *ātmanepada*, due to the absence of the *ātmanepada* [suffix]. [The example given is: *prāpnoṣīṣṭa*.

In the sense of benediction (*āśis*), the suffix *liṅ* is used; by [Pāṇini 1.3.13], the *ātmanepada* endings are applied; by [Pāṇini 3.4.107], *suṭ* is added before *ti* and *tha*; then *ṣatva* and *ṣṭutva* are applied.
Thus we have *prakramiṣīṣṭa*.
Here, by [Pāṇini 1.3.42], the *ātmanepada* ending is used because the agent is intended, as the prefixes *pra-* and *upa-* are semantically connected.
Regarding the form *praśnoṣyate*:
the suffix *lṛṭ* is applied by the rule *lṛṭ śeṣe ca* [Pāṇini 3.3.13].
Regarding *pracikraṃsate*: [this example does not appear in the Kāśikā].

[The form] *pracikraṃsiṣyate* exists; [here] the desiderative suffix (*san*) takes the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) by the rule *pūrvavatsanaḥ* (Pāṇini 1.3.62). [Regarding the phrase] "in all cases," and so forth.

In forms such as *yuktaṃ prakraṃsīṣṭa* and *prasnīṣīṣṭa*, the roots *snū* and *kram* serve as the cause for the middle voice (*ātmanepada*), because the middle voice is prescribed [after them]. But in the case of *pracikraṃsata*, how can the root *kram* be the cause for the middle voice? For here the middle voice does not occur by depending on the root *kram*; rather, what is it? It is another verbal root ending in the suffix *san*. To this he says: "Even from that which ends in *san*" and so forth.
For even the middle voice that is prescribed after a root ending in *san*—by the rule *pūrvavatsanaḥ* (Pāṇini 1.3.62)—[is caused by the underlying root].

Because of the statement "there too, as before," the nature of the verbal root (*dhātu*) is relied upon as the cause for the middle voice (*ātmanepada*). Although the middle voice is prescribed after a root with the suffix *san*, the intention is that the absence of that cause still exists there in the sequence.
Now, for what purpose is the mention of "cause" (*nimitta*) employed; why not simply say "in the middle voice"? To this he says: "The mention of the cause," and so forth.

Regarding *sīyuṭ*: that which has *sīyuṭ* as its initial element is *sīyuḍādi*; that after which the *ātmanepada* endings follow is *tatpara*, namely the suffix *syapratyaya*; that after which [the *ātmanepada*] follows further is *tatparapara*, namely the suffix *sanpratyaya*. The mention of "cause" (*nimitta*) is for the purpose of ensuring that there be a prohibition of both these [suffixes]. Among them, for the sake of prohibiting *sīyuḍādi*, [examples are] *prasnoṣīṣṭa* and *prakraṃsīṣṭa*; and for the sake of prohibiting *tatparapara*, [an example is] *pracikraṃsiṣyata*. For in this case, if the mention of "cause" were not made, then the word "in the *ātmanepada*" would be understood as a locative of reference (*parasaptamī*).

Furthermore, in forms such as *pra-snīṣīṣṭa* and *prakram-sīṣṭa*, since there is an *ārdhadhātuka* suffix following the *ātmanepada* [suffix], and since the augment *sīyuṭ* belongs to that *ātmanepada*, a prohibition [of *iṭ*] pronounced with reference to the *ātmanepada* would not apply because it is only a part of that [augment].

In the case of *pracikraṃsiṣyata*, if "in the *ātmanepada*" were understood as a locative of reference (*parasaptamī*), then—given that the mention of the "specified" (in P. 1.1.66) is for the purpose of immediate sequence—the prohibition of *iṭ* after the *saN* would not occur when there is an intervention by the [suffix] *syen*. However, when "cause" (*nimitta*) is taken [as the meaning of the locative], it does occur.
For in all these cases, *snau* and *kram* possess the status of being causes for the *ātmanepada* affix as appropriate.
Therefore, the mention of "cause" (*nimitta*) must be made.

Someone might have the misconception that since the *ātmanepada* affix is observed after the root *snau* in the form *prasnavitrīyate*, the root *snau* must therefore be the cause of the *ātmanepada*, and thus the prohibition [of the *yaṅ* suffix] would apply. To dispel this, he says: "In this case, one acts like one who emits urine," and so forth.

In some places, the reading is "he acts like one who asks questions" (*praśnavitāram ivācarati*); however, that is not tenable. For the suffix *kyaṅ* is not prescribed after an object (*karman*), but rather after a word ending in a case-suffix (*subanta*) denoting the agent (*kartṛ*).
Therefore, this reading is due to a scribal error.

The form *prasnavitēva ācarati* is derived from the root ending in the suffix *tṛc*. By the rule *kartuḥ kyaṅ salopaśca* [Pāṇini 3.1.11], the suffix *kyaṅ* is applied; by the rule *rīṅ ṛtaḥ* [Pāṇini 7.4.27], the substitution *rīṅ* occurs.

While the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) is prescribed for roots ending in *kyaṅ*, it is prescribed specifically for those that end in the marker *ṅ*. But is the root *snau* itself marked with *ṅ*? No; rather, it is the form ending in *kyaṅ* that is so marked.
Therefore, since only that which ends in *kyan* is the cause for the middle voice (*ātmanepada*), and not the root *snau*, the prohibition does not apply.
As for the phrase "but in the case of *kram*" and so forth:
because of the mention of the "cause" (*nimitta*), the prohibition must occur only when the middle voice is actually present, and not when it is absent.
The prohibition [of the *ṇiṅ* affix] regarding the agent (*kartṛ*) does not apply here; therefore, it is added as a supplement (*upasaṃkhyāna*).
In the examples "she has begun" (*prakrāntā*) and "she has commenced" (*upakrāntā*), [the rule] Pāṇini 1.3.42 applies.

Is this not the domain of the *ātmanepada* for the root *kram* when preceded by the prefixes *pra-* and *upa-*, since that rule prescribes the *ātmanepada* for *kram*? Indeed, this is the domain of the *ātmanepada* for *kram*.
"Having the middle voice as its domain" (*ātmanepadaviṣaya*) means that for which the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) is the domain;
[as in the examples] "one should begin" (*prakramitavyam*) and "one should undertake" (*upakramitavyam*).
By the rule *[[3.4.70]]*, the *kṛtya* suffix is used here in the sense of the abstract state (*bhāva*) or the object (*karman*). Regarding the form *niṣkramitā*:
by the rule *idudupadhasya* *[[8.3.41]]*, the *visarjanīya* is replaced by *ṣ*.

Why [is it] "preceded by *ni-*"? Because there is no occurrence of the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) for the root *kram*, this [suffix] does not apply here to the middle voice. Now, why does it not occur in cases such as *prasnusūṣati*, *prasnutaḥ*, and *prasnutavān*, since the root *snau* is not here within the domain of the middle voice? To this he says: "of *snau*" and so forth.

Now, one might object: since the prohibition of *iṭ* by the rules "śrayukaḥ kiti" [Pāṇini 7.2.11] and "na vṛdbhyaḥ" [Pāṇini 7.2.12] finds its scope in other roots ending in long *ū*, shouldn't this very [prohibition] apply here by virtue of being subsequent, rather than the [general] prohibition? This is not so; for it was stated previously that the prohibitive rule is stronger. The purpose is so that the prohibition may apply to the specific prescription based on the mere presence of the root *iṇ*. By stating "graha uttarasya" and "graha," he demonstrates that the fifth case (*pañcamī*) is intended.

If this is so, then should the mention of *iṅ* (the verbal root *i*) be made? It need not be made; for that [mention] follows by anuvṛtti from the preceding context. For that was indicated in the nominative case, while here the purpose is served by an indication in the genitive (*ṣaṣṭhī*). This is not a fault; because of the rule "The fifth case [is used] in the sense of the sixth" (Pāṇini 1.1.67), the word *grahaḥ*—which is in the fifth case—will effect the status of the sixth case for the [preceding term].
Thus: *jagṛhiva*, *jagṛhim*.

By the rule *grahādisūtra* [Pāṇini 6.1.16], there is vocalization (*samprasāraṇa*). Thus, in forms such as *grāhitā* and *grāhiṣyate*, why does the augment *iṭ* (of the *ciṇvadiṭ* type) not occur? To this he says: "Of that which is the subject under discussion," and so forth. This lengthening applies to that *iṭ* which is the subject under discussion as being part of the *ārdhadhātuka* suffix; it does not apply to the *ciṇvadiṭ*, because that is not the subject under discussion.
By the term *ciṇvat*, the state of being like *ciṇ* (*ciṇvadbhāva*) is indicated.
The augment *iṭ* is said to be present when [the suffix] behaves like *ciṇ*.

In the form *grāhita*, the suffix *tās* is applied by [Pāṇini 3.1.33], the ātmanepada is applied because it denotes the state (*bhāva*) or the object (*karman*) by [Pāṇini 1.3.13], the substitution of *ḍā* is applied by [Pāṇini 2.4.85] et seq., there is the elision of the *ṭi* (the penultimate vowel), and the augment *iṭ* is applied by [Pāṇini 6.4.62] et seq.; due to the *ciṇ*-like behavior, there is vṛddhi.

Now, regarding the forms *jarīgṛhitā* and *jarīgṛhītum*: why does the long vowel not occur here after the root *gṛh* with the suffix *yaṅ*, when the suffixes *tṛn* and *tumun* have been applied and the elision of *ya* and the elision of *a* have taken place? [Answer: Because the word "optionally" (*vā*) in the subsequent rule applies as a remainder (*śeṣabhūta*) to both rules, and thus it is understood as a restricted option (*vyavasthitavibhāṣā*). Alternatively, the view that the term "prescribed" (*vihita*) serves as a qualifier is explained here:
the augment *iṭ* is prescribed for the meaning of the root *gṛh*; for that [augment], the long vowel occurs.

And the augment *iṭ* is not prescribed here for the root *grah*; from what, then, would it arise? It would arise from the *yaṅ*-intensive form. Therefore, there is no possibility of lengthening (*dīrgha*) here. Now, why was it not stated simply as "for *grah*, [the augment *iṭ* occurs] before *īṭ* and *liṭ*"? What is the purpose of mentioning "lengthening" (*dīrgha*)? It cannot be done in this way; for if that were so, the operation of *īṭ* would not apply to *iṭ*. Consequently, in the form *agrahīt*, the elision of *sic* by the rule "before *īṭ*" (Pāṇini 8.2.28) would not occur, and the prohibition "not before *iṭ*" (Pāṇini 7.2.4) would also apply. Furthermore, in the forms *agrahīḍhvam* and *agrahīdhvam*, the substitution of the retroflex (*mūrdhanya*) by the rule "of *iṭ*" (Pāṇini 8.3.79) would also follow.

Since the substitution of the long vowel (*dīrgha*) occurs, the grammatical operation of *iṭ* is applicable to it by virtue of its status as a *sthānivadbhāva*; thus, only the long vowel is prescribed. [In forms such as] *variṣīṣṭa* (the example given in the *Kāśikā* is *vivariṣīṣṭa*), the augment *iṭ* is applied according to [Pāṇini 7.2.42]. [The form] *vistariṣīṣṭa* is the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) in the passive sense. [The form] *prāvāriṣṭām* is likewise.

By the rule *tasthasthamipāṃ tāntantāmaḥ* [Pāṇini 3.4.101], the suffix *tas* becomes *tām*; is the augment *iṭ* applied here as prescribed generally? [The answer is yes]. Then there is the *vṛddhi* strengthening by the rule *sici vṛddhiḥ*. Thus we have *prāvāriṣuḥ*.
By the rule *sijabhyastavidibhyaśca* [Pāṇini 3.4.109], the suffix *jhi* is replaced by *jus*.
No example for the root *vṛṅ* has been presented, because the formation of the *parasmaipada* endings is impossible for it.
[The forms] *prāvariṣṭa* and *prāvarīṣṭa* [are derived] by [the rule] Pāṇini 7.2.42, which prescribes the augment *iṭ*. [The form] *vuvūrṣate* [is derived as follows:]...

By [Pāṇini 1.2.9], there is the *kittva* (the status of being marked with *k*) of the suffix *san*; by [Pāṇini 6.4.16], there is lengthening (*dīrgha*); by [Pāṇini 7.1.102], there is the substitution of *u* [for the vowel of the root] when preceded by a labial (*oṣṭha-pūrva*), followed by the substitution of *ra* for the semivowel (*raparatva*). Why does this not occur here in the cases *cikīrṣati* and *jihīrṣati*, since the application [of the rule] would exist once the lengthening has been performed? To this he says: "*cikīrṣati, jihīrṣati*. The meaning is already explained. Since the augment *iṭ* would otherwise be required due to the root being marked with an acute accent (*udātta*), this rule is commenced to provide an option.
The term "in the ātmanepada" is a locative of proximity (*parasaptamī*).
This is also a qualifier of *sic*.

If this were so, then *liṅ* would not be qualified, and consequently, *liṅ* would also apply in the case of parasmaipada endings. This is not the case; for there is the governing rule "after [a root] beginning with *val*" (Pāṇini 7.2.35), and because *liṅ* in the parasmaipada lacks the addition of *yāsuṭ* and the like.

Regarding the phrase "ātmanepadapare": that [suffix] after which the *ātmanepada* follows is so described. And this [condition] is connected only with the term *sic*, not with the term *liṅ*; for the mention of *ātmanepada* functions as a qualifier specifically with respect to *sic*.
Regarding "vṛṣīṣṭa":
because of the *kittva* (the property of being marked with *k*) by the rule "uśca" [Pāṇini 1.2.12], there is an absence of *guṇa*.
Regarding "āstīrṣīṣṭa".
As before? [This refers to] the substitution of *kit* and lengthening (*dīrghatva*), and so forth.

Regarding "after *avṛt*": the elision of *sic* occurs by [Pāṇini 8.2.27], "after a short vowel, from a stem. Since roots ending in *ṛ* are *anudātta*, a prohibition [of the augment *iṭ*] would otherwise apply; therefore, this statement is made for the purpose of providing an option.
Regarding "dhvṛṣīṣṭa":
the root *dhvṛ* means "to be distressed" (*hūcrchane*; Dhātupāṭha 1.39).
By [Pāṇini 1.3.13], the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) is applied.
In this way, the ātmanepada ending should be understood in other instances as well. As before, due to the *kittva* designation, there is an absence of *guṇa*. Thus: *smṛṣīṣṭa*.
The root *smṛ* means "to remember" (*cintāyām*;
Dhātupāṭha 933). Regarding the form *cyoṣīṣṭa*, it belongs to the group beginning with *cyuṅ*, *chyaṅ*, and *jyuṅ* (the *cyuṅ* and *chyaṅ* do not exist in the Dhātupāṭha).
(Dhātupāṭha 955, 956).
Here, because of the *ṅit* designation, the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) is used in the active sense (*kartari*).
Thus: "akṛṣata."
[This is] the substitution of *it* and so forth.

Now, why does [the substitution] not occur in *saṃskṛṣīṣṭa* and *samaskṛta*, since the root *kṛ* here has the prefix *suṭ* added by the rule "after *sam*, *pari*, and *upa*, when *kṛ* means 'to adorn'" (Pāṇini 6.1.137), and thus begins with a conjunct consonant (*saṃyogādi*)? To this he says: "*saṃskṛṣīṣṭa*" and so forth.

The term *upadeśa* (in the state of being taught) is understood to carry over from the rule *ekāca upadeśe 'nudāttāt* [Pāṇini 7.2.10]. Therefore, this [prohibition] must apply only to that which begins with a conjunct consonant (*saṃyogādi*) in the state of being taught; however, the root *kṛ* does not begin with a conjunct consonant in the state of being taught. What then? It follows after such a [conjunct]; hence, the prohibition does not apply. As for the phrase "and because it is not a part" (*abhaktatvācca*), etc., this is the resolution regarding the form *saṃskṛṣīṣṭa*, but not regarding *samaskṛta*.

[Objection: Is it not the case that, by the rule *amra hraḍāgamaḥ* ("the augment *hraḍ* occurs after *am*"), and by the principle *tadbhaktastadgrahaṇena gṛhrate* (Vārttika 20)—"that which is a part of it is included by the mention of it"—the augment *aṭ* is also included by the mention of the *aṅga* (stem)? And by the principle *tanmadhyapatitastadgrahaṇena gṛhrate* (Vārttika 21)—"that which falls within it is included by the mention of it"—the augment *suṭ* is also included by the mention of the *aṅga*? Thus, *karoti* would indeed have a *saṃyoga* (consonant cluster) at its beginning. Furthermore, because of the governing context (*adhikāra*) of *aṅga*, even a *saṃyoga* that is a constituent part of the *aṅga* is included here, due to proximity (*pratyāsatti*). Yet, in *saṃskṛṣīṣṭa*, the *saṃyoga* at the beginning is not a constituent part of the *aṅga*; and that which is a constituent part of the *aṅga* does not occur at the beginning of a *saṃyoga*. Therefore, the undesired application of *iṭ* does not arise here.
Here, by the rule "the substitution of *s* for the *m* of *sam* when followed by a labial" (Vārttika 936), the *m* of *sam* becomes *s*, and the preceding vowel becomes nasalized.

In the case of *samaskṛta*, as before, there is the elision of the suffix *sic*. The letter *ca* serves to carry forward the mention of the *ātmanepada*; therefore, the subsequent rule applies without distinction. This is because that which is carried forward (*anukṛṣṭa*) does not recur in what follows. The root *svṛ* ("to sound" and "to afflict") is from the first class (Bhvādi, No. 932); *ṣūṅ* ("the delivery of the fetus by living beings") is from the first class (Adādi, No. 1031); and *ṣūṅ* ("the procreation of living beings") is from the fourth class (Divādi, No. 1132).
The root *ghūñ* in the sense of "trembling" (*kampane*) belongs to the *svādi*, *kryādi*, and *curādi* groups (Dhātupāṭha 1255, 1487, 1385).
Among these, because of the governing rule *ekācaḥ* [Pāṇini 7.2.10], the first two groups are intended for inclusion, not the latter.

Examples of roots marked with an indicatory *ū* (*ūditaḥ*) include *gāhū* in the sense of "stirring" (*viloḍane*; Dhātupāṭha 649) and *gupū* in the sense of "protecting" (*rakṣaṇe*; Dhātupāṭha 395), and so forth.

Since these [roots] have anudātta svaritas as their accents, a prohibition [of iṭ] would otherwise apply; however, since the others have udātta accents, iṭ would necessarily apply. Therefore, this statement is for the purpose of providing an option.
Regarding "vigāḍhā," the application of ḍhatva and so forth should be understood as before.

Alternatively, for what purpose is the word *vā* (or) stated here? Since the word *vā* is understood from the rule *iṭ sani vā* [Pāṇini 7.2.41], why is it repeated? To this he says: "While *vā* is being understood," and so forth. For that previous mention of *vā* is connected with the optative (*liṅ*) and the aorist (*sic*); therefore, if it were to carry over, those two suffixes would also carry over. Consequently, this new mention of *vā* is for the purpose of excluding the *liṅ* and *sic* that were connected with the previous *vā*.

But would there not be a recurrence (*anuvṛtti*) of *liṅ* and *sic*? Therefore, this mention of *vā* is for the purpose of excluding *liṅ* and *sic*, which were connected with the preceding [rule]. But if there is a recurrence of *liṅ* and *sic*, then the mention of *svarati* would become redundant, since the option is already established by the preceding rule? This is not so; by the authority of the explicit statement (*vacana-prāmāṇyāt*), the mention of *svarati* is understood to be for the purpose of making it obligatory (*nityārtham*).

Alternatively, because of the mention of the *svarita* accent, the word "optionally" (*vā*) is excluded. Now, for what purpose is there a specific mention of the *vikaraṇas* (verbal suffixes) for the roots *sūti* and *sūyati*, rather than simply saying "after *sū*"? To this he says: "of *sūti* and *sūyati*" and so forth. If it were stated as "after *sū*," then according to the rule "when a root without an *anubandha* is mentioned, it does not include one with an *anubandha*" (Vyāḍiparibhāṣā 53), only the root *sū* "to impel" (Dhātupāṭha 1408) [or *ṣū* "to impel"] would be understood.

Therefore, for the purpose of excluding that [other root], the mention of the *vikaraṇa* must be made. If this is the objective, should one not simply mention *sūṅ*? This cannot be done; for if such a mention were made, according to the principle "when there is a choice between a root with a *vikaraṇa* and one without a *vikaraṇa*, the one with the *vikaraṇa* is taken," only *sūyati* would be included, and not *sūte*.
Therefore, the mention of the *vikaraṇa* is for the sake of excluding that.

The existence of this paribhāṣā is indicated by this very mention [of *dhūñ*]. If this [paribhāṣā] were not present, one would have mentioned *sūṅ*. Furthermore, if the mention of *dhūñ* with its anubandha were not made, then, by the "paribhāṣā of the one without an anubandha" (Vyāḍīya-paribhāṣā 53), there would be the apprehension of *ṣū* in the sense of "shaking" (*vidhūnane*) alone from the Dhātupāṭha (1398), and this is undesirable.
Therefore, the mention of the suffix with its *anubandha* (the letter *ṇ*) is for the purpose of excluding the meaning of "shaking off" (*vidhūnana*).
Regarding the rule beginning with *svarateḥ*:

the scope of this optional rule (*vikalpa*) is [the forms] *svaritā* and *svartā*; the scope of the rule *ṛddhanoḥ sye* [Pāṇini 7.2.70] is [the forms] *kariṣyati* and *hariṣyati*. When both [rules] would apply to the root *svarati*, the latter [rule] prevails by way of conflict (*vipratiṣedha*), resulting in the form *svariṣyati*.

Regarding the passage beginning with *kiti tu pratyaye*: the scope of the rule *śrayukaḥ kiti* [Pāṇini 7.2.11] is, for example, *sūtaḥ*, *sūtadāni*; the scope of this optional rule is, for example, *svartā*, *svaritā*; *sotā*, *savitā*; *dhautā*, *dhavitā*. When both rules would apply here, the prohibition by *śrayukaḥ kiti* [7.2.11] applies invariably by means of a *pūrvavipratiṣedha* (prior exclusion), resulting in *svṛtvā*, *sūtvā*, *dhūtvā*. And this is established precisely because the section containing the prohibitions (*pratiṣedhakāṇḍa*) is formulated before [the section containing the optional rules].

For it was stated previously—earlier—that the purpose of the formulation of the prohibition is so that there may be a prohibition of the mere root *iṇ*, which has not been specified by any particular rule of application.

This very matter—the formulation of the prohibition [of the *ṇic* suffix] for these roots—is referred to here by the term "prior prohibition" (*pūrvavipratiṣedha*), because it yields the same result as the prior prohibition. The roots are: *hiṃs* in the sense of injury (*hiṃsā*) and accomplishment (*saṃrāddhi*) (DhP 1193); *ṇaś* in the sense of disappearance (*adarśana*) (DhP 1194); *tṛp* in the sense of gratification (*prīṇana*) (DhP 1195); *dṛp* in the sense of exhilaration and delusion (*harṣa-mohana*) (DhP 1196); *duh* in the sense of wishing to harm (*jighāṃsā*) (DhP 1197); and *muh* in the sense of loss of consciousness (*vaicittya*).

(dhātupāṭhaḥ-1198), `ṇṇuha ddhadgiraṇe` (dhātupāṭhaḥ-1199), and `ṣṇiha prītau` (dhātupāṭhaḥ-1200)—these are the roots beginning with *radh*. Among these, since *tṛpyati* and *dṛpyati* are anudātta, the prohibition of *iṭ* would apply; however, for the remaining roots, since they are udātta, *iṭ* would apply obligatorily. Therefore, this statement is made to provide an option (*vikalpa*). Thus, [we have] "naṣṭā."
The augment *num* is applied by the rule *masjinaśor jhali* [Pāṇini 7.1.60].
The substitution of *ṣ* is applied by the rule *vraścādi-sūtra* [Pāṇini 8.2.36], followed by the substitution of *ṣṭu*. Thus, the form is *traptaḥ*.
Thus, by [Pāṇini 6.1.78], there is the substitution of *yaṇ*.
In the word “*tarpitā*,” there is the *guṇa* substitution for the light penultimate vowel.

In the case where the suffix *it* is absent, [the forms] are *drogdhā*, *megdhā*, *snodhyā*, and *snegdhetī*. Regarding the absence of the *it*-suffix: by the rule *vā druhamuhaṇṇuhaṇṇihām* [Pāṇini 8.2.33], there is the substitution of *gh*; by *jhaṣastathordho’dhaḥ* [8.2.40], there is the substitution of *dh*; and by *jhalāṃ jaś jhaśi* [8.4.53], there is the substitution of the *jaś* sound, which is the letter *g*.
Thus, one obtains *droḍhā*, *ñoḍhā*, *snoḍhā*, and *sneḍhā*.
As before, the application of the *ḍhatva* (substitution of *ḍh*) and other rules should be understood accordingly.

"Because of the restriction [imposed by] the *krādiniyama*, some desire an option for the *liṭ* [perfect tense] due to its subsequent position after the roots beginning with *radh*; thus, in the alternative case, forms such as *raradhva* and *raradhma* should also occur. "But others," and so forth.
For this indeed is the purpose of the preceding rule that prescribes the prohibition of *iṭ*: so that the prohibition may be stronger.
Therefore, because of the greater strength of this restrictive prohibition (*pratiṣedhaniyama*), there must invariably be *iṭ*.

In this regard, the intention of the earlier [authorities] is as follows: the strength of the prohibition arises from the force of the preceding rule prescribing the prohibition of *iṭ*, and not from the restrictive prohibition itself.

The intention of others is as follows: because the prohibition (*pratiṣedha*) is stronger, the restriction (*niyama*) regarding that property is also stronger, and not the prohibition alone; thus, when that [restriction] is stronger, its application occurs, and by that, it is proper for the *iṭ* augment to be present invariably. The restriction concerning the prohibition is precisely the restriction regarding roots beginning with *krā-* (Pāṇini 7.2.13), as in "rarandhiva" and "rarandhima."

The augment *num* [is applied] by [Pāṇini 7.1.58]. Why is the mention of *iṭ* repeated here when [the term] *iṭ* was already present [in the previous rule]? To this he says: "The mention of *iṭ* is for the sake of making it obligatory (*nitya*). For if the mention of *iṭ* were absent, since an option (*vikalpa*) is the subject under discussion, the application of *iṭ* would be optional.
Therefore, the mention of *iṭ* must be made for the sake of obligatoriness.

But surely, since the [substitution of] *iṭ* has already been established by the previous rule, this rule must necessarily be a permanent (*nitya*) injunction simply by virtue of its formulation? To this, he says: "For the formulation... and so forth. Since the previous rule allows for the optional application (*vikalpitatva*) of *iṭ* in the case of the *niṣṭhā* suffixes, this present formulation is made as a permanent rule to prevent the prohibition that would otherwise apply according to [Pāṇini 7.2.15]. In that context, if the mention of *iṅ* were not made here, then this present formulation would merely serve as an exception (*bādhaka*) to that very same prohibition; consequently, there would only be an option, and not a permanent injunction.

Therefore, the mention of *iṅ* must be made for the sake of making [the rule] obligatory (*nitya*). For if the mention of *iṅ* were made for the sake of obligatoriness, then because that would exclude the optionality, the prescription would be obligatory even in subsequent cases. To this he says: "In that very case," and so forth.

Moreover, optionality cannot be excluded by this mention of *iṅ*; because it is marked with a circumflex accent (*svarita*), it is by the power of the mention of *iṅ* itself [that the optionality is established].
Even though the mention of "option" (*vikalpa*) does not follow [from the previous rule], this rule is obligatory (*nitya*).
However, the recurrence of that very option is for the sake of what follows;

therefore, in the subsequent cases, there is indeed an option. The roots *iṣ* in the sense of "desire" (DhP 1351) and *ṣah* in the sense of "endurance" (DhP 852); as well as both *lubh* in the sense of "greed" (DhP 1238) and *lubh* in the sense of "delusion" (DhP 1305)—all are included, because no specific distinction is made.

The roots *ruṣa* in the sense of "anger" (*dhātupāṭha* 1670) and *ruṣa*, *riṣa* in the sense of "injury" (*dhātupāṭha* 1230, 1231)—all of these are udātta [roots]. Since the augment *iṭ* would apply obligatorily [to the suffixes mentioned], this rule is commenced for the purpose of making it optional.
The phrase "for that purpose" refers to this.
The purpose [of the word "vā"] is so that the option (*vikalpa*) may apply only to the root meaning "to desire" (*icchārtha*), and not to the other two.

However, those who do not read it as *uditam* explain it thus: since the option applies to what has been mentioned, they understand it as a fixed option (*vyavasthitavibhāṣā*) for the present context; or, because of its association with the root *sah* belonging to the *bhūvādigaṇa*, it will apply optionally only to the root meaning "to desire," and not to the other two.
Thus: *soḍhā*.
When the substitutions of *ḍha* for *dha*, *ṣṭu* for *ṣṭa*, and the elision of *ḍh* have been applied,
[the term] "ending in *i*" refers to roots such as *div* (DhP 1107) and *siv* (DhP 1108).

The roots *ṛdh* in the sense of "to increase" (Dhātupāṭha 1245); *bhrasj* in the sense of "cooking" (Dhātupāṭha 1284); *dambh* [or *dambhana*] in the sense of "deceiving" (Dhātupāṭha 1270); *śri* in the sense of "service" (Dhātupāṭha 897); *svṛ* in the senses of "sound" and "affliction" (Dhātupāṭha 932); *yū* in the sense of "mixing" [and "not mixing"] (Dhātupāṭha 1033); *ūrṇu* in the sense of "covering" (Dhātupāṭha 1039); *śriñ* in the sense of "supporting"; and *jñap* with the causative marker (*ṇic*) in the senses of "killing," "desiring," and "ascertaining."

The roots *ṣaṇ* in the sense of "giving" (Dhātupāṭha 1464) and *vana* and *ṣaṇa* in the sense of "sharing" (Dhātupāṭha 463, 444)—both are included here because no distinction is made between them. In this context, since *bhrasj* is anudātta, and since *lū*, *yū*, *ṛṇu*, and *bhṛñ* end in long vowels (*ugantatva*), the prohibition [of *iṭ*] by Pāṇini 7.2.12, *sani grahaguhīśca*, would apply. However, since the remaining roots are udātta, *iṭ* would be obligatory; it is for this reason that this optional rule is commenced. Thus: *dudyūṣati*.

From the root *div*, with the suffix *san*, there is the *kittva* (treatment as *kit*) of *san* by the rule *halāntacca* [Pāṇini 1.2.10]. Then, by the rule *cchvoḥ śūḍanunāsike* [Pāṇini 6.4.19], *ūṭh* is substituted, followed by the *yaṇ* replacement. There is reduplication of this form *dyūṣa*. By the rule *coḥ kuḥ* [Pāṇini 8.2.30], there is *cartva*—the substitution of *d* for the letter *dh*.

In the form *vibhrajjiṣati*, by the rule *stoḥ ścunā ścuḥ* [Pāṇini 8.4.40], there is *ścutva*—the substitution of *j* for the letter *d*. By the rule *sivādīnāṃ vāvyavāye’pi* [Pāṇini 8.3.71], there is the substitution of *d* for the letter *s*. Thus, *vibhrajjiṣati* is formed.
Regarding the form *bibharjati*:

by the rule *bhrasjo ropadhāyā ram anyatarasyām* (Pāṇini 6.4.47), the augment *ram* follows the letter *a*; because of the genitive case-nirdeśa in the phrase *ropadhayoḥ*, this *ram* causes the elision of both the *repha* (the letter *r*) and the upadhā (*s*), resulting in the form *bhartsati*. Then, by the rule *iṇkoḥ* (Pāṇini 8.3.57) and subsequently *ādeśapratyayayoḥ* (Pāṇini 8.3.59), the substitution of *ṣ* occurs. Regarding the forms *ghitsati* and *ghīpsati*: [these are derived from the root *ghas* with the desiderative suffix].

By this [rule], there is the substitution of *it* and *īt*. By the rule *khari ca* [Pāṇini 8.4.54], there is the substitution of *c*; the letter *bh* becomes *p*. As before, there is the elision of the reduplication (*abhyāsa*). By the rule *halāntācca* [Pāṇini 1.2.10], because of its status as *kit*, there is the elision of the nasal (*anunāsika*).

Thus: *ucchiśrīṣati*. Here, by the rule [1.2.9], there is the status of *kit*, and by the rule [6.4.16], there is lengthening; then follows the doubling (*dvirvacana*) and the operations pertaining to the reduplication.

The substitution of *ṣ* occurs by [Pāṇini 8.3.59] *ādeśapratyayoḥ*; then, by [8.4.63], the *c*-substitution of the *d* results in the letter *c*. Then, by [8.4.63], the *ś* is replaced by *cch*. Thus we have *sisvariṣati*.
Regarding the reduplication: for this [root] *svṛ*, there is the substitution of *at* by *urat* [Pāṇini 7.4.66], and *ra* follows as the substitute for *ṛ*.

Thus, *susvūrṣati*. As in the previous case, there is lengthening; then, by *udoṣṭhapūrvasya* [Pāṇini 7.1.102], there is the substitution of *u*, followed by *ra*; then, by *hali ca* [Pāṇini 8.2.77], there is lengthening; and then reduplication of *svūrṣa*. The operations pertaining to the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*) apply, and by *ādeśapratyayayoḥ* [Pāṇini 8.3.59], there is the substitution of *ṣ*.
In *yiyaviṣati*,
there is the substitution of *i* for the reduplicated syllable by [Pāṇini 7.4.80].
In *prorṇunūṣati*, [the same applies].
By the rule "of a second [element] beginning with a vowel" (Pāṇini 6.1.2), there is reduplication of the second monosyllabic element *nuṣ*, but the letter *r* is not reduplicated before it.

In the form *prorṇunaviṣati*, when the suffix *iṭ* is present and the marker *ṅ* is optionally applied according to Pāṇini 1.2.3, then *uvaṅ* substitution occurs; otherwise, *guṇa* substitution takes place.
"The root *bhuji* belonging to the *bhūvādika* class is what is intended here.
Now, why is the root *ṅubhṛñ* belonging to the *jauhotyādika* class not intended? To this he says: "Because of the mention with the affix *śap*" and so forth.

If the intention were to include the root *bhṛ* of the *jauhotyādika* class, which has the meaning of supporting and nourishing, then one would have made the mention simply as "*bhṛ*"; one would not have made the mention as "*bhara*" with the affix *śap*. Since the mention is indeed made with *śap*, it is understood that the root belonging to the *bhūvādika* class is intended.
In *bubhūrṣati*,
the lengthening of the vowel occurs as before due to the suffix *ut*.
In *jñīpsati*, [the same applies].

From the root *jñā*, the suffix *ṇic* is applied; by the rule *artihvṛ...* and so forth, the augment *puk* is added, followed by the substitution of the first vowel (*ādittva*) and the elision of the reduplication (*abhyāsalopa*).
Thus, one forms *siṣāsati*.
By the rule *janasanakhanāṃ sañjhaloḥ*, the substitution of *ā* occurs.
"Some here," and so forth. By the word "some," it is implied that some do not recite [this].
However, those who do not recite it provide a supplementary rule (*upasaṃkhyāna*) here for the roots *tan*, *pat*, and *daridrā*.
In the forms *titaṃsati* and *titāṃsati*,
the long vowel [of the root] occurs optionally by the rule *tenoter vibhāṣā* (Pāṇini 6.4.17).
In the form *pitsati*, [the short vowel occurs].
By rules such as *sanimīmā* [Pāṇini 7.4.54], there is the substitution of *īs*, the elision of the reduplication, and by *skoḥ* [Pāṇini 8.2.29] etc., the elision of *s*.
Thus we have *didaridriṣati* and *didaridrāsati*.
By the rule *daridrāterārdhadhātuke* (Vārttika 789), there is optionally the elision of the vowel *ā*. [The form] *kliṣṭvā* is derived as follows.

The substitution of *ṣ* [for *s*] is by the rule *vraścādi-sūtra* (Pāṇini 8.2.36). Regarding the form *kliśitvā*, the *kittva* status is established by [the rule] *kliśaḥ ktvāniṣṭhayoḥ* (Pāṇini 1.2.26).

"The option is already established for the *ktvā* suffix" means: if the option is already established for the *ktvā* suffix by [Pāṇini 7.2.44] *svarati* etc. because of its being marked with *ū*, then for what purpose is the mention of *ktvā*? To this he says: "But of *kliś* in the sense of 'affliction' (*upatāpa*)... and so forth. "The augment *iṭ* would necessarily apply."
Because the root *kliś* has an udātta accent when it means "to afflict," [the word] "for that purpose" (*tadartham*) means for the purpose of that *kliś* which signifies affliction.

That which has this as its purpose or motive is "tathoktam" (so stated). Alternatively, it means for the sake of preventing that which would otherwise necessarily result in the augment *iṭ* for the root *kliś*, whose meaning is "to afflict"; this is because the word *artha* here signifies "prevention. Since [the root] ends in a long vowel (*ū*), the prohibition of *iṭ* by the rule *śryukaḥ kiti* [Pāṇini 7.2.11] would apply; therefore, this statement is made to ensure that the augment occurs optionally before the suffixes *ktvā* and *niṣṭhā*. Examples are: *pavitvā*, *paktiḥ*, and *pavitavān*.
Because of the prohibition of *kittva* by this rule [1.2.22], the *guṇa* substitution indeed takes place.

The mention of *pūṅ* with its *anubandha* is for the purpose of excluding *pūñ*. Regarding the roots *vasa* "to dwell" (DhP 1005) and *kṣudha* "hunger" (DhP 1190), since they are *anudātta*, the prohibition of *iṭ* would otherwise apply; therefore, this statement is made to prescribe *iṭ* for the suffixes *ktvā* and *niṣṭhā*.
Thus, we have *uṣitvā*.

Regarding *ktvā*, although the prohibition of *kittva* would apply by [Pāṇini 1.2.18], *kittva* is established by [Pāṇini 1.2.7] (*muḍ amṛt-vabhyās-avyavāye 'pi*). Then, by the rule for the *vac*-class [Pāṇini 6.1.15], there is *saṃprasāraṇa* because it belongs to the *yajādi* group; and by [Pāṇini 8.3.60] (*śāsivasighasīnāṃ ca*), there is the substitution of *ṣ*.
Thus we have *kṣudhitvā*. Here too, *kittva* applies optionally by [Pāṇini 1.2.26].

Regarding the statement, "The mention of the *vikaraṇa* [suffix] is for the purpose of indicating the verbal root (*dhātu*)," and so forth—it has been stated that "the mention of the *vikaraṇa* serves only to indicate the verbal root.

Now, one might raise the objection: "Why is this not understood as being for the purpose of excluding the root *vasa* in the sense of 'covering' (Dhātupāṭha 1023)? To such a person, he replies with the words "of *vasteḥ*" and so forth.

Now, one might raise the objection: "Why is it not understood that [the mention of] *vāvastaḥ* and *vāvastavān* is for the purpose of excluding the *yaṅluṅ* (the elision of the *yaṅ* suffix)? To such an objector, he replies with the words "of *vasteḥ*" and so forth. The intention is that even by understanding the rule as a qualification of what is prescribed (*vihitaviśeṣaṇapakṣa*), the exclusion of the *yaṅluṅ* can be accomplished. Furthermore, since the term *iṭ* is already being carried over (*anuvartamāna*) from the previous rule, for what purpose is *iṭ* mentioned again? To this he says: "The repetition of the mention of *iṭ* is for the sake of making it obligatory (*nityārtham*)."
The previous mention of *iṅ* was connected with [the rule] as an option; therefore, if that were to recur, its [optional status] would also recur.
Consequently, the mention of *iṅ* is repeated here in order to exclude that [optionality]. Regarding "honored" (*añcitāḥ*), the meaning is "revered."
The suffix *kta* is applied by [Pāṇini 3.2.188].
The elision of the nasal [of the root] does not occur by [Pāṇini 6.4.24], because of the prohibition [stated] in [Pāṇini 6.4.30].
[The word] "asya" [is used].

The genitive case [in the compound *lobhitavya*] is by virtue of the rule *ktasya ca vartamāne* (Pāṇini 2.3.67). Regarding the forms *lubhitvā* and *lobhitvā*, the absence of guṇa due to the kit-status [of the suffix] occurs in one alternative by the rule *ralo vyupadhāt* (Pāṇini 1.2.26) and so forth. As for the form *gārdheya*, it remains exactly as prescribed.
In the case of the suffix *kvā*, there is an option;

however, according to [Pāṇini 7.2.15] regarding the *niṣṭhā* suffix, there is a permanent prohibition. Thus we have *jarītvā* and *jaritvā*. The root *jṛ* (meaning "to grow old") belongs to the *kryādi* class (Dhātupāṭha 1494).
In the alternative view provided by the rule *vṛto vā* [Pāṇini 7.2.38], the vowel is long.

However, for one who reads *jṛṣ* in the sense of "loss of vitality" (*vayohāni*) as belonging to the *vivādi* group in the Dhātupāṭha (no. 1130), there is no inclusion here because it possesses an *anubandha*; thus, for him, the form is *jaurtvā*.
As for *vraścitvā*:

Regarding the root *vraścū* in the sense of "cutting" (*dhātupāṭha* 1292), because of the prohibition [stated] in [Pāṇini 1.2.18], the *samprasāraṇa* substitution does not occur by virtue of the rule *grahijyā-* etc. [Pāṇini 6.1.16]; this is because that rule is prescribed for an affix marked with *k*. Now, what is the purpose of including the mention of *ktvā*, since the mention of *ktvā* already continues from [Pāṇini 7.2.50]? To this he says: "The mention of *ktvā*" and so forth.
For that mention of *ktvā* is connected with *niṣṭhā*; therefore, when it is carried over [by *anuvṛtti*], there would be a carry-over of that (*niṣṭhā*) as well.
This being the case, [the rule] would apply even to the *niṣṭhā* suffixes.

Consequently, another mention of *ktvā* is made here for the purpose of excluding the *niṣṭhā* suffixes. The root *kṛtī* in the sense of "cutting" belongs to the Taudādika class (Dhātupāṭha 1435), and *kṛtī* in the sense of "encircling" belongs to the Raudhādika class (Dhātupāṭha 1447); since no distinction is specified, both are included.

The root *cṛt* is used in the senses of "injury" and "tying together" (*hiṃsā-saṃgranthanayoḥ*; the Dhātupāṭha reads *hiṃsā-śranthanayoḥ*, 1324); *chṛd* is used in the senses of "shining" and "playing" (*dīpti-devanayoḥ*, 1445); and *tṛd* is used in the senses of "injury" and "giving" (*hiṃsā-dānayoḥ*; the Dhātupāṭha reads *hiṃsā-anādarayoḥ*, 1446).
The letter *u* [in these roots] is for the purpose of specification according to [Pāṇini 7.2.56];
the letters *i* and *r* are likewise for the very same purpose of specification according to [Pāṇini 3.1.57].
The root *nṛt* (meaning "to move the limbs") is listed as 1116 in the Dhātupāṭha.

Since all these [roots] are marked with an anudātta accent, the augment *iṭ* would necessarily apply; therefore, this rule is stated to provide an option for the suffixes beginning with *s*, excluding *sic*. In the word *se*, the vocalization of the vowel *a* is not intended to be restrictive (*atantram*), as it is not meant to be significant.

Therefore, there arises a doubt regarding this [rule]. However, its lack of independence (*atantratva*) is to be understood from the prohibition of *sic* in the rule "asici. For if the pronunciation of the letter *a* were not independent, then why was it not stated simply as "svasici"? [It is] for fear of ambiguity.
If it were stated as *hrucyamāne*, the meaning "in both the *sic* and the *sye*" might also be suspected.

However, when it is stated as *se'sici*, because two locative cases (*saptamī*) are employed, the intended meaning is understood to be "in a verbal root beginning with *s* other than *sic*". But would there not still be doubt here? Even if it were stated thus, one might ask: "Why is it not so in the case of *sic*? For if it were to apply even in the case of *sic*, the mention of that [term *sic*] would be purposeless; one could simply have said *si*.
"Katsyati" is the *lṛṭ* (future tense);
"akatsryat" is the *luṅ* (aorist).

In the form *cikṛtsati*, the suffix *san* [is applied]; because it is marked with the *k*-sign, there is an absence of *guṇa* substitution by [Pāṇini 1.2.10]. The root *gam-lṛ* (meaning "to go," Dhātupāṭha 982) is *aniṭ* (lacking the augment *iṭ*) because it is unaccented (*anudātta*).

Even that substitution of *gam* for the root *iṇ* "to go" (DhP 1045) by the rule *sani ca* (Pāṇini 2.4.47), as well as that for the root *ik* "to remember" (DhP 1047) by the statement *iṇvadika iti vaktavyam* (Vārttika 167), and that for the root *iṅ* "to study" (DhP 1046) by the rule *iṅaśca* (Pāṇini 2.4.48)— all these would, due to the status of being a substitute (*sthānivadbhāva*), be treated as if they lacked the *iṭ* augment.
This statement is made so that the *iṭ* augment may occur before a following sārvadhātuka suffix beginning with *s*, excluding the *sic* augment, in forms such as *gamiṣyati* and *agamiṣyat*.

An example of *gam* without a substitute is *jigamiṣati*. Is this [an example] of its substitution by *iṇ* or its substitution by *ig*? Now, while [the rule] concerns that which is not followed by *it*, for what purpose is *iṅ* mentioned again? To this he says: "The mention of *iṅ* is for the sake of making it obligatory (*nitya*)."

For that previous mention of *iṅ*—connected with the mention of the option (*vā*) in [Pāṇini 7.2.56], "The augment *iṭ* is optionally applied after a root ending in an *udit* vowel"—would continue to apply when that [sūtra] is followed; consequently, its application would also persist, and thus the optional addition of *iṭ* would result. Therefore, a new mention of *iṅ* is made in order to exclude that [previous rule].

Regarding "saṃgaṃsīṣṭa": from the root *gam* preceded by the prefix *sam*, the optative suffix *liṅ* with the augment *sīyuṭ* is applied; the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) is prescribed by the rule *samo gamṛcchi* [Pāṇini 1.3.29]; the augment *suṭ* is added by [Pāṇini 6.1.138]; then the substitution of *gh* for *g* and the retroflexion (*ṣṭutva*) of the *s* occur. Regarding "sañjigāsate": [this is derived from the desiderative of the same root].
By the rule *pūrvavatsanaḥ* [Pāṇini 1.3.62], the ātmanepada ending is applied;
thus, we have *adhijigāṃsate*.
This is a counter-example for the substitution of *iṅ* for the root *gam*.

Now, why does the lengthening [of the vowel] not occur here in *sañcigamsate* by virtue of the rule *pūrvatrāsiddham* (Pāṇini 6.4.22)? To this he says: "Of the substitute *iṅ* for the root *gam*, etc.
For that lengthening is desired for the substitute *iṅ* of the root *gam*, and not for any other.
Thus it has been stated there: "It should be said: 'of the substitute *iṅ* for the root *gam*.'"

If it is stated that [the rule applies] "in the case of parasmaipada endings," then it would not apply to *kṛt* suffixes or where there is elision (*luk*) of the parasmaipada ending? To this he says: "by the ātmanepada," and so forth. "Situated in the same word" means situated in one and the same word.
"It is desired everywhere else" means that this is made clear by the passage beginning with "for even in the case of kṛtya suffixes," as in the examples "sañjigamiṣitā" and "adhijigamiṣitā."
There are two examples of the *kṛtya* suffixes:
"jigamiṣitavyam tvayā" (you must desire to go). This [example] occurs when there is the elision (*luk*) of the *parasmaipada* suffix.

Because *gam* ends in a suffix marked with *n*, there is the imperative (*loṭ*), the ending *sip*, the replacement of *sip* by *hi* according to [Pāṇini 3.4.87], and the elision of *hi* according to [Pāṇini 6.4.105].

But how is it that when it is stated "in the case of parasmaipada endings," the elision of the parasmaipada suffix after a *kṛt* suffix is also obtained? He thinks as follows: a split of the rule (*yogavibhāga*) must be made: one part is "after *gam*, there is *iṭ*"; there, "after *s*" is carried over, meaning that the augment *iṭ* occurs after *gam* before an *ārdhadhātuka* suffix beginning with *s*.
Then, "in the case of parasmaipada endings" is a second rule for the purpose of restriction.
And if this restriction were to apply without qualification, then the preceding rule (pūrvayoga) would be rendered useless.

Therefore, the restriction is with respect to those of the same class (*tulyajātīya*). And since that which belongs to the same class occurs in the domain of *tiṅ* and *siṅ*, [the restriction] applies only to the *parasmaipada* endings and not to the *ātmanepada* endings.
In the case of *kṛt* suffixes and when there is elision (*luk*) of the *parasmaipada* ending, it certainly does not occur [by the preceding rule], because it has not been excluded by the restriction.
Regarding the passage beginning with "But the author of the *Padaśeṣa* [says]...":

the author of the *Padaśeṣa*, moreover, thinks as follows: "In the case of the *parasmaipada*s"—this is not a locative of reference (*parasaptamī*), but rather a locative of domain (*viṣayasaptamī*). That is to say, when the root *gam-* is observed—that is, found—in the domain of the *parasmaipada*s, then the augment *iṭ* occurs before an *ārdhadhātuka* suffix beginning with *s*.

This being the case, even without a formal separation of rules (*yogavibhāga*), according to that view, the *iṭ* augment occurs after every *kṛt* suffix—even when there is no *parasmaipada*—and even when there is elision of the *parasmaipada*, provided that a *gam* root was characterized as having a *parasmaipada* ending. This is because the *ārdhadhātuka* suffix beginning with *s* is not specified as being "governed by" (*paratvena*) a *parasmaipada*. According to that view, the forms *sañjigamiṣitā* and *adhijigamiṣitā vyākaraṇasya* should result; for the *gam* roots preceded by *sam-* and *adhi-* were not characterized as having *parasmaipada* endings.
For instance: after the root *gam* preceded by the prefix *sam*, the Ātmanepada is prescribed by the rule *samo gamyucchi* (Pāṇini 1.3.29) and others;

likewise, after the root preceded by *adhi*, the Ātmanepada is applied by the rule *anudāttaṅitaḥ* (Pāṇini 1.3.12) due to its status as a substitute (*sthānivadbhāva*). Because of the use of the plural number in the expression *vṛdbhyaḥ*, the sense of "and so forth" (*ādi*) is understood.
For this very reason, he says: "from *vṛt* and the rest."
The four roots beginning with *vṛt*—namely, *vṛtu* vartane (DhP 758), *vṛdhu* vṛddhau (DhP 759), *śṛdhu* śabdakutsāyām (DhP 760), and *syandū* sravaṇe (DhP 761)—are all acute-accented (*udātta*).

Among these, for the first three, the augment *iṭ* is invariably required; however, for *syand*, since it is marked with an indicatory *u* (*udid*), the *iṭ* is optionally required. This prohibition is stated [in the following rule] regarding that case. Thus, one says: *vartsyati*.

The suffix *lṛṭ* is applied by [Pāṇini 3.3.13] *śeṣe ca*; the active voice (*parasmaipada*) is optionally used by [Pāṇini 1.3.92] *vadbhyāḥ syasanoḥ*. In the form *vivṛtsati*, there is an absence of *guṇa* due to the *kit* status of the suffix *san* according to [Pāṇini 1.2.10].

In the case of *vṛdhi* and *śṛdhi*, the letter *dh* undergoes *cartva* (substitution by a voiceless unaspirated consonant) according to the rule *khari ca* [Pāṇini 8.4.54], resulting in the letter *t*. Regarding the statement "it need not be said that 'after *catur*' [the substitution occurs]," he states the reason for this: "For the inclusion of *vṛt*," and so forth.

If that very [term] is understood as being for the purpose of completing the *vṛddhi* and so forth as well, then—whether by way of *tantra* (simultaneous application) or because words possess multiple powers (*anekaśakti*)—nothing undesirable follows. Even when understood in this way, the intention is that only what is desired is established.
Thus, the mention of the word "four" (*catur*) having been rejected, he states its purpose: "That is done," and so forth.

If the mention of "four" (catur) were not made, then the optional substitution [of *i* for the root] characterized by the *ūdit* designation would apply to the root *spand*, because it is *antaraṅga*.
Its *antaraṅga* status arises from its dependence solely upon an *ārdhadhātuka* suffix beginning with a consonant (*valādi*).
However, this prohibition is *bahiraṅga* because it depends upon a specific type of *ārdhadhātuka* suffix.

Therefore, the mention of *catur* (four) is made so that the prohibition may set aside the optional application (*vikalpa*) characterized by the *ūdittva* (the property of having *ū* as an indicatory letter), even though that [optional application] is internal (*antaraṅga*).
But how is this meaning obtained even when the mention of *catur* is made? To this he says: "In the mention of *catur*" and so forth.

That which has *syandi* as its subsequent [element] is *tatpara*; the state of being that is *tātparya* (intentionality); by that *tātparya*, that is, by way of having that as its primary focus—this is the meaning.
Regarding the term "sannidhāpitaḥ," it means "brought near" or "presented.
And the purpose of this very prohibition is precisely this: how might the conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) of that which has been thus presented be sublated?
Therefore, because of the mention of "four" (in the rule *caturgrahaṇāt*), the prohibition (*pratiṣedha*) overrides even the internal (*antaraṅga*) substitution of *vikalpa*.
Regarding the phrase "here too" (*atrāpi*) and so forth:

how, then, is a universal prohibition obtained elsewhere while the term "in the case of parasmaipada endings" (*parasmaipadeṣu*, Pāṇini 7.2.58) continues to apply? He thinks as follows: the word "of *gam*" (*gameḥ*) continues to apply; there, the connection will be made in this way: "In whatever manner *iṭ* occurs after *gam* when followed by a suffix beginning with *s*, in that very same manner, *iṭ* does not occur after *vṛt* and the others."

Therefore, just as the ātmanepada [terminations] are excluded from the root *gam* while the augment *iṭ* occurs everywhere else, so too is there a prohibition [of *iṭ*] after the roots beginning with *vṛt*. Regarding the root *kṛpū* in the sense of "capability" (Dhātupāṭha 762): since it is marked with *ū* (ūdittva), *iṭ* would optionally apply; thus, this prohibition is commenced.
[The form is] *kalptā*.

In the *luṭ* [future] tense, the *parasmaipada* ending is optional by the rule *luṭi ca kḷpaḥ* [Pāṇini 1.3.93]; [then], by the rule *laṭaḥ śatṛśānacāv aprathamāsamānādhikaraṇe* [Pāṇini 3.2.124], there is the substitution of *latva*. Thus, one forms *cikḷpsati*. As before, there is *kittva*.
Regarding the phrase "of *kḷp* also," and so forth:

this meaning is obtained through the continued application (*anuvṛtti*) of the rule for *vṛt* and the others; only when that [rule] continues in application will the connection be made—namely, that just as there is a prohibition for *vṛt* and the others, so too is there this [prohibition] for *kḷp*.

If, then, the mention of *vṛt* and the others continues here, would not the prohibition also apply to *vṛt* and the others in that [context]? It will not apply, by virtue of the power of making a formal division of the rule (*yogavibhāga*).

If this [prohibition] were to apply to *vṛt* and the others as well, then one would have formulated the rule as *na vṛdbhyaḥ pañcabhyaḥ tāsi ca*. Since the augment *iṭ* is required by the rule *krādiniyamāt*, a prohibition is prescribed for the *thali* suffix after roots ending in *j* that are invariably without *iṭ* (*nityāniṭ*) when *tāsi* follows—such as in *pātā* and so forth. The mention of the *luṅ* (aorist) is for the purpose of demonstrating that [the root] is invariably without *iṭ* (*nityāniṭ*) in *tāsi*; and its lack of *iṭ* is due to the prohibition of *iṭ* by the rule *ekācaḥ* [Pāṇini 7.2.10].
Regarding the forms *lūtvā* and *lulavitha*,
because of the statement "as in those cases," the prohibition does not apply here.
Otherwise, if it were not stated that [the rule applies] "to those [roots] ending in *t* or *s*," the prohibition would also apply here— namely, in *bhavati* and *lunāti*.

[The printed reading is: "Because of the prohibition [stated in the rule] *śrayukaḥ kiti* (Pāṇini 7.2.11), which applies to those that are invariably aniṭ (*nityamaniṭaḥ*) before a *kit* suffix. [Objection: Would there not also be a prohibition here? For *lunāti* is invariably aniṭ before a *kit* suffix due to the prohibition in *śrayukaḥ kiti*; [as in the examples] *papiva*, *papima*.
There is elision of the vowel *ā* by [Pāṇini 6.4.64].
Regarding the phrase "the mention of *aniṅ* by the word 'nityam' (*aniṅgrahaṇaṃ nityamityanena*)," etc.:
the meaning is that the mention of *aniṅ* is for the purpose of specifying how the root's lack of the augment *iṭ* (*aniṭtva*) is to be qualified by the word "nityam."

Now, regarding *savitā* [from the root *su*]: why is the mention of *aniṭ* (unaccented) not made for the sake of preventing the prohibition of *thal* with the *seṭ* (accented) suffix? It ought not to be for that purpose. For it is stated that *thal* does not occur after those [roots] ending in *tās*. And the prohibition that applies to that which ends in *tās* with a *seṭ* suffix cannot be designated as "after those ending in *tās*" (*tāsvat*). Rather, the suffix *-vat* expresses a similarity based precisely on the absence of *iṭ* in the case of that *thal* which is prescribed after roots such as *hras*, *miñj*, and *bhā*.

However, by the very inclusion of the word *vat*, there will be no prohibition of those [roots] ending in *iṭ* before the suffix *sthali*; otherwise, that similarity which is expressed by the term *vat* would not exist.

Therefore, it is rightly said that this is indeed the purpose of including *aniṅ*. Now, if the inclusion of *aniṅ* were not made, of what would the word "always" (*nityam*) be understood as a qualifier? It would be a qualifier of the prohibition.

But surely, the prohibition (*pratiṣedha*) is established as being permanent (*nitya*); in that case, if the prohibition were not qualified by the mention of "permanent," then the mention of "permanent" would be purposeless. This is not so; it is for the purpose of ensuring that the prohibition in the preceding rule (*pūrvasūtra*) be understood as non-permanent (*anitya*). And thus, by the preceding rule, the augment *iṭ* would indeed apply in certain instances. Therefore, the purpose of the mention of "non-*iṭ*" (*aniṭ*) is exactly as previously stated.
Regarding the rule *tāsau vibhāṣiteṭ* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 7.2.43): in the sūtra beginning with *svarati-* (7.2.44), the augment *iṭ* is optionally prescribed for the root *dhūñ*.

Because of the mention of "always" (*nitya*) in that [subsequent rule], the augment *iṭ* necessarily occurs in the case of *thali* when it is a root for which *iṭ* is optionally prescribed (*vibhāṣiteṭ*).

And even in the absence of the mention of "permanence" (*nitya*), the prohibition would indeed apply; for even by virtue of an optional absence of *iṭ*, the designation of *niṅ* certainly occurs. For instance, even though the root *guh* optionally takes *iṭ*, the suffix *kso* still occurs: *adhukṣat*.

Now, for what purpose is the instruction using the suffix *vat* (the possessive suffix *matup* used adverbially)? Why not simply say "in those [roots]" (*tāsu*)? To this he says: "In those" (*tāsvat*), etc.

If the instruction with *vat* were not present, then even for that [root] which is "non-existent" (*asan*) in those [roots], and which is therefore always *aniṭ* (lacking the augment *iṭ*), there would be a prohibition of *iṭ* in the *thali* [suffix].

But when the instruction with *vat* is present, since *vat* signifies complete similarity, it follows that just as *iṭ* does not occur for such a [root] in the *tās*, so too *iṭ* must not occur in the *thali*; thus, the undesirable consequence does not arise at all.

For if that [root] which is *asat* (non-existent) in the *tās-* [affixes] were indeed non-existent, then because of its non-existence, it would be eternally *aniṭ*; consequently, there would be a prohibition of *iṭ* even for the *thali* [affix].

This being the case, while there is an absence of *iṭ* for that which is *asat* in *tās-* etc., whereas for another it is *sat*, then just as there is an absence of *iṭ* for such a form in *tās-* etc., so too it would not occur for that same form in *thali*. The intention is that for that which is *asat* in *tās-* and is eternally *aniṭ* due to its non-existence, there is no prohibition of *iṭ* in *thali*—as in the example *jaghasitha*—by virtue of the subsequent rule; therefore, he says: "In the subsequent rule also," and so forth.
Thus, this instruction by means of the suffix *vat* is for the sake of what follows;

however, in this case, there is no purpose in the instruction by *vat*, because the prohibition does not apply to the roots *ghas* and *vyay* simply due to their not ending in a vowel (*anajantatvāt*).
[The example is] *jaghasitha*.
In the form *udayitha*, the root *ghas* is substituted [for *ad*] by the rule *liṭanyatarasyām* (Pāṇini 2.4.40);
then, by the rule *liṭi dhātor anabhyāsasya* (Pāṇini 6.1.8), the substitution of *vayi* occurs; and finally, by the rule *liṭabhyāsasyobhayeṣām* (Pāṇini 6.1.17), *saṃprasāraṇa* takes place.
Why [is this so]? Because *ghas* and *vay* do not exist in those [roots], they are eternally *aniṭ*. To this he says: "For [the substitute] *ad*" and so forth.
Their non-existence in those [roots] should be understood from the fact that they are not prescribed there. This undertaking is for the purpose of excluding roots ending in a consonant (*anajanta*).
[The example is] *iyaṣṭha* (or *iyaṣṭa*, according to the *Padamañjarī*).
As before, there is *samprasāraṇa* of the practice [of the root], *ṣatva* by the rule *vraśca-* etc. [Pāṇini 8.2.36], and *ṣṭutva*.
Regarding "cakarṣitha":
the root is *kṛṣa vilekhane* (Dhātupāṭha 990).

This [root] possesses the vowel *a* after the guṇa substitution has been applied, but not during its original enunciation (*upadeśa*). Why then is the term "enunciation" (*upadeśe*) included here? Indeed, it could have been omitted; for one could certainly have carried forward the mention of "enunciation" from the rule *ekāca upadeśe* [Pāṇini 7.2.10]. Why is it nevertheless included? It is done for the sake of clarity.
If that were absent, someone might think—since it was of no use in the preceding rule—that it had ceased to apply, and thus they might understand the rule even as *tāsāmatvataḥ*.
"Rarādhitha"— the root *rādha* (and *sādha*) is used in the sense of "accomplishment" (*saṃsiddhi*) [Dhātupāṭha 1262,
1263]. "Jighṛkṣati."

> [[Pāṇini 7.2.12]] Because of this prohibition of *iṭ*, [the root *añj*] is invariably without *iṭ* (*nityāniṭ*) in the *tās-* [aorist], but not in the *sac-* [perfect]; rather, it is [without *iṭ*] in the *saci*. Regarding the root *añj* [meaning] "to manifest, to smear," etc. [the Dhātupāṭha reads: "to manifest, to perish, to desire, to go"] (Dhātupāṭha 1458), there is lengthening of the reduplicated syllable by [Pāṇini 7.4.70], and the augment *nuṭ* is added by [Pāṇini 7.4.71] because it consists of two consonants (*dvihala*). This root possesses the vowel *a* in its original form (*upadeśa*), yet it is not invariably without *iṭ* in the *tās-* [aorist], because *iṭ* is optionally applied to it by the rule for the *svarati*-class [Pāṇini 7.2.44]. Thus, [we have the form] *sasmartha*.
The root *smu* is used in the sense of "thinking" (Dhātupāṭha 933).
Regarding the form *dadhvartha*:
the root *dhvṛ* is used in the sense of "reeling" or "fainting" (Dhātupāṭha 939).
Now, although among those roots ending in *a*, the roots *vṛṅ* and *vṛñ* are udātta, even so, *vṛṅ* cannot possibly occur in that context, because it is ātmanepada.

As for the root *vṛñ*, because of the Vedic irregularity (*nipātana*) stated in [Pāṇini 7.2.64], "In the Veda, *vavartha*," it must necessarily take the augment *iṭ* in the secular language (*bhāṣā*). Therefore, this [prohibition] is not applicable for the purpose of prohibiting *iṭ* after those two. As for other roots ending in ṛ, since they are *anudātta*, they are invariably without *iṭ* (*aniṭ*); thus, the prohibition of *iṭ* by [Pāṇini 7.2.61], "After a root ending in a vowel other than *ac*, when followed by *tās* or *thali*, there is invariably no *iṭ*," is already established. One should not raise the objection that [the prohibition] would fail because, once the *guṇa* substitution has occurred and the replacement of *ṛ* by *ra* (*raparatva*) has been applied, the root no longer ends in *ac*.

Because of the connection with the word *acaḥ* (of a vowel), which is drawn forward from the preceding rule regarding the acceptance of instruction (*upadeśagrahaṇa*); or alternatively, the ablative case [in *acaḥ*] is a qualifier of that which is prescribed, and thus we shall understand it as follows: "from that which is preceded by a vowel. Therefore, since the prohibition for those ending in *ṛ* is already established by the very rule *ataḥ tv-as-vas-anaḥ*, for what purpose is this new undertaking? To this he says: "When something is already established, a new undertaking is for the sake of restriction (*niyamārthaḥ*).

[The restriction is: "not from others. Who, then, are these? They are those other than those ending in *ṛ*—namely, those ending in a vowel (*ajanta*) and those not ending in a vowel (*anajanta*) that end in *at* in their original form (*upadeśe*).

Now, why is this restriction (*niyama*) not understood as: "The substitution of *ṛ* [for *ar*] occurs for Bhāradvāja alone, and not for other teachers"? He thinks as follows: from the previous sūtra, the phrase "and that which has *at*" (*atvataḥ*) carries over (*anuvartate*). The purpose of that carry-over is precisely this: by means of this restriction, due to proximity (*sannidhānāt*), it applies only to that which was previously mentioned—the root (*dhātu*) ending in *ā* that carries over, and that which has *at*. And thus, that carry-over would otherwise be purposeless.
Therefore, he says "that," etc., meaning that this very restriction is understood: "For Bhāradvāja, only when there is *ṛ*."
The word *tat* indicates the reason (*hetu*).
Since such a restriction (*niyama*) applies here— namely, that the prohibition of *iṭ* occurs only for the root *bhṛ* (of the Bharadvāja school) and not for other roots— therefore,
even though a permanent prohibition of *iṭ* was established by the two preceding rules, this option (*vikalpa*) arises by virtue of the force (*sāmarthya*) of those two preceding rules.
Although in that [sūtra] the mention of *vāk* is absent and the mention of *ācārya* is made, it is nevertheless obtained by implication.
Now, what is the purpose of including the *tapara* (the long *ṝ*)? Why not simply say "of Bhāradvāja" (*urbhāradvājasya*)? To this he says: "The inclusion of the *tapara*," and so forth.

For if only *hruḥ* were stated, then because the rule "an [vowel] includes its homogeneous counterparts" (*aṇ savarṇān gṛhṇāti*) would apply, there would be the inclusion of even those words ending in the vowel *ṛ*.
Therefore, the addition of *t* (in *tapara*) is for the purpose of excluding that [possibility].
But what would happen if there were no inclusion of those ending in *u*? To this he says: "For thus," and so forth.
The word *tathā* is used in the sense of "in this manner."
The word *hi* has the sense of "because.

Why is this so? Because even without the inclusion of the long vowel marker (*tapara*), since there would already be a grasping of those sounds including the long *ṛ*-vowels, one might suspect that this [rule] is for the purpose of an injunction (*vidhi*).
For a restriction (*niyama*) occurs only when there is nothing else to be enjoined.
If there were a mention of all roots ending in *ṛ*, then a prohibition would have to be prescribed for those alone, for their prohibition is not established by the preceding rule. [One might argue:
"Is it not the case that for all roots ending in *ṛ*, the suffix *iṭ* is obligatory because they are *seṭ*?

However, when the letter *t* is added as a marker (*taparakaraṇa*), long vowels are excluded by that *t*; since there is then no longer anything to be prescribed, this becomes a restrictive rule (*niyama*). In forms such as *babhūtha*, the absence of *iṭ*—which would otherwise be required everywhere by the rule governing roots beginning with *krī* and others—is here established as an irregularity (*nipātana*).
In *babhūtha*, by [Pāṇini 7.4.73] *bhavateraḥ*, there is the substitution of *ā* for the vowel of the reduplicated syllable. In *babhūvitha*: [the same applies].
The suffix *vuk* is applied by [Pāṇini 6.4.88].
