Regarding the form *ātatantha*: it is derived from the root *tanu* (meaning "to expand," Dhātupāṭha 1463) preceded by the prefix *āṅ*.
In *atenitha*,
there is the substitution of *et* and the elision of the reduplication by [Pāṇini 6.4.121].
In *jagṛbhma*, [the same applies].
The suffix *vuk* is applied by the rule *bhuvo vug luṅliṭoḥ* (Pāṇini 6.4.88). Regarding the form *ātatantha*:
the root is *tanu* (Dhātupāṭha 1463) meaning "to expand," preceded by the prefix *ā*.
In *atenitha*,
there is the substitution of *e* (by Pāṇini 6.4.121) and the elision of the reduplication.
In *jagṛbhma*, [the same applies].
In *graherliṭ*, the substitution of *mā* for *mas* occurs by the rule *parasmaipadānām* [Pāṇini 3.4.82], and the semivowel-vocalization (*samprasāraṇa*) occurs by the rule *grahijyā* [Pāṇini 6.1.16].
Regarding *vavārtha*:

*vṛñ* is "to choose" (Dhātupāṭha 1254); *sṛj* is "to emit" (Dhātupāṭha 1414); and *dṛśir* is "to see" (Dhātupāṭha 988). For these two, since the augment *iṭ* would necessarily apply according to the rule governing roots beginning with *krī* (*krādiniyama*), this statement is made to allow for an option.
In *saruāṣṭha* and *dadraṣṭha*, the substitution of *ṣ* [for *s*] occurs by Pāṇini 8.2.36 (*vraśca* etc.), and the substitution of *i* [for *ṛ*] occurs by Pāṇini 6.1.58. In *āditha* and *āritha*,
[the roots are] *ada* "to eat" (Dhātupāṭha 1011) and *ṛ* "to go" (Dhātupāṭha 1098).
By [Pāṇini 7.4.70], there is lengthening of the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*).

In the form *viṣyayitha*, the root is *vyeñ* "to cover" (Dhātupāṭha 1007); the semivowel substitution (*samprasāraṇa*) occurs by [Pāṇini 6.1.17], which states that both types of roots undergo this change in the reduplicated syllable of the perfect tense (*liṭ*).

Why, then, does the substitution of *ā* [for the vowel]—prescribed by the rule *ādeca upadeśe* [Pāṇini 6.1.45]—not occur here for the root *vyeñ*? To this he says: "By the rule *vyeño na vyo liṭi* [Pāṇini 6.1.46], etc.;
and there is also a constant prohibition for *ṛ* by the rule *arterapi nityaṃ pratiṣedhaḥ* [Vārttika 7.2.63]."

"Here, the mention of *iṅ* is for the sake of clarity. [The opponent objects: "But surely the mention of *iṅ* must be for the purpose that the augment *iṭ* should always (*nityam*) occur; for without the mention of *iṅ*, this rule for *iṅ* could not be understood as being obligatory (*nitya*). To this he replies: "For when there is the prescription of an option (*vikalpa*)," and so forth.

For by this [mention], is the prescription of an immediately following option made, or rather the permanent prohibition (*nityapratiṣedha*) established previously or subsequently? Even that [prohibition] can be carried over by the maxim of the frog-leap (*maṇḍūkapluti*).

In this regard, if the former alternative were intended, then the mention of *ārtti* would be purposeless; for the option would already be established by the rule itself: "In the case of [the substitution of] *ṛ*, [there is optionally no *guṇa*] according to Bhāradvāja" (Pāṇini 7.2.62). If, on the other hand, the latter alternative were intended, then the mention of *ārtti* would likewise be purposeless; for the prohibition would already be established by the rule: "In the case of [the substitution of] *ṛ*, [there is no *guṇa*] according to Bhāradvāja" (Pāṇini 7.2.63).
Since, therefore, neither the prescription of an option nor that of a prohibition is logically tenable, neither is applicable here.
Even without the inclusion of the term *iṅ*, it could be understood that this rule for *iṅ* is obligatory (*nitya*).

However, since such an understanding would result in a complexity of comprehension (*pratipatti-gaurava*), the inclusion of *iṅ* is made for the sake of clarity. [The sūtra states: "Of monosyllabic roots (*ekāc*) that have undergone reduplication.
From what is this determined? From the force (*sāmarthya*) of the mention of "monosyllabic" (*ekāc*).

Indeed, there is no root that possesses more than one vowel (*anekāc*) before the doubling (*dvirvacana*) has taken place, for the purpose of excluding which the mention of "one-voweled" (*ekāc*) would be made.

But surely *jāgarti* exists; therefore, would that [mention] not be for the purpose of excluding it? This is not so; for the commencement of a grammatical rule (*yogārambha*) is not prompted by a single example alone.
If this were the intended purpose, he would have simply said, "after *jāgr*, [the suffix does not take the augment *it*]."
In that case as well, this is the meaning: the burden of understanding is avoided.
But could it not also serve to exclude the root *ūrṇu*? No, for it was stated previously: "The substitution of *ūrṇu* for *ūrṇu* [is applied] as if it were *ṇuv*.
Therefore, what was said is correct: "of monosyllabic roots that have undergone reduplication."
Regarding the forms *ādivān* and *aśivān*:
the roots are *ada* (meaning "to eat," Dhātupāṭha 1011) and *aś* (meaning "to eat," Dhātupāṭha 1523).
The suffix *kvasu* is applied by Pāṇini 3.2.107; there is reduplication, as well as the strengthening of the reduplicated syllable, and lengthening of the initial vowel according to Pāṇini 7.4.70.

There is lengthening by the rule for homogeneous vowels (*savarṇadīrghatva*), the augment *iṭ*, the *num* suffix by the rule *ugidacām* [Pāṇini 7.1.70], lengthening by the rule *sāntamahataḥ* [Pāṇini 6.4.10], and the elision of the final consonant (*saṃyogāntalopa*) by the rules *halṅyādi* [Pāṇini 6.1.68] and [Pāṇini 8.2.23].
Thus we have *pecivan* and *śokivān*.
Then, by the rule *ata ekahalmadhye* [Pāṇini 6.4.120] and others, there is the substitution of *et* and the elision of the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsalopa*).

"Once the single-substitute [ekādeśa] has been made between the stem and the suffix," and so forth. Now, regarding the rule for reduplication (*dvirvacana*) in the sixth book, the author of the *Vṛtti* has adopted the position that "reduplication is a double application" (*dviḥprayoga*). In this case, even before the single-substitute between the stem and the suffix has occurred—and even before the substitution of *ai* (*aitva*) and the elision of the reduplicated syllable have taken place—these monosyllabic roots (*ekācaḥ*) already possess their reduplication. For if reduplication were a substitute (*sthāne dvirvacane*), then another word (*śabdāntara*) consisting of multiple vowels (*anekāc*) would be extended [to the root], and thus these roots, having undergone reduplication, would indeed become polysyllabic (*anekāctva*). But this is not the case under the view that reduplication is a double application (*dviḥprayoge dvirvacane*).

For in that case, it is the very same root that is stated twice; and even if it were pronounced a hundred times, it would not lose its status as a single vowel (*ekāc*), much less when it is stated twice. Why, then, is it said: "When the single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) of the root and the reduplication has been applied, and when the *et* and the elision of the reduplication (*abhyāsalopa*) have been performed, these [roots] become single-vowel after the reduplication has taken place"? There is no fault here, for this was stated by relying on the fact that the status of being a single vowel is produced by the repetition itself.

For indeed, even due to a difference in properties (*dharma*), there occurs the conventional usage of a difference in the substratum (*dharmin*). To illustrate: speakers say, "He was clever last year, he is more clever this year, and he is most clever the year before next; thus you have become someone else entirely. Alternatively, the position of reduplication in place (*sthāne dvirvacana*) is also adopted there, on the grounds that reduplication consists of a double utterance. By the word "and" (*ca*), it is indicated that the position of reduplication in place is also applicable there.
As for those defects that might arise from that position, they have already been countered there.
Regarding the form *tasthivān*:
by the rule *śarpūrvāḥ khayaḥ* [Pāṇini 7.4.61], the *khya* is the remainder; then, by the rule *ato lopa iṭi ca* [Pāṇini 6.4.64], the vowel *ā* is elided.

Regarding the form *jakṣivān*: as before, there is the substitution of *ghasl* for the root *ad*; then, by the rule *gamahana* [Pāṇini 6.4.98], there is the elision of the penultimate vowel; then, by the rule *jhalāṃ jaś jhaśi* [Pāṇini 7.4.62], there is the substitution of *jaś*—namely, *jh* for *dh*; then, by the rule *jhaṣastathordho 'dhaḥ* [Pāṇini 8.2.40], there is the substitution of *j* for *jh*.

For the following *dh*, there is the substitution of *c* by the rule *khari ca* [Pāṇini 8.4.55]—namely, *k*; and finally, there is the substitution of *ṣ* by the rule *śāsivasighasīnāṃ ca* [Pāṇini 8.3.60].

But surely, since the augment *iṭ* is already established here by the rule for the *kṛ*-class and others, what is the purpose of this new undertaking? To this he says: "Since [it is] established," and so forth. By the phrase "prescribed by the rule for the *kṛ*-class and others," he clarifies exactly that which is stated in the *Kātantra-pariśiṣṭa* (59): "When [a form] is already established, a new undertaking is for the purpose of restriction (*niyama*).
The word "prescribed" (*prasakta*) means...
The meaning is "attained.

Regarding the term "is restricted" (*niyamyate*): the meaning is that, having been excluded from other verbal roots, it is established as applying only to those beginning with a single vowel (*ekāj-ādi*).

Now, what is the purpose of including the mention of *āt* (the long vowel *ā*), given that even those [bases] ending in short *a* become single-syllabic (*ekāc*) once the elision of *at* has occurred and reduplication has been applied; thus, wouldn't the rule be established by the mention of *ekāc* alone? To this he says: "The mention of *āt* is for the sake of including those with more than one syllable (*anekāc*).
But how do they come to have more than one syllable? To this he says: "In the case of reduplication," and so forth.

Since the elision of the vowel *ā* is caused by the presence of the augment *iṭ*, those [roots] should undergo the elision of *ā* only when *iṭ* exists, not when it is absent; therefore, as long as *iṭ* has not been applied, there would be no elision of *ā*. Consequently, if the mention of "beginning with *ā*" (*ād*) were not present, these roots—which have more than one vowel (*anekāc*) after reduplication—would not be included. Therefore, the mention of "beginning with *ā*" must be made for the sake of including those with multiple vowels.
If this is so, would it not follow that *iṭ* would also apply to the root *daridrāti*? To this, he says: "But in the case of *daridrāti*," and so forth.

The formation of *kvasu* after the root *daridrā-* is impossible; for, by the rule "the inclusion of multiple [roots] ending in *kāsi*" (Vārttika 305), there must be the substitution of *ām* for *daridrā-*, and when that occurs, the suffix *liṭ* must undergo elision (*luk*) by the rule "after *ām*" (Pāṇini 2.4.81). So how could this occasion for the augment *iṭ* arise? [In the example] "daridrāñcakāra," the root *kṛ-* is employed subsequently because of the rule "and *kṛ-* is employed subsequently" (Pāṇini 3.1.40), following a *liṭ* suffix. Even granting the absence of *ām* for *daridrā-*, he states another solution: "Or, even if *ām* is not applied," and so forth.
In this context, *iṭ* is prescribed for roots ending in long *ā*. [One might argue:

"Since there is the rule ‘*lopaḥ siddhaśca pratyayavidhau*’ (the elision is established even before the formation of the suffix), the long *ā* is elided even prior to the arising of the suffix; therefore, because the cause [for *iṭ*] is absent, *iṭ*-augmentation does not occur.

[The opponent suggests: "Let the mention of *ad* be made, but the mention of *ghas* need not be done. For when reduplication has been performed and the penultimate vowel has been elided by the rule ‘*ghasibhasohaṃli ca*’ [Pāṇini 6.4.100], the *iṭ*-augmentation would be established by the rule ‘*ekācaḥ*’ [Pāṇini 7.2.35]. To this, he replies: “*Ghaseḥ api*,” etc. [meaning: the mention of *ghas* is also necessary].
"Because it lacks a vowel" (*anackatvāt*):
this is the reason for the absence of reduplication.
Reduplication is prescribed for monosyllabic roots (*ekāc*), because of the governing rule [*ekācaḥ*] at Pāṇini 6.1.1.

Therefore, the intention is that once the elision of the *upadhā* vowel has occurred, there would be no reduplication because the root would lack a vowel; consequently, forms such as *jakṣivān* would not be established. Now, one might ask: "Even if the mention of *ghas* is made, why does this same fault not occur? To this he says: "Even when [it is] being made," etc. [This phrase is absent in the Kāśikā; however, in the Padamañjarī, the reading *kriyamāṇe tu* is found as the pratīka].
This is clear. Since, by the previous restrictive rule (*niyama*), the augment *iṭ* does not occur after roots such as *gam*, this optional rule (*vibhāṣā*) is commenced.

Regarding the form *jagmivān*: because it is subsequent [in the order of rules], *iṭ* is applied first; then, by the rule *gamahana-* (Pāṇini 6.4.98), there is the elision of the penultimate vowel (*upadhā-lopa*); thereafter, reduplication (*dvirvacana*) takes place.
Regarding the forms *jaghanvān* and *jaghnuvān*,
the substitution of *gh* for *h* occurs by rule [Pāṇini 7.3.55].
[The term] "of that which has the sense of obtaining" refers to...
Of the root *vidlṛ* in the sense of "acquisition" (*dhātupāṭha* 1432);
[it applies] "not to that which has the meaning of knowledge," namely,
of the root *vida* in the sense of "knowledge" (*dhātupāṭha* 1064).

Regarding *vida sattāyām* (Dhātupāṭha 1171) and *vida vicāraṇe* (Dhātupāṭha 1450): because these two roots take the ātmanepada endings, the suffix *kvasu* does not occur after them when they are conjugated in the ātmanepada; thus, they are not introduced [in this context]. Regarding the rule *dṛśeśca* and so forth:
the meaning is that it should be explained as having the sense that the augment *iṭ* is added after the suffix *kvasu* following the root *dṛś* (*vṛśir prekṣaṇe*, Dhātupāṭha 988).

In this regard, the following is the explanation: the term "vibhāṣā" is treated as a *yogavibhāga* (a split of the rule), whereby [the substitution] will also apply to the root *dṛś*. And even so, the rule "of *gam*, *han*, *vid*, and *viś*" (*gamahanavidaviśām*) is not rendered purposeless; for it serves to indicate that the preceding rule does not have universal application. In this way, the over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) is avoided. [The mention of] "of *san*" (*sanoteḥ*).

By the utterance of the second-case form of the root *ṣaṇu* (meaning "to give," Dhātupāṭha 1464) preceded by the suffix *san*, [the sūtra] indicates a fixed sequence (*ānupūrvī*). This is so that the rule may apply only where such a sequence is fixed. Since this sequence is fixed only in Vedic usage (*chandas*), this nipātana is understood to pertain exclusively to that domain.
For this very reason, the author of the Vṛtti has shown a Vedic usage:
*senivāṃsam*. As before, there is the substitution of *e* for the vowel and the elision of the reduplication.
The augment *iṭ* is applied by the rule *vasvekājādghasām* [Pāṇini 7.2.67]. The word *vibhāṣā* has ceased to apply here.

Since roots ending in *ṛ* and the root *han* are anudātta, this sūtra is intended to prescribe *iṭ* for the suffix *sya*, which was otherwise prohibited by the rule *ekāca upadeśe ’nudāttāt* [Pāṇini 7.2.10].

Now, one might ask: is *iṭ* optionally prescribed for the root *svar* by the rule *svaratisūtisūyatidhūñūdito vā* [Pāṇini 7.2.44]? To this he says: "No; by this [present rule], it is obligatory. Thus, this sūtra is for the purpose of prescribing *iṭ* for the root *svar* before the suffix *sya*.

Now, regarding the root *svarati*, the augment *iṭ* is optionally applied by the rule *svarati-prabhṛtibhyaḥ* [Pāṇini 7.2.44]. To show that it is instead obligatory by this present rule, he says: "*svarateḥ*" and so forth.

Since the optional application of *iṭ* was prescribed for the root *svarati* by the rule *svarati-prabhṛtibhyaḥ* [7.2.44], the present rule establishes the obligatory application of *iṭ* after roots ending in *ṛ* when the suffix *sya* follows, according to the principle of conflict (*vipratiṣedha*).
The purpose of the word "also" (*api*) is stated here again—despite its having been mentioned in the rule *svarati-prabhṛtibhyaḥ*—for the benefit of those who are prone to forgetfulness.

Now, what is the purpose of adding the *tapara* (the long vowel marker) [to the letter ṛ]? If you say it is so that [the rule] does not apply to the long vowels (*dīrgha*), this is not correct; for because they are acute (*udātta*), the augment *iṭ* must necessarily follow them. If that is the case, then in the absence of the *tapara*, just as in the rule *svarati-sūti-sūyati-dhūnūdito vā* (Pāṇini 7.2.44), there would be a reference to the verbal root *ṛ* due to its association with *svarati* and others, so too here, due to its association with the root *han*, there would be a reference to the verbal root *ṛ*. However, when the *tapara* is present, it is understood that this is a reference to the phoneme (*varṇa*) itself.
For it is well known that the use of *t* as a marker (*taparatva*) occurs in the specification of a phoneme (*varṇa*).

And since the mention of a phoneme everywhere necessitates a rule of "specification by the final element" (*tadantavidhi*), the augment *iṭ* is established for those [roots] ending in the vowel *ṛ*. The root *añjū*—meaning "to manifest, to smear, to shine, to go" (Dhātupāṭha 1458)—is marked with an indicatory *ū*. Since this root is included among those beginning with *svarati* (Pāṇini 7.2.44), an option would have applied; therefore, this statement is made to ensure its compulsory occurrence.

Regarding *āñjīt*: there is the elision of the vowel *i* by [Pāṇini 6.4.65] *itaśca*; is there the augment *iṭ* by [Pāṇini 7.2.35]? There is the elision of *sic* by [Pāṇini 8.2.28] *iṭa īṭi*; is there the augment *āṭ* by [Pāṇini 6.4.72]? There is the *vṛddhi* strengthening by [Pāṇini 6.1.87] *āṭaśca*. Regarding *āñjiṣṭām*.

By the rule *tasthasthamipām*, the suffix *jhi* is replaced by *jus*. Regarding the roots *ṣṭuñ* "to praise" (DhP 1043) and *ṣuñ* "to press" (DhP 1247), since they are anudātta (unaccented), a prohibition [of the substitution] would otherwise apply; however, since an option is already established for the root *dhūñ* by the rule *svarati-sūti-sūyati-dhūnūdito vā* (Pāṇini 7.2.44), this [present sūtra] is commenced. Regarding *yama* "to cease" (DhP 984), *ramu* "to play" (DhP 853), and *ṇama* "in bowing and sound" (DhP 981); there are also roots ending in long *ā*, such as *yā* "to go" (DhP 1049), and so forth.

Since all [roots] ending in a non-anudātta vowel would otherwise be subject to the prohibition of *iṭ*, this rule is commenced. Here, because of the mention of the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī-nirdeśa*), the augment *iṭ* applies to *yam* and the others; however, due to the governing context of *ārdhadhātuka*, it applies only to *sic*.
Thus, we have "vyaraṃsīt."
By [Pāṇini 1.3.83], the *parasmaipada* (active voice) suffixes are applied.

An example involving the dual and plural numbers is appropriate, for there is indeed a distinction there in the audible presence of the augment *s* and the augment *iṭ*; however, an example of the singular number is inappropriate because there is no such distinction. To one who might think this, he says "of *yam*, etc. and so forth, in order to show that even there, in the singular, there is a distinction consisting in the prohibition of *vṛddhi*. [The form is] *āyaṃsta* [the *Kāśikā* and *Padamañjarī* also cite *āyaṃsta* as the very reading].
Thus, the *ātmanepada* [is applied].
Regarding "araṃsta," here too [the rule] beginning with "anudātta" [1.3.12] applies. [The roots are]: *ṇmiṅ* "to smile slightly" (Dhātupāṭha 948) and *pūṅ* "to purify" (Dhātupāṭha 966).
The mention of the suffix *an* is for the purpose of excluding the root *pū*.

Both the root *ṛ* belonging to the *bhvādi* class (*ṛ gatiprāpaṇayoḥ*, Dhp. 936) and the root *ṛ* belonging to the *juhotyādi* class (*ṛ gatau*, DhP. 1098) are included here, because no distinction is made between them.
However, this inclusion does not apply to roots ending in long *ṛ* (*ṝ*); for in the subsequent rules, *iṭ* is prescribed for roots such as *kṝ* and others.

The roots *añj* [meaning "to smear," according to the Dhātupāṭha 1458: *vyaktimarṣaṇakāntigatiṣu*] and *aś* [meaning "to pervade" (*vyāptau*) or "to join" (*saṃdhe*), according to the Dhātupāṭha 1264] are intended here.

The root *aś* [meaning "to eat" (*bhojane*), Dhātupāṭha 1523] is not included; is this because the augment *iṭ* is already established for it simply by virtue of its being accented? In that case, since *añj* and *aś* would optionally take *iṭ* due to having an indicatory letter *it*, while the remaining roots would [optionally take it] due to ending in the vowel *u*, and since a prohibition would then apply by the rule *sanigrahaguhośca* [Pāṇini 7.2.12], this [sūtra] is commenced.
Regarding *sismiyiṣate*:
the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) is applied by the rule *pūrvavatsanaḥ* [Pāṇini 1.3.62].
Regarding *pipaviṣate*.
By [Pāṇini 7.4.80], the *it*-augment is applied to the reduplication,
resulting in *aririṣati*.
When the augment *iṭ* is present and *guṇa* has been applied, there is reduplication of the second monosyllabic (*ekāc*) vowel of the root beginning with a vowel (*ajādi*).

Regarding "he desires to anoint" (*añjijiṣati*), it is said "he desires to eat" (*aśiśiṣati* [or *aśiśiṣate*—Kāśikā; not found in the printed edition]). Here, the letter *n* of the root *añj* is not reduplicated because of the prohibition stated in [Pāṇini 6.1.3]. The roots are as follows: *rudir* (Dhātupāṭha 1067) in the sense of shedding tears; *ñi ṣvap* (Dhātupāṭha 1068) in the sense of sleeping; *ās* (Dhātupāṭha 1069) in the sense of breathing; *ana* (Dhātupāṭha 1070); and *jakṣ* (Dhātupāṭha 1071) in the sense of eating [or, according to the Dhātupāṭha, eating and laughing].
The roots beginning with *rud* are listed among the *adādi* (third class) verbs.

According to the principle "when both [case endings] are mentioned, the mention of the ablative is stronger" (*Śākapārthivādhikaraṇa* 97), the ablative in *rudādibhyaḥ* supersedes the locative *sārvadhātuke*, thereby effecting its conversion into a genitive.
The mention of the locative is for the sake of what follows.

Because it is understood that *iṅ* [is substituted] for a *sārvadhātuka* suffix beginning with a consonant (*val*) by that [rule], he says "from the five beginning with *rud*" and so forth. In the word "prāṇiti," there is the substitution of *ṇ* [for *n*] by [Pāṇini 8.4.19] *aniteḥ*.
Regarding the form *svaptā*:

because of the mention of the term *sārvadhātuka*, the augment *iṭ* does not apply to the *ārdhadhātuka*. Furthermore, the general rule for *iṭ* simply does not apply here, due to the prohibition [stated in Pāṇini 7.2.10] beginning with *ekācaḥ*.

However, since other roots such as *rud* and others have an udātta vowel, the augment *īṭ* must necessarily occur for the ārdhadhātuka suffix as well; therefore, *svapa* alone serves as the counter-example. Regarding the form *se*:
this is a citation without a case ending, having applied the substitution of the genitive case by the rule *supāṃ suluk* [Pāṇini 7.1.39].
Regarding the form *īśiṣe*.

Regarding *īśa aiārye* (Dhātupāṭha 1020): in the present tense (*laṭ*), because the root is marked with an indicatory vowel *anudātta*, the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) is used. By [Pāṇini 3.4.80], *thās* is replaced by *se*. Because the root belongs to the *adādi* class, there is elision (*luk*) of the suffix *śap*. Thus we have *īśiṣva*. This is the imperative (*loṭ*). With the suffix *se*, when the substitution of *va* for *as* is applied according to [Pāṇini 3.4.91], the principle that "that which undergoes a partial modification is not different from the original" applies here as well. Regarding *dhve*: [the same process applies].
This is a non-inflected reference, just as before:
*īḍidhve*.
[The root] *īḍ* is used in the sense of "praising" (*stuti*; Dhātupāṭha 1019). The middle voice (*ātmanepada*) is applied as before, and the elision of the *śap* suffix is likewise as before.
In *īḍidhvam*,
the suffix *loṭ* takes the substitute *am* according to [Pāṇini 3.4.91]. In *janiṣvam*, [the same applies].

The ātmanepada [suffixes] apply as before, by the rule *chandasyubhayathā* (Pāṇini 3.4.117); and the absence of the elision of the penultimate vowel (*upadhālopa*) occurs by the rule *śyanparasmaipadeṣu* (Pāṇini 7.4.78). Thus:
"and there is no elision of the penultimate vowel."

By the rule *gamahana* [Pāṇini 6.4.98], elision of the penultimate vowel (*upadhā-lopa*) would apply; its absence occurs precisely because of the status of the Vedic text (*chāndasa-sattva*), according to the principle: "All rules are optional in the Veda" (*sarve vidhayaś chandasi vikalpyante*). Regarding the phrase "of the root *jan* in the sense of 'begetting,'" etc.: one might object that because this [root *jan*] possesses an indicatory letter (*anubandha*), it alone should be understood by the mention [of the form *jana*], and not the preceding one [the root *janī*]. Is the vowel *a* merely for the purpose of pronunciation and not an indicatory letter? This is not a fault; for here, since the word *jana* consists of fewer syllables, it would normally be placed first in a compound, but its placement after [the other member] is intended to demonstrate an exception to the general rule.
Because the paribhāṣā "that which has no subsequent [application]" (vyā|pa|53) does not apply here, both [roots] are included. Thus, we have *vyatijajñidhvam*;
the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) is used according to [Pāṇini 1.3.14], "the middle voice is used when there is a reciprocal action (*karmavyatīhāra*) in the sense of the agent."
Regarding the passage beginning with "tatra" and so forth:

in that very context of the sūtra-reading, according to the rule *yasmin vidhis tadādāvallgrahaṇe* (Vyāḍīya-paribhāṣā 127), when there is a mention of the sound *s*, there is a mention of the word *se* which begins with *s*.
And that word *se* beginning with *s* can only be the word *se* itself, as it is designated as *sārvadhātuka*; for no other [word] is possible.

"But is it not possible that the word *sva* itself [is intended]? This is not so; for that which is modified in one part is not different [from the original] (Vyāḍi-Patañjali 16). That [word *sva*] is indeed the word *se*, and therefore it must also be included by the mention of that [term].
As for those who recite the rule as "īḍajanodhrye ca," they include the particle *ca* for the purpose of carrying over (*anukarṣaṇa*) that very same rule, namely "īśaḥ sa" (Pāṇini 7.2.77).
The augment *iṭ* also occurs after the root *īś* before the ending *dhve*.

If, then, the augment *iṭ* is desired even after *īś* before *dhve*, why do they not read a single sūtra as "īś-īḍ-janāṃ sedhvayoḥ"? In this way, a separate case-ending would not have to be uttered, and the particle *ca* would not need to be employed? To this he says: "The sūtra is diverse," and so forth;
"dhve [is used] for that which has the substitution of *e* for *ṭ*," and so forth.

The sole purpose of this substitution of *et* for the final vowel (*ṭerettvam*) is that it should apply only where the substitution of *et* for the final vowel has already been made. Since the substitution of *et* for the final vowel does not occur in the *laṅ* [tense], the augment *iṭ* should not be applied there.

If this is so, then it should also not occur in the *loṭ* [imperative], because once the replacement by *am* has been made, the substitution of *et* for the final vowel is absent? To this he says: "But in the *loṭ*," and so forth. [This refers to the rule] "that which is the *liṅ* in a *sārvadhātuka* [suffix]."

In this context, the locative case in *sārvadhātuke* [Pāṇini 7.2.76] is used in the sense of selection (*nirdhāraṇe*), and the singular number is used for the genus (*jātāvekavacanam*), as in the rule *kārake* [1.4.23].
Alternatively, by means of a transposition of case endings (*subvyatyayena*), the singular is applied to what would otherwise be a plural.
This is not a locative of sequence (*parasaptamī*)—meaning "when a *sārvadhātuka* follows"—because a preceding *liṅ* is impossible.
Regarding the form *kuryāt*:

in the sūtra beginning with the injunction (vidhi), the suffix *liṅ* is applied; then *yāsuṭ* is added; by the rule *itaśca* [Pāṇini 3.4.100], there is the elision of the *i*; then the *guṇa* substitution for the verbal root; then, after the change of the *r* to the following vowel (*raparatva*), by the rules *ata ut sārvadhātuke* [Pāṇini 6.4.110] and *ato guṇe* [Pāṇini 6.1.97], there is the substitution of the subsequent form (*pararūpatva*).
Regarding the form *kurvīta*: [the same process applies].
The substitution of *yaṇ* for the vowel *u* occurs,
as in the forms "kurvīran," "kuryuḥ," and "kuryāḥ."

Here, because of the inclusion of the term "infinitude" (ānantya), the substitution of *jus* and *sip* does not occur; for example, in *kriyāstām* and *kriyāsuḥ*. [In these cases,] by the rule *āśiṣi liṅ* [Pāṇini 3.3.173], the *liṅ* suffix is applied, and by the rule *riṅśayagliṅkṣu* [Pāṇini 7.4.28], the *riṅ* substitute is applied.
Because of the mention of the term *sārvadhātuka*, this substitution does not occur in the *ārdhadhātuka* domain.
And because the designation *ārdhadhātuka* is prescribed by the rule *ārdhadhātukatvaṃ ca* (P.

3.4.116), [the suffixes] *kṛṣīṣṭa* and *hraṣīṣṭa* [are formed]. By the rule *uśca* (P. 1.2.12), there is the status of being *kit*, resulting in the absence of *guṇa*. As for "that which is *sārvadhātuka*," that which was under discussion is here understood in the genitive case through a change of grammatical number (*vibhaktivipariṇāma*).
Therefore, it says: "of the *sārvadhātuka* suffix following an *aṅga* ending in the vowel *a*.

As in *paceta* (or *paṭhet*, as found in the older printed edition). Once the substitution of *iy* has been made, the *y* is elided by [Pāṇini 6.1.87] and [Pāṇini 6.1.66], together with the preceding *a*.
"cinuyāt" (he should pile);
"yāyāt" (he should go)— in these cases,
there is elision of the *śap* suffix due to their belonging to the *adādi* class.

Regarding the form *cikīrṣyāt*: this is the optative (*liṅ*) in the sense of a benediction derived from a desiderative stem (*sananta*). [Objection: "But surely, there ought to be elision of the *a* here."
The intention is that there is no purpose in including the term *sārvadhātuka* [in the rule].

Regarding the phrase "even in the case of *pacet*" and so forth: although this is intended as an example for *pacet*, since the lengthening [of the vowel] must occur by rule Pāṇini 6.4.101 (*ato dīrgho yañi*), this substitution of *iy* would have no scope, as its entire domain is already occupied by another rule.
Therefore, this [rule] must necessarily set aside another rule.
And thus, just as it is a sublater of the long vowel, so too would it be a sublater of the elision (*ato lopa*).
Consequently, the sense is that the mention of *sārvadhātuka* must be carried over [from the previous rule].
"It might be so," and so forth.

If the term *sārvadhātuka* were to be supplied from the rule *turustunnamyamaḥ sārvadhātuke* [Pāṇini 7.3.95] and applied here as well, then what you have said would indeed be the case; for the substitution of *iy* would then have no scope of application.

If, following the rule *atha* [Pāṇini 7.3.88], the mention of *tiṅ* is understood as a governing term (*anuvartana*) and the lengthening is prescribed, then this would be a rule prescribing lengthening for *tiṅ* alone when it is about to disappear (*abhāvi*). Since this [rule] is commenced when the substitute [prescribed by Pāṇini 6.4.105] has not yet applied, it becomes a sublater of that very substitute according to the maxim *yena nāprāpta* (Vyāḍiparibhāṣā 49), but not of the elision of *ataḥ*.
This [present rule] is commenced when the elision of *ataḥ* after *iy* is both applicable and inapplicable.

For [the rule] applies when an *ārdhadhātuka* affix follows, but not when a *sārvadhātuka* affix follows. Now, regarding the expression *yeyi*: what is this grammatical reference (*nirdeśa*)? Here, the substitute *yā* takes the genitive case; thus, having [the form] *yā-as*, and with *iya* substituted [for *yā*], the long *ā* is either elided by the rule *āto lopaḥ* [P. 6.4.48] or by splitting the rule *ātaḥ dhātoḥ* [P. 6.4.140]. Then, the *s* of the genitive case ending becomes *r* by the rule *sasajuṣo ruḥ* [P. 8.2.66], and finally, the *y* is substituted [for the *r*] by the rule *bho-bhago-agho-apūrvasya yo 'śi* [P. 8.3.17].

In that case as well, when there is elision by [Pāṇini 8.3.19] *lopaḥ śākalyasya*, the form should be indicated as *ya iyaḥ* according to the rule [Pāṇini 6.4.81], and not as *yataḥ*; for here, the substitution of *guṇa* (the single substitute *e*) for *a* and *i* cannot possibly occur, because the elision of *y* [by 8.3.19] is considered non-existent (*asiddha*) [for the purposes of the preceding rule 6.1.87]. To this he says: "The indication *yeyaḥ* is without a case-ending (*avibhaktika*). In the expression *yeyaḥ*, by the combination of the original base (*sthānin*) and the substitute (*ādeśa*), the word *yā* is understood.
This designation is without case endings because the case ending has been elided by the rule *supāṃ suluk* [Pāṇini 7.1.39].
And having accepted that the designation possesses case endings, he states another resolution,
beginning with "yaḥ" and "vā."

But how can one avoid relying on the fact that the elision (*lopa*) is treated as non-existent (*asiddha*)? To this he says: "This is a Vedic-style (*sautra*) designation. The particle *iti* indicates a reason. Why?

Because "all rules are optional in the Veda" (*PuPāVṛ 56*), and "the Sūtras are like the Veda" (*Mahābhāṣya*). Therefore, because this is a Sūtra-style designation, the [operation] at [Pāṇini 6.1.87] was performed without relying on its being non-existent.
In this rule, the vowel *a* [in *iyādeśe*] is for the purpose of pronunciation (*uccāraṇārtha*). The two genitives in *ātaḥ* and *ṅitaḥ* are in different grammatical relations (*vyadhikaraṇa*).
The genitive in *ātaḥ* is a genitive of the place (*sthāna-ṣaṣṭhī*) with respect to the substitute *iy*.
The genitive in *ṅitaḥ* is a partitive genitive (*avayava-ṣaṣṭhī*) with respect to the vowel *ā*, because a mere *ṅ*-sound alone cannot exist.

The term *ṅit* is understood here as a genitive (*ṣaṣṭhī*) in connection with the word *avayava*—that is, "of a part that has *ṅ* as its *it*. A suffix whose *it* is the letter *ṅ* is called *ṅit*; a part of such a suffix is a *ṅidavayava*.

[Examples are] *pacete*, *pacethe*. [This is formed from] *laṭ*; because it has a circumflex accent (*svaritet*), the *ātmanepada* endings are used; [the endings] *ātām* and *thām*; [and by the rule] *sārvadhātukamapit* (Pāṇini 1.2.4).
4) Thus, there is the status of being marked with *ṅ* (ṅittva).

In the forms "pacetām" and "pacethām," the imperative (*loṭ*) is applied; once the substitution of *e* for the final syllable (*ṭi*) has been made by [Pāṇini 3.4.79], the suffix *ām* is added by [Pāṇini 3.4.90].

But surely, the vowel *a* here is not a constituent part (*avayava*) of that which has the marker *ṅ*; for in the rule *gāṅkuṭādibhyaḥ...* [Pāṇini 1.2.1], the meaning "as if having *ṅ*" (*ṅidvat*) is accepted as being like "having *ṅ*" (*ṅiti*), and this same meaning applies here in [Pāṇini 1.2.4] as well. Likewise, in this rule too, that very mention of *ṅit* carries over; and if that meaning were accepted, then whatever operation is prescribed for what has *ṅ*, that would indeed be observed for the preceding element when followed by a *sārvadhātuka* suffix, but not because that *sārvadhātuka* suffix itself possesses the property of *ṅit*. To this he says: "In the rule *sārvadhātukam apit*... and so forth.
"In the preceding rule alone" means...

In the rule *gāṅkuṭādibhyaḥ* (Pāṇini 1.2.1), if it were accepted that "an affix following *gāṅ* and the roots beginning with *kuṭ* is treated as having the marker *ṅ*," then the *san* affix following the *kuṭ*-roots would possess the *ṅ*-marker (*ṅittva*). If it possessed the *ṅ*-marker, by the rule *anudāttaṅita ātmanepadam* (1.3.12), the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) would be required; consequently, forms such as *uccukuṭipati* would not be established. Therefore, for the sake of establishing this, it is accepted that "that which has the *ṅ*-marker is treated as having the *ṅ*-marker" (*ṅiti ṅidvat*). However, in the rule *sārvadhātukamapit* (1.2.4), the meaning accepted is that "that *sārvadhātuka* [affix] becomes one having the *ṅ*-marker."
Therefore, it is indeed correct that the vowel *ā* is a constituent part of the *ṅit* [suffix]. In forms such as *pacante* and *yajante*,
although the vowel *ā* of the substitute *akta* is a constituent part of the *ṅit* suffix, nevertheless, because of the rule stating "of *āt*" (*ātaḥ*), [the substitution does not apply here].
In the forms *pacāvahai* and *pacāmahai*,

the suffixes *loṭ* are *vah* and *mahiṅ*. By the rule *āḍuttamasya pi ca* [Pāṇini 3.4.92], the augment *āṭ* is applied, and the first person (*uttama*) suffix becomes marked with the *pi* designation.
In this case, because [the root] ends in *p*, it does not possess the *ṅit* quality; consequently, the rule *āto ṅidadayavākāraḥ* does not apply.
Thus we have *mimāte* and *mimāthe*.
[The root] *māṅ* [meaning] "measuring" [and also "sound," according to the Dhātupāṭha] (Dhātupāṭha 1088) undergoes *ślu* substitution for *śap* due to its belonging to the *juhotyādi* class.

By the rule *ślau* [Pāṇini 6.1.10], there is reduplication; by *bhṛñāmit* [Pāṇini 7.4.76], the *it*-augment is applied to the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*); and by *śnābhyastayorātaḥ* [Pāṇini 6.4.112], there is elision of the long *ā*. Regarding the phrase *aṅgasyātaḥ*:
this is a genitive of different case-relation (*vyadhikaraṇa-ṣaṣṭhī*), meaning that when there is an *at* belonging to an *aṅga*, the augment *muk* occurs.
In that case, should the mention of *ad* (the vowel *a*) be made here? It need not be made; for the word *ataḥ* will be carried over (*anuvartate*) from the preceding rule [Pāṇini 7.2.80].

But is it not the case that in that [rule] the ablative (*pañcamī*) is specified, whereas here the meaning is expressed by the genitive (*ṣaṣṭhī*)? This is not so; for the ablative *ataḥ* has its purpose fulfilled there in the substitution of *iy* and so on, whereas *āne* is a locative (*saptamī*) whose purpose is not yet fulfilled. Therefore, this locative *āne* will be treated as a genitive in relation to the ablative *ataḥ*, because of the rule: "The locative case-ending is used in the sense of the genitive" (Pāṇini 1.1.66).

But surely, the letter *a* is a phoneme (*varṇa*), and the letter *m* is also a phoneme; yet *mu* has its marker (*liṅga*) at the end, and the "end" (*anta*) is a constituent part (*avayava*). Now, it is not logical for a phoneme to be a constituent part of another phoneme—[the printed text reads *varṇasyāvayavī*, but the correct reading is *varṇasyāvayava*]—because one phoneme does not initiate another. Therefore, is it not incorrect to say that "therefore the augment *mu* occurs"? This is not a fault; for in every case, when an augment is prescribed, whether it is that after which the augment is prescribed or the augment itself, its status as being "at the beginning" (*ādita*) or "at the end" (*antata*) is prescribed with reference to the entire complex [of the base and the augment].
Therefore, the intended meaning of the statement "the augment *muk* is inserted" is this: this aggregate, beginning with the vowel *a*, comes to end with the letter *s*.
As for the form *pacamānaḥ*:
it is the present tense suffix *laṭ*, which takes the substitute *śānac*.

When it is stated that the augment *muk* occurs after the suffix *āna* when it follows a stem (*aṅga*) ending in *a*, one who considers these two genitive cases to be in apposition (*samānādhikaraṇa*) might grasp the meaning of the rule as: "the augment *muk* occurs after a stem ending in *a* when *āna* follows. Such a person might then teach as follows: "If the stem were to end in *a*, then in the form *pacamānaḥ*, the suffix would not be unaccented according to the rule *adupadeśāllasārvadhātukamanudāttam* [Pāṇini 6.1.180], because the vowel *a* would be separated from the suffix by the augment *muk*.
For in that context, it is established that the rule applies to what ends in *a* at the time of its original enunciation (*upadeśa*), and not to a stem that merely ends in *a* at that point."

Nor can it be argued that this *nuk* is a partial (*bhakta*) constituent of the suffix *aṅ*, and therefore there is no intervention; for while this [nasal] being a partial constituent would not intervene with respect to the suffix *aṅ* itself, it certainly does intervene with respect to the letter *a*. Indeed, one part of a whole does not become an intervener for that same whole, yet it certainly becomes an intervener for another part. Therefore, he says: "This [nasal] is a partial constituent of the letter *a* alone," and so forth.
The word *mātra* is used here to exclude the status of being a constituent part (*aṅga-bhaktatva*).
And in this context, "constituent part" (*aṅga*) refers to a specific phonetic form;
it is the vowel *a* itself that is the augment (*āgamī*), not the constituent part.

Therefore? Because it is not a part of that [the *muk*]. Since the *muk* is grasped precisely by the non-grasping of that [the *ā*], there is no intervention; thus, the *lasārvadhātuka* suffix becomes unaccented (*anudātta*).

But surely, even when the *muk* is attached as a part of the long *ā*, it must necessarily be unaccented by rule [P. 6.1.186]; and since the *muk* is considered as if non-existent in the application of accent rules—according to the principle "in the prescription of accents, a consonant is as if non-existent" (Vyāḍi-Pāṇini-Paribhāṣā 37)—there would still be no intervention because the *muk* is non-existent? The author thinks as follows: this paribhāṣā is not accepted by the author of the Bhāṣya.
For instance—having rejected that rule, he has adopted this other rule: "When a vowel is to be obtained after a consonant [hal-svara-prāptau], the consonant is as if non-existent" (Nī.pā.vṛ. 68).
But here there is no obtaining of a vowel after a consonant; rather, it is of a vowel.
[The objection begins with] "If this is so," and so forth.

If this [substitution] were devoted to the letter *a*, then by the inclusion of that [term], in the case of *pacamāna*, the substitution of *iy* for *ana*—which follows immediately after the *ā* according to Pāṇini 7.2.81 (*āt-i-y-anaḥ*)—would apply because *muk* does not act as an intervention. To this, [the author] says: "It does not occur because of the specification with the *tapara* marker.
For here, the letter *a* is specified as having a duration of one *mātrā* (short) by the *tapara* marker; when *muk* is present, it becomes half a *mātrā*.
Therefore, due to this difference in duration, [the rule] will not apply.
That which has more than half [a mora] is *adhyardhā*; that which has an *adhyardhā* mora is *adhyardhamātra*.

Even so, the rule that "a *sārvadhātuka* suffix is unaccented" would not apply; therefore, in the formulation of that rule as well, there is the mention of *tapara* (the vowel *a* with a following *t*).
[The phrase] "the mention of *upadeśa*" and so forth [is used].
In that context, the instruction is given for the purpose of perceiving its prior state;

therefore, although there is a difference in duration once *muk* has been applied at a later time, nevertheless, because it possesses the duration of one *mātrā* during the stage of instruction (*upadeśāvasthā*), the quality of being unaccented (*anudātta*) indeed applies here.
"And so," etc.

Since, according to that [rule], after the instruction [of the preceding rule], even when there is a difference in time, the substitution must occur by virtue of being *anudātta*, and having established this, even in cases such as *pacāvaḥ* where a difference in time exists once the lengthening (*dīrghatva*) has been applied by [Pāṇini 7.3.101], the substitution still takes place. The ablative case in *āsaḥ* (from *ās*), though its purpose is already fulfilled, will cause the locative case in *āne* (from Pāṇini 7.2.82), whose purpose was already fulfilled in the preceding rule, to be interpreted as a genitive, according to the statement [Pāṇini 1.1.67]. Therefore, this substitution is prescribed specifically for *āna*. Thus he says: "Of the word *āna* following *ās*.
As in the example *āsīnaḥ*.
The root *ās* is used in the sense of "sitting" (*upaveśane*; Dhātupāṭha 1021).

Because it is marked with an anudātta vowel, the ātmanepada endings are applied; by [Pāṇini 1.1.54], the vowel *ā* is replaced by *i*. Due to its inclusion in the *ad*-class, there is elision (*luk*) of the suffix *śya*.

The inclusion of the long vowel marker (taparakaraṇa) is for the sake of ease of pronunciation. "The statement 'ā' is a reference to a specific individual instance (vyakti)" means that there is a reference only to the pure, non-nasalized (*niranunāsika*) individual instance of the phoneme *ā*.

Now, what would be the fault if there were a reference to the generic form (*ākṛti*), such that this reference to a specific individual instance was adopted to avoid that [fault]? To this he says: "For if there were a reference to the generic form," and so forth.
In this context, "genus" (*jāti*) is intended, and not "configuration" (*saṃsthāna*).

Since it is impossible to indicate a pure genus when a genus is being specified, the grammatical operation is understood to apply to the individual instances (*vyakti*) which serve as its substratum. In that case, if the specification of the genus were relied upon here, then since all instances of the vowel *a* would have attained the status of being the substratum for the genus, by the rule *alo 'ntyasya* [Pāṇini 1.1.52], the substitute for the nasalized *n*—which is the closest in similarity (*āntaratamya*)—would be a nasalized *ā* alone.

If, however, there were a reference to a specific individual (*vyakti-nirdeśa*), this fault would not arise; yet [the objection] that "this and so forth is not established" remains, for there is no word here expressing an alternative (*vikalpa*), nor is the subject under discussion (*prakṛta*) absent? To this he says: "by way of an alternative" (*vikalpena*), and so forth. By the rule *aṣṭana ā vibhaktau* (Pāṇini 7.2.84), the acute accent (*udāttatva*) is prescribed for the long vowel of *aṣṭan* before case-endings other than those called *sarvanāmasthāna*. If the substitution of *āt* were obligatory (*nitya*), the qualification "after a long vowel" (*dīrghāt*) would be purposeless.

Furthermore, in the rule *aṣṭābhya auś* (Pāṇini 7.1.21), the mention of the form with the substitution of *ātva* (*aṣṭā-*) would be purposeless; since there is nothing to be excluded [by such a specification], one could simply have said *aṣṭanaḥ*. Therefore, by the inclusion of the long vowel (*dīrgha-grahaṇa*) and the mention of the form with *ātva*, it is indicated that this *ātva* substitution occurs optionally.
Therefore, the phrase "by eight," and so forth, is also included as an alternative, because of the use of the singular number.
For otherwise, since there would be a plurality of objects, he would have said "of the eight. Consequently, this [term] refers primarily to its own essential form (*svarūpa*).

In that context, when the member (*aṅga*) under discussion is qualified by this [rule], the rule of "application to what ends with that" (*tadantavidhi*) is obtained; for it has been stated that when there is a qualifier, the rule of application to what ends with that applies. [The example *priyāṣṭā* is not seen in the root text.]
The long vowel [is substituted] by the rule *sarvanāmasthāne* [6.4.8], etc., resulting in *yuṣmad* and *asmat*. Regarding the forms *yuṣmad* and *asmat*:

by the rule *pañcamyā at* [7.1.31], the substitution of *at* for the ablative plural suffix *bhyas* occurs; then, after the final *t* is elided by *ato guṇe* [6.1.97], the *para-rūpa* (single-substitute) operation applies. If [one objects]: "Since the governing context is *halī* (before a consonant), would not the substitution of *āt* also fail to apply here? What then is the purpose of including the mention of *anādeśa* (non-substitute)? To this he says: "But in the subsequent [rules]," and so forth.
Regarding the statement that the purpose [of the present rule] is for the sake of non-substitution in the subsequent sūtra *yo'ci* [Pāṇini 7.2.89]:

if this were so, it should have been formulated right there; why is it done here? The intention is that it is for the sake of clarity. [The forms] *tvām* and *mām* [are derived] by the substitution of *tvam* and *mām* [as prescribed in Pāṇini 7.2.97].
Regarding "yuvām" and "āvām":
the substitutes *yu* and *āv* are applied by the rule *yuvāvau dvivacane* [Pāṇini 7.2.92].

In all cases, when the case-ending *ṅe* (dative) follows, the substitution of *am* occurs by the rule *ṅe prathamayoram* [Pāṇini 7.1.28]; and once *am* has been made, the preceding form is applied by the rule *ami pūrvavatvam* [Pāṇini 6.1.107]. This statement is also intended for the purpose of providing these specific substitutes.
Regarding the forms *yuvayoḥ* and *āvayoḥ*:

one might object that the substitution of *ya* (by Pāṇini 7.2.89, *yo'ci*) will serve as an exception here. But then, even in the case of the dual nominative, the elision of the remainder (*śeṣe lopaḥ*, 7.2.90) would likewise be an exception.
Just as the elision of the remainder is set aside by this [present rule] due to the force of the specific injunction, so too would the substitution of *ya* be set aside.

"Exceptions that precede [a rule] sublate the immediately following rules, but not those that follow" (Vyāḍipāda 9); thus, even the substitution of *y* would be sublated. Therefore, it must be stated: "of the first case," as in "thou" (*tvam*) and "I" (*aham*).

> [[7.2.94]] The substitutes *tvā* and *āha*. Although it would have been sufficient to say "au," the use of the dual number in the first case is for the sake of variety. Regarding the passage beginning with "In the rule *yuṣmadasmador ām ādeśaḥ*... and so forth:

> [[7.2.86]] If the mention of *hal* from the preceding rule [[7.2.85]] is carried over here, then the substitution of *ya*, being prescribed without distinction, is understood as the general rule (*utsarga*).
But the substitution of *āt* is prescribed specifically for a following consonant-initial case ending (*hal-ādi*), and thus it is an exception even to this [rule].

In this way, even without the mention of *ac*, the *yakāra* would remain only before a vowel-initial [suffix]; therefore, could one not simply omit the word *aci*? That is true; however, it is included for the sake of clarity, as in the examples: *svad gacchati* and *mad gacchati*.
By [Pāṇini 7.1.32], *ṅasi* is replaced by *āt*. "Those which are duals" means the singular and plural cases.
"In this case" refers to the following.
"In the case of the fifth and subsequent case endings,
their elision is prescribed," because only those [suffixes] remain as the remainder (śeṣa).
Regarding "tubhyam" and "mahyam":
by the rule "tubhyamahrau ṅayi" [Pāṇini 7.2.95], the substitutes *tubhyam* and *mahyam* occur.
Regarding "yuṣmabhyam" and "asmabhyam": [these are formed by the substitution of *bhyas* for the case-ending].
By [Pāṇini 7.1.30], *bhyām* is substituted;
thus, "tava" and "mama. By [Pāṇini 7.2.96], *tva* and *ma* are substituted.
Regarding the forms *yuṣmākam* and *asmākam*, [the rule] states: "After [the words] *yuṣmad* and *asmad*, [there is elision].

Now, what is the purpose of including the term *śeṣa* (remainder)? Why not simply say "elision" (*lopa*)? It should not be suspected that if this were stated, the elision would apply without distinction; for while the elision being prescribed generally would constitute a general rule (*utsarga*), its exceptions (*apavāda*)—namely the *yakāra* and *akāra*—would apply specifically to particular case-endings (*vibhakti*) where no substitute has been taught. Thus, even without the inclusion of *śeṣa*, the elision would be established as applying only to the remainder. To this he says: "The inclusion of *śeṣa* is for the sake of clarity."

"When the elision of the final [phoneme] has been performed, why does the suffix *ṭāp* not occur for the feminine?"— the sense is that once the final [phoneme] has been elided, because the word ends in *at*, the suffix *ṭāp* ought to apply by the rule "ajādyaṭaṣṭāp" [Pāṇini 4.1.4]. [The author replies with] "sannipāta," etc.
For when there is immediate proximity to the case-ending (*vibhakti*), the words *yuṣmad* and *asmad* become those ending in the vowel *a*.
In that situation, if they were to produce the suffix *ṭāp*, then the immediate proximity to the case-ending would be destroyed by them.
And since that which is characterized by the occurrence of something else cannot be the cause for its own destruction, the suffix *ṭāp* does not occur.

If this is so, would [the suffix] not also fail to occur after words such as *tyad* and the rest? This is not a fault; for by making the rule-statement *yadayam* (Pāṇini 7.3.45), he indicates that the suffix *ṭāp* occurs after *tyad* and the rest. Furthermore, this resolution was stated while assuming that *yuṣmad* and *asmad* possess feminine gender.
Now, to show that the suffix *ṭāp* does not occur precisely because they lack feminine gender, he says: "in the absence of gender," and so forth.
"However, some desire the elision of the remainder (*śeṣalopa*) as the elision of the *ṭi* [suffix].
This is for the purpose that the *ṭāp* suffix should not occur in such instances as "you are a Brāhmaṇī" (*tvaṃ brāhmaṇī*) or "I am a Brāhmaṇī" (*ahaṃ brāhmaṇī*).

It is also for the purpose that when the substitute *bhyam* is applied in "to you all" (*yuṣmabhyam*) and "to us all" (*asmabhyam*), the substitution of *et* by the rule "in the plural, before a consonant, *et*" (*bahuvacane jhalyet*) should not occur.
"How so?

He thinks as follows: "That [suffix] in which neither the vowel *ā* nor the consonant *y* has been prescribed is the 'remainder' (*śeṣa*). In that case, when elision (*lopa*) is prescribed for the remainder, the elision of *ṭi* is not obtained.

By the technical rule (*paribhāṣā*) beginning with "[1.1.52]," it would follow that only the final [letter] is affected. Therefore, he clarifies the meaning of the term "remainder" (*śeṣa*)—in relation to the substitutions (*ādeśa*) to be stated later—by means of the words "And those," and so forth.

"That which is other than [the cases] beginning with the locative (maparyanta) is the remainder (śeṣa). This, moreover, is precisely the *ṣṭi* [suffix]. Here, since this remainder (*śeṣa*) is the locus for the elision (*lopa*)—meaning "the elision of the *ṣṭi* occurs"—the seventh case is used because the remainder is intended to be expressed as the locus (*adhikaraṇa*) with respect to the elision.

But for what purpose is elision (*lopa*) stated, given that [the form] would be established simply by the substitution of *yat* for words beginning with *tyad*? It is not established; because [the word *atyad*] does not belong to the class of words beginning with *tyad*.
For the status of being a word beginning with *tyad* is defined as "the words beginning with *tyad* extend up to *dvā*.
In this regard, the very mention of elision of the remainder (*śeṣalopa*) serves as the indicator (*jñāpaka*).

Therefore, the substitution of *tyadādi* (the *yatva* and subsequent changes) does not apply to the word *bhavat*—as in *bhavān*. Regarding the forms *yuvakām* and *āvākām*, the suffix *akac* is applied by the rule *avyayasarvanāmnām akac prāk ṭeḥ* [Pāṇini 5.3.71].

Here, if the expression "of that which ends in *map*" (*maparyantasya*) were not stated, then because no limit would be specified, the suffix would apply even to the form with *akac* (*sākacka*). Therefore, he says: "Let it not apply to the whole form when it has *akac*."
If the inclusion of "without limit" (aparyanta) were not present, then because no boundary would be established and because a substitute is manifold, the substitution would apply to everything.
But what fault would there be in the substitution applying to everything? To this, he says: "And thus," and so forth;
"the undesired form would result."
If the letter *ya* were substituted for the vowel *a* by the rule *yo 'ci* [Pāṇini 7.2.89], then the forms would have to be *tv-y-ā* and *m-y-ā*.

However, when the term "ending in *m*" (*maparyanta*) is included, since the portions of *yuṣmad* and *asmad* ending in *m* are established as the substituends (*sthānin*), the substitutions to be described hereafter apply to these very forms; thus, there is no fault whatsoever. Now, what is the purpose of including the word *pari* ("around" or "including")? Could one not simply say "ending in *m*" (*māntasya*)? Even if this were stated, since the word *anta* signifies "proximity," and because one relies on a *bahuvrīhi* compound that includes the quality of its members (*tadguṇasaṃvijñāna*), the desired result would be achieved. To this, he says: "Of that which ends in *m*," and so forth.

In this context—either regarding the absence of substitution for *sākacka* (the form with the *it* augment), or else regarding word-forms such as *yuvakām* and *avakām*—the inclusion of the term "ending in *m*" (*māntasya*) which has already been established is for the purpose of indicating a limit. It serves to indicate the limit of the substituends, namely the constituent parts of *yuṣmad* and *asmad*. Therefore, it is for the sake of ensuring that the operation to be described hereafter does not apply to the words *yuṣmad* and *asmad* when they end in *m*.

When? To this [the author] replies with "when [the forms] ending in *ṇi*, etc."—that is, when the suffix *ṇic* has been added to *yuṣmad* and *asmad* in the sense of "he speaks [them]," the elision of the final vowel occurs by virtue of the treatment as an *iṣṭhan*-derivative (*iṣṭhavadbhāva*) according to the rule "the operation of the base applies before *ṇa*" (Vār. 813). Then, after the addition of *kvip*, the suffix *ṇic* is elided by Pāṇini 6.4.51. Thus, one might think that the substitutes should apply whenever *yuṣmad* and *asmad* end in *m*. To prevent this from occurring, the word "ending in *m*" (*mānta*) is included [in the sūtra]. Even if the inclusion [of the word *mānta*] were not there, the restriction to the state of ending in *m* would still be obtained through the very mention of *yuṣmadasmadoḥ*. Consequently, the substitutions to be taught hereafter would only take place where *yuṣmad* and *asmad* actually end in *m*.

If, however, the inclusion [of the term *parigrahaṇa*] is intended to indicate a limit (*avadhi*), then it must necessarily be something that is to be excluded (*vajryamāna*); for a forest cannot possibly serve as a limit by that [term].
In that case, what stands in the place of a whole and its parts is being specified:
it will apply only where the word *ācch* is to be excluded, and not only in the case of *yuṣmad* and *asmad* ending in *m*.

But surely, the substitutes for *yuṣmad* and *asmad* are prescribed when followed by case-endings (*vibhakti*), and in the state of being followed by the suffix *-m*, there is no following of a case-ending; because of the status of the elision of the *ṇi*-suffix as being "as if it were the original" (*sthānivadbhāva*). So, what is the purpose of including the mention of the form ending in *-m* as something to be excluded? To this he says: "And the status of being 'as if the original' (*sthānivattva*)," and so forth. Because of the rule "When [a suffix] is elided by *kvi*, it is not as if it were the original" (Vārttika 1.1.59), the status of being "as if the original" does not apply here. Therefore, the intention is that the condition of being followed by a case-ending indeed exists. [The term] "in the dual" (*dvivacane*)...

If this were to be understood as referring to the technical term *dvi-vacana* (the dual number), then those two substitutes (*tv-ādeśau*) would occur only when that [dual] follows. Consequently, when *yuṣmad* and *asmad* denote two things in a compound, since the meaning of the compound possesses a different number, the singular or plural would arise from the compound rather than the dual; thus, they would not occur. Furthermore, when *yuṣmad* and *asmad* refer to a single entity or to many, while the meaning of the compound is in the dual, the dual would indeed occur after the compound, and in such cases they would necessarily appear as *yuvā-* and so forth—which is undesirable.
The expression of two meanings is "dual" (*dvivacana*). [This refers to] the rule:
"When *yūṣmad* and *asmad* are in the dual," and the term "in the dual."
This is the seventh case [locative] based on the object (*viṣaya-saptamī*).
To clarify that this very [term] has the status of being a locative based on the object, he says: "in the domain of the expression of two meanings" (*dvyarthābhidhānaviṣaye*).
The expression of two meanings is *dvyarthābhidhānam*; those which have that as their domain—namely, the pronouns *yuṣmad* and *asmad*—are described in that way.
"Of those two," and so forth:
of those two, *yuṣmad* and *asmad*, the portion ending with the penultimate letter (*maparyanta*) is the base (*sthānin*); for that, *yuvā* and *āvā* are substituted.
With the words "when," etc., he demonstrates what is desired to be established when there is the inclusion of the meaning (*arthagrahaṇa*).

If, then, when the singular and plural endings have arisen from a compound, the forms *yu* and *ava* replace *yusmad* and *asmad* because they concern the expression of two referents, this being the case, would these two forms also occur in the domain of the following rules: *yūyavayau jasi* (Pāṇini 7.2.93), *tubhyamahau ṅayi* (Pāṇini 7.2.95), and *tavamamau ṅasi* (Pāṇini 7.2.96)? To this he says: "But if *tvā* and *āh* [are used] in the nominative singular," and so forth.
Regarding the example *atiyuvām* and *atyāvām*:
it is a *prādi-samāsa* (prepositional compound) according to the rule *ātyādayaḥ krāntādyarthe* (Vārttika 91).

In that case, although that referent which transcends the meanings of *yuṣmad* and *asmad* is delimited by the number one—and thus the singular number (*ekavacana*) occurs there—nevertheless, because the scope of expression involves two referents, the forms *yuvān* and *āvān* indeed occur for *yuṣmad* and *asmad*.
For here, by the rule "and in the accusative" (*dvitīyāyāñca*, Pāṇini 7.2.87), the substitution of *āt* takes place;
thus we have *atiyuvān* and *atyāvān*.
The substitution of *n* [for *s*] occurs by the rule *śaso na* [Pāṇini 7.1.29].
In the form *atyāvayā*,
the substitution of *y* [for *v*] occurs by the rule *yo'ci* [Pāṇini 7.2.89].
In *atiyuvābhir atyāvābhiḥ*,
the substitution of *āt* [for *au*] occurs by rule 7.2.86.
In *atiyuvabhyam atyāvabhyam*, [the same applies].
In the case of *atiyuvatibhyaḥ*,
the substitution of *ad* for the *ṅasi* ending is by rule [Pāṇini 7.1.32],
whereas for the plural, it is by rule [Pāṇini 7.1.31]: *pañcamyā at*.
"Excessive water, excessive speech"—
thus "excessive youth, excessive protection.
By [Pāṇini 7.1.32], there is the substitution of *ad* for the genitive case ending (*ṅasi*).
But for the plural, [the substitution is] by the rule *pañcamyā ut* (Pāṇini 7.1.31);
thus we have *atiyuvākam*, *atyāvākam*,
and *atiyuvayi*, *atyādayi*.
The state of being *pūrvavat* (as before) [is seen] in the forms *atiyuvāsu* and *atyāvāsu*.
The state of being *pūrvavat* (as before) [applies] to the acute accent (*udātta*).

Regarding what was stated by the words "in the domain of *tvāhā* and so forth," namely that "if [the rules] *yadi tvahau* [Pāṇini 7.2.94] and so on were not superseded by other substitutes," he clarifies this with the words "but when" and so forth.
He demonstrates what is achieved when the term "meaning" (*artha*) is included by means of the example "atitvāmatamām.

In this case, since the two meanings of *yuṣmad* and *asmad*—which have been transcended—are the referents of the compound and thus possess the number two, a dual ending does indeed occur for the compound; nevertheless, because *yuṣmad* and *asmad* themselves do not possess a dual meaning, the substitutions *yuvā* and *āvā* do not take place.
The vowel substitution [ā] occurs by the rule *tvamāv eka-vacane* [Pāṇini 7.2.97].
Alternatively, this is the dual form of the second case; hence, the substitution is applied by the rule *dvitīyāyāṃ ca* [Pāṇini 7.2.87].
Regarding the phrase "evam asunyeyam," he demonstrates the absence of substitution even in other grammatical rules:
"Look at those who have surpassed you" (*atiyuṣmām*), and "those who have surpassed us" (*atyasmām*).
By those two who have surpassed you, by *atitvābhyām*; by those two who have surpassed me, *atimābhyām*.
By those two who have surpassed you all—[the action] was done by *kṛtamatiyuṣmābhyām*. Give to those two who have surpassed you: give by *atitvābhyām*, give by *atimābhyām*.
[He said: "Give to those who have surpassed you. [Examples: *atiyuṣmābhyām* (to those two who have surpassed you), *atyasmābhyām* (to those two who have surpassed us).
"He has come to those who have surpassed you": *atisyābhyām āgataḥ*, *atimābhyām āgataḥ*.
"He has come to those who have surpassed you all": *atiyuṣmābhyām āgataḥ*, *atyasmābhyām āgataḥ*.

The possessive suffix *sva* is applied to the forms *atitvām*, *atitvayoḥ*, *atimām*, and *atimayoḥ*. The possessive suffix *sva* is applied to the forms *atyasmām*, *atyasmayoḥ*, *atitvām*, *atitvayoḥ*, *atimām*, and *atimayoḥ*. Place [the object] beyond you (*atitvām*), place it beyond the two of you (*atitvayoḥ*), place it beyond me (*atimām*), and place it beyond the two of us (*atimayoḥ*).
"Place [the suffix] after *atikrānta-yuṣmad*, place it after *atiyuṣmad*, and place it after *atyasmad*. Regarding the form *paramayuṣmad*:

by the rule "In the context of *aṅga*, [the substitution applies] to that [stem] and its following member" (Pāṇini 7.2.98), the substitutions occur for the two following members as well. Alternatively, the term *jasi* here is a locative of reference (*parasaptamī*); therefore, the substitutions occur when *jas* follows even when [the stem] is compounded.

Even in cases such as *paramayūyam*, the suffix *jas* indeed follows the words *yuṣmad* and *asmad*; this [rule] will be stated [in Pāṇini 7.2.93], and the present [sūtra] is an exception (*apavāda*) to that. Now, what is the purpose of including the mention of *tvā*? One might ask: why not simply say "after *asau*, *ah* [is substituted]"? For the substitution of *tvā* would then occur by [the rule] *tvāhau sau* (Pāṇini 7.2.94). It is impossible to state it thus; for if the mention of *tvā* were absent, the substitution of *ah* would apply to *yuṣmad* as well.
Or alternatively, could one not simply say here "after *asmad*, *ah* [is substituted] after *asau*"? Even so, there would be prolixity (*gaurava*).

Therefore, let it be exactly as stated otherwise. This statement is made because the two [suffixes] *tvam* and *aham* are about to be mentioned immediately thereafter, as if they were already present. By saying "the mention is by way of the meaning (*artha*) 'in the singular'," he shows that the term *ekavacana* (singular) is taken here in its sense, and not in its technical (*pāribhāṣika*) grammatical sense.
The intention is that the fault which would arise from taking the technical sense has already been stated under the rule *yuvāvau dvivacane* [Pāṇini 7.2.92].
In this context, however, the mention of "meaning" (*artha*) is understood from the mention of "word" (*vacana*).

If the mention of "suffix" (*pratyaya*) were intended here, one would simply have said "in the case of singularity" (*ekatve*). The term "in a case-ending" (*vibhaktau*) is understood [from a previous rule]; there, the connection will be made as follows: "the case-ending that occurs in the sense of singularity."
Alternatively, one should not say *etad*; for since the two substitutes are already established by the rule *ekavacane hi* [Pāṇini 7.2.98],
[the forms] *tvām* and *mām* [are derived] with the substitution of *āt* by the rule *dvitīyāyāñca* [Pāṇini 7.2.87].

By the rule beginning with *yadā samāsa ekārthe*, he demonstrates what is achieved when the mention of "meaning" (*arthagrahaṇa*) is present. Even when a dual or plural ending occurs after a compound that possesses a different number, these two substitutes for *yuṣmad* and *asmad* still occur provided they have a single meaning (*ekārtha*). This being the case, one might think that these two would also fall within the scope of other substitutes such as those prescribed by [Pāṇini 7.2.94], *yūyavayau jasi* [7.2.93], *tubhyamahyau ṅayi* [7.2.95], and so forth; therefore, he says: "*ādeśāntarāṇāṃ tu*" and so on.
The statement "because of the prior prohibition" (pūrvavipratiṣedha) is made because a subsequent prohibition (paravipratiṣedha) is impossible;
that impossibility arises because these two [rules] themselves are subsequent [to one another].
However, the "prior prohibition" is obtained by virtue of the word *para* signifying "that which is desired" (*iṣṭa*).

In this regard, the scope of [Pāṇini 7.2.94] *tatra* is where *yuṣmad* and *asmad* do not occur in a single referent (*ekārtha*), as in *atikrānto yuṣmān* → *atitvam*, *atyaham*. The scope of [Pāṇini 7.2.97] *tvamāvekavacane* is where a different case-ending occurs after two single-referent stems, as in *tvām*, *mām*. When both rules would apply simultaneously in cases such as *atikrāntastvām* → *atitvam* and *atikrānto mām* → *atyaham*, the forms *tvah* and *au* (for *tvam* and *aham*) occur by means of a prior counter-exception (*pūrvavipratiṣedha*). By another method, when other substitutes are applicable, a prior counter-exception must be stated.
Regarding the expression “*atikrānto tvāmatitvām*, *atimām*”:

although here the dual number occurs due to the compound (*samāsa*), nevertheless, because the pronouns *yuṣmad* and *asmad* refer to a single entity, the substitutes *tvam* and *mām* indeed take place.
If one were to adopt the technical sense of the singular number, these two would not occur; for that [technical singular] is not present here.
"Examples such as these should be cited":

*atikrāntau tvāṃ paśya* (look at those who have surpassed you), *atitvām* (having surpassed you); *atimāṃ paśya* (look at those who have surpassed me); *atitvābhir atimābhiḥ kṛtam* (done by those who have surpassed you and by those who have surpassed me).

I give you to those who have surpassed you; I give you to those who have surpassed me. I give you to those who have surpassed you; I give you to those who have surpassed me. You have come to those who have surpassed you; you have come to those who have surpassed me.
From those who have surpassed you (*atikrāntebhyaḥ*), [the gift] comes to you as *atitvadāgataḥ*, *atimadāgataḥ*.
From the two who have surpassed you (*atikrāntayoḥ*), [the gift] comes from you as *atitvayoḥ svam*, *atimayoḥ svam*.
From those who have surpassed you (*atikrāntānām*), [the gift] comes from you as *atitvākam svam*, *atimākam svam*.
"Place you beyond two [years], place you beyond two [years], place you beyond me.
"Place you beyond three [years], place you beyond three [years], place you beyond me. Regarding the phrase "occurring in the singular number," the meaning is:
occurring within the scope of denoting a single object.

Regarding the forms *tvadīyaḥ* and *madīyaḥ*, the suffix *cha* is applied by [Pāṇini 4.2.114], because [the bases] are designated as *vṛddha* by [Pāṇini 1.1.74]. Regarding the forms *tvattaraḥ* and *mattaraḥ*: [the suffix *taraP* is applied].

The suffix *tarap* is applied by the rule "When a word expressing a dual number is present as an upapada, the suffixes *tarap* and *īyasun* are used" (Pāṇini 5.3.57). Thus, one says "tvadyati, madyati" and "tvadyate,
madyate."

The suffix *kyan* [is applied] by the rule "kartuḥ kyaṅ salopaśca" [Pāṇini 3.1.11]. Now, one might ask: since the two [desired] locations are already established by the preceding rule, for what purpose is this present undertaking? To this he says: "Because of the governing authority of the term 'vibhaktau' (in a case-ending)," and so forth.
The phrase beginning with "nanu ca" (but surely... is the objector's statement.
"That which occurs between the base and the suffix, or between the preceding and following words, is the 'internal case-ending' (antarvartinī vibhaktiḥ).
"This cannot be so," says the other;
"it must be elided by *luk*," he says, providing the reason for its invisibility.

The intention [of the opponent] is that, by the rule *[[2.4.71]]*, the elision (*luk*) ought to occur even before the two substitutions; consequently, the two substitutions conditioned by that [elision] would not take place.
The proponent [of the correct view] states, "The elision is external," and so forth.

For the two substitutions, the sole basis is the case-ending (*vibhakti*), whereas for the elision, there are two further bases: the status of being a verbal root (*dhātutva*) and the status of being a nominal stem (*prātipadikatva*).

Thus, since [the suffix] is a *dhātu* or a *pratipadika*, it is *bahiraṅga* because it depends on the *bāhulaka* suffixes and because it depends on the compound (*samāsa*). But how can the elision (*luk*) be *bahiraṅga* in relation to that? By the principle "that which is *bahiraṅga* is as if unestablished (*asiddha*) with respect to that which is *antaraṅga*" (Vyāḍi-Pāṇini 42), the two substitutions will indeed occur first.
"This very [point], etc."—this is said by the other [party] as well.

Since the rule "even internal operations (*antaraṅga*) are not barred by an external elision (*bahiraṅga-luk*)" would have already established the point, he would not have stated the rule for the substitute (*adeśa*); yet he did state it, and that very fact indicates: "Even internal operations are barred by an external elision" (Vyāḍipāda 128).
What is the purpose of this indicator (*jñāpaka*)? To this, he says: "By that," and so forth.

If this meaning were not made known, then in the case of *gomatpriyaḥ* (one who has cows as his beloved), because the elision (*luk*) [of the matup suffix] is internal (*antaraṅga*), the augment *num* [would apply] by the rule *ugidacām* [Pāṇini 7.1.70], followed by lengthening by *ato dīrgho yañi* [Pāṇini 7.3.101]; and once the elision of the final consonant cluster (*saṃyogāntalopa*) is effected by *saṃyogāntasya lopaḥ* [Pāṇini 8.2.23], the undesirable form *gomānpriyaḥ* would result. However, when this meaning is made known, even the internal *num* and other operations are superseded by the external elision (*luk*), and thus this undesirable consequence does not arise.
By the first word "ādi" (and so forth), there is the inclusion of forms such as *gomatyati*—meaning "he desires one who possesses cows"—and *gomatyate*—meaning "he acts like one who possesses cows.
By the second [word], there is the inclusion of lengthening and the elision [of the suffix] by the rule *halṅyābbhyo dīrghāt sutisyapṛktaṃ hal* [Pāṇini 6.1.68].

If, on the grounds of being *antaraṅga* (more internal), the elision by *halṅyābbhyo* [6.1.68] were to occur first, then by the principle of *pratyayalakṣaṇa* (the suffix being present despite its elision), *num* and other such operations would apply, and consequently, that very same undesirable form would result.
And because there is elision (*luk*), [the rule] "when there is *luk*" (Pāṇini 1.1.63) prohibits the application of grammatical operations based on the presence of an affix; thus it does not occur.

Regarding the phrase "and so forth" (*evaṃ ca*): since this elision (*luk*), though external (*bahiraṅga*), subverts even internal (*antaraṅga*) rules, and having done so, the following substitutions do not occur when a suffix or a subsequent member of a compound follows: [the forms derived from] Pāṇini 7.2.94, 7.2.93, and the substitutions "tubhyam" and "mahyam" in place of "tvam" and "aham" before the dative suffix *ṅe* (Pāṇini 7.2.95–96).

Regarding the passage beginning with "atha" and so forth: an indicator (*jñāpaka*) occurs when there is no other purpose; however, in this case, there *is* a purpose—namely, the sublation (*bādhana*) of these alternative substitutes (*ādeśa*). Since this purpose exists, the sense is that it is appropriate to understand this [sūtra] for that very purpose, and not for the sake of providing an indication.
Regarding the phrase "with reference to the status of the target form" (*lakṣyasthityapekṣayā*):

the "status of the target form" (*lakṣyasthiti*) is the location or state of that which is to be explained (*vyutpādya*). "With reference to that" (*tadviṣaye'pekṣā*) means *lakṣyasthityapekṣā*; [the rule operates] by means of that as its cause.
This is not understood as being for the purpose of subverting other substitute rules (*ādeśāntara*).
Forms such as *gomatpriyaḥ* and *gomatyati*, which exist in common usage as correct words (*sādhu*),
would not be included if this [rule] were understood merely for the purpose of subverting other substitutes.
However, he shows that even these are included when it is intended as a metarule (*jñāpanārtha*)— this is expressed by the passage beginning with "if this is intended as a metarule."

But how, even when such a purpose exists and there is a requirement for the maintenance of the *lakṣya* (the form to be characterized), can this [sūtra] be understood as being for the sake of providing a *jñāpaka* (an indicator)? It is possible to understand it thus: [the author] thinks that this is not indeed a [primary] purpose, because the inclusion of the syllable *ca* is for the sake of drawing in (*anukarṣaṇa*) the term "ending in *m*" (*maparyanta*). This very purpose of drawing it in is so that the two substitutes may apply to those ending in *m*. And if this were for the sake of subverting other substitutes, then that drawing in would be purposeless.
Why is this sūtra formulated for the purpose of preventing other substitutions? Those other substitutions are applied only to that which ends in *m*, and not to anything else.

Therefore, even without the continued application of the mention of "ending in *m*," since exceptions (*apavāda*) share the same locus as their general rules (*utsarga*), the rule will apply only to that which ends in *m*. So what is the use of continuing the mention of "ending in *m*"? If it were for the purpose of preventing other substitutions, then it would be appropriate to continue the mention of "ending in *m*" so that the rule applies to everything.
Therefore, since this [rule] follows from the inclusion of the limit "up to *mā*," its purpose is not to subvert other rules regarding different locations (*adeśāntara*).
Consequently, it is understood as an indicator (*jñāpaka*).
