Now, an objection is raised by another: "But why is it not understood that this [rule] is for the purpose of subverting these [suffixes], namely *tvā*, *āha*, and so forth?"

His intention is this: Is this [rule] for the purpose of setting aside other substitutes for that which ends in *m*? Why does it not occur? In that regard, the meaning is as follows: the particle *ca* need not be employed for the purpose of carrying forward (*anukarṣaṇa*) the mention of "ending in *m*" (*maparyanta*). If the mention of "ending in *m*" were to continue [from the previous rule], this [present rule] would not be applicable for the purpose of setting aside other substitutes; however, when that [mention] has ceased, it certainly becomes applicable. Regarding "three" (*trayaḥ*):
the guṇa substitution occurs by the rule "and before *jas*" (*jasi ca*, Pāṇini 7.3.109).
Regarding "four" (*catvāraḥ*), the suffix *ām* is applied by [Pāṇini 7.1.98]. Regarding "three" (*trīṇi*).

By [Pāṇini 7.1.20], there is the substitution of *śi*; by [7.1.72], the augment *num*; and by [6.4.7] and [6.4.8], "and in the case of a nominal stem ending in *su*, *au*, or *as*, except for the vocative," there is lengthening. Is this [the condition] "in the feminine" (*striyām*) a qualifier of the words "three" (*tri*) and "four" (*catur*)?
Yes, because those two alone are what are heard [in the rule].
[And it is not a qualifier] of the "stem" (*aṅga*), as stated [in the commentary].
He shows what is excluded by the particle *eva* with the words "by that" (*tena*).
[This occurs] through the relationship of qualifier and qualified (*viśeṣaṇaviśeṣyabhāva*).

For if only the word *aṅgam* were qualified by the word *striyām*—[the printed edition reads *viśeṣyeta*]—then even when the words *tri* and *catur* refer to the masculine or neuter gender, while the *aṅgam* (the base) refers to the feminine, these two substitutes would still occur.
The two [suffixes] do not occur when [the words] *tri* and *catur* are qualified by the rule "tricaturoḥ striyām. For example: *priyatriḥ*, etc.
Because "feminine" (*strī*) is the meaning of the external member (*anyapadārtha*), the base (*aṅga*) refers to the feminine, whereas the words *tri* and *catur* are in another gender.
When the word *aṅga* refers to a masculine or neuter [noun], while the words *tri* and *catur* refer to a feminine, then these two alone [are substituted]:
*priyāstisro brāhmaṇya asya* becomes *priyatisā*, *priyatisrau*, *priyatisnaḥ*;
[and] *priyatisṛ brāhmaṇakulam* becomes *priyatisṛṇī*, *priyatisṛṇi*.
*Priyacatasṛ*, *priyacatasṛṇī*, *priyacatasṛṇi*.
Regarding the rule "in the state of *tisṛ*" and so forth:

when the suffix *kan* is applied to the word *tri* by the rule *saṃjñāyāṃ kan* (Pāṇini 5.3.87), the [substitution of *tisṛ*] would not apply because there is no case-ending present; therefore, this [rule] is commenced.

The purpose of the word *upasaṃkhyāna* is to provide an additional rule (*pratipādana*). In this regard, the following is the additional rule: the particle *ca* ("and") from the preceding sūtra is carried over here, and it serves to include what has not been explicitly mentioned.
By means of that, the suffix *kan* will also occur when a name (*saṃjñā*) is intended.
"Tisṛkā" is a name for a village. Regarding the statement "there is the irregular prescription (nipātana) of the acute accent on the first syllable of 'catasṛ'":

In the case of *cataruāḥ paśya*, the rule [Pāṇini 6.1.167] would result in an udātta accent on the final syllable; however, an udātta on the initial syllable is desired. Therefore, the designation of the initial udātta (*ādyudāttanipātana*) must be made for that purpose.
This is so that, by the accent of the designated particle (*nipātanasvara*), the final udātta may not occur.

If that is so, then just as the accent of the *nipātana* (the specific substitution) subverts the accent of the *śasi*, so too would it subvert that initial acute accent (*ādyudāttatva*) which is prescribed for what is not a case-ending by the rule [Pāṇini 6.1.179]. Consequently, in the form *catasṛṇām*, the acute accent of the *ām* ending would not occur? To this he says: "But in the case of *catasṛṇām*, etc. [The reason is: "By virtue of the inclusion of the term 'beginning with a consonant' (*halādi*).
This is the very reason for that.
For in that context, the mention of "beginning with a consonant" (hal-ādi) is made for the purpose of excluding [words] beginning with a vowel (aj-ādi).
Furthermore, this word "four" (catuḥ) refers to the plural number;
all plurals other than the nominative, accusative, and genitive plurals are those beginning with a consonant.

In that case, when the augment *nuṭ* is applied by means of a prior counter-exception (*pūrvavipratiṣedha*) over the rules for the *num* augment, the long vowel, and the treatment as *ṛjvat*, the word should have an acute accent on the first syllable because it begins with a consonant (*halādi*).

However, because the term "not a sarvanāmasthāna" (*asarvanāmasthāna*) is understood to carry over from Aṣṭādhyāyī 6.1.170 (*jasaḥ śī*), the acute accent on the first syllable does not occur [for the nominative plural].
Therefore, the mention of "beginning with a consonant" (*halādi*) was made there in order to prevent this accentuation from applying to the nominative plural suffix *śas*.

And if the accent of the particle (*nipātana-svara*) were not to occur, then let there be no purposelessness in the mention of "beginning with a consonant" (*hal-ādi*). Here, due to the incapacity of the mention of "beginning with a consonant," the accent of the particle is superseded by the accent of the case-ending (*vibhakti-svara*); therefore, in the form *catasṛṇām*, there is the udātta accent on the final syllable. But for what purpose is the substitution of *ac* stated, since it would already be established by the substitution of *yaṇ*? To this he says: "the homogeneous with the preceding" (*pūrvasavarṇa*), and so forth.

If this [substitution] did not exist, then in the case of *sūtre* + *śasi*, there would be the substitution of the homogeneous vowel (*pūrvasavarṇa*) by Pāṇini 6.1.102, and the substitution of *u* (*ut*) by 6.1.107, as well as the *guṇa* substitution when a *sarvanāmasthāna* or the locative ending *ṅi* follows by 7.3.110.

Therefore, this substitution of *r* is commenced as an exception (*apavāda*) to these [rules]. Now, one might object: "It is appropriate that this substitution of *r* serves as an exception here to the rules for the homogeneous vowel and the substitution of *u*, but it is inappropriate as an exception to the rule for *guṇa*; for it is said: 'Exceptions occurring in the middle sublate preceding rules, but not subsequent ones' (Vyāḍiparibhāṣā 10). To this, he says: "Even though it is subsequent," and so forth.
The scope for the *guṇa* [substitution] is: *kartārau*, *hartārau*, *kartarī*; the scope for the *repha* [substitution] is: *tisraḥ paśya*, *tiruāstiṣṭhanti*; and *priyatiriuā nidhehi*.

Here, when both would apply, the *repha* occurs by virtue of the *pūrvavipratiṣedha* (the former prevails over the latter), and it thus blocks even the subsequent *guṇa* [substitution] conditioned by the *ṅi*-case endings and the *sarvanāmasthāna* [terminations]. [Question: "Why does the rule specify *ṛtaḥ* ('of an *ṛ*' sound)?"
He thinks as follows: "The words *tisṛ* and *catasṛ* will follow [the rule for] *ah*.
Since those two end in the vowel *ṛ*, by the paribhāṣā regarding the final letter (A 1.1.52), the substitution will apply only to the *ṛ*.
[Thus, the mention of] *tisṛcatasroḥ* is for the sake of ensuring their application."
The term *ṛtaḥ* is stated so that the application—meaning the attainment—of *tisṛ* and *catasṛ* may occur even when followed by a vowel (*aci*).

Otherwise, as indicated by the phrase "for otherwise" and so forth, if *ṛtaḥ* were not stated, this exception would be understood to apply only to those two [forms, *tisṛ* and *catasṛ*]; consequently, they would not occur before vowels. [This is because] "the substitution of *jaras* occurs by way of conflict (vipratiṣedha) with the rule prescribing the augment *num*."

*Numo’vakāśaḥ*: *trapūṇi*, *jatūni*; *jarasāveśasyāvakāśaḥ*: *jarasau*. In cases where both [rules] apply simultaneously, the subsequent substitution of *jaras* occurs by virtue of the prohibition (*vipratiṣedha*). For if *num* were applied first, the substitution of *jaras* would not be obtained because it would be separated by *num*; nevertheless, it is obtained by resorting to the qualification of the prescribed element (*vihitaviśeṣaṇa*). Even so, according to the principle that "substitutions apply to the specific form as it is pointed out" (*nirdiśyamānasyādeśā bhavanti*), once the substitution of *jaras* for the word *jarā* has been made, the *num* would be heard following the letter *s*.

[The printed reading is *śrūyate*. Even so, could there be an injunction (*ādeśa*) for the whole [stem]? Even in that case, since the rule for *num* would have already accomplished its purpose, it would not apply again once the substitution has been made; thus, the form *jaras* would not occur, and an undesired form would result. Now, in this instance—*atijarasam brāhmaṇakulam paśya*—once the substitution of *jaras* has been applied, why does *su* not become *am* by the rule *svamornapuṃsakāt* [Pāṇini 7.1.23]? To this he says: "In this case," and so forth.

The compound *jarāmatikrāntam* is a *prādi-samāsa*. By the rule *hrasvo napuṃsake prātipadikasya* [Pāṇini 1.2.47], the final vowel is shortened; thus, we arrive at the form *jarām*. At this stage, because a modification of a single part does not alter the identity of the whole (*ekadeśavikṛtasyānanyatvāt*), three operations—shortening, the substitution of *am*, and the substitution of *jaras*—simultaneously apply. Among these, shortening is superseded by the substitution of *am* according to the rule *ato'm* [Pāṇini 7.1.24], as the latter is an exception (*apavāda*) to the former. Furthermore, the substitution of *am* is itself superseded by the substitution of *jaras*, because the latter follows later in the sequence of rules.

Now, once the substitution of *jaras* has been applied, why does elision (*luk*) not occur again? To this he says: "The rule for elision," and so forth. The rule for elision does not apply again because its opportunity has passed; in the third-person plural, it should be *kimatajaraibbrāhmaṇakulaiḥ*, or rather, should it be *atijarasam*, *atijarasaiḥ*, and so on? To this he says: "*Atijarasam*," and so forth. "According to the opinion of Gonardīya."
For it is stated thus in the Bhāṣya: "Godatīya says: 'Is this not included [in the rule]? It should be [stated that] *atijaram* and *atijaraiḥ* must occur.
What, then, is the reasoning for this? To this he says: "Based on the occasioning cause (*sannipātalakṣaṇa*)," and so forth.

If the substitution of *am* and the substitution of *ais* were merely the causes for the replacement by *jaras*, then the status of the stem as ending in the vowel *a* would be destroyed by those two substitutions.
And this is incorrect; for once those two have arisen at that moment of falling [into the womb], they are unable to obstruct it.
"Others" refers to those who follow the opinion of the author of the Sūtras.
Why do they think thus again? To this he says: "Because of its impermanence," and so forth.
Furthermore, its impermanence has been established in [the sūtra] 7.1.9. Regarding the word "asyāḥ":
by [the rule] 7.2.106, the *t* is replaced by *s*.
Regarding "tyaḥ":
the substitution of *śī* occurs by the rule *jasaḥ śī* [Pāṇini 7.1.17],
as in "imau".
The substitution of *m* [for *n*] occurs by the rule *daśca* [Pāṇini 7.2.109].
Thus: *asau*;
*amū*.
Having applied the substitution of *u* for *at* by [Pāṇini 7.2.102], there is lengthening by [Pāṇini 6.1.102].
Thus, "amī" [is formed]; then, by [Pāṇini 8.2.81], there is the substitution of *i* for the final vowel.
Now, why does this not occur here in the case of *bhavān*? To this he says: "of those ending in two [consonants]," and so forth. This has already been made known previously under [Pāṇini 7.2.90].
Thus: *bhavān*.

The augment *num* is applied by [Pāṇini 7.1.70] *ugidacām*, and the lengthening is applied by [Pāṇini 6.4.14]. Now, why does this not also apply here to those that have become technical terms (*saṃjñā*) or secondary members (*upasarjana*), such as in the case of *tyad* and its derivatives—namely, *tyad*, *atisyad*, and *atityadaḥ*? To this he says: "Those that have become technical terms or secondary members," and so forth.
This is because the words beginning with *tyad* fall within the group starting with *sarva*.

The words beginning with *sarva* are recited as non-technical terms (*asaṃjñībhūta*) and as non-subordinate members (*anupasarjanībhūta*). For it is thus: the purpose of assigning them the great technical designation "pronouns" (*sarvanāmāni*, Pāṇini 1.1.27) is so that the designation may apply to all those that have become names;
however, it should not apply to those which are themselves the names of something else or which have become subordinate members.

Therefore? Words such as *tyad* and so forth, when they have become subordinate to a noun (*saṃjñā*), are excluded by the very fact of their being listed [in the rule]; the meaning is that they are cast outside the scope of *tyad* and the others.
Consequently, because they are not among *tyad* and the rest, the grammatical operations prescribed for *tyad* and so forth do not apply to them.
However, "it certainly does apply when the word has *tyad* and the others as its primary referent."

In which word do "tyad" and the others constitute the primary element? That word is "tyadādipradhāna"; in such a case, the substitution of *at* certainly occurs, because it has not been excluded by the recitation [of the list]. Its non-exclusion, however, follows from the acceptance of the designation "sarvanāman" (pronoun) for words beginning with "sarva," based on the rule that a designation applies to a compound ending in [the named items]. Now, why is the substitution of the vowel *a* alone not prescribed for "kim"? For in that way the sūtra would be more concise, as the [substitution of] *a* is already understood from the preceding context; thus, the sūtra could have been formulated simply as "kimo't. To this he replies: "[The substitution] is of 'kim' when accompanied by the suffix *kaC*. Therefore, the substitution of the vowel *a* is not prescribed for "kim" [in its simple form].

This substitution of *hrā* [for *kim*] occurs because, according to the principle "that which falls in the middle of something is included by the mention of that thing" (*vyā|pā|21*), the form with the *akac* suffix is also included by the mention of *kim*. Therefore, the substitution is applied even to the form with *akac*; thus, it is not the case that only the vowel *a* is prescribed as the substitute for *kim*.

For if it were so prescribed, then after the substitution had been made for the form without *akac*, if *akac* were subsequently added, the undesirable form *kaka* would result—this is the intended meaning.

But how is it that when *āt* is substituted for *kim*, the form becomes *ka*, given that if *āt* were substituted for the *m* and the *yaṇ*-substitution were applied to the *ta*, the result would be *kya*? This is not a fault; for the substitution of *āt* is prescribed for the *i* as well. If [one objects] that "the substitution of *āt* does not apply to the final letter of a word," [we reply]: why then is the mention of the vowel *a* made here again? By this, the rule "when there is a modification of a non-final letter, it applies to that which stands in the vicinity of the final" (*vyā.pa.* 63) applies to the *i*. Thus, with the two *a*s, by the application of *para-pūrva-tva*, the form *ka* is established.
By some, the reading is "imaḥ.

Regarding that, this is the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*): Why is not simply the vowel *ā* prescribed as "imaḥ"? For in this way the sūtra would be concise, since the previously mentioned *ā* is carried over here; in that case, the sūtra should indeed be formulated as "imaḥ."

If that were the case, then even for the forms *tīn*, *timau*, and *timaḥ* derived from the root *tima ṣṭima ādrībhāve* (Dhātupāṭha 1123, 1124) with the suffix *kvip*, the rule would undesirably apply; however, this does not happen because the pronouns beginning with *tyad* (*tyadādi*) qualify the *im*. [Objection: Is it not so that the *im* belonging to the *tyadādi* group is meant? [Response: No; for if the substitution of *mat* were applied by the rule *daśca* (Pāṇini 7.2.109), then it would undesirably apply even in the case of *imau* and *imaḥ* derived from *idam*.

One should not suspect that by the *lakṣaṇapratipadokta-paribhāṣā* (Vyāḍi-Pāṇini 3), when *imaḥ* is prescribed [by P. 7.2.85], the rule *iti* (P. 1.1.52) would apply; for it is said that "there is no application of the final-alphabetic rule (*alontyavidhi*) to what is meaningless" (Vyāḍi-Pāṇini 62). Therefore, he says: "even of that which has the augment *kaC*" (*sākackasyāpi*), and so forth. The former reading alone is more correct. However, in the other reading, after the substitution of *kvā* by the subsequent sūtra and the replacement of *imaḥ*, there would result the hearing of two *k* sounds joined together (*saṃyukta*), and that is undesirable. This [present rule] is an exception (*apavāda*) to the former.
Because the word *ti* lacks a case ending (*vibhakti*), the vowel *i* is for the sake of pronunciation;
the purpose belongs solely to the letter *t*.

In that regard, according to the rule "In an *al*-designation, an operation prescribed for something applies to that which begins with it" (Vyāḍipāda 127), the substitution of *t* is prescribed as an operation to be applied when a case ending (*vibhakti*) follows.
Therefore he says: "at the beginning of *t*," and so forth;
"from where? and "where?"
In the rule *kimo't* [Pāṇini 5.3.12], the word *vā* ("optionally") is drawn forward from the subsequent rule. Consequently, in one alternative, the suffix *tral* [Pāṇini 5.3.10] also occurs,
as in *kuha*.
The word *ha* is derived from [Pāṇini 5.3.13] *vā ha ca cchabdasi*.

Furthermore, these suffixes beginning with *tasil* receive the technical designation "vibhakti" (case-ending) according to [Pāṇini 1.1.38] *eṣāṃ ca tasilādīnām*. This is an exception (*apavāda*) to the substitution of *ka* [prescribed by Pāṇini 5.3.4].
Thus, we have the form *kva*.

Regarding the rule *kimo't* [Pāṇini 5.3.12]: Now, for what purpose is a different substitute prescribed, rather than simply prescribing the original *ku* itself? For even in that case, the substitution of *yaṇ* would be established as *kvā*; furthermore, a split of the sūtra (*yogavibhāga*) would not need to be made, as one could simply formulate a single rule: *kutihātsu*. To this, he says: "The prescription of a different substitute," and so forth.
If the substitute *ku* were applied, it would subvert the *yaṇ* substitution, and by [Pāṇini 6.4.146], the *guṇa* substitution would instead take effect.
Therefore, for the sake of its removal, the substitution *kv-* is prescribed.
Even so, when the suffix is being enjoined, the suffix *ḍvat* should be prescribed by the rule *kimo ḍvat*; there too, once the *ṭi*-elision has been performed, the form *kva* is indeed established.

If it is argued that this is not established because, when the designation *pada* applies, the rule *ku-pvoḥ...* [Pāṇini 8.2.39] would require the change of the letter *k* to *g*, and thus it would not be established—this is not so; because of the principle *asiddhaṃ bahiraṅgam antaraṅge* (the external is non-existent with respect to the internal), the *ṭi*-elision is considered non-existent (*asiddha*), and therefore the *jaś*-substitution does not occur.
For the elision of *ṭi* is prescribed when a *ḍit* suffix follows; thus, by depending on that *ḍit* suffix, it becomes *bahiraṅga*.

However, since *jaś*-ness (*jaśtva*) is prescribed at the end of a word (*padānte*), it does not depend on any other cause and is therefore *antaraṅga*. To this he says: "The suffix *ḍvat* is a different suffix [added] to *kim*" and so forth.
If *ḍvat* were prescribed as a different suffix, the form *kvā* with the augment *sākacka* would not be established.

For if *asaci* were applied, when *kim* remains and the suffix *ḍvat* follows, the undesirable form *kakva* would result after the elision of the *ṭi*. However, since the substitution of *kvā* is prescribed when the suffix *at* follows—and because this consists of more than one phoneme—it becomes a substitute for the whole (*sarvādeśa*) of that which possesses the *k* (i.e., *kim* with its *kacc*), and thus the undesirable form does not arise. Therefore, *ḍvat* is not prescribed as a separate suffix for the sake of including the *kacc*.
That whose purpose (*artha*) is a specific meaning (*sākacka*) is "sākackārtha. Regarding the word "sai":
does this refer to the nominative singular, or the locative plural, or both? In this context, it is the nominative singular that is referred to;
for indeed, there is no general reference to both cases.
If it were so, Pāṇini would have stated it thus:
"In this way, an operation prescribed for that which begins with *s* will apply to both of them.
Therefore, there is the mention of only one of the two.

For instance, because of such grammatical indications as *so'ci lope cet* (Pāṇini 6.1.134), it is appropriate to understand that only the nominative singular is being referred to, as in *he sa, sā*. Here, the word *he* is a collection of indeclinables (*nipāta*) used in the sense of emphasis (*avadhāraṇa*).

But will not the substitution of *yat* and so forth for *tyad* and so forth (*tyadādyatva*) serve as an obstacle here? This is not so; for rules that have no scope (*anavakāśa*) are indeed obstructive, whereas the substitution of *at* has scope.
What is its scope? The word *dvi*: namely, *dvau*.
Even though that [final] position exists, and although there is room for *sakara* as well, nevertheless, because the final [element] is subsequent, *satva* would occur.
Consequently, in the case of *he saḥ*, the elision of the *su* suffix by [Pāṇini 6.1.69] would not take place.
Therein, once the elision of the *hal-ṅy-ādi* [suffixes] has been performed, and the *rutva* and *visarjanīya* have been applied, an undesirable form would result.

In this case, however, the suffix *ṭāp* would not apply for the feminine according to [Pāṇini 4.1.4], *ajādyataṣṭāp*. Therefore, it must be stated that [the rule applies] "to the two non-final [sounds]. [The word] *sau* alone [is used]. The substitution of *aut* for *adas* is prescribed as an exception to the substitution of *at* for *tyad*-type stems.
Regarding the word "asau": by the preceding rule, the *d* is replaced by *s*, and [by Pāṇini 6.1.88] there is *vṛddhi*. Regarding the phrase "yadā ca" and so forth:
Regarding the phrase "and sweetness" (*sādutvañca*):
the particle *ca* (and) serves the purpose of conjunction (*sanniyoga*).
Consequently, in that very same alternative where there is a prohibition of *aut*, in that same alternative, the substitution of *ut* for the following vowel *ā* is prescribed.
Regarding the phrase "of those [words] whose final member has not occurred," and so forth:

here, in the case of *paramāham*, *paramānena* (by the rule *paramāham, paramāneneti* [Pāṇini 7.2.94]), and *ido'y puṃsi* (by the rule *ido'y puṃsi* [Pāṇini 7.2.111]), the substitutes *eta* occurring for that case-ending which arises from the compound are considered *bahiraṅga* (external); however, this occurs even before the production of the case-ending. The lengthening (*dīrghatva*) of a vowel (*akaḥ*) when followed by a homogeneous vowel (*savarṇe*) is *antaraṅga* (internal) and would therefore occur first; the substitutes would occur afterwards. Consequently, undesirable forms such as *paramaham*, *paramayam*, and *paramanenā* would result.

Therefore, the substitutes for *tyad* and so on—which have become final words (*uttapada*) and for which the internal sandhi (*savarṇa-sandhi*) has not yet been applied—must be stated; that is, they must be explained. This indicates the teacher’s practice: first the grammatical operation (*kārya*) takes place between the preceding and following words, and only afterwards does the single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) occur.
This is because he teaches the prohibition [of the single-substitute] in the rule *na gośvansāvavarṇa-rāḍ-aṅ-ḍuhāṃ daḥ* (Pāṇini 8.2.22).

How does this serve as an indicator (*jñāpaka*)? In the word *indra*, there are two vowels; of these, one is removed by the elision [of the final vowel] according to Pāṇini 6.4.148, while the other is replaced by a single substitute (*ekādeśa*). Thus, the word *indra* becomes devoid of vowels (*anacka*); in that case, what occasion would there be for the application of *vṛddhi*? However, the Teacher perceives that the grammatical operation first applies to the preceding and following words, and only afterwards does the single substitute take place; for this reason, he teaches the prohibition of *vṛddhi* by the rule [Pāṇini 7.3.22]. From this indicator, it follows that the substitutes for pronouns such as *tyad* and others occur when they have become the second member of a compound (*uttarapada*), provided that the vocalic sandhi (*svarasandhi*) has not yet been performed.
"From *adas*, there shall be *aut* for *su*, etc.
Here, a restrictive sense (*avadhāraṇa*) is to be understood:
from the word *adas*, *aut* shall occur only for the following *su*.
"Let it be so, or let it not be.

Once the substitution of *tyadādi* [for the pronoun *adas*] has been applied according to Pāṇini 7.2.102, and the *vṛddhi* increment has been applied according to 6.1.88, the form *asau* is indeed established. Therefore, for what purpose is the elision of the nominative suffix (*su*) prescribed? Since it would be redundant, the elision of *su* should not be prescribed in this way; rather, only the substitution of *aut* [for the final vowel] should be prescribed. To this, he states the fault: "The vocative ending would be elided after a short vowel."

In the case of *he 'sau*, would the elision of the nominative suffix (*su*) not apply by [Pāṇini 6.1.69], and consequently, the vocative form *he 'sau* would not be established? [Reply: "No, because that [elision] applies after a consonant (*hal*). This is not a fault; for once the substitution of *aut* (i.e., *o*) has been applied to the vocative ending after a consonant, it becomes an *aṇ* vowel, and no longer a *hal* consonant. Therefore, how could there be any occasion for elision there? [Objection: Then the mention of *hal* must be made. [Reply: It need not be made; because that is already under discussion (*prakṛta*). The mention of *hal* is indeed still in force from [Pāṇini 6.1.68].

Although [the word *hal*] was originally mentioned in the nominative case there, its meaning here is expressed by a genitive indication (*ṣaṣṭhī-nirdeśa*). Nevertheless, by the rule "eṅ hrasvāt" (Pāṇini 6.1.67), the ablative case (*pañcamī*) will be treated as if it were a genitive (*ṣaṣṭhī*) for the sake of the nominative *hal*, according to the statement: "In this grammar, an earlier case-number is understood as a subsequent one. If that is so, then there is this fault: "There would be the substitution of *e* for *āp* when that [suffix] follows," and so forth. When the substitution of *yat* for the pronouns beginning with *tyad* has been applied before the vowel *u*, and the feminine suffix *ṭāp* is added, then in the form "he asau brāhmaṇī," the substitution of *e* for *ā* (by Pāṇini 7.3.106) would occur, just as it does in the example "he khaṭve. [To this, the answer is: "No, because of the continued application of the phrase 'not when followed by a *jhal* [consonant]' (*na jhali*)."

This is not a fault; for in the rule *sambuddhe ca* [Pāṇini 7.3.106], the phrase *bahuvacane jhalyet* [Pāṇini 7.3.103] is understood as a governing rule (*anuvartate*). Therefore, the substitution of *e* must occur only when the vocative (*sambuddhi*) begins with a *jhal* sound. Now, once the substitution of *o* has been made, the vocative no longer begins with a *jhal* sound; rather, it begins with an *ac* vowel. Consequently, the rules *pratyayasthācca kāt* [Pāṇini 7.3.44] and the substitution of *śī* would apply [which they should not]. [The reading *prasajyeta* is preferred over *prasajyate* in the Pradīpa.]
[The reading is marked as *mudritaḥ* (authenticated)].
The first *ca* has the sense of *tarhi* (then/in that case), while the other is for conjunction (*samuccaye*).

Well then, this would be a fault: in the case of *asakau brāhmaṇī*, when *akac* is applied to express meanings such as "unknown" (*ajñāta*) and so on, and then *ṭāp* is applied, the rule "pratyayasthāt kāt" [Pāṇini 7.3.44] and others would result in the substitution of *i* for the vowel preceding the *kā*. [Objection: In the case of *asau brāhmaṇī*, by the rule "auṅa āpaḥ" [Pāṇini 7.1.18], the substitution of *śī* occurs; however, since the *okāra* (o) is an integral part (*avayava*) of *adas*, there is no *ṭāp* at all, so these two faults do not arise.

Furthermore, the occurrence of the substitution *śī* should be understood as being optional (*pākṣika*). In which case? In that case where the marker *ṅ* is attached to the suffix for the purpose of indicating its general application.

However, when it follows the instruction of the preceding rule, the substitution *śī* occurs only for the two dual endings; for it was precisely those two that were assigned the marker *ṅ* by the former teachers.

There is no possibility at all for another [substitute]; because of the presence of the augment *āṅ*. By the rule *alo’ntyaparibhāṣā* (P. 1.1.52), this *m* must replace only the final *m*; yet, once the substitution of *m* for *m* has been made, there is no difference [in the result]. Why, then, is it stated that "the *m* [is replaced] by *m*"? To refute this objection, he says: "*of the m*," and so forth. The meaning is already explained. The word "*idamaḥ*" (from P. 7.1.2) continues [to apply], while "*sau*" (from P. 7.1.11) is discontinued, because the word "*sau*" is mentioned again in the subsequent sūtra.

Therefore, in this case, the letter *m* replaces the letter *d* merely when a case-ending (*vibhakti*) follows. Because of the mention of "in the masculine" (*puṃsi*) in the subsequent rule, this [substitution] becomes *y* in the feminine. Now, why is it not understood to apply in the neuter? It is impossible to understand it thus; for in the neuter, by the rule *svamornapuṃsakāt* (Pāṇini 7.1.23), there must be elision (*luk*) of the nominative suffix *su*. Since *su* is being elided here, how could the letter *y* occur when that [suffix] has been dropped? If one argues that it occurs by the principle of "the appearance of the suffix" (*pratyayalakṣaṇa*), we say no; because of the prohibition of the principle of the appearance of the suffix by the rule *na lumatāṅgasya* (Pāṇini 1.1.62).
Therefore, it is rightly said: "In the feminine, this [word] has the letter *y*. Regarding the word "by this" (*anena*):

after the substitution of *tad*-stem elements and the subsequent substitution of the single substitute for the preceding and following forms (*pararūpa*), the form *id-* undergoes the substitution of *ina* according to Pāṇini 7.1.12, and then the substitution of *ina* according to 6.1.87.
Regarding the word "of these two" (*anayoḥ*).
By the rule *osi ca* [Pāṇini 7.3.104], there is the substitution of *i*, the absence of the substitute [for the case-ending], and the elision of *su*.
Regarding the phrase "by the letter *p*":
why does this not occur by means of the letter *p* of the suffix *kap*? Because there is no purpose for it.

Is it not the case that the purpose [of the rule] "nanu ceha" is so that [the form] "iha" may occur when a *prāgdiśīya* case ending follows? Thus, by the rule "iti" (5.3.3), there ought to be an exception here.

And in this context, in the rule "amehakvatisitrebhyaḥ" (Kārikā 4.2.115), the mention of the form "iha"—which is the substitution for *idam* ending in *ha* before the elision of the *id*-portion—is the indicative mark (*liṅga*). Since the previous rule would have required no substitution at all, the elision of the *id*-portion is prescribed before consonant-initial endings. For example: "ābhyām."

The state of being *tyad* and so forth [is established]; hence, by the rule *guṇe* [Pāṇini 6.1.94], there is the substitution of the single subsequent form (*pararūpa*), and by the rule *supi ca* [Pāṇini 7.3.102], there is lengthening.

Now, why does this elision not occur for the final [sound] according to the maxim *alo'ntyaparibhāṣā* [Pāṇini 1.1.52]? To this he says: "In the case of that which is meaningless," and so forth. Having granted the application of the rule regarding the final sound even in the case of what is meaningless, he states another solution: "Or rather," and so forth.
And the mention of *aṅ* need not be made, since that [word] follows [from the previous rule]. To this he says: "*anāpyakaḥ*" and so forth.

Although in that [previous rule] it was designated by the nominative case (*prathamā-nirdiṣṭa*), whereas here the sense requires it to be designated by the genitive (*ṣaṣṭhī-nirdiṣṭa*), nevertheless, by the statement "[1.1.66] *saptamīsthāne prathamā*," the word *hal* being in the locative (*saptamī*) will cause the word *an* to be treated as if it were in the genitive (*ṣaṣṭhī*).
This resolution should be understood according to the opinion of the author of the Bhāṣya, because this particular *paribhāṣā* is not accepted [by him].

In this view, however, having applied the single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) rule to the forms of the three *akara*s [the final vowel of the stem and the initial vowel of the suffix], the lengthening and other operations must be prescribed. Regarding the form *mārṣṭā*: from the root *mṛj* (meaning "to cleanse") [Dhātupāṭha 1066], there is the substitution of *ṣ* by the rule *vraścādi-* [Pāṇini 8.2.36], followed by the substitution of *ṣṭu*. When a case-ending arises after the *kvip*-derived form of *mṛj*, as in *kaṃsaparimṛṅbhyām* and *kaṃsaparimṛṅbhiḥ*, the rule for *vṛddhi* would apply; yet the prohibition of *vṛddhi* based on the condition of *kvip*—namely, *na ca kvibāśrayaḥ* [Pāṇini 1.1.5]—is not able to take effect. Why? Because the term *kṅiti* is a locative of cause (*nimitta-saptamī*).

And in this case, the *vṛddhi* substitution caused by the *kvip* suffix does not apply; what then [applies]? That caused by the case-ending (*vibhakti*). Therefore, since its prohibition must be stated, he says: "The mention of 'dhātu' [in Pāṇini 6.4.132] refers to the verbal root," and so forth. This point is indicated by the irregular formation (*nipātana*) in the word *bhrauṇahatya* (Pāṇini 6.4.174): that an operation stated for a verbal root applies only when a suffix follows a verbal root. Consequently, [the rule] does not apply in the case of *kaṃsamṛṅbhyām*.
For that which is prescribed by the rule "after a verbal root" (*dhātoḥ*) is a suffix of a verbal root (*dhātupratyaya*).

Now, [suffixes] such as *bhyām* and so forth are not prescribed after a verbal root; rather, they are prescribed after a nominal stem (*prātipadikāt*). Therefore, they are not suffixes of a verbal root. Examples include *kaṃsaparimṛḍbhyām* and so forth.

As before: when *ṣatva* (the substitution of *ṣ* for *s*) has been applied, the *jaśtva* (substitution of the voiced unaspirated stop) of the letter *ṣ* results in *ḍ*. Regarding the forms *niścāyaniṣpāvau*—[the *Kāśikā* explains: "one winnowing of a single grain of rice, two winnowings with a winnowing-basket"]—the suffix *dhañ* is added after the roots *ci* preceded by *nis* and *pū* according to [Pāṇini 3.3.20]. Then, by [Pāṇini 8.3.41], the *visarjanīya* undergoes *ṣatva*.

"Kāraḥ, hāraḥ"— here the suffix *ghañ* is applied to the roots *kṛ* and *hṛ* in the sense of abstract action (*bhāve*). "Gauḥ, gāvaḥ, gāvaḥ"— [these are examples of the declension of the word for cow].
The designation *ṇit* applies to the *sarvanāmasthāna* [case endings] by the rule *goto ṇit* [Pāṇini 7.1.90]. Thus, we have *sakhāyau* and *sakhāyaḥ*;
here too, the rule *ato dīrgho yañi* [Pāṇini 7.1.92] applies.
"Of *jaya* and *yau*":
*ji* in the sense of "victory" (Dhātupāṭha 561); *yu* in the sense of "mixing" [and "non-mixing"] (Dhātupāṭha 1033).
"Of *cyava*"—thus [it is said].
The roots *cyuṅ*, *jyuṅ*, *pruṅ*, and *pluṅ* mean "to go" (*gatau*). [Note: These are not found in the Dhātupāṭha.
The mention of the suffix *ac* is so that the form may also occur with the suffix *ani*.

One might object: "Will this not already occur there simply by the force of the marker *ṇ*? This is not the case; for there is another purpose for the marker *ṇ*. What is it? It is so that when the substitution of *ava* has been applied in forms such as *gāvau* and *gāvaḥ*, the rule [Pāṇini 7.2.116] may apply to produce the *vṛddhi* vowel.

If this is so, then in the case of *gauraḥ*, since this *vṛddhi* has already fulfilled its purpose regarding the domain of non-guṇa, would it not be sublated by the *guṇa* in forms such as *kārayati* due to its subsequent status? [One might argue: "It will not occur because of the force of the marker *ṇit*. But this is no answer; for the application of the marker *ṇit* in rules such as Pāṇini 6.4.51 already has its own established purpose. This fault does not arise; for the activity of the Teacher (Pāṇini) indicates that *vṛddhi* occurs even in the domain of *guṇa*; otherwise, why would he again introduce the rule for *guṇa* in 7.3.85 (*jāgarteśca*), which covers both the domain of *vṛddhi* and the domain of prohibition?

For if there were no occurrence of *vṛddhi* with respect to the domain of *guṇa*, then since *guṇa* already exists in forms such as *jāgarayati*, the initiation of *guṇa* in that domain would be purposeless.
Furthermore, that the scope of the rule is the domain of *vṛddhi* is understood from the prohibition [of *guṇa*] in the case of *ciṇ* and *ṇal*.

Now, for what purpose is this division of rules (*yogavibhāga*) made? Could one not simply say: "After a root ending in *ñ* or *ṇ*, [the *ṭi*] is replaced by *upadhā*" (Pāṇini 6.4.7)? It is impossible to state it thus; for if that were said, although forms like *gāvaḥ* (from *go*), *gāvaḥ* (from *go*), *cāyakaḥ* (where *av* is substituted), and *lāvakaḥ* (where *guṇa* is substituted) would be correctly formed once the substitutions of *av* and *guṇa* have taken place—resulting in *gauḥ* and *sakhāyau*—forms such as *jaitram* would not be established, because the substitution of *av* and *guṇa* would be impossible as required. Therefore, the division of rules must be made according to the specific requirements of each case. In *pākaḥ* and similar forms, the suffix *ghañ* is used in the sense of an abstract action (*bhāve*), and by [Pāṇini 7.3.52], there is the substitution of *ku* (i.e., *k*).
As for *rāgaḥ*: [it is derived from *rañj* with the suffix *ghañ*].
> [[6.4.27]] Thus there is the elision of the nasal (anunāsika). [The form] "pācayati" [is derived] by [the addition of] the suffix *ṇic* according to [[3.1.26]].

Regarding the form *cakāsayati*: because of the mention of the *upadhā* (penultimate vowel) here, the substitution does not apply to the letter *a* following the letter *c*. The inclusion of the *tapara* marker (*at*) is for the sake of brevity.
For if it were stated that "when this [vowel] is absent, there is the substitution of the penultimate vowel" (*upadhā*), there would be prolixity (*gaurava*).

However, the use of the *tapara* marker (the *ṛ*) is not for the purpose of excluding the long vowel; for once the *vṛddhi* has been applied to a long vowel, no distinction remains. The genitive case in *acām* expresses selection (*nirdhāraṇa*); thus, [the meaning is]:
"in place of the initial vowel among the vowels."

But surely, since the technical rule regarding *ik* (*ik-paribhāṣā*) applies, the substitution should occur for the place of *ik*; therefore, one should say "in the place of *ik*" (*ikaḥ sthāne*), and not "in the place of *ac*" (*acaḥ sthāne*)? The [author] thinks as follows: from the rule [Pāṇini 7.2.115], the second mention of *aj* is carried over (*anuvartate*) for the purpose of indicating the substituendum (*sthānin*). Therefore, just as in that [previous] rule the *ik-paribhāṣā* does not apply because of the indication of the substituendum, so it is here as well; thus there is no fault. Examples: *gārgyaḥ*, *vātsyaḥ*; *dākṣiḥ*, *plākṣiḥ*.
Regarding the rule *ata iñ* [4.1.95], we have examples such as *aupagavaḥ* and *kāpaṭavaḥ*.

Now, consider *prāgdīvyatīyo’ṇ* [4.1.83]. Then, in the case of *tvāṣṭraḥ* and *jāgataḥ*, when the suffix *aṇ* is applied by *tasyedam* [4.3.120], the vowel *a* of *tvaṣṭṛ* and *jagat* respectively undergoes the *vṛddhi* substitution prescribed by *taddhiteṣvacāmādeḥ* [7.2.117]. Why does the *vṛddhi* substitution characterized by the penultimate vowel (*upadhā*) not occur instead? To this he says: "The *vṛddhi* of the first vowel among the vowels (*acāmādeḥ*) subverts the *vṛddhi* of the penultimate vowel."
But how can that which is stated for one thing serve as a sublater for another? It is because of an indicator (*jñāpaka*).

The fact that [Pāṇini] recites the word *puṣkarasat* in the *anuśatikādi* group indicates that where there is initial *vṛddhi*, no other *vṛddhi* occurs. What is the purpose of its inclusion in the *anuśatikādi* group? It is so that there may be *vṛddhi* in both members of the compound, as in *pauṣkarasādi*, meaning "the descendant of Puṣkarasat."

The suffix *iñ* is applied by [Pāṇini 4.1.96] *bāhvādibhyaśca*. If initial *vṛddhi* were not the sublater (*bādhaka*) of other *vṛddhi*, then since the *vṛddhi* would already be established by the rule concerning the penultimate vowel (*upadhā*), the word *pauṣkarasādi*—and thus the word *puṣkarasat*—would not be listed among the *anuśatikādi* group.
The Teacher perceives that where there is initial *vṛddhi*, no other *vṛddhi* occurs; for this reason, he lists the word *puṣkarasat* among the *anuśatikādi* group.

But surely, since the suffix *ṭhak* is prescribed there [in the rule for "carati"], the *vṛddhi* substitution characterized by the penultimate vowel (*hrupadhā*) would not apply because *ṭhak* is not marked with *ñ* or *ṇ*. Thus, from "he moves about as a Puṣkarasat" (*puṣkarasadā carati*), one would expect the form *pauṣkarasādikaḥ*. This is not so; for if the suffix *ṭhak* were produced after the word *puṣkarasat* in the sense of "moving about," why is it not produced again? Because of non-usage (*anabhidhāna*). For derivatives formed by *kṛt*, *taddhita*, and compound suffixes are governed by actual usage (*abhidhāna*).

Therefore, the reading of the word *puṣkarasat* in the *anuśatikādi* group is merely indicative (*jñāpaka*). Although the term *taddhiteṣu* [Pāṇini 7.3.117] is established as having a plural ending, nevertheless, because of the mention here in the singular, the scope of the plural is understood through a transformation (*vipariṇāma*) to refer to the singular; hence he says: "when a *taddhita* suffix beginning with *k* follows. Examples: *nāḍāyanaḥ*, *jārāyaṇaḥ*.
[The suffix] *phak* is applied by [Pāṇini 4.1.99].

*Ākṣikaḥ*, *śālākikaḥ*: from the words *akṣi* and *śalākā*, the suffix *ṭhak* [is applied] by [Pāṇini 4.4.2], "He plays with that, he digs with that, he wins with that, or it has been won thereby"; [then the substitution of *ik* for *ṭha* occurs] by [Pāṇini 7.3.50]. In the *Kāśikā-vivaraṇapañjikā* composed by the venerable Master Jinendrabuddhi, who is like a Bodhisattva, this concludes the second quarter of the seventh chapter. Now begins the third quarter of the seventh chapter. By [Pāṇini 7.2.117], when the rule for *vṛddhi* would apply to the vowel *ai* on account of proximity (*āntaratamya*), the substitution of *ā* is prescribed for the words beginning with *devikā*. Here, three possible positions (*pakṣa*) are considered: 1. [...]

The elements beginning with *devikā* are qualified by the preceding term "aṅga" (suffixal element)—that is, "of the suffixal elements beginning with *devikā*. Alternatively: 2) By those [elements], the suffixal element [is qualified]—meaning "of the suffixal element ending in *devikā* and so forth"; or else:
3) By those, the initial vowel [is qualified]—meaning "the first vowel (*ac*) among the vowels belonging to the elements beginning with *devikā*."

In that regard, if the first position were adopted, then the expression "rice growing on the banks of the Devikā" (*dāvikākūlāḥ śālayaḥ*) would not be established; for in that case, the word *devikā* alone would not be the subordinate member (*aṅga*), but rather the compound *devikākūla*.

[Objection: Is it not the case that *aṅgasya* is a partitive genitive (*avayava-ṣaṣṭhī*), and that the relationship between qualifier and qualified will be established thus: "those which are parts of the *aṅga*, namely Devikā and so forth"? And since the word *devikā* here is indeed a part of the *aṅga*, this fault does not apply. [Response: This is true; however, there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). It would also apply in a case such as *saudevikaḥ*, meaning "born in Sudevikā.
Alternatively, if the second position were adopted, even then the form *dāvikākūlāḥ śālayaḥ* ("rice growing on the banks of the Dāvikā") would not be established.

When the *aṅga* (base) is qualified by [the suffixes] beginning with *devikā*, since there is the rule of "extension to that which ends in it" (*tadantavidhi*) for both the qualified and the qualifier, it would follow that the rule applies to an *aṅga* ending in *devikā* and so forth, but not to one beginning with it. Therefore, a further effort must be undertaken so that it may apply even to that which begins with it.
However, when the third alternative is adopted, even without a further effort, the rule applies to both the simple [suffix] and to that which begins with it as well as to that which ends with it.

In all cases, because the vowel at the beginning of *ācāma* and so forth belongs to the *devikā*-group, he says—referring specifically to that [initial vowel]—"of these, namely *devikā*, *śiṃśapā*, *ādityavāṭ*, *dīrghasattra*, and *śreyas*," and so on. Among the vowels of these *devikā*-type words, whatever vowel is the first, when there is the occasion for *vṛddhi* (the substitution of *ai*), its form *ā* is prescribed. Thus, we have "pūrvaśāṃśapa."

As before, there is vṛddhi of the subsequent member (uttarapada). That [vṛddhi] occurs specifically as *ā* because it is obtained through the continued application (*anuvṛtti*) of the rule for the subsequent member (*uttarapadādhikāra*) regarding the group beginning with *devika*. Thus, the statement "the word *vahīnara* must be formulated" is made.
This is for the purpose of precluding that *vṛddhi* which would otherwise apply to the letter *a*;
however, once the letter *i* has been substituted, the *vṛddhi* that applies there indeed takes place.
As for the phrase "some, however," and so forth:

*Kuṇaḍa*, *vāḍava*, and so forth. [The form] *vihīna* is derived from *vihīnaḥ naro kāmakrodhābhyām* ("a man devoid of desire and anger"), where the *n* is elided due to its inclusion in the *pṛṣodarādi* group; the descendant of *vihīnara* is *vaihīnariḥ*, according to *Pāṇini 4.1.95*: *ata iñ*. In the rule *kekayamitrayupralayānām*, the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) denotes a part in relation to "the beginning" (*yādi*). The genitive case in *yādeḥ* is a locative of substitution (*sthāna-ṣaṣṭhī*) in relation to the substitute (*ityādeśa*). That which has *ya* as its initial is *yādi*.
The letter *ya* accompanied by *a* and the letter *u* accompanied by *a* [are the substitutes].

For the descendants of Kekaya and others, there is the substitution of *iy* for that which begins with *ya* and so forth, provided it is a constituent part [of the base]. Now, one might object: the word *mitrayu* is the ultimate base (*paramaprakṛti*), not a lineage (*gotra*); since the technical term "lineage" is prescribed for a specific type of offspring in the rule "That which begins from the grandson is the lineage" (Pāṇini 4.1.162), how can a suffix prescribed after a "lineage" be applied to the ultimate base? To this, he says: "For it is worldly," and so forth.

What, then, is the mundane lineage (*laukika-gotra*)? To this he says: "And in the world," and so forth. Here, the mundane lineage is intended. And in the world, the word *ṛṣi* is designated as "lineage" (*gotra*).
Furthermore, this word *mitrayu* signifies a seer (*ṛṣi*). Therefore, even when the suffix is stated [to be applied] from that *gotra*, the suffix occurs.
Regarding the form *prāleya*:

by the rule *ata āgataḥ* (Pāṇini 4.3.74), the suffix *aṇ* is applied. When a *taddhita* suffix beginning with *ñ* or *ṇ* follows, an increase (*vṛddhi*) would otherwise be required; however, this prohibition is now stated, and along with that prohibition, the substitutions *ai* and *au* (*aijāgamau*) take place.
By the rule "the vowel *ai* [is substituted] for the letter *ya*" and so forth, he demonstrates the connection according to their respective order.
Regarding the term "vaiyasanam":
the root *asu* means "to cast" (Dhātupāṭha 1209).

The word *vaiyākaraṇa* is derived as follows: from the prefix *vi-* and the root *as-* (in the sense of "to be thrown" or "cast"), with the suffix *lyuṭ* in the instrumental sense (*karaṇe*), forming a *prādi-samāsa*, followed by the substitution of *yaṇ* and the suffix *aṇ* according to Pāṇini 4.3.53. In this context, the *vṛddhi* substitution does not occur for the vowel *a* following the final *y*; therefore, the augment *aij* is inserted before that [final *a*]. Thus, we have *vaiyākaraṇaḥ*.

*Vyākaraṇa*: that by which words (*śabda*) are specifically formed or derived; the suffix *lyuṭ* is used in the sense of the instrument (*karaṇe*). This is a *prādi-samāsa* (compound with a prefix), followed by the suffix *aṇ* according to Pāṇini 4.2.59. In this case, because the application of grammatical rules proceeds like a rain-cloud (*parjanya-vat*), the *vṛddhi* that would otherwise result from the vowel *a* at the end of the first member of the compound does not occur; therefore, the augment *aij* (*ai* or *au*) is inserted before that. *Sauvāḥ*: "good" (*su*) + "self" (*ātmā*) = *svāḥ*; the compound is as previously explained. Then, the suffix *aṇ* is applied in the sense of "descendant" (*apatya*) according to Pāṇini 4.1.112.
In this case, *vṛddhi* does not occur after a *va*-sound that is at the end of a word; therefore, the augment *aij* (*ai* or *au*) occurs before it. Regarding the form *ārthi*:
one whose purpose (*artha*) is "no" (*na*) is *anartha*; his descendant is formed with the suffix *iñ* [Pāṇini 4.1.95].
Regarding "yāṣṭakaḥ":
[the suffix] *īkak* is applied after *śakti* and *yaṣṭi* by Pāṇini 4.4.59.
Regarding "yātāḥ": [this refers to those who have gone].

By the rule *iṇaḥ parasya laṭaḥ śatrādeśaḥ* (Pāṇini 3.2.124), there is the substitution of *śatṛ* for the *laṭ* [present tense] following a root ending in *iṇ*; then, by *aci śnu-dhātu-bhruvāṃ y-v-oḥ* (Pāṇini 6.4.77), *yaṇ* is substituted; and subsequently, by *taddhiteṣvacām ādeḥ* (Pāṇini 7.2.117), the augment *aṇ* is added. In both these instances, the letter *y* will be at the end of a word (*padānta*). For example: "Let curd be given to the Brāhmaṇas, but buttermilk to Kauṇḍinya. Here, the giving of buttermilk sets aside the giving of curd. Even if these two were not cases of setting aside (*bādha*), nevertheless, because the *aic* vowels (*ai* and *au*) are applied first due to their being obligatory (*nitya*), the *vṛddhi* substitution occurs afterwards, and it will apply to those very vowels.

Nor should it be suspected here that even those two [vowels *ai* and *au*] are non-eternal (*anitya*) due to the application of another rule; for they are not prescribed as substitutes for another word-form, but rather they are themselves the original elements (*abhakta*) preceding the *y* and *v*.

Even if there were the application of another rule, nevertheless, because the two [substitutions] are non-eternal, once the *ai* and *au* have been produced by the subsequent rule, the principle "when two rules apply simultaneously, that which is sublated remains sublated" (*vipratiṣedhe yadbādhitaṃ tadbādhitameva*) applies, and thus the *vṛddhi* substitution does not occur again.

Even if there were an increase [of the vowel] due to the cognition of recurrence (*punar-prasaṅga*), nevertheless the desired result would indeed be established, because there is no difference [in the outcome]. To this he says: "the statement of the prohibition," and so forth.

*Prakḷpti* means conceptualization (*prakalpana*), that is to say, determination (*vyavasthā*). The purpose is: how might that very domain of *ai* and *au*, where the prohibition of the increase (*vṛddhi*) of what follows *y* and *v* occurs, be properly established through conceptualization?
A prohibition is being stated; for what purpose, then, is this determination of the scope (*viṣaya-parakalpanā*) for *aic* (the diphthongs *e* and *o*) made? To this he says: "lest [it] occur here.
If the determination of the scope for *aic* were not established by means of the statement of the prohibition, then [the substitution] would occur even in cases such as *dādhyaśviḥ* and *mādhvīkā*.
Therefore, so that this fault does not arise, the determination of the scope for *aic* is established by means of the statement of the prohibition.
*Dadhipriya* is derived from *dadhi-āśa*, and *madhupriya* is derived from *madhu-āśa*.

According to the rule "In the section on grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇa*), there is a compound of words such as *śākapārthiva* and elision of the middle member" (Vārttika 83), this is a compound with elision of the middle term.

Now, even though the prohibition [of *vṛddhi*] is being stated, why does it not apply here, given that there is no *vṛddhi* following the vowels *y* and *v*? To this he says: "For in this case," and so forth.

For a prohibition of *vṛddhi* occurs only when there is the possibility (*prasaṅga*) of its application, not when there is none; and here there is no possibility of *vṛddhi* following the [suffixes] *y* and *v*, therefore the intention is that the prohibition simply does not apply.

Now, one might object: the rule *acām ādeḥ* [Pāṇini 7.2.117] is understood [in the present context], by which *y* and *v* are qualified as "those *y* and *v* which occur in place of the initial vowel among the vowels";
and such [substitutes for an initial vowel] do not exist in forms like *dadhyai* and *dadhyau*.

And if there were not this [separate mention of *yvoḥ*], then there would be no purpose [for it]. This is not so; for there is the mention of "of the vowels" (*acām*) and so forth. Therefore, if *y* and *v* were qualified [by that], then the *vṛddhi* [substitution] would remain unqualified.
Consequently, there would also be a prohibition of *vṛddhi* in this case: *dve aśītī bhṛto bhṛto bhāvī vā* → *dvyāśautikaḥ*.
Now, if *vṛddhi* is qualified—either by "of the vowels" (*acām*) or as "the *vṛddhi* [substitution]"—then this fault does not occur.

For in this context, the *vṛddhi* substitution is not applied by the rule "after *āc* and so forth" (*na hy atrācām āder ity evaṃ vṛddhiḥ*). What then? It is by the rule "of a numeral and that which has the number of years as its final member" (*saṃkhyāyāḥ saṃvatsarasaṃkhyasya ca*) [Pāṇini 7.3.15].
Why then would *y* and *v* not be specified? And consequently, in forms such as *dādhyai* and *dādhyaḥ*, the diphthongs *ai* and *au* would indeed occur.
Therefore, in order to establish the proper domain for those two, it must be stated that "not" (*na*) applies.

"It is intended that this prohibition applies even to the *vṛddhi* [vowel substitution] of the final member of a compound. And this is obtained because it continues to apply within the governing rule (*adhikāra*) concerning the final member of a compound.
As in the example: "pūrvatraiyalinde."

In this context, there is a prohibition regarding the rule *viśo’madrāṇām* [Pāṇini 7.3.13], which would otherwise require the vṛddhi (vowel strengthening) of the final syllable of the second member of the compound. If this prohibition were to apply even to the vṛddhi of the second member, then in the case of *dvyāśītikaḥ* as well, the vṛddhi of the second member that is obtained by the rule *dvyāśīteḥ khañ ca* [Pāṇini 5.1.32] would also be prohibited. Therefore, he says: “But where,” and so forth.

How, then, is it that the desired prohibition does not occur here? Because the vowels of the second member (*uttarapada*) are qualified by the first vowel among them, and it is that [first vowel] which is specified by the terms *y* and *v*.

When there is a vowel at the beginning of the vowels of the *uttarapada* (the second member of a compound), the *vṛddhi* substitution does not occur for that *uttarapada* after the *y* or *v* [of the *taddhita* suffix]. Furthermore, in the case of *dvyāśītikaḥ*, since the letter *y* stands in place of the initial vowel of the *uttarapada*, the prohibition of *vṛddhi* does not apply here. [The form] *dauvārikaḥ* is derived by the application of the suffix *ṭhak* [according to Pāṇini 4.4.69].
"Belonging to the door-keeper" is *dauvārapāla*,
according to [Pāṇini 4.3.120] which prescribes the suffix *aṇ*.
However, in most manuscripts, it appears as "belonging to the door-keeper" is *dauvārapālika*.

The reading [found there] is incorrect; for no suffix *ṭhak* has been prescribed by any rule in the sense of "his" (tasyeda) after the word *dvārapāla*. However, in another place, the reading is "the offspring of the door-keeper (*dvārapāla*) is *dauvārapālikaḥ*," where *ṭhak* is applied according to Pāṇini 4.1.146: *revatyādibhyaṣṭhak*.
But [one might object]:...

In that context, the word *dvārapālī* is recited, but not the word *dvārapāla*. If this is so, then it is thought that the word *dvārapāla* ought to have been recited there, as it will also include the form *dvārapālī*; for according to the rule, "When a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) is mentioned, that which is qualified by gender is also included" (Vyāḍipāda 29), such is the logical principle. However, those who do not recite the word *dvārapāla* there cite the form *dauvārapāliḥ*, ending in the suffix *iñ*, in the sense of offspring.

How, then, does it apply to the *gaṇa* "dvāra" [in the rule] for the door-keeper (*dvārapāla*)? Here too, the initial vowel is qualified by "door and so forth" (*dvārādi*); that is, among the vowels of the words beginning with "door," it is the first vowel which is not *aj*. This is because of the upcoming rule concerning "that which begins with it" (*tadādividhi*), as indicated by the term "*sauvaraḥ*" (pertaining to the *svarita*).
Since the treatise was composed concerning (*adhikṛtya*) accent (*svara*), the suffix *aṇ* is applied according to [Pāṇini 4.3.87]: *adhikṛtya kṛte granthe*. Thus we have *saurīyāḥ*.
The feminine suffix *ṅīp* is applied according to [Pāṇini 4.1.15]: *ṭiḍḍhāṇañ*.
From "vaiyalkaśaḥ," [the suffix] aṇ is applied by [Pāṇini 4.3.53]. From "sauvastikaḥ," [the suffix] aṇ is applied.
The suffix *ṭhak* is applied by the rule "An addition [to the list] after words such as *mā-śabda*" (Vārttika 482), resulting in *sauvargamanikaḥ* (or *sauvargamikaḥ* according to the Kāśikā).

The suffix *ṭhak* is applied by the rule "An addition [to the list] after words such as *prabhūta-* when followed by *āha*" (Vārttika 483). [Objection: "This is already established by the preceding rule."

[Objection: Is it not because the letter *va* is at the end of a word (*padānta*)? To this, [the author] says: "In that case, it might be so. If the derivation is made thus—"one's own study is *svādhyāya*"—then, because it is not at the end of a word, [the rule] would not apply. Is the reading of the word *svādhyāya* meaningful in that derivation? Therefore, he says: "But even if it is thus," and so forth. How, then, is the word *svādhyāya* derived from the word *sva*? To this, he says: "For even at the beginning of that," and so forth.
Regarding "sphaiyakṛtaḥ" [the Kāśikā reads "sphaikṛtaḥ"], the suffix *aṇ* is applied by [Pāṇini 4.1.114]. Regarding "sauvādumṛdavaḥ" [the Kāśikā reads "sovādumṛdavam"].
Here too, the suffix *aṇ* is applied by [Pāṇini 4.3.120] *tasyedam*. Similarly, in the case of *śauvanam*, [the suffix *aṇ* is applied]; thus, one also has *śauvam*.
By [Pāṇini 6.4.144], there is the elision of the *ṭi* suffix.
In the word *śauvādaṃṣṭraḥ*, by [Pāṇini 6.3.137], there is lengthening. In the word *naiyagrodhaḥ*, [the same applies].

> [[4.3.134]] The suffix *aṇ* [is applied]. "It grows downwards, thus it is *nyagrodha*"—from the root *añc*, by [the rule] *ṛtvig-ādinā* [[3.2.59]], there is the suffix *kvin*; by [the rule] *iti kutvam* [[8.2.62]], there is the substitution of *k* for *c* (i.e., the *ku*-substitution), and the *yaṇ*-substitution of *e* for *ni*.
The word *nyagrodha* is derived from the root *ruh* with the prefix *nyak*, followed by the suffix *pacādyac*.

In this formation, the substitution of *dh* for *h* occurs by Pāṇini 7.3.53 (*nyaṅkvādīnāṃ ca*), the substitution of *g* for *k* occurs by 8.2.39 (*jhalāṃ jaś jhaśi*), and the *guṇa* strengthening of the light penultimate vowel (*laghūpadhaguṇa*) applies. Thus, when the word *nyagrodha* is etymologically derived in this manner, since the rule 7.3.3 (*na yvābhyām*) already establishes the desired form due to the fact that the letter *y* is at the end of a word, this present rule is for the purpose of restriction (*niyamārtham*). It ensures that the elision of *y* occurs only when it stands alone [as the final member], and not when it begins a compound (such as *nyagrodhamūla*). Regarding the view that the word is not etymologically derived (*avyutpattipakṣe*), it is said that "this [rule] serves as an original injunction (*vidhyartham*)."
Because the letter *ya* is at the end of a word (*apadāntatvāt*). Regarding what was stated: there is a prohibition of *vṛddhi* and the introduction of the augment *aij*.
[The form is] *vyāvakrośī* (or *vyākrośī*, as in the manuscript).

[The forms] such as *pāṭhaḥ* [are derived as follows]: from the roots *kruśa* "to call" (DhP 856; according to some lists, also "to weep"), *likha* "to arrange letters" (DhP 1365), *carca* "to study" (DhP 1712, belonging to the *curādi* class), and *hasa* "to laugh" (DhP 721)—from these preceded by the prefix *vyava*, the suffix *ṇac* is applied, and from that ending in *ṇac*, the suffix *añ* is added.
Here, when the aforementioned operation is prohibited, only *vṛddhi* (vowel strengthening) occurs, because two prohibitions are understood to imply the original state (*prakṛtyartha*).
The suffix *ṅīp* is applied by the rule *ṭiḍḍhāṇañ* [Pāṇini 4.1.15]. Regarding the word *svāgatikaḥ*: "a welcome" (*svāgatam*) means a beautiful arrival (*śobhanam āgatam*).
The suffix *ṭhak* is applied according to the Vārttika: "In the sense of 'he said that' and so forth, there is an addition [to the list] of words beginning with *prabhūta*" [Vārttika 483].
Regarding the term *svādhvarika*: here too, the suffix *ṭhak* is applied by [Pāṇini 4.4.8] *carati*. A beautiful sacrifice (*adhvara*) is a *svadhvara*.
"Having a limb as its own," and so forth;
[this refers to] "the suffix *ryāṅ* after a word denoting one's own limb" (Pāṇini 5.3.78);
[and the vowel lengthening is by] "after *at*, the suffix *iṅ*" (Pāṇini 4.1.95).
One whose limbs (*aṅga*) are beautiful is *svaṅga*; one whose limbs are gone is *vyaṅga*; one from whom a foot (*aṅghri*) has departed is *vyaṅgha*.

"Vyavahāra" means the act of dealing (*vyavaharaṇa*); the suffix *ghañ* is used here to denote the abstract state (*bhāve*). Now, one might object: this word *vyavahāra* occurs in the sense of "mutual exchange of actions" (*karmavyatīhāra*), and in that case, the prohibition established by the rule *na karmavyatīhāre* [Pāṇini 7.3.6] would already be effective; why then is it mentioned here? To this he says: "This word *vyavahāra*... [is used here in a different sense].

What, then, is the worldly (*laukika*)? Furthermore, the worldly conduct is that behavior by which one is called "worldly" (*vyāvahārika*) in terms of social transactions; that is how it should be understood. Regarding the term *svāpateyam*: how is its application [to the word *sva*] established here, given that the letter *v* does not occur at the end of this word? To this he says: "Its application is established because the word *sva* is listed among the *dvārādi* group."
The intended meaning is that this follows the rule for "that-initial" (tadādi-vidhi). How it constitutes a "that-initial" formation has been stated in that very same place: *ābhāstriḥ*, *ādaṃṣṭriḥ*.

[In these cases,] *bhastrā* is that which belongs to him, and *śuna iva daṃṣṭrā* (fangs like a dog's) belong to him; thus they form *bahuvrīhi* compounds, with the shortening of the initial member (*upasarjana-hrasvatvam*).

But by what means does the prohibition of *vṛddhi* apply from the very beginning, such that this prohibition is stated, since its [the word *āśā*] final sound is not the letter *v*? To this he says: "The word *āśā* is recited among the *drārādi* group."

But surely the word *ā* alone is listed among the *dvārādi* group; what possibility is there for a rule of "starting from that" (*tadādividhi*) to apply there? If you argue that this is because of the rule "when a grammatical operation is prescribed with reference to a certain element, it applies to that element and what begins with it, provided the mention of the element is not by means of its initial letter" (*Vyākaraṇa-paribhāṣā* 127), this is not so. A rule of "starting from that" occurs when there is a mention of a consonant (*hal*) specified in the locative case (*saptamī-nirdiṣṭa*), and neither of these two conditions exists here. Therefore, he says "And in that case," etc.
The intention is that if the rule of "starting from that" did not apply there, then this statement of prohibition would be meaningless, since there would be no possibility for the operation to occur.

The purpose of the indicator (jñāpaka) is to prevent the application of *vṛddhi* in cases such as *śauvādaṃṣṭro maṇiḥ*. [Regarding the statement] "the inclusion of the initial vowel *i* must be made": this means that a *taddhita* suffix beginning with *i* is to be understood, and thus an explanatory rule (*vyākhyāna*) must be formulated to include those beginning with *i*.
He asks, "For what purpose? and says: "for the sake of [the vowels] beginning with *ā* and *āṬ*. That which has the purpose or aim of those beginning with *ā* and *āṬ* is so described.
However, their actual purpose is simply the initial *vṛddhi* [strengthening].

The explanation there is as follows: the mention of *iñ* here is intended as an indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*) for *taddhita* suffixes beginning with *i*; therefore, the prohibition applies elsewhere as well, even to other *taddhita* suffixes.
Regarding the phrase "of that which ends in it":
this refers to [a word] ending in *iñ*, such as *anyannāyī*.

But how can that which is desired be obtained elsewhere, given that even elsewhere, when a *taddhita* suffix is produced, there ought to be elision by the rule *iñaḥ* [Pāṇini 6.4.148]? This is not a fault; for this [mention of] *iñ* is not a locative of cause (*nimitta-saptamī*), but rather a locative of sequence (*para-saptamī*). If it were a locative of cause, there would be no prohibition of the prohibition of *vṛddhi* caused by the absence of the *aṇ* suffix. But if it is a locative of sequence, although the elision is performed, the prohibition is nevertheless established through the status of being a *sthānivadbhāva*.

Regarding the word *ābhastram*: the suffix *aṇ* is applied by [Pāṇini 4.2.111] *iñaśca*. Since a permanent prohibition would have been required by the preceding rule, an option is now stated. [The phrase] *padāntasya* [is used].
The meaning is "that which ends with the word *pada*.
Regarding the term *āāpadam*:
one who has a *pada* (foot) like that of a dog (*śvan*) is *āpadaḥ*; this [word] belongs to him, thus it is *āāpadam*.

Regarding the term *śauvāpada*, the long vowel [is applied] by [Pāṇini 6.3.137]. This is stated because, although an increase (*vṛddhi*) would have been applicable to the initial vowel of the stem (*aṅga*), this [rule] is now being formulated. Now, one might object: since in rules such as *avayavād ṛtoḥ* [7.3.11], a locative case is employed, even without the governing heading (*adhikāra*) of "the latter member" (*uttarapada*), the operation will apply to the latter member itself by virtue of [Pāṇini 1.1.67]; so what is the purpose of the heading "the latter member"? To this, he says: "In cases where," and so forth.
By the word "etc. (*ādi*), rules such as *ahmadbhagasindhvante pūrvapadasya* [Pāṇini 7.3.19], *anunnatikādīnāñca* [7.3.20], and *devatādvandve ca* [7.3.21] are included.

Since there is no mention of the ablative case (*pañcamī*) in these rules, if the governing heading *uttarapada* (the subsequent member) were not in effect, the *vṛddhi* substitution would apply only to the first vowel of the *aṅga* (the nominal stem), and not to the subsequent member.

Why is that? For that purpose, the governing rule for subsequent words (*uttarapadādhikāra*) is established. If this is so, one might raise the objection: "In this case, the rule *iha* (Pāṇini 7.3.11) need not be cited, because a mention of the ablative case (*pañcamīnirdeśa*) is already present here. Anticipating this objection, he states that even where there is a mention of the ablative case, this [governing rule] performs its function incidentally (*prāsaṅgika*), as in the passage beginning with "even in mentions of the ablative case" (*pañcamīnirdeśeṣv api*). He further states another purpose in the passage beginning with "and of *vṛddhi*" (*vṛddheś ca*).

The section concerning the final member (*uttarapadādhikāra*) is established so that this designation "vṛddhi" may apply to the *vṛddhi* [vowel] prescribed therein. But what is the reason for thus requiring the designation of *vṛddhi*? He says: "In the case of the *vṛddhi* of the final member," and so forth.

This is for the purpose of ensuring that when the final member contains a *vṛddhi* vowel as prescribed in the section on the final member, the preceding member (*pūrvapada*) shall have its final syllable accented (*antodātta*).

In the rule *uttarapadavṛddhau sarvañca* [Pāṇini 6.2.105], it is prescribed that "the vṛddhi which is ordained under the governing heading (*adhikāra*) of 'the final member' (*uttarapada*). How can this be understood? It can only be understood if the governing heading of 'the final member' is established for the sake of designation (*vyapadeśa*), and not otherwise. Therefore, the governing heading of 'the final member' must be made for the sake of designation.
*Bālamano ramā* [commentary on] *Pāṇini Sūtra* 7.3.10, *uttarapadasya* (1376):
"This is a governing rule (*adhikāra*).
These initial sūtras belong to the section on initial *vṛddhi* in the seventh book.
From the *Bālamano ramā*: "After the negative particle *nañ*, [the suffix *aṇ* is applied] to *śuci*, *kṣāra*, *kṣetra-jña*, and *kuśala-nipuṇa*. (Pāṇini 5.4.153).

This sūtra occurs within the section on initial *vṛddhi*, where the options "of the subsequent member" (*uttarapadasya*) and "or of the preceding member" (*pūrvasya tu vā*) are understood as being carried over. Thus: *ā-śauca*—*āśaucam*.
The meaning is "come from the impure.
According to the rule *tata āgataḥ*, when the suffix *aṇ* is applied, there is an option for the initial vowel of the first member (*pūrvapada*) to undergo vṛddhi;
however, for the subsequent member (*uttarapada*), the initial vṛddhi is obligatory.
Similarly, in the subsequent cases as well, the meaning should be understood as "come from one who is not a knower of the field (akṣetrajña), who is unskilled (akuśala), and who is inept (anipuṇa).

However, in the term *ānaiāryam*, the suffix *ṣyañ* is applied in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāva*) according to the rule for the *brāhmaṇa*-class of words; [the mention of] *ṛtoḥ* [is absent in the manuscript labeled 'mu'].

This is not a grasping of the essential nature (*svarūpa*), but rather a grasping of the object (*artha*). For it is said that [the suffix] *vati* occurs after a part (*avayava*), and this very thing becomes a part of the *ṛtu*; thus, these two function as parts of the whole.

When the meaning is being understood, this instruction regarding the referent is comprehended; therefore, it is understood that the grammatical operation applies to a word denoting a season that follows a preceding member which denotes a part [of that season]. Thus he says, "denoting a part," and so forth.
"An *ekadeśi*-compound" refers to the rule *pūrvāparādibhiḥ* (Pāṇini 2.2.1).

But surely, by the rule *grahaṇavatā prātipadikena tadantavidhiḥ pratiṣidhyate* (Vyā.pa. 89), the extension of a grammatical operation to that which ends with a word-form is prohibited; so how can a suffix prescribed after the words *varṣā* and *hemanta* be understood as applying to words ending in them? To this he says: "In that context, regarding the seasons (*ṛtu*), when there is a prescription involving *vṛddhi*, [it applies to] the constituent parts. For example, *paurvavarṣikaḥ* (or *paurvavārṣikam*, according to the Kāśikā). Having formed a descriptive compound (*viśeṣaṇasamāsa*)—namely, "those which are both prior (*pūrva*) and the rains (*varṣā*)"—the secondary derivative (*taddhita*) is to be prescribed in the sense of "belonging to" (*bhava*). Here, the word *pūrva* denotes time and not a constituent part; thus, the *vṛddhi* substitution occurs only at the beginning of the base (*aṅga*).

Now, one might ask: why does the suffix *ṭhak* not apply here as well by means of the rule regarding the inclusion of what follows (*tadantavidhi*)? To this he says: "For [the rule applies] only when preceded by a constituent part," and so forth. Regarding the term "of a country" (*janapadasya*), this is not a literal mention of the specific form itself, because of the prohibition in the subsequent sūtra: "not for those that are not Madra" (*amadrāṇām*).

In the subsequent sūtra, this very mention of "janapada" (country) is carried forward; therefore, if here [in the present sūtra] there were a mention of the word-form itself (*svarūpa-grahaṇa*), then the prohibition regarding the Madras would be purposeless. Consequently, this is a mention of the meaning (*artha-grahaṇa*); thus, it is understood that the grammatical operation applies to that which denotes a country. Hence he says: "Of that which follows after *su*, *sarva*, *ardha*, and these [others], provided it denotes a country," and so forth.
Regarding the example *supāñcālakaḥ*: "excellent Pañcālas" is a *prādi-samāsa* (compound with a prefix).
In the case of *sarvapāñcālakaḥ*,
it is a *karmadhāraya* compound according to the rule beginning with *pūrvakālaika* [Pāṇini 2.1.48].
In the case of *ardhapāñcālakaḥ*, [the same applies].

In the rule *ardhaṃ napuṃsakam* [Pāṇini 2.2.2], a *tatpuruṣa* compound is formed with the word *ardha*. In all cases, when a secondary suffix (*taddhita*) is applied in the sense of "born there" (*jāta*) and so forth, how is it that the suffix prescribed by the rule *janapadatadavadhyośca* [Pāṇini 4.2.124] occurs after a word ending in *janapada*? To this he says: *su-sarvārdha-dik-śabdebhyaḥ*, etc. The term *janapadasya* [Pāṇini 7.3.12] is understood [from the previous rule]; therefore, it is understood that the mention of *prācām* (of the Easterners) refers to a location and not to the teachers themselves. Thinking thus, he says: *prācāṃ deśe grāmāṇām*, etc.
"Pūrveṣukāmaśamī":

this is a compound formed according to [Pāṇini 2.1.50], "That which is both *pūrvā* and *iṣukāmaśamī*," and then the suffix *aṇ* is applied according to [Pāṇini 4.2.107] in the sense of "originating there.
"Pūrvapāṭaliputrakaḥ" is likewise formed.

Regarding "pūrvasmin pāṭaliputre bhavaḥ" (originating in the eastern Pāṭaliputra): this is a *tatpuruṣa* compound in the sense of a secondary derivative (*taddhita*). By the rule [Pāṇini 4.2.123], the suffix *vuñ* is applied.

Now, one might object: since there is only one Pāṭaliputra, and thus no other Pāṭaliputra exists to be excluded, how can the word "Pāṭaliputra" be qualified by the word "eastern"? There is no fault here, because the word "Pāṭaliputra" refers to a specific part of Pāṭaliputra.

Now, for what purpose is the mention of "cities" (*nagara*)? It is not established by simply saying "of villages" (*grāmāṇām*), for a city is indeed a village; a village is conventionally understood as a settlement of a community of people, and a city is likewise a settlement of a community of people. Therefore, a city is also a village, because those rules which are not intended to apply to a village are not applied to a city either.

For instance: when it is said, "The village cock is not to be eaten" (*abhakṣyo grāmyakukkuṭaḥ*) or "The village pig is not to be eaten" (*abhakṣyo grāmyaśūkaraḥ*), even the city [cock or pig] is not eaten; and when it is said, "One should not study in the village" (*grāme nādhyetavyam*), one does not study even in the city. Therefore, the city is also a village. And having established this, [the author] says, "Precisely because it is a village," etc., meaning that in rules such as *udīcyagrāmācca bahvaco'ntodāttāt* (Pāṇini 4.2.108), *dikpūrvapadādasaṃjñāyāṃ ñaḥ* (4.2.107), and *dikśabdā grāmajanapadākhyānacānarāṭeṣu* (6.2.103), the mention of "village" (*grāma*) includes the city as well.

If, then, a city (*nagara*) is also a village (*grāma*), would it not follow that the mention of "city" (*nagara-grahaṇa*) is required in the rule *viśiṣṭaliṅgo nadīdeśo 'grāmāḥ* [Pāṇini 2.4.7]? This is true; however, in that case, an exclusion of cities must be stated there. But for what reason does this very distinction of relationship arise, such that the separate mention of "village" and "city" is made for the sake of its comprehension? To this he says: *dikpūrvapado hi*, etc.

For if, just as a compound with "diś" (direction) as its first member—such as *pūrvottara*—is the name of a village like *Pūrveṣukāmaśamī*, so too were it the name of a city, then the relationship [between the two] would not differ.

Just as a word-form such as *Pāṭaliputra*, when functioning as a final member (*uttarapada*), denotes a city, so too, if the name of a village were likewise [to denote] a village, even then the relationship would not differ. But this is not the case; for the word denoting a village consists of a different kind of aggregate of preceding and following members, whereas the word denoting a city consists of a different kind of final member.
Therefore, because of the difference between village and city, there is a difference in the relationship.
Having thus shown the cause for the difference in relationship, he states the difference in relationship itself with the words beginning with "In that case" (*tatra*).
"Of those denoting a village" refers to [words] such as *pūrvauṣukāmaśamī* and so forth. "Of a part" refers to...
