[The suffix *cha* is applied] after [words such as] *iṣukāmaśamī*, *kṛṣṇamṛttikā*, and so forth; and after words denoting directions (*dikśabda*), such as *pūrva* and others.
"But in other cases," and so forth; [this refers to] cities. "The region [is the name] of northern cities."
In this context, the connection "vṛddhi occurs" is made; this is what is required.

In examples such as *pūrveṣukāmaśama*, because the internal operation (*antaraṅga*) of *guṇa* substitution takes place first between the two members of the compound, the conditions for the application of *vṛddhi*—namely, that a directional word (*dik-śabda*) and the word "village" (*grāma*) must be the subsequent member (*uttara-pada*)—no longer obtain. For *vṛddhi* is a "external" (*bahiraṅga*) operation when it occurs after a secondary suffix (*taddhita*) has been applied, depending upon that suffix; whereas *guṇa*, which applies prior to the production of the *taddhita*, is an "internal" (*antaraṅga*) operation. Nor can it be argued that *vṛddhi* will nonetheless occur by virtue of an explicit rule, for the scope of such a rule is limited to cases where the single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) does not exist, such as in *pūrvakārṣṇamṛttika* and similar forms.

Furthermore, the status of being "as if the end or the beginning" (*antādivadbhāva*) does not apply here, because of the prohibition: "When there is a dependence on both [parts], it is not as if they were the end or the beginning" (Pāṇini 6.1.84).

Therefore, one might raise the objection: "In this case, are both the preceding member (*pūrvapada*) and the following member (*uttarapada*) being relied upon? To such an objector, he replies: "In cases such as *Pūrveṣukāmaśamī*," and so forth. Just as this meaning was indicated by the rule [Pāṇini 6.3.22], so too has it been established under [Pāṇini 7.2.107].

The plural number in "of villages and towns" (*grāmanagarāṇām*) is for the purpose of excluding a rule that would apply to the singular form. Regarding "biennial" (*dvisāṃvatsarikaḥ*): as before, there is a compound in the sense of a secondary derivative (*taddhita*), and from that, the suffix *ṭhañ* is applied according to the rules for words beginning with *prāgvatīya*.

Regarding the forms *dviṣāṣṭikaḥ* and *dvisāptatikaḥ*: one might object that since the rule *kālāt* (Pāṇini 5.1.77) applies to the rule *[[5.1.80]]*, and since words such as *dviṣaṣṭi* are not words denoting time (*kālaśabda*), but rather words denoting number (*saṃkhyāśabda*), how can they produce a suffix prescribed under the heading of *kāla*? To this, he says: "The word *dviṣaṣṭi* etc. and so forth.

In this context, a word expressing time is understood by the term "time" (*kāla*). For when a word such as "sixty-two" refers to years—which are countable units—it is a word expressing time; therefore, it is called "time. Consequently, it generates the suffix prescribed under the heading of "time" (*kāla*).

Now, for what purpose is the mention of the "year" (*saṃvatsara*)? Since, in the rule *yāvataḥ* [Pāṇini 7.3.17], the word "measure" (*parimāṇa*) denotes any cause of delimitation whatsoever, and not specifically a cause of delimitation by height and circumference as in the case of a *prastha* measure; otherwise, the prohibition of the *śāṇa* would be meaningless, for the *śāṇa* is not a measure that delimits by height and circumference. Therefore, time (*kāla*) is also a cause of delimitation, and consequently, it too is a "measure"—this is the sense of the word "year."
Is this not already established by the rule *parimāṇasyāsaṃjñāśāṇayoḥ* [Pāṇini 7.3.17]? To refute such an objection, he says: "The mention of *saṃvatsara*, etc.
The mention of *saṃvatsara* is for the purpose that the mention of *parimāṇa* (measure) should not include the measure of time (*kālaparimāṇa*).
By the mention of *saṃvatsara*, this meaning is made known: "In the mention of *parimāṇa*, the measure of time is not included."
Consequently, where there is the apprehension of measurement (*parimāṇa*), the measurement of time (*kāla*) is not apprehended.
By the words "by that" (*tena*) and so forth, he demonstrates what is established when, upon the apprehension of measurement, the measurement of time is not apprehended:
"the *vṛddhi* substitution occurs in the final member of the compound."

By the rule beginning with *parimāṇāntasya* [Pāṇini 7.3.17], [the suffix *ṭhak* is applied]. Regarding the form *dvivarṣā*: it means "one who has been hired for two years," or "one who has existed for two years," or "one who will exist for two years. The suffix *ṭhak* is applied as before; then, while the rule *tasya* [Pāṇini 5.1.88] is still in effect, the elision (*luk*) is applied by [Pāṇini] 5.1.89.
Regarding the statement "it is not a *paryudāsa* (exclusion)":

when the prohibition of the suffix *ṅīp* is to be applied, that prohibition indeed takes effect; thus, by the rule [Pāṇini 4.1.21], the suffix *ṅīp* does not occur. For example: "A person who has been hired or engaged for two years to perform work is called *dvivarṣikaḥ*."

In this case, when a secondary derivative (*taddhita*) suffix is produced for the meanings of "appointed" (*adhīṣṭa*) and "hired" (*bhṛta*), the future tense is understood; therefore, someone might have the misconception that these two [meanings] should also be subject to the prohibition [of the *luṅ*]. To dispel that, he says: "In the case of 'appointed' and 'hired,'" and so forth.

What, then, is the reason why [the prohibition] does not apply? He says: "For it is understood," and so forth. In that regard, if another word were used—such as "he will perform the work, having been appointed or hired for two years"—then the future tense would be understood, but not otherwise.

Therefore, since that [suffix] is not for the sake of a secondary derivative (*taddhita*), it would apply to [the meanings of] "appointed" (*adhīṣṭa*) and "maintained" (*bhṛta*); thus, the prohibition does not occur.

But surely, when a human being (*manuṣya*) is to be expressed, there ought to be elision (*luk*) of the suffix *ṭhañ* by rule 5.1.89; so how is the form *dvivārṣikaḥ manuṣyaḥ* ("a two-year-old human") established? This is not a fault; for this elision does not occur without qualification, but rather only in a specific domain.

How so? In that case, the mention of "nitya" (always) should have been made; for [the elision] would have occurred always by the force of the very commencement [of the rule], even though it was already established by the preceding [rule]. Why then was it done? It was done so that [the elision] might apply specifically when the sense is "past" (*bhūta*), and not in cases such as "requested for study" (*adhīṣṭa*) and so on. Therefore, in cases such as *adhīṣṭa*, the elision occurs only optionally (*vibhāṣā*) by rule 5.1.88. Since posteriority (*paratva*) is not possible for a technical name (*saṃjñā*), he says "in the domain of a name" (*saṃjñāyāṃ viṣaye*), etc., thereby showing that "in the domain of a name and of *śāṇa*" is a locative of domain (*viṣaya-saptamī*).
He further states: "and when *śāṇa* is the subsequent member."
The word "object" (*viṣaya*) is required [to complete the sense].

Although it might be argued that the status of being subsequent (*paratva*) is possible for the following member (*uttarapada*), namely *śāṇa*, nevertheless, it is difficult to maintain that a single locative case functions both as a locative of object (*viṣayasaptamī*) and as a locative of sequence (*parasaptamī*).
Therefore, it is more appropriate to regard this locative as a locative of object with respect to the following member *śāṇa* itself.
Regarding the term *dvikauḍavikam*:
[the suffix] *ṭhañ* is applied according to Pāṇini 5.1.18 (*prāgvateṣṭhañ*).
Furthermore, because the suffix does not denote "worthiness" (*anārhīyatva*), the elision (*luk*) prescribed by Pāṇini 5.1.28 (*adhyardhapūrvadvigoḥ*) does not occur.

Regarding the term *dvisauvarṇikaḥ* (or *dvisauvaraṇikam* according to the *Kāśikā*), the suffix is the same [as in the previous case]. But how is there vowel lengthening (*vṛddhi*) here, since it is stated that [the rule applies] to "that which ends in a measure word" (*parimāṇānta*), and *suvarṇa* is a weight-measure (*unmāna*) because it measures heaviness, not a measure-word (*parimāṇa*)? There is no fault here; the activity of the Teacher indicates that "even a measure of heaviness is taken as a 'measure' (*parimāṇa*) in this context because it is a means of delimitation. This is shown by the fact that he begins the prohibition regarding *śāṇa* with the rule: *asaṃjñāśāṇayoḥ*.

Now, why does elision (*luk*) not occur by the rule *adhyardhapūrva* [Pāṇini 5.1.28]? To this he says: *vibhāvā*, etc. In the case of *dvinaiṣkikam*, the suffix *ṭhak* is applied by the rule *asamāse niṣkādibhyaḥ* [Pāṇini 5.1.20].

Regarding the term *pāñcalohitika* [the Kāśikā reads *pāñcalohitikam*]: when the suffix *ṭhak* is applied, by the rule *bhasyāḍhe taddhite* (Vār. 731), there occurs the substitution of the masculine form (*puṃvadbhāva*). Consequently, the feminine suffix *ṅīp* and the augment *nakāra*, which were prescribed by the rule *varṇādanudāttāt topadhāt to naḥ* (Pāṇini 4.1.39), are both removed. Regarding the term *dvaikulijikam* [the Kāśikā reads *dvaikulijikaḥ*]: [the same process applies].
"Prāgvatīyaṣṭhañ ca": the [rule] "saṃkhyāyāḥ" [Pāṇini 5.2.45] is no longer in force. Regarding the statement "je" indicates the sense of *jāta* (born/produced):
this is the usage of "je," which is a single phoneme (*ekadeśa*) from the word *jāta*.
For there is indeed the usage of even a single part of a word, as for example: *bhīma* for *bhīmasena*, and *satyabhāmā* for *bhāmā*.
Therefore, it should be understood that by the use of a portion of the word *jāta*, the meaning "born" (*jāta*) is indicated.
[This applies to the form] *proṣṭhapadāsu*.

In the case of *yuktavat* [meaning "as if joined with"], the absence of the suffix is according to Pāṇini 1.2.51: *yuktavad vyaktivacane*. Thus, for *bhadrayādāḥ*, since time is joined with the word *bhadra*, the grammatical operations such as the addition of the suffix *aṇ* should be applied as before. Similarly, for *sauhārdam*.
The suffix *aṇ* is applied by the rule *tasyedam* [Pāṇini 4.3.120].
When the suffix *aṇ* follows the word *suhmada*, then by the rule *yadādeśas tadvat* [Pāṇini 1.1.56], the substitution of *hm* for *dh* occurs,
resulting in the form *sauhādryam*.
By [Pāṇini 4.1.124], the suffix *ṣyañ* is applied; by [Pāṇini 6.3.51], the substitution of *hrasva* (short vowel) for *hm* occurs. Thus, we have "saubhāgineyaḥ" and "dīrbhāginayaḥ.
When the suffix *ḍhak* is applied by [Pāṇini 4.1.126], "kasyāṇyādīnāminaṅ ca," the substitution of *inaṅ* takes place.
Regarding "saktu-sindhavaḥ":
this is a compound with the middle term elided (madhyamapadalopa), formed according to the *śākapārthivādi* group.
Regarding "sāktusaindhavaḥ": [this is likewise a compound].

Since the suffix *ṭhañ* would [otherwise] apply by [Pāṇini 4.2.118], the suffix *aṇ* applies by [Pāṇini 4.2.133]. But surely, only the word *sindhu* is listed there; how then can [the suffix] apply to that which ends in it? To this he says: "by that," and so forth. But how is the rule of extension to what ends in that (*tadantavidhi*) obtained through that word *sindhu*, given that the rule of extension to what ends in [a stem] is prohibited by the principle: "there is no extension to what ends in a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) when that stem is itself used as a marker" (Vyāḍiparibhāṣā 89)? This is not a fault; for the particle *ca* there has the sense of including what was not explicitly mentioned. Therefore, [the suffix] occurs after the word *sindhu* and also after that which ends in it. [The example is] *ānuśatika*.

"Purchased for a hundred" (*śatena krītaḥ*) results in *śatikaḥ* by [Pāṇini 5.1.21] via the suffix *ṭhan*. "Followed by that which is purchased for a hundred" (*anugataḥ śatikena*) becomes *ānuśatikaḥ*, from which [the suffix] *aṇ* is applied by [Pāṇini 4.3.120], yielding *ānuśātikam*; likewise, *ānuhauḍikam*.
[The suffix] *ṭhak* is applied by [Pāṇini 4.4.8] in the sense of "he travels."
Regarding the term *ānusāṃvatsarikam*:

is it [formed] by the extended application (*atideśa*) of the rule *tatra ca dīyate kāryaṃ bhavavat* (Pāṇini 5.1.96), and [consequently] the suffix *ṭhañ* by the rule *bahvaco'ntodāttāt* (Pāṇini 4.3.67)?
[The example is] *āṅgāravaiṇavaḥ*.
The suffix *aṇ* [is applied] by [Pāṇini 4.1.92].
"To be eaten" (*āśitavyam*)—
the suffix *aṇ* [is applied] by [Pāṇini 4.3.53].

Regarding the term *āsyahātyam*: if the reading is *āsyahaitikam*, then the suffix *ṭhañ* is applied according to [Pāṇini 5.1.108], *tadasya prayojanam*. Now, one might object: since the rule *prātipadikāt* ("from a nominal stem") is understood to carry over, and since *āsyahatyā* and *āsyaheti* are compounds of words rather than nominal stems (*prātipadika*), how can a suffix be added here? Or even if the suffix were added, how could there be no elision (*aluk*) of the case-ending? To this he says: "For this very reason," and so forth.
Regarding "Vādhyauga":
[the suffix] *añ* is applied after [names beginning with] *Bida* and so forth when expressing immediate descent from a human being (Pāṇini 4.1.104).
Regarding "Pauṣkarasādi" and "Rānuhārati": [these are derived by adding the patronymic suffix *iñ*].
By rule 4.1.96, the suffix *iṇ* is applied;
thus we have *kaurukātyam* (the *kāśikā* reads *kaurukātyaḥ*).
The suffix *ayañ* is applied because the word belongs to the *gara-ga-ādi* group.

Regarding the term *kaurupāñcālaḥ*: the suffix *aṇ* is applied by [Pāṇini 4.3.53]. Now, one might object that the suffix *vuñ* ought to apply here because of [Pāṇini 4.2.124], which prescribes *vuñ* for words denoting a country (*janapada*). To this he replies: “A collection of countries is included under the designation ‘country’,” and so forth.

The word *kurupañcāla* denotes a collection of territories (*janapada-samudāya*), and since a collection of territories is not included under the term "territory" (*janapada*) itself, how could there be any occasion for the suffix *vuñ*? In the case of *audakaśauddhiḥ*, the suffix *iñ* is applied by [Pāṇini 4.1.95]. In the cases of *aihalaukikaḥ* and *pāralaukikaḥ*, the suffix *ṭhañ* is applied by the Vārttika: "Also after a compound whose final member is *loka*" (Vārttika 459).
Is this so? He recites that this is the intended meaning in the verse beginning with "samānasya tadādeśca," namely:
"it is universal" (sārvalaukikaḥ) and "it pertains to all persons" (sārvapauruṣam).
By [Pāṇini 4.3.120], the suffix *aṇ* is applied;
thus, "sārvabhaumaḥ. By [Pāṇini 5.1.41], the suffixes *aṇ* and *añ* are applied.
Regarding "prāyaugikaḥ": the suffix *ṭhañ* is applied because it belongs to the group beginning with *adhyātma* (Pāṇini 4.3.60). Regarding "pārastraiṇeyaḥ": [the suffix *ḍhak* is applied].
The suffix *inaṅ* is applied by [Pāṇini 4.1.127] "kulaṭāyā vā. In that context, [the rule] "tatra" [from 4.1.120] and [the rule] "4.1.126" are understood to follow. Thus, we have "rājapauruṣyam."
The suffix *ṣyañ* [is applied] due to the rule *brāhmaṇādibhyaś ca* [Pāṇini 5.1.123],
as in *sautranāḍiḥ*;
and the suffix *iñ* [is applied] by the rule *ata iñ* [Pāṇini 4.1.95], as in *ābhigāmikaḥ*.
The suffix *iṣṭhan* is applied [to form *ārhīya*] in the sense of "one who deserves to be approached" (*abhigamamarhati*).
In the expressions "pertaining to the divine" (*ādhidaivikam*) and "pertaining to the elemental" (*ādhibhautikam*),
the suffix *ṭhañ* is applied in the sense of "being so" (*bhava-artha*), according to the rule beginning with *adhyātma-ādi* (Pāṇini 4.3.60).
Regarding "cāturvedyam":
the suffix *ṣyañ* is prescribed;

it should be stated that it is used in its own sense (*svārthika*) for the sake of establishing forms such as *cāturvaṇrya*, and thus *ṣyañ* is used in its own sense here. Regarding "āgnimārutīm": [the suffix *cha* is applied].

"Agni and Marut" is a *dvandva* compound. By the rule [Pāṇini 4.2.24], the suffix *aṇ* is applied because these two are its deities (*devatā*). Consequently, by the rule [Pāṇini 7.3.28], there is *vṛddhi* (vowel strengthening) for both the preceding and following vowels. Furthermore, in the domain of the *anaṅ* substitution, the vowel *i* replaces the final syllable of the word "Agni" according to [Pāṇini 7.3.119]. Finally, the feminine suffix *ṅīp* is added by [Pāṇini 4.1.15] (*ṭiḍḍhāṇañ*), resulting in the form *āgnimārutī*. Regarding the phrase "which *dvandva* of deities is connected to a *sūkta*," and so forth: that which partakes of a *sūkta* is "connected to a *sūkta*" (*sūktasambandhī*); that for which the oblation (*havis*) is prepared is "connected to the oblation" (*havissambandhī*).
And this qualification of the *dvandva* compound is mediated by its meaning, as in the statement “and here it does not occur,” and so forth.

But how is this specific distinction obtained when there is a general statement? The thought is as follows: after [Pāṇini 7.3.22], the rule *na* should be separated as a distinct *yogavibhāga*; by that, it is established that [the substitution] does not occur elsewhere in connection with *sūkta* or in connection with *havis*.
In the case of *skāndaviśākhaḥ*,
the suffix *aṇ* is applied according to [Pāṇini 4.3.120].
In the case of *brāāhṛprajāpatyam*, [the suffix *aṇ* is applied].

Regarding the rule *dityadityādityapatyuttarapadāṇṇyaḥ* [Pāṇini 4.1.85]: *sāindrah*, *āgnendraḥ*. Here, by the rule *aṇ* [Pāṇini 4.2.24], the suffix *aṇ* is applied; then, by the rule *devatādvandve ca* [Pāṇini 7.3.21], the substitution *ānaṅ* is applied for the final vowel of the first member, and the *guṇa* substitution occurs for the vowel of the preceding member. Thus: *aindrāgnam*.

Here too, as before, the operation of *aṇ* and so forth applies; since it was stated previously that "there are two vowels in the word *indra*," etc., this is easily understood. [Examples include] *aindrāvaruṇam* and *maitrāvaruṇam*.

When the substitution of *ānaṅ* is applied by the rule *devatādvandve ca* [Pāṇini 7.3.21], the word *varuṇa* follows a long vowel. If the mention of "the teachers" (*ācārya*) were present in the phrase *prācām* [in 7.3.25], then the author would not have stated *vibhāṣitam* in the subsequent rule [7.3.26]; rather, that very mention of *prācām* would have been carried over there for the purpose of providing an option. Therefore, he says "in the region of the Easterners" (*prācāṃ deśe*), etc., to indicate that the mention is of a geographical location.

In this context, by the mention of "nagara," its own form (*svarūpa*) is understood, according to the rule *svarūpagrahaṇam* (Pāṇini 1.1.68). By the word "uttara," the final member of a compound (*uttarapada*) is indicated; however, because that final member is always present [in a compound], the status of being "optional" (*vibhāṣitatva*) would not be applicable to it. Therefore, since the *vṛddhi* [substitution] related to it is optional, it is stated as "it is optional. For this very reason, he says: "There is an option regarding the final member."
The word "increase" (vṛddhi) is connected with the subject under discussion. Regarding the term "half-a-droṇa" (ārdhadrauṇika):
it is a compound formed by the rule "a neuter [word] expressing a part [is compounded with its whole]" (Pāṇini 2.2.2). Then, by the rule [5.1.18], the suffix *ka* is applied.

Alternatively, what is the purpose of stating "or" (*vā*)? One might argue that since the word "optionally" (*vibhāṣitam*) is understood from the preceding rule [Pāṇini 7.3.25] by virtue of its being carried over (*anuvartate*), it is connected with this word "subsequent" (*uttara*); therefore, if it were carried over, the option would apply only to the subsequent member. This is not so; the compound "subsequent member" (*uttarapada*) will not be accented, but the particle *tu* is used here, and it will serve the purpose of restriction—meaning that it applies only to the preceding member, not to the subsequent one.

In that case, since the option (*vā*) is indeed more concise than the alternative of performing or not performing the rule regarding the nature of the vowel in a compound, the word "option" (*vā*) is stated once again. While the preceding rule would have prescribed an increase (*vṛddhi*) of the measure (*parimāṇa*), it is prohibited because it would apply to the vowel *a* at the beginning of the *ac*-group.
However, the option for the first member of the compound still occurs, because of the continued application (*anuvṛtti*) of the phrase "of the preceding" (*pūrvasya tu*). For example:
*ārdhaprasthikaḥ*.

The compound [in *vṛddhi*] is formed by the rule *ardhaṃ napuṃsakam* (Pāṇini 2.2.2), as before; [the suffix *t*] is an affix (*pratyaya*). [The question] "What would be the consequence? is asked because he thinks as follows: since the vowel *ā* is necessarily a *vṛddhi* [vowel], there is no difference whether or not the prohibition of *vṛddhi* applies; the form remains the same. Therefore, even if the *tapara* designation (*t*) were not present, nothing undesirable would result.
[This is addressed by the statement] "of that which has a *vṛddhi* as its cause," and so forth.
He shows what undesirable consequence would follow if the *tapara* (the long vowel marker) were not employed for the sake of indicating that specific time.
But what is the reason why the prohibition of the masculine form (*puṃvadbhāva*) would not apply? To this he says: "For where... and so forth.
Indeed, it is only while effecting a *vṛddhi* (vowel strengthening) that a secondary derivative (*taddhita*) becomes the cause of *vṛddhi*.
Therefore, wherever a prohibition of *vṛddhi* is made in a *taddhita* suffix, that [suffix] is not the cause (*nimitta*) for *vṛddhi*.

Consequently, since the *puṃvadbhāva* (masculine-like treatment) is not prohibited for a *taddhita* suffix whose cause is *vṛddhi*, the *puṃvadbhāva* would indeed occur. Where? In the examples beginning with "yathā" and so forth.
"His wife is a grammarian (*vaiyākaraṇī*).
Furthermore, the prohibition of *vṛddhi* here is by the rule "not after *y* or *v*" (*na yvābhyām*, Pāṇini 7.3.3) and so forth.

Now, for what purpose is the word "of the subsequent" (*parasya*) used, so that it might not apply to the preceding [syllable]? This is not the case; because of the force of employing the qualifier "from this" (*ataḥ*), it will not apply to the preceding one.

For no other increase (*vṛddhi*) is possible for this [word] *pūrva* than that which follows from the word *ardha*; furthermore, the optional rule *pūrvasya tu vā* (Pāṇini 7.3.26) would be rendered meaningless if there were a prohibition of it.

Well then, is the purpose [of the prohibition] so that the rule of "specification by the final letter" (*tadantavidhi*) might not apply? If the rule of specification by the final letter were in effect here as well, the prohibition would apply even in the case of *ardhadrauṇikam*.

The previous rule, however, would mean "purchased for half a *muṣṭi*," i.e., *ārdhamauṣṭika*; this would be the sense [if the rule were applied as before]. But when the word *para* (following) is included, that which follows after the half—that is, the immediately subsequent element—is what is resorted to; thus, there is no possibility of the application of the rule regarding the end of a compound (*tadanta-vidhi*). In the case of the word *pravāhaṇa*, when the suffix *ḍha* follows, the two genitives in the expression *uttarapadasya* are in different cases (a *vyadhikaraṇa* construction). The meaning is: "of that which is the *uttarapada*—that is, the constituent part—of the word *pravāhaṇa*. [The resulting form is] *pravāhaṇeyaḥ*.

From the root *vah* with the prefix *pra* and the causative suffix *ṇic*, we derive *pravāhayati* ("he causes to flow forth"), from which comes *pravāhaṇa*. Here, the suffix *lyuṭ* is applied in the sense of the agent according to [Pāṇini 3.3.113], followed by a *prādi*-compound [2.2.18], and then the substitution of *ṇ* for *n* according to [8.4.30]. Subsequently, the suffix *ḍhak* is added in the sense of "offspring" (*apatya*). But why is the vṛddhi (vowel strengthening) of the second member specifically prescribed, given that it already possesses vṛddhi by its very nature? Even though this is so, the vṛddhi must still be explicitly stated so that the prohibition of the masculine form (*puṃvadbhāva*) may apply according to [6.3.39], since the taddhita suffix is the cause of the vṛddhi.

If the *vṛddhi* of the subsequent member (*uttarapada*) were not prescribed, then in that case where the *vṛddhi* of the prior member (*pūrvapada*) is not prescribed—such as in the example *pravāhaṇeyī-bhāryaḥ* ("one whose wife is a *pravāhaṇeyī")—the prohibition of the masculine form (*puṃvadbhāva*) would not apply; for the *vṛddhi* [of the first member] would not be the cause (*nimitta*) of the secondary derivative (*taddhita*). This is just as in the case of *vaiyākaraṇa-bhāryaḥ*.

[Objection: But even if there is no cause for the application of the suffix *taddhita*, the prohibition of the masculine form (*puṃvadbhāva*) will still occur by the rule "after [a word ending in] *vṛddhi* [the feminine suffix is not replaced], when a *taddhita* follows" (Pāṇini 6.3.41). For here too, there is the status of a genus (*jāti*) according to the principle "a lineage (*gotra*) together with a school (*caraṇa*). [Response: If that is so, then this teaches that the prohibition is non-permanent (*anitya*).

Therefore, in the case of *hāstikam* ("a collection of female elephants"), the prohibition of the masculine form—which is introduced by the supplementary rule (*aupasaṃkhyānika*) "when a *bha*-stem [followed by] a *taddhita* other than one beginning with *āḍha*" (Vārttika 731)—does not take effect. [Example: *prāvāhaṇeyiḥ*. [Derivation: [From *prāvāhaṇeya*] by the rule "from *at*, *iñ*" (Pāṇini 4.1.95).

Regarding the term *prāvāhaṇeyaka*: [the suffix] *aṣuñ* is applied [by Pāṇini 4.3.126] after a *gotra* or *caraṇa*. Now, for what purpose is this stated? For it is not appropriate to undertake it for the sake of ensuring that the final member (*uttarapada*) of the word *pravāhaṇeya*—which ends in the suffix *ḍha*—is invariably *vṛddhi*-augmented; nor is its undertaking appropriate for the sake of making the *vṛddhi* of the prior member (*pūrvapada*) optional.

One might argue: "Even in the case of *iñ* and other such secondary suffixes (*taddhita*), the optionality will apply to the cause itself by the preceding rule, overriding the *vṛddhi* caused by that [suffix]; for when the secondary suffix *iñ* has occurred, the status of being 'subsequent' (*paratva*) to the element *ḍha* does not disappear. To this he says: "*bāhrataddhita*" and so forth.
That [vṛddhi] which has as its cause a secondary suffix beginning with *bāhṛ* is described thus.
Furthermore, the quality of beginning with *bāhṛ* belongs to this secondary suffix because the word *prāvāhaṇeya* is not included among those beginning with *it*.
That [substitution], being dependent upon an external cause—the taddhita suffix—is itself external (bahiraṅga).
However, the option (vikalpa) based on the letter ḍha, which occurs prior to the production of the brāhma-taddhita suffix, is internal (antaraṅga) and is thus unable to be sublated by it.
Consequently, if this [rule] were not commenced, that [substitution] would indeed occur.
Therefore, this is undertaken for the sake of providing alternatives. The examples will be explained later.
The passage beginning with "In this regard, some say" and so forth is a mnemonic verse (*grahaṇaka-vākya*).

The commentary on this [sūtra] is: "Not from a *tatpuruṣa* compound preceded by the negative particle *nañ*. By the rule *na nañpūrvāt tatpuruṣāt* [Pāṇini 5.1.120], any suffix expressing an abstract state (*bhāvapratyaya*) other than *tva* and *tal* is prohibited; therefore, one who desires an abstract suffix after these words must apply it only after *śūci* and so forth, but not an abstract suffix after *nañ*-compounds. If that were done first, the *nañ*-compound would be formed afterwards, and consequently, the *vṛddhi* (vowel strengthening) prescribed for the initial vowel of the base (*aṅga*) would not take effect.

For when the suffix denoting the abstract state (*bhāvapratyaya*) has been applied first, and subsequently the *nañ* compound is formed, the initial vowel of the *nañ* member does not become subject to *vṛddhi*, because only the final member (*uttarapada*) possesses the status of being the base (*aṅga*). Yet this rule is stated; therefore, by the force of that statement, *vṛddhi* occurs for the base even in the case of the *nañ* member. Regarding the phrase "others, however" (*tadapare*), etc.:

other teachers do not accept the claim that this optional (*vibhāṣā*) *vṛddhi* is prescribed for the first member of the compound where it was previously unobtained. Why? He says: "For there is also [the case] other than one expressing an abstract state," and so forth.
The particle *eva* is displaced and should be understood immediately after the word *vidyate*.

If, on account of a *nañ*-compound, no other *taddhita* suffix denoting a state (*bhāva*) than one that causes *vṛddhi* were to exist in meanings such as "offspring" and so forth, then likewise no other [suffix] would exist from a *bahuvrīhi* or a *nañ*-compound denoting a state; consequently, it would be logical that words such as *aśuci* and others, not being *aṅga*s, would subvert the governing rule for *aṅga*, since the prescription of *vṛddhi* would have no purpose [otherwise].

But this is not so; there indeed exists a secondary derivative (*taddhita*) caused by *vṛddhi* from a negative compound (*nañsamāsa*) in the sense of "offspring" and so forth—such as *ākauśaliḥ*, meaning "the offspring of one who is unskilled," and *ākauśalam*, meaning "that which belongs to one who is unskilled.

And from a negative compound that is a *bahuvrīhi*, there also exists a word expressing an abstract state (*bhāva*); for example, "one whose pure [qualities] do not exist" is *aśuciḥ*, and its abstract state is formed with the suffix *aṇ* according to [Pāṇini 5.1.131], resulting in *āśaucam*.

Since this is the case, another secondary derivative expressing an abstract state is also found to exist from a negative compound, and likewise, one caused by *vṛddhi* is found from a negative *bahuvrīhi* compound expressing an abstract state.

Therefore, since the purpose has been achieved there, it is logical that the [general rule for] the suffix *añ* is set aside by the specific eligibility for the *aṅga* [suffix]. Furthermore, as for what was stated—"the suffix denoting abstract state (*bhāvapratyaya*) follows only after a *tatpuruṣa* compound that does not begin with the negative particle *nañ*"—showing that this too is incorrect, he says: "akṣetrajña-anīśvarau" (or "akṣetrajñānīśvarau," according to the *Kāśikā*), and so forth.

For these two words are listed in the *brāhmaṇādi* group specifically as *tatpuruṣa* compounds; therefore, the suffix *ṣyañ* occurs only after these two *tatpuruṣas*. Otherwise, their inclusion in the *brāhmaṇādi* list would be purposeless.

Therefore, this *vṛddhi* substitution, which is invariably applicable to the stem itself, is prescribed optionally for the abstract suffix (*bhāvapratyaya*) and for other *taddhita* suffixes, as appropriate.

Regarding the term *tad-aśauca*: if it is formed as a *tatpuruṣa* compound—meaning "not pure" (*na śuciḥ aśuciḥ*)—then when the suffix *aṇ* is applied by [Pāṇini 4.3.120], there is *vṛddhi* (vowel strengthening). If, however, it is a *bahuvrīhi* compound—meaning "one for whom purity does not exist" (*nāsti śuciḥ asya aśuciḥ*)—then, if the abstract sense (*bhāvārtha*) is intended, the suffix *aṇ* is applied by [Pāṇini 5.1.131]. But if the sense of [the quality] itself is intended, then the suffix *aṇ* is applied by [Pāṇini 4.1.83], *prāgdīvyato’ṇ*, as in *ānaiyāyyam* and *ākṣaitrajñyam*.
In the case of the two *tatpuruṣa* compounds, since they belong to the *brāhmaṇādi* group, the suffix *vyañ* is applied, and there is *vṛddhi*.

Regarding the term *ākīśalamānaipuṇam*: whether this is a *bahuvrīhi* or a *tatpuruṣa*, in either case, by [Pāṇini 5.1.120], only the suffix *aṇ* is applicable. Even though the words *kuśala* and *nipuṇa* are listed among the *brāhmaṇādi* group and the *yudhādi* group, nevertheless, a suffix denoting an abstract state (*bhāvapratyaya*) is not justified after a *tatpuruṣa* ending in those words, nor even after a *bahuvrīhi* ending in them, because there is no rule for *tadantavidhi* (extension of a grammatical operation to that which ends with such a word). It is said: "In the *brāhmaṇādi* list, these two should be regarded as negative compounds (*nañsamāsa*).
The meaning is that the suffix *ṣyañ* occurs after these two negative compounds.
"‘These two’ refers to the indeclinables *yathātathā* and *yathāpura*.
[The phrase] ‘*yathā’sāvṛśyate*’ refers to avyayībhāva compounds."

But would not the prohibition [stated in Pāṇini 2.1.7], "asādṛśye" (when there is no similarity), apply here? This is not a fault; for in this case, similarity is not understood. To explain: "yathātatham" is said to mean "truthfully," and "yathāpuram" means "of old. How, then, is it known that these are *avyayībhāva* compounds? To this he says: "For thus," and so forth.
For here, by the rule "the neuter stem takes the short vowel" (Pāṇini 1.2.47), the shortening is applied on the basis of its being neuter;
and since the status of being neuter is prescribed for the *avyayībhāva*, it is understood that these are *avyayībhāva* compounds.
As for the phrase "In the Bhāṣya, however," and so forth:

The phrase "the state of being otherwise than it is" (*ayathātathābhāva*) does not undergo shortening; rather, as shown, a compound (*samāsa*) is indicated by [Pāṇini 2.1.4] *sup supā*, not an *avyayībhāva* compound.

For in an *avyayībhāva*, there would have to be shortening based on its neuter gender. However, in this view, because the formulation is that of the Sūtra—according to the Mahābhāṣya principle that "Sūtras are like Vedic"—one should understand that the short vowel occurs in place of the long one due to a phonetic substitution (*varṇavyatyaya*). [The word] "in the case of secondary suffixes" (*taddhiteṣu*) has ceased to apply.
Because it is not marked with the svarita accent.
Regarding the phrase "that which is connected [to the condition] 'when ki follows'":
one must understand that this has ceased [to apply].

Furthermore, its connection [to that rule] is due to the recurrence (*anuvṛtti*) of the term "in secondary suffixes" (*taddhiteṣu*) from [Pāṇini 7.2.117] into [7.2.118], which states "and when a *kit* [suffix follows].

If, however, the term "*kit*" were to recur [into 7.2.117], then, because the suffix *ṭak* would be applied by the rules "after *jāyā* and *patnī*, *ṭak*" [3.2.52] and "[the suffix *ṭak* is applied] when the agent is not a human being" [3.2.53], the form *jāyāghnaḥ tilakālakaḥ* ("a mole on the forehead that destroys one's wife") would also [incorrectly] result. The mention of the markers *ñ* and *ṇ* (*ñṇit*), however, is connected only with the suffix itself.
Therefore, even when the rule *taddhiteṣu* [Pāṇini 7.2.117] has ceased to apply, that [rule] continues to follow. As in the example *ghātayati*,
which contains the causative suffix *ṇic*.
The suffix *kṛt* [is applied] by the rule *hanter ñiṇṇiṇṇukṣu* [Pāṇini 7.3.54]. Thus, "ghātakaḥ" is formed with the suffix *ṇḍul*.
The term *sādhughātī* is formed by the suffix *ṇini* according to [Pāṇini 3.2.78]. The term *ghātaṃghātam* is formed as follows:

By the rule *ābhīkṣṇye ṇamul ca* [Pāṇini 3.4.22], and by the statement *ābhīkṣṇye dve bhavataḥ* (Vārttika 887), there is reduplication. Regarding the form *ghātaḥ*, the suffix *ghañ* is applied after the verbal root *han* with the prefix *ā*.

Regarding "adhāni": this is the *luṅ* [aorist] tense; the substitution of *ciṇ* occurs by the rule "ciṇ bhāvakarmaṇoḥ" [Pāṇini 3.1.66]; the *ātmanepada* [middle voice] ending occurs by the rule "bhāvakarmaṇoḥ" [Pāṇini 1.3.13], and the elision (*luk*) of the *takāra* [the *ta* suffix] occurs by the rule "ciṇo luk" [Pāṇini 6.4.104].
Regarding "jaghāna": this is the *liṭ* [perfect] tense.

In the case of *liṭ*, *tip*, and its replacement by *ṇal*, the substitution of *gh* for *k* occurs according to [Pāṇini 7.3.55]. Now, why does this not occur here in the forms *vātrradhnaḥ* and *bhrauṇadhnaḥ*—derived from *vṛtraṃ hatavān* and *bhrūṇaṃ hatavān* respectively? These are formed by adding *kvip* after the roots *han* with the objects *brahma*, *bhrūṇa*, and *vṛtra* according to [3.2.87], then adding *aṇ* after that suffix according to [4.3.120], and finally eliding the final vowel (*al*) according to [6.4.135]. To this, he replies: "Of the root," and so forth.
A suffix prescribed after a verbal root (dhātu) is called a "verbal-root suffix" (dhātupratyaya).
An operation stated with respect to a verbal root applies specifically to that verbal-root suffix.
This is indicated by the irregular form (nipātana) *bhrūṇahatyam* [Pāṇini 6.4.174].

Therefore, [the substitution does not occur] in cases such as *vātrradhnaḥ* and *bhrauṇadhnaḥ*. For in these instances, the suffix is not prescribed after a verbal root (*dhātu*)—what then? It is prescribed after a nominal stem (*prātipadika*). Regarding the rule *ciṇi kṛti ca*:
the mention of *ciṇ* is for the purpose of excluding *kṛt* suffixes.
However, its non-occurrence (*akṛttvam*) is because it is not prescribed under the heading of the second verbal root class (*dvitīyadhātu*). [Examples:
*adāyi*, *adhāyi*.
For the roots *dadāti* and *dadhāti*, the operations such as the *luṅ* (aorist) suffixes and so forth proceed as before.
"Dāyaḥ" and "dhāyaḥ":
[these are formed] with the suffix *dhañ*.
"Dāyakaḥ" and "dhāyakaḥ": [these are formed] with the suffix *ṇvul*.
In the case of *ṣvul*,
as in "he gave" (*adadau*) and "he placed" (*dadhau*),
the substitution of *au* occurs by rule 7.1.34.
"Cauṅgiḥ, Bālākiḥ"—the suffix *iñ* is applied here after *cūḍā* and *balākā* because they belong to the *bāhv-ādi* group.

One might think that [the suffix] will not apply here due to the continued application of the rule "of the first vowel among the *ac* vowels" (*acāmādeḥ*); to such a person, he states another example: "He whose deity is *jñā* is *jñaḥ*."
Here, by virtue of the principle of "behaving like that which is designated" (*vyapadeśivadbhāva*), the vowel *ā* becomes the first of the vowels (*acāmādi*).
In this case, even if the term *aciṇ-kṛt* were not present, and even though the phrase *acāmādeḥ* continues to apply, the suffix *yuk* would indeed occur here.

The rule *vyapadeśivadbhāvo’prātipadikena* (Pāṇini 1.2.52) has been stated to apply specifically to the domain of suffixal operations (*pratyayavidhi*). Thus, we have the forms *aśami*, *atami*, and *adami*.
The roots are *śamu* (DhP 1201) "to calm," *tamu* (DhP 1202) "to desire," and *damu* (DhP 1203) "to calm"; the *luṅ* and other tenses are formed as before.
In forms such as *śamakaḥ*, the suffix *ṇvul* is applied.
In *śamaḥ* and similar forms, the suffix *ghañ* is applied.
In *yāmakaḥ* and *rāmakaḥ*,
[the roots are] *yama* in the sense of "ceasing" (Dhātupāṭha 984) and *ramu* in the sense of "sporting" (Dhātupāṭha 856).
These two are taught with anudātta vowels. Now, how is it that there is exertion and cessation? To this he says: "exertion and cessation," and so forth;
"those ending in anu," and so forth.

The word "as correct" (*sādhutvena*) is to be understood as the ellipsis. The meaning is that these two [forms] are to be known as correct by virtue of their being treated as *nipātana*s (irregularities). This is so that [the forms] *śamī*, *tamī*, and *damī* may occur;
for [the suffix] *dhinuṇ* is prescribed after the eight roots beginning with *śam* by [Pāṇini 3.2.141]: *śamityaṣṭābhyo dhinuṇ*.

If "in the original instruction" (*upadeśa*) were not included here, [the prohibition] would not apply; for once the accent of the suffix has been applied, the verbal root (*dhātu*) is *anudātta* (unaccented).

However, when "in the original instruction" is included, that initial state is what is characterized; thus, even though the *anudātta* status occurs at a later time, the prohibition still holds because the root is *udātta* (accented) at the stage of the original instruction.
Regarding the phrase "here," etc.:

If the mention of "instruction" (*upadeśa*) were not made, then [the rule] would apply even in cases such as *yāmaka-* and *rāmaka-*, because of the prescription of an acute accent for the syllable preceding the suffix by the rule *liti* (Pāṇini 6.1.193). However, when the mention of "instruction" is included, it does not occur, because [the vowel] is grave (*anudātta*) in the original instruction (*upadeśa*). Thus it is said: "It should be stated that this does not apply to the roots *ā-cami*, *kami*, and *vami*."

The meaning is that this form should be explained as having the sense of "there is no prohibition" for these three roots: *kamu* (Dhātupāṭha 443), *ṭuvama* (Dhātupāṭha 849), and *cama*, *chamu*, *camu*, *jhamu* (Dhātupāṭha 469, 470, 471, 472).
Here is the explanation: first, regarding *cam*, because it is mentioned in the very sūtra *anācamer* [Aṣṭādhyāyī 6.1.142], there is no prohibition.
As for the other two, however, it is due to the irregular formation (*nipātana*) by the rule *dhāma-devāṅ ḍaḍaḍaau* [Aṣṭādhyāyī 4.2.8] and [Aṣṭādhyāyī 5.2.65].
Now, how is *āma* [derived]? He says: "The root *āma* belongs to the *caurādika* class," and so forth.

From the root *ama* meaning "disease" (*ama roge*, Dhātupāṭha 1720), which belongs to the *caurādika* class, when the causative suffix *ṇic* is applied and *vṛddhi* occurs, and then the suffix *ac* is added by [Pāṇini 3.3.56] *erac*, the form *āma* is obtained.
For even with the causative suffix *ṇic*, there is no prohibition of *vṛddhi*; because that [prohibition] applies only when *ac* follows immediately after the root (*aciṇkṛt*).
But the absence of *kṛttvam* (the status of being treated as *kṛt*) should be understood as before.

Now, one might object: "Since the designation *mit* applies by the rule *janījṛṣksasurañjo'mantāśca* (following Dhātupāṭha 817), shouldn't there be shortening of the vowel here in the causative (*ṇi*) by the rule *mitāṃ hrasvaḥ* [Pāṇini 6.4.92]? To this he says: "For in this case, there is no *mittvam*.
Why is there none? He says: "Not others," and so forth.

As for the root *bhvādi* listed as *ama* in the sense of "motion and so forth" (*ama gatyādiṣu*, Dhātupāṭha 465), its form should be *ama* alone. Now, how is it that there is the word *viśrāma*? For it cannot be said that this is ungrammatical, since the usage "the earth is the resting place of the sun" (*sūryaviśrāmā bhūmiḥ*) is observed. To this he says: "such usage as this," and so forth. Someone might suspect that this [root] is the substitute *han* for *vadhi*, and that this [form] refers to that; therefore, in order to dispel that doubt, he says: "*vadhi* is another verbal root," and so forth.

Is there also another root-form (*prakṛtyantara*)? If it were one ending in the vowel *a*, the prohibition would be purposeless, for [the substitution of *vṛddhi*] would not occur simply because it has a consonant as its penultimate (*dhupadhatvāt*). Thinking this, he says: "of that which ends in a consonant. But from what is it determined that there exists such another root-form? To this he says: "and [the word] *bhakṣaka*," etc.
Now, why does this prohibition not apply specifically to the substitute *vadhi* for *han*? To this he says: "of the substitute for *han*," etc.

"jajāna garbham," etc., is a Vedic usage. The mention of "ṛtī" is for the sake of specific indication; it is so that the term ending in the vowel *ṛ* should not be understood [as including other forms], as in the rule at [Pāṇini 7.4.16].

Regarding the form *arpayati*: it is derived from the root *ṛ* with the causative suffix *ṇic*; the *guṇa* substitution occurs by the rule *pugantalaghūpadhasya* [Pāṇini 7.3.86]. Examples include *hyepayati* and *vlepayati*.
The root *hrī* is used in the sense of shame (*lajjāyām*) [Dhātupāṭha 1085]; *vlo* is used in the sense of covering (*varaṇe*) [Dhātupāṭha 1502]. Regarding the forms *knopayati* and *kṣmāpayati*:
*knūyo* is used in the sense of sound (*śabde*) [Dhātupāṭha 4.85], and *kṣmāyī* is used in the sense of shaking (*vidhūnane*) [Dhātupāṭha 4.86].
By [Pāṇini 6.1.66], there is the elision of the letter *y*. The phrase "the mention of both roots" is used because there is no distinction [between them].
It must be understood that both roots are included here: namely, *rī* in the sense of "movement and drying" (*dhātupāṭha* 1500) and *roṅ* in the sense of "hearing" (*dhātupāṭha* 1138).

But is it not the case that, according to the rule "when a [term] without an *anubandha* is mentioned, one without an *anubandha* is not [intended]" (Vyāḍīya-paribhāṣā 53), the mention of *rīṅ* would not be applicable? This is not a fault. Here, although *hrasva* (short vowel) should have been placed first because it has fewer syllables (*alpāctara*) when choosing between *hrasva*, *olī*, and *yāt*, the fact that the word *ārti* is placed first—disregarding the rule *alpāctaram* [Pāṇini 2.2.34]—indicates that no other statement from this grammar is being followed here.
By this, it is indicated that the paribhāṣā regarding [terms] without *anubandhas* is not required; thus, the mention of *rīṅ* also occurs.

Now, for what purpose is the augment *puK* prescribed as having the initial position (*pūrvānta*), rather than being prescribed as having the final position (*parādi*)? [One might argue: "Let it be prescribed as *parādi*; when *puṭ* is present, the mention of 'that which ends in *puK*' (*puganta*) need not be made in the rule prescribing *guṇa*, because it would already be established by [Pāṇini 7.3.86]. If you say: "In the case of *puṭ*, the mention of *puṭ* must necessarily be made; otherwise, by [Pāṇini 7.2.115], there would be *vṛddhi*," this is not so.

Since the condition for *vṛddhi* with respect to the causative suffix (*ṇic*) has not yet been reached, the statement that *puṭ* is an augument (*āgama*) will serve as an exception to what follows; thus, there is no occasion for *vṛddhi*.

In that case, there is this fault at the beginning of the subsequent [rule]: in forms such as *dāpyate* and *dāpyata*, since the *ṇi* has been elided, the *pakāra* (the letter *p*) would not be heard. This is not a fault; for the elision of *ṇi* does not cause the total disappearance [of the suffix], such that upon the cessation of *ṇi*, the augment *puṭ* would also cease. Since the suffix is still present in its trace (*lakṣaṇa*), even though *ṇi* has ceased, the *puṭ* will be heard. Thus he says: "The making of *puṭ* a part of the preceding element," and so forth.

The *luṅ* suffix after the root *dāpayati*, the *cli* augment, its replacement by *caṅ* according to Pāṇini 3.1.48 (*ṇiśridrusrubhyaḥ kartari*), the elision of the *ṇi* affix, the shortening of the penultimate vowel according to 7.4.1 (*ṇau caṅyupadhāyā hrasvaḥ*), reduplication according to 6.1.11 (*caṅi*), the substitution of *i* for the penultimate vowel according to 7.4.93 (*sanvallaghuni caṅpare*), and the lengthening of that *i* according to 7.4.94 result in *adīdapat*.

In this context, if the augment *puṭ* were applied, the shortening would not occur because the vowel would no longer be penultimate (*anupadhātva*). However, when *puk* is present, the shortening does indeed take place.

Therefore, the addition of *puk* at the beginning [of the stem] is for the sake of shortening the vowel. Regarding the roots *śo* (DhP 1145) "to thin," *cho* (DhP 1146) "to cut," *ṣo* (DhP 1147) "in the sense of finishing," *hveñ* (DhP 1008) "in the sense of rivalry," *vyeñ* (DhP 1007) "in the sense of covering," *veñ* (DhP 1006) "in the sense of weaving," *pā* (DhP 925) "to drink," and both forms of *pai* (DhP 920, 921) "to dry"—since these end in long *ā*, the rule for *yuk* would otherwise apply; hence, *puk* is prescribed.

In the passage beginning with *niśāyayati*, there is the substitution of *ā* [for the vowel] according to [Pāṇini 6.1.45]. Some authorities maintain that this rule also includes the inclusion of the roots *pā* (in the sense of "drinking") and *ovai* (in the sense of "drying").
Where the inclusion of *hras* is not desired, he says "of *pibati*"; the intention is as in the rule "there is elision [of the penultimate] of *pibati*, and [the vowel] becomes *ī*" (Pāṇini 7.4.4).

Now, why is there not also the inclusion of the root *pā* in the sense of "protection" (Dhātupāṭha 1056)? To this he says: "But of *pā* in the sense of protection," and so forth. "However, its augment *luk* must be stated."

But surely, since the root *pāl* is listed in the *cur*-class [of the Dhātupāṭha] with the meaning "to protect" (*pāla rakṣaṇe*, DhP 1609), the form *pālayati* will result from that? True, this is so; however, the augment *luk* is added specifically to prevent the *puk* augment. Otherwise, from the root *pā* [in the first class], one would get *pāyayati*.
Regarding the statement "the augment *nuk* should be stated for *dhūñ* and *prīñ*":
*dhūñ* means "to shake" (DhP 1835) and *prīñ* means "to satisfy" (DhP 1836). The meaning is that the augment *nuk* must be stated—that is, explained—for these two roots.

In this regard, the explanation is as follows: since the roots *dhūñ* in the sense of "shaking" (*dhātupāṭha* 1398) and *tṛp* in the sense of "satisfying" (*dhātupāṭha* 1195) are irregularly formed (*nipātana*), there will be the elision (*luk*) of these two [suffixes].
The phrase "these too" refers to the *yuga*-class and others.
In forms such as *niśāyayati*, the substitution of *ā* [for the penultimate vowel] occurs by rule 6.1.45.
Forms such as *nyaśīśayat* are to be derived in the same manner as *adīdapat*, having first applied the rules for the *luṅ* tense and so forth as previously described.
Regarding the form *adūdhanat*:
Because it does not end in the vowel *ā*, there is no treatment of the reduplication as being like that of the *saN* suffix (*sanvadbhāva*) here.

In the case of *apipriṇat*, there is also no lengthening because of the lack of a heavy syllable (*alaghutva*). Now, one might object: "The roots *śā*, *śās*, *sā*, *hvā*, and *vyā* are listed in the [Dhātupātha] list as ending in *e*; how then can they be understood here when they have undergone the change to *ā*? To this he says: "*śācchāsāhvā*," etc. (the printed edition reads *śāhvetyādi*).

But how is the application of *puK* explained by means of the inclusion of those [roots] that have undergone the substitution of *itva* (short *i*)? It is because *puK* is prescribed for roots ending in long *ā*.
By the example "adhyāpayati" and so forth, he demonstrates the purpose of this indicator (*jñāpaka*).
In "adhyāpayati," the substitution of *itva* occurs according to Pāṇini 6.1.48.

By the word "ādi" (and so forth), terms such as *jāpayati* are included. Now, if the inclusion of roots beginning with *śā*, which have undergone the change to *kṛtātva*, was made in order to state the attainment of the augment *puK*, then would it not be proper to include only *veñ* when it has likewise undergone *kṛtātva*? This cannot be so; for if it were stated simply as *ve*, there would be the inclusion of *pai* and *ovai* in the sense of "drying" (*śoṣaṇe*) [Dhātupāṭha 920, 921]. Therefore, it is proper to include only *veñ* when it has not yet undergone *kṛtātva*. Thus, the rule for the augment *jug* is prescribed to apply when *puK* is attained.
Regarding the phrase "or of this [root] *vah*":
it refers to the root *vah* in the sense of "going" and "smelling" (Dhātupāṭha 1050).
Regarding the phrase "in the sense of shaking": [it refers to the same root].
The meaning is "trembling.

Now, one might object: since the form *upavājayati* is established from the root *vaja* or *vraja* in the sense of "motion" (*gatau*)—as seen in the Dhātupāṭha (252, 253)—for what purpose is this [rule] stated? It is for the purpose that the augment *puK* should not apply to the root *vāti*.
The rule for the insertion of *jUK* is stated so that [the form] may be understood as belonging to the root *pai* in the sense of "drying," with *o* changed to *ava*. Thus, this is its form.

But surely, since that which is derived from a technical definition (*lākṣaṇika*) ends in a different vowel form, the augment *juk* should not apply here? This is not so; for it has just been stated in this very context that the paribhāṣā regarding "that which is taught by a technical definition versus that which is taught as a specific word-form" does not apply. Regarding the phrase "in the sense of causing the flow of oil": what is this so-called "causing the flow of oil"? It is the act of causing the flowing of oil that is about to disappear—that is, its application. For instance, when the suffix *lyuṭ* is applied in the sense of the abstract state (*bhāva*) to the root *pat* preceded by the prefix *vi*, one obtains the form *vipātanam*.
Regarding the form *vilīnayati*:
there are the substitution of *guṇa* and the replacement by *ā*.

Now, once the substitution of *at* (as prescribed by Pāṇini 6.1.51) has been applied, why does the augment *nuk* not occur in *vilāpayati*, given that what is partially modified remains essentially the same? To this, he says: "the root *lī*" and so forth.

In the rule *lī*, the vowel *ī* is elided (*praśliṣyate*)—is this so that [the rule] applies only to that which ends in *ī*? It does not apply to that which has undergone the change to *u*. [The commentary states: "By *lī*, there is the inclusion of both *lī* and *līṅ*. Now, one might object: by the *niranubandhaka-paribhāṣā* (the paribhāṣā regarding roots without an indicatory letter), it would be more appropriate to include only the root *lī* "to adhere" belonging to the *kryādika* class (DhP 1501), and not the root *līṅ* "to adhere" belonging to the *daivādika* class (DhP 1139). To this, he replies: this is considered to be a single root that is taught twice for the sake of two different conjugational suffixes (*vikaraṇa*) and for the sake of the middle voice (*ātmanepada*).
And having established this, the ātmanepada suffix occurs by both rules: "After the root *lī* [in the senses] of honoring and making firm" (Pāṇini 1.3.70).
[The form] *lā* refers to the root *lā*, and also to *lo* when its vowel has been changed to *ā* (*loyati*).
The connection is with the word "grahaṇam" (the taking) which is under discussion. A cause (*hetu*) is that which instigates an independent agent.
That from which one fears is *bhaya* (fear); that which is both a cause (*hetu*) and fear (*bhaya*) is *hetubhaya*. In that *hetubhaya*:

although the substitution of *vṛddhi* would apply by rule Pāṇini 7.3.34 (*ñibhī bhaye*), and the substitution of *ā* would also apply by rule Pāṇini 6.1.56, the substitution of *ghu* is optionally prescribed after the causative suffix (*ṇi*).
Thus: *muṇḍo bhīṣayate* ("the bald man causes fear").
By [Pāṇini 1.3.68], the *ātmanepada* [suffix] is applied.

Now, once *āttva* has been performed, why does [the substitution of *bhī* for *bhīṣ*] not occur in the case of *muṇḍo bhāpayate*? To this he says: "In this case also," and so forth. Regarding *sphāvayati*: [it is derived from] *sphāyo*, *o pyāyī vṛddhau* (Dhātupāṭha 487, 488). But for what purpose is this stated, since [the desired form] could result from the very *nipātana* (irregular derivation) of *śadlṛ śātane* (Dhātupāṭha 1428), whereby the letter *t* would occur? [If you say: "So that it may apply elsewhere than in the sense of 'motion' (*gati*), and not in the sense of motion"? No; for the word *śātana* expresses a meaning other than motion.
In that case, this indicates: "Even exceptions (*nipātana*s) are non-sublating (*abādhaka*).

(Pāṇini 1.1.58). Therefore, from the word *purā*, the substitution of *tu* prescribed by the rule "in the case of [words] anciently proclaimed" (Pāṇini 4.3.105) does not sublate the *ṭu* and *ṭul* suffixes prescribed by the rule "for *sāyaṃ*, *ciraṃ*, etc.
(Pāṇini 4.3.23). By this, the form *purātana* is also established. [The example] "he causes to grow" (*ropayati*).
The root *ruh* [is used] in the sense of birth (*janman*) and manifestation (*prādurbhāva*) [Dhātupāṭha 859].

Why, then, is this stated, given that among the *divādi* roots, *rup* and *lup* are listed in the sense of "deluding" (*vimohana*) [Dhātupāṭha 1236, 1237], so that from the latter one would derive *ropayati*, while from *ruh* one would derive *rohayati*? [This is stated] so that the usage *ropayati* may also occur in the sense of birth; otherwise, it would apply only to the sense of deluding.

If it is argued that since verbal roots have multiple meanings, *rup* will function in the sense of birth—this is not so; for although roots have multiple meanings, they do not possess every possible meaning.

For when it is said "it undergoes transformation" (*rūpyati*), no other meaning is understood; rather, it means precisely "for the purpose of deluding. [The phrase] "it does not follow after a *sup*" means that it does not follow after a word ending in a *sup* (nominal suffix). And this meaning is to be understood through the paribhāṣā rule concerning the mention of a suffix (*pratyayagrahaṇaparibhāṣā*).

In the sense of "one who is unknown" and so forth, [the suffix] *ka* is applied after words beginning with *prāg* (i.e., *prāk*), according to Pāṇini 5.3.70: *prāgivāt kaḥ*. Thus we have *jaṭilikā*, *muṇḍikā*, *kārikā*, and *hārikā*.
Regarding the suffix *ṇvul*:
[the form] "etikā" is derived as follows:

from the pronoun *etad*, the suffix *akac* is added by [Pāṇini 5.3.71], followed by the replacement of the final vowel and consonant with the following vowel (*tyādādyatva*) by [Pāṇini 6.1.97], then the substitution of the subsequent form (*pararūpatva*) by [Pāṇini 6.1.97], the addition of the feminine suffix *ṭāp*, and finally the lengthening of a vowel before a homogeneous vowel (*akaḥ savarṇe dīrghatvam*) by [Pāṇini 6.1.101].
The word *śakā* is derived from the root *śak* with the suffix *ac* (as in the *pacādi* group) and the feminine suffix *ṭāp*.
The inclusion of the term *stha* is for the sake of clarity.

In this context, why is it not the case that [the rule] "where there is merely the letter *ka*, let there be no suffix" is applied for that very purpose? To this he says: "For 'merely the letter *ka*'" and so forth.
The mention of the phoneme is "kādi"; the vowel *a*, however, is for the sake of pronunciation.

However, there is no such thing as a suffix consisting solely of the letter *ka* for the purpose of whose exclusion the mention of *stha* would be necessary. If it were said, "after a suffix (*kātaḥ pratyayāt*)," the word "suffix" would apply to a part of a suffix; therefore, even without the mention of *stha*, it would be possible to understand that the letter *ka* must belong to a suffix.
Consequently, the mention of *stha* is for the sake of clarity.
"Maṇḍanā, ramaṇā"— from roots such as *nand*, the suffix *layu* is applied [according to Pāṇini 3.1.134]. "Paṭukā, mṛdukā, gokā, naukā"— [these are formed with the suffix *ka*].

As before, [the suffix] *ka* is applied. From the roots *rālā* in the sense of "taking" (*dhātupāṭha* 1057, 1058) and *daṣ* in the sense of "giving," the *ka* suffix is added according to the *uṇādi* rule *kṛdādhārārcikalibhyaḥ kaḥ* (Dhātupāṭha 3.18). Now, etc.
The opponent asks: "Why [is it] 'the letter *ka*'? Since the letter *ka* is what is heard, isn't it more appropriate to apply the qualification 'of that very [letter]'? This is the intended meaning.
In order to reveal the intention with which the questioner asked, he says, "If this were so," and so forth.
By the word *yadyapi*, the letter *ka* is qualified—namely, that *ka* which follows an *ā*.
This being the case, [the rule] would not apply in the word *karikā*, because the *ka* is separated from the *ā* by the letter *i*.
The other [teacher] says: "When the single-substitute (ekādeśa) has been made," and so forth.
For when there is a hiatus (vyavasarga), there is an intervention;
however, since there is no hiatus once the single-substitute has been made, there is no intervention.
"An *ekādeśa* is like the preceding [element]," and so forth— this is the challenger's position;
however, the status of being "as if occupying the place" (*sthānivadbhāva*) is established by [Pāṇini 1.1.56].
The other [opponent] says: "Because of the statement.

This statement is indeed uttered, yet the letter *k* does not immediately follow [the *a*]. Therefore, once the status of being like the original (*sthānivadbhāva*) has been established by the force of that statement, one does not rely on an intervention by a single phoneme in all cases. [The opponent asks: "If, then, by the force of the statement it occurs even when there is an intervention—as in *kārikā* and so forth—then would it also occur in *rathakaṭaā* and *putrakāmyā*? To this he replies: "In the case of *rathakaṭaā* and so forth," etc.
From *rathānāṃ samūhaḥ* [Pāṇini 4.2.51], the suffix *kaṭac* is applied, followed by *ṭāp*.
Regarding *putram icchati*, the suffix *kāmyac* is applied according to [Pāṇini 3.1.9];
then, by [Pāṇini 3.3.102], the suffix *a* is added, followed by *ṭāp*.

In that case, because there is an intervention by multiple phonemes (*varṇa*) produced by hearing, the shortening (*it-tva*) does not occur. According to the principle "that by which there is no intervention of constituent parts [is considered non-intervening] even when separated," an intervention by a single phoneme is relied upon.
Since there is no intervention by constituent parts but rather an intervention everywhere, it is logical that [the operation] should take place when separated by a single phoneme.

In every case, there is an intervention by at least one phoneme (varṇa) caused by the substitution being as if it were the original (sthānivat); however, with respect to a cluster (saṅghāta), such intervention may or may not exist.
Therefore, that [distinction] is not taken into account here. Thus:
"this [suffix] follows what ends in a *sup*."

Regarding the word *parivrājaka* [with the suffix] *āp*: by the rule for the application of suffixes (*pratyayalakṣaṇa*), it should be understood as ending in a case-suffix (*subanta*). And this is a "prohibitive negation" (*prasajyapratiṣedha*):
namely, that if *āp* does not follow immediately after a word ending in a case-suffix, [the rule does not apply].

Furthermore, what is the fault in [interpreting this as] an exclusion by negation (*paryudāsa*), such that it is not accepted as such? To this he says: "For in the case of *paryudāsa*," and so forth. If this were a *paryudāsa*, then [the analysis would be]: *su* + *apaḥ* = *asap*; and from that, the suffix *udāt* would follow, because it occurs after [a word ending in] *ap*. Consequently, even in the case of *bahuparivrājaka*, the feminine suffix (*īp*) would necessarily occur, on the grounds that the suffix *āp* follows a collection of preceding and succeeding words that does not end in *su*. However, the status of not ending in *su* belongs to the entire collection, because the suffix *su* has not yet been produced [at that stage]; for here, the production of *su* occurs from the constituent word *parivrājaka*, and not from the collection.
"Since 'asu' means that in which breath (*asu*) is not present, this [term] *asub* is also not accepted";
the meaning is that even the *bahuvrīhi* compound is not accepted.
But what is the fault in accepting it, such that it is not accepted? To this he says: "For instance," and so forth.
The meaning is: "In that case, then.

Since, in a *bahuvrīhi* compound, the designation of being a word ending in a *suptiṅ* (a nominal stem) exists for both the prior and subsequent members by virtue of the rule regarding suffixal characteristics (*pratyayalakṣaṇa*), such a member is not "not-sup" (*asup*); rather, it is precisely one that possesses a present *sup*.
Consequently, in the example *bahucarmikā*, the substitution of long *ī* (ittva) would not occur, because [the suffix] *āp* does not follow what is "not-sup."
The term *bahuvrīhi* [is used] because there are many skins (*carman*) in this [place];
by [Pāṇini 5.4.154], the suffix *kap* is added, followed by *ṭāp*.
Thus, "māmikā" [is formed].

Regarding *mameyam* [meaning "this is mine"]: from the rule *tasyedam* [Pāṇini 4.3.120], the suffix *aṇ* is applied; then, by the rule *tavakamamakau* [Pāṇini 4.3.3], the substitute *mamaka* is applied. Now, one might object: since the word *mamaka* ends in *aṇ*, shouldn't the suffix *ṅīp* be applied according to the rule *ṭiḍḍhāṇañ* [Pāṇini 4.1.15]? If so, how does the suffix *ṭāp* occur? [The answer is: "Because of the restriction [imposed] by the rule *kevalamāmaka...*," and so forth. [The example] *narikā* is as follows.
From the roots *gai* and *śabd*, [the suffix *ṅīṣ* is applied] by [Pāṇini 4.1.45], resulting in the shortening of the vowel;
then, by [Pāṇini 4.1.4], the suffix *ṭāp* is added. Thus, one obtains *dākṣiṇātyikā* and *ihatyikā*.
In the sense of "belonging to the southern direction," the suffix *tyak* is applied according to [Pāṇini 4.2.98];
for the form *iha-bhava*, [the suffix *cha* is applied] according to [Pāṇini 4.2.104];
and in both cases, when the meanings such as "unknown" (*ajñāta*) and so forth are intended, [the suffix *aṇ* is applied] according to [Pāṇini 5.3.70].
The purpose of the term *upasaṃkhyāna* (supplementation) is to provide an explanation.

The explanation therein is as follows: because of the understanding of a fixed option (*vyavasthitavibhāṣā*) in the rule "udīcām ātaḥ sthāne" [Pāṇini 7.3.46], the suffixes *-tya* and *-tya* will necessarily occur. When an option is applicable to *yetya* by the rule "udīcām ātaḥ sthāne" [7.3.46] and so forth, and when a necessity is applicable to *setya* by the preceding rule, this prohibition is commenced; for a prohibition presupposes a prior application.
When the suffix *-akac* occurs after those two, then this prohibition is understood to apply.
"Yakā" and "sakā": here, *akac* is applied to *yat* and *tad* as before; then *su*, and the substitution of *a* for the initial of *tyad*-class words.
Regarding the statement, "The mention of 'yāsa' is not restrictive," it means that the specific form cited is not intended to limit the rule.
The meaning is that it is not the primary factor.
What is the reason? He says: "This is for the purpose of indicating both 'yat' and 'tat'.
Why is it explained in this way? He says: "In this case as well," and so forth.
*Yāse* is a form ending in the nominative singular.

Now, if this grammatical indication were a *tantra* (a fixed rule), then because of the inclusion of the nominative singular form, the [substitution] would not apply in cases such as *yakām* and *takām* where other case endings occur; yet that is desired even there.
Therefore, it is said that this indication is not a *tantra*, but is intended as an illustration (*upalakṣaṇa*) of the nominal stems *ya-* and *ta-*.

Regarding the passage beginning with "yāsayorittvapratiṣedhe" (in the prohibition of the substitution of *i* for *yās*), the word *upasaṃkhyāna* means "explanation" or "demonstration. What is being stated here is this: when the prohibition [of the *it*-augment] for *yad* and *tad* is being formulated, an explanation must be provided regarding the prohibition of that which ends in the suffix *tyakan*.

In this regard, the following is the explanation: here the separation of the rule (*yogavibhāga*) is made as "not" (*na*); by means of that, the prohibition will apply to that which ends in the suffix *tyakan*.
In the same way, it should be understood that even in subsequent cases, the purpose of the supplementary statement (*upasaṃkhyāna*) is for the sake of providing an explanation.
This very explanation must also be carried out by relying on the application of the separation of the rule.
Regarding "upatyakā" and "adhatyakā":
the suffix *tyakan* is applied by the rule "upādhibhyāṃ tyakannāsannārūḍhayoḥ" [Pāṇini 5.2.34].
Regarding "pāvakā": [the suffix *kan* is applied].
The suffix *ṇvul* [is applied here].
Regarding the term "aloma-kā":
it is a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "one who has no body hair" (*na asyāḥ lomāni santi*).
The suffix *kap* is applied by [Pāṇini 5.4.154],
resulting in "jīvakā" and "nandakā. The suffix *vun* is applied by [Pāṇini 3.1.150].
"Devaka, Yajñaka":

when the suffix *kan* is applied to the words *devadatta* and *yajñadatta* according to Pāṇini 5.3.76 (*anukampāyāṃ kan*), the elision of the final member of the compound occurs according to the Vārttika 614 (*anajādau ca vibhāṣā lopo vaktavyaḥ*).
"Kṣipakā" and "dhruvakā. [The roots] "kṣipa" in the sense of "impelling" (Dhātupāṭha 1285) and "dhruva" in the sense of "steadiness" (Dhātupāṭha 943).
After those [roots], in the sense of "unknown" and so forth, the suffix *ka* is applied by [Pāṇini 5.3.70]: *prāgivāt kaḥ*.
"Tārakā" [is derived] from the root *tṛ* with the suffix *ṇvul*. "Varṇakā" refers to a woven textile.
The suffix *añ* is applied [by Pāṇini 4.3.137] in the sense of "a product of threads," [with the resulting form] *tāntavaḥ*,
which is a specific type of cloak.
In that context, the word *varṇaka* should be added as an exception (*upasaṃkhyātavyā*).

The root *varṇ* belongs to the *curādigaṇa*, as stated in the Dhātupāṭha (1938): "In the senses of color (*varṇa*), describing the act of coloring (*varṇakriyā*), presiding over (*adhiṣṭhāra*), and speaking of qualities (*guṇavacana*). From this root, with the suffix *ṇvul*, we derive *varṇikā*, meaning "an expounder" (*vyākhyatrī*). [Similarly,] *vartakā*.
From the root *vṛt* in the sense of "turning" (*vartane*; Dhātupāṭha 758), with the suffix *ṇvul*, we have *varttikā*. The meaning is "one who studies."

Regarding the statement "the *aṣṭakā* [is] that which has the ancestors as its deity" (*pitṛdaivatya*): *pitṛdaivatya* refers to a specific Vedic ritual procedure; therein, the term *aṣṭakā* is enumerated.

From the root *aśū* in the sense of "pervasion" (Dhātupāṭha 1264), the suffix *takan* is applied according to the rule *iṣyasibhyāṃ takan* (Daiva-Uṇādi 3.30). By the rule concerning the *vraścādi* group (Pāṇini 8.2.36), the substitution of *ṣ* occurs, followed by the change to *ṣṭ*.
Regarding "aṣṭakā":

[the suffix] *ka* is applied according to Pāṇini 5.1.57 (*aṣṭābhyaḥ kap*), meaning "that whose measure is eight," and then the suffix *kan* is applied according to 5.1.22 (*saṃkhyāyā atiśadantāyāḥ kan*).
Regarding "vā sūtakā" and so forth.
The purpose [of this rule] is to provide an additional enumeration (*upasaṃkhyāna*) of words.

In this regard, the demonstration is as follows: words such as *sūtakā* and *sūtikā* fall within the class beginning with *pṛṣodara*; therefore, by virtue of belonging to the *pṛṣodarādi* group, this option is established. Since the preceding rule would have required the substitution of *it* (the short *i*) obligatorily, this statement is made for the sake of providing an option. [In the case of the suffixes] *yak* and *ak*, [the preceding vowel] is long.
That [vowel] which has *ya* preceding it is called *yakapūrvā*.
What is the referent of the other word (*anyapadārtha*)? It is the aggregate (*samudāya*).
For in this way, the word "preceding" (*pūrva*) refers to a constituent part (*avayava*).
And that constituent part belongs to the whole, not to another constituent part;
for one phoneme does not become a constituent part of another phoneme.
Rather, its designation as "prior" is in relation to another constituent part.

Furthermore, since it is the subject under discussion, that other constituent (*avayava*) is understood to be the vowel *sthānī* [the original element] itself. As for the feminine gender indication, it should be understood as the feminine nature belonging to the meaning of the whole (*samudāya*), starting from the word *tasya* up to *tu*.
Its purpose, however, will be stated later.
Regarding the phrase "ātaḥ sthāne": the word "yo'kāra" (the letter *a* which is) is connected with the distant [term]. [The examples are] "ibhyikā," and so forth.
From words such as *ibhya* and others, by the rules *prāgivāt kaḥ* [Pāṇini 5.3.70] and *ke'ṇaḥ* [Pāṇini 7.4.13], there is shortening. In the case of *sāṃkāśyikā*,
since there is no *a* in place of the *ā*, the substitution of *it* (the feminine suffix *ī*) occurs invariably.

Now, for what purpose is the mention of *sthāna* (place/position), given that this very genitive case will establish the connection with *sthāna* by virtue of the rule: "The sixth [case-ending] denotes the place of substitution" (*ṣaṣṭhī sthāneyogā*)? To this he says: "The mention of *sthāna*" and so forth.
The mention of the letter *a*—which has been prescribed in place of [the original] *a* by another rule—is an *anuvāda* (restatement).
The inclusion of the word "in place" (*sthāne*) here is for the purpose that the relationship [of substitution] may be understood even in this case.
But what is the reason why, in the absence of the word "in place," the understanding of the relationship would not occur in an *anuvāda*? To this he says: "By the expression *ātaḥ*," and so forth.

In rules for prescription (*ādeśavidhi*) such as [Pāṇini 2.4.52] and so forth, this technical rule (*paribhāṣā*) [Pāṇini 1.1.49] applies, but not in a restatement (*anuvāda*); for this [technical rule] constitutes a supplement to prescriptive sentences. Furthermore, in this case, an *a*-sound is not prescribed by this [rule] in place of an *a*-sound; what then? That which has been produced by another grammatical rule is qualified by this: "the *a*-sound that occurs in place of an *āt*. Therefore, the application of that technical rule does not occur here. In that regard, if the mention of "place" (*sthāna*) were not made, then there would be an understanding of a relationship of proximity, namely, "the *a*-sound which is near to an *āt*."

Or is it as before? When this question is raised, he says: "by the term *ātaḥ*" and so forth. The vowel *a*, which was taken as the substituendum (*sthānin*) for the vowel *i*, is specified by the term *ātaḥ*.
Thus, because it is the substantive (*viśeṣya*), the vowel *a* is primary; because the vowel *ā* is the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*), it is secondary.

In that case, even if that technical rule (*paribhāṣā*) were to apply as a restatement (*anuvāda*) when the mention of "place" (*sthāna*) is absent—since the understanding of the operation occurs primarily with respect to the principal element—the connection with "place" would be understood for this very genitive [in *ātaḥ*] alone, and not for the genitive in *ātaḥ*.
However, when the mention of "place" is present, it is understood for this one as well; it is for this purpose that the mention of "place" is made.
[The example is: *ai-ākāḥ*.

As before? Who [is the referent], and what is the shortening? Now, for what purpose is the feminine gender used in the expression *yakapūrvāyāḥ*? He says: "The use of the feminine gender [is for this reason]:

if that were not there, one might understand the status of the original element (*sthānitva*) to belong to the letter *a* alone in place of the vowel *ā*. Consequently, in the case of the verbal root *yā*, when preceded by the words *śubham* or *bhadram*, the suffix *vic* would apply according to the rules *vijupe chandasi* [Pāṇini 3.2.73] and *āto maninkvanibvanipaśca* [Pāṇini 3.2.74]."
If [the suffix] *ka* were applied after that [stem], then an undesirable option (*vikalpa*) would also apply in cases such as *śubhaṃyikā* and *bhadraṃyikā*.
Therefore, for the sake of excluding that, there is the mention of the feminine gender.
The words *śubham* and *bhadram* are indeclinables (*nipāta*) ending in the letter *m*.
"Of that which has *yak* as its predecessor," and so forth,
is the statement of the rule (*grahaṇavākya*).
Of that [rule], there is the phrase "of the *yakāra* and *kakāra* at the end of a verbal root," and so forth.
"Commentary":
"'To be stated' means 'to be explained.'"

In this regard, the following is the explanation: because the option (*vibhāṣā*) is understood as being restricted (*vyavasthita*), there would follow a prohibition of the *it*-designation for the vowel *a* that follows even the *y* and *v* at the end of a verbal root; however, that shall not occur. For example: *sunayikā*, *suśayikā*.
[The suffix] *-ac* is applied by [Pāṇini 3.3.56] *erac* after the roots *ṇīñ* and *śīṅ*.

"She whose manner (*naya*) is beautiful" and "she whose reclining (*śaya*) is beautiful" form *sunayā* and *suśayā*. From these, by the rules *prāgivāt kaḥ* [Pāṇini 5.3.70] and *ke'ṇaḥ* [Pāṇini 7.4.13], the shortening of the vowel occurs. Examples are *supākikā* and *aśokikā*.
[The roots] *ḍupacaṣ pāke* (Dhātupāṭha 996) and *śuca śoke* (Dhātupāṭha 183) take the suffix *ghañ* in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāva*).

The term *śobhanapākā* (one whose cooking is excellent) and *avidyamānaśokā* (one whose sorrow is non-existent) are *bahuvrīhi* compounds; by [Pāṇini 5.4.154], the suffix *kap* is added, and by [Pāṇini 7.4.15], the shortening of the vowel occurs. Thus we have *bhastrakā* and *bhastrikā*.
Is it as before? [Yes,] the suffix *ka* is applied.
Thus we have *abhastrakā* and *abhastrikā*.
As before, there is the suffix *kap*, forming either a *bahuvrīhi* or a *tatpuruṣa*.

Now, why are these two examples with a preceding negative particle (*nañ*) not cited? To this he says: "These two [compounds] with a preceding negative particle do not necessitate [the application of the rule]. Since the subject under discussion is the option regarding the prohibition of *it*-ness (*ittva-pratiṣedha-vikalpa*), this is how it should be understood.
"What is the reason?"—
with this, he asks for the reason why the two [reasons] preceded by the negative particle (*nañ*) are not probative.
With the words "For here," etc., he demonstrates that very reason.

Regarding the phrase "by the case-ending existing within": although that case-ending which constitutes the meaning of the compound is elided, by the rule of *pratyayalakṣaṇa* (the presence of a suffix), this [suffix] would follow immediately after the word *etad*, which ends in a case-ending (*sup*), and likewise after the word *dvi*. Consequently, there would be no possibility for the substitution of *it*; this is because of the prohibition [stated in Pāṇini 7.3.44], "not after a word ending in a case-ending" (*asupaḥ*). Therefore, what is the point of the optional application of that prohibition? For this reason, these two words—*etad* and *dvi*—when preceded by the negative particle *nañ*, do not trigger [the application of the suffix]. If this is so, then by this same logic, the word *sva* should also not trigger it? To this he says: "But the word *sva*," and so forth.

Is it not logical that these two [suffixes] do not apply when preceded by *nañ*, because there is no intervention here? For, considering that *āP* occurs after a word ending in a *su*-affix (*subanta*), the *akaC* suffix—which occurs before the *tiṅ* affix—cannot possibly be an intervening element.

However, by the rule *svaśabdastu* [Pāṇini 1.1.35], the word *sva-*—when it does not function as a pronominal (*asarvanāman*)—denotes either a kinsman or wealth. Therefore, from that [base], only the suffix *kap* should occur, and not *akac*.
