In that case, if one forms a negative compound (*nañsamāsa*) and then applies the suffix *kap*, and subsequently adds the feminine suffix *ṭāp* to that which ends in *kap*, then this [suffix *ṭāp*] would not follow immediately after a form ending in a case-suffix (*subanta*), because it is separated by the suffix *kap*. Consequently, even when preceded by the negative particle *nañ*, the word *sva-*—not being a pronominal—triggers the optional application [of the suffix]. As for the statement "the word *bhastrā* is one whose masculine form has not been mentioned," this is because it always occurs only in the feminine.
If this is so, since the option is already established by [Pāṇini 7.3.48], for what purpose is it mentioned here? To this he says: "of that," and so forth.
That whose meaning or purpose is the *upasarjana* (secondary member) is described as such.

When the word *bhastrā* is not an *upasarjana*, then this option—being one where the feminine form has not been previously stated as masculine—is indeed established by the subsequent rule (*Pāṇini 7.3.48*), because the phrase "of those preceded by the negative particle" (*nañpūrvāṇām*) is understood to carry over there as well.
But when it is an *upasarjana* (secondary member of a compound), it does not attain the status of having been previously used in the masculine form; thus, the desired result is not established.
Therefore, the word *bhastrā* is included here so that the rule may apply even to an *upasarjana* that has been previously used in the masculine, as in the examples *abhastrakā* and *abhastrikā*.

Regarding the meaning of *alpe* [Pāṇini 5.3.85], the suffix *ka* is applied after words beginning with *prāg* [Pāṇini 5.3.70] as in the example *atra*. Once the shortening of the *upasarjana* has been performed, [the form is established].

When the *bahuvrīhi* compound *avidyamānā bhastrā asya* is formed, [the word *abhastra*] is [derived] by the rule *ana upadhālopino 'nyatarasyām* (Pāṇini 7.1.83). Regarding the phrase "again," and so forth:
the word *abhastra* is indeed a *bahuvrīhi*; since it also occurs in the masculine, it is "one whose masculine form has been stated" (*bhāṣitapuṃska*).
Therefore, when the suffix *ṭāp* is produced from a word that has already expressed the masculine (*bhāṣitapuṃska*),

even though that *ṭāp* is produced from such a word, the shortening prescribed by the rule *ke'ṇaḥ* [Pāṇini 7.4.13] does not occur in place of an *at* that was ordained after a word that has not expressed the masculine (*abhāṣitapuṃska*).
Consequently, this is not established by the phrase "from a word that has not expressed the masculine"— this is the intended meaning.

"By the word 'also' (*api*) in the rule *nañpūrvāṇām api*, it is intended that this rule applies to those preceded by *nañ*, as well as to others preceded by different words and to simple [words] alone.
Regarding this, he provides the example: *nirbhastrikā*, etc.
That from which a bellows (*bhastrā*) has gone out is *nirbhastrikā*.
That which has many bellows (*bhastrā*) is *bahubhastrikā*.
By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), forms such as *subhastrakā*, *subhastrikā*, *bhastrakā*, and *bhastrikā* are included.
If, then, the rule is intended for both those preceded by another word and for simple [stems], then the statement "of those preceded by the negative particle *nañ*" would be redundant.

One might object: "The rule will apply to those preceded by *nañ* and so forth through the principle of *tadantavidhi* (extension to what ends with that), and to the simple word *nañ* itself by the principle of *vyapadeśivadbhāva* (treating a thing as identical to its designation). However, this cannot be established because of the two Paribhāṣās: 'There is no *tadantavidhi* when a nominal stem (*pratipadika*) is accompanied by a suffix' (Vyāḍi-Pāṇini 89), and 'The principle of *vyapadeśivadbhāva* does not apply when a nominal stem is involved' (Dharmakīrti-Pāṇini 65). This objection should not be raised, for both of these Paribhāṣās apply only to the domain of the prescription of suffixes (*pratyayavidhi*). Therefore, he says "here," etc.

Since the operation of the prefix *prakara-* is already established here by *tadantavidhi* and *vyapadeśivadbhāva*, the statement "even for those preceded by *nañ*" is merely a restatement (*anuvāda*) of that which is already proven.

For what purpose? For the sake of comprehension by those of dull intellect. The phrase "also [the words] preceded by the negative particle *nañ*" is stated so that even those of dull intellect who are unable to comprehend the meaning just mentioned may still achieve comprehension. The particle *ca* is for the purpose of carrying over the phrase "also [the words] preceded by the negative particle *nañ*. Examples: *khaṭvakā*, *khaṭvikā*.

As before? Who [is the example]? This word *khaṭvā*, having its gender specified, always occurs only in the feminine and therefore is not one that has been mentioned as having a masculine counterpart (*bhāṣitapuṃska*). Thus, [the form] is *akhaṭvikā*.
"Non-couch" (*akhaṭvā*) is a negative compound (*nañ-samāsa*).
In "supreme couch" (*paramakhaṭvikā*), and so forth,
the compound is formed by [Pāṇini 2.1.61] *āpinā*.

In all cases, the short vowel [is substituted] by the rule *ako 'ṇaḥ* [Pāṇini 7.4.13]. Someone might have the misconception that because a *bahuvrīhi* compound is *bhāṣitapuṃska* (having a masculine form), this optional [substitution] should not apply here; therefore, he says "in a *bahuvrīhi*" etc., in order to dispel that doubt. But how is it that when it is stated "[after a word] not having a masculine form" (*abhāṣitapuṃskāt*), [the substitution] occurs even after a *bahuvrīhi* that *does* have a masculine form? To this he says: "here too, even from one not having a masculine form," and so on.
The particle *iti* is used here in the sense of a reason (*hetau*).

Although [the word] is a *bahuvrīhi* that has been stated as masculine (*bhāṣitapuṃska*), nevertheless, when the short vowel is applied by the rule *kapi* (Pāṇini 7.4.15), then there occurs an option (*vikalpa*) precisely for that *a* which stands in place of the *ā* prescribed after a word that is not stated as masculine (*abhāṣitapuṃska*).
The *bahuvrīhi* compound "one for whom no bed exists" (*avidyamānā khaṭvā asya*) takes the suffix *kap* by the rule *śeṣādvibhāṣā* (Pāṇini 5.4.154); from that, the short vowel is applied.
And that [suffix] occurs only after a word that is not inherently masculine (abhāṣitapuṃska),
which is why the option between *akhaṭvakā* and *akhaṭvikā* indeed arises.
As for the phrase "But when," etc.

In the case of the *bahuvrīhi* compound *avidyamānakhaṭvā* ("one for whom there is no bed"), the shortening of the penultimate vowel occurs, followed by the suffix *ṭāp*. Then, regarding *alpākhaṭvā* ("a small bed"), one might ask: "Why is it not like the previous case? [The answer is: it becomes *akhaṭvikā* according to Pāṇini 5.3.70 (*kaḥ*). Here, the optional application will not occur; because the *bahuvrīhi* has been previously treated as masculine (*bhāṣitapuṃska*), the vowel *a* is prescribed in place of the feminine suffix *ā*.

Showing that [the rule] does not apply even in the case of a *prādi*-compound, he says "likewise" (*tathā*) and so forth. Regarding the example "atikhaṭvikā": here too, once the *prādi*-compound has been formed and the shortening of the subordinate member (*upasarjana*) has occurred, the optional application [of the feminine suffix] does not take effect, because the vowel *a* is prescribed in place of the final *ā* of a *tatpuruṣa* compound that is originally masculine (*bhāṣitapuṃska*). Furthermore, the phrase "even for those preceded by *nañ*" is no longer operative, because it was carried over from the preceding sūtra.
This *yoga* is an exception (*apavāda*) to [the rule] "it" [Pāṇini 7.1.86];
and it is also an exception to the shortening [prescribed by] "ke'ṇaḥ" [Pāṇini 7.4.13]. The mention of the Teacher (*ācārya*) is for the sake of making the rule obligatory (*nitya*).
For if that [mention of the teacher] were absent, there would be an option due to the governing rule "of the Northerners" (udīcām, Pāṇini 7.3.46).

But when the mention of the teacher is present, by means of it the phrase "of the Northerners" is set aside, and thus this rule becomes obligatory. Here, if the letter *ṭha* were taken without distinction, it would apply even to the end of a verbal root, as in *paṭhitā* and *paṭhitum*.
Therefore, wishing to avoid this fault, he says—"the *ṭha* which is the cause of the stem"—in order to show that the *ṭha* of an affix is intended, and not merely the letter *ṭha* itself.
The genitive case in *aṅgasya* denotes a relationship characterized by connection.

Although a portion of a verbal root (*dhātu*) may indeed be related to a stem (*aṅga*), nevertheless, due to proximity (*pratyāsatti*), only that which serves as the cause for the very acquisition of the status of a stem—that is, that in relation to which something becomes a "stem"—is understood here as the related factor of the stem, and not even its constituent part.
[This is expressed by the question: "And what is it that becomes the cause of the stem?"

He thinks as follows: "If that which is the cause (*nimitta*) of a stem (*aṅga*) in general were taken here, then it would apply even to the *ṭha* at the end of a verbal root (*dhātu*), for the parts (*avayava*) are indeed the causes of the whole (*avayavin*), since the whole is initiated by them. To this he says: "The suffix (*pratyaya*). His intention is this: although the parts exist, as long as the suffix has not arisen, the acquisition of the nature of a stem does not occur for that whole; however, once that [suffix] has arisen, it does occur. Therefore, the suffix alone is the cause of the stem, not the part. [Examples: *ākṣikaḥ*, *śālākikaḥ*.
He plays with dice; [in the sense of "he plays with dice," the suffix *ṭhak* is applied—this is the reading in the *mu* manuscript];
in the sense of "he plays with counting-sticks (*śalākā*)," the suffix *ṭhak* is applied, as in "a maker of salt" (*lāvaṇika*).

In this case as well, regarding the rule *lavaṇaṃ paṇyam asya* [Pāṇini 4.4.52], does the mention of *ṭhasya* here refer to a single phoneme (*varṇamātra*) or to the entire cluster (*saṅghāta*)? In the former view, the reference to *ṭhasya* would be untenable; in the latter, however, there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) to Uṇādi derivatives such as *kaṇeṣṭhaḥ* (Dhātupāṭha 5–6) and *kaṇṭha*.

But here, in the case of *māthitika*—derived from the sense "his merchandise has been churned" (*mathitaṃ paṇyam asya*)—once the suffix *ṭha* is applied, the substitution of *i* for *ṭha* is made; then, when the *a* of the base is elided by *ato lopaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.4.148), the form ends in *t*. At this point, one might object: "Since the substitute *i* is treated as the original element (*sthānivadbhāva*), it is included by the mention of the suffix *ṭha*; therefore, by the rule *isusuktāntāt kaḥ* (Pāṇini 7.3.51), the substitution of *ka* for *ṭha* should follow. To such an objection, he replies with the words beginning "In the case of *ṭhak* and so on," etc.

By the word "ādi" (and so forth), suffixes such as *ṭhañ* are included. If, in those cases, only the phoneme (*varṇa*) is the suffix (*pratyaya*) while the vowel *a* is merely for the sake of pronunciation (*uccāraṇārtha*), then in the rule [Pāṇini 7.3.50] *ataḥ*, the *a* is likewise for the sake of pronunciation. Thus, only the phoneme is taken as the substituendum (*sthānin*). Here too, the *a* is indeed for the sake of pronunciation; therefore, whatever fault the opponent will raise regarding the inclusion of only the phoneme, that fault applies when only the phoneme is taken as the substituendum.

In this case as well, the vowel *a* is intended solely for the purpose of pronunciation; thus, the objection that the opponent will raise regarding the fault of grasping the mere phoneme (*varṇamātra*) is refuted.
Even though there is the grasping of the mere phoneme, the designation *ṭhasya* is employed by means of an adventitious *a* that serves the purpose of pronunciation.
As for the passage beginning with "But if there were the grasping of a cluster," etc.:

Now, in the case of suffixes such as *ṭhak* and others, the word *sākaṭya* is a complex formation (*saṅghāta*) that functions as the suffix; this being so, it is appropriate here in the rule as well to take the complex formation as the element undergoing substitution (*sthānin*). Desiring to remove the first objection that the opponent wishes to raise against this position, he says "In that case," and so forth.

Having exposed the second objection under this position with the example "mathita is his merchandise" (*mathita-paṇyam asya*), he refutes it with the principle "an operation conditioned by a grammatical combination" (*sannipātalakṣaṇo vidhiḥ*), and so on.

The [suffix] *ṭāp* arises because it follows a word beginning with *aj* (a vowel) and ending in *takāra* (t); it is not able to obstruct that status of beginning with *aj*, and thus the substitution of *kā* does not occur. Regarding the phrase "due to the status of being a *sthānivadbhāva* of the elision [of the final *i*] by the rule *yasyeti ca*," the connection is with the previously mentioned statement "the substitution of *kā* does not occur"; for [the condition of ending in *takāra*] is obstructed by the status of being a *sthānivadbhāva*.

The status of being a *sthānin* (original element) occurs again by [Pāṇini 1.1.56], which states that "in the application of a grammatical operation concerning what precedes, the substitute (*ādeśa*) behaves like the original (*sthānin*). However, here there is no operation concerning what precedes; rather, what is the case? It is an operation concerning what follows what precedes. Therefore, he asks: "Whence does the status of being a *sthānin* arise? He replies with the words "even from what precedes" and so forth.

The intention is that the term *pūrvavidhi* ("operation concerning what precedes") is not intended solely as a genitive compound meaning "an operation of what precedes," but also as a locative compound meaning "an operation after what precedes. When a single substitution (*ekādeśa*) would otherwise apply according to the preceding rule, the substitution of *is* for the final and initial letters is prescribed.
Regarding *sarpiṣkaḥ*:

by the rule *tadasya pacyam* [Pāṇini 4.4.51], the suffix *ṭhak* (which becomes *ika*) is applied as a *prāgvahatīya* derivative; then the substitution of *ru* and *visarjanīya* occurs, and by the rule *visarjanīyasya saḥ* [Pāṇini 8.3.44], the *visarjanīya* is replaced by *ṣ*.
Regarding *dhānuṣkaḥ*: [the same process applies].
The suffix *ṭhak* is applied by [Pāṇini 4.4.57] *tadasya grahaṇam*,
resulting in *yājuṣkaḥ*;
the suffix *ṭhak* is applied by [Pāṇini 4.4.2] *tena dīvyati*.

"naiṣādakarṣukaḥ, śābarajambūkaḥ"—meaning "born of a Niṣādakarṣu woman" and "born of a Śābarajambu woman," [the suffix *uka* is applied according to Pāṇini 4.2.119]; the shortening [of the vowel] occurs by [Pāṇini 7.4.13]: *ke'ṇaḥ*. [Examples: "mātṛkam" (maternal) and "paitṛkam" (paternal).
"Derived from the mother," "derived from the father"—
[this refers to] the suffix *ṭhak* [prescribed] by [Pāṇini 4.3.78]. [The form] "from *udaka*" is derived by [the rule] "after *uda*, *kaḥ*" [prescribed by Pāṇini 4.2.19].

[The examples] "śākṛtkaḥ" and "yākṛtkaḥ" [are formed] by the suffix *ṭhak* according to the rule "śakṛtā yakṛtā saṃsṛṣṭe" (Pāṇini 4.4.22). Now, why does this not apply here in cases such as "āśiṣā carati" → "āśiṣikaḥ" and "uṣā carati" → "auṣikaḥ"? To this he says: "of *is* and *us*, etc. (referring to Pāṇini 7.3.51).

By the rule *arcisucihusṛpichādichardibhya isiḥ* (Dhātupāṭha 9.30), *janerusiḥ* (Dhātupāṭha 9.37), and *arttipṛvapiyajitanidhanitapibhyo nit* (Dhātupāṭha 9.39), as well as other such rules in this section, two suffixes, *isi* and *usi*, are prescribed. According to the maxim *lakṣaṇapratipadoktaparibhāṣā* (Vyāḍīya-paribhāṣā 3), there is a preference for the mention of those suffixes that are explicitly stated (*pratipadokta*) over those that are merely indicated by a general rule (*lākṣaṇika*). Consequently, [the suffix] does not apply in cases such as *āśiṣikaḥ* and *auṣikaḥ*, because the *isi* and *usi* in these instances are merely indicated by a rule.

Likewise, from the root *śās* meaning "to desire" (Dhātupāṭha 1022) preceded by *hrāṅ*, and from the simple root *vas* meaning "to dwell" (Dhātupāṭha 1005), when the suffix *kvip* is applied, followed by *samprasāraṇa* and the substitution of the preceding vowel for the following one (*parapūrvatva*), the forms *āśiṣikaḥ* and *auṣikaḥ* are obtained. [This is governed by the rule] *śāsivasidhasīnāṃ ca*.

Thus, by [Pāṇini 8.3.60], there is the substitution of *ṣ*. However, because that [substitution] is considered asiddha (not yet established), the possibility of the substitution of *ka* was raised; hence the statement: "An addition must be made regarding the word *doṣa*."
The purpose of the word *upasaṃkhyāna* (supplementary addition) is to provide an explanation.

In this regard, the explanation is as follows: the term *ap* is understood to follow from [Pāṇini 7.3.47] *nañpūrvāṇām api*; and that term has the sense of including what has not been explicitly mentioned (*anuktasamuccayārtha*). By means of that, the form *doṣaḥ* will also occur—as in "pākaḥ" (cooking) and "tyāgaḥ" (renunciation), where the suffix *ghañ* is applied in the sense of an abstract action (*bhāve*).
Regarding the forms *pākyam* and *vākyam*:

[the suffix] *ṇyat* is applied by the rule *ṛhalorṇyat* [Pāṇini 3.1.124]. Now, one might object: since the bases *ca* and *ja* are equal in number to the affixes *ghi* and *ṇyat*, would there not be an application according to their respective order—namely, *ca* before *ghi* and *ja* before *ṇyat*? If so, how can there be an exception, such that in the case of *rāgaḥ* (formed with *ghañ*), the substitution of *k* for *j* (the *kutva* change) would apply? This is not the case; because of an indicator (*jñāpaka*), the rule of respective order does not apply here.

By prescribing the absence of *kutva* for the letter *ja* in the case of the suffix *ghañ* through the rules *yat* [Pāṇini 7.3.61] and *yaṅo 'ci ca* [7.3.62], and by providing the technical indication (*nirdeśa*) in the rule *tena raktaṃ rāgāt* [4.2.1], he makes known that there is no application of "correspondence in order" (*yathāsaṃkhya*) here. This undertaking is for the sake of the sense of "over" (*adhi*). [This is shown by the statement: "The suffix *u* does not follow *avañcati*";
for in that context, the rule *bhṛmṛśītṛcaritsaritanidhanimimasjibhya uḥ* [Dhātupāṭha 1.92] continues to apply.
Regarding the word *madguḥ*:
from the root *ṭumasjo śuddhau* (Dhātupāṭha 1415), the substitution of *da* for *sa* occurs by [Pāṇini 8.4.53];
then, the suffix *u* is applied by the rule *mimasjibhya uḥ*.
By this, he indicates the rule beginning with *bhṛ-mṛ-śī-tṛ-car-* (Pāṇini 3.2.162).
Regarding *bhṛguḥ*:
[it is derived from] *bhrasj* "to cook" (Dhātupāṭha 1284).
In the sūtra beginning with *pratibhṛdi* (*Pāṇini 4.1.113*), the suffix *ap* is carried over from that very sūtra (*Pāṇini 4.1.92*). In the example *dūrepākaḥ* (variant reading:
*dūrepākāḥ*), the suffix *ac* is applied according to the rule for roots beginning with *pac* (*Pāṇini 3.1.134*), in the sense of the agent who is also the object (*karmakartṛ*).
Regarding the rule "after *apa* ending in *u*": it is understood that [the suffix *kyap*] is applied after the root *i* (to go) in the sense of "studying" (*adhīyate*).
Regarding the rule "after *tan*" (*tañcateḥ*): [the suffix *kyap* is applied].

Regarding "tancu" and "tvancu" in the sense of "motion" (*gatau*) [Dhātupāṭha 191, 192], and "vañcu" in the sense of "deceiving" (*pralambhane*) [Dhātupāṭha 1703]: does this refer to a portion of the rule "sphāyitañcivañci... [Pāṇini 6.1.25], namely the rule "sphāyitañcivañciśakikṣipikṣudisṛpidṛpitṛpivanyundiiātivṛtyajinīpadimadimudikhidibhidichidimandicandidahidasidambhivahavasivāśiśīṅhasasidhiśubhibhyo rak" [Uṇādi-sūtra 8.31]? It indicates that [the root *vañc*] is included there. Regarding "vyatiṣaṅgaḥ," [it refers to the root] "ṣanja" in the sense of "attachment" (*saṅge*) [Dhātupāṭha 987]. Regarding "avasargaḥ": [it refers to the root *sṛj*].
From the root *sṛj* in the sense of "emission" (*visarga*) [Dhātupāṭha 1178], the suffix *ac* is applied according to the rule *pacādyac*, resulting in *sarga*.
From the root *medh* [Dhātupāṭha 992], which means "to sprinkle" (*secana*), [the suffix *ghañ* is applied to form *medhaḥ*].
From the root *miha* in the sense of "sprinkling" (*secana*) [Dhātupāṭha 992]... [the suffix *ghañ* is applied to form *meghaḥ*].
"Right now," [as in] "āpākaḥ. The suffix *aṇ* is applied by the rule *karmaṇyaṇ* [Pāṇini 3.2.1], since "cooking" (*pāka*) is the object (*karman*) of the action.
Regarding "arhateḥ": the root *arh* means "to worship" (Dhātupāṭha 740). Regarding "daheḥ": [the root *dah*].
In *dahabhasmīkaraṇe* (Dhātupāṭha 992); [and] regarding *ruheḥ*:

*ruha* means "to grow from seed" and "to appear" (Dhātupāṭha 859). Now, one might object: since words such as *nyaṅku* and others are listed in the list of nominal stems (*prātipadika-gaṇa*) with their *kutva* changes already applied, for what purpose is this [rule]? For just as other operations occur by virtue of being *nipātana*s, so too will the *kutva* change occur. This is stated for the purpose of authorizing that very reading in the list of nominal stems.
If this [sūtra] were not present, the reading would be understood as *pramāda* (an error). The examples such as *dhātayati* have been explained under [Pāṇini 7.3.32].
As for *dhnanti*:
this is the present tense (*laṭ*), with the substitution of *anti* for *jhi*, and the elision of the penultimate vowel according to [Pāṇini 6.4.98], etc.
"May they destroy," this is the imperative mood (*loṭ*).
"On the road," this is [the locative].

In *laṅ*, there is the elision of the vowel *i* by [Pāṇini 6.4.100] *itaśca*. Regarding *prahāraḥ* and *prahārakaḥ*, the suffixes *ghañ* and *ṇvul* are applied to the root *hṛ*. Here, the mention of *ñ-ṇ-it* could either be a qualifier of the root *han*—meaning "the *han* that has *ñ*, *ṇ*, or *it* as its subsequent element"—or it could be a qualifier of the letter *h*—meaning "the *h* that has *ñ*, *ṇ*, or *it* as its subsequent element," provided that this *h* belongs to the root *han*. If the former alternative were adopted, the rule would not apply in forms such as *dhnanti*, because here the root *han* does not have *na* as its subsequent element; for it is impossible for a whole (*samudāya*) to stand in a relation of priority or posteriority with respect to one of its own parts (*avayava*), and furthermore, there is no other *na* present.
If, on the other hand, the alternative view were adopted, it would not apply anywhere; for it is impossible for the letter *ha* to be followed by *ñ*, *ṇ*, *n*, or *na*.

This impossibility arises because, in forms such as *dhnanti*, the elision of the vowel *a* (by P. 6.4.98) is treated as *sthānivadbhāva* with respect to the preceding rule [P. 6.4.103], and thus there is an intervention by the letter *a*; and in forms such as *ghātayati*, there is likewise an intervention after the *ha* by the element *ana* which is a constituent part of the root *han*.

Now, one might object: "By the force of the statement, the suffix *kṛt* should apply even when there is an intervention; even so, in the case of *hananamicchati*, [the rule] *supa ātmanaḥ kyac* [Pāṇini 3.1.8] would apply, followed by *ittva* by *kyaci ca* [Pāṇini 7.4.33], and then with the addition of *ṇvul* to the form ending in *kyac*, the elision of the vowel *a* by *ato lopaḥ* [Pāṇini 6.4.48] would result in *hananīyaka*. To such an objector, he states another alternative view, beginning with: "The *ñṇit* suffix is here a qualifier of the root *han*.
For it is not possible for all *ñṇit* suffixes containing the letter *n* to be qualifiers of *han*, nor is it possible for them to be qualifiers of the letter *h*.

Therefore, since only some [element] can be a qualifier for something else according to possibility, and since a *ñṇit* affix occurs after the root *han*, that [affix] is its qualifier— meaning "when a *ñṇit* affix follows immediately after *han*. However, the letter *n* cannot be a qualifier for *han*, for the reason stated previously.
However, since it is stated that "it is applicable to the *ik* vowel," this is a qualification of that very [vowel]: "of the *h* sound which immediately precedes a *n* sound.
This [rule] is obtained because the mention of "what is specified" (*nirdiṣṭagrahaṇa*) in Pāṇini 1.1.66 has the purpose of indicating immediate sequence (*ānantarya*).
When immediate sequence is thus relied upon, over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*)—which would otherwise apply to forms such as *hantā* and *hantum*—is eliminated.

But surely, immediate succession between the letter *ha* and the letter *ṇa* is not possible, because when the elision of the vowel *a* occurs, there is an intervention by the vowel *a* due to the status of the original element (*sthānivadbhāva*)? To this he says: "And that," etc.
"Produced by conjunction" (*sannipātakṛtam*) means produced by actual audition (*śruti*).

But surely, even when the immediate succession (*ānantarya*) caused by the *sannipāta* is accepted, would not the quality of being a *kutva* (the substitution of *k* for *g*) be obstructed by that which is produced by the rule of *sthānivadbhāva*, namely the non-immediate succession [restored] by that very rule? To this he says: "But that which is produced by the rule of *sthānivadbhāva," and so forth.
Why is it not an obstructor? He says: "By virtue of the force of the explicit statement.

If the non-immediate succession produced by the rule of *sthānivadbhāva* were an intervening factor or an obstructor, then the explicit mention of the letter *n* would be purposeless; for it would have no scope of application (*niravakāśatvāt*).
Therefore, by the force of the statement, it is not obstructive.
Regarding the two positions proposed by the words "even though" (*yadyapi*) and so forth, this is the refutation of the fault that exists in the second position.
In that context, the fault that arises when the letter *ha* is qualified by the negative particle *na* has already been refuted.

Now, however, he removes the fault that arises when the letter *ha* is qualified by a *ñṇit* affix. This portion of the root *han* which follows *ha* and begins with *a* and ends with *n* creates an intervention between the *ñṇit* affix and the root in all instances. But an intervention is possible through the word *ananīya*; and since such an intervention does not occur [in cases like *ghātayati*], the rule "that by which there is no intervention applies even when there is an intervention" (*Vyāḍipāda* 46) serves as the authoritative basis for the occurrence of *kutva* in forms such as *ghātayati*.
However, since an intervention by the word *hanīya* is not possible, whereas an intervention by [the suffix] *anīya* is indeed possible, the rule will not apply in the case of *hananīyaka*.
As for the fault stated regarding the first alternative, it has no occasion, precisely because that position is not accepted.

The mention of the root *han* by means of the affix *śtip* is solely for the purpose of indicating the verbal root (*dhātu*), and not for the purpose of excluding the *yaṅ*-lopa (the elision of *yaṅ*).
In that case, there must indeed be the substitution of *ku* (the guttural *g*) by [Pāṇini 7.3.55]. Regarding the form *jighāṃsati*:

the suffix *san* is applied, followed by lengthening [by 6.4.16], reduplication, the substitution of *cu* (the palatal *c*) for *jh* by [7.4.62]—resulting in the letter *jh*; then the substitution of *jaś* (the voiced unaspirated *j*) for *jh* by [8.4.54]—resulting in the letter *j*; and finally, the substitution of *it* (the vowel *i*) for the radical *a* by [7.4.79]—resulting in *jighāṃsati*. Regarding the form *jaṅghanyate*: [the process is as follows].
The augment *nuṭ* is applied by [Pāṇini 7.4.85]. Regarding the form *jaghāna*:
this is the example for when there is no *ṇiṭ*-status due to the use of the first person singular (*uttamapuruṣa*) in the *parasmaipada*.

But in the view that [the *ṇi*] is present, it is already established by the preceding rule. Why does [the substitution] not occur in *jihananīyiṣati*—formed by adding *kyac* after the word *agrahanana*, and then *san* after that? For in this case, the letter *h* of the root *han* follows the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*). To this he replies: "In this case, when there is an affix caused by the reduplication," and so forth. Here, the words "of *han*" (from Pāṇini 7.3.54) and "of the stem" (*aṅgasya*) are understood to carry over.

A cognition (pratyaya) brought about by repetition (*abhyāsa*) serves as the cause for that [repetition]; because that cognition is the cause of the specific [modification], the root *han* is qualified as a stem (*aṅga*) by that cognition which has repetition as its cause.
[As stated in the Kāśikā: "When there is a cognition caused by repetition, the root *han* is the stem.
By such a *han* as well, the repetition is qualified.

When there is a relationship of qualifier and qualified such that "the reduplication of the stem *han* which is characterized by the aforementioned qualifications," then, on account of that reduplication, the substitution of *ku* (kutva) must occur in the suffixes beginning with *san* and others. Consequently, it does not occur here in the form *jihananīyiṣati*, because in this case, when the suffix *san* is conditioned by the reduplication, *han* is not the stem (*aṅga*); rather, what is the stem? It is the word *hananīya*.
However, since the root *han* is a subordinate element (*aṅga*), it is not the cause for the reduplication when the suffix *lyuṭ* is applied. Regarding "prajighīṣati":
the root *hi* (meaning "to go," Dhātupāṭha 1257) takes the desiderative suffix *san*; the lengthening of the vowel occurs as before.
Regarding "prajedhīyate": [the same applies].

The long vowel [of the root] is applied by the rule *akṛtsārvadhātukayoḥ* [Pāṇini 7.4.25]; then there is reduplication, and by the rule *dvirvacane 'ci* [Pāṇini 1.1.59], the *guṇa* substitution occurs for the reduplicated syllable. Thus, *prajighāya*:
[the suffix] *ṇal*, with the *vṛddhi* and *āy-ādeśa* substitutions.

In the word *prācīhayat*, there is the causative suffix *ṇic* [from the root *hi*]; the substitution of *caṅ* occurs by the rule *ṇiśri* etc. [Pāṇini 3.1.48]; the shortening of the penultimate vowel occurs by the rule *ṇau caṅyupadhāyāḥ* [Pāṇini 7.4.1]; and reduplication occurs by the rule *caṅi* [Pāṇini 6.1.11].
Furthermore, that which was performed in the presence of *ṇic* is treated as *sthānivadbhūta* [Paribhāṣā 21]; thus, by the rule *hi* [Pāṇini 7.4.94], the long vowel is substituted for the *hi* sound.
Regarding the phrase "on account of the reduplication in the *caṅ*" (*caṅyabhyāsanimitte*), etc.:

in the case of *prājīhayat*, the root *hi* is the base (*aṅga*) with respect to the *ṇic* that follows on account of the reduplication in the *caṅ*; it is not [the base] with respect to that very *caṅ* which is the cause of the reduplication, because in this sūtra there is a governing heading (*adhikāra*) for "reduplication. When the cause of reduplication—which is implied by the reduplication itself—is understood as the affix (*pratyaya*) [to which the root belongs], and it is thus understood that the root *hi* is the base, then what occasion would there be for [the rule] to apply to something outside the *caṅ*? Since it does not apply in this way, there is no purpose in the prohibition "not when there is no *caṅ*" (*acaṅi*).
Having thus rejected the inclusion [of the augment], he states its purpose with the words "that is done," and so forth.
What, then, is made known by this? He says: "after *hi*, except when *aṅ* follows," and so forth.
"After *hi*, except when *aṅ* follows," and so forth.

By the rule "heracaṅi," it is indicated that the substitution of *k* for *h* occurs in the root *hi* even when followed by more than *ṇi*, provided it is not in the context of *caṅ* or the *san*-class suffixes. By the words "by that" (*tena*) and so forth, he demonstrates the purpose of this indicator (*jñāpaka*).
The example is "he desires to cause [him] to send" (*prajighāyayiṣati*).

In the expression "desiring to cause to abandon" (*prahāyayitum icchati*), the desiderative suffix *san* is applied after the causative form (*ṇyantāt*). Regarding the forms "he desires to conquer" (*jigīṣati*) and "he conquered" (*jigāya*):

according to [Pāṇini 7.3.54], there is the substitution of *k* for the initial *j* of the following root. This is the periphrastic perfect (*liṭ*) of the root *jyā* ("loss of vigor," Dhātupāṭha 1499).

When the semivowel substitution (*samprasāraṇa*) is performed by the rule concerning *grahi*, *jyā*, and so forth [Pāṇini 6.1.16], and the preceding vowel is substituted for the following one, this specific form *jirati* arises.

Therefore, the substitution of *ku* would also apply to this [form], because it is included by the mention of *ji*. Nor can it be argued: "Once the lengthening has been applied by [Pāṇini 6.4.2] *halaḥ*, there will be no inclusion by the mention of *ji*, because that which is modified in one part is not different [from the original]. For otherwise, even in the case of *jinīṣati*, once the lengthening has been applied by [Pāṇini 6.4.16] *ato lopaḥ*, there would likewise be no inclusion by the mention of *ji*. Alternatively, if someone were to object: "The substitution of *ku* must occur even before the lengthening, because it is subsequent [to the rule for lengthening]," he says in response: "*jināteḥ*" and so forth.

By the technical rule *lakṣaṇapratipadoktaparibhāṣā* (Pāṇini 1.1.68), this [rule] refers only to that which is read as *ji jaye* (Dhātupāṭha 561), being the specifically mentioned form (*pratipadokta*), and not to *jināti*. This is because the form *jī-* which results when *samprasāraṇa* is applied is *lākṣaṇika* (derived from a rule).
Thus: *jijyatuḥ*, *jijyuḥ*.

By the rule *liṭ, atus, us* [Pāṇini 6.4.82], there is the substitution of *yaṇ*. When the substitution of *kutva* was about to apply by [the rule] *kuhoścuḥ* [Pāṇini 7.3.52], this prohibition is commenced. Examples are: *kūjaḥ*, *khajaḥ*, *garjaḥ*. [The roots are:
*kūja* "inarticulate sound" (Dhātupāṭha 223), *kharja* "pain" (Dhātupāṭha 229), and *garja* "sound" (Dhātupāṭha 226). [Examples are also: *samājaḥ*, *udājaḥ*.
From the root *aj* in the sense of "going" and "throwing" (Dhātupāṭha 230),
the suffix *ghañ* is applied by [Pāṇini 3.3.69],
resulting in the forms *parivrājaḥ* and *parivrājyam*.
The roots *vaja* and *vraja* mean "to go" (*gatau*) [Dhātupāṭha 252, 253].
Now, one might ask: why has no example been provided for the root *aj* with the suffix *ṇyat*? To this he says: "of the substitution of *vī*" (*vībhāvasya*), and so forth.

In that regard, the substitution of *vī* is prescribed by the rule *ajeḥ ṣṭran ghañapoḥ* [Pāṇini 2.4.56]; therefore, an example for that [root with *ṇyat*] is not applicable, and thus it was not shown—this is the intended meaning.
The letter *ca* has the sense of including what has not been explicitly mentioned; by it, there is also a prohibition regarding the root *vāj*, as in *vājaḥ* and *vācyam*. Regarding *bhujaḥ*:
the root *bhuj* is listed in the Dhātupāṭha (1454) as "to protect" and "to eat. The suffix *ghan* is applied according to [Pāṇini 3.3.121] *halaśca*.
Here, the suffix *ghan* is understood from the preceding rule [3.3.120] *ave tṛstrorghañ*.
Regarding the word *nyubja*:

when it is stated that the term *udja* (meaning "straightness") has the letter *da* as its penultimate (*dakāropadha*), then the substitution of *ba* for the letter *da* is prescribed by way of a grammatical irregularity (*nipātana*).

Alternatively, according to the rule [*asiddhebha udjeḥ*—this statement appears in the Mahābhāṣya under the sūtra *iyavaraṭ*], once the letter *bha* is substituted for *da*, the letter *ba* arises through the application of the *jaś*-rule.

If, however, [the root] is *ubj* with the vowel *a* as its penultimate (*bakāropadha*), namely *ubja* in the sense of "straightening," then in the case of *samudga* and others, the substitution of *da* for the letter *ba* must be stated. [In the words] *prayājaḥ* and *anuyājaḥ*, the suffix *ghañ* is applied according to Pāṇini 3.3.19 (*yajayācarucaśca*) after the roots preceded by *pra-* and *anu-*. In those cases, the change to *ku*-sounds (*kutva*) is prescribed as an irregularity (*nipātana*). [The phrase] "for the sake of illustration" means...
The meaning is that this is for the purpose of indicating other similar cases as well.
Consequently, the substitution of *kutva* does not occur in other sacrificial components (*yajñāṅga*) of the same type, such as the *prayāja* and *anuyāja* offerings.

Furthermore, it should be understood that the mention of the words *prayāja* and *anuyāja* is intended as an illustration (*pradarśanārthatā*), since they are included among the sacrificial components; for that [mention] is made for this very purpose.
How indeed could it be understood that the mention of *prayāja* and *nṛyāja* is intended as an illustration (*upalakṣaṇa*)?

For otherwise, since the status of being a constituent part of the sacrifice (*yajñāṅga*) would be understood through the very power of the irregular derivation (*nipātana*), that [mention] would simply not need to be made. Regarding the word *vañcam*:
*vañcu*, *cañcu*, *tañcu*, *tvañcu*, *mruñcu*, *mlañcu*, *bhrucu*, *mlucu*—these are roots meaning "to go" (Dhātupāṭha 1.89–1.96).
The suffix *ghañ* is used in the sense of the object (*karman*).
The meaning is that they deceive what is to be deceived, and they go to what is to be gone to.
[Regarding] "caṅkam": [it is derived from the root *kram* with the prefix *caṃ*].
The suffix *ghañ* is applied by [Pāṇini 3.3.121] *halaśca*. Regarding the word *nyokaḥ*:

it is derived from the root *uc* preceded by the prefix *ni*, as in the Dhātupāṭha (1223) "√uc samavāye" (to dwell together). By [Pāṇini 3.1.135] *igupadhajñāprīkiraḥ kaḥ*, we have *nyocatīti nyokaḥ*; the meaning is "he dwells. Alternatively, by the rule *ghañarthe kavidhānam* (Vārttika 306), the suffix *ka* is applied—*nyucantyasminniti nyokaḥ*; the meaning is "they dwell in this."

"Why again... and so forth. He thinks as follows: "This is a conventional term (*rūḍhi-śabda*); there is no meaning here for its constituent parts (*avayava-artha*). Only an etymological derivation (*vyutpatti*) must be performed, and that is indeed possible even when the suffix *ghañ* is applied by [Pāṇini 3.3.121], *halaśca*. Therefore, there is no purpose for this specific rule (*yoga*). [The opponent replies: "If *ghañ* were used, the word would have the acute accent (*udātta*) on the first syllable."
By this [rule], *it* [is established].

Now, in cases such as *divaukasaḥ* ("dwelling in heaven") and *jalaukasaḥ* ("living in water"), how is there the substitution of *ṣ* for *k*, given that there is no suffix *kap* here, nor the suffixes *dhiṇ* or *ṇyat*; what then? It is the suffix *asun*. To this he says: "In *divaukasaḥ*" and so forth;
the meaning is already explained. "In *avaśyapacyam*" and so forth.

The root *ḍupacaṣ* is listed as "pāke" (in the meaning of cooking) [Dhātupāṭha 996], and *vac* is listed as "paribhāṣaṇe" (in the meaning of speaking) [Dhātupāṭha 1842]. Following the rule *āvaśyakādhamaṇryayorṇiniḥ* [Pāṇini 3.3.170], the suffix *ṇyat* is applied by the subsequent rule [3.3.171] in the sense of necessity (*āvaśyaka*). A compound is formed because the term belongs to the *mayūravyaṃsakādi* group [Pāṇini 2.1.71]. By the rule *lubhyedavaśyamaḥ kṛtye tumkāmamanasorapi* (Kāśikā on 6.1.149), the letter *m* of *avaśyam* is elided before a word ending in a *kṛtya* suffix. The mention of *ṇye* alone is for the purpose of excluding cases where the sense is not one of necessity.
Regarding the passage beginning with *yājyam*:

the roots are *yaja* (to worship the gods, etc., DhP 1002), *ṭuyāc* (to beg, DhP 863), *ruca* (to shine, DhP 745), *vaca* preceded by *pra-* (to speak, DhP 1842), and *ṛc* (to praise, DhP 1302). But how can there be the suffix *ṇyat* after *ṛc*, given that by the rule *ṛdupadhāccākḷpicṛteḥ* (Pāṇini 3.1.110), the suffix *kyap* should apply instead of *ṇyat* after a root ending in *ṛ* with a penultimate *ṛ*? To this he says: "after a root with a penultimate *ṛ*" (*ṛdupadhāt*), etc.

Now, what is the purpose of including the mention of *pravac* (to speak), since the prohibition would already be established by the rule [Pāṇini 7.3.67]? To this he says: "The mention of *pravac* is for the sake of a technical term (*śabda-saṃjñā*) for the word.
One might object: "Is there not any word at all whose denotation (*vācya*) is its very name? To this he says: "There is one called *pravācya*," and so forth.
With the words "others, however," and so forth, he shows another opinion.
Regarding the phrase "but this":
this form is beyond dispute.

What, then, is this distinction? He says: "of the *daśarātra*," and so forth. In which [context] do the ritualists (*yājñika*) not disagree? It is in that *daśarātra* sacrifice where this form of the word *śas* is intended, and not elsewhere. If this is so, the mention of *pravaci* is redundant for the sake of restriction (*niyamārtha*). One must certainly exert effort so that its application occurs only in a specific domain; will not the substitution of *k* (*kutva*) also occur there by virtue of that very effort? This is not the case; for by means of the restriction (*niyama*), the prohibition of *kutva* for other prefixes (*upasarga*) is set aside.
The determination of the meaning, however, will be understood through common usage alone.

Regarding the rule "in the case of a prohibition when the suffix *ṇyat* is applied," and so forth: if this prohibition of *ṇyat* were to be applied, an additional rule (*upasaṃkhyāna*) must be made for the root *tyaj* (meaning "to abandon," Dhātupāṭha 986).
The purpose of the word *upasaṃkhyāna* is to provide an explanatory addition (*pratipādana*).

In this regard, the following is the explanation: the particle *ca* has the sense of including what has not been explicitly mentioned; by means of it, a prohibition will also apply to the root *tyaj*. In the case of the roots *yuj* "to join" (Dhātupāṭha 1444) preceded by *pra-* and *ni-*, the absence of *kutva* (the substitution of *g* for *y*) is prescribed as a *nipātana* (irregularity), provided that the suffix *ṇyat* occurs in the sense of possibility (*śakyārtha*).
Furthermore, the suffix *ṇyat* in the sense of possibility is to be understood by the rule *śaki liṅ ca* [Pāṇini 3.3.172].

For in that context, the rule *tatra hi* (Pāṇini 3.3.171) continues to apply. Now, for what purpose is this new *nipātana* (irregular formation), given that the term *ṇye* (Pāṇini 7.3.65) already continues to apply? In that case, while one could simply state "after the roots *pra-yuj* and *ni-yuj*, [the suffix *ṇyat* is applied] in the sense of capability," the *nipātana* is for the sake of establishing a conventional meaning (*rūḍhi*).

This is so that the form occurs even where the sense of capability is not the primary factor—such as in *prayojyaḥ bhṛtyaḥ* ("an employee who is to be employed") and *niyojyaḥ dāsaḥ* ("a servant who is to be directed").
The term *niyojya* does not apply to a master (*svāmin*).
For in that context, the words *prayojya* and *niyojya* are not technical terms (*rūḍha*); rather, they are derived from [the sense of] being subordinate (*guṇabhūta*). Regarding the word *bhojya*:

from the root *bhuja* in the sense of "protecting" and "eating" (Dhātupāṭha 1454), when the suffix *ṇyat* is applied and the meaning to be expressed is "that which is to be eaten," the absence of *kutva* (the change of *j* to *g*) is prescribed as a grammatical irregularity (*nipātana*).

"Gruel (*yavāgū*) is to be eaten. Now, one might object: this root *bhakṣ* refers to solid food (*kharaviśada*), not to a liquid substance, as in the rule [Pāṇini 4.2.16]. Therefore, how can it apply to gruel when it is stated "in what is to be eaten" (*bhakṣye*)? To this he says: "In this context, 'what is to be eaten' (*bhakṣyam*)" and so forth.
The root *bhakṣ* does not necessarily refer only to solid food.
For instance, its usage is observed even with respect to liquid substances,
as in "one who eats foam," "one who eats air," and "an eater of air.
Therefore, since the root *bhakṣ* (to eat) applies to the general category of things that are consumed, it occurs [in the sense of "eating"] even with respect to barley-gruel (*yavāgū*).

Although it should have been stated as "bhujo bhakṣye," this is a formal derivation (nipātana) for the sake of conventional usage (rūḍhi). This is so that [the suffix] applies when the object (karman) is food to be consumed (abhyavahārya), but not when it is something to be protected; for example, *bhogyā apūpāḥ*, which means "cakes to be guarded" (i.e., kept safe). Regarding the word "dadat": [it is derived from the root *dā* with the suffix *śatṛ*].

The root *ḍudāñ* is used in the sense of "giving" (*dāne*; Dhātupāṭha 1091). By the rule *liṅarthe leṭ* [Pāṇini 3.4.97], the *leṭ* suffix is employed. The substitution of *jhi* by *ant* [7.1.3] occurs; then, by *ādiprabhṛtibhyaḥ* [3.4.97], there is the elision of the *i* of *leṭ*. By *āḍajādīnām* [3.4.94], the augment *āṭ* is added, followed by the *śap* suffix. Because this belongs to the *juhotyādi* class, there is *ślu* (elision of *śap*). By *ślau* [6.1.10], reduplication occurs. Then, the elision of the final consonant of the *saṃyoga* [8.2.23] takes place. Finally, by *ṅamo hrasvādaci ṅamuṇ nityam* [8.3.32], the *ṅmuṭ* augment is added. Thus, we have: *somo dadad gandharvāya*.
The suffix *sip* is applied to the root *dadāti*, while the remainder is as previously explained.
Regarding the phrase "yad agnir agnaye dadāt": when *dadāt* is established, does [the rule] "akaḥ savarṇe dīrghaḥ" [Pāṇini 6.1.101] apply for the lengthening of the vowel? The remainder is as before.

If, even after the augment *āṬ* (or *yaṅ* according to the Prāṃu reading) has been applied and the elision (*lopa*) has occurred, the form *dadāt* is still established, for what purpose then is the word *vā* stated? To this he says: "In that case," and so forth.

This might be the case: why then is the inclusion of the term *vāk* (speech) not appropriate for the sake of clarity, since there is no possibility of doubting the non-establishment of the form *vadādīnām*? To this he says: "For this," and so forth. This is easy to understand.

Regarding "it sharpens" (*niśyati*), and so forth: the root *śo* means "to thin out" (Dhātupāṭha 1145); *cho* means "to cut" (this root does not appear in the printed edition of the Dhātupāṭha, which lists 1146 as *cho chedane*); *do* means "to break apart" (Dhātupāṭha 1148); and *ṣo* means "to bring to an end" (Dhātupāṭha 1147).

Now, for what purpose is it stated as "in *śyan*" (*śyani*), rather than simply stating "in *śit*" (*śiti*)? For if it were stated thus, the elision would occur only in *śyan*, since no other suffix beginning with *ś* exists after a root ending in *o*. Furthermore, the rule would be more concise in this way. In that case, the mention of *śit* in [Pāṇini 7.3.75] *ṣṭhivuklamucamāṃ śiti* need not be made, as this very term will be understood there by context. True, it would indeed be established; however, there would be a burden of comprehension (*pratipatti-gaurava*). Therefore, "in *śyan*" is stated in order to avoid such a burden of comprehension.

Regarding the term *otaḥ*: the inclusion of the long vowel marker (*t* in *ta*) is for the sake of ease of pronunciation, for there is nothing else that could be excluded by it, nor anything else that could be prescribed. [Examples: *adhukṣātām*, *adhukṣāthām*.

In the case of *duh* (to milk), the suffixes are *luṅ* and *cliḥ*. By the rule *svaritañitaḥ* [Pāṇini 1.3.72], the Ātmanepada endings are applied: *ātām* and *āthām*. For the *cliḥ*, there is the substitution of *ksa* by the rule *śāla igupadhādaniṭaḥ ksaḥ* [Pāṇini 3.1.45]. Its elision occurs by this rule [1.1.52]. By the rule *dāderghātorghaḥ* [Pāṇini 8.2.32], the letter *h* becomes *dh*. By the rule beginning with *ekāco vaśo bhaṣ* [Pāṇini 8.2.37], the *bhaṣ*-substitution occurs—the *h* becomes *dh*. By the rule *khari ca* [Pāṇini 8.4.54], there is *cartva* (the substitution of a voiceless stop)—the *dh* becomes *k*. By the rule *iṇkoḥ* [Pāṇini 8.3.57], there is *ṣatva* (the substitution of *ṣ*)—resulting in *adhikṣi*. This is the third person singular (*uttamapuruṣaikavacana*) with the augment *iṭ*.
Regarding *adhukṣat*: there is the suffix *tip*, and by [Pāṇini 3.4.100] *itaśca*, there is the elision of the *ik* vowel. Regarding *adhukṣatām*.

By the rule *tasthasthamipām* [Pāṇini 3.4.101], *tas* is replaced by *tām*. The inclusion of the letter *k* is for the purpose of excluding cases such as *haṃsau*, *haṃsāḥ*, *vatsau*, and *vatsāḥ*. The roots *duh* (to milk, DhP 1014), *diha* (to smear, DhP 1015), *liha* (to lick, DhP 1016), and *guhū* (to conceal, DhP 896)—all these are marked with the *svarita* accent.
Because they are *svaritet*, by the rule *svaritajitaḥ kartrabhiprāye kriyāphale* [Pāṇini 1.3.72], they take the *ātmanepada* endings when the fruit of the action accrues to the agent.

Regarding *adugdha*: the substitution of *bh* is as before; by [Pāṇini 8.2.40], *t* is replaced by *dh*; and by [Pāṇini 8.4.53], *dh* is replaced by *g*. Regarding *adugdhām*: [the same process applies].
*thās*, as before; *dhatvādi* (beginning with *dha*). "Adugdhvam": [this is] *dhvam*.
"aduhvahi"— the suffix *vahi*; "adigdha."
As before, there is the substitution of *gh* for *t* and so forth.

Regarding the term "alīḍha": the *h* of *hata* becomes *ḍh* by [Pāṇini 8.2.31], as before; then there is the substitution of *dh* for *t* and the substitution of *ṣṭu* for *th* by [Pāṇini 8.3.13]; finally, a long vowel is substituted by [Pāṇini 6.3.110] and the following rules.
Regarding "nyagūḍha":
this also is the same as the preceding [case]. Regarding "vyatyapukṣata": [this is explained as follows].
The root *puṣ* in the sense of "nourishing" (Dhātupāṭha 1182) is preceded by the prefix *vyati*.
The middle voice (*ātmanepada*) is applied according to [Pāṇini 1.3.14], *kartari karmaṇyatihāre*, and the change of *ṣ* to *k* is applied according to [Pāṇini 8.2.41].
Thus, we have *ajukṣāmahi*.
[The author] says: "Now, what is the purpose of including the mention of *luk*, given that the term *lopa* continues [from the previous rule]? He replies:

"While *lopa* is understood [to carry over]," for if *lopa* were prescribed by carrying over the mention of *lopa* itself, then [by the rule] *alo 'ntyasya* [Pāṇini 1.1.52], it would apply only to the final [element].

However, it applies to every [suffix] because the designation *luk* is prescribed for the non-appearance of a suffix. Therefore, the mention of *luk* was made so that the elision (*lopa*) of every *k*-suffix might occur.
[The example is] "bahvartham."
The meaning is: "for the sake of the dual number of the first person.
That which has an external object as its purpose is described as such.
Now, why does it not serve another purpose? To this he says: "But in other cases," and so forth.
Whatever *ātmanepada* [suffix] begins with a dental is necessarily preceded by a *jhal* [consonant].
In that case, once the final vowel *a* has been elided, the desired form is indeed established by the elision of the *s* according to Pāṇini 8.2.26.

One might object: "In other cases as well, it would not be established without an elision (*luk*), because when the elision of the *s* is to be performed following the elision of the vowel *a*, the status of being like the original (*sthānivadbhāva*) applies by virtue of Pāṇini 1.1.57. To this he replies: "There is no status of being like the original even for the elision of the vowel *a*."
Why is it not so? He says: "In the absence of what precedes, [a substitute] is not like the original (sthānivadbhāva).

Therefore, the mention of *luk* (elision) is not for the sake of anything else, but rather for the sake of the word *vah* itself. For here, because [the suffix] begins with *hrasva-hal* (a short vowel followed by a consonant), the elision of the *s* [of *vah*] by Pāṇini 6.1.68 would not occur; thus, the form is not established. [Objection: But even if the mention of *luk* were made, there should still be no *luk* in *vah*, because it does not begin with a dental (*adantyādi*); for the letter *v* is both dental and labial (*dantyauṣṭhya*), and it is not included under the term "dental. To this he replies: "Even though it is dental-labial," and so forth.
He states the reason for this very point with the words "If," and so forth:
if the dental-labial *d* were not included by the mention of "dental" (*dantya*), then he would have said "those two" (*tau*) instead of "the dental" (*dantya*).
Even if those two [the labials] were mentioned, everything intended would indeed be established.

For there is no other dental [consonant] belonging to the *ātmanepada* suffixes besides that [s]. Therefore, even the letter *v*, though being both dental and labial, is included by the mention of "dentals. In this regard, the following objection is raised: as for what was stated—that "elsewhere, when the elision of the dental [s] has been performed according to [Pāṇini 8.2.26], the desired result is indeed established through the elision of the *sakāra*"—that is incorrect. For by the rule [Pāṇini 8.2.26], the elision of the *sakāra* alone is not prescribed; rather, it is the elision of the *sic* [suffix]. Indeed, he will state in that very same place: "This is the elision of the *sic* itself. This is not so.

Since the mention of *sij* is intended as an indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*) for the substitutes beginning with *cli*, the meaning there should be understood as follows: the elision of the *s* occurs only when it belongs to that which is a substitute for *cli*. He says "of *śam* and the others," etc., because the plural number and the mention of *aṣṭan* indicate that the sense of "beginning with" (*ādi*) is understood.

The eight roots beginning with *śam* are: *śamu* (to become calm, DhP 1201); *tamu* (to desire, DhP 1202); *damu* (to become calm, DhP 1203); *śramu* (to exert oneself and to feel fatigue, DhP 1204); *kṣamu* (to endure, DhP 1206); *bhramu* (to wander or lack stability, DhP 1205); *klamu* (to be weary, DhP 1207); and *madī* (to rejoice, DhP 1208). The term *asyati* refers to the root *asu* (to throw, DhP 1209).

This is recited after the eight [roots]: "it wanders" (*bhramati*). Is this [form] derived by [the addition of] *śyan* according to the rule *vā bhrāśa-* (Pāṇini 3.1.70)? This is a counter-example for that alternative in which [the application of *śyan*] does not occur.

The inclusion of *śyan* is for the sake of clarity. For it is possible to carry forward the previously mentioned mention of *śan*—even though it is separated by the mention of *luk*—to this point by means of the "frog-leap" maxim (*maṇḍūkapluti-nyāya*). Regarding the roots: *ṣṭhivu* (DhP 1110) in the sense of spitting; *klamu* (DhP 1207) in the sense of exhaustion; and *camu*, *chamu*, *jamu*, *jhamu* (DhP 469–472) in the sense of eating, preceded by the prefix *ā*.
In the form *klāmati*, since there is an absence of *śyan* by virtue of the rule *vā bhrāśa-* (Pāṇini 3.1.70), the suffix *śap* is applied.
"The inclusion of *klam* is for the sake of [the suffix] *śa*;

it is not for the sake of *śyan*, because that is already established by the preceding rule. By stating 'of *cam* preceded by *āṅ*', etc., he shows that the mention of *cam* preceded by *āṅ* is intended so that [the suffix] does not apply to *cam* alone or when preceded by any other prefix. Thus, [he gives the example] *krāmati*."
The root *kram* (meaning "to step" or "to stride") is listed as number 473 in the Dhātupāṭha.
The form *ākramate* is preceded by the prefix *āṅ*.

The suffix *ātmanepada* is applied by [Pāṇini 1.3.40]. An objection is raised with the words "Come forth (*utkrāma*), come together (*saṅkrāma*)," and so on. From the root *kram* preceded by *ud-* and *sam-*, in the imperative (*loṭ*), the substitution of *hi* for *si* occurs according to [Pāṇini 3.4.87]: *sehir apicca*. When the *hi* is elided by [Pāṇini 6.4.105], the prohibition of the application of the suffix-characteristic (*pratyayalakṣaṇa*) applies by [Pāṇini 1.1.63]; consequently, in the forms "come forth" (*utkrāma*) and "come together" (*saṅkrāma*), the lengthening of the vowel would not occur. For when the *hi*—which causes the suffix-characteristic—is elided, it is impossible for the root *kram* to be followed by a *parasmaipada* suffix.

"This is not a fault," and so forth, is the rebuttal. One might object: "When a suffix is elided by *lumat*, the sequence [of operations] applies; therefore, in this case, only the two [roots] would be the *aṅga*. To this he says: "And *krami* is not the *aṅga*," because it is separated by the *śap* suffix.
"What then? It is 'śapi'. Because only *śap* exists there, separated [from the preceding element]. "He desires," "he goes," "he restrains."

Regarding the rule *kartari śap* [Pāṇini 3.1.68]: now, for what purpose is there the inclusion of the root *iṣ* in the sense of "desire" (Dhātupāṭha 1351), which is marked with the *udittva* indicator? To this he says: "*iṣeḥ*" and so forth.
This is so that the rule does not apply to the root *iṣ* meaning "to go" (Dhātupāṭha 1127) belonging to the Divādi class, as in the form *iṣyati*.

The root *iṣ* belonging to the kryādigaṇa, as seen in the Dhātupāṭha under the rule *iṣa ābhīkṣṇye* (1525), is not intended here; rather, it is the root *iṣ* with the marker *u* that is taken, so that [the substitution of *ś* for *ṣ*] does not occur in forms such as *iṣṇāti*. If so, for those who do not read the root *iṣ* as having the marker *u* (*udit*) here, would the substitution not also apply in *iṣyati* and *iṣṇāti*? To this he says: "But those who [do not read *iṣ* as *udit*]," and so forth. Those who do not read the root *iṣ* here as being distinguished by the marker *u*—in order to prevent the substitution of *ś* for *ṣ* in *iṣyati* and *iṣṇāti*—they carry forward the mention of the vowel (*ajgrahaṇa*) from rule 7.3.72.

Even while this [term *śit*] is being followed [in the rule], if by it the word *śit* is qualified—meaning "the substitution of *cha* occurs for *śit*, and in what kind of [suffix]? In one beginning with a vowel (*ajādau*)"—then, when the substitution of *hi* for the *sip* of the imperative (*loṭ*) of the root *iṣ* has been made, and subsequently the substitution of *śānac* for the *śnā* suffix has been made according to [Pāṇini 3.1.83], one might think that in the form *iṣaṇa*, the substitution of *cha* would certainly occur by the rule of "application to the beginning" (*tadādividhi*), based on the principle: "In a reference to a term beginning with a letter, a grammatical operation applies to that which begins with it" (Vyāḍiparibhāṣā 127). Anticipating this, he says:
"And they explain that this primary mention of the suffix (*anga-grahaṇa*) is qualified by the word *śit*"—that is, the substitution of *cha* occurs for a vowel, provided that the suffix is *śit*.
Furthermore, the predominance of the non-vowel (*ac*) [in the rule *aci*] is due precisely to its being qualified;
thus, in the phrase "and so being," etc.,
when this predominant element "non-vowel" (*ac*) is qualified by the term "before *śit*" (*śiti*), the rule of "beginning with that" (*tadādividhi*) does not apply.
What is the reason? He says: "In which there is a rule," and so forth.

It is not only the rule *tadanta-vidhāna* (Pāṇini 1.1.72) that is intended by means of a qualifier; rather, the rule *tadādi-vidhāna*—namely, *yasmin vidhis tadādāv algrahaṇe* (Vyāḍiparibhāṣā 127)—is also intended by means of a qualifier alone.
And because of the absence of that *tadādi-vidhi*, the substitution of *ch* does not occur in the word *aṣāṇa*.

Even though there is no rule prescribing that [the suffix] begins with *ta* (tadādividhi), why does the substitution of *cha* not occur for this vowel *ā*, which is the initial sound of the substitute *śānac*, when followed by a *śit* affix? To this he says: "For this... and so forth.
The letter *ś* is a marker (*anubandha*) of the entire complex, not of the vowel *ā*.

Therefore, the substitution of *ś* does not apply to a single vowel (*aj*), but rather to the entire cluster; thus, the change to *cch* does not occur. [The following are the roots: *pā* "to drink" (DhP 925), *ghrā* "to smell" (DhP 926), *dhmā* "in sound and contact with fire" (DhP 927), *ṣṭhā* "cessation of motion" (DhP 928), *mnā* "repetition" (DhP 929), *dāṇ* "giving" (DhP 930), *dṛśir* "seeing" (DhP 988).

The roots *ṛ* in the sense of "motion" and "attaining" (*dhātupāṭha* 936), *ṛ* and *sṛ* in the sense of "motion" (*dhātupāṭha* 1298, 1099); *śadlṛ* in the sense of "cutting" (*dhātupāṭha* 1428); *ṣadlṛ* in the sense of "falling" (*dhātupāṭha* 1427), which belongs to the Tudādigaṇa; and *ṣadlṛ* in the sense of "falling," "motion," and "exhaustion" (*dhātupāṭha* 854), which belongs to the Bhvādigaṇa—in place of these roots, the substitutes beginning with *piba* occur respectively.

But surely, since there are two roots *sad*, how can a one-to-one correspondence (*yathāsaṃkhyam*) not fail due to this disparity? This is not a fault; for indeed, the single root *sad* is mentioned twice for the sake of two different suffixes (*vikaraṇa*).
[Thus we have] "he sits" (*śīyate*), which takes the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) by [Pāṇini 1.3.60]. Or else, etc. [as follows].
Regarding the statement, "The root *pibati* would incur the fault of having its penultimate syllable unaccented," there is another solution:

if the initial acute accent were not prescribed as a nipātana (irregular formation), then, by the natural accent of the root (*dhātusvara*), the word would be oxytone; subsequently, when the suffix *śap* is added, the single-substitute (*ekadeśa*) rule [P. 6.1.97] would apply, resulting in an acute accent on the final syllable of the stem. Consequently, the form *pibati* would become a word with an acute accent on the middle syllable (*madhyodātta*). However, an initial acute accent (*ādyudātta*) is desired; therefore, the initial acute accent is prescribed as a nipātana so that this irregular accent may override the natural accent of the root.
Regarding the passage beginning with *sarttaḥ*:

"vega" means speed (*java*); that which possesses this is "vegin," and its state is "vegitā. In that sense of motion, they desire the substitution of *dhāv* for the root *sṛ*. It should be understood that this [substitution] is obtained through the application of the option (*vā*) from the rule *lugvā duhadiha* (Pāṇini 7.3.73), because that option is a fixed alternative (*vyavasthitavibhāṣā*).
The mention of *arttisarti* with the marker *śit* is solely for the purpose of indicating the verbal root (*dhātu*), not for the purpose of excluding the *yaṅ*-luṅ (the elision of the *yaṅ* suffix).

For in the case of *yaṅ*-luṅ, a suffix marked by *śit* cannot occur; does it not follow that [the suffix] is like *adādi* (belonging to the class beginning with *ad*)? No, because the elision (*luk*) of *śap* is prescribed for what is ordained after that [root].
If it is argued that the elision of *śap* will not occur by rule P. 7.4.78, we say no, because in the Vedic language (*chandas*) one follows exactly what is observed.

Because in the Vedic language (*chandas*), no usage of a form ending in *yaṅluk* is observed for roots beginning with *arti*. Regarding the statement "the root *jan* belonging to the *divādi* class is intended":
there are two roots *jan*—the *divādi* root *janī* in the sense of "manifestation" (Dhātupāṭha 1149) and the *juhotyādi* root *jana* in the sense of "birth" (Dhātupāṭha 1105).
Here, it is the *divādi* root that is intended, not the other.
For there cannot be a short vowel (*śit*) after that [root], because of the prescription of *ślu*.

He will state later the purpose for the long-vowel pronunciation. Regarding the statement, "Some desire [the root] *vlī* in the sense of 'going' up to *vṛt*," according to them, there should be no shortening for the two roots read after that—namely *vrī* in the sense of 'covering' (DhP 1504) and *bhrī* in the sense of 'fear' (DhP 1505)—[and thus they remain as] *vrīṇāti* and *bhrīṇāti*.

[Objection: Is not the formation of the *vṛt* (grouping) for the sake of completing the *lvādi* group? Otherwise, [if it were for the sake of the *pvādi* group] up to the end of the *gaṇa*, the state of having a *niṣṭhā*-nasal (*ṇatva*) would apply to those [consonants]. And if that *vṛt* were for the sake of completing the *lvādi* group, then it would be more appropriate for the *pvādi* group to extend only up to the end of the *gaṇa*. To this, he says: "The formation of the *vṛt," etc. The intention is that being for the sake of completing both groups is not contradicted by anything. [Objection: "Others," etc. The sense is that since the *lvādi* group follows immediately after, it is more logical that the formation of the *vṛt* is for the sake of completing that [specific] group.

For those who maintain this view, since *vṛ* (to choose) and *bhṛ* (to fear)—these two roots—must also possess a short vowel [in the present tense], as in *vṛṇāti* and *bhināti*, because both are included among the *pvādi* group;
[the opponent objects: "In the case of *jānāti*, a short vowel would result.
To this he replies: "Because of their inclusion in the *pvādi* group," starting with the rule *jñā-janor jā*.

If, when the substitute *jā* is applied, there were to be a short vowel (*hrasva*), then the long vowel pronunciation would be purposeless; one should have simply said *ja*. Therefore, by the force of the long vowel pronunciation, there will be no short vowel in the case of *jānāti*.

[Objection: But surely the long vowel pronunciation is for the sake of *janya*; for the form *jāyate* is not established merely by applying the substitute *ja* to the root *jan*. To this, he says: "Even when the substitute *ja* is applied," and so forth.

But for those [grammarians] who perform the formation of *vr̥t* (vowel-lengthening) for the sake of completing both groups, what is the purpose of pronouncing the long vowel in *jā*? Is it so that the long vowel may occur in *jānāti*? This is not the case; the long vowel will occur by [Pāṇini 7.3.101]. But is it not true that, according to the principle "when a rule has applied to a base (*aṅga*), there is no further application [of another rule] to that which has already been established" (Vyāḍi-Patañjali 38), it would not apply? This is not so; it is said "[to that which is] established," and when the substitute *ja* has been made, the base (*aṅga*) is not yet established, because it is unfit for usage. The long vowel is pronounced for the sake of ease of comprehension. [As in the example: *pramiṇanti*.
The substitution of *ṇ* [for *n*] occurs by the rule *hinu mīnā* [Pāṇini 8.4.15], and the elision of the vowel *ā* occurs by the rule *śnābhyastayor ātaḥ* [Pāṇini 6.4.112].

Here, the citation of the suffix *mīnāti* is for the purpose of including the root *mīñ hiṃsāyām* (Dhātupāṭha 1476) belonging to the *kryādi* class, so that the root *mīṅ hiṃsāyām* (Dhātupāṭha 1137) belonging to the *devādi* class might not be included.

The specific mention of *mīñaḥ* is made for the sake of variety. There are two roots, *ñimidā* "to moisten": one belonging to the Bhūvādigaṇa and the other to the Divādigaṇa (Dhātupāṭha 743 and 1243). Here, the one from the Divādigaṇa is intended; as for the other, because it is marked with an *ṅ*, the substitution of *guṇa* is already established by Pāṇini 7.3.86 (*śap* [is replaced] after [roots ending in] *ṅ*). Regarding the form *midyate*:

the ātmanepada suffix is applied by Pāṇini 1.3.13, and the *ik* [of the rule] qualifies the *aṅga* (stem) under discussion which is present here. Since a qualification implies that the rule applies to that which ends in the qualified element, he says: "ending in an *ik*" (*igantasya*), and so forth.
Regarding "ajuhavuḥ":

this is the *laṅ* [imperfect] tense; by the rule "sijabhyastavidabhyaśca" [Pāṇini 3.4.109], the suffix *jhi* is replaced by *jus*; there is *ślu*-elision of the *śap* [present marker]; and by the rule "ślau" [Pāṇini 6.1.10], reduplication occurs.
Regarding "abibhayuḥ": [the same analysis applies].
The root *ñibh* is used in the sense of "fear" (*bhaye*; Dhātupāṭha 1084). Regarding the form *abibharuḥ*:

the root *ḍubhṛñ* is used in the senses of "supporting" and "nourishing" (*dhāraṇapoṣaṇayoḥ*; Dhātupāṭha 1087); the substitution of *i* for the reduplicated syllable is applied by the rule *bhuñām it* (Pāṇini 7.4.76).
Regarding the forms *cinuyuḥ* and *sunuyuḥ*:
[the suffix] *liṅ* [is applied], followed by *yāsuṭ*, and then *jus* for *jhi* according to Pāṇini 3.4.108 and 6.1.96, resulting in the substitution of the subsequent form (*pararūpatva*).
As for the phrase "tatra nāprāpte" and so forth...
That which has the *sārvadhātuka* as its basis is called *sārvadhātukāśraya*. That prohibition for which the state of having the marker *ṅ* (*ṅittva*) is the cause is described in that way.

Since that [prohibition] would apply everywhere, including before *jusi*, this *guṇa* is commenced while that [prohibition] is not yet applicable; therefore, it will be a sublater of that [prohibition] alone, but not of that [prohibition] for which the state of having the marker *ṅ* is the cause based on *yāsuṭ*.
For here [the rule] is commenced regarding both what is already established and what is not yet established:
in cases such as *cinuyuḥ*, it concerns what is already established; in cases such as *ajuhavuḥ*, it concerns what is not yet established.
The particle *ca* serves for conjunction.
Is it not so that there is nothing else to be combined? He states the recurrence of this very definition;
therefore, it also applies to the negation of the original definition, as in "adīdhayuḥ."

The root *dīdhīṅ* is listed [in the Dhātupāṭha] as "to shine" and "to play" (No. 1076). In the *laṅ* [tense], by transposition (*vyatyaya*), the *parasmaipada* [ending] is used; the suffix *jhi* follows, which receives the designation *abhyasta* according to Pāṇini 6.1.6. By Pāṇini 3.4.109, *jhi* is replaced by *jus*. Because the root belongs to the *adādi* class, there is elision (*luk*) of the *śap* suffix.

Then, the substitution of *guṇa* [for the *ik* vowels] would have been applicable by Pāṇini 7.3.84, but that is prohibited by Pāṇini 1.1.5. That prohibition, however, is overridden by Pāṇini 1.1.6 when the rule is re-applied, because the particle *ca* has the sense of inclusion (*samuccaya*). Thus we obtain the forms *cetā* and *stetā*, formed with the suffix *tṛc*.

The *anaṅ* substitution [of *an* for *as*] occurs by the rule *ṛduśanaspurodaṃso'nehasāñca* [Pāṇini 7.1.94], and the lengthening of the vowel occurs by the rule *sarvanāmasthāne* [Pāṇini 6.4.8] and so forth. [Question: "Why is it said, 'before a *sārvadhātuka* or *ārdhadhātuka* suffix'? [Answer: It is thought thus: one should have stated "before a suffix" (*pratyaye*) or "before *saṅ*" (*saṅi*). If this were stated, then in forms such as *bhavati*, the *guṇa* substitution would already be established. The term *saṅ* is a technical abbreviation (*pratyāhāra*) beginning with the *sakāra* of *san* and ending with the *ṅakāra* of *mahiṅ*.
In the word *agnitvam*, the suffix *tva* is applied according to [Pāṇini 5.1.119]. In the word *agnikāmyati*:
> [[3.1.9]] Thus [is formed] *kāmyac*.
Regarding "if" (*yadi*) and so forth:
if it were stated that [the suffix] is a *pratyaya* (affix), then it would apply even to *tvā-kāmya* and *cora*.

Moreover, if it were said that [the suffix] *saṅ* is prescribed, it would apply to the *kāmyac* suffix as well, because that too is included within the *pratyāhāra*. [Examples: "jāgarayati" (he causes to wake) [is formed with] *ṇic*;
"jāgarakaḥ" (a wakeful one).
The suffix *ṇvul* [is applied] as in "sādhujāgarī";
the suffix *ṇini* is used in the sense of habitual disposition (*tācchīlya*).

In the expression *jāgarañjāgaram*, the suffix *ṇamul* is applied according to Pāṇini 3.4.22 (*ābhīkṣṇye ṇamul*) because of the sense of repetition; the doubling of the word occurs according to the Vārttika 887 (*ābhīkṣṇye dve bhavataḥ*). Thus, it means "he remains awake repeatedly."

The suffix *dhañ* is used in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāva*). These are examples in the scope of the rule for *vṛddhi*: *jāgaritā* and *jagaritavān* are examples in the scope of the prohibition [of *vṛddhi*].

What, then, is the reason that examples are presented specifically regarding the domain of *vṛddhi* and the domain of prohibition? To this he says: "In the domain of *vṛddhi* and in the domain of prohibition," and so forth.
Elsewhere than in the domains of *vṛddhi* and prohibition, *guṇa* is established by the preceding rule (*pūrvasūtra*).
Therefore, this *guṇa* is commenced for the sake of the domains of non-*vṛddhi* and prohibition; hence, only examples belonging to those specific domains are presented.

In forms such as *jāgarayati*, once the *guṇa* substitution has been applied and the replacement by *r* (*raparatva*) has occurred, someone might have the misconception that the *vṛddhi* substitution [prescribed by P. 7.2.116] must then take effect. To dispel this, he says: "When that [guṇa] has been performed," and so forth.

What, then, is the reason why it does not occur when that has been performed? He says: "For if," and so forth. If, even after this *guṇa* has been performed, the *vṛddhi* [of P. 7.2.116] were to occur, then forms such as *jāgarayati* would not exist; and thus the *guṇa* would be rendered purposeless, because the form would already be established by the *vṛddhi* [of P. 7.2.115] itself.
Regarding the rule *ciṇṇaloca* and so forth:
what is the purpose of this prohibition concerning *ciṇ* and *ṇal*? It is so that the *vṛddhi* [vowel] may be heard.

For if, even after *guṇa* has been applied, the rule *ata upadhāyāḥ* [Pāṇini 7.2.116] were to apply, the prohibition of *ciṇ* and *ṇal* would be useless; let there be *guṇa* here, and even when that exists, the *vṛddhi* must again take place by the rule *ata upadhāyāḥ*, and thus the hearing of the *vṛddhi* will occur.
Regarding "ajāgāri":

[the suffix] *luṅ*, [then] *cli*; by the rule "ciṇ bhāvakarmaṇoḥ" [Pāṇini 3.1.66], *cli* is replaced by *ciṇ*; [then] by the rule "ato lopaḥ" [Pāṇini 6.4.48], there is elision (*luk*) of the letter *t*.
[The forms] "jāgṛtaḥ" and "jāgṛthaḥ" [are derived similarly].

By the rule *laṭ, tasthasau, tayoḥ* [Pāṇini 3.4.78], the marker *ṅit* is applied; due to the root belonging to the *adādi* class, there is elision (*luk*) of the *śnā* suffix. Regarding the statement, "Some explain that the vowel *i* in *vī* is for the sake of pronunciation," what is it that is desired to be established by this, such that they explain it in this way? He says: "*kvasāv apa*" and so forth.
If the *vi* belonging to the entire complex were to be understood here in the same way as a suffix (*pratyaya*), where would this prohibition of *guṇa* not apply? However,

if the letter *i* is for the sake of pronunciation and this is the apprehension of the mere phoneme (*varṇa*) itself, then by the rule "where there is an injunction, it applies to that which begins with [the element mentioned] when there is an apprehension of what precedes" (Vyāḍiparibhāṣā 127), this prohibition of *guṇa* is established even in that case, as in *jajāgṛvān*.

The substitution of *kvasu* for *liṭ* occurs by [Pāṇini 3.2.107]; the augment *num* is added by [Pāṇini 7.1.70], resulting in *jajāgṛvān*. The substitution of *kvasu* for *liṭ* occurs by [Pāṇini 3.2.107]; the augment *num* is added by [Pāṇini 7.1.70]; lengthening occurs by [Pāṇini 6.4.10]; and the elision of the final consonant (*saṃyogāntalopa*) and the following vowel (*halṅyādi*) occur.
By the statement "some," it is implied that others do not consider the [final *n*] to be for the purpose of pronunciation.

They think as follows: "The suffix *kvasu* is Vedic (*chāndasa*), and in the Veda, even [suffixes] that are *sārvadhātuka* are treated as such; because of the rule [Pāṇini 1.2.4], the prohibition will occur precisely due to its being marked with the *ṅit* indicator, as in the case of *ajāgaruḥ* and so forth. Thus they think: "Because of the *ṅit* indicator [in the rule Pāṇini 7.3.85], the prohibition will occur."
Regarding the passage beginning with *ajāgaruḥ*:

he thinks as follows—this [rule] *aviciṇṇalṅitsu* is a prohibitive negation (*prasajyapratiṣedha*), meaning "it does not occur in the presence of *vici*, *ṇal*, or *ṅit*. Consequently, even in the case of *ajāgaruḥ*, there would result a prohibition of the *guṇa* substitution that is otherwise applicable by the rule *jusi ca* [Pāṇini 7.3.83]. Likewise, in the case of *evamahaṃ jajāgare*, when the *ṇit*-designation is absent according to the rule [7.1.91], a *guṇa* is desired by the rule *sārvadhātukārdhadhātukayoḥ* [7.3.84]; yet, due to this [proposed] prohibition, that *guṇa* would not occur.
"No, because there is no negation"—this is the rebuttal.
This is not a fault; why? Because there is no negation.
The meaning is that it is a non-presuppositional negation (*aprasajyapratiṣedha*).

If it is not a *prasajya-pratiṣedha* (absolute negation), what then is it? To this he says: "In the rule *aviciṇṇalṅitsu*, this is a *paryudāsa* (relative negation). For in an absolute negation, there would be a prohibition of even that which is applicable by another rule; this is not the case in a relative negation.

Indeed, in a relative negation, a *guṇa* (strengthening) is prescribed elsewhere than before *vi*, *ciṇ*, *ṇal*, and *ṅit* suffixes, but it is not prohibited within those *vi*, *ciṇ*, *ṇal*, and so forth.

And this is a *paryudāsa* (an exclusion). Therefore, the *guṇa* substitution indeed occurs both in the case of *jus* and in the *ṇal* [affix]. Even assuming, for the sake of argument, that it is a *prasajya-pratiṣedha* (a simple prohibition), he states another solution, beginning with "Or rather" (*atha vā*).

Is this because of proximity (*ānantarya*), according to the principle that "a rule or a prohibition applies to what is immediately preceding" (Vyāḍipāda 19)? This is a prohibition of the application [of *guṇa*] that would otherwise occur by the rule *jāgraḥ* [6.1.10]; however, the application that occurs through another grammatical rule such as *jusi ca* [7.3.83] is not prohibited.
Thus, we have the form *ajāgaruḥ*.

The designation *abhyasta* [is applied] by [Pāṇini 6.1.6]: *laṅ, >*. By [Pāṇini 3.4.109]: *sijabhyastavidibhyaśca*, the suffix *jhi* becomes *jus*. Regarding the two [rules], "of a stem ending in *pu*" and "of that which has a light penultimate (*laghūpadha*)": both are *bahuvrīhi* compounds—namely, "that of which the end is *pu*" is so stated, and "that of which the penultimate is light" is *laghūpadha*. [Examples are] *bhettā*, *chettā*.
