Now, one might object: since the designation *guru* (heavy) applies when there is immediate succession between a consonant at the beginning of an affix and a constituent of the stem [by Pāṇini 1.4.11], the designation *laghu* (light) is sublated; therefore, *guṇa* substitution should not occur here. To this he says: "Of the beginning of an affix," etc.

The very purpose of making the *kit* markers of the suffixes *knū* and *san* (in rules such as Pāṇini 3.2.140 and 1.2.10) is this: so that there may be no *guṇa* substitution in forms such as *gṛdhnuḥ* and *vibhatsati*. If the *laghūpadha-guṇa* were not to occur when there is immediate sequence between a consonant at the beginning of a suffix and a consonant that is a member of the stem (*aṅga*), then he [Pāṇini] would not have made them *kit*; yet he has done so. Therefore, by making *knū* and *san* *kit*, it is indicated that the *laghūpadha-guṇa* is not precluded even when there is immediate sequence between a consonant of the suffix and a consonant of the stem.

But would not the *kit* designation of *san* be for the purpose of preventing the augment *ām* in forms such as *sisṛkṣati*? This is not so; for if this were the intended purpose, he would have formulated the prohibition in that very context as: "In the case of *sṛj* and *dṛś*, when followed by a *jhal* suffix, there is *am*, provided *san* is not *kit*.
Therefore, the *kit* designation of *san* is indeed an indicator (*jñāpaka*) that the rule [Pāṇini 7.3.86] prescribing *guṇa* for a light penultimate vowel applies here.

This being the case, when rule 1.1.3 is present, a single *guṇa* substitution would apply wherever [the condition] exists; consequently, it would also apply here in the word *bhinatti*, because the base (*aṅga*) has a light penultimate vowel (*laghūpadha*). Nor can it be argued that—by virtue of rule 1.1.7—the designation *saṃyoga* being present, this [base] will not have a light penultimate vowel, and thus the *guṇa* will not occur.

Has this not already been made known—that when there is immediate succession between two consonants (*hal*) that are parts of a stem (*aṅga*), the *guṇa* substitution for a light penultimate vowel (*laghūpadha*) is not excluded? To this he says: "And here, the penultimate (*upadhā*)... and so forth.

For, because of the presence of the rule regarding *ik* vowels (*ik-paribhāṣā*), only a vowel (*ic*) is understood as the penultimate here, since it has been brought to mind by that rule. Therefore, in the case of *bhinatti*, there is no *guṇa*; for in this instance, the penultimate of the stem is not an *ik* vowel, but rather the letter *a*.
Regarding the phrase "But others say" (*apare tu*), and so forth:

The connection with what is to be stated here is that they explain the meaning of the sūtra. [In the term] *puganta*, *puk* is the end (*anta*); the compound is formed by the split of the rule (*yogavibhāga*) "after a seventh-case word" (Pāṇini 2.1.40).
This word *anta* denotes a part; thus, the meaning is "that which is a part following *puk*."

Of what is it a member (*avayava*)? Because of the continued application (*anuvṛtti*) of the term "of a stem" (*aṅgasya*) and because of the mention of *puk*, it refers to a stem that possesses the augment *puk*.

It should not, however, be understood as referring only to that which begins with a short vowel (*ik*), as that would be restricted by the technical rule (*paribhāṣā*) concerning stems ending in *puk*. [The compound] *laghvī upadhā* means "a light penultimate vowel" (*laghūpadhā*).
This is a descriptive compound (*viśeṣaṇasamāsa*).
Regarding the rule "pugantalaghūpadha," this is a collective copulative compound (*samāhāradvandva*).
Regarding the phrase "the meaning of the sūtra":
the term "meaning of the sūtra" (*sūtrārtha*) refers to only a portion of the sūtra’s meaning, for the meaning of the sūtra is not exhausted by this much alone, as it remains incomplete.

This incompleteness arises because the statement "there is guna substitution for a root ending in a *puk* affix and for that [root] which has a light penultimate vowel" expresses only a single part of the sūtra’s full meaning.
"They describe" means "they explain. This is for the purpose of ensuring that the *guṇa* substitution does not occur in the case of the word *bhinatti*.
For in this sense of the Sūtra, [if it were taken as a Bahuvrīhi], the fault of "guṇa" (vṛddhi substitution) would undesirably apply to the word *bhinatti*.

If a Bahuvrīhi were not intended here, then for whatever vowel (*ik*) belonging to the stem—which is the referent of the other member of the compound—wherever that [vowel] might be situated, the fault of "guṇa" would undesirably apply.

If a Bahuvrīhi were indeed intended, then for whatever vowel (*ik*) belonging to the stem—which is the referent of the other member of the compound—wherever that [vowel] might be situated, the fault of "guṇa" would undesirably apply.

But this fault does not apply in the case of a *tatpuruṣa* compound; for there, the stem (*aṅga*) is qualified by two light vowels (*laghūpadha*), and thus the *guṇa* substitution is prescribed for that [vowel] alone—namely, "the *guṇa* occurs for that *ik* which is a light vowel of the stem. In the word *bhinatti*, the light vowel of the stem is not that [vowel], and although that [vowel *i*] is light, it is not the *upadhā*.
Therefore, when a *tatpuruṣa* is resorted to, there is no occasion for *guṇa* here.

This applies specifically by the rule *sārvadhātukārdhadhātukayoḥ*: *agnicit-tvam*, *agnicit-kāmyati*. The mention of *puganta* (roots ending in *pu* or *g*) is for the sake of [strengthening] a light penultimate vowel (*laghūpadha*): as in *nenijāni*, *vevijāni*, and *pariveviṣāṇi*.

From the roots *ṇijir* (Dhātupāṭha 1093) meaning "to purify" or "to wash," *vijir* (Dhātupāṭha 1094) meaning "to separate," and *viṣu* (Dhātupāṭha 1095) meaning "to pervade"— from these, the *loṭ* [imperative] mood, the *mip* suffix, the augment *aṭ*, the substitution of *ślu* for *śap*, reduplication by the rule *ślau*, and the *guṇa* substitution for the reduplicated syllable by the rule *abhyāsasya guṇaḥ* [Pāṇini 7.4.75] result in the forms *anenijam*, *avevijam*, and *paryaveṣiṣam*. In the *laṅ* [imperfect], the substitution of *am* for *mip* occurs by the rule *tasthasthamipāṃ tāntantāmaḥ* [Pāṇini 3.4.101].
Regarding the word *vedāni*: the root *vid* means "to know" (*dhātupāṭha* 1064).
As before, the imperative suffixes (*loṭ*) and so forth are applied as appropriate; because it belongs to the *ad*-class, there is elision (*luk*) of the *śap* augment.
Regarding the form *nenekti*: [the suffix] *laṭ*, [then] *tip*; by [Pāṇini 8.2.30], there is *kutva* (the substitution of *k* for *n*).

Now, what is the purpose of including the term *pit* [in the rule], since when there is *ṅittva* by [Pāṇini 1.2.4], a prohibition must apply by [Pāṇini 1.1.5]? And yet, there is no distinction between these two prohibitions. To this, he says: "The inclusion of *pit*... [is for the following reason].
He will state this [sūtra] as 7.3.92; the mention of *pit* is for the purpose that [the rule] should apply when there is a *pit* suffix, and not when there is no *pit*.
For example: *nineja* (he has led), which is the *liṭ* [perfect tense].
And that [suffix] is designated as *ārdhadhātuka* by the rule *liṭ ca* [Pāṇini 3.4.115].
[The form] *juhavāni* [is derived from] the root *hu* "to give" (Dhātupāṭha 1083).
The suffixes *loṭ* and so forth are as before;
"ajuhoṣam" likewise has the suffixes *laṅ* and so forth as before.

In this context, because the rule *laghūpadhasya* [Pāṇini 7.3.86] is understood as a governing rule (*anuvṛtti*), the prohibition does not apply to that *guṇa* which is prescribed for a stem ending in *i* by the rule *sarvadhātukārdhadhātukayoḥ* [Pāṇini 7.3.84]. Regarding the statement "*bahulaṃ chandasi vaktavyam*" (it should be stated that [the prohibition] is frequent in the Vedic language), the meaning is that this point must be explained as signifying that in the domain of the Veda, the prohibition of *guṇa* occurs frequently.

Regarding this, the explanation is as follows: here, this sūtra is divided into two rules (*yoga*s). The first rule is "na" (not); the second is "abhyastasyāci piti sārvadhātuke" (in the case of a reduplicated root, before a *pit* sārvadhātuka suffix beginning with a vowel), and the word "na" is understood to carry over (*anuvartate*) into this second rule. Furthermore, this second rule is intended to indicate that the scope of the preceding rule is not universal. Consequently, there will be a frequent prohibition (*pratiṣedha*) in the Vedic language (*chandas*). For example: *jujoṣat*.

The root *juṣ* is used in the sense of "serving" or "enjoying" (*pratisevanāyām*; Dhātupāṭha 1288). [In the formation of the word *juṣasva*: the suffix *leṭ* with the ending *tip* is applied; by [Pāṇini 3.4.94], the augment *aṭ* is added; because it belongs to the *tudādi* class, the suffix *śa* is applied; by [Pāṇini 7.4.78], this *śa* undergoes *ślu*-elision; by [Pāṇini 6.1.10], reduplication (*dvirvacana*) occurs due to the presence of *ślu*;
and the *guṇa* substitution of the light penultimate vowel (*laghūpadhaguṇa*) takes place.

If one maintains that there is a prohibition of *guṇa* for a reduplicated (*abhyasta*) root when followed by a *pit* sārvadhātuka suffix, [then] since the shortening of the penultimate vowel (*upadhā-hrasvatva*) is desired in forms such as *paspaśāte*, *cakāśīti*, and *vāvaśīt*, that would not be obtained. Therefore, one must state that for reduplicated roots there is only the shortening of the penultimate vowel, and not a prohibition of *guṇa*; for if there were shortening, forms such as *nenijāni* and so on would be established, as would *paspaśāte* and so on. To one who might raise this objection, he replies with "paspaśāte" and so forth.
If someone should object: "How is it that forms such as *nenijāni* and so forth are established, as well as *paspaśāte* and so forth?"—to him he replies with the words beginning with "*paspaśāte*."

The verbal root *spāś* (the reading *spāś* is found in the Prātipadika-pāṭha) indeed exists as a distinct root listed in the Gaṇapāṭha. From it, the suffix *yaṅ* is applied; by [Pāṇini 2.4.74], there is elision (*luk*) of that suffix; then reduplication occurs; by [Pāṇini 7.4.61], all consonants except the first (*khayaḥ śeṣaḥ*) remain; once the shortening of the reduplicated syllable has been performed, by [Pāṇini 7.4.83], lengthening occurs; by [Pāṇini 3.1.85], through a transposition of sounds (*varṇavyatyaya*), the penultimate vowel and the vowel of the reduplicated syllable become short; then the suffix *leṭ* is added; and by transposition itself, the Ātmanepada voice is used; finally, the augment *āṭ* is added, resulting in *cākaśīti*.

From the root *kāśṛ* in the sense of "shining" (Dhātupāṭha 1162), the substitution of *cu* for the reduplicated syllable occurs by [Pāṇini 7.4.62], followed by the suffix *tip*; the augment *iṭ* is optionally applied by [Pāṇini 7.3.94].
Thus we have *vāvaśīti*.
From the root *vāśṛ* in the sense of "sound" (Dhātupāṭha 1163), the remainder is to be understood as before, according to the appropriate rules.

Regarding the statement "In *paspaśāte*, there is shortening of the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*)," the word "and" (*ca*) implies that there is also shortening of the penultimate vowel (*upadhā*). In other instances, however, there is only shortening of the penultimate vowel, not shortening of the reduplicated syllable.
"Or [it could be] from other verbal roots (*prakṛtyantara*).

[The roots] *spaś* in the sense of "afflicting or touching" (Dhātupāṭha 887), *kaś* in the sense of "moving or sitting" (Dhātupāṭha 1024), and *vaś* in the sense of "desire" (Dhātupāṭha 1080)—these are other verbal roots that have a short vowel as their penultimate letter (*hrasvopadha*). Therefore, these forms belong to these very roots. Consequently, let it remain exactly as it was stated [in the original rule]. [Regarding the form] *abhūt*: [it is derived from the root *bhū*].
There is elision (*luk*) of *sic* by the rule "the elision of *sic* after roots ending in *gā*, *sthā*, etc.

[Pāṇini 2.4.77]. Regarding "suvāvahai" and "suvāmahai": the root is *ṣūṅ* (meaning "to release the fetus of a living being," Dhātupāṭha 1031). In the imperative (*loṭ*), the suffixes *vahimahiṅ* are applied; the *ṭi* portion is replaced by *e* [Pāṇini 3.4.79]; *e* is replaced by *ai* [Pāṇini 3.4.93]; because the root begins with a vowel (*ādi*), there is elision of *śap* [Pāṇini 3.4.92]; and *āṭ* is prefixed [Pāṇini 6.4.71], followed by the replacement of *u* by *uvaṅ* according to the rule "in place of *u* following a vowel, before a suffix beginning with a vowel, in verbal roots and dhātus" [Pāṇini 6.4.77].

Now, why is the introduction made of *sū* belonging to the first class (*adādi*), and not of *sū* and *sū* belonging to the sixth (*tudādi*) and fourth (*divādi*) classes respectively? To this he says: “of *sū*, which has the *luṅ* suffix,” and so forth.

But surely, by the paribhāṣā regarding those with the *luṅ* suffix (*vyā.pa.* 50), the inclusion of the *śap*-suffix-bearing *ṣū* ‘to impel’ from the sixth class and the *śyan*-suffix-bearing *ṣūṅ* ‘the birth of living beings’ from the fourth class would be appropriate? To this he says: “of *sūti* and *sūyati*,” and so forth.
Because of the mention of the locative case ending *-tiṅ-i*, there ought to be a prohibition regarding an immediately following *tiṅ* (verbal suffix).

Furthermore, no *tiṅ* can possibly follow immediately after *sū-* or *sūyati-*, because they are separated by a *vikaraṇa* (verbal suffix). Therefore, the intention is that those two are not included here; rather, it is appropriate to understand the root *sū-* alone as being intended.

It might be argued: "Since the authority of the verbal suffix (*vacana*) prevails, even when there is an intervention by a *vikaraṇa*, the prohibition will still apply; therefore, it is appropriate to include only those two [roots]. To this he says: "Of the *vikaraṇa* alone," and so forth.

For in the case of those two [roots], the *kit*-status of the *vikaraṇa* is established by the rule *tayoḥ...* (P. 1.2.4), and the prohibition is already accomplished by the rule *tatra...* (P. 1.1.5). Thus, the inclusion of those two would be purposeless; therefore, they are not included here. [The example] is "bhavati."
Because of the mention of *tiṅ* [in the rule], this prohibition does not apply here when *śap* follows a *tiṅ* suffix; for example,
*vyatibhaviṣīṣṭa*, which is the *liṅ* used in the sense of benediction (*āśis*).

And that [suffix] is designated as *ārdhadhātuka* by [Pāṇini 3.4.116]; [the suffix] *sīyuṭ*; the *ātmanepada* by [Pāṇini 1.3.14], "in the sense of the agent when there is a reciprocal action"; [then] *suṭ*, *ṣatva*, and *ṣṭutva*. Regarding the words "atha" and so forth:
the point is that since the rule "when the base is mentioned, the form ending in *yaṅluk* is also included" (Vyāḍipañjikā 79) applies, the prohibition must also apply there [to the *yaṅluk* form].
In the form *bobhavīti*,
there is the *guṇa* substitution for the reduplication according to [Pāṇini 7.4.82].
Regarding the phrase "from the indicator" (*jñāpakāt*) and so forth:

If this prohibition were to apply even in the case of *yaṅ*-elision (*yaṅluk*), the author would not have made an irregular derivation (*nipātana*) for the purpose of preventing *guṇa*; yet he has done so. Therefore, it indicates that this prohibition does not apply when there is *yaṅ*-elision. When *guṇa* is about to occur, the rule for *vṛddhi* is commenced.
In forms such as *yauti*, the elision of *śap* is as previously stated. [The example is] *sunoti*.
The suffix *śnu* [is applied];
"yavāni" is the imperative (*loṭ*).
The third person singular ending:
*yutaḥ*, *rutaḥ*. [This is formed by] the present tense marker (*laṭ*) and the suffix *tas*.
The inclusion of the long vowel *ā* (in the term *tapara*) is for the purpose that [the rule] should not apply in the case of *sūtrī*.

Now, why does it not apply in the case of *api stuyād rājānam*, since here too there is *yāsuṭ*, which is a portion of a *tiṅ*? It would follow that it is included by the mention of *tiṅ* according to [P. 1.1.62]. Nor can one say: "The prohibition [of P. 1.1.5] will apply," because that prohibition concerns a *vṛddhi* characterized by *it*, whereas this [vṛddhi] is not characterized by *it*; for it has been stated that "a *vṛddhi* whose substitute is not explicitly mentioned is characterized by *it*," since this [vṛddhi] has its place (*sthānin*) explicitly indicated. To this he says: "api stuyāt," etc.

For here, by the rule *yāsuṭ parasmaipadeṣūdātto ṅicca* [Pāṇini 3.4.103], the sārvadhātuka suffix is marked with *ṅ*; and because of the statement *ṅicca pinna bhavati*, the status of being *pit* is sublated by the status of being *ṅit*. Therefore, the *vṛddhi* substitution prescribed for a *pit* suffix does not occur here either. Now, why does it not occur in cases such as *yoyoti* and *roroti*, since when the *luk* elision takes place, these two bases end in the vowel *u*? To this he says: *nābhayastasya*, etc.
The meaning is understood.

By the word "ādi" (and so forth), forms such as *nonoti* [the reading *cokoti* etc. is found in the Prāṅu manuscript] are included. Since the preceding rule would have necessitated obligatory *vṛddhi*, this [present rule] is stated for the purpose of providing an option. For example: *prorṇoti*.
As before, there is the elision of *śap*.
In the form *prorṇavāni*, this is the first person singular of the imperative (*loṭ*). The term *vibhāṣā* ("optionally") has ceased to apply.

This is an exception (*apavāda*) to the optional *vṛddhi* obtained by the preceding rule. Now, one might object: "The term *hal* indeed continues [from the previous rule]; therefore, by virtue of its capacity (*sāmarthya*), it will apply only to a *apṛkta* [consonant], and not to that which begins with it. For a collection beginning with *hal* is not itself *hal*. So what is the purpose of including the mention of *apṛkta*? To this he says: "While *hal* continues," and so forth.
The inclusion of the term *apṛkta* is made for this very purpose: so that, due to the continuation of *hal*, [the rule] does not apply to that which begins with it.

If this technical rule (paribhāṣā) did not exist, the mention of "uncombined" (apṛkta) would be purposeless, for what occasion would there be for a guna vowel occurring even at the beginning of such a [consonant] cluster, since it is already covered by the rule *hali ca*? It would not apply at all, because that [cluster] consists of consonants (*hal-ātmaka*). Yet, this mention of "uncombined" has been made; therefore, it is indicated that this technical rule does not exist.

Now, why was it not stated simply as "not before a non-singular" (*anāpṛkte*)? What is the purpose of mentioning the term *guṇa*? For once the *vṛddhi* substitution is prohibited, the desired form would be established by the general rule (*utsarga*) of *guṇa* itself. This is not so; for there would be understood a prohibition of the optional (*vibhāṣā*) rule mentioned previously, and consequently, *vṛddhi* would occur invariably. The root *tṛha* in the sense of "injury" belongs to the *rudhādi* class; while *tṛhū* and *tṛbhū* in the sense of "injury" belong to the *tudādi* class. Of these two, this [rule] refers to the former, not the latter. Because that [latter] is separated by its verbal suffix (*vikaraṇa*), a consonant (*hal*) immediately following it is not possible.

Regarding *tṛṇeḍhi*: by [Pāṇini 7.2.31], *ḍha* replaces *ha*; by [8.2.40], *ḍha* becomes *ṭa*; by [8.4.41], *ṣṭu* replaces [the *ṭa*]; by [8.3.13], *im* is the augment; and by [6.1.87], the *ṭi* is elided. Regarding *tṛṇekṣi*.
The substitution of *k* occurs by [Pāṇini 8.2.41] *dhaḍhoḥ kaḥ si*.
Regarding *atṛṇeṭ*:

this is the *laṅ* tense, the suffix *tip*, followed by the elision of the *hal* and *ṅit* suffixes [6.1.66]. Once the substitution of *ḍh* has been applied [8.2.39], there is the substitution of *jaś*—the *ḍh* becomes *ḍ*. Then, by [8.4.55] *vāvasāne*, there is the substitution of *car*—the *ḍ* becomes *ṭ*.

But is it not the case that here, because [the suffix] has been elided, the augment *iṭ* should not occur for the *sārvadhātuka* suffix? If it is argued that even though it is elided, it will still apply there by virtue of the "characteristic of a suffix" (*pratyayalakṣaṇa*), we say: no; because there is no application of the "characteristic of a suffix" when the operation depends on a phoneme (*varṇāśraya*). Therefore he says: "In the case of that which depends on a phoneme," and so forth. He thinks as follows: the statement "there is no application of the characteristic of a suffix when it depends on a phoneme" (Vyāḍipāda 96) does not constitute a total prohibition of the application of the characteristic of a suffix when it depends on a phoneme; rather, it explains the purpose of the mention of the word "suffix" (*pratyaya*) in rule [Pāṇini 1.1.62].

When a suffix (*pratyaya*) is elided, two kinds of operations are understood: those caused by the suffix and those not caused by the suffix. Among these, that which is caused by the suffix is intended so that it may occur when the suffix is elided, while the other [non-suffix-caused] should not. Therefore, in the example *gave hitam* (beneficial for a cow), which becomes *go-hitam*, the substitution of *ava* does not take place once the case-ending has been elided.
Because of the governing rule *hraci* (Pāṇini 6.1.110), in the case of the substitution of *ava*, the phoneme (*varṇa*) is the cause, not the affix alone.

However, here, because of the governing rule concerning the *aṅga* (Pāṇini 6.4.1), it is specifically an affix beginning with a consonant (*hal-ādi*) that is relied upon; thus, the augment *īm* has the affix as its cause.
Therefore, by the rule of "affix-characteristics" (*pratyaya-lakṣaṇa*), that [augment] indeed occurs.

If this *hras* [the substitution of *i* for *ṛ*] were caused by the suffix (*pratyaya-nimitta*), how could it be stated that "it applies even when there is no suffix" (*varṇāśraye 'py etad yuktam*)? For in the example *atṛṇeḍ*, the suffix is merely a phoneme (*varṇamātratvāt*). This was stated because the phoneme is resorted to as a qualifier of the suffix (*pratyaya-viśeṣaṇatvena*), and not because it is not caused by a suffix; for the phoneme *t* [in *atṛṇeḍ*] does not lose its status as a suffix. In *tṛṇahāni*, that very same form is the first person singular of the imperative (*loṭ*). [The form] *tṛṇḍhaḥ* [is likewise].

[The process is as follows: by *tas*, [the suffix *ta*]; by *śnasoranlopaḥ* [Pāṇini 6.4.111], there is the elision of the final letter; by *pūrvavaḍḍhatvādi* [Pāṇini 8.3.24], there is the substitution of *ḍha*; by [Pāṇini 8.4.58], there is the *anusvāra*; and by [Pāṇini 8.4.58], there is the *parasavarṇa* substitution resulting in the letter *ṇ*. Now, for what purpose is the root *tṛh* with the affix *śnam* included here, rather than simply saying *tṛha*? To this he says: "If *tṛṇaha*" and so forth.

If the inclusion of the form with the affix *śnam* were not made, then this [rule] would be commenced when *śnam* was not yet applicable; and since there is a conflict between the two based on their position, *śnam* would be superseded by *ṇam*.
Even in the absence of a contradiction, an undesirable arrangement would result—[the question being] whether *śnam* comes first or *im* later? [If the former,] then an undesirable form would arise.

When *śnam* has already occurred and the root *tṛh* is subsequently followed by *im*, there would be a simultaneous occurrence (*samāveśa*) of both, and the desired arrangement would be achieved: *śnam* first, and *im* later.

Therefore, for the purpose that the augment *iṭ* should occur when *śnam* has been applied, the *śnam* which has arrived is taken as being repeated (*tṛh*). The ablative *brūvaḥ*—which has not yet served its purpose—is intended to effect a change of the seventh case (*saptamī*) of the previously established term *sārvadhātuke* into a sixth case (*ṣaṣṭhī*), according to the rule "after that [term], of what follows" (*tasmād ity uttarasya*, Pāṇini 1.1.66). Consequently, this *iṭ* is understood to apply specifically to a *sārvadhātuka* affix beginning with a consonant (*hal*) that follows the root *brū*. To this end, he says: "of that which follows *brū*, beginning with a consonant," and so forth.

But how, then, is that which begins with *hal* obtained by virtue of being an *āgama*? It is stated [in the Vārttika] that "when there is a rule regarding something, in the case of a mention of *al*, it refers to that which begins with it" (*yasmim vidhistadādāvalgrahaṇe*), and not "that of which there is a rule. For if there were no rule regarding what begins with that (*tadādividhi*), [the substitution] would apply only in cases such as *abravīt*, but not in cases such as *bravīti*. This is not a fault; for since the term *apṛkta* is mentioned later on, the possibility of a rule regarding what begins with that is understood. Otherwise, if there were no rule regarding what begins with that, even without the mention of *apṛkta*, it would necessarily be *apṛkta* [by its very nature], and the mention of *apṛkta* would be redundant. Thus, [we have] *bravīti*.
As before, there is the elision of *śap*.
"Brāvāṇi" is likewise the first person singular of the imperative (*loṭ*).
Regarding the term *brāūtaḥ*: [it is derived from] the present tense marker *laṭ*, with the suffix *tas*. Regarding *lālapīti* and so forth:

the intensive (*yaṅ*) suffix is applied after the roots *lap*, *vad*, and *ru*; for the first two, there is lengthening of the reduplicated syllable according to Pāṇini 7.4.83, while for *ru*, there is *guṇa* substitution according to 7.4.82, followed by the elision of *yaṅ* according to 2.4.74.
Regarding the forms *varvartti* and *carkatti*:

when there is elision (*luk*) of the *yaṅ* suffix after the roots *vṛñ* and *kṛñ*, the augment *rug* is added to the reduplicated syllable by [Pāṇini 7.4.92] *ṛtaśca*. But what is the reason that these are cited only for the case of *yaṅ*-elision and not for the *yaṅ*-ending form? To this he says: "beginning with *halādeḥ*" and so forth.

Since the *ātmanepada* occurs because of the *ṅit* designation for the *yaṅ* suffix, and there exists no *pit* *sārvadhātuka* beginning with a consonant (*hal*) in the *ātmanepada*, there can be no example here of a form ending in *yaṅ*. Why is that? Because a *pit* *sārvadhātuka* beginning with a consonant is impossible [in the *ātmanepada*]. Rather, the example refers to a form ending in *yaṅ-luk*. For in that case, a *pit* *sārvadhātuka* beginning with a consonant is possible, since forms ending in *yaṅ-luk* are *parasmaipada* according to the rule "and *carkarīta* is *parasmaipada*. Therefore, it is precisely a form with *yaṅ-luk* that is cited as the example.

*Carkarītam* is the technical name for the *yaṅ-luk* (elision of the *yaṅ* suffix) according to the ancient masters. Some say that the root *tu* mentioned in the Sūtra is used in the sense of "growth," while others say it is used in the sense of "injury. It is traditionally taught that this root belongs to the *luṅ-vikaraṇa* class; and since the term *bahulam* (variously) in [Pāṇini 2.4.73] allows for the elision (*luk*) even in the common language (*bhāṣā*), its status as a *luṅ-vikaraṇa* is thereby established. [The example is] *śamīṣpam*.
The imperative form is *aśamīdhvam*;
the imperfect form is *aśamīdhvam*.
"Abhyamīti" is the imperative (loṭ);
"aśamīdhvam" is [the same].
Regarding *laṅ*:
"he goes" (*abhyamīti*). [The root] *ama* [is used] in the sense of "going" and so forth (Dhātupāṭha 465); [the suffixes] *laṭ*, *tip*.

But how can a sārvadhātuka affix beginning with *ha*, such as *śap*, occur immediately after *śam* and *yam*, given that there must necessarily be an intervention by *śyan*? Is not *śap* also applied to the root *am*? To this he says: "of *śap* and *śyan*" (*śadhyamoḥ*), etc.
Here, the elision (*luk*) of the *vikaraṇa* occurs by the rule [Pāṇini 7.4.78].

Regarding the phrase "in the case of *sārvadhātuka* [affixes]," this is a specification in the feminine gender; for the word *sārvadhātuka* is well known in the feminine gender as a technical term (saṃjñā) used by Apiśali.
Now, for what purpose is the mention of *sārvadhātuka*, given that [the term] continues from the rule [Pāṇini 7.3.87]? He says: "While *sārvadhātuka* is being carried over," and so forth.
For that mention of *sārvadhātuka* is connected with the word *pit* [in the preceding rule];
therefore, if that were to continue, the mention of *pit* would also continue, and consequently, the rule would not apply in the case of *apit*.
Therefore, the mention of *sārvadhātuka* is made so that this [rule] may apply even in those cases. Regarding the term *apṛkte*:
by means of a substitution of case endings (*sup-vibhakti-vyatyaya*), the locative case is used in the sense of the genitive; thus, this *iṭ* augment applies only to an *apṛkta* suffix.
The mention of *asti* is for the sake of the *laṅ* (imperfect) tense.
Regarding the form *āsīt*:

from the root *as* meaning "to be" (*dhātupāṭha* 1065), in the *laṅ* tense, there is elision of the *śap* suffix because it belongs to the *adādi* class; then, by [Pāṇini 6.4.72], *āṭ* is prefixed; and by [Pāṇini 6.1.87], *vṛddhi* is substituted for both vowels.
Regarding "akārṣīt":
there is vṛddhi [substitution] due to the suffix *sic*. Regarding "alāvīt" and "apādhīt": [there is vṛddhi substitution].
By the rule *iṭa īṭi* [Pāṇini 8.2.28], there is the elision of the *sic* suffix. Regarding the form *āttha*:

here, when the *sip* suffix following a reduplicated (*bruva*) root is replaced by *thal* according to *bruvaḥ pañcānām adita āho bruvaḥ* [Pāṇini 3.4.84], and when the *bruva* substitute *ah* is applied, does the augment *īṭ* not apply because the *thal* is included under the term *bruva* through its status as a *sthānivadbhāva* (as if it were the original element), since it is also captured by the mention of *sārvadhātuka*? Thus, *īṭ* would seem to be required.
Regarding the form *abhūt*:

since the root *as* undergoes the substitution of *bhū* by Pāṇini 2.4.52 (*aster bhūḥ*), and because that [substitute] is treated as the original (*sthānivadbhāva*) and is thus included by the mention of the root *as*, the augment *īṭ* would be required. Why, then, does it not occur? To this he says: "In the case of *āhi* and *bhū*," etc.
[The rule states: "There is a prohibition regarding *īṭ*."
In the case of *āherbhuvaśceṭi*, there is a prohibition of the rule of "acting like the original" (*sthānivadbhāva*).
Therefore, it does not occur here in the form *ātva*.
By the rule *āhasthaḥ* [Pāṇini 8.2.35], the *ha* is replaced by *tha*; then, by the rule *khari ca* [Pāṇini 8.4.55], that *tha* is replaced by *ta*.
Regarding *abhūt*: by [Pāṇini 2.4.77] *gātisthā*, there is the elision (*luk*) of *sic*. Regarding *sarvamāḥ*: this is the *laṅ* suffix of the root *as*;

as before, there is *āṭ*; the elision of *si* and the following vowel according to [Pāṇini 6.1.68] *halṅyābbhyo dīrghāt sutisyapṛktaṃ hal*; and for the *s*, there is *ru*-substitution followed by *visarjanīya*. Regarding *gobhirakṣāḥ pratyañcamatsāḥ*: [the same analysis applies].

In *kṣara* (meaning "to move," Dhātupāṭha 851) and *tsara* (meaning "to go by guile," Dhātupāṭha 554), there is the elision of *sic* by [Pāṇini 6.1.66], followed by *vṛddhi* by [Pāṇini 7.2.2]; the visarga is as before. Regarding *abhaiṣīḥ*:
from *ñibhī* (meaning "fear," Dhātupāṭha 1084), there is *vṛddhi* due to *sic*.

Now, regarding the form *mā putraka* [in the phrase] *athābhaiṣīrmā putraka*, how is there the augment *aṭ* here, since that [augment] is prohibited by [Pāṇini 6.4.74]? Furthermore, in the forms *akṣāḥ* and *atasāḥ*, why does the augment *iṭ* not occur after the *sic* suffix ending in *at*? To this he says: "Because of its being Vedic" (*chāndasatvāt*), and so forth. The connection with the present context is that the absence of the augment *iṭ* in *akṣāḥ* and *atasāḥ* is due to their being Vedic. Although one could simply say "optionally in the Veda" (*vā chandasi*), the use of the term *bahulam* (variously) is for the sake of subsequent rules.
And we shall demonstrate its purpose for what follows later on. In the rule *rudah*, the singular number is used for the plural by means of a transposition of case endings (*sub-vyatyaya*).
This is understood from the plural form *pañcabhyaḥ*. Since the augment *iṭ* would otherwise apply [by Pāṇini 7.2.76], the augment *īṭ* is prescribed as an exception to that.

*rud* (Dhātupāṭha 1067) means "to shed tears"; *svap* (Dhātupāṭha 1068) means "to sleep"; *ās* (Dhātupāṭha 1069) means "to breathe"; *an* (Dhātupāṭha 1070) [means "to breathe"]; and *jakṣ* (Dhātupāṭha 1071) means "to eat" and "to laugh"—these are the roots beginning with *rud*, belonging to the second class (*adādigaṇa*).
In the form *arodīt*, the suffix is *laṅ*.
Regarding "prāṇīt":
the substitution of *ṇ* [for *n*] occurs by [Pāṇini 8.4.19], which states that [the *n* of] the root *an* is replaced by *ṇ*.
Regarding "ajāgarbhavān": [this is formed from the root *jṛ* with the suffix *kvasu*].
Regarding the term *ajāgarbhavān*: this root *jāgarti* is recited after the five [roots beginning with *budha*].

When the *guṇa* substitution and the replacement by *r* have been applied, the elision of the suffix by rule 6.1.68 (*halṅyādi-lopa*) occurs. Since the augment *iṭ* would have been required by the preceding rule, the augment *aṭ* is here prescribed.

The mention of Gārgya and Gālava is for the sake of honor (*pūjārtha*), not for the sake of providing an option (*vikalpārtha*). Because *aṭ* and *iṭ* serve as indicators (*liṅga*) that the rule applies to the beginning of a word, and because they share the same domain (*ekaviṣayatva*), their simultaneous occurrence is impossible; furthermore, since an option is already established even without the mention of the teachers, their inclusion serves only to show respect. The mention of all [the teachers] is for the sake of honor, not for the sake of making the rule obligatory (*nityārtha*), because the mention of Gārgya and Gālava is intended to preclude an option. The addition of the long vowel marker *t* (*taparakaraṇa*) is for the sake of subsequent rules;
its purpose is to prevent the substitution of *e* by the rule *bahuvacane jhalyet* (Pāṇini 7.3.103) in forms such as *khaṭvābhiḥ*.
Regarding "aṅganā":
the suffix *na* is applied according to [Pāṇini 5.2.99] because she possesses excellent limbs (*aṅgāni*), despite the presence of hair and so forth.
Regarding "keśava": [the suffix *aṇ* is applied].
The suffix *vap* is applied according to [Pāṇini 5.2.109], "He who has hair (*keśā yasya santi*). Some maintain that the term *tiṅ* is carried over from [Pāṇini 7.3.88].

Regarding the form *teṣāṃ bhavān*: since the suffix *kvasu* is a *sārvadhātuka*, there should not be lengthening [of the vowel] by rule P. 7.3.84; this is because *kvasu* is not an *atiṅ* (non-finite) element. In the case of *bhagavān*: from the root *bhū*, the suffix *liṭ* is applied, followed by *kvasu*. By P. 6.4.86, *kvasu* optionally receives the designation *sārvadhātuka*. Consequently, by P. 3.1.68, the *śap* augment is added for the agent (*kartṛ*). Then, by P. 6.4.10, the vowel is lengthened. Finally, the rules for the elision of *hal* and *ṅī* etc., and the elision of the final consonant of a cluster (*saṃyogāntalopa*), apply (P. 6.1.68; 8.2.23).

Although "ādi" could have been stated [instead of "ādī"], the inclusion of the long vowel (*dīrgha*) is so that it may be *only* long. Why? So that whatever else might otherwise apply shall not occur. What else might apply? The *pluta* (protracted) vowel prescribed by "[8.2.97] *anantarasyāpyekaikasya prācām*" and "[8.2.105] *praśnākhyānayoḥ*". Furthermore, why is the original *aj*-augment not prescribed here? Because even in that case, there would be a long vowel by "[6.1.97] *akaḥ savarṇe dīrghaḥ*", and then there would be elision by "[7.3.72] *vahīti*"; moreover, in a form such as *atijarābhyām*, there would be the substitution of *jaras* by "[7.2.101] *acīti*". To prevent these [undesired results], the inclusion of the long vowel (*dīrgha*) has been made.

And in this case, *pluta* (protracted vowel) would result [as an exception]. But surely, in the case of *vṛkṣāṇām*, the rule *nāmi* [Pāṇini 6.4.3] will serve as an annulment (*bādhaka*) [of the *pluta*]; so what is the use of including the mention of *jhal* for the purpose of excluding that? This is not so; the rule *nāmi* has its scope in cases such as *agnīnām*, whereas if the mention of *jhal* were absent, *ettva* (the substitution of *e* for *ai*) would prevail over *dīrghatva* (lengthening) due to its higher status [in the order of rules], resulting in forms such as *pacadhvam* and *yajadhvam*. [In these,] there is the imperative (*loṭ*), the substitution of *e* for *ṭi* [by Pāṇini 3.4.91], and the replacement of the suffix with *ām*. The phrase "by the designation of the ancient teachers as *āṅ*" and so forth [is explained as follows].
For the ancient teachers used to provide the third-case singular ending as *āṅ*.
Therefore, by that usage of *āṅ*, the third-case singular is understood.
"By the bed" (*khaṭvayā*) is an example of a word ending in the feminine suffix *ṭāp*.

Regarding the term *bahurājyā*: this is an example of a word ending in the suffix *jāt* (the feminine suffix *jāp*). The suffix *ḍāp* is applied by the rule *ḍābubhābhyāmanyatarasyām* [Pāṇini 4.1.13].
Regarding the form *kārīṣagandhyayā*:
it is derived from a word ending in *cāp*.

[First,] from *karīṣasyeva gandho 'sya* ("his scent is like that of dried cow dung"), by [Pāṇini 5.4.137], the suffix *it* is applied, resulting in *karīṣagandhiḥ*; then, by [Pāṇini 4.1.92], the suffix *aṇ* is applied; then, by [Pāṇini 4.1.78] and following rules, *vyaṅ* is substituted for *aṇ* and *iñ*; and finally, from that which ends in *vyaṅ*, the suffix *cāp* is applied by [Pāṇini 4.1.74].

Regarding the term *kīlālapā*: it means "one who drinks *kīlāla*. From the rule *ato maninkvanibvanipaśca* [Pāṇini 3.2.74], the suffix *vic* is applied; from that form ending in *vic*, the third-case singular ending is added, and by the rule *ṭāṅasiṅasām...* [Pāṇini 6.4.140], the vowel *a* is elided. Now, why does this [elision] not occur here in the case of *atikhaṭvena* (by one who has passed beyond a bed), after the shortening of the *upasarjana* has been performed, due to the status of being a *sthānivadbhāva*? Would it not follow? To this he says: "*ṅyābgrahaṇam*," etc.

Some say: "The rule 'when there is a mention of *ṅī* or *āp*, there must be a mention of the long [vowels]' should be formulated; by that, when shortness (*hrasvatva*) has been applied, [the elision] does not occur. Others, however, say: "A split of the rule (*yogavibhāga*) should be made for [Pāṇini 6.1.68]: 'Whatever operation applies to *ṅī* and *āp* in the treatise, let all of that apply to the long vowels, and not to the short ones. Then follows the second rule: 'A suffix consisting of a single phoneme (*apṛkta*) following *su*, *ti*, or *si*' (6.1.66). In this context, 'from [stems ending in] consonants, *ṅī*, or *āp*' is understood to carry over. The letter *c* is for the purpose of drawing in [the word] 'also' (*api*) from [Pāṇini 7.3.104]. This is an exception (*apavāda*) to the preceding [rule]."
*Ambārthāḥ* means those whose meaning is "mother" (*mātṛ*).
Regarding the phrase *ḍalakavatīnām* and so forth: those vowels which possess the phonemes *ḍa* and *la* are called *ḍalakavatyaḥ*.
Here, the *ḍa* and *la* sounds that do not constitute parts of a conjunct (*saṃyoga*) are understood;
otherwise, [the rule] would also apply in cases such as "he akka" and "he alla. The meaning of the word "vaktavya" (to be stated) is "it should be explained."

The same meaning should be understood for the two subsequent verbal roots as well. In this regard, the following explanation applies: from [Pāṇini 7.4.78], the term *bahulam* ("diversely") is carried over by the principle of the frog-leap (*maṇḍūkapluti*), whereby all operations, including prohibitions and so forth, will also take place.
Thus, "for one who is worthy" (*arhate*).
The meaning is: "to one who has become a vessel for praise.

Regarding the example *gārgīmātā*: he who deserves praise by being designated as having a mother who is a Gārgī is spoken of in this way. The mention of the short vowel (*hrasva*) is a qualifier of the stem under discussion (*prakṛta-aṅga*); and since a rule involving a qualifier applies to that which ends with it, he says: "of that which ends in a short vowel," and so forth.
In this way, the rule of *tadantavidhi* (application of a grammatical operation to that which ends with the specified element) should be understood in subsequent cases as well.
Now, why does [the elision] not occur in cases such as "he kumāri" or "he brāhmaṇabandhu"? To this, he says: "he kumāri," etc.
If the *guṇa* substitution were to take place after the short vowel (*hrasva*) has been applied, then the application of the short vowel would be purposeless.

But is this not for the sake of the *guṇa* [substitution]? It might be so; for if that [suffix] were absent, the *guṇa* prescribed by "the *guṇa* of a short vowel" (Pāṇini 7.3.108) would not occur, because [the stem] would not end in a short vowel. Thus he says: "If," and so forth.

The intention is that in this way, the complexity of the grammatical derivation (*prakriyā-gaurava*) is avoided. Regarding the phrase "in *jas* and so forth," the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) indicates a class or type.
The meaning is "in the various types of suffixes.
"From this context" refers to [the rules] beginning with *ambārthanadyorhrasvaḥ* (Pāṇini 7.3.107).
"It should be stated as 'in the Veda' (chandasi)" means that it must be explained that the grammatical operation occurs optionally within the scope of the Veda;
however, this explanation is to be made by relying on that very term "bahulam" (diversely).
In the passage beginning with "ambe," etc.,
the shortening [of the vowel] does not occur by the rule *ambārthanadyorhrasvaḥ* (Pāṇini 7.3.107).
In the word *darvī*, there is the substitution of a guṇa for the short vowel.
In the case of *śatakratvaḥ*, [the substitution of *o* for *as*] is also governed by [Pāṇini 7.3.109] *jasi ca*.
Regarding *pao*,
there is the *guṇa* [substitution] by [Pāṇini 7.3.111] *dherṅiti*.

In the word *kikidīvyā*, the substitution of *nā* [for *na*] occurs by [Pāṇini 7.3.120]. Regarding the statement "the inclusion of the marker *t* (taparakaraṇa) is for the sake of ease of pronunciation," this is because a long *ṛ*-vowel cannot occur after the suffixes *ṅi* and the case-endings known as *sarvanāmasthāna* such that it would need to be replaced by one followed by *t*. [Examples are: *sakhye*, *patye*.

The words *sakhi* and *pati* do not possess the technical designation *ghisamjñaka*; this is because of the exclusion (*paryudāsa*) in [Pāṇini 1.4.7], "The remainder is *ghi*, except for *sakhi*," and because of the restrictive rule (*niyama*) in [Pāṇini 1.4.8].
Regarding the form *paṭvī*:
the suffix *ṅīṣ* is applied by [Pāṇini 4.1.44], "After a word denoting a quality (*guṇavacana*), [the feminine suffix] *ṅīṣ* is optionally [added]."

In this case, there is no *guṇa* substitution; because the term *supi* is understood from the rule *supi ca* [Pāṇini 7.3.102], as in the example *kurutaḥ*. Here, from the root *kṛ*, there is the suffix *u*, *guṇa* of the root, *raparatva* (substitution of *r*), and by the rule *ata ut sārvadhātuke* [Pāṇini 6.4.110], there is the substitution of *u*. Even here, due to the understanding of *supi*, there is no *guṇa* for the element ending in the *vikaraṇa* when followed by *tas*. The word *nadyāḥ* is in the ablative case (*pañcamī*). Since its purpose has not yet been fulfilled, it will effect a change of the seventh case (*saptamī*) of the word *ṅiti*—which has already served its purpose in the preceding rule—into a sixth case (*ṣaṣṭhī*).

Therefore, this augment *āṭ* is understood to apply only to that which ends in *ṅ*; thus he says: "of what follows after a stem ending in *nadī*," and so forth. In forms such as *kumāryai*, there is *vṛddhi* by [Pāṇini 6.1.87] *āṭaśca*.

Now, for what purpose is the long vowel [ā] pronounced? Could it not simply be stated as *a*? For [the forms] *kumāryai* and *kumāryāḥ* would be established by the *vṛddhi* [substitution] according to [Pāṇini 7.2.115], which itself results from the *savarṇadīrgha* [rule]. Furthermore, one should not suspect that *pararūpa* (the single substitute of the subsequent form) would apply here by [Pāṇini 6.1.97]; for even if *pararūpa* were to apply here, it would not occur due to the force of this specific rule. This is not a fault, for there is another purpose for the statement. What is that? [It is so that] in the case of *śriyai* and *śriyāḥ*, the acute accent (*udātta*) prescribed by [Pāṇini 6.1.168] does not occur.

The statement "augmentals (*āgama*) are udātta in their initial syllable" is intended so that they may remain *anudātta*. For it is possible for a single substitute (*ekādeśa*) to be included by the term "augmental" through the application of the *antādivadbhāva* (the treatment of a substitute as being like the end of the preceding element and the beginning of the following). Now, just as the *anudātta* nature of an augmental subverts the accent of a suffix—as in *lavitā*, *lavitum*, and so on—it would likewise subvert the accent of a case-ending (*vibhakti*).
Therefore, this [rule] is for the purpose of *vṛddhi* by [Pāṇini 6.1.87]: *āṭaśca*. Regarding the example "in *khaṭvāyām*":
the *vṛddhi* is applied by [Pāṇini 6.1.88].

In the case of *khaṭvāyāḥ*, the long vowel (*dīrgha*) is explicitly stated in [Pāṇini 6.1.97]: *akaḥ savarṇe*; its purpose is so that both *vṛddhi* and *savarṇa-dīrgha* may occur, and not merely the substitution of the subsequent form (*pararūpatva*).

If it is argued that [the substitution] will not occur due to the force of the pronunciation of the letter *a*, we say no; for there is another purpose for the pronunciation of this *a*. What is it? It is so that in forms such as *jñāyai* and *jñāyāḥ*, the acute accent (*udātta*) prescribed by [Pāṇini 6.1.168] shall not apply, and instead the anudātta accent of the augment (*āgama*) shall occur. Now, why does it not occur in *atikhaṭvāyāḥ* (from *atikrāntā khaṭvām*), since once the shortening of the subordinate member (*upasarjana-hrasvatva*) has been applied, the substitute would, by virtue of its status as a *sthānin*, be included by the mention of *ā*, and thus the rule would apply? To this he says: "*atikhaṭvāyā*" and so forth.

When, first of all, lengthening is not applied by the rule *supi ca* [Pāṇini 7.3.102], then, because of the statement that "the mention of *ṅī* and *āp* includes the long vowel," this [substitution] does not occur.

When lengthening is applied, then it does not occur because it is *lākṣaṇika* (derived); according to the principle: "Between that which is mentioned by a general rule (*lakṣaṇa*) and that which is mentioned directly (*pratipadokta*), only the directly mentioned one is to be understood. [The substitution of *yāṭ*] is an exception (*apavāda*) to [the addition of] *yāṭ*.
The explicit utterance of the letter *ā* is so that [the rule] may apply in the case of *sarvasyāḥ*; otherwise, the substitution of the single subsequent form (*pararūpatva*) would result.

One might think that [the rule] would not apply by virtue of the power of the pronunciation of the vowel *a*—but this should not be suspected. For [the present rule] is intended so that, in the case of *taddhi tasyām*, the acute accent (*udātta*) of the case-ending prescribed by Pāṇini 6.1.171 (*taddhita-svareṇa saha samāsāntodāttatvam*) shall not occur, and instead the enclitic grave accent (*anudātta*) of the augment (*āgama*) shall take effect. This statement is for the sake of excluding pronouns (*asarvanāma*).

However, those who prescribe the designation "pronoun" (*sarvanāma-saṃjñā*) for ordinal numbers ending in *-tīya* by means of the Vārttika, "In the section concerning 'optionally' (*vā-prakaraṇe*), there is an addition (*upasaṃkhyāna*) of the rule for *ṅit* suffixes for *-tīya*" (Vārttika 6), reject this sūtra; for [the desired result] is already established by that very [Vārttika].

Furthermore, this supplementary rule (*upasaṃkhyāna*) must necessarily be formulated so that *smāy* and the other suffixes may optionally apply when a *ṅit* [suffix] follows—resulting in forms such as *dvitīyasmai*, *dvitīyāya*, *dvitīyasmin*, and *dvitīye*. Others, however, reject the need for a supplementary rule altogether, asserting that *smāy* and the others are established by this very sūtra alone. How so? The term *sarvanāmnaḥ* ("of a pronoun") is understood here [from the previous sūtra], while *syāṭ* is no longer operative; thus, the connection is made as follows: "That which has been prescribed for a pronoun before a *ṅit* suffix applies optionally after the words *dvitīya* and *tṛtīya*."

Therefore, since the forms *syā* and so forth will be produced by the very substitution of *ap*, there is no need for a supplementary rule (*upasaṃkhyāna*). The term *ṅeḥ* refers to the singular locative case ending.
This is understood from such indications as [the rule] *striyām*. For example: *grāmaṇyām*.

In the expression *grāmaṃ nayati* ("he leads to the village"), the suffix *kvip* is applied by the rule *satsūdviṣa* [Pāṇini 3.2.61], and the substitution of *ṇ* is applied by the rule *agragrāmābhyāṃ ca* [Pāṇini 6.4.82]. Then, regarding the forms *kumāryām*, *khaṭvāyām*, and *sarvasyām*, how are they established? Once the case-ending *ām* is applied, would there not have to be the augment *nuṭ* by the rule *hrasvanadyāpo nuṭ* [Pāṇini 7.1.54]? This is not a fault; because the augment *nuṭ* is subsequent [in the order of rules], the augments *āṭ*, *yāṭ*, and *syāṭ* take effect first.

In the case of those [suffixes], there is no possibility of the application of *nuṭ* at all; for the simultaneous occurrence (*samuccaya*) of both initial markers (*ādi-liṅga*) is not tenable. The term "nadī" (feminine noun) is understood here by way of anuvṛtti.
Therefore, if the vowels *i* and *u* are qualified [by it], the meaning is: "those *i* and *u* vowels which belong to feminine nouns designated as *nadī*."

If this is so, is this [rule] useless because it is already established by the preceding one? This is not the case; for the vowel *au* would have applied by the subsequent rule due to its posteriority, whereas [the present rule] applies only when this [condition] exists. Because of the mention of a different substitute in the form "āṅ," there occurs here a transformation of the case-ending for the sake of the sense; thus, that which was previously introduced as "gher" in the genitive case becomes here introduced in the ablative case. Therefore, he says: "of what follows after *ghi*," and so forth.

Now, for what purpose [is this]? One might think: "Since it is stated that [the suffix] does not occur in the feminine (*astriyām*), one could simply say 'in the masculine after *āṅ* (*āṅo nā puṃsi*)'; if this were said, one need not suspect that forms such as *trapuṇā* and *jatunā* would not be established, because they are already established by the addition of *num* according to [Pāṇini 7.1.73]. To refute such a view, the example *amunā brāhmaṇakulena* is introduced.
For here, after the substitution of *ya* for the pronoun stem (according to 7.2.102), the substitution of *u* and *atva* have occurred (according to 6.1.97).
In that case, if it were stated "in the masculine," then *amunā* would not be established in the neuter, because the substitution of *m* (*mubhāva*) is considered non-existent (*asiddha*).

Is it because of the absence of *num*? When it is stated "not in the feminine" (*astriyām*), it is established that even in the neuter, the absence [of the feminine suffix] does not occur, as in the form *amunā*. For there is no lack of established status (*asiddhatva*) for the *mubhāva* when the *nābhāva* is to be applied; such is the intention based on the rule [Pāṇini 8.2.3].

Thus ends the third quarter of the seventh chapter in the *Kāśikā-vivaraṇapañjikā* composed by the venerable master Jinendrabuddhi, who is like a Bodhisattva. Now begins the fourth quarter of the seventh chapter: "When a *ṇi*-affix follows that which has *caṅ* as its subsequent element. In this compound, *caṅ* is that after which the *ṇi*-affix occurs; thus it is so described. Examples include *acīkarat*, and so forth.

From the roots *kṛñ*, *hmañ*, *lūñ*, and *pañ*, the causative suffix *ṇic* is applied (*hetumaṇṇic*). From that, the aorist suffix *luṅ* is added, followed by *cli*. By the rule *ṇiśri* [Pāṇini 3.1.48] et cetera, *cli* is replaced by *caṅ*, and by the rule *ṇeraniṭi* [Pāṇini 6.4.51], the *ṇi* is elided.

Here, when both reduplication (*dvirvacana*) and the shortening of the penultimate vowel (*upadhāhrasvatva*) are applicable, the shortening of the penultimate vowel takes precedence due to its higher status in the order of rules. Following that, reduplication occurs. Then, because of the principle that "what is done to a root in the presence of *ṇi* is treated as non-existent (*sthānivat*)," the forms *kṛ*, *hma*, and so forth—the original, unmodified verbal roots—are themselves what undergo reduplication.

In this context, for the roots *kṛ* and *hṛ*, when the substitution of *at* [by Pāṇini 7.4.66] has been applied to the reduplicated syllable, followed by the substitution of *ra* [as the final element], and the application of *halādiśeṣa*, then by the rule "like *sa*" [Pāṇini 7.4.93] and so forth, there is the *it*-augment due to the treatment as *san*. For the roots *pū* and *lū* as well, when the shortening [of the reduplicated syllable] has been applied, there is the *it*-augment [by Pāṇini 7.4.80].
In all cases, there is the lengthening [of the penultimate vowel] by [Pāṇini] 7.4.94.

"Here, when both reduplication (*dvirvacana*) and the shortening of the penultimate vowel (*upadhā-hrasvatva*) are applicable," and so forth. In examples such as *acīkarat*, reduplication is obligatory because it applies whether [the subsequent operation] has occurred or not; likewise, the shortening of the penultimate vowel is also obligatory. Between these two, the shortening of the penultimate vowel occurs because it is the subsequent rule; once that has been applied, reduplication follows—this is the sequence in which the grammatical operations take effect. However, in the case of *mā bhavān aṭiṭat*, reduplication alone is obligatory, but the shortening does not apply after the second monosyllabic stem (*ekāc*) has been reduplicated, because it is intervened by the form of the word *ṭi*, which stands before it.

Therefore, in the case of *mā bhavān aṭiṭat*, because [the root] is eternal (*nitya*), reduplication of the second *ekāc* (single-consonant) syllable would result. What fault would there be if that reduplication were to occur? To this he says: "And that being so," and so forth.
And thus, when reduplication has been performed, the penultimate vowel (*upadhā*) of that stem (*aṅga*) which occurs before a *ṇi* followed by *caṅ* is subject to shortening.

Furthermore, if shortness (*hrasvatva*) were not present, the form *mā bhavān aṭiṭat* would not be established. The [augment] *āṭ* is for the purpose of preventing the application of *āṇ*; however, when *āṭ* is present, there is no difference [in the result].
Whether the short vowel [of the suffix] is present or not, there ought to be a *vṛddhi* substitution by the rule *āṭaśca* [Pāṇini 6.1.87].
The word *bhavat* is for the purpose of removing doubt.
[The author says: "This is not a fault."
How is that which was just mentioned obtained? To this he says: "The addition of the marker *ṛ* in *oṇṛ*" and so forth.

The purpose of adding the marker *ṛ* to the root *oṇṛ* (meaning 'to remove,' Dhātupāṭha 454) is so that, by virtue of being marked with *ṛ*, there may be a prohibition of shortening according to the rule *nāglopiśāsvṛditām* (Pāṇini 7.4.2).
For if even the obligatory reduplication were not superseded by the shortening of the penultimate vowel, then the addition of the marker *ṛ* in *oṇṛ* would be purposeless.

"If reduplication (dvirvacana) were performed first, then because of the intervention by the subsequent form *ṇi*, the shortening (*hrasva*) would not occur anyway; so what is the purpose of making the root *oṇ* marked with the *ṛt* indicatory letter (*ṛdit*)? [The answer is: The activity of the Teacher indicates that even obligatory reduplication is superseded by the shortening of the penultimate vowel (*upadhā-hrasvatva*), since he makes the root *oṇ* marked with the *ṛt* indicatory letter. [Question: "What is the purpose of [the condition] 'in the presence of *ṇi*' (*ṇau*)?"

He thinks as follows: Is the mention of *ṇi* (the causative suffix) made for the purpose that, when the substitution of *luṅ* and *laṅ* has occurred but the *ṇilopa* has not yet occurred, and when the *vṛddhi* and *āvādeśa* have not yet occurred—leaving the form *alū i + at*—the shortening of the *ūkāra* should not take place? Or is it for the purpose that, once the *vṛddhi* of the *ūkāra* has occurred, the shortening of the resulting *aukāra* should not take place? Neither of these two purposes is necessary; for in this case, by virtue of being *antaraṅga* (internal), the *vṛddhi* and *āvādeśa* must necessarily occur first.

Furthermore, the internal nature (*antaraṅgatva*) of those two [the *ṇi* and the *aṅga*] is due to their depending solely on the *ṇic*; whereas the external nature (*bahiraṅgatva*) of the short vowel (*hrasva*) is due to its depending on the *caṅ*.
Regarding the statement "when it is said that 'there is a shortening of the penultimate (*upadhā*) in the presence of *caṅ*'" and so forth:
if only this much were stated, in the absence of the mention of *ṇic*, the meaning would be that there is a shortening of the penultimate of that stem (*aṅga*) which occurs when *caṅ* follows.

And thus, in the case of *alīlavat*, where it is stated that "the short [vowel] has no scope," the substitution of *au* for the *ṛ*-vowel alone would occur by the force of the rule, even overriding the internal (*antaraṅga*) *vṛddhi*. Even if, somehow, the *vṛddhi* were not overridden, once *vṛddhi* had been applied, it would still follow that *au* alone would be substituted, overriding even the internal *āv* replacement; otherwise, this specific rule would be rendered meaningless. As in the example *adīdapat*.

In this case, when the causative suffix *ṇic* is added to the root *dā*, and the *luṅ* (aorist) suffix with *caṅ* is applied, resulting in the form *a-dā-i-at*, the short vowel [prescribed by Pāṇini 7.3.70] would apply by the authority of that specific rule (*vacanaprāmāṇyāt*), even though it is an internal operation (*antaraṅga*), thereby overriding the augment *puk*. Once that shortening has occurred, the *puk* augment would not apply because its cause (*nimitta*) has been destroyed. Consequently, in forms such as *apīpacat*, the shortening would never occur at all; for when *caṅ* follows, the base (*aṅga*) beginning with *pāc* and so on consists of an initial vowel (*ā*) which is not subject to shortening.
The word "ādi" (etcetera) is intended to include [the forms] *apīpaṭhat* and so forth.
Therefore, it should be stated that [the suffix] *ṇi* follows; [one might ask:
"What is the purpose of [specifying] *caṅ*?"

This is the intended meaning: the term *caṅ* is stated for the purpose that the shortening (*hrasva*) should not occur when there is only the suffix *ṇi*. However, this purpose for the mention of *caṅ* is not tenable; because the activity of the Teacher indicates that shortening does not occur after *ṇi* alone—since he teaches the shortening in the rule "the short vowel of *mit* roots" (Pāṇini 6.4.92). The intention is that, consequently, it will not occur in forms such as *kārayati* and *hārayati*. If, on the basis of this indicator (*jñāpaka*), shortening does not occur in *kārayati* and so forth, then it would likewise not occur in *acīkarat*.
Could it be that this [result] will occur here by the force of the statement? Even so, it would certainly occur in cases such as *kārayati*.

For when the rule *mitāṃ hrasvaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.4.92) is being stated, it is not possible to understand a distinction of scope based on the fact that [the shortening] does not occur in forms such as *acīkarat*.
Therefore, the mention of *caṅ* must be made.

"What is the purpose of including the term *upadhā*? [The opponent] thinks thus: "The term *upadhā* is included so that [the rule] does not apply to the final letter (*alo’ntyasya*); however, this is unnecessary. For when there is a *ṇi* followed by *caṅ*, whatever is the *aṅga*—as in *acīkarat* and the like—even after the internal operations (*antaraṅga*) such as *vṛddhi* have taken place, it is impossible for a short vowel to exist as the final element of the *aṅga*. This is because a *ṇic* is produced only after a stem ending in a vowel (*ajanta*); how much more so in cases like *apapaṭhat*, where a *ṇic* is produced after a consonant-final stem (*halanta*)! Therefore, since a short vowel cannot be the final element, the inclusion of the term *upadhā* is redundant even without it."
By virtue of this statement, the short vowel will occur specifically for that which has become an *upadhā* [penultimate],
as in "acakāṅkṣat" and "avavāñchat.
[The roots] *krākṣi*, *vākṣi*, and *mākṣi* are used in the sense of "desiring" (*kāṅkṣāyām*) [Dhātupāṭha 667, 668, 669].

Although there exists no root ending in a short vowel that is not followed by a nasal, nevertheless, just as [the rule] applies to forms such as *acakarat* due to the explicit statement (*vacana*) regarding what is not final, so too would it apply to forms such as *acakāṅkṣat*.
Therefore, the intention is that the mention of the "penultimate" (*upadhā*) is made so that this fault shall not occur.

Now, an objection is raised: "Is it not the case that the shortening is prescribed for an *ac* that belongs to an *aṅga* when a *ṇi* followed by *caṅ* follows? In that regard, although an immediate *ac* is not possible, nevertheless, according to the principle ‘where there is no intervention [by more than one letter], even if there is intervention [by one], the rule applies because of the authority of the statement’ (Vyāḍiparibhāṣā 46), the shortening should occur even when there is intervention, provided that the intervention is by only a single phoneme. [Response: It is true that intervention by only a single phoneme is possible everywhere. However, intervention by a cluster (*saṅghāta*) of phonemes is sometimes possible and sometimes not. In this specific case, there is always intervention [by more than one phoneme]. Therefore, since the intervention is by a cluster, the shortening does not apply, despite the authority of the statement. This is because the condition "where there is no intervention" excludes cases where the intervention is by a cluster. Intervention by a single phoneme is indeed possible, but intervention by a cluster is not possible here. Thus, the shortening does not take place.

In examples such as *acakāṅkṣat*, the intervention is by a cluster (*saṅghāta*) itself; therefore, there is no possibility of the short vowel [substitution] at all. Why, then, is the mention of the *upadhā* (penultimate) required? To this he says: "This very [point]," and so forth.

The mention of the *upadhā* must necessarily be made for the sake of subsequent rules. But if it were made here for the purpose of forms like *acakāṅkṣat*, the maxim "that by which there is no intervention" (Vyāḍiparibhāṣā 46) would not need to be resorted to.
Since the short vowel of the penultimate syllable (*upadhā*) has already been replaced here by the very act of adding *ṇiC*, this *guṇa* substitution is obtained;
therefore, it is applied only here and not elsewhere.
[This is stated in the rule: "An addition must be made regarding the shortening of the penultimate vowel when *ṇiC* follows *ṇiC*."

When a *ṇi*-affix follows a *caṅ* (the reduplication of the aorist), it should be added as an exception that the penultimate vowel (*upadhā*) of the stem (*aṅga*) becomes short before that *ṇi*. For example, in *avīvadat*:

the root *vad* takes *ṇic* by [Pāṇini 3.1.26]; from that form ending in *ṇic*, because he caused one who had already spoken (*vāditavantam*) to speak, *ṇic* is applied again by [Pāṇini 3.1.26]; then the *luṅ* (aorist) suffixes follow; and finally, the *ṇi* is elided by [Pāṇini 6.4.51].

But what is the reason that [the rule] does not apply, given that once the *ṇi*-elision has been performed, the vowel of the base (*aṅga*) preceding the *caṅ* suffix indeed becomes a short penultimate (*upadhā*)? To this he says: "That which... and so forth. Even by the rule *acaḥ parasmin pūrvavidhau* (P. 1.1.57), because the *ṇi*-elision would be treated as if it were still present (*sthānivadbhāva*) when the shortening is to be applied, there is no intervention by the *ṇic*, and thus the shortening does not occur. Or rather, by that very *ṇi*-elision, this base becomes one whose initial vowel is elided (*aglopyaṅga*); for this reason, the state of being short (*hrasvatva*) does not apply.

Is it because of the prohibition that will be stated immediately following [in the rule] beginning with *aglopi* (Pāṇini 6.4.69)? He rejects the supplementary statement (*upasaṃkhyāna*) "it is established by the indication of the class-form (*ṇyākṛti-nirdeśāt*") by saying: "In the case of *ṇau*.
By "the class-form of *ṇi*," the universal (*jāti*) of *ṇi* is indicated, not the individual instance (*vyakti*) of *ṇi*.
Therefore, there is no intervention in the case of the individual instance, for there is none in the case of the universal; since the universal of *ṇi* is one.
For it is not logical that a thing should be separated from itself by that very same thing.

[Objection: But surely, separation is indeed possible even with respect to the locus of the universal *ṇi*, by means of a higher form (*ṇyākṛti*)—that is, a universal—which serves as the substratum for the lower individual (*ṇivyakti*)? [Reply: This is not so; because the universal inheres in that individual as well.
Thus, there is no such separation with respect to the locus of the higher form (*ṇyākṛti*).

The status of being "aglopī" (having its initial portion elided) does not exist here at all; for in this case, there is no other "aṅga" (base) present apart from the causative suffix *ṇic*, which could become an "aglopī-aṅga" through the elision [of that suffix].
Nor is there an elision of the class-sign *ṇi*; because it is actually heard [in the utterance], and it is impossible for that which is being heard to undergo elision, according to the rule:
"That which is heard is not elided" (Pāṇini 1.1.60).

But surely, even apart from the genus (*jāti*), the individual (*vyakti*) which serves as its substratum does indeed exist; for it is not the case that the genus and the individual are non-different, since the Sāṃkhya doctrine is being adopted here.

Alternatively, when there is a reference to the *ṇyākṛti* (the generic form of the suffix), the shortness of the vowel in the augment (*upadhā-hrasvatva*) is accepted as having that *ṇyākṛti* as its cause. Therefore, by the maxim of "the cow and the bull" (*gobalīvardanyāya*), while that *ṇyākṛti* is mentioned as the cause [of the shortening], the elision of another [vowel] is understood to be the cause for the prohibition [of the shortening]; and that [elision] does not exist here.

Therefore, because the reference is to the *ākṛti* (general form), the [rule] is established. The term *ag* is a *pratyāhāra* (abbreviated designation). *Aglopa* means the elision (*lopa*) of an *ak* (vowel); those *aṅga*s (bases) which possess such an elision are called *aglopī*.

[The root] *śās* in the sense of "instruction" (Dhātupāṭha 1075) has an *ṛt* vowel; those [roots] beginning with *bādhṛ* in the sense of "stirring" (Dhātupāṭha 5) have an *ṛt* vowel. Thus, these are the *ṛdinti*.
Regarding the forms *amamālat* and *amamātarat*:

the suffix *ṇic* is applied by the rule *tat karoti tad ācaṣṭe* (Gaṇasūtra 187); then, by the rule *ṇāviṣṭhavat kāryaṃ prātipadikasya* (Vārttika 813), the status of being like the superlative suffix *iṣṭhan* (*iṣṭhavadbhāva*) applies; consequently, by the rule *turiṣṭhemeyaḥsu* (Pāṇini 6.4.154), there is elision of the final *ṛ* (*ṭilopa*); after that, the *luṅ* tense suffixes and so forth are added.
In forms such as *atayararājat*, the suffix *ṇic* is applied by the rule *prātipadikād dhātvarthe bahulam iṣṭhavacca* (Gaṇasūtra 186).
Regarding the term *anvalulomat*:
the suffix *ṇic* is applied by the rule *satyāpapāśarūpa* [Pāṇini 3.1.25]. Regarding the phrase "where only *aṅ* itself [is elided]," etc.:

here, the elision of *aṅ* occurs in two ways—sometimes only *aṅ* itself is elided, as in *amāmālīt* and so forth; sometimes both *aṅ* and the following consonant (*hal*) are elided, as in *atyararājat* and so forth.

Is it not already established that where only [the vowel] *a* is elided (*lupyate*), there the rule does not apply because of the status of the elision as being like its original (*sthānivadbhāva*)? For when there is the status of being like the original, the [substitution of] *yaṇ* simply does not occur due to the intervention caused by the elision; therefore, the statement "where [the vowel] *a* is elided" (*aglopi*) is not for that purpose.

However, in the other case, since the substitute applies to both the consonant (*hal*) and the vowel (*ac*), the result is achieved because there is no status of being like the original (*asthānivadbhāva*).

For it has been stated that the status of being "as if the original" (sthānivadbhāva) applies to a substitute for a vowel (*aj*) when it is conditioned by a subsequent element, but not to a substitute for a consonant (*hal*) or a vowel (*ac*).
Therefore, this statement is intended for cases where there are substitutes for both consonants and vowels.
Is it for another purpose? Since it is being formulated, it will also serve the purpose of cases where only the initial [vowel] is elided; thus, an example for that purpose has been presented.
*adudhaukat*.

[The roots] *kaki*, *vaki*, *āki*, *traki*, *ḍhaukṛ*, *traukṛ*, *ṣvaṣka*, *vaska*, *maska*, *ṭikṛ*, *ṭīkṛ*, *tikṛ*, *raghi*, and *laghi* have the meaning of motion (*gatyarthāḥ*). (Dhātupāṭha 94–108).

By [Pāṇini 8.4.54], the *jaś*-substitution occurs, resulting in the letter *ḍ*. Is this root *bhrāj* listed in the *Bhvādi* class as being *anudātta*? It is indeed listed there as an *ātmanepada* root with the marker *ṛ*, namely `ṭubhrāju ṭubhrāsu dīptau` (Dhātupāṭha 823, 824). Furthermore, it is also listed prior to the *phaṇādi* group as `ejṛbhrejṛ bhrājṛ dīptau` (Dhātupāṭha 179, 180, 181).

Its inclusion in the *phaṇādi* group must necessarily be accepted for the sake of the operations pertaining to that specific section (*tantra*), since by that very inclusion, the grammatical operations of the *gaṇa*—such as the addition of the suffix *śap*—are also established.

The reading of this [root] elsewhere appears to be non-Vedic (*anārṣa*). Regarding the roots *bhāsṛ* (in illumination) [DhP 6.24], *bhā* (in distinct speech) [DhP 6.12], *dīpī* (in illumination) [DhP 2.150], *jīva* (in sustaining life) [DhP 6.562], *mīla*, *śmīla*, *smīla*, *kṣmīla* (in closing the eyes) [DhP 6.517–520], and *pīḍa* (in pressing) [DhP 9.1544]—since the shortening [of the penultimate vowel] would have been obligatory for these, this optional rule (*vibhāṣā*) is commenced. Thus, we have the form *abibhrajat*.
When there is shortness (*hrasvatva*), then, as before, the substitution of *it* occurs by virtue of the treatment as *san*-like (*sanvadbhāva*).
Thus, "abībhavat":

here, as before, there is lengthening (*dīrgha*). Now, for what purpose is the designation of *ṛt* applied to the roots *bhrāj* and *bhās*, given that this [designation] serves as their *ṛt*-marker? The purpose is so that, by virtue of being marked with *ṛt*, the prohibition of shortening may apply according to the preceding rule.

If the shortening of those two vowels were prescribed by the *Vibhāṣā* [rule], then the inclusion of the marker *ṛt* would indeed be purposeless; therefore, he says "of *bhrāja* and *bhās*" and so forth.

Regarding the term "un-Pāṇinian" (*apāṇinīyam*): this is "Pāṇinian" (*pāṇinīyam*) because it belongs to Pāṇini; "un-Pāṇinian" means not belonging to Pāṇini. This is because he does not accept it, and not because he did not compose it.

Otherwise, the designation of these roots as having an indicatory *ṛ* (ṛdit), such as in "bādhṛ viloḍane" (Dhātupāṭha 5), would be un-Pāṇinian. For it was established previously (under Pāṇini 6.1.106) that the author of the *gaṇa*-lists is not Pāṇini; thus, the author of the *gaṇa*-lists is one person and the author of the *sūtra*s is another. Furthermore, when shortening (*hrasvatva*) would otherwise apply, its exception is prescribed: the elision (*lopa*) of the root *pibati* is ordained, as is the substitution of the vowel *ī* for the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*).
Because of the governing rule concerning the *upadhā* (the penultimate vowel), [the substitution] would apply only to the *upadhā*.
The inclusion of the term *adhi* is for the purpose that the two letters *l* and *i* should not optionally replace [the *upadhā*] simultaneously—
as in the form *apīpyat*.

The root *pā* in the sense of "drinking" (Dhātupāṭha 925) takes the suffix *ṇic*. By the rule *śācchāsāhvāvyāvepām* [Pāṇini 7.3.37], the augment *yuk* is applied. Now, one might object: since the elision of the penultimate vowel (*upadhālopa*) is obligatory and occurs earlier due to its higher priority, the root would then lack a syllable (*anackatva*), and thus reduplication should not take place. To this, he says: "When the elision of the penultimate vowel has been made," and so forth.
This is easily understood.

The mention of *pibāteḥ* with the *śtip* affix is for the purpose of excluding the *yaṅ*-luṅ form—namely, *apāpayat*. However, that [mention] cannot serve to exclude the two roots *pā* "to protect" (DhP 1056) and *pai* "to dry up" (DhP 920, 921); for in those cases, the former will not apply simply because it belongs to the *luk*-class (*adādi*), while the latter is excluded because it is a derivative (*lākṣaṇika*) form. This [rule] is also an exception to the shortening [of the vowel].
The rule *īccābhyāsasya* [Pāṇini 7.4.4] is no longer in force.

The mention [of the root] with the *śtip* affix is solely for the purpose of excluding the *yaṅ*-lopa (the elision of the *yaṅ* suffix), as in the example *atāsthapat*. This too is an exception (*apavāda*) to the rule concerning short vowels (*hrasva*). Here, too, the purpose of the mention with *śtip* is the same—as in *ajāghrapat*. In this case, the vowel *ṛ* is presented as the substituend (*sthānin*), and because it is an internal element (*antaraṅga*), only *i*, *r*, *ā*, or *ā* would be expected to occur; for the short vowel is not an external element (*bahiraṅga*). Therefore, since these [rules for *i*, *r*, *ā*, and *ā*] are understood to be exceptions to those [short vowels], he says: "It is an exception to *i*, *r*, *ā*, and *ā*."

The substitution of *i* by [Pāṇini 7.1.101] *upadhāyāśca*, the substitution of *a* (guṇa) by [Pāṇini 7.3.86] *pugantalaghūpadhasya*, and the substitution of *ā* by [Pāṇini 7.2.114] *mṛjerbṛddhiḥ*—these, which would respectively replace the vowel *ṛ* with *ir*, *ar*, and *ār* according to [Pāṇini 1.1.50] *uraṇ raparaḥ*, are here set aside as exceptions. An example is *acīkṛtat*.
The root *kṛt* (meaning "to sound") is from the *cur*-class (Dhātupāṭha 1653); the suffix *ṇic* is added.
Regarding "avīvṛtat": the root *vṛt* means "to turn" (Dhātupāṭha 758). Regarding "amīmṛjat":
the root *mṛj* means "to cleanse" (Dhātupāṭha 1066), followed by the causative suffix *ṇic*.

But surely, because they are *antaraṅga* (internal), the substitutions *i*, *ī*, and *ar* ought to occur; for their *antaraṅga* status is due to their depending solely on the suffix *ṇi*. However, the substitution of *ṛ* depends upon the *ṇic* that follows *caṅ*, and is therefore *bahiraṅga* (external).
So how can it be that by this [substitution of *ṛ*], *i*, *ī*, and *ar* are superseded? To this he says: "By the force of the explicit statement," and so forth.
If [the operations] such as being "internal" (antaraṅga) were to apply [first], then the explicit statement [of the rule] would be purposeless, because it would have no scope [otherwise].
Therefore, even those [operations] that are internal are superseded.
[This is shown by the phrase] "the inclusion of *t* [in the term *tapara*]," and so forth.

For if the *tapara* marker were not present, then wherever a long vowel (*dīrgha*) is the substitute, a long vowel would result by virtue of being the closest [to the original] due to similarity of place (*antaratamya*). Therefore, the *tapara* marker is employed so that even when a long vowel is the substitute, only a short vowel may occur. Now, one might object: "Since it is said that 'an *aṇ* being pronounced does not include its homogeneous counterparts' (*vyā.pa.* 35), even when a long vowel is the substitute, only a short vowel will occur, not a long one. To this he replies: "And this [short vowel] is not being pronounced," and so forth. What is the reason? To this he says: "In order to exclude other possible substitutes."
Thus [it is said]:

there are other substitutes such as *ira*, *ār*, and so on; for the purpose of excluding those, it is permitted that the vowel *ī* retains its very own form (*asmīyarūpa*), and a previously non-existent *ṛ* is not prescribed at all—so how could this [substitute] be something yet to be produced (*bhāvyamāna*)? Regarding the form *avīvṛdhat*:
the root *vṛdhu* (meaning "to grow," Dhātupāṭha 759) takes the causative suffix *ṇic*, followed by the aorist (*luṅ*) and other suffixes.

The inclusion of the word *nitya* ("always") is for the purpose of making known that the particle *vā* from the preceding sūtra does not carry over [to this one]; otherwise, it might be understood that even there [in the preceding rule], this [particle] does not carry over. Regarding the example *avadigye*: the root *deṅ* is used in the sense of "protection" (*rakṣaṇe*; Dhātupāṭha 962). The suffix *liṭ* is applied; because of its *ṅit*-character, the Ātmanepada voice is used; the third person singular ending is added; by [Pāṇini 3.4.81], *eś* and *irec* are substituted [for the *liṭ* endings]; and by [Pāṇini 6.4.82], *yaṇ* substitution occurs [of *i* for *e*]. It is said: "By the mention of *dayateḥ*, the root *deṅ* is intended, and not the root *daya* in the sense of 'giving' (*dāna*')."
But surely, why is there not an inclusion of the root *daya*—meaning "giving, going, protecting, harming, and taking" (Dhātupāṭha 481)? To this he says: "For of that," and so forth.

It is stated [in the rule] "in the *liṭ* [perfect tense]," yet there is no *liṭ* immediately following the root *daya* "in giving" (Dhātupāṭha 481). Why?
