Because its [the *ām* suffix's] application is prescribed by the rule "of that" (Pāṇini 3.1.37). Objection: But does not the word "not in a mantra" (*amantra*) carry over into that [rule 3.1.37]? Therefore, since there is no *ām* in a mantra, would there not indeed be immediate succession? Response: He thinks as follows: "In the Vedic language (*chandas*), one follows what is actually observed. Thus, even though the word "not in a mantra" applies, because an *ām* is not observed in mantras, the immediate succession does not occur.
The intention is that the substitution of *diś* for the root *dā*, as in "dāy" (meaning "to give," Dhātupāṭha 481), is not observed in the mantra.

Regarding the objection: "In *avadigye*, since the substitution of *digi* would have no scope, the reduplication should occur first; just as in *cakhyau*, where the substitution of *khyāñ* for *cakṣiṅ* (Pāṇ. 2.4.54) has no scope, the reduplication occurs after that substitution has been applied—so too here, once the substitution of *digi* is made in *avadigye*, by what could the subsequent reduplication be blocked?"—to one who might raise this objection, he replies: "The blocking of the reduplication by the substitution of *digi* is intended. But how is this obtained, even though it is merely intended? By the continued application (*anuvṛtti*) of the term "obligatory" (*nitya*).

In this context, the term *nitya* ("obligatory") is carried over from the preceding sūtra, and an option (*vibhāṣā*) does not apply here. Therefore, the inclusion of the term *nitya* is understood to serve the purpose of excluding whatever else might otherwise apply. Consequently, regarding whatever grammatical operation would otherwise apply in the *liṭ* (perfect) tense, the inclusion of *nitya* is understood to exclude that; thus, the connection is made as follows: "Among the operations applicable in the *liṭ*, only the substitution of *dig* etc. occurs obligatorily, and no other operation. In this way, the prevention of reduplication (*dvirvacana*) is achieved.

Since the substitution of *yaṇ* is not prescribed here because it is stated that [the rule] applies only when *liṭ* follows, the form becomes [as follows] in the presence of an *ac* vowel: *sasvaratuḥ*, *sasvaruḥ*. [The root] *svṛ* [is used] in the sense of "sound" and "affliction" (*dhātupāṭha* 932). By [the rule] *urat* [7.4.66], there is the substitution of *at* for the reduplicated syllable, followed by the substitution of *ra* for *ṛ*, and then the *halādiśeṣa* operation. [Similarly:
*dadhvaratuḥ*, *dadhvaruḥ*.
The root *dhvṛ* is listed as "to be distressed" (Dhātupāṭha 939).
[Examples: *sasmaratuḥ*, *sasmaruḥ*. The root *smṛ* is listed as "to remember" (Dhātupāṭha 807).

But is it not the case that everywhere the reduplication (*abhyāsa*) is a member (*aṅga*), and yet that [member] does not have the status of being "beginning with a conjunct" (*saṃyogādi*)? This is not a fault, for the position here is that "the double usage is the reduplication" (*dviḥprayogo dvirvacanam*); in that view, even the subsequent [portion] indeed receives the designation of a member (*aṅga*).

Alternatively, even if one holds that "the reduplication occurs in place [of the whole]" (*sthāne dvirvacanam*), there is still no fault; for in every instance, the reduplication of the *liṭ* [perfect] prevents the status of being "beginning with a conjunct. And this rule is stated; therefore, we shall understand it thus: before the reduplication, the status of being "beginning with a conjunct" exists, and here too, prior to the reduplication, the status of being "beginning with a conjunct" exists—as in *cikṣipatuḥ*, *cikṣipuḥ*.
The root *kṣi* means "to perish" (*dhātupāṭha* 236); here, the substitution of *iyaṅ* applies.
Regarding the phrase "even in the domain of prohibition," etc.:
in cases such as *thal*, which do not fall within the scope of the prohibition [of *guṇa*] by the rule *kṅiti ca* (Pāṇini 1.1.5), the *guṇa* is established by the rule [7.3.84].

Therefore, this [sūtra] is commenced so that [the rule for *guṇa*] may apply even in the domain of the prohibition of *guṇa*. For someone might have the misconception that even in the domain of *vṛddhi*, *guṇa* ought to occur because it is subsequent; thus, in order to dispel that, he says: "But in the domain of *vṛddhi*" and so forth. The scope of *guṇa* is, for example, *sasvaratuḥ* and *sasvaruḥ*; the scope of *vṛddhi* before a suffix marked with *ñ* or *ṇ* is, for example, *svārakaḥ* and *dhvārakaḥ*. In cases such as *sasvāra* and *dadhvāra*, where both would apply, *vṛddhi* alone occurs by virtue of the "prior exception" (*pūrvavipratiṣedha*).

Now, what is the purpose of including the *tapara* (the long vowel *ā*)? If it is for the sake of preventing [the substitution] from applying even to the long vowel—as in the case of the root *stṛñ* "to cover" (DhP 1484), where one would have *ātastaratuḥ* and *ātastaruḥ* by the subsequent rule—this is not so; for the long vowel must indeed be included by the subsequent rule. But surely, because of this *tapara*, it would not apply? And the subsequent rule has its own scope, namely before a consonant cluster (*asaṃyoga*), as in *kṛ* "to scatter" (DhP 1409), where we have *nicakaratuḥ* and *nikaruḥ*. If that is the case, then this is not a *tapara* at all; rather, this is a reference made with the suffix *tasin*.
Regarding the phrase "of *saṃyoga*, etc. and so forth:

here, within the context of the *aṅga* (stem), the *aṅga* is qualified by being "that which begins with a *saṃyoga*. Now, since the root *kṛ* does not have an *aṅga* beginning with a *saṇyoga*, [the rule] would not apply; therefore, the inclusion of the term "preceded by a *saṃyoga*" (*saṃyogopadha*) must be made so that the *guṇa* substitution may also occur for the root *kṛ*.

Regarding the forms *sañcaskaratuḥ* and *sañcaskaruḥ*, the augment *suṭ* is applied by [Pāṇini 6.1.137], and by the rule [6.1.136], that *suṭ* occurs even when there is an intervention by the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*). But what is the reason that the *guṇa* substitution is not established here, given that once *suṭ* has been added, the root *kṛ* becomes preceded by a conjunct consonant (*saṃyoga*) according to the principle: "That which falls in the middle of something is included by the mention of that thing" (Vyāḍipāda 21)? To this, he says: "For in this case," and so forth.

By this, he demonstrates that *suṭ* is extrinsic (*bahiraṅga*). For if it were extrinsic, then by the rule "that which is extrinsic is unestablished (*asiddha*) with respect to that which is intrinsic" (Vyāḍi-Pāṇini 42), since the extrinsic *suṭ* would be unestablished when the intrinsic *guṇa* is to be applied, the status of the root *kṛ* as beginning with a conjunct consonant (*saṃyogādi*) would not be possible. According to the view that "first the verbal root is joined with a prefix (*upasarga*), and afterwards with an instrument (*sādhana*)" (Jainendra-Pāṇinian Vṛtti 98), the operation concerning the root and the prefix is intrinsic; therefore, since *suṭ* is also an operation concerning the root and the prefix, it would [otherwise] be considered intrinsic.

In the view that "the verbal root (*dhātu*) is joined with the *sādhana* [kāraka] first, and subsequently with the prefix (*upasarga*)," the *suṭ* augment becomes *bahiraṅga*. For in this view, since the meaning of the root alone—without a prefix—is joined with the *sādhana*, the *liṭ* suffix denoting the *sādhana* must first be applied. Once that has been done and reduplication (*dvirvacana*) based upon it has occurred, the *suṭ* is then applied through the rule "even when there is intervention by *aṭ* or a reduplicated element" (*aḍabhyāsavayavāye’pi*, Pāṇini 6.1.136).
And this being the case, because it depends on multiple words and requires many factors, the *suṭ* augment is established as being "external" (*bahiraṅga*).

Guṇa, however, occurs at the very moment immediately following the production of the *liṅ* suffix; it requires nothing else. Because it depends on a single word and requires few factors, it is "internal" (*antaraṅga*). Consequently, while that [guṇa] is to be applied, since the *suṭ* is not yet established, the root *karoti* does not have a stem beginning with a conjunct consonant.
Therefore, that [guṇa] does not apply.

"And having done so," etc. Since *suṭ* is thus external (*bahiraṅga*), and having done so, when the internal (*antaraṅga*) augment *iṭ* is to be applied, because that [augment] is non-existent (*asiddha*) due to the absence of an initial conjunct consonant (*asaṃyogāditvāt*), the augment *iṭ* does not occur in *karoter upaskṛṣīṣṭa* or *saṃskṛṣīṣṭa* by virtue of [Pāṇini 7.2.43]. By this, the very externality of *suṭ* is demonstrated.

[Objection: But surely, because the context concerns *aṅga* (the stem), by proximity only a *saṃyoga* that is a part of the *aṅga* is understood. Furthermore, by the mention of "preceding *k*" (*kātpūrva*), it has been indicated therein that the *suṭ* augment is not a part of the stem (*abhakta*); therefore, precisely because it is not a part of the stem and thus does not begin with a *saṃyoga*, the *iṇ* [augment] will not apply to the root *kṛ*. Why then is the status of being "external" (*bahiraṅga*) and consequently "unestablished" (*asiddha*) brought forward here? [Reply: This is true; however, the following is considered: let the *suṭ* indeed be a part of the *karoti* stem; nevertheless, because it is unestablished, there will be no occasion for the *iṭ* augment in the form *saṃskṛṣīṣṭa*. Therefore, the mention of "having a *saṃyoga* as a penultimate letter" (*saṃyogopadha*) must be made.

This is its meaning: the root *kṛ* with a conjunct consonant (*saṃyogopadha*) is intended to be included in the rule; that is to say, an explanation for the inclusion of those with a conjunct consonant must be provided. In this regard, the following explanation should be given: the letter *ca* is added here, and it serves to include the root *kṛ* when it has a conjunct consonant as its penultimate. Thus, once the augment *suṭ* is applied to it as well, the *guṇa* substitution will take place for that which has a conjunct consonant as its penultimate. [The root] *ṛcch* [is listed] in the sense of "going," "loss of the senses," and "becoming embodied" (Dhātupāṭha 1296).
The elision (*praśleṣa*) of the vowel *ṛ* should also be applied here, because of the use of the plural number.
For this very reason, he says: "of the root *ṛcchati*, of that which has *ṛ* as its [stem-final], and of those ending in the vowel *ṛ*.
Those ending in *ṛ* include, for example, *kṝ* "to scatter" (Dhātupāṭha 1409) and *gṝ* "to swallow" (Dhātupāṭha 1410), and so forth.
*ānarcchatuḥ*, *ānarcchuḥ*, and so forth.

[The suffixes] *atus* and *us*: there is *guṇa* substitution, reduplication, and the treatment of the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsakārya*) as before; then, by [Pāṇini 7.4.70], there is lengthening (*dīrgha*), and by [Pāṇini 7.4.71], *nuṭ* is inserted because [the root] has two consonants (*dvihala*).
Thus: *āratuḥ*, *āruḥ*.

As before, there is lengthening by virtue of repetition (*abhyāsa*), and then [the substitution] of the homogeneous vowel with the preceding one. Regarding the statement "because *ṛcchati* does not have a light penult," and so forth: its lack of a light penult is due to its being an internal (*antaraṅga*) operation.

It should be understood that when the *tuk* augment is applied by the rule *che ca* [Pāṇini 6.1.71], and the designation *guru* is established by the rule *aciśnudhātubhruvāṃ yvoriyaṅuvaṅau* [Pāṇini 6.4.77], the [substitution] does not apply because the root has a heavy penultimate vowel (*gurūpadha*).
Regarding the passage beginning with *ṛtāṃ tu*:
since the [substitution] is indeed prohibited for roots ending in *ṛ*, it is expected that the *guṇa* substitution is prescribed.

The prohibition of their [the suffixes] *guṇa* substitution, however, should be understood from the rule *asaṃyogālliṭ kit* (Pāṇini 1.2.5) when *kit*-ness is established by the rule *ārdhadhātukasyeḍ valādeḥ* (Pāṇini 7.2.35).
Regarding the phrase "but in the domain of *vṛddhi*" and so forth:

just as in the domain of *vṛddhi*, the rule *ṛtaśca saṃyogādeḥ* (Pāṇini 7.4.10) prescribes *vṛddhi* itself by means of a prior counter-exception (*pūrvavipratiṣedha*), so too should it be understood for the vowels *ṛ* and *ṝ*.

The scope for *guṇa* is, for example, *nicakaratuḥ* and *nicakaruḥ*; the scope for *vṛddhi* is, for example, *kārakaḥ* and *hārakaḥ*. In cases such as *nicakāra* and *nijagāra*, where both rules would apply, *vṛddhi* alone is prescribed by means of the "priority of the preceding" (*pūrvavipratiṣedha*). Regarding the roots *śṛ* (in the sense of injury), *dṛ* (in the sense of tearing), and *pṛ* (in the senses of protecting and filling)—as listed in the Dhātupāṭha at numbers 1488, 1490, and 1489 respectively—the *guṇa* substitution occurs invariably by the preceding rule [Pāṇini 7.3.84]. Thus, we have *viśaśratuḥ*;
once the shortening (*hrasvatva*) has taken place, the *yaṇ* substitution follows.

Regarding the phrase "the mention of *hrasva*," and so forth: if the mention of *hrasva* were not made, then in the alternative (*pakṣa*) where the option (*vikalpa*) provided by the word *vā* results in the absence of *guṇa*, the substitution of *i* [by *ṛta iddhātoḥ* 7.1.100] would undesirably apply, as would the substitution of *u* [by *udīṭhpūrvasya* 7.1.102]. Therefore, for the purpose of preventing that, the word *hrasva* is stated. Furthermore, although one could have simply said *ṛt*, the mention of *hrasva* is for the sake of subsequent rules.
"Which ones? and so forth.
But how, when this [rule] is rejected, are forms such as *viśaśratuḥ* established? To this he says: "In the sense of cooking," and so forth.

Although forms such as *viśaśratuḥ* are established by applying the elision of the suffix *ak* according to Pāṇini 6.4.64, even so, the meaning would not be correct; therefore, suspecting that the rejection of the rule for the perfect tense (*liṭ*) would be untenable, he states that "roots have multiple meanings."
With the words "And this being so," and so forth, he refutes the rejection [of the rule] by means of counter-examples.

If the rejection of the sūtra were made, how could the form *viśaśṛṣān* be established when it has been formed? For instance: if the shortening of the vowel for the root *śṛṇāti* is not applied, then the form would be *viśaśarvān*;
if, however, it is applied to the root *śrāti*, the form would be *viśaśrivān*.
Therefore, its rejection is improper. The term *aṇ* includes the preceding *ṇ* by means of a pratyāhāra; otherwise, one would have said simply "ke caḥ.
Alternatively, one would not even have said "acaḥ," for it is only vowels (*ac*) that possess short, long, and protracted durations.
[The example is] "jñakā."
"One who knows" is *jña*; from that [word] ending in *-jña*, the suffix *ṭāp* is applied.
Thus, *ajñātā jñā* ("one who was unknown, but now known") takes the suffix *ka* according to *prāgivāt kaḥ* (Pāṇini 5.3.70).
Alternatively, *anukampitā jñā* ("pitied as a knower") takes the suffix *kan* according to [Pāṇini 5.3.76]. Once *kan* has been applied, *ṭāp* is added to that which ends in it.

Now, why does this not occur here: by the rule *kṛdādhārārcikalabhyaḥ kan* (Pāṇini 3.3.18), the suffix *kan* is applied after the roots *rāti* and *dadhāti*, and from that which ends in *kan*, the feminine suffix *ṭāp* is added, resulting in forms such as *rākā* and *dhākā*? This is easily understood. Someone might have the misconception that because the root *kan* without an indicatory letter (*niranubandhaka*) is being taken here, the paribhāṣā "the rule applies only to that which lacks an indicatory letter" (*niranubandhakaparibhāṣā*) should preclude the application of *kan*. To dispel this doubt, he says: *na kapi*, etc.
If this technical rule (*paribhāṣā*) were to apply here, then the prohibition in [Pāṇini 7.4.14], *na kapi*, would be purposeless;
the intention is that the suffix *kap* will not be included [in the application of the rule] precisely because it possesses an *anubandha*. Regarding the example *bahukumārīkaḥ*:
it means "one who has many daughters" (*bahvyaḥ kumāryo yasya saḥ*).

By [Pāṇini 5.4.153], the suffix *kap* is applied, and there is the elision of the *anubandha*. Now, if the shortening (*hrasvatva*) here is prohibited, why does the shortening of the *upasarjana* not occur? If you argue that it will not occur precisely because of this prohibition, we say no; according to the principle "a rule or a prohibition applies only to what is immediately preceding" (Vyāḍiparibhāṣā 19), this prohibition applies only to the immediately preceding short vowel, and not to every short vowel.

If it is argued that, by the force of the word *kapi*, there will be no shortening of the subordinate member (*upasarjana*) because of the rule *hrasvo napuṃsake prātipadikasya* [Pāṇini 1.2.47], since the rule for shortening [1.2.48] uses the term *strī* to include suffixes such as *ṭāp* and others prescribed under the heading of *strī* (feminine); therefore, in the case of *bahukumārīka*, the shortening of the subordinate member ought to occur—[the author] says: "Of the subordinate member of a cow-word or a feminine word," and so forth. Why does it not occur? He says: "For, in the sense of the compound," and so forth.

For the shortening of the *upasarjana* is prescribed for a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) that ends in a feminine suffix when it is a compound. In the formulation of that rule, because the term "nominal stem" (*prātipadika*) is understood from the previous rule *hrasvo napuṃsake prātipadikasya* [Pāṇini 1.2.47], the shortening of the *upasarjana* would apply only to a compound nominal stem that ends in a feminine suffix. However, in examples such as *bahukumārīkaḥ*, the compound nominal stem does not end in a feminine suffix; why is this so? Because the suffix *kap* is prescribed in this very context by the governing rule *kaḥ karṇoḥ...* [Pāṇini 5.4.68].

Regarding the inclusion of the word *anta* ("end") in the rule *samāsāntāḥ*, this is its purpose: that the suffix should be the final part (*anta*) of the compound. But how does that [suffix] become a constituent part (*avayava*) of the compound? Only if the designation "compound" (*samāsa-saṃjñā*) applies to it as well. And how does the designation "compound" apply to it? If the suffix *kap* occurs after the final member (*uttarapada*) which expresses the meaning of the compound, even before the compound has been formed; and subsequently, the compound is formed with that which ends in *kap*, and not otherwise. Therefore, since *kap* is prescribed under the governing heading (*adhikāra*) of "compound suffixes" (*samāsānta*), once *kap* has been applied to the final member expressing the meaning of the compound, the compound must subsequently be formed.

And therefore, since a compound ending in a feminine suffix does not exist here as a single subsequent member of a compound, the shortening of the *upasarjana* does not occur. In the case of "bahukhaṭvākaḥ," the suffix *kap* is applied by [Pāṇini 5.4.154]. Since the prohibition [of this shortening] would have applied by [Pāṇini 1.1.5], this specific rule is prescribed as an exception. In the case of "akarot," [the same applies].

From the root *kṛ*, there is the suffix *luṅ*; [then] *cli* [is applied]; [and then] *tip* [is applied] according to Pāṇini 3.1.59, whereby *cli* is replaced by *aṅ*. Thus, "asarat" [is formed]. The root *sṛ* means "to go" (Dhātupāṭha 935).

Regarding "ārat": from the root *ṛ* in the sense of "motion" and "attaining" (Dhātupāṭha 936), the suffix *aṅ* is applied by [Pāṇini 3.1.56] *sarttiśāstyarttibhyaśca*. Since *ṛ* begins with a vowel other than *a*, the augment *āṭ* is added by [Pāṇini 6.1.87] *āṭaśca*, resulting in the vṛddhi strengthening. Regarding "adarśat": the suffix *aṅ* is applied by [Pāṇini 3.1.57].

Now, for what purpose is the mention of *guṇa* (vocalic strengthening)? Why not simply say "the letter *a*"? It cannot be done in this way; for if one were to say "the letter *a*," it would apply to the final [letter] of the root *duś*. But when *guṇa* is mentioned, because there is a restriction in the formulation of a technical designation (*saṃjñā*), it occurs only in place of *iK* (the vowels *i*, *u*, and *ṛ*). As in the example: *āsthat*.
In the case of *asu* (meaning "to throw," Dhātupāṭha 1209), the substitution of *aṅ* for *cl* occurs by the rule *asyativaktikhakyātibhyo'ṅ* [Pāṇini 3.1.52]. Regarding *āṭ*:

the root *ṭu oā* (meaning "motion" and "increase," Dhātupāṭha 1010) takes the suffix *aṅ* by the rule *jṛstambhubhrucu* [Pāṇini 3.2.58] et cetera; there is then the formation of a single substitute (*pararūpa*) for the two vowels *a*. Regarding *apaptat*: [the same process applies].
The roots *śal*, *hul*, and *patlṛ* mean "to go" (*gatau*; Dhātupāṭha 843, 844, 845); the suffix *aṅ* is applied by virtue of their belonging to the *puṣādi* group.
The letter *m* [in the root] is for the purpose of indicating the specific grammatical operation (*deśavidhyartha*). Regarding the form *avocat*:
the root *vac* means "to speak" (*paribhāṣaṇe*; Dhātupāṭha 1842); the suffix *aṅ* is applied by the rule *asyatiktikhyātibhyaḥ* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 3.1.52) and so forth.

The purpose of the letter *m* is precisely that. Since the prescription of *guṇa* has not yet reached its scope, this rule applies when a *sārvadhātuka* suffix beginning with *ṅ* follows. However, in the case of a suffix beginning with *p*, the *guṇa* is already established by the general rule alone. [In the case of] *loṭ*, after the augment *āṭ*—as in *śayai* and *śayāvahai*.
Therefore, where a grammatical operation (*guṇa*) does not otherwise apply, it is prescribed here:
"they lie down" (*śerate*).

Due to its belonging to the *adādi* class, there is the elision (*luk*) of the *śap* suffix; and by the rule "in the *ātmanepada* endings, [the final vowel] other than *a* [is replaced]" (*ātmanepadeṣvanataḥ*), the replacement of *jha* with *ad* occurs.
In this context, the augment *ru* is inserted [according to Pāṇini 7.1.6]. As in the example *śiśye*:
the suffix is *liṭ*; by the rule *liṭ ca* [3.4.115], it receives the designation of *ārdhadhātuka*; it is either the first person singular or the third person singular.

When there is the singular number of the third person, [the suffix] is *aiś*. As before, there is the dual number, and by rule 6.4.82 (*aci śnu-dhātu-...*), the *yaṇ* substitution occurs; for the other [suffixes], *iṭ* is added, and the final vowel (*ṭi*) becomes *e*. Now, what is the purpose of including the mention of *guṇa* (vocalization)? Why not simply say, "for *śīṅ*, *e* is substituted before a *sārvadhātuka* suffix"? The thought is this: in the mention of "*śīṅ*" with its *anubandha* (indicatory letter), the genitive case is employed. However, an *anubandha* has the nature of being subject to removal; once it has been assigned the technical name *it*, its removal would follow through elision (*lopa*). In that case, this other method of removal might be disregarded.
For that [genitive ending], the *it*-designation is not what causes its removal; rather, it is the letter *e* [that does so].
If that were so, then the vowel *e* would replace the position of the letter *ṅ*;

therefore, the mention of "guṇa" brings forward [the rule] *it*. But if it is argued that the letter *ṅ* is eliminated for that very reason, and thus the letter *ṅ* will not be pronounced, such that the instruction would be made as *jhiyaḥ*, this is not possible; for if the instruction were made in that way, it would apply even in the case of *yaṅ*-elision—as in *śeśīta* and *śeśyati*. [The correct form is] *śayyate*.

Regarding the form *śāśayyate*: this is the intensive (*yaṅ*) suffix. Because it is both subsequent and obligatory, the reduplication occurs first; prior to that, the substitution of *ayaṅ* takes place. Then, there is the reduplication of the element *śayya*, and by [Pāṇini 7.4.83], the long vowel is substituted for the abhyāsa (the reduplicated syllable).
In the case of *praśayya*:

the compound is formed by [Pāṇini 3.4.21] "The suffix *ktvā* is used after two verbs having the same agent when the action denoted by the former precedes in time," and by [Pāṇini 2.2.18]. Then, by [Pāṇini 7.1.37] "In a compound where the preceding member is not *nañ*, *lyap* is substituted for *ktvā*," the form *yem* results.
The suffix *yat* is applied according to Pāṇini 3.1.97 (*ñyādyat*), as in the word *śayyā* (note: this example is not found in the *Kāśikā*).

The suffix *kyap* is applied by the rule beginning with Pāṇini 3.3.99 (*saṃjñāyāṃ samajanisada...*) to form words such as *samaja*. The phrase "gone to the assembly" (*samūhaṃ gataḥ*) is thus explained.

The root *ūh* is used in the sense of "reflection" (*vitarke*) [Dhātupāṭha 648]. Although this form is established by the vocalization (*saṃprasāraṇa*) of the semivowel due to its inclusion in the *yajādi* group before a *kit* suffix, this rule for the short vowel is nevertheless prescribed so that the long vowel might also be heard after the root *ūh*.
Thus we have the form *samīhrate*.
The root *īh* is used in the sense of "exertion" (Dhātupāṭha 632).
The form *samūhitaḥ* is derived from the suffix *kta*.
"This meaning is a collection [of rules]": namely, "after roots ending in ṛ or consonants, the suffix -ya is used" (Pāṇini 3.1.124),
and "only after [roots ending in] aṇ," and so forth.
The mention of *aṇ* continues from the rule *ke'ṇaḥ* [Pāṇini 7.4.13]. Thus, in *ā uhrate*, *ohrate*, and *samohrate*,
the shortening of the vowel does not take place.

If the mention of *ava* were to continue [from the previous rule], then the prescription of the short vowel would be purposeless. Should one not rather say: "after a preposition, [the substitution of] *ud* occurs for the root *ūh*"? It is not purposeless; because it serves the purpose of what follows—namely, that he will state "for the root *eti* before the suffix *liṅ*" (Pāṇini 7.4.24), and there the term "short vowel" (*hrasva*) must be understood as continuing so that it applies there as well. Thus: *udiyāt*. The root is *iṇ* "to go" (Dhātupāṭha 1045); the suffix is *liṅ* in the sense of benediction (*āśis*), and by [Pāṇini 8.2.29] there is the elision of the *s*.
Thus: *abhīyāt*.
If the lengthening by *savarṇadīrgha* has not yet occurred, the short vowel remains.
By the rule beginning with "in the *liṅ* [optative] expressing a blessing" (*āśiṣi liṅi*), he shows the scope of the sūtra;
for since lengthening of the root *iṇ* is impossible in a *sārvadhātuka* *liṅ*, this [sūtra] has no application here.

In cases where lengthening would otherwise apply to the non-full (*akṛt*) or the sārvadhātuka suffixes [by Pāṇini 7.4.25], once that lengthening has occurred, this rule causes shortening. For example: *bhṛśāyate* (he acts intensely), where the suffix *kyaṅ* [is applied by Pāṇini 3.1.12];
and *sukhāyate* (he feels happy).
By the rule *sukhādibhyaḥ kartṛvedanāyām* [Pāṇini 3.1.18], the suffixes *kṛt* and *ṅit* are applied; thus,
in the form *cīyate*,
the *lakāra* (verbal suffix) denotes the object (*karman*).
In *cecīyate*,
there is guna of the reduplicated syllable according to [Pāṇini 7.4.82].
In *toṣṭūyate*, likewise.
The root *ṣṭuñ* in the sense of "praising" (*stutau*) [Dhātupāṭha 1043], by [Pāṇini 7.4.61], undergoes the retention of the final consonant (*khayaḥ śeṣaḥ*). Thus, one forms *cīyāt* and *stūyāt*;
these are the optative (*liṅ*) in the sense of benediction (*āśiṣi*).
Regarding the term *prakṛtyā*:
it is formed by adding the suffix *lyap* [Pāṇini 7.1.37];
and that [suffix] receives the technical designation *kṛt* by rule 3.1.93.

But surely, when *aj* is presented by the long vowel [in Pāṇini 6.4.3], the *aṅga* is qualified by it; and since there is the rule of "ending-in-that" (*tadantavidhi*) with respect to that qualifier, lengthening should apply to an *aṅga* ending in *ac*. However, in this case, once the *tuk* augment has been applied [by 6.1.71], the status of ending in *ac* no longer exists. Consequently, because it does not end in *ac*, lengthening should not occur.
Why, then, is the term *akṛt* included for the purpose of excluding this? To this, he says: "Because of its priority," and so forth.

What is the scope for the *tug* augment? It is in the case of *agnicit*. What is the scope for the long vowel (*dīrgha*)? It is in the case of *cīyate*. Since both would apply in cases such as *prakṛtya* and *prahmatya*, if the term *akṛt* were not included [in the rule], the *tug* would be superseded by the long vowel due to its posteriority in the order of rules.
Therefore, the inclusion of the term *akṛt* must be made.
As in the example: *cinuyāt*.

The suffix *liṅ* is used for the injunctive (*vidhi*) and so forth; and by the rule *tiṅ-śit-sārvadhātukam* [Pāṇini 3.4.113], it receives the technical designation *sārvadhātuka*. In the forms *uruyā* and *dhṛṣṇuyā*, the substitution of *yā* occurs for the third-case singular ending of the words *uru* and *dhṛṣṇu* by the rule *supāṃ suluk* [Pāṇini 7.1.39] and others. In the form *śucīkaroti*, [the same applies].
The suffix *cvi* is applied by the rule *ubhūtatadbhāve* (Pāṇini 5.4.50) and so forth.

The letter *ca* serves the purpose of conjunction (*samuccaya*) with respect to what precedes. The mention of *kyac* is understood as a continuation [from the previous rule], as is the phrase *akṛtsārvadhātukayoḥ*.
Thus, we have the form *mātrīyati*.

Regarding "pitrīyate": the suffix *kyaṅ* is applied by [Pāṇini 3.1.11], "The suffix *kyaṅ* is added after a verbal root [ending in] a *kartṛ* [agentive marker], and there is elision of the [final] *s*. Regarding "cekrīyate": [the suffix *yaṅ* is applied].

The suffix *yaṅ* is applied after the root *kṛ*; [in the word] "pitryam," the suffix *yat* is applied by [Pāṇini 4.3.79]; when the substitution of *rīṅ* has been made, the elision of the vowel *i* occurs by [Pāṇini 6.4.148].
But how, when the condition *kṅiti* is stated, does the substitution occur therein? To this he says: "The term *kṅiti* is discontinued here.

If this is so, then the mention of *yi* would also have to be discontinued, because they are mentioned in a single grammatical rule (*ekayoganirdiṣṭa*). This is not the case; for the continued application (*anuvṛtti*) of words is dependent upon their being marked with the *svarita* accent.

And here, since the *svarita* quality is specifically attributed to the mention of *yi*, that alone continues to apply; whereas since the *svarita* quality is not attributed to the mention of *kṅit*, that does not continue to apply here.
Regarding the form *cekīryate*:

the root *kṛ* means "to scatter" (*vikṣepe*; Dhātupāṭha 1409). By the rule *ṛta iddhātoḥ* [Pāṇini 7.1.100], the substitution of *i* for *ṛ* occurs, followed by the substitution of *ra* for *ṛ*. Then, by the rule *hali ca* [Pāṇini 8.2.77], the vowel is lengthened.
Regarding the form *nijegilyate*:

the root is *gṛ* in the sense of "swallowing" (*nigaraṇe*; Dhātupāṭha 1410). The intensive suffix *yaṅ* is applied according to [Pāṇini 3.1.24] *lupasada* etc., and the substitution of *la* for the *ra* is applied according to [Pāṇini 8.2.20] *yo yaṅi*.

Now, what is the purpose of including the long vowel (*dīrgha*) in the rule? Could one not simply say *riṅ*? [The desired form] would be established by the lengthening prescribed by the rule *akṛtsārvadhātukayoḥ* [Pāṇini 7.4.25]. In that case, too, the meaning would be this: the mention of *riṅ* need not be repeated in the subsequent rule, as this very [term] will carry over (*anuvarttiṣyate*) there. [Objection: It is not so established. Since the application of *riṅ* begins when the lengthening has not yet taken effect, it would act as an exception (*bādhaka*) to that lengthening.

Granted that [the rule for] *ṛ* is an exception (*bādhaka*) to its own long vowel, but how can it be an exception to another substitute that applies once the [long vowel] replacement has already occurred? Is it not the case that *riṅ* is commenced while this [long vowel] is still applicable? If so, then the pronunciation of the long vowel is for the sake of easy understanding by those of dull intellect;

the letter *ṅ* is for the sake of indicating that the substitution applies to the final [element]. Here too, the mention of *yi* and the term *akṛtsārvadhātuka* carry over. Among these, because of the possibility of deviation, the qualification applies only to *liṅ*, and not to *śayak*.
Regarding the forms *ādriyate* and *ādhriyate*:

the root *dṛṅ* meaning "to respect" (Dhātupāṭha 1411) and the root *dhṛṅ* meaning "to stand firm" (Dhātupāṭha 1412) are preceded by the prefix *āṅ*; the suffix *śa* is applied because they belong to the *tudādi* class.
Regarding the form *kriyāt*: [it is derived from the root *kṛ* with the optative suffix].
"Liṅ is used in the sense of benediction" (Pāṇini 3.3.173). Regarding the form *bibhṛyāt*:

here, the liṅ suffix denotes an injunction (*vidhi*) and so forth; because the root belongs to the *juhotyādi* class, there is *ślu* elision; by the rule "when *ślu* follows" (6.1.10), there is reduplication; and by the rule "for the roots *bhṛ*, etc., [the penultimate vowel] becomes *i*" (7.4.76), the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*) receives the vowel *i*.

Regarding "kṛpīṣṭa": the suffix *liṅ* is used in the sense of a benediction according to Pāṇini 3.3.173. By the rule 1.2.12 (*uśca*), the suffix is marked with the *kittva* indicator, which results in the absence of *guṇa* substitution. The roots *ṛ* (meaning "to go" and "to cause to reach," Dhātupāṭha 936) and *ṛ*/*sṛ* (meaning "to go," Dhātupāṭha 1098, 1099)—both belonging respectively to the Bhvādigaṇa and the Jauhotyādigaṇa—are what is intended here.

Because of the statement in the *Mahābhāṣya*, "Sūtras are like poetic license" (*chandovat sūtrāṇi bhavanti*), the elision (*luk*) of the suffix *śyan* has been applied and the term is indicated as *ṛt*. Otherwise, if the indication were made as *ucchati*, then the root belonging to the *juhotyādi* class would not be included.
Furthermore, even if the indication were made as *iyarti*, the root belonging to the *bhvādi* class would still not be included.
However, the indication as simply *ṛ* was not made for the sake of variety (*vaicitryārtha*).

This is an exception (*apavāda*) to what was previously established by the rule [Pāṇini 6.1.58]. It is said that "the [application of] *ś* is withdrawn because of impossibility. The impossibility, however, arises because the roots *ṛ* and *saṃyoga* (as well as others) do not have *ś* as their *vikaraṇa*.
The suffix *yak* [is applied] because of the rule "it is honored" (*aryate*); thus,
[the form] "he should honor" (*aryāt*).
The *liṅ* [suffix] is used in the sense of a benediction (*āśis*).

Now, why does [the substitution of *sa* for *s*] not occur in *saṃskriyate* or *saṃskriyāt*, since even the root *kṛ-* becomes a "base beginning with a conjunct" (*saṃyogādyaṅga*) once *suṭ* has been applied? To this he says: "In this case," etc.
However, *suṭ* is considered extrinsic (*bahiraṅga*) because it depends upon two words.

Furthermore, the guna [substitution] is internal (*antaraṅga*) because it depends on a single word (*ekapada*). According to the principle "that which is external (*bahiraṅga*) is as if non-existent (*asiddha*) with respect to that which is internal" (Vyākaraṇa-paribhāṣā 42), the augment *suṭ* is as if non-existent; therefore, the base (*aṅga*) does not possess the status of beginning with a conjunct consonant (*saṃyogādi*). Even if, for some reason, *suṭ* were to be considered existent, even then, because *suṭ* is not a suffix (*abhakta*), the base still does not begin with a conjunct consonant. Consequently, the guna substitution does not take effect.
Because of the governing context of "aṅga" (stem), the term "saṃyoga" (conjunction) is understood here as a part of the stem.
For if [the augment] *suṭ* were not a portion of the stem, it would not be logical for the conjunction to be a part of the stem in the form "iyṛyāt.
Thus, [the example is] "iyṛyāt."

The root *ṛ* means "to go" (Dhātupāṭha 1098). The suffix is the optative (*liṅ*) in the sense of injunction and so forth. Because the root belongs to the *juhotyādi* class, there is *ślu*-elision of the *śap* suffix; by the rule *ślau* [Pāṇini 6.1.10], reduplication occurs; by *arttipiparttyośca* [7.4.77], the *it* augment is applied to the reduplicated syllable; then the suffix *tīyaṅ* is added; and by *liṅaḥ salopo'nantyasya* [7.2.79], the *s* is elided. Although the rule *arttisaṃyogādyorat* [7.4.78] should have been sufficient, the explicit mention of *guṇa* is for the sake of variety. This [rule] is an exception to the *rīṅ* substitution that would otherwise apply.

Regarding the form *arāryate*: there is the *guṇa* substitution for the *yaṅ* suffix, followed by the replacement of *y* with *ra*. Then, by the rule "the second [syllable] of a reduplicated root beginning with a vowel" (Pāṇini 6.1.2), there is reduplication; the *halādiśeṣaḥ* (retention of the first consonant) applies, and finally, by the rule "of a long vowel before a suffix marked with ṅ or ñ" (Pāṇini 7.4.83), there is the lengthening of the vowel.

Now, one might object: "Since *ṛt* begins with a consonant (*ahala*), does not *yaṅ* fail to apply? To this he says: "*arteḥ*" and so forth. Granted that *yaṅ* occurs by virtue of an augmentative rule (*upasaṃkhyāna*), yet the substitution of *r* should not undergo reduplication because of the prohibition [in Pāṇini 6.1.3]: "There is no doubling of the first element of a conjunct consonant (*saṃyoga*) beginning with *n*, *d*, or *r*. To this he says: "*na ndrāḥ saṃyogādayaḥ*. For it has been stated therein: "A prohibition must be stated regarding the *r* that follows a *y*."

Therefore, after the *repha* (the letter *r*), there is a doubling of this [element] *yaṃ*. In the form *jaṅghanyate*, [the suffix] *nuk* is applied by [Pāṇini 7.4.85], and *kutva* (the substitution of *gh* for *h*) is applied by [Pāṇini 7.3.55]. In this regard, what is the purpose of the long-vowel (*dīrgha*) pronunciation? Is it so that the long vowel may occur and the short vowel (*hrasva*) may not? This is not the case; for even if the short vowel were prescribed, the result would be established by [Pāṇini 7.4.25]: *akṛtsārvadhātukayordīrghaḥ* ("there is lengthening of the penultimate vowel before non-*kṛt* affixes and *sārvadhātuka* affixes"). Furthermore, the long vowel will occur as appropriate by [Pāṇini 7.4.26]: *cvau ca* ("and when the suffix *cvi* follows"). If this is so, then this [long-vowel pronunciation] indicates the following: "A rule conditioned by a technical name (*saṃjñā*) is not universally obligatory" (*saṃjñāpūrvako vidhiranityaḥ*).
By this, *svāyambhuva* is established. [The rule] *cvau ca* (Pāṇini 7.4.26) is an exception to the lengthening [prescribed by] *ityasyāyamapavādaḥ* [referring to 7.4.25].
The letter *ca* is for the purpose of carrying over (*anukarṣaṇa*) the word *asya* from [the rule] *asya* (Pāṇini 7.4.32).

Now, what is the purpose of making a separate rule (*pṛthagyogakaraṇa*), instead of simply making a single rule such as *ccikyacoḥ asya*? To this he says: "The making of a separate rule," and so forth.

The separation of the rule (*yogavibhāga*) was made so that subsequent operations such as those beginning with *na chandasy-aputrasya* [Pāṇini 7.4.35] would apply to *kyac*, but not to *cvī*. Thus: the desire to eat is *bubhukṣā*;
the desire to drink is *pipāsā*;
the act of coveting is *gardhaḥ*.
The meaning is "he desires. [Regarding the statement] "that which was prescribed for the *kyac* suffix does not occur here," what then is that? He says: "the lengthening and the substitution of *ī*."

But surely, according to the principle that "a rule or a prohibition applies to what is immediately preceding" (Vyākaraṇa-paribhāṣā 19), there ought to be a prohibition of the *ītva* (the substitution of *ī*) which is immediate, and not of the lengthening (*dīrghatva*) which is separated by other elements? This is not a fault; the statement of both *ā* and *ādh* in the rule "ātaśca" [Pāṇini 7.4.37] is an indicator (*jñāpaka*) that this prohibition applies to the lengthening as well. Otherwise, since the form would already be established by the lengthening alone, the employment of the letter *ā* would be purposeless.
In the word "mitrayuḥ," the suffix *up* is applied by [Pāṇini 3.2.170], and the elision of the vowel *a* occurs by [Pāṇini 6.4.48].

The phrase "it should be stated as 'of those beginning with *aputra*'" means that this should be explained as having the sense that there is no prohibition for [words] beginning with *putra*. Here is the explanation: immediately after [the rule] *[[7.4.33]]*, it should be stated "*putrasya*" (of *putra*). For what purpose is this? It is for the purpose of setting aside the prohibition that will be stated in the rule "*na chandasi*" (not in the Vedic language).
Thus, the negative particle *nañ* need not be explicitly uttered in the form "of one who has no son" (*aputrasya*).

This [form] occurs because, although one should have stated "of a son" (*putrasya*) immediately after [the rule] Pāṇini 7.4.33, the statement here as "of one who has no son" (*aputrasya*) is for the purpose of ensuring that the prohibition applies to "son" (*putra*) and the others.
And this is obtained because "son" (*putra*) serves as an illustration (*upalakṣaṇa*). "This very singular number is the indicator (*jñāpaka*)," and so forth.

How does this function as an indicator (*jñāpaka*)? If this prohibition applied only to the *it* (the short *i*) immediately preceding [by Pāṇini 7.4.35], then the mention of *āt* would be purposeless, because [the lengthening] would already be established by [Pāṇini 7.4.25]: "before a non-*kṛt* suffix and before a *sārvadhātuka* suffix. Yet, it is indeed mentioned; therefore, it indicates that this prohibition applies to the long vowel (*dīrgha*) as well. When the prohibition [of 7.4.35], "not in the Veda" (*na chandasi*), would have applied, the mention of *āt* is undertaken for *deva* and *sumna*.
Regarding the word "in the *Kāṭhaka*": this is a qualifier specifically for the *Yajus* (Vedic prose).
"This Yajus belongs to Kaṭha" is *kāṭhakam*—[formed] by [Pāṇini 4.3.126]: *gotracaraṇād vañ*. [In the word *kāvyantaḥ*,] there is elision according to [Pāṇini 1.1.52].

From the base ending in *kyac*, the suffix *śatṛ* is applied, and from that [base] ending in *śatṛ*, the suffix *jas* is applied. The terms "in Vedic literature," "in the Yajus," and "in the Ṛc" are all withdrawn; therefore, this rule applies generally.
The root *do* in the sense of "cutting" (Dhātupāṭha 1148); *ṣo* in the sense of "concluding an action" (Dhātupāṭha 1147);

*mā* in the sense of "measurement" (Dhātupāṭha 1062), *māṅ* in the sense of "measurement" (Dhātupāṭha 1142), and *meṅ* in the sense of "bestowing" (Dhātupāṭha 961)—all three are included because of the rule "there is no distinction in the mention of roots beginning with *gam* and *dā*" (Vyāḍīyapañjikā 124);
and *ṣṭhā* in the sense of "cessation of motion" (Dhātupāṭha 928).

In that regard, for the first [root], the substitution of *da* is applicable by the rule "do dadghoḥ" (Pāṇini 7.4.46); for the remaining [roots], the substitution of *ī* is applicable by the rule "ghumāsthā" (Pāṇini 6.4.66) and others; therefore, the substitution of *it* is prescribed [here].
Regarding "avadāya":
as before, the suffix *ktvā* becomes *lyap*.
Regarding "avadātā": [it is derived from the same root].
The mention of *dyatisyatati* with the *śtip* affix is for the purpose of excluding the elision (*luṅ*) of *yaṅ*.
Consequently, for those two [roots], it remains exactly as it applies: *dādattaḥ*, *dādattavān*, *sāsītaḥ*, *sāsītavān*.

The addition of the *ta* (the long vowel marker) is for the sake of ease of pronunciation (*mukhasukhārtha*), and not for the purpose of excluding the long vowel (*dīrghanivṛttyartha*), because [according to] the rule "an *aṇ* being taught [as a substitute] does not include its homogeneous counterparts" (Vyāḍipāda 35), the long vowel would not otherwise be applicable. [Furthermore, regarding the roots: *śo* in the sense of "making thin" (Dhātupāṭha 1145) and *cho* in the sense of "cutting" (Dhātupāṭha 1146);
[and] "the substitution of *it* for the root *śyai* is obligatory when [the suffix] *vrat* follows."

The word *brāta* is not taken as the final member of a compound; rather, it refers to its domain (*viṣaya*). Within the domain of *vrata*, the substitution of *i* for *n* in the root *śyā* occurs invariably, as in the example: *saṃśito brāhmaṇaḥ*.

One who is indeed diligent regarding the specific conduct known as a *vrata* (vow) is called *saṃśitavrata*. He is so called because he is one by whom, or for whom, the *vrata* has been properly undertaken with diligence (*saṃśita*). Now, one might object: since the *vrata* is already indicated by the suffix *-it* prescribed in the rule governing *vrata*, the use of the word *vrata* itself would not be appropriate. This is not a fault; for while the suffix *-it* occurs elsewhere, it is always stated [with the word] *vrata*, and thus this becomes a general term.

In this context, the word *vrata* is employed in a specific sense. Its placement at the end of the compound (paranipāta) should be understood as being due to its inclusion in the group beginning with *āhitāgni*. [This is] established by understanding it as a case of restricted optionality (*vyavasthitavibhāṣā*).
In order to confirm this with a scriptural statement, he says: "Devatrāta," and so forth. [The root] *traiṅ* means "to protect" (Dhātupāṭha 965); the suffix *kta* is applied.

Regarding the rule *nudavidondatrāghrāhyībhyo'nyatarasyām* (Pāṇini 8.2.56), the substitution of *na* for *n* does not occur at all when the word is a proper name (*saṃjñā*). Thus, one protected by the gods (*devaiḥ*) is Devatrāta; here, the word *deva* is intended as an illustration of a proper name.

Even when the word *trāta* occurs alone as a proper name (*saṃjñā*), the substitution of *ṇatva* (the change of *t* to *ṇ*) is not applied. Thus, in a proper name, both forms occur elsewhere: *trāṇaḥ* and *trātaḥ*.
[The form] *galaḥ* [is derived similarly].
From the root *gṛ* (to swallow), the suffix *ac* is applied according to Pāṇini 3.1.134;
by 6.1.65 and 6.1.67, the substitution of *la* for *ra* is obligatory when referring to a limb of a living being, resulting in *gala*.
However, when referring to poison (*viṣa*), the form *gara* indeed occurs.
Regarding the word *grāha*: the suffix *ṇa* is applied by [Pāṇini 3.1.143]. The suffix *ṇa* occurs invariably for the aquatic creature *nakra* (crocodile), as in the form *grāha*.

In the case of *āditya*, *soma*, and so forth, the suffix *ac* (by Pāṇini 3.1.134) indeed occurs—hence the word *graha*. Regarding the statement "the rule for *sat* does not apply when used with *iti*": in examples such as *varṣatīti dhāvati* ("he runs because it rains") and *hantīti palāyate* ("he flees because he is being struck"), the suffixes *śatṛ* and *śānac*, which are designated as *sat* by [Pāṇini 3.2.127], do not occur at all when used with *iti*, due to the fixed optionality (*vyavasthitavibhāṣā*) of the rule.

In this context, the term *vibhāṣā* (optionally) is understood to carry over from [Pāṇini 3.2.121]. Thus, we have: *arjayan vasati* ("he lives while earning") and *adhīyāno vasati* ("he lives while studying"). In the construction with *asati* ("not being"), these two [suffixes] occur invariably. Now, one might object: since the sense of cause (*hetu*) is already indicated by the word *iti* itself, the rule for the present tense (*sat-vidhi*) will not apply in cases such as *varṣati* ("it rains") or *hanti* ("he strikes"); however, where the word *iti* is not employed, the rule certainly applies—as in *arjayan vasati*, etc. Therefore, even without the governing heading (*adhikāra*) of *vibhāṣā*, the optionality is indeed obtained here.

Therefore, the mention of *vibhāṣā* (optionality) should certainly not be carried over [from the previous rule]; thus, this is not an example of *vyavasthitavibhāṣā* (restricted optionality). What, then, is the example? It is: *kariṣyāmīti vrajati* ("He goes, thinking 'I shall do'").

Here, by the word *ca* in the rule *lṛṭ śeṣe ca* [Pāṇini 3.3.13], when another action is the *upapada* (governing word) for the sake of a future action, the suffix *lṛṭ* is applied; however, the rule for *sat* (the present participle) will not apply to that *lṛṭ* due to *vyavasthitavibhāṣā*.

By virtue of the rule *aprathamāsamānādhikaraṇena*, [the suffix] occurs invariably in other cases—for example, *kariṣyantaṃ paśya* ("see him who will do"). However, when there is coreferentiality with a word in the nominative case (*prathamāsamānādhikaraṇe*), there is an option: *brāhmaṇaḥ kariṣyan* or *brāhmaṇaḥ kariṣyati*. Regarding the phrase "mutually" (*mithaḥ*) and so forth:
"mutually" means by way of co-occurrence.
The meaning is that *devatrāta*, *galagrāha*, and others are not prescribed as optional alternatives for the same referent (*viṣaye*) along with *trāṇa*, *garagraha*, and so forth.

Regarding "gavākṣaḥ": while the rule [Pāṇini 6.1.122] is in effect, [by Pāṇini 6.1.123] *avaṅ* is applied invariably for a window (*vātāyana*), as in *gavākṣa*; however, in the case of a limb of a living being (*prāṇyaṅga*), as in *go'kṣam*, it does not occur. Elsewhere, both forms are used: *gavākṣam* and *go'kṣam*. Regarding "saṃśitavrataḥ": [this refers to one whose vow is sharpened].
The suffix *ni* is invariably applied after *tan* [in the sense of sharpening];
elsewhere it is optional— e.g., *niśitam*, *niśātam*,
meaning "sharpened" or "sharp."
All of this is obtained through *vyavasthita-vibhāṣā*.

In some cases there is only an injunction (*vidhi*), in some cases only a prohibition (*pratiṣedha*), and in some cases both; such a variety of meanings established as optional is called *vyavasthita-vibhāṣā*.
And this various establishment should be understood to apply to the generic form (*ākṛti*) of the word-meaning.

For in that context, having unified and condensed the entire range of things to be characterized (*lakṣya-rāśi*), both of these—affirmation (*vidhi*) and negation (*pratiṣedha*)—are taught. The function of the treatise (*śāstra*) consists in establishing this much meaning: that both affirmation and negation occur when the word-meaning (*padārtha*) is a genus (*jāti*). As for the systematic arrangement (*vyavasthāna*) without confusion—where in some instances there is only affirmation, in some only negation, and in some both—this is obtained from the instruction of an unbroken lineage of teachers (*ācārya-pāramparya*). By the rule *dhur-mā-sthā* [Pāṇini 6.4.66], the substitution of *it* would have been required; however, the substitution of *hi* for the root *dadhati* is prescribed.

The mention of *śtip* is for the purpose of excluding the *yaṅ*-luṅ (the elision of *yaṅ*). Consequently, the substitution of *hi* does not occur for the *yaṅ*-luṅ form: *dādhītaḥ*, *dādhītavān*, and *dādhītva*. Since the substitution of *ī* would apply as before, the substitution of *hi* is prescribed specifically for the *ktvā* suffix. Although the form *hitvā* is also established from the root *hi* (meaning "to go," Dhātupāṭha 1257), this statement is nevertheless made to prevent the substitution of *i* in the case of the root *jahāti*.
Now, for what purpose is the root *jahāti* specified by means of the *śtip* affix (*jahāteḥ*), rather than simply saying "of *haḥ*"? To this he says: "*jahāteḥ*" and so forth.
By this, he shows that the specification is made in order to exclude *ohāṅ gatau* (Dhātupāṭha 1089).
For if the specification were simply "*haḥ*," then because that [term] is common to both, it would apply to *jihāti* as well.
Regarding the form *jahāti*: when there is a reference by means of the *śtip* affix, [the rule] does not apply. By this [rule], only *jahāti* is referred to, not *jihāti*.
For if such a reference were made, it would not apply to the *yaṅluk* (reduplication with elision) form, as in *jāhātu*.

The substitution of *ī* also does not occur here; for even in that rule, there is a reference by means of the *śtip* affix. And here, once the *iṭ* augment has been applied, the elision of the vowel *ā* occurs by [Pāṇini 6.4.64]. By the word *ca*, the phrase "in the Veda" (*chandasī*) is drawn over from the previous context. Thus: "the augment *iṭ* is optionally applied."
When there is the augment *iḍ*, then by [Pāṇini 6.4.64], there is the elision of the vowel *ā*.
Thus, "sudhitam" is a compound according to [Pāṇini 2.2.18].
Likewise, "vasudhitam."
This is a descriptive compound (*viśeṣaṇasamāsa*).
As before, there is the elision of the suffix *ākara*.
[The form is] "nemadhitam."

The term *sāmi* [Pāṇini 2.1.26] forms a second-case (accusative) compound. It has been stated that in this context, the word *sāmi* signifies "half" (*tatrārthagrahaṇa*). Furthermore, this word *nema* is a synonym for the word *sāmi*.

Regarding "dhiṣva": [the substitution] *se* replaces *thās* by Pāṇini 3.4.80, and the letter *v* is substituted [for the *s*] by 3.4.91. Regarding "absence of reduplication": [this refers to the fact that the root does not undergo reduplication].

There is the elision of the vowel *a* by [Pāṇini 6.4.112] *ślau*; the change of the letter *gh* to *t* by [Pāṇini 8.4.54] *khari ca*; and the change of the reduplicated syllable to *dh* by [Pāṇini 8.2.38], which effects the substitution of *bhaṣ* for *jhal*. Thus we have *dhiṣīya*.

This is the optative (*liṅ*) in the sense of a benediction (*āśis*), with the change of *iṭ* to *at* by [Pāṇini 3.4.106]. The phrase "in Vedic usage" (*chandasi*) is no longer in force, because it was drawn back [into the previous rule] by the particle *ca* in the preceding sūtra.
"Dattaḥ" and "dattavān" [are formed with] the suffixes *kta* and *ktavatu*. "Dattiḥ" [is formed with] the suffix *ktin*.
In the forms *dhītáḥ* and *dhītavān*,
the substitution of *īt* occurs as previously described.

Why does the substitution of *hi* not occur by [Pāṇini 7.4.42]? To this he says: "This is the form of the root *dheṭ*," and so forth. It is the form of the root *dheṭ* "to drink" (Dhātupāṭha 902), not of the root *dhā*.
Therefore, the meaning is that the substitution of *hi* does not take place.

Regarding the word *dātam*: this is the form of the root *dāp* "to cut" (Dhātupāṭha 1059); it does not have the designation *ghu*, because of the prohibition [stated] as *adāp* [Pāṇini 1.1.20]. Now, since the rule *do dadghoḥ* [Pāṇini 7.4.46] prescribes this by means of the *jaś* sound, someone might be confused—thinking, "Is this substitute (*ādeśa*) one ending in *takāra*? Or is it one ending in *dakāra*? Or perhaps one ending in *dhakāra*? Or one ending in *thakāra*? Therefore, in order to dispel that confusion, he says: "This substitute," and so forth.
How is this known? He says: "For it has been stated thus," and so forth.

If this *ādeśa* (substitute) were to end in the letter *t*, then in the word *sudatta*, the rule *dāsti* [Pāṇini 6.3.123]—which is understood from the preceding context—would require the lengthening of the vowel *i*.
On the other hand, if it were to end in the letter *d*, then by the rule *radābhyām* [Pāṇini 8.2.42], the substitution of *ṇatva* for the dental *t* would occur.

Now, if it ends in *dh*, then by the rule "jhaṣas tathor dho 'dhaḥ" [Pāṇini 8.2.40], the *t* of the *niṣṭhā* suffix would undergo substitution with *dh* after a word ending in a *jhaṣ* sound. [To this it is replied: "There is no fault when it ends in *th*. Here, the negative particle (*nañ*) is to be supplied.
The meaning is that there is no fault in the case of *thā*.
Regarding the phrase "therefore" (*tasmāt*) and so forth:
since there is a fault in the three preceding alternative positions (*pakṣa*), this substitute (*ādeśa*) is therefore [the one] ending in *th*.
In the example *dattaḥ* (given) and *dattavān* (having given), the substitution of *t* for *th* occurs by the rule *khari ca* [Pāṇini 8.4.54].
Regarding the phrase "if, however" (*yadi tu*) and so forth:
two alternative views (*pakṣau*) were presented in the Bhāṣya under the rule *dasti* [Pāṇini 6.3.123], namely: [the suffix] *dā* followed by a suffix beginning with *t*, or ending in *t*.

In this regard, if the position is adopted that lengthening occurs when the element *dā* ends in *t*, then there is the fault of the undesired application of lengthening. However, if the position is adopted that lengthening occurs when the element *dā* begins with *t*, then there is no fault even in the case of [forms] ending in *t*;
for lengthening occurs where the element *dā* begins with *t*, as in *nīttam*, *vīttam*, and so forth, but not in *sudatta* and the like.
Therefore, there is the partial fault of obtaining [the result] too far back,
as in the rule "also for *dānta* and *dhānta*" and so forth.
For these two substitutes, *dānta* and *dhānta*, being prescribed in conjunction with the letter *t* and others, are not capable of becoming the cause for the destruction of that very [conjunction].

Therefore, there is no fault even in the forms *dānta* and *dhānta*. Regarding *avadatta* and so forth: [this occurs] at the beginning of the action (*ādikarman*), that is, at the commencement of the activity.
The meaning is "the moment of the initial action.

Here, although the substitution of *t* [for *d*] would have been required by Pāṇini 7.4.47, these forms beginning with *avadatta* are established as irregular (*nipātana*). Furthermore, the term "in the sense of the initial action" (*ādikarmaṇi*) is a qualifier for all [these forms], and not only for *pradatta*.

Except in the case of the first action (*ādikarma*), the substitution of *t* occurs by the rule *aca upasargāt taḥ* [Pāṇini 7.4.47], and not the change to *d*—as in *avattam*, *vīttam*, *sūttam*, and *anūttam*.

Regarding the phrase "not preceded by a prefix" (*anupasargāḥ*) and so forth: alternatively, *ava* and the others are not even designated as prefixes (*upasarga*) in relation to the root *dadāti*; this is because they pertain to another action expressed by *gam* (to go) which is distinct from the action expressed by those prefixes—as in *avagataṃ dattam* ("given after being understood"), and so it should be understood in other cases as well.
Therefore, these [prefixes] have the designation of "prepositions" (upasarga) with respect to the root *gam*, not with respect to *dā*.
Thus it has been said: "Those particles beginning with *pra* which are connected with an action have the designation of 'prepositions' with respect to that [action].

Consequently, since the designation of "preposition" does not apply here, the substitution of *t* would not even arise; so what is the purpose of this specific rule (*nipātana*)? It is an exception (*apavāda*) to the substitution of *da*.
"The substitution *ta* occurs here"—the vowel *a* is for the sake of pronunciation.
In forms such as *prattam*, when the vowel *ā* is replaced by *t*, the *d* undergoes *cartya* (substitution by *t*), resulting in *ta*; thus [we have] *nīttam*.
The lengthening [of the vowel] occurs by [Pāṇini 6.3.123] *dasti*.
Regarding the word *avadāttam*,
this is the form of the root *daip* "to purify" (Dhātupāṭha 924).
"An *al* [substitute] applies to the beginning," according to the rule [Pāṇini 1.1.54]. "The term *ac* must be repeated twice."

When the word *acaḥ* is repeated twice, there arise two word-forms: *acaḥ* and *ac*. Among these, one ends in the fifth case (ablative) and the other in the sixth case (genitive). Therein, by means of the former, the prefix (*upasarga*) is qualified—as "from a prefix ending in a vowel."
This substitution occurs in the form "the other [consonant] also indicates the place of articulation," namely,
"or [it is] two *t*s" (*dvitakāraḥ*);
or else, [it is governed by the rule] "after a prefix, *t* is substituted for *s*" (*aca upasargāt taḥ*).

Only that which consists of two *t* sounds (*dvitakāra*) is indicated as the substitute for the entire complex; therefore, because this [substitute] has more than one phoneme (*anekāl*), it would apply to the whole. If, then, this indication consists of two *t* sounds, then by the rule *apo bhi* [Pāṇini 7.4.48], a substitution for the whole would also result, since it too has more than one phoneme. To address this, he says: "In *apo bhi*, etc. In the rule *apo bhi*, the word *acaḥ* (of a vowel) is understood from the previous context; therefore, even though it has more than one phoneme, by the rule *anekāl śit sarvasya* [Pāṇini 1.1.55], the substitution will apply to the *p* alone, not to the whole. "Of *dyati*, etc. [refers to the following].

The scope for the rule *dyateḥ* (Pāṇini 8.2.43) is where there is no prefix (*upasarga*) ending in *a*, such as in *nirditam* and *durditam*. The scope for this substitute (*ādeśa*) [of *t* for *d*] is when it follows a prefix ending in *a* that is other than one designated as *ghu*—such as the root *ḍudāñ* "to give" (Dhātupāṭha 1091)—as in *avattam* and *parīttam*. When both rules would apply to the root *dyati* following a prefix ending in *a*, the letter *t* alone occurs by way of the *vipratiṣedha* (the rule of mutual exclusion). Thus, in *avattam* and *prattam*, the substitution of *d* for *t* occurs by the rule *adbhiḥ* (Pāṇini 8.2.39), which effects the change of *t* to *d* through the process of *jaśtva*.
But in the view that there are two *t* sounds, by [Pāṇini 8.4.53] "pūrvasya api," the *jaś*-substitution occurs—resulting in the letter *d*.
Then, by [Pāṇini 8.4.65], the preceding *d* is elided:
*suvaḥ* (or *svavaḥ*).

[Kāśikā] and so forth. It is desired that for these words—*suvas*, *svatavas*, *māsa*, and *uvas*—the substitute *ta* occurs when followed by a word beginning with *bha*, in the domain of Vedic usage (*chandas*). And it should be understood that this [substitution] is obtained precisely by [Pāṇini 3.1.85]. Here too, in the view that there are two *t*s, since it consists of more than one phoneme (*anekāl*), it would follow that it is a replacement for the whole (*sarvādeśa*); therefore, [the rule specifies] "of the vowel" (*acaḥ*).
The word ending in the fifth case (pañcamyanta) is to be understood as carrying over [from the previous rule].
Alternatively, according to the principle that "substitutes apply to that which is being pointed out" (*nirdiśyamānasyādeśā bhavanti*), it will apply to the *s* sound alone,
as in the form *vatsyati*.
The root *vas* is listed as number 1942 in the Dhātupāṭha (*vasanivāse*).
Regarding the form *jighatsati*: it is derived from the root *ad* with the suffix *san*; by [Pāṇini 2.4.37], *ghaslṛ* is the substitute for *ad* before the suffix *luṅ* and *san*.
"He will say" (*vakṣyati*):
[the root] *vac* in the sense of "speaking" (Dhātupāṭha 1842); by [Pāṇini 8.2.30], there is the substitution of *k* for *c*. [Examples:
*ghāsaḥ*, *vāsaḥ*.

The suffix *ghañ* is applied in the sense of an action (*bhāve*) according to Pāṇini 3.3.18 (*bhāve ghañ*), resulting in the substitution of *ghas* for the root [according to 2.4.38]. Thus we have *āsse* and *vasse*.

The roots *ās* (meaning "to sit," Dhātupāṭha 1021) and *vas* (meaning "to wear" or "to clothe," Dhātupāṭha 1023) take the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) because they are marked with an indicatory vowel *u* (*anudāttet*). By Pāṇini 3.4.80 (*cāsaḥ se*), the suffix *si* is substituted for *liṭ*; and because these roots belong to the *ad*-class, there is elision (*luk*) of the *śap* augment.

Now, why was it not stated that "it is *sa* when followed by a *tiṅ*"? It cannot be done so; for in this case as well, [the substitution] would not occur—as in *vyativatsīṣṭhāḥ*. [The forms] *kartāse* [are derived thus]: [from *kartāsi*,] *thāsaḥ se* [applies].
Regarding "tvam asi":
[the root] *bhu* (Dhātupāṭha 1065) is used; as before, there is elision of the *śap* suffix.
Regarding "vyatisethe": [the same applies].

The Ātmanepada suffix occurs by the rule *kartari karmavyatīhāre* [Pāṇini 1.3.14]. By the rules *thāsaḥ se* [3.4.80] and *ato guṇe* [6.1.97], there is the elision of the vowel *a*. Now, why does the substitution of *ṣ* not occur by the rule *atha* [8.3.59]? To this he replies: "In the case of the *a* and *s* of the root *as*," and so forth.

The intention is that when the *a* and *s* are elided, only the suffix remains; that alone constitutes the word (*pada*). Therefore, due to the prohibition [stated in] *ataḥ* [Pāṇini 8.3.111], the substitution of *ṣ* will not occur. Thus: *kartārau*, *kartāraḥ*.
Here, from the suffix *luṭ*, the suffixes *tas* and *jhi* undergo the substitutions *rau* and *ras* respectively by [Pāṇini 7.1.3]: *ataḥ* [2.4.85]. Similarly: *adhyetārau*, *adhyetāraḥ*.

Is the *ātmanepada* [ending] applied because the suffix *iṅ* has the marker *ṅit*? [The endings] *ātām* and *jhaḥ*, as well as *ra* and *ras* for those two, follow as before. Since a suffix beginning with *repha* (*r*) cannot occur after the root *as*, there is no example [of such an application].
However, some show the example "vyatire"; this would be appropriate if the word *ccha* were used in that way, but since it is not so used, it is incorrect.

The substitution of *re* is prescribed for Vedic usage by [Pāṇini 6.4.76], according to the principle that "in the Veda, one follows what is observed" (Vyākaraṇa-paribhāṣā 68). The particle *ca* has the sense of conjunction (*samuccaya*) with respect to what precedes. Regarding the form *kartāhe*:
it is derived from the root *kṛ* with the suffix *luṭ*, in the middle voice (*ātmanepada*), first person singular; the augment *iṭ* is applied, and the final *e* of the suffix is replaced by *ā*.
Here, by this [rule], the *s* becomes *h*, resulting in *vyatihe*. The middle voice (*ātmanepada*) is applied according to [Pāṇini 1.3.14] *asteḥ*; the elision of the vowel *a* is as before.
Regarding the word "eti":
the inclusion of the long vowel *t* (taparakaraṇa) is for the purpose of avoiding the substitution of *ay* (*ayādeśa*) in the locative case.

For if the *ay* substitution were to occur, there would be doubt as to which [term] this reference pertains to—whether it refers to the *ay* substitution itself, or to the phoneme *e*? Because of its svarita accent, the term *lopa* (elision) is understood to carry over, but not the immediately preceding *ha*, since that is neither svarita nor so declared.
In the case of the letter *ya*, the vowel *i* is for the sake of pronunciation.

When the letters *yi* and *ivuṛṇ* follow—namely, these two letters *yo* (*yi* and *vu*)—there occurs the elision of the roots *dīdhīṅ* ("to shine, to play," DhP 1076) and *vevīṅ* ("to go, to move similarly," DhP 1077). And that [elision] applies to the final [letter] by [Pāṇini 1.1.52].

Since there would otherwise have been the hearing of the *ya* at the beginning, and since the substitution of *yaṇ* would have applied to the beginning of the *ivarṇa* by [Pāṇini 6.4.82], this statement regarding elision is made.
"Ādīdhya, āvevya"— here the suffix is *lyap*.
"Ādīdhyata, āvevita"— here [the suffixes are] *kta* and *ktavatu*.
> [[1.3.13]] Thus, the *ātmanepada* [is applied]; > [[3.1.67]] | "ādīdhita, āvevita" [are examples]. > [[1.3.13]] Thus, the *ātmanepada* [is applied]; > [[3.1.67]] |
"ādīdhita, āvevita"— these are [forms with] the suffix *tṛc*.
"ādīdhyanam, ādevyanam"— these are [forms with] the suffix *lyuṭ*.
The suffix *lyuṭ* [is applied]; because of the prohibition of *guṇa* by the rule *daudhīvevīṭām* [Pāṇini 1.1.6], the substitution of *yaṇ* occurs.

Although there is equality between the two causes (*nimitta*) and the two subjects of the operation (*kārin*), nevertheless, the correspondence according to order (*yathāsaṃkhyam*) does not take place here, because it is not intended (*asvaritatvāt*).

The mention of the term *varṇa* (letter) is so that the rule applies when the vowel *i* is actually heard, but it should not apply here: *ādīdhayateḥ* and *āvevayateḥ*, derived from the causative forms (*ṇijanta*) with the suffix *ṇvul*, resulting in *ādīdhyakaḥ* and *ādevyakaḥ*.

For here, since [the suffix] is *nitya*, once the *ṇi*-elision has been performed, the rule regarding the elision of an affix (*pratyayalopalakṣaṇa*, Pāṇini 1.1.62) would apply; therefore, because of the mention of the "letter" (*varṇagrahaṇa*), it does not occur. From the rule *saḥ syārdhadhātuke* (Pāṇini 7.4.49), the word *si* is understood as a carry-over (*anuvartate*); and that is a qualifier of *soḥ*. Regarding *mīti mīnātiminatyoḥ*:
this refers to the two roots *mīñ* in the sense of "injuring" (Dhātupāṭha 1476) and *ḍumiñ* in the sense of "placing" (Dhātupāṭha 1250).

But surely, when the word *mī* is being uttered, its inclusion [in the rule] for the root *mi* (to measure) is not justified? This is not so; for once the lengthening prescribed by [Pāṇini 6.4.16] has been applied, it indeed takes the form *mī*.

Even so, does not its inclusion fail to be justified by the rule regarding "that which is taught by a technical definition versus that which is taught by its specific form" (*lakṣaṇapratipadokta-paryudāsa*)? This is not the case; for here, because it bears the designation *ghu*, the fact that the author did not place the word *ghu* first in the compound indicates that just as the rule of prior placement is disregarded here, so too is some other technical statement of the grammar.

Therefore, it is logical that this technical definition (*paribhāṣā*) is not required here, and thus the root *mi* (from *minoti*) is also included. This is based on the principle: "For in the case of roots beginning with *mā*, there is no distinction among those that begin with *ā*. Thus, there is the inclusion of the three previously mentioned roots beginning with *meṅ*.

The terms *ghu* refer to the roots *dā* and *dhā*. In the case of the roots *rabha* (in the sense of "rashness," DhP 974), *ḍulabhaṣ* (in the sense of "attainment," DhP 975), *śaklṛ* (in the sense of "ability," DhP 1261), *śala*, *hula*, and *patlṛ* (all in the sense of "motion," DhP 843, 844, 845), and *pada* (in the sense of "motion," DhP 1169), the vowel (*ac*) is replaced by *sanīṣ* before an affix beginning with *s*. The inclusion of the term *ac* is for the purpose of ensuring that this is a replacement of the entire vowel (*sarvādeśa*).
For if that [substitution] were not present, because there would be more than one *al* (phoneme), there would be a substitution for the whole [stem].
In the form *pramitsani*,
there is the elision of the reduplication (*abhyāsalopa*) by the rule *atra lopo'bhyāsasya* [Pāṇini 7.4.58], and its replacement by *s* by the rule *saḥ syārdhadhātuke* [Pāṇini 7.4.49].
Regarding the form *apamitsate*:
the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) is applied by the rule *pūrvavatsanaḥ* (Pāṇini 1.3.62). The same applies to *āripsate* and *ālipsate*.

The substitution of *c* for *khar* [Pāṇini 8.4.54]—that is, the change of *bh* to *p*—and the elision of *s* [Pāṇini 8.2.29] by the rule "of *t* and *k*, when they are the first members of a conjunct consonant, and at the end of a word. Thus: *īpsati*.
[The root] *āplṛ* means "to pervade" (Dhātupāṭha 1260).
*Jñīpsati*.

The root *jñā* is listed in the *Dhātupāṭha* as "in the sense of understanding" (1507). With the addition of the causative suffix (*ṇic*), the augment *puk* is applied by the rule *arttihvṛ...* (Pāṇini 7.3.36). Then, from the root *jñā* listed as "in the senses of killing, heating, and calming" (811), the designation *mit* is applied by the rule *mitaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.4.92), resulting in a short vowel; subsequently, the suffix *ṇi* is elided by the rule *ṇeraniṭi* (6.4.51). Regarding the form *īrtsati*:

from the root *ṛdh* "to increase" (Dhātupāṭha 1271), the vowel *ī* is substituted, followed by the replacement of *r* (*raparatva*). Then, the letter *k* is substituted for the letter *ś* by the rule *khari ca* (8.4.54), resulting in the letter *t*.
And here, the vowel (*ac*) must be qualified by the cause of cognition (*jñāpinaṅga*), but the cause of cognition is not qualified by the vowel, because there is no deviation [in that case].
For the state of being a cause of cognition never deviates from the vowel.

However, if the vowel were qualified by the cause of cognition, then every vowel related to the cause of cognition would have to undergo *īttva* (the substitution of *ī*); and if *īttva* were thus applied even to the suffix *ṇi*, the form *jñīpsati* would not be established. Anticipating this objection, he says: "In the sense of 'making known,' after the root *jñap*, before *vā* and *vac*," and so forth.

In that case, the scope for the [substitution of] *aj* and so forth is [in forms like] *kārayati*; the scope for the elision (*lopa*) of the *ṇi* suffix is [in forms like] *kāraṇā*, *hāraṇā*. When both would apply to the second vowel, the elision of the *ṇi* suffix alone occurs by virtue of the "priority of the preceding" (*pūrvavipratiṣedha*), as in *jñīpsati*.
"Of the other" means of the vowel *a*.

Regarding the form *ardidhiṣati*: there is the guṇa substitution for the light penultimate vowel, followed by the replacement of the semivowel with a vowel (*raparatva*). Then, according to [Pāṇini 6.1.2], the element *dhi* is reduplicated.
However, the doubling of the *repha* (the letter *r*) does not occur, because of the prohibition stated in [Pāṇini 6.1.3].
The *jaś*-ness of the practice is the letter *ja*. The letter *ta* is for the sake of ease of pronunciation. Regarding the form "mokṣate":
it is derived from the root *muc-lū* in the sense of "releasing" (Dhātupāṭha 1430).

By [Pāṇini 8.2.30], there is the substitution of *k* for *c*; by [Pāṇini 8.3.57], there is the substitution of *ṣ* for *s*. The middle voice (*ātmanepada*) is used because of the extended application (*atideśa*) of the status of the object (*karmavat*) according to [Pāṇini 3.1.87] and following rules.
The expression "by itself" (*svayameva*) is intended to demonstrate its status as both object and agent (*karmakartṛ*).

When one desires to release the calf, and that calf—which is the object of the desire to release—attains a state of favorability toward the action of releasing, then, due to its independence, when it is intended to be expressed as the agent in this action, the root *muc* (to release) becomes transitive (*sakarmaka*).

Now, for what purpose is the mention of *guṇa* (substitution)? Why not simply say "na u" (na u)? [Objection: But in that case, by the rule "the vowel *o* takes the place of *u* and *a*" (P. 6.1.87), the substitution of *o* would apply here; however, because of the mention of *guṇa*, only the *guṇa* vowel (*o*) occurs, due to the restriction inherent in the formulation of technical definitions (*saṃjñāvidhāna*). [Response: This is not so; the term *ac* (vowel) is understood to carry over from the previous rule. Therefore, it will not apply to the final letter. If this is the case, then this [mention of *guṇa*] indicates that the word *ac* has ceased to apply [to the subsequent rules].

In the rule *tena* [Pāṇini 7.4.58], the elision of the augment *at* of the reduplication does not occur. However, if there were the governing authority (*adhikāra*) of *at*, one might ask: "Let it not happen"? But then the continued application (*anuvṛtti*) of that [authority] would be purposeless, and thus the elision would apply only to *at*. To demonstrate what is indicated by the word *atra* here, he says: "That which is this," and so forth. Now, what is the purpose of including the term *atra*? If it is argued that it is so that [the elision] may apply within the section beginning with *sani mīmā* [Pāṇini 7.4.54] and so on, but not in cases such as *dadau* or *dadatuḥ*, we say: no.

If this were the intended purpose—that is, if one were to aim for the rule "In the presence of *san*, [the long vowel is substituted] for the roots *mī*, *mā*, *dhū*, *rū*, *bha*, *labh*, *śak*, *pat*, and *pad*, and there is elision of the reduplication (*abhyāsa-lopa*)"—then this would have been stated right here in this section and not elsewhere. Consequently, the mention of "here" (*atra*) would be purposeless; therefore, he says: "In the presence of *san*, *mī*, *mā*, *dhū*, *rū*, *bha*, *labh*," etc., adding:
"For the sake of determining the scope (*viṣaya-avadhāraṇārtham*).
This means it is for the sake of a restriction (*niyama*) regarding the scope of the elision of the reduplication.
In order to demonstrate that very fact—that [the rule] serves to restrict its scope—he says "atraiva" and so forth.
By the word "atra," the domain beginning with "is" is indicated.

He says "it does not occur in the domain of *sanvadbhāva*" in order to show, by means of this restriction, what is excluded so that the elision of the augment (*abhyāsalopa*) may occur only in the domain beginning with "is."
Regarding *amīmapat*:

from the root *bhīñ* in the sense of "to injure" (*bhīñ hiṃsāyām*, Dhātupāṭha 1476), there is the substitution of *ā* [for the radical vowel] by Pāṇini 6.1.50; then the causative suffix *ṇic*; as before, the augment *puk*; the *luṅ* tense marker; *caṅ* for *cli*; elision of *ṇi*; shortening of the penultimate vowel; reduplication; the augment *aṭ*; then, due to the condition of being like the *sa*-present (*sanvadbhāva*) by Pāṇini 7.4.93 and following, the substitution of *i* for the radical vowel by Pāṇini 7.4.79, and finally the lengthening by Pāṇini 7.4.94.
Thus, *adīdapat*. Regarding *adīdapat*: [the formation is similar].
The root *ḍudāñ* in the sense of "giving" (Dhātupāṭha 1091) takes the suffix *ṇic* and so forth as before.

Because of the inclusion of the word *atra* ("here"), the elision of the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsalopa*) does not occur here. But how could the elision of the reduplicated syllable, which is prescribed for the *saN* affix, apply here, such that the inclusion of the word *atra* is made for the purpose of its exclusion? To this, he says: "*sanvallaghuni*" and so forth.

For just as the property of *it* (the augment *it*) occurs due to the extension (*atideśa*) of the status of being like the perfect tense (*saṇvat*), so too would there be the elision of the reduplication (*abhyāsalopa*). Here, someone might have the misconception that by the rule "of the final [al]" (*alontyaparibhāṣā*, P. 1.1.52), there ought to be an elision [only of the final letter]; therefore, in order to dispel that, he says "of the whole" (*sarvasya*), etc.
But how is "of the whole" obtained? To this he says: "for that very purpose," etc.
By this very word *eva*, he sets aside the interpretation that it serves to restrict the scope of the object.

If this is so, would it not follow that [the rule] would apply even in the domain of the *sanvadbhāva* (the treatment as having the suffix *san*)? He thinks thus: even in the domain of *sanvadbhāva*, the undesirable consequence of the elision of the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsalopa*) can be avoided; for there, by the term *sanvat*, the grammatical operation dependent upon *san* is extended by analogy.
Furthermore, the elision of the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsalopa*) does not depend solely on the presence of *san*; what then? It depends on the substitution of *is* and so forth as well.
Therefore, even in the absence of the mention of *atra*, the elision of the reduplicated syllable will not occur in forms such as *amīmapat*, because those [substitutions] are absent.
