Consequently, the mention of *atra* is indeed redundant and should not be made at all.
Why is it done? So that there may be the elision of the whole [substitute].

But how, even when the mention of *atra* (here) is made, is the elision of the whole obtained? Some say: "From an increase in the text comes an increase in the meaning. By the mention of *atra*, it is indicated through the effort of this great sūtra: "This elision must be performed for a large original element (*sthānin*)."
Furthermore, some maintain that this [term *at*] is made applicable to a large domain only if the elision of the entire suffix (*sarvasya abhyāsalopa*) is performed, and not otherwise.
Others say, "The rule regarding the final letter applies when there is more than one meaning.
Who, then, are these? They are to be understood as those who explain the inclusion of the word *at* as being for the purpose of determining the scope of the application.

The meaninglessness of the reduplication (abhyāsa) is to be understood in the alternative view that it is a substitute (sthāne dvirvacana). For in this case, that other word which is prescribed in place of [the original] is meaningful as a whole; however, the partial element that is the reduplication is indeed meaningless.

Even in the view that there are two applications (dvi-prayoga) and two occurrences (dvi-vacana), the repetition is devoid of meaning because it expresses no different sense. For example: *ḍuḍhaukiṣate*, *tutraukiṣate*.

From the roots *ḍhaukṛ* and *traukṛ*, which are marked with an anudātta vowel and thus take the ātmanepada endings, the suffix *san* is added; the ātmanepada ending is applied by the rule *pūrvavatsanaḥ* [Pāṇini 1.3.62].
Examples are: *aḍuḍhaukat*, *atutraukat*.
From these two roots with the causative suffix *ṇic*, the *luṅ* (aorist) is formed, and the operations such as *caṅ* substitution and so forth are applied as before; for example:
*ḍuḍhauke*, *tutrauke*.
[In the case of] *liṭ* (perfect), the singular ending is used, and for that, *aiś* is substituted.

Regarding the phrase "of the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*) when followed by a non-vowel" (*abhyāsasyānaci*), etc.: the meaning is that this should be explained as having the sense that whatever operation is prescribed for the reduplicated syllable occurs when it is not followed by a vowel.

In this regard, the explanation is as follows: by virtue of the prescription of the augment in the rule "optionally for *car*, *cal*, *pat*, and *dad* when followed by a non-vowel in a verbal derivation" (*vā caricalipatidadonāmacyākhyābhyāsasya*, Vārttika 658), the *halādiśeṣa* (retention of the initial consonant) should not take place.

For if the *halādiśeṣa* (the rule of retaining only the initial consonant) were in effect, there would be no distinction between a substitute (*ādeśa*) and an augment (*āgama*), both being introduced by the suffix *kai*; thus, one would simply have prescribed the substitute itself.

And in that case, since there would be no elision of the reduplication (*abhyāsalopa*), it would—by the principle of elimination (*pāriśeṣya*)—occur only in places other than a vowel. [The term] "beginning with a consonant" (*halādiḥ*) means "that which is both a consonant (*hal*) and an initial (*ādi*)," i.e., a *karmadhāraya* compound, and not a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*) meaning "the first among consonants" (*halām ādiḥ*).

If this were a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*), then the meaning would be: "Among the consonants (*hal*) of the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*), the first one remains. And in that case, in forms such as *ānakṣatuḥ* and *ānakṣuḥ*, since the root *akṣū* (meaning 'to pervade,' Dhātupāṭha 654) begins with a vowel (*aj*), there is no second monosyllabic (*ekāc*) element; thus, when doubling occurs for the first monosyllabic element, although the reduplicated syllable does not begin with the letter *k*, it nevertheless begins with a consonant (*hal*). Consequently, it would follow that this [consonant] should remain [by the rule].

But there is no fault in this being a *karmadhāraya* compound; for in that case, the status of beginning with a consonant (*hal-āditva*) is prescribed in relation to the reduplication (*abhyāsa*), and here the letter *k* is not the first element of the reduplication.
Therefore, this is a *karmadhāraya*:
as in *jaglau* and *mamlau*.

From the roots *glai* in the sense of "to fade" (Dhātupāṭha 903) and *mlai* in the sense of "to bend the limbs" (Dhātupāṭha 904), there is the substitution of *ā* [for the radical vowel] by [Pāṇini 6.1.45], and the substitution of *au* [for the reduplicated syllable] by [Pāṇini 7.1.34]. In the forms *āṭatuḥ* and *āṭuḥ*,
once the lengthening of the reduplicated syllable has been applied by [Pāṇini 7.4.70], there is the application of the long vowel resulting from homogeneous vowels (*savarṇadīrghatvam*).

But surely, "remainder" (*śeṣa*) means persistence, and that is already established for the fire; so for what purpose is it enjoined? To this he says: "This [elision] has as its cause the remainder of the first," and so forth.
That elision for which the remainder of the first is the cause is described in that way.
For here, the remainder of the first is not being enjoined; rather, this elision of everything except the first is enjoined on account of that [remainder].

Since the retention of the first consonant (*halādi-śeṣa*) is already established by the rule "the retention of the first [consonant] when there is a state [of reduplication]," this present rule is understood as being for the purpose of restriction: "only the first consonant is retained, not one that is not the first. In this way, the non-appearance of what is not the first is prescribed as the cause for the retention of the first. If, however, this elision of what is not the first were prescribed as caused by the retention of the first, then in forms such as *ādutuḥ* and *āraruḥ*, the elision would not occur; because the cause is absent—the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*) does not even have a first consonant, so how could there be its retention? To this, he says: "In that case," and so forth.

When the elision of the augment *āṭ* (anādi-lope) is to be performed, recourse is taken to the class (*jāti*) of the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*), not to the individual instance (*vyakti*) of that reduplication.

Therefore, although the initial consonant (*hal-ādi*) does not occur in every single instance of reduplication, nevertheless, when it occurs in some instances such as *papāca*, it effects the removal of the initial *āṭ* in all cases, including forms like *āṭatuḥ* and *āṭuḥ*; for the class of the reduplicated syllable is non-different [in all instances].
Indeed, the very same class of reduplicated syllable that exists in *papāca* and so on is also present in *āṭatuḥ*, *āṭuḥ*, and the like.
"But others," and so forth.
Others maintain that [the rule] is stated in order to establish the elision of everything except the initial [syllable] in forms such as *āṭatuḥ* and *āṭuḥ*.

This word "remainder" (*śeṣa*) does not denote mere persistence; what then? It denotes a persistence qualified by cessation. If this is so, then because persistence is the substantive (*viśeṣya*), it possesses primacy, whereas cessation, being the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*), lacks primacy.

And likewise: because they follow the principal element, subordinate elements (*guṇas*) lack primacy. In cases such as *papāca*, where there is the presence of an abhyāsa (reduplication) beginning with a consonant (*hal*), there ought to be the removal of the consonant beginning with *i* (in *āṭ*); consequently, that same fault remains—namely, that in forms such as *āṭatuḥ* and *āṭuḥ*, the removal of the consonant beginning with *a* (*anādi-hal*) would not occur. To this, he says: "its presence" (*tadavasthānam*), and so forth. Although that presence is the principal element because it is designated by the word "remainder" (*śeṣa*) as the thing to be qualified (*viśeṣya*), nevertheless, it is non-principal because it is not something to be enjoined (*avidheya*).
But its non-prescriptiveness [is established] because it is already established.
Even though cessation (*nivṛtti*) serves as a qualifier, it is the primary element because it is what is to be prescribed.

Thus it has been said: "That which is established, which assists, and which exists for the sake of another is a subordinate member (*aṅga*); whereas that which is to be accomplished, which does not assist [in this way], and which is the principal is the primary element (*pradhāna*)."

In that case, since cessation (*nivṛtti*) is what is to be enjoined—being the primary element—this meaning arises for the present sūtra: "There is the cessation of the *hal* [consonant] of the beginningless repetition. Consequently, having attained primacy because it is the object of the injunction, how could it require a non-injunctional, non-primary non-cessation (*anivṛtti*) such as "of the initial [sound]" and so forth?
For what reason would it require it? The meaning is: for no reason at all.
For it is not logical that the principal [element] should follow the subordinate [elements].

Therefore, the sense is that even though the *hal* (consonant) and so forth remain, there must be elision (*lopa*) of the *av* (vowels) and so forth. Since the previous rule would have resulted in the retention of the *śar* (sibilants and *h*), this rule for the retention of *khay* (the *kh*, *ph*, and *ch*-series) is now commenced.
Furthermore, this non-initial retention (*anādiśeṣa*) supersedes the initial retention (*ādiśeṣa*).
For when both [the object and the cognition] persist, the term "remainder" cannot logically function as a qualifier.
It has already been stated that this term expresses a persistence qualified by cessation;
however, when both persist, there can be no persistence qualified by cessation.
Therefore, this [rule] is an exception (*apavāda*) to the previous rule concerning the initial [consonant].
[The example is] *cuścotiṣati*. [The root] *ścut* (meaning "to ooze," Dhātupāṭha 41) takes the suffix *san*, followed by *iṭ*.
Regarding "tiṣṭhāsati":
[the root] *sthā* is used in the sense of "ceasing from motion" (Dhātupāṭha 928).
Regarding "pispandiṣate": [the root] *spand* is used in the sense of "throbbing."

The root *spadi*, meaning "to move slightly" (*dhātupāṭha* 14), is marked with the *anudātta* accent; because it is marked with the *it* letter, the augment *num* is added by [Pāṇini 7.1.58], and the *ātmanepada* voice is applied by [Pāṇini 1.3.62]. Regarding the form *sasnau*:
the root *ṣṇā*, meaning "to cleanse" (*dhātupāṭha* 1052), is used.
The substitution of *au* for *pūrvevaṇ* occurs [by the rule] beginning with "kharpūrvāḥ. Thus,
one says "ucchivati."

Regarding the root *ucchi* in the sense of "to dwell" (Dhātupāṭha 216), when the form *san-ucchi-sa* is established, both reduplication (*dvirvacana*) and the *tuk* augment become applicable. Therein, because it depends on a phoneme (*varṇa*), the *tuk* is internal (*antaraṅga*). Once that has been applied, reduplication and the substitution of *ch* for *c* (*cutva*) are applicable. Since the latter [the *cutva*] is subsequent, when reduplication is to be performed, the *cutva* is considered as if non-existent (*asiddha*); thus, reduplication applies to the word *chiṣ*. In that case, the substitution of *ś* for *ch* (*śeṣa*) does not apply to the *ch*; because it is not preceded by a sibilant (*aśarpūrva*).

The letter *t* does not become *h*; therefore, when the "remainder of the initial consonant" (*halādi-śeṣa*) has been applied by the preceding rule, the letter *t* would be heard in the form *satyabhāse*. However, there is this [rule]: "This [operation] is as if non-existent (*asiddha*) with respect to what precedes it, except for reduplication" (*pūrvatrāsiddhoyamadvirvacane*, Jai. Pa. Vṛtti 70). Thus, the substitution of *c* (*cutva*) is performed first, and reduplication occurs afterwards. Even so, once the letter *ch* has been eliminated by the "remainder of the initial consonant," the substitution of *c* (*cutva*) would also be eliminated according to the principle "when the cause is removed, the effect is also removed" (*nimittāpāye naimittikasyāpyapāyaḥ*, Vyā. Pa. 47); consequently, in the word *ucicchiṣati*, only the letter *t* would be heard in the reduplicated syllable.
Therefore, it must be stated: "When preceded by a *khari* [consonant], the *khaya* [consonants] [are replaced by the corresponding *khari*]."
For this being the case, when the substitution of *cha* is made for the remaining [letter], the *ta*-sound is replaced; thus, there is no occurrence of an undesired consequence. Regarding "cakhāna":
from the root *khanu* in the sense of "digging" (*avadāraṇe*, DhP 878), there is reduplication, and its *cu*-substitution yields *cha*; then, by [Pāṇini 8.4.54], the *cha* is replaced by *ca*.
Regarding "jaghāti": [the same process applies].
By the rule *liṭ anyatarasyām* [Pāṇini 2.4.40], there is the substitution of *ghas* for the root *ad*; the change of the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*) to a palatal (*cutva*) occurs.
In place of a voiced aspirated consonant (*nādavat*), a similarly characterized *jhakāra* is substituted, which then undergoes the change to a voiced unaspirated (*jaśtva*)—becoming *jakāra*.
Thus, we have the form *jahāra*.
The root *hṛ* is listed as *hmañ? haraṇe* (Dhātupāṭha 899). From the form *jihīrṣati*:

by [Pāṇini 1.2.9], there is *kittva* for the suffix *san*; by [6.4.16], there is lengthening (*dīrghatva*) of the vowel; by [7.1.100], there is the substitution of *i* for *ṛ* of the root (*ṛta iddhātoḥ*); then *raparatva* (substitution of *r* as the final element); by [8.2.77], there is lengthening (*hali ca*); and then there is reduplication (*dvirvacana*) of the stem *hīrṣ*. This is a prohibition of the *cutva* (change to *c*) that would otherwise have been obtained by the preceding rule.
Regarding the form *kokūyate*:
the lengthening [of the vowel] is by [Pāṇini 7.4.25] *akṛtsārvadhātukayoḥ*, and the guṇa substitution for the reduplicated syllable is by [Pāṇini 7.4.82].
Now, for what purpose is the mention of the *vikaraṇa* (suffix) [the *ya*]? Why not simply say *koḥ*? To this he replies with the words *kavateḥ* and so forth.

The root *kuṅ* (Dhātupāṭha 1401) belongs to the Taudādika class; *ku* (Dhātupāṭha 1042) belongs to the Adādika class; and *kuṅ* (Dhātupāṭha 151) belongs to the Maudādika class—all having "sound" as their meaning. The specific mention of the verbal suffix (*vikaraṇa*) is for the purpose of ensuring that the Bhauvādika root is understood, while the other two are excluded.

Is this not the result of the exclusion of these two [roots], so that even this form *cokūyate* may occur? And since this is indeed established by the mention of *koḥ*, provided that by the paribhāṣā "the one without an anubandha" only the root *kauti* without an anubandha is grasped, should the mention *koḥ* alone be made? This is not so; for even though they share the same word-meaning, their denotable objects (*abhidheya*) are indeed distinct.

For instance: the root *kavati* occurs in the sense of an indistinct sound, as in "the camel cries out" (*uṣṭraḥ kokūyate*); the root *kuvatī* also occurs in the sense of a cry of distress, as in "the low-born man groans" (*cokūyate vṛṣalaḥ*), meaning he is afflicted; whereas *kauti* refers to sound in general.
Therefore, the specific mention of the suffix (*vikaraṇa*) must be made so that there may be the inclusion of the intended specific meaning.

[Objection: But surely, by the paribhāṣā regarding suffixes with a *luk* elision, [the substitution] will not apply to *kauti*; so for what purpose is it appropriate that the mention of the suffix (*vikaraṇa*) serves to exclude that? [Response: It is thought thus: the mention of the suffix must necessarily be made for the purpose of excluding *kuvi*. When it is employed for another purpose, it also serves to exclude *kauti*. Consequently, the paribhāṣā regarding suffixes with *luk* elision (Pāṇini 1.1.63) need not be relied upon here for the purpose of excluding *kauti*. Thus, [we have] *cukuve*.
As before? [The substitution of] *ai* for the vowel *ta* occurs; by the rule "aci śnudhātu" [Pāṇini 6.4.77], etc., there is the substitution of *uVaṅ*. Regarding "karīkṛṣyate":

from the root *kṛṣ* in the sense of "plowing" (Dhātupāṭha 990), the augment *rīk* is applied by the rule "rīgṛdupadhasya" [Pāṇini 7.4.90]. The letter *ca* is for the purpose of drawing forward [the application of] the rule "chandasi" [from Pāṇini 7.4.78]. Regarding "dhārayateḥ": [this refers to the root *dhṛ*].

The forms *dhṛñ* "to hold" (Dhātupāṭha 900), *dhṛṅ* "to stand" (Dhātupāṭha 1412), and *dhṛṅ* "to fall apart" (Dhātupāṭha 960)—the inclusion of these [roots] when they are causative (*ṇyanta*) is intended by the rule "or after *dhṛṅ*" (*dhṛṅo vā*). This refers to the two roots mentioned immediately prior that are not causative (*aṇyanta*). The phrase "optionally in *ślau* or in the elision of *yaṅ*" (*ślau yaṅluki vā*) applies as well.

In that regard: concerning *dādharti*—when it is derived from the root *dhṛ* with the suffix *ślu*, then the elision of the *ṇi*-affix, the lengthening of the reduplicated syllable, and the irregularity are prescribed.

However, when it occurs in the *yaṅ*-lopa (elision of *yaṅ*), then because the root has more than one vowel (*anekāc*), the *yaṅ* suffix would not apply; therefore, that too is prescribed as an irregularity, as is the shortening of the penultimate vowel (*upadhā*).
As for the elision of the *ṇi*-affix, it is established by the rule *yaṅo'ci ca* [Pāṇini 2.4.74], since the *yaṅ* is an *ārdhadhātuka* suffix.

The lengthening of the reduplicated syllable is established by the rule *abhyāsasya dīrghatvam api* (Pāṇini 7.4.83). Regarding the forms *dardharti* and *dardharṣi*: here too, when there is *ślu* (elision) of the suffix after the root *dhṛ*, the augment *ruk* is added to the reduplicated syllable and the *ṇi* suffix is elided.
The elision (*ślū*) is to be understood by the rule itself: *śluḥ sarvatra* [Pāṇini 7.4.78].

However, when there is *yaṅluk*, then although lengthening would have been required by the rule *yaṅo 'ci ca* [Pāṇini 7.4.30], its absence is prescribed as a *nipātana*. When *dhṛṅ* is used with *ślau*—as in *dādharti*—then, after reduplication has occurred, the lengthening of the reduplicated syllable is prescribed as a *nipātana*.

But when the root *dhṛṅ* itself occurs with the elision of *yaṅ* (*yaṅluk*), then the absence of the augment *rug* and so forth—which would otherwise be required by [Pāṇini 7.4.92] *ṛtaśca*—is prescribed as a grammatical anomaly (*nipātyate*).
Thus we have *dardharti*, *dardharṣi*.

Here too, when *dhṛṅ* occurs with *ślau* (reduplication), the augment *rug* is prescribed for the reduplicated syllable; but when there is *yaṅluk*, then—as before—the absence of the long vowel (*dīrgha*) that would otherwise be required is prescribed as an anomaly, and not the augment *rug*, because that [augment *rug*] is already established by [Pāṇini 7.4.91] *guṇo yaṅlukor* and so forth. Furthermore, the use of the parasmaipada endings is due to the rule *vyatyayo bahulam* [Pāṇini 3.1.85].
"Let it be so," and "elsewhere"—
the state of being "elsewhere" should be understood with reference to the third person singular of the imperative mood.
Regarding the form *bobhavīti*:

because it belongs to the *adādi* class, the *śap* suffix is elided by [Pāṇini 2.4.72]; however, due to the word *bahulam* (in various ways), it does occur here. Furthermore, the augment *īṭ* is optionally applied by [Pāṇini 7.3.94]. Regarding the form *tetisate*: [the same applies].

Regarding the word "tijeḥ": it refers to the root *tij* in the sense of "sharpening" (*niśāne*; Dhātupāṭha 971). Now, one might ask: since the suffix *yaṅ* is marked with the *ṅit* indicatory letter, is not the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) already established by the rule [Pāṇini 1.3.62], which states that a suffix marked with *ṅ* causes the verb to take the middle voice? If so, for what purpose is this form prescribed as an irregularity (*nipātana*)? To this he replies: "Because of the *ṅit*-ness of *yaṅ*" and so forth.

The middle voice (*ātmanepada*) is established for the purpose of indicating [a specific rule]. He shows that the middle voice is prescribed as a *nipātana* (irregular formation) for the sake of indication.
As for the purpose of this indication: the intention is that the middle voice does not occur elsewhere except in the case of the *yaṅ*-lopped form—as in *bobhavīti*.

Regarding the word *ālarṣi*: from the root *ṛ* (meaning "to go," Dhātupāṭha 1098, 1099), which belongs to the *juhotyādi* class, when the substitution of *at* is applied by [Pāṇini 7.4.66] and the substitution of *ra* for *ṛ* follows, the rule *halādiśeṣaḥ* would apply; therefore, as an exception to that, the substitution of *la* for the *repha* is prescribed by nipātana. Why, then, is this citation with the suffix *sip* explained as being non-essential (*atantra*)? To this he says: *tippy api*, etc.
Regarding "phaṇateḥ":
this refers to the root *phaṇa* "to move" (Dhātupāṭha 821).
Regarding "syandeḥ": [this refers to the root *syand*].
This refers to the root *syandū* in the sense of "flowing" (*praruāvaṇe*) from the Dhātupāṭha (761).
Why, then, is it explained that the prefix *sam-* is not a necessary condition here? To this he says: "For even here," and so forth.
[The example is] *karikrat*.
The root *ḍukṛñ* is used in the sense of "making" (Dhātupāṭha 1472).

When the *yaṇ* substitution has been applied, because the root no longer ends in *ṛ*, the augment *ri* for the reduplicated syllable prescribed by [Pāṇini 7.4.92], *ṛtaśca*, would not apply; therefore, it is introduced as an irregularity (*nipātana*). This is indicated by the rule "of *krand*" (*krandeḥ*).
This refers to the roots *kadi*, *kradi*, and *kladi* in the sense of calling out and weeping (*dhātupāṭha* 772, 773, 774).
How, then, is it known that this is a *nipātana* (irregular formation) in the *luṅ* tense? To this he says: "For of this," and so forth.
Since the meaning of the root *krand* is indicated by means of a form ending in *luṅ*, it is therefore known that this is a *nipātana* in the *luṅ* tense.
And here, the augment *rīk* is indeed prescribed as a nipātana for the reduplication;
this refers to the root *ḍubhṛñ* in the sense of "supporting and nourishing" (Dhātupāṭha 1087), as in the form *bibhartteḥ*.
Regarding "from *dhvarati*":
*dhvṛ* means "to be distressed" (Dhātupāṭha 939).
Regarding "from *dyute*": [it means] "to shine."
Regarding the root *dyuta* in the sense of "to shine" (Dhātupāṭha 741),
there is an absence of *samprasāraṇa*. Since *samprasāraṇa* would otherwise be required by [Pāṇini 6.1.15], its absence is here established as an irregularity (*nipātana*).
Regarding "tarateḥ":
this refers to the root *tṛ* in the sense of "floating" and "crossing over" (Dhātupāṭha 969).
Regarding "sṛpeḥ": [this refers to the root *sṛp*].
Of the root *gamlṛ* and *sṛplṛ* in the sense of "going" (*gatau*) [Dhātupāṭha 982, 983];
and of "of *vṛji*"—
that is, of the root *vṛji* in the sense of "avoiding" (*varjane*) [Dhātupāṭha 1812].
"marmṛjya" is the form of the root "mṛjū śuddhau" (Dhātupāṭha 1066) with the suffix ṇal. "āganīganti" [is likewise].
This too is correct.
To show that the particle *iti* has the sense of "kind" (*prakāra*), he says: "of such kinds," and so forth.
The meaning is that those for whom an ungrammatical operation is observed in the Veda—just as in the case of *dādharti* and others—are "of such kinds," that is, similar to *dādharti*.

What are these? They are *galagartī* and so forth. From the root *gṛ* "to swallow" (*dhātupāṭha* 1410), when there is elision of the *yaṅ* suffix and reduplication (*ślau*), the form *galagartī* is derived; here, the absence of *c*-substitution for the reduplicated syllable, the exception to *halādiśeṣa*, and the substitution of *la* for the *ra* are all treated as irregularities (*nipātana*). The term "in the Veda" (*chandasi*) is no longer applicable, because it was drawn over from the previous rule by the particle *ca*. Examples are: *vavṛte*, *vavṛdhe*, and *śaśṛdhe*.

The roots *vṛtu* in the sense of "turning" (Dhātupāṭha 758), *vṛdhu* in the sense of "growing" (Dhātupāṭha 759), and *śṛdhu* in the sense of "contemptuous sound" (Dhātupāṭha 760) take the *liṭ* suffix. Among these, the first two take the *ātmanepada* because they are *anudātetta* (having an indicatory vowel with the low-pitched accent), while the latter takes it because it is *svaritetta* (having an indicatory vowel with the circumflex accent).

As before, there is reduplication; once *halādiśeṣa* has been applied and the state of ending in an *ṛ*-vowel (*ṛvarṇāntatā*) has arisen, there is the substitution of *at*, followed by *raparatva* (substitution of *r*), and then *halādiśeṣa*. In forms such as *narnarti*, *narinartti*, and *narīnartti*, someone might have the misconception that since the exceptions (*apavāda*) beginning with *rīg*—namely [Pāṇini 7.4.90] and [7.4.91]—apply subsequently, and since the root no longer ends in an *ṛ*-vowel once those exceptions have been applied, this [rule, Pāṇini 6.1.2], should not apply. To dispel that misconception, he says: "in *narnarti*," after *halādiśeṣa* has taken place.
When that [substitution] has been obtained, the *samprasāraṇa* of *dyuti* and *svāpi* is commenced.
In the case of *vididyute*:

the root *dyuta* (meaning "to shine," Dhātupāṭha 741) takes the *liṭ* suffix; because it is marked with an *anudātta* vowel, the *ātmanepada* endings are used. Therein, the *samprasāraṇa* is applied by this rule, and by [Pāṇini 6.1.108], the preceding element (*para-pūrva-tva*) is substituted.

Regarding "vyadyutat": it is formed from the causative (*ṇyanta*) of the root *dyut* with the suffix *luṅ*; there is reduplication (*caṅ*), elision of the causative marker (*ṇilopa*), shortening of the penultimate vowel (*upadhāhrasvatva*), reduplication (*dvirvacana*), and the addition of the augment *aṭ*.
[The forms] "vididyutiṣate" and "vididyotiṣate" are likewise derived.

In the case of *san*, there is optionally *kittva* by the rule "ralo vyupadhāt" [Pāṇini 1.2.26]. When *kittva* does not apply, there is the *guṇa* substitution for the light penultimate vowel (*laghūpadhaguṇa*), and the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) applies by the rule "pūrvavatsanaḥ" [Pāṇini 1.3.62].
Thus, one forms *susvāpayiṣati*.
The root *ñiṣvap* means "to lie down" (*śaye*; Dhātupāṭha 1068). From that which ends in *ṇic*, the suffix *san* is applied.

For what reason is an example of the form ending in *ṇic* presented? To this he says: "That which ends in *svap* with *ṇic* is understood. The intention is that by this, an example of the form ending in *ṇic* has been demonstrated.
That the term refers to the causative form is understood precisely from the mention of *svāpeḥ*;

for such a designation would not be possible for the non-causative root alone. Moreover, the substitution of *sampasāraṇa* for the reduplicated syllable of the non-causative root is established by this very rule.

For instance: first, regarding the *liṭ* [perfect] suffix, this is already established by the rule "liṭabhyāsasyobhayeṣām" [Pāṇini 6.1.17]. Regarding the *san* [desiderative] suffix, however, since the *san* is *kit* by the rule "rudavida" [Pāṇini 1.2.8], the root undergoes *samprasāraṇa* by the rule "vacisvapi" [Pāṇini 6.1.15] and then becomes *sup* before being reduplicated; likewise, in the case of the *yaṅ* [intensive] suffix, it is that which has undergone *samprasāraṇa* that is reduplicated by the rule "yaṅi ca" [Pāṇini 6.1.19]. Therefore, because the *samprasāraṇa* of the root ending in *aṇ* is established by this grammatical system, the form ending in *svāpin* is what is intended to be included. If the form ending in *svāpin* is indeed intended to be included...

Then, from the root *svap* with the suffix *ṇvul*, we have *svāpaka*. From *svāpakam icchati* (he desires the sleeper), there is the suffix *kyac*, resulting in the form *svāpakīya*. When one then adds the desiderative suffix *san*—thinking "he desires to desire the sleeper"—one arrives at *siṣvāpakīyiṣati*. Does not *samprasāraṇa* (vowel contraction) apply here as well? To this he says: "Of that," and so forth. This *samprasāraṇa* is desired when there is immediate succession—that is, non-intervention—by a suffix that begins with *ni* following the reduplicated stem (*abhyāsa*) of that root *svap*. Therefore, in *siṣvāpakīyiṣati*, it does not occur.
That causal condition which arises from practice is not the one immediately preceding sleep here, because it is separated by the suffixes *ṇvul* and *kyac*.

But how is it that *saṃprasāraṇa* is obtained when there is an immediate [suffix] by means of a suffix conditioned by reduplication (*abhyāsa*), given that this specific qualification is not explicitly stated in the rule? He thinks as follows: because the suffix brought into proximity by the reduplication is itself a condition for the specific suffix, the base *svāpi* is qualified therein by that suffix conditioned by reduplication—namely, "the base *svāpi* which occurs when there is a suffix conditioned by reduplication."

And thus, when there is a relationship of qualifier and qualified based on the cause of repetition (*abhyāsa*), provided that no other intervening suffix exists, the *samprasāraṇa* (vocalization) must occur only for that which is the repetition of the root belonging to its own base (*svāṅga*).

However, it is not by means of an intervening suffix that a suffix which is separated [from the root] becomes the cause for reduplication (*abhyāsa*); with respect to that [intervening suffix], *svāpi* does not become the base (*aṅga*). Nor is it by means of another intervening suffix separated from *sidh* and *vāpa* that a suffix which is being repeated as the cause of reduplication becomes the base with respect to that; nor is the suffix which is the cause of reduplication in *siṣvāpayiṣati* immediately following the base of *svāpi*. But what about the *ṇvul* suffix which is immediately after *svāpi*?
In comparison with that [the root *svap*], *svāpi* is a member (*aṅga*), and this [root *svap*] does not become the cause for reduplication (*abhyāsa*).

Why, then, does it not occur here: *svapanam* (the act of sleeping), *svāpaḥ* (sleep) [formed with the suffix *ghañ*]; *svāpam karoti* (he performs sleeping) [with the suffix *ṇic*]; and *svāpayitum icchati* (he desires to cause to sleep) [with the suffix *san*, resulting in *siṣvāpayiṣati*]? It is said: because of the status of the elision of the vowel *a* as being like the original (*sthānivadbhāva*), there ought to be vocalization (*samprasāraṇa*) of the reduplication belonging to *svāpi*. However, when the elision of the vowel *a* has the status of being like the original, the reduplication does not belong to *svāpi*; rather, it belongs to another word, namely *svāpa*. [The example] "vivyathe" [is explained as follows].
The root *vyath* (meaning "to tremble" or "to fear") is listed as number 764 in the Dhātupāṭha; because it is marked with an anudātta vowel, it takes the ātmanepada endings.

Now, someone might have the misconception that the letter *y* must be eliminated by the rule *halādiśeṣaḥ*, while the letter *v* undergoes *samprasāraṇa*; therefore, to dispel that doubt, he says: "of the letter *y*" and so forth. [The resulting form is] *vāvyathyate*.

Furthermore, since only the short vowel [of the root] *iṇ* would have been heard [if no rule intervened], the lengthening is prescribed [by this rule], as in *īyatuḥ* and *īyuḥ*. Now, one might object: "But surely, because the substitution of *yaṇ* [for *i*] applies by virtue of being a subsequent rule (P. 6.4.81), the reduplication would not apply due to the resulting lack of a syllable (*anackatvāt*)"? To this, he says: "The *yaṇ* of *iṇ*, etc. (referring to P. 6.4.81).

The status of being a *sthānivadbhāva* (as if occupying the place of the original), however, is by virtue of [Pāṇini 1.1.56]. And that [status] applies only when the doubling (*dvirvacana*) is to be performed at its fixed time; once that has been performed, it remains only in the form of the substitute (*ādeśa*), as in *iyāya* and *iyayitha*.

In *ṇali* and *thali*, after the application of *vṛddhi* and *guṇa* respectively, the reduplication [of the root] occurs by virtue of the status of the original element (*sthānivadbhāva*), resulting in the vowel *i*. For that [reduplicated *i*], the substitution of *iyaṅ* applies by the rule "for the reduplicated syllable, when followed by a non-homogeneous vowel" (*abhyāsasyāsavarṇe*, Pāṇini 6.4.78). The term "*liṭ*" is understood to carry over [from the previous sūtra].
However, the mention of "*kit*" has ceased [to apply].

When the substitution of the subsequent form (*pararūpa*) would otherwise be required by the rule "[before *liṭ* ending in *k* or *ṅ*, there is] the single substitute of the subsequent form" (Pāṇini 6.1.97), the present rule initiates the substitution of a long vowel (*dīrghatva*).

The inclusion of the long vowel marker (*tapara*) is for the purpose that a long vowel which is short by its very nature—such as the long *v* taught [in the root list]—does not become short even when its shortness is applied. For example, in the case of the root *ā-chi* (Dhātupāṭha 209) meaning "to stretch," we have *āccha*, *ācchatuḥ*, and *āccuḥ*.

Here, after the *liṭ* suffix, *tip* becomes *ṇal*, *tas* becomes *atus*, and *jhi* becomes *us*; then, following reduplication and the application of *halādiśeṣa*, the rule *hrasvaḥ* [Pāṇini 7.4.59] applies. What would happen if there were a long vowel here? [If so], the augment *nuṭ* would apply by the rule *tasmānnuḍ dvihalaḥ* [Pāṇini 7.4.71].

Because of the statement "of the first [consonant]," the long vowel does not occur here for the final [consonant]—as in *papāca* and so forth. That which has two *hal*s (consonants) is called *dvihal*. [Examples are:

*ānaṅga*, *ānaṅgatuḥ*, *ānaṅguḥ*. [The roots] *agi*, *ragi*, and *lagi* have the meaning "to go" (*gatyarthāḥ*) [Dhātupāṭha 146, 144, 145]; because they are marked with the indicatory letter *it*, the augment *num* is applied.

Regarding the forms *ānañja*, *ānañjatuḥ*, and *ānañjuḥ*: the root *añjū* is listed in the Dhātupāṭha (1458) as meaning "to manifest, to smear, to shine, and to go. In the context of Māheśvara Sūtra 4 (*ai-au-c*), it is stated: "In a pratyāhāra [list] of phonemes, those which are partial portions of phonemes and have the same form as other phonemes do not undergo the grammatical operations prescribed for those [full] phonemes; for they merely imitate their shadow, and are not those [phonemes] themselves. Indeed, the Teachers maintain that a phoneme is produced by a distinct effort. Having said this, it is further stated: "An exception must be made regarding the vowel *ṛ* in the rules for the augment *nuṭ*, the substitution of *la*, and the process of *vināma*."

In this context, having reached the appropriate occasion, he provides a solution regarding the rule for the insertion of *nuṭ* before the letter *ṛ*: "The *repha* (the sound *r*) which is a part of the letter *ṛ* is included by the mention of *hal*.
[This applies in forms such as] *ānudhatuḥ*, *ānṛdhuḥ*.
[The root is] *ṛdhu* (meaning "to increase") from the Dhātupāṭha (1271).

But how, then, by the mention of *hal* (consonant), is the *ṛ*-substitute *repha*—which is not of the nature of a *varṇa* (phoneme)—included among those whose nature consists of *varṇas*? The intention is that this is due to the force of the mention of "two *hals*" (*dvihal*).

In this regard, one should have stated simply "after that, *nuṭ*" (*tasmānnuṭ*). Even if this were so, there would be no undesirable application of *nuṭ* in forms such as *āṭatuḥ* and *āṭuḥ*; for the rule "after the root *aś*" (*aśnoteḥ*) serves a restrictive purpose: if *nuṭ* occurs after something consisting of two *hals*, then it occurs only after *aś*, and not after anything else.
"He eats" for the purpose of cessation—this should not be doubted. If this were the only purpose, he would simply say "nāśnaḥ. Therefore, its purpose is indeed restriction (*niyama*).

Thus, since the rule is established even without the mention of "dvihal," the reason he employs the mention of "dvihal" is so that it may apply even to those [roots] that have the same form as a "dvihal" [root].

This is for the sake of ensuring that the same applies even to that [word] which has one *hal* as its primary constituent and a second as non-primary, which—because it imitates the shadow of the former—is fit to be designated as a *hal* only by way of metaphorical designation (*upacāra*).

How is this [attained]? If the term *dvihala* (containing two *hals*) is heard here, it applies to the *repha* (the letter *r*), which is a constituent part of the vowel *ṛ* and imitates its shadow, and not otherwise.

Therefore, by the force of the inclusion of the term *dvihala*, the *repha*—which is a single part of the *ṛ*-vowel—is understood here by the mention of *hal*; otherwise, the mention of *dvihala* would be purposeless. This undertaking is intended for the sake of those words that do not contain two *hals*.

Regarding "vyānaśe": the root *aś* means "to pervade" (*aśū vyāptau*, Dhātupāṭha 1264). Because it is marked with an indicatory vowel *ṭ* (anudāttettva), the Ātmanepada endings are applied; thus we have the suffix *ta*, which becomes *eś*.
The mention of the suffix *aśnoteḥ* is for the purpose of excluding the root *aś* meaning "to eat" (*aśa bhojane*, Dhātupāṭha 1523) belonging to the Kryādi class.
The letter *ca* serves to carry forward the augment *nuṭ*. Thus, in *babhūva*, [the substitution of] *vṛk* applies by [Pāṇini 6.4.88].
In *anubabhūve*, [the same applies].
The *ātmanepada* [suffixes] are used after this verbal root.
The mention of the suffix *śtip* is for the purpose of excluding the *yaṅ*-lopa [formation]: as in *vobhāveti*. Regarding "of *sūti*":
this refers to the root *ṣūṅ* in the sense of "the delivery of a fetus by a living being" (Dhātupāṭha 1031).

Regarding the word "suṣuve": the middle voice (ātmanepada) occurs because of the *ṅit* designation, and the substitution of *uvaṅ* takes place. The particle *iti* is used for the purpose of including other similar forms.
By this, forms such as *jāgrāmaḥ* and *adarśama* are established. In *jāgrāmaḥ*, the suffix *āna* is substituted for the root *jāgṛ*.
In *adarśama*, there is an absence of the substitute *paśya* for the root *dṛś* when the *laṅ* suffix is applied.
In the common language (*bhāṣā*), one says "we have awakened" (*jāgṛma*) or "we have seen" (*apaśyāma*);

however, in the *Ṛgveda*, in forms such as *dādharti*, the inclusion of *sasuva* and *grahīṣyaṇa* was not made for the sake of variety (*vaicitrya*). Since the meaning of "and so forth" (*ādi*) is understood from the mention of the plural number, he says "of these" (*evām*) and so on.

*Ṇijir* (Dhātupāṭha 1093) "in cleaning and nourishing," *Vijir* (Dhātupāṭha 1094) "in separation," and *Viṣlṛ* (Dhātupāṭha 1095) "in pervasion"—these, beginning with *ṇij*, belong to the *Jauhotyādi* class.
"The mention of 'three' (tri) is for the sake of what follows.

[In the rule] *bhṛñām it* [Pāṇini 7.4.76], there is the substitution of *i*. The mention of "three" is for the purpose that this [substitution] should apply to exactly three [roots] and not to more than that.
Why does this not also apply for this purpose? To this he says: "In this way," and so forth.

If the mention of the three [suffixes] is made here, for what purpose is the inclusion of *bṛt* at the end of *nij* and the others? This must be asked of the author of the *gaṇa* list, not of the author of the *sūtra*.
For it was stated previously that "the author of the *gaṇa* list is one person and the author of the *sūtra* is another."
It should be understood that the formation of *vṛt* was also performed by the author of the *Gaṇapāṭha* for the sake of variety, for the work of the author of the *Gaṇapāṭha* is indeed diverse.

Now, for what purpose is the mention of the term "guṇa" [in the rule]? Why could it not simply say "ekāra"? This cannot be said; for if it were stated in this way, someone might understand it to mean that "the substitution of *ekāra* for the roots beginning with *ni-*" is an exception (*apavāda*) to the rule of "retaining the initial consonant" (*halādiśeṣa*).

For when a technical designation (*saṃjñā*) is prescribed based on the inclusion of a specific quality (*guṇa*), there is a restriction such that only *ika* [is affected]; however, as for *hal*, its exclusion occurs by means of the remainder [of the rule] beginning with *hal*. The roots *ḍubhṛñ* "to support and nourish" (DhP 1087), *māṅ* "to measure" (DhP 1088), and *ohāṅ* "to go" (DhP 1089)—these *bhṛñ*-class roots belong specifically to the *juhotyādi* (third) class. Thus, [we have the forms] *mimīte* and *jihīte*, where the substitution of *i* [for the radical vowel] occurs by [Pāṇini 6.4.113]. [We also have] *iyarti* and *piparti*.

The roots *ṛ* and *sṛ* mean "to go" (Dhātupāṭha 1098, 1099); *pṛ* means "to protect" or "to fill" (Dhātupāṭha 1086). Because they belong to the *juhotyādi* class, there is *ślu*-elision of the *śap* suffix; then there is *guṇa*, reduplication, the substitution of *at* by *uraṇ raparaḥ* [Pāṇini 7.4.66], the substitution of *it* by this rule, and the substitution of *rapara*. Then, by *arti-pipartyośca* [Pāṇini 6.4.78], there is the substitution of *iyaṅ*.
Now, what is the purpose of including the mention of *arti*, since this suffix is taught as following after roots beginning with *nij*?

And all those [forms] that follow *nij-* and so on are exclusively Vedic (*chāndasa*); for indeed, having recited them, it was stated [by Pāṇini] "in the Chandas" (*chandasi*). Since they are Vedic, [the form] is established by the rule *arter vṛddhir chandasi* [Pāṇini 7.4.78]. If this is so, then this [usage] indicates that the employment of the root *ṛ* occurs even in the common language (*bhāṣā*). Regarding the form *viviṣṭi*: the root is *vaś* in the sense of "desire" (Dhātupāṭha 1080); there is *ślu*-elision of the *śap* suffix by the rule *arter vṛddhir chandasi* [7.4.78], and the substitution of *ṣ* is effected by the rule *vraśca-* etc. [8.2.36].
Regarding "vivakti": the root *vac* is used in the sense of "speaking" (Dhātupāṭha 1842). Regarding "siṣakti": [the root *sac*].
Or [it is derived] from *saca* in the sense of "to join" (Dhātupāṭha 997) or *saca* in the sense of "to sprinkle" (Dhātupāṭha 163);
thus [we have] *jigartti*, *jighartti*.
[These are derived from] *gṛ* and *ghṛ* in the sense of "to sprinkle" (Dhātupāṭha 937, 938).
In all cases, as before, there is the *śap* suffix and *ślu* elision. For example: *jajanam*, *dadhanam*.
[These derive from] the roots *jan* "to be born" (Dhātupāṭha 1105) and *dhan* "to possess grain" (Dhātupāṭha 1104).

In *luṅmipo'm*, because [the root] belongs to the *juhoty-ādi* class, there is *ślu*-elision of *śap*; the prohibition of *aṅ* is by the rule "in the Veda, [the augment *aṭ* is] frequently absent even when not preceded by *māṅ*" (Pāṇini 6.4.75). [The forms] *pipakṣati* and so forth are the forms of the roots *pac* and *yaj*.
[The form] *pipāsati* [is derived from the root *pā*].
From the root *pāti* or *pibati*.
Regarding "lulūṣati":
[it is derived from] *lūñ* "to cut" (Dhātupāṭha 1483).
By [Pāṇini 1.2.9], there is an absence of *guṇa* due to the *kittva* designation;

by [Pāṇini 7.2.12], there is a prohibition of the *iṭ* augment. For what purpose is the inclusion of *ta* (the *tapara* marker) [in the rule]? [It is] so that [the augment] does not occur in forms such as *pāpaciṣate*, derived from the desiderative (*san*) of the root *pāpacyate*.

What, then, is the reason that a short vowel does not occur here? It is because of the force of the prescription for a long vowel. If it were understood as "the reduplication which occurs before *san*," then [the long vowel would be prescribed]; however, the rule "before *pu*, *yaṇ*, and *ji*" [is stated] for the sake of ease of pronunciation. (The Kāśikā does not contain the phrase "pu-yaṇ-ji.")
The locative case ending is used here by treating *pu*, *yaṇ*, and *ja* as a single compound (*ekavadbhāva*).
Regarding the term *apara*: "that from which *a* follows" is *apara*; thus, *aparamavarṇapara* means that which is followed by a vowel other than *a*.

Regarding the form *pipaviṣate*: from the root *pūṅ* in the sense of "purifying" (*padane*; Dhātupāṭha 966), the suffix *san* is added. By the rule *smipūṅrañjvaśāṃ sani* [Pāṇini 7.2.74], the augment *iṭ* is inserted, followed by *guṇa* and the replacement (*avādeśa*).
Due to the status of being a *sthānivadbhāva*, there is reduplication (*dvirvacana*) of the element *pū*; this *sthānivadbhāva* is established by the rule *sthānivad ādeśo’nalvidhau* [Pāṇini 1.1.56].
Regarding the form *pipāvayiṣati*:

this is the desiderative (*san*) suffix added after the causative (*ṇic*) of the root *pū*. Here too, by virtue of the status of being a substitute (*sthānivadbhāva*), the element *pū* is reduplicated.
Regarding "bibhāvayiṣati":
from the root *bhū* in the sense of "existence" (*sattāyām*), with the causative suffix (*ṇic*) added, the desiderative suffix (*san*) is applied.
Regarding "yiyāvayiṣati": [it is formed similarly].

From the root *yu* (to join) with the suffix *nic*, followed by *san*: by the rule "a root ending in *san*" [Pāṇini 7.2.49], the augment *iṭ* is added, resulting in *rirāvayiṣati*; from *lū* (to cut), *lilāvayiṣati*.
The suffix *san* is added after the two roots *rauti* and *lunāti* when they are followed by the causative marker *ṇic*. Thus, we have *jijāvayiṣati*.

Here, *ju* is a root mentioned in the *sūtra* (Pāṇini 3.2.150), as it is listed in the rule *jucaṃkramya-ādayaḥ* (3.2.150) and others; from that [root], the causative *ṇic* is applied, and then *san*.

But how is it that the reduplicated syllable ends in *u* in forms such as *pipādayiṣati*, given that when the suffix *ṇiC* follows, the internal operation (*antaraṅga*) of *vṛddhi* and the substitution of *ā* would first take effect, resulting in a form ending in *v*, which would then have to be reduplicated? If it is argued that the reduplication of the form ending in *u* will occur by virtue of the status of the original element (*sthānivadbhāva*), [the answer is] no; for there is no *sthānivadbhāva* for what has been effected after *ṇiC*. This is because *ṇiC* itself is the cause of the non-reduplication. Therefore, he says: "This very [point]," etc. Indeed, without *ṇiC*, not all [roots] followed by the vowels *u*, *a*, *ṇ*, *j*, or *o* are possible.

For in that case, if the status of being *sthānivat* (as if occupying the original position) did not apply to what is performed upon the causative suffix (*ṇi*), then for those [roots] where the vowels *p*, *u*, *ṇ*, *j*, and *o* can all occur before a vowel (*avarṇa*) even without the causative suffix, there would be no problem. However, for those [roots] where the state of being followed by a vowel is not possible without the causative suffix, their reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*) would not end in *u*; yet this rule, "of *o* when *p*, *y*, *ṇ*, *j*, or *jha* follows" (*oḥ puyaṇjya-pare*), is stated.
Therefore, this is an indicator (*jñāpaka*) that even when the causative suffix is the cause of non-reduplication, it retains its *sthānivat* status.
By this, forms such as *tutāvayiṣati* and *bibhāvayiṣati* are established.

Furthermore, for which [roots] is the condition of having a vowel (*avarṇa*) followed [by *y* or *v*] not possible without the addition of the causative suffix (*ṇic*)? It is for all others except those ending in *yakāra* and *pakāra*.
For example: *pāpaciṣate*.

By [Pāṇini 6.4.48], there is the elision of the vowel *a*, and by [Pāṇini 6.4.49], there is the elision of the consonant *y*. Thus we have *tutāvayiṣati* (the reading *avatutāvayiṣati* is found in the Kāśikā and Padamañjarī). The verbal root is *tu*, which belongs to the *tudādi* class, as it is listed in the rule beginning with *turustuśamyamaḥ* [Pāṇini 7.3.95].
Regarding "juhāvayiṣati":
from the root *hu* meaning "to give" (Dhātupāṭha 1083), with the causative suffix (*ṇic*), the desiderative suffix (*san*) is added.
Regarding "bubhūṣati": [it is derived similarly from the root *bhū*].

As before, there is an absence of the qualities of *iṅ* and *guṇa*. [The examples are: from the roots *sru* "to flow" (DhP 940), *śru* "to hear" (DhP 942), *du* and *dru* "to run" (DhP 944, 945), and *pruṅ*, *pluṅ*, and *cyuṅ* "to move" (DhP 957, 958, 956), we have *sisrāvayiṣati* and so forth.

From these causative (*ṇic*) forms, the desiderative suffix (*san*) is applied in all cases. Now, one might object: "But here there is an intervention by a consonant beginning with *s* between [the root] and the *yaṇ* [vowel]; how can the substitution of *it* (short *i*), which is prescribed when a *yaṇ* followed by a vowel (*avarṇa*) follows, occur when there is such an intervention? To this, he says: "By the force of the explicit statement (*vacanasāmarthyāt*)."

For in every case there is an intervention by a single phoneme beginning with *s*, and this rule is stated; therefore, here, by the force of the statement, an intervention by a single phoneme is resorted to. Otherwise, this statement would be purposeless.
By the words "by the preceding rule" (*pūrvasūtreṇa*), etc., he shows that this is an optional rule (*vibhāṣā*) for what was not previously established.
[The example is] *śuśruṣati* (or *śuśrūyate*, according to the Kāśikā).
As before, there is an absence of the two qualities [of being a root and having an *it* augment].
The mention of *śtip* is for the purpose of indicating the verbal root (*dhātu*), not for the purpose of excluding the *yaṅ* suffix.
In this case, once the *guṇa* has been applied, because the state of ending in the vowel *u* no longer exists, the *it* designation does not occur.

Regarding the statement *sorū aviṣati* [this is not found in the Kāśikā]: this rule prescribes the substitution of *guṇa* for the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*). Therefore, although the term *luk* here is general, it is understood specifically as referring to the elision of *yaṅ* (*yaṅluk*).
For one considers that a reduplicated syllable cannot occur when there is *luk* [of the suffix], and thus he says: "in *yaṅ* and in *yaṅluk*," and so forth.

Regarding *caukruśīti*: the root *kruś* (meaning "to call out") [DhP 856] takes the *yaṅ* suffix; by [Pāṇini 2.4.74], the *yaṅ* is replaced by *lṛ*; by [Pāṇini 7.3.94], the augment *iṭ* is optionally added; and because the prohibition of the application of a suffix-characteristic (*pratyayalakṣaṇa*) applies once the *yaṅ* has been elided, the *guṇa* substitution would not otherwise take effect—hence the mention of the elision (*luk*). Furthermore, although *guṇa* would have applied by [Pāṇini 7.3.86], it is prohibited by [Pāṇini 7.3.87]. Regarding *yaṃyamyate*: the root *yam* (meaning "to cease") [DhP 984] takes the augment *nuk* by [Pāṇini 7.4.85].
With the words "But surely" (*nanu ca*), etc., he refutes this [objection] regarding the term *akitaḥ*.
The term *akitaḥ* is stated for the purpose that [the rule] should not apply in cases such as *yaṃyamyate*.

In this case, since the substitution of *nuṭ* would take effect as an exception (*apavāda*), the word would not end in *añ* and thus the long vowel (*dīrgha*) would not occur anyway; therefore, there would be no purpose in the mention of *akitaḥ*.

With the words "In that case, then" (*evaṃ tarhi*) and so forth, he shows that the term *akitaḥ* is stated in order to indicate this *paribhāṣā*: "Exceptions (*apavāda*) do not subvert general rules (*utsarga*) in cases of modification through repetition (*abhyāsa-vikāra*)" (Vyāḷī-Pañjikā 23). Regarding the example *ḍoḍhaukyate*:

after applying *yaṅ* to the root *ḍhaukṛ* (meaning "to go," Dhātupāṭha 98) and performing the *halādiśeṣa* operation, there is shortening by [Pāṇini 7.4.59] *hrasvaḥ*, and then *guṇa* substitution by the preceding rule.

In that case, if this indicator (*jñāpaka*) did not exist, the shortening [prescribed by] *Pāṇini 6.4.120* (*hrasvatvaṃ*)—which has its scope in forms such as *pipāsati*—would be sublated by the lengthening of the *sandhyakṣara* vowels [prescribed by *Pāṇini 6.4.157*]. If it is argued:

"Since there is no purpose for prescribing lengthening of a long vowel, the lengthening will not occur," we reply: No, this is not so. There is indeed a purpose for prescribing the lengthening of a long vowel. What is that? It is so that the short vowel does not occur. And if this indicator did not exist, then even in a form like *acīkarat*, the substitution of *it* [for the penultimate vowel], which has its scope in forms such as *acikṣaṇat*, would be sublated by the lengthening [prescribed by] *Pāṇini 7.4.94* (*dīrgho laghoḥ*).

If this indicator (*jñāpaka*) did not exist, then in cases such as *pipakṣati*, the shortening (*ittva*) prescribed by the rule *sanyataḥ* [Pāṇini 7.4.79] would have scope; however, it is sublated by the lengthening (*dīrghatva*) ordained by the rule for the *mān-badh-ādi* group [Pāṇini 6.4.97].

Likewise, in the case of *ajīgaṇat*, if this indicator did not exist, the substitution of the remaining consonant (*halādiśeṣaḥ*) [Pāṇini 7.4.60], which has scope in forms such as *papāṭha*, would be sublated by the aforementioned shortening.
But when this indicator exists, none of this is sublated.

But surely, a rule becomes informative (jñāpaka) only when there is no other purpose; yet there is indeed a purpose for this [rule]. What is it? That, with regard to the status of *kit*, it should not apply to the root *jahāti*—as in *jāhāti* and *jāheti*. This is not so. If this were the purpose, then [the author] would have formulated the prohibition as "of *ahā*" (*ahākaḥ*).

Furthermore, the term "*akitah*" ought to be a qualifier of the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*), provided that the status of *kit* arises during the state of reduplication. However, the status of *kit* for the root *jahāti* does not depend upon the reduplicated syllable, for it occurs prior to the reduplication itself.
Therefore, from the root *jahāti*, the forms should be *jāhāti* and *jāheti*.
Consequently, the statement "not when followed by *kit*" (*akitah*) is merely an indicator (*jñāpaka*).
However, the inclusion of the *kit* marker [in Pāṇini 6.4.116] is for the purpose of preventing the obstruction of the general reference in the rule *jahāteh* (Pāṇini 3.1.148).

Now, what is the purpose of including the mention of "long" (dīrgha)? It might be argued that it could simply be understood as "of the vowel *ā*" (*ādita eva*). This cannot be so, for otherwise the status of the rule "not after *ki*" (*akitaḥ*) as an indicator (*jñāpaka*) would not be tenable. For when the mention of "long" is present, once the augment *nuK* has been applied, there is no possibility of lengthening because the stem no longer ends in a vowel (*anajanta*); thus, the prohibition "not after *ki*" functions as an indicator. However, if only the vowel *ā* were prescribed, it would apply to an abhyāsa (reduplicated syllable) that already ends in a vowel, and consequently, the rule "not after *ki*" could not serve as an indicator.

Therefore, the mention of "long" (*dīrgha*) must be made. Since lengthening would apply by the rule *tasmāddīrghagrahaṇaṃ kartavyam* (Pāṇini 7.4.83), this statement is commenced. Forms such as *tantanyate* and so forth belong to the roots *tam*, *gam*, *yam*, and *ram*. If [the mention of "long"] were not made, then in forms such as *yamyate*, the *anusvāra* prescribed by the rule *jhalāṃ jaś jhaśi* (Pāṇini 8.4.53) would not be established because it would not be followed by a *jhal* sound. To address this, he says: "That which is called *nuk*," and so forth.
But how can this *nuk* be understood as having the purpose of indicating the *anusvāra*? To this he says: "For by the original element (*sthānin*)," and so forth.
For here, the substitute (*ādeśa*), the *anusvāra*, is indicated by the original element *nuk*.
Therefore, it is the *anusvāra* itself that is prescribed here as the augment (*āgama*), and not *nuk*.
In examples such as *yamyamyate*, although there is the condition of being followed by a non-*jhal* sound (*ajhal-paratā*), the *anusvāra* is nevertheless established.

Likewise, [the rule] P. 8.4.58 would apply, yet the audible presence of the *anusvāra* is desired in one alternative; that, however, is not established because [the rule] is an exception (*apavāda*). To this, he says: "And like a word-final [consonant]," etc.
The meaning is that this should be explained as having the sense that the *anusvāra* becomes as if it were at the end of a word (*padāntavat*).

In this regard, the explanation is as follows: since the rule for the final element (*tadanta-vidhi*) already ensures that *anusvāra* occurs at the end of a word ending in a nasal (*anunāsika*), there would be no purpose in explicitly mentioning "the end" (*anta-grahaṇa*). It is stated, however, so that whatever property belongs to an *anusvāra* at the end of a word should also apply to the *nuK* augment. Consequently, the *anusvāra* will be audible in one alternative (*pakṣe*). Regarding the form *tetimyate*: it is derived from the roots *tima* and *ṣṭima*, meaning "to become moist" (*ārdībhāve*). (Dhātupāṭha 1123, 1124).

Now, for what purpose is the addition of *t* (*tapara*) made, given that there is nothing else to be excluded from this [term], since short vowels are absent everywhere? To this he says: "The addition of *t*," and so forth. Since there is no present long vowel [to be excluded], the addition of *t* will serve to exclude even a long vowel that existed previously. Regarding the word "bābhāmyate": *(Note: This refers to the grammatical context where the term *tapara*—meaning "followed by *t*"—is used to specify a short vowel, thereby excluding any long vowel, whether current or previously existing.)*
The root *bhām* is used in the sense of "anger" (*krodhe*; Dhātupāṭha 441). This [entry] begins with a nasalized vowel.

The roots *jap* and *jalp* mean "articulate speech" (Dhātupāṭha 397, 398); *jabh* and *jṛbhī* mean "bending of the limbs" (Dhātupāṭha 388, 389); *dah* means "reducing to ashes" (Dhātupāṭha 991); *daṃś* means "biting" (Dhātupāṭha 989); *bhavj* means "crushing" (Dhātupāṭha 1453); and *paś* is a root found in the Sūtras. In forms such as *jañjapyate* up to *daṃdaśyate*, the suffix *yaṅ* is applied according to Pāṇini 3.1.24 (*lupasada...*).

In the other case, it is by way of a general characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*). [The roots] *cara* in the sense of "going" (Dhātupāṭha 559) and both *ñi phalā* in the sense of "falling apart" (Dhātupāṭha 516) and *phala* in the sense of "ripening" or "accomplishment" (Dhātupāṭha 530) are included.

The letter *ā* in the root *niṣ* is for the purpose of pronunciation (*uccāraṇārtha*), not an *anubandha*, because there is no purpose [for it as such]. Consequently, by the paribhāṣā concerning roots without *anubandhas* (Pāṇini 1.2.53), only this root *niṣ* in the sense of "accomplishing" (*niṣpatti*) would be grasped, and not the one in the sense of "falling apart" (*viśaraṇa*). This is not a fault; the letter *c* is added here, and it will serve as a conjunctive particle (*samuccaya*) to include the root in the sense of "falling apart. Thus, in the form *cañcūryate*, the suffix *yaṅ* is applied according to Pāṇini 3.1.24 (*lupasada...*).
When the vowel *a* is changed to *u* by the subsequent sūtra, a long vowel is substituted according to [Pāṇini 8.2.77] *hali ca*.

The portion of the rule concerning the connection (*yogabhāga*) is for the sake of what follows; the intention is that, were the term *para* not included, the operation would apply only to the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*) because of the governing context (*adhikāra*) of the reduplicated syllable. Thus, it says: "Let it not be [the case] for the reduplicated syllable."
"Lest [the substitute] apply to the final *al*.

If "from *at*" (*ataḥ*) were not stated, one would think that by the maxim "of the final *al*" (*alo'ntyasya*), the substitution would apply to that final *al* which belongs to the verbal form following the reduplication. Now, for what purpose is the inclusion of the *t* (the *tapara* marker) made, since even in the place of a single-mora vowel, by virtue of internal similarity (*āntaratamya*), only a single-mora vowel will result? To this, he says: "The inclusion of the *t*," and so forth.

If the *tapara* marker were not applied to the vowel *u*, then in forms such as *cañcūrti* and *pampulati*, the *guṇa* substitution prescribed by [Pāṇini 7.3.86], *pugantalaghūpadhasya*, would occur; it is for the purpose of preventing this that the *tapara* marker is employed. Now, one might object: "In the case of *cañcūrti*, the long vowel itself will serve as the blocker of the *guṇa*; so what is the use of this *tapara* marker for the sake of its exclusion? To this, he says: "The long vowel," and so forth.
[The reason for its non-application is] by the rule [Pāṇini 6.4.22], *asiddhatvaṃ tu...* (the subsequent is considered as if not having taken effect).

If, then, a quality (*guṇa*) that is obtained by another rule is set aside by the addition of *t* (the *tapara* marker), then longness (*dīrghatva*) would likewise not occur. This is not a fault; for when the *tapara* marker is employed, longness is also established.
Therefore, it cannot be said that the long vowel is excluded.

And thus, considering that it is impossible to exclude longness by means of the *tapara* marker in the rule *ata ut sārvadhātuke* [Pāṇini 6.4.110], the prohibition of longness for the root *kṛ* is undertaken in the rule *na bhakurchurām* [Pāṇini 8.2.79].

Therefore, the inclusion of *ta* in the rule (*ataḥ*) is intended here to prevent [the application of the rule] in cases such as: *phalantaṃ prayuṅkte* → *phālayati*; then, from the root *phālayati*, there is *kvip*, and from that which ends in it, by the Vārttika "In the sense of conduct (*ācāra*), *kvip* is added after all nominal stems," there is *kvip*; and from that which ends in it, there is *yaṅ*: *panphālyate*, *pampāloti*. How, then, would [the rule] apply [undesirably]? Because that which has undergone a partial modification is not different [from the original]. This introduction [of the rule] is for the purpose of preventing *yaṅ* and *luk*. [The example is] *cūrttiḥ*.
> [[3.3.94]] A long vowel [is substituted] as before.
Regarding "prakṛtāḥ": [the root *kṛ* takes] the suffix *niṣṭhā*; from that which ends in it, the feminine suffix *ṭāp* is added; then the nominative plural suffix *jas*.
"By the force of the statement, [the term 'abhyāsa'] is not connected here.

The intention is this: if both the mention of *yaṅ-luk* and the mention of *abhyāsa* were connected here, then the statement would be redundant; for by the preceding rule alone, the [doubling of] the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*) for both *yaṅ* and *yaṅ-luk* is already established. Forms such as *varīvṛtyate* are derived from the roots *vṛt*, *vṛdh*, and *nṛt* (Dhātupāṭha 758, 759, 1116).

"It should be stated that 'it applies to those containing the element *ṛ*'"—the meaning is that this must be explained so that the substitutions *rīg* and so forth may apply even to other roots containing *ṛ*, not only to those with *ṛ* as a penultimate vowel (*ṛdupadha*).

In this regard, the explanation is as follows: the particle *ca* ("and") is used here, and it serves to include (*samuccaya*) other roots containing *ṛ* besides those with *ṛ* as a penultimate vowel; thus, the substitutions *rīg* and so forth occur for *vṛśc* and other such roots that contain *ṛ*.
The rule *rīgṛtvataḥ* was not formulated [separately]; it is for the sake of variety.
In the rule *ṛdupadhasya*, the addition of the *tapara* marker (*ṛt*) is for the sake of avoiding ambiguity.

Once the *yaṇ* substitution has been applied before the vowel *u*, there might arise a doubt: does this refer to that which has *ṛ* as its penultimate letter (*ṛkāropadha*), or rather to that which has *r* as its penultimate letter (*rephopadha*)? [The answer is: it is only when there is elision (*luk*).
By the letter *ca*, the operations such as *rīk* and others are drawn forward [from the previous rule].
Thus: *carkarti*.
[The root] *ḍukṛñ* "to do" (Dhātupāṭha 1472). *jarhati*.
"Hmañ? haraṇe" (Dhātupāṭha 899);
"and [the substitution of] 'akarti' for 'kirati'" refers to the root "kṛ?
vikṣepe" (Dhātupāṭha 1409).
Regarding the phrase "kirati" and so forth:

the mention of *kirati* is for the purpose of illustration (*upalakṣaṇārtha*). Therefore, it should be understood that this includes other roots ending in the vowel *ṛ*, such as *gṛ* (Dhātupāṭha 1410) in the sense of "swallowing."

"Ending in *carkarīta*" means that which ends in the *yaṅ*-lopa (the elision of the *yaṅ* suffix). This technical term "*carkarīta*" was indeed coined by the ancient masters specifically for the *yaṅ*-lopa.
Thus:
"pacati" (he cooks) is the third person singular present indicative.
This too is intended as an illustration;
for other statements are also included here.

Thus, the meaning is that one who would bring about—that is, would produce—forms such as *nayati* and *karoti*, which end in ṛ (as in *kṛ*) and so forth, in the first person singular of the present tense (*laṭ*), and so on.
"I consider him one who knows what has been attained.
One who knows what has been attained (*prāpta*) is "one who knows what has been attained" (*prāptijña*).
However, since diseases and so forth are the subject under discussion here, he who knows their attainment should be understood as "one who knows what has been attained."
I understand it thus:
"The seizure has been commenced by him.
By this, he states the reason for its attainment.

*Saṃgraha* is that by which the characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) is correctly grasped and made known; thus, it is the science of grammar (*vyākaraṇa-śāstra*). It is "commenced" (*prārabdha*) in an excellent manner (*prakarpa*), because it has been heard many times from many [teachers].
What, then, is this "attainment" (*prāpti*) for the sake of whose full knowledge I understand the one who knows attainment? To this he says: "In this regard, this... and so forth.
Two things are under discussion here: the *aṅga* (the base) and the repetition (*abhyāsa*).
The term *ṛtaḥ* is employed as a qualifier; although both are under discussion there, nevertheless, this *ṛtaḥ* is a qualifier of the *aṅga* alone, not of the repetition.
Why? Because of the force of the inclusion of the long vowel marker (*taparakaraṇa*).

In every case, by the rule *hrasvaḥ* [Pāṇini 7.4.59], the vowel of the reduplication (*abhyāsa*) ought to be short; therefore, there is no long vowel in the reduplication. If the term *ṛtaḥ* were a qualifier of the reduplication, then the inclusion of the *tapara* marker (the lengthened *ṝ*) would be purposeless. Consequently, by the force of the *tapara* marker, the term *ṛtaḥ* qualifies the stem (*aṅga*) itself, not the reduplication.
And this being the case, there is no application [of the rule] to *kṛ* (the root *kirati*); for *rug* and the others have been excluded by the addition of the marker *t* (*taparakaraṇa*).

By the word "and the rest" (*ādi*), *rig* and so forth are included. Thus, when it is said, "there is no application to *kṛ*, *rug*, and the others," what is meant by Bhaṭṭoji is that, by process of elimination, the application belongs only to those roots ending in a short vowel, such as *kṛ*. By the three rules beginning with *sanyataḥ* [Pāṇini 7.4.79], whatever operation is prescribed for the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*) when followed by the suffix *san*, that is extended [by analogy] to cases where a *caṅ* follows a light syllable.

Regarding the phrase "laghuni caṅpare": these are two locative case endings in apposition (*vyadhikaraṇe*). It means that when a *ṇi* (causal suffix) followed by *caṅ* (the aorist marker) follows, whatever [vowel] was light (*laghu*) immediately preceding it, the subsequent reduplication (*abhyāsa*) of that [vowel] becomes like *san* (as if it were followed by *san*). The term "caṅpare" is a *bahuvrīhi* compound: "that after which *caṅ* follows is *caṅpara*. It is not a *tatpuruṣa* compound meaning "that which is both *caṅ* and *para*."

By implication, this extension (*atideśa*) is understood to apply only to that which ends in a *ṇic* affix; for otherwise, if this extension were to apply to that which ends in a verbal root (*prakṛti*), then he would have stated, "as in the case of *san* and *caṅ*.
The phrase "when there is no elision of *an*" (*ananlope*) is a qualifier of the term "when followed by *caṅ*" (*caṅpare*).
The term *ag* is a technical abbreviation (*pratyāhāra*) for vowels. The elision of an *ak* vowel is called *aglopa*; that which does not have this is *anaglopa*.
An example is *apīpacat*.

From the root *pac* (with the *ṇit* suffix), in the *luṅ* tense, after applying *cleścaṅ*, the shortening of the penultimate vowel (*upadhāhrasvatvam*), reduplication with its attendant operations (*dvirvacanamabhyāsakāryam*), and the application of *halādiśeṣa*, there occurs by this [rule] the treatment as *sanvadbhāva*. By the rule *sanyataḥ* [Pāṇini 7.4.79], there is the substitution of *i* for the vowel, and by the subsequent rule [7.4.94], there is lengthening. Thus we have *atatakṣat* and *ararakṣat*.

However, because the *repha* and *takāra* are followed by a conjunct consonant (*saṃyogaparatvāt*), when they receive the designation of "heavy" (*gurusaṃjñā*), the treatment as *sanvadbhāva* does not take place.
Regarding the form *ajajāgarat*:
here, the syllable *ja* is heavy because of the length of its vowel.
As for the passage beginning with "In this regard, some [say]... and so forth:
For them, the form should be *ajījāgarat*.

But what is the reason they desire this, given that it is stated [in Pāṇini 7.3.86] that "when a light syllable precedes a *caṅ*," and yet here the light syllable is separated by intervening elements? To this he says: "In all cases indeed," and so forth.

Even in forms such as *acīkarat*, because of the intervention of a letter such as *k*, there is no immediate succession of the light syllable to the reduplication (*abhyāsa*). Yet this rule is stated; therefore, by the authority of this statement, the *sanvadbhāva* (treatment like the *san* suffix) must occur even when there is an intervention of two letters.
And therefore, just as in forms such as *acīkarat* the [strengthening] occurs even when there is an intervention, so too here the operation of *sanvadbhāva* ought to occur despite the intervention.
If, however, it does not occur because of the intervention, then the intention is that it should likewise not occur in this case either.
[The author says: "That is incorrect."

Regarding the [form] *ajajāgarat*, they desire the application of the rule for treating a root as if it were *san*-ending (*san-vadbhāva*) by relying on the fact that the root *gṛ* is light (*laghu*); and regarding the reason stated by the words "in all cases" (*sarvatraiva*) and so forth, both of these are unsatisfactory here because they are illogical.
Why? He explains this with the words "by which" (*yena*) and so forth:
there is an intervention by a single phoneme (*varṇa*) in every case.
There is both the presence and absence of intervention by a cluster of phonemes (*varṇasaṅghāta*).

In that regard, according to the principle "that by which there is no intervention [is considered non-intervening] even when there is intervention" (Vyāḍipāda 46), one resorts only to that intervention by a single phoneme which is invariably present and impossible to avoid, and not to intervention by a cluster of phonemes.
In the example *ajajāgarat*, there is intervention by a cluster of phonemes.

If, then, one does not rely on the intervention of a cluster of vowels (*varṇasaṅghāta*), would it not fail to be established when there is intervention by a cluster of consonants (*vyañjanasaṅghāta*)? With this intention, he says: "How [could there be] *acikṣaṇat*? and so forth.
This is a form of the root *kṣaṇu* in the sense of "to injure" (Dhātupāṭha 1465).
Since it is also established here by means of an indicator (*jñāpaka*), he says: "The activity of the Teacher," and so forth.
Those suffixes such as *saṃyoga* and others that are similar to *kṣaṇoti* are of this same class;
that is to say, they are of the same type as *kṣaṇoti*.

If they did not possess the vowel *it*, then for the purpose of excluding them [from the application of *atva*], the rule *atsmṛdṛtvaraprathabhrada* (Pāṇini 7.4.95) and so forth would not have prescribed *atva*; yet it does prescribe it.

Therefore, this very prescription for the substitution of *at* indicates the teacher’s intention: "The substitution of *it* occurs for roots of this class. For example, in the form *ahaṃ papaca*, when the *ṇal* suffix is in the first person singular, there is no *ṇit*-characteristic [by virtue of Pāṇini 7.1.91]; thus, this serves as a counter-example.

In this context, the suffix *laghu* follows immediately after [the verbal root], but not when followed by *caṅ*. For example, in forms such as *acakamata*, the *luṅ* and *caṅ* affixes are applied directly from the verbal root itself—specifically from *kam* in the sense of "desire" (*kāntau*), as per the statement "there is an addition for the root *kam*" (Vārttika 208). Thus, the *luṅ* and *caṅ* are applied to the very base of the root.

Regarding the form *acakathat*: the root *kath* in the sense of "continuous discourse" (*vākyaprabandhe*) belongs to the *curādi* group and ends in a long vowel (*adanta*). Here, by [Pāṇini 6.4.48], there is the elision of the vowel *a*.

In this case, however, if the *sthānivadbhāva* (the status of being as if the original element) were applied to the elision of the *t* (*tvaglopa*), the rule would not apply even when there is an intervention [of a letter].
Therefore, he states another counter-example: "He called the stone 'adadṛṣat'.
Here, the suffix *ṇic* is added according to the rule *tat karoti tad ācaṣṭe* (Vārttika 200).

Regarding the statement "Is it not as if [the suffix] iṣṭhan? The operation [pertains] to the nominal stem" (Vārttika 811), there is elision of the *ṭi* due to the treatment as if [the suffix] iṣṭhan were present.

Here, there is elision of both vowels (*ac*) and consonants (*hal*), and since this applies only to the word *nāka* in its entirety, there is no application of the rule regarding the status of the original element (*sthānivadbhāva*).
However, the mention of the elision of *ak* being made for other purposes serves to preclude the application of the *sanvadbhāva* rule even in cases such as *acakathat*.
Regarding the form *avīvadat*:

one might think that since the root *vad* takes the causative suffix (*ṇic*) in the sense of "he caused [someone] who had spoken (*vāditavantam*) to speak," and then another causative suffix (*ṇic*) is added, the initial *ṇic* is elided by Pāṇini 6.4.51; even though this occurs, the base (*aṅga*) does not lose its initial vowel (*aglopi*), and therefore the treatment as *sanvadbhāva* (the behavior of the *san* suffix) should not apply. To address such an objection, he says: "he caused [someone] who had spoken to speak," and so forth.
By the rule beginning with *caṅpare*, he states the reason why the elision of the *ṇic* is not considered an elision of the initial vowel (*aglopi*).
By the rule *caṅpare*, the class of *ṇic* is implied by means of the *sanvadbhāva* (the treatment as if followed by *san*).
Therefore, according to the maxim of the cow and the bull (*gobalīvardanyāya*), the class of *ṇic* is accepted as the cause [of the substitution].
Consequently, the elision of any other *ak* (vowel) than that of the *ṇic*-class is adopted as the cause for the prohibition, but not the elision of that very *ṇic*-class itself.
Therefore, since the elision of *ṇi* is not treated as making the base (*aṅga*) "eliding" (*aglopin*), when that [ṇi] is elided, the base does not become "eliding.
Consequently, the treatment as *san*-like (*sanvadbhāva*) certainly applies here.

To one who might object—arguing that just as the substitution of *it* (the vowel *i*) occurs for the reduplication in forms like *acīkarat* by means of the extension (*atideśa*) "as if *san*-like," so too should it apply to forms like *amīmapat* despite the elision of the reduplication in *mīmā* and others—he says: "*mīmādīnām*" and so forth.
By the word "etc. (*ādi*), the inclusion of *dhva* and others is intended.
With the words "Furthermore" (*kiñca*) and so forth, another solution is presented.
For, by the extended application (*atideśa*) of the term "like *san*" (*sanvat*), the grammatical operation dependent upon *san* itself is what is extended.
And what is the purpose of [the rule] requiring a suffix (*san*) as its basis? It is that which requires *san* and nothing else.

Furthermore, the elision (*lopa*) prescribed by the rule *atra lope 'bhyāsasya* [Pāṇini 7.4.58] does not require *san* alone; rather, it also requires the substitution of *is*, and so forth. By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), the inclusion of *dhv* and other such substitutions is intended.
With the words "Furthermore," etc., another solution is presented.
For, by the extension (*atideśa*) expressed as "as if having *san*," only that grammatical operation which depends upon *san* is extended.
And what is the operation that depends upon *san*? It is that which requires *san*, and nothing else.

Furthermore, the elision (*lopa*) prescribed by the rule *atra lope'bhyāsasya* [Pāṇini 7.4.58] does not depend on the suffix *san* alone; rather, it depends on the substitution of *is* and so forth as well. By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), the substitution of *ī* according to *ajñapyṛdhāmīt* [Pāṇini 7.4.55] and the *guṇa* substitution according to *muco'karmakasya* [Pāṇini 7.4.57] are included.
Consequently, in forms such as *abhīmapat*, the substitution of *is* does not occur.

The intention is that [the suffix] does not occur even when there is an elision of the reduplication (*abhyāsa*). [The roots are: *smṛ* in the sense of "thinking" (DhP 933); *dṛ* in the sense of "fear" (DhP 808); *ñi tvara* in the sense of "haste or agitation" (DhP 775); *pratha* in the sense of "becoming manifest" (DhP 1553); *mrada* in the sense of "crushing" (DhP 767); *stṛñ* in the sense of "covering" (DhP 1484); and *spaś* in the senses of "afflicting" and "touching" (DhP 887).

Now, as to why the lengthening [of the vowel] does not occur in the case of *adadarat* by virtue of [Pāṇini 6.4.15], he says: "By the force of the inclusion of *ta* after the letter" (*taparakaraṇasāmarthyāt*), and so forth.

For by that very rule [6.4.15], the long *au* would have been obtained, and its prevention is effected by the inclusion of *ta*. This is because, according to the principle "an *aṇ* being taught [as a substitute] does not include its homogeneous counterparts" (*bhāvyamāno 'ṇ savarṇān na gṛhṇāti*), those vowels being taught [as substitutes] do not include their homogeneous sounds; furthermore, in all cases, the short vowel is substituted for the [long] vowels beginning with *sthā*.
