In that case, if [the vowel] were obtained even by another characteristic, the addition of *t* (taparakaraṇa) would not serve to exclude the long [vowel]; rather, the addition of *t* would be merely for the purpose of exclusion.

Why is that? Because of the force of the inclusion of *ta* [in Pāṇini 6.1.71], the long vowel is not applied by [Pāṇini 7.4.94]; this is the intended meaning. Regarding the roots *veṣṭa* "to surround" (Dhātupāṭha 255) and *ceṣṭa* "to move" (Dhātupāṭha 256), since their reduplicated syllables (*abhyāsa*) do not have a light vowel following them, the status of being like *san* (*sannvadbhāva*) does not apply at all; therefore, by this [rule], the optional substitution of *a* is prescribed. The root *gaṇa* "to count" (Dhātupāṭha 1853) belongs to the *curādi* group and ends in a long vowel (*adanta*).

In that case, when the elision [of the penultimate vowel] has been effected by the rule *tatrākārāt* (Pāṇini 6.4.48), this substitution of *ī* is prescribed because the rules for the treatment as a reduplicated stem (*sanvadbhāva*) and the lengthening of the vowel—both of which would otherwise not apply due to the statement *anaglopaḥ*—are here set aside.
The particle *ca* serves to carry forward the optionality (*vibhāṣā*) from the preceding rule.

Thus ends the fourth quarter of the seventh chapter in the *Kāśikā-vivaraṇapañjikā* composed by the venerable master Jinendrabuddhi, who is like a Bodhisattva. And the seventh chapter is completed. The Eighth Chapter, First Quarter: Since this [section] is understood to be a governing rule (*adhikāra*) due to its connection with the indicatory mark of the circumflex accent (*svarita*), he says "of all" (*sarvasya*), etc.
"We shall state" (*vakṣyāmaḥ*) means "we shall explain."
"Prior to *pada*. [The *Kāśikā* explains: "Prior to the word *pada*"—that is, prior to the rule that is about to be stated as "*padasya*" [Pāṇini 8.1.16].
This is a citation of the rule "*padasya*" which is about to be stated.

However, because the difference between the original form (*anukārya*) and the imitation (*anukaraṇa*) is not intended [to be expressed], there is no case-ending (*vibhakti*) since the item lacks the status of a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) due to the absence of meaning, as in the example: *gavityayamāha* ("He says, 'Go! [where *go* is an imitation of the word]).
It should be understood that this is according to the rule "everything is doubled" (*sarvasya dve bhavataḥ*). The particle *iti* is used for the purpose of indicating the meaning.
The meaning of the phrase "every [word] has two [forms]" is that which is understood; the sense is that this form of meaning is to be known as that which will be stated hereafter.
"He will state" refers to the author of the Sūtras.
Regarding the word "therein" (*tatra*):
in this grammatical rule (yoga), two alternatives are possible— doubling (*dvirvacana*) by way of substitution (*sthāne*), and doubling as a dual occurrence (*dviḥprayoga*).
How so? Because this is the context of the instruction on words (*śabdānuśāsana*), it is understood that "of all" refers to "all words.

Now, this word *dvi* ("two")—according to the rule "numbers up to ten denote the numbered objects" (*Hevāmbuga* 90)—is a term for a numbered object (*saṃkhyeya*). In this case, that numbered object must be either the form of a word or a repetition (*āvṛtti*). Furthermore, the expression "two" (*dve*) could be indicated either in the neuter gender or in the feminine gender. Among these, when it is indicated in the neuter gender, the numbered object is the form of a word.

If the reference is made in the feminine gender, then there are two actions characterized by utterance (*uccāraṇa*) belonging to the word. In that case, when [the operations] are prescribed with respect to the form of the word, this genitive case in *sarvasya* becomes a genitive of location (*sthāna-ṣaṣṭhī*), according to the principle: "Because the relationship is not otherwise fixed" (Pāṇini 1.1.49). In this view, the position is that "doubling occurs in place [of the original]."

But when two occurrences (*āvṛtti*) are prescribed, then the position arises that "doubling is the use twice. In this view, there is no relationship of original element (*sthānin*) and substitute (*ādeśa*),
for occurrence is an action (*kriyā*), and in this context, the word is its instrument (*sādhana*).
Furthermore, the relationship of original and substitute (sthānyādeśabhāva) is not possible between an action and its instrument.
For if such a relationship were to exist, since the original word possesses the nature of ceasing, there would be only cessation; and consequently, there would be an absolute absence of the action.
Indeed, the act of utterance is not possible without the word, because that action is a property of the word.
Therefore, when two occurrences (*āvṛtti*) are prescribed, then the position that "doubling (*dvirvacana*) is the double employment [of the word]" arises.

In this view, with respect to the word *āvṛtti*, the genitive case in *sarvasya* should be understood as the agentive genitive characterized by its connection to a *kṛt*-suffix, according to Pāṇini 2.3.65 (*kartṛkarmaṇoḥ kṛti*).
For every word, when it is being repeated, becomes the agent of the act of repetition.
This was stated by resorting to the alternative view that [the reduplication] occurs in place of the whole.

But how is the view that the reduplication occurs in place of the whole resorted to? And why should it not be resorted to? Because it is faulty. For if the reduplication were in place of the whole, then because of the rule *āliṭi cchvoḥ śūḍ* [Pāṇini 6.4.19], which is treated as *asiddha*, [the forms] *dāg* and *vāg* would not be established. If the reduplication were performed first before the substitution of *ḍha* and so on, then the substitutions of *ḍha* and so on would not be established here, because the element would no longer be at the end of a word (*apadāntatvāt*). This is not a fault; for he will state this: "That which is *asiddha* with respect to what precedes it does not apply when there is reduplication" (*pūrvatrāsiddhīyam advirvacane*).

Furthermore, reduplication is prescribed for a word that occurs in the sense of "perpetual" (*nitya*) or "repetition" (*vīpsā*); however, as long as the substitution of *ḍha* and so forth has not yet taken place, the application of the term "word" (*pada*) to such a form in the sense of "perpetual" and so on is not possible. Therefore, the sequence must be that the substitution of *ḍha* and so forth occurs first, and reduplication follows afterward. If this is so, then in cases such as *visaṃvisam* and *musalambhulam*, the substitution of *ṣa* [for *s*] would apply by rule 8.3.59? This too is not a fault, because the substitution of *ṣa* is prescribed for that *s* which is a substitute (*ādeśa*), whereas here the *s* is not a substitute itself, but rather a part (*avayava*) of that [substitute].

In that case, would not the substitution of *ṇ* (ṇatva) apply here in the word *nṛbhirnṛbhiḥ* [by Pāṇini 8.4.1]? This too is not a fault. When the *nakāra* which is the subject of the operation is always in the same word as the cause such as the letter *r*, then it would indeed be subject to the substitution of *ṇ*. This too is not a fault; for when the *nakāra* which is the subject of the operation is always in the same word as the cause such as the letter *r*, then it ought to become *ṇ*. Is this something that needs to be explicitly stated? No. How then is it obtained without being stated? By the force of the inclusion of the term "same" (*samāna*).

For if this were the case even where there is both the state of being in the same word (*samānapadasthatva*) and the state of not being in the same word (*asamānapadatva*), then the mention of "same" (*samāna*) would be purposeless. In the case of the word *nṛbhiḥ*, the state of being in the same word with respect to the letter *r* as the cause exists only when the doubling (*dvirvacana*) of the letter *n* has already taken place, and not when it has not yet taken place. Therefore, the position that doubling occurs in its place (*sthāne*) is indeed faultless, and it is proper to adopt it.

Regarding the phrase "two [are] two," he thinks as follows: "Only two specific [cases] are intended; however, since no specific distinction is mentioned here, any two whatsoever that possess the form of words would be included.

With the intention that the restriction must be established by means of the *paribhāṣā* (metarule) "iti paribhāṣayā vyavasthā bhavitavyā" (the restriction must be determined by this metarule), he says: "those which [possess the form] both in terms of the word (*śabda*)... and so forth.
In this regard, for some words, the closest similarity (*sādṛśya*) is based solely on the word-form, as in the case of words such as *akṣa* and others which denote the *bibhītaka* tree;
for some, it is based solely on the meaning and not the word-form, as in the case of words such as *taru* and *pādapa*;
and for some, it is based on both, as in the case of two finite verb forms (*tiṅanta*) of the root *paj*.
The mention of "both" (*ubhaya*) is for the purpose that the rule should apply where there is similarity on both counts;

this is understood from the inclusion of the superlative suffix *-tama* in the technical rule (*paribhāṣā*) *sthāne 'ntaratamaḥ* (P. 1.1.50). To demonstrate those two types of closest similarity, he says: "Of one," and so forth.

Now, why does the substitution of the word *dvis* itself not occur, given that the rule *atha* (Pāṇini 1.1.68) prescribes the inclusion of the actual form (*svarūpagrahaṇa*)? Because the word is indicated by means of reduplication (*dvirvacana*).
If there were inclusion of the actual form, there would be the undesirable consequence of substituting the word *dvis*.
Furthermore, since the author states [the rules] *tasya paramāmreḍitam* (8.1.2) and *anudāttañca* (8.1.3), it is understood from this that there is no substitution of the word *dvis*.

For if there were a substitution (*ādeśa*) of the word *dvis*, since [the designation of] "subsequent" (*para*) is based on distinction, and because the subsequent word *dvis* would not be distinct [from itself], the status of being "subsequent" could not even exist in the case of the substitution of *dvis*; how much less, then, could there be the designation of "repeated" (*āmreḍita*) or the property of being unaccented (*anudātta*)? Furthermore, if *dvis* were the substitute, then while [the rule] Pāṇini 6.1.98 is in force, the prohibition of the single-substitute form (*pararūpa*) for the vowel *a* which is a constituent part of the repeated element—stated in Pāṇini 6.1.99—would be untenable, because the vowel *a* is not a constituent part of the word *dvis*.
By this same reasoning, the interpretation that the word *sarva* refers to its own phonetic form (*svarūpagrahaṇa*) is also refuted.

For if there were a reference to the actual form (*svarūpa*) of the word *sarva*, then its very form would have to be doubled. Consequently, as before, the prohibition of the substitution of the subsequent form (*pararūpatva*) for the vowel *a* belonging to the reduplicated member (*āmreḍita*) would be untenable; furthermore, the inclusion of the term "always" (*nitya*) in [Pāṇini 8.1.4] would be purposeless, since doubling is prescribed there for that which occurs in the sense of "always" (*nitya*) and in the sense of "distribution" (*vīpsā*).

Furthermore, the word *sarva* does not apply to an eternal (*nitya*) object, for eternality resides in verbal suffixes (*tiṅ*), according to the rule: "Repetition (*vīpsā*) occurs in the case of indeclinables, primary suffixes (*kṛt*), secondary suffixes (*suc*), and nominal case endings (*sup*).
Therefore, in the expression *sarvasya*, the term "object" (*artha*) is understood.
Here, the word *sarva* refers to the whole (*sakala*) or that which possesses all parts (*kalāvati*); thus, there is reduplication of the entire word such as *pacati*. Enough with this digression.

Thus far, it has been stated—relying on the view that doubling occurs in place [of the original]—"both [elements] occur in place of the whole. Now, relying on the view that "doubling is the employment twice," he says "but when," and so forth.
The word *tu* ("but") indicates the distinction from the previous position; in that case, two forms of the word are prescribed according to the principle of closest proximity (*antaratamya*).
But here, that very same word is repeated twice; the meaning is that it is uttered twice. "There are two repetitions" means there are two acts of pronunciation.

Furthermore, how is the position that "doubling is the dual utterance" (*dviṣprayogo dvirvacanam*) to be adopted, and how is it not to be adopted? Because it is faulty. For if there were a dual utterance—in the case of *ām? pacasi pacasi devadatta*—the prohibition of the *nighāta* accent [by Pāṇini 8.1.55] would not apply; because the vocative is separated by two words, there is an absence of the condition of being "separated by one interval" (*ekāntaratā*).

Regarding the doubling [of a word] in its original position (*sthāne dvirvacane*), this substitution (*ādeśa*) applies to a single word (*ekapada*). Thus, although there is a distinction inherent in the substitution itself, because of the status of being "as if the original" (*sthānivadbhāva*), there is the designation of oneness (*ekatvavyapadeśa*). Consequently, since it becomes "one or the other," the prohibition of the *nighāta* accent is established. This is not a fault; for here, the distinction is merely figurative (*upacarita*) due to a difference in properties (*dharmabheda*), whereas the intrinsic nature (*svagata*) is indeed non-different. Otherwise, composition (*vṛtti*) would not even be possible. For it is precisely one and the same entity that undergoes repetition and so forth. Therefore, because the entity is [in fact] distinct, the state of having an interval of one syllable (*ekāntaratā*) is established here all the more clearly.

In that case, how is the suffix applied here in the word *paunaḥpunyam*? Here, the suffix *ṣyañ* [prescribed by Pāṇini 5.1.124] in the sense of an action (*karman*) after words denoting qualities (*guṇavacana*) and the class beginning with *brāhmaṇa* does not apply. Furthermore, the suffix *ṭhañ* [prescribed by Pāṇini 4.3.11] in the sense of "repetition" (*paunaḥpunika*) does not apply either, because it is not a nominal stem (*aprātipadikatvāt*).

Its status as not being a nominal stem follows from the fact that for meaningful aggregates, only a compound (*samāsa*) is considered a nominal stem, since the mention of "compound" in the rule serves as a restrictive definition (*niyamārthatvāt*).

In the case of reduplication (*dvirvacana*), although the designation *prātipadika*—which depends on its own base—is absent because the word ends in a case-suffix (*subanta*), nevertheless, by virtue of the principle of "behaving like the original" (*sthānivadbhāva*), it becomes a *prātipadika*, since the term *prātipadika* is included in the rule for reduplication.

And although its locus (sthānin) is a word ending in a *sup* suffix by virtue of the characteristic of being a suffix (*pratyayalakṣaṇa*), nevertheless, the prohibition of the designation "nominal stem" (*prātipadika*) by [Pāṇini 1.2.45] *apratyayaḥ* does not apply; for the fact that the prohibition of the designation "nominal stem" by [Pāṇini 1.2.45] *apratyayaḥ* does not apply when there is the characteristic of a suffix has been indicated by [Pāṇini 8.2.8] *naṅi saṃbuddhau*. Even though there is a doubling (*dvirvacana*) due to double application (*dvi-prayoga*), there is no fault;
for in this context, the mention of "compound" (*samāsa*) serves to exclude the designation "nominal stem" only from those of the same kind.
And what is that which is of a similar nature? It is that for which the meaning of a collection arises by way of differentiation and integration.
And for what does such a meaning arise? For the sentence (*vākya*). Furthermore, this meaning—beginning with "eternal" and so forth—is certainly not observed in the state of individual words.
Since that which is seen at the time of reduplication is neither split by another word nor joined with it, how could there be an exclusion of such a form by the mention of a compound (*samāsa*)?

Alternatively, the activity of the Teacher (*ācārya*) indicates that suffixes (*taddhita*) are indeed produced from such types of words, as he includes the word *kautaskuta* among the items beginning with *kasya* [Pāṇini 4.2.95]. Although the suffix *tyap* would have been expected by [Pāṇini 4.2.104], the suffix *aṇ* occurs precisely because of this specific grammatical exception (*nipātana*).

Does the word *sarvasya* here serve to exclude [the application of] *1.1.52*, or does it serve to establish the sense of the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhy-artha*)? In that regard, it cannot possibly be for the purpose of excluding *talo* (the suffix *tal*).
For instance, there ought to be two forms of words that are most similar both phonetically and semantically;
and since those of such a nature necessarily consist of multiple *al*s (phonemes), this would occur even without the inclusion of the word *sarva* [in 1.1.55].
It would apply to every future [word], not just to the last one.
Furthermore, the inclusion of the word *sarva* (all) is not justified even for the sake of conveying the sense of the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhyartha*).

For instance, in cases where the genitive is explicitly uttered, such as in the rule *tasyāpatyam* (Pāṇini 4.1.92), the sense of the genitive will be understood from the very utterance of the genitive itself.

In the rule *nityavīpsayoḥ* [Pāṇini 8.1.4], although the genitive case is not explicitly uttered, nevertheless, even without the mention of the word *sarvasya*, the meaning of the genitive can be understood. How so? The term *dve* is an indication of a substitute (*ādeśa*), and a substitute requires a related original (*sthānin*). Furthermore, these are indications of meaning; and in an indication of meaning, a relationship between an original and a substitute is not logically possible. Therefore, the meaning of the sentence is understood as follows according to the view that the doubling is a substitute: "Of that word which occurs in the sense of 'constant' or 'repetition,' there are two."
Even when it is held that "doubling is the double application [of a word]," the genitive sense is indeed understood even without the statement "of all" (*sarvasya*).
For repetition is an action (*kriyā*), and an action must necessarily have a means (*sādhana*) as its correlate, since the very acquisition of its own existence (*ātmalābha*) depends upon that means.

Therefore, the understanding of the genitive sense is perfectly clear through the realization that "there are two [applications] of that which is the means of that action. With this intention, he asks: "What is the purpose of 'of all'? (*sarvasyeti kim*)?

Regarding the phrase "for the sake of clarity": the intention is that for one who is unable to understand the universal application (*sarvādeśa*) or the genitive sense (*ṣaṣṭhyartha*), the word *sarvasya* is stated for the sake of easy comprehension.
The passage beginning with "Now" (*atha*) and so forth follows.

He thinks as follows: "By stating 'of a word' (*padasya*), the application of the dual number is excluded for compounds (*samāsa*), secondary derivatives (*taddhita*), and sentences (*vākya*); furthermore, it need not be stated again later that 'of a word' applies [at 8.1.16].
For this very statement 'of a word' will be carried over (*anuvartayiṣyate*) there."

If the term "of a word" (*padasya*) were not stated here, reduplication would apply even to compounds—for instance, in the case of *saptaparṇa* (meaning "having seven leaves on each joint"), as in *parvaṇi-parvaṇi sapta-sapta parṇāny asya santi*. It would also apply to secondary derivatives (*taddhita*), such as *dvipadikāṃ dadāti* ("he gives two paces"), where the suffix *-van* is applied according to the rule *pāda-śatasya saṃkhyāder-van* [Pāṇini 5.4.1]. Furthermore, it would apply to entire sentences, such as *grāme-grāme pānīyam* ("there is water in every village"). Consequently, the rule *padasya* [Pāṇini 8.1.16] need not be stated later.
To this, he replies: "It cannot be so."
Regarding this, he states the reason: "For here," and so forth.
"'He cooks thoroughly' (*prapacati*)"—this is a sentence, because it consists of a collection of words.
In this context, if the term "of a word" (*padasya*) were stated [as a governing rule], the doubling (*dvirvacana*) of this [word *saptaparna*] would not occur.

Therefore, it is impossible to say "of a word. However, in cases such as *saptaparnaḥ* ("seven-leaved") and *dvipadikāṃ dadāti* ("he gives two paces"), if "of a word" were stated, the doubling would not take place; for [in those cases] the meaning is already expressed by means of a compound (*samāsa*) or a secondary derivative (*taddhita*).

The intention is that [the rule] will not apply even in cases such as *grāme grāme pānīyam* ("water in every village"), because the distributive repetition (*vīpsā*) is already indicated by the reduplication of the individual member itself. Regarding the passage beginning with "here" (*iha*): from the root *druh* (Dhātupāṭha 1197) meaning "to injure," the suffix *tṛc* is added. When the form *dru-h-tṛ* is established, both the substitution of *gh* for *h* and the substitution of *ḍh* for *h* would apply, as would the reduplication. In that situation, since the substitutions of *y* and *ḍh* are considered *asiddha* (non-existent) when the reduplication [prescribed by P. 6.1.1] is to be performed, the reduplication would first apply while those two substitutions have not yet taken place.
If that [rule] were applied later—or even if there were the optionality provided by *vā druhamuhaṣṇuṣṇihām* (Pāṇini 8.2.33)—an undesirable result would also follow.
This restriction must necessarily be obtained so that it is not merely the desired outcome;

for when the substitution of *gh* occurs for one [letter], then the second must also undergo the substitution of *gh*, and when the substitution of *ḍh* occurs for one, then the second must also undergo the substitution of *ḍh*—only then would it be the desired result.
However, this restriction cannot be established, because there is no cause for such a restriction.
Therefore, at times even an undesirable result might occur.
In that regard, when one of the preceding or following [sounds] becomes *gh* and the other becomes *ḍh*, then an undesirable result would also follow.

If both [the preceding and the following] were to possess the quality of *ghatva* or *ḍhatva*, would that not be desired? Therefore, for the purpose of excluding what is undesired, it must be stated: "That which is *pūrvatrāsiddhīya* is not [operative] with respect to reduplication" (*pūrvatrāsiddhīyam advirvacane*).
Within this governing rule (*adhikāra*) [beginning with Aṣṭādhyāyī 8.2.1], the operation such as the elision of *n* (*nalopa*) is *pūrvatrāsiddhīya*.

By virtue of its belonging to the *gahādi* group, the suffix *cha* is applied [according to Pāṇini 4.2.137]. Consequently, it is non-existent (*asiddha*) in relation to everything other than reduplication, but not with respect to reduplication itself.

Alternatively—the meaning is that this should be explained as having the following sense: in the preceding section, namely the seven chapters and a quarter, that which is "not established" (asiddha) is what is called *pūrvatrāsiddham*; the very same operations such as the elision of *n* (*nalopa*) are included therein. That which pertains to this is *pūrvatrāsiddhīyam*. Furthermore, that non-establishment (*asiddhatva*) of the elision of *n* and so forth occurs when something other than reduplication (*dvirvacana*) is to be performed, but not specifically in the case of reduplication itself. This is how it should be interpreted.

In this regard, the following is the explanation: In rule [8.2.3], the word *na* should be separated from *yaṅoḥ* (by means of *yogavibhāga*). By that, when reduplication (*dvirvacana*) is to be applied, the status of being "not established" (*asiddhatva*) will not occur.

And since the status of being "not established" does not apply, when the suffix *tṛc* is added to the root *druh*, first there is optionally the substitution of *gh* by [8.2.32]; then, by [8.2.40] (*jhaṣastathordho'dhaḥ*), there is the substitution of *dh*; then, by [8.4.53], there is the substitution of *jaś*—the letter *g* for the letter *dh*; then follows reduplication, resulting in *drogdhādrogyoti*.
However, when the substitution of *gh* does not take place, then by [8.2.31] (*ho ḍhaḥ*), there is the substitution of *ḍh*, and as before, the substitution of *dh*.
And by [the rule] *ṣṭutvañ ca* (Pāṇini 8.4.41), there is the elision of the preceding *ḍhakāra*, followed by reduplication—resulting in *droḍhādroḍha*; thus, the desired form is indeed established.

If, then, it must be stated that "the rule regarding what is not established in the preceding [is applied] except in the case of reduplication" (*pūrvatrāsiddhīyamadvirvacane*), then would this not contradict what will be said under [Pāṇini 8.2.1] regarding *aujaḍhavat*—namely, "because the substitution of *ḍha*, the *ṣṭu*-operation, the elision of *ṣa*, and so forth, are not established, the elision of *ya* after the causative suffix (*ṇi*) occurs, and due to its status as a *sthānivadbhāva*, the *ha* is reduplicated twice"? There is no contradiction; for the rule "the rule regarding what is not established in the preceding [is applied] except in the case of reduplication" does not have universal application.
How is this known? From the introduction of the sūtra [Pāṇini 8.4.21].

For if the rule *pūrvatrāsiddhīyam advirvacane* (Jainendra-vyākaraṇa 70) were to apply to all cases, then, since the doubling [of the root] must occur after the application of the substitution of *ṇ* for *n* by the rule *aniteḥ* (Pāṇini 8.4.19), the forms such as *prāṇiṇiṣati* would already be established; what then would be the purpose of formulating the subsequent rule *kim* (Pāṇini 8.4.21)? Yet, that rule has indeed been formulated. Therefore, it is understood that the rule *pūrvatrāsiddhīyam advirvacane* does not have universal application.

As for the one who thinks that this statement was made with reference to the doubling [of the root] occurring in the eighth [chapter], that is incorrect. For regarding the rule *su-vi-ni-dur-bhyaḥ supi-sūti-samāḥ* (Pāṇini 8.3.88), he will state—in order to establish the form *viṣuṣupuḥ*—"that which has become *ṣup* is doubled. This would contradict [the opponent's view]; for if the status of being unestablished (*asiddhatva*) did not apply to the substitution of *ṣ* when the doubling prescribed in the sixth chapter is to be performed, then the doubling of that which has become *ṣup* would be obtained, and not otherwise.
Therefore, the previous resolution alone is correct.
"Or rather, this [is the meaning] of *sarvasya* alone"—so say the *Kāśikā* and the *Padamañjarī*.
The word *vā* (or) has the sense of an alternative with respect to the previously mentioned purpose.
Alternatively, it is not so; the inclusion of the term *sarva* is for the sake of clarity.
What then? It is performed for the sake of understanding that which has completed all its operations.

The inclusion of the word "all" (*sarva*) should be understood as being for the purpose that there may be an understanding—that is, a realization—of that which has performed every operation, such as reduplication (*dvitva*) and so forth. How is this so? This word *sarva* ends in the suffix *-a*, which expresses possession; thus, *sarvaḥ* means "one who possesses all operations. By the rule [Pāṇini 5.2.127], the suffix *ac* is applied because it belongs to the *arśādi* group. Therefore, what is stated is that reduplication occurs for that which has performed all its operations. The term *tasya* ("of that") is a genitive of specification (*avayava-ṣaṣṭhī*).

Regarding that which is uttered twice: the designation *ābhreḍita* is prescribed for that form of the word which constitutes its ultimate constituent part (*paramāvayavabhūta*). Now, under the view that reduplication consists in the double employment [of the same word], how can there be the designation "the latter" (*para*)? And why should it not be so? Because that [designation] is based on distinction (*bhedanibandhana*).
Indeed, the designation "the latter" is based on distinction.

And in the view that there is a double application (*dvirvacana*), there is no difference in the word itself; for in that case, only the repetition (*āvṛtti*) differs, not the word. This is not a fault; even though the word is not different, there will be a figurative distinction based on the difference in its properties (*dharma*).
For indeed, there is a conventional usage of distinction regarding an object that is not different, due to a difference in its properties.
Thus, speakers say: "Were you not clever last year? But this year you have become even more clever; you have truly become someone else."

In the expression *caura caura*, there is elision of the suffix *su* by [Pāṇini 6.1.69]; there is reduplication due to the sense of reproach by [Pāṇini 8.1.8] et seq.; and there is the protracted (*pluta*) vowel by [Pāṇini 8.2.95]: "The repeated word (*āmreḍita*) is protracted when expressing reproach. The same applies to *dasyo dasyo*.
By [Pāṇini 7.3.106], there is *guṇa* substitution.

Now, what is the purpose of including the word *tasya* (of that), given that the word *dve* (two) will continue to apply, and one might understand it thus: "that which follows the two"? This cannot be so; for then, by [Pāṇini 6.1.1], even in that case, the subsequent [word] would receive the technical designation *āmreḍita*.
When *tasya* is included, it is understood that "the subsequent [word] to that which undergoes this doubling about to be described" is meant.
Therefore, there is no over-extension [of the term].
The use of the long technical designation "āmreḍita" is for the purpose of understanding it as a descriptive (anvartha) name:
that which is spoken with emphasis (*ādhikyena*) is called *āmreḍita*.

Therefore, here too it occurs: "Aho darśanīyā, aho darśanīyā; mahad rocate, mahad rocate. The doubling [of the word] should be understood here as intended to illuminate the excellence of its beauty and its brilliance. This very formation of a long technical name (*mahatī saṃjñā*) serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*) that doubling occurs when expressing excellence. When the natural accent (*prakṛtisvara*) would otherwise apply, the fact that the subsequent syllable is stated to be unaccented (*anudātta*) indicates this.

Furthermore, because the word *anudātta* here stands in grammatical apposition with the word *para*, it does not denote the technical (śāstrīya) *anudātta* accent; rather, it is understood according to its etymological meaning (*anvartha*) as "that which has no *udātta* [in it]. For if the technical *anudātta* were intended, the genitive case would have had to be uttered for the sake of establishing the relationship, as in "of the subsequent" (*parasya*).
And if that were the case, [the rule] would become: *syāt* [1.1.52].

Moreover, even if the term "of all" (*sarvasya*) were to carry over [from the previous rule], even so, by virtue of the authority of the explicit statement, it would follow that the substitution of all [sounds] occurs at one and the same time.
Therefore, it is proper to accept only that which is etymologically meaningful (*anvartha*). As in the example: *bhuṅktebhuṅkte*.

By [Pāṇini 1.3.66], the *ātmanepada* suffix is applied. When that has been applied, because it is a "subsequently taught" (*śiṣṭa*) accent, it subverts the accent of the verbal root (*dhātusvara*), and thus the accent of the suffix (*pratyayasvara*) prevails. Although the accent of the *śnam* augment is subsequently taught once it has been applied, nevertheless—according to the principle that "the accent of a *vikaraṇa* does not subvert the accent of a *sārvadhātuka*"—the accent would have belonged to the word *te* itself. Then, by [Pāṇini 6.1.186], the *sārvadhātuka* suffix becomes *anudātta* (unaccented). Once the elision (*lopa*) of both *śna* and *as* has occurred, by [Pāṇini 6.1.161], the word *te* becomes *udātta* (accented) again. Since reduplication applies to a permanent (*nitya*) element, when that is performed, the subsequent syllable becomes *anudātta* by this [rule].
Regarding the form *paśūnpaśūn*:

following the rule *kubhraśca* (Dhātupāṭha 1.107), with *ku-* being carried over, the suffix *ku* is applied by the rule *arjidṛśikasamyamipaśibādhamṛjipaśitugdhugdīrghahakārāśca* (Dhātupāṭha 1.112). Here, *dṛśi* is replaced by *paśi*. The word *paśu*, due to the accent of the suffix, is udātta on its final syllable; this undergoes a single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) with the vowel *a* of the case-ending. Then, there is reduplication for the sake of distributive repetition (*vīpsā*), and by this [rule], the subsequent syllable becomes anudātta. This is stated in the phrase: "In the sense of 'constant' (*nitya*) and in distributive repetition (*vīpsā*)."

By this [statement], he shows that the locative case in "nityadīpsayoḥ" is for the purpose of indicating the meaning [of the suffix], and not that it is a genitive. For if this were a genitive, then a rule regarding the actual form of the word (svarūpavidhi) would result; consequently, the grammatical indications such as "nityaṃ kroḍājīvikayoḥ" [Pāṇini 2.2.17] and "pādaśatasya saṃkhyādervīpsāyām" [Pāṇini 5.4.1] would be untenable.

In this context, this word *nitya* is seen used in common worldly usage even with reference to those things—such as the self (*ātman*) and space (*ākāśa*)—which are held to exist at all times and whose production and destruction are not perceived by agents; for example: "the self is eternal," "space is eternal," and "the sky is eternal.
It is also used in the sense of frequency (*ābhīkṣṇya*), as in: "he laughs constantly" and "he speaks constantly."

In this regard, if "eternality" (*nityatā*) were present here in a general sense as the denotable meaning (*abhidheyabhāvena*), then there would be the inclusion of that which expresses the meaning of "eternal," and consequently, even words such as *ātman* and *ākāśa* would incur the undesirable consequence of being subject to reduplication. With this intention, he asks: "In what [words] is there eternality? The other, having understood the intention, replies: "In verbal suffixes (*tiṅ*), in indeclinables (*avyaya*), and in primary derivatives (*kṛt*). This is a *karmadhāraya* compound: those which are both indeclinables and primary derivatives.

Although in words such as *ātman* and *ākāśa*, the term "eternality" (*nityatā*)—characterized by existing at all times—occurs as the expressed meaning, nevertheless, in this context, it is precisely that eternality characterized by repetition (*abhīkṣṇya*) which is relied upon in the case of verbal suffixes (*tiṅ*) and indeclinable kṛt-suffixes where the state [of the action] is predominant.
Thus, the intention is that there is no over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).
Now, one might object: this word "eternal" (*nitya*) is a general term.

Furthermore, general terms are not capable of being restricted to a specific meaning without context and the like. And here, there is no such context or the like by which a restriction to a specific meaning might occur; so, from what source could the adoption of the specific sense of "permanence" (nityatā) be obtained? Thinking thus, he asks: "Whence is this? The ellipsis to be supplied is: "The sense intended here is that 'permanence' (nityatā) means frequency (ābhīkṣṇya)."

Because the word *nitya* is understood here as signifying "repetition" (*ābhīkṣṇya*)—since it is taken from its etymological sense of pervasion—the "permanence" (*nityatā*) intended here is that characterized by repetition; for it is said that there is reduplication of a *pada*.

And that *pada* is either ending in a nominal suffix (*subanta*) or ending in a verbal suffix (*tiṅanta*). Among these, he will state later that [reduplication applies] to those ending in *sup*, such as *dīpsa*. Now, if this word *nitya* were taken to mean "unchanging" (*kūṭastha*), then, since the term "unchanging" would apply to nouns (*subanta*) by way of being their denoted meaning, reduplication would occur only for nouns ending in *sup*, and not for those ending in *tiṅ*, nor for indeclinables formed with primary suffixes (*kṛt*).
However, when the word *nitya* is understood as denoting frequency (*ābhīkṣṇya*), the reduplication characterized by "constancy" applies to both verbal roots and undeclinables;
whereas for others, it is characterized by "repetition" (*vīpsā*). Thus, the entire range of words is accommodated.
Therefore, because of this pervasiveness, since the word *nitya* is taken here as denoting frequency, the statement "frequency is constancy" (*ābhīkṣṇyaṃ nityatā*) is justified.

"In this context, 'constancy' (*ābhīkṣṇya*) means 'perpetuity' (*nityatā*). And that [constancy] applies to verbal suffixes (*tiṅ*) and to primary suffixes added to indeclinables (*avyaya*). Why is this so? To this he says: "And constancy," and so forth.

For "repetition" (*ābhīkṣṇya*) means occurring again and again, and since that is possible only for an action (*kriyā*) which is of the nature of something to be accomplished (*sādhya*), it is a property of that [action] alone, and not of a substance (*dravya*); because a substance, being of an already established nature (*siddha-rūpa*), is denoted by a nominal suffix (*subanta*).
And since that action is expressed only by verbal endings (*tiṅanta*) and the like, permanence resides in those [verbal forms] alone.
What, then, is that action? It is that which, by virtue of its connection with constancy characterized by repetition, is expressed by the word "eternal. Thus he says: "that which," and so forth.
"Without ceasing" means "not making a pause."
"‘That is eternal’ means that the entity whose nature is action is eternal.
‘Primarily’ [means...]"
That with reference to which an action is undertaken is the primary [purpose]; its state is "being such.

Although one who desires to go to a village repeatedly performs the act of approaching the foot of a tree, nevertheless, that [approaching] is not the primary [purpose]. This is what is meant: he does not perform it as the primary [object], because the action is not undertaken with reference to that.
In the expression "going to the village, he approaches the roots of the trees," although there is repetition (*ābhīkṣṇya*), the reduplication does not occur.

For by the phrase "whatever action" (*yāṃ kriyām*), the action is shown as the substratum (*dharmin*); and by the phrase "performing without ceasing" (*anuparaman karoti*), its quality of repetition (*ābhīkṣṇya*) is shown.
"pacatipacati" is an example of a form ending in a verbal suffix (*tiṅanta*).
"bhuktvābhuktvā" and "bhojaṃbhojam" are [examples of forms ending in absolutives].

In this context, the suffixes *ktvā* and *ṇamul* are applied by the rule *ābhīkṣṇye ṇamul ca* [Pāṇini 3.4.22]. In the form *lunīhi lunīhi*, the imperative (*loṭ*) is used according to the rule *kriyāsamabhihāre* [Pāṇini 3.4.2], which prescribes the substitution of *hi* for that [imperative]; it is stated therein that *hi* and *sva* possess the properties of the imperative. Consequently, the verbal suffix (*vikaraṇa*) is added, and the substitution of *ī* occurs by the rule *ī halyaghoḥ* [Pāṇini 6.4.113].

These three are examples of indeclinables (*avyaya*). The designation *kṛt* is applied to these, including those ending in *-ktvā*, by the rule Pāṇini 3.1.93. However, the designation *avyaya* is applied to the suffix *-ktvā* by the rule Pāṇini 1.1.40.
Regarding *ṇamul*, it is governed by [Pāṇini 3.4.22] *namul tu*.
Regarding *loṭ*, however, it is because its repetition (*ābhīkṣṇya*) is recited among the items beginning with *svar* [in the list of indeclinables].

Now, one might object: these suffixes—*ktvā*, *ṇamul*, and *loṭ*—are prescribed specifically for repetition (*ābhīkṣṇya*). In that case, just as in the example *pāpacyate*, where reduplication does not occur because the repetition is already manifested by the *yaṅ* suffix prescribed for the intensification of action (*kriyā-samabhihāra*), so too, since the repetition is manifested by *ktvā* and the others, reduplication should not occur here either.
Now, even though that [repetition] has been explained, would it not also apply here in the case of *pāpacyate*? To this he says: "In the case of *ktvā* and *ṇamul*," and so forth.

For the powers (*śakti*) of entities are indeed diverse. To illustrate: a certain person performs a specific action, such as carrying a load, while depending on assistance, whereas another performs that very same action independently of assistance. Therefore, although the suffixes *ktvā*, *ṇamul*, and *loṭ* are prescribed to express repetition (*abhīkṣṇya*), nevertheless, repetition is not manifested by them alone.
Only those [suffixes] that require reduplication have the capacity to manifest repetition (*paunaḥpunya*), not those alone [without such a requirement].

Therefore, reduplication indeed occurs for that which ends in them; however, since the suffix *yaṅ* possesses the power to manifest repetition even when independent of reduplication, because repetition is already expressed by that very [suffix], [reduplication] does not occur in forms such as *pāpaṇyate*.

For reduplication is prescribed to indicate frequency (*ābhīkṣṇya*); and since this [frequency] is already indicated by the *yaṅ* suffix itself, what is the purpose of reduplication? Now, one might object: "Is it not the case that reduplication is indeed desired even for a *yaṅ*-stem in certain instances? And would that not fail to be established if the *yaṅ* were capable of indicating repetition (*paunaḥpunya*) independently of reduplication? To this he says: "But when," and so forth. Repetition of action (*kriyāsamabhihāra*) is of two kinds: frequency and intensity (*bhṛśārtha*). Among these, when reduplication occurs after a *yaṅ*-stem, then the *yaṅ* suffix is used in the sense of intensity.

The intention is this: the reduplication applies only to that sense of intensity (*bhṛśārtha*) which pertains to frequency (*paunaḥpunya*), for that [frequency] is not manifested by the *yaṅ* suffix; since the latter is known to express intensity.
Thus it is said: "In the case of the intensification of action (*kriyāsamabhihāra*), frequency is to be understood."

In this regard, although the term *kriyāsamabhihāra* (intensive repetition of action) is general, nevertheless, by virtue of the contextual requirement (*sāmarthya*), its application is understood to refer specifically to that which does not mean "intense" (*abhṛśa*). For it is not possible for one repetition to exist within another repetition. Now, how is it that the suffix *yaṅ* occurs in the sense of repetition (*paunaḥpunya*)? And why should it not occur? Because it is superseded by the reduplication (*dvirvacana*) prescribed for non-initial words. If it is asked, "What then is the scope (*avakāśa*) for *yaṅ*?"—is it not simply in the sense of intensity (*bhṛśārtha*)? This is not a fault; for reduplication is prescribed for the word (*pada*), whereas *yaṅ* is prescribed for the verbal root (*dhātu*).

Likewise, because there is a great difference between the two types of objects (*kāryin*), from what [source] does the sublation arise? It has been stated: "In the sense of permanence (*nitya*) and repetition (*vīpsā*). Among those, permanence has been explained as applying to verbal suffixes (*tiṅ*) and indeclinable *kṛt*-suffixes.

However, repetition (*vīpsā*) is not understood—[namely], in what way does it function as the expressed meaning (*abhidheya*)? Therefore, for the sake of understanding that, he asks: "Now, in which [elements] does repetition occur? The other, having understood his intention, says: "Repetition occurs in the case of nominal suffixes (*sup*)."
This is because the capacity for that very repetition is present in the expression itself.

If *vīpsā* (repetition) were intended as a general pervasion, then the word *cikīrṣā* would also have to undergo reduplication, since its function there consists in the desire to pervade the mat and so forth by means of the action of "making. Anticipating this, he asks: "What, then, is *vīpsā*?
He replies: "It has as its object a specific kind of pervasion," and so on.

The term *vīpsā* refers to that desire whose object is the simultaneous pervasion (*vyāpti*) or non-pervasion (*avyāpti*) of various substrates (*adhikaraṇa*) bearing diverse names, through their connection with an action or other factors. Such a desire is called "the speaker's *vīpsā*.
By the word "speaker" (*prayoktuḥ*), he demonstrates that *vīpsā* is a property of the speaker, not a property of the denoted object.

But how is this distinction—that [the desire] has as its object a specific pervasion—obtained? It is obtained from the use of the word *vi* (in *vīpsā*). For if the intended meaning of *vīpsā* were simply the desire to pervade without qualification, he would have said merely "of the two eternal and desired" (*nityepsayoḥ*). Since it has been stated that "the speaker's desire regarding a specific pervasion is *vīpsā*," yet that specific nature is not understood because its form has not been specified, and because that [specificity] being unknown, the *vīpsā* qualified by it is also not known, he asks: "What, then, is that?"
Regarding the phrase "of those expressing diversity" (*nānāvācinām*) and so forth:
"of those expressing diversity" and "of substrata" (*adhikaraṇānām*) are two genitive cases in grammatical apposition (*vyadhikaraṇa*).
"Diversity" (*nānā*) means being distinct (*pṛthagbhūta*); those words whose nature it is to express such [distinct things] are "those expressing diversity."

The meaning is: "of the substrata (adhikaraṇa) related to those [actions], which are the expressed meanings. In the phrase "by means of action or quality" (kriyāguṇābhyām), the suffix *tīyā* is used in the sense of the instrumental case (*karaṇe*).
"Simultaneously" means at one and the same time. "Of the agent" means...
Of the speaker; that is, of one who employs a reduplication.
"In order to pervade."
"To obtain through a specific relation" means to connect completely. "Desire" [is the word used].
*Abhilāṣaḥ* means desire. Regarding *vīpsā*:
it is a *prādi*-compound; *vīpsā* is a specific kind of desire (*viśiṣṭā īpsā*).
With the words "of those expressing various distinct meanings" (*nānābhūtārthavācinām*), he explains the statement just mentioned.
Since such repetition (*vīpsā*) occurs [only when multiple referents are involved], there is no doubling [of the suffix] in the case of *cikīrṣā*;
for *cikīrṣā* is the desire of the agent (*kartṛ*), not that of the prompter (*prayoktṛ*).
And because such repetition (*vīpsā*) is present, there is no doubling even for words denoting a genus (*jāti*), as in *niṣpanno yavaḥ* ("the barley is ripe").
For words denoting a genus do not express multiple distinct objects.
Even when there is a desire to pervade [the objects] sequentially, doubling does not occur, as in: "this village is beautiful, and this village is beautiful."

This [fault] does not occur even in the case of *dvandva* compounds or *ekaśeṣa* formations—for instance, "In this forest, the *dhava*, *khadira*, and *palāśa* trees are beautiful," or "In this forest, the trees are beautiful. Even when the intention to pervade all specific particulars (*viśeṣa*) is not desired, such usage is nevertheless employed; thus, there is no denotation of all specific particulars (or, according to the Kāśikā reading, no non-denotation of all specific particulars). Consequently, the speaker’s desire to pervade all specific particulars does not arise.
However, generally relying on their excellence, the speaker employs the sentence thus: "Every village is beautiful.

For here, there is the speaker's desire (*lipsā*) to simultaneously pervade all villages—which are distinct from one another due to differences in direction, location, and so forth—by means of the quality of beauty. [Similarly:
"Every country, every country... and so on.
In this case as well, it is for the sake of the people:
"A man approaches a man seated in *nidhana*.
Here, it is by means of the act of *nidhana* performed upon the men.
*Nidhana* means destruction; this is the sense.
The mention of "action" (*kriyā*) and "quality" (*guṇa*) is for the purpose of illustration.
Even in the case of substances, when there is a speaker's desire to simultaneously pervade multiple loci denoted by various words, that is indeed *vīpsā* (repetition/distribution).

By this, the double mention [of the word] in the expression *grāme grāme pānīyam* ("water at every village") is also established. As for the one who says, "A substance does not have a connection with another substance because it is already established in its own form," his statement—that "absolute connection (*atyantasaṃyoga*) is the complete connection of time and distance with actions, qualities, and substances"—is contradicted; furthermore, this usage by the learned, *grāme grāme pānīyam*, would not be possible.

Now, how is it that this word *grāma* functions in the sense of distributive repetition (*vīpsā*), given that distributive repetition is not its denoted meaning (*abhidheya*)? What then? It is a region of land crowded with people. This is true; nevertheless, because it is manifested through the medium of the realization of reduplication, it is said that it "functions" in that sense. For the village, by undergoing reduplication, manifests distributive repetition; thus, it functions in that sense by way of manifestation.

Now, regarding the expression "grāmo grāmaḥ" (village after village), why is there the singular number, given that because there are many villages, the plural number ought to be used? Or [is it used] when the doubling [of the word] has been performed? This is not so; for in this case, plurality arises only with respect to the aggregate (*samudāya*), not with respect to each individual part. Indeed, singularity is not contradicted by plurality in a constituent part that has already assumed the number one. Therefore, the plural does not occur from the perspective of the parts.
If you ask, "Then why does it not occur from the perspective of the aggregate?"—it is because plurality is already understood through the distributive repetition (*vīpsā*).

For that collection [of words] cannot exist through distributive repetition (*vīpsā*) without plurality; thus, while manifesting that [repetition], it implies plurality as a necessary concomitant (*āntarīyakatva*).
Consequently, since the meaning has already been understood, the plural suffix is not employed.
Now, regarding that which is a verbal form (*tiṅanta*) characterized by both necessity and intensity: once reduplication has been applied there, should the suffix of intensity be added?

Alternatively, [one might ask]: "Does the suffix [denoting] excellence (*prakarṣa*) apply after the reduplication has already taken place? To this he says: "That which ends in a verbal suffix" (*yattiṅantaṃ*), etc. Here, the reason is the conflict of rules (*vipratiṣedha*).

In that regard, the scope for reduplication is where the sense of "constancy" (*nitya*) is intended to be expressed, not excellence—such as *pacati-pacati* ("he cooks repeatedly"); the scope for the suffix of excellence is where there is a connection with excellence, not constancy—such as *pacatitarām* ("he cooks more excellently"); but where there is a connection with both, reduplication occurs by virtue of the conflict of rules—such as *pacati-pacatitarām* ("he cooks most excellently").

In that case, would not a suffix of excellence (*prakarṣapratyaya*) apply even to a nominal stem (*subanta*) that is joined with both distributive repetition (*vīpsā*) and excellence, precisely for that reason—that it has already undergone reduplication? Consequently, forms such as *āḍhataramāḍhataram ānaya* ("bring it more and more") would not be established. To this, he says: "But here," and so forth. If the connection of a nominal stem with both distributive repetition and excellence were simultaneous, then this undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) would indeed follow; however, it does not occur. For it is maintained that a nominal stem first joins with a suffix of excellence, and only subsequently with distributive repetition.

How so? For here, what is called *vīpsā* (repetition/distribution) is a human attribute, a particularity of intention. And it proceeds from a learned speaker in such a way that no undesirable consequence arises for the word, nor for the speaker. If *vīpsā* were to occur prior to the suffix expressing excellence (*prakarṣa-pratyaya*), or simultaneously with it, an undesirable consequence would arise for the word, and through that, for the speaker as well—just as [the error] occurs among men who say "helayo helaya" regarding water, and an undesirable consequence occurs in the case of sacrifices.

Therefore? It is established that when there is a desire to express excellence (*prakarṣa*), the repetition (*vīpsā*) must occur after [the word] has been used by the learned speaker; thus, forms such as *āḍhataram āḍhataram ānaya* ("bring it more and more") are established. Another view: "In this case too, for that very same reason, the suffix of excellence would occur only after the doubling has already taken place; consequently, *āḍhataram āḍhataram ānaya* would not be established. To this objection, the author says "But here," and so forth. Because of its association with excellence, the suffix of excellence is expressed by the word "excellence" (*prakarṣa*).
For, due to its association with repetition, the doubling is expressed by the word "repetition" (*vīpsā*).
This is what is meant: it is intended that the application of reduplication belongs to that which is joined with a suffix expressing excellence (*prakarṣa*).

And here the intention is this: the reason why reduplication occurs first for that which is simultaneously joined with excellence and with permanence—that conflict (*vipratiṣedha*) does not exist here, because the two rules are not of equal strength.
Their lack of equal strength, however, is due to the suffix expressing excellence being *antaraṅga* (internal) and the reduplication being *bahiraṅga* (external).
For instance, the suffixes expressing excellence (*ātiśāyika*) are applied to nominal stems (*prātipadika*) ending in *ṅī* or *āp*, whereas reduplication (*dvirvacana*) applies to a word (*pada*).

Since "that which is external (*bahiraṅga*) is as if unestablished (*asiddha*) with respect to that which is internal (*antaraṅga*)" (Vyāḍipāda 42), a conflict (*vipratiṣedha*) between what is established and what is unestablished is improper. Therefore, first the suffix of excellence must be applied to the form ending in a case-suffix (*subanta*), and subsequently, reduplication must be applied to that which ends in it.

But is it not the case that the *atiśāyika* suffixes are not *antaraṅga* (internal), since they arise from a base that possesses *sāmarthya* (semantic capacity), according to the governing rule [Pāṇini 4.1.82], and this *sāmarthya* exists only with a *subanta* (inflected nominal)? This is not so; for it has been stated in that very same context [under 4.1.82]: "This governing rule extends as far as *prāgdiśo vibhaktiḥ* [Pāṇini 5.3.1], which marks the limit of *svārthika* (self-referential) suffixes; it has no application among the *svārthika* suffixes. And the *atiśāyika* suffixes are indeed *svārthika*. Therefore, because it is *antaraṅga*, once that suffix has arisen, the reduplication of the *subanta* must subsequently take place, as in: *pari pari trigartebhyaḥ*.
When, by the rule *[[1.4.88]]*, *pari* receives the designation of *karmapravacanīya*, then by the rule *[[2.3.10]]*, the fifth case (*pañcamī*) [is employed]. In the example *pariṣiñcati*,
the meaning is "he sprinkles all around" (*sarvatra siñcati*).
The substitution of *ṣ* [for *s*] occurs by the rule "after a preverb (*upasarga*), before *sunoti*" (Pāṇini 8.3.65), and so forth.

Regarding the rule "optionally after *pari* when meaning 'exclusion' (*varjana*), provided there is no compound" (Pāṇini 8.1.5), the meaning is that this sūtra should be explained as having the sense: "when *pari* has the meaning of exclusion and there is no compound, reduplication (*dvirvacana*) optionally takes place."

In this regard, the explanation is as follows: from the rule *vibhāṣā veṣṭiceṣṭyoḥ* [Pāṇini 7.4.96], the term *vibhāṣā* (optionally) is carried over by "frog-leap" (*maṇḍūkapluti*) [i.e., skipping intervening rules]. Therefore, in the case of a non-compound (*asamāsa*), the doubling (*dvirvacana*) of *pari* when used in the sense of exclusion (*varjana*) is optional. Regarding the statement "in a non-compound": someone might have the misconception that because of this specific mention, there must necessarily be doubling in the case of a compound. To dispel that notion, he says: "But in a compound," and so forth.

Just as in the case of *dadhyodana* ("curd-rice"), where the word *upasikta* ("mixed with") is included within the compound, so too, when a compound is formed according to [Pāṇini 2.1.12], there is an exclusion [of that word]. However, the word *pari* is entirely meaningless within the compound; therefore, the doubling (*dvirvacana*) which is prescribed for a word functioning in the sense of exclusion does not occur in a compound. Even if the word *pari* were meaningful in the sense of exclusion, since the sense of exclusion would already be conveyed by the compound itself, there should still be no doubling.
In the case of *paritrigartam*,
the substitution of *am* for the *s* that arises from the compound is applied by the rule *nāvyayībhāvādato 'stvapañcamyāḥ* [Pāṇini 2.4.83]. In the case of *prasamupodaḥ*,

the compound-ending suffix (*samāsānta*) prescribed by the rule *dvandvāccudaṣahāntāt samāhāre* [Pāṇini 5.4.106] is not applied, because the rules governing compound-endings are not universally obligatory (*anitya*).
Regarding "for the purpose of filling the verse":
this is a locative case used according to Pāṇini 2.3.37, *yasya ca bhāvena bhāvalakṣaṇam*.
By the state of "filling the verse"—characterized by its occurrence—the possibility of reduplication is indicated.

But surely, [it might be argued], it is because of reduplication (*dvirvacana*). [We reply: That which precedes [the reduplication] is merely for the purpose of filling the metrical foot (*pādapūraṇa*) and is non-existent; how then could its existence be the defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) of reduplication? For that is not a real existence; this is a hollow argument. Here, "existence" (*bhāva*) refers to the process of arising (*utpatti*), and that occurs only for that which has not yet attained its perfected existence (*aniṣpannasattāka*), not for that which has already attained its perfected existence. Indeed, jars and the like do not arise while they are still in the state of clay. Furthermore, although no specific [type of verse] is mentioned here, by implication (*sāmarthya*), only a *ṛc* is understood, not a *śloka*.

For this is a worldly verse, and in common usage, since words are intended to convey meaning, the employment of a meaningless expression is not appropriate. Thinking that if the formation of a bahuvrīhi-like compound were prescribed for a single word without distinction, it would then apply even to the word *eka* (as in *ekam ekam*), the author—desiring to avoid such an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*)—states: "The word *eka*, when repeated, becomes a bahuvrīhi-like compound."

But how is it that the specific condition "only when it is reduplicated" (*dvirukta*) is obtained, given that this is not explicitly mentioned in the sūtra? The thought is as follows: the term *vīpsā* (repetition) continues [from the previous rule]. And since reduplication has already been prescribed for the case of *vīpsā*, and that [reduplication] is not sublated by this present rule through the application of the *bahuvrīhi*-like behavior (*bahuvrīhivad-bhāva*) to the word *eka*, otherwise the rule "of each one, according to the Easterners" (*ekaikasya prācām*, Pāṇini 8.1.86) would be untenable.
Therefore, because the mention of *vīpsā* continues, this *bahuvrīhi*-like behavior is understood to apply specifically to the word *eka* when it is reduplicated.
He asks, "What, then, is the purpose of the treatment as a *bahuvrīhi*? and replies with the words beginning "In the case of being like a *bahuvrīhi*.

Although the elision of the case-ending (*sup-luk*) and the masculine form (*puṃvadbhāva*) are not explicitly stated [in the rule] as occurring in a *bahuvrīhi*, nevertheless, since these two are observed there, their application is the purpose of this extended application (*atideśa*).
[The example is] "ekaikam" (each one).

When reduplication is performed for the sake of distributive repetition (*vīpsā*), just as the elision of the case-ending (*subluk*) occurs in a *bahuvrīhi* compound such as *citraguḥ* by the rule *supo dhātuprātipadikayoḥ* [Pāṇini 2.4.71], so too does it occur here by means of extended application (*atideśa*).

Because the word is a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) due to that very extended application within the compound, the case-ending *su* is applied; then, by the rule *ato'm* [Pāṇini 7.1.24], the substitution of *am* for *su* takes place.
Thus: "ekaikayā" (by each one).

As before, there is elision of the case-ending (*luk*). Just as in the example *darśanīyabhārya*—where, in a *bahuvrīhi* compound, the transformation into the masculine form (*puṃvadbhāva*) occurs by means of [Pāṇini 6.3.34] *striyāḥ puṃvat* and so forth—so too here, by extension (*atideśa*), the third-case singular ending undergoes the substitution of *et* [by Pāṇini 7.3.105], followed by the substitution of *ay*. Now, one might object: "Even if the transformation into the masculine form does not occur, would this not still be established even after the *vṛddhi* substitution [of *ai* for *e*] has been applied by [Pāṇini 6.1.88] *ety-edhaty-ūṭsu*? Although this would indeed be established, it would nevertheless not be established once the reduplication (*dvirvacana*) has been applied by [Pāṇini 8.1.10] *gatagata* and so forth.

Therefore, in the subsequent sūtra, the application of the masculine form (*puṃvadbhāva*) is stated as the very purpose of this extended application (*atideśa*), namely that [the compound] is "like a *bahuvrīhi*.
As for the expression *ekaikayā*, however, it was stated in order to indicate that the mention of the neuter gender in the word *ekam* is not intended to be restrictive;
indeed, the non-restrictive nature of the gender mention in the sūtra is made known by the inclusion of the term "neuter" (*napuṃsaka*) in the rule *ardhaṃ napuṃsakam* (Pāṇini 2.2.2).

If the mention in the Sūtra were intended as a *tantra* (a governing rule), then since the specific gender would already be established by that very mention in the word "half" (*ardha*), he would not have stated "neuter" (*napuṃsaka*).
Furthermore, why would the preservation of the original accent of the first member (*pūrvapadaprakṛtisvaratva*) not also be mentioned as a purpose? Because there is no distinction;
once the elision (*nighāta*) of the following member has been applied, the original accent of the first member will naturally remain.

If, then, that which is observed in a *bahuvrīhi* is extended [to other compounds], would it not follow that the prohibition of the designation *sarvanāman*, the accent, and the compound-final suffix (*samāsānta*) would also be extended? To this he says: “The designation *sarvanāman*,” and so forth.

But how can these—the prohibition of the designation *sarvanāman* and the others—be understood as applying to the *bahuvrīhi* prescribed under the governing rule for compounds (*samāsādhikāra*)? It is said: first, the prohibition of the designation *sarvanāman* can indeed be understood from the fact that, while the rule *bahuvrīhau* (Pāṇini 1.1.29) is still in effect, the term *bahuvrīhi* is mentioned again in the rule *bahuvrīhiḥ* (Pāṇini 1.1.28).

The purpose of this [rule] has been stated: so that the prohibition may apply only to that which is a *bahuvrīhi* compound itself, and not to that which becomes a *bahuvrīhi* by virtue of being treated as a *bahuvrīhi* (*bahuvrīhivadbhāva*). Thus, by implication, the prohibition is understood to apply only to a *bahuvrīhi* prescribed under the governing heading of compounds (*samāsādhikāra*).

For no other [type of word] besides a *bahuvrīhi* can be a *bahuvrīhi* in its own right; for instance, in cases such as *ekaikasmai*, although it possesses the status of a *bahuvrīhi* through *bahuvrīhivadbhāva*, it is not a *bahuvrīhi* per se.

By this rule [Pāṇini 6.2.172], while the term *bahuvrīhi* is being carried over from the previous rule [Pāṇini 6.2.162: *bahuvrīhāvidametattadbhyaḥ*], the final acute accent (*antodāttatva*) is prescribed for what follows *nañ* and *su* within a *bahuvrīhi*, but not for those two [suffixes] themselves. Why? Because *su* and *nañ* are here taken as causes (*nimitta*). And it is not logical for that which serves as a cause to also be the recipient of the grammatical operation (*kāryin*). As it was stated by the author of the Bhāṣya regarding the sūtra *hayavaraṭ* (Māheśvara Sūtra 5): "In this sūtra, *ra* and *ha* are not the recipients of the operation; rather, these two are the causes of reduplication (*dvirvacana*)."

Therefore, in which *bahuvrīhi* [compound], because only *su* and *nañ* follow [the first member], there is doubling according to [Pāṇini 8.1.10] and the treatment as a *bahuvrīhi* [according to 5.4.75].
Alternatively, since the term "compound" (*samāsa*) is understood from the rule for accentuation [Pāṇini 6.1.223], we shall qualify the *bahuvrīhi* by that: "that compound which is a *bahuvrīhi*."

But surely, *nana* and *susvit*, even though they are indeed compounds, have already received the designation "compound" (*samāsa*) through the application of the rule for treating them as if they were *bahuvrīhi*. Consequently, even when the term "compound" is specified [in the rule], would it not follow that the accent does not apply to the *bahuvrīhi*? This is not a fault. For by the specification of "compound," the *bahuvrīhi* is indeed distinguished; there is no *bahuvrīhi* that is not a compound. In this context, by the force of the qualification and by way of an extended application (*atideśa*), the accent does not occur for that which has received the designation "compound. And it is understood that this *bahuvrīhi* is prescribed within the governing heading (*adhikāra*) on compounds.

But surely, when the term *bahuvrīhi* is qualified by the mention of *samāsa*, it is determined merely that this refers to a specific *bahuvrīhi* by virtue of the power of the qualification; however, does not doubt still persist regarding that specific *bahuvrīhi*? It is said in reply: a specific understanding arises from the commentary (*vyākhyāna*), for there is no fault in the rule being inapplicable due to doubt, according to the principle that "one does not abandon a grammatical rule because of doubt" (Pāṇini 1.4.2). Furthermore, in the rule prescribing the compound-ending suffix (*samāsānta*), the word *samāsa* is understood to carry over from the previous rule, "And [the suffixes apply] after a compound referring to that [same thing]" (Pāṇini 5.4.68).

In this context, since the status of being a compound-final suffix (*samāsānta*) would already be established for the suffixes to be mentioned here simply by virtue of the governing rule on compounds (*samāsādhikāra*), the continued reference to the term "compound" (*samāsagrahaṇa*) is understood to serve the purpose of ensuring that the status of being a compound-final suffix applies specifically to that particular kind of compound which is qualified by the continued application of the governing rule.
Furthermore, that specific compound is to be understood, according to the explanation, as only that which is prescribed within the governing rule on compounds.

Now, one might ask: why does the elision of *n* not occur here by the rule *atha naneti* [Pāṇini 6.3.73], since that rule is also seen to apply in the case of a *bahuvrīhi* compound? This is not a fault. For in the rule *nalopo nañaḥ* [Pāṇini 6.3.73], the governing heading (*adhikāra*) from the preceding rule [6.3.72] continues to apply—that is, the elision of *n* is prescribed when there is a subsequent member (*uttarapada*). Furthermore, the negative particle *nañ* is presented here as the subject of the operation (*kāryin*); and since a subject of an operation cannot simultaneously function as its own cause (*nimitta*), the elision must occur when *nañ* is followed by a different subsequent member, as in *abrāhmaṇaḥ*, but not when it is itself that member. Therefore, how could there be any occasion for the elision of the *n* in this case? [The commentary continues: "Because there is no state of being afflicted (*ābādhanabhāvāt*)."

The suffix *ghañ* is used here in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāve*). If the property of being subject to obstruction (*abādha*) is taken as a characteristic of the expressed meaning (*abhidheya-dharma*), then reduplication would apply only to words such as *bādhitapīḍita*, and not to words such as *gata*. However, when the property is taken as a characteristic of the speaker (*prayoktṛ-dharma*), it occurs in all cases.

Therefore, rather than [relying on] the pervasion (*vyāpti*) and the pervaded (*vyāpya*), the property of the speaker (*prayoktṛdharma*) alone is resorted to; thus he says, "the property of the speaker. Regarding the phrase "of that which exists therein," its manifestation occurs by way of understanding the reduplication (*dvirvacana*) and by way of understanding the treatment as a *bahuvrīhi* compound; therefore, its occurrence (*vṛtti*) should be understood as being "therein," and not from the denotation of that [compound].
For words such as *gata* do not in any way express contradiction.
The particle *ca* indicates a split in the sentence;
thus, two things are prescribed here: by one sentence, reduplication (*dvirvacana*), and by the other, the treatment as a *bahuvrīhi* compound (*bahuvrīhivadbhāva*).
In examples such as *gatagataḥ*, the elision (*luk*) of the case-ending *s* occurs as before;
however, in examples such as *gatagatā*, the masculine form (*puṃvadbhāvaḥ*) likewise applies as before.
[This refers to the phrase] "by the departure and so forth of the beloved," and so on.
By this, he shows that there is no sublation of the property of the agent (*prayoktṛdharma*).

By the word "etc. (*ādi*), destruction and so forth are included. By the phrase "it becomes like a *karmadhāraya*," he explains that this is an extension of the effect (*kāryātideśa*). The fruit of this extension of the effect will be shown later.

"Regarding the purpose [of treating the compound] as if it were a *karmadhāraya*, etc."—in that context, the common purpose applies both to the elision of the suffix *sug* (*sug-luk*) by virtue of the treatment as a *bahuvrīhi* and to this present extended application (*atideśa*). However, the phenomenon of "masculine-like behavior" (*puṃvadbhāva*) is sometimes common and sometimes uncommon. It is common where there is no prohibition of *puṃvadbhāva*, as in examples such as *paṭu-paṭvī*; it is uncommon where there is a prohibition of *puṃvadbhāva* by rules such as Pāṇini 6.3.37, as in examples such as *kālakā-kālikā*.

For instance, although the masculine-like treatment (*puṃvadbhāva*) is prohibited for a certain [word], the masculine-like treatment is nevertheless prescribed in a *karmadhāraya* compound by the rule beginning with *striyāḥ puṃvat...* (Pāṇini 6.3.34).
However, the property of having the udātta accent on the final syllable (*antodāttatva*) is indeed unique [to the *karmadhāraya*].

Why? Because the rule *karmadhāraye 'niṣṭhā* (Pāṇini 6.1.223) prescribes the final-udātta accent specifically for the *karmadhāraya*, not for the *bahuvrīhi*; for in the case of the latter, the rule *tatra* (Pāṇini 6.2.1) prescribes an exception to that final-udātta accent by applying the original accent of the first member (*pūrvapada-prakṛtisvara*).
In this regard, only that purpose which is unique [to this rule] necessitates this extension (*atideśa*), and not any other.

For even when the extension "as in the case of a *bahuvrīhi*" is carried over, that [purpose] is indeed accomplished. However, since its commencement serves another purpose, the continued application of the extension "as in the case of a *bahuvrīhi*" would be redundant; for by this very [rule], the common [purpose] is also established.
Therefore, even the elision of case endings (*subluk*) and so forth is not a common purpose for the status of being a *karmadhāraya*.
In the example "paṭupaṭvī," the suffix *ṅīṣ* is applied by the rule "voto guṇavacanāt" [Pāṇini 4.1.44].
And that [feminine suffix] is replaced by the masculine form (*puṃvadbhāva*) in the preceding word, as in *kālakakālikā*.

In the sense of "unknown" and so forth, the suffix *ka* is applied after a word ending in *prāgīvat* by Pāṇini 5.3.70; then the feminine suffix *ṭāp* is added, followed by the shortening of the vowel according to 7.4.13, and the substitution of *it* as before.
By the rule of *puṃvadbhāva* (masculine treatment), the feminine suffixes *ṭāp* and *ṅīp* are removed from the first member [of the compound].

But how can there be *puṃvadbhāva* here, given that a prohibition has been made by the rule *na kopadhāyāḥ* [Pāṇini 6.3.37]? To this he says: "Of a word ending in *ka*" [and so on—this refers to the counter-exception *na kopadhāyāḥ* etc., as found in the Pradīpa and other commentaries].

In the reading beginning with "pāṭha," etc., the rule *karmadhāraye hi* (Pāṇini 6.3.42) and others prescribes the masculine form (*puṃvadbhāva*) in cases where a prohibition would otherwise apply; by that, the masculine form occurs even for a word ending in the suffix *kopadha*.

But surely, the rule for the unaccented nature of the *ābhreḍita* (the reduplicated word) belongs to the eighth book (*āṣṭamikam*), whereas the rule for the acute accent on the final syllable of a compound (*samāsāntodāttatva*) belongs to the sixth book (*ṣāṣṭhikam*); therefore, by virtue of its higher status, there ought to be only the unaccented nature of the *ābhreḍita*. And if this were so, would not the extended application (*atideśa*) of the rule "as in the case of a *karmadhāraya*" become redundant? For that [extended application] has its purpose fulfilled elsewhere. To this, he says: "The acute accent on the final syllable of the compound is by this [rule]," and so forth. For when an extension of a science (*śāstrātideśa*) occurs, the operations are performed by those very rules of the science as they are extended, while remaining in their own original locations. Thus, because the unaccented nature of the *ābhreḍita* is [governed by] the acute accent on the final syllable of the compound, the former would indeed be subsequent [and thus superseded].

And this is not an extension of the treatise (śāstra); what then? It is an extension of the operation (kārya). When there is an extension of the operation, it is prescribed by the very rule of extension itself.
Therefore, the final udātta accent alone remains.
Therefore, for that reason, being subsequent [in the sequence of rules], it subverts the lack of acute accent (*anudāttatva*) belonging to the *ābhīkṣṇya* (repetition) compounds.

Now, one might object: even without the mention of "subsequent" (*uttara*), just as the governing rules (*adhikāra*) such as "[3.1.1] *taddhita-*" and so forth persist in what follows, so too will this [rule] persist; for we observe the continued application of governing rules in subsequent sections. So, for what purpose is the expression "in the subsequent ones" (*uttareṣu*) stated? To this he replies: "By the governing rule alone," and so forth.

In some cases, there is the conventional usage of designating governing rules (*adhikāra*) as "indicatory" (*lakṣaṇa*); for example, the governing rule *śeṣe* [Pāṇini 4.2.91] possesses the status of an indicatory rule, yet this is not clearly evident, because such a status is not observed in other governing rules such as *anyeṣv api* [Pāṇini 3.1.1] and so forth.
Therefore, the expression *uttareṣu* (in the subsequent ones) is stated so that its status may be made clear.
Indeed, this is done for the purpose of preventing this very [governing rule] from being considered an indicatory rule.
If, however, the characteristic were impossible to apply to the subsequent sections, the statement "in the following" would be meaningless, as there would be nothing to exclude.
Alternatively, one may supply the phrase "according to the maxim of the lion’s glance.

For generally, the recurrence of a rule in subsequent sections is considered faulty when it lacks a specific purpose for exclusion; thus, the application of the maxim of the lion’s glance is not always clear, since it is not observed in certain cases, such as with suffixes (*pratyaya*).
Therefore, for the sake of making this clear, the words "in the subsequent [rules]" are stated.

If, by the logic of the "lion's glance" (*siṃhāvalokita*), there were no possibility at all for governing rules (*adhikāra*) to recur to what precedes, then the statement "in the subsequent [rules]" would be purposeless, as there would be nothing to exclude. "Mode" (*prakāra*) means "difference" (*bheda*) and also "similarity" (*sādṛśya*).
For the word *prakāra* is seen to be used in both senses.
In that regard, its usage is observed in the sense of "difference" (*bheda*): "He eats in many *prakāras*.
The meaning is: "He eats by means of many differences (*bhedas*), that is, by means of many particulars (*viśeṣas*)."
Even in the case of similarity— as in "this boy is of the type [of a Brāhmaṇa]," which means "he is similar to a Brāhmaṇa"—
here, "type" (prakāra) is understood to mean "similarity" (sādṛśya).

Whence is this [known]? From conformity with the observed usage (*lakṣya*). For here, no distinction is understood between "one who has undergone reduplication" (*kṛtadvirvacana*) and "one who expresses a quality" (*guṇavacana*); rather, what is understood is similarity (*sādṛśya*). And in this matter, the inherent nature of the word's expressive power (*śabdaśaktisvābhāvya*) is the reason.

Is it because that [quality] is indicated by means of the understanding of the dual number in the phrase "of one existing in a mode" (*prakāre vartamānasya*)? In that case, its occurrence (*vṛtti*) therein is to be understood.

Regarding the passage beginning with "one whose qualities are complete" (*paripūrṇaguṇa*), by this example he demonstrates the occurrence of a word denoting a quality (*guṇavacana*) in the sense of similarity (*sādṛśye*).
