For analogy (*upamāna*) is similarity. One who possesses all qualities such as proficiency is called "complete" (*paripūrṇa*); one who lacks them—being incomplete or unfinished—is not so called.

If someone were to object: "Since the suffix *jātīya* is also prescribed as expressing a variety (*prakāra*), this [present rule] is commenced even though that [suffix] has not yet been reached; therefore, does it not follow that it would sublate that [suffix]?"—to such a person he replies: "The sublation of *jātīya* by this [rule] is not intended. But how is it that sublation, even if intended, does not take place? Because the term *anyatarasyām*, which will be mentioned later, is a supplement (*śeṣa*) to both rules.

What, then, is the reason that sublation (*bādhana*) is not accepted here? To this he says: "For there occurs [the case where one says] 'it is of a sharp kind' or 'it is of a dull kind,' and so forth. As for the reading found in most manuscripts, "sharp-sharp-ness of kind" (*paṭupaṭujātīya*) or "dull-dull-ness of kind" (*mṛdumṛdujātīya*), that is an error caused by negligence.
Why? Because the relationship of the sublated and the sublator (*bādhyabādhakabhāva*) occurs when multiple effects are obtained from a single causal agent.

But here, since the variety [of the quality] is already indicated by the words *paṭu-daṭu-mṛdu-mṛdu* themselves, reduplication (*dvirvacana*) does not apply to those two, nor does the suffix *-jātīya-*; therefore, this is a corrupt reading. [The examples are:
*agnirmāṇavakaḥ* ("the boy is fire") and *gaurvāhikaḥ* ("the Vāhika is a cow"). Here, the word *agni-* and the word *go-* function in the sense of a type of food (*anna-prakāra*).

Likewise, by means of the word "fire" (*agni*), a boy (*māṇavaka*) is understood as being clearly similar [to fire], and by means of the word "cow" (*go*), a Vāhīka [is understood as being clearly similar to a cow].

For these two are not words denoting qualities (*guṇavacana*); rather, they are words denoting substances (*dravyavacana*), because the boy and the Vāhīka are substances. But surely, even these two are indeed words denoting qualities. For instance, the word "fire" (*agni*) applies to the boy through the relation of metaphorical identification (*abhedopacāra*), either by way of the relationship of comparison (*upamānopameyabhāva*) or by taking up a specific quality of that same class—such as heat—which was observed in the fire, and applying it to the boy. This is because the word is employed for the purpose of manifesting that very same specific quality.

In the same way, the word "cow" (*go*) also, by taking up a specific quality of that same class which was observed in a dew-lapped animal (*sāsnādimat*)—such as dullness (*jāḍya*) and so forth—subsists in a draft-ox (*vāhīka*) through either of the two previously mentioned relations, for the purpose of communicating that very same specific quality.

Therefore, since these two [words] are engaged in communicating a specific quality, they too are indeed "quality-expressing" (*guṇavacana*); thus he says: "Even though here," and so forth. For that meaning which is understood from a word by its mere hearing (*śrutimātra*) is its primary, non-deviant meaning.
That which is perceived as a primary reality through some cause, such as metaphorical identification (*abhedopacāra*), is called "secondary" (*gauṇa*); this means it is figurative.
From the word *agni*, fire is perceived by the mere hearing of the sound; and from the word *go*, that which possesses a dewlap and so forth [is perceived].
Therefore, for the word *agni*, "the purifier" (*pāvaka*) is the primary meaning; likewise, for the word *go*, "the carrier" (*vāhika*) is the primary meaning.

The connection of the secondary [meaning], such as a young boy (*māṇavaka*), with the primary meaning, such as "redness" (*yāvaka*), etc., constitutes one of the two types of relations previously mentioned:
the relation with the primary meaning.
By that cause or instrument, the specific difference or particularity of a quality such as sharpness or dullness is determined; thus it is so described.

But how does its determination occur through that connection? Because of the cognition of that [connection], for that specific quality is the cause of that connection; since, when that [quality] exists, that [connection] is present.
Therefore, when the relationship, though being of two kinds, is cognized, it brings about the cognition of that [object], just as smoke [brings about the cognition] of fire.

Although the word *go* (cow) and the word *agni* (fire) are employed to denote a secondary meaning (*gauṇārtha*) other than their primary referent—namely, such specific qualities as those mentioned—it does not follow that they are always expressive of qualities (*guṇavacana*). Therefore, it is not stated that they are [always] so. For instance, when these words are used in a non-primary sense for a young Brahmin (*māṇavaka*) or a Bāhīka on the basis of similarity (*sādharmyeṇa*), they are not expressive of qualities; however, when they are used in a non-primary sense for a young Brahmin or a Bāhīka on the basis of similarity, they do become expressive of qualities.
And when [the word] refers to fire and to that which possesses a dewlap and so forth, it denotes either a genus (jāti) or a substance (dravya).
In that regard, when the word *agni* functions with respect to "fire-ness" (*agnitva*) and the word *go* likewise with respect to "cow-ness" (*gotva*), they are denoters of a genus;
but when they denote a genus or a substance, [they function as such].

In that regard, when the word *agni* refers to "fire-ness" (*agnitva*) and the word *go* also refers to "cow-ness" (*gotva*), they are denoters of universals (*jāti*). But when they refer to a substance (*dravya*) characterized by those universals—that is, possessing them—then they are denoters of substances. Therefore, because they do not denote qualities at all times, the doubling [of these words] does not occur.

And this is obtained from the mention of the term *guṇavacana* (quality-word). For any word existing in the sense of "kind" (*prakāra*) becomes a *guṇavacana*; yet it is stated here that the rule applies to "the *guṇavacana*. In that context, the understanding of "all kinds" is recognized—namely, that which is more properly a *guṇavacana*.
And what is more properly a *guṇavacana*? That which is always a *guṇavacana*. [This sentence does not exist in the Bhūṣaṇa.]

If it is the case that a word must undergo reduplication only when it always denotes a quality, then the word *paṭu* would not even obtain reduplication; for it too is a quality-denoting word only when it refers to the specific quality of cleverness (*pāṭava*), whereas when it refers to the substance possessing that quality, it is merely a substance-denoting word. This is not so; for it is impossible to denote the qualified object (*viśeṣya*) without denoting its qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*). Therefore, while denoting the substance as the qualified object, the qualifier must necessarily be denoted as well.
Therefore, even when occurring with reference to a substance (*dravya*), the word *paṭu* (sharp/clear) indeed denotes its qualifying quality (*guṇa*) as well.
This, however, is the distinction: it denotes the quality as a subordinate element (*upasarjanībhūta*), whereas it denotes the substance as the primary element (*pradhānabhūta*).
[The same applies to] "succession" (*ānupūrvya*), and so forth.
This is for the purpose of excluding distributive repetition (*avīpsārtham*), because distributive repetition is impossible here.

For distributive repetition occurs between distinct things belonging to the same class, such as [the repetition] "villages" (*grāmāṇām*). Indeed, all [villages] are occupied by the single universal (*jāti*) of "village-ness. However, those belonging to the same class are distinguished by differences of direction, location, and so forth.

In expressions such as "thick at every root" (*mūle mūle sthūlāḥ*), however, the word "root" (*mūla*) refers to that which is the primary root of the bamboos and so forth— of which no other lower part exists— and likewise to that which is the primary tip— of which no other upper part exists. For instance, when "the root of the bamboo" (*veṇormūlam*) is said, the cognition arises precisely with respect to that [part] below which there is no further portion.
Likewise, when "the top of a bamboo" is mentioned, the cognition of a "top" arises only in that part for which there is no other part above it, and not elsewhere.

As for the designation of "root" and "top" among those parts, it is relative: the designation "root" is made in relation to what is situated below, and the designation "top" is made in relation to what is situated above.
Therefore, all parts of the bamboo do not possess the same status as [the designation] "villages" do.

For indeed, the state of being a village (*grāmatva*) among villages is not produced by dependence [on anything else]. However, for parts (*bhāga*), the primary status of being a root and being foremost is produced without dependence;
but for multiple parts, both [statuses] exist.
That which is produced by dependence is therefore of a different nature from the parts.

Furthermore, there is no distributive repetition (*vīpsā*) among things of different classes, as in the case of "the dewlap-possessing [cows]" and "the Vāhīkas. For when it is said, "a cow, a cow," the distributive sense pertaining to the Vāhīkas is not understood. Moreover, this much meaning is intended to be expressed: that the bamboo, reeds, and so forth are perceived as being either thick or thin in their respective order; but it is not distributive repetition.
"Point out the eldest, the eldest"—here, it is merely the sequence that is intended.
First, point out whoever is the eldest among all; then, point out whoever is the eldest among those others.

Otherwise, if there were a repetition (*vīpsā*) of the "eldest" (*jyeṣṭha*) here, there would be no entry for the very youngest, because he would not be included by that repetition, as he is not an "eldest.
Therefore, even here there is no repetition.
Consequently, the meaning of this passage should be explained as follows: "In the case of sequence (*anupūrvya*), two [words] occur. This is the intended sense.

In this regard, the explanation is as follows: just as the rule *śeṣe* [Pāṇini 4.2.92] is both a defining rule (*lakṣaṇa*) and a governing heading (*adhikāra*), so too is this rule *tathā* [Pāṇini 8.1.4] both a defining rule and a governing heading.
Therefore, regarding the subsequent rules for reduplication—such as "two [words] occur in sequence"—the explanation should be applied accordingly in each case.

If, then, *sarvasya dve* [Pāṇini 8.1.1] is also a defining rule, then rules such as *tathā* [8.1.4] and others would not be redundant, precisely because there are applications for them, such as the rule *nityadīpsayoḥ* [8.1.4].
"From this [reason], do not give 'mā māvam' to both of you here"—in this context, "both" is emphasized.
The meaning is: "Give to both alone; neither to one, nor to many."

Even without the employment of the particle *eva*, restriction (*avadhāraṇa*) is understood because it is intended to be expressed, as in the example: "Pārtha is the archer. [The opponent asks: "But what is the reason that repetition (*vīpsā*) is not possible here? To this he says: "For in this case," and so forth. By this, he demonstrates the absence of repetition.
A *kārṣāpaṇa* is indeed a collection consisting of multiple *māṣas*.

However, it is not intended that all the *māṣas* be pervaded by the act of giving; rather, it is two [that are intended]. Thus, there is no distributive repetition (*vīpsā*) here—as in "give a *māṣa*, give two *māṣas*, buy [how many] *māṣas*?"—where the meaning intended is "give one *māṣa*, or two, or three," and not a restrictive determination (*avadhāraṇa*). Therefore, the double mention does not occur. [The phrase] "due to agitation" (*sambhrameṇa*) [is used].
"Activity with haste" means the act of setting forth.

"‘ahirahiḥ budhyasva budhyasva’—if this person does not wake up, I shall not awaken him today; thinking that he has surely been bitten by a snake, one utters this sentence out of agitation. Regarding the two rules—"it should be stated that there is reduplication in the case of frequent repetition" (Vārttika 886) and "it should be stated that there is reduplication in the case of constant repetition" (Vārttika 887)—it is argued that since this necessity is already indicated by the imperative (*loṭ*) and other such suffixes themselves, reduplication would not otherwise apply.
By the rule beginning with *nitya* (Pāṇini 6.1.4), he demonstrates that reduplication is established in this very context.
How it is established is explained in that same section by the passage beginning with *ktvāṇamulor loṭaś ca dvirvacanāpekṣayā*. For example:
*paṭapaṭākaroti*.
When the suffix *ḍāc* is to be applied to the word *paṭaccha*, reduplication occurs even before it has been produced.

Then, by the rules "after an imitation of an indistinct sound consisting of two or more syllables, provided it does not end in *it*, *ḍāc* is added" (Pāṇini 5.4.57) and "when *ḍāc* follows, the final vowel and the consonant following it are always replaced by the single substitute of the subsequent vowel" (Pāṇini 6.1.96), the *t* is replaced by the subsequent vowel form (*pararūpa*).
Thus: *paṭapaṭāyate*.

The ātmanepada ending is applied by the rule *lohitādi-ḍājbhyaḥ kyaṣ* (Pāṇini 1.3.90). Regarding the phrase "of that which ends in ḍāc," this was stated with reference to a form where ḍāc is yet to be applied (*bhāvi-ḍājanta*). Therefore, this reduplication is intended to occur precisely when ḍāc has not yet been produced, while it remains the subject of application.
For this very reason, the author of the *Vṛtti* stated regarding the sūtra *avyaktānukaraṇa* [Pāṇini 5.4.57] and others: "The locative [in the word] *ḍāci* is a locative of scope (*viṣayasaptamī*).
In this regard, the prescription of the single-substitute *pararūpa* by [the rule] *ato guṇe* [Pāṇini 6.1.97] is the indicator (*jñāpaka*).
There, the words *hraḥ* and *antasya* are understood to carry over.

If reduplication is intended to occur when *ḍāc* follows, then once *ḍāc* has been prescribed, the word *paṭa* must first undergo elision of the suffixal *ṭi* by virtue of its obligatory application (*nityatva*); and such being the case, since the form *paṭac* would no longer exist, that [resulting] form would not be possible. Therefore, this is a locative of scope (*viṣaya-saptamī*). By adopting this view, what was stated under [Pāṇini 6.1.100]—namely, "reduplication is desired to occur prior to the elision of the *ṭi*"—becomes logically consistent.

For in this way, the reduplication is established prior to the elision of the *ṭi* [portion]; provided that the rule for that [reduplication] is applied when *ḍāc* is the domain. Otherwise, if it were to be applied when that [suffix] follows, then because it would be obligatory, the elision of the *ṭi* alone would occur prior [to reduplication], and not the reduplication. [The examples] such as *dvitīyākaroti* and so forth are formed by *ḍāc* according to the rule *kṛño dvitīyatṛtīya* (Pāṇini 5.4.58).
Regarding the phrase "for that purpose":

it is for the sake of ensuring that reduplication occurs only for an *avyakta-anukaraṇa* (imitation of an indistinct sound) ending in a *ḍāc* suffix. By the mention of "some," it is implied that some do not read [the rule] as *bahulam* (optionally).
Their argument is essentially this: from the rule "sarvasya dve," the term *vibhāṣā* (optionally) is understood to carry over, and that is a *vyavasthitavibhāṣā* (a restricted option).
Consequently, reduplication will occur here only for an *avyaktānukaraṇa* (imitation of an indistinct sound) ending in *ḍāc*, and not for anything else.
Therefore, there is no purpose in the inclusion of the term *bahulam* (variously).

Regarding the phrase "of *pūrva* and *prathama*" and so forth, and the expression "when there is a desire to express an excellence of meaning": the meaning is that the "excellence" (*atiśaya*)—that is, the pre-eminence (*prakarpa*)—of the expressed meanings of the words *pūrva* and *prathama*; the "desire to express" (*vivakṣā*) that [excellence] is the speaker's wish to speak of it; and when that [desire] exists, the two forms [the suffix -tama and the doubling of the word] occur. This is how the form of the rule's meaning is to be explained.
The explanation has already been provided previously.

To one who might think, "Since this rule for reduplication is being introduced when the suffixes of excellence (*ātiśāyika*) have not yet been reached, it must necessarily supersede them," he says in response: "The suffixes of excellence are also seen.
How so? Reduplication is prescribed by the very rule "the whole [word] is doubled" (Pāṇini 8.1.1).
Here, because of the governing rule of *vibhāṣā* (optionality), there is an alternative;
thus, when the doubling (*dvirvacana*) does not occur, the suffixes expressing excellence (*atiśāyika*) are applied. This refers to the rule beginning with "of *ḍatara* and *ḍatama*," and so forth.
The suffix *itac* is prescribed by the rule *kiṃyattadoḥ* [Pāṇini 5.3.92],
and the suffix *ḍatamac* is prescribed by the rule *vā bahūnāṃ jātiparipraśne* [Pāṇini 5.3.93].

*Sampradhāraṇā* (comparative deliberation) is that process of determining which of two or more things possesses a quality such as intensity (*āḍhya-tva*) and so forth, in the manner of "this one is more intense" and so on.

A word with a feminine gender (*strīliṅgaśabdaḥ*) is called "feminine" (*strī*) because of its connection with the feminine gender. It is called *nigada* because it is expressed by means of it; the suffix *gha* is applied according to [Pāṇini 3.3.118], *puṃsi saṃjñāyāṃ ghaḥ prāyeṇa*. That state (*bhāvaḥ*) which has a feminine expression (*strīnigadaḥ*) is "feminine-expression."

When two words ending in the suffixes *ḍatara* and *ḍatama*, which denote feminine gender and express a state (*bhāva*), are used in a context of comparative deliberation (*sampradhāraṇā*), they become doubled.
The mention of *ḍatara* and *ḍatama* here should be understood as an illustration (*upalakṣaṇa*).
For this very reason, the author will later state: "The [doubling] of words other than those ending in *ḍatara* and *ḍatama* is also observed" (with the addition of the word *hi* in the Kāśikā).
In this context, for some, excellence (*āḍhatva*) is produced by the application of means; for some, it is produced by effort; and for some, it is produced by the abundance of fortune.

When it is said, "Both of these possess excellence," the listener, while understanding what has produced their excellence, employs the sentence, "Which of these two possesses greater excellence? In that case, excellence is a state (*bhāva*) expressed by a feminine noun as a synonym for prosperity (*vibhūti*);
and it resides in words ending in the suffixes *-tara* and *-tama*, because one proceeds to ask about it.
"Karmavyatihāre," etc.
Karmavyatihāra is the exchange of actions;
for instance, when one person provides food for another's meal, and the other likewise provides food for the first.

By this [sūtra], the status of being like a compound (*samāsavadbhāva*) is prescribed extensively (*bahulam*). However, reduplication (*dvirvacana*) is already established by the rule *dvirvacanam* (Pāṇini 8.1.1).
Furthermore, that status of being like a compound does not occur at all in the word *anyonya* due to the extensive application (*bahulavacana*) of the rule.
In the case of the word *itaretara*, however, it is always [used] thus:
in the absence of compound formation, the nominative singular of the first member must be employed, as in:
"these Brāhmaṇas feed one another."
The word *anyam*, which ends in the second case singular, is reduplicated.
Since there is no application of the *samāsavadbhāva* (treatment as a compound) here, the first member retains its nominative singular ending.

For that [first member], the rules >[[8.2.66]], >[[6.1.113]], >[[6.1.87]], and >[[6.1.109]] must be applied, resulting in the substitution of *u* (*utvam*) and the formation of the single preceding form (*pūrvarūpatvam*).
Regarding the term "anyo'nyasya": it is a reduplication of the word ending in the genitive case. They cause each other's relatives, such as sons and so forth, to eat.
The meaning is that "another also [eats] with him. Regarding the expression *itaretaraṃ bhojayanti*:

when the word ending in the second case (*dvitīyānta*) is reduplicated, it becomes a singular form of the second case; then, by [Pāṇini 6.1.103], there is the substitution of the preceding vowel (*ami pūrvatvam*).

Regarding the term *itaretarasya*: this is the reduplication of the word ending in the genitive case. Once the *su*-affix has been elided (*luk*), because it is now a nominal base (*prātipadika*) belonging to a compound, the genitive singular affix is applied once again. The phrase "in the feminine and neuter" (*strīnapuṃsakayoḥ*), and so forth, follows.

Regarding the [term] *strīnapuṃsakayoḥ*: when a pronoun (*sarvanāman*) is used in the sense of mutual exchange of action (*karmavyatihāra*), it should be stated that the substitution of *ām* optionally occurs for the final syllable of the subsequent member (*uttarapada*).

The genitive case in the word *uttarapadasya* expresses a relationship with a part; therefore, this substitution takes the place of whatever case-ending belongs to the subsequent member as its constituent part.
If it were a genitive of location (*sthāne-ṣaṣṭhī*), then because the substitute *ām* consists of more than one phoneme (*anekāl*), it would result in a total replacement of the entire original form.
Regarding the form *anyonyāmime brāhmaṇyo bhojayataḥ*:

there is reduplication of the word *anyām*, the substitution of *ām* for the case-ending, the shortening of the first member of the compound due to the rule of diversity (*bahulavacana*), and the application of *rutva* (the addition of *r*) and so forth as before. In the form *anyo'nyam*, the second member also undergoes shortening and other changes as previously described.
Regarding the expression "itaretarāṃ bhojayataḥ" (they feed one another):

when the status of a compound (*samāsavadbhāva*) is present, the feminine suffix *ṭāp* is elided due to the masculine-like transformation (*puṃvadbhāva*) that occurs in all derivative forms (*vṛttimātra*) of pronouns (Jainendravyākaraṇa 1.2.103).
The same applies to the form "itaretaram. Here, the negative particle *nañ* functions as an antonym (*vipakṣa*), just as in the cases of *adharma*, *anṛta*, and so forth.

*Kṛcchra* means suffering (*duḥkha*), and *prayatna* means exertion (*prayāsa*); furthermore, this is a property of sentient beings (*prāṇidharma*). *Akṛcchra* is the opposite of *kṛcchra*; it is also a property of sentient beings, in the presence of which one accomplishes acts such as giving even without exertion.
In that context, the forms *priya* and *sva* become [the bases] for the two suffixes (*dv-e*).

"He gives with affection" means he gives without effort. When the word ending in the third case singular is reduplicated and the *sub*-suffixes are elided (*luk*), it again becomes the third case singular by virtue of its status as a compound (*samāsavadbhāva*).

"‘A dear son,’ ‘a comfortable chariot’—in these cases, the words *priya* (dear) and *sukha* (comfortable) do not refer to specific qualities of sentient beings that are the opposites of suffering (*kṛcchra*), but rather to substances.
For a son is called ‘dear’ because he causes delight, and a chariot is called ‘comfortable’ because it provides pleasure. [This concludes the section on] "according to their respective [meanings]."
The term *yathā* forms an avyayībhāva compound with *yatha* in the sense of repetition (*vīpsā*), according to the rule *yathāsādṛśye* [Pāṇini 2.1.7].
To demonstrate that the word *sva* here denotes either "self" (*ātman*) or "one's own" (*ātmīya*), he says: "whichever self," and so forth.
[This results in] the form *yathāyatham*.

By the rule *hrasvo napuṃsake* [Pāṇini 1.2.47], the neuter forms are short. Regarding the statement "the substitution of *amb-* for the first member," etc.: once reduplication has been performed, we have the form *dvi-au*. When the case-ending elision (*sup-luk*) has occurred, both the substitution of *amb-* and the substitution of *at-* are applied to the vowel *ī*; from the whole [form] *su-* is added respectively, by the rule *ato'm* [Pāṇini 7.1.24] when *am* follows, and by the rule *pūrva-para-yaṇ-aḥ* [Pāṇini 6.1.103]. Otherwise, the form *dvandvam* would not be established. Now, is this form *dvandvam* prescribed as an irregularity (*nipātana*) in these instances where the elision of *ra* and so forth is taught, or is it prescribed when they serve as the domain [of application]? To this he says: "In that case," etc.
*Rahaḥ* means secrecy; that which is appropriate for it is *rahasyam*, according to [Pāṇini 4.4.98] *prāgdhitādyat*.
Alternatively, it is derived as "that which exists in secret" (*rahasi bhavam*), with the suffix *yat* according to [Pāṇini 4.3.54] because it belongs to the *dig-ādi* group.
[The rule applies] in the sense of "defining a limit" (*maryādāvacane*).
*Maryādā* means not exceeding a limit; the expression of that is *maryādāvacana*.

The inclusion of the word "expression" (*vacana*) is so that [the designation] may apply when the limit is conveyed by the actual words, and not when it is understood through the sense, context, and so forth—as in the case of *ācaturam*.
> [[2.1.13]] Thus ends the *avyayībhāva* [compound]; > [[5.4.107]] the suffix *ṭac* is applied as a final member of the compound.
To clarify the meaning of the limit (*maryādā*) in the example, he says: "The mother [is limited] by the son," and so forth.
For a mother obtains four descendants born from her union—namely, the son, the grandson, the great-grandson, and that grandson's son—but no more than those.
"Having the sense of a limit" (*maryādārtha*) means that whose purpose is a limit is "having the sense of a limit.
"He employs" (*prayunakti*)— thus [it is said].
The meaning is "he prepares.
Regarding the term "pairs" (dvandvāni),
it means cold, heat, and so forth— the causes of pleasure and pain.

[The meaning is "the causes of pleasure and pain"—this is the reading of the Prāṅmukha school. If a *yogavibhāga* (separation of rules) were made, would the mention of *rahasya* and so forth be purposeless? It is not purposeless, because it serves to provide detailed exposition (*prapañca*).
Alternatively, it is for the purpose of making known that this *yogavibhāga* of the rule "dvandvam" does not apply to all cases. Regarding the phrase "prior to the jurisdiction of *apadānta*":
it means prior to the rule "apadāntasya mūrdhanyaḥ" (Pāṇini 8.3.55).

In the subsequent rules, whatever operation is prescribed for a word ending in a *su*-affix (a nominal) or a verbal suffix (*tiṅanta*) beginning with an invocation (*āmantrita*), there the operation is understood to apply to a "word" (*pada*) even without an explicit heading (*adhikāra*) on "word"; therefore, bypassing those [rules], that very heading where it is useful is now introduced.

As it will be stated: "There is elision of a final consonant cluster" (*Pāṇini 8.2.23*). By the restrictive rule (*niyama*) [of the preceding sūtra], the term "of a word" (*padasya*) is a genitive of locus (*sthāna-ṣaṣṭhī*).

And what would be the sixth position for this [rule]? The meaning of the rule *udāttasvaritayoryaṇaḥ svarito 'nudāttasya* [Pāṇini 8.2.4] would arise as follows: "An acute (*svarita*) accent occurs for that which is unaccented (*anudātta*) following a *yaṇ* (vowel) that itself follows an acute or a *svarita* vowel; thus, the entire word ending in that unaccented vowel becomes *svarita*. If this were the case, it would apply here in *kumāryau*, but it would not apply in *kumāryaḥ*.
For in this latter instance, the word does not end in an unaccented vowel that follows a *yaṇ* after an acute or *svarita* vowel; rather, it ends in the letter *s*.

> [[8.2.5]]] Here too, this is the meaning arising from the genitive case of *sthāna*: "the syllable that is the single substitute (*ekadeśa*) for both the acute (*udātta*) and the grave (*anudātta*) becomes acute for the word ending in that [substitute].
If this were so, it would apply only here in the case of *vṛkṣau*, but not in the case of *vṛkṣāḥ*.

For in this latter case, the word does not end in that single substitute for the acute and grave; what then? It ends in *-s*. To one who might raise this objection, he replies with the words: "with reference to the rule to be stated," and so forth.
This is the third [case-ending], the instrumental.

By means of that which serves as the cause—the requirement for the sentences to be stated hereafter—the determination of the genitive sense for the word under discussion (adhikṛta-pada) is to be understood.
"Determination" (vyavasthā) means a restrictive rule (niyama).

For among the rules to be stated hereafter, some—such as [Pāṇini 8.2.23] *padasya* and so forth—require a genitive case expressing the sense of "in place of" (*sthāna-ṣaṣṭhī*). Others—such as [Pāṇini 8.2.4] *udāttasvaritayoryaṇaḥ* and so forth—require a genitive case expressing the sense of "part of" (*avayava-ṣaṣṭhī*).
Therefore, by virtue of this dependence on another factor, there is a restriction regarding the meaning of the genitive.
For rights exist for the sake of others;
and their being for the sake of others occurs only if they appropriate the object for themselves in accordance with the requirements of others.
With the words "in some cases" (*kvacit*) and so forth, he demonstrates that very establishment of the genitive sense.

What, then, is the reason that this restriction—"the sixth [case ending] is not used when there is no connection" (Pāṇini 2.3.39)—does not apply here? He thinks as follows: this restriction depends upon another related element (*sambandhin*).
For "connection" (*yoga*) is indeed a relation, and that rests upon multiple related elements.

Since no other related element exists within this governing rule (*adhikāra-sūtra*), its application does not occur here at all. This is expressed in the rule: "Before a word denoting contempt, provided it is a *sup*-ending word and not a *gotra* name, etc. (Pāṇini 2.1.53).

Whence is this [conclusion]? On this point, some say: "Because the status of being a cause (nimittabhāva) for the ablative case *padāt* is sublated by the locative case *supi* [Pāṇini 8.1.69], it is not able to function; therefore, the causal status of the ablative is sublated. But this is incorrect; for there is no contradiction whatsoever when both the locative and the ablative are accepted as having the status of a cause.

In this regard, the connection would be as follows: "That which follows a word (*padāt*)—namely, a finite verb (*tiṅanta*)—is elided when followed by a vocative ending in a *sub* suffix expressing contempt. Consequently, this would apply only here: *devadattaḥ pacati pūtīti*, but not here: *pacati pūtīti*.
Furthermore, in the rule *canacidivagotrāditaddhitābhreḍiteṣvagateḥ* [Pāṇini 8.1.57], the term *padāt* would also fail to recur;
for the locative *padāt* would have been superseded by the ablative [of the current rule]. As a result, the rule would serve only the purpose of expressing contempt.
When there is the employment of *cana* and so forth, it would be understood as "therefore" (*tasmāt*).
Therefore, it must be resolved that the engagement and withdrawal of the governing rules (*adhikāra*) occur [only] from this point.
Alternatively, is this [the word] *pāda-ādeḥ* connected with the prohibition?

Therefore, when the prohibition [of the *nighāta* accent] by the rule *kutsane* (Pāṇini 8.1.69) has ceased, the requirement that the word must be "after a *pada*" (*padāt*) also ceases. This applies to the phrase *yat te niyatam*, and so forth. Here, the vocative word *mṛtyo* follows the word *rajasam*; however, because *mṛtyo* stands at the beginning of the word *anavadhṛṣya*, the substitution of the *nighāta* accent does not occur.

When *asminnasati* (Pāṇini 8.1.19) applies, the first syllable of the vocative case retains its original udātta accent. For example: *rudro vaḥ*. Here, although the word *yuṣmākam* follows the word *devaḥ*, because it occurs at the beginning of the verse-quarter (*pāda*) "yuṣmākaṃ kuladevatā," the substitution of *vas* does not take place.
Even in the immediately following counter-example, in the verse "asmākaṃ śatrumarvanaḥ," the word *asmākam* occurs at the beginning of the quarter-verse (*pāda*).
Therefore, even though it follows the word *bhagavān*, the substitution of *naḥ* for *asmākam* does not take place.
Regarding this, it is said: "By the mention of 'pāda' here, both the quarter of a Vedic hymn (*ṛkpāda*) and the quarter of a verse (*ślokapāda*) are included."
Because no specific distinction is made.

Now, for what purpose is the mention of "all" (*sarva*), given that by [Pāṇini 6.1.158], in words (*pada*) there occurs only either a circumflex (*svarita*) or an acute (*udātta*) accent; and when an unaccented (*anudātta*) vowel is prescribed for that [circumflex or acute], the entire word becomes unaccented? To this he says: "The mention of 'all' (*sarvagrahaṇam*)," etc.
By the phrase "that which is being restated" (*anūdyamānam*), etc., he explains the purpose of the mention of "all."
That word is of two kinds: that which is being restated (*anūdyamāna*) and that which is being prescribed (*vidhīyamāna*).

Among these, that which is already established and is mentioned for the sake of another operation is the word being restated; whereas that which is previously unknown and is being enjoined is the word being prescribed. The inclusion of the term "all" (*sarva*) is for the purpose of ensuring that both of these [types of words] be unaccented. What is thereby established? To this he says: "By that," and so forth.
For the substitutes for *yuṣmad* and *asmad*, being currently prescribed, do not yet possess established existence (*asiddhasattāka*).

Indeed, a further property (*dharmāntara*) is sought to be applied to an entity that already exists, just as dyeing applies to a cloth whose form is already complete, but not to one that is unformed; likewise, it applies to that very entity when it has not yet reached its [final] state.

In that context, if the term "all" (*sarva*) were not present, then only that word which possesses established existence—such as a vocative (*āmantrita*) and so forth—which is being referred to (*anūdyamāna*), would have the prescription of the enclitic accent (*anudātta*) applied to it, but not to the substitutes for *yuṣmad* and *asmad*.
"But when 'all' (sarva) is included, that [anudātta quality] is prescribed for those [yuṣmad and asmad] as well.

Now, even if "all" is included, how can the anudātta nature of the substitutes for *yuṣmad* and *asmad* be prescribed? For their status as "not yet established" (*asiddhatva*) at the time of their prescription has certainly not been removed by that [inclusion]. To this he says: "By means of a split in the sentence" (*vākyabhedena*), and so forth.
By the force of including "all," a split in the sentence is intended here; otherwise, the anudātta nature could not be understood through the inclusion of "all."
In this context, the substitutes are prescribed by the first sentence, and their unaccented nature (*anudāttatva*) is prescribed by the second.

How then can it be said that they are "being prescribed," given that the unaccented nature of the substitutes *yuṣmad* and *asmad*—which have already been prescribed—is being prescribed by a subsequent sentence? It should be understood that the intention here is as follows: that which is being prescribed in this section, having already been prescribed, should subsequently be unaccented.

If that which is not yet established cannot be prescribed, then how is the acute accent of the augment *aṬ* prescribed in the rule "In the *luṅ*, *laṅ*, and *lṛṅ* [tenses], *aṬ* is acute" (P. 6.4.71)? In that case too, by the authority of the statement, a split of the sentence (*vākyabheda*) must be made: by one sentence the augment *aṅ* is prescribed, and by the other, the acuteness of what has been prescribed. But here, if the term "all" (*sarva*) were absent, a split of the sentence would not be possible, and thus the lack of accentuation would simply not occur, since the prescription of the non-acute accent would already have found its application in cases such as vocatives (*āmantrita*). [This explains] the phrase "and the substitutes for *yuṣmad* and *asmad*."

The word *ca* (and) serves to collect another purpose. And what is this other purpose for including the term *sarva* (all)? It is so that the substitutes *vām*, *nau*, and so forth, may apply to the entire word ending in a case-suffix (*subanta*) when it is *yuṣmad* or *asmad*. Otherwise, if the inclusion of *sarva* were omitted, because of the genitive indication in the rule *yuṣmadasmadoḥ* [Pāṇini 7.2.90], the substitutes would apply only to those two words in their isolated state, setting aside the case-ending.

But surely, since the term *pada* from [Pāṇini 8.1.16] is understood here, and a "word" (*pada*) is indeed that which ends in an inflection, then even without the mention of *sarva* ("all"), the rule would apply to the entire word along with its inflection? To this he says: "In cases where," and so forth. A word beginning with *su* is a *svādi-pada*; the compound is formed by the split of the rule [Pāṇini 2.1.40], *saptamī*. Furthermore, the technical designation *pada* is prescribed for it by [Pāṇini 1.4.17], *tasya param āmreditaṃ...*. If the mention of *sarva* were not present, the suffixes would apply only to the word ending in an inflection where such a word exists.
Wherever a case-ending (*vibhakti*) follows, the preceding word would not [be subject to the rules], yet it is desired that they apply there as well to the whole (*sarvasya*).
Therefore, even where the word beginning with *su* occurs in forms such as the dative dual, the term "all" (*sarvam*) is stated so that the rules may apply to every inflected noun (*subanta*).
Now, one might object: will it not be stated that what follows a vocative (*āmantrita*) after a word is unaccented (*anudātta*)?

In this regard, since the rule for the anudātta (unaccented) nature of "idam" is commenced before the udātta accent of the vocative has even arrived, that [anudātta] applies to what is not at the beginning of a word (*apādādi*). Consequently, when that [anudātta] subverts [the udātta], the natural accent (*prakṛtisvara*) would apply to the vocative. However, because of the inclusion of the word "sarva" (all), the attainment of all accents is subverted by the anudātta nature of the vocative. Why, then, is the inclusion of "sarva" not also intended for the purpose of subverting the attainment of all accents? It cannot be so; for this word "anudātta" is in grammatical apposition with "vocative," and it will subvert the attainment of all accents.

When the acute accent on the first syllable (*ādyudāttatva*) has been prohibited and the original accent (*prakṛtisvara*) is being applied, the term "anudātta" (unaccented) refers to the vocative (*āmantrita*).
Therefore, the purpose of including the word "sarva" (all) is exactly as stated previously. When the acute accent on the first syllable of the vocative would otherwise apply, this [rule] is stated.

Here, since the rules for elision (*nighāta*) and the substitutes for *yuṣmad* are prescribed based merely on the governing heading of "word" (*pada*), they would apply even in cases where their application is not desired.

Even where [certain operations] are prescribed, they do not apply in some instances; therefore, with the desire to avoid this fault, he says: "In the same sentence," and so forth. Why? Because the operations such as *nighāta* (accentual suppression) are prescribed for what follows a word beginning with a vocative (*āmantrita*), it must be stated that these operations are prescribed only when those two reside in a single common substratum, namely, one and the same sentence. For what purpose? He says: "In this [context]," and so forth.
"In this [expression], 'this is a staff,' the word 'exists' is required;
although it is not explicitly employed, it is understood, and thus it has been so stated."

"Where there is no other verbal form (*kriyāpada*), the verb *as* (to be) in the present tense is employed; thus, even when not explicitly used, it is understood. Therefore, "this is a staff" (*ayaṃ daṇḍaḥ*)—accompanied by this understood *asti*—constitutes one sentence, while "take this" (*harānena*) is another. In that case, if the suppression of accent (*nighāta*) and so forth were not prescribed for a single sentence, then the suppression of the accent of the finite verb *hara*, which follows the non-finite word *daṇḍa*, would undesirably follow.

If it is argued: "This is a rule concerning words (*padavidhi*), and such a rule occurs only when there is semantic competency (*sāmarthya*); however, here that does not exist. Therefore, because of this lack of competency, the substitution [of *m* for *t*] will not take place"—then in that case, it would also not occur in these instances: "O Devadatta, your mother tells you," "He stands on the bank of the river," and "I shall give you rice-gruel."

For here, the vocative "Devadatta" has no syntactic capacity (sāmarthya) with the word "iha" (here). Moreover, this stick certainly possesses syntactic capacity in the sentence "harānena daṇḍaḥ" (bring this stick), because the pronoun "anena" (by this), which refers back to the instrument, requires that which is to be brought, and by proximity, that is understood to be the stick itself; thus, there exists between the stick and the word "hara" a syntactic capacity characterized by mutual expectancy (vyapekṣā). [As in:
"Cook the rice; it will be yours."
"Cook the rice" is one sentence; "it will be yours" is another. [Or:
"Cook the rice, it will be mine"—here too, "cook the rice" is one sentence, and "it will be mine" is another.

In this regard, if the substitutes for *yuṣmad* and *asmad* were not prescribed within a single sentence (*ekavākya*), then from the word *paceti*, the substitutes *te* and *me* would apply to the following *yuṣmad* and *asmad* by the rule *tvamāvekavacanasya* (Pāṇini 7.2.97), for there is indeed semantic connection (*sāmarthya*) here as well. To explain: there exists a mutual expectancy (*vyapekṣā*) between the cooking and the words *yuṣmad* and *asmad*, in the sense that "by means of this cooking, which is the instrument, the rice will become yours" or "mine"—wherein the referent denoted by the word *yuṣmad* and the referent denoted by the word *asmad* are connected.
However, when the term *samānavākya* ("within a single sentence") is included, no undesirable consequence arises.
Regarding the phrase "And here," etc.:
the word "and" (ca) is used for conjunction.
This shows that this is another purpose of the desired [proof] according to the opponent's view.
"O Devadatta, your mother says this here" is one sentence; "he stands on the bank of the river" is the second;
"I will give you rice porridge" is the third.

In that regard, the purpose [of the rule] is so that, in the first sentence, there may be the *nighāta* (elision of accent) for the vocative *devadatta* following the word *iha*; and in the second, so that the substitution of *ta* for the word *yuṣmad* following *nadyāḥ*—by the rule "*temayāvekavacanasya*" [Pāṇini 8.1.22]—may take place. Thus, *nighāta* and other such operations are to be understood as occurring within a single sentence (*samānavākya*).

An example for the substitutes of the word *asmad* has not been presented here, because it is understood by means of the examples for the substitutes of the word *yuṣmad*. Furthermore, such examples as "O Śālīna, give me rice" (*śālīna odanaṃ me dehi*) are to be seen there. Now, what would happen if the suppression of accent (*nighāta*), as well as the substitutes for *yuṣmad* and *asmad*, were not stated within a single sentence? To this, he says: "The end of an *āmantrita*," and so forth.

First, regarding the first sentence: here, the word *iha* (here) has location as its primary meaning, and a location requires something to be located within it (*ādheya*). That which is to be located is the mother, not Devadatta.
The meaning is: "Your mother is staying here; tell her.
Therefore, the vocative *Devadatta* lacks syntactic connection (*sāmarthya*) with the word *iha*.
In the second example, however, the word ending in a verbal suffix (*tiṅanta*) is *tiṣṭhati*, which follows the word *nadyāḥ*.
Yet, that [suffix] has no syntactic connection (*sāmarthya*) with *nadyāḥ*; rather, it has a connection with *kūle*.
In the third example as well, the word *yuṣmad* follows the word *śālīnām*, but it has no syntactic connection with *śālīnām*; rather, it has a connection with *odanasya*.

Then, due to the absence of that capacity, the *nighāta* (elision) and other operations dependent upon it would not occur. Regarding the phrase "dependent upon that": here, the word "here" (*iha*) is the basis for the [application of] the rules concerning *nadyāḥ* and *ecchālīnām*; they are described as such because they have that as their cause.

Alternatively—what is meant by "those whose basis is semantic capacity" (*sāmarthya*)? It refers to those [rules] for which semantic capacity is the foundation. For if the present rule were not stated, then, because the governing authority (*adhikāra*) pertains to words (*pada*), operations such as *nighāta* (accentual suppression) would apply only when there is a grammatical word-formation; and that [word-formation] is dependent upon semantic capacity. Since that semantic capacity does not exist here, how could there be any occasion for *nighāta* and the like? Therefore, it must be stated that operations such as *nighāta* apply within a single sentence (*samānavākya*) so that they may occur even in the absence of semantic capacity. Thus: "In the case of the genitive, dative, and accusative endings. (*ṣaṣṭhī-caturthī-dvitīyāsyayoḥ*)
The two [roots] *sthā* and *gā*, which occur in the sixth [section] and those following, are stated in that manner.

The suffix *ka* is applied by the rule *supi sthā* (Pāṇini 3.2.4). But what is the reason that examples are presented only for the two forms ending in the dual number? To this he says: "In the case of those ending in the singular and plural," and so forth.

Now, what is the purpose of including the term *stha* (standing/remaining)? Why not simply say, "In place of *yuṣmad* and *asmad*, [substitutes occur] when the sixth, fourth, and second cases are present"? Since the *yuṣmad* and *asmad* stems would necessarily remain in their original state (*tātsthya*) when the sixth case and so forth are being prescribed, he says: "The inclusion of *stha*," etc. That which has the audible case-ending as its meaning, purpose, or cause is described in that way.

This is what is meant: the mention of *sthā* (in the rule *yuṣmadasmador sthāne*) is for the purpose of ensuring that the sixth (*ṣaṣṭhī*) and other case-endings (*vibhakti*), which are being heard, may serve as the cause (*nimitta*) for the substitution. Consequently, where the case-ending is not heard, the substitutions do not occur—as in the examples *ayaṃ yuṣmatputraḥ* ("this is your son") and *ayam asmatputraḥ* ("this is our son").
However, if the mention of *sthā* were absent, the two substitutions would still occur even when the case-ending is elided, by virtue of the rule *pratyayalope pratyayalakṣaṇam* (Pāṇini 1.1.62).

Furthermore, in this case, the case-ending (*vibhakti*) is not heard because it has been elided after forming a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*) by the rule *supo dhātuprātipadikayoḥ* (Pāṇini 2.4.71). How is it that, even with the inclusion of the word "sthā" (*sthagrahaṇa*), the case-ending—which is not being heard—is understood as the cause (*nimitta*) for the substitution? Because the state of "being located therein" (*tātsthyam*) is possible only when that case-ending is actually being heard.

Alternatively, this verb *tiṣṭhati* functions in the sense of "not abandoning": as in the passage, "Wait at the appointed time, O Sugrīva" (*samaye tiṣṭha sugrīva*). [And: "The path by which Vālī was slain is not narrow; wait at the appointed time, O Sugrīva, do not follow the path of Vālī. (Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa, Kiṣkindhākāṇḍa, Sarga 30, Verse 81). The meaning is: "Do not abandon the agreement."
By this, it is understood that [the rule] "yuṣmadasmador ādeśau" applies when the sixth (genitive), fourth (dative), and second (accusative) case endings have not been abandoned.

And when it is understood in this way, the case ending (*vibhakti*) is taken as the cause for the substitution only when it is actually heard [in the utterance]. But what is the reason that examples are presented only for those ending in the genitive and dative, and not for those ending in the accusative? To this he says: "Of that ending in the second [case]," and so forth. The analysis is: *tvām* and *mām* are [the substitutes] for the second case; that is, *tvā* and *mā*.
The term *ekavacanasya* (of the singular) is understood [from the previous rule].

Thus he says, beginning with "the second," etc. Now, he provides examples according to the sequence of the second, fourth, and sixth cases, and according to the sequence of the singular, dual, and plural numbers—beginning with *śrīśa*, etc.
Therein, the first quarter-verse is: *śrīśas tvāvatu mām apīha*.
The Lord of Śrī—the Master—is Viṣṇu; the grammatical connection is "may He protect you and me as well.
Here, *tvām* and *mām* are the forms of the second person singular accusative with the substitutes *tvā* and *mā*. [The verse continues:
"May He grant welfare to you and to me as well."

The grammatical construction is: "May that Lord of Śrī grant (*dattāt*) welfare (*śarma*) and happiness (*sukha*) to you and to me as well. The form *dattāt* is derived from the root *du dāñ* (to give) in the imperative mood (*loṭ*) used as a benediction (*āśis*).
In some readings, the form *dadyāt* (optative) appears instead.
In this instance, for the forms *tubhyam* and *mahyam*, which end in the singular dative case, there are the substitutes *te* and *me* respectively, as in:
*svāmī te me 'pi sa hariḥ* ("That Lord Hari belongs to you and to me").
Here, for the forms *tava* and *mama*, which end in the singular genitive case, there are the substitutes *te* and *me*.
"May the All-pervasive One protect both you and us. The grammatical construction is: "May the All-pervasive One (*vibhuḥ*), who is omnipresent, protect both *vām* (you two) and *nau* (us two).
Here, the forms *vām* and *nau* are the substitutes for the second-person dual and first-person dual accusative cases, respectively, namely *yuvām* and *āvām*.
"May the Lord grant happiness to you two and to us.
After the word "nau," the word "api" (also) is to be supplied. Thus, "vām" and "nau" are the dual forms of the fourth case (dative) ending in the sense of "to you two" and "to us two" respectively.
In the phrase *patir vām api nau hariḥ*, the forms *vām* and *nau* are the dual sixth-case endings for "you two" and "us two" respectively; likewise,
in *so 'vyād vo naḥ*.
May he protect us— meaning,
may he guard us; here, *vas* and *nas* are the forms for the second person plural and first person plural respectively,
as in "may he grant auspiciousness to you and to us."
*Śivam* means "auspicious.
After the word *na*, the word *api* is to be supplied as an ellipsis.
Here, *yuṣmabhyam* and *asmabhyam* are the forms of the dative plural ending in *-bhyas*, which become *-vas* and *-nas* respectively.
"He is to be served by you here"—that Hari is to be served (*sevya*) by you as well as by us; that is to say, he is to be worshipped (*bhajanīya*).
The genitive case is used according to the rule: "The genitive may optionally be used for the agent of gerundives (*kṛtya*)."

In this case, *yuṣmākam* and *asmākam* are the forms ending in the sixth case plural (*ṣaṣṭhī-bahuvacana*) with the substitutes *vas* and *nas*. In the phrases "may he protect you" (*tvām pātu*) and "may he protect me" (*mām pātu*), because *yuṣmad* and *asmad* do not follow immediately after a word (*padāt paratvābhāvāt*), the rule "the second case [substitutes] *tvā* and *mā*" does not apply; this is the meaning.
Although here the word *asmacchabda* follows the word *pātu*, there is no fault because two sentences of different times are intended here.
[In the phrase] *saṃvedyo 'smān*,
there is no substitution because the word *asmacchabda* stands at the beginning of a quarter-verse (*pāda*).

Although this verse is in the *anuṣṭubh* meter, the established rule is that each quarter-verse (*pāda*) therein consists of eight syllables. In that regard, in the absence of euphonic combination (*saṃdhi*), the phrase "asmān kṛṣṇaḥ sarvadāvatu" contains nine syllables and thus cannot constitute a quarter-verse.
However, if the *saṃdhi* is performed such that the vowel *o* is treated as the latter part of the preceding word, the status of having eight syllables is violated.

Because *saṃvedya* lacks the status of being a word (*pada*), there is no occurrence of the pronoun *asmad* following a word. However, if [the compound] were treated as having its prior boundary (*pūrvānta*), then *smān*, situated at the beginning of the quarter-verse (*pāda*), would not have the form of the word *asmac*. Nevertheless, because *saṃvedyaḥ*—as qualified by the single-substitute (*ekādeśa*)—is treated as having its prior boundary, it possesses the status of a word.
Furthermore, by the maxim of "that which is modified in one part" (*ekadeśavikṛtanyāya*), *smān* retains the form of the second-case singular of the word *asmad*.
In reality, however, because the vowel *o* belongs to the preceding part, *saṃvedyaḥ* possesses the status of a word (*padatva*), and *smāt* and so forth consist of eight syllables.
Furthermore, because it belongs to the subsequent part, it takes the form of the word *asmad*.

As for the rule "when both [preceding and following] are relied upon, it is neither like the end nor like the beginning," this does not apply here; we shall explain this in the section on the root *iṇ*.
Some, however, offer counter-examples such as: "What [is the point of the restriction] 'not at the beginning of a word'? [Consider: *yuṣmān rakṣatu govindo'smān kṛṣṇassarvadāvatu*.
That is incorrect; for in the case of *yuṣmān*, the rule simply does not apply because it does not follow a word (*pada*).
As for *asmān*, although it does follow a word, it does not follow a word situated within the same sentence (*samānavākya*).

One might object: "Why not simply formulate the rule as *yuṣmadasmadoḥ ṣaṣṭhīcaturthīdvitīyāntayoḥ*? What is the purpose of including the word *sthā* (standing), since even with *sthā*, that same meaning can somehow be obtained? To this he replies: [the sense of] "remaining" (*tiṣṭhati*) is understood from *hāsīḥ*. Therefore, the intended etymological derivation is: those which "stand," meaning they do not abandon, the sixth, fourth, and second case endings.
The meaning is "without abandoning the sixth (genitive) and other case-endings.
The intention is that this results in [the two words] being characterized by non-elided sixth and other case-endings.
Thus: *yuṣmat-putraḥ*.
The word "iti" is used to ensure that [the preceding element] follows immediately after a word ending in a case-suffix (*padāt-paratvam*).
The analysis (*vigraha*) is either *yuvayoḥ putraḥ* (the son of you two) or *yuṣmākam putraḥ* (the son of you all), or *āvayoḥ putraḥ* (the son of us two) or *asmākam putraḥ* (the son of us all).

Here, because the case-suffix has been elided by *luk*, there is no occurrence of the substitute [for the genitive] since the condition of having an audible case-suffix (*śrūyamāṇa-vibhaktikatva*) is absent.

The analysis [of the compound] as "your son" (*tava putraḥ*) and "my son" (*mama putraḥ*) is not intended here, because the substitutes *tvad* and *mad* will be prescribed there by the rule *pratyayottarapadayośca*. "In a single sentence" (*samānavākye*) means that the cause (*nimitta*) and the element possessing the cause (*nimittin*) must reside within the same sentence.
The word *nighāta* denotes the *anudātta* (unaccented) tone.
Regarding the expression "a single finite verb" (*ekatiṅ*): by the term *tiṅ*, a word ending in a *tiṅ* suffix is intended.
The analysis of the compound is "that which has one *tiṅ*.
This is a definition of a sentence (*vākya*), and it is indeed useful for this science [of grammar].
Consequently, there is no lack of extension (*avyāpti*) in cases such as "Look, the deer is running," as is clear in the *Mahābhāṣya* on the *Sūtra* concerning semantic competency (*samartha*).

Regarding "odanam": "odanaṃ paca" is one sentence, and "tava bhaviṣyati" is another sentence. Consequently, because the word *yuṣmad* (in the form *tava*) does not follow a word situated within the same sentence, there is no substitution [of *te* for *tava*]; this is the intended meaning.
"Of *śālī* rice":

this means "of *vrīhi* rice. The genitive case is used here to express the relationship between the material cause (*prakṛti*) and its modification (*vikāra*). "These, namely *vānīva* and so forth," refers to the specific varieties.

And this is established in the Bhāṣya on the sūtra *sapūrvāyāḥ*. Regarding the word *dhāta*, this is an address to Mahādeva; he provides an example for the rule *anvādeśe tu nityam* as follows: *tasyai te namaḥ* (salutations to you for that).

In this context, the preceding sentence—"He who is Agni, the carrier of oblations; he who is Indra, whose arm wields the thunderbolt"—is to be understood. Thus, because there is a restatement (*anvādeśa*) for the purpose of making known another action after something has been employed to enjoin a certain action, the sense is that the substitution (*ādeśa*) is mandatory in that case. Regarding the phrase "when joined with these" (*ebhir yukte*), the meaning is "in connection with these."

Alternatively—the suffix *kta* is used in the sense of the object according to [Pāṇini 3.4.70], "The *kṛtya*, *kta*, and *khalartha* suffixes occur after roots in the sense of the object. When joined with, that is, connected with, these [suffixes], with what? With the word *yuṣmad* and the word *asmad*.
Although those two [forms] end in the dual number by their original nature (*prakṛti*), nevertheless, because they are connected here with each [person] individually, the singular number is employed:
"of you" (*tava*) and "of me" (*mama*),
as well as "of you two" (*yuvayoḥ*) and "of us two" (*āvayoḥ*).

In the forms "yuṣmākam asmākam" and "tubhyam mahyam," the substitution of *am* occurs by the rule "ṅeprathamayoram" [Pāṇini 7.1.28], and the forms *tubhyam* and *mahyam* occur in the dative singular (*ṅayi*) by the rule "tubhyamahau ṅayi" [Pāṇini 7.2.95].
In the forms *yuṣmabhyam* and *asmabhyam*,
as well as in *tvām* and *mām*,
the substitutes *tvam* and *mām* are applied by [Pāṇini 7.2.97], and the substitution of *āt* (long *ā*) is applied by [Pāṇini 7.2.87].
Regarding "yuṣmān" and "asmān":
by [Pāṇini 7.1.29] *śaso na*, the *na* replaces *śas*; the acute accent (*udātta*) is as before.
It is said that "the mention of *yukta* is for the purpose of understanding the direct connection."
The term *yoga* (connection) refers to a connection with [words] such as *ca* (and) that is direct (*sākṣāt*) and without intervention (*avyavadhāna*).
The mention of *yukta* (connected) is for the purpose that its application (*pratipatti*) may occur in this manner.

But how, by the mention of *yukta*, does the understanding of a direct connection come about? He thinks as follows: because this sentence is incomplete, the very mention of the instrumental case (*tṛtīyā-nirdeśa*) will imply the inclusion of the word *yukta*, just as in the rule "In the sense of 'equal' [the suffix *vat* is used] after words other than *tulya* and *upamā*" (Pāṇini 5.1.117).

Therefore, should the mention of "joined" (*yukta*) not be made at all? It is made so that there may be a direct understanding of the connection (*yoga*). But another says: "This is a rule concerning words (*pada-vidhi*), and a rule concerning words applies only to those [words] that are semantically connected (*samartha*). Since the connection is already obtained through the fact that it is a rule concerning words, if the mention of 'joined' is made, is it for the sake of a direct understanding of the connection? This too is incorrect; for it has been stated that even in the absence of semantic connection, operations such as *nighāta* (elision of accent) and so forth occur within a single sentence (*samāna-vākya*).

When, then, is there a direct connection between the particles beginning with *ca* and the pronouns *yuṣmad* and *asmad*? It is when they illuminate meanings such as conjunction (*samuccaya*) that reside within the referents of those pronouns. Here, these particles beginning with *ca* possess meaning through the meaning to be illuminated, namely conjunction and so forth; therefore, when they illuminate properties (*dharma*) such as conjunction that are indeed inherent to *yuṣmad* and *asmad*, then there is a direct connection between the particles beginning with *ca* and *yuṣmad* and *asmad*. But when [the properties] belong to others related to villages and so forth, then it is an indirect connection, not a direct one.
In that case, there is no prohibition regarding connection with *ca* (and): "The village is yours and the city is mine.
Here, the word "village" and the word "city" are joined by the word *ca*; for the meaning of that [word *ca*] is to illuminate their conjunction (*samuccaya*).

However, the words *yuṣmad* (you) and *asmad* (I) are joined with "village" and "city," because here the meaning of a relationship of ownership between those two [words] and those two [nouns] is possible.

But surely, the mention of *yukta* (connected) is for the purpose of understanding direct connection (*sākṣādyoga*), so that it may not apply to what is connected by means of another connection (*yuktayukta*). How then is this done? For a prohibition being stated regarding connection with *ca* and so forth does not extend to what is connected by another connection; indeed, a connection with *ca* and so forth that is itself connected by another connection does not constitute a "connection with *ca* and so forth. Therefore, what is the use of the mention of *yukta* for the sake of understanding direct connection? In that case, this very mention of *yukta* indicates that in this section on prohibitions, a prohibition applies even to what is connected by another connection (*yuktayukta*).

Therefore, what will be stated in the subsequent sūtra—"there is also a prohibition [of the *karmapravacanīya* designation] when joined with words having the sense of 'seeing' (*paśyārtha*)"—becomes logically consistent. The term "having the sense of seeing" (*paśyārthaiḥ*) is a *bahuvrīhi* compound.

In that context, if "seeing" (*paśya*) were derived from the root *dṛś-* with the suffix *śa* (as prescribed by Pāṇini 3.1.137: *pādhradhmādheṭvṛśaḥ śaḥ*) in the sense of the agent (*kartṛ*), then its meaning would be "words having the sense of a seer" (*draṣṭrarthaiḥ*). And in that case, the prohibition "not in the sense of looking at" (*anālocane*) would be difficult to justify.

Therefore, this word *ālocana* is derived from the abstract action (*bhāva-sādhana*)—that is, "the act of perceiving" (*ālocitiḥ ālocanam*). In that case, when a prohibition is stated regarding [the word] joined with terms denoting the agent of seeing (*draṣṭṛ-artha*), what possibility is there for it to apply to something joined with the functions of perception (*ālocana-vṛtti*)? It would not apply at all. When that very same prohibition is stated as "non-perception" (*anālocana*), what possibility is there for it to apply to something joined with the functions of perception? It would not apply at all. How, then, is this prohibition "non-perception" justified? Only if the word *paśyat* is a *bhāva-sādhana*, and not otherwise.

Therefore, by virtue of this very irregular formation (*nipātana*) [according to Pāṇini 3.3.113], the suffix *śa* is applied here in the sense of an abstract action (*bhāva*). In that case, there is the substitution of *paśya-* for the root *dṛś-* according to [Pāṇini 7.3.78], and the single-substitute form (*pararūpatva*) of the two *a*-vowels occurs according to [Pāṇini 6.1.94].
The meaning is: those whose purpose is "seeing" (*paśya-*) are "those whose purpose is seeing" (*paśyārthāḥ*), i.e., those whose purpose is vision.
This word *darśana* is a synonym for the eye (*cakṣus*), as seen, for example, in the rule [Pāṇini 5.4.76]: *akṣṇo'draśanāt*.
Therefore, lest there be a misconception even regarding the eye, he says: "Vision is knowledge.

And that [vision] is subsequently specified as "ocular knowledge" (*cakṣurjñāna*), because the term "ocular knowledge" is mentioned separately; thus, it is understood to be something other than that [general vision].
An example of what was stated directly is: "The village has come after seeing you," and so forth.
The statement, "Having observed that the village was his own, he arrived," and so forth, is logically consistent.
Regarding the phrase "having observed":
the meaning is that he arrived after having ascertained [the situation] with his mind.
"The village sees you" means that it perceives you by means of visual cognition (*cakṣurjñāna*). "And thus it has been illustrated."

The meaning is that the example has been cited in accordance with the very nature of this *iṣṭi* (intended application). Here, the word *saha* signifies "existing together," while the word *pūrva* signifies "preceding" or "position.

*Sapūrvā* is a *bahuvrīhi* compound in the sense of the fifth case (*pañcamyarthe*), meaning "that which has a preceding [word] existing together [with it]. According to [Pāṇini 6.3.82], there is the substitution of *sa-* for *saha*.
"[Of the first case]" (*prathamāyāḥ*).
By the paribhāṣā regarding the inclusion of that which ends in a suffix (Pāṇini 1.1.72), it is understood that the term refers to that which ends in [the suffix].
For this very reason, he says: "from a word ending in the nominative case," and so on, including "optionally for *yuṣmad* and *asmad*."

*Ādeśaḥ* means "instruction" (or statement), and *anvādeśaḥ* means "subsequent instruction" (or reference). *Ananvādeśaḥ* is the negation of *anvādeśaḥ*. In that case, it should be stated that when there is no subsequent instruction (*ananvādeśe*), the case-endings (*vibhaktyāḥ*) of *yuṣmad* and *asmad* occur.
To the question "For what purpose?", he says: "In this [context]," and so forth;

"All indeed," and so forth. Those substitutes that apply to *yuṣmad* and *asmad* when they follow a word ending in the nominative case (*prathamā*) preceded by another word, as well as those others [that apply] when not preceded by such a word—all these indeed should be stated as optional (*vibhāṣā*) when the substitution of *ana* does not occur.

If this is so, one might think that since the option (*vikalpa*) is established everywhere by this very statement, this sūtra is useless; thinking thus, he says: "In that case, not... and so forth. [He asks:

"Is it for the sake of subsequent reference (*anvādeśa*)? If this were not stated, then because of the designation "non-subsequent reference" (*ananvādeśa*), there would be no option regarding subsequent reference after a word ending in the nominative case when preceded by another word.

Why is this so? Even when an *upasaṃkhyāna* (supplementary rule) is made for the sake of ensuring that the option (*vikalpa*) applies even in the case of subsequent reference (*anvādeśa*) from a word ending in the nominative case preceded by *sa-* (as in *sapūrvāt*), this very sūtra must still be formulated.
However, when this [sūtra] is formulated, that *upasaṃkhyāna* need not be made.
How so? By the principle of the "lion's glance" (*siṃhāvalokita-nyāya*), the mention of the option (*vibhāṣā-grahaṇa*) extends back to the preceding rule as well.

In this matter, because the term *vyavasthita-vibhāṣā* (restricted option) is employed, there will be an option in all cases where there is no subsequent reference (*ananvādeśa*); however, in the case of subsequent reference (*anvādeśa*), *dāmnī-āva-* and so on apply invariably, while for a nominative preceded by another word, even in subsequent reference, there is an option. This [sūtra] is commenced since the various accents such as the udātta would otherwise apply according to their respective rules. Regarding the example *pacati gotram*:
one who is unable to provide a livelihood through his own personal effort, but provides it instead by means of falsely claiming to belong to a noble lineage (*gotra*), is described in this way.
"pacati" means "he makes manifest.
The root *pac* (in the Dhātupāṭha, no. 174) signifies "making manifest. Thus: "He makes his lineage known."
The doubling occurs when the sense is that of permanence (*nitya*). Only he who repeatedly proclaims his lineage (*gotra*) is liberated.
[This is stated] because "there is no substitution of the verbal root."

Regarding the form *brāuvo vaciḥ* [Pāṇini 2.4.53], the substitution of *vac* would otherwise apply; its absence is due to a specific irregularity (*nipātana*). In the case of *vicakṣaṇa*, here too, the absence of the substitution of *khyāñ*—which would otherwise apply by the rule *cakṣiṅaḥ khyāñ* [Pāṇini 2.4.54]—is to be understood as resulting from a specific irregularity.

"The word 'nāma' is struck down [as an option] here," because the term *vibhāṣā* (optionally) is carried over [from the previous rule]. And there is no over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) resulting from that carry-over, because it is understood as a *vyavasthitavibhāṣā* (an option restricted to specific cases).

"In this case, it is indeed udātta on the first syllable," because the word *nāman* is udātta on the first syllable by the rule "nabviṣayasyānisantasya" (Phiṭ-sūtra 2.26). [The compound means] "a contemptible lineage."

From the verbal root *guṅ* in the sense of "an indistinct sound" (*avyakte śabde*) [Dhātupāṭha 949], when the suffix *ṣṭran* is applied according to the *uṇādi* rules, the form *gotra* arises. Consequently, by the accent rule for *nit* suffixes, the word *gotra* here has its first syllable accented acute (*ādyudātta*).
[The example is: "he cooks evil" (*pacati pāpam*).
The word *pāpa* is used in the sense of censure; since it follows a form ending in a *siṅ* suffix and does not belong to the *gotra*-class and so forth, it is not elided [by sandhi].

Regarding this mention of "contempt" (*kutsanā*) and "frequency" (*abhīkṣṇya*), there are two possibilities: either it is a qualifier for "unaccented" (*anudātta*)—meaning that words such as *gotra* following a finite verb (*tiṅ*) become unaccented when contempt or frequency is expressed—or else it is a qualifier for the listing (*pāṭha*) of *gotra* and the others—meaning that these [words] function as *gotra*, etc., in these two senses, and they become unaccented when they follow a finite verb. The point is that the specific sequential order in which these are listed among the nominal stems (*prātipadika*) constitutes their designation as *gotra*, etc., only when they occur in those two senses.

In that regard, in the former view, under the rules *cana-cid-iva-gotrādi-taddhita-amreḍiteṣv-agateḥ* [Pāṇini 8.1.57] and [the subsequent rule 8.1.69], the grammatical operation would apply even to those words that signify contempt (*kutsana*) or repetition (*abhīkṣṇya*), because no specific distinction is mentioned. However, in the other view, this fault does not arise;

for those words which do not signify contempt or repetition do not even possess the designation "gotra" and so forth, since only those occurring in the sense of contempt or repetition are recited in the list (*gaṇa*).
Having taken all this into account, he said: "And the inclusion of the terms *kutsana* (censure) and *abhīkṣṇya* (frequency)," and so forth.
"Recitation" (*paṭhata*) refers to the specific arrangement (*sanniveśaviśeṣa*).
That must be understood as being qualified by the word "proper" (*sat*).
He asks, "What is desired by that [sūtra]? and replies with the words beginning with "by that.

But how is it possible for both the recitation of *gotra* and the others, as well as their being unaccented (*anudātta*), to be prescribed by a single effort? He thinks as follows: a split of the rule (*yogavibhāga*) must be made: first, "words beginning with *gotra* that follow a finite verb (*tiṅ*) become unaccented"; then, "in the cases of contempt (*kutsana*) and frequency (*abhīkṣṇya*)," [the rule continues] with "words beginning with *gotra*" alone.
And since there is nothing else to be prescribed in this second connection, the words beginning with *gotra* themselves are qualified by the mention of contempt and frequency.

Alternatively, the Teacher has presented the Sūtra in two ways for his students; both of these are authoritative, and therefore they will accept both. As for the commentary (*vṛtti*), however, it should be understood through a division of sentences as follows: "Words such as *gotra* and so on occur after a finite verb (*tiṅanta*) when expressing contempt or frequency"—meaning that those very words, when following a finite verb, become unaccented (*anudātta*).

But surely, words such as *gotra* and others denote only their own primary meanings, such as lineage and so forth, which are not different from themselves; how then could they denote contempt (*kutsanā*) or frequency (*abhīkṣṇya*)? There is no fault here, for when those very same primary meanings are expressed as qualified by contempt or frequency, then [the words] function with respect to those two qualities. For example, in the expression "a blue lotus" (*nīlam utpalam*), the word *utpala* is acute-accented on its first syllable according to the rule *navviṣayasyānisantasya* (Phiṭ-sūtra 2.26).
In the expressions "it exists" (*bhavati*) and "he cooks" (*pacati*), [the verbal suffixes are similarly treated].
The meaning of this is that "pacatikriyā" (the action of cooking) occurs.

In the word *pacati*, the suffix *śap* and the augment *tiP* are unaccented (*anudātta*); the vowel *a* is accented acute (*udātta*) by the accent of the verbal root; and according to [Pāṇini 8.4.66], the syllable *śa* becomes circumflex (*svarita*).

But surely, *nighāta* (the low-pitched accent) and other such phenomena are prescribed for compound sentences (*samāsa-vākya*), and this [present case] is not even a sentence at all. Therefore, what is the purpose of including the term *atiṅ* (not ending in a finite verb) [in the rule]? Furthermore, for what reason is this not a sentence? [The opponent replies: Because in the definition of a sentence—namely, "A sentence is a finite verb (*ākhyāta*) accompanied by indeclinables (*avyaya*), objects (*kāraka*), and qualifiers (*viśeṣaṇa*)"—singularity (*ekatva*) is intended to be expressed, whereas here there are two finite verbs. [The author replies: This is not a fault. Here too, that which is a finite verb devoid of an object (*akāraka*) is what is intended.
And in this case, that [verb] is only one, namely the word *bhavati*; however, *pacati* is an object (*kāraka*).
For it is stated in the Bhāṣya: "Verbs such as *pacati* (he cooks) become actions; they become the agents of an action.

Furthermore, regarding that which was stated—"A sentence is a collection of words containing a single finite verb (*tiṅ*)"—here too, the term "containing a single finite verb" is used with reference to that finite verb which is the principal element.

And here, only one finite verb (*tiṅanta*) is primary. If this is so, then which among these is the finite verb? It is "bhavati" (he exists). As for "pacati" (he cooks), it is secondary because it serves as a means (*sādhana*). [Objection: "But the agent (*kartā*) is [the primary factor]."

From the root *kṛ*, there is the suffix *luṭ* and the suffix *tās*. By [Pāṇini 2.4.85], the singular ending is replaced by *ḍā*; when *ḍit* follows, there is elision of the final vowel (*ṭilopa*). Regarding the rule "after *tās*" and so forth:
the augment (āgama) is udātta on its first syllable by virtue of the accent of the suffix (*pratyayasvara*).

In cases where there is no elision of the suffix *ṭi*—as in *irtāraḥ*, *kartāraḥ*, and so on—the *lasārvadhātuka* affixes become unaccented by the rule "nāsyanudāttenṅit" (Pāṇini 6.1.180), and consequently, the accent falls on the *tās* suffix itself. However, where there is elision of the *ṭi*, the *lasārvadhātuka* becomes accented by the rule "anudāttasya ca yatrodāttalopaḥ" (Pāṇini 6.1.155). Although the capacity of words such as *yad* depends upon their connection with particles (*nipāta*), nevertheless, because they convey meaning, their composition with the word *yukta* is indeed appropriate.
Alternatively, there is no compound here; rather, because these words are indeclinables (*avyaya*), their case-endings are elided and are not heard.

However, the inclusion of the term "joined" (*yukta*) here is for the purpose of ensuring the direct perception of the connection [with the word *saha*]; therefore, the prohibition does not apply to that which is joined with what is itself joined.
We shall clarify this point even in the subsequent examples.

In this context, the inclusion of the term *yatrayatra* is for the purpose that there may be a prohibition of what is joined with those two [particles] even when it precedes them. For while the prohibition of what follows after them—that which is marked by a *tiṅ* affix—is already established by the rule *yadvṛttānnityam* (Pāṇini 8.1.66), that same rule does not establish the prohibition for what precedes them;
because in that case, by the rule *yadvṛttādibhiḥ pañcamī* (Pāṇini 1.1.67), the prohibition of the *nighāta* accent is taught only for the subsequent element, and not for the other.
Regarding the phrase "yat karoti":
because the suffix *u* in the word *karoti* is udātta, the word is middle-udātta (*madhyodātta*).
Regarding the phrase "nejjihvāyanto narakam patāma" [the reading in the Prātiśākhya is "nojjihrāyanto"].
The substitution of *paterlaṭ*, *mas*, and *śap* [by Pāṇini 7.3.101] results in a long vowel.

Since the root is taught with an indicatory *ṅit* and the suffix is a *lasārvadhātuka*, it becomes unaccented by [Pāṇini 6.1.180]; consequently, this word is acutely accented on its first syllable due to the accent of the verbal root (*dhātusvara*).
"And if he eats" (*sa ceḍ bhuṅkte*).

By [Pāṇini 1.3.66], the *ātmanepada* suffix is applied; because it belongs to the *rudhādi* class, the *śnam* augment is added. As before, the *lasārvadhātuka* suffix is unaccented (*anudātta*). Then, by [Pāṇini 6.4.111], "the elision of *al* after *ina* and *as*," and by [Pāṇini 6.1.161], once the acute accent (*udātta*) has been applied, the word *bhuṅkte* is accented on its final syllable.
Regarding the phrase "if he studies": [this follows].
