For when the locative case (*saptamī*) is employed, the dependence on a subsequent cause is not resorted to if the inclusion of *gatis* is present.

Furthermore, if only "in *gati*" were stated, although the word *mandra* is not a *gati*, the following cause—the *anudātta* accent—would still apply to it here because it depends upon that [preceding] member (*aṅga*). However, when the word "*gateḥ*" (of a *gati*) is present, this fault does not arise; for the following cause is dependent upon a *gati*, and such a [following] cause is absent here. With the words "when that exists," etc., he explains the meaning of the expression "it becomes as if non-existent.
He says: "as if non-existent" (*avidyamānavat*).
This is a designation using the suffix *vati*; "as if non-existent" (*avidyamānavat*) means it exists as something equivalent to what is non-existent.
And the suffix *vati* occurs in the sense of similarity. Thus, its similarity to what is non-existent occurs if, even when that [cause] is present, the effect based upon it does not occur.
And when that [cause] is absent, whatever effect there is, if that same effect occurs even when it [the cause] is present, then it is based on that [cause].

By means of the rule "by the elision of the vocative" (*āmantritanighātena*)—as stated in the *Kāśikā* and *Padamañjarī*—he demonstrates the purpose of the treatment as non-existent (*avidyamānavadbhāva*), which is the absence of whatever grammatical operation would otherwise apply when that [vocative] is present. For example: *devadatta yajñadatta*.

Here, because the preceding word is treated as non-existent, the elision of the accent (*nighāta*) does not occur; consequently, the word *yajñadatta* retains its acute accent on the first syllable by the rule governing the vocative case (*āmantritādyudāttatva*, Pāṇini 6.1.198).
"Devadatta, my village is my own property"— in such cases, the substitutes *tad* and *mam* are prescribed by rule 7.2.96. "In such instances as these," and so forth.

By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), examples such as "Devadatta, this is given to you" are included, [showing that] "the substitutes for *yuṣmad* and *asmad* do not occur," according to rules such as Pāṇini 8.1.22. By the statement beginning with "The purpose [of the rule] is to prohibit [the substitution] immediately before an honorific expression," he demonstrates the purpose of the treatment as if non-existent (*avidyamānavadbhāva*) even when that vocative exists— that is, the grammatical operation which would otherwise apply when the vocative is absent.

Regarding the passage beginning with "even in [the case of] 'yāvad devadatta pacasi'," the meaning of the word *api* should be understood as follows: even where the vocative (*āmantrita*) acts as an interrupter [of the connection]. For example: *devadattaḥ pacati*.
In this case, because of the absence of non-existence (*avidyamānatva*), the lack of accentuation (*anighāta*) for the finite verb indeed occurs. Regarding the word "prior" (*pūrva*):
is it not the case that Devadatta is prior even to what follows? No; since there is nothing subsequent here, Devadatta does not possess the status of being "prior."
When the acute accent on the first syllable of a vocative (*āmantrita*) is to be applied, [the preceding word] does not behave as if it were non-existent.

For example, in "devadatta pacasi" (O Devadatta, you cook), the word *devadatta* possesses the quality of being prior with respect to the word *pacasi*; therefore, by virtue of the rule regarding non-existence (*avidyamānavadbhāva*), that [prior status] would have to occur, and consequently, the acute accent on the first syllable of the vocative would not apply to it.

Regarding the two objections raised here—namely, that in the phrase “*imaṃ me gaṅge yamune*,” the word *gaṅgā* would lose its proximity to the word *yamunā*, and thus it might obstruct the status of being a cause for the *nighāta* (elision of accent), resulting in the word *yamunā* not undergoing *nighāta*—he says “*pūrvatvaṃ ca*,” etc., having anticipated these two points.
The particle *ca* is used in the sense of restriction (*avadhāraṇe*) and is displaced in its position [in the verse].
It should be understood as meaning “only in relation to what follows.”
The particle *iti* is used here in the sense of a reason (*hetu*).

When the state of being something belongs to certain things in relation to another thing, then for those things whose state is being restated (*anūdyamāna*), the property (*dharma*) that is being enjoined (*vidhīyamāna*) is understood as pertaining specifically to that [related] object.

For example: "The son is attentive to his duties. Here, the son's state of being a son is dependent upon [the father]; thus, when he is restated by way of his state of being a son, the attentiveness to duties enjoined for him is understood as being attentive to those specific duties in relation to which his status as a son exists, and not to other duties.
And this "precedence" (pūrvatva) is indeed relative to something else.

Therefore, when the status of being as if non-existent (avidyamānavadbhāva) is prescribed for that which is addressed (āmantrita) by way of reference, that very thing to which the precedence is relative becomes the "other" (para) with respect to whose operation it occurs, and not with respect to anything else.
With respect to what kind of operation? With respect to an operation conditioned by itself, or one conditioned by another.
That which has its own [vowel] as its cause is *svanimittam*; this means it is an *āmantrita* (vocative).
That which has another word as its cause is *antanimittam*.

Since, when an operation (*kārya*) must be performed for a subsequent element, that *āmantrita* becomes as if non-existent, but not when an operation must be performed for itself—therefore, in the example *devadatta pacasīti*, the acute accent on the first syllable of the *āmantrita* is not an operation belonging to the subsequent element; rather, it belongs to the *āmantrita* itself.

Since the quality of being unaccented (*anudātta*) belongs to what follows [the vocative], that [preceding word] indeed becomes as if non-existent. Having thus refuted the first objection, he says "imaṃ me gaṅge yamune," etc., in order to refute the second.
Here too, the state of being "prior" is relative to what follows; this is precisely the reason.
It should be connected as follows: the word *gaṅge*, ending in a vocative case, because it is itself as if non-existent, does not serve as the cause [for the accentuation of the following word].

In what context does [the preceding word] not function as a cause (*nimitta*)? It is when the subsequent word *sumuneḥ* must be made unaccented (*anudātta*). And it does not obstruct the status of *me* as a cause; thus, the word *gaṅge*, being previously addressed (*āmantrita*), behaves as if non-existent (*avidyamānavat*) when the word *yamune* is to be made unaccented—this depends on everything [stated in the rule]. Here, because the word *pūrva* (preceding) is a relative term (*sambandhiśabda*), the status of being as if non-existent is prescribed for the preceding vocative (*āmantrita*) when an operation (*kārya*) is to be performed upon the subsequent [word].

In the verse beginning "imaṃ me gaṅge yamune," although the word *me*—which is other than the word *gaṅge*—is the cause for the unaccented (anudātta) status of the word *yamune*, nevertheless, that unaccented status is an operation (*kārya*) belonging solely to the vocative (*āmantrita*). Therefore, when that [operation] is to be performed, the word *gaṅge* becomes as if non-existent.

For this very reason, it was stated previously: "Even when there is another cause, because it is treated as non-existent by this [rule], it does not obstruct the causal status of the word *me* with respect to its own accentuation (*nighāta*)."
What is the purpose of employing the particle *vat*? It is so that [the treatment] may apply even to its own substratum (*svāśraya*). For example: *ām bho devadatta tri*.

In this case, the prohibition of the low-pitched accent (*nighāta*) based on the rule "an *āmantrita* separated by one word from an *ām* is not [low-pitched] when not in close proximity" (*āma ekāntaram āmantritam anantike*, Pāṇini 8.1.55) becomes established.

Furthermore, this [word *tri*] should be understood as having a plural ending; for if it ended in the singular, there would be no such status of being "as if non-existent" (*avidyamānavat*), due to the prohibition [of that status] stated in "after *ām*, [there is no *avidyamānavat* treatment] for a vocative" (*āmreḍite ca*, Pāṇini 8.1.73).

However, [the form] exists according to the rule *bahuvacanānte tu* (Pāṇini 8.1.74). Now, one might object: words employed for the sake of another convey an extension (*atideśa*), as in "The Vāhīka is an ox. In that case, an extension is understood from the statement "that which exists [in the original] is [treated as] that which does not exist [in the derivative]. And since the property of extension implies the cessation of the word's own original basis (*svāśraya-nivṛtti*), there would be no need for the suffix *-vat*. True, this is so; however, he thinks as follows: without the suffix *-vat*, there would be an uncertainty regarding usage, such that it might be thought that something preceded by an address (*āmantrita*) does not [function as such] in certain instances.

And thus, for that which is addressed by another address, there would not be the state of being separated by one word from the preceding. "In a coreferential construction" (*samānādhikaraṇa*)—according to the *Kāśikā*—means having the same denotation.
For example: "O Agni, Lord of the House."

Is the word *agni* here denotative of fire in general? Although it expresses a universal, when it is delimited by the word *gṛhapati*, which denotes a particular, it remains restricted to that specific fire called the *gārhapatya*; thus, the word *gṛhapati* stands in grammatical apposition (*samānādhikaraṇa*) with it. In the same way, the state of apposition should be understood in the expression "the student, the matted-hair ascetic, the teacher" (*māṇavaka jaṭilādhyāpaka*). Here, due to the difference in perspective, the word *jaṭilaka* is neither a universal nor a particular; rather, it is a particular relative to the student, while it possesses the status of a universal relative to the teacher.

In this case, when *jaṭilaka* is in apposition (*samānādhikaraṇa*), the status of being as if non-existent (*avidyamānavat*) does not apply to *māṇavaka* with respect to [the following], but rather to the word *jaṭilaka* with respect to the preceding [word]. By the rule beginning with "of the preceding" (*pūrvasya*), he demonstrates the result of the prohibition. For example: *devadatta pacasi*.

In that context, since the *lakāra* (verbal suffix) is prescribed for the agent (*kartṛ*) precisely where the referent of the word "Devadatta" resides, the form *pacasi* ("you cook") stands in grammatical apposition (*samānādhikaraṇa*) with the word "Devadatta.
However, it does not become a vocative (*āmantrita*), as in "O Devadatta, Yajñadatta!

Here, the word "Devadatta" is not taken as a proper name (*saṃjñāśabda*); what then? It is based on action (*kriyānimittaka*). Otherwise, because a proper name refers to a single specific entity, it would not be a term expressing a general property (*sāmānyavacana*).
"These are synonyms"—
by this he shows the absence of being a general term;
for a general term is dependent upon particulars.

And no distinction whatsoever should be stated here regarding that in relation to which [something] might be a "universal" (sāmānya), because all [terms] have an absolutely non-different meaning; otherwise, they would not be synonyms.

But how are these known to be synonyms? To this he says: "For it has been said thus," and so forth. This statement is intended as an alternative to the previous [position], which held that [the deity] exists eternally as if present: "The gods are the refuge."

When there is the quality of being as if non-existent (*avidyamānavattva*), then the vocative *śaranyāḥ* has its first syllable acute (*ādyudātta*); otherwise, there is the suppression accent (*nighāta*).

Similarly, in the case of "brāhmaṇā vaiyākaraṇāḥ," one should understand that the word *vaiyākaraṇa* has its first syllable acute and may optionally have the suppression accent. Now, for what purpose is the mention of "specific term" (*viśeṣavacana*), since the term "general term" (*sāmānyavacana*) continues to apply, and a general term depends upon a specific term, such that even without the mention of a "specific term," a "specific term" would be understood? To this, he says: "Precisely because of the governing rule of 'general term,'" and so forth.

For one of dull intellect who is unable to understand it in this way, the inclusion of specific words with clear meaning is made. If, then, because a general term requires a specific one, the operation is understood from the mention of the general term, then the same operation would be understood in the previous rule [Pāṇini 8.1.73] as well; and in that case, the counter-example "devadatta yajñadatta" would be deficient in two respects; for just as the word "yajñadatta" is not in apposition, so too is the specific term.

Now, is this [the word *devadatta*] a term of specification (*viśeṣavacana*)? If that were so, then just as in the expression "O Agni, lord of the house" (*agne gṛhapate*), the word *agni*, although a general term, becomes a qualifier for that specific fire when delimited by the word *gṛhapati*, which denotes a specific [role], and thus the word *gṛhapati* stands in grammatical apposition (*samānādhikaraṇa*) with it; likewise, the word *devadatta*, being delimited by the word *yajñadatta*, which denotes a specific [individual], would remain fixed upon that very specific referent, and thus the word *yajñadatta* would stand in grammatical apposition with it—this is what must be considered.

Thus ends the first quarter of the eighth chapter in the *Kāśikā-vivaraṇapañjikā* composed by the venerable master Jinendrabuddhi, who was like a second Bodhisattva. Now begins the second quarter of the eighth chapter: Is this a rule (*yoga*), or a general metarule (*paribhāṣā*), or perhaps a governing heading (*adhikāra*)? These two alternatives are to be considered.

In this regard, if this were a *paribhāṣā* (a metarule), then throughout the entire *Aṣṭādhyāyī*, whatever follows would be considered non-existent (*asiddha*) with respect to what precedes it. Consequently, in the rule [7.1.9] *tadoḥ saḥ sāvanantyayoḥ*, because the substitution of *yatva* for *tyadādi* words would be non-existent, the substitution of *ais* in forms such as *taiḥ* and *yaiḥ* would not occur. Having observed this defect in the view that it is a *paribhāṣā*, and having determined through its *svarita* accent that it is an *adhikāra* (a governing heading) according to [1.3.11], he says: "This is an *adhikāra* [heading] stating 'non-existent in what precedes'. The phrase "until the end of the book" is intended to indicate the limit [of its scope].
The word "therein" (*tatra*) is used to introduce the sentence.
Regarding "with a quarter" (*sapādā*): it is called *sapādā* because it exists together with a quarter (*pāda*), namely, the one that was just introduced immediately preceding it.
Regarding the term *saptādhyāyī*:
it is a collective compound (*samāhāra*) of seven chapters, with the feminine suffix *ṅīp* applied according to Pāṇini 4.1.21.

In some places, the reading is *sapādasaptādhyāyī*; in that case, it is a descriptive determinative compound (*viśeṣaṇasamāsa*) meaning "that which consists of seven chapters plus one quarter," with the masculine form applied by virtue of the rule on *puṃvadbhāva*.
"This" refers to that which is about to be stated:
"the chapter minus one quarter."
"Deficient by one quarter" (*pādonah*) means an incomplete chapter, i.e., lacking one quarter.
By the statement "it becomes unestablished" (*asiddho bhavati*), and so forth,

he demonstrates that here the status of being unestablished within the grammatical system (*śāstrāsiddhatva*) is intended, both by the mention of a chapter deficient by one quarter and by the mention of subsequent rules (*uttarottarayoga*).

For if one resorts to the non-establishment (*asiddhatva*) of the effect, then just as when the killer of Devadatta is slain, Devadatta does not reappear, so too, once the non-establishment of the effect has been set forth, there is no restoration of the original form (*prakṛti*). Consequently, since the rule for the substitution of *t* by *tuṣm* applies precisely because the [original] state is not established, and not because it is non-established according to the rules, this undesirable consequence does not arise. Moreover, the primacy belongs to the rule (*śāstra*), while the priority belongs to the effect (*kārya*) only in a figurative sense.

The grammatical operation (*kārya*) for which the rule (*śāstra*) is prior is also called "prior" by way of metaphorical designation (*upacāra*), but its priority does not exist inherently; for there is no specific spatial arrangement (*sanniveśaviśeṣa*).
Indeed, the operation resides in the target form (*lakṣya*); and just as the target form lacks such an arrangement, so too does the operation residing therein.
Furthermore, when primary priority exists, the adoption of a figurative sense is not permissible.
Therefore, the word "prior" (*pūrva*) is employed in the rule by means of the inclusion of the word "prior.
And its status as "prior" occurs only in relation to a subsequent rule (*para-śāstra*).
Consequently, it is logical that this [rule] should establish the non-validity (*asiddhatva*) of that very subsequent rule in relation to which its own status as "prior" exists.
And once the non-establishment of the treatise has been established, the non-establishment of its purpose is effectively established as well, because the latter is dependent upon the former.
The word *siddha* signifies "accomplished";
its meaning is "that which has been brought to completion."
That which is unestablished is called "unaccomplished.
Furthermore, another treatise—that which is already accomplished—cannot be rendered into a state of non-accomplished existence even by a hundred words.
Otherwise, no one would ever experience a state of being overwhelmed by suffering; for by the mere statement that it is "unestablished," one cannot bring about the non-accomplishment of suffering.

Therefore, just as when it is said, "This is a non-Brāhmaṇa given by a Brāhmaṇa," an extension (atideśa) is understood, so too here, when "asiddha" is stated, an extension is understood; thus he says, "it becomes as if unestablished" (*asiddhavat bhavati*).
To clarify this very point, he says, "the operation of what is established" (*siddhakāryam*), and so forth.
For it becomes as if unestablished only if it does not perform that operation which belongs to what is established.
Regarding the phrase "tad etat" and so forth:

"tat" (that) refers to the reason; because the meaning of the word *asiddha* has just been stated, therefore this statement of *asiddha* is for the purpose of prohibiting that which has a grammatical operation (*ādeśa*) as its cause (*lakṣaṇa*). That which has a grammatical operation as its cause or condition is called *ādeśalakṣaṇa*; [the term refers to] the prohibition of such [an operation].

That which has this as its purpose or motive is described as such. Regarding the phrase "and for the sake of the occurrence of that which is characterized by an original rule (*utsarga-lakṣaṇa-bhāva*)," an *utsarga* is that which is set aside or superseded; thus, *utsarga* refers to the characteristic of the original element (*sthānin*). That whose characteristic or cause is an *utsarga* is "characterized by an original rule" (*utsarga-lakṣaṇa*), namely an operation (*kārya*). The "occurrence" (*bhāva*) of that is its arising, which is the "occurrence of that which is characterized by an original rule. That which has this as its purpose or motive is described as such.

In the phrase "asmā uddhara" and so forth, the word *asmai* is the dative case of the pronoun *idam*. Following the word *uddhara*, the substitution of *ā* occurs according to [Pāṇini 7.1.29], and by [Pāṇini 6.1.66], there is the elision of the letter *v*.

When that has been performed, the rule for the lengthening of a vowel with its homogeneous counterpart (Pāṇini 6.1.101) would apply; however, because the elision of *v* is considered non-existent (*asiddha*) for the purposes of this rule, it does not take effect.
"Because the elision of *v* (vyalopa) is not established (*asiddhatvāt*).
By virtue of its purpose, the rule concerning the elision of *v* is referred to by the term "elision of *v*.
Alternatively, because the rule for the elision of *v* is not established, it is said that "the elision of *v* is not established."
In these examples, the purpose of stating that [the substitute] is *asiddha* is the prohibition of the characteristics of the substitute (*ādeśalakṣaṇapratiṣedha*).
Now, in order to show those examples for which the presence of the general rule (*utsargalakṣaṇabhāva*) is the purpose, he says: "amudhmai," etc.
These are the singular forms of the fourth, fifth, and seventh cases of the pronoun *adas*.
Regarding the rule *tyadādīnām atvaṃ* [Pāṇini 7.2.102]:

even though the status of being "not established" (*asiddhatva*) does not apply here, the substitution of *u* [for *t*] occurs by virtue of its higher position [in the *Aṣṭādhyāyī*], namely *ato guṇe* [Pāṇini 6.1.97]. Consequently, because there is no longer a stem ending in the vowel *a*, the suffixes *smāi* and others—such as *smāi* and *smaḥ* prescribed by *sarvanāmnaḥ smai* [Pāṇini 7.1.14] and *ṅeprathamayoram* [Pāṇini 7.1.28]—would not occur.
However, when the preceding rule is considered "not established," those suffixes do indeed occur.

"Because the substitution of *u* (utva) is not established"— here too, by virtue of its subservience to that [rule], the word "substitution of *u*" refers to the grammatical rule (*śāstra*) for such substitution.
This is the verse beginning with "śuṣkikā."
In this context, the term "illustration" (*nidarśanam*) is connected individually with each [example] beginning with *śuṣkikā*.
Regarding the rule "and for *jhal* sounds when there is *ca*-substitution," the fact that [the former rule] is not established (*asiddha*) here has not been stated for fear of breaking the meter.

Even though not explicitly stated, it is understood from the context as "śuṣkikā. From the root *śuṣ* in the sense of "drying" (Dhātupāṭha 1183), the suffix *kta* is applied; by [Pāṇini 8.2.51], there is the substitution of *ka*; then the feminine suffix *ṭāp*. In the sense of "unknown," the suffix *ka* is added by [Pāṇini 5.3.70]; then, by [Pāṇini 7.4.13], there is shortening [of the vowel]; then again *ṭāp*. By [Pāṇini 7.3.44] and following, the substitution of *it* occurs invariably, and not optionally by [Pāṇini 7.3.46] and following, because [the latter rule] is considered asiddha with respect to [the former].

Regarding the term *śuṣkajaṅghā*: this is a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "she whose shanks are dry. According to [Pāṇini 6.3.37], the prohibition of *puṃvadbhāva* (masculine-like substitution) does not apply here;
this should be connected with the present context because [the rule at] 8.2.51 is considered *asiddha* (non-existent for the purposes of the preceding rule).

But surely, even if the [reason] is unestablished (*asiddhatva*), the prohibition of the former state (*pūrvadbhāvapratiṣedha*) would still not apply here, because of the statement: "In the prohibition regarding [roots] having *ka* as an upadhā, the mention of *taddhita* suffixes must be made" (Pāṇini Dhātupāṭha 7.3.3)? No; this is the opinion of the author of the Vārttika, but according to the opinion of the author of the Sūtras and the author of the Ślokavārttika, this purpose has not been set forth here. For these two accept the prohibition regarding [roots] having *ka* as an upadhā in a general sense. As in: *kṣāmimān*.

From the roots *kṣai*, *jai*, and *ṣai* in the sense of "wasting away" (*kṣaye*)—as per Dhātupāṭha 913, 914, and 915—the vowel substitution prescribed by [Pāṇini 6.1.45] applies, and by [Pāṇini 8.2.53], the *t* of the past passive participle suffix (*niṣṭhā*) is replaced by *m*. Thus, when the form *kṣāma-* is established, one should apply either the suffix *iñ* according to [Pāṇini 4.1.95], or the suffix *ini* according to [Pāṇini 5.2.115], or the possessive suffix *matup*.
This applies to the root *vah* and so forth.

From the root *vah* (meaning "to carry," Dhātupāṭha 1004), the suffix *niṣṭhā* (the past passive participle suffix -ta) is applied; there is vocalization (*samprasāraṇa*) [of the *v*]. By the rule *ho ḍaḥ* (Pāṇini 8.2.31), the substitution of *ḍha* occurs; by *ḍho ḍhe lopaḥ* (8.2.40), the first *ḍha* is elided; by *ṣṭunā ṣṭuḥ* (8.4.41), the substitution of *ṣṭu* occurs; by *ḍhalope pūrvasya dīrgho 'ṇaḥ* (6.3.111), the preceding vowel is lengthened. Thus, the form *ūḍha* is established. Then, the causative suffix *ṇic* is added in the sense of "he causes that to be done" (*tam ācaṣṭe*). By the Vārttika *ṇāviṣṭhavat kāryaṃ prātipadikasya* (Vārttika 813), because of the status of being like the superlative suffix *iṣṭhan*, the *ṭi*-portion (*ū*) is elided.
From that [base ending in *ṇic*], the suffix *luṅ* (past tense) is applied, and by the rule *ṇiśridrusubhyaḥ* (3.1.48), the suffix *caṅ* is applied.

In this case, because the status of being a verbal root (*dhātu*), the *aṣṭu* designation, and so forth, are not established [by the time the *caṅ* suffix is applied], that *ṇ* which undergoes *ṭilopa*—by virtue of the rule "that which is performed upon the *ṇ* is as if it were the original" (*sthānivadbhavati*; Pāṇini 1.1.56)—undergoes reduplication of the element *hata* according to "when *caṅ* follows" (Pāṇini 6.1.11), and the substitution of *cu* according to "the *cu* replaces the *jhal*" (Pāṇini 7.4.62). Thus, in place of the aspirated (*mahāprāṇa*) *ha*, there is the aspirated *jha*; in place of *jha*, there is *ja* according to "the *ja* replaces the *jhal*" (Pāṇini 8.4.54); then the augment *āṭ* is added according to "after *āṭ*" (Pāṇini 6.4.72), and the *vṛddhi* replacement occurs according to "and after *āṭ*" (Pāṇini 6.1.87).

Now, one might ask: why does the treatment as *saN*-like (*sanvadbhāva*), prescribed by the rule *sasvalladhuni caṅpare* [Pāṇini 7.4.93], not occur here? To this he says: "In the absence of elision of a vowel" (*anaglope*), and so forth.

If, then, because of the prohibition by the rule "in the absence of elision of a vowel," the *sanvadbhāva* does not take place, would it not follow that the form *aujiḍhat* (or *aujaḍhat*, as read in the Prācīna manuscript) could not be established? To this he says: *aujiḍhat*, and so forth. [The example given is] *guḍaliṇmān*.

The word *guḍaṃ leḍhi* [one who licks molasses] is formed with the suffix *kvip*; from that stem, the possessive suffix *matup* is added; as before, there is the substitution of *ḍh* by rule 8.2.39, resulting in *guḍaḍ-mat*. Then, when the *vatva* (substitution of *v*) for the *mat* is to be applied, the substitutions of *ḍha* and *jaś* are considered *asiddha* (unestablished); therefore, the *vatva* prescribed by rule 8.2.10 (*jhayaḥ*) does not occur. In the *Kārikā*, the mention of the *jaśtva* of *jhal* sounds is for the purpose of illustration (*upalakṣaṇa*). By this, he shows: "This is merely an illustration for words such as *śuṣkikā* and others, but it is not an exhaustive enumeration (*parigaṇana*)."

For if it were said that when the seven chapters and a quarter (sapādā saptādhyāyī) are to be applied, the [remaining] three-quarters of a chapter are unestablished (*asiddha*), then those applications of the genitive (*ṣaṣṭhī-nirdeśa*), locative (*saptamī-nirdeśa*), and ablative (*pañcamī-nirdeśa*) which are made here would also be unestablished. Consequently, in the rule *ato bhisa ais* [Pāṇini 7.1.9], because the genitive reference would be unestablished, the rule *ṣaṣṭhī sthāneyogā* [Pāṇini 1.1.49] would not apply. Thus, this genitive would instead signify proximity (*sāmīpya-yoga*), and consequently, even that which is proximate to a *saṃyogānta* (a word-final conjunct consonant) would undergo elision (*lopa*).

> [[8.2.26]] Even here, because the reference by the locative case is not established as valid, the paribhāṣā "tasminniti nirdiṣṭe pūrvasya" (P. 1.1.65) would not apply. Consequently, since there would be no restrictive rule stating that [the operation] must occur only for the preceding [element] in immediate proximity, there would be elision of either the preceding or the following [element]—whether in immediate proximity or separated—before a *jhal* consonant in general.

Regarding the rule *hrasvādaṅgāt* [Pāṇini 8.2.27] and others, since the designation by the ablative case (*pañcamīnirdeśa*) would not be subject to the status of being "not established" (*asiddhatva*) due to the application of [the principle] *pūrvatrāsiddham* [Pāṇini 1.1.67], there would be no restriction; consequently, the elision (*lopa*) might undesirably apply either to what precedes or what follows, whether immediately contiguous or separated. Therefore, he says: "Those here which are designations by the genitive case," and so forth.
But what is the reason that the status of being "not established" does not occur? To this he says: "For at the time of the operation," and so forth.

For if it were the case that "the technical terms and rules of interpretation (*saṃjñā-paribhāṣa*) are according to their enunciation" (*yathoddeśaṃ saṃjñāparibhāṣam*; Vyākaraṇa-mahābhāṣya, Pāṭha 59), then these rules of interpretation, being situated in the preceding portion [of the grammar], would not be considered *asiddha* with respect to the mention of the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī-nirdeśa*) and so forth. However, it is not the case that the technical terms and rules of interpretation are according to their enunciation; rather, it is "the technical terms and rules of interpretation are at the time of the operation" (*kāryakālaṃ saṃjñāparibhāṣam*; Vyākaraṇa-mahābhāṣya, Pāṭha 58). For technical terms and rules of interpretation are indeed occasioned by the operations (*kārya*). Therefore, they are employed precisely where the operation occurs; thus, they exist only in the [context of] instruction (*upadeśa*).

Therefore, since the rules (*nirdeśa*) occupy the same location [as the technical terms], there is no priority (*pūrvatva*) for the technical rules (*paribhāṣā*) here; consequently, how could there be the contingency of those [rules] being treated as *asiddha* when they ought to be applied? If the technical terms and rules (*saṃjñā-paribhāṣā*) were to apply at the time the operation is to be performed (*kāryakāla*), would not this rule [P. 1.1.56], "the technical terms and rules stand [in their place]," apply here? What would be the fault in that? From the roots *sphur* and *sphul* in the sense of "trembling" (Dhātupāṭha 1389, 1390), and *gur* in the sense of "lifting up" (Dhātupāṭha 1396), if the suffix *ṇyat* were applied by P. 3.1.124 (*ṛhalorṇyat*), then forms such as *disphoryam* and *avagoryam* would not be established.

For when this technical rule (*paribhāṣā*) is present, the lengthening [of the vowel] by the rule *hali ca* [Pāṇini 8.2.77] would apply, overriding the *guṇa* substitution due to its higher status; therefore, he says: “But this [rule], ‘In case of conflict, the latter [prevails]’,” and so forth.
The connection with the subject at hand is that this technical rule, *vipratiṣedhe param* [Pāṇini 1.4.2], does not operate here.
Why does it not operate? He says: “By which,” and so forth.

For a conflict occurs between two rules of equal strength. But here, the subsequent rule— such as *hali ca* [Pāṇini 8.2.77] and so forth— which competes with the preceding rule such as *pugantasya* [Pāṇini 7.3.86] and desires to override it, is itself considered *asiddha* (non-existent) with respect to that preceding rule.

Therefore, because their strengths are unequal, there is no conflict; thus, this technical rule (*paribhāṣā*), "In case of conflict, the latter [prevails]" (*vipratiṣedhe param* [Pāṇini 1.4.2]), does not apply.
The phrase "and so forth" (*tathā ca*) and so on means: such being the case, when this *paribhāṣā* does not operate.

If, then, when a preceding operation is to be performed, that which follows is considered unestablished (*asiddha*), this being the case, when a general rule (*utsarga*) is to be applied, the subsequent exception (*apavāda*) would be unestablished.

Consequently, in the forms *dogdhā* and *dogdhṛm*, because the *gha* [substitution] prescribed by "gha for roots beginning with *da*" (Pāṇini 8.2.32) would be unestablished, the substitution of *ḍha* would occur for the *dha*. To this, he says: "But regarding the object of an exception," and so forth. Even if that which follows—even within the domain of an exception—were unestablished when a general rule is to be applied, the statement of the exception would be rendered useless due to its lack of scope (*nirviṣayatvāt*).

Therefore, even for the subsequent exception (*apavāda*), there is no lack of established validity (*asiddhatva*) due to the authority of the statement. [Objection: But if it is by virtue of the authority of the statement, would their existence not occur alternately (*paryāyeṇa*)? In that case, how could there be the consequence of redundancy (*vaiyarthyaprasaṅga*)? [Reply: This is not so; for if the exception were to occur alternately, the prescription of the *dhatva* [substitution] by the rule "vā druhamuha" (Pāṇini 8.2.33) would be purposeless. Furthermore, the word "kṛtaḥ" is connected only with the mention of *tug* just mentioned immediately before, and not with all the [suffixes] beginning with *su*.
Otherwise, just as the connection of the word *vidhi* with each [element] was shown, he should likewise show its connection here.

In this case, when this word *vidhi* is connected with *su*-suffixes and so forth, would it be connected as having the sense of an abstract action (*bhāvasādhana*), or as having the sense of an object (*karmasādhana*)? If the first alternative is adopted, then in the forms *rājabhiḥ* and *takṣabhiḥ*, when the substitution of *ais* is to be applied, the non-application of the rule regarding the non-validity (*asiddhatva*) of the elision of *n* (*nalopa`) would not be obtained; for when [the term *vidhi*] has the sense of an abstract action, the status of non-validity must apply where there is the prescription of something that does not yet exist, but not where something already existing is concerned.

And here, there is no prescription for *sup* when it is non-existent; what then? It is prescribed only when it exists. Therefore, even in cases such as *rājabhyām* and *rājabhyaḥ*, where *ais* replaces [the case-ending] and where lengthening by *supi ca* [Pāṇini 7.3.102] and the change to *e* by *bahuvacane jhalyet* [Pāṇini 7.3.103] are to be applied, the status of being "asiddha" (non-existent for the purpose of the preceding rule) does not apply at all. This is because here, the prescription of lengthening and the change to *e* occurs when *sup* follows, but not when *sup* is non-existent.

In the other view, however, since the rule prescribes [the substitution] only for those vowels that are actually present (*satām*), the elision (*lopa*) is intended to be treated as non-existent (*asiddhatva*); yet this is not established. For when the word *vidhi* (prescription) is used in the sense of the object (*karmasādhana*), and is connected with those [vowels], then while they are present, another operation would have to be prescribed for them, and they must consequently be regarded as non-existent due to that non-existence. It cannot, however, be said that the word *vidhi* is connected with the object (*karma*) in the sense of the *sup*-suffixes, while it is connected with the abstract state (*bhāva*) in the case of *svara* and the others.

"One single term *vidhi* is included in the Sūtra; and that [term] must be either an abstract noun (*bhāvasādhana*) or an object noun (*karmasādhana*), but not both, for it is not possible for one single thing to function as both. To refute this objection, he says: "This word *vidhi*, etc.

If indeed the word *vidhi* were connected with the collection [of suffixes] such as *sup* and *svar*, then this fault would arise. But it is not connected with the collection; rather, it is connected with each [suffix] individually, beginning with *sub*.

And when this [principle] is applied individually, for as many auxiliaries as it is connected with, there arise such statements as: "In the rule concerning vowels (*svarādi*), the elision of *m* (*malopa*) is as if non-existent (*asiddha*)," and so forth.

The statement "The elision of *n* (*nalopa*) is as if non-existent in the rules concerning case-endings (*sup*), accent (*svara*), technical names (*saṃjñā*), and the suffix *tuG*" is itself a summary statement (*grahaṇakavākya*) serving as the basis for those very rules.
And since those sentences are distinct, the injunctive word (*vidhi-śabda*) is likewise distinct.
Among them, some are formed by means of the action (*bhāva-sādhana*), and some are formed by means of the object (*karman-sādhana*).

In that context, while the injunction of the very [roots] *svar*, *saṃjñā*, *tu*, *kāma*, and *sati* ought to be carried out, the non-establishment (*asiddhatva*) of the elision of *n* (*nalopa*) is stated; and because they are being enjoined by that [injunction], they attain the status of objects (*karman*) or states (*bhāva*).

Therefore, since the object (*karman*) is not expressed by a word denoting an action (*vidhiśabda*) that functions as an abstract noun (*bhāvasādhana*), the genitive case must apply to these [words] by the rule *kartṛ-karmaṇoḥ kṛti* [Pāṇini 2.3.65].

Consequently, the abstract-noun-denoting [action] is connected with those [words] joined by the genitive of the object (*karma-ṣaṣṭhī*), and [it is also connected] with the nominal suffix (*sup*) which expresses a general relation through a genitive ending.
Thus it is said: "that which functions as an action" (*karmasādhanaḥ*).

It denotes merely the connection with the action being enjoined by the *sup* suffix. However, it should be understood that the genitive (*ṣaṣṭhī*) is used where the genitive is prescribed by the rule *śeṣe* [Pāṇini 2.3.50]. The compound *sambandhasāmānyavacanī ṣaṣṭhī* is a genitive-tatpuruṣa compound; furthermore, *sā cāsau ṣaṣṭhī ca* is a descriptive (karmadhāraya) compound. Thus, the term refers to that *sup* suffix at the end of which stands a genitive expressing a general relation.

A connection with a word expressing an injunction (*vidhiśabda*) that has "action" as its efficient cause (*karmasādhana*) is not possible for a nominal suffix (*sup*) joined with a genitive of action (*karmaṣaṣṭhī*); for such a genitive of action is untenable. If indeed the *sup* were the object (*karman*), then the genitive of action would apply to it; however, that *sup* is not the object, because it is being prescribed [by the rule]. Rather, it is the operation (*kārya*) related to that [prescribed suffix] which is the object.

Because it is being prescribed, that action is expressed by the word of its injunction; therefore, even in that case, a genitive of action (*karma-ṣaṣṭhī*) is not possible, let alone in the case of a *sup*-ending word that does not denote an action. [The reading in the Kāśikā-pāṭha is *akarmaṇi supi*. This refers to the phrase beginning with "by that" (*tena*).

Why is this so? Because the word *vidhi* (rule) is connected with a *sup* ending that possesses a genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) expressing mere relationship; for that reason, every rule—whether it be the substitution of *ais* for *bhisa* in place of a *sup*, or rules such as lengthening (*dīrghatva*) occurring when a *sup* follows, or any rule for which a *sup* is the cause—is related to a *sup*. Consequently, [the former] is everywhere considered "not yet established" (*asiddha*) [with respect to the latter].

But is it not the case that, by the statement "The genitive [case] denotes that which takes the place" (*ṣaṣṭhī sthāneyogā*), the genitive must denote a specific type of relationship and not a general relationship?

And so, would the status of being "not established" (*asiddhatva*) apply only in the place where the case-endings (*sup*) themselves are substituted, and not elsewhere? This is not the case. For the operation of this *paribhāṣā* applies in cases such as [Pāṇini 1.1.56] *yatra hādeśo vidhīyate*, where a substitute is prescribed; it does not apply, however, in a case where an operation already prescribed by another rule is employed for the sake of another operation. Otherwise, there would be the apprehension of the vowel *ū* in the word *ūdīcām*. Now, in this instance, no substitute for the case-endings (*sup*) is being prescribed; what then? It is the establishment (*siddhatva*) of that which has been prescribed by another rule.

Therefore, the technical rule (*paribhāṣā*) concerning "the place of the substitute" (*sthāne-yoga*) [Pāṇini 1.1.48] has no application here. In the case of *rājavatī* and so forth: after the suffix *matup* is added to the word *rājan*, when the feminine suffix *ṅīp* is applied, the rule "acute accent on the final syllable" (*antodātta*) [Pāṇini 6.1.214] would apply.

Because the elision (*nalopa*) is considered *asiddha* (non-existent for the purposes of subsequent operations), this word is not *rājavatī*; thus, in its absence, the word *rājavatī* remains initially acute (*ādyudātta*) because the stem *rājan*—ending in the *kanin* suffix according to the rule *kaninyuvṛṣitakṣirājidhanvidyupratidivaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.1.157)—is acutely accented on the first syllable by the *nit-svara* (the accentuation of a suffix marked with *n*). [Examples: *pañcārbham*, *daśārmam*.
Regarding the word *māsa* [formed by the rule] *māsa-ja-hni-yu-ya-vas-na-ṭ-kha-cha-vāḥ* [Pāṇini 2.1.50]:

here, once the elision of the *n* has been applied, the preceding member (*pūrvapada*) ends in the vowel *a*. Consequently, by the rule *arur-maṇi-vy-ri-ṣu ca, arvāṇaś-ca, avarṇam ca* [Pāṇini 6.2.90], the initial udātta accent would be required for that [first member]. However, because [the elision of *n*] is considered "unestablished" (*asiddha*), that does not occur; rather, the final udātta accent of the compound [as prescribed by] *samāsasya* [Pāṇini 6.1.217] takes effect. Thus we have *pañcadaṇḍi* (or *pañcadaṇḍī*, as in the Kāśikā).

The compound *pañcānāṃ daṇḍinām samāhāraḥ* (the collection of five staff-bearers) is formed by [Pāṇini 2.1.51] *taddhitārtha-*, etc.; it is a *dvigu* because it denotes a collective (*samāhāre dviguḥ*), and it takes the neuter gender by [Pāṇini 2.4.17] *sa napuṃsakam*.

Once the elision of the *n* (*nalopa*) has occurred, the condition of ending in an *ik* vowel (*igantatā*) arises; consequently, one might expect the original accent of the preceding member (*prakṛtisvara*) to apply according to [Pāṇini 6.2.29]. However, because the elision of the *n* is considered non-existent (*asiddha*), that does not happen, and instead the final acute accent of the compound (*samāsāntodāttatva*) applies by [Pāṇini 6.1.217]. This is what is meant by the phrase "that very thing," and so forth.

In this regard, some hold the view that a single technical term (*saṃjñā*) performs the function of multiple terms—that is, "whatever functions are performed by technical terms, a single term alone operates therein. Others, however, hold the view that just as a single function is performed by one term, so too is another; therefore, "as many functions as there are technical terms, just so many terms operate therein."

In that regard, this purpose does not apply to the former view; for by the very same technical name (*saṃjñā*) through which the elision (*luk*) of *jaś* and *śas* was effected by the rule "elision after six" (*ṣaḍbhyo luk*, Pāṇini 7.1.22), the prohibition of the feminine suffix *ṭāp* will likewise be accomplished. Therefore, it serves as a purpose in the other view.
To the question, "How does it serve as a purpose even here? he says: "For that which... and so forth.

The word *hi* has the sense of "because"; the particle *iti* marks the reason. Because the designation *ṣaṭ* (six), which was applied for the purpose of eliding the case endings *jas* and *śas*, does not result in the prohibition of feminine suffixes, therefore that [designation] must be applied once again.
Why? Because it must be applied; therefore, this is the purpose—this is the meaning. Regarding "vṛtrahābhyām" and "vṛtrahabhiḥ":

[the word] "vṛtra-han" means "one who has slain Vṛtra. From the base ending in *kvip* by [Pāṇini 3.2.87], after adding the suffixes *bhyām* and *bhis*, and once the *n* has been elided [by 6.4.24], [the rule 6.1.71] would apply; however, because [the elision] is considered non-existent (*asiddha*), it does not take effect.
Regarding the phrase "In this regard, some [say]" and so forth:
*sannipāta* means immediate succession; that which has such a characteristic as its cause is described as "not having that [as its cause].
The elision of the *n* is due to the *sannipāta* of the *sup* [case-ending].

If it were to apply *tuka*, it would obstruct the *saṃnipāta* [condition]. And since "a rule characterized by *saṃnipāta* is a cause for the non-application of that which obstructs it" (*Vyāḍīyapāda* 12), the elision of *n* does not trigger the application of *tuka*. Therefore, the mention of *tuka* is purposeless.

But is it not the case that *tuk* belongs to the preceding limit [of the stem]? What is this *tuk*? It is included by the very mention of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*). Therefore, how could there be an obstruction of that combination (*sannipāta*)? For it is not possible for something to be separated from itself by its own constituent part. This is not so; for *tuk* is a short vowel (*hrasva*) as an augment (*āgama*), not the entire composite ending in that [vowel]. Consequently, how could it be included by the mention of the nominal stem? Or rather, because it is "unestablished" (*asiddha*) due to the rule concerning what is external (*bahiraṅga*), the elision of the nasal (*nalopa*) is [unestablished] with respect to *tuk*. Thus, the mention of the rule for *tuk* would be purposeless.

The elision of *n* (*nalopa*) is considered "external" (*bahiraṅga*) because it is prescribed in dependence upon the case-ending suffix of the word (*pada*), whereas the insertion of the *tuk* augment for the phoneme is considered "internal" (*antaraṅga*) because it is prescribed in dependence upon the word situated within. Thus, the principle applies: "That which is external is as if non-existent with respect to that which is internal" (*asiddhaṃ bahiraṅgam antaraṅge*, Vyākaraṇa-paribhāṣā 42). If this is so, and [the rule] is indeed correctly understood, then for what purpose is the mention of *tuk* made? To this he says: "That is done," and so forth.

However, the purpose of the paribhāṣā "characterized by conjunction" (*sannipātalakṣaṇaparibhāṣā*) in making [the rule] non-eternal is as follows: in the case of *dṛkṣāya*, the lengthening [of the vowel] is established by [Pāṇini 7.3.102], *supi ca*.

For it is when there is a conjunction with an *a*-stem that the substitution of *ya* for the genitive ending *ṅi* is prescribed [by 7.1.13]. Therefore, on account of being caused by that [conjunction], [the rule of non-eternality] would not effect its destruction by way of removing the status of being the cause of that lengthening.
Because it is non-eternal, however, it does so.
Furthermore, another purpose for this will be stated later on.

By means of the paribhāṣā regarding external (bahiraṅga) characteristics, the fact that [the suffix] *sup* is not *anit* is made known; thus, in the case of *eṣā* and *dve*, the formation of *ṭāp* is established.
For here, the substitution of *tyadādyatva* is external because it depends upon the case-ending (*vibhakti*), whereas *ṭāp* is internal because it depends upon the nominal stem (*prātipadika*).
In that case, when the suffix *ṭāp* is to be applied, the substitution of *tyadādi* [for the initial phoneme] would be considered *asiddha*; consequently, the suffix *ṭāp* would not be established.
However, it is established because of its *anitya* (non-universal) nature.
Furthermore, in the word *pratidīvnā*, the purpose is the establishment of the lengthening [of the vowel] by the rule *hali ca* [Pāṇini 8.2.77].

If that [rule] were not optional, then when the lengthening prescribed by *hali ca* was to be applied, the elision of *al* (*āllopaḥ*)—being *bahiraṅga*—would be considered *asiddha*; consequently, since there would be no verbal root ending in *v* followed by a consonant (*hal*), the lengthening would not occur. However, because it is optional, it is established, as in the form *rājīyati*.
The suffix *kyac* is applied by [Pāṇini 3.1.8], and the substitution of *i* for the final vowel occurs by [Pāṇini 7.4.33]. Regarding the form *rājāyate*:

the suffix *kyaṅ* is applied by [Pāṇini 3.1.11], "The suffix *kyaṅ* is added after a word denoting the agent, and there is elision of the *sa*-suffix," and the lengthening of the vowel occurs by [Pāṇini 7.4.25], "In place of the penultimate short vowel of a verbal root before a non-*kṛt* or non-*sārvadhātuka* suffix."
Regarding "rājaśyaḥ":
this is a citation of the word *mu* without its case ending,
as in the form *amunā*.

The substitution of *yat* for *adas* occurs; then, by the rule *adaso 'ser dād u do maḥ* [Pāṇini 8.2.80], the substitutions of *utva* and *matva* take place. Following this, since the word *gher* is being carried over from [Pāṇini 7.3.119] into [Pāṇini 7.3.120], the substitution of *nā* occurs.

If the meaning of the sūtra were simply "if a substitute (*mubhāva*) is not *asiddha* when its absence (*nābhāva*) is to be applied," then this being the case, when the absence has been effected, why would that which is to be accomplished not lack *asiddhatva*? Consequently, in the form *amunā*, the lengthening of the stem ending in *ā*—which is prescribed by the rule *supi ca* [Pāṇini 7.3.102]—would result. Therefore, he says: "But when the absence has been effected," and so forth.

For since the presence of a short vowel is not the cause for the destruction of that short vowel, even though it is [technically] unestablished (*asiddha*), there is no contingency of its becoming long.
"Or rather," and so forth.

Just as when one person is asked, "Who is running this way? and another asks, "What kind of person is running?", a certain clever-minded individual answers both questions simultaneously with a single utterance: "A man with long ears (*ota*) is running. In the same way, here too, these two rules have been uttered by means of a *tantra* (a simultaneous or shared application).

In that regard, regarding the second rule (*yoga*), what is not obtained from another [rule]—in that case, the substitution of *bhu* must be applied because [the original form] is not yet established; such is the meaning of the sūtra.
By this, the lengthening (*dīrghatva*) will not occur. To preclude the occurrence of lengthening within the very same rule, he says: "Or rather," and so forth.

Now, one might object: if the status of *mubhāva* as established (*siddhatva*) were included by this rule when the substitution of *na* is to be performed, then the very absence (*abhāva*) of *na* would not even occur; how much less, then, could there be the non-establishment of *mubhāva* when something else is to be performed subsequent to that [absence]? To this he says: "But when *na* is to be performed," and so forth.

Just as an old maiden, while praying for the boon that her sons might eat rice with plenty of milk, ghee, and curds from a golden vessel, has in effect already secured a husband, sons, cattle, and wealth; so too here, when an operation is to be performed on something that results in another, the fact that the *subhāva* (the state of being a substitute) is established is accepted, whereas the fact that the *subhāva* is not established when the operation is to be performed on the original form (*sthānin*) is not relied upon.
This is expressed by the word "thereby" (*tena*).

For this very reason is the meaning of the sentence: "Is it not the case that the established status (*siddhatva*) of the substitution of *m* [for *n*] when [the suffix] *yat* follows a word ending in *kṛt* is understood for the sake of that [substitution], and by that cause there is neither the absence [of the nasalization] nor the occurrence of lengthening?
Regarding the term "one part" (*ekadeśa*), it refers to the rule:
"In the case of the final syllable of a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) and the locative singular ending, [there is the substitution of] an acute and grave [vowel]."

The word *vṛkṣa* is oxytone (*antodātta*) by virtue of the accent of the nominal stem (*prātipadika-svara*); thus, its final vowel, the letter *a*, is acute (*udātta*). The singular locative case ending is grave (*anudātta*) according to Pāṇini 6.1.158 (*anudāttau suppitau*). When these two [vowels] undergo substitution by a single substitute (*ekādeśa*) according to Pāṇini 6.1.87, a circumflex (*svarita*) would result due to the principle of closest proximity (*āntaratamya*). However, since the rule "a single substitute for an acute vowel is acute" (Pāṇini 8.2.5) applies, that single substitute would remain acute. If, on the other hand, that [acute accent] were considered as not yet established (*asiddha*), then when the substitution of *ay* is to be performed, that single substitute would still be circumflex; consequently, by closest proximity, the substitution of *ay* in its place would also result in being circumflex. Furthermore, the single substitute possesses an "internal" status (*antaraṅgatva*) because it depends upon both [the preceding and following elements].
The *guṇa* substitution [of *ā* for *a* + *ā*] is internal (*antaraṅga*), because it depends on a single word;
whereas the *ay* substitution is external (*bahiraṅga*), because it is the opposite of that. For example: "this belonging to Kumārī" (*kumāryā idam*).

The word *kumāra* has its final syllable accented (*antodātta*), like the word *vṛkṣa*. From that [word], by [Pāṇini 4.1.20] the suffix *ṅīp* is applied; by [6.4.148] the vowel *a* is elided; by [6.1.161] the vowel *ī* becomes accented; and then the singular dative case ending is added. When the form *kumārī-e* is established, by [7.3.112] the augment *āṭ* is inserted, and by [6.1.74] the *yaṇ* substitution occurs. By [6.1.174] the case ending becomes accented. And by [1.1.54], this accentuation applies specifically to the *āṭ* which is part of the case ending. Then, by [6.1.87] "and after *āṭ*," the single substitute *vṛddhi* (ā) is formed.

And that [substitution], as before, would result in a circumflex (svarita) accent being applied by the rule *svarite prāpte* [P. 8.2.5]; therefore, its status as established (*siddhatva*) must be stated—so that in the case of *kumāryā idam*, the substitution of *ay* may occur on an acute (udātta) vowel. Otherwise, as in the previous case, there would be a circumflex (or, according to the Kāṃu manuscript, "there would be no [circumflex]"). [The word] "yadi" and so forth [introduces the following].

If the acute accent (*udāttatva*) is applied first and the single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) operation follows, then—as shown in the immediately preceding derivation of the form—the substitution of *ay* becomes established precisely when the form is being finalized; thus, this example is appropriate.
Regarding the phrase "Now, however" (*atha tu*), etc.:
when *kumārī-e* is the state [of the base], the augment *āṭ* is added, and then the *yaṇ* substitution occurs.
"In that case, the accent of the case-ending [applies] by [Pāṇini 6.1.174] *tatraikādeśe*.
If the accent of the case-ending is applied after the single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) has been formed, then this supplementary rule (*upasaṃkhyāna*) would serve no purpose.

For in the derivation of this form, since the udātta-accent of the single-substitute—which must be treated as established when the *ay*-substitution is to be performed—is already established, he explains that this supplementary rule does not have that as its purpose.
And this is logical;
for instance, because it is internal (*antaraṅga*), the single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) must indeed occur first, and subsequently the accent of the case-ending (*vibhaktisvara*).
Since the single-substitute occurs by depending upon individual phonemes (*varṇa*), it possesses the status of being internal.
Is the acute accent (*udāttatva*) of the case-ending due to its being dependent [on something else]? It belongs to the word (*pada*), and thus it is considered *bahiraṅga* (external).
In the example "vṛkṣāvidam," this should be understood according to the analysis "vṛkṣaḥ idam"; furthermore, in this case, there is *vṛddhi* by the rule "[6.1.88] eka-adeśaḥ punar atra."
The rule *prathamayoḥ pūrvasarvadīrghaḥ* [Pāṇini 6.1.102] does not apply here, because the long vowel is prohibited by the rule *nādici* [Pāṇini 6.1.103].
Thus we have *gāṅge'nūpaḥ*.
When the suffix *aṇ* is applied in the sense of "born in the Gaṅgā," the word *gāṅga-* becomes oxytone (*antodātta*) due to the accent of the suffix.

The term *anūpa* is a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "that in which water (*āpas*) has followed (*anugata*). By the rule *ūd-anordeśe* [Pāṇini 6.3.97], the vowel *ū* is substituted for *ud*. Then, by the rule *ṛkpūrabdhūḥpathām-ānakṣe* [Pāṇini 5.4.74], the suffix *a* is added; thus, the word *anūpa* is also oxytone (accented on the final syllable) due to the accent of the suffix, while the remainder of the word is unaccented (*anudātta*). Regarding the phrase "because that [element] is established":

the vowel *e* that was produced in the word *gāṅga* when followed by the locative singular ending [by Pāṇini 6.1.87] is already established. Consequently, the single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) [produced by Pāṇini 6.1.109] with the vowel *a* of the word *anūpa* becomes subject to the rule *saḥ* [Pāṇini 8.2.5].

For this reason, by the rule *svarito vānudātte padādau* [Pāṇini 8.2.6], the circumflex (*svarita*) occurs in one alternative. If, however, there were non-establishment (*asiddhatva*), then that single vowel (*ekāra*) would become circumflex by virtue of being the substitute for both an acute (*udātta*) and a grave (*anudātta*) sound, due to its internal proximity (*āntaryataḥ*). Furthermore, as for the single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) resulting from *yaḥ punaḥ* [Pāṇini 6.1.109], it does not arise from a grave following an acute; thus, by the rule *svarito vānudātte padādau* [8.2.6], the circumflex would not occur in that alternative. Rather, since it arises in place of both a circumflex and a grave, it would necessarily be circumflex by virtue of internal proximity (*āntaratamya*).

Regarding the term *śatṛsvara*: it is a compound (*samāsa*) in which the latter member is elided (*uttarapadalopa*), following the rule for compounds such as *śākapārthiva* (Pāṇini 2.1.69), meaning "an accent based on the *śatṛ* [suffix].
Examples are *tudatī* and *nuktī*.

From the roots *tud* and *nud* (*dhātupāṭhaḥ* 1281, 1282), the suffix *laṭ* is applied; because they belong to the *tud*-class, the suffix *śa* is added, which is acutely accented on its final syllable by the accent of the affix (*pratyayasvara*). When the *lasārvadhātuka* suffix is made unaccented, the single substitute (*ekādeśa*) is formed by the rule of *pararūpa*.

This substitute is acutely accented according to the rule "the single substitute for [a vowel] with an acute [vowel] is acute" (*ekādeśa udāttanodāttaḥ*). Since that acute accent is established, and while the phrase "from what is acutely accented on the final syllable" (*antodāttāt*) is being carried over, the vowel *ī* becomes acutely accented by the rule "after that which ends in the present participle suffix *śat*" (*iti śatrantād antodāttād īkārasyodāttatvam bhavati*).

If the single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) were unestablished (*asiddha*), however, its acute accent (*udāttatva*) would not occur; for there is the governing rule (*adhikāra*) "from that which has an acute accent at the end" [Pāṇini 6.1.163].
[The author] refutes this purpose by relying on the *jñāpaka* (indicatory evidence) provided by the rule "after *anu*, etc.
He asks, "How, then, is this a *jñāpaka*? and says: "For not... and so forth.

The word *hi* indicates the reason. This is the purpose of the prohibition [of the accent] in the case of *anuma*: so that when *num* is applied by [Pāṇini 7.1.80] in the forms *tudantī* and *nudantī*, the acute accent (*udāttatva*) of the form accompanied by *num* (*sanuma*) does not occur.

For if the accent of the *śatṛ* [suffix] were [to apply], the accent of the single substitution (*ekādeśasvara*) would be considered unestablished (*asiddha*), and the prohibition would be rendered meaningless; because without the accent of the single substitution, there is no final acute accent for the *śatṛ* suffix.
Therefore, it is determined from this prohibition that the accent of the single-substitute (ekādeśa) is established.
For, apart from the accent of the single-substitute, there is no word ending in *śatṛ* with the augment *num* that has an udātta on the final syllable.
Consequently, the statement of the prohibition "anum" is merely an indicator (*jñāpaka*). [Examples are: *tudanti*, *likhanti*.
Here too, as before, when the anudātta quality of the sārvadhātuka suffix has been applied and the [root] accentuation has been applied, the single substitute for an udātta and an anudātta is udātta.
By the word "tena" (by that),
it is meant by the established accent of the single substitute.
Regarding the term "vajryamānatā":
this indicates the meaning of [Pāṇini 6.1.158].
The sense is that, with one syllable excluded (*vajrayitvā*), the remainder becomes unaccented (*anudātta*).

If, however, [the rule] were to be unestablished (*asiddha*)—in the case of the rule "A word is unaccented, with the exception of one [vowel]" (*anudāttaṃ padam ekavarjam*)—then since the accent of the single-substitute (*ekādeśasvara*) would be unestablished and the [exceptional] vowel to be excluded (*vajryamāna*) would not exist, there would follow the undesirable consequence (*prasajyeta*) of hearing two acute (*udātta*) vowels.

But has it not been stated that the mention of *asiddha* is for the purpose of establishing the general rule (*utsarga-lakṣaṇa*) regarding the meaning of the action? And here, the substitute (*sthānin*) is circumflex (*svarita*). For instance, by the very rule [P. 6.1.97] *pararūpa*, a circumflex vowel is prescribed in place of the final *e* or *o*; then, by the rule [P. 8.2.5] *ekadeśa udāttenodāttaḥ*, an acute (*udātta*) substitute is prescribed for that circumflex. In that case, if—on account of the acute substitute being *asiddha*—the status of being excluded (*varjyamānatā*) caused by that [circumflex] does not occur, let it not be so.

But that which is the substitute (*sthānin*) for this circumflex (*svarita*) will be caused by that [substitution]; how then does this purpose hold? It is explained as follows: there are four views regarding the rule *[[8.2.5]]*. First view: By rules such as *[[6.1.87]]*, a single substitution (*ekādeśa*) occurs between an acute (*udātta*) and a grave (*anudātta*) vowel due to their closest similarity (*āntaratamya*). Consequently, the two qualities (*guṇa*) of the circumflex are removed; then, by the rule *tasya* *[[8.2.5]]*, an acute quality is prescribed as the substitute in the place of the circumflex. This is the first view.
The second [view] is that once the quality of the *svarita* has been produced, one arrives at a different word through the disappearance of that other quality.
The third [view] is that this is a *paribhāṣā* (technical rule) stating that "the single substitute for an *anudātta* and an *udātta* is *udātta*.

In this view, because the *paribhāṣā* is a subordinate member of the whole, it forms a single syntactical unit (*ekavākyatā*) with the rules concerning single substitutes; therein, the following meaning is established: "An *ādguṇa* occurs," and "But [an *udātta* occurs] in the place of an *udātta* and an *anudātta*" [Pāṇini 6.1.87].

The fourth view, however, is that when a single substitute (*ekādeśa*) occurs between an acute (*udātta*) and a grave (*anudātta*) vowel, it becomes acute and is not endowed with the quality of circumflex (*svarita*). This rule establishing acuteness is introduced as an exception (*apavāda*) to the circumflex.
It is by relying on this very view—according to the principle "that which applies where another does not" (*yena nāprāpte*)—that this purpose has been set forth.

And how is this possible in this view? For here, indeed, the acute accent (*udāttatva*) is prescribed at the very same time as the rule [of substitution]; it is not the case that the quality of acuteness is an *ādeśa* (substitute) for that which has already been prescribed as having the quality of circumflex (*svarita*). Thus, it is impossible for the circumflex, as the *sthānin* (original element), to be excluded; because the accent of the single substitute (*ekādeśasvara*) is established [prior to any other operation]. [It is said: "Once that [substitution] has taken place, there is the suppression (*nighāta*) of the finite verb by the rule *tiṅṅatiṅaḥ*.

However, if that [suppression] were not established, the accent of the single substitute would occur later, and consequently, the state of being acutely accented in the middle (*madhyodāttatā*) would result.
In the word *pacati*, the vowel *i* in the suffix *ti* is unaccented (*anudātta*) because it is "left over" (*satiśiṣṭa*).

The word *iti* is acutely accented on its first syllable (*ādyudātta*) according to the rule *nipātā ādyudāttāḥ*. The single substitute (*ekādeśa*) resulting from the lengthening of similar vowels (*savarṇadīrghatva*) between these two is *bahiraṅga* because it depends on two bases (*dvipādaśrayatva*). Since that [substitute] is *bahiraṅga*, the accent dependent upon it is also *bahiraṅga*. Consequently, the vowel *i* remains as if non-existent (*asiddha*), and thus it does not fall under the prohibition of the rule *tena* (Pāṇini 6.1.158).

In the case of *prapacati*, because [the *kṛt* suffix] is *asiddha* due to being *bahiraṅga*, the rule *tiṅi codāttavati* (Pāṇini 8.1.71) does not apply, and thus the *gati* does not become unaccented; rather, only the *nighāta* (elision of accent) applies here by the rule *tiṅaṅatiṅaḥ* (Pāṇini 8.1.28). As in the example: *harivo medinam*.

From the word *hari*, there is the suffix *matup*, then *su*, and *num*. [The *num*] is elided by *halṅyābbhyo dīrghāt sutisyapṛktaṃ hal* [Pāṇini 6.1.68], and the final consonant (*saṃyogānta*) is elided by *saṃyogāntasya lopaḥ* [Pāṇini 8.2.23]. When that has been done, *rutva* (the substitution of *r*) occurs. Then, by the rule *haśi ca* [Pāṇini 6.1.110], there is the substitution of *utva* (the substitution of *u*). [Objection: "Because the elision of the final consonant (*saṃyogāntalopa*) is considered non-existent (*asiddha*), the substitution of *utva* by the rule *haśi ca* does not apply. This is because, while the elision of the final consonant is treated as non-existent, the *m* of *iś* is separated from the *t* by the intervening *k*; furthermore, the *t* is not a *ha*-letter (it is a *ta*-class consonant).

Regarding the form *ālādīt*: this is the *luṅ* (aorist) tense. From the root *lad*, the suffix *sic* is applied; then *iṭ* is added by [Pāṇini 7.2.35]. Following this, the *vṛddhi* substitution occurs due to *sic*. Then, by [Pāṇini 8.2.28], there is the elision of *sic* before *īṭ*, and the long vowel *ā* results from the rule of homogeneous lengthening (*akaḥ savarṇadīrghatvam*).
Regarding the forms *vṛkṇaḥ* and *vṛkṇavān*: [these are derived from the root *vraśca* with the suffixes *kta* and *ktavat*, respectively].

The root *ovraścū* in the sense of "cutting" (*chedane*) [Dhātupāṭha 1292] takes the *niṣṭhā* suffix; there is vocalization (*samprasāraṇa*) by the rule *grahijyā...* [Pāṇini 6.1.16], followed by the substitution of *k* [Pāṇini 8.2.30], then the substitution of *n* [Pāṇini 8.2.45], and finally the substitution of *ṇ* by the rule *aṭkupvāṅ...* [Pāṇini 8.4.2]. If the substitution of *ṣ* had not occurred, there would have been the elision of *s* by the rule *skoḥ saṃyogādyoḥ* [Pāṇini 8.2.29].
Thus, it is said that "the substitution of *k* is indeed not established."

He demonstrates the purpose of including the mention of "the prescription of *ṣatva*, vowels, suffixes (*pratyaya*), and *iḍ*" by stating: "In the prescriptions for vowels, suffixes, and *iḍ*, the word *kṣība* is cited as an example.
But how is it possible for the single word *kṣība* alone to serve as an example for all three types of prescriptions? To this he says: "In that regard," and so forth.

In the rule *anupasargāt phulla-kṣība-...* (Pāṇini 8.2.55), the word *kṣība* is established as a *nipāta* (irregularly formed word) when the suffix *kta* follows the root *kṣīb* (meaning "to be intoxicated") from the Dhātupāṭha (root list).
And in that regard, various types of derivation (*nipātana*) have been resorted to.
In some instances of derivation, in the prescription of suffixes, and in the prescription of accents, the word *kṣība* is cited; in others, in the prescription of the augment *iṭ*.
How so? He says: "When," and so forth.
The inclusion of the phrase "in a technical name" (*saṃjñāyām*) and so forth is due to the continued application (*anuvṛtti*) of the term "technical name" from the rule [Pāṇini 6.1.204].
"This accent" means it is *ādyudātta* (accented on the first syllable).

For in that context, the term *udātta* (accented) is understood from rule 6.1.159, and the term *ādi* (initial) is applicable from rule 6.1.197; this is because, while the elision of the word *uc-* is considered non-existent (*asiddha*), the word *kṣība* does not consist of two syllables. Indeed, while the elision of *uc-* is non-existent, the word *kṣība* does not become two-syllabled; rather, it is three-syllabled—as in the form *kṣībikaḥ*.

"The augment *iṭ* would apply," because the elision of the letter *t* is considered non-existent (*asiddha*), and thus the following *ārdhadhātuka* suffix begins with a consonant (*balādi*). For example: *agnātri icchatram* (agnātricchatram) and *paṭātri ucchatram* (paṭātricchatram).

In the case of *agnipatu* and *agniśabda* when in the vocative (*sambuddhi*), once the *guṇa* substitution has been applied to the short vowel, the vocative suffix is elided by the rule *eṅhrasvāt sambuddheḥ* [Pāṇini 6.1.69]. Then, by the rule *eco 'pragṛhyasyādūrāddhūte pūrvasyārdhasyād uttarasyedūttau* [Pāṇini 8.2.107], the *ā* that results from the first half of the *ec* vowels (the *e* and *o*) is replaced respectively by *i* and *u*. Thus, there arises the question: "Does the *tuka* augment apply obligatorily? It is desired that it apply obligatorily; however, it would apply optionally by the rule *naśchavyapraśān* [Pāṇini 8.3.7], and that [optionality] is not desired.
Therefore, it must be stated that in the rule for *tuṅ* (the insertion of *t*), the substitution of the protracted vowel (*pluta*) is established as valid.
Why [is the condition] "after *cha*" specified? So that in other rules for *tuṅ*, the substitution of the protracted vowel remains indeed invalid—as in the example: *khalaṃ punāti brāhmaṇakulam*.

[In this case,] there is the elision (*luk*) of the suffix *kvip* by [Pāṇini 6.1.67], followed by the substitution of *guṇa* for the short vowel by [Pāṇini 7.3.108]; as before, the substitution of the protracted vowel [would apply].

Because this [rule] is unestablished (*asiddha*), the *tuk* augment does not occur in the case of *khalapu* according to Pāṇini 6.1.71. [The rule] "the substitution of *ścu* occurs before a *dhuṭ* [consonant]" and so forth applies in examples such as *aṭ-ścyotati* and *raṭ-ścyotati*.

The suffix *kvip* is applied after the two roots *aṭ* and *raṭ*, meaning "to go" (*dhātupāṭha* 295, 297). The augment *su-* is added, followed by the elision of the consonant and following vowels according to *halṅyābbhyo dīrghāt sutisyapṛktaṃ hal* [Pāṇini 6.1.68]. Then, by *jhalāṃ jaśo'nte* [Pāṇini 8.2.39], the letter *ṭ* is changed to *ḍ*.

In that case, when the word *ścyotati* follows, because the substitution of *ścu* (the change of *c* to *ś*) is considered *asiddha* (non-existent) for the purposes of the application of *dhuṭ* (the augment *ḍ*), the augment *dhuṭ* would not apply. Therefore, it must be stated that the substitution of *ścu* is *siddha* (established) when the application of *dhuṭ* is to be performed.
But for what purpose is this [rule] stated? And so forth.
The intention is that this *sakāra* is not heard anywhere at all. Regarding the form *madhuścyut*:

by applying the rule *tat karoti tad ācaṣṭe* (Vārttika 209), one forms the causative (*ṇic*) from the sense "he causes honey to flow," resulting in *madhuścyutayati*. Then, by the rule *ṇāviṣṭhavad bhātipadikasya* (Vārttika 813), [the substitution of *yuvan* for *yuva* applies].

When *ṇilopa* has occurred and we have *madhuścyut*, the suffix *kvip* is added again; then, by [Pāṇini 6.4.51], there is the elision of *ṇi*. Because the substitution of *ścutva* is considered *asiddha*, the *s* at the beginning of the *saṃyoga* is elided by [Pāṇini 8.2.29] (*skor saṃyogādyoḥ*), followed by the elision of the final consonant of the *saṃyoga* by [Pāṇini 8.2.23] (*saṃyogāntasya lopaḥ*). Then, by [Pāṇini 8.2.30], the *k*-substitution (*kutva*) occurs, resulting in the desired form *madhuk*.
This is the intended meaning for why this [root] is recited with an initial *s*.
Does this form occur even when [the root] begins with the letter *ś*? To this he says: "But when this [root] begins with *ś*, etc.

First, there is the elision of the final *y* by the rule *saṃyogāntasya lopaḥ* [Pāṇini 8.2.23]. Once the *y* is elided, the *c* becomes the final member of a conjunct (*saṃyoga*), and thus it too is elided. Then, when the *ś* undergoes the change to *ṣ* by the rule *vraścādi-* [Pāṇini 8.2.36], and subsequently [by 8.2.39] the *ṣ* changes to *ḍ*, the form *madhuṅ* would also necessarily occur. [The forms] *babhaṇatuḥ* and *babhaṇuḥ* [are explained as follows].

From the roots *aṇ*, *raṇ*, and *bhaṇ* (Dhātupāṭha 444, 445, 447), the *liṭ* suffix is applied. Upon its reduplication (*dvirvacana*), by [Pāṇini 8.4.54], the *jaś*-treatment occurs, resulting in the letter *ba*. Since that [substitution] is considered non-existent (*asiddha*), this [root] is treated as beginning with a non-substitute vowel; thus, by [Pāṇini 6.4.120], *etva* (the substitution of *e* for *a*) would apply in the case of *liṭ* when there is a single consonant between [the root-initial and the affix]. Regarding the form *vicicchitsati*: the desiderative (*san*) suffix is added to the root *chid*. There is reduplication of *chid*. By [Pāṇini 8.4.54], the *car*-treatment occurs, resulting in the letter *ca*. Because that [substitution] is considered existent (*siddha*), the *tuṅ* augment does not apply to the syllable *ci* within the reduplicated portion, according to [Pāṇini 6.1.71] "che ca" (when *ch* follows, *tuṅ* is inserted after the preceding vowel).

Regarding the form *ucicchiṣati*: the root *ucchī* is used in the sense of "to abandon" (*dā|pā|216*). With the desiderative suffix *san*, by the rule *ajāderdvitīyasya* [Pāṇini 6.1.2], the reduplication applies to the second part because *ucch* is an internal element (*antaraṅga*). Once the augment *tuk* has been applied, the syllable *tchis* is reduplicated. In that context, by the rule *kharpūrvāḥ khayaḥ* [Vārttika 878], the letter *ch* remains; as before, there is the substitution of *c* for *t*. Because that [substitution] is established as valid (*siddha*), the augment *tuk* does not apply to the vowel *u*. Examples include *saya~yyantā* and *sava~vvatsaraḥ*.

In the case of *sam* followed by *yanti*, and also when followed by the word *vatsara*—as in *yal lokam tal lokam*—where the second singular forms of *yat* and *tat* are followed by the word *loka*, the *m* becomes an *anusvāra* by Pāṇini 8.3.23. Then, by 8.4.58, when the *parasavarṇa* (the following sound) is applied as a nasalized *yay* according to internal similarity (*āntarya*), because that [substitution] is considered "unestablished" (*asiddha*) by 8.4.45, the rule 8.4.46 (*anaci ca*)—which prescribes the doubling of a *yar* (semivowel or spirant)—does not apply.
Consequently, in this instance, the doubling of the three *y*-sounds and the others would not occur in one alternative.

"‘If [the term] *pada* were under the governing heading (*adhikāra*)’," and so forth. If the word "of a *pada*" (*padasya*) from [Pāṇini 8.1.16] does not recur in the rules concerning *latva* and so on, then, because reduplication of a *pada* would be equivalent to reduplication of a non-*pada*, the reduplication would be *bahiraṅga* (external), while *latva* and so on would be *antaraṅga* (internal). According to the principle "that which is *bahiraṅga* is as if non-existent (*asiddha*) when that which is *antaraṅga* is to be applied" (Vyāḍiparibhāṣā 42), since the reduplication would be *asiddha* when *latva* and so on are to be performed—[the reading in the Prāṇu is "dvirvacanasyāsiddham"].

Since [the desired form] is established by means of reduplication (*dvirvacana*), the rule *kū~ḥ pāṭhaḥ* [Pāṇini 8.2.1] does not apply; consequently, the substitution of *l* and so forth must first take place. Once those have occurred, the desired result is indeed established by means of reduplication. Since the section on words (*pada-adhikāra*) is in effect, the substitutions of *l* and so forth are also considered "external" (*bahiraṅga*); thus, by the principle that "that which is external is as if non-existent" (*asiddhaṃ bahiraṅgam antaraṅge*, Vyāḍiparibhāṣā 42), reduplication is established once those [substitutions] have taken place.

However, *latva* and the other [substitutions] are not established when this [doubling] is to be performed, because they are *asiddha* (not yet established) with respect to what precedes them [by P. 6.4.22]. Consequently, if doubling were performed first and *latva* and the others were subsequently prescribed, an undesirable result would also follow due to the subsequent [application of those rules].
Therefore, if there is an extension of the heading of "word" (*pada-adhikāra*), it must be stated that *latva* and the others are established [even in this context], as in the example:
*galo galaḥ*.
The root *mṛ* is used in the sense of "swallowing" (*nigaraṇe*; Dhātupāṭha 1410). Regarding the form *nunnaḥ*:
by [the rule] *muda-vida-vi-bhū-māsy-tapis-tasu-kas-paś-ca* (Pāṇini 8.2.56), the substitution of *na* occurs, and optionally, the substitution of *ta*.
