Regarding the forms *abhino’bhinah*: this is the root *bhid* (to split) with the suffix *laṅ*, the suffix *sip*, the augment *śnam*, and the elision of the consonant by rule 6.1.66 (*halṅyābbhyo dīrghāt sutisyapṛktaṃ hal*); then, by rule 8.2.74 (*sipi dhātorurvaṇ*), there is optionally the substitution of *ru* for the final consonant, and by rule 8.2.75 (*daśca*), the dental *d* is replaced by *ru*. As before, the substitution of *u* occurs by rule 6.1.113 (*ato roraplutādaplute*). Regarding the forms *mātṛṣṣvasā* and *pitṛṣṣvasā*.
In the alternative view provided by *mātuḥpitṛbhyāmanyatarasyām* [Pāṇini 8.3.85], there is the substitution of *ṣ*.
Thus, we have *māṣavāpāṇi*.
When *prātipadikāntanumbibhaktiṣu* [Pāṇini 8.4.11] is being applied while *māṣa vāpāṇi* [8.4.10] is still in force, there is the substitution of *ṇ* in the alternative view.
In the alternative view [of Pāṇini 8.4.45], there is an anusvāra: *vāṅnayanam*.
In the other case, it is *vākchayanam*.
While the rule [Pāṇini 8.4.59] is in effect, there is optionally the substitution of *cha* by [Pāṇini 8.4.63], *śaś choṭi*.
Regarding the phrase "of the substitution of *la*, etc.," this demonstrates the fault that arises for the substitutions of *la* and so forth if they were considered *asiddha*.

Because [the substitution of] *lat* and so forth would be unestablished. If reduplication were performed first, then because this rule—being an optional injunction (*vikalpa-vidhi*)—would apply at a later time, just as it applies in the preceding case, it would likewise not apply in the subsequent case due to the absence of a restrictive injunction (*niyoga*). Consequently, an undesirable option (*aniṣṭa-vikalpa*) would result: because it would apply in one of the two cases (the preceding) and fail to apply in the other (the subsequent). An undesirable option is not desired.
If that were the case, undesirable results such as *garo galaḥ* and *galo garaḥ* would follow.
In that regard, the rule "na" should be formulated as a sūtra concerning undesirable cases.
For what purpose? To prohibit the application of the principle of "asiddha" (non-validity) with respect to undesirable cases.
In this case, the status of being "not established" (*asiddha*) with respect to what precedes has an undesirable scope. Therefore, the phrase *bhu-ne* continues to apply in this rule.

If this is so, for what purpose is this [rule], since the prohibition is already established by the preceding rule? It is for the purpose of making known that [the previous rule] does not apply everywhere.

Therefore, this [rule] operates wherever non-ascertainment (*asiddhatva*) is intended; elsewhere, however, the opposite occurs, due to the division of the rule (*yogavibhāga*) in this sūtra: "of *udāttayaṇ* and *svaritayaṇ*" (*udāttayaṇaḥ, svaritayaṇaśca*). The meaning is: that *yaṇ* which stands in the place of an *udātta* vowel is *udāttayaṇ*; that *yaṇ* which stands in the place of a *svarita* vowel is *svaritayaṇ*.

In the forms *kumāryau* and *kumāryaḥ*, by the rule *anudāttau suppitau* [Pāṇini 3.1.4], the case endings *au* and *jas* are unaccented (*anudātta*). When these follow a vowel that is the result of *udāttayaṇ* (a vowel substituted for an *udātta* *ī*), a *svarita* accent occurs. This is according to the rule regarding the accent of the disappearance of an *udātta* (*udāttanivṛttisvara*).

Regarding the term *udāttalopanimitta-svara* ("the accent caused by the elision of an acute vowel"): that which is prescribed in the rule *pūrvam udāttasya lopo yasmāt sa punar udāttanivṛtti-svaraḥ* (Pāṇini 6.1.161) is not to be understood [in this context—according to the reading in the *Nākām*].
[The words in question] are "acute at the end due to the accent of the kṛt suffix."
Regarding the form *lvyā pvyā*: from the roots *lū* and *pū*, which are oxytone by virtue of their verbal accent (*dhātusvara*), the suffix *kvip* is applied; thus it is a compound.

Because the rule [Pāṇini 6.2.139] prescribes the preservation of the original accent (*prakṛtibhāva*) for the final member of a *kṛt*-derived word, these two [words] become oxytone by the accent of the *kṛt* suffix.

Regarding the rule *udāttayaṇādeśaś ca*: by this sūtra, a circumflex (svarita) accent is prescribed for that which follows two anudātta vowels or for a vowel following an udātta *yaṇ*; furthermore, he shows that by the preceding method, a circumflex is also prescribed for the locative singular (*saptamyekavacana*) following a circumflex *yaṇ*.
[The phrase] *tasya yo yaṇ* means "the *yaṇ* which belongs to that."
By the word "tasya" (of that), there is a reference to the genitive singular case-ending.
Regarding the phrase "of the anudātta vowel 'ā' belonging to the word *āśā*":

since the word *āśā* is udātta on its first syllable according to the rule *āśāyā adigvācyā cet* (Phiṭ-sūtra 1.18), the vowel 'ā' [in the form *āśā-ā-*, i.e., *āśāyāḥ*] becomes anudātta by virtue of [Pāṇini 6.1.158].
Regarding the passage beginning with "nanu ca":

the circumflex (*svarita*) accent prescribed by this rule, *udāttayaṇaḥ*, for the locative singular [ending], is considered *asiddha* (non-existent) when the substitution of *yaṇ* according to Pāṇini 6.1.77 is to be applied. Consequently, since this is not a *yaṇ* substitution in place of a circumflex, the circumflex does not occur in *khalapvyaśā* and *khalapvyaśe* due to the principle of non-repetition (*sakṛdgatinyāya*).
Regarding the passage beginning with "āśrayāt":...
[Objection: "In the rule *āhāyam-svaritayaṇ*, [the circumflex accent] is not established anywhere? [Response: The circumflex accent is established.
In that case, its establishment will occur by virtue of its dependence [on another rule], just as the substitution of *ru* is established in the rule *ato ror aplutād aplute*.
[Objection: "If this is so," and so forth.
By this, he points out an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) when [the accentuation] is assumed to be established on the basis of the substratum (*āśraya*). Regarding the example *dadhyāśā*:

the word *dadhi* is acute-accented on its first syllable by the rule *nabviṣayasyānisantasya* (Phiṭ-sūtra 2.26); the remainder is unaccented (*anudātta*) by [Pāṇini 6.1.158]; and by [Pāṇini 8.4.66], the vowel *i* following the letter *dh* becomes circumflex-accented (*svarita*).
If its status as established (*siddhatva*) were due to that basis, then the vowel *ā* of the word *āśā*, which follows the *aṇ* substituted for it, would have to be circumflex (*svarita*).
Therefore, and so forth:

since such an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) occurs when establishment based on that [subsequent] basis is resorted to, it must be stated that this very circumflex accent (*yaṇ-svara*) which is prescribed by this rule (Pāṇini 8.2.4) is established when the substitution of *yaṇ* is to be performed.
The meaning of the phrase "it should be stated" (*vaktavyam*) is its explanation.
That, however, should be carried out as before by relying on the division into *yoga* and so forth.
Regarding the words "some, however" (*kecittu*), and so on.

With the words "If this were so," etc., he refutes the objection of over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) that was raised, according to the opinion of certain scholars. Over-extension is the occurrence of activity even with respect to an unintended object. Now, by the rule *na ca* [Pāṇini 8.4.66], the circumflex (*svarita*) which is prescribed after an acute (*udātta*) is not considered established merely by virtue of its being dependent on that [acute]; for the circumflexness of the unaccented vowel following the *svaritayaṇ* (the semivowel *y* substituted for a circumflex) that follows an acute is what is intended. Consequently, because of its status as a substitute (*sthānitva*), the circumflexness of the letter *ā* in the word *aśā* following that *yaṇ* is recited in the *Taittirīyaka*, a different Vedic branch.
Furthermore, that non-udātta quality belongs to the vowel *ā* of the word *agni*; for that [vowel] is udātta on the final syllable by virtue of the accent of the nominal stem (*prātipadika-svara*).
"Likewise in the case of *brāhmaṇa*" — [the word *iti* is not present in the Prāṃu manuscript reading] — here, by the word *brāhmaṇa*, a specific part of that [same category] is intended.
Regarding the form *dadhyāśayati*:

from the root *aś* with the causative suffix (*ṇic*), the vowel is either accented on the final syllable by the rule for verbal roots (*dhātusvara*) or by the rule for *cit* suffixes (*citsvara*). The following vowel *a* is unaccented (*anudātta*).
According to the Brāhmaṇa, when this [unaccented *a*] follows a *svarita* *yaṇ*, it is taught to be *svarita*.
The phrase "But as...
and so forth serves to support that very same over-extension [of the argument].

The Vārttikakāra stated: "If it is argued that [the rule] is established by the word 'until' (ākṣayāt), then there is a fault regarding the circumflex accent (svarita) following an acute accent (udātta)."

This is its meaning: if [the rule were applied] on the basis of the substratum (*āśraya*), then it would follow that when a *svarita* follows an *udātta*, and there is a *yaṇ* (vowel) after that [svarita], the subsequent *anudātta* would be intended to become *svarita*. In that case, there would be a fault.

Therefore, it is established by this [previous] rule that *svaritatva* does not occur [in such instances]. For by this Vārttika, the meaning "there is *svaritatva* for the *anudātta* following a *yaṇ* that is *svarita* and comes after an *udātta*" is not understood.
Therefore, this is not so;

for it is established that, according to how it ought to be, a circumflex (svarita) does not arise for a following unaccented (anudātta) vowel after a circumflex semivowel (svaritayaṇ) by means of this [rule].
With the words "in that way" (*tathā*) and so forth, he immediately confirms the very point just made.

For in the Bhāṣya, by means of the passage beginning with "the mention of *svarita* will not be made," the mention of *svarita* in the rule is rejected on the grounds that it is superfluous (*asiddhatva*). And this rejection is only logical if one does not desire the *svarita* quality of an unaccented vowel following a *yaṇ*-substitute for a *svarita* that arises from an acute (*udātta*) vowel; otherwise, if the *svarita* produced by that cause were indeed desired, the rejection would not be justified at all.

Why, then, is the inclusion of the *svarita-yaṇ* rejected in the Bhāṣya? For if that [inclusion] were rejected, then in forms such as *sakṛllvyāśā*, the *svarita* of the unaccented vowel would not be established. To this he says: "In *sakṛllvyāśā* and so forth," etc.

Here, the *udātta-yaṇ* is the single *yakāra* following the vowels *u* and *v*. But surely, because there is an intervention by that which arises in place of the locative singular ending, it should not be established? To this he says: "The *svarita-yaṇ*," etc.
He states the very reason for this: "In the rule concerning accentuation" (*svaravidhau*), and so forth.
The particle *iti* indicates a cause.
If [the desired result] is established even without the mention of *svarita*, why is its mention made in the sūtra? To this he says: "But that is done," and so forth.
For the meaning intended by [Pāṇini 1.1.57] is this: "When an operation (*vidhi*) is to be performed based on what precedes, a substitute (*ādeśa*) for *ac* is treated as the original (*sthānivat*).

In the rule prescribing the *svarita* accent for an unaccented vowel following an *udātta-yaṇ*, there is an intervention by the vowel *i* due to the *sthānivadbhāva* of that *yaṇ* substitute which occurs in place of the locative singular ending. [One might object: "Since a consonant is treated as non-existent (*avidyamānavat*) in rules concerning accents" (Vyāḍiparibhāṣā 37), does this not constitute an intervention?
Because of that intervention, in the case of *sakṛllvyāśā*, the rule "udāttayaṇaḥ" would not apply; therefore, the term *svarita* is included [in the rule].

But surely, by the rule *napadāntaradvirvacanam* (Pāṇini 1.1.57) and others, the status of being a substitute (*sthānivadbhāva*) is prohibited in the application of vowel rules (*svaravidhi*). So how can there be an intervention? To this he says: "In the case of vowel changes, lengthening, and the elision of *y*, etc. For the status of being a substitute is prohibited for a substitute that consists of the elision of a vowel (*aco lopa*) when a vowel rule is to be applied. [This portion does not appear in the printed edition.]

For it has been stated there: "It must be stated that in the case of the elision of a vowel (*svara*), a long vowel (*dīrgha*), or *y*, a substitute for an elided element (*lopādeśa*) does not behave like the original (*sthānivat*). (Vārttika 1 on Pāṇini 1.1.59). Now, in this instance, there is no substitute for an elided vowel; rather, there is a substitute *yaṇ*. Therefore, there is no prohibition of *sthānivadbhāva*. [The example is] "vaidyāśā."

Regarding *vidasyāyati*: because it belongs to the *vidādi* group, the suffix *añ* is applied by the rule *anṛṣyānantarye* [Pāṇini 4.1.104]; from that form ending in *añ*, the suffix *ṅīn* is applied by the rule *śāṅgaravādyaño ṅīn* [Pāṇini 4.1.73].

Here, once the acute accent (*udātta*) has been assigned to the initial syllable due to the *ṅit* status [of the suffix], the remaining syllables become unaccented (*anudātta*). Thus, in the word *baidyāśā*, the *yaṇ* substitute occurs in place of an unaccented vowel, not in place of an acute (*udātta*) or a circumflex (*svarita*) vowel.
This is what is meant by "here."

"This [word] has its first syllable udātta by virtue of the *lit-svara* rule" (Pāṇini 6.1.193). This is because it ends in the suffix *tral* (Pāṇini 5.3.10). The form *id-* is elided by the rule "before a consonant, there is elision of *loḥ*" (Pāṇini 7.2.113). Regarding the term "of the anudātta":

When there is a single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) for an acute (*udātta*) vowel together with an acute-less (*anudātta*) vowel, that substitute shall be acute, and not circumflex (*svarita*). This rule is commenced because the circumflex would otherwise have applied.

In the examples, words such as *agni* and others are oxytone (*antodātta*) by the accent of nominal stems (*prātipadika-svara*) according to *Phiṭ-sūtra* 1.1; however, the case-ending (*vibhakti*) is grave (*anudātta*) by the rule "The *sup* and *tiṅ* endings are grave" (*Pāṇini* 3.1.4).
In *agnī* and *vāyū*,
[the long vowel is applied] by [Pāṇini 6.1.102].
In *vṛkṣau* and *plakṣau*, [the same applies].
By [Pāṇini 6.1.88], there is *vṛddhi*:
"pacanti," "yajanti.
By [Pāṇini 6.1.97], there is the substitution of the subsequent form (*pararūpatva*).
"This single substitute [ekādeśa] belongs to two anudātta vowels.

Now, one might object: since the letter *śa* has been made svarita by rule 8.4.66, this single substitute would belong to a svarita and an anudātta; how then can it be said that it belongs to "two anudātta vowels"? To this he replies: "Because the svarita is considered non-existent (*asiddha*) when the subsequent form (*pararūpa*) is to be applied. For example, in the word *sūtthitaḥ*, there is a compound according to rule 2.2.18.
"In this case, the word *su* is a *karmapravacanīya*. By this, he removes the status of *su* as a *gati*.
For if it were a *gati*, then by [Pāṇini 8.1.70], there would be a *nighāta* (elision of the accent); consequently, this single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) would not be between an udātta and an anudātta.
Regarding the phrase "in a *prādi*-compound" and so forth:
the word *su-* is acutely accented on its first syllable.

For when a *prādi*-compound is formed, there occurs acute accentuation on the first syllable due to the rule "in a *tatpuruṣa* compound [the first member retains its original accent] when it has the sense of 'equal' (or similar meanings)" (Pāṇini 6.2.2).

Therefore, by virtue of that reason of having the *prakṛtisvara* accent, this is a substitute (*ādeśa*), because when the long vowel resulting from the homogeneity of vowels (*savarṇadīrghatva*) occurs after an initial unaccented (*anudātta*) word, the word *su-*—which is originally udātta on its first syllable—retains its original accent (*prakṛtisvaratva*), and thus it is logical that the remainder becomes unaccented (*anudātta*). Now, an objection may be raised: "In the case of a *prādi* compound, a prohibition must be stated for *karmapravacanīya*s" (Vārttika 96). How then can there be a *prādi* compound here? This is not a fault, because that prohibition is not universal (*anitya*).

The impermanence (*anityatva*) of the word *su* should be understood from its inclusion in the *suṣāmādi* group [Pāṇini 8.3.98]. For in that context, since the form would have been established by [the rule] *upasargātsunoti* (8.3.65) and others, its recitation there is for the sake of cases where it is not a prefix (*anupasarga*). And its status as not being a prefix follows from its being designated as a *karmapravacanīya* by [the rule] *soḥ* (1.4.94).
Alternatively, this prohibition applies to those *prādi* prefixes other than *su* and *ati*.

For it is stated in that context [Pāṇini 2.2.18] that *su* and *ati* form a compound when expressing praise (*pūjā*), and in the case of praise, their status as *karmapravacanīya*s is intended. As in the example:
*dīkṣate*.
The word *vi* is acutely accented on its first syllable by virtue of being a *nipāta*.

Here too, one should connect [the explanation] as follows: since the *nighāta* (elision of accent) has been applied by the rule *tiṅṅatiṅaḥ* [Pāṇini 8.1.28], and because this occurs when there is a single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) with an unaccented initial of the following word, it becomes unaccented.
[Thus we have] *vasuko 'si*.

The word *vasu* is oxytone (*antodātta*) by virtue of the accent of the nominal stem (*prātipadika-svara*). Then, because it ends in the suffix *su*, there is the substitution of *u* for *as* when followed by *hrasva* [according to Pāṇini 6.1.113]. By virtue of its status as a substitute (*sthānivadbhāva*), that *u* is considered to have the nature of *sup*, and thus it is anudātta. Together with the preceding vowel, [the resulting form is *vasū*]. And that [form] is oxytone by the previous rule [Pāṇini 8.2.5]. Regarding the form *asi*:
once the *s* has been elided by the rule "elision of *tās* and *tāsī*" [Pāṇini 7.4.50], it is the form of the present tense (*laṭ*) in the second person singular (*sip*).

In this case, by the rule *tiṅṅatiṅaḥ* [Pāṇini 8.1.28], the vowel *ā* is unaccented (*anudātta*); through the rule *tasyākāreṇa saha* [Pāṇini 6.1.109], there is the substitution of the subsequent vowel for both. Regarding the phrase "the mention of *svarita*," etc.: how is it that the substitute becomes *svarita* even when the mention of *svarita* is absent? Furthermore, the repeated mention of *svarita* is for the sake of clarity; it is not, however, for the purpose of prescribing the *svarita* accent as an alternative option. To this, he says: "For if it were *udātta*," and so forth.

For when an acute accent (*udātta*) is optionally applied, in that case where it does not occur, there must be that which is most similar to both the acute and the grave; and that is precisely the circumflex (*svarita*). Therefore, even without the explicit mention of the circumflex, it will indeed be circumflex. In the expressions "of the nominal stem" (*prātipadikasya*) and "of the word" (*padasya*), the two genitives are in apposition.
As in the example: *ahan ahim* ("he slew the serpent").
In *hanterlaṅ*, after the elision of the suffix by *halṅyādilopaḥ* [P. 6.1.68], there is the elision of *śap* because it belongs to the *adādi* class.
Due to the prohibition stated in *adhātuḥ* [P. 1.2.45], the status of being a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) does not apply here.
Thus: *rājā*, *rājānau*, *rājānaḥ*.

Because the designation *pada* is prohibited here [in Pāṇini 1.4.17] when it is not a *sarvanāmasthāna*, the final *n* belongs to the stem (*prātipadika*). Regarding the rule "of the final of a stem" (*prātipadikāntasya*),

since this is a genitive *tatpuruṣa* compound, it is appropriate that this very word (*prātipadika*)— being the predominant member (*uttarapada*)— is qualified by it, and not the subordinate member (*guṇabhūta*).

In this context, the letter *n* is qualified by both the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) and the word "end" (*anta*); and that letter *n* is included within the nominal stem. Regarding the term "of a word" (*padasya*):

even though the two [qualifiers]—the end of the nominal stem and the word—are undesirable as being in different grammatical relations (vyadhikaraṇa), they must stand in the relation of qualifier and qualified, namely: "of the end of the nominal stem" and "of the word."
The meaning is that whatever is a constituent part (*avayava*) of a word (*pada*) is also [a constituent part] of a nominal stem (*prātipadika*).

This being the case, even if the mention of "the end" (*anta*) were made, the elision of *n* (*nalopa*) would still occur in forms such as *rājānau* and *rājānaḥ*, because here too the letter *n* is the final element of a nominal stem which is a constituent part of a word. To refute this objection, he says: "The mention of 'nominal stem' (*prātipadika*) is indeed not in composition. And therefore, its being a coreferential qualifier (*samānādhikaraṇa-viśeṣaṇa*) of the term "of the word" (*padasya*) is indeed appropriate; such is the intention.

If the intention is that, in that case, the mention of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) would necessarily involve the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) in its entirety, he says: “*supāṃ suluk*. By this rule, since the genitive case is elided (*luk*), the mention of the nominal stem is indicated by that elision; therefore, there is no occasion for the genitive case to apply. [The example is] *ahar*.

By the rule *svamīrvapuṃsakāt* [Pāṇini 7.1.23], there is elision (*luk*) of the nominative singular suffix (*su*). Then, by the rule *naśca* [Pāṇini 8.2.69], the *n* is replaced by *r*. Due to the principle of *pratyayalakṣaṇa* (the suffix being considered present for grammatical operations), the condition of having a case-ending (*sup*) following *ahan* [as required by Pāṇini 6.4.75] does not exist here; this is because of the statement: *lumatā lupte pratyayalakṣaṇaṃ nāsti* [Pāṇini 1.1.62]. Thus, we have *ahobhyām* and *ahobhiḥ*.
By the rule *ahan* [Pāṇini 8.2.68], there is the substitution of *r*; by *haśi ca* [6.1.110], there is the substitution of *u*.

Now, an exception (*pratiṣedha*) occurs only when there has been a prior application (*prāpti*). In this case, once the substitution of *r* for the *n* has occurred, the elision of *n* (*nalopa*) cannot even apply because the letter *n* no longer exists. So what is the purpose of the prohibition? To this he says: *ahan* [8.2.68] and *ro'supi* [8.2.69] are prescribed as substitutes.

Thus, both of these—the substitution of *r* and the substitution of *u*—are without scope (*anavakāśa*) regarding the elision; otherwise, their prescription would be meaningless. Therefore he says: "it has its own scope," and so forth.
For there is a prohibition [against elision] in the case of the vocative dual, according to the rule *sambuddhau hi lopo na* (Pāṇini 8.2.8).
Therefore, in that case, both of these [rules] have their scope of application, as in:
*he dīrghāho nidāgha*.

The term *nidāgha* is a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "one in whom the days are long"; this is its vocative case. Although the [final] vowel is elided by rule Pāṇini 6.1.68 (*halṅyābbhyo dīrghāt sutisyapṛktaṃ hal*), the condition of being followed by a *sup*-suffix still exists by virtue of the *pratyayalakṣaṇa* (the presence of a suffix as if it were not elided). Consequently, rule Pāṇini 8.2.69 (*ro'supi*) does not apply, and by rule Pāṇini 8.2.68 (*ahann ahnaḥ*), the substitution of *ru* occurs, resulting in the form *ahan*. Thus, it is called *ahan*.
Regarding the phrase "ending in the nominative singular," and so forth:

in that context, although it would have been sufficient to state simply that the term *ahan* which is employed in the rule prescribing the substitution of *r* (Pāṇini 8.2.68) is repeated, the statement "the nominative singular ending, without the elision of *n*" is made in order to demonstrate the justification for the fact that by this sūtra (*ahan*), not only is the substitution of *r* prescribed, but rather—by virtue of the principle of repetition—the word-form *ahan* itself is being formally explained (*anvākhyāyate*).

If the substitution of *hr* were enjoined by the rule *ahan* [Pāṇini 6.4.125], then, because of its connection with that substitute, the genitive case would have to be employed; thus, the genitive would have been used instead of the nominative. If the nominative were used to introduce *hr*, it would refer to the form where the *n* has already been elided, since the elision of *n* is the very characteristic being defined. But this is not what was done. Therefore, it is understood from the employment of the nominative-ending form where the *n* has not yet been elided that the grammatical derivation (*anvākhyāna*) of the form *ahan* is being performed. "Is derived" (*anvākhyāyate*) means it is established as being correct (*sādhutvena pratipādyate*).
For what purpose? To prevent the elision of the *n*. That is, so that the elision [of the *n*] prescribed by this rule—[[8.2.7]]—does not occur. Regarding the form *carman*:
the substitution of *luk* for the case-ending *ṅi* is applied by the rule *supāṃ suluk...* [[7.1.39]].

Now, in the case of *surājñi*, the designation of a nominal stem (*prātipadika-saṃjñā*) indeed exists, because there is no prohibition by the rule "that which is not a suffix" (*apratyaya*) [Pāṇini 1.2.45] due to the application of the rule "as if a suffix were present" (*pratyayalakṣaṇa*) [Pāṇini 1.1.61].

However, in the case of *ādre carman*, the aforementioned designation of a nominal stem does not exist at all; for it is sublated by the designation of a "nominal base" (*bha-saṃjñā*), which is triggered by the same rule regarding suffixes.
Therefore, the meaning is that there is no possibility at all for the elision of the *n* (nalopa).
How is the prohibition established? To this he says: "Precisely because of this," and so forth;
"and the designation *bha* does not occur."
In this case as well, [the phrase] "it is made known by the definition of the suffix" is connected to this very same prohibitive statement.
By the words "and likewise," etc., he demonstrates the purpose of that making known. Thus, from this prohibition, two matters are made known.
And having done so—since the designation of a nominal stem (*prātipadika-saṃjñā*) applies in the case of *rājapuruṣa*, the elision of the *n* also takes place.
If the designation *bha* were not present, the elision [of the final *n*] by [Pāṇini 6.4.134] would not occur.

One should understand that the purpose of the statement "not due to the absence of the *bha* designation" (*na bhasaṃjñābhāvāt*) is to be found in the view that "the technical designations and rules (*saṃjñā-paribhāṣā*) apply according to their original enunciation" (*yathoddeśaṃ saṃjñāparibhāṣam*).

However, in the view that "the technical designations and rules apply at the time the operation is to be performed" (*kāryakālaṃ hi saṃjñāparibhāṣam*), the *bha* designation is an operation dependent on the stem (*aṅga-kārya*); therefore, by the very prohibition of the *pratyayalakṣaṇa* rule [Pāṇini 1.1.62], the *bha* designation does not occur. Thus, there is no need for the instruction regarding the absence of the *bha* designation in that context.
By the rule beginning with *ṅāvuttarapade*, this prohibition of the prohibition of *na*-elision is stated when *ṅi* follows.
That prohibition must be stated regarding that *ṅi* which occurs before an *uttarapada*.
[The word] "must be stated" (*vaktavyaḥ*) means:
The meaning is that it must be explained.

Here is the explanation: from the rule *svarito vānudātte padādau* [Pāṇini 8.2.6], the word *vā* (or) is understood to carry over; and since this is a *vyavasthitavibhāṣā* (a restricted option), the [application of the rule] will not occur when *ṅī* is the final member of a compound. Thus: "one who has sesame seeds on his skin" is *carmatilaḥ*.
Is it because there is intelligibility even when there is a lack of grammatical coreferentiality (*vaiyadhikaraṇya*) that the compound is formed?

But is it not the case that this statement is far too brief—namely, that "a prohibition must be stated when a *nā* [feminine suffix] occurs as the final member of the compound"? [This portion does not appear in the printed edition.]

Even in the case of *sambuddhi* (vocative singular), this prohibition must indeed be stated when the subsequent member (*uttarapada*) follows; otherwise, in the analysis *he rājan? vṛndāraka*, once the compound is formed by the rule *vṛndārakanāgakuñjaraiḥ* [Pāṇini 2.1.62], the elision of the *n* in *herājan? vṛndāraka* would not occur. Therefore, he says: "But in the case of *he rājan? vṛndāraka*," and so forth.
A compound must be formed with a sentence that has the same meaning; for only in this way does there exist the necessary semantic connection (*sāmarthya*), and not otherwise.

And so it has been said: "That which is capable of expressing the meaning of the sentence to be grasped should be understood as 'samartha' (capable). Now, the meaning that is understood here by the sentence *he rājan vṛndāraka* is not known through the compound *he rājavṛndāraka*. For in a sentence, because there is no unification of meaning (*ekārthībhāva*), the vocative is understood; whereas in a compound, it is the opposite—the vocative is the collective meaning of the whole.

Therefore, the compound should be formed by analyzing it exactly as "rājā" (king) and "vṛndārakaḥ" (excellent), followed by the vocative case ending. Thus, the first member of the compound ends in the vocative. In the expression "he rājan vṛndāraka," the compound will indeed occur; consequently, since there is no vocative case ending following the second member of the compound, the prohibition of the elision of the *n* (nalopa) does not even apply, and thus there is no purpose in that prohibition. [The rule] "vā napuṃsakānām" and so forth [is stated].

Alternatively, this should be explained as having the sense that "the elision of *n* is prohibited for neuter gender [stems]. Regarding this, the explanation is as follows: here too, one must proceed by relying on the recurrence of the word *vā* (or) and its status as a *vyavasthitavibhāṣā* (an option restricted by specific conditions). The intended meaning is this: after a stem ending in *m*, a stem having *m* as its penultimate letter, a stem ending in *a*, or a stem having *a* as its penultimate letter, the *m* of the suffix *matup* undergoes the substitution of *ca*. To demonstrate how exactly that comes about, he says: "*mato r iha*" and so forth.
In this context, the suffix *matup* is introduced as the subject of the operation (*kāryin*).

And that [suffix] cannot exist without the status of being a nominal stem (*prātipadika*), because the rule for its introduction occurs within the governing heading (*adhikāra*) of "nominal stems" (Pāṇini 4.1.1).

Therefore, prior to the suffix *matup*, there must be a nominal stem obtained by implication through syntactic competency (*sāmarthya*); that [stem] is then qualified by the letter *m* and the vowel *a*—that is, as "that which has *m* as its final element" (*makārānta*) and "that which has *a* as its final element" (*avarṇānta*).
The capacity [of the rule] lies in the fact that the *upadhā* (penultimate vowel) is qualified by the letter *m* and by the vowel *a*.
How so? It should be connected thus: first, the end of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) is qualified;
then, that *upadhā* which is qualified by the qualifier *m* and by the qualifier *a* is further qualified—namely, "that which has *m* as its *upadhā*" and "that which has *a* as its *upadhā*."

Is it not so that [the addition of] the suffix *matup* after what is qualified by the letter *m* should not occur in the rule *upadhāyāśca* (Pāṇini 7.1.101)? This is because the meaning "this [suffix] obtains its own desired object" is what results. The particle *iti* is used in the sense of a reason (*hetu*).
Since the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) itself—which is obtained through the force of the context—is being qualified, therefore this meaning which is about to be stated will also apply to the Sūtra.

Regarding the form *kiṃvān*: the suffix *matup* is added in the sense of "what does this possess? (*kim asyāsti*). By the rule *ugidacām* [Pāṇini 7.1.70], the augment *num* is inserted; then, by the rules *halaṅyābbhyo dīrghāt* [6.1.68] and *saṃyogāntasya lopaḥ* [8.2.23], the final consonant is elided, and finally, by *sarvanāmasthāne cāsambuddhau* [6.4.8], the vowel is lengthened. Regarding the form *nārmatam*: one who possesses men is *nṛmān*. From *nṛmataḥ* (belonging to one who possesses men), the suffix *aṇ* is applied according to [Pāṇini 4.3.120]. Once the vṛddhi strengthening has been applied, the base becomes *nārmatam*. Here, since the suffix *matup* has an *avarṇa* (a or ā) as its penultimate letter, it forms a nominal stem (*prātipadika*), and thus the substitution of *v* for *m* should apply. Why, then, does it not occur? To this he says: "In this case," and so forth.
In the case of *nārmata*, here the substitution of *vat* occurs precisely because of the rule for *vṛddhi*; and that [vṛddhi] is caused by a *bahu-vrīhi* or a *taddhita*.

Therefore, the state of having an *a*-vowel as a penultimate (*avarṇopadhatva*) is "external" (*bahiraṅga*), whereas the state of being the cause for the application of the suffix (*vatva*) is "internal" (*antaraṅga*). And according to the principle that "the external is not established in the presence of the internal" (*asiddhaṃ ca bahiraṅgam antaraṅge*), the suffix *vat* does not occur in *nārmata*. As for *agnicitvān*, [the term *agni-cit* receives] the designation *bha* by [Pāṇini 1.4.19].

Because of that, by the rule *tena padasaṃjñānibandhanaṃ* (Pāṇini 8.2.39), the substitution of *jaś* does not occur. In the word *ahīvatī*, the suffix *matup* is added in the four senses [of possession, etc. according to *cāturarthikaḥ* (Pāṇini 4.2.85), and the vowel is lengthened according to *dīrghaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.3.120). In the phrase *udadhāvarthe*, the meaning is "in that object for which water is held."

Likewise, when the suffix *kip* is applied by the rule *tathā hyudake karmaṇyupapade* [Pāṇini 3.3.93], and when the substitution of *uda-* for *udaka-* is made by the rule *ityudakasyoda-* [Pāṇini 6.3.58], the word *udadhi* is derived. He shows that by the particle *ca*, [the word *saṃjñāyām*] from rule 8.2.11 is drawn in,
as in the phrase "and in the case of a name" (*saṃjñāyāṃ ca*), etc.
"udadhāvarthe," etc. The inclusion of the term *udadhi* is for the sake of technical designation (*saṃjñā*).
"udandān" [is the form].
When there is the intention to express the meaning "that which has water (ḍadaka) as its substrate (dheya) exists in this," the suffix *matup* is applied; thus,
it is that very [substratum] which is denoted,
and not the Ganges or other such things.

If that in which water is placed were itself called "possessing water" (*udakavān*), then the designation "pot" would apply even to the water, since water is also placed within a pot. Therefore, he says: "The pot possesses water," and so forth.
In this context, the speaker’s intention (*vivakṣā*) is the primary cause for the derivation of a word, not the actual existence of the object.

And that meaning of "holding" (*dadhati*) by which the ocean (*udadhi*) is so called is not intended here in the case of the pot; rather, there is intended merely the connection with the existence of water.
Only this much is intended to be expressed: "there is water in this.

Therefore, since the sense of "containing" (dadhāti) is not intended, the status of being an ocean (*udadhi*)—though it may exist in the jar—is simply not to be conceptualized; thus, this is not the domain for the irregular derivation (*nipātana*).
Consequently, one says, "the jar possesses water" (*udakavān*).
But when the meaning of "bearing" (dadhāti) is intended to be expressed, then it should be stated as "udanvān."
In the *Bālamano ramā*, under rule 8.2.13 (*saṃjñāyām*), it is stated:
"The forms beginning with *ahīvatī* are names (*saṃjñā*) of a particular river or a particular city.
[This is] because [the word *ahi*] belongs to the *śara*-group.

"And for *śara* and others," the meaning is that there is a long vowel [in the penultimate]. From the *Bālamanoramā*: "In *udanvān*, and when meaning 'ocean' (1876), 8.2.13: *udanvān* [is formed] and when meaning 'ocean'.
This means [the suffix *matup* is applied] when it is a proper name (*saṃjñā*) and when it signifies the ocean.

In reality, however, it would have been more appropriate to formulate the rule simply as *udanvāṃśca*, since the form *udanvat* is already established for "ocean" by the continued application (*anuvṛtti*) of the condition *saṃjñāyām* ("in the sense of a name"). Regarding the statement, "the form *rājanvān* is an irregular derivation (*nipātyate*)," what is irregularly derived here? The absence of the elision (*lopa*) of the *n*, and optionally the substitution of *nuṅ*.
[The example is] "*saurājyam*" ("good governance").

A king who is excellent is a "good king" (*surājā*); the state of being that is "good kingship" (*saurājyam*). The suffix *vyañ* is applied here according to Pāṇini 5.1.124 (*brāhmaṇādibhyaś ca*), resulting in the elision of the final *n*.
Furthermore, this good kingship consists in the connection of the country with an excellent king.

According to the rule "In compounds, primary derivatives (*kṛt*), and secondary derivatives (*taddhita*), the relation [of the base] is what is expressed" (Pāṇini-vārttika 130), the word *rājanvān* denotes only the country, not the good kingship itself.
But that region, though not directly expressed by the word, is understood because it is invariably concomitant with good governance (*saurājya*);
and since that [good governance] implies it, he says: "when it is being understood. The term *rājanvān* is in the masculine gender.
To demonstrate its lack of necessity, the example "the earth is possessed of a king" (*rājanvatī pṛthivī*) is introduced. This has been explained in the rule *harivo medinam* (Pāṇini 8.2.3),
as in the phrase *ārevānetu mā viśat*.

Regarding the word *rayi*, there is vocalization (*samprasāraṇa*) by the rule "vocalization occurs diversely for *rayi* before the suffix *mat*" (Pāṇini 6.1.37), followed by the substitution of the preceding vowel (*parapūrvatva*).

Now, why does this not occur here in the case of *saptarṣimantam* and *dyāvāpṛthivīmantam*? He says: when the dvandva compound *dyauśca pṛthivī ca* is formed, the substitution *dyāvā* for *div* takes place by the rule "in a dvandva of deities, *dyāvā* is substituted for *div*" (Pāṇini 6.3.29).
[Examples include] *gorvān*, *dhūrvān*, and *āśīrvān*.

The roots *gṛ* (in the sense of "sound," Dhātupāṭha 1498), *dhurvī* (in the sense of "harming," Dhātupāṭha 573), and *āṅ-pūrvaka-śās* (in the sense of "commanding," Dhātupāṭha 1022)—from these, the suffix *kvip* is applied because they belong to the *sampadādi* group.

In the case of *gṛṇāti*, the substitution of *i* for *ṛ* occurs by [Pāṇini 7.1.100]: *ṛta iddhātoḥ*. In the case of *dhurvī*, the letter *v* is elided by [Pāṇini 6.4.21]. In the case of *śās*, when the suffix *kvip* follows, the substitution of *i* for the root *śās* preceded by *āṅ* is established by the Vārttika [781]: *āśāsaḥ kvāvupasaṃkhyānam*. When the possessive suffix *matup* is added, the substitution of *ru* for the final consonant occurs by [Pāṇini 8.2.66]: *sasajuṣo ruḥ*. Thus, we have the form *akṣaṇvantah*.

By [Pāṇini 7.1.75], *chandasyāpi dṛśyate* [7.1.76], the augment *āṅ* is seen; the augment *nuṭ*; the elision of the *n* of *anaṅ*; and the *ṇ*-substitution for the *n* of *num*. Regarding the form *asthanvantam*:
with the exception of the *ṇ*-substitution, *anaṅ* and the other operations must be applied to the word *asthi* as before.

Regarding the word *śīrṣaṇvatī*, it is established as an irregular form (nipātita) by [Pāṇini 6.1.60]. Now, one might object: since the augment *nuṭ* is immediately preceding, it would be logical for that very *nuṭ* to undergo the substitution of *v* (vatva), and not for the letter *m* which is separated from it; so why does the substitution of *v* not apply to *nuṭ* here, while it does not apply to what follows it? To this, he says: "Because *nuṭ* is considered non-existent (*asiddha*)," and so forth.

Now, what about this *nuṭ*? Why does it not become an exception (*apavāda*) because it occurs later? Because they belong to different classes (*bhinnajātīyatva*). For a particular (*viśeṣa*) that has achieved a result of the same class can indeed sublate a general rule (*sāmānya*), but here there is a difference in the results: since *vatva* is a substitute (*ādeśa*) while *nuṭ* is an augment (*āgama*), there is no relationship of sublation between them. The placement of *nuṭ* at the beginning [of the word] is for the purpose that *ṇatva* may occur; otherwise, the prohibition [stated in Pāṇini 8.4.37] would apply. [Thus we have the form] *supanthitaraḥ*.

*śobhanaḥ panthāḥ* ("a beautiful path") is a *prādi-samāsa* (compound with prefixes). From the word *su-*, because of the prohibition in *na pūjanāt* [Pāṇini 5.4.69], the compound-ending suffix (*samāsānta*) prescribed by *ṛkpūrabdhūḥ* [Pāṇini 5.4.74] and so forth does not occur. [The form] *dalayuhantamaḥ* is derived from *dasyuṃ hatavān* ("one who has slain the Dasyu") with the suffix *kvip*, and from that [base ending in *kvip*], the superlative suffix *tamap* is added.

Regarding "bhūridāvattaraḥ": because he gives much (*bhūri dadāti*), the suffix *vanip* is applied by [Pāṇini 3.2.74] *āto maninkvanibvanipaśca*; then, the augment *tuṭ* is added to the final syllable of the subsequent member of the compound.
Regarding "rathītaraḥ": [the same suffix is applied].

[The objection: Is [the form *rathin*] derived from the word *rathin* by adding the possessive suffix *ini*, followed by the comparative suffix *tarap*, the elision of the *n*, and the substitution of *ī*—or rather, is it that the *ī* itself replaces the *n*, resulting in a long vowel by the rule of homogeneous vowels (*savarṇadīrghatva*)? In this case, the phoneme *ra* is taken as the original element (*sthānin*), and *la* is its substitute (*ādeśa*) of exactly the same nature; consequently, the substitution of *la* would apply only to that which is the isolated phoneme *repha* (the sound *r*) and not a constituent part [of a larger unit], but the *la* would not apply to the *ṛ*-vowel, because those two are not presented in the sutra as having the relationship of original element and substitute.

Furthermore, one might object that [if this were not the case], forms such as *kḷptaḥ* (prepared) and *kḷptavān* (has prepared) would not be established. To such an objection, he replies: "The universal 'ra' is employed.

Setting aside the distinction created by being a phoneme (*varṇatva*) or not being a phoneme (*avarṇatva*), that universal which resides in both individual instances of the letter *ra*—whether consisting of a phoneme or not consisting of a phoneme—is what is employed; for it is because of this [universal] that the name and cognition "ra" remain identical for both of those two, even though they are differentiated by the distinction of being a phoneme or not being a phoneme. It is not, however, the phonemic instance itself that is so. This is the specific point. [Regarding the word] "by that": [Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly; the translation reflects the portion available.]

By means of the inclusion of the general property (*sāmānya*), there is the apprehension of both; for that general property exists in both. [The phrase] "even 'la' is indeed a general property" implies that it is "included."

In this case as well, should it not be stated that there is the inclusion of both—the *l* sound alone and that which resides in the *ḷ* sound? It is not stated because its meaning is understood by following the previous rule.
Regarding the phrase "therefore this," etc.:
since there is thus the inclusion of both the *r* sounds and the *l* sounds, the substitution of the *l* sound alone is prescribed for the *r* sound alone.
By virtue of internal similarity, the *ḷ* sound also [substitutes] for the *ṛ* sound.

Now, even if both are included in the designation, one might object that it would not be possible to state that the *ṛ* sound is prescribed as the substitute in the place of the *ṛ* sound; for the *repha* (the sound *r*) residing within the *ṛ* sound does not itself become the *ṛ* sound—what then? It is merely a constituent part (*avayava*) of it.

In that case, since both [the *ṛ* and *ḷ* sounds] are included, the meaning obtained is that the *l*-sound residing in the *ḷ*-vowel is indeed similar to the *r*-sound residing in the *ṛ*-vowel due to their internal similarity (*antaratama*), but not the meaning that the *ḷ*-vowel occurs in place of the *ṛ*-vowel as well. To refute this objection, it is stated: "by way of a modification of one part.
Here, "one part" refers to the *r*-sound, which is a constituent of the *ṛ*-vowel; its "modification" is the *l*-sound, which is a constituent of the *ḷ*-vowel.
Alternatively, "one part" refers to the *l*-sound, which is a constituent of the *ḷ*-vowel, and that itself is the modification.
The letter *ṛ* undergoes a partial modification of its *r*-element. "Door" means the entrance or, in other words, the means;
by that [door], the substitution of the letter *ḷ* is prescribed in place of the letter *ṛ*.

If the separation of the *r* and *l* sounds residing within the phonemes *ṛ* and *ḷ* from those very *ṛ* and *ḷ* sounds were possible, then—due to that inseparability—the entire *ṛ* sound would be prescribed as the substitute for the entire *ḷ* sound by means of a partial modification (*ekadeśavikāra*). To strengthen this very point, he says: "And thus," and so forth.

Since, in this way, the sound *ḷ* is prescribed in place of *ṛ* by means of a partial modification (*ekadeśavikāra*), there is thus the inclusion of forms such as those governed by the rule *luṭi ca kḷpaḥ*. Having thus resolved the objection, that which was stated— namely, "In the case of the prescription of *nuṅ*, the substitution of *la*, and the modification (*vināma*), the vowel *ṛ* [or *ṛkāra* according to the Kāśikā and Padamañjarī] must be provided for" (Vārttika 1)— has now been addressed on the occasion of the substitution of *la*, as in the forms *kalptā*, *kalptārau*, and *kalptāraḥ*.
The suffix is either *tṛc* or *luṭ*.
Regarding the form *cikḷpsati*:
the suffix *san* [is applied], and because it is *kit* by rule 1.2.10, there is an absence of *guṇa*.
"Prepared," "has prepared"— these are the forms with the suffixes *kta* and *ktavatu*.
"Pity" (*kṛpā*)— this is [the form with the suffix] *a*.

How is this established? Since, in this case as well, there ought to be *latva* [the substitution of *l* for *ṛ*], he says: "‘Kṛpa’—this," and so forth. By this, he demonstrates that from the root *krapa* (Dhātupāṭha 771), meaning "to pity" or "to go," the form *kṛpa* arises when the suffix *aṅ* is applied according to Pāṇini 3.3.104 (*ṣidbhidādibhyo 'ṅ*) and the vocalization (*samprasāraṇa*) occurs simultaneously with it; thus, he shows that this form *kṛpa* is derived through grammatical rules (*lākṣaṇika*). If this is so, then why does *latva* not occur here? To this he replies: "For of that," and so forth.

Since the form *kṛp-* arises from the root *kṛp-* after the *samprasāraṇa* has been applied, it is therefore derivative (*lākṣaṇika*). Consequently, by the maxim "that which is derived from a rule does not include that which is taught explicitly" (*lakṣaṇapratipadoktaparibhāṣā*, Vyāḍi-Pāṇini 3), it is not included; thus, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of [the application of] *la*. In words such as *kṛpaṇa*, *kṛpīṭa*, and *karpūra*, this form *kṛp-* is indeed original (*aupadeśika*), not derivative.

For instance, regarding the suffix *kvun* prescribed by the rule "rañje kvun" (*rajaḥ kyun* is the reading in the Daurgasiddhi; there are alternative readings as *rajeḥ* or *rañjeḥ*) [Daurgasiddhi 5.24], because of the use of the word "bahulam" (in various cases), when it is applied specifically after the root *kṛp*, the form *kṛpaṇa* arises. Furthermore, regarding the suffix *kīṭan* prescribed by the rule "kṛtṛkṛpibhyaḥ kīṭan" (*kṛtṛkṛpikampibhyaḥ kīṭan* is the reading in the Daurgasiddhi; there is an alternative reading as *kapikampibhyaḥ*) [Daurgasiddhi 5.3], when this *kīṭan* is applied after the root *kṛp*, the form *kṛpīṭa* arises.

He states that when the suffix *ura* is applied according to the rule *kharjipiñjādibhya ūrolacau* (Dhātupāṭha 10.10), the form *karpūra* arises—namely, in the passage beginning with *kṛpaṇakṛpīṭa*. He considers the following: by virtue of the word *bahula* ("variously"), the suffix *kyun* (or *kvun*, as the reading in the Prātipadika-pāṭha suggests) is added to the root *kṛp* itself, and therein its semivowel is vocalized (*samprasāraṇa*). Furthermore, in the rule *kṛ-tṛkṛpibhyaḥ kīṭan* (Dhātupāṭha 5.3), the mention of *kṛpi* will be removed and replaced by the mention of *kḷpi*; the vocalization, however, will occur precisely because of the *bahula* rule.

Even in the rule *kharjipiñjādibhya ūrolacau*, by the inclusion of the word "etc. (*ādi*), only the root *kṛp* will be understood, and the vocalization (*samprasāraṇa*) will occur as before. Even though forms such as *kṛpaṇa* and *kṛpāṇa* would result [from that], he says—starting with *jaṇādayo bahulam iti vā*—to show that this would be a fault. Not conceiving it possible for two things of entirely different forms to have an identical nature, he asks: *kim idam* etc., and [answers] *samānaviṣayatvam*.

He demonstrates here that by the word "one" (*eka*), what is intended is the state of having an identical object-domain (*abhinna-viṣayatva*), and not an identical intrinsic nature (*abhinnasvabhāvatva*).

But for what purpose is the substitution of *l* prescribed with reference to *kṛp*, rather than *kṛp* itself being the referent? Only the state of being *l* (*latva*) should be applied in the place of *gu*; and that must necessarily be stated for the sake of [the application of] such forms as *upalkārīyati*.
And thus, in the rule *ṛdupadhāccakḷpi cṛteḥ* (Pāṇini 6.1.59), the prohibition regarding *kḷp* need not be formulated.

Therefore, it is possible [to argue] as follows: since the rule *ṛkāraḷkārayoḥ savarṇasaṃjñā* (P. 1.1.9) prescribes that the phonemes *ṛ* and *ḷ* share the designation "homogeneous" (*savarṇa*), the *u-ra-ṛtva* (the substitution of *u* for *ṛ*) being prescribed for the phoneme *ṛ* would also apply to the phoneme *ḷ*. Consequently, the phoneme *ḷ* would undesirably be classified as an *ṛ-varṇa*. However, if one teaches the form ending in *ṛ* and then prescribes the substitution of *l* for it, then the *la-tva* (the substitution of *l* for *ṛ*) of that *ḷ* is also established. In this regard, two alternatives are possible: one view is that the mention of *ayati* is a qualifier of the letter *r*; the second view is that it is a qualifier of the prefix (*upasarga*).

Regarding this, in the first view, the commentary (*vṛtti*) passage beginning with "after *ayi*" should be interpreted as follows: "When *ayi* follows, there is the substitution of *la* for that *ra* which belongs to a prefix. In the second view, it should be interpreted thus: "When *ayi* follows, there is the substitution of *la* for the *ra* belonging to that prefix which begins with *ma*. [Examples are: *plāyate*, *palāyate*.
The *ātmanepada* suffix occurs after the root *aya-ṇya* because it is marked with an *anudātta* vowel.

[An objection is raised: "How can there be *latva* (the substitution of *l* for *r*) here in the first view, since when that [substitution] is to be applied, the status of being a *sthānin* (original element) must apply by virtue of Pāṇini 1.1.57? Consequently, once there is a separation (*vibhāga*) between the verbal base and the prefix, the letter *r* would be separated from the letter *a*, and thus its being followed by *aya* would not be possible. To this he says: "In this case, that which... and so forth.
"Separation" (*vibhāge*) means disjunction (*viśleṣa*).

The mention of "single" (*ekagrahaṇa*) in the rule *pratyaya* is for the purpose of demonstrating that when there is a cluster [of consonants], the substitution of *l* does not occur if there is an intervention. For by that [rule], where there is indeed an intervention and no non-intervention, the substitution of *l* must take place because the statement lacks authority in the case of intervention. By what is there such an intervention? By a single phoneme (*varṇa*).
Furthermore, regarding whether there is an intervention by means of conjunction (*saṅghāta*) or not: because of that, [the rule] applies when there is an intervention.
Thus, in the first position, *latva* occurs when there is an intervention by a single phoneme (*varṇa*).

The rule does not apply only where there is an ungrammatical (aśāstrīya) intervention by means of the substitution of *sthānivadbhāva*; rather, it applies even where there is a worldly (laukika) intervention by a phoneme that is actually heard—this is the meaning of the word "also" (*api*). Now, one might object: by the mention of "niraḥ" in the rule *niraḥ kuṣaḥ* [Pāṇini 7.2.46], it is indicated that there exists another prefix ending in *r*, namely *nir-*; therefore, since the term [the rule] would find its scope in forms such as *nilaya*, how [could the rule apply to *niṣkuṣita*]?

"By that which [is intended] as non-intervention, [the rule applies] even when there is intervention, because of the authority of the statement" (Vyā|Pā|46)—so it has been said. He thinks thus: a single example does not necessitate a general definition; for if this were the only purpose, he would simply have used the term *nir*.

Having thus established the validity of everything under the first alternative (*pakṣa*), he says "But in the case of the qualifier of a prefix," etc., in order to establish it under the second alternative.
This word *tu* functions in the sense of the word *api*.

Not only is everything established—such as *palyayate* and so forth—when *ati* is understood as qualifying the letter *r*, but when that same [term] qualifies the prefix (*upasarga*), all this is likewise established.
Alternatively, the word "but" (*tu*) indicates the distinction of this position from the previous one;
for in that case, the objection arises that *latva* (the substitution of *l* for *r*) would apply due to the intervention of a vowel.

Therefore, all this—that which is to be established—is already proven; the meaning is that here there is no occasion at all for this objection, so it does not require further effort to establish. The objector [says]: "Does it not also follow from the prefix *pra*?"

The word *tu* (but) serves to distinguish [the present case] from the preceding one; in the previous instance, the suffix *prati* did not apply because it was separated by a compound (*saṅghāta*). Here, however, there is no separation by anything, and therefore they consider that *prati* also applies.
The phrase "others" refers to those who are adherents of the second position.
Regarding the rule "after *ni* and *dus*, [the *r* of *gira* becomes *l*]":

if one were to object, "Whether the mention of *ati* is a qualifier of the *repha* (the letter *r*) or a qualifier of the prefix (*upasarga*), in either case, once *ratva* (the substitution of *r*) has occurred, *latva* (the substitution of *l*) would follow," the author replies to such an objection with "after *ni* and *dus*" and so forth. The meaning is already explained. As for the example "he swallows" (*girati*).
It is a form derived from the sense of "swallowing" (*nigaraṇa*);
it is the word *nigaraṇam*,
formed with the suffix *lyuṭ*.
"Nigāraka" [is derived] with the suffix *ṇvul*;
it means "one who swallows down" (*nigāryate*).

For here, once the *ṇi*-elision has been performed, the optional rule (*vikalpa*) would not be established because there is no vowel (*ac*) following [the elided element]. To refute this objection, he says: "it is caused to be made to flow" (*nigāryate*), "it is caused to be strained" (*nigālyate*).
The status of being as if occupying the original position (*sthānivadbhāva*) is, however, as before.
This might be the case.

Is it not the case that there is no application of the *sthānivadbhāva* rule here, because of the prohibition stated in *Pūrvatrāsiddhe na sthānivat* (Paribhāṣenduśekhara 48)? To this he replies with the words "In the case of what is not established in what precedes," and so forth.
*Sāpavādam* means "accompanied by an *apavāda*"; *apavāda* here signifies a fault (*doṣa*).
The meaning is that this very [prohibition] constitutes a flaw in this Paribhāṣā.
The word *api* is used for conjunction.

Not only is that objection accompanied by an exception, but this statement as well—namely, "that which was previously established is not treated as a substitute" (*pūrvatrāsiddhaṃ na sthānivat*)—is indeed accompanied by an exception.
To demonstrate that very fact of being accompanied by an exception through the words of an authoritative teacher, he says: "of that," and so forth.

In that regard, this fault arises in the rule for the elision of a *saṃyoga* (consonant cluster) and so forth: [the forms] *kākyarthaḥ* and *vāsyarthaḥ*. Here, if there were no *sthānivadbhāva* (the status of being like the original element) for the *yaṇ* substitute, the elision of the *k* and *s* sounds would undesirably apply by the rule *skoḥ saṃyogādyoḥ* [Pāṇini 8.2.29]. In the rule for the substitution of *l* (*latva*), [in the forms] *nigāryate* and *nigālyate*, if there were *sthānivadbhāva* for the elision of the *ṇi* suffix, the optional substitution of *l* would not occur. In the rule for the substitution of *ṇ* (*ṇatva*), [in the forms] *prahiṇoti* and *pramīṇīta*, if there were no *sthānivadbhāva* for the *guṇa* and *it* qualities, the substitution of *ṇ* would not be obtained by the rule *raṣābhyāṃ no ṇaḥ samānapade* [Pāṇini 8.4.1].

"Or because of its being internal," and so forth. This is another solution. The status of being internal (*antaraṅgatva*) belongs to the optionality of *latva* (the substitution of *la*), because it depends on the phoneme (*varṇa*).
However, the elision (*ṇilopa*) is extrinsically conditioned (*bahiraṅga*), because it depends upon the *ārdhadhātuka* suffix.
Now, why does the substitution of *l* not occur in the forms *girau* and *giraḥ*? To this he says: "In *girau*, *giraḥ*, etc.
The particle *iti* indicates the reason.
When a root is understood in its own form (*svarūpa*), then regarding that suffix, the operation is understood to apply only to that suffix which is prescribed immediately after the root.

Therefore, it does not occur in *agiraḥ* and *giraḥ*. For in these cases, the nominative and accusative singular endings (*au* and *jas*) are not prescribed after the root *gṛ* ending in *kvip* by the rule *śrato rītaḥ* [Pāṇini 7.1.91]; rather, they are prescribed under the governing heading (*adhikāra*) of "nominal stem" (*prātipadika*) [Pāṇini 4.1.1]. [This refers to the rule] *saṃyogāntasya* [Pāṇini 8.2.23].

That whose end is a *saṃyoga* (a conjunct consonant) is described as such. The inclusion of the term "end" (*anta*) is for the sake of clarity; for the term "of a word" (*padasya*) [from Pāṇini 8.1.16] is understood to carry over, and since the word is qualified by the *saṃyoga*, the status of being "ending in a *saṃyoga*" is obtained for the word by [Pāṇini 1.1.72].

In the case of *gomān*, once the elision of the *hal* and *ṅī* etc. has been performed, the long vowel [is applied] by [Pāṇini 6.4.14], which states that "the final [vowel] of that which ends in *al* is elided" [and the subsequent rule 6.4.15 applies].
In the cases of *kṣeyān* and *bhūyān*, [the same process applies].

In this case, [the substitution of] *r* would not apply due to the elision of the final consonant of the conjunction (*saṃyogāntalopa*). To one who might think that it is superseded by the substitution of *ru* because of its higher status [in the order of rules], he says: "It is better, it is more," and so forth. If, then, even though it is subsequent, the substitution of *ru* does not supersede the elision of the final consonant of the conjunction because it is considered unestablished (*asiddha*), then for that very reason it would also not supersede the substitution of the voiced stops (*jaśtva*). Consequently, in the cases of *yaśaḥ* and *payaḥ*, there would be only the substitution of *jaś* (the voiced stops *j* and *g*), and not the substitution of *ru*. To this he says: "But as for the substitution of *jaś*," and so forth. For the substitution of *ru* is commenced whether the elision of the final consonant of the conjunction has already applied or has not yet applied.

It is appropriate that *rutva* (the substitution of *r*) does not subvert [the rule for] *jaśtva* (the substitution of voiced stops), because in cases such as *śreyān*, *jaśtva* is already applicable, whereas in the case of *payaḥ*, it is not yet applicable. It is appropriate that *rutva* does not subvert [the rule for] *jaśtva*, because in cases such as *śreyān*, *jaśtva* is already applicable, whereas in the case of *payaḥ*, it is not yet applicable.
Since the substitution of *jaś* (the voiced unaspirated stops) is already applicable everywhere, that [substitution of *rut*] is then commenced.
Therefore, by virtue of possessing the character of an exception (*bādhaka*), the substitution of *rut* indeed becomes an exception to the substitution of *jaś*.

In the case of *śreyān*: the suffix *iyasun* is applied according to [Pāṇini 5.3.60], resulting in the elision of *śra*; then, by [Pāṇini 6.1.87] and [Pāṇini 6.4.10], "of that which ends in *s* or *mahat*," the long vowel (*dīrgha*) is substituted.
*bhūyān* [is derived as follows]: by [Pāṇini 6.4.158], there is the elision of the vowel *ī* in the suffix *īyasun*, and the substitution of *bhū-* for *bahu*.

Now, why does the elision of the final consonant of a conjunct (*saṃyogāntalopa*) not occur in cases such as *dadhy atra* and *madhv atra*? To this, he says: "*dadhy atra*" and so forth. However, the substitution of *yaṇ* is considered "extrinsic" (*bahiraṅga*) because it depends upon two words.
However, the elision of a final consonant cluster (*saṃyogāntalopa*) possesses the status of being "internal" (*antaraṅga*) because it depends upon a single word (*ekapada*).

Why [is there the mention of] "of a word" (*padasya*)? [Consider the examples: *gomantau*, *gomantaḥ*. Regarding the rule "of a word ending in a consonant cluster" (*saṃyogāntasya padasya*), and so forth:
here, the "word ending in a consonant cluster" is a qualifier for the letter *r* (*repha*), and the letter *r* is also a qualifier for the letter *s* (*sakāra*).

The final letter *s* of a word that ends in a conjunct consonant (*saṃyoga*)—specifically, the *s* that follows the *r* which is a member of that conjunct—is elided. For example: *akṣāḥ*, *atsāḥ*. [Derivation: From the roots *kṣara* (to move, DhP 851) and *tsara* (to go stealthily, DhP 554), we derive the aorist (*laṅ*). By [Pāṇini 7.2.2], there is *vṛddhi* strengthening; by [6.1.66], the suffix *tiP* is elided after a consonant or *ṅ*; and by this [rule], the *s* of the *sic* augment is also elided. Then the augment *aṬ* is added, and the *r* becomes a *visarga* by [8.3.15].
Is this not already established by the preceding rule? Why, then, is this [rule] commenced? To this he says: "In the case of what is established," and so forth.
This shows the nature of the restriction: "only after *r* there is *s*.

However, one should not suspect here a contrary restriction—namely, "only after *s* there is *r*"—because the word *pum̐s*, which has undergone the elision of its final consonant cluster according to Pāṇini 8.2.23 (*uraḥprabhṛtiṣu*), is listed [in the *gaṇapāṭha*] under 5.4.151.
For, under that reversed rule, the elision of the final consonant due to the presence of *saṃyoga* would not be applicable.

Regarding the word *ūrk*: from the root *ūrj* (meaning "to strengthen" and "to give life"—the reading is *ūrja-prāṇanayoḥ*), the suffix *kvip* is applied according to the rule beginning with *bhrājabhrāsa* [Pāṇini 3.2.177].

In this case, by rule, the elision of the letter *ja* does not occur; when that [elision] is absent, there is *kutva* according to [Pāṇini 8.2.30], whereby the letter *ja* becomes *ga*. Then, by [Pāṇini 8.4.55] (*vāvasāne*), there is *cartva*, whereby it becomes *ka*. Thus: *nyamārṭ* [the root *mṛj*—*kāśikā* and *padamañjarī*]. The root *mṛj* (meaning "to cleanse") is listed as number 1066 in the *Dhātupāṭha*. Due to its belonging to the *adādi* class, there is elision of the *śap* suffix. By [Pāṇini 6.1.66], there is elision of the *tip* ending according to the rule beginning with *halṅyābbhyo dīrghāt...* [and 7.2.114]. By [Pāṇini 8.2.36] (*vraśca...*), there is *ṣatva*, whereby [the *ga*] becomes *ṣ*. There is *jaśtva* for that [ṣ], whereby it becomes *ḍ*. There is also *cartva* for that [ḍ], whereby it becomes *ṭ*. [Examples: *alavidhvam*, *alaviḍhvam*.

Regarding *luṅ*, sic? [Pāṇini 3.1.44]: by the rule *sasya dhi ca* [Pāṇini 8.3.79], there is elision of the *s*. Thus, in one alternative, *bhū* becomes *dhanyaḥ*. With the words "if here" (*yadyatra*) and so forth, he demonstrates what is obtained when the elision of the *sakāra* takes place. For if the elision of the *sakāra* did not occur, then after applying the substitution of *ṣ* by *sicaḥ* [Pāṇini 8.3.59], and then the substitution of the *jaś*-class sound *ḍ* by *ṣṭun* [Pāṇini 8.4.53], and then the substitution of *ṣ* for the *dhakāra* by *ṣṭun* [Pāṇini 8.4.41], there would have to be a *ḍhakāra*. Consequently, even in the alternative where the *mūrdhanya* (retroflex) does not occur, the *dhakāra* would not be heard.
The inclusion of the term *vibhāṣā*, however, would serve the purpose of the *liṭ* [perfect tense] and the *liṅ* [optative mood].
Therefore, so that the sound *dh* may be heard in the alternative where the retroflex [ṣ] does not occur, the elision is prescribed;
[this is indicated by the statement]: "From this point onward, the elision of the *s* of *sic* is desired."
And that [result] is obtained through the continuation of the term *vibhāṣā* from rule 8.2.21 and by understanding it as an optionally fixed (*vyavasthitavibhāṣā*) rule.

Regarding the form *cakādhi*: the root is *cakāsṛ* (meaning "to shine," Dhātupāṭha 1074); the suffix is the imperative (*loṭ*), second person singular (*sip*); the replacement *hi* occurs by 3.4.87 (*sehir apicca*); the change to *dhi* occurs by 6.4.101; as before, there is the elision of the *śap* augment; and as before, there is the substitution of a voiced stop (*jaśtva*)—the *s* becomes *d*.
Regarding the example *payo dhāvati*: the substitution of *r* for the final syllable of the word *payaḥ* occurs, and by [Pāṇini 6.1.110] *haśi ca*, the substitution of *u* occurs.

Anticipating the objection that if the elision of *s* (of the suffix *sic*) were desired from this point onward, then in the forms *sagdhiḥ* and *babdhām*, the elision of the *s* by [Pāṇini 8.2.26] would not apply, he says: "*sagdhir babdhām*," etc.

The root *ad* is listed as "ada bhakṣaṇe" (Dhātupāṭha 1011). In the feminine, by the rule *ktin* (Pāṇini 3.3.94) followed by *ghaslādeśaḥ* (Pāṇini 2.4.37), there is the substitution of *ghas*. By the rule *upadhālopaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.4.100), the penultimate vowel is elided. The elision of the *s* is Vedic, according to the rule *bahulaṃ chandasi*.
Sometimes something else is stated; this too is the meaning of *bahulam*.
By the rule *iṣyate* (Pāṇini 8.2.40), the *t* is changed to *dh*, and as before, by the rule for *jaś*-substitution, the *gh* becomes *g*.

*samānā gdhiri* is a descriptive determinative compound (*viśeṣaṇasamāsa*). The substitution of *sa-* for *samāna-* occurs by the rule *samānasya chandasi* [Pāṇini 6.3.84]. Regarding *babdhām*: the root is *bhas* (meaning "to devour" and "to shine," Dhātupāṭha 1100). It is in the imperative (*loṭ*), which, by the extension *loṭo laṅvat* [Pāṇini 3.4.85], takes the endings of the imperfect (*laṅ*); thus, the ending *tas* becomes *tām*. Because it belongs to the *juhotyādi* class, there is the elision of the suffix *śap*. By the rule *ślau* [Pāṇini 6.1.10], there is reduplication. As before, there is the elision of the penultimate vowel (*upadhāsalopa*) and, likewise, the substitution of *da* for *ta*. Then, by the rule *bhakārasya dakāraḥ* [Pāṇini 8.4.54], there is the substitution of *jaś*-hood (*jaśtva*), whereby *bha* becomes *da*.
Thus, this much has been shown as the view intended by the author of the Ślokavārttika.
Now, in order to show the view of the Bhāṣyakāra, he says: "But the Bhāṣyakāra says," and so forth.
By this, he demonstrates that the Bhāṣyakāra intends the elision of the letter *s* alone, without any such distinction.
Regarding the passage beginning with "by that" (*tena*):
for one who intends the elision of every *s* without distinction, the rule would apply even in the case of *payo dhāvati*.
Therefore, another effort must be undertaken so that [the rule] does not apply here.
However, the recourse to the *vyavasthita-vibhāṣā* (the optionality restricted by rule) in this other effort is exactly as in the previous case.

This, however, is the distinction: in the former instance, by virtue of the *vyavasthita-vibhāṣā*, the elision of *s* will occur only after the root *dhī*, and not after any other; whereas here, the elision of the mere *s* occurs without distinction only where the cause (*nimitta*) and the effect (*nimittin*) reside within the same word (*samāna-pada*), such as in *papau* and *adhāvīt*. But in cases where they reside in different words (*bhinna-pada*), such as *payodhāvati*, it does not occur at all.

To this extent, the established linguistic usage is called "another effort" (*yatnāntara*). In order to state this matter—which has been summarized here—in detail, along with objections and their refutations, he says: "*dhi sakāre sico lopaḥ*" and so forth.
It should be understood that the word *dhi* serves as an indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*) for the point from which the elision of the *sakāra* is to be prescribed when *dhi* follows.
Why is this so? Because of the statement made previously: "From this point onward, the elision of the *sakāra* of *sica* is desired."

Because the *sakāra* is intended to be expressed as the locus (*adhikaraṇa*) with respect to the elision (*lopa*), there is an indication by means of the locative case. What is the purpose [of this]? He says: "For from *cakāt*" and so forth.

If there is elision of the *sic*, how then is *āśādhvam* formed? From the root *āṅ-pūrvaka-śās* in the sense of "desire" (*icchā*; Dhātupāṭha 1022), in the imperative (*loṭ*), the ending *dhvam*, the substitution of *e* for *ṭi* [by P. 3.4.91], and the elision of *śap* as before.

In this case, the elision (*lopa*) of the letter *s* is desired, but it does not occur if the elision is prescribed only for the *s* of the suffix *sic*. [Objection: "The substitution of a *jaś* sound (*jaśtva*) will take place for the *s*. [Response: By the rule [Pāṇini 8.4.53], the *jaśtva*—that is, the substitution of *d* for the *s*—is established, resulting in the form *āśābdam*.
To refute the rule regarding the elision of the *s* from here on, he says: "Everything would thus be established."
If [the substitution] were to occur for the letter *s*, then by that very rule of *jaś*-ness, the entire object of the rule would be accomplished;
consequently, the intention is that this grammatical rule for the elision of *s* would not even need to be composed.

To this, one might object: "If *jaś*-ness were to apply, there would be a difference in the audible form (*śruti*); for instance, when doubling of the *s* occurs according to [Pāṇini 8.4.46], and then *jaś*-ness is applied to the two *s*s, the hearing of two *d*s would result. To this he replies: "And yet, the audible form does not differ."
The sense is that there is no difference in the perception of a single or multiple consonants when they follow a vowel.
"And *luṅ* is also not included in the [rule for] the cerebralization" means that it must be done [to include it]; this is the ellipsis.
And this is another advantage when *jaś*-ness applies:

in the rule "After an *iṇ*-stem, the *dh* of *ṣīdhvam*, *luṅ*, and *liṭ* [is replaced by a retroflex] when following an *aṅga*" (Pāṇini 8.3.78), there would be no need to mention *luṅ* because the retroflex substitution is already established in cases such as *accoḍhvam* and *aploḍhvam* through the sequence of *ṣatva*, *jaśtva*, and *ṣṭutva*.

[The roots] *cyuṅ*, *jyuṅ* [are not found in the Dhātupāṭha], and *pruṅ-pluṅ* "to go" [are not found in the Prācīna manuscript]. (Dhātupāṭha 955, 956, 957, 958). Regarding *luṅ*: [after the suffix] *dhvam*, there is *sic*. By [Pāṇini 8.3.59], there is the substitution of *ṣ* [for *s*]; by [Pāṇini 8.4.53], there is the substitution of a *jaś*-sound for the letter *ṣ*, namely the letter *i*; and by the rule of *ṣṭu*-substitution, the letter *dh* becomes *ḍh*.

Thus, through the sequence of operations such as the substitution of *ṣ*, in the *luṅ* tense, the cerebralization of the letter *gh* results in *sidh-dha*. Therefore, what is the purpose of mentioning *luṅ*? In this way, *luṅ* is rejected.
As for the one who maintains that the mention of *luṅ* (the aorist suffix) must be made [in the rule], he says: "It is defective with respect to *seṭ*.

If the mention of *laṅ* were not made for the cerebralization (*mūrdhanya*) and the insertion of *iṭ*, then in the case of [Pāṇini 8.3.79] *vibhāṣeṭaḥ*, the cerebralization would not apply; consequently, as before, once the rules for *ṣatva* and so forth have been applied, there would always be the form *alavidhvam* alone, and never the form *apalaviḍhvam*.
Therefore, the mention of *luṅ* must be made for the sake of subsequent rules.
The elision of the *s* in [Pāṇini 8.2.25] *dhi ca* must be stated for the sake of establishing forms such as *alaviḍhvam*;
for this would not be established if the elision of the *s* did not occur. Consequently, what was said—that "everything would be thus established"—is incorrect.

And when the rule *śrica* [Pāṇini 8.2.25] is being applied, the mention of *sic* must be made so that [the substitution of *ru* for *s*] does not occur after *hu*. Thus, according to the opinion of the author of the *Ślokavārttika*, it is established that the mention of *sic* must be made. As for the other [view], he says—in order to show another fault when that [rule] is applied: "*ghasibhasor na sidhyet*" [sic would not be established], etc.
The word *tu* (but/however) is used in the sense of a reason (*hetu*).

Why? For the reason stated—that if the mention of *sij* were made, the elision of the *sakāra* in *dhasi* and *bhasi* would not be established in forms such as *sagdhiḥ* and *babdhām*—is not a valid reason. Because even if the elision [of the *sakāra*] by the rule *dhasi-bhasoḥ* (Pāṇini 8.2.26) does not occur when the mention of *sij* is made, nevertheless, an elision of the phoneme (*varṇalopa*) will occur according to Vedic usage (*cchāndasa*). By that [Vedic elision], both these forms, *sagdhiḥ* and *babdhām*, are indeed established. To the question "In what way is there a Vedic elision of a phoneme?", he says "Just as," and so forth.

Just as in the application regarding the sacrificial ritual (*adhvara*), there is a Vedic elision of a phoneme in the phrase *iṣkartāram adhvarasya*, so too will [the elision] occur in *sagdhīḥ* and *babdhām* for the roots *ghas* and *bhakṣ*.

Here, the word *vā* indicates another justification; that other justification is this: *sagdhīḥ* is not a form derived from *ghas*, but rather from the root *ṣagha* (meaning "to injure," Dhātupāṭha 1268).

But surely there is a difference in meaning and a difference in accent: in the former derivation, the meaning is "equal bending," and it has an udātta accent on the final syllable due to the *tas* suffix; whereas when the suffix *ktin* is applied to the root *ṣadhi*, it means "injury" and has an udātta accent on the first syllable due to the *nit* suffix. [Response: Since verbal roots have multiple meanings, the root *ṣadhi* will function here in the sense of "equal bending," and the final udātta accent will occur through a shift in accent; thus, there is no fault.

Furthermore, this form *bandhāma* does not arise from [the root] *bandh*; what then? It is derived from the root *badha* in the sense of "binding" (*badha bandhane*, Dhātupāṭha 973), with the imperative suffix *loṭ* and the first-person plural ending *mas*. By applying [Pāṇini 8.2.36] which changes the final *t* to *d*, and then by applying [Pāṇini 8.2.40] which changes the *dh* of the root to *b*, the form *babdhāma* is produced.

Thus, even if the inclusion of the term *sic* were to fail to establish the forms of *ghas* and *bhas*, there would still be no undesirable consequence; for by this etymological derivation as well, that [undesirable result] is avoided.
As it has been said: "The forms *ghasit* and *bhasit* would not be established; therefore, the mention of *sic* [in the rule] is not for that purpose.

Consequently, the view of the author of the Ślokavārttika—that the purpose [of the mention of *sic*] is stated in *Pāṇini 8.2.25*, namely, "there is the elision of *sic* after a root ending in *ghu* when followed by *s*"—is thus established. For example: *abhitta*, *abhitthāḥ*.

In the *luṅ* (aorist) of the root *bhid*, the *ātmanepada* ending is used because it has a *svarita* indicatory vowel (*svaritet*). Similarly, in *avāttām*: from the root *das*, in the *luṅ*, the suffix *tas* is replaced by *tām*. By the rule "khari ca" [Pāṇini 8.4.54], the *d* is changed to *t*—that is, the letter *t*. Thus, "avāttām.
In *avāttām*, from the root *das*, in the *luṅ*, *tas* becomes *tām*.
Regarding the form *adātta*:
the *th* is replaced by *t*, and a *vṛddhi* vowel is substituted according to [Pāṇini 7.2.3], *vadavraja* etc.

Here, one might have the misconception that once the *s* has been elided, the rule [Pāṇini 7.4.49], *saḥ syārdhadhātuke*, would not apply to change the *t* to *s*. To address such a person, he says: *avāttām*, and so forth.
"amaṃsta, amaṃsthāḥ"—[from] *mana* "to know" (Dhātupāṭha 1176); because it is anudāttet, it takes the ātmanepada endings.
"abhitsātām"—[from] *bhid* "to split."
*bhiderātām* and *abhitsata*: by [Pāṇini 7.1.5], there is the substitution of *ad* for the *jha* suffix. *Alāviṣṭām*.

Regarding *tasaḥ tāṃ*, there is vṛddhi in the case of *sic*. Here, since the sequence is established by direct audition (*śruti*), the *sakāra* follows a short vowel and the augment *iṭ*; it does not follow from the stem (*aṅga*), because the addition of *iṭ* is a part of the suffix (*pratyayabhakta*) and thus not part of the stem itself. For example: *alāviṣuḥ*.
