In *akṛṣātām*, the suffix *jhi* is replaced by *jus* according to Pāṇini 3.4.109 (*sijabhyastavidibhyaśca*). Due to the rule *uśca* (1.2.12), the suffix is marked with the *kittva* indicator, which results in the absence of *guṇa* substitution.

Regarding "dviṣṭacām": [the suffix] *suc* is applied after words ending in two, three, or four [syllables] by Pāṇini 5.4.18; then *tarap* is added for the sense of excellence (*atiśāyana*). By the rule beginning with 5.4.11 (*kimettiṅ...*), the suffix *amu* is added, and by 8.3.101, the *s* is replaced by a retroflex (*mūrdhanya*) sound. Regarding "adevīt": when the prohibition of *vṛddhi* is applied by 7.2.4 (*neṭi*), the *guṇa* substitution of the light penultimate vowel occurs; then *iṭ* is added by 7.3.96. The term *jhal* continues to apply [from the previous rule].

The term *saṃyogādyoḥ* is a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*). Although here the conjunction (*saṃyoga*)—being the meaning of the latter member—is subordinate (*guṇabhūta*), nevertheless, because the mention of "the first of a conjunction" (*saṃyogādi*) does not serve as a qualifier for *skorantagrahaṇam*, it is understood that even though it is subordinate, the conjunction itself is qualified by it. Thus he says: "that conjunction which is at the end of a word. Regarding the word "at the end":
The meaning is "at the end. Regarding the phrase "when followed by a *jhal* [consonant]," it requires the word "of a *pada*" (*padasya*).

Regarding the phrase "of those two, the first": the meaning is "of that aforementioned conjunction, of the two [moments] constituting its beginning. Regarding the word "attached" (*lagna*): [it means] joined.

The roots *olasja* and *olajī* mean "to be ashamed" (*dhātupāṭhaḥ* 1290, 1291). Here, with the suffix *niṣṭhā*, when a *jhali* consonant follows the letter *j*, there is elision of the *s* that is part of the conjunction of *s* and *j* at the beginning of the word, according to [Pāṇini 8.2.45]. Then, by [Pāṇini 8.2.42], the change to *n* occurs. By [Pāṇini 7.2.14], the augment *iṭ* is prohibited because the root ends in *śvī* or *ī*. Finally, by [Pāṇini 8.2.30], the change to *k* (kutva) occurs, resulting in the letter *g*. Thus, the form is *sādhulak*.
The suffix *kvip* is applied after the root *lajj* with the sense of "agent" (*sādhu*).

Here, the *num* augment is added by the rule *atra padasyādasāne saṃyogaḥ* [Pāṇini 7.1.60]. And that *num* is indeed present; for it is stated in the Vārttika: "The *num* is placed before the final letter of the root *masj*, for the purpose of [preventing] the elision of the *anubandha* and the initial of the *saṃyoga*."
7) According to this statement, [the augment] occurs before the final letter *j*. And for that [root], there is the elision of the nasal by the rule *aniditām* [Pāṇini 6.4.24].
Thus we have *taṣṭaḥ*.

[The roots] *takṣū* and *tvakṣū*, meaning "to make thin" (Dhātupāṭha 655, 656), have an indicatory vowel *ū*; therefore, by the rule *svaratyādi-* [Pāṇini 7.2.44], the augment *iṭ* is optional. Consequently, by the rule *niṣṭhāyām* [Pāṇini 7.2.15], there is a prohibition of *iṭ*.

Regarding the example *kāṣṭhaśavasthātā*: the suffix *kvip* is applied because [the root] *śak* can take *kāṣṭha* as its object (*kāṣṭhaṃ śaknoti*). The compound *kāṣṭhaśaki-sthātā* is formed by means of a *yogavibhāga* (separation of rules) from the rule *saptamī* (Pāṇini 2.1.40). With the words *tad atra* and so forth, he refutes what was stated [in the Vārttika]: "it should be stated that [the substitution of *ṣa* for *śa* occurs] before a *jhal*-ending [suffix]" (Vārttika 917). The word *tat* is used here to introduce the statement.
"There is no usage at all of the root *śak* with the suffix *kvip*.

[This objection is raised because] the suffix *kvip* would apply by the rule "after *śak*" (Pāṇini 3.2.130). However, the purpose of including the word "is seen" (*dṛśyate*) here is this: that the rule should apply only where the usage of a form with *kvip* is actually observed in common worldly usage; and in the world, no such usage of *śak* with *kvip* as *kāṣṭhaśak* is observed.

Therefore, since there is no usage of the root *śak* with the *kvip* suffix at all, for this reason the author of the Bhāṣya says—intending to reject [the necessity of] the statement "it should be stated that [the substitution occurs] before a *jhal* letter followed by *saṅ*" (Vārttika 917)—"There is not even a *kāṣṭhaśak*; how then could this *kāṣṭhaśak* exist? Its function consists in being dependent upon a substratum (*ādhāra*) such as a hole (*udghana*). Therefore, where the substratum itself, namely the *kāṣṭhaśak*, does not exist, its dependent, the agent who stands (*sthātṛ*), is all the more non-existent. Consequently, it need not be stated that [the substitution occurs] before a *jhal* letter followed by *saṅ*; for there is nothing to be excluded (*vyāvartyābhāvāt*).

Why does [the substitution] not occur here in *vāksthātā*? Because the *kutva* (the substitution of *k* for *s*) is treated as non-existent (*asiddha*) when there is the elision of the initial member of a *saṃyoga*. Why then does it not occur here in *vāsyārtham* and *kākyartham*? He says: "In the case of *dāsyartham*, *kākyartham*, etc. Now, what is the purpose of [specifying] *skor*? It is so that it does not occur in *narnarti*.

This form is derived after the substitution of *ru* for the reduplication of the root *nṛt* when it is in its yaṅ-luk (intensive without suffix) form, according to [Pāṇini 7.4.91]. Why is it said "of the first member of a conjunct"? Consider the example *payaḥśak*;
this is a word ending in the *kvip* suffix.
For there is no usage at all of the root *śak* when it is accompanied by a prefix and ends in *kvip*;
however, it would certainly occur when it is used alone.
Why [is it said] "if it is at the end"? [Consider] *takṣitā*, *takṣakaḥ*. [This applies] "before a consonant (*jhal*) and at the end of a word (*padānte*)."

The term "parataḥ" (after) is connected with each [term]. Now, one might object: since *jhal* was drawn forward by the particle *ca* in the preceding sūtra, its recurrence here is improper? This is not so; for in that [preceding] case, *jhal* was not drawn forward by the particle *ca*. What then? It was because of its being marked as *svarita* that it continued to apply; thus, the mention of "end" (*anta*) does not obstruct it, and this has been explained by the particle *ca*. [The example is] "vāk".
From the root *vac*, the suffix *kvip* is applied by the rule "kvib vaci" (Vārttika 288), and there is lengthening of the vowel.

Regarding the form *kruñca*: here some read the root as *kuñc* with a *repha* (*ra*) and the vowel *a* as its penultimate, according to the Dhātupāṭha entry "kuñca kauṭilyālpībhāvayoḥ" (186); others read it as *kuñc* without the *repha* and with the vowel *na* as its penultimate, according to the Dhātupāṭha entry "kuñca kauṭilyālpībhāvayoḥ" (185).

In this regard, if someone were to raise an objection based on the earlier reading—asking why [the substitution] does not occur in the case of *kruñca*—he replies with the words beginning with *ṛñca*.
By this, he demonstrates the purpose here of that which was previously rejected by the statement: "It need not be said that [the rule applies] before a *jhal* letter followed by *saṅ*.
Alternatively, it is due to the irregular formation (*nipātana*) prescribed by the rule *yujikruñcāñca* [Pāṇini 3.2.59].

In the word *kruñc*, the connection is that the substitution of *k* (kutva) does not occur for the letter *ñ*. Having accepted the reading of the word as having *ñ* as its penultimate (*ñakāropadha*) and containing the letter *r* (*sarepha*), two such solutions were stated to address the resulting contingency. Now, however, there is no contingency of *kutva* at all; for this word is not read with *ñ* as its penultimate, but rather with *n* as its penultimate. To demonstrate this, he says: "Or, it has *n* as its penultimate," and so forth.

But what is the reason for reading it with the letter *na* as the penultimate? What then? He says "or with the letter *na* as the penultimate" (*nakāropadho vā*) and so forth, in order to demonstrate that it has *na* as its penultimate. Furthermore, he asks:
"What is the reason for reading it with the letter *na* as the penultimate? and answers: "For if there were elision of the letter *na*" (*nakāralope hi*) and so forth.
Indeed, this usage *nikucita* exists.

While the rule *dhātorniṣṭhāntasya* [Pāṇini 6.4.23] is being carried over, the elision of the letter *n* is observed here by the application of *aniditām* [Pāṇini 6.4.24]. Therefore, this root is recited with *n* as its penultimate letter; otherwise, this usage would not be tenable. For there is no grammatical rule (*lakṣaṇa*) for the elision of the letter *ñ*.

If, then, *kuñc* is recited as being devoid of the letter *r* and having *n* as its penultimate (*nakāropadha*), then the forms *kruṅ*, *kruñcau*, and *kruñcaḥ* would not be established; for when the suffix *kvip* is applied by the rule [Pāṇini 3.2.59] beginning with *ṛtvig*, and the *n* is elided by the rule [6.4.24] beginning with *aniditām*, the result would be *kuk*, *kuc-au*, and *kuc-aḥ*. Therefore, he says: "*yujikruñcām*," and so forth.

It might be argued: "Even if the non-elision of the letter *n* is treated as an irregularity (*nipātana*), nevertheless, when the *n* becomes an *anusvāra*, and that [anusvāra] undergoes the *parasavarṇa* substitution (becoming *ñ*) before a *yay* sound according to Pāṇini 8.4.58, would not the *kutva* (the change to a guttural) still apply? To this he says: "In that case," and so forth; the meaning is already explained. Regarding the word *soḍhā*:

once the substitution of *ḍha* for *ha* has been made by Pāṇini 8.2.40, the *t* of the suffix *tṛc* becomes *d* [by Pāṇini 8.2.41], then *ṣṭu* substitution occurs [by Pāṇini 8.4.41], and finally the substitution of *ū* for *o* occurs [by Pāṇini 6.3.112].

Regarding "jalāṣāṭ": it means "one who endures water. [The suffix] *ṇvi* is applied by [Pāṇini 3.2.62] and [3.2.63]; there is vṛddhi of the penultimate vowel; it is a compound with an upapada; [by Pāṇini 6.3.137] there is lengthening of the first member; the *jaś*-tva of the letter *ḍha* results in the letter *ḍa*; its *caturtha*-tva results in the letter *ṭa*; [by Pāṇini 8.3.56] this becomes a retroflex (*mūrdhanya*). Regarding "praṣṭhavāṭ": [it is derived similarly].

The suffix *ṇvi* is applied by [Pāṇini 3.2.64] *vahaśca*. Although the rule *cuhoḥ kuḍhau* could have been formulated as a single yoga, its formulation as separate rules is for the purpose of preventing an equal number of operations.
For if they were a single yoga, then due to the equality of number, there would be *kutva* before *jhal*-beginning suffixes and *ḍhatva* at the end of a word; [the examples are] *dagdhā*, *dagdhum*.
As before, there is the substitution of *dha* for *dh*; and by the rule that a *jhaś* sound replaces [the final consonant] before a *jhaś* sound, the *ghakāra* becomes *gakāra*.
Thus, "kāṣṭhadhak" is a form ending in the *kvip* suffix.

By the rule *ekāco baśo bhaṣ* [Pāṇini 8.2.37] and others, the letter *d* becomes *bhaṣ*, which is *dh*; the letter *gh* undergoes *jaś*-substitution to become *g*; and that *g* undergoes *cutva*-substitution to become *k*. Since the rule says *dādeḥ* ("of those beginning with *d*"), the substitution of *gh* would not be established in the case of *adhog*, because this word does not begin with *d* and thus is not governed by that rule; therefore, he says "of the root" (*dhātoḥ*) and so forth.
That [term "root"] is indeed a qualifier.

The meaning is that it is a qualifier of *dāder* (of what begins with *da*). Of what kind is it? It means "ending in a genitive case [expressing] a part" (*avayava-ṣaṣṭhy-antam*); that is, it ends in a genitive case that relates to a constituent part (*avayava*).
"What is accomplished [by this]? means: "If this is so, what desired result is established?
[The answer is: "In this way, the phoneme *gh* is also established in the word *adho-gu*."

In this case as well, since the letter *d* is a constituent part of the word *dādi*, which itself is a constituent part of the verbal root (*dhātu*), the substitution of the *bhaṣ*-class sound applies to *d*.

[The derivation is as follows: *duh* with the suffix *laṅ*, followed by *tip*; due to its being of the *adādi* class, there is elision of *śap*; then the elision of the final consonant and the following vowel according to Pāṇini 6.1.68; as before, the substitution of the *bhaṣ*-class sound; and the augment *aṭ*.
[Regarding the objection] "How [is this so? and so forth:
The substitution of *gh* occurs for the letter *h* that is a constituent part of that word beginning with *da* which itself is a constituent part of a verbal root (*dhātu*).
This being the case, the meaning is that the substitution of *gh* cannot possibly occur in forms such as *dagdhā* and *dagdhum*;
for in these instances, the letter *h* is not a constituent part of that word beginning with *da* which is a constituent part of the verbal root.
However, that composite [form] of which the letter *ha* is a constituent part is indeed a verbal root (*dhātu*), not something that has *ha* as its constituent part.
To this, he gives the answer: "By virtue of being treated like that which possesses a designation" (*vyapadeśivadbhāvāt*).
By this principle of being treated like that which possesses a designation, even this [composite] becomes a constituent part of the verbal root, such as *vā*.
Even when there is no actual difference, usage in the world is observed as if there were a distinction; for example:
"the body of a stone statue" and "the head of Rāhu. Alternatively, and so forth:
*dhātūpadeśa* refers to the list of verbal roots (*dhātupāṭha*).
In that context, it is understood as "that which begins with *d*.

But how is the qualification "beginning with *d*" obtained in the list of verbal roots (*dhātupāṭha*)? It is obtained through the force of the mention of "verbal root" (*dhātu*). For its purpose would be this: so that [the rule] does not apply to what is not a verbal root.

And this [objection] is without merit, for it is not possible for the letter *ha* to be a constituent part of a verbal root (*dhātu*) when the letters beginning with *jha* follow, or at the end of a word, such that the mention of "verbal root" (*dhātu*) would be intended to exclude it.

That superfluous mention leads one to understand this meaning: that the quality of beginning with the letter *da* is a qualifier applied specifically to the verbal root as it appears in the Dhātupāṭha.

When understood in this way, although there is grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) between "of a verbal root" (*dhātoḥ*) and "beginning with *da*" (*dādeḥ*), nevertheless, the substitution of *gha* does indeed apply in the case of *adhoṅ*, because in the Dhātupāṭha, the root *duh* begins with the letter *da*.
"And so," and so forth.

And when it is understood in this way, although *dāmaliha* begins with the letter *da*, nevertheless the substitution of *dha* does not occur in the case of *dāmaliḍ*; for in the original enunciation of the verbal root (*dhātūpadeśa*), it does not begin with *da*.
Its status as a verbal root is established by [Pāṇini 3.1.32].

The word "also" (*api*) indicates that the substitution of *ḍha* occurs not only after the root *adhi*, but also after *dāmaliḥ*. [The derivation is as follows: from *dāma* and the root *lih* (to lick), *kvip* is applied to form *dāmaliḥ*. From that [stem ending in *kvip*], *kyac* is applied according to *supa ātmanaḥ kyac* [Pāṇini 3.1.8] to form *dāmaliham icchati* ("he desires to lick the rope"). From the stem ending in *kyac*, *kvip* is applied again; then, by *lopo vyor vali* [Pāṇini 6.1.66], there is the elision of the vowel *a*; by *lopaḥ śākalyasya* [Pāṇini 8.3.19], there is the elision of the *y*; by *ho ḍhaḥ* [Pāṇini 8.2.31], there is the substitution of *ḍha* for *ha*; and by *jhalāṃ jaś jhaśi* [Pāṇini 8.4.53], there is the substitution of the voiced unaspirated stop (*jaś*) for the *ḍha*. Regarding the term "*druheḥ*": this refers to the root *druh* meaning "to wish to harm" (*jighāṃsā*), as listed in the Dhātupāṭha (no. 1197).
Regarding the phrase "of the others":

this is because [the suffix] does not apply to these—namely, *muh* in the sense of "bewilderment" (Dhātupāṭha 1198), *ṣṇuha* in the sense of "vomiting" (Dhātupāṭha 1199), and *ṣṇiha* in the sense of "affection" (Dhātupāṭha 1200).

Furthermore, these [roots] would have the form *ghatva* because they do not begin with the letter *da*: *vraścū* "to cut" (DhP 1292), *bhrasj* "to cook" (DhP 1284; the root in the Dhātupāṭha is indeed *bhrasj*), *sṛj* "to emit" (DhP 1178), *mṛj* "to cleanse" (DhP 1066), *yaj* "to worship the gods, to associate, to give" (DhP 1002), *rāj* "to shine" (DhP 822), and *ṭu bhrājṛ*, *ṭṛbhrāśṛ*, *ṭubhlāśṛ* "to shine" (DhP 823, 824, 825).
The term *cha* denotes words ending in the letter *ch*; the term *śa* denotes words ending in the letter *ś*.

Here, since the substitution of the voiced unaspirated stop (*jaś*) would apply to the letter *ś*, while the substitution of the unaspirated stop (*kaṭ*) would apply to the others, the letter *ṣ* is prescribed as an exception to those [rules].
Thus, [the form] *vraṣṭā* is derived.

There is elision of the *sakāra* by the rule *skoḥ saṃyogādyoḥ* [Pāṇini 8.2.29]. Because it has an *ūdit* vowel, there is optionally the absence of *iṭ*. Thus we have *mīlabṛṭ* and *dhānābhṛṭ*. There is vocalization (*samprasāraṇa*) by the rule *grahijyā* [Pāṇini 6.1.16].
In *ruāṣṭā*, the augment *iṭ* is applied by [Pāṇini 6.1.58]. As for *mārṣṭā* (or *mārṣṭīti*).
Regarding the reading *mudritapāṭha*: the term *upayaṭ* is derived from the root *i-* by means of the suffix *vic*, according to [Pāṇini 3.2.73].

Regarding the word *samrāṭ*: by the rule [Pāṇini 8.3.25], the *m* of *sama-* is replaced by *m*. Now, what is the reason that no example with a *jhal*-beginning suffix is shown for the roots *rāj-* and *bhrāj-*? To this he says: "of *rāj-* and *bhrāj-*," etc.
He asks why the status of being a *jhal* does not apply, and replies: "because [the suffix] begins with a *jhal* after these two," etc.
That which follows these two and begins with a *jhal* consonant is encompassed by the augment *iṭ*; therefore, *iṭ* is prescribed for them because they possess the property of being *seṭ*.

Regarding the others, in the first and fourth [groups], *iṭ* is optional (*vibhāṣiteṭau*), according to the rule beginning with *svarati* (Pāṇini 7.2.44). But the remaining ones are *aniṭ*, because of the prohibition of *iṭ* by the rule *ekācaḥ* (Pāṇini 7.2.10).
Therefore, for both purposes, their inclusion [is necessary],

as in the forms *rāṣṭiḥ* and *bhrāṣṭiḥ*. The suffix *ktin* is applied by the rule *kvibantān-nāb-ādibhyaś-ca* (Vārttika 307), and the prohibition of the augment *iṭ* is applied by the rule *titutra-tatasa-thasisusarakaseṣu ca* (Pāṇini 7.2.9).
Regarding the term *śabdaprāṭ*:

[it is derived] from the sense "one who asks (*pṛcchati*) about sound (*śabda*)," with the suffix *kvip* applied by the rule *kvivvaci* (Vārttika 288), and the vowel is lengthened. Now, for what purpose is the inclusion of the letter *ch* [in the rule], since—given that the *ch* in *pṛccha* is changed to *ś* by the rule *cchvoḥ śūḍanūmāsike ca* (Pāṇini 6.4.19)—the substitution of *ṣ* will occur in forms such as *pṛṣṭa* simply because the word ends in *ś*? To this he says: "In the case of *cchada*, *śūṭ*, etc.
and so forth; "In this case," etc.
The particle *iti* indicates a reason (*hetau*).

For in that context, the rule *hi* (Pāṇini 6.4.15) is understood to follow, and by means of it, the mention of *ch* is made; otherwise, forms such as *pṛṣṭaḥ* and *pṛṣṭavān* would be established, but not *praṣṭā*, *praṣṭum*, and so forth, because the substitution of *ś* does not occur before suffixes beginning with *tṛc* when they are not marked with *k* or *ṅ*.
And this has been stated according to the opinion of the author of the Sūtras.

Some teachers indeed reject the inclusion of the syllable *ch* in this sūtra. For instance, it is stated under [Pāṇini 6.4.19], *cchvoḥ śūḍanunāsike ca*: "Some do not carry forward the condition *kṅiti* here.
How then [is the form] *dyubhyām*, *dyubhiḥ* derived when *ūṭh* has been applied? [The answer is: "Because of the use of the long vowel marker (*tapara*), it will have the duration of one mātrā."

"In the rule *chaśāṃ ṣaḥ* [Pāṇini 8.2.36], the mention of *ch* need not be made; for by this very [rule], the substitution of *ṣ* is prescribed everywhere. Regarding *leṣṭā*: [the root] *liś* "to become small" (Dhātupāṭha 1179). Regarding *veṣṭā*: [the root] *viś* "to enter" (Dhātupāṭha 1424). If the term *dhātoḥ* [from Pāṇini 8.2.32] is understood here as a governing word (*anuvartate*), then it is a genitive of part (*avayava-ṣaṣṭhī*) qualifying the single vowel (*ekāc*).
The term *jhaṣantasya* is also in apposition and serves as a qualifier of that very [term];
*ekācaḥ* has a genitive of part (*avayava-ṣaṣṭhī*) in relation to *baś*. Thus, [the meaning is] "of that which is a part of it."

"An *avayava* (part) of that is *tadavayava*. That which is a part of the verbal root (*dhātu*) consisting of a single vowel (*ekāj*) and ending in a *jhaṣ* letter is connected with the word "that" (*tat*). By the phrase "when *jhal* follows," the term *jhal* is understood from [Pāṇini 8.2.26]; he shows that this is a qualifier of the letter *s*.

Why, then, is "before a *jhal* consonant" (*jhalī*) continued [in the rule]? It is so that the continuation of "at the end of a word" (*padāntasya*) may occur; otherwise, if "before a *jhal*" were withdrawn, the mention of "end of a word" (*padāntagrahaṇa*), which is connected to it, would also be withdrawn, and consequently, the rule would not apply at the end of a word.
But surely, because of its *svarita* accent, the continuation of "at the end of a word" will take place? Indeed, it is explained in this manner for the easy comprehension of those of dull intellect.
[The rule states: "and in the word *dhva*."

In this context, the requirement "when a *jhal* [consonant] follows" is not required, because it is impossible. For there is no such word as *dhva* that consists of a *jhal* sound; it is not included within the *pratyāhāra*s (phonetic groupings).
[The example is] *bhotsyate* (or *bhotsyante*, according to the *Kāśikā* and *Padamañjarī*).

In the case of the root *budha* in the sense of "understanding" (*budha avagamane*, Dhātupāṭha 858), the suffix *lṛṭ* is applied, followed by the suffix *sya*. By the rule *khari ca* (Pāṇini 8.4.54), there is the substitution of *ca* for the dental *ta*, resulting in the letter *tha*. Because the root begins with an anudātta vowel, the Ātmanepada voice is employed. Here, by the principle of *vryapadeśivadbhāva* (treating a part as if it were the whole), the very form of the root *budh* itself is considered to have a single-consonant (*ekāc*) portion ending in a *jhaṣ* sound; its constituent *ba* is a *baś* sound. Due to the principle of *āntaratamya* (closest proximity), in place of the labial [consonant], there will be a labial *bha* sound.
This should be understood similarly in other cases as well.
In *abhudhvam* [the older reading is *abuddha*], there is the substitution of *k* by [Pāṇini 8.2.41], and the substitution of *ṣ* by [Pāṇini 8.3.59].
In *nyaghūḍhvam*,
and in *dhokṣyate*, [the same rules apply].

Regarding *duho lṛṭ*: by [Pāṇini 8.2.32], *dh* is substituted for the initial *d* of a root; then, by [8.4.54], the *c*-substitution (*cartvam*) applies to that *dh*, resulting in the letter *k*. Thus, we have *ajarghāḥ*. The root *gudhu* in the sense of "desire" (Dhātupāṭha 1246) takes the *yaṅ* suffix. There is reduplication, followed by the application of *halādiśeṣaḥ*. By [7.4.66], *u* is substituted for the reduplicated syllable (*urat*), and by [7.4.62], the *c*-substitution (*cutvam*) applies. Then, by [2.4.74], there is *yaṅ-luk* (elision of *yaṅ*), and by [7.4.91], *ruk* is inserted.
With *jagṛdha* established, the rules beginning with *iṅ* (for the formation of the aorist) are to be applied.
In this context, the primary [meaning] is "vulture" (*gṛdhra*); this is a derivative form ending in the suffix *jhaṣ*.

Regarding the term "from *gardabhayati*": it is derived from the word *gardabha* with the causative suffix *ṇic* in the sense of "he causes that to be expressed. Then, by the rule "the nominal stem undergoes the same changes as in the *iṣṭhan* suffix" (Vārttika 813), there is the elision of the *ṭi* (the final vowel and following consonant).
In this context, due to the fear of [the application of] *garva*, this very suffix *jhaṣ* is the primary member of the verbal root. Regarding the term "not a suffix" (*apratyaya*),
that which does not end in a suffix— such as *kvip* and others— is called "not a suffix."

Regarding the word *dāmaliṭ*: here, once the substitution of *ḍha* for *ha* has been applied by [Pāṇini 8.2.31], the condition of ending in a *jhaṣ* sound (*jhaṣantatā*) arises; however, because of the inclusion of the term *ekāj* ("consisting of a single vowel"), the *bhaṣ*-substitution does not take place.

Now, one might object: "In this case, there are two parts consisting of a single vowel—the first beginning with *da* and ending with *m*, and the second beginning with *la* and ending in a *jhaṣ* sound; and even if the term *ekāj* were not present, the *bhaṣ*-substitution would certainly not apply to these."

For instance: that which ends in *jhaṣ* has no *vaś*; however, that which begins with *da* and ends in *ma* does have *vaś*, yet it lacks the property of ending in *jhaṣ*. Is the mention of "single-vowel" (*ekāj*) then purposeless? To this he says: "If the mention of 'single-vowel' were not there," and so forth. *Vaś* is a qualifier for the sake of exclusion (*vyavaccheda*).
That whose purpose (*artha*)—that is, its motive (*prayojana*)—is exclusion is described as such.

If the mention of "a single vowel" (*ekāj*) were not there, then—because nothing else is heard in this context, and because *baś* is what is actually heard—it would be *baś* itself that is qualified by the term "of the root" (*dhātoḥ*), rather than a "portion of the root" (*dhātor avayavaḥ*) being *baś*. And in that case, since it would be impossible for *baś* to have a final *jhaṣ*, the word "ending in *jhaṣ*" (*jhaṣanta-*) would qualify the root itself; for nothing else is possible here. Thus, the meaning of the sūtra would be as follows: "Of a root ending in *jhaṣ*, that portion which is *baś*, [becomes *bha*] when followed by a *jhal* consonant, *s*, or *ṣv*, and at the end of a word."

And according to this interpretation of the sūtra, the [substitution] would also apply in the case of *dāmaliṭ*. Is there not a *baś* sound here? Yes, there is; it is a member of the root ending in a *jhaṣ* sound.
When the condition "of a one-syllable [root]" (*ekācaḥ*) is present, the phrase "of a root ending in a *jhaṣ*" becomes a qualifier for both ends [of the *baś*], and that too is a *baś*.
Thus, the meaning of the sūtra arises exactly as demonstrated by the author of the commentary (*vṛttikāra*); consequently, nothing undesirable follows.

For in the case of *dāmaliṭ*, that which ends in *jhaṣ* and has a single vowel (*ekāc*) as its constituent part does not have a *baś* sound [as its penultimate], whereas that which has a *baś* sound, such as one beginning with *da* and ending in *m*, is not one that ends in *jhaṣ*. [The example] "he will be angry" (*krotsyati*) is given: the root *krudh* means "to be angry" (Dhātupāṭha 1189).
In the case of *dādadvi*,
there is lengthening of the reduplicated syllable according to [Pāṇini 7.4.83].
The inclusion of the term "end" (*anta*) is for the sake of avoiding ambiguity.

For if that were not the case, there would be doubt: "Is it the *baś* [the root *bhṛ*] here that has the status of the original (*sthānin*), or is it the *jhaṣ* [the root *dhā*]? This form also belongs to the root *dadhāti*, which has undergone reduplication; however, there is also the form of the root *dadha* ("to hold," Dhātupāṭha 8) which has not undergone reduplication. In that latter case, because it is separated by the *śap* suffix, the immediate *t* and *th* cannot occur. Therefore, it is understood that only the root *dadhāti* is intended, as he says: "The root *dadhāti*, having undergone reduplication, is included [by the term *dadha*]. As in: *dhattaḥ*.

The suffixes *laṭ* and *tasthasthasau* follow; for the root *śap*, there is reduplication when *ślu* is applied (*śapaḥ ślulupi dvirvacanam*). By the rule *ślau* [Pāṇini 6.1.10], reduplication occurs, and by *abhyāsasyāsavarṇe* [Pāṇini 6.4.78], the *jaś*-substitution of the reduplicated syllable results in the letter *d*. By the rule *śnābhyastayor ātaḥ* [Pāṇini 6.4.112], there is elision of the long *ā*. The *bhaṣ*-substitution of the *d* in the reduplicated syllable results in the letter *dh*. By the rule *stoḥ ścunā ścuḥ* [Pāṇini 8.4.40], the *cartva*-substitution of the *dh* in the verbal root results in the letter *t*. Thus, the form is *dhatse*.
Regarding *thāsaḥ se* [Pāṇini 3.4.80], there is the substitution of *e* for the final vowel (*ṭi*), resulting in *dhadhve*. Regarding *dhadhvam*, [the same applies].
The substitution of *it* occurs by [Pāṇini 3.4.91].

But how can there be the change to a *bhaṣ*-sound (*bhaṣbhāva*) here, since it is stated that "the *bhaṣ*-change applies to the *da* of a root ending in a *jhaṣ* sound which is the substitute for *dhā*, and not here, because there is neither an ending in a *jhaṣ* sound—due to the status of being a *sthānivadbhāva* (acting like the original) following the elision of the vowel *ā* [by Pāṇini 1.1.57]—nor a *baś* sound, because the *jaś*-substitution for the reduplication is considered asiddha"? To this he says: "By the force of the statement," etc.
One must understand that "the *asiddha* status of the *jaś*-substitution for the reduplication does not apply" due to the force of that specific statement.

If the status of being "as if in the original" (*sthānivadbhāva*) were to apply to the elision of the vowel *ā*, then the substitution of the voiced unaspirated stop (*jaś*) for the reduplication would be considered unestablished (*asiddha*).
This being the case, this specific rule would be rendered meaningless; for without the elision of the vowel *ā* from the root *dhā*, there could never be a *baś* sound [in the reduplication].
Therefore, by virtue of the authority of this very statement, both [the *sthānivadbhāva* and the *asiddha* status] do not occur.

In this context, *jhal* and *ut* are understood as recurring, as well as *jhaṣantasya*. That *jhal* which is other than the letters *t* and *th* is that in which the substitution of *bhaṣ* for the final *jhaṣ* of the root *dhā* is not desired.
Therefore, with the intention that the desired result is established even without the statement "of *t* and *th*," he asks: "What is the purpose of [the rule] 'of *t* and *th*'? He replies:
"Because of immediate succession," and so forth.

For in the immediately preceding sūtra, it was stated: "of *s* and *dh*" [Pāṇini 8.2.37]. Consequently, according to the principle that "a rule applies to what is proximate, or a prohibition applies to what is proximate" (Vyāḍiparibhāṣā 19), the substitution of *bhaṣ* would be understood to apply only to *s* and *dh*, and not to *t* and *th*; therefore, the words "of *t* and *th*" (*tathoḥ*) are stated. If this were so, when another cause (*nimitta*) is introduced, there should be the cessation of the previous cause; consequently, the substitution would occur only for *t* and *th*, and not for *s* and *dh*. To this, he says: "The letter *c*," etc. This is the resolution. [Regarding the term] "in the perfect" (*āliṭ*).
Once the substitution of *ḍha* has been made, the substitution of *jaś* follows.

Now, what is the purpose of including the word "end" (*anta*)? Is it not the case that the mention of "end" continues from [Pāṇini 8.2.29] onwards? To this he says: "The mention of 'end,' etc. For that mention of "end" is connected with the term *jhal*; therefore, when that [mention of "end"] recurs, the term *jhal* would also recur. Consequently, another mention of "end" is made in order to exclude that [term *jhal*].
And because of that [prohibition], it does not occur in *vasateḥ*, *vastā*, or *vastum*. Regarding the word "athaḥ":
by this, he shows that this is a prohibition of the verbal root (*dhātu*), not a prohibition of the letter *dhakāra*.
For if it were a prohibition of the letter *dhakāra*, the rule would mean that when *t* and *th* follow a *dhakāra*, the *dhakāra* itself does not become [the substitute].
Consequently, grammatical indications such as *matibuddhipūjārthebhyaśca* [Pāṇini 3.2.188] and *ityevamādayo nirdeśā nopapadyeran* [Pāṇini 1.1.73],
as well as forms like *alabdha*, *alabdhāḥ*—
where the *sakāra* is elided by the rule *luṅ, tasya tathāsau* [Pāṇini 8.2.26]— would not be possible.
Regarding "alīḍha, alīḍhāḥ": the substitution of *ḍha*, the substitution of *ṣṭu*, the elision of *ḍh*, and the lengthening of the vowel must be applied. Regarding "pekṣyati":
the root is *piṣlṛ* in the sense of "crushing" (*sañcūrṇana*; Dhātupāṭha 1452); this is the future tense (*lṛṭ*).
"apekṣyat" is [an example of] the conditional (lṛṅ);
"pipikṣati" is [an example of] the desiderative.

In the case of *san*, according to [Pāṇini 1.2.10], there is an absence of guṇa due to its being marked with the *k* indicator (*kittvāt*). In the case of *pinaṣṭi*, the suffix *śnam* is applied because it belongs to the *rudh*-class.
In the case of *leḍhi*: [the suffix *śnu* is applied].
Because [the root] begins with *ad*, there is elision (*luk*) of the suffix following *śap*. Regarding the form *āstīrṇam*:
the root is *stṛñ* in the sense of "covering" (Dhātupāṭha 1484).
By the rule *ṛta iddhātoḥ* [Pāṇini 7.1.100], there is the substitution of *it* for *ṛ*; then by *hali ca* [8.2.77], there is lengthening.
"Viśīrṇam" [means] "destroyed";
[the root] "śṛh" is used in the sense of "injury" (Dhātupāṭha 1488).
"Nigīrṇam" [means] "swallowed."
The root *gṛ* is used in the sense of "swallowing" (*nigaraṇe*) [Dhātupāṭha 1410].

In these cases, there is a prohibition of the augment *iṭ* by the rule *śrayukaḥ kiti* [Pāṇini 7.2.11], as in the form *avagūrṇam*. The root *gurī* is used in the sense of "lifting up" (*udyamane*) [Dhātupāṭha 1396].

There is a prohibition of the augment *iṭ* by the rule *śvīdito niṣṭhāyām* [Pāṇini 7.2.14]. Now, just as in the rule *atha yathā* [Pāṇini 8.2.18], the term *ra* is employed as a general category, setting aside the distinction between being a phoneme (*varṇatva*) and not being a phoneme (*avarṇatva*), so too here. Since the letter *r* exists within the phoneme *ṛ*, one might think that in forms such as *kṛtaḥ* and *kṛtavān*, the substitution must necessarily be *na* and not *en*. To address such a person, he says: "*ra ityatra*" and so forth.

If "ra" were taken here as a general category (*sāmānya*), then that very objection would apply; however, it is not the general category of the sound *ra* that is being taken up. What then? It is the consonant consisting of half a mora (*ardhamātrā*).

And since there is no identical form [between the two instances], how could the objection regarding the substitution of *na* (*natva*) arise? Even granting that a general category is indeed being taken up, he says—"Even when there is a reference to a general category," and so forth, in order to demonstrate that the substitution of *na* does not follow in this case.

In this context, the letter *ṛ* consists of parts, and the *repha* situated in its middle consists of one-fourth of a *mātrā*. Because there is an intervention by that third part which follows the *repha*, [the rule] does not apply. [Examples are] *caritam* and *muditam*. [The roots are] *cara* (meaning "to move," Dhātupāṭha 559) and *muda* (meaning "joy," Dhātupāṭha 16).

For if the mention of *ta* were absent, the word *niṣṭhā* would be qualified by the rule *radābhyām*—namely, "that *niṣṭhā* which follows *ra* or *da*"—and consequently, in cases such as *caritam*, the substitution of *na* would apply only to the augment *iṭ* by the rule [8.2.42]; because that *iṭ* is a part of the *niṣṭhā*.

Now, when the word "ta" is mentioned [in the rule], why does [the substitution] not occur for the letter *t* in words such as *caritam*? Because it is separated by the augment *iṭ*. For that [augment], being a part of the suffix (*pratyayabhakta*), would not separate the suffix itself; however, its status as a constituent part (*avayava*) of that [suffix] would indeed cause separation.
"Let it not apply to the subsequent [sound].

For if the mention of "preceding" (*pūrva*) were absent, and the letter *d* were qualified by the immediately preceding *niṣṭhā*—that is, "the *d* which belongs to the *niṣṭhā*"—then once the substitution of *jaś* has been applied, the rule would apply only to the subsequent [sound], as in *bhinnavadbhyām*, *bhinnavadbhiḥ*, and so forth.
On the other hand, if it were not qualified, then because no specific distinction is provided, just as it would apply to the preceding [sound], so too would it apply to the subsequent one.
Therefore, the mention of "pūrva" (the preceding) was made for the purpose that this [rule] should not apply to another.
Now, why does [the suffix] *iñ* [prescribed by Pāṇini 4.1.95, *ata iñ*,] not occur in the case of *kārttiḥ*, which means "the descendant of Kṛta"? To this he says: "In this case," and so forth.

For *vṛddhi* (vowel strengthening) occurs by depending upon a *taddhita* suffix as its cause, and is therefore *bahiraṅga* (external); however, since *naṭvam* (the substitution of *naṭ*) will occur without depending on any external cause, it is *antaraṅga* (internal).

Therefore, because the *vṛddhi* [substitution] is extrinsic (*bahiraṅga*), the *repha* is considered non-existent (*asiddha*) when the substitution of *natva* is to be applied. [Objection: But if that [vṛddhi] is indeed characterized as extrinsic, then it alone ought to be non-existent, not the *repha* as well; for the *repha* itself does not constitute the *vṛddhi*. [Reply: This is not a fault; for the *repha* is dependent upon the *vṛddhi*. Consequently, since the *vṛddhi* is extrinsic, the *repha* must also be regarded as extrinsic. In the word *pradrāṇaḥ*: the root is *drā* in the sense of "going with contempt" (Dhātupāṭha 1054).
The substitution of *ṇ* [for *n*] occurs as per [Pāṇini 8.4.29].
Regarding the word "mlānaḥ": the root is *mlai*, meaning "to bend the limbs" [or "to lose one's vigor," according to the Dhātupāṭha] (Dhātupāṭha 904).
"Passed away (*cyutaḥ*), gone beyond (*plutaḥ*). [The roots] *cyuṅ* and *pluṅ* mean "to go" (Dhātupāṭha 955, 958).
"Departed (*niryātaḥ*)."
The root *yā* is listed as "in the sense of reaching" (Dhātupāṭha 1049).
Regarding the word *nirvātaḥ*,
the root *vā* is listed as "in the sense of moving and scenting" (Dhātupāṭha 1050).
In this context, the status of being a verbal root (*dhātu*) does not belong to these two: *ryā* and *rvā*.

For the aggregate *ryā* begins with a conjunct consonant (*saṃyoga*), and this is not a verbal root; what then is? It is *yā*. Likewise, the aggregate *rvā* begins with a conjunct consonant, and this is not a verbal root; what then is? It is *vā*.

But is it not the case that here the status of being "beginning with a conjunct" (*saṃyogāditva*) is extrinsic (*bahiraṅga*), because it depends on two words, whereas *natva* is intrinsic (*antaraṅga*) due to the opposite reason? Since it is stated that "the extrinsic is as if non-existent (*asiddha*) in the presence of the intrinsic" (Vyāḍipāda 42), *natva* would simply not occur because the status of being "beginning with a conjunct" is non-existent [by virtue of being extrinsic]; so what is the purpose of including the mention of "dhātu"? If this is so, then it serves to indicate this: whatever property arises for the aggregate of root and prefix through its connection with a prefix, that [property] causes grammatical operations to apply to the root, even though that root itself does not possess that property.
In the expression *tenopāsyate guruḥ* (the teacher is attended by him), the *lakāra* suffix in the passive sense (*karmaṇi*) is established by the fact that [the root] is overcome by the enemy;
here, the property of being transitive (*sakarmakatva*) arises through its connection with the prefix (*upasarga*).
And that [property] belongs to the combination of the verbal root and the prefix, not to the verbal root alone.

In that case, if this meaning were not made known, the *lakāra* (verbal suffix) would not occur in the sense of the object (*karman*), because the verbal root (*dhātu*) would be intransitive (*akarmaka*). However, when this meaning is made known, it occurs, as in the example "he has bathed" (*snātaḥ*).
The root *snā* is used in the sense of "cleansing" (Dhātupāṭha 1052). Regarding the word *jīnaḥ*:

from the root *jyā* in the sense of "loss of vitality" (Dhātupāṭha 1499), there is vocalization (*samprasāraṇa*) by the rule *grahijyā* [Pāṇini 6.1.16], and lengthening by the rule *halaḥ* [Pāṇini 6.4.2].
As for the phrase "from roots beginning with *ṛ* and *lpa*," and so forth.
The meaning is that this rule must be explained as having the sense: "The *ktin* suffix following roots ending in *ṛ* and those beginning with *l*, etc., becomes *niṣṭhā*.
The explanation is based on the fact that in the rule *nuḥ* (Pāṇini 8.2.45), the particle *ca* has the function of including what is not explicitly mentioned.

Just as the substitution of *n* for the *t* of the *niṣṭhā* occurs after roots ending in *ṛ* and those beginning with *l*, etc., so too the substitution of *n* for the *t* of *ktin* occurs. [This is indicated by the phrase] "*dugvoḥ*."
The root *du* [in the sense of] "affliction" (*ṭu ṭu upatāpe*; however, in the *Padamañjarī*, this root *du* in the sense of "going" [944] is cited, not *ṭu ṭu upatāpe*) (Dhātupāṭha 1256).
*Gu* [means] "excretion of feces" (Dhātupāṭha 1399).
"Pūnāḥ" means "destroyed."
"Purified grain" means that which has been winnowed. [The term] "of the root *si*" [is used].
This refers to the root *viñ* in the sense of "binding" (*bandhane*; Dhātupāṭha 1248).
The phrase "that which has 'swallowing' as its object-agent" (*grāsakarmakartṛka*) means that for which "swallowing" (*grāsa*) is the object-agent; it is described in that way.
This [designation] is based on the sense [of the action].
It should be understood that its qualification is "having the act of swallowing as its agent.

Just as a swallowed morsel attains suitability for the act of binding through its connection with a particular type of food, so too, although it is an object (*karman*), its agency is intended to be expressed; thus, it becomes a "self-acting object" (*karmakartṛ*).
"Like a morsel of food" means it is caught by oneself.
"A sow bound by a snare."
This is a counter-example for the whole [rule].
To show a counter-example for the parts, he says: "Even the morsel," and so forth.

Even if the morsel were only the object (*karman*) and not the object-agent (*karmakartṛ*), even then [the rule] would not apply; because its status as having the morsel as its object-agent is absent in that case.

For at that time, by virtue of the act of eating (*grāsakarma*), he becomes the agent of the act of eating (*grāsakarmakartṛka*). Regarding the word "āpīna," there is the substitution of *pī* [for *pyai*] according to [Pāṇini 6.1.28]. Regarding the phrase "the roots beginning with *svad* are marked with *o*," [it refers to the rule defining those as *odita*].

Furthermore, those beginning with *ṣūṅ* "to give birth to living beings" (Dhātupāṭha 1132) and ending with *vrīṅ* "in the sense of pleasing" [or "covering"] (Dhātupāṭha 1140) are listed among the *divādi* roots. Regarding the term *kṣiyaḥ*:

both *kṣi* "in the sense of destruction" (Dhātupāṭha 236) and *kṣi* "in the senses of dwelling and going" (Dhātupāṭha 1407) are included, because no specific distinction is made. As in the example: "the afflictions (*kleśāḥ*) have been destroyed."

Because [the roots] are intransitive according to the rule *kto’dhikaraṇe ca* [Pāṇini 3.4.76], the *niṣṭhā* suffix occurs in the sense of the agent (*kartari*). By the rule *niṣṭhāyām aṇyadarthe* [Pāṇini 6.4.60], there is lengthening of the vowel. Examples include "the rogue is exhausted" (*kṣīṇo jālmaḥ*) and "the ascetic is exhausted" (*kṣīṇas tapasvī*).
Regarding this, the rule *vā’krośadainyayoḥ* [Pāṇini 6.4.61] applies.

But surely, from the very mention of *kṣiyaḥ*, the inclusion of the long vowel (*dīrgha*) is understood; so what is the purpose of explicitly mentioning the long vowel? If the short vowel were to be included in this way, then, since the rule *pugantalaghūpadhasya ca* [Pāṇini 7.3.86] applies later, the *guṇa* substitution would take effect, and the form mentioned in the rule would have to be *kṣeḥ*. To address this, he says: "For even of the short," and so forth.

If the mention by means of *iyaṅ* were necessarily intended only for the long vowel as a representation of the verbal root (*dhātu*), then one would understand from that mention that this refers to the long vowel. However, the mention by means of *iyaṅ* does not apply to the long vowel alone.

For this [suffix] is seen following the root *kṣi* when it ends in a short vowel, as in the rule *niṣṭhāyām aṇyadarthe* (Pāṇini 6.4.60). Is it not established there that this is an imitation (*anukaraṇa*) of [the root] ending in a short vowel, and not of one ending in a long vowel? It is replied: it is proper to imitate [the root] exactly as it is;
and since [the root] ends in a short vowel, its lengthening must be prescribed.
Therefore, it is understood that this is an imitation (*anukaraṇa*) of that very [word].

If, then, there is a designation by means of *iyaṅ* even for a verbal root imitation (*dhātvanukaraṇa*) ending in a short vowel—as in rules such as Pāṇini 6.4.19 and 7.3.58—why does it not also occur in cases such as "after *vi* and *parā*, [the suffix] *ji*" (Pāṇini 1.3.19), and so forth? Here, in the phrase "after *vi* and *parā*," and so on, the word *asaṅkalpam* ("not being a conceptualization") is to be supplied (*adhyāhārya*).

For regarding the imitation (*anukaraṇa*) of a verbal root, there is the rule "the imitation is like the original" (*prakṛtivadanukaraṇaṃ bhavati*, Vyāḍipāda 113), and thus the designation is made by means of the *iṅ* suffix.

And what can this imitation of a verbal root be, such that it remains as the very object being imitated within the verbal root? The status of being a verbal root (*dhātutva*), characterized by the expression of action (*kriyāvācitva*), is intended [to apply].
However, in cases such as *ityevamādau*, although the status of being a verbal root residing in the object being imitated exists, it is not taken into account because it is not intended.

Therefore, this is not an imitation (*anukaraṇa*) of a verbal root (*dhātu*). Rather, it should be understood as an imitation of that form-commonality (*rūpasāmānya*)—which is devoid of meaning—belonging to suffixes such as *ṅī* and to other words denoting action that resemble them, such as *ṅī*.
Consequently, because it is not an imitation of a verbal root, the substitution of *iyaṅ* does not occur; this is the intended meaning.

If, then, it were an imitation (*anukaraṇa*) of a verbal root (*dhātu*), then because "an imitation is like its original" (*prakṛtivadanukaraṇam bhavati*), this being the case, the prohibition of the designation *prātipadika* by [Pāṇini 1.2.45] *na dhātoḥ* would also apply; and consequently, the case-ending (*vibhakti*) would not be possible? No, there is no fault, because the designation *prātipadika* will apply by virtue of relying on the meaningfulness [of the imitation] through its meaning as the object of imitation, indicated by the suffix *-vat*. Regarding the form *śīnam*: from the root *śyaiṅ* "to go" (Dhātupāṭha 963), there is vocalization (*samprasāraṇa*) by [Pāṇini 6.1.24] *dravamūrtisparśayoḥ śyaḥ*, and lengthening by [Pāṇini 6.4.2] *halaḥ*.
"In 'coldness exists' (*śītaṃ vartate*),
the past passive participle (*niṣṭhā*) denotes the state (*bhāva*);
however, in the preceding case, it denotes the agent (*kartṛ*)."
The same applies to cases such as "the wind is cold" (*śīto vāyuḥ*), and so forth;
and to cases such as "the water is cold" (*śītam udakam*). [The phrase] "even though it is subordinate" (*guṇabhūto 'pi*) means:

The meaning is: "even though it is not the primary factor. Now, an objection might be raised: since grammatical operations (*kārya*) are understood to apply to the primary element, it is not logical for that which is not primary to serve as the cause (*nimitta*) for an operation such as the prohibition of *natva* (the substitution of *na* for *na*). This is not a fault. For if the term "asparśe" were an exclusion (*paryudāsa*), then in examples such as "cold wind" (*śīto vāyuḥ*), there would be *natva* because there exists a substance other than touch (*sparśa*). However, this is not an exclusion; rather, it is a simple negation (*prasajyapratiṣedha*). Therefore, wherever there is even a trace of touch, there must be a prohibition of *natva* based upon that [touch].

And here, the stop-consonant (*sparśa*) is subordinate (*guṇabhūta*); therefore, there is indeed a negation of its being the basis [for the designation of the compound]. Let it be so that there is a negation of its being the basis; however, how can the stop-consonant, which is subordinate to the *samprasāraṇa*, be the cause [of the rule]? By the abandonment of the restrictive rule (*niyama*). Here, the rule is "that which has fewer syllables" (*alpāctaram*, Pāṇini 2.2.34)—namely, that in a *dvandva* compound, that which has fewer syllables must be placed first. In this case, by placing the word *sparśa*, which has fewer syllables, at the end, the author has abandoned this restrictive rule.

For what purpose was this [term] employed? It is for the purpose of indicating that here, the *sparśa* (contact/obstruction) is the cause of *samprasāraṇa* (vocalization), whether it be primary (*pradhāna*) or secondary (*upasarjana*).
By this, even a *sparśa* that is subordinate becomes a cause for *samprasāraṇa*.
This word *sparśa* is used both as a term for a quality (*guṇa*) and as a term for a disease (*roga*); since no specific distinction is made here, both meanings are understood.

Anticipating the objection that, "then [the word] would also apply to a disease (*roga*), and thus the form *pratiśīna* would not be established," he says: "And in the case of a quality (*guṇa*)," and so forth.
The meaning is: "only in the case of a quality.
But how is the restriction to a quality alone obtained? From an indicator (*jñāpaka*).

The fact that [the author], having prescribed the *samprasāraṇa* in the rule "In place of *śyai*, there is [guṇa] before *drava*, *mūrti*, *sparśa*, and *vaḥ*" (Pāṇini 6.1.24), prescribes again with "before *śya*" (6.1.25), indicates this: wherever there is the mention of the root *śyai*, the word *sparśa* employed therein does not signify a disease. For if it did signify a disease, the second prescription would be purposeless, since the result would already be established by the former rule.
Indeed, the root *śyai* preceded by *prati* occurs only in the sense of a disease and nowhere else. Thus it is said: "provided that it is not an *apādāna* (ablative) in that context."

By the word "therein" (tatra), the root *añc* is referred to. Through the medium of the word, it is understood—by the force of the prohibition regarding the ablative—that this [prohibition] applies precisely to the meaning of the root *añc*. For the status of being an ablative (*apādānatva*) is not possible for the root *añc*; what then? It is because the case-factors (*kāraka*s) have as their domain the action belonging to that [meaning].

This is what is meant: it is not the case that when the sense of "bending" (*añcati*) is present as the object, the ablative (*apādāna*) does not occur. The word "samaknau" means "joined together" (*saṅgatau*).

The root *añc* (given as *ancū* in the Kāśī edition of the Dhātupāṭha, no. 188), meaning "to go" and "to worship," has an indicatory letter *ū*. Because it is marked with *ū*, the augment *iṭ* is optional (*vibhāṣiteṭ*).

Consequently, by [Pāṇini 7.2.15], there is a prohibition of *iṭ* in the case of the past passive participle (*niṣṭhā*). Furthermore, by [Pāṇini 6.4.24], there is the elision of the nasal (*anunāsika-lopa*) for roots not having an indicatory *it*.
Thus we have the form *udaktam udakam* ("the water has been drawn up").
The meaning is "water that has been drawn out.
Now, as for the word *vyakta*, why does the suffix *naṭ* not occur here? To this he says: "*vyaktam ityetat*" and so forth.
[The root] *añjū* [is used] in the senses of manifestation (*vyakti*), smearing (*mrakṣaṇa*), beauty (*kānti*), and motion (*gati*). [Note: some manuscripts read *añcū*.]

The reading "kāśīmudritaḥ pāṭhaḥ" (as found in the Dhātupāṭha, sūtra 1458) refers to this very form; the meaning is that the form [of the root] is such that the *natva* (the substitution of *n* for *ṇ*) does not occur here. Regarding the forms "ādyūnaḥ" and "paridyūnaḥ," the sense is "one who does not desire to win. The vowel *ū* is substituted by the rule "cchavoḥ śūḍanunāsike ca" [Pāṇini 6.4.19].

"The game of dice is underway. In this context, the intended meaning is the desire for victory; therefore, the prohibition [against gambling] does not apply. But how can there be a desire for victory here, given that no playful activity characterized by the casting of dice is perceived? To this he says: "For in the case of the desire for victory... and so forth (as found in the Kāśī edition).
The desire to conquer is *vijigīṣā*; [it occurs] in that [state].
In that context, activities such as the casting of dice are performed during play.
Therefore, the sense is that it exists for the purpose of the desire to conquer (*vijigīṣārtha*).

By the word "etc. (*ādi*), the casting of lots (*śalākāpāta*) and so forth are included. [The phrase] "of the root following *dā*" refers to this very root *vā* from the Dhātupāṭha (1050), meaning "to go" and "to scent.
[The passage beginning with] "And not," etc. [is explained as follows].
That whose substratum (ādhāra) is the non-performance of the action (dhātvarthācikirṇa) is so described.
This is what is meant: if the meaning of a verbal root is inherent (samaveta) in that very root—this is the sense.
For example: "the fire has gone out" (nirvāṇo 'gniḥ), "the lamp has gone out" (nirvāṇaḥ pradīpaḥ).
In this context, that which is the pacification of the intrinsic nature, characterized by cessation, is the meaning of the verbal root;
as in "this monk is extinguished" (*nirvāṇa*).
This also applies here.
Alternatively, the meaning of the verbal root is the abandonment of passion and so forth;
as in the expression "the wind has ceased," because the verb is intransitive, the past participle suffix (*niṣṭhā*) denotes the agent.
"In *nirvātaṃ vātena* (blown out by the wind)," here [the suffix] denotes the state (*bhāva*). In both cases here, the obstruction of motion is the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*).
Regarding the phrase "the lamp is extinguished by the wind," here the word "by the wind" (*vātena*) is in the instrumental case denoting the agent (*kartṛ*).

Consequently, someone might be deluded into thinking that the wind itself is the locus (*adhāra*) of the action of extinguishing, and therefore [the lamp] ought to be expressed in the locative case (*saptamī*). To dispel this misconception, he says: "The lamp is extinguished" (*niryāṇaḥ pradīpaḥ*), and so forth.
In this context, the meaning of the word *nirvāṇa* is "the element" (*dhātu*). And that [element] has fire as its substratum, not wind as its substratum.

For if, in the case of wind being the substratum, the suffix *niṣṭhā* were applied in the sense of the agent (as in *nirvāṇa* = "one who has blown out"), then, because the agent would already be expressed by that very suffix, the third case ending would not occur for the word *vāta* (wind).
Alternatively, if it were applied in the sense of the action itself according to Pāṇini 3.3.114, then, in that case, *nirvāṇa* would not be masculine.
Therefore, the lamp itself is the agent and the locus of the meaning of the verbal root.

If this is so, how is there an instrumental case (*tṛtīyā*) in the word *vātena*? To this he says: "But the wind," and so forth. By this, he shows that this instrumental case is not used for the agent. Regarding the rule for the suffix *niṣṭhā* following the root *śuṣa* (meaning "to dry up," Dhātupāṭha 1183), when the substitution of *ṣṭu* would have occurred for the letter *t*, the letter *k* is prescribed instead.
The syllable *a* is for the sake of pronunciation, as in "śuṣkaḥ" and "śuṣkavān.

It is appropriate that "śuṣvān" is the example, but "śuṣka" is not; for it would not be proper to introduce this rule for that meaning, since it is already established by the specific grammatical derivation (*nipātana*) in [Pāṇini 6.1.206]. This is not so; for if the letter *k* were present by virtue of that derivation, then in the case of "śuṣkikā," there would be the optional substitution of *i* (short *i*) according to [Pāṇini 7.3.46], and in the case of "śuṣkajaṅghā," there would be a prohibition of the masculine form (*puṃvadbhāva*) according to [Pāṇini 6.3.37].
But here, since the substitution of *k* for *p* has been prescribed, that [substitution of *ś*] is considered non-existent (*asiddha*), and therefore neither of these two [operations] occurs.
Consequently, the commencement of this rule is also justified for the sake of forms such as *śuṣkaḥ*. [Examples: *pakvaḥ*, *pakvavān*.
[Root: *ḍupaṭacaṣ* in the sense of "cooking" (Dhātupāṭha 996).

If this is so, [one might ask] how the form *pakva* is established? It is indeed established by means of the irregular derivation (*nipātana*) [Pāṇini 6.1.141]. Nevertheless, this rule must necessarily be commenced for the sake of the form *pakvavān*. Furthermore, since it is commenced for another purpose, it also serves the purpose of the form *pakva*; thus, the word *pakva* has been presented as its example. The intention is that if its derivation were effected through an irregular derivation, there would be an excessive burden on the learner’s understanding. [The roots] *kṣai*, *jai*, and *vai* mean "to perish" (Dhātupāṭha 913–915). [The form] *prastīmaḥ*.
The roots *ṣṭai* and *styai* mean "to congeal" and "to sound," respectively (*dhātupāṭha* 911, 910).
By [Pāṇini 6.1.23], there is vocalization (*samprasāraṇa*); as before, there is lengthening. In this case, when the suffix *matup* does not occur.

In that case, by the rule *tadā* [Pāṇini 7.2.43], there ought to be the substitution of *n*; and consequently, forms such as *prastīnaḥ* and *prastīnavān* would be desired—such might be the misconception of someone. Therefore, in order to refute that, he says: "When the state of having *mat* does not exist," and so forth. [Objection:

Once the *samprasāraṇa* has been performed first, why does the substitution of *n* not occur? [Response: He says: "When that has been performed," and so forth. Regarding the form *phullaḥ*: the root *ñiphalā* is used in the sense of "falling apart" (*viśaraṇe*) [Dhātupāṭha 516]; there is a prohibition of the augment *iṭ* by [Pāṇini 7.2.16], and the substitution of *u* for the following *a* occurs by [Pāṇini 7.4.88].
"It is intended that this substitution of *l* for *t* applies even to that which ends in *ktavat*.

But how can this be obtained when it is not even intended, for the word ending in *ktavat* is not explicitly mentioned in the *sūtra*? It is said in reply: Here, regarding the form of a word ending in *t* that belongs to the *niṣṭhā* [past participles], the form *phulla* is prescribed as an irregularity (*nipātana*); and as for *ktavat*, it is the same. However, if the meaning of *ktavat* is to be qualified, let it be so qualified; for there is no purpose served by whether that [meaning] is identical or different.
Therefore, this substitution of *l* occurs even for that which ends in the suffix *ktavatu*.

If this same logic were applied, then even those forms such as *kṣība*, *kṛśa*, and *ullāgha*, which are prescribed as nipātanas (irregularly formed words), would also result in being treated as ending in *ktavatu*. This is not a fault; for the term *anyatarasyām* (optionally) which will be mentioned later is a supplement (*śeṣa*) to both rules.
Furthermore, since the restricted option (*vyavasthitavibhāṣā*) is not known [to apply here], there will be no over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). [The rule begins with] "from the roots *kṣī* and *kṛś*."
Regarding the roots *kṣībṛ* (in the sense of "intoxication," Dhātupāṭha 382) and *kṛśa* (in the sense of "making thin," Dhātupāṭha 382 and 1227):
it is stated that "the absence of *iṭ* is also prescribed as a nipātana.

Since the elision of the suffix *kta* is considered *asiddha*, an *ārdhadhātuka* suffix beginning with a consonant (*valādi*) would require the augment *iṭ*; therefore, its absence is also prescribed as a nipātana.
"Or, when *iṭ* has been applied, there is the elision of the word *ic*";
the connection is that it is "irregularly formed" (*nipātyate*). This option depends on the absence of *iṭ*.
Alternatively—the absence of *iṭ* is not prescribed as a nipātana (irregularity).
What then? When *iṭ* has been applied, there is the elision of the word *iccha*. [This is because] "an upasarga other than *ud* is prohibited after the root *lāgh*" is stated.
The inclusion of the prefix *ud-* is for the sake of its specific mention;
otherwise, the mention of that which is preceded by *ud-* would be purposeless—this is the intended meaning.

Since it is stated [in the rule] "when not preceded by a prefix" (*anupasargāt*), one might ask why the form *parikṛśa* is not established there? To this he says: "In the case of *parikṛśa*, etc. and so forth.

The action characterized by "making thin" (tanūkaraṇa) has another action, namely the action characterized by "going" (gamana), as its distinct counterpart; this [prefix *pari*] is connected with that [other action], not with the word *kṛśa*. Therefore, considering that it functions as a preposition (*upasarga*) in relation to the root *kṛś*, we have the form "parigataḥ kṛśaḥ.
By this, he demonstrates that connection with that other action.

Now, for what purpose is this *nipātana* (irregular formation)? For [the forms] such as *phulla* could be established from the root *phull* "to blossom" (*phulla vikasane*, Dhātupāṭha 532) by adding the suffix *ac* according to *pacādyac*; *kṣība* could be established by adding the suffix *ka* characterized by the rule for roots ending in *i* or *u* (*igupadhalakṣaṇe ke*) from the root *kṣīv*; and *kṛśa* could also be established simply by adding *ac* to the root *kṛś*. Likewise, *ullāgha* would certainly be established by adding *ac* to the root *lāgh*. This is indeed true; however, in the case of the past passive participle (*niṣṭhā*), if this rule did not exist, undesirable forms would result for roots such as *phal*.
Therefore, this has been commenced in order to prevent that. [Examples: *samunnaḥ*, *samuttaḥ*.
There is elision of the *n* by [Pāṇini 6.4.24] *aniditām*. Regarding the statement "of *hrī*"— [the *Kāśikā* and *Padamañjarī* read *hyī*]—
it refers to the root *hrī* in the sense of "shame" (Dhātupāṭha 1085).
"Unattained" means because it has not been prescribed by anyone. "Of the others" means...

In this context, regarding the roots *nuda* (*ṇuda*) "to impel" (DhP 1426) and *undī* "to moisten" (DhP 1457), [the substitution of *na* for the root-final consonant] would necessarily apply by [Pāṇini 8.2.42, *radābhyām*].

Regarding the roots *traiṅ* "to protect" (DhP 965) and *ghrā* "to smell" (DhP 926), [the substitution of *na*] applies by [Pāṇini 7.2.43, *traiṅpāghrādhmāsthāmnādāṇdṛśyartisaṃsarterṇiṅ*]. It is intended that here the root *vid* "to discern" (DhP 1035) is the one being referred to.

But how is its inclusion intended? Is it by means of the *ślu*-conjugation marker (*śluvikaraṇa*), through association with this [root] *hī* (as read in the Prācya recension as *hyīṇā*)? This is not so; for, due to association with the *śa*-conjugation marker (*śavikaraṇa*) in the case of *nud*, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of including the root *vid* in the sense of "obtaining. Therefore, the option (*anyatarasyām*) is a restricted option (*vyavasthitavibhāṣā*); thus, it must apply only to the sense of "investigating" (*vicāraṇā*), and not to any other. Since it is logical to include only that which is intended to be so included, that very [root] is what is taken.
But how is it known that the inclusion of the root *vid* is intended in the sense of "investigation"? To this he says: "For thus," and so forth.

The word "is intended" (*iṣyate*) is to be connected with each of the following terms. By the word "past passive participle" (*niṣṭhā*), he indicates that which ends in a past passive participle; [this applies] to "of the root *vid*" (*vetteḥ*), and so forth.

Regarding the root *vida* in the sense of "knowledge" (*dhātupāṭha* 1064), the form *viditaḥ* is desired; this is because the augment *iṭ* is compulsory, and since there is an intervention by that *iṭ*, the substitution of *n* for the *t* of the *niṣṭhā* suffix is impossible.

Regarding *vidyateḥ*: for the root *vida* in the sense of "existence" (*dhātupāṭha* 1171), which takes the *śyan* suffix, the form *vinnaḥ* is desired when ending in the *niṣṭhā* suffix; this is because the prohibition of *iṭ* applies by the rule *ekācaḥ* [Pāṇini 7.2.10], and because the substitution of *n* is prescribed compulsorily by the rule *radābhyām* [Pāṇini 8.2.42].

Regarding the forms *vintevinnaśca vittaśca*: these two forms of the word ending in the *niṣṭhā* suffix are desired as derived from the root *vid* in the sense of "investigation" (*vicāraṇe*, Dhātupāṭha 1450). This is because, as in the previous case, there is a prohibition of the augment *iṭ*, and by this rule [Pāṇini 8.2.56], the substitution of *n* for *t* is optionally prescribed. As for the phrase *bhogivittaśca vindateḥ*: [this refers to the root] *vindati*.
By the word "vibhateḥ," he shows the root *vid* in the sense of "obtaining. For when the augment *num* is applied by [Pāṇini 7.1.59], the form becomes *vindati*.

Regarding the term *bhogavitta*: it is a compound formed as "one who is known (*vitto*) for enjoyment (*bhoge*)," based on the division of the rule (*yogavibhāga*) [Pāṇini 2.1.40] beginning with "the locative case" (*saptamī*).
The mention of "enjoyment" (*bhoga*) is merely illustrative;
"conviction" (*pratyaya*) is also included.

For the root *vid* in the sense of "acquisition" (*lābha*)—as per the Dhātupāṭha (1432)—the form *vitta* is desired when used with the meanings of enjoyment or conviction in the past passive participle (*niṣṭhā*). This is because of the specific grammatical prescription (*nipātana*) in [Pāṇini 8.2.58] that prevents the substitution of *n* for *t* in the words "enjoyment" and "conviction," and because of the prohibition of the augment *iṭ* in the past passive participle by [Pāṇini 7.2.15].

Regarding the root *vid* [in the sense of "finding"], it is optionally treated as having an indicatory *i* (*iṅ*) by the rule *vindater hi kvasau* [Pāṇini 7.2.68]. By the statement, "and the word *bhogavit* is from *vid*", it is meant that according to Bhoja, this form *vinna* is desired in meanings other than those conveyed by the suffixes *bhoga* and *pratyaya*. As for the roots *dhyai* in the sense of "thinking" (Dhātupāṭha 908) and *khyā* in the sense of "speaking" (Dhātupāṭha 1060), both are included because of the rule *cakṣiṅaḥ khyāñ* [Pāṇini 2.4.54].

But is it not the case that because the substitute for *cakṣiṅ* possesses an *anubandha*, the rule does not apply due to the *paribhāṣā* regarding the inclusion of forms without *anubandhas* (P. 1.1.68)? This is not a fault; for in this context, when the status of being subsequent (*paratva*) is to be established for the *t* of the *niṣṭhā* suffix, the ablative case (*pañcamī*) is appropriate, as in [the rule] *radābhyām* (P. 8.2.42).
Since the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) is employed here where the ablative ought to be used, it is intended to express a general relationship (*sambandhasāmānya*).
And a general relationship is not possible without the related entities (*sambandhin*).

Furthermore, when a root with its suffixal extensions (*sānubandhaka*) is being abandoned, a distinction between related forms is not possible; therefore, it is correct that those [roots] should also be included. For instance, in the cases of *pṛ* (DhP 1489) "to protect and to fill," *mucch* (DhP 212) "to faint and to rise up," and *madī* (DhP 1208) "to rejoice"—in these roots such as *dhyai* and others, this prohibition is commenced because the substitution of *na* would otherwise apply to the first two by rule 6.1.43 (*āditaśca*), and to the others as well by rule 8.2.42 (*radābhyām*). Thus, we have the form *pūrtaḥ*.

There is a prohibition of *iṭ* by the rule *śrayukaḥ kiti* [Pāṇini 7.2.11]; there is *utva* (substitution of *u*) by the rule *udoṣṭhapūrvasya* [Pāṇini 7.1.102], and as before, there is lengthening. In the word *mūrttaḥ*, there is the elision of the letter *cch* by [the rule *cchoḥ śūḍanunāsike ca*] 6.4.19, and there is a prohibition of *iṭ* by [the rule *na ktvā seṭ*] 7.2.16. Thus, *mattaḥ*.
In this case as well, [the rule] "after roots ending in *śū* and *ī*, the suffix *niṣṭhā* takes the augment *it*" (Pāṇini 7.2.14) applies. The meaning is "his wealth (*dhana*) is abundant.

But how can that which is derived in the sense of "enjoyment" (*bhoga*) have its application in the sense of "wealth"? To this he says: "For *ghana*," and so forth. By showing that the word *bhoga* functions as a *karmasādhana* (an object-based derivation), he demonstrates its application to "wealth."
"The meaning is 'well-known' (*pratīta*).
By this, he explains that the word *pratyaya* functions as a passive derivative (*karmasādhana*).
In the term *pratīta*, the suffix *-ta* is the past passive participle (*niṣṭhā*) used in the sense of the object (*karman*).

"Pratīta" means "explained. And how does this meaning arise when the word is derived from the suffix? It occurs if the word *prati* is also derived as a passive (karmasādhana)—that is, *pratyaya* is that which is understood (*pratīyate*).
Therefore, the status of the word *pratyaya* as a passive derivative should be understood. "The form *bhittam* is thus established as an irregularity (*nipātyate*)."

What is being set aside? Since [the rule] *radābhyām* [Pāṇini 8.2.42] would require the substitution of *n*, its absence is what is intended. "If it becomes a *śakala*" means: if the meaning of the word *śakala*—which has the alternative name *khamaṇḍa*—is the same as the meaning of the word *bhitta*.

But how is it that the word *bhitta* has "fragment" (*śakala*) as its meaning? To this he says: "This is a synonym for *śakala*. The word *bhitta* is indeed a synonym for *śakala*; therefore, just as the word *śakala* has "fragment" as its denotation, so too does the word *bhitta*.

But is it not the case that this word *śakala* is a generic term (*jātiśabda*), because it functions toward its own denotation by taking a generic property as the cause for its application; whereas the word *bhitta* is an action term (*kriyāśabda*), because its application is caused by an action? For instance, since the root *bhid* has the meaning "to split," when the suffix *kta* is prescribed, the form *bhitta* is derived as an irregularity (*nipātana*). Furthermore, an action term cannot logically be a synonym for a generic term. To this, he says: "In this case," and so forth. "Etymology of the word" (*śabdavyutpatti*) means the grammatical refinement (*saṃskāra*) of the word; in the case of this word *bhitta*, that [refinement] has the action of splitting (*bhidikriyā*) as its cause, but it does not have the actual occurrence of that action as its cause, because such an occurrence is non-existent [in the case of a finished product].
Rather, it is the genus (*jāti*) alone that is the cause for its application, because that [genus] exists.
Therefore, like the word *śakala*, the word *bhitta* is also a genus-word (*jāti-śabda*) and not an action-word (*kriyā-śabda*); thus, its synonymy with it is logical.

If, then, the act of splitting (*bhidi-kriyā*) does not exist here at all, how can even the refinement of the word (*śabda-saṃskāra*) have that as its cause? This is not so; for this restriction is not being asserted—that only an existing action can be the cause of the refinement of a word.

For instance, although the word *tailapāyikā* is conventionally established (*rūḍha*) for a particular kind of living creature, the word denoting the act of drinking oil does not exist there; nevertheless, the act of drinking oil is resorted to as the basis for its formation (*saṃskāra*).

But how is it that the word *bhitta* does not have the act of splitting (*bhidikriyā*) as its ground for application (*pravṛttinimitta*)? To this he says: "For when there is the intention to express the act of splitting," and so forth.
Here, the word *bhinnam* (split) is connected individually with both the words *bhitta* and *śakala*.

Regarding that [statement], "it becomes 'bhinnam' or 'bhittam'," both of these two usages are established when there is an intention to express the action of splitting (*bhidikriyā*). For when a fragment has been split apart,

the usages *bhinnam* and *bhittam* are employed with the intention of expressing the state of being split (*vidīrṇatā*) of that fragment, provided there is an intention to express the action of splitting.

Furthermore, if the word *bhitta* were to have the activity of splitting (*bhidi*) as its basis for application (*pravṛttinimitta*), then the state of being split (*vidīrṇatā*) of a fragment would already be conveyed by the word *bhitta* itself, which is based on the act of splitting; thus, this usage [of the word *bhinna*] would not be tenable, for there is nothing to which the word *bhinna* could apply unless it has first been conveyed by the word *bhitta*.

Moreover, the usage "the split fragment" (*bhinnaṃ śakalam*) would also be untenable; because the word *bhitta*, derived from the root *śakl* (to break) and based on the act of splitting, would have already sublated the application of the word *bhinna*.
And since this twofold application exists, it is not understood that the word *bhitta* has as its cause the act of splitting (*bhidikriyā*).
[The term] "from this root *ṛ*" means either from *ṛ* "to go" (Dhātupāṭha 1098) or from *ṛ* "to go and to cause to reach" (Dhātupāṭha 936).
[The example] "one who is low (*adham*) with respect to debt (*ṛṇa*) is an *adhamarṇa*."

But by what [rule] is there a compound here, since there is no characteristic of a compound at all? [One might argue: "The compound [is formed] due to the *yogavibhāga* [separation of rules] in the rule *saptamī*. However, this too should not be said, because it would result in the locative case (*saptamī*) being placed first in the compound. To this he says: "Precisely for this reason," and so forth.
"'*Tadbhāva* means indebtedness'—that is, the connection with the act of taking a loan, thinking 'he will repay that.'"
Through connection with that [future time], this person is called a debtor (*adhamarṇa*) even when the thing exists [now].

Regarding the phrase "at another time" (*kālāntare*), etc.: the time other than that time at which the debtor receives is "another time" (*kālāntara*); that which is to be given at that [other] time is "to be given at another time" (*kālāntaradeya*). The mention of the "debtor" is employed solely for the purpose of indicating the exchange—that is, the reversal—involved therein, and not for the purpose of expressing its own primary meaning.

For what reason is it explained in this way? To this he says: "It is also [used] in the sense of 'creditor' (*uttamarṇa*). For in the case of a debt, one person becomes the debtor (*adhamarṇa*), who, having received [the loan], will repay it; whereas he who, having given [the loan], will receive it back is the creditor (*uttamarṇa*). In that context, if the mention of *adhamarṇya* were taken solely for the purpose of establishing its own meaning, then the form *uttamarṇa* would not be established, because *adhamarṇya* is not intended to be expressed here.

Therefore, this [term] *uttamarṇa* (creditor) also applies even in the case of a debt (*adhamarṇa*), because the mention of "debt" is intended as an illustration for any exchange involving a future delivery; for here there is indeed an exchange between two points in time.
Thus, even the creditor, when giving, effects an exchange with that which is to be given at a later time. Regarding the root *sad-*:
it is derived from *ṣadlṛ* "to dissolve, to go, to perish" (Dhātupāṭha 854).
Regarding "niṣattaḥ":
the substitution of *ṣ* occurs according to [Pāṇini 8.3.66] *sadiraprateḥ*.
Regarding "anuttam": [the same rule applies].
In the root *undī* (meaning "to moisten," Dhātupāṭha 1457), there is the elision of the nasal [of the suffix] according to [Pāṇini 6.4.24], *aniditām*.
Regarding the word *pratūrtam*:

when it is derived as a *nipātana* (irregular formation) from the root *ñitvarā* (meaning "agitation," Dhātupāṭha 775), then by [Pāṇini 6.4.20], *jvaratvara*, etc., there is the substitution of *u* for the vowel *va* and for the penultimate vowel (*upadhā*).

When [the root] is *urvī*, *turvī*, or *thurvī*—meaning "to injure" (Dhātupāṭha 569, 570, 571)—then by [Pāṇini 6.4.21], there is the elision of the letter *r*, and as before, there is lengthening of the vowel. Thus, *sūrtam*.

[The root] *sṛ* means "to go" (Dhātupāṭha 935); in connection with the substitution of *u*, there is the replacement of *r* (raparatva), and as before, there is lengthening of the vowel. Thus, *gūrtam*.

Regarding the entry *gurī udyamāne* [the variant reading is *gūrī*; Dhātupāṭha 1396], the example given is *ghṛtaspṛk*. Here, for the sibilant *ś*, which is produced with the mouth wide open (*vivṛta-karaṇa*), with breath as its external effort (*ā-sānupradāna*), and is voiceless (*aghoṣa*), there is the corresponding voiceless unaspirated stop *kh*. This undergoes *jaśtva* (substitution by a voiced unaspirated stop), becoming *g*.

Then, for the *g*, *cartva* (substitution by a voiceless unaspirated stop) applies, resulting in *k*. Now, what is the purpose of mentioning the suffix (*pratyaya*) in the rule? Why not simply say "after *kvip*"? For *kvip* never deviates from being a suffix.

When this is being stated, one should not suspect that the substitution of *k* for *t* (*kutva*) would apply only to the *kvip* suffix as an exception to its elision (*lopa*). For indeed, in the case of the mention of the suffix *kvip*, where there is a mention of a suffix, the suffix-mention-paribhāṣā (Pāṇini 1.1.72) brings to mind the word ending in *kvip*. Since the substitution of *k* for *t* (*kutva*) is considered non-existent (*asiddha*) when the elision of *kvip* is to be performed, the elision must first take place.
