Once that has occurred, the subsequent substitution of *k* for *t* will apply only to the remaining verbal root (*dhātu*). Therefore, he says: "It should be stated that *k* [is substituted] for *kvip*," and so forth.

For if the mention of "affix" (*pratyaya*) were not made, the rule would apply only to a word-final element ending in the *kvin* affix, and not to one ending in any other affix, even though that too is intended. Therefore, the mention of "affix" is made. When the mention of "affix" is present, a *bahuvrīhi* compound is obtained.
By means of that *bahuvrīhi* compound, the verbal root from which [the formation] is prescribed is indicated; thus, everything is established. In the examples *māno aruṣāk* and *māno adrāk*:

[from the roots] *sṛj* (DhP 1414) "in emission" and *dṛkṣi* (DhP 988) "in seeing," there is the *luṅ* [tense]; *sic* replaces *cli* [by Pāṇini 3.1.44]; *tip* [is the personal ending]; the augment *iṭ* is added [by Pāṇini 6.1.58]; the *vṛddhi* substitution occurs [by Pāṇini 7.2.3, etc.]; the elision of the *hal* and *ṅit* suffixes occurs [by Pāṇini 6.1.66]; the augment *aṭ* is added; and by this [rule], the *kṛtva* [suffix] is applied.
"The suffix *kvin* is prescribed after the roots *sṛj* and *dṛś*. Thus, *kvin* is prescribed for *sṛj* by [Pāṇini 3.2.59], "The suffix *kvin* is applied after *ṛtvij*, etc.";
and for *dṛś* as well, by [Pāṇini 3.2.60], "After *dṛś*, when not meaning 'to look,' the suffixes *kañ* and *kvin* are applied among *tyap* and the others."
But how is there the augment *aṭ* here, given that it is prohibited by the rule *na māṅyoge* [Pāṇini 6.4.74]? To this he says: "Even when there is *māṅ*, etc. These two usages are Vedic (*chāndasa*).
Therefore, even though *māṅ* is present, the augment *aṭ* indeed occurs by the rule *bahulaṃ chandasyāmāṅyoge'pi* [Pāṇini 6.4.75].

If [it is asked], "Does the augment *iṭ* [apply] by [Pāṇini 7.3.96]? Why then does it not occur? he says: "And *iṭ* does not occur," and so forth. Because of the mention of "affix" (*pratyaya*), just as the status of being a *kṛt* suffix applies to *kvip* when it has undergone elision (*luk*), as in *dṛgbhyām* and similar forms derived from the root *dṛś* with *kvip*, [the same applies here].
"In this way," and so forth.

Is it because of the mention of *pratyaya* (suffix)? Once it is established that "the substitution of *k* occurs even for a word ending in another suffix, provided that the suffix *kvip* has been prescribed after it," then in the case of *rajjusṛḍbhyām*, the substitution of *ṣ* which would result from the rule *brāccha-ādi-sūtra* (Pāṇini 8.2.36) must be set aside by the substitution of *k*.

"But if this is not desired, a counter-argument (*pratividhāna*) must be made. [This is not in the *Prāmu-pāṭha*]. The counter-argument is that the mention of the word *vā* ("or") in the subsequent sūtra is a remainder (*śeṣa*) applicable to both rules.
And since this is a rule of fixed option (*vyavasthitavibhāṣā*), it will not apply here.
This being so, the forms should be *rajjusṛbhyām* and *rajjusṛṅbhyaḥ*. Regarding the example *jīvanaṅāhutiḥ*:

here, in the alternative where the change to *ku* does not occur, the substitution of *ṣ* is applied by the rule *vraśca-* [Pāṇini 8.2.36], after which the substitution of the voiced unaspirated stop (*jaś*)—namely, the letter *ḍ*—occurs. The term *padasya* (of a word) is understood to carry over.
And that [term], which is in grammatical apposition with "root" (*dhātu*), is qualified by the letter *m*—meaning "of a word ending in *m* that is a root. For example: *praśān*, *pratān*.

[The roots] *śamu* (in the sense of "pacification," DhP 1201) and *tamu* (in the sense of "longing," DhP 1202) take the suffix *kvip*; then, by [Pāṇini 6.4.15], there is lengthening of the penultimate vowel, and by [Pāṇini 6.1.68], the elision of the consonant and the following vowel.

Why does the elision of the letter *n* not occur here in the word *atheha* (according to Pāṇini 8.2.7)? To this he says: "of the *natva*" (*natvasya*), and so forth. In the word *aganma*, there is the elision of the letter *s* (according to Pāṇini 3.4.98).
In the word *jaganvān*:

The suffixes *gamer liṭ*, *kvasuḥ*, [the rule] *halṅyādi* [Pāṇini 6.1.66], the elision of the final consonant of a conjunct [by] *saṃyogāntalopaḥ* [8.2.23], the lengthening [of the vowel] by *sāntamahataḥ* [6.4.10], and the elision of the penultimate vowel (*upadhālopa*) by *gamahana* [6.4.98] etc., [apply].
[By this,] the status of being a *sārvadhātuka* suffix does not occur [for *kvasuḥ*].
The letter *ca* serves to draw forward the term "in a verbal root" (*dhātau*). [Thus we have] *sajūḥ*.

The root *juṣ* is listed in the Dhātupāṭha (1288) with the meanings "to love" and "to serve. From the derivation *saha juṣate*, the suffix *kvip* is applied, followed by an *upapada* compound. By [Pāṇini 6.3.78], the substitution of *sa-* for *sa-* occurs.
Once the substitution of *ru* has been made, the lengthening of the vowel is applied by [Pāṇini 8.2.76]: *rvorupadhāyāḥ*.
The inclusion of the term *sajuṣaḥ* is for the purpose of including forms that do not end in the letter *s*.

And this *yoga* is an exception (*apavāda*) to the substitution of *jaś*. Regarding the form "dāśeḥ" [the Kāśikā reads "dāśateḥ"]: it is derived from the root *dāśṛ* "to give" (Dhātupāṭha 882) with the suffix *ṇvin*. From the roots *vah* and *dāś*, the suffix *ṇvin* is applied by the rule "In a mantra, after *ota*, *vah*, *uktha*, *śas*, and *puroḍāś*, the suffix *ṇvin* is added" (Pāṇini 3.2.71); and from the root *yaj*, the suffix *ṇvin* is applied by the rule "After *yaj*, the suffix *ṇvin* is added when *āva* follows" (Pāṇini 3.2.72). From these words ending in the suffix *ṇvin*, the vocative case (*sambuddhi*) is formed; then, by the rule "elision of *hal* and *ṅi*" (Pāṇini 6.1.66), there is elision of the case-ending. Thereafter, by the Vārttika "for *ota*, *vāha*, etc., there is elision of the *ṭi* of the word-form *ḍas*" (Vārttika 263), there is elision of the *ṭi* of the word-form *ḍas*.

For what purpose are these [words] treated as *nipātana*s (irregularly formed items), given that forms such as *otavobhyām* and *otavobhiḥ* could be accounted for by the rule *otavāhādīnāṃ ḍaspadasya*? Since this would already be established by the rule *ḍasi ca* [Pāṇini 7.3.109], why is this stated? To this he replies: "Of *otavāh* and so forth," etc. These are not treated as *nipātana*s for the sake of the substitution of *ru*; rather, they are for the sake of lengthening (*dīrghatva*) in the vocative singular.
But is not lengthening also already established for these by the rule *ḍrīrghatvamapi eṣāṃ* [Pāṇini 6.4.14]? To this he replies: "And of a stem ending in *at* or *as*," etc.

For in that context, the term *asambuddhau* ("except in the vocative singular") is understood to carry over from the rule *tatra hi* [Pāṇini 6.4.8]; consequently, lengthening would apply in the vocative, and it is for this purpose that these forms are treated as irregular (*nipātana*). Regarding the form *puroḍāḥ*:
by the very sūtra *mantre otavahokthaśas* [Pāṇini 3.2.71], the substitution of *ḍa* for *da* is prescribed.
Regarding the term *ukthaśāḥ*: the root *śans* means "to praise" (*dā-pā-śān-vayati*, Dhp. 728).

Because one praises the *ukthas*, the suffix *ṇvin* is applied by the rule *mantré ṣeṇi ca* (Pāṇini 3.2.71); from that, as before, the vocative case ending and so forth are applied. When the elision of the *n* would otherwise occur by the rule *na lopaḥ prātipadikāntasya* (Pāṇini 8.2.7), this [preservation] is ordained.
In the forms *ahobhyām* and *ahobhiḥ*,
the substitution of *u* [for the final *o*] occurs by [Pāṇini 6.1.110] *haśi ca*. Thus,
we have *dīrghāho nidāghaḥ* (or *dīrghāhā*, as found in the Kāśikā and the ancient printed reading of the Nyāsa).

This is a *bahuvrīhi* compound. By [Pāṇini 6.1.68], there is the elision of the final consonant (*hal*) and the vowels beginning with *i* (*ṅy-ādi*). Because the substitution of *r* (*rutva*) is considered as if not having taken effect (*asiddha*), the lengthening occurs by [Pāṇini 6.4.8] (*sarvanāmasthāne ca*). Then, by [Pāṇini 8.3.7] (*bho-bhago-agho...*), the *r* is replaced by *y*, and that *y* is elided by [Pāṇini 8.3.22] (*lopaḥ śākalyasya*).

Thus we have: "O Dīrghāho Atri! (he *dīrghāho* *atri*). Then, by [Pāṇini 6.1.113] (*eṅaḥ padāntādati*), *u* is substituted; and by [Pāṇini 6.1.87] and [6.1.109], the subsequent vowel becomes the single substitute (*parapūrvatva*).

One might have the misconception that when *tip* is elided by [Pāṇini 6.1.66] *halṅyādilopaḥ*, and after the *luk*-elision of *tip* and the addition of the augment *aṭ*, the form *ahan* is produced, and therefore it ought to undergo the substitution of *ru*. To dispel this doubt, he says: "*ahan*" and so forth. Here, the word *upasaṃkhyāna* means "stating" or "explaining. The meaning is that when the substitution of *ru* is to be applied to the form *ahar*, its application must be stated for the forms beginning with *rūpa*.

In this regard, the following is the demonstration: the particle *ca* from the preceding sūtra is carried over here, and it serves the purpose of including what has not been explicitly mentioned; by means of it, the substitution of *r* will occur for [the final *s*] of *ahan* before words such as *rūpa*.
The example is *ahorūpam*.
This is a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*) meaning "the form of the day" (*ahnaḥ rūpam*).

But how does the substitution of *r* (rutva) that is prescribed for the word *rātri* apply to the word *rātra*? It occurs either by virtue of the principle of "treating as the original" (*sthānivadbhāva*), or because a form that has undergone a partial modification is not considered different from the original.
The word *rātra* was not explicitly included [in the rule], so that it might also apply to the word *rātri*, as in: "The day has passed; night has arrived. [An example is:
"The *rathantara* [sāman] of the day."
It is a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*),
or alternatively, it is not a compound at all;
[the rule] *ro'supi* is superseded by the substitution of *ru*, and so forth.
Whether *ahorūpa* and so forth constitute a compound (*samāsa*) or not a compound (*asamāsa*), in every case there must be elision (*luk*) of the case-ending.
When elision occurs, by the rule *lumatā lupte pratyayalakṣaṇasya pratiṣedhaḥ* [Pāṇini 1.1.62], the application of a grammatical operation conditioned by a suffix is prohibited.
Consequently, because the condition of being followed by a *sup*-suffix (*supparatva*) is absent, the rule *roḥ supi* [Pāṇini 8.2.69] would apply; therefore, the substitution of *ru* is prescribed.
For what purpose? So that the substitution of *u* (utvam) may occur by the rule *haśi ca* [Pāṇini 6.1.110].

If this were to apply to the *ru* that has arisen [from the substitution of *ru* for *visarga*], then in the rule prescribing *utvam*, there would be the recurrence of a *repha* (*r*) characterized by the indicatory letter *u* (as in *roḥ*). The word *bhuvaḥ* is an indeclinable that resembles a genitive case ending; since the substitution of *ru* would be obligatory for it, this sūtra is intended so that the *repha* may optionally occur. The particle *ca* serves to draw forward the term *ubhayathā* ("in both ways").
Therefore, it does not recur in what follows:
"bhuvo vikhyasya.
Here, the word *mū* is used either in the genitive case or in the ablative case.

If this is so, then because it is *lākṣaṇika* (derived from a rule), this [augment] will not occur; therefore, what is the purpose of including the term *mahāvyāhṛti* for its exclusion? In that case, this teaches that the paribhāṣā "the specifically mentioned (*pratipadokta*) takes precedence over the *lākṣaṇika*" is not eternal. By this, the augment *puK* in the form *krāpayati* is established; for if that [paribhāṣā] were eternal, it would not occur here, because this [form] ending in *ā* is *lākṣaṇika*. What kind of word *bhuvas* is a *mahāvyāhṛti*? To this he says: "The word *bhuvas*... and so forth.
For the intermediate space (*antarikṣa*) is great (*mahat*); because its utterance is vast (*vyāhmati*), it is therefore called *mahāvyāhṛti*. [Regarding the forms] "vidvadbhyām":
by [Pāṇini 7.1.36], there is the substitution of *vasu*. [Examples:
"papivadbhyām", "papivadbhiḥ".

From the roots *pivati* or *pāti*, there is the suffix *liṭ*, followed by *kvasu*; the augment *iṭ* is applied according to Pāṇini 7.2.67 (*vasvekājādghasām*), and the elision of the vowel *ā* occurs according to 6.4.64. By virtue of the status of being a substitute (*sthānivadbhāva*), this form *pā* is reduplicated. From the roots *ruś* and *dhvaṃs*, as in the examples *ukhāruṭ* and *parṇadhvat*: [the forms] *ukhāruṭ* (one who breaks a pot) and *parṇadhvat* (one who withers leaves) are derived from *ruś* and *dhvaṃs* respectively with the suffix *kvip*, meaning "he breaks a pot" (*ukhāyāḥ ruśati*) and "he withers the leaves" (*parṇāni dhvaṃsate*). The elision of the nasal (*n*) occurs according to 6.4.24 (*aniditām*).

In this context, the status of being an "unoccupied scope" (*anavakāśa*) for the rule [of] *vasu* is untenable, because every object [of application] is already occupied by another rule. Nevertheless, in cases such as *vidvān*, the elision of a final consonant cluster (*saṃyogāntalopa*) would apply, whereas in cases such as *vidvadbhyām*, the substitution of *r* (*rutva*) would apply. Therefore, since that [rule of *vasu*] lacks an unoccupied scope, when *rutva* sublates [the former], then the elision of the final consonant cluster must also be sublated by it; consequently, *vidvān* would not be established, which would lead to confusion. To address this, he says: "When *rutva* has not yet applied," and so forth.

"When a rule is commenced while another [rule] has not yet taken effect, it becomes a sublater of that [other rule]" (Vyāḍīya-paribhāṣā 49). And this [present rule] is not commenced while *rutva* (the substitution of *r*) has not yet taken effect; therefore, that very [*rutva*] is sublated by *datva* (the substitution of *d*).
"But the elision of a final consonant cluster (*saṃyogāntalopa*) is not like this"—the word *tu* ("but") shows the distinction from *rutva*.
The particle *iti* is used here in the sense of a reason (*hetu*).
Just as *rutva* (the substitution of *r*) applies everywhere, the elision of the final syllable of *sy-ogantah* does not apply in the same way.
For that [elision] applies only in cases such as *vidvān*, but not in cases such as *vidvadbhyām*.

Why is that? The intention is this: by that very [substitution], the *datva* (the substitution of *d* for *t*) is sublated, but not the *datva* itself; for when the elision of a final consonant in a conjunct (*saṃyogāntalopa*) is to be applied, the *datva* is considered as if non-existent (*asiddha*).

Therefore, just as the letter *d* in the rule *ho ḍhaḥ* [Pāṇini 8.2.31] is an exception (*apavāda*) here, why does the same not apply to the rule *sa...* [Pāṇini 7.1.82]? Since the letter *d* sublates the *ḍhatva* because it has a specific scope (*hravakāśatva*), it would be logical that it should likewise sublate the *num* [augment] as well? To this he replies: "But it does not occur because of the force of its prescription (*vidhānasāmarthya*)."
For indeed, *num* is prescribed at every step by the rule *sāvanaḍuhaḥ*. If this [present] *d* were an exception (*apavāda*) to that, then the prescription of *num* would be purposeless.

Thus, for "anaḍvān": the suffix *ām* is applied by [Pāṇini 7.1.98], followed by the *yaṇ* substitution, and then the elision of the final consonant (*halṅyādi*) and the final member of the conjunct (*saṃyogānta*).
"He is an ox" (*anaḍvān*).
[This is] according to [Pāṇini 7.1.99]. The rest is as before. [The rule] *rvor upadhāyāḥ* [applies].
The analysis of the compound is: *r* and *v* are *rvau*; [the word] "of those two" (*tayoḥ*) is the analysis.
From the rule "after a verbal root, *ru* is optionally substituted before *siP*" (*sipi dhāto rurvā*), the term "verbal root" (*dhātoḥ*) is understood by anuvṛtti.
The term *rvau* is its qualifier; therefore, the rule of "specification by the final element" (*tadantavidhi*) applies.
The term "of a word" (*padasya*) is supplied as a governing heading.

From the rule "of *sk* and *k*, when they are the first members of a conjunction" (*skoḥ saṃyogādyoḥ*), the word "at the end" (*ante*) is understood to carry over. Thus he says, beginning with "the letter *r*" (*repha*), and so forth.
Regarding "pipaṭhīḥ":
the intention is that the vowel *i* following the letter *ṭha* becomes long, and the *repha* (the letter *r*) becomes a *visarga*. Regarding "pipaṭhībhyām": [the same rule applies].

The intention is that because [the word] *pipaṭhiṣ* is a *pada*, the rule *rvor upadhāyāḥ* applies, resulting in a long vowel when *bhyām* and other case endings follow, as they are characterized as being at the end of a *pada*.
Regarding the specific rule for the *sup* (case) endings, he says: *vā śari*.

When *pipaṭhiṣ-su* is in this state, since the substitution of *ṣ* is considered *asiddha*, *r* is substituted; then, after the lengthening and the *visarjanīya*, the rule *vā śari* optionally replaces the *visarjanīya* by preventing its substitution with *s*.
The meaning is that in the alternative where that [visarjanīya] is absent, there is the substitution of *s* for the *visarjanīya*.

In that case, when the form *pipaṭhiḥ-su* is established under the *visarjanīya* alternative, since it is not preceded by the letter *iṇ* or the *ka*-group, the substitution of *ṣ* [prescribed by] "ādeśapratyayayoḥ" does not apply. Thus, [the example] is "acakāḥ tvam.
Once *ru* has been applied, its *visarjanīya* is replaced by *s* according to [Pāṇini 8.3.34].
The subsequent application of the word *tvam* is for the purpose of making the *sip* suffix manifest.

Now, what is the purpose of including the term *dhātu* (verbal root), given that the substitution of *r* and *d* is prescribed even for a suffix ending in *s*, and there is nothing other than a verbal root ending in *s* before the *sip* suffix? To this, he says: "The inclusion of the term *dhātu*," and so forth.
Furthermore, its utility for a subsequent rule will be demonstrated under [Pāṇini 8.2.76]: *asva-rvor upadhāyāḥ*.

"Let the mention of the verbal root (*dhātu*) be made for the sake of what follows, but the mention of *ru* need not be made; for since it would be purposeless, when the substitution of *d* is optionally applied, the substitution of *ru* is obtained in its alternative case exactly as prescribed. To this he says: "And the mention of *ru*," which implies that it is not merely for the sake of what follows. He will state [later] "and after *da*" (*daśca*); the purpose is so that in that alternative case, the substitution of *ru* may take place.

For if that [condition] were absent—meaning, if the state of being *dat* did not exist—then the state of being *cat*, as it is obtained, would not occur. By means of the letter *ca*, the term *daḥ* (from Pāṇini 8.2.72) is drawn forward; therefore, its recurrence does not take place in what follows. In the example *abhinastvam*, there is the *laṅ* suffix; because the root belongs to the *rudhādi* class, the suffix *śnam* is applied. The rule applies only to a "word" (*pada*) and also to a "verbal root" (*dhātu*); both of these are here coreferential and are qualified by the letters *r* and *v*. Since a qualification implies a rule concerning that which ends with the qualifier, he says: "of that which ends in *r* or *v*."
Why was an example for the letter *v* not shown? To this he says: "The inclusion of the letter *d* is for the sake of what follows.
The implication is that an example ending in *v* was therefore not shown.
However, that is not for this specific purpose, because a word ending in *v* cannot be a verbal root (*dhātu*).
Regarding *abibhar*:

this is the root *bhṛ* in the *laṅ* tense, with the suffix *tip*, followed by *guṇa*, *raparatva*, reduplication, *urat* (substitution of *at*), *bhṛñām it* (substitution of *it*), and the elision of the consonant and following vowels (*halṅyādilopa*). Regarding *divyati* and *caturyati*:
here both *div* and *catur* are nominal stems (*prātipadika*); therefore, [the application of the rule] does not occur.
In the word *smaryate*, the suffix *yak* is applied in the sense of the abstract action (*bhāve*), and the *guṇa* substitution occurs according to [Pāṇini 7.3.84]: *guṇo’rtisaṃyogādyoḥ*.
In the word *bhavyam*, [the same applies].

By [Pāṇini 3.1.97] *aco yat*, there is *guṇa*; by [Pāṇini 6.1.80], there is the substitution of *ava*. Because the rule for lengthening had previously been prescribed for roots ending in *r* or *v*, this [rule] is for the sake of those not ending in *r* or *v*.
In the phrase "in the *upadhā*," the locative singular is used in place of the genitive dual through a transposition of case endings (*sub-vyatyaya*).
[The meaning is] "becoming the *upadhā*."
The meaning is "having attained the status of a *upadha*. This refers to the two [sounds] preceding the final vowel (*alo'ntyāt*).
"Followed by a consonant" (*halpara*) means...
The term *hal* [in the rule] is a bahuvrīhi compound meaning "that which follows these two. Furthermore, that *hal* should be understood as being an integral part of the verbal root (*dhātu*) itself.
For in cases where the suffix is followed by a *hal* that comes after the letters *r* or *v*, the desired result is already established by the preceding rule.
Regarding "hūrchitā":
the root is *hurch* in the sense of "crookedness" (*kauṭilye*) [Dhātupāṭha 211].
Regarding "mūcchatā": [the root is *murch*].
The root *murch* [is used] in the sense of fainting (*mūrchā*) and increase (*samucchrāya*) [Dhātupāṭha 212].

Now, one might object: "Once reduplication has been applied by [Pāṇini 6.1.2], the letter *r* is no longer the penultimate (*upadhā*) here? This is not so; because reduplication is considered non-existent (*asiddha*) when the lengthening [of the vowel] is to be performed, there is only one consonant (*hal*) here, namely the letter *ś*, and thus the letter *r* indeed retains its status as the penultimate.
[Examples: *ciriṇoti*, *jiriṇoti*.

Regarding the roots *ri*, *kṣi*, *ciri*, *jiri*, *dāśa*, and *dṛ* in the sense of "injury" (*hiṃsāyām*) (Dhātupāṭha 1275–1280), the suffix *śnu* is applied because they belong to the *svādi* group. Here, from the roots *rī* in the sense of "motion" (*gatau*) (Dhātupāṭha 1500) and *dhī* in the senses of "motion, procreation, etc. (*gatiprajanādiṣu*) (Dhātupāṭha 1048), when the suffixes *liṭ*, *atus*, and *us* are applied, the substitution of *yaṇ* occurs by Pāṇini 6.4.82 (*eranekācaḥ*). Because of the status of that [substitute] as if it were the original (*sthānivadbhāva*), when reduplication (*dvirvacana*) is performed, the forms *riryatuḥ* and *riyuḥ*; and *vivyatuḥ* and *vivyuḥ* are established. At this point, a long vowel would result for the *ik* of the reduplicated syllable, because the *repha* and *vakāra* (the letters *r* and *v*) are followed by a consonant (*hal*) and thus constitute the *upadhā* (penultimate).

Why does this not occur? To this he says: "ririyatuḥ, ririyaḥ," and so forth, by means of the rule *sthānivadbhāvaḥ* [Pāṇini 1.1.56]. But surely, the status of being a substitute (*sthānivadbhāvaḥ*) is prohibited in the case of the prescription of a long vowel by the rule *na padānta...* [Pāṇini 1.1.58]; so how can its application be possible here? This is not so; for in that context a specific enumeration is made: "In the cases of vowel-change, lengthening, and the elision of *y*, a substitute for an elided letter is not treated as the original" (Kāśikāvṛtti on 1.1.59), or "because it is considered as if non-existent" (*asiddhatvāt*), and so on.

In this case, the substitution of *yaṇ* is extrinsic (*bahiraṅga*), because that which is prescribed within the governing rule for *aṅga* depends upon an affix. The lengthening (*dīrghatva*), however, is intrinsic (*antaraṅga*), because it depends upon the base (*prakṛti*).

According to the principle "and what is extrinsic is as if non-existent (*asiddha*) with respect to what is intrinsic" (Vyāḍipāda 42), when the lengthening is to be applied, the *yaṇ* substitution is considered non-existent; therefore, the *r* and *v* are not followed by a consonant (*hal*), so how could there be the application of the lengthening?

In that case, why does the lengthening [of the vowel] not occur in *caturyitā*? For here, when the suffix *tṛc* follows the verbal root *caturya* ending in *kyac*, after the elision of the vowel *a* by Pāṇini 6.4.48, the *repha* (the letter *r*) becomes a penultimate (*upadhā*) sound followed by a consonant (*halpara*), and thus there is the possibility of lengthening. To this, he says: "In *caturyitā* as well," and so forth.
Therefore, the elision is *bahiraṅga* because it depends on an *ārthadhātuka* suffix;
the lengthening is *antaraṅga*, as before.
In that case, even in *pratidīvnā*, there would not be lengthening.

For just as in *caturyitā* the vowel *ṛ* is not the penultimate (*upadhā*) of the root, so too in *pratidīvnā* the *v* is not [the penultimate]. To explain: is *divya* alone the root? But the *n* belongs to the suffix; and the *v* is not the penultimate of the root *div*, but rather it is internal [to the root]. Therefore, he says: "In *pratidīvnā*, etc."

From the root *div* preceded by *prati*, the suffix *kvin* is applied according to [Aṣṭādhyāyī 3.2.61] *pratipūrvād divaḥ kanin yuvuṣitakṣi*, etc.; subsequently, the elision of the vowel *a* occurs according to [6.4.134].

Now, one might object: since the elision of *a* (*al-lopa*) is treated as if it were present (*sthānivadbhāva*) by [1.1.57], the verbal root here does not end in *v* when followed by a consonant (*hal*);
therefore, how can there be lengthening by [8.2.77] *hali ca*? To this he says: "In the rule for lengthening," and so forth.

The prohibition of the status of being *sthānivat* (as if occupying the original position) is, however, by the rule "not at the end of a word" (*na padānta*, P. 1.1.57). Now, one might object: even so, because the elision of *a* (*al-lopa*) is established as being external (*bahiraṅga*), a verbal root ending in *v* cannot occur before a consonant (*hal*) in this instance. To this he says: "An external [operation] is not established," and so forth.
The reason for not resorting to this [rule] is the non-universality (*anityatva*) of this maxim (*paribhāṣā*).
However, the non-eternality (*anityatva*) [of this rule] is indicated by the inclusion of the term *tugvidhi* in rules such as *nalopaḥ supsvara-* (Pāṇini 6.3.71).

Now, regarding forms such as *jivriḥ* and *kiryoh*, why does the lengthening [of the vowel] prescribed by *hali ca* (Pāṇini 6.4.2) not occur? For the word *jivri* is also derived in this very manner: "from the root *jṝ* [with the suffix] *krin*, and *ra* is replaced by *va*" (Dhātupāṭha 1.80).

From the verbal roots *jṛṣ* and *jhṛṣ* in the sense of "loss of vitality" (*vayohāni*)—as found in the *Dhātupāṭha* (1130, 1131)—the suffix *krin* is applied. By the rule *ṛta iddhātoḥ* [Pāṇini 7.1.100], the substitution of *it* occurs; then there is the substitution of *ra* for *ṛ*, and subsequently the substitution of *va* for *ra*. In this derivation, for the root *jivri* ending in *va*, when a consonant (*hal*) follows the *ra*, the possibility of lengthening arises by the rule *hali ca* [Pāṇini 8.2.77].
The same derivation is applied to words such as *kiri* and *giri*.
[The suffix] *i* is added after a vowel (*aca iḥ*). [Daiva-nighaṇṭu].

1–67) Thus, while the suffix *i* is being carried over, these [words] are derived by prescribing the suffix *i* after the verbal roots *kirati* and others— namely *bhuj*, as per the rule *bhujeḥ kicca* (Daiva 1.71), and *kṛ, gṛ, śṛ, pṛ, kuṭi, bhid, chid*, as per the rule *kṛgṛśṛpṛkuṭibhidicchidibhyaśca* (Daiva 1.72)— by means of the rule *bhujeḥ kicca*.

If this is the derivation—once the *yaṇ* substitution has been applied, would not words such as *kṛ*, which end in *r*, undergo lengthening by the rule *hali ca* [Pāṇini 6.4.2] when followed by a consonant (*hal*)? To this he says: "The *uṇādi* suffixes are underived," and so forth.

But surely, even in the view that [the suffixes] are derived (*vyutpattipakṣa*), the lengthening of the vowel does not apply in cases such as *kiryoḥ* and *giryor*; for here, when followed by a consonant (*hal*), the roots *kṛ* and *gṛ* do not end in *r*. This is because, when lengthening is to be applied, the substitution of *yaṇ* (semivowels) would be treated as the original element (*sthānivadbhāva*). For indeed, in the case of elisions of vowels (*svarāvilopa*), a substitute for an elided element (*lopājādeśa*) is not treated as the original, whereas any other substitute is indeed treated as the original. True, this is so; however, this resolution was stated while merely conceding the point. He thinks as follows: although the prohibition of being treated as the original (*sthānivadbhāva-pratiṣedha*) applies without distinction, nevertheless, lengthening would still not apply here; because the *uṇādi* derivatives are considered *avyutpanna* (non-derived/unanalyzed).

If the *uṇādi* suffixes are considered unanalyzed nominal stems (*avyutpanna-prātipadika*), then it is certainly not appropriate to adopt the view of etymological derivation (*vyutpatti-pakṣa*) for that very same rule. Even if one were to derive the word *pratidivan*—ending in the *kvanip* suffix—according to the rules "āto maninkvanibvaniyaśca" [Pāṇini 3.2.74] and "anyebhyo'pi dṛśyante" [3.2.75], its long vowel would still not be established; for once the *v* is elided by the rule "lopo vyorvali" [6.1.66], the verbal root would end in *av*, rather than *ā*. Therefore, an effort must be made in this regard.

Thus it is done: in the rule *hali ca* [Pāṇini 8.2.77], the view that "the meaning of a word is already manifested" (*vyaktaḥ padārthaḥ*) is relied upon. And according to this view, since there is a difference in grammatical rules for each individual instance (*pratilakṣyam*), they teach as many rules as there are instances to be explained. Among those various instances, in accordance with the specific forms to be accounted for: in some cases, such as *pratidīvnā*, the view that words are derived from their constituent parts (*vyutpattipakṣa*) is adopted; in other cases, however, such as *jivriḥ*, *kiryauḥ*, *giryauḥ*, and so on, the view that words are underived primitives (*avyutpattipakṣa*) is adopted.

The letter *ca* is for the purpose of drawing forward [the rule] *halo* [from Pāṇini 6.1.113]. Since the lengthening [of the vowel] would have applied by [the rule] *hali ca* [Pāṇini 6.1.71], this prohibition is commenced. Regarding the word *dhuryaḥ*:
it means "one who carries the yoke" (*dhuraṃ vahati*), and the suffix *yat* is applied by [the rule] *dhuro yaḍḍhakau* [Pāṇini 4.4.77].

Regarding the form *kuryāt*: this is the optative (*liṅ*) of the root *kṛ*. By the rule *tanādikṛñbhya u* [Pāṇini 3.1.79], the suffix *u* is added; the root undergoes *guṇa*; there is substitution of *ra* for the semivowel; by the rule *ata ut sārvadhātuke* [Pāṇini 6.4.110], the vowel *u* is replaced by *ū*; and by the rule *ye ca* [Pāṇini 6.4.109], the *u* is elided. Thus, one obtains *kuryāt*.
The *liṅ* [suffix] is used in the sense of a benediction (*āśis*).

The mention of the root *kṛ* by means of its *vikaraṇa* (the suffix *śn*) is for the purpose that the prohibition [of the augment *iṭ*] should not apply in cases such as *cikīrṣati*. In the term *aseḥ*, the vowel *i* is for the sake of pronunciation;
that which has no *s* is thus described as *as-* (i.e., *aseḥ*).
And since that which is of such a nature does not end in the letter *s*, he says: "of that which does not end in *s*" (*asakārāntasya*), and so forth.

Regarding "this" (*amum*) and so on: when the substitution of *t* for *tyad*-type stems has been applied to *adas* before the case-endings beginning with *ām*, and the subsequent form (*pararūpa*) has been applied, the substitution of *asi* [for *adas*] occurs by virtue of [Pāṇini 6.1.103].
By the rule *auṭ* (Pāṇini 6.1.88), there is *vṛddhi*.
In the case of the nominative plural (*śas*), there is the substitution of a long vowel homogeneous with the preceding one (*pūrvasavarṇadīrghatva*).

Here, by the paribhāṣā regarding the "most similar substitute" (*sthāne 'ntaratama*) [Pāṇini 1.1.49], in the singular number, a one-mora vowel (*mātrika*) is replaced by a one-mora vowel, while elsewhere, a two-mora vowel (*dvimātrika*) is replaced by a two-mora vowel. But surely, only a one-mora vowel is mentioned in the sūtra; how then can a two-mora vowel be obtained? If it is argued that this is due to the inclusion of the term "homogeneous" (*savarṇa*) in the rule *aṇuditsavarṇasya cāpratyayaḥ* [Pāṇini 1.1.69], we say no.
Because of the prohibition [stated in] *bhāvyamāno’ṇ savarṇān na gṛhṇāti* (Vyāḍi-Pāṇini 35), [the author] says: "*bhāvyamāno’pi*," etc.
And this has been indicated by the inclusion of the long vowel marker (*tapara*) in the rule *ṛta ut* (Pāṇini 6.1.107). Regarding the form *adasyati*:
[it is derived] by *supa ātmanaḥ kyac* (Pāṇini 3.1.8). [The Vārttika states: "It should be stated that for the word *adas*, [the substitution of] *an* occurs in place of *aru*."
This is a *dvandva* compound of the vowels *o*, *ā*, and the consonant *r*. It is a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "one for whom there are no *oruās*" (*avidyamānā oruā asya*).

[Regarding the form *oruā*: because it is neuter, the suffix *su* is elided by *svamornapuṃsakāt* [Pāṇini 7.1.23]. Then, the substitution of *ru* for *s* occurs by *sasajuṣo ruḥ* [Pāṇini 8.2.66], followed by the substitution of *u* for *r* by *ato roraplutādaplute* [Pāṇini 6.1.113], and finally the substitution of the preceding vowel for the following one (*parapūrvatvam*) by *pūrvasavarṇe* [Pāṇini 6.1.102].
This is a counter-example (*pratyudāharaṇa*) for the prohibition of the long vowel *ī*.
Regarding the word "adaḥ": this [rule] is for the prohibition of the substitution of *r*. Once the substitution of *ru* has been applied, the *visarjanīya* follows.
"Regarding the phrase 'for that purpose':
this is for the sake of ensuring that the prohibition applies to the *sakāra* and *repha* as well. [The rule] 'of that which has *i* after *aḥ*'..."
The letter *sa* [is present; it is not in the reading *nāsti-kāṃu*] for the purpose of pronunciation.
The letter *a* signifies "that of which the *sa* is the [initial]," meaning "belonging to whom.
[This explains] the passage beginning with "How," and so forth.

When the substitution of *adr* for *adas* is made, does the *mutva* (the substitution of *m* for *u*) apply separately to both *adas* and *adr*, or only to that which is in the final position (*antyasadeśa*), or rather, does it not occur at all in the domain where the *adr* substitution applies? This is what he asks with the words "of *adas*, of *adr*" (*adaso'draḥ*), etc.
*Ma* and *u* constitute *mu*; the state of being that is *mutva*.

The meaning is that some authorities desire the substitution of *m* for both *adas-* and *adreḥ*. For even without the particle *ca*, its sense is understood, as in the sentence: "Day after day, bringing a cow, a sheep, a man, and a beast," and so forth.

How so? He says "as follows": regarding the term *lattvavat*, just as in the case of the rule *calīkḷpyate* (Pāṇini 8.2.18), some authorities maintain that the substitution of *l* applies to both the *r* of the verbal root and the syllable *rī*; likewise, there is the substitution of *m* for *daśaḥ* and *adreḥ*. Regarding the phrase "some [hold it applies] to the final homogeneous part," this refers to the following.
The substitute *adra* ends in the vowel *i*; some desire its change to *u*.
Furthermore, that [change] concerns the letter *d* and the letter *r* belonging to the substitute *adra*.
"Some say no," they claim.
Others, however, maintain that when the substitution of *adra* for *adas* is made, the substitution of *mut* should certainly not occur;
he states the reason for this very point: "for it is seen after *as*. That which has *as* as its *si* (locative case ending) is *asi*; [the rule applies] to that *asi*.
The word *hi* is used in the sense of "for which reason.

Why? Because the substitution of *a* for the *s* of that *adas-* is observed by scholars to undergo the change to *m* (*mutva*). Furthermore, the substitution of *a* does not occur for the *s* of *adas-* when it has already undergone the replacement [of its final vowel] by *ā*, because the cause—the following case-ending—is absent.
Therefore, it should not be [understood] as having the letter *m*. With the words "by those" (*yaiḥ*) and so forth, he explains the first half of the verse.
By those who explain it thus: "the prohibition of the letter *s* is made for the word *asi* (sword), meaning that the letter *s* does not exist in this [word].
Regarding the phrase "of both":

*adas*, and *adri*. Regarding the form *amumuyaṅ* and so forth: from the root *añc* in the sense "he moves toward that" (*adoñcati*), the suffix *kvin* is applied by the rule beginning with *ṛtvig-* (Pāṇini 3.2.59). By the rule *aniditām-* (6.4.24), there is elision of the nasal (*n*). Then, a *tatpuruṣa* compound is formed. Subsequently, the augment *num* is added by the rule *ugidacām-* (7.1.70), and the elisions of the consonant and the following vowel (*halṅyādi*) as well as the final consonant (*saṃyogānta*) are applied.
In the singular, by the rule *akṛt-saṃjñāyāḥ kuḥ* [Pāṇini 8.2.62], there is the substitution of *ku*—that is, the letter *ṅ* replaces the letter *n*.

Elsewhere, [the form] *amumuyaṅ* and *amumuyañcau* arises as follows: first, there is the *anusvāra* by [Pāṇini 8.3.24], then the *parasavarṇa* *ñakāra* (or *ṅakāra*, according to the Kāśikā reading) by [8.4.58]. Then, while the term *sarvanāmnaḥ* is being carried over from [6.3.91], the *ṭi*-portion of the word *adas-* is replaced by *adr-ā-* by [6.3.92]. Following the initial *d*-sound, the *u*-vowel (*utva*) is substituted for the following vowel, and the *d*-sound becomes *m* (*matva*). After the second *d*-sound as well, the *u*-vowel (*utva*) is substituted for the *ra*-phoneme, and the *d*-sound becomes *m*. Thus, *amumuyaṅ* and *amumuyañcau* are formed.
By the words "just as" (*yathā*) and so forth, he explains the meaning of the phrase "like the substitution of *l*" (*latvavat*).
Regarding the form *calīkḷpyate*:
the root *kṛpū* is used in the sense of "capacity" (*sāmarthye*; Dhātupāṭha 762).

From the sense "it is extremely capable" (*atyantaṃ kalpate*), the intensive suffix *yaṅ* is applied. This results in reduplication, the substitution of *at* for the vowel by Pāṇini 7.4.66, the substitution of *rīk* by 7.4.90, the substitution of the guttural by the palatal by 7.4.62, and the substitution of the labial *ra* by *la* by 8.2.18 for both instances [of the *ra*], because the technical rule (*paribhāṣā*) "when there is a change not affecting the final letter, it affects the letter situated in its place" (Vyāḍiparibhāṣā 63) is not invoked here.
With the words "But those who," etc., they explain the meaning of the phrase "some [hold that this applies] to the final *s* in the same position.
[The examples are] "adamuyaṅ" and "adamuyañcau.
In these cases, there is the substitution of *u* for the vowel following the *d* of *adri*, and the substitution of *m* for the *d* of *adri* itself.

The rest is as before. The passage beginning with "But for those" (*yeṣāṃ tu*)—as found in the reading of the Prācīna manuscript—is an explanation of the phrase "some" (*eke*). For whom, then, must there be substitution by *m* specifically in the domain of the *tyadādi* (pronouns) rules? It is for those who explain [the forms] in this way: *aḥ seyaṃsya so'yamasistasyāseḥ*.

Regarding the word "atra": it means that [the substitution] should not occur at all in the domain of the *adradra* substitute, because the *tyadādyatva* (the replacement of the initial *t* of *tyad* etc. with *a*) does not apply. Thus, one has the forms *adadraṅ*, *adadraāñcau*, and *adadrañcaḥ*.
As before; however,
the distinction lies in the forms "amuyā" and "amuyoḥ."

When the suffix *osi* follows the word *adas*, it undergoes the substitution of *yat* (the *ad-ādyatva* rule). Then the feminine suffix *ṭāp* is added, followed by a single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) operation. Regarding that [single substitute], by the rule *tasya* (Pāṇini 6.1.85), the preceding element is treated as if it were the final element of the whole; thus, it is indeed included by the mention of "dād" (beginning with *da*).

In this context, if the word "dād" were not stated, then after the substitution of *it* by the rules *osi ca* (7.3.104) and *ṅe-prathamayoḥ* (7.3.105)—which apply to a *ṅit* suffix—and subsequently the substitution of *ay* for that *it*, the substitution of *ut* would apply to the letter *ya* alone, according to the *alontyaparibhāṣā* (Pāṇini 1.1.52). However, because of the explicit mention of "dād," this does not occur.

The addition of the vowel *u* (in *uditi*) is for the sake of ease of pronunciation. The statement "the term 'plural' (*bahuvacana*) is a designation based on its meaning" means that it is a designation according to its etymological sense.

This is what is intended: this is not a reference to the technical, conventional term "plural"; rather, it is a reference to the etymological sense—that which expresses many objects is "plural" (*bahuvacana*).
For what reason is it explained in this way? He says: "Because [it applies] to the technical term," and so forth.
If this were a reference to the technical term *bahuvacana* (plural), then it would not apply in the case of *amī*;
for in this instance, there is no technical plural following the vowel *e*.
If, however, the term is taken in its literal sense (*anvarthagrahaṇa*), then here too the designation of many vowels is established.

The literal sense is obtained through the principle of pervasion (*vyāptinyāya*)—that is, so that the status of the substitute (*sthānivattva*) may be understood as applying specifically to the vowel *e*.
If it were stated simply as *eḥ*, one might suspect that the vowel *i* would also be considered a substitute.

And what would happen? Once the substitution of *adr* has been made, the substitution of *yaṇ* for the *ī* that is a constituent part of that [substitute] would be obstructed. The letter *t* in *īd* is for the sake of ease of pronunciation. Regarding the phrase "the mention of *vākya*" and so forth:
for if the mention of *vākya* were not there, the protracted vowel (*pluta*) would undesirably apply to all the words whatsoever that exist within a sentence.
However, in the case of grasping a sentence (*vākya*), it will apply only to the final [syllable], not to a non-final one.
For the *yaṣṭi* of only the final word becomes the *vākyaṣṭi*, and not that of any other.
Therefore, this is for the purpose that there be no prolation (*pluti*) of a non-final word, but rather that it should occur only in the final one.
Why does it not apply to the final [word] of an infinite [sentence]? Because it is undesired.

For the cessation of the governing rule for words (*pada-adhikāra*) is not intended; thus it was stated previously: "The governing rule for words extends up to the governing rule for word-finales (*apadānta*). Furthermore, because it is unreal; for by the mention of a sentence, it does not refer to all those which are word-finales within that sentence.

For there is only one *ṭi* in a sentence, and that necessarily belongs to the word as well; therefore, it is not logical for [the mention of] *ṭi* to serve the purpose of excluding the word from the jurisdiction [of the rule].

Now, what is the purpose of mentioning *ṭi*, since by the paribhāṣā "the final letter of the base" (*alo’ntyaparibhāṣā*) alone, the protracted vowel (*pluta*) will occur for the *ṭi* in the example *āyuṣmānedhi devadatta3*? To this, he says: "The mention of *ṭi*" and so forth.

For if the mention of *pluta* were not present, then just as in the rule "the final vowel of a neuter stem is short" (*hrasvo napuṃsake prātipadikasya*), where the mention of "short" (*hrasva*) brings to mind the rule "of a vowel" (*acaḥ*), and when the stem is thus qualified by the vowel, the shortening occurs only for that which ends in a vowel—such as *suvāk* (neuter) or *brāhmaṇakulam*—and not for that which does not end in a vowel;

so too here, since the mention of *pluta* brings to mind the rule "of a vowel" (*acaḥ*), and the sentence is thus qualified by the vowel, the *pluta* would occur only for that which ends in a vowel, and not for that which ends in a consonant.
But when the mention of *ṭi* occurs, it is the vowel (*ac*) that is qualified by the term *ṭi*, and not the *ṭi*-named element by the vowel.
For if the *ṭi*-named element were qualified by the vowel, then the prolation (*pluta*) would apply to that *ṭi* which ends in a vowel; in that case, the mention of *ṭi* would be purposeless.

Even without it, since the sentence is qualified by the vowel (*ac*), the prolation occurring for that which ends in a vowel is established as applying to the final vowel by the paribhāṣā "the operation applies to the final [element]" (Pāṇini 1.1.52).
Therefore, the mention of *ṭi* is not purposeless. The vowel (*aj*) is qualified by the designation *ṭi*—that is, "the vowel which bears the designation *ṭi*.
This being the case, the protracted (*pluta*) vowel is established even for that vowel which follows a consonant (*vyañjana*) that has the designation *ṭi*.
Regarding the example *agnici3tta*:
even though the word ends in a non-consonant (*avyañjana*), by virtue of the principle of "behaving like that which possesses a designation" (*vyapadeśivadbhāva*), it is treated as *devadatta3*.

Therefore, the mention of the term *ṭi* is made so that the protracted vowel (*pluta*) may occur for the final vowel (*ac*) of even a word ending in a consonant. However, the mention of *udātta* (acute) is for the purpose of excluding other accents; this necessitates that [the word] be acute on the penultimate syllable (*anantodātta*). As for a word that is acute on the final syllable (*antodātta*), it becomes acute on the penultimate by the very principle of "behaving like the original" (*sthānivadbhāva*). This is illustrated by the rule beginning with *yadabhivādyamāno guruḥ*.
In this context, because a specific [term] is not mentioned following a general introduction, there is a reference using the neuter gender in the word *yat*. "May you live long, Devadatta!"—
this is the example here, as it is a sentence for returning a greeting (*pratyabhivāda*).
In this context, the statement "I, Devadatta, salute you" is presented merely to demonstrate that the teacher is the one being saluted.
The *pratyabhivāda* (return greeting) is the blessing which the teacher, being saluted, bestows.
In that regard, the fact that the teacher is being saluted must necessarily be demonstrated; otherwise, the *pratyabhivāda* would not be understood.

"Edhi" means "be. It is derived from the root *as* in the sense of "to be" (Dhātupāṭha 1065), in the imperative mood (*loṭ*), second person singular. By [Pāṇini 3.4.87], *si* is replaced by *hi*, which is also indicatory (*apit*). By [6.4.119], the substitution of *e* for the root vowel occurs, and by [6.4.111], the *a* of the reduplicated syllable is elided. Finally, by [6.4.101], the substitute *dhi* is applied.

"It must be stated" means it must be explained. Here is the explanation: from [Pāṇini 8.2.74], the word "or" (vā) is carried over by the maxim of the frog's leap; and that is a restricted option (*vyavasthitavibhāṣā*), therefore it will not apply in the feminine.
Regarding the phrase "even toward one who is envious":
one who envies is called *asūyaka*.
He who treats his teacher with indignation through improper conduct is termed *asūyaka*.

By the words "In that case" (*tasmin*) and so forth, he shows that even though a prohibition might be desired, it need not be stated. When this saluter is not recognized as being envious, then the teacher who is to be saluted indeed performs the protracted vowel (*pluta*) in his return greeting (*pratyabhivādana*). But when it is known, "This man is envious and intends to trouble me," then there is simply no return greeting here; so what is the use of a prohibition? How, then, is it known that there is no return greeting when he is recognized as being envious? To this he says: "And thus," and so forth.

A certain ill-mannered person approached and, with improper intent, greeted him by saying, "O sir, I salute this cooking pot. When he had thus saluted, the teacher, unaware of his malice and thinking that "sthālī" was simply the man's name, replied with a protracted vowel (*pluta*) as part of the formal greeting: "May you live long, O Sthālī! Then that ill-mannered man said, "This is not my name; I intended to employ the 'stick-bearer' logic (*daṇḍinyāya*).
Thereupon, the teacher offered a reply without the protracted vowel: "May you live long, O Sthālī! (i.e., "O Sthālī-bearer").

Again he said: "It is not that I did not intend to apply the rule regarding the *daṇḍin* (the person with a staff); this is merely my name. Then the teacher, perceiving his malice (*asūyakatva*), spoke to him: "You are a malicious wretch! You do not deserve a return greeting (*pratyabhivāda*). May you be split apart, O low-born one (*vṛṣala*), like a cooking pot! Now, when one employs a return greeting such as "O Devadatta, are you well? or "O Devadatta, may you live long!", why is there no protracted vowel (*pluta*)? To this he says: "In the case of those who utter a greeting," and so forth.
That by which one salutes is "salutation" (*abhivādana*); and that which is both the salutation and the sentence is the "salutation-sentence" (*abhivādanavākya*).
In that regard, first: the "name" (*nāman*) is that which is uttered or mentioned, such as "I am Devadatta"; the "clan-name" (*gotra*) is such as "I am a Vātsya.
When these are employed at the end—that is, at the conclusion—of the sentence of response to a salutation (*pratyabhivāda*), this protracted vowel (*pluta*) is desired there.

However, in cases such as "Devadatta, are you well? (*devadatta kuśalyasi*), the name mentioned in the salutation—the word *devadatta*—is employed at the beginning of the response-greeting (*pratyabhivādana*), not at its end. Therefore, the protracted vowel (*pluta*) does not occur there.
From what, then, is this understood? It is understood from the recurrence of the particle *vā*, from the recognition of a fixed option (*vyavasthitavibhāṣā*), or from its predominance (*prādhānya*).

For here, because the understanding of the action pertains to the principal [element], the *ṭi* (the final vowel with its following consonant) of the principal word occurring at the end of the sentence must undergo prolation (*pluta*). And the primacy of a word is determined by way of its meaning.

That word which expresses the principal meaning is the principal [word]. Furthermore, the principal meaning is the saluter, because the response to the salutation (*pratyabhivāda*) is for the sake of favoring that [saluter].
Likewise, when a teacher returns a greeting, he employs a response that favors the one who offered the salutation.

Therefore, the one who offers the salutation is the object of the refinement (*saṃskārya*), while words such as "well-being" (*kuśalin*) or "long-lived" (*āyuṣmat*) are the means of that refinement. Consequently, because the one who offers the salutation is the object of the refinement, he is the primary factor; the words denoting him—namely, his name-word (*saṃjñā-śabda*) and his lineage-word (*gotra-śabda*)—are the ones at the end of the sentence for which the protracted vowel (*pluta*) occurs.

Although the meaning expressed by a verbal suffix (*tiṅanta*) is something to be accomplished (*sādhya*), its status as something to be accomplished is not what is intended here as the primary factor; rather, it is simply its character as a refinement (*saṃskāraka*). Therefore, even that [verbal meaning] does not possess primacy.

Regarding the rule *bhorājanyaviśām* and so forth: *bhoḥ* is a mention of the actual form (*svarūpagrahaṇa*); *rājanya* refers to one whose name is Kṣatriya; and *viś* refers to one whose name is Vaiśya.

In this case, the option (*vibhāṣā*) regarding the word *bhoḥ* applies because it is neither a technical term (*saṃjñā*) nor a word denoting a lineage (*gotra*). For the others, however, [the substitution] applies because they are technical terms. "From afar" (*dūrāt*) means "from nearby" (*ārāt*).
The fifth case (pañcamī) is used [after the word *hūta*] according to the rule "the second case is also used after words meaning 'far' and 'near'" (Pāṇini 2.3.35).
*Hūtam* means "calling";
the past passive participle (*niṣṭhā*) is used here in the sense of an abstract action (*bhāve*).
It is said to be "far," yet "far" is not fixed.
That which is far for one overcome by laziness is near for one endowed with enthusiasm.
For instance, someone says to another: "Bring that water-pot over there."
He said: "Get up and take [it]; I will not be able to go far.
Therefore, because "far" is not fixed, it is not known in which state one must leap;
hence he says "far," and so forth.
"Hūtam" means an invocation;
that which is distant in relation to that [invocation] is what is relied upon here. The particle "iti" is used in the sense of a reason.

Because that which depends on effort (*dhūta*) is here considered "distant" from what is natural (*prākṛta*)—that is, from what arises by its own nature (*prakṛti*)—therefore, when a specific effort superior to the natural effort is not resorted to, that place where the calling of a word is heard is called "distant.
Consequently, the intention is that there is no lack of stability regarding what is distant.

Now, how could there be a *pluta* (protracted) vowel here—as in "piba devadatta3 saktūn"? It is not merely the utterance of a sound that constitutes a call (*hūta*), but rather a specific word (*śabdaviśeṣa*) by which one is enjoined to come when [the call] follows; that specific word is the call, and such does not exist here. To this he says: "And the mention of 'called' (*hūtagrahaṇam*)," etc. A call is a means of addressing (*sambodhana*) effected by a word.
The word "and" (*ca*) has the sense of "therefore."
Therefore, since that which is to be accomplished by it—namely, the vocative—is indicated, the mention of "the summoned" (hūta) should be understood as an indication of the vocative in general.

Here, this *pluta* [vowel] is also prescribed for a distant address (*dūrāt-sambodhane*); there is also the rule for *ekaśruti*: "In a distant address and in a vocative, *ekaśruti* [applies]" (Pāṇini 1.2.33). In that case, since several rules would apply to the same instance, one of the following must occur: sublation (*bādha*), option (*vikalpa*), or combination (*samuccaya*). It is not known here whether these two are combined, whether they are optional, or whether one sublates the other. To ascertain this, he says: "And in this [case]," etc. First of all, there cannot be sublation, because the scope of application (*viṣaya*) is the same.

For the relationship of the sublated and the sublator (*bādhyabādhakabhāva*) exists only when there is a difference in scope (*viṣayabheda*). For example, in the rules *karmaṇyaṇ* [Pāṇini 3.2.1] and [the subsequent rule 3.2.3], one has a specific (*viśeṣa*) scope and the other has a general (*sāmānya*) scope; thus, there is a difference in scope. But since there is no such difference in scope between these two [rules under discussion], a sublation is improper.
An option (*vikalpa*) is also improper, because they do not apply simultaneously (*asahaprāpti*).
For a choice arises when two things are obtained simultaneously, as in the case of *tat* and *tyad* and so forth.
But here, there is no simultaneous attainment with respect to the single accent (*ekaśruti*), because the protracted vowel (*pluta*) is not established [as valid in this context].
Therefore, by the principle of elimination (*pāriśeṣya*), it is simply a substitution (*samādeśa*).

Furthermore, "conjunction" (*samāveśa*) here refers to the operation [of two rules] within a single sentence, but not within a single constituent part (*avayava*); for it is impossible for two contradictory operations to apply to one and the same thing, whereas a sentence consists of multiple constituents. Thus, "the final vowel (*ac*) becomes *pluta*."

However, it is logical that there should be a single enunciation for what remains; for by the preceding rule, the protracted vowel (*pluta*) was prescribed only for that which is being offered as the primary element, since its primacy arises from the employment of the sentence for the purpose of directing attention toward it. Therefore, the [protraction] does not apply to the two particles *hai* and *he*; this present rule is commenced for that very purpose.

Now, for what purpose is the mention of *hai* and *he* repeated, given that [the rule] would apply even without it because they are already heard [in the sūtra]? [One might argue: "It will apply to those two alone. To this he says: "*Punar*... etc. (referring to the variant reading *punastu* etc.).

If it were stated simply as "*haihe-prayoge*," then by virtue of the governing context (*adhikāra*) of [Pāṇini 8.2.82], it would apply only to the final [two syllables] and not to the non-final ones; the repetition of *haihe* is for the sake of ensuring it applies to those [non-final ones] as well. Furthermore, the inclusion of the word *prayoga* in the mention of *haihe* is so that it may apply even when [the particles] are meaningless. And they are meaningless only when they constitute the end of a vocative (*āmantrita*).
Since the meaning intended by that very [particle] has already been understood, and because there is no other meaning to be illuminated, those two would be meaningless.
However, others say: "The combinations of particles *hanta* and *haiha* also exist.
In that case, if the mention of "usage" (*prayoga*) were not made, those two would not be included; for they are derivative (*lākṣaṇika*).

Therefore, the mention of "in usage" (*prayoga*) is for the purpose that it may apply even to those [sounds] characterized by their specific phonetic properties (*lākṣaṇika*) when they occur in actual usage. In greetings in return (*pratyabhivāda*) and similar cases, the final syllable (*ṭi*) of a sentence becomes protracted (*pluta*) and acute (*udātta*).

That very [protracted vowel], however, is said to be the protracted form of a heavy (*guru*) vowel—excluding the sound *ṛ*—even if it is not final. This is expressed by the rule: "Even of a non-final *ṭi*."
By this [use of] the word *api*, he shows that it performs a conjunction (*samuccaya*).

For if a conjunction with "also" (*api*) is made with respect to the guru, such that it applies to both the non-final and the final guru, then by this [rule], there is a protracted vowel (*pluta*) for a non-final guru;
whereas a final light syllable remains protracted only by the preceding rule.
Furthermore, it would follow that the hearing of two protracted vowels (*pluta*) would occur simultaneously.
Nor can it be argued that this will not happen because of the rule *na ca* (Pāṇini 6.1.158); for while that [subsequent rule] is to be applied, the protracted vowel remains unestablished (*asiddha*).

When the term *ṭi*, which bears the designation *ṭi*, is also included by the word "also" (*api*), then by this very rule, a protracted vowel is prescribed for the final *ṭi* as well as for a non-final heavy syllable (*guru*).

In that context, because of the expression "of each one," just as there is no simultaneity for the first [syllable], so too there is none for the last; thus, the undesirable consequence of simultaneity does not arise.
Regarding the phrase "the mention of 'each one,'" etc.:
if the mention of "each one" were not made, then in some cases it would follow that all [syllables] occur simultaneously.
Therefore, the singular mention [of each] is for the purpose of ensuring that [the rule] applies alternately (*paryāyeṇa*).
This should be understood as having been formulated on the basis of the principle: "Technical names and paribhāṣās follow the order in which they are enunciated" (*yathoddeśaṃ saṃjñāparibhāṣam*).
In another system of interpretation (*darśanāntara*), when the [rule] *[[6.1.158]]* is present, there is no possibility of the simultaneous occurrence of two protracted vowels (*pluta*).

Now, what is the purpose of [specifying] "of the Easterners" (*prācām*), since the option (*vibhāṣā*) would be established even by the mention of each individual case? To this he says: "of the Easterners. The intention is that [the option applies] to every *pluta* vowel.
For this very reason he says: "by this," and so forth.
"Engaging in an action without reflecting on its cause of ruin is recklessness. Regarding the phrase "the commencement":
of what is there a commencement? Of the study of one's own Veda (*svādhyāya*) and so forth. Regarding the phrase "in the performance of a sacrifice":
the word *karman* here denotes an action (*kriyā*).

The meaning is "in the performance of a sacrifice. It should be understood that this protracted vowel (*pluta*) is intended only in the case of the phrase *ye yajāmahe*, because of the continued application of the rule for "the Easterners" (*prācām*) and because of the understanding of the rule as having a fixed option (*vyavasthitavibhāṣā*). "What is this so-called *praṇava*?"—this is a question, arising because the *praṇava* has not been defined in this treatise and is not well-known in common worldly usage.

By the phrase "or of the foot" (pādasya vā)— the reading in the Prāṃu is "and of the foot" (pādasya ca), etc.— he demonstrates the nature of the *praṇava* according to the technical rules (*paribhāṣā*) of other treatises.
Regarding the expression "the final syllable," the vowel is intended here by the word "syllable" (*akṣara*).
Furthermore, its status as "final" (antya) is in relation to the other vowels. Regarding the term "upasaṃgṛhya," it means "having grasped."

That which has its final syllable at the beginning of the remaining syllables is "tad-ādi" (beginning with that). "Akṣara-śeṣa" is a collective *dvandva* compound meaning "the syllable and the remainder. Here, "akṣara" refers to a vowel (*svara*), and its "remainder" (*śeṣa*) is the consonant (*vyañjana*). Thus, it is both the vowel and the remainder of the syllable. That very [vowel] is [the subject] where there is no consonant following the final vowel.
In that case, the "beginning with that" (tadādi) refers to the external referent (anyapadārtha) of the bahuvrīhi compound.
By the principle of "designation as if possessing the designation" (vyapadeśivadbhāva), the designation "beginning with that" applies there as well.

Where there is a consonant following the final vowel, the external referent consists of that consonant together with the vowel, because a bahuvrīhi with "inclusion of its own qualities" (tadguṇasaṃvijñāna) is relied upon here.

That which is expressed by this treatise as being designated by the term *ṭi*—namely, that which follows the final syllable [of a word]—if one performs the substitution of a three-mora vowel for it, whether it be *u* or *o*, they call that the *praṇava*. For example: *jinvato3m*. Here, there is the present tense (*laṭ*) following the root *jinva*; its replacement is the suffix *śatṛ*; by irregularity (*vyatyaya*), the suffix *śnu* is applied; then the *yaṇ* substitution occurs. When the form *jinvan* is established, the *praṇava* is substituted for the final syllable of the word *an*.

Regarding the form *sumnayo3m*: from the word *sumna*, the suffix *kyac* is applied; then, by the rule *kyācchandasī* [Pāṇini 3.2.170], the suffix *u* is added; subsequently, by the rule *ātaḥ* [Pāṇini 7.4.38], the *ā* is elided. When the form *sumnāyuḥ* is established, the *praṇava* (the syllable *om*) is substituted for the final vowel and the following consonant of the portion beginning with *u*. Now, an objection is raised: "A grammatical maxim (*paribhāṣā*) has been established stating that the *praṇava* replaces only those long vowels (*o* and *au*) that stand in the place of *ṭi* (the final vowel of a nominal stem). In that case, even without the mention of *ṭi*, the substitution would apply to the *ṭi* itself; so what is the purpose of mentioning *ṭi*? To this, he replies with the words beginning "The mention of *ṭi*" (*ṭigrahaṇam*), and so forth.
If the mention of *ṭi* were not present here, then by the paribhāṣā "the substitute [applies] to the final [element]" (*alo 'ntyaparibhāṣā*), it would apply only to the final letter.
Therefore, the mention of *ṭi* is made so that it may apply to the entire *ṭi* suffix,
and not merely to its final letter.

Since the syllable *oṃ* consists of multiple phonemes (*anekāl*), it will undergo substitution for the whole word; thus, the mention of *ṭi* is for the sake of the vowel *o*. Here, does the mention of "end" (*anta*) serve to set aside the rule regarding *ṭi*, or does it act as a qualifier? In the first case, since the end is qualified by the vowel (*ac*), the prolation (*pluta*) would apply only to a *yājyā* that ends in a vowel. In the other case, the mention of "end" would be purposeless, for a *ṭi* cannot possibly occur at the very end [of a word]; this is because the technical name *ṭi* is prescribed specifically for the form of a word ending in a consonant according to [Pāṇini 1.1.64]. With this intention, he asks: "What is the purpose of mentioning 'end'? (*antagrahaṇaṃ kim*)?

The other [author], having understood this intention, speaks—beginning with "That which is called *yājyā*"—in order to demonstrate that the purpose of the mention of the "extremes" (*antagrahaṇa*) is indeed something else. The meaning has already been explained. *Śrauṣaṭ* and *vauṣaṭ* are indeclinables (*nipāta*); the others are third-person singular forms of the imperative mood. Some, however, say that the word *āvaha* is also an indeclinable.
Regarding the word *preṣya*:

the root *īṣ* means "to go" (it is read as *iṣa gatāu* in the Divādi class; Dhātupāṭha 1127). Because it belongs to the Divādi class, the suffix *śyan* is applied, and [the initial vowel] coalesces with the vowel of the prefix according to Pāṇini 6.1.87. Now, why does this [substitution] not occur here in the following cases: *āvaha devān yajamānāya* (Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā 5.12), *āvaha jātavedaḥ* (Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 1.3.22), and *suyajā yaja*? To this he says: [the rule applies] in cases such as *āvaha devān*, etc. [but not in these].

The inclusion of the word "ādi" (beginning) is so that [the rule] does not apply to the beginning of a sentence and so forth. In the sense of "agnim indhe" (he kindles the fire), *agnīdh* refers to a specific officiating priest; his *preṣaṇa*, meaning his commissioning or directing, is what is meant by *agnītpreṣaṇa*.
Since "ādi" is mentioned in proximity, he says "tasmādevādeḥ" (from that very beginning) and so on, implying that the subsequent [term] is understood in relation to that alone.
"In this very case" means...
In order to demonstrate what is excluded by the particle *eva* in the two examples just mentioned, he says: "O Agnīdh, spread the fires; strew the sacrificial grass.
But how is this obtained? He says: "For that purpose," and so forth.

And how the protracted vowel (*pluta*) can be understood as optional (*vibhāṣā*) in all cases has been explained in the sūtra beginning with "of a long [vowel], not being *ṛ*, which is not final" (Pāṇini 8.2.86).

If, then, the *pluta* vowel were understood as optional (*vibhāṣā*) in all cases, would the mention of "optionally" (*vibhāṣā*) in the subsequent rule be purposeless? No; it is for the sake of detailed exposition (*prapañca*). Now, how is there a *pluta* here in the examples: *uddhara3 uddhara*, *abhihara3 abhihara*? This *pluta* occurs at the time of Vedic recitation (*svādhyāya*), not in the command to the *Āgnīdhra* priest, nor is it of the initial syllable (*ādeḥ*), nor even of the final syllable (*antaḥ*). What then? It is of something other than those. To this he says: because *diḥ* (the word beginning with *d-*) is proximate. He says—starting with "from that very initial syllable"—that by reference to that alone, the *paraḥ* (the following syllable) is also understood. "In this very case," etc.
In order to show what is excluded by the particle *eva* in the two examples just mentioned, he says: "O Agnīdh, spread the fires; strew the sacrificial grass.
But how is this obtained? He says: "For that purpose," and so forth.

Furthermore, why would the mention of the option (*vibhāṣā*) later on be redundant, since the protracted vowel (*pluta*) is understood to be optional everywhere? It is not redundant, because it is for the sake of detailed exposition (*prapañca*).

Now, how is there a protracted vowel (*pluta*) here—as in "uddhara3 uddhara" (lift up, lift up) and "abhihara3 abhihara" (bring toward, bring toward)? This protraction occurs at the time of Vedic recitation (*svādhyāya*), not in the *agnītpreṣaṇa* (the call to the Agnīdhra priest), nor is this [protraction] of the initial syllable, nor is it [governed by] Pāṇini 1.2.32 (*plutaḥ praśnāntābhipūjitayoḥ*). What then? Is it of something other than those? To this he says: "But here," etc., for the sake of clarity. Regarding "an answer to a question":
an answer to a question is an explanation given in response to what has been asked; that is "an answer to a question."

This word *prativacana* is used even for a contradictory statement—namely, "a contradictory statement is a *prativacana*"—for here the prefix *prati* indicates opposition (*virodha*), as in the cases of *pratimalla* (an opposing wrestler) and *pratigaja* (an opposing elephant). It is also used in the sense of distributive repetition (*vīpsā*)—"in response to each and every statement" is *prativacana*; this is an *avyayībhāva* compound with an indeclinable in the sense of "according to" (*yathārthe yad avyayam*, Pāṇini 2.1.6).

It also occurs in the sense of "resolution" (*samādhi*): when one says, "I have given a reply to what was stated by him," it is understood that a resolution has been made. In that case, if only the word "reply" (*prativacana*) were used, it would apply everywhere. Therefore, the term "questioned" (*pṛṣṭa*) is included for the sake of specifying the particular kind of reply; so that it may apply only to the statement of the meaning of what was asked, and not elsewhere. [The word] "having refuted" (*nigṛhya*).
This is the end of the section.
Regarding the term "from oneself" (*svataḥ*):
it means from one's own cognition (*svāvagamāt*).
"Prācyāvanam" (or "Pracyācanam," according to the Prāṃu reading) means removal;
"āviṣkaraṇam" means manifestation.
"Manifestation.
"Śrāddha" refers to a specific type of ritual action.
"Thus it is investigated" means that [the matter] is treated as having its own position established in this manner. The particle *ca* serves to carry over the term *vibhāṣā*.
Therefore, the subsequent rule becomes obligatory. [The example is] *caura caura3*.
By the rule *vākyāder āmantritasya* (Pāṇini 8.1.8) and others, there is reduplication for the purpose of addressing.

Although the mention of "the beginning of a sentence" (*vākyādi*) here is intended to prevent the prolated vowel (*pluta*) from applying to the final word, nevertheless, by the force of this specific statement, it occurs even for that which is not at the end.

For an *āmreḍita* (reduplication) is not possible at the end of a sentence, because the rule for doubling a word applies only to a word that begins a sentence when it is used in reproach (*bhatrsana*).

The phrase "for that purpose" means so that [the designation] may apply alternately to both the preceding and the following words; it also serves as an indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*) for anything that is doubled.
From the mention of *bhatrsana* (reviling) in connection with the term *āmreḍita* (reduplication), it is understood that *āmreḍita* refers to that which follows a reduplicated word.
However, the application [of the rule] cannot occur merely by that much, because reviling is what is expressed by the reduplication itself.
Therefore, the mention of *āmreḍita* is understood to serve as an indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*) for the reduplicated form.
And because that doubling occurs even regarding both the preceding and the following subject, the *pluta* (protracted) vowel applies to both.
Furthermore, it occurs alternately and not simultaneously, because the purpose of the *pluti* is to indicate contempt (*bhartṣaṇa*).
For that contempt is already indicated by the protraction of just one of the two. [The word] "expecting" (*ākāṅkṣam*) [is used].

The term *ākāṅkṣam* means "that which desires" or "that which expects," derived from the root *kāṅkṣ* with the suffix *pacādyac*. In examples such as *aṅga kūja3* and so forth—specifically *aṅga kūja3* and *aṅga vyāhara3*—both of these expect the thought: "Now this fool will understand."
"Come, Devadatta"—this too is [an example of] "you speak falsely";
"study"—this too is [an example of] "I will give you rice";
"he does not desire anything further than this."
Because the intended meaning is already complete.

Now, for what purpose is the mention of *yukta* (joined), since the connection (*yoga*) will be understood simply because it is a rule concerning words (*padavidhi*)? If this is so, then by including the term *yukta*, [the author] indicates that the technical rule (*paribhāṣā*) "that which is taught after a word-final element applies to that which follows immediately" (P. 1.1.67) is not universally obligatory (*anitya*).

Therefore, even though the word *sūrya* (sun) lacks [direct] semantic connection with the negative particle *nañ*, the compound in the expression *asūryampaśyāni mukhāni* ("faces that do not see the sun") is established. "Investigation" (*vicāra*) is the examination of an object by means of a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).

"Being made the object of that" means being investigated. The use of the plural number is for the purpose of including those things whose investigation pertains only to their meaning and not to their essential form (*svarūpa*); otherwise, it would apply only to those things whose investigation pertains to their essential form.

Indeed, when the primary sentence is being investigated, it is not proper to include that which is secondary by way of its meaning; for it is the primary that is to be investigated. Regarding the example "gṛhā3i":
in the word *gṛha*, the vowel *e* occurs; according to the rule *eco'pragṛhrasya* [Pāṇini 6.1.109], the first half of this vowel becomes *ā*, while the second half becomes *i*.
By this [rule], the *pluta* vowel occurs for that specific form (*ākāra*). Although this is already established by the preceding rule, this present one is for the sake of restriction (*niyamārtha*).

The word "tu" (but/however) serves to restrict according to the intended meaning. For if it were not there, a contrary restriction might be understood: namely, that [the *pluta*] occurs only in the colloquial language (*bhāṣā*) before [the particle].

And "being prior" (pūrvatva) is relative to usage. Between the two sentences "Is it a snake? and "Is it a rope?", the *pluta* occurs only for the *ṭi* of that which is used first. However, because the word "prior" (*pūrva*) is not mentioned here [in the current rule], it is understood from the previous rule that this applies to the Vedic language (*chandas*). "Pratiśruti" means listening back.

The word *pratijñā* is formed by adding the suffix *lyuṭ* in the sense of an abstract action (*bhāva*) to the root *śru* preceded by the prefix *prati*; it is a *tatpuruṣa* compound according to the rule *kugati* (Pāṇini 2.2.18).
When the root *śru* preceded by *prati* intends to express favoring others, it then functions in the sense of "acceptance" (*abhyupagama*).
However, when there is no intention to express favoring others, it then functions in the sense of "promise" (*pratijñāna*).

When the word *śravaṇa* is formed as an instrument (*bhāvasādhana*) meaning "listening"—and the compound *pratiśravaṇam* is formed with the indeclinable *prati* according to Pāṇini 2.1.14—then it means "engaged in listening," that is, being oriented toward hearing. Since no specific object is mentioned here, the prolated (*pluta*) vowel occurs at the end of the sentence in every instance of such listening, as in:
*devadatta bhoḥ kimāttha3* ("O Devadatta, what are you saying?").
This is an example of being directed toward listening. The vocative "O venerable sir" is addressed for the purpose of hearing;
thus he says, "What do you say? in order to hear that.
It becomes directed toward [the goal] because it is undertaken with the aim of hearing [the teaching] in one place.
As for the example in the case of acceptance: "O sir, give me a cow; I shall give one to you.
In the case of a formal proposition (*pratijñā*): "Sound must be eternal."
The letter *ca* is for the purpose of drawing forward [the rule] "in the spoken language" (*bhāṣāyām*). Regarding *agama3*:

this is the *luṅ* (aorist) of the root *gam*, with *aṅ* by virtue of its being marked with *ḷ* in the *puv-ādi-sūtra* (Pāṇini 1.2.55), followed by the suffix *sip*. Regarding *agnibhūtā3i* and *paṭā3u*.

In the case of *sambuddhau* (the vocative singular), there is *guṇa* substitution by [Pāṇini 7.3.108] *hrasvasya guṇaḥ*, and by [Pāṇini 8.2.107] *eco 'pragṛhyasya* etc., the vowel *a* is substituted for the *ec* vowels, as well as *i* and *u*. In the example sentences, the protracted (*pluta*) vowel of the preceding words occurs by this very rule. Should someone object, "How is it that here the protraction occurs even for a non-final syllable, given that the rule *vākyasya ṭeḥ* (Pāṇini 8.2.82) continues to apply?"—to him he replies with the words: "In the case of *agnibhūte* and *paṭo*," and so forth. [The word] *cit* means "indeed" (*iti*).
The employment of the particle *iti* serves to indicate the meaning that the word *etat* (this) is a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*).

For if this particle *iti* were not present for this purpose, and some other word in the sense of "resemblance" (*upamā*) were employed instead, it would be understood that the word *cit* itself is protracted (*pluta*).
By employing that [particle *iti*] here, when that [word *etat*] is thus qualified, the protraction of the final syllable (*ṭi*) of the sentence is established.
Regarding the phrase "katathañcidāhaḥ," here the word *cit* is used in the sense of difficulty (*kṛcchre*). An example is: "The boy Agni might cause fear."

The meaning is that "the boy should shine like fire"; although there is here the sense of a comparison (*upamā*), nevertheless, because the word *cit* is not employed, the protracted vowel (*pluta*) does not occur. However, if the mention of "being employed" (*prayujyamāna*) were absent, then even though the sense of comparison is present here—and even if the employment of all other things signifying comparison could be understood—the protraction would certainly occur based on the employment of the word *cit* itself. The particle *ca* serves to include this very protraction.
