And since a conjunction (*samuccaya*) is based on a distinction (*bheda*), this [rule] is stated immediately after the rule concerning the protracted vowel (*pluta*); otherwise, one might understand that in the very same domain as the previously mentioned causes for protraction, only the quality of being unaccented (*anudāttatva*) is prescribed. The particle *iti* is for the purpose of indicating the subject of the operation (*kāryin*);
for in order to prescribe an operation, the subject must necessarily be indicated in the genitive case.
Alternatively, by means of the particle *iti*, the sense of "or" (*vā*) is recalled.

In this context, the word *upari-svit* and others, which are primarily concerned with sound (*śabda-pradhāna*), are intended as the grammatical operation (*kārya*) and are indicated by the particle *iti*, so that the protracted vowel (*pluta*) may be understood. For example: *adhaḥ-svid-āsīt* and so forth.

Here, it is deliberated whether it was "below" (*adhaḥ-svit*) or "above" (*upari-svit*). In the former sentence, the protracted vowel is acute (*udātta*) according to [Pāṇini 8.2.97] and other rules; however, in the latter case, it is grave (*anudātta*) by this [present rule], which serves as an exception (*apavāda*) to that very [acute rule].

The purpose of the particle *ca* is exactly as before. Words such as *asūyā* and others are designated as "verbal" (*ākhyāta*) by the rule beginning with *vākyāder āmantritasya* (Pāṇini 8.1.8). Consequently, the doubling [of the vocative] in examples such as *māṇavaka3 māṇavaka* is to be understood through that very same rule. [The author notes: "The mention of the option (*vā*) must be made."
The phrase "or" (*vā*) is an indicator for this alternative;
it means that there is an explanation (*vyākhyāna*).
What is intended here is this: an explanation of the alternatives must be provided.

In this regard, the following is the explanation: from the rule *vibhāṣā pṛṣṭaprativacane heḥ* [Pāṇini 8.2.93], the term *vibhāṣā* (optionally) is carried over by the "frog-leap" (*maṇḍūkapluti*) method; therefore, there will be an option. *Kṣiyā* is a breach of proper conduct. *Āśīḥ* is the expression of a desired blessing. *Niyoga* is an injunction or command.
It requires another verbal form (tiṅanta) alone. Why is this so? Precisely because of the mention of "expectancy" (ākāṅkṣā).
For when there is a nominal stem ending in a case-suffix (subanta), there is necessarily an expectancy for a verbal form that conveys the means of accomplishment (sādhana).
"And wealth, father"—
here, the word "may you obtain" (*lapsīṣṭa*) is understood.
"And grammar."
In this case as well, there is the request "adhyeṣīṣṭa";
[and] "lunīhi3" (with the protracted vowel), where the substitution of *i* occurs by [Pāṇini 6.4.113]:
*ī halyadhoḥ*.
In "piba," the substitution of *piba* is according to the rule [Pāṇini 7.3.78] beginning with *pāghrā*.
In "astu," [the substitution of *stu* for *as* occurs].

In *aster loṭ*, by [Pāṇini 3.4.86] *eruḥ*, there is the substitution of *u*; due to its belonging to the *adādi* class, there is the elision (*luk*) of the *śap* suffix; and this does not depend on any other verbal ending (*tiṅanta*). The same applies to *vihara*. As for the phrase "but of the final," etc., the word *tu* ("but") indicates a distinction from the other words.

By the rule *antyasya* [P. 1.1.52], the circumflex (*svarita*) is prescribed, and by the rule *tasyādita udāttamardhahrasvam* [P. 1.2.32], the grave (*anudātta*) is prescribed. Since these two cannot coexist in a single location simultaneously, the grave accent does not occur in that position even as an alternative option, nor does the circumflex, due to the authority of the specific injunctions. Thus, when the protracted vowel (*pluta*) is being prescribed by such rules as [P. 8.2.84], since the rule *acaśca* [P. 1.2.28] is present, the protraction would apply only to that very vowel which has been specified as protracted—namely, to the composite whole consisting of the *eC* vowels—but it is desired that it apply to its constituent parts.
Since this cannot be established without a specific statement, this sūtra is commenced.

The cause for that prolation (*pluta*) is the contingency of *ec* vowels being [subject to] prolation from afar; the meaning is that this occurs when prolation has been established by the preceding section. In the examples "ai3tikāyana" and "au3pamanyava," since prolation of the *ec* vowels would have applied by the rule "guroranṛto 'nantyasya" (Pāṇini 8.2.86), this [present rule] effects the prolation of the *i* and *u* sounds that constitute those parts.

In the case of *ai3tikāyana* and *au3pamanyava*, if the prolated vowel (*pluta*) is applied to the *i* and *u* which are constituent parts of the diphthongs *ai* and *au*, then the *e*-vowel and *o*-vowel would result in being either four morae (*caturmātra*) or three and a half morae (*sārdhatrimātra*).
However, here the *ai* and *au* are composite sounds (*samāhāravarṇa*), wherein one mora belongs to the vowel (*a*) and one mora each belongs to the *i* and *u* vowels.
Others, however, say: "One half-mora belongs to the vowel (*a*), and one and a half morae belong to the *i* and *u* vowels."

In this first view, when this [prolongation] is performed, since *i* and *u* have three morae (*mātrā*) each and the vowel *a* has one, a total of four morae would result. In the other view, however, the vowel *a* has half a mora, while *i* and *u* have those same three; thus, a total of three and a half morae would result. Therefore, he says: "In this case, when... and so forth. Now, an objection might be raised: "The designation 'prolonged' (*pluta*) was established for that which has three morae; how then can two morae or three morae also be made 'prolonged' by this rule? To this, he replies with the words: "For [the term] 'prolonged'... and so forth.

By this, he shows that the worldly (*laukika*) *pluta* vowel is intended here, not the technical (*pāribhāṣika*) one. How, then, is this obtained? Because the mention of *pluta* again would otherwise be purposeless; for in common usage, the *pluta* is understood to possess lengthening (*vṛddhi*). Therefore, he says: "The meaning is that *i* and *u* undergo lengthening."
Since verbal roots have multiple meanings, the root *plu* also functions in the sense of "increase.

[Objection: Even so, an unrestricted increase would result, because no specific limit is expressed; consequently, whatever the extent of the increase might be, how could two vowels ever become four morae (*mātrā*)? To this, he says: "In this regard," and so forth.
The meaning is that *pluti* is an increase.

How, then, is this restriction obtained? It is thought as follows: the genitive case [in *aij-oh*] is used in relation to the *pluta* vowel. *I* and *u* are lengthened (*plavete*) in such a way that they become the *pluta* of *eṅ*; and they thus become *ai* and *au* provided that there is an increase in quantity (*vṛddhi*) sufficient for *ai* and *au* to become three-mora (*trimātra*).

For if no such increase were made, they would remain merely *ai* and *au* (without being *pluta*), because the *ai* and *au* have a fixed measure; and consequently, the *pluta* would not belong to *ai* and *au*.

Regarding the phrase "measuring two and a half morae" (*ardhatṛtīyamātrau*): those two whose measure (*mātrā*) is two and a half are "measuring two and a half morae"; those two [syllables] which possess that [measure] are "measuring two and a half morae.
This explanation has been stated by relying upon the opinion of the author of the Vārttika.
Showing that the author of the Bhāṣya indeed accepts the duration of four mātrās for the protracted (pluta) vowel, he says: "But it is stated in the Bhāṣya," and so forth.
He asks: "How is that?"—that is, if that is the opinion of the author of the Bhāṣya, in what manner would it be established? This is what he asks.

With the words "In the view of equal division" (*samparavibhāgapakṣe*) and so forth, he demonstrates how that [pluta] is produced. For in the view of equal division, by this rule a *pluta* vowel of three morae (*trimātra*) is made from the *i* and *u*; consequently, the two morae belonging to that [vowel] together with the preceding *a*-mora, when all combined, become four morae. And thus, the *pluta* becomes four-moraic (*caturmātra*).

In this view of the author of the Bhāṣya, however, the mention of *pluta* (protracted vowel) again is for the purpose of including all *pluta* vowels; otherwise, because of the context of the *svarita* [rule], this *pluta* would apply only to that [svarita] when it occurs, just as in the case of *i* and *u*. But by mentioning *pluta* again, it applies even to the *udātta* and *anudātta* [vowels]. The inclusion of the marker *t* (*tapara*) is for the sake of clarity. The diphthongs (*ec*) are composite sounds; therein, for the *ekāra* and *okāra*, this *pluta* belongs to the whole according to the preceding section, whereas for the *ekāra* and *okāra*, it belongs to the constituent parts, namely *i* and *u*.
This is commenced by the immediately preceding sūtra with the statement: "The enumeration of the objects must be made.
This is the rule for inclusion (*grahaṇavākya*).
He provides its explanation with the words beginning "praśnāntābhipūjita," stating that "it must be done" (the Kāśikā reads "it must be stated").
The meaning is that this must be explained. Here is the explanation: the rules beginning with [Pāṇini 8.2.100] are carried over (*anuvartante*) here; therefore, they do not apply elsewhere.
"According to their respective scope" (*yathāviṣayam*).

"Whatever is the object of whatever [word], according to that object"—this is an *avyayībhāva* compound formed by the rule *yathā’sādṛśye* (Pāṇini 2.1.7). Regarding the protracted (*pluta*) vowel: in cases of questioning or praise, it is *anudātta* (unaccented) by *praśnāntābhipūjitayoḥ* (Pāṇini 8.2.100); however, in the case of a question, it is *svarita* (circumflex) by *praśne tu* (Pāṇini 8.2.105), while in all other remaining cases it is *udātta* (acute).
As for the statement, "But these two, *iti* and *tu*, are acute," [it means they are always *udātta*].
And because of the governing rule *ṭerudāttaḥ* [Pāṇini 8.2.82],
as in *viṣṇubhūte viṣṇubhūte3*.
Here, the protracted vowel (*pluta*) is applied by the rule *āmreḍitaṃ bhartsane* [Pāṇini 8.2.95].
"Come, O young brahmin Viṣṇubhūti!"—here [the rule] *dūrād dhūte ca* [Pāṇini 8.2.84] applies.

Now, one might object: even if there were no such enumeration (*parigaṇana*), the protracted vowel (*pluta*) would not be applicable anyway, because of the statement *adūrād dhūte* ("when calling from a short distance"). Therefore, he asks: for what purpose is this counter-example given regarding the enumeration? He replies: "And in the case of the enumeration," and so forth.

If there were no enumeration [of specific cases], one would say, "it will apply by means of 'not far' (adūrāddhūta)"—this is the reading in the Kāśikā-vṛtti. But since this [enumeration] exists, this need not be stated; for precisely because of the enumeration, it will not apply in the case of "far" (dūrāddhūta).

"It must be done" means "it must be explained. In this regard, the explanation is as follows: the term "end" (*anta*) is carried over from the rule [Pāṇini 6.1.115] *yājyāntaḥ*; therefore, it will apply only to that which is at the end.

In the example "bhadraṃ karoṣi gauḥ," the protracted vowel (*pluta*) occurs by the rule "in [cases of] honoring" (Pāṇini 8.2.100). This rule does not apply here because of the continued application of the mention of "the end" (from the previous sūtra); for in this case, the word *iti* does not follow immediately after the vowel, but rather follows a consonant.
In "śobhane khalu staḥ khaṭve," here too, the protracted vowel (*pluta*) occurs by the rule "when [a word] is being honored" (Pāṇini 8.2.100).
This is also governed by the rule beginning with "and when [a word] is addressed" (Pāṇini 8.1.52), and so forth.
That which is both protracted (*pluta*) and a modification (*vikāra*) is called a "protracted modification" (*plutavikāra*).
The designation "protracted" for the vowels *i* and *u* should be understood as being due to their association with the protracted vowel.
The mention of *i* and *u* is for the purpose that these substitutions do not apply to the *ai*, *o*, and *au* vowels, whether preceding or following [the *i* and *u*].
The inclusion of the long vowel marker (*tapara*) here is also for the sake of ease of pronunciation. Regarding the word "of those two":
it refers back to the *i* and *u* vowels that were prescribed immediately preceding. Examples are: *agnā3yāśā*, *paṭā3vāśā*.

When *agne āśā* and *paṭo āśā* are established, if any one of these—namely, "at the end of a question, at the end of what is highly honored, at the end of what is being deliberated, at the end of a response, or at the end of a sacrificial offering" (Vārttika 932)—is intended, then the vowel *a* of the preceding meaning becomes a protracted (*pluta*) vowel, while the vowels *i* and *u* of the following meaning remain; by this [rule], *y* and *v* are substituted for those two. But why is this commenced again? Is it not already accomplished by [the rule] *etau* (Pāṇini 6.1.77)? To this he says: "Because *i* and *u* are not established," and so forth. [Objection: But surely the protracted vowel is established in the context of vowel-sandhis (*svarasandhi*).

In rules such as those prescribing *yaṇ* substitution (*yaṇādeśādiṣu*), [the author] states that there is the preservation of the original form (*prakṛtibhāva*) for a protracted vowel (*pluta*) by the rule *yadayam?* (P. 6.1.125). For an operation must apply to something that exists, not to something that does not exist; and since the *pluta* vowel is a single phoneme (*ekaḥ*), these two [rules, namely *akaḥ savarṇe dīrghaḥ* and *plutapragṛhyā aci nityam*] would already be established among the vowel-sandhis (*svarasaṃdhi*). To this he replies with "But even so" (*athāpi*) and so forth.

If this were not stated, then in the case of *agnā3 i indram* and *paṭā3 u udakam*, once they have reached that stage, the rule for lengthening before a homogeneous vowel (*akaḥ savarṇe dīrghatvam*, P. 6.1.97) would apply, overriding the *yaṇ* substitution prescribed in the sixth chapter. And here, in the case of *agnā3 iti* and *āśā iti*, the preservation of the original form (*prakṛtibhāva*) would apply by the rule *plutapragṛhyā aci nityam* (P. 6.1.127).

Therefore, even though these two [the *pluta* vowel and the *śākala* rule] are established, this [new rule] must indeed be stated so that lengthening (*dīrghatva*) and the *śākala* operation do not occur.

Now, one might ask: "Is there not already another effort for the purpose of excluding those? What is it? It is said: An addition (*upasaṃkhyāna*) is made to the rule *iko yaṇ aci* [Pāṇini 6.1.77]: "The substitution of *yaṇ* should be stated for an *ik* preceded by a *pluta* vowel, for the purpose of excluding the *śākala* and lengthening" (Vārttika 673). This addition must necessarily be made.
The *ik* [vowel] following the word *bhoḥ* is *pluta*.

Here, the vowel *i* following the word *bhoḥ* is a particle (*nipāta*), not a modification resulting from *pluta*. It is desired that there be a *yaṇ*-substitution for it; that would not occur if this supplementary rule (*upasaṃkhyāna*) were not stated.
Therefore, that [rule] must necessarily be applied.

And since, when it is applied, the *pluta* and *vikāra* forms of *i* and *u* must also become [the same], this [present rule] need not be stated; to address this, he says "even so" (*tathāpi*), and so forth.

When *agnā3* and *āśā* are present, if the substitution of *yaṇ* were to be made here for the place of the udātta *i* by means of that supplementary rule from the sixth [book], then, because it would be established as a completed operation, the circumflex (*svarita*) accent would undesirably result for the anudātta vowel of the word *āśā*, according to the rule [Pāṇini 8.2.4]: "In place of an anudātta vowel following an udātta-yaṇ... etc.
The word *āśā* is oxytone according to the rule *āśāyā digākhyā cet* (Phiṭ-sūtra 1.18).

Furthermore, the remaining portion is unaccented (*anudātta*) by the rule *anudāttam* (Pāṇini 6.1.152), so the vowel *ā* is unaccented. Consequently, there arises the contingency of [the final syllable] being svarita; therefore, this [rule] is stated in order to prevent that.
"Kintu yaṇā," and so forth;
these are two summary verses (*saṃgrahaśloka*).
"Kim" is used in the sense of an interrogative particle.

The word *tu* is used here in the sense of deliberation (*vitarke*). [Question: Why is it not already established in examples such as *agnā3yāśe* by means of the substitution *yaṇ* [prescribed by Pāṇini 6.1.77], for which reason the Teacher prescribes *ir* and *uv* for *i* and *u*? [Answer: The intention is that everything is indeed established.
It might be argued: "The substitution *yaṇ* does not apply because, when that [substitution] is to be performed, *i* and *u* are not established. To this, he says: "*tau ca*," etc.
The word *tu* indicates the reason (*hetau*). When an *ik* vowel is preceded by a protracted (*pluta*) vowel, then [the substitution] would apply to it.

Therefore, regarding the supplementary rule (*upasaṃkhyāna*) which states, "The substitution of *yaṇ* must be prescribed for an *ik* preceded by a protracted vowel, in order to prevent the application of the *śākala* rule and the long-vowel rule" (Vārttika 673), this [present sūtra] provides an exception (*apavāda*) to both the *yaṇ* substitution and the rules concerning the long vowel and the *śākala* phenomenon.
For that reason, the rules for *śākala* (elision) and *dīrgha* (lengthening) will not apply to those two [cases] beginning with *it*.

The word *ca* (and) is used in the sense of conjunction (*samuccaya*); it should be understood as displaced from its position and placed immediately after the negation. [The meaning is: "And those two are established for me in the cases of vowel-sandhi (*svarasandhi*)."
And the rules for the Śākala and the long vowel do not serve as their purpose;
the same applies to the exception (apavāda).
Since the cessation of the Śākala and the long vowel is their purpose, he states another purpose: "But the reason is precisely the sublation of the *yaṇ* [substitution] and the accent."

The accent based on the substitution of *yaṇ* is the *yaṇ-svara*; its "obstruction" (*bādhana*) is the cause or reason. Of what? From the context, it is understood to be the reason for the commencement of the Sūtra.
The word *tu* (but/however) is used for emphasis.
The meaning is that the very fact of not contradicting [the Sūtra] itself is the reason for the commencement of this Sūtra.

Thus ends the second quarter of the eighth chapter in the *Kāśikā-vivaraṇapañjikā*, composed by the venerable master Jinendrabuddhi, who is like a Bodhisattva. Now begins the third quarter of the eighth chapter. Regarding the rule *yudhoḥ* [Pāṇini 7.1.1], that which was stated for the purpose of avoiding an undesirable result (*dveṣyaparīhāra*) should also be understood to apply to the rule *matuvasoḥ*. For example: *indramarutva*.

From the word *marut*, the suffix *matup* is applied; by [Pāṇini 8.2.10] (*jhayaḥ*), there is the substitution of *ya*; by [Pāṇini 7.1.70] (*ugidacām*), there is the augment *num*; by [Pāṇini 6.1.66] (*halṅyādi*) and [Pāṇini 8.2.23] (*saṃyogānta*), there is elision; for the letter *n*, there is the substitution of *r* (by [Pāṇini 8.2.66]); for that *r*, there is the substitution of *y* by [Pāṇini 8.3.17] (*bhobhago* etc.); and for that *y* as well, there is elision by [Pāṇini 8.3.19] (*roḥ supi*). Thus: *hariṣo medinaṃ tvā*. From the word *hari*, the suffix *matup* is applied; by [Pāṇini 8.2.15] (*vasusraṃsu* etc.), there is the substitution of *va*; and as before, there is *num* and so forth.

However, the distinction here is as follows: by the rule *haśi ca* [Pāṇini 6.1.110], there is the substitution of *u* for *ru*; and by the preceding rule [6.1.87], *sa* is substituted for *ha*. Thus we have *mīḍhvastokāya*. The root *miha* (meaning "to sprinkle," Dhātupāṭha 992) takes the suffix *kvasu* after the perfect tense (*liṭ*). By the rule *dāśvān sāhvān mīḍhvāṃśca* [Pāṇini 6.1.12], the reduplication is prohibited, the root is marked as *aniṭ*, and the lengthening of the penultimate vowel (*upadhādīrghatva*) is prescribed as an irregularity (*nipātana*). Then, by the rule *ho ḍhaḥ* [8.2.31], *ha* is replaced by *ḍha*. When *ru* is replaced by *visarjanīya*, that *s* is substituted by *ś* according to the rule *kharavasānayor visarjanīyaḥ* [8.3.15] and its subsequent replacement by *ś* under the conditions specified in [8.3.34].
Since there is no usage of the substitute *śatṛ* for *vasu* in the vocative case within the domain of the Veda (*chandas*), there is no example for it.

For this very reason, the metarule (*paribhāṣā*) "when a term with one *anubandha* is mentioned, [it does not include] a term with two *anubandhas*" (Vyāḍiparibhāṣā 52) does not apply here; because in the Veda, no usage of *vasu* followed by the vocative suffix is observed that possesses only one *anubandha*. Examples are: *vidvān* and *he papivan*.

The augment *iṭ* is applied to the suffix *kvasu* following the roots *pā* or *pā* (to drink) by [Pāṇini 7.2.67], and the elision of the vowel *ā* occurs by [Pāṇini 6.4.64]. Due to the status of the substitute being as if it were the original (*sthānivadbhāva*), reduplication takes place. Regarding the statement "the addition of *van*," since a *van* suffix without an indicatory letter (*ananubandhaka*) is impossible, the terms *kvanip* and *vanip* are understood here in their general sense.

The suffixes *kvanip* and *vanip* are also included here, as they are prescribed by the supplementary rule (*aupasaṃkhyānika*) "In the Vedic language, *kvanip* and *vanip* should be stated [after roots] in the sense of possession" (Vār. 582). For example, in the word *prātaritva*:

the root *iṇ* (meaning "to go," Dhātupāṭha 1045) is preceded by *prātaḥ*; then, while the rule *āto maninkvanibdhanipaśca* (Pāṇini 3.2.74) is in force, the suffix *kvanip* is applied by rule 3.2.75, followed by the substitution [of *ī* for *a*] according to 6.1.71.

However, because this [word *bhavat*] belongs to the group beginning with *sampadādi*, the suffix *kvip* is applied; then, after the addition of *tuk*, the suffix *matup* follows. By the rule *jhayaḥ* (Pāṇini 8.2.10), the substitution of *vat* occurs, and the form is thus established from that which ends in *matup*. Therefore, no supplementary rule (*upasaṃkhyāna*) is required. Regarding the phrase "optionally" (*vibhāṣā*) and so forth:
the word *bhavat* is derived from the root *bhā* with the suffix *ḍavatup*, as stated in the rule *bhāterḍavatup* (Pāṇini 5.2.64).

A nominal stem (*prātipadika*) is that which is not yet analyzed [into its constituent parts] and is followed by case-endings (*vibhakty-anubandha*); however, the other two [forms cited] end in the suffix *matup*.
Regarding the form "he bhoḥ":

once the substitution of *ru* for *num* has been applied, the vowel *o* is substituted for the entire word *ava*, and not for the final phoneme alone, because of the rule "there is no application of a rule concerning the final phoneme when [the element to be replaced] is meaningless" (*nānarthake 'lontyavidhiḥ*).
"Is it established from the consciousness of non-attachment?
This is the summary statement.
"Or else," [he says].
This is its explanation:
"even though they are unrelated," and so forth.
By this, he demonstrates the reason for their status as particles (*nipāta*).

If [the vocative particle] *bho* and so forth were to arise solely from the addition (*upasaṃkhyāna*), it would not occur in the dual and plural numbers, because of the absence of the vocative case ending (*sambuddhi*). Furthermore, it would not occur in the feminine vocative either—as in *bho brāhmaṇī*; for in this case, words characterized by the feminine gender are not included [in the rule]. If it is argued that "when a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) is mentioned, that which is qualified by gender is also included" (Vyāḍi’s Paribhāṣā 29), we say no; for there is a prohibition of that in the context of case endings (*vibhakti*). This technical rule (*paribhāṣā*) is prohibited regarding any grammatical operation prescribed for a case ending, according to the statement: "When a case ending is concerned, that which is qualified by gender is not included" (Vyāḍi’s Paribhāṣā 30).

Furthermore, even if it is not prohibited [by the rule *na ṅisambuddhyoḥ*], even so, since it remains as *bhavati*, when the substitution of *ru* is applied to the *i* (or *ī*) and the substitution of *au* is applied to the word *ava*, the undesired form would result because the substitution of *ru* is considered non-existent (*asiddha*), and thus the elision of the final consonant of the conjunct (*saṃyogāntalopa*) would not occur; consequently, the substitution of *visarjanīya* would take place. Therefore, because they are observed in forms other than the vocative and in the feminine, these must be understood as particles (*nipāta*). Their status as particles, moreover, is due to their being counter-parts of case-endings (*vibhaktipratirūpaka*), as they are included among the *ca*-group by the *Gaṇasūtra*: "And those that are counter-parts of case-endings and accents" (Gaṇasūtra 16).

Furthermore, the word *bhoḥ* would have the status of a particle (*nipāta*); for when the suffix *vic* is applied to the root *bhū* and the vowel substitution (*guṇa*) occurs, the word *bhoḥ* itself exists as a form ending in a case-suffix (*vibhaktyanta*), whereas the other two [words, *bhagoḥ* and *aghoḥ*] would not.

Indeed, if this supplementary rule (*upasaṃkhyāna*) were not stated, the words *bhagoḥ* and *aghoḥ* do not exist as forms ending in a case-suffix that could serve as the prototypes (*pratirūpaka*) for these particles.
Therefore, these should be understood as particles mentioned in the Sūtras themselves, because they are recited in the Sūtra: *bhobhagoaghoapūrvasya* (Pāṇini 8.3.17).

Alternatively, since the particle *ca* in the rule "and those that resemble prefixes, case-endings, and short vowels" has the sense of an inclusive conjunction (*anuktasamuccaya*), these [words] should be understood as being *nipātas*.

If, then, the supplementary rule (*upasaṃkhyāna*) is rejected by relying on their status as *nipātas*, would not the suffixes *tasil* and others—prescribed when used in connection with words such as *bhavat* in the rules *samostāt* [Pāṇini 5.3.7], *bhostataḥ* [Pāṇini 5.3.14], and *bhostatra* [Pāṇini 5.3.14]—fail to be established when the word *bhoḥ* is employed? This is not a fault, because it is not desired [that they apply].

Indeed, he who rejects the supplementary rule (*upasaṃkhyāna*) on the grounds that [the word *bhoḥ*] is a particle (*nipāta*), would certainly not desire the suffixes beginning with *tasil* when the word *bhoḥ* is employed. The state of being "prior" (*pūrvatva*) is relative to the word *idam*. Here, the element *ru* is also understood to carry over [from the previous rule].

However, its status as prior cannot be understood in relation to that [*ru*]; for since the nasalized vowel (*anunāsika*) and *ru* are prescribed simultaneously—both continuing from what follows—the *ru* is not yet established at the time the nasalization is prescribed.
Therefore, it is impossible to understand this [nasalization] as being prior in relation to it.
Therefore, "priority" is understood in relation to that for whose place *ru* is prescribed; thus he says: "of that which precedes that for whose place *ru* is prescribed.
The word *tu* (but) shows the distinction of the preceding element from the subsequent one that undergoes the operation:
the effect of *ru*-substitution applies to the subsequent [element], whereas the nasalization (*anunāsika*) applies to the preceding one.

Alternatively, [the author] shows the distinction between the *rutva* (the substitution of *r*) and the nasal (*anunāsika*). Is *rutva* obligatory? But the nasal is optional (*vibhāṣā*). Why is the group of letters beginning with *ach*, *chak*, and *dak* mentioned? If it is argued that this is for the sake of [the rule] applying within this section on *rutva*, [we reply]: No; this is already established by the governing context (*adhikāra*) alone.

For just as the rule "the nasal [is substituted] for the preceding" (Aṣṭādhyāyī 6.1.102), which is introduced [in that context], continues to apply in what follows, so too does this term *ru*. In that case, one might argue that even without the statement "here" (*atra*), [the rule] will occur within the section on *ru*; therefore, he says "here" (*atra*) and so forth.
"Conjunction" (*sanniyoga*) means simultaneity.
The mention of "together" (*saha*) is for the purpose of showing how that [object] could possibly be perceived simultaneously with the redness;
furthermore, a restriction (*avadhāraṇa*) should be understood here: "with the redness *alone*."
For the co-occurrence (*sanniyoga*) of *ru* and the nasalized vowel (*anunāsika*) is established merely by their presence together, since both continue to apply in what follows.

Because there is no contradiction due to the difference in their respective domains (*sthānin*), this is indeed obtained even without the inclusion of the word "here" (*atra*). Now, one might object: "Since the nasalized vowel (*anunāsika*) is not marked with the *svarita* accent after the section on *ru*, its co-occurrence will not be understood [automatically]; so what is the purpose of including the word 'here'? To this, he says: "If the extent of the governing rule (*adhikāra*) were not delimited," and so forth.

The "measure" (*parimāṇa*) of an application (*adhikāra*) is its extent; its "comprehension" (*parigraha*) is its full understanding or determination. In the absence of that [determination], learners of dull intellect, having given rise to doubt as to whether the *svarita* accent for a nasalized vowel (*anunāsika*) exists in what follows or not, might suspect that even in rules such as *ḍho ḍhe lopaḥ* [P. 8.3.13]—where an operation such as the elision of *ḍh* is prescribed for something—the nasalization would apply to the preceding [vowel].

Alternatively, what is the purpose of including the word *atha* (or *atha vā*)? Since the option (*vikalpa*) for this rule will be understood from the very mention of the word *nitya* (obligatory) in the subsequent sūtra, is it not so? This is not the case; for if it were so, the option would be understood as applying to the preceding sūtra. Therefore, should one say "or" (*vā*)? It need not be said; the activity of the Teacher (*ācārya*) indicates that this rule is optional, because in the subsequent sūtra he teaches the introduction of the *anusvāra* after the *ru* following that [consonant] for which the nasalization (*anunāsika*) has not been applied. Indeed, that is not possible if this rule were obligatory, because [the condition] "for which the nasalization has not been applied" would refer to the [consonant] preceding the *ru*.
In that case, the mention of *vā* (optionally) is for the sake of clarity, as in the example: *devamacchā dīvyati*.

Here, when the vowel *a* is followed by the suffix *aṭ*, the rule *dūrghādadi samānapāde* [Pāṇini 8.3.9] causes the *r*-substitution (*rutva*) of the letter *n*. Following that, by this [rule], the nasalization (*anunāsikatva*) of the preceding *a* is applied; then, as before, the *y* is substituted for the *ru*, and its elision occurs just as previously.
If it is said that "some recite *anusvāra* in *mahāṃ indro ya ojasā*," then one must explain how that form is established; therefore, he says "that" (*saḥ*), and so forth.

This is to be understood by means of the rule *vyatyayo bahulam* [Pāṇini 3.1.85]. Regarding the example *yo vā vanaspatīṃranu*: when *vanaspatīn* and *anu* stand together, the *n* is changed to *r* by the rule *naśca apadāntasya jhali* [Pāṇini 8.3.9], and then an *anusvāra* follows the vowel *i* by the rule *anunāsikāt paro 'nusvāraḥ* [Pāṇini 8.3.4], resulting in *bhavāṃścarati*.

By the rule *naśchavyapraśān* [Pāṇini 8.3.7], the *n* undergoes *ru*-substitution (*rutvam*); for that *visarjanīya*, there is *s*-substitution; and for that *s*, by the rule *stoḥ ścunā ścuḥ* [Pāṇini 8.4.40], there is *ścu*-substitution (i.e., *ś*). The inclusion of the word *nitya* is for the sake of clarity (*vispaṣṭārtham*). Since this would have been established even by the preceding optional rule (*vikalpa*), this rule must be understood as obligatory (*nitya*) simply by virtue of its formulation. [Objection: But surely, for this very reason, the formulation of this rule should serve to establish a restriction (*niyama*) such that it applies only when *aṭ* follows, or only when *aṭ* itself is followed by *at*—that is, so that the rule might apply only in these specific cases? [Response: This is not so; for a restriction (*niyama*) occurs only when there is something else to be prescribed (*vidheya*). If there were nothing else to be prescribed, a restriction could not exist.
But here there is something to be enjoined; what is it? It is the "perpetual nasal" (*nityo'nunāsikaḥ*).
Therefore, an injunction alone is appropriate, not a restriction (*niyama*).
And so it has been said: "When both an injunction and a restriction are possible, the injunction alone is superior" (Vyāḍipāda 130).
In the word "ātaḥ," the letter *t* is for the purpose of removing doubt.

If only "ā" were stated, a doubt would arise: "Is this a reference to the genitive form *ākārasya* (of the vowel *ā*) which is the subject of the operation, or is it a reference to the nominative form *ādeśāntasya* (of that which ends in *ā*)? [To resolve this,] the word "anya" (other) must be supplied here. For if the word "anya" were not supplied, since the word "para" has already been dropped, this ablative case in "anunāsikāt" would have to depend on that very [word "para"]; because no other basis for the ablative case is possible here.

Is it not the case that, according to [Pāṇini 1.1.67], the ablative case would apply only with respect to the word *para* (subsequent) when this [paribhāṣā] is present? This is not so; for if the present paribhāṣā were to apply here, the mention of the word *para* would be purposeless.
Therefore, the ablative must indeed be used with respect to the word *para*.

And being thus [the word *para*], would it, by means of the rule beginning with "anyārāditarartediśy... [Pāṇini 2.3.29], denote a direction (*dig-vṛtti*) in connection with the word *para*, or would it denote something other than that (*anyārtha-vṛtti*)? In the first case, the *anusvāra* would be understood as occurring immediately after the *ru* (the substitute for *r*) which itself follows an *anunāsika* (nasalized vowel); yet it is not desired that it follow from that [nasalized vowel]. In the second case, however, this meaning would result: "it occurs after an *anunāsika*; the meaning is that the *anusvāra* becomes something other than the *anunāsika*. And in this way, the mention of the word *para* would be purposeless; for the *anusvāra* does not differ from the *anunāsika* in relation to the *anunāsika* itself.

Furthermore—because of its being explicitly stated [in the rule], the anusvāra would be understood as belonging to that very nasalized vowel (*anunāsika*), since *ru* is the subject under discussion (*prakṛta*). And this is undesirable. However, if another word is supplied (*adhyāhāra*), then it is understood that the anusvāra belongs to that which has not yet been nasalized and follows immediately after this [vowel].
Therefore, another word must be supplied here.
Even when another word is supplied, it is understood that the anusvāra belongs to that which has not yet been nasalized and follows immediately after this [vowel].
Therefore, another word must be supplied here.

Even though another word has been supplied, if this ablative case in *anunāsikāt* were dependent solely on the word *para*, that same fault would remain exactly as before; thinking this, he says: "And this [is] with reference to that," and so forth.
The word *ca* is used for emphasis.
The meaning is: "only with reference to the word *anya*, and not with reference to the word *para*.
By the phrase "that which is other than *anunāsika*," he demonstrates that very dependence on the word *anya* through the use of the ablative case (*pañcamī*).
By the phrase "preceding *ru*," he also indicates the continued application (*anuvṛtti*) of the term "preceding" (*pūrva*).
And "being prior" (*pūrvatvam*) is relative to *ru*.
By the phrase "for which the nasalization has not been made," he also demonstrates that the meaning is denoted by another word.
Furthermore, by the word "from that" (*tataḥ*), he indicates that the term "prior" (*pūrva*) undergoes a transformation into the ablative case ending here for the sake of the sense.

By the word *para*, the fact that the word *anya*—which is not displaced—is in the ablative case (*pañcamyantatā*) is indicated; by the word *āgama*, the fact that the ablative case belonging to that word *anya* is dependent upon the word *para* is indicated;
and by the word *āgama*, the absence of substitution (*ādeśābhāva*) is also indicated.
The mention of *para* (the following) could have been omitted.

For, by supplying the word *anya* (other) ending in the ablative case (*pañcamyantāt*) and by transforming the word *pūrva* (preceding) into the nominative case (*prathamāntatayā*), the rule would be understood as follows: "When there is another [consonant] following that which begins with a nasal (*anunāsika*), the augment *anusvāra* occurs before that [other consonant]. And this being understood, even without the mention of *para*, forms such as *saṃskartṛ* would indeed be established; so what is the use of mentioning *para*? It is done for the sake of clarity. Thus, when *anusvāra* would otherwise have applied, this statement [is made].
Regarding the form *saṃskartā*—this reading is printed in the *Nyāsa* and the *Padamañjarī*.

It is derived from the root *kṛ* preceded by the prefix *sam*, with the suffixes *tṛc* and so forth. By the rule *samo gamyṛcchi...* [Pāṇini 6.1.137], the augment *suṭ* is applied. Then, by the rule *samo makārasya...* [Pāṇini 1.1.52], the *m* of *sam* becomes *r*; following that, the preceding vowel becomes nasalized (*anunāsika*), and the *r* becomes a *visarjanīya*.
When the *visarjanīya* is optionally changed to *s* by the rule *vā śari* [Pāṇini 8.3.36], the commentary demonstrates how the *s* occurs invariably.
But how is the letter *s* indicated in this sūtra? To this he says: "In the presence of *suṭ*, [the *s* of the suffix] is like *sam*" (*samaḥ ssuṭi*), and so forth.

This is stated with reference to that alternative in which, after the *visarjanīya* has been substituted for the *s* of the case-ending, the rule "before a *śar* [consonant], [the preceding *r* becomes *s*]" (*vā śari*) is not applied to produce the letter *s*. Otherwise, one would have to say that this indication contains three *s*s, because of the conjunction of three *s*s:
for one *s* belongs to the case-ending, the second belongs to the substitute, and the third belongs to *suṭ*.
But when one recites the Sūtra after having performed [the substitution] three times, then the word *dvi* (twice) should be understood as indicating the inclusion of the additional *sakāra*.

If, then, the *sakāra* is prescribed as a substitute, the nasalized form (*anunāsika*) would not occur in the case of *saṃskartā*; for in this context, the mention of *atru* was stated for the purpose of conveying a necessary connection (*sanniyoga*) with *ru* alone. There is no fault here, because the mention of *ru* in this section serves as an indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*) for whatever is prescribed in that context.

"With *ru*": the meaning is "together with that which is prescribed in the section on *ru*. Furthermore, although it was stated in the preceding rule (*vṛtti*) that "the preceding [element] of *ru*," there too the mention of *ru* should be understood as an indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*) for whatever is prescribed in this present section; otherwise, in the case of "saṃskartā," there would be no *anusvāra* according to that alternative view. "From *pum*": [this refers to the elision of *m*].

This is the specification of that portion which remains after [the elision of] the *sakāra* of the word *puṃsaḥ*; for when the *sakāra* has undergone elision due to being at the end of a conjunct (*saṃyogāntalopa*), it alone is the subject of the grammatical operation. Regarding the term *ampare*: that after which *am* follows is so described.

The term *am* here refers to the *pratyāhāra* (abbreviated designation), not to the singular case-ending (*dvitīyaikavacana*). Why is this so? Because of the principle of pervasion (*vyāpti*) and because of its association with the *pratyāhāra* *khayi*. For example, in the word *puṃścalī*.
The root *cala* is recited in the *pacādi* group.

From this root *cala* meaning "to shake" (*dhātupāṭha* 832), the suffix *ac* of the *pacādi* class is applied; because it ends in a *ṭi* vowel, the suffix *ṅīp* is added according to Pāṇini 4.1.15 (*ṭiḍḍhaṇañ...*). Thus, *puṃścalī* is a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*).
Regarding the term *puṃskāmā*:

it is a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "one who has desire (*kāma*) for a man. Alternatively, it is derived from the root *kām* with the suffix *ṇa*, according to the rule "the suffix *ṇa* should be stated after [roots] such as *śīli*, *kāmi*, and *bhikṣācari*" (Vārttika 229); from that, the feminine suffix *ṭāp* is applied.
In this example, "puṃskāmā," it is stated that "the substitute is indeed the letter *s*"; this requires the addition of the word "of the *visarjanīya*."

"It should be stated" means it should be explained. In this regard, the explanation is as follows: in the rule *kupvoḥ ka pau ca* [Pāṇini 8.3.37], the term *vā* ("or") is carried over from the preceding rule *vā śari* [Pāṇini 8.3.36]; and that [application of] *vā* is a restricted option (*vyavasthitavibhāṣā*).

Therefore, in this case as well, there will be only the *sakāra* for the *visarjanīya*, and not the *visarjanīya* or the *jihvāmūlīya*. First, the counter-argument was stated when the alternative involving two *sakāras* was not adopted in the preceding rule; however, when that alternative—namely, "the instruction contains two *sakāras*"—is adopted, he states the following counter-argument: "But in the case of the instruction containing two *sakāras*," and so forth.

But surely, since *ru* also continues [from the previous rule], just as the letter *s* continues there, so too would *ru* optionally apply; and consequently, when *ru* applies and *visarjanīya* is substituted, the *jihvāmūlīya* would certainly occur? To this he says: "But *ru*, though continuing," and so forth. He states the reason for that very point: "The continuation of its connection," and so forth. The particle *iti* indicates a cause; for it (the *ru*) continues here in connection with its own related elements, namely *matup* and *vasu*, from the rule "In the vocative, *ru* replaces *matup* and *vasu*" (Pāṇini 8.2.1).
Therefore, it is not capable of experiencing a relationship with another related entity. "Puṃdāsaḥ" is a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*), meaning "the servant of a man."
Or it is a *karmadhāraya* compound; thus [we have] "pūgavaḥ. But here, by [Pāṇini 5.4.92], the suffix *ṭac* is applied as a compound-final element (*samāsānta*).
"puṃkṣīram, puṃkṣuram"— these are genitive compounds (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*). [The rule] "khayyami" applies here.
The mention of "para" (subsequent) is for the purpose of excluding contrary interpretations.

If the mention of "para" were absent, it would be understood as "before a *khay* [consonant] following an *am*," and consequently, the rule would apply even in cases such as *pumākhyah* and *pumācāraḥ*. Therefore, the mention of "para" is made. Regarding the word "sa" (he/that):

[The word] *nivṛttam* (ceased) [is used]; only *ru* continues [to apply]. That too is indeed not connected with *matup* or *vasu*, because those two have also ceased [to apply]. The term *naḥ* is a mention of the phoneme *n*; and that is a qualifier of the word under discussion (*prakṛta*), and by means of a qualifier, the rule of "ending in that" (*tadantavidhi*) applies. Thus he says: "of a word ending in the letter *n*" (*nakārāntasya padasya*), and so forth.
[Example: *bhavāñ chādayati*.
The root *jhada* is used in the sense of "to exclude" (*apavāraṇe*) [Dhātupāṭha 1833], with the causative suffix *ṇic*.
Regarding the form *bhavāṃṣṭīkate*:
the roots *ṭikṛ*, *ṭīkṛ*, *radhi*, and *laghi* have the meaning of "motion" (*gatyarthāḥ*) [Dhātupāṭha 103, 104, 107, 108].
The *ātmanepada* ending is used because the root is marked with the *anudātta* accent.

Regarding the form *praśān*: from the root *śam* preceded by the prefix *pra*, the suffix *kvip* is applied. By the rule *anunāsikasya kvijhaloḥ kṅiti* [Pāṇini 6.4.15], there is lengthening of the vowel; then, by the rule *naśca* [8.2.64], the *m* is replaced by *n*. Because that [substitution] is considered *asiddha*, the elision of the *n* (*nalopa*) does not occur.

"Are you a *tsaruka*? [The suffix] *kan* is applied according to Pāṇini 5.2.64: "After *tsaru*, the suffix *kan* is added in the sense of 'skillful'. This statement is for the purpose of providing an option (*vikalpa*), since the previous rule would have made the application obligatory. Regarding the phrase "in the same foot" (*samānapāde*), this is a locative case derived from a *karmadhāraya* compound.

And this word *samāna* is understood here as occurring in the sense of "one" (*eka*). The meaning is that [the cause and the effect] reside in a single foot (*pāda*), that is, in one and the same locus.
Although the term *eka* ("one") could have been used there, the term *samāna* was employed so that [the rule] might apply even in some cases where they are not in the same foot.
Therefore, here also *ru* occurs—as in "yajāmahai yajñiyā indradevān ilāmahai īkṣām anājyā.
Here, the cause (*nimitta*) and the effect (*nimittin*) reside in two distinct *pādas*.
Alternatively, the word *samāna* is understood in the sense of similarity; otherwise, he would have used the term *eka* (one).
And here, there is a similarity between the two verbs because they share the same meaning.
Just as the verb *yajāmahai* functions in the sense of worship (*pūjā*), so too does *ilāmahai*.

[The root] *īḍ* [is used] in the sense of praise (*stuti*) [Dhātupāṭha 1019]; it is in the imperative (*loṭ*), and by [Pāṇini 3.4.96], the *ṭe* suffix is replaced by *et*, resulting in the substitution of the vowel *i* with *e*.
Through the transposition of the phonemes of the root, the letter *ḍa* becomes *la*.

The short vowel [in *nṛṇām*] occurs because it is Vedic (*chāndasa*). Regarding the form *nṝn*: the genitive case ending is elided by the rule "supāṃ suluk... (Pāṇini 7.1.39) and so forth; thus, the reference is made after performing that elision.
Alternatively, no case-ending at all is produced here, because the distinction between the original (anukārya) and the imitation (anukaraṇa) is not intended to be expressed.
This is as in examples such as *gavity ayam āha* ("He says 'cow'"). In the term *pe*, only the phoneme *p* is taken as the cause [of the grammatical operation], not the entire aggregate.

The letter *a*, however, serves the purpose of pronunciation (*uccāraṇārtha*). For otherwise, if the entire cluster beginning with *a* were relied upon as the cause (*nimitta*), then [the substitution] would occur only in cases such as *nṛḥ pacati*, but not in cases such as *nṛn prīṇīhi*. Furthermore, the term *aṭi* has ceased to apply here, because another cause has been introduced. Now, why is it not understood that this is a qualifier of that very same cause—namely, "that which is the letter *p* when followed by *aṭ"*? It is impossible to understand it in this way; for in that case, it would not apply here: *nṛḥ psāti* and *nṛḥ plāvayati*.

Therefore, the inclusion of the term *nivṛtti* (exclusion) for this *aṅgagrahaṇa* (mention of the stem) is appropriate. The forms *svatavān* and so forth should be understood as being explained as before. Likewise, it applies to the subsequent rule *kān* [Pāṇini 8.3.12] as well:
*svatavāḥ, pāyur agne*.

The *num* augment [is applied] by *dṛksvaḥsavatavasāñ chandasi* [Pāṇini 7.1.83]; then the elision of the final consonant (*halṅyādi* [6.1.68]) and the elision of the final member of the conjunction (*saṃyogāntalopa* [8.2.23]) apply. Regarding the form *kāṃskān*: the substitution of *ka-* for *kim-* occurs by *kimaḥ śasi* [7.2.103]; the long vowel [of the first two cases] occurs by *prathamayoḥ pūrvasavarṇaḥ* [6.1.102]; the substitution of *na-* for the *s-* occurs by *ato ror aplutād aplute* [6.1.113]; there is reduplication due to distributive repetition (*vīpsā*); the substitution of *ru-* occurs; the visarga occurs; and the substitution of *sa-* for that [visarga] occurs by *tasya* [8.3.34].

But how can there be the letter *s* here, given that by the rule *kupvoḥ ka pau ca* [Pāṇini 8.3.37], there ought to be either a *visarjanīya* or a *jihvāmūlīya*? To this he says: "Of this," and so forth. Although it is not explicitly recited there, he says "In the case of *samaḥ suṭi*" and so forth to demonstrate that an undesirable consequence would nonetheless follow. He asks: "If the letter *s* were to carry over (*anuvarttiṣyate*) here, would it not follow that the letter *s* would also apply everywhere in the preceding rules because it carries over from this very point? To this he replies: "In the preceding rules," and so forth.

For in the preceding rules, by the statement *pūrvayogeṣu hi* (in the previous rules), there is the recurrence (*anuvṛtti*) of that very [element] which is connected with its own related term and with the augment *suṭ*; therefore, it does not become connected with another related term.
When it should have been said simply "kān? kān," the inclusion of the term *āmreḍita* (reduplicated) is so that [the rule applies] only where there is a doubling;
thus, it does not apply here in the case of *kān? kān paśyati*.
In this context, one *ka* is used for inquiry (*praśna*) and the second for censure (*kutsā*).
What [does he see]? He sees those who are censurable. In the rule "after *ḍha*," only the phoneme *ḍha* is taken as the cause, not a collection of phonemes.
Why is this so? Because of pervasion (*vyāpti*).

The syllable *a* is for the purpose of pronunciation (*uccāraṇārtha*). However, when there is the mention of a phoneme (*varṇagrahaṇa*), it applies even in cases such as *līḍhvā* and *mīḍhva*; otherwise, if a collection of phonemes (*varṇasamudāya*) were intended as the cause (*nimitta*), then it would apply only in cases such as *lauḍham* and *mīḍham*, but not in cases such as *līḍhavā*.
[Examples include] *līḍham*, etc.

From the roots *lih* "to lick" (DhP 1016), *mih* "to sprinkle" (DhP 992), and *guh* "to conceal" (DhP 896), the suffix *kta* is applied. By the rule *ṣṭunā ṣṭuḥ* (Kātantra Pāṭha), there is the substitution of *ṣṭu* for *ṣṭu*. Then, by *ho ḍhaḥ* (Pāṇini 8.2.31), *h* is replaced by *ḍh*; by *jhaṣastathordho'dhaḥ* (Pāṇini 8.2.40), *t* is replaced by *dh*; and by *ṣṭunā ṣṭuḥ* (Pāṇini 8.4.41), there is the substitution of *ṣṭu*. Following this, there is the elision of *ḍh*, and by *ḍhralope pūrvasya dīrgho'ṇaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.3.110), a long vowel is substituted for the preceding *aṇ*.

But how can the example beginning with *līḍham* be justified, given that the letter *ḍh* cannot serve as the cause for the subsequent operation here, because when the elision of *ḍh* (*ḍhalopa*) is to be performed, the substitution of *ṣṭu* (*ṣṭutva*) is not yet established? To this, he says: "of the substitution of *ṣṭu*. Here, the letter *ḍh* is not relied upon as the cause for the elision of *ḍh*; nor is it possible for it to be established anywhere where this elision of *ḍh* would have to be performed by this very rule. Therefore, it should be understood that the establishment of the substitution of *ṣṭu* occurs precisely through the reliance on the letter *ḍh* as the cause; otherwise, this statement would be purposeless, as it would have no scope of application.

It might be argued: "The elision of the letter *ḍh* will occur by [the rule] *ālīḍhaukate*; for here the letter *ḍh* is already established, so why would the statement be purposeless? To this he replies with the words "*ālīḍhaukte*" and so forth.

Even though the letter *ḍh* is established as the cause (*nimitta*) here, nevertheless the elision of *ḍh* is not possible; because once the substitution of the *jaś*-sounds has been applied, the letter *ḍh*, which is the subject of the operation (*kāryin*), no longer exists.

But surely, because it lacks an object [of application], the elision of *ḍ* will be an exception (*apavāda*) to the rule for *jaś*-substitution? To this he says: "And not," and so forth. Why is this so? He says: "For of that," and so forth.
For if its scope were not possible, then it could be understood as an exception to the *jaś*-rule.

Furthermore, its scope includes forms such as *līḍha* and the like; therefore, it cannot be understood that this [rule] applies to cases where the substitution of the *jaś*-sounds has already occurred.

But how can forms like *līḍha* be its scope, given that—just as in the case of *āliṅḍhaukate*, where the elision of *aṭ* is not applicable because the subject of the operation no longer exists once the *jaś*-substitution has been applied—the same would hold for *līḍha* and so on, since the cause [for the elision] would be absent due to the *asiddha* status of the *ṣṭutva* rule?

Now, is the fact that the *ṣṭutva* rule is not established due to the elision of *ḍha* here [in the case of *liḍha*, etc. overridden by the power of the specific statement? Why then is the *jaśtva* rule not also overridden in the other case? Therefore, if the domain of the elision of *ḍha* in *liḍha* and so forth must necessarily be the same as the domain of the other [rule], and not merely the domain of *liḍha* and so forth, then he says: "For in that case," and so on. Here, because of the mention of the locative case in the word *ḍhe*, immediate proximity (*ānantarya*) is relied upon; however, [the objection] that it is not merely the domain of *liḍha* and so forth applies to the other case as well—hence he says: "For in that case," and so on.

In this context, because of the mention of the locative case in the term *ḍhe*, the operation must occur within its scope, and not merely in cases such as *līḍha* and others even elsewhere. Therefore, he says: "For in that case," and so forth.

Here, by the mention of the locative case in *ḍhe*, immediate sequence (*ānantarya*) is relied upon; for the mention of the word *nirdiṣṭa* (in the rule) has the purpose of indicating immediate sequence.
Consequently, when there is immediate sequence, the elision of *ḍh* (*ḍhalopa*) must take place.

And there is proximity (*ānantarya*) produced by direct audition (*śruti*) in *loḍhā* and similar forms, because both the cause (*nimitta*) and the effect (*kāryin*), namely the two *ḍha* sounds, are heard.

Therefore, is this alone the scope for the elision of *ḍha*? True, here there is no proximity produced by direct audition; however, there is also non-proximity produced by the technical rule (*śāstra*). This is because the rule treats the substitution of *ṣṭu* as non-existent (*asiddha*). And when that [non-proximity] exists, even that is not the scope for the elision of *ḍha*. To this he says: "Produced by the technical rule; because the rule treats the substitution of *ṣṭu* as non-existent."

And since that [intervening element] exists, even that [intervening element] is not within the scope of the elision of *ḍh*; therefore, he says: "produced by the grammatical rule" (*śāstrakṛta*), and so forth.
Even though there is an immediate sequence produced by the rule, it is set aside by the elision of *ḍh*; for otherwise, the statement [of the rule] would be purposeless.

Just as the elision of *ḍh* occurs by setting aside the immediate sequence produced by the rule through the force of the statement, so too in the case of *āliṅḍhaukate*, the elision of *ḍh* would occur by setting aside the immediate sequence produced by the audible phonemes (*śruti*); thus he says: "But in the case of *āliṅḍhaukate*," and so forth.
The word "tu" (but) indicates the distinction of this [case] from cases such as *līḍha*.
For in those cases like *līḍha*, although there is no immediate succession (*ānantarya*) established by a grammatical rule (*śāstra*), there is indeed that established by direct audition (*śruti*).

Here, however, there is neither immediate succession established by direct audition—since two sounds of the letter *ḍh* are not heard—nor is it established by a rule, because the rule does not provide for the non-application of the substitution of the voiced unaspirated stop (*jaś*) as being unestablished (*asiddha*).

Therefore, this is certainly not the domain for the elision of *ḍh*. But what is this: is it the inclusion of the *repha* (the letter *r*) with its *anubandha*, or rather that without an *anubandha*? Furthermore, if there is an inclusion of the one with the *anubandha*, then forms such as *agnīrathaḥ* and *indūrathaḥ* are established, but *nīraktaṃ* and *dūraktaṃ* are not established.

Now, what if the inclusion [of the rule] were for that which lacks an *anubandha* (indicatory letter)? In that case, forms such as *nīraktam* and *dūraktam* would be established, but *agnīrathaḥ* and *indūrathaḥ* would not be established. This is not a fault. Here, by means of this method, the Teacher has pronounced two rules—*ro ri*—wherein in one instance there is the inclusion of that with an *anubandha*, and in the other, that without an *anubandha*.
In *nīraktam* and so forth, the lengthening [of the vowel] occurs by [Pāṇini 6.3.111].

In this context, if the genitive case in *padasya* were a locative genitive (indicating position), then, by rule 6.1.52 (*ato ror aplutād aplute*), the elision of the *repha* would occur only for a *repha* at the end of a word—as in *nīraktam* and similar forms. However, in cases such as *ajardhāḥ*, where the *repha* is not at the end of a word, the elision would not occur. Anticipating this objection, and considering that in this instance the genitive is one of qualification (*viśeṣaṇa-ṣaṣṭhī*), the author says "of the word" (*padasya*) and so forth.

For the genitive case in *viśeṣaṇa-ṣaṣṭhī* is construed with this very rule, *padasya*, as follows: "The elision occurs when a *repha* (the sound *r*) which is a constituent part (*avayava*) of a word (*pada*) stands before another *repha*. By this, the elision occurs even for a *repha* that is not at the end of a word (*apadānta*), as in *ajardhāḥ*.
This has been explained in a rule such as *ekāco baśo bhaṣ* [Pāṇini 8.2.37], namely in the example *apāspāḥ*. [The derivation is as follows:

from the root *spadi* (meaning "to tremble" or "to move," Dhātupāṭha 3), with the suffix *yaṅ*; reduplication; the retention of the remaining consonant (*khayaḥ śeṣaḥ*) by [Pāṇini 7.4.61]; lengthening by [Pāṇini 7.4.83]; and the elision of *yaṅ* by [Pāṇini 2.4.74].

With *pāspardha* established, the suffix *laṅ* is applied; *sip* follows. Due to its recitation in the list beginning with *carkarītañ ca* (Dhātupāṭha 1081), there is elision (*luk*) of *śap*. By [Pāṇini 6.1.66], *sip* is elided by *iṭ* and so forth. By the rule of *jaś*-substitution, the letter *dh* becomes *d*. By [Pāṇini 8.2.75], *daś ca*, that same *d* undergoes *rutva* (becoming *r*). Here, the *r* is elided by this [present rule], and as before, the lengthening of the vowel occurs.

The separation of the rule (*yogavibhāga*) is for the sake of what follows, so that the recurrence of *repha* may occur in the subsequent sūtra; otherwise, there would also be a recurrence of *ḍha*, and consequently, *visarjanīya* would undesirably apply to that as well. If, in this context, the genitive were a partitive genitive—meaning "the *repha* which is a constituent of a word"—then *visarjanīya* would also apply to the *repha* in words like *arkaḥ*, even though it is not at the end of a word.

There is no fault here in [the rule being] a genitive of location (*sthāna-ṣaṣṭhī*); for in this case, the word (*pada*) is qualified by the letter *r*, and by means of a qualifier, the rule of "extension to that which ends in it" (*tadantavidhi*) applies. Thus, when an operation is prescribed for that which ends in *r*, it occurs only at the final letter (*alo'ntyasya*). Therefore, this genitive in the phrase "of the word" (*padasya*) is a genitive of location. And showing that this word is qualified by *r*, he says: "of the word ending in *r*" (*rephāntasya padasya*). [The conditions are: "when *khari* follows or at the end of a word" (*khari parato'vasāne ca*).

Regarding this term *pataḥ*: it is connected only with what precedes, not with the subsequent *avasāna* (pause), because there can be no sequence between them (*paurvāparya*). For that by which one ceases [speaking] would be the *avasāna*; and cessation (*virati*) or pause (*virāma*) is simply the non-utterance of a phoneme.

Therefore, [the rule] beginning with the word "rephāntāt" is initiated by the first letter of the word; that much is designated as *avasāna* (pause), for no further [element] is possible, since that alone is never employed in usage.
Its non-employment, however, is due to its being devoid of meaning.
In other cases, moreover, *avasāna* is of the nature of absence.

Moreover, priority and posteriority (paurvāparya) are not possible in the case of non-existence, because that [priority and posteriority] is a property of phonemes (varṇadharma). Therefore, that [non-existence] also cannot occur after a word ending in the letter *r*. However, some, relying on a priority and posteriority imagined by the intellect (*buddhikalpita*), connect this [term "after"] even with the rule "and at the end" (*avasāne ca*).

In this regard, if the temporal sequence (*paurvāparya*) imagined by the learned (*vṛddhi-kalpita*) is not resorted to, then even this single locative case in the rule *kharavasānayoḥ* would be divided according to the difference in the loci: the locative in *khari* occurs in the sense of a proximate locus (*upaśleṣika-adhikaraṇa*), meaning "when *kha* follows"; whereas in *avasāne*, the locative occurs in the sense of a situational locus (*vaiṣayika-adhikaraṇa*), meaning "in the situation of word-finality.

However, when the temporal sequence imagined by the learned is resorted to even in the case of non-existence (*abhāva*) and even in the case of word-finality (*avasāna*), then in both instances it is simply a locative of posteriority (*parasaptamī*).

In the examples, when *visarjanīya* is substituted [by Pāṇini 8.3.34], the *sakāra* is applied; then, when a *cavarga* follows, the *ścutva* (substitution of *ś*) occurs. Regarding *nārkuṭaḥ*, derived from *nṛkuṭāṃ bhavaḥ* by adding the suffix *aṇ* [Pāṇini 4.3.53], and regarding *nārpatyaḥ*, derived from *nṛpater apatyam* by adding the suffix *ṇya* [Pāṇini 4.1.85] because the word *nṛpati* follows after *diti*, *āditya*, or *ādityapatya*—why does *visarjanīya* not occur here? To this he says: "In this case," and so forth.

The substitution of *vṛddhi* is *bahiraṅga* because it depends upon a *taddhita* suffix prescribed for the sense of "originating from" (*bhavādau*), and since that [suffix] is *bahiraṅga*, the *repha* (*r*) which is its locus is also *bahiraṅga*; this is because it depends upon the *vṛddhi*, and furthermore, because the *repha* is a constituent part of that [suffix], and because it is caused by it. However, the *visarjanīya* is *antaraṅga* because it arises depending upon the *khari* sounds and the *adhamā* (voiced unaspirated stops). According to the principle "that which is *bahiraṅga* is as if non-existent (*asiddha*) with respect to that which is *antaraṅga*" (Vyākaraṇa-paribhāṣā 42), when the *visarjanīya* is to be applied, the *repha* is as if non-existent; therefore, the *visarjanīya* does not occur here.

But surely, when *vṛddhi* is to be applied, the *visarjanīya* is intended to be *antaraṅga* (internal), yet it is non-existent [at that stage]. If it is non-existent, then the designation of *vṛddhi* as *bahiraṅga* (external) is not tenable, because that [designation] depends upon its being *antaraṅga*. If that [designation] is non-existent, then the *repha* would also not possess that [designation].

For the external nature (*bahiraṅgatva*) of the *repha* is established by way of the external nature of the *vṛddhi*; consequently, because both factors are deficient, it was stated that the *paribhāṣā* regarding external elements (*vyā|pa|42*) does not apply. As for what was said—"because the *vṛddhi* is characterized as external"—that is untenable. This is not so; [the rule] "na" (Pāṇini 6.1.107) is divided into separate *yoga*s for the sake of other operations.
By means of this, when *vṛddhi* is to be applied, the *visarjanīya* will not be considered non-existent (*asiddha*).
For this very reason, it should be understood that even under the *bahir-aṅga-paribhāṣā*, the *asiddhatva* (non-validity) of the *visarjanīya* will not occur;
this is because the view expressed in *kāryakālaṃ saṃjñāparibhāṣam* (Vyāḍi-Pāṇini 58) is adopted here.
And this is logical, for since technical names (*saṃjñā*) and rules (*paribhāṣā*) are prompted by specific operations, it is proper that they should reside precisely where those operations occur.

For wherever non-identity (*asiddhatva*) is effected by this [rule], that is its domain of operation (*kāryadeśa*). And where is non-identity effected by this? In the rule for the *visarjanīya*. Therefore, this [rule] belongs to that very domain; it does not belong to the domain where it is [merely] enumerated as "in 1.4.2," nor does it belong to the domain where it is made known—as in the case of "vāha ūṭh" (6.4.132)—such as in the examples "payaḥsu" and "yaśaḥsu."
In some places, one reads two *s* sounds.
In that case, the *s* replaces the *visarga* by the rule *vā śari* [Pāṇini 8.3.36],
as in *sarpiḥṣu*.

Where the *visarjanīya* is recited, there the substitution of *ṣ* for the *s* of the suffix occurs by the rule *num-visarjanīya-śav-yavāye 'pi* [Pāṇini 8.3.58]. Where two *ṣ*s are recited, as in *sarpiṣṣu*, there—just as before—the *visarjanīya* is changed to *s*, and then, just as before, the *s* of the suffix is changed to *ṣ*, while the preceding [sibilant] undergoes the change to *ṣṭu* [by Pāṇini 8.4.40]. He says "in *sup*" (*supi*) etc., in order to dispel the suspicion that the term *sup* refers to the entire *pratyāhāra*.

And this is obtained through the continued application (*anuvartana*) of the rule *khari*; for there is no *sup* [suffix] other than the locative plural (*saptamī-bahuvacana*) that begins with a *kṣara*. Let it not be so, because of the continued application of *khari*.
Why does the inclusion of the *pratyāhāra* [of consonants] by means of the letter *pa* not occur in the locative case? It is possible that the *sup* beginning with *khara* [is intended there].
If it were so, what would happen? In cases such as *agīḥkaḥ* and *adhaḥkaḥ*, the visarga would not occur due to the restrictive rule.
Therefore, the [traditional] commentary alone is the refuge.
But for what purpose is this [rule], since the visarga is indeed already established by the preceding rule? To this he says: "Since it is already established," and so forth.

A contrary rule is not to be suspected, because of the mention of the *visarjanīya* in [Pāṇini 8.3.15] *gīrṇu*, *dhūrṣu*; the lengthening is by [Pāṇini 8.2.76] *rthor upadhāyāḥ*. In *bho atra* and so forth, the elision of *y* is obligatory by [Pāṇini 8.3.20] *oto gārgyasya*.
The mention of Gārgya in that rule is for the sake of honor.
Even in cases such as *bho dadāti*, the elision of *y* (*yalopa*) is indeed obligatory by [Pāṇini 8.3.22].

Now, what is the purpose of mentioning *aś* [in this rule], given that when *aś* followed by *am* occurs before a *khar* consonant, a *visarga* must occur there by [Pāṇini 8.3.15]; and once the *visarga* has been substituted, since that substitute would be treated like the original (*sthānivadbhāva*), it would be included by the mention of *ru* [in 8.3.16]? No; because there is an indicator (*jñāpaka*).

When [the author] makes this statement—namely, that in the rule *atrānunāsikaḥ pūrvasya tu vā* (P. 8.3.2), he provides the instruction without employing the *visarjanīya* or the letter *y*—it indicates that the *yakāra* does not replace the *visarjanīya* before a *khari* sound.
If one objects, "In that case, would it [then] occur at the end of a word (*avasāne*)? No; because of the governing context (*adhikāra*) of P. 6.3.114.
Therefore, even without an explicit statement, [the absence of the substitution] occurs by implication; hence he says: "The mention of *at* is for the sake of what follows."
By the passage beginning with "[8.3.22] ityādinā," he demonstrates that very same fact of being for the sake of what follows:
"dṛkṣavṛṭ."

The root *ovraścū* in the sense of "cutting" (*chedane*) [Dhātupāṭha 1292] takes the suffix *kvip*. By the rule *grahādibhyaḥ* [Pāṇini 6.1.16], there is vocalization (*samprasāraṇa*). By the rule *skoḥ saṃyogādyor ante ca* [Pāṇini 8.2.29], the letter *s* is elided. By the rule *vraścabhrasjasṛjamṛjayajarājabhrājacchaśāṃ ṣaḥ* [Pāṇini 8.2.36], the letter *c* becomes *ṣ*, which by the rule *jhalāṃ jaś jhaśi* [Pāṇini 8.4.53] becomes *ḍ*. Then, by the rule *ṣṭunā ṣṭuḥ* [Pāṇini 8.4.41], that *ḍ* also becomes *ṭ*. Thus, we have *vṛkṣavṛṭ*. To express "he causes that to be done" (*tam ācaṣṭe*), the causative suffix *ṇic* is added. By the rule *ṇāviṣṭhavat prātipadikasya* [Vārttika on Pāṇini 7.1.2], the base undergoes the same changes as it would before the superlative suffix *iṣṭhan*. By the rule *ṭeḥ* [Pāṇini 6.4.155], the final vowel and following consonant (*ṭi*) are elided. From the derived form *vṛkṣavayati* ending in *ṇic*, the suffix *kvip* is added again.
By the rule *ver apṛktasya* [Pāṇini 6.1.67], the *ṇic* is elided. Thus, one says: *vṛkṣav karoti* ("he makes a tree-cutter").
In this case, because of the inclusion of *aś*, the elision (*lopa*) of the *vakāra* does not occur when followed by the letter *kakāra*.
Precisely because of this inclusion of *aś*, the elision [prescribed] by [Pāṇini 6.1.66] does not indeed take place.
Otherwise, the inclusion of *aś* would be purposeless.

If the mention of *aś* were for the sake of the subsequent [rule], then it should have been placed right there; for in that case, the *svarita* accent would not need to be applied for the purpose of carrying the term forward (*anuvṛtti*). With this intention, he says "Now" (*atha*), and so forth.
Regarding "for the sake of the subsequent":
that which has its purpose or utility in the rule following the sūtra beginning with [Pāṇini 8.3.22] is described as such.
By the passage beginning with >[[8.3.23]], he clarifies that very point regarding its purpose for what follows.

For if the mention of *aś* were made in >[[8.3.22]], then, just as there would be a recurrence (*anuvṛtti*) of the mention of *hal* in >[[8.3.23]], so too there would be a recurrence of the mention of *aś*.
Consequently, the *anusvāra* of *m* would occur only before a *hal* that is preceded by *aś*, and not before every *hal* in general.
But when the mention of *aś* is not made there, then the *anusvāra* is established for every following consonant (*hal*).

He shows again that the mention of *aś* is for the sake of what follows—namely, the rule "for *v* and *y*, [there is] a substitute with less articulatory effort" (*vyor laghuprayatnataraḥ*), and so forth. The meaning has already been explained. Regarding the phrase "with less articulatory effort" (*laghuprayatnataraḥ*):
*Prayatnaḥ* means effort (*prayatana*). By the rule *yajayāca* [Pāṇini 3.3.90], the suffix *naṅ* is applied.
That which has light effort is "light-effort" (*laghuprayatna*); that which possesses light effort to a superlative degree is "more light-effort" (*laghuprayatnatara*).

What, then, is this "state of being produced with even less effort" (*laghuprayatnataratva*), by virtue of which a sound becomes produced with even less effort? To this he says: "The state of being produced with even less effort," and so forth. The *sthāna* (place of articulation) is the palate and so on; the *karaṇa* (instrument of articulation) is the root of the tongue and so on. Slackness (*śaithilya*) in the pronunciation of these two is the "state of being produced with even less effort. The *sthāna* is the palate and so on; the *karaṇa* is the root of the tongue and so on; slackness in the pronunciation of these two is the "state of being produced with even less effort."

In these examples, by virtue of internal similarity (*āntaratamya*), the *v* remains as *v*, and the *y* remains as *y*. The mention of Śākaṭāyana is for the sake of honor. For by this [sūtra], the state of being produced with less effort (*laghuprayatnatara*) is prescribed for *v* and *y*; and by the subsequent sūtra, their elision (*lopa*) is also prescribed. In that case, precisely because both are prescribed, it will be understood that the [present] rule applies optionally. He will later state that the elision of *v* and *y* following an *o*-vowel is obligatory (*nitya*).
Therefore, he says "preceded by an *a*-vowel" (*avarṇapūrvayoḥ*) and so forth, indicating that this rule is understood to apply to those instances where *v* and *y* are preceded by an *a*-vowel.
"The mention of Śākalya is for the sake of providing an option (*vibhāṣā*).

[Objection: But according to the opinion of Śākaṭāyana, [the form] is prescribed with even less effort (*laghuprayatnatara*). In that case, even without the mention of Śākalya, the rule would be understood as being merely optional; otherwise, the prescription of less effort would be purposeless—so what is the use of mentioning Śākalya? To this, he says: "By that," and so forth.

For if the mention of Śākalya were not present, since the option (*vibhāṣā*) would apply when [the elision] is released by a lighter effort, the elision would be obligatory; consequently, the hearing of the two sounds *v* and *y* with a heavier effort would not occur in the alternative case.
But when the mention of Śākalya is present, the elision is made optional;
thereby, their hearing in that alternative case is established.

And thus there are three forms: one on the side of the lighter effort (*laghuprayatnatara*), a second on the side of elision (*lopa*), and a third on the side of the absence of both. Since there is no *va* following *o*, this rule will be understood as applying specifically to the *ya* that occurs at the end of a word (*padānta*); therefore he says: "of the *ya* following *o*.

Now, since the elision of the *ya* following *au* is already established by the preceding rule alone, for what purpose is this [present] commenced? To this he replies: "This commencement is for the sake of the *mit* designation (*mit-artho'yam ārambhaḥ*)."
If so, what is the purpose of mentioning Gārgya? To this he says: "The mention of Gārgya," and so forth.

In this section, since the elision (*lopa*) is prescribed as being of lighter articulation (*laghuprayatnatara*), one might ask: "Of which [elision] is this obligatory elision (*nityalopa*) the sublater? To this he says: "This which... and so forth. Alternatively, if this introduction were for the sake of making [the elision] obligatory, then the lighter articulation would not occur optionally; therefore he says: "This which... and so forth.

Because the optional elision (*lopavikalpa*) follows immediately [after the preceding rule], the intention is that its very cessation (*nivṛtti*) is what ought to be effected. Regarding the phrase "But some," etc.:

how can there be a sublation (*bādhana*) of that which possesses a lighter effort (*laghuprayatnatara*), even though it is desired, when—given its immediate proximity—it would be logical for this [present rule] to sublate the optional elision? There is no fault, because the entire set of operations (*kāryasamudāya*) involving *v* and *y* is required [by the present rule]. If it were to require only the optional elision, then that alone would be sublated, not the one with the lighter effort, because it would be separated by the elision.

But when, in a particular context, an operation is prescribed with reference to a collection [of sounds], then that very collection is excluded because of its immediate proximity. The inclusion of *t* (the *tapara* marker) is for the sake of avoiding ambiguity.

For if "oḥ" were stated [without the visarga], doubt would arise: "Is this a reference to the vowel *o* (okāra), or rather to the syllable *u* (ukāra)? It should not be so; since the rule "bho-bhago-agho-apūrvasya" [Pāṇini 8.3.17] is understood [as a governing rule], and there is no *u*-vowel in words such as "bhoḥ," how could there be any doubt? If that is the case, then [the visarga] is for the sake of ease of pronunciation (*mukhasukha*). Since [the desired form] is already established by the rule "uñi pada eva" [Pāṇini 8.3.19], [the mention of the visarga] is for the purpose of restriction (*niyamārtha*): [the substitution occurs] only before *uñ*, and not elsewhere. [The phrase] "preceded by *avaṛṇ*" [is used].

Since a *va* preceded by an *o* is impossible, and since [the substitution] for a *ya* preceded by an *a* is already established by the preceding rule, this elision (*lopa*) is understood to apply only to those preceded by an *a*-vowel; thus, it is stated "preceded by an *a*-vowel" (*avarṇapūrvayoḥ*).

Regarding "that *u*" (*sa u*): the word *tat* becomes *su* [by sandhi], then *tyadādyatvam* [is applied], then by Pāṇini 7.2.106 it becomes *saḥ*, then *rutvam* [is applied], then a *ya* is substituted for that *r*, and its elision occurs by this [rule].

Regarding the term *tantrayutam*: when the word *tantrya*, ending in the locative case, is followed by the word *uta* ending in the suffix *niṣṭhā* (the past passive participle suffix *kta*), the substitution of *ay* occurs. Now, one might object: "It is stated that this rule applies before the suffix *uñ* [as in the form *kāṃ-u*], but this is not *uñ* because of the absence of the letter *ñ*. Therefore, what is the purpose of including the mention of the word *pada* for the sake of excluding that case? To this, he says: "In the case of the root *veñ* when there is vocalization (*samprasāraṇa*)," and so forth.
The *samprasāraṇa* substitution, however, occurs by [the rule] *vacisvapi-* (Pāṇini 6.1.15) and so forth.
Thus far, the purpose of including the term *pada* has been shown without regard for the existence of the specific nipāta *uñ*.
But when its existence is taken into account, he says—"for the sake of what follows"—in order to demonstrate another purpose.

The rule *ṅamo hrasvādaci ṅamuṇ nityam* [Pāṇini 8.3.32] is intended so that the suffix *ṅamuṭ* occurs before a word beginning with a vowel, but not here in the case of *paramadaṇḍin*.
