If this were for the sake of the subsequent rule, why was it not formulated right there? What, then, is the advantage of doing it here? The advantage is that the status of being *svarita* is not declared. Even if it were done here, the fact that one need not rely on the *lakṣaṇapratipadokta-paribhāṣā* (Vyāḍi-paribhāṣā 3) remains the same.

The letter *ca* is for the purpose of indicating that which is preceded by the vowel *a*; otherwise, because [the vowels] *hrasva* and *dīrgha* (*hrotaḥ*) are not immediately followed [by *ya*], one might understand the elision (*lopa*) to apply to the *ya* that follows them. This is not the case; for if it were understood in this way, this sūtra would be entirely purposeless, since the result would already be established by the preceding rule.

It is not purposeless, however, because it serves as a restrictive rule (*niyamārtha*): so that the elision occurs only when *uṅ* (the vocative ending) follows a word (*pada*), as in "bho u padacyati.
If this restrictive purpose did not exist, the elision would occur invariably even in cases such as "bho yutam" and "bhago yutam."

If, however, this *u* is the inclusion of the particle *uñ*, then there is nothing to be excluded by the restrictive rule; therefore, in relation to what precedes it, the particle *ca* should be understood as having the sense of conjunction (*samuccaya*). The letter *ñ* in *uñ* is for the sake of avoiding ambiguity. For if that were absent, the reference would be "au" in the locative case (*saptamī*), and consequently, a doubt might arise: "Is this a reference to the vowel *u*, or to the vowel *ū*? Thus, ambiguity would result.

But even if that [term] were employed, would there not still be a doubt as to whether the inclusion of the particle *uñ* is intended, or rather the inclusion of the *ñ* from *ukārāt* up to *jhabhañ* (Mā. Sū. 8)? It is not so; first, you must be asked this: does the obligatory elision apply only to those consonants (*hal*) included within the pratyāhāra *uñ*, or to others as well? What should be said here? "To others as well. For he will state this later: [Pāṇini 8.3.22].

If that were the case, then if a pratyāhāra were intended to be included here, one would have used the letter *c* in the rule *eauc* (Mā. Sū. 4) to form the pratyāhāra, as in the rule *uci ca pade*. Furthermore, regarding the rule *hali api*, it would be covered by the rule *hali sarveṣām*.
In that case too, this purpose is achieved: doubt is eliminated.

Alternatively, if the intention here were to include the *u*-class vowels (*u*, *ū*, *ū3*) by means of the pratyāhāra *uÑ*, [the author] would have formed this single rule as `uli ca pade sarveṣām`, having taken the pratyāhāra *ul* by means of the letter *l*. Indeed, we do not see any purpose for the division of the rules (*yogavibhāga*).
Therefore, the inclusion of the *u*-class vowels (*u*, *ū*, *ū3*) via a pratyāhāra is not intended here.

Therefore, it is beyond doubt that this refers exclusively to the particle *uñ*. This is because, in the rule "of *bho*, *bhago*, *agho*, and that preceded by *a*," a *v* sound preceded by *bho*, *bhago*, or *agho* is impossible;
however, a *v* sound preceded by an *a*-vowel is possible.

However, it has already been shown by the rule *hali sarveṣām* that elision does not occur for that [visarga]. Therefore, in this case, only the *yakāra* is understood and not the *vakāra*, as it has been shown that its elision does not take place in such rules as *bho-bhago-agho-apūrvasya* (Pāṇini 8.3.17). In that context, what is the purpose of including the mention of *aś*? It is so that this elision prescribed by *hali sarveṣām* may occur when followed by a consonant (*hal*) after an *aś* vowel, but it should not occur here: *vṛkṣa vṛścati* becomes *vṛkṣavṛṭ*; from this, with the causative suffix (*ṇic*), we have *vṛkṣavayati*; and from *vṛkṣavayati* with the deletion of the suffix (*apratyaya*), we get *vṛkṣav*. Thus, one might say: *vṛkṣav karoti*.

Thus, by demonstrating the purpose of the inclusion of *aś*, it is stated by this very rule that the elision (*lopa*) of the letter *v* preceded by a vowel (*avaṇa*) does not occur before a consonant (*hal*) in the case of the *āśis* suffix.

Now, one might object: "Is it not improper for the term 'preceded by a vowel' (*avaṇapūrvasya*) to be carried over [from the previous rule], since it was not explicitly drawn forward (*anukṛṣṭa*) in the preceding rule? Therefore, how can there be an elision of what is preceded by a vowel? This is not so; for the statement "that which is drawn forward from a preceding rule does not carry over to the subsequent one" (Vyāḍiparibhāṣā 76) is merely a general tendency (*prāyika*).

How is this known? In the rule [8.4.12], although *ṇaḥ* is already established by context, the word *ṇaḥ* is mentioned again. This is done to exclude the optionality (*vā*) that was carried over from [8.4.10]. If this were not a general principle (*prāyika*), the repetition of *ṇaḥ* would be purposeless; for since the optionality (*vā*) would not be carried over due to its being drawn back in the preceding rule, what would be the point of repeating *ṇaḥ*? Yet it is repeated, and from this it is understood that the paribhāṣā regarding "that which is drawn back" (*anukṛṣṭa*) is not universally obligatory (*anitya*). Thus: "So that the elision (*lopa*) may also occur according to Śākaṭāyana."

Because of the word *api* (also), [the rule applies] to Śākalya as well. However, if the term *sarva* (all) were not included, it would be understood that the elision (*lopa*) applies only according to the opinion of Gārgya, who is proximate [to Śākalya]. The term *pada* is a genitive of location (*sthāna-ṣaṣṭhī*). That *pada* is qualified by the letter *m*; and because of the qualification, the rule of "ending-in-that" (*tadanta-vidhi*) applies. Thus, when the substitution of *anusvāra* is prescribed for a word ending in *m*, by the paribhāṣā *alo’ntyasya* [Pāṇini 1.1.52], it is understood to apply to the final *m* itself. Therefore, he says: “of a word ending in *m*” (or, according to the *Kāśikā* and *Padamañjarī*: “of the final *m* of a word”). “Of the word.”
Thus [ends the previous rule]. The word *hali* has ceased to apply, because of the mention of *jhal*.
The letter *ca* is for the purpose of carrying forward the letter *m*.

For if that were not present, there might be the apprehension that since an *ikāra* (the vowel *i*) not at the end of a word is being taken here as the subject of the operation, the letter *m* has been excluded.
Regarding "payāṃsi":
[the suffix] *num* is applied by [Pāṇini 7.1.20], and [the vowel] is lengthened by [Pāṇini 6.4.10].
Regarding "ākraṃsyate": [it is derived from the root *kram* with the prefix *ā*].

From the root *kram* preceded by the prefix *āṅ*, the suffix *lṛṭ* is applied; the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) is used according to [Pāṇini 1.3.40], "The prefix *āṅ* [is used] in the sense of exertion.
Thus, one says *ācikraṃsate*.
The middle voice is used here according to [Pāṇini 1.3.62], "The desiderative suffix *san* follows the same rules as the original verb."
The same applies here in the case of *athijigāṃsate*:

after the root *iṅ* followed by the suffix *san*, there is the substitution of *gam* by the rule *iṅaśca* [Pāṇini 2.4.48]; then, by the rule *ata upadhāyāḥ* [Pāṇini 7.2.116], there is lengthening; then reduplication and the operations pertaining to the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsakārya*). [The form] *rājan* [is derived as follows].

From the root *rāj* with the suffix *śatṛ*, followed by the vocative case ending, there is elision according to Pāṇini 6.1.68 (*halṅyābbhyo dīrghāt sutisyapṛktaṃ hal*). Thus, "samrāṭ. From the root *rāj* preceded by the prefix *sam*, the suffix *kvip* is applied according to Pāṇini 3.2.61 (*satsūdviṣadruhaduhayujavidabhidachidajinīrājām uṣṇik-kvib-antānāṃ ca*), resulting in *samrāj*. By Pāṇini 8.2.36 (*vraścabhrasjasṛjamṛjayajarājabhrājacchaśāṃ ṣaḥ*), the change to *ṣ* occurs; the *ṣ* undergoes the *jaś*-change to *ḍ*, and that *ḍ* undergoes the *car*-change to *ṭ*.
Thus, "samrāṭ. Regarding "sābhrājyam": [it is derived from the root *bhrāj* with the prefix *sa-*].
Is it because [the preceding vowel] belongs to the *brāhmaṇa*-class and so forth? It is a consonant (*vyañjana*).
But for what purpose is the letter *m* pronounced again? To this he says: "The utterance of *m* for the sake of *m*" and so forth.
By the rule [Pāṇini 8.3.23], an *anusvāra* would result; so that this [substitution] may not occur, the letter *m* is prescribed for the letter *m*.

If this is so, then the prohibition "na" (not) should be stated, for in this way the sūtra becomes concise by not having to utter the case-ending. [Objection: If that is the case, then is this indicated by the rule for the insertion of *m* through the addition of the specific instruction? [Response: It indicates that in this context, an additional rule applies. Thus, it is established that when *y*, *v*, or *l* follow, *y*, *v*, or *l* may optionally occur—as in the word *saṃyat*.

From the root *yam* preceded by *sam*, the suffix *kvip* is applied; the letter *m* is elided by the rule *anudāttopadeśa...* [Pāṇini 6.4.37], and the augment *tuk* is added to the vowel *a* by the rule *ata upadhāyāḥ* [Pāṇini 6.1.71]. The term *maḥ paraḥ* is a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "that after which *m* follows.

To the question "What [is it]? the answer is *hralayati*. Regarding the roots *hvala* and *hrala* meaning "to move" (Dhātupāṭha 805, 806), the designation *mit* is optionally applied by the rule *jvalahvalahralanamāmanupasargādvā* [Gaṇasūtra following Dhātupāṭha 817]; consequently, the vowel is shortened by the rule *mitāṃ hrasvaḥ* [Pāṇini 6.4.92].

Regarding the phrase "yavalapare" and so forth: that which has *ya*, *va*, or *la* following it is called *yavalapara*; in such a case, the meaning of the rule is to be explained as "the *ya*, *va*, or *la* optionally [occur] in place of the letter *m*. As for the explanation itself, it has already been provided previously.

And why are these *yavals* [the nasalized *ya*, *va*, and *la*] of yours [taught] due to internal similarity (*āntaratamya*)? They are indeed nasalized (*sānunāsika*). Is it because of the mention of the option (*vāvacana*)? In that case, the *anusvāra* certainly occurs as an alternative. Now, why was it not simply stated as "before *bha*" (*he bhaḥ*)? For in that way, the mention of the subsequent element (*paragrahaṇa*) would not have to be made; for its purpose would be conveyed by the locative case itself—namely, "the vowel *a* which occurs before the letter *m*. This is not so; if it were stated as "before *ma*" (*he maḥ*), the reverse would also be understood—namely, "the letter *m* followed by the letter *ha*"—and consequently, [the rule] would apply only in cases such as *kimahnaḥ*.

If it is argued that [the rule] will not apply because of the intervention of the letter *a*, we say no; for according to the principle, "that by which there is no intervention applies even when there is intervention" (*Vyāḍipāda* 46), an intervention by a single phoneme is accepted, but not one by multiple phonemes.

If it is asked: "What of the first position? In cases such as *hralayati*, the rule has already served its purpose; therefore, it is not possible to rely on an intervention [of more than one letter]," we say no. For one who has understood the meaning of the sūtra to be that the letter *m* [is substituted] in the word *hakāra*, no other alternative is possible for him.

Therefore, the mention of *para* (following) must indeed be made so that there may be no misconception regarding the contrary. The term *naḥ* is a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "that which follows *na*. The mention of *para* is for the purpose of ensuring that [the substitution] occurs when *na* is followed by a *nakāra*; otherwise, if it were stated simply as *ne naḥ*, it would be understood that the substitution applies only when a solitary *nakāra* follows, because *na* is introduced as a distinct cause. [Objection: Does this not result in the removal of the word *he*? [Response: This is not the case; for if it were so, this statement would be rendered meaningless.
Is the *nakāra* established by the rule *kṛte hranuttvāre nakāre parataḥ* (P. 8.4.58)? True; this [mention of *para*] is for the sake of providing an option (*vikalpa*).

For here, when the *nakāra* is not applied by this [rule], then by the force of the statement (*vacanasāmarthyāt*), it is established that the *parasavarṇa* does not occur; thus the option is achieved. Therefore, the mention of *para* must be made so that [the rule applies] when *hakāra* is followed by *na*, but not when it is alone.
Regarding the form *kin hnute*:
the root *hnuṅ* means "to remove" (*apanayane*; Dhātupāṭha 1082); due to its belonging to the *adādi* class, there is elision of the *śap* suffix.

Here, some raise the objection: "Why is it not understood as the prohibitive particle *na*? This is incorrect, because the word is read with a *visarga*, and a *visarga* cannot logically occur after a *nakāra* that expresses a prohibition.

Furthermore, even if it is read without the visarga (*avisarga*), the apprehension of a prohibition remains unjustified because there is no possibility [of the rule applying]. *Ṅ* and *ṇ* are those two, *ṅṇau*; *ka* and *ṭa* are those two, *kaṭau*. Each of these is connected with the letter *u* and the letter *k* respectively—thus, *ku-ṭ-gi-ti*.
The letter *u* is for the sake of pronunciation (*uccāraṇārtha*), and the letter *k* is for the sake of prescribing the place of articulation (*deśavidhyartha*).
[The example is: *prāṅk śete*.
The word *prāk* has been explained in [Pāṇini 8.2.62]. Regarding the form *vaṇṭ chete*: it is derived from the root *vaṇ* with the suffix *vic*.
But for what purpose are these two made from the beginning of the preceding element (*pūrvāntāt*)? To this he says: “*pūrvāntakaraṇam*,” etc.

Furthermore, what is the reason that *chatvam* occurs when it belongs to the beginning of the preceding element (*pūrvāntatve*), and not when it belongs to the end of the following element (*parāditve*)? To this he says: “*śaścho’ṭi*,” etc.
But for what purpose is this understood? [The Kāśikā reading is *vijñāyeta*]. To this he says: “*iha*,” etc.

If the rule *padāntājjhayaḥ* [Pāṇini 8.2.10] were not applied there, then in the word *virapśin*, the substitution of *ch* would be understood to apply; however, when it is understood in this way, it does not occur, because there is no *jhay* at the end of a word here.

In the form *viriṣśin*, the suffix *śatṛ* replaces the *lṛṭ* (future) by the rule *lṛṭaḥ sadvā* [Pāṇini 3.3.14], and then, by the rule *sya-sic-sīyuṭ-tāsiṣu* [Pāṇini 7.3.96], the *s* of the suffix *syap* is replaced by *ś*, and the *y* is replaced by *i*.

Regarding the example *prāṅk sāyaḥ*: if [the augment] were *parādi* (belonging to the subsequent element), then the prohibition by *naśca* [8.3.111] would not apply to the *ṣatva* (substitution of *ṣ* for *s*) that would otherwise be required by *iṇkoḥ* [8.3.57] and *ādeśapratyayayoḥ* [8.3.59], because it would not be at the beginning of a word (*apadāditvāt*). [The correct form is] *praṅk sāyaḥ*. Regarding the example *vaṇṭk sāyaḥ*: [the same logic applies].

In this case as well, the prohibition by rule 8.4.42 would not apply to the *ṣṭutva* obtained by rule 8.4.41, because [the letter *ḍ*] is not at the end of a word (*apadānta*). Therefore, in forms such as *prāṅkśeta*, the treatment of the suffix as part of the preceding element (*pūrvānta*) is performed for the sake of establishing the substitution of *cha* and so forth. Regarding the principle that "when there is a mention of both [cases], the mention of the ablative (*pañcamī*) is stronger" (Śākaṭāyana Paribhāṣā 97), since the ablative *ṅaḥ* is stronger than the locative *sī*, the locative is interpreted as a genitive, and the *dhuṭ* augment is prescribed for the letter *ś* itself. Thus he says: "from that which ends in *ḍ*" and so forth.
If this is so, what is the purpose of the locative mention? It is for the sake of brevity (*lāghava*).
If it were stated as *ṅaḥ so dhuṭ*, there would be the disadvantage of prolixity (*gaurava*) due to the addition of the letter *dh*.

Now, why is this seventh-case (*saptamī*) indication not understood to mean "when a rule applies to something, it applies to that which begins with it," according to the principle *yasmin vidhistadādāvalgrahaṇe* (Vyākaraṇa-paribhāṣā 127)? Because that [application] is established simply by the absence of a solitary *s* [at the beginning of a word], since the governing term *pada* is in force.

In the case of *āliṭatyāya*, once *dhuṭ* is applied, the *c*-substitution (*cartva*) of the letter *dh* results in the letter *t*. However, although *tuṭ* could have been prescribed for the sake of brevity in the process (*prakriyālāghava*), the mention of *dhuṭ* is for the sake of subsequent rules—so that when the rule *naśca* (Pāṇini 8.3.30) applies, it may be *dhuṭ* and not *tuṭ*.

If it were so, what would follow? In the case of *bhavānsāya*, would the substitution of *ru* not apply by [Pāṇini 8.3.7], *naśchavyapraśāna*? This is not the case; for the condition *ampare* (when followed by *am*) does not recur here, and there is no *t* sound here that is followed by *am*.

Now, might it be argued that even here the *t* is followed by *am* by virtue of having previously been an *u* sound? Even so, because the augment *tuṭ* is not yet established (*asiddha*), the substitution of *ru* will not occur.
Therefore, the augment *tuṭ* alone must be prescribed.
If that is so, then the mention of *dhuṭ* is for the sake of variety.

Now, for what purpose is *dhuṭ* [stated]? Why is it made as a subsequent element (*parādi*), rather than being made as a prior element (*pūrvānta*) simply as *dyuṭ*? For if it were so, the mention of *tug* in rule 8.3.31 would not need to be made, since *dyuṭ* alone would be carried over there. To this he says: "The making of it a subsequent element," and so forth. If it were made a prior element, then in the form *āliṭtsāya*, the *ṣṭutva* substitution would apply to the *dhuk*.

However, since the status of being a word-final (*padāntatva*) has not been prescribed for the letter *ṭ* in the case of *parādi-karaṇa*, the prohibition [of doubling] by [Pāṇini 8.4.42] is established. For that purpose, *parādi-karaṇa* is employed. The letter *ca* is for the purpose of carrying forward (*anukarṣaṇa*) the term *dhuṭ*. Now, one might object: "But surely it will be carried forward simply because it is marked with a *svarita* accent, and it will not be carried forward in what follows because another augment is introduced or because it lacks the *svarita* mark. This is true; however, there would be excessive cognitive burden (*pratipatti-gaurava*) for those of dull intellect.

Now, regarding the form *bhavānsāya*, why does the substitution of *ru* not occur by [Pāṇini 8.2.7], which states that *ru* is substituted for a *dhuṭ* [consonant] when followed by a *cari* [consonant]? To this he says: "Because both the *dhuṭ* and the *cartva* are *asiddha*," and so forth.

If there were *asiddhatva* (non-application) only of the *cartva* or only of the *dhuṭ*, even then the occurrence of *rutva* would be impossible; how much more so when both are *asiddha*? The mention of both is intended to demonstrate the absolute impossibility of the occurrence of *rutva*. In some places, the reading is: "Because of the *asiddhatva* of the *dhuṭ* and the *cartva*."

In this case as well, the following meaning should be understood: for even without the particle *ca*, that meaning is understood, as in the sentence beginning with "day after day leading away a cow, a horse, a man, or an animal.
Alternatively, the meaning of this reading is: "because the substitution of *c* for *t* (*cartva*) is considered non-existent (*asiddha*) when it comes to the *dhuṭ* augment.

[Objection: But isn't the *dhuṭ* augment itself also non-existent? Why, then, is the non-existence of the substitution of *c* for *t* mentioned, and then again the non-existence of the *dhuṭ*? [Response: This is not so; for even if the *dhuṭ* were present, without the substitution of *c* for *t*, the occurrence of the *ru*-substitution (*rutva*) would simply not take place.

The sense is this: it is appropriate to raise the objection regarding the substitution of *ru* because that [substitution] is dependent on the existence of something else; however, since the substitution of *ru* is declared to occur when followed by an *am*-sound (*ampare*) before a *chv*-sound (*chavi*), and such a condition does not exist here, how can the substitution of *ru* be questioned even though the substitution of *ca* is *asiddha*? This doubt is raised on the grounds that the status of being followed by an *am*-sound (*amparatva*) exists by virtue of a preceding *u* that has already occurred.

But surely, when there is no present [application], one resorts to what has occurred previously (*bhūtapūrva*); is there not a present state of being followed by *am* elsewhere for the substitution of *ru*? This is true; however, this was stated by way of superimposition (*adhyāropya*). He thinks as follows: "Let it be granted that being followed by *am* would result from the previously mentioned *u*; [nevertheless,] he says, 'because the *dhuṭ* augment is not established here'. The locative case in *śi*, which has not yet fulfilled its purpose, effects a change of the ablative case in *naḥ*—which had fulfilled its purpose in the preceding rule—into a genitive case.

Because of the statement [Pāṇini 1.1.66], it is understood that the letter *n* alone is the augment (*āgama*); thus he says: "of that which ends in *n*," and so forth. Now, for what purpose is *tuk* made a prior-final element (*pūrvānta*), rather than the previously mentioned *dhuṭ* being made a posterior-initial element (*parādi*)? Even so, would it not be established by the rule of *cartya* (the substitution of *c* for *t*)? To this he replies: "The making of it a prior-final element," and so forth. "Prior-final" means the end of the preceding [element]; furthermore, by the context, *tuk* is understood. Its "making" = its prescription, is for the sake of ensuring that the substitution of *ch* (*chatva*) occurs.
If *dhuṭ* alone were prescribed as the original element (*prakṛta*), then the substitution of *ch* according to [Pāṇini 8.4.63] would not occur;
the reason for this has already been stated previously.
"If it is so," and so forth.

If the *tuk* augment is applied as a prior element (*pūrvānta*), then in the form *kurvaṃś-cete*, the letter *n* would undergo the substitution of *ṇ* by the rule *aṭ-ku-pvāṅ-num-vyavāye ’pi* [Pāṇini 8.4.2], because the *tuk* prevents the status of being a word-final (*padāntatā*). However, if it is treated as a subsequent element (*parādi*), this fault does not arise; for, according to the principle that "the prohibition of *ṇatva* applies when [the cause] follows" [Pāṇini 8.4.37], the substitution of *ṇ* is blocked. The intention is as follows: while the word *neti* ("not") is understood from the preceding sūtra [8.4.34], a separate rule (*yogavibhāga*) is made with [8.4.40]. By means of this, in the case of *kurvaṃś-cete*, where there is a connection with the *ca*-group (the palatals), the substitution of *ṇ* does not occur at all.

But surely, even if the *yogavibhāga* (separation of rules) is not performed, the substitution of *ṇ* would still apply, because here there is no connection with the *ca*-class [consonants], since the substitution of *ś* for *t* (*ścutva*) is considered *asiddha* (non-existent for the purposes of the preceding rule)? [Answer: No fault arises, because by the force of performing the *yogavibhāga*, the prohibition of *ṇatva* will occur despite the *asiddha* status of *ścutva*. In the expressions "imaḥ" and "ṅamuṭaḥ," both are references to *pratyāhāras* (abbreviated terms).
The element *uṭ* is connected individually with each of the letters beginning with *ṅ*.

The term *hrasvāt* is a qualifier for *ṅam*. Although *ṅam* is qualified by *hrasva*, it is also a qualifier of the word (*pada*). And because a rule involving a suffix applies to that which ends with the qualified element, it is understood as "from a word ending in [a ṅam-]". Even though the word *padasya* is established in the genitive case, it is nevertheless transformed here into the ablative case for the sake of the sense—according to the principle: "In the mention of two cases, the ablative mention is stronger" (Śākaṭāyana Paribhāṣā 97). By means of the ablative *ṅamaḥ*, the locative *aci* is mentally converted into a genitive, whereby the vowel (*ac*) itself becomes the recipient of the augment.

The mention of the seventh case (locative), however, is for the sake of brevity and for the sake of what follows; having kept all this in mind, he says: "from that which ends in a *ṅam* which follows a short vowel. For here, a correspondence according to numerical order (*saṃkhyātānudeśa*) is to be understood, because the number of the substitutes (*āgaminaḥ*) and the augments (*āgamānām*) is equal.
As in the example: *pratyaṅṅāste*.
The root *ās* is used in the sense of "sitting" (Dhātupāṭha 1021); due to its belonging to the *adādi* class, there is elision of the *śap* suffix.
Thus, one says "he sits drawing" (*kṛṣan āste*).
The root *kṛṣ* is used in the sense of "plowing" (Dhātupāṭha 990); it belongs to the *tudādi* class, and the suffix *śatṛ* is applied.

Now, regarding the form *paramadaṇḍinā*: when the compound *paramadaṇḍin* is formed by [Pāṇini 2.1.61] *sanmahat* etc., why does the augment *nuṭ* not occur after the final *ṅa*-class letter (*n*) in the third case singular? For here, even though the preceding element is a *bha*-stem by [Pāṇini 1.4.18], the *ṅa*-class letter—the letter *n*—is followed by a short vowel (*i*) at the end of the compound; and although the case-ending following this *daṇḍin-* has been elided, the term "word" (*pada*) is still applicable to it by the rule of "characteristic of an affix" (*pratyayalakṣaṇa*, Pāṇini 1.1.62). Thus, since the third case singular ending follows a word ending in a vowel, there would seem to be an occasion for the application of *ṅamuṭ*. To this, he says: "*paramadaṇḍinā*" and so forth.

The meaning of the sentence is this: when the designation "uttarapada" (subsequent member) is to be applied, the *pratyayalakṣaṇa* (the rule that a suffix-endings still function as such) does not apply in any operation other than those prescribed for the beginning of a word (*padādi*).

Since the *pratyayalakṣaṇa* does not apply here, the technical term "pada" is not assigned to *daṇḍinā*. Consequently, the augment *ṅamuṭ*, which is prescribed to follow a word-final [consonant], does not occur.
Thus, first of all, the resolution has been stated according to the opinion of Kātyāyana.
Now, in order to demonstrate that which is according to the opinion of the author of the Sūtras, he says: "Or rather," and so forth.

Since the word *pade* is understood [from the previous rule] and *pada* is being qualified here, by the principle "in a rule where there is a mention of 'that which begins with X,' the operation applies to that which begins with X" (Vārttika 14), the grammatical operation must apply to a *pada* beginning with a vowel (*aj-ādi*). However, in this case, there is no *pada* beginning with a vowel; therefore, how could there be the possibility of the insertion of *nuṭ*? Now, what is the purpose of the mention of *nitya* ("obligatory")? One might argue that since the word *vā* ("optionally") occurs in the subsequent sūtra (Pāṇini 8.3.33), the present rule will be understood as an obligatory one. This is true; however, [if *nitya* were not mentioned here], the status of obligatoriness would also be understood for the preceding sūtra (Pāṇini 8.3.31). Thus, the mention of *nitya* is necessary to ensure that the distinction between the two rules is maintained.

Why is this? The term "nitya" (always) is included for the purpose of indicating that the word "vā" (optionally) continues from the preceding sūtras, starting from [8.3.26]. The term "mayaḥ" refers to the *pratyāhāra* (abbreviated designation), and not to the verbal root *aya*, *vaya*, or *maya*.
Why is this so? Because of the principle of pervasion (*vyāpti*).

For what purpose is this stated, given that the *v* of *uñ* is already established by [Pāṇini 6.1.77]? If it is argued that it is for the sake of providing an option (*vikalpa*), one might think: "If [the rule] *iko yaṇ aci* were obligatory (*nitya*), then this statement would indeed be for the sake of an option. But this is not so; for the word *vā* from [Pāṇini 6.1.76] will be carried over (*anuvartate*), and that is understood as a restricted option (*vyavasthita-vibhāṣā*). Therefore, he says "because of its being a *pragṛhya*" and so forth, to show that the *yaṇ* substitution occurs optionally for *uñ*. Its status as a *pragṛhya*, moreover, is due to the prescription of the technical term *pragṛhya* by [Pāṇini 1.1.17]: *uñaḥ*.
When that [substitution] occurs, the status of the original form (*prakṛtibhāva*) would apply by rule 6.1.125. Since that would result, the substitution of *v* is prescribed.

Even so, immediately after the rule "iko yaṇ aci" (6.1.77), the *yaṇ* for *uṅ*—namely *v*—should simply be prescribed; for in this way, the word "va" need not be used, because *yaṇ* is the subject under discussion. Furthermore, the mention of "vā" need not be made, as the term "vā" from rule 6.1.76 follows here by means of "frog-leap" (*maṇḍūkapluti*). To this he replies: "Because it is not established," and so forth.

In that case, when *hrucyamāne* is uttered, since the substitution of *v* is established (siddha), the anusvāra prescribed before a consonant (*hal*) would occur; however, this is not desired. Therefore, it is performed right here. When it is performed here, the anusvāra for *m* does not occur, because the substitution of *v* is not yet established (*asiddha*). "The word *khari* is understood to carry over" means: *hrucyamāne* → *hrucyamāne* (by the rule *anaci ca*, where *m* becomes *anusvāra* before a consonant). *hrucyamāne* → *hrucyamāne* (by the rule *mo'nusvāraḥ*). *hrucyamāne* → *hrucyamāne* (by the rule *vā padāntasya*). *hrucyamāne* → *hrucyamāne* (by the rule *anusvārasya yayi parasavarṇaḥ*). *hrucyamāne* → *hrucyamāne* (by the rule *vā padāntasya*). *hrucyamāne* → *hrucyamāne* (by the rule *khari ca*). *hrucyamāne* → *hrucyamāne* (by the rule *vā padāntasya*). *hrucyamāne* → *hrucyamāne* (by the rule *anusvārasya yayi parasavarṇaḥ*). *hrucyamāne* → *hrucyamāne* (by the rule *vā padāntasya*). *hrucyamāne* → *hrucyamāne* (by the rule *khari ca*). *hrucyamāne* → *hrucyamāne* (by the rule *vā padāntasya*). *hrucyamāne* → *hrucyamāne* (by the rule *anusvārasya yayi parasavarṇaḥ*). *hrucyamāne* → *hrucyamāne* (by the rule *vā padāntasya*). *hrucyamāne* → *hrucyamāne* (by the rule *khari ca*). *hrucyamāne* → *hrucyamāne* (by the rule *vā padāntasya*). *hrucyamāne* → *hrucyamāne* (by the rule *anusvārasya yayi parasavarṇaḥ*). *hrucyamāne* → *hrucyamāne* (by the rule *vā padāntasya*). *hrucyamāne* → *hrucyamāne* (by the rule *khari ca*). *hrucyamāne* → *hrucyamāne* (by the rule *vā padāntasya*). *hrucyamāne* → *hrucyamāne* (by the rule *anusvārasya yayi parasavarṇaḥ*). *hrucyamāne* → *hrucyamāne* The recurrence (*anuvṛtti*) of the rule *khar-avasānayor visarjanīyaḥ* [Pāṇini 8.3.15] should be understood either by the "frog-leap" method (*maṇḍūkapluti*) or through its own inherent connection; otherwise, the operation would be understood as applying to *khari* even in the preceding rule [8.3.33]. The term *śar* is a bahuvrīhi compound meaning "that after which *śar* [the sibilants] follow. Now, for what purpose is the mention of *para* ("following") used? Could it not simply be stated as *śari*? It is impossible to state it thus; for if it were stated in that way, only *śar* itself would be understood as the cause (*nimitta*), and not *khari*, due to the recurrence [of *khari* from the previous rule] and because of the prescription *vā śari* [8.3.36].

In that case, a reversal might be understood—namely, that [the rule applies] only where there is a *ś* sound; and thus [the rule] would apply only in cases such as *nityaḥ sphoṭaḥ* and *puruṣaḥ sthūlaḥ*, but not in cases such as *vāsaḥ kṣaumam*. Therefore, the word *para* is included so that such a reversal is not understood. Now, for what purpose is *visarjanīya* mentioned? One might simply say "not" (*na*), for when the prohibition of the *s* sound is established, the *visarjanīya* will remain in its own form. To this he says: "Of the *visarjanīya*" and so forth.

The modification (*vikāra*) of that *visarjanīya* consists of the *jihvāmūlīya* and other such sounds; the mention of *visarjanīya* is for the purpose of excluding those. Otherwise, if only "not" (*na*) were stated, then according to the principle that "a rule or a prohibition applies only to what is immediately preceding" (*Vyākaraṇa-paribhāṣā* 29), it would be understood as applying only to the *sakāra*. Consequently, the *jihvāmūlīya* and other modifications would still occur in place of the *visarjanīya*. However, when *visarjanīya* is explicitly mentioned, [the modification] does not occur precisely by the force of that very mention. Thus: "and the *visarjanīya*."

By this, he shows that the letter *ca* is for the purpose of drawing in (*anukarṣaṇa*) the *visarjanīya*. Alternatively, one might argue: "The mention of *atha* (in Pāṇini 8.3.17) should be understood as recurring [here]; why then should the *jihvāmūlīya* and *upadhmānīya* not be treated as optional? And in this way, the letter *ca* would not need to be used for the purpose of drawing in the *visarjanīya*; for when these two are excluded, the *visarjanīya* itself will occur in that alternative case? This is not so; for in this manner, it would apply only when followed by *śap* and *rap*, and only when *kup* follows. However, in the case where they are not followed by *śap* and *rap*, the rule *aśarpare vā* (Pāṇini 8.3.34) would result in the substitution of *sakāra* (*s*) in that alternative case.
Therefore, the letter *ca* must be added [to the rule].

Here, since the letters *ka* and *pa*—which are the jihvāmūlīya and upadhmānīya—are pronounced in the sūtra, someone might have the doubt: "Are these two [letters] understood to be substitutes for the *visarjanīya*? In order to dispel that doubt, he says: "The letters *ka* and *pa* are for the purpose of pronunciation.
The sense is that it would be impossible to pronounce those two [substitutes] without these [two letters].
What kind of substitutes (*ādeśau*) are those two? To this he says: "The *jihvāmūlīya* and *upadhmānīya* alone are the substitutes.
The word "but" (*tu*) indicates a distinction from the two composite forms of substitutes that were previously suspected.
The particle "only" (*eva*) serves for the purpose of restriction.

The meaning is that the *jihvāmūlīya* and *upadhmānīya* sounds occur only in their individual forms, and not as parts of a composite unit. Since every possible subject here is already occupied by another rule, [the rule] *visarjanīyasya saḥ* [Pāṇini 8.3.34] would have no scope; therefore, just as in examples such as *vṛkṣaḥ karoti*, this rule [8.3.34] is superseded and the rule *kupvoḥ ka pau ca* [8.3.37] applies, why does one not ask: "In cases such as *vāsaḥ kṣaumam* and *adbhiḥ psātam*, why does this rule [8.3.35], *śarpare*, not also supersede [the former]? To one who might raise such an objection, he replies:

"—*visarjanīyasya*," etc. This [rule] is commenced whether [the previous rule] has already applied or has not yet applied. It applies where it has already applied, as in *vāsaḥ kṣaumam* ("linen garment") and *adbhiḥ psātam* ("eaten with water"); and it applies where it has not yet applied, as in *vṛkṣaḥ karoti* ("the tree does") and *vṛkṣaḥ pacati* ("the tree cooks")."

Since this [rule] would otherwise apply everywhere, its qualification is thus established because it is prescribed for the case of *kha* alone; therefore, this is an exception to that very rule, and not to any other injunction, as the definition of an exception is inapplicable with respect to the latter.

It might be argued: "In the rule *śarpare visarjanīyasya* (P. 8.3.35), a *khar* followed by a *śar* other than the *ka*-class and *pa*-class is the scope for the *visarjanīya*; whereas in the rule *kupvoḥ ka pau ca* (P. 8.3.37), the *ka*-class and *pa*-class not followed by a *śar* are the scope. Thus, in examples such as *vāsaḥ kṣaumam* and *adbhiḥ psatam*, both rules would apply. In such a case of conflict (*vipratiṣedha*), according to the principle *paraṃ kāryam* (P. 1.4.2), it would be proper for the *jihvāmūlīya* and *upadhmānīya* to occur, overriding the *visarjanīya*. To this he replies with the words "*pūrvatrāsiddhe*" and so forth. He provides the justification for this very point with the statement "*abhāvād uttarasya*" ("because of the non-existence of the subsequent [rule]").

A conflict arises when two rules of equal strength apply simultaneously to the same object; however, there is no simultaneous application here, because while the preceding rule is yet to be applied, the succeeding one is non-existent due to its lack of established status. The particle *iti* indicates a reason:

since there is no conflict (*vipratiṣedha*) when the preceding rule is not yet established, therefore, in the cases of *vāsaḥ kṣaumam* and *adbhiḥ psātam*, only the rule [8.3.35] applies, and not the rules for the *jihvāmūlīya* and *upadhmānīya* sounds.

Regarding the phrase "some" (*kecit*) and so forth: *vāsaḥ* means linen cloth (*kṣauma*). In the rule *adbhiḥ psātam*, they perform a split of the rule (*yogavibhāga*) in the rule *kupvoḥ ka pau ca* for the purpose that the *visarjanīya* should occur. They state: there is one rule, *kupvoḥ*, and a second rule, *ka pau*. In the former rule, the word *visarjanīyaḥ* from [Pāṇini 8.3.34] is understood as a carry-over (*anuvartate*).
Therefore, after *ś* and *r*, when followed by *k* or *p*, only the *visarjanīya* occurs, and not the *jihvāmūlīya* or *upadhmānīya*. This is an exception (*apavāda*) to the preceding rule.

The term "not at the beginning of a word" (*apadādau*) is in the singular number by way of a substitution for the dual (of the two letters *k* and *p*); otherwise, it would not be possible for "not being at the beginning of a word" to qualify *k* and *p*.

When there is duality [of suffixes], one should apply the rule "before *apa* and so forth. The phrase "in the case of *pāśa*, *kalpa*, *ka*, and *kāmya*" is an illustration of possible instances, not an exhaustive enumeration, because there is nothing else to be excluded.
For example: *payaspāśam*.

the suffix *ka* is applied according to [Pāṇini 5.3.73] to the word *payaḥ* when it is unknown.
Regarding "payaskāmyati": [the suffix *kāmyac* is applied].

Regarding *pā* in the sense of drinking (*pāne*, Dhātupāṭha 925), the substitution of *piba-* occurs by the rule [Pāṇini 7.3.78]. As for the statement, "It should be stated that 'the substitute *s-* occurs in place of the visarga of a non-indeclinable when followed by a word beginning with a consonant other than at the beginning of a word,'" this means that in the rule *so'padādau*, it must be explained that the substitute *s-* occurs in place of the visarga of a non-indeclinable.

In this regard, the explanation is as follows: the word *vā* (or) from the rule *vā śari* [Pāṇini 8.3.36] is understood here, and that is a restricted option (*vyavasthitavibhāṣā*). Therefore, it will apply only to what is not an indeclinable (*anavyaya*), and not to an indeclinable.
The phrase "for the sake of restriction in the case of *kāmya* after *ru*" is a mnemonic statement (*grahaṇakavākya*).
"Only that [is the meaning]"—
this is its explanation.
The same meaning applies here for the word "vaktavya" (to be stated) as well.
The explanation should be made as in the previous rule.
In the expression "of *ru*," the genitive case indicates the place of articulation (*sthāna-ṣaṣṭhī*). The meaning is: "of that *visarjanīya* which belongs to *ru*."
"He recites [the root] with *uj* as its penultimate and *upadhmānīya* as its final.

Here, this is the view of some: namely, that the root is *ubja* in the sense of "straightness" (Dhātupāṭha 1303), but the *upadhmānīya* is not heard [in the form], because it is indicated through the application of the rule for changing a guttural to a palatal (*kṛtajaśtva*). However, the view of others is that the root is *udja* in the sense of "straightness."

In that regard, according to the first position, by applying the suffix *ghañ* via Pāṇini 3.3.121 (*halaśca*), and then applying *kutva* (the substitution of *k*) via 7.3.52 (*cajoḥ ku ghiṇṇyatoḥ*), the rule 8.4.53 would change the *upadhmānīya* into *ba*, resulting in the undesirable forms *abhyubgaḥ* and *samubgaḥ*.

Therefore, it must be stated that when a *ka*-class consonant follows, the *upadhmānīya* becomes *sa*; once the *upadhmānīya* has become *sa*, it is changed to *da* by the rule for *jaś*-substitution. In this way, the desired forms *abhyudgaḥ* and *samudgaḥ* are established.

The prohibition of doubling for the *upadhmānīya* must also indeed be stated; otherwise, in the case of *hrubjijiṣati*, the doubling of the *upadhmānīya* would undesirably follow by rule [Pāṇini 6.1.2]. However, according to the other view—that *bha* should be stated for the root *ubj* in the section on "unestablished" (*asiddha*) rules—otherwise forms such as *ubjijiṣati* and *ubjita* would not be established.
And so it has been said: "In the *asiddha* section, *bha* is substituted for *ubj*."
The mention of *asiddha* is because the sound *bh* is not established [as a substitute].
This is so that, in the case of *ubjijiṣati*, there may be a prohibition of reduplication for the second monosyllabic (*ekāc*) element according to Pāṇini 6.1.3.
Should this *bh* be explicitly stated? No, it need not be stated; for it is established by means of a technical designation (*nipātana*).

What, then, is the purpose of this specific rule (*nipātana*)? It is the rule: "The forms *bhuja* and *nyuja* are used in the senses of 'causing pain' (*pāci*) and 'afflicting' (*upatāpa*)," [Pāṇini 7.3.61]. If that were so, would it not follow here as well—that *abhyudgaḥ* and *samudgaḥ*—would they not require the substitution of *ṣ*? There is no fault, because this is a specific rule (*nipātana*) applying where the substitution of *k* does not occur. Since the substitution of *s* would have applied by the preceding rule, the substitution of *ṣ* is prescribed as its exception, as in:
"*sarpistatra*" (or "*sarpiste*" according to the Kāśikā).
Thus, that very [rule] applies.
From this point onward, if only the letter *ṣ* is carried over and not the letter *s*, then in rules such as *ataḥ kṛkamikaṃsa* (Pāṇini 8.3.46), the mention of the letter *s* must be made.
Even if it were made, if the letter *ṣ* does not carry over there, then a confusion would arise regarding that [letter *s*] as well.

Now, from this point forward, if only the letter *s* (sakāra) continues to apply and not the letter *ṣ* (ṣakāra) as well, then in the rules [Pāṇini 8.3.41], [8.3.43], [8.3.44], and [8.3.45], the mention of *ṣ* must be made. Even if that were done, if the letter *s* also continued to apply, then *s* would also occur there; thus, this same confusion (*saṅkara*) would result. To this he says: "The answer," and so forth.
By this, the objection regarding the application of both *s* and *ṣ* is refuted.
Regarding the fault of confusion (*saṅkara*) that was pointed out, he states its refutation with the words "In that case" (*tatra*), and so forth.

But how is this distinction of scope obtained when both [terms] continue to apply equally in what follows? It is because they continue by way of the "frog-leap" maxim (*maṇḍūkapluti*). The rule "not at the beginning of a word" (*apadādau*, Pāṇini 8.3.38) has ceased to apply. The term *namaḥ* receives the designation of *gati* by the rule "after the word *namaḥ*" (Pāṇini 1.4.74), while the term *puraḥ* receives it by the rule "after the word *puraḥ*" (Pāṇini 1.4.67). Thus: "He makes a city, cities, or before. (*pūḥ purau, puraḥ karoti*).

The root *pṛ* is listed in the Dhātupāṭha as "to protect and to fill" (1086). By the rule *bhrājabhrāsa-* [Pāṇini 3.2.177], the suffix *kvip* is applied. Then, by *udoṣṭhapūrvasya* [7.1.102], the vowel *u* is substituted for the radical *ṛ*. This is followed by the substitution of *ra* (*raparatvam*). The nominal suffixes beginning with *su* (*svādayaḥ*) are added, and by *halṅyādilopaḥ* [6.1.66], the case-ending is elided. Finally, by *rvorupadhāyā dīrghaḥ* [8.2.76], a long vowel is substituted in the singular form. Thus, we have *pūḥ* and *purau*. In the case of *purā*, because it is not designated as a *gati* (preverb), the substitution of *s* (*satvam*) does not occur for the word *purā*; in its absence, there would only be the visarga (*visarjanīya*), though in some grammatical views, the *upadhmānīya* may also occur.

In the case of *puraḥ karoti*, because it possesses the designation *agati* (non-gati), the substitution of *s* does not occur; in its absence, there is only the *visarjanīya*, though optionally the *jihvāmūlīya* may also occur.
However, for the word *namaḥ*, the counter-example should be understood as *namaḥ kṛtvā*;
the author of the Vṛtti did not show it because it is easily understood. *ic ca uc ca*—these two are *iduttau*.
That which has *ik*, *uk*, and so forth as its preceding elements (*upadha*) is described as such.
The rule beginning with "ni-duḥ-bahis" and so on is for the purpose of illustrating possible cases, not an exhaustive enumeration, because there are no exceptions to be excluded.
"He acts for his mother," "He acts for his father"—as to why it is not so in these cases, he will explain later. [Examples: "Desirous of a male," "Desirous of repeatedly."
In this case as well, he will explain how it does not occur:

"catuṣkapālam" (four potsherds) and "catuṣkaṣṭakam" (four thorns). Here, there is either a *bahuvrīhi* compound of the word *catur* with the words *kapāla* and *kaṇṭaka*, or a *dvigu* compound in the sense of a collective (*samāhāra*).

The feminine gender does not apply here because of the rule: "A *dvigu* compound whose final member ends in the vowel *a* is stated to be feminine" (*Vārttika* 156)—this is negated by the statement: "There is a prohibition for *pātra* and so forth" (*Vārttika* 159). The forms *mātuḥ karoti* and *pituḥ karoti* are colloquial (*deśya*). [In this case,] the genitive singular is formed from the words *mātṛ* and *pitṛ*; the substitution of *u* by the rule *ṛta ut* (Pāṇini 6.1.107) results in a single substitute; then there is the replacement of *u* by *r* (*raparatva*); the elision of *s* by the rule *rātsasya* (Pāṇini 8.2.24); and finally, the visarga replaces the *r*.
And because the *repha* (the letter *r*) is not a suffix (*apratyayatvāt*), the *visarjanīya* is not a suffix; therefore, the substitution of *ṣa* would apply.
Why does that not occur? To this he says: "In the *kaskādi* group," and so forth. This is the resolution.
This is a *karmadhāraya* compound meaning "that which is both a single substitute (*ekādeśa*) and the cause (*nimitta*).

If *ṣatva* were to occur because the single substitute for *iṇ* were the cause, then the word *bhrātuṣputra* would not have been included among the words in the *kaskādi* group; for [the desired form] would already be established by this very rule. Yet it has been included there, and this very fact indicates that *ṣatva* does not occur when caused by a single substitute. [The examples beginning with] "pum-muhusāḥ" and so forth [are given].
"Should be stated" means "should be explained.

In this regard, the explanation is as follows: the mention of *anyatarasyām* ("optionally") in the subsequent rule [Pāṇini 8.3.42] should be understood as applying as a remainder (*śeṣabhūta*) to both rules.
That is a restricted option (*vyavasthitavibhāṣā*), and therefore [the substitution] does not occur for the words *pum* and *muhuḥ*.
But for others, it will always be so.
The inclusion of the word *pum* was made by relying on the alternative that substitutes *ru* [for *s*];
for in the alternative where there is a substitute *s*, since there is no *visarjanīya*, the *sakāra* [is applied] by the rule *saṃhitāyām* [Pāṇini 8.3.34].
How it is that the *jihvāmūlīya* does not occur has already been explained previously.
In the word *muhukāmā*,
when the substitution of *ṣ* is prohibited, the *jihvāmūlīya* occurs.
In some places, the word "muhuḥkāmā" is read with the letter *s*. In that case,
just as the absence of the *jihvāmūlīya* (the *visarga* sound) was previously established for the term *puṃskāmā*, it must likewise be established here.

Regarding the forms *naiṣkulyam* and *dauṣpuruṣyam*, one might object: "Since these are derived from *niṣkuṭa* and *duṣpuruṣa* by adding the suffix *ṣyañ* (Pāṇini 4.3.75), and since the condition for the substitution of *ṣ* [for *s*]—namely, that the word ends in *i* or *u* (*idudupadha*)—is absent once the *vṛddhi* strengthening has occurred due to that suffix, the rule for *ṣatva* does not apply. Furthermore, one might argue that even in cases like *niśṣkulam* and *duśṣpuruṣaḥ*, where a protracted vowel (*pluta*) is prescribed by the rule *guroranṛtaḥ* (Pāṇini 8.2.86), the *ṣatva* would likewise not occur because the condition of ending in *i* or *u* is no longer met. To such an objector, the author replies with the words "*naiṣkulyam*" and so on. In this regard, the *vṛddhi* strengthening is indeed "external" (*bahiraṅga*) because it depends upon the secondary derivative suffix (*taddhita*). Furthermore, the secondary derivative suffix itself is external because it depends upon meanings such as "belonging to" (*bhava*) and the like. Thus, the substitution of *ṣ* occurs first, before the external operations take effect.

Therefore, even though the *vṛddhi* [substitution] depends upon that [vowel], it is considered *bahiraṅga*. The *pluta* [protracted vowel] is also *bahiraṅga*, because it is prescribed for a sentence (*vākya*) in the sense of calling from afar or greeting from afar. However, the substitution of *ṣatva* (the change to *ṣ*) depends on fewer factors, as it is prescribed for a single phoneme (*varṇa*) belonging to a word (*pada*); thus, it is *antaraṅga*. Consequently, since the *vṛddhi* and *pluta* are *asiddha* (non-existent) with respect to the *antaraṅga* *ṣatva* that is to be performed, the *ṣatva* indeed takes place.

[This portion is not found in the Kāśikā reading. The inclusion of the *tapara* (the long vowel marker) is for the purpose that [the rule] should not apply in cases such as *āśīḥ karoti*, *goḥ karoti*, and *dhūḥ karoti*. [This portion is not found in the Kāśikā reading. By the rule beginning with *idudupadhasya*, he rejects the inclusion of the words *dvi*, *tri*, and *catur*.
For this [inclusion] is made for the following purpose: so that the substitution of *ṣ* for the *visarjanīya* occurs only for *dvi* and the others, and not in a case such as *pañcakṛtvaḥ karoti*.

But surely, while the rule *idudupadhasya* [Pāṇini 8.3.41] is being carried over, if the *visarjanīya* is qualified by the word "occurring in the domain of *kṛtvas-artha*"—meaning "the *visarjanīya* of that word which has a *kṛtvas-artha* suffix"—then it would not apply to anything else; for there is no possibility of another word containing *i*, *u*, or *ū* as its penultimate (*upadha*) that occurs in the sense of *kṛtvas-artha*. Therefore, even without the explicit mention of *dvi*, *tri*, and *catur*, the change to *ṣ* will occur only for their *visarjanīya*. Thus, the words *dvi*, *tri*, and *catur* could have been omitted.

"Why does he state the option regarding *ṣatva* [the substitution of *ṣ*] in the sense of *kṛtvasuc*?"—in this rule prescribing the option for *ṣatva*, he asks for the reason for stating "in the sense of *kṛtvasuc*. Why? What is the purpose for which he states this option for *ṣatva* by saying "in the sense of *kṛtvasuc*"? That is to say, what is the motive because of which he includes the mention of "in the sense of *kṛtvasuc*" in this rule prescribing the option for *ṣatva*? This is the meaning.
The intended meaning here is precisely what will be stated later.
Therefore, he states the reason: "In the case of *catuṣkapāla*, etc.
If the mention of the sense of the suffix *kṛtvas* were not made, the optional substitution of *ṣ* would apply even to *catuṣkapāla*, whereas it is prescribed as obligatory.
Therefore, in this context, the term *kṛtvo'rtha* is stated for the purpose that the substitution of *ṣatva* (the change to *ṣ*) should not occur by way of an option (*vibhāṣā*).

With the intention for which he questioned [the opponent] further, he says: "But is it not already established there by the preceding rule? The word *na* is used in the sense of conceding the point (*abhyupagama*).

By this, he demonstrates the following: let there be the optional (*vibhāṣā*) substitution of *ṣ* by this [rule]; nevertheless, by the preceding rule, the substitution of *ṣ* will be obligatory, and thus its pronunciation will occur. For even when the substitution of *ṣ* does not take place by this [rule], the substitution of *ṣ* is established for "catuṣkapāle" by the preceding rule [Pāṇini 8.3.41]. The phrase "he prescribes this even though it is already established" means that it is already obtained (*prāpta*).

This explains as follows: since the rule *idudupadhasya* etc. would otherwise necessitate the obligatory substitution of *ṣ*, this present rule prescribes an optional alternative for that *ṣ*-substitution.

Because [the former] has not already been established by that [latter], according to the maxim *yena nāprāpte* (Vyāḍi-pāda 49), this [present rule] would be a sublater (*bādhaka*) of it. Thus, by this, what was stated—that "it is established there by the preceding [rule]"—is refuted.
Therefore, the mention of *kṛtvo'rtha* (words having the sense of "times") is for the purpose of excluding the *vibhāṣā* (optionality).

This might be argued: when the suffix *suc* is applied with the intention of expressing *kṛtvo'rtha*, and its *visarjanīya* is subsequently produced, then [the substitution of *ṣ*] would not apply by the preceding rule (*pūrveṇa*), because of the prohibition [contained in] *apratyayasya* (Pāṇini 8.3.41); furthermore, since the rule *taparaḥ* (Pāṇini 1.1.70) establishes that "this [rule] enjoins what is already established," that [prohibition] is not applicable. Why then would the constant *ṣatva* be sublated by this optional rule? To this he says: "*yadāpi kṛtvo'rthe*" and so forth.
The word "the word *catuḥ* occurs" is to be supplied as the remainder [of the sentence].

And this [rule] is connected with the present context: "When *hras* is established, one prescribes four; [thereby] the substitution of *ṣ*. The meaning of this is as follows: what is being said is that this optional prescription for the substitution of *ṣ* is not only prescribed when the word *catur* functions in the sense of a numeral (*kṛtvo'rtha*)—where it would already have been obtained by the preceding rule—but rather also when it does not function in the sense of a numeral. He provides the justification for this very point with the words: "when the suffix expressing the sense of *kṛtvas* is elided," and so forth.
And so forth.

The word *hi* indicates the reason (*hetau*). [The term] *kṛtvo'rthīya* means "that which exists in the sense of *kṛtvas*" (i.e., adverbs of frequency). [In the formation of the word *gahvarīya*], *ka* and *suca* are added; then, by virtue of its inclusion in the *gahādi* group, the suffix *cha* is applied.

Why? Because by the rule *rātsasya* [Pāṇini 8.2.24], when the suffix denoting frequency (*kṛtvo'rtha*) is elided, the *visarjanīya* of the non-suffixal *repha* occurs; therefore, even in the case of frequency, since the preceding rule would have made the substitution of *ṣa* obligatory, this present option for *ṣa* is prescribed. Consequently, since this option would begin where the preceding *ṣa*-substitution had not already applied—whether in the case of frequency or non-frequency—it would necessarily be an annulment (*bādhaka*) of that preceding rule. And if the mention of "frequency" (*kṛtvo'rtha*) were not present here, the optional *ṣa*-substitution would undesirably apply even in a word like *catuṣkapāla*.
Therefore, it is established that the mention of the sense of *kṛtvas* (times) is for the purpose of excluding that [other case].

Regarding the passage beginning with "In this way" (*evam*): if the mention of the sense of *kṛtvas* is made, then, in that case, what is the use now of the rule stating "twice, thrice, four times"? Nothing at all; because there is nothing to be excluded.

Therefore, the intended meaning is simply that "this should not be done. [The reading *mā bhūd* for *na kartavyam* is found in the Prācīna manuscript. One might object: "If this were not the case, then even in examples such as *pañcakṛtvaḥ karoti*, there would be optional (*vibhāṣā*) ṣatva; therefore, is it not the case that the present rule effects its exclusion? To this he replies with the words beginning "For another... (*anyo hi*), and so forth.

The rule *idudupadhasya* [Pāṇini 8.3.41] is understood here, and it is stated that this applies "in the sense of a kṛtvas-pratyaya. However, there is no word other than those beginning with *dvis* (twice) etc. that has *i* or *u* as its penultimate vowel (*idudupadha*) while functioning in the sense of a kṛtvas-pratyaya. Therefore, by virtue of the semantic fitness (*sāmarthya*), the rule will apply only to these [words] and not to others; thus, the explicit mention of *dvis* and so on would be redundant.
With the words "If it were not done" (*akriyamāṇe*) and so forth, he demonstrates the fault that would arise if the mention of *dvis* and so on were omitted.

If the mention of "twice" (*dvis*) and so forth were not made, then, since the *visarjanīya* is the subject under discussion, that very *visarjanīya* would be qualified by the term "in the sense of *kṛtvas*"—that is, "the *visarjanīya* which occurs in the sense of *kṛtvas*.
What, then, would be the fault in this case? To this he says: "The form *caturaḥ* would not be established.
"In that way," [he continues].

In that same way, when the *visarjanīya* is qualified by the inclusion of the word "meaning" (*artha*) as just described, the optional substitution of *ṣ* for the word *catur* is not established. Why is it not established? To this he says: "Of the *repha*," and so forth.

The word *hi* indicates the reason: because, according to [Pāṇini 8.2.24] *rātsasya*, when the *s* of *suc* is elided, the *visarjanīya* arises from the *repha* which is a constituent part of the base; therefore, it is not established.
This *visarjanīya* does not signify the sense of "times" (*kṛtvas-artha*).
Now, even if that [suffix] were applied, why would this fault not arise? To this, he says: "Therefore," and so forth.
When the words *dvi*, *tri*, and *catur* are employed in that [context], it is logical that the mention of the sense of "times" (*kṛtvas-artha-grahaṇa*) serves as a qualifier for the word *catuḥ*.

For instance—is it because that [number] has been heard [in the rule]? It is that very word which is qualified: namely, the word *catuḥ* when it occurs in the sense of a *kṛtvas-artha* (adverbial frequency).
Even though the *kṛtvas-artha* suffix is elided, the word *catuḥ* still functions in the sense of *kṛtvas-artha*; thus, there would be no fault even if the mention of *dvis-* and so on were made.
Therefore, the mention of *dvis-* and so on must be made so that the mention of *kṛtvas-artha* may serve as its qualifier.
Showing that this also cannot be its purpose, he says: "The word under discussion ends with that.
"Ending with that" means ending with the *visarjanīya*.

Therefore, it is logical that it too should be qualified by that; he provides the justification: "The fact that the word ends with that is obtained because the word is qualified by the *visarjanīya*."
The word "api" is used for emphasis;
it means "of that very [person]. Why is this so? Because of the principle of pervasion (vyāpti).
For if the *visarjanīya* were qualified [by the word "word"], the form *caturaḥ* would not be established; however, when the "word" (*pada*) is qualified, it occurs everywhere.

Therefore, we shall qualify that very [word]: "a word which occurs in the sense of the suffix *kṛtvas*. When the "word" is thus qualified, the substitution of *ṣ* for the *visarjanīya* of *caturaḥ* is indeed established.

Even when the suffix *kṛtvas* has been elided, the word *catuḥ* still functions in the sense of *kṛtvas*. Therefore, the author of the *Ślokavārttika* rejected the inclusion of "twice" (*dvi*) and so forth [in the rule], arguing that it is unnecessary. However, the intention of the author of the Sūtra is as follows: because the *visarjanīya* is the object of the grammatical operation (*kāryin*), and because it is qualified by the word *pada*, it possesses primacy.

In that case, if the mention of "dvir" and so forth were not made, then—due to its predominance—the *visarjanīya* alone would be qualified by the term "kṛtvo'rtha" (having the sense of repetition). However, since that [mention] exists, by virtue of the necessity of including it, and because it is directly stated (*sākṣāt*), this qualification applies only to the word beginning with "dvir," and not to the *visarjanīya* which is merely inferred through its *svarita* accent.
Therefore, it is correct to include the mention of "dvir" and so forth.

With the passage beginning with "But thus" (*evaṃ tu*), he establishes the mention of "two," "three," and "four" according to the opinion of the author of the Sūtras. The phrase "by the preceding [rule]" refers to the rule beginning with *idudupadhasya* (Pāṇini 8.3.41).

In this regard, one might ask: what is the scope of the rule *idudupadhasya* [Pāṇini 8.3.41]? It is, for example, in *niṣkṛtam* and *duṣkṛtam*. What is the scope of the present rule (*naśca dhātusthoruṣubhyaḥ*)? It is, for example, in *dviṣkaroti* and so forth. One might then argue that in the case of *catuṣkaroti*, because the present rule is subsequent, it will override the preceding rule and this option alone will apply. To address this, he says: "When the preceding is not established" (*pūrvatrāsiddhe*), and so on.

What is the reason that [the rule] does not apply? To this he says: "Because of the absence of what follows. If one holds the view that words such as *sapiḥ*, *yajus*, and so forth—which end in the suffixes *is* and *us*—are derived according to the rules "after the roots *aci*, *śuci*, *husṛ*, *yiccha*, *ādiccha*, and *śṛdi*, the suffix *isi* is added" (*Daiva 9.30*), and while the rule for *usi* is still in force, "after the roots *ati*, *tapa*, *pṛ*, *vap*, *yaj*, *tan*, *dhā*, *ni*, and *pā*, the suffix *us* is added, and it is *nit*" (*Daiva 9.39*), then this statement is made because, although the substitution of the *ṣatva* sound has not yet occurred, the substitution of the *jihvāmūlīya* and other sounds would otherwise have applied by the rule "in place of *k* and *p* before *v* and *y*" (*Pāṇini 8.3.37*).

Now, according to the view that "the words beginning with *atha* are underived nominal stems" (*pu|pa|vṛ|70*), since [the word *atha*] would not be followed by a suffixal *visarjanīya*, the rule *aprātyayavisarjanīyatvāt* (Pāṇini 8.3.41) would necessitate the obligatory substitution of *ṣ*. This [present sūtra] is therefore commenced [to provide an exception]. [The phrase] "when there is semantic connection" (*sāmarthye sati*) [is used].
Because *k* and *p* are relied upon as causes [of substitution], their capacity must be understood only in relation to another word that begins with them.

In the example *sarpiṣkaroti*, [the word] *sarpiḥ* requires an action to be accomplished (*sādhyā kriyā*) in the sense of "he performs an action for which clarified butter is the instrument" (*sarpiḥ sādhanaṃ karoti*). Since the meaning of the verb "to do" (*karoti*) is also something to be accomplished (*sādhya*), there exists a semantic connection (*sāmarthya*) between the instrument (*sādhana*)—which is the clarified butter—and the action. For instance: "Let the clarified butter remain; you drink water."

In this case, there is no semantic compatibility (*sāmarthya*) between *sarpiḥ* and *piba*. For instance, the word *piba* requires [the object] "water," whereas *sarpiḥ* implies "let it remain. Now, why does the optional substitution of *ṣ* not occur in the compound *paramasarpiḥkuṇḍikā* according to the rule of optionality (*vibhāṣā*)? To this he says: "Semantic compatibility is required here," and so forth.
The word *dā* also functions in the sense of "also" (*api*), because indeclinables possess multiple meanings.
Its connection is with the phrase "not, however" (*na punaḥ*) by way of forming a single conceptual unit (*ekārthībhāva*), and also with the word "both" (*ubhaya*).
Furthermore, a restrictive emphasis (*avadhāraṇa*) is to be understood here, since all sentences have exclusion (*vyavaccheda*) as their result.

Therefore, this is the meaning here: in this context, semantic competency (*sāmarthya*) is based solely on mutual expectancy (*vyapekṣā*). Why, then, would it not be appropriate to base it on both [expectancy and proximity]? For general terms do not settle upon specific meanings without the aid of context (*prakaraṇa*) and so forth; yet, there is no such context or similar factor here by which one should grasp semantic competency as being defined solely by expectancy. This is not a fault.

Regarding the rule *kāryakālaṃ saṃjñāparibhāṣam* (Vyāḍiparibhāṣā 58), the term *padasya* ("of a word") is understood here. Since the governing heading (*adhikāra*) of "word" (*pada*) itself brings to mind the technical rule concerning semantic competency (*samarthaparibhāṣā*), competency is already established. Nevertheless, the purpose of explicitly including the mention of "competency" (*sāmarthya*) is so that there may be an inclusion of the specific type of competency intended. In this context, the intended competency is defined solely by mutual expectancy (*vyapekṣā*); therefore, it is proper to rely on that alone, and not on syntactic unity (*ekārthībhāva*), nor on both. For example, in the case of *sapiṣkuṇḍikā*, it is a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*).
The same applies to cases such as *dhanuṣkapāla* ("bow-case") and so forth.

Regarding *paramam apiḥ kuṇḍikā* ("the supreme ghee-pitcher"): having first formed a *karmadhāraya* compound of the words *parama* and *sarpiḥ* by means of [Pāṇini 2.1.60] *sanmahatparamottamotkṛṣṭāḥ pūjyamānaiḥ*, one then forms a *ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa* (genitive compound) with the word *kuṇḍikā*.

In this case, with respect to the word *parama*, the word *sarpiḥ* is the subsequent member (*uttarapada*), and since the visarga resides therein, the substitution of *ṣ* does not occur. Now, one might object: in the rule [Pāṇini 8.3.44], the mention of the suffixes *is* and *us* is a reference to suffixes (*pratyayagrahaṇa*); therefore, by the restrictive principle that "when there is a reference to a suffix, it refers to that which begins with the element from which that suffix is prescribed and ends with it," only those instances where *is* and *us* are prescribed should be understood, and nothing more than that. Furthermore, the word *parama* is an additional element.

For the suffix *sa* is prescribed after the word *kevala* alone, not after words such as *parama*; and thus, since there would be no base for the final member (*uttarapada*) at all, what would be the point of the prohibition? To this he says: "This very [point]," and so forth. If this were a restrictive rule (*niyama*) here, the phrase "not standing after a preceding member" (*anuttarapadasthasya*) would not have been stated, yet it has been stated. Therefore, this makes it known that this is not a restrictive rule here. What is the purpose of this indicator (*jñāpaka*)? To this he says: "By that," and so forth.

Since this restriction does not apply here, for that reason, even when an additional element is included in the sentence—as in *paramasarpiḥ karoti* and *paramasarpiṣkaroti*—there occurs an option regarding the substitution of *ṣ* by the preceding rule (*pūrvasūtra*); however, if the restriction were in force, it would not occur.

[Objection: "In that case, even in a compound, as in *paramasarpiḥkuṇḍikā*, there ought to be an option regarding the substitution of *ṣ* because of the absence of the restriction. To this he says: "And there, *vyapekṣā*," etc.
The particle *ca* (and) has the sense of emphasis (*avadhāraṇa*).

The particle *iti* is used here in the sense of a reason (*hetau*). In that regard, because the term "sāmarthya" (semantic expectancy) is mentioned in the rule beginning with *isusoḥ* [Pāṇini 8.3.44], it is precisely this *vyapekṣā* (mutual expectancy) that is adopted as the basis for the optional application of the status of having semantic expectancy. Therefore, it does not apply in a compound (*samāsa*), because that [expectancy] is absent there. This statement is made because [the rule] *kupvoḥ ka pau ca* [Pāṇini 8.3.37] would otherwise apply. For example: *ayaskāraḥ*.
The suffix *aṇ* [is applied] by [Pāṇini 3.2.1]: *karmaṇyaṇ*.
Thus, it is also the case here in *ayaskāmaḥ*.
However, the rule "the suffix *ṇa* should be prescribed after [roots ending in] *śīli*, *kāmi*, *bhikṣi*, and *ācari*" (Vārttika 229) does not apply here.
In that supplementary rule (*upasaṃkhyāna*), the form *kāmayate* is used because it is derived from the root *kam* with the suffix *ṇic*; here, however, it is used without *ṇic*.

When, by the rule "the suffixes *āya*, etc., are optional before an *ārdhadhātuka* suffix" (*āyādaya ārdhadhātuke vā*), the suffix *ṇiṅ* is absent for *kam*, then *kam* remains without *ṇic*. Thus we have the example *ayaskaṃsaḥ*.
This is a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*).

[Objection: But surely, once the suffix *sa* is applied by the rule "from the roots *vṛ*, *vadi*, *hani*, *kami*, and *kaṣi*, the suffix *sa* [is added]" (Dhātupāṭha 9.29), the form *kaṃsa* is established; since this is already accomplished by the mention of the root *kami* alone, the mention of *kaṃsa* is redundant. [Response: No; it is for the purpose of providing an indication (*jñāpana*).
By this it is made known that there is also this view: "The *uṇādi* suffixes are unanalyzed; they are not [derived from] nominal stems," as in the case of *ayaskumbhaḥ*.

The term *kumbha* is a modification (*vikāra*) of iron (*ayasa*). It is a compound formed by the elision of intermediate words (*padalopa*), according to the rule: "In the section on compounds with a common substratum (*samānādhikaraṇa*), there is an addition [to the list] for *śākapārthiva* and similar compounds, and there is elision of the final member" (Vārttika 83). Alternatively, it is a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*), namely *ayas-kumbhī*.
The suffix *aṅīṣ* is applied because [the word] belongs to the *gaura*-class;
the compound is like *ayaskumbha*. Thus, "ayaspātrī" (an iron vessel).

The word *pātra* ends in the suffix *ṣṭun*; [the feminine suffix] *ṅīṣ* is applied by the rule *ṣidgaurādibhyaśca* [Pāṇini 4.1.41]. Regarding the term *ayaskuśā*, the letter *i* in *ayas-* is not intended to be significant here.
By that rule [Pāṇini 4.1.42], *jānapadāvisūtra*, the suffix *ṅīṣ* is applied;
thus we have *ayaskuśā*.
Here, the letter *i* in *ayas* is not intended to be significant.
By that rule [Pāṇini 4.1.42], *jānapadī* etc., the suffix *ṅīṣ* does not apply.
In the case of *ayaskarṇī*, meaning "one whose ears are like iron," the suffix *ṅīp* is applied by the rule [Pāṇini 4.1.55] *nāsikodara* etc.;
this is because the word *karṇa* ending in the vowel *ī* is what is being referred to.

Therefore, someone might have the misconception that in the word *śunaḥkarṇa*, there must be the presence of the suffix *sat* [to form the compound]; in order to refute this, he says: "But this *śunaskarṇa*," and so forth.
Regarding the term "the making of light" (*bhāḥkaraṇam*), it is a compound with a word ending in the suffix *lyuṭ*.

If, then, the inclusion of the *tapara* (the long vowel marker) were not made, would [the suffix] *ṭa* not also apply in the case of *bhāskaraḥ*—as in the example "he makes light" (*bhāsaṃ karoti*)—by virtue of the rule *vica-karap-ataḥ* [Pāṇini 3.2.21]? To this he says: "But this word *bhāskaraḥ*," and so forth.
This is easy to understand. Regarding the expression "*athaḥśirasaḥ*":
by means of a transposition of cases, the nominative stands in place of the genitive.
By the phrase "when followed by the word *pada*," he shows that the term *pada* refers to its own form (*svarūpa*) and not to the technical (*pāribhāṣika*) definition.

For if it were the technical definition that were being referred to, the mention of *pada* would be redundant; the intention is that [the technical sense] is already obtained from the governing rule concerning compounds (*samāsa*).

Regarding "śiraspadam": this is a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*). It is an exception (*apavāda*) to [the rule] *kutvoḥ* (Pāṇini 8.3.37). Regarding "according to the application" (*yathāyogam*): [it means] as appropriate.

The meaning of "according to the application" (*yathāyogārtha*) is as follows: the *visarjanīya* that follows the vowel *iṇ* is replaced by *ṣakāra*, whereas any other [visarjanīya] is replaced by *sakāra*.

Thus, in the case of *kaskaḥ*, when the nominative suffix *su* follows, there is the substitution of *ka* [for the final *a*] according to Pāṇini 7.2.103, and there is reduplication due to the desire for emphasis (*dīpsā*).
As for *kautaskutaḥ*: [it is derived from *kutas kutaḥ*].

By [Pāṇini 5.3.7] and [7.2.104], *ku* replaces *kimaḥ*; as before, there is reduplication; and when the suffix *aṇ* is applied by [4.3.74], the *ṭi*-portion is elided according to the Vārttika [842]: "The elision of the *ṭi* of indeclinables occurs only when a *bha*-affix follows. Thus we have *bhrātuṣputraḥ*.
When this is a compound, the sixth case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) is not elided by [6.3.23].
Regarding the term *śuvas-kaṇaḥ*:
[the suffix] *aluk* is applied by the rule *saṃjñāyām* (Pāṇini 6.3.21).
However, when it is not a proper name (*asaṃjñā*), in a compound it becomes simply *ākarṇa*.

But surely, since the letter *ṣ* is already established for words such as *sarpiṣkuṇḍika-* by the rule *sarpiṣkuṇḍikādīnām* [Pāṇini 8.3.45], what is the purpose of including these here? To this he says: "of these," and so forth.
Those who play with the *pārāyaṇa* are called *pārāyaṇikāḥ*; the suffix *ṭhak* is applied according to the rule *tena dīvyati* [Pāṇini 4.4.2].
This refers to the statement "in the Bhāṣya and in the Vṛtti."

What is the purpose of the phrase "of one who stands on the unsurpassed state" (*anuttarapadasthasya*)? It is illustrated as a counter-example in both the *Bhāṣya* and the *Vṛtti* with the compound *paramasarpiḥkuṇḍikā*; thus, he shows that the reading of those two [compounds] is not intended here by these [authorities].
By the words "not having its formation prescribed by a rule" (*avihitalakṣaṇaḥ*), etc., he declares that the *kaska-* group is an *ākṛtigaṇa* (an open class).
The particle *ca* (and), serving to include what has not been mentioned, indicates this very meaning.

The technical term *upacāra* is prescribed for the *s* and *ṣ* sounds that take the place of the visarga (*visarjanīya*). In the case of *ayaspātram*, once a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*) has been formed, the rule *ataḥ kṛkamikaṃsa...* [Pāṇini 8.3.46] would necessitate the obligatory substitution of *ṣ*; however, by this present rule, an option is established. Similarly, in cases such as *vātaspātram*, if a compound is formed, [the substitution of *ṣ*] would otherwise apply; whereas in *uruṇaskāraḥ*, since it is not a compound, [the substitution] does not apply at all.
From the word *uru*, the substitution of *nas* for the following *asmat* occurs according to [Pāṇini 7.1.21], and the change to *ṇ* occurs according to [Pāṇini 8.4.27].

Now, why does this not occur in cases such as *harikeśaḥ purastāt* (Ṛgveda 10.139.1) and *sa naḥ pāvaka* (Ṛgveda 1.12.10)? To this he says: "In *harikeśa*, etc. The word *vā* ("or") is no longer in effect. [The substitute is] *kar*.

From the root *kṛ* with the suffix *luṅ*: by the rule beginning with "cli luṅi" [3.1.43], *cli* is substituted; then by "tasya" [2.4.80] and following, there is elision (*luk*); then *tip* is added; *guṇa* is applied; *raparatva* (substitution of *ra*) occurs; *tilopa* (elision of *ti*) occurs by "halṅyābbhyo dīrghāt sutisyapṛktaṃ hal" [6.1.66]; the *repha* becomes a *visarjanīya*; and by "bahulaṃ chandasyāmāṅyoge 'pi" [6.4.75], there is an absence of the augment *aṭ*. Thus, "karat. From the root *kṛ* with the suffix *laṅ*: by "āḍajādīnām" [6.4.72], *āṭ* is added; by "ṛdṛśoraṅi guṇaḥ" [7.4.16], *guṇa* is applied; and as before, there is an absence of the augment *aṭ*.
Alternatively, there is the substitution of *śatṛ* for *laṭ*, with *śap* by way of transposition;
thus "karati.
Here, *laṭ* occurs, followed by *tip*, and *śap* as before.

Regarding "kṛdhi": this is the imperative (loṭ) of the root *kṛ*. By the rule *sehrappricca* [Pāṇini 3.4.87], the suffix *sip* is replaced by *hi*. For that [suffix], there is the substitution of *dhi* by the rule *śruśṛṇupṛkṛvṛbhyaśchandasi* [Pāṇini 6.4.102], and then the elision of the verbal suffix (*vikaraṇa*) by the rule *tasthasthamipāṃ tāmtamtāmaḥ* [Pāṇini 3.4.101]. Regarding "kṛtam": [this is the past passive participle].
This ends with the suffix *niṣṭhā*.
Regarding the word "viātaskaḥ":
[it is formed] by the rule "pañcamyāstasil" (Pāṇini 5.3.7).
In *uruṇaskṛdhi*,
as before, there is the substitution of *nas* and the change to *ṇ*. In *sadaskṛtam*, [the same applies].

In the expression *sadasi kṛtam*, the compound is formed by means of a *yogavibhāga* (separation of rules) based on the rule *saptamī* [Pāṇini 2.1.40]. Regarding *adhyartham*, this is a qualifier for *pari*. As in the example *himavatas pari*.
The meaning is "above the Himavat. The ablative case (*pañcamī*) should be understood as standing in place of the genitive (*ṣaṣṭhī*) due to a grammatical substitution (*subvyatyaya*).
[This applies to] "of heaven and earth," and so forth.

In this context, the word *pari* signifies "in every respect" (*sarvatobhāve*). Regarding the form *divaspātu*: it is the imperative (*loṭ*) of the root *pā*, with the suffix *tip*; by [Pāṇini 3.4.86] *eruḥ*, the *u*-substitution occurs; and because it belongs to the *adādi* class, there is elision (*luk*) of the *śap* augment. Regarding *vācaspatim*:

by the rule [Pāṇini 6.3.14], due to the mention of *bahula* (variously), there is elision of the *kṛt* suffix *yat*. This statement is intended to provide an option (*vikalpa*), as the previous rule would have made the application compulsory (*nitya*).

If this is so, then the inclusion of the word *vā* (or) is redundant, for by the very force of the commencement [of the rule], this injunction will be understood as optional.
