This is not so; for if the mention of *vā* were absent, the preceding injunction would be understood as applying extensively (*bahulam*), because the term *bahulam* is the subject under discussion. But here, since *vā* is mentioned, the preceding injunction would be understood as obligatory (*nitya*); therefore, it is not redundant. The word *mūrdhanyaḥ* means "located on the head" (*mūrdhani bhavaḥ*). By the rule *śarīrāvayavād yat* [Pāṇini 4.3.55], the suffix *yat* is applied, and by *prakṛtyaikāj* [Pāṇini 6.4.163], there is the preservation of the original form (*prakṛtibhāva*). As in the example: *siṣeca*.

The root *ṣic* is defined as "to sprinkle" (*kṣaraṇe*, Dhātupāṭha 1434); *ṣvap* is defined as "to sleep" (*śaye*, Dhātupāṭha 1068). By the rule "the *ṣ* at the beginning of a verbal root becomes *s*" (*dhātvādeḥ ṣaḥ saḥ*, Pāṇini 6.1.66), the *ṣ* is changed to *s*. Then follows the *liṭ* suffix, the *tip* affix, and the *ṇal* replacement. For the root *svap*, there is vocalization (*samprasāraṇa*) by the rule "for both classes [of roots], there is vocalization of the reduplicated syllable in the *liṭ*" (*liṭabhyāsasyobhayeṣām*, Pāṇini 6.1.17). Now, for what purpose is the mention of *śru* and *artha*? One might ask: why not simply say "*ṣa*" alone? Even if *ṣ* were used, forms such as *siṣeca* would be established, and the sūtra would be more concise. To this, he replies: "Even though it could be established by saying simply *ṣa*... [and so forth].

If only "ṣ" were stated [in the rule], then in forms such as *acakṛḍhvam* and *cakṛḍhve*, the substitution of *ṣ* would undesirably apply by the rule *iṇaḥ ṣīdhvaṃ luṅliṭāṃ dho 'ṅgāt* (P. 8.3.78). However, the substitution of *ḍh* is desired, and that is indeed established when there is the mention of the "cerebral" (*mūrdhanya*) [in P. 8.3.29]. For in this case, by the principle of closest proximity (*āntaratamya*), a *ḍh*—which possesses the same articulatory effort (*anupradāna*), place of articulation (*sthāna*), and is voiced and aspirated (*ghoṣavat*, *mahāprāṇa*)—is substituted for the *gh*. If, on the other hand, the mention of *ḍh* were made in the rule *iṇaḥ ṣīdhvam*, then the mention of the "cerebral" could be omitted from the present rule.
And thus, the mention of *ḍha* has not been made for the sake of variety. [Objection:
But surely, since the mention of *ḍha* would exclude the letter *ṣa*, one would have to provide the mention of *ṣa* in all subsequent rules. [Response:
Let it be so; nevertheless, by mentioning the "head" (*mūrdhanya*), the mention of the actual form itself is more concise.

For in the case of grasping the actual form (*svarūpa*), there are six morae (*mātrā*): here, when "ṣa" is uttered, there are two morae; in the subsequent sūtra, when "ḍha" is uttered, there are two; and further on, when "ṣa" is uttered, there are two.
All these, when added together, amount to six morae.
When the retroflex (*mūrdhan*) is grasped, there are seven.
Therefore? When there is the apprehension of the actual form (*svarūpa*), there is brevity.

However, even if the letters *ṣ* and *ḍh* were present in the original form (*prakṛti*), if it were assumed that this [subsequent] application occurs because of the circumflex (*svarita*) accent of the letter *ṣ*, then there would be even greater brevity in apprehending the actual form. Thus:
"not becoming *kṛt*."
By the rule *hrasvādaṅgāt* [Pāṇini 8.2.27], there is the elision of *sic*.

Now, what is the purpose of including the term *anta-* (end) [in the rule]? If it were stated simply as "the *mūrdhanya* [retroflex] for what is not a word (*apadasya*)," it would be understood that the *mūrdhanya* applies to that *s* which belongs to what is not a word.
Consequently, in forms such as *kariṣyati*, the substitution would not occur, because the *s* belongs to a word (*pada*).

Where, then, would it apply? It would apply in cases such as *kariṣyati*, where the designation *pada* does not exist; for in such instances, the designation *bha* would subvert the designation *pada*. Therefore, the mention of the word "end" (*anta*) is made [in the rule]. [The rule] is: *sāḍapasya*.
The meaning is "of one who has attained this form, *sāṭ*.

Regarding the word *jalāṣāṭ*: [it is derived as follows: from the root *sah-* (to endure) with the prefix *jala-*, the suffix *ṇvi* is applied while *bhajo ṇviḥ* [Pāṇini 3.2.62] is being carried over by [3.2.63]; then there is *vṛddhi* [strengthening] by [7.2.116]; *ḍhatva* (the substitution of *ḍha*) by *ho ḍhaḥ* [8.2.31]; its *jaśtva* (substitution of the voiced unaspirated stop *ḍa*); and finally lengthening by [6.3.137].
Because of the internal similarity (*āntaratamya*) between the voiced aspirated sibilant *sakāra* and [the corresponding sound], the *ṣakāra* is of that very same nature.

Regarding the rule "with *ḍa*" (*saha ḍena*), etc.: when the rule *ḍīṅaḥ* (Pāṇini 3.2.97) is being carried over, the suffix *ḍa* is applied by [the rule] *ḍvitaḥ ktriḥ* (Pāṇini 3.2.101); this is because the word "also" (*api*) is intended to indicate the deviation from all restrictive conditions (*sarvopādhivyabhicāra*).

The term *sāḍi* is derived as follows: it is a *bahuvrīhi* compound based on the rule *saha ḍena vartate* [Pāṇini 2.2.28]; the substitution of *sa-* for the word *saha-* occurs by the rule *sahasya saḥ* [Pāṇini 6.3.78]; the suffix *iñ* is applied to form *saḍasyāpatyam* according to the rule *ata iñ* [Pāṇini 4.1.95]; then, by the rule *yasyeti ca* [Pāṇini 6.4.148], the final vowel *a* is elided; and finally, with the application of *ādivṛddhi*, the form *sāḍi* is obtained. If the word *saher* (from the rule *saher dīrghāt*) were not present, the retroflex substitution (*mūrddhanya*) would undesirably apply.

If it is argued that because of the status of the substitute as the original (sthānivadbhāva) according to Pāṇini 1.1.57 (*acaḥ parasmin pūrvavidhau*), the form *sāṭ* does not exist [after the substitution], we say no; for there is a prohibition of the status of the original by the rule *pūrvatrāsiddhe na sthānivat* (Jainendra-vyākaraṇa-paribhāṣā 48).

But even so, one might still object that this form *sāṭ* does not exist here at all; for when the substitution of *ṣ* is to be applied, the external (bahiraṅga) vowel lengthening (*vṛddhi*) is considered non-existent (*asiddha*).

In that case, would there not also be [the undesired form] *jalāṣāḍ*? [No,] because when the substitution of *ṣ* is to be applied, the external (*bahiraṅga*) *vṛddhi* is indeed non-existent (*asiddha*). For that [vṛddhi] occurs by depending on the *aṅga* (stem), and the designation *aṅga* exists only when there is an affix (*pratyaya*), and the affix depends on the *upapada*; thus, it is clear that the *vṛddhi* of the penultimate vowel (*upadhā*) is external. However, the substitution of *ṣ* is internal (*antaraṅga*), as it is prescribed for that which has become an *aṅga*. Therefore, by the rule "what is external is non-existent with respect to what is internal" (*asiddhaṃ bahiraṅgam antaraṅge*), the substitution of *ṣ* will not occur—[if this were so,] this statement [of yours] would be purposeless.
Therefore, lest the statement be rendered purposeless, this paribhāṣā does not apply.
In the case of *turāsāham*,
this is the nominative singular ending of a stem ending in *tṛ*.
In some places, the reading is *jalāsāham*, but that is incorrect; for here, the substitution of *ṣ* is desired.

And so he will state [at 8.3.110]: "The mention of *āsani* in the list beginning with *savana* is for the purpose of indicating that the substitution of *ṣ* occurs even for roots other than those ending in *iṇ*.
By this, [the form] *jalāṣāham* [is established]."

[The question is: "Is this [the word] *āṣāham* established? [The answer is: "It is established. [The question is: "What about the word *sa*? He thinks as follows: by the paribhāṣā "of the final [element]" (P. 1.1.52), the final [element] must first be [replaced] by the letter *ḍ*. Since it would apply to the final [element], the letter *ḍ* would have to be [substituted] by virtue of proximity (*āntaratamya*); however, this is incorrect, because there is no purpose in prescribing the letter *ḍ* for the letter *ḍ*.

Therefore, even without the inclusion of the word "sa" [in the rule], the substitution will apply to the letter *s* alone. However, if the word "sa" were absent, one might object: "In the absence of a modification of a non-final element, [the substitute] takes the place of that which is in the vicinity of the final" (*Vyāḍīya-paribhāṣā* 63). Due to the principle of *āntaratamya* (closest similarity), would not a retroflex *ṛ*-vowel of the same duration as the two-moraic vowel *ā* replace it? With this intention, he says: "Let it not be so for the vowel *ā*. The term "iṇkoḥ" is a singular compound formed from a *dvandva*, hence it is expressed in the singular number. As for the augment *num*, although there is neuter gender, it is not applied because of the maxim: "The teaching regarding augments is not mandatory" (*Vyāḍīya-paribhāṣā* 99).
The term *iṇ* is a pratyāhāra (abbreviated designation) formed by the subsequent letter *ṇ*.

The term *ku* refers to the *ka*-varga (the guttural class). From what is this determined—that there is a reference to these [two terms], and not to the letters *i*, *k*, and *u*? It is from the [traditional] commentary (*vyākhyāna*).

In all cases of doubt, this principle applies: "For a specific understanding arises from a detailed explanation; indeed, there is no absence of a defining characteristic (*alakṣaṇa*) due to doubt" (Vyāḷīpa 75).
[Thus,] in the forms *vākṣu* and *tvakṣu*, the substitution of *k* occurs by rule 8.2.30.
"He will give" (*dāsyati*).

But how is this counter-example (*pratyudāharaṇa*) justified, given that in the rule [Pāṇini 1.1.69], an *ā*-vowel is included by the inclusion of the letter *ha*; for there is indeed homogeneity (*savarṇatva*) between the *ā* and the *ha*, because they have the same place and effort of articulation (*sthāna-prayatna*), since their place is the same, as stated in "the letters *a*, *kuh*, and the visarga are gutturals" (*akuhavisarjanīyāḥ kaṇṭhyāḥ*)?

The effort (*prayatna*) is also the same—[namely], that the articulatory organ (*karaṇa*) is open for the sibilants (*ūṣman*) and for the vowels (*svara*). Therefore, even though there is a difference in *īṅ*, the retroflex [ṣ] would indeed result [by rule P. 8.4.63]. In the rule [P. 1.1.10], "when a letter is mentioned by its own form, it includes its homogeneous counterparts," the vowel *ā* is included by the mention of the letter *ha*; for there is homogeneity (*savarṇatva*) between *ha* and *ā*, because their place of articulation (*sthāna*) and effort (*prayatna*) are identical. Their place of articulation is the same, according to the rule: "the letters *a*, *ku* (i.e., *ka-ṭa-pa-yā*), and the visarga are gutturals (*kaṇṭhya*)."

The effort [of articulation] is also equal—if the organ of articulation (*karaṇa*) for the sibilants (*ūṣman*) and the vowels is the same. Therefore, even though there is *iṇ* [as a cause], the retroflex (*mūrdhanya*) would indeed result. If it is argued that this is not so because of the prohibition of the designation "homogeneous" (*savarṇa-saṃjñā-pratiṣedha*) according to the rule *na jhalāṃ jaś jhaśi* (Pāṇini 8.4.53), we say: no. This is not a fault, because the prohibition applies only to those whose homogeneous status has not been grasped; [the portion of the text stating otherwise does not exist in the Kāśikā reading]. This is not a defect.

Since he provides this instruction—*yadayam* [Pāṇini 4.4.127]—without applying the cerebralization (*mūrdhanya*) to the *s* following the vowel *a*, it is understood that in the rule *mūrdhno matup* [Pāṇini 4.4.126], he likewise provides the instruction without applying cerebralization to the *s* following the vowel *a*. From this, it is concluded that when the letter *h* is being mentioned, it does not include the vowel *a*; otherwise, he would not have provided the instruction *vayasyāsu*.
[The example is] *asau*.

By [Pāṇini 7.2.106], the *d* becomes *s*; by [Pāṇini 7.2.107], there is the substitution of *au* and the elision of the case-ending *su*. Because the mention of *iṇkoḥ* is in the ablative case (pañcamī), and because the term "as specified" (*nirdiṣṭa*) is intended to mean "immediate proximity," this rule is commenced since the previous one would not apply when there is an intervention. A cerebral (*mūrdhanya*) sound replaces the *s* that follows *iṇ* or *k*, even when there is an intervention by the augment *num*, an intervention by the *visarjanīya*, or an intervention by a *ś* or *v*.
The word *api* is connected with each of these [terms] individually; thus, three sentences are formed.
We shall demonstrate the purpose of these three sentences later. The mention of *num* should be understood as an indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*) for the *anusvāra* that stands in the place of *num*;
for there is no intervention by *num* whatsoever, since the rule [Pāṇini 8.3.24] prescribes the *anusvāra* in all such cases.
In the case of *sarpīṣi*,
the augment *num* is applied by [Pāṇini 7.1.72], and the lengthening of the vowel occurs by [Pāṇini 6.4.10].
In the case of *sarpiḥṣu*:

In *sarpiṣṣu*, the *visarjanīya* is applied by [Pāṇini 8.3.36] *dāśari*. Because of the mention of the option (*vāgrahaṇāt*) in [Pāṇini 8.3.34] *visarjanīyo ‘nte*, there is optionally a *sakāra* in place of the *visarjanīya*; once the following *sakāra* has been changed to *ṣakāra*, the preceding one is changed to *ṣakāra* by [Pāṇini 8.4.40].

Now, why does this not apply here in the cases *nisse* and *niṃssva*? To this he says: “*numādibhiḥ*” and so forth. And this [rule] is obtained because the completion of the sentence applies to each [condition] individually; for when the completion of the sentence applies to each individually, there are three distinct sentences: “Even when there is an intervention by *num*, a cerebral [substitute] occurs for what follows *iṇ* and *ku*; and likewise in other cases as well. The statement “even when there is an intervention by *num*, *visarjanīya*, *śa*, or *v*” is the governing rule (*grahaṇakavākya*) that serves as the basis for those very [individual rules].

In that context, by the first rule, a retroflex [substitute] is prescribed when there is an intervention by *num*; by the second, however, when there is an intervention by *visarjanīya*; and by the third, when there is an intervention by the *śar* sounds.
Therefore, it does not occur here—namely, a retroflex [substitute] when there is an intervention by *num* together with *visarjanīya* and so forth—as in *niṃsse*.

Regarding *ṇisi cumbane* (Dhātupāṭha 1025): because it is marked with the indicatory letter *it*, the augment *num* is added; then [the suffix] *laṭ*, [and then] *thās*; by [Pāṇini 3.4.80], *thāsaḥ se*, *thās* is replaced by *se*; and because it belongs to the *adādi* class, there is elision (*luk*) of the *śap* suffix.
Thus, we have *niṃssva*. Regarding *loṭ*: by [Pāṇini 3.4.91], the final vowel (*ṭi*) is replaced by *e*; then, by the same rule, the *e* is replaced by *va*.

Furthermore, what is the purpose of the word *api*? If it is argued that it is so that [the rule] may apply even when there is no intervention, this is not the case; for since the rule is already established by the preceding one in the absence of intervention, its restatement must be understood as having a restrictive purpose (*niyamārtha*), namely, that it applies only when there is an intervention by *num* and the like.

If that were the case, would not the substitution [of ṣ] for *iṇ* and *ku* fail to occur when there is no intervention by *num* and the like? This is not so. For if the cerebral [substitution] were intended even when there is intervention by *num* and the like, he would have formulated a single rule as "when there is intervention by *num*, *u*, *visarjanīya*, or *ś*," and indeed he did so. Therefore, by the force of making a division of the rules (*yogavibhāga*), the former [rule] will be understood as having the purpose of [excluding] intervention; thus, the word *api* (even) is not necessary. However, for one who understands the matter in this way and finds the process of comprehension too cumbersome, the word *api* serves to avoid that difficulty.
Since it would have been sufficient simply to mention the letter *s*, the use of the pratyāhāra *śar* is for the sake of variety;
for there is no intervention by the letters *ś* and *v* between the cause (*nimitta*) and the effect (*kāryin*). In this regard, four possible interpretations arise:

1) In both instances of the rule *ādeśapratyayayoḥ*, this genitive case might be construed as relating to a part (*avayava*) with respect to the letter *s*: namely, "the *s* which is a part of a substitute (*ādeśa*)" and "the *s* which is a part of an affix (*pratyaya*)."

Alternatively: (3) "In a suffix (*pratyaya*), when there is a substitute (*ādeśa*) in grammatical coreference (*samānādhikaraṇa*)," [means] the *sakāra* which is part of the suffix, and the *sakāra* which is part of the substitute. (4) Or, it may be the reverse: [the *sakāra*] which is part of the substitute, and [the *sakāra*] which is part of the suffix.
But how can a single genitive case be both in grammatical coreference or connected to a part? It is because the objects [of the two relations] are distinct.

For just as in the rule *kharavasānayoḥ* [Pāṇini 8.3.15], even though there is only one locative case, it is divided according to the difference in its substrates (*adhikaraṇa*), so too here, one must understand that although there is only one genitive case, it is divided according to the difference in its objects (*viṣaya*).

Therefore, if the first alternative (the *sthāne dvirvacana* view) were adopted, then once reduplication had been applied by the rule *nityavīpsayoḥ* [Pāṇini 8.1.4], the substitution of *ṣatva* would undesirably apply in cases such as *basaṃbisam* and *musalaṃmusalam*, because in these instances the letter *s* is indeed a constituent part of the substitute (*ādeśāvayava*).
Thus, the alternative of reduplication in place of the original (*sthāne dvirvacana*) has certainly been adopted.

In the second [alternative], however, [the rule] would not apply in cases such as *kariṣyati*, because the mere letter *s* is not an affix (*pratyaya*). In the third alternative, both faults mentioned regarding the first two [alternatives] would follow. Having observed that all three alternatives are defective, he adopts the fourth alternative and says: "The *sakāra* which is not a substitute (*adeśa*)," and so forth. Even when the fourth alternative is adopted, [the rule] would not apply in cases such as *indro mā vakṣat* and *sadevām yakṣat* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 3.4.6), because here the *sakāra* is an affix (*pratyaya*) and not a constituent part of an affix (*pratyayāvayava*); therefore, he says: "*indro mā vakṣat*," and so forth.

The particle *iti* is used here in the sense of a reason (*hetu*). Because even in this case, by the principle of "behaving like that which possesses a designation" (*vyapadeśivadbhāva*), the *s* belonging to the suffix is a part of the suffix; therefore, it becomes a retroflex (*mūrdhanya*) sound. Regarding the form *vakṣāt*: from the root *vah*, there is the *leṭ* suffix, followed by *tip*; then the elision of the *i* vowel [by Pāṇini 3.4.97]; then the augment *aṭ* [by 3.4.94]; then the substitution of *sip* [by 3.1.34]; then the change of *h* to *ḍh* [by 8.2.31]; and finally the change to *k* [by 8.2.41].
Regarding *yakṣat*: by the rule *yaj-eḥ* [Pāṇini 8.2.30], there is *kutva*—the change of the letter *j* to *g*; then, by *cartva*, that *g* becomes *k*.

The remainder is as before, according to the appropriate application. Regarding *anvaśiṣat*: the root *śās* is used in the sense of "instruction" (Dhātupāṭha 1075). This is the *luṅ* (aorist) tense; by the rule *sartti-śāsty-artibhyaś-ca* [Pāṇini 3.1.56], *cl* is replaced by *aṅ*; then, by [Pāṇini 6.4.34], there is the substitution of *i* for the penultimate vowel.
Regarding "anvaśiṣatām," the suffix *tas* becomes *tām*. Regarding "śiṣṭaḥ": [it is derived from the root *śās*].
The substitution of *ṣ* [for *s*] occurs, and as before, the substitution of *it* [the augment *i*].
Regarding "uṣitaḥ":

from the root *vas* "to dwell" (Dhātupāṭha 1005), the augment *iṭ* is applied by [Pāṇini 7.2.52], and the semivowel substitution (*samprasāraṇa*) occurs by the rule concerning *vac* and other roots [Pāṇini 6.1.15].

Regarding the forms *jakṣatuḥ* and *jakṣuḥ*: [the root] *ghas* (meaning "to eat," Dhātupāṭha 715) and its substitute *ghas*—both of these are included here. Now, one might object that since a substitute (*ādeśa*) is defined by a grammatical rule (*lākṣaṇika*), its inclusion is improper. This is not a fault; for the paribhāṣā concerning "that which is taught by a rule versus that which is directly stated" (*lakṣaṇapratipadokta*) is not universally obligatory (*anitya*).
Its impermanence is indicated by the mention of the particle (*nipāta*) in [Pāṇini 6.3.109];
it is also indicated by the mention of "mahāvyāhati" in [Pāṇini 8.2.71].

Furthermore, since one of the two roots *ghas* or *vas* here consists of fewer syllables, the root *śās* is placed first despite the rule for prior placement (*pūrvanipāta*) being applicable; by doing so, the author indicates independence from the formal rules—that is, to show that we need not rely on any particular grammatical rule in this instance.
Therefore, since the technical rule *lakṣaṇapratipadoktaparibhāṣā* (Pāṇini 1.1.3) is not invoked here, it is logical that the substitute (*ādeśa*) is also included.

When the *liṭ* suffix follows the root *ad*, the substitution of *dhas* occurs by *liṭanyatarasyām* (7.3.97); then, the elision of the penultimate vowel occurs by *gamahana* (6.4.98). Because of the status of being a *sthānivadbhāva* (as if occupying the place of the original), there is reduplication; then, by *jhalāṃ jaś jhaśi* (8.4.53), the change to *cutva*—namely, the letter *jha*—occurs, followed by *jaśtva* for that [jha], resulting in the letter *ja*; and for the letter *gh*, there is *cartva*, resulting in the letter *k*. It should be understood that because this [substitute] serves as the basis [for the subsequent operations], the desired form is established.
Regarding the form *akṣan*:

[the suffix] *luṅ* undergoes the substitution of *ghasl* by [Pāṇini 2.4.37], the substitution of *jhi* by *ant* [by 7.1.3], and the elision of the final consonant of the *saṃyoga* by [8.2.23]. By the rule *mantra ghasahvara...* [2.4.80], there is the elision of *cli*, followed by the elision of the penultimate vowel by [6.4.100], and the change of *k* by *cartva*. When it is stated that "this statement is for the sake of preventing the substitution," someone might object: "It is appropriate that the statement is made for the sake of preventing the substitution of *śās* and *vas*; however, the statement regarding *ghas* is made for the sake of the affix, because it is a substitute. To this, he replies: "*ghasiḥ*," etc.

For the collection of phonemes beginning with *gha* is indeed the substitute (*ādeśa*) *ghas*, whereas the *s* is a part (*avayava*) of that [substitute], not itself a substitute; thus, this statement is made to indicate that even with respect to the substitute *ghas*, [the *s*] is not a substitute. Regarding the term "having become *ṣ*" (*ṣabhūte*), the meaning is: having attained this form, namely *ṣ*.
As for "he desires to praise" (*tuṣṭuṣati*).

By the rule *sanaḥ kittvam* (Pāṇini 1.2.9), the suffix *san* is marked with the *k*-sign; by *dīrghaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.4.16), there is lengthening; then reduplication; and by *śapūrvāḥ khayaḥ* (Pāṇini 7.4.61), the remaining consonants (*khayaḥ*) are retained [of the reduplicated syllable]. Thus, from the root *sic*, one forms *sivecayiṣati*:
the suffix *ṇic* is added by *sivecayiṣati* (Pāṇini 3.1.26), followed by *san*, the augment *iṭ*, and the substitution of *guṇa* and *ay-ādeśa*.
By the rule *ṇau kṛtaṃ sthānivadbhavati* (Pāṇini 1.1.56), there is reduplication of the suffix *sic*. Thus, we have *siṣañjayiṣati*.
[The root] *sañj* (meaning "to adhere," Dhātupāṭha 987) takes the suffix *san*, followed by reduplication; then, by the rule *sanyataḥ* (Pāṇini 7.4.79), the change to *i* occurs.

Regarding the form *suṣvāpayiṣati*: there is vocalization (*samprasāraṇa*) of the reduplication according to [Pāṇini 7.4.67], which applies to the causative of the root *svap*. Now, one might ask: "Is not the cerebral substitution here already established by the preceding rule alone? What, then, is the purpose of this new rule? To this, he says: "Since it is already established," and so forth.

Regarding "sisikṣati": the suffix *san* is added to the root *sic*; while the rule [Pāṇini 1.2.9] is in effect, [Pāṇini 1.2.10] applies, and due to its *kittva* status, there is an absence of *guṇa*. Then, by [Pāṇini 8.2.30], the substitution of *ku* (i.e., *ṣ*) occurs.
Regarding "susūṣate" [the Kāśikā reads "susūṣati"]: [the same analysis applies].
The root *ṣūṅ* is defined as "to release the embryo of living beings" (*dhātupāṭha* 1031). By the rule *pūrvavatsanaḥ* (Pāṇini 1.3.62), the Ātmanepada ending is applied.
Why is there an exception (*pratyudharaṇa*) such as *susūṣati*, which ends in the suffix *tip*? That should be understood as belonging to the root *ṣū* meaning "to impel" (*dhātupāṭha* 1408).

Now, what is the purpose of employing the particle *eva* [in the rule], since a restriction (*niyama*) would be understood simply by the force of beginning the rule when [the desired result] is already established? To this he says: "The employment of the particle *eva*," and so forth.

But what is the fault in this restriction—that the substitution occurs *only* before the suffix *san* after the roots *stu* and *ṇī*—such that it is not desired? To this he says: "In the case of *stu* and *ṇī*, [the substitution occurs] only before *san," and so forth.

By this restrictive rule (*avadhāraṇa*) stating "only before *san*," the exclusion of other suffixes is effected for *stu* and *ṇī*: if a retroflex (*mūrdhanya*) occurs after *stu* and *ṇī*, it must be only before *san*, and not before any other suffix.
Consequently, [the form] *tuṣṭāva* would not occur in the *liṭ* [perfect tense].
In this case, however, *sisikṣati* would indeed [be formed]; for by the restrictive rule (*avadhāraṇa*), the substitution of *ṣ* is not excluded.
Regarding the phrase "elsewhere" (*anyatra*) and so forth:
if it were not stated that "in the case of *ṣaṇ*", then the restriction would apply everywhere without distinction.

Furthermore, because the restriction has not been revoked, just as in *sisikṣati* the substitution of *ṣ* for the following *s* does not occur after the reduplication (*abhyāsa*), so too it would not occur in *siṣeca* even when the suffix *liṭ* follows.
Therefore, the term *ṣaṇi* is stated so that [the rule] might not apply elsewhere, such as before *liṭ* and other suffixes. [The question is:
"What is the purpose of this compliance regarding *vinati*?"
*Vinata* is the designation used by the ancient teachers for the substitution of *ṣa*-sounds and *ṇa*-sounds. *Anurodhaḥ* means "conformity" or "purpose.
The intended meaning is: what is the purpose of the *ṣa*-substitution such that the form with the *ṣa*-substitution already applied is taken up here?
"Let there be no restriction for *arvinata*," [it is said]. *Arvinata* means "that in which the quality of *sat* (existence) is absent.
If it were simply stated as *san*, the restriction would apply to existence (*sat*) in general.
In that case, just as [a sound] does not become *mūrdhanya* due to the practice of another element (*dhātu*) when *ṣatva* is present, so too it would not occur when *ṣatva* is absent.

Therefore, [the rule] states "not having become *ṣ*" (*aṣatvabhūta*) so that this restriction (*niyama*) does not apply when *ṣatva* has not occurred. The term *avinata* means "that in which *ṣatva* is non-existent."
If only "san" were stated, the restriction would apply to the suffix *san* in its general form.

In that case, just as the cerebralization does not occur for another root after the repetition of *san* when it has become *ṣa*-bhūta (i.e., changed to *ṣ*), it would likewise not occur when it has not become *ṣa*-bhūta.
Therefore, the mention of "vinata" is for the purpose that the restriction should not apply when it has not become *ṣa*-bhūta.

Regarding the form *suṣupsati*: the desiderative suffix (*san*) is added to the root *svap*; due to the rule *rudavidamuṣagrahi...* [Pāṇini 1.2.8], the suffix is marked with the *k*-sign, which triggers the vowel substitution (*samprasāraṇa*) by the rule *vacisvapiyajādīnām...* [Pāṇini 6.1.15].
[The opponent asks: "What is the point of insisting on the inclusion of the *anubandha* (indicatory letter)?"
The letter *na* is an *anubandha*. What is the purpose, what is the utility, of including the letter *na* as an *anubandha?
[It is so that] the restriction may not apply to every instance of the word *ṣa* alone."

When the word "ṣa" is mentioned, does it not refer to whatever [sound] bears that name? In that case, the rule would apply everywhere to the sound *ṣ*. However, when there is a mention of a sound accompanied by an *anubandha* (indicatory letter), the rule applies only to that specific instance and not elsewhere.
Therefore, even in the case of the bare sound *ṣ* without an *anubandha*, the cerebral (*mūrdhanya*) substitution certainly occurs for other [sounds] as well.

Regarding the form *suṣupiṣa indram*: it is derived from the root *svap* with the *liṭ* suffix; the *ātmanepada* ending is applied by transposition (*vyatyaya*). By the rule *thāsaḥ se* [Pāṇini 3.4.80], the *thās* is replaced by *se*. By the rule *asaṃyogālliṭ kit* [1.2.5], the *liṭ* suffix is marked as *kit*, which triggers *samprasāraṇa* (vowel substitution) by the rule beginning with *vac* [6.1.15]. The augment *iṭ* is added according to the restriction for roots beginning with *krī* and others. Reduplication (*dvirvacana*) follows. The retroflex (*mūrdhanya*) replaces the *s* of the suffix. When the word *indra* follows, the *ayādeśa* (substitution of *ay*) occurs, and subsequently, the *yakāra* is elided by the rule *lopaḥ śākalyasya* [8.3.19]. Thus, the form *suṣupiṣa indram* is established. Here, because there is no restrictive rule regarding the absence of an *anubandha*, the retroflex replacement certainly occurs after the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*).

"Regarding the phrase 'the occurrence [of *i*] in the reduplicated syllable' (*abhyāsasya yā prāptiḥ*), and so forth: if the mention of 'reduplicated syllable' (*abhyāsa*) were not made, the restriction would apply even to that *i* which belongs to the verbal root (*dhātu*). This is not desired. Therefore, the mention of 'reduplicated syllable' is made so that the restriction may apply specifically to that occurrence of *i* which takes place in the reduplicated syllable."
Regarding "pratīṣiṣati": this is the desiderative (saN) of the root *i* preceded by the prefix *prati*. Regarding "adhoṣiṣati": [this is the desiderative of the root *vas*].

Being preceded by *adhi* and so forth, [the root *iṣ*] is reduplicated because it begins with *aj* and consists of a single vowel, according to the rule *sanyaṅoḥ* [Pāṇini 6.1.9]. Then, by the rule *sanyataḥ* [Pāṇini 7.4.79], the vowel *i* is replaced by *ī*. Following this, the single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) of the root and the prefix occurs. When the forms *adhīṣiṣa-* and *pratīṣiṣa-* are established, since there is no restriction regarding the application of the augment *ṣat*, even when the desiderative suffix (*san*) has become *ṣat*, the sibilant following the root indeed becomes a retroflex (*mūrdhanya*). This mention of *sa* is an indication made without a case-ending. One might suggest that the prohibition alone should be formulated as *na*; however, there is no difference in terms of brevity (*lāghava*). Examples include *sisvedayiṣati* and others.

The roots *niṣvidā* in the sense of "oozing from the body" (*dhātupāṭha* 1188), *ruvad* and *svard* in the sense of "tasting" (*dhātupāṭha* 18, 19), and *ṣaha* in the sense of "endurance" (*dhātupāṭha* 852)—from these, the suffix *ṇic* is applied, and then the desiderative suffix *san*.
Now, one might ask: since there is no difference in the rule whether a *s* is prescribed for a *s*, for what purpose is the *s* explicitly mentioned? To this he says: "Of the *s*" and so forth.

Since the letter *s* was substituted [by P. 8.3.59] according to the rule *ya eṣām* [P. 8.2.64], the substitution of a retroflex (*mūrdhanya*) would apply because it is a substitute; therefore, this statement is made. Because the ablative case is specified in the rule *iṇkoḥ* [P. 8.3.57], and because the mention of the specific term [in that rule] implies immediate proximity (*ānantarya*), the rule would not apply when there is an intervention; hence this [present rule] is commenced. By the mention of *aṅ*, the augment (*āgama*) is included, not the *pratyāhāra* [of vowels];
this is to be understood from the traditional commentary (*vyākhyāna*).
"Prior to the mention of *saṃ*":
this refers to the rule beginning with *parinivibhyaḥ sevasitasaya* [Pāṇini 8.3.70].
The examples will be explained later on.

The word "api" (even) is for the purpose that [the rule] should apply even when there is no intervention; otherwise, if it were not so, then even for one whose substitution-sibilant (*ādeśa-sakāra*) is already obtained by the preceding rule, it would not occur in the absence of an intervening vowel, because it would be barred by the *takrakauṇḍinya-nyāya* (the maxim of the curd and Kauṇḍinya). How much more so, then, for a non-substitution sibilant belonging to words such as *senā*, for which the occurrence of a retroflex (*mūrdhan*) is absolutely impossible? [The phrase] "it continues from 'before *sit*' (*prāk sitāt*)" applies here.

Regarding the rule *sthāsenayasedhasica* [Pāṇini 8.3.65], those verbal roots (*dhātu*) which are indicated in the sūtra by the word *sthā*—that is, from that point up until the mention of *sita* in *prāk sitasaṃśabdanāt* [Pāṇini 8.3.70]—are to be understood as "the *sthā*-class" (*sthādayaḥ*). Now, for what purpose is the substitution of *ṣ* (ṣatva) stated when there is an intervention by the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*), given that in forms such as *paritiṣṭhāsatī*, the substitution of *ṇ* (ṇatva) is already established by the general rule *iṇkoḥ* [Pāṇini 8.3.57]? To this, he says: "When there is an intervention by the reduplicated syllable," and so forth.

Since the *sakāra* of that which is not taught with a *ṣakāra* as its upadeśa is not established by the preceding rule, the rule for *ṣatva* is stated for that purpose when there is intervention by the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*), as in the example *abhiṣiṣeṇayiṣati*. [In this case: "he intends to march against with an army. By the rule *satyāpapāśarūpavīṇātūlaślokasenālomatvacavarmavarṇacūrṇacurādibhyo ṇic* [Pāṇini 3.1.25], the causative suffix (*ṇic*) is applied; due to the treatment as if it were the suffix *iṣṭhan*, there is elision of the penultimate vowel (*ṭilopa*); then the desiderative suffix (*san*); and as before, the augment *iṭ* is added. Furthermore, it is stated "and for the sake of [reduplicated syllables] ending in a vowel" (*avarṇāntābhyāsārthaṃ ca*).
With reference to the rule concerning the suffix *ṣu*, it has been stated:

although there is a substitution of *s* for that [root-final], nevertheless this is not established by the general rule (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*), because the reduplication does not end in *iṇ* and because it is separated by that [substitute]. For example:
*abhitaṣṭhau*.

By [Pāṇini 7.1.34], *au* is substituted; as before, there is the elision of the remaining consonants (*khayaḥ śeṣaḥ*). Regarding the phrase "and for the sake of prohibiting [the substitution] in the case of *ṣaṇ*"—this means that by the restrictive rule [Pāṇini 8.3.61], "only in the case of *stau* and *ṇi*," that which was prohibited and excluded is now intended to apply in the case of *ṣaṇ*. What, then, was that which was prohibited? The substitution of *ṣ*.
Alternatively, [the suffix] *niṣṭhā* occurs in the sense of negation (*pratiṣedha*), which is what is negated.
The word *artha* functions here in the sense of "cessation" (*nivṛtti*), as in the expression "smoke for the sake of mosquitoes" (*maśakārtho dhūmaḥ*).
Thus it has been said: "The prohibition of *ṣatva* that was made for a root other than *stu* and *ṇi* when *ṣaṇ* follows—that is for the purpose of its cessation."
Regarding the form *abhiṣiṣikṣati*:

if it were not stated here that [the substitution of *ṣ*] occurs even when there is an intervention by the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*), then the *ṣ*-substitution would not take place, as it does not in the case of *sisikṣati*. Why is the word "of the reduplicated syllable" (*abhyāsasya*) mentioned, given that the word "and" (*ca*) is used here, which serves to draw in the word "also" (*api*) from the previous rule? By this, the meaning becomes: "both when there is no intervention and also when there is an intervention. If one objects: "In that case, even without the mention of 'of the reduplicated syllable,' the [ṣ-substitution] will apply to what follows a cause situated in a prefix (*upasarga*), because of the prohibition [stated in Pāṇini 8.3.111]? No; [that is not so].

Because the rule *upasargāt sunoti* [Pāṇini 8.3.65], which is intended for the prescription of the cerebral *ṣ*, serves as a prohibition [of that very cerebralization], and since that very prohibition would otherwise apply, the rule *upasargāt sunoti* is commenced in order to override it. Therefore, from where could there be the application of the prohibition? To this he says: "But of the reduplication," and so forth. One should not suspect a reversed restriction (viparītaniyama) such as "only of the reduplication in the case of *sthā* and the others"; for if such a reversed restriction were in effect, the prescription of the cerebral *ṣ* for *sthā* and the others in the context of reduplication would be entirely purposeless. "Abhisusūṣati."
The root *ṣū* is used in the sense of "impelling" (*preraṇe*; Dhātupāṭha 1408). Regarding the form *abhisiṣāsati*:

the root *ṣo* is used in the sense of "concluding an action" (*antakarmaṇi*; Dhātupāṭha 1147); and the roots *ṣuñ* in the sense of "pressing out" (*abhiṣave*; Dhātupāṭha 1247) and *ṣū* in the sense of "impelling" (*preraṇe*; Dhātupāṭha 1408).

Is it because of the instruction [in the rule] regarding the addition of the suffix *śap* that there is no inclusion of the two roots *ṣūṅ*—namely, *ṣūṅ* "to release the embryo of living beings" (Dhātupāṭha 1031) and *ṣūṅ* "to bring forth" (Dhātupāṭha 1132)—from the first (*adādi*) and fourth (*divādi*) conjugations? This is because of the principle: "When a root is cited without an *anubandha*, it does not include the same root with an *anubandha*" (Vyāḍiparibhāṣā 53).

The root *ṣo* in the sense of "ending" (*antakarmaṇi*) [DhP 1147], *ṣṭuñ* in the sense of "praising" (*stutau*) [DhP 1043], *ṣṭubhu* in the sense of "obstructing" (*stambhe*) [DhP 394; note that the Kāśikā and Prācīnāmnāya read *ṣṭuma*] [DhP 394], and *ṣṭhā* in the sense of "cessation of motion" (*gatinivṛttau*) [DhP 928]—the causative form *senayati* has already been shown previously.

Regarding *ṣi* in the sense of "motion" (*gatyām*) [DhP 47] and *ṣidhū* in the sense of "scriptural authority and accomplishment" (*śāstre māṅgalye ca*) [DhP 48], both are included. However, it should be understood that because of the prohibition [by Pāṇini 8.3.113], the substitution of *ṣ* occurs for these two roots in cases other than motion.
The mention of *śap* is for the purpose of excluding the root *ṣidhu* "to complete" belonging to the *divādi* class.

Regarding the roots *vicir* "to flow" (*dhātupāṭha* 1434) and *sañj* "to adhere" (*dhātupāṭha* 987), since they are taught with an initial *ṣ*, the rule *ṣṭuanunāsikaḥ* [Pāṇini 8.3.59] would apply; however, since the prohibition by *na ṣatvaṃ kupvoḥ* [Pāṇini 8.3.111] would then apply, this statement [is made]—[this is not found in the Kāśikā reading].
Since that instruction regarding *at* is not applicable from the very beginning,
the mention of *sunoti* and so forth by means of the *śtip* affix is for the purpose of excluding the *yaṅ*-lopa (the elision of the *yaṅ* suffix).
[The rule] "after a cause situated in a prefix," and so on, applies.

By this, he shows that when the cause for the retroflex [nasal] is situated within a preverb (*upasarga*), the word "preverb" is used here by way of metaphorical designation (*upacāra*) because of its location therein.
For indeed, there is the application of a term to that which is located therein, as in the example: "The beds cry out.
[The example is] *abhyaṣuṇot*.
In *laṅ*, there is the substitution of *ṣ* [for *s*] by the rule *prāksitād aṅvyavāye 'pi* [Pāṇini 8.3.63].
In *abhiṣuvati*,
the substitution of *uvaṅ* occurs by the rule *aci śnudhātubhruvām* [Pāṇini 6.4.77], etc.
In *abhiṣyati*,
there is the elision of the vowel *o* by [Pāṇini 6.1.71]. In *abhiṣṭauti*, [the same applies].

Because it belongs to the *ad-ādi* class, there is *luk* (elision) of the *śap* suffix; [then] by [Pāṇini 7.3.89], there is *vṛddhi*. Regarding "he praises" (*abhiṣṭobhate*), the *ātmanepada* ending occurs because the root is *anudāttet*.
Regarding "abhiṣiñcati," [the suffix] *num* is applied by [Pāṇini 7.1.59]. Regarding "abhiṣajati."
There is the elision of the letter *n* by the rule *daṃśasañjasvañjāṃ śapi* [Pāṇini 6.4.25].
The same applies in the case of *abhiṣvajate*. The middle voice (*ātmanepada*) is used as before.
Regarding "abhiṣiṣvaṅkṣate":
here too, the ātmanepada ending is applied by the rule "pūrvavatsanaḥ" (Pāṇini 1.3.62).
Regarding "dadhi siñcati."

There is a prohibition [of the *suṭ* augment] by the rule *iti pratiṣedhaḥ* (8.3.111). In the example "a place that is drained" (*niḥsecako deśaḥ*), the prefix *nis-* is connected with the action of going (*gam-*) and not with the action of sprinkling (*sic-*); therefore, it receives the designation of a preverb (*upasarga*) only with respect to *gam-*, and not with respect to *sic-*.

Because of the rule stating, "Those particles such as *pra* and others, when joined with an action, receive the technical designations of 'motion' (*gati*) and 'prefix' (*upasarga*) in relation to that [action]" (Pāṇini-vṛtti 1.4.99),
[the form] *abhisāvakīyati* is derived from the root *su* with the suffix *ṣvul*.

Regarding *sāvakamicchati*: by [Pāṇini 7.4.33], the substitution of *i* occurs; thus, with *sāvakīya* established, there is a connection with the prefix *abhi*, and from that, the present tense suffix (*laṭ*). Here too, the designation "prefix" (*upasarga*) applies to *abhi* in relation to the desiderative *sāvakīyati*, because of its connection with the action toward that [desiderative], and not in relation to the root *su* (to press), because of the reversal [of the sequence].
Therefore, the change to *ṣ* does not occur.

If this is so, then [the rule] would not apply even in the case of *abhiṣāvayati*, because here too there is a reversal with respect to the root *sāvati*? To this he says: "But in the case of *abhiṣāvayati*, etc. For here, the root *su-* first undergoes connection with the prefix (*upasarga*), and only afterwards does it undergo connection with the meaning of commanding (*preṣaṇa*) or requesting (*adhyeṣaṇa*), thereby giving rise to the causative suffix (*ṇic*). Therefore, one is commanded or requested with respect to the action itself as qualified by the prefix.

Therefore, since *sunoti* itself is designated as a preverb (*upasarga*), the substitution of *ṣ* for *s* indeed occurs. This statement is made because the prohibition [of the substitution] would otherwise apply according to [Pāṇini 8.3.111].
In the word *sadiḥ*, by means of a transposition of case endings (*sub-vyatyaya*), the nominative stands in place of the genitive;
thus: "in *niṣīdati*."
The root *ṣad* is listed as "to perish, to go, and to sink" (Dhātupāṭha 1427). By the rule [Pāṇini 7.3.78], *sīd* is substituted for it. Thus we have "niṣasāda."

Due to the prohibition [stated in] *sadisvañjoḥ parasya liṭi* (Pāṇini 8.3.118), the substitution of *ṣ* does not occur for the letter following the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*). In connection with the rule *sadiraprateḥ* (Pāṇini 8.3.66), which appears in the *Bālamanoramā*, he says: "After *sad-* when not preceded by *prati*.
[He adds: "From a prefix" (*upasargāt*); the meaning is: "following an *iṇ*-vowel situated in a prefix."
Intending that the nominative case in *sadiḥ* signifies the sense of the genitive (*ṣaṣṭhyarthe prathamā*), he says: "of the root *sad*, the *s*" (*sadeḥ sasya*).
The example is *niṣīdati*.
Regarding the rule *bāla-manoramā*: "before *sit*, even when there is intervention by *aṭ*" (Pāṇini 8.3.66), it says "before *sat*" (*prāksitāt*).
The phrase "included in the sūtra beginning with 'upasargāt sunoti'" is the ellipsis [to be supplied].
Regarding the word "teṣām" (of them),
it means "of the fifteen."
"He prohibited" (nyaṣedhat):

because it is separated by the letter *a*, the letter *i* does not follow immediately; thus, since [the rule] would otherwise not apply, this is a specific statement. "He heated thoroughly" (abhyuṣuṇot) is also to be cited as an example. *Stanbhi* is a verbal root belonging to the Vedic (sautra) tradition.

If [it is argued that] it is a *ṣopadeśa* (a root taught with an initial *ṣ*) because of the definition [in the Bhāṣya]: "those which have *aj* as their penultimate and end in a *sādit* [consonant]," then it is a *ṣopadeśa* for him; consequently, as before, since the prohibition of *ṣatva* would apply, this statement [is made]. Alternatively, if it is not a *ṣopadeśa* because it is read as such in the Sūtra, then [the prohibition] does not apply at all. By the word *ca* ("and") in [Pāṇini 3.1.82], the *śnā* suffix is added in conjunction [with the others].
By the rule *aniditām* [Pāṇini 6.4.24], there is the elision of the nasal. It is stated that "the word *aprateḥ* does not recur here" [as noted in the *Kāśikā* and *Padamañjarī*].
This is understood precisely from the division of the sūtra (*yogavibhāga*); for otherwise, he would have included the mention of *prati* in the preceding sūtra itself.

It might be argued: "The rule *avāccālambanāvidūryayoḥ* (Pāṇini 8.3.68) will prescribe the substitution of *ṣ* for *s*. Therefore, the separation of the *yoga* (the rule) is intended so that [the substitution] occurs only after the root *stanbh*, and not after *sad*. But this is not correct; even if it were a single *yoga*, the substitution would apply only to that [root] whose function pertains to proximity (*ālambana*) or distance (*avidūrya*). And to which [root] do these two [conditions] belong? To *stanbh* alone. The particle *ca* serves to carry forward (*anukarṣaṇa*) the root *stanbh*."
This undertaking is not fruitless.
"Support" (ālambana) means taking refuge.
"Distant" (vidūra) means far removed; that which is other than that is "not distant" (avidūra).

Furthermore, that which is near and yet not too far should be understood as such; it is not merely being near. If mere proximity were intended, he would have used the term "near" alone. The state of not being distant is "non-distantness" (*an-avidūrya*).

Precisely for this reason, by virtue of irregular derivation (*nipātana*), the suffix denoting an abstract state (*bhāvapratyaya*) follows even a *tatpuruṣa* compound preceded by the negative particle (*nañ*);
or alternatively, it is due to its inclusion in the *brāhmaṇa*-class [of words].
Thus: "having taken hold" (*avaṣṭabhya*).
This is the end of the section.
The meaning is "having resorted to.
[As in the phrase] "the autumn was seized."
The meaning is "near.
Alternatively, the meaning is "neither too near nor too far.
This distinction of meaning, however, is to be understood from the context and other such factors.

The substitution of *dh* for the final *ṣṭh* occurs by [Pāṇini 8.2.40], and the substitution of *v* for *bh* occurs by [Pāṇini 8.4.53]. Regarding the word *avastabdhaḥ*, the meaning is "oppressed" (*abhyardita*). The letter *c* serves to draw forward the rule [Pāṇini 8.3.68] *avāt*.
This is because, otherwise, the substitution would not apply to the root *svan* following *vi*, as it does not have the substitute *sa* for its initial.

Because of the word *ava* and because it is not a *niṣṭhā*-formed word (*aniṇanta*), this [rule] is commenced even though [the application of the suffix] was not otherwise required. By stating, "a specific action of consuming is denoted," he shows that its purpose is eating.
Regarding the word "viṣvaṇati": it means he eats with sound. Since verbal roots have multiple meanings, the root *svan* here functions in the sense of a specific action of consuming.

With the words "yatra" and so forth, he demonstrates that very specific kind of food. Regarding the roots *ṣevṛ* and *sevṛ*, meaning "to serve" or "to resort to"—though these are not found in the standard *dhātupāṭha* (they are listed as 501)—they are taught in the *bhvādi* class as *ātmanepada* verbs.

Since the rule *yo 'ti vā* (Pāṇini 8.3.111) would apply to the former (*ṣevṛ*) to prohibit the change of *ṣ* to *s*, while for the latter (*sevṛ*) the change to *s* was already unobtainable, this statement serves as a formal rule (*vacana*).
Thus, we have the form "sita."
Regarding the root *ṣiñ* in the sense of "binding" (*dhātupāṭha* 1248), this statement is made because the [prohibition of *ṣatva*] previously mentioned would otherwise apply.

Others, however, maintain that *syati* is also included; thus, when the suffix *kta* is added and the substitution of *ī* for *ya* is applied by the rule *dyatisyatimāsthām it ti kiti* [Pāṇini 7.4.40], the form *sita* is obtained.

But for what purpose is its inclusion, since the desired result is already established by the rule *upasargāt sunoti* [Pāṇini 8.3.65]? It is for the sake of restriction (*niyamārtham*), so that [the substitution] occurs only after the prefixes *pari*, *ni*, and *vi* as prepositions, and not after others.
Regarding the word *saya*:
this is the inclusion of the form ending in *ac* [by Pāṇini 3.3.56] derived from the root *sū*, for the purpose of excluding forms ending in other suffixes.
Regarding the word *sivu*: [it is included as the base form].
The root *ṣivu* means "to weave" (*tantusantāne*; Dhātupāṭha 1108), as before. Since a prohibition would otherwise apply, the mention of this [root] is made.
Regarding *saha*: it is not present in the Prāṅmukha recension;
it means "to endure" (*marṣaṇe*; Dhātupāṭha 852).
Regarding the term *suṭ*:

it refers to the augment *suṭ* (or *ruṭ*, according to the reading in the Kāśikā), because since its *s* is not a substitute for an original *s*, the rule for changing it to *ṣ* (*ṣatva*) would not otherwise apply; therefore, it is explicitly mentioned here.

As for the roots *stu* and *svañj*, the change to *ṣ* is already established by rules such as Pāṇini 8.3.65 (*upasargāt sunoti...*), so their inclusion in this context is intended so that the subsequent rule may provide an optional alternative even when there is an intervening vowel (*avyavāye*).
Regarding "pariṣodhyati":
the lengthening [of the vowel] occurs by the rule *hali ca* [Pāṇini 8.2.77].
Regarding "pariṣkaroti": [the same applies].

By [Pāṇini 6.1.137], *suṭ* is applied. Due to proximity (*pratyāsatti*), the roots beginning with *sivu*—namely *sivu*, *saha*, *suṭ*, *stu*, and *svañj*—are understood in that very preceding sūtra [8.3.70] as being those ending in *niṣṭhā* when preceded by *san*; they are not the *stu* and *svañj* found listed in the Dhātupāṭha. Since the rule [8.3.63] "before *sit*, even when there is intervention by *aṭ*" would apply to *stu* and *svañj*, while for the remaining roots it would not, this optional rule (*vibhāṣā*) is commenced. The root *syandū* (Dhātupāṭha 761) means "to flow" (*ruāvaṇe*). Because this root is not taught with an initial *ṣ* (*aṣopadeśa*), the substitution of *ṣ* for *s* was not applicable; therefore, this specific statement is made. Example: *anusyandate matsya udake* ("the fish flows along in the water").

Now, how is this counter-example justified? If the term *aprāṇiṣu* is understood as a *prasajya-pratiṣedha* (an absolute negation), meaning "it does not occur among non-living beings"; for in an absolute negation, wherever there is even a trace of a living being (*prāṇin*), the substitution of *ṣ* by *ūrdhanya* (the retroflex sibilant) must not take place. And here, since the fish (*matsya*) is a living being, the substitution of *ṣ* does not apply.

If, however, a *paryudāsa* (exclusion) is resorted to—meaning "it occurs other than with respect to living beings"—then a collection consisting of both living and non-living beings would indeed be "other than living beings," and thus the cerebral [substitution] would apply here in that object which consists of a collection of living and non-living beings. [The root] *skandir* (in the sense of "going" and "drying up") [Dhātupāṭha 971] has its upadeśa (original enunciation) with the vowel *a*. Therefore, since the cerebral substitution had not yet been established for it, this rule is stated.

Regarding the term *viṣkaśaḥ*: there is the elision of the nasal [of the root *kaś*] by the rule *aniditām* [Pāṇini 6.4.24], and the substitution of *n* [for *ś*] by the rule *radābhyām* [Pāṇini 8.2.42], and so forth. The phrase "by the force of making a separate rule" (*pṛthagyogakaraṇasāmarthyāt*), and so on, [is used].

The intention is that if the cerebral [substitution] were not intended for *skand* even after another preposition when followed by a non-*niṣṭhā* suffix, then one would have formulated a single rule as "after *vi* and *pari*, [the substitution occurs] before *skand* in a non-*niṣṭhā* context.

The particle *ca* serves to carry over (*anukarṣaṇa*) the word *skand*. Since the previous rule had established an option regarding the substitution of *ṣ*, this [present rule] prescribes its absence in the example "pariṣkandaḥ."
The suffix *ac* is applied according to the rule *pacādyac*.

In the rule *bahvaca iñaḥ prācyabharateṣu* [Pāṇini 2.4.66], it is indicated by the inclusion of the term "Easterners" (*prācām*) that the Bharatas are not included therein. Therefore, although the Bharatas are Easterners, they are mentioned separately. The roots *sphura* and *sphula*, meaning "to move," belong to the Taudādika class (Dhātupāṭha 1389 and 1390).
In these two cases as well, as before, the rule for the substitution of *ṣ* for *s* is prescribed even when the *mūrdhan* (the hard palate) has not been reached.

The mention of *śtip* is solely for the purpose of indicating the verbal root (*dhātu*); it is not intended to exclude the *yaṅ*-luṅ (the intensive without the *yaṅ* suffix). For in the *yaṅ*-luṅ, once the elision of the remaining *khaya* consonants of the reduplicated syllable has occurred, a *sakāra* following *ni* and the others is not possible. [Example: *viṣkambhitā*.

Is it because of the reading in the sūtra *stanmabhustunbhuskanbhuskunbhuskuñbhyaḥ śnuśca* [Pāṇini 3.1.82]? This is a verbal root mentioned in the sūtras (*sautra-dhātu*) that is taught with the letter *ṣ*. Since the substitution of the retroflex (*mūrdhanya*) for its *s* had not yet been established, it is prescribed for the *s* that follows the suffix *vi*. The inclusion of the word "always" (*nitya*) is for the purpose of excluding optionality.

The purpose of the mention of *śtip* is the same as before. By the rule "after an *aṅga* ending in *iṇ*, [the substitution of *ṣ* occurs] for those that follow," he shows that the *aṅga* ending in *iṇ* is the qualifier of *ṣī*, *suṅ*, *aṅ*, and *luṅ*, and these in turn are qualifiers of the letter *dh*. Now, why is it not understood that the *aṅga* ending in *iṇ* is the qualifier of the letter *dh* itself—[meaning] "that *dh* which follows what ends in *iṇ*"? He thinks as follows: if the *aṅga* ending in *iṇ* were a qualifier of the letter *dh*, then [the substitution would not apply] in forms such as *cyoṣīḍhvam* and *ploṣīḍhvam*; because of the intervention by the word *ṣī*.

Furthermore, according to the principle that "that by which there is no intervention [is considered immediate], even when there is intervention, because of the authority of the statement" (Vyā.pa. 46), the operation would indeed occur even when there is an intervention by a single *ṣī* suffix.
Even so, if the meaning were understood solely through the authority of the statement, those of dull intellect would experience a burden in their comprehension.
Since this fault does not arise when *ṣīdhvam* and the others are specifically qualified, it is appropriate that the *iṇ*-ending element itself be the qualifier for them.

If it is argued that this is incorrect because [the letter *h*] is a quality (*guṇa*), the following might be said: since the letter *dh* is the object of an operation (*kāryin*) and is qualified by those [suffixes], it possesses primacy;
whereas for those [suffixes], due to the reverse being the case, there is a lack of status as a quality.
Therefore, it is logical that the suffix ending in *iṇ* is the qualifier of the letter *h* itself.

And this is not so; for in a case where, having experienced a connection with the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*), the subordinate element (*guṇa*) becomes capable of performing a greater service for the principal (*pradhāna*), it first experiences a connection with the qualifier—which is itself subordinate—and only afterwards does it experience a connection with the principal. And thus: "The subordinate element, having undergone its own refinement (*saṃskāra*), reaches the principal."
For it thus operates more extensively in the service of the primary element.

Thus, here, by means of the member (*aṅga*) qualified by *iṇ*, the forms *ṣīdhvam* and so forth are specified; they bring about a specific grammatical operation for the letter *dh*, one that is free from the fault of requiring excessive cognitive effort.

Therefore, it is precisely the forms *ṣīdhvam* and so forth that are qualified by the member qualified by *iṇ*; and by those [forms], the letter *dh* is indeed properly qualified. This alone is logical.

"cyoṣīḍhvam, ploṣīḍhvam"— from the roots *cyu* and *plu*, the optative (*liṅ*) in the sense of a benediction, the suffix *sīyuṭ*, the ending *dhvam*, the prohibition of *iṭ* by [Pāṇini 7.2.10] "ekācaḥ," and then *guṇa*. "acyoḍhvam, aploḍhvam"— [these are from the same roots in the aorist].

By the rule *dhi ca* [Pāṇini 8.2.25], there is the elision of the *sakāra*, resulting in *cakṛḍhve* and *vavṛḍhve*. These are the forms of the root *kṛñ* and the root *vṛñ* in the perfect tense (*liṭ*).
The prohibition of the augment *iṭ* is applied by the rule *kusṛbhṛvṛ* [Pāṇini 7.2.13] and others.

The doubling [of the root] is the operation pertaining to the reduplication (*abhyāsa*). Now, one might object: does not the previous mention of *iṇ* from [Pāṇini 8.3.57], namely *iṇkoḥ*, indeed carry over here? How then is the mention of *iṇ* made again? To this he says: "The mention of *iṇ*" and so forth.

For that previous mention of *iṇ* was connected with the *ka*-group; therefore, when it recurs [in the present rule], that [connection] would also recur. Consequently, a new mention of *iṇ* is made here in order to exclude that [connection].
[Examples: *pakṣīdhvam*, *yakṣīdhvam*.

By the rule *paciyajibhyām āśiṣi liṅ* [Pāṇini 8.2.30], there is the substitution of *k* (*kutva*). When that has been applied, because the *ka*-class (*kavarga*) has ceased to exist here, the retroflex (*mūrdhanya*) does not occur.
As for *studhvam*: this is the imperative (*loṭ*) of the root *stu*; due to its belonging to the *adādi* class, there is the elision (*luk*) of the suffix *śap*.
"astudhvam" is the imperative (loṭ);
"pariveviṣodhvam" is the imperfect (laṅ).

The root *viṣlṛ* (Dhātupāṭha 1095) in the sense of "to pervade" takes the optative suffix *liṅ* in the imperative mood (*vidhi-lakāra*) with the augment *sīyuṭ*. By the rule *juhotyādibhyaḥ* (Pāṇini 2.4.75), there is *ślu* (elision of the suffix); by *ślau* (6.1.10), reduplication occurs; by *ṇijāṃ trayāṇāṃ guṇaḥ* (7.4.75), the *guṇa* substitution is applied to the reduplicated syllable; by *lopo vyor vali* (6.1.66), the *y* is elided; and by *saḥ syārdhadhātuke* (7.4.49), the *s* is elided.
In this context, the word *ṣīdhvam* exists as a composite consisting of the *ṣ* of the verbal root and the portion *īdhvam*; however, it is not an *aṅga* (stem) followed by a suffix ending in *ṇ*.
For instance, the designation *aṅga* applies to the entire form *veviṣi*, but not to the portion preceding the letter *ṣ* consisting merely of *veṣī*.

[The statement] "This is also established by the inclusion of meaningful units (*arthavadgrahaṇāt*)" is the objection of the challenger (the *codaka*). [Note: This phrase "this" does not appear in the *Kāśikā*.]
"Grasping" (*grahaṇa*) means that by which something is grasped; "the grasping of that which possesses meaning" (*arthavad-grahaṇa*) refers to the inclusion of meaningful elements.

This, moreover, is the technical rule (*paribhāṣā-sūtra*): "When there is the mention of that which possesses meaning, [there is no application] of that which is meaningless" (*arthavadgrahaṇe nānarthakasya*).
By this as well, the form *pariveviṣīdhvam* is established.

By the paribhāṣā "that which possesses meaning" (Vyā.pa.1), since only a meaningful word *ṣīdhva* would be grasped, it would necessarily have to undergo the substitution of *ḍha*. However, this word *ṣīdhva* is not meaningful here; rather, it is the constituent part *īdhva* that is meaningful. Thus, the intention [of the objector] is: "What is the purpose of including the term 'aṅga' (stem) in order to exclude this?
To this, he gives the reply: "But this has not been relied upon."

"This" refers to the statement in the Bhāṣya: "When there is the mention of something meaningful, that which is meaningless is not included" (Vyāḍipāda 1). Alternatively, *gṛhītiḥ* means "mentioning"; thus, "the mentioning of that which is meaningful" is a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhī-samāsa*).
Therefore, this too is established; here, the intention is indeed the same as before. "But this has not been adopted" [but that has not been adopted—Kāśikā] is the reply.

It is not accepted that there is a "taking" (*grahaṇa*) of only those [elements] possessing meaning (*arthavat*), because the technical rule (*paribhāṣā*) regarding the taking of meaningful elements (Pāṇini 1.2.45) is not invoked here.
This non-invocation, however, is for the sake of avoiding the fault of excessive cognitive burden (*pratipatti-gaurava*).

For a listener whose intellect is slow (*manvadhī*), if they were to understand every desired meaning by relying on words not explicitly mentioned in the sūtra, there would be a heavy cognitive burden.
In this context, when the mention of *aṅga* (the stem) is made, the intended meaning is understood precisely as "pleasure" (*sukha*).

While it would have been sufficient to mention only *liṅ*, the mention of *ṣīdhvam* is for the purpose of ensuring that the rule applies to the *dhakāra* of this specific form. Consequently, [the substitution] does not occur in forms such as *ayīdhvam* and *stuvīdhvam*. In some cases, where the preceding rule would apply invariably, and in other cases where it would not apply at all, this statement is made for the sake of providing an option (*vikalpa*).

We shall clarify this in the examples. Here, the mention of *iṇ* is a qualifier for *iṭ*, and that [qualifier] is also for *ṣīdhvam* and the others, while those [in turn] are qualifiers for the letter *dh*. Showing this, he says: "after what follows *iṇ*," and so forth. Now, one might object: "Is it not the case that posteriority (*paratva*) with respect to *iṭ* is impossible for *ṣīdhvam* and the *liṭ* [affix], since they are included by the very mention of that [term *iṭ*]? Even though such posteriority is not possible in terms of the technical rules of grammar (*śāstra-kṛta*), nevertheless, it certainly exists in terms of audible sequence (*śruti-kṛta*); thus there is no fault.

In the forms *laviṣīdhvam* and *laviṣīḍhvam*, once the augment *iṭ* has been applied to the word *ṣīdhvam*, there is no intervention [between the root and the suffix] because that [augment] is included by the term *tadgrahaṇa*; thus, the [substitution of *ḍh* for *dh*] would necessarily apply by the preceding rule. In the form *alavidhvam*, however, the augment *iṭ* is applied specifically to the *sic* suffix, not to the *luṅ* [tense]; since that [augment] is not included by the term *tadgrahaṇa*, the [substitution] does not apply by the preceding rule.

In the case of *luluviḍhve* as well, since the augment *iṭ* belongs specifically to the *liṭ* [perfect], and because that [augment] is included by the mention of that [root], the rule would apply invariably by the preceding [sūtra] even in the absence of *vyadhāna*. As for *āsiṣīdhvam*:

[it is derived from] the root *ās* in the sense of "eating" (*dhātupāṭha* 1021), in the *liṅ* [optative] with *sovuṭ*; because the *iṇ* [vowel] of the root-sakāra is not situated before the *san* suffix, the augment *iṭ* does not occur here after that *iṇ*.

"Now, how should it be here?"—the intention is: "Should this be [formed] with an optional augment (*vikalpa*), or should it be formed with a compulsory augment (*nitya*)? [The root is] *dīṅ* "to perish" (Dhātupāṭha 1134); [in the] *liṭ* [perfect tense], there is the augment *iṭ* by the rule [beginning with] *krādi-niyama* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 7.2.13).
By [Pāṇini 6.4.63], *guṭ* is added, and the final letter (*ṭi*) is replaced by *e*.

When *upadidīyidhvam* is thus established, some say that there should indeed not be an option for *ḍha*-substitution here; because when there is immediate succession (*ānantarya*) between the augment *iṭ* and the stem (*aṅga*) ending in *iṇ*, that [succession] is interrupted by *yuṭ*. [Objection:
Is this *yuṭ* a part of the whole (*samudāyabhakta*)? [Response: It does not interrupt the whole itself.
But it certainly intervenes as a constituent part (*avayava*).

Now, why does it not necessarily occur with the preceding [suffix]? Because here, the *liṭ* follows an *aṅga* ending in *at*, and the letter *dh* is related to that; thus it must be so. And in this way, the meaning of the rule was demonstrated by the author of the *Vṛtti*.
But if this is not accepted, then the mention of *vibhāṣā* (optionally) cannot be connected with the preceding rule;
and that [optionality] is a restricted option (*vyavasthitavibhāṣā*), therefore it does not apply here.
Thus, in other cases, it will necessarily occur.
Regarding the phrase "of others" (*apareṣām*) and so forth:

when the mention of *aṅga* (stem) has ceased here, only the term *iṇaḥ* (after the root *iṇ*) continues to apply; thus, the augment *iṭ* is qualified by *iṇ* alone—meaning "the *iṭ* that follows *iṇ*.
And in this way, there must necessarily be the optional substitution of *ḍha* in this case.

For in this case, there is the augment *iṭ* following the *ṇa* (the suffix *ana*) which begins with *ya*, provided it is immediately subsequent. In the word *saṅgaḥ*, the nominative case is used in place of the genitive by means of a metrical substitution (*sub-vyatyaya*).
This should be understood in the same way for what follows as well.
Since the prohibition [of the augment] by rule 8.3.111 would otherwise apply, this new rule is commenced.
The same applies to the following as well.

*Sañjanam* means "attachment" (*saṅga*), derived from the root with the suffix *dhañ* in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāve*). It is a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "that which has an attachment—that is, a close contact—among the fingers. Regarding the term *bhīruṣṭhānam*:
it is a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*) consisting of the word *sthāna*, used here as a locus (*adhikaraṇasādhana*).
The formulation of separate rules is for the purpose of preventing the application of "correspondence according to order" (*yathāsaṃkhya*).

For if they were combined into a single rule, even though there would be equality between the cause (*nimitta*) and the effect (*naimittika*), the application of correspondence according to order might still occur due to the presence of the *svarita* accent.

Now, if the *svarita* accent is postulated for that very purpose, then the employment of the rule-splitting (*yogavibhāga*) is for the sake of variety. Since a prohibition would otherwise apply because the *s* sound belongs to the beginning of a word (*pada*), this [rule] is commenced.
The same applies to the subsequent cases as well.

The words *stoma* and *soma* are derived from the verbal roots *stu* ("to praise") and *su* ("to press") respectively, by applying the suffix *man* according to Pāṇini 3.2.181: "The suffix *man* is applied after the roots *ṛ*, *stu*, *su*, *hu*, *sṛ*, *duh*, *kṣi*, *kṣubh*, *āyā*, *pad*, *i*, *yakṣi*, and *ni*. Thus, they are etymologically explained.
However, according to the view that [the suffix] does not arise [from the root], the substitution of *ṣ* is prescribed for these two even when they have not yet been obtained from the very beginning;
as in "agniṣṭut. Here, the suffix *kvip* is applied to the root *stu* with *agni* as an upapada.
By the rule *hyas-asya* [Pāṇini 6.1.69], the suffix *tuka* is applied; this is a *upapada-samāsa*,
as in the word *agniṣṭomaḥ*.
The compound *agniṣomau* is a genitive determinative (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*).
It is a copulative (*dvandva*) compound; the substitution of *i* [for the final vowel of *agni*] occurs by the rule *īdagneḥ somārudrayoḥ* [Pāṇini 6.3.27].
[It is argued: "Is the lengthening of *agni* intended for the sake of applying the *ṣatva* [substitution of *ṣ* for *s*] in the word *soma*?"
And this [result] is obtained from the *bhāṣya* through the continued application of the term "optionally" (*vibhāṣā*) from the rule *vibhāṣeṭaḥ* (Pāṇini 8.3.79).

Nor would there be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) resulting from that continued application, because the option is understood as being restricted (*vyavasthitavibhāṣā*). Examples are: *jyotiṣṭomaḥ* and *āyuḥstomaḥ*, which are genitive compounds (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*).
The *sakāra* undergoes *rutva*, becoming a *visarjanīya*; then, by the rule *vā śari* (Pāṇini 8.3.36), it optionally becomes a *sakāra*.

For that [subsequent] *takāra* and the [preceding] *sakāra*, the rule for *ṣṭutva* applies. This statement is made because the substitution of *ṣatva* was not otherwise applicable, as the *sakāra* is not a substitute (*anādeśa*). The root *ṣṭana* (Dhātupāṭha 461), belonging to the *bhūvādigaṇa*, is what is intended here.

In the case of the word *devaśabda* [derived from] the root *gadī* meaning "to lament" (*gadī parivedane*, Dhātupāṭha 1860), this does not apply to the root belonging to the *curādika* class (Dhātupāṭha 1859). If that [latter root] were included, then because it ends in the vowel *a*, the rule *na vṛddhir ecācām ātaḥ* (Pāṇini 7.2.116) would prevent the occurrence of *vṛddhi*.
This substitution of *ṣ* is prescribed only after the prefixes *abhi* and *nis*.

For when the head of that subsequent *stuti* (praise) has been formed from the individual [elements], the technical designation of the word is not understood [from the rule] "after *abhi* and *ni*" (*abhinisaḥ*), and so forth. The meaning is:
"after this aggregate of prefixes which is *abhi-ni*."
Regarding the term *abhiniṣṭāna*:
it is derived with the suffix *ghañ* according to [Pāṇini 3.3.19], *abhinistīryate 'nena*,
and is a *prādi-samāsa* (compound with a prefix).
But surely, because of the common governing rule (*samānādhikāra*), [the suffix] will not occur in the case of *abhiniḥstanati*;

so what is the purpose of including the term "technical name of a word" (*śabda-saṃjñā*) for the sake of its exclusion? To this he says: "From the rule beginning with *samāsa*, [the previous rule] has ceased. This too is a statement made because [the application] was not otherwise established, as in the previous cases. That which ends in *yat* and *ca* is *yac*; that after which *ca* and *cau* follow is *yacpara*.
Because the word *prāduḥ* is not a prefix (*anupasarga*), it is mentioned separately. Regarding the form *abhiṣanti*:

[it is derived from] the root *as* in the sense of "being" (Dhātupāṭha 1065); due to its belonging to the *adādi* class, there is elision of the *śap* suffix, and by the rule *śnasorallopaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.4.111), there is elision of the vowel [of the root].
4|111) Thus [is the form] of the root *i*;
"abhiṣyāt" is the optative (*liṅ*).

Regarding the word *anusṛtam*: [the root] *sṛ* means "to go" (Dhātupāṭha 935). But surely, because the letter *s* is prolated (*prṛta*), [the prefix *anu*] is dependent upon that very [letter]? It is not the case that the designation "prefix" (*upasarga*) for the word *anu* applies with respect to the letter *s* in *anusṛtam*; for that [letter] alone does not denote an action, and the rule prescribing the designation "prefix" for words such as *pra* and others applies only with respect to what denotes an action.

"Those particles beginning with *pra* which are employed in relation to something [else] receive the technical designations of *gati* and *upasarga* in relation to that thing" (Mahābhāṣya 1.4.40). Therefore, even if the mention of the root *as* were absent, a retroflex (*mūrdhanya*) substitution would not occur here.

So what is the purpose of mentioning *as*? One might argue: "In its absence, a retroflex would apply to the *s* of another verbal root following the word *prāduḥ*; therefore, the mention of *as* is for the sake of preventing that. But this is not the case, because the word *prāduḥ* has a restricted scope of application.
For that [suffix] is always employed only in relation to the roots *kṛ*, *bhū*, and *as*.
Why, then, does this objection arise? He shows the opponent's view with the words "Now," etc., for one who wishes to point out that [objection].
Wishing to state another counter-example, he says: "Elsewhere."
In the counter-example "anusutam," [the phrase] "even so" means "even in this way."

By this, he shows the following: even if one were to assume this [interpretation], is it not still necessary to include the mention of *asti*? There is indeed a counter-example. Therefore, the mention of *asti* must certainly be made.

From the root *ṣūṅ* "to release the fetus of living beings" (Dhātupāṭha 1031), with the prefix *anu*, the suffix *kvip* is applied; thus, *anusūtaḥ* becomes *anusūḥ*. His descendant is formed by adding the suffix *ḍhak* because of the rule *śubhrādibhyaśca* [Pāṇini 4.1.123]; *ḍhak* is replaced by *eya*; and by the rule *ḍhe lopenā'kadravāḥ* [Pāṇini 6.4.147], the vowel *ū* is elided.

In this context, if the term *asti* were not included [in the rule], the designation of *anu* as a prefix (*upasarga*) with respect to the letter *s* would still exist, and consequently, the cerebralization (*mūrdhanya*) would indeed occur. Since the prohibition [of cerebralization] by the rule *supiṣūtayoḥ* (Pāṇini 8.3.111) would otherwise apply, the word *sama*—derived from the verbal root *sam* and listed among the *sarvādi* group—is treated as a nominal stem (*prātipadika*). Therefore, since the [prohibition of] *ṣatva* does not apply to it from the very beginning, this specific statement is made. Alternatively, if the word *sama* is derived from the verbal root *ṣama ṣṭama avaikalpe* (Dhātupāṭha 829, 830) using the suffix *ac* (the *pacādi* class), then even though the prohibition [of cerebralization] would apply to that form as well when followed by the suffix *san*, this statement is provided.

Regarding "suṣuptaḥ": [the root is] *ṣvap* (meaning "to sleep") [as listed in the Dhātupāṭha as number 1068]. It takes the suffix *niṣṭhā*; there is vocalization (*samprasāraṇa*) by the rule [Pāṇini 6.1.15] beginning with *vaci-*; and the prohibition of the augment *iṭ* is by the rule [Pāṇini 7.2.10] beginning with *ekācaḥ*. Regarding "suṣūtiḥ": [the root is] *sū* (meaning "to bring forth"). It takes the suffix *ktin*. There is vocalization (*samprasāraṇa*) by the rule [Pāṇini 6.1.15] beginning with *vaci-*. The substitution of *u* for *ū* is by the rule [Pāṇini 6.4.19] beginning with *ūdupadhāyā gohaḥ*. The form is thus *suṣūtiḥ*.

The form *sūtī* is derived from either the root *sū* or *sūyati* by the rule *striyāṃ ktin* [Pāṇini 3.3.94]. This is a citation of the specific word-form (*svarūpagrahaṇa*). Where this particular form does not occur, the suffix is not applied—as in *susūnam* and *visūtam*.

But how is it known that this is a mention of the root's own form (*svarūpa*), and not a mention of the *sūtra*, the *lu*-affix, or the *vikaraṇa*? Does it not also apply to that [root] when the *śtip* affix is added by the rule "The affixes *śtip* and *itap* are used for the indication of a verbal root" (*iviśtapau dhātunirdeśe*) (Vārttika 319), such that there would be this mention as *sūtiḥ*? [It is known] because of its association with the word *sama*; for in this case, the own form of the root is what is being taken.

Although it might be argued that by association with the *sup* (nominal suffix), the verbal root (*dhātu*) should also be understood [as included], nevertheless, according to the "prohibition of the subsequent" (*paravipratiṣedha*) regarding words, that association which pertains to the word itself is stronger; thus, through association with the word *su* alone, its own form (*svarūpa*) is grasped, and not the verbal root through association with the *sup* suffix.
Now, for what purpose is the substitution of *ṣ* for the *s* of *su-pi* stated? To this he says: "The substitution of *ṣ* for *su-pi* is so that it may not apply to *svapi*" and so forth.

In the forms *susvāpaḥ*, *visvapanam*, *nisvapanam*, and *duḥsvapanam*, the substitution of *ṣ* for the *s* of the root *svap* should not occur when the semivowel has not been vocalized (*akṛta-samprasāraṇa*). For this reason, the substitution of *ṣ* is prescribed for *svap* when the semivowel has been vocalized (*kṛta-samprasāraṇa*). If this is so, why is it not [the case] in *visuṣvāpa*? [The derivation is as follows: from *svap* with the suffix *liṭ*, the suffix *tip*, the suffix *ṇal*, reduplication, and then vocalization (*samprasāraṇa*) by [Pāṇini 6.1.17]. Why does the substitution of *ṣ* not occur for the reduplicated syllable of *svap* once the semivowel has been vocalized? The intention is that there is simply no such reason by which the substitution would not occur in *visuṣvāpa*.
However, for the *s* of another [word], *ṣatva* certainly occurs by the rule *parasya tu sakārasya* (Pāṇini 8.3.59); this present deliberation does not concern that case.
The phrase "because of *halādiśeṣa*, there is no *supiḥ*" shows the reason why *ṣatva* does not occur here.

> [[6.1.17]] For, because this *samprasāraṇa* occurs later, once *halādiśeṣa* has been applied, even if the *samprasāraṇa* is subsequently performed, the form "sup" does not result; because the *pakāra* occurs later than the *samprasāraṇa*, once *halādiśeṣa* has been applied, even if the *samprasāraṇa* is subsequently performed, the form "sup" still does not result, due to the absence of the *pakāra*.
