Therefore, the intention is that *ṣatva* (the substitution of *ṣ* for *s*) will not occur.
Thus, the absence of the form "sup" for "sup" is stated as the reason for the absence of *ṣatva*.

The proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣavādin*), however, having first applied *samprasāraṇa* and subsequently considering that the letter *p* has been eliminated by the rule for the retention of the first consonant (*halādiśeṣa*), raised this objection.

[The opponent asks: "But even after [the application of *halādiśeṣa*], there is the elimination of the letter *p*; therefore, this is not truly a *sup* because of the absence of the letter *p*. So why was this objection raised? [The response is: Because of the principle that "that which is modified in one part is not different [from the original]" (*ekadeśavikṛtasyānanyatvāt*), the intention is that this is indeed a *sup*.

But when, due to its higher priority, the *halādiśeṣa* (the replacement of all consonants except the first by the first alone) has been performed and then the *samprasāraṇa* occurs, then—because that which has undergone a partial modification is not considered different from the original—this [application of the rule] does not apply to *supi*. For in that case, the modification is not of *supi* itself; rather, it is of *svapi*.
Therefore, he says: "The *samprasāraṇa* is desired first.
That is to say, the *samprasāraṇa* itself is desired prior to the *halādiśeṣa* and other operations.
Likewise, the mention of both [hal and ādi] there was made for this purpose: so that even setting aside the subsequent *halādiśeṣa* rule, the *samprasāraṇa* alone should occur first.
Therefore, it has been stated that before the *halādiśeṣa*, the *abhyāsa* must indeed undergo *samprasāraṇa*;
and consequently, the objection—"Why is it not *visuṣvāpa*?"—remains exactly as it was.

If that is the case, then does this restriction—namely, that the rule *sthādiṣvabhyāsena cābhyāsasya* [Pāṇini 8.3.64] applies only to the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*) of roots beginning with *sthā* and not to others—prevent the change of the reduplicated syllable in *visuṣvāpa* from becoming *ṣ*? To answer this, he says: "of *sthā* and the rest," and so forth. The restriction caused by *sthā* and the rest is called the "restriction of *sthā* and the rest" (*sthādiniyama*), and it is designated by those roots because the restriction is formulated by taking them as its basis. The restriction that applies to *sthā* and the rest does not operate here.

How will there not be *ṣatva* (the substitution of *ṣ* for *s*) of the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*) in the form *visuṣvāpa*? Why, then, does the restriction (*niyama*) regarding *sthādi* roots not apply here? To this he says: "prior to *sit*" (*prāk sitāt*). The ellipsis to be supplied is: "because among those [roots], a restrictive rule (*niyamavidhāna*) has been prescribed. [The full rule is: "In the case of *sthādi* roots and the reduplicated syllable, [the *ṣatva* applies] by means of the reduplicated syllable."
In this context [of rule 8.3.64], the phrase "prior to *sita*" [from rule 8.3.63] is understood to carry over.

Consequently, since the term *sita* is mentioned in rule 8.3.70 (*sevāsata*), the restriction applies specifically to those roots beginning with *su-noti*, *su-vati*, *syati*, and *stobhati* that are situated prior to it; thus, it shows that the substitution of *ṣ* for the reduplicated syllable is excluded for these alone, and not for others. However, the proponent of the established doctrine (the Siddhāntin) maintains the intention that the restriction is general.

It might be argued: "Even *suṣi* is established from the very same [root] as *sita*; therefore, the restriction (*niyama*) will also apply here. To this, he says: "*uttaraḥ suṣiḥ*" ("the subsequent *suṣi*"). This refers back to the word *sita*. The *suṣi* is recited after the word *sita*; how then could the restriction apply there? Therefore, since the restriction does not exclude the *ṣatva* (palatalization) of its reduplication, the objection—"Why is it not *visuṣvāpa*?"—remains entirely valid.

If that is so, then [one might object]: "According to the principle *arthavadgrahaṇe nānarthakasya* (Vyāḍīya-paribhāṣā 1), since the term *sup* is understood as signifying that which possesses meaning (*arthavat*), and since here [in the case of *su-puṃs-au*] it is meaningless, the substitution of *ṣ* will not occur;

for in this instance, *sup* does not possess meaning. To explain: when there is reduplication in place of the whole, then the aggregate alone is meaningful, while the individual part is indeed meaningless."

But when *dvirvacana* (reduplication) means the double application [of the word], even then it is the repetition of the word (*śabda*), not of the meaning (*artha*). Consequently, even when reduplication has occurred, the meaningfulness belongs only to the entire complex (*samudāya*), and not to the base (*prakṛti*) alone, nor to the reduplicated portion (*abhyāsa*) alone. Therefore, he says: "In the case of the meaningless [elements], as in *viṣuṣupuḥ*. The remainder of the sentence is: "How is there the substitution of *ṣ*? (i.e., how does the rule Pāṇini 8.3.64 apply?).

If [it is argued that] the rule applies because of the inclusion of *sup* when it has meaning—such that there is no *ṣatva* (the substitution of *ṣ*) in *vi-suṣvāpa*—then how will there not be *ṣatva* in *vi-ṣuṣupuḥ*? For here too, due to being meaningless (*anarthakatva*), there should certainly be no *ṣatva*, just as in *vi-suṣvāpa*. To this, he says: "That which has become *sup* is reduplicated" [*ṣupi* is the reading in the *Prātipadika-pāṭha*].
The meaning is that the form *pupī* having been reached, it is reduplicated.

The *liṭ* suffix [is applied] to the root *svap*. There is reduplication (*dvirvacanam*). By the rule *asaṃyogālliṭ kit* [Pāṇini 1.2.5], there is *kit*-tva. By the rule concerning the *vac-ādi* group [Pāṇini 6.1.15], there is *saṃprasāraṇa*. By this [present rule], there is *ṣatva*. When the form *viṣuṣupuḥ* is established, by the principle of closest proximity (*āntaratamya*), there is reduplication of the element *ṣup*. Thus, when it has become *pupi* and is being reduplicated, the *ṣatva* of the reduplicated syllable in *viṣuṣupuḥ* is established. In *piṣuṣvāpa*, however, there is no reduplication of that which has become *ṣupi*; for that which has become *pupi* does not exist [in that context].

Thus, how could there be a substitution of *ṣ* when the semivowel-vocalization (*samprasāraṇa*) has already taken place, since [the suffix] would have become *sup*? Because the *ṇal* suffix lacks the *kittva* designation, there is no semivowel-vocalization at all; how then could there be the substitution of *ṣ*? Therefore, it is precisely the word *sup* that is repeated [in the rule], even though after the semivowel-vocalization has occurred, it becomes *supī*; nevertheless, because that [form] is devoid of meaning, the cerebral substitution (*mūrdhanya*) does not apply to it. Thus, if the substitution of *ṇ* were to occur for that which has undergone semivowel-vocalization, the objection—"Why is it not 'visuṣvāpa'?"—is resolved by relying on the interpretive maxim (*paribhāṣā*) regarding the inclusion of meaningful elements (*arthavadgrahaṇa*).

But surely, when reduplication is to be performed, the substitution of *ṣ* is not established; why then is it said that "that which has become *ṣu* is reduplicated"? To this he says: "That which is unestablished (*asiddha*) in what precedes," and so forth. [The root] *ṣṇā* in the sense of "cleansing" (Dhātupāṭha 1052): since the prohibition of *ṣ*-substitution would apply to this as before, this rule is commenced. *Kauśalam* means skill or proficiency.

"In skilled at making mats" (*niṣṇātaḥ kaṭakaraṇe*), it is understood that he is "proficient. In "skilled in bathing in the river" (*nadīṣṇaḥ*), it is likewise [understood] that he is "proficient in bathing in the river."

By [Pāṇini 6.4.64], there is the elision of the vowel *ā*; this is a compound with an upapada. In the case of *nadīsnātaḥ* as well, the compound is formed by the rule *saptamī* [2.1.40] through a split of the yoga (*yogavibhāga*). Regarding *pratiṣṇātam*:
as before, since the prohibition of the substitution of *ṣ* would have applied, it is here established as an irregular form (*nipātana*).

While the term *snāteḥ* [Pāṇini 8.3.89] is being carried over, if it were stated in the sūtra simply as "after *prati*," forms such as *pratiṣṇātam* would indeed be established. However, this would also undesirably apply to forms with suffixes such as *-tṛc*; therefore, the irregular form (*nipātana*) *pratiṣṇātam* is resorted to in order to prevent that over-extension. If the root *ṣṭhala* "to stand" (Dhātupāṭha 836) is considered a *ṣopadeśa* (a root taught with an initial *ṣ*) according to the rule "roots beginning with *s* and ending in *d* are *ṣopadeśas*" (Kāśikā on 6.1.66), and if this is its form, then—as in the previous case—a prohibition [of ṣatva] would apply, and thus this specific statement is made.

Now, since it is not so recited in the *gaṇa*, the word *sthala* is either derived from the rule "there is the designation *ayopadeśa*" (Pāṇini 1.3.2) or is a newly coined term (*adhyutpanna*). Therefore, this statement is made because the substitution of *ṣ* had not yet been established at the very beginning.
Regarding the phrase "if it refers to a lineage (*gotra*)," the meaning is: if the word *kapiṣṭhala* pertains to a lineage, then [the form is valid].
And here, by the mention of *gotra*, the worldly (*laukika*) lineage is intended, not the technical (*pāribhāṣika*) one.
In the world, those men who are the originators of a line of progeny—those from whom a line of progeny proceeds—are designated as "lineage" (*gotra*).
And which word *Kapiṣṭhala* is the subject of lineage? It is that which is a proper name (*saṃjñā-śabda*) recited in the *Pravarādhyāya*.
Since the technical sense of being a *gotra* (lineage) is not possible without the application of a patronymic suffix (*apatyapratyaya*), it is this technical *gotra* that is intended here.

Regarding the phrase "named Kapiṣṭhala": one who stands on firm ground is *sthala*; [the suffix] *ac* is added according to Pāṇini 3.1.134 (*pacādyac*). One who stands like a monkey (*kapiriva sthalaḥ*) is *kapiṣṭhalaḥ*.

The compound is formed by the rule *upamitaṃ vyaghrādibhiḥ* (Pāṇini 2.1.55) and so forth. This has been done merely for the sake of etymological derivation; however, no meaning of the individual components exists [in this case]. The word *nāman* is employed to show that the word *kapiṣṭhala* is a proper name (*saṃjñāśabda*).
Because the word *kapiṣṭhala* is not well-known, he states—"of whom Kāpiṣṭhali is the offspring"—in order to explain it by means of its well-known descendant.
The meaning is that he whose offspring is Kāpiṣṭhali is the one named Kapiṣṭhala.
[The reading] is *kapisthalam*.

"Of the monkeys" (*kapīnām*): the meaning is "the place" or "the station. Because the prefix *pra-* ends in a vowel, the rule for the substitution of *ṣ* (ṣatva) does not apply; therefore, it is specifically prescribed here. One whose nature is to go in front (*agre gantum śīlam yasya*) is called *agragāmī*, meaning a leader or one who goes before. [In the word] *praṣṭhaḥ*, the suffix *ka* is applied according to [Pāṇini 3.2.4], and as before, there is the elision of the vowel *a*. Regarding the word *viṣṭaraḥ*: [it is derived from *vi-√stṛ* with the suffix *ghañ*].

Regarding the root *stṛñ* (meaning "to cover," Dhātupāṭha 1484), even though its initial consonant is not followed by a dental, it does not possess the status of being taught with a *ṣ* (*ṣopadeśatva*), because of the rule: "With the exception of *sṛp*, *sṛj*, *stṛ*, *styai*, *kṛ*, *sṛ*, and *vṛ*" (Kāśikā on Pāṇini 6.1.66). Therefore, the substitution of *ṣ* for *s* is not prescribed here as an irregularity (*nipātana*).
Thus, from *vi-stīryate* comes *viṣṭaraḥ*, according to the rule *ṛdorap* (Pāṇini 3.3.57).

This is a conventional term (*rūḍhi-śabda*) which may be etymologically derived in some way or another; one should not insist upon the meaning of its constituent parts here. By the mention of "meter" (*chandas*), the *bṛhatī* and other such meters are included, for the name "Veda" does not refer to the Veda itself, but rather to the meters such as the *bṛhatī*.
[An objection: But "seat" (*viṣṭara*) was the subject under discussion; how then can it be substituted by "expansion" (*viṣṭāra*)? To this he says: "from the prefix *vi-*," and so forth.

> [[3.3.32]] Following from this, while the term `straḥ` is being carried over, [the suffix] `ghañ` is applied to the root `stṛ` by virtue of the rule `prathane vāṇaśabde` [[3.3.33]] and the rule `vā` [[8.3.94]], which establishes the `ṇit` designation.
And it is not the case that the form *viṣṭara* results simply from the suffix `ghañ`.
Therefore, although *viṣṭara* was already established as the base form, it is nonetheless treated as a *nipātana* (an irregularly formed word).

But surely, even when the suffix *ghañ* is prescribed, by this very same irregular derivation (*nipātana*), once the shortening is applied, the form *viṣṭara* indeed occurs; so how can it be understood that [the word] is *viṣṭāra*? It is because of the statement "and in the name of a meter" (*chandonāmni ca*). For *viṣṭara* is not the name of a meter; rather, it is *viṣṭāra*. Is this the word *sthira*? If it is derived from the root *sthā* with the suffix *kirac* according to the rule "ajira-śiśira-" (Pāṇini 6.4.127), then this statement is made because the prohibition [of retroflexion] by the rule "sātpadādyoḥ" (Pāṇini 8.3.113) would otherwise apply.
Now, since the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) itself is not yet derived [by suffixation], this statement is made because [the desired forms] have not been obtained from the very beginning:
*gaviṣṭhiraḥ*, *gudhiṣṭhiraḥ*. In these cases, it is a compound (*samāsa*) used as a proper name (*saṃjñā*).

Now, one might ask: why is there no elision (*aluk*) of the locative case ending in *gaviṣṭhira* here, given the rule "the locative [ending] is not elided when a name is formed after a word ending in a consonant or the letter *a*" (Pāṇini 6.3.9)? The answer is: no, because the word *go* does not end in a consonant (*ahalanta*). To this he says: "from the word *go*" and so forth. This is a statement made because the prohibition [of elision] would otherwise apply by the rule "after the word *go*" (Pāṇini 8.3.111).
How this is so has been explained under the rule "as before" (Pāṇini 8.3.91). Examples are *viṣṭhalam* and *kuṣṭhalam*.

The word *sthala* ends in the suffix *ac* (by Pāṇini 3.1.134). Therefore, when the two words *vi* and *ku* are understood as indeclinables (*nipāta*), there is a compound according to [Pāṇini 2.2.18], *kugatiprādayaḥ*. However, if they are not indeclinables but denote "bird" and "earth" respectively, then it is a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*).
Thus: *śamiṣṭhalam*.
The compound is *śamīnāṃ sthalam* (the place of *śamī* trees). By [Pāṇini 6.3.63], there is shortening of the vowel.

The purpose of pronouncing the short vowel is so that it does not occur in the alternative case where the long vowel is intended; otherwise, due to the rule of diversity (*bahulavacanāt*), the long vowel might also be understood as an option.
Regarding the term "pariṣṭhalam":
it is a *prādi* compound (a prefix compound).

This statement is made because, when a *upapada* compound is formed here with the word *sthala* as the subsequent member (*uttarapada*), the elision of the locative case-ending (*aluk*) occurs; and for those [roots] ending in the suffix *iṇ*, although the substitution of *va* would have been obtained by the rule *iṣkoḥ* [Pāṇini 8.3.57], a prohibition based on the status of being at the beginning of a word (*padādi*) would have applied, hence this statement is made.

Even from the word *barhis*, although a prohibition based on the status of being at the beginning of a word would have applied by the rule *nuḍ-vi-sarjanīya-śaṣ-avāye 'pi* [Pāṇini 8.3.58], this statement is made. However, for the remaining [roots], the [substitution of *va*] was not applicable at all.

Is this the mention of the verbal root *sthā*, or is it the mention of the word-form itself? If, having applied the elision of the vowel *ā* by [Pāṇini 6.4.140], the sixth case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) is used for *tiṣṭhateḥ* as a designation, then it is the mention of the verbal root.

If, however, by means of a substitution of case endings (*subvyatyaya*), the first case (*prathamā*) is made for the sixth case *sthaḥ*, and it is the word *stha* ending in the suffix *kapratyaya* that is designated, then it is the mention of the word-form itself. Considering that if the verbal root were mentioned here, it would undesirably apply even in cases such as *gosthānam*, he says "from these" (*ityetebhyaḥ*) and so forth, thereby demonstrating that it is the mention of the word-form.

In the examples, regarding the word *goṣṭha*, when the word *go* ending in the nominative case is an *upapada*, the suffix *ka* is prescribed in the sense of *ghañ*. According to the Vārttika, "The suffix *ka* is prescribed in the sense of *ghañ* for the sake of [forming] *svasr*, *āsnā*, *āp*, *avyathi*, *havir*, and *yu*," the suffix *ka* is applied here in the locative sense (*adhikaraṇe*) to mean "that in which cows stand.
In the word *apaṣṭha*, meaning "he does not stand," the suffix *ka* is added by [Pāṇini 3.2.4], *supi sthaḥ*.
In some places the reading is *āpaṣṭhaḥ*;
[here] the long vowel is applied by [Pāṇini 6.3.137].
In all other instances as well, the suffix *ka* is applied by [Pāṇini 3.2.4].

If the word *ku* is a particle (*nipāta*), then the suffix *kaṇi* is applied when this [word] ending in *praṇama* is the attendant term (*upapada*); if, however, it is not a particle, then it is applied when [the attendant term] ends in the locative case (*saptamī*).
In the case of *ambā* and so forth, it is applied only when they end in the locative case.
For example: *jambaṣṭhaḥ*.
By the rule *[[6.3.63]]*, the vowel is shortened.

Regarding the word *stha*: since the term is used here to denote its own form (*svarūpagrahaṇa*), the [shortening] would not apply to other [forms]. Therefore, he says: "of *sthā*, *sthin*, and *sthṛ*," and so forth.
The substitution of *ṣ* for these [letters] must also be stated; that is to say, it must be explained.
In this regard, the explanation is as follows: because the group beginning with *suṣāmā* is an *ākṛtigaṇa*, the substitution of *ṣ* will occur for these as well.
For example: *savryeṣṭhāḥ* (or *savyeṣṭhāḥ*, according to the Kāśikā).

Regarding the word *savyeṣṭhṛ*: while the rule *diverḍau* (Dhātupāṭha 2.7) is in effect, the rule *nayaterḍicca* (Dhātupāṭha 2.8) applies; furthermore, by the rule *savye sthaśchandasī* (Dhātupāṭha 2.9), the suffix *ṛ* is added to the root *sthā* when the word *savya* is used as an upapada. Because the suffix is marked with *ṭ*, there is elision of the *ṛ* vowel (*ṭilopa*). By the rule *tatpuruṣe* (Pāṇini 6.3.13) et seq., there is no elision (*aluk*) of the locative case ending. When *savyeṣṭhṛ* is established, the substitution of *abnaṅ* is applied by the rule *ṛduśanaspurudaṃśo’nehasām* (Pāṇini 7.1.94), and the lengthening of the vowel occurs by the rule *sarvanāmasthāne cāsambuddhau* (Pāṇini 6.4.8). Thus, the form *parameṣṭhī* [or *parameṣṭhīḥ* according to the Kāśikā] is derived.

While the rule *gameridhiḥ* (Pāṇini 3.2.17) is being carried over, the suffix *ini* is applied by the rule *parame sthaḥ kicca* (Pāṇini 3.2.19)—where *kit* alone is intended [according to the Daiva-nighaṇṭu]. Due to the *kit* designation, there is elision of the *ā*.
When *parameṣṭhin* is established, the lengthening occurs by the rule *sau ca* (Pāṇini 6.4.13). Thus we have *savyeṣṭhṛsāradhiḥ*.

As before: having established the word *savyeṣṭhṛ*, a *karmadhāraya* compound is formed with the word *sārathi*. In some cases, where the substitution of the retroflex *ṣ* would otherwise be prohibited, and in other cases where it would not apply from the very beginning, the retroflex is prescribed.
Regarding the word *suṣāmā*:
this word *sāman* is derived by applying the suffix *manin* to the root *ṣo* in the sense of "concluding" (*antakarmaṇi*) [Dhātupāṭha 1147].
Since a prohibition [of sandhi] would otherwise apply based on the definition of "at the beginning of a word" (*padādi*), this entry is recited here in order to override that rule:
*niṣṣāmā* and *duṣṣāmā*.

When the *repha* (the letter *r*) has been replaced by *visarjanīya*, and when, according to the option provided by the rule *vā śari* [Pāṇini 8.3.36], a *sakāra* (*s*) is substituted, then once the *ṣatva* (change to *ṣ*) of the following sound has occurred, the *ṣṭutva* (change to *ṣṭ*) of the preceding sound follows. Now, one might ask: since the cerebralization (*mūrdhanya*) for the three words beginning with *suṣedha* is already established by the rule *upasargāt sunoti* [Pāṇini 8.3.65] and others, what is the purpose of including them here? To this he replies with the words "the word *su*" and so forth. Because the word *su* functions as a *karmapravacanīya* (a particle governing a specific relation), it is not an *upasarga* (preverb); therefore, the reading is *suṣedha*.

However, since *niḥ* and *duḥ* have other functions as prefixes (*upasarga*), they are excluded from being [treated as] *anu* and *ava*; thus, the connection should be made that the reading is *duḥṣedhaḥ*.

In words such as *suṣedha*, there is no prefix-status (*upasargatva*) for *sthā* and the others; therefore, if their inclusion here were not made, then the substitution of *ṣ*—which is prescribed by rules such as *upasargāt sunoti* [Pāṇini 8.3.65] based on a cause situated in a prefix—would not occur, yet it is desired. Consequently, these words beginning with *suṣedha* are included here so that the substitution of *ṣ* may occur even when the cause is not a prefix.

In that case, since the word *su* functions as a *karmapravacanīya*, it does not receive the designation of *upasarga*; this is because of the governing rule that "there is only one designation" (Pāṇini 1.4.1).

Furthermore, its status as a non-*upasarga* follows from the specific prescription of the *karmapravacanīya* designation in the rule "anupasargatvaṃ tvasya" (Pāṇini 1.4.94). As for the words *nis* and *dur*, however, they lack the status of *upasarga* because their scope pertains to other actions.

*Nirgataḥ sedhaḥ* becomes *niṣsedhaḥ*, and *durgataḥ sedhaḥ* becomes *duṣsedhaḥ*; for these two are the objects of the action of going (*gami-kriyā*). Therefore, they possess the status of prefixes (*upasarga*) only with respect to the root *gam*, not with respect to the root *sidh*. This is because of the rule stated in the Mahābhāṣya (1.4.61): "Prepositions (*prādi*) which are connected with an action [are designated as] 'motion' (*gati*) and 'prefix' (*upasarga*) only with respect to that [root] toward which they are directed."

Thus, first of all: regarding the root *ṣidhu* in the sense of "to accomplish" (*saṃrāddha*) [Dhātupāṭha 47], when it occurs in the sense of "going" (*gati*), the form *sedha* arises; therefore, he says "of *sedhati*" and so forth to show that the listing [of these roots] is for the purpose of setting aside the prohibition.
Alternatively, since he will state the prohibition [by the rule] *atha vā* [Pāṇini 8.3.113], this listing is for the purpose that such a prohibition should not apply.
Examples are: *suṣandhiḥ*, *niṣṣandhiḥ*, *duṣṣandhiḥ*.

These [words] end in the *kṛt* suffix [by virtue of Pāṇini 3.3.92]. Therefore, since their *s* is not a substitute [for a dental], the rule for changing it to a retroflex (*ṣatva*) would not otherwise apply; hence, they are listed here. "It is joined" (*sandhīyate*) is *sandhi*; "a beautiful junction" (*suṣandhiḥ*) is a *prādi* compound.
The same applies elsewhere as well.

However, regarding the words *suṣṭhu* and *duṣṭhu*, their placement at the end [of the list] is for the purpose of excluding them from the rule concerning initial members of a compound (*padādi-lakṣaṇa*). It is said that "these two are derived from the root *sthā* in the *uṇādi* suffixes."
The term *ku* is understood from the rule *kubhraśca* (Pāṇini 6.4.107).
The two words ending in the suffix *ku*, namely *mṛgayu* and others, are derived according to the rule *mṛgayvādayaśca* (Pāṇini 3.1.121). Regarding the form *gauriṣakyaḥ*:
in the case of the word *gauriṣakya*, the substitution of *ṣ* for the letter *s* occurs when it is a proper name (*saṃjñā*).
"Gaurī-sakthī" is a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*).

In the rule beginning with "acpratyayān-vavapūrvāt" (Pāṇini 5.4.75), the term *ac* is separated as a distinct yoga-rule; thus, the suffix *ac* is added as a compound-final element (*samāsānta*). However, when it is a possessive compound (*bahuvrīhi*)—meaning "one whose thigh is like that of Gaurī"—then it ends in the suffix *ṣac*, according to the rule "bahuvrīhau sakthyakṣṇoḥ svāṅgāt ṣac" (Pāṇini 5.4.113).

Is this word *sakti* derived from the suffix *vithan* according to [Pāṇini 5.2.30], *asisañcibhyāṃ kthina*, or is it an underived form? In the former case, the inclusion of the word *gauriṣaktha* [in the Gaṇapāṭha] is for the purpose of setting aside the prohibition [of ṣatva]. In the latter case, however, ṣatva does not apply at all.

Regarding the word *pratiṣṇikā*: for this as well, the suffix *kap* is applied by the rule *pratisnātīti* (Pāṇini 3.2.106) [the reading *pratiṣṇātīti* is found in the Kāśikā; the reading here is *pratisnātīti*]. Then, by the rule *āp* (Pāṇini 4.1.4), the feminine suffix *āp* is added after that which ends in *kap*. Finally, by the rule *ke'ṇaḥ* (Pāṇini 7.4.13), the vowel is shortened.
The substitution of *ī* [for the vowel] occurs by the rule beginning with *pratyasthāt* (Pāṇini 7.3.44).
The reading *jalāvāham* is intended for cases where the root does not end in *i*.
Furthermore, this [form] is observed to be non-Vedic (anārṣa).
For instance, its status as a *ṣ* will be established by the indicative power (*jñāpaka*) of the inclusion of the word *āsani* in the rule *savanādiṣu* (Pāṇini 8.3.112).

Others, however, justify its reading here for the purpose of showing an alternative view: either the word *āsani* should be recited in the *savanādi* group for the sake of providing that indication, or else the word *jalāṣāhi* should be included here. Thus they support its presence in this text as a means of demonstrating an option.
And the reading here is for the sake of illustration;
by that, it should be understood that there is also the reading "āvāhanam," as in "nauṣecanam" and "dundubhiṣeṣaṇam."

These are genitive compounds (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*). The inclusion of the root *vevṛ* in the sense of "service" (*sevane*) [in the Dhātupāṭha, no. 501] after *sic* is for the purpose of overriding the prohibition regarding the suffix *syuṭ*. The rule beginning with *eti saṃjñāyām* is a mnemonic statement (*grahaṇakavākya*).
The explanation of this very [term] is provided by the passage beginning with "ekāraparasya" (of that which has 'e' following).
The term "ekāraparaḥ" is a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "that after which 'e' follows. By this, he demonstrates that the locative case in "etena" is a *parasaptamī* (a locative of sequence).
Regarding "hariṣeṇaḥ":

it is a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "one whose army (*senā*) consists of tawny ones (*harayaḥ*"); the shortening of the penultimate vowel occurs due to its being a *sarvanāman* (in this case, *hari*).
Regarding "puṣvasenaḥ": [it is formed similarly].

The substitution of the masculine form (*pūṃvadbhāvaḥ*) occurs by [Pāṇini 6.4.79] and subsequent rules. Regarding the term *viṣvaksenaḥ*: the suffix *kvin* is applied by [Pāṇini 3.2.59], *ṛtvig-*, etc., to the root *viṣvañc-* (to go in all directions).
There is elision of the *n* by [Pāṇini 6.4.24] *aniditām* and [6.3.45].
The suffix *ṅīp* is applied, followed by the elision of the vowel *a* by [6.4.138] *acaḥ*. Then, by [6.3.137] *cau*, there is lengthening of the vowel.
The term *viṣūcīsenā* is a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "one whose army faces in all directions."
The shortening of the penultimate vowel [occurs] by [Pāṇini 6.4.79], *tyādinā*, etc.; there is the substitution of the masculine form (*puṃvadbhāva*);
and the substitution of *k* for *kv* occurs by [Pāṇini 8.2.62], *kvitvasya kuḥ*.
By [Pāṇini 8.2.39], there is *jaś*-ness, resulting in the letter *ga*.
By [Pāṇini 8.4.54], "and before a *khar* [consonant]," there is *car*-ness, resulting in the letter *ka*.
Because that [substitution] is considered as if not yet established (*asiddha*), there is the letter *ya*. [The rule] "optionally after *nakṣatra*" [is applied].
Since the rule would have applied permanently by the preceding [sūtra], this option is now stated.

In the sūtra *suṣāmādiṣu ca* (Pāṇini 8.3.98), the particle *ca* has the sense of conjunction (*samuccaya*); moreover, it indicates that the group *suṣāmādi* is an *ākṛtigaṇa* (an open-ended class). Therefore, he says: "those for which no [specific] rule has been prescribed," and so forth. Because of the governing heading *apadāntasya* (Pāṇini 8.3.55), the substitution of the retroflex nasal (*mūrdhanya*) does not apply at the end of a word; since it would otherwise not apply, this [present sūtra] is commenced. To demonstrate those secondary suffixes (*taddhita*) beginning with *ta* for which the retroflex nasal ought to occur, he says: "*tarap-tamapau*."

Regarding the form *sarpiṣṭaram*: the suffix *tarap* is applied by the rule *dvivacanavibhajyopapade* [Pāṇini 5.3.57]. The original *s* undergoes *rutva* (becoming *r*), followed by *visarjanīya*. By the rule *tasya ca* [Pāṇini 8.3.34], that *visarjanīya* becomes *s*. By this present rule, that *s* becomes *ṣ*, and then *ṣṭutva* (the substitution of *ṭ* for *t*) occurs.
Regarding "sarpiṣṭamam":
the suffix *tamap* is applied according to the rule beginning with "atiśāyane" (Pāṇini 5.3.55).
Regarding "catuṣṭaye": [it refers to the fourfold set].

The suffix *tayap* is applied [by Pāṇini 5.2.42] in the sense of a part of a number; the suffix *jam* (i.e., *śas*) follows that which ends in *tayap*, or it may be the singular locative case (*saptamyekavacana*). When it is the nominative plural (*jas*), there is the substitution of *śī* by [Pāṇini 7.1.17]: *jaśaḥ śī*. In some places, the reading is *catuṣṭayī*.
For in that case, the suffix *ṅīp* is applied by [Pāṇini 4.1.15] *ṭiḍḍhāṇañ*.
[Examples are] *sarpiṣṭvam*, *sarpiṣṭā*.
In the usage *sarpiṣṭas*, while [the rule] *tasau matvarthe* [5.4.45] is being carried over from [the previous sūtra], the suffix *tasi* is applied by [the rule] *pṛthvādibhya imanijvā* [5.1.122].
Regarding the word "āviṣṭa":
[the suffix] *tyap* occurs after the word *ādi* in the sense of "origin" (*bhava*) and so forth, according to Pāṇini 4.3.104.

But surely it is stated in the mnemonic verse (Kārikā 4.2.115): "The application of the suffix *tyap* is traditionally taught after the words *ama*, *iha*, *kvata*, *si*, *tre*, and from indeclinables"? Since that [verse] provides an exhaustive enumeration, how can *tyap* occur after the word *ādi*? This is not a fault.

Is it because of having fewer syllables (*alpāctaratvāt*)? Since the rule requires that the word *ku* or the word *tra* be placed first when forming a compound, the fact that this is not done demonstrates a deviation from the general grammatical rule (*lakṣaṇavyabhicāra*). By showing this, it is indicated that that enumeration [of conditions for precedence] is indeed subject to exceptions; therefore, the suffix occurs even after the word *aviḥ*. In the example *sarpismāt*, the suffix *sāti* is applied according to [Pāṇini 5.4.52].

But surely, because of the upcoming rule [8.3.111], the retroflex [ṣ] will not occur simply due to that very prohibition; so what is the purpose of the expression *tādau* for the sake of excluding that? To this he says: "of the *s* of an affix," and so forth.

For by the word *sāt*, the status of being a *ṣ* is prohibited for two things: the *s* that belongs to the affix *sāt*, and that which is characterized as being at the beginning of a word (*padādi*), but not for the original *s* (*prakṛti-sakāra*) preceding the affix *sāt*.
Therefore, if the expression *tādau* were not stated, then, while the *s* of the affix would not become a *ṣ*, the original *s* would indeed [become a *ṣ*].
And that being the case, the status of being *ṣṭu* would also apply to the *s* of the suffix.
"It must be stated" means it must be explained.

In this regard, the following is the explanation: here, the mention of "beginning" (*ādi*) need not be made; for by the rule *yasmin vidhis tadādāv algrahaṇe* (Vārttika 14), [the operation] will occur when [the suffix] begins with that [letter]. Why, then, is it done? It is done so that the mention of "beginning" may clearly indicate an extension of the scope [of the rule], thereby ensuring that the prohibition applies to forms ending in a verbal suffix (*tiṅanta*). Alternatively, in rules such as *na rapara* (Pāṇini 7.3.110), a separation of the yoga (*yogavibhāga*) will be made by means of the word "not" (*na*), whereby the prohibition does not apply to forms ending in a verbal suffix. In this explanation, however, the mention of "beginning" is for the sake of clarity.
"May they break more, may they cut more"—

this is formed from the roots *bhid* and *chid* with the suffix *liṅ*, the augment *yāsuṭ*, the replacement of *jhar* by *jus* [Pāṇini 3.4.108], and the elision of *s* by the rule "the *s* of *liṅ* is elided" [Pāṇini 7.2.79], etc.;
then the substitution of the subsequent form (*pararūpa*) occurs by [Pāṇini] 6.1.96.

There is elision of the vowel *i* [by Pāṇini 6.4.111]. The suffix *tarap* is applied by [Pāṇini] 5.3.56 (*tiṅaśca*), and the suffix *ām* is applied by [Pāṇini] 5.4.11 (*kimettiṅavyaya...*) and so forth. This rule is also commenced for the sake of forms ending in a word-final position, as in *niṣṭapati*.
[The root] *tapa* (meaning "to heat" or "to torment") is found in the Dhātupāṭha at numbers 985 and 396.

When *rut* occurs, the *visarjanīya* is substituted [by Pāṇini 8.3.34]; then the dental *s* becomes a retroflex (*mūrdhanya*), and the rule for *ṣṭu* applies. Now, in cases such as *niṣṭaptaṃ rakṣaḥ* and *niṣṭaptā arātayaḥ*, why does this not apply to the root *tap* ending in the suffix *niṣṭhā*? For is there not indeed repetition (*āsevana*) here? To this, he says: "In *niṣṭaptam*" and so forth.
For in this case, the mere existence of the thing is not the primary cause for the derivation of the word; rather, it is the speaker's intention (*vivakṣā*).

And since there is no intention here to express repetition (*āsevanā*), the retroflex *ṣ* occurs. If, however, repetition were intended, then this retroflex *ṣ* would not occur; therefore, he says: "Or it is Vedic" (*cchāndaso vā*), and so forth.
When the doubling [of the *s*] has been performed by [Pāṇini 8.4.47] *samāse ca*, the retroflex *ṣ* is applied again. This rule is also commenced for the sake of the word-final position.
"Antaḥpādam" means "in the middle of a foot. This is an *avyayībhāva* compound used in the sense of a case ending (*vibhaktyartha*).
By the term "pāda," there is a general inclusion of both the quarter of a *ṛc* verse and the quarter of a *śloka*.
However, the property of beginning with the letter *t* is here a qualification of *yuṣmad* alone, and not of the other two [words], because of its non-deviation [from them].
Since the word *yuṣmad* also begins with *t* when it undergoes substitutions such as *tvad*, he says: "the substitutes of *yuṣmad*" and so forth.
In *agniṣṭvam*,
the substitution of *tvā* [for *tvam*] occurs by [Pāṇini 7.2.94], and the change of the nominative suffix *su* to *am* occurs by [Pāṇini 7.1.28]. In *agniṣṭvaḥ*, [the same applies].
By [Pāṇini 8.1.23], there is the substitution of *tvā* for that which ends in the second case;
thus, "agniṣṭe. By [Pāṇini 8.1.22], there is the substitution of *tayā* for that which ends in the sixth case.

Regarding the form *agniṣṭava*: by [Pāṇini 7.2.96], there is the substitution of that [suffix]; and by [Pāṇini 7.1.27], *akṣ* is substituted for the genitive (*ṅas*) after *yuṣmad* and *asmad*. Thus, we have *agniṣṭat*—an example cited in the *Kāśikā* as "O Agni, you are present here" (*agne sadhiṣṭava*), while the reading in the *Kaumudī* is *agniṣṭva*.
This word *tat* is either a particle (*nipāta*) or a pronoun (*sarvanāman*),
as in the expression "they have fashioned" (*niṣṭatakṣuḥ*).
The *liṭ* [perfect] suffix of the root *takṣ* with the *us* affix:
"agnistatpunaḥ.
Here, the word *agni* occurs at the end of the preceding member.
Therefore, this *sakāra* occurs at the end of a quarter-verse (*pāda*), not in the middle of a quarter-verse. Regarding the word "in the *yajus*":
this refers to the *Yajurveda*.
Since quarters (*pādas*) do not occur there, this rule for the substitution of *ṣakāra* is commenced even though it was not previously applicable.

The inclusion of the word *ekeṣām* (of some) is for the purpose of providing an option (*vikalpa*). This [sūtra] is commenced because the prohibition [stated in 8.3.111], "when *eṣām*," would otherwise apply. Now, one might object: "Is it not the case that the substitution of *ṣ* is already established by the subsequent sūtra (*8.3.106*) in examples such as *anubhiḥṣṭutam* and *gobhiḥṣṭomam*? Therefore, what is the purpose of commencing this [present sūtra]? One might argue: 'This occurs when there is a compound, where there is a prior member (*pūrvapada*) and a subsequent member (*uttarapada*), but here there is no compound; therefore, it is not established by the subsequent rule, *pūrvapadād iḥ*. But this is incorrect, because even in the absence of a compound, that which is a prior member is still included therein."

He will say: "Even in a non-compound (*asamāse*)—[the *Kāśikā* states: 'even that which is the prior member (*pūrvapada*) in a non-compound'—the reading in the *Prāmāṇyāsa* is: 'that which is the prior member, even that is included there']—even that which is the prior member, that too is included here" (*Kāśikā* 8.3.104). To this he says: "Only from a prior member," and so forth; [the example is] "dviṣaṃdhiḥ."
It is either a genitive tatpuruṣa compound or a bahuvrīhi compound.
As for the form "madhuṣṭhānam," it is a genitive compound.
Regarding the term *dvivāharuā*:

the compound is formed in the sense of a secondary derivative (*taddhita*), meaning "that which exists in two *saharuās*. By [Pāṇini 4.3.53], the suffix *aṇ* is applied; by [Pāṇini 7.3.15], there is vowel strengthening (*vṛddhi*) of the final syllable of the second member of the compound.

Now, how is there the substitution of *ṣ* here in the expression *triḥ ṣamuddhatvāya*? For [one might argue] that in a compound (*samāsa*), the term "prior member" (*pūrvapada*) is conventionally established (*rūḍha*) for that which constitutes the prior member; yet this is not a compound, but rather a sentence (*vākya*). To this, he says: "Even in the absence of a compound," and so forth. How, then, is this obtained? Because here the term "prior member" is understood in the sense of a fixed position (*vyavasthā*). For just as in common usage the word *pūrva*—by virtue of conventional meaning (*rūḍhi*)—occurs in some cases to denote a collective whole, as in *pūrvapañcālāḥ* ("the eastern Pañcālas"), and in other cases to denote a fixed position, as in *asmāt pūrvam* ("prior to this"); so too in the grammatical treatise (*śāstra*).
Therefore, the word *vyavasthā* (establishment/limitation) is understood here.
Why? Because of pervasion (*vyāpti*).
If only a conventional (*rūḍhi*) word were accepted, it would apply only to a compound (*samāsa*) and not to a non-compound (*asamāsa*).

Since this is already established by the rule *vyavasthāśabde tu sarvatra bhavati* (Pāṇini 8.3.106), this [present rule] is for the sake of elaboration (*prapañca*). It is stated that "the particle *suñ* is understood here" (as noted in the Kāśikā). Now, why is the verbal root *ṣuñ* (meaning 'to press', Dhātupāṭha 1247) not understood here? He thinks as follows: wherever he intends to include this root, he provides the citation using the suffix *ktin*.

This is the style of the Teacher: as seen in the rules *upasargāt sunoti* [Pāṇini 8.3.65] and *upasargād bahulam* [8.3.117]. Therefore, if the intention here were to refer to the verbal root (*dhātu*), he would have made the reference using the suffix *śtip*; but he has not done so. Consequently, it is determined that this refers to the particle (*nipāta*) itself, as in the example *abhīṣuṇaḥ*.

In the case of the genitive plural of the word *asmad*, [the substitution] *nas* occurs by [Pāṇini 7.1.28], the lengthening of the vowel occurs by [Pāṇini 6.3.134], and the change to *ṇ* occurs by [Pāṇini 8.4.27]. Regarding the term *anaḥ*:
it means that which has no letter *n*.

Regarding the word *goṣāḥ*: [it is derived from] the root *ṣaṇu* in the sense of "giving" (*dhāne*, Dhātupāṭha 1464). [The form is derived as] "one who wins cows" (*gāṃ sanoti*), with the suffix *kvanip*; then, by the rule *viṅavanoranunāsikasyāt* (Pāṇini 6.4.41), there is the substitution of *ā* for the nasal vowel.

Regarding the word *goṣāṇi*: while the suffix *in* is being carried over from [Pāṇini 5.2.24], the suffix *in* is applied by [Pāṇini 5.2.27]: *chandasi vanasanarakṣimanthibhyaśca*. Now, one might object: is not the substitution of *ṣ* for *s* already established in forms such as *goṣāḥ* by [Pāṇini 8.3.106]?
To the question "For what purpose is this [rule]? he says: "Only after a preceding word.
This is for the sake of establishing the restriction that [the suffix *ṭhak*] occurs only after a word that does not contain the letter *n*, and not after any other; so that such a rule may apply.
If this is the case, then "gosanim" is not a result of the restriction, because it begins with *savanādi*? To this he says: "In this case," and so forth.
The particle *iti* is used here in the sense of a reason (*hetu*).

Because the word *gosani* is recited in the *savana* and other sections [of the Veda], it does not constitute the result of a restrictive rule (*niyama*); for this reason, some offer the counter-example *sisānayiṣatīti*, while others say, "*sisanīrityapare*."
The form *sisānayiṣati* is derived from the desiderative (*san*) of the causative (*ṇyant*) of the root *san*.
If this [rule] were not stated for the sake of restriction, then the substitution of *ṣ* would apply only to the roots *stu* and *ṇyanta* (as per Pāṇini 8.3.61).
Since this [rule] exists, it does not occur; thus, this is an example of a causative form.

Is this not because of the very restriction [stated in] *amyantasya stītiṇyoreva* [Pāṇini 8.3.61]? No, because the cessation of the *ṣatva* (the substitution of *ṣ* for *s*) is already established. Regarding *sisanoḥ*: from the root *san*, there is the suffix *san*, then *iṭ*, reduplication, and the *ṇatva* (substitution of *ṇ* for *n*) of the *s* of *san*. When *sisaniṣ* is established, the *kvip* suffix is added; by *ato lopaḥ* [6.4.48], the *a* is elided. Since the *ṣatva* is treated as *asiddha* (not yet applied), the *rutva* (substitution of *r* for *ṣ*) occurs. Then, by *rvorupadhāyā dīrgho'ṅkhaḥ* [8.2.76], a long vowel is substituted. When *sisanīḥ* is established, since the *san* that was subject to *ṣatva* no longer exists here, the restriction *stītiṇyoreva* [8.3.61] does not apply.

If this were not stated here, there would be a retroflex [ṣ] by the rule *mūrdhanyaḥ* (Pāṇini 8.3.59); however, because this [rule] exists, it does not occur. It is for the sake of *asāḍ* and for the sake of [roots] other than those beginning with *iṇ*. For example, in *pṛtanāṣāham*, the suffix *ṇvi* is applied by the rule *pṛtanāṣāḍ* (Pāṇini 3.2.63).
In the word *ṛtīṣāham*, by [Pāṇini 6.3.137], there is a long vowel *ī*. Thus:
*ṛtīṣaham*.
By [Pāṇini 3.2.178], the suffix *kvip* is applied;
by [Pāṇini 6.3.138], there is lengthening of the vowel *i*.
It is said: "In *saṃhitā*, this lengthening and the substitution of *ṣ* [for *s*] occur."
When both [the rules] are prescribed, the establishment of the long vowel is for the purpose of demonstrating that this is an application of the word *ṛti* according to the section on *saṃhitā*.
Otherwise, one might suspect that this is merely another word, *ṛti*.

As for the one who thinks that the change to *c* will occur here simply through the transposition of phonemes (*varṇavyatyaya*), and asks what is the use of this separation of the rule (*vākyavibhāga*), for him it is demonstrated that the *ṣatva* substitution is a feature of *saṃhitā*.

For if the letter *ṣ* were applied by the rule *yadi hi* [Pāṇini 3.1.85], then it would occur only in non-sandhi (*asaṃhitā*), because the governing heading for sandhi (*saṃhitā*) does not apply there. Therefore, the intention is that a separation of the rule (*yogavibhāga*) must be made so that it may apply within the scope of the sandhi heading.
The phrase "for the purpose of including what has not been mentioned" means this.
This substitution of *ṣ* occurs not only after the root *iṇ* (*i*, *ī*) and after another [vowel], but also after the roots *pṛtanā* and *ṛta*.

As for those who do not perform the split of the rule (*yogavibhāga*), they explain that the particle *ca* has the sense of "and" (*samuccaya*), meaning that [the substitution occurs] even after *ṛta*. The term *rapara* means "that which has *r* as its subsequent element. Regarding the roots: *sṛplṛ* ("to move") [DhP 983], *sṛj* ("to emit") [DhP 1414], *spṛś* ("to touch") [DhP 1415], and *spṛha* ("to desire")—which is listed in the *curādi* class with a final short *a* [DhP 1871].

The term *savanamādi* is a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "those for which the *savana* is the beginning. Regarding the word *viruāṃsikā*, it is derived from the root *ruāṃsu* (meaning "to cover," according to the Dhātupāṭha 754) preceded by the prefix *vi-*; the suffix *ṇvul* is applied according to the rule *royakhyāyāṃ ṇvul bahulam* [Pāṇini 3.3.108].

Regarding the word *viruābdhaḥ*: the root *ruānbhū* [or *viāāsa*, according to the Dhātupāṭha] (Dhātupāṭha 757) means "to trust" or "to rest. By the rule *aniditām* (Pāṇini 6.4.24), there is elision of the nasal (*n*). By the rule *jhaṣastathortho'dhaḥ* (Pāṇini 8.2.40), the letter *th* is replaced by *dh*. Then, by the rule *jhalāṃ jaś jhaśi* (Pāṇini 8.4.53), the letter *bh* is replaced by *b*. Regarding the word *visṛpaḥ*: [the derivation follows similarly].
The suffix *kasun* [is applied] as in *iti*;
*visarjanāt* [is formed with] the suffix *lyuṭ*.
Regarding "divispṛśam":
by [Pāṇini 6.3.14], there is no elision (*aluk*) of the locative case ending. Regarding "niḥspṛhaḥ" (the *Kāśikā* reads *niḥspṛham*).
*Spṛhaṇam* is *spṛha*; by the rule *er ac* [Pāṇini 3.3.56], the suffix *ac* is applied, and there is the elision of the *ṇi*. One from whom desire has departed is *niḥspṛhaḥ*.

Regarding the expression *savane savane*: it is derived from the root *su* with the suffix *lyuṭ*, followed by the locative singular case ending; the reduplication occurs due to distributive repetition (*vīpsā*).
Regarding "sūtesūte":
it is from the root *ṣūṅ* (Dhātupāṭha 1131), meaning "the release of the embryo of living beings," or from the root *sū*, with the suffix *niṣṭhā*.
Regarding "somesome": [it is from the root *su*].

Why is it called *suñ*? The word *soma* is derived by [the rule] beginning with *arttis tu* (Pāṇini 6.4.126). Regarding the phrase "at each commencement of the *savana*," it is a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*) meaning "the commencement of the *savana*."
Regarding the form *kiṃsaṃ kiṃsam*: the root *ṣo* is used in the sense of "ending" (*antakarmaṇi*; Dhp 1.147). By the rule *āto 'nupasarge kaḥ* (Pāṇini 3.2.3), the suffix *ka* is applied.

In that context, when the nasalization (*anusvāra*) is applied to the word *kim*, the question arises as to whether the substitution [of *saṃ* for *sam*] is obtained due to the cause residing in the preceding member, by virtue of the rule: "Because the *ayogavāha* sounds are taught with the augment *aṭ*, [the substitution occurs] even when there is an intervention by a *ṅ* sound."
Regarding the expression *anusavanam anusavanam*— [the reading *anusavanam iti* is found in the Prācīna manuscript]—
this is a form ending in the suffix *lyuṭ*. Its etymological derivation is based on the sense of "going" (*aśyāsana*), similar to the word *gosani*.

What is the purpose of including *agā* in the rule? For in this case, the substitution of *ṣ* for *s* does not apply; that is to say, the substitution of *ṣ* applies to a *s* that follows an *iṇ*-vowel preceded by a word-final [consonant], and yet this *s* does not follow an *iṇ*-vowel. To this he says: "The inclusion of *agā*" and so forth.
What is the purpose of this indication? To this he says: "*jalāṣāham*" and so forth. In some places, the reading is "*visaṃbisam, musalamusalam*."

In the view that there is doubling [of the suffix], a prohibition must be stated for the *ṣatva* (the substitution of *ṣ* for *s*) that would otherwise apply by virtue of the *s* being part of an *ādeśa*, according to the rule *ādeśaprahatyayayoḥ* [Pāṇini 8.3.59]. Thus, this is a prohibition of the *ṣatva* that would have been obtained by that rule. Furthermore, this is a prohibition of the *ṣatva* that would have been obtained by the rule *upasargāt sunoti* [Pāṇini 8.3.65] in the case of *sesicyate*; the application [of that rule] is established by *ādeśaprahatyayayoḥ*.
Regarding the form *abhiseicyate*:
here [the substitution of *ṣ*] would apply by the rule *upasargāt sunoti* (Pāṇini 8.3.65) and so forth.

But how, then, does the prohibition operate here, given that the rule *upasargāt* (8.3.65) and others prescribe the substitution of *ṣ* even in cases where a prohibition [of *ṣ*] would otherwise apply?

Anticipating the objection that "just as the attainment [of the rule] *atropasargasthān nimittāt* (Pāṇini 8.3.111) sets aside this prohibition characterized by being 'at the beginning of a word' (*padādi*), so too should it set aside the rule *ataḥ* (Pāṇini 8.3.112)," he says: "The attainment [of the rule] concerning prepositions," and so forth.

By the principle of *yenanāprāpti* (Vyāḍipāda 49), it is logical that there should be a sublation of the prohibition characterized by being 'at the beginning of a word' alone; in that case, the rule *ataḥ* (8.3.112) is indeed commenced for the sake of prepositions, whether that [prohibition] has already been attained or not yet attained.

Alternatively—the meaning is as follows: according to the principle that "exceptions [apavāda] set aside the rules immediately preceding them, not those that follow" (Vyāḍipāda 9), the application of *ṣatva* resulting from the prefix [in the rule] "after a prefix" (*upasargāt*) sets aside only the prohibition characterized by the initial position of a word (*padādilakṣaṇa*) for the suffix *sic*, but it does not set aside the prohibition for *sic* in the context of the *yaṅ* affix. The prohibition of *ṣatva* which would otherwise apply by the rule "after a prefix, in *sunoti*" (*upasargāt sunoti* 8.3.65) is [intended here]. The term "because of non-performance" (*akāryāt*) functions as a warding off of that very prohibition. Examples are: *pratistabdham* and *nistabdham*.

This is prescribed as an exception (*apavāda*) to the *ṣatva* (the substitution of *ṣ* for *s*) that would otherwise apply by rule 8.3.67. It is introduced when *ṣatva* would have applied by rule 8.3.70 (*parinivibhyaḥ*). Regarding the form *soḍhaḥ*:
even in the case of the past passive participle (*niṣṭhā*), this specific form arises when the nominative singular ending is applied.
To dispel the apprehension that this [rule] might apply, he says: "sahiṛyam," and so forth. Regarding the phrase "soṅbhūtaḥ" (or "soḍhabhūtaḥ" according to the reading in the Prāṃu):
the meaning is that it has attained that form which results when the letter *ha* is changed to the letter *ḍha*.

The letter *ḍh*, however, is not heard when the substitution of *jaś* occurs, as in the example *parisoḍhaḥ*. After the substitutions of *gh*, *ḍh*, *ṣṭu*, and the elision of *ḍh* have been performed, the vowel *o* is substituted [by P. 6.3.112]. Here, while the substitution of *ṣ* would apply to the first [root] by P. 8.3.67 (*stanbheḥ*), and the prohibition applies to the other two by P. 8.3.70 (*parinivibhyaḥ*), this [rule] is commenced.

Regarding the form *abhyatastambhat*: the suffix *ṇic* is applied, followed by *luṅ* (the aorist marker). By the rule *ṇiśridrusrubhyaḥ kartari caṅ* [Pāṇini 3.1.48], the *caṅ* affix is added; there is the elision of *ṇi*. By the rule *caṅi* [Pāṇini 6.1.11], reduplication occurs. As before, the remaining consonant (*khayaḥ śeṣaḥ*) remains, and the augment *aṭ* is added. In the case of *paryasīṣivat* and so forth, although the substitution of *ṣ* for *s* would have been required due to the intervention of the prefix (*upasarga*)—by the rule *sthādiṣvabhyāsena cābhyāsasya* [Pāṇini 8.3.64]—it does not take place here. *paryasīṣivat*, etc.

As in the previous case, there is *luṅ* and so forth; for *siv*, there is the *guṇa* substitution of the light penultimate vowel; for *sah*, however, there is *vṛddhi* by [Pāṇini 7.2.116]; then, by [Pāṇini 7.4.93], there is the substitution of *it*; for both, there is the shortening of the penultimate vowel by [Pāṇini 7.4.1];
and finally, there is the lengthening by [Pāṇini 7.4.94].

Here too, by [Pāṇini 8.3.71], which states "for *siv* and others even when there is an intervention by *aṅ*," the substitution would apply to those following the cause of the prefix even when there is an intervention by *aṅ*; in that case, it occurs.
Regarding the rule *sivusahoh* and so forth:

the meaning is that one must explain the form of this [rule] in such a way that the substitution of *ṣ* (ṣatva) does not occur for these two roots, *sivu* and *sah*, when following a prefix (*upasarga*) that serves as the cause [of the change].
For what purpose? He says: "The application [of the rule] from a prefix," and so on.

In this regard, the explanation is as follows: from the rule *upasargāt sunoti* [Pāṇini 8.3.65], the term *upasargāt* is carried over here by the principle of the "frog-leap" (*maṇḍūkapluti*). Therefore, the prohibition will apply specifically to that occurrence which is preceded by a prefix (*upasarga*). "And thus it has been illustrated."

That which is to be explained as having that meaning has been stated accordingly; the meaning is that an example of that very form of the meaning has been cited. Regarding "abhyasoṣyat," this is the conditional (lṛṅ) mood.
In the form *abhisusūṣati*, the suffix *san* [is added];
by the rule *san* (Pāṇini 1.2.9), there is an absence of *guṇa* due to its being *kit*.
Then, by the rule *ñj-jhan-gamāṃ sani* (Pāṇini 6.4.16), there is lengthening of the vowel *i*.
Regarding the passage beginning with "atra" and so forth: the particle *iti* is used here in the sense of a reason (*hetau*).

Why is this? Because, due to the restriction [*niyama*] "only after [the roots] *stu* and *ṇī* when followed by a *ṣat* [suffix], and not after the reduplicated syllable" (*stautiṇyoreva ṣaṇyabhyāsāt*, Pāṇini 8.3.61), the [application of the rule] does not otherwise obtain; and because of the restriction "in the case of *sthā* and others, [the substitution occurs] after the reduplicated syllable" (*sthādiṣvabhyāsena*, Pāṇini 8.3.64), there is likewise no application [of the desired rule]. Therefore, they cite *abhisusūḥ* as an example.

It might be argued: "In this case as well, does [the *s*] not exist? Therefore, that example is also untenable. To this he says: "The *s* that has become *ṣ* does not occur," and so forth. For the restriction "only for the roots *stu* and *ṇī*" (Pāṇini 8.3.61) applies when the *s* has become *ṣ*; however, here the *s* has not become *ṣ*. Therefore, in the absence of the mention of *saṅ*, the substitution of *ṣ* by rule 8.3.59 (*abhyāsasthānnimittāt*) would not apply.
Is the mention of "repetition" (*abhyāsa*) [intended] for the sake of the prefix (*upasarga*)? No, because that would be impossible.

Therefore, the substitution of *ṣ* for the *s* of the verbal root (*dhātu*) after a cause situated in a prefix does not apply here; for it is separated by the repetition, and furthermore, the *s* of this repetition has been excluded by the restrictive rule concerning *sthā* and other roots.
Thus: *abhisusūḥ*.

In *abhisusūṣa*, the suffix *kvip* is applied by [Pāṇini 3.2.178] *sthaḥ* [sic: *sthaḥ* is a typo for *sthaḥ*], and because the substitution of *ṣ* is not yet established (*asiddha*), the substitution of *r* and the *visarjanīya* occur. Regarding the phrase "if they reside in the same word" (*samānapadasthau cet*) and so forth:
this word *samāna* is a synonym for "one" (*eka*);
its meaning is "identical" (*abhinnam*).

The term *samānapada* is a *karmadhāraya* compound meaning "that which is both identical (*samāna*) and a word (*pada*). Those two [sounds] which stand within such a word are called *samānapadasthau*; the suffix *kap* is applied according to the rule *tatra tiṣṭhati* (Pāṇini 4.3.53).
Here, the cause (*nimitta*) consists of the letter *repha* (r) and the letter *ṣakāra* (ṣ).
That *nakāra* (n), which possesses that cause, is the "possessor of the cause" (*nimittī*) when it undergoes transformation into the state of *ṇatva* (the substitution of *ṇ* for *n*).
By this, the following is meant: wherever the letters *repha* (*r*) and *ṣakāra* (*ṣ*) occur in a word, if the letter *nakāra* (*n*) also occurs there [the rule applies]. For example:
*āstīrṇam*, *viśīrṇam*.
[The roots are] *stṛñ* "to cover" (Dhātupāṭha 1484) and *śṛ* "in the sense of injury" (Dhātupāṭha 1488).

The suffix *niṣṭhā* [the *kta* and *ktavatu* affixes] follows the roots preceded by the prefixes *vi-* and *ā-*; there is a prohibition of *iṭ* by the rule *śryukaḥ kiti* [Pāṇini 7.2.11]. There is the substitution of *it* for the root vowel by *ṛta iddhātoḥ* [Pāṇini 7.1.100], and the substitution of *ra* for the semivowel *ṛ*. Regarding the form *avagūrṇam*: the root *gurī* (meaning "to lift up") is listed as number 1396 in the Dhātupāṭha; there is a prohibition of *iṭ* by the rule *śvīdito niṣṭhāyām* [Pāṇini 7.2.14].

The vowel lengthening is by [Pāṇini 8.2.77] *hali ca*; the substitution of *na* for the *t* of the *niṣṭhā* suffix is by [Pāṇini 8.2.42] *radābhyāṃ niṣṭhāto naḥ*, and its change to *ṇ* is by this very rule (*aṭkupvāṅnumvyavāye ’pi*).
Thus: *kuṣṇāti*, *puṣṇāti*.
[The roots are] *kuṣa* "to extract" (Dhātupāṭha 1518) and *puṣa* "to nourish" (Dhātupāṭha 1529).
"The suffix *śna* [is introduced].

Regarding the statement "the mention of *ṣ* is for the sake of what follows," one might ask: why is it not also for this very purpose? To this he replies: "because it is already established by the rule of *ṣṭu*."

If this is so, for what purpose is the citation of *kuṣṇāti* and the like? It is for the purpose of demonstrating that the mention of the letter *ṣ* (*ṣagrahaṇa*), while being made for the sake of subsequent rules, also serves this present purpose. In the absence of the mention of *ṣ*, forms such as *kuṣṇāti* would be established by the rule for *ṣṭu* substitution alone. However, since that [mention of *ṣ*] is made for the sake of subsequent rules, the substitution of *ṇ* must be performed by this very rule.

In this operation, because the substitution of *ṣṭu* is not established (*asiddha*), and because its purpose is fulfilled elsewhere, its priority (*paratva*) is not tenable; for it is said: "Regarding that which is unestablished in what precedes it, there is no conflict (*vipratiṣedha*), because of the absence of a subsequent [rule]" (Jaiminīya-Paribhāṣā 67).
[The rule] "It should be stated: 'and after a vowel containing *ṛ*" (*ṛvarṇācca*) and so forth [is necessary].
The substitution of *ṇa* being prescribed after *ra* and *ṣa* does not apply after a vowel containing *ṛ*, because that [vowel with *ṛ*] is a different phoneme (*varṇāntara*).

Nor can it be argued that [the substitution] will arise from the *repha* situated within the vowel *ṛ*, for in the Sūtra, the *repha* as a phoneme (*varṇa*) is relied upon as the cause for the substitution of *ṇ*.

Indeed, the *repha* residing within the vowel *ṛ* is not a complete phoneme; what is it then? It is a portion of a phoneme (*varṇaikadeśa*). Because it is a mere portion of that [phoneme], a portion of a phoneme is not grasped by the mention of the phoneme itself.
Thus it has been said: "Regarding those portions of phonemes within phonemes which have the same form as other phonemes, does that operation apply to them or not?"
For those [sounds] merely imitate its shadow; they are not that very thing itself.
The teachers maintain that a phoneme is produced by a distinct effort.
Therefore, it must be stated: "and after a vowel containing *ṛ*."
In the forms "tisṛṇām" and "catasṛṇām," the substitutes [tisṛ and catasṛ] occur by rule 7.2.99.
Due to the prohibition "na tisṛcatasṛ" (6.4.4), the lengthening [of the vowel] prescribed by "nāmi" (6.4.3) does not take place.

"Established by the indication of commonality of sound. By this, he rejects the proposed addition (*upasaṃkhyāna*). "Ra-śruti" is a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "that which has 'ra' as its audible perception (*śruti*) or apprehension (*upalabdhi*)."

Alternatively—*śruti* means "that which is heard," and *ra-śruti* is that which is both *ra* and *śruti*. Here, setting aside the distinction between being a phoneme (*varṇatva*) and not being a phoneme (*avarṇatva*) that arises from the mere vowel *ṛ*, that universal which is simply the hearing of *ra* (*raśrutimātra*) is what is indicated, and not the specific individual instance of the phoneme *repha* itself.
By this, the substitution of *ṇ* is established even in cases such as *tisṛṇām*, because that universal of the hearing of *ra* exists within the vowel *ṛ*.

It might be argued: "In the sound *ṛ*, there are three vowel-portions (*ajbhāga*), and the fourth, situated in their midst, is the *repha*. Since the designation is made based on the commonality of the sound *ra* [in that *repha*], the substitution of *ṇa* would not be established even by that, because of the intervention of that vowel-portion which follows the *repha*? To this, he says: "possessing the *a*-vowel" (*avarṇabhāk*), and so forth.

Since he provides the mention of *nṛnamana* and *tṛpnoti* in the rule for the prohibition of *ṇatva* (the substitution of *ṇ* for *n*) in the *kṣubhnādi* group, this indicates that *ṇatva* occurs even when there is an intervention by a portion containing an *a*-vowel; otherwise, the inclusion of these two would be purposeless, as there would be no possibility [of *ṇatva*] to begin with, and prohibitions must be preceded by a possibility.

Now, although the specific instance of the letter *r* (*repha-vyakti*) is indicated as being composed of phonemes (*varṇātmikā*), he says "Or rather" (*atha vā*) and so forth to demonstrate that *ṇatva* nevertheless occurs.

Previously, it was established by the mention of a commonality of sound (*śruti-sāmānya*) included in the rule that *ṇatva* occurs even when there is an intervention by a portion of a vowel (*avarṇa-bhāga*). Now, however, the distinction is simply that it occurs from a non-*ṛ*-vowel (*ad-ṛ-varṇa*) that is not separated [by such an intervention].
Now, for what purpose is the mention of *ṇa*? For the retroflex (*mūrdhanya*) which is the subject under discussion (*prakṛta*) will continue to apply here.

That alone is what is to be prescribed; in that case, by the principle of closest proximity (*antaratama*), would it not be the *ṇakāra* itself that occurs for the *nakāra*? This is true; however, in the preceding sūtra, the mention of the "cerebral" (*mūrdhanya*) was connected with the prohibition. Therefore, if that [term] were to carry over [into this sūtra], one might suspect that the prohibition also carries over.
Consequently, the term is mentioned again in order to dispel the suspicion of such a prohibition.

But surely, since there is no possibility of occurrence, there will be no suspicion of a prohibition; for prohibitions are preceded by a possibility of occurrence, and there is no possibility of the retroflex [ṣ] being obtained after the two sibilants (ś and ṣ) by anyone. This is true; it is precisely from this very prohibition that the positive rule is inferred. Alternatively, because of the word "optionally" (*vā*) in the immediately preceding sūtra, this rule should be understood as applying optionally.

Therefore, [the mention of] "by both" (*rāvābhyām*) is either for the purpose of excluding alternative options (*vikalpa*) or for the sake of clarity. Because the ablative case (*pañcamī*) in the rule indicates that the term *nirdiṣṭa* (specified) implies immediate proximity (*ānantarya*), this rule prescribes the substitution of *ṇa* even when it was not otherwise obtained due to intervention by the augment *āṭ* and so forth, as in the case of *paryāṇaddham*. In *paryāṇaddham*: from the root *ṇaha* (meaning "to bind," Dhātupāṭha 1166), with the suffix *niṣṭhā* (-ta). By the rule *naho dhaḥ* (Pāṇini 8.2.34), the letter *ha* is replaced by *dha*. Then, by the rule *jhaṣastathordho’dhaḥ* (Pāṇini 8.2.40), the letter *ta* is replaced by *dha*. Finally, by the rule *ṇo naḥ* (Pāṇini 8.4.53), the preceding *dha* is replaced by *da*.

But surely, the substitution of *ṇ* is already established here by the intervention of *aṅ*, because according to the rule *aṇ savarṇān gṛhṇāti* (Pāṇini 1.1.69), *aṅ* is also included by the mention of *aṅ*. For what purpose, then, is the mention of *āṅ* made? To this he says: "The mention of *āṅ*" and so forth.

If the mention of *āṅ* were absent, there would be a prohibition [of the *ṇ* substitution] due to the intervention of *āṅ* by the rule *āṅ-māṅ-ohśīṭi* (Pāṇini 8.4.38). Therefore, the mention of *āṅ* is for the purpose of setting aside that [prohibition].

Regarding the term *bṛṃhaṇam*: the roots *bṛha* and *bṛhi* mean "to grow" (*vṛddhau*) [and *vahi* means "to grow" and "to sound," according to the Dhātupāṭha (735, 736)]. By the rule *idito num dhātoḥ* [Pāṇini 7.1.58], the augment *num* is applied, followed by the suffix *lyuṭ*, which results in the substitution of *anusvāra* [by Pāṇini 8.3.24]. Now, one might raise the following objection: "How can this be an example of the mention of *num*, since here there is an intervention by the *anusvāra*, not by the *num*; and furthermore, because there is no *num* in the word *tṛṃhaṇam*, the rule would apply only to *prenvanam*, where there is indeed an intervention by *num*? Anticipating this criticism, he says: "*numgrahaṇam*," etc.
For here, the mention of *num* is for the purpose of indicating the *anusvāra*, not for the purpose of establishing *num* itself.
What is thereby established? To this he says: "By that," and so forth.
"[The strengthening] of *dṛṃhaṇam*" (the *Kāśikā* and *Padamañjarī* read *tṛṃhaṇam*).
The roots *tṛh* and *dṛh* mean "to injure" (*hiṃsāyām*) [Dhātupāṭha 1455 and 1350]. The suffix *lyuṭ* is applied, and as before, there is an *anusvāra*.
Here, because the mention of *num* serves as an indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*) for the *anusvāra*, the substitution of *ṇ* occurs even when *num* is absent, provided there is an intervening *anusvāra*.
This word *api* indicates that in the case of *vṛṃhaṇam*, the substitution of *ṇ* occurs even when the *anusvāra* derived from *num* intervenes.
Regarding the term "prenvanam":
the root *vi* means "pervasion" (*vyāptau*; Dhātupāṭha 587).
The suffix *pūrvavaśun* is applied; because it is not followed by a non-vowel (*ajhalpara*), the *anusvāra* does not occur.

In this case as well, because the *anusvāra* serves as a mere indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*), even though the nasal sound (*nu*) exists, there is no intervention by an *anusvāra*; thus, the rule for *ṇatva* does not apply.

For just as in the expression, "Having seen the star, they should release their speech," since the time of seeing the star serves as a mere indicator, they release their speech when that specific time occurs even if the star is not visible, and they do not release their speech when the star is visible if that specific time is absent.

Likewise here as well, since the mention of *num* serves as an indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*) for *anusvāra*, it should be understood that even in the absence of *num*, the rule does not apply where there is no intervention by an *anusvāra*.
But what is the case here: does the sentence conclude with the entire group [of conditions], or with each one individually? If the former position is adopted, then it would never apply;
for it is impossible for an intervention by all [the factors] beginning with *aṭ* to occur in a single example.

Now, if [the rule] were restricted to the second [case], then it would not apply in examples such as *arkeṇa*, because there is an intervention by more than one [element]. To this he says: "Because its purpose is to indicate intervention," and so forth.

This means: "in the case of an intervention by these [elements], namely *aṭ* and the others. And these [elements] are capable [of causing intervention] both individually and when combined with one another.
Those who are used for the purpose of indicating that [object] which is to be indicated—whether by one, two, or many—are indeed included [in the prohibition].

For instance, when it is said, "One must not study together with Devadatta, Yajñadatta, and Viṣṇumitra," even if one studies together with just one among those mentioned for the purpose of indicating the prohibition of studying together—namely, Devadatta and the others—one does not study with two or with many.

Therefore, in this case as well, since the *aṭ* augment and so forth serve to indicate the intervention (*vyavāya*), the substitution of *ṇ* occurs when there is an intervention by those [augments] either individually or collectively.
"By the separate ones" means that non-intervention is indicated by each one individually. "By the combined ones" means—
"By those joined together with one another. The mention of "all" is for the purpose of indicating more than two;
for an intervention by all [of them] is not possible anywhere.
And thus, it is stated that in some cases there is the completion of the sentence for each [word] individually, while in other cases it occurs through the collection [of words] as far as possible.

Now, what is the purpose of including the word *api* (also)? If it is argued that it is so that [the rule] may apply when there is no intervention (*avyavāya*), we say no; for this is already established by the preceding rule alone. If that is so, then the inclusion of *api* is for the sake of the subsequent rule. For if it were not there, the rule "after a preverb, even in a non-compound" (*upasargādasamāse 'pi*, Pāṇini 8.4.14) would apply only here—such as in *praṇayati*—where there is an intervention [of sounds].

But here [the rule] would not apply in the case of *nirṇayati*, for there is no intervention here by any one of the [prefixes] beginning with *ā*. Is it not because the cause beginning with *r* (the *repha*) continues to apply here, and since it is impossible for that alone to be the "prior member" (*pūrvapada*), the meaning is understood by implication to be "after what follows a cause situated in the prior member"? Thus he says: "from a cause situated in the prior member," and so forth.
Regarding *drūṇasaḥ*:
it is a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "one whose nose is like a tree" (*dur* = tree).

In this context, the word *dru* signifies a branch. [The suffix] *ac* is applied by the rule *añ nāsikāyāḥ saṃjñāyāṃ nasañ cāsthūlāt* (Pāṇini 5.4.118), and there is the substitution of *nas* for *nāsikā* as a compound-final element. Thus, [the form] is *carmanāsikaḥ*.

The compound *nāsikāsyā carmavikāraḥ* ("a leather product for the nose") is formed by the rule "A *bahuvrīhi* may also be used with a genitive denoting a modification of a whole, and there is elision of the final member" (*samudāyavikāraṣaṣṭhāśca bahuvrīhir uttarapadalopaśca*, Pāṇini 2.1.51).
There is shortening of the *upasarjana* [by Pāṇini 1.2.48].
Thus: *ṛgayanam*.

The term *ṛco'yana* is a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*). One might ask: could the word *aga* be omitted? Would the absence of *ṇatva* (the substitution of *ṇ* for *n*) in *ṛgayanam* not be established simply by the rule of irregular derivation (*nipātana*) [Pāṇini 8.4.2]? This is not the case; for it has been stated that "irregular derivations do not necessarily override [other rules]. Therefore, if the word *aga* were not mentioned, then in some instances *ṛgayaṇam* might also be understood as a valid form. Consequently, the word *aga* must be explicitly stated.
Now, is this for the purpose of restriction (*niyamārtha*) or for the purpose of an injunction (*vidhyartha*)? To this he says: "Some," and so forth.
Others describe this as being for the purpose of an injunction;
therefore, he said "some."

[Objection: But surely, by the preceding sūtra, *ṇatva* was prescribed only when the cause (*nimitta*) and the effect (*nimittin*) reside within the same word (*samānapada*). However, in compounds such as *druṇasaḥ*, once the compound has been formed, the cause and the effect do not reside in the same word; for the cause resides in the prior member (*pūrvapada*), while the *n* (the effect) resides in the subsequent member (*uttarapada*). Thus, since *ṇatva* is not even applicable by the preceding sūtra, how can this [present rule] be understood as having a restrictive purpose (*niyamārthatā*)? To this, he says: "Even in a compound," and so forth.

Even though there is a lack of "samāna-pada" (identity of word) with respect to the individual components of the compound—since the designation *pada* applies to each of those two words by virtue of the *pratyayalakṣaṇa* rule even when their case-endings have been elided—the identity of word certainly exists with respect to the whole, because the designation *pada* applies to the aggregate by virtue of the case-ending produced after the compound.

Therefore, since the relationship between cause and effect (the condition and that which is conditioned) exists within the same word even in a compound, the application [of the rule] by the preceding [sūtra] would occur; consequently, it is established that this [present sūtra] is for the purpose of restriction (*niyamārtha*).

If this is so, then just as in the case of *carmanāsika*, where the substitution of *ṇ* for the *n* situated in the final member (*uttarapada*) does not occur because it has been specifically excluded by a restrictive rule, likewise [the substitution] would not occur even for a *taddhita*-suffixal *n* in cases such as *kharapasyāpatyaṃ khārapayaṇaḥ*—by the rule *naḍādibhyaḥ phak* [Pāṇini 4.1.99]—or in *mātṛbhogāya hito mātṛbhogīṇaḥ*—by the rule *ātmanviājanabhogottarapadāt khaḥ* [Pāṇini 5.1.9]; and likewise, in a case such as *karaṇaṃ priyamasya karaṇapriyaḥ*, where the *n* is situated in the prior member (*pūrvapada*), it would also not occur? To this, he says: "And that," and so forth.

For a correlative term (*sambandhiśabda*) necessarily brings its counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) to mind—[the reading *sannidhāpayanti* is found in both the Kāṃu and Prāṃu editions]. Just as when it is said, "One should behave with devotion toward one's mother," although the word "one's own" is not explicitly stated, it is nevertheless understood that it refers to "one's own mother";

so too here, these two are correlative terms—"prior member" (*pūrvapada*) and "subsequent member" (*uttarapada*). For the status of being a subsequent member is possible only when there is the status of being a prior member, and the status of being a prior member is possible only when there is the status of being a subsequent member.

When the subsequent member (*uttarapada*) is brought into proximity by the presence of the preceding member (*pūrvapada*), this restriction prevents the change to *ṇ* for that very *n* situated in the subsequent member—as in *carmanāsika* and so forth—but not for one situated in a preceding member that ends in a *taddhita* suffix.
In examples such as *khārapāyaṇa* and *mātṛbhogīṇa*, the *n* is situated in a preceding member ending in a *taddhita* suffix according to the circumstances, and not in the subsequent member.
Therefore, there is this fault regarding the purpose of this restriction: namely, the word "agaḥ" (not after a word denoting a mountain).

The prohibition would apply only to the restriction (*niyama*) and not to the substitution of *ṇ* for *n*, because the prohibition constitutes a part of the restrictive rule itself. Consequently, the substitution of *ṇ* for *g* would occur both when [the word] is a technical term (*saṃjñā*) and when it is not. For this very reason, he says "agaḥ" and so forth.
The prohibition "aga" applies specifically to the substitution of *ṇ* (ṇatva), not to the restrictive rule (*niyama*).
Therefore, the undesirable consequence (*doṣaprasaṅga*) does not arise at all.

But how can this prohibition, being merely a part of the restrictive rule, be understood as applying to the substitution of *ṇ*? To this question, he provides the following answer: "By means of a split of the yoga (*yogavibhāga*)," and so forth.

The rule *pūrvapadātsaṃjñāyām* constitutes one *yoga*, while *agaḥ* constitutes the second. By this [second rule], whatever occurrence of *ṇatva* (the substitution of *ṇ* for *n*) might be applicable is entirely prohibited, and not merely the immediately following operation.
Otherwise, the division of the rules (*yogavibhāga*) would be purposeless.
As for the phrase "others, however," and so forth:
The word *tu* indicates a distinction from what preceded.

However, other teachers maintain that in the previous sūtra, whatever is a single word (*nitva-pada*) is precisely what constitutes a "single word" (*samāna-pada*). This is what is being stated: whether the consideration is made with respect to the individual components or whether it is made with respect to the aggregate, they accept as a "single word" exactly that which is a single word.
Why? To this he says: "Because of the mention of 'samāna' (identical)," and so forth.
The mention of *samāna* is made for this purpose:

that when there is the status of having a single word as their locus (*ekapadādhikaraṇatva*), the state of being *ṇatva* (the substitution of ṇ for n) should occur between the cause (*nimitta*) and the effect (*nimittin*), but it should not occur when they are in separate words (*bhinnapadatva*).
And this [objection] is without merit; for the meaning of "non-different" is already obtained simply by the mention of the word *pada*.

If *ṇatva* were to occur whenever there is a difference of substratum (*padādhāra*), then the mention of the word *pada* would be purposeless, as there would be nothing to exclude; for those two [the cause and the effect] do not exist when they are not situated within a word (*apada*).
Therefore, by the very force of the mention of the word *pada*, *ṇatva* is understood to occur between a cause and an effect that reside within non-different words.
