Regarding that: since the condition "in the same word" (*samānapada*) is already obtained simply by the mention of *pada*, the explicit mention of *samāna* (same) is made for the purpose of restriction; the intention is that [the rule applies] only to that which is always (*nityam*) in the same word. By the words "of those" (*teṣām*) and so forth, he shows that, according to the opinion of those who rely on the preceding sūtra, this [present rule] serves as an injunction (*vidhi*).

It might be argued: "Even in a compound (*samāsa*), the basis for the relationship between the cause and the effect is always necessarily within the same word (*samānapada*); therefore, this was stated here for the sake of restriction (*niyamārtha*), not for the sake of an injunction (*vidhyartha*. To this, he says: "For in a compound," and so forth.

For in a compound, there exists a division such as "this is the prior member (*pūrvapada*) with respect to its constituent parts" and "this is the subsequent member (*uttarapada*). Therefore, there is also the state of being different words (*asamāmapadatva*).
By the word "also" (*api*), it is implied that there is also the state of being the same word (*samānapadatva*).

In that regard, when there is a mutual dependence between the preceding and the following [members], then, due to the distinction between the preceding and the following, there is a lack of identity of word (*asamānapadatva*).
However, when there is dependence upon the aggregate [as a whole], then, because of the absence of a distinction between preceding and following, there is identity of word (*samānapadatva*).
Therefore, in a compound (*samāsa*), identity of word is not necessarily constant. In the word *vanaṃ*, the nominative case is used by way of a substitution (*vyatyaya*) for the genitive case.
"Puragāvaṇam" is a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*).
According to [Pāṇini 6.3.117], there is lengthening of the vowel in the first member (*pūrvapada*).
"Agrevaṇam" is likewise formed.

This is a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*). When that has been formed, the word *vana* is placed last according to the rule beginning with *rājadantādi* (Pāṇini 2.2.31). By the rule [Pāṇini 6.3.9], there is no elision (*aluk*) of the locative case ending.

But surely, since the substitution of *ṇ* is already established by the preceding rule, for what purpose is this one? To this he says: "Since [it is] established," and so forth. One should not suspect a reverse restriction—that the *ṇ* applies only to the *v* and *n* of words beginning with *puraga*—because the forms *puraga*, etc., are cited with their long vowels already applied. Thus, this purpose is served: that the restriction should apply only where these words have their long vowels, and not elsewhere.

Since the lengthening [of the vowel] would already be established by the rule *anyatā* (Pāṇini 6.3.117), the explicit utterance of the long vowel would result in nothing but unnecessary complexity (*gaurava*).
Therefore, the restriction applies only to those instances where these [vowels] undergo lengthening.

Therefore, because there is no object to be excluded (*vyavacchedya*), there is no suspicion of a reversed restriction (*viparītaniyama*); for these preceding words do not possess their long vowel when occurring after anything other than "forest" (*vana*). As for those words *oṣadhi* and *vanaspati* which are not *pra*-type words, [the rule applies] in the sense of a proper name (*saṃjñā*): whether the preceding sūtra is for the purpose of restriction (*niyamārtha*) or for the purpose of an injunction (*vidhyartha*), in either case, the *ṇatva* (nasalization) not otherwise obtained is prescribed by this [rule].
This is likewise in the case of non-proper names (*asaṃjñā*) under the view that it is an injunction.

However, if the rule were restricted (niyamapakṣe), its formulation would be purposeless with respect to the term *asaṃjñā*, because there is no restriction regarding *asaṃjñā*; for the substitution of *ṇ* would be established as appropriate by the first two rules alone. Among the others beginning with *śara*, the words *ikṣu* and *śara* denote grasses (*oṣadhi*).
The remaining ones, beginning with *plakṣa*, denote trees (*vanaspati*).

In the case of these [words], when they are not names (*asaṃjñā*), the substitution of *ṇ*—which would otherwise not apply under either the rule for positive prescription (*vidhipakṣa*) or the rule for restriction (*niyamapakṣa*) regarding names—is prescribed by this [sūtra].
However, when they are names (*saṃjñā*), the optional (*vibhāṣā*) substitution of *ṇ* prescribed by Pāṇini 8.4.6 would apply; therefore, this sūtra prescribes it as obligatory.

He demonstrates the function of the word "also" (*api*) in the phrase "even when not a name" (*asaṃjñāyām api*): if the word "also" were absent, then because of the governing heading (*adhikāra*) concerning names, the rule would not apply when the word is not a name.

But if, having set aside the governing rule on technical names (*saṃjñā*), a rule were stated in a general sense, would it always be possible to omit the mention of "technical name"? It is nevertheless stated for the sake of clarity:
*pravaṇam*, *nirvaṇam*. This is an *avyayībhāva* compound formed by [Pāṇini 2.1.6] *avyayam* etc., in the sense of a case ending.

The meaning is "in the middle of the forest. Furthermore, *śaravaṇam* and similar forms are genitive compounds (*ṣaṣṭhī-samāsa*). Regarding the rule for technical names (*saṃjñā*)—namely, *vanaṃ puragāmiśrakā-* (Pāṇini 8.4.4)—since there is no substitution of *ṇ* for the *n* of *vana* following words denoting herbs or trees due to this specific restriction, it should be understood that the option (*vibhāṣā*) applies in non-technical names by the principle of elimination (*pāriśeṣya*). One should not suspect that because of this optional rule, which takes precedence, the substitution must also occur in technical names; for when a restrictive rule (*niyama*) is to be applied, the optional rule (*vibhāṣā*) is considered non-existent (*asiddha*).
If, however, this option (*vibhāṣā*) is intended to apply both when there is a name (*saṃjñā*) and when there is no name, then a further effort must be undertaken for that purpose.

What, then, is that? It is the application of a *yogavibhāga* (splitting of the rule). When a *yogavibhāga* is made, one rule is understood as being for the purpose of subverting the restriction; thus, the option is established even in the case of a name.

However, the status of being unestablished (*asiddhatva*) will not apply here due to the force of the word-splitting (*yogavibhāga*). Regarding this, for those who rely on the interpretation that "samānapada" means "that which is always the same word," this is an option (*vibhāṣā*) where [the rule] was not previously applicable; for others, however, it is an option where [the rule] was already applicable. The mention in the plural number is intended to exclude the word's own form (*svarūpa*).

“*Dūrvāvaṇam*” and so forth are genitive compounds (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*). Regarding the statement, “it should be stated that [the suffix applies] after two-syllable and three-syllable [stems],” the word *akṣara* here refers to syllables (*akṣu*).

The meaning is that this rule must be explained as having the following sense: "the substitution of *ṇ* for the letter *v* occurring after words consisting of two syllables or three syllables, such as the words *oṣadhi* and *vanaspati*.
Regarding this, the explanation is as follows: due to the understanding of the fixed linguistic usage (*vyavasthitavibhāṣā*), the substitution occurs only after words of two or three syllables.
This same principle regarding the word *vyākhyeya* (to be explained) should be stated in subsequent cases as well.

The explanation, however, should be made by relying on the *vyavasthitavibhāṣā* (the rule of fixed optionality). Now, one might object: trees such as the *śirīṣa* are indeed trees (*vṛkṣa*), but they are not forest-possessors (*vanaspati*); and when the term "forest-possessor" is mentioned, the term "tree" is not included, because there is an absolute difference between them.
Thus it is stated in another treatise: "A fruit-bearing plant is to be known as a *vanaspati*, while trees are those that bear both flowers and fruit."

How then is it that examples such as *śirīṣavanam* (a grove of *śirīṣa* trees) and *vadarīvanam* (a grove of *badarī* trees) are cited? To one who asks this, he replies: "A tree (*vanaspati*) is to be understood as that which bears fruit.
Although the distinction between a tree (*vṛkṣa*) and a forest-tree (*vanaspati*) is shown by this verse, nevertheless, for the present purpose, they should be understood here as non-distinct.

Regarding their treatment as non-distinct, the very statement of the Commentator (*bhāṣyakāra*) serves as the evidence; for it has been stated by the Commentator under [Pāṇini 4.2.67]: "What is the purpose of the mention of 'ending in -vat'? A village not far from *śirīṣa* trees is called *śirīṣāḥ*; a grove belonging to them is *śirīṣavanam*."

If it were not stated here that "it refers to the individual," then the status of being a *vanaspati* (tree/forest-plant) would be extended [to the plural]; consequently, the status of being a *vanaspati* would be extended, and by rule [Pāṇini 8.4.6], the substitution of *ṇ* would undesirably apply.

Furthermore, if here there were no inclusion of *vṛkṣa* and *vanaspati* as being identical, then—due to the extension of the status of being a *vanaspati*—the optional application of the *ṇ* substitution would be untenable; for *śiṃśapā*s are not *vanaspati*s.
"A fruit-bearing *vanaspati* is to be known [by this definition].
That which possesses fruit alone without flowers is to be known as a fruit-bearing *vanaspati*, such as the *udumbara* and others.
"Trees (*vṛkṣa*) are those endowed with both flowers and fruit."
They are called *puṣpaphalopagāḥ* because they approach (*upagacchanti*) or obtain (*prāpnuvanti*) flowers and fruits.

The suffix *ḍa* is applied here by means of the supplementary rule (*upasaṃkhyāna*) "it is seen in other cases as well" (*anyeṣv api dṛśyate*), which follows rules such as *antātyanta-* (Pāṇini 3.2.48).
Furthermore, it is not only those that produce flowers and fruits that are trees; what then? Those that produce either one—whether flowers or fruits—are also trees.
In this regard, the *vetasa* and others produce only flowers, while the *plakṣa* and others produce only fruit; however, the *āmra* and others produce both.

In this context, whatever is a *vanaspati* is necessarily a tree (*vṛkṣa*), but what is a tree is not necessarily a *vanaspati*. For example: reeds (*vetasa*) and the like are trees that bear flowers; *plakṣa* trees and the like are those that bear fruit; and mango trees (*āmra*) and the like are those that bear both flowers and fruit. Regarding the statement "herbs (*oṣadhyaḥ*) end with the ripening of their fruit":

from the word *oṣadhi*, the feminine suffix *ṅīṣ* is applied because it belongs to the *bahv-ādi* group, according to the rules: "The suffix *ik* is added after a stem ending in a consonant [to form a feminine noun]" (Gaṇasūtra 50), and "The suffix *ika* is optionally added after any [stem] except those ending in *aktin*" (Gaṇasūtra 51).
Those plants whose end is destruction through the ripening of their fruit are to be known as *phalapākāntā* (fruit-ripening-ending) herbs, such as the *kavalya* and others.
Regarding the phrase "creepers (*latā*), shrubs (*gulma*), and spreading vines (*vīrudh*"): creepers (*latā*) are those possessing tendrils, such as the *mālatī* and others.

*Gulmas* are trees with short trunks. *Vīrudhas* are to be understood as those that possess many stems. The word "of the day" (*ahnaḥ*) is in the nominative case instead of the genitive, as previously explained. This [rule] is for the purpose of prescribing [the elision] for those who rely on the mention of the word *samāna*, namely those for whom it is always the same word.
But for others, it is for the purpose of restriction (*niyamārtham*).
In the same way, in the subsequent cases as well, both the status of being a restriction and the status of being an injunction (*vidhyarthatā*) should be understood according to the context.
[This applies to] "the forenoon," and so forth.
In the rule *pūrvāparādi* (Pāṇini 2.2.1), there is a *ekadeśin* compound.

The suffix *ṭac* is applied by the rule *rājāhaḥsakhibhyaṣṭac* (5.4.91) as a compound-final suffix (*samāsānta*). By the rule [5.4.88], the substitution of *ahan* occurs, followed by the application of *savarṇadīrgha* (vowel coalescence).
Regarding "nirahnaḥ": it is a *prādi* compound meaning "from which the day has departed" (*nirgata-mahna*). The remainder is as previously explained.
Regarding the term *dīrghāhna*:
it is a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "that in which the days (*ahāni*) are long (*dīrgha*).
The reference to the *tatpuruṣa* [compound] continues from the rule *ṭaj-ic-au* (Pāṇini 5.4.86).
Therefore, the suffix *ṭac* does not occur in this *bahuvrīhi* compound.
By the rule *ana upadhālopino 'nyatarasyām* [Pāṇini 4.1.28], the feminine suffix *ṅīp* is applied, and by the rule *ṭeḥ* [Pāṇini 6.4.134], the penultimate vowel *a* is elided.
In this case, because the word is understood to end in *ā*, the substitution of *ṇa* for *na* does not take place.

If, however, [the substitution] were to apply to that which does not end in the vowel *a*, then just as the substitution of *ṇ* for the *n* of the stem *ahan-* occurs in the word *pūrvāhṇaḥ* (forenoon) because the *n* remains as it was established prior to the suffix, so too would it occur in *dīrghāhnī śarat* (an autumn with long days). Therefore, its inclusion [in the rule] is understood through interpretation. Because of the use of the *tapara* marker (*t*), the substitution does not occur in *parāhnaḥ* (afternoon), where the word ends in *ā*.
The inclusion of the term *anta* (end) is for the sake of clarity.

Since the preceding word (*pūrvapada*) is qualified by the letter *a* followed by *t*, the rule of "specification by the final element" (*tadantavidhi*) will apply; thus, even without the mention of *anta*, the status of being "ending in that" is obtained. [The form] *udvaha* is derived with the suffix *lyuṭ* in the sense of an instrument (*karaṇe*), as in "that by which one carries. Precisely because of this, there is a lengthening of the penultimate vowel (*upadhādīrgha*) due to irregular derivation (*nipātana*).

Regarding the term *ikṣuvāhaṇam*: it is a compound formed with the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) characterized by its connection to a verbal derivative (*kṛt*), meaning "the carrying of sugarcane" (*ikṣūṇāṃ vāhanam*). It is said that "that which has been placed upon a vehicle is called 'deposited' (*āhitam*)."
Because verbal roots have multiple meanings, the root *dhā* occurs there [in the sense of "to place"];
in the word *āhita*, the past tense (*bhūtakāla*) is not intended to be expressed,
for according to [Pāṇini 3.3.113], the suffix *kta* is prescribed in the sense of time in general.

Therefore, even when sugarcane and the like have not been loaded onto a vehicle for the purpose of transport, but are merely placed on the ground for that purpose alone, the designation still applies— namely, "the vehicle of Dākṣi. In this case,
only a vehicle belonging to Dākṣi is understood, not the state of being loaded.
Therefore he says: "The meaning is 'a vehicle belonging to Dakṣi-svāmin'.

In this case, the power of the word (*śabda-śakti*) is the cause [of the understanding]. Regarding the phrase "when there is the denotation of a place," the word "being understood" (*gamyamāna*) is to be supplied as the remainder.
In the phrase "those whose drink is milk" (*kṣīraṃ pānaṃ yeṣām*), the genitive case is used according to the rule for the agent (*kartari*) in connection with a *kṛt* suffix.
As in the example "the Uśīnaras are milk-drinkers" (*kṣīrapāṇā uśīnarāḥ*),
an excellence (*atiśaya*) is understood here, and not merely the relation of drinking milk, since that [mere relation] is possible elsewhere as well.

But surely, words such as *kṣīrapāṇa* (milk-drinker) and others refer to humans, and because they are in grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with [the word] *uśīnara* and so forth, those too must refer to that very same [human]; how then is it understood here that they denote a country? This is not so; because the inhabitants of countries such as Uśīnara reside there, they are perceived in that way. Thus, by means of their connection to the country of Uśīnara and so forth, the name "Uśīnara" applies to humans. Furthermore, words such as *uśīnara* were originally applied only to the countries as proper names (*saṃjñā*).

In the expression "the platforms cry out" (*krośanti*), by way of their connection with the platforms, those words "platform" (*mañca*) which are applied to the men [standing upon them] are understood to denote the platforms themselves.

If it were not understood that they denote the platforms, then how could the men, as qualified by the support of the platforms, be cognized? This undertaking is for the purpose of providing an illustration:
"drinking milk" (*kṣīrapāṇam*).

*Pītiḥ* means "drinking. When the rule *napuṃsake bhāve ktaḥ* [Pāṇini 3.3.114] is in force, the suffix *lyuṭ* is applied by the rule *lyuṭ ca* [Pāṇini 3.3.115]. Thus we have the example "the bronze vessel for drinking milk" (*kṣīrapāṇaḥ kaṃsaḥ*).
Here, *pānaḥ* is derived with the suffix *lyuṭ* according to the rule *karaṇādhikaraṇayoś ca* [Pāṇini 3.3.117], meaning "that by which one drinks" (*pīyate 'nena iti pānaḥ*).
Regarding the phrase "in the section on *vā*" (*vāprakaraṇe*),
the meaning here is the presentation of an *upasaṃkhyāna* (supplementary rule).
The sense is that within this section on *vā*, one must provide a presentation of the change to *ṇ* (*ṇatva*) for the letter *n* found in words such as *giri-nadī* and others.

In this regard, the following is the explanation: the particle *ca* in the subsequent sūtra has the sense of an inclusive conjunction (*anuktasamuccaya*). By means of it, the substitution of *ṇ* for the *n* in words such as *giri-nadī* and others will optionally occur. The word *anta* denotes a constituent part (*avayava*).
[The example is] *māṣavāpiṇau*.

The suffix *ṇini* is applied by [Pāṇini 3.2.78], and not by [Pāṇini 3.2.78] (*supyajātī ṇinistācchīlye*), because the subordinate member (*upapada*) denotes a genus (*jāti*). "Māṣavāpāṇi" is a compound with an subordinate member (*upapadasamāsa*), derived from "those who sow beans" (*māṣān vapanti*) [by Pāṇini 3.2.1]; there is the substitution of *śir* [for the root *vap*] by [Pāṇini 7.1.20]; the augment *num* by [Pāṇini 7.1.72]; and the lengthening by [Pāṇini 6.4.8]. Thus: "māṣavāpeṇa."

Is it because of the incorrect form *mādhavā*? [The rule] *tṛtīyaikavacanasya* [Pāṇini 7.1.12] prescribes the substitution of *in*. Now, why does this not also occur in the case of *gargāṇāṃ bhaginī gargabhaginī*? Here too, the word *bhaginī* follows the word *garga*, which is a nominal stem (*prātipadika*), and since its final letter is *n*, the application [of the rule] would seem to be valid. To this he says: "Because of the governing heading of *pūrvapada*," and so forth.

From the rule *pūrvapadātsaṃjñāyāmagaḥ* [Pāṇini 8.4.3], the term *pūrvapadāt* is understood by way of *anuvṛtti*. Because the word *pūrva* is a relative term, it brings to mind that very thing in relation to which it has the status of being a "prior member" (*pūrvapada*), namely, the "subsequent member" (*uttarapada*). Therefore, although no specific nominal stem (*prātipadika*) is mentioned here, the substitution of *ṇ* for *n* occurs only for the *n* at the end of that nominal stem which constitutes the subsequent member. Thus, it is said: "In this case, it does not occur."

The word *hi* indicates the reason. Why? Because, due to the governing influence of the preceding rule (*pūrvapadādhikāra*), it is understood that the substitution of *ṇ* for *n* applies only to the *n* at the end of that nominal stem (*prātipadika*) which serves as the subsequent member (*uttarapada*). Therefore, in the case of *gargabhaginī*, the substitution does not occur. For here, the word-form *bhagin* is not the subsequent member; rather, the word is simply *bhaginī*, and that is not a nominal stem, because of the prohibition [stated in Pāṇini 1.2.45]: "That which is not an affix [is called a nominal stem]."
And its final letter is not *na*, but rather *ī*. [Objection:
But surely the usage *gargabhaginī* is also observed; if this is the case, that form would not be possible. To this he says: "But when," and so forth.
When the derivation is indeed *gargāṇāṃ bhaginī* (the sister of the Gargas), then the substitution of *ṇa* should not occur.

But when the word *gargabhaginī* is derived by first forming a genitive compound with the word *bhaga*—as in *gargasya bhagaḥ*—and then applying the suffix *iñ* in the feminine sense to express possession (*matvarthe*), then, this derivation being established, just as the substitution of *ṇ* occurs invariably in the case of *mātṛbhogīṇa*, so too should it occur here in *gargabhaginī*.
By the phrase "like *mātṛbhogīṇa*," he shows that even then, the substitution of *ṇ* does not occur by this very rule, but rather by another grammatical rule (*lakṣaṇāntareṇa*).

Therefore, this is what is meant: when such an etymological derivation occurs, then just as in the case of *mātṛbhogīṇa*—where, by [Pāṇini 8.4.2], the substitution of *ṇ* for the *n* of a taddhita suffix is obligatory due to the presence of *a*, *ṭ*, *k*, *p*, or *v*—the same applies here to *gargabhaginī*.
In this instance, the *n* belongs specifically to the taddhita suffix and does not reside in the subsequent member (*uttarapada*) of the compound.
For this very reason, one should not suspect that the cause (*nimitta*) and the effect (*nimittin*) reside in separate words.

Just as the rule *pūrvapadāt saṃjñāyām agaḥ* [Pāṇini 8.4.3] does not preclude the substitution of *ṇ* by means of that very restriction, so too has it been explained in that same place. If it were the case that the substitution of *ṇ* must occur for the *n* at the end of whatever nominal stem (*prātipadika*) constitutes the second member (*uttarapada*), then in forms such as *māṣavāpiṇī* and *māṣavāpinī*, the optional substitution of *ṇ* would not apply. Is it not the case here that the word *vāpin* alone is the second member, and not the form *vāpinī*? To this he says: "But in the case of *māṣavāpinī*," and so forth.

For here, since the compound is formed with the *kṛt*-affix ending itself—namely, by the rule *vāpin*—before the production of the nominal suffix (*sup*), the final sound of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) becomes *n*. This is because *vāpin* possesses the status of a nominal stem according to [Pāṇini 1.2.46]. Therefore, the substitution of *ṇ* (ṇatva) certainly occurs in this case. But how is it possible for the final sound of the subsequent member (*uttarapada*) to be *n* when the compound is formed before the production of the nominal suffix? For, by the rule [Pāṇini 1.4.14], the technical designation "word" (*pada*) is prescribed only for that which ends in a nominal suffix (*sup*) or a verbal suffix (*tiṅ*).
In that case, since there is no actual production [of a new entity], the status of being a "word" (*padatva*) is not possible here.
Why, then, is this specific distinction made—that "this is the subsequent word" (*uttarapada*)? There is no fault, because it is due to conventional usage (*rūḍhi*).

The terms "prior word" (*pūrvapada*) and "subsequent word" (*uttarapada*) are conventional terms; for when a compound (*samāsa*) has been formed, whatever word is established as the first part is known as the "prior word," and whatever is established as the latter part is known as the "subsequent word."

And that conventional usage (rūḍhi) is not possible only for the constituents of a compound that end in vowels (*subanta*); rather, it applies to some even among those that do not end in vowels (*asubanta*).

Why, then, would the designation of "prior member" (*pūrvapada*) and "subsequent member" (*uttarapada*) not be applicable here? By the words "in the same way here" (*tathātra*) and so forth, he confirms what was stated [previously]: "because of the governing rule concerning the prior member, [the suffix applies] to the subsequent one.
Since this is so, the meaning here is that the substitution of *ṇ* occurs only for the final *n* of the subsequent nominal stem (*prātipadika*), and not for any other.
And having established this, the inclusion of the term *num* was made.
Why, however, was that [term] included when, even with this meaning, *num* would not otherwise be established? To this he says: "For that," and so forth;
because *num* is prescribed for the *aṅga*.

In the case of *māṣavāpān*, since it is the entire compound (*samudāya*) that functions as the subordinate member (*aṅga*), the augment *num* is added to that which constitutes the whole compound as the subordinate member, and not to the final member (*uttarapada*). Consequently, the *num* does not belong to the end of the final member.
The intention here is that if the mention of *num* were not made [in the rule], then the substitution of *ṇ* (the *ṇatva*) would not occur.

If, however, the substitution of *ṇ* is prescribed for the letter *n* that constitutes the final sound of a nominal stem (*prātipadika*), even when it is not followed by another word (*anuttarapada*), then the mention of *num* need not be made at all, since the rule would be established simply by the phrase "of the end of a nominal stem" (*prātipadikāntasya*).

For in a compound such as *māṣavāpinī*, when the compound is formed, the letter *n* is indeed the final sound of the nominal stem. The term "it must be stated" (*vaktavyam*) means that it must be explained [in the commentary].

In this regard, the following is the explanation: the term *vā* [Pāṇini 8.4.10] is understood here, and it is a restricted option (*vyavasthitavibhāṣā*). Therefore, the substitution of *ṇ* for the *y* of words such as *yuvan* should not occur. In the example *āryayūnā*, there is a descriptive compound (*viśeṣaṇasamāsa*). The semivowel *y* is replaced by its corresponding vowel (*samprasāraṇa*) according to [Pāṇini 6.4.133], and the resulting form becomes the single substitute of the preceding and following sounds (*pūrvarūpatva*) according to [Pāṇini 6.1.108]. Similarly, in *prapakvāni*, [the same process applies].

This is a summary of the grammatical derivation (*gatisamāsa*). The purpose of the particle *ca* is exactly as stated previously. Regarding the form "vṛtrahaṇau," the suffix *kvip* is applied by [Pāṇini 3.2.87] *brāhṛbhrūṇa*.
In the word *kṣīrapāṇi*,
there is the elision of the vowel *ā* [by Pāṇini 6.4.64] following the roots *piba-* or *pā-*.
In the word *surāpāṇi*, [the same applies].

[The suffix] *ṭak* [is applied] after the root *pā-* (to drink) by Pāṇini 3.2.8 (*gāpoṣṭak*). Or rather, is it after the root *pā-* (to protect) as before? [In that case,] what [suffix] is it? Now, for what purpose is the mention of *ṇa* [in the rule], since the term *ṇaḥ* [from 8.4.1] continues to apply? If it is argued that it is for the sake of making it obligatory (*nitya*), one might say this: since *vā* ("or") is the topic under discussion, if the mention of *ṇa* were not repeated, an option (*vikalpa*) would result; therefore, the mention of *ṇa* is made again so that it may be obligatory. But this is incorrect, because the option is already established by the preceding rule alone.

In that case, would this rule not be obligatory simply by the force of its being newly introduced (*ārambha-sāmarthya*)? To this he says: "While *ṇ* is being carried over," and so forth. The re-mention of *ṇ* is for the sake of clarity regarding the cessation of the scope of the optional rule (*vikalpa-adhikāra*), because that [scope] lacks the indicatory vowel *svarita*.

For if *ṇ* were not mentioned, some person of dull intellect might think: "The mention of 'or' (*vā*) is indeed still carried over; and even while that is carried over, this rule will be obligatory by the force of its new introduction, whereas the subsequent one will be merely optional. The purpose of the introduction [of this rule] is to provide for cases where the second member of the compound has more than one vowel (*anekāc-uttarapada*).

The letter *ca* serves to carry forward [the rule] from "at the end of a nominal stem (*prātipadika*), before *num*, and in a case-ending" (Pāṇini 8.4.11). Consequently, there is no recurrence [of that rule] in what follows, according to the maxim regarding what has been carried forward (*cānukṛṣṭaparibhāṣā*). [Thus we have the example:
"two garments" (*vastrayugiṇau*).

> [[5.2.115]] *iti iniḥ* | Although one could have simply said *kaḥ*, the inclusion of *kumati* is for the purpose that [the suffix] should apply even when the word begins with a letter other than the *ka*-group (*kakāravarga*). Otherwise, by the rule *yasmin vidhis tadādvalgrahaṇe* (Vyākaraṇa-paribhāṣā 127), it would apply only when beginning with the *ka*-group. For example:
*dapana-vāpaḥ*, *kumbhasya vāpaḥ* = *kumbhavāpaḥ*, *māṣāṇāṃ kumbhavāpaḥ* = *māṣakumbhavāpaḥ*—[these are formed] by the suffix *ini* according to *ata ini-ṭhanau* [[5.2.114]].

In the case of *māṣakumbhavāpinau*, [the suffix] would apply, but in the case of *vastrayugiṇau*, it would not. Regarding the term *ṇopadeśasya*: that which has *ṇ* in its original instruction (*upadeśa*) is called *ṇopadeśa*. This is a *bahuvrīhi* compound with different coreferential members (*vyadhikaraṇa-bahuvrīhi*), because it functions as a descriptive indicator (*gamaka*). Alternatively, *upadeśa* means that which is taught or first uttered; thus, *ṇopadeśa* refers to that whose original instruction contains *ṇ*, and this is a *bahuvrīhi* compound with identical coreferential members (*samānādhikaraṇa-bahuvrīhi*).
Regarding "praṇamati": the root *ṇam* (Dhātupāṭha 981) means "to bow" and "to sound.
Regarding "prāṇāyakaḥ": [it is derived from the same root with the prefix *pra-*].

The root *ṇī* [is used] in the sense of "leading" (*prāpaṇe*) [Dhātupāṭha 901]; [the suffix] *ṇvul* is added, and it forms a *prādi-samāsa*. In the example "a region with a leader" (*praṇāyako deśaḥ*), because the prefix *pra-* is connected to the action with respect to the root *gam*, it has the designation of a preverb (*upasarga*) only with respect to *gam*, and not with respect to *nī*; for the rule prescribes the technical terms "motion" (*gati*) and "preverb" (*upasarga*) only with respect to that verb which the prefixes (*prādayaḥ*) are employed to qualify.
"What is the purpose of [the phrase] 'even in a non-compound'?"—

the sense is that since no specific distinction is mentioned even without this [phrase], it will apply both in compounds and in non-compounds. "[Because of the governing rule of the prior member]" and so forth.
The phrase "from a preceding member" (*pūrvapadāt*) is understood [from the previous rule].

The status of being a "preceding member" (*pūrvapadatva*) occurs in a non-compound (*asamāsa*). For the word *pūrvapada* is a conventional term (*rūḍhiśabda*) that was previously established; that very same term is carried over here, and it is possible only in a compound. Therefore, when it is stated "even in a compound," the implication is that it would apply only in a compound.

The particle *iti* is used here in the sense of a reason (*hetau*). Since this fault would occur if that [condition] were absent, the phrase "even when there is no compound" (*asamāse 'pi*) is stated in order to indicate the cessation of that preceding condition. By using the term "indication" (*dyotana*), he explains this: the cessation of that [condition] is not actually effected by this rule; rather, its mere non-existence is simply made manifest because it lacks the *svarita* accent.

This is what is meant: for the sake of making it clear to one of dull intellect who is unable to understand it in this way, it is stated that [the suffix] applies even when there is no compound (*asamāse*).
Regarding the word *praṇardati*: the roots *nard* and *gard* mean "to sound" (*śabde*; Dhātupāṭha 56, 57).

Even though it follows a vowel (*ac*), this is not an *ṇopadeśa* (a root taught with an initial *ṇ*) because of the formulation of an exception: "with the exception of *nṛt*, *nard*, *nand*, *nak*, *nāth*, and *ṇu*" (Mahābhāṣya). Thus, in *praṇiṇoti*, from the root *hi* [meaning 'to go' and 'to increase'—Dhātupāṭha 1257], there is *guṇa* substitution by [Pāṇini 7.3.84].
In *pramīṇāti*: [the same applies].
The root *mī* in the sense of "injury" [from the *Dhātupāṭha*, root 1476, belonging to the *kryādi* class] takes the suffix *śnā*. Thus, in the form *pramīṇītaḥ*,
there is the substitution of *ī* by rule [Pāṇini 6.4.113].

Now, how is it that there is the substitution of *ṇ* in the forms *prahiṇoti* and *pramīṇīta*, given that the rule *hinu-mīnā* refers to the specific forms [of the roots] themselves, and these two forms do not exist here once the modification of *guṇa* and so forth has been applied? Therefore, shouldn't it be only in cases such as *prahiṇutaḥ* and *pramīṇāti*? There is no fault, because the substitute (*ajādeśa*) possesses the status of the original (*sthānivadbhāva*), or because a form modified by a partial change remains essentially identical to the original.

Is it not the case that the status of being a substitute (*sthānivadbhāva*) is prohibited by the rule "that which is not established in what precedes is not like its original" (*pūrvatrāsiddhe na sthānivat*) [Paribhāṣā 48]? This very Paribhāṣā is indeed faulty; as it has been stated: "The fault of this [Paribhāṣā] lies in the cases of the elision of the first member of a conjunct consonant (*saṃyogādilopa*), and in the substitution of *ṇ* for *n*" [Vārttika on 1.1.59].

Now, why was it not stated simply as "after *him* and *mī*"? It is impossible to state it thus, because the *n* of the augment (*āgama*) would also be subject to change—as in *prahenardanam* and *pramīnardanam*.

The term *praheḥ* means "from *prahiṇoti*" (he sends forth). According to the rule *anyebhyo 'pi dṛśyante*, the suffix *vic* may also be applied even when there is no intermediate *a*-vowel (*avikaraṇa*) or the letter *n*. Thus we have *prahanardanam* and *pramīnardanam*.
[The form] *praheḥ* is derived from *prahiṇoti* by the application of the suffix *vic* according to [Pāṇini 3.2.75], followed by *guṇa* substitution.
*Pramīḥ* is derived from *pramīṇāti* with the suffix *kvip*.
*Praher-nardanam* is a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*) meaning "the roaring of the lion" (*pramyaḥ* = lion). Regarding the word *pravapāṇi*, it is the imperative (*loṭ*) form of the root *vapi*.
The augment *āṭ* is applied by the rule *āḍuttamasya picca* [Pāṇini 3.4.92]; thus,
we have *prayāṇi*.
The root *vapa* is listed in the Dhātupāṭha as "in the sense of reaching" (1049).
Regarding the form *pravapāni māṃsāni*:

it is a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "those whose *vapā* (omentum) is excellent. By the rule *jaśśasoḥ śi* [Pāṇini 7.1.20], the *śi* replacement occurs; by the rule *napuṃsakasya jhalacaḥ* [7.1.72], the *num* augment is added; and by the rule *sarvanāmasthāne cāsambuddhau* [6.4.8], the vowel is lengthened—thus we have *pravapāni*.
In this case, [the substitution] does not occur because of the mention of the *loṭ* [imperative] suffix.

If one asks, "Why then does it not occur by the rule *prātipadikāntanumvibhaktiṣu ca* [Pāṇini 8.4.11]?"—it indeed occurs in one alternative view. But surely the term *upasargāt* ("after a preverb") is still understood [from the previous rule], and the word *pra* is not a preverb (*upasarga*) in relation to the root *ni*.

What then? [The reading *apiṃ* is supported by the Prācīna-pāṭha. It is with respect to *api*; therefore, because it lacks the status of a prefix (*upasarga*), the [suffix] will not occur anyway—so what is the point of mentioning *loṅ*? This is not so; for in that case, it would not occur even in the root examples cited in the sūtra, since here there is the status of a prefix with respect to the verbal root (*dhātu*), but not with respect to *ani*. Therefore, by implication, the mention of "prefix" (*upasarga*) understood here as a recurring term is recognized as being intended to indicate *pra* and the others—as in the rule: *añ-nāsikāyāḥ saṃjñāyāṃ nasañ-cāsthūlāt* (Pāṇini 5.4.118).

In this rule [Pāṇini 8.4.17], the mention of *upasarga* is intended as an illustration (*upalakṣaṇa*) for *pra* and the other prefixes. Consequently, if the mention of *loṭ* were not present, the substitution of *ṇa* would indeed occur; therefore, *loṭ* is stated in order to prevent that. Now, even so, the mention of *loṭ* need not be made, because of the principle "when there is the mention of something meaningful, the meaningless is not included" (*arthavadgrahaṇe nānarthakasya*). For here, it is the meaningful word *āni* that is being mentioned, not the letter *i*; for in the example *pravapāni māṃsāni*, the word *āni* is not meaningless—what then? It is the vowel *i*. If this is the case, then this teaches us that the aforementioned paribhāṣā is not universally valid (*anityā*).

Since the term *in* is understood even when it is meaningless in the rule *tena* [Pāṇini 6.4.12], the lengthening of the vowel is established even in the case of *bahuvāgmīni brāhmaṇakulāni*. What is the purpose of pronouncing the vowel *ā* in *ān*? It is for the sake of ensuring that [the lengthening occurs] even for the bare word *ni* when the augment *āṬ* does not occur. But surely the augment *āṬ* must always occur, for there is no optionality in its prescription. If this is so, then this [mention of *ān*] indicates that the teaching regarding augments is not mandatory (*anityam*).

By this [rule], usages such as "śākaṃ pacānasya sukhā vai madhavan gṛhāḥ" ("To one cooking vegetables, the houses of Madhava are indeed pleasant") become established. The term *dhu* refers to those [roots] designated by the technical name *dhu*.

The term *mā* refers to the inclusion of *māṅ māne* (DhP 1142) and *meṅ praṇidāne* (DhP 961); however, it does not refer to *mīñ hiṃsāyām* (DhP 1476) or *ḍu miñ prakṣepaṇe* (DhP 1250) when they have undergone the substitution of *āt* [by P. 6.1.50], nor does it refer to *mā māne* (DhP 1062).

But surely, according to the rule "In the case of the mention of *ga*, *mā*, and *ā*, there is no distinction" (Vyāḍīyapāṭha 124), there ought to be a mention of all [the roots] alike. How then is the mention of only *māṅ* and *meṅ* obtained? This is not so; for here, by not placing the term *ghu* first—despite the presence of the rules "In a Dvandva compound, [the word with fewer syllables]" (Pāṇini 2.2.34) and "The word that begins with a vowel... (Pāṇini 2.2.32)—it is indicated that one should not proceed here out of compliance with the wording of the rule, but rather according to one's own intention.
Therefore, whichever [root] one intends, that alone is taken.

It is logical that, by following the indication of the intended meaning (*icchālakṣya*), only *māṅ* and *meṅ* are understood [as being included]. For this very reason, as an indication that one should proceed according to one's intention, even when the form *meti* is not possible due to the absence of the *āttva* substitution for *meṅ*, it is nevertheless indeed included—as in the example *praṇimayate*.
[The word] "he understands" (*pratipadyate*) [is used here].
The suffix *śyan* is applied because the root belongs to the *divādi* class; the *ātmanepada* ending is used because the root is marked with an *anudātta* vowel.
Regarding the form *praṇimimīte*:

the *ślu* replacement occurs because the root belongs to the *juhotyādi* class; there is reduplication by the rule *ślau* [Pāṇini 6.1.10]; the substitution of *i* for the radical vowel of the reduplicated syllable occurs by the rule *bhṛñām it* [Pāṇini 7.4.76], and the substitution of *i* for the penultimate vowel of the reduplicated syllable occurs by the rule *ata ādeḥ* [Pāṇini 7.4.70].
In *praṇiṣyati*,

there is the elision of the vowel *o* by [Pāṇini 7.3.71], and the substitution of *ṣ* for *s* by [Pāṇini 8.3.65]. In forms such as *praṇihanti* up to *praṇipsāti*, there is the elision of the suffix *śap* because they belong to the *adādi* (second) class of roots.
In *praṇiśābhyati*,
the lengthening occurs by the rule *śamāmaṣṭānāṃ dīrghaḥ* [Pāṇini 7.3.74].
In *praṇidegdhi*, [the same applies].

In the case of *diha* (Dhātupāṭha 1015), with the suffix *laṭ*, the elision of *śap* occurs as before; then, by the rule *dāderdhātorghaḥ* (8.2.32), there is the substitution of *gh*; by *śaṣastathordho'dhaḥ* (8.2.40), there is the substitution of *dh*; and by [8.4.53], there is the substitution of *jaś*-ness, resulting in the letter *g*. Someone might have the misconception that because *gad* and the others are specified in the locative case, and because the mention of "specification" (*nirdiṣṭa*) in [1.1.66] implies immediate proximity (*anantarya*), the operation should not occur here due to the intervention of the augment *aṭ*. To dispel this doubt, he says: "*aḍvyavāye 'pi*" ("even when there is intervention by *aṭ*").

But how, then, is the substitution of *ṇ* (ṇatva) obtained when there is an intervening vowel (*aḍ-vyavāya*) that is desired? Here, because the letter *ca* has the sense of an inclusive "and" (*anukta-samuccaya*), there is the rule: "After *ni*, *vi*, and *abhi*, even when there is an intervening vowel" (*nivyabhibhyaḥ aḍvyavāye api*), or according to the Vedic usage: "In the Veda, after *ni*, *vi*, and *abhi*, even when there is an intervening vowel. From this, either by the maxim of the leaping monkey (*maṇāḍūka-pluti-nyāya*), the term "when there is an intervening vowel" (*aḍvyavāye*) is understood to carry over (*anuvṛtti*). Now, an objection might be raised: since the augment *aṭ* is a part of the root *gad* and so forth, its inclusion would necessarily include the augment itself; therefore, how can there be an "intervention"? This is not so; for the augment *aṭ* is prescribed as belonging to the stem (*aṅga*), and the stem ends with the verbal suffix (*vikaraṇa*). Thus, there is indeed an intervention.
It is a part of the entire compound, not merely of the mace (*gadā*) and so forth;
therefore, it cannot be grasped by the mention of the mace and so on. The term "from a preverb" (*upasargāt*) [from Pāṇini 8.4.14] continues to apply.
And the status of being a preverb (*upasargatva*) belongs toward that [action] with which the words beginning with *pra* are connected.

The verbal root (*dhātu*) alone expresses the action, and it is with respect to that very root that prefixes (*prādi*) possess the status of *upasargas*. Consequently, when the root is brought to mind by the mention of the term *upasarga*, its specific qualifications—namely, that it does not begin with *k* or *kh*, and that it does not end in *ṣ*—are understood. Therefore, he says: "That verbal root which, in its original enunciation (*upadeśa*), does not begin with *k* or *kh*, and does not end in *ṣ*. Both the mention of the beginning and the end are for the sake of clarity, since the rule would have been established simply as "not *ka* or *kha*" and "not ending in *ṣ*" (*a-ka-khe a-ṣe*).

If the rule of initial inclusion (*tadādividhi*) or the rule of final inclusion (*tadantavidhi*) were to apply to all [elements] beginning with *a* and so forth, then one would have stated "akakhaṣe" after forming a *dvandva* compound of all of them. From the expression "akakhe aṣe," however, it is understood that by one [element] there is initial inclusion, and by another there is final inclusion. In this case, there might be this much doubt—namely, which [element] effects initial inclusion and which effects final inclusion—but that too will be resolved through the commentary (*vyākhyāna*).
The inclusion of the word "remainder" (śeṣa) is for the sake of clarity.
Furthermore, if there were an optionality regarding the mace (gadā) and so forth, the preceding rule would be rendered meaningless.
The inclusion of the term "instruction" (upadeśa) is likewise for the sake of clarity alone.

The term "upadeśe" (in the original instruction) can be carried over from the rule *śakyate taddhi* [Pāṇini 8.4.14] by means of the "frog-leap" (*maṇḍūkapluti*) maxim. Regarding the example *pranipinaṣṭi*:
the root *piṣlṛ* is used in the sense of "crushing" (Dhātupāṭha 1452).
And regarding the phrase "here there is a prohibition," etc.
Regarding the form *pratipekṣyati*:

if the rule *piṇeḥ ṣakārasya* [Pāṇini 8.2.41] were applied to change the *ṣ* to *k*, then because it would no longer end in *kh* or *av*, and because the term "in the original instruction" (*upadeśagrahaṇa*) were not present, the prohibition [of the substitution of *ṣ* for *s*] would not apply.
However, since that term is present, the substitution does not occur, because [the root *piṣ*] ends in *ṣ* in its original instruction (*upadeśe*).
"And let there not be [this] here"—
thus "prohibition" is required;
[the word] "one who prohibits."

In this context, regarding the root *viś* in the sense of "entering" (*viśa praveśane*, Dhātupāṭha 1424), once the substitution of *ṣ* has been effected by the rule *vraścādi-sūtra* [Pāṇini 8.2.36], because the root would end in *ṣ*, a prohibition [of the doubling of the nasal] would apply if the term "in its original enunciation" (*upadeśagrahaṇa*) were absent. However, since that term is present here, the prohibition does not apply. Furthermore, if "in its original enunciation" were absent, then in forms such as *praṇicakāra* and *pracicakhāda*, there would be no prohibition of the *cutva* (substitution of *c*) for the reduplicated syllable according to [Pāṇini] 7.4.62, because the root would not belong to the *akakhādi* group.
But when this [nasal] exists, it occurs. This nasal "n" is such that not even one of the [rules] beginning with Aṅ (A 6.4.72) applies.

Consequently, once reduplication has been performed, because the other "n" would be separated by the nasal of the reduplicated syllable, the rule would not apply; yet it is desired that it should. Therefore, this [sūtra] is commenced so that it may also apply to that [nasal].
In *prāṇiṇiṣati*,
by the rule *samy-aṅoḥ* [Pāṇini 6.1.9], which follows from *sam-iṭaḥ* [Pāṇini 6.1.2], the word *ni* is reduplicated.
In *prāṇiṇat*, likewise.

The suffix *luṅ* follows a root ending in the causative marker *ṇic*; there is the elision of *ṇic*. Because of the status of being "as if occupying the original position" (*sthānivadbhāva*) according to [Pāṇini 1.1.59], the word *ni-* undergoes reduplication.
Regarding the rule "what is established in what precedes is as if non-existent" (*pūrvatrāsiddhīyam*), etc.:

if this principle—namely, "that which is established in what precedes is as if non-existent except for reduplication" (*pūrvatrāsiddhīyam advirvacane*)—did not exist, then since the substitution of *ṇ* would be as if non-existent when reduplication was to be performed, the reduplication would have to occur first.

In this case, if this sūtra did not exist, then because of the intervention [of the vowel] by the first *na*, the substitution of *ṇ* for the second [nasal] by the rule *aniteḥ* [Pāṇini 8.4.19] would not occur; consequently, forms such as *prāṇiṇiṣati* would not be established.

However, since this [sūtra] serves as an exception (*apavāda*) to the rule *ata upadhāyāḥ* [Pāṇini 7.2.116], the substitution of *ṇ* is indeed performed by *aniteḥ* [8.4.19] due to its superior status (*paratva*).
Then, once the substitution of *ṇ* has been made and reduplication (*dvirvacana*) is applied, this form is established even without this sūtra.
If this is so, for what purpose is this [work] undertaken? To this he says: "But this," and so forth.
The *kṛtya* suffix is used here in the sense of possibility (*śakya*). The particle *iti* indicates the reason (*hetu*).
The word *tu* here is used for emphasis (*avadhāraṇe*).
Since that statement of an exception (*apavāda*) cannot possibly be relied upon, this sūtra is therefore commenced.

For if that [exception] were relied upon—[the reading in the Prācīna commentary is: "if that very thing were relied upon"]—then this sūtra would not need to be composed; consequently, it would not be understood that this statement of an exception does not apply to all cases.

If it were stated in this manner, then in the case of *aujaḍhat*, because the rule of *ḍha*-ness (*ḍhatva*) and so forth would not be established—due to the absence of what is "not established" (*asiddha*) in the preceding [rule]—there would be no doubling (*dvirvacana*) of the element *hat*.
However, when this sūtra exists, it is understood that the statement of that exception (*apavāda*) does not apply universally.
Consequently, in *aujaḍhat*, because the rules for *ḍha*-ness and so forth are not established, the doubling of *hat* does indeed occur.

For what purpose is the word *ubhau* ("both") used here, since the ṇatva of the preceding *n* is already established by the previous rule alone, while for the other [the subsequent *n*], it is due to the force of this new commencement? One might think: even without the mention of *ubhau*, the ṇatva of the *ṇakāra* would occur by this very rule even when there is an intervention [of letters]. However, the intention is as follows: if only "of the one with the reduplication" (*sābhyāsasya*) were stated, then just as the reduplication prescribed by [P. 6.1.2] is understood to be an exception (*apavāda*) to the first reduplication, so too here, the ṇatva of the second *n* being commenced even when there is an intervention such as *anaḍ* etc., would be understood as an exception to the preceding [rule].

The mention of "of that which has repetition" (*sābhyāsasya*) is for the sake of clarity, since it is already established by the word "both" (*ubhau*). Indeed, it is not possible for both *n* sounds to occur in the case of the root *han* when it lacks repetition. The genitive case in "of *han*" (*hanter*) is a partitive genitive (*avayava-ṣaṣṭhī*). [The rule continues with] "preceded by *at*" (*atpūrvasya*).
The term *atpūrva* is a bahuvrīhi compound meaning "that which has 'a' as its preceding member.
The letter *n* constitutes the referent of the other member of the compound.
[This refers to the rule] "it is struck" (*prahaṇyate*).

The root *han* is listed as "hana hiṃsāgatyoḥ" (Dhātupāṭha 1012). The ātmanepada ending is applied by [Pāṇini 1.3.13]. Regarding the form *pradhananti*, the penultimate vowel is elided by [Pāṇini 6.4.98], "gama-hana," etc.
The substitution of *k* for *h* occurs by the rule *ho hanter ñṇitsu* [Pāṇini 7.3.54].

Regarding the form *prādhāni*: this is the *luṅ* (aorist) tense; the suffix *ciṇ* is substituted for *cli* by the rule *ciṇ bhāvakarmaṇoḥ* [Pāṇini 3.1.66]; the *vṛddhi* strengthening occurs by the rule *aco ñṇiti* [Pāṇini 7.2.116]; and the elision of the letter *t* occurs by the rule *tiṅśit sārvadhātukam* [Pāṇini 3.4.113] followed by *ārdhadhātukaṃ śeṣaḥ* [Pāṇini 3.4.114] and *ārdhadhātukasyeḍ valādeḥ* [Pāṇini 7.2.35], which results in the application of *āḍ ajādīnām* [Pāṇini 6.4.72] and subsequently *āṭaśca* [Pāṇini 6.4.104]. Thus, the *t* is elided.
The mention of *śit* is for the purpose of indicating the verbal root (*dhātu*), not for the purpose of excluding the *yaṅluṅ* (the absence of the *yaṅ* suffix).

Regarding the example *prajaṅghanīti*: once the doubling (*dvirvacana*) has occurred and the changes to *cu* and *jaś* have been applied, the substitution of *ṇatva* will not take place because the following *n* is separated by the letter *j*.

However, because there is an *anusvāra* by the rule *pūrvasya tu* (P. 8.3.24), and because [the preceding vowel] has become possessed of an *anusvāra*, the word "of the preceding" (*pūrvasya*) is used instead of "from this" (*ataḥ*) for the sake of variety. Since the preceding rule would have made the application obligatory, this statement is for the purpose of providing an option. The inclusion of the word "optionally" (*vā*) is intended to indicate that the preceding rules are obligatory; otherwise, by the very force of commencing this new rule, its own application would be understood as obligatory, while the preceding rules—due to the continued application (*anuvṛtti*) of the term "optionally" (*vibhāṣā*) from P. 8.1.50—would remain optional.

But here, since the word *vā* ("optionally") is not used, those rules which fall between two optional rules are understood to be compulsory (*nitya*). Regarding this, [one might ask]: "In the rule *antaḥśabdasyāṅkividhiṇatveṣūpasargasaṃjñā vaktavyā* (Vārttika 71), because the designation *upasarga* is present for the application of the rule concerning *ṇatva*, would the *ṇatva* not already be established by [Pāṇini 8.4.22] itself? In response: although the *ṇatva* is indeed established by that very rule, this present *yoga* is commenced for the sake of the specific location (*adeśa*) and for the sake of *arca*.
Thus, we have *antarhaṇanam*; here, the suffix *lyuṭ* is used in the sense of an abstract action (*bhāva*).

The meaning is "killing in the middle. Because [the word *antar*] has the technical designation of a *gati* by [Pāṇini 1.4.65], there is a compound formation by [Pāṇini 2.2.18]. Thus: "a region where killing occurs internally (*antarhananaḥ deśaḥ*)."

The suffix *lyuṭ* is used here in the sense of an action (*adhikaraṇe*). Regarding the form *antardhanaḥ*, although it denotes a place, the substitution of *ṇa* for *na* occurs precisely by virtue of the grammatical irregularity (*nipātana*) in the rule "the place [called] *antardhana*. As for the word *ayanaṃ*, it is a form derived from the root *aya-* or *iṇ-* with the suffix *lyuṭ*.
Although this is already established by the preceding rule [8.4.28], this statement is made for the purpose of providing an exception regarding non-substitutes (*adeśa*).
By means of the particle *ca*, the mention of "substitute" (*ādeśa*) and the mention of "preverb" (*upasarga*) are drawn over from the previous rule.

This is for the purpose of preventing their recurrence in the subsequent rules. An *avagraha* is that which is recited by separating [words]; since it is both a verse-quarter (*ṛc*) and an *avagraha*, it is called an *ṛdavagraha*.
The words "from the vowel *ṛ*," "from an *avagraha*," and "from the preceding word" (*pūrvapada*) are three locative case forms used here in apposition.

By the force of the context, since the preceding word itself cannot be merely the vowel *ṛ*, he shows that the term "preceding word" (*pūrvapada*) refers to a portion of the preceding word when that portion is the vowel *ṛ*.
For words that apply to wholes sometimes also apply to parts, just as in the expression "the cloth is burnt," the word "cloth" refers to a single part of the cloth.

Regarding the term *nṛmaṇāḥ*: it is a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "one whose mind (*manas*) is directed toward men (*nṛ-*)" (i.e., benevolent toward men). The lengthening of the vowel [of the first member] is according to Pāṇini 6.4.14.
Regarding the term *pitṛyāṇa*:
it is a *yāna* because one goes (*yānti*) by means of it; the suffix *lyuṭ* is used in the sense of an instrument (*karaṇe*).
"The path of the fathers" (*pituryānam*) is a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*).
With the words "For here," etc., he demonstrates that the vowel *ṛ* is subject to the *avagraha* (separation).

Regarding the phrase "the mention of *avagraha*," etc.: if the mention of *avagraha* were not made, then [the rule] would apply to the vowel *ṛ*—provided it is not at the end of a word and is not separated (*anavagṛhya*)—but since this [mention] exists, it does not occur.
The *avagraha* occurs only at the end of a word (*padānta*), not at the end of what is not a word (*apadānta*).

Regarding this, the view of some is as follows: although the rule [6.3.114] *atra* continues to apply here, it is not connected [to the present context], because of the explicit mention of *avagraha*.
Therefore, the substitution of *ṇ* occurs only when the vowel *ṛ* is subject to *avagraha*, and not otherwise.

Others, however, hold this view: just as one who is not currently dancing is still called a "dancer" because he is fit for dancing, so too the syllable *ṛ*, even when not being elided (*avagṛhyamāṇa*), is called an "elision" (*avagraha*) because it is fit for elision. Therefore, what is meant is this: from the syllable *ṛ* that is fit for elision, the substitution of *ṇ* occurs; this being the case, since the rule for elision falls under the jurisdiction of *saṃhitā*, the substitution of *ṇ* occurs only in *saṃhitā*, and not from an elision (*avagraha*). [The term] *dhātusthaḥ* means "standing in a root" (*dhātau tiṣṭhati*); the suffix *kap* is applied according to [Pāṇini 3.2.4].
In the words *ūrvi* and *ṣvi*, there is the mention of the actual forms (*svarūpagrahaṇa*).
The term *nas* is a general designation for both the substitute *nāsikā* and the substitute *asmad*.

Consequently, in this instance, only the substitute *asmad* is subject to the grammatical operation (*kāryin*), not the other; for the other is impossible [to occur] after elements such as *dhātu*, *stha*, and so forth.
For the status of being the subject of the operation will belong to the substitute *nāsikā* in the subsequent rule.

Regarding "rakṣā naḥ": from the root *rakṣa* in the sense of "to protect" (Dhātupāṭha 658), there is the imperative mood (*loṭ*), ending in the second person singular. For the following word *naḥ*, which is the accusative plural of the pronoun *asmad*, the substitution of *nas* occurs according to [Pāṇini 8.1.21], and the lengthening of the preceding vowel occurs according to [Pāṇini 6.3.135]. Regarding "śikṣā naḥ": [the same analysis applies].

Is it from the root *śikṣ* in the sense of "learning" or "acquiring knowledge" (*dhātupāṭha* 605)? From such a root, the substitution of *nas* for *asmat* occurs, as in *uruṇaskṛdhi*. This is the imperative (*loṭ*) of the root *kṛ*; *sip* is the ending, which is replaced by *hi* according to *sehrapicca* [Pāṇini 3.4.87].
The substitution of *hi* for *hi* [the imperative suffix] occurs by the rule *śruśṛṇupṛkṛbṛbhyaśchandasi* (Pāṇini 6.4.102).
The change of the visarga to *s* occurs by the rule *kaḥkarat* (Pāṇini 8.3.50), etc.
Thus: *abhīṣu ṇaḥ*.
By [Pāṇini 6.3.134], there is lengthening; by [Pāṇini 8.3.109], *suñaḥ*, there is the substitution of *ṣ*.
Likewise, in the case of *ūṣrva ūṣu ṇaḥ*, there is lengthening of the vowel *u* by [Pāṇini 6.3.136], and the substitution of *ṣ* by [Pāṇini 8.3.109].

By means of the letter *ca*, the word *chandasi* is drawn over from [Pāṇini 8.4.25], for the purpose of excluding its recurrence in the subsequent rules. Since the substitute *naṣ* does not denote an action, it cannot function as a prefix (*upasarga*) with respect to that [verb]; therefore, this mention of "prefix" (*upasargagrahaṇa*) is understood to be an illustration (*upalakṣaṇa*) intended to include the group beginning with *pra*.
Regarding "prathaḥ":
as before, *nas* is substituted for *asmad*. Regarding "praṇasam": [the same applies].
The term *pragata-nāsikaḥ* is a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "one whose nose is protruding.

By [Pāṇini 5.4.119], the suffix *ac* is applied as a compound-final element (*samāsānta*), and the word *nāsikā* undergoes the substitution of *nas*. Regarding the rule "the *nakāra* situated within a *kṛt*-suffix which follows a vowel," this serves as a qualification for the *nakāra* in the word *adya*.
He shows, however, that [the suffix] is not *kṛt*.
If the qualifier were indeed *kṛt*, then in the word *pravapaṇam*, the substitution of *ṇ* would not occur, for here a *kṛt* suffix does not follow a vowel (*ac*);
yet the presence of the letter *n* is certainly possible.

If this were a qualifier of *kṛt*, then in rules such as [Pāṇini 8.4.34], the mention of *kam* and so forth would be purposeless, because there is no possibility of its application. For a *kṛt* suffix that is prescribed after these [roots] cannot possibly follow a vowel (*ac*), since they do not end in a vowel.
Therefore, it is appropriate that this be a qualifier of the letter *n*.

In order to show those *kṛt* suffixes for which the substitution of *ṇ* is possible, he says: "ana, māna, ānīya," and so forth. *Ana* refers to the substitute for *lyu*. *Māna* refers to the suffixes *āna*, *śānac*, *kānac*, and *cānaś*.

That which is prescribed by the rule *anīyar-tavyadādi* [Pāṇini 3.1.96]; that which is prescribed by *aniḥ* [3.3.112], *iniḥ* [3.2.78], *iniḥ* [3.3.170], *iniḥ* [3.2.78], and *āvaśyakādhamaṇryayoriniḥ* [3.3.170]—this suffix has its *anubandha* dropped. A *niṣṭhā*-substitute is that which is prescribed in the section beginning with *radābhyāṃ niṣṭhāto naḥ* [8.2.42].
Regarding "prayāṇam": [it is formed] from the root *yā* with the suffix *lyuṭ*, as before. Regarding "prayāyamāṇam": [it is formed] from the same root with the suffix *śānac*.
The *lakāra* (verbal suffix) is used in the sense of the object (*karman*).
[The suffix] *śānac* is applied, followed by *yak*, and then *muk* is added according to Pāṇini 7.2.82.
Thus, the form "prayāṇīyam" is derived.
The suffix *anīyar* [is applied] as in "aprayāṇiḥ" (one who does not go forth). [This is formed by] *nañ-aniḥ* [Pāṇini 3.3.112] when expressing an insult.
In the word *prayāyiṇau*,
the suffix *yuk* is applied according to [Pāṇini 7.3.33], *āto yukciṇkṛtoḥ*.
In the word *prahīṇaḥ*, [the suffix *kta* is applied].
The root *ohāk* means "to abandon" (*tyāge*; Dhātupāṭha 1090).
By [Pāṇini 8.2.45], the letter *t* is replaced by *n*; by [Pāṇini 6.4.66] and following rules, the substitution of *ī* occurs. Thus, we have the form *pramagnaḥ*.

From the root *ṭu masjo* in the sense of "cleansing" (*dhātupāṭha* 1415), the augment *num* is applied by [Pāṇini 7.1.60]. This *num* occurs before the letter *j*; for there is a rule stating: "They desire that *num* should be placed before the final letter of the root *masj*, for the purpose of preventing the elision of the *anuṣaṅga* (the nasal) and the initial consonant of the *saṃyoga* (consonant cluster). By the rule beginning with [Pāṇini 6.4.24], *aniditāṃ hala upadhāyāḥ kṅiti*, there is the elision of the *n* of this root, and by the rule beginning with [Pāṇini 8.2.29], *skoḥ saṃyogādyor* etc., there is the elision of the *s*.
The substitution of *ku* [for *v*] occurs by rule 8.2.30. Regarding the form *paribhukvaḥ*:
the root *bhuñj* is used in the sense of "crookedness" (*kauṭilya*) [according to Dhātupāṭha 1417].

Regarding the word "nirviṇṇaḥ": this is a form derived from one of the roots meaning "to lose" or "to be deprived of" (such as *vidī* or *vin*), and not from the root *vida* in the sense of "knowledge" (Dhātupāṭha 1064); for if it were that root, it would be marked with the *iṭ* augment (*seṭ*), which would result in the form *nirviṇṇasya*.

Since the suffix *as* does not occur here [in the expected form], it follows that an addition (*upasaṃkhyāna*)—meaning an explanatory rule (*pratipādana*)—must be made to establish the form *nirviṇṇasya*.

In this regard, the following is the demonstration: the term *bahulam* (diversely) is carried over from the preceding sūtra; by that, [the substitution] will occur even for a subsequent [element] that does not end in a vowel (*anac*). Since the previous rule would have made the operation obligatory (*nitya*), this [present sūtra] is commenced for the sake of making it optional (*vikalpa*).

If this were so, the mention of *vibhāṣā* (optionally) would be purposeless, as the optionality would be understood simply by the force of the commencement [of the rule]. This is not so; for the opposite [i.e., that the rule is not optional] might also be possible.

But this is a mandatory rule (*nityavidhi*), whereas the preceding sūtra is optional (*vibhāṣā*) due to the continued application of the term *bahulam*. By saying "that which is prescribed after a causative [suffix] (*ṇyanta*)," he shows that the word *ṇeḥ* functions as a qualifier of what is prescribed (*vihitaviśeṣaṇatva*).
And its purpose will be stated in the commentary [under the rule] *prayāpyamāṇam* (Pāṇini 3.1.26),
where the suffix *ṇic* is applied.

By the rule *artihyī* [Pāṇini 7.3.36], the suffix *puk* is applied. The letter *c* in the sūtra is for the purpose of drawing forward the option (*vibhāṣā*); by means of this, the subsequent rule becomes obligatory.
Thus: *prakopadham*.
The root *kup* means "anger" (*dhātupāṭhaḥ* 1233).
[Examples include] *prahaṇam* and *prohaṇam*. The root *īh* means "effort" (*dā|pā|632*), and *ūh* means "reflection" (*dā|pā|648*).

In this case, [the substitution] prescribed by [Pāṇini 8.4.29] occurs invariably. But how is it known that the mention of *hal* here is a qualifier of the initial [sound], and not of the final? To this he says: "of that which has *ij* as its penultimate," and so forth. Since all roots having *ij* as their penultimate are necessarily those ending in a consonant (*halanta*), the fact that they already possess the status of being consonant-final is established by the very presence of *ij* as the penultimate; therefore, the explicit mention of *hal* being made serves to understand it as a qualifier of the initial. [The word] "of a consonant" (*halaḥ*) is understood to carry over [from the previous rule].
He will state the purpose for its continued application later on.

Now, one might object: "In the previous rule, the mention of *hal* was a qualifier of the initial [sound], whereas here, what is the point of qualifying the final [sound]? To this he says: "By that," and so forth.

For there exists no root beginning with a consonant that is preceded by a consonant; this is established by implication. Therefore, by the continued application of the term *hal*, the rule of "specification by the final element" (*tadantavidhi*) applies.
Thus, it says "*sanumaḥ*."
The meaning is "together with the *anusvāra*. Why is this so? Because the mention of *num* is intended as an indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*) for the *anunāsika*.
Why, again, is it explained in this way? Because this rule (*yoga*) is for the purpose of restriction (*niyamārtha*).
And thus its status as a restrictive rule (*niyamārthatā*) holds only if the mention of *num* is intended as an indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*) for the *anusvāra*, and not otherwise.
A restrictive function is understood when there is nothing else to be prescribed (*vidheya*).
If the mention of *num* were merely expressive of *mum* itself and not intended as an indicator for the *anusvāra*, then it would not serve as an indicator for the *anusvāra*.

And this being the case, wherever [the doubling] is not established by the rule *yatra* [Pāṇini 8.4.29], there this [rule under discussion] must indeed be prescribed as an injunction. Where is it not established by that [rule]? In the case of the root *ivi* (meaning "to pervade," Dhātupāṭha 587) in the form *predhvanam*. Although the phrase *aṭkuṣvanumvyavāye 'pi* [Pāṇini 8.4.2] continues to apply here, nevertheless, it does not apply in this instance; for the mention of *num* in that rule is intended as an indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*) for the anusvāra, and here there is an absence of the anusvāra.
Therefore, for one who desires this [rule] to have a restrictive (niyamārtha) purpose, it must be understood that the mention of *num* serves as an indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*) for the *anusvāra*.
Thus, in cases such as *preṅkhaṇam*, although [the form] is established by [Pāṇini 6.1.90], this [present rule] results in being a restriction.
And that *num* serves as an indicator for the *anusvāra* is inferred from the composition of the extensive sūtra: *ijādeḥ sanumaḥ* [Pāṇini 6.4.73].

For if the mention of *num* were intended to indicate *num* alone and not as a secondary indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*) for the *anusvāra*, then one would have simply said "of *ivi*"; for there exists no other root beginning with *ivi* that ends in a consonant and possesses *num*. If it is argued that roots such as *ikhi* exist [and could be meant], we say no; because once the *anusvāra* has been applied, the *num* is no longer present. As in the example: *preṅkhaṇam*.

In forms such as *akha vakha*—where the root *ikhi* is recited with a guttural (*kavarga*) ending—the suffix *it* causes the augment *num* by Pāṇini 7.1.58. By 8.3.24, this becomes an *anusvāra*. Then, by 8.4.58, there is the substitution of the homogeneous sound (*parasavarṇatva*). However, because that substitution is considered "not established" (*asiddha*), this remains simply an *anusvāra*.
Thus we have *prombhaṇam*.
In the case of *ubha* and *unbha* in the sense of "filling" (Dhātupāṭha 1319, 1320), the *anusvāra* occurs as before.
But is this not already established by the rule *nanu ca* (Pāṇini 8.4.29)? For what purpose is this [new rule] commenced? To this he says: "In the case of what is already established," and so forth.
Regarding the term *pramaṅganam*:
in that very list of roots meaning "to go" (*gatyarthavarga*), the root *magi* is recited; in some places, however, the reading is *pramaṅkanam*.

This [rule] is to be understood as belonging to the root *maṅk* (*maṇḍane*, Dhātupāṭha 89). Now, an objection is raised: "A restrictive rule (*niyamārthatā*) applies only when there is nothing else to be prescribed (*vidheya*). Here, since the substitution of *ṇatva* is already optionally applicable due to the suffix *ṇi*, a mandatory *ṇatva* ought to be prescribed—according to the principle that 'when both a mandatory rule (*vidhi*) and a restrictive rule (*niyama*) are possible, the mandatory rule is superior' (Vyāḍiparibhāṣā 130). Therefore, why does this not serve as a mandatory prescription for the forms ending in *ṇi*? To this he replies: "Because of the governing influence (*adhikāra*) of the word *hal*," and so forth. The word *hal* is carried over (*anuvartate*) from the preceding sūtra, and it has been stated that this implies a rule regarding what ends in that (*tadantavidhi*). However, a verbal root (*dhātu*) ending in the suffix *ṇi* cannot end in a consonant (*hal*). Thus, the restriction does not apply here.

What then? [The suffixes] *sa* and *jha*. And that which is prescribed after a base ending in a consonant (*halanta*) cannot apply to one ending in a vowel (*ajanta*); therefore, in this case, the rule does not serve as a permanent injunction for the causative (*ṇyanta*) form.

But surely, once the *ṇi*-suffix is elided, even the causative base becomes one ending in a consonant, and thus—even under the heading "after a consonant" (*halaḥ*)—it would indeed serve as an injunction? This is not so; because we rely on the qualification of what has been specifically prescribed.

To refute this objection, he says: "A *kṛt* suffix prescribed after a root beginning with a vowel other than *i* or *ī*, which ends in a consonant, [is called *niṣṭhā*]. Thus, the term "prescribed" (*vihita*) is employed as a qualifier. Regarding the roots *ṇisi* (to kiss, DhP 1025), *ṇikṣi* (to be angry, DhP 659), and *ṇidi* (to blame, DhP 66)—since these have *ṇ* as their initial marker (*ṇopadeśa*), the suffix would necessarily be *niṣṭhā* by the rule *upasargād ṛti dhātau* (Pāṇini 8.4.14). This [sūtra] is commenced for the purpose of providing an option (*vikalpa*) where that necessity would otherwise apply.

If this is so, there is no need to mention the root *vā*; for would not the option (*vikalpa*) follow simply from the fact that two separate rules (*yoga*) are formulated? This is not the case; for the opposite might also be understood: "this rule is obligatory (*nitya*), while that one is optional (*vibhāṣā*).

[Should this not have been placed] immediately after the rule "upasaragādasamāse" (Pāṇini 8.4.14)? Its placement here is for the purpose of making known the obligatoriness of the preceding rule—namely, that those rules which fall between two optional rules are indeed obligatory. [Regarding the statement: "By the mention of *pū*, the mention of *pūñ* is to be understood."

The root *pū* read in the *Bhvādi* class as "pūḍ? pavane" (Dhātupāṭha 966) is not intended to be included here; rather, the inclusion of the one belonging to the *Kryādi* class is intended. How is it that when only "pū" is mentioned, the inclusion of *pūñ* alone is obtained? It is because of the separation of the rule (*yogavibhāga*) [in Pāṇini 3.3.104] into "kṛti" [following the previous rule].

Regarding the statement "the desired result is established through the splitting of the rule" (*yogavibhāgād iṣṭasiddhiḥ*, Vyākaraṇa-pradīpa 87), it means that by means of a *yogavibhāga*, the substitution of *ṇ* occurs specifically for the root *pūṅ*.

Thus, when the substitution of *ṇ* for the *n* situated in a *kṛt*-suffix following *pūṅ* has not yet been established through such a *yogavibhāga*, the reference is understood to apply to *pūṅ* alone by the principle of elimination (*pāriśeṣyāt*). This is expressed in the passage beginning with "and [the rule] regarding those ending in the causative suffix *ṇi*" (*ṇyantānāṃ ca*), and so forth.
Since the forms derived from the causative suffix (ṇic) are distinct words [from the roots], the rule does not apply to them;
therefore, an addition (*upasaṃkhyāna*) must indeed be made. This means that its formulation is necessary.

In this regard, the following is the demonstration: the rule should be analyzed by splitting it as *na iti* (not [the suffix] *ṇya*). By this, the suffix will not apply even to roots ending in *ṇi*. Nor, this being the case, would the mention of roots beginning with *bhā* be purposeless; for it serves to indicate that the preceding rule does not have universal application (*asarvaviṣayatva*).
In this way, the over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) is avoided. Examples are: *niṣpānam*, *duṣpānam*.

The substitution of *ṣ* for the *visarjanīya* occurs by the rule *idudupadhasya* [Pāṇini 8.3.41]. Here, the application is by the rule *iṇkoḥ* [Pāṇini 8.4.29], as in the examples *sarpiṣpānam* and *yajuṣpānam*.

This is a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*). While the rule *nityaṃ samāse* [Pāṇini 8.3.45] and its successors are in force following *it* [8.3.44], the substitution of *ṣ* for the *visarjanīya* occurs here by the application of *atra* [8.4.10].

Thinking that "padāntāt" is a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*), someone might object: "Why then is there no prohibition of *ṇatva* (the substitution of *ṇ* for *n*) here in the case of *susarpiṣkeṇa*, since the letter *ṣ* is at the end of a word (*pada*)? To him, he replies with the words "pade antaḥ," etc. For if it were a genitive compound, there would be a prohibition of *ṇatva*; however, this is not a genitive compound. What then? It is a compound formed by the rule "saptamī" [Pāṇini 2.1.40] through a split in the yoga (*yogavibhāga*). The compound means: "at the end when a word (*pada*) follows" (*pade parabhūte'ntaḥ padāntaḥ*).

Furthermore, in this case, the letter *ṣ* is not the final element of a word (*pada*), because the word *ka-* does not bear the designation of a *pada*. Therefore, the prohibition of *ṇatva* (the substitution of *ṇ*) does not apply here.

[The compound] "one whose clarified butter (*sarpiḥ*) is excellent" is a *bahuvrīhi*; the suffix *kap* is added by [Pāṇini 5.4.154]. Thus, the prohibition of *ṇatva*—which would otherwise have applied by [Pāṇini 8.4.14], "after a prefix, in a non-compound," and so forth—is established.

Regarding the word *praṇaṣṭaḥ*: the root *ṇaś* is used in the sense of "disappearance" (*adarśane*; Dhātupāṭha 1194). From this, the suffix *niṣṭhā* is applied. The augment *num* is added by the rule *masjinaśorjhali* [Pāṇini 7.1.60], and the elision of the nasal (*n*) occurs by the rule *ṇo naḥ* [Pāṇini 6.4.24]. The substitution of *ṣ* for *n* is effected by the rule *vraścādi* [Pāṇini 8.2.36]. Regarding the form *praṇaśyati*: [the same process applies].
The suffix *śyan* is applied because [the root] belongs to the *divādi* class.

Now, what is the purpose of including the mention of "the end" (*anta*)? For, even if it were stated simply as "of *naś*, *ṣaḥ*," the prohibition of *ṇatva* for that which ends in *ṣ* would occur through the rule of "specification of the end" (*tadantavidhi*), namely, "when there is a specification of *naś*" (Pāṇini 1.1.72). To this, he says: "The mention of 'the end'... He gives the example: *pranaṅkṣyati*.
As before, by [Pāṇini 8.2.41] *ṣatve*, there is the substitution of *k*.

Here, if the mention of "end" (*anta*) were not made, then since the state of ending in *ṣ* would no longer exist once the *k*-substitution had taken place, the prohibition would not apply. But because this [mention of "end"] exists, it applies even after the *k*-substitution has been performed.

For this indeed is its purpose: so that there may be a prohibition even when a *ṣa* (the letter *ṣ*) has occurred previously. This is stated as a prohibition of the *ṇatva* (the substitution of *ṇ* for *n*) which would otherwise apply by the rule "even when separated by *aṭ*, *kṛ*, *pū*, *āṅ*, *an*, or *uñ*" [Pāṇini 8.4.2].

In the case of "vṛkṣān," there is lengthening by [Pāṇini 6.1.102] and the substitution of *n* for *s* by [Pāṇini 6.1.103]. Since both the cause (*nimitta*) and the effect (*nimittin*) have been produced subsequently, the separation of both is understood; therefore, he says: "when there is a separation by a word (*pada*) between the cause and the effect," and so forth.

Regarding the expression *māṣakumbhaṣāpena*: "a jar of beans" is *māṣakumbhaḥ*; one who sows that [jar] is *māṣakumbhavāpaḥ* (by *[[3.2.1]]*). From that [compound ending in *-vāpa-*], the third case singular ending is applied.
Here, the substitution [of *ś* for *s*] is obtained by *[[8.4.11]]*.

Regarding the phrase "by means of the fourfold yoga" (*caturaṅgayogena*): here, the suffix *ṭac* is applied according to [Pāṇini 5.2.137]. It is a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "that which has four limbs" (*catvāryaṅgānyasya*). By that [term], there is a "fourfold yoga" (*caturaṅgayoga*), which is a third-case (*tṛtīyā*) compound according to [Pāṇini 2.1.32].
In the former case there is separation by the word *kumbha*, but in the latter case by the word *aṅga*.
Regarding the term *prāvanaddham*:

from the verbal root *ṇaha* in the sense of "binding" (Dhātupāṭha 1166), the suffix *niṣṭhā* is applied; then the rules *naho dhaḥ* [Pāṇini 8.2.34], *ṇatvam* [8.4.1], and *ṇo naḥ* [8.4.53] must be applied, and it is a *gati-samāsa*.

In this context, the word *ava* signifies separation (*vyavāya*). The application of the rule for *ṇatva* (the substitution of *ṇ* for *n*) occurs by the rule "after a prefix, even in a non-compound" (*upasargādasamāse’pi*, Pāṇini 8.4.14) and so forth.
The same applies in the case of "we go forward" (*pragānnayāmaḥ*).
The intervention, however, is caused by the word *gām*.
This is an example from the Vedic (Chāndasa) language;

for in the common language (*bhāṣā*), there is no usage of prepositions (*upasarga*) separated from the verbal root, nor is there usage of them before the root. Rather, since the term "in the Vedic" (*chandasi*) is carried over from [Pāṇini 1.4.81] to [1.4.82], by this rule [the preposition] becomes separated in the Vedic language.
In the word *go*, the vowel *o* undergoes substitution by *ā* according to [Pāṇini 6.1.93].
Regarding the rule beginning with *padavyavāye*:
