the meaning to be explained is that this prohibition which is stated regarding the intervention of a word (*padavyavāye*) applies when there is no *taddhita* suffix. This is the intended sense.
The meaning is that this is the explanation for that.
The meaning is that this is the explanation for that.

Regarding "this is the explanation for that": from [Pāṇini 8.4.33], the word *vā* ("or") is understood by the principle of the frog-leap (*maṇḍūkapluti*); and since that is a restricted option (*vyavasthitavibhāṣā*), there will be no prohibition in the case of a secondary derivative (*taddhita*).
Regarding the phrase "by means of fresh cow-dung": *gomaya* is derived from *go* (cow) with the suffix *mayaṭ* according to Pāṇini 4.3.145.
The term *ārdra-gomaya* is a *karmadhāraya* compound meaning "that which is both fresh and cow-dung."
There is an intervention by the word *go*.

And its designation as a "word" (*pada*) is established by the rule *padasaṃjñā cāsya* (P. 1.4.17). This [rule] states a prohibition of the substitution of *ṇ* for *n*, which would otherwise have been required by the rule *raṣābhyāṃ no ṇaḥ* (P. 8.4.1) and others.

The form *kṣubhnā* here is a mention of the specific form itself, not a mention of the verbal root; otherwise, the prohibition would apply even in the case of *kṣobhaṇam*. Thus, there is a prohibition.

If this is so, then in the case of *kṣabhnanti*, when the long *ā* is elided by [Pāṇini 6.4.112] *śnābhyastayor ātaḥ*, and in the case of *kṣubhnītaḥ* (variant reading: *kṣudhvanītaḥ*) when the *ī* is substituted by [Pāṇini 6.4.113] *ī haly adhoḥ*, the prohibition of *ṇatva* would not apply because the original form (*svarūpa*) is absent. This objection is invalid, because the substitute (*ajādeśa*) is treated as the original (*sthānivadbhāva*), or because that which is modified by a substitute is not different from the original (Vyāḍipāda 16). The phrase "these are subsequent words" (*uttarapadāni*) and so forth demonstrates the application of [Pāṇini 8.4.3] *pūrvapadāt saṃjñāyām agaḥ*.
In the word *harindī*,
the suffix *ṇini* is used in the sense of habitual action (*tācchīlya*).
In the word *harinandanaḥ*, [the suffix *ṇa* is used].
The compound is formed with a word ending in *tyuṭ*.

Similarly, in the case of *harinagaram* (or *girinagaram*, according to the *Kāśikā* and *Padamañjarī*), there is also a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*) with *nagara*. [Regarding the form] *narīnṛtyate*:
By [Pāṇini 7.4.90], the augment *rīg* is added to the reduplicated syllable, as in the case of *aṭkupvāṅ* [8.4.2] in *tṛpnoti*.
The root *tṛp* (meaning "to satisfy," Dhātupāṭha 2195) takes the suffix *śnu* by way of transposition (*vyatyaya*). Thus:
*parinartanam*, *parigahanam*.
The acquisition [of the designation *gati*] occurs by the rule *gatisamāsau* (Pāṇini 2.2.18). Compounds such as *śaraniveśa* and others, ending with *darbhānūpa*, are genitive (*ṣaṣṭhī*) compounds.
Regarding the term *anūpa*:

it is a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "that in which water has gone" (*amugatā āpo yasmin*). The suffix *a* is applied as a compound-final element (*samāsānta*) by [Pāṇini 5.4.74], *ṛkpūrabdhūḥpathāmānakṣe*. Then, the substitution of *u* for *o* occurs by [Pāṇini 6.3.98], followed by the lengthening of the homogeneous vowels (*savarṇadīrghatvam*). Regarding the rule "and the absence of *ṇ* after *ācārya*":
because of the word "and" (*ca*), there is also the presence of *ṇ*; thus, an option (*vibhāṣā*) is established.
Because the *vibhāṣā* (optionality) is fixed [by other rules], the substitution of *ṇ* occurs invariably according to the Teacher [Pāṇini].
Thus, we have "ācāryabhogaunaḥ. [The suffix] *kha* [is applied] by the rule *ātmanvī-ājāna-bhogottarapadāt khaḥ* [Pāṇini 5.1.9].
The application [of the rule] occurs by [Pāṇini 8.4.2], *aṭkupvāṅ*, and so forth. Similarly, in the case of *ācāryānī* as well,
the suffix *ṅīṣ* and the augment *ānuk* are applied by [Pāṇini 4.1.49], *indravaruṇa*, and so forth.

Considering that the particle *ca* has the sense of including what has not been explicitly mentioned (*anuktasamuccaya*), and thus indicates that [the list] is not yet complete, he says: "The *kṣubh*-class is an *ākṛtigaṇa*. [Note: *kṣudhvanītaḥ* is the reading in the *Prātipadika-pāṭha*. Regarding the rule "when there is a conjunction with the letters *ś* and *c*" and so forth: "conjunction" (*sannipāta*) means immediate proximity (*ānantarya*).
For example: *vṛkṣaśśete*.
By the rule *vā śari* [Pāṇini 8.3.36], the visarga is replaced by *s*;
that *s* is then replaced by *ś* by this [present rule].
Thus: *yajjati*.
In the root *masj* (meaning "to cleanse") [Dhātupāṭha 1415], the *s* is replaced by *d* according to Pāṇini 8.2.53, and that *d* is replaced by *j* by this [present rule].

One should not suspect that the *jaś*-substitution is non-applicable (*asiddha*) when the *ścutva*-substitution is to be applied; for in the rule 7.1.60, the form *majjeḥ* is cited with the *ścutva* already applied.
If [the present rule] were non-applicable (*asiddha*), this citation would be untenable.
In *bhṛjjati* and *vṛścati*,
there is vocalization (*saṃprasāraṇa*) by the rule [Pāṇini 6.1.16] beginning with *grah*. In *yajñaḥ* and *pāñjā*, [the same applies].

In the case of *yaj* and *yāc*, the suffix *naṅ* is applied by the rule *yajayāca* [Pāṇini 3.3.90]. Here, there are two subjects of transformation (*kāryin*), namely the letter *s* and the *tavarga* (the retroflex class), and likewise two causes (*nimitta*), namely the letter *ś* and the *cavarga* (the palatal class). Consequently, due to this equality, a correspondence based on numerical order (*saṃkhyātānudeśa*) would apply; why then does the *tavarga* not undergo substitution by the *cavarga* when the letter *s* comes into contact with the letter *ś*? To this he says: "By *śāt*" and so forth.
For prohibitions are always preceded by a prior possibility of application.

If there were a correspondence according to the respective order of the causes (*nimitta*), then, since a change to *c* for the *tavarga* following a *ś* would never occur, he would not have formulated the prohibition in [Pāṇini 8.4.43], "after *ś*" (*śāt*). Yet it has been formulated; therefore, this indicates that there is no correspondence based on numerical order.

Furthermore, although the rule "of *s* and *t*" (*stoḥ*) could have been stated in the locative case as "in *c*" (*cau*) for the sake of brevity, the statement in the instrumental case as "by *c*" (*ścunā*) is made so that the operation may occur even through a preceding conjunction (*sannipāta*)—as in *yajñaḥ* and *yācñā*.

For in the rule *saptanīnirdeśe hi* (P. 1.1.66), [the designation] would apply only to what follows, not to what precedes. Here too, the prohibition in *toḥ ṣi* (P. 8.4.42) is the indicator (*jñāpaka*) for the absence of the designation according to numerical correspondence (*saṃkhyātānudeśa*). If, even here, there were a designation according to numerical correspondence with respect to the cause, then in the case of contact with the letter *ṣ*, the substitution of *ṣṭu* (as in *ṣṭunā ṣṭuḥ*) would not apply to the *tavarga*. [The author] would not have made the prohibition in *toḥ ṣi*; yet he has done so. Therefore, that very fact is the mark here for the absence of designation according to numerical correspondence.

Regarding "vṛkṣaṣṭīkate": the roots *tikṛ*, *ṭikṛ*, *ṭīkṛ*, *ragi* [the reading *radhi* is found in the Dhātupāṭha], and *ladhi* have the meaning of "motion" (Dhātupāṭha 105, 103, 104, 107, 108). Regarding "peṣṭā":
the root *piplṛ* has the meaning of "crushing" (Dhātupāṭha 1452).

"Kṛṣīṣṭa, kṛṣīṣṭhāḥ"—this is the optative (liṅ) in the sense of benediction (āśis) from the root *kṛ*; for it, there is the suffix *sīyuṭ*, the elision of *ya* by [Pāṇini 6.1.66], *suṭ* by [3.4.107], and the change to *ṣ* by [8.3.59]; by this [rule], the change to *ṣṭu* occurs. "Agniciḍḍīnaḥ."

[From the *Dhātupāṭha*: *ḍīṅ* √*ḍī*, meaning "to move through the air" (968)]. Because it belongs to the *svādi* group, [the rule] "after [roots] beginning with *svādi*, [the suffix *iṭ* is inserted]" (Pāṇini 7.2.45) applies, resulting in the form *agni-ciḍḍhaukte*. [The root] *ḍhaukṛ* means "to go" (98). [Examples: *aṭṭati*, *aḍḍhati*.

The roots *atṭa* (listed as *atikramahiṃsayoḥ* in the Dhātupāṭha, no. 254) and *aḍḍa* (Dhātupāṭha, no. 254), as well as *adaḍa* (listed as *aniyoge* in the Dhātupāṭha, no. 348)—the inclusion of these two in this group with *t* and *v* as their penultimate vowels is for the purpose of hearing (*śravaṇa*) the *s* and *d* sounds after the elision of the final consonant (*saṃyogāntalopa*) when they take the suffix *kvip*. The phrase "not after *ān*" (*anām*) is a prohibition against the application of the augment *nuṭ* when it occurs in the genitive plural (*ṣaṣṭhībahuvacana*). The example given is *āliṭsāye*;
this is an illustration for the case when the augment *dhuṭ* does not occur by rule Pāṇini 8.3.29.
Regarding the form *īṭṭe*:
the root is *iḍ* in the sense of "praising" (*iḍa stutau*, Dhātupāṭha 1029).

Because it is marked with an anudātta vowel, the ātmanepada ending is applied; because it belongs to the *ad*-class, there is elision of the *śap* suffix; and by the rule *khari ca* (Pāṇini 8.4.54), the *ḍ* is changed to *ṭ*.

In the word *sarpiṣṭamam*, the suffix *tamap* is applied according to Pāṇini 5.3.55 (*atiśāyane tamap*), and the *s* is replaced by a retroflex (*mūrdhanya*) according to 8.3.101; thus it becomes *ṣ*.
Regarding the rule *ṣatṣu ṇaḥ*: [the *ṣ* is changed to *ṇ*].

By the rule *ṣaṭcatumryaśca* [Pāṇini 7.1.55], the suffix *guṭ* is applied; by *jhalāṃ jaśo'nte* [Pāṇini 8.2.39], the sibilant *ṣ* is changed to *ḍ*; and by *ṣṭunā ṣṭuḥ* [Pāṇini 8.4.45], the *ḍ* is changed to *ṇ*. Thus we have *ṣaṇṇavatiḥ*. This is a compound with elision of the second member (*uttarapadalopa*), formed according to the *śākapārthiva* class, meaning "ninety plus six."

The compound *ṣaṇṇagarī* is formed by the rule [Pāṇini 4.1.21], which prescribes the suffix *ṅīp* for the collective sense of six cities. In the examples *agnicicchaṇḍe* and *somasucchaṇḍe*, the suffix *kvip* is applied according to [Pāṇini 3.2.91]. [Note:
This example *somasucchaṇḍe* does not appear in the Kāśikā.]
The suffix *kvip* is applied by [Pāṇini 3.2.90].

Here, because of the mention of the locative case in the word "pi," the substitution of *ṣṭu* indeed occurs due to the presence of the complete combination—thus: *peṣṭā*, *peṣṭum*. In the cases of *viśnaḥ* and *praśnaḥ*:

from the roots *viccha* (to go, Dhātupāṭha 1423) and *praccha* (to desire to know, Dhātupāṭha 1413), the suffix *naṅ* is applied as before; then, by [Pāṇini 6.4.19], the letter *c* is replaced by *ś*.

Although this meaning—that there is no substitution of *c* for the *ś* following [the *taddhita* suffix] *yañ*—is obtained precisely from the rule of irregular formation (*nipātana*) at Pāṇini 3.2.117, nevertheless, this [present rule] is commenced in order to avoid the cognitive burden for those of dull intellect.
Alternatively, it has been stated that "irregular formations (*nipātanas*) may even be non-contradictory."

If this [rule] were not commenced, forms such as *praśnaḥ* and *viśnaḥ* would also be possible. By the phrase "of a word-final [consonant]" (*padāntasya*), the mention of "word-final" (*padāntagrahaṇa*) is carried over from [Aṣṭādhyāyī 8.4.42]; he shows that this, by implication, undergoes the status of being in the genitive case. In the examples beginning with *vāṅnyati*, once the substitution of the corresponding non-nasal (jaś) for the letter *g* has been applied according to [Aṣṭādhyāyī 8.2.39], its nasalized form (*anunāsika*) must be made.
Thus: *vāṅmayam*.
The suffix *mayaṭ* is applied by [Pāṇini 4.3.144].

Regarding the term *tvaṅmayam*, here too [the suffix is applied] by [Pāṇini 4.3.141], which begins with "In the case of *mayaṭ* and *vati*... [and so on]. [This applies when] "there are the letters *r* and *h* following a vowel (*ac*)."

By this, he shows that *ra* and *ha* are qualifiers (*viśeṣaṇa*). [The rule] "of the following *ya* and *ra*, except for another vowel" (*ānyāmuttarasya yaraḥ*) also indicates that *ya* and *ra* are qualifiers of *ra* and *ha*.
Regarding "barkkaḥ":
from the root *arc* in the sense of "worship" (*pūjāyām*) [Dhātupāṭha 204], with the suffix *dhañ*, and the substitution of *ku* for *c* and *j* by [Pāṇini 7.3.52] *cajoḥ ku ghiṇṇyatoḥ*.
Regarding "markkaḥ": [the same derivation applies].

*marci-* is a root belonging to the *sautra* class, meaning "to give. From that [root], the suffix *kan* is applied according to *iṇ-bhī-kā-pā-śyā-ati-marcibhyaḥ kan* (Pāṇini 3.2.171), and by *coḥ kuḥ* (Pāṇini 8.2.30), there is the substitution of *ku* (the guttural *k*).
Here, the letter *r* follows the vowel *a*, and the letter *k* follows that *r*; thus, it is a *yar*.
[The form] is *brāhṛā*.
In this case as well, the letter *ha* follows immediately after the letter *a*, and the letter *ma* follows that *ya*.
Regarding the form *apahnuve*:
here too, the letter *ha* follows the letter *a*; as before, there is the elision (*luk*) of the suffix *śap*, and consequently, there is the doubling (*dvirvacana*) of the following letter *na*.
Regarding the term *kiṃ hnute*: here, because the letter *ha* does not follow the vowel *a*, the letter *na* is not doubled. Regarding *kiṃ hralayati*.
The roots *hval* and *hral* mean "to move" (*sañcalane*; Dhātupāṭha 805, 806).

With the causative suffix *ṇic*, the rule "*jvala-hvala-hrala-namāmanupasargād vā*" (immediately following Dhātupāṭha 817)—where the reading in the Prāṅmukha-pāṭha is "*jvala-hnala-hvala*"—prescribes the designation *mit*. Consequently, by the rule "*mitāṃ hrasvaḥ*" [Pāṇini 6.4.92], shortening (*hrasvatva*) occurs. Regarding the phrase "*anacparasya*": *anac* means other than a vowel (*aca*). That which has an *anac* after it is called *anacpara*. Thus, it refers to [the root] followed by a non-vowel.

Regarding the example *daddhyatra*: here, the letter *dh* following the vowel [in *dadhi*] undergoes doubling when followed by the non-vowel *y*. Then, by the rule *jhalāṃ jaś jhaśi* (Pāṇini 8.4.53), the *dh* is changed to *d*.
Regarding "maddhvatra": here there is reduplication of the letter *dh*, which follows a non-*an* vowel. This is according to the rule "yaṇo mayaḥ," and so forth.

Here, the doubling of a *yar* (semivowel or spirant) following an *u* has been stated. However, since the rule for the substitution of a *yaṇ* for a semivowel does not apply when a *ma* follows an *anac* (non-consonant) and is followed by a vowel, this must be added as a supplementary rule (*upasaṃkhyāna*).
What, then, is the example here? To this he says: "Some," and so forth.
In cases such as *utkkā* and *valmmaukaḥ*, there is doubling of the *m* (ma) following a *k* (ka) or *y* (ya) that follows an *a* (a). For example: *dadhyyatra* and *madhvvatra*.

After the letter *dh*, there is reduplication of the following semivowel (*yaṇ*) and the letter *y*. [This is governed by] rules such as "after a sibilant (*śara*), the *khaya* [consonants]... and so forth.
In the forms *stthālau* and *stthātā*, there is reduplication of the letter *th*, which is a *khaya* following a sibilant (*śara*). In the form *vatssaḥ*, [there is reduplication of the *s*].

After the letter *takāra* (*t*), when followed by a *khaya*, there is doubling of the *śara* *sakāra* (*s*) and *kakāra* (*k*). For example: *ikṣūn*, *ikṣvīram*. After the letter *kakāra* (*k*), when followed by a *khaya*, there is doubling of the *śara* *ṣakāra* (*ṣ*).
Regarding the term *apsarāḥ*: after the letter *p*, there is reduplication (*dvirvacana*) of the sibilant (*śara*) following the *khaya* sounds;
[and] "two [consonants] at the end of a word" (*avasāne dve*), and so forth.
And [the phrase] "he said" (*avaci ca*) is appropriate by resorting to a *paryudāsa* (exclusion).
However, in the case of a *prasajya-pratiṣedha* (absolute negation), this could have been avoided by continuing the word *vā* from [Pāṇini 8.1.45].
This is not so.

For if it were a *prasajya-pratiṣedha* (absolute negation), the status of the sūtra as an injunctive statement (*vidhi-vākya*) would not be tenable; and if that were so, would there not be reduplication by some [other rule]? Therefore, it is untenable that the status of this [sūtra] as an injunctive statement should be inferred from a prohibitive statement. Furthermore, when a *prasajya-pratiṣedha* occurs, one resorts to *paryudāsa* (exclusion) for fear of the excessive complexity of the understanding. [Note: In the printed *Kāśikā* and likewise in the *Padamañjarī*, the word *ādinī* is taken as ending in the feminine suffix *ṅīp*. This is a locative absolute. Hence he says: "When *ādi* follows."
Regarding the term "putrādinī": it means "one whose habit is to eat her own sons," where the suffix *ṇini* is used in the sense of habitual action (*tācchīlye*).
Thus, "putrādinī" refers to a "crocodile."
This is an explanation of the true state of affairs, not a mere reproach. [The point is:

"It should be stated that 'when followed by *tatpara*'"—meaning that since the word *ādinī* follows the word *putra*, the rule of reduplication (*dvirvacana*) does not apply there; this is how the meaning should be explained.

In this regard, the following is the explanation: the word "na" (not) is separated [from the preceding rule] by *yogavibhāga* (splitting the rule), so that [the doubling] will not apply when followed by *tatpara*.

Regarding the phrase "or when followed by *hata*" and so forth, the meaning is that it should be explained as having the sense that the doubling of the word *putra* does not occur when followed by the words *hata* and *jagdha*.
The explanation, however, should be made by carrying over the mention of *vāc* from the previous rule, or by resorting to a split of the yoga (*yogavibhāga*) with the word "not" (*na*).
Nor does this result in an undesirable option (*vikalpa*) even in the case of *puttrādinī*,
because we understand the rule to be a fixed option (*vyavasthitavibhāṣā*).

What is both killed and eaten? That which is "killed-eaten" (*hatajagdha*). And that which is "other than" (or "supreme over") the killed-eaten is "killed-eaten-supreme" (*hatajagdhapara*); [the term refers] to that which is *hatajagdhapara*. In the examples "putrahatī" and "putrajagdhī," the analysis is a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "one by whom a son has been killed" (*putro hataḥ*) or "one by whom a son has been eaten" (*putro jagdhaḥ*). The suffix *ṅīṣ* is applied according to the rule beginning with "asvāṅgapūrvapadāt" (Pāṇini 4.1.53).

Regarding the passage beginning with "the *caya* [consonants] are the second," the term *caya* is a genitive of location (*sthāna-ṣaṣṭhī*), meaning that *kh*, *cha*, *ṭh*, *th*, and *ph* are the "second" [class members].
Their status as "second" occurs in relation to the first consonants of their respective classes.
Regarding "vapsaḥ": when *c* (the *ca*-class) follows *t*, and *ś* or *s* follows, the second *th* is substituted for the *t*. Regarding "khṣīram": [this is formed by the same rule].
The doubling of the letter *k* before the letter *v*, when followed by a sibilant (*śar*), results in a second *s*:
as in *apsarāḥ*.
The doubling of the letter *p* before the letter *s*, when followed by a sibilant (*śar*), results in a second *ph*: as in *karvati*.
The root *kṛṣ* is used in the sense of "plowing" (*vilekhana*) [Dhātupāṭha 990].
Regarding the form *varvati*:
the roots *pṛṣ*, *vṛṣ*, and *mṛṣ* are used in the sense of "sprinkling" (*secana*) [Dhātupāṭha 705–707].
Regarding the word "ādarśaḥ": the root *dṛś* is used in the sense of "seeing" (Dhātupāṭha 988). The suffix *dhañ* is applied here in the sense of the locus (*adhikaraṇe*).

Regarding the term *darśaḥ* [it is absent in the Kāśikā], for this very reason the suffix *dhañ* is applied in the sense of an instrument (*karaṇe*). In cases such as *indraḥ*, there is the application of the rule *anaci ca* [Pāṇini 8.4.46]. Thus:
*indraḥ*, *candraḥ*, *mandraḥ*.
The roots are: *idi paramārye* (Dhātupāṭha 63), *cadi āhlāde* [and *dīptau ca*] (Dhātupāṭha 68), and *madi stutimodadasyapnakāntigatiṣu* (Dhātupāṭha 13).
The suffix *rak* is applied according to the rule *sphāyitañci* etc.
(Pāṇini 6.1.27), as in the examples *rāṣṭraḥ* and *bhrāṣṭraḥ* [the forms *rāṣṭram* and *bhrāṣṭram* according to the Kāśikā].
The roots *rājṛ* and *bhrājṛ* mean "to shine" (*dīptau*) [as listed in the Dhātupāṭha as 822 and 823].
The suffix *ṣṭran* is added according to the rule *sarvadhātubhyaḥ ṣṭran* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 3.2.178).
The substitution of *ṣ* for *s* occurs by the rule *vrācādi-sūtra* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 8.2.36).
The mention of Śākaṭāyana is for the sake of honor.
This rule is indeed obligatory;
otherwise, since it would already be established by the subsequent sūtra, its commencement would be purposeless. This commencement is for the sake of [the forms] beginning with *atri*.
In examples such as *arkaḥ*, there is the application [of the rule] by [Pāṇini 8.4.46].

Although the [desired result] would be established even for words beginning with *atri* simply by the force of the initial formulation [of the prohibition], the inclusion of the term *sarvatra* ("everywhere") is for the purpose that this prohibition should apply even when the previous [rule, Pāṇini 8.4.46], is applicable—so that the prohibition may occur even when [the condition of] that [previous rule] is met.

If that [term *sarvatra*] were absent, then due to proximity (*pratyāsatti*), this prohibition would apply only to the application of [Pāṇini 8.4.46] itself, namely "also when *a* does not follow" (*anaci ca*).

The mention of Śākalya is for the sake of honor, not for the sake of providing an option (*vikalpa*). Both a positive injunction (*vidhi*) and a prohibition (*pratiṣedha*) are stated by means of two rules; here, an option will arise by virtue of the very context (*sāmarthya*); otherwise, there would be no scope for the injunction. This undertaking is for the purpose of making [the rule] obligatory (*nitya*).
In this case, although the [application of the rule] is established by the very force of the commencement [of the treatise], the mention of the Teacher (ācārya) is for the sake of honor.
In examples such as *dātadram*, there is the application of [Pāṇini 8.4.46]: *anaci ca*. Regarding *labdhā* and so forth:
the suffixes *tṛc*, *tumun*, and *tavya* are applied after the root *labh*.

By the rule *iti dhakāre jhaśi* [Pāṇini 8.4.53], the *jaś*-ness of the letter *bha* results in the letter *ba*. Thus, we have *degdhā* [the Kāśikā reads *dogghā*]. The root *diha* (meaning "to increase") is listed as number 1015 in the Dhātupāṭha; by the rule *dāderdhātordhaḥ* [Pāṇini 8.2.32], the letter *ha* is replaced by the letter *dha*.

Regarding the term *boddhā*: by the rule *jaśtva*, the letter *dh* becomes *d*. Because of the letter *ca*, the inclusion of *ca* is carried over [from the previous rule], and therefore its application does not continue in what follows. Regarding *cikhaniṣati*: [this is formed from the root *khan* with the desiderative suffix].

From the root *khan* with the suffix *san*: reduplication, the substitution of the remaining initial consonant (*halādiśeṣa*), and by [Pāṇini 7.4.62], the change of *kh* to *ch*—the letter *ch*; in its place, the letter *c*. Thus:
*cicchitsati* (or *cicchitsati* as read in the Kāśikā, Pradīpa, and Uddyota).
From the root *chid* with the suffix *san*: reduplication, the insertion of *tuk* by [Pāṇini 6.1.71], and the change of *ch* to *c*.

Regarding "ṭhiṭhakārayiṣati": the suffix *ṇic* is applied according to the rule "that which one does, that which one describes" (*tatkaroti tadācaṣṭe*) [Dhātupāṭha 200, 201], meaning "he describes the sound ṭha. Due to the treatment as if it were the superlative suffix *iṣṭhan*, there is elision of the final vowel (*ṭilopa*). Then follows the desiderative suffix *san*, the augment *iṭ*, *guṇa* strengthening, and the replacement with *ay*.
Thus we have "tiṣṭhāsasi."
> [[7.4.61]] *śeṣaḥ* (remainder). In the case of *pipha-kārayiṣati*, it has the same grammatical derivation as *ṭiṭha-kārayiṣati*.

However, this is the distinction: the suffix *ṇic* is applied after the word *phakāra*. According to the rule "those that move in the original form (*prakṛti*) remain in the original form (*prakṛticaraḥ*)," the meaning is that the substitutes (*ādeśas*) have the same form as the original (*sthānin*), being non-different from it; this is for the purpose of preventing the application of the *jaś*-rule, by the operation of the principle that "a grammatical rule applies like Parjanya (the rain-god, i.e., universally). Thus, "those moving in the original form" (*prakṛticaraḥ*) refers to those whose form is identical to the original.
In *cicīṣati*,
there is lengthening according to [Pāṇini 6.4.16].
In *titīrṣati* [this is not recorded in the Kāśikā].

By the rule *ṛta iddhātoḥ* [Pāṇini 7.1.100], there is the substitution of *it* (short *i*) and the replacement by *ra*; then, by *hali ca* [8.2.77], there is lengthening. Thus we have *jijhakārayiṣati*. This has the same grammatical derivation as *ṭiṭhakārayiṣati*.
In this context, there is a specific rule regarding the suffix *ṇic* applied to the verbal root *jhakāra*.
Thus, we have the form *jighatsati*.

Here, the desiderative suffix *san* is added to the root *ad*, and by the rule *luṅ-sanorghaslṛ* [Pāṇini 2.4.37], the substitute *ghaslṛ* is applied. As before, the semivowel of the reduplicated syllable undergoes *cutva* (becoming a sibilant), resulting in the letter *jh*; this then undergoes *jaśtva* (becoming a voiced stop), resulting in the letter *j*. Finally, by the rule *saḥ syārdhadhātuke* [Pāṇini 7.4.49], the *s* of the suffix is replaced by *t*.
Regarding the form *ḍuḍhaukiṣate*:
it is the desiderative (*san*) of the root *ḍhauk*.
According to the rule "the unaspirated stops (*jaś*) of the base remain unaspirated stops (*jaś*)," [the *kh* becomes *g*].

Is this for the purpose of *carva* (reversion) as before? *Jaśaḥ prakṛtijaśaḥ* means those *jaś* sounds which, by their very nature (*prakṛtyā*), are non-different in form from the original (*sthānin*).
[The example is] *jijaniṣate*.
The middle voice (*ātmanepada*) is applied by the rule *pūrvavat sanaḥ* [Pāṇini 1.3.62].
Regarding "bubudhe":
because it has an anudātta indicatory vowel (it), the ātmanepada ending is applied; by [Pāṇini 3.4.81], the substitution of *e* for *a* occurs.
Regarding "dadau": [the same rule applies].
By [Pāṇini 7.1.34], *auttva* (the substitution of *au*) occurs.
Regarding *ḍiḍe*:

the root *ḍīṅ* means "to move through the air" (Dhātupāṭha 968). As before, there is an elision of the initial vowel (*ādeśa*), and by the principle of *sthānivadbhāva*, *ḍī* undergoes reduplication. In *yuyutsate*, the suffix *san* is added to the root *yudh*; the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) applies by [Pāṇini 1.3.62], "as before, after *san*."

Regarding the form *āripsate*: the suffix *san* is added by [Pāṇini 3.1.7] *ratrilabhibhyāṃ san*. Then, by [Pāṇini 7.4.54] *sani mīmā*, the substitution of *i* occurs; subsequently, the letter *s* is elided by [Pāṇini 8.2.29] *skoḥ saṃyogādyoranta ca*.

In this context, there is the elision of the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*) according to [Pāṇini 7.4.58] *atra lopo'bhyāsasya*. The particle *ca* (and) has the sense of conjunction; it indicates that the *cara* substitutes do not occur only for the reduplicated syllable, but also before a *khar* (voiceless consonant). If the particle *ca* were absent, there might arise the misconception of some dull-witted person that the *cartva* (substitution of *c*, *ṭ*, *t*, *t*, *p*) prescribed immediately [in the preceding rule] would apply only when a *khari*-beginning suffix follows the reduplicated syllable—as in *tiṣṭhāsatī* and so on—and not even in cases such as *cakhāda*. Therefore, since the substitution of *jaś* (voiced unaspirated stops) would be obligatory by [Pāṇini 8.2.39], these *cara* substitutions are prescribed as optional in the *avasāna* (pause/final position).

Because of the mention of the word *vā* (or), in some instances, *jaś*-ness (*jaśtva*) indeed occurs as well. The term *aṇaḥ* is a technical abbreviation (*pratyāhāra*) formed by the preceding letter *ṇ*;
otherwise, for the sake of avoiding ambiguity, one would have used *acaḥ*. Furthermore, there are no *hal* (consonants) at the end of a word that are *aṇ*.

In the case of *dīrgha*, [the form] is *madhu* because of the rule *svamornapuṃsakāt* [Pāṇini 7.1.23], which prescribes the elision (*luk*) of the suffixes *su* and *am*. In the case of *agni* and *vāyu*, [the forms are *agnī* and *vāyū*].

The vowel lengthening occurs by [Pāṇini 6.1.102]. The designation *pragṛhya* is applied by [Pāṇini 1.1.11]: "A dual ending with *ī*, *ū*, or *e* is called *pragṛhya*. Regarding the examples beginning with *śaṅkitā*:

from the roots *śaki* (to suspect) [Dhātupāṭha 86], *uchi* (to glean) [Dhātupāṭha 215], *kuḍi* (to burn) [Dhātupāṭha 270], *ṭunadi* (to rejoice) [Dhātupāṭha 67], and *kapi* (to move) [Dhātupāṭha 375], the suffixes *tṛc* and others are added. Because they are marked with the indicatory letter *it*, the augment *num* is inserted; then, by [Pāṇini 8.3.24], an *anusvāra* is substituted. This *anusvāra* is then replaced by a homogeneous sound (*parasavarṇa*) according to the present rule.

Regarding the forms *kurvanti* and *kṛṣanti*: from the root *kṛ*, and from the root *kṛṣ* belonging to the Taudādika class (*kṛṣa vilekhane*, Dhātupāṭha 1286), there is the substitution of *jhi* for the suffix *laṭ*. When the *n* of *jhi* becomes an *anusvāra*, and that *anusvāra* is replaced by a nasal homogeneous with the following sound (*parasavarṇa*), i.e., *n*, the rule *aṭkupvāṅnumvyavāye ’pi* (Pāṇini 8.4.2) would require the change of *k* to *ṇ*. Why does this not occur? To this he says: "In this case," and so forth.

Does the substitution of *ṇ* (ṇatva) occur here before or after the anusvāra? First, it does not occur before; because when the anusvāra is to be applied, the substitution of *ṇ* is considered non-existent (*asiddha*), therefore the anusvāra itself is applied to the *n* first.

Even after the *n* has been changed to its corresponding homogeneous sound (*parasavarṇa*) by the rule for *parasavarṇa*, [the substitution of *ṇ*] still does not occur; because when the substitution of *ṇ* is to be applied, that which occupies the place of the anusvāra is considered non-existent. [This refers to the phrase] "by the corresponding homogeneous sound."
The meaning is: "by means of the grammatical rule intended for the purpose of *parasavarṇa*.
Does it follow that because of being for that purpose, it receives that designation?
Yes; as in the case of a jasmine flower intended for a lamp being called a "lamp."

The word "punaḥ" means "after the occurrence of the anusvāra. By the phrase beginning with "evam," the Bhāṣya states that the *ṇatva* (the substitution of ṇ for n) is bypassed by the *n* which has become an *anusvāra*; thus, the bypassing of *ṇatva* is predicated of the *n* that has turned into an *anusvāra*.
Is that [the substitution] itself unestablished? He shows that the substitution of *ṇ* for the nasal *n*—which is a *parasavarṇa*—does not take place, by saying "it transcends.
The meaning is that it exists having transcended [the preceding condition].

Regarding the form *ārkrasyate*: from the root *kram* preceded by the prefix *ā*, the suffix *luṭ* is applied, and by [Pāṇini 1.3.40], the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) is used. Thus we have *ācikraṃsate* (the Kāśikā reads *ācikraṃsyate*).

The ātmanepada [suffix] is applied by [Pāṇini 1.3.62]: *pūrvavat sanaḥ*. The mention of the word "optionally" (*vā*) is for the purpose of making known that the preceding rule is compulsory; this is because, considering that those rules which fall between two optional rules are compulsory. If the word "optionally" were not included, the opposite might be suspected—that the preceding rule is optional, while this present rule is compulsory by virtue of its very formulation. [Example: *utthātā* ("one who will rise").

By the rule *ādeḥ padasya* [Pāṇini 1.1.53], the initial sibilant (s), which is a voiceless aspirate (*mahāprāṇa*), is replaced by a dental stop (th) of the same class as the preceding sound. By the rule *khari ca* [Pāṇini 8.4.54], this *th* is changed to *t*. Then, by the rule *anaci ca* [Pāṇini 8.4.46], the preceding *t* undergoes doubling (*dvirvacana*). According to the rule *vā* [Pāṇini 8.4.65], one of the two is optionally elided. Thus we have *uttambhitā*. The root *stambh* is a Vedic (sautra) verbal root.

Regarding the term *utsnātā*: the root *ṣṇā* is used in the sense of "cleansing" (*śauce*; Dhātupāṭha 1052). The inclusion of the word *pūrva* is for the purpose of precluding the *parasavarṇa* [substitution]. [The rule applies to] that which is preceded by *ud*, and so forth.

When the rule for *pūrvasavarṇa* (the substitution of the preceding vowel) is to be applied, there must be an addition (*upasaṃkhyāna*)—meaning an explanatory statement—regarding the word *skand* in the Vedic language (*chandas*). The demonstration of this is as follows: by means of transposition (*vyatyaya*), the *pūrvasavarṇa* will occur for the vowel following *ud-* when *skand* is used in the Vedic context. For example: *utkanda* [the form *utkandaḥ* according to the Kāśikā].
The imperative suffix *sip* undergoes the substitution of *hi* by [Pāṇini 3.4.87], and that *hi* is elided by [Pāṇini 6.4.105]. Regarding the rule "and in the case of disease" (*roge ca*), etc.:

the meaning is that this should be explained as having the sense that, without distinction between Vedic and common usage, when "disease" is to be expressed, there is a substitution of the homogeneous vowel with the preceding one for the root *skand* following *ud*.

In this regard, the explanation is as follows: it will be formed according to the rule *pṛṣodarādīni yathopadiṣṭam* [Pāṇini 6.3.109]. Regarding the word *utkandakaḥ*, the suffix *ṇvul* is applied by the rule *rogākhyāyāṃ ṇvul bahulam* [Pāṇini 3.3.108].
*Bālamano ramā*: "In all cases, according to Śākalya" (Pāṇini 8.4.61). The word "not" (*na*) is understood to carry over [from the previous rule].
The meaning is that wherever reduplication has been prescribed, in those instances, according to the opinion of the sage Śākalya, reduplication does not take place.
"According to some teachers, [the doubling does not occur] after a long vowel. The word "not" (na) is understood from the previous rule.
According to the opinion of certain teachers, the doubling of a *yara* (any consonant except *ya*, *ra*, *la*, and *va*) following a long vowel does not take place.
According to another opinion, however, Kaiyaṭa maintains in the commentary on the rule *nājjhalau* that the word *vā* ("or") is understood from the rule *anaci ca*.

Thus, since the option regarding doubling would be established by the rule *anaci ca* alone, the three subsequent rules beginning with *triprabhṛtiṣu* need not have been commenced; this is the position established in the *Prakriyā-prakāśa* (the *Prakriyā-kaumudī*).
Due to the contradiction with these three sūtras, it appears reasonable that the term *vā* (optionally) should not be carried over (*anuvartyam*) from the rule *anaci ca* (Pāṇini 8.4.47).
*Bālamanoramā*: *udaḥ sthāstambhoḥ pūrvasya* (Pāṇini 8.4.61). Regarding *udaḥ sthāstambhoḥ*:

although the term *savarṇa* was mentioned as part of a compound in the rule *anusvārasya yayi parasavarṇaḥ* (Pāṇini 8.4.58), it is extracted here and connected [to the present rule], because it has been promised (*pratijñāna*) that the svarita accent applies to a portion [of a compound].
The term *udaḥ* is in the ablative case;

therefore, by the technical rule (*paribhāṣā*) "from that [ablative], [the operation applies] to what follows," the phrase *udaḥparayoḥ* ("of those following *ud*") is obtained. Thus he says: "of those following *ud*."
Regarding the word *pūrva*:
the meaning is that the substitute shall be that which is homogeneous (*savarṇa*) with the preceding letter, namely the *u* of *uda*.

Furthermore, this [substitute] is "homogeneous with the preceding" (*pūrvasavarṇa*); by the maxim regarding the final letter (*alo'ntyaparibhāṣā*), it does not become a substitute for the final letter of the roots *sthā* and *stambh*, as he states: "of the subsequent, the first" (*ādeḥ parasya*).

By this rule of exception, it means that [the substitution] occurs only for the initial *s* of the roots *sthā* and *stambh*. As for "utthānam," [it is derived from] the root *ṣṭhā* in the sense of "cessation of motion."

The suffix *lyuṭ* is used in the sense of an abstract action (*bhāva*). Thus, "supporting" (*uttambhanam*) is derived from the root *ṣṭabhi* in the sense of "obstructing" (*pratiṣṭambhe*), with the suffix *lyuṭ* applied in the sense of an abstract action.

The root *stambh* is specified in the rule for the introduction of the *śnu* suffix, either as a Vedic (sautra) root or because the mention of the labial stop (*pavargīya*) in the phrase "sthā-stambhoḥ" applies to both [roots *sthā* and *stambh*]. Now, in the case of *ud-sthānam*, when applying the rule for the homogeneous substitute (*pūrvasavarṇa*), the preceding cause is the letter *d*; and its homogeneous letters are only five: *t, th, d, dh, n*.

This is because of the similarity of their dental place of articulation (*sthāna*) and the similarity of their contact effort (*spṛṣṭa-prayatna*); however, this does not apply to the phoneme *ḷ* or the phoneme *s*, for although they share a similar place of articulation with *d*, they possess the effort of being "open" (*vivṛta*).
Nor does it apply to the phoneme *l*, because its effort is "slightly contacted" (*īṣatspṛṣṭa*).
Furthermore, all other phonemes besides these are not homogeneous (*savarṇa*) with *d*, because they have different places of articulation.

Consequently, all five sounds—ta, tha, da, dha, and na—which share the same place of articulation (*sthāna*) as the letter *da*, which serves as the *pūrvanimitta* (the preceding cause), would have been eligible to replace the letter *sa*. This is because the similarity (*āntarya*) based on the place of articulation—the dental region—is indistinguishable across all five with respect to the letter *sa*, which is the original element (*sthānin*). Furthermore, there is no similarity based on internal effort (*ābhyantara-prayatna*), because the original letter *sa* possesses the effort of being "uncontracted" (*vivṛta*), whereas these five possess the effort of being "contacted" (*spṛṣṭa*).

Therefore, having taken internal effort (*antaryama*) from external effort (*bāhyaprayatna*) itself, he states the determination among the five [types of effort] here with the words "of the unvoiced" (*aghoṣasya*).
By the term "unvoiced," it is effectively stated that [the sound] possesses aspiration and is characterized by a wide opening (*vivara*), because these properties are co-occurrent (*samaniyata*).

The substitute *sakāra* here, being the locus of substitution (*sthānin*), possesses a fourfold set of efforts consisting of being unvoiced (*aghoṣa*), aspirated (*āśvasita*), characterized by a wide opening (*vivāra*), and strongly articulated (*mahāprāṇa*).
Among those [consonants], the first, third, and fifth do not belong to it (the *ta* class), because they possess little breath (*alpapraṇa*).
Nor does the fourth belong to it, because it possesses the effort of being voiced (*ghoṣa*), nasalized (*anunāsika*), and non-spreading (*saṃvāra*).

However, the second, the letter *tha*, possesses the fourfold effort consisting of being voiceless (*aghoṣa*), non-nasalized (*anunāsika*), spreading (*vivāra*), and having great breath (*mahāpraṇa*).

Therefore, the meaning is that this very *thakāra* (the letter *th*) occurs in place of the *sakāra*, being homogeneous (*savarṇa*) with the preceding *dakāra* which served as the cause for its substitution.

Thus, when *ud-sthānam* is established, the *dakāra* is replaced by a *takāra* according to the rule *khari ca*; then, the *sakāra* is replaced by a *thakāra* homogeneous with the preceding [letter]. Consequently, the forms *utththānam*—containing one *takāra* and two *thakāras*—are established. The same principle should be applied to *utthatambhanam* as well.
In that regard, the distinction is that there are two *takāra*s and one *thakāra*. Regarding the word "tasya" (of that): it means of the *thakāra* which is the substitute for the *sakāra*.
And thus, the intention is that when there is elision of the first *thakāra*, the resulting forms are those with one *takāra* and one *thakāra*.
Now, an objection might be raised: "But if there is no elision of the first *thakāra*, it is untenable to claim that the forms have one *takāra* and two *thakāras*;

for, by the rule *khari ca*, the first *thakāra* would undergo *cartva* [substitution of *t*], resulting in the undesired consequence of having two *takāras* and one *thakāra*. To this, he says: "In the case of non-elision... [and so forth].

"Because it is not established" means that, in relation to the rule "khari ca," the form *udasthāḥ* is subsequent [to the application of the former rule]; this is the intended meaning. Furthermore, the reading with three *t*s in the word *uttambhanam* is erroneous.

This is because the aforementioned procedure is common to both cases. However, some scholars, accepting a *yogavibhāga* (splitting the rule) of the word "not" (*na*) in the rule *na mune*, maintain that since the substitution of the preceding homogeneous vowel (*pūrvasavarṇa*) for the letter *th* is not considered *asiddha* with respect to the change to *c* (*cartva*), they somehow establish the form *uttambhanam* as having three *t*s. But that is not approved by the author of the root-text (*mūlakṛt*), because in the root-text the procedure is explained as being common to both.

In reality, however, the sequence of the sūtras as accepted in the *Bhāṣya* on the sūtra *halo yamām* is as follows: after the six-sūtra group beginning with *dīrghād ācāryāṇām*, *anusvārasya yayi parasavarṇaḥ*, *vā padāntasya*, *tor li*, *udaḥ sthāstambhoḥ pūrvasya*, *jhayo ho 'nyatarasyām*, and *śaś cho 'ṭi*, there follows the five-sūtra group beginning with *jhalāṃ jaś jhaśi*, *abhyāse car ca*, *khari ca*, *vā 'vasāne*, and *aṇo 'pragṛhyasyānunāsikaḥ*. This is the order of the sūtras.

And thus, when the substitution of *c* for *khari* (P. 8.4.55) is to be applied, because the *th* in *udaḥ sthāstambhoḥ* (P. 8.4.61)—which is a substitute with the same preceding vowel (*pūrvasavarṇa*)—is not considered *asiddha*, the form *utththānam* contains two *th*s and one *th*, while the form *uttūmbhanam* contains three *t*s; this has been explained in detail in the *Śabdenduśekhara*. In examples such as *vāgdhasati*, by the principle of closest similarity (*antaratama*), the fourth letters of the consonant classes (*varga*) such as *gh* arise from the *mahāprāṇa* (aspirated) *h*.

The inclusion of the term *anyatarasyām* (optionally) is for the purpose of making known the obligatory nature (*nityatva*) of the two preceding rules. Regarding the statement "it should be stated that *chatva* [the substitution of *ch* for *ś*] occurs when *am* follows": the meaning is that this must be explained as having the sense that *chatva* occurs when *am* follows. In this regard, the following is the explanation: a *yogavibhāga* (splitting of a rule) is made of the rule *śaśchaḥ*. By this, [the substitution] will occur even when *l* and other sounds—which are not included in the pratyāhāra *aṭ*—follow. Therefore, the second rule, *aṭi*, is for the purpose of removing over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*); by it, [the substitution occurs] only when *aṭ* follows, and not otherwise.
Furthermore, due to the power of the word-split (*yogavibhāga*), the suffix *am* occurs even in certain instances within the *anaḍ* etc. group included under *pratyāhāra*;
otherwise, the performance of the word-split would be purposeless.
The form *amī* was not mentioned [in the rule] for the sake of variety.

From this point [in the rule *atra* 8.4.59], the term *padānta* (end of a word) is understood by way of anuvṛtti, for the purpose of qualifying *jhay*. Consequently, in the case of *tu* [added] in [the rule *jhayo ho* 8.3.31], making it a *pūrvānta* (part of the preceding element) becomes justified for the sake of applying the substitution of *cha*. [Otherwise,] because of the continued application of the term *dhuṭ* from [the rule *jhalāṃ jaś jhaśi* 8.3.29], the subsequent [element] would be considered *asiddha*; thus, making it a *pūrvānta* would be useless. Regarding the statement "In *śayyā*, there are two *yakāra*s": one is a constituent part of the *kyap* suffix prescribed by [the rule *saṃjñāyāṃ samajaniṣadanipatamanavidhāñkruśibhyo lyuṇinyacaḥ* 3.3.99], while the other is the *apṛkta* [suffix].
"Third, that which is produced by sequence (*kramaja*). Sequence means *ānupūrvī* (succession); that which is born from that is "produced by sequence.
Furthermore, that which is prescribed by the rule *anaci ca* [Pāṇini 8.4.46] is indeed "produced by sequence," because it arises after the two preceding *y* sounds.
"The letter *ya* following the letter *ta* is one" [one *ya*, according to the *Kāśikā*];
it is a constituent part of the suffix *ṇya* prescribed by the rule "after *diti*, *aditi*, and *āditya*" (*Pāṇini* 4.1.85). Thus, there are two *ya*s.
The first [instance] is a part of that which is prescribed by the rule *dityadityādityapatyuttarapadāñ ñyaḥ* [Pāṇini 4.1.85] in the sense of "from the word *aditi*.
The second, however, is a part of the *ṇya*-suffix prescribed by that very same rule in the sense of "from the word *āditya*" [Pāṇini 4.2.24].
"The third is born from the sequence" means this.
That which is prescribed by the rule *yaṇo mayaḥ* (Pāṇini 8.4.64),
namely "of the middle [m] or of both middles," is optional (*anyatarasyām*) because of the governing authority (*adhikāra*) of that rule.

If it belongs to one, then [the suffix] *madhyama* is used; if it belongs to two, then [the suffix] *madhyamau* is used. Regarding the form *āśnam*: because of the irregular formation (*nipātana*) in the rule *annāṣṇaḥ* (Pāṇini 4.4.85), the substitution of *jagdhi* [for the root *ad*] by the rule *ado jagdhiḥ* (Pāṇini 2.4.36) does not occur; rather, the substitution of the nasal *ṇ* for the final consonant occurs by the rule *radābhyām* (Pāṇini 8.2.42), etc.

This *nakāra* occurs when followed by *yam*, provided that it is not preceded by a consonant (*hal*); what then? It is preceded by a vowel (*ac*). In the word *adhryam*, the suffix *yat* is applied according to [Pāṇini 5.4.25]: *pādārdhābhyāṃ ca*.

In this case, the letter *gh* follows the letter *r*, when a *y*-sound (*yam*) follows. But is this not a *y*-sound? It is the letter *dh*; for that [the *gh*] is situated within the *y*-sounds (*yams*). As in the word "śāṅgam."

The suffix *aṇ* is applied in the sense of "a modification of *śṛṅga*," resulting in initial *vṛddhi* and the substitution of *r* for *ṇ*. Here, the letter *ṅ* is a *yama*; it follows a consonant (*hal*), but the letter *g* is not a *yama* following that [consonant], because it is not included in the *yam* pratyāhāra. Furthermore, the initial *vṛddhi*—being dependent on the secondary suffix (*taddhita*)—is an external member (*bahiranga*); yet the letter *g* is not a *yama* following that [vowel], because it is not included in the *yam* pratyāhāra.

The *vṛddhi* substitution [of *ai*] in *pra-ṇati*, which depends on a *taddhita* suffix, is *bahiraṅga*; however, the elision (*lopa*) is *antaraṅga*. Consequently, when the *antaraṅga* elision is to be applied, the *vṛddhi* is considered non-existent (*asiddha*). Because that [vṛddhi] is non-existent, the *repha* (*r*) dependent upon it is likewise non-existent. This being the case, how can it be said that the *ṅakāra* is not followed by a *hal* (consonant)? Some raise this objection, but their view should not even be presented; for such a possibility exists even in the primary example, namely *prattam* and *avattam*.

From the root *dadāti*, the suffix *kta* is applied; by [Pāṇini 7.4.47], the letter *a* is replaced by *t*, and by [Pāṇini 8.4.54] (*khari ca*), the letter *d* is also changed to *t*. Thus, there are three *t*s in total: two are substitutes, and one is part of the suffix. That which is produced by [Pāṇini 8.4.47] (*anaci ca*) is the fourth, arising from the sequence of sounds.
"Of the middle [syllable], or of the two middles"—
this is to be understood as being due to the continued application of the option (*anyatarasyām*) from the preceding rule.
"In *marutta*, there are four *t*-sounds."

The first three [sounds] are as before; the fourth is a constituent part of the word *marut*; and the fifth is produced by the sequence [of sounds], being that which is prescribed by the rule *anaci ca* [Pāṇini 8.4.46].

Now, one might object: "But [the rule for doubling applies] after a prefix ending in a vowel (*ajanta*)"? To this it is replied: the word *marut* does not end in a vowel (*ajanta*); rather, what is it? It ends in a consonant (*halanta*). If so, how can the doubling occur? To this he says: "Of the word *marut*" and so forth.
In this context [of Pāṇini 8.4.59], there is an extension (*upasaṃkhyāna*) of the word *marut* for the sake of the grammatical operation pertaining to prefixes.

If *tatva* (the substitution of *t*) were not to occur even when that [condition] exists, then it would be useless. Therefore, by the force of the supplementary rule (*upasaṃkhyāna*), *tatva* certainly occurs even after a stem ending in a vowel other than *an*. Well then, just as *tatva* occurs here by the force of the supplementary rule for the prefix, so too in the case of *bharu-nayati*, there would be *ṇatva* (the substitution of *ṇ*) due to the *t* in [Pāṇini 8.4.14], even when there is an intervention by a vowel such as *aṇ*.
If it is desired, let it be so;
if it is not desired, then it should be understood as included among the *kṣubhna*-type words [Pāṇini 8.4.39].
"Śārṅgam."

The letter *ṅ* is subject to elision when followed by a *hal* (consonant) that is a *jhar* (any consonant except *y*, *v*, *r*, *l*, and semivowels) and is homogeneous (*savarṇa*) with it; however, since this [following *ñ*] is not a *jhar*, the elision does not occur.

In the form *priyapañcñā*, the compound *bahuvrīhi* "one to whom five beloved ones belong" is formed; then follows the singular instrumental case ending. By [Pāṇini 6.4.134], there is the elision of the vowel *a*; by [Pāṇini 8.4.40], the *tavarga* (the dental stop class) undergoes the substitution of *ścutva* (becoming a retroflex).
According to the rule *vargo vargeṇa savarṇaḥ*, the letter *ñ* is homogeneous (*savarṇa*) with the *c*-group;
however, this *ñ* is not a *jhar*.
Therefore, when it follows, there is no elision (*lopa*) of the letter *c* even though it is separated from the preceding consonant by that [intervening *ñ*].

[Objection: But even if this rule *jharī* were not formulated, would not the elision (*lopa*) still fail to apply here? [Response: No, for the elision does not occur, because the mention of "specified" (*nirdiṣṭa-grahaṇa*) is intended to ensure immediate proximity (*ādantarya*). An elision should occur when a homogeneous vowel (*savarṇa*) follows immediately after; however, in this case, the letter *ñ* is not immediately following, because once the preceding [vowel] has been elided, the elision of the *a*-vowel (by P. 6.1.109) becomes a *sthānivadbhāva* (as if it were the original element). So what is the use of the word *jharī*? To this he says: “of the elision” (*lopasya*), etc.
In the context of rules that are not established for what precedes (*pūrvatrāsiddhe*), the *sthānivadbhāva* of the elision of a short vowel (*hrasva-lopa*) is prohibited.
If the term "jhar" were not stated here, then there would indeed be elision (*lopa*) in this case, as in "tarptā.

[The root] *tṛp* in the sense of "pleasing" (Dhātupāṭha 1271) undergoes the substitution of *takāra* for *pakāra* due to a difference in place of articulation (*sthānaveda*). Since they are not homogeneous (*savarṇa*), elision does not occur here.

But surely, since the causes (*nimitta*) and the effects (*kāryin*) are identical here, there ought to be a correspondence according to their respective numbers; in that case, even in the absence of the mention of "homogeneous" (*savarṇa*), no elision would apply at all in examples such as *tarptā*. So why is the mention of "homogeneous" necessary to exclude that [undesired result]? To this he says: "By the force of the mention of 'homogeneous' (*savarṇa-grahaṇa-sāmarthyāt*)," and so forth.

If there were numerical correspondence (*yatāsaṃkhyam*) here, then only the phoneme *jh* would be subject to elision for the phoneme *jh*. However, since only the phoneme *jh* is a homogeneous (*savarṇa*) sound of the phoneme *jh*, and this being the case, the mention of "homogeneous" (*savarṇagrahaṇa*) would be purposeless; for there is nothing to be excluded, as it is impossible for a phoneme *jh* to be non-homogeneous with another phoneme *jh*. Therefore, by the force of the mention of "homogeneous" in this context, there is no numerical correspondence.
Therefore, in the forms *śiṇḍhi* and *piṇḍhi*, when there is a *ḍha* belonging to the homogeneous class (*savarṇa*), the *ḍa* is elided.

[The roots are] *śiṣlṛ* "to fall apart" (or "to distinguish") [DhP 1451] and *piṣlṛ* "to grind" [DhP 1452]. In the *loṭ* mood, with the suffix *sip*, the substitution of *hi* occurs by [Pāṇini 3.4.87], followed by the addition of *śnam*. Then, by [Pāṇini 6.4.111], the *a* is elided; by [Pāṇini 6.4.101], *hi* is changed to *dhi*; and by [Pāṇini 8.4.53], the *jaś*-substitution occurs—changing the *ṣ* to *ḍ*. Finally, by [Pāṇini 8.3.24], the *anusvāra* is added.

By [Pāṇini 8.4.41], the *dh* becomes *ḍh*; by [8.4.58], the *ṇ* is inserted; and by this [rule], there is the elision of the *ḍ* when it becomes *ḍh*. Thus we have "Gārgyaḥ" and "Vātsyaḥ. From the words *garga-* and *vatsa-*, [the suffix] *yañ* is applied by [4.1.105]. By [6.1.191], "that which begins with *ñ* or *ṇ* is always acute," the first syllable is acute; by [6.1.158], the remainder is unaccented (*anudātta*), and that [unaccented vowel] becomes a circumflex (*svarita*). [Examples: "pacati" (he cooks), "paṭhati" (he reads).

The two *tip* suffixes are *anudātta* (unaccented) because they are *anudātta* by nature. The vowel *ā* of the letter *p* is also *udātta* (accented) due to the accent of the verbal root (*dhātusvara*). Consequently, the letter *ś* of the suffix *śap* following that [vowel] becomes *svarita* (circumflex).

What, then, is the reason this sūtra is stated here, rather than being stated immediately after [Pāṇini 6.1.185]? For in that case, the mention of *svarita* would not have to be made; the subject matter under discussion (*prakṛta*) would simply carry over. To this he replies with the words beginning "of this" (*asya*). If it were placed there, then [the rule] 6.1.158 would apply here, and consequently, the *anudātta* and *svarita* accents would be heard, not the *udātta* and *svarita*.

But here, since the *svarita* [accent] would be unreal (*asiddha*) when this [rule] is being applied, the rule *tadāśrayam* (P. 6.1.158) does not apply; therefore, both its acute (*udātta*) and circumflex (*svarita*) accents are heard. Regarding the phrase "having an acute or circumflex as its following element" (*udāttasvaritodayam*): it is a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "that from which an acute or circumflex arises. To show that the word *udaya* is connected with each [member of the compound], he says: "of that which has an acute as its following element," and so forth.
In this context, the word *udaya* functions in the sense of the word *para*.
In the phrase "gāgryas tatra," the word *tatra* is udātta on its first syllable by virtue of the accent of the suffix *tral*,
according to [Pāṇini 6.1.197].

Regarding "gārgyaḥ kva": the word *ka* has a svarita accent by virtue of its own inherent accent; the suffix *at* is added to the word *kim* according to [Pāṇini 5.3.12], and *kim* undergoes the substitution *kva* according to [Pāṇini 7.2.105].

While it would have been sufficient to say "acute and circumflex" (*udātta-svarita*), the inclusion of the term *udaya* is for the sake of brevity and clarity; thus it is said, "the mention of *udaya* is for the sake of auspiciousness" (*maṅgalārtham*).

Auspiciousness is the cause for the accomplishment of the desired object. Furthermore, the desired objects are the expansion of the science (*śāstra*) and the possession of heroic men and the like. Accordingly it has been said: "Those sciences which begin with an auspicious word, have an auspicious word in their middle, and end with an auspicious word, endure; they come to possess heroic men and long-lived men" (Mahābhārata 1.1.1).
Just as [scriptural works] such as the *Maṅgala* begin with auspicious elements, so too do they conclude with them.
When the word "udaya" is employed here for the sake of auspiciousness, the commencement of what follows becomes preceded by an auspicious element.

Consequently, that which was stated—"the inclusion of the long (*dīrgha*) and protracted (*pluta*) vowels by this [term] *ā* is not intended; rather, the inclusion of the *ṇa* is intended by the closed (*saṃvṛta*) vowel, whereas the inclusion of the vowel *ā* is intended when it possesses all its qualities" (Kāśikā on Pāṇini 8.4.69), becomes logically consistent.
For when undertakings are commenced preceded by auspicious rites, the accomplishment of the desired goal occurs.
Furthermore, this word *u* is well-known in the world as having an auspicious meaning, just like the word *vṛddhi*. Therefore, its inclusion is made for the sake of auspiciousness.
